title: Exam technique: Communication and Networking
content:
### What earns the marks
For switching and protocols, describe earns marks for the mechanism plus its consequence: packets carry addresses and sequence numbers so routers forward independently and the receiver reassembles. For TCP vs UDP, justify earns marks for matching reliability to the use case, not for declaring one better. For security, name earns the control plus what it inspects: packet-filtering checks headers against rules.
### Traps
Error: circuit-switching features credited to packet switching. Correction: dedicated path and guaranteed bandwidth are circuit properties. Error: TCP recommended for live video. Correction: delay hurts more than loss there, so UDP. Error: claiming wireless uses collision detection. Correction: senders cannot listen while sending, so avoidance (RTS/CTS).

title: A Level Mathematics: Hypothesis Testing
content:
A Level Mathematics: Hypothesis Testing

A hypothesis test is a formal way of deciding whether data are surprising enough to overturn an assumption. The logic is legal rather than mathematical in spirit: assume the claim is true, compute how unlikely the observed evidence would be under that assumption, and reject the claim only if the evidence is unlikely enough. This note sets out the machinery — null and alternative hypotheses, significance levels, tails, critical regions — and then applies it to the binomial and normal cases the exam uses.

The logic of a test

The null hypothesis H0 is the assumption of no change, no effect, no bias: the status quo. The alternative H1 is what you would conclude if the data are too extreme. The significance level α is the risk of rejecting a true H0 that you are willing to accept.

H0: the parameter equals its old value
H1: the parameter is greater, less, or simply different
alpha: the maximum acceptable probability of a Type I error (often 0.05 or 0.01)
test statistic: the observed value computed from the sample
p-value: probability of a result at least as extreme, assuming H0

The analogy that makes the asymmetry clear: a criminal trial presumes innocence. The presumption is not a belief, it is the default that evidence must overcome. Failing to reject H0 is not proof of H0 — it is a verdict of "not proven".

One-tailed and two-tailed tests

The alternative decides the tail. A one-tailed test is used when the direction of the change is specified in advance; a two-tailed test when any change would matter.

AlternativeTest typep-value
p > p0one-tailed, upperP(X ≥ observed)
p < p0one-tailed, lowerP(X ≤ observed)
p ≠ p0two-tailed2 × the smaller tail

Worked example (choosing the alternative). A coin is suspected of favouring heads. Which alternative applies?

the suspicion has a direction, so H1: p > 0.5, a one-tailed upper test
a two-tailed test would be right only if any bias mattered

Errors and their consequences

Every test can go wrong in two ways, and the significance level controls only one of them. Understanding which is which is a frequent exam question and a genuine conceptual point.

Type I error: reject H0 when it is true  (probability alpha)
Type II error: fail to reject H0 when it is false
reducing alpha reduces Type I errors but increases Type II errors
increasing the sample size reduces both

Worked example. A test at the 5% level concludes a die is biased when it is fair. Which error is this?

H0 (fair) was true and was rejected
that is a Type I error, with probability at most 5%

Worked example 2 (effect of sample size). Explain why the same observed proportion can be significant in a large sample and not in a small one.

a larger sample reduces the standard error, so the same deviation
becomes more standard errors away from the null value
the evidence is measured in standard errors, not in raw counts

Testing a binomial proportion

The test statistic is the observed number of successes, the null distribution is binomial, and the p-value is a cumulative binomial probability.

H0: p = p0;  X ~ B(n, p0)
upper tail p-value = P(X >= x)
lower tail p-value = P(X <= x)
reject H0 if p-value <= alpha

Worked example. A manufacturer claims 90% of components are fault-free. In a sample of 20, only 15 are fault-free. Test at the 5% level whether the claim is too high.

H0: p = 0.9;  H1: p < 0.9
X ~ B(20, 0.9)
P(X <= 15) = 0.0432
0.0432 < 0.05, so reject H0
there is evidence the fault-free rate is below 90%

Worked example 2 (critical region). Find the 5% critical region for that test.

P(X <= 15) = 0.0432 (below 0.05)
P(X <= 16) = 0.1330 (above 0.05)
critical region: X <= 15

Worked example 3 (actual significance level). State the actual significance level of that test.

the probability of a Type I error is P(X <= 15) under H0 = 0.0432
so the actual level is 4.32%, just inside the 5% requirement

Testing a normal mean

When the variable is continuous and the population is normal — or the sample is large — the test statistic is standardised with a z-score and compared with critical values.

test statistic z = (x-bar - mu)/(σ/sqrt n)   (σ known)
or z = (x-bar - mu)/(s/sqrt n)                  (σ estimated, large n)
critical values at 5% one-tailed: 1.6449;  two-tailed: 1.96
at 1% one-tailed: 2.3263;  two-tailed: 2.5758

Worked example. A machine fills bags with a mean of 500 g and standard deviation 8 g. A sample of 16 bags has mean 496 g. Test at the 5% level whether the mean has fallen.

H0: mu = 500;  H1: mu < 500
standard error = 8/sqrt 16 = 2
z = (496 - 500)/2 = -2
critical value at 5% one-tailed is -1.6449
-2 < -1.6449, so reject H0: the mean has fallen

Worked example 2 (two-tailed). Same data, tested two-tailed at 5%.

critical values are +/-1.96
|-2| > 1.96, so still reject H0
the evidence is that the mean is not 500, in either direction

Worked example 3 (interpreting a p-value). A test gives z = 1.72 for H1: μ > μ0. Find the p-value and conclude at 5%.

p-value = P(Z > 1.72) = 0.0427
0.0427 < 0.05, so reject H0
the result is significant at the 5% level but not at 1%

Choosing the right test

The exam does not label the test; the shape of the data decides it. Getting the distribution wrong makes every later mark unreachable, so the decision is worth making explicitly.

count of successes in n trials with constant p  →  binomial test
count of events in an interval at a constant rate  →  Poisson test
mean of a continuous measurement  →  normal test (z)
correlation between two variables  →  product-moment test

Worked example. A nurse records the number of patients arriving in an hour on 30 separate days. Which test?

counts of arrivals in equal intervals at a roughly constant rate
use a Poisson test on the mean count, not a binomial test
a normal test on the mean of the 30 counts is also defensible for large n

Writing a conclusion that earns the marks

The final mark of a hypothesis test is for the conclusion, and it has three components: a decision about H0, a reference to the significance level, and the finding stated in the context of the question. Dropping any one of them costs a mark even when the arithmetic is perfect.

Compare these two endings. "0.0201 < 0.05, so reject H0" scores the comparison. "There is sufficient evidence at the 5% level that the call rate has increased" scores the comparison and the interpretation. "The rate has increased" scores neither, because it reports a certainty the test cannot deliver.

The opposite case is often mishandled too. When the p-value is above the level the correct wording is that there is insufficient evidence to reject H0 — never that H0 is true, and never that nothing has happened. A non-significant result from a small sample is weak evidence either way, and saying so is better than overclaiming in either direction.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Hypotheses) A coin might be biased against heads. State H0 and H1. Answer: H0: p = 0.5; H1: p < 0.5.
  2. (Error) Define a Type II error. Answer: failing to reject H0 when it is false.
  3. (Binomial) 8 of 20 seeds germinate; test p = 0.6 against p < 0.6 at 5%. Answer: X ~ B(20, 0.6), so P(X ≤ 8) = 0.0565; since 0.0565 > 0.05 there is insufficient evidence to reject H0.
  4. (Critical region) X ~ B(15, 0.4): 5% lower critical region. Answer: test P(X ≤ c) ≤ 0.05: P(X ≤ 2) = 0.0271 ≤ 0.05, but P(X ≤ 3) = 0.0905 > 0.05, so the critical region is X ≤ 2.
  5. (Actual level) For that region, state the actual significance level. Answer: actual significance level = P(X ≤ 2) = 0.0271 = 2.71%.
  6. (Normal) μ0 = 20, σ = 4, n = 25, mean 21.5: test at 5% one-tailed. Answer: z = (x̄ − μ0)/(σ/√n) = (21.5 − 20)/(4/√25) = 1.5/0.8 = 1.875, and 1.875 > 1.6449, so reject H0.
  7. (Two-tailed) Same data two-tailed: Answer: z = (21.5 − 20)/(4/√25) = 1.875, and 1.875 < 1.96, so do not reject H0.
  8. (p-value) z = 2.4, H1: μ > μ0. Find the p-value. Answer: p-value = P(Z > 2.4) = 1 − 0.9918 = 0.0082.
  9. (Sample size) Why can a larger sample turn a non-significant result significant? Answer: the standard error shrinks, so the same deviation is more standard errors away.
  10. (Conclusion wording) Write a valid conclusion for a rejected H0. Answer: there is sufficient evidence at the 5% level that the mean has fallen.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Concluding H0 is true: failing to reject means the evidence is insufficient; it is never proof of the null.
  • Wrong tail: compute P(X ≥ x) for an increase and P(X ≤ x) for a decrease; using the other tail inverts the conclusion.
  • Doubling without a two-tailed alternative: the p-value is doubled only when H1 is "not equal".
  • p-value compared with the wrong threshold: 5% is 0.05; comparing 0.043 with 5 instead of 0.05 reverses the verdict.
  • Standard error omitted: the z-score divides by σ/√n, not by σ.
  • Critical value for the wrong tail: the 5% one-tailed value is 1.6449, the two-tailed is 1.96; the sign matters too.
  • Type I and Type II swapped: Type I is rejecting a true null — the error the significance level controls.
  • Conclusion beyond the data: a rejected H0 says the parameter has changed, not why, and never that the change is important.

Setting up the hypotheses before any calculation

Hypotheses are the first lines a marker reads, and a wrong direction or a sample statistic written where a parameter belongs loses marks before any arithmetic is checked. The subsections set out how to define the parameter, write H₀ as a single value and read H₁ from the wording of the question.

Defining the parameter in words first

Before writing any symbol, say what the parameter measures. Let p be the proportion of seeds that germinate, or let μ be the mean mass of a bag in grams. The parameter belongs to the population the claim is about, not to the sample you were given. The definition is the line that makes the rest of the working easy to follow, so write it first.

Writing H₀ as a single value

H₀ names one value for the parameter with an equals sign, such as H₀: p = 0.6 or H₀: μ = 50. It is the value the test assumes is true when it calculates the probability of the data. The probability can only be worked out at one specific value, so the test is always carried out at the value stated in H₀, and the working should say so.

Reading the direction of H₁ from the wording

Words map to symbols in a fixed way. “Greater than”, “more than”, “has increased” and “above” give >. “Less than”, “fewer”, “has decreased” and “below” give <. “Different from”, “has changed” and “is not equal to” give ≠. A question that asks whether a proportion has changed, without saying which way, needs H₁: p ≠ p₀, and that choice fixes a two-tailed test.

Hypotheses for a mean from a normal model

When X is normal with a known standard deviation, the hypotheses concern μ, and the variance belongs to the model: X ~ N(μ, σ²). Write the assumption that the population is normal with known σ, or that the sample is large enough for the central limit theorem to apply. The hypotheses for a sample mean are the same as for the population mean, because the test is about μ.

Hypotheses set before the data are used

The direction of H₁ must come from the claim in the question, not from the sample. If the sample mean is 49 and the claim is μ = 50, it is tempting to choose H₁: μ < 50 after looking at the data. That choice invalidates the test, because it lets the data pick the tail. Settle the direction from the wording, and show it in the working before the test statistic.

Critical regions and the significance level

A critical region is the set of outcomes that leads to rejecting H₀. For a discrete distribution it is a set of whole numbers, and for a normal test it is a range of z-values. The subsections show how each is built from the significance level, and where the sign and boundary errors come from.

Building a critical region from tail probabilities

For a lower-tail test at level α, find the largest value k with P(X ≤ k) ≤ α, assuming H₀. The critical region is then {0, 1, …, k}. For X ~ B(10, 0.5) at the 5% level, P(X ≤ 1) = 11/1024 = 0.0107 and P(X ≤ 2) = 56/1024 = 0.0547. The second value is greater than 0.05, so k = 1 and the critical region is {0, 1}.

The actual significance level is rarely the stated level

Because X takes only whole-number values, the probability in the critical region is usually below the stated level. Here it is 0.0107, about 1.07%, not 5%. Say so in the working, using the phrase “actual significance level”. A discrete test that falls short of 5% is correct; a candidate who claims the level is exactly 5% makes a false statement.

Critical values for a normal test

For a normal test with known σ, a critical value of z replaces the critical count. The standard values are 1.645 for a one-tailed test at 5%, 2.326 for one-tailed at 1%, 1.96 for two-tailed at 5% and 2.576 for two-tailed at 1%. A lower-tailed test rejects when z ≤ −1.645; an upper-tailed test rejects when z ≥ 1.645. The normal distribution is continuous, so the actual level equals the stated level exactly.

Two-tailed critical regions for a discrete test

For a two-tailed test at 5%, each tail may carry probability at most 0.025. For X ~ B(10, 0.5), P(X ≤ 1) = 0.0107 is at most 0.025, while P(X ≤ 2) = 0.0547 is not. The lower critical region is {0, 1}, and by symmetry the upper one is {9, 10}. The combined probability is 0.0215, which is below 0.05, so the test can reject for 0, 1, 9 or 10 successes.

Checking the boundary and the sign

A common slip is to put the boundary in the wrong region or to use the wrong sign. For a lower-tailed normal test at 5%, the boundary z = −1.645 is itself in the critical region, because the test rejects when z ≤ −1.645. A critical value of +1.645 on a lower-tailed test is the commonest sign error. Write the inequality with the boundary included, then check that its sign matches the tail named in H₁.

p-values, step by step

A p-value gives the same decision as a critical region, but it reports how unlikely the data are on the assumption that H₀ is true, rather than only whether they fall inside a region. Many A2 questions ask for a p-value directly, and some ask for a comparison with the level in a single sentence.

What a p-value is and is not

The p-value is the probability, assuming H₀ is true, of a result at least as extreme as the one observed, in the direction stated in H₁. It is not the probability that H₀ is true, and it is not the probability that the result happened by chance. A p-value of 0.03 means that a result this extreme would occur 3% of the time if H₀ were true.

A p-value for a lower-tailed binomial test

For X ~ B(10, 0.5) with H₁: p < 0.5, suppose 2 successes are observed. The p-value is P(X ≤ 2) = 56/1024 = 0.0547. That is greater than 0.05, so the result is not significant at the 5% level. At the 10% level, 0.0547 is less than 0.10, so H₀ is rejected. The same observation gives different decisions at different levels, which is why the level must always be stated.

A p-value for a two-tailed binomial test

For the same observation with H₁: p ≠ 0.5, the p-value is twice the smaller tail probability: 2 × 0.0547 = 0.1094. A two-tailed p-value is never the value of one tail alone, and it is capped at 1 if doubling would exceed 1. Here 0.1094 is greater than 0.05, so the result is not significant at 5%. A two-tailed p-value is always at least as large as the one-tailed value, which is why a two-tailed test is the harder one to pass.

A p-value for a normal test

Suppose z = −2.1 is found for a lower-tailed normal test. The p-value is Φ(−2.1) = 1 − Φ(2.1) = 1 − 0.9821 = 0.0179. For a two-tailed test the p-value would be 2 × 0.0179 = 0.0357. Use the symmetry of the normal curve, and show the Φ step so that the table lookup can be checked.

Comparing a p-value with the significance level

If the p-value is less than or equal to the significance level, reject H₀. Write the comparison as a statement with both numbers, for example 0.0547 > 0.05, so do not reject H₀. Then give the decision in words, in the context of the question. The comparison in numbers is what the working shows, and the sentence is what the conclusion mark asks for.

The normal test as a standardised calculation

When the population is normal with a known standard deviation, the sample mean is itself normal, and the test standardises it before comparing with a critical value. This section shows the standardisation and the figure that makes the critical region visible.

Standardising the sample mean

If X ~ N(μ, σ²), then the mean of n independent values satisfies X̄ ~ N(μ, σ²/n) when H₀ is true. The test statistic is z = (x̄ − μ₀)/(σ/√n), where μ₀ is the value stated in H₀. Standardising converts any normal model to the standard normal distribution, so the critical values in the tables apply to every normal test.

Using the standard error, not the standard deviation

The denominator is σ/√n, the standard error of the mean, and not σ on its own. Dividing by σ alone gives a z-value that is √n times too small, and the test becomes too cautious. If σ is given, use it directly. If only the sample standard deviation s is given and the sample is large, use s as an estimate of σ and say so in the working.

A worked normal test

A machine fills bags with a mean of 500 g and a known standard deviation of 12 g. A sample of 36 bags has mean 496 g. Test at the 5% level whether the mean fill is less than 500 g. The standard error is 12/√36 = 2, so z = (496 − 500)/2 = −2. The critical value is −1.645, and −2 is less than −1.645, so H₀ is rejected. The p-value is Φ(−2) = 0.0228, which is less than 0.05.

Reading the critical region from the figure

The figure shows the standard normal curve with the lower 5% tail shaded. The boundary at −1.645 separates the critical region from the rest of the curve, and the observed z-value of −2 lies inside the shaded tail, which is why the test rejects H₀. Sketching this shape with the boundary and the observed value marked is a quick check that the direction of the test is right.

Reading the answer back in the units of the question

The conclusion must be in the units of the question: “There is evidence at the 5% level that the mean fill is less than 500 g.” Do not write “the mean is less than 500”, because a test never establishes a fact about the population. Name the quantity the evidence is about, the mean fill mass, and state the level.

Power and the probability of a Type II error

A test that rejects H₀ rarely is also unlikely to detect a real change. The power of a test measures how often it detects a specified change, and it is the quantity that questions about Type II errors ask for.

Defining power

The power of a test is the probability of rejecting H₀ when a specified alternative value is true. A power of 0.149 at p = 0.3 means the test rejects H₀ 14.9% of the time when p really is 0.3. The probability of a Type II error at that value is 1 − power, which is 0.851 here. Power is always calculated at a stated alternative, so name the value of the parameter you used.

Calculating power for a binomial test

Take the lower-tailed test from the previous section: X ~ B(10, 0.5) with H₀: p = 0.5, H₁: p < 0.5 and critical region {0, 1}. To find the power at p = 0.3, use X ~ B(10, 0.3) and find the probability of the critical region. P(X = 0) = 0.7¹⁰ = 0.02825 and P(X = 1) = 10 × 0.3 × 0.7⁹ = 0.12107. Adding these gives 0.1493, so the power is 0.149 to 3 significant figures.

Factors that increase power

Power rises when the sample is larger, when the true value is further from the value in H₀, and when the significance level is larger. A larger sample shrinks the standard error, so a real shift is more likely to land in the critical region. A larger level widens the critical region, but it also raises the chance of a Type I error. This is the trade-off: a test that is hard to pass by chance is also hard to pass when H₁ is true.

Why a non-significant result is not proof

If the power is low, a non-significant result is weak evidence. At p = 0.3 the test above fails to reject H₀ with probability 0.851, so that outcome is very likely even though H₀ is false. A result that does not reject H₀ does not show that p = 0.5. It shows only that the data were not strong enough to reject H₀ at this level.

Sample size and the size of the difference

A test that must detect a small difference needs a large sample. A difference that is large compared with the standard error is detected easily, while a small difference relative to the standard error may not be. In an exam, the question will say whether the power or the Type II error probability is wanted, so check the wording before you calculate, and state the alternative value you used.

Marked questions with full answers

Each question below is set at the level an A2 paper uses, with the marks shown. Work the method yourself before reading the answer, and compare the steps you wrote with the answer's steps rather than only its final value.

Question 1: a binomial test of a seed claim [4 marks]

Question. A seed company claims that 80% of its seeds germinate. In a random sample of 15 seeds, 8 germinate. Test at the 5% level whether the proportion that germinate is less than 0.8.

Answer. Let p be the proportion of seeds that germinate. H₀: p = 0.8 and H₁: p < 0.8. Under H₀, X ~ B(15, 0.8), and the p-value is P(X ≤ 8). Let Y = 15 − X, so Y ~ B(15, 0.2) and P(X ≤ 8) = P(Y ≥ 7) = 1 − P(Y ≤ 6) = 1 − 0.9820 = 0.0180. Since 0.0180 is less than 0.05, reject H₀. There is evidence at the 5% level that the proportion of seeds that germinate is less than 0.8.

Question 2: a two-tailed normal test with known σ [5 marks]

Question. The mass of a bag of sugar is normally distributed with standard deviation 2 g. The manufacturer claims the mean mass is 1000 g. A random sample of 16 bags has mean 1001.5 g. Test the claim at the 5% level.

Answer. H₀: μ = 1000 and H₁: μ ≠ 1000. Under H₀, X̄ ~ N(1000, 2²/16), so the standard error is 2/4 = 0.5. Then z = (1001.5 − 1000)/0.5 = 3. The two-tailed critical values at 5% are ±1.96, and 3 is greater than 1.96, so reject H₀. The p-value is 2 × (1 − Φ(3)) = 2 × 0.00135 = 0.0027. There is evidence at the 5% level that the mean mass differs from 1000 g.

Question 3: the critical region for a sample mean [4 marks]

Question. X is normal with standard deviation 3. H₀: μ = 20 and H₁: μ > 20 are to be tested at the 5% level using the mean of a sample of 9 values. Find the critical region for the sample mean x̄.

Answer. Under H₀, X̄ ~ N(20, 3²/9), so the standard error is 3/3 = 1. The upper critical value of z is 1.645, which gives the boundary x̄ = 20 + 1 × 1.645 = 21.645. The critical region is x̄ > 21.645. Stating the region in terms of x̄, not z, is what the mark asks for.

Question 4: reading a p-value at two levels [2 marks]

Question. A test gives a p-value of 0.03. State the conclusion at the 5% level and at the 1% level.

Answer. At the 5% level, 0.03 is less than 0.05, so reject H₀: there is evidence that the parameter differs from the claimed value. At the 1% level, 0.03 is greater than 0.01, so do not reject H₀: there is not enough evidence at the 1% level. The result is significant at 5% but not at 1%.

Question 5: false rejections over many tests [3 marks]

Question. A test at the 5% level is applied to 200 independent samples, and H₀ is true in every case. (a) State the expected number of samples that lead to rejection of H₀. (b) Show that the probability that at least one sample leads to rejection is 1 − 0.95²⁰⁰, and state its value to 5 decimal places.

Answer. (a) Each sample rejects H₀ with probability 0.05, so the expected number is 200 × 0.05 = 10. (b) The probability that no sample rejects is 0.95²⁰⁰, so the probability of at least one rejection is 1 − 0.95²⁰⁰ = 1 − 0.0000351 = 0.99996 to 5 decimal places. Rejection on at least one of 200 tests is almost certain, even though each test has only a 5% chance of a false rejection.

Question 6: a large-sample z-test using s [5 marks]

Question. A sample of 100 measurements has mean 52.4 and standard deviation 6. Test at the 1% level whether the population mean is 50, against the alternative that it is not 50.

Answer. H₀: μ = 50 and H₁: μ ≠ 50. The sample is large, so s = 6 is used as an estimate of σ. The standard error is 6/√100 = 0.6, so z = (52.4 − 50)/0.6 = 4. The two-tailed critical values at 1% are ±2.576, and 4 is greater than 2.576, so reject H₀. There is evidence at the 1% level that the population mean is not 50.

Equations and symbols

A hypothesis test is a decision rule, and these are its moving parts: the test statistic, the standard error, the tail probability and the comparison that produces the verdict.

The decision

reject H0 if p-value <= alpha Key: H0 = the null hypothesis, the assumption of no change; p-value = the probability of a result at least as extreme, assuming H0 is true; alpha = the significance level, the acceptable risk of rejecting a true H0 (often 0.05 or 0.01). Failing to reject is not proof that H0 is true — it means the evidence was insufficient.

P(X <= 15) = 0.0432 Key: X = number of fault-free components in a sample of 20; 0.0432 = the lower-tail probability under H0: p = 0.9. Because 0.0432 < 0.05 the null is rejected, and the same figure is the actual significance level of the test.

The normal test

standard error = 8/sqrt 16 = 2 Key: 8 = population standard deviation σ (g); 16 = sample size n (bags); 2 = the standard error of the mean (g). The standard error, not σ, is the denominator of the test statistic — omitting the √n is the classic lost mark.

z = (496 - 500)/2 = -2 Key: z = the test statistic, in standard errors; 496 = sample mean (g); 500 = hypothesised mean μ (g); 2 = the standard error (g). Compare |z| with the critical value: 1.6449 one-tailed at 5%, 1.96 two-tailed at 5%.

p-value = P(Z > 1.72) = 0.0427 Key: Z = the standard normal variable; 1.72 = the observed test statistic; 0.0427 = the area beyond it, for an upper-tail alternative. Significant at 5% but not at 1% — say which level you are concluding at.

Errors

A Type I error rejects a true H0 and has probability alpha; a Type II error fails to reject a false H0. Lowering alpha reduces Type I errors and increases Type II; a larger sample reduces both, because it shrinks the standard error so the same deviation counts as more standard errors.

The slip worth naming

Comparing a p-value with 5 instead of 0.05, or doubling the tail without a two-sided alternative. Both reverse a correct conclusion, which is exactly the mark the question is testing.

title: IGCSE Biology: Diseases and Immunity
content:
IGCSE Biology: Diseases and Immunity

You are under constant attack: bacteria, viruses and fungi try to colonise you every hour of every day, and the only reason you survive is a layered defence system that is part physical wall, part chemical weapon, part mobile army with a memory. This note explains what pathogens are and how they spread, walks through every non-specific and specific defence in the order an infection meets them, describes how vaccination produces immunity without illness, and ends with antibiotics and the resistance crisis that is one of the most-examined topics of the decade. Every immune mechanism is described as a step-by-step sequence so you can write it out in the exact order the mark scheme expects.

Pathogens: the four types

A pathogen is any organism or particle that causes disease. Bacteria: living cells that reproduce by binary fission, causing disease by damaging tissues or producing toxins (cholera, tuberculosis, food poisoning). Viruses: not living — a core of DNA or RNA in a protein coat; they reproduce only inside a host cell, hijacking its machinery to make copies, bursting out and destroying it (measles, influenza, HIV). Fungi: eukaryotic organisms that feed on living or dead tissue (athlete's foot, ringworm). Protoctista: single-celled eukaryotes, often carried by a vector (Plasmodium causing malaria, carried by Anopheles mosquitoes). The difference matters for treatment: antibiotics kill bacteria (targeting walls, ribosomes or DNA replication) but have no effect on viruses, because viruses use the host's own machinery.

How pathogens spread: transmission routes

Direct contact: touching an infected person (skin, sexual contact — STIs), or contact with body fluids (blood, saliva, semen). Droplet infection: coughs and sneezes aerosolise droplets containing pathogens (influenza, tuberculosis, COVID-19). Airborne: pathogens travel on dust or droplet nuclei over longer distances. Contaminated food and water: cholera, typhoid, food poisoning (poor hygiene, untreated sewage). Vectors: organisms that carry and transmit pathogens without suffering themselves (mosquitoes for malaria, fleas for plague, tsetse flies for sleeping sickness). Blood-borne: needles, transfusions (HIV, hepatitis B). Water supply sanitation (chlorination, sewage treatment), hygiene (handwashing, food hygiene), and vector control (bed nets, insecticides) break these routes — and identifying which route a given disease uses is a standard exam question.

Non-specific (innate) defences

Non-specific defences protect against all pathogens in the same way — the body's first three lines. Skin: a physical barrier of dead, keratinised cells; intact skin cannot be penetrated by most pathogens; sebaceous glands secrete sebum (slightly acidic, antimicrobial). Mucous membranes: line the airways and gut; goblet cells secrete mucus trapping pathogens, cilia sweep the mucus to the throat (in the trachea) or it is swallowed; stomach acid (hydrochloric acid, pH 2) kills most swallowed pathogens. Chemical defences: lysozyme in tears and saliva digests bacterial walls; bile in the small intestine is antimicrobial. Inflammation: damaged cells release histamine, causing vasodilation (redness, heat, swelling) and increased blood flow, which delivers more white blood cells and clotting factors to the site. Phagocytosis: phagocytes (a type of white blood cell) are attracted by chemicals from damaged tissue and bacteria, engulf the pathogen into a vacuole, fuse it with a lysosome whose enzymes digest the pathogen (a phagosome becoming a phagolysosome). Non-specific responses have no memory and do not distinguish one pathogen from another.

Specific (adaptive) defences: the two arms

Specific defences target one particular pathogen and produce memory — the basis of immunity. The two types of white blood cell involved are phagocytes (non-specific, above) and lymphocytes (specific). Antigens are molecules (usually proteins) on the surface of pathogens — or on transplanted tissues — that identify them as foreign. When a lymphocyte meets "its" antigen it divides rapidly (clonal selection) and mounts one of two responses. The antibody response (humoral): lymphocytes in the blood and lymph nodes produce antibodies — Y-shaped proteins with a variable region complementary to one antigen; each antibody binds only its specific antigen (lock-and-key), forming an antigen-antibody complex that clumps pathogens (agglutination) so phagocytes can engulf them faster, or neutralises toxins. The cell-mediated response: phagocytes first engulf the pathogen and display its antigen (antigen presentation); T-lymphocytes (helper T cells) then coordinate the response, activating B-lymphocytes to make antibodies and stimulating phagocytes, and killing infected body cells directly. Antibody specificity means one type of lymphocyte (and its antibody) responds to one antigen only — which is why you can catch influenza many times in your life (many strains, each with different antigens).

Immunity: active, passive, natural, artificial

TypeHow acquiredMemory cells?Duration
Active naturalRecovering from the diseaseYesLong-lasting (often lifelong)
Active artificialVaccination (dead/attenuated pathogen or antigen)YesYears; boosters extend it
Passive naturalAntibodies across the placenta or in breast milkNoWeeks to months
Passive artificialInjection of antibodies (antiserum/antitoxin)NoShort — a few weeks

Active immunity involves the person's own lymphocytes making antibodies and memory cells (slow to develop but long-lasting); passive immunity transfers ready-made antibodies (immediate but temporary) — used for snake venom antitoxin, tetanus after a deep wound, and protecting newborn babies.

Vaccination and its population effects

A vaccine contains dead or attenuated (weakened) pathogens, or fragments of their antigens. On injection, they stimulate the primary response: lymphocytes with complementary receptors multiply, make antibodies, and — crucially — leave memory cells. If the real pathogen later enters, the secondary response is faster (memory cells divide immediately), stronger and longer, so the pathogen is destroyed before symptoms appear: the person is immune. Vaccination programmes also produce herd immunity: when a high proportion of a population is immunised, the pathogen cannot spread easily, protecting those too young, too ill or allergic to be vaccinated. Measles needs about 95 % coverage for herd immunity to hold. Exam questions love the "why vaccinate the whole population" line: it reduces the number of susceptible hosts, breaking the transmission chain.

Antibiotics and resistance

Antibiotics are chemicals (often from fungi such as Penicillium) that kill or inhibit bacteria — by breaking cell-wall synthesis (penicillin), blocking protein synthesis (tetracycline), or preventing DNA replication. They do not work on viruses, because viruses replicate using host machinery that antibiotics cannot target without harming the patient — which is why doctors do not prescribe antibiotics for influenza. Resistance evolves by natural selection: in any bacterial population, random mutations may let a few bacteria survive an antibiotic; those survivors reproduce, passing the resistance gene on (and plasmids carrying resistance can transfer between bacteria even across species); repeated or incomplete antibiotic courses select strongly for resistance. MRSA is a resistant Staphylococcus aureus strain causing hospital infections. Slowing resistance: only prescribe when necessary, complete the full course, do not share or use leftover antibiotics, develop new drugs, and use antibiotics less in agriculture. The misuse examples examiners expect: stopping a course early (leaving the most resistant bacteria alive), prescribing for viral infections, and broad overuse.

Worked example: following an infection through every defence

Scenario: a person inhales influenza virus droplets. Step 1 (barriers): mucus and cilia in the airway trap and sweep many virions to the throat; those remaining attach to airway epithelium. Step 2 (infection): the virus injects its RNA, hijacks the cell to make copies, and bursts out destroying cells — hence sore throat and cough. Step 3 (innate): damaged cells release histamine; inflammation brings phagocytes which engulf virions and present antigens. Step 4 (adaptive): helper T-lymphocytes detect the antigen and activate B-lymphocytes, which divide and secrete antibodies specific to the viral surface antigen; antibodies bind virions, clumping them for phagocytosis; T-killer cells destroy infected host cells. Step 5 (recovery and memory): after recovery, antibody levels fall but memory cells persist. Step 6 (secondary response): on re-exposure to the same strain, memory cells mount a rapid secondary response and no symptoms develop. Vaccination applies steps 3–6 with a harmless antigen instead of the live virus. Answer planning tip: an "explain how the body responds to a pathogen" question wants barriers first, then phagocytosis, then the specific response with antibodies and memory — in that order.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Calling viruses "bacteria" or claiming antibiotics kill viruses — the treatment distinction is a guaranteed question.
  • Writing that antibodies "kill" pathogens: they bind, clump and neutralise; phagocytes do the killing.
  • Confusing antigen (on the pathogen) with antibody (made by lymphocytes) — the single most common error in this topic.
  • Saying vaccination injects the disease: it injects dead or weakened pathogens or antigens that cannot cause the full disease.
  • Leaving "memory cells" out of any immunity explanation — they are the mechanism of long-term protection.
  • Describing passive immunity as "better": it is immediate but short-lived; active takes days but lasts.
  • Explaining antibiotic resistance as "the person becomes resistant": it is the bacteria that evolve resistance by selection of mutants.
  • Forgetting herd immunity when asked why healthy people should be vaccinated.

Exam-style questions and answers

Q1. Describe how phagocytes destroy bacteria. (3 marks) Answer: attracted by chemicals, engulf the bacterium into a vacuole (1); a lysosome fuses with the vacuole releasing digestive enzymes (1); the bacterium is digested and soluble products are absorbed (1).

Q2. Explain how vaccination produces immunity. (4 marks) Answer: vaccine contains dead/attenuated pathogen or antigens (1); stimulates lymphocytes to produce complementary antibodies (1); memory cells are produced (1); on re-infection the secondary response is faster and stronger so the pathogen is destroyed before symptoms appear (1).

Q3. Explain why antibiotics are ineffective against viruses. (2 marks) Answer: viruses replicate inside host cells using host machinery (1); antibiotics target bacterial structures/processes such as cell walls or bacterial ribosomes which viruses lack (1).

Q4. Explain how bacteria become resistant to antibiotics. (4 marks) Answer: random mutations produce resistant bacteria in the population (1); antibiotic kills non-resistant bacteria leaving resistant ones to reproduce (1); resistance gene passed on to offspring (1); overuse and incomplete courses increase the selection pressure (1).

Q5. Describe two ways in which malaria is transmitted and how its spread can be reduced. (4 marks) Answer: bitten by infected female Anopheles mosquitoes carrying the protoctistan Plasmodium (1); breeding-site reduction and insecticides (1); bed nets impregnated with insecticide (1); vaccines and prompt treatment of infected people (1).

title: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Ratio, Rate and Proportion
content:
Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Ratio, Rate and Proportion

Ratio, rate and proportion are the mathematics of comparison: how two quantities share a whole, how fast one changes with another, and what happens when one stays on the same path to infinity. They appear in nearly every Paper 2, usually as multi-step word problems where the arithmetic is easy and the interpretation is not. This note builds the topic from zero: simplifying and dividing in ratios, the unitary method for direct and inverse proportion, the algebra forms y = kx and y = k/x, and rates — speed, density, flow — with their unit conversions.

Ratio fundamentals

A ratio compares quantities of the same kind. The notation a : b means "a for every b". Equivalent ratios are made by multiplying or dividing all parts by the same number; the simplified ratio has no common factor (other than 1) and, for measurements, the same units.

  • Simplify: 24 : 36 = 2 : 3 (divide both by 12).
  • Three-part: 2 : 3 : 5 means five shares in total; each share is total ÷ 10.
  • Units first: 500 g : 1.5 kg = 500 : 1500 = 1 : 3. Convert before simplifying, never after.

Worked example. Share £84 in the ratio 3 : 4.

total parts = 3 + 4 = 7
one part = 84/7 = 12
shares = 3 x 12 = 36 and 4 x 12 = 48
check: 36 + 48 = 84

Worked example 2 (three parts). A sum of $240 is divided among A, B and C in the ratio 2 : 3 : 5. Find each share.

parts = 2 + 3 + 5 = 10
one part = 240/10 = 24
A = 2 x 24 = 48, B = 3 x 24 = 72, C = 5 x 24 = 120

Combining ratios and ratio changes

Two ratios sharing a middle term can be combined by making that term common:

A : B = 2 : 3 and B : C = 4 : 5
LCM of the B terms (3 and 4) is 12:
A : B = 8 : 12 and B : C = 12 : 15
so A : B : C = 8 : 12 : 15

Worked example (change). A bag contains red and blue counters in the ratio 5 : 3. After 6 red counters are removed, the ratio becomes 1 : 1. Find the original numbers.

let red = 5x, blue = 3x
(5x - 6)/3x = 1  ->  5x - 6 = 3x  ->  2x = 6  ->  x = 3
original: red = 15, blue = 9
check: after removing 6 red, 9 : 9 = 1 : 1

Direct proportion

Two quantities are in direct proportion when one is a constant multiple of the other: double one, double the other. The algebra form is y = kx, a straight line through the origin.

y = k x        k = y/x (the constant of proportionality)
unitary method: find the value of one unit, then multiply

Worked example. 5 pens cost $3.25. Find the cost of 12 pens.

one pen = 3.25/5 = $0.65
12 pens = 12 x 0.65 = $7.80

Worked example 2 (algebra form). y is directly proportional to x, and y = 18 when x = 6. Find y when x = 11.

y = kx  ->  18 = 6k  ->  k = 3
y = 3 x 11 = 33

Worked example 3 (proportion with powers). The mass of a sphere is proportional to the cube of its radius; a sphere of radius 2 cm has mass 40 g. Find the mass of a sphere of radius 3 cm.

m = k r^3  ->  40 = k x 8  ->  k = 5
m = 5 x 27 = 135 g

Inverse proportion

Inverse proportion means one quantity falls as the other rises: double one, halve the other. The algebra form is y = k/x (the product xy is constant).

y = k/x        x y = k
unitary method: find the total "work" (product), then divide

Worked example. Six workers build a wall in 8 days. How long will 4 workers take (same rate)?

total work = 6 x 8 = 48 worker-days
time for 4 = 48/4 = 12 days

Worked example 2 (algebra). y is inversely proportional to x; y = 5 when x = 4. Find y when x = 10.

xy = k  ->  4 x 5 = 20  ->  y = 20/10 = 2

The shape on a graph distinguishes the two: direct proportion is a straight line through the origin; inverse proportion is a curve that never touches either axis (a hyperbola).

Rates

A rate compares quantities with different units: speed (distance per time), density (mass per volume), pressure (force per area), flow rate (volume per time). Each is a division, and each can be rearranged.

speed = distance/time        density = mass/volume
pressure = force/area        flow rate = volume/time

average speed over a journey = total distance/total time
(not the average of the speeds, unless the times are equal)

Worked example 1 (speed). A car travels 150 km in 2 hours 30 minutes. Find its average speed in km/h and m/s.

time = 2.5 h
speed = 150/2.5 = 60 km/h
in m/s: 60 x 1000/3600 = 16.7 m/s

Worked example 2 (density). A block of volume 250 cm³ has mass 675 g. Find its density, and the mass of 400 cm³ of the same material.

density = 675/250 = 2.7 g/cm3
mass = 2.7 x 400 = 1080 g = 1.08 kg

Worked example 3 (average speed trap). A cyclist rides 20 km at 20 km/h, then 20 km at 10 km/h. Find the average speed for the whole journey.

time 1 = 20/20 = 1 h;  time 2 = 20/10 = 2 h
total distance = 40 km; total time = 3 h
average speed = 40/3 = 13.3 km/h (not 15!)

Flow rates and filling problems

Flow-rate questions combine a rate with a volume: a tap fills at 4 litres per minute, a pump empties at 6 litres per minute, a pipe delivers water at 2.5 m s⁻¹ through a cross-section. The method is the same division, but the units demand attention — litres per minute into litres and minutes, cubic metres per second into m³ and s, with 1 m³ = 1000 litres and 1 minute = 60 s.

Worked example. A bath holds 180 litres. A tap fills it at 9 litres per minute, but the plug leaks 1.5 litres per minute. How long does the bath take to fill?

net rate = 9 - 1.5 = 7.5 litres per minute
time = 180/7.5 = 24 minutes

Best buys and multi-step comparisons

Ratio reasoning powers the practical comparison questions: which packet is better value, which journey is faster per kilometre, which contract costs less per month. The method is always to reduce both options to the same unit before comparing, and to compare like with like (price per 100 g, cost per km, cost per month).

Worked example. A 750 g box of cereal costs $3.60 and a 1.2 kg box costs $5.28. Which is better value?

large: 5.28/1.2 = $4.40 per kg
small: 3.60/0.75 = $4.80 per kg
better value: the 1.2 kg box (lower cost per kg)

Worked example 2 (multi-step). Two phone contracts: A charges $12 per month plus $0.10 per GB; B charges $20 per month with 15 GB included. For someone using 20 GB per month, which is cheaper over a year?

A: 12 + 0.10 x 20 = $14 per month; yearly = 168
B: $20 per month; yearly = 240
A is cheaper for a 20 GB user by $72 per year.
(check the crossover: 12 + 0.1g = 20 -> g = 80 GB, so B
only wins for very heavy users)

The crossover point is a favourite extension: set the two cost expressions equal and solve, then interpret which side of the crossing each customer sits on.

Worked examples: mixed problems

Worked example. A recipe for 4 people uses 300 g of rice. How much is needed for 10 people, and how many people can be served with 2.1 kg?

per person = 300/4 = 75 g
for 10: 750 g
2100 g / 75 = 28 people

Worked example 2 (currency). An exchange rate is £1 = $1.25. Convert £240 to dollars and $500 to pounds.

240 x 1.25 = $300
500/1.25 = £400

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Divide) Share 360 in the ratio 5 : 7. Answer: parts 12; one part 30; shares 150 and 210.
  2. (Simplify with units) Simplify 40 minutes : 2 hours. Answer: 40 : 120 = 1 : 3.
  3. (Direct) 8 m of cloth costs $52. Find the cost of 13 m. Answer: per metre $6.50; 13 × 6.50 = $84.50.
  4. (Inverse) 4 taps fill a tank in 45 minutes. How long for 6 taps? Answer: total = 4 × 45 = 180 tap-minutes; 180/6 = 30 minutes.
  5. (Algebra) y ∝ x² and y = 50 when x = 5. Find y when x = 8. Answer: 50 = k × 25 → k = 2; y = 2 × 64 = 128.
  6. (Rate) A train covers 210 km in 2 h 20 min. Find its average speed. Answer: 2⅓ h; 210 ÷ 7/3 = 90 km/h.
  7. (Density) 150 cm³ of a liquid has mass 120 g. Find the mass of 1 litre. Answer: density 0.8 g/cm³; 1000 cm³ × 0.8 = 800 g.
  8. (Reverse) A map scale is 1 : 50 000. Two points are 7 cm apart on the map. Find the real distance in km. Answer: 7 × 50 000 = 350 000 cm = 3.5 km.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Averaging speeds: average speed is total distance over total time, never the mean of the two speeds unless the times are equal. The classic 20/10 km/h trap answers 15 instead of 13.3.
  • Ratio direction: dividing 84 in 3 : 4 is not 84 × 3/4 for both shares; identify which share is which before writing the answer.
  • Units in ratios: 500 g : 1.5 kg simplifies only after conversion to 500 : 1500 = 1 : 3. Mixing units gives 1 : 0.003.
  • Direct versus inverse: ask "if one doubles, what happens to the other?" Doubling both means direct; one doubling while the other halves means inverse.
  • Proportional to a power: for y ∝ x², doubling x multiplies y by 4; for y ∝ √x it multiplies by √2. Find k from the given pair first.
  • Currency direction: multiplying by the rate converts one way; the reverse needs division. Check with a rough estimate.
  • Time units: 2 h 30 min is 2.5 h, not 2.3 h. Convert minutes to a decimal fraction of an hour before dividing.
  • Rounding mid-calculation: keep full accuracy until the final answer, then round to 3 s.f. or as instructed; money answers usually need 2 decimal places.

title: IGCSE Mathematics: Simplifying and Expanding
content:
IGCSE Mathematics: Simplifying and Expanding

Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580 (2025–2027), section 2 Algebra and graphs: statements 2.1 Introduction to algebra, 2.2 Algebraic manipulation and 2.3 Algebraic fractions (Extended). Algebra is the language the rest of the course is written in, and this note is its grammar: what letters mean, how expressions are simplified and expanded, how they are factorised, and how algebraic fractions are handled. Every manipulation below is written out line by line, because on Paper 2 (non-calculator) the method marks are the marks — and on Paper 4 an unexplained jump is where sign errors hide.

What a letter means: an introduction to algebra

A letter in algebra is a placeholder for a number whose value can change (a variable) or for a number that is fixed but unknown (a constant). The expression 3x + 2 says: take a number, multiply it by 3, then add 2. Substitution is the reverse: if x = 5, then 3x + 2 = 3 × 5 + 2 = 15 + 2 = 17. Work in the given order — multiplication before addition — because the conventions of algebra are just the conventions of arithmetic with letters standing in for numbers.

  • 3x means 3 × x. Writing 3 × x with a multiplication sign is unnecessary, but writing 3x as 3 + x is a serious error.
  • x² means x × x, and 2x² means 2 × x × x — the index applies only to the x, not to the 2.
  • xy means x × y, and x(y + 2) means x multiplied by the whole bracket.
  • A term is a product of numbers and letters, such as 3x²; terms are separated by + and − signs.
  • Like terms have exactly the same letter part: 3x² and −7x² are like terms; 3x² and 3x are not.

Why letters work at all. A rule like a(b + c) = ab + ac is not a trick to memorise — it is the distributive property of arithmetic, true for every number, so writing it once with letters proves it for all cases at once instead of checking each one. That is the whole power of algebra: one line of symbols replaces a million examples.

Simplifying: collecting like terms

To simplify, gather the like terms and add their coefficients (the numbers in front). Work one letter part at a time and keep every sign with its term.

Simplify:  5x + 3y - 2x + 7 - y + 4

Group the x terms, then the y terms, then the numbers:
= 5x - 2x + 3y - y + 7 + 4        [terms rearranged; each sign travels with its term]
= (5 - 2)x + (3 - 1)y + (7 + 4)   [coefficients collected]
= 3x + 2y + 11

For expressions with powers, only identical letter parts can join:

Simplify:  4x^2 + 3x - x^2 + 2x - 9

= 4x^2 - x^2 + 3x + 2x - 9
= (4 - 1)x^2 + (3 + 2)x - 9
= 3x^2 + 5x - 9

The x² and x terms never combine: x² counts squares while x counts lengths, and they are different kinds of quantity — exactly why the index must match before terms are collected.

Expanding brackets

Expanding uses the distributive law: every term outside the bracket multiplies every term inside. The golden rule of signs is that a minus sign in front of a bracket changes the sign of everything inside.

Expand:  3(2x - 5)

= 3 x 2x + 3 x (-5)        [each term inside multiplied by 3]
= 6x - 15
Expand:  -(4x - 7)

= -1 x 4x + (-1) x (-7)    [a bracket with no number means x (-1)]
= -4x + 7

Two brackets multiply every term of the first by every term of the second. Writing each product on its own line prevents the classic dropped-term error:

Expand and simplify:  (2x + 3)(x - 5)

= 2x x x + 2x x (-5) + 3 x x + 3 x (-5)     [four products: each term x each term]
= 2x^2 - 10x + 3x - 15
= 2x^2 - 7x - 15

The pattern is sometimes called FOIL (First, Outer, Inner, Last), but the safe habit is the one above: systematic, complete, and it scales to three brackets:

Expand:  (x + 1)(x - 2)(x + 3)

First expand the first two brackets:
(x + 1)(x - 2) = x x x + x x (-2) + 1 x x + 1 x (-2) = x^2 - 2x + x - 2 = x^2 - x - 2
Now multiply by the third bracket, term by term:
(x^2 - x - 2)(x + 3) = x^2 x x + x^2 x 3 + (-x) x x + (-x) x 3 + (-2) x x + (-2) x 3
= x^3 + 3x^2 - x^2 - 3x - 2x - 6
= x^3 + 2x^2 - 5x - 6

Perfect squares deserve instant recognition: (x + 5)² = (x + 5)(x + 5) = x² + 10x + 25. The middle term is 2 × 5 × x = 10x, so (x + a)² = x² + 2ax + a². Writing (x + 5)² as x² + 25 is the single most common error in the whole of algebra.

Factorising

Factorising is expanding in reverse: writing a sum as a product. Every factorisation can be checked by expanding again, and on an exam that check costs seconds.

Common factors. Take out the highest factor of every term:

Factorise:  12x^3 - 8x^2

Highest common factor of 12x^3 and 8x^2 is 4x^2:
= 4x^2(3x) + 4x^2(-2)        [showing the division of each term]
= 4x^2(3x - 2)

Factorising quadratics of the form x² + bx + c. Find two numbers that multiply to c and add to b:

Factorise:  x^2 + 7x + 12

Two numbers with product +12 and sum +7: 3 and 4 (both positive, since c and b are positive)
Check: 3 x 4 = 12 and 3 + 4 = 7
= (x + 3)(x + 4)

Expand to verify: (x + 3)(x + 4) = x^2 + 4x + 3x + 12 = x^2 + 7x + 12  ✓

Signs follow from the product and sum: for x² − 2x − 15 the product is −15 and the sum is −2, so the numbers are −5 and +3 (the larger number carries the sign of the sum), giving (x − 5)(x + 3).

Factorising ax² + bx + c. When the coefficient of x² is not 1, multiply a × c and split the middle term:

Factorise:  6x^2 + 11x - 10

a x c = 6 x (-10) = -60; find two numbers with product -60 and sum +11: +15 and -4
Split the middle term:  6x^2 + 15x - 4x - 10
Factorise in pairs:     3x(2x + 5) - 2(2x + 5)        [first pair gives 3x, second gives -2]
Take out (2x + 5):      (2x + 5)(3x - 2)

Expand to verify: 6x^2 - 4x + 15x - 10 = 6x^2 + 11x - 10  ✓

Difference of two squares. Whenever an expression is two squares subtracted, x² − a² = (x + a)(x − a), because the middle terms cancel when expanded: (x + a)(x − a) = x² − ax + ax − a² = x² − a². So 9x² − 25 = (3x + 5)(3x − 5).

Completing the square (Extended). Rewrite x² + bx as a square minus a correction:

Write x^2 + 6x - 7 in the form (x + p)^2 + q

x^2 + 6x - 7 = (x + 3)^2 - 3^2 - 7        [half of 6 is 3; (x+3)^2 introduces +9, so subtract 9]
= (x + 3)^2 - 9 - 7
= (x + 3)^2 - 16

This form reads off the turning point at once: the minimum value is −16, at x = −3. For 2x² + 8x − 5, take the 2 out first: 2(x² + 4x) − 5 = 2[(x + 2)² − 4] − 5 = 2(x + 2)² − 13.

ExpressionFactorisationHow to spot it
ax² + bxx(ax + b)Common factor: every term shares an x
x² + bx + c(x + p)(x + q) with pq = c, p + q = bFind the number pair with product c and sum b
ax² + bx + c(px + q)(rx + s)Split the middle term using a × c, then factorise in pairs
x² − a²(x + a)(x − a)Difference of two squares: a subtraction of two square terms
x² + 2ax + a²(x + a)²Perfect square: first and last terms are squares and the middle is twice their product

The order matters: take out a common factor before looking for any pattern, and check every factorisation by re-expanding. A table like this is worth copying into revision cards, because recognising the shape is faster in the exam than deriving it.

Algebraic fractions (Extended)

Algebraic fractions obey exactly the same rules as ordinary fractions — and it is worth knowing why those rules are what they are. Multiplication multiplies tops and bottoms because a fraction is a product. Division asks how many of one fraction fit into another, and the answer is the reciprocal: 3/4 ÷ 1/2 asks how many halves fit into three quarters, and the answer is 1½, which is 3/4 × 2/1 = 3/2. Dividing by a fraction is the same as multiplying by its reciprocal — the rule is not arbitrary; it is what division means.

Simplify:  (x^2 - 9) / (x^2 + 5x + 6)

Factorise top and bottom completely first:
= (x + 3)(x - 3) / [(x + 3)(x + 2)]
Cancel the common factor (x + 3):
= (x - 3) / (x + 2)        valid except where x + 3 = 0

Cancellation divides top and bottom by the same thing, which is legitimate; cancelling individual terms across a sum (writing (x + 3)/(x + 2) as 3/2) is not, because the top is not a product.

Express as a single fraction:  2/(x - 1) - 3/(x + 2)

The lowest common denominator is (x - 1)(x + 2):
= 2(x + 2) / [(x - 1)(x + 2)] - 3(x - 1) / [(x - 1)(x + 2)]     [each fraction multiplied by the missing factor]
= [2(x + 2) - 3(x - 1)] / [(x - 1)(x + 2)]                       [single denominator; brackets protect the signs]
= [2x + 4 - 3x + 3] / [(x - 1)(x + 2)]                           [expanding: -3 x -1 = +3]
= (7 - x) / [(x - 1)(x + 2)]
Multiply and divide:  (x^2 - 4)/(x + 5)  x  (x + 5)/(x + 2)

= [(x + 2)(x - 2)(x + 5)] / [(x + 5)(x + 2)]     [factorise, then multiply tops and bottoms]
= x - 2

Worked example: a full simplification

Simplify and factorise completely: 3(x + 2)² − 2(x + 2)(x − 1) − 5x.

Expand (x + 2)^2 first:   (x + 2)(x + 2) = x^2 + 2x + 2x + 4 = x^2 + 4x + 4
So 3(x + 2)^2 = 3x^2 + 12x + 12

Expand (x + 2)(x - 1):    x x x + x x (-1) + 2 x x + 2 x (-1) = x^2 - x + 2x - 2 = x^2 + x - 2
So -2(x + 2)(x - 1) = -2x^2 - 2x + 4

Put everything together:
3x^2 + 12x + 12 - 2x^2 - 2x + 4 - 5x
= 3x^2 - 2x^2 + 12x - 2x - 5x + 12 + 4
= x^2 + 5x + 16

The expression x^2 + 5x + 16 does not factorise over the integers (no pair multiplies to 16 and adds to 5),
so the simplified form is the final answer.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Writing (x + 5)² as x² + 25. Squaring a bracket gives a middle term: x² + 10x + 25.
  • Dropping a minus sign when expanding a bracket with a minus in front: −(3x − 4) = −3x + 4, not −3x − 4.
  • Cancelling a single term across a sum: (x + 3)/(x + 2) cannot be simplified by cancelling x.
  • Collecting unlike terms: 3x² + 5x is already simplified; nothing more can join.
  • Losing the sign of a term when rearranging: 5 − 2x written as 2x − 5 flips the expression.
  • Forgetting to divide every term when taking out a common factor: 12x³ − 8x² = 4x²(3x − 2), and the −2 must be checked by re-expanding.
  • On Paper 2, leaving a decimal where an exact fraction or surd is required — without a calculator, exact answers are the point.
  • Assuming x² + bx + c always factorises; when no integer pair works (or the discriminant is negative), the expression is already final.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 2, 3 marks). Simplify fully: 4(2x − 3) − 3(x − 5).

Answer: 8x − 12 − 3x + 15 = 5x + 3. (Distribute the −3 correctly: −3 × −5 = +15.)

Question 2 (Paper 2, 4 marks). Factorise completely: 3x² − 27.

Answer: Take out the common factor 3: 3(x² − 9). Recognise the difference of two squares inside: 3(x + 3)(x − 3). Taking only one factor loses the second mark.

Question 3 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Expand and simplify (2x − 1)(x + 4).

Answer: 2x × x + 2x × 4 + (−1) × x + (−1) × 4 = 2x² + 8x − x − 4 = 2x² + 7x − 4.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Write (2x − 3)/(x + 1) − 2/(x − 2) as a single fraction in its simplest form.

Answer: Common denominator (x + 1)(x − 2): [(2x − 3)(x − 2) − 2(x + 1)] / [(x + 1)(x − 2)] = [2x² − 4x − 3x + 6 − 2x − 2] / [(x + 1)(x − 2)] = (2x² − 9x + 4) / [(x + 1)(x − 2)], which factorises to (2x − 1)(x − 4)/[(x + 1)(x − 2)] and no longer cancels.

Question 5 (Paper 2, 3 marks). Express 2x² + 12x − 7 in the form 2(x + a)² + b.

Answer: 2(x² + 6x) − 7 = 2[(x + 3)² − 9] − 7 = 2(x + 3)² − 18 − 7 = 2(x + 3)² − 25. So a = 3, b = −25.

Question 6 (Paper 4, 3 marks). Given f(x) = (x² − 4)/(x² + x − 2), simplify f(x) and state the value of x for which it is undefined.

Answer: f(x) = (x + 2)(x − 2)/[(x + 2)(x − 1)] = (x − 2)/(x − 1). It is undefined where the original denominator is zero: x² + x − 2 = (x + 2)(x − 1) = 0, so x = −2 or x = 1.

Once expressions are in hand, equations solve for the unknowns they contain.

title: IGCSE Biology: Enzymes
content:
IGCSE Biology: Enzymes

Enzymes are the reason you can digest a meal in hours rather than centuries: they are biological catalysts, proteins that speed up chemical reactions without being consumed. This note starts with the lock-and-key picture of how they work, moves to the factors that change their rate (temperature, pH, substrate concentration, enzyme concentration), gives the graph-reading rules examiners use to separate A-grade answers from C-grade ones, and closes with the Paper 6 enzyme-investigation design you can be asked to write from scratch. Every graph is described in words as well as axes, so you can reconstruct it in the exam.

What an enzyme is, physically

Each enzyme is a globular protein folded so that part of its surface forms a pocket called the active site — a groove whose shape and charge match one particular molecule, the substrate. When substrate meets active site they form an enzyme-substrate complex, the reaction happens (bonds broken or made), and the products leave, freeing the unchanged enzyme to repeat. The lock-and-key analogy imagines the substrate as the key and the active site as the lock; the induced-fit model is the modern refinement — the active site flexes slightly to grip the substrate, straining its bonds so less energy is needed to break them. That lowering of activation energy is the whole catalytic trick: enzymes do not add energy, they lower the hill the reaction must climb.

Specificity and the naming rule

Each enzyme acts on one substrate only, because the active site is complementary to that substrate's shape — this is enzyme specificity. The naming convention is worth a free mark: the enzyme is named after its substrate with the suffix –ase. Starch is digested by carbohydrase (specifically amylase); protein by protease; lipid by lipase; and a specific sugar like lactose by lactase. Maltase digests maltose, sucrase digests sucrose. If a question names a substrate and asks for its enzyme, answer by adding –ase and you will almost always be right.

Temperature and enzyme rate

Temperature works in two stages. Below the optimum, heating increases the kinetic energy of both enzyme and substrate, so they collide more often and with more energy — the rate rises (roughly doubling per 10 °C near the optimum). At the optimum temperature (around 37 °C for human enzymes, 25 °C for many plant enzymes), the rate is fastest. Above the optimum, the bonds holding the tertiary structure (hydrogen and ionic bonds) break: the active site changes shape, the substrate no longer fits, and the enzyme is denatured — this is permanent. The graph of rate against temperature is therefore a steep rise, a rounded peak, then a fall to zero. Exam phrasing: "denatured" must be paired with "active site changes shape" and "substrate no longer fits" to earn all the marks.

pH and enzyme rate

Each enzyme has an optimum pH — around pH 2 for pepsin in the stomach, pH 7–8 for salivary amylase and trypsin in the small intestine. Changing pH alters the charges on the amino acids of the active site; far from the optimum, ionic and hydrogen bonds break and the enzyme denatures, exactly as with temperature. The rate-pH graph is a bell curve centred on the optimum. The trap: do not write that acid "kills" the enzyme or that pH "denatures the substrate" — it is the enzyme's structure that fails.

Substrate and enzyme concentration

With enzyme constant and substrate concentration rising: the rate rises in direct proportion at first (more substrate means more frequent collisions, every active site busy), then the curve levels off (a plateau) when all active sites are occupied — the enzyme is saturated, and adding substrate cannot help. With substrate in excess and enzyme concentration rising: the rate rises linearly and does not plateau while substrate remains available. Recognising which factor is limiting is a standard three-mark "explain the shape of the graph" question: name the limiting factor at each stage (substrate concentration below saturation; number of active sites above it).

Every factor at a glance

FactorEffect on rate below the optimumEffect above the optimumReason
TemperatureRate rises with heatingRate falls to zeroMore energetic collisions, then denaturation of the active site
pHRate rises towards the optimumRate falls to zeroCharges on the active site change, then bonds break
Substrate concentrationRate rises in proportionRate plateausAll active sites occupied — the enzyme is saturated
Enzyme concentrationRate rises in proportionRises while substrate remainsMore active sites available for the substrate

Inhibitors

Competitive inhibitors have a shape similar to the substrate and bind to the active site, blocking it; their effect can be reduced by raising substrate concentration (more substrate outcompetes them). Non-competitive inhibitors bind elsewhere on the enzyme (an allosteric site), changing the active site's shape so the substrate cannot fit; raising substrate concentration does not overcome them. At IGCSE, know both in one line each and be able to say which one is affected by substrate concentration — that distinction is a favourite Paper 2 and Paper 4 probe.

Investigating enzyme rate: the Paper 6 method

A standard investigation: measure 5 cm³ of starch solution into a water bath at a set temperature; add 1 cm³ of amylase solution; start the timer; every 30 seconds take a drop of the mixture and test on a spotting tile with iodine; record the time until the iodine stays yellow-brown (all starch hydrolysed). Rate = 1 ÷ time (the standard reciprocal, in s⁻¹). Variables: independent = temperature (or pH, or enzyme concentration); dependent = time for starch to disappear (converted to rate); controls = volume and concentration of starch, volume and concentration of enzyme, pH (use buffer), identical timing technique. Repeat and take a mean. A water bath (not a Bunsen flame) is required for temperature control, and each test tube must reach the set temperature before mixing.

Worked example: reading and calculating from an enzyme experiment

At 25 °C, starch disappeared in 240 s; at 35 °C, in 120 s; at 45 °C, in 150 s; at 55 °C, in 600 s. Step 1: convert to rate using rate = 1 ÷ time: 1/240 = 0.00417 s⁻¹; 1/120 = 0.00833 s⁻¹; 1/150 = 0.00667 s⁻¹; 1/600 = 0.00167 s⁻¹. Step 2: read the pattern — the rate rises from 25 to 35 °C (kinetic energy up), peaks between 35 and 45 °C, then collapses at 55 °C. Step 3: explain each point as the examiner wants: from 25 to 35 °C, more energetic collisions occur; at the peak the enzyme is at its optimum; at 55 °C the enzyme has denatured, its active site has changed shape and the substrate no longer fits, so the rate is lowest. Step 4: state the trend as a sentence with a number: "the fastest rate was at 35 °C (0.00833 s⁻¹) and the slowest at 55 °C (0.00167 s⁻¹), a five-fold difference." Always quote at least one figure when asked to "use the data".

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Writing that enzymes "are used up" — catalysts are unchanged at the end; say "recovered unchanged".
  • Explaining high temperature as "the enzyme dies" — enzymes are not alive; say the enzyme is denatured because bonds in the tertiary structure break.
  • Forgetting to state "the active site changes shape, so the substrate can no longer fit" — the two extra clauses are the extra marks.
  • Confusing "rate of reaction" with "time taken": rate = 1 ÷ time, so a longer time means a slower rate; plotting time and calling it rate loses interpretation marks.
  • Leaving units off rates (s⁻¹ or per second) or off concentration (mol/dm³) in Paper 4 calculations.
  • In a design question, not controlling pH or temperature — even if you are not investigating them, they must be listed and held constant.
  • Calling the lock-and-key model "wrong": at IGCSE, induced fit is the more precise description, but both are accepted if you explain specificity.
  • Saying competitive inhibitors "kill" enzymes; they only block the active site temporarily.

Exam-style questions and answers

Q1. Explain why the rate of an enzyme-controlled reaction increases as temperature rises from 20 °C to 30 °C. (2 marks) Answer: molecules gain kinetic energy so move faster (1); collisions between enzyme and substrate are more frequent and more energetic, so more enzyme-substrate complexes form (1).

Q2. Explain what happens to an enzyme at 60 °C and why the reaction stops. (3 marks) Answer: the enzyme is denatured (1); bonds maintaining the tertiary structure break so the active site changes shape (1); the substrate no longer fits so no enzyme-substrate complexes form (1).

Q3. Describe how you would investigate the effect of pH on amylase activity. (4 marks) Answer: use buffers to set a range of pH values (1); keep starch concentration, amylase volume and temperature constant (1); time how long starch takes to be hydrolysed, testing with iodine (1); repeat and calculate rate = 1 ÷ time, plot rate against pH (1).

Q4. Explain why adding more substrate eventually stops increasing the reaction rate. (2 marks) Answer: the enzyme becomes saturated — all active sites are occupied at any moment (1), so additional substrate has to wait and cannot raise the rate further (1).

Q5. A reaction takes 40 s. Calculate the rate and state its unit. (2 marks) Answer: rate = 1 ÷ 40 = 0.025 (1); unit s⁻¹ or per second (1).

Equations and symbols

Every relation this topic is examined on, written with its real notation and followed by a key naming each symbol, its unit and what it means. Where a law has a second useful form both are given, so the rearrangement in the exam is mechanical rather than a thing to rediscover under time pressure.

Measuring enzyme rate

rate = amount of product formed / time taken
Key: rate = the speed of the reaction (units per second or per minute, e.g. cm³ s⁻¹ of gas, or g min⁻¹ of product); amount of product = the measured change (volume of gas, mass lost, colour change); time = the interval over which it happened. The quantity measured in Paper 6 is almost always one of these three.

rate = 1 / time to completion
Key: time to completion = how long the reaction takes to finish, judged by a fixed end point (all the substrate gone, the colour stops changing). A convenient rate in arbitrary units: if one tube finishes in 20 s and another in 40 s, the first is twice as fast.

mean rate = (total product) / (total time)
Key: the average over the whole experiment. It is smaller than the initial rate, because the substrate concentration falls as the reaction proceeds — which is why the initial rate is the fair comparison between two conditions.

initial rate = gradient of the tangent at t = 0 on a product-against-time graph
Key: gradient = change in y divided by change in x, taken at the steepest point (the start). Drawing the tangent by eye is a mark-scheme skill: use a ruler, take points far apart, and give the unit.

Comparing rates between conditions

Q₁₀ = rate at (T + 10 °C) / rate at T
Key: Q₁₀ = the temperature coefficient; T = the lower temperature in °C. A Q₁₀ of about 2 for a enzyme-catalysed reaction means the rate doubles for a 10 °C rise — until the enzyme denatures, above which Q₁₀ falls below 1 and the comparison becomes meaningless.

% change = ((new value − original value) / original value) × 100
Key: new value = the rate under the changed condition; original value = the control rate. The correct way to say "how much faster", and the check that a percentage has not been confused with a rate.

optimum temperature: the peak of the rate-against-temperature graph
Key: rate rises to a maximum as kinetic energy and collision frequency increase, then falls sharply as the enzyme's tertiary structure breaks and the active site loses its shape. The fall is not gradual: denaturation is irreversible, which is why the graph is asymmetric.

optimum pH: the peak of the rate-against-pH graph
Key: pH changes the charges on the amino acids in the active site, so the substrate no longer fits; extremes also denature the enzyme. Pepsin works near pH 2, salivary amylase near pH 7, and a question that gives the wrong optimum for the named enzyme is a common trap.

title: IGCSE Physics: Measurement and Units
content:
IGCSE Physics: Measurement and Units

Cambridge IGCSE Physics 0625 (2026–2028), Topic 1 Motion, forces and energy, statement 1.1 Physical quantities and measurement techniques — plus the experimental skills that Paper 6, Alternative to Practical, examines directly. Every physics result rests on a measurement, and every measurement is uncertain. This note builds the vocabulary of quantities and units, the practical techniques for length, volume and time, and then the full Paper 6 method: variables, safety, tables, graph plotting, gradients and intercepts, conclusions and error analysis. Paper 2 and Paper 4 carry the theory marks; Paper 6 carries these skills as a written exam of their own.

Physical quantities and SI units

A physical quantity is a property that can be measured, and every measurement needs a number and a unit. Physics uses the SI system, whose base units include the metre (m) for length, the kilogram (kg) for mass, the second (s) for time, the ampere (A) for electric current, the kelvin (K) for temperature and the mole (mol) for amount of substance. All other units are derived from these: speed in metres per second (m s⁻¹) is a base unit divided by a base unit, and force in newtons is defined so that 1 N = 1 kg m s⁻².

QuantitySymbolSI unitHow the unit is built
Lengths or lmetre (m)base unit
Massmkilogram (kg)base unit
Timetsecond (s)base unit
VolumeVcubic metre (m³)m³; litres and cm³ are everyday alternatives (1 litre = 0.001 m³)
Speedvmetre per second (m s⁻¹)m ÷ s
Frequencyfhertz (Hz)1 Hz = 1 cycle per second (s⁻¹)
ForceFnewton (N)kg m s⁻²
EnergyEjoule (J)N m = kg m² s⁻²
Pressureppascal (Pa)N m⁻²

Large and small quantities use standard prefixes or standard form: kilo (×1000), centi (÷100), milli (÷1000), micro (÷10⁶). Standard form writes a quantity as a number between 1 and 10 multiplied by a power of ten, so the speed of light is 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. Units obey ordinary algebra: dividing metres by seconds gives m s⁻¹, and a unit written as m/s and one written as m s⁻¹ are the same thing.

Measuring length, area and volume

Length is measured with a ruler or a tape. The three rules of good practice are fixed: place the scale edge along the line being measured, start from the zero mark rather than the worn end of the ruler, and take the reading at eye level directly above the point to avoid parallax error. A ruler reading should be quoted to the nearest half millimetre with an uncertainty of about ±0.5 mm; a vernier caliper or a micrometer screw gauge reads to 0.01 mm and is used when the length is small.

Areas and volumes are calculated from measured lengths. The area of a rectangle is length × width; the volume of a rectangular block is length × width × height; the volume of a cylinder is π r² l. For an irregular solid, the volume is found by displacement: water is poured into a measuring cylinder, the starting volume is read, the object is lowered in, and the rise in level is the object's volume. Read the bottom of the curved meniscus at eye level. The technique fails for objects that float (use a sinker), objects that absorb water or dissolve (use sand or oil), and objects that splash water out on entry (lower them gently on a thread).

Area scales with the square of a length and volume with the cube, so a small length error is amplified: a 2 per cent error in each of the three dimensions of a cube gives about a 6 per cent error in its volume. This is exactly the kind of reasoning Paper 6 rewards in its evaluation questions.

Measuring time intervals

Short times are measured with a stopwatch, and human reaction time of about 0.2 s dominates a single reading. Two standard techniques control it. First, repeat and average: time several oscillations of a pendulum and divide by the number of swings, because the reaction error is then spread over many periods. Second, use a larger quantity: time 20 trolley passes rather than one, or measure the time for 50 dots from a 50 Hz ticker timer, where consecutive dots are 0.02 s apart. Timing devices built into the apparatus — light gates, data loggers and ticker timers — remove reaction time entirely and are the expected answer when a question asks how to improve a timing measurement.

Errors, precision and percentage uncertainty

Every measurement carries an uncertainty, usually taken as the range of the scale: ±0.5 mm on a ruler, ±0.5 s on a stopwatch read to seconds, ±0.5 of the smallest scale division on a measuring cylinder. Two kinds of error behave differently. A random error scatters readings in both directions and is reduced by repeating and averaging; a systematic error shifts every reading the same way — a zero error on a balance, a bent ruler, parallax — and is removed by correcting the instrument, never by averaging. An anomaly is a result that does not fit the pattern; it is discarded only with a stated reason, never because it is inconvenient.

The size of an uncertainty is compared using percentage uncertainty, a technique Paper 6 tests whenever results are combined:

percentage uncertainty in one reading = (uncertainty / reading) × 10⁰
percentage uncertainty in a sum or difference = (largest absolute uncertainty / answer) × 10⁰
percentage uncertainty in a product or quotient = sum of the individual percentage uncertainties

Worked example: a cube of side 2.0 ± 0.05 cm has a mass of 24.0 ± 0.1 g. The side's percentage uncertainty is 0.05/2.0 × 100 = 2.5 per cent, so the volume (a product of three lengths) carries 3 × 2.5 = 7.5 per cent. The mass carries 0.1/24.0 × 100 = 0.4 per cent. The density = mass/volume carries 7.5 + 0.4 = 7.9 per cent, so ρ = 24.0/8.0 = 3.0 g cm⁻³ ± 0.2 g cm⁻³. The volume term dominates: improving the ruler improves the result far more than improving the balance.

Scalars and vectors (Supplement)

A scalar has size only: distance, speed, mass, energy, temperature, pressure. A vector has size and direction: displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, momentum, weight. Vectors are added by direction: two forces in a line add or subtract; two forces at right angles combine by Pythagoras, with the direction found from an angle. If a boat is pushed 3.0 m north and 4.0 m east, its resultant displacement is 5.0 m on a bearing of about 53° from north. Drawing the vector triangle to scale is a complete method on Paper 4 whenever the angle is not 90°.

Paper 6: how the practical exam is written

Paper 6 is a written exam about practical physics; you handle no apparatus but you must think like an experimenter. The question types repeat, and each has a method.

  • Choosing apparatus. Match the instrument to the quantity and its size: a ruler for lengths of centimetres, a micrometer for wires, a measuring cylinder for volumes, a balance for masses. State the range and the precision you expect.
  • Variables. Name the independent variable (what you change), the dependent variable (what you measure) and the control variables (what you keep fixed). A fair test changes one thing only, and every control earns a mark: same material, same temperature, same apparatus, same operator.
  • Safety. Link each hazard to a control: hot water and burners — use tongs and keep hands clear; masses and clamps — secure the clamp to the bench and stand clear of falling masses; lasers and ultrasound — never look into the beam; electricity — low voltages only, and switch off between readings.
