  • Tables. Draw a box with a column per quantity and a heading of quantity divided by unit, e.g. length / cm. Numbers sit in the cells without units. Give each column enough rows for repeats, quote consistent significant figures, and record raw readings before any calculated column.
  • Graphs. The independent variable goes on the horizontal axis. Choose a scale that fills at least half the sheet, label both axes with quantity and unit, plot points with a fine cross, and draw a single smooth line of best fit — a thin ruled line for a linear relationship, a smooth curve otherwise. Never join dots dot to dot.
  • Gradient and intercept. The gradient = (change in vertical quantity) / (change in horizontal quantity), taken between two distant points on the line, not between plotted points. For a straight line through the origin the two variables are directly proportional; a non-zero intercept has physical meaning — on a speed–time graph it is the initial speed, on a cooling curve the ambient temperature — and the equation of the line is written as vertical quantity = gradient × horizontal quantity + intercept.
  • Conclusions. State the relationship the graph shows in words and symbols, quote the gradient with its unit, and relate the result to the physics (for example, a load–extension graph through the origin shows extension proportional to load, and its gradient is the spring constant).
  • Evaluation. Name the largest source of uncertainty with a reason, say which way it pushes the answer, and propose a specific improvement — more repeats, a longer measurement interval, a sensor or data logger, a wider range of values — not a vague plea for more care.

Worked example: reading a graph and its gradient

A student measures the speed of a trolley pulled down a runway, plotting speed on the vertical axis against time on the horizontal axis. The plotted points lie close to a straight line crossing the vertical axis at 0.10 m s⁻¹ and passing through (2.0 s, 1.30 m s⁻¹) and (6.0 s, 3.30 m s⁻¹).

gradient = (3.30 - 1.30) / (6.0 - 2.0) = 2.00 / 4.0 = 0.50 m s⁻²
intercept = 0.10 m s⁻¹
equation: speed = 0.50 x time + 0.10

The gradient is the trolley's acceleration, 0.50 m s⁻², and the intercept is its initial speed, 0.10 m s⁻¹. A conclusion that says only speed increases with time earns no mark; the mark is for the number, its unit and its physical meaning.

Common mistakes

  • Writing a number without its unit, or putting units into the cells of a results table whose heading already carries the unit.
  • Starting a ruler scale from the broken zero end, or reading at an angle and introducing parallax error.
  • Joining plotted points with a zig-zag line instead of drawing one smooth line of best fit, which hides anomalies rather than revealing them.
  • Calculating a gradient between two neighbouring plotted points; use two distant points on the line to shrink the reading error.
  • Reducing a systematic error by repeating readings; averaging shrinks random error only, and a zero error must be corrected at the instrument.
  • Keeping an anomaly with no comment, or discarding one without a stated physical reason.
  • Confusing scalar and vector: adding a speed to a velocity, or giving a direction for energy.
  • Reporting a percentage uncertainty but never saying which measurement dominates the final result.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 6, 3 marks). Describe how you would measure the average speed of a trolley on a runway.

Answer: Mark a fixed distance along the runway and measure it with a metre ruler. Release the trolley from the same point each time and time its passage over the marked distance with light gates and a data logger (or a stopwatch, repeated and averaged to reduce reaction error). Average speed is the distance divided by the time. Repeat for several distances or heights and record results in a table.

Question 2 (Paper 6, 3 marks). A student measures the period of a pendulum once and gets 1.3 s. Suggest two improvements to the method.

Answer: Time 20 complete oscillations and divide by 20, so reaction time error becomes a small fraction of the total; repeat the whole measurement several times and take a mean. Keep the pendulum length fixed and time from the release point to avoid a variable starting condition.

Question 3 (Paper 4, 2 marks). A length is recorded as 2.50 cm. State the instrument used and its uncertainty.

Answer: A ruler reading to 0.1 cm (or a vernier caliper if the precision demands it), with an uncertainty of ±0.05 cm, half the smallest scale division.

Question 4 (Paper 6, 4 marks). The volume of a small stone is found from 30 cm³ to 45 cm³ in a measuring cylinder and its mass is 36 g. Calculate the density and its percentage uncertainty if each volume reading is uncertain by ±0.5 cm³.

Answer: Volume = 15 cm³. The uncertainty in the difference is 0.5 + 0.5 = 1.0 cm³ (worst case for a difference), so the percentage uncertainty is 1.0/15 × 100 = 6.7 per cent. Density = 36/15 = 2.4 g cm⁻³, so the answer is 2.4 g cm⁻³ ± 0.2 g cm³ (about ±7 per cent). Using a larger volume difference would shrink the percentage uncertainty.

Question 5 (Paper 2 style). Which quantity is a vector? A energy; B temperature; C momentum; D pressure. Answer: C. Momentum has size and direction; the rest are scalars.

With measurements trustworthy, the next topic is what heat does to matter: thermal physics.

Equations and symbols

Measurement is the one topic whose equations are mostly about the arithmetic of uncertainty rather than a physical law. Paper 6 marks the method, the significant figures and the uncertainty, so each relation below is given with the symbols it uses and the unit each symbol carries.

Averages and rates

x̄ = (x₁ + x₂ + … + xₙ) / n
Key: x̄ = mean value (same unit as the readings); x₁ … xₙ = individual readings, all in the same unit; n = number of readings (no unit). Anomalous readings are discarded before averaging, never included and then blamed on the mean.

v = d / t
Key: v = average speed (m/s); d = total distance travelled (m); t = total time taken (s). On a two-leg journey this is total distance over total time, not the mean of the two speeds.

T = t / N
Key: T = period of one oscillation (s); t = total time for N oscillations (s); N = number of oscillations counted (no unit). Timing twenty swings and dividing moves the reaction-time error from each swing to the whole interval.

Uncertainty

percentage uncertainty = (Δx / x) × 100%
Key: Δx = absolute uncertainty of the reading, taken as ± half the smallest division for a single reading (same unit as x); x = the reading itself; the result is a percentage (no unit).

percentage uncertainty of a product or quotient = %A + %B
Key: %A, %B = the percentage uncertainties of the measured quantities being multiplied or divided. Adding the percentages is the rule whenever the quantities are combined by × or ÷.

percentage uncertainty of a power = n × (%x)
Key: n = the power to which the quantity is raised (2 for an area, 3 for a volume); %x = the percentage uncertainty in the measured length. This is why a 5% uncertainty in a diameter becomes 15% in a volume.

Geometry needed to find a volume

V = πr²h
Key: V = volume of a cylinder (m³ or cm³); r = radius, half the diameter (m or cm); h = height (m or cm); π = 3.14 (no unit).

V = (4/3)πr³
Key: V = volume of a sphere (m³ or cm³); r = radius (m or cm). The cube is what makes the percentage uncertainty three times the radius's.

A = πr²
Key: A = area of a circle (m² or cm²); r = radius (m or cm).

V = V₂ − V₁
Key: V = volume of an irregular solid (cm³); V₂ = cylinder reading with the solid submerged (cm³); V₁ = cylinder reading before it was added (cm³).

Converting units before substituting

1 km/h = 1000 m / 3600 s = 0.278 m/s
Key: divide a speed in km/h by 3.6 to get m/s. Converting after substituting is the commonest arithmetic error on Paper 2.

1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³
Key: multiply a density in g/cm³ by 1000 to use it with masses in kg and volumes in m³.

1 cm² = 1 × 10⁻⁴ m² and 1 cm³ = 1 × 10⁻⁶ m³
Key: areas scale with the square of the length conversion and volumes with the cube, which is why 100 cm² is 0.01 m², not 1 m².

The one derived quantity this topic measures

ρ = m / V
Key: ρ (ρ) = density (kg/m³ or g/cm³); m = mass (kg or g); V = volume (m³ or cm³). The units must match before dividing: 250 g in 30 cm³ is 8.3 g/cm³, which is 8300 kg/m³.

title: Coordination, Response and Gene Technology — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Coordination, Response and Gene Technology — Quick Revision Summary

All of Edexcel International A2 Biology Topic 8 (8.1–8.22) in one pass: the statement each specification point asks for, in the order of the notes. The explanation, worked detail and exam practice stay in the full notes — use this to check recall.

8.1 Neurones

  • Sensory — cell body to one side of a long axon, long dendron; receptor to CNS.
  • Relay — cell body central, short axon, many short dendrites; inside the CNS.
  • Motor — cell body in the CNS, long axon; CNS to effector.
  • All: nucleus and many mitochondria (ATP for the Na⁺/K⁺ pump), dendrites carry impulses in, axon out; Schwann cells make the myelin sheath, the gaps are nodes of Ranvier.

8.2 From stimulus to response

Stimulus → receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone in the CNS → motor neurone → effector. A muscle contracts or a gland secretes.

8.1, 8.5 Saltatory conduction

Myelin insulates the axon, so an impulse can only start at bare nodes and jumps node to node — faster than depolarising every stretch of membrane. Larger diameter and higher temperature also speed conduction.

8.3 The spinal reflex arc

  • Rapid and involuntary, completed before the brain is aware: it protects the body.
  • Grey matter (inner) holds the cell bodies and synapses of relay and motor neurones; white matter (outer) holds myelinated axons to and from the brain.
  • Withdrawal: pain receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone in the cord → motor neurone → flexor contracts, extensor relaxes.

8.4 The action potential

  • Resting potential about −70 mV: the pump moves 3 Na⁺ out for 2 K⁺ in, and the membrane is more permeable to K⁺.
  • Threshold opens voltage-gated Na⁺ channels: Na⁺ in, depolarisation to about +40 mV.
  • Na⁺ channels close, K⁺ channels open: K⁺ out, repolarisation, brief hyperpolarisation, then the pump restores the gradients.
  • All-or-nothing: a stronger stimulus gives more impulses per second, not a bigger impulse. In the refractory period the Na⁺ channels are inactivated, so conduction stays one-way.

8.6 Synapses and the pupil

  • Impulse → Ca²⁺ channels open → Ca²⁺ in → vesicles fuse and release acetylcholine → binds postsynaptic receptors → Na⁺ in → new impulse; acetylcholinesterase ends the signal.
  • Bright light: parasympathetic → circular muscles contract → pupil constricts. Dim light: sympathetic → radial muscles contract → pupil dilates.

8.7 Drugs acting on transmission

  • Nicotine — mimics acetylcholine at nicotinic receptors; stimulant, addictive.
  • Lidocaine — blocks voltage-gated Na⁺ channels, so no impulse forms; local anaesthetic.
  • Cobra venom α-toxin — blocks acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction; paralysis.
  • L-DOPA — crosses the blood–brain barrier and becomes dopamine; relieves Parkinson's symptoms.
  • MDMA — floods the synapse with serotonin, then depletes and damages serotonin neurones.

8.8 Rods and the optic neurone

Rhodopsin is opsin plus retinal (11-cis). Light makes retinal all-trans, which lowers cGMP, so the Na⁺ channels open in the dark close: the rod hyperpolarises, releases less glutamate, and the bipolar cell passes the change on until impulses fire in the optic neurone. The rod itself hyperpolarises — its impulse appears later in the pathway.

8.9 Habituation

A decreasing response to a repeated, harmless stimulus: the animal learns to ignore it. Not muscle fatigue and not sensory adaptation — the receptor still responds; the change is at the synapse between the sensory and motor neurones. Investigate by repeating a harmless stimulus, timing the response, and showing a new stimulus still works.

8.10 CNS and PNS

The CNS (brain, spinal cord) integrates and coordinates. The PNS links it to receptors and effectors: somatic control is voluntary, autonomic is not — sympathetic prepares for action, parasympathetic promotes rest and digestion, often with opposite effects on the same organ.

8.11–8.12 Coordination in plants

  • Phytochrome — Pr + red light (660 nm) → Pfr, the active form; far-red light (730 nm) reverses it. Pfr enters the nucleus and acts on transcription, switching germination and flowering genes on or off.
  • Auxin (IAA) — made in the shoot tip, moved polarly; cells on the shaded or lower side elongate more (acid growth), so shoots bend to the light and upwards. In roots higher auxin inhibits elongation, so roots bend down.
  • Gibberellins — stem elongation and germination: GA from the embryo reaches the aleurone layer, which makes amylase to hydrolyse starch into maltose for the embryo.
  • Core practical 18 — germinating grains on starch agar + iodine: a clear zone shows amylase activity, boiled grains give none.

8.13 Nervous and hormonal coordination

Nervous: electrical, fast, short-lived, targeted. Hormonal: chemical, blood-borne, slower, longer-lasting, widespread. They combine — fight or flight, where sympathetic impulses raise the heart rate and adrenaline sustains it. Plants coordinate with hormones only.

8.14 The brain

  • Cerebral hemispheres — thought, memory, reasoning, language, conscious sensation; each controls the opposite side.
  • Hypothalamus — homeostasis (temperature, water balance, hunger, sleep) and control of the pituitary.
  • Pituitary — hormones such as growth hormone and ADH.
  • Cerebellum — coordination of movement, posture and balance.
  • Medulla oblongata — heart rate, breathing, coughing and swallowing reflexes.

8.15 Imaging the brain

  • CT — X-rays: structure, bone and bleeding; quick, but ionising.
  • MRI — magnetic field and radio waves: detailed soft tissue, no ionising radiation; slower.
  • fMRI — blood-oxygen change after neural activity, so it shows which areas are active: good spatial, poor temporal resolution.
  • PET — a radioactive tracer such as labelled glucose shows metabolism and receptors; ionising and expensive.

8.16 Brain chemicals and disease

Parkinson's: loss of dopamine neurones in the substantia nigra, treated with L-DOPA. Depression: low serotonin and noradrenaline, treated with SSRIs that block reuptake. Identifying the chemical at fault is what lets a drug replace it, mimic it or slow its loss.

8.17–8.19 GMOs and recombinant DNA

  • Drugs from GMOs — the human insulin gene in a bacterial plasmid, grown in a fermenter, then extracted and purified; identical to human insulin, so fewer immune reactions than animal insulin. Growth hormone and clotting factors likewise.
  • Making it — a restriction endonuclease leaves sticky ends on the gene; the same enzyme cuts the plasmid, the two base-pair, and DNA ligase seals the backbone.
  • Inserting it — transformation of competent bacteria (calcium chloride and heat shock, or electroporation), viral vectors, microinjection, gene gun; antibiotic-resistance markers show which cells took it up.

8.20 Microarrays

mRNA from two samples → cDNA with two fluorescent dyes → hybridises to the probes on the chip. Green or red: that gene is more active in that sample; yellow: similar; brightness: how active. Used to compare which genes are switched on, e.g. diseased against healthy tissue.

8.21 Bioinformatics

Computers storing and analysing biological data — DNA and protein sequences, gene expression, structures. It identifies genes by comparison, builds phylogenetic trees, predicts protein structure and interprets microarrays, working on data from projects such as the Human Genome Project.

8.22 GM risks and benefits

  • Benefits — pest- and herbicide-resistant crops, better nutrition, higher yields; human proteins for medicine; research organisms.
  • Risks — genes escaping to wild populations, harm to non-target species, pest resistance, possible allergens; ethical and regulatory concerns, long-term effects uncertain.

Typical mistakes

  • Saying light depolarises a rod cell — it hyperpolarises it.
  • Putting saltatory conduction under the myelin instead of at the nodes.
  • Swapping the circular muscles (constrict) and radial muscles (dilate).
  • Claiming a stronger stimulus gives a bigger action potential.
  • Calling habituation fatigue or sensory adaptation.
  • Giving auxin a promotive effect on elongation in roots, where it inhibits it.
  • Swapping the roles of restriction enzymes and DNA ligase.
  • Using fMRI to image structure — MRI does that; fMRI shows activity.

Exam-style questions

  • Why does a myelinated axon conduct faster? Myelin insulates the membrane, so an impulse can only start at the nodes; it jumps node to node rather than depolarising every region.
  • How does MDMA alter synaptic transmission? It increases serotonin release and blocks reuptake, over-stimulating the postsynaptic cell; repeated use depletes serotonin and damages neurones.
  • What is the aleurone layer's role in germination? Gibberellin from the embryo makes the aleurone layer synthesise amylase, which hydrolyses starch to maltose for the embryo.
  • How does PET show the active part of the brain? Labelled glucose is taken up more by active cells, and the radiation detected from it maps where metabolism is highest.

title: Summary Writing — Study Notes
content:
A summary task tests whether you can select the relevant information and express it concisely in your own words. Accuracy and economy matter more than style.

Reading the task first

Read the question before the text. It tells you which points to select, and it sets the word limit. Mark the text lightly as you read, looking for the points the question asks for and ignoring examples and illustrations unless they are needed.

Selecting points

  • Include main points that answer the question directly.
  • Leave out anecdotes, examples and repeated ideas.
  • Keep the order logical, usually following the text's order unless the question asks otherwise.

Paraphrasing

Paraphrasing means rewriting an idea in your own words and sentence structure. Changing one or two words is not enough.

Techniques

  • Replace phrases with equivalent expressions, for example "in the not-too-distant future" becomes "soon".
  • Combine two sentences into one where the ideas are connected.
  • Use a general word for a list of specific examples where the question allows it.

Staying concise

Cut filler such as "in my opinion" or "it is important to note that". Each sentence should carry a required point. Count your words and stay within the limit.

Checking your summary

Read your summary alone. Does it answer the question? Could a reader understand it without the original text? Is every sentence necessary?

title: Alkenes — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Alkenes

Chemistry — AS. Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH11, Topic 5. Alkenes contain a carbon–carbon double bond, which makes them far more reactive than alkanes. Their addition reactions are a central part of organic synthesis.

Key areas to revise

  • Structure and bonding
  • Addition reactions
  • Polymerisation
  • Isomerism

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

title: Differentiation II
content:
Differentiation II

Product and Quotient Rules

  • (uv)′ = u′v + uv′
  • (u/v)′ = (u′v − uv′)/v²

Example: y = x² e^x gives dy/dx = 2x e^x + x² e^x = e^x(2x + x²).

Standard Derivatives

  • sin x → cos x; cos x → −sin x; tan x → sec²x
  • e^x → e^x; ln x → 1/x

Chain Rule Everywhere

d/dx [ln(3x)] = 3/(3x) = 1/x; d/dx [e^(2x)] = 2e^(2x); d/dx [sin²x] = 2 sin x cos x.

Implicit Differentiation

Differentiate both sides w.r.t. x, treating y as a function of x (terms in y pick up dy/dx).

Example: x² + y² = 25 → 2x + 2y(dy/dx) = 0 → dy/dx = −x/y.

Parametric Curves

For x = f(t), y = g(t): dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt).

Example: x = t², y = t³ gives dy/dx = 3t²/2t = 3t/2.

Exam tips: quote the rule you use; for tangent/normal on parametric curves, find t at the point first, and simplify implicit answers using the original equation.

title:
Cell Structure, Reproduction and Development — AS Level Biology

This revision note belongs to the Edexcel International Advanced Subsidiary (IAS) Biology specification, WBI12 Unit 1, Topic 3 Cell Structure, Reproduction and Development. It covers the cell as the unit of life, eukaryotic and prokaryotic ultrastructure, microscopy and measurement, the cell cycle and mitosis, meiosis and genetic variation, gametes and fertilisation in mammals and flowering plants, stem cells, and the genetic control of development through gene expression, epigenetics and inheritance. Every statement below the topic owns is covered in its own section or paragraph.

1. Cells as the units of life and the levels of organisation

All living organisms are made of cells, and all cells share some common features: a plasma membrane (cell surface membrane) enclosing the cell, cytoplasm in which most chemical reactions occur, and ribosomes for protein synthesis. Differences between cell types are explained from these common features — for example the presence or absence of a cell wall, a nucleus, or membrane-bound organelles decides what a cell can do. In multicellular organisms, cells are organised into tissues, tissues into organs, and organs into organ systems, each level carrying out a particular function. A tissue is a group of similar cells working together; an organ is made of several tissues with a combined function; an organ system is a group of organs whose functions are linked, such as the digestive system. Understanding this hierarchy matters because a structure at one level is shaped by the level below it — the properties of a tissue follow from the cells it contains.

2. Eukaryotic cell ultrastructure and the functions of the organelles

Eukaryotic cells have a membrane-bound nucleus that contains the chromosomes, and a range of membrane-bound organelles, each with a distinct function. The plasma membrane (cell surface membrane) is a phospholipid bilayer with proteins embedded in it, controlling what enters and leaves the cell. The nucleus is surrounded by a double nuclear envelope with nuclear pores, and contains the cell's DNA; the nucleolus inside the nucleus is the site of ribosome assembly. Ribosomes, made of a large and a small subunit, are the sites of protein synthesis and occur free in the cytoplasm or attached to the rough endoplasmic reticulum. The rough endoplasmic reticulum (rER) is a stack of membrane-bound sacs studded with ribosomes; it synthesises proteins and passes them on in vesicles. The smooth endoplasmic reticulum (sER) lacks ribosomes and synthesises lipids and carbohydrates. Mitochondria have a double membrane, the inner one folded into cristae to increase surface area, and a matrix that contains the enzymes for aerobic respiration; they supply ATP. Centrioles are paired microtubule cylinders that organise the spindle fibres during nuclear division. Lysosomes are membrane-bound sacs containing hydrolytic enzymes that digest worn-out cell components and pathogens. The Golgi apparatus modifies, sorts and packages proteins into vesicles for secretion or for delivery to other parts of the cell; it is also involved in the formation of extracellular enzymes. The cytoskeleton of microtubules and microfilaments maintains cell shape, holds organelles in place and enables movement within the cell.

3. Prokaryotic cell ultrastructure and how to tell the two apart

Prokaryotic cells are much smaller than eukaryotic cells and lack a membrane-bound nucleus. Their genetic material is a single, circular DNA molecule that lies free in the cytoplasm, not associated with histones. The cell wall is made of peptidoglycan and gives rigidity and shape. Many prokaryotes have a protective capsule outside the cell wall. Plasmids are small circles of DNA separate from the main chromosome; they can be transferred between cells and often carry genes for antibiotic resistance. Flagella — rigid helical tails that rotate — give motility in some prokaryotes, and pili help cells attach to surfaces and to each other and mediate conjugation. Prokaryotic ribosomes are 70S, smaller than the 80S ribosomes of eukaryotes. A bacterium therefore shows, in EM images: cell wall, capsule, plasma membrane, circular DNA free in the cytoplasm, 70S ribosomes, plasmids, and, where present, flagella and pili — and none of the membrane-bound organelles found in a eukaryotic cell.

4. Seeing the ultrastructure: light and electron microscopy

A light microscope uses visible light passed through a specimen; its maximum useful magnification is around ×1500 and its resolution is about 0.2 µm, limited by the wavelength of light. An electron microscope uses a beam of electrons, giving far higher resolution and magnification; transmission electron microscopes (TEM) show the internal ultrastructure of thin sections, and scanning electron microscopes (SEM) show the surface detail of a specimen. Staining is essential in light microscopy because most cells are transparent — stains such as methylene blue for animal cells or iodine solution for starch make structures visible and show up nuclei, starch grains and cell walls. The electron microscope can show the organelles listed in 3.3 — nucleus, nucleolus, ribosomes, rER, sER, mitochondria, centrioles, lysosomes, Golgi apparatus — and, in prokaryotes, the cell wall, capsule, plasma membrane, circular DNA, 70S ribosomes, flagella and pili, so that students can recognise the organelles from electron micrographs. In a light microscope the total magnification equals eyepiece magnification × objective magnification; a graticule (eye-piece graticule) fitted with a stage micrometer lets you calibrate it so real sizes can be measured, and specimens can be drawn to scale from the microscope.

5. Core Practical 5 — observing and drawing animal cells

Use a light microscope to make observations and labelled drawings of suitable animal cells, for example cheek epithelial cells. The steps are: sterilise by wiping the mouth, smear a thin layer of cells onto a slide, stain with methylene blue, lower a coverslip at an angle to avoid air bubbles, and observe under the microscope. Draw what you see with the correct relative sizes of nucleus, cytoplasm and cell membrane, label the parts, and add a title and magnification. Core Practical 5 also develops the skill of using a graticule with a microscope to make measurements and understand the concept of scale — the graticule is calibrated against a stage micrometer at each objective, so the real size of a cell or organelle can be calculated from the number of graticule divisions it spans.

6. Cell division: mitosis, the cell cycle and genetic variation by meiosis

Mitosis produces genetically identical daughter cells for growth and asexual reproduction and is one part of the cell cycle, which is the regular sequence of events in a dividing cell: interphase (during which the cell grows, and DNA is replicated — G1, S and G2), mitosis and cytokinesis. Mitosis itself has stages — prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase — in which the copied chromosomes line up on the equator, separate and move to opposite poles, and new nuclei form, followed by division of the cytoplasm. A useful calculation is the mitotic index, the proportion of cells in a sample that are dividing: mitotic index = number of cells undergoing mitosis ÷ total number of cells in the field of view. This is used in Core Practical 6, the root tip squash, to see and count the stages of mitosis. Meiosis, by contrast, produces genetically non-identical gametes and is the source of variation: in metaphase I the homologous chromosomes line up as pairs and assort independently (independent assortment), and in prophase I crossing over exchanges alleles between the chromatids of a homologous pair, so that gametes carry new combinations of alleles. A locus is the fixed position of a gene on a chromosome; genes on the same chromosome are linked and tend to be inherited together, so linked genes do not assort independently.

7. Gametes, fertilisation in mammals and fertilisation in flowering plants

Mammalian gametes are specialised for their function. Sperm are small and motile, with a haploid nucleus, a lot of mitochondria to power the flagellum, and an acrosome at the head containing enzymes that digest a path through the egg's outer layers. Egg cells are larger, with cytoplasm containing food reserves; the zona pellucida is a glycoprotein layer around the egg that sperm must penetrate. Fertilisation in mammals begins when the acrosome reaction releases enzymes that digest the zona pellucida, then the cortical reaction releases cortical granules into the space around the egg, hardening the zona pellucida and preventing more than one sperm from entering; finally the sperm and egg nuclei fuse, restoring the diploid number. In flowering plants, fertilisation begins with pollination and the growth of a pollen tube from the pollen grain down through the style to the embryo sac; two male nuclei travel down the tube, one fertilising the egg to form the zygote (which develops into the embryo) and one fusing with the two polar nuclei to form the triploid endosperm that will feed the developing seed — double fertilisation, unique to flowering plants.

8. Stem cells and what society does with them

A stem cell is an undifferentiated cell that can divide to produce more stem cells and differentiated cells. Totipotent stem cells can develop into any cell type and form a complete organism; the zygote and the cells of the early embryo up to the 16-cell morula are totipotent. Pluripotent stem cells can give rise to many, but not all, cell types; cells of the blastocyst are pluripotent, and in plants many meristem cells are totipotent, which is why a whole plant can be grown from a single cell or tissue. Stem cells are used medically — for example in bone marrow transplants for leukaemia — and their use raises ethical and social questions: the source of embryonic stem cells, the balance of benefit against risk, and decisions made by individuals, committees and governments all draw on scientific knowledge but also on values. Students should be able to discuss these issues from a range of ethical viewpoints.

9. Gene expression: how one gene makes more than one protein and how proteins control cells

Cells become specialised through differential gene expression — different genes are switched on or off in different cells, producing active mRNA and then proteins that control cell processes or determine cell structure. One gene can give rise to more than one protein through post-transcriptional changes to messenger RNA (mRNA) such as alternative splicing, in which the same primary transcript is spliced in different ways to make different mRNAs and therefore different polypeptides. Transcription factors switch genes on or off by binding to DNA and promoting or blocking transcription, so they control which proteins a cell makes. Epigenetic modification — including DNA methylation and histone modification — alters the activation of certain genes without changing the DNA sequence itself, and these modifications can be passed on following cell division, so that a cell's gene activity can be inherited by its daughter cells and, in some cases, across generations.

10. Inheritance: alleles, genotypes, phenotypes and how they vary

A gene is a sequence of bases on a DNA molecule that codes for a sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide. The allele is one of the different forms of a gene; the genotype is the alleles an organism has; the phenotype is the observable feature that results from the genotype and the environment. Recessive alleles only show in the phenotype when homozygous; dominant alleles show even in the heterozygous state; codominance is when both alleles in the heterozygote contribute to the phenotype. Sex linkage is the inheritance of a gene carried on the X chromosome, such as red-green colour blindness in humans, which appears more often in males because they have only one X chromosome and so express a recessive allele on it. Some phenotypes are affected by multiple alleles for the same gene, and others by polygenic inheritance, where many genes each contribute a small effect, giving rise to continuous variation in the phenotype — height in humans is a classic example. The environment can also affect phenotype, so that a feature is the result of an interaction between genotype and environment rather than genotype alone.

11. Mutations: how they arise and what they can do

Errors in DNA replication can give rise to mutations — changes to the base sequence of DNA. A substitution replaces one base with another and may change one amino acid or none (because the code is degenerate); an insertion adds one or more bases, and a deletion removes one or more, and these can cause a frameshift that changes every amino acid after the mutation and often produces a non-functional protein. Mutations are the source of new alleles, and some mutations give rise to cancer or genetic disorders, while many have no observable effect. Cystic fibrosis is a genetic disorder caused by a recessive allele; the faulty allele affects chloride ion channels, so the functioning of the gaseous exchange, digestive and reproductive systems is impaired — thick mucus blocks the airways, the pancreas duct is blocked so digestion is affected, and fertility in males is reduced because the vas deferens is absent or blocked.

12. Genetic screening and the questions it raises

Genetic screening can identify carriers of a recessive allele, and prenatal testing — including amniocentesis (sampling the fluid around the embryo) and chorionic villus sampling (taking a sample of placental tissue) — can check an embryo or fetus for genetic disorders. Pre-implantation genetic diagnosis (PGD) is used during IVF to test embryos before implantation so that only unaffected embryos are used. These techniques raise ethical and social questions: the reliability and risk of the test, the right to know or not to know, who decides what is a disorder worth preventing, the cost and access to treatment, and the risk of starting down a path toward selecting traits rather than preventing disease. Students should be able to identify and discuss these issues from religious, moral and social viewpoints.

13. How to use this note and what to revise next

Use these notes by working section by section through the topic, checking that you can name every organelle, state its function, and recognise it in an electron micrograph. Practise the calculations — magnification, real size from image size and magnification, mitotic index, and the index of diversity and the calculations that appear in the genetics sections. Revise by drawing and labelling an animal cell and a plant cell from memory, annotating each organelle with its function, then testing yourself on meiosis and on how variation arises. After this topic, revise Topic 4 Plant structure, biodiversity and conservation, and Topic 5 Energy flow, ecosystems and the environment, because the genetics here underpins inheritance in those later topics.

Egg cells are larger, with cytoplasm containing food reserves; the zona pellucida is a glycoprotein layer around the egg that sperm must penetrate. Fertilisation in mammals begins when the acrosome reaction releases enzymes that digest the zona pellucida, then the cortical reaction releases cortical granules into the space around the egg, hardening the zona pellucida and preventing more than one sperm from entering; finally the sperm and egg nuclei fuse, restoring the diploid number. In flowering plants, fertilisation begins with pollination and the growth of a pollen tube from the pollen grain down through the style to the embryo sac; two male nuclei travel down the tube, one fertilising the egg to form the zygote (which develops into the embryo) and one fusing with the two polar nuclei to form the triploid endosperm that will feed the developing seed — double fertilisation, unique to flowering plants.

8. Stem cells and what society does with them

A stem cell is an undifferentiated cell that can divide to produce more stem cells and differentiated cells. Totipotent stem cells can develop into any cell type and form a complete organism; the zygote and the cells of the early embryo up to the 16-cell morula are totipotent. Pluripotent stem cells can give rise to many, but not all, cell types; cells of the blastocyst are pluripotent, and in plants many meristem cells are totipotent, which is why a whole plant can be grown from a single cell or tissue. Stem cells are used medically — for example in bone marrow transplants for leukaemia — and their use raises ethical and social questions: the source of embryonic stem cells, the balance of benefit against risk, and decisions made by individuals, committees and governments all draw on scientific knowledge but also on values. Students should be able to discuss these issues from a range of ethical viewpoints.

9. Gene expression: how one gene makes more than one protein and how proteins control cells

Cells become specialised through differential gene expression — different genes are switched on or off in different cells, producing active mRNA and then proteins that control cell processes or determine cell structure. One gene can give rise to more than one protein through post-transcriptional changes to messenger RNA (mRNA) such as alternative splicing, in which the same primary transcript is spliced in different ways to make different mRNAs and therefore different polypeptides. Transcription factors switch genes on or off by binding to DNA and promoting or blocking transcription, so they control which proteins a cell makes. Epigenetic modification — including DNA methylation and histone modification — alters the activation of certain genes without changing the DNA sequence itself, and these modifications can be passed on following cell division, so that a cell''s gene activity can be inherited by its daughter cells and, in some cases, across generations.

10. Inheritance: alleles, genotypes, phenotypes and how they vary

A gene is a sequence of bases on a DNA molecule that codes for a sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide. The allele is one of the different forms of a gene; the genotype is the alleles an organism has; the phenotype is the observable feature that results from the genotype and the environment. Recessive alleles only show in the phenotype when homozygous; dominant alleles show even in the heterozygous state; codominance is when both alleles in the heterozygote contribute to the phenotype. Sex linkage is the inheritance of a gene carried on the X chromosome, such as red-green colour blindness in humans, which appears more often in males because they have only one X chromosome and so express a recessive allele on it. Some phenotypes are affected by multiple alleles for the same gene, and others by polygenic inheritance, where many genes each contribute a small effect, giving rise to continuous variation in the phenotype — height in humans is a classic example. The environment can also affect phenotype, so that a feature is the result of an interaction between genotype and environment rather than genotype alone.

11. Mutations: how they arise and what they can do

Errors in DNA replication can give rise to mutations — changes to the base sequence of DNA. A substitution replaces one base with another and may change one amino acid or none (because the code is degenerate); an insertion adds one or more bases, and a deletion removes one or more, and these can cause a frameshift that changes every amino acid after the mutation and often produces a non-functional protein. Mutations are the source of new alleles, and some mutations give rise to cancer or genetic disorders, while many have no observable effect. Cystic fibrosis is a genetic disorder caused by a recessive allele; the faulty allele affects chloride ion channels, so the functioning of the gaseous exchange, digestive and reproductive systems is impaired — thick mucus blocks the airways, the pancreas duct is blocked so digestion is affected, and fertility in males is reduced because the vas deferens is absent or blocked.

12. Genetic screening and the questions it raises

Genetic screening can identify carriers of a recessive allele, and prenatal testing — including amniocentesis (sampling the fluid around the embryo) and chorionic villus sampling (taking a sample of placental tissue) — can check an embryo or fetus for genetic disorders. Pre-implantation genetic diagnosis (PGD) is used during IVF to test embryos before implantation so that only unaffected embryos are used. These techniques raise ethical and social questions: the reliability and risk of the test, the right to know or not to know, who decides what is a disorder worth preventing, the cost and access to treatment, and the risk of starting down a path toward selecting traits rather than preventing disease. Students should be able to identify and discuss these issues from religious, moral and social viewpoints.

13. How to use this note and what to revise next

Use these notes by working section by section through the topic, checking that you can name every organelle, state its function, and recognise it in an electron micrograph. Practise the calculations — magnification, real size from image size and magnification, mitotic index, and the index of diversity and the calculations that appear in the genetics sections. Revise by drawing and labelling an animal cell and a plant cell from memory, annotating each organelle with its function, then testing yourself on meiosis and on how variation arises. After this topic, revise Topic 4 Plant structure, biodiversity and conservation, and Topic 5 Energy flow, ecosystems and the environment, because the genetics here underpins inheritance in those later topics.

title: A Level Mathematics: The Binomial Distribution
content:
A Level Mathematics: The Binomial Distribution

A binomial distribution counts successes in a fixed number of independent trials, each with the same probability of success. Coins, multiple-choice guesses, defective items in a sample and free throws all fit the same template, and once a problem is recognised as binomial the calculation is a formula plus a cumulative table. This note builds the distribution from its four conditions, derives the formula from counting, and then uses it for the two things exams actually ask: probabilities and hypothesis tests.

The four conditions

Before writing X ~ B(n, p) you must be able to name the conditions, because most exam questions include a part asking whether the model is appropriate. The conditions are not red tape: drop any one and the formula is simply wrong.

1. a fixed number of trials n
2. each trial has exactly two outcomes (success / failure)
3. the probability of success p is constant for every trial
4. the trials are independent
then X = number of successes has X ~ B(n, p)

Worked example (checking the model). A bag holds 5 red and 15 blue counters. Four counters are taken without replacement. Is the number of red counters binomial?

n = 4 is fixed and each draw is red or not red
but p changes: 5/20, then 5/19 if a red was taken, ...
the trials are not independent, so NOT binomial (it is hypergeometric)

Taking with replacement would fix it: p stays 0.25 on every draw.

The formula, and where it comes from

The probability of a particular sequence of r successes and n − r failures is p^r (1−p)^(n−r), because independence lets you multiply. The number of such sequences is the number of ways to choose which r trials succeed, which is nCr. Multiplying gives the formula.

P(X = r) = nCr p^r (1 - p)^(n - r)
the nCr counts arrangements; the powers give the probability of one arrangement

Worked example. X ~ B(10, 0.3). Find P(X = 3).

P = 10C3 (0.3)³ (0.7)⁷
= 120 × 0.027 × 0.08235
= 120 × 0.002223 = 0.2668

Worked example 2 (a single trial count). A fair die is rolled 8 times. Find the probability of exactly two sixes.

X ~ B(8, 1/6)
P(X = 2) = 8C2 (1/6)² (5/6)⁶ = 28 × 0.02778 × 0.3349 = 0.2605

Worked example 3 (why nCr appears). For n = 3 and r = 1, list the sequences and confirm the coefficient.

sequences: SFF, FSF, FFS - three of them
each has probability p(1-p)²
so P(X = 1) = 3p(1-p)², and 3C1 = 3

Cumulative probabilities

Questions almost always ask for a range, not a single value, and the cumulative distribution is what the calculator or the tables supply. The skill is rewriting the question into the form the table gives you.

P(X <= r) is tabulated directly
P(X >= r) = 1 - P(X <= r - 1)
P(X < r)  = P(X <= r - 1)
P(a <= X <= b) = P(X <= b) - P(X <= a - 1)
P(X = r) = P(X <= r) - P(X <= r - 1)

Worked example. X ~ B(20, 0.4). Find P(X ≥ 8).

P(X >= 8) = 1 - P(X <= 7)
= 1 - 0.4159
= 0.5841

Worked example 2 (between). For the same X, find P(5 ≤ X ≤ 10).

= P(X <= 10) - P(X <= 4)
= 0.8725 - 0.0510
= 0.8215

Worked example 3 (the strict inequality trap). For the same X, find P(X > 6).

P(X > 6) = 1 - P(X <= 6) = 1 - 0.2500 = 0.7500
note this is different from P(X >= 6) = 1 - P(X <= 5) = 0.8746

Mean and variance

The binomial has the simplest mean and variance in the syllabus, and they are worth knowing both forwards and backwards: a question can give the mean and variance and ask for n and p.

E(X) = np
Var(X) = np(1 - p)
standard deviation = √(np(1-p))

Worked example. X ~ B(50, 0.2). Find the mean and standard deviation.

mean = 50 × 0.2 = 10
variance = 10 × 0.8 = 8
sd = 2.828

Worked example 2 (backwards). A binomial variable has mean 12 and variance 9. Find n and p.

np = 12;  np(1-p) = 9
divide: 1 - p = 9/12 = 0.75  →  p = 0.25
then n = 12/0.25 = 48

Hypothesis testing with the binomial

A one-tailed test asks whether p has increased or decreased; the test statistic is the observed count, and the p-value is the probability of a result at least as extreme in the direction of the alternative.

H0: p = p0      H1: p > p0 (or p < p0)
X ~ B(n, p0) under H0
p-value = P(X >= observed) or P(X <= observed)
compare with the significance level; reject H0 if p-value <= alpha

Worked example. A coin is tossed 20 times and lands heads 15 times. Test at the 5% level whether the coin is biased towards heads.

H0: p = 0.5;  H1: p > 0.5
X ~ B(20, 0.5)
P(X >= 15) = 1 - P(X <= 14) = 1 - 0.9793 = 0.0207
0.0207 < 0.05, so reject H0
there is evidence at the 5% level that the coin favours heads

Worked example 2 (two-tailed). The same data tested two-tailed.

double the smaller tail: 2 × 0.0207 = 0.0414
0.0414 < 0.05, so still reject H0 at the 5% level

Worked example 3 (critical region). For X ~ B(20, 0.5), find the critical region for a 5% one-tailed test of p > 0.5.

P(X >= 14) = 0.0577 (above 0.05)
P(X >= 15) = 0.0207 (below 0.05)
critical region: X >= 15

Note that the critical region is chosen so the probability of a Type I error is at most 5%, which is why 14 is excluded even though it is close.

When the model breaks down

Examiners like the question that asks why a binomial model is only an approximation. The usual culprits are dependence, a varying probability, or a fixed sample drawn without replacement from a small population.

SituationProblemEffect
sampling without replacementtrials not independentp drifts; use the hypergeometric instead
clustered data (pupils in classes)responses correlatedvariance underestimated
probability varies between trialsp not constantformula invalid
large n, p near 0.5computation heavynormal approximation is reasonable

Worked example (normal approximation). X ~ B(200, 0.4). Use a normal approximation to estimate P(X ≤ 70).

mean = 80;  variance = 200 × 0.4 × 0.6 = 48;  sd = 6.928
continuity correction: X <= 70 becomes X < 70.5
z = (70.5 - 80)/6.928 = -1.371
P(Z < -1.371) = 0.0852

The continuity correction is compulsory: a discrete count needs a half-unit boundary before it can be treated as continuous.

Expected frequencies and the shape of the distribution

A binomial distribution is not symmetric unless p = 0.5, and that shape decides which tail an exam question is fishing in. The most likely value — the mode — is the integer near (n + 1)p, and expected frequency multiplies the probability by the number of samples taken. Both are quick marks that are frequently missed because students jump straight to the formula.

mode is near (n + 1)p, checked by comparing consecutive probabilities
expected number in a sample of size N = N x P(X = r)

Worked example. X ~ B(12, 0.3). Find the most likely value of X and the expected number of 3s in 500 independent observations.

(n + 1)p = 13 × 0.3 = 3.9, so check r = 3 and r = 4
P(X = 3) = 220 × 0.027 × 0.1176 = 0.2397
P(X = 4) = 495 × 0.0081 × 0.1681 = 0.2311
mode = 3
expected number of 3s = 500 × 0.2397 = 120 (to the nearest whole)

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Model) State the distribution for the number of sixes in 12 rolls of a fair die. Answer: X ~ B(n, p) with n = 12 rolls and p = 1/6 the chance of a six on each, so X ~ B(12, 1/6).
  2. (Single value) X ~ B(8, 0.25): find P(X = 2). Answer: P(X = 2) = ⁸C₂ (0.25)² (0.75)⁶ = 28 × 0.0625 × 0.1780 = 0.3115.
  3. (Cumulative) X ~ B(15, 0.3): find P(X ≤ 4). Answer: P(X ≤ 4) = Σₖ₌₀⁴ ¹⁵Cₖ (0.3)ᵏ (0.7)¹⁵⁻ᵏ = 0.5155 from cumulative binomial tables.
  4. (Complement) Same X: find P(X ≥ 3). Answer: P(X ≥ 3) = 1 − P(X ≤ 2) = 1 − 0.2969 = 0.7031 — the complement, because the tables give the lower tail only.
  5. (Mean) X ~ B(40, 0.35): find E(X) and Var(X). Answer: 14 and 9.1.
  6. (Backwards) Mean 18, variance 12: find n and p. Answer: mean np = 18 and variance np(1 − p) = 12; dividing, 1 − p = 12/18 = 2/3, so p = 1/3 and n = 18 ÷ (1/3) = 54.
  7. (Test) 12 of 20 seeds germinate; test p = 0.5 against p < 0.5 at 5%. Answer: H₀: p = 0.5 against H₁: p < 0.5; under H₀, X ~ B(20, 0.5) and P(X ≤ 12) = 0.8684, which is far above 0.05, so there is no evidence to reject H₀.
  8. (Critical region) X ~ B(10, 0.2): find the 5% critical region for p < 0.2. Answer: the smallest possible tail is P(X ≤ 0) = (0.8)¹⁰ = 0.1074, which already exceeds 0.05, so no critical region exists at the 5% level for this n.
  9. (Approximation) X ~ B(100, 0.5): approximate P(X ≥ 60). Answer: μ = np = 50 and σ = √(np(1 − p)) = √25 = 5; with the continuity correction z = (59.5 − 50)/5 = 1.9, so P(X ≥ 60) ≈ P(Z > 1.9) = 0.0287.
  10. (Assumption) Give one reason a binomial model may fail for defects in boxes of 20. Answer: defects may cluster, so trials are not independent.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Forgetting nCr: the coefficient counts arrangements; without it the answer is the probability of one specific sequence.
  • nCr on the wrong factor: it is p^r (1−p)^(n−r), with the success probability raised to the number of successes.
  • Inequality direction: P(X ≥ 8) uses 1 − P(X ≤ 7), not 1 − P(X ≤ 8).
  • Variance confused with standard deviation: np(1−p) is the variance; the test and the normal approximation need the square root.
  • Continuity correction omitted: any normal approximation to a discrete count needs the half-unit adjustment.
  • One-tailed evidence read as two: halving or doubling the tail without checking the alternative direction is a silent error.
  • Independence asserted, not checked: sampling without replacement from a small population breaks the model, and the question usually invites you to say so.
  • p-value compared with the wrong threshold: the significance level is given as a percentage; 5% means 0.05, not 5.

Recognising a binomial situation in context

Most binomial marks are lost before any arithmetic starts, because the question was not identified as binomial. The subsections below give a checklist for reading a question and writing the model in the standard form X ~ B(n, p) before you calculate anything.

Writing the model in the form X ~ B(n, p)

Once you decide a situation is binomial, state the model in full: X ~ B(n, p), where X is the number of successes, n is the number of trials and p is the probability of a success on each trial. Define X in words in your answer, for example “X is the number of defective bulbs in a box of 20”. A model with no definition of X loses the communication mark even when the probabilities are right.

Identifying the number of trials, n

The value of n is the fixed number of times the experiment is repeated: the number of bulbs tested, the number of patients treated, or the number of games played. Read the question for the phrase that fixes it, such as “of 20 bulbs chosen at random”. If the question keeps going until a result occurs, the number of trials is not fixed and the binomial model does not apply directly.

Identifying the probability of success, p

The value of p is the probability of the outcome you have chosen to call a success on one trial. It must stay the same for every trial. A fair coin gives p = 0.5, and a bag where 15% of items are faulty gives p = 0.15 for each item drawn with replacement. If the question gives a percentage, convert it to a decimal before you use it in any formula.

Checking for fixed trials

The number of trials must be decided before the experiment starts. Counting the number of successes in a fixed sample is binomial, whereas recording how many trials it takes to get the first success is not. A question about the number of heads in ten tosses is binomial; a question about how many tosses are needed for the first head is a different model. Make the fixed-n check before any other check.

Checking for independent trials

Each trial must not affect the next. Independence is what allows you to multiply the probabilities of several outcomes together, and it is the assumption most often ignored. Drawing items with replacement keeps p constant, and that is what the model needs. Drawing without replacement changes p after each draw, so the binomial model is only an approximation when the sample is small compared with the population.

Worked identification

A survey finds that 30% of adults own a bicycle. Twelve adults are chosen at random from a large town and asked whether they own one. Let X be the number who own a bicycle. Here n = 12, p = 0.3 and the answer is X ~ B(12, 0.3). The population is large, so the probability for each adult stays close to 0.3 and the model is a reasonable one to use. State that assumption, because a marker looks for it.

Equations and symbols

The distribution, its conditions and the four tail identities. Every question on this topic is one of these lines plus a calculator.

P(X = r) = nCr p^r (1 - p)^(n - r) Key: n = number of trials, fixed in advance; p = probability of success in one trial, constant; r = the number of successes asked for; nCr = n!/(r!(n − r)!), the number of orders the successes can occur in. The (1 − p) term is the failures, and its power must be n − r.

X ~ B(n, p) Key: X = the count of successes; the tilde means "is distributed as"; n and p as above. Write this line before calculating — it is often a mark on its own, and it fixes which parameters go into the calculator.

P = 10C3 (0.3)³ (0.7)⁷ Key: n = 10, p = 0.3, r = 3, so the failures are 7 and their probability is 0.7. The coefficient 10C3 = 120 accounts for the order of the three successes among the ten trials.

P(X >= r) = 1 - P(X <= r - 1) Key: a complement, so the two probabilities add to 1; the boundary moves by one because the binomial is discrete. Using 1 − P(X ≤ r) instead is the classic off-by-one error.

P(a <= X <= b) = P(X <= b) - P(X <= a - 1) Key: subtract the part below the interval; again the "− 1" is there because P(X ≤ a − 1) is everything before a. Check with a small case you can list by hand before trusting the calculator.

title: IGCSE Physics: Energy, Work and Power
content:
IGCSE Physics: Energy, Work and Power

Cambridge IGCSE Physics 0625 (2026–2028), Topic 1 Motion, forces and energy, statement 1.7 Energy, work and power. Energy is the currency of every physical process: it is never created or destroyed, only moved between stores and converted between forms. This note builds the whole idea from scratch — stores, transfers, the two energy equations, work, power, the world's energy resources and efficiency — because Paper 4 rewards candidates who can both calculate an energy change and explain where the energy went.

Energy stores and transfers

Think of energy as money held in different bank accounts. It can sit in a store, and it can move between stores along a transfer pathway, but the total across all accounts never changes. The examined stores and transfers are:

Energy storeWhat it meansExample
KineticEnergy of a moving object; more mass or more speed means moreA moving lorry
Gravitational potentialEnergy stored by virtue of height in a gravitational fieldA book on a shelf
Elastic potentialEnergy stored by stretching, compressing or twistingA drawn bow, a compressed spring
Thermal (internal)Energy of the random motion of particles in a substanceHot water in a kettle
ChemicalEnergy stored in chemical bondsFood, fuel, a battery
NuclearEnergy stored in the nucleus of an atomUranium fuel

The four transfer pathways are mechanical work (a force acting over a distance), heating (energy transferred by a temperature difference), radiation (energy carried by waves, mainly infrared and light) and electrical work (charge moving through a potential difference). When a ball is thrown upwards, chemical energy in the muscles does mechanical work on the ball, and that energy becomes kinetic; as the ball rises, kinetic becomes gravitational potential; as it falls back, gravitational potential becomes kinetic again; on impact the kinetic spreads into the thermal stores of the ball, the ground and the air, and some is radiated as sound.

Conservation of energy and Sankey diagrams

The law of conservation of energy states that energy cannot be created or destroyed, and the total energy in a closed system stays constant. This is the most powerful statement in the syllabus: whenever a question says a machine loses energy, it means the energy has been transferred to less useful stores, not destroyed. A Sankey diagram draws the total energy input as one wide arrow, splits it into useful output and wasted arrows, and is drawn so the arrow widths are proportional to the energies.

Useful energy is the energy transferred to the store the device was designed to fill; wasted energy is transferred to stores that were not the goal, usually thermal energy of the surroundings, and it is eventually transferred to the environment, often by radiation. Wasted energy is not destroyed — it has simply become too spread out to be harnessed easily.

Kinetic and gravitational potential energy

Both equations are Supplement statements, and both appear constantly in Paper 4 calculations.

kinetic energy = 1/2 x mass x speed squared        EK = 1/2 m v²
gravitational potential energy = mass x gravitational field strength x height        EP = m g h
  • EK: kinetic energy in joules (J); m: mass in kilograms (kg); v: speed in metres per second (m s⁻¹). Energy is a scalar, so the speed is squared and the direction of travel does not matter.
  • EP: gravitational potential energy in joules (J); g: gravitational field strength in newtons per kilogram (N kg⁻¹, use the value given in the question); h: vertical height in metres (m), measured between the two positions being compared.

Only the difference in height matters. Lifting a 2 kg book from a table to a shelf 0.50 m above it raises EP by 2 × 9.81 × 0.50 = 9.8 J, whatever the height of the room. The sign convention is simple: EP increases as an object rises and decreases as it falls, and the change is ΔEP = m g Δh.

Energy methods are often faster than forces and equations of motion. For a falling object with no air resistance, m g h = ½ m v², and the mass cancels: every object falls at the same rate in a vacuum. For a roller coaster of mass 500 kg dropping 20 m from rest, v = √(2 g h) = √(2 × 9.81 × 20) = 19.8 m s⁻¹.

Work done

Work is done when a force moves an object. It is energy transferred by mechanical work, and it is measured in joules:

work done = force x distance moved in the direction of the force        W = F s
  • W: work done in joules (J). One joule is the work done when a force of 1 newton moves its point of application 1 metre in the direction of the force.
  • F: force in newtons (N); s: distance moved in metres (m), measured in the direction of the force.

Work is a scalar, but the two quantities must line up: carrying a box horizontally at constant height does no work against gravity, because the motion is perpendicular to the weight. Pushing a trolley with 50 N against 20 N of friction over 4 m does 200 J of work in total, of which 80 J goes to heating the bearings and floor through friction and 120 J remains as kinetic energy. If you carry shopping upstairs, the work done against gravity is your weight multiplied by the vertical height gained, not the length of the staircase.

Power

Power measures how fast energy is transferred — the rate of doing work. A car engine that lifts the same load in half the time is twice as powerful.

power = work done / time taken = energy transferred / time taken        P = W / t = E / t
  • P: power in watts (W). One watt is one joule per second (1 W = 1 J s⁻¹). A kilowatt is 1000 W.
  • W: work done in joules (J); E: energy transferred in joules (J); t: time taken in seconds (s).

Power is a scalar. For a vehicle moving at constant speed against a constant force, the same idea gives P = F v (Supplement), with F in newtons and v in metres per second, giving watts directly. Doubling the speed of a car at constant driving force doubles the power needed; a car climbing a hill at constant speed needs power P = mgv sin θ to raise its weight.

Energy resources and electricity generation

Most electrical energy is generated the same way: a fuel heats water, the steam spins a turbine, and the turbine spins a generator that converts the kinetic energy of rotation into electrical energy. What differs is the energy store the heat comes from.

ResourceStore usedAdvantagesDisadvantages
Coal, oil, gas (fossil fuels)Chemical, burned to give heatReliable, cheap to run, existing infrastructureFinite supply; carbon dioxide and pollutants released; contributes to climate change and acid rain
BiofuelChemical, from plant or animal materialRenewable; carbon dioxide released was recently absorbed by the plantsLand and water needed to grow crops; energy cost of farming and transport
HydroelectricGravitational potential of stored waterRenewable, reliable, no fuel cost, no emissions in useDams flood valleys and disrupt habitats; high construction cost; depends on rainfall
GeothermalThermal energy inside the EarthRenewable, reliable, small land useOnly practical near volcanic regions; drilling cost; possible release of underground gases
Nuclear fuelNuclear, released by fissionVery large energy per kilogram; no carbon dioxide in operationRadioactive waste that must be stored safely for centuries; high decommissioning cost; accident risk
Solar cellsLight radiation converted directly to electricityRenewable, silent, no emissions in use, low maintenanceOutput varies with light and season; expensive to manufacture; large area needed for high output
Solar panels (heating)Light radiation heating water directlyRenewable and cheap to runOnly heats water; ineffective at night and in cloudy climates

Non-renewable resources exist in finite stock and are used faster than they form; renewable resources are replenished as they are used. Supplement statements add the deep connection: the Sun is the principal source for almost all of these resources. Sunlight drives the water cycle behind hydroelectric power and biofuels, heats the ground behind wind and geothermal gradients, and fossil fuels are the remains of organisms that grew in sunlight. The Sun releases energy by nuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium, and research into fusion on Earth aims to provide a fuel that is abundant and produces no long-lived radioactive waste, though sustained fusion power is still experimental.

Efficiency

Efficiency compares what a device delivers with what it is given:

efficiency = useful energy output / total energy input
efficiency = useful power output / total power input

Efficiency has no unit; multiply by 100 for a percentage. No real device is 100 per cent efficient, because some energy is always transferred to thermal stores of the surroundings by friction, resistance and radiation. A filament lamp is about 5 per cent efficient (most energy becomes heat, not light); an electric motor might reach 80 per cent. The most efficient heating device is a simple heater, because its useful output is thermal energy — the same store as its waste. A Sankey diagram makes this visible at a glance, and the arrows must sum to the total input.

Worked example: lifting and efficiency

A crane lifts a 500 kg load through 12 m at constant speed in 20 s. Take g = 9.81 N kg⁻¹.

weight = m g = 500 × 9.81 = 4905 N
useful work = force x distance = 4905 × 12 = 58 860 J
useful power = work / time = 58 860 / 20 = 2943 W (about 2.9 kW)

The motor takes 150 000 J of electrical energy to do this lift. Its efficiency is 58 860 / 150 000 = 0.39, or 39 per cent. The remaining 91 140 J is not destroyed: it warms the motor windings, the cables and the surrounding air.

Second stage, using energy conservation: if the load is dropped from rest through the same 12 m with negligible air resistance, m g h = ½ m v² gives v = √(2 × 9.81 × 12) = 15.3 m s⁻¹. The mass cancels, so any object dropped through 12 m reaches the same speed.

Common mistakes

  • Saying energy is used up or lost; energy is transferred to other stores, and the total is conserved. Examiners award the mark for transferred, not lost.
  • Putting speed rather than speed squared into EK = ½mv², and forgetting the ½.
  • Measuring h in EP = mgh along a slope or a staircase; h is the vertical height difference.
  • Using the wrong mass in W = mg: the mass in kilograms, multiplied by g, never the weight in newtons multiplied by g again.
  • Confusing work done with power: joules measure energy, watts measure the rate of energy transfer.
  • Calculating efficiency as total in over useful out; the useful output goes on top, so efficiency is always less than 1.
  • Forgetting that a percentage efficiency needs multiplying by 100, and leaving the answer as 0.39 when 39 per cent is asked for.
  • Mixing units: power in watts needs energy in joules and time in seconds, so kilowatts and minutes must be converted first.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 4, 3 marks). A ball of mass 0.15 kg is moving at 10 m s⁻¹. Calculate its kinetic energy and the height through which it would need to be raised to store the same energy. Take g = 9.81 N kg⁻¹.

Answer: EK = ½mv² = ½ × 0.15 × 10² = 7.5 J. Setting mgh = 7.5 gives h = 7.5 / (0.15 × 9.81) = 5.1 m.

Question 2 (Paper 4, 4 marks). A 60 kg student runs up a flight of stairs of vertical height 3.0 m in 4.0 s. Calculate the useful power developed. Take g = 10 N kg⁻¹.

Answer: work = mgh = 60 × 10 × 3.0 = 1800 J. Power = 1800 / 4.0 = 450 W. (Real power is higher, because the student also gains kinetic energy and warms their muscles.)

Question 3 (Paper 2 style). A machine takes in 2000 J and delivers 1500 J of useful work. Its efficiency is: A 25 per cent; B 75 per cent; C 133 per cent; D 175 per cent. Answer: B. 1500/2000 = 0.75 = 75 per cent. Option C comes from putting input over output — the classic trap.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 6 marks). Explain why a solar cell is described as renewable, and discuss whether it is a good replacement for a coal-fired power station.

Answer: A solar cell converts light energy directly into electrical energy and consumes no fuel, so its energy source, sunlight, is replenished continuously and it is renewable. It produces no carbon dioxide or pollutants in operation. Against that, output depends on light intensity and falls at night and in cloudy weather, so storage or backup generation is needed; manufacturing the cells is energy-intensive, and a large area is required for high output. Coal is reliable and dispatchable but burns a finite resource, releasing carbon dioxide that drives climate change plus sulfur dioxide and particulates. A balanced conclusion weighs reliability and land use against emissions and fuel sustainability.

Question 5 (Paper 4, 3 marks). A car engine produces a driving force of 2000 N while travelling at 30 m s⁻¹. Calculate the useful power output.

Answer: P = F v = 2000 × 30 = 60 000 W = 60 kW.

Question 6 (Paper 6 style). Suggest how you would determine experimentally the efficiency of an electric motor lifting a small mass.

Answer: Measure the mass with a balance and the height lifted with a ruler, and record the time with a stopwatch. The useful output is mgh, calculated from the measured mass and vertical height. Measure the electrical energy input with a joule meter, or with an ammeter and voltmeter readings and E = V I t. Efficiency is mgh divided by V I t. Repeat for several masses and quote an average, keeping the input voltage constant.

With energy accounted for, the next question is what happens when forces are spread over area and depth: pressure and density.

Reading a Sankey diagram — and why its widths are the physics

A Sankey diagram looks like decoration and is actually an equation. The width of each band is the amount of energy in that transfer, which means conservation of energy is visible as a shape: whatever goes in on the left comes out on the right, split into useful and wasted. Once you read the widths as numbers, efficiency stops being a formula to memorise and becomes a comparison of two lengths.

Why the bands widen and narrow. Energy is never created or destroyed, only transferred between stores. A machine takes energy in one store, moves some of it to the store you wanted, and the rest to a store you did not — usually the thermal store of the surroundings. In the motor above, 200 J of electrical energy becomes 150 J of kinetic energy and 50 J of heating: 150 + 50 = 200, and the diagram cannot be drawn any other way.

Efficiency = useful output ÷ total input Key: efficiency = the fraction of the energy supplied that ends up in the useful store (no unit, or %); useful output = energy in the store you wanted (J); total input = energy supplied (J).

Worked example. For the motor above, find the efficiency and the energy wasted each second if it is supplied with 200 J every second.

efficiency = useful ÷ total = 150 ÷ 200 = 0.75 = 75%
wasted per second = 200 J − 150 J = 50 J

The same number read as power: the motor is supplied with 200 W and delivers 150 W of useful mechanical power, so 50 W is transferred to the surroundings by heating. Efficiency is the same whether you use energy or power, because both sides are divided by the same time.

The word the examiner wants for "wasted". Energy that does not reach the useful store is dissipated — spread out into the surroundings, usually by heating, at a slightly higher temperature. It has not disappeared, and writing "lost" invites the follow-up "where did it go?". Writing "dissipated to the surroundings by heating" earns it in one phrase.

Chained efficiency: the reason a lamp is worse than it looks. Machines are usually in series, and efficiencies multiply. A power station converts fuel at about 40%, transmission through the grid keeps about 95%, and a filament lamp turns about 5% of what reaches it into light. The overall figure is
0.40 × 0.95 × 0.05 = 0.019
so roughly 2% of the chemical energy in the fuel leaves the lamp as light. Multiplying fractions that are all less than one gives an answer smaller than any of them, which is the arithmetic behind every "why is this so inefficient?" question.

Where marks are lost. Drawing a Sankey whose output bands do not add up to the input band — it is a conservation diagram, and the mark scheme checks the widths. Quoting efficiency as a fraction when the question asks for a percentage, or the other way round. And describing the wasted arrow as "energy lost", which is both wrong and, in an exam, a marked error.

Equations and symbols

Statement 1.7 is a small set of equations used in a large number of combinations. The two rules that carry most of the marks are that work needs a force along the displacement, and that power is a rate, so every time must be in seconds before dividing.

Work and the energy stores

W = Fd
Key: W = work done (J); F = force in the direction of motion (N); d = distance moved along that direction (m). A force at right angles to the motion does no work.

KE = ½mv²
Key: KE = kinetic energy (J); m = mass (kg); v = speed (m/s). The speed is squared, so doubling the speed quadruples the energy — the reason braking distance rises so steeply.

GPE = mgh
Key: GPE = gravitational potential energy (J); m = mass (kg); g = gravitational field strength (9.8 N/kg); h = height gained (m). A fall is a loss of GPE, so state the sign or the word.

KE lost = GPE gained (no friction)
Key: the conservation statement used to link the two stores. With friction or air resistance, part of the energy is transferred to the thermal store of the surroundings and the equality becomes an inequality.

v = √(2gh)
Key: v = speed at the bottom of a frictionless fall (m/s); g = 9.8 m/s²; h = height fallen (m). It comes from ½mv² = mgh, and the mass cancels — which is why a feather and a hammer match on the Moon.

Power

P = E / t = W / t
Key: P = power (W); E or W = energy transferred or work done (J); t = time taken (s). One watt is one joule per second.

E = Pt
Key: E = energy transferred (J); P = power (W); t = time (s). With P in kilowatts and t in hours the energy comes out in kilowatt-hours, which is what a meter measures.

P = Fv
Key: P = useful power output (W); F = driving force (N); v = constant speed (m/s). For a car at steady speed the driving force equals the total resistive force.

1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J
Key: one kilowatt-hour is the energy of a 1000 W appliance running for one hour; 1 kW × 3600 s = 3.6 MJ.

Efficiency

efficiency = (useful energy output / total energy input) × 100%
Key: both energies in joules (or both powers in watts, since the time cancels); the result is a percentage and can never exceed 100. A figure above 100 means the wrong quantity was used as the input.

wasted energy = input − useful output
Key: the remainder is transferred by friction, air resistance or sound to the thermal store of the surroundings. Energy is not destroyed, so the widths of a Sankey diagram must balance.

useful power of a lifting motor = mgh / t
Key: m = load mass (kg); g = 9.8 N/kg; h = height lifted (m); t = time taken (s). Comparing this with the electrical input VI gives the motor's efficiency.

title: Databases and Data Definition — Study Notes
content:
Databases and Data Definition

Syllabus note: in 9618, databases is AS content (section 8, AS Paper 1). This is the condensed companion to the full AS Databases note, not separate A2 content.

Relational Concepts

A table (relation) stores rows (tuples) and columns (attributes). The primary key uniquely identifies each row; a foreign key references a primary key in another table, creating the relationship. A composite key uses two or more columns together.

Normalisation

  • 1NF: atomic values, no repeating groups.
  • 2NF: 1NF plus every non-key attribute depends on the whole key (kills partial dependency in composite keys).
  • 3NF: 2NF plus no transitive dependency — non-key attributes must not depend on other non-key attributes.

Normalisation reduces redundancy and prevents update, insert and delete anomalies.

DDL and DML

DDL defines structure: CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE, DROP. DML manipulates data: SELECT ... FROM ... WHERE, INSERT INTO, UPDATE, DELETE. Joins combine related tables: FROM Student s JOIN Enrolment e ON s.id = e.StudentID. Aggregates: COUNT, SUM, AVG with GROUP BY and HAVING.

Transactions and Concurrency

A transaction is a unit of work obeying ACID: Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (rules preserved), Isolation (concurrent transactions do not interfere), Durability (committed data survives crashes). Record locking blocks conflicting simultaneous edits; a deadlock occurs when two transactions each hold a lock the other needs.

Exam tips: normalise a small table through 1NF, 2NF, 3NF naming the dependency removed at each step; write a two-table SELECT with JOIN; state which ACID property a scenario breaks.

DDL and DML

Data Definition Language (DDL) creates and changes the structure of a database: CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE and DROP TABLE. Data Manipulation Language (DML) works with the data inside the structure: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE.

Example: CREATE TABLE Student (ID INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, Name VARCHAR(30)); is DDL; INSERT INTO Student VALUES (1, 'Ana'); is DML.

Exam tip: classify each statement by whether it changes structure or changes data.

Worked example: a SELECT query

To list the names of students in Year 11 who study Physics, sorted by surname, a query joins two tables and filters the result: SELECT Name FROM Student INNER JOIN Enrolment ON Student.StudentID = Enrolment.StudentID WHERE Year = 11 AND Subject = 'Physics' ORDER BY Name. Read the question word by word and map each condition onto a clause.

Keys and integrity

  • A primary key uniquely identifies each record in a table and cannot be null.
  • A foreign key holds the primary key of another table, which links the two tables together.
  • A candidate key is any field, or combination of fields, that could serve as the primary key.

Entity-relationship modelling

A one-to-many relationship, such as one teacher and many classes, is shown by placing the primary key of the "one" side in the "many" table. A many-to-many relationship, such as students and courses, needs a third, linking table that holds a foreign key for each side. Without it the database would repeat data or store several values in one field, which breaks normalisation.

Exam point: CREATE TABLE statements declare the data types, the primary key and each foreign key. DROP and ALTER change the structure; INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE and SELECT work with the records.

title: Binomial Distribution — Study Notes
content:
The Binomial Distribution

When Binomial Applies

X ~ B(n, p) counts successes in n independent trials when:

  • a fixed number n of identical trials,
  • each trial ends in success or failure,
  • constant success probability p,
  • trials are independent.

Check all four before using the model — "justifying a binomial model" is a real exam question.

The Formula

P(X = r) = ⁿCᵣ pʳ(1 − p)ⁿ⁻ʳ for r = 0, 1, ..., n. The ⁿCᵣ counts which r of the n trials were the successes.

Example: X ~ B(5, 0.3). P(X = 2) = ¹⁰C₂? No — ⁵C₂ × 0.3² × 0.7³ = 10 × 0.09 × 0.343 = 0.3087.

Cumulative Probabilities

P(X ≤ 2) = P(0) + P(1) + P(2). "At least" questions convert by the complement: P(X ≥ 2) = 1 − P(X ≤ 1). Keep one extra decimal place in intermediate steps to avoid rounding drift.

Expectation and Variance

  • E(X) = np and Var(X) = np(1 − p)

For X ~ B(20, 0.4): E(X) = 8 and Var(X) = 4.8.

Modelling Decisions
