If trials are dependent (drawing without replacement from a small population) binomial is not appropriate. If p changes between trials it is not binomial. When n is large and p small, the binomial is approximately Poisson — but at A2 you usually stay exact.

Exam tips: identify n and p in words before touching the calculator. For P(X ≥ k) always rewrite as 1 − P(X ≤ k − 1). Tables give cumulative values — use them rather than summing by hand.

title: Further Trigonometry — Study Notes
content:
Further Trigonometry

Compound Angles

  • sin(A ± B) = sin A cos B ± cos A sin B
  • cos(A ± B) = cos A cos B ∓ sin A sin B

Example: sin 75° = sin(45° + 30°) = (√2/2)(√3/2) + (√2/2)(1/2) = (√6 + √2)/4.

Double Angles

  • sin 2A = 2 sin A cos A
  • cos 2A = cos²A − sin²A = 2cos²A − 1 = 1 − 2sin²A

Example: express 4 sin x cos x in one term: 2 sin 2x.

The R-Form

a sin x + b cos x = R sin(x + α) with R = √(a² + b²) and tan α = b/a.

Example: 3 sin x + 4 cos x = 5 sin(x + 0.927). This instantly gives the maximum 5 and minimum −5.

Reciprocal Functions

sec θ = 1/cos θ, cosec θ = 1/sin θ, cot θ = 1/tan θ. Key identity: 1 + cot²θ = cosec²θ.

Exam tips: choose the cos 2A form that eliminates the unwanted function; when solving with R-form, divide by R before using inverse trig, and translate intervals carefully.

Exam method: reciprocal functions and identities

The reciprocal functions are sec x = 1/cos x, cosec x = 1/sin x and cot x = 1/tan x. Rewrite them in terms of sine and cosine when a question mixes functions, because this usually shows which identity to use.

The Pythagorean identities are sin² x + cos² x = 1, 1 + tan² x = sec² x and 1 + cot² x = cosec² x. Divide the first identity by cos² x or sin² x to obtain the second or third.

To solve an equation such as sec x = 2, first rewrite it as cos x = 1/2, then find the acute angle and the other solutions in the required range. For cos x = k the solutions in 0 to 2π are α and 2π − α, where α is the acute angle.

To prove an identity, work on the more complicated side only, and keep rewriting until it matches the other side.

Exam cue: Give each solution in the range asked for, using exact values such as π/3 when the angle is standard.

title: Chemical Equilibria A2 Level Chemistry Revision Notes
content:
Chemical Equilibria A2 Level Chemistry Revision Notes

This revision note belongs to Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH14, Topic 13 Chemical Equilibria, covering homogeneous and heterogeneous systems, equilibrium constants Kc and Kp, the factors affecting equilibrium composition and constant values, total entropy links, and reaction extent predictions.

Expressions for Kc in Homogeneous and Heterogeneous Systems

When a reversible reaction takes place in a closed system, it eventually reaches a dynamic equilibrium where the rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction, and the concentrations of reactants and products remain constant. The equilibrium constant Kc allows you to deduce the position of equilibrium quantitatively.

  • Be able to deduce an expression for Kc, for homogeneous and heterogeneous systems, in terms of equilibrium concentrations.
  • For a general homogeneous system where all species are in the same phase, such as aA + bB reversible cC + dD, the expression is Kc = [C]^c [D]^d / ([A]^a [B]^b), where square brackets denote equilibrium concentrations in mol dm⁻³.
  • For heterogeneous systems containing species in different phases, pure solids and pure liquids are omitted from the Kc expression because their concentrations remain essentially constant throughout the reaction. For example, for the decomposition of calcium carbonate, CaCO3(s) reversible CaO(s) + CO2(g), the expression is simply Kc = [CO2].

Expressions for Kp in Homogeneous and Heterogeneous Systems

For systems involving gases, it is often more convenient to use partial pressures rather than concentrations to define the equilibrium position.

  • Be able to deduce an expression for Kp for homogeneous and heterogeneous systems, in terms of equilibrium partial pressures in atm.
  • The mole fraction of a gas in a mixture is calculated as the number of moles of that individual gas divided by the total number of moles of all gases present in the mixture.
  • The partial pressure of an individual gas is its mole fraction multiplied by the total pressure of the gas system, measured in units of atmospheres or atm.
  • For a homogeneous gas phase reaction such as N2O4(g) reversible 2NO2(g), the partial pressure expression is Kp = p(NO2)² / p(N2O4).
  • For a heterogeneous gas-solid equilibrium such as C(s) + CO2(g) reversible 2CO(g), pure solid carbon is omitted from the expression, giving Kp = p(CO)² / p(CO2).

Calculating Equilibrium Constants from Experimental Data

Calculations involving Kc and Kp require systematic tracking of initial moles, change in moles, and equilibrium moles, converting them to concentrations or partial pressures.

  • Be able to calculate a value, with units where appropriate, for the equilibrium constants Kc and Kp for homogeneous and heterogeneous reactions, from experimental data.
  • For Kc calculations, divide equilibrium moles by the total volume in dm³ to find equilibrium concentrations, substitute into the Kc formula, and cancel out units or combine them using indices such as mol⁻² dm⁶.
  • For Kp calculations, find total moles at equilibrium, determine mole fractions for each gas, multiply by total pressure to find partial pressures in atm, substitute into Kp, and derive units like atm or atm².

Worked Example for Kc Calculation

For H2 + I2 reversible 2HI, suppose 1.00 mol of hydrogen and 1.00 mol of iodine are heated in a 2.00 dm³ flask. At equilibrium, 1.60 mol of hydrogen iodide has formed.

  • Step 1: Set up an ICE table. Initial moles: H2 = 1.00, I2 = 1.00, HI = 0.00.
  • Step 2: Equilibrium moles: HI = 1.60. Since stoichiometry shows 2 mol of HI form, 0.80 mol of H2 and 0.80 mol of I2 must have reacted.
  • Step 3: Calculate remaining equilibrium moles: H2 = 1.00 − 0.80 = 0.20 mol; I2 = 1.00 − 0.80 = 0.20 mol.
  • Step 4: Convert to concentrations by dividing by the volume of 2.00 dm³: [HI] = 1.60 ÷ 2.00 = 0.80 mol dm⁻³, [H2] = 0.20 ÷ 2.00 = 0.10 mol dm⁻³, [I2] = 0.20 ÷ 2.00 = 0.10 mol dm⁻³.
  • Step 5: Substitute into Kc expression: Kc = [HI]² / ([H2] × [I2]) = 0.80² / (0.10 × 0.10) = 0.64 / 0.01 = 64. The units cancel out entirely because the number of moles of reactants equals the number of moles of products.

Effects of Changes on Equilibrium Composition

Le Chatelier's principle helps predict how a system responds to external stresses, altering equilibrium composition without changing the constant itself unless temperature changes.

  • Understand how, if at all, a change in temperature, pressure or the presence of a catalyst affects the equilibrium composition in a homogeneous or heterogeneous system.
  • Adding reactant or removing product shifts the position towards the products. Adding product shifts it towards the reactants.
  • Increasing pressure or decreasing volume favours the side of the reaction with fewer gas molecules. Changing the volume has the same effect as changing pressure.
  • Raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium in the endothermic direction. Lowering the temperature shifts it in the exothermic direction.
  • A catalyst changes the rate at which equilibrium is reached by providing an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy, but it has no effect on the equilibrium position or composition.

Independence of Equilibrium Constants from Concentration and Pressure

While altering conditions shifts the position of equilibrium, the underlying constant remains strictly invariant under specific conditions.

  • Understand that the value of the equilibrium constant is not affected by changes in concentration or pressure or by the addition of a catalyst.
  • A change in concentration or pressure shifts the equilibrium composition to counteract the change, but the ratio of products to reactants at the new equilibrium exactly equals the original Kc or Kp value.
  • A catalyst speeds up both the forward and reverse rates equally, leaving the equilibrium constant completely unchanged.

Effect of Temperature on Equilibrium Constants

Temperature is unique because it alters the actual value of the equilibrium constant Kc and Kp, reflecting a change in the position of equilibrium.

  • Know the effect of changing the temperature on the equilibrium constant Kc and Kp for both exothermic and endothermic reactions.
  • Understand that the effect of temperature on the position of equilibrium is explained using a change in the value of the equilibrium constant.
  • For an exothermic forward reaction, raising the temperature decreases the value of Kc and Kp, as the equilibrium shifts to the left. Lowering the temperature increases Kc and Kp.
  • For an endothermic forward reaction, raising the temperature increases the value of Kc and Kp, as the equilibrium shifts to the right. Lowering the temperature decreases Kc and Kp.

Entropy, Total Entropy, and Equilibrium Constants

Thermodynamics links the position of equilibrium to total entropy change and the magnitude of the equilibrium constant.

  • Understand the effect of a change in temperature on the value of Stotal and the magnitude of the equilibrium constant, since Stotal = R ln K.
  • The equation Stotal = R ln K bridges kinetics, equilibrium, and thermodynamics, where R is the universal gas constant and ln K is the natural logarithm of the equilibrium constant.
  • When temperature changes, it alters Stotal, which in turn directly alters the magnitude of K. A larger positive Stotal corresponds to a much larger equilibrium constant, meaning the reaction goes virtually to completion.

Predicting the Extent of Reaction

The numerical value of an equilibrium constant gives immediate insight into whether a reaction proceeds far towards products or stays mostly as reactants.

  • Be able to apply knowledge of the value of equilibrium constants to predict the extent to which a reaction takes place.
  • When an equilibrium constant value is very large, greater than 10 to the power of 10, the numerator is vastly larger than the denominator, indicating that the reaction goes essentially to completion with very few reactants remaining.
  • When an equilibrium constant value is very small, less than 10 to the power of minus 10, the denominator dominates, indicating that virtually no reaction takes place and the system remains almost entirely as reactants.
  • When an equilibrium constant is around 1, significant amounts of both reactants and products are present at equilibrium.

Typical mistakes

  • Mistake: Including pure solids or pure liquids in Kc or Kp expressions. Correction: Omit pure solids and pure liquids because their active masses do not change.
  • Mistake: Forgetting to divide equilibrium moles by volume when calculating Kc. Correction: Always divide moles by the volume in dm³ to obtain concentration values before substituting into Kc.
  • Mistake: Believing that increasing pressure changes the value of Kc. Correction: Pressure changes the position of equilibrium and shifts concentrations, but Kc remains constant at a fixed temperature.
  • Mistake: Using mass in grams instead of mole fractions or partial pressures for Kp calculations. Correction: Always convert mass to moles, find mole fractions, and multiply by total pressure in atm.

Exam-style questions

  1. Write the expression for Kc for the heterogeneous reaction C(s) + H2O(g) reversible CO(g) + H2(g).

    Answer: Kc = [CO] [H2] / [H2O]. Solid carbon is omitted.

  2. State and explain the effect of increasing the temperature on the value of Kc for an endothermic forward reaction.

    Answer: Kc increases. Raising temperature favours the endothermic direction, increasing product concentrations and decreasing reactant concentrations, raising the numerator of Kc.

  3. Calculate the units of Kp for the equilibrium N2(g) + 3H2(g) reversible 2NH3(g) when pressure is measured in atm.

    Answer: Kp = p(NH3)² / (p(N2) × p(H2)³). Units are atm² / (atm × atm³) = atm⁻².

  4. Explain why a catalyst has no effect on the numerical value of Kc.

    Answer: A catalyst speeds up the forward and reverse rates equally by lowering the activation energy, leaving the equilibrium constant ratio unchanged.

  5. Explain what a Kc value of 10 to the power of 15 indicates about the extent of a reaction.

    Answer: The reaction goes almost entirely to completion, with the equilibrium position lying far to the right.

Use these revision notes to test your understanding of equilibrium expressions, unit derivations, and thermodynamic links via Stotal. Next, revise reaction kinetics and acid-base equilibria.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Kc expression, applied to H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g): Kc = [HI]² ÷ ([H₂][I₂]). The units depend on the equation, here none, because the moles cancel. Write the units only when they do not cancel, and state the units explicitly when you give Kc.
  • Kp, applied to N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃: partial pressure of a gas = mole fraction × total pressure. Kp = p(NH₃)² ÷ (p(N₂) × p(H₂)³), and its units are Pa⁻² here. Give the units with Kp, because the pressures do not cancel.
  • Le Chatelier and Kc, applied to an exothermic reaction: raising the temperature moves the equilibrium to the left and decreases Kc. Adding a catalyst does not change Kc, because it speeds up the forward and backward reactions equally. Adding more reactant changes the position but not Kc.
  • Pressure effects: for N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, four gas molecules become two, so higher pressure favours the product. The equilibrium moves to the side with fewer gas molecules, and Kp stays the same at a fixed temperature.

Equations and symbols

Every equilibrium expression is one fraction: products over reactants, each raised to its stoichiometric number, with pure solids and liquids left out. These are the forms the questions use, plus the two relations that connect the constant to thermodynamics and to partial pressure.

Kc

Kc = [C]^c [D]^d / ([A]^a [B]^b) Key: Kc = equilibrium constant in concentration terms; [X] = equilibrium concentration of each species (mol dm⁻³); the lower-case letters are the stoichiometric numbers from the balanced equation, not arbitrary powers. Units are derived from the powers and often cancel.

Kc = [CO2] Key: the heterogeneous case CaCO3(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO2(g): the two solids are omitted, so the expression is a single concentration. Writing the solids in is the commonest lost mark on the topic.

Kc = [HI]² / ([H2] × [I2]) = 0.80² / (0.10 × 0.10) = 0.64 / 0.01 = 64 Key: the worked case H2 + I2 ⇌ 2HI in a 2.00 dm³ flask: concentrations in mol dm⁻³, squared because two moles of HI form. The units cancel because the moles are equal on both sides, so Kc is dimensionless here.

Kp

partial pressure of a gas = mole fraction × total pressure Key: partial pressure in atm (or Pa); mole fraction = moles of that gas ÷ total moles of gas (no units); total pressure in the same unit as the answer.

Kp = p(NO2)² / p(N2O4) Key: p(X) = partial pressure of that gas (atm); the square reflects 2NO2 in N2O4 ⇌ 2NO2. Units work out as atm, because two moles of gas become one.

Kp = p(CO)² / p(CO2) Key: the heterogeneous case C(s) + CO2 ⇌ 2CO: solid carbon is omitted, so only the two gases appear. Note that a solid has no partial pressure at all — that is why it vanishes.

Kp = p(NH3)² / (p(N2) × p(H2)³) Key: N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3: the cube comes from 3H2, and the units are atm⁻², because 4 mol of gas become 2. Write the units — they are a mark.

The thermodynamic link

Stotal = R ln K Key: Stotal = total entropy change of the system and surroundings (J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹); R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; K = the equilibrium constant (Kc or Kp). A large positive Stotal means a large K, so the reaction goes nearly to completion; raising the temperature changes Stotal and therefore changes the value of K.

The slip worth naming

Believing a pressure change alters K. Pressure shifts the position of equilibrium but the constant is unchanged at fixed temperature; only temperature changes the value of Kc or Kp.

title: Binomial Distribution — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Binomial Distribution

Mathematics — A2. X ~ B(n, p) counts successes in n independent trials when:

Key areas to revise

  • When Binomial Applies
  • The Formula
  • Cumulative Probabilities
  • Expectation and Variance
  • Modelling Decisions

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

### Worked example For X ~ B(n, p), P(X = r) = nCr pʳ(1 − p)ⁿ⁻ʳ, with mean np and variance np(1 − p). For n = 5 and p = 0.2, P(X = 2) = 10 × 0.2² × 0.8³ = 10 × 0.04 × 0.512 = 0.2048. The mean is 5 × 0.2 = 1.

title: Chemical Energetics
content:
Chemical Energetics

Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry 0620, Extended route, topic 5 (statement 5.1). Energy changes, exothermic and endothermic reactions, reaction pathway diagrams, activation energy and bond energy calculations.

5.1 Exothermic and endothermic reactions

  • Exothermic reactions release energy to the surroundings; the temperature of the surroundings rises. Combustion and neutralisation are exothermic. Endothermic reactions take in energy; the temperature falls. Thermal decomposition and photosynthesis are endothermic.
  • Enthalpy change, ΔH, is the energy change for a reaction. Exothermic: ΔH is negative. Endothermic: ΔH is positive.
  • Bond breaking is endothermic (energy is put in); bond making is exothermic (energy is released).
  • A reaction pathway (energy profile) diagram plots energy against progress: the reactants sit at one level, the products at another, and the difference is ΔH. The hump between them is the activation energy, Ea.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Bond energy calculation, applied to H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl: bonds broken are H–H (436 kJ/mol) and Cl–Cl (242 kJ/mol), total in = 678 kJ/mol. Bonds made are two H–Cl bonds (431 kJ/mol each), total out = 862 kJ/mol. ΔH = 678 − 862 = −184 kJ/mol. The reaction is exothermic, and the negative sign must be written.
  • Sign convention, applied to an endothermic decomposition: energy in is greater than energy out, so ΔH is positive. When the question asks "is the reaction exothermic or endothermic?", the sign of ΔH is your evidence — quote it.
  • Activation energy reasoning, applied to why a catalyst does not change ΔH: a catalyst provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy, so more collisions are successful and the rate rises. The energy of reactants and products is unchanged, so ΔH is the same. State both halves of that argument.
  • Experimental enthalpy change, applied to an acid–alkali neutralisation measured in a polystyrene cup: q = mcΔT, with m the mass of the solution (use the volumes added, 1 cm³ ≈ 1 g), c = 4.2 J/g°C. If 50.0 cm³ rises by 6.8 °C, q = 50.0 × 4.2 × 6.8 = 1428 J. Divide by the moles of water formed to get ΔH per mole; the sign is negative because the solution warmed.

Common errors

  • Getting the ΔH sign backwards — energy out means negative.
  • Adding bond energies that are broken and made together instead of subtracting.
  • Calling the activation energy "the energy of the reaction". It is the minimum energy needed to start the reaction.

title: A Level Physics: Astronomy and Cosmology
content:
A Level Physics: Astronomy and Cosmology

Astronomy is physics at the largest scale: measuring the distance to a star by its brightness, its size by its temperature, and the age of the universe by how fast galaxies recede. This note builds the toolkit from zero: luminosity and the inverse-square law, standard candles (Cepheid variables and Type Ia supernovae) and the distance ladder, stellar radii from Stefan's law, Hubble's law and redshift, and the evidence for the Big Bang. Every calculation is worked in full, because the papers test exactly these three or four formulas.

Brightness, luminosity and the inverse-square law

A star's luminosity L is the total power it radiates (watts). What a telescope receives is intensity (or flux) I — power per unit area at the observer's distance:

I = L/(4 π d²)

I in W m⁻², L in W, d in m
doubling the distance quarters the intensity

The analogy: a light bulb's power is fixed, but the same light spreads over a sphere of radius d — four times the area at twice the distance, so a quarter of the brightness per square metre. This one law underlies every distance measurement in astronomy.

Worked example. A star has luminosity 4.0 × 10²⁶ W. Find its intensity at 10 parsecs (1 pc = 3.09 × 10¹⁶ m).

d = 10 × 3.09 × 10¹⁶ = 3.09 × 10¹⁷ m
I = L/(4 π d²) = 4.0 × 10²⁶/(4 × 3.14 x (3.09 × 10¹⁷)²)
  = 4.0 × 10²⁶/(1.20 × 10³⁶) = 3.3 × 10⁻¹⁰ W m⁻²

Standard candles and the distance ladder

A standard candle is an object whose luminosity is known, so its observed intensity gives its distance by rearranging the inverse-square law. Two are examinable:

  • Cepheid variables: pulsating stars whose period of variation is tightly related to their luminosity (longer period, more luminous). Measuring the period gives L; measuring I gives d. Cepheids calibrated the first rungs of the cosmic distance ladder.
  • Type Ia supernovae: exploding white dwarfs that reach a consistent peak luminosity, bright enough to be seen in distant galaxies; they extended the ladder to cosmological distances and revealed the accelerating expansion.
distance from a standard candle:
d = √(L/(4 π I))

Worked example. A Cepheid has luminosity 1.0 × 10²⁹ W and observed intensity 2.5 × 10⁻¹² W m⁻². Find its distance in parsecs.

d = √(L/(4 π I)) = √(1.0 × 10²⁹/(4 × 3.14 × 2.5 × 10⁻¹²))
  = √(1.0 × 10²⁹/3.14 × 10⁻¹¹) = √(3.18 × 10³⁹)
  = 5.64 × 10¹⁹ m
in parsecs: 5.64 × 10¹⁹/3.09 × 10¹⁶ = 1825 pc
          = 1.8 kpc (2 s.f.)

Stellar radii and Stefan's law

A star radiates approximately as a black body. Stefan's law relates its luminosity to its surface area and absolute temperature:

L = 4 π r² σ T⁴

σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴ (Stefan-Boltzmann constant)
r = stellar radius (m), T = surface temperature (K)

so r = √(L/(4 π σ T⁴))

The fourth power is the headline: doubling a star's temperature multiplies its radiated power per square metre by 16. That is why hot blue stars are vastly more luminous than cooler red ones of similar size — and why a red giant can outshine the Sun despite its low temperature, because its radius is enormous.

Worked example. The Sun has L = 3.8 × 10²⁶ W and T = 5800 K. Find its radius.

r = √(L/(4 π σ T⁴))
T⁴ = (5800)⁴ = 1.13 × 10¹⁵
4 π σ T⁴ = 4 × 3.14 × 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ × 1.13 × 10¹⁵
              = 8.05 × 10⁸
r = √(3.8 × 10²⁶/8.05 × 10⁸) = √(4.72 × 10¹⁷)
  = 6.87 × 10⁸ m  (about 7 × 10⁸ m; the accepted value is 6.96 × 10⁸ m)

Worked example 2 (comparison). A star has the same temperature as the Sun but 100 times its luminosity. Find its radius in solar radii.

L = 4 π r² σ T⁴, same T and σ:
r² proportional to L  →  r = 10 R_sun

Redshift and Hubble's law

Light from distant galaxies is shifted toward longer wavelengths — redshift — because the galaxies are receding. For speeds much less than c:

z = Δλ/λ = v/c     (v << c)

Hubble's law: v = H0 d

H0 = Hubble constant (about 70 km s⁻¹ Mpc-1)
d = distance (Mpc)

Worked example 1. A galaxy's spectral line at 656 nm is observed at 689 nm. Find its recession speed.

Δλ = 689 - 656 = 33 nm
z = 33/656 = 0.0503
v = z c = 0.0503 × 3.0 × 10⁸ = 1.51 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹
  = 1.5 × 10⁴ km s⁻¹

Worked example 2. A galaxy at 100 Mpc recedes at 7000 km s⁻¹. Find H₀ and the Hubble time.

H0 = v/d = 7000/100 = 70 km s⁻¹ Mpc-1
Hubble time = 1/H0:
70 km s⁻¹ Mpc-1 = 70 000/(3.09 × 10²²) s⁻¹ = 2.27 × 10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹
t = 1/H0 = 4.4 × 10¹⁷ s = 1.4 × 10¹⁰ years = 14 billion years

The Big Bang and its evidence

Hubble's law implies that galaxies were once much closer together — the universe expanded from a hot, dense state. Three pieces of evidence are examinable:

  • Redshift of galaxies: nearly all galaxies recede, and recession speed increases with distance — expansion from a common origin.
  • Cosmic microwave background (CMB): a uniform 2.7 K radiation filling the sky — the cooled remnant of the hot early universe, predicted before it was found.
  • Abundance of light elements: the observed ratios of hydrogen, helium and lithium match predictions of Big Bang nucleosynthesis.

The expanding universe has no centre: space itself stretches, so every observer sees distant galaxies receding in all directions. The age estimate 1/H₀ assumes constant expansion; accelerating expansion (dark energy) modifies it, and the measured value is about 13.8 billion years.

The theory makes a further testable claim: the CMB should be an almost perfect black-body spectrum with tiny temperature ripples, and it is — the ripples themselves are the seeds of galaxy formation, and their pattern matches the theory's predictions for the mix of ordinary matter, dark matter and dark energy. That agreement across independent observations is why the Big Bang is accepted as the standard cosmological model rather than a single unexplained measurement.

Worked examples: the standard exam types

Worked example. Two stars have the same radius; star A is twice as hot as star B. Find the ratio of their luminosities.

L = 4 π r² σ T⁴; same r and σ
L_A/L_B = (T_A/T_B)⁴ = 2⁴ = 16
Star A is 16 times more luminous.

Worked example 2. A star's luminosity is 4.0 × 10³⁰ W and its surface temperature 10 000 K. Find its radius and compare it with the Sun's (7.0 × 10⁸ m).

T⁴ = (10⁴)⁴ = 1.0 × 10¹⁶
4 π σ T⁴ = 4 × 3.14 × 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ × 1.0 × 10¹⁶ = 7.12 × 10⁹
r = √(4.0 × 10³⁰/7.12 × 10⁹) = √(5.62 × 10²⁰)
  = 2.37 × 10¹⁰ m
r/R_sun = 2.37 × 10¹⁰/7.0 × 10⁸ = 34 solar radii

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Inverse square) A star at 20 pc has intensity I. What is its intensity at 60 pc? Answer: Three times the distance gives 1/9 of the intensity: I/9.
  2. (Luminosity) Define luminosity and state its unit. Answer: The total power radiated by a star across all wavelengths, measured in watts (W).
  3. (Standard candle) Explain how a Cepheid variable is used to find distance. Answer: Its pulsation period determines its luminosity from the period–luminosity relation; comparing that luminosity with the observed intensity gives d = √(L/4πI).
  4. (Stefan) A star has twice the Sun's radius and half its temperature. Compare luminosities. Answer: L ∝ r²T⁴ → (2)² × (1/2)⁴ = 4 × 1/16 = 1/4: the star is a quarter as luminous.
  5. (Redshift) A line at 500 nm appears at 505 nm. Find v. Answer: z = 5/500 = 0.010; v = 0.010 × 3.0 × 10⁸ = 3.0 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹.
  6. (Hubble) A galaxy at 50 Mpc recedes at 3500 km s⁻¹. Find H₀. Answer: H₀ = 3500/50 = 70 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹.
  7. (Age) Estimate the age of the universe from H₀ = 70 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹. Answer: t = 1/H₀ ≈ 14 billion years (with unit conversions: 70 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹ = 2.27 × 10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹).
  8. (Big Bang evidence) State two observations supporting the Big Bang. Answer: The redshift–distance relation (Hubble's law) and the cosmic microwave background; the light-element abundances are a third.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Parsecs versus metres: convert before substituting; 1 pc = 3.09 × 10¹⁶ m, 1 Mpc = 3.09 × 10²² m, 1 AU = 1.50 × 10¹¹ m.
  • Luminosity versus intensity: L is the star's total power; I is what arrives per square metre. The inverse-square law connects them and d must be in metres.
  • T⁴ not T: Stefan's law is a fourth power — doubling temperature multiplies luminosity by 16, not 2. Most arithmetic errors here are exponent slips.
  • Kelvin: surface temperatures in Stefan's law must be absolute; a temperature given in °C needs +273 first.
  • Redshift approximation: z = v/c holds for v ≪ c; at large redshifts the relativistic formula is needed. State the assumption.
  • H₀ units: km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹ — mismatched units in 1/H₀ give absurd ages. Convert km to m and Mpc to m.
  • Hubble time is an estimate: 1/H₀ assumes constant expansion; note the acceleration caveat when discussing the age.
  • Centre of the universe: the Big Bang happened everywhere — there is no centre or edge; expansion stretches space between galaxies.
  • Precision: 2 or 3 s.f. with units (W, W m⁻², m, km s⁻¹, years); the data sheet supplies σ, c and H₀.

title: A Level Mathematics: Complex Numbers
content:
A Level Mathematics: Complex Numbers

Complex numbers exist because the real number line is not big enough to solve every quadratic. The equation x² + 1 = 0 has no real solution, and rather than declaring it unsolvable mathematicians invented a number whose square is −1 and then discovered that the resulting system is not a curiosity but the natural home of rotation, oscillation and alternating current. This note builds the arithmetic from that single definition, then shows the two representations — Cartesian a + bi and modulus-argument — and why switching between them turns multiplication into something you can do in your head.

Why the number system needed extending

The real numbers are ordered: given any two, one is bigger. That ordering is exactly what a complex number gives up, and it is why complex numbers cannot be drawn on a line but can be drawn on a plane. The analogy that makes the extension feel inevitable is the one that produced negative numbers: subtracting a larger number from a smaller one was once impossible, so the integers were invented to close the gap. Square-rooting a negative number closes the next gap in the same way.

i is defined by  i² = -1
a complex number is z = a + bi, where a and b are real
a = Re(z)  the real part;  b = Im(z)  the imaginary part
two complex numbers are equal only when both parts match:
a + bi = c + di  means  a = c and b = d

The last line is not a triviality — it is the standard method for finding unknown constants in complex equations, because one equation in complex numbers carries two real equations inside it.

Arithmetic in Cartesian form

Addition and subtraction work component by component, exactly like vectors. Multiplication works by expanding the brackets and then replacing i² with −1; nothing else is needed.

(3 + 2i) + (1 - 5i) = 4 - 3i
(3 + 2i)(1 - 5i) = 3 - 15i + 2i - 10i² = 3 - 13i + 10 = 13 - 13i

Worked example. Expand (2 + 3i)².

(2 + 3i)(2 + 3i) = 4 + 6i + 6i + 9i²
= 4 + 12i - 9
= -5 + 12i

Worked example 2 (a product that comes out real). Expand (4 + 3i)(4 − 3i).

= 16 - 12i + 12i - 9i² = 16 + 9 = 25

That result is not a coincidence: it is the complex analogue of the difference of two squares, and it is the engine of division.

Powers of i cycle with period four, which saves a great deal of work:

PowerValueReason
i¹idefinition
i²−1definition
i³−ii² × i
i⁴1(i²)² = 1

So i^99 = i^(96+3) = (i⁴)^24 × i³ = −i, because 99 divided by 4 leaves remainder 3.

Complex conjugates and division

Division is made possible by the conjugate: the number with the imaginary part negated, written with a bar over the z. Multiplying a number by its own conjugate always gives a real, non-negative result, which is what allows the i to be cleared from a denominator.

conjugate of z = a + bi is z-bar = a - bi
z x z-bar = a² + b²  (always real, always >= 0)
to divide: multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator

Worked example. Write (3 + 4i)/(1 − 2i) in the form a + bi.

multiply by (1 + 2i)/(1 + 2i):
numerator: (3 + 4i)(1 + 2i) = 3 + 6i + 4i + 8i² = 3 + 10i - 8 = -5 + 10i
denominator: (1 - 2i)(1 + 2i) = 1 + 4 = 5
result: (-5 + 10i)/5 = -1 + 2i

Worked example 2 (solving an equation). Find real x and y such that (x + iy)(2 − i) = 5 + i.

expand: 2x - xi + 2yi - i² y = (2x + y) + (2y - x)i
match parts:  2x + y = 5  and  2y - x = 1
from the second: x = 2y - 1
substitute: 2(2y - 1) + y = 5  →  5y = 7  →  y = 1.4, x = 1.8

The Argand diagram and modulus-argument form

A complex number is a point, and the plane it lives in is the Argand diagram: real part across, imaginary part up. That picture immediately supplies two other ways to describe the same point — how far it is from the origin and at what angle — and those are the coordinates that make multiplication behave.

modulus |z| = √(a² + b²)     (distance from the origin)
argument arg z = θ, the angle from the positive real axis
principal argument: -180 < θ <= 180 degrees (or -π < θ <= π)

tan θ = b/a, but the quadrant decides the actual angle

Worked example. Find the modulus and argument of z = −1 + √3 i.

|z| = √(1 + 3) = 2
the point is in the second quadrant (a negative, b positive)
reference angle: tan⁻¹(sqrt3/1) = 60 degrees
argument = 180 - 60 = 120 degrees
so z = 2(cos 120 + i sin 120)

Worked example 2 (fourth quadrant). Find the argument of z = 3 − 3i.

|z| = √(9 + 9) = 4.243
tan⁻¹(-3/3) = -45 degrees, and the point is in the fourth quadrant
so the principal argument is -45 degrees (equivalently 315 degrees)

Multiplying and dividing in modulus-argument form

In Cartesian form multiplication is a bracket expansion; in modulus-argument form it is two separate, simple operations. That is the whole reason the form exists.

z1 z2:  multiply the moduli, add the arguments
z1/z2:  divide the moduli, subtract the arguments
z^n:    modulus^n, argument x n     (de Moivre's theorem)

Worked example. z1 = 2(cos 30° + i sin 30°) and z2 = 3(cos 80° + i sin 80°). Find z1z2 and z1/z2.

z1 z2 = 6(cos 110 + i sin 110)
z1/z2 = (2/3)(cos(-50) + i sin(-50)) = 0.667(cos 50 - i sin 50)

Worked example 2 (de Moivre). Find (1 + i)⁸.

|1 + i| = sqrt 2, arg = 45 degrees
(1 + i)⁸ = (sqrt2)⁸ (cos 360 + i sin 360) = 16(1 + 0i) = 16

Worked example 3 (geometric reading). Describe what multiplying by i does to a point on the Argand diagram.

i has modulus 1 and argument 90 degrees
so multiplying by i keeps the distance from the origin and adds 90 degrees
that is a quarter turn anticlockwise - multiplication as rotation

Roots of polynomial equations

Real-coefficient polynomials have complex roots in conjugate pairs. That single fact lets you go from one known root to two, halve the degree by dividing out a quadratic factor, and often finish the job with ordinary factorisation.

if a + bi is a root of a polynomial with real coefficients, then a - bi is too
the pair supplies the quadratic factor (z - (a+bi))(z - (a-bi)) = z² - 2az + (a² + b²)

Worked example. 2 + i is a root of z³ − 5z² + 9z − 5. Find all three roots.

conjugate pair: 2 + i and 2 - i
quadratic factor: z² - 4z + 5
divide: (z³ - 5z² + 9z - 5) / (z² - 4z + 5) = z - 1
roots: 2 + i, 2 - i, 1

Worked example 2 (forming an equation). Find the quadratic with roots 3 ± 2i.

sum = 6, product = 9 + 4 = 13
z² - 6z + 13 = 0

Loci on the Argand diagram

A locus question asks for the set of points satisfying a condition on a complex number, and every standard condition has a shape you should recognise without algebra.

ConditionShapeWhy
|z − a| = rcircle, centre a, radius rconstant distance from a point
|z − a| = |z − b|perpendicular bisector of abequidistant from two points
arg(z − a) = θhalf-line from a at angle θconstant direction, one-way
|z − a| ≤ rclosed discthe inequality includes the boundary

Worked example. Sketch the locus of |z − 3 − 4i| = 5 and state its centre and radius.

rewrite: |z - (3 + 4i)| = 5
circle, centre 3 + 4i, radius 5
it passes through the origin because |0 - 3 - 4i| = 5

Worked example 2 (inequality region). Describe the region |z − 1| < 2 and arg z > 45°.

inside the circle centre 1 radius 2 (not the boundary)
AND above the half-line from the origin at 45 degrees
the answer is the part of the disc lying above that ray

Exponential form and Euler's relation

The modulus-argument form is usually written more compactly as re^(iθ), using Euler's relation. That notation is not decoration: it makes the multiplication rules obvious, because exponentials multiply by adding their powers.

Euler: e^(i θ) = cos θ + i sin θ
so z = r e^(i θ)
z1 z2 = r1 r2 e^(i(theta1 + theta2))
z^n = r^n e^(i n θ)
z-bar = r e^(-i θ)

Worked example. Write z = 1 + i in exponential form and hence find z⁶.

r = sqrt 2, θ = π/4  →  z = sqrt2 e^(i π/4)
z⁶ = (sqrt2)⁶ e^(i 6 π/4) = 8 e^(i 3pi/2) = 8(cos 270 + i sin 270) = -8i

Worked example 2 (cos and sin from exponentials). Use Euler's relation to express cos θ in terms of exponentials.

e^(i θ) = cos θ + i sin θ
e^(-i θ) = cos θ - i sin θ
adding: 2 cos θ = e^(i θ) + e^(-i θ)
cos θ = (e^(i θ) + e^(-i θ))/2

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Powers) Simplify i^35. Answer: 35 = 4 × 8 + 3, so i^35 = i³ = −i.
  2. (Arithmetic) Write (5 − 2i)(3 + 4i) in the form a + bi. Answer: 15 + 20i − 6i − 8i² = 23 + 14i.
  3. (Division) Write (2 + i)/(3 − i) in the form a + bi. Answer: multiply by (3 + i): (5 + 5i)/10 = 0.5 + 0.5i.
  4. (Modulus) Find |4 − 3i|. Answer: √(16 + 9) = 5.
  5. (Argument) Find arg(−2 − 2i) in the principal range. Answer: third quadrant, so −135°.
  6. (De Moivre) Find (√3 + i)⁴. Answer: r = 2, θ = 30°, so 16(cos 120 + i sin 120) = −8 + 8√3 i.
  7. (Roots) 1 − 2i is a root of z² − 2z + 5 = 0. State the other root. Answer: 1 + 2i.
  8. (Locus) Describe |z + 2| = 3. Answer: circle centre −2, radius 3.
  9. (Locus) Describe arg(z − 1) = π/3. Answer: half-line from 1 at 60°, excluding the point itself.
  10. (Exponential) Write 2 − 2i as re^(iθ). Answer: r = 2√2, θ = −45°, so 2√2 e^(−iπ/4).

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Squaring the imaginary part only: (2i)² = −4, not 4i² left uncollected, and (a + bi)² has a middle term 2abi that is easy to drop.
  • Conjugate applied to the numerator: divide by multiplying both parts by the conjugate of the denominator only.
  • Argument in the wrong quadrant: tan⁻¹(b/a) returns a first-quadrant angle; add or subtract 180° to place it correctly.
  • Principal range ignored: an argument of 300° is written −60°, not 300°, when the question asks for the principal value.
  • Modulus of a sum: |z1 + z2| is not |z1| + |z2|; only products and quotients distribute over modulus.
  • Conjugate pairs assumed for complex coefficients: the pairing holds for real coefficients, which is the case in every exam question — but say so when justifying.
  • Locus with the wrong centre: |z − a| is a circle centred at a, not at −a; the sign inside the modulus flips the centre.
  • °/rad mode: de Moivre in radians while the question is in degrees gives a phase that is wrong by a factor of 57.3.

Equations and symbols

Complex numbers are one definition and two representations. Everything else — division, powers, roots, loci — is a consequence of the lines below, and the marks are for knowing which representation makes the operation easy.

Definition and Cartesian form

i² = -1 Key: i = the imaginary unit, defined so that its square is −1. This single line is why every quadratic has a root and why powers of i cycle with period four.

z = a + bi Key: z = the complex number; a = the real part, Re(z); b = the imaginary part, Im(z); both a and b are real numbers with no units. Two complex numbers are equal only when both parts match, which turns one complex equation into two real ones.

z x z-bar = a² + b² Key: z-bar = the conjugate a − bi; the product is always real and never negative. This is the engine of division: multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator only, and the i leaves the bottom.

Modulus, argument and rotation

|z| = √(a² + b²) Key: |z| = modulus, the distance from the origin on the Argand diagram (no units); a and b = the real and imaginary parts. It is Pythagoras, so the sign of a or b never matters.

z1 z2: multiply the moduli, add the arguments Key: z1 and z2 = the two complex numbers; moduli multiply, arguments add — which is why division divides the moduli and subtracts the arguments, and why z^n raises the modulus to n and multiplies the argument by n (de Moivre).

e^(i θ) = cos θ + i sin θ Key: θ = the argument, the angle from the positive real axis (radians in this form); e = 2.718…; the identity is Euler's relation, so z = r e^(i θ) with r = |z|. Exponentials then multiply by adding powers, which is the same rule in a shorter notation.

Roots

z² - 6z + 13 = 0 Key: the quadratic with roots 3 ± 2i: the sum of the roots is 6, giving −6z, and the product is 3² + 2² = 13, giving the constant. Real coefficients force conjugate pairs, so one known complex root always gives two.

The slip worth naming

Taking tan⁻¹(b/a) as the argument. It returns a first-quadrant angle, so add or subtract 180° when the point lies in the second or third quadrant, and keep the principal range the question asks for.

title: Hypothesis Testing — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Hypothesis Testing

Mathematics — A2. The null hypothesis H₀ is the default claim (no change, p = p₀). The alternative H₁ is what a suspicious observation suggests (p > p₀, p < p₀, or p ≠ p₀). The significance level α is the probability of rejecting a true H₀ — the false-alarm rate, usually 5% or 1%.

Key areas to revise

  • The Framework
  • Test for a Binomial Proportion
  • One-Tailed vs Two-Tailed
  • Critical Regions
  • Conclusions in Context

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

### Worked example A test of a claimed mean has a null hypothesis H₀ and an alternative H₁. Choose a significance level such as 5%, calculate the test statistic and its p-value, then reject H₀ if p < α. A two-tailed test looks for a change in either direction, so the 5% is split between the two tails. ### Worked example A test of a claimed mean has a null hypothesis H₀ and an alternative H₁. Choose a significance level such as 5%, calculate the test statistic and its p-value, then reject H₀ if p < α. A two-tailed test looks for a change in either direction, so the 5% is split between the two tails.

title: Waves & Sound — Study Notes
content:
Waves & Sound

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): general wave properties; reflection/refraction/diffraction; sound.

1. Wave basics

v = fλ. Transverse (oscillation ⊥ travel — light, water, S-waves) vs longitudinal (parallel — sound, P-waves). Amplitude, wavelength, frequency f = 1/T; wavefront diagrams.

2. Ripple tank behaviours

  • Reflection: angle in = angle out; speed/frequency unchanged, direction changes.
  • Refraction: speed change at boundary bends wavefronts (shallow water slows ripples).
  • Diffraction: spreading through gaps ≈ λ wide; around edges.

3. Electromagnetic spectrum (order)

Radio → micro → IR → visible (red 700 nm – violet 400 nm) → UV → X → gamma. All travel at 3 × 10⁸ m/s in vacuum; transverse; uses and dangers (IR heating; UV skin; X/gamma ionising).

4. Sound

  • Longitudinal; needs a medium (bell in vacuum demo). Speed ~340 m/s air, faster in liquids/solids.
  • Range 20 Hz–20 kHz; ultrasound > 20 kHz (sonar, prenatal scans, cleaning).
  • Pitch ↔ frequency; loudness ↔ amplitude.

5. Echo problems

Distance = (v × t)/2 (there and back).

Example: echo after 0.6 s, v = 340 → cliff 102 m away.

Exam tips: in diagrams always label wavelength as crest-to-crest; for refraction, state "changes speed" first, then direction; quote EM uses with the hazard.

Wave equation and sound

The wave equation is v = fλ, where v is the wave speed, f the frequency and λ the wavelength. Sound is a longitudinal wave that needs a medium, so it cannot travel through a vacuum. All electromagnetic waves travel at the speed of light in a vacuum, about 3 × 10⁸ m/s. In reflection the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. For an echo, the sound travels to the reflecting surface and back, so the distance to the surface is half the total distance travelled.

title: IGCSE Mathematics: Equations
content:
IGCSE Mathematics: Equations

Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580 (2025–2027), section 2 Algebra and graphs, statement 2.5 Equations — linear equations, changing the subject, simultaneous equations and quadratic equations, with the Extended additions of fractional equations and simultaneous linear–non-linear pairs. Solving an equation is finding the value of an unknown that makes a statement true, and every technique in this note is one idea applied repeatedly: do the same to both sides. The worked lines below are written out in full, because the method marks on both Paper 2 and Paper 4 are earned line by line.

What solving means: the balance principle

An equation is a balance. The equals sign says the left and right sides hold the same value, so any operation — add, subtract, multiply, divide — is legal only if it is applied to both sides. Solving then uses inverse operations to peel away everything around the unknown: addition undoes subtraction, multiplication undoes division, and a square root undoes a square. The golden rule of order: undo addition and subtraction first, then multiplication and division, then powers and roots.

Solve:  3x + 7 = 22

3x + 7 - 7 = 22 - 7        [subtract 7 from both sides]
3x = 15
3x / 3 = 15 / 3            [divide both sides by 3]
x = 5

Check in the original: 3 × 5 + 7 = 15 + 7 = 22  ✓

The check is not optional decoration: it costs five seconds and catches sign errors, which are the most common mark lost on Paper 2.

If the equation contains...First moveWhy
BracketsExpand every bracketSeparate terms can then be collected
FractionsMultiply every term by the lowest common denominatorOne step clears all fractions
Unknowns on both sidesCollect unknowns on one side, numbers on the otherThe equation must end as x = number
Powers of the unknownBring to one side as a quadratic and factorise or use the formulaLinear methods cannot isolate x inside x²

Linear equations with brackets, fractions and unknowns on both sides

The strategy is always the same: expand, collect, solve. Write one step per line and keep the equation balanced.

Solve:  5(2x - 3) = 3x + 11

10x - 15 = 3x + 11        [expand the bracket]
10x - 3x = 11 + 15        [subtract 3x from both sides, add 15 to both sides]
7x = 26
x = 26/7 = 3 5/7          [exact fraction, not a rounded decimal]
Solve:  (x + 4)/3 - 2 = x/5

Multiply every term by 15, the lowest common denominator of 3 and 5:
15 x (x + 4)/3 - 15 × 2 = 15 x x/5
5(x + 4) - 30 = 3 × 5x + 20 - 30 = 3x        [expand]
5x - 10 = 3x             [collect constants]
5x - 3x = 10
2x = 10
x = 5

Check in the original: (5 + 4)/3 - 2 = 3 - 2 = 1 and 5/5 = 1  ✓

Multiplying by the common denominator clears fractions in one step — a technique worth using deliberately, since working with fractions line by line is where slips happen.

Changing the subject of a formula

Making x the subject means rearranging until the formula reads x = ... . Unwrap x the same way: undo additions, then multiplications, and if x appears in more than one place, collect all x-terms on one side first and factorise.

Make x the subject:  y = (2x + 3)/(x - 1)

Multiply both sides by (x - 1):
y(x - 1) = 2x + 3
yx - y = 2x + 3          [expand the left side]
yx - 2x = y + 3          [bring x terms left, others right]
x(y - 2) = y + 3         [factorise: x taken out of both terms]
x = (y + 3)/(y - 2)

Every line is a legitimate balanced move, and the final answer is a formula valid for any y except y = 2. Formula rearrangement is a Paper 4 staple — often disguised as a physics or mensuration problem.

Simultaneous equations

Two unknowns need two equations. There are two standard methods, and both produce both unknowns.

Elimination — make one unknown's coefficients match and subtract:

Solve:  3x + 2y = 16   and   5x - 2y = 8

The y coefficients already match (+2 and -2), so add the equations:
(3x + 2y) + (5x - 2y) = 16 + 8
8x = 24
x = 3

Substitute x = 3 into the first equation:
3(3) + 2y = 16
9 + 2y = 16
2y = 7
y = 3.5

Check in the second equation: 5(3) - 2(3.5) = 15 - 7 = 8  ✓

Substitution — make one unknown the subject of one equation:

Solve:  x + y = 10   and   y = x² - 4        [one linear, one non-linear: Extended]

From the first equation: y = 10 - x
Substitute into the second:
10 - x = x² - 4
0 = x² + x - 14        [rearranged: x² - 4 + x - 10 = x² + x - 14]
x = [-1 ± √(1 + 56)]/2 = [-1 ± √57]/2       [quadratic formula]

Numerically x ≈ 3.275 or x ≈ -4.275, with the matching y values y = 10 - x ≈ 6.725 and 14.275.

For a pair of straight lines there is exactly one solution unless the lines are parallel (no solution) or identical (infinitely many) — a common Paper 2 short question.

Quadratic equations

A quadratic has the form ax² + bx + c = 0 and may have two solutions, one, or none. Three methods are examinable.

1. Factorising.

Solve:  x² - 5x + 6 = 0

(x - 2)(x - 3) = 0        [factors of +6 that sum to -5]
A product is zero only when a factor is zero:
x - 2 = 0  or  x - 3 = 0
x = 2  or  x = 3

2. Completing the square.

Solve:  x² + 6x + 2 = 0

(x + 3)² - 9 + 2 = 0        [(x+3)² = x² + 6x + 9, so subtract 9 to keep equality]
(x + 3)² - 7 = 0
(x + 3)² = 7
x + 3 = ±√7                  [both roots, positive and negative]
x = -3 ± √7
x ≈ -0.354  or  x ≈ -5.65

3. The quadratic formula. It is completing the square, done once and for all. Starting from ax² + bx + c = 0 and dividing by a:

x² + (b/a)x + c/a = 0
x² + (b/a)x = -c/a
x² + (b/a)x + (b/2a)² = -c/a + (b/2a)²        [add the completing-the-square term]
(x + b/2a)² = (b² - 4ac)/(4a²)
x + b/2a = ±√(b² - 4ac)/(2a)
x = [-b ± √(b² - 4ac)] / (2a)

The discriminant b² − 4ac decides how many solutions there are before any solving: if it is positive there are two distinct roots, if it is zero there is one repeated root, and if it is negative there are no real roots.

Solve:  2x² - 3x - 5 = 0

a = 2, b = -3, c = -5;  b² - 4ac = 9 + 40 = 49, so two roots
x = [3 ± √49] / 4 = [3 ± 7]/4
x = (3 + 7)/4 = 2.5    or    x = (3 - 7)/4 = -1

Fractional equations (Extended)

An equation with x in a denominator is cleared the same way as any fraction equation — multiply through by the denominator — but the solutions must be checked against it, because a value that makes the denominator zero is not a solution at all.

Solve:  3/(x - 1) + 2 = 5/(x + 2)

Multiply every term by (x - 1)(x + 2):
3(x + 2) + 2(x - 1)(x + 2) = 5(x - 1)
3x + 6 + 2(x² + x - 2) = 5x - 5
3x + 6 + 2x² + 2x - 4 = 5x - 5
2x² + 5x + 2 = 5x - 5
2x² + 7 = 0
x² = -7/2

No real solutions. (Had a value like x = 1 appeared, it would be rejected as it makes x - 1 = 0.)

Worked example: an exam-style multi-step equation

A rectangle has length (2x + 1) cm and width (x − 3) cm. Its area is 30 cm². Find x and the dimensions.

(2x + 1)(x - 3) = 30
2x² - 6x + x - 3 = 30        [expand]
2x² - 5x - 3 = 30
2x² - 5x - 33 = 0            [subtract 30 from both sides]
(x - 3.5)(2x + 11) ... check by formula instead:
Factorise the quadratic: we need two numbers with product 2 x (-33) = -66 and sum -5.
The pair -11 and +6 works: (-11) × 6 = -66 and -11 + 6 = -5.
Split the middle term:  2x² + 6x - 11x - 33 = 0
Factorise in pairs:     2x(x + 3) - 11(x + 3) = 0
(x + 3)(2x - 11) = 0
x = -3  or  x = 11/2 = 5.5
x = 22/4 = 5.5   or   x = -12/4 = -3

The negative answer is rejected: a length of x − 3 with x = −3 gives −6 cm, which is impossible. So x = 5.5, the length is 12 cm and the width is 2.5 cm. Checking the area: 12 × 2.5 = 30 ✓. Interpreting the solutions in context is a mark in its own right.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Applying an operation to one side only. The single most common algebraic error; the equation must stay balanced.
  • Sign errors when expanding: −3(x − 4) = −3x + 12, not −3x − 12.
  • Forgetting the ± when taking a square root: x² = 9 gives x = 3 or x = −3.
  • Rejecting or accepting context solutions carelessly: lengths, counts and times must be positive, and the rejected root should be stated as rejected with a reason.
  • Leaving a fractional answer as a rounded decimal on Paper 2, where exact fractions are expected.
  • Ignoring the discriminant's role: if b² − 4ac is negative the quadratic has no real roots — say so rather than hunting for errors.
  • Missing a denominator restriction in a fractional equation and quoting x = 1 as a solution of 1/(x − 1) = ... .
  • Rounding too early: keep exact values (fractions, surds) until the final line of a multi-step question.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 2, 3 marks). Solve 4x − 7 = 2x + 9.

Answer: 4x − 2x = 9 + 7, so 2x = 16 and x = 8. Check: 32 − 7 = 25 and 16 + 9 = 25 ✓.

Question 2 (Paper 2, 4 marks). Solve x² + 2x − 15 = 0.

Answer: (x + 5)(x − 3) = 0, so x = −5 or x = 3. (Factor pairs of −15 summing to +2: +5 and −3.)

Question 3 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Solve the simultaneous equations 2x + 3y = 12 and 4x − y = 5.

Answer: Multiply the second equation by 3: 12x − 3y = 15. Add to the first: 14x = 27, so x = 27/14. Substitute: 2(27/14) + 3y = 12 gives 27/7 + 3y = 12, so 3y = 12 − 27/7 = 57/7 and y = 19/7.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Solve 2x² − 8x + 3 = 0, giving answers to 2 decimal places.

Answer: b² − 4ac = 64 − 24 = 40. x = [8 ± √40]/4 = [8 ± 6.325]/4, so x ≈ 3.58 or x ≈ 0.42.

Question 5 (Paper 4, 5 marks). Make r the subject of V = (1/3)πr²h.

Answer: 3V = πr²h (multiply by 3); 3V/(πh) = r² (divide by πh); r = √[3V/(πh)] (take the positive square root, since a radius is positive).

Question 6 (Paper 4, 5 marks). The length of a rectangle is 3 cm more than twice its width. Its perimeter is 54 cm. Find its area.

Answer: Let the width be w; the length is 2w + 3. Perimeter: 2[w + (2w + 3)] = 54, so 2(3w + 3) = 54, 3w + 3 = 27, 3w = 24 and w = 8. The length is 19 cm and the area is 8 × 19 = 152 cm².

Inequalities generalise equations from exact equality to a range of permitted values.

title: Work, Energy and Power — Study Notes
content:
Work, energy and power

Work

  • Work done = force × displacement in the direction of the force, W = Fs cos θ. Unit: joule (J), where 1 J = 1 N m.
  • No work is done by a force that acts perpendicular to the displacement, such as the normal contact force on a body moving along a horizontal surface.

Energy stores and transfers

Gravitational potential energy, kinetic energy, elastic potential energy, chemical energy and thermal energy are energy stores. Work done transfers energy from one store to another.

Conservation of energy

Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred. Where only conservative forces such as gravity act, the total mechanical energy is constant. Where non-conservative forces such as friction or air resistance act, the energy they dissipate appears as thermal energy.

Kinetic and gravitational potential energy

  • Kinetic energy: Ek = ½mv².
  • Gravitational potential energy change near the Earth's surface: ΔEp = mgΔh.

Power and efficiency

  • Power = work done ÷ time = energy transferred ÷ time. Unit: watt (W), where 1 W = 1 J s⁻¹.
  • Efficiency = useful energy output ÷ total energy input × 100%. It is always less than 100%.

Worked example: a 2.0 kg object falls freely from rest through 5.0 m. Its speed at the bottom, from energy conservation: ½mv² = mgh, so v = √(2gh) = √(2 × 9.81 × 5.0) ≈ 9.9 m s⁻¹.

Exam tips: check whether the question says air resistance is negligible before using conservation of energy. Always convert minutes to seconds in power calculations. Give efficiency as a percentage.

Power, efficiency and energy transfer

Power is the rate at which work is done or energy is transferred, P = W/t = Fv for a force moving at constant velocity. Efficiency is the useful energy output divided by the total energy input, and it is always less than 1 because some energy is dissipated, usually as thermal energy from friction. When a body is raised, its gain in gravitational potential energy is mgh, and a kinetic energy change is ½m(v2 - u2). Both can be used to find the work done against resistive forces.

Exam tip: state the percentage efficiency with units, and check that it is below 100 percent.

title: Differentiation II — Study Notes
content:
Differentiation II

Edexcel International A Level Mathematics — Pure Mathematics 3 (WMA13), sat at A2.

Product and Quotient Rules

  • (uv)′ = u′v + uv′
  • (u/v)′ = (u′v − uv′)/v²

Example: y = x² e^x gives dy/dx = 2x e^x + x² e^x = e^x(2x + x²).

Standard Derivatives

  • sin x → cos x; cos x → −sin x; tan x → sec²x
  • e^x → e^x; ln x → 1/x

Chain Rule Everywhere

d/dx [ln(3x)] = 3/(3x) = 1/x; d/dx [e^(2x)] = 2e^(2x); d/dx [sin²x] = 2 sin x cos x.

Implicit Differentiation

Differentiate both sides w.r.t. x, treating y as a function of x (terms in y pick up dy/dx).

Example: x² + y² = 25 → 2x + 2y(dy/dx) = 0 → dy/dx = −x/y.

Parametric Curves

For x = f(t), y = g(t): dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt).

Example: x = t², y = t³ gives dy/dx = 3t²/2t = 3t/2.

Exam tips: quote the rule you use; for tangent/normal on parametric curves, find t at the point first, and simplify implicit answers using the original equation.

Exam method: exponential, logarithmic and trigonometric rules

The derivative of eˣ is eˣ, and the derivative of e^(kx) is k e^(kx). The derivative of ln x is 1/x, and for ln(f(x)) the chain rule gives f′(x)/f(x). The derivative of sin x is cos x and of cos x is −sin x; for a function of kx, multiply by k.

When a product contains an exponential or trigonometric function, use the product rule d/dx(uv) = u dv/dx + v du/dx. Factorising the result, such as eˣ(1 + x), makes it easier to evaluate at a point.

Quotients use d/dx(u/v) = (v du/dx − u dv/dx)/v². Write tan x as sin x/cos x when the quotient rule is easier, and remember that d/dx(tan x) = sec² x.

Second derivatives follow by differentiating again. Use them to classify stationary points, or to check the concavity of a curve, when the question asks for it.

Exam cue: Show each rule as you apply it. Method marks are awarded for a correct product or chain step even if the final arithmetic is wrong.

Worked examples: combining rules

Example 1 (product rule). Differentiate y = x²(3x − 1)⁴.

Let u = x² and v = (3x − 1)⁴. Then du/dx = 2x and dv/dx = 4(3x − 1)³ × 3 = 12(3x − 1)³ (chain rule inside the product). So dy/dx = x² × 12(3x − 1)³ + (3x − 1)⁴ × 2x = 2x(3x − 1)³[6x + (3x − 1)] = 2x(3x − 1)³(9x − 1). Factorising at the end is what the examiner expects; leave a fully expanded answer only if asked.

Example 2 (quotient rule). Differentiate y = (x + 2)/(x² + 1). Let u = x + 2 and v = x² + 1. dy/dx = [1(x² + 1) − (x + 2)(2x)]/(x² + 1)² = (x² + 1 − 2x² − 4x)/(x² + 1)² = (1 − 4x − x²)/(x² + 1)². Check the numerator by substituting a value of x into the original and the answer: it is easy to lose the minus sign on the second term.

Trigonometric and exponential derivatives in context

  • d/dx (sin 3x) = 3 cos 3x, so the chain rule multiplies by the derivative of the inside. Writing sin 3x as sin(3x) makes the inside visible.
  • d/dx (e4x − 1) = 4e4x − 1. The derivative of e to a power is the same expression times the derivative of the power.
  • d/dx (ln(2x + 5)) = 2/(2x + 5). The derivative of ln x is 1/x, and the chain rule supplies the factor 2.
  • d/dx (cos² x) = 2 cos x × (−sin x) = −2 sin x cos x. Write powers of functions as (function)ⁿ and apply the chain rule once for each layer.

Implicit differentiation worked through

For x² + xy + y² = 7, differentiate each term with respect to x. A term in y is differentiated as a function of x and so gives dy/dx through the chain rule: 2x + (x dy/dx + y × 1) + 2y dy/dx = 0. Collect the dy/dx terms: dy/dx(x + 2y) = −(2x + y), so dy/dx = −(2x + y)/(x + 2y). The gradient is then found at a given point by substituting both coordinates.

Parametric differentiation

If x = t² and y = 2t³, then dx/dt = 2t and dy/dt = 6t², so dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt) = 6t²/(2t) = 3t. This is a chain-rule statement, not a new formula, and it is the reason the division is by dx/dt, not multiplied.

Common errors that lose marks

  • Forgetting the inner derivative in the chain rule, for example differentiating sin(3x) as cos(3x).
  • Writing the quotient rule with the denominator on the wrong side, or dropping the square on the denominator.
  • Treating dy/dx as a fraction and cancelling dy with dx in an implicit step; differentiate term by term instead.
  • Substituting the point into dy/dx before simplifying, which is fine, but forgetting to substitute both x and y when the expression still contains y.

title: Functions
content:
Functions

A function maps each input in the domain to exactly one output in the range.

Composite Functions

fg(x) means f(g(x)) — apply g first, then f. Order matters.

Example: f(x) = 2x + 1, g(x) = x². Then fg(x) = 2x² + 1 but gf(x) = (2x + 1)².

Inverse Functions

f⁻¹ reverses f: f⁻¹f(x) = x. To find it, swap x and y in y = f(x) and rearrange.

Example: f(x) = 3x − 2 gives f⁻¹(x) = (x + 2)/3.

An inverse exists only if f is one-one. If not, restrict the domain (e.g. f(x) = x² for x ≥ 0 has f⁻¹(x) = √x). Graphically, y = f⁻¹(x) is the reflection of y = f(x) in the line y = x, and the range of f becomes the domain of f⁻¹.

Transformations

NotationEffect on y = f(x)
f(x) + atranslation up by a
f(x + a)translation left by a
a f(x)vertical stretch, factor a
f(ax)horizontal stretch, factor 1/a
−f(x)reflection in the x-axis
f(−x)reflection in the y-axis

Exam tips: state the domain of any inverse; when combining transformations, translations inside the bracket act in the opposite direction to the sign.

title: International GCSE English as a Second Language: Word Formation: Prefixes and Suffixes
content:
International GCSE English as a Second Language: Word Formation: Prefixes and Suffixes

Word formation is the skill of building the word a sentence needs from the word you are given — turning decide into decision, happy into unhappy, careful into carefully. It is tested directly in gap-fill tasks across the 9280 papers and it underpins the range mark in writing: a candidate who can deploy accurate, varied word families reads as a competent user of English. This note builds the system from zero: how English derives nouns, verbs, adjectives and adverbs from base words, which prefixes flip meaning, how spelling changes behave, and the decoding procedure that solves every word-formation question under time pressure.

Word families: one idea, four outfits

Most English base words belong to a family whose members are different parts of speech. The first step of any word-formation question is deciding which member the sentence is dressed for.

Base verbNounAdjectiveAdverb
decidedecisiondecisive / decideddecisively
createcreationcreativecreatively
carecarecareful / carelesscarefully
succeedsuccesssuccessfulsuccessfully
developdevelopmentdeveloping / developed—
comparecomparisoncomparablecomparatively
relaterelation / relationshiprelative / relatedrelatively
beautybeautybeautifulbeautifully

The productive pattern: verbs end in -ify, -ise, -en (justify, modernise, widen); nouns of action end in -tion, -ment, -ance, -ence, -ing (decision, development, performance, existence); adjectives end in -ful, -less, -ous, -ive, -able, -ible, -al, -ic (careful, careless, dangerous, active, readable, possible, natural, scientific); adverbs end in -ly (carefully).

Suffixes by part of speech

Part of speechCommon suffixesExamples
Nouns (people)-er, -or, -ist, -ant, -eeteacher, actor, scientist, assistant, employee
Nouns (things/ideas)-tion, -ment, -ness, -ity, -ance, -ence, -ismeducation, achievement, happiness, ability, importance, difference, tourism
Adjectives-ful, -less, -ous, -ive, -able, -ible, -al, -ic, -y, -ishhopeful, hopeless, famous, attractive, comfortable, sensible, cultural, economic, rainy, childish
Adverbs-lyquickly, easily, surprisingly
Verbs-ise/-ize, -ify, -enorganise, simplify, widen

Note the pairs that change meaning with the suffix: -ful (full of) versus -less (without) — hopeful and hopeless; -ous (having the quality) — danger → dangerous. And the -ing/-ed adjective pair: -ing describes the thing that causes (a tiring day), -ed describes the person affected (a tired student).

Prefixes that flip or shift meaning

PrefixMeaningExamples
un-not, reverseunhappy, unable, unlock
in- / im- / il- / ir-notindependent, impossible, illegal, irregular
dis-not, oppositedisagree, dishonest, disappear
mis-wronglymisunderstand, misspell, mislead
re-againrewrite, rebuild, reapply
over- / under-too much / too littleoverestimate, overcrowded, underestimate
pre- / post-before / afterpreview, precaution / postpone, post-war
anti-againstantibiotic, anti-social
co-, ex-, inter-with, out of, betweencooperate, export, international

The negative prefix is chosen by habit as much as by rule: in- becomes im- before m and p (impossible, impatient), il- before l (illegal), ir- before r (irregular). There is no rule for which words take un- rather than in- — unhappy but inactive — so learn negatives as pairs: unhappy, uncomfortable, unfriendly / inactive, inconvenient, informal / dishonest, disrespectful / misbehave.

Spelling changes when adding suffixes

  • Silent -e dropped before a vowel suffix, kept before a consonant suffix: hope + ful → hopeful (the e goes because a vowel follows) but hope + less → hopeless (the e stays because a consonant follows); like + able → likable (e dropped), manage + ment → management (e kept). Compare the same base twice and the rule becomes visible.
  • y → i before a consonant suffix: happy + ness → happiness; beauty + ful → beautiful; but y stays before -ing and -ous: carrying, curious.
  • Final consonant doubled after a single vowel + consonant in stressed syllables: big + er → bigger; begin + ing → beginning; but visit + or → visitor (stress not on last syllable).
  • -ce/-ge keep the e before -a/-o: courage + ous → courageous (the soft c sound is protected).

Worked example. Build the adjective from beauty and the noun from decide. Step 1: beauty ends in a consonant + y → change y to i before -ful: beautiful. Step 2: decide drops the final e before -tion: decision. Both spellings are the marks; the morphology is only the map.

The decoding procedure for gap-fill word formation

  1. Decide the part of speech the gap needs: read the sentence around the gap. After an article or adjective → noun. After a linking verb (is, seems, becomes) → adjective. After a verb object or sentence end → adverb. Before a noun → adjective.
  2. Decide the meaning direction: positive or negative? prefix needed? does the context say although / but / despite (which often signals the opposite meaning)?
  3. Build the word: apply the family suffix, then the prefix if needed.
  4. Spell-check against the three changes: e-drop, y→i, consonant doubling.
  5. Read the finished sentence once — the built word must fit both grammar and meaning.

Worked example 1. "Her ___ (explain) of the theory was completely ___ (understand)." Step 1: after Her + of the theory → noun; explain → explanation (note the -ation after a plain explanation form: explain → explanation, a family with its own spelling). Step 2: after was completely → adjective; understand with the context "completely ... of the theory" and the likely positive framing → understandable. If the sentence had a but clause ("... was completely ___ , so no one followed it"), the negative would be needed: un-understandable is wrong English; use incomprehensible — some negatives cannot be built, which is why step 5 (read it back) exists.

Worked example 2. "The ___ (industry) revolution changed society ___ (dramatic)." Step 1: before the noun revolution → adjective: industry → industrial (the y becomes i before the -al suffix). Step 2: after the verb changed → adverb: dramatic + ally → dramatically (the adjective dramatic gains -ally, not just -ly — read the finished word back and it must sound right). Answer: industrial, dramatically.

Worked example 3 — the double trap. "It is ___ (possible) to finish in ten minutes." Step 1: after is → adjective. Step 2: the context means cannot be done → negative prefix. Step 3: possible takes im- before p: impossible. Many candidates write unpossible — the prefix table exists to prevent exactly that.

Word formation in the writing tasks

The same skill powers the range band in writing and speaking. Families let one idea appear in several grammatical clothes inside one paragraph: "The decision was difficult. We decided slowly and decisively, and the decisive factor was cost." Deciding (or better, deciding not to repeat the root four times) is a range demonstration; the mark scheme rewards varied and accurate structures, and family variation is the cheapest variety available.

  • Upgrade weak adjective stacks: "very big problem" → "significant problem"; "very good results" → "excellent results"; "very tired" → "exhausted". Precision beats intensifiers.
  • Nominalise for formality: "Because prices rose, we lost customers" → "The rise in prices led to a loss of customers." The -tion and -ness nouns are the engine of formal style.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. Build the word: "The ___ (manage) of the company ___ (success) launched a ___ (create) campaign." Answer: management / successfully / creative. Why: after The → noun; after the subject + verb → adverb; before a noun → adjective.
  2. Build with negative prefix: "His answer was ___ (correct) and showed ___ (complete) ___ (understand) of the topic." Answer: "His answer was incorrect and showed complete misunderstanding of the topic." Why: correct takes the negative in- (incorrect); complete is used as an adjective before the noun and needs no prefix (complete, not completely — an adjective describes the noun misunderstanding); understand becomes the noun misunderstanding with the mis- prefix that signals wrongness.
  3. Spelling focus: happy → happiness; big → bigger; beauty → beautiful; decide → decision. Why: y→i, consonant doubling, y→i before -ful, silent-e drop.
  4. Choose the negative: "It is ___ (legal) to park here and ___ (polite) to shout." Answer: illegal / impolite. Why: il- before l, im- before p.
  5. -ing or -ed: "The trip was ___ (exhaust), and the ___ (sleep) children ___ (immediate) fell asleep." Answer: exhausting / sleepy (or sleeping — but sleepy fits tired children) / immediately.
  6. Rewrite with a noun: "He decided to resign because the job was badly paid." Answer: "His decision to resign was caused by the low pay." Why: decide → decision nominalises the clause for formal style.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Right family, wrong form: writing "explaination" or "decission" — the morphology is right but the spelling loses the mark. Learn each family's spelling as vocabulary.
  • Impossible negatives: unpossible, unlegal, unregular. Learn the prefix with the word: impossible, illegal, irregular.
  • -ing / -ed adjectives swapped: "I am boring in this lesson" says the speaker bores others. The person feels -ed; the thing causes -ing.
  • Double suffixes: "carefulness" when carefulness is fine but "beautifulness" is not (beauty → beauty is a noun already; no -ness). When the gap already has the family noun, add nothing.
  • Adverb after linking verbs: "The results were surprising good" → surprisingly good (adverb modifies the adjective), but "The results were surprisingly good" versus "The results were good" — know that after be/seem/become an adjective follows: "The food smells good", not "well".
  • Spelling changes ignored: write the finished word once in the check step; the three changes (e-drop, y→i, doubling) account for most spelling losses.
  • Capital letters and plurals: if the built word starts a sentence it keeps its capital; if the gap sits after a number or many, the noun needs the plural form — a whole-mark detail in note-completion tasks.
  • Over-engineering: sometimes the base word is correct as given (complete in question 2). If the built form sounds wrong read aloud, try the unchanged word.

title: Waves & Sound — Study Notes
content:
Waves & Sound

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): general wave properties; reflection/refraction/diffraction; sound.

1. Wave basics

v = fλ. Transverse (oscillation ⊥ travel — light, water, S-waves) vs longitudinal (parallel — sound, P-waves). Amplitude, wavelength, frequency f = 1/T; wavefront diagrams.

2. Ripple tank behaviours

  • Reflection: angle in = angle out; speed/frequency unchanged, direction changes.
  • Refraction: speed change at boundary bends wavefronts (shallow water slows ripples).
  • Diffraction: spreading through gaps ≈ λ wide; around edges.

3. Electromagnetic spectrum (order)

Radio → micro → IR → visible (red 700 nm – violet 400 nm) → UV → X → gamma. All travel at 3 × 10⁸ m/s in vacuum; transverse; uses and dangers (IR heating; UV skin; X/gamma ionising).

4. Sound

  • Longitudinal; needs a medium (bell in vacuum demo). Speed ~340 m/s air, faster in liquids/solids.
  • Range 20 Hz–20 kHz; ultrasound > 20 kHz (sonar, prenatal scans, cleaning).
  • Pitch ↔ frequency; loudness ↔ amplitude.

5. Echo problems

Distance = (v × t)/2 (there and back).

Example: echo after 0.6 s, v = 340 → cliff 102 m away.

Exam tips: in diagrams always label wavelength as crest-to-crest; for refraction, state "changes speed" first, then direction; quote EM uses with the hazard.

title: Statistics — Probability — Study Notes
content:
Statistics — Probability

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): probability scale, combined events, tree diagrams, conditional probability, relative frequency.

1. Basics

P(event) = favourable/total; 0 ≤ P ≤ 1; P(not A) = 1 − P(A). Probabilities of a complete set sum to 1 — use to find a missing probability.

2. Combined events

  • Independent: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).
  • Mutually exclusive: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B).
  • With replacement ⇒ independent; without replacement ⇒ denominators shrink.

Example: bag 4 red, 6 blue; two draws without replacement: P(both red) = 4/10 × 3/9 = 2/15.

3. Tree diagrams

Multiply along branches; add between outcome paths. Label end products like 4/10 × 6/9 = 4/15.

4. Conditional probability

P(A|B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B). From tree diagrams it is the "given the first branch happened" re-weighting.

5. Relative frequency (experimental)

Relative frequency = successes ÷ trials. More trials → closer to theoretical probability; compare with expected counts (n × P).

Exam tips: always reduce fractions for final answers; in tree diagrams write the multiplication line before the product — that is where the marks are.

title: IGCSE Physics: Electricity and Circuits
content:
IGCSE Physics: Electricity and Circuits

Cambridge IGCSE Physics 0625 (2026–2028), Topic 4 Electricity and magnetism: statements 4.2 Electrical quantities, 4.3 Electric circuits and 4.4 Electrical safety. Electric circuits are the most calculation-dense part of the Paper 4 paper, and every result in them flows from one picture: a battery pushes charge round a circuit, the charge pays a price (p.d.) to get through each component, and the rate of flow is the current. This note builds charge, current, e.m.f., p.d., resistance, energy and power from scratch, then builds real circuits from them and finishes with the mains safety that saves lives.

Electric charge and the electron model

There are two kinds of charge, positive and negative, and the rule is simple: like charges repel, unlike charges attract. Rubbing a polythene rod with a cloth transfers electrons from the cloth to the rod, so the rod becomes negatively charged and the cloth positive; nothing is created — charge is transferred. A conductor (metal, graphite, the human body, tap water) lets charge move through it because it contains free electrons; an insulator (plastic, rubber, dry air, glass) does not. Charging by friction works only when the object is isolated on an insulating support, or the charge leaks away instantly.

Supplement adds the two deeper ideas. Charge is measured in coulombs (C); one coulomb is the charge that flows when a current of 1 ampere passes for 1 second, and the charge on one electron is 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. A charged object also creates an electric field in the space around it — a region where other charges experience a force — and the field of a point charge is drawn as radial lines pointing away from a positive charge and towards a negative one.

Electric current

Electric current is the rate of flow of charge. In metals the charge carriers are free electrons drifting slowly around the circuit while the electric field travels almost at the speed of light, which is why a lamp lights the instant a switch is closed.

current = charge / time        I = Q / t
  • I: current in amperes (A); Q: charge in coulombs (C); t: time in seconds (s). Current is treated as a scalar in circuit calculations.
  • Conventional current flows from the positive terminal, round the circuit, to the negative terminal; electrons drift the opposite way. Both descriptions are accepted, but conventional current is the one used in circuit diagrams.

An ammeter measures current and is connected in series, so the whole current passes through it. Direct current (d.c.) flows in one direction only, as from a battery; alternating current (a.c.) reverses direction repeatedly, as from the mains, which in the UK completes 50 cycles per second at 230 V.

Electromotive force and potential difference

The electromotive force (e.m.f.) of a source is the energy transferred from other forms to electrical energy per unit charge driven round the whole circuit; the potential difference (p.d.) across a component is the energy transferred from electrical to other forms per unit charge passing through that component. Both are measured in volts, and a voltmeter is connected in parallel with the component being measured.

potential difference = energy transferred / charge        V = W / Q
electromotive force = energy transferred from other forms / charge driven
  • V: potential difference in volts (V); W: energy in joules (J); Q: charge in coulombs (C). One volt is one joule per coulomb (1 V = 1 J C⁻¹).

The distinction that earns marks: e.m.f. is about energy supplied to the circuit (a battery's rating, 1.5 V for a dry cell), while p.d. is about energy delivered to a component. In a series circuit the p.d.s across the components add up to the supply e.m.f., because each coulomb spends its energy bit by bit around the loop.

Resistance

Resistance is how much a component opposes current. It is measured in Ω (Ω): a 12 Ω resistor passes less current than a 4 Ω resistor at the same p.d.

resistance = potential difference / current        R = V / I
  • R: resistance in Ω (Ω); V: p.d. across the component in volts (V); I: current through it in amperes (A). Resistance is a scalar.

Resistance is measured by setting up a circuit with the unknown resistor, an ammeter in series and a voltmeter across it, then changing the supply with a variable resistor and taking several pairs of readings. The resistance is found from the gradient of a graph of V against I, which averages the whole data set.

The wire's dimensions matter. A longer wire has greater resistance (resistance is proportional to length); a thicker wire has less (resistance is inversely proportional to cross-sectional area); and the material matters because of how many free electrons it provides. Nichrome wire is used for heating elements because it has a high resistance and resists oxidation when hot.

Supplement: current–voltage graphs. A metallic conductor at constant temperature gives a straight line through the origin — ohmic. A filament lamp curves over: as it heats, its resistance rises, so the graph flattens. A diode conducts in one direction only, giving almost zero current in reverse; a light-dependent resistor falls in resistance as light intensity rises; a thermistor falls in resistance as temperature rises. All three are basis-of-operation questions for sensors.

Electrical energy and power
