Every component turns electrical energy into something else — heat in a resistor, light and heat in a lamp, kinetic energy in a motor. The rate of that transfer is electrical power:

electrical power = potential difference x current        P = V I
electrical energy = power x time = V I t        E = V I t
  • P: power in watts (W); V: volts (V); I: amperes (A); E: energy in joules (J); t: time in seconds (s).
  • Combined with R = V/I this gives P = I²R and P = V²/R, useful when the resistance is known instead of the p.d.

The kilowatt-hour is the domestic unit of energy: one kWh is the energy used by a 1000 W device running for one hour (3.6 × 10⁶ J). Electricity bills charge cost = number of kWh × price per kWh, and a Paper 4 question usually asks for the cost of running a named appliance for a stated time.

Circuit components and circuit rules

Circuit diagrams use standard symbols: cell, battery, lamp, resistor, variable resistor, thermistor, LDR, diode, LED, ammeter, voltmeter, switch, motor. The two rules for series and parallel circuits are the spine of every calculation:

SeriesParallel
CurrentThe same through every componentShared between the branches; the branch currents add up to the total
Potential differenceShared between the components; the p.d.s add up to the supplyThe same across every branch
ResistanceR(total) = R1 + R2 + ...1/R(total) = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + ... (Supplement); two equal resistors in parallel give half the resistance of one

Adding lamps in series makes all of them dimmer, because the total resistance rises and the current falls; adding lamps in parallel leaves each at full brightness (each has the full p.d. across it) but draws more current from the supply. A variable resistor in series with a lamp dims it by reducing the current; a potential divider (Supplement) is two resistors in series with the output tapped between them:

output voltage = supply voltage x R2 / (R1 + R2)

A potential divider feeding a sensor gives an output voltage that changes with light or temperature, which is the basis of automatic night lights and thermostats.

Electrical safety

The domestic mains in the UK is 230 V a.c., enough to kill. The three wires in a three-core cable are colour-coded: live (brown) carries the alternating p.d. at about 230 V; neutral (blue) completes the circuit and is held near 0 V; earth (green and yellow) is a safety wire connected to the metal case of the appliance and to the ground.

  • Fuse: a thin wire in the live path that melts and breaks the circuit if the current exceeds its rating, protecting against overheating and fire. Choose a rating just above the normal working current.
  • Circuit breaker: a magnetic or electronic switch that trips and can be reset; faster and reusable, doing the same job as a fuse.
  • Earthing: if a fault connects the live wire to a metal case, the earth wire carries a large current that blows the fuse instead of giving the user a shock.
  • Double insulation: appliances with plastic cases need no earth wire, because no fault can make the case live.

Everyday hazards to name in an exam: frayed cables, damaged plugs, wet hands, water near electrical equipment, overloaded adapters, and touching a live conductor. The physics of the danger is current through the body: even a few tens of milliamperes through the heart can be fatal, and wet skin lowers body resistance and raises that current.

Worked example: a mixed circuit

Two resistors, 6.0 Ω and 3.0 Ω, are connected in parallel across a 12 V supply.

1 / R(total) = 1/6.0 + 1/3.0 = 0.167 + 0.333 = 0.500, so R(total) = 2.0 Ω
total current = V / R = 12 / 2.0 = 6.0 A
current in the 6.0 Ω resistor = 12 / 6.0 = 2.0 A
current in the 3.0 Ω resistor = 12 / 3.0 = 4.0 A   (branch currents add to 6.0 A)
power in the circuit = V I = 12 × 6.0 = 72 W
energy in 5 minutes = P t = 72 × 300 = 21 600 J

Each resistor has the full 12 V across it, as the parallel rule demands. If the two were instead in series, the total resistance would be 9.0 Ω, the current 1.33 A, and each p.d. would add to 12 V — a useful check before trusting any circuit answer.

Common mistakes

  • Putting an ammeter in parallel or a voltmeter in series; ammeters join in series, voltmeters across the component.
  • Using the supply voltage as the p.d. across one component in a series circuit; the supply is shared.
  • Adding resistances in parallel by simple addition; the reciprocals add, so the total is always less than the smallest branch.
  • Confusing current direction with electron drift, or saying charge is used up; the current is the same everywhere in a series circuit, and energy is transferred, not the charge.
  • Using watts and minutes in E = VIt; power in watts needs energy in joules and time in seconds (convert kWh and hours carefully in cost questions).
  • Forgetting that a filament lamp's resistance rises as it heats, so its I–V graph is a curve, not a straight line.
  • Choosing a fuse rating far above the working current for safety; too high a rating defeats the protection.
  • Mixing e.m.f. and p.d.: the battery has an e.m.f.; each component has a p.d. across it.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 4, 3 marks). A lamp is marked 24 W, 12 V. Calculate the current it takes and its resistance.

Answer: P = VI gives I = 24/12 = 2.0 A. R = V/I = 12/2.0 = 6.0 Ω.

Question 2 (Paper 4, 3 marks). A charge of 360 C passes through a lamp in 3.0 minutes. Calculate the current.

Answer: I = Q/t = 360/180 = 2.0 A. (Convert minutes to seconds first.)

Question 3 (Paper 2 style). In a series circuit of two resistors, which statement is true? A the current is largest through the smaller resistor; B the p.d. across each is the same as the supply; C the current is the same in both; D the total resistance is less than either. Answer: C. Current is the same everywhere in series; the p.d. is shared and the total resistance is the sum.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 4 marks). A 3.0 kW kettle runs for 4.0 minutes from 230 V. Find the charge that flows and the energy transferred.

Answer: I = P/V = 3000/230 = 13 A. Q = It = 13 × 240 = 3120 C. Energy = Pt = 3000 × 240 = 720 000 J (0.20 kWh).

Question 5 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Explain why a metal-cased washing machine has an earth wire but a plastic hairdryer does not.

Answer: The metal case is a conductor; if a fault brings the live wire into contact with it, the case would become live at 230 V and anyone touching it would receive a shock. The earth wire connects the case to the ground, so a large fault current flows to earth and melts the fuse, isolating the supply. The hairdryer has a plastic (double-insulated) case which cannot conduct, so no fault can make the outside live and no earth wire is needed.

Question 6 (Paper 6 style). Describe how you would determine the resistance of a coil of wire.

Answer: Connect the coil in series with an ammeter, a cell and a variable resistor, with a voltmeter across the coil. Vary the current and record several pairs of current and p.d. readings. Plot p.d. against current; the gradient is the resistance of the coil. Taking several readings and using the graph removes the effect of random errors and of the coil warming up (which would otherwise change its resistance).

Where charge flows, fields follow: next is Magnetism and Electromagnetism.

I–V characteristics: what the shape of the graph proves

A current–voltage graph is the fastest way to see what a component does, because its shape is the answer. A straight line through the origin says the resistance is constant; a curve says the resistance changes, and the direction of the bend says whether it rises or falls. This is one of the few places on the paper where you are asked to describe a shape and then explain it with particles.

Ohm's law is a statement about constancy. For a metallic conductor kept at constant temperature, the current is directly proportional to the potential difference:

R = V / I Key: R = resistance (Ω); V = potential difference across the component (V); I = current through it (A). A component obeys Ohm's law when R is the same at every point — that is, when the graph is a straight line through the origin, as the resistor's is.

Why the lamp bends. As the current through a filament lamp increases, the filament gets hotter. In a metal, current is carried by electrons drifting through a lattice of vibrating ions; the hotter the metal, the more violently the ions vibrate and the more often they collide with the electrons. More collisions mean a harder push needed for the same current, so the resistance rises. On the graph, that shows up as the current increasing more and more slowly for each extra volt — the gradient falls. The lamp does not disobey Ohm's law; it simply does not meet the law's condition, because its temperature is not constant.

The trap that costs a mark every year. On a curved characteristic, the resistance at a point is V ÷ I at that point — the ratio of the coordinates, not the gradient of the curve. The gradient has units of A V⁻¹, which is conductance, and using it here produces a number that is not a resistance at all. Read the coordinates off the curve and divide them.

Worked example. Use the lamp's curve to find its resistance at 1.0 V and at 4.0 V, and explain the change.

At 1.0 V the curve gives I = 0.22 A, so R = V ÷ I = 1.0 ÷ 0.22 = 4.5 Ω.
At 4.0 V the curve gives I = 0.51 A, so R = V ÷ I = 4.0 ÷ 0.51 = 7.8 Ω.

The resistance has almost doubled because the filament is far hotter at 4.0 V than at 1.0 V, so its ions vibrate more strongly and obstruct the electron drift more. The temperature rise, not the voltage itself, is the cause — say so explicitly, because "the resistance goes up because V goes up" is the answer that gets no credit.

The two other shapes worth knowing. A diode conducts almost nothing in one direction and then, above about 0.6 V in the forward direction, its current rises steeply: its resistance falls as the voltage rises, the opposite of the lamp. A thermistor's resistance falls as its temperature rises, which is what makes it useful in a thermostat — the shape on its own graph is not the point, the direction of change is.

Where marks are lost. Reading the gradient instead of V ÷ I. Describing the lamp's curve as "Ohm's law fails" without saying why. And forgetting the units: potential difference in volts, current in amperes, resistance in ohms — a characteristic read in milliamps gives a resistance a thousand times too small.

Equations and symbols

Statements 4.2 to 4.4 rest on five equations and three circuit rules. Charge, current, voltage and resistance are defined by the first three; the power relations all follow from them, so a question that gives two quantities can almost always be finished without memorising a fourth formula.

Charge, current and voltage

Q = It
Key: Q = charge flowing (C); I = current (A); t = time (s). One coulomb is one ampere for one second.

I = Q / t
Key: I = current (A); Q = charge passing a point (C); t = time (s). Current is a rate of charge flow, not a quantity of charge.

V = W / Q
Key: V = potential difference (V); W = work done or energy transferred (J); Q = charge moved (C). One volt is one joule per coulomb, which is the definition the mark scheme wants.

E = QV
Key: E = energy transferred by the charge (J); Q = charge (C); V = potential difference (V).

Q = Ne
Key: Q = total charge (C); N = number of electrons (no unit); e = elementary charge, 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. Used when a question asks how many electrons carry a given charge.

Resistance and Ohm's law

V = IR
Key: V = potential difference across the component (V); I = current through it (A); R = resistance (Ω). Ohm's law holds only when temperature is constant, which is why a filament lamp's I–V graph curves.

R = V / I
Key: R = resistance (Ω); V = potential difference (V); I = current (A). For a curved I–V graph, R is still V/I at the chosen point, not the gradient.

1 Ω = 1 V / 1 A
Key: the definition of the Ω; a component has 1 Ω when 1 V drives 1 A through it.

Power and energy in a circuit

P = VI
Key: P = power (W); V = potential difference (V); I = current (A).

P = I²R
Key: P = power dissipated as heat (W); I = current (A); R = resistance (Ω). This is the form that explains why transmission cables carry a low current at high voltage.

P = V² / R
Key: P = power (W); V = potential difference (V); R = resistance (Ω). Use it when the current is not given.

E = Pt = VIt
Key: E = energy transferred (J); P = power (W); t = time (s); V = potential difference (V); I = current (A).

cost = P(kW) × t(h) × price per kWh
Key: P in kilowatts (W ÷ 1000); t in hours; the price is per kilowatt-hour. A 2000 W heater for 3 hours uses 6 kWh.

fuse rating: I = P / V
Key: I = normal operating current (A); P = appliance power (W); V = supply voltage (V). Choose the next standard fuse above this value, never below it.

The three circuit rules

series: R(total) = R₁ + R₂ + …
Key: resistances in Ω (Ω); the current is the same everywhere in the series path and the supply voltage divides between the components.

parallel: 1 / R(total) = 1 / R₁ + 1 / R₂ + …
Key: resistances in Ω (Ω); the potential difference is the same across each branch and the current divides. Two 6 Ω resistors in parallel give 3 Ω, which is less than either — a parallel combination always has a lower resistance.

V(total) = V₁ + V₂ (series) and I(total) = I₁ + I₂ (parallel)
Key: the voltage rule for series and the current rule for parallel, both in the units of the quantity. The companion rules — voltage equal in parallel, current equal in series — follow from charge and energy conservation.

title: Exam technique: Abstract Data Types
content:
### What earns the marks
For ADT choice, the access pattern stated earns the mark: LIFO for stacks, FIFO for queues, keyed jumps for BSTs. For traversals, the visit order written (root-left-right for preorder) earns each mark. For linked structures, pointer relinking described earns the insertion mark without any shifting claim.
### Traps
Error: queues for undo. Correction: undo is LIFO, so stack. Error: inorder claimed as root-first. Correction: preorder is root-first. Error: arrays claimed best for mid-list churn. Correction: shifting costs every insert.
### Worked example
Trace a stack. Push A, push B, push C, then pop, then push D, then pop. After the three pushes the top is C, so the first pop returns C. Pushing D leaves the stack as A, B, D, so the second pop returns D and B is left on top. A stack is last in, first out, so the top item always leaves first.
### Check yourself
State which structure a printer queue uses and why, in one sentence that names the order of service. A print queue serves the first job submitted first, so it is first in, first out.

title: AS Level Mathematics: Proof
content:
AS Level Mathematics: Proof

Proof is the difference between "it works for these numbers" and "it must work for all". AS proof covers four methods — direct proof, proof by exhaustion, proof by counter-example (disproof) and proof by deduction from definitions — plus the algebra of odd, even and consecutive numbers, and completing the square as a tool for inequalities. This note builds each method from zero with templates, full worked examples and the precise wording examiners expect, because proof marks are awarded for structure as much as for algebra.

The language of proof

TermMeaning
ConjectureA statement believed true but not yet proved
TheoremA statement that has been proved
ProofA logical argument from known facts to the conclusion
DisproofOne counter-example that makes the statement false
ExhaustionChecking every possible case

A single counter-example disproves a "for all" statement; no number of examples proves one. That asymmetry is the heart of the topic and the first thing examiners test.

Odd, even and consecutive numbers

even: 2n           (n integer)
odd:  2n + 1       (or 2n - 1)
consecutive integers: n, n + 1, n + 2
consecutive even: 2n, 2n + 2
consecutive odd: 2n + 1, 2n + 3

These forms are not optional decoration: a proof about parity must start from them, because "let the number be x" proves nothing about oddness.

Worked example 1. Prove that the sum of two consecutive odd numbers is a multiple of 4.

let the numbers be 2n + 1 and 2n + 3
sum = 4n + 4 = 4(n + 1)
which is a multiple of 4 for every integer n

Worked example 2. Prove that the product of two odd numbers is odd.

let them be 2m + 1 and 2n + 1
product = 4mn + 2m + 2n + 1 = 2(2mn + m + n) + 1
of the form 2k + 1 with k = 2mn + m + n, an integer
so the product is odd

Worked example 3. Prove that the difference between the squares of consecutive integers is the sum of the integers.

(n + 1)² - n² = n² + 2n + 1 - n² = 2n + 1 = n + (n + 1)

Direct proof

Start from the definitions, manipulate algebraically, and arrive at the required form. Write the conclusion explicitly ("hence ... as required") so the argument is closed.

Worked example. Prove that if x is odd then x² is odd.

let x = 2n + 1
x² = 4n² + 4n + 1 = 2(2n² + 2n) + 1
which is 2k + 1, hence odd

Worked example 2. Prove that the sum of any three consecutive integers is divisible by 3.

n + (n + 1) + (n + 2) = 3n + 3 = 3(n + 1)
which is divisible by 3

Proof by exhaustion

When the domain is small enough to list, check every case. The proof is only complete if the list is genuinely exhaustive — state why nothing is missed.

Worked example. Prove that every prime between 20 and 30 is the sum of two square numbers or state otherwise.

primes in the range: 23, 29
23 = 9 + 14 (not two squares); 25 + (-2)? no
23 = 4 + 19? no; squares below 23: 1, 4, 9, 16
1 + 16 = 17; 4 + 16 = 20; 9 + 16 = 25; 4 + 9 = 13
so 23 is not a sum of two squares; 29: 4 + 25 = 29  yes
conclusion: the conjecture fails for 23; the true statement is
"29 is the only prime between 20 and 30 expressible as a sum of two squares"

Worked example 2. Prove that n² + n is even for all integers n by exhaustion of the two parity cases.

case 1: n even, n = 2k → n² + n = 4k² + 2k = 2(2k² + k), even
case 2: n odd, n = 2k + 1 → 4k² + 4k + 1 + 2k + 1 = 4k² + 6k + 2
        = 2(2k² + 3k + 1), even
both cases covered, so the statement holds for all integers

The two-case parity split is exhaustion in its most common exam form: every integer is even or odd, so the cases exhaust the domain.

Disproof by counter-example

To disprove a "for all" claim, produce one case where it fails and show the arithmetic. One is enough; a hundred confirming cases prove nothing.

Worked example. Disprove: "if n² is a multiple of 4 then n is a multiple of 4."

try n = 6: n² = 36, a multiple of 4? 36/4 = 9, yes
but 6 is not a multiple of 4
so n = 6 is a counter-example and the statement is false

Worked example 2. Disprove: "n² − n + 11 is prime for all positive integers n."

n = 11: 121 - 11 + 11 = 121 = 11², not prime
counter-example n = 11 disproves the conjecture

Proof by completing the square

Inequalities about quadratics are proved by completing the square: a squared term is never negative, so the expression's minimum (or maximum) is visible.

x² + bx + c = (x + b/2)² + c - b²/4
since (x + b/2)² >= 0, the minimum value is c - b²/4

Worked example 1. Prove that x² + 4x + 7 > 0 for all real x.

x² + 4x + 7 = (x + 2)² + 3
(x + 2)² >= 0, so the expression is at least 3 > 0

Worked example 2. Prove that 2x − x² ≤ 1 for all real x.

2x - x² = -(x² - 2x) = -[(x - 1)² - 1] = 1 - (x - 1)²
since (x - 1)² >= 0, this is at most 1

Worked example 3. Find the values of k for which x² + kx + 9 > 0 for all x.

completing the square: (x + k/2)² + 9 - k²/4 > 0 for all x
requires the constant term positive: 9 - k²/4 > 0
k² < 36  →  -6 < k < 6

That last question is the discriminant argument in disguise: "always positive" means no real roots, so b² − 4ac < 0. Either method earns the marks; the completing-the-square route often reads more clearly.

Divisibility and multiples

A statement of the form "is a multiple of k" is proved by putting the expression in the shape k times an integer. Do the algebra first, then identify the factor; never assume the factor exists.

Worked example. Prove that for any integer n, n(n + 1)(n + 2) is a multiple of 6.

among any three consecutive integers there is at least one even
number and exactly one multiple of 3
so the product contains a factor 2 and a factor 3
since 2 and 3 are coprime, the product is divisible by 6

Worked example 2. Prove that 3^(2n) - 1 is a multiple of 8 for positive integers n.

3^(2n) - 1 = 9^n - 1 = (9 - 1)(9^(n-1) + ... + 1)
= 8 x (a positive integer), so divisible by 8

Worked example 3. Prove that the sum of five consecutive integers is always divisible by 5.

n + (n+1) + (n+2) + (n+3) + (n+4) = 5n + 10 = 5(n + 2)

Proof by contradiction: the irrationality of root 2

Contradiction assumes the statement is false, derives an impossibility, and concludes the statement is true. The classic example is examinable and worth knowing in full.

assume √(2) is rational: √(2) = p/q in lowest terms, p, q integers
square: 2 = p²/q²  →  p² = 2q²
so p² is even  →  p is even (a square is even only if its root is)
write p = 2k: 4k² = 2q²  →  q² = 2k²
so q² is even  →  q is even
but p and q cannot both be even if p/q is in lowest terms
contradiction  →  √(2) is irrational

The two logical hinges are that an even square implies an even root, and that "lowest terms" forbids a common factor of 2. State both; the marks live in them.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Parity) Prove that the sum of an odd and an even number is odd. Answer: write the odd number as 2m + 1 and the even one as 2n, m, n integers; then (2m + 1) + 2n = 2(m + n) + 1 = 2k + 1 with k = m + n, which is the definition of odd.
  2. (Consecutive) Prove that the product of two consecutive integers is even. Answer: of two consecutive integers one is even, so n = 2k or n + 1 = 2k; then n(n + 1) = 2k(n + 1) or 2kn, either way 2 × integer, so the product is even.
  3. (Direct) Prove that (3n + 1)² − 1 is a multiple of 3. Answer: (3n + 1)² − 1 = 9n² + 6n + 1 − 1 = 9n² + 6n = 3(3n² + 2n), a multiple of 3 for every integer n.
  4. (Counter-example) Disprove "all primes are odd". Answer: 2 is prime and even.
  5. (Counter-example) Disprove "n² + 1 is prime for all n". Answer: n = 3 gives 10, not prime.
  6. (Completing the square) Prove x² − 6x + 10 > 0. Answer: x² − 6x + 10 = (x − 3)² − 9 + 10 = (x − 3)² + 1; a square is never negative, so the expression is at least 1 and therefore > 0 for every real x.
  7. (Exhaustion) Prove that n³ − n is divisible by 6 for n = 1, 2, 3, 4. Answer: 0, 6, 24, 60 — each divisible by 6 (a finite check is exhaustion).
  8. (Discriminant) Find k so that x² + 2kx + 4 = 0 has no real roots. Answer: no real roots needs b² − 4ac < 0: (2k)² − 4 × 1 × 4 = 4k² − 16 < 0, so k² < 4 and −2 < k < 2.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Proving by example: two or three numbers never prove a "for all" statement; the argument must use algebra with a general n.
  • Not defining the variable: "let n be an integer" and "let n be odd, so n = 2k + 1" are required openings; an undefined x cannot carry a parity argument.
  • Assuming what you must prove: working backwards from the result to a true statement does not prove the original unless every step is reversible — say so if it is.
  • Counter-example not checked: show the arithmetic that makes the case fail; asserting "n = 6 fails" without the calculation loses the mark.
  • Incomplete exhaustion: if the domain has cases you did not cover (e.g. negatives, zero), the proof is incomplete — state the cases and why they exhaust.
  • Completing the square sign: a negative leading coefficient flips the inequality; factor out the minus first.
  • Conclusion missing: close with "hence ... as required"; an unclosed argument reads as unfinished.
  • Notation: write ≡ for identities and ⇒ for implications correctly; mixing them muddles the logic examiners follow.

The three shapes of a proof — and how to choose between them

A proof is not a longer calculation; it is an argument with a shape. There are only three shapes in this specification, each fits a different kind of statement, and recognising which one a question wants is most of the mark.

Shape 1: direct proof. Start from the definition, do algebra, arrive at the thing you were asked to show. It is the right choice whenever the statement is about all numbers of a kind, because a variable stands for all of them at once. "The sum of two consecutive integers is odd" is three lines: let them be n and n + 1, then n + (n + 1) = 2n + 1, which is odd by definition.

Shape 2: exhaustion. When there are finitely many cases, check them all and say so. It is a real proof — but only because the list is complete.

Shape 3: contradiction. When the statement denies something ("there is no greatest prime", "√2 is irrational"), assume the opposite and show it cannot stand. The template above is the whole method; the work is entirely in step 2.

The sentence that makes step 2 work. Whatever you deduce must contradict something already established — a definition, a theorem you have proved, or the assumption you made in step 1. In the √2 proof the contradiction is that a fraction is shown to be reducible when it was written in lowest terms, and the words that carry it are "but this contradicts the assumption that a and b have no common factor".

Why a counter-example is not a proof. One example can disprove a universal statement and can never prove one: "n² + n + 41 is prime for n = 1, 2, 3" is true and worthless, because n = 41 breaks it. If a question says "prove", an example earns nothing; if it says "disprove", one counter-example is a complete answer.

Worked example. Prove that if n² is even then n is even.

Suppose instead that n is odd. Then n = 2k + 1 for some integer k, so
n² = (2k + 1)² = 4k² + 4k + 1 = 2(2k² + 2k) + 1
which is odd, because it is one more than a multiple of 2. But we were told n² is even, and a number cannot be both odd and even — a contradiction. Therefore n cannot be odd, so n is even. ∎

Two details earn marks that students routinely drop: stating the form of the variable ("n = 2k + 1 for some integer k", not "n is odd so write it as something odd"), and naming the contradiction rather than stopping at the algebra. The ∎ is optional; the sentence that says what was contradicted is not.

Where marks are lost. Assuming what you are proving (writing "n² = 2m and n = 2k" straight away). Using the converse by accident — proving "n even ⇒ n² even" when the question asked the other way round. And ending with "therefore it is true" without saying what is true and why the assumption failed.

Equations and symbols

The algebraic moves that carry a P1 proof. Each line is a rewrite of one expression, so the marks are for the factorisation at the end, not the expansion.

sum = 4n + 4 = 4(n + 1) Key: sum = the combined expression from two consecutive even numbers; 4n + 4 is the unsimplified result; 4(n + 1) is the form that proves divisibility by 4. Always finish in the "k × integer" shape the question names.

product = 4mn + 2m + 2n + 1 = 2(2mn + m + n) + 1 Key: m, n = integers, so 2m + 1 and 2n + 1 are the two odd numbers; the final form is 2k + 1 with k = 2mn + m + n, which is the definition of odd. The factorisation, not the arithmetic, is the proof.

(n + 1)² - n² = n² + 2n + 1 - n² = 2n + 1 = n + (n + 1) Key: the difference of consecutive squares; the result is the sum of the same two numbers, which is the identity being proved. Two independent routes to 2n + 1 is stronger than one.

n + (n + 1) + (n + 2) = 3n + 3 = 3(n + 1) Key: three consecutive integers; the middle term is n + 1, so the sum is three times the middle. The last form proves divisibility by 3 for every n without testing any value.

let x = 2n + 1 Key: the standard opening for an odd number; n is an integer, so 2n is even and 2n + 1 is odd. State "for some integer n" — the clause is part of the proof, not decoration.

title: AS Level Physics: Forces and Equilibrium
content:
AS Level Physics: Forces and Equilibrium

Equilibrium is the physics of things that stay put — or move steadily — because everything acting on them cancels. The two conditions it obeys (no resultant force, no resultant moment) turn architecture, cranes and ladders into solvable puzzles. This note builds the toolkit from zero: what a moment is and why doors have handles at their edges, couples and torque, the centre of gravity, and the two equilibrium conditions applied to beams and multi-force systems, with every worked example solved in full.

Moment: the turning effect of a force

A force that does not act through a pivot makes a body turn. The measure of that turning effect is the moment:

moment of a force = force x perpendicular distance from the pivot
M = F d          (unit: newton metre, N m)

The analogy: a door. Push at the handle (far from the hinges) and it swings easily; push near the hinges and the same force barely turns it. The perpendicular is the load-bearing word: the distance must be measured along the line perpendicular to the force's line of action. If a force acts at an angle, resolve it first and use the perpendicular component.

Worked example. A door handle is 0.80 m from the hinges. A student pushes with 30 N at 40° to the door's surface. Find the moment about the hinges.

component perpendicular to the door: F_perp = 30 sin(40) = 19.3 N
(the angle is measured from the door itself, so the perpendicular
 component carries the sine)
M = F_perp d = 19.3 x 0.80 = 15.4 N m  (2 s.f.: 15 N m)

Direction matters in sign conventions: anticlockwise moments are usually taken as positive, clockwise as negative (or vice versa — consistency is what the marker checks).

Couples and torque

A couple is a pair of equal and opposite forces whose lines of action do not coincide: it produces pure rotation with no resultant force. The moment of a couple (its torque) is one force times the perpendicular distance between the two forces:

torque of a couple = F x d_between        (or 2 x F x (d/2))
unit: N m

Everyday couples: turning a steering wheel (both hands push oppositely), winding a clock key, the compass needle between two poles. The commonest exam error is halving or doubling the separation — measure between the two forces, full stop.

Centre of gravity

The centre of gravity is the point where the entire weight of a body may be taken to act. For uniform regular shapes it sits at the geometric centre; for irregular shapes it can be found experimentally (plumb-line method: hang the shape freely from two different points; the verticals from the suspension points meet at the centre of gravity). Stability questions follow from its position: an object topples when its line of action of weight falls outside its base — wide bases and low centres of gravity give stability (racing cars, furniture anti-tip brackets).

Worked example. Explain why a double-decker bus is more likely to topple on a sharp bend when fully loaded on the upper deck. Answer: Loading the upper deck raises the combined centre of gravity; on the bend, the turning effect of the weight about the outer wheels increases with the perpendicular distance to the pivot; if the weight's line of action passes beyond the outer wheels, the net moment topples the bus.

Equilibrium of forces: the two conditions

A body is in equilibrium when both conditions hold:

  1. Translational equilibrium: the vector sum of forces is zero — ΣF = 0 in every direction.
  2. Rotational equilibrium: the sum of moments about any pivot is zero — ΣM = 0 (total anticlockwise = total clockwise).

The practical routine for any beam problem: (1) draw the diagram and mark every force; (2) take moments about a chosen pivot — choosing one where an unknown force acts eliminates it; (3) write ΣM = 0 and solve; (4) use ΣF = 0 to find the remaining unknowns.

Worked examples: beam problems in full

Worked example 1. A uniform beam of weight 40 N and length 2.0 m rests on two supports, one at each end. A 20 N load sits 0.50 m from the left support. Find the reaction forces.

Let the reactions be R_L (left) and R_R (right).
Take moments about the left support (eliminates R_L):
anticlockwise = clockwise
R_R x 2.0 = (40 x 1.0) + (20 x 0.50)
R_R x 2.0 = 40 + 10 = 50
R_R = 25 N
Vertical equilibrium: R_L + R_R = 40 + 20 = 60 N
R_L = 60 - 25 = 35 N
Check: moments about the right support:
35 x 2.0 = 70 clockwise, and (40 x 1.0) + (20 x 1.5) = 70
anticlockwise. Balanced.

Worked example 2 (non-uniform). A 3.0 m plank of weight 60 N rests with one end on a pivot and the other on a scale. Its centre of gravity is 1.2 m from the pivot end. Find the scale reading.

Take moments about the pivot:
R_scale x 3.0 = 60 x 1.2 = 72
R_scale = 72/3.0 = 24 N
(and the pivot takes the remaining 60 - 24 = 36 N)

Worked example 3 (angled force). A horizontal beam is held by a rope at 30° to the beam at its far end; the beam's weight W acts at its centre. Find the rope tension T in terms of W.

Moments about the beam end at the wall:
anticlockwise (rope): T sin(30) x L
clockwise (weight):  W x L/2
T sin(30) x L = W L/2
T x 0.5 = W/2  ->  T = W

The habit that prevents errors: cancel the common factor (L) only after writing both moment lines fully.

Multi-force equilibrium: triangles and resolution

When three non-parallel forces hold a body in equilibrium, they can be arranged tip-to-tail into a closed triangle — a graphical method with marks attached. For more forces, resolve into perpendicular components (usually horizontal and vertical) and set each sum to zero:

sum of horizontal components = 0
sum of vertical components   = 0

Worked example. A 100 N weight hangs from two ropes, one at 30° and one at 60° to the horizontal. Find the tensions.

Let tensions be A (30 deg rope) and B (60 deg rope).
Horizontal: A cos(30) = B cos(60)
            0.866 A = 0.5 B  ->  B = 1.732 A
Vertical:   A sin(30) + B sin(60) = 100
            0.5 A + 0.866 x 1.732 A = 100
            0.5 A + 1.5 A = 100 -> 2.0 A = 100
A = 50 N,  B = 1.732 x 50 = 86.6 N

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Moment) A spanner grips a nut 0.25 m from its pivot end; a mechanic pushes at 60° to the spanner with 80 N. Find the moment. Answer: perpendicular component = 80 sin 60 = 69.3 N; M = 69.3 × 0.25 = 17.3 N m ≈ 17 N m.
  2. (Definition) Define centre of gravity. Answer: The point at which the whole weight of a body may be taken to act.
  3. (Couple) Two opposite 15 N forces act 0.40 m apart on a wheel rim. Find the torque. Answer: τ = Fd = 15 × 0.40 = 6.0 N m.
  4. (Beam) A uniform 4.0 m beam (weight 100 N) rests on supports 0.50 m from each end. A 50 N load sits at the midpoint. Find the reactions. Answer: By symmetry each reaction = (100 + 50)/2 = 75 N.
  5. (Stability) Explain why a racing car is built low and wide. Answer: A low centre of gravity and wide base increase stability: the weight's line of action must move further before it falls outside the base, so larger moments are needed to topple it.
  6. (Equilibrium conditions) State the two conditions for a rigid body to be in equilibrium. Answer: The resultant force on the body is zero (ΣF = 0), and the resultant moment about any point is zero (ΣM = 0).
  7. (Resolution) A single rope holds a 20 N weight stationary, the rope making 40° with the horizontal. Find the tension. Answer: Vertical equilibrium: T sin 40 = 20, so T = 20/0.643 = 31.1 N ≈ 31 N. (For a picture hung on a cord fixed at both ends, resolve both halves' tensions instead.)
  8. (Practical) Describe how to find the centre of gravity of an irregular lamina. Answer: Hang the lamina freely from a pin through a hole near its edge; hang a plumb line from the same pin and draw the vertical line; repeat from a second hole; the intersection of the two vertical lines is the centre of gravity.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Perpendicular distance: the moment is Fd with d perpendicular to F. Using the slant distance when a force acts at an angle is the commonest error — resolve the force or find the true perpendicular first.
  • Couple geometry: d in Fd for a couple is the full separation of the two forces, not the radius. Turning a steering wheel with hands 0.60 m apart: τ = F × 0.60.
  • Pivot choice: take moments about a point where an unknown force acts to eliminate it; taking them about the wrong point creates simultaneous equations unnecessarily.
  • Uniform assumption: a uniform beam's weight acts at its midpoint; a non-uniform one's does not — read which the question gives.
  • Reaction direction: assume upward reactions; a negative result simply means the force acts downward (a tether, not a support). Do not panic at minus signs.
  • Forces without directions: ΣF = 0 is a vector statement — write horizontal and vertical sums separately rather than one jumble.
  • Three-force triangle conditions: the forces must be coplanar and non-parallel for the triangle method; parallel forces need the moment approach.
  • Units and precision: moments in N m (not J — even though the units are dimensionally identical, the mark requires the moment unit), forces in N, 2 or 3 s.f.
  • Method marks: state "taking moments about the pivot" and write ΣM = 0 explicitly before substituting numbers.

title: Exam technique: Dynamics
content:
### What earns the marks
For resultant force, subtract opposition before applying F = ma to earn both marks. For collisions, total momentum before equated to total after earns the method mark. For rebounds, the sign change included earns the second mark.
### Traps
Error: friction ignored in acceleration. Correction: use the resultant, not the push alone. Error: rebound treated as stopping. Correction: add the speeds with the sign flip. Error: kinetic energy claimed conserved generally. Correction: momentum always, kinetic only when elastic.
### Worked example
A car of mass 800 kg has a driving force of 2400 N and a resistance of 400 N. The resultant force is 2400 - 400 = 2000 N, so a = F/m = 2000 / 800 = 2.5 m/s^2. Subtract the opposing force before you divide by the mass.
### Check yourself
A 2 kg trolley moving at 3 m/s hits a stationary 1 kg trolley, and they stick together. Total momentum before is 2 x 3 = 6 kg m/s, so the joint speed is 6 / 3 = 2 m/s. Show the momentum equation even when the speed looks obvious.

title: Integration — Study Notes
content:
Integration

Cambridge International AS & A Level Mathematics 9709, Paper 1. Integration reverses differentiation. Questions want a general antiderivative, a specific curve through a point, a definite integral, or an area. Most lost marks come from the constant of integration, the limits, and the sign of a region below the axis.

Start from a question

A curve passes through (1, 1) and has dy/dx = 3√x − 2/x² for x > 0.

  1. Find y in terms of x.
  2. Evaluate the integral of (3√x − 2/x²) from x = 1 to x = 4.
  3. Find the area between the curve y = x² − 4 and the x-axis, from x = 0 to x = 3.

Part 1. Integrate term by term: 3x^(1/2) gives 2x^(3/2), and −2x⁻² gives 2x⁻¹. So y = 2x^(3/2) + 2/x + c. Substituting (1, 1) gives 2 + 2 + c = 1, so c = −3 and y = 2x^(3/2) + 2/x − 3.

Part 2. The antiderivative at 4 is 16 + ½ = 33/2. At 1 it is 4 = 8/2. The definite integral is 33/2 − 8/2 = 25/2. No +c is needed.

Part 3. The curve y = x² − 4 crosses the x-axis at x = 2. Between 0 and 2 it lies below the axis, so that part of the integral is negative. The area is |∫ from 0 to 2| + ∫ from 2 to 3. The first integral is [x³/3 − 4x] from 0 to 2 = −16/3, so its area is 16/3. The second is [x³/3 − 4x] from 2 to 3 = −3 − (−16/3) = 7/3. The total is 23/3. Taking the integral from 0 to 3 directly gives −3, which is the wrong answer for an area.

Indefinite integrals

∫axⁿ dx = a xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + c, for n ≠ −1. Add one to the power, divide by the new power, and write +c. Multiply out brackets and rewrite roots as powers first. Example: ∫(x − 2)(x + 4) dx = ∫(x² + 2x − 8) dx = x³/3 + x² − 8x + c.

Area between two curves

Find where the curves meet, then integrate the upper curve minus the lower curve between those x-values. Example: y = 2x and y = x² meet at x = 0 and x = 2. Between them 2x ≥ x², so the area is ∫ from 0 to 2 of (2x − x²) dx = [x² − x³/3] from 0 to 2 = 4/3.

Trapezium rule

With strips of width h and ordinates y₀, y₁, …, yₙ, the estimate is (h/2)[y₀ + 2(y₁ + … + yₙ₋₁) + yₙ]. Example: ∫ from 0 to 2 of (x² + 1) dx with h = 1. The ordinates are 1, 2 and 5, so the estimate is ½(1 + 4 + 5) = 5. The exact value is 14/3. The curve bends upwards, so the estimate is too large.

Traps that cost marks

  • Integrating a product term by term without expanding the brackets first.
  • Writing +c in a definite integral, or forgetting it in an indefinite one.
  • Subtracting the limits in the wrong order.
  • Quoting a negative answer for an area that lies below the x-axis.

title: Astronomy and Cosmology — Study Notes
content:
Astronomy and Cosmology

Luminosity and Intensity

Luminosity L is total power radiated (W). Intensity at distance d: I = L/(4πd²) — the key to distances.

Standard candles (Cepheid variables, Type Ia supernovae) have known L, so measuring I gives d.

Example: the Sun: I = 1370 W m⁻² at d = 1.5 × 10¹¹ m gives L ≈ 3.9 × 10²⁶ W.

Stellar radii (25.2)

A star radiates as a black body of surface temperature T, so L = 4πR²σT⁴. Rearranged, R = √(L / 4πσT⁴). Luminosity therefore depends on both radius and temperature.

Example: with L = 3.9 × 10²⁶ W and T = 5800 K, R = √(3.9 × 10²⁶ / (4π × 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ × 5800⁴)) ≈ 7.0 × 10⁸ m.

Doubling the temperature at fixed radius multiplies L by 2⁴ = 16. A cool red giant can be far more luminous than the Sun because its radius is very large.

Wien and Stefan–Boltzmann

  • Wien: λ_max T = 2.9 × 10⁻³ m K — hotter stars are bluer
  • Stefan: L = σAT⁴, σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸

Hubble's Law

Galaxies recede with v = Hd, H₀ ≈ 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹. Redshift z = Δλ/λ ≈ v/c for small z.

Example: a galaxy at 100 Mpc recedes at v = 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ × 100 × 3.09 × 10²² ≈ 6800 km s⁻¹.

The Big Bang

Evidence: Hubble expansion, cosmic microwave background (2.7 K), hydrogen/helium abundance. Age estimate: t ≈ 1/H₀ ≈ 14 billion years. The fate question: critical density, Ω.

Exam tips: convert Mpc to metres (×3.09 × 10²²) before Hubble arithmetic; distinguish redshift of light from distance ladder methods.

title: Exam technique: Probability
content:
### What earns the marks
For combined events, each branch probability with the changed denominator earns a mark: write 3/5 then 2/4 for no-replacement draws. For expectation, probability times trials stated earns the mark even with arithmetic slips. For conditional probability, restricting the denominator to the given condition earns the method mark: write 12/20 before simplifying. For P(A or B), the overlap subtracted earns the final mark.
### Traps
Error: unchanged denominator after a no-replacement draw. Correction: both numerator and denominator drop. Error: dividing by 50 for a given-glasses probability. Correction: condition first, population second. Error: adding P(A) + P(B) without subtracting the overlap. Correction: both-occurring counted twice. Error: adding single-coin probabilities for two coins. Correction: multiply along branches.
