A teacher samples 50 students from the first 50 names on the register. Name the sampling method and the main source of bias. This is a convenience sample, and the bias comes from the register order, which may not represent the whole school.

title: AS Level Mathematics: Circular Measure
content:
AS Level Mathematics: Circular Measure

Radians measure angles by the arc they cut: one radian is the angle subtended when the arc equals the radius. That definition makes every circle formula simpler — arc length becomes s = rθ and sector area becomes ½r²θ, with no 360 in sight. This note builds the topic from zero: the radian definition and conversions, arc length and sector area with derivations, the segment area formula, and the applied problems (belts, pendulums, cones) that combine circular measure with trigonometry. Every worked example keeps the calculator in radian mode, which is the first habit this topic demands.

Radians and conversion

one full turn = 2 π radians = 360 degrees
π radians = 180 degrees

degrees → radians: multiply by π/180
radians → degrees: multiply by 180/π

common values: 30 ° = π/6, 45 ° = π/4,
60 ° = π/3, 90 ° = π/2, 180 ° = π

Worked example. Convert 150° to radians and 2.4 radians to degrees.

150 x π/180 = 5 π/6 = 2.618 rad
2.4 × 180/π = 137.5 °

Why radians: the arc length formula s = rθ only works when θ is in radians. In degrees the same arc is (θ/360) × 2πr — the same quantity, but with the conversion built in.

Arc length and sector area

arc length: s = r θ
sector area: A = (1/2) r² θ
perimeter of a sector: s + 2r

(θ in radians, r in the same length unit as s)

Worked example 1. A sector has radius 8 cm and angle 1.5 radians. Find the arc length and area.

s = r θ = 8 × 1.5 = 12 cm
A = (1/2) r² θ = 0.5 × 64 × 1.5 = 48 cm²

Worked example 2 (perimeter). Find the perimeter of the same sector.

perimeter = arc + 2 radii = 12 + 16 = 28 cm

Worked example 3 (working backwards). A sector of radius 6 cm has area 27 cm². Find the angle in radians and degrees.

27 = (1/2)(36) θ  →  27 = 18 θ  →  θ = 1.5 rad
in degrees: 1.5 × 180/π = 85.9 °

Segment area

segment area = sector area - triangle area
             = (1/2) r² θ - (1/2) r² sin(θ)
             = (1/2) r² (θ - sin θ)

The triangle is formed by the two radii and the chord; its area uses ½r² sin θ (the sine rule area formula). The subtraction is always the same picture: the segment is the sector with the triangle removed.

Worked example. Find the area of the segment cut off by a chord in a circle of radius 10 cm when the angle at the centre is 1.2 radians.

sector area = (1/2)(100)(1.2) = 60 cm²
triangle area = (1/2)(100) sin(1.2) = 50 × 0.932 = 46.6 cm²
segment = 60 - 46.6 = 13.4 cm²

Worked examples: the standard exam types

Worked example 1 (belt around pulleys). Two pulleys of radius 0.20 m and 0.50 m have centres 1.5 m apart. Find the length of the belt around them (straight sections plus arcs).

straight sections: 2 × 1.5 = 3.0 m (approximately, for the
common external tangents when the radii differ the geometry
needs the tangent length, but the exam version usually gives
equal pulleys or the tangent length directly)
equal-pulley version: belt = 2d + 2 π r = 3.0 + 1.26 = 4.26 m

Worked example 2 (pendulum arc). A pendulum of length 0.80 m swings through 0.6 radians. Find the arc length travelled by the bob.

s = r θ = 0.80 × 0.6 = 0.48 m

Worked example 3 (cone sector). A sector of radius 12 cm and angle 2.0 radians is folded into a cone. Find the base radius.

arc length becomes the base circumference:
s = 12 × 2.0 = 24 cm² π r_base = 24  →  r_base = 24/(2 π) = 3.82 cm

Radian trigonometry and small angles

In radian mode, the trigonometric functions take radian inputs, and small-angle approximations become available: for small θ, sin θ ≈ θ and tan θ ≈ θ (with θ in radians), and cos θ ≈ 1 − θ²/2. These approximations underpin pendulum motion and lens theory later, and they appear in exam questions as "show that for small θ ...".

Worked example. Show that for small θ, the arc length and the chord length are approximately equal.

arc = r θ
chord = 2r sin(θ/2) ~ 2r (θ/2) = r θ  for small θ
so chord ~ arc, with the difference of order θ³

Composite shapes with sectors

Exam figures combine sectors with triangles, rectangles and semicircles. The method is always the same: shade the required region, split it into standard pieces, compute each piece with the radian formulas, then add or subtract. Perimeter questions require the boundary only — internal lines are not part of it.

Worked example. A shape is a rectangle 12 cm by 8 cm with a quarter-circle of radius 8 cm removed from one corner. Find the area and perimeter of the remaining shape.

rectangle area = 96 cm²
quarter circle = (1/4) π r² = (1/4)(3.142)(64) = 50.3 cm²
remaining area = 96 - 50.3 = 45.7 cm²

perimeter: straight edges 12 + 4 + 8 = 24 cm (the 4 cm is the
remaining part of the 8 cm side)
plus the arc: quarter circumference = (1/4)(2 π)(8) = 12.6 cm
total perimeter = 36.6 cm

Worked example 2 (two sectors). Two circles of radius 5 cm have centres 8 cm apart. Find the area common to both.

the overlap is two identical segments. In each circle the chord
subtends an angle θ where cos(θ/2) = 4/5, so θ/2 =
0.6435 and θ = 1.287 rad.
segment area = (1/2)(25)(1.287 - sin 1.287)
             = 12.5(1.287 - 0.960) = 4.09 cm²
common area = 2 × 4.09 = 8.18 cm²

Arc, chord and sector in practice

Three quantities are easy to confuse and each has its own formula. Keep them side by side:

QuantityFormula (θ in radians)What it measures
Arc lengths = r θthe curved boundary
Chord lengthc = 2r sin(θ/2)the straight line joining the arc's ends
Sector areaA = (1/2) r^2 θthe pie-slice region

Worked example. A sector has radius 10 cm and angle 1.0 rad. Find the arc length, chord length and the difference between them.

arc = 10 × 1.0 = 10.0 cm
chord = 2 × 10 x sin(0.5) = 20 × 0.4794 = 9.59 cm
difference = 0.41 cm (the arc bulges beyond the chord)

Worked example (angular speed). A wheel of radius 0.35 m turns at 12 rad s⁻¹. Find the linear speed of a point on its rim and the angle turned in 5 s.

v = r ω = 0.35 × 12 = 4.2 m s⁻¹
angle = ω t = 12 × 5 = 60 rad (about 9.5 full turns)

Angular speed links circular measure to mechanics: one radian per second means one radius of arc per second, so the rim speed is rω. Exam questions on rotating wheels, pulleys and centrifuges all reduce to this one relation, and it also explains why a point near the rim of a wheel moves faster than a point near the hub despite both completing a turn in the same time. The same relation converts between the two ways of measuring rotation: revolutions per minute to radians per second is a factor of 2π/60.

The difference is the sagitta-related gap that appears in lens and bridge questions; it grows as the angle grows, which is why the small-angle approximation fails for large sectors.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Convert) Convert 72° to radians. Answer: θ(rad) = θ(°) × π/180°, so 72 × π/180 = 72π/180 = 2π/5 ≈ 1.257 rad.
  2. (Arc) Radius 5 cm, θ = 2.0 rad. Find the arc length. Answer: arc length s = rθ = 5 × 2.0 = 10 cm.
  3. (Sector) Radius 4 cm, θ = 3.0 rad. Find the area. Answer: sector area A = ½r²θ = ½ × 4² × 3.0 = ½ × 16 × 3 = 24 cm².
  4. (Reverse) A sector of radius 9 cm has arc length 13.5 cm. Find θ in radians. Answer: θ = 13.5/9 = 1.5 rad.
  5. (Segment) Radius 6 cm, θ = π/3. Find the segment area. Answer: sector = ½ × 36 × π/3 = 6π ≈ 18.85; triangle = ½ × 36 × sin(π/3) = 18 × 0.866 = 15.59; segment ≈ 3.26 cm².
  6. (Perimeter) Find the perimeter of a sector of radius 7 cm and angle 0.8 rad. Answer: the perimeter is the arc plus two radii: rθ + 2r = 7(0.8) + 14 = 5.6 + 14 = 19.6 cm.
  7. (Cone) A sector of radius 10 cm and angle 1.8 rad forms a cone. Find the base radius and slant height. Answer: arc = 18 cm → base radius 18/(2π) = 2.86 cm; slant height = 10 cm.
  8. (Small angle) Use sin θ ≈ θ to estimate sin(0.10) and compare with the calculator value. Answer: in radians sin θ ≈ θ for small θ, so sin(0.10) ≈ 0.10 against the calculator's 0.0998 — an error of about 0.2%, small because 0.10 rad is small.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Degree mode: every radians formula requires the calculator in RAD mode. A sin of 1.2 in degree mode gives an entirely different number.
  • Mixing units: s = rθ silently assumes r in metres and s in metres; cm and m mixed in one calculation produces a factor-of-100 error.
  • Half forgotten: sector area is ½r²θ, not r²θ. The ½ comes from the triangle comparison.
  • Angle in degrees in the formula: θ must be radians; convert first, and only convert the final answer back if asked.
  • Perimeter includes the radii: the perimeter of a sector is arc + 2r; the arc alone is not the perimeter.
  • Segment triangle: use ½r² sin θ for the triangle, with θ the same central angle; a different angle changes the answer.
  • Exact versus decimal: when the question says "in terms of π", keep π symbolic; converting to 3.14 loses the required form.
  • Small-angle validity: sin θ ≈ θ is good only for small θ (roughly under 0.2 rad); do not apply it to 1.5 rad.

Reading a sector: the one drawing this topic is built on

Every formula in circular measure comes from a single picture, and nearly every mistake comes from mixing up the two curves in it. Draw the sector once, label the radius, the angle and the arc, and the rest is arithmetic on that drawing.

Why the radian exists. An angle in radians is defined as the arc it cuts off divided by the radius:

θ = s / r Key: θ = angle at the centre (rad); s = arc length (m); r = radius (m). The units cancel, so a radian is a pure ratio — one radius-length of arc per radius. That is why a full turn is 2π radians and not 360: the whole circumference is 2πr, so the angle it subtends is 2πr ÷ r = 2π.

Turn the definition around and you get the arc formula, which is the one you actually use:

s = r θ Key: s = arc length (m); r = radius (m); θ = angle at the centre in radians. Using degrees here gives an answer 57 times too large — the single most common error in the topic.

Where ½r²θ comes from. Cut the sector into many thin triangles, each with height r and a sliver of arc as its base. A triangle's area is ½ × base × height, so each sliver is ½ × (rΔθ) × r, and adding them all up gives ½r² × (total θ):

A = ½ r² θ Key: A = area of the sector (m²); r = radius (m); θ = angle at the centre (rad). Notice that the arc is in this formula too — A = ½ r × (rθ) = ½ r s, which is the "thin triangle" statement written algebraically.

Worked example. A sector has radius 9.0 cm and angle 1.2 rad. Find its arc length, its area, and the length of its chord.

arc: s = rθ = 9.0 × 1.2 = 10.8 cm
area: A = ½r²θ = ½ × 81 × 1.2 = 48.6 cm²
chord: the two radii and the chord form an isosceles triangle with sides 9.0, 9.0 and included angle 1.2 rad, so chord = 2 × 9.0 × sin(1.2/2) = 18 × 0.5646 = 10.2 cm

That last line is the step students skip, and it is the step the paper is testing: the chord is a straight line, so it needs trigonometry, not the arc formula. The segment area is then sector minus triangle, A = ½r²(θ − sin θ) = 48.6 − ½ × 81 × sin 1.2 = 48.6 − 37.7 = 10.9 cm².

The perimeter of a sector is three sides, not one. A sector's boundary is the arc plus the two radii: P = 2r + rθ. For the example above, P = 18.0 + 10.8 = 28.8 cm. Answering with 10.8 alone is the most frequently lost mark on this topic, because the word "perimeter" invites you to think of the curve only.

Where marks are lost. Degrees in an equation that needs radians (check the calculator is in RAD mode the moment a question says "radians"). Reading "arc" as "chord". Forgetting the two radii in a perimeter. And using ½r²θ for a segment — the segment is the sector minus the triangle, and the triangle's area is ½r² sin θ.

Deriving the arc and sector formulae from the fraction of a circle

Both formulae come from one idea: a sector is the same fraction of its circle as its angle is of a full turn. Seeing that fraction is more useful than memorising two formulae, because the same reasoning works when a question changes the circle or the angle.

Arc length as a fraction of the circumference

The full circumference is 2πr, and a full turn is 2π radians. A sector of angle θ takes the fraction θ/(2π) of the circle, so s = (θ/2π) × 2πr = rθ. The π cancels, which is why radians make the arc formula so short.

Sector area as a fraction of the disc

The whole disc has area πr². The sector takes the same fraction, so A = (θ/2π) × πr² = ½r²θ. Check it with θ = 2π: ½r²(2π) = πr², the whole disc.

What goes wrong if the angle is in degrees

In degrees a full turn is 360, not 2π, so the fraction becomes θ/360 and the arc is (θ/360) × 2πr. Putting a degree value straight into rθ gives an answer about 57.3 times too large, because one radian is 180/π degrees.

The area formula from integration

Adding thin sectors of area ½r² dθ from 0 to θ gives ∫₀^θ ½r² dθ = ½r²θ. This is the same result reached by integration, and it is the method behind the formula rather than a separate rule.

Recovering the radius and angle from the arc and area

Dividing the area by the arc gives A/s = ½r, so r = 2A/s, and then θ = s/r. A sector with arc 15 cm and area 75 cm² has r = 2 × 75 / 15 = 10 cm and θ = 15/10 = 1.5 rad.

Checking the units of the answer

An arc is a length, so its unit is the radius unit. A sector's area has square units. An area with no square unit usually means the arc formula was used by mistake.

title: Circular Motion and SHM — Study Notes
content:
Circular Motion and SHM

Circular Motion Recap

Angular speed ω = 2π/T; v = ωr; a = ω²r = v²/r; F = mv²/r toward the centre.

Simple Harmonic Motion

Acceleration is proportional to displacement and opposite: a = −ω²x.

Solutions: x = x₀ sin ωt (start at centre) or x = x₀ cos ωt (start at extreme), with ω = 2πf.

Velocity and acceleration:

  • v_max = ωx₀ at the centre
  • a_max = ω²x₀ at the extremes

Example: a pendulum with x₀ = 0.02 m, f = 0.5 Hz has a_max = (2π × 0.5)² × 0.02 ≈ 0.20 m s⁻².

Energy in SHM

E = ½mω²x₀² total (constant), exchanged between KE (max at centre) and PE (max at extremes).

Damping and Resonance

Damping removes energy: light damping → slow decay; critical → fastest return without oscillation. Resonance: driving at the natural frequency gives maximum amplitude (microwave ovens, swing pushing, bridge disasters).

Exam tips: quote a = −ω²x as the defining condition; time period questions often need only T = 2π/ω.

title: AS Level Physics: Work, Energy and Power
content:
AS Level Physics: Work, Energy and Power

Energy is the currency of physics: it is never created or destroyed, only changed in form and moved from place to place, and every calculation in mechanics is really an accounting exercise in that currency. This note builds the energy toolkit from zero: what work actually is (a transfer, not a thing), the conservation principle that governs every process, the two energy formulas you will use daily — kinetic and gravitational potential — and power, the rate at which the currency is spent. Every worked example is a full energy audit with each line shown.

Work: energy in transit

Work is done when a force moves its point of application: energy is transferred from one store to another. The definition that earns the mark:

work done = force x distance moved in the direction of the force
W = F s cos(theta)

W in joules (J), F in newtons (N), s in metres (m)
theta = angle between the force and the displacement

The analogy: pushing a shopping trolley. Push along the direction of travel (θ = 0, cos θ = 1) and all your effort does work; push sideways (θ = 90°, cos θ = 0) and you do no work on its forward motion — you merely warm your arms. One joule is the work done when a force of one newton moves its point of application one metre: 1 J = 1 N m.

Worked example. A woman pushes a trolley with 80 N along 15 m of horizontal floor, the force angled 30° above the horizontal. Find the work done.

W = F s cos(theta) = 80 x 15 x cos(30)
  = 80 x 15 x 0.866 = 1039 J  (2 s.f.: 1.0 kJ)

If instead the question were a box pushed horizontally with 80 N over 15 m, the answer is simply 80 × 15 = 1200 J. Read whether an angle is given; the cos θ line is where method marks live.

Conservation of energy

Energy cannot be created or destroyed; the total energy of a closed system is constant. Energy transfers between stores — kinetic, gravitational potential, elastic potential, thermal, internal — and every real transfer leaks some energy to thermal stores of the surroundings through friction. The exam phrasing: "energy is transferred usefully to X and dissipated to the surroundings as heat" — learn the transfer vocabulary (transferred, dissipated, stored) because the mark schemes use it deliberately.

StoreChange that fills itExample
Kinetican object speeds upa falling stone
Gravitational potentialan object is lifteda book on a shelf
Elastic potentiala spring is stretched or compresseda drawn bow
Thermal (internal)friction, or heatingbrake pads after a descent

Kinetic energy and gravitational potential energy

kinetic energy:  KE = (1/2) m v^2
gravitational potential energy (near a planet's surface):
                 GPE = m g h     (change in GPE = m g Delta h)

m in kg, v in m s-1, g = 9.81 m s-2 (or the value given),
h = vertical height change in metres

Two traps live in the definitions. First, h is vertical: moving a box 10 m along a shelf adds no gravitational potential energy however far it slides. Second, GPE is defined as a change — only differences matter, so the question's reference level (where h = 0) is yours to choose; pick the lowest point and every height stays positive.

Worked example 1 (falling object). A 0.50 kg ball is dropped from 20 m. Find its speed just before impact (ignore air resistance).

energy at top:   GPE = m g h = 0.50 x 9.81 x 20 = 98.1 J
energy at bottom: KE = (1/2) m v^2, and KE = GPE
(1/2)(0.50) v^2 = 98.1
0.25 v^2 = 98.1 -> v^2 = 392.4 -> v = 19.8 m s-1

Worked example 2 (with friction). A 2.0 kg trolley starts at the top of a 5.0 m slope at 30° and reaches the bottom at 3.0 m s⁻¹. Find the energy dissipated by friction.

vertical height: h = 5.0 sin(30) = 2.5 m
initial GPE = m g h = 2.0 x 9.81 x 2.5 = 49.05 J
final KE = (1/2)(2.0)(3.0)^2 = 9.0 J
energy lost to friction = 49.05 - 9.0 = 40.05 J
                        = 40 J (2 s.f.)

Note the structure of every friction question: start energy minus end energy is the dissipation. Nothing is destroyed — it went to thermal stores.

Bringing things to rest: work done by braking

A whole family of questions asks how far a vehicle takes to stop, or what force stops it. The engine of the calculation is always the same: the kinetic energy the vehicle loses becomes work done by the braking force.

KE lost = work done by braking
(1/2) m v^2 = F s        (F = average braking force, s = stopping distance)

Worked example. A 1200 kg car travelling at 20 m s⁻¹ brakes to a halt over 40 m. Find the average braking force.

initial KE = (1/2) m v^2 = 0.5 x 1200 x 20^2 = 240 000 J
(1/2) m v^2 = F s  ->  240 000 = F x 40
F = 240 000/40 = 6000 N = 6.0 kN

The same equation rearranged answers the safety version: since KE grows with v², doubling the speed quadruples the energy the brakes must absorb and hence the stopping distance at constant force. That single statement is a full mark in most questions about speed limits.

Power: the rate of transfer

power = work done / time = energy transferred / time
P = W/t          (watts, W; 1 W = 1 J s-1)

also, for a force moving at constant speed:
P = F v          (derivable: W/t = F s/t = F v)

Worked example 1. A motor lifts a 200 kg crate through 8.0 m in 12 s at constant speed. Find its useful power output (g = 9.81 m s⁻²).

useful work = gain in GPE = m g h = 200 x 9.81 x 8.0 = 15 696 J
P = W/t = 15 696/12 = 1308 W = 1.3 kW (2 s.f.)

Worked example 2 (P = Fv). A car engine provides 20 kN of thrust at a steady 30 m s⁻¹. Find the power developed.

P = F v = 20 000 x 30 = 6.0 x 10^5 W = 600 kW

Efficiency closes the topic: efficiency = useful energy output / total energy input, always a fraction (or ×100%). Real machines are between 0 and 1 — an efficiency of 1.2 is a red flag in your own answer.

Worked example 3 (efficiency). A lift uses 40 kJ of electrical energy to raise a 500 kg load through 6.0 m. Find its efficiency.

useful output = m g h = 500 x 9.81 x 6.0 = 29 430 J
input = 40 kJ = 40 000 J
efficiency = 29 430/40 000 = 0.74  (74%)

Worked examples: the mixed audit

Worked example. A 1.5 kg trolley is pushed by a 6.0 N force along a 4.0 m horizontal track. It starts from rest and ends at 3.0 m s⁻¹. Account for the energy.

work input from the push: W = F s = 6.0 x 4.0 = 24 J
final KE = (1/2)(1.5)(3.0)^2 = 6.75 J
energy to friction/thermal = 24 - 6.75 = 17.25 J = 17 J (2 s.f.)
comment: most of the push became heat - the track is rough.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Work) A 40 N force acts at 60° to the horizontal, moving a box 5.0 m horizontally. Find the work done. Answer: W = Fs cos θ = 40 × 5.0 × cos 60 = 40 × 5.0 × 0.5 = 100 J.
  2. (Conservation) A cyclist freewheels down a hill. Describe the energy transfers. Answer: Gravitational potential energy is transferred to kinetic energy as the cyclist descends; some energy is dissipated to the thermal stores of the brakes, tyres and air through friction and drag, so the final kinetic energy is slightly less than the initial GPE.
  3. (GPE/KE) A 0.20 kg ball is thrown up at 15 m s⁻¹. Find the maximum height reached (no air resistance). Answer: ½mv² = mgh → h = v²/(2g) = 225/(2 × 9.81) = 11.5 m.
  4. (Power) A crane lifts 800 kg through 12 m at constant speed in 20 s. Find the useful power (g = 9.81). Answer: W = mgh = 800 × 9.81 × 12 = 94 176 J; P = W/t = 4709 W = 4.7 kW.
  5. (Efficiency) A generator takes in 50 kJ and delivers 38 kJ of electrical energy. Find the efficiency and state where the rest goes. Answer: 38/50 = 0.76 (76%); the remaining 12 kJ is dissipated as heat to the surroundings (thermal stores) through friction and electrical resistance.
  6. (P = Fv) A car moves at constant speed against a total drag of 500 N. Find the engine power at 25 m s⁻¹. Answer: P = Fv = 500 × 25 = 12 500 W = 12.5 kW.
  7. (Vertical height) A 3.0 kg suitcase is carried 4.0 m horizontally across a room. Find the change in its GPE. Answer: Zero — the vertical height did not change, and GPE depends only on vertical displacement.
  8. (Full audit) A 1.0 kg block slides 2.0 m down a 25° slope and reaches 2.5 m s⁻¹. Find the energy dissipated. Answer: h = 2.0 sin 25 = 0.845 m; GPE lost = 1.0 × 9.81 × 0.845 = 8.29 J; KE gained = ½ × 1.0 × 6.25 = 3.13 J; dissipated = 8.29 − 3.13 = 5.2 J.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • h is vertical: sliding along a level floor changes no GPE. Convert slope distance to vertical height with sin θ before mgh.
  • Speed squared: KE = ½mv² — doubling v quadruples KE. Candidates who double the energy on doubling speed lose marks in multi-step questions.
  • W = Fs versus W = mgh: the work done by a lifting force equals the gain in GPE only at constant speed; if the load accelerates, some work also becomes KE.
  • Forgetting the energy audit structure: friction questions want input energy minus output energy as a stated subtraction — show both energies first.
  • Power units: kW into W before dividing by seconds (1 kW = 1000 W). 1300 W is 1.3 kW, not 13.
  • Efficiency as a percentage over 100: impossible; check the ratio direction (output over input, never the reverse).
  • g value: use 9.81 m s⁻² unless the paper supplies another value; a question giving g = 10 expects 10.
  • Significant figures and units: answers to 2 or 3 s.f. with units (J, W, m s⁻¹) — unrounded calculator output costs marks.
  • Method visibility: write the formula (W = Fs cos θ, P = W/t) as its own line before substitution; formulae earn credit independently of arithmetic.

title: Edexcel IAL Computer Science: Processor Fundamentals and Architecture
content:
Edexcel IAL Computer Science: Processor Fundamentals and Architecture

Pearson Edexcel International Advanced Level in Computer Science, Unit 1 Principles of Computer Science (with Unit 3 systems architecture depth): CPU architecture and the fetch–decode–execute cycle, assembly language and bit manipulation, and processors, parallel processing and virtual machines. Every cycle below is traced register by register, and every assembly instruction is annotated with its effect on memory and the accumulator — because the exam hands you a memory dump and asks for the cycle's exact state at each step.

The stored-program machine

The Von Neumann architecture stores program instructions and data in the same memory, fetched by the CPU over shared buses: CPU (control unit, ALU, registers), main memory, backing storage, and input/output, joined by the address, data and control buses. Its weakness, the Von Neumann bottleneck, is that instruction and data traffic contend for one path — the motivation for caches, pipelines and Harvard-style split paths (separate instruction and data caches) in modern designs.

CPU components and registers

RegisterRole in the cycle
Program counter (PC)Holds the address of the next instruction; incremented after the fetch
Memory address register (MAR)Holds the address being accessed on this bus transfer
Memory data register (MDR/MBR)Holds the instruction or data just fetched or about to be written
Current instruction register (CIR)Holds the instruction being decoded and executed
Accumulator (ACC)Holds the running result of ALU operations

The control unit fetches, decodes and orchestrates; the ALU performs arithmetic and logic; the clock paces each micro-step; the address bus is one-way (CPU → memory/devices), the data bus two-way, the control bus carries read/write/interrupt/clock signals.

The fetch–decode–execute cycle, traced

Memory (opcode / operand; opcode 01 = LOAD, 10 = ADD, 11 = STORE):

  5: 01 001000   LOAD 8
  6: 10⁰⁰¹⁰⁰¹   ADD 9
  7: 11 001010   STORE 10⁸: 0000 0101   (5)
  9: 0000 0011   (3)
 10: 0000 0000   (empty)

Cycle 1 - LOAD 8:
  FETCH:   PC = 5 → MAR = 5; control bus READ; MDR = 01 001000;
           CIR = 01 001000; PC = PC + 1 = 6.
  DECODE:  opcode 01 = LOAD: copy memory[operand] to ACC.
  EXECUTE: operand 001000 = 8; MAR = 8; READ; MDR = 5; ACC = 5.

Cycle 2 - ADD 9:
  FETCH:   PC = 6 → MAR = 6; READ; MDR = 10⁰⁰¹⁰⁰¹; CIR = same; PC = 7.
  DECODE:  opcode 10 = ADD: ACC = ACC + memory[operand].
  EXECUTE: MAR = 9; READ; MDR = 3; ALU: ACC + MDR = 5 + 3 = 8; ACC = 8.

Cycle 3 - STORE 10:
  FETCH:   PC = 7 → MAR = 7; READ; MDR = 11 001010; CIR = same; PC = 8.
  DECODE:  opcode 11 = STORE: memory[operand] = ACC.
  EXECUTE: MAR = 10; MDR = 8 (from ACC); WRITE; memory[10] = 0000 10⁰⁰.

Interrupts fit between cycles: complete the current instruction, save the PC,
run the interrupt service routine, restore the PC, resume.

The examiner's checklist: PC → MAR for the fetch; MDR → CIR; PC incremented at fetch (not execute); execute behaviour depends entirely on the opcode; the MAR is reused in execute to address the operand.

Assembly language

Assembly is a thin, human-readable veneer over machine code: one mnemonic per instruction (LOAD, ADD, STORE, JMP, CMP), assembled to binary by an assembler. It is low-level (tied to the processor's instruction set), fast, and used where direct hardware control matters — embedded firmware, drivers, performance-critical inner loops. Instruction sets: CISC (many complex instructions, variable length, microcoded — x86) versus RISC (few simple instructions, one cycle each, hardwired — ARM). Mobile devices favour RISC for power efficiency; the trade-off is instructions-per-task versus cycles-per-instruction.

Assembly concepts with a small program (accumulator machine):

  START:  LOAD  X      ; ACC = value at X
          ADD   Y      ; ACC = ACC + value at Y
          STORE Z      ; Z = ACC
          CMP   K      ; compare ACC with K (sets flags)
          JMPLE DONE   ; jump to DONE if ACC <= K (flag-driven)
          LOAD  Z      ; otherwise adjust
          SUB   K
          STORE Z
  DONE:   HALT

Key ideas the exam tests: labels are addresses (START, DONE are memory
locations); operands address memory; jumps make selection and loops; flags
(Z for zero, C for carry, N for negative, V for overflow) are set by CMP and
tested by conditional jumps - the mechanism behind every IF and WHILE once
compiled.

Bit manipulation (statement 4.3) is done with logical shifts and masks: AND with a mask to extract bits (flags, packed fields), OR to set a bit, XOR to toggle, NOT to invert, shift left/right to multiply/divide by powers of two. Extracting the third byte of a packed word: shift right 16, then AND 0xFF — each step traced in binary in exam answers.

Performance and parallelism

  • Factors: clock speed (ticks per second), cores (independent instruction streams), cache size and levels (L1 fastest/smallest, L3 slowest/largest), bus width (bits per transfer), word length (bits the CPU processes at once), instruction set (CISC/RISC trade-off), and pipelining (overlapping fetch/decode/execute of consecutive instructions — stalls occur on branches).
  • Parallel processing: bit-level (wider words process more bits at once), instruction-level (pipelines and superscalar execution), data-level (SIMD — same operation on many data items: GPU rendering), task-level (different programs or subtasks on different cores). Amdahl's law bounds the gain: the sequential fraction limits speed-up regardless of core count.
  • Virtual machines: a software emulation of another machine. Hardware VMs (hypervisors like VMware/KVM) run several OS instances on one physical host — server consolidation, isolation, easy backup and migration. Language VMs (the JVM, the CLR) execute bytecode portably: compile once to bytecode, run anywhere the VM exists — platform independence at the cost of a translation overhead versus native code.
Worked: a program is 25% sequential. Speed-up with 8 cores (Amdahl):

  speed-up = 1 / (0.25 + 0.75 / 8) = 1 / (0.25 + 0.09375) = 1 / 0.34375 = 2.91

Eight cores give under a threefold gain - the parallel hardware cannot help
the sequential quarter, which is the whole point of the question.

Worked example: one program through the whole stack

Source (high level):     z = x + y
Assembly (low level):    LOAD X / ADD Y / STORE Z
Machine code:            01 001000 / 10⁰⁰¹⁰⁰¹ / 11 001010  (as above)

The assembler resolves labels to addresses; the CPU executes each instruction
through fetch-decode-execute; the compiler that produced the assembly chose the
register usage and the instruction order. Three representations, one behaviour -
and the exam question naming "which stage produced which artefact" targets
exactly these three columns.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Saying the PC increments during execute; it increments after the fetch.
  • Confusing MAR (address) with MDR (data) — the most-marked pair in Unit 1.
  • Claiming assembly is "almost high level"; it is one-to-one with machine instructions and hardware-specific.
  • Forgetting that CMP sets flags and conditional jumps read them — without that link, selection and loops have no mechanism.
  • Answering parallelism questions with "more cores = faster" only; Amdahl's law and the type of parallelism (bit/instruction/data/task) are the marks.
  • Describing a language VM as an emulator of hardware only; the JVM executes bytecode — portability is its purpose.
  • Using a logical shift to halve a negative two's-complement number (must be arithmetic shift, preserving the sign bit).

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Unit 1, 5 marks). Describe the fetch–decode–execute cycle of an instruction that adds the contents of address 200 to the accumulator.

Answer: Fetch: the PC's value is copied to the MAR; a READ signal fetches the instruction from memory into the MDR; it is copied to the CIR; the PC increments. Decode: the control unit interprets the opcode as ADD with operand 200. Execute: MAR ← 200; READ fetches the data into the MDR; the ALU adds MDR to the accumulator and stores the result in it.

Question 2 (Unit 1, 3 marks). Explain the purpose of the MAR and the MDR.

Answer: The MAR holds the memory address currently being read from or written to, driving the address bus. The MDR holds the data or instruction transferred in that access — fetched values arrive there and outgoing values are placed there before a write.

Question 3 (Unit 1, 4 marks). Explain two differences between CISC and RISC processors and state one use for each.

Answer: CISC has many complex instructions, often multi-cycle and microcoded, so programs need fewer instructions — suiting desktops (x86). RISC has few simple instructions, each executed in one clock cycle with hardwired control and heavy pipelining — suiting power-sensitive mobile/embedded devices (ARM). The trade-off: fewer instructions per task versus fewer cycles per instruction.

Question 4 (Unit 1, 4 marks). Explain how 8 cores can fail to give 8× speed-up.

Answer: Amdahl's law: the speed-up is limited by the sequential fraction of the program, which no extra core can accelerate — only the parallel fraction divides among cores. Coordination overhead (thread synchronisation, communication) and memory-bus contention further reduce gains, so real speed-up depends on how much of the work is genuinely parallel.

Question 5 (Unit 1, 4 marks). Describe what a hypervisor provides and one benefit and one drawback of virtualisation.

Answer: A hypervisor runs multiple virtual machines, each with its own OS, on one physical machine by arbitrating CPU, memory and storage. Benefit: server consolidation and isolation — one hardware outlay, VMs start, migrate and snapshot independently. Drawback: each VM competes for shared physical resources, so performance is lower than bare metal, and the hypervisor itself consumes resources and expands the trusted computing base.

Question 6 (Unit 1, 3 marks). Explain how a conditional jump implements IF mark ≥ 50 in assembly.

Answer: CMP compares the accumulator with 50 by subtraction, setting flags (zero, negative, carry, overflow) without storing the result. The test mark ≥ 50 becomes a jump-if-greater-or-equal (reading N and V or C flags) to the "pass" label; if the condition fails, execution falls through to the "fail" code. Flags are the bridge between comparison and branching.

Below the assembly sits the digital logic every instruction is built from: hardware components, gates and Boolean algebra.

title: Data Types and File Organisation — Study Notes
content:
Data Types and File Organisation

User-Defined Types

A user-defined type is derived from existing types. An enumerated type lists named values in order: TYPE Months = (Jan, Feb, Mar ...). Internally each value is an integer index starting at 0. Pointer types store a memory address; the dereference operator returns the value at that address, which is how linked structures reference their nodes. Set types store unordered collections of distinct values from an ordinal base type, supporting union, intersection and difference.

Records

A record groups related fields of different types under one identifier, for example a Student record with name : STRING and mark : INTEGER. Arrays of records are the standard structure for storing a table of items in memory.

File Organisation

  • Serial: records in insertion order; searching checks every record. Simple but slow.
  • Sequential: records kept in key order; binary search possible, but insertion needs rewriting.
  • Random (direct): a hashing function converts the key into a storage address, giving near-instant access. A poor hash causes collisions — two keys hashing to the same address — resolved by chaining or overflow areas.

Hashing

A common method is division hashing: Address = Key MOD TableSize. A good hash distributes keys evenly; load factor above roughly 70 percent degrades performance.

Exam tips: state the internal integer representation of enumerated values; define a collision before describing its resolution; compare the three file organisations in terms of search and insert cost.

title: Exam technique: Pressure and Density
content:
### What earns the marks
For solids, p = F/A with substitution earns both marks. For liquids, proportionality with depth stated earns the explanation mark. For hydraulics, pressure equated across pistons earns the method mark.
### Traps
Error: force and pressure interchanged. Correction: pressure divides by area. Error: depth effect inverted. Correction: deeper means greater pressure. Error: atmospheric pressure guessed at 10 Pa. Correction: about 100 kPa at sea level.

title: Electric Fields and Capacitance — Study Notes
content:
Electric Fields and Capacitance

Coulomb's law

The force between two point charges is F = kQ₁Q₂/r², with k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻². Like charges repel and unlike charges attract. The force acts along the line joining the charges.

Example: +2.0 μC and −3.0 μC, 0.30 m apart, attract with F = 0.60 N.

Electric field strength

Field strength E is the force per unit positive charge: E = F/Q, in N C⁻¹ (or V m⁻¹). For a point charge E = kQ/r², radially outward for positive charge.

Uniform field: between parallel plates, E = V/d, with the field constant in magnitude and direction. A charge q in it feels F = qE.

Example: plates 4.0 cm apart with p.d. 600 V have E = 1.5 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹.

Electric potential and potential energy

Electric potential V at a point is the work done per unit positive charge in bringing a small charge from infinity to that point: V = kQ/r for a point charge. Potential is a scalar. Field strength is the negative potential gradient, E = −dV/dr, so a steep potential-distance graph means a strong field. The field points from high to low potential.

Capacitance

Capacitance C = Q/V, measured in farads (C V⁻¹). The energy stored is W = ½QV = ½CV² = ½Q²/C. The area under a graph of V against Q equals the stored energy.

Example: a 10 μF capacitor charged to 200 V stores 0.20 J.

Capacitors in series and parallel

  • In parallel the capacitances add: C = C₁ + C₂.
  • In series the reciprocals add: 1/C = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂. The total is smaller than the smallest.

Discharge: through a resistor R, the charge falls exponentially, Q = Q₀e^(−t/RC). The time constant RC is the time for the charge or p.d. to fall to 37% of its initial value.

Exam tips: convert μF and cm to SI units before calculating. Check whether a question asks for field strength (vector) or potential (scalar). Series capacitors share the charge; parallel capacitors share the p.d.

title: Formal Writing: Register and Linking Words — Study Notes
content:
Formal writing uses a measured register: full forms instead of contractions, precise vocabulary, and connectives that show how ideas relate. Using the right register is as important as using correct grammar.

Formal and informal register

Informal writing uses slang, contractions and abbreviations. Formal writing avoids them.

  • Informal: Hey, we can't go tomorrow.
  • Formal: We are unable to attend the meeting tomorrow.

Linking words

Linking words show the relationship between ideas.

  • Addition: moreover, furthermore, in addition
  • Contrast: however, nevertheless, although
  • Result: consequently, therefore, as a result
  • Sequence: first, then, meanwhile
  • Similarity: similarly, likewise

Choosing a connective

Ask what the relationship is. If the second idea contradicts the first, use a contrast word. If it follows from the first, use a result word. Avoid starting every sentence with the same word.

Opening and closing formal letters

  • Use Dear Sir or Madam when you do not know the name.
  • Use Dear followed by a name when you do.
  • End with Yours faithfully for Dear Sir or Madam, and Yours sincerely for a named person.

Checking an essay

Remove contractions. Replace casual words with precise ones. Check that each connective matches the logic between the sentences.

title: Exam technique: Poisson Distribution
content:
### What earns the marks
For lambda scaling, the rate times the interval stated earns the first mark. For probabilities, e^-lambda lambda^x / x! with values earns the method mark. For approximations, the condition named (n large, p small, lambda = np) earns credit.
### Traps
Error: unscaled lambda over a new interval. Correction: scale first. Error: binomial coefficients inside Poisson work. Correction: Poisson formula only. Error: mean and variance treated as different. Correction: both equal lambda.

title: IGCSE Physics: Waves and Sound
content:
IGCSE Physics: Waves and Sound

Cambridge IGCSE Physics 0625 (2026–2028), Topic 3 Waves: statements 3.1 General properties of waves, 3.2 Light, 3.3 Electromagnetic spectrum and 3.4 Sound. Waves are how energy travels from place to place without moving matter along with it, and everything from a ripple on a pond to a gamma ray obeys the same few rules. This note builds the general wave behaviour first, then light (reflection, refraction, lenses, colour), then the electromagnetic spectrum and finally sound, with the calculations and the ray constructions that Paper 4 and Paper 6 reward.

General properties of waves

A wave transfers energy without transferring matter. Drop a cork into a ripple tank and the ripples pass under it while the cork only bobs: the water moves up and down, not outward. Every wave is described by the same vocabulary:

TermMeaningUnit
AmplitudeMaximum displacement from the rest position; relates to energy (loudness for sound, brightness for light)metre (m)
Wavelength (λ)Distance between two equivalent points on neighbouring waves, e.g. crest to crestmetre (m)
FrequencyNumber of complete waves passing a point per second; equals the source's number of oscillations per secondhertz (Hz)
PeriodTime for one complete wave to pass a pointsecond (s)
Wave speedDistance a wave crest travels per secondmetre per second (m s⁻¹)
wave speed = frequency x wavelength        v = fλ
period = 1 / frequency        T = 1 / f
  • v: wave speed in metres per second (m s⁻¹); f: frequency in hertz (Hz, = s⁻¹); λ: wavelength in metres (m). All scalars, so there are no signs to worry about — but all three quantities must be in SI units before multiplying.

Transverse waves have the vibration perpendicular to the direction of travel: water waves, light and all electromagnetic waves, waves on a shaken rope. Longitudinal waves have the vibration parallel to the direction of travel: sound in air, the push-pull of a slinky. Longitudinal waves show compressions (where particles are pushed together) and rarefactions (where they are spread apart).

Three behaviours describe what happens when waves meet things. Reflection is bouncing off a surface; the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, measured from the normal. Refraction is the change of direction when a wave passes into a different medium at an angle, because its speed changes; moving into a slower medium bends the ray towards the normal and the wavelength shortens while the frequency stays constant. Diffraction is the spreading of waves through a gap or around an obstacle, and it is most pronounced when the gap width is comparable to the wavelength. Ripple tanks demonstrate all three: straight barriers give reflection, shallow regions give refraction, and narrow gaps give circular wavefronts after diffraction (Supplement: wider gaps give less spreading, and an edge produces noticeable diffraction only for longer wavelengths).

Reflection of light

Light travels in straight lines and reflects from smooth surfaces with the law of reflection: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, both measured between the ray and the normal (an imaginary line perpendicular to the surface at the point of incidence). A plane-mirror image is upright, the same size as the object, laterally inverted (left and right swapped), and as far behind the mirror as the object is in front.

Supplement: the ray construction. To locate the image, draw a ray from the object to the mirror, continue it behind the mirror at the same angle, and drop a perpendicular from the image position to the mirror; repeat with a second ray. Where the reflected rays appear to come from behind the mirror is where the image sits. Drawing the construction to scale with a protractor gives the image position exactly.

Refraction of light

When light passes from air into glass at an angle it slows and bends towards the normal; passing back out it speeds up and bends away from the normal. The amount of bending is fixed by the material's refractive index:

refractive index = sin(angle of incidence in vacuum or air) / sin(angle of refraction)        n = sin i / sin r
critical angle:        sin c = 1 / n
  • n: refractive index, a scalar with no unit, always greater than 1 for a material like glass or water.
  • i and r: angles in degrees measured from the normal, not from the surface.
  • c: critical angle in degrees, defined for a ray passing from the material into air.

Total internal reflection happens when a ray inside a material hits the boundary at an angle greater than the critical angle: none of it escapes and all reflects. Two applications are examinable: optical fibres, where light bounces along the core with total internal reflection and carries data over long distances with little loss, and prisms in periscopes and binoculars, where a 45° prism turns light through 90° or 180° by total internal reflection with almost no energy loss compared with a mirror.

Thin lenses and vision

A converging lens brings parallel rays to a focus at its principal focus; a diverging lens spreads them out as if they came from a focus on the near side. Three standard rays build any image on a converging lens:

  • A ray parallel to the axis refracts through the principal focus on the far side.
  • A ray through the centre of the lens passes straight through undeviated.
  • A ray through the near-side principal focus emerges parallel to the axis.

Where two refracted rays cross, a real image forms — it can be shown on a screen. Where they only appear to diverge from a point behind the lens, a virtual image forms — it cannot be caught on a screen and is seen only by looking through the lens. An object beyond twice the focal length gives a smaller inverted real image (a camera); an object between the focus and the lens gives a larger upright virtual image (a magnifying glass, Supplement). Short sight (myopia) is corrected with a diverging lens, long sight (hyperopia) with a converging lens (Supplement).

Dispersion and the electromagnetic spectrum

White light passing through a prism disperses into a spectrum from red to violet because different colours refract by different amounts: red light is refracted least (it travels fastest in glass) and violet most. Light of a single colour is monochromatic (Supplement). The visible spectrum sits inside a much larger family — the electromagnetic spectrum, all waves travelling at 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ in a vacuum, all transverse, arranged by increasing frequency (and decreasing wavelength) as: radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays.

RegionWavelength scaleUsesHazards
Radio wavesmetres to hundreds of metresRadio and TV broadcasting, communicationsLittle evidence of harm at normal levels
Microwavesmillimetres to centimetresMobile phones, satellite communications, microwave ovens, radarHeating of body tissue; dangerous at high intensity
InfraredmicrometresHeating, night-vision cameras, remote controls, optical fibresBurns and skin heating at high intensity
Visible light400–700 nmVision, photography, fibre-optic dataDazzle; eye damage from lasers and the Sun
Ultraviolet10–400 nmFluorescent lamps, sterilisation, security markingSunburn, skin ageing and skin cancer, eye damage
X-rays0.01–10 nmMedical imaging, airport security, detecting cracks in metalIonising: cell damage and cancer risk; dose kept low
Gamma raysbelow 0.01 nmSterilising equipment, cancer radiotherapy, food irradiationIonising: severe cell damage; shielded with lead and concrete

Supplement: signals and communication. An analogue signal varies continuously with the quantity it carries; a digital signal is a stream of on/off pulses. Digital signals are preferred because they can be regenerated without amplifying noise, can be compressed to carry more information, can be encrypted, and can carry text, sound and images in the same stream. Satellite links work by beaming a microwave signal to an orbiting satellite, which amplifies and retransmits it back to a distant ground station.

Sound

Sound is a longitudinal wave produced by vibrating objects and travelling through a medium — air at about 340 m s⁻¹ at room temperature, faster in liquids and fastest in solids, because the particles are closer together and pass the vibration on more quickly. Sound cannot travel through a vacuum. The frequency of a sound sets its pitch (high frequency, high pitch), and the amplitude sets its loudness. The human range of hearing is roughly 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz.

Echoes and distance measurement. Sound reflects from hard surfaces, giving echoes. The depth of the sea under a ship is found by sending a pulse and timing its return:

distance to the surface = (speed of sound x total time) / 2        s = v t / 2

The halving is essential — the pulse travels down and back — and forgetting it is the classic error in this topic. Measuring the time between two microphones a known distance apart gives the speed of sound directly: v = distance/time.

Ultrasound is sound above the human hearing range (above 20 kHz). Its short wavelength means it reflects well from small internal boundaries, which makes it useful for prenatal scanning (reflection at tissue boundaries builds an image), cleaning delicate items (high-energy vibrations dislodge dirt), flaw detection in metal castings (an internal crack reflects the pulse), and sonar depth sounding. All uses share the same principle: send a pulse, time the echo, calculate the distance with s = vt/2.

Worked example: wave calculation and echo depth

A ship's sonar sends ultrasound of frequency 50 kHz. The echo returns from the seabed after 0.12 s. The speed of sound in seawater is 1500 m s⁻¹.

total distance travelled = v t = 1500 x 0.12 = 180 m
depth of the sea = 180 / 2 = 90 m

Second calculation: a ripple tank wave has a wavelength of 0.040 m and the dippers oscillate 25 times per second. The wave speed is v = f λ = 25 × 0.040 = 1.0 m s⁻¹. The frequency of the wave equals the frequency of the source, and it stays unchanged when the wave passes into deeper water — only the speed and the wavelength change there.

Common mistakes

  • Measuring a wavelength from crest to trough; that is half a wavelength. Measure between two equivalent points on neighbouring waves.
  • Forgetting that frequency never changes on refraction. The speed and wavelength change; the frequency is set by the source and stays constant.
  • Mixing up the angle of incidence with its complement: all angles in reflection and refraction are measured from the normal.
  • Using v = fλ with mismatched units: hertz times centimetres gives cm s⁻¹, not m s⁻¹. Convert the wavelength to metres first.
  • Forgetting to halve the total distance in an echo calculation.
  • Drawing a converging lens ray diagram without the two special rays, or putting the image on the wrong side: real images form on the far side where rays actually cross, virtual images on the same side as the object.
  • Claiming light travels slower in a vacuum than in glass; it is fastest in a vacuum and slower in denser media, which is what causes refraction.
  • Describing a digital signal as continuously varying; it is discrete pulses, which is precisely why it resists noise.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 4, 3 marks). A water wave has a frequency of 4.0 Hz and a wavelength of 0.25 m. Calculate its speed and its period.

Answer: v = fλ = 4.0 × 0.25 = 1.0 m s⁻¹. Period T = 1/f = 1/4.0 = 0.25 s.

Question 2 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Explain why sound cannot be heard on the Moon but sunlight still reaches it.

Answer: Sound is a longitudinal wave that needs a medium, because it travels by particles passing vibrations to their neighbours. The Moon is surrounded by a vacuum, with no particles to carry the vibration, so sound cannot travel there. Light is an electromagnetic transverse wave that carries energy without needing a medium, so it crosses the vacuum of space easily.

Question 3 (Paper 2 style). Light passes from air into glass at an angle. Which quantity does not change? A speed; B wavelength; C frequency; D direction. Answer: C. The frequency is set by the source and is unchanged; speed and wavelength both fall in glass and the ray bends.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Ultrasound of speed 1500 m s⁻¹ is used to find the depth of the sea. The echo returns in 0.40 s. Calculate the depth and explain why ultrasound is used rather than audible sound.

Answer: Depth = v t / 2 = 1500 × 0.40 / 2 = 300 m. Ultrasound has a very short wavelength, so it reflects well from small boundaries and gives a clear echo pattern without diffracting uselessly around small features; it also does not interfere with ordinary sound and is harmless at the intensities used.

Question 5 (Paper 6 style). Describe how to measure the speed of sound in air using two microphones and a data logger.

Answer: Place two microphones a measured distance apart in a straight line from a sound source (a clapping board or signal generator and loudspeaker). Trigger the data logger with the sound at each microphone and record the time interval between the arrivals, or display both pulses on an oscilloscope and measure the time from the trace. Speed is the distance between the microphones divided by the time interval. Repeat at several separations and find the speed from the gradient of a distance–time graph, which averages out the reaction error.

Question 6 (Paper 4, 3 marks). State two differences between a transverse and a longitudinal wave, and give one example of each.

Answer: In a transverse wave the vibrations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer; in a longitudinal wave they are parallel to it. Transverse waves have crests and troughs; longitudinal waves have compressions and rarefactions. Examples: light (transverse) and sound in air (longitudinal).

Waves carry energy without matter; the next topic is the energy that drives circuits: Electricity and Circuits.

Equations and symbols

One equation, v = fλ, carries the whole of wave physics; the rest of this topic is refraction, the lens and the echo. Frequency and period are reciprocals, so a question that gives one and asks for the other is testing whether you inverted it correctly.

The wave equation

v = fλ
Key: v = wave speed (m/s); f = frequency (Hz, waves per second); λ (lambda) = wavelength (m). The speed is set by the medium, so when a wave crosses into a new medium f stays the same and λ changes.

f = 1 / T
Key: f = frequency (Hz); T = period, the time for one complete oscillation (s). A 0.004 s period is 250 Hz.

T = 1 / f
Key: the same relation rearranged; T in seconds, f in hertz.

d = vt
Key: d = distance travelled by the wave (m); v = wave speed (m/s); t = time (s). For an echo the sound travels to the surface and back, so the distance to the surface is half of vt.

s = vt / 2
Key: s = distance to the reflecting surface (m); v = speed of sound in the medium (m/s); t = total time between the pulse and its echo (s). The factor of 2 is the most frequently dropped mark in echo questions.

v(sound in air) ≈ 340 m/s and v(light in vacuum) = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s
Key: the two speeds that explain thunder arriving after lightning; light is nearly a million times faster, so the flash is seen almost instantly.

audible range for a human = 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz
Key: f below 20 Hz is infrasound and above 20 kHz is ultrasound; both are outside human hearing but ultrasound is used in medical scanning and sonar.

Refraction

n = sin i / sin r
Key: n = refractive index of the material (no unit); i = angle of incidence in the less dense medium, measured from the normal (°); r = angle of refraction in the material (°). Both angles are always measured from the normal, never from the surface.

n = 1 / sin c
Key: c = critical angle (°), the angle of incidence in the denser medium for which the refracted ray runs along the surface. A larger n means a smaller critical angle.

n = c / v
Key: c = speed of light in a vacuum (3.0 × 10⁸ m/s); v = speed of light in the material (m/s). Light slows on entering a denser medium, which is what bends it towards the normal.

total internal reflection when i (greater than) c
Key: i = angle of incidence inside the denser medium (°); c = critical angle (°). Beyond c no light escapes, which is the rule behind optical fibres and reflecting prisms.

Lenses and images

m = h(image) / h(object)
Key: m = magnification (no unit); h(image) = image height (m or cm); h(object) = object height in the same unit. m greater than 1 means enlarged, less than 1 means diminished.

real image: formed where rays actually meet, and can be projected on a screen
Key: a converging lens gives a real image when the object is beyond the focal length; the image is inverted. A virtual image is where rays only appear to come from, and cannot be projected.

title: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Statistics and Data Handling
content:
Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Statistics and Data Handling

Statistics is the art of describing a pile of numbers with a few well-chosen ones: an average to say where the middle lies, a spread to say how tightly the data cluster, and a chart to make the shape visible. The IGCSE questions test exactly that pipeline — classify the data, compute the averages and spread, draw or read the chart, and compare two distributions. This note builds the whole subject from zero: the data types, every average and measure of spread with the frequency-table method, the standard charts, cumulative frequency curves, and histograms with unequal class widths.

Classifying statistical data

TypeMeaningExamples
Qualitative (categorical)describes a quality, not a numberfavourite colour, blood group
Quantitativemeasured or counted as a numberheight, number of siblings
Discretecountable, separate values (usually integers)number of children, shoe size
Continuouscan take any value in a range (measured)height, time, mass

The classification decides which charts and averages are legal: a mode for categorical data, a median for ordered data, class intervals for continuous data. Discrete data are plotted as bar charts with gaps; continuous data as histograms with no gaps (and frequency density on the vertical axis).

Averages and range

mean = sum of values / number of values
median = middle value when ordered (mean of the two middle
         values for an even count)
mode = most frequent value (or class); none if no repeats
range = largest - smallest

quartiles: Q1 = lower quartile (25%), Q3 = upper quartile (75%)
interquartile range (IQR) = Q3 - Q1  (spread of the middle 50%)

The mean uses every value (sensitive to outliers); the median ignores extreme values (robust); the mode is the only average available for categorical data. When comparing two data sets, quote an average and a spread: "school A has a higher median but a larger IQR, so its results are higher on average but less consistent."

Worked example. Find the mean, median, mode and range of: 4, 7, 7, 9, 12, 15, 18.

mean = (4+7+7+9+12+15+18)/7 = 72/7 = 10.3 (3 s.f.)
median = 4th value = 9
mode = 7 (appears twice)
range = 18 - 4 = 14

Worked example 2 (even count). Find the median of 3, 5, 8, 10, 12, 15.

even count: average the 3rd and 4th values
median = (8 + 10)/2 = 9

Averages from frequency tables

mean = sum of (value x frequency) / sum of frequencies
median = the value at position (n + 1)/2 in cumulative order
mode = the value with the highest frequency

Worked example. The table shows goals scored: 0 (5 players), 1 (8), 2 (6), 3 (2). Find the mean and the median.

total players = 5 + 8 + 6 + 2 = 21
total goals = 0 × 5 + 1 × 8 + 2 × 6 + 3 × 2 = 0 + 8 + 12 + 6 = 26
mean = 26/21 = 1.24 (3 s.f.)
median position = (21 + 1)/2 = 11th value
cumulative: 5 (0 goals), 13 (1 goal) - the 11th value is 1
median = 1

For grouped data, use midpoints: the mean = Σ(midpoint × frequency)/Σfrequency, and the median comes from the cumulative frequency curve (below). The grouped mean is an estimate because the midpoint stands in for every value in the class.

Charts and diagrams

  • Bar chart: bars with gaps for categorical or discrete data; height = frequency.
  • Pie chart: angle = (frequency/total) × 360°; label the sectors with the category.
  • Pictogram: a symbol represents a fixed number; a half symbol represents half that number.
  • Stem-and-leaf: a sorted display that keeps the actual values; the key explains the split (e.g. 3|4 means 34).
  • Frequency polygon: plot frequency against the midpoint of each class and join with straight lines.

Worked example (pie chart). 40 students choose a sport: football 16, tennis 10, swimming 8, other 6. Find the angle for football.

angle = (16/40) × 360 = 144 °

Worked example 2 (pie chart reverse). A sector of 72° represents 9 students. How many students in total?

72 ° represents 9  →  360 ° represents 9 × 360/72 = 45 students

Cumulative frequency diagrams

A cumulative frequency table adds frequencies as you move up the classes. Plot cumulative frequency against the upper class boundary and join with a smooth curve; then read positions:

median at n/2
lower quartile at n/4
upper quartile at 3n/4
IQR = Q3 - Q1

Worked example. A cumulative frequency curve for 60 students' marks: Q1 = 42, median = 55, Q3 = 68. Find the IQR and interpret it.

IQR = 68 - 42 = 26 marks
The middle 50% of students scored within 26 marks of each other;

Always read across to the curve and then down to the horizontal axis — and use the class boundaries, not the midpoints, for the plot positions.

Histograms and frequency density

When class widths differ, the height of a bar cannot be the frequency — a wide class would dominate unfairly. Instead, the area of each bar is proportional to the frequency:

frequency density = frequency / class width
frequency = frequency density x class width (area of the bar)

Worked example. Class 0–10 has frequency 20; 10–20 has frequency 30; 20–40 has frequency 40. Find the frequency densities.

0-10: 20/10 = 2.0
10-20: 30/10 = 3.0
20-40: 40/20 = 2.0

Reading a histogram backwards is the standard question: measure a bar's width and height, multiply to get the frequency, and read the class from the horizontal axis. Remember that the axes often use class boundaries, so a bar from 20 to 40 covers width 20.

Stem-and-leaf diagrams and frequency polygons

A stem-and-leaf diagram sorts data while keeping every value visible: the stem is the leading digit and the leaf the final digit, with a key such as 3|4 meaning 34. Interpreting one means reading the ordered leaves to find the median, the quartiles and the shape: the median is the middle leaf, Q1 and Q3 sit at the quarter and three-quarter positions, and the distribution's skew shows in where the leaves bunch.

A frequency polygon plots frequency against the midpoint of each class and joins the points with straight lines; it is the grouped-data equivalent of a line graph and makes comparisons between two distributions easy (plot both polygons on the same axes).

Worked example. The leaves for stem 4 are 1, 3, 3, 6, 8 and for stem 5 are 0, 2, 5. List the data in order and find the median.

values: 41, 43, 43, 46, 48, 50, 52, 55
n = 8, so the median is the mean of the 4th and 5th values:
(46 + 48)/2 = 47

Worked example 2 (interpreting). Explain what a long right-hand tail of leaves in a stem-and-leaf diagram indicates.

A long right tail means a few unusually high values: the data
are positively skewed, and the mean will be greater than the
median because the high values pull it upward.

Comparing distributions

Comparison questions want two statements: one about the average (which is higher) and one about the spread (which is more consistent). Use median and IQR together — they are robust to outliers — or mean and standard deviation when the data are symmetric and the syllabus supplies it.

Worked example. Class A: median 62, IQR 18. Class B: median 58, IQR 9. Compare.

Class A has the higher typical score (median 62 vs 58), but its
results are more spread out (IQR 18 vs 9), so Class B is more
consistent even though its middle score is lower.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Averages) Find the mean and range of 12, 15, 11, 19, 13. Answer: mean = (12 + 15 + 11 + 19 + 13)/5 = 70/5 = 14; range = largest − smallest = 19 − 11 = 8.
  2. (Frequency table) Values 1, 2, 3 with frequencies 4, 7, 9. Find the mean. Answer: mean = Σfx/Σf = (1 × 4 + 2 × 7 + 3 × 9)/(4 + 7 + 9) = (4 + 14 + 27)/20 = 45/20 = 2.25.
  3. (Median) Find the median of 2, 4, 4, 6, 9, 10. Answer: there are six values, so the median is the mean of the 3rd and 4th: (4 + 6)/2 = 5.
  4. (Pie chart) A sector of 90° represents 15 people. Find the total. Answer: 90° is 90/360 = ¼ of the circle, so the total is 15 ÷ ¼ = 15 × 4 = 60 people.
  5. (Cumulative frequency) For 80 values, where do you read the median? Answer: At cumulative frequency 40, reading across to the curve and down to the axis.
  6. (Histogram) A bar of width 5 has frequency density 4. Find its frequency. Answer: frequency = frequency density × class width = 4 × 5 = 20.
  7. (Frequency density) Class 30–50 has frequency 24. Find the frequency density. Answer: class width = 50 − 30 = 20, so frequency density = frequency/width = 24/20 = 1.2.
  8. (Compare) Two runners' times: A median 42 s, IQR 3 s; B median 40 s, IQR 8 s. Compare. Answer: B is faster typically (lower median) but less consistent (larger IQR); A is more reliable.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Median without ordering: the median is the middle of the ordered list. Forgetting to sort is the commonest data-handling error.
  • Even-count median: average the two middle values; do not pick one of them.
  • Grouped mean: use midpoints and label the answer an estimate — the midpoint is not the actual mean of the class.
  • Histogram heights: the vertical axis is frequency density, not frequency; area is the frequency. Reading the height as the frequency is the classic histogram error.
  • Cumulative frequency positions: plot against upper class boundaries and read the median at n/2 (not (n+1)/2 on the graph).
  • Pie chart arithmetic: check that the angles sum to 360° before answering the next part.
  • IQR direction: IQR = upper − lower quartile; a negative IQR means the quartiles are swapped.
  • Comparison claims: quote actual values ("median 62 vs 58"), not "better" without evidence.

Collecting and classifying data

Every statistical question starts with data, and the type of data decides which averages and diagrams are sensible. Before any calculation, decide where the data came from, what kind of values it holds, and whether the sample is fair. The subsections below set out these decisions in the order an examiner expects them to be made.

Primary and secondary data

Primary data is collected by the person who uses it, for example by a survey or an experiment carried out in class. Secondary data is taken from an existing source such as a census, a published table or a sports website. Primary data suits a question that needs a specific answer, while secondary data is quicker but may not match the exact question being asked. State which kind you have used when you describe an investigation.

Discrete and continuous data

Discrete data takes separate values that are usually counted, such as the number of goals scored or the number of people in a family. Continuous data can take any value in a range and is measured, such as height, mass or time. The distinction matters for grouping: a discrete table can use single values, while a continuous table needs class intervals with clear boundaries such as 10 ≤ t < 20.

Qualitative and quantitative data

Qualitative data describes a quality, such as eye colour or favourite subject, and cannot be averaged. Quantitative data is numerical and can be ordered and added. A mean is only meaningful for quantitative data, so a question that asks for the mean colour is answered by naming the mode or by stating that no mean exists.

Reading the question before the data

Underline what the question asks for before reading the table: a mode, a median, a range, a comparison or a conclusion. Many marks are lost by calculating the right number and then answering a different question. Note the units and the sample size at the same time, because the sample size is needed for a relative frequency and the units for a correct final statement.

Bias in samples and questionnaires

A sample is biased when some members of the population are more likely to be chosen than others. Asking only students in one class about a school-wide question is biased, and so is a question that leads the respondent, such as asking whether people agree that the bus service is too slow. A fair sample is random, large enough to represent the group, and drawn from the whole population being studied.

Judging the reliability of a conclusion

A conclusion is only as reliable as the data behind it. A small sample, an unrepresentative group or a question with an obvious bias weakens any statement drawn from it. A good answer names one weakness and suggests a change, such as taking a larger sample across a wider range of times or places.

Drawing a conclusion from a table

A conclusion must be supported by a number from the table and must answer the question asked. If the mean time for group A is 14 minutes and for group B is 18 minutes, the statement that group B took longer on average is supported, but a statement about all pupils in the school is not, because only two groups were measured.

Equations and symbols

Seven formulas cover the whole paper: the three averages with their range and interquartile range, the two histogram relations, and the pie-chart angle. Every one carries the same mark-scheme requirement — substitute, then state the answer in the units of the data, not as a bare number.

mean = sum of values / number of values Key: mean = the arithmetic average, in the same units as the data; sum of values = the total of every reading; number of values = how many readings there are. Uses every value, so one outlier moves it.

median = the value at position (n + 1)/2 in cumulative order Key: n = the number of values; the position is a count through the ordered list, not a value. For an even n the position falls between two values, so average them — picking one of the two is the commonest lost mark.

mode = the value with the highest frequency Key: mode = the most frequent value, in the same units as the data; for grouped data it is the modal class. The only average available for categorical data.

range = largest - smallest Key: largest and smallest = the extreme values of the data set; the range is their difference, in the data's units. It uses only two values, so a single outlier destroys it.

IQR = Q3 - Q1 Key: IQR = interquartile range, the spread of the middle 50% of the data (same units); Q3 = upper quartile at the 75% position; Q1 = lower quartile at the 25% position. A negative IQR means the quartiles have been swapped.

IQR = 68 - 42 = 26 marks Key: 68 = Q3, the mark at the 75% position; 42 = Q1, the mark at the 25% position; 26 marks = the IQR. Interpret it in words: the middle half of the students scored within 26 marks of each other.

frequency density = frequency / class width Key: frequency density = the height of the bar (no units, since it is a count divided by a width); frequency = the number of readings in the class; class width = upper boundary minus lower boundary (in the data's units). Use it only when the class widths differ — with equal widths the height may be the frequency.

frequency = frequency density x class width (area of the bar) Key: the same relation rearranged; reading a histogram backwards means measuring a bar's width and height and multiplying. In a histogram it is the area, never the height, that represents the frequency.

angle = (frequency/total) × 360° Key: frequency = the count in the sector; total = the total count for the whole chart; angle in degrees, and the sectors must sum to 360°. To go the other way, total = frequency × 360/angle.

mean = sum of (value x frequency) / sum of frequencies Key: value = each reading, or the midpoint of a class for grouped data (same units); frequency = how many times it occurs. With midpoints the answer is labelled an estimate, because the midpoint stands in for every value in the class.

title: Differentiation II — Study Notes
content:
Differentiation II

Product and Quotient Rules

  • (uv)′ = u′v + uv′
  • (u/v)′ = (u′v − uv′)/v²

Example: y = x² e^x gives dy/dx = 2x e^x + x² e^x = e^x(2x + x²).

Standard Derivatives

  • sin x → cos x; cos x → −sin x; tan x → sec²x
  • e^x → e^x; ln x → 1/x

Chain Rule Everywhere

d/dx [ln(3x)] = 3/(3x) = 1/x; d/dx [e^(2x)] = 2e^(2x); d/dx [sin²x] = 2 sin x cos x.

Implicit Differentiation

Differentiate both sides w.r.t. x, treating y as a function of x (terms in y pick up dy/dx).

Example: x² + y² = 25 → 2x + 2y(dy/dx) = 0 → dy/dx = −x/y.

Parametric Curves

For x = f(t), y = g(t): dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt).

Example: x = t², y = t³ gives dy/dx = 3t²/2t = 3t/2.

Exam tips: quote the rule you use; for tangent/normal on parametric curves, find t at the point first, and simplify implicit answers using the original equation.

Exam method: exponential, logarithmic and trigonometric rules

The derivative of eˣ is eˣ, and the derivative of e^(kx) is k e^(kx). The derivative of ln x is 1/x, and for ln(f(x)) the chain rule gives f′(x)/f(x). The derivative of sin x is cos x and of cos x is −sin x; for a function of kx, multiply by k.

When a product contains an exponential or trigonometric function, use the product rule d/dx(uv) = u dv/dx + v du/dx. Factorising the result, such as eˣ(1 + x), makes it easier to evaluate at a point.

Quotients use d/dx(u/v) = (v du/dx − u dv/dx)/v². Write tan x as sin x/cos x when the quotient rule is easier, and remember that d/dx(tan x) = sec² x.

Second derivatives follow by differentiating again. Use them to classify stationary points, or to check the concavity of a curve, when the question asks for it.

Exam cue: Show each rule as you apply it. Method marks are awarded for a correct product or chain step even if the final arithmetic is wrong.

Worked examples: combining rules

Example 1 (product rule). Differentiate y = x²(3x − 1)⁴.

Let u = x² and v = (3x − 1)⁴. Then du/dx = 2x and dv/dx = 4(3x − 1)³ × 3 = 12(3x − 1)³ (chain rule inside the product). So dy/dx = x² × 12(3x − 1)³ + (3x − 1)⁴ × 2x = 2x(3x − 1)³[6x + (3x − 1)] = 2x(3x − 1)³(9x − 1). Factorising at the end is what the examiner expects; leave a fully expanded answer only if asked.

Example 2 (quotient rule). Differentiate y = (x + 2)/(x² + 1). Let u = x + 2 and v = x² + 1. dy/dx = [1(x² + 1) − (x + 2)(2x)]/(x² + 1)² = (x² + 1 − 2x² − 4x)/(x² + 1)² = (1 − 4x − x²)/(x² + 1)². Check the numerator by substituting a value of x into the original and the answer: it is easy to lose the minus sign on the second term.

Trigonometric and exponential derivatives in context

  • d/dx (sin 3x) = 3 cos 3x, so the chain rule multiplies by the derivative of the inside. Writing sin 3x as sin(3x) makes the inside visible.
  • d/dx (e4x − 1) = 4e4x − 1. The derivative of e to a power is the same expression times the derivative of the power.
  • d/dx (ln(2x + 5)) = 2/(2x + 5). The derivative of ln x is 1/x, and the chain rule supplies the factor 2.
  • d/dx (cos² x) = 2 cos x × (−sin x) = −2 sin x cos x. Write powers of functions as (function)ⁿ and apply the chain rule once for each layer.

Implicit differentiation worked through

For x² + xy + y² = 7, differentiate each term with respect to x. A term in y is differentiated as a function of x and so gives dy/dx through the chain rule: 2x + (x dy/dx + y × 1) + 2y dy/dx = 0. Collect the dy/dx terms: dy/dx(x + 2y) = −(2x + y), so dy/dx = −(2x + y)/(x + 2y). The gradient is then found at a given point by substituting both coordinates.

Parametric differentiation

If x = t² and y = 2t³, then dx/dt = 2t and dy/dt = 6t², so dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt) = 6t²/(2t) = 3t. This is a chain-rule statement, not a new formula, and it is the reason the division is by dx/dt, not multiplied.

Common errors that lose marks

  • Forgetting the inner derivative in the chain rule, for example differentiating sin(3x) as cos(3x).
  • Writing the quotient rule with the denominator on the wrong side, or dropping the square on the denominator.
  • Treating dy/dx as a fraction and cancelling dy with dx in an implicit step; differentiate term by term instead.
  • Substituting the point into dy/dx before simplifying, which is fine, but forgetting to substitute both x and y when the expression still contains y.

title: Programming Concepts — Study Notes
content:
Programming Concepts

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): variables/constants, data types, selection/iteration, arrays, file handling, subroutines, scope, IDE tools.

1. Basics

Constants vs variables; types: INTEGER, REAL, CHAR, STRING, BOOLEAN, DATE; casting between them. Declaration with meaningful names.

2. Selection and iteration

IF score >= 50 THEN
  grade ← "pass"
ELSE
  grade ← "fail"
ENDIF

CASE OF grade
  "A" : OUTPUT "excellent"
  OTHERWISE : OUTPUT "keep going"
ENDCASE

REPEAT
  INPUT pin
UNTIL pin = storedPin

FOR i ← 1 TO 10 STEP 2 ... NEXT i

WHILE: condition first (may not run); REPEAT: runs at least once.

3. Arrays

Fixed size, indexed (0- or 1-based per spec); 2D arrays: row, column. Bounds errors when index leaves range. Traversal with FOR loops.

4. Files

OPENFILE "data.txt" FOR READ
READFILE "data.txt", line
CLOSEFILE "data.txt"

OPENFILE "log.txt" FOR APPEND
WRITEFILE "log.txt", record

Modes: READ, WRITE (overwrites), APPEND (adds).

5. Subroutines

Procedure (no return) vs function (returns value). Parameters by value (copy) vs reference (original). Local scope inside; global shared — declare deliberately, avoid overuse.

6. IDE tools

Syntax highlighting, autocompletion, breakpoints, single stepping, variable watch — name the tool and its debugging benefit.

Exam tips: use the exam pseudocode style exactly; for 2D arrays, loop rows outer/columns inner; choose WHILE vs REPEAT by "must it run once?"

Selection and iteration in practice

Selection uses IF and CASE structures to choose between paths, and a branch runs only when its condition is true. Iteration repeats a block of code. A count-controlled loop, such as FOR, runs a known number of times. A condition-controlled loop, such as WHILE or REPEAT, runs until a condition changes. A WHILE loop may run zero times, but a REPEAT loop always runs at least once.

A well-written program uses meaningful identifiers, indents its code to show structure, and includes comments that explain why a piece of code exists. Subroutines split a large problem into smaller tasks that can be tested separately.

Exam tip: choose the loop type from whether the number of repetitions is known in advance.

Worked example: a loop that totals marks
