Students can also sanity-check their answers by graphing the related functions or using a calculator to verify their solutions.
### Timing
This topic typically accounts for 10-15% of the total exam time. Students should budget around 20-30 minutes to answer questions on this topic, depending on the difficulty and complexity of the questions. It is essential to read the questions carefully and allocate time accordingly to ensure that all parts of the question are answered.

title: IGCSE Biology: Biological Molecules
content:
IGCSE Biology: Biological Molecules

Your body is a chemical machine, and the machine runs on four families of large molecules: carbohydrates for fuel and structure, lipids for membranes and long-term energy stores, proteins for everything from muscles to enzymes to antibodies, and nucleic acids (DNA) for information. This note takes each family from its smallest building block to its full structure and function, defines every bond by name, explains the food tests you will perform in Paper 6, and expands the DNA double helix base-by-base. By the end you should be able to look at any food test result or structural diagram and derive the reasoning rather than memorise it.

Elements, small molecules and large molecules

Life is built mainly from carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen (plus smaller amounts of sulfur and phosphorus). Small molecules (glucose, amino acids, fatty acids, nucleotides) join end-to-end to form large molecules (starch, protein, lipid, DNA) in condensation reactions — one molecule of water is removed each time a bond forms. The reverse, splitting a molecule by adding water, is hydrolysis; every digestive enzyme in the body is named after the bond it hydrolyses. Learn the pairing now and it pays off twice: in this topic and again in human nutrition.

Carbohydrates: sugars, starch, glycogen, cellulose

Monosaccharides are single sugars: glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆) is the body's immediate fuel. Disaccharides are two sugars joined: maltose (glucose + glucose), sucrose (glucose + fructose) and lactose (glucose + galactose), each joined by a glycosidic bond formed in condensation. Polysaccharides are long chains: starch (the plant store, a mixture of amylose and amylopectin), glycogen (the animal store, highly branched, in liver and muscle) and cellulose (the plant structural fibre, straight chains that cross-link for strength). Starch is tested with iodine solution: yellow-brown turns blue-black. Function summary: sugars for transport and instant energy; starch and glycogen for storage; cellulose for cell walls.

Lipids: fats, oils and membranes

A lipid is built from one glycerol joined to three fatty acids by ester bonds (three condensation reactions, three water molecules removed). Saturated lipids have no carbon-carbon double bonds in the tails (straight, pack tightly, solid at room temperature — animal fats); unsaturated lipids have one or more double bonds (kinks in the tails, loose packing, liquid — plant oils). Lipids store twice the energy per gram of carbohydrates, form waterproof layers, insulate (blubber, subcutaneous fat), protect organs, and make up the phospholipid bilayer of every cell membrane. The test for lipids is the ethanol emulsion test: dissolve the sample in ethanol, then add water — a milky-white emulsion means lipid present.

Proteins: amino acids to polypeptides

A protein is one or more polypeptide chains folded into a specific 3-D shape. Each amino acid has the same backbone — a central carbon with an amino group (–NH₂), a carboxyl group (–COOH), a hydrogen and a variable R group. In a condensation reaction the –NH₂ of one amino acid reacts with the –COOH of the next, releasing water and forming a peptide bond; repeat it and you have a polypeptide. The sequence of R groups (the primary structure) dictates how the chain folds (secondary and tertiary structure), and that fold dictates function: haemoglobin's shape cradles iron to carry oxygen; enzymes' active sites fit one substrate; antibodies' variable regions fit one antigen; keratin's coil makes hair and nails. The biuret test detects peptide bonds: add biuret solution (sodium hydroxide then copper(II) sulfate) — blue turns to purple if protein is present.

Enzymes as biological molecules (see the Enzymes note for the full kinetics)

Enzymes are globular proteins that act as biological catalysts: they speed reactions without being used up by lowering activation energy. Their active site is a specific-shaped pocket formed by the tertiary structure; only a substrate with a complementary shape fits (the induced-fit model shows the site flexing slightly as the substrate binds). Digestive enzymes hydrolyse their named bonds: carbohydrases (amylase) break glycosidic bonds in starch; proteases (pepsin, trypsin) break peptide bonds in proteins; lipases break ester bonds in lipids. Naming rule: the suffix –ase is an enzyme, the suffix –ose is a sugar, and the stem names the substrate.

Water and mineral ions — the small molecules that matter

Water is the biological solvent for a reason: its molecules are polar (slightly negative oxygen, slightly positive hydrogens), so they surround and dissolve ions and polar molecules, forming the cytoplasm, blood plasma and tissue fluid. Water's high specific heat capacity buffers temperature swings; its high latent heat of vaporisation makes sweating and transpiration effective coolers; its cohesion (hydrogen bonding between molecules) helps the water column in xylem; and it is a reactant in photosynthesis and hydrolysis. Mineral ions have named roles worth memorising: iron for haemoglobin, calcium for bones and clotting and muscle contraction, sodium for nerve impulses, phosphate for DNA and ATP, nitrate for amino acids and chlorophyll in plants, magnesium for chlorophyll, potassium for stomatal opening.

The four food tests at a glance

MoleculeTest reagentPositive resultTechnique note
StarchIodine solutionYellow-brown to blue-blackAdd the solution to the food on a white tile
Reducing sugarBenedict's solutionBlue to brick-red precipitateMust be heated in a water bath; green or orange for lower amounts
ProteinBiuret (sodium hydroxide then copper(II) sulfate)Blue to purpleDo not heat
LipidEthanol then waterWhite milky emulsionShake the sample with ethanol first, then add water

Worked example: the food-test decision tree and one full calculation

A student tests a mystery food for starch, reducing sugars, protein and lipid. Result log: iodine stays orange-brown; Benedict's solution turns from blue to brick-red after heating; biuret turns purple; the emulsion test gives no white cloud. Reading it step by step: iodine unchanged means no starch (the only positive is blue-black). Benedict's brick-red after heating means a reducing sugar is present (glucose gives the strongest red; moderate heat gives yellow-green). Biuret purple means peptide bonds, so protein is present. No emulsion means no lipid. Conclusion: a protein-rich food containing glucose — egg white with sugar, for instance. Now a calculation you can be asked to do with any of these: a 10 g food sample releases 2.5 kJ when burnt under a calorimeter that heated 50 g of water by 12 °C. Energy released = mass of water × specific heat capacity × temperature change = 50 g × 4.2 J/g°C × 12 °C = 2520 J = 2.52 kJ. Because 1 g of lipid yields about 38 kJ and 1 g of carbohydrate about 17 kJ, a high energy per gram means a fatty food.

DNA: the information molecule

DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) is a polymer of nucleotides. Each nucleotide has three parts: a deoxyribose sugar, a phosphate group, and one of four organic bases — adenine (A), thymine (T), cytosine (C), guanine (G). The nucleotides form a long chain by phosphodiester bonds between the sugar of one and the phosphate of the next (one sugar-phosphate backbone on each strand). Two strands then twist into a double helix, held by hydrogen bonds between complementary base pairs: A–T (two hydrogen bonds) and C–G (three hydrogen bonds). The pairing rule is strict and examinable: A only ever bonds with T, C only ever with G. Genes are short sections of DNA whose base sequence codes for the amino acid sequence of a protein; chromosomes are long DNA molecules wound around proteins; a gene is to a chromosome as one sentence is to a book.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Confusing "condensation" with "digestion": condensation builds polymers; digestion (hydrolysis) breaks them; every digestive enzyme performs hydrolysis.
  • Writing the Benedict's result as "turns red" without heating: the test must be heated (water bath), or it scores nothing.
  • Calling a protein's shape "its secondary structure" when the question wants "tertiary structure, which determines the active site".
  • Mixing up the base pairing: writing A–C or G–T in a DNA question is an instant lost mark.
  • Describing iodine for starch as turning "brown to black" — the required wording is "yellow-brown to blue-black".
  • Saying lipids "give more energy because they are bigger" — they store more per gram because their tails are more reduced (more C–H bonds).
  • In Paper 6, omitting the control (a known positive and negative sample) in a food-test plan; examiners award a mark for "compare with a known sample".
  • Writing "DNA is a protein": DNA is a nucleic acid; it is made of nucleotides, not amino acids.

Exam-style questions and answers

Q1. Describe how you would test a food sample for reducing sugar. (3 marks) Answer: dissolve or crush the sample in water and filter (1); add Benedict's solution and heat in a water bath (1); a brick-red (or orange/green) precipitate confirms reducing sugar (1).

Q2. Explain how a change in an amino acid sequence can change an enzyme's function. (3 marks) Answer: the sequence determines the tertiary fold (1); a different R group alters the shape or charge of the active site (1); so the substrate no longer fits and the rate of reaction falls (1).

Q3. State the two base-pairing rules in DNA and the number of hydrogen bonds in each. (2 marks) Answer: A–T with two hydrogen bonds; C–G with three hydrogen bonds (1 per pair).

Q4. Explain why lipids are better energy stores than carbohydrates. (2 marks) Answer: lipid tails contain more carbon-hydrogen bonds per gram so more energy is released per gram on oxidation (1); and they are insoluble so they do not affect water potential in cells (1).

Q5. Describe the role of water in living organisms. (3 marks) Answer: solvent for transport in blood and cytoplasm (1); high specific heat capacity buffers temperature (1); reactant in photosynthesis and hydrolysis, and cohesion aids water movement in xylem (1).

Equations and symbols

The quantitative side of this topic is small but examinable: one energy calculation from a calorimeter, and the two food-energy figures that let you say why a fatty food releases more. Everything else here is a symbol-and-unit reference for the structures and quantities the questions name.

Energy released = mass of water × specific heat capacity × temperature change Key: energy released = the chemical energy transferred from the burning food, in joules (J); mass of water = the mass heated in the calorimeter (g); specific heat capacity = 4.2 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹ for water; temperature change = rise in the water's temperature (°C). Keep grams and joules together — using kilograms here is the commonest arithmetic slip.

50 g × 4.2 J/g°C × 12 °C = 2520 J = 2.52 kJ Key: the numbers are the worked case in the note — 50 g of water warmed by 12 °C releases 2520 J, and 1 kJ = 1000 J, so the stored energy in that 10 g sample is 2.52 kJ. Divide by the mass of food burned to quote energy per gram, which is the figure the question then compares.

The quantities and their units

QuantitySymbol or phraseUnit
Energy released by a food sampleEJ, or kJ per gram
Mass of water heatedmg
Temperature riseΔT°C
Energy value of a nutrient—kJ g⁻¹ (lipid ≈ 38, carbohydrate ≈ 17)
Glucose formulaC₆H₁₂O₆—

The bonds and the molecules, written as formulae

  • Condensation removes one water molecule per bond formed; hydrolysis adds one back. The bond names are examinable: glycosidic (carbohydrate), ester (lipid), peptide (protein), phosphodiester (DNA).
  • Monosaccharide C₆H₁₂O₆ → disaccharide by one glycosidic bond; a polysaccharide is many such bonds in a chain.
  • DNA base pairing: A–T with two hydrogen bonds, C–G with three. Write the dash as the bond, never as "equals", because the pair is not a formula.

title: Functions — Study Notes
content:
Functions

A function maps each input in the domain to exactly one output in the range.

Composite Functions

fg(x) means f(g(x)) — apply g first, then f. Order matters.

Example: f(x) = 2x + 1, g(x) = x². Then fg(x) = 2x² + 1 but gf(x) = (2x + 1)².

Inverse Functions

f⁻¹ reverses f: f⁻¹f(x) = x. To find it, swap x and y in y = f(x) and rearrange.

Example: f(x) = 3x − 2 gives f⁻¹(x) = (x + 2)/3.

An inverse exists only if f is one-one. If not, restrict the domain (e.g. f(x) = x² for x ≥ 0 has f⁻¹(x) = √x). Graphically, y = f⁻¹(x) is the reflection of y = f(x) in the line y = x, and the range of f becomes the domain of f⁻¹.

Transformations

NotationEffect on y = f(x)
f(x) + atranslation up by a
f(x + a)translation left by a
a f(x)vertical stretch, factor a
f(ax)horizontal stretch, factor 1/a
−f(x)reflection in the x-axis
f(−x)reflection in the y-axis

Exam tips: state the domain of any inverse; when combining transformations, translations inside the bracket act in the opposite direction to the sign.

title: Edexcel IAL Computer Science: Data Types, Records and Arrays
content:
Edexcel IAL Computer Science: Data Types, Records and Arrays

Pearson Edexcel International Advanced Level in Computer Science, Unit 2 Practical Programming and Problem Solving: data types and records, and arrays. Choosing how data is represented decides what code can do with it — so this note follows each structure from declaration through memory layout to the algorithms that use it, with every index and pointer traced on a drawn memory diagram.

Primitive data types

TypeValuesOperationsWatch for
INTEGERWhole numbers in a fixed rangeArithmetic, comparisonOverflow at range limits
REAL/FLOATApproximate decimalsArithmeticRounding error; equality tests unreliable
CHAROne symbolComparison by code'A' ≠ 'a' in ASCII
STRINGSequences of charactersConcatenation, slicing, length, searchImmutable in Python; indexing from 0
BOOLEANTRUE / FALSEAND, OR, NOTTruthiness of 0 and ""
DATE/TIMECalendar valuesComparison, differenceTime zones and formats

Type casting: int→float widening is exact; float→int truncates (7.9 → 7) unless rounded; string→number raises errors on bad input (hence validation first); char→int yields the character code. Python's dynamic typing assigns without declaration, but the underlying values still have types — the difference between language convenience and data semantics is examinable.

Records

An array groups values of one type; a record groups values of different types describing one entity. A student record: {studentID: STRING, name: STRING, mark: INTEGER, isEnrolled: BOOLEAN}. Records give structure and meaning; fields are accessed by name, eliminating the "which index was the mark?" problem.

Memory view of one student record:

  +-----------+--------+------+------------+
  | studentID | name   | mark | isEnrolled |
  +-----------+--------+------+------------+
  | "S1024"   | "Chen" |  72  |    TRUE    |
  +-----------+--------+------+------------+

A file of records is the same shape repeated: each line/record one student -
the bridge between in-memory structures and file organisation (covered in
depth at A²).

Python dictionaries play the record role:
  student = {"studentID": "S1024", "name": "Chen", "mark": 72}
  student["mark"] = 75         # field update by name
  if student["mark"] >= 70: ...

Strings as character arrays

A string is conceptually an array of characters, so every array operation has a string analogue: indexing (name[0] is the first character), traversal (examining each character), searching (finding a substring), and length. String-specific operations the exam expects: concatenation, slicing, case conversion, and comparison by character code. Python immutability matters here — methods like upper() return new strings rather than modifying the original — and off-by-one errors appear in slicing (s[2:5] gives characters at indices 2, 3 and 4, not 5). Converting between characters and their codes (ord('A') = 65, chr(66) = 'B') links this note back to the representation work in Unit 1.

Array algorithms in full

Four operations cover most exam questions, and each has a cost worth stating. Traverse: visit every slot once — O(n), one loop. Search: linear search compares each slot until a match (O(n)); on sorted arrays, binary search halves the remaining range each comparison (O(log n)) — examined fully at A2. Sort: ordering an array (bubble, insertion, selection) so search and output are possible. Aggregate: count, sum, min, max, mean — one pass with a running value. Each pattern is a loop with a purpose; the trace table is the proof.

Arrays: declaration, indexing and processing

An array reserves a contiguous block, one slot per index, accessed in constant time. Declaration fixes the size and element type; index conventions matter (pseudocode often 0..n−1 or 1..n — always state which). Standard patterns: traverse, search, insert, delete, and compute aggregates.

Array of 6 marks, 0-based, after filling:

  index:  0    1    2    3    4    5
  value: 55   72   41   68   90   55

Linear search for 68 - every step:
  i=0: marks[0]=55, not 68
  i=1: marks[1]=72, not 68
  i=2: marks[2]=41, not 68
  i=3: marks[3]=68 - found; return index 3 (and stop)

  Worst case: searching for a value not present walks all 6 slots - n
  comparisons for n items: O(n). (Complexity is examined fully at A².)

Counting above the pass mark - aggregate pattern:
  count = 0
  for i in range(6):
      if marks[i] >= 50:
          count += 1
  # trace: i=0:55 yes (1); i=1:72 yes (2); i=2:41 no; i=3:68 yes (3);
  #        i=4:90 yes (4); i=5:55 yes (5) → count = 5

Insert shifting (insert 60 at position 2): shift elements right from the end -
  [55, 72, 41, 68, 90] → [55, 72, 60, 41, 68] with 90 dropped if full.
  Deleting at position 1 shifts left: [55, 60, 41, 68] - O(n) moves either way.

Bounds and traps: marks[6] on the array above is out of range (undefined behaviour in many languages; Python raises IndexError); an array is fixed size in classic languages (overflow/underflow on insert/delete), while Python lists are dynamic. Two-dimensional arrays are grids: declaration ARRAY[0:3, 0:2] gives 4 rows × 3 columns; a value needs both indices — board[row][col] — and traversal nests a loop within a loop.

2D array worked: seating plan 3 rows x 4 columns, mark every empty seat.

  seats = [[0, 1, 0, 0],
           [1, 1, 0, 1],
           [0, 0, 0, 0]]

  empty = 0
  for row in range(3):
      for col in range(4):
          if seats[row][col] == 0:
              empty += 1
  # row 0: 3 empty; row 1: 1 empty; row 2: 4 empty → empty = 8

Memory is linear (row-major: row 0's four cells, then row 1's...), which is
why nested loops traverse row by row.

Static versus dynamic structures

Static arrays: fixed size set at declaration, contiguous, fast indexed access, wasted or insufficient space decided in advance. Dynamic structures (Python lists, linked lists at A2) grow as needed with allocation overhead. Choosing: known fixed bounds and heavy indexing → static array; unpredictable growth and frequent inserts → dynamic. The exam wants the reason in terms of allocation and access cost.

Worked example: choosing a structure for three jobs.

1. Storing 30 daily temperatures with heavy day-by-day access:
   static array of 30 REALs - known size, constant-time indexed reads.

2. A task queue where items arrive and leave unpredictably:
   a dynamic structure (list or queue) - a fixed array would overflow.

3. Storing 200 employee records keyed by staff number:
   an array/FILE of records, or a dictionary - records give typed fields,
   a dictionary gives name-based access; sequential arrays suit batch
   processing, dictionaries suit lookups.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Off-by-one indices: an array declared [0:5] has six slots; a loop for i in range(6) covers exactly those.
  • Assuming the language's array bounds are checked; pseudocode questions want you to state the guard, not assume one.
  • Using float for money (rounding error) or equality tests on floats (use a tolerance).
  • Confusing records with arrays: uniform typed slots versus named mixed fields of one entity.
  • 2D indexing order: seats[row][col], and nested loops must match that order.
  • Forgetting that insertion/deletion in arrays shifts elements (O(n)) — cost statements earn marks.
  • Declaring a fixed array for data of unpredictable size without discussing the overflow risk.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Unit 2, 3 marks). Explain the difference between a record and an array.

Answer: An array stores multiple values of the same data type under one name, accessed by index — suited to lists of like values. A record groups fields of different types describing one entity (a student: string name, integer mark, boolean status), accessed by field name. Arrays suit collections; records suit entities.

Question 2 (Unit 2, 4 marks). An array holds 5 values at indices 1–5. Describe what happens when a value is inserted at index 2.

Answer: To make room, elements at indices 5 down to 2 are each shifted one position up (5→6 slot if space, else the last is lost in fixed arrays); the new value is written at index 2. The operation takes O(n) moves, and a bounds check must confirm the array is not full before shifting.

Question 3 (Unit 2, 4 marks). Write pseudocode to find the smallest value in an array of 100 numbers and explain the role of the first element.

Answer: smallest <- numbers[1]; FOR i <- 2 TO 100; IF numbers[i] < smallest THEN; smallest <- numbers[i]; ENDIF; NEXT i; OUTPUT smallest. Initialising smallest with the first element guarantees a real value from the array is the starting benchmark (initialising with 0 would fail for all-negative data).

Question 4 (Unit 2, 3 marks). Explain two differences between static and dynamic data structures.

Answer: A static structure's size is fixed at declaration — memory is reserved once, giving fast indexed access but overflow risk or wasted space. A dynamic structure grows and shrinks during execution by allocating memory as needed — flexible for unpredictable data volumes, at the cost of allocation overhead and (for linked structures) slower indexed access.

Question 5 (Unit 2, 4 marks). Describe how a 2D array could represent a noughts-and-crosses board and how a win is checked.

Answer: A 3×3 array stores each cell's state (empty, X, O), addressed board[row][col]. A win check tests the eight lines: three rows (board[0][0]=board[0][1]=board[0][2], etc.), three columns, and two diagonals — each test comparing three cells for equality and not-empty.

Question 6 (Unit 2, 3 marks). Explain why money should not be stored in a float variable.

Answer: Binary floating point cannot represent many decimal fractions exactly (0.1 has no finite binary expansion), so repeated arithmetic accumulates rounding error and balance checks drift out. Money is stored as integer minor units (pence) or a decimal type, with rounding rules applied explicitly at defined points.

Records in files are the raw material of information systems; the next note shows how databases organise them at scale.

title: Astronomy and Cosmology — Study Notes
content:
Astronomy and Cosmology

Luminosity and Intensity

Luminosity L is total power radiated (W). Intensity at distance d: I = L/(4πd²) — the key to distances.

Standard candles (Cepheid variables, Type Ia supernovae) have known L, so measuring I gives d.

Example: the Sun: I = 1370 W m⁻² at d = 1.5 × 10¹¹ m gives L ≈ 3.9 × 10²⁶ W.

Stellar radii (25.2)

A star radiates as a black body of surface temperature T, so L = 4πR²σT⁴. Rearranged, R = √(L / 4πσT⁴). Luminosity therefore depends on both radius and temperature.

Example: with L = 3.9 × 10²⁶ W and T = 5800 K, R = √(3.9 × 10²⁶ / (4π × 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ × 5800⁴)) ≈ 7.0 × 10⁸ m.

Doubling the temperature at fixed radius multiplies L by 2⁴ = 16. A cool red giant can be far more luminous than the Sun because its radius is very large.

Wien and Stefan–Boltzmann

  • Wien: λ_max T = 2.9 × 10⁻³ m K — hotter stars are bluer
  • Stefan: L = σAT⁴, σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸

Hubble's Law

Galaxies recede with v = Hd, H₀ ≈ 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹. Redshift z = Δλ/λ ≈ v/c for small z.

Example: a galaxy at 100 Mpc recedes at v = 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ × 100 × 3.09 × 10²² ≈ 6800 km s⁻¹.

The Big Bang

Evidence: Hubble expansion, cosmic microwave background (2.7 K), hydrogen/helium abundance. Age estimate: t ≈ 1/H₀ ≈ 14 billion years. The fate question: critical density, Ω.

Exam tips: convert Mpc to metres (×3.09 × 10²²) before Hubble arithmetic; distinguish redshift of light from distance ladder methods.

Standard candles and the cosmic distance ladder

A standard candle is an object whose luminosity is known, such as a Type Ia supernova or a Cepheid variable star. Comparing its known luminosity with its observed brightness gives its distance, using the inverse-square law. Stellar radii can be found in the same way: the luminosity L = 4πR2σT4 links radius, surface temperature and output power.

Exam tip: state which assumption you are making, such as that the star radiates as a black body, before you calculate the radius.

Worked example: distance from parallax

A star has a parallax angle of 0.25 arcseconds when observed from opposite sides of the Earth's orbit. The distance in parsecs is d = 1/p = 1/0.25 = 4.0 pc. One parsec is about 3.26 light-years, so the star is roughly 13 light-years away. Parallax is the most direct distance method, and it works only for nearby stars.

Inverse-square law for brightness

The apparent brightness of a star falls as the inverse square of its distance. A star that is four times as far away appears 4² = 16 times fainter, for the same luminosity. This is why luminosity, which is intrinsic, must be distinguished from apparent brightness, which depends on distance.

Hubble's law and the expanding universe

  • Hubble's law states that v = H₀d, where v is the recession speed and d is the distance.
  • With H₀ ≈ 70 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹, a galaxy 100 Mpc away recedes at about 7000 km s⁻¹.
  • Redshift shows that most galaxies are moving away from us, which is evidence that the universe is expanding.

Exam point: the Big Bang model gives an age for the universe of about 13.8 billion years, consistent with the cosmic microwave background, which is the faint, nearly uniform radiation left from the early universe.

Quick revision: Integration II

Mathematics — A2 (9709). With linear arguments: ∫ e^(3x) dx = e^(3x)/3 + c; ∫ cos 2x dx = sin 2x/2 + c.

Key areas to revise

  • Standard Integrals
  • Substitution
  • Integration by Parts
  • Partial Fractions

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Key points to remember

Integration by substitution reverses the chain rule. Choose u as the inner function, find du/dx, and replace dx so that the integral is in terms of u only. Change the limits when you use a definite integral, or substitute back into x before you evaluate it.

Integration by parts uses ∫u (dv/dx) dx = uv − ∫v (du/dx) dx. Choose u to be the part that becomes simpler when differentiated, such as a polynomial, and dv/dx the part that is easy to integrate, such as eˣ or sin x. Partial fractions can be used first to make an integral of a rational function manageable.

title: IGCSE Physics: Forces and Motion
content:
IGCSE Physics: Forces and Motion

Cambridge IGCSE Physics 0625 (2026–2028), Topic 1 Motion, forces and energy: statements 1.2 Motion, 1.3 Mass and weight, 1.5 Forces and 1.6 Momentum. This is the mechanics spine of the whole course, and it is where the Paper 4 structured calculation marks are won and lost. Almost every mechanics question begins the same way: label the velocities, find the resultant force, then choose the equation. The ideas below are built from absolute zero, but the definitions are examinable word for word, so learn them exactly as stated.

Speed, velocity and acceleration

Start with an analogy. A car's speedometer tells you how fast the car is covering ground; it says nothing about which way the car points. That everyday reading is speed. Add a compass direction to it and you have velocity. Speed is a scalar (size only); velocity is a vector (size and direction), and that single distinction runs through the entire course.

QuantityDefinitionSymbol and unitScalar or vector
DistanceTotal length of the path travelleds, metre (m)Scalar
DisplacementDistance in a stated straight-line direction from a start points, metre (m)Vector
SpeedDistance travelled per unit timev, metre per second (m s⁻¹)Scalar
VelocityRate of change of displacement, i.e. speed in a stated directionv, metre per second (m s⁻¹)Vector
AccelerationRate of change of velocitya, metre per second squared (m s⁻²)Vector

The two equations every question uses are:

average speed = total distance travelled / total time taken        v = s / t
acceleration = (final velocity - initial velocity) / time taken    a = (v - u) / t

Here u is the initial velocity, v is the final velocity, and t is the time taken. The SI units must be metres, seconds and metres per second before the equations are used; convert kilometres to metres and minutes to seconds first. The sign convention is the student's choice but must be stated: pick one direction as positive (upwards or forwards is usual), then velocities and accelerations in the opposite direction are negative. A negative acceleration that slows an object is often called a deceleration. An object thrown upwards has g = 9.81 m s⁻² downwards throughout its flight, so if up is positive its acceleration is −9.81 m s⁻² at every point, including the instant it stops at the top.

Average speed over a whole journey is not the average of the speeds. It is total distance divided by total time, so a car that covers 100 km at 50 km h⁻¹ and the next 100 km at 100 km h⁻¹ has an average speed of 200 km in 3 hours, which is 67 km h⁻¹, not 75 km h⁻¹.

Describing motion with graphs

Graphs are the language of this topic, and Paper 4 nearly always carries one. Two kinds do all the work.

FeatureDistance–time graphSpeed–time graph
GradientSpeed (or velocity)Acceleration
Area under the graphNot meaningfulDistance travelled
Horizontal lineObject at restConstant speed, zero acceleration
Straight sloping lineConstant speedConstant acceleration
CurveChanging speed (draw a tangent to find the speed at a point)Changing acceleration

On a distance–time graph the gradient is the distance moved divided by the time taken, which is the speed. On a speed–time graph the gradient is the change in speed divided by the time taken, which is the acceleration, and the area under the graph is made of rectangles (speed × time = distance) and triangles (½ × base × height), so it gives the total distance travelled. Drawing a tangent to a curve at a point is a Paper 6 skill: place the ruler so it just touches the curve, extend the line well past the curve on both sides, and take two distant points on the tangent to work out its gradient.

Paper 6 link. A trolley pulled by a falling mass leaves dots on ticker tape from a 50 Hz timer, so consecutive dots are 0.02 s apart. The distance between successive dots gives the speed over that interval, and a speed–time graph of those speeds has a gradient equal to the trolley's acceleration. Measuring a short distance with a ruler and dividing by 0.02 s is exactly the averaging technique in statement 1.1.

Mass, weight and gravitational field strength

Mass is the amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms with a balance. It does not change wherever the object is taken: the mass of an astronaut is the same on the Moon as on Earth. Weight is the force of gravity on that mass, measured in newtons with a spring balance, and it is a vector because gravity always pulls towards the centre of the attracting body. The astronaut's weight on the Moon is about one sixth of that on Earth because the Moon's gravitational field is weaker.

weight = mass x gravitational field strength        W = m g
  • W: weight in newtons (N). Weight is a vector, and its direction is straight down towards the centre of the Earth.
  • m: mass in kilograms (kg). Mass is a scalar.
  • g: gravitational field strength in newtons per kilogram (N kg⁻¹); on Earth g ≈ 9.81 N kg⁻¹, which is numerically the same as the free-fall acceleration 9.81 m s⁻².

Examination questions give the value of g to use, and many IGCSE papers round it to 10 N kg⁻¹ to keep the arithmetic simple. Always use the value printed in the question, and quote it in your answer when you substitute. Never confuse the two instruments: a balance compares masses and would give the same reading on the Moon, while a newton meter compares weights and would not.

Forces and their effects

A force is a push or a pull, measured in newtons, and it is a vector: direction matters. Forces can change an object's speed, change its direction of travel, or change its shape. Newton's first law states that an object remains at rest, or continues at constant velocity in a straight line, unless a resultant (net) force acts on it. Motion only changes when forces are unbalanced; a book resting on a table has weight and an equal upward normal contact force acting on it, so its resultant force is zero and it does not accelerate.

The resultant force is the single force that has the same effect as all the real forces combined. Two people pushing a trolley the same way add; pushing opposite ways subtract; forces at right angles combine by Pythagoras on the diagonal (Supplement). Newton's second law, in the form examined at IGCSE, is a Supplement statement:

resultant force = mass x acceleration        F = m a
  • F: resultant force in newtons (N), positive in the chosen positive direction.
  • m: mass in kilograms (kg).
  • a: acceleration in metres per second squared (m s⁻²), in the same direction as F.

The equation only works with the resultant force and only in SI units. If a car's engine produces 3000 N while drag is 1000 N, the resultant is 2000 N, and it is that 2000 N that goes into F = ma.

Friction and drag. Friction acts where surfaces touch and always opposes the motion or the tendency to move. Drag (air resistance or water resistance) opposes motion through a fluid and grows as the speed grows. A falling object released from rest therefore accelerates at first, because weight exceeds drag; as speed rises, drag rises until it equals the weight. From that moment the resultant force is zero, the acceleration is zero, and the object falls at terminal velocity. This is a Supplement explanation and it is a regular Paper 4 six-mark question: describe the motion in stages and use the words resultant force, drag and terminal velocity.

Springs and extension. A load hung on a spring stretches it. The relationship is summarised on a load–extension graph: a straight line through the origin shows extension proportional to load, up to the limit of proportionality. The stiffness of the spring is its spring constant:

force = spring constant x extension        F = k x
  • F: force applied to the spring in newtons (N).
  • k: spring constant in newtons per metre (N m⁻¹); larger k means a stiffer spring.
  • x: extension in metres (m). Extension = stretched length − original length, so it is a scalar in practice.

Beyond the limit of proportionality the line curves: the spring is permanently deformed and does not return to its original length when the load is removed. Doubling the load doubles the extension only while the graph is still a straight line. Two identical springs in series share the load and stretch twice as far; in parallel they share the load and stretch half as far (Supplement).

Turning effects of forces: moments

A force that does not act through a pivot makes an object turn. The size of that turning effect is the moment of the force:

moment of a force = force x perpendicular distance from the pivot        M = F d
  • M: moment in newton metres (N m). A moment is a vector in the sense that it turns clockwise or anticlockwise, and that sense must be carried through the calculation as a sign.
  • F: force in newtons (N).
  • d: perpendicular distance from the line of action of the force to the pivot in metres (m).

The word perpendicular is the whole mark. If a 10 N force acts at 30° to a spanner handle, the moment uses the perpendicular component of the force, or equivalently the perpendicular distance. For an object in equilibrium the principle of moments applies: the sum of the clockwise moments about any pivot equals the sum of the anticlockwise moments, and the resultant force is zero. A see-saw balances when the anticlockwise moment of the near child equals the clockwise moment of the far child; moving either child outwards increases that child's moment without changing their weight. Two equal and opposite forces whose lines of action do not coincide form a couple, which produces rotation without translation, as when a steering wheel is turned with both hands.

Centre of gravity and stability

The centre of gravity of an object is the single point through which its entire weight may be taken to act. For a uniform object it is the geometric centre; for a lamina (a flat sheet) it can be found experimentally by the plumb-line method, which is a classic Paper 6 task: hang the lamina freely from one hole, hang a plumb line from the same pin, and mark the line; repeat from a second hole; the lines cross at the centre of gravity.

Stability depends on where that point sits relative to the base. An object topples when the line of action of its weight falls outside its base, because the weight then produces a resultant moment that overturns it. Wide bases and low centres of gravity make objects stable (racing cars carry ballast low; tall trucks are loaded low), and top-heavy objects with narrow bases topple easily.

Momentum and impulse

Momentum is the quantity of motion a moving object carries: a lorry at 20 m s⁻¹ is far harder to stop than a bicycle at the same speed. Momentum is a Supplement statement for 0625 and is a favourite for Paper 4 calculation questions.

momentum = mass x velocity        p = m v
impulse = change in momentum = resultant force x time        F t = m v - m u
  • p: momentum in kilogram metres per second (kg m s⁻¹). Momentum is a vector, in the same direction as the velocity, so the sign convention chosen at the start must be applied to every velocity.
  • m: mass in kilograms (kg); v and u: final and initial velocity in metres per second (m s⁻¹), positive in the chosen positive direction.
  • Impulse: newton seconds (N s), equal to the change in momentum.

The principle of conservation of momentum: in a closed system, where no external resultant force acts, the total momentum before an event equals the total momentum after it. Total means the vector sum: momenta in opposite directions carry opposite signs. This one statement solves collisions, explosions and recoil problems. Newton's second law in its full form is implied here: the resultant force equals the rate of change of momentum, F = (mv − mu)/t, which is why increasing the time of impact reduces the force for the same change in momentum — that is how airbags, crash barriers and landing on a bent knee work.

Worked example: collision and impact force

Collision. A 1200 kg car travelling at 15 m s⁻¹ runs into a stationary 800 kg car and the two lock together. Find their common velocity. Take the first car's direction as positive.

total momentum before = 1200 × 15 + 800 × 0 = 18 000 kg m s⁻¹
total momentum after = (1200 + 800) v = 2000 v
2000 v = 18 000, so v = 9 m s⁻¹, in the original direction

The combined cars move at 9 m s⁻¹ in the direction the first car was travelling. Note that kinetic energy is not conserved in this collision — most of it is lost to sound and deformation — but momentum is always conserved.

Impact force. A 0.50 kg ball travelling at 12 m s⁻¹ hits a wall and rebounds at 8 m s⁻¹ in the opposite direction. The contact lasts 0.050 s. Find the average force on the ball. Take the initial direction as positive, so the rebound velocity is −8 m s⁻¹.

change in momentum = m v - m u = 0.50 x (-8) - 0.50 × 12 = -4.0 - 6.0 = -10 kg m s⁻¹
average force = change in momentum / time = -10 / 0.050 = -200 N

The minus sign shows the force acts opposite to the ball's initial motion, which is what a wall does. The magnitude is 200 N. Getting the sign of the rebound velocity wrong is the single most common error in this topic, and it doubles the answer.

Common mistakes

  • Confusing mass and weight: mass is in kilograms and never changes; weight is in newtons and equals mg. A mass of 5 kg has a weight of about 50 N, not 5 kg.
  • Using the average of speeds for the average speed of a journey; it is always total distance over total time.
  • Reading the wrong quantity from a graph: gradient on a distance–time graph is speed, gradient on a speed–time graph is acceleration, and only the speed–time graph has a meaningful area.
  • Putting any force into F = ma. Only the resultant force gives the acceleration, so add and subtract the forces first.
  • Using a slanted distance in a moment calculation; d is measured perpendicular to the line of action of the force.
  • Losing the sign of a velocity in a momentum calculation. Reversal of direction is a sign change, and the total momentum is a vector sum, not a sum of sizes.
  • Using g = 9.81 when the question says take g = 10 N kg⁻¹, and forgetting to state which value was used.
  • Adding a force in newtons to a momentum in kg m s⁻¹; if the units do not match, the physics does not either.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 4, 3 marks). A cyclist starts from rest and reaches 8.0 m s⁻¹ in 5.0 s. Calculate the average acceleration and the distance travelled.

Answer: a = (v − u)/t = (8.0 − 0)/5.0 = 1.6 m s⁻². Distance = average speed × time = ½(0 + 8.0) × 5.0 = 20 m. (A speed–time graph of the motion is a triangle of area ½ × 5.0 × 8.0 = 20 m.)

Question 2 (Paper 4, 4 marks). A skydiver of mass 80 kg falls. Explain, using forces, why she reaches a terminal velocity, and state the size of the drag force at that moment.

Answer: Weight W = mg = 80 × 9.8 = 784 N downwards (≈ 800 N if g = 10 is taken). At first weight exceeds drag, so there is a downward resultant force and she accelerates. As speed increases, drag increases. When drag equals the weight the resultant force is zero, acceleration is zero, and she falls at constant terminal velocity. The drag force is then 784 N (or 800 N) upwards.

Question 3 (Paper 2 style). Which statement about a ball thrown straight up is correct? A: its acceleration at the top is zero; B: its velocity at the top is zero; C: its momentum at the top is maximum; D: its weight is zero at the top. Answer: B. The velocity is instantaneously zero at the top, but g still acts there, so the acceleration is 9.81 m s⁻² downwards and the weight is unchanged. Paper 2 setters rely on this confusion between velocity and acceleration.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 4 marks). A 1500 kg car travelling at 20 m s⁻¹ brakes to a stop in 4.0 s. Calculate the braking force.

Answer: change in momentum = mv − mu = 1500 × 0 − 1500 × 20 = −30 000 kg m s⁻¹. Force = change in momentum / time = −30 000 / 4.0 = −7500 N. The braking force is 7500 N opposite to the motion.

Question 5 (Paper 6 style). Describe how you would find the centre of gravity of an irregular lamina.

Answer: Hang the lamina from a pin through a hole near its edge so it swings freely. Hang a plumb line from the same pin and, when everything is at rest, mark the plumb-line position on the lamina. Repeat with the lamina hung from a second hole. The point where the two marked lines cross is the centre of gravity. The plumb line marks the vertical through the pivot, and the centre of gravity lies on it in both cases.

Question 6 (Paper 4, 3 marks). A 0.20 kg ball moving at 6.0 m s⁻¹ collides with an identical ball at rest and stops dead. Find the velocity of the second ball after the impact.

Answer: total momentum before = 0.20 × 6.0 = 1.2 kg m s⁻¹. After the impact the first ball has zero momentum, so 0.20 × v = 1.2 and v = 6.0 m s⁻¹ in the original direction.

Momentum, moments and Newton's laws are the tools; the next step is what those forces actually do to energy.

Reading a motion graph line by line

A velocity–time graph is not a picture of the journey. It is a table of two quantities, drawn so that the arithmetic can be done with a ruler. That is the whole idea, and it is why the graph rewards a student who knows what to look for and punishes one who reads it like a map.

Read the graph above in the order the journey happened, and at every segment ask two questions: what is the gradient and what is the area underneath. The answers are always the same two quantities, just measured over different intervals.

SegmentGradient (Δv ÷ Δt)What it meansArea under that segment
0 s to 4 s24 ÷ 4 = 6 m s⁻²Constant acceleration: the velocity rises by 6 m s⁻¹ every second½ × 4 × 24 = 48 m
4 s to 8 s0 ÷ 4 = 0Constant velocity — not at rest. The car is still moving at 24 m s⁻¹4 × 24 = 96 m
8 s to 10 s−24 ÷ 2 = −12 m s⁻²Deceleration: the velocity falls 12 m s⁻¹ each second½ × 2 × 24 = 24 m

a = (v − u) / t Key: a = acceleration (m s⁻²); v = final velocity (m s⁻¹); u = initial velocity (m s⁻¹); t = time taken (s). The gradient is this equation rearranged — nothing more.

Worked example. Find the total distance travelled and the average speed over the ten seconds.

Distance is the area under the whole line, so add the three segments:
s = 48 m + 96 m + 24 m = 168 m

Average speed is total distance over total time, never the mean of the speeds:
vavg = s / t = 168 m ÷ 10 s = 16.8 m s⁻¹

Notice what that number is not. The car spent most of the journey at 24 m s⁻¹, yet its average is 16.8 m s⁻¹, because the first four seconds and the last two were slower. A student who averages 6, 0 and −12 (or 24 and 0) gets a number with no meaning at all.

The self-check that proves the area rule. For the first four seconds, u = 0, a = 6 m s⁻² and t = 4 s, so the equation of motion gives
s = u t + ½ a t² = 0 + ½ × 6 × 4² = 48 m
which is exactly the triangle's area. The area rule is not a separate law — it is that equation, drawn.

Where marks are lost. Three traps account for almost every lost mark on this topic. Reading a flat line as "stopped" (it is constant velocity; only a line on the time axis is stationary). Measuring distance from the height of the line rather than the area under it. And forgetting that a negative velocity means travel in the opposite direction, so a journey out and back has a displacement near zero even though the distance is large — the areas on either side of the axis cancel, and the examiner asks for "distance" or "displacement" precisely to see whether you noticed.

Equations and symbols

Every equation 0625 uses across statements 1.2, 1.3, 1.5 and 1.6, in the form the mark scheme expects. Motion equations assume constant acceleration in a straight line; the force equations are vector equations, so direction is part of the answer.

Motion

v = Δs / Δt
Key: v = speed or velocity (m/s); Δs = change in displacement (m); Δt = time interval (s). Velocity is a vector, so a change of direction is a change of velocity even at constant speed.

a = Δv / Δt = (v − u) / t
Key: a = acceleration (m/s²); v = final velocity (m/s); u = initial velocity (m/s); t = time taken (s). A negative a means deceleration.

v² = u² + 2as
Key: v = final velocity (m/s); u = initial velocity (m/s); a = constant acceleration (m/s²); s = displacement (m). Use it whenever time is neither given nor asked for.

s = ut + ½at²
Key: s = displacement (m); u = initial velocity (m/s); t = time (s); a = acceleration (m/s²). For a body released from rest, u = 0 and the distance is ½at².

s = ½(u + v)t
Key: s = displacement (m); u, v = initial and final velocity (m/s); t = time (s). This is the area under a velocity–time graph for constant acceleration, which is why the area is always a valid route to distance.

g = 9.8 N/kg (9.8 m/s²)
Key: g = gravitational field strength near the Earth's surface; numerically equal to free-fall acceleration, so a dropped body gains 9.8 m/s of speed each second in the absence of air resistance.

Mass, weight and force

W = mg
Key: W = weight (N); m = mass (kg); g = gravitational field strength (N/kg), 9.8 on Earth and about 1.6 on the Moon. Mass stays in kilograms and does not change with location; weight is the force and does.

F = ma
Key: F = resultant force (N); m = mass (kg); a = acceleration (m/s²). F is the resultant after friction and air resistance are subtracted, which is the single most common lost mark in this topic.

R = √(F₁² + F₂²)
Key: R = magnitude of the resultant (N); F₁, F₂ = two perpendicular forces (N). For forces along one line, add them when they point the same way and subtract when they oppose.

Balanced forces: ΣF = 0 implies a = 0
Key: ΣF = the vector sum of all forces (N); a = acceleration (m/s²). Zero resultant means at rest or at constant velocity — never "no forces acting".

Moments and springs

M = F × d
Key: M = moment of the force (N m); F = the force (N); d = the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force (m). A distance measured along a slant gives the wrong moment.

Σ clockwise moments = Σ anticlockwise moments
Key: the principle of moments, for a body in equilibrium. Each term is a force times its perpendicular distance (N m).

F = kx
Key: F = load or tension (N); k = spring constant (N/m or N/cm); x = extension beyond the natural length (m or cm). Valid only up to the limit of proportionality; beyond it the graph curves and the equation stops applying.

k = F / x
Key: k = spring constant (N/m); found as the gradient of the straight part of a force–extension graph, not from a single point beyond the limit.

Momentum

p = mv
Key: p = momentum (kg m/s); m = mass (kg); v = velocity (m/s). Momentum is a vector: opposite directions need opposite signs.

F = Δp / Δt
Key: F = average force acting (N); Δp = change in momentum (kg m/s); Δt = time over which it acts (s). This is the form that explains crumple zones and seatbelts: the same Δp spread over a longer Δt gives a smaller F.

m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂
Key: m₁, m₂ = masses (kg); u₁, u₂ = velocities before the collision (m/s); v₁, v₂ = velocities after (m/s). Total momentum is conserved when no external resultant force acts; kinetic energy is not necessarily conserved.

title: Data Types and File Organisation — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Data Types and File Organisation

Computer Science — A2. A user-defined type is derived from existing types. An enumerated type lists named values in order: TYPE Months = (Jan, Feb, Mar ...). Internally each value is an integer index starting at 0. Pointer types store a memory address; the dereference operator returns the value at that address, which is how linked structures reference their nodes. Set types store unordered collections of distinct values from an ordinal base type, supporting union, intersection and difference.

Key areas to revise

  • User-Defined Types
  • Records
  • File Organisation
  • Hashing

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

### Worked example A hash function maps each key to a storage address. If the file has 100 slots and the key is an integer n, the address could be n mod 100. Two keys that give the same address are a collision, and the file must provide a method such as an overflow area to store the second record.

title: Oscillations and Waves II — Quick Revision Summary

Physics — A2. Progressive waves transfer energy; stationary waves store it in loops. Stationary patterns arise from two identical waves travelling in opposite directions (reflections on strings, air columns).
