title: Biotechnology and Genetic Modification
content:
Biotechnology and Genetic Modification

Cambridge IGCSE Biology 0610, Extended route, topic 21 (statements 21.1–21.3). Biotechnology and microorganisms, industrial fermentation with aseptic technique, and genetic modification with its applications and risks.

21.1 to 21.2 Biotechnology

  • Biotechnology uses living organisms or their products industrially. Microorganisms ferment sugars to make bread, beer, yoghurt and cheese, and are used to produce insulin and antibiotics.
  • Industrial fermentation controls temperature, pH, nutrient supply and oxygen, with aseptic technique preventing contamination by unwanted microbes. Sterilise equipment before, work near a flame, and autoclave waste after.

21.3 Genetic modification

  • Genetic modification transfers a gene for a desired characteristic into another organism: extract the gene, insert it into a vector (plasmid or virus), introduce the vector into host cells, and select the modified cells. Examples include insulin-producing bacteria, GM crops with pest resistance, and Golden Rice enriched with beta-carotene.
  • Benefits include higher yields and improved nutrition; risks include genes spreading to wild populations, effects on biodiversity, and consumer concerns.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Process chain, applied to producing human insulin in bacteria: the human insulin gene is cut with a restriction enzyme, joined to a plasmid with DNA ligase, and the recombinant plasmid is put into bacteria which then produce the insulin as they multiply. Name restriction enzyme and DNA ligase — both appear as separate marks every year.
  • Evaluation reasoning, applied to GM crops in a developing country: weigh higher yield and lower pesticide use against seed costs, gene flow to wild relatives, and farmer dependency. Reach a justified judgement; both sides must appear for the top band.
  • Aseptic technique reasoning, applied to why a fermenter must be sterilised first: unwanted microbes would compete for nutrients and could produce toxic or unwanted products, ruining the batch. Link each technique step to the reason it exists.

Common errors

  • Saying GM "changes the animal's own genes by breeding". GM transfers a gene directly across species boundaries.
  • Confusing restriction enzymes (cut) with DNA ligase (join).
  • Forgetting aseptic technique is needed AFTER as well as before fermentation, for safe disposal.

title: Materials: Deformation — Study Notes
content:
Materials: deformation

Edexcel International A Level Physics — Unit 1 (WPH11), sat at AS.

Stress and strain

  • Stress = F ÷ A, where A is the cross-sectional area perpendicular to the force. Unit: pascal (Pa), where 1 Pa = 1 N m⁻².
  • Strain = extension ÷ original length. It has no unit.

Young modulus

Young modulus E = stress ÷ strain, measured in the region where stress is proportional to strain. Unit: Pa.

Force–extension behaviour

  • Up to the limit of proportionality, extension is proportional to force (Hooke's law), and the graph is a straight line through the origin.
  • Up to the elastic limit, the material returns to its original length when unloaded. This is elastic deformation.
  • Beyond the elastic limit, the material is plastically deformed and does not return to its original length. The graph curves, and the energy in the extension is not recovered.

Energy stored

The elastic energy stored in a stretched material equals the area under its force–extension graph up to the point of interest. For a spring obeying Hooke's law, E = ½Fx = ½kx².

Worked example: a wire of cross-sectional area 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ m² is pulled by 500 N. Stress = 500 ÷ (2.0 × 10⁻⁴) = 2.5 × 10⁶ Pa. If it extends by 1.0 mm from an original length of 2.0 m, strain = 0.001 ÷ 2.0 = 5.0 × 10⁻⁴, so E = 2.5 × 10⁶ ÷ 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ = 5.0 × 10⁹ Pa.

Exam tips: convert the area to m² and the extension to m before calculating. Strain has no unit, so do not write a unit for it. Say "the limit of proportionality" and "the elastic limit" as separate ideas.

Stored elastic energy and Hooke's law

Within the limit of proportionality, extension is proportional to force, F = kx, and the stiffness k depends on the material and its dimensions. The elastic strain energy stored in a stretched wire is equal to the area under the force-extension graph, E = ½Fx. For a material, the Young modulus E = stress / strain. Beyond the elastic limit the material deforms plastically and does not return to its original length.

Exam tip: state the limit of proportionality on the graph, because the energy formula only applies while the material obeys Hooke's law.

Worked example: a stretched wire with a load

A steel wire 1.5 m long and 0.80 mm in diameter is loaded with a 20 kg mass. The cross-sectional area is π(0.40 × 10⁻³)² ≈ 5.03 × 10⁻⁷ m². The force is F = mg = 20 × 9.81 = 196 N, so the stress is 196 ÷ (5.03 × 10⁻⁷) ≈ 3.9 × 10⁸ Pa.

If the wire stretches by 1.1 mm, the strain is 0.0011 ÷ 1.5 ≈ 7.3 × 10⁻⁴, and E = stress ÷ strain = 3.9 × 10⁸ ÷ 7.3 × 10⁻⁴ ≈ 5.3 × 10¹¹ Pa. Quote the Young modulus with its unit and to two significant figures, and check that the value is in the range expected for the material: steel is roughly 2 × 10¹¹ Pa, so a result far from that points to an area or unit error.

Comparing materials

  • A stiff material has a large Young modulus: for a given stress, it produces a small strain.
  • A brittle material fractures soon after the elastic limit, with little or no plastic deformation, so its graph stops abruptly.
  • A ductile material, such as copper, undergoes large plastic deformation before it breaks, so its graph shows a long curved section after the elastic limit.

Area under the graph

For a non-linear force–extension graph, the energy stored is still the area under the curve. Count the squares, or split the region into a triangle and a rectangle, and convert the result to joules using the scale factors. Only the energy up to the elastic limit can be recovered when the load is removed; the rest is dissipated as heat.

Hysteresis and loading cycles

When a material is loaded and then unloaded, the unloading curve may not retrace the loading curve. The region enclosed between the two curves is energy dissipated per cycle, often as heat. Rubber bands and car tyres show this, which is why they warm up when repeatedly deformed.

  • Strain is extension divided by the original length, so do not use the stretched length.
  • Young modulus has the unit of pascal, the same as stress, because strain is dimensionless.
  • Only a sample loaded within its elastic region returns to the same length; a permanent set after unloading means plastic deformation has occurred.

Common errors that lose marks

  • Using the diameter as the radius in the area formula, which quadruples the area.
  • Calling the gradient of the stress-strain graph the "stiffness". Stiffness belongs to the force-extension graph; the gradient of stress against strain gives E.
  • Quoting Hooke's law as valid beyond the limit of proportionality, where extension is no longer proportional to force.

title: IGCSE Computer Science: Networking and Data Transmission
content:
IGCSE Computer Science: Networking and Data Transmission

Cambridge IGCSE Computer Science 0478 (2026–2028), Paper 1 Computer Systems: statement 2.1 Types and methods of data transmission, 2.2 Methods of error detection, 2.3 Encryption, and 3.4 Network hardware. This note explains how data travels between machines — the modes and media it moves over, how errors in transit are spotted and fixed, how it is kept secret from eavesdroppers, and the hardware that carries it. Every parity bit and checksum below is worked line by line, because Paper 1 asks you to produce the check bits, not just name the method.

Why network computers at all

Networking lets machines share resources and communicate: shared files, printers and internet connections; centralised backup and security; email and messaging; and collaboration on the same data. The three sizes you must distinguish: a LAN (local area network) covers one site — a school or office — over its own cabling; a WLAN is a LAN using wireless links; a WAN (wide area network) spans many sites over public infrastructure such as telephone lines and fibre, with the internet the largest WAN of all.

Two ways to organise a LAN. In a client–server network, dedicated servers hold shared files, user accounts and backups, and clients request services from them: central control, easy backups, better security, but expensive hardware and an administrator is required — a server failure can stop everyone. In a peer-to-peer network every computer is equal and shares its own resources: cheap and simple, but no central control, each machine backed up separately, and security is harder to enforce.

Serial and parallel transmission

Serial sends one bit at a time down a single wire (or channel). It needs fewer wires, so it is cheaper and works over long distances without the signals interfering with each other; modern systems use serial links for almost everything outside the chip (USB, Ethernet, SATA). Parallel sends several bits at once — one per wire. It looks faster, and is over very short distances such as the paths inside a computer, but over long cables the wires pick up each other's signals (crosstalk) and the pulses arrive at slightly different times (skew), so the receiving end misreads them. Memory buses and internal data paths stay parallel; anything long-distance is serial.

Simplex, half-duplex and full-duplex

ModeDirectionExample
SimplexOne direction onlyKeyboard to computer; a TV broadcast
Half-duplexBoth directions, but one way at a timeWalkie-talkie; older Ethernet hubs
Full-duplexBoth directions simultaneouslyTelephone call; modern switched Ethernet

Two more distinctions the syllabus names. Synchronous transmission sends a continuous stream of data with a shared clock signal synchronising sender and receiver — fast and efficient for large transfers. Asynchronous transmission sends one character at a time wrapped in a start bit and stop bit (with a parity bit), so no shared clock is needed; it is slower because of the overhead but simple and cheap for bursty traffic such as a keyboard. Baseband means the whole medium carries a single digital signal (ordinary Ethernet); broadband splits the medium into several frequency channels so different signals travel at once (the cable TV and ADSL line into a house).

Transmission media

MediumHow it carries dataStrengthsWeaknesses
Twisted pair (Ethernet cable)Electrical pulses in paired copper wiresCheap, easy to install, fine for LANsLimited distance and speed; electrical interference
Coaxial cableElectrical pulses in a shielded copper coreBetter shielding than twisted pair; TV and cable networksThicker, dearer, still limited bandwidth compared with fibre
Fibre opticPulses of laser light down glass fibresHuge bandwidth, very long distances, immune to electrical interference, hard to tapExpensive; needs specialist skills to join and repair
Wireless (radio, microwave, infrared)Electromagnetic waves through the airMobility; no cabling costInterference and obstacles; slower; eavesdropping risk; coverage limits

Bandwidth is the maximum data rate of a link, in bits per second (bps, kbps, Mbps, Gbps) — the width of the pipe. Latency is the delay before data arrives. High bandwidth with high latency still feels sluggish: size of pipe versus distance the water travels. Time to send a file is roughly file size in bits divided by bandwidth:

Worked example: how long to send a 45 MB file over an 8 Mbps link?

45 MB = 45 x 8 = 360 megabits                [bytes to bits: multiply by 8]
360 / 8 = 45 seconds

Note the two eights doing different jobs: one converts bytes to bits,
the other is the 8 Mbps bandwidth. Confusing them is the classic error.

Error detection: parity

Signals degrade in transit — crosstalk, interference, dirty connectors — so receiving systems must check whether what arrived is what was sent. The simplest method, parity checking, appends one extra bit (the parity bit) to each byte so that the number of 1-bits in the group is always odd (odd parity) or always even (even parity). The sender works the bit out; the receiver recounts.

Send 0110 1011 with EVEN parity.

Count the 1-bits: 0+1+1+0+1+0+1+1 = 5 ones (odd).
For the group to have an even number of ones, the parity bit must be 1.
Transmitted byte (with parity bit at the front): 1 0110 1011

Now suppose one bit is flipped in transit: 1 0010 1011.
The receiver counts the ones: 1+0+0+1+0+1+0+1+1 = 5 (odd), but even parity was
agreed, so an error is detected and the byte is retransmitted.

With ODD parity for the same byte, the parity bit would be 0 (already 5 ones),
and the receiver expects an odd total.

Parity catches any single bit flip (the total changes parity), but two flips cancel out and pass unnoticed — a limitation worth a mark on its own.

Error detection: checksums

A checksum covers a whole block of data rather than one byte. The sender adds the data values together and sends the sum (or its complement) with the block; the receiver repeats the addition and compares. A corrupted value gives a different total.

Send the block 25, 47, 12 with a checksum.

Sender: 25 + 47 + 12 = 84. Transmit 25, 47, 12, 84.
Suppose 47 is corrupted to 48.
Receiver: 25 + 48 + 12 = 85, which does not match the received checksum 84:
error detected, request retransmission.

A plain sum can miss compensating errors (25 up by 1 and 12 down by 1), so real
systems use the one's complement of the sum, which catches more patterns.

Checksums detect most multi-bit errors in a block but not all; they are used together with retransmission (below), not instead of it.

Error correction and ARQ

Automatic repeat request (ARQ) is the protocol that turns detection into recovery. The receiver acknowledges each correctly received packet with an ACK; a corrupted packet gets a NAK (negative acknowledgement), and the sender resends it. If the packet or its ACK is lost entirely, the sender's timeout expires and it resends anyway. Sequence numbers on packets let the receiver spot duplicates caused by those resends and discard them. Stop-and-wait ARQ sends one packet and waits for its ACK before the next; continuous ARQ keeps a window of packets flowing and retransmits only the missing ones — faster on long links.

Error-correcting codes go further: extra bits are added so the receiver can repair a single-bit error without retransmission (vital where no return channel exists, such as on CDs). The trade-off in every method: more check bits means more reliability and less room for data.

Encryption

Anything crossing a network can be intercepted, so sensitive data is encrypted: the readable plain text is scrambled by an algorithm (a cipher) using a key into unreadable cipher text; the receiver uses a key to decrypt it back. The algorithm is public — the security lives in the key, like a lock whose design everyone knows but whose key you alone hold.

Symmetric encryptionAsymmetric encryption
KeysOne shared secret key for both encrypting and decryptingA matched pair: a public key (encrypts) and a private key (decrypts)
SpeedFast, suited to bulk dataSlow, suited to short messages and key exchange
ProblemGetting the shared key to the other party securely in the first placeNothing is secret to distribute, but the private key must be kept safe
ExamplesAES, DESRSA

Real systems combine them: HTTPS uses the asymmetric pair to agree a symmetric session key, then encrypts the whole conversation with the fast cipher. Hashing is a third tool — a one-way function producing a fixed-length value (the hash) from any input; it cannot be reversed, so passwords are stored as hashes (with a salt against rainbow tables) and any change to a message changes its hash, proving integrity. Digital certificates issued by certificate authorities bind a public key to a real identity, so a browser knows it is talking to the genuine bank and not an impostor.

Network hardware (statement 3.4)

  • Network interface card (NIC) — gives a device a network connection and a MAC address; it frames data onto the medium.
  • Switch — connects devices within a LAN and forwards each frame only to the port holding the destination MAC address; filters traffic and reduces collisions.
  • Router — connects different networks (your LAN to the internet) and forwards packets between them by choosing the best path using IP addresses.
  • Wireless access point — lets Wi-Fi devices join the wired LAN.
  • Hub — an older, simple repeater broadcasting every frame to all ports; largely replaced by switches.

Two addresses appear in exam answers and they belong to different layers: the MAC address is the permanent hardware identifier of a NIC used within a LAN, while the IP address is the logical address of a device on a network, used by routers to deliver packets across networks. Domains and DNS sit on top of that (see the internet note).

Worked example: a school LAN sends a file from room 1 to a server.

The file is split into numbered packets. Each packet is given the server's IP
address. The sending switch looks up the server's MAC address and forwards the
frame within the LAN. Along the way each packet may take a different route;
the server uses the sequence numbers to reassemble the file in order, and ACKs
any packet that fails its checksum so the sender retransmits only that packet.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Saying parity "corrects" errors; parity detects most single-bit errors — correction needs error-correcting codes or retransmission.
  • Getting the parity bit backwards: count the existing ones first; even parity needs the total to be even, so an odd count means the parity bit is 1.
  • Claiming two flipped bits are detected by parity; they change the count by two, which parity cannot see.
  • Confusing bandwidth with latency, or forgetting to convert bytes to bits (×8) before dividing by a bits-per-second rate.
  • Describing a router's job as "connects computers in a LAN" — that is the switch; the router connects networks and routes packets by IP address.
  • Swapping MAC and IP: MAC is fixed hardware identity on a LAN; IP is logical and can change, and is what routing uses.
  • Saying symmetric encryption is more secure than asymmetric (or vice versa); they are secure in different ways — the exam wants the key-distribution and speed trade-off.
  • Forgetting the timeout case in ARQ questions: a lost packet or lost ACK is recovered by the sender's timer, not by a NAK.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 1, 4 marks). Describe the difference between serial and parallel transmission and state one use for each.

Answer: Serial transmission sends the bits of a byte one after another down a single channel, so it is cheaper, immune to crosstalk between wires and reliable over long distances — used for USB, Ethernet and all long-distance links. Parallel transmission sends several bits simultaneously down multiple channels, which is faster over short distances but suffers skew and crosstalk over long cables — used for data buses inside a computer.

Question 2 (Paper 1, 3 marks). The byte 1011 0010 is to be sent using odd parity. State the parity bit and the transmitted group.

Answer: The byte contains five 1-bits (odd). Odd parity requires an odd total, so the parity bit is 0 and the transmitted group is 0 1011 0010 (parity bit shown first).

Question 3 (Paper 1, 4 marks). Explain how ARQ recovers from (i) a corrupted packet and (ii) a lost packet.

Answer: (i) The receiver's checksum test fails, so it returns a NAK; the sender retransmits that packet. (ii) No packet arrives, so no ACK is returned; the sender's timeout expires and it retransmits. In both cases the packet carries a sequence number so the receiver can discard duplicates and reassemble the data in order.

Question 4 (Paper 1, 4 marks). Explain why a bank uses asymmetric encryption to start a secure connection but symmetric encryption to transfer the data.

Answer: Asymmetric encryption (a public/private key pair) needs no shared secret to be distributed, so the bank can safely agree a session key with any customer who encrypts with the bank's published public key — only the bank's private key decrypts it. That process is slow, so once the session key is agreed both sides switch to fast symmetric encryption for the bulk of the transaction, which is efficient for large amounts of data.

Question 5 (Paper 1, 2 marks). Calculate the time to send a 12 MB file over a 4 Mbps link.

Answer: 12 MB = 96 megabits (12 × 8), and 96 ÷ 4 = 24 seconds.

Question 6 (Paper 1, 4 marks). Compare a switch and a router in a school network.

Answer: A switch connects devices within the LAN and forwards each frame only to the port of the destination MAC address, keeping local traffic off the rest of the network. A router connects the school LAN to other networks such as the internet and forwards packets between them, choosing routes using IP addresses. A switch works within one network; a router works between networks.

With the data safely moved, the next question is what runs on the machines: the software and the operating system that manages everything.

title: IGCSE Biology: Organisms and their Environment
content:
IGCSE Biology: Organisms and their Environment

Ecology is the accounting of life: where the energy comes from, how much of it moves from level to level, and how the materials (carbon, nitrogen) are endlessly recycled while the energy flows through and out. This note builds food chains and food webs from producers up, explains why only about 10 % of energy passes between levels (with the transfer-efficiency calculations fully worked), traces the carbon and nitrogen cycles step by step, and finishes with population measurement and the factors that control population size. Every cycle is written as a numbered sequence so you can reproduce it in the exam.

Energy flow: producers, consumers and decomposers

Almost all ecosystems are powered by the Sun. Producers (green plants and algae) trap light energy by photosynthesis and convert it into chemical energy in glucose — the base of every food chain. Consumers eat other organisms: primary consumers (herbivores) eat producers; secondary consumers (carnivores) eat herbivores; tertiary consumers eat other carnivores. Decomposers (bacteria and fungi) break down dead organisms and waste, releasing nutrients back to the environment and respiring energy as heat. Detritivores (earthworms, woodlice) feed on detritus (dead material), fragmenting it for decomposers. The flow is one-way: light → chemical energy in producers → consumers → heat lost at every stage; materials, in contrast, cycle.

Food chains, food webs and trophic levels

A food chain shows the transfer of food energy from one trophic level to the next: maize (producer) → locust (primary consumer) → lizard (secondary) → hawk (tertiary). Arrow direction is critical — always point from the organism being eaten to the eater, representing the direction of energy flow. A food web is many interconnected food chains (more realistic); removing one species can cascade through the web — a favourite "explain the consequence" question. Each organism occupies a trophic level: level 1 producers, level 2 primary consumers, and so on. DDT and other persistent poisons accumulate up the chain (biomagnification): the top predator has the highest concentration, which is why raptor eggshells thinned after DDT use.

Pyramids and energy transfer efficiency

Pyramids of numbers count organisms (can be inverted — one tree feeding many caterpillars); pyramids of biomass show the dry mass at each level (usually upright, measured in g/m²); pyramids of energy (kJ/m²/year) are always upright because energy is lost at each transfer. Where does the energy go between levels? Much of the food is not digested (egested in faeces); some is lost in respiration as heat (the largest loss); some goes into growth, but parts are inedible (bones, fur) or become detritus. The result: only about 10 % of the biomass/energy at one level passes to the next. Calculation: if producers contain 20 000 kJ, primary consumers receive about 2 000 kJ, secondary consumers about 200 kJ, tertiary about 20 kJ — divide by 10 at each step. Percentage efficiency = (energy transferred to next level ÷ energy available at this level) × 100. This is why food chains rarely exceed four or five levels: not enough energy remains at the top, and it is why eating lower on the chain (plant-based diets) can feed more people — a linked food-supply question.

Energy at each trophic level

Trophic levelRoleTypical energy (kJ per m² per year)
1Producers (photosynthetic)20 000
2Primary consumers (herbivores)2 000
3Secondary consumers (carnivores)200
4Tertiary consumers (top carnivores)20

Worked example: energy-transfer calculations

A grassland fixes 25 000 kJ per m² per year. Grasshoppers assimilate 2 500 kJ; frogs 250 kJ; snakes 25 kJ. Step 1: check each transfer: 2 500 ÷ 25 000 = 0.10 = 10 %; 250 ÷ 2 500 = 10 %; 25 ÷ 250 = 10 % — consistent with the 10 % rule. Step 2: what happens to the rest? At each level, energy is lost as heat in respiration, in faeces (undigested material), and in uneaten parts. Step 3: question variants: if the snake level must support 10 000 kJ of snake biomass, how much producer is needed? 10 000 → 100 000 (frogs) → 1 000 000 (grasshoppers) → 10 000 000 kJ of grass — show the three multiplications. Step 4: biomass units: dry mass is used (water varies and is not energy), measured by drying samples to constant mass in an oven — a standard Paper 6 method note. Efficiency questions always want the working shown: division by the level below and the percentage written with its unit.

The carbon cycle

Carbon cycles between the atmosphere, living things and the oceans. Step 1: photosynthesis removes carbon dioxide from the air and fixes carbon into glucose and biomass. Step 2: feeding passes carbon along food chains. Step 3: respiration by all organisms returns carbon dioxide to the atmosphere. Step 4: decomposers respire the carbon in dead organisms and waste back to the air as carbon dioxide. Step 5: combustion of fossil fuels (coal, oil, gas) releases carbon that was locked away for millions of years. Step 6: carbon is also stored (sequestered) in fossil fuels, carbonate rocks, oceans (dissolved carbon dioxide and carbonates) and forests. Human impact: burning fossil fuels and deforestation have raised atmospheric carbon dioxide, intensifying the greenhouse effect and global climate change — cutting this cycle's balance is the core of the climate topic.

The nitrogen cycle

Nitrogen is essential for proteins and nucleic acids, and although the air is 78 % nitrogen gas, animals and plants cannot use it directly — the nitrogen cycle has four key bacterial steps. Step 1: nitrogen fixation — nitrogen-fixing bacteria (Rhizobium in root nodules of legumes, Azotobacter in soil) convert nitrogen gas into ammonia and then ammonium compounds in the soil. Step 2: nitrification — nitrifying bacteria (Nitrosomonas: ammonium to nitrite; Nitrobacter: nitrite to nitrate) oxidise ammonium compounds to nitrates, the form plants absorb by root hairs (active transport). Step 3: assimilation — plants take up nitrates and build them into amino acids and proteins; animals obtain nitrogen by eating plants or other animals. Step 4: ammonification — decomposers break down proteins in dead organisms and urea in waste, releasing ammonia/ammonium compounds. Step 5: denitrification — anaerobic bacteria (in waterlogged/poorly aerated soil) convert nitrates back to nitrogen gas, returning it to the air — a loss for farmers, which is why ploughing and drainage (aeration) and fertilisers are used. Fertilisers (natural: manure and compost; artificial: NPK) replace the nitrates removed at harvest.

Populations and population size

A population is all the organisms of one species in an area at a given time; a community is all the populations of different species living together; an ecosystem is the community plus the abiotic (non-living) environment — light, temperature, water, soil pH, mineral ions, carbon dioxide. Population size depends on: birth rate, death rate, immigration and emigration; and it is limited by competition (for light, water, space, nutrients), predation, disease and climate. A typical population growth curve: a lag phase (establishment), a log (exponential) phase (resources plentiful), a stationary phase (births = deaths, resources limiting) and sometimes a decline (resources exhausted). Sampling methods: quadrats (random sampling for plants and slow organisms — throw the quadrat randomly, count within, repeat for a mean), and mark-release-recapture (trap, mark, release, recapture later; population = (number in first catch × number in second catch) ÷ number marked in second catch) for mobile animals. The assumptions of mark-release-recapture: marks do not rub off or harm the animal, the marked animals mix fully with the population, and there are no significant births, deaths or migrations between samplings.

Worked example: population estimation

Ecologists trap 40 mice, mark them and release them. A week later they trap 50 mice, of which 20 are marked. Step 1: the formula — total population = (first catch × second catch) ÷ marked in second catch. Step 2: substitute — (40 × 50) ÷ 20 = 2000 ÷ 20 = 100 mice. Step 3: evaluate the reliability — the sample sizes are small and marks may have rubbed off, giving a wide confidence; repeat the recapture and take a mean. Quadrat example: five 1 m² quadrats contain 12, 15, 9, 14 and 10 dandelions; mean = (12 + 15 + 9 + 14 + 10) ÷ 5 = 60 ÷ 5 = 12 dandelions per m²; for a 200 m² field, the estimated population is 12 × 200 = 2 400. Always show the sum and the division, and quote units (organisms per m²).

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Pointing food-chain arrows from eater to eaten — the arrow shows energy flow, so it points to the eater.
  • Writing that energy "cycles" like carbon: energy flows through and is lost as heat; only materials cycle.
  • Using wet mass for biomass pyramids: dry mass is required because water content varies.
  • Skipping the 10 % rule in energy questions: always divide by 10 (or multiply by 0.1) per level and show it.
  • Confusing nitrogen gas with nitrates: plants absorb nitrates (and ammonium), not atmospheric nitrogen; bacteria convert the gas.
  • Mixing up nitrification (bacteria making nitrates) and denitrification (bacteria releasing nitrogen gas).
  • Confusing population (one species) with community (all species) in definitions.
  • Forgetting the assumptions of mark-release-recapture when evaluating a population estimate.

Exam-style questions and answers

Q1. Explain why food chains rarely have more than five trophic levels. (2 marks) Answer: only about 10 % of energy passes to each successive level (1); so insufficient energy remains at higher levels to support another population (1).

Q2. Describe the role of nitrifying bacteria in the nitrogen cycle. (2 marks) Answer: they oxidise ammonium compounds first to nitrites and then to nitrates (1); the form of nitrogen that plant roots absorb (1).

Q3. A grassland producer level contains 50 000 kJ. Calculate the energy available to secondary consumers. (2 marks) Answer: 50 000 ÷ 10 ÷ 10 (1); = 500 kJ (1).

Q4. Describe how you would estimate the population of dandelions in a field. (3 marks) Answer: use quadrats thrown at random coordinates (1); count dandelions in each and calculate the mean per m² (1); multiply by the total field area (1).

Q5. Explain the effect of deforestation on the carbon cycle and climate. (3 marks) Answer: fewer trees means less photosynthesis removing carbon dioxide (1); burning or rotting trees releases stored carbon (1); atmospheric carbon dioxide rises intensifying the greenhouse effect and global warming (1).

title: A Level Physics: Magnetic Fields and Electromagnetism
content:
A Level Physics: Magnetic Fields and Electromagnetism

Magnetism and electricity are one phenomenon seen from two sides: every current makes a magnetic field, and every changing magnetic field makes a current. This note builds the subject from zero: what a magnetic field is and how flux density measures it, the forces on currents and on moving charges with their right-hand rules, the fields produced by wires and solenoids, electromagnetic induction through Faraday's and Lenz's laws, and the alternating-current ideas — rms values, rectification and smoothing — that connect the physics to the mains supply. Every calculation type is worked in full.

The magnetic field and flux density

A magnetic field is a region where a magnetic force acts on moving charges, currents and magnetic materials. Field lines run from north to south outside a magnet and never cross; their density indicates strength. The strength of the field is measured by the magnetic flux density B, in tesla (T): one tesla is one newton per ampere-metre of conductor, or one weber per square metre. Magnetic flux Φ through an area is the field passing through it:

Phi = B A cos(theta)        weber (Wb)

theta = angle between the field and the NORMAL to the area
flux linkage = N Phi        (N turns of a coil)

Force on a current-carrying conductor

F = B I L sin(theta)

B in T, I in A, L = length of conductor in the field (m)
theta = angle between the current and the field

The force is maximum when the current is perpendicular to the field (sin 90° = 1) and zero when parallel. Its direction comes from Fleming's left-hand rule: first finger = field, second finger = current, thumb = force (all mutually perpendicular). The analogy: think of the wire as a sail in a river of field lines — the force is perpendicular to both the flow and the sail.

Worked example. A 0.20 m wire carrying 3.0 A sits perpendicular to a 0.50 T field. Find the force.

F = B I L = 0.50 x 3.0 x 0.20 = 0.30 N

Force on a moving charge

F = B Q v sin(theta)

for a charge moving perpendicular to the field:
F = B Q v, and this force is centripetal:
B Q v = m v^2/r  ->  r = m v/(B Q)

A charged particle moving perpendicular to a uniform field follows a circular path; the radius grows with momentum and shrinks with field strength and charge. This is the working principle of the mass spectrometer (ions of different mass follow different radii) and the cyclotron.

Worked example. An electron moves at 2.0 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ perpendicular to a 0.10 T field. Find the force and the radius of its path.

F = B e v = 0.10 x 1.6 x 10^-19 x 2.0 x 10^6 = 3.2 x 10^-14 N
r = m v/(B e) = (9.11 x 10^-31 x 2.0 x 10^6)/(0.10 x 1.6 x 10^-19)
  = 1.82 x 10^-24/1.6 x 10^-20 = 1.14 x 10^-4 m  (0.11 mm)

Magnetic fields due to currents

  • Straight wire: concentric circular field lines around the wire; the right-hand grip rule (thumb along current, fingers curl with the field) gives direction; strength falls with distance, B = μ₀I/(2πr).
  • Solenoid: a uniform field inside, like a bar magnet, with the field direction set by the right-hand grip rule; adding an iron core concentrates the field (an electromagnet).
  • Parallel wires: currents in the same direction attract, opposite directions repel — a direct consequence of each wire's field acting on the other's current.

Worked example. Find the flux density 0.050 m from a long straight wire carrying 10 A (μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹).

B = mu0 I/(2 pi r) = (4 pi x 10^-7 x 10)/(2 pi x 0.050)
  = (2 x 10^-6)/0.050 = 4.0 x 10^-5 T

Electromagnetic induction

Faraday's law: the induced e.m.f. is proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux linkage. Lenz's law: the induced current opposes the change producing it (a statement of energy conservation — the induced current's field pushes back).

epsilon = - N dPhi/dt

moving a rod of length L at speed v perpendicular to B:
epsilon = B L v

rotating coil (peak e.m.f.): epsilon_0 = N B A omega

Worked example. A 0.50 m rod moves at 4.0 m s⁻¹ perpendicular to a 0.20 T field. Find the induced e.m.f.

epsilon = B L v = 0.20 x 0.50 x 4.0 = 0.40 V

Worked example (flux change). A 200-turn coil of area 0.010 m² sits in a 0.50 T field; the field is reversed in 0.10 s. Find the average e.m.f.

initial flux linkage: N B A = 200 x 0.50 x 0.010 = 1.0 Wb-turn
field reversed: change = 2 x 1.0 = 2.0 Wb-turn
epsilon = change/time = 2.0/0.10 = 20 V

Alternating current: peak and rms values

Mains electricity is sinusoidal: the voltage and current reverse direction periodically. The average of a sine wave is zero, so power calculations use the root-mean-square value, which is the steady d.c. value that would deliver the same power:

V_rms = V_0/sqrt(2) = 0.707 V_0
I_rms = I_0/sqrt(2)

average power: P = V_rms I_rms = I_rms^2 R = V_rms^2/R

Worked example. A 230 V rms mains supply feeds a 2.0 kW heater. Find the peak voltage and the rms current.

V_0 = 230 x sqrt(2) = 325 V
I_rms = P/V_rms = 2000/230 = 8.7 A

Rectification and smoothing

A diode allows current in one direction only, so a single diode halves the a.c. wave (half-wave rectification); a bridge of four diodes produces full-wave rectification — the output always has the same polarity. A capacitor in parallel with the load then smooths the output: it charges at the peaks and discharges through the load between them, reducing the ripple. Larger capacitance and larger load resistance give less ripple (τ = RC longer relative to the cycle).

  • Half-wave: one diode; half the wave is missing; more ripple.
  • Full-wave: bridge of four diodes; both halves used; easier to smooth.
  • Smoothing: capacitor across the load; ripple reduced as C and R increase.

Worked examples: combined electromagnetism

Worked example. A generator coil of 50 turns and area 0.020 m² rotates at 60 rad s⁻¹ in a 0.40 T field. Find the peak e.m.f. and the rms e.m.f.

epsilon_0 = N B A omega = 50 x 0.40 x 0.020 x 60
         = 24 V
epsilon_rms = 24/sqrt(2) = 17 V

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Force on wire) A 0.30 m wire carrying 2.0 A is perpendicular to a 0.80 T field. Find the force. Answer: F = BIL = 0.80 × 2.0 × 0.30 = 0.48 N.
  2. (Direction) State Fleming's left-hand rule. Answer: With the first finger along the field and the second along the current, the thumb points along the force — used for motors (the left hand gives the force on the conductor).
  3. (Charge) Explain why a moving charge in a uniform magnetic field moves in a circle. Answer: The magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work and changes only direction; a constant perpendicular force produces circular motion with r = mv/(BQ).
  4. (Solenoid) Describe the magnetic field inside a current-carrying solenoid. Answer: Strong, uniform, and directed along the axis; outside it resembles a bar magnet's field, with the end determined by the right-hand grip rule.
  5. (Faraday) State Faraday's law and Lenz's law. Answer: The induced e.m.f. is proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux linkage; the induced current opposes the change that produces it.
  6. (Lenz) Explain why Lenz's law is a consequence of energy conservation. Answer: If the induced current aided the change, it would generate energy from nothing; opposing it means work must be done to produce the change, and that work becomes electrical energy.
  7. (rms) An a.c. supply has peak voltage 340 V. Find the rms voltage. Answer: V_rms = 340/√2 = 240 V.
  8. (Smoothing) Explain how a capacitor smooths a rectified output. Answer: The capacitor charges as the rectified voltage rises to its peak and discharges through the load as the voltage falls, filling the gaps between peaks and reducing the ripple.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Angle in F = BIL sin θ: θ is between the current and the field; perpendicular means sin θ = 1. A wire parallel to the field feels no force.
  • Left hand versus right hand: use the left-hand rule for the force on a current (motor effect) and the right-hand grip rule for the field around a current. Mixing them reverses the answer.
  • Flux versus flux density: Φ = BA (weber), B is tesla; flux linkage multiplies by N turns. Do not call B flux.
  • Change of flux sign: reversing a field doubles the change (from +BA to −BA), a factor candidates often forget.
  • rms factor: peak over √2; the peak is rms × √2. Power uses rms values, not peak.
  • Induced e.m.f. needs change: a stationary coil in a steady field induces nothing; there must be a changing flux linkage (movement, rotation, or a changing current).
  • Lenz direction questions: state the opposing field direction and then the current direction; the reasoning chain is the mark.
  • Rectification understanding: diodes conduct one way only; a bridge gives full-wave, a single diode half-wave — do not claim a single diode gives full-wave output.
  • Precision and units: tesla, weber, volt; 2 or 3 s.f.; μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹ from the data sheet.

title: Cell Structure, Reproduction and Development Revision Notes
content:
Cell Structure, Reproduction and Development

Biology AS Edexcel IAL Topic 3 covers the ultrastructure of eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells, microscopy, cell division by mitosis and meiosis, fertilisation, stem cells, and genetic control through gene expression, epigenetics and inheritance.

  • Cells are the basic units of all living organisms sharing common features, organised hierarchically from cells to tissues, organs, and organ systems.
  • Eukaryote ultrastructure includes nucleus, nucleolus, ribosomes, rough and smooth endoplasmic reticulum, mitochondria, centrioles, lysosomes, and Golgi apparatus, with rER and Golgi cooperating in protein transport and extracellular enzyme formation.
  • Prokaryote ultrastructure features a cell wall, capsule, plasmid, flagellum, pili, ribosomes, and circular DNA.
  • Microscopy relies on magnification and resolution, using light and electron microscopes, with specimen staining essential for contrast, alongside Core Practical 5 for light microscopy, graticule measurements, and cell drawing.
  • Genetics involves gene loci, linkage, and meiosis ensuring genetic variation through independent assortment in metaphase I and crossing over in prophase I.
  • Mammalian gametes feature adaptations like the acrosome in sperm and zona pellucida in eggs, leading to fertilisation via the acrosome and cortical reactions and nuclear fusion, paralleled in flowering plants by pollen tube growth and double fertilisation.
  • The cell cycle and mitosis produce genetically identical daughter cells for growth and asexual reproduction, assessed quantitatively via mitotic indices and Core Practical 6 root tip squashes.
  • Stem cells can be totipotent or pluripotent, found in morula and blastocysts, enabling specialisation through differential gene expression, alternative splicing post-transcription, and epigenetic DNA methylation and histone modification.
  • Phenotypes reflect interactions between genotype, environment, multiple alleles, polygenic inheritance displaying continuous variation, and heritable epigenetic changes.

Worked example

Calculate the actual length of an organelle measuring 45 mm in an electron micrograph with a magnification of ×30,000. Using the formula actual size = image size ÷ magnification, convert 45 mm to micrometres by multiplying by 1000 to get 45,000 um. Then calculate 45,000 um ÷ 30,000 = 1.5 um.

Key points to remember

Students frequently lose marks by confusing the roles of the rough endoplasmic reticulum and the Golgi apparatus; rER folds and transports newly synthesized proteins, whereas the Golgi apparatus modifies, packages them into vesicles, and produces extracellular enzymes. In microscopy calculations, always ensure image size and scale bar units match before dividing by magnification. Remember that crossing over occurs between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes during prophase I of meiosis, not mitosis, and independent assortment happens in metaphase I. For epigenetics, be precise: DNA methylation involves methyl groups added to cytosine bases inhibiting transcription, while histone modification affects chromatin condensation, and both can be passed on following cell division.

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

title: Organic Synthesis — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Organic Synthesis

Chemistry — A2. Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH15, Topic 20. Organic synthesis plans a route from a starting material to a target molecule. You need to choose reagents and conditions, track functional groups and calculate the overall yield.

Key areas to revise

  • Planning a route
  • Key interconversions
  • Yield calculations

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

title: Exam technique: Algorithms & Programming
content:
### What earns the marks
To earn full marks on this topic, students need to demonstrate their ability to design and problem-solve using algorithms, as stated in statement 7. For calculate questions, show working and justify answers. For explain and describe questions, provide clear and concise pseudocode or flowcharts. For justify and state questions, provide a reason or explanation for the answer. 
### Traps
Common mistakes include not using ENDIF/NEXT/ENDWHILE terminators in pseudocode, not recording condition results in trace tables, and not testing boundary values. Correction: always use terminators, record condition results, and test boundary values. 
### Memory hooks
To remember the difference between validation and verification, use the mnemonic 'valid' for checking data format and 'verify' for checking data accuracy. To remember the linear search algorithm, think of 'looking for a book on a shelf'. To sanity-check an answer, test it with a simple example. 
### Timing
This topic typically accounts for 20-30% of the paper, and students should budget around 30-40 minutes to answer the questions. Make sure to read the questions carefully and manage time effectively to earn the maximum marks.

title: Exam technique: Mensuration
content:
### What earns the marks
For circles, sectors and arcs, the fraction of 360 stated earns the method mark: write 60/360 before multiplying. For cylinders, cones and spheres, the formula quoted earns a mark on its own, so write Volume = (1/3) pi r squared h even when confident. For compound shapes, split earns marks: compute each part separately, then add or subtract with a clear statement.
### Traps
Error: 2 pi r used for area. Correction: circumference versus area check first. Error: omitting 1/3 for cones and pyramids. Correction: quote the formula every time. Error: using diameter as radius in a semicircle cut-out. Correction: halve the diameter before any pi work. Error: forgetting the square root in a Pythagoras step. Correction: label squared lines as squared.
### Worked example
A cylinder has radius 3 cm and height 10 cm. Its volume is πr²h = π × 9 × 10 = 90π ≈ 282.7 cm³. A sector of angle 60° in a circle of radius 6 cm has arc length (60/360) × 2π × 6 = 2π cm.
### Check yourself
A trapezium has parallel sides 5 cm and 9 cm and a perpendicular height of 4 cm. Find its area. Use ½(a + b)h = ½ × (5 + 9) × 4 = 28 cm². State the units and show the substitution before the final value.

title: AS Level Mathematics: The Normal Distribution
content:
AS Level Mathematics: The Normal Distribution

Many measurements cluster symmetrically about a mean: heights, reaction times, measurement errors, the fill of a production line. The normal distribution is the mathematical shape of that clustering — a symmetric bell curve defined entirely by its mean and standard deviation. This note builds the topic from zero: the shape and its properties, standardising to the standard normal, reading probabilities from tables, working backwards from a probability to an unknown mean or standard deviation, and combining normal variables.

Properties of the normal distribution

X ~ N(mu, σ²)   (mean mu, variance σ²)

symmetric about the mean: P(X < mu) = P(X > mu) = 0.5
total area under the curve = 1
inflection points at mu +/- σ
about 68 per cent within 1 sd, 95 per cent within 2, 99.7 within 3

The notation takes the variance, not the standard deviation: N(10, 4) means mean 10 and standard deviation 2. Writing N(10, 4) while treating 4 as the standard deviation is the single commonest error in the topic.

Worked example. X ~ N(20, 9). State the mean and standard deviation and find P(X < 20).

mu = 20, σ = 3
P(X < 20) = 0.5 by symmetry

Standardising

z = (x - mu)/σ

Z ~ N(0, 1), the standard normal, tabulated in most formula booklets
P(X < x) = P(Z < z) = Φ(z)

Standardising answers "how many standard deviations above the mean is this value?" Every normal probability question reduces to that one number.

Worked example. X ~ N(50, 16). Find P(X < 58).

σ = 4;  z = (58 - 50)/4 = 2
P(Z < 2) = 0.9772

Worked example 2 (above). For the same X, find P(X > 45).

z = (45 - 50)/4 = -1.25
P(Z > -1.25) = P(Z < 1.25) = 0.8944

Between two values

P(a < X < b) = Φ(z_b) - Φ(z_a)

below a value, subtract from 1
between two values, subtract the smaller cumulative from the larger

Worked example. X ~ N(100, 225). Find P(85 < X < 115).

σ = 15
z1 = (85 - 100)/15 = -1;  z2 = (115 - 100)/15 = 1
P = Φ(1) - Φ(-1) = 0.8413 - 0.1587 = 0.6826

Worked example 2 (both tails). X ~ N(30, 25). Find P(X < 25 or X > 38).

σ = 5
z1 = -1  →  Φ = 0.1587
z2 = 1.6  →  Φ = 0.9452, so upper tail = 0.0548
total = 0.2135

Working backwards: finding x from a probability

given P(X < x) = p, find z from the inverse table, then
x = mu + z σ

Worked example. X ~ N(40, 64). Find the value exceeded by 10 per cent of the distribution.

P(X > x) = 0.10  →  P(X < x) = 0.90  →  z = 1.2816
x = 40 + 1.2816(8) = 50.25

Worked example 2 (middle 80 per cent). X ~ N(50, 100). Find the range containing the middle 80 per cent.

tails of 10 per cent each: z = +/-1.2816
x = 50 +/- 1.2816(10)  →  37.2 to 62.8

Finding the mean or standard deviation

When mu or σ is unknown, each probability statement gives an equation in z, and two statements give simultaneous equations.

Worked example 1 (find σ). X ~ N(20, σ²) and P(X > 26) = 0.05. Find σ.

P(X < 26) = 0.95  →  z = 1.6449
(26 - 20)/σ = 1.6449  →  σ = 6/1.6449 = 3.648

Worked example 2 (simultaneous). X ~ N(mu, σ²) with P(X < 10) = 0.20 and P(X < 20) = 0.90. Find mu and σ.

z values: -0.8416 and 1.2816
(mu - 0.8416 σ) = 10
(mu + 1.2816 σ) = 20
subtract: 2.1232 σ = 10  →  σ = 4.71
mu = 10 + 0.8416(4.71) = 13.96

The signs matter: a value below the mean has a negative z, so 10 = mu − 0.8416 σ. Setting both equations up with the same sign convention is what makes the simultaneous solve work.

Combining normal variables

if X ~ N(m¹, s¹²) and Y ~ N(m², s²²) are independent:
X + Y ~ N(m¹ + m², s¹² + s²²)
X - Y ~ N(m¹ - m², s¹² + s²²)
aX + b ~ N(a m¹ + b, a² s¹²)

The variance of a difference adds, exactly as in the probability-distributions topic: independent uncertainties compound in either direction.

Worked example. The masses of apples are N(120, 100) grams and of pears N(150, 144), independent. Find the probability that a random apple and pear together weigh more than 300 g.

T = A + P ~ N(270, 244)
sigma_T = 15.62
z = (300 - 270)/15.62 = 1.921
P(T > 300) = 1 - Φ(1.921) = 0.0274

Worked example 2 (difference). Two machines fill bottles: A ~ N(500, 25) ml, B ~ N(505, 36) ml, independent. Find P(A's fill exceeds B's).

D = A - B ~ N(-5, 61);  σ = 7.81
P(D > 0):  z = (0 + 5)/7.81 = 0.640
P = 1 - 0.7389 = 0.261

Normal approximations and modelling assumptions

The normal model is used for continuous measurements that arise from many small independent influences. Before applying it, check the assumptions: the variable is continuous (or discrete with enough values to ignore the gaps), the distribution is roughly symmetric, and the mean and standard deviation are known or estimable.

Worked example (quality control). A machine produces rods of mean 25.0 mm and standard deviation 0.2 mm. Rods outside 24.7–25.3 mm are scrapped. Find the proportion scrapped.

z1 = (24.7 - 25.0)/0.2 = -1.5  →  0.0668
z2 = (25.3 - 25.0)/0.2 = 1.5   →  upper tail 0.0668
total scrapped = 0.1336, about 13.4 per cent

Interpretation matters: state the proportion and, where asked, the expected number in a batch — 13.4 per cent of 1000 rods is about 134 rods.

Reading the table and using symmetry

The standard normal table gives Φ(z) = P(Z < z) only for positive z. Two symmetries cover every other case:

Φ(-z) = 1 - Φ(z)
P(Z > z) = 1 - Φ(z)
P(-z < Z < z) = 2 Φ(z) - 1

Worked example. Find P(-1.5 < Z < 0.5).

Φ(0.5) = 0.6915;  Φ(-1.5) = 1 - 0.9332 = 0.0668
P = 0.6915 - 0.0668 = 0.6247

Worked example 2 (inverse with symmetry). Find z such that P(Z > z) = 0.75.

Φ(z) = 0.25, so z is negative
z = -0.6745  (the value with Φ = 0.6745 is 0.6745)
check: P(Z > -0.6745) = 1 - 0.25 = 0.75

A rough sketch of the bell with the required region shaded prevents sign errors; the area asked for must match the area you extract from the table.

Normal approximation to the binomial

For a large number of trials the binomial distribution becomes bell-shaped and can be approximated by a normal with the same mean and variance, with a continuity correction because the binomial is discrete.

X ~ B(n, p):  mu = np,  σ² = np(1 - p)
use the normal when np > 5 and n(1 - p) > 5
continuity correction: X >= k becomes X > k - 0.5
                        X <= k becomes X < k + 0.5

Worked example. X ~ B(100, 0.3). Estimate P(X ≥ 35).

mu = 30, σ² = 21, σ = 4.583
with continuity: P(X > 34.5)
z = (34.5 - 30)/4.583 = 0.982
P = 1 - 0.8370 = 0.163

Without the 0.5 shift the estimate is noticeably worse, and the correction is explicitly credited in mark schemes. State both the approximation and the correction.

Is the normal model appropriate?

Before using the bell curve, check four things: the variable is continuous (or a discrete variable with many values); the distribution is roughly symmetric with a single peak; the mean and standard deviation are known or estimated from a large sample; and the values extend, in principle, in both directions. Heights and measurement errors satisfy these; incomes and waiting times do not, because they are skewed.

Worked example. A shop's daily sales figures have a mean of 400 pounds and an sd of 250 pounds, and the normal model gives P(sales < 0) = 0.055. Is the model appropriate?

the calculation implies a 5.5 per cent chance of negative sales,
which is impossible, so the normal model is a poor fit here
sales are right-skewed with a floor at zero; a model with a lower
bound, or a transformation, would be more honest

Recognising when a model fails is examinable: the arithmetic can be flawless and the modelling still wrong, and the marks for that judgement are separate.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Notation) X ~ N(12, 25). State the sd. Answer: 5.
  2. (Standardise) X ~ N(12, 25): find P(X < 17). Answer: z = 1; 0.8413.
  3. (Above) X ~ N(12, 25): find P(X > 9). Answer: z = −0.6; 0.7257.
  4. (Between) X ~ N(12, 25): find P(10 < X < 15). Answer: z = −0.4 and 0.6; 0.7257 − 0.3446 = 0.3811.
  5. (Inverse) X ~ N(12, 25): find the 90th percentile. Answer: z = 1.2816; x = 18.4.
  6. (Unknown σ) X ~ N(50, s²), P(X > 60) = 0.10. Find s. Answer: z = 1.2816; s = 10/1.2816 = 7.80.
  7. (Combination) X ~ N(10, 4), Y ~ N(15, 9), independent. Find P(X + Y < 30). Answer: sum ~ N(25, 13), sd 3.606, z = 1.387, P = 0.917.
  8. (Difference) Same X, Y: find P(Y − X > 10). Answer: D ~ N(5, 13), z = (10 − 5)/3.606 = 1.387; P = 0.083.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Variance mistaken for sd: N(mu, σ²) — square-root the second parameter before standardising.
  • Forgetting the tails: P(X > x) = 1 − Φ(z); the table gives "less than".
  • Wrong z sign: values below the mean have negative z; symmetrise using Φ(−z) = 1 − Φ(z).
  • Subtracting variances of a difference: Var(X − Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) when independent.
  • Not stating independence: combinations need it; without the assumption the variance rule does not hold.
  • Continuity: for a discrete variable approximated by the normal, use a continuity correction (P(X ≥ 5) becomes P(X > 4.5)) — required in A2, and stating it early avoids the habit.
  • Rounding z: use four decimal places from tables or the full calculator value; rounding z to 2 d.p. shifts the probability noticeably.
  • Answer without context: convert the probability into a proportion, a number of items or a percentage, as the question asks.
