title: IGCSE Chemistry (OxfordAQA): Atomic Structure and the Periodic Table
content:
Atomic Structure and the Periodic Table

Everything in chemistry comes back to this topic. The particle model explains why ice melts and why perfume crosses a room; the model of the atom explains why sodium loses an electron and chlorine gains one; and the periodic table turns those two ideas into predictions you can make for an element you have never seen. In the OxfordAQA 9202 papers this material is not a single question — it is the language the rest of the paper is written in, so a shaky answer here shows up in bonding, electrolysis, quantitative chemistry and organic chemistry too. This note covers specification statements 3.1.1, 3.1.2 and 3.1.3, works through the calculations the examiner actually sets, and ends with exam-style questions with full working.

1. The three states of matter

Matter is classified into three states by how its particles are arranged and how freely they move. The particles themselves do not change when a substance changes state — only their arrangement and their energy do. That is why melting ice is a physical change and not a chemical one: H₂O is still H₂O.

PropertySolidLiquidGas
ArrangementRegular lattice, particles touchingIrregular, particles still touchingFar apart, random
MovementVibrate about fixed positionsSlide past one anotherMove quickly in straight lines
ShapeFixedTakes the shape of the containerFills the container
VolumeFixedFixed (almost)Fills the container
CompressibilityAlmost noneAlmost noneEasily compressed

The state a substance is in at room temperature depends on the balance between the forces holding its particles together and the kinetic energy they have. Strong forces and low energy give a solid; weak forces and high energy give a gas. Heating raises the average kinetic energy of the particles, so it is always the route from solid to liquid to gas.

2. Changing state, and the energy it costs

Each change of state has its own name, and the examiner expects the exact word rather than "it turns into":

  • melting — solid to liquid; freezing — liquid to solid
  • boiling or evaporating — liquid to gas; condensing — gas to liquid
  • subliming — solid straight to gas (dry ice and iodine both do this); depositing — gas straight to solid

During a change of state the temperature does not rise even though energy is being supplied. The energy is being used to overcome the forces between particles rather than to speed them up. On a heating curve this appears as a flat section: the first flat section is melting, the second is boiling, and the boiling one is longer because vaporisation needs more energy than melting.

The energy needed to change the state of a mass without changing its temperature is given by the specific latent heat: E = m L → Key: E = energy (J); m = mass (kg); L = specific latent heat (J/kg). For boiling the value used is the specific latent heat of vaporisation, and for melting the specific latent heat of fusion.

3. Diffusion and the evidence for particles

Diffusion is the spreading of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration because of their random motion. It is the simplest evidence that particles exist and that they move:

  • bromine vapour in air — the brown colour spreads through the gas jar without stirring
  • ammonia and hydrogen chloride at opposite ends of a tube — a white ring of ammonium chloride forms nearer the hydrogen chloride end, because ammonia particles are lighter and travel faster
  • potassium manganate(VII) in water — the purple colour spreads slowly through the liquid

Diffusion is faster at a higher temperature, because the particles have more kinetic energy, and faster for a lighter particle at the same temperature. In a liquid it is much slower than in a gas, because the particles are close together and collide constantly. The kinetic energy of a particle is Eₖ = ½ m v² → Key: Eₖ = kinetic energy (J); m = mass (kg); v = speed (m/s). Two particles at the same temperature have the same average kinetic energy, so the lighter one must have the greater speed — which is exactly why the ammonia particles reach the middle of the tube first.

4. A simple model of the atom

An atom is the smallest part of an element that can exist. An element contains only one kind of atom; a compound contains atoms of two or more elements chemically combined in fixed proportions; a mixture contains substances that are not chemically combined. The atom itself is built from three subatomic particles.

ParticleRelative massRelative chargeWhere it is
Proton1+1Nucleus
Neutron10Nucleus
Electron1/1836 (negligible)−1Shells around the nucleus

Two numbers describe any atom. The atomic number (Z) is the number of protons, and it is what makes the element what it is — every carbon atom has six protons and no other element does. The mass number (A) is the number of protons plus the number of neutrons, because the electron's mass is negligible. So for a neutral atom: neutrons = A − Z, and electrons = Z. In an ion the protons never change; only the electrons do.

Electrons occupy shells, filled from the inside out. The first shell holds 2, the second 8, the third 8, and the fourth fills after the third has eight (potassium and calcium are the two you meet at this level). The configuration of an element is written as a list of shell occupancies, for example sodium is 2,8,1 and calcium is 2,8,8,2. The number of electrons in the outer shell is the same as the group number for the main-group elements, and the number of shells is the same as the period number.

5. Isotopes and relative atomic mass

Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. Carbon-12 and carbon-14 both have six protons, but carbon-14 has eight neutrons instead of six. Isotopes have identical chemical properties, because chemistry is decided by the electrons, and slightly different physical properties, because mass affects how fast particles move and diffuse.

Because a sample of an element usually contains a mixture of isotopes, the mass quoted in the periodic table is a weighted mean called the relative atomic mass: Aᵣ = (mass₁ × abundance₁ + mass₂ × abundance₂ + …) ÷ 100 → Key: Aᵣ = relative atomic mass (no units); mass = mass number of each isotope; abundance = percentage of that isotope in the sample. That is why chlorine's relative atomic mass is 35.5 and not a whole number.

6. Ions, and why atoms form them

Atoms react to reach the stable electron arrangement of a noble gas. Metals lose electrons and become positively charged ions; non-metals gain electrons and become negatively charged ions. Sodium (2,8,1) loses its outer electron to become Na⁺ with the arrangement 2,8; chlorine (2,8,7) gains one to become Cl⁻ with 2,8,8; magnesium (2,8,2) loses two to become Mg²⁺; oxygen (2,6) gains two to become O²⁻.

The charge on an ion tells you the ratio in which ions combine, because the total charge in a compound must be zero: Na⁺ with Cl⁻ gives NaCl; Mg²⁺ with O²⁻ gives MgO; Al³⁺ with O²⁻ needs two aluminium ions and three oxide ions, giving Al₂O₃.

7. The Periodic Table

Mendeleev arranged the elements in order of atomic weight but left gaps for elements that had not been discovered, and predicted their properties from their neighbours — and the predictions turned out to be right, which is why his table became the basis of the modern one. The modern table arranges elements in order of atomic number, which removes the few places where Mendeleev had to break his own weight order.

A group is a vertical column and contains elements with the same number of outer electrons, so they react in similar ways. A period is a horizontal row, and going across a period the atoms gain a proton and an electron and the elements change from metals to non-metals.

  • Group 1, the alkali metals (lithium, sodium, potassium): one outer electron, so they are very reactive; reactivity increases down the group because the outer electron is further from the nucleus and lost more easily; they are soft, low density, and react with water to give a hydroxide and hydrogen: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂
  • Group 7, the halogens (fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine): seven outer electrons, so they gain one; reactivity decreases down the group; a more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive one from its salt: Cl₂ + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br₂
  • Group 0, the noble gases (helium, neon, argon): full outer shells, so they are unreactive; used where a non-reactive atmosphere is needed, such as argon in a filament lamp
  • Transition metals (the block between groups 2 and 3): hard, dense, high melting points, coloured compounds, variable oxidation states and useful catalysts — iron in the Haber process is the example the paper uses

The table is a prediction machine: an element's group tells you its outer electrons and therefore its ion, and its position tells you whether it is a metal or a non-metal. That is how the properties of an unfamiliar element are answered without memorising it.

8. Worked examples

Worked example 1 — counting the particles in an ion. Give the number of protons, neutrons and electrons in ²⁴Mg²⁺. The mass number is 24 and the atomic number of magnesium is 12. Protons = Z = 12; neutrons = A − Z = 24 − 12 = 12; electrons = Z − charge = 12 − 2 = 10. The ion has 10 electrons and the arrangement 2,8, the same as neon.

Worked example 2 — relative atomic mass from abundances. A sample of chlorine contains 75% ³⁵Cl and 25% ³⁷Cl. Aᵣ = (35 × 75 + 37 × 25) ÷ 100 = (2625 + 925) ÷ 100 = 3550 ÷ 100 = 35.5. The answer is not rounded to a whole number, because a relative atomic mass is a weighted mean and chlorine really is a mixture.

Worked example 3 — electron configuration. Calcium has atomic number 20, so it has 20 electrons: 2 in the first shell, 8 in the second, 8 in the third, and the remaining 2 in the fourth, giving 2,8,8,2. The Ca²⁺ ion has lost the two outer electrons, so its configuration is 2,8,8 and it is isoelectronic with argon.

Worked example 4 — energy to boil a liquid. How much energy is needed to boil 0.50 kg of water if its specific latent heat of vaporisation is 2.3 × 10⁶ J/kg? Using E = m L: E = 0.50 × 2.3 × 10⁶ = 1.15 × 10⁶ J. Show the substitution — the mark scheme pays for the numbers being put into the relation, not for the final value alone.

9. Exam-style questions

Question 1. An atom of an element has 17 protons and 18 neutrons. State its mass number, its number of electrons, and the charge on the ion it forms. Answer: mass number = 17 + 18 = 35; electrons = 17; the atom has seven outer electrons, so it gains one and forms a 1− ion.

Question 2. Explain why the melting point of sodium is lower than the melting point of magnesium. Answer: both are metals, but magnesium contributes two delocalised electrons per atom and has a smaller ion, so the electrostatic attraction between the ions and the delocalised electrons is stronger and more energy is needed to break the lattice.

Question 3. Bromine exists as ⁷⁹Br and ⁸¹Br in a 1:1 ratio. Calculate its relative atomic mass. Answer: Aᵣ = (79 × 50 + 81 × 50) ÷ 100 = (3950 + 4050) ÷ 100 = 8000 ÷ 100 = 80.0.

Question 4. Describe what happens to the particles of a solid as it is heated to its melting point and then melted. Answer: the particles vibrate more vigorously as the temperature rises, until the vibrations are strong enough to overcome the forces holding them in the lattice; at the melting point the temperature stays constant while the energy supplied breaks those forces, and the particles can then slide over one another.

Question 5. Chlorine water is added to potassium bromide solution. State what is observed and write the equation. Answer: the solution turns orange-brown because bromine is displaced; Cl₂ + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br₂. Chlorine is above bromine in group 7, so it is the more reactive halogen.

Question 6. Explain why argon is used as the atmosphere inside a filament lamp. Answer: argon has a full outer shell so it is unreactive, and it will not react with the hot filament; it also stops the filament oxidising, which would shorten its life.

10. Common mistakes

  • Writing "the particles get bigger" when a substance is heated. They do not — they move faster.
  • Giving the number of electrons in an ion as the atomic number. In a positive ion the electron count is lower than Z.
  • Confusing mass number with relative atomic mass: the first belongs to one atom, the second is a weighted mean for the element.
  • Saying reactivity increases down group 7. It decreases; the halogen nearer the top of the group displaces the one below.
  • Explaining a flat section on a heating curve as "the substance is not being heated". Energy is still being supplied; it is being used to change state.
  • Giving a relative atomic mass with units. Aᵣ has no units, because it is a comparison with carbon-12.

11. Exam technique for this topic

  • When asked to explain a trend, name the force and say what happens to it: "the attraction between the ions and the delocalised electrons is stronger, so more energy is needed".
  • For "describe the arrangement and movement", answer both parts — examiners award a mark for arrangement and a separate one for movement.
  • In a calculation question, write the relation, then the substitution, then the result with its unit. A bare answer can score zero even when the number is right.
  • For an unfamiliar element, use its group number for outer electrons and its period for shells instead of trying to recall it.
  • If a question says "explain", a statement of fact is not enough: link the observation to the particle-level reason.

title: AS Level Mathematics: Mechanics M1 — Kinematics, Dynamics and Statics
content:
AS Level Mathematics: Mechanics M1 — Kinematics, Dynamics and Statics

Mechanics describes motion and the forces causing it. M1 covers three linked strands: kinematics (describing motion with graphs and the constant-acceleration equations), dynamics (Newton's second law applied to single particles and connected bodies), and statics (equilibrium of a particle and moments of forces). This note builds each from zero, with the modelling assumptions stated, the sign conventions fixed, and worked examples written out line by line — because in mechanics the marks are in the diagram and the equation, not the answer.

Modelling assumptions and units

standard assumptions unless told otherwise:
  the object is a particle (no size, no rotation)
  air resistance is negligible
  the string is light and inextensible; the pulley is smooth
  g = 9.8 m s^-2 (use 9.81 if the question says so)

State the assumption when you use it: "modelling the stone as a particle, so air resistance is ignored". Marks are awarded for identifying what the model simplifies.

Kinematics: the constant-acceleration equations

v = u + at
s = ut + (1/2) a t^2
v^2 = u^2 + 2as
s = ((u + v)/2) t

u initial velocity, v final velocity, a acceleration,
s displacement, t time

The equations hold only for constant acceleration. Choose the equation by listing what you know and what you want: exactly one equation omits the quantity you neither know nor need.

Worked example 1. A car accelerates uniformly from 8 m/s to 20 m/s in 6 s. Find the acceleration and the distance.

a = (v - u)/t = (20 - 8)/6 = 2 m/s^2
s = ((u + v)/2)t = 14 x 6 = 84 m

Worked example 2 (falling). A stone is dropped from rest from a cliff and takes 3 s to land. Find the height, taking g = 9.8.

u = 0, a = 9.8 (downward positive), t = 3
s = 0 + (1/2)(9.8)(9) = 44.1 m

Worked example 3 (upward). A ball is thrown vertically upwards at 15 m/s. Find the maximum height and the total time in the air.

at the top v = 0: 0 = 225 - 2(9.8)s  ->  s = 11.48 m
time up: 0 = 15 - 9.8t  ->  t = 1.53 s
total time = 3.06 s (symmetric flight)

Fix the positive direction before substituting. Upward-positive makes g = −9.8; the alternative is consistent arithmetic but must not be mixed mid-question.

Velocity-time and displacement-time graphs

displacement-time: gradient = velocity
velocity-time: gradient = acceleration; area = displacement
speed-time: area = distance

Worked example. A cyclist accelerates from rest to 12 m/s in 5 s, travels at 12 m/s for 10 s, then decelerates to rest in 4 s. Find the total distance.

area 1: (1/2)(5)(12) = 30
area 2: 12 x 10 = 120
area 3: (1/2)(4)(12) = 24
total = 174 m

Area below the time axis is negative displacement: the particle has reversed direction, and distance sums the magnitudes.

Newton's second law and forces

resultant force F = m a
weight W = m g
friction opposes motion: F <= mu R (limiting case F = mu R)
normal reaction R acts perpendicular to the surface

Worked example 1 (horizontal). A 5 kg box is pushed with 30 N along a rough floor with friction 8 N. Find the acceleration.

resultant = 30 - 8 = 22 N
a = 22/5 = 4.4 m/s^2

Worked example 2 (on a slope). A 4 kg particle slides down a smooth slope inclined at 30°. Find its acceleration.

component of weight along the slope = 4g sin 30 = 19.6 N
a = 19.6/4 = 4.9 m/s^2  (= g sin 30)

Worked example 3 (with friction on a slope). Same slope, friction 6 N.

resultant = 19.6 - 6 = 13.6 N
a = 3.4 m/s^2

Connected particles

Two bodies joined by a string have the same magnitude of acceleration (the string is inextensible) and the same tension throughout (the string is light and the pulley smooth). Write one equation per body and add them to eliminate T.

Worked example (pulley). Masses 5 kg and 3 kg hang either side of a smooth pulley. Find the acceleration and the tension.

for 5 kg (downward positive): 5g - T = 5a
for 3 kg (upward positive):   T - 3g = 3a
add: 2g = 8a  ->  a = 2.45 m/s^2
T = 3(g + a) = 3(9.8 + 2.45) = 36.75 N

Worked example 2 (on a table). A 4 kg block on a smooth table is connected over a pulley to a 2 kg hanging mass. Find the acceleration.

hanging mass: 2g - T = 2a
block: T = 4a
add: 2g = 6a  ->  a = 3.27 m/s^2

Worked example 3 (lift). A 60 kg person stands in a lift accelerating upward at 2 m/s². Find the reaction force.

R - 60g = 60(2)  ->  R = 60(11.8) = 708 N
the person feels heavier; in free fall R would be zero

Statics: equilibrium of a particle

equilibrium: the resultant force is zero
resolve horizontally and vertically, or along and perpendicular to
a slope, and set each total to zero

Worked example. A 10 N weight hangs from two strings making 40° and 50° with the horizontal. Find the tensions.

horizontal: T1 cos 40 = T2 cos 50
vertical: T1 sin 40 + T2 sin 50 = 10
from the first: T2 = T1 cos40/cos50 = 1.1918 T1
T1(0.6428) + 1.1918 T1(0.7660) = 10
T1(0.6428 + 0.9129) = 10  ->  T1 = 6.43 N, T2 = 7.66 N

Moments

moment = force x perpendicular distance from the pivot
for equilibrium of a rigid body: sum of clockwise moments = sum of
anticlockwise moments

Worked example. A uniform plank 4 m long of weight 200 N rests on two supports 1 m from each end. A 300 N load is placed 0.5 m from the left end. Find the reactions.

supports at 1 m and 3 m from the left; load at 0.5 m
moments about the left support:
  load: 300 x 0.5 = 150 anticlockwise
  weight: 200 x 1 = 200 clockwise (weight acts at the centre, 2 m)
  right reaction R2 at 2 m: clockwise
  150 = 200 + 2 R2  ->  R2 = -25 N, so the plank would tip
check total: R1 + R2 = 500 needed; with R2 negative the support
cannot hold, so the load must be moved inward - a tipping question

Moments about a support is the standard trick: it eliminates that support's reaction, leaving one unknown. If the required reaction is negative, the body is not in equilibrium and tipping is the intended conclusion.

Friction and limiting equilibrium

Friction is a variable force: it takes whatever value is needed to prevent motion, up to a maximum. Only at the point of slipping does it reach its limiting value.

F <= mu R  on a rough surface
limiting friction: F = mu R   (on the point of moving)
R is found by resolving perpendicular to the surface

Worked example 1 (horizontal, limiting). A 10 kg block rests on a rough horizontal floor with mu = 0.4. Find the smallest horizontal force needed to move it.

R = 10g = 98 N
limiting friction = 0.4 x 98 = 39.2 N
so a force just above 39.2 N starts it moving

Worked example 2 (slope). A block sits on a rough slope inclined at 25° with mu = 0.5. Does it slide?

component down the slope: mg sin 25 = 0.4226 mg
maximum friction: mu mg cos 25 = 0.5 x 0.9063 mg = 0.4531 mg
maximum friction exceeds the driving component, so it stays at rest
and friction takes the value 0.4226 mg

The comparison is the answer: if mu >= tan θ the particle remains in equilibrium on the slope, because the friction ceiling covers the driving component. That inequality is a standard exam demand.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (suvat) u = 4, a = 3, t = 5. Find s. Answer: 20 + 37.5 = 57.5 m.
  2. (suvat) u = 10, v = 30, s = 100. Find a. Answer: 900 = 100 + 200a → a = 4 m/s².
  3. (graph) A v–t graph rises 0 to 20 m/s in 4 s, then falls to 0 in 2 s. Distance? Answer: 40 + 20 = 60 m.
  4. (F = ma) 12 kg, resultant 36 N. Find a. Answer: 3 m/s².
  5. (slope) Smooth slope at 20°, mass 5 kg. Find a. Answer: g sin 20 = 3.35 m/s².
  6. (pulley) 6 kg and 4 kg over a smooth pulley. Find a. Answer: 2g = 10a → 1.96 m/s².
  7. (tension) For that pulley, find T. Answer: T = 4(9.8 + 1.96) = 47.0 N.
  8. (moments) A 2 m lever with a 50 N force at 1.5 m from the pivot balances a force F at 0.5 m. Find F. Answer: 50 × 1.5 = 0.5F → F = 150 N.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • No diagram: draw the forces before writing equations; nearly every mechanics error is a missing or misdirected force.
  • Sign convention drift: fix positive direction once and keep it; a sign flip mid-question produces a wrong acceleration.
  • Using suvat with varying acceleration: the equations need constant a; if a changes, split into stages or use a graph.
  • Forgetting weight on a slope: the component along the slope is mg sin θ; the perpendicular component mg cos θ is balanced by the reaction on a smooth slope.
  • Tension assumed equal to weight: in an accelerating system T ≠ mg; solve the equations.
  • Adding instead of eliminating T: write one equation per body with consistent directions, then add to cancel T.
  • Moments with the wrong distance: the perpendicular distance from the pivot, not the distance along the rod.
  • Units and g: use the g the question gives; mixing 9.8 and 9.81 changes answers at the third figure.

Formula summary

v = u + at;  s = ut + at^2/2;  v^2 = u^2 + 2as;  s = (u + v)t/2
F = ma;  W = mg;  F = mu R at limiting friction
moment = force x perpendicular distance

Every M1 calculation begins with a diagram showing the forces, the chosen positive direction and the known quantities. The formula is the last step; the model is the first.

title: Probability — Study Notes
content:
Probability

Basic Rules

For an event A with P(A) = p: 0 ≤ p ≤ 1, and P(A′) = 1 − P(A). For mutually exclusive events, probabilities add: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B). For events that can occur together, subtract the overlap:

  • P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B)

Venn Diagrams

Draw the universe first, then the events. Fill from the intersection outwards: if P(A) = 0.6, P(B) = 0.5 and P(A ∩ B) = 0.25, then only-A = 0.35, only-B = 0.25, neither = 0.15. Every region must sum to 1.

Tree Diagrams

Branch probabilities multiply along a path; outcomes at the end of complete paths add. Draw one branch set per stage of the experiment. For two draws without replacement from a bag of 5 red and 3 blue: P(RR) = (5/8)(4/7) = 20/56.

Conditional Probability

P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B) — the probability of A given that B has occurred. The condition shrinks the sample space.

Example: P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.4, P(A ∩ B) = 0.2. Then P(A | B) = 0.2/0.4 = 0.5, so A and B are independent since P(A | B) = P(A).

Independence

A and B are independent exactly when P(A ∩ B) = P(A)·P(B). Do not confuse independent (no influence on probabilities) with mutually exclusive (cannot co-occur). Mutually exclusive events with non-zero probabilities are never independent.

Exam tips: convert every "given that" into a conditional. With trees, label the second-stage branches with conditional probabilities; they are usually different from the first stage when drawing without replacement.

Exam method: combined events

The addition rule gives P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B). For mutually exclusive events the intersection is empty, so P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B). Draw a Venn diagram to place each probability in its region before calculating.

Independent events satisfy P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B). Test independence by checking this equation rather than assuming it, because the question may give the joint probability and ask you to decide.

The conditional probability P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B). Events are independent exactly when P(A | B) = P(A).

Tree diagrams suit sequential events without replacement. Multiply along each branch and add the branches that give the outcome required.

Exam cue: State whether events are independent or mutually exclusive, because the two are different and the formula depends on it.

title: Operating Systems — Study Notes
content:
Operating Systems

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2023–2025): OS roles, memory/process management, hardware–software layer, interrupts, buffers, utility software.

1. What an OS does

Manages memory, processes/files, I/O via drivers, security (users, permissions), and provides the UI (CLI/GUI) between user, applications and hardware.

2. Memory and process management

  • Paging/segmentation move programs in/out; virtual memory extends RAM to disk when RAM is full.
  • Multitasking: scheduler gives each process time slices; context switching saves/restores state.

3. Interrupts and buffers

Interrupts signal events (I/O complete, timer); CPU saves context, services via ISR, resumes. Buffers hold data in transit (printing) so slow devices don't block the CPU; spooling queues jobs.

4. Utility software

Disk formatter, defragmenter (reduces head movement on HDDs; unnecessary for SSD), backup scheduler, compression, antivirus, file compression.

5. UI and drivers

CLI: precise, scriptable, low overhead. GUI: icons/windows, discoverable, more resources. Device drivers translate OS calls to hardware specifics — each device needs its own.

Exam tips: "manage" verbs earn marks: manages memory, manages processes, manages peripherals; explain virtual memory by RAM-full scenario, not definition alone.

title: Organic Chemistry
content:
Organic Chemistry

Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry 0620, Extended route, topic 11 (statements 11.1–11.8). Formulae and functional groups, naming, fuels and fractional distillation, alkanes, alkenes, alcohols, carboxylic acids and polymers.

11.1 to 11.2 Formulae and naming

  • A homologous series shares a general formula and functional group, with similar chemical properties and a gradual change in physical properties. Alkanes CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ (saturated), alkenes CₙH₂ₙ (unsaturated, C=C), alcohols CₙH₂ₙ₊₁OH, carboxylic acids CₙH₂ₙ₊₁COOH.
  • Structural isomers have the same molecular formula but different structural formulae — butan-1-ol and butan-2-ol are a syllabus example.

11.3 to 11.5 Fuels, alkanes and alkenes

  • Petroleum is a mixture of hydrocarbons separated by fractional distillation. Fractions with shorter chains have lower boiling points, are more volatile, less viscous and burn more easily. From the top: refinery gas, gasoline, naphtha, kerosene, diesel, fuel oil, bitumen.
  • Alkanes are saturated and burn; complete combustion gives carbon dioxide and water, incomplete combustion gives carbon monoxide and soot. Substitution with chlorine in ultraviolet light: methane + chlorine → chloromethane + hydrogen chloride.
  • Alkenes have a carbon–carbon double bond and decolourise orange bromine water — the test for unsaturation. Cracking breaks long-chain alkanes into shorter alkanes and alkenes, using a hot catalyst of silica or alumina.

11.6 to 11.8 Alcohols, acids and polymers

  • Ethanol by fermentation (yeast, 25–35 °C, no air) or by hydration of ethene (300 °C, 60 atm, phosphoric acid catalyst). Fermentation uses a renewable feedstock but is slow and gives dilute ethanol; hydration is fast and pure but uses a finite feedstock.
  • Ethanoic acid forms from ethanol oxidation; it reacts with metals (salt + hydrogen), bases (salt + water) and carbonates (salt + water + carbon dioxide). Carboxylic acid + alcohol gives an ester (the syllabus example is ethyl ethanoate).
  • Addition polymerisation: many ethene monomers join to make poly(ethene); the repeat unit keeps all atoms. Condensation polymerisation releases a small molecule (water or HCl) per link — nylon and PET are the syllabus examples, and proteins are natural condensation polymers of amino acids.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Repeat unit reasoning, applied to a polymer shown with a backbone: find the two carbons of the monomer double bond, keep the other groups attached, and redraw as a repeat unit with single bonds and extension bonds on each side. Deduce the monomer from the repeat unit by restoring the double bond — the exam habit that prevents lost marks.
  • Cracking equations, applied to C₁₀H₂₂ cracking to octane: C₁₀H₂₂ → C₈H₁₈ + C₂H₄. Atoms must balance on both sides, so the second product must be an alkene. Check carbon and hydrogen counts before writing the final answer.
  • Fermentation yield calculation, applied to 100 g of glucose (Mr 180) giving ethanol: moles = 100 ÷ 180 = 0.556 mol. From C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂, ethanol = 1.11 mol, mass = 1.11 × 46 = 51.1 g. Percentage yield compares this theoretical mass with the actual mass obtained.
  • Homologous series trends, applied to naming and properties: as chain length increases in alkanes, boiling point rises (stronger intermolecular forces), viscosity rises and flammability falls. Use intermolecular forces as the reason, not "molecules get bigger".

Common errors

  • Breaking the polymer chain when drawing a repeat unit. The extension bonds must remain.
  • Forgetting the ultraviolet light in the alkane substitution conditions, or the catalyst and conditions in cracking.
  • Saying alkenes "react with bromine water by substitution". It is addition, and the decolourisation is the test.

title: AS Level Physics: Materials and Deformation
content:
AS Level Physics: Materials and Deformation

Edexcel International A Level Physics, Unit 1 (WPH11) Mechanics and Materials — Hooke's law, stress and strain, Young modulus, elastic and plastic behaviour, and elastic strain energy. This is where mechanics meets the laboratory: the definitions are precise, the graphs carry most of the marks, and the measurement of Young modulus is one of the unit's core practicals and a favourite of WPH13.

Hooke's law

Stretch a spring and it extends; double the load and (at first) the extension doubles. That proportionality is Hooke's law:

force = spring constant x extension        F = k x
  • F: load in newtons (N); k: spring constant (the stiffness) in newtons per metre (N m⁻¹); x: extension in metres (m), where extension = loaded length − original length. Extension is positive for stretching and negative for compression.
  • The law holds only up to the limit of proportionality: beyond it the load–extension graph curves, and past the elastic limit the material is permanently deformed — the extension remains when the load is removed.

A load–extension graph is a straight line through the origin up to the limit of proportionality, and its gradient is the spring constant. Springs in series share the load and add their extensions (1/k = 1/k₁ + 1/k₂); springs in parallel share the load and add their spring constants. Hooke's law applies to all elastic materials, not just coils: a wire, a beam and a rubber band all show the same initial proportionality.

Stress and strain

Extension depends on the size of the sample as well as the material, so materials are compared using quantities that are independent of dimensions. Stress is the force per unit cross-sectional area; strain is the extension per unit original length:

tensile stress = force / cross-sectional area        σ = F / A
tensile strain = extension / original length        ε = x / L
  • Stress (σ): pascals (Pa = N m⁻²); strain (ε): dimensionless, often quoted as a percentage. Both are scalars in a tensile test, but the sign distinguishes tension (positive) from compression (negative).
  • A: cross-sectional area in square metres (m²); L: original length in metres (m); x: extension in metres (m).

Strain has no unit because it is a ratio of two lengths — a common examination trap. Engineering strain uses the original length; so does the AS definition.

Young modulus

The stiffness of a material itself, as opposed to a particular sample, is Young modulus:

Young modulus = stress / strain        E = σ / ε = F L / (A x)
  • E: Young modulus in pascals (Pa), usually quoted in gigapascals (1 GPa = 10⁹ Pa). Steel is about 200 GPa, aluminium about 70 GPa, rubber about 0.01 GPa.
  • E is the gradient of the straight-line (linear) portion of the stress–strain graph, and it is constant for a given material within the limit of proportionality.

Measuring Young modulus (core practical). A long steel wire is clamped at one end, loaded with known masses over a pulley, and its extension measured with a travelling microscope, a vernier scale or an extensometer attached directly to the wire. The long wire is deliberate: a 2 m wire stretches far more than a 30 cm one for the same stress, so the percentage uncertainty in the extension is small. Diameter is measured with a micrometer at several points and orientations and averaged, because A = πd²/4 and the diameter enters squared. Plot load against extension; the gradient is k, and E = FL/(Ax) is evaluated from the gradient and the measured dimensions. The procedure repeats the readings, checks the wire returns to its original length (elastic region), and keeps the load below the limit of proportionality.

Stress–strain and load–extension graphs

FeatureMeaning
Initial straight lineElastic deformation: stress is proportional to strain; gradient = Young modulus; unloaded material returns to its original length
Limit of proportionalityEnd of the straight line: stress and strain are no longer proportional
Elastic limitBeyond this point deformation is plastic: permanent set remains after unloading
Yield pointA sudden large extension for little extra load; the material flows
Ultimate tensile stressThe maximum stress on the graph, where necking begins (the wire thins locally)
Fracture pointThe wire breaks

The area under a load–extension graph is the work done in stretching the sample; the area under a stress–strain graph is the energy stored per unit volume. Material types read straight off the graph: a ductile material (copper) has a long plastic region before breaking; a brittle material (glass, cast iron) fractures with little plastic deformation; a polymeric material (rubber) shows a long, curved elastic region and large strain at low stress.

Elastic strain energy

Work must be done to stretch a material, and while the deformation is elastic that work is stored as elastic strain (potential) energy in the stretched bonds:

elastic strain energy = 1/2 x force x extension        E = 1/2 F x = 1/2 k x²
  • E: energy in joules (J); F: load in newtons (N); x: extension in metres (m); k: spring constant in newtons per metre (N m⁻¹).
  • It equals the area under the load–extension graph (a triangle, ½ × base × height), and the energy per unit volume is the area under the stress–strain graph, ½ × stress × strain in the linear region.

This is why an elastic band gets warm when stretched repeatedly — hysteresis — and why a bow stores energy in its limbs. On release, the stored energy converts to kinetic energy: ½kx² = ½mv² gives the launch speed of a spring-loaded trolley.

Unit 3 skills: uncertainty in a materials experiment

WPH13 regularly uses a materials experiment as the context for data-analysis questions. The skills it marks:

  • Choosing instruments to match the expected size of the quantity (micrometer for wire diameter, vernier or extensometer for extension), and explaining why (small quantities carry large percentage uncertainties otherwise).
  • Percentage uncertainty propagation for E = FL/(Ax): add the percentage uncertainties of F, L, A and x, remembering that A ∝ d² so the diameter's percentage uncertainty is doubled.
  • Error bars on both axes, best-fit line, and the uncertainty in the gradient from the steepest and shallowest lines through the error bars.
  • Control variables: same wire material and diameter throughout, same temperature, avoid overloading beyond the elastic limit, allow the wire to settle before each reading.
  • Safety: long wires under heavy loads store large energies and can snap — wear eye protection, stand behind a barrier, use a safety cage on the pulley, add masses gently.

Worked example: Young modulus and its uncertainty

A steel wire of length 1.80 m and diameter 0.40 mm extends 2.1 mm under a load of 60 N.

area = π d² / 4 = 3.14 x (0.00040)² / 4 = 1.26 × 10⁻⁷ m²
stress = F / A = 60 / 1.26 × 10⁻⁷ = 4.8 × 10⁸ Pa
strain = x / L = 0.0021 / 1.80 = 1.17 × 10⁻³
Young modulus = stress / strain = 4.8 × 10⁸ / 1.17 × 10⁻³ = 4.1 × 10¹¹ Pa (about 400 GPa)

A sanity check flags the result: steel is about 200 GPa, so a value of 400 GPa suggests an error — in fact the extension here is half the realistic value, which is exactly the sort of conclusion an evaluation question wants. Uncertainties: with the extension measured as 2.1 ± 0.1 mm its percentage uncertainty is 4.8 per cent; the diameter 0.40 ± 0.01 mm gives 2.5 per cent, doubled to 5.0 per cent through d²; the length contributes about 0.3 per cent. The total is about 10 per cent, dominated by the extension — so an extensometer rather than a ruler would improve the result most.

Common mistakes

  • Confusing the spring constant (a property of a particular spring, N m⁻¹) with Young modulus (a property of a material, Pa).
  • Using the stretched length instead of the original length in strain, or forgetting to square the diameter when finding the cross-sectional area.
  • Quoting strain with a unit; it is dimensionless.
  • Applying E = FL/(Ax) or F = kx beyond the limit of proportionality.
  • Forgetting the ½ in elastic strain energy: the load rises from zero linearly, so the work is the triangle's area, not the full rectangle.
  • Reading the gradient of a load–extension graph as Young modulus; Young modulus is the gradient of stress against strain. Convert first.
  • Missing that A = πd²/4 means the diameter's uncertainty doubles in the final percentage.
  • Assuming a brittle material stores much energy before fracture; the area under its graph is tiny.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (WPH11, 3 marks). A 2.0 N load stretches a spring from 12.0 cm to 15.0 cm. Calculate the spring constant and the extension produced by a 5.0 N load.

Answer: Extension = 3.0 cm = 0.030 m, so k = F/x = 2.0/0.030 = 67 N m⁻¹. With 5.0 N, x = F/k = 5.0/67 = 0.075 m = 7.5 cm (assuming the limit of proportionality is not exceeded).

Question 2 (WPH11, 4 marks). A copper wire of length 2.00 m and cross-sectional area 0.50 mm² is loaded with 100 N and extends 1.2 mm. Calculate the stress, the strain and Young modulus.

Answer: Stress = F/A = 100 / (0.50 × 10⁻⁶) = 2.0 × 10⁸ Pa. Strain = x/L = 0.0012/2.00 = 6.0 × 10⁻⁴. Young modulus = 2.0 × 10⁸ / 6.0 × 10⁻⁴ = 3.3 × 10¹¹ Pa ≈ 330 GPa.

Question 3 (WPH13, 4 marks). Explain why a long thin wire is used to measure Young modulus, and why the diameter is measured at several positions.

Answer: The extension is proportional to length and inversely proportional to area, so a long thin wire gives a measurable extension under a modest load, keeping the percentage uncertainty in the extension small. The diameter is measured at several positions and in two perpendicular directions and averaged, because the wire's diameter is not perfectly uniform and the area depends on d², so a single unrepresentative measurement would skew the result.

Question 4 (WPH11, 3 marks). A spring of constant 400 N m⁻¹ is compressed by 0.12 m. Calculate the elastic potential energy stored and the speed it can give to a 0.50 kg ball.

Answer: E = ½kx² = ½ × 400 × 0.0144 = 2.9 J. Setting ½mv² = 2.9 gives v = √(2 × 2.9/0.50) = 3.4 m s⁻¹.

Question 5 (WPH11, 4 marks). Describe the difference between elastic and plastic deformation, and explain how a stress–strain graph shows which is occurring.

Answer: In elastic deformation the atoms are displaced slightly from their equilibrium spacing and return when the load is removed, so no permanent change occurs; the stress–strain graph is a straight line whose gradient is Young modulus. In plastic deformation the atomic planes slide over one another, so the material is permanently changed when unloaded; on the graph this is beyond the elastic limit, where the line curves and the strain grows faster than the stress. The limit of proportionality marks the end of the linear region; the elastic limit marks the onset of permanent set.

Question 6 (WPH13, 3 marks). A student's value of Young modulus is 30 per cent below the accepted value. Suggest two likely sources of error.

Answer: The extension was measured with a ruler over too short a gauge length, underestimating it (a systematic underestimate of extension gives an underestimate of E); the wire may already have been stretched beyond its elastic limit on earlier runs, giving extra extension for the same load. Use an extensometer over a longer gauge length, keep loads within the elastic region, and take repeated readings at each load.

Unit 1's remaining strand — energy, power and turning effects — continues the mechanics.

Equations and symbols

The materials topic is six equations and one graph. Every one of them is a straight-line relation used inside the limit of proportionality, so the first thing to state in any answer is that the deformation is still elastic.

F = k x Key: F = applied load (N); k = spring constant, the stiffness of this spring (N m⁻¹); x = extension, meaning loaded length minus original length (m). The gradient of a load–extension graph is k; beyond the limit of proportionality the line curves and the equation stops applying.

σ = F / A Key: σ = tensile stress (Pa, where 1 Pa = 1 N m⁻²); F = tensile force (N); A = cross-sectional area (m²). Stress removes the size of the sample so two wires of different diameter can be compared.

ε = x / L Key: ε = tensile strain (dimensionless — a ratio of two lengths); x = extension (m); L = original length, not stretched length (m). Quoting a unit for strain is a lost mark.

E = σ / ε = F L / (A x) Key: E = Young modulus (Pa, usually GPa); σ = stress (Pa); ε = strain (dimensionless); F = load (N); L = original length (m); A = cross-sectional area (m²); x = extension (m). E is the gradient of the straight part of a stress–strain graph — not of a load–extension graph, which gives k.

A = π d² / 4 Key: A = cross-sectional area of the wire (m²); d = diameter (m); π = 3.14. Because d is squared, the percentage uncertainty in the diameter doubles in the final answer — the standard WPH13 data-analysis mark.

E = 1/2 F x = 1/2 k x² Key: E = elastic strain energy stored (J); F = load at that extension (N); x = extension (m); k = spring constant (N m⁻¹). It is the area of the triangle under the load–extension graph, so the ½ is not optional: the load rose from zero.

1/k = 1/k₁ + 1/k₂ Key: k = combined spring constant of two springs in series (N m⁻¹); k₁, k₂ = their individual constants (N m⁻¹). Springs in series add extensions for the same load; springs in parallel add constants instead.

½kx² = ½mv² Key: k = spring constant (N m⁻¹); x = compression or extension (m); m = mass of the launched object (kg); v = its launch speed (m s⁻¹). Energy stored in the spring becomes kinetic energy, which is the launch-speed question in one line.

title: Organisms and their Environment
content:
Organisms and their Environment

Cambridge IGCSE Biology 0610, Extended route, topic 19 (statements 19.1–19.4). Energy flow, food chains and webs, nutrient cycles, and populations with sampling.

19.1 to 19.3 Energy and nutrient cycles

  • Energy flows one way through an ecosystem: from the Sun to producers, then consumers, with about 10% passed on at each transfer; most is lost in respiration and as heat. Nutrients, by contrast, are recycled.
  • Trophic levels: producers (plants), primary consumers (herbivores), secondary consumers (carnivores), decomposers (bacteria and fungi) which break down dead material and return nutrients to the soil.
  • The carbon cycle: photosynthesis removes carbon dioxide, respiration and combustion return it, and decomposition releases carbon from dead organisms. The nitrogen cycle involves nitrogen-fixing bacteria in root nodules, nitrifying bacteria, and denitrifying bacteria returning nitrogen to the air.

19.4 Populations

  • A population is all the organisms of one species in an area; a community is all the populations; an ecosystem includes the abiotic factors too. Sampling uses quadrats for plants and random selection for mobile animals.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Energy calculation, applied to 3000 kJ reaching producers: 300 kJ reach primary consumers and 30 kJ reach secondary consumers. Explain the 10% rule with the losses — respiration, uneaten parts, faeces, heat. State the losses explicitly; quoting the percentage alone is not the explanation.
  • Cycle reasoning, applied to why adding fertiliser can cause eutrophication: nitrates wash into the water, algae bloom, light is blocked, plants die, and decomposer bacteria multiply and use up dissolved oxygen, killing fish. Give the full chain — each step is a separate mark.
  • Sampling evaluation, applied to a quadrat survey: randomise positions by throwing a marker or using random coordinates, take a large number of quadrats, and state that this reduces bias and improves reliability. Name both randomisation and sample size as improvements.

Common errors

  • Saying energy is recycled in an ecosystem. Only nutrients cycle; energy flows out as heat.
  • Forgetting decomposers when describing a nutrient cycle.
  • Placing quadrats in a line "to be systematic" without justifying; systematic sampling suits gradient studies, random sampling suits population estimates.

title: Inheritance
content:
Inheritance

Cambridge IGCSE Biology 0610, Extended route, topic 17 (statements 17.1–17.4). DNA, genes and chromosomes, mitosis and meiosis, and monohybrid inheritance with genetic diagrams and probability.

17.1 Chromosomes, genes and proteins

  • DNA is a double helix of two strands made of nucleotides; genes are sections of DNA that code for proteins. Chromosomes carry many genes. An allele is a version of a gene; genotype is the allele combination; phenotype is the expressed characteristic.

17.2 Mitosis

  • Mitosis produces two genetically identical diploid cells for growth, repair and asexual reproduction. It follows DNA replication, then one division.

17.3 Meiosis

  • Meiosis produces four genetically different haploid gametes. Two divisions follow replication; crossing over and independent assortment create variation. Fertilisation restores the diploid number.

17.4 Monohybrid inheritance

  • A genetic diagram shows parents' genotypes, the gametes, the Punnett square, then offspring genotypes and phenotypes with ratios. For two heterozygotes Bb × Bb, offspring are 1 BB : 2 Bb : 1 bb, phenotypic ratio 3 : 1.
  • Sex determination: females XX, males XY. A father's gamete decides the sex of the offspring — 50% chance of a girl, 50% of a boy.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Genetic diagram, applied to albinism (recessive a): two heterozygous parents Aa × Aa have offspring in the ratio 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa, so 1 in 4 is albino. If the question asks for the chance from several children, each conception is independent — multiply the probabilities, and state that assumption.
  • Crossing over reasoning, applied to why meiosis increases variation: non-sister chromatids exchange sections during prophase I, so alleles that were on the same chromosome appear on different ones. That recombination, with independent assortment of chromosome pairs, produces new combinations.
  • Sex-linked reasoning, applied to haemophilia (Xᴴ normal, Xʰ affected): a carrier mother XᴴXʰ and a normal father XᴴY have a 25% overall chance of an affected son — 1 in 4 of all children, or 1 in 2 of their sons. State which denominator you are using; the ambiguity loses marks otherwise.

Common errors

  • Writing gametes with paired alleles. Gametes carry one allele of each gene.
  • Saying meiosis makes identical cells. Genetic variation is the point of meiosis.
  • Confusing the phenotypic ratio (3:1) with the genotypic ratio (1:2:1).

title: Complex Numbers — Study Notes
content:
Complex Numbers

Board note: complex numbers are not examined in the Edexcel International A Level main specification — they sit in Further Mathematics (FP1, WFM01). Cambridge examines them at A2 (9709); this note serves both boards.

Basics

i² = −1. A complex number z = a + bi has real part a and imaginary part b. Two numbers are equal iff both parts match.

Arithmetic: add/subtract parts; multiply with brackets and replace i² with −1.

Example: (2 + 3i)(1 − i) = 2 − 2i + 3i − 3i² = 5 + i.

Conjugates

z̄ = a − bi. zz̄ = a² + b² (real). Dividing: multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate.

Example: 1/(3 − i) × (3 + i)/(3 + i) = (3 + i)/10.

Argand Diagram

Plot z as the point (a, b). |z| = √(a² + b²) is the modulus (distance from origin); arg z = tan⁻¹(b/a) is the argument (angle). Multiply two numbers: moduli multiply, arguments add.

Modulus–Argument Form

z = r(cos θ + i sin θ), r = |z|, θ = arg z. Useful for powers and roots.

de Moivre and Roots

[r(cos θ + i sin θ)]ⁿ = rⁿ(cos nθ + i sin nθ).

Example: (1 + i)⁸: |1 + i| = √2, arg = π/4, so z⁸ = (√2)⁸ cis 2π = 16.

An nth root gives n evenly spaced solutions, 2π/n apart on a circle of radius r^(1/n).

Exam tips: always give arguments in the required interval; when solving equations, remember complex roots come in conjugate pairs for real polynomials.

Exam method: arithmetic and modulus

Treat i as a symbol with i² = −1 and collect real and imaginary parts separately. When multiplying complex numbers expand like brackets, then replace i² by −1. To divide, multiply the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator, which turns the denominator into a real number.

For z = a + bi the modulus is |z| = √(a² + b²) and the argument is the angle θ in the Argand diagram with tan θ = b/a, placed in the correct quadrant. The conjugate z* = a − bi reverses the sign of the imaginary part, and z z* = a² + b², which is always real.

Equal complex numbers have equal real parts and equal imaginary parts. Use this to solve for unknown real values, comparing coefficients on both sides of an equation.

Exam cue: State the final answer in the form a + bi, and check the sign of the imaginary part after every multiplication.

Worked example: square root of a complex number

Find z such that z² = −9 + 40i. Let z = a + bi. Then a² − b² = −9 and 2ab = 40, so ab = 20. Trying a = 4 and b = 5 gives 16 − 25 = −9, which works. So z = 4 + 5i or z = −(4 + 5i). Check by squaring: (4 + 5i)² = 16 + 40i − 25 = −9 + 40i.

Quadratic equations with complex roots

For x² + 2x + 5 = 0, the discriminant is 4 − 20 = −16, which is negative, so the roots are not real. Use √(−16) = 4i to get x = (−2 ± 4i)/2 = −1 ± 2i. The two roots form a conjugate pair, as they always do when the coefficients are real.

Loci in the Argand diagram

  • |z − 2| = 3 is the circle with centre 2 and radius 3, since it gives the distance of z from the point 2.
  • arg(z) = π/4 is a half-line from the origin at 45° above the positive real axis.
  • |z − 1| = |z + i| is the perpendicular bisector of the points 1 and −i.

Exam point: when a locus question gives an inequality, shade the correct region on the diagram and label the boundary as a solid or dashed line depending on whether it is included.

title: Hypothesis Testing — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Hypothesis Testing

Mathematics — A2. The null hypothesis H₀ is the default claim (no change, p = p₀). The alternative H₁ is what a suspicious observation suggests (p > p₀, p < p₀, or p ≠ p₀). The significance level α is the probability of rejecting a true H₀ — the false-alarm rate, usually 5% or 1%.

Key areas to revise

  • The Framework

  • One-Tailed vs Two-Tailed
  • Critical Regions
  • Conclusions in Context

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

### Worked example A test of a claimed mean has a null hypothesis H₀ and an alternative H₁. Choose a significance level such as 5%, calculate the test statistic and its p-value, then reject H₀ if p < α. A two-tailed test looks for a change in either direction, so the 5% is split between the two tails. ### Check yourself Define a Type I error in words. It is rejecting H₀ when H₀ is actually true. title: Energy, Work & Power — Study Notes
content:
Energy, Work & Power

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): stores and transfers, KE/PE, work, energy sources, power, efficiency.

1. Energy stores & transfers

Stores: kinetic, gravitational, elastic, chemical, nuclear, thermal. Transfer mechanisms: mechanically, electrically, heating, waves. Energy is conserved overall; transfers via work done.

2. Formulas

  • KE = ½mv²; PE = mgh.
  • Work W = Fd (force along displacement, joules).
  • Power P = W/t = E/t; P = Fv for constant speed.

Example: 0.5 kg at 4 m/s: KE = 4 J. Lift 2 kg by 3 m: PE = 60 J (g = 10).

3. Energy sources

Renewable: solar, wind, hydro, geothermal, biofuel, tidal — replenished. Non-renewable: fossil fuels, nuclear — finite. Discuss reliability, cost, pollution for "evaluate" questions.

4. Efficiency

Efficiency = useful output ÷ total input (×100%). Sankey diagrams show losses.

Example: motor: 150 J useful from 600 J → 25%.

5. Energy-chain problems

Equating KE loss to PE gain: v = √(2gh) for frictionless drop; braking distance grows with v².

Exam tips: define work as "force × distance moved in the direction of the force"; use g = 10 unless told otherwise; efficiency is a ratio — no units.

title: Numerical Measures of Central Tendency — Study Notes
content:
Central Tendency: Mean, Median and Mode

The Mean

For data x₁, ..., xₙ the mean is

  • x̄ = Σx/n

For a frequency table with midpoints x and frequencies f: x̄ = Σfx/Σf. The mean uses every value, so a single extreme value drags it — that is its main weakness.

The Median

The median is the middle value: position (n + 1)/2 for ordered raw data. With n even, average the two middle values. The median ignores the size of extreme values, so it describes skewed data more honestly. For grouped data, estimate the median by linear interpolation within the median class.

The Mode

The most frequent value. A dataset may have no mode or several. For grouped data the modal class is the one with the highest frequency density (frequency ÷ class width), not the highest frequency.

Effects of Data Changes

Adding a constant a to every value adds a to the mean and median (the mode too) but leaves the spread untouched. Multiplying every value by b multiplies mean and median by b.

Coding

Subtract a constant and divide by a convenient width: y = (x − a)/b. Then x̄ = b·ȳ + a. Coding simplifies arithmetic and always preserves the relationship — the coded mean decodes exactly.

Example: data 2, 4, 4, 10: mean = 5, median = 4, mode = 4. Change 10 to 100: mean = 27.5, median and mode unchanged — the mean chased the outlier.

Exam tips: always state which average you used and why. When asked to compare two distributions, pair a central measure with a spread measure; a mean without a spread is only half an answer.

Exam method: mean, median and mode

For ungrouped data, the mean is the sum of the values divided by the number of values. The median is the middle value of the ordered list, at position (n + 1)/2, and the mode is the value that occurs most often. Always order the data before finding the median.

For grouped data, the mean is Σfx/Σf using the class midpoints. The modal class is the class with the highest frequency, and the median class is the one containing the (n + 1)/2 th value.

Each average suits different data. The mean uses every value, so an outlier pulls it away from the centre, while the median is unaffected by extreme values. Say which average is more representative when the question asks you to comment.

Changing one value changes the mean but may not change the median, which is useful to check a calculation.

Exam cue: When the question gives a mean and asks for a missing value, form the equation Σx = n × mean and solve for the unknown.

title: IGCSE Chemistry: Acids, Bases and Salts
content:
IGCSE Chemistry: Acids, Bases and Salts

Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry 0620 (2026–2028), Extended route, Topic 7 Acids, bases and salts: statement 7.1 The characteristic properties of acids and bases, 7.2 Oxides, and 7.3 Preparation of salts. This note builds from what an acid physically is (a proton donor) through every reaction type worth marks, to the four salt-preparation methods with their procedures — and it is those procedures that carry Paper 6 as well as Paper 4. Every equation is balanced and every calculation line is explicit.

What acids and bases are

The everyday definition: acids taste sour, turn litmus red and react with metals and carbonates; bases are metal oxides or hydroxides that neutralise acids; alkalis are soluble bases (they dissolve to give hydroxide ions). The Extended definition that earns the extra mark: an acid is a proton (H⁺) donor and a base is a proton acceptor — in water an acid donates H⁺ to the solvent, forming H₃O⁺ but conventionally written as H⁺(aq).

Dissociation of acids in water - the strong/weak distinction:

  STRONG acid - fully dissociated (every molecule releases its proton):
    HCl(aq) → H⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq)          [single arrow]
    HNO₃(aq) → H⁺(aq) + NO₃⁻(aq)
    H₂SO₄(aq) → 2H⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq)

  WEAK acid - only partially dissociated (an equilibrium):
    CH₃COOH(aq) ⇌ H⁺(aq) + CH₃COO⁻(aq)   [equilibrium arrow]
    H₂CO₃(aq) ⇌ H⁺(aq) + HCO₃⁻(aq)

Strong vs weak is about the DISOCIATION, not the concentration:
  dilute HCl is strong but dilute; concentrated ethanoic acid is weak but
  concentrated. Strong acids attack metals and carbonates faster (more H⁺
  ions per volume); weak acids are safer (vinegar, lemon juice).

Reactions of acids: the four types

Reacts withProductsWorked equation
MetalsSalt + hydrogenMg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g)
Bases (metal oxides/hydroxides)Salt + waterCuO(s) + H₂SO₄(aq) → CuSO₄(aq) + H₂O(l)
CarbonatesSalt + water + carbon dioxideCaCO₃(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl₂(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g)
Ammonia (alkali)Ammonium saltNH₃(g) + HCl(aq) → NH₄Cl(aq)

Neutralisation is acid + base → salt + water; the ionic essence is H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O. Indicators: litmus (red in acid, blue in alkali), thymolphthalein (colourless in acid, blue in alkali), methyl orange (red in acid, yellow in alkali), universal indicator for a pH estimate. pH measures acidity: pH 7 neutral, below 7 acidic, above 7 alkaline; each unit is a tenfold change in H⁺ concentration.

Oxides: the four classes

  • Basic oxides — metal oxides (CuO, CaO) that react with acids to give salt and water.
  • Acidic oxides — non-metal oxides (SO₂, CO₂, NO₂) that react with alkalis to give salt and water.
  • Amphoteric oxides — react with both acids and alkalis (Al₂O₃, ZnO) — the Extended favourite.
  • Neutral oxides — neither (CO, NO, H₂O).
Amphoteric behaviour worked, both directions:

  Al₂O₃ + 6HCl → 2AlCl₃ + 3H₂O         [acts as a base, with acid]
  Al₂O₃ + 2NaOH → 2NaAlO₂ + H₂O        [acts as an acid, with alkali]

The oxide's character tracks the element's position: metallic oxides basic,
non-metallic oxides acidic, and the metal/metalloid border (Al, Zn) gives
amphoteric behaviour.

Preparation of salts: four methods

The method is chosen by the salt's solubility and the acid type — a decision tree the exam expects you to reason through, not recite.

Decision tree:

  Soluble salt?
  |-- YES → use an ACID + excess INSOLUBLE base/metal/carbonate, then
  |          filter off the excess and crystallise.
  |-- NO  → precipitation: mix two solutions of soluble salts, filter,
             wash and dry the precipitate.

Worked procedure 1 - soluble salt from an insoluble base:
  copper(II) sulfate from copper(II) oxide + dilute sulfuric acid.
  1. Warm dilute H₂SO₄ in a beaker.
  2. Add CuO powder a little at a time with stirring - it reacts and
     dissolves: CuO + H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + H₂O
  3. Keep adding until NO MORE DISSOLVES (the excess solid remains) -
     this guarantees all the acid is used up.
  4. FILTER off the excess CuO (the filtrate is pure copper(II) sulfate
     solution).
  5. Heat the filtrate to the point of crystallisation, leave to cool and
     crystallise; dry the crystals between filter papers.

  The excess-solid trick is the key exam point: a pure salt needs either
  reagent fully consumed, and only an insoluble excess can be filtered off.

Worked procedure 2 - insoluble salt by precipitation:
  barium sulfate from barium chloride + sodium sulfate solutions.
  BaCl₂(aq) + Na₂SO₄(aq) → BaSO₄(s) + 2NaCl(aq)
  Mix solutions, filter the precipitate, wash with distilled water, dry.

Worked procedure 3 - titration (soluble salt from acid + soluble alkali):
  sodium chloride from hydrochloric acid + sodium hydroxide.
  Both are solutions, so there is no excess solid to filter - use EXACT
  volumes from a titration (see the techniques note), then evaporate.

Worked procedure 4 - acid + excess metal (hydrogen given off):
  zinc sulfate from zinc + dilute sulfuric acid; filter excess zinc.

Water of crystallisation

Many salts crystallise with water locked into their lattice — hydrated salts (CuSO₄·5H₂O blue; CoCl₂·6H₂O pink). Heating drives the water off as anhydrous salt (white CuSO₄), and the change is reversible — the water test from the environment topic. In calculations the water counts in the formula mass: Mᵣ of CuSO₄·5H₂O = 160 + 5 × 18 = 250, not 160.

Worked example: a full salt-preparation calculation

10.0 g of calcium carbonate reacts with excess hydrochloric acid:
  CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂

(a) moles CaCO₃ = 10.0 / 100 = 0.100 mol
(b) ratio 1:1 → moles CaCl₂ = 0.100 mol
(c) mass CaCl₂ (Mᵣ = 111) = 0.100 × 111 = 11.1 g   [theoretical yield]
(d) if 9.4 g of dry salt is collected:
    percentage yield = 9.4 / 11.1 × 10⁰ = 84.7%

Where the mass is lost: crystals left in solution, spills, incomplete
reaction, or wet product if not dried - the usual evaluation question.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Confusing acid strength with concentration — strong = fully dissociated; concentrated = lots of acid per volume. The two are independent axes.
  • Writing weak acid dissociation with a single arrow; weak acids are equilibria.
  • Salt formula errors from ion charges: Al³⁺ + Cl⁻ → AlCl₃, not AlCl — check charge balance.
  • Forgetting carbon dioxide in acid + carbonate answers (three products, not two).
  • Adding excess soluble alkali in salt prep (then the salt is contaminated and cannot be filtered) — only insoluble reagents can be used in excess.
  • Leaving water of crystallisation out of formula mass or percentage-composition calculations.
  • Describing neutralisation as "acid + metal" — that is a separate reaction type; neutralisation is acid + base.
  • In precipitation questions, not washing the precipitate (residual soluble ions contaminate it).

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 4, 3 marks). Explain the difference between a strong acid and a concentrated acid.

Answer: A strong acid dissociates completely in water, releasing all its protons (e.g. hydrochloric acid); a concentrated acid contains a large amount of acid per unit volume of solution. A dilute solution of a strong acid is strong but dilute; a concentrated solution of a weak acid (ethanoic) is concentrated but weak.

Question 2 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Write equations for sulfuric acid reacting with (i) magnesium (ii) copper(II) oxide (iii) sodium carbonate.

Answer: (i) Mg + H₂SO₄ → MgSO₄ + H₂. (ii) CuO + H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + H₂O. (iii) Na₂CO₃ + H₂SO₄ → Na₂SO₄ + H₂O + CO₂.

Question 3 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Describe how pure crystals of copper(II) sulfate are prepared from copper(II) oxide and dilute sulfuric acid.

Answer: Warm the dilute acid; add copper(II) oxide with stirring until it no longer dissolves (excess solid ensures all acid reacts); filter off the excess copper(II) oxide; heat the filtrate to the point of crystallisation; leave the solution to cool and crystallise; filter and dry the crystals between filter papers.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 3 marks). Explain why aluminium oxide is described as amphoteric.

Answer: Aluminium oxide reacts with acids to form a salt and water (acting as a base), e.g. Al₂O₃ + 6HCl → 2AlCl₃ + 3H₂O, and also reacts with alkalis to form a salt and water (acting as an acid), e.g. Al₂O₃ + 2NaOH → 2NaAlO₂ + H₂O. Oxides with both behaviours are amphoteric.

Question 5 (Paper 4, 5 marks). Calculate the mass of anhydrous sodium sulfate formed when 21.2 g of sodium carbonate is neutralised by excess sulfuric acid. (Mᵣ: Na₂CO₃ = 106, Na₂SO₄ = 142)

Answer: Na₂CO₃ + H₂SO₄ → Na₂SO₄ + H₂O + CO₂. Moles Na₂CO₃ = 21.2 ÷ 106 = 0.200 mol. Ratio 1:1 → 0.200 mol Na₂SO₄. Mass = 0.200 × 142 = 28.4 g.

Question 6 (Paper 6, 3 marks). A student prepares lead(II) iodide by precipitation. State the reagents and describe the steps after mixing.

Answer: Mix solutions of lead(II) nitrate and potassium iodide. Filter to collect the yellow precipitate; wash it with distilled water to remove soluble nitrate/iodide ions; dry it between filter papers or in a warm oven.

Acids and salts live in the wider map of the elements — the Periodic Table's groups and their trends.

title: Continuous Random Variables — Study Notes
content:
Continuous Random Variables

Probability Density Functions

A continuous variable X is described by a density f(x) with f(x) ≥ 0 and ∫f(x)dx = 1 over all x. Probabilities are areas:

  • P(a ≤ X ≤ b) = ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx

Single points have zero probability, so strict or loose inequalities make no difference: P(X < 2) = P(X ≤ 2).

Finding Unknown Constants

Piecewise densities carry an unknown k: impose that the total area is 1 (and continuity at joins where required). One equation, one unknown.

Example: f(x) = kx on 0 ≤ x ≤ 2. Total area: k·(2²/2) = 2k = 1, so k = ½.

Expectation and Variance

  • E(X) = ∫x·f(x) dx
  • E(X²) = ∫x²·f(x) dx
  • Var(X) = E(X²) − (E(X))²

The mean is the balancing point of the area under the density. For symmetric densities the mean sits at the symmetry point — worth spotting before integrating.

The Median and Mode

The median m solves ∫₋∞ᵐ f(x) dx = 0.5 (left half of the area). The mode is the x maximising f(x). For uniform densities the median is the midpoint.

Uniform Distribution

If f(x) = 1/(b − a) on [a, b], every point is equally likely. Then E(X) = (a + b)/2 and Var(X) = (b − a)²/12 — memorise both; they are quick exam marks.

Exam tips: always verify ∫f = 1 before computing anything else. Sketch the density — area intuitions catch algebra slips. Median questions are integration-to-0.5 questions; set them up before calculating.

Exam method: density functions

A probability density function f must satisfy f(x) ≥ 0 for all x and the total area under it must equal 1, so the integral of f over its whole domain is 1. Use this to find an unknown constant before asking for any probability.

For a continuous variable, P(a ≤ X ≤ b) is the integral of f(x) from a to b. The endpoints carry no probability, so strict and non-strict inequalities give the same answer. Outside the given domain f(x) = 0.

The cumulative distribution function F(x) = P(X ≤ x) is the integral of f from the lower end of the domain up to x. The median m satisfies F(m) = 0.5, and the mode is where f is largest.

Expected value E(X) is the integral of x f(x) over the domain, and the variance is E(X²) minus the square of E(X). Write each integral with its limits before evaluating.

Exam cue: Sketch the density over its domain first. A linear density is a triangle or trapezium, and the area of the shape gives the total probability quickly.

title: AS Level Mathematics: Trigonometry
content:
AS Level Mathematics: Trigonometry

Trigonometry at AS level extends the triangle ratios of IGCSE into functions of any angle: the sine and cosine waves that model tides, sound and alternating current, the identities that let you simplify expressions and solve equations, and the sine and cosine rules that handle triangles without a right angle. This note builds the whole topic from zero: the graphs and their properties, exact values, the two core identities, the interval method for solving equations, the sine/cosine rules with the ambiguous case, and transformations of trigonometric graphs. Radian answers are expected wherever the question uses radians.

The three graphs and their properties

FunctionPeriodRangeKey features
sin θ360° (2π)−1 to 10 at 0°, 180°, 360°; maximum at 90°
cos θ360° (2π)−1 to 11 at 0°; 0 at 90°, 270°
tan θ180° (π)all real values0 at 0°, 180°; asymptotes at 90°, 270°

The graphs encode the symmetries the papers test: sin(180° − θ) = sin θ, cos(−θ) = cos θ, sin(−θ) = −sin θ, tan(180° + θ) = tan θ. A quick sketch of the relevant wave inside the required interval solves most equation problems before any algebra.

Worked example. Sketch y = sin x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 360° and mark where sin x = 0.5.

the sine wave crosses 0.5 on its rising part at x = 30 °
and on its falling part at x = 150 ° (symmetry about 90 °)
solutions in the interval: x = 30, 150

Exact values

The exact values come from two special triangles and must be known in both degrees and radians:

Anglesincostan
30° = π/61/2√3/21/√3
45° = π/41/√21/√21
60° = π/3√3/21/2√3

Beyond the first quadrant, use the symmetry rules with the reference angle: sin 150° = sin 30° = ½; cos 240° = −cos 60° = −½; tan 135° = −tan 45° = −1. The quadrant sign pattern ("CAST" or a sketch) decides the sign.

Worked example. Find the exact value of cos 300°.

300 ° is in the fourth quadrant; reference angle 60 °
cos is positive in the fourth quadrant: cos 300 = cos 60 = 1/2

The two identities

sin²(θ) + cos²(θ) = 1
tan(θ) = sin(θ)/cos(θ)     (cos θ not 0)

useful rearrangements:
sin² = 1 - cos²;  cos² = 1 - sin²
1 + tan² = sec² (beyond AS but built from the same identity)

Worked example 1 (simplify). Simplify (1 − cos²θ)/sin θ.

1 - cos² = sin²
sin²/sin = sin θ   (θ not a multiple of 180 °)

Worked example 2 (prove). Prove that (sin θ + cos θ)² = 1 + 2 sin θ cos θ.

expand: sin² + 2 sin cos + cos²
rearrange: (sin² + cos²) + 2 sin cos = 1 + 2 sin cos

Worked example 3 (solve with the identity). Solve 2 sin²θ + cos θ = 2 for 0 ≤ θ ≤ 360°.

replace sin² = 1 - cos²:
2(1 - cos²) + cos = 2
2 - 2cos² + cos = 2  →  -2cos² + cos = 0
cos(1 - 2cos) = 0  →  cos = 0 or cos = 1/2
cos = 0: θ = 90, 270
cos = 1/2: θ = 60, 300

Solving trigonometric equations in an interval

The method that never misses solutions: find the principal value, then use the symmetry of the wave to generate every solution in the interval.

  1. Isolate the trigonometric part (use identities if needed).
  2. Find the principal value with the inverse function.
  3. Use the symmetries: for sin, solutions are θ and 180° − θ (plus 360° steps); for cos, θ and 360° − θ; for tan, θ + 180° steps.
  4. Check every solution lies in the stated interval, and count them.

Worked example. Solve cos 2x = 0.5 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 360°.

let u = 2x, so 0 <= u <= 720
cos u = 0.5  →  u = 60, 300, 420, 660
x = 30, 150, 210, 330

The doubled-angle trap: the interval for u doubles too. Expand the interval whenever the argument is multiplied.

Worked example 2 (shifted). Solve sin(x − 30°) = 0.6 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 360°.

u = x - 30, so -30 <= u <= 330
sin u = 0.6  →  u = 36.9 or 143.1
x = 66.9 or 173.1

The sine and cosine rules

sine rule: a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C
cosine rule: a² = b² + c² - 2bc cos A
area of a triangle: (1/2) a b sin C

How to choose: two sides and a non-included angle (SSA) or two angles and a side (AAS) use the sine rule; three sides (SSS) or two sides and the included angle (SAS) use the cosine rule. The area formula uses two sides and the included angle.

Worked example 1 (cosine rule). A triangle has sides 8 cm, 11 cm and an included angle of 60°. Find the third side and the area.

a² = 8² + 11² - 2(8)(11)cos 60
    = 64 + 121 - 176(0.5) = 185 - 88 = 97
a = 9.85 cm
area = (1/2)(8)(11) sin 60 = 44 × 0.866 = 38.1 cm²

Worked example 2 (sine rule). In a triangle, angle A = 40°, side a = 7 cm, side b = 10 cm. Find angle B.

sin B / b = sin A / a
sin B = b sin A / a = 10 × 0.643/7 = 0.918
B = 66.7 ° or B = 113.3 ° (ambiguous case)

The ambiguous case

When you know two sides and a non-included angle, the sine rule can produce two valid triangles: angle B could be 66.7° or its supplement 113.3°. Both satisfy the sine rule, and the question must be read to decide which is intended — often a given angle sum rules one out, or the diagram shows an obtuse angle. State both and choose, with a reason.

Worked example. In the triangle above, find the two possible values of angle C and side c.

if B = 66.7: C = 180 - 40 - 66.7 = 73.3 °
  c/sin 73.3 = 7/sin 40  →  c = 7 × 0.958/0.643 = 10.4 cm
if B = 113.3: C = 26.7 °
  c = 7 × 0.449/0.643 = 4.89 cm

Transformations of trigonometric graphs

y = a sin(bx + c) + d
amplitude = |a|;  period = 360/b (or 2 π/b)
phase shift = -c/b;  vertical shift = d

Worked example. State the amplitude, period and range of y = 3 sin 2x + 1.

amplitude 3; period 360/2 = 180 °
range: 3 sin 2x ranges -3 to 3, so y ranges 1 - 3 = -2 to 4

Worked example 2 (phase). Describe the transformation y = sin(x + 45°).

a translation of 45 ° to the left (inside the bracket, so the
shift is opposite in sign to the constant)

Worked examples: applied trigonometry

Worked example. A ship sails 30 km on a bearing of 040°, then 20 km on a bearing of 130°. Find its distance and bearing from the start.

the two legs are 90 ° apart (130 - 40), so resolve into east and north
leg 1: east 30 sin 40 = 19.28;  north 30 cos 40 = 22.98
leg 2: east 20 sin 130 = 15.32;  north 20 cos 130 = -12.86
total: east 34.60;  north 10.12
distance = √(34.60² + 10.12²) = √(1197.2 + 102.4) = 36.1 km
bearing: tan(θ) = 34.60/10.12 = 3.419  →  θ = 73.7 °
(measured from north towards east)  →  bearing 074 °

The component method works for any number of legs; the cosine rule on the included angle is quicker only for exactly two. Either way, bearings are measured clockwise from north at every stage, never from the previous heading.

Radians, arc length and sector area

Radian measure is the natural unit for the trigonometric functions: one radian is the angle subtended at the centre of a circle by an arc equal in length to the radius, and a full turn is 2π radians. The conversions and the two circle formulas are used constantly in P1:

π radians = 180 °;  1 radian = 57.3 °
arc length s = r θ  (θ in radians)
sector area = (1/2) r² θ
segment area = sector area - triangle area

Worked example. A sector has radius 6 cm and angle 2 radians. Find its arc length, perimeter and area.

arc = 6 × 2 = 12 cm
perimeter = 12 + 6 + 6 = 24 cm
area = (1/2)(36)(2) = 36 cm²

Worked example 2 (segment). Find the area of the segment cut off by a chord subtending 1.2 radians in a circle of radius 5 cm.

sector = (1/2)(25)(1.2) = 15 cm²
triangle = (1/2)(5)(5) sin 1.2 = 12.5 × 0.932 = 11.65 cm²
segment = 15 - 11.65 = 3.35 cm²

The radian formulas only work in radians; in degrees the arc length is (θ/360)2πr and the sector area (θ/360)πr². Mixing the two is a silent error that costs the accuracy mark.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Exact) Find sin 240° exactly. Answer: third quadrant, reference 60°: −√3/2.
  2. (Identity) Simplify sin²θ/(1 − sin²θ). Answer: sin²θ/cos²θ = tan²θ.
  3. (Solve) Solve tan θ = 1 for 0 ≤ θ ≤ 360°. Answer: θ = 45°, 225°.
  4. (Solve with identity) Solve 3 cos²θ = sin²θ for 0 ≤ θ ≤ 360°. Answer: 3cos² = 1 − cos² → cos² = ¼ → cos = ±½ → θ = 60°, 120°, 240°, 300°.
  5. (Cosine rule) Sides 5 cm and 7 cm with included angle 120°. Find the third side. Answer: a² = 25 + 49 − 70(−0.5) = 109 → a = 10.4 cm.
  6. (Sine rule) A = 35°, B = 80°, a = 9 cm. Find b. Answer: b = 9 sin 80/sin 35 = 9 × 0.985/0.574 = 15.4 cm.
  7. (Area) Find the area of a triangle with sides 6 cm and 9 cm and included angle 50°. Answer: ½ × 54 × sin 50 = 20.7 cm².
  8. (Graph) State the period and amplitude of y = 4 cos 3x. Answer: period 120°, amplitude 4.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Losing solutions: an equation often has more than one solution in the interval; use the symmetry rules or sketch the wave. The commonest mark loss in this topic.
  • Not expanding the interval: for sin 2x over 0 ≤ x ≤ 360°, the argument runs to 720°; solutions are lost without that.
  • Degree/radian mode: the question's units decide the calculator mode; a radian interval (0 to 2π) needs RAD.
  • Wrong rule: sine rule for AAS/SSA, cosine rule for SAS/SSS; using the sine rule on SAS fails silently.
  • Forgetting the ambiguous case: SSA can give two triangles; state both and justify the choice.
  • Identity rearrangement slips: sin² = 1 − cos², not cos² − 1. Sign errors here propagate through the whole solution.
  • Amplitude and period: y = a sin bx has amplitude |a| and period 360/b; the b is not an amplitude.
  • Rounding mid-solution: keep full accuracy until the final answer; angles to 1 d.p. unless told otherwise.

title:
Respiration, Muscles and the Internal Environment — Edexcel International A2 Level Biology

This revision note covers the biology topics that sit behind the energy use of cells and animals and behind the maintenance of the internal environment. It is built around the specification statements rather than around a loose theme, so each numbered section reflects one or more things the specification expects a candidate to be able to do. The note is deliberately at exam depth: it explains the reasoning, gives the worked examples and comparisons that examiners look for, and lists the common mistakes that lose marks in this topic. Use it to check what you actually know and to practise the kinds of answer the specification rewards.

1. Why respiration matters and what the topic is for

Respiration is the set of reactions that release energy from nutrient molecules and couple that energy to the work cells do. The main nutrient in most questions is glucose, and the main energy currency that respiration produces is ATP. The practical point is that cells do not get energy directly from glucose; they get it from ATP, and respiration is the process that links the fuel to the currency. Understanding respiration therefore means understanding where the energy comes from, how the cell captures it, and how that energy is used in muscles and in the rest of the body.
