  2. Explain why respiration is an energy-releasing process but still needs to be staged rather than happening in one reaction. Answer: Respiration releases energy from glucose but a single reaction releasing all the energy at once would mostly waste it as heat; the stages release energy in manageable amounts that the cell can use to phosphorylate ADP to ATP, the energy currency for cell work. Stage-by-stage release also allows regulation of the rate to match the cell’s needs. (4 marks)
  3. Describe the sliding filament model of muscle contraction and state the role of ATP in it. Answer: During contraction the actin and myosin filaments slide past each other rather than shortening themselves, so the sarcomere shortens. Myosin heads bind to actin, pivot and pull the thin filament toward the centre, then detach and re-cock. ATP is required for the myosin head to detach from actin and be re-cocked for the next cycle, so the contraction is powered by ATP hydrolysis. (5 marks)
  4. Explain the roles of calcium and ATP in the control of muscle contraction and relaxation. Answer: When a muscle is stimulated, calcium is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum and exposes the binding sites on actin so myosin heads can bind; ATP is used to power the cross-bridge cycle and to detach the myosin heads. Relaxation occurs when calcium is removed and the binding sites are covered again; ATP is still required for detachment, which is why a muscle without ATP stays contracted, as in rigor mortis. (5 marks)
  5. Describe the response of the body during exercise in terms of heart rate and breathing rate, and explain why each increases. Answer: During exercise heart rate increases to deliver more oxygenated blood to the muscles and to remove more carbon dioxide and heat, and breathing rate increases along with breathing depth to bring in more oxygen and remove more carbon dioxide. Both responses increase because the muscles’ ATP demand rises and the supply and waste-removal systems must keep up with the increased metabolism. (5 marks)
  6. Describe how the skin blood vessels help control body temperature and state the direction of the response in each case. Answer: Blood vessels near the skin surface dilate in heat, increasing blood flow near the surface and increasing heat loss to the environment; they constrict in cold, reducing blood flow near the surface and reducing heat loss. This is part of thermoregulation and homeostasis, along with other responses such as sweating or shivering and behavioural changes. (4 marks)
  7. Define homeostasis and explain the principle of negative feedback with one example. Answer: Homeostasis is the maintenance of a stable internal environment within limits. Negative feedback is the control principle in which a change from the set point is detected and the response reduces the change, returning the variable toward the set point; for example in temperature control, if body temperature rises, effectors such as sweating and vasodilation increase heat loss, reducing the temperature back toward normal. (5 marks)
  8. Explain why water and solute balance are part of homeostasis and what happens if the internal environment becomes too concentrated or too dilute. Answer: Cells depend on the water potential of the internal environment; if it becomes too concentrated, water moves out of cells by osmosis, and if it becomes too dilute, water moves into cells. Either change can disrupt cell function, so the concentrations of water and solutes must be controlled. The body loses water in breathing, sweating and urine, so water balance is dynamic and must be regulated. (5 marks)
  9. Explain the link between respiration and muscle activity during exercise and why sustained vigorous exercise can exceed the body’s aerobic capacity for a time. Answer: Muscle activity uses ATP, so respiration must increase to supply ATP; aerobic respiration is efficient and sustainable if oxygen supply is sufficient, but during vigorous exercise oxygen delivery may not keep up with demand, so the muscle relies relatively more on pathways that do not need oxygen and produces different products, which is why breathing and heart rate rise and why the body shifts its metabolism. (5 marks)
  10. State what the kidneys do to help maintain the internal environment. Answer: The kidneys remove waste from the blood and help control water and solute balance by adjusting the composition of the urine, so they are important for maintaining the composition of the internal environment and for disposing of the waste products of metabolism including the CO2-related and other wastes that result from respiration. (4 marks)
  11. Describe one example of negative feedback in the human body and identify the receptor, control centre and effector in that example. Answer: In temperature control, temperature receptors detect a rise in core or skin temperature, the hypothalamus acts as the control centre, and effectors such as sweat glands and skin blood vessels respond by increasing heat loss, returning temperature toward the set point. If temperature falls, effectors such as shivering and vasoconstriction reduce heat loss or increase heat production. (5 marks)

Revise this topic by matching each numbered specification point to one mechanism, one location and one reason. Practise the respiration stages and their products, the sliding filament idea with ATP and calcium, the exercise responses and the thermoregulation responses, and the homeostasis and negative feedback principle with examples. Check that you can say where each process happens and why, not just what happens. Then move on to the next topic and the related practicals, because the practicals are the way the specification ties the ideas to hands-on work.

title: Edexcel IAL Computer Science: Simulation, Sensors and Real-World Data
content:
Edexcel IAL Computer Science: Simulation, Sensors and Real-World Data

Pearson Edexcel International Advanced Level in Computer Science, Unit 3/Unit 4: computer simulation and modelling, sensors and data capture, and the handling of real-world data — its messiness, validation, and the visualisation that makes it usable. These are the topics where the exam's scenario questions live: a flood model, a weather station, a clinical trial dataset. Every model below is walked through its loop, because simulation questions mark the loop, not the name.

Simulation and modelling

A model is a simplified representation of a system; a simulation runs that model over time to observe behaviour that may be impossible, dangerous, slow or expensive to observe on the real system. Why simulate: safety (crash tests, disaster planning), cost (flight training without aircraft), speed (compressing years of climate into hours), and experimentation with impossible scenarios (a dam's failure, a pandemic's spread).

Model typeMethodSuits
Continuous (mathematical)Differential equations stepped through timePhysics, climate, population dynamics
Discrete-eventState changes at event times; a clock jumps to each eventQueues, factories, network traffic
Monte CarloThousands of random samples; aggregate the outcomesRisk, finance, uncertainty estimates
Agent-basedAutonomous agents following local rules; macro behaviour emergescrowds, ecosystems, markets
Discrete-event simulation traced: a bank queue.

  State: queue length, teller busy/idle, clock.
  Events: ARRIVAL, DEPARTURE.

  clock 08:00  ARRIVAL A -> queue 1; teller idle -> serve A; schedule
               DEPARTURE 08:05
  clock 08:02  ARRIVAL B -> queue 1 (teller busy); B waits
  clock 08:04  ARRIVAL C -> queue 2
  clock 08:05  DEPARTURE A -> teller free -> serve B (queue 1);
               schedule DEPARTURE 08:09
  clock 08:09  DEPARTURE B -> serve C (queue 0)
  ...
  Collect: average wait, max queue, teller utilisation.

  Run it again with different arrival rates (or random draws) to find the
  teller count meeting a "95% wait under 5 minutes" target - the purpose of
  the exercise.

Monte Carlo method, traced: to estimate pi, sample random (x, y) points in the unit square and count those with x² + y² ≤ 1 — the ratio converges to π/4. More seriously: sampling thousands of market or epidemic paths gives outcome distributions rather than single predictions — the technique behind risk models.

Simulation validity is the critical-thinking mark: a model is only as good as its assumptions; verification (does the model do what was intended?) differs from validation (does it match reality?); random inputs need realistic distributions; and outputs carry uncertainty that must be reported, not presented as fact.

Model design and its assumptions

Building a model is choosing what to leave out — and the exam rewards naming those choices. A flood model treats the river channel as a shape and rain as an input rate; it ignores debris, tides and the farmer's culvert. Each abstraction is an assumption with a validity range: outside it (an unprecedented storm) the model's output is extrapolation, not prediction. Sensitivity analysis tests which assumptions matter — vary each parameter and watch the output; a result that swings wildly on one uncertain input is fragile and must be reported as such. Documentation of assumptions is what turns a demonstration into an artefact a decision-maker can trust.

Sensors and data capture

A sensor converts a physical quantity into an electrical signal the system reads: temperature (thermistor/thermocouple), light (LDR/photodiode), pressure, humidity, motion (PIR/accelerometer), sound, pH, flow. The signal chain from world to data: sensing → analogue signal → conditioning (amplify, filter noise) → analogue-to-digital conversion (sample and quantise — the Unit 1 representation work in hardware) → microcontroller → storage or transmission.

  • Sampling settings: rate (must exceed twice the fastest change — Nyquist) and resolution (bits of the ADC decide measurement granularity).
  • Calibration: mapping raw readings to true values against known references; drift requires periodic recalibration.
  • Error sources: noise (random — smoothed by averaging or filtering), bias (systematic — fixed by calibration), drift, quantisation, and placement (an unshielded temperature sensor reads the sun, not the air).
  • Logging and transmission: local buffering when offline, batch upload, and battery/scheduling trade-offs in remote deployments (a weather station sleeps between readings).
Worked: a river flood-warning station.

  Sensors: water-level ultrasonic ranger (sampled every 5 min), rainfall
  tipping-bucket (event-counted), temperature for compensation.
  Signal chain: analogue level -> amplifier -> 12-bit ADC -> microcontroller.
  Noise handling: median of 5 readings per sample (rejects a stuck-ping
  outlier); moving average for the displayed trend.
  Validation: level must be 0-8 m (range check); sudden 3 m jumps rejected
  as sensor faults unless the rainfall counter agrees (cross-check).
  Transmission: hourly GPRS batch upload; local ring buffer of 7 days.
  Alerting: threshold + rate-of-rise rule (level rising 0.5 m/hour warns
  earlier than a simple high-water mark).
  Calibration: manual staff-gauge reading weekly; offset corrected in code.

Real-world data: messy, then usable

Real data breaks textbook assumptions: missing values, duplicates, inconsistent formats (dates in three styles, units mixed), outliers, and errors of capture. The pipeline the exam expects:

  • Collection — decide what to measure and the granularity; document the method.
  • Cleaning — handle missing values (delete, impute mean/median, or model), remove duplicates, standardise formats and units, correct or flag outliers (decide: error or genuine extreme?).
  • Integration — merge sources with matching keys; reconcile conflicting values.
  • Analysis — descriptive statistics (mean, median, mode, range, standard deviation); identify trends and correlations — with the warning that correlation is not causation.
  • Visualisation — choose the chart for the question: line (trends over time), bar (comparison), histogram (distribution), scatter (relationship), pie (composition of a whole — sparingly).
  • Interpretation — state conclusions with their uncertainty and the limitations of the data.
Worked: cleaning a hospital admissions dataset.

  raw rows: 12,411
  1. duplicates (same patient ID + timestamp): 213 removed -> 12,198
  2. date formats ("03/04/26", "2026-04-03", "3 Apr 26") standardised to ISO
  3. ages: 4 rows "150", "−3", "n/a" -> out-of-range rejected; n/a imputed
     from the median age ONLY for aggregate analysis (flagged, not invented)
  4. admission_ward: inconsistent casing/spelling ("A&E", "a and e") mapped
     to a controlled vocabulary
  5. stay_duration recalculated from standardised dates (derived field beats
     trusting the raw column)
  6. descriptive stats on the clean set: mean stay 4.2 days, median 3.0,
     std dev 3.1 - the mean/median gap reveals the skewed long-stay tail.

  The rule: document every cleaning decision; deleting outliers silently is
  how honest data becomes misleading data.

Big data context: volume, velocity, variety, veracity (the four Vs) describe why traditional tools fail; sampling and streaming strategies, and privacy obligations over personal data, accompany every real-world dataset. Correlation versus causation earns its own marks: two series moving together may share a third cause, and the experiment or domain reasoning must justify a causal claim.

Worked example: from sensor to decision

A greenhouse climate model: temperature, humidity and CO2 sensors feed a
simulation that predicts tomorrow's conditions and controls vents/heaters.

1. Capture: sensors sampled each minute; ADC resolution 0.1 C.
2. Clean: range checks; median filter; calibration offsets applied.
3. Model: a discrete-time heat/moisture model (loss per hour depends on the
   delta to outside temperature and wind).
4. Simulate: run the model forward with forecast weather; Monte Carlo over
   forecast uncertainty to get a spread of outcomes.
5. Decide: if the 5th percentile of predicted overnight temperature drops
   below 4 C, pre-heat before sunset (acting early beats reacting).
6. Verify: compare yesterday's prediction with today's measured reality;
   re-fit parameters weekly - the model earns trust by tracking truth.

Statistical measures in practice

Real-world analysis rests on a small kit of measures, each answering one question. The mean summarises central tendency but is pulled by outliers; the median resists them (a skewed stay-length distribution reads median 3.0 against mean 4.2); the mode names the most common value (category data). Range and standard deviation describe spread — the standard deviation being the typical distance from the mean. Correlation (Pearson's r between −1 and +1) measures linear association, not cause. Choosing the right pair and reading their disagreement is a recurring exam skill: when mean and median diverge, the data is skewed and the honest summary says so.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Saying simulation "predicts the future"; it explores model behaviour under assumptions — output uncertainty must be reported.
  • Confusing verification with validation: built right versus matches reality.
  • Ignoring sampling rate vs signal frequency (aliasing) or ADC resolution vs required precision in sensor answers.
  • Treating missing values as zero; zeros are data, blanks are absence — the handling changes statistics.
  • Quoting correlation as causation in data questions.
  • Choosing visualisations that mislead (truncated y-axes, pie charts for many categories); the chart must fit the question.
  • Silent outlier removal: state the criterion and the effect, because genuine extremes may be the finding.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Unit 3, 4 marks). Explain why a flight simulator is used instead of real training flights.

Answer: Simulation safely reproduces rare and dangerous situations (engine failure, severe weather) that cannot be risked for training, at a fraction of the cost of operating aircraft, with unlimited repetition and instant reset. The model's fidelity is validated against real flight data, and trainees can pause and review — none of which is possible in the air.

Question 2 (Unit 3, 4 marks). Describe the difference between discrete-event and continuous simulation.

Answer: Continuous simulation advances the whole system state in fixed time steps governed by differential equations — suiting smoothly varying systems like climate or population. Discrete-event simulation jumps the clock directly between state-changing events (arrivals, departures) and processes each in order — suiting queues, factories and networks where nothing happens between events. Discrete-event is efficient for sparse activity; continuous fits dense, gradual change.

Question 3 (Unit 3, 4 marks). Explain two sources of error in sensor measurements and how each is handled.

Answer: Random noise (electrical interference, fluctuation) distorts individual readings — handled by sampling multiple readings and filtering (median or moving average). Systematic bias (the sensor reads consistently high due to calibration drift) shifts all readings — handled by calibrating against a known reference and applying a correction, with periodic recalibration. Range checks reject physically impossible values before use.

Question 4 (Unit 3, 5 marks). Describe the steps in preparing real-world data for analysis.

Answer: Collect with a documented method and granularity. Clean: remove duplicates, standardise formats and units, resolve missing values (delete, impute or flag — never treat as zero), handle outliers with a stated criterion. Integrate sources by matching keys. Analyse with descriptive statistics and trends. Visualise with charts fitted to the question. Interpret with uncertainty and limitations stated, and avoid causal claims from correlation alone.

Question 5 (Unit 3, 4 marks). Explain what is meant by verification and validation of a simulation model.

Answer: Verification checks the model is built correctly — the code implements the intended equations and rules (tested against hand calculations). Validation checks the model is a good representation of reality — its outputs match real observations within tolerance. A model can be verified yet invalid (the wrong equations faithfully implemented), so both are required before trusting results.

Question 6 (Unit 3, 3 marks). Explain why a Monte Carlo simulation runs thousands of trials.

Answer: Random sampling of uncertain inputs produces a distribution of outcomes rather than a single number; thousands of trials make that distribution stable enough to estimate probabilities (e.g. the 5% worst-case flood height) and quantify uncertainty. The aggregate statistics converge as trials increase — one run would be an anecdote, not a risk estimate.

With this note the Computer Science estate is complete: IGCSE 0478 Papers 1 and 2, and the Edexcel IAL Units 1–4 framework, each note at the exam-grade depth standard.

title: IGCSE Chemistry: Organic Chemistry
content:
IGCSE Chemistry: Organic Chemistry

Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry 0620 (2026–2028), Extended route, Topic 11 Organic chemistry: statements 11.1 Formulae, functional groups and terminology, 11.2 Naming organic compounds, 11.3 Fuels, 11.4 Alkanes, 11.5 Alkenes, 11.6 Alcohols, 11.7 Carboxylic acids, and 11.8 Polymers. Organic chemistry is a system, not a list — one structural logic generates every name, formula and reaction in this note. Each homologous series is derived from its general formula, and every reaction shows the functional-group change explicitly.

The organic framework: homologous series and functional groups

A homologous series is a family of similar compounds with the same functional group and general formula, differing by CH₂ units, showing gradual physical-property trends and similar chemistry. A functional group is the atom or group of atoms responsible for the characteristic reactions (C=C for alkenes, –OH for alcohols, –COOH for acids).

SeriesGeneral formulaFunctional groupSuffix
AlkanesCₙH₂ₙ₊₂None (single bonds)-ane
AlkenesCₙH₂ₙC=C-ene
AlcoholsCₙH₂ₙ₊₁OH–OH-ol
Carboxylic acidsCₙH₂ₙ₊₁COOH–COOH-oic acid

Saturated = all single C–C bonds (alkanes); unsaturated = at least one C=C (alkenes). Structural isomers share the molecular formula but have different structural formulae (butane and methylpropane, both C₄H₁₀) — the reason displayed formula alone is not enough. Naming: count the carbons (meth- 1, eth- 2, prop- 3, but- 4), add the suffix for the functional group.

Fuels and fractional distillation

Petroleum = a mixture of hydrocarbons, separated by FRACTIONAL DISTILLATION.

  The crude oil is vaporised and fed into the column:
   - hot at the bottom, cooler at the top;
   - each fraction condenses at the height where its boiling range matches
     the temperature.

  Fractions (lightest at top): refinery gas (C¹-C⁴, bottled gas),
  gasoline/petrol (C⁵-C10, car fuel), naphtha (chemical feedstock),
  kerosene/paraffin (jet fuel), diesel oil (lorry fuel), fuel oil (ships),
  lubricating fraction (oils, waxes), bitumen (road surfaces).

  Trend up the column (towards longer chains):
   - BOILING POINT RISES (bigger molecules, stronger intermolecular forces);
   - VISCOSITY INCREASES (thicker, flows less easily);
   - VOLATILITY FALLS (evaporates less readily);
   - COMBUSTION gets less clean (more soot/carbon).

Fractional cracking breaks long alkane chains into shorter, more useful ones (alkanes + alkenes): C₁₀H₂₂ → C₈H₁₈ + C₂H₄ — driven by the need for petrol and alkene feedstock.

Alkanes: substitution

Alkanes are generally unreactive (strong, non-polar C–C and C–H bonds) but burn (combustion) and undergo substitution with halogens in UV light.

Complete combustion (all hydrocarbons):
  CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O
Incomplete combustion (limited O₂):
  2CH₄ + 3O₂ → 2CO + 4H₂O   (carbon monoxide - toxic)
  or soot (C) forms - a visible flame with yellow tips.

Chlorination of methane (photochemical substitution):
  CH₄ + Cl₂  --UV light-→  CH₃Cl + HCl
  One H is REPLACED by Cl - the definition of substitution. The UV light
  provides the activation energy to split the Cl-Cl bond into radicals.
  Further substitution gives CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃, CCl₄ - the products are a
  mixture, which is why the reaction is poor for synthesis.

Alkenes: addition

Alkenes react via the C=C double bond in addition reactions — two reactants join to give one product (nothing is lost).

Addition to ethene - each with its conditions:

  + bromine (test for unsaturation):
    C₂H₄ + Br₂ → C₂H₄Br₂        (1,2-dibromoethane)
    OBSERVATION: orange bromine water is DECOLOURISED - the test that
    distinguishes alkenes from alkanes.

  + hydrogen (nickel catalyst, heat):
    C₂H₄ + H₂ → C₂H₆            (ethane; hydrogenation - margarine making)

  + steam (phosphoric acid catalyst, heat + pressure):
    C₂H₄ + H₂O → C₂H₅OH         (ethanol)

In every case the double bond opens to single bonds and the atoms add on -
draw the product by "opening" the C=C and attaching one atom to each carbon.

Alcohols

Two production routes for ethanol, with the trade-off the exam always asks:

1. FERMENTATION of glucose (yeast, no oxygen, 25-35 °C):
     C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂
   Advantages: renewable feedstock (sugar/corn), low energy conditions,
   batch process.
   Disadvantages: slow (days), dilute product (needs distilling), depends on
   crop supply and weather.

2. CATALYTIC HYDRATION of ethene (H₃PO₄ catalyst, 300 °C, 60 atm):
     C₂H₄ + H₂O → C₂H₅OH
   Advantages: fast, continuous, high purity and yield.
   Disadvantages: ethene comes from crude oil (finite), high energy/pressure
   costs.

Ethanol itself: burns cleanly (C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O) as a fuel;
a solvent (perfumes, paints); in alcoholic drinks.

Carboxylic acids and esters

Carboxylic acids are weak acids: they react with metals (salt + hydrogen), bases (salt + water) and carbonates (salt + water + carbon dioxide — the fizz test that identifies an acid).

Oxidation of ethanol to ethanoic acid:
  ethanol + [O] → ethanoic acid     e.g. by acidified potassium
  manganate(VII), or by bacterial action in vinegar production (air + 
  Acetobacter).

Esterification (acid + alcohol, concentrated H₂SO₄ catalyst):
  ethanoic acid + ethanol → ethyl ethanoate + water
  CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O

  Naming esters: the FIRST word comes from the ALCOHOL (ethyl, from ethanol),
  the second from the ACID (ethanoate, from ethanoic acid).
  Propyl methanoate = propanol + methanoic acid.

  Esters: sweet smells (fruits, perfumes), solvents, plasticisers.

Polymers

A monomer is the small molecule that repeats; a polymer is the very long chain of joined monomers. Addition polymerisation joins many alkene molecules by opening the double bonds — nothing else is produced.

Deducing the repeat unit - the master method:

  Monomer: propene, CH₂=CH-CH₃
  1. Open the double bond: -CH₂-CH(CH₃)-
  2. Extend the "bonds" at both ends to show the chain continuing:
     [ -CH₂-CH(CH₃)- ]ₙ

  Reverse (monomer from repeat unit): find the two backbone carbons of one
  unit, restore the double bond between them, and cap the ends with the
  substituents that were drawn.

  poly(ethene):  n CH₂=CH₂ → [ -CH₂-CH₂- ]ₙ
  poly(propene): n CH₂=CHCH₃ → [ -CH₂-CH(CH₃)- ]ₙ
  poly(chloroethene) (PVC): n CH₂=CHCl → [ -CH₂-CHCl- ]ₙ

Condensation polymerisation (two different bifunctional monomers):
  a small molecule (usually water) is LOST at each link.
  Nylon (a polyamide): diamine + dicarboxylic acid → nylon + water.
  PET (a polyester): diol + dicarboxylic acid → PET + water.
  Proteins are natural polyamides from amino-acid monomers.

Disposal: plastics are non-biodegradable — landfill accumulates, plastics in the ocean harm wildlife, burning releases toxic gases (HCl from PVC, CO from incomplete combustion). Options: recycling (sorted by type), depolymerisation (PET can be broken back to monomers and re-polymerised), and biodegradable alternatives.

Worked example: one route map, every reaction type

From ethane to ethyl ethanoate:

  ethane --(cracking/heat)-→ ethene      [thermal decomposition]
  ethene + steam --(H₃PO₄, 300 °C)-→ ethanol   [addition / hydration]
  ethanol + [O] --(bacterial)-→ ethanoic acid  [oxidation]
  ethanol + ethanoic acid --(conc. H₂SO₄)-→ ethyl ethanoate [esterification]

  Each arrow names its type, conditions and the functional-group change:
  alkane → alkene (C-C to C=C), alkene → alcohol (C=C to C-OH),
  alcohol → acid (-OH to -COOH), acid + alcohol → ester (-COOH/-OH to
  -COO-). Tracking the functional group through a route map is the skill
  the exam tests.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Forgetting that addition reactions need the C=C — alkanes substitute, alkenes add; mixing them up loses every mark on the question.
  • Bromine water: decolourised by alkenes (addition) but NOT by alkanes — the observation sentence must name the colour loss.
  • Counting general formula wrong for the first members (methane CH₄ fits CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ with n = 1).
  • Writing polymers without the extending bonds at both ends of the repeat unit (it must show continuation).
  • In ester naming, swapping which part comes from the acid and which from the alcohol.
  • Leaving reaction conditions off (UV for substitution, Ni/heat for hydrogenation, concentrated H₂SO₄ for esterification) — conditions are marks.
  • Claiming fermentation is fast/pure — the comparison with catalytic hydration needs both sides.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 4, 3 marks). Define a homologous series and state three general characteristics.

Answer: A homologous series is a family of similar compounds with the same functional group and general formula, each member differing from the next by a CH₂ unit. Characteristics: similar chemical properties; gradual trend in physical properties (boiling point rises with chain length); can be made by similar methods.

Question 2 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Describe the test that distinguishes ethene from ethane, with equations.

Answer: Add aqueous bromine and shake. Ethene decolourises the orange bromine (addition: C₂H₄ + Br₂ → C₂H₄Br₂); ethane shows no change (no reaction in the dark at room temperature). The C=C double bond is responsible for the addition.

Question 3 (Paper 4, 5 marks). Compare fermentation and catalytic hydration as routes to ethanol.

Answer: Fermentation (C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂, yeast, 25–35 °C) uses renewable sugar crops and mild conditions, but is slow, gives dilute ethanol needing distillation, and varies with crop supply. Catalytic hydration (C₂H₄ + H₂O → C₂H₅OH, H₃PO₄, 300 °C, 60 atm) is fast, continuous and high-yield, but depends on crude-oil-derived ethene and costly high-pressure conditions.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Draw the repeat unit of poly(propene) and name the polymerisation type.

Answer: Monomer propene CH₂=CHCH₃ opens at the double bond giving repeat unit [–CH₂–CH(CH₃)–]ₙ, with the chain bonds extending at both ends. This is addition polymerisation — many monomers join with no other product.

Question 5 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Describe how ethyl ethanoate is made and state its uses.

Answer: Warm ethanol with ethanoic acid in the presence of concentrated sulfuric acid catalyst (esterification): CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O. The ester is distilled off. Ethyl ethanoate is used as a solvent (nail-varnish remover), in perfumes and flavourings (sweet smell).

Question 6 (Paper 4, 3 marks). Explain why burning PVC can be more harmful than burning poly(ethene).

Answer: PVC contains chlorine; burning it releases hydrogen chloride gas, which is toxic and forms acidic fumes, plus carbon monoxide from incomplete combustion. Poly(ethene) contains only carbon and hydrogen and burns to CO₂ and water if complete — less acutely toxic though still a CO₂ source.

Organic molecules can be burned as fuels — the next topic is what happens when electrons move instead: electrochemistry.

title: A Level Mathematics: Sequences and Series
content:
A Level Mathematics: Sequences and Series

This note extends the AS work on arithmetic and geometric sequences into the A2 demands: sums to infinity with their conditions, recurrence relations and their closed forms, the σ notation manipulations, and the applied models — savings, depreciation, loan repayment and pendulum decay. It assumes the AS formulas and concentrates on the reasoning that distinguishes a secure A2 answer: why a series converges, when a model is valid, and how a recurrence becomes a formula.

Recap of the core formulas

arithmetic: u_n = a + (n - 1)d;  S_n = (n/2)[2a + (n - 1)d]
geometric:  u_n = a r^(n - 1);   S_n = a(1 - r^n)/(1 - r)
            S_inf = a/(1 - r) for |r| < 1

Worked example (mixed). The 4th term of a geometric series is 24 and the 7th is 192. Find a, r and S∞ if |r| < 1 (or state that it diverges).

ar³ = 24;  ar⁶ = 192
divide: r³ = 8  →  r = 2;  a = 3
|r| > 1, so the series diverges and S_inf does not exist

Convergence and the sum to infinity

A geometric series converges exactly when |r| < 1, because rⁿ → 0 and the term a rⁿ/(1 − r) vanishes. The condition is worth proving in words: each term is a fixed fraction of the last, so the running total approaches a limit rather than growing without bound.

S_inf = a/(1 - r)   exists only for |r| < 1

recurring decimals are geometric series in disguise

Worked example. Express 0.2̇7̇ (0.272727…) as a fraction.

= 0.27 + 0.0027 + 0.000027 + ...
a = 0.27, r = 0.01
S_inf = 0.27/0.99 = 27/99 = 3/11

Worked example 2 (find the range). For what values of x does 1 + 3x + 9x² + ... converge, and what is the sum?

r = 3x;  convergence needs |3x| < 1  →  |x| < 1/3
S_inf = 1/(1 - 3x)

Recurrence relations

u_(n+1) = a u_n + b

fixed point: L = aL + b  →  L = b/(1 - a)  (a not 1)
converges to L when |a| < 1

Worked example. u₁ = 5 and u_(n+1) = 0.5u_n + 6. Find the limit and the first four terms.

terms: 5, 8.5, 10.25, 11.125
limit L = 6/(1 - 0.5) = 12
the sequence rises towards 12 without reaching it

Worked example 2 (periodic). u_(n+1) = 1/(2 − u_n) with u₁ = 1. Find the first four terms and describe the behaviour.

u2 = 1/(2 - 1) = 1
so every term is 1: a constant sequence, a fixed point

σ notation and manipulation

sum from k = 1 to n of (ak + b) = a n(n+1)/2 + bn

split sums, factor constants, and shift the index as needed

Worked example. Evaluate the sum from k = 1 to 20 of (4k − 3).

= 4(20)(21)/2 - 3(20) = 840 - 60 = 780
check with the arithmetic formula: a = 1, d = 4, n = 20
S = 10(2 + 77) = 790  →  recheck: last term 4(20) - 3 = 77,
first term 1; S = (20/2)(1 + 77) = 780, agreement

Worked example 2 (geometric sum). Evaluate the sum from k = 1 to 8 of 3(2)^(k−1).

a = 3, r = 2, n = 8
S = 3(2⁸ - 1)/(2 - 1) = 3(255) = 765

Applied models

Worked example (savings with interest). 500 pounds is invested at the start of each year at 5% annual interest. Find the value after 10 years.

the first deposit earns 10 years, the last earns 1 year
value = 500(1.05¹⁰ + 1.05⁹ + ... + 1.05)
geometric: a = 500(1.05), r = 1.05, n = 10
S = 525(1.05¹⁰ - 1)/(0.05) = 525 × 12.578 = 6603 pounds

Worked example 2 (depreciation). A machine worth 20000 pounds depreciates 12% per year. When is it worth less than 5000?

20000(0.88)^n < 5000  →  0.88^n < 0.25
n ln 0.88 < ln 0.25  →  n > 1.386/0.1278 = 10.8
so after 11 years

Worked example 3 (bouncing ball). A ball is dropped from 3 m and rebounds to 70% of its previous height. Find the total distance travelled before it stops.

down 3, then up and down 3(0.7), 3(0.7)², ...
total = 3 + 2[3(0.7) + 3(0.7)² + ...]
= 3 + 2[3(0.7)/(1 - 0.7)] = 3 + 2(7) = 17 m

The doubling of the rebound terms is the standard trap: each bounce is travelled twice, up and down, except the initial drop. Sketching the first two bounces on a height axis makes the pattern obvious before any algebra is attempted.

Deriving the sum formulas

Both sum formulas are reconstructable in a few lines, which is worth more than memorising them: a candidate who can derive them never panics in an exam.

arithmetic: S = a + (a + d) + ... + [a + (n - 1)d]
write it backwards and add: 2S = n[2a + (n - 1)d]

geometric: S = a + ar + ... + ar^(n-1); multiply by r and subtract
S(1 - r) = a(1 - r^n)  →  S = a(1 - r^n)/(1 - r)

Worked example. Use the derivation to find S_12 for 4 + 10 + 16 + ...

a = 4, d = 6, n = 12
S = (12/2)[2(4) + 11(6)] = 6(74) = 444

Letting n grow in the geometric formula sends rⁿ → 0 when |r| < 1, leaving a/(1 − r): convergence falls out of the derivation rather than being a separate fact.

When is an arithmetic sum greatest?

If the common difference is negative, the terms eventually become negative and the running total peaks. Finding that peak is a standard A2 question.

terms stop increasing when a + (n - 1)d first becomes negative
sum is greatest just before the terms turn negative

Worked example. Find the greatest value of the sum of 50 + 47 + 44 + ...

d = -3; terms positive while 50 - 3(n - 1) > 0  →  n < 17.67
so keep 17 terms (last term 50 - 48 = 2)
S_17 = (17/2)(50 + 2) = 442

The 18th term is −1, so including it lowers the total: the maximum is at 17 terms. State the reason, not just the number.

Finding the number of terms

Many questions give the first and last terms and ask how many there are. Solve the nth-term formula for n rather than counting.

Worked example. How many terms are in 7, 11, 15, ..., 143?

143 = 7 + (n - 1)4  →  136 = 4(n - 1)  →  n = 35

Worked example 2 (geometric). How many terms of 2, 6, 18, ... are less than 5000?

2(3)^(n-1) < 5000  →  3^(n-1) < 2500
(n - 1) ln 3 < ln 2500  →  n - 1 < 7.13  →  n <= 8

For geometric sequences the log step is compulsory; for arithmetic ones simple rearrangement suffices. Round down for "less than" and up for "at least", and state the counting either way.

Three consecutive terms and the arithmetic mean

Many sequence questions give three consecutive terms involving an unknown and ask for the value that makes the sequence arithmetic or geometric. The condition is the definition, written as an equation.

arithmetic: middle = (first + third)/2
after canceling: the two consecutive differences are equal
geometric: middle² = first x third
after canceling: the two consecutive ratios are equal

Worked example. Find x so that x, x + 3 and 2x + 1 are consecutive terms of an arithmetic sequence.

(x + 3) - x = (2x + 1) - (x + 3)
3 = x - 2  →  x = 5
terms: 5, 8, 11 (difference 3) - check passes

Worked example 2 (geometric). Find x so that 4, x, 9 are consecutive geometric terms.

x² = 36  →  x = 6 or x = -6
both work; the sign changes whether the ratio is positive or negative

The geometric condition gives a square, so both signs survive unless context rules one out. That is exactly why the question usually adds a condition such as "all terms positive".

Formula summary

arithmetic: u_n = a + (n-1)d;  S_n = (n/2)[2a + (n-1)d]
geometric:  u_n = a r^(n-1);   S_n = a(1 - r^n)/(1 - r)
S_inf = a/(1 - r), |r| < 1
recurrence limit: L = b/(1 - a), |a| < 1

In applied questions the model choice decides everything: additive change is arithmetic, proportional change is geometric. Read the wording — "increases by 200 each year" versus "increases by 4% each year" — before writing a single formula, and check the first term corresponds to the first period rather than the starting quantity.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (S∞) Find S∞ of 5 + 2 + 0.8 + ... Answer: r = 0.4; 5/0.6 = 8⅓.
  2. (Convergence) For what x does 2 + 6x + 18x² + ... converge? Answer: |3x| < 1 → |x| < ⅓.
  3. (Recurring decimal) Write 0.4545... as a fraction. Answer: 45/99 = 5/11.
  4. (Recurrence) u_(n+1) = 0.2u_n + 8, find the limit. Answer: 8/0.8 = 10.
  5. (σ) Evaluate Σ from 1 to 10 of 5. Answer: 50.
  6. (σ arithmetic) Evaluate Σ from 1 to 15 of (2k + 1). Answer: 2(120) + 15 = 255.
  7. (Depreciation) 8000 pounds loses 10% annually. Value after 6 years? Answer: 8000(0.9)⁶ = 4252 pounds.
  8. (Unknown n) The sum of 3 + 6 + 12 + ... exceeds 1000 first at which term? Answer: S_n = 3(2ⁿ − 1) > 1000 → 2ⁿ > 334.3 → n = 9.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Using S∞ without checking |r| < 1: a divergent series has no finite sum; saying so earns the mark.
  • Off-by-one in applied models: count how many periods each payment earns; the first deposit earns one more year than the last.
  • Rebound counted once: every bounce after the first contributes twice to the distance.
  • Recurrence limit without the convergence condition: L = b/(1 − a) is only the limit when |a| < 1.
  • Mixing the models: growth uses (1 + r), decay and depreciation use (1 − r); inverting them changes the answer entirely.
  • Logs with a negative base factor: take ln of a positive quantity only; 0.88ⁿ is fine, (−0.88)ⁿ is not.
  • n must be a positive integer: inequality solutions are rounded up for "after how many years" questions.
  • Exact versus approximate: keep fractions and powers until the final money value, then round to the nearest penny or pound as asked.

Equations and symbols

Every relation this topic is examined on, written with its real notation and followed by a key naming each symbol, its unit and what it means. The sections above explain why each one is true; this sheet is the version to revise from, where the answer depends on reproducing the exact form and substituting into it without losing a unit.

Arithmetic and geometric, in both directions

uₙ = a + (n − 1)d and Sₙ = (n/2)(2a + (n − 1)d) = (n/2)(a + l)
Key: uₙ = the nth term; a = the first term; d = the common difference, uₙ₊₁ − uₙ; n = the term number; Sₙ = the sum of the first n terms; l = the last term included, uₙ. The (n − 1) is why the first term has no d added, and the second sum form is Gauss's pairing of the ends.

uₙ = a rⁿ⁻¹ and Sₙ = a(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r), r ≠ 1
Key: a = the first term; r = the common ratio, uₙ₊₁/uₙ; n = the number of terms; Sₙ = the sum of the first n. Each step multiplies by r, so the power is one less than the term number; r = 1 makes every term a and the sum na, which is the excluded case.

S∞ = a/(1 − r), valid only for |r| < 1
Key: S∞ = the sum to infinity; a = the first term; r = the common ratio. The condition is part of the answer, not a footnote: at |r| ≥ 1 the terms do not shrink and no finite sum exists, so writing the value without the condition loses a mark.

remainder after n terms = S∞ − Sₙ = a rⁿ/(1 − r)
Key: S∞ = the infinite sum, a and r as above; Sₙ = the sum of the first n; the difference is the tail still to be added. It shrinks geometrically, which is the algebraic form of the convergence argument.

arⁿ⁻¹ = X ⇒ n = 1 + log(X/a)/log r
Key: a = the first term; r = the common ratio, r > 0 for this form; X = the value of the term whose position is wanted; n = that position. Taking logarithms is the only way to free n from the exponent, and rounding up is usually required because n must be a whole number of terms.

Recurrence relations and their closed forms

uₙ₊₁ = a uₙ + b ⇒ limit L = b/(1 − a), reached only when |a| < 1
Key: uₙ = the current term; a = the multiplier; b = the constant added; L = the fixed point, the value satisfying L = aL + b. A recurrence with |a| < 1 creeps towards L without reaching it, one with |a| > 1 diverges, and |a| = 1 either repeats or drifts linearly.

uₙ = aⁿ⁻¹(u₁ − L) + L
Key: u₁ = the given first term; a, b = the recurrence constants; L = its fixed point b/(1 − a); n = the term number. Subtracting the limit turns the recurrence into a geometric sequence, which is why the closed form has this shape — it is the bridge between the two halves of the topic.

|uₙ − L| = |a|ⁿ⁻¹|u₁ − L|
Key: L = the limit; a = the recurrence multiplier; u₁ = the first term; the modulus is the distance from the limit after n terms. It is how "how many terms until it is within 0.01 of the limit" is answered, by solving an inequality in n with logarithms.

Sums in σ notation

Σ_{r=1}^{n} r = n(n + 1)/2, Σ r² = n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6, Σ r³ = [n(n + 1)/2]²
Key: Σ = the sum; r = the index running from 1 to n; n = the last index. The three standard results every polynomial sum is built from; the cube sum being the square of the linear sum is worth recognising as a check.

Σ_{r=1}^{n} (A r + B) = A n(n + 1)/2 + B n
Key: A, B = constants; r = the index; n = the number of terms. Sums are linear, so a linear expression splits into the standard r-sum plus a repeated constant — no new formula needed.

Σ_{r=m}^{n} f(r) = Σ_{r=1}^{n} f(r) − Σ_{r=1}^{m−1} f(r)
Key: m = the first index wanted; n = the last; f = the term expression. Subtracting two running totals is the safe way to handle a sum that does not start at 1, rather than re-deriving.

Models and disguised series

0.ẋẏ̇ = a/(1 − r) with a = the repeating block over its place value and r = 10⁻ᵏ
Key: a = the first occurrence of the repeating block as a decimal; r = the ratio between consecutive blocks (10⁻² for a two-digit block, 10⁻³ for three); k = the block length. Every recurring decimal is a geometric series, which is why the fraction is always a rational number.

appreciation or depreciation: Aₙ = A₀(1 ± p/100)ⁿ
Key: Aₙ = the value after n periods; A₀ = the starting value, in the currency unit; p = the percentage change per period; n = the number of periods. It is a geometric sequence with r = 1 ± p/100, so the same convergence and log methods apply.

loan or savings balance: Bₙ₊₁ = Bₙ(1 + i) − R
Key: Bₙ = the balance after n payments, in currency; i = the interest rate per period as a decimal; R = the fixed repayment or withdrawal. This is uₙ₊₁ = auₙ + b with a = 1 + i and b = −R, so its long-term behaviour and closed form come straight from the recurrence results above.

title: AS Level Physics: Superposition
content:
AS Level Physics: Superposition

Superposition is what happens when two waves occupy the same space at the same time: the displacements add, and from that single rule emerge stationary waves, diffraction, interference and the diffraction grating — the four phenomena of this topic. The mental picture to keep is two people shaking ropes that cross: at the crossing, the rope's shape is the sum of both shapes, instant by instant. This note builds each phenomenon from that rule, with the derivations and calculations line by line and the practical skills the papers demand.

The superposition principle

When two or more waves meet, the resultant displacement at any point is the vector sum of the individual displacements at that point. The waves pass through each other unchanged afterwards — they do not bounce off or alter each other. Everything in this topic is that sentence applied to different geometries:

  • Constructive interference: crest meets crest — displacements add, amplitude is a maximum.
  • Destructive interference: crest meets trough — displacements cancel, amplitude is a minimum (zero for equal waves).

Interference is sustained (a stable pattern) only when the sources are coherent: same frequency and a constant phase difference. Two unrelated lamps are incoherent and produce no stable pattern — this distinction is examinable every session.

Stationary waves

A stationary (standing) wave forms when two progressive waves of the same frequency and amplitude travel in opposite directions — classically a wave and its reflection. The pattern oscillates but does not travel: there are fixed points of zero displacement (nodes) and fixed points of maximum displacement (antinodes), and the wave profile stays in place while the medium oscillates within it.

FeatureProgressive waveStationary wave
Energytransferred along the wavestored in the oscillating regions; not transferred
Nodesnonefixed zero-displacement points, half a wavelength apart
Antinodescrests move alongfixed maximum points, half a wavelength apart
Phaseneighbouring points vary smoothly in phaseall points between two adjacent nodes oscillate in phase

Harmonics give the numbers. For a string fixed at both ends (or a pipe closed at both ends), the fundamental has nodes at both ends and one antinode between: the string length L fits half a wavelength, so λ = 2L. The next mode fits a full wavelength (λ = L), the next 3λ/2 (λ = 2L/3), and in general λₙ = 2L/n with fₙ = n v/(2L). For a pipe closed at one end, the closed end is a node and the open end an antinode: the fundamental fits a quarter wavelength, λ = 4L, and only odd harmonics appear, fₙ = n v/(4L) with n = 1, 3, 5 ...

Worked example. A guitar string 0.65 m long has a wave speed of 320 m s⁻¹. Find the fundamental and second harmonic frequencies.

fundamental: lambda = 2L = 1.30 m
f1 = v/lambda = 320/1.30 = 246 Hz
second harmonic: lambda = L = 0.65 m
f2 = 320/0.65 = 492 Hz   (exactly 2 x f1, as expected)

Worked example (closed pipe). A pipe 0.50 m long, closed at one end, has sound speed 340 m s⁻¹. Find the fundamental and state the next allowed frequency.

fundamental: lambda = 4L = 2.00 m
f1 = 340/2.00 = 170 Hz
only odd harmonics allowed -> next is the 3rd: f3 = 3 x 170 = 510 Hz

Diffraction

Diffraction is the spreading of waves as they pass through a gap or around an obstacle. It is significant when the gap (or obstacle) size is comparable to the wavelength — the wave bends generously around a 1 cm gap if λ is a few centimetres, but barely at all for light through a doorway. The rule to quote: noticeable diffraction requires gap size approximately equal to the wavelength. Consequences: long-wavelength radio diffract around hills; short-wavelength microwaves need line-of-sight aerials; light through everyday doors shows negligible diffraction, which is why shadows exist.

The single-slit pattern is examinable in outline: a broad central maximum of width related to λ/a (slit width a), with the intensity falling away on either side; a narrower slit produces a wider spread. Water waves in a ripple tank photograph the same behaviour macroscopically.

Interference: two sources

Two coherent sources produce a stable pattern of maxima and minima. The controlling quantity is the path difference — the difference in distance from the two sources to the point in question:

  • Constructive (maximum): path difference = nλ (n = 0, 1, 2 ...), i.e. a whole number of wavelengths.
  • Destructive (minimum): path difference = (n + ½)λ — a whole number plus half.

Worked example. Two speakers sit 4.0 m apart, driven in phase at 170 Hz (sound speed 340 m s⁻¹). A listener stands on the perpendicular bisector, then moves until the first minimum. Find the path difference at the first minimum.

lambda = v/f = 340/170 = 2.0 m
first minimum: path difference = lambda/2 = 1.0 m

On the perpendicular bisector the path difference is zero, so the centre is a maximum; the first minimum occurs where the difference reaches half a wavelength — 1.0 m of extra path.

Young's double-slit experiment

Light through two closely spaced slits forms fringes of alternating bright and dark bands on a screen. The fringe spacing formula, derived from path difference across a distant screen, is the calculation the papers test:

fringe spacing  w  = lambda D / d

D = slit-to-screen distance (m)
d = slit separation (m)
lambda = wavelength (m)

Worked example 1. Light of wavelength 600 nm falls on slits 0.25 mm apart; the screen is 1.8 m away.

lambda = 600 nm = 6.0 x 10-7 m
d = 0.25 mm = 2.5 x 10-4 m
w = lambda D/d = (6.0 x 10-7 x 1.8)/(2.5 x 10-4)
  = 1.08 x 10-6/2.5 x 10-4 = 4.32 x 10-3 m = 4.3 mm

Worked example 2 (working backwards). Fringe spacing 2.0 mm is measured with D = 2.0 m and λ = 500 nm. Find the slit separation.

d = lambda D/w = (5.0 x 10-7 x 2.0)/(2.0 x 10-3)
  = 1.0 x 10-6/2.0 x 10-3 = 5.0 x 10-4 m = 0.50 mm

Examiner note: the formula assumes small angles and a distant screen; when asked to describe the effect of moving the screen away, the answer is that fringes spread out (w increases with D) — a proportionality answer, not a guess.

The diffraction grating

A diffraction grating has many equally spaced slits; the interference from all of them produces sharp, bright maxima at angles given by

n lambda = d sin theta

n = 0, 1, 2, ... (the order)
d = slit spacing (grating spacing), the distance between
    adjacent slits (m)
theta = angle of the maximum from the central beam

The number of orders is a standard question: since sin θ ≤ 1, the maximum order n is the largest integer with nλ ≤ d, i.e. n = floor(d/λ); each order appears twice (either side) plus the central beam.

Worked example 1. A grating has 300 lines per millimetre. Light of wavelength 550 nm is incident normally. Find the angles of the first- and second-order maxima.

grating spacing: d = 1 mm/300 = 3.33 x 10-6 m
first order (n = 1):
sin theta = lambda/d = 5.5 x 10-7/3.33 x 10-6 = 0.165
theta = sin-1(0.165) = 9.5 degrees
second order (n = 2):
sin theta = 2 x 0.165 = 0.330
theta = 19.3 degrees

Worked example 2 (counting orders). With the same grating and λ = 550 nm, how many maxima are visible in total?

max order: n lambda <= d  ->  n <= d/lambda = 3.33 x 10-6/5.5 x 10-7 = 6.06
largest integer n = 6
orders: -6 to +6 plus n = 0  ->  13 maxima in total

Practical skill: measuring d from a grating quoted as N lines per metre, d = 1/N. A grating with 500 lines per mm has d = 2.0 × 10⁻⁶ m. Getting that reciprocal wrong doubles every downstream answer.

Worked examples: comparing the phenomena

Worked example. White light falls on a double slit and, separately, on a diffraction grating. Describe and explain the difference between the two patterns.

double slit: equally spaced fringes; the central fringe is white,
             outer fringes coloured because fringe spacing depends
             on lambda - blue (shorter lambda) fringes sit closer
             to the centre than red
grating:     sharply defined maxima at angles set by sin theta =
             n lambda/d, so each order spreads into a spectrum
             with violet least deviated and red most

Why the marks land: the description names the pattern shape, then the mechanism (spacing proportional to λ) and the colour ordering — explanation, not just observation.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Definitions) State the principle of superposition and define coherence. Answer: When waves meet, the resultant displacement is the sum of the individual displacements. Coherent waves have the same frequency and a constant phase difference.
  2. (Stationary waves) Describe the formation of a stationary wave in a string. Answer: A wave produced at one end travels along the string and reflects at the fixed end; the incident and reflected waves of equal frequency and amplitude superpose; at nodes the two are in antiphase and cancel, at antinodes in phase and reinforce; the pattern oscillates without propagating.
  3. (Closed pipe) The fundamental of a closed pipe is 220 Hz. State the frequency of the next possible harmonic and why. Answer: 660 Hz — closed pipes support odd harmonics only, so the next is the third harmonic, 3 × 220.
  4. (Diffraction) State and explain why long-wave radio signals can be received behind hills but microwave signals cannot. Answer: Radio wavelengths (hundreds of metres) are comparable to hill sizes, so they diffract noticeably around them; microwaves (centimetres) diffract negligibly and need line of sight.
  5. (Double slit) Blue light (450 nm) is replaced by red (650 nm) with no other change. State the effect on fringe spacing and explain. Answer: The spacing increases because w = λD/d and λ has increased; the fringes spread out proportionally.
  6. (Grating) A grating has 600 lines per mm and is illuminated with 500 nm light. Calculate the angle of the first-order maximum. Answer: d = 1/600 000 = 1.67 × 10⁻⁶ m; sin θ = 5.0 × 10⁻⁷/1.67 × 10⁻⁶ = 0.300; θ = 17.5°.
  7. (Orders) In question 6, how many maxima are visible altogether? Answer: d/λ = 3.33, so n = 3; orders −3 to +3 plus the central beam make 7 maxima.
  8. (Practical) Describe how you would measure the fringe spacing of a double-slit pattern. Answer: Measure the distance across several fringes (e.g. from the centre of one bright fringe to the centre of the nth bright fringe) with a ruler or travelling microscope, then divide by n — measuring many fringes reduces the fractional uncertainty.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Grating spacing inversion: 300 lines per mm means d = 3.33 × 10⁻⁶ m, not 3.33 × 10⁻³ m. Write the reciprocal step as its own line.
  • Units in the grating formula: d and λ must both be in metres. Nanometres into the formula directly gives sin θ in the thousands.
  • sin θ vs tan θ: fringe positions at large angles cannot use the small-angle approximation; use sin⁻¹ from the grating equation and w = λD/d only where angles are small.
  • Counting orders: remember the central beam (n = 0) and both sides; and round the order down (floor of d/λ), never up.
  • Node/antinode language: nodes are zero displacement and exist because of antiphase superposition; antinodes vibrate with double amplitude. Swapping the two is a definition mark lost.
  • Closed-pipe harmonics: an open–closed pipe supports odd harmonics only (1st, 3rd, 5th); answering with the second harmonic loses the mark.
  • Incoherent sources: two separate lamps cannot produce a stable interference pattern — coherence is the condition, and it is worth a stated mark.
  • Path difference conditions: maxima at whole wavelengths, minima at half-integer. State the condition in words and symbols.
  • Method marks: write the formula (nλ = d sin θ or w = λD/d) before numbers; a correct formula with failed arithmetic still earns credit.

Equations and symbols

The whole of this topic as equations, each written with its real symbols and each followed by a key naming every symbol and its unit. Where a law has more than one useful form both are given, because which one is quickest depends on which quantities the question hands you. Learn the form here and the algebraic rearrangement becomes mechanical in the exam.

8.1 Wave quantities and stationary waves

v = f λ
Key: v = wave speed (m s⁻¹); f = frequency (Hz); λ = wavelength (m). For a wave crossing a boundary the speed and wavelength change but the frequency is set by the source and does not.

T = 1 / f
Key: T = period, the time for one complete oscillation (s); f = frequency (Hz).

y = y₁ + y₂
Key: y = resultant displacement at a point (m); y₁, y₂ = displacements the two waves would separately produce there (m). The superposition principle itself: displacements add as vectors, so two troughs make a deeper trough and a crest meeting a trough cancels.

node spacing = λ / 2, antinode spacing = λ / 2, node to nearest antinode = λ / 4
Key: λ = wavelength of the waves forming the stationary wave (m). A stationary wave stores energy rather than transporting it, because the two travelling waves carry equal energy in opposite directions.

λ_n = 2 L / n, so f_n = n v / (2 L)
Key: λ_n = wavelength of the nth harmonic (m); L = length of the string or pipe (m); n = 1, 2, 3 … (all integers); f_n = its frequency (Hz); v = wave speed on the string or in the air (m s⁻¹). Applies to a string fixed at both ends and to a pipe open at both ends; f₁ = v/2L is the fundamental, and every harmonic is present.

λ_n = 4 L / n, so f_n = n v / (4 L) with n = 1, 3, 5 …
Key: λ_n = wavelength (m); L = length of the pipe closed at one end (m); n = odd integers only; f_n = frequency (Hz); v = speed of sound (m s⁻¹). A closed end must be a node and an open end an antinode, so only odd harmonics exist — the missing even harmonics are the standard exam trap.

f_n = n f₁
Key: f_n = frequency of the nth harmonic (Hz); f₁ = fundamental frequency (Hz); n = harmonic number. Use it to jump straight from the fundamental to the harmonic a question asks for.

8.2 Diffraction and 8.3 interference

path difference = n λ (constructive), path difference = (n + ½) λ (destructive)
Key: path difference = difference in distance travelled by the two waves to the point (m); λ = wavelength (m); n = 0, 1, 2 … For sources in phase, a whole number of wavelengths arrives in step and reinforces; a half-odd number arrives in antiphase and cancels.

Δφ = 2π Δx / λ
Key: Δφ = phase difference between the two waves at the point (rad); Δx = path difference (m); λ = wavelength (m). The bridge between the two languages of interference: distances in metres and phase in radians, related by 2π per wavelength.

Δφ = 2π Δt / T
Key: Δφ = phase difference (rad); Δt = time delay between the two waves arriving (s); T = period (s). The same idea in time: one whole period of delay is one whole cycle of phase.

w = λ D / d
Key: w = fringe spacing, centre to centre of adjacent bright fringes (m); λ = wavelength (m); D = distance from the double slits to the screen (m); d = separation of the two slits (m). Young's double-slit result, valid when D ≫ d and the fringes are close together.

λ = w d / D
Key: λ = wavelength of the light (m); w = measured fringe spacing (m); d = slit separation (m); D = slit-to-screen distance (m). The measuring form: w and D are easy to measure, d is given, so λ comes out of three lengths.

I ∝ A²
Key: I = intensity, power per unit area (W m⁻²); A = amplitude of the oscillation (m). Doubling the amplitude quadruples the intensity, which is why two identical waves in phase give four times the intensity of one rather than twice.

I = P / (4 π r²)
Key: I = intensity at distance r from a point source (W m⁻²); P = power radiated by the source (W); r = distance from the source (m). The inverse-square law that follows from the energy spreading over a sphere.

coherence: constant phase difference, same frequency
Key: two sources are coherent when the phase difference between them does not vary with time, which requires identical frequency and a fixed path relationship. Independent lamps are not coherent, which is why a stable fringe pattern needs one source split into two paths — a laser, or a single slit feeding a double slit.

8.4 The diffraction grating

d sin θ = n λ
Key: d = grating spacing, the distance between adjacent slits (m); θ = angle between the normal and the nth-order maximum (degrees); n = order of the maximum, 0, 1, 2 …; λ = wavelength (m). Constructive interference from many slits at once, which is why the maxima are sharp where two-slit fringes are broad.

d = 1 / N
Key: d = slit spacing (m); N = number of lines per metre (m⁻¹). For a grating quoted in lines per millimetre, N = 1000 × lines mm⁻¹.

n_max = d / λ (largest integer below it)
Key: n_max = highest order that can be seen; d = slit spacing (m); λ = wavelength (m). It follows from sin θ ≤ 1: an order whose d sin θ would exceed d cannot exist, and the largest integer that fits is the answer.

total maxima = 2 n_max + 1
Key: n_max = highest visible order; the +1 counts the central zero-order maximum; the factor 2 counts the orders on either side of it. The standard final part of a grating question.

sin θ ∝ λ
Key: θ = diffraction angle (degrees); λ = wavelength (m); at fixed order n and spacing d, since sin θ = nλ/d. This is why white light spreads into a spectrum with red deviated most and violet least — the opposite of a prism, where violet is deviated most.

title: AS Level Mathematics: Integration
content:
AS Level Mathematics: Integration

Integration is differentiation in reverse: it recovers a function from its gradient, and it accumulates a rate into a total — the area under a curve, the distance from a velocity, the cost from a marginal. This note builds the topic from zero: the indefinite integral and the constant of integration, the power rule, definite integrals and the fundamental theorem, areas above and below the axis, the area between two curves, and kinematics. Every worked example shows the antiderivative line before any substitution of limits.

The indefinite integral

if dy/dx = x^n then y = x^(n+1)/(n+1) + c   (n not -1)

integral of x^n dx = x^(n+1)/(n+1) + c
integral of k f(x) dx = k integral of f(x) dx
integral of a sum = sum of integrals

The +c is mandatory for indefinite integrals: every antiderivative differs by a constant, and the constant is fixed by a boundary condition (a point on the curve).

Worked example 1. Find ∫(6x² − 4x + 3) dx.

= 6x³/3 - 4x²/2 + 3x + c
= 2x³ - 2x² + 3x + c

Worked example 2 (negative and fractional powers). Find ∫(1/x² + √x) dx.

rewrite: integral of (x⁻² + x^(1/2)) dx
= -x⁻¹ + (2/3)x^(3/2) + c
= -1/x + (2/3)x^(3/2) + c

Worked example 3 (finding c). dy/dx = 3x² + 2 and the curve passes through (1, 5). Find y.

y = x³ + 2x + c
5 = 1 + 2 + c  →  c = 2
y = x³ + 2x + 2

Definite integrals and area

integral from a to b of f(x) dx = F(b) - F(a)

area under the curve between x = a and x = b (above the axis)
= definite integral; a negative value means the region is
below the x-axis, and the area is the magnitude

Worked example. Evaluate ∫ from 1 to 3 of (2x + 1) dx.

antiderivative: x² + x
F(3) = 9 + 3 = 12;  F(1) = 1 + 1 = 2
value = 12 - 2 = 10

Worked example 2 (area under a curve). Find the area under y = x² between x = 0 and x = 3.

integral: x³/3
from 0 to 3: 27/3 - 0 = 9 square units

Worked example 3 (below the axis). Find the area between y = x² − 4 and the x-axis from x = 0 to x = 2.

integral: x³/3 - 4x
from 0 to 2: 8/3 - 8 = -16/3
the value is negative because the region is below the axis;
area = 16/3 = 5.33 square units

Areas crossing the axis

When a curve crosses the x-axis inside the interval, integrate each piece separately and add the magnitudes — a single integral would cancel positive and negative areas.

Worked example. Find the total area between y = x² − 1 and the x-axis from x = −2 to x = 2.

crossings at x = -1 and x = 1
piece 1 (-2 to -1): F = x³/3 - x; F(-1) - F(-2) = (2/3) - (-2/3) = 4/3
piece 2 (-1 to 1): F(1) - F(-1) = (-2/3) - (2/3) = -4/3 → magnitude 4/3
piece 3 (1 to 2): F(2) - F(1) = (2/3) - (-2/3) = 4/3
total area = 4/3 + 4/3 + 4/3 = 4 square units

Area between two curves

area between y = f(x) and y = g(x) from a to b
= integral of (f(x) - g(x)) dx from a to b
where f is the upper curve and g the lower

Worked example. Find the area between y = x² and y = x from x = 0 to x = 1.

upper curve on this interval is y = x
integral of (x - x²) dx = x²/2 - x³/3
from 0 to 1: 1/2 - 1/3 = 1/6 square units

Worked example 2 (intersections). Find the area enclosed by y = x² and y = 2x.

intersections: x² = 2x → x(x - 2) = 0 → x = 0, 2
upper on (0, 2) is y = 2x
integral of (2x - x²) dx = x² - x³/3
from 0 to 2: 4 - 8/3 = 4/3 square units

Kinematics with integration

velocity v = ds/dt  →  displacement s = integral of v dt
acceleration a = dv/dt  →  velocity v = integral of a dt

definite integral of v from t1 to t2 = displacement
integral of |v| = distance travelled

Worked example. A particle has velocity v = 3t² − 6t (m/s). Find its displacement from t = 0 to t = 3 and its distance travelled.

s = integral of (3t² - 6t) dt = t³ - 3t²
from 0 to 3: 27 - 27 = 0  →  net displacement zero
sign of v: 3t(t - 2), negative between 0 and 2, positive after
distance = |integral 0 to 2| + integral 2 to 3
= |8 - 12| + (27 - 27) - (8 - 12) = 4 + 4 = 8 m

The distinction between displacement and distance is examinable: displacement is the signed integral, distance is the sum of the absolute pieces.

Worked examples: mixed integration

Worked example. The curve y = f(x) has f'(x) = 6x − 4 and passes through (2, 3). Find f(x) and the area under the curve from x = 1 to x = 2.

f(x) = 3x² - 4x + c;  3 = 12 - 8 + c → c = -1
f(x) = 3x² - 4x - 1
area = integral 1 to 2: x³ - 2x² - x
F(2) = 8 - 8 - 2 = -2; F(1) = 1 - 2 - 1 = -2
area = -2 - (-2) = 0  (the curve is below the axis and the
signed areas cancel); the geometric area needs the crossing
checked - a useful reminder to sketch first

Integrating expressions that need rearranging

Integration has no product or quotient rule at AS level, so expressions must first be written as sums of powers. Two standard rearrangements cover almost every case:

product: expand, then integrate term by term
quotient with a single term denominator: divide through first

(x + 2)(x - 5) = x² - 3x - 10
(3x² + 4x)/x = 3x + 4
√(x)(x + 1) = x^(3/2) + x^(1/2)

Worked example. Find ∫ (x + 3)(x − 1) dx.

expand: x² + 2x - 3
integrate: x³/3 + x² - 3x + c

Worked example 2. Find ∫ (4x³ + 2x)/x dx.

divide: 4x² + 2
integrate: (4/3)x³ + 2x + c

Two boundary conditions

When the second derivative is given, integrate twice and use two pieces of information to fix both constants. The order matters: the first integration produces the gradient function and its constant, the second the curve and its constant.

Worked example. d²y/dx² = 6x, dy/dx = 2 when x = 1, and y = 5 when x = 1. Find y.

first: dy/dx = 3x² + c;  2 = 3 + c  →  c = -1, so dy/dx = 3x² - 1
second: y = x³ - x + k;  5 = 1 - 1 + k  →  k = 5
y = x³ - x + 5

Finding limits and constants from area information

Area questions are often inverted: the area is given and a limit or coefficient must be found. Set up the definite integral with the unknown, evaluate, and solve the resulting equation — rejecting any root outside the geometric context.

Worked example. The area under y = kx² from x = 0 to x = 3 is 36. Find k.

integral: kx³/3
from 0 to 3: 27k/3 = 9k
9k = 36  →  k = 4

Worked example 2 (unknown upper limit). The area under y = 2x from x = 0 to x = a is 25. Find a.

integral: x²;  from 0 to a: a² = 25
a = 5  (the negative root is rejected: a is an x-coordinate to
the right of the origin in this setup)

Kinematics: recovering velocity from acceleration

Worked example. A particle starts from rest with acceleration a = 6t − 4 (m/s²). Find its velocity at t = 3 and the distance travelled in the first 3 seconds.

v = integral of (6t - 4) dt = 3t² - 4t + c
at rest at t = 0: c = 0  →  v = 3t² - 4t
v(3) = 27 - 12 = 15 m/s
distance = integral of |v| from 0 to 3
v = 0 at t = 0 and t = 4/3; v is negative on (0, 4/3)
piece 1: [t³ - 2t²] from 0 to 4/3 = 64/27 - 32/9 = -32/27 → 32/27
piece 2: [t³ - 2t²] from 4/3 to 3 = (27 - 18) - (-32/27) = 9 + 32/27
distance = 32/27 + 9 + 32/27 = 9 + 64/27 = 11.4 m

The sign analysis is the whole question: sketch v against t, mark where it crosses zero, and integrate each piece with its sign removed.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Indefinite) Find ∫(4x³ − 2) dx. Answer: integrate term by term and add the constant: ∫4x³ dx = x⁴ and ∫2 dx = 2x, so the result is x⁴ − 2x + c.
  2. (Negative power) Find ∫x⁻² dx. Answer: raise the power by one and divide by the new power: ∫x⁻² dx = x⁻¹/(−1) + c = −1/x + c.
  3. (Definite) Evaluate ∫ from 0 to 2 of 3x² dx. Answer: integrate, then substitute the limits: ∫₀² 3x² dx = [x³]₀² = 2³ − 0³ = 8.
  4. (Area) Find the area under y = x + 2 from x = 0 to x = 3. Answer: [x²/2 + 2x] = 4.5 + 6 = 10.5.
  5. (Below axis) Find the area between y = x − 3 and the x-axis from x = 0 to x = 2. Answer: integral = [x²/2 − 3x] = 2 − 6 = −4; area 4.
  6. (Between curves) Find the area between y = x² and y = x³ from 0 to 1. Answer: upper is x²; ∫(x² − x³) = 1/3 − 1/4 = 1/12.
  7. (Constant) dy/dx = 4x and y = 7 when x = 1. Find y. Answer: y = 2x² + c → 7 = 2 + c → c = 5 → y = 2x² + 5.
  8. (Kinematics) v = 2t + 1. Find the displacement from t = 0 to t = 4. Answer: [t² + t] = 16 + 4 = 20 m.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Forgetting +c: an indefinite integral without the constant loses a mark; with a boundary condition, the constant is required for the answer.
  • Power rule reversal: integrate xⁿ to x^(n+1)/(n+1); adding one and dividing is the opposite of differentiating, and mixing them up produces nonsense.
  • Limits order: F(b) − F(a), never the reverse. A negative area often means the limits were swapped.
  • Ignoring crossings: a definite integral over a region that crosses the axis gives the signed area; split at the crossings and add magnitudes for the geometric area.
  • Wrong upper curve: subtract lower from upper; sketching between the intersection points avoids the sign error.
  • Distance versus displacement: displacement is the signed integral; distance sums the absolute pieces. Read which is asked.
  • Expanding before integrating: products must be expanded or divided first; there is no product rule for integration at AS level.
  • Units: areas are square units, displacements in metres; attach and interpret units in applied questions.

Reverse differentiation and the constant of integration

Integration undoes differentiation. Every indefinite integral is found by asking which function differentiates to the one given, and every answer carries a constant of integration, because a constant disappears when a function is differentiated.

Integrating powers of x

For any power other than −1, ∫xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + c. Raise the power by one and divide by the new power. For example ∫x³ dx = x⁴/4 + c, and ∫x⁻² dx = x⁻¹/(−1) + c = −1/x + c. Students often forget to add one to the power, which gives a result that does not differentiate back to the start.

Integrating a sum and a constant multiple

Integrate term by term and keep constant multipliers outside. ∫(3x² − 4x + 5) dx = x³ − 2x² + 5x + c. Check it by differentiating: 3x² − 4x + 5 is returned exactly, which is the test that the answer is correct.

Why the constant of integration is needed

The derivative of x³ + 7 is the same as the derivative of x³ − 2, so the integral of 3x² must be x³ plus some unknown constant. Writing +c records that the answer is a whole family of curves, one for each value of c. A question that gives one point on the curve fixes c, and that step is worth marks in its own right.

Integrating (ax + b)ⁿ

When the bracket is linear, the chain rule runs backwards and needs one extra division by a. ∫(2x + 3)⁴ dx = (2x + 3)⁵/(2 × 5) + c = (2x + 3)⁵/10 + c. Differentiating (2x + 3)⁵/10 gives 5 × 2 × (2x + 3)⁴/10, which is (2x + 3)⁴, so the answer is confirmed.

Integrating expressions that need rearranging

Expand brackets and split fractions before integrating, because the power rule works only on single powers. (x + 1)² is x² + 2x + 1 before integration, so ∫(x + 1)² dx = x³/3 + x² + x + c. Writing (x + 1)² as a power of a bracket and applying the linear rule gives the same answer, but expanding is the safer route when the bracket is not linear.

Checking an integral by differentiating

Differentiate the answer and compare it with the integrand. If the two do not match, the error is in the power, the division or a missing coefficient. This check takes a few seconds and catches most sign and division slips before they reach the final line.

Definite integrals: meaning and evaluation

A definite integral has limits and gives a number. It is the signed area between the curve and the x-axis between those limits, and it is evaluated by substituting the upper limit, substituting the lower limit and subtracting. The constant of integration cancels in that subtraction, so it is not written for a definite integral.

Evaluating between limits

Write the result in square brackets with the limits at the top and bottom, then substitute. ∫₁³ (2x + 1) dx = [x² + x]₁³ = (9 + 3) − (1 + 1) = 12 − 2 = 10. Put the subtraction in brackets when the limit is negative, so that the sign is not lost.

Reversing the limits

Swapping the limits changes the sign of the answer: ∫₃¹ f(x) dx = −∫₁³ f(x) dx. This is useful when the limits are given in the wrong order, and it is also a common source of a wrong sign when a question asks for an area, because an area is always positive.

Integrals over an interval of zero width

If the two limits are equal, the integral is zero, because the interval has no width. ∫₂² f(x) dx = 0 for any function f. The rule is used as a quick check: an answer that is not zero for equal limits has a mistake in the evaluation.

Using the fundamental theorem

The definite integral equals F(b) − F(a), where F is any antiderivative of f. The choice of antiderivative does not matter, because adding a constant to F adds the same constant to both values and cancels. This is why the constant can be left out of definite integrals.

Finding a constant from a definite integral

If ∫₀² (kx) dx = 4, then [kx²/2]₀² = 2k = 4, so k = 2. Set up the integral with the unknown inside it, evaluate it in terms of the unknown, and then solve the resulting equation as a normal linear or quadratic equation.

Area as a definite integral from a graph

When a question asks for the area between a curve and the x-axis, first sketch the curve to see whether it is above or below the axis on the interval. Only then write the integral. A region above the axis gives a positive integral, and a region below gives a negative one, so the area is the absolute value.

Areas: below the axis, between curves and crossing points

Most area questions on this topic are a sketch, a set of limits and one subtraction. The difficulty is identifying which function is on top and where the curve crosses the axis, so those two steps should be written out before any integral is set up.

Area below the x-axis

When the curve is below the axis, its integral is negative, and the area is the positive value of that integral. For y = x² − 4 between x = 0 and x = 2, the integral is [x³/3 − 4x]₀² = (8/3 − 8) = −16/3, so the area is 16/3 square units.

Area that crosses the axis

Split the integral at each point where the curve meets the x-axis, and take the absolute value of each piece before adding them. For y = x² − 4 from x = 0 to x = 3, the two pieces are 16/3 (below the axis) and 7/3 (above it). The total area is 23/3, although the single integral from 0 to 3 gives −3. A single integral across the crossing gives the net signed value, not the area.

Area between a curve and a line

The area between two curves is the integral of the top curve minus the bottom curve, taken between the points where they meet. The subtraction is what makes the method work: the integral of the top curve gives the area under it, and subtracting the bottom curve removes the part that lies beneath the bottom curve.

Finding intersection points first

Set the two equations equal and solve for x. For y = x² and y = 2x, x² = 2x gives x = 0 and x = 2. These values are the limits of integration. Solving the intersection first prevents limits being guessed from the sketch, which is the usual cause of a wrong answer on a question that is otherwise correct.

Area enclosed by two curves

For y = 6 − x and y = x², the intersections satisfy x² + x − 6 = 0, so x = −3 and x = 2. The line is on top throughout this interval, so the area is ∫ from −3 to 2 of (6 − x − x²) dx = [6x − x²/2 − x³/3] from −3 to 2 = 22/3 + 27/2 = 125/6 square units.

Choosing the top and bottom curve

Test a point between the intersections in both equations to find which curve is higher. The answer depends on this choice: subtracting the wrong way round gives the negative of the area. If the curves swap over inside the interval, split the integral at the second intersection and treat each part separately.

Equations and symbols

Integration is four formulas and two decisions: which power rule, and whether the answer is signed. Learn the rule with its condition attached — the exception at n = −1 is the mark most often lost.

integral of x^n dx = x^(n+1)/(n+1) + c Key: x = the variable of integration (no units for a pure function); n = the power, any real number except −1; c = the constant of integration, fixed by a boundary condition. Raise the power by one, then divide by the new power — the reverse of differentiating, and n = −1 is excluded because it would divide by zero.

if dy/dx = x^n then y = x^(n+1)/(n+1) + c (n not -1) Key: dy/dx = the gradient function; y = the function recovered from it; n = the power; c = the constant. The same statement read from the other end: differentiating the answer returns the question.

integral of k f(x) dx = k integral of f(x) dx Key: k = a constant multiplier (no units); f(x) = the function being integrated. Constants pass through the integral sign, which is why a polynomial is integrated term by term.

integral from a to b of f(x) dx = F(b) - F(a) Key: a = the lower limit; b = the upper limit; f(x) = the integrand; F(x) = any antiderivative of f(x). Upper value minus lower value, never the reverse — a negative area usually means the limits were swapped.

velocity v = ds/dt Key: v = velocity (m s⁻¹); s = displacement (m); t = time (s). The gradient form; integrate it in reverse to recover displacement.

displacement s = integral of v dt Key: s = displacement (m); v = velocity (m s⁻¹); t = time (s). The signed integral, so motion backwards subtracts from the total.

acceleration a = dv/dt Key: a = acceleration (m s⁻²); v = velocity (m s⁻¹); t = time (s). The link that lets a question give acceleration and ask for velocity or displacement.

velocity v = integral of a dt Key: v = velocity (m s⁻¹); a = acceleration (m s⁻²); t = time (s). Integrate, then use "starts from rest" or a stated value to fix the constant.

integral of |v| = distance travelled Key: |v| = the magnitude of the velocity, so every piece counts positive (m s⁻¹); the integral gives distance (m), not displacement. Split the integral wherever v = 0, because that is where the sign changes.

9k = 36 → k = 4 Key: 9k = the definite integral of kx² from 0 to 3, written with the unknown constant k; 36 = the given area (square units); k = 4 (no units). The inverted-area question: set the integral equal to the stated area and solve, rather than integrating a known function.
