title: IGCSE Biology: Transport in Animals
content:
IGCSE Biology: Transport in Animals

Your body contains about 5 litres of blood travelling through roughly 100 000 km of vessels, driven by a pump the size of your fist that beats around 100 000 times a day. This note builds the circulatory system from first principles: why large animals need a double circulation, how the heart is wired (with every chamber, valve and vessel named and the blood path traced through it), how arteries, veins and capillaries are each built for their job, what blood is made of and what each component does, and how coronary heart disease develops and is prevented. The heart-cycle sequence is expanded beat by beat so you can follow the pressure changes rather than memorise a diagram.

Single and double circulations

Small organisms rely on diffusion alone; larger animals need a mass-transport system. A single circulation (fish): blood passes through the heart once per circuit — heart → gills → body → heart. Gas exchange at the gills drops the pressure, so flow to the body is slow; a double circulation solves this. A double circulation (mammals, birds): blood passes through the heart twice per full circuit. The right side pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs (pulmonary circulation); oxygenated blood returns to the left side, which pumps it at high pressure around the body (systemic circulation). Advantage: blood pressure is restored after the lungs, so oxygen reaches tissues fast; and the two circuits can operate at different pressures (low in the delicate lungs, high for the body). An open circulation (insects) bathes organs directly in haemolymph; a closed circulation keeps blood in vessels at all times — the mammalian system is closed.

Heart structure and the double circulation

The heart has four chambers: two thin-walled atria (singular: atrium) that receive blood, and two thick-walled ventricles that pump it out. The right atrium receives deoxygenated blood from the vena cava; the right ventricle pumps it to the lungs via the pulmonary artery. The left atrium receives oxygenated blood from the pulmonary veins; the left ventricle pumps it to the whole body via the aorta — its wall is thickest because it generates the highest pressure. Four valves ensure one-way flow: the atrioventricular valves (tricuspid on the right, bicuspid/mitral on the left) between atria and ventricles, and the semilunar valves at the base of the pulmonary artery and aorta. Valves open when pressure behind them exceeds pressure ahead, and close to prevent backflow — the "lub" of the heartbeat is the atrioventricular valves closing; the "dub" is the semilunar valves closing. Coronary arteries wrap over the heart muscle itself and deliver oxygenated blood to the cardiac muscle, which cannot absorb oxygen from the blood inside its chambers.

The cardiac cycle, step by step

Step 1 — atrial systole: the atria contract, pushing the last of the blood into the ventricles (atrioventricular valves open; semilunar valves closed). Step 2 — ventricular systole: the ventricles contract, pressure rises above the atria (atrioventricular valves slam shut — "lub"), blood is ejected into the pulmonary artery and aorta (semilunar valves forced open). Step 3 — diastole: the ventricles relax, pressure drops below that in the arteries (semilunar valves snap shut — "dub"), blood fills the atria again from the veins, and the cycle repeats. Duration: about 0.8 s at rest (0.1 s atrial systole, 0.3 s ventricular systole, 0.4 s diastole). During exercise the cycle shortens (more beats per minute) and stroke volume rises, so cardiac output (heart rate × stroke volume) increases to deliver more oxygen.

Blood vessels: structure fits function

VesselWallLumenSpecial featuresFunction
ArteryThick, muscular, elasticNarrowElastic recoil smooths pressure pulsesCarries blood at high pressure away from the heart
ArterioleMuscularNarrowSmooth muscle contracts/relaxes to control flowDiverts blood to active organs
CapillaryOne cell thick (endothelium)Very narrow (one cell wide)Huge total surface area, slow flowExchange of gases, nutrients and wastes with tissue fluid
VeinThin, less muscle/elasticWideValves prevent backflowReturns blood at low pressure to the heart

Artery walls are thick and elastic to withstand and smooth the pulsing pressure (elastic recoil maintains flow between beats); veins have valves and rely on skeletal muscle contraction to squeeze blood back against gravity. Capillaries are exactly one cell thick so the diffusion distance is minimal, and their slow flow gives time for exchange — structure and function matched at every level.

Blood: plasma, cells and their roles

Plasma is the straw-coloured liquid: about 55 % of blood volume; it carries water, dissolved glucose, amino acids, fatty acids, glycerol, hormones, carbon dioxide (as hydrogencarbonate ions), urea, plasma proteins (fibrinogen for clotting, albumin for osmotic balance), and antibodies. Red blood cells (erythrocytes): biconcave discs with no nucleus and packed haemoglobin; haemoglobin binds oxygen at high partial pressure in the lungs and releases it at low partial pressure in the tissues (oxyhaemoglobin ↔ haemoglobin + oxygen). White blood cells (leucocytes): part of immunity — phagocytes engulf pathogens; lymphocytes produce antibodies and antitoxins. Platelets (cell fragments): clotting — they stick to a wound, trap red cells and activate fibrinogen → fibrin threads, forming a scab that seals the vessel and blocks pathogen entry. Tissue fluid: plasma minus large proteins, formed at the arteriole end of capillaries where pressure forces it out; most is reabsorbed at the venule end; excess drains into the lymphatic system.

Coronary heart disease

The coronary arteries supply the heart muscle itself. Coronary heart disease develops when fatty deposits (atheroma/cholesterol plaques) build up in the artery walls, narrowing the lumen and restricting blood flow; the muscle is starved of oxygen and glucose, causing angina (chest pain on exertion) and, if a coronary artery blocks completely (a thrombus/clot), a myocardial infarction — heart attack — and muscle death. Risk factors: diet high in saturated fat and salt, smoking (carbon monoxide reduces oxygen-carrying capacity; nicotine raises heart rate and constricts vessels), obesity, stress, lack of exercise, alcohol, age, and inherited family history. Prevention and treatment: a balanced diet low in saturated fat, regular exercise, not smoking, statins (lower cholesterol), anticoagulants (aspirin/warfarin), angioplasty (balloon to widen the artery, often with a stent), and coronary bypass surgery (grafting a vessel to detour the blockage). The exam wants risk factor linked to mechanism — not just a list.

Worked example: cardiac output calculation and reading a heart diagram

At rest a person has a heart rate of 70 beats per minute and a stroke volume of 70 cm³. Step 1: cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume = 70 × 70 = 4900 cm³ per minute = 4.9 dm³/min ≈ the whole blood volume circulated each minute. Step 2: during exercise, rate rises to 150 and stroke volume to 110: output = 150 × 110 = 16 500 cm³/min — 3.4 times the resting output. Step 3: explain the benefit: more oxygen and glucose delivered to muscles per minute, more carbon dioxide removed, so respiration rate can stay high. Diagram-reading practice: trace one drop of blood — vena cava → right atrium → (tricuspid valve) → right ventricle → (semilunar valve) → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary veins → left atrium → (bicuspid valve) → left ventricle → (semilunar valve) → aorta → body. Name the valves in order and you answer almost any "trace the path" question for full marks.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Saying arteries "carry oxygenated blood": the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood; arteries carry blood away from the heart, whatever its oxygen content.
  • Confusing atrium and ventricle roles: atria receive; ventricles pump.
  • Explaining the left ventricle's thick wall as "it is bigger" — the answer is higher pressure needed for the systemic circulation.
  • Forgetting the coronary arteries in a heart-structure question — they are often the last mark.
  • Describing blood flow in veins as due to "suction" or gravity alone; mention valves and skeletal muscle contraction.
  • Writing that platelets "carry oxygen": they clot blood; red blood cells carry oxygen.
  • Listing heart-disease risk factors without explaining the mechanism (e.g. saturated fat raises blood cholesterol which deposits in artery walls).
  • In valve questions, writing "valves stop the blood going back" without the pressure context: they open forward when pressure behind them is higher and close to prevent backflow.

Exam-style questions and answers

Q1. Describe the route of blood through the heart, naming the chambers and vessels. (4 marks) Answer: vena cava to right atrium (1); to right ventricle and out via the pulmonary artery to the lungs (1); pulmonary veins to left atrium (1); to left ventricle and out via the aorta to the body (1).

Q2. Explain why the wall of the left ventricle is thicker than that of the right. (2 marks) Answer: it pumps blood at higher pressure to the whole body (1), while the right ventricle only pumps to the nearby lungs at lower pressure (1).

Q3. Compare the structure of an artery and a vein. (4 marks) Answer: artery has thicker muscular/elastic wall, vein thinner (1); artery narrower lumen, vein wider (1); veins have valves, arteries generally do not (1); arteries carry blood under high pressure from the heart, veins return it at low pressure (1).

Q4. Explain how a diet high in saturated fat can lead to a heart attack. (3 marks) Answer: raises blood cholesterol (1); fatty deposits build up in coronary artery walls narrowing the lumen (1); a clot can block the vessel completely, starving the muscle of oxygen (1).

Q5. Describe the role of platelets and plasma in blood clotting. (3 marks) Answer: platelets stick to the damaged vessel wall and release clotting factors (1); fibrinogen is converted to fibrin threads (1); the mesh traps red blood cells forming a scab; plasma carries the fibrinogen and other clotting proteins (1).

Equations and symbols

This topic is mostly structure and sequence, so there is only one calculation in it — but it is examined almost every year, and the units are where the marks go.

Cardiac output

cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume Key: cardiac output = volume pumped by one ventricle per minute (cm³ min⁻¹, or dm³ min⁻¹); heart rate = contractions per minute (beats min⁻¹); stroke volume = volume ejected per contraction (cm³ per beat).

cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume = 70 × 70 = 4900 Key: the resting case: 70 beats min⁻¹ × 70 cm³ per beat = 4900 cm³ min⁻¹, which is 4.9 dm³ min⁻¹ — roughly the whole blood volume passing through once a minute.

output = 150 × 110 = 16 500 cm³/min Key: the same person exercising: rate 150 beats min⁻¹ and stroke volume 110 cm³ give 16 500 cm³ min⁻¹, about 3.4 times resting output — the number the explanation is built on.

Reversible and one-way reactions in blood

oxyhaemoglobin ↔ haemoglobin + oxygen Key: the double arrow is essential — loading runs left to right in the lungs (high oxygen partial pressure) and unloading runs right to left in the tissues (low partial pressure). One direction only would mean the blood could never deliver its oxygen.

fibrinogen → fibrin threads Key: a one-way conversion, catalysed by thrombin released from platelets; the insoluble fibrin mesh traps red blood cells and forms the scab, so this arrow never reverses.

The slip worth naming

Stroke volume is per beat and cardiac output is per minute, so mixing the two units gives an answer out by a factor of the heart rate. Quote cm³ min⁻¹ and dm³ min⁻¹ explicitly in the answer line.

title: Cell Structure, Reproduction and Development — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Cell Structure, Reproduction and Development — Quick Revision Summary

Biology — AS Edexcel IAL, WBI12 Unit 1 Topic 3. The cell as the unit of life, eukaryotic and prokaryotic ultrastructure, light and electron microscopy and measurement, mitosis and the cell cycle, meiosis and variation, gametes and fertilisation in mammals and flowering plants, stem cells and their uses, and genetic control through gene expression, epigenetics and inheritance patterns.

  • 3.1 Common features of all cells: a plasma membrane, cytoplasm and ribosomes are shared by every cell; differences such as a nucleus, cell wall and organelles explain cell function.
  • 3.2 Levels of organisation: cells form tissues, tissues form organs, organs form organ systems; each level carries out a particular function and shapes the level above it.
  • 3.3 Eukaryotic ultrastructure: nucleus with nuclear envelope and nucleolus, ribosomes (80S) on rER and free, rER (protein synthesis and transport), sER (lipid synthesis), mitochondria (double membrane, cristae, matrix, aerobic respiration), centrioles (spindle organisation), lysosomes (digestive enzymes), Golgi (modifies, sorts and packages proteins, forms extracellular enzymes).
  • 3.4 rER and Golgi: the rER makes proteins and passes them to the Golgi in vesicles; the Golgi modifies, sorts and packages them, and is involved in forming extracellular enzymes.
  • 3.5 Prokaryotic ultrastructure: no membrane-bound nucleus — a single circular DNA free in the cytoplasm; cell wall of peptidoglycan; capsule; plasmids (small rings of DNA, often carrying resistance genes); flagella (rotate for motility); pili (attachment and conjugation); 70S ribosomes — smaller than eukaryotic 80S.
  • 3.6 EM recognition: in EM images, recognise nucleus, nucleolus, ribosomes, rER, sER, mitochondria, centrioles, lysosomes, Golgi and — in prokaryotes — the cell wall, capsule, circular DNA, 70S ribosomes, flagella and pili.
  • 3.7 Microscopy and staining: light microscopes use visible light and have low resolution (~0.2 µm, ~×1500 max); electron microscopes (TEM for internal ultrastructure, SEM for surface detail) give far higher resolution and magnification. Staining with methylene blue (animal cells) or iodine (starch, cell walls) makes transparent structures visible; a graticule calibrated with a stage micrometer lets you measure real sizes.

Worked example

Calibrate a graticule: one eyepiece division at ×400 equals 2.5 µm (calibrated against a stage micrometer). A cell spans 20 divisions, so its real length = 20 × 2.5 µm = 50 µm. To find real size from image size, real size = image size ÷ magnification, so a cell drawn 50 mm long at ×2000 is 50 mm ÷ 2000 = 0.025 mm = 25 µm.

Key points to remember

  • Magnification ≠ resolution; resolution is the ability to distinguish two close points and sets the useful limit of detail.
  • In a light microscope total magnification = eyepiece × objective; always calibrate the graticule at each objective before measuring.
  • A stain makes transparent structures visible — methylene blue shows nuclei in animal cells, iodine shows starch grains and cell walls.
  • Staining matters in electron microscopy too: heavy-metal stains increase contrast in TEM and SEM images.
  • The plasma membrane is an active, protein-studded barrier; without it the cell cannot control what enters and leaves.
  • The nucleus holds the DNA and nucleolus; the nucleolus makes ribosomes, which then leave the nucleus.
  • Ribosomes are the same fundamental structure in all living things (though smaller in prokaryotes: 70S), and that is part of the evidence for common ancestry.
  • Mitochondria have a double membrane and cristae that increase surface area for aerobic respiration — the energy for cell activities.
  • The Golgi modifies and packages proteins; extracellular enzymes (such as digestive enzymes) are secreted by exocytosis after Golgi packaging.
  • Endocytosis and exocytosis move materials in vesicles, and both need ATP — another place ATP is used beyond respiration.

Key points to remember

Know the cell cycle: interphase (G1, S, G2 — growth and DNA replication) then mitosis (prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase) then cytokinesis; mitosis makes genetically identical cells for growth and asexual reproduction. Meiosis makes genetically non-identical gametes and is the source of variation, through independent assortment in metaphase I and crossing over in prophase I. A locus is the position of a gene on a chromosome; linked genes do not assort independently. Sperm are specialised: small, motile, with an acrosome of digestive enzymes, mitochondria for energy and a haploid nucleus; eggs are large with food reserves and the zona pellucida. Fertilisation in mammals: acrosome reaction digests the zona pellucida, cortical reaction blocks further sperm, nuclei fuse to form the zygote. In flowering plants: pollen tube grows to the embryo sac, double fertilisation — one male nucleus fertilises the egg (zygote → embryo), one fuses with the two polar nuclei to form triploid endosperm. Mitotic index = number of cells dividing ÷ total cells; used in Core Practical 6 root tip squash to count mitotic stages. Totipotent cells (zygote, early embryo, plant meristems) can form a whole organism; pluripotent cells (blastocyst cells) can form many but not all cell types. Stem cells are used in bone marrow transplants, and their use raises ethical and social questions.

Key points to remember

Cells become specialised by differential gene expression — different genes switched on or off produce different proteins; one gene can give several proteins through alternative splicing of mRNA. Transcription factors switch genes on or off. Epigenetic modification — DNA methylation and histone modification — changes gene activity without changing the DNA sequence, and the modification can be passed on after cell division. Phenotype is genotype plus environment: multiple alleles (ABO blood groups), polygenic inheritance (height — continuous variation) and environment all contribute. Mutations are changes in DNA base sequence: substitution may change one amino acid or none, insertion/deletion may cause a frameshift. Mutations are the source of new alleles and can cause cancer or genetic disorders such as cystic fibrosis (faulty chloride channel — lung, gut and reproductive problems). Pedigree diagrams show inheritance patterns; sex linkage (red-green colour blindness, haemophilia) is carried on the X and is more common in males. Genetic screening can identify carriers and test embryos (PGD) or a fetus (amniocentesis, CVS); this raises ethical and social questions — consent, the right to know, what counts as a disorder, the choice to terminate, access and cost, and the risk of selecting for non-medical traits.

How to use this

Read the summary list first, then open the full revision notes for any point that feels weak, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself. Revise next by: drawing and labelling a plant cell and an animal cell from memory with each organelle''s function; carrying out the graticule calibration and mitotic index calculations; and working through a monohybrid cross, a sex-linked cross and a pedigree to explain the ratios and the logic for each.

title: Data Structures — Study Notes
content:
`# Data Structures

Cambridge International AS & A Level Computer Science 9618: section 10 (Data types and structures), examined in AS Paper 2.

Arrays and Lists

Contiguous, indexed, O(1) access; fixed size. 2D arrays: element (i, j) — rows × columns.

Stack (LIFO)

push/pop/peek at one end. Uses: call stacks, undo, expression evaluation, DFS.

Example: evaluating 3 4 + : push 3, push 4, pop both, push 7.

Queue (FIFO)

enqueue at rear, dequeue at front. Uses: print queues, schedulers, BFS. A circular queue reuses vacated slots with head/tail pointers modulo capacity.

Linked List

Nodes with data + pointer. Insert/delete O(1) at a known node; search O(n). Traversal follows next pointers until null.

Hash Table

Hash function maps keys → index. Collisions resolved by chaining or open addressing. Average O(1) lookup, worst O(n).

Complexity

OperationArrayLinked ListHash
Access by indexO(1)O(n)—
SearchO(n)O(n)O(1) avg
Insert/deleteO(n)O(1)O(1) avg

Exam tips: trace pointers carefully in linked-list diagrams; for circular queues, show head/tail movement and overflow/underflow checks.

Two-dimensional arrays and records

A two-dimensional array stores values in rows and columns, and each element is found with two indexes, usually written A[row, column]. A table of marks for five students in three subjects is a 5 by 3 array. Indexes normally start at 0, so the last element of an array with 8 elements has index 7.

A record groups fields of different data types under one name. A student record might hold a name as a string, an age as an integer and a pass flag as a Boolean. An array of records lets a program store a whole list of students, each with several fields, in one structure.

Exam tip: an array holds one data type throughout, while a record can mix types. Say this when asked to compare them.

Worked example: a stack trace

Start with an empty stack. Push A, push B and push C, so the stack holds A, B, C with C on top. Pop returns C, and a second pop returns B. Push D, and the stack now holds A and D. A trace table with one row per operation is the method examiners expect in a trace question.

Choosing a structure

  • Use a queue for tasks processed in arrival order, such as a print queue.
  • Use a stack for reversing data, undo operations and backtracking, because the last item added is the first removed.
  • Use a hash table for fast lookup by key. A good hash gives average-case constant-time access, but collisions must be handled, usually by chaining or open addressing.

Linked list pointers

Each node holds a data item and a pointer to the next node. Inserting or deleting a node means changing pointers rather than moving elements, so the change is quick once the position is known. Finding a node by its position still means following pointers from the start of the list, which is a linear search.

Exam point: state the behaviour precisely. Describing a queue as first in, last out loses the mark; the correct description is first in, first out (FIFO).

title: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Bearings, Constructions and Loci
content:
Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Bearings, Constructions and Loci

Bearings are how navigators describe direction, and geometrical constructions are how geometers draw exact figures with only a ruler and a pair of compasses. Together they fill the practical geometry questions on both papers: a bearing calculated from a diagram, a locus sketched and shaded, a perpendicular bisector constructed and justified. This note builds the topic from zero: the three rules of bearings and the back-bearing calculation, the compass-and-ruler constructions with their standard arcs, scale drawings and their measurements, and the four loci the syllabus requires, with every step shown.

Bearings: the three rules

A bearing is a direction written as a three-figure angle. Three rules define it:

  1. Measured from North (the north line, drawn as an upward arrow).
  2. Clockwise.
  3. Written with three figures — 035°, 090°, 245° (never 35° or 9°).

Bearings are always between 000° and 360°; a direction due east is 090°, due south 180°, due west 270°.

Worked example. A ship sails from A on a bearing of 060° for 12 km to B, then on a bearing of 150° for 8 km to C. Describe the position of C relative to A qualitatively.

060 ° is between north and east; 150 ° is between east and
south. So C lies south-east of A, and the two legs turn 90 °
(150 - 60 = 90) - the path is two perpendicular legs, making a
right angle at B.

Back bearings

The bearing of A from B is not the bearing of B from A — they differ by 180° (add if under 180°, subtract if 180° or more):

back bearing = bearing + 180  (if bearing < 180)
             = bearing - 180  (if bearing >= 180)

Worked example. The bearing of B from A is 072°. Find the bearing of A from B.

72 + 180 = 252 °

Worked example 2 (three-figure check). The bearing of P from Q is 310°. Find the bearing of Q from P.

310 - 180 = 130 °

Bearings with trigonometry

Bearing problems become right-triangle problems once you draw the north lines and mark the angles between the path and north. Use Pythagoras for distances and trigonometry for angles, then convert the angle into a bearing.

Worked example. A boat sails 5 km due north, then 12 km due east. Find its distance and bearing from the start.

distance = √(5² + 12²) = √(169) = 13 km
angle east of north: tan(θ) = 12/5  →  θ = 67.4 °
bearing = 067 ° (to the nearest degree)

Worked example 2 (reverse). A helicopter is 9 km from base on a bearing of 145°. How far east and how far south of the base is it?

angle from south = 180 - 145 = 35 °
east = 9 sin(35) = 5.16 km
south = 9 cos(35) = 7.37 km

Constructions: ruler and compasses only

Constructions are marked on the accuracy of the arcs and the visibility of the construction lines. Keep your compasses sharp and do not rub out the arcs.

ConstructionStandard method (in order)
Perpendicular bisector of ABcompasses wider than half AB: arc from A, same-radius arc from B, both sides; join the two intersections
Angle bisectorarc across both arms from the vertex; same-radius arcs from those two crossings; join the vertex to their intersection
Perpendicular from a point to a linearc from the point cutting the line twice; equal arcs from those cuts; join the point to their intersection
Perpendicular at a point on a lineequal arcs either side of the point; then the perpendicular-bisector method between them
60° anglearc from the endpoint across the line; same radius arc from the crossing; join
Triangle given SSSdraw the base; arcs of the other two lengths from each end; join the intersection

Worked example. Construct the perpendicular bisector of a segment AB of length 8 cm and explain why every point on it is equidistant from A and B.

Construction: arcs of radius > 4 cm from A and from B, above and
below the segment; the two intersections join to form the bisector.
Why: the arcs are circles of equal radius centred at A and B, so
their intersection points are equidistant from A and B; the line
through them is the locus of all such points.

Scale drawings

A scale drawing represents a real situation to a ratio: 1 : 50 000 means 1 cm on paper represents 50 000 cm in reality (0.5 km). The method: convert the scale to a usable unit, measure or construct to scale, then read back with the reverse conversion.

Worked example. A map has scale 1 : 25 000. Two towns are 6.4 cm apart on the map. Find the real distance in km.

6.4 cm x 25 000 = 160 000 cm
160 000 cm = 1600 m = 1.6 km

Worked example 2 (drawing). A field is 400 m by 250 m. Draw it at scale 1 : 5000. What are the drawing dimensions?

400 m = 40 000 cm; /5000 = 8 cm
250 m = 25 000 cm; /5000 = 5 cm
The drawing is 8 cm by 5 cm.

Loci

A locus is the set of all points satisfying a condition. Four standard loci are examinable, and each has its construction:

  • Fixed distance from a point: a circle (arc) of that radius, centred on the point.
  • Equidistant from two points: the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining them.
  • Equidistant from two lines: the angle bisector(s) of the angle between them.
  • Fixed distance from a line: two parallel lines at that distance, one on each side (with semicircular ends for a segment).

Region questions combine loci: "shade the region closer to A than B and within 3 cm of C" means intersect the perpendicular bisector's half-plane with the circle's interior.

Worked example. A goat is tethered to a corner of a 6 m by 4 m shed with a 5 m rope. Describe the region it can reach.

A three-quarter circle of radius 5 m around the corner, minus
the part blocked by the shed: the rope wraps the shed's⁴ m and
6 m walls. The reachable region is the quarter circle of radius
5 m outside the shed plus smaller arcs where the rope wraps
(radius 1 m around the far 4 m corner, no reach around the far
6 m corner since 5 - 6 < 0).

Worked examples: bearings and loci together

Worked example. Two radio transmitters A and B are 10 km apart, with B due east of A. A signal is received equally strongly at points equidistant from A and B, and within 6 km of A. Describe the region.

Equidistant from A and B: the perpendicular bisector of AB - a
north-south line 5 km east of A.
Within 6 km of A: a circle of radius 6 km centred at A.
The region is the part of the circle on one side of the bisector:
a circular segment of radius 6 km, cut by the line 5 km from A.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Bearing definition) State the three rules for a bearing. Answer: Measured from north, clockwise, written as three figures.
  2. (Back bearing) The bearing of X from Y is 128°. Find the bearing of Y from X. Answer: a back bearing reverses direction, so add 180° when the bearing is below 180°: 128° + 180° = 308° (if the bearing exceeds 180°, subtract 180° instead).
  3. (Calculation) A plane flies 30 km north then 40 km east. Find its distance from the start and its bearing. Answer: distance = √(900 + 1600) = 50 km; tan θ = 40/30 → θ = 53.1°, bearing 053°.
  4. (Components) A ship is 15 km from port on a bearing of 210°. Find its distance west of the port. Answer: angle from south = 210 − 180 = 30°; west = 15 sin 30 = 7.5 km.
  5. (Construction) Describe how to construct the perpendicular bisector of a 6 cm segment. Answer: set the compasses to more than half the segment — more than 3 cm — and draw arcs from each end both above and below it; the two crossings of the arcs give the points the bisector passes through, so join them, and every point on that line is equidistant from both ends.
  6. (Locus) Describe the locus of points equidistant from the sides of an angle. Answer: The angle bisector — every point on it is the same perpendicular distance from both arms.
  7. (Scale) On a 1 : 20 000 map, a lake is 3.5 cm long. Find its real length in km. Answer: 3.5 × 20 000 = 70 000 cm = 0.7 km.
  8. (Region) Shade the region inside a triangle that is closer to side AB than to side AC and within 2 cm of vertex A. Answer: closer to AB than to AC means the half-plane on AB's side of the angle bisector of angle A, and within 2 cm of A means inside the circle of radius 2 cm centred on A; the shaded region is the intersection of those two, bounded by the bisector and the compass arc.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Two-figure bearings: 35° must be written 035°. Three figures, always.
  • Measuring from the wrong north: bearings start at north, not east. A bearing of 090° is east, not north.
  • Back-bearing addition: add 180 if the bearing is below 180, subtract if above; the result must stay between 000 and 360.
  • Anticlockwise angles: bearing questions are clockwise; a clockwise angle and its anticlockwise partner sum to 360.
  • Rubbing out construction arcs: the arcs are the evidence. Leave them visible and use a sharp pencil.
  • Locus shading: shade the region, not the boundary line; the question usually says "shade the region".
  • Scale unit slips: convert the real measurement to the same unit as the drawing before applying the ratio, and remember 1 km = 100 000 cm.
  • Diagram not to scale: measure only when told to; otherwise calculate. A protractor reading on a "not to scale" diagram earns nothing.

Bearings drawn properly: clockwise from north, three digits, always

A bearing is not an angle inside a triangle — it is a direction on the page, and almost every lost mark on this topic comes from measuring it from the wrong place or turning the wrong way. One drawing fixes the idea for good.

The three rules, in the order they bite. A bearing is measured from the north line at the point you are leaving, it turns clockwise, and it is written with three digits (060°, not 60°, and 025° rather than 25°). The third rule is not fussiness: 070° and 007° are different directions, and the leading zeros are how a reader tells them apart.

The back bearing is the return journey. If B is on a bearing of 060° from A, then A is on a bearing of 240° from B:

back bearing = bearing + 180° (or − 180° if the result would exceed 360°) Key: both are the same line measured from opposite ends. Adding 180° cannot go wrong; subtracting can, so add and then subtract 360° if necessary. For 060°: 60 + 180 = 240°. For 300°: 300 + 180 = 480, and 480 − 360 = 120°.

Worked example. A ship sails 12 km from port P on a bearing of 060°, then 9 km on a bearing of 150°. How far is it from P, and on what bearing?

Draw the two legs nose-to-tail. The turn between them is 150 − 60 = 90°, so the two legs are perpendicular and the distance closes as a right-angled triangle:
distance = √(12² + 9²) = √(144 + 81) = √225 = 15 km

The overall bearing is the angle from north to the closing line, which needs the angle at P inside the triangle: tan θ = 9 / 12, so θ = 36.9°, and the bearing is 60 − 36.9 = 023.1° on the far side — which is why the sketch, not the arithmetic, decides between adding and subtracting. Candidates who skip the sketch get 15 km and then guess the direction.

Where marks are lost. Measuring anticlockwise (bearing 060 becomes the 300° direction). Measuring from the horizontal or from another bearing rather than from north. Writing two digits. And finding the distance with a scale drawing but then reading the bearing off the wrong vertex — the bearing of A from B is not the bearing of B from A, and the question always says which.

Bearings in more depth

A bearing gives a direction as an angle measured clockwise from north, written as three figures. Bearings are the commonest context for angle questions in navigation, and they combine with the sine and cosine rules when the journey is not at right angles. The subsections below cover measuring, reversing and using bearings in a calculation, which are the three skills the mark scheme checks.

Measuring a bearing with a protractor

Place the centre of the protractor on the point where the bearing starts, with the zero line pointing north. Read the angle clockwise from north to the line that joins the start point to the target. A bearing of 65° is read on the outer scale of a protractor when the north line points up the page. Always check which scale you are reading, because the inner scale gives the anticlockwise angle and loses marks.

Three-figure bearings in exam answers

Exam bearings are written with exactly three figures, so a bearing of 8° is written 008°, and 65° is written 065°. The three-figure form is required even when the answer has a leading zero. A bearing given with two figures will normally be marked wrong, so write the final answer in the form the question asks for and keep the degree sign.

The bearing of A from B and of B from A

The bearing of B from A and the bearing of A from B are not the same. The first is measured at A, the second at B. They differ by exactly 180°, so if the bearing of B from A is 070°, the bearing of A from B is 250°. Draw a north line at each point, because the question usually asks for one direction and the reversed direction is the common error.

Back bearings

A back bearing is the bearing of the start point from the end point, and it is found by adding or subtracting 180°. If the bearing is less than 180°, add 180°. If it is more than 180°, subtract 180°. The back bearing is used when a journey is reversed, and it is also used as a check on a diagram, since the two north lines at the points are parallel.

Bearings with trigonometry

A bearing often describes one side of a triangle, and the other sides are found with the sine or cosine rule. Put the north lines on the diagram, mark the bearing as an angle between the north line and the side, and then find the interior angle of the triangle. Once the angle is known, the rule is applied in the usual way, and the bearings are only used to find that angle.

A worked navigation problem

A ship sails 12 km on a bearing of 040° and then 9 km on a bearing of 130°. The angle between the two legs at the turning point is found from the bearings: the turn is 130° − 040° = 090°, so the path is at right angles and the distance back to the start is √(12² + 9²) = 15 km. Each step uses one bearing to find an angle, and then Pythagoras or a rule gives the length.

Checking a bearing answer

A bearing must lie between 000° and 360°. Check that the answer is measured clockwise from north, that it has three figures, and that a diagram drawn to scale agrees with the value. A bearing of 200° points roughly south-south-west, so a diagram showing it pointing north-east is a sign that the angle was measured from the wrong line.

Geometrical constructions with ruler and compasses

A construction is a drawing made with a ruler and a pair of compasses only, with no protractor and no measurement. The method is what gets the mark, so the arcs must be left visible on the final diagram. The subsections below give the standard constructions the syllabus asks for, with the steps for each and the checks that show the result is accurate.

The perpendicular bisector of a line

To construct the perpendicular bisector of a line AB, open the compasses to more than half the length of AB. Draw an arc from A above and below the line, then draw the same arc from B so that the two pairs of arcs cross at two points. The line joining those two crossing points is the perpendicular bisector. It cuts AB into two equal parts at a right angle.

The bisector of an angle

To bisect an angle, put the compass point on the vertex and draw an arc that cuts both arms of the angle. From each of those two points draw a further arc of equal radius, so the arcs cross inside the angle. The line from the vertex through the crossing point bisects the angle into two equal parts. The construction works for any angle, because the two triangles formed are congruent.

A perpendicular from a point to a line

To draw the perpendicular from a point P to a line, place the compass on P and draw an arc that cuts the line at two points. Then construct the perpendicular bisector of those two points. The bisector passes through P and meets the line at right angles, so it is the required perpendicular. This method works whether P is above or below the line.

Constructing 60° and 90° angles

A 60° angle is constructed by drawing an equilateral triangle. Draw a line, put the compass on one end, and mark an arc of radius equal to the line. From the other end draw a second arc of the same radius to cross it. Joining the crossing point to the two ends gives an equilateral triangle, so the angle at the end is 60°. A 90° angle is constructed as a perpendicular to a line through a point on it.

Constructing a triangle from three sides

To construct a triangle with sides 6 cm, 5 cm and 4 cm, draw the 6 cm base. Open the compass to 5 cm, place the point at one end, and draw an arc. Open to 4 cm, place the point at the other end, and draw a second arc to cross the first. Join the crossing point to the two ends. A triangle is fixed by its three sides, so the construction gives one unique shape.

Accuracy and the arcs left on the diagram

Examiners check the construction arcs, not only the final line. Leave every arc visible, use a sharp pencil, and keep the compass radius constant when it is supposed to be constant. A line drawn without its construction arcs can earn no method marks, even if it is in the correct place. Make the arcs light but clear, so a marker can see which steps were followed.

Common construction errors

The commonest errors are opening the compass by different amounts for arcs that should be equal, forgetting that the perpendicular bisector needs arcs from both ends, and drawing a bisector from the wrong vertex. Check each construction by measuring afterwards: the bisected parts should be equal, and the angle at a right-angle construction should be 90° when you check it with a protractor.

Loci: the set of points that obey a rule

A locus is the set of all points that satisfy a given condition. In this note, loci are drawn with ruler and compasses, and the answer is a region or a line that a student must shade or describe. The subsections below cover the standard loci the syllabus names: points at a fixed distance, points equidistant from two points or two lines, and combined loci that give a region.

A locus defined by a fixed distance

The locus of points that are exactly 3 cm from a fixed point O is a circle of radius 3 cm with centre O. Every point on the circle is 3 cm from O, and no other point is. The locus of points within 3 cm of O is the region inside that circle, including the circle itself. Read the word "exactly" as a circle and the words "within" or "less than" as a region.

Points equidistant from two points

The locus of points equidistant from two points A and B is the perpendicular bisector of AB. Every point on that line is the same distance from A as from B. A question that asks for the points closer to A than to B asks for the half-plane on A's side of the bisector, so the answer is a region and not just the line.

Points equidistant from two lines

The locus of points equidistant from two intersecting lines is the pair of angle bisectors of the angles between them. The bisector of the angle between two lines passes through their intersection point. For two parallel lines, the locus is the single line midway between them, parallel to both.

Combining loci to find a region

Many questions ask for the region that satisfies two or more conditions at once. Draw each locus on the same diagram, using a light line for each. The required region is where all the conditions are true at the same time, so it is the overlap of the individual regions. Shade it and label it, since the marks are given for the correct region and not just for the lines.

Loci with a distance from a line

The locus of points at a fixed distance from a straight line is two lines, one on each side, parallel to the original line and at that distance. Within a given distance the region is the strip between those two lines. This type of question is often combined with a circle or a perpendicular bisector, so draw the strip first and then the other constraint.

Reading a locus question in words

The key phrases are "equidistant", "closer to", "within", "at a fixed distance" and "at equal distances from". Each phrase maps to one locus: equidistant from points gives a bisector, equidistant from lines gives an angle bisector, and within a distance gives a circle or a strip. Underline the phrase in the question, name its locus, and then construct it.

Checking a locus diagram

Test a point in each region of your answer and confirm it satisfies the conditions. A point inside the shaded area must be closer to the stated point, and a point outside it must fail. Leaving the construction arcs visible also lets the marker check the construction, so keep them even when the answer is a shaded region.

title: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Area, Perimeter and Volume
content:
Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Area, Perimeter and Volume

Measurement questions are the most reliable marks on the paper — provided you convert units correctly and choose the right formula. This note builds the mensuration toolkit from zero: the unit system and its tricky area and volume conversions, the area formulas for every plane shape with derivations, circles, arcs and sectors, the volume and surface area of every solid in the syllabus, and compound shapes — how to add and subtract the pieces. Every worked example shows the substitution and the units, because units and premature rounding are where the marks disappear.

Units of measure

Length, area and volume units are linked by powers of the linear conversion factor:

ConversionLengthAreaVolume
1 m = 100 cm× 100× 100² = 10 000× 100³ = 1 000 000
1 cm = 10 mm× 10× 100× 1000
1 km = 1000 m× 1000× 10⁶× 10⁹

Capacity: 1 litre = 1000 cm³ = 1000 ml; 1 m³ = 1000 litres. The classic trap is converting area with a length factor — 1 m² is 10 000 cm², not 100 cm².

Worked example. Convert 3.5 m² to cm² and 2500 cm³ to litres.

3.5 m² = 3.5 × 10⁰⁰⁰ = 35 000 cm²
2500 cm³ = 2500/1000 = 2.5 litres

Area and perimeter of plane shapes

ShapePerimeterArea
Rectangle2(l + w)l × w
Trianglesum of sides½ × base × perpendicular height
Parallelogram2(a + b)base × perpendicular height
Trapeziumsum of sides½(a + b) × h (parallel sides a, b)
Circle2πrπr²

The triangle and parallelogram formulas both need the perpendicular height — not a slanted side. That single word accounts for more lost marks than any other in mensuration.

Worked example. Find the area of a trapezium with parallel sides 7 cm and 11 cm and height 5 cm.

A = (1/2)(a + b) h = 0.5 x (7 + 11) × 5
  = 0.5 × 18 × 5 = 45 cm²

Worked example 2 (triangle). A triangle has sides 6 cm, 8 cm, 10 cm. Is it right-angled, and what is its area?

6² + 8² = 36 + 64 = 100 = 10², so yes - right-angled
at the 6-8 corner. Area = (1/2) × 6 × 8 = 24 cm².

Circles, arcs and sectors

An arc is a fraction of the circumference; a sector is the same fraction of the area. The fraction is the angle over a full turn:

circumference = 2 π r;  area = π r²

arc length  = (θ/360) × 2 π r
sector area = (θ/360) x π r²
perimeter of a sector = arc length + 2r
segment area = sector area - triangle area

Worked example. A sector has radius 9 cm and angle 140°. Find its arc length, sector area and perimeter (π = 3.142).

arc = (140/360) × 2 × 3.142 × 9 = 0.3889 × 56.56 = 21.99 cm
area = (140/360) × 3.142 × 81 = 0.3889 × 254.5 = 98.97 cm²
perimeter = 21.99 + 18 = 39.99 cm = 40.0 cm (3 s.f.)

The perimeter of a sector includes the two radii — students routinely answer only the arc length.

Worked example 2 (segment). Find the area of the segment cut off by a chord in a circle of radius 6 cm when the sector angle is 90°.

sector area = (90/360) × 3.142 × 36 = 28.28 cm²
triangle area = (1/2) × 6 × 6 = 18 cm² (right angle at centre)
segment = 28.28 - 18 = 10.28 cm²

Surface area and volume of solids

SolidVolumeSurface area
Cuboidl × w × h2(lw + lh + wh)
Prism (any cross-section)area of cross-section × length2 × cross-section + perimeter × length
Cylinderπr²h2πr² + 2πrh
Cone⅓πr²hπr² + πrl (l = slant height)
Sphere⁴⁄₃πr³4πr²
Pyramid⅓ × base area × heightsum of face areas

Slant height versus vertical height is the cone trap: volume uses the perpendicular height h, surface area uses the slant height l, and l² = r² + h² connects them.

Worked example 1 (cylinder). A cylinder has radius 4 cm and height 10 cm. Find its volume and total surface area.

V = π r² h = 3.142 × 16 × 10 = 502.7 cm³
SA = 2 π r² + 2 π r h = 2 × 3.142 × 16 + 2 × 3.142 × 4 × 10
   = 100.5 + 251.4 = 351.9 cm²  (352 cm², 3 s.f.)

Worked example 2 (cone). A cone has radius 5 cm and vertical height 12 cm. Find its volume and slant height.

V = (1/3) π r² h = (1/3) × 3.142 × 25 × 12 = 314.2 cm³
l = √(5² + 12²) = √(169) = 13 cm

Worked example 3 (sphere). Find the volume of a sphere of radius 6 cm.

V = (4/3) π r³ = (4/3) × 3.142 × 216 = 904.8 cm³

Compound shapes: add and subtract

Compound figures are split into standard shapes (add) or standard shapes with a piece removed (subtract). The discipline: draw the split lines, label each sub-shape's dimensions, compute each area separately, then combine.

Worked example. An L-shape is made from a 10 cm × 8 cm rectangle with a 4 cm × 3 cm rectangle removed from one corner. Find its area and perimeter.

area = 10 × 8 - 4 × 3 = 80 - 12 = 68 cm²
perimeter: trace the outline:
10 + 8 + 6 + 5 + 4 + 3 = 36 cm
(6 = 10 - 4 along the removed edge; 5 = 8 - 3)

Worked example 2 (semicircle on a rectangle). A running track is a 60 m by 30 m rectangle with a semicircle of diameter 30 m at each end. Find its area.

rectangle = 60 × 30 = 1800 m²
two semicircles = one full circle of radius 15:
  π x 225 = 706.9 m²
total = 1800 + 706.9 = 2507 m²  (2510 m², 3 s.f.)

Worked examples: composite solids

Composite solids combine the standard formulas: a silo is a cylinder with a hemisphere on top; a pencil is a cylinder with a cone; a capsule is a cylinder with two hemispheres. The method: split the solid, compute each volume, add; for surface area, add only the faces that are actually exposed (the join is hidden).

Worked example. A capsule is a cylinder of radius 3 cm and length 10 cm with a hemisphere at each end. Find its total volume and surface area.

cylinder volume = π r² h = 3.142 × 9 × 10 = 282.8 cm³
two hemispheres = one sphere: (4/3) π r³ = (4/3) × 3.142 × 27
               = 113.1 cm³
total volume = 282.8 + 113.1 = 395.9 cm³

surface area: cylinder curved surface 2 π r h = 188.5 cm²
plus one full sphere 4 π r² = 113.1 cm²
total = 301.6 cm²  (the circular joins are internal, not exposed)

Worked example 2 (frustum-free method). A cone of radius 6 cm and height 9 cm has its top 3 cm cut off parallel to the base. Find the volume removed.

the removed cone is similar to the whole cone, scale k = 3/9 = 1/3
volume of whole cone = (1/3) π x 36 × 9 = 339.3 cm³
removed volume = k³ x whole = (1/27) × 339.3 = 12.6 cm³
(the same as computing directly with radius 2 cm and height 3 cm)

Worked examples: reverse problems and density

Worked example. A cylindrical tank of radius 1.5 m holds 20 m³ of water. Find the depth.

V = π r² h  →  h = V/(π r²) = 20/(3.142 × 2.25)
h = 20/7.07 = 2.83 m

Worked example 2 (density). A metal cuboid 5 cm × 4 cm × 2 cm has mass 312 g. Find its density in g cm⁻³ and kg m⁻³.

volume = 5 × 4 × 2 = 40 cm³
density = 312/40 = 7.8 g cm⁻³
in kg m⁻³: 7.8 × 10⁰⁰ = 7800 kg m⁻³

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Units) Convert 2.4 m² to cm² and 0.75 litres to cm³. Answer: 24 000 cm²; 750 cm³.
  2. (Trapezium) Parallel sides 12 cm and 8 cm, height 6 cm. Find the area. Answer: ½(12 + 8) × 6 = 60 cm².
  3. (Sector) Radius 7 cm, angle 72°. Find arc length and sector area. Answer: arc = (72/360) × 2π × 7 = 8.80 cm; area = (72/360) × π × 49 = 61.6 cm².
  4. (Cylinder) Radius 3 cm, height 12 cm. Find the volume. Answer: π × 9 × 12 = 339 cm³ (3 s.f.).
  5. (Cone) Radius 8 cm, height 15 cm. Find the volume and slant height. Answer: V = ⅓π × 64 × 15 = 1005 cm³; l = √(64 + 225) = 17 cm.
  6. (Sphere) Diameter 10 cm. Find the surface area. Answer: r = 5; SA = 4π × 25 = 314 cm².
  7. (Compound) A rectangle 14 m × 6 m has a semicircle of diameter 6 m removed from one end. Find the area. Answer: 84 − ½π × 9 = 84 − 14.14 = 69.9 m².
  8. (Reverse) A sphere has volume 288 cm³. Find its radius. Answer: 288 = ⁴⁄₃πr³ → r³ = 288 × 3/(4π) = 68.75 → r = 4.10 cm.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Slant versus perpendicular height: triangle/parallelogram areas use perpendicular height; cone surface area uses slant height; cone volume uses perpendicular height.
  • Area unit conversion: 1 m² = 10 000 cm² and 1 cm² = 100 mm². Multiplying by 100 instead of 10 000 is the single most common mensuration error.
  • Sector perimeter: add the two radii to the arc length. The question asks for the perimeter of the sector, not the arc.
  • Using the diameter as radius: halve the diameter first; every circle formula uses r.
  • π precision: use 3.142 or the calculator's π; rounding π to 3 loses accuracy on multi-step questions. Round only the final answer (usually 3 s.f. or as stated).
  • Compound shape subtraction: remove the correct region and keep the outline consistent — recompute the perimeter from the actual boundary, not the sum of the sub-shapes' perimeters.
  • Volume of a prism: cross-section area × length, where the length is perpendicular to the cross-section (a slanted prism uses the perpendicular distance).
  • Units in the answer: cm² for area, cm³ for volume, and capacity conversions (1000 cm³ = 1 litre). A correct number with the wrong unit loses marks on Paper 2.

title: Exam technique: Data Representation
content:
### What earns the marks
For full marks on number systems (1.1), show full working in conversions, e.g. binary to decimal to hex. For text, sound and images (1.2), explain how character sets and colour depth affect file size. For data storage and compression (1.3), justify the use of lossless or lossy compression. Command words like calculate, show that, explain, describe, justify, and state are used, with working and reasons required for full marks.
### Traps
Error: incorrect conversion between number systems. Correction: double-check place values and use the correct conversion method. Error: forgetting to include metadata in file size calculations. Correction: remember to include width, height, and depth in bitmap image calculations. Error: using lossy compression for text files. Correction: use lossless compression for text files to preserve exact data.
### Memory hooks
Use the mnemonic BIC (Binary, Integer, Character) to remember the different number systems. For binary to decimal conversion, use the pattern of doubling the previous place value. To sanity-check file size calculations, use the formula: file size (bits) = W x H x depth. Write down the conversion method before starting a question to ensure accuracy.
### Timing
This topic typically accounts for 20-30% of the paper, with 2-3 questions. Budget around 30-40 minutes to answer these questions, depending on the complexity and your familiarity with the topic.

title: Nuclear Physics
content:
Nuclear Physics

The Nucleus

Protons + neutrons (nucleons). Nuclide notation: ᴬZX — Z protons, A nucleons. Isotopes share Z, differ in N.

Nuclear densities are enormous (~10¹⁷ kg m⁻³) — nearly all mass in a tiny volume.

Radioactive Decay

Random and spontaneous:

Half-life: time for half the nuclei to decay. N = N₀ e^(−λt), λ = ln 2 / t½.

Respiration, Muscles and the Internal Environment — Edexcel International A2 Level Biology

This short revision note is the companion to the longer respiration, muscles and internal environment notes and is written to be used when you want a focused summary of the topic rather than a full working-through of every specification statement. It is built around the same specification points, so each section corresponds to one or more things the specification expects a candidate to be able to do. The note stays at exam depth, but more compactly: it gives the reasoning, the key contrasts and the common mistakes that lose marks, without re-covering every detail of the longer note. Use it to check the core of the topic and to practise the kinds of answer the specification rewards when time is short.

1. What the topic is for and how the three parts connect

Respiration is the set of reactions that releases energy from nutrient molecules and links that energy to the ATP the cell uses for work. Muscles are where a large share of that ATP is used in movement, and they cannot work unless the supply of ATP, oxygen and fuel keeps up with demand. The internal environment is the fluid and conditions around the body’s cells, and it has to stay within limits while respiration and muscle activity push it around with heat, carbon dioxide, water and changes in solute balance. The topic is therefore a connected system: respiration powers the cell, the muscle is a big ATP user, and the internal environment has to cope with what the muscle and the respiration produce. If you see the topic as one connected system, the links between the parts become easier to answer, and that is where many of the better marks sit.

2. Aerobic respiration as a sequence of stages

Aerobic respiration is a sequence of stages: glycolysis in the cytoplasm, the link reaction and the Krebs cycle in the mitochondrial matrix, and oxidative phosphorylation on the inner mitochondrial membrane. Glycolysis breaks glucose down to pyruvate, producing a small amount of ATP and reduced NAD. The link reaction and the Krebs cycle produce the reduced coenzymes and carbon dioxide. Oxidative phosphorylation uses the reduced coenzymes to make most of the ATP and reduces oxygen to water. The important idea is that respiration is staged and aerobic, and that oxygen is the final electron acceptor in oxidative phosphorylation, which is what allows the bulk of ATP to be made.

A good answer says that respiration is a sequence of stages, states the four stages and where they happen, and says that oxygen is used in oxidative phosphorylation as the final electron acceptor. It does not say that respiration is one reaction that turns glucose straight into ATP, because it is not, and it does not say that the Krebs cycle is where oxygen is used, because it is not. If you can give the stages in order and say where each happens, you have the respiration idea in a form that scores marks.

3. Glycolysis and the link reaction and the Krebs cycle: what each contributes

Glycolysis phosphorylates glucose and splits it, then oxidises the triose phosphate, producing pyruvate, a small ATP yield by substrate-level phosphorylation and reduced NAD. The link reaction converts pyruvate to acetyl coenzyme A, releasing carbon dioxide and reducing NAD. The Krebs cycle oxidises the acetyl group, releasing more carbon dioxide, making a small amount of ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation, and producing reduced NAD and reduced FAD. The main conceptual point is that the stages after glycolysis exist largely to supply the reduced coenzymes and to release carbon dioxide, and that the ATP from substrate-level phosphorylation in the cycle is small compared with the ATP from oxidative phosphorylation.

A good answer says that glycolysis produces pyruvate, ATP and reduced NAD; that the link reaction produces acetyl coenzyme A, CO2 and reduced NAD; and that the Krebs cycle produces reduced coenzymes, a little ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation and CO2. It does not say that the Krebs cycle makes most of the ATP, because it does not, and it does not say that the cycle happens in the cytoplasm, because it happens in the mitochondrial matrix. If you can say what each stage contributes, you have the pathway in a form that scores marks.

4. Oxidative phosphorylation and the role of the inner membrane and oxygen

Oxidative phosphorylation happens on the inner mitochondrial membrane. The reduced coenzymes deliver hydrogen and the energy from the electrons is used to pump protons from the matrix to the intermembrane space, creating a proton gradient. As protons flow back through ATP synthase, ATP is made. Oxygen is the final electron acceptor and combines with protons to form water. The important point is that ATP is made by chemiosmosis using the proton gradient, not by the electron transport chain directly handing a phosphate to ADP, and that oxygen is essential because it keeps the chain working as the final acceptor.

A good answer says that the inner membrane is folded into cristae to provide surface area, that the energy from the electrons pumps protons, that the proton gradient drives ATP synthesis through ATP synthase, and that oxygen is the final electron acceptor forming water. It does not say that ATP is made directly by the chain itself; that is one of the most common mark-losers on this topic. If you can keep the chain and ATP synthase in their separate roles, you have the oxidative phosphorylation idea in a form that scores marks.

5. ATP as the energy currency and why respiration is staged

ATP is the immediate energy currency that respiration supplies to the cell. The energy for most cellular processes does not come directly from glucose; it comes from the hydrolysis of ATP. Respiration exists to regenerate ATP from ADP using the energy in food, and then the ATP is used for active transport, movement, biosynthesis and other endergonic processes. Respiration is staged so that the energy from food is released in manageable amounts that the cell can use to phosphorylate ADP, and so that the rate can be controlled according to the cell’s needs. A good answer says that respiration is staged so the energy can be captured in ATP and that ATP is the energy currency used by the cell. It does not say that the cell could simply burn glucose in one step for the same practical result, because the control and capture are the point.

6. Muscle contraction: sliding filaments, ATP and calcium

Muscle contraction works by the sliding filament mechanism. The actin and myosin filaments slide past one another, so the sarcomere shortens, but the filaments themselves do not shorten. Myosin heads bind to actin, pivot and pull, then detach and re-cock, pulling the thin filament past the thick one in a cycle powered by ATP. Calcium exposes the actin binding sites so the myosin heads can bind, and relaxation happens when calcium is removed and the binding sites are covered again. A good answer says that the filaments slide, that ATP is used for detachment and re-cocking and for the cycle, and that calcium is needed for the binding. It does not say that the filaments shorten during contraction; that is one of the most common mistakes on this topic. If you can say that the filaments slide and that ATP and calcium are both needed, you have the contraction idea in a form that scores marks.

7. The response to exercise: heart rate, breathing rate and breathing volume

During exercise, heart rate, breathing rate and the volume of air breathed per breath all increase. The heart pumps faster and often harder to deliver more oxygenated blood to the muscles and to remove more carbon dioxide and heat. Breathing increases in frequency and depth so that more oxygen is brought in and more carbon dioxide is removed. The point is that the body responds on several fronts at once, because exercise raises the ATP demand and therefore the oxygen demand and the waste production. A good answer says that both rate and depth of breathing increase, and that heart rate increases, and that these raise the supply of oxygen and the removal of carbon dioxide and heat. It does not say that breathing rate alone is the response, because depth matters too, and it does not say the heart only beats faster without considering the increased delivery overall. If you can say that the response is multi-system and that it serves the supply and removal needs, you have the exercise response in a form that scores marks.

8. Thermoregulation and the control of heat loss and heat production

Thermoregulation is the control of body temperature, which is part of homeostasis. When the body needs to lose heat, blood vessels near the skin surface dilate, increasing blood flow near the surface and heat loss; this is vasodilation. When the body needs to conserve heat, those vessels constrict, reducing blood flow near the surface and heat loss; this is vasoconstriction. The body can also produce more heat by shivering, which uses ATP and therefore links back to respiration, and it can make behavioural changes such as putting on clothing. A good answer says that vasodilation increases heat loss and vasoconstriction reduces it, that shivering produces heat, and that these are part of homeostasis. It does not invert the relationship, so vasodilation is not linked to cold and vasoconstriction to heat. If you keep the direction correct, you avoid one of the most common mistakes on this part of the topic.

9. Homeostasis, negative feedback and the internal environment

Homeostasis is the maintenance of a stable internal environment within limits. Negative feedback is the main control principle: a change from the set point is detected, and the response reduces the change and returns the variable toward the set point. The internal environment matters because cells can only work properly within a limited range of conditions, so water balance, temperature, pH and solute concentrations have to be controlled. Respiration and exercise put demands on all of these, because they produce heat, carbon dioxide and water and change the balance of solutes. A good answer says that homeostasis is stability within limits, that negative feedback opposes the change, and that the body keeps variables within a normal range rather than making them absolutely constant all the time. It does not say that the internal environment never changes, because it does; it says that it is kept within limits. If you can say that, you have the homeostasis idea in a form that scores marks.

10. Water and solute balance and the role of the kidneys

The body has to manage water and solute balance because cells depend on the water potential of the internal environment. If it becomes too concentrated, water leaves cells by osmosis; if too dilute, water enters. Either change can disrupt cell function. Water is also lost through breathing, sweating and urine, so the balance is dynamic. The kidneys help by removing waste from the blood and by adjusting the water and solute content of the urine, so they are part of the internal environment control system. A good answer says that water and solute balance are part of homeostasis, that cells depend on the water potential around them, and that the kidneys remove waste and help control water and solute balance. It does not say that water balance is only about drinking, because breathing and sweating also matter. If you can say that, you have the water-balance idea in a form that scores marks.

11. How the topic fits together: supply, work and control

The topic is really about a chain. Respiration makes ATP from glucose, muscles use ATP to do work, and the work changes the internal environment so the supply and control systems have to respond. The heart and lungs respond to the oxygen demand and the carbon dioxide production. Thermoregulation responds to the heat. Water and solute balance are affected by sweating and by the increased rate of exchange. Homeostasis keeps the whole thing within limits while the muscles demand more and the metabolism produces more waste. If you can trace that chain, you can answer the questions that span the parts, which are often the best-marked ones. If you treat respiration, muscles and internal environment as three unrelated topics, you lose the reasoning that makes them connected.

  • Saying respiration is one reaction that turns glucose straight into ATP, instead of a sequence of stages.
  • Saying the filaments shorten during contraction, instead of sliding past each other.
  • Saying ATP alone starts contraction, without mentioning calcium exposing the binding sites.
  • Saying the Krebs cycle happens in the cytoplasm or is where oxygen is used.
  • Saying ATP is made directly by the electron transport chain, instead of by ATP synthase using the proton gradient.
  • Forgetting that oxygen is the final electron acceptor in oxidative phosphorylation.
  • Saying breathing rate alone is the response to exercise, forgetting breathing depth and heart rate.
  • Inverting vasodilation and vasoconstriction so vasodilation goes with cold and vasoconstriction with heat.
  • Treating homeostasis as meaning the internal environment never changes, rather than staying within limits by negative feedback.
  • Forgetting that sweating and breathing both affect water balance, not just drinking and urine.
  • Saying positive feedback is the main homeostatic mechanism, when negative feedback is.
  • Saying glycolysis makes most of the ATP from respiration; it does not.
  • Describing thermoregulation responses without saying whether they conserve or produce heat.
  • Missing the link that exercise stresses the internal environment so the control systems have to cope.

13. Exam-style questions

  1. Describe aerobic respiration and state the role of oxygen in the process. Answer: Aerobic respiration is a sequence of stages: glycolysis in the cytoplasm, the link reaction and the Krebs cycle in the mitochondrial matrix, and oxidative phosphorylation on the inner mitochondrial membrane. Glycolysis produces pyruvate, ATP and reduced NAD; the link reaction and Krebs cycle produce reduced NAD and reduced FAD and release CO2; oxidative phosphorylation uses the reduced coenzymes to make ATP and uses oxygen as the final electron acceptor, forming water. (5 marks)
  2. Explain why respiration is an energy-releasing process but still needs to be staged. Answer: Respiration releases energy from glucose, but a single reaction releasing all the energy at once would mostly waste it as heat. The stages release energy in manageable amounts that the cell can use to phosphorylate ADP to ATP, the energy currency for cell work, and the staging also allows the rate to be controlled to match the cell’s needs. (4 marks)
  3. Describe the sliding filament model of muscle contraction and state the role of ATP. Answer: During contraction the actin and myosin filaments slide past each other rather than shortening themselves, so the sarcomere shortens.   4. Explain the roles of calcium and ATP in contraction and relaxation. Answer: When a muscle is stimulated, calcium is released and exposes the binding sites on actin so myosin heads can bind. (5 marks)
  5. Describe the body’s response during exercise in terms of heart rate and breathing, and explain why each increases. Answer: During exercise heart rate increases to deliver more oxygenated blood to the muscles and to remove more carbon dioxide and heat, and breathing rate and depth increase to bring in more oxygen and remove more carbon dioxide. Both increase because the muscles’ ATP demand rises and the supply and waste-removal systems have to keep up with the increased metabolism. (5 marks)
  6. Describe how the skin blood vessels help control body temperature and state the direction of the response. Answer: In heat, blood vessels near the skin surface dilate, increasing blood flow near the surface and increasing heat loss. This is part of thermoregulation and homeostasis, along with other responses such as sweating or shivering and behavioural changes. (4 marks)
  7. Define homeostasis and explain the principle of negative feedback, with one example. Answer: Homeostasis is the maintenance of a stable internal environment within limits. Negative feedback is the control principle in which a change from the set point is detected and the response reduces the change, returning the variable toward normal. Example: in temperature control, if body temperature rises, sweating and vasodilation increase heat loss, returning temperature toward the set point; if it falls, shivering and vasoconstriction reduce heat loss or increase heat production. (5 marks)
  8. Explain why water and solute balance are part of homeostasis and what happens if the internal environment becomes too concentrated or too dilute. Answer: Cells depend on the water potential of the internal environment. If it becomes too concentrated, water moves out of cells by osmosis; if too dilute, water moves into cells. Either can disrupt cell function, so the concentrations of water and solutes must be controlled. The body loses water in breathing, sweating and urine, so water balance is dynamic and has to be regulated. (4 marks)
  9. State what the kidneys do to help maintain the internal environment. Answer: The kidneys remove waste from the blood and help control water and solute balance by adjusting the composition of the urine, so they are important for maintaining the internal environment and for disposing of waste products of metabolism. (3 marks)
  10. Describe the link between respiration and muscle activity during exercise. Answer: Muscle activity uses ATP, so respiration must increase to supply ATP. Aerobic respiration is efficient and sustainable if oxygen supply is sufficient, but during vigorous exercise oxygen delivery may not keep up with demand, so the muscle relies relatively more on pathways that do not need oxygen and produces different products, which is why breathing and heart rate rise and the body shifts its metabolism. (4 marks)

Revise this topic by matching each numbered specification point to one mechanism, one location and one reason. Practise the respiration stages and their products, the sliding filament idea with ATP and calcium, the exercise responses and the thermoregulation responses, and the homeostasis and negative feedback principle with examples. Check that you can say where each process happens and why, not just what happens. Then move on to the next topic and the related practicals, because the practicals are the way the specification ties the ideas to hands-on work.

  9. State what the kidneys do to help maintain the internal environment. Answer: The kidneys remove waste from the blood and help control water and solute balance by adjusting the composition of the urine, so they are important for maintaining the internal environment and for disposing of waste products of metabolism. (3 marks)
  10. Describe the link between respiration and muscle activity during exercise. Answer: Muscle activity uses ATP, so respiration must increase to supply ATP. Aerobic respiration is efficient and sustainable if oxygen supply is sufficient, but during vigorous exercise oxygen delivery may not keep up with demand, so the muscle relies relatively more on pathways that do not need oxygen and produces different products, which is why breathing and heart rate rise and the body shifts its metabolism. (4 marks)

Revise this topic by matching each numbered specification point to one mechanism, one location and one reason. Practise the respiration stages and their products, the sliding filament idea with ATP and calcium, the exercise responses and the thermoregulation responses, and the homeostasis and negative feedback principle with examples. Check that you can say where each process happens and why, not just what happens. Then move on to the next topic and the related practicals, because the practicals are the way the specification ties the ideas to hands-on work.

title: Computational Thinking and Problem-Solving — Study Notes
content:
Computational Thinking and Problem-Solving

Thinking Ahead, Abstractly, Systematically

  • Abstraction: keep essential features, drop detail — a metro map ignores street geometry.
  • Decomposition: split the problem into sub-problems solved independently.
  • Thinking ahead: pre-plan inputs, outputs and reusable components; pre-calculate tables where possible.

Recursion

A recursive routine calls itself with a smaller input and a base case that stops the recursion. Elegant for trees and divide-and-conquer, but each call consumes stack space — deep recursion can overflow. Any recursion can be rewritten with a loop and explicit stack.

Searching and Sorting

  • Linear search: O(n), works unsorted.
  • Binary search: O(log n), needs sorted data.
  • Bubble sort: O(n²) average; simple; detects a sorted pass.
  • Insertion sort: O(n²) average; fast on nearly-sorted data.
  • Merge sort: O(n log n) always; needs extra memory.

Testing

White-box tests trace internal paths; black-box tests check specification behaviour. Choose normal, boundary and erroneous data. Dry runs use trace tables recording variables line by line; a trace of recursion should log each call and its return.

Exam tips: write the base case before the recursive call in pseudocode; give the Big-O with a one-line justification; construct a trace table for a small loop or recursive call.

Recursion

A recursive routine calls itself on a smaller version of the problem. It needs a base case that stops the calls and a recursive case that moves towards the base case. Without a base case the routine never terminates and the call stack overflows.

Example: factorial(n) = 1 if n = 0, otherwise n × factorial(n − 1).

Recursion and iteration can solve the same problems. Recursion is often clearer for tree-shaped problems; iteration uses less memory because it does not build up stack frames.

Worked example: binary search on sixteen items

A sorted list has 16 items. Each comparison with the middle item halves the search range: 16 to 8, 8 to 4, 4 to 2, 2 to 1. At most ⌈log₂16⌉ = 4 comparisons are needed to find the item or confirm it is absent. A linear search on the same list may need 16 comparisons, so binary search is much faster, but only when the list is sorted.

Recursion: factorial

A recursive function calls itself on a smaller problem. For factorial, fact(n) returns 1 when n is 0 (the base case), and otherwise returns n × fact(n − 1). Each call waits for the next one to return, so the calls build up on the call stack. Without a base case the recursion never ends.

Testing a solution

  • Normal test data checks the typical case.
  • Boundary test data checks the limits, such as the first item, the last item and an empty list.
  • Erroneous test data checks that invalid input is rejected, for example a letter typed where a number is expected.

Exam point: a test plan lists the input, the expected output and the reason for each test, so that the result can be checked against the design.

title: Further Algebra — Study Notes
content:
Further Algebra

Polynomial Division and the Remainder Theorem

Divide to rewrite p(x) = (x − a)q(x) + r. The remainder when dividing by (x − a) equals p(a).

Example: p(x) = x³ − 2x² + 5. p(2) = 8 − 8 + 5 = 5, so dividing by (x − 2) leaves remainder 5.

If p(a) = 0, then (x − a) is a factor — that is the factor theorem. Divide out fully to reduce a cubic to a quadratic and factorise completely.

The Modulus Function

|x| measures distance from zero: |x| = x for x ≥ 0, −x for x < 0. Its graph is V-shaped.

Solving |2x − 1| = 5: split into 2x − 1 = 5 or 2x − 1 = −5, giving x = 3 or −2.

Inequalities: |2x − 1| < 5 becomes −5 < 2x − 1 < 5, so −2 < x < 3.

Partial Fractions

Reverse of combining fractions — needed before binomial expansion of rational functions.

  • Repeated linear: (4x + 1)/(x + 1)² = A/(x + 1) + B/(x + 1)²
  • Distinct linear: (7x + 4)/(x + 1)(x + 2) = A/(x + 1) + B/(x + 2)

Example: cover the (x + 1) factor with x = −1: B = 3; then compare coefficients for A = 4.

Exam tips: for |ax + b| > c, remember two separate regions; check factor-theorem roots by substitution before long division.
