title: A Level Physics: Oscillations and Waves II
content:
A Level Physics: Oscillations and Waves II

Simple harmonic motion is the master oscillation: the movement of a pendulum, a mass on a spring, a guitar string, a child on a swing — every system that accelerates back toward an equilibrium position with a restoring force proportional to displacement. This note builds SHM from zero: the defining condition and its equations, the displacement, velocity and acceleration graphs and their calculus links, the energy bookkeeping within a cycle, and the real-world finishing topics — damping and resonance — with the applications and disasters that make them examinable.

What simple harmonic motion is

A body performs simple harmonic motion (SHM) when its acceleration is proportional to its displacement from a fixed equilibrium point and always directed toward that point:

a = - ω² x

a = acceleration (m s⁻²), x = displacement from equilibrium (m)
ω = angular frequency (rad s⁻¹); the minus sign means the
acceleration always points back toward equilibrium

The analogy: a ball in a bowl. Push the ball up the side (displacement) and gravity pulls it back with a force proportional to how far up the slope it is — push twice as far, and the restoring force doubles. That proportionality is the whole defining feature; friction-less mass-spring systems and small-angle pendulums obey it.

QuantitySymbolRelation
Displacementxx = A sin(ωt) (from equilibrium at t = 0)
AmplitudeAmaximum displacement
PeriodTT = 2π/ω; mass on a spring: T = 2π√(m/k); pendulum: T = 2π√(L/g)
Frequencyff = 1/T = ω/(2π)
Angular frequencyωω = 2πf = √(k/m) (spring), √(g/L) (pendulum)

SHM equations and graphs

Starting from equilibrium at t = 0, the kinematics follows by differentiation (or by reading the graphs):

displacement:  x = A sin(ω t)
velocity:      v = A ω cos(ω t)
acceleration:  a = - A ω² sin(ω t) = - ω² x

velocity-displacement relation:
v = ω √(A² - x²)

Graph discipline is a mark source in its own right: displacement is a sine wave; velocity leads displacement by a quarter cycle (cosine); acceleration is the inverted displacement (anti-phase, scaled by ω²). At the extremes (x = ±A): velocity is zero and acceleration is maximum; at equilibrium (x = 0): velocity is maximum and acceleration is zero. Learn the four positions (centre, both extremes, mid-point) as a table of states.

Worked example. A mass oscillates with amplitude 0.10 m and frequency 2.0 Hz. Find ω, the maximum speed, and the maximum acceleration.

ω = 2 π f = 2 × 3.14 × 2.0 = 12.6 rad s⁻¹
v_max = A ω = 0.10 × 12.6 = 1.26 m s⁻¹
a_max = A ω² = 0.10 × 158 = 15.8 m s⁻²

Worked example 2 (using v = ω√(A² − x²)). With the same oscillation, find the speed at x = 0.06 m.

v = ω √(A² - x²) = 12.6 x √(0.010 - 0.0036)
  = 12.6 x √(0.0064) = 12.6 × 0.08 = 1.01 m s⁻¹

Worked example 3 (pendulum). Find the period of a 0.90 m pendulum (g = 9.81 m s⁻²).

T = 2 π √(L/g) = 2 × 3.14 x √(0.90/9.81)
  = 6.28 x √(0.0917) = 6.28 × 0.303 = 1.90 s

Energy in simple harmonic motion

Energy shuttles between kinetic and potential stores while the total stays constant (undamped SHM):

total energy:  E = (1/2) m ω² A² = (1/2) k A²
kinetic:       KE = (1/2) m ω² (A² - x²)
potential:     PE = (1/2) m ω² x²   (spring: (1/2) k x²)

The energy curves are examinable as graphs: total energy is a horizontal line over x; KE is an inverted parabola peaking at equilibrium; PE is an upright parabola peaking at the extremes; against time both are sine-squared curves oscillating at twice the frequency of x. Doubling the amplitude quadruples the total energy (E ∝ A²) — a favourite multiple-choice item.

Worked example. A 0.50 kg mass on a spring (k = 200 N m⁻¹) oscillates with amplitude 0.08 m. Find the total energy and the kinetic energy at x = 0.04 m.

E = (1/2) k A² = 0.5 × 200 × 0.0064 = 0.64 J
PE at x = 0.04: (1/2) k x² = 0.5 × 200 × 0.0016 = 0.16 J
KE = E - PE = 0.64 - 0.16 = 0.48 J

Damping

Real oscillations lose energy to drag and friction — damping. The three regimes matter:

  • Light damping: amplitude decays exponentially while the system keeps oscillating at almost the natural frequency (a child's swing gradually slowing).
  • Critical damping: the system returns to equilibrium in the minimum time without overshooting — deliberately engineered for car suspension, door closers and moving-coil meters.
  • Heavy (over) damping: a slow, sluggish return without oscillation.

The energy lost per cycle is the exam phrasing: light damping reduces amplitude gradually because each cycle transfers energy to the surroundings; the total energy falls exponentially with time even though the frequency barely changes.

Resonance

A driven oscillation responds most strongly when the driving frequency matches the system's natural frequency — resonance. The amplitude–frequency curve shows a peak at resonance; sharper peaks mean lighter damping. The mechanism: at resonance the driving force is in phase with the velocity, so energy is transferred most efficiently each cycle.

ApplicationUse or effect
Musical instrumentsair columns and strings resonate at their natural frequencies to amplify sound
Radio tuningan LC circuit selects the broadcast frequency that resonates with it
Microwave ovensdrive water molecules near their resonant absorption frequency
Car suspensiondesigned so road-frequency inputs never match the car's natural frequency; damping controls the peak
Tacoma Narrows (1940)wind-driven resonance (with aeroelastic flutter) destroyed the bridge — the cautionary case study
Bridges and buildingsseismic design detunes natural frequencies from earthquake oscillations

Worked example. Explain why soldiers break step crossing a bridge. Answer: Marching produces a periodic driving force at the step frequency; if it matched the bridge's natural frequency, resonance would build large-amplitude oscillations and structural damage; breaking step makes the driving frequency irregular and removes the coherent input.

Worked examples: combined SHM problems

Worked example. A 0.25 kg mass on a spring completes 20 oscillations in 8.0 s. Find the spring constant k.

T = 8.0/20 = 0.40 s
T = 2 π √(m/k)  →  k = m (2 π/T)²
k = 0.25 x (6.28/0.40)² = 0.25 × 246.4 = 61.6 N m⁻¹
  = 62 N m⁻¹ (2 s.f.)

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Definition) State the defining condition for SHM. Answer: The acceleration is proportional to the displacement from equilibrium and directed toward it: a = −ω²x.
  2. (Graphs) Sketch or describe the velocity–time graph of an oscillating mass starting at maximum displacement. Answer: Velocity is a cosine-like curve starting at zero, reaching extremes of ±v_max as the mass passes equilibrium, one quarter cycle ahead of the displacement.
  3. (Calculations) An oscillator has amplitude 0.12 m and ω = 8.0 rad s⁻¹. Find the maximum acceleration. Answer: a_max = Aω² = 0.12 × 64 = 7.68 m s⁻² ≈ 7.7 m s⁻².
  4. (Energy) State how the total energy of an SHM system depends on amplitude and explain the effect of doubling it. Answer: E = ½kA², so energy is proportional to A²; doubling the amplitude quadruples the total energy.
  5. (Pendulum) Explain why a pendulum clock keeps worse time on a warm day. Answer: Warmth lengthens the pendulum L, and T = 2π√(L/g), so the period increases and the clock runs slow.
  6. (Damping) Distinguish light and critical damping. Answer: Light damping: oscillations continue with amplitude decaying exponentially; critical damping: the system returns to equilibrium in the shortest time without oscillating.
  7. (Resonance) Sketch qualitatively the amplitude–frequency response for a lightly and a heavily damped driven system, and state one use of resonance. Answer: Both peak at the natural frequency; the lightly damped peak is tall and sharp, the heavily damped one short and broad. Use: radio tuning circuits selecting a station's frequency.
  8. (Practical) Describe how you would determine g using a simple pendulum. Answer: Measure pendulum length L from pivot to bob centre; time N complete oscillations with a stopwatch and find T = t/N; repeat for several L values; plot T² against L — the gradient is 4π²/g, so g = 4π²/gradient.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • ω versus f: ω = 2πf. In a = −ω²x the ω is angular frequency; using f directly misses a factor of 4π².
  • Phase of the graphs: at maximum displacement, speed is zero and acceleration is maximum — candidates often invert this. Anchor on the extremes first: nothing moves at the turning points.
  • Energy ∝ A²: doubling amplitude quadruples energy; the amplitude of displacement does not scale energy linearly.
  • Pendulum validity: T = 2π√(L/g) assumes small angles (under about 10°) and a point mass; large angles lengthen the period.
  • Period independence: a pendulum's period is independent of bob mass and amplitude (small angle) — the classic conceptual question.
  • Damping and frequency: damping reduces amplitude and slightly shifts the peak frequency; in light damping the frequency is almost unchanged — do not claim the oscillation stops instantly.
  • Resonance condition: resonance requires the driving frequency to match the natural frequency; merely being "vibrated" does not guarantee it.
  • Spring constant from period: rearrange algebraically first (k = m(2π/T)²) and write the formula line — the rearrangement itself carries marks.
  • Precision: 2 or 3 s.f. with units (rad s⁻¹, m s⁻², N m⁻¹, J); keep π in the working until the final step.

title: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Right-Angled Trigonometry
content:
Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Right-Angled Trigonometry

Right-angled triangles are the most useful triangles in mathematics: Pythagoras relates the three sides, and the sine, cosine and tangent ratios relate sides to angles. Between them they solve every distance and angle problem the IGCSE sets, from ladders against walls to angles of elevation and three-figure bearings. This note builds the topic from zero: Pythagoras with its converse and 3D use, the SOHCAHTOA ratios with the selection method, exact values derived rather than memorised, and the multi-step problems that combine Pythagoras with trigonometry.

Pythagoras' theorem

in a right-angled triangle: a^2 + b^2 = c^2
where c is the hypotenuse (the side opposite the right angle)

The theorem is a statement about areas: the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides. The converse identifies right angles: if a² + b² = c² for the longest side c, the triangle is right-angled — the standard test for 3-4-5 and 5-12-13 triangles.

Worked example 1. A right-angled triangle has legs 6 cm and 8 cm. Find the hypotenuse.

c^2 = 6^2 + 8^2 = 36 + 64 = 100
c = 10 cm

Worked example 2 (finding a leg). The hypotenuse is 13 cm and one leg is 5 cm. Find the other leg.

a^2 = 13^2 - 5^2 = 169 - 25 = 144
a = 12 cm

Worked example 3 (converse). Is a triangle with sides 7, 24, 25 right-angled?

7^2 + 24^2 = 49 + 576 = 625 = 25^2
yes - right-angled, with the right angle opposite the 25 side

Pythagoras in three dimensions

In a cuboid, the space diagonal uses Pythagoras twice: first across the base, then up the height.

space diagonal = sqrt(l^2 + w^2 + h^2)

Worked example. A cuboid is 3 cm by 4 cm by 12 cm. Find the length of the space diagonal.

d = sqrt(9 + 16 + 144) = sqrt(169) = 13 cm

The three ratios: SOHCAHTOA

sin(theta) = opposite/hypotenuse      (SOH)
cos(theta) = adjacent/hypotenuse      (CAH)
tan(theta) = opposite/adjacent       (TOA)

Label the sides relative to the angle in question: the hypotenuse is always opposite the right angle; the opposite is across from the angle; the adjacent is the remaining side touching the angle. The selection method: mark the known side and the wanted side, then ask which ratio contains both.

Worked example 1 (finding a side). In a right-angled triangle, the angle is 35° and the hypotenuse is 12 cm. Find the opposite side.

known: hypotenuse; want: opposite  ->  sine
sin(35) = opposite/12
opposite = 12 sin(35) = 12 x 0.574 = 6.88 cm

Worked example 2 (finding a side with cosine). Angle 40°, hypotenuse 20 cm; find the adjacent side.

cos(40) = adjacent/20
adjacent = 20 cos(40) = 20 x 0.766 = 15.3 cm

Worked example 3 (finding an angle). Opposite 5 cm, adjacent 9 cm. Find the angle.

tan(theta) = 5/9 = 0.5556
theta = tan-1(0.5556) = 29.1 deg

For angles, use the inverse functions (sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹, tan⁻¹) and check the calculator is in degree mode — a radian-mode calculator turns 90° into 1.57 and ruins the paper.

Exact trigonometric values

Three angles have exact values worth knowing, derived from two special triangles:

Anglesincostan
30°1/2√3/21/√3
45°1/√21/√21
60°√3/21/2√3

Derivation: a 45-45-90 triangle with legs 1 has hypotenuse √2 (Pythagoras), giving sin 45 = 1/√2. An equilateral triangle of side 2 split in half gives a 30-60-90 triangle with sides 1, √3, 2, giving all six values. Deriving them once beats memorising them badly.

Two sanity checks keep the table honest: sine increases from 0 to 1 as the angle grows from 0° to 90°, so sin 30 must be smaller than sin 60; and cosine runs the other way, so cos 30 must be larger than cos 60. If an exact value breaks either ordering, the table has been misremembered.

Worked example. Find the exact value of sin 60° × tan 30°.

sin 60 = sqrt(3)/2;  tan 30 = 1/sqrt(3)
product = (sqrt(3)/2) x (1/sqrt(3)) = 1/2

Angles of elevation and depression

An angle of elevation is measured upward from the horizontal to an object; an angle of depression is measured downward. Both are measured from the observer's eye line, and the angle of depression from A to B equals the angle of elevation from B to A (alternate angles).

Worked example. From a point 40 m from the base of a tower, the angle of elevation to the top is 32°. Find the tower's height.

tan(32) = height/40
height = 40 tan(32) = 40 x 0.625 = 25.0 m

Worked example 2 (depression). A cliff is 60 m high; the angle of depression to a boat is 25°. Find the horizontal distance to the boat.

the angle at the boat is also 25 deg (alternate)
tan(25) = 60/d  ->  d = 60/tan(25) = 60/0.466 = 128.7 m

Choosing the method: a decision routine

Most lost trigonometry marks come from choosing the wrong tool, not from arithmetic. The routine below takes ten seconds and removes the guesswork:

  1. Is there a right angle? If not, the question needs the sine or cosine rule (a different topic) — do not force SOHCAHTOA onto a triangle without a right angle.
  2. What do you know — two sides, or a side and an angle? Two sides with no angle means Pythagoras. A side and an angle means trigonometry.
  3. Which ratio? Mark the known side and the target relative to the given angle, then pick the ratio containing both: sin uses opposite and hypotenuse, cos uses adjacent and hypotenuse, tan uses opposite and adjacent.
  4. What is the unknown — a side or an angle? A side comes from multiplying; an angle needs the inverse function.

Worked example. A roof rafter is 4.5 m long and meets the horizontal at 38°. Find the vertical rise and the horizontal run.

rise: sin(38) = rise/4.5  ->  rise = 4.5 sin(38) = 2.77 m
run:  cos(38) = run/4.5   ->  run = 4.5 cos(38) = 3.55 m
check: 2.77^2 + 3.55^2 = 7.67 + 12.60 = 20.27 ~ 4.5^2

Worked example 2 (finding the angle of a ladder). A 6 m ladder reaches 5.2 m up a wall. Find the angle it makes with the ground.

sin(theta) = 5.2/6 = 0.867  ->  theta = 60.1 deg

Multi-step problems: Pythagoras and trigonometry together

Many questions need both tools: Pythagoras to find a side in one triangle, trigonometry to use it in another. The method: draw and label every triangle, find the shared side first, then proceed.

Worked example. A ladder 5 m long leans against a wall, with its foot 2 m from the wall. Find the height reached and the angle the ladder makes with the ground.

height: h^2 = 5^2 - 2^2 = 25 - 4 = 21  ->  h = 4.58 m
angle: cos(theta) = 2/5 = 0.4  ->  theta = 66.4 deg

Worked example 2 (two triangles). From a point P, the angle of elevation to the top of a building is 30°; from a point Q, 20 m closer, it is 45°. Find the height.

let h be the height and x the distance from Q to the base.
tan(45) = h/x  ->  h = x
tan(30) = h/(x + 20)
h = (x + 20) tan(30) = (h + 20)(1/sqrt(3))
h sqrt(3) = h + 20  ->  h(sqrt(3) - 1) = 20
h = 20/(1.732 - 1) = 20/0.732 = 27.3 m

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Pythagoras) A right-angled triangle has legs 9 and 12. Find the hypotenuse. Answer: √(81 + 144) = √225 = 15.
  2. (Leg) Hypotenuse 17, one leg 8. Find the other. Answer: √(289 − 64) = 15.
  3. (Ratio) Angle 28°, adjacent 15 cm. Find the opposite side. Answer: tan 28 = o/15 → o = 15 × 0.532 = 7.98 cm.
  4. (Angle) Opposite 7, hypotenuse 10. Find the angle. Answer: sin θ = 0.7 → θ = 44.4°.
  5. (Exact) Find cos 30° exactly. Answer: √3/2.
  6. (Elevation) From 25 m away, the angle of elevation to a tree top is 40°. Find the height. Answer: 25 tan 40 = 25 × 0.839 = 21.0 m.
  7. (3D) A cuboid is 2 cm by 3 cm by 6 cm. Find its space diagonal. Answer: √(4 + 9 + 36) = √49 = 7 cm.
  8. (Combined) A ship sails 30 km east then 40 km north. Find its distance from the start and the bearing of its final position. Answer: distance = 50 km; tan θ = 40/30 → θ = 53.1°, bearing 053°.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Calculator mode: check DEG, not RAD or GRAD, before any trigonometric calculation. A radian answer is usually obviously wrong (tiny or huge), but only if you check.
  • Wrong ratio: label the sides relative to the angle before choosing SOH, CAH or TOA; picking by habit is the commonest trigonometry error.
  • Hypotenuse identification: the hypotenuse is opposite the right angle, not necessarily the longest-looking side on the diagram.
  • Pythagoras with the hypotenuse as a leg: c² = a² + b² only when c is the hypotenuse; finding a leg requires subtraction.
  • Rounding early: keep full calculator accuracy until the final answer; round to 3 s.f. (or 1 d.p. for angles unless told otherwise).
  • Angle of depression drawn from the wrong line: it is measured from the horizontal, not from the cliff face; the alternate-angle equality fixes the geometry.
  • Exact values with decimals: "exact" means surds and fractions, not 0.866; leaving √3/2 is required.
  • Missing units and labels: state cm, m, km and degrees; name the side or angle found, especially in multi-step problems.

title: Web Technologies and Security — Study Notes
content:
Web Technologies and Security

The Three Layers

  • HTML gives structure and content: elements, attributes, forms for user input.
  • CSS gives presentation: selectors, properties, responsive layout.
  • JavaScript gives client-side behaviour: validation before submission, DOM updates without reload.

Server-side scripting (PHP) runs on the server: reads form fields ($_POST), queries the database, outputs HTML. The client never sees PHP source.

SQL Injection

An attack where crafted input changes the meaning of a query. If a login query concatenates the username directly, entering X OR 1=1 can match every row. Defences: parameterised queries (prepared statements) that separate code from data, validation, and least-privilege database accounts.

Encryption

  • Symmetric: one shared key (AES). Fast, but key distribution is the weak point.
  • Asymmetric: public/private key pair (RSA). Anyone encrypts with the public key; only the holder decrypts with the private key. Slower, so used to exchange a symmetric session key.
  • SSL/TLS combines both: certificates verify the server, asymmetric key exchange establishes a symmetric session key, then traffic is encrypted. HTTPS = HTTP over TLS on port 443.

Hashing vs Encryption

Hashing (e.g. SHA-256) is one-way: passwords should be stored hashed with a unique salt, never encrypted reversibly.

Exam tips: explain why parameterised queries stop injection; describe the TLS handshake in three steps; distinguish hashing from encryption with password storage as the example.

Symmetric and asymmetric encryption

Symmetric encryption uses one shared key to encrypt and decrypt. It is fast, but the key must be shared securely. Asymmetric encryption uses a public key to encrypt and a private key to decrypt. TLS uses asymmetric encryption to agree a shared symmetric key at the start of a session.

A digital certificate binds a public key to an organisation. A trusted certificate authority signs it so that a browser can check the site's identity.

Exam tip: explain the hybrid approach: asymmetric for the key exchange, symmetric for the bulk data.

Exam method: choosing a defence

Match each threat to the control that stops it. Parameterised queries stop SQL injection because user input is passed as data and never run as part of the command. Input validation rejects unexpected characters before they reach the database. HTTPS uses encryption to protect data in transit, so an eavesdropper on the network sees only ciphertext. Passwords should be stored as salted hashes, so a stolen database does not reveal the original passwords.

Answer the question that is asked. If the question is about protecting data sent over a network, encryption is the answer. If it is about checking a password without storing it, a hash is the answer. Giving the wrong defence for the threat loses the marks even when the explanation is accurate.

Common errors

  • Describing a hash as reversible. A hash is one-way, so the original value cannot be recovered from it.
  • Calling a web page secure simply because it uses a padlock. The padlock shows encryption, not that the site is free of flaws.

title: IGCSE Biology: Human Influences on Ecosystems
content:
IGCSE Biology: Human Influences on Ecosystems

Humans now change every ecosystem on Earth — feeding ourselves at scale, destroying habitats, polluting air, water and soil, and altering the climate. This note works through food supply and intensive farming, the mechanisms of habitat destruction and species extinction, each pollutant with its cause-effect chain (from eutrophication to acid rain to greenhouse gases), and the conservation strategies that reverse the damage — reserves, breeding programmes, recycling and international agreements. The exam marks lie in chains of causation, so every impact is stated as mechanism → effect on the ecosystem → consequence.

Food supply and intensive farming

The growing human population (over 8 billion) needs more food; intensification maximises yield per hectare. Methods: fertilisers (replace soil nitrates and other ions removed at harvest — but excess runs off into waterways causing eutrophication), pesticides (kill insect pests, fungal diseases and weeds — but can poison non-target species, accumulate in food chains and drive resistance), herbicides (kill competing weeds), and livestock in confined conditions (high efficiency but welfare and antibiotic-resistance concerns). Monoculture (one crop over large areas) maximises short-term yield but depletes specific soil minerals and is vulnerable to a single pest or disease. Traditional/extensive farming (crop rotation, hedgerows, composting) sustains soil fertility and biodiversity at lower yields. The tension is the exam's favourite evaluation question: food security versus environmental cost.

Habitat destruction and species extinction

Habitat loss is the largest cause of biodiversity decline: deforestation for timber, cattle, soy and palm oil (tropical rainforests), wetland drainage for agriculture and housing, coral-reef destruction by trawling, warming and acidification, and urbanisation. Consequences: populations fragment (isolated groups cannot interbreed — reduced genetic diversity), food webs collapse (losing a keystone species cascades through the web), soil erosion follows tree removal (dust bowls, landslides, siltation of rivers), and species become extinct — extinction is forever. Human drivers in full: hunting and overfishing, pollution, introduced (invasive) species outcompeting natives (rats on islands, water hyacinth in lakes), and climate change shifting habitats faster than species can migrate or adapt. Rates of extinction today are estimated at 100–1000× the background (natural) rate.

Pollution of water: eutrophication

Excess nitrates and phosphates (from fertiliser run-off, sewage, detergents) enter rivers and lakes. Step 1: nutrients stimulate algal bloom — dense growth of algae covering the surface. Step 2: light is blocked, so submerged plants below die. Step 3: decomposer bacteria break down the dead plants and algae, multiplying rapidly. Step 4: bacterial respiration uses up the dissolved oxygen in the water. Step 5: fish and other aquatic animals suffocate and die (fish kills), and the water becomes anoxic and foul-smelling. Prevention: buffer strips of vegetation along waterways, careful fertiliser application (right amount, right time), tertiary sewage treatment (removing nitrates and phosphates), and phosphate-free detergents.

Air pollution: acid rain and greenhouse gases

Acid rain: sulfur dioxide (from burning fossil fuels containing sulfur, and smelting) and nitrogen oxides (from vehicle engines and power stations) dissolve in rainwater forming sulfuric and nitric acids, lowering rain pH below about 5.6. Effects: damages limestone buildings and statues (calcium carbonate + acid → soluble salts), leaches essential minerals (magnesium, calcium) from soil so plants weaken, acidifies lakes and rivers killing fish and amphibians (and mobilising toxic aluminium), and damages leaf cuticles and respiratory surfaces. Prevention: flue-gas desulfurisation (limestone scrubbers in power stations), catalytic converters in cars (converting carbon monoxide, nitrogen oxides and unburnt hydrocarbons to carbon dioxide, nitrogen and water), and low-sulfur fuels and renewables. The greenhouse effect: gases (carbon dioxide, methane, water vapour, nitrous oxide) absorb re-radiated infrared energy from the Earth's surface, warming the lower atmosphere — a natural effect that makes Earth habitable, but human emissions amplify it. Enhanced greenhouse effect and global warming: rising average temperatures cause ice-cap melting and sea-level rise, altered rainfall and more extreme weather, shifts in species distributions (poleward and uphill), coral bleaching, and threats to agriculture and water supplies. Sources of the extra greenhouse gases: fossil-fuel combustion (carbon dioxide), deforestation (carbon dioxide), rice paddies and ruminant livestock and landfill (methane), fertilisers (nitrous oxide).

Pollution summary

PollutantSourceEffectPrevention
Nitrates and phosphatesFertiliser run-off, sewageEutrophication, fish killsBuffer strips, phosphate-free detergents
Sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxidesPower stations, vehiclesAcid rain: damaged buildings, lakes, soilScrubbers, catalytic converters
Carbon dioxide, methaneFossil fuels, livestock, landfillEnhanced greenhouse effect, climate changeRenewables, reforestation
CFCsAerosols, refrigerationOzone-layer depletion, more UV reaching EarthInternational bans, replacement chemicals

Conservation and sustainability

Conservation maintains biodiversity and ecosystem services. Methods: nature reserves and national parks protecting habitats (with buffer zones and wildlife corridors connecting fragmented habitats), captive breeding and reintroduction programmes (saving critically low populations — giant panda, golden lion tamarin, Arabian oryx), seed banks and gene banks preserving genetic material, legal protection (CITES trading bans, protected species and habitats legislation), sustainable resource use (selective logging, fishing quotas and no-take zones, rotation), reducing pollution (cleaner energy, recycling), and education and international agreements (Kyoto Protocol, Paris Agreement, Rio conventions on biodiversity and climate). Sustainability means meeting present needs without compromising future generations: renewable energy (solar, wind, hydro, biofuels), recycling (paper, glass, metals, plastics — reducing extraction energy and landfill), reforestation and afforestation, and permaculture and organic farming. Individual-level actions (recycling, less meat, public transport) and governmental policy (carbon taxes, protected areas) are both fair comparison material.

Worked example: evaluating a conservation decision

Scenario: a lake suffers annual fish kills and algal blooms; farmland surrounds it. Step 1: diagnose — nitrate and phosphate run-off from fertilisers causes eutrophication (algal bloom → light blocked → decomposers multiply → oxygen depleted → fish die). Step 2: propose controls with mechanisms — buffer strips of vegetation along the watercourse trap run-off; precision fertiliser application reduces excess; phosphate-free detergents cut the phosphorus load; tertiary sewage treatment removes nutrients; aeration of the lake replenishes oxygen. Step 3: evaluate — buffer strips are cheap and create habitat (biodiversity bonus) but take land out of production; precision farming costs equipment but reduces fertiliser bills; aeration treats symptoms, not causes. Step 4: conclude with a balanced judgement citing productivity versus biodiversity, exactly as an evaluation question demands. Writing technique: for "assess" or "evaluate" questions, give both sides with mechanisms and finish with a justified judgement — a one-sided answer caps at half marks.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Describing eutrophication without the oxygen step: the fish die because decomposer bacteria deplete dissolved oxygen, not because algae "eat" them.
  • Saying the greenhouse effect itself is bad: it is natural and beneficial; it is the enhanced (human-boosted) effect that causes dangerous warming.
  • Confusing the ozone layer (stratospheric ozone absorbing UV) with the greenhouse effect (warming) — different phenomena, both pollution-related.
  • Listing pollutants without the mechanism: acid rain requires naming sulfur dioxide/nitrogen oxides dissolving in rainwater.
  • Writing that conservation means "leaving everything alone": active management (breeding, reserves, corridors, quotas) is the exam's expected answer.
  • Forgetting invasive species and overhunting when listing causes of extinction — habitat loss is biggest but not the only one.
  • Answering an "evaluate" question from one side only.
  • Confusing methane sources: ruminant livestock, rice paddies and landfill (anaerobic decomposition) — not fossil-fuel burning (that is mainly carbon dioxide).

Exam-style questions and answers

Q1. Explain how fertiliser run-off leads to the death of fish in a river. (4 marks) Answer: nitrates and phosphates leach into the river (1); algal bloom grows covering the surface (1); submerged plants die and decomposers multiply breaking them down (1); bacterial respiration depletes dissolved oxygen so fish suffocate (1).

Q2. Describe two ways in which humans reduce biodiversity. (4 marks) Answer: habitat destruction by deforestation or drainage (1) removing food and shelter so species die out (1); pollution of air/water/soil (1) poisoning organisms or acidifying lakes (1).

Q3. Explain how carbon dioxide contributes to global climate change. (3 marks) Answer: burning fossil fuels raises atmospheric carbon dioxide (1); carbon dioxide absorbs re-radiated infrared heat from the Earth (1); average global temperature rises, changing weather patterns and sea levels (1).

Q4. Describe the methods used to conserve endangered species. (4 marks) Answer: habitat protection in reserves and national parks (1); captive breeding and reintroduction programmes (1); seed/gene banks and legal protection from hunting and trade (1); international agreements limiting exploitation (1).

Q5. Evaluate the use of pesticides in farming. (4 marks) Answer: benefits — higher yields, less crop loss to pests and disease, more reliable food supply (1); costs — non-target species poisoned, biomagnification up food chains, resistant pests evolve (1); alternatives — biological control and integrated pest management (1); balanced judgement weighing food security against biodiversity (1).

title: A Level Mathematics: Permutations and Combinations
content:
A Level Mathematics: Permutations and Combinations

Counting is the part of probability that requires no formula to start with, only a decision: does the order matter? Every question in this topic is answered by that one question. If order matters the count is a permutation; if it does not the count is a combination. Everything else — repetitions, restrictions, arrangements around a circle — is a variation on the same counting principle, and this note sets out each variation with the reasoning behind it.

The multiplication principle

If a choice can be made in a ways and, independently, a second choice in b ways, the pair can be made in a × b ways. That is the whole foundation; the formulas are shortcuts for repeated applications of it.

arrangements of n distinct objects in a row: n! = n x (n-1) x ... x 2 × 1
0! = 1 by convention, so that formulas stay consistent
choosing r from n with order: nPr = n!/(n - r)!
choosing r from n without order: nCr = n!/(r!(n - r)!)

Worked example. A password is 4 distinct letters from the 26-letter alphabet. How many passwords are possible?

order matters, so 26P4 = 26 × 25 × 24 × 23 = 358,800

Worked example 2 (no order). How many ways can 4 students be chosen from 26?

order does not matter, so 26C4 = 14,950

Worked example 3 (a leading zero is not allowed). A code uses four distinct digits from 0 to 9 and cannot begin with zero. How many codes?

first digit: 9 choices (1 to 9)
remaining three: 9P3 = 9 × 8 × 7 = 504
total = 9 × 504 = 4536

Worked example 4 (the link). Explain why nPr = nCr × r!.

every unordered selection of r objects can be arranged in r! orders
so counting ordered selections = counting unordered ones then arranging them

Deciding whether order matters

The decision is not about the words "choose" or "arrange" in the question — those are hints, not rules. The safe test is to imagine two selections differing only by swapping two items: if that counts as a different outcome, order matters.

SituationOrder?Count
finishing order of a raceyesnPr
a committee of 3nonCr
a 4-digit PINyespermutation, with repetition allowed
a hand of cardsnonCr
seating 5 people in a rowyes5!

Worked example. A team of 11 is chosen from 16 players, and one of the 11 is captain. Count the possibilities.

choose the 11: 16C11 = 4368
choose the captain from them: 11 ways
total = 4368 × 11 = 48,048

The multiplication principle is doing the work here: two independent choices, multiplied.

Repetition and identical items

When some objects are identical, arranging them as if all were distinct overcounts by the number of ways the identical ones can be swapped. Dividing by those factorials corrects it.

arrangements of n items with groups of identical items:
n!/(a! b! c! ...) where a, b, c are the group sizes
with repetition allowed, choosing r from n: n^r

Worked example. How many distinct arrangements of the letters in BANANA?

6 letters: B once, A three times, N twice
6!/(1! 3! 2!) = 720/12 = 60

Worked example 2 (repetition allowed). A 3-digit code uses digits 0-9, repeats allowed. How many codes?

10 × 10 × 10 = 1000
if repeats were not allowed: 10 × 9 × 8 = 720

Worked example 3 (identical plus restriction). How many arrangements of the letters of LEVEL begin with L?

fix L at the front; remaining letters E, V, E, L
that is 4 letters with E twice: 4!/2! = 12
but the leading L is one of the two Ls, so there is only one choice for the front
answer 12

Restrictions: the "glue" method

When certain items must be together, treat the group as a single object, arrange the objects, then arrange within the group. When certain items must not be together, count the total and subtract the "together" case.

together: glue the group, arrange the objects, multiply by the internal arrangements
not together: total arrangements minus the together arrangements
specific positions: fix those items first, then arrange the rest

Worked example. Five books, two of which must stand together, are arranged on a shelf. How many orders?

glue the pair: now 4 objects, arranged in 4! = 24 ways
the pair interchange in 2! = 2 ways
total = 48

Worked example 2 (not together). The same five books with the pair not together.

total arrangements = 5! = 120
together = 48
not together = 120 - 48 = 72

Worked example 3 (fixed positions). Four men and three women sit in a row of seven. How many arrangements have all three women together?

glue the women into one block: now 5 objects (4 men + block), 5! = 120
internal arrangements of the women: 3! = 6
total = 720

Circular arrangements

Around a circle, rotations of the same arrangement are not distinguishable, so fixing one item removes the rotational symmetry and the count drops by a factor of n.

n distinct items around a circle: (n - 1)!
a necklace (where reflection also counts as the same): (n - 1)!/2

Worked example. In how many ways can 6 people sit around a round table?

(6 - 1)! = 5! = 120

Worked example 2 (with a fixed seat). How many ways if one particular person must sit in a specified chair?

fix that person, arrange the other 5 around: 5! = 120
the specified chair removes the rotational freedom entirely, so the answer is unchanged here

Worked example 3 (two people together at a round table). Six people, two of whom must sit together.

glue the pair: 5 objects around a circle = 4! = 24
internal order of the pair: 2
total = 48

Combinations with conditions

Committee questions combine cases: choose so many from one group and so many from another, then add the disjoint alternatives. The discipline is to make the cases genuinely disjoint, or the same selection gets counted twice.

choose a from group A and b from group B: C(a-group, a) x C(b-group, b)
several allowed compositions: add the separate cases
at least one: total minus none

Worked example. From 6 men and 5 women, how many committees of 4 contain exactly 2 women?

choose 2 women from 5: 10
choose 2 men from 6: 15
total = 150

Worked example 2 (at least one). How many committees of 4 contain at least one woman?

total committees: 11C4 = 330
none: 6C4 = 15
at least one = 330 - 15 = 315

Worked example 3 (cases added). How many committees of 3 contain more women than men?

3 women: 5C3 = 10
2 women and 1 man: 5C2 × 6C1 = 10 × 6 = 60
total = 70

Counting inside probability

Combinations are usually the denominator of a probability question: count the favourable selections, count all selections, divide. Doing the counting separately from the probability keeps both parts clean and makes partial credit possible.

Worked example. A bag holds 5 red and 7 blue counters. Four are drawn at random. Find the probability of exactly 2 red.

total selections: 12C4 = 495
favourable: 5C2 × 7C2 = 10 × 21 = 210
probability = 210/495 = 0.4242

Worked example 2 (at least one). For the same bag, find the probability of at least one red.

complement: no red means all four blue
7C4 = 35
P(no red) = 35/495 = 0.0707
P(at least one red) = 1 - 0.0707 = 0.9293

Worked example 3 (order matters in the numerator). Three cards are drawn from a standard deck without replacement. Find the probability they are drawn in increasing order of value.

every set of three distinct cards has exactly one increasing order out of 3! orders
so the probability is 1/6, independent of the deck

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Factorial) Evaluate 7!. Answer: 7! = 7 × 6 × 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 5040.
  2. (Permutation) In how many orders can 5 runners finish? Answer: 5P5 = 5! = 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 120.
  3. (Combination) Evaluate 10C3. Answer: 10C3 = 10!/(3! × 7!) = (10 × 9 × 8)/(3 × 2 × 1) = 720/6 = 120.
  4. (Choice) From 8 books, how many ways to choose 3? Answer: 8C3 = 8!/(3! × 5!) = (8 × 7 × 6)/(3 × 2 × 1) = 336/6 = 56.
  5. (Arrangement) How many arrangements of the letters of STATISTICS? Answer: 10!/(3! × 3! × 2!) = 3 628 800/(6 × 6 × 2) = 3 628 800/72 = 50,400.
  6. (Glue) 6 people in a row with two together: Answer: glue the pair: 5! × 2! = 120 × 2 = 240.
  7. (Not together) Same 6, not together: Answer: total − together = 6! − 5! × 2! = 720 − 240 = 480.
  8. (Circle) 7 people around a table: Answer: (n − 1)! = 6! = 720.
  9. (Committee) 3 from 5 men and 4 women, exactly 2 men: Answer: 5C2 × 4C1 = 10 × 4 = 40.
  10. (At least) 4 from the same 9 with at least one woman: Answer: all − none = 9C4 − 5C4 = 126 − 5 = 121.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Using nPr where order does not matter: a committee is unordered; using permutations overcounts by r!.
  • Forgetting to divide by repeated factorials: identical letters need the divisor or the count is inflated.
  • Glue method without the internal factor: the block also has an internal arrangement, and dropping the 2! halves the answer.
  • Circular arrangements with n! instead of (n − 1)!: rotations are the same seating.
  • Adding what should be multiplied: independent stages multiply; alternative cases add.
  • Overlapping cases: cases must be disjoint, or selections are counted twice.
  • "At least one" counted directly: the complement is almost always faster and safer.
  • Restrictions applied after the count: fix the restricted positions first, then count what remains.

Choosing between nPr, nCr and a plain product

Most lost marks in this topic come from using the right formula for the wrong question. Before any calculation, decide whether you are selecting, arranging or doing both, and whether the answer depends on the order. The subsections below set out the decision in the order a careful candidate works through it.

Selecting without arranging: nCr

If you only need to choose a group and the order inside the group does not matter, use ⁿCᵣ = n! / (r!(n − r)!). Choosing a committee of 4 from 10 people gives ¹⁰C₄ = 210. The result counts groups, so two committees with the same members in a different order are the same committee.

Selecting and arranging: nPr

If the chosen items are then placed in distinct positions, the order matters and you use ⁿPᵣ = n! / (n − r)!. Choosing a chair, a vice-chair and a secretary from 10 people gives ¹⁰P₃ = 720. Each committee of 3 from the previous example can be arranged in 3! = 6 ways, so 720 = 120 × 6, which is a useful check.

A plain product for independent choices

When each decision is made separately and the number of options for one does not depend on the others, multiply. Three shirts and four trousers give 3 × 4 = 12 outfits. Do not reach for a combination formula here: nothing is being chosen from a single pool of identical kinds of object.

Checking the order question

Ask whether swapping two chosen items changes the outcome. A password changes if its letters are swapped, so it is an arrangement. A team does not change when two members swap places, so it is a selection. If the words in the question say “the first, second and third” or “positions”, the order matters.

Worked decision

Seven runners compete for gold, silver and bronze. The medals are different, so the order matters and the count is ⁷P₃ = 7 × 6 × 5 = 210. If the question asked for three runners to go through to a final with no ranking, the count would be ⁷C₃ = 35. The same seven people give 210 or 35 depending only on whether the medal order is asked for, so state which one you have chosen before you write the number.

Common error: dividing when you should not

Students often divide by a factorial out of habit. Divide only when items are truly identical or the outcome groups are truly unordered. Dividing ⁷P₃ by 3! to get the medal count gives 35 and throws away the difference between gold and silver, which the question asked you to keep.

Keeping items apart and placing them together

Restriction questions usually ask that certain people or letters are together, or that they are not. Two methods work, and the complement is often shorter. Choose the method from the wording before you start counting.

Together: treat the pair as one object

If two items must sit together, glue them into one block. Arrange the block with the others, then multiply by the number of internal orders of the block. Seven people in a row with two particular people side by side give 6! × 2! = 720 × 2 = 1440 arrangements. Omitting the 2! halves the answer.

Not together: subtract the together cases

For the same seven people with the two not allowed together, the total is 7! = 5040. Subtract the 1440 arrangements in which they are together, giving 5040 − 1440 = 3600. This is usually quicker than building the arrangements directly, because the gaps between people are hard to count without listing them.

Not together: place people in the gaps

An alternative for the same question is to arrange the other five people first, which gives 5! = 120 orders. There are six gaps, including the two ends, and the two special people must go into different gaps. Choose 2 of the 6 gaps in order, 6P2 = 30 ways, and this gives 120 × 30 = 3600. Both methods agree, and showing the second one earns the method marks even if the first has an error.

Letters that must not be adjacent

For the word HEART with the vowels E and A not next to each other, count the arrangements with the vowels together (4! × 2! = 48) and subtract from 5! = 120, giving 72. The same subtraction pattern applies to any pair that must be kept apart.

Position restrictions

If one person must stand at one end, fix that person first and arrange the rest. A person fixed at one end leaves 6 people for 6 places, giving 6! = 720. Fixing the restricted item before counting the free ones avoids double counting, which is the usual cause of an answer that is too large.

Interpreting “together” and “next to”

“Side by side” and “next to each other” mean adjacent in the order given. They do not mean the same chair or a shared seat. Read the wording carefully, because a question about two people sitting “with one seat between them” needs a different count altogether.

Groups, teams and sharing into sets

Questions that divide people or objects into groups are where the difference between labelled and unlabelled groups decides the answer. A group that is named, such as “team A” or “the first group”, is labelled. A group that is only described by its members is unlabelled, and the count must not treat two identical splits as different.

Choosing one team from a pool

Choosing a team of 3 from 10 people is a plain selection, so the count is ¹⁰C₃ = 120. No ordering inside the team is counted, and the team is simply the set of three names.

Two teams with names: labelled groups

If the two teams are called Red and Blue, the choice of Red fixes the rest. Choosing 3 for Red from 6 people and 3 for Blue from the remaining 3 gives ⁶C₃ × ³C₃ = 20 × 1 = 20 ways. The name of each team matters, so there is no further division.

Two identical teams: unlabelled groups

If the two teams are not named, the same 20 splits are counted twice, once with each team as Red. Divide by 2 to get 10 ways to split six people into two unlabelled teams of three. Check that the answer is even, since the teams can be swapped in pairs.

Sharing into several sets of equal size

Dividing 9 people into three unlabelled groups of three gives ⁹C₃ × ⁶C₃ × ³C₃ / 3! = 84 × 20 × 1 / 6 = 280 ways. The divisor 3! is needed because the three groups can be listed in 3! orders without changing the split.

Groups with a fixed member

If a particular person must be in the team, choose the other two from the remaining nine: ⁹C₂ = 36. Fixing the person first removes the need for a subtraction later and keeps the count clear.

Worked example: a committee of mixed teachers

A committee of 4 is chosen from 5 men and 4 women and must contain at least one woman. The complement is the committee with no women, which is all men: ⁵C₄ = 5. The total committees are ⁹C₄ = 126. So the answer is 126 − 5 = 121. Writing the complement out in words, “no women”, stops the most common slip, which is counting the all-women case as if it had been excluded.

Pascal's triangle and binomial coefficients

The numbers ⁿCᵣ are the same numbers that appear in the binomial expansion and in Pascal's triangle. Seeing the link lets you check a count quickly, and it appears in both the algebra and the probability questions in A2.

Building the triangle from addition

Each entry in Pascal's triangle is the sum of the two entries above it. Row 0 is 1, row 1 is 1 1, row 2 is 1 2 1, row 3 is 1 3 3 1, and row 4 is 1 4 6 4 1. The entry in row n, position r (counting from 0) is ⁿCᵣ, so row 4 gives ⁴C₂ = 6 directly.

The binomial theorem

The expansion of (a + b)ⁿ has the coefficient ⁿCᵣ on the term aⁿ⁻ʳbʳ. For (1 + x)⁵, the coefficient of x² is ⁵C₂ = 10, and the full expansion is 1 + 5x + 10x² + 10x³ + 5x⁴ + x⁵. Check one value by substituting x = 1, which gives 2⁵ = 32, the sum of the row.

Using the row sum as a check

The sum of row n is 2ⁿ, because it counts all the subsets of an n-element set. Row 5 sums to 1 + 5 + 10 + 10 + 5 + 1 = 32 = 2⁵. If a count you calculated does not fit the row pattern, look again before you write it down.

Symmetry: ⁿCᵣ = ⁿCₙ₋ᵣ

Choosing r items to take is the same as choosing n − r items to leave, so ⁿCᵣ = ⁿCₙ₋ᵣ. For example ⁸C₆ = ⁸C₂ = 28. Use the smaller of r and n − r when you calculate by hand, because the factorials are shorter.

Coefficient questions

A question might ask for the coefficient of x³ in (2 + x)⁶. The general term is ⁶Cᵣ 2⁶⁻ʳ xʳ, so for r = 3 the coefficient is ⁶C₃ × 2³ = 20 × 8 = 160. The combination gives the number of ways and the power of the constant gives the rest; both are needed.

Why the link matters in probability

The binomial probability P(X = r) = ⁿCᵣ pʳ qⁿ⁻ʳ uses the same coefficient as the expansion of (q + p)ⁿ. The coefficients count the ways the successes can be placed among the trials, and the powers of p and q give the chance of each arrangement. Keeping the two roles separate prevents the error of leaving out the combination.

Equations and symbols

Every formula here is a shortcut for the multiplication principle, and each one carries a condition that decides whether it applies. The condition is the mark: "order matters" and "items are identical" change the count by a factorial.

n! = n x (n-1) x ... x 2 × 1 Key: n = the number of distinct objects (a count, no units); n! = the number of orders they can be arranged in (a count). The falling product stops at 1, and 0! = 1 by convention so the formulas stay consistent.

nPr = n!/(n - r)! Key: n = how many objects are available; r = how many are being chosen; nPr = the number of ordered selections (a count). Read it as "start at n and write down r factors": 26P4 = 26 × 25 × 24 × 23.

nCr = n!/(r!(n - r)!) Key: n = objects available; r = objects chosen; nCr = the number of unordered selections (a count). The extra r! in the denominator is exactly what removes the orderings — which is the whole difference between a permutation and a combination.

nPr = nCr × r! Key: nPr = ordered selections; nCr = unordered selections; r! = the ways to order each selection. The identity explains both formulas at once: count the sets, then arrange each one.

26P4 = 26 × 25 × 24 × 23 = 358,800 Key: 26 = letters available; 4 = letters chosen without replacement; 358,800 = ordered passwords (a count). The factors fall because each letter is used once — repetition allowed would give 26⁴ instead.

26C4 = 14,950 Key: 26 = students available; 4 = students chosen; 14,950 = unordered groups (a count). The same numbers as the password question, 24 times smaller, because a group of four has 4! orderings that all count as one group.

n!/(a! b! c! ...) Key: n = total items; a, b, c = the sizes of the groups of identical items. Dividing by the factorials of the repeats removes the arrangements that look identical — 6!/(1! 3! 2!) = 60 arrangements of BANANA, not 720.

6!/(1! 3! 2!) = 720/12 = 60 Key: 6 = letters in BANANA; 1! = the single B; 3! = the three As; 2! = the two Ns; 60 = distinct arrangements (a count). Every repeated letter needs its own factorial in the denominator, or the count is inflated.

n^r Key: n = choices available at each stage; r = number of stages; the result counts selections with repetition allowed (a count). It is the multiplication principle applied r times — three digits from 0 to 9 with repeats gives 10³ = 1000.

(n - 1)! Key: n = people or objects around a circle; the result counts distinct circular arrangements (a count), because rotating a seating does not create a new one. For a necklace, where a reflection is also the same, divide once more: (n - 1)!/2.

5! × 2! = 120 × 2 = 240 Key: 5! = the arrangements of four single items plus the glued pair as one object; 2! = the internal orders of the pair; 240 = total arrangements (a count). Gluing without the internal factor halves the answer, which is the classic lost mark in this topic.

title:
Appendix U — Cross-strand reasoning in one long integrated answer

A question that crosses the strands is the one that tests whether the topic is a connected whole or three separate lists. The best way to answer such a question is to write one integrated answer that moves between the strands without losing the thread, and the best way to practise that is to take a cross-strand question and write the integrated answer from the durable ideas and the cross-strand appendix. Suppose the question asks you to relate the immune recognition of antigens to the forensic comparison of DNA patterns, and to say what the two kinds of recognition have in common and what they do not. A good integrated answer says that both are about telling things apart by recognising specific features, and that the immune system recognises antigens and produces specific antibodies and memory cells, while DNA profiling compares patterns of variation in DNA and uses the differences between individuals to identify or exclude. A good answer then says that the common point is recognition and comparison, while the differences are that one is a biological response inside the body and the other is a technical comparison of extracted DNA, and that one is about defence and the other is about identification. If you can write that, you have the cross-strand answer, and you have the kind of answer that question is built from. If you only write two separate descriptions, you have lost the connection, and the connection is what the question is after.

If you write that integrated answer with the common point and the differences in the right places, you hit the marks that the cross-strand question is after. You hit the recognition-and-comparison idea, which is the common point. You hit the biological-response-versus-technical-comparison idea, which is one of the differences. You hit the defence-versus-identification idea, which is the other of the differences. You hit the connection, because you have said both the common point and the differences without treating them as unrelated.
