title: Sequences and Series — Study Notes
content:
Sequences and Series

Arithmetic Progressions (AP)

Terms increase by a common difference d.

  • nth term: uₙ = a + (n − 1)d
  • Sum: Sₙ = n/2 [2a + (n − 1)d]

Example: AP 5, 8, 11: the 20th term is 5 + 19 × 3 = 62.

Geometric Progressions (GP)

Terms multiply by a common ratio r.

  • nth term: uₙ = arⁿ⁻¹
  • Sum: Sₙ = a(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r)
  • Sum to infinity (|r| < 1 only): S∞ = a/(1 − r)

Example: a = 8, r = 1/2 gives S∞ = 8/(1/2) = 16.

Binomial Expansion

(1 + x)ⁿ = 1 + nx + n(n − 1)/2! x² + n(n − 1)(n − 2)/3! x³ + …, valid for |x| < 1.

For positive integer n, coefficients come from Pascal's triangle: (1 + 2x)⁴ = 1 + 8x + 24x² + 32x³ + 16x⁴.

Exam tips: identify a, d or r first; for "sum to infinity" questions check |r| < 1 explicitly, and for binomial expansions give terms up to the power asked (usually x² or x³).

Formulae and exam method

Arithmetic progression: the nth term is Tₙ = a + (n − 1)d, where a is the first term and d the common difference. The sum of the first n terms is Sₙ = n/2 [2a + (n − 1)d], or Sₙ = n/2 (a + l) when the last term l is known.

Geometric progression: Tₙ = arⁿ⁻¹, and Sₙ = a(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r) for r ≠ 1. The sum to infinity exists only when |r| < 1, and then S∞ = a/(1 − r).

To find the number of terms, substitute the known sum or term and solve for n. When n sits in an exponent, take logarithms. Check that n is a positive integer.

Sigma notation: Σ from r = 1 to n of (ar + b) is evaluated with the standard sums, but write out the first few terms when the pattern is unclear.

Exam cue: Identify whether the question is AP or GP before choosing a formula, and state the value of r when using the sum to infinity.

Exam method: arithmetic and geometric sums

For an arithmetic sequence with first term a and common difference d, the nth term is a + (n − 1)d and the sum of the first n terms is S_n = n/2 (2a + (n − 1)d). For a geometric sequence with ratio r, the nth term is ar^(n − 1) and S_n = a(1 − r^n)/(1 − r) for r ≠ 1.

The sum to infinity exists only when |r| < 1, and then S∞ = a/(1 − r). If |r| ≥ 1, say so explicitly rather than applying the formula.

Exam cue: Identify whether the sequence is arithmetic or geometric from the common difference or ratio before choosing a formula. Check the number of terms n carefully when you set up the equation.

title: A Level Mathematics: Hypothesis Testing
content:
A Level Mathematics: Hypothesis Testing

A hypothesis test is a formal way of deciding whether data are surprising enough to overturn an assumption. The logic is legal rather than mathematical in spirit: assume the claim is true, compute how unlikely the observed evidence would be under that assumption, and reject the claim only if the evidence is unlikely enough. This note sets out the machinery — null and alternative hypotheses, significance levels, tails, critical regions — and then applies it to the binomial and normal cases the exam uses.

The logic of a test

The null hypothesis H0 is the assumption of no change, no effect, no bias: the status quo. The alternative H1 is what you would conclude if the data are too extreme. The significance level α is the risk of rejecting a true H0 that you are willing to accept.

H0: the parameter equals its old value
H1: the parameter is greater, less, or simply different
alpha: the maximum acceptable probability of a Type I error (often 0.05 or 0.01)
test statistic: the observed value computed from the sample
p-value: probability of a result at least as extreme, assuming H0

The analogy that makes the asymmetry clear: a criminal trial presumes innocence. The presumption is not a belief, it is the default that evidence must overcome. Failing to reject H0 is not proof of H0 — it is a verdict of "not proven".

One-tailed and two-tailed tests

The alternative decides the tail. A one-tailed test is used when the direction of the change is specified in advance; a two-tailed test when any change would matter.

AlternativeTest typep-value
p > p0one-tailed, upperP(X ≥ observed)
p < p0one-tailed, lowerP(X ≤ observed)
p ≠ p0two-tailed2 × the smaller tail

Worked example (choosing the alternative). A coin is suspected of favouring heads. Which alternative applies?

the suspicion has a direction, so H1: p > 0.5, a one-tailed upper test
a two-tailed test would be right only if any bias mattered

Errors and their consequences

Every test can go wrong in two ways, and the significance level controls only one of them. Understanding which is which is a frequent exam question and a genuine conceptual point.

Type I error: reject H0 when it is true  (probability alpha)
Type II error: fail to reject H0 when it is false
reducing alpha reduces Type I errors but increases Type II errors
increasing the sample size reduces both

Worked example. A test at the 5% level concludes a die is biased when it is fair. Which error is this?

H0 (fair) was true and was rejected
that is a Type I error, with probability at most 5%

Worked example 2 (effect of sample size). Explain why the same observed proportion can be significant in a large sample and not in a small one.

a larger sample reduces the standard error, so the same deviation
becomes more standard errors away from the null value
the evidence is measured in standard errors, not in raw counts

Testing a binomial proportion

The test statistic is the observed number of successes, the null distribution is binomial, and the p-value is a cumulative binomial probability.

H0: p = p0;  X ~ B(n, p0)
upper tail p-value = P(X >= x)
lower tail p-value = P(X <= x)
reject H0 if p-value <= alpha

Worked example. A manufacturer claims 90% of components are fault-free. In a sample of 20, only 15 are fault-free. Test at the 5% level whether the claim is too high.

H0: p = 0.9;  H1: p < 0.9
X ~ B(20, 0.9)
P(X <= 15) = 0.0432
0.0432 < 0.05, so reject H0
there is evidence the fault-free rate is below 90%

Worked example 2 (critical region). Find the 5% critical region for that test.

P(X <= 15) = 0.0432 (below 0.05)
P(X <= 16) = 0.1330 (above 0.05)
critical region: X <= 15

Worked example 3 (actual significance level). State the actual significance level of that test.

the probability of a Type I error is P(X <= 15) under H0 = 0.0432
so the actual level is 4.32%, just inside the 5% requirement

Testing a normal mean

When the variable is continuous and the population is normal — or the sample is large — the test statistic is standardised with a z-score and compared with critical values.

test statistic z = (x-bar - mu)/(σ/sqrt n)   (σ known)
or z = (x-bar - mu)/(s/sqrt n)                  (σ estimated, large n)
critical values at 5% one-tailed: 1.6449;  two-tailed: 1.96
at 1% one-tailed: 2.3263;  two-tailed: 2.5758

Worked example. A machine fills bags with a mean of 500 g and standard deviation 8 g. A sample of 16 bags has mean 496 g. Test at the 5% level whether the mean has fallen.

H0: mu = 500;  H1: mu < 500
standard error = 8/sqrt 16 = 2
z = (496 - 500)/2 = -2
critical value at 5% one-tailed is -1.6449
-2 < -1.6449, so reject H0: the mean has fallen

Worked example 2 (two-tailed). Same data, tested two-tailed at 5%.

critical values are +/-1.96
|-2| > 1.96, so still reject H0
the evidence is that the mean is not 500, in either direction

Worked example 3 (interpreting a p-value). A test gives z = 1.72 for H1: μ > μ0. Find the p-value and conclude at 5%.

p-value = P(Z > 1.72) = 0.0427
0.0427 < 0.05, so reject H0
the result is significant at the 5% level but not at 1%

Choosing the right test

The exam does not label the test; the shape of the data decides it. Getting the distribution wrong makes every later mark unreachable, so the decision is worth making explicitly.

count of successes in n trials with constant p  →  binomial test
count of events in an interval at a constant rate  →  Poisson test
mean of a continuous measurement  →  normal test (z)
correlation between two variables  →  product-moment test

Worked example. A nurse records the number of patients arriving in an hour on 30 separate days. Which test?

counts of arrivals in equal intervals at a roughly constant rate
use a Poisson test on the mean count, not a binomial test
a normal test on the mean of the 30 counts is also defensible for large n

Writing a conclusion that earns the marks

The final mark of a hypothesis test is for the conclusion, and it has three components: a decision about H0, a reference to the significance level, and the finding stated in the context of the question. Dropping any one of them costs a mark even when the arithmetic is perfect.

Compare these two endings. "0.0201 < 0.05, so reject H0" scores the comparison. "There is sufficient evidence at the 5% level that the call rate has increased" scores the comparison and the interpretation. "The rate has increased" scores neither, because it reports a certainty the test cannot deliver.

The opposite case is often mishandled too. When the p-value is above the level the correct wording is that there is insufficient evidence to reject H0 — never that H0 is true, and never that nothing has happened. A non-significant result from a small sample is weak evidence either way, and saying so is better than overclaiming in either direction.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Hypotheses) A coin might be biased against heads. State H0 and H1. Answer: H0: p = 0.5; H1: p < 0.5.
  2. (Error) Define a Type II error. Answer: failing to reject H0 when it is false.
  3. (Binomial) 8 of 20 seeds germinate; test p = 0.6 against p < 0.6 at 5%. Answer: P(X ≤ 8) = 0.0565, not significant.
  4. (Critical region) X ~ B(15, 0.4): 5% lower critical region. Answer: P(X ≤ 2) = 0.0271, P(X ≤ 3) = 0.0905, so X ≤ 2.
  5. (Actual level) For that region, state the actual significance level. Answer: 2.71%.
  6. (Normal) μ0 = 20, σ = 4, n = 25, mean 21.5: test at 5% one-tailed. Answer: z = 1.875 > 1.6449, reject.
  7. (Two-tailed) Same data two-tailed: Answer: 1.875 < 1.96, do not reject.
  8. (p-value) z = 2.4, H1: μ > μ0. Find the p-value. Answer: 0.0082.
  9. (Sample size) Why can a larger sample turn a non-significant result significant? Answer: the standard error shrinks, so the same deviation is more standard errors away.
  10. (Conclusion wording) Write a valid conclusion for a rejected H0. Answer: there is sufficient evidence at the 5% level that the mean has fallen.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Concluding H0 is true: failing to reject means the evidence is insufficient; it is never proof of the null.
  • Wrong tail: compute P(X ≥ x) for an increase and P(X ≤ x) for a decrease; using the other tail inverts the conclusion.
  • Doubling without a two-tailed alternative: the p-value is doubled only when H1 is "not equal".
  • p-value compared with the wrong threshold: 5% is 0.05; comparing 0.043 with 5 instead of 0.05 reverses the verdict.
  • Standard error omitted: the z-score divides by σ/√n, not by σ.
  • Critical value for the wrong tail: the 5% one-tailed value is 1.6449, the two-tailed is 1.96; the sign matters too.
  • Type I and Type II swapped: Type I is rejecting a true null — the error the significance level controls.
  • Conclusion beyond the data: a rejected H0 says the parameter has changed, not why, and never that the change is important.

title: Programming and Algorithms — Study Notes
content:
`# Programming and Algorithms

Design Approaches

  • Top-down (stepwise refinement): decompose into modules — planned structure
  • Object-oriented: classes encapsulating state + behaviour — reusability
  • WAD (write all down): rapid prototyping — evolves during coding

Pseudocode Conventions

DECLARE x : INTEGER
IF x > 10 THEN ... ELSE ... ENDIF
WHILE ... ENDWHILE
FOR i ← 1 TO n ... NEXT i
FUNCTION f(a) RETURNS INTEGER

Searching

  • Linear: check each item, O(n), works unsorted
  • Binary: halve a sorted list each step, O(log n)

Example: 1,000,000 items: binary search needs ≤ 20 comparisons.

Sorting

AlgorithmBestAverageIdea
BubbleO(n)O(n²)swap neighbours
InsertionO(n)O(n²)insert into sorted prefix
MergeO(n log n)O(n log n)divide and merge

Merge sort example: [5,2,9,1] → [5,2][9,1] → [2,5][1,9] → [1,2,5,9].

Recursion

A function calling itself with a base case. Factorial: f(0)=1, f(n)=n·f(n−1). Stack frames handle state.

Exam tips: state the Big-O and justify it; for traces, tabulate variable changes per iteration.

Testing with normal, boundary and erroneous data

Normal test data is typical valid input that the program should accept and process correctly. Boundary (extreme) test data sits at the edges of the valid range, such as the lowest and highest permitted values, because errors often occur there. Erroneous test data is invalid input that the program should reject, such as text entered where a number is required.

A trace table records the value of each variable at each step of an algorithm. Tracing a algorithm by hand with test data shows where it departs from the intended result, and it is a common exam task.

Exam tip: a complete test plan includes all three kinds of data, with the expected output written beside each test value.

title: AS Level Mathematics: Mechanics M1 — Kinematics, Dynamics and Statics
content:
AS Level Mathematics: Mechanics M1 — Kinematics, Dynamics and Statics

Mechanics describes motion and the forces causing it. M1 covers three linked strands: kinematics (describing motion with graphs and the constant-acceleration equations), dynamics (Newton's second law applied to single particles and connected bodies), and statics (equilibrium of a particle and moments of forces). This note builds each from zero, with the modelling assumptions stated, the sign conventions fixed, and worked examples written out line by line — because in mechanics the marks are in the diagram and the equation, not the answer.

Modelling assumptions and units

standard assumptions unless told otherwise:
  the object is a particle (no size, no rotation)
  air resistance is negligible
  the string is light and inextensible; the pulley is smooth
  g = 9.8 m s⁻² (use 9.81 if the question says so)

State the assumption when you use it: "modelling the stone as a particle, so air resistance is ignored". Marks are awarded for identifying what the model simplifies.

Kinematics: the constant-acceleration equations

v = u + at
s = ut + (1/2) a t²
v² = u² + 2as
s = ((u + v)/2) t

u initial velocity, v final velocity, a acceleration,
s displacement, t time

The equations hold only for constant acceleration. Choose the equation by listing what you know and what you want: exactly one equation omits the quantity you neither know nor need.

Worked example 1. A car accelerates uniformly from 8 m/s to 20 m/s in 6 s. Find the acceleration and the distance.

a = (v - u)/t = (20 - 8)/6 = 2 m/s²
s = ((u + v)/2)t = 14 × 6 = 84 m

Worked example 2 (falling). A stone is dropped from rest from a cliff and takes 3 s to land. Find the height, taking g = 9.8.

u = 0, a = 9.8 (downward positive), t = 3
s = 0 + (1/2)(9.8)(9) = 44.1 m

Worked example 3 (upward). A ball is thrown vertically upwards at 15 m/s. Find the maximum height and the total time in the air.

at the top v = 0: 0 = 225 - 2(9.8)s  →  s = 11.48 m
time up: 0 = 15 - 9.8t  →  t = 1.53 s
total time = 3.06 s (symmetric flight)

Fix the positive direction before substituting. Upward-positive makes g = −9.8; the alternative is consistent arithmetic but must not be mixed mid-question.

Velocity-time and displacement-time graphs

displacement-time: gradient = velocity
velocity-time: gradient = acceleration; area = displacement
speed-time: area = distance

Worked example. A cyclist accelerates from rest to 12 m/s in 5 s, travels at 12 m/s for 10 s, then decelerates to rest in 4 s. Find the total distance.

area 1: (1/2)(5)(12) = 30
area 2: 12 × 10 = 120
area 3: (1/2)(4)(12) = 24
total = 174 m

Area below the time axis is negative displacement: the particle has reversed direction, and distance sums the magnitudes.

Newton's second law and forces

resultant force F = m a
weight W = m g
friction opposes motion: F <= mu R (limiting case F = mu R)
normal reaction R acts perpendicular to the surface

Worked example 1 (horizontal). A 5 kg box is pushed with 30 N along a rough floor with friction 8 N. Find the acceleration.

resultant = 30 - 8 = 22 N
a = 22/5 = 4.4 m/s²

Worked example 2 (on a slope). A 4 kg particle slides down a smooth slope inclined at 30°. Find its acceleration.

component of weight along the slope = 4g sin 30 = 19.6 N
a = 19.6/4 = 4.9 m/s²  (= g sin 30)

Worked example 3 (with friction on a slope). Same slope, friction 6 N.

resultant = 19.6 - 6 = 13.6 N
a = 3.4 m/s²

Connected particles

Two bodies joined by a string have the same magnitude of acceleration (the string is inextensible) and the same tension throughout (the string is light and the pulley smooth). Write one equation per body and add them to eliminate T.

Worked example (pulley). Masses 5 kg and 3 kg hang either side of a smooth pulley. Find the acceleration and the tension.

for 5 kg (downward positive): 5g - T = 5a
for 3 kg (upward positive):   T - 3g = 3a
add: 2g = 8a  →  a = 2.45 m/s²
T = 3(g + a) = 3(9.8 + 2.45) = 36.75 N

Worked example 2 (on a table). A 4 kg block on a smooth table is connected over a pulley to a 2 kg hanging mass. Find the acceleration.

hanging mass: 2g - T = 2a
block: T = 4a
add: 2g = 6a  →  a = 3.27 m/s²

Worked example 3 (lift). A 60 kg person stands in a lift accelerating upward at 2 m/s². Find the reaction force.

R - 60g = 60(2)  →  R = 60(11.8) = 708 N
the person feels heavier; in free fall R would be zero

Statics: equilibrium of a particle

equilibrium: the resultant force is zero
resolve horizontally and vertically, or along and perpendicular to
a slope, and set each total to zero

Worked example. A 10 N weight hangs from two strings making 40° and 50° with the horizontal. Find the tensions.

horizontal: T¹ cos 40 = T² cos 50
vertical: T¹ sin 40 + T² sin 50 = 10
from the first: T² = T¹ cos40/cos50 = 1.1918 T¹
T¹(0.6428) + 1.1918 T¹(0.7660) = 10
T¹(0.6428 + 0.9129) = 10  →  T¹ = 6.43 N, T² = 7.66 N

Moments

moment = force x perpendicular distance from the pivot
for equilibrium of a rigid body: sum of clockwise moments = sum of
anticlockwise moments

Worked example. A uniform plank 4 m long of weight 200 N rests on two supports 1 m from each end. A 300 N load is placed 0.5 m from the left end. Find the reactions.

supports at 1 m and 3 m from the left; load at 0.5 m
moments about the left support:
  load: 300 × 0.5 = 150 anticlockwise
  weight: 200 × 1 = 200 clockwise (weight acts at the centre, 2 m)
  right reaction R2 at 2 m: clockwise
  150 = 200 + 2 R2  →  R2 = -25 N, so the plank would tip
check total: R1 + R2 = 500 needed; with R2 negative the support
cannot hold, so the load must be moved inward - a tipping question

Moments about a support is the standard trick: it eliminates that support's reaction, leaving one unknown. If the required reaction is negative, the body is not in equilibrium and tipping is the intended conclusion.

Friction and limiting equilibrium

Friction is a variable force: it takes whatever value is needed to prevent motion, up to a maximum. Only at the point of slipping does it reach its limiting value.

F <= mu R  on a rough surface
limiting friction: F = mu R   (on the point of moving)
R is found by resolving perpendicular to the surface

Worked example 1 (horizontal, limiting). A 10 kg block rests on a rough horizontal floor with mu = 0.4. Find the smallest horizontal force needed to move it.

R = 10g = 98 N
limiting friction = 0.4 × 98 = 39.2 N
so a force just above 39.2 N starts it moving

Worked example 2 (slope). A block sits on a rough slope inclined at 25° with mu = 0.5. Does it slide?

component down the slope: mg sin 25 = 0.4226 mg
maximum friction: mu mg cos 25 = 0.5 × 0.9063 mg = 0.4531 mg
maximum friction exceeds the driving component, so it stays at rest
and friction takes the value 0.4226 mg

The comparison is the answer: if mu >= tan θ the particle remains in equilibrium on the slope, because the friction ceiling covers the driving component. That inequality is a standard exam demand.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (suvat) u = 4, a = 3, t = 5. Find s. Answer: 20 + 37.5 = 57.5 m.
  2. (suvat) u = 10, v = 30, s = 100. Find a. Answer: 900 = 100 + 200a → a = 4 m/s².
  3. (graph) A v–t graph rises 0 to 20 m/s in 4 s, then falls to 0 in 2 s. Distance? Answer: 40 + 20 = 60 m.
  4. (F = ma) 12 kg, resultant 36 N. Find a. Answer: 3 m/s².
  5. (slope) Smooth slope at 20°, mass 5 kg. Find a. Answer: g sin 20 = 3.35 m/s².
  6. (pulley) 6 kg and 4 kg over a smooth pulley. Find a. Answer: 2g = 10a → 1.96 m/s².
  7. (tension) For that pulley, find T. Answer: T = 4(9.8 + 1.96) = 47.0 N.
  8. (moments) A 2 m lever with a 50 N force at 1.5 m from the pivot balances a force F at 0.5 m. Find F. Answer: 50 × 1.5 = 0.5F → F = 150 N.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • No diagram: draw the forces before writing equations; nearly every mechanics error is a missing or misdirected force.
  • Sign convention drift: fix positive direction once and keep it; a sign flip mid-question produces a wrong acceleration.
  • Using suvat with varying acceleration: the equations need constant a; if a changes, split into stages or use a graph.
  • Forgetting weight on a slope: the component along the slope is mg sin θ; the perpendicular component mg cos θ is balanced by the reaction on a smooth slope.
  • Tension assumed equal to weight: in an accelerating system T ≠ mg; solve the equations.
  • Adding instead of eliminating T: write one equation per body with consistent directions, then add to cancel T.
  • Moments with the wrong distance: the perpendicular distance from the pivot, not the distance along the rod.
  • Units and g: use the g the question gives; mixing 9.8 and 9.81 changes answers at the third figure.

Formula summary

v = u + at;  s = ut + at²/2;  v² = u² + 2as;  s = (u + v)t/2
F = ma;  W = mg;  F = mu R at limiting friction
moment = force x perpendicular distance

Every M1 calculation begins with a diagram showing the forces, the chosen positive direction and the known quantities. The formula is the last step; the model is the first.

Equations and symbols

Every relation these topics are examined on, gathered into one reference sheet, each written with its real notation and followed by a key that names every symbol, its unit and what it measures. The sections above build the reasoning; this is the exam-hall version, where what you need is the exact form of a line rather than the story behind it.

The four constant-acceleration equations

v = u + at
Key: u = the initial velocity (m s⁻¹); v = the final velocity (m s⁻¹); a = the constant acceleration (m s⁻²); t = the time taken (s). It follows from acceleration being the gradient of the velocity–time graph, so it carries no information about displacement — reach for it when the distance is neither given nor wanted.

s = ut + ½at²
Key: s = the displacement from the starting point (m); u = the initial velocity (m s⁻¹); a = the constant acceleration (m s⁻²); t = the time (s). The area under the velocity–time graph written as a formula. Use it when the final velocity is unknown or irrelevant; a negative s means the particle finished behind its starting point, not that the formula failed.

v² = u² + 2as
Key: the symbols as above; s = displacement (m). It is the time-free equation, which is why it is the one for "find the speed after a given distance" and for a body projected vertically where the time to the highest point is not asked. It gives v², so both signs of v must be considered when taking the square root.

s = ½(u + v)t
Key: u = initial velocity (m s⁻¹); v = final velocity (m s⁻¹); t = time (s); s = displacement (m). The trapezium area under a straight-line velocity–time graph, i.e. the average velocity times the time. It is the quickest route whenever u, v and t are all known.

s = vt − ½at²
Key: the same five quantities. Algebraically identical to s = ut + ½at² once v = u + at is substituted; it exists so that a question giving v, a and t never forces you to compute u first.

What the motion graphs give you

gradient of a displacement–time graph = velocity; gradient of a velocity–time graph = acceleration
Key: gradient = the slope of the line, in m s⁻¹ for the first graph and m s⁻² for the second; a negative gradient means motion in the negative direction (for the second graph, deceleration in the positive direction). A curved graph has no single gradient, so either draw a tangent or split the motion into stages.

area under a velocity–time graph = displacement; area under a speed–time graph = distance
Key: area = the region between the graph and the time axis, in m; signed for velocity (below the axis counts negative), unsigned for speed. Distance is the sum of the magnitudes of the areas on both sides of the axis, so a particle that reverses has travelled further than its displacement.

Force, weight and Newton's second law

ΣF = ma
Key: ΣF = the resultant force on the body (N), i.e. the vector sum, not the largest force; m = the mass (kg); a = the acceleration (m s⁻²), always in the direction of the resultant. The whole of dynamics is this one line written separately along each direction of interest, with friction, tension and weight each given their own sign.

W = mg
Key: W = the weight (N); m = the mass (kg); g = the gravitational field strength, 9.8 m s⁻² unless the question states 9.81. Weight is a force and acts vertically downwards from the centre of mass; mass never changes with location, weight does.

R = m(g + a) in a lift accelerating upward, R = m(g − a) accelerating downward
Key: R = the normal reaction from the floor (N); m = the mass of the occupant (kg); g = 9.8 m s⁻²; a = the lift's acceleration (m s⁻²), positive upward. Take upward as positive throughout and the two cases are one equation, R − mg = ma. In free fall a = g and R = 0, which is the "apparent weightlessness" result.

on a slope at angle θ: component along the slope = mg sin θ, component perpendicular = mg cos θ
Key: m = the mass (kg); g = 9.8 m s⁻²; θ (theta) = the angle of the slope to the horizontal (degrees). The two components swap when the angle is measured from the vertical, which is the single commonest source of a wrong slope equation. On a smooth slope the perpendicular components balance, so R = mg cos θ.

F ≤ μR, with F = μR at limiting friction
Key: F = the friction force (N), which takes whatever value is needed to prevent sliding up to its ceiling; μ (mu) = the coefficient of friction, dimensionless, different for each pair of surfaces; R = the normal reaction (N), found by resolving perpendicular to the surface. The inequality is the physics: friction is not always μR, only at the point of slipping.

the particle stays at rest on a rough slope if and only if μ ≥ tan θ
Key: μ = the coefficient of friction; θ = the angle of the slope. It comes from comparing mg sin θ with μmg cos θ and cancelling mg. A slope of 25° with μ = 0.5 therefore holds the block, since tan 25° = 0.466 is less than 0.5, and the friction actually acting is only mg sin θ.

Connected particles

(m₁ − m₂)g = (m₁ + m₂)a ⇒ a = g(m₁ − m₂)/(m₁ + m₂)
Key: m₁ = the heavier mass (kg); m₂ = the lighter mass (kg); g = 9.8 m s⁻²; a = the common acceleration (m s⁻²), m₁ descending. It comes from writing m₁g − T = m₁a and T − m₂g = m₂a with opposite directions positive for each body, then adding to cancel T. It is only valid for a light inextensible string over a smooth pulley.

T = m₁(g − a) = m₂(g + a)
Key: T = the tension in the string (N); m₁, m₂ = the two masses (kg); a = the common acceleration (m s⁻²); g = 9.8 m s⁻². Substitute into either body's equation — the two expressions must agree, which makes them a free arithmetic check. In equilibrium (a = 0) both reduce to T = mg, and in a rapidly accelerating system T is not the weight.

block m₁ on a smooth table joined to hanging mass m₂: a = m₂g/(m₁ + m₂), T = m₁a
Key: m₁ = the mass on the table (kg); m₂ = the hanging mass (kg); a = the common acceleration (m s⁻²); T = the tension (N). The table's normal reaction balances m₁g, so the only driving force is m₂g acting on the combined mass. With friction present, replace m₂g by m₂g − F in the numerator and keep the same denominator.

write one equation per body with its own positive direction, then add to eliminate T
Key: T = the tension (N), the internal force that appears in both equations with opposite signs. This is the method rather than a formula: it generalises to three connected masses, to a body on a slope and to a pulley with friction, where a memorised formula does not.

Statics: equilibrium, resolution and moments

equilibrium of a particle: ΣF_x = 0 and ΣF_y = 0
Key: ΣF_x = the sum of the horizontal components (N); ΣF_y = the sum of the vertical components (N); the particle has no acceleration, so both totals vanish. Choose axes along the most forces — for a body on a slope, along and perpendicular to the slope rather than horizontal and vertical.

a weight W hanging from two strings at angles α and β to the horizontal: T₁ cos α = T₂ cos β and T₁ sin α + T₂ sin β = W
Key: T₁, T₂ = the tensions in the two strings (N); α (alpha), β (beta) = the angles each string makes with the horizontal (degrees); W = the hanging weight (N). The first line says the horizontal pulls cancel, the second that the vertical components carry the weight. Two equations, two unknowns — solve the first for one tension in terms of the other, then substitute.

three forces in equilibrium form a closed triangle, so their magnitudes are proportional to the sines of the angles opposite
Key: the three force magnitudes (N) and the angles between the lines of action. Reversing one force turns equilibrium into a triangle; this is a check on a resolved solution, not usually a required method, but it catches a sign or angle error immediately.

moment of a force = F × d, where d is the perpendicular distance from the pivot
Key: F = the force (N); d = the perpendicular distance from the line of action to the pivot (m); the moment is in N m, and its sense is clockwise or anticlockwise. If the force is at an angle to the rod, use the component perpendicular to the rod, F sin θ, with θ measured between the force and the rod.

a rigid body in equilibrium: sum of clockwise moments = sum of anticlockwise moments, and ΣF = 0
Key: each moment = force × perpendicular distance (N m); the force condition gives the total reaction. Take moments about a support so that its own reaction has zero distance and drops out, leaving one equation in one unknown — the standard first move on every plank question.

uniform rod of length L and weight W has its weight acting at L/2 from either end
Key: L = the length of the rod (m); W = its weight (N), acting vertically through the midpoint because the mass is evenly distributed; a non-uniform rod's centre of mass is wherever the question puts it. Placing a load outside a support makes the required reaction negative, which is the signal that the rod tips about the other support.

title: Edexcel IAL Computer Science: Operating Systems, Translators and Data Security
content:
Edexcel IAL Computer Science: Operating Systems, Translators and Data Security

Pearson Edexcel International Advanced Level in Computer Science, Unit 1 Principles of Computer Science: operating systems and their purposes, language translators, and data security and integrity. This note goes below the GUI: what an operating system actually allocates and protects, how source code becomes machine instructions, and how data is kept correct and confidential — with the security section structured as threat → mechanism → defence, the shape examiners mark against.

The operating system as resource manager

An operating system is the system software that manages the hardware and provides services to applications. Two complementary views: the resource manager (allocating CPU time, memory, storage and peripherals fairly and efficiently) and the extended machine (hiding hardware complexity behind clean interfaces so applications never program the disk controller directly).

  • Processor management — scheduling processes onto the CPU; time slicing and priorities give multitasking; a process moves between ready, running and blocked states.
  • Memory management — allocating RAM to processes, protecting one process's space from another, and using virtual memory (paging to backing store) when RAM is exhausted.
  • File management — directories, file naming, access permissions, and tracking free space.
  • Device management — device drivers translate OS requests into device-specific commands; a buffer smooths speed differences between CPU and peripherals; interrupts and spooling coordinate them.
  • User interface — GUI (intuitive, direct manipulation) or CLI (scriptable, low overhead, precise).
  • Security — authentication, access rights, audit logs.

Interrupts underpin responsiveness: a device raises an interrupt; the CPU completes its current instruction, saves state, runs the interrupt service routine (ISR), restores state and resumes. Priorities arbitrate simultaneous interrupts. Polling (asking devices in turn) wastes cycles; interrupts let devices signal need.

Utility software

Utilities maintain and protect the system: antivirus (signature and heuristic scanning), defragmentation (recontiguating scattered files on magnetic disks — pointless on SSDs), backup (full vs incremental; the 3-2-1 rule: three copies, two media, one off-site), compression, file management, firewalls and disk partitioning tools. The exam wants each utility's function stated as an effect on performance, security or reliability.

Language translators

TranslatorMechanismOutputConsequence
CompilerWhole-program translation before executionStandalone machine-code executableFast execution; errors reported across the whole program at compile time; recompilation needed per change
InterpreterLine-by-line translation and immediate executionNone saved (translator needed each run)Slower; errors surface exactly at the failing line; ideal for development and portability
AssemblerOne mnemonic to one machine instructionMachine code for that processorFull hardware control; tied to the instruction set
Same program, two translation paths:

  source:  total = 0
           for i in 1..5: total = total + i
           print(total)

Compiler:  scans the whole file → syntax check all lines → optimises →
           emits executable → the executable runs at machine speed. The
           compiled file runs again and again with no translator present.

Interpreter: takes line 1, translates and runs it (total = 0 in memory);
           takes line 2's loop, translating and running each iteration; then
           line 3 prints 15. Every rerun repeats the translation.

Intermediate languages (bytecode for the JVM) sit between: compiled once,
interpreted or JIT-compiled at run time - portable without source exposure.

Choosing a translator: worked factors

Exam questions ask which translation approach suits a given project; the answer weighs four factors. Execution speed: compiled code runs at machine speed — pick it for number-crunching or embedded targets. Development cycle: interpreters give immediate feedback and pinpointed errors — pick them for prototyping and teaching. Portability: an interpreter or bytecode VM runs anywhere the runtime exists; native executables need rebuilding per platform. Intellectual property: distributing an executable or bytecode keeps source private; distributing interpreted source exposes it. Hybrid systems (Java's compile-to-bytecode then JIT, or Python's compiled .pyc cache) mix the trade-offs — mention them when the question allows.

Data security and integrity

Security protects confidentiality, integrity and availability of data; integrity means data is accurate, complete and unaltered — maintained by validation at input, verification, access control and transaction controls. The two ideas interlock: a security breach often destroys integrity (tampering), and integrity measures (checksums, audit trails) also reveal breaches.

ThreatMechanismDefence
Malware (virus/worm/trojan/ransomware)Malicious code: attaches and replicates / spreads over networks / disguises itself / encrypts for ransomAntivirus, patching, firewalls, least privilege, offline backups
Phishing / social engineeringManipulating people into revealing credentialsTraining, verification procedures, spam filters, 2FA
Brute force / dictionary attacksAutomated password guessingLong complex passwords, lockouts, rate limiting, hashing with salt
Interception / sniffingEavesdropping on trafficEncryption (TLS, VPNs), secure protocols
DoS / DDoSOverwhelming a service with trafficTraffic filtering, rate limiting, redundancy
SQL injectionHostile input executed as codeParameterised queries, input validation
Insider misuseAuthorised users exceeding needLeast privilege, auditing, separation of duties

Access-control mechanisms: authentication (knowledge, possession, inherence — and two-factor combinations), authorisation (rights matrices and role-based access), encryption (symmetric AES for bulk; asymmetric RSA for key exchange and signatures; hashing for password storage and integrity), and physical security. Passwords are stored as salted hashes so a database leak does not yield usable passwords.

Worked: protecting a payroll database, defence in depth.

Layer 1 physical: locked server room, encrypted backups off-site.
Layer 2 network: firewall rules; payroll VLAN; TLS for all access.
Layer 3 host: patched OS; antivirus; full-disk encryption.
Layer 4 application: parameterised queries (SQL injection), session timeouts.
Layer 5 data: least-privilege roles (clerk sees one department; only the
              payroll officer sees salaries); all changes audit-logged.
Layer 6 people: security training, two-factor admin logins, separation of
              duties (the person who adds employees is not the one who
              approves pay changes).

An attacker must beat every layer; a defender must hold each one - asymmetry
the answer should name.

Integrity in databases: validation (type, range, length, presence, check digits), verification (double entry, visual checks), and access-controlled updates. Recovery: backups, transaction logs, journaling — restoring to the last consistent state after failure.

Worked example: analysing a breach

Incident: an admin's credentials are phished; an attacker copies the customer
table overnight; data appears on a leak site.

Analysis against the layers:
  phishing succeeded → no 2FA on admin accounts (authentication gap);
  overnight copy unnoticed → no anomaly alerting on bulk reads (monitoring);
  full table visible → excessive rights; data not encrypted at rest;
  customer impact → notification obligations triggered.

Remediation: enforce 2FA on all admin access; alert on bulk export; encrypt
the table at rest; reduce each account to least privilege; staff refresher on
phishing; restore confidence with a published incident report.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Describing the OS as "the software you click on"; frame it as resource management and services — scheduling, memory, files, devices.
  • Saying virtual memory makes a computer faster; it prevents crashes when RAM is full at the cost of speed.
  • Confusing compilation with interpretation in a comparison; the deliverable (executable versus nothing saved) is the decisive point.
  • Claiming compiled code can never be interpreted or vice versa — hybrid systems (JVM) exist; the question wants the primary mechanism.
  • Answering security questions with antivirus alone; map each threat to its mechanism and defence.
  • Storing passwords encrypted rather than hashed (reversible storage is a vulnerability), or hashing without a salt (rainbow tables).
  • Conflating validation with verification: validation checks plausibility of the value; verification checks it matches the source.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Unit 1, 4 marks). Describe two operating system functions and why each matters.

Answer: Memory management allocates RAM to each running process and protects one process's memory from another, so programs cannot corrupt each other and available RAM is used fully; virtual memory lets processes exceed physical RAM. Processor scheduling allocates CPU time among processes (time slicing, priorities), so several programs appear to run at once and urgent tasks are not starved.

Question 2 (Unit 1, 4 marks). Explain how an interrupt improves the efficiency of I/O.

Answer: Instead of the CPU repeatedly polling each device (wasting cycles on idle devices), a device raises an interrupt when it needs service. The CPU finishes its current instruction, saves the program counter, runs the device's ISR, and resumes exactly where it left off — so the CPU does useful work until attention is genuinely required.

Question 3 (Unit 1, 4 marks). Compare compiled and interpreted approaches for a cross-platform scientific application.

Answer: A compiled version runs at full machine speed — critical for heavy computation — but needs a separate build per platform and a recompile for each change. An interpreter runs unchanged anywhere the interpreter exists, simplifying distribution and debugging, but executes more slowly because translation repeats at run time. For number-crunching, compile; for portability and rapid iteration, interpret — or compile to portable bytecode.

Question 4 (Unit 1, 4 marks). Explain how hashing protects stored passwords.

Answer: Passwords are never stored in plain text; a one-way hash function maps each password to a fixed-length digest that cannot be reversed. A random salt per user defeats rainbow-table and precomputed-dictionary attacks, and equal passwords then hash differently. At login the submitted password is hashed with the stored salt and compared. Even a database leak yields only digests, which must be cracked one guess at a time.

Question 5 (Unit 1, 5 marks). Describe how a company can protect data against both external attack and internal misuse.

Answer: External: firewalls and patched systems block and contain attacks; TLS/VPNs stop interception; 2FA and strong password policies defeat credential theft; tested off-site backups defeat ransomware. Internal: least-privilege roles ensure staff access only what their job needs; audit logs and anomaly alerts deter and detect misuse; separation of duties prevents any one person completing a sensitive action alone; training builds a reporting culture. Together these give defence in depth across technology and people.

Question 6 (Unit 1, 3 marks). Explain the difference between validation and verification with examples.

Answer: Validation checks that data is plausible before storage — a range check rejects a mark of 250, a type check rejects "abc" as an integer. Verification checks the data captured matches the source — double-entering a new bank account number, or visually checking a scanned form against the record. Validation enforces integrity of values; verification enforces accuracy of capture.

The last Unit 1 domain steps back from mechanisms to consequences: who owns data, what is fair use, and what AI changes.

title: Further Trigonometry — Study Notes
content:
Further Trigonometry

Compound Angles

  • sin(A ± B) = sin A cos B ± cos A sin B
  • cos(A ± B) = cos A cos B ∓ sin A sin B

Example: sin 75° = sin(45° + 30°) = (√2/2)(√3/2) + (√2/2)(1/2) = (√6 + √2)/4.

Double Angles

  • sin 2A = 2 sin A cos A
  • cos 2A = cos²A − sin²A = 2cos²A − 1 = 1 − 2sin²A

Example: express 4 sin x cos x in one term: 2 sin 2x.

The R-Form

a sin x + b cos x = R sin(x + α) with R = √(a² + b²) and tan α = b/a.

Example: 3 sin x + 4 cos x = 5 sin(x + 0.927). This instantly gives the maximum 5 and minimum −5.

Reciprocal Functions

sec θ = 1/cos θ, cosec θ = 1/sin θ, cot θ = 1/tan θ. Key identity: 1 + cot²θ = cosec²θ.

Exam tips: choose the cos 2A form that eliminates the unwanted function; when solving with R-form, divide by R before using inverse trig, and translate intervals carefully.

title: Networks and the Internet — Study Notes
content:
Networks and the Internet

The TCP/IP Stack

Four layers: Application (HTTP, FTP, SMTP, DNS), Transport (TCP reliable, connection-oriented with sequence numbers and acknowledgements; UDP fast, connectionless), Internet (IP addressing and routing), Link (physical delivery on the local network). Layering separates concerns so each layer can change independently.

Switching

  • Circuit switching: a dedicated path is held for the call (traditional telephone) — wasteful if idle.
  • Packet switching: data split into packets routed independently; each carries source/destination addresses and a sequence number, reassembled at the destination. Efficient and fault-tolerant; packets may arrive out of order (TCP fixes ordering).

Addressing and Subnetting

IPv4 addresses are 32 bits, written dotted decimal, split into network + host portions by the subnet mask. ANDing an IP with the mask yields the network ID. 192.168.4.0/26 means the first 26 bits are network, leaving 6 host bits: 64 addresses, 62 usable. NAT maps private addresses to one public IP.

Models and Protection

Client-server centralises services (web, email, files); peer-to-peer shares directly (torrents, small LANs). Firewalls filter traffic by rules; proxy servers sit between clients and the internet, caching and filtering; ports identify services (80/443 web, 25 SMTP).

Exam tips: compute usable hosts from a given prefix; trace a packet through the four layers naming one protocol per layer; explain one advantage of packet over circuit switching.

Protocols and switching

A protocol is a set of rules that devices follow to communicate. TCP/IP is the suite used on the internet, and protocols define how data is addressed, formatted and checked for errors.

In circuit switching a dedicated path is set up for the whole call, as in the traditional telephone network. In packet switching the message is split into packets, each carrying a header with source and destination addresses and a sequence number. Packets can take different routes and are reassembled at the destination.

Exam tip: packet switching uses the network efficiently because no path is reserved, but packets can arrive out of order.

Exam method: dividing a network into subnets

Take 192.168.1.0/24 and split it into four equal subnets. A /24 prefix leaves 8 host bits, so borrowing 2 bits gives a /26 prefix and 6 host bits, which means 64 addresses per subnet. The four networks are 192.168.1.0, 192.168.1.64, 192.168.1.128 and 192.168.1.192. In each subnet the first address is the network address and the last is the broadcast address, so the usable hosts are 62 per subnet.

Always work out the block size first: 256 minus the last octet of the subnet mask gives the step between subnet addresses. For a mask ending in 192, the step is 64.

Common errors in networking questions

  • Forgetting that the network and broadcast addresses cannot be assigned to hosts, so the usable count is 2 to the power of the host bits, minus 2.
  • Confusing packet switching with circuit switching. Packet switching splits data into packets that may take different routes; circuit switching reserves a fixed path for the whole call.
  • Stating that a router works at the data link layer. Routers forward packets using IP addresses, so they operate at the network layer.

title: Number — Sets — Study Notes
content:
Number — Sets

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): set notation, Venn diagrams, shading, universal set, subsets.

1. Notation

  • ∈ belongs to; ∉ not in; ∅ empty set; ξ (or U) universal set; n(A) = number of elements.
  • A ∩ B intersection (AND); A ∪ B union (OR); A′ complement (NOT A).
  • A ⊆ B: every element of A is in B.

2. Venn diagrams

Fill the intersection first, then work outwards. Two sets: only A, both, only B, neither.

Example: 30 students; 18 maths, 15 physics, 7 both ⇒ neither = 30 − (11 + 7 + 8) = 4.

3. Shading

For A ∩ B′ shade where A and outside-B overlap. (A ∪ B)′ = A′ ∩ B′ (De Morgan) — check every region.

4. Regions algebra

With region variables x, y, z: use the totals to form equations, e.g. n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B).

5. Probability links

P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B) — inclusion–exclusion from the diagram.

Exam tips: "neither" sits outside both circles — subtract from the universal set last; label regions with numbers, not expressions, as you fill.

The number sets

Natural numbers are 1, 2, 3 and so on; integers add zero and negatives; rational numbers can be written as a fraction p/q with q not zero; irrational numbers, such as π and √2, cannot. Terminating and recurring decimals are rational. Prime numbers have exactly two factors, 1 and themselves.

Prime factors and HCF/LCM

Write a number as a product of primes using a factor tree. The highest common factor uses the common primes at their lowest powers; the lowest common multiple uses every prime at its highest power. Venn diagrams sort numbers by properties such as even, square or prime.

Square roots and cube roots

The square root of a number is positive or negative: √16 = 4 but x² = 16 gives x = ±4. Check whether a root is exact or needs a calculator, and give a non-exact answer to the accuracy asked.

Worked example: a two-set Venn diagram

In a group of 30 students, 18 play football (set F) and 12 play cricket (set C), and 5 play both. Fill the diagram from the centre outwards: the intersection is 5, so football only is 18 − 5 = 13 and cricket only is 12 − 5 = 7. The union has 13 + 5 + 7 = 25 students, so 30 − 25 = 5 play neither sport. Answer questions by reading from the diagram: the number who play football or cricket but not both is 13 + 7 = 20.

Notation in words and symbols

  • A ∩ B: elements in both A and B. Written as "and" in the question.
  • A ∪ B: elements in A or B or both. Written as "or" in the question.
  • A′: the complement, everything in the universal set ξ that is not in A.
  • n(A) means the number of elements in A; the total of all regions in the diagram is n(ξ).

Shading regions

To shade (A ∪ B)′, first shade A ∪ B, then leave the shaded region outside both circles. To shade A′ ∩ B, shade B and take away the part that lies inside A. A quick test: list the regions by number (1 for A only, 2 for the intersection, 3 for B only, 4 outside) and write each expression as the list of regions it covers. Expressions that match the same list describe the same set.

Factors, HCF and LCM

Write each number as a product of primes. 360 = 2³ × 3² × 5 and 84 = 2² × 3 × 7. The HCF takes the lowest power of each common prime: 2² × 3 = 12. The LCM takes the highest power of every prime that appears: 2³ × 3² × 5 × 7 = 2520. The HCF multiplies to the smallest number that both divide; the LCM is the smallest number both divide into.

Surds and roots

Simplify √72 by finding a square factor: √72 = √(36 × 2) = 6√2. A surd is left in exact form until the question asks for a decimal. Cube roots follow the same logic: ∛54 = ∛(27 × 2) = 3∛2. Do not split a sum under a root: √(9 + 16) is 5, not √9 + √16 = 7.

Common errors

  • Writing 13 as the answer to "football only" by reading the total for football, not the region.
  • Confusing HCF with LCM, usually by taking the highest power for both.
  • Treating 0 as a natural number when a question asks for the set of natural numbers; state which convention is used if the mark scheme is strict.

title: Coordinate Geometry — Study Notes
content:
Coordinate Geometry

Gradients and Equations of Lines

Gradient m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁). From ax + by + c = 0, the gradient is −a/b.

Point-slope form: y − y₁ = m(x − x₁).

Example: through (4, 3) with m = −1/2: y − 3 = −(x − 4)/2, i.e. y = −x/2 + 5.

Parallel and Perpendicular

  • Parallel lines: equal gradients.
  • Perpendicular lines: m₁m₂ = −1 (gradients are negative reciprocals).

Example: perpendicular to y = 2x + 1 has gradient −1/2.

Midpoint and Distance

Midpoint of (x₁, y₁), (x₂, y₂): ((x₁+x₂)/2, (y₁+y₂)/2).

Distance: √((x₂−x₁)² + (y₂−y₁)²). The line from (0,0) to (3,4) has length 5 — recognise 3-4-5 triangles.

Intersections and Bisectors

Intersections: solve the equations simultaneously. The perpendicular bisector of AB passes through the midpoint of AB with gradient −1/m(AB) — equate distances PA = PB for the locus method.

Exam tips: rationalise gradients as fractions; check perpendicularity by multiplying gradients to get −1.

Key results and exam method

Distance between (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂) is √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²). The midpoint is ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2). The gradient is (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁); a vertical line has no gradient and a horizontal line has gradient 0.

Parallel lines have equal gradients. Perpendicular lines have gradients m₁ and m₂ with m₁m₂ = −1, so a line perpendicular to gradient 3/4 has gradient −4/3. The perpendicular bisector of a chord passes through the midpoint of the chord, is perpendicular to it, and always passes through the centre of the circle.

A circle with centre (a, b) and radius r has equation (x − a)² + (y − b)² = r². Expand and compare with x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 to read the centre (−g, −f) and the radius √(g² + f² − c). To test whether a line meets a circle, substitute the line into the circle equation and examine the discriminant.

Exam cue: Sketch the situation first. Many marks are for stating which point is the midpoint, which gradient is perpendicular, and which radius is used.

Worked example: midpoint, distance and the perpendicular bisector

Let A = (2, 5) and B = (8, −1). The midpoint is ((2 + 8)/2, (5 − 1)/2) = (5, 2). The length AB is √((8 − 2)² + (−1 − 5)²) = √(36 + 36) = 6√2.

The gradient of AB is (−1 − 5)/(8 − 2) = −1. The perpendicular bisector has gradient 1 and passes through (5, 2), so its equation is y − 2 = x − 5, which gives y = x − 3. Check that C = (0, −3) lies on it: 0 − 3 = −3, so it does.

Intersection of two lines

To find where y = 2x + 1 meets y = −x + 7, set the two right-hand sides equal: 2x + 1 = −x + 7, so 3x = 6 and x = 2. Substitute back: y = 2(2) + 1 = 5. The lines meet at (2, 5). Always substitute back into the second equation as a check.

Area of a triangle from coordinates

For the triangle with vertices (1, 1), (5, 1) and (3, 4), the base from (1, 1) to (5, 1) has length 4 and the height is the vertical distance from (3, 4) to that base, which is 3. The area is ½ × 4 × 3 = 6 square units.

When the base is not horizontal, use the shoelace method: list the coordinates in order, multiply diagonally, subtract, and halve the absolute value. It works for any triangle, so it is safer than estimating the height.

Parallel and perpendicular lines in exam questions

  • Parallel lines have equal gradients, so 2y = 4x + 1 and y = 2x − 7 are parallel.
  • Perpendicular gradients multiply to −1, so a line perpendicular to gradient 3/4 has gradient −4/3.
  • If a question asks for a line through a given point perpendicular to a line, find the gradient first, then substitute the point into y = mx + c or y − y₁ = m(x − x₁).

Common errors that lose marks

  • Subtracting the coordinates in different orders for the gradient, for example using (−1 − 5)/(2 − 8), which gives the wrong sign.
  • Stating the distance as the difference of the x-coordinates only, rather than using Pythagoras on both differences.
  • Leaving a midpoint as a fraction when it is a whole number, or giving a line equation in a form that is not what the question asks for.

title: Exam technique: Hardware and Logic Gates
content:
### What earns the marks
For device choice, sense-process-store-output each matched earns credit: sensors for capture, processor for decisions, storage for logs, transmitter for remote output. For logic, the gate-by-gate evaluation shown earns method marks; the law named (absorption, De Morgan) earns the final mark. For architecture, each register with its single role earns precision.
### Traps
Error: office peripherals for sensing tasks. Correction: sensing needs sensors. Error: MAR/MDR roles swapped. Correction: address out via MAR, instruction back via MDR. Error: B claimed for A AND (A OR B). Correction: absorption gives A.

title: Superposition — Study Notes
content:
Superposition

Edexcel International A Level Physics — Unit 2 (WPH12), sat at AS.

Principle of superposition

When two or more waves meet at a point, the resultant displacement is the vector sum of the individual displacements. Constructive interference occurs where the waves are in phase; destructive interference occurs where they are in antiphase.

Stationary waves

  • A stationary wave forms when two progressive waves of the same frequency, amplitude and wavelength travel in opposite directions and superpose.
  • Nodes are points of zero amplitude; antinodes are points of maximum amplitude. Adjacent nodes (or antinodes) are separated by λ/2.
  • On a string fixed at both ends, the fundamental frequency is f = v/(2L), so the wavelength is λ = 2L.

Interference

For coherent sources (same frequency and a constant phase difference) with slit separation a and screen distance D, the fringe spacing is Δx = λD/a.

Diffraction

Diffraction is the spreading of a wave after it passes through a gap or round an edge. It is greatest when the gap width is comparable to the wavelength.

Diffraction grating

For a grating with slit spacing d, the angle θ of the nth-order maximum satisfies nλ = d sin θ. A grating with more lines per metre gives a smaller d and larger angles of diffraction.

Worked example: light of wavelength 600 nm passes through two slits 0.30 mm apart, with a screen 1.5 m away. Fringe spacing Δx = λD/a = (600 × 10⁻⁹ × 1.5) ÷ (3.0 × 10⁻⁴) = 3.0 mm.

Exam tips: convert nm and mm to metres before using Δx = λD/a. Check the order n when using a grating. Coherence is a requirement for interference, so state it.

The diffraction grating equation

A diffraction grating has many closely spaced slits. Light of wavelength λ leaves the grating at angle θ to form bright maxima when d sin θ = nλ, where d is the slit spacing and n is the order of the maximum. Each order is sharper and more widely separated than a double slit, because the many slits reinforce the bright positions. The number of orders visible is limited by the condition that sin θ cannot exceed 1.

Exam tip: convert the slit spacing to metres before using the grating equation, and note that the central maximum is n = 0.

Two-source interference: a worked calculation

Two coherent loudspeakers emit sound of frequency 680 Hz. The speed of sound is 340 m s⁻¹, so λ = v/f = 340/680 = 0.50 m. A listener walks along a line parallel to the line joining the speakers. At a point where the path difference is 0.75 m, the waves arrive in antiphase, because 0.75 is an odd multiple of λ/2 (0.25 m). The listener hears a minimum there.

Use the path difference, not the distance from one source, to decide the outcome. Path difference = nλ gives a maximum; path difference = (n + ½)λ gives a minimum. Writing the test as a multiple of λ, and not as a raw distance, is the step examiners look for.

Phase difference and path difference

A phase difference of 360° (2π radians) corresponds to a path difference of one wavelength. A phase difference of 180° corresponds to a path difference of λ/2. In general, phase difference = (path difference / λ) × 360°. Questions often give one and ask for the other, so be ready to convert between them.

  • Coherence needs a constant phase difference, which is why two independent light bulbs do not produce a stable fringe pattern.
  • Monochromatic light is needed for sharp fringes, because each wavelength produces its own fringe spacing and the patterns blur together.
  • Fringe spacing is directly proportional to wavelength and to screen distance, and inversely proportional to slit separation. Halving a doubles the spacing.

Stationary waves: harmonics on a pipe

An open pipe has antinodes at both ends, so its fundamental wavelength is 2L and its harmonics are f, 2f, 3f and so on. A pipe closed at one end has a node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end, so its fundamental wavelength is 4L, and it produces only odd harmonics: f, 3f, 5f.

Example: a pipe of length 0.85 m, open at both ends, with speed of sound 340 m s⁻¹. The fundamental is f = v/(2L) = 340/1.7 = 200 Hz, and the second harmonic is 400 Hz.

Common errors that lose marks

  • Using the slit spacing a where the question gives the slit-to-screen distance D, or the reverse. Read the labels in the diagram before substituting.
  • Stating that a stationary wave transfers energy along the string. It does not: energy is confined between the nodes, and the wave transfers no net energy along the medium.
  • Calling the points between two adjacent nodes "in phase" without qualification. Particles between the same two nodes are in phase; particles either side of a node are in antiphase.
