title: Algebra — Simplifying and Expanding — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Algebra — Simplifying and Expanding

Mathematics — OL. substitution, collecting like terms, expanding brackets, factorising (common factor, quadratics, difference of two squares), algebraic fractions.

  • 1. Substitution
  • 2. Collecting like terms
  • 3. Expanding
  • 4. Factorising
  • 5. Algebraic fractions

How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

### Worked example Expand (x + 3)(x − 5) to get x² − 2x − 15. Check at x = 1: the left side is 4 × (−4) = −16, and the right side is 1 − 2 − 15 = −16. Simplify 3a²b × 4ab³ = 12a³b⁴ by multiplying coefficients and adding the powers of each letter. Factorise 6x² + 9x = 3x(2x + 3).

Key points to remember

To expand a single bracket, multiply every term inside by the term outside, keeping the signs. To expand two brackets, multiply each term of the first by each term of the second, then collect like terms. Factorising reverses this: take out the highest common factor first, then check whether the remaining bracket can be factorised again.

A common error is to drop a sign when the outside term is negative, for example writing -2(x - 3) as -2x - 6 instead of -2x + 6. Substitute a simple value such as x = 1 into both the original and the answer to check your expansion or factorisation.

title: AS Level Mathematics: Circular Measure
content:
AS Level Mathematics: Circular Measure

Radians measure angles by the arc they cut: one radian is the angle subtended when the arc equals the radius. That definition makes every circle formula simpler — arc length becomes s = rθ and sector area becomes ½r²θ, with no 360 in sight. This note builds the topic from zero: the radian definition and conversions, arc length and sector area with derivations, the segment area formula, and the applied problems (belts, pendulums, cones) that combine circular measure with trigonometry. Every worked example keeps the calculator in radian mode, which is the first habit this topic demands.

Radians and conversion

one full turn = 2 π radians = 360 degrees
π radians = 180 degrees

degrees → radians: multiply by π/180
radians → degrees: multiply by 180/π

common values: 30 ° = π/6, 45 ° = π/4,
60 ° = π/3, 90 ° = π/2, 180 ° = π

Worked example. Convert 150° to radians and 2.4 radians to degrees.

150 x π/180 = 5 π/6 = 2.618 rad
2.4 × 180/π = 137.5 °

Why radians: the arc length formula s = rθ only works when θ is in radians. In degrees the same arc is (θ/360) × 2πr — the same quantity, but with the conversion built in.

Arc length and sector area

arc length: s = r θ
sector area: A = (1/2) r² θ
perimeter of a sector: s + 2r

(θ in radians, r in the same length unit as s)

Worked example 1. A sector has radius 8 cm and angle 1.5 radians. Find the arc length and area.

s = r θ = 8 × 1.5 = 12 cm
A = (1/2) r² θ = 0.5 × 64 × 1.5 = 48 cm²

Worked example 2 (perimeter). Find the perimeter of the same sector.

perimeter = arc + 2 radii = 12 + 16 = 28 cm

Worked example 3 (working backwards). A sector of radius 6 cm has area 27 cm². Find the angle in radians and degrees.

27 = (1/2)(36) θ  →  27 = 18 θ  →  θ = 1.5 rad
in degrees: 1.5 × 180/π = 85.9 °

Segment area

segment area = sector area - triangle area
             = (1/2) r² θ - (1/2) r² sin(θ)
             = (1/2) r² (θ - sin θ)

The triangle is formed by the two radii and the chord; its area uses ½r² sin θ (the sine rule area formula). The subtraction is always the same picture: the segment is the sector with the triangle removed.

Worked example. Find the area of the segment cut off by a chord in a circle of radius 10 cm when the angle at the centre is 1.2 radians.

sector area = (1/2)(100)(1.2) = 60 cm²
triangle area = (1/2)(100) sin(1.2) = 50 × 0.932 = 46.6 cm²
segment = 60 - 46.6 = 13.4 cm²

Worked examples: the standard exam types

Worked example 1 (belt around pulleys). Two pulleys of radius 0.20 m and 0.50 m have centres 1.5 m apart. Find the length of the belt around them (straight sections plus arcs).

straight sections: 2 × 1.5 = 3.0 m (approximately, for the
common external tangents when the radii differ the geometry
needs the tangent length, but the exam version usually gives
equal pulleys or the tangent length directly)
equal-pulley version: belt = 2d + 2 π r = 3.0 + 1.26 = 4.26 m

Worked example 2 (pendulum arc). A pendulum of length 0.80 m swings through 0.6 radians. Find the arc length travelled by the bob.

s = r θ = 0.80 × 0.6 = 0.48 m

Worked example 3 (cone sector). A sector of radius 12 cm and angle 2.0 radians is folded into a cone. Find the base radius.

arc length becomes the base circumference:
s = 12 × 2.0 = 24 cm² π r_base = 24  →  r_base = 24/(2 π) = 3.82 cm

Radian trigonometry and small angles

In radian mode, the trigonometric functions take radian inputs, and small-angle approximations become available: for small θ, sin θ ≈ θ and tan θ ≈ θ (with θ in radians), and cos θ ≈ 1 − θ²/2. These approximations underpin pendulum motion and lens theory later, and they appear in exam questions as "show that for small θ ...".

Worked example. Show that for small θ, the arc length and the chord length are approximately equal.

arc = r θ
chord = 2r sin(θ/2) ~ 2r (θ/2) = r θ  for small θ
so chord ~ arc, with the difference of order θ³

Composite shapes with sectors

Exam figures combine sectors with triangles, rectangles and semicircles. The method is always the same: shade the required region, split it into standard pieces, compute each piece with the radian formulas, then add or subtract. Perimeter questions require the boundary only — internal lines are not part of it.

Worked example. A shape is a rectangle 12 cm by 8 cm with a quarter-circle of radius 8 cm removed from one corner. Find the area and perimeter of the remaining shape.

rectangle area = 96 cm²
quarter circle = (1/4) π r² = (1/4)(3.142)(64) = 50.3 cm²
remaining area = 96 - 50.3 = 45.7 cm²

perimeter: straight edges 12 + 4 + 8 = 24 cm (the 4 cm is the
remaining part of the 8 cm side)
plus the arc: quarter circumference = (1/4)(2 π)(8) = 12.6 cm
total perimeter = 36.6 cm

Worked example 2 (two sectors). Two circles of radius 5 cm have centres 8 cm apart. Find the area common to both.

the overlap is two identical segments. In each circle the chord
subtends an angle θ where cos(θ/2) = 4/5, so θ/2 =
0.6435 and θ = 1.287 rad.
segment area = (1/2)(25)(1.287 - sin 1.287)
             = 12.5(1.287 - 0.960) = 4.09 cm²
common area = 2 × 4.09 = 8.18 cm²

Arc, chord and sector in practice

Three quantities are easy to confuse and each has its own formula. Keep them side by side:

QuantityFormula (θ in radians)What it measures
Arc lengths = r θthe curved boundary
Chord lengthc = 2r sin(θ/2)the straight line joining the arc's ends
Sector areaA = (1/2) r^2 θthe pie-slice region

Worked example. A sector has radius 10 cm and angle 1.0 rad. Find the arc length, chord length and the difference between them.

arc = 10 × 1.0 = 10.0 cm
chord = 2 × 10 x sin(0.5) = 20 × 0.4794 = 9.59 cm
difference = 0.41 cm (the arc bulges beyond the chord)

Worked example (angular speed). A wheel of radius 0.35 m turns at 12 rad s⁻¹. Find the linear speed of a point on its rim and the angle turned in 5 s.

v = r ω = 0.35 × 12 = 4.2 m s⁻¹
angle = ω t = 12 × 5 = 60 rad (about 9.5 full turns)

Angular speed links circular measure to mechanics: one radian per second means one radius of arc per second, so the rim speed is rω. Exam questions on rotating wheels, pulleys and centrifuges all reduce to this one relation, and it also explains why a point near the rim of a wheel moves faster than a point near the hub despite both completing a turn in the same time. The same relation converts between the two ways of measuring rotation: revolutions per minute to radians per second is a factor of 2π/60.

The difference is the sagitta-related gap that appears in lens and bridge questions; it grows as the angle grows, which is why the small-angle approximation fails for large sectors.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Convert) Convert 72° to radians. Answer: θ(rad) = θ(°) × π/180°, so 72 × π/180 = 72π/180 = 2π/5 ≈ 1.257 rad.
  2. (Arc) Radius 5 cm, θ = 2.0 rad. Find the arc length. Answer: arc length s = rθ = 5 × 2.0 = 10 cm.
  3. (Sector) Radius 4 cm, θ = 3.0 rad. Find the area. Answer: sector area A = ½r²θ = ½ × 4² × 3.0 = ½ × 16 × 3 = 24 cm².
  4. (Reverse) A sector of radius 9 cm has arc length 13.5 cm. Find θ in radians. Answer: θ = 13.5/9 = 1.5 rad.
  5. (Segment) Radius 6 cm, θ = π/3. Find the segment area. Answer: sector = ½ × 36 × π/3 = 6π ≈ 18.85; triangle = ½ × 36 × sin(π/3) = 18 × 0.866 = 15.59; segment ≈ 3.26 cm².
  6. (Perimeter) Find the perimeter of a sector of radius 7 cm and angle 0.8 rad. Answer: the perimeter is the arc plus two radii: rθ + 2r = 7(0.8) + 14 = 5.6 + 14 = 19.6 cm.
  7. (Cone) A sector of radius 10 cm and angle 1.8 rad forms a cone. Find the base radius and slant height. Answer: arc = 18 cm → base radius 18/(2π) = 2.86 cm; slant height = 10 cm.
  8. (Small angle) Use sin θ ≈ θ to estimate sin(0.10) and compare with the calculator value. Answer: in radians sin θ ≈ θ for small θ, so sin(0.10) ≈ 0.10 against the calculator's 0.0998 — an error of about 0.2%, small because 0.10 rad is small.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Degree mode: every radians formula requires the calculator in RAD mode. A sin of 1.2 in degree mode gives an entirely different number.
  • Mixing units: s = rθ silently assumes r in metres and s in metres; cm and m mixed in one calculation produces a factor-of-100 error.
  • Half forgotten: sector area is ½r²θ, not r²θ. The ½ comes from the triangle comparison.
  • Angle in degrees in the formula: θ must be radians; convert first, and only convert the final answer back if asked.
  • Perimeter includes the radii: the perimeter of a sector is arc + 2r; the arc alone is not the perimeter.
  • Segment triangle: use ½r² sin θ for the triangle, with θ the same central angle; a different angle changes the answer.
  • Exact versus decimal: when the question says "in terms of π", keep π symbolic; converting to 3.14 loses the required form.
  • Small-angle validity: sin θ ≈ θ is good only for small θ (roughly under 0.2 rad); do not apply it to 1.5 rad.

Reading a sector: the one drawing this topic is built on

Every formula in circular measure comes from a single picture, and nearly every mistake comes from mixing up the two curves in it. Draw the sector once, label the radius, the angle and the arc, and the rest is arithmetic on that drawing.

Why the radian exists. An angle in radians is defined as the arc it cuts off divided by the radius:

θ = s / r Key: θ = angle at the centre (rad); s = arc length (m); r = radius (m). The units cancel, so a radian is a pure ratio — one radius-length of arc per radius. That is why a full turn is 2π radians and not 360: the whole circumference is 2πr, so the angle it subtends is 2πr ÷ r = 2π.

Turn the definition around and you get the arc formula, which is the one you actually use:

s = r θ Key: s = arc length (m); r = radius (m); θ = angle at the centre in radians. Using degrees here gives an answer 57 times too large — the single most common error in the topic.

Where ½r²θ comes from. Cut the sector into many thin triangles, each with height r and a sliver of arc as its base. A triangle's area is ½ × base × height, so each sliver is ½ × (rΔθ) × r, and adding them all up gives ½r² × (total θ):

A = ½ r² θ Key: A = area of the sector (m²); r = radius (m); θ = angle at the centre (rad). Notice that the arc is in this formula too — A = ½ r × (rθ) = ½ r s, which is the "thin triangle" statement written algebraically.

Worked example. A sector has radius 9.0 cm and angle 1.2 rad. Find its arc length, its area, and the length of its chord.

arc: s = rθ = 9.0 × 1.2 = 10.8 cm
area: A = ½r²θ = ½ × 81 × 1.2 = 48.6 cm²
chord: the two radii and the chord form an isosceles triangle with sides 9.0, 9.0 and included angle 1.2 rad, so chord = 2 × 9.0 × sin(1.2/2) = 18 × 0.5646 = 10.2 cm

That last line is the step students skip, and it is the step the paper is testing: the chord is a straight line, so it needs trigonometry, not the arc formula. The segment area is then sector minus triangle, A = ½r²(θ − sin θ) = 48.6 − ½ × 81 × sin 1.2 = 48.6 − 37.7 = 10.9 cm².

The perimeter of a sector is three sides, not one. A sector's boundary is the arc plus the two radii: P = 2r + rθ. For the example above, P = 18.0 + 10.8 = 28.8 cm. Answering with 10.8 alone is the most frequently lost mark on this topic, because the word "perimeter" invites you to think of the curve only.

Where marks are lost. Degrees in an equation that needs radians (check the calculator is in RAD mode the moment a question says "radians"). Reading "arc" as "chord". Forgetting the two radii in a perimeter. And using ½r²θ for a segment — the segment is the sector minus the triangle, and the triangle's area is ½r² sin θ.

Deriving the arc and sector formulae from the fraction of a circle

Both formulae come from one idea: a sector is the same fraction of its circle as its angle is of a full turn. Seeing that fraction is more useful than memorising two formulae, because the same reasoning works when a question changes the circle or the angle.

Arc length as a fraction of the circumference

The full circumference is 2πr, and a full turn is 2π radians. A sector of angle θ takes the fraction θ/(2π) of the circle, so s = (θ/2π) × 2πr = rθ. The π cancels, which is why radians make the arc formula so short.

Sector area as a fraction of the disc

The whole disc has area πr². The sector takes the same fraction, so A = (θ/2π) × πr² = ½r²θ. Check it with θ = 2π: ½r²(2π) = πr², the whole disc.

What goes wrong if the angle is in degrees

In degrees a full turn is 360, not 2π, so the fraction becomes θ/360 and the arc is (θ/360) × 2πr. Putting a degree value straight into rθ gives an answer about 57.3 times too large, because one radian is 180/π degrees.

The area formula from integration

Adding thin sectors of area ½r² dθ from 0 to θ gives ∫₀^θ ½r² dθ = ½r²θ. This is the same result reached by integration, and it is the method behind the formula rather than a separate rule.

Recovering the radius and angle from the arc and area

Dividing the area by the arc gives A/s = ½r, so r = 2A/s, and then θ = s/r. A sector with arc 15 cm and area 75 cm² has r = 2 × 75 / 15 = 10 cm and θ = 15/10 = 1.5 rad.

Checking the units of the answer

An arc is a length, so its unit is the radius unit. A sector's area has square units. An area with no square unit usually means the arc formula was used by mistake.

Converting angles and keeping exact values

Most lost marks on this topic are not hard mathematics. They come from an angle left in the wrong unit, or from a decimal where the question wanted π. These habits prevent both.

Degrees to radians, exactly

Multiply degrees by π/180. For example 150° × π/180 = 5π/6. When the question asks for an exact value, keep π in the answer and evaluate it only at the end.

Radians to degrees

Multiply radians by 180/π. For example 1.2 rad × 180/π = 68.75°. As a check, 1 rad is about 57.3°, so 1.2 rad must be a little more than 60°.

Multiples of π in an answer

A sector with r = 6 cm and θ = π/3 has arc length 6 × π/3 = 2π cm, which is about 6.28 cm. Give the exact form 2π cm when the question asks for it, and the decimal only when it asks for a decimal.

Estimating the size of a radian

π/2 ≈ 1.57 is a right angle and π ≈ 3.14 is a straight line. Since 1 rad is about 57°, an angle of 0.5 rad is roughly 29°. A quick estimate like this catches a wrong calculator mode before the answer is written.

Setting the calculator to radians

Check the mode before every trigonometric step. In RAD mode sin(π/6) = 0.5. In DEG mode, sin 0.5236 gives 0.0091, which shows the calculator was not in radians.

Mixed units in one question

A question may give the radius in metres and the angle in degrees. Convert the angle first, find the arc in the radius unit, and then state the answer in the unit the question asks for.

The triangle and the segment inside a sector

A chord joins the two ends of the arc, which turns the sector into a triangle plus a segment. Most questions on this topic that look hard are one of these three shapes in disguise, so identify the shape before choosing a formula.

The triangle inside a sector

The two radii and the chord form an isosceles triangle with sides r, r and included angle θ. Its area is ½r² sin θ, and it is always smaller than the sector.

Segment area as sector minus triangle

The segment between the chord and the arc has area ½r²θ − ½r² sin θ = ½r²(θ − sin θ). With r = 10 cm and θ = 1.2 rad, sin 1.2 = 0.9320, so the segment is ½ × 100 × (1.2 − 0.9320) = 13.4 cm².

Chord length from the cosine rule

The chord satisfies c² = r² + r² − 2r² cos θ, which simplifies to c = 2r sin(θ/2). With r = 10 cm and θ = 1.2 rad, c = 20 sin 0.6 = 11.29 cm.

Choosing the sector, triangle or segment

Read the shaded region before choosing a formula. Bounded by the two radii and the arc, it is the sector. Bounded by the chord and the arc, it is the segment. Bounded by the two radii and the chord, it is the triangle. Choosing the wrong one is the most common cause of a lost method mark.

Angles in the isosceles triangle

The two base angles of the triangle are equal, and each is (π − θ)/2. Those angles are needed when a question asks for an angle at the chord rather than at the centre.

Reflex angles and the major segment

The segment formula ½r²(θ − sin θ) applies for θ less than π. For a reflex angle, find the minor segment using 2π − θ, and subtract it from the whole disc to get the major part.

title: Exam technique: Sequences and Series
content:
### What earns the marks
For AP terms, a + (n-1)d with the brackets evaluated earns the mark; sums use n/2(2a + (n-1)d) quoted. For GP work, the ratio found by division earns one mark and the formula applied earns the next. For sum to infinity, the |r| < 1 check stated earns the method mark.
### Traps
Error: n used instead of (n-1) in terms. Correction: first term needs zero gaps. Error: infinity sums with |r| >= 1. Correction: check convergence first. Error: differentiating S_n for the nth term. Correction: subtract S_{n-1}.

title: A Level Physics: Electric Fields and Capacitance
content:
A Level Physics: Electric Fields and Capacitance

Electric fields are the invisible architecture around every charge: the reason a balloon sticks to a wall, the reason a capacitor can store energy in a camera flash, the reason lightning finds a path. This note builds the topic from zero: what a field is and how field lines encode it, uniform and radial fields with their formulas, Coulomb's law and electric potential, and then capacitance — what it means to store charge, where the energy lives, and how a capacitor discharges exponentially. Every formula is derived or justified, and every calculation type is worked in full.

Electric fields and field lines

A field is a region where a force acts on a suitable object: an electric field exerts a force on a charge. Field lines are the map, drawn with three rules: they point in the direction of the force on a positive charge; their density indicates field strength (closer lines, stronger field); and they never cross. A positive point charge has lines radiating outward; a negative charge has them pointing inward; between two parallel plates the lines are equally spaced and parallel — a uniform field.

  • Uniform field: same magnitude and direction everywhere (between charged plates).
  • Radial field: strength falls with distance, direction along the radius (around a point charge or sphere).

Uniform electric fields

Between parallel plates separated by distance d with potential difference V, the field strength is constant:

E = V/d        (V m⁻¹ or N C⁻¹)

force on a charge in the field: F = Q E
so the acceleration of a particle of mass m: a = QE/m

The analogy: the field is a slope; a charge is a ball. Between parallel plates the slope is uniform, so the ball accelerates steadily — exactly like projectile motion with gravity replaced by QE, which is why electron beams deflect in parabolic arcs between deflection plates.

Worked example. Two plates 4.0 cm apart have a p.d. of 200 V. An electron enters the field.

E = V/d = 200/0.040 = 5000 V m⁻¹
force: F = eE = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ x 5000 = 8.0 × 10⁻¹⁶ N
acceleration: a = F/m_e = 8.0 × 10⁻¹⁶/9.11 × 10⁻³¹
            = 8.8 × 10¹⁴ m s⁻²  (toward the positive plate)

Coulomb's law: force between point charges

F = Q1 Q2 / (4 π ε₀ r²)

ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹ (permittivity of free space)
1/(4 π ε₀) = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²
r = separation between the charges (m)

The law is an inverse-square law like gravitation, but with two crucial differences: the force can attract or repel (like charges repel), and the constant is enormously larger. The 10³⁶ ratio between electric and gravitational forces between two protons is why gravity dominates the cosmos while electricity dominates chemistry.

Worked example. Two charges of +3.0 μC and −2.0 μC are 0.15 m apart in air. Find the force.

F = k Q1 Q2/r² = 8.99 × 10⁹ x (3.0 × 10⁻⁶ x 2.0 × 10⁻⁶)/0.15²
  = 8.99 × 10⁹ x 6.0 × 10⁻¹²/0.0225
  = 0.0539/0.0225 = 2.4 N  (attractive)

Electric field of a point charge

From Coulomb's law, the field strength at distance r from a point charge Q is the force per unit charge:

E = Q / (4 π ε₀ r²)        (N C⁻¹)

Compare with gravitational field strength g = GM/r²: same inverse-square shape, different constant and source. Field strength is a vector (direction is the force on a positive charge); field lines are denser near the charge, matching the 1/r² fall.

Worked example. Find the field strength 0.20 m from a +5.0 nC charge.

E = k Q/r² = 8.99 × 10⁹ x 5.0 × 10⁻⁹/0.040
  = 44.95/0.040 = 1.1 × 10³ N C⁻¹ (away from the charge)

Electric potential

Potential is the potential energy per unit charge at a point in a field, measured relative to infinity:

V = Q / (4 π ε₀ r)        (volts, J C⁻¹)

work done moving a charge: W = Q ΔV
relation to field strength: E = - dV/dr  (field is the
potential gradient; the minus sign means E points toward
decreasing potential)

The potential around a positive charge is positive and falls with distance; around a negative charge it is negative and rises toward zero at infinity. Equipotential surfaces are perpendicular to field lines — no work is done moving a charge along one.

Worked example. Find the potential 0.50 m from a −4.0 nC charge and the work needed to move a +2.0 nC charge there from infinity.

V = k Q/r = 8.99 × 10⁹ x (-4.0 × 10⁻⁹)/0.50 = -71.9 V
W = Q ΔV = 2.0 × 10⁻⁹ x (-71.9 - 0) = -1.4 × 10⁻⁷ J
The negative work means the field does the work - the charges attract.

Capacitors and capacitance

A capacitor stores charge on two conductors separated by an insulator. Its capacitance is the charge stored per volt:

C = Q/V        farad (F); 1 F = 1 C V⁻¹

parallel plates: C = ε₀ epsilon_r A/d

epsilon_r = relative permittivity of the dielectric,
A = plate area (m²), d = plate separation (m)

The analogy: a capacitor is a tank for charge, and capacitance is the tank's width — a wide tank (large C) holds more charge for the same pressure (voltage). The dielectric matters: inserting a material with ε_r > 1 (typically 2–10) multiplies the capacitance because the molecules polarise and reduce the effective field between the plates.

Worked example. A parallel-plate capacitor has plates of area 0.020 m² separated by 0.10 mm of air. Find C.

C = ε₀ A/d = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² x 0.020/1.0 × 10⁻⁴
  = 1.77 × 10⁻¹³/1.0 × 10⁻⁴ = 1.77 × 10⁻⁹ F = 1.8 nF

Combining capacitors reverses the resistor rules: capacitors in parallel add (C = C₁ + C₂ — bigger plates), while in series the reciprocals add (1/C = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂).

Worked example (series). Find the total capacitance of 4.0 μF and 12.0 μF in series.

1/C = 1/4.0 + 1/12.0 = 0.25 + 0.0833 = 0.333
C = 3.0 uF   (always smaller than the smallest capacitor)

Energy stored in a capacitor

Charging a capacitor means pushing charge onto a conductor that already repels it — the voltage rises as charge accumulates, so the work done is the area under the Q–V graph, a triangle:

W = (1/2) Q V = (1/2) C V² = Q²/(2C)

The energy is stored in the electric field between the plates. The Q–V graph is a straight line through the origin for a fixed capacitor; the stored energy is the triangular area beneath it — which is why the factor is ½ and not 1.

Worked example. A 100 μF capacitor is charged to 12 V. Find the energy stored and the charge.

Q = C V = 100 × 10⁻⁶ x 12 = 1.2 × 10⁻³ C
W = (1/2) C V² = 0.5 × 10⁰ x 10⁻⁶ x 144 = 7.2 × 10⁻³ J
  = 7.2 mJ

Discharging a capacitor

A capacitor discharging through a resistor follows an exponential decay, like radioactive decay:

Q = Q0 e^(-t/RC)        V = V⁰ e^(-t/RC)        I = I0 e^(-t/RC)

time constant tau = RC   (seconds)
after one tau: about 37% of the starting value remains
after five tau: under 1% remains (effectively discharged)

Worked example. A 470 μF capacitor charged to 9.0 V discharges through 2.2 kΩ. Find the time constant and the voltage after 2.0 s.

tau = R C = 2200 × 470 × 10⁻⁶ = 1.03 s
V = 9.0 x e^(-2.0/1.03) = 9.0 x e^(-1.94)
  = 9.0 × 0.144 = 1.29 V  (1.3 V, 2 s.f.)

The discharge graph questions are standard: plot ln V against t and the gradient is −1/(RC); the area under a current–time graph is the charge that left the capacitor.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Field strength) Two plates 2.0 cm apart have a p.d. of 100 V. Find E. Answer: E = V/d = 100/0.020 = 5000 V m⁻¹.
  2. (Coulomb) Two +2.0 μC charges are 0.10 m apart. Find the force between them. Answer: F = 8.99 × 10⁹ × (2.0 × 10⁻⁶)²/(0.10)² = 8.99 × 10⁹ × 4.0 × 10⁻¹²/0.010 = 3.6 N, repulsive.
  3. (Potential) Explain why electric potential, unlike field strength, is a scalar. Answer: Potential is energy per unit charge, and energy is a scalar; it has sign (positive near positive charge) but no direction. Field strength is a vector because force has direction.
  4. (Capacitance) A capacitor stores 5.0 mC at 25 V. Find its capacitance. Answer: C = Q/V = 5.0 × 10⁻³/25 = 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ F = 200 μF.
  5. (Dielectric) Explain why inserting a dielectric increases capacitance. Answer: The dielectric's molecules polarise, creating an opposing field that reduces the net field for the same charge; since V = Ed falls while Q stays, C = Q/V rises (multiplied by ε_r).
  6. (Energy) A 2.0 μF capacitor is charged to 50 V. Find the energy stored. Answer: W = ½CV² = ½ × 2.0 × 10⁻⁶ × 2500 = 2.5 × 10⁻³ J = 2.5 mJ.
  7. (Discharge) A 2.0 kΩ resistor discharges a 100 μF capacitor. Find the time constant and the percentage remaining after 0.60 s. Answer: τ = RC = 2000 × 100 × 10⁻⁶ = 0.20 s; after 0.60 s = 3τ, remaining fraction = e⁻³ = 0.050, so 5.0%.
  8. (Graph) State how the gradient of a ln V against t graph relates to the time constant. Answer: ln V = ln V₀ − t/RC, so the gradient is −1/(RC) = −1/τ.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • V/d in centimetres: d must be in metres; 4.0 cm is 0.040 m, and the classic factor-of-100 error follows.
  • Charge units: μC = 10⁻⁶ C, nC = 10⁻⁹ C. Substituting μC as C inflates answers by a million.
  • Sign conventions: field strength is defined by the force on a positive charge; around a negative charge the lines point inward. State directions explicitly.
  • E = V/d only in uniform fields: between plates yes; around a point charge use E = kQ/r².
  • Series/parallel reversal: capacitors behave oppositely to resistors — series gives the reciprocals, parallel simply adds.
  • Energy factor ½: W = ½QV, not QV — the voltage rises during charging, so averaging matters. Forgetting the ½ doubles the answer.
  • Time-constant confusion: τ = RC in seconds means R in Ω and C in farads; the pair must be SI.
  • Discharge graph linearisation: a plot of V against t is a curve; only ln V against t is a straight line whose gradient gives −1/τ.
  • Precision: 2 or 3 s.f. with units (N, V m⁻¹, F, J, s); use ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹ from the data sheet.

title: AS Level Chemistry: Intermolecular Forces
content:
AS Level Chemistry: Intermolecular Forces

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH12, Topic 7 explains the forces that hold molecules to one another, as distinct from the covalent bonds inside them. These forces are far weaker than covalent bonds, yet they decide boiling temperature, volatility, solubility and the anomalous behaviour of water, and they are the reason a molecule with polar bonds is not necessarily a polar molecule. Examiners test the explanation rather than the label, so every answer should name the force, say what causes it, and relate it to the property asked about.

Three types of intermolecular force

All intermolecular forces are electrostatic: they arise from the attraction between regions of opposite charge. They differ in what creates those regions.

ForceOriginTypical strength
London forces (instantaneous dipole–induced dipole)Fluctuating electron density in one molecule induces a dipole in a neighbourVery weak, but increases with the number of electrons
Permanent dipole–permanent dipolePermanently polar bonds and an asymmetric shape leave one end of the molecule slightly positive and the other slightly negativeWeak, roughly 5–20 kJ mol⁻¹
Hydrogen bondingA hydrogen atom bonded to N, O or F is attracted to a lone pair on N, O or F in another moleculeStrongest of the three, up to about 40 kJ mol⁻¹

London forces

Electrons are in constant motion, so at any instant the electron distribution in a molecule may be uneven. That creates an instantaneous dipole, which in turn distorts the electron cloud of a neighbouring molecule and induces a dipole in it. The two dipoles then attract. The effect is present in every substance, including the noble gases and non-polar molecules such as methane, and it is the only intermolecular force in a non-polar substance.

The strength of London forces depends on how easily the electron cloud can be distorted, which is called polarisability. Two factors control it:

  • Number of electrons: more electrons means a larger, more polarisable cloud. Iodine (I₂) is a solid and chlorine (Cl₂) a gas at room temperature for this reason.
  • Surface area and shape: a long unbranched chain has more surface contact between neighbouring molecules than a compact branched isomer with the same formula, so it has stronger London forces.

London forces are also the reason why a noble gas such as argon can be liquefied at low temperature, even though its atoms have no permanent dipole and no bonds to break.

Permanent dipole–dipole interactions

A bond between atoms of different electronegativity is polar: the more electronegative atom carries a partial negative charge, δ−, and the less electronegative atom carries δ+. If the molecule is not symmetrical, the individual bond dipoles do not cancel, and the molecule as a whole has a permanent dipole. Neighbouring molecules then line up with opposite ends together, and the attraction is a permanent dipole–permanent dipole interaction.

Hydrogen chloride, HCl, is polar and its molecules attract this way. Carbon dioxide has two polar C=O bonds, but the molecule is linear and symmetrical, so the dipoles cancel exactly and CO₂ has no permanent dipole; its molecules are held only by London forces. Tetrachloromethane, CCl₄, is also symmetrical and non-polar for the same reason, while trichloromethane, CHCl₃, is polar because the fourth substituent is hydrogen rather than chlorine and the symmetry is broken. Whether a molecule is polar therefore needs two checks: are the bonds polar, and is the shape symmetrical?

Hydrogen bonding

Hydrogen bonding is a particularly strong form of permanent dipole attraction. It occurs only when two conditions are satisfied:

  • A hydrogen atom is covalently bonded to a highly electronegative atom, limited to nitrogen, oxygen or fluorine.
  • A lone pair is available on an N, O or F atom in a neighbouring molecule, which the δ+ hydrogen can approach.

The result is a strong attraction between the δ+ hydrogen and the lone pair, often drawn as a dotted line: O–H···O. The bond is directional, which is why hydrogen bonding produces specific structures rather than a random arrangement.

Water, ammonia and hydrogen fluoride all hydrogen bond:

SubstanceHydrogen-bonding unitNumber of hydrogen bonds per molecule in the liquid
H₂OO–H···OTwo hydrogen atoms and two lone pairs allow an extensive network
NH₃N–H···NThree hydrogen atoms but only one lone pair, so fewer bonds than water
HFF–H···FOne hydrogen atom and three lone pairs; chains of HF molecules

Hydrogen bonding is not the same as a covalent bond to hydrogen. It is an intermolecular attraction, so it is broken when a substance melts or boils, while the O–H covalent bond stays intact. That distinction is worth stating explicitly in an answer.

The anomalous properties of water

Water's properties do not follow the pattern of similar molecules, and hydrogen bonding is the explanation.

High melting and boiling temperatures. Compared with hydrogen sulfide, H₂S, which has a similar formula, water boils about 160 °C higher. The molecules of H₂S are held only by London forces and weak dipole–dipole attractions, whereas each water molecule can hydrogen bond to several neighbours. Breaking those attractions needs far more energy, so the melting and boiling temperatures are unusually high, and water is a liquid at room temperature while H₂S is a gas.

Ice is less dense than liquid water. In ice, each water molecule hydrogen bonds to four neighbours in a regular tetrahedral arrangement, which holds the molecules further apart than in the liquid and leaves open hexagonal spaces. When ice melts, much of that open framework collapses and the molecules pack more closely, so liquid water is denser than ice. This is why ice floats, and why a lake freezes from the top, insulating the water beneath and allowing aquatic life to survive.

Hydrogen bonding also gives water a high surface tension, a high specific heat capacity and a high enthalpy of vaporisation, all of which follow from the energy needed to overcome the network of hydrogen bonds.

Predicting hydrogen bonding

To decide whether a molecule can hydrogen bond, look for an O–H, N–H or F–H group and for a lone pair on O, N or F. Ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH, can hydrogen bond because of its O–H group; ethanal, CH₃CHO, has a C=O bond with lone pairs but no hydrogen attached to an electronegative atom, so it cannot donate a hydrogen bond, although its oxygen can accept one. A molecule such as CH₃F has no H–F bond, so it does not hydrogen bond. Methanol and water mix in all proportions because both can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds, whereas methane, with only C–H bonds, cannot.

Intermolecular forces and physical properties

Boiling temperature is a measure of the energy needed to separate molecules, so it reports the strength of the intermolecular forces, not the strength of the covalent bonds. Four trends are examined.

Boiling temperature of alkanes increases with chain length. Each additional CH₂ group adds electrons and surface area, so the London forces between the molecules become stronger and more energy is needed to separate them. Methane boils at −162 °C, ethane at −89 °C and decane at 174 °C.

Branching lowers the boiling temperature. Pentane and 2,2-dimethylpropane have the same molecular formula, but the branched molecule is more compact. Its molecules have less surface contact, so its London forces are weaker and it boils at 9.5 °C compared with 36 °C for pentane. The same reasoning explains why branched isomers have lower boiling temperatures throughout the alkanes.

Alcohols have higher boiling temperatures than alkanes of similar electron count. Ethanol (46 electrons) boils at 78 °C while propane (26 electrons) boils at −42 °C. The comparison is not quite like for like, but the key point is that ethanol molecules hydrogen bond through the O–H group, while propane molecules have only London forces. The hydrogen bonding more than compensates for the smaller number of electrons.

Boiling temperatures of the hydrogen halides are not a simple trend. HF is the highest because of hydrogen bonding. From HCl to HBr to HI, London forces grow as the number of electrons increases, so the boiling temperatures rise in that order: HCl −85 °C, HBr −67 °C, HI −35 °C. HF, at 20 °C, sits far above the smooth trend, and that outlier is the evidence for hydrogen bonding.

Choosing a solvent

Dissolving depends on the solute particles being separated and surrounded by solvent particles, so the solute–solvent attractions must be comparable to the forces they replace. In practice, like dissolves like.

  • Water dissolves ionic compounds because the polar water molecules attract the ions: the partially negative oxygen surrounds a cation and the partially positive hydrogens surround an anion. This is hydration, and it releases hydration enthalpy that helps to compensate for the lattice enthalpy that must be overcome.
  • Water dissolves simple alcohols such as methanol and ethanol, because the alcohol's O–H group can both donate a hydrogen bond to water and accept one from it. As the hydrocarbon chain grows, the non-polar part becomes a larger fraction of the molecule and solubility falls: ethanol mixes with water in all proportions, but hexan-1-ol is only slightly soluble.
  • Water is a poor solvent for halogenoalkanes and other polar organic molecules such as chloroethane. The molecule has a dipole, so it is attracted to water to some extent, but it has no O–H group and cannot hydrogen bond with water, and its hydrocarbon part cannot interact favourably with the water network. The solute–solvent attractions are too weak to overcome the hydrogen bonding between water molecules.
  • Non-aqueous solvents are used when the solute's intermolecular forces resemble the solvent's. Iodine, a non-polar molecule held by London forces, dissolves in hexane, which is also non-polar; bromine dissolves in cyclohexane for the same reason. Propanone is a useful intermediate case, dissolving both polar and many non-polar substances because it has a polar C=O group and a hydrocarbon part.

A good answer states the force between solvent molecules, the force between solute and solvent, and whether the second is strong enough to replace the first.

Typical mistakes

  • Saying a substance has hydrogen bonds when the hydrogen is bonded to carbon; only N–H, O–H and F–H count.
  • Describing hydrogen bonding as a covalent bond, or claiming that boiling water breaks O–H bonds.
  • Assuming that a molecule with polar bonds must be polar, without checking whether the shape cancels the dipoles.
  • Attributing the trend in alkane boiling temperatures to stronger covalent bonds rather than to stronger London forces.
  • Explaining branching by saying the molecule has fewer electrons; the number of electrons is the same, the surface contact is not.
  • Explaining the lower density of ice as an expansion on freezing without mentioning the open hydrogen-bonded lattice.
  • Describing London forces as "weak covalent forces" or as attractions between permanent dipoles.

Exam-style questions

  1. Explain why the boiling temperature of iodine is higher than that of chlorine. Answer: iodine has more electrons and a larger, more polarisable electron cloud, so the London forces between its molecules are stronger; more energy is needed to separate the molecules.
  2. Explain why 2-methylbutane has a lower boiling temperature than pentane. Answer: both have the molecular formula C5H12 and the same number of electrons. 2-methylbutane is more branched and more compact, so its molecules have less surface area in contact, the London forces between them are weaker, and less energy is needed to separate them.
  3. Explain, in terms of intermolecular forces, why ethanol is soluble in water but chloroethane is not. Answer: ethanol has an O–H group and can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds with water, so the solute–solvent attractions are strong enough to replace the hydrogen bonds between water molecules. Chloroethane is polar but has no O–H group, so it cannot hydrogen bond with water; its attractions to water are too weak to compensate for breaking the water–water hydrogen bonds.
  4. Explain why ice is less dense than liquid water. Answer: in ice each water molecule forms hydrogen bonds to four neighbours in a tetrahedral arrangement, producing an open lattice with spaces between the molecules. When ice melts the lattice collapses and the molecules pack more closely, so the liquid is denser.
  5. Identify the strongest intermolecular force in each of the following and justify your answer: (a) HCl, (b) CH₃OH, (c) CCl₄. Answer: (a) permanent dipole–permanent dipole, because the molecule is polar and has no O–H, N–H or F–H group; (b) hydrogen bonding, because of the O–H group; (c) London forces, because the molecule is symmetrical and the bond dipoles cancel, so it is non-polar.

When revising, practise the three-part answer: name the force, explain what causes it in these molecules, then link it to the property in the question. Move on to Introduction to Kinetics and Equilibria next, where the same molecular picture explains why reactions need collisions with sufficient energy.

Worked example: hydrogen bonding and the energy to boil water

Calculate the energy needed to heat 100 g of water from 25 °C to 100 °C and then to convert it to steam at 100 °C. The specific heat capacity of water is 4.18 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹ and the enthalpy of vaporisation is 40.7 kJ mol⁻¹.

Step 1, heating: q = mcΔT = 100 × 4.18 × 75 = 31 350 J = 31.4 kJ
Step 2, boiling: n(H2O) = 100 / 18.0 = 5.56 mol
                 energy = 5.56 × 40.7 = 226 kJ
Total = 31.4 + 226 = 257 kJ, of which 226 kJ (88 %) is used to separate molecules

The result is the quantitative version of the argument in the text. Almost nine tenths of the energy goes into overcoming intermolecular forces rather than into raising the temperature, and for water those forces are hydrogen bonds. Compare hydrogen sulfide, whose enthalpy of vaporisation is about 18.7 kJ mol⁻¹: the same 5.56 mol would need only 104 kJ to vaporise, which is why water boils 160 °C higher.

Two exam conclusions follow from the same numbers. Steam at 100 °C causes worse burns than water at 100 °C because condensing it releases 40.7 kJ mol⁻¹, and sweating cools the body effectively because each gram of water that evaporates carries away about 2.3 kJ.

title: Exam technique: Mensuration
content:
### What earns the marks
For circles, sectors and arcs, the fraction of 360 stated earns the method mark: write 60/360 before multiplying. For cylinders, cones and spheres, the formula quoted earns a mark on its own, so write Volume = (1/3) pi r squared h even when confident. For compound shapes, split earns marks: compute each part separately, then add or subtract with a clear statement.
### Traps
Error: 2 pi r used for area. Correction: circumference versus area check first. Error: omitting 1/3 for cones and pyramids. Correction: quote the formula every time. Error: using diameter as radius in a semicircle cut-out. Correction: halve the diameter before any pi work. Error: forgetting the square root in a Pythagoras step. Correction: label squared lines as squared.

title: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Sets and Venn Diagrams
content:
Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Sets and Venn Diagrams

Set notation is the language of sorting: it describes which elements belong together, which belong to both groups, and which belong to neither. The IGCSE questions are almost always Venn-diagram problems in disguise — a survey of students, a group of numbers, a club membership — and the marks come from filling every region correctly. This note builds the topic from zero: the notation and symbols, the two-set and three-set Venn diagrams and how to shade them, the counting formulas, and the word-problem method that never misses a region.

Set notation and vocabulary

SymbolMeaningExample
∈is an element of3 ∈ {1, 2, 3}
∉is not an element of5 ∉ {1, 2, 3}
ξ (or U)the universal set — everything under discussionξ = {1, 2, ..., 12}
∅the empty setodd multiples of 2 = ∅
A′the complement of A — everything in ξ not in AA′ = ξ A
A ∪ Bunion — in A or B or both{1,2} ∪ {2,3} = {1,2,3}
A ∩ Bintersection — in both{1,2} ∩ {2,3} = {2}
n(A)the number of elements of An({2, 4, 6}) = 3

Two rules follow directly: A ∩ A′ = ∅ (nothing is both in and out), and A ∪ A′ = ξ (everything is one or the other). Subsets: A ⊂ B means every element of A is also in B. The empty set has no elements, so n(∅) = 0, and it is a subset of every set — a fact worth stating explicitly when a question asks whether ∅ ⊂ A is true.

Two-set Venn diagrams

A two-set diagram divides the universal set into four regions: only A, only B, both, and neither. Filling them from the inside out is the reliable method:

  1. Write the number in the intersection (both) first.
  2. Work outward: only A = n(A) − both; only B = n(B) − both.
  3. Neither = total − (only A + only B + both).

Worked example. In a class of 32, 18 study French, 15 study Spanish, and 7 study both. Find the number studying only French, only Spanish, and neither.

both = 7
only French = 18 - 7 = 11
only Spanish = 15 - 7 = 8
neither = 32 - (11 + 8 + 7) = 32 - 26 = 6

Worked example 2 (reverse). In a group, 20 like tea, 14 like coffee and 5 like neither. Everyone likes at least one of the two? Then find n(tea ∩ coffee).

n(T union C) = 20 + 14 - both
total = 20 + 14 - both + 5 = 39 - both
If the group has 30 people: 30 = 39 - both → both = 9

The inclusion–exclusion formula

n(A union B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A intersection B)

for three sets:
n(A u B u C) = n(A) + n(B) + n(C)
             - n(A n B) - n(A n C) - n(B n C)
             + n(A n B n C)

The subtraction corrects double counting; the final addition corrects the triple-counted centre. Knowing the formula lets you answer "how many in total" questions without a full diagram, but a diagram is still the safer route for word problems.

Worked example. A survey of 50 people: 30 read newspapers, 25 read magazines, 12 read both. How many read at least one?

n(N union M) = 30 + 25 - 12 = 43
neither = 50 - 43 = 7

Three-set Venn diagrams

The three-set diagram has eight regions (counting "none of the three"). The fill order that never fails:

  1. Start with the triple intersection (all three).
  2. Find the "exactly two" regions by subtracting the triple from each pair.
  3. Find the "only one" regions by subtracting the pair and triple totals from each set total.
  4. Find "none" from the grand total.

Worked example. 40 students choose subjects: 20 take Maths, 18 take Physics, 15 take Chemistry; 8 take Maths and Physics, 6 take Maths and Chemistry, 5 take Physics and Chemistry; 3 take all three. Find how many take exactly one subject and how many take none.

triple = 3
exactly M and P = 8 - 3 = 5
exactly M and C = 6 - 3 = 3
exactly P and C = 5 - 3 = 2
only M = 20 - (5 + 3 + 3) = 9
only P = 18 - (5 + 2 + 3) = 8
only C = 15 - (3 + 2 + 3) = 7
exactly one = 9 + 8 + 7 = 24
total counted = 24 + 5 + 3 + 2 + 3 = 37
none = 40 - 37 = 3

Sets of numbers and shading

Questions often use number sets inside the universal set: ξ = {1, 2, ..., 20}, A = multiples of 3, B = multiples of 4. List them, then use the same four regions:

A = {3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18}
B = {4, 8, 12, 16, 20}
A n B = {12}
A u B = {3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 12, 15, 16, 18, 20}
neither = {1, 2, 5, 7, 10, 11, 13, 14, 17, 19}

Shading questions ask for a region described in symbols. Translate the symbols into words first: A′ ∩ B means "not in A, but in B" — the part of B outside A. A ∪ B′ means "in A, or outside B" — everything except the part of B that is not in A.

Listing sets and set-builder notation

Sets can be written in three ways, and questions move between them. The roster method lists the elements: A = {2, 4, 6, 8}. The description method states the rule in words: A is the set of even numbers from 2 to 8. Set-builder notation states the rule symbolically: A = {x : x is an even number, 2 ≤ x ≤ 8} — read as "the set of all x such that x is even and between 2 and 8".

  • Roster for finite sets: list every element once, in braces, separated by commas; order does not matter and repeats are not counted twice.
  • Description for patterns: "multiples of 3 less than 30" is clearer than listing ten numbers.
  • Set-builder for precision: the colon means "such that"; the condition after it does the work.

Worked example. Write the set of odd numbers between 1 and 11 in roster and set-builder form, and find its size.

roster: {3, 5, 7, 9}  (strictly between, so 1 and 11 excluded)
set-builder: {x : x odd, 1 < x < 11}
n(A) = 4

Reading the inequalities is the trap: "between" usually excludes the endpoints, "from ... to ..." usually includes them, and the question's wording decides. When in doubt, list both interpretations and choose the one consistent with the other numbers in the question.

Worked examples: word problems

Worked example. In a hostel of 60 students, 35 play football, 28 play basketball, and 12 play both. How many play neither?

at least one = 35 + 28 - 12 = 51
neither = 60 - 51 = 9

Worked example 2 (with a variable). In a group of 25, x people like both tea and coffee, 12 like tea only and 8 like coffee only. Find x if everyone likes at least one.

12 + 8 + x = 25  →  x = 5

Worked example 3 (conditional language). Of 40 students, 24 study History, 18 study Geography and 6 study neither. How many study both?

at least one = 40 - 6 = 34
34 = 24 + 18 - both  →  both = 42 - 34 = 8

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Notation) ξ = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8}; A = {2, 4, 6, 8}; B = {1, 3, 5, 7}. Find A ∩ B and A ∪ B. Answer: A ∩ B = ∅; A ∪ B = ξ.
  2. (Complement) With A = {2, 4, 6, 8} in ξ above, list A′. Answer: A′ is everything in ξ that is not in A: ξ = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8} and A = {2, 4, 6, 8}, so A′ = {1, 3, 5, 7}.
  3. (Two sets) n(A) = 14, n(B) = 9, n(A ∩ B) = 4. Find n(A ∪ B). Answer: the overlap is counted twice when the sizes are added, so take it off once: n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B) = 14 + 9 − 4 = 19.
  4. (Neither) In a class of 30, 17 like cricket, 12 like tennis and 5 like both. Find the number who like neither. Answer: at least one = 24; neither = 6.
  5. (Three sets) 30 students: 15 like Maths, 12 like Physics, 10 like Chemistry; 5 like Maths and Physics, 4 like Maths and Chemistry, 3 like Physics and Chemistry, 2 like all three. Find the number who like exactly one. Answer: only M = 15 − (3 + 2 + 2) = 8; only P = 12 − (3 + 1 + 2) = 6; only C = 10 − (2 + 1 + 2) = 5; total = 19 (with exactly-two counts 3, 2, 1 and triple 2).
  6. (Shading) Describe the region A′ ∩ B in words. Answer: Elements in B but not in A — the part of B outside A.
  7. (Numbers) ξ = {1, ..., 20}; A = even numbers; B = multiples of 5. Find n(A ∩ B). Answer: A ∩ B holds the numbers that are both even and a multiple of 5, i.e. multiples of 10; up to 20 those are 10 and 20, so n(A ∩ B) = 2.
  8. (Reasoning) Explain why n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) is wrong when A and B overlap. Answer: The elements in both sets are counted twice in n(A) + n(B), so the intersection must be subtracted once: n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B).

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Filling the intersection last: start at the centre. Adding both set totals and forgetting the overlap counts shared elements twice.
  • Forgetting the "neither" region: the universal set includes elements outside all named sets; if the question gives a total, subtract to find them.
  • Confusing ∪ and ∩: union is "or" (everything), intersection is "and" (only the middle). A quick mnemonic: ∪ looks like a cup that holds everything.
  • Shading the wrong side for A′: the complement is everything outside A, including parts of other sets and the region outside them all.
  • Triple intersection double subtraction: when subtracting pairs, remember each pair already includes the triple; subtract the triple from each pair before using them.
  • Reading "only": "only A" means A and nothing else — exclude the overlaps. The word only is a region instruction, not decoration.
  • Notation in answers: list elements with braces and commas; do not write 1, 2, 3 as an unbraced list when the answer is a set.
  • Assuming everyone likes something: unless stated, some may be outside both sets — check whether the total equals the sum of the regions.

The four regions: reading a Venn diagram as a counting grid

A two-set Venn diagram is not a picture of two sets. It is a grid with four cells, and every question about it is answered by putting a number in each cell and adding.

Name the four cells before you write anything. For sets A and B inside a universal set ξ, every element is in exactly one of: only A, both, only B, neither. In the figure that is 7, 5, 9 and 4. The moment all four numbers are on the page, every part of the question is a sum:

n(A) = 7 + 5 = 12 Key: n(A) counts everything inside circle A, including the overlap.
n(A ∩ B) = 5 Key: the intersection — the region inside both circles.
n(A ∪ B) = 7 + 5 + 9 = 21 Key: the union — everything inside at least one circle.
n(ξ) = 21 + 4 = 25 Key: the universal set also counts what is in neither set.

Why the formula has a minus sign. Adding n(A) and n(B) counts the overlap twice — once with each circle — so it has to come back off:

n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B) Key: n(A ∪ B) = elements in at least one set; n(A ∩ B) = elements in both. In the figure, 12 + 14 − 5 = 21, which is exactly the sum of the three inner cells. The subtraction is not a rule to remember; it is the double count being removed.

Worked example. In a class of 30, 18 study French, 15 study Spanish and 6 study both. How many study neither?

French only = 18 − 6 = 12
Spanish only = 15 − 6 = 9
at least one = 12 + 6 + 9 = 27
neither = 30 − 27 = 3

Going the other way — "9 study neither" — is the same arithmetic in reverse, and it is the version that appears when the examiner wants an unknown: if the total is 30 and 9 study neither, then 21 study at least one, and 18 + 15 − x = 21 gives x = 12 studying both. Filling the grid from the overlap outwards always works, because the overlap is the only cell that belongs to both circles.

Where marks are lost. Treating "18 study French" as 18 in the French-only region, which double-counts 6. Forgetting the neither region, so the four numbers do not add to the total. And shading the wrong side for A′ ∩ B: the complement of A is everything outside A, so A′ ∩ B is the B-only region, not the overlap.

title: A Level Physics: Astronomy and Cosmology
content:
A Level Physics: Astronomy and Cosmology

Astronomy is physics at the largest scale: measuring the distance to a star by its brightness, its size by its temperature, and the age of the universe by how fast galaxies recede. This note builds the toolkit from zero: luminosity and the inverse-square law, standard candles (Cepheid variables and Type Ia supernovae) and the distance ladder, stellar radii from Stefan's law, Hubble's law and redshift, and the evidence for the Big Bang. Every calculation is worked in full, because the papers test exactly these three or four formulas.

Brightness, luminosity and the inverse-square law

A star's luminosity L is the total power it radiates (watts). What a telescope receives is intensity (or flux) I — power per unit area at the observer's distance:

I = L/(4 π d²)

I in W m⁻², L in W, d in m
doubling the distance quarters the intensity

The analogy: a light bulb's power is fixed, but the same light spreads over a sphere of radius d — four times the area at twice the distance, so a quarter of the brightness per square metre. This one law underlies every distance measurement in astronomy.

Worked example. A star has luminosity 4.0 × 10²⁶ W. Find its intensity at 10 parsecs (1 pc = 3.09 × 10¹⁶ m).

d = 10 × 3.09 × 10¹⁶ = 3.09 × 10¹⁷ m
I = L/(4 π d²) = 4.0 × 10²⁶/(4 × 3.14 x (3.09 × 10¹⁷)²)
  = 4.0 × 10²⁶/(1.20 × 10³⁶) = 3.3 × 10⁻¹⁰ W m⁻²

Standard candles and the distance ladder

A standard candle is an object whose luminosity is known, so its observed intensity gives its distance by rearranging the inverse-square law. Two are examinable:

  • Cepheid variables: pulsating stars whose period of variation is tightly related to their luminosity (longer period, more luminous). Measuring the period gives L; measuring I gives d. Cepheids calibrated the first rungs of the cosmic distance ladder.
  • Type Ia supernovae: exploding white dwarfs that reach a consistent peak luminosity, bright enough to be seen in distant galaxies; they extended the ladder to cosmological distances and revealed the accelerating expansion.
distance from a standard candle:
d = √(L/(4 π I))

Worked example. A Cepheid has luminosity 1.0 × 10²⁹ W and observed intensity 2.5 × 10⁻¹² W m⁻². Find its distance in parsecs.

d = √(L/(4 π I)) = √(1.0 × 10²⁹/(4 × 3.14 × 2.5 × 10⁻¹²))
  = √(1.0 × 10²⁹/3.14 × 10⁻¹¹) = √(3.18 × 10³⁹)
  = 5.64 × 10¹⁹ m
in parsecs: 5.64 × 10¹⁹/3.09 × 10¹⁶ = 1825 pc
          = 1.8 kpc (2 s.f.)

Stellar radii and Stefan's law

A star radiates approximately as a black body. Stefan's law relates its luminosity to its surface area and absolute temperature:

L = 4 π r² σ T⁴

σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴ (Stefan-Boltzmann constant)
r = stellar radius (m), T = surface temperature (K)

so r = √(L/(4 π σ T⁴))

The fourth power is the headline: doubling a star's temperature multiplies its radiated power per square metre by 16. That is why hot blue stars are vastly more luminous than cooler red ones of similar size — and why a red giant can outshine the Sun despite its low temperature, because its radius is enormous.

Worked example. The Sun has L = 3.8 × 10²⁶ W and T = 5800 K. Find its radius.

r = √(L/(4 π σ T⁴))
T⁴ = (5800)⁴ = 1.13 × 10¹⁵
4 π σ T⁴ = 4 × 3.14 × 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ x 1.13 × 10¹⁵
              = 8.05 × 10⁸
r = √(3.8 × 10²⁶/8.05 × 10⁸) = √(4.72 × 10¹⁷)
  = 6.87 × 10⁸ m  (about 7 × 10⁸ m; the accepted value is 6.96 × 10⁸ m)

Worked example 2 (comparison). A star has the same temperature as the Sun but 100 times its luminosity. Find its radius in solar radii.

L = 4 π r² σ T⁴, same T and σ:
r² proportional to L  →  r = 10 R_sun

Redshift and Hubble's law

Light from distant galaxies is shifted toward longer wavelengths — redshift — because the galaxies are receding. For speeds much less than c:

z = Δλ/λ = v/c     (v << c)

Hubble's law: v = H0 d

H0 = Hubble constant (about 70 km s⁻¹ Mpc-1)
d = distance (Mpc)

Worked example 1. A galaxy's spectral line at 656 nm is observed at 689 nm. Find its recession speed.

Δλ = 689 - 656 = 33 nm
z = 33/656 = 0.0503
v = z c = 0.0503 × 3.0 × 10⁸ = 1.51 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹
  = 1.5 × 10⁴ km s⁻¹

Worked example 2. A galaxy at 100 Mpc recedes at 7000 km s⁻¹. Find H₀ and the Hubble time.

H0 = v/d = 7000/10⁰ = 70 km s⁻¹ Mpc-1
Hubble time = 1/H0:
70 km s⁻¹ Mpc-1 = 70 000/(3.09 × 10²²) s⁻¹ = 2.27 × 10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹
t = 1/H0 = 4.4 × 10¹⁷ s = 1.4 × 10¹⁰ years = 14 billion years

The Big Bang and its evidence

Hubble's law implies that galaxies were once much closer together — the universe expanded from a hot, dense state. Three pieces of evidence are examinable:

  • Redshift of galaxies: nearly all galaxies recede, and recession speed increases with distance — expansion from a common origin.
  • Cosmic microwave background (CMB): a uniform 2.7 K radiation filling the sky — the cooled remnant of the hot early universe, predicted before it was found.
  • Abundance of light elements: the observed ratios of hydrogen, helium and lithium match predictions of Big Bang nucleosynthesis.

The expanding universe has no centre: space itself stretches, so every observer sees distant galaxies receding in all directions. The age estimate 1/H₀ assumes constant expansion; accelerating expansion (dark energy) modifies it, and the measured value is about 13.8 billion years.

The theory makes a further testable claim: the CMB should be an almost perfect black-body spectrum with tiny temperature ripples, and it is — the ripples themselves are the seeds of galaxy formation, and their pattern matches the theory's predictions for the mix of ordinary matter, dark matter and dark energy. That agreement across independent observations is why the Big Bang is accepted as the standard cosmological model rather than a single unexplained measurement.

Worked examples: the standard exam types

Worked example. Two stars have the same radius; star A is twice as hot as star B. Find the ratio of their luminosities.

L = 4 π r² σ T⁴; same r and σ
L_A/L_B = (T_A/T_B)⁴ = 2⁴ = 16
Star A is 16 times more luminous.

Worked example 2. A star's luminosity is 4.0 × 10³⁰ W and its surface temperature 10 000 K. Find its radius and compare it with the Sun's (7.0 × 10⁸ m).

T⁴ = (10⁴)⁴ = 1.0 × 10¹⁶
4 π σ T⁴ = 4 × 3.14 × 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ x 1.0 × 10¹⁶ = 7.12 × 10⁹
r = √(4.0 × 10³⁰/7.12 × 10⁹) = √(5.62 × 10²⁰)
  = 2.37 × 10¹⁰ m
r/R_sun = 2.37 × 10¹⁰/7.0 × 10⁸ = 34 solar radii

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Inverse square) A star at 20 pc has intensity I. What is its intensity at 60 pc? Answer: Three times the distance gives 1/9 of the intensity: I/9.
  2. (Luminosity) Define luminosity and state its unit. Answer: The total power radiated by a star across all wavelengths, measured in watts (W).
  3. (Standard candle) Explain how a Cepheid variable is used to find distance. Answer: Its pulsation period determines its luminosity from the period–luminosity relation; comparing that luminosity with the observed intensity gives d = √(L/4πI).
  4. (Stefan) A star has twice the Sun's radius and half its temperature. Compare luminosities. Answer: L ∝ r²T⁴ → (2)² × (1/2)⁴ = 4 × 1/16 = 1/4: the star is a quarter as luminous.
  5. (Redshift) A line at 500 nm appears at 505 nm. Find v. Answer: z = 5/500 = 0.010; v = 0.010 × 3.0 × 10⁸ = 3.0 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹.
  6. (Hubble) A galaxy at 50 Mpc recedes at 3500 km s⁻¹. Find H₀. Answer: H₀ = 3500/50 = 70 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹.
  7. (Age) Estimate the age of the universe from H₀ = 70 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹. Answer: t = 1/H₀ ≈ 14 billion years (with unit conversions: 70 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹ = 2.27 × 10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹).
  8. (Big Bang evidence) State two observations supporting the Big Bang. Answer: The redshift–distance relation (Hubble's law) and the cosmic microwave background; the light-element abundances are a third.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Parsecs versus metres: convert before substituting; 1 pc = 3.09 × 10¹⁶ m, 1 Mpc = 3.09 × 10²² m, 1 AU = 1.50 × 10¹¹ m.
  • Luminosity versus intensity: L is the star's total power; I is what arrives per square metre. The inverse-square law connects them and d must be in metres.
  • T⁴ not T: Stefan's law is a fourth power — doubling temperature multiplies luminosity by 16, not 2. Most arithmetic errors here are exponent slips.
  • Kelvin: surface temperatures in Stefan's law must be absolute; a temperature given in °C needs +273 first.
  • Redshift approximation: z = v/c holds for v ≪ c; at large redshifts the relativistic formula is needed. State the assumption.
  • H₀ units: km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹ — mismatched units in 1/H₀ give absurd ages. Convert km to m and Mpc to m.
  • Hubble time is an estimate: 1/H₀ assumes constant expansion; note the acceleration caveat when discussing the age.
  • Centre of the universe: the Big Bang happened everywhere — there is no centre or edge; expansion stretches space between galaxies.
  • Precision: 2 or 3 s.f. with units (W, W m⁻², m, km s⁻¹, years); the data sheet supplies σ, c and H₀.

title: IGCSE Chemistry (OxfordAQA): Rate and Extent of Chemical Change
content:
The Rate and Extent of Chemical Change

This topic holds two questions that look alike and are not. The first is how fast a reaction goes — the rate — which is measured by how quickly a reactant is used up or a product appears. The second is how far it goes — the extent — which for a reversible reaction is decided by where the equilibrium sits. A catalyst changes the first and not the second, a temperature change usually changes both, and an exam that asks about one is testing whether you can tell them apart. The second half of the topic applies the equilibrium idea to the two industrial processes the specification names, then closes with redox, which is the electron bookkeeping underneath displacement, extraction and corrosion.

1. What a rate is, and how it is measured

The rate of a reaction is the change in the amount of a reactant or product per unit time. Anything that can be measured as the reaction proceeds can be turned into a rate, so the practical you are given decides the measurement rather than the other way round.

  • Volume of gas collected in a gas syringe or over water, read against a stopwatch. Good for metal plus acid, or carbonate plus acid.
  • Loss in mass on a balance, when a gas escapes. Good for marble chips plus acid, where carbon dioxide leaves.
  • Time to a visible change, such as the cross disappearing behind precipitated sulfur, measured by looking down through the flask.
  • Colour change measured with a colorimeter, which turns "it went paler" into a number.

The rate is fastest at the start and slows as the reaction proceeds, because the reactants are being used up and their concentration falls. That is why a rate graph curves rather than running straight, and why the tangent at the start gives the initial rate.

2. Collision theory: why any factor works

Particles react only when they collide, and only when they collide with at least the activation energy — the minimum energy needed to break the bonds that must break. Every factor in this topic changes one of those two things: how often collisions happen, or what fraction of them carry enough energy.

  • More frequent collisions come from crowding the particles together: higher concentration, higher pressure, or a larger surface area.
  • More energetic collisions come from higher temperature, which gives the particles more kinetic energy, so a larger fraction of collisions exceeds the activation energy.
  • A catalyst does neither: it provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy, so a larger fraction of the existing collisions is now sufficient.

Notice that a temperature rise does both — particles move faster, so they collide more often, and each collision is more energetic. The second effect is much larger, which is why "more collisions" alone is an incomplete answer when the factor is temperature.

3. Concentration and pressure

Increasing the concentration of a solution means more particles of the reactant in the same volume, so collisions between reactant particles are more frequent and the rate rises. Increasing the pressure of a gas does the same thing by squeezing the same number of particles into a smaller volume. Neither changes the activation energy, and neither changes how much product you eventually get — only how quickly you get it.

A common exam version gives you a graph and asks you to compare two curves. Say which is steeper and why, and then say that both level off at the same height, because the same amount of reactant was used in each case.

4. Surface area

A reaction between a solid and a solution can only happen at the surface of the solid, so breaking the solid into smaller pieces exposes more surface for the same mass and the rate rises. Powdered calcium carbonate reacts faster than marble chips of the same mass, and the total volume of gas collected is unchanged.

  • Same mass, more surface: the rate increases because more particles are available to collide.
  • Same mass, same product: the final volume of gas or mass of product is identical, so the two curves meet at the same level.
  • Powder is not always better: in a school practical a fine powder can froth over or block a filter, which is why the method specifies chips even though the powder is faster.

5. Catalysts

A catalyst increases the rate of a reaction without being used up, by lowering the activation energy. It is not a reactant, it does not appear in the balanced equation, and it is recovered chemically unchanged at the end — which is why a catalyst can be reused indefinitely and why only a small amount is needed.

The effect on a rate graph is specific and examinable: the catalysed curve is steeper and levels off sooner, but it reaches exactly the same final amount, because a catalyst changes the rate and not the yield. Enzymes are biological catalysts, and they are specific — one enzyme catalyses one reaction — which is the usual link question into Biology.

6. Worked example: calculating a rate

Magnesium ribbon is added to excess dilute hydrochloric acid and the hydrogen is collected in a gas syringe. After 24 s, 72 cm³ of gas has been collected. Calculate the mean rate of reaction over that time.

rate = volume ÷ time = 72 cm³ ÷ 24 s = 3.0 cm³/s

Key: rate = the mean rate of reaction (cm³/s); volume = the volume of gas collected (cm³); time = the time taken (s).

The word "mean" matters: this is the average over the whole 24 s, and the instantaneous rate at the start was higher. If the same experiment were repeated with powder instead of ribbon, the mean rate over the first 24 s would be larger, but the total volume collected when the reaction finished would be the same.

A second form appears when the measurement is a mass loss: if a flask loses 1.20 g in 30 s, the mean rate is 1.20 g ÷ 30 s = 0.040 g/s. The units always carry the answer — a rate with no unit, or with the wrong one, loses a mark.

7. Reversible reactions and dynamic equilibrium

Some reactions can go both ways. When the forward and reverse reactions happen in the same container, the mixture eventually reaches a state where both are still occurring but at the same rate, so the amounts of reactants and products stop changing. That state is a dynamic equilibrium, and "dynamic" is the word that earns the mark: the reactions have not stopped.

Two conditions are needed for an equilibrium to be reached: the reaction must be reversible, and it must take place in a closed system so nothing escapes. If a gas is allowed to leave, the reverse reaction cannot keep up and there is no equilibrium.

At equilibrium the concentrations are constant, not equal. It is entirely normal for a mixture to be mostly reactants, or mostly products, and the position of equilibrium describes which.

8. Factors affecting equilibrium

Le Chatelier's principle says that if a change is made to a system at equilibrium, the position of equilibrium shifts to oppose that change. It tells you the direction of the shift, and the exam usually then asks what happens to the yield. The factors that matter are concentration, pressure and temperature.

  • Concentration. Adding more of a reactant shifts the equilibrium to the right, using it up. Removing a product as it forms also shifts it to the right.
  • Pressure. Increasing pressure shifts the equilibrium towards the side with fewer gas molecules, because that reduces the pressure. If both sides have the same number of gas molecules, pressure has no effect.
  • Temperature. Raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium in the endothermic direction, absorbing the extra heat. Lowering it shifts it in the exothermic direction.
  • Catalyst. A catalyst has no effect on the position of equilibrium at all. It reaches the same equilibrium sooner, which is a rate effect and not an extent effect.

Count the gas molecules before you answer a pressure question, and check the sign of ΔH before you answer a temperature question. Both are one line of working that decides the answer.

9. The Haber process: making ammonia

Ammonia is made from nitrogen from the air and hydrogen from natural gas, over an iron catalyst. The reaction is reversible and exothermic in the forward direction.

N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃   ΔH = −92 kJ/mol

Key: ΔH = the enthalpy change for the forward reaction (kJ/mol); ⇌ = the reaction is reversible.

Four gas molecules on the left become two on the right, so a high pressure shifts the equilibrium to the right and increases the yield. The forward reaction is exothermic, so a low temperature would also increase the yield — but a low temperature makes the reaction far too slow to be useful. The compromise is about 450 °C and 200 atmospheres with an iron catalyst: the temperature is a rate compromise, the pressure is a yield choice, and the catalyst recovers the rate that the temperature costs.

The ammonia is removed by cooling it to a liquid and taking it out of the mixture, which pulls the equilibrium further to the right because the product is being removed. That is the industrial version of the concentration rule above.

10. The Contact process: making sulfuric acid

Sulfur is burned to sulfur dioxide, the dioxide is oxidised to sulfur trioxide over a vanadium(V) oxide catalyst, and the trioxide is dissolved in concentrated sulfuric acid to make more acid.

2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃   ΔH = −197 kJ/mol

Key: ΔH = the enthalpy change for the forward reaction (kJ/mol); ⇌ = the reaction is reversible; V₂O₅ is the catalyst.

This is the same compromise as the Haber process. Three gas molecules become two, so high pressure raises the yield; the forward reaction is exothermic, so high temperature lowers the yield but raises the rate. The process runs at about 450 °C and 1 to 2 atmospheres, with the pressure kept modest because the yield is already high at ordinary pressure and compressing gas is expensive.

The sulfur trioxide is not added to water directly, because the reaction is violent and produces a fine mist of acid that is hard to condense. It is dissolved in concentrated sulfuric acid instead, which is a practical detail the exam does ask about.

11. Redox: oxidation, reduction and oxidation states

Oxidation is the loss of electrons, and reduction is the gain of electrons — remember them as OIL RIG. They always happen together, which is why the whole class of reactions is called redox: whatever loses electrons is oxidised, and whatever gains them is reduced.

  • Oxidising agent takes electrons from something else, so it is itself reduced. Potassium manganate(VII) and chlorine are common examples.
  • Reducing agent gives electrons to something else, so it is itself oxidised. Carbon and hydrogen are common examples.

For simple ions, oxidation state is just the charge: Na⁺ is +1, Cl⁻ is −1, Fe³⁺ is +3. For an element, it is 0. In a compound, hydrogen is usually +1, oxygen is usually −2, and the states of everything else must add up to the overall charge. That bookkeeping identifies what has been oxidised even when no electrons appear in the equation.

12. Worked example: oxidation states and half equations

Find the oxidation state of sulfur in sulfuric acid, H₂SO₄, and of manganese in potassium manganate(VII), KMnO₄.

For H₂SO₄: 2(+1) + x + 4(−2) = 0, so x = 6 and sulfur is +6. For KMnO₄: (+1) + x + 4(−2) = 0, so x = 7 and manganese is +7.

Key: x = the unknown oxidation state; the numbers in brackets are the known states of hydrogen (+1), oxygen (−2) and potassium (+1); the total equals the overall charge of the species, which is 0 for a neutral compound.

Now the electron half-equations for iron displacing copper from copper(II) sulfate. The iron atom loses two electrons and the copper ion gains them:

Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻ (oxidation)   and   Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu (reduction), giving Fe + Cu²⁺ → Fe²⁺ + Cu.

Key: e⁻ = an electron; the two half-equations must transfer the same number of electrons, which is why no coefficients are needed here.

The blue colour of the solution fades and a pink-brown solid appears, because copper(II) ions are blue and iron(II) ions are pale green. That observation plus the two half-equations is a full-mark answer.

13. Typical mistakes

  • Saying a catalyst increases the yield. It increases the rate and leaves the equilibrium position alone.
  • Explaining a temperature rise only as "more collisions". The dominant effect is that a larger fraction of collisions now exceeds the activation energy.
  • Answering a pressure question without counting gas molecules, or a temperature question without knowing which direction is exothermic.
  • Saying the reaction has stopped at equilibrium. Both directions are still running at equal rates.
  • Calling oxidation "gain of oxygen" as if that were the definition. It works for some reactions, but the electron definition is the one the specification uses and the one that covers all of them.
  • Mixing up the agent with what happens to it: the oxidising agent is reduced, and the reducing agent is oxidised.
  • Giving a rate with no unit, or with the unit of the quantity rather than of the rate.

14. Exam-style questions

  1. Explain why increasing the temperature increases the rate of a reaction. Answer: The particles have more kinetic energy, so they move faster and collide more often, and a much larger fraction of those collisions has at least the activation energy, so more collisions are successful.
  2. Marble chips and powdered calcium carbonate of the same mass are added to separate samples of excess acid. State two differences between the rate curves. Answer: The powdered sample's curve is steeper and levels off sooner, but both curves reach the same final volume of gas.
  3. Explain the effect of increasing the pressure on the equilibrium N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃. Answer: There are four gas molecules on the left and two on the right, so increasing the pressure shifts the equilibrium to the right, towards the fewer molecules, and the yield of ammonia increases.
  4. Explain why the Haber process is not run at the temperature that would give the highest yield. Answer: The forward reaction is exothermic, so a low temperature would shift the equilibrium to the right and increase the yield, but the rate would be far too slow, so a compromise of about 450 °C is used with an iron catalyst.
  5. State the catalyst used in the Contact process and write the equation for the reaction it catalyses. Answer: Vanadium(V) oxide, V₂O₅: 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃.
  6. Zinc is added to copper(II) sulfate solution. Write the two half-equations and say which species is oxidised. Answer: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ and Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu. Zinc is oxidised because it loses electrons.
  7. Calculate the oxidation state of chromium in potassium dichromate, K₂Cr₂O₇. Answer: 2(+1) + 2x + 7(−2) = 0, so 2x = 12 and x = +6.
  8. 0.80 g of magnesium reacts with excess acid and 640 cm³ of hydrogen is collected in 40 s. Calculate the mean rate. Answer: rate = 640 ÷ 40 = 16 cm³/s.

15. Revision checklist

  • I can describe three ways to measure a rate and say which suits which reaction.
  • I can explain every factor using collision theory, distinguishing frequency from energy.
  • I can calculate a mean rate and give its unit.
  • I can define dynamic equilibrium and say why a closed system is needed.
  • I can predict the effect of concentration, pressure, temperature and a catalyst on an equilibrium.
  • I can describe the Haber and Contact processes with their equations, conditions and catalysts.
  • I can explain each industrial compromise in terms of rate against yield.
  • I can assign oxidation states and write half-equations for a redox reaction.
  • I can name the oxidising and reducing agent in a reaction and say what happens to each.

title: A Level Mathematics: The Binomial Distribution
content:
A Level Mathematics: The Binomial Distribution

A binomial distribution counts successes in a fixed number of independent trials, each with the same probability of success.
