Coins, multiple-choice guesses, defective items in a sample and free throws all fit the same template, and once a problem is recognised as binomial the calculation is a formula plus a cumulative table. This note builds the distribution from its four conditions, derives the formula from counting, and then uses it for the two things exams actually ask: probabilities and hypothesis tests.

The four conditions

Before writing X ~ B(n, p) you must be able to name the conditions, because most exam questions include a part asking whether the model is appropriate. The conditions are not red tape: drop any one and the formula is simply wrong.

1. a fixed number of trials n
2. each trial has exactly two outcomes (success / failure)
3. the probability of success p is constant for every trial
4. the trials are independent
then X = number of successes has X ~ B(n, p)

Worked example (checking the model). A bag holds 5 red and 15 blue counters. Four counters are taken without replacement. Is the number of red counters binomial?

n = 4 is fixed and each draw is red or not red
but p changes: 5/20, then 5/19 if a red was taken, ...
the trials are not independent, so NOT binomial (it is hypergeometric)

Taking with replacement would fix it: p stays 0.25 on every draw.

The formula, and where it comes from

The probability of a particular sequence of r successes and n − r failures is p^r (1−p)^(n−r), because independence lets you multiply. The number of such sequences is the number of ways to choose which r trials succeed, which is nCr. Multiplying gives the formula.

P(X = r) = nCr p^r (1 - p)^(n - r)
the nCr counts arrangements; the powers give the probability of one arrangement

Worked example. X ~ B(10, 0.3). Find P(X = 3).

P = 10C3 (0.3)³ (0.7)⁷
= 120 × 0.027 × 0.08235
= 120 × 0.002223 = 0.2668

Worked example 2 (a single trial count). A fair die is rolled 8 times. Find the probability of exactly two sixes.

X ~ B(8, 1/6)
P(X = 2) = 8C2 (1/6)² (5/6)⁶ = 28 × 0.02778 × 0.3349 = 0.2605

Worked example 3 (why nCr appears). For n = 3 and r = 1, list the sequences and confirm the coefficient.

sequences: SFF, FSF, FFS - three of them
each has probability p(1-p)²
so P(X = 1) = 3p(1-p)², and 3C1 = 3

Cumulative probabilities

Questions almost always ask for a range, not a single value, and the cumulative distribution is what the calculator or the tables supply. The skill is rewriting the question into the form the table gives you.

P(X <= r) is tabulated directly
P(X >= r) = 1 - P(X <= r - 1)
P(X < r)  = P(X <= r - 1)
P(a <= X <= b) = P(X <= b) - P(X <= a - 1)
P(X = r) = P(X <= r) - P(X <= r - 1)

Worked example. X ~ B(20, 0.4). Find P(X ≥ 8).

P(X >= 8) = 1 - P(X <= 7)
= 1 - 0.4159
= 0.5841

Worked example 2 (between). For the same X, find P(5 ≤ X ≤ 10).

= P(X <= 10) - P(X <= 4)
= 0.8725 - 0.0510
= 0.8215

Worked example 3 (the strict inequality trap). For the same X, find P(X > 6).

P(X > 6) = 1 - P(X <= 6) = 1 - 0.2500 = 0.7500
note this is different from P(X >= 6) = 1 - P(X <= 5) = 0.8746

Mean and variance

The binomial has the simplest mean and variance in the syllabus, and they are worth knowing both forwards and backwards: a question can give the mean and variance and ask for n and p.

E(X) = np
Var(X) = np(1 - p)
standard deviation = √(np(1-p))

Worked example. X ~ B(50, 0.2). Find the mean and standard deviation.

mean = 50 × 0.2 = 10
variance = 10 × 0.8 = 8
sd = 2.828

Worked example 2 (backwards). A binomial variable has mean 12 and variance 9. Find n and p.

np = 12;  np(1-p) = 9
divide: 1 - p = 9/12 = 0.75  →  p = 0.25
then n = 12/0.25 = 48

Hypothesis testing with the binomial

A one-tailed test asks whether p has increased or decreased; the test statistic is the observed count, and the p-value is the probability of a result at least as extreme in the direction of the alternative.

H0: p = p0      H1: p > p0 (or p < p0)
X ~ B(n, p0) under H0
p-value = P(X >= observed) or P(X <= observed)
compare with the significance level; reject H0 if p-value <= alpha

Worked example. A coin is tossed 20 times and lands heads 15 times. Test at the 5% level whether the coin is biased towards heads.

H0: p = 0.5;  H1: p > 0.5
X ~ B(20, 0.5)
P(X >= 15) = 1 - P(X <= 14) = 1 - 0.9793 = 0.0207
0.0207 < 0.05, so reject H0
there is evidence at the 5% level that the coin favours heads

Worked example 2 (two-tailed). The same data tested two-tailed.

double the smaller tail: 2 × 0.0207 = 0.0414
0.0414 < 0.05, so still reject H0 at the 5% level

Worked example 3 (critical region). For X ~ B(20, 0.5), find the critical region for a 5% one-tailed test of p > 0.5.

P(X >= 14) = 0.0577 (above 0.05)
P(X >= 15) = 0.0207 (below 0.05)
critical region: X >= 15

Note that the critical region is chosen so the probability of a Type I error is at most 5%, which is why 14 is excluded even though it is close.

When the model breaks down

Examiners like the question that asks why a binomial model is only an approximation. The usual culprits are dependence, a varying probability, or a fixed sample drawn without replacement from a small population.

SituationProblemEffect
sampling without replacementtrials not independentp drifts; use the hypergeometric instead
clustered data (pupils in classes)responses correlatedvariance underestimated
probability varies between trialsp not constantformula invalid
large n, p near 0.5computation heavynormal approximation is reasonable

Worked example (normal approximation). X ~ B(200, 0.4). Use a normal approximation to estimate P(X ≤ 70).

mean = 80;  variance = 200 × 0.4 × 0.6 = 48;  sd = 6.928
continuity correction: X <= 70 becomes X < 70.5
z = (70.5 - 80)/6.928 = -1.371
P(Z < -1.371) = 0.0852

The continuity correction is compulsory: a discrete count needs a half-unit boundary before it can be treated as continuous.

Expected frequencies and the shape of the distribution

A binomial distribution is not symmetric unless p = 0.5, and that shape decides which tail an exam question is fishing in. The most likely value — the mode — is the integer near (n + 1)p, and expected frequency multiplies the probability by the number of samples taken. Both are quick marks that are frequently missed because students jump straight to the formula.

mode is near (n + 1)p, checked by comparing consecutive probabilities
expected number in a sample of size N = N x P(X = r)

Worked example. X ~ B(12, 0.3). Find the most likely value of X and the expected number of 3s in 500 independent observations.

(n + 1)p = 13 × 0.3 = 3.9, so check r = 3 and r = 4
P(X = 3) = 220 × 0.027 × 0.1176 = 0.2397
P(X = 4) = 495 × 0.0081 × 0.1681 = 0.2311
mode = 3
expected number of 3s = 500 × 0.2397 = 120 (to the nearest whole)

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Model) State the distribution for the number of sixes in 12 rolls of a fair die. Answer: X ~ B(n, p) with n = 12 rolls and p = 1/6 the chance of a six on each, so X ~ B(12, 1/6).
  2. (Single value) X ~ B(8, 0.25): find P(X = 2). Answer: P(X = 2) = ⁸C₂ (0.25)² (0.75)⁶ = 28 × 0.0625 × 0.1780 = 0.3115.
  3. (Cumulative) X ~ B(15, 0.3): find P(X ≤ 4). Answer: P(X ≤ 4) = Σₖ₌₀⁴ ¹⁵Cₖ (0.3)ᵏ (0.7)¹⁵⁻ᵏ = 0.5155 from cumulative binomial tables.
  4. (Complement) Same X: find P(X ≥ 3). Answer: P(X ≥ 3) = 1 − P(X ≤ 2) = 1 − 0.2969 = 0.7031 — the complement, because the tables give the lower tail only.
  5. (Mean) X ~ B(40, 0.35): find E(X) and Var(X). Answer: 14 and 9.1.
  6. (Backwards) Mean 18, variance 12: find n and p. Answer: mean np = 18 and variance np(1 − p) = 12; dividing, 1 − p = 12/18 = 2/3, so p = 1/3 and n = 18 ÷ (1/3) = 54.
  7. (Test) 12 of 20 seeds germinate; test p = 0.5 against p < 0.5 at 5%. Answer: H₀: p = 0.5 against H₁: p < 0.5; under H₀, X ~ B(20, 0.5) and P(X ≤ 12) = 0.8684, which is far above 0.05, so there is no evidence to reject H₀.
  8. (Critical region) X ~ B(10, 0.2): find the 5% critical region for p < 0.2. Answer: the smallest possible tail is P(X ≤ 0) = (0.8)¹⁰ = 0.1074, which already exceeds 0.05, so no critical region exists at the 5% level for this n.
  9. (Approximation) X ~ B(100, 0.5): approximate P(X ≥ 60). Answer: μ = np = 50 and σ = √(np(1 − p)) = √25 = 5; with the continuity correction z = (59.5 − 50)/5 = 1.9, so P(X ≥ 60) ≈ P(Z > 1.9) = 0.0287.
  10. (Assumption) Give one reason a binomial model may fail for defects in boxes of 20. Answer: defects may cluster, so trials are not independent.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Forgetting nCr: the coefficient counts arrangements; without it the answer is the probability of one specific sequence.
  • nCr on the wrong factor: it is p^r (1−p)^(n−r), with the success probability raised to the number of successes.
  • Inequality direction: P(X ≥ 8) uses 1 − P(X ≤ 7), not 1 − P(X ≤ 8).
  • Variance confused with standard deviation: np(1−p) is the variance; the test and the normal approximation need the square root.
  • Continuity correction omitted: any normal approximation to a discrete count needs the half-unit adjustment.
  • One-tailed evidence read as two: halving or doubling the tail without checking the alternative direction is a silent error.
  • Independence asserted, not checked: sampling without replacement from a small population breaks the model, and the question usually invites you to say so.
  • p-value compared with the wrong threshold: the significance level is given as a percentage; 5% means 0.05, not 5.

Recognising a binomial situation in context

Most binomial marks are lost before any arithmetic starts, because the question was not identified as binomial. The subsections below give a checklist for reading a question and writing the model in the standard form X ~ B(n, p) before you calculate anything.

Writing the model in the form X ~ B(n, p)

Once you decide a situation is binomial, state the model in full: X ~ B(n, p), where X is the number of successes, n is the number of trials and p is the probability of a success on each trial. Define X in words in your answer, for example “X is the number of defective bulbs in a box of 20”. A model with no definition of X loses the communication mark even when the probabilities are right.

Identifying the number of trials, n

The value of n is the fixed number of times the experiment is repeated: the number of bulbs tested, the number of patients treated, or the number of games played. Read the question for the phrase that fixes it, such as “of 20 bulbs chosen at random”. If the question keeps going until a result occurs, the number of trials is not fixed and the binomial model does not apply directly.

Identifying the probability of success, p

The value of p is the probability of the outcome you have chosen to call a success on one trial. It must stay the same for every trial. A fair coin gives p = 0.5, and a bag where 15% of items are faulty gives p = 0.15 for each item drawn with replacement. If the question gives a percentage, convert it to a decimal before you use it in any formula.

Checking for fixed trials

The number of trials must be decided before the experiment starts. Counting the number of successes in a fixed sample is binomial, whereas recording how many trials it takes to get the first success is not. A question about the number of heads in ten tosses is binomial; a question about how many tosses are needed for the first head is a different model. Make the fixed-n check before any other check.

Checking for independent trials

Each trial must not affect the next. Independence is what allows you to multiply the probabilities of several outcomes together, and it is the assumption most often ignored. Drawing items with replacement keeps p constant, and that is what the model needs. Drawing without replacement changes p after each draw, so the binomial model is only an approximation when the sample is small compared with the population.

Worked identification

A survey finds that 30% of adults own a bicycle. Twelve adults are chosen at random from a large town and asked whether they own one. Let X be the number who own a bicycle. Here n = 12, p = 0.3 and the answer is X ~ B(12, 0.3). The population is large, so the probability for each adult stays close to 0.3 and the model is a reasonable one to use. State that assumption, because a marker looks for it.

Probabilities of at least one, and of more than r

Questions that ask for “at least” or “more than” are the ones where the complement saves the most time. The subsections set out the choice between a direct sum and the complement, and the checks that stop an off-by-one error.

Probability of at least one success

“At least one” is the complement of “none”, so P(X ≥ 1) = 1 − P(X = 0) = 1 − qⁿ, where q = 1 − p. For X ~ B(5, 0.2), P(X ≥ 1) = 1 − 0.8⁵ = 1 − 0.32768 = 0.672 to 3 significant figures. Adding the probabilities of X = 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 gives the same answer but takes five calculations instead of one.

Probability of more than r successes

“More than 3” means 4 or more, so P(X > 3) = 1 − P(X ≤ 3). For X ~ B(10, 0.3), P(X ≤ 3) = 0.6496 to 4 decimal places, so P(X > 3) = 0.3504. The number 3 is included in the part you subtract from 1; forgetting that is the typical error on “more than” questions.

Choosing between a direct sum and the complement

Use the complement when the part you do not want is short: “at least one”, “at most one but not zero” and similar phrases. Use a direct sum when the wanted region has only a few terms, such as P(X = 2) + P(X = 3). With a calculator table of cumulative probabilities, most “at most” and “at least” questions reduce to one lookup and one subtraction.

Probability of exactly r on a calculator

For X ~ B(n, p), P(X = r) = ⁿCᵣ pʳ qⁿ⁻ʳ. The combination ⁿCᵣ counts the ways the r successes can be arranged among n trials. For X ~ B(10, 0.3), P(X = 3) = 120 × 0.3³ × 0.7⁷ = 120 × 0.027 × 0.0823543 = 0.2668 to 4 decimal places. Enter the combination with the nCr key so the arrangement count is not mistyped.

The most likely number of successes (the mode)

The most likely value of X is the mode. For a binomial distribution it is the whole number part of (n + 1)p, and if (n + 1)p is itself a whole number there are two modes, (n + 1)p − 1 and (n + 1)p. For X ~ B(10, 0.3), (n + 1)p = 3.3, so the mode is 3. Check against the probabilities: P(X = 3) = 0.2668 is larger than P(X = 2) = 0.2335 and P(X = 4) = 0.2001.

Checking that the probabilities add to 1

A complete check is that P(X = 0) + P(X = 1) + … + P(X = n) = 1. You rarely add every term in an exam, but the check is useful when you build a table of probabilities for a whole distribution. If a column does not total 1 to the rounding used, one of the terms was calculated with the wrong value of q or the wrong combination count.

Adding independent binomial variables

A question can combine two or more binomial counts, for example the total number of faults from two machines. The result is binomial only under particular conditions, and the subsections below say what those conditions are and how to check them.

Same probability, different numbers of trials

If X ~ B(n, p) and Y ~ B(m, p) are independent, and both use the same probability of success p, then X + Y ~ B(n + m, p). Two batches tested for the same fault, with the same chance of that fault on each item, combine into one larger binomial. The shared p is the key condition: the trials must all be a success or failure with the same chance.

The rule for X + Y

Write the result as X + Y ~ B(n + m, p). For example, X ~ B(4, 0.5) and Y ~ B(6, 0.5), independent, give X + Y ~ B(10, 0.5). Add the trial counts, not the probabilities. The probability of success stays the same because each trial still has the same chance of success.

When the probabilities differ

If X ~ B(n, p) and Y ~ B(m, q) with p ≠ q, the sum is not binomial, and you cannot use the rule above. The number of successes comes from trials that have different chances, so no single p describes all of them. A question that asks for the distribution in this case expects a table of values, not a single binomial statement.

Worked example: two batches

Batch A has 8 items and batch B has 12 items. Each item in either batch is defective with probability 0.05, and the items are independent. Let T be the total number of defective items. Then T ~ B(20, 0.05), because both batches share p = 0.05. The probability of no defective items at all is P(T = 0) = 0.95²⁰ = 0.358 to 3 significant figures.

Why the mean and variance add

The mean of a sum is always the sum of the means, whether or not the variables are independent. The variance of a sum is the sum of the variances only when the variables are independent. For the batch example, E(T) = 20 × 0.05 = 1 and Var(T) = 20 × 0.05 × 0.95 = 0.95, which is the same as adding the separate variances 8 × 0.0475 and 12 × 0.0475.

Contrast with a normal approximation

For a large n, a binomial count is often approximated by a normal distribution with the same mean np and variance npq. The approximation is weak when np or nq is small, as in the batch example where np = 1. In that case use the exact binomial probabilities, and quote the normal approximation only when the question asks for it or when n is large enough for both np and nq to be well above 5.

A one-tailed hypothesis test, step by step

A binomial hypothesis test asks whether an observed count is too unlikely for the claimed probability to be true. The method has the same steps every time, and each step earns its own mark, so write them in order.

State H₀ and H₁ in terms of the parameter

H₀ states the claimed value of p, and H₁ states the direction of the alternative. For a claim that a coin or process produces fewer successes than stated, write H₀: p = 0.4 and H₁: p < 0.4 in your working, with the symbols defined. The hypotheses are always about p, never about X, and H₀ always contains the equals sign.

Find the tail the alternative points to

The direction of H₁ tells you which tail of the distribution is critical. A “less than” alternative uses the lower tail, which contains small values of X. A “greater than” alternative uses the upper tail. Decide the tail before you look at the observed value, because choosing it afterwards invalidates the test.

Compute the probability of the observed value or more extreme

For a lower-tail test, find P(X ≤ x), where x is the observed count, assuming H₀ is true. Suppose X ~ B(12, 0.4) and 1 success is observed. Then P(X ≤ 1) = 0.6¹² + 12 × 0.4 × 0.6¹¹ = 0.00218 + 0.01741 = 0.0196 to 3 significant figures. The working must show both terms, because a single number with no method earns only a fraction of the method marks.

Compare the probability with the significance level

If the probability is less than or equal to the significance level, reject H₀. Here 0.0196 is less than 0.05, so the result is significant at the 5% level and H₀ is rejected. If the question gives a 1% level, the same probability would not be significant, because 0.0196 is greater than 0.01. Always compare with the level the question states.

Write the conclusion in the context of the question

A complete conclusion states what the result means for the claim, not just whether H₀ was rejected. For example: “There is evidence at the 5% level that the proportion of successes is less than 0.4.” Use the word “evidence” and refer to the proportion, because a test gives evidence about a population, not a proof about it.

Find the critical region and the actual significance level

The critical region is the set of values of X that lead to rejection. For B(12, 0.4), P(X ≤ 1) = 0.0196 is at most 0.05 but P(X ≤ 2) = 0.0196 + 66 × 0.16 × 0.6¹⁰ = 0.0835 is more than 0.05, so the critical region at the 5% level is {0, 1}. The actual significance level is 0.0196, which is 1.96%, because the discrete distribution cannot be cut at exactly 5%.

Equations and symbols

The distribution, its conditions and the four tail identities. Every question on this topic is one of these lines plus a calculator.

P(X = r) = nCr p^r (1 - p)^(n - r) Key: n = number of trials, fixed in advance; p = probability of success in one trial, constant; r = the number of successes asked for; nCr = n!/(r!(n − r)!), the number of orders the successes can occur in. The (1 − p) term is the failures, and its power must be n − r.

X ~ B(n, p) Key: X = the count of successes; the tilde means "is distributed as"; n and p as above. Write this line before calculating — it is often a mark on its own, and it fixes which parameters go into the calculator.

P = 10C3 (0.3)³ (0.7)⁷ Key: n = 10, p = 0.3, r = 3, so the failures are 7 and their probability is 0.7. The coefficient 10C3 = 120 accounts for the order of the three successes among the ten trials.

P(X >= r) = 1 - P(X <= r - 1) Key: a complement, so the two probabilities add to 1; the boundary moves by one because the binomial is discrete. Using 1 − P(X ≤ r) instead is the classic off-by-one error.

P(a <= X <= b) = P(X <= b) - P(X <= a - 1) Key: subtract the part below the interval; again the "− 1" is there because P(X ≤ a − 1) is everything before a. Check with a small case you can list by hand before trusting the calculator.

title: Exam technique: Data Representation
content:
### What earns the marks
For conversions, the working (place values or division remainders) earns the method mark before the answer. For images, resolution times colour depth quoted earns each mark. For sound, sample rate times resolution times time earns the calculation marks.
### Traps
Error: hex read as denary directly. Correction: convert via binary. Error: bits and bytes mixed. Correction: divide by 8 for bytes. Error: compression types swapped. Correction: lossy loses data, lossless keeps it.

title: Exam technique: Right-Angled Trigonometry
content:
### What earns the marks
For finding sides or angles, the correct ratio chosen (sin, cos, tan) with sides labelled earns the method mark: write sin(angle) = opposite / hypotenuse before substituting. For Pythagoras, the squared equation earns the mark before the root. For exact values, the surd form (root 3 / 2) earns the exactness mark; decimals lose it. For angles of elevation and depression, the diagram with the equality stated earns credit.
### Traps
Error: sine used where cosine belongs (adjacent involved). Correction: label O, A, H on the diagram first. Error: 225 given as the hypotenuse. Correction: root last. Error: 0.866 accepted for sin 60. Correction: exact means surd. Error: sin used for a tan situation in height problems. Correction: opposite over adjacent when the hypotenuse is absent.

title: Electricity & Circuits
content:
Electricity & Circuits

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2023–2025): simple circuits, current, p.d., resistance, series/parallel, electrical safety, practical electricity.

1. Circuit symbols & current

Conventional current: + → − (electron flow opposite). I = Q/t. Ammeter in series; voltmeter in parallel.

2. Current, p.d., e.m.f.

  • Current: rate of charge flow; same everywhere in series.
  • p.d.: energy per coulomb across a component; e.m.f.: electrical energy per coulomb given by the source.

3. Resistance

  • R = V/I. Ohmic conductor: V ∝ I at constant temperature.
  • Series: R = R₁ + R₂ + …; same current; p.d. shares in proportion to R.
  • Parallel: 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂; same p.d.; current splits (inverse-R share).
  • Resistance ∝ length, ∝ 1/area (wires).

4. Components

Fixed/variable resistors, LDR (light ↑ R ↓), thermistor (T ↑ R ↓), diode/LED (one-way), relay, filament lamp (R grows as T rises — V–I curve flattens).

5. Power and energy

P = VI = I²R = V²/R; E = VIt. Fuse rating just above normal current; earth wire, double insulation, circuit breakers (trip quickly, resettable).

Example: 230 V, 2 A heater: P = 460 W; correct fuse 3 A or 5 A.

6. Digital electronics basics (syllabus 4.5 context)

Analogue vs digital; logic gates drive outputs from inputs (see CS link); sensors feed comparator-style circuits.

Exam tips: series: current same; parallel: p.d. same — say which before calculating; always compute total resistance first in mixed circuits.

title: Numerical Methods — Study Notes
content:
Numerical methods

When an equation cannot be solved algebraically, numerical methods locate roots to required accuracy. You must know three families: change of sign, fixed-point iteration and Newton-Raphson.

Change of sign (decimal search)

If f is continuous and f(a) and f(b) have opposite signs, there is a root in (a, b). Bisection repeatedly halves the interval; a decimal search tests x = 1.0, 1.1, 1.2, ... until the sign changes. The method fails for repeated roots (the graph touches the axis without crossing).

Fixed-point iteration

Rearrange f(x) = 0 into x = g(x), then iterate x_(n+1) = g(x_n). Near the root the iteration converges when |g'(x)| < 1 at the root; if |g'(x)| > 1 it diverges. The iteration staircase/cobweb diagrams show this.

Newton-Raphson

x_(n+1) = x_n - f(x_n) / f'(x_n).

It uses the tangent at the current estimate and converges quadratically (fast), but it can fail: if f'(x_n) = 0 the tangent is vertical, and a poor starting point can send the sequence to a different root or into a loop.

Accuracy and error bounds

  • A sign change over an interval of width w brackets the root to within w; quoting the midpoint gives error at most w/2.
  • Iterate until successive values agree to the required accuracy (e.g. 3 s.f.).
  • Always substitute the final value back into f to confirm f(root) is close to 0.

Choosing a method

  • Bisection: guaranteed on a bracketed interval but slow.
  • Newton-Raphson: fast, needs f' and a good starting value.
  • Iteration: simple, but convergence depends on the rearrangement.

title: Exam technique: Processor Fundamentals
content:
### What earns the marks
For the fetch stage, the register chain PC to MAR to MDR to CIR stated in order earns full marks. For assembly traces, the arithmetic shown earns one mark and the addressing mode named (direct for memory addresses, immediate for hash values) earns the second. For shifts, the bit pattern written out earns the method mark before any multiply-or-divide claim.
### Traps
Error: MAR and MDR roles swapped. Correction: address travels out, instruction travels back. Error: overflow ignored after a left shift past 8 bits. Correction: state the overflow explicitly. Error: cores credited with adding RAM. Correction: cores add parallelism; pipelining overlaps stages.

title: Alkenes Quick Revision
content:
Alkenes

Edexcel International AS Level Chemistry revision notes covering the structure, bonding, isomerism, addition reactions, mechanisms, and polymer disposal of alkenes.

  • Alkenes and cycloalkenes are unsaturated hydrocarbons with a general formula CnH2n containing a carbon-carbon double bond consisting of one sigma bond and one pi bond.
  • Geometric isomerism arises due to restricted rotation around the C=C double bond and different substituents on each carbon atom of the double bond.
  • The E-Z naming system uses Cahn-Ingold-Prelog priority rules, becoming necessary when the cis- and trans- naming system breaks down due to non-identical groups on the carbon atoms.
  • Alkenes undergo addition reactions including hydrogenation with a nickel catalyst, halogenation to di-halogenoalkanes, addition of hydrogen halides to mono-halogenoalkanes, hydration with steam and an acid catalyst to form alcohols, and oxidation with acidified potassium manganate(VII) to diols.
  • Bromine or bromine water acts as a qualitative test for a C=C double bond, turning from orange/brown to colourless.
  • Electrophilic addition mechanisms for bromine and hydrogen bromide with ethene, and hydrogen bromide with propene, involve curly arrows starting from bonds or lone pairs and proceed via carbocation intermediates whose stability increases in the order primary < secondary < tertiary.
  • Addition polymerisation produces long-chain polymers from alkene monomers, requiring the ability to draw repeat units from monomers and vice versa.
  • Polymer disposal problems are mitigated by developing biodegradable polymers and removing toxic waste gases produced by incineration.

Worked example

Deduce the E-Z isomer designation for (E)-1-bromo-1,2-dichloroethene. Step 1: Assign priorities to the groups attached to each carbon of the C=C double bond using atomic numbers. On carbon 1, bromine (atomic number 35) outranks chlorine (atomic number 17). On carbon 2, chlorine outranks hydrogen (atomic number 1). Step 2: Locate the highest priority groups on each carbon. Since the bromine on carbon 1 and the chlorine on carbon 2 are on opposite sides of the double bond, the isomer is designated as (E).

Key points to remember

Students often forget that a pi bond is formed by the sideways overlap of p-orbitals, which restricts rotation and causes geometric isomerism. When drawing curly arrows for electrophilic addition, ensure the arrow starts precisely from the electron source, either a bond or a lone pair, and points to the electron-deficient species. In addition of hydrogen bromide to propene, remember that the major product is formed via the more stable secondary carbocation intermediate rather than the less stable primary carbocation. When naming geometrical isomers, always apply the E-Z priority rules systematically rather than relying on cis and trans prefixes when more than two different groups are attached to the double-bonded carbons.

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

title: Exam technique: Programming and Algorithms
content:
### What earns the marks
For validation, the rejected range stated plus the rejection loop earns both marks. For structure, single entry and exit modules using only sequence, selection and iteration earn the design marks. For traces, each variable tracked per line earns method credit. For testing, the stage named with its setting (isolated module vs live users) earns each mark.
### Traps
Error: fixed FOR loops for unknown-attempt validation. Correction: WHILE-until-valid loops. Error: binary search on unsorted data. Correction: sort first or use linear search. Error: unit and acceptance settings swapped. Correction: unit is isolated with test data; acceptance is live with real users.

title: A Level Mathematics: Differentiation II
content:
A Level Mathematics: Differentiation II

A2 differentiation adds the rules for products, quotients and functions of functions, then applies them to implicit equations, parametric curves and rates of change. Every rule in this note is stated with the condition for using it and derived where the derivation is short, because the exam tests recognition as much as execution.

The chain rule

if y = f(g(x)) then dy/dx = f'(g(x)) g'(x)

or with u: dy/dx = dy/du x du/dx

Worked example 1. Differentiate y = (3x + 2)⁵.

dy/dx = 5(3x + 2)⁴ × 3 = 15(3x + 2)⁴

Worked example 2 (trigonometric). Differentiate y = sin(2x).

dy/dx = 2 cos(2x)

Worked example 3 (exponential). Differentiate y = e^(x²).

dy/dx = 2x e^(x²)

Worked example 4 (power of a trig function). Differentiate y = cos³x.

treat as (cos x)³: dy/dx = 3(cos x)² x (-sin x) = -3 sin x cos² x

The product rule

d(uv)/dx = u dv/dx + v du/dx

"first times derivative of second plus second times derivative of first"

Worked example 1. Differentiate y = x² sin x.

dy/dx = 2x sin x + x² cos x

Worked example 2. Differentiate y = x ln x.

dy/dx = ln x + x(1/x) = ln x + 1

Worked example 3. Differentiate y = x²e^(3x).

dy/dx = 2x e^(3x) + 3x² e^(3x) = x e^(3x)(2 + 3x)

Factorising the answer is not cosmetic: stationary points need the factorised form to be solved.

The quotient rule

d(u/v)/dx = (v du/dx - u dv/dx)/v²

the numerator's order matters: v times derivative of u minus u times
derivative of v

Worked example 1. Differentiate y = sin x/x.

dy/dx = (x cos x - sin x)/x²

Worked example 2 (a common form). Differentiate y = (2x + 1)/(x − 3).

dy/dx = [(x - 3)(2) - (2x + 1)(1)]/(x - 3)²
      = (2x - 6 - 2x - 1)/(x - 3)² = -7/(x - 3)²

Worked example 3 (exponential quotient). Differentiate y = e^x/ln x.

dy/dx = [ln x e^x - e^x(1/x)]/(ln x)²

Implicit differentiation

differentiate both sides with respect to x, treating y as a function
of x: each y term contributes its derivative times dy/dx

then solve for dy/dx

Worked example 1. Find dy/dx for x² + y² = 25.

2x + 2y dy/dx = 0
 dy/dx = -x/y

Worked example 2 (product inside). Find dy/dx for xy + y² = 6.

differentiate: y + x dy/dx + 2y dy/dx = 0
dy/dx (x + 2y) = -y
dy/dx = -y/(x + 2y)

Worked example 3 (tangent). Find the tangent to x² + xy = 6 at the point (2, 1).

2x + y + x dy/dx = 0
at (2, 1): 4 + 1 + 2 dy/dx = 0  →  dy/dx = -2.5
tangent: y - 1 = -2.5(x - 2)  →  5x + 2y = 12

Parametric differentiation

if x = f(t) and y = g(t): dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt)

Worked example. For x = t², y = t³ − t, find dy/dx in terms of t.

dx/dt = 2t;  dy/dt = 3t² - 1
dy/dx = (3t² - 1)/(2t)

Worked example 2 (tangent). Find the tangent at t = 2.

point: x = 4, y = 6
gradient: (12 - 1)/4 = 2.75
tangent: y - 6 = 2.75(x - 4)  →  y = 2.75x - 5

Worked example 3 (second derivative). Find d²y/dx² in terms of t for the same curve.

d/dx(dy/dx) = [d/dt(dy/dx)] / (dx/dt)
d/dt[(3t² - 1)/(2t)] = (6t x 2t - (3t² - 1)2)/(4t²) = (6t² + 2)/(4t²)
divide by 2t: (6t² + 2)/(8t³)

Stationary points with the new rules

Worked example. Find and classify the stationary point of y = x e^(−x²).

dy/dx = e^(-x²) + x(-2x)e^(-x²) = e^(-x²)(1 - 2x²)
stationary at x = +/- 1/sqrt 2 = +/- 0.707
at x = 0.707: y = 0.707 e^(-0.5) = 0.429  →  maximum
by symmetry x = -0.707 is a minimum with y = -0.429

Worked example 2 (product inside a log). Show y = x ln x has a minimum at x = e^(−1).

dy/dx = ln x + 1 = 0  →  x = e⁻¹ = 0.368
y = e⁻¹ ln(e⁻¹) = -e⁻¹ = -0.368
second derivative = 1/x > 0 at this point, so minimum

Connected rates of change

chain rule in rate form: dV/dt = dV/dr x dr/dt
strategy: write the quantity as a function of one variable, differentiate,
link the rates, substitute

Worked example. A spherical balloon is inflated so that its volume increases at 100 cm³/s. Find dr/dt when r = 5 cm.

V = (4/3) π r³  →  dV/dr = 4 π r²
at r = 5: dV/dr = 10⁰ π = 314.2
dr/dt = (dV/dt)/(dV/dr) = 10⁰/314.2 = 0.318 cm/s

Worked example 2 (area). A circular ripple's radius grows at 2 cm/s. How fast is the area growing when r = 10 cm?

A = π r²  →  dA/dr = 2 π r = 62.83
dA/dt = 62.83 × 2 = 125.7 cm²/s

Exponentials and logarithms to other bases

Every exponential can be rewritten with base e, because a = e^(ln a). That one identity turns an unfamiliar derivative into something the chain rule already handles, and it explains why base e is the natural choice: the conversion factor disappears.

y = a^x = e^(x ln a)
dy/dx = ln a x e^(x ln a) = a^x ln a

y = log_a(x);  write x = a^y and differentiate implicitly:
1 = a^y ln a dy/dx   →   dy/dx = 1/(x ln a)

special cases: d/dx(e^x) = e^x;  d/dx(ln x) = 1/x

The factor ln a is what students leave out. For a = e it equals 1, which is exactly why base-e derivatives come out clean and every other base drags a constant along.

Worked example. Differentiate y = 3^x.

y = e^(x ln 3)
dy/dx = ln 3 x e^(x ln 3) = 3^x ln 3 = 1.0986 × 3^x

Worked example 2 (chain rule inside the exponent). Differentiate y = 2^(x²).

y = e^(x² ln 2)
dy/dx = e^(x² ln 2) x (2x ln 2) = 2x ln 2 × 2^(x²) = 1.386 × 2^(x²)

Worked example 3 (logarithm of a linear function). Differentiate y = ln(3x + 2) and state where the derivative is valid.

inner u = 3x + 2, du/dx = 3
dy/dx = (1/u) × 3 = 3/(3x + 2)
valid for 3x + 2 > 0, i.e. x > -2/3

The second derivative test and curve sketching

At a stationary point the first derivative vanishes, so it cannot distinguish a peak from a trough. The second derivative does: it measures how the gradient itself is changing, which is the curvature of the graph at that point.

Condition at a stationary pointShape of the curveConclusion
d²y/dx² < 0concave down (∩)local maximum
d²y/dx² > 0concave up (∪)local minimum
d²y/dx² = 0test inconclusivecheck the sign of dy/dx either side

Worked example. Find and classify the stationary points of y = x³ − 3x, then sketch the curve.

dy/dx = 3x² - 3 = 3(x - 1)(x + 1)
stationary at x = 1 and x = -1
at x = 1:  y = 1 - 3 = -2;  y'' = 6x = 6 > 0  →  minimum (1, -2)
at x = -1: y = -1 + 3 = 2;  y'' = -6 < 0      →  maximum (-1, 2)
y intercept: x = 0, y = 0 (also a root)
end behaviour: x -> +inf gives y -> +inf; x -> -inf gives y -> -inf

Worked example 2 (where the test fails). Classify the stationary point of y = x⁴.

dy/dx = 4x³ = 0 only at x = 0, where y = 0
y'' = 12x² = 0 at x = 0, so the test is inconclusive
look at dy/dx: negative for x < 0, positive for x > 0
so the curve falls then rises: (0, 0) is a minimum

The failed case is examinable: y = x³ has no sign change in dy/dx at the origin, so it is a point of inflection, not an extremum. Reporting "stationary point" for x³ without that check loses the mark.

Kinematics with calculus

When displacement is given as a function of time, velocity is its derivative and acceleration the derivative of velocity. Those two definitions replace the constant-acceleration formulas the moment the motion stops being uniform, which is the whole point of the calculus treatment.

s(t) displacement;  v = ds/dt;  a = dv/dt = d²s/dt²
reverse: s = integral of v dt;  v = integral of a dt
maximum displacement occurs where v = 0
distance travelled = integral of |v| dt, split where v changes sign

Worked example. A particle moves with s = t³ − 6t² + 9t metres. Find when it is instantaneously at rest and its acceleration at those instants.

v = 3t² - 12t + 9 = 3(t - 1)(t - 3)
at rest: t = 1 and t = 3
a = 6t - 12   →   a(1) = -6 m/s²;  a(3) = 6 m/s²
s(1) = 4 m;  s(3) = 0 m

Worked example 2 (total distance versus displacement). For the same motion, find the distance travelled in 0 ≤ t ≤ 3.

v is positive on (0, 1) and negative on (1, 3)
distance = [s(1) - s(0)] + [s(1) - s(3)] = (4 - 0) + (4 - 0) = 8 m
note the displacement s(3) - s(0) = 0, so displacement alone would report 0

That last result is the standard trap: a question asking for distance needs the sign changes found first, or the positive and negative parts cancel and the answer is nonsense.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Chain) Differentiate (2x − 1)⁴. Answer: 8(2x − 1)³.
  2. (Product) Differentiate x³e^x. Answer: x²e^x(3 + x).
  3. (Quotient) Differentiate (x + 1)/(x − 1). Answer: −2/(x − 1)².
  4. (Implicit) x² + y² = 16: find dy/dx. Answer: −x/y.
  5. (Implicit tangent) Same circle at (2, √12): gradient? Answer: −2/3.46 = −0.577.
  6. (Parametric) x = t², y = 2t + 1: find dy/dx. Answer: 2/(2t) = 1/t.
  7. (Rates) V = s³, ds/dt = 1.5, s = 4. Find dV/dt. Answer: 3s² × 1.5 = 72.
  8. (Stationary) y = x²e^x: find the stationary points. Answer: e^x(x² + 2x) = 0 → x = 0 (min), x = −2 (max).

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Chain rule forgotten: differentiating sin 2x as 2 cos 2x, not cos 2x — the inner derivative is compulsory.
  • Quotient rule order reversed: v du − u dv, not u dv − v du; the sign flips if you swap.
  • Implicit y terms: each differentiated y term needs a dy/dx factor, including products like xy.
  • Parametric dy/dx inverted: it is (dy/dt)/(dx/dt), not the reciprocal.
  • Second derivative by differentiating dy/dx with respect to t: must divide by dx/dt, or the answer is d/dt, not d/dx.
  • Rates linked backwards: dV/dt = dV/dr × dr/dt; inverting gives an answer in the wrong units.
  • Stationary points unfactorised: equations like x e^x(2 + x) = 0 are solved only when factorised.
  • Domain of ln: differentiating ln x is valid only for x > 0; for negative arguments use ln|x|.

title: Circular Measure — Study Notes
content:
Circular Measure

Cambridge International AS & A Level Mathematics 9709, Paper 1: radian measure, arc length, and the areas and perimeters of sectors and segments. Every formula here takes its angle in radians — that is the single fact most marks hinge on.

Radians

One radian is the angle at the centre of a circle subtended by an arc whose length equals the radius. The full circumference is 2πr, so a full turn is 2π radians and π radians = 180°.

  • Degrees → radians: multiply by π/180. Example: 150° = 150π/180 = 5π/6 ≈ 2.618 rad.
  • Radians → degrees: multiply by 180/π. Example: 1.5 rad = 1.5 × 180/π ≈ 85.9°.

Learn the common values: 30° = π/6, 45° = π/4, 60° = π/3, 90° = π/2, 180° = π, 360° = 2π. Leave answers in terms of π unless the question asks for a decimal — and when it does, give three significant figures.

Arc Length

s = rθ (θ in radians).

Example: r = 6, θ = π/3 gives s = 6 × π/3 = 2π.

A chord splits the circumference into a minor arc and a major arc, and their lengths add to 2πr. If a question gives the major angle, use θ_major = 2π − θ_minor before substituting.

Sector Area

A = ½r²θ.

Example: r = 5, θ = 1.2 gives A = ½ × 25 × 1.2 = 15.

Minor and major sector areas add to πr². The perimeter of a sector is P = 2r + s = 2r + rθ — the two straight edges count, so an arc length alone is not a perimeter.

Segment Area

A = ½r²(θ − sin θ). For r = 2, θ = π/2: A = 2(π/2 − 1) = π − 2.

The segment is the sector minus the triangle ½r²sin θ — that subtraction is where the formula comes from, and writing it down earns method marks even if the arithmetic slips. Its perimeter is the arc plus the chord, with chord length 2r sin(θ/2).

Putting It Together

Worked example: a sector has radius 8 cm and angle 1.1 rad. Arc length s = 8 × 1.1 = 8.8 cm. Area A = ½ × 64 × 1.1 = 35.2 cm². Perimeter P = 2 × 8 + 8.8 = 24.8 cm.

Rearranging

  • θ = s/r (must be radians)
  • θ = 2A/r²
  • r = s/θ, and r = √(2A/θ) — isolate the squared term first, then take the positive root only, since a radius is a length.

Exam traps: never mix degrees into s = rθ or A = ½r²θ — convert first, and check the calculator is in radian mode. Sketch the sector and mark r and θ before computing. Read whether the question asks for the major or the minor arc, sector, or segment, and confirm area answers carry squared units while arcs and perimeters are plain lengths.

title: Microbiology, Immunity and Forensics
content:
Microbiology, Immunity and Forensics

This A2 Level Biology revision note covers Edexcel IAL Topic 6, focusing on culturing microorganisms, immunity, antibiotics, decomposition, forensic DNA profiling, and determining the time of death.

  • 6.1 Culturing microbes requires strict aseptic technique using autoclaved equipment and nutrient agar to prevent contamination.
  • 6.2 Microbial growth is measured via cell counts, dilution plating, mass, and optical turbidity methods.
  • 6.3 Bacterial growth curves consist of lag, exponential, stationary, and death phases; exponential growth rate constants are calculated using (ln(N_t) − ln(N_0)) / t.
  • 6.4 Core Practical 13 investigates the growth rate of liquid cultures safely and ethically.
  • 6.5 Pathogens include bacteria and viruses (Ebola, TMV, HIV, lambda phage), exhibiting lytic cycles or latency.
  • 6.6 M. tuberculosis and HIV infect host cells, destroying immune cells and causing fatal systemic symptoms.
  • 6.7 Pathogen entry routes are protected by physical and chemical barriers including skin, stomach acid, and flora.
  • 6.8 Non-specific responses feature inflammation, lysozyme action, interferon release, and phagocytosis.
  • 6.9 Antigens provoke immune responses involving macrophages, antigen-presenting cells, plasma cells, and specific antibodies.
  • 6.10 B cells and T cells (helper, killer, memory) coordinate humoral and cell-mediated immune responses.
  • 6.11 Immunity is acquired naturally or artificially, through active or passive mechanisms.
  • 6.12 Pathogen evasion mechanisms drive an evolutionary race between hosts and pathogens.
  • 6.13 Bacteriostatic antibiotics stop bacterial reproduction while bactericidal antibiotics kill bacteria outright.
  • 6.14 Core Practical 14 investigates the inhibition zones of different antibiotics on bacteria.
  • 6.15 Hospital-acquired infection prevention requires strict hygiene codes and controlled antibiotic prescription.
  • 6.16 Microorganisms decompose organic matter, recycling carbon within ecosystems.
  • 6.17 Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) amplifies DNA fragments exponentially using thermal cycling.
  • 6.18 Gel electrophoresis separates DNA fragments by length through an agarose gel using an electric current.
  • 6.19 DNA profiling uses short tandem repeats to identify individuals and establish genetic relationships.
  • 6.20 Time of death is estimated using decomposition stages, succession, forensic entomology, body temperature, and rigor mortis.

Worked example

Calculate the exponential growth rate constant for a bacterial culture where the initial cell number N_0 is 1000 cells, rising to 50000 cells after 4 hours. Using the formula k = (ln(N_t) − ln(N_0)) / t, we get k = (ln(50000) − ln(1000)) / 4 = (10.82 − 6.91) / 4 = 3.91 / 4 = 0.978 per hour.

Key points to remember

Students often confuse bacteriostatic and bactericidal antibiotics; remember bacteriostatic prevents division whereas bactericidal causes cell lysis. When calculating exponential growth, ensure you use natural logarithms (ln) rather than base-10 logs unless converting appropriately. In PCR, remember the steps of denaturation at 95 °C, annealing at 55 °C, and extension at 72 °C using Taq polymerase. For forensics, remember that rigor mortis is temporary muscle contraction caused by ATP depletion, which peaks and then reverses as decomposition begins.

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

title: Exam technique: Operating Systems
content:
### What earns the marks
For OS functions, each of processor, memory, device and file management stated earns credit. For interrupts, the cause plus the handler action earns both marks. For utilities, the named tool matched to its job earns the mark.
### Traps
Error: operating system confused with utility software. Correction: the OS manages hardware; utilities do jobs. Error: buffer and spooling swapped. Correction: buffers smooth speed gaps, spooling queues print jobs. Error: one function listed for describe questions. Correction: give the full set.

title: IGCSE Mathematics: Trig Graphs, Sine and Cosine Rules
content:
IGCSE Mathematics: Trig Graphs, Sine and Cosine Rules

Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580 (2025–2027), section 6 Trigonometry, Extended statements E6.4 Trigonometric functions (the graphs of sine, cosine and tangent over 0° to 360°, and solving trigonometric equations) and E6.5 Non-right-angled triangles (the sine rule, the cosine rule and the area formula ½ab sin C). The right-angled toolkit SOH CAH TOA only works when a right angle is present; these are the tools that work for every triangle. The note also covers the bearing and three-dimensional applications that appear in Paper 4, with every worked example fully recalculated.

From right-angled ratios to any angle

In a right-angled triangle, sin θ = opposite/hypotenuse, cos θ = adjacent/hypotenuse and tan θ = opposite/adjacent. The graphs in this note extend those definitions to every angle from 0° to 360°, which is what makes them useful for waves, rotating objects and periodic motion later in the course. The exact values to know by heart:

Anglesincostan
0°010
30°1/2√3/21/√3
45°√2/2√2/21
60°√3/21/2√3
90°10undefined

These come from two triangles worth knowing: the half-equilateral (30°–60°–90° with sides 1, √3, 2) and the isosceles right triangle (45°–45°–90° with sides 1, 1, √2).

The trigonometric graphs, 0° to 360°

  • y = sin x starts at 0, rises to 1 at 90°, falls through 0 at 180°, to −1 at 270°, and back to 0 at 360°. It is a wave, maximum 1 and minimum −1.
  • y = cos x is the sine wave shifted: it starts at 1, falls through 0 at 90°, to −1 at 180°, through 0 at 270°, back to 1 at 360°.
  • y = tan x is 0 at 0° and 180° and 360°, rises steeply towards +∞ just before 90°, and comes from −∞ just after 90°; it has vertical asymptotes at 90° and 270° because cos x = 0 there and tan = sin/cos.

The symmetries behind solving equations:

sin x = sin (180° - x)        e.g. sin 40° = sin 140°
cos x = -cos (180° - x)       e.g. cos 60° = -cos 120°
cos x = cos (360° - x)        e.g. cos 40° = cos 320°

Solving trigonometric equations. Find the first solution from the calculator or the exact-value table, then use the symmetry to find the others in 0° ⩽ x ⩽ 360°:

Solve sin x = 0.5 for 0° ⩽ x ⩽ 360°:

First solution: x = 30° (from the exact values)
Sine is positive in the first and second quadrants, so the second solution is
x = 180° - 30° = 150°
Answers: x = 30° and x = 150°
Solve 2 cos x + 1 = 0 for 0° ⩽ x ⩽ 360°:

2 cos x = -1
cos x = -1/2
First solution: x = 120° (cosine is negative in the second quadrant; cos 60° = 1/2)
Cosine is also negative in the third quadrant: x = 360° - 120° = 240°
Answers: x = 120° and x = 240°

A sketch of the graph before solving is the safest habit: it shows how many answers to expect, which is exactly what examiners check for.

Area of a triangle: ½ab sin C

The familiar area formula is ½ × base × height. For a triangle with sides a and b and included angle C, the height above base b is a sin C (from SOH in the right-angled triangle formed by the height), so:

area = 1/2 x a x b x sin C
  • a, b: the two known sides, in any units as long as both match; C: the angle between those two sides, in degrees; area: in the square of the side units.
Worked example: a = 8 cm, b = 5 cm, C = 48°:

area = 1/2 × 8 × 5 x sin 48°
     = 20 × 0.7431        [sin 48° = 0.7431 to 4 d.p.]
     = 14.86 cm²  ≈ 14.9 cm² (3 s.f.)

The angle must be the included one; using a non-included angle gives a different (wrong) triangle.

The sine rule

For any triangle with sides a, b, c opposite angles A, B, C:

a / sin A = b / sin B = c / sin C

or, when looking for an angle:  sin A / a = sin B / b = sin C / c

Use it when you know a matching side–angle pair (a side and the angle opposite it) plus one other item. It generalises SOH CAH TOA to triangles without a right angle.

Worked example: A = 40°, a = 7 cm, B = 65°. Find b.

a / sin A = b / sin B
7 / sin 40° = b / sin 65°
b = 7 x sin 65° / sin 40°
  = 7 × 0.9063 / 0.6428      [4 d.p. values]
  = 6.3441 / 0.6428
  = 9.87 cm (3 s.f.)

The ambiguous case. When you know two sides and an angle that is not between them (SSA), the triangle may not be unique: if the given angle is acute and the opposite side is shorter than the other side but longer than the perpendicular distance, there are two possible triangles. Since sin θ = sin (180° − θ), the calculator's answer θ may need supplementing with 180° − θ. Check both candidates against the angle sum of 180° before accepting them.

The cosine rule

For any triangle with sides a, b, c and angle A opposite side a:

a² = b² + c² - 2 b c cos A
rearranged for an angle:  cos A = (b² + c² - a²) / (2 b c)

Use it when you know SAS (two sides and the included angle) or SSS (all three sides). It is the general form of Pythagoras: with A = 90°, cos 90° = 0 and the formula collapses to a² = b² + c².

Worked example (SAS): b = 7 cm, c = 5 cm, A = 52°. Find a.

a² = 7² + 5² - 2 × 7 × 5 x cos 52°
    = 49 + 25 - 70 × 0.6157        [cos 52° = 0.6157 to 4 d.p.]
    = 74 - 43.10
    = 30.90
a = √30.90 = 5.56 cm (3 s.f.)
Worked example (SSS): a = 8 cm, b = 5 cm, c = 7 cm. Find angle B.

cos B = (a² + c² - b²) / (2 a c)
      = (64 + 49 - 25) / (2 × 8 × 7)
      = 88 / 112
      = 0.7857
B = cos^(-1)(0.7857) = 38.2° (3 s.f.)

The rule never fails for a valid triangle, and the angle found is always the one opposite the side that appears alone with the minus sign.

Bearings and multi-step problems

A bearing is measured clockwise from north, written as three figures (070°, 150°). The method: draw both north lines (they are parallel), transfer angles using parallel-line facts (alternate angles are equal), then choose the sine or cosine rule for the triangle formed.

Worked example: from a port Q, a ship sails 60 km on a bearing of 070° to P,
then 45 km on a bearing of 150° to R. Find the distance PR.

Both legs start at Q, so the angle at Q between them is the difference of the
bearings: angle PQR = 150° - 070° = 80° (draw the north line at Q and measure
clockwise to each leg; the angle inside the triangle is the gap between them).
PR² = 60² + 45² - 2 × 60 × 45 x cos 80°        [cosine rule at angle Q]
     = 3600 + 2025 - 5400 × 0.1736
     = 5625 - 937.7
     = 4687.3
PR = 68.5 km (3 s.f.)

The 3-D extension uses the same toolkit: a space diagonal has length d = √(x² + y² + z²), and the angle between a line and a plane is found by projecting the line onto the plane and solving the right-angled triangle that remains. Sketch the relevant 2-D triangle separately — that is the step most answers skip and most marks follow.

Worked example: choosing the right rule

In triangle PQR, PQ = 5 cm, PR = 8 cm and angle QPR = 60°. Find QR and the area.

QR is opposite the known angle 60° with the two other sides known (SAS):
QR² = 8² + 5² - 2 × 8 × 5 x cos 60°
     = 64 + 25 - 80 × 0.5        [cos 60° = 0.5]
     = 89 - 40
     = 49
QR = 7 cm exactly.

Area = 1/2 × 8 × 5 x sin 60° = 20 × 0.8660 = 17.3 cm² (3 s.f.)

Note the exact answer: when the numbers conspire, the square root is whole and leaving it as √49 would be an incomplete answer. Now find angle PQR with the sine rule: sin Q / 8 = sin 60° / 7 gives sin Q = 8 × 0.8660/7 = 0.9897, so Q = 81.8° or 98.2° (ambiguous case); the cosine rule resolves it: cos Q = (25 + 49 − 64)/(2 × 5 × 7) = 10/70 = 0.1429, so Q = 81.8°.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Using the sine rule without a matched pair: you need a side and the angle opposite it; otherwise use the cosine rule.
  • Forgetting the ambiguous case: two triangles may satisfy the data when two sides and a non-included angle are given — check both.
  • Mixing degrees and calculator mode: the calculator must be in degrees mode, and answers should be given to 3 s.f. unless told otherwise.
  • Losing a minus sign in the cosine rule: a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A; for an obtuse angle cos A is negative, which makes the side longer, and an answer that contradicts that is a sign slip.
  • Using ½ab sin C with a non-included angle; C must be the angle between a and b.
  • Writing bearings without three figures (070°, not 70°) or measuring anticlockwise.
  • Rounding intermediate values too early; keep 4+ d.p. through the working and round only the final answer.
  • Reading sin⁻¹ as 1/sin; it is the inverse function giving an angle from a ratio.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 2, 4 marks). Solve cos x = 0.6 for 0° ⩽ x ⩽ 360°.

Answer: First solution x = 53.1° (3 s.f.). Cosine is positive in the first and fourth quadrants, so the second is x = 360° − 53.1° = 306.9°. Answers: 53.1° and 306.9°.

Question 2 (Paper 2, 3 marks). Sketch y = sin x for 0° ⩽ x ⩽ 360° and state its maximum and minimum.

Answer: A wave starting at (0, 0), peaking at (90°, 1), crossing (180°, 0), bottoming at (270°, −1), ending at (360°, 0). Maximum 1, minimum −1.

Question 3 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Triangle ABC has AB = 9 cm, AC = 7 cm and angle BAC = 50°. Find BC.

Answer: Cosine rule: BC² = 9² + 7² − 2 × 9 × 7 × cos 50° = 81 + 49 − 126 × 0.6428 = 130 − 81.0 = 49.0, so BC = 7.0 cm (3 s.f.).

Question 4 (Paper 4, 4 marks). In triangle PQR, angle P = 30°, angle Q = 105° and PR = 12 cm. Find QR.

Answer: Angle R = 45°. By the sine rule, QR/sin 30° = 12/sin 45°, so QR = 12 × 0.5/0.7071 = 8.49 cm (3 s.f.).

Question 5 (Paper 4, 4 marks). A triangle has sides 6 cm, 8 cm and 11 cm. Find its area.

Answer: Find the angle between two known sides first. cos C = (36 + 64 − 121)/(2 × 6 × 8) = −21/96 = −0.2188, so C = 102.6°. Area = ½ × 6 × 8 × sin 102.6° = 24 × 0.9763 = 23.4 cm² (3 s.f.).

Question 6 (Paper 4, 5 marks). A boat sails 2.8 km due south from a point A to a point B. A lighthouse L is 4.2 km from A on a bearing of 120°. Find the distance BL and the bearing of the lighthouse from B.

Answer: At A the due-south direction is bearing 180°, so angle BAL = 180° − 120° = 60°. Cosine rule: BL² = 2.8² + 4.2² − 2 × 2.8 × 4.2 × cos 60° = 7.84 + 17.64 − 11.76 = 13.72, so BL = 3.70 km (3 s.f.). For the bearing, find angle ABL: cos B = (2.8² + 13.72 − 17.64)/(2 × 2.8 × 3.704) = 3.92/20.74 = 0.1890, so B = 79.1°. Since B is due south of A, the direction from B to A is due north, and the lighthouse lies east of that line, so its bearing from B is 079° (3 s.f.).

Angles and sides are the language of shape; the next note measures those shapes — area, volume and mensuration.

title: Statistics — Data Handling — Study Notes
content:
Statistics — Data Handling

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): averages from lists and tables, quartiles/IQR, charts, cumulative frequency, histograms.

1. Averages

  • Mean = Σfx/Σf from frequency tables. Median = middle value (ordered data). Mode = most frequent. Range = max − min.
  • Choose the best average: mode for shoe sizes, median when outliers distort the mean.

Example (table): goals 0,1,2,3 with f 5,8,4,3: mean = (0+8+8+9)/20 = 1.25.

2. Quartiles and IQR

Q₁ at n/4, Q₃ at 3n/4 (position); IQR = Q₃ − Q₁ — less affected by outliers than the range.

3. Charts

Bar charts, pie charts (angle = fraction × 360°), time series, pictograms. Compare data sets with like-for-like totals; comment on trends.

4. Cumulative frequency

Running totals vs upper class boundaries; the curve ends at (max, n). Median at n/2; Q₁/Q₃ at n/4 and 3n/4; box plot from the five-figure summary.

5. Histograms

Bar area ∝ frequency: FD = frequency ÷ class width. Recover frequencies as FD × width; unequal widths need FDs on the axis.

Exam tips: read cumulative-frequency answers with dashed construction lines; always compare spreads, not just averages, when asked to compare data.

Mean, median, mode and range

For ungrouped data, the mean is the sum of values divided by the number of values; the median is the middle value after ordering (the average of the two middle values if there is an even count); the mode is the most frequent value; the range is the largest minus the smallest value.

Frequency tables and grouped data

For a frequency table, the mean is the sum of (value × frequency) divided by the total frequency. For grouped data, use the midpoint of each class as the value and state that the answer is an estimate.

Charts and diagrams

Pie charts use angles: each sector angle is the category frequency divided by the total, multiplied by 360°. Bar charts have gaps between bars; histograms have no gaps, and for unequal class widths the height shown is frequency density.

Worked example: a full set of averages

Take the data 2, 4, 4, 7, 9, 10. There are six values. The mean is (2 + 4 + 4 + 7 + 9 + 10)/6 = 36/6 = 6. The median is the average of the third and fourth values, (4 + 7)/2 = 5.5. The mode is 4, the only value that occurs twice. The range is 10 − 2 = 8.

Stem-and-leaf diagrams

A stem-and-leaf diagram keeps every original value while showing the shape of the data. For values 23 and 27 on the stem 2, write 2 | 3 7. Always include a key such as 2 | 3 means 23, and put the leaves in ascending order so that the median and quartiles can be read directly.

Pie charts and scatter diagrams

  • In a pie chart, the angle for each category is (frequency/total) × 360°. Check that all the angles add up to 360°.
  • A scatter diagram shows the relationship between two variables. A positive correlation means that y tends to increase as x increases.
  • A line of best fit should pass close to the middle of the points. Use it to interpolate within the data, which is reliable, and be cautious about extrapolating beyond it.

Exam point: when you compare two distributions, comment on both an average and a spread, for example the median and the IQR, in the context of the data.

title: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Bearings, Constructions and Loci
content:
Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Bearings, Constructions and Loci

Bearings are how navigators describe direction, and geometrical constructions are how geometers draw exact figures with only a ruler and a pair of compasses. Together they fill the practical geometry questions on both papers: a bearing calculated from a diagram, a locus sketched and shaded, a perpendicular bisector constructed and justified. This note builds the topic from zero: the three rules of bearings and the back-bearing calculation, the compass-and-ruler constructions with their standard arcs, scale drawings and their measurements, and the four loci the syllabus requires, with every step shown.

Bearings: the three rules

A bearing is a direction written as a three-figure angle. Three rules define it:

  1. Measured from North (the north line, drawn as an upward arrow).
  2. Clockwise.
  3. Written with three figures — 035°, 090°, 245° (never 35° or 9°).

Bearings are always between 000° and 360°; a direction due east is 090°, due south 180°, due west 270°.

Worked example. A ship sails from A on a bearing of 060° for 12 km to B, then on a bearing of 150° for 8 km to C. Describe the position of C relative to A qualitatively.

060 ° is between north and east; 150 ° is between east and
south. So C lies south-east of A, and the two legs turn 90 °
(150 - 60 = 90) - the path is two perpendicular legs, making a
right angle at B.

Back bearings

The bearing of A from B is not the bearing of B from A — they differ by 180° (add if under 180°, subtract if 180° or more):

back bearing = bearing + 180  (if bearing < 180)
             = bearing - 180  (if bearing >= 180)

Worked example. The bearing of B from A is 072°. Find the bearing of A from B.

72 + 180 = 252 °

Worked example 2 (three-figure check). The bearing of P from Q is 310°. Find the bearing of Q from P.

310 - 180 = 130 °

Bearings with trigonometry

Bearing problems become right-triangle problems once you draw the north lines and mark the angles between the path and north. Use Pythagoras for distances and trigonometry for angles, then convert the angle into a bearing.

Worked example. A boat sails 5 km due north, then 12 km due east. Find its distance and bearing from the start.

distance = √(5² + 12²) = √(169) = 13 km
angle east of north: tan(θ) = 12/5  →  θ = 67.4 °
bearing = 067 ° (to the nearest degree)

Worked example 2 (reverse). A helicopter is 9 km from base on a bearing of 145°. How far east and how far south of the base is it?

angle from south = 180 - 145 = 35 °
east = 9 sin(35) = 5.16 km
south = 9 cos(35) = 7.37 km

Constructions: ruler and compasses only

Constructions are marked on the accuracy of the arcs and the visibility of the construction lines. Keep your compasses sharp and do not rub out the arcs.

ConstructionStandard method (in order)
Perpendicular bisector of ABcompasses wider than half AB: arc from A, same-radius arc from B, both sides; join the two intersections
Angle bisectorarc across both arms from the vertex; same-radius arcs from those two crossings; join the vertex to their intersection
Perpendicular from a point to a linearc from the point cutting the line twice; equal arcs from those cuts; join the point to their intersection
Perpendicular at a point on a lineequal arcs either side of the point; then the perpendicular-bisector method between them
60° anglearc from the endpoint across the line; same radius arc from the crossing; join
Triangle given SSSdraw the base; arcs of the other two lengths from each end; join the intersection

Worked example. Construct the perpendicular bisector of a segment AB of length 8 cm and explain why every point on it is equidistant from A and B.

Construction: arcs of radius > 4 cm from A and from B, above and
below the segment; the two intersections join to form the bisector.
Why: the arcs are circles of equal radius centred at A and B, so
their intersection points are equidistant from A and B; the line
through them is the locus of all such points.

Scale drawings

A scale drawing represents a real situation to a ratio: 1 : 50 000 means 1 cm on paper represents 50 000 cm in reality (0.5 km). The method: convert the scale to a usable unit, measure or construct to scale, then read back with the reverse conversion.

Worked example. A map has scale 1 : 25 000. Two towns are 6.4 cm apart on the map. Find the real distance in km.

6.4 cm x 25 000 = 160 000 cm
160 000 cm = 1600 m = 1.6 km

Worked example 2 (drawing). A field is 400 m by 250 m. Draw it at scale 1 : 5000. What are the drawing dimensions?

400 m = 40 000 cm; /5000 = 8 cm
250 m = 25 000 cm; /5000 = 5 cm
The drawing is 8 cm by 5 cm.

Loci

A locus is the set of all points satisfying a condition. Four standard loci are examinable, and each has its construction:

  • Fixed distance from a point: a circle (arc) of that radius, centred on the point.
  • Equidistant from two points: the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining them.
  • Equidistant from two lines: the angle bisector(s) of the angle between them.
  • Fixed distance from a line: two parallel lines at that distance, one on each side (with semicircular ends for a segment).

Region questions combine loci: "shade the region closer to A than B and within 3 cm of C" means intersect the perpendicular bisector's half-plane with the circle's interior.

Worked example. A goat is tethered to a corner of a 6 m by 4 m shed with a 5 m rope. Describe the region it can reach.

A three-quarter circle of radius 5 m around the corner, minus
the part blocked by the shed: the rope wraps the shed's⁴ m and
6 m walls. The reachable region is the quarter circle of radius
5 m outside the shed plus smaller arcs where the rope wraps
(radius 1 m around the far 4 m corner, no reach around the far
6 m corner since 5 - 6 < 0).

Worked examples: bearings and loci together

Worked example. Two radio transmitters A and B are 10 km apart, with B due east of A. A signal is received equally strongly at points equidistant from A and B, and within 6 km of A. Describe the region.

Equidistant from A and B: the perpendicular bisector of AB - a
north-south line 5 km east of A.
Within 6 km of A: a circle of radius 6 km centred at A.
The region is the part of the circle on one side of the bisector:
a circular segment of radius 6 km, cut by the line 5 km from A.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Bearing definition) State the three rules for a bearing. Answer: Measured from north, clockwise, written as three figures.
  2. (Back bearing) The bearing of X from Y is 128°. Find the bearing of Y from X. Answer: 128 + 180 = 308°.
  3. (Calculation) A plane flies 30 km north then 40 km east. Find its distance from the start and its bearing. Answer: distance = √(900 + 1600) = 50 km; tan θ = 40/30 → θ = 53.1°, bearing 053°.
  4. (Components) A ship is 15 km from port on a bearing of 210°. Find its distance west of the port. Answer: angle from south = 210 − 180 = 30°; west = 15 sin 30 = 7.5 km.
  5. (Construction) Describe how to construct the perpendicular bisector of a 6 cm segment. Answer: Set compasses wider than 3 cm; draw arcs from each endpoint, both above and below; join the two crossing points.
  6. (Locus) Describe the locus of points equidistant from the sides of an angle. Answer: The angle bisector — every point on it is the same perpendicular distance from both arms.
  7. (Scale) On a 1 : 20 000 map, a lake is 3.5 cm long. Find its real length in km. Answer: 3.5 × 20 000 = 70 000 cm = 0.7 km.
  8. (Region) Shade the region inside a triangle that is closer to side AB than to side AC and within 2 cm of vertex A. Answer: The intersection of the half-plane on AB's side of the angle bisector of A with the circle of radius 2 cm centred at A.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Two-figure bearings: 35° must be written 035°. Three figures, always.
  • Measuring from the wrong north: bearings start at north, not east. A bearing of 090° is east, not north.
  • Back-bearing addition: add 180 if the bearing is below 180, subtract if above; the result must stay between 000 and 360.
  • Anticlockwise angles: bearing questions are clockwise; a clockwise angle and its anticlockwise partner sum to 360.
  • Rubbing out construction arcs: the arcs are the evidence. Leave them visible and use a sharp pencil.
  • Locus shading: shade the region, not the boundary line; the question usually says "shade the region".
  • Scale unit slips: convert the real measurement to the same unit as the drawing before applying the ratio, and remember 1 km = 100 000 cm.
  • Diagram not to scale: measure only when told to; otherwise calculate. A protractor reading on a "not to scale" diagram earns nothing.

Bearings drawn properly: clockwise from north, three digits, always

A bearing is not an angle inside a triangle — it is a direction on the page, and almost every lost mark on this topic comes from measuring it from the wrong place or turning the wrong way. One drawing fixes the idea for good.

The three rules, in the order they bite. A bearing is measured from the north line at the point you are leaving, it turns clockwise, and it is written with three digits (060°, not 60°, and 025° rather than 25°). The third rule is not fussiness: 070° and 007° are different directions, and the leading zeros are how a reader tells them apart.

The back bearing is the return journey. If B is on a bearing of 060° from A, then A is on a bearing of 240° from B:

back bearing = bearing + 180° (or − 180° if the result would exceed 360°) Key: both are the same line measured from opposite ends. Adding 180° cannot go wrong; subtracting can, so add and then subtract 360° if necessary. For 060°: 60 + 180 = 240°. For 300°: 300 + 180 = 480, and 480 − 360 = 120°.

Worked example. A ship sails 12 km from port P on a bearing of 060°, then 9 km on a bearing of 150°. How far is it from P, and on what bearing?

Draw the two legs nose-to-tail. The turn between them is 150 − 60 = 90°, so the two legs are perpendicular and the distance closes as a right-angled triangle:
distance = √(12² + 9²) = √(144 + 81) = √225 = 15 km

The overall bearing is the angle from north to the closing line, which needs the angle at P inside the triangle: tan θ = 9 / 12, so θ = 36.9°, and the bearing is 60 − 36.9 = 023.1° on the far side — which is why the sketch, not the arithmetic, decides between adding and subtracting. Candidates who skip the sketch get 15 km and then guess the direction.

Where marks are lost. Measuring anticlockwise (bearing 060 becomes the 300° direction). Measuring from the horizontal or from another bearing rather than from north. Writing two digits. And finding the distance with a scale drawing but then reading the bearing off the wrong vertex — the bearing of A from B is not the bearing of B from A, and the question always says which.

title: IGCSE Chemistry (OxfordAQA): Chemical Analysis
content:
Chemical Analysis

This topic is about finding out what a substance is without being told. Half of it is a set of tests you must know exactly — the gas tests, the flame tests, the hydroxide precipitates and the anion tests — because the examiner asks for the observation and the conclusion, and a test you half-remember produces the wrong colour and no marks. The other half is the two techniques that separate mixtures from pure substances: melting and boiling point as a measure of purity, and chromatography as a way of splitting a mixture into its components and identifying them by an Rf value. Both halves reward precision over explanation: a colour must be right, a calculation must be laid out, and the order of a test (acid first, then barium chloride) must be correct.

1. What "pure" means in chemistry

In everyday speech "pure" means "nothing added", which is why orange juice can be labelled pure while containing dozens of compounds. In chemistry a pure substance is a single element or a single compound, with nothing else mixed in. Pure water is H₂O and nothing else; orange juice is a mixture, however natural it is, because it contains water, sugars, acids and pigments together.

A mixture contains two or more substances that are not chemically joined, so it can be separated by physical means — filtration, distillation, crystallisation or chromatography — and the proportions can be anything. A compound is chemically joined, has a fixed formula, and can only be separated by a chemical reaction. That distinction is the reason a mixture has a melting range while a pure compound melts at one temperature.

Alloys are a useful test of the definition: brass is a mixture of copper and zinc, so it is not pure, even though it is a single solid material with a definite colour and it looks completely homogeneous.

2. Melting and boiling points as a purity test

A pure substance melts and boils at a single fixed temperature, and both values are a property of that substance. An impurity lowers the melting point and raises the boiling point, and it also spreads each one over a range, because the impurity disturbs the arrangement of particles and the substance no longer changes state all at once.

So the test is not just "get a number and look it up": the sharpness is the evidence. A sample that melts between 78.5 and 79.5 °C is almost certainly a pure substance, because that range is 1 °C wide and near the melting point of naphthalene at 80 °C; a sample that starts to soften at 70 °C and is fully liquid at 85 °C is impure, whatever its average. The value identifies the substance and the width of the range judges its purity, so two samples with different ranges are not equally pure, and the wider and lower the range, the more impurity is present.

Boiling point is measured the same way, and distillation uses this: a pure liquid distils at a constant temperature, so a thermometer reading that climbs during distillation is evidence that the liquid was a mixture. That is why fractional distillation can separate crude oil into fractions at all.

3. Formulations and mixtures

Many useful materials are deliberately mixtures, designed to have the properties no single substance has. These are called formulations, and each component is present in a measured amount: paints contain a pigment, a solvent, a binder and additives; medicines contain an active ingredient plus fillers; fertilisers contain several compounds to supply nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium together; alloys are formulated for strength or resistance to corrosion.

Because a formulation is a mixture, its composition can be checked by analysis rather than by a formula — the percentage by mass of each component can be measured, and a product that does not match its specification is out of specification even if every ingredient is present. The exam wording to watch for is "state why the paint is a formulation rather than a compound": the answer is that the components are mixed and not chemically combined, and each is present in a chosen proportion.

4. Paper chromatography — how it separates

Chromatography separates the components of a mixture by letting them travel at different speeds through a material. In paper chromatography the paper is the stationary phase (the water held in the paper fibres does most of the work) and the solvent that creeps up it is the mobile phase.

The method matters, because the marks are in the detail: draw a pencil line near the bottom of the paper (pencil, not pen, because ink would dissolve and run), put a small spot of the mixture on the line, and lower the paper into the solvent so that the solvent is below the line and the spot is not submerged. Let the solvent rise, then take the paper out and mark the solvent front before it dries.

A component that is strongly attracted to the stationary phase moves slowly; one that dissolves well in the mobile phase moves quickly. The result is a series of spots at different heights. If a substance is colourless, a locating agent is needed to make the spots visible — ninhydrin for amino acids, for example — which is why an "explain why a locating agent is used" question appears so often.

Chromatography is used to identify the dyes in an ink or a food colouring, to separate the amino acids from a protein digest, to check the purity of a drug, and in forensic work to compare a sample from a scene with a reference. In every case the identification works by comparison: the unknown's spots are compared with spots from known substances run on the same paper.

5. Rf values and reading a chromatogram

The position of a spot is summarised by its Rf value — the retention factor — which is the distance the spot moved divided by the distance the solvent moved:

Rf = distance moved by the substance ÷ distance moved by the solvent front → Key: both distances are measured in the same units (usually cm) from the pencil line, to the centre of the spot and to the solvent front; Rf has no units and is always less than 1, because nothing can travel further than the solvent.

The Rf value is a property of the substance under those conditions, which is the sentence that earns the mark. Change the solvent, the temperature or the type of paper and the value changes, so an Rf is only comparable with a reference value obtained the same way. That is why an unknown is run alongside known substances on the same sheet rather than matched against a table from a textbook.

Reading a chromatogram also involves counting: three spots in a vertical line means three components, and two spots at the same height means the same substance, whether the mixture is a single sample or two samples side by side.

6. Worked examples — purity and chromatography

Example 1. On a chromatogram the solvent front is 7.8 cm above the pencil line and the centre of a spot is 4.7 cm above it. Calculate the Rf value.

Rf = distance moved by the substance ÷ distance moved by the solvent front = 4.7 ÷ 7.8 = 0.60. The answer has no units, and it must be below 1; a value above 1 means the distances were measured from the wrong place, usually from the bottom of the paper rather than from the pencil line.

Example 2. A sample of a solid melts between 74 °C and 81 °C. The pure substance melts at 79 °C. State what the result shows and explain it.

The sample is impure. A pure substance melts sharply at a single temperature, whereas this sample melts over a range of 7 °C and starts to melt below the true value; an impurity lowers the melting point and broadens the range, so both features point the same way.

Example 3. Why must the solvent level be below the spot when the paper is placed in the tank?

If the solvent covers the spot, the sample dissolves into the bulk solvent in the tank instead of travelling up the paper, so the components never separate and no chromatogram forms.

7. Tests for the common gases

Six gases are examined, and each has one test and one observation. Learn them as pairs, because a test without its observation scores nothing:

GasTestPositive result
Hydrogen, H₂Hold a lighted splint at the mouth of the tubeA squeaky pop as it burns
Oxygen, O₂Insert a glowing splintThe splint relights
Carbon dioxide, CO₂Bubble through limewater (calcium hydroxide solution)The limewater turns milky or cloudy
Chlorine, Cl₂Hold damp litmus paper in the gasThe paper is bleached; the gas is pale green
Ammonia, NH₃Hold damp red litmus paper in the gasThe paper turns blue
Sulfur dioxide, SO₂Bubble through acidified potassium dichromate(VI) solutionOrange turns green
