The limewater test has a chemistry behind it, and it is worth knowing because it explains the word "milky": CO₂ + Ca(OH)₂ → CaCO₃ + H₂O → Key: the calcium carbonate is the white, insoluble solid that makes the solution cloudy, and it dissolves again if excess carbon dioxide is bubbled through, which is why a long bubbling can clear the liquid.

Two of these tests are easily confused. Chlorine bleaches damp litmus (it goes white), while ammonia turns damp red litmus blue; using blue litmus for chlorine and red for oxygen is the usual slip. Notice too that the litmus must be damp for both, because the gas has to dissolve to form an acid or an alkali before it can change the indicator.

8. Flame tests for metal ions

A clean nichrome or platinum wire is dipped in the sample and held in a non-luminous flame; the colour of the flame identifies the metal ion. The wire must be cleaned in concentrated hydrochloric acid between tests, otherwise the previous sample contaminates the next colour.

IonFlame colour
Lithium, Li⁺Crimson (deep red)
Sodium, Na⁺Yellow, persistent and bright
Potassium, K⁺Lilac
Calcium, Ca²⁺Orange-red
Copper, Cu²⁺Green or blue-green

Flame tests work because heating supplies energy that excites electrons; as they fall back they emit light of a wavelength characteristic of that ion. That explanation is not required at IGCSE, but it does explain the limitation: a mixture of two metal ions shows the dominant colour, so sodium's yellow can mask everything else, and a very small amount of an ion may give no visible colour at all. Flame tests are quick but not sensitive, which is exactly the gap that instrumental methods fill.

9. Hydroxide precipitate tests

Adding a few drops of sodium hydroxide solution to a solution of a metal salt produces an insoluble hydroxide, and the colour of that precipitate identifies several ions at once:

IonPrecipitate with NaOH(aq)Behaviour in excess NaOH(aq)
Copper(II), Cu²⁺BlueInsoluble
Iron(II), Fe²⁺Green, turning brown on standing in airInsoluble
Iron(III), Fe³⁺Red-brown (rust coloured)Insoluble
Aluminium, Al³⁺WhiteDissolves to a colourless solution
Zinc, Zn²⁺WhiteDissolves to a colourless solution
Calcium, Ca²⁺WhiteInsoluble
Magnesium, Mg²⁺WhiteInsoluble

The behaviour in excess is the part students leave out and the part that carries the marks. Aluminium and zinc hydroxides are amphoteric — they dissolve in excess alkali — so a white precipitate that disappears in excess sodium hydroxide is evidence for Al³⁺ or Zn²⁺, and a white precipitate that stays is evidence for Ca²⁺ or Mg²⁺. To separate aluminium from zinc, add ammonia solution instead: the zinc hydroxide dissolves in excess ammonia, the aluminium hydroxide does not.

Iron(II) is worth a second look: the green precipitate is iron(II) hydroxide, and it darkens to brown because the iron(II) is oxidised to iron(III) by oxygen in the air. If a question says the precipitate "turns brown on standing", the answer is iron(II) and the explanation is oxidation, not a mistake by the student.

10. Tests for anions

Three anion tests cover the syllabus, and each has a required order of addition:

  • Carbonate, CO₃²⁻: add dilute acid. If a carbonate is present, effervescence occurs and the gas turns limewater milky — the same CO₂ test as above. Nothing else in these tests fizzes with acid, so this one is a good first check.
  • Sulfate, SO₄²⁻: add dilute hydrochloric acid first, then barium chloride solution. A white precipitate of barium sulfate confirms a sulfate. The acid is added first to remove any carbonate, which would also give a white precipitate and a false positive.
  • Halides: add dilute nitric acid, then silver nitrate solution. Chloride gives a white precipitate, bromide gives cream, and iodide gives yellow. The acid removes carbonate for the same reason as above, so a white precipitate here really is silver chloride rather than a mixture of silver chloride and carbonate.

To tell the halides apart with certainty, add ammonia solution: silver chloride dissolves in dilute ammonia, silver bromide only in concentrated ammonia, and silver iodide does not dissolve at all. That single extra step is often the difference between a 2-mark and a 3-mark answer.

11. Putting the tests together — identifying an unknown

Most exam questions give an unknown solid and a list of results, and the answer is built from them in order. Work through the observations systematically:

  1. Colour of the solid or solution — a blue solution suggests Cu²⁺, pale green Fe²⁺, yellow or brown Fe³⁺. A colourless solution rules those out but not much else.
  2. Flame test — identifies Li⁺, Na⁺, K⁺, Ca²⁺ or Cu²⁺ even in a mixture.
  3. Hydroxide precipitate — confirms the cation and gives information the flame test cannot, especially for Al³⁺, Zn²⁺, Mg²⁺ and Fe²⁺, which have no useful flame colour.
  4. Carbonate test with acid — decides whether the anion might be a carbonate before anything else is added.
  5. Sulfate and halide tests — with the acid first in each case, so the result is not confused by a carbonate.

The one modern addition in the spec is instrumental analysis, and flame emission spectroscopy is the example to know. The sample is heated in a flame and the light emitted is passed through a spectrometer, which separates it into wavelengths. Each metal ion emits a characteristic set of wavelengths, so the ion can be identified from the pattern, and the intensity of the light gives the concentration.

Compared with the tests above, instrumental methods are more sensitive (they detect amounts far too small to see), faster, and more accurate, and they can analyse a mixture without separating it or even without a trained eye reading a colour. The cost is the equipment, which is why a school laboratory still uses a wire and a flame.

12. Worked examples — identification

Example 1. A white solid dissolves in water to give a colourless solution. Adding sodium hydroxide gives a white precipitate that does not dissolve in excess. Adding dilute nitric acid then silver nitrate gives a white precipitate that dissolves in dilute ammonia. Identify the solid.

A white precipitate with sodium hydroxide that is insoluble in excess is calcium or magnesium; the flame test would separate them, but with no flame colour reported, the anion decides the identity. The white precipitate with silver nitrate that dissolves in dilute ammonia is silver chloride, so the anion is Cl⁻. A compound of Ca²⁺ (the more common of the two in this test) with Cl⁻ gives calcium chloride, CaCl₂.

Example 2. Three unlabelled solutions contain copper(II) sulfate, iron(II) sulfate and iron(III) sulfate. Describe one test that identifies all three.

Add sodium hydroxide solution to each. Copper(II) gives a blue precipitate, iron(II) gives a green precipitate that turns brown on standing, and iron(III) gives a red-brown precipitate immediately. One reagent, three colours, and the precipitates are all insoluble in excess, so the excess step is not needed here.

Example 3. A fertiliser is suspected of containing ammonium sulfate. Explain why the sulfate test must come after the carbonate test.

If a carbonate were present, adding barium chloride would give a white precipitate of barium carbonate, which looks exactly like barium sulfate; adding dilute acid first destroys any carbonate, so a white precipitate afterwards can only be barium sulfate. The carbonate test is not optional housekeeping: it is what makes the sulfate result mean something.

13. Exam-style questions

  1. State what is meant by a pure substance in chemistry, and explain why a sample that melts over a range of 8 °C is not pure. Answer: a pure substance is a single element or compound with nothing else mixed in; a pure substance melts at one fixed temperature, so a range of 8 °C shows an impurity is present, which lowers the melting point and spreads it over a range.
  2. Describe how paper chromatography can show that a green ink contains three dyes. Answer: place a spot of the ink on a pencil line near the bottom of the paper, stand the paper in a solvent with the solvent level below the spot, and let the solvent rise; the dyes travel at different speeds according to their attraction to the paper and the solvent, so three spots appear at different heights, and each can be identified by comparing its Rf value with those of known dyes run on the same paper.
  3. Give the test and the observation for carbon dioxide, and write the equation for the reaction involved. Answer: bubble the gas through limewater; it turns milky. CO₂ + Ca(OH)₂ → CaCO₃ + H₂O, and the white calcium carbonate is what makes it cloudy.
  4. A solution gives a white precipitate with sodium hydroxide that dissolves in excess, and no precipitate with silver nitrate. Identify the two ions that could be present and explain how to distinguish them. Answer: Al³⁺ or Zn²⁺, since both give a white hydroxide that is amphoteric; add ammonia solution instead, because zinc hydroxide dissolves in excess ammonia and aluminium hydroxide does not.
  5. Explain why the wire used in a flame test must be cleaned between samples. Answer: a trace of the previous sample would remain on the wire and give its flame colour, so the observed colour might belong to the contaminant rather than to the substance being tested.
  6. State two advantages of flame emission spectroscopy over a flame test. Answer: it is more sensitive, so it detects ions at concentrations too low for a visible colour; and it is more accurate and can measure concentration as well as identify the ion, whereas a flame test only gives a colour.
  7. A white solid fizzes with dilute hydrochloric acid and the gas turns limewater milky. Identify the anion and write the ionic equation for the reaction with acid. Answer: carbonate, CO₃²⁻; CO₃²⁻ + 2H⁺ → CO₂ + H₂O. The fizzing and the milky limewater together are the evidence, since neither observation on its own is conclusive.

14. Common mistakes

  • Using the wrong litmus for a gas. Chlorine bleaches damp litmus paper; ammonia turns damp red litmus blue.
  • Giving a test without its observation. "Bubble through limewater" scores nothing until you add "and it turns milky".
  • Mixing the halide colours. Chloride is white, bromide cream, iodide yellow — not the other way round.
  • Adding silver nitrate before the acid. Without the acid first, a carbonate produces a white precipitate and looks like a chloride.
  • Forgetting the excess step in a hydroxide precipitate test, which is the only way to separate aluminium and zinc from calcium and magnesium.
  • Measuring Rf from the bottom edge of the paper rather than from the pencil line, or to the top of the spot rather than its centre. Both give a value that is wrong and sometimes greater than 1.
  • Saying a substance is pure because it looks uniform. Brass is uniform and is a mixture.
  • Claiming an impurity raises the melting point. It lowers it, and raises the boiling point.

15. Exam technique for this topic

  • Write tests as a pair: reagent, then observation, then conclusion. Three short sentences score three marks; "it goes cloudy" alone scores one.
  • Give colours precisely, with the standard words: blue, green, red-brown, cream, yellow, lilac, crimson, orange-red. "Dark" or "light" is not a colour in a mark scheme.
  • When the question says "excess", it is asking about the extra observation, not about the amount. Say whether the precipitate dissolves.
  • In an Rf calculation, show the fraction with the words in place before substituting the numbers, and check the answer is below 1.
  • If the data identify two possible ions, say how to tell them apart rather than guessing. A named second test is a mark; a guess is not.
  • For "state one advantage of an instrumental method", the safe answers are sensitivity, speed, accuracy and the ability to work with very small samples.

title: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Bearings, Constructions and Loci
content:
Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Bearings, Constructions and Loci

Bearings are how navigators describe direction, and geometrical constructions are how geometers draw exact figures with only a ruler and a pair of compasses. Together they fill the practical geometry questions on both papers: a bearing calculated from a diagram, a locus sketched and shaded, a perpendicular bisector constructed and justified. This note builds the topic from zero: the three rules of bearings and the back-bearing calculation, the compass-and-ruler constructions with their standard arcs, scale drawings and their measurements, and the four loci the syllabus requires, with every step shown.

Bearings: the three rules

A bearing is a direction written as a three-figure angle. Three rules define it:

  1. Measured from North (the north line, drawn as an upward arrow).
  2. Clockwise.
  3. Written with three figures — 035°, 090°, 245° (never 35° or 9°).

Bearings are always between 000° and 360°; a direction due east is 090°, due south 180°, due west 270°.

Worked example. A ship sails from A on a bearing of 060° for 12 km to B, then on a bearing of 150° for 8 km to C. Describe the position of C relative to A qualitatively.

060 ° is between north and east; 150 ° is between east and
south. So C lies south-east of A, and the two legs turn 90 °
(150 - 60 = 90) - the path is two perpendicular legs, making a
right angle at B.

Back bearings

The bearing of A from B is not the bearing of B from A — they differ by 180° (add if under 180°, subtract if 180° or more):

back bearing = bearing + 180  (if bearing < 180)
             = bearing - 180  (if bearing >= 180)

Worked example. The bearing of B from A is 072°. Find the bearing of A from B.

72 + 180 = 252 °

Worked example 2 (three-figure check). The bearing of P from Q is 310°. Find the bearing of Q from P.

310 - 180 = 130 °

Bearings with trigonometry

Bearing problems become right-triangle problems once you draw the north lines and mark the angles between the path and north. Use Pythagoras for distances and trigonometry for angles, then convert the angle into a bearing.

Worked example. A boat sails 5 km due north, then 12 km due east. Find its distance and bearing from the start.

distance = √(5² + 12²) = √(169) = 13 km
angle east of north: tan(θ) = 12/5  →  θ = 67.4 °
bearing = 067 ° (to the nearest degree)

Worked example 2 (reverse). A helicopter is 9 km from base on a bearing of 145°. How far east and how far south of the base is it?

angle from south = 180 - 145 = 35 °
east = 9 sin(35) = 5.16 km
south = 9 cos(35) = 7.37 km

Constructions: ruler and compasses only

Constructions are marked on the accuracy of the arcs and the visibility of the construction lines. Keep your compasses sharp and do not rub out the arcs.

ConstructionStandard method (in order)
Perpendicular bisector of ABcompasses wider than half AB: arc from A, same-radius arc from B, both sides; join the two intersections
Angle bisectorarc across both arms from the vertex; same-radius arcs from those two crossings; join the vertex to their intersection
Perpendicular from a point to a linearc from the point cutting the line twice; equal arcs from those cuts; join the point to their intersection
Perpendicular at a point on a lineequal arcs either side of the point; then the perpendicular-bisector method between them
60° anglearc from the endpoint across the line; same radius arc from the crossing; join
Triangle given SSSdraw the base; arcs of the other two lengths from each end; join the intersection

Worked example. Construct the perpendicular bisector of a segment AB of length 8 cm and explain why every point on it is equidistant from A and B.

Construction: arcs of radius > 4 cm from A and from B, above and
below the segment; the two intersections join to form the bisector.
Why: the arcs are circles of equal radius centred at A and B, so
their intersection points are equidistant from A and B; the line
through them is the locus of all such points.

Scale drawings

A scale drawing represents a real situation to a ratio: 1 : 50 000 means 1 cm on paper represents 50 000 cm in reality (0.5 km). The method: convert the scale to a usable unit, measure or construct to scale, then read back with the reverse conversion.

Worked example. A map has scale 1 : 25 000. Two towns are 6.4 cm apart on the map. Find the real distance in km.

6.4 cm x 25 000 = 160 000 cm
160 000 cm = 1600 m = 1.6 km

Worked example 2 (drawing). A field is 400 m by 250 m. Draw it at scale 1 : 5000. What are the drawing dimensions?

400 m = 40 000 cm; /5000 = 8 cm
250 m = 25 000 cm; /5000 = 5 cm
The drawing is 8 cm by 5 cm.

Loci

A locus is the set of all points satisfying a condition. Four standard loci are examinable, and each has its construction:

  • Fixed distance from a point: a circle (arc) of that radius, centred on the point.
  • Equidistant from two points: the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining them.
  • Equidistant from two lines: the angle bisector(s) of the angle between them.
  • Fixed distance from a line: two parallel lines at that distance, one on each side (with semicircular ends for a segment).

Region questions combine loci: "shade the region closer to A than B and within 3 cm of C" means intersect the perpendicular bisector's half-plane with the circle's interior.

Worked example. A goat is tethered to a corner of a 6 m by 4 m shed with a 5 m rope. Describe the region it can reach.

A three-quarter circle of radius 5 m around the corner, minus
the part blocked by the shed: the rope wraps the shed's⁴ m and
6 m walls. The reachable region is the quarter circle of radius
5 m outside the shed plus smaller arcs where the rope wraps
(radius 1 m around the far 4 m corner, no reach around the far
6 m corner since 5 - 6 < 0).

Worked examples: bearings and loci together

Worked example. Two radio transmitters A and B are 10 km apart, with B due east of A. A signal is received equally strongly at points equidistant from A and B, and within 6 km of A. Describe the region.

Equidistant from A and B: the perpendicular bisector of AB - a
north-south line 5 km east of A.
Within 6 km of A: a circle of radius 6 km centred at A.
The region is the part of the circle on one side of the bisector:
a circular segment of radius 6 km, cut by the line 5 km from A.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Bearing definition) State the three rules for a bearing. Answer: Measured from north, clockwise, written as three figures.
  2. (Back bearing) The bearing of X from Y is 128°. Find the bearing of Y from X. Answer: a back bearing reverses direction, so add 180° when the bearing is below 180°: 128° + 180° = 308° (if the bearing exceeds 180°, subtract 180° instead).
  3. (Calculation) A plane flies 30 km north then 40 km east. Find its distance from the start and its bearing. Answer: distance = √(900 + 1600) = 50 km; tan θ = 40/30 → θ = 53.1°, bearing 053°.
  4. (Components) A ship is 15 km from port on a bearing of 210°. Find its distance west of the port. Answer: angle from south = 210 − 180 = 30°; west = 15 sin 30 = 7.5 km.
  5. (Construction) Describe how to construct the perpendicular bisector of a 6 cm segment. Answer: set the compasses to more than half the segment — more than 3 cm — and draw arcs from each end both above and below it; the two crossings of the arcs give the points the bisector passes through, so join them, and every point on that line is equidistant from both ends.
  6. (Locus) Describe the locus of points equidistant from the sides of an angle. Answer: The angle bisector — every point on it is the same perpendicular distance from both arms.
  7. (Scale) On a 1 : 20 000 map, a lake is 3.5 cm long. Find its real length in km. Answer: 3.5 × 20 000 = 70 000 cm = 0.7 km.
  8. (Region) Shade the region inside a triangle that is closer to side AB than to side AC and within 2 cm of vertex A. Answer: closer to AB than to AC means the half-plane on AB's side of the angle bisector of angle A, and within 2 cm of A means inside the circle of radius 2 cm centred on A; the shaded region is the intersection of those two, bounded by the bisector and the compass arc.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Two-figure bearings: 35° must be written 035°. Three figures, always.
  • Measuring from the wrong north: bearings start at north, not east. A bearing of 090° is east, not north.
  • Back-bearing addition: add 180 if the bearing is below 180, subtract if above; the result must stay between 000 and 360.
  • Anticlockwise angles: bearing questions are clockwise; a clockwise angle and its anticlockwise partner sum to 360.
  • Rubbing out construction arcs: the arcs are the evidence. Leave them visible and use a sharp pencil.
  • Locus shading: shade the region, not the boundary line; the question usually says "shade the region".
  • Scale unit slips: convert the real measurement to the same unit as the drawing before applying the ratio, and remember 1 km = 100 000 cm.
  • Diagram not to scale: measure only when told to; otherwise calculate. A protractor reading on a "not to scale" diagram earns nothing.

Bearings drawn properly: clockwise from north, three digits, always

A bearing is not an angle inside a triangle — it is a direction on the page, and almost every lost mark on this topic comes from measuring it from the wrong place or turning the wrong way. One drawing fixes the idea for good.

The three rules, in the order they bite. A bearing is measured from the north line at the point you are leaving, it turns clockwise, and it is written with three digits (060°, not 60°, and 025° rather than 25°). The third rule is not fussiness: 070° and 007° are different directions, and the leading zeros are how a reader tells them apart.

The back bearing is the return journey. If B is on a bearing of 060° from A, then A is on a bearing of 240° from B:

back bearing = bearing + 180° (or − 180° if the result would exceed 360°) Key: both are the same line measured from opposite ends. Adding 180° cannot go wrong; subtracting can, so add and then subtract 360° if necessary. For 060°: 60 + 180 = 240°. For 300°: 300 + 180 = 480, and 480 − 360 = 120°.

Worked example. A ship sails 12 km from port P on a bearing of 060°, then 9 km on a bearing of 150°. How far is it from P, and on what bearing?

Draw the two legs nose-to-tail. The turn between them is 150 − 60 = 90°, so the two legs are perpendicular and the distance closes as a right-angled triangle:
distance = √(12² + 9²) = √(144 + 81) = √225 = 15 km

The overall bearing is the angle from north to the closing line, which needs the angle at P inside the triangle: tan θ = 9 / 12, so θ = 36.9°, and the bearing is 60 − 36.9 = 023.1° on the far side — which is why the sketch, not the arithmetic, decides between adding and subtracting. Candidates who skip the sketch get 15 km and then guess the direction.

Where marks are lost. Measuring anticlockwise (bearing 060 becomes the 300° direction). Measuring from the horizontal or from another bearing rather than from north. Writing two digits. And finding the distance with a scale drawing but then reading the bearing off the wrong vertex — the bearing of A from B is not the bearing of B from A, and the question always says which.

Bearings in more depth

A bearing gives a direction as an angle measured clockwise from north, written as three figures. Bearings are the commonest context for angle questions in navigation, and they combine with the sine and cosine rules when the journey is not at right angles. The subsections below cover measuring, reversing and using bearings in a calculation, which are the three skills the mark scheme checks.

Measuring a bearing with a protractor

Place the centre of the protractor on the point where the bearing starts, with the zero line pointing north. Read the angle clockwise from north to the line that joins the start point to the target. A bearing of 65° is read on the outer scale of a protractor when the north line points up the page. Always check which scale you are reading, because the inner scale gives the anticlockwise angle and loses marks.

Three-figure bearings in exam answers

Exam bearings are written with exactly three figures, so a bearing of 8° is written 008°, and 65° is written 065°. The three-figure form is required even when the answer has a leading zero. A bearing given with two figures will normally be marked wrong, so write the final answer in the form the question asks for and keep the degree sign.

The bearing of A from B and of B from A

The bearing of B from A and the bearing of A from B are not the same. The first is measured at A, the second at B. They differ by exactly 180°, so if the bearing of B from A is 070°, the bearing of A from B is 250°. Draw a north line at each point, because the question usually asks for one direction and the reversed direction is the common error.

Back bearings

A back bearing is the bearing of the start point from the end point, and it is found by adding or subtracting 180°. If the bearing is less than 180°, add 180°. If it is more than 180°, subtract 180°. The back bearing is used when a journey is reversed, and it is also used as a check on a diagram, since the two north lines at the points are parallel.

Bearings with trigonometry

A bearing often describes one side of a triangle, and the other sides are found with the sine or cosine rule. Put the north lines on the diagram, mark the bearing as an angle between the north line and the side, and then find the interior angle of the triangle. Once the angle is known, the rule is applied in the usual way, and the bearings are only used to find that angle.

A worked navigation problem

A ship sails 12 km on a bearing of 040° and then 9 km on a bearing of 130°. The angle between the two legs at the turning point is found from the bearings: the turn is 130° − 040° = 090°, so the path is at right angles and the distance back to the start is √(12² + 9²) = 15 km. Each step uses one bearing to find an angle, and then Pythagoras or a rule gives the length.

Checking a bearing answer

A bearing must lie between 000° and 360°. Check that the answer is measured clockwise from north, that it has three figures, and that a diagram drawn to scale agrees with the value. A bearing of 200° points roughly south-south-west, so a diagram showing it pointing north-east is a sign that the angle was measured from the wrong line.

Geometrical constructions with ruler and compasses

A construction is a drawing made with a ruler and a pair of compasses only, with no protractor and no measurement. The method is what gets the mark, so the arcs must be left visible on the final diagram. The subsections below give the standard constructions the syllabus asks for, with the steps for each and the checks that show the result is accurate.

The perpendicular bisector of a line

To construct the perpendicular bisector of a line AB, open the compasses to more than half the length of AB. Draw an arc from A above and below the line, then draw the same arc from B so that the two pairs of arcs cross at two points. The line joining those two crossing points is the perpendicular bisector. It cuts AB into two equal parts at a right angle.

The bisector of an angle

To bisect an angle, put the compass point on the vertex and draw an arc that cuts both arms of the angle. From each of those two points draw a further arc of equal radius, so the arcs cross inside the angle. The line from the vertex through the crossing point bisects the angle into two equal parts. The construction works for any angle, because the two triangles formed are congruent.

A perpendicular from a point to a line

To draw the perpendicular from a point P to a line, place the compass on P and draw an arc that cuts the line at two points. Then construct the perpendicular bisector of those two points. The bisector passes through P and meets the line at right angles, so it is the required perpendicular. This method works whether P is above or below the line.

Constructing 60° and 90° angles

A 60° angle is constructed by drawing an equilateral triangle. Draw a line, put the compass on one end, and mark an arc of radius equal to the line. From the other end draw a second arc of the same radius to cross it. Joining the crossing point to the two ends gives an equilateral triangle, so the angle at the end is 60°. A 90° angle is constructed as a perpendicular to a line through a point on it.

Constructing a triangle from three sides

To construct a triangle with sides 6 cm, 5 cm and 4 cm, draw the 6 cm base. Open the compass to 5 cm, place the point at one end, and draw an arc. Open to 4 cm, place the point at the other end, and draw a second arc to cross the first. Join the crossing point to the two ends. A triangle is fixed by its three sides, so the construction gives one unique shape.

Accuracy and the arcs left on the diagram

Examiners check the construction arcs, not only the final line. Leave every arc visible, use a sharp pencil, and keep the compass radius constant when it is supposed to be constant. A line drawn without its construction arcs can earn no method marks, even if it is in the correct place. Make the arcs light but clear, so a marker can see which steps were followed.

Common construction errors

The commonest errors are opening the compass by different amounts for arcs that should be equal, forgetting that the perpendicular bisector needs arcs from both ends, and drawing a bisector from the wrong vertex. Check each construction by measuring afterwards: the bisected parts should be equal, and the angle at a right-angle construction should be 90° when you check it with a protractor.

title: AS Level Chemistry: Energetics
content:
AS Level Chemistry: Energetics

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH12, Topic 6 covers the heat energy exchanged in chemical reactions: how enthalpy change is defined and measured, how calorimetry data is turned into a value per mole, how Hess's Law lets you find an enthalpy change you cannot measure directly, and what bond enthalpies can and cannot tell you. The calculations are straightforward once the definitions are exact, because most marks are lost through signs, units and the direction of a cycle rather than through arithmetic.

Enthalpy change and standard conditions

Enthalpy change, ΔH, is the heat energy change measured at constant pressure. In an open beaker the pressure is constant, so the heat exchanged is an enthalpy change; the units are kJ mol⁻¹.

Standard conditions are a pressure of 100 kPa and a stated temperature, usually 298 K. A standard enthalpy change symbol has a plimsoll mark, as in ΔH⦵. The substance must also be in its standard state, which is its usual physical state at 100 kPa and 298 K: water is liquid, bromine is liquid, carbon is graphite.

  • Exothermic: heat is released to the surroundings, the temperature rises, and ΔH is negative by convention.
  • Endothermic: heat is absorbed from the surroundings, the temperature falls, and ΔH is positive.

An enthalpy level diagram shows the two states as horizontal lines: products below reactants for an exothermic reaction with an arrow pointing down, products above reactants for an endothermic reaction with an arrow pointing up. The vertical axis is enthalpy, and the arrow is labelled with the value of ΔH including its sign.

The sign convention is worth remembering in one sentence: breaking bonds always absorbs energy, making bonds always releases it, and whether a reaction is exothermic depends on which of those two totals is larger.

The five standard enthalpy definitions

These definitions are marked word for word, so learn each one with its standard state and its "per mole of" condition.

QuantityDefinition
Standard enthalpy change of reaction, ΔrH⦵The enthalpy change when the reaction occurs in the molar quantities shown in the chemical equation, under standard conditions.
Standard enthalpy change of formation, ΔfH⦵The enthalpy change when one mole of a compound is formed from its elements in their standard states under standard conditions.
Standard enthalpy change of combustion, ΔcH⦵The enthalpy change when one mole of a substance is completely burned in oxygen under standard conditions.
Standard enthalpy change of neutralisation, ΔneutH⦵The enthalpy change when one mole of water is formed by the reaction of an acid with an alkali under standard conditions.
Standard enthalpy change of atomisation, ΔatH⦵The enthalpy change when one mole of gaseous atoms is formed from the element in its standard state under standard conditions.

By definition, the standard enthalpy change of formation of an element in its standard state is zero, because no change occurs in forming an element from itself. Atomisation is always endothermic, because bonds or intermolecular forces must be broken: ΔatH⦵ of sodium is the energy to turn Na(s) into Na(g), and for a diatomic element such as chlorine it is half the bond enthalpy of Cl–Cl, since only one mole of chlorine atoms is formed from half a mole of Cl2 molecules.

Calorimetry: measuring an enthalpy change

Two experiments are examinable. In the first, two solutions are mixed in an insulated container, typically a plastic cup, and the maximum temperature reached is recorded. In the second, a fuel is burned in a spirit burner beneath a copper calorimeter containing water, and the temperature rise of the water is recorded along with the change in mass of the burner.

The energy transferred to the surroundings is calculated with the specific heat capacity equation:

energy transferred (J) = mass (g) × specific heat capacity (J g-1 °C-1) × temperature change (°C)

The specific heat capacity of water is 4.18 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹. Then the enthalpy change of the reaction is the energy transferred divided by the number of moles that reacted, converted to kJ mol⁻¹ and given the correct sign.

Worked example (mixing). 50.0 cm³ of 1.00 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid is mixed with 50.0 cm³ of 1.00 mol dm⁻³ sodium hydroxide. The temperature rises by 6.8 °C. Assume the solution has a density of 1.00 g cm⁻³ and the same specific heat capacity as water.

q = 100 × 4.18 × 6.8 = 2842 J
n(H2O) = c × V = 1.00 × 0.0500 = 0.0500 mol
ΔH = -2842 / 0.0500 = -56 840 J mol-1 = -56.8 kJ mol-1

The temperature rose, so the reaction is exothermic and the answer must be negative. The accepted value is about −57.3 kJ mol⁻¹ for a strong acid and strong alkali, so the result is close.

Worked example (combustion). Burning 0.500 g of methanol raises the temperature of 100 g of water by 20.0 °C.

q = 100 × 4.18 × 20.0 = 8360 J
n(CH3OH) = 0.500 / 32.0 = 0.0156 mol
ΔH = -8360 / 0.0156 = -536 000 J mol-1 = -536 kJ mol-1

The data book value is −726 kJ mol⁻¹. The measured value is much less exothermic, and the evaluation should explain why: heat is lost to the surroundings and to the apparatus, the combustion is incomplete because a spirit burner burns in air and produces soot and carbon monoxide, methanol evaporates from the wick without burning, and the experiment is not carried out under standard conditions.

Assumptions and error evaluation

  • The solution is assumed to have the density of water (1.00 g cm⁻³) and the specific heat capacity of water (4.18 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹); a solution that is not mostly water makes this less valid.
  • All the heat released is assumed to raise the temperature of the solution or water; in practice the container absorbs some heat, so a plastic cup is used to reduce conduction losses. A lid reduces losses by evaporation and convection.
  • Heat loss means the measured temperature rise is too small, so the magnitude of ΔH is underestimated.
  • Temperature is read to the nearest 0.5 °C with a simple thermometer, which is a large percentage uncertainty for a small rise. Use a larger amount of reactant or a digital thermometer to improve the precision.
  • The reaction is assumed to be complete and instantaneous, and the mass of water is assumed constant.

Hess's Law

Hess's Law states that the total enthalpy change of a reaction is independent of the route taken, provided the initial and final conditions are the same. It follows from the law of conservation of energy and allows an enthalpy change that cannot be measured directly, such as the formation of carbon monoxide or the hydration of an anhydrous salt, to be calculated from values that can be measured.

An enthalpy cycle is a diagram of alternative routes. Two forms are examined:

  • From formation data: the elements in their standard states are the bottom of the cycle. Reactants and products both form from the elements, so ΔH(reaction) = Σ ΔfH(products) − Σ ΔfH(reactants).
  • From combustion data: the combustion products, usually carbon dioxide and water, are the bottom of the cycle. Both reactants and products burn to the same products, so ΔH(reaction) = Σ ΔcH(reactants) − Σ ΔcH(products).

Notice that the two expressions are mirror images. In both, you go from the reactants down to the reference state and back up to the products, which is why the subtraction reverses. Learn the direction rather than memorising a formula you may apply backwards under pressure.

Worked example (formation). Calculate ΔH for the combustion of methane: CH4(g) + 2O2(g) → CO2(g) + 2H2O(l), given ΔfH⦵ values of −75 kJ mol⁻¹ for methane, −394 kJ mol⁻¹ for carbon dioxide and −286 kJ mol⁻¹ for water.

ΔH = [ΔfH(CO2) + 2 × ΔfH(H2O)] - [ΔfH(CH4) + 2 × ΔfH(O2)]
ΔH = [-394 + 2(-286)] - [-75 + 0]
ΔH = -966 + 75 = -891 kJ mol-1

The answer is negative, as expected for a combustion. The accepted value is −890 kJ mol⁻¹.

Worked example (combustion data). Calculate ΔH for the reaction C2H4(g) + H2(g) → C2H6(g) given ΔcH⦵ values of −1411 kJ mol⁻¹ for ethene, −286 kJ mol⁻¹ for hydrogen and −1560 kJ mol⁻¹ for ethane.

ΔH = [ΔcH(C2H4) + ΔcH(H2)] - [ΔcH(C2H6)]
ΔH = [-1411 + (-286)] - [-1560] = -1697 + 1560 = -137 kJ mol-1

The reaction is the addition of hydrogen across a double bond, so a modest exothermic value is a sensible check.

Core Practical 2: enthalpy change using Hess's Law

The enthalpy change of hydration of anhydrous copper(II) sulfate cannot be measured directly, because the anhydrous solid reacts violently with water and the hydration step cannot be isolated. It is found from two measurable dissolution experiments and a cycle.

Route 1: CuSO4(s)  + aq  → CuSO4(aq)      ΔH1 (dissolving anhydrous)
Route 2: CuSO4(s)  → CuSO4.5H2O(s) → CuSO4(aq)   ΔH(hydration) then ΔH2 (dissolving hydrated)

Both routes start with anhydrous copper(II) sulfate and end with the same aqueous solution, so the total enthalpy changes are equal:

ΔH1 = ΔH(hydration) + ΔH2      so      ΔH(hydration) = ΔH1 - ΔH2

Each dissolution is carried out in a insulated cup with a known mass of solid added to a known volume of water, recording the temperature change and calculating the enthalpy change per mole as in the calorimetry section. Since dissolving anhydrous copper(II) sulfate is strongly exothermic and dissolving the hydrated salt is slightly endothermic, the difference is large and negative. The evaluation must mention heat loss, the assumption about the specific heat capacity of the solution, and the uncertainty in reading a small temperature change.

Bond enthalpies

Bond enthalpy is the energy required to break one mole of a specified covalent bond in the gas phase. Mean bond enthalpy is the average energy required to break one mole of a specified covalent bond, averaged over a range of different compounds. The two are not the same: the O–H bond in water, in methanol and in ethanoic acid has a slightly different enthalpy in each, so data books quote averages.

For a reaction in the gas phase:

ΔH = Σ bond enthalpies broken - Σ bond enthalpies formed

Breaking bonds is endothermic (positive), making bonds is exothermic (negative). If more energy is released in forming the products' bonds than is absorbed in breaking the reactants' bonds, the reaction is exothermic and the value is negative.

Worked example. Calculate ΔH for the hydrogenation of ethene, C2H4 + H2 → C2H6, using mean bond enthalpies in kJ mol⁻¹: C=C 612, C–C 348, C–H 413, H–H 436.

Bonds broken: 1 × C=C (612) + 4 × C-H (1652) + 1 × H-H (436) = 2700 kJ mol-1
Bonds formed: 1 × C-C (348) + 6 × C-H (2478) = 2826 kJ mol-1
ΔH = 2700 - 2826 = -126 kJ mol-1

The arithmetic is simple but the bookkeeping is not: count the C–H bonds on both sides carefully, because the product has two more than the reactants. A quick check is that the number of bonds formed should equal the number broken plus one, since the double bond becomes a single bond and an H–H bond is lost.

Limitations of bond enthalpy calculations

  • The values are averages, so a calculation using mean bond enthalpies gives an approximate answer; the true value differs because the environment of a bond changes its strength.
  • The calculation assumes all species are gaseous. If the reaction produces a liquid, the enthalpy of condensation is not included, so the result differs from the standard enthalpy change.
  • Values are quoted for the gas phase, so reactions involving solids or liquids need additional enthalpy terms to be accurate.

Reversing the equation is the other examined skill: given ΔH and every bond enthalpy except one, substitute into the bond enthalpy equation and solve for the unknown. For example, if ΔH for a reaction is known and the bonds broken total 2000 kJ mol⁻¹, then the bonds formed total 2000 − ΔH.

Bond enthalpy data also gives a qualitative indication of which bond will break first in a reaction: the bond with the lowest bond enthalpy is the easiest to break, so it breaks first and the reaction proceeds more rapidly at room temperature. This is why the C–I bond in iodoalkanes breaks more readily than the C–Cl bond in chloroalkanes, and why alkanes react only slowly with halogens in the dark: the C–H and C–C bonds are strong and need ultraviolet light or heat to start the reaction.

Typical mistakes

  • Giving an exothermic enthalpy change a positive sign, or an endothermic one a negative sign.
  • Using the mass of the fuel burned instead of the mass of water heated in q = mcΔT.
  • Forgetting to divide the energy transferred by the number of moles, and reporting a value in kJ rather than kJ mol⁻¹.
  • Mixing up the formation and combustion cycles, or adding the values instead of subtracting in the correct direction.
  • Quoting a standard enthalpy of formation for an element as non-zero.
  • Treating a mean bond enthalpy as an exact value for a specific molecule.
  • Omitting the sign when writing the final answer, even when the working is correct.

Exam-style questions

  1. Define the standard enthalpy change of combustion. Answer: the enthalpy change when one mole of a substance is completely burned in oxygen, with all reactants and products in their standard states at 100 kPa and a stated temperature, usually 298 K.
  2. A student dissolves 4.00 g of ammonium nitrate in 50.0 g of water and the temperature falls from 21.0 °C to 16.5 °C. Calculate the enthalpy change of solution in kJ mol⁻¹. Answer: q = 50.0 × 4.18 × 4.5 = 941 J absorbed from the surroundings, so the solution is endothermic. n = 4.00 / 80.0 = 0.0500 mol, so ΔH = +941 / 0.0500 = +18 800 J mol⁻¹ = +18.8 kJ mol⁻¹.
  3. Explain why the enthalpy of combustion of methanol measured with a spirit burner is less exothermic than the data book value. Answer: heat is lost to the surroundings and apparatus, combustion is incomplete because of limited oxygen, some methanol evaporates without burning, and the experiment is not carried out under standard conditions.
  4. Use the bond enthalpies C–H 413, Cl–Cl 242 and C–Cl 328 kJ mol⁻¹, and H–Cl 432 kJ mol⁻¹, to calculate ΔH for CH4 + Cl2 → CH3Cl + HCl. Answer: bonds broken = 4(413) + 242 = 1894; bonds formed = 3(413) + 328 + 432 = 1999; ΔH = 1894 − 1999 = −105 kJ mol⁻¹.
  5. The standard enthalpy change of formation of ethyne, C2H2, is +227 kJ mol⁻¹ and that of benzene, C6H6, is +49 kJ mol⁻¹. Explain what these values show about the stability of the two compounds relative to their elements. Answer: both are endothermic relative to their elements, so both are thermodynamically unstable with respect to decomposition into carbon and hydrogen. Ethyne is much less stable than benzene, which is consistent with benzene's delocalised ring and with ethyne's tendency to polymerise or decompose.

Practise by writing the cycle before any numbers: a correctly drawn cycle makes the sign obvious. Then revise Kinetics, where activation energy and reaction profiles use the same enthalpy ideas to explain rate rather than feasibility.

title: IGCSE Biology (OxfordAQA): Ecology
content:
Ecology

An ecosystem is a community of organisms interacting with each other and with their physical surroundings, and almost every question about one is a question about energy or about a limit. Energy enters as sunlight, is captured by producers, and loses most of itself at every step up a food chain; organisms compete for the rest, and their adaptations decide who wins. This topic also contains two calculations that are easy marks if you keep the units straight — the efficiency of energy transfer and a population estimate from quadrats — and one cycle, carbon, that links every living thing to the atmosphere. The last subsection turns the same ideas on us: what happens to an ecosystem when a forest is cleared or a river is polluted.

1. Feeding relationships

Photosynthetic organisms are producers: they capture light energy and store it in glucose, which becomes the starting point of every food chain. Organisms that eat others are consumers, and decomposers break down dead material and return nutrients to the soil.

  • Primary consumer — eats a producer (a herbivore).
  • Secondary consumer — eats a primary consumer (a carnivore).
  • Tertiary consumer — eats a secondary consumer.
  • Decomposer — bacteria and fungi that break down dead organisms and waste, releasing minerals such as nitrates and carbon dioxide.

Each step is a trophic level. A food chain shows one route; a food web shows all of them, which is why removing one species from a web affects many others — that is interdependence. A pyramid of biomass shows the mass of living material at each level and is almost always widest at the bottom.

2. Energy transfer and efficiency

Only about 10 % of the energy at one trophic level is passed to the next. The rest is lost as heat from respiration, used in movement, lost in waste materials, or left in parts that are not eaten. This is why food chains rarely have more than four or five levels: there is simply not enough energy left.

efficiency = (energy transferred to the next level ÷ energy available at the previous level) × 100

Key: efficiency = the percentage of energy passed on (%); energy transferred = the energy in the organisms at the next trophic level (kJ); energy available = the energy in the organisms being eaten (kJ).

A pyramid of biomass is not the same as a pyramid of energy. Biomass is a snapshot of mass at one moment; energy flow is measured over time. A pyramid of biomass can occasionally be inverted — for example where the producers are tiny phytoplankton that reproduce very fast — while a pyramid of energy never is.

3. Adaptations, competition and interdependence

An adaptation is a feature that helps an organism survive in its habitat. Examiners want three words: the feature, the advantage, and the reason it matters.

  • Structural — a physical feature. A polar bear's thick fur and fat layer reduce heat loss; a cactus has spines instead of leaves to reduce water loss.
  • Behavioural — what the organism does. Desert animals are active at night to avoid the heat; some birds migrate to find food.
  • Functional — a physiological process. A camel conserves water by producing concentrated urine; some fish can change the amount of salt they excrete.

Competition happens when organisms need the same resource that is in short supply — light, water, space, food or a mate. Organisms that compete successfully are more likely to survive and reproduce, which is natural selection in one sentence. Extremophiles are adapted to conditions that would kill most life, such as high temperature, high salt or high pressure.

4. Sampling: quadrats and transects

You cannot count every organism, so ecologists sample. A quadrat is a square frame placed at random; counting within several quadrats gives an estimate for the whole area. A transect is a line across a habitat, with quadrats placed along it, used when conditions change from one place to another — for example from a path into a wood.

estimated population = (mean number per quadrat × total area) ÷ area of one quadrat

Key: estimated population = the total number in the habitat (individuals); mean per quadrat = the average count from the samples; total area = the area of the whole habitat (m²); area of one quadrat = the area covered by the frame (m²).

Random placement matters. Throwing the quadrat over the shoulder, or always placing it where the flowers are, produces a biased estimate — and "state one way to make the sampling more reliable" wants either random placement or a larger number of samples.

5. Worked example: population estimate and energy efficiency

A student places ten 0.25 m² quadrats in a 400 m² field and counts 4, 6, 5, 7, 3, 5, 4, 6, 5, 5 dandelions. Estimate the population.

mean per quadrat = 50 ÷ 10 = 5. Then estimated population = (5 × 400) ÷ 0.25 = 2 000 ÷ 0.25 = 8 000 dandelions.

Key: mean per quadrat = the total count divided by the number of quadrats; 400 m² = the area of the field; 0.25 m² = the area of one quadrat.

Now the energy side. If the grass in a field contains 80 000 kJ of energy and the rabbits eating it contain 8 000 kJ, the efficiency is (8 000 ÷ 80 000) × 100 = 10 %. The other 72 000 kJ was lost as heat from respiration, used in movement, or passed out in waste — and it is not available to the foxes.

6. The carbon cycle

Carbon moves between the atmosphere, living organisms, the soil and the oceans. The processes are few, and the exam asks you to name the one that moves carbon in a given direction.

  • Photosynthesis removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and stores the carbon in glucose.
  • Respiration releases carbon dioxide back to the atmosphere from plants, animals and decomposers.
  • Feeding passes carbon compounds along a food chain.
  • Decomposition releases carbon dioxide as microorganisms break down dead material.
  • Combustion of fossil fuels releases carbon that was locked away for millions of years, which is why it adds to the atmospheric store rather than recycling it quickly.

7. Decay

Decomposers break down dead material faster when the conditions suit them: warm, moist and aerobic. That is why compost heaps are kept damp and turned to add oxygen, and why food lasts longer in a freezer — cold slows the microorganisms down.

  • Temperature — warmer means faster decay, up to the point where the microorganisms are killed.
  • Water — decomposers need moisture; a dry compost heap barely decays.
  • Oxygen — most decomposers are aerobic, so turning a heap or leaving it open speeds decay.

The standard practical measures the rate of decay of milk or bread at different temperatures, using the time taken for an indicator to change colour. The point of the result is that decay is enzyme-controlled, so it has an optimum rather than simply rising with temperature forever.

8. Humans and their effects on the environment

The specification's biology-only subsection asks for the effects, and each effect is best remembered as a cause, a consequence and a cost to biodiversity.

  • Deforestation destroys habitats, reduces carbon dioxide uptake and can increase soil erosion and flooding.
  • Air pollution — sulfur dioxide from burning fossil fuels dissolves in rain to form acid rain, which damages leaves and kills aquatic life in acidified lakes.
  • Water pollution — fertiliser run-off adds nitrates, causing eutrophication: algae grow, block light, die, and their decomposition uses up oxygen, killing fish.
  • Land pollution — landfill takes land and releases methane; plastics persist for centuries because they are not biodegradable.
  • Greenhouse gases — carbon dioxide and methane trap heat; rising global temperature shifts habitats and raises sea levels.

Biodiversity is the variety of species and of the genetic variation within them. It matters because a more diverse ecosystem is more resilient: if one species fails, others can fill its role. Conservation — protected areas, breeding programmes, hedgerows and seed banks — is the response, and it works best when it protects a whole habitat rather than one animal.

9. Typical mistakes

  • Writing "energy is lost" without saying where: heat from respiration, movement, waste, uneaten parts.
  • Confusing a pyramid of biomass with a pyramid of energy, or claiming energy pyramids can be inverted.
  • Giving an adaptation without its advantage — "the cactus has spines" earns nothing on its own.
  • Sampling only where the plants are obvious, then describing the estimate as accurate.
  • Saying plants only take carbon dioxide out of the atmosphere. They also respire, day and night.
  • Describing eutrophication as "algae poison the water" rather than the oxygen being used up by decomposers.
  • Calling decay "rotting by chemicals" — it is microorganisms, and their enzymes, that do it.

10. Exam-style questions

  1. Explain why a food chain rarely contains more than five trophic levels. Answer: Only about 10 % of the energy is passed to the next level, the rest being lost as heat from respiration, in movement and in waste, so there is too little energy left for more levels.
  2. Grass contains 60 000 kJ and the cows eating it contain 6 600 kJ. Calculate the efficiency of energy transfer. Answer: efficiency = (6 600 ÷ 60 000) × 100 = 11 %.
  3. Give two adaptations of a polar bear and explain each. Answer: Thick fur traps a layer of warm air, reducing heat loss; a thick layer of fat insulates and stores energy for when food is scarce.
  4. A 0.5 m² quadrat is used 8 times in a 200 m² field, giving a mean of 6 plants. Estimate the population. Answer: (6 × 200) ÷ 0.5 = 2 400 plants.
  5. Describe how carbon dioxide is returned to the atmosphere from a dead tree. Answer: Decomposers such as fungi and bacteria break down the dead wood and respire, releasing carbon dioxide.
  6. Explain why a compost heap decays faster when it is turned regularly. Answer: Turning adds oxygen, and the decomposers are aerobic, so respiration and therefore decay are faster.
  7. Explain how fertiliser run-off can kill fish in a river. Answer: Nitrates cause algae to grow and cover the surface, blocking light so plants die; decomposers break them down and use up the dissolved oxygen, so fish suffocate.
  8. Why does deforestation reduce biodiversity? Answer: It removes the habitat and food sources of many species, so populations fall and some species disappear locally.

11. Revision checklist

  • I can define producer, consumer, decomposer and trophic level.
  • I can explain the 10 % rule and calculate efficiency.
  • I can give structural, behavioural and functional adaptations with their advantages.
  • I can describe quadrat and transect sampling and calculate a population estimate.
  • I can name every process that moves carbon and say which way it moves.
  • I can describe the conditions that speed up decay and explain why.
  • I can describe four human effects on ecosystems and their consequences.
  • I can explain why biodiversity makes an ecosystem more resilient.

title: Motion in a Circle and Gravity — Study Notes
content:
Motion in a circle and gravity

Edexcel International A Level Physics, A2: circular motion in Unit 4 (WPH14) and gravitational fields in Unit 5 (WPH15).

Circular motion

  • A body moving in a circle at constant speed has a centripetal acceleration of v²/r, directed towards the centre.
  • The centripetal force is F = mv²/r = mω²r, and it is provided by a real force such as tension, friction or gravity. It does no work on the body, because it is always perpendicular to the velocity.

Gravitational field

The gravitational field strength at a point is the force per unit mass placed at that point: g = F/m. Unit: N kg⁻¹. Field lines point towards the mass that creates the field.

Newton's law of gravitation

F = GMm/r², where r is measured from the centre of each point mass. Doubling the separation reduces the force to one quarter.

Gravitational field of a point mass

g = GM/r². Outside a uniform sphere, its field is the same as that of a point mass at its centre.

Gravitational potential

Gravitational potential at a point is the work done per unit mass in bringing a small mass from infinity to that point. It is always negative, is zero at infinity, and becomes more negative closer to the mass: V = −GM/r. Gravitational potential energy of a mass m is Ep = mV.

Worked example: a 2.0 kg object moves in a circle of radius 0.50 m at 3.0 m s⁻¹. The centripetal force is F = mv²/r = (2.0 × 3.0²) ÷ 0.50 = 36 N.

Exam tips: use r as the distance from the centre, not the surface. State that gravitational potential is negative and rises to zero at infinity. Field strength and potential are different quantities: do not mix their units.

Gravitational potential and escape velocity

Gravitational potential at a point is the work done per unit mass in moving a small mass from infinity to that point, so φ = -GM/r. Potential is negative because work must be done against gravity to remove a mass to infinity. The change in gravitational potential energy between two radii is GMm(1/r1 - 1/r2). A body escapes a planet when its kinetic energy equals the potential energy needed to reach infinity, which gives the escape speed v = √(2GM/r).

Exam tip: use the zero of potential at infinity, and keep the sign of the potential negative in every calculation.

Worked example: orbital speed and period

A satellite of mass m orbits a planet of mass M at radius r. Gravity provides the centripetal force: GMm/r² = mv²/r, so v = √(GM/r). The orbital period follows from T = 2πr/v, which gives T² = (4π²/GM) r³. This is Kepler's third law in the form used at AS level.

Example: a satellite at radius 7.0 × 10⁶ m around a planet of mass 6.0 × 10²⁴ kg. The speed is v = √((6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 6.0 × 10²⁴)/(7.0 × 10⁶)) = √(5.7 × 10⁷) ≈ 7.6 × 10³ m s⁻¹. The period is T = 2π × 7.0 × 10⁶ / 7.6 × 10³ ≈ 5.8 × 10³ s, about 97 minutes.

Geostationary orbit

A geostationary satellite has a period of exactly 24 hours and orbits in the equatorial plane. Its radius is fixed by the period, so every geostationary satellite has the same radius and speed, regardless of its mass. Its orbit must lie above the equator, which is why communication satellites sit over one point on the ground.

Why orbiting bodies are weightless

Astronauts in orbit are not outside the pull of gravity; gravity supplies their centripetal acceleration. The spacecraft and its occupants fall freely together, so there is no contact force, and the apparent weightlessness follows from that free fall.

Circular motion: banked roads and conical pendulums

On a banked road with no friction, the horizontal component of the normal reaction supplies the centripetal force: N sin θ = mv²/r, while the vertical component balances weight: N cos θ = mg. Dividing gives tan θ = v²/(rg). The design speed depends only on the angle, the radius and g, not on the mass of the vehicle.

  • For a conical pendulum, tension has a vertical component that balances weight and a horizontal component that supplies the centripetal force.
  • Always draw a free-body diagram and resolve forces into components along the radius and the vertical before writing equations.
  • The centripetal force is not an extra force on the diagram; name the real forces that supply it.

Common errors that lose marks

  • Including centripetal force as a separate force in the free-body diagram, which double-counts the force.
  • Using the planet's surface radius where the question gives the distance from the centre, or the reverse.
  • Stating that the satellite is stationary in orbit. It is moving at constant speed, so its velocity changes direction continuously and it is accelerating.

title: AS Level Mathematics: Proof
content:
AS Level Mathematics: Proof

Proof is the difference between "it works for these numbers" and "it must work for all". AS proof covers four methods — direct proof, proof by exhaustion, proof by counter-example (disproof) and proof by deduction from definitions — plus the algebra of odd, even and consecutive numbers, and completing the square as a tool for inequalities. This note builds each method from zero with templates, full worked examples and the precise wording examiners expect, because proof marks are awarded for structure as much as for algebra.

The language of proof

TermMeaning
ConjectureA statement believed true but not yet proved
TheoremA statement that has been proved
ProofA logical argument from known facts to the conclusion
DisproofOne counter-example that makes the statement false
ExhaustionChecking every possible case

A single counter-example disproves a "for all" statement; no number of examples proves one. That asymmetry is the heart of the topic and the first thing examiners test.

Odd, even and consecutive numbers

even: 2n           (n integer)
odd:  2n + 1       (or 2n - 1)
consecutive integers: n, n + 1, n + 2
consecutive even: 2n, 2n + 2
consecutive odd: 2n + 1, 2n + 3

These forms are not optional decoration: a proof about parity must start from them, because "let the number be x" proves nothing about oddness.

Worked example 1. Prove that the sum of two consecutive odd numbers is a multiple of 4.

let the numbers be 2n + 1 and 2n + 3
sum = 4n + 4 = 4(n + 1)
which is a multiple of 4 for every integer n

Worked example 2. Prove that the product of two odd numbers is odd.

let them be 2m + 1 and 2n + 1
product = 4mn + 2m + 2n + 1 = 2(2mn + m + n) + 1
of the form 2k + 1 with k = 2mn + m + n, an integer
so the product is odd

Worked example 3. Prove that the difference between the squares of consecutive integers is the sum of the integers.

(n + 1)² - n² = n² + 2n + 1 - n² = 2n + 1 = n + (n + 1)

Direct proof

Start from the definitions, manipulate algebraically, and arrive at the required form. Write the conclusion explicitly ("hence ... as required") so the argument is closed.

Worked example. Prove that if x is odd then x² is odd.

let x = 2n + 1
x² = 4n² + 4n + 1 = 2(2n² + 2n) + 1
which is 2k + 1, hence odd

Worked example 2. Prove that the sum of any three consecutive integers is divisible by 3.

n + (n + 1) + (n + 2) = 3n + 3 = 3(n + 1)
which is divisible by 3

Proof by exhaustion

When the domain is small enough to list, check every case. The proof is only complete if the list is genuinely exhaustive — state why nothing is missed.

Worked example. Prove that every prime between 20 and 30 is the sum of two square numbers or state otherwise.

primes in the range: 23, 29
23 = 9 + 14 (not two squares); 25 + (-2)? no
23 = 4 + 19? no; squares below 23: 1, 4, 9, 16
1 + 16 = 17; 4 + 16 = 20; 9 + 16 = 25; 4 + 9 = 13
so 23 is not a sum of two squares; 29: 4 + 25 = 29  yes
conclusion: the conjecture fails for 23; the true statement is
"29 is the only prime between 20 and 30 expressible as a sum of two squares"

Worked example 2. Prove that n² + n is even for all integers n by exhaustion of the two parity cases.

case 1: n even, n = 2k → n² + n = 4k² + 2k = 2(2k² + k), even
case 2: n odd, n = 2k + 1 → 4k² + 4k + 1 + 2k + 1 = 4k² + 6k + 2
        = 2(2k² + 3k + 1), even
both cases covered, so the statement holds for all integers

The two-case parity split is exhaustion in its most common exam form: every integer is even or odd, so the cases exhaust the domain.

Disproof by counter-example

To disprove a "for all" claim, produce one case where it fails and show the arithmetic. One is enough; a hundred confirming cases prove nothing.

Worked example. Disprove: "if n² is a multiple of 4 then n is a multiple of 4."

try n = 6: n² = 36, a multiple of 4? 36/4 = 9, yes
but 6 is not a multiple of 4
so n = 6 is a counter-example and the statement is false

Worked example 2. Disprove: "n² − n + 11 is prime for all positive integers n."

n = 11: 121 - 11 + 11 = 121 = 11², not prime
counter-example n = 11 disproves the conjecture

Proof by completing the square

Inequalities about quadratics are proved by completing the square: a squared term is never negative, so the expression's minimum (or maximum) is visible.

x² + bx + c = (x + b/2)² + c - b²/4
since (x + b/2)² >= 0, the minimum value is c - b²/4

Worked example 1. Prove that x² + 4x + 7 > 0 for all real x.

x² + 4x + 7 = (x + 2)² + 3
(x + 2)² >= 0, so the expression is at least 3 > 0

Worked example 2. Prove that 2x − x² ≤ 1 for all real x.

2x - x² = -(x² - 2x) = -[(x - 1)² - 1] = 1 - (x - 1)²
since (x - 1)² >= 0, this is at most 1

Worked example 3. Find the values of k for which x² + kx + 9 > 0 for all x.

completing the square: (x + k/2)² + 9 - k²/4 > 0 for all x
requires the constant term positive: 9 - k²/4 > 0
k² < 36  →  -6 < k < 6

That last question is the discriminant argument in disguise: "always positive" means no real roots, so b² − 4ac < 0. Either method earns the marks; the completing-the-square route often reads more clearly.

Divisibility and multiples

A statement of the form "is a multiple of k" is proved by putting the expression in the shape k times an integer. Do the algebra first, then identify the factor; never assume the factor exists.

Worked example. Prove that for any integer n, n(n + 1)(n + 2) is a multiple of 6.

among any three consecutive integers there is at least one even
number and exactly one multiple of 3
so the product contains a factor 2 and a factor 3
since 2 and 3 are coprime, the product is divisible by 6

Worked example 2. Prove that 3^(2n) - 1 is a multiple of 8 for positive integers n.

3^(2n) - 1 = 9^n - 1 = (9 - 1)(9^(n-1) + ... + 1)
= 8 x (a positive integer), so divisible by 8

Worked example 3. Prove that the sum of five consecutive integers is always divisible by 5.

n + (n+1) + (n+2) + (n+3) + (n+4) = 5n + 10 = 5(n + 2)

Proof by contradiction: the irrationality of root 2

Contradiction assumes the statement is false, derives an impossibility, and concludes the statement is true. The classic example is examinable and worth knowing in full.

assume √(2) is rational: √(2) = p/q in lowest terms, p, q integers
square: 2 = p²/q²  →  p² = 2q²
so p² is even  →  p is even (a square is even only if its root is)
write p = 2k: 4k² = 2q²  →  q² = 2k²
so q² is even  →  q is even
but p and q cannot both be even if p/q is in lowest terms
contradiction  →  √(2) is irrational

The two logical hinges are that an even square implies an even root, and that "lowest terms" forbids a common factor of 2. State both; the marks live in them.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Parity) Prove that the sum of an odd and an even number is odd. Answer: (2m + 1) + 2n = 2(m + n) + 1, which is odd.
  2. (Consecutive) Prove that the product of two consecutive integers is even. Answer: n(n + 1): one of n, n + 1 is even, so the product is even.
  3. (Direct) Prove that (3n + 1)² − 1 is a multiple of 3. Answer: 9n² + 6n = 3(3n² + 2n).
  4. (Counter-example) Disprove "all primes are odd". Answer: 2 is prime and even.
  5. (Counter-example) Disprove "n² + 1 is prime for all n". Answer: n = 3 gives 10, not prime.
  6. (Completing the square) Prove x² − 6x + 10 > 0. Answer: (x − 3)² + 1 ≥ 1 > 0.
  7. (Exhaustion) Prove that n³ − n is divisible by 6 for n = 1, 2, 3, 4. Answer: 0, 6, 24, 60 — each divisible by 6 (a finite check is exhaustion).
  8. (Discriminant) Find k so that x² + 2kx + 4 = 0 has no real roots. Answer: 4k² − 16 < 0 → k² < 4 → −2 < k < 2.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Proving by example: two or three numbers never prove a "for all" statement; the argument must use algebra with a general n.
  • Not defining the variable: "let n be an integer" and "let n be odd, so n = 2k + 1" are required openings; an undefined x cannot carry a parity argument.
  • Assuming what you must prove: working backwards from the result to a true statement does not prove the original unless every step is reversible — say so if it is.
  • Counter-example not checked: show the arithmetic that makes the case fail; asserting "n = 6 fails" without the calculation loses the mark.
  • Incomplete exhaustion: if the domain has cases you did not cover (e.g. negatives, zero), the proof is incomplete — state the cases and why they exhaust.
  • Completing the square sign: a negative leading coefficient flips the inequality; factor out the minus first.
  • Conclusion missing: close with "hence ... as required"; an unclosed argument reads as unfinished.
  • Notation: write ≡ for identities and ⇒ for implications correctly; mixing them muddles the logic examiners follow.

The three shapes of a proof — and how to choose between them

A proof is not a longer calculation; it is an argument with a shape. There are only three shapes in this specification, each fits a different kind of statement, and recognising which one a question wants is most of the mark.

Shape 1: direct proof. Start from the definition, do algebra, arrive at the thing you were asked to show. It is the right choice whenever the statement is about all numbers of a kind, because a variable stands for all of them at once. "The sum of two consecutive integers is odd" is three lines: let them be n and n + 1, then n + (n + 1) = 2n + 1, which is odd by definition.

Shape 2: exhaustion. When there are finitely many cases, check them all and say so. It is a real proof — but only because the list is complete.

Shape 3: contradiction. When the statement denies something ("there is no greatest prime", "√2 is irrational"), assume the opposite and show it cannot stand. The template above is the whole method; the work is entirely in step 2.

The sentence that makes step 2 work. Whatever you deduce must contradict something already established — a definition, a theorem you have proved, or the assumption you made in step 1. In the √2 proof the contradiction is that a fraction is shown to be reducible when it was written in lowest terms, and the words that carry it are "but this contradicts the assumption that a and b have no common factor".

Why a counter-example is not a proof. One example can disprove a universal statement and can never prove one: "n² + n + 41 is prime for n = 1, 2, 3" is true and worthless, because n = 41 breaks it. If a question says "prove", an example earns nothing; if it says "disprove", one counter-example is a complete answer.

Worked example. Prove that if n² is even then n is even.

Suppose instead that n is odd. Then n = 2k + 1 for some integer k, so
n² = (2k + 1)² = 4k² + 4k + 1 = 2(2k² + 2k) + 1
which is odd, because it is one more than a multiple of 2. But we were told n² is even, and a number cannot be both odd and even — a contradiction. Therefore n cannot be odd, so n is even. ∎

Two details earn marks that students routinely drop: stating the form of the variable ("n = 2k + 1 for some integer k", not "n is odd so write it as something odd"), and naming the contradiction rather than stopping at the algebra. The ∎ is optional; the sentence that says what was contradicted is not.

Where marks are lost. Assuming what you are proving (writing "n² = 2m and n = 2k" straight away). Using the converse by accident — proving "n even ⇒ n² even" when the question asked the other way round. And ending with "therefore it is true" without saying what is true and why the assumption failed.

title: IGCSE Chemistry: Electrochemistry
content:
IGCSE Chemistry: Electrochemistry

Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry 0620 (2026–2028), Extended route, Topic 4 Electrochemistry: statement 4.1 Electrolysis and 4.2 Hydrogen–oxygen fuel cells. Electrolysis is chemistry driven by electricity — forced electron movement — and every question asks three things: what is the electrolyte, what forms at each electrode, and why. The product rules below are derived from ion behaviour, not memorised lists, and every half-equation is balanced for atoms and charge.

What electrolysis is

Electrolysis is the breakdown of an ionic compound (molten or aqueous) by passing electricity through it. Vocabulary: the electrolyte is the ionic compound that conducts when molten or in solution (ions free to move); the cathode is the negative electrode (reduction: cations are attracted to it); the anode is the positive electrode (oxidation: anions are attracted to it). Electrons flow through the wires; ions carry the charge through the liquid.

The electron bookkeeping, spelled out:

  CATHODE (negative): positive ions (cations) drift here.
    Each cation GAINS electrons -> reduction:  Mⁿ⁺ + n e⁻ -> M
  ANODE (positive): negative ions (anions) drift here.
    Each anion LOSES electrons -> oxidation:  X⁻ -> X + e⁻

  Mnemonic that never fails: OIL RIG
    Oxidation Is Loss (of electrons) - at the ANODE
    Reduction Is Gain - at the CATHODE

  And the electrode names:
    PANC - Positive Anode, Negative Cathode.

Molten electrolysis

Case study: molten lead(II) bromide, PbBr₂ (electrolysis of the melt)

  Ions present: Pb²⁺ and Br⁻

  CATHODE: Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ -> Pb(l)    [lead metal, grey liquid]
    OBSERVATION: grey molten lead collects.
  ANODE:   2Br⁻ -> Br₂(g) + 2e⁻    [bromine vapour]
    OBSERVATION: orange-brown vapour with choking smell.

  Overall: PbBr₂ -> Pb + Br₂  (electrons supplied by the circuit)

General molten-binary rule: the METAL forms at the cathode (reduced);
the NON-METAL forms at the anode (oxidised).

Aqueous electrolysis: the competition

In solution, water provides H⁺ and OH⁻ alongside the salt's ions, so both electrodes have competing species. The rules, applied in order:

  • Cathode: the less reactive ion is discharged (e.g. copper over hydrogen in copper sulfate); if the metal is above hydrogen (Na, K, Ca, Mg, Al), hydrogen is discharged from water.
  • Anode: concentrated halide solutions give halogen (Cl₂ from concentrated NaCl); otherwise (sulfate, nitrate, dilute solutions) hydroxide/oxygen is discharged from water.
Three standard aqueous cases, worked:

1. Concentrated sodium chloride solution (brine):
   CATHODE: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ -> H₂(g)         [hydrogen - sodium is too reactive]
   ANODE:   2Cl⁻ -> Cl₂(g) + 2e⁻        [chlorine - concentrated halide]
   Left in solution: NaOH (sodium hydroxide) - a useful by-product.
   Uses: chlorine (water treatment, plastics), hydrogen (ammonia), NaOH.

2. Dilute sulfuric acid (electrolysis of water):
   CATHODE: 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ -> 2H₂
   ANODE:   2H₂O -> O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻  (or 4OH⁻ -> O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻)
   Volume ratio H₂ : O₂ = 2 : 1 (the classic exam volume question).

3. Aqueous copper(II) sulfate with INERT (platinum/graphite) electrodes:
   CATHODE: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ -> Cu(s)        [copper coats the electrode]
   ANODE:   4OH⁻ -> O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻    [oxygen bubbles; solution goes
                                         acidic as Cu²⁺ removed and H⁺
                                         remains from water]

   With COPPER electrodes (electroplating setup):
   CATHODE: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ -> Cu          [object being plated gains copper]
   ANODE:   Cu -> Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻          [copper anode dissolves, refilling
                                        the solution - the classic
                                        electroplating arrangement]

Ionic half-equation discipline: atoms balanced first, then charges balanced
with electrons on the correct side (right for oxidation, left for reduction).
ElectrolyteElectrodesCathode productAnode product
Molten PbBr₂InertLead (Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb)Bromine (2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻)
Conc. NaCl(aq)InertHydrogen (2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂)Chlorine (2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻)
Dilute H₂SO₄(aq)InertHydrogenOxygen (2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻)
CuSO₄(aq)InertCopper (Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu)Oxygen (from OH⁻)
CuSO₄(aq)Copper anodeCopperNone — anode dissolves (Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻)

Electroplating

Electroplating coats an object with a thin layer of another metal (cutlery with chromium, jewellery with silver, cans with tin) — for appearance, corrosion resistance and reduced cost. The object is the cathode; the plating metal is the anode; the electrolyte contains the plating metal's ions. Its purpose in the syllabus: protection, looks and cost.

Hydrogen–oxygen fuel cells

The fuel cell reaction, both half-equations:

  At the anode (hydrogen side):  2H₂ -> 4H⁺ + 4e⁻
  At the cathode (oxygen side):  O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ -> 2H₂O
  Overall:  2H₂ + O₂ -> 2H₂O     (electrical energy + heat - a redox
                                   reaction whose electrons travel through
                                   an external circuit instead of direct
                                   contact)

  Key point: the ONLY product is WATER - no CO₂ at the point of use.

Comparison with petrol engines (the "advantages and disadvantages" question):
  + no pollutants at point of use (only water),
  + more efficient than combustion engines (no thermal cycle limits),
  + refuel in minutes (unlike battery charging).
  - hydrogen storage is hard (high pressure/low temperature; bulky tanks),
  - hydrogen is usually made from natural gas (so CO₂ is emitted at the
    production stage) unless made by electrolysis with renewables,
  - fuel cells and hydrogen infrastructure are expensive.

Worked example: predicting products systematically

Question: predict all products of electrolysis of aqueous copper(II) sulfate
with copper electrodes, and write the equations.

Step 1 - ions in solution: Cu²⁺, SO₄²⁻, and from water H⁺, OH⁻.
Step 2 - cathode (reduction): competing Cu²⁺ and H⁺; copper is BELOW
  hydrogen in the reactivity series, so Cu²⁺ is discharged:
    Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ -> Cu
Step 3 - anode (oxidation): sulfate is not discharged; OH⁻ from water would
  give O₂ - BUT the anode is copper, and the copper anode OXIDISES first:
    Cu -> Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻
Step 4 - overall: copper is transferred from anode to cathode (electroplating
  geometry). The solution concentration stays constant (Cu²⁺ lost at the
  cathode is replaced from the anode).
Observations: cathode gains mass (reddish coating); anode loses mass.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Swapping electrodes: cathode is negative (reduction of cations); anode is positive (oxidation of anions) — PANC and OIL RIG together prevent this.
  • Putting electrons on the wrong side of half-equations (reduction gains them — left; oxidation loses — right) or leaving charge unbalanced.
  • Ignoring the "concentrated" in brine questions: dilute NaCl gives oxygen at the anode, not chlorine.
  • Discharging the reactive metal (Na) instead of hydrogen at the cathode in aqueous solutions.
  • Forgetting the electrodes' material in aqueous cases: copper anodes dissolve rather than producing oxygen.
  • Claiming fuel cells produce "no products" — water is the product; and ignoring that hydrogen production may still emit CO₂.
  • Misreading gas volumes: electrolysis of dilute acid gives H₂:O₂ = 2:1 by volume (twice as much hydrogen).

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 4, 3 marks). Define electrolysis and name the electrode where reduction occurs.

Answer: Electrolysis is the decomposition of an ionic compound (molten or aqueous) by passing an electric current through it. Reduction occurs at the cathode (the negative electrode), where cations gain electrons.

Question 2 (Paper 4, 5 marks). Write the half-equations and observations for the electrolysis of molten lead(II) bromide.
