Oil (about 0.8 g cm⁻³) floats on water; syrup (about 1.4 g cm⁻³) sinks below it. A carefully poured column of syrup, water and oil layers in the order syrup, water, oil, and a grape that is denser than water but less dense than syrup will float at the syrup–water boundary. The rule is the same in every case: each substance finds the level where the density below it is greater and the density above it is smaller.

Pressure: force spread over area

Pressure is what a force does when it is spread over a surface. The same force over a smaller area produces a greater pressure, which is why a drawing pin drives into a board point-first and why snowshoes stop you sinking into snow. A sharp knife cuts because the small edge area turns a modest force into enormous pressure.

pressure = force / area        p = F / A
  • p: pressure in pascals (Pa). One pascal is one newton per square metre (1 Pa = 1 N m⁻²). Pressure is a scalar.
  • F: force in newtons (N), acting perpendicular to the surface.
  • A: area in square metres (m²) over which the force acts.

Area must be in square metres: 1 cm² = 0.0001 m², so 25 cm² = 0.0025 m². Atmospheric pressure at sea level is about 100 000 Pa (100 kPa), which presses on every square metre with a force of 100 000 N — the reason a vacuum flask is crushed if the air is pumped out, and the reason the body needs equal pressure inside as well.

Pressure is transmitted through liquids: a force applied at one point in a confined liquid is passed on undiminished in every direction, which is the principle of hydraulic brakes and car jacks, where a small force on a small piston gives a large force on a large piston because the pressure is the same on both.

Pressure in a liquid

Supplement. The pressure in a liquid rises with depth because the liquid above presses down. For a liquid of uniform density the increase is:

pressure due to a liquid column = density x gravitational field strength x depth        p = rho g h
  • p: pressure in pascals (Pa); rho: density of the liquid in kilograms per cubic metre (kg m⁻³).
  • g: gravitational field strength in newtons per kilogram (N kg⁻¹, use the value given in the question).
  • h: vertical depth below the surface in metres (m). Depth is measured vertically, not along a slope or the container wall.

Only the vertical height of the column counts, which is why the pressure at the bottom of a swimming pool depends only on the water's depth, not on the shape or the width of the pool. The total pressure at depth includes the atmosphere pressing on the surface: total pressure = atmospheric pressure + ρgh. A diver at 20 m in fresh water experiences ρgh = 1000 × 9.81 × 20 = 196 200 Pa from the water alone, about three times atmospheric pressure in total, which is why the ears must be equalised during descent. A manometer measures a pressure difference by the height difference of a liquid column; a barometer measures atmospheric pressure by the height of a mercury column (about 760 mm at sea level).

Worked example: density and pressure together

A rectangular brass block measures 4.0 cm × 5.0 cm × 10.0 cm and has a mass of 1.20 kg.

volume = 0.040 x 0.050 x 0.100 = 0.00020 m3
density = mass / volume = 1.20 / 0.00020 = 6000 kg m-3  (6.0 g cm-3)

Notice the unit conversion before the division: centimetres were converted to metres first, so the density comes out in kg m⁻³ directly. The same calculation in laboratory units gives the same answer: the volume is 4.0 × 5.0 × 10.0 = 200 cm³ and the mass is 1200 g, so the density is 1200 / 200 = 6.0 g cm⁻³, which converts to 6000 kg m⁻³. Keep the arithmetic in one unit system end to end and the conversion error cannot appear.

Now the block rests on a table on its largest face. The force is its weight, 1.20 × 9.81 = 11.8 N, spread over 5.0 cm × 10.0 cm = 0.0050 m²:

pressure = F / A = 11.8 / 0.0050 = 2350 Pa

Turned onto its smallest face, the area is 4.0 × 5.0 = 0.0020 m² and the pressure rises to 5875 Pa — the same weight, a smaller area, a larger pressure. Finally, the pressure 2.0 m below the surface of a fresh-water lake is ρgh = 1000 × 9.81 × 2.0 = 19 620 Pa, about 20 kPa above atmospheric pressure.

Common mistakes

  • Dividing by mass instead of volume, or reversing the density equation. Density is mass over volume; the heavy object with the same volume has the higher density.
  • Forgetting to convert g cm⁻³ to kg m⁻³ (multiply by 1000) or centimetres to metres before using SI equations. A volume in cm³ must become m³ by dividing by 10⁶.
  • Using area in cm² in p = F/A. The pascal is a newton per square metre, so the area must be in m².
  • Measuring h along the slope of a container or along the wall; depth is the vertical distance below the free surface.
  • Ignoring the atmosphere when asked for the total pressure at a depth: total pressure is atmospheric plus the liquid contribution.
  • Assuming heavy objects sink and light ones float; it is density, not mass, that decides. A huge ship floats on air-filled hull volume.
  • Treating density as a vector or attaching a direction to pressure; both are scalars.
  • Quoting more than two significant figures from readings taken with a ruler or a measuring cylinder, ignoring the precision of the apparatus.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 4, 3 marks). A glass block of mass 150 g has dimensions 5.0 cm × 4.0 cm × 2.0 cm. Calculate its density in g cm⁻³ and in kg m⁻³.

Answer: Volume = 5.0 × 4.0 × 2.0 = 40 cm³. Density = 150 / 40 = 3.75 g cm⁻³ ≈ 3.8 g cm⁻³. In SI units: 3.75 × 1000 = 3750 kg m⁻³.

Question 2 (Paper 4, 3 marks). A student stands on one foot; her weight of 500 N acts on an area of 0.015 m². Calculate the pressure, and state what happens when she stands on both feet with a total area of 0.030 m².

Answer: p = F/A = 500 / 0.015 = 33 000 Pa (33 kPa). On both feet the area doubles, so the pressure halves to about 17 000 Pa. The force is unchanged; only the area changes.

Question 3 (Paper 2 style). An object floats with half its volume submerged in water of density 1000 kg m⁻³. Its density is: A 2000 kg m⁻³; B 1000 kg m⁻³; C 500 kg m⁻³; D zero. Answer: C. Floating means the average density is less than the liquid's; an object that floats with half its volume submerged has an average density of 500 kg m⁻³.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Calculate the pressure due to the water at a depth of 3.0 m in a lake, and the total pressure at that depth. Take g = 10 N kg⁻¹ and atmospheric pressure as 100 kPa.

Answer: p = ρgh = 1000 × 10 × 3.0 = 30 000 Pa = 30 kPa. Total pressure = 100 kPa + 30 kPa = 130 kPa.

Question 5 (Paper 6 style). Describe how you would determine the density of an irregular stone that is denser than water.

Answer: Measure the mass of the dry stone on a balance. Partly fill a measuring cylinder with water and record the volume at eye level with the meniscus bottom. Lower the stone in gently (tied with thread if needed) and record the new volume. The stone's volume is the difference. Density is mass divided by the volume change. Repeat the volume readings and average to reduce random error, and check that no water is splashed out or carried away on the stone.

Question 6 (Paper 4, 3 marks). Explain why a steel needle sinks in water while a steel ship of 10 000 tonnes floats.

Answer: Steel has a density of about 7800 kg m⁻³, far greater than water, so a solid needle sinks. The ship's hull encloses a large volume of air, so the average density of the ship and the air inside it is much less than 1000 kg m⁻³. The ship therefore floats and displaces a weight of water equal to its own weight.

Density decides what floats and pressure decides what pushes; the next stop is the particle model that explains both when matter is heated.

Equations and symbols

Density and pressure share one theme: a quantity spread over a volume or an area. Every equation below is a ratio, so the units of the two quantities must match before dividing.

Density

ρ = m / V
Key: ρ (rho) = density (kg/m³ or g/cm³); m = mass (kg or g); V = volume (m³ or cm³). 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³.

ρ(water) = 1.0 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³
Key: the reference value that decides floating and sinking for most questions; a body denser than this sinks in water.

V = m / ρ
Key: the same relation rearranged to find a volume (m³ or cm³) from a mass (kg or g) and a density. Useful when a question gives the mass of displaced water.

Pressure on a surface

p = F / A
Key: p = pressure (Pa, where 1 Pa = 1 N/m²); F = force acting perpendicular to the surface (N); A = area of contact (m²). Halving the area doubles the pressure for the same force, which is the whole physics of a sharp blade.

F = pA
Key: F = force on a surface (N); p = pressure (Pa); A = area (m²).

1 kPa = 1000 Pa and 1 MPa = 1 × 10⁶ Pa
Key: prefixes applied to the pascal; atmospheric pressure is about 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa, which is 100 kPa.

Pressure in a liquid

p = ρgh
Key: p = pressure due to the liquid (Pa); ρ (rho) = density of the liquid (kg/m³); g = 9.8 N/kg; h = depth below the surface (m). The pressure depends on depth and density only — not on the shape or width of the container.

Δp = ρgΔh
Key: Δp = pressure difference between two depths (Pa); Δh = vertical separation of the two points (m). This is the equation behind a manometer reading and behind the pressure on a diver's eardrum.

F₁ / A₁ = F₂ / A₂
Key: F₁, F₂ = forces on the input and output pistons (N); A₁, A₂ = their areas (m² or cm²). The pressure is transmitted unchanged, so a larger area gives a larger force — the hydraulic press.

Upthrust and floating

U = ρ(fluid) × V(displaced) × g
Key: U = upthrust (N); ρ(fluid) = density of the fluid (kg/m³); V(displaced) = volume of fluid pushed aside (m³); g = 9.8 N/kg. This is Archimedes' principle written as an equation.

floating: ρ(object) (less than) ρ(fluid)
Key: ρ(object) = the object's average density, including any trapped air (kg/m³). A steel ship floats because its average density is below water's, not because steel is light.

V(submerged) / V(total) = ρ(object) / ρ(fluid)
Key: V(submerged) = volume below the surface (m³); V(total) = whole volume (m³). A body floating half-submerged in water has half water's density, about 500 kg/m³.

sinking: weight (greater than) maximum upthrust
Key: weight = mg (N); maximum upthrust = the upthrust when the body is fully submerged. A body sinks when its density exceeds the fluid's, because even fully submerged the upthrust cannot reach its weight.

title: Probability Distributions — Study Notes
content:
Discrete Random Variables

Probability Distributions

A discrete random variable X takes values xᵢ with probabilities pᵢ where each pᵢ ≥ 0 and Σpᵢ = 1. A probability distribution can be given as a table, a formula, or a function. Any missing probability is found by subtraction.

Example: X = number of heads in 2 fair tosses: P(0) = 1/4, P(1) = 1/2, P(2) = 1/4.

Expectation

The mean of X is

  • E(X) = Σxᵢpᵢ

It is a weighted average — the long-run average value over many repetitions. E(X) need not equal any value X can actually take.

Variance

  • Var(X) = E(X²) − (E(X))²

where E(X²) = Σxᵢ²pᵢ — square the values before multiplying by probabilities. The standard deviation is √Var(X).

Linear Transforms

For constants a and b:

  • E(aX + b) = a·E(X) + b and Var(aX + b) = a²·Var(X)

Adding a constant shifts but does not spread; multiplying scales the spread by |a|.

Independent Variables

If X and Y are independent: E(X + Y) = E(X) + E(Y) and Var(X + Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y). The addition rule for expectation always holds; the variance addition needs independence. The same applies to differences: Var(X − Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) — the subtraction does not cancel spread.

Exam tips: first verify Σp = 1 in any given table. Write E(X²) and (E(X))² separately; merging them is the most common exam error. In games of chance, set the expected profit to zero to find a fair entry fee.

Exam method: discrete distributions

A discrete probability distribution gives P(X = x) for each value x. Each probability lies between 0 and 1, and the probabilities sum to 1. Use the sum to find an unknown constant before calculating any other probability.

The expected value is E(X) = Σ x P(X = x), and E(X²) = Σ x² P(X = x). The variance is Var(X) = E(X²) − [E(X)]². Set out the values, probabilities and products in a table to keep the working clear.

For a function of X, such as Y = 2X + 3, the expected value is E(Y) = 2E(X) + 3. The variance changes as Var(2X + 3) = 4 Var(X), because adding a constant does not change the spread.

When a question asks for P(X ≤ x) or P(X ≥ x), add the probabilities for the values in the range.

Exam cue: Check that the probabilities sum to 1 before reporting any expected value, because a missing or wrong probability makes the rest of the answer wrong.

Worked example: expectation and variance of a discrete variable

Let X take the values 0, 1, 2 and 3 with probabilities 0.1, 0.4, 0.3 and 0.2. The expectation is E(X) = 0(0.1) + 1(0.4) + 2(0.3) + 3(0.2) = 0 + 0.4 + 0.6 + 0.6 = 1.6. To find the variance, first find E(X²) = 0 + 0.4 + 1.2 + 1.8 = 3.4, then Var(X) = E(X²) − [E(X)]² = 3.4 − 2.56 = 0.84. Calculating E(X²) directly and subtracting the square of the mean is quicker than summing squared deviations, and it is the method to use when the probabilities are given as a table.

Checking a probability distribution

Every probability must lie between 0 and 1 inclusive, and the probabilities must sum to 1. If a question gives an unknown probability, use the sum to find it before calculating any expectation. Writing the check on the page shows the examiner that the distribution is valid, and it protects you from losing the later method marks when a slip appears in the first line.

The binomial distribution

If X is the number of successes in n independent trials, each with success probability p, then X follows a binomial distribution. Its mean is np and its variance is np(1 − p). The probability of exactly r successes is the binomial coefficient multiplied by p to the power r and by (1 − p) to the power n − r. State the conditions of independence and constant probability when you use this model.

title: AS Level Mathematics: Circular Measure
content:
AS Level Mathematics: Circular Measure

Radians measure angles by the arc they cut: one radian is the angle subtended when the arc equals the radius. That definition makes every circle formula simpler — arc length becomes s = rθ and sector area becomes ½r²θ, with no 360 in sight. This note builds the topic from zero: the radian definition and conversions, arc length and sector area with derivations, the segment area formula, and the applied problems (belts, pendulums, cones) that combine circular measure with trigonometry. Every worked example keeps the calculator in radian mode, which is the first habit this topic demands.

Radians and conversion

one full turn = 2 π radians = 360 degrees
π radians = 180 degrees

degrees → radians: multiply by π/180
radians → degrees: multiply by 180/π

common values: 30 ° = π/6, 45 ° = π/4,
60 ° = π/3, 90 ° = π/2, 180 ° = π

Worked example. Convert 150° to radians and 2.4 radians to degrees.

150 x π/180 = 5 π/6 = 2.618 rad
2.4 × 180/π = 137.5 °

Why radians: the arc length formula s = rθ only works when θ is in radians. In degrees the same arc is (θ/360) × 2πr — the same quantity, but with the conversion built in.

Arc length and sector area

arc length: s = r θ
sector area: A = (1/2) r² θ
perimeter of a sector: s + 2r

(θ in radians, r in the same length unit as s)

Worked example 1. A sector has radius 8 cm and angle 1.5 radians. Find the arc length and area.

s = r θ = 8 × 1.5 = 12 cm
A = (1/2) r² θ = 0.5 × 64 × 1.5 = 48 cm²

Worked example 2 (perimeter). Find the perimeter of the same sector.

perimeter = arc + 2 radii = 12 + 16 = 28 cm

Worked example 3 (working backwards). A sector of radius 6 cm has area 27 cm². Find the angle in radians and degrees.

27 = (1/2)(36) θ  →  27 = 18 θ  →  θ = 1.5 rad
in degrees: 1.5 × 180/π = 85.9 °

Segment area

segment area = sector area - triangle area
             = (1/2) r² θ - (1/2) r² sin(θ)
             = (1/2) r² (θ - sin θ)

The triangle is formed by the two radii and the chord; its area uses ½r² sin θ (the sine rule area formula). The subtraction is always the same picture: the segment is the sector with the triangle removed.

Worked example. Find the area of the segment cut off by a chord in a circle of radius 10 cm when the angle at the centre is 1.2 radians.

sector area = (1/2)(100)(1.2) = 60 cm²
triangle area = (1/2)(100) sin(1.2) = 50 × 0.932 = 46.6 cm²
segment = 60 - 46.6 = 13.4 cm²

Worked examples: the standard exam types

Worked example 1 (belt around pulleys). Two pulleys of radius 0.20 m and 0.50 m have centres 1.5 m apart. Find the length of the belt around them (straight sections plus arcs).

straight sections: 2 × 1.5 = 3.0 m (approximately, for the
common external tangents when the radii differ the geometry
needs the tangent length, but the exam version usually gives
equal pulleys or the tangent length directly)
equal-pulley version: belt = 2d + 2 π r = 3.0 + 1.26 = 4.26 m

Worked example 2 (pendulum arc). A pendulum of length 0.80 m swings through 0.6 radians. Find the arc length travelled by the bob.

s = r θ = 0.80 × 0.6 = 0.48 m

Worked example 3 (cone sector). A sector of radius 12 cm and angle 2.0 radians is folded into a cone. Find the base radius.

arc length becomes the base circumference:
s = 12 × 2.0 = 24 cm² π r_base = 24  →  r_base = 24/(2 π) = 3.82 cm

Radian trigonometry and small angles

In radian mode, the trigonometric functions take radian inputs, and small-angle approximations become available: for small θ, sin θ ≈ θ and tan θ ≈ θ (with θ in radians), and cos θ ≈ 1 − θ²/2. These approximations underpin pendulum motion and lens theory later, and they appear in exam questions as "show that for small θ ...".

Worked example. Show that for small θ, the arc length and the chord length are approximately equal.

arc = r θ
chord = 2r sin(θ/2) ~ 2r (θ/2) = r θ  for small θ
so chord ~ arc, with the difference of order θ³

Composite shapes with sectors

Exam figures combine sectors with triangles, rectangles and semicircles. The method is always the same: shade the required region, split it into standard pieces, compute each piece with the radian formulas, then add or subtract. Perimeter questions require the boundary only — internal lines are not part of it.

Worked example. A shape is a rectangle 12 cm by 8 cm with a quarter-circle of radius 8 cm removed from one corner. Find the area and perimeter of the remaining shape.

rectangle area = 96 cm²
quarter circle = (1/4) π r² = (1/4)(3.142)(64) = 50.3 cm²
remaining area = 96 - 50.3 = 45.7 cm²

perimeter: straight edges 12 + 4 + 8 = 24 cm (the 4 cm is the
remaining part of the 8 cm side)
plus the arc: quarter circumference = (1/4)(2 π)(8) = 12.6 cm
total perimeter = 36.6 cm

Worked example 2 (two sectors). Two circles of radius 5 cm have centres 8 cm apart. Find the area common to both.

the overlap is two identical segments. In each circle the chord
subtends an angle θ where cos(θ/2) = 4/5, so θ/2 =
0.6435 and θ = 1.287 rad.
segment area = (1/2)(25)(1.287 - sin 1.287)
             = 12.5(1.287 - 0.960) = 4.09 cm²
common area = 2 × 4.09 = 8.18 cm²

Arc, chord and sector in practice

Three quantities are easy to confuse and each has its own formula. Keep them side by side:

QuantityFormula (θ in radians)What it measures
Arc lengths = r θthe curved boundary
Chord lengthc = 2r sin(θ/2)the straight line joining the arc's ends
Sector areaA = (1/2) r^2 θthe pie-slice region

Worked example. A sector has radius 10 cm and angle 1.0 rad. Find the arc length, chord length and the difference between them.

arc = 10 × 1.0 = 10.0 cm
chord = 2 × 10 x sin(0.5) = 20 × 0.4794 = 9.59 cm
difference = 0.41 cm (the arc bulges beyond the chord)

Worked example (angular speed). A wheel of radius 0.35 m turns at 12 rad s⁻¹. Find the linear speed of a point on its rim and the angle turned in 5 s.

v = r ω = 0.35 × 12 = 4.2 m s⁻¹
angle = ω t = 12 × 5 = 60 rad (about 9.5 full turns)

Angular speed links circular measure to mechanics: one radian per second means one radius of arc per second, so the rim speed is rω. Exam questions on rotating wheels, pulleys and centrifuges all reduce to this one relation, and it also explains why a point near the rim of a wheel moves faster than a point near the hub despite both completing a turn in the same time. The same relation converts between the two ways of measuring rotation: revolutions per minute to radians per second is a factor of 2π/60.

The difference is the sagitta-related gap that appears in lens and bridge questions; it grows as the angle grows, which is why the small-angle approximation fails for large sectors.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Convert) Convert 72° to radians. Answer: θ(rad) = θ(°) × π/180°, so 72 × π/180 = 72π/180 = 2π/5 ≈ 1.257 rad.
  2. (Arc) Radius 5 cm, θ = 2.0 rad. Find the arc length. Answer: arc length s = rθ = 5 × 2.0 = 10 cm.
  3. (Sector) Radius 4 cm, θ = 3.0 rad. Find the area. Answer: sector area A = ½r²θ = ½ × 4² × 3.0 = ½ × 16 × 3 = 24 cm².
  4. (Reverse) A sector of radius 9 cm has arc length 13.5 cm. Find θ in radians. Answer: θ = 13.5/9 = 1.5 rad.
  5. (Segment) Radius 6 cm, θ = π/3. Find the segment area. Answer: sector = ½ × 36 × π/3 = 6π ≈ 18.85; triangle = ½ × 36 × sin(π/3) = 18 × 0.866 = 15.59; segment ≈ 3.26 cm².
  6. (Perimeter) Find the perimeter of a sector of radius 7 cm and angle 0.8 rad. Answer: the perimeter is the arc plus two radii: rθ + 2r = 7(0.8) + 14 = 5.6 + 14 = 19.6 cm.
  7. (Cone) A sector of radius 10 cm and angle 1.8 rad forms a cone. Find the base radius and slant height. Answer: arc = 18 cm → base radius 18/(2π) = 2.86 cm; slant height = 10 cm.
  8. (Small angle) Use sin θ ≈ θ to estimate sin(0.10) and compare with the calculator value. Answer: in radians sin θ ≈ θ for small θ, so sin(0.10) ≈ 0.10 against the calculator's 0.0998 — an error of about 0.2%, small because 0.10 rad is small.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Degree mode: every radians formula requires the calculator in RAD mode. A sin of 1.2 in degree mode gives an entirely different number.
  • Mixing units: s = rθ silently assumes r in metres and s in metres; cm and m mixed in one calculation produces a factor-of-100 error.
  • Half forgotten: sector area is ½r²θ, not r²θ. The ½ comes from the triangle comparison.
  • Angle in degrees in the formula: θ must be radians; convert first, and only convert the final answer back if asked.
  • Perimeter includes the radii: the perimeter of a sector is arc + 2r; the arc alone is not the perimeter.
  • Segment triangle: use ½r² sin θ for the triangle, with θ the same central angle; a different angle changes the answer.
  • Exact versus decimal: when the question says "in terms of π", keep π symbolic; converting to 3.14 loses the required form.
  • Small-angle validity: sin θ ≈ θ is good only for small θ (roughly under 0.2 rad); do not apply it to 1.5 rad.

Reading a sector: the one drawing this topic is built on

Every formula in circular measure comes from a single picture, and nearly every mistake comes from mixing up the two curves in it. Draw the sector once, label the radius, the angle and the arc, and the rest is arithmetic on that drawing.

Why the radian exists. An angle in radians is defined as the arc it cuts off divided by the radius:

θ = s / r Key: θ = angle at the centre (rad); s = arc length (m); r = radius (m). The units cancel, so a radian is a pure ratio — one radius-length of arc per radius. That is why a full turn is 2π radians and not 360: the whole circumference is 2πr, so the angle it subtends is 2πr ÷ r = 2π.

Turn the definition around and you get the arc formula, which is the one you actually use:

s = r θ Key: s = arc length (m); r = radius (m); θ = angle at the centre in radians. Using degrees here gives an answer 57 times too large — the single most common error in the topic.

Where ½r²θ comes from. Cut the sector into many thin triangles, each with height r and a sliver of arc as its base. A triangle's area is ½ × base × height, so each sliver is ½ × (rΔθ) × r, and adding them all up gives ½r² × (total θ):

A = ½ r² θ Key: A = area of the sector (m²); r = radius (m); θ = angle at the centre (rad). Notice that the arc is in this formula too — A = ½ r × (rθ) = ½ r s, which is the "thin triangle" statement written algebraically.

Worked example. A sector has radius 9.0 cm and angle 1.2 rad. Find its arc length, its area, and the length of its chord.

arc: s = rθ = 9.0 × 1.2 = 10.8 cm
area: A = ½r²θ = ½ × 81 × 1.2 = 48.6 cm²
chord: the two radii and the chord form an isosceles triangle with sides 9.0, 9.0 and included angle 1.2 rad, so chord = 2 × 9.0 × sin(1.2/2) = 18 × 0.5646 = 10.2 cm

That last line is the step students skip, and it is the step the paper is testing: the chord is a straight line, so it needs trigonometry, not the arc formula. The segment area is then sector minus triangle, A = ½r²(θ − sin θ) = 48.6 − ½ × 81 × sin 1.2 = 48.6 − 37.7 = 10.9 cm².

The perimeter of a sector is three sides, not one. A sector's boundary is the arc plus the two radii: P = 2r + rθ. For the example above, P = 18.0 + 10.8 = 28.8 cm. Answering with 10.8 alone is the most frequently lost mark on this topic, because the word "perimeter" invites you to think of the curve only.

Where marks are lost. Degrees in an equation that needs radians (check the calculator is in RAD mode the moment a question says "radians"). Reading "arc" as "chord". Forgetting the two radii in a perimeter. And using ½r²θ for a segment — the segment is the sector minus the triangle, and the triangle's area is ½r² sin θ.

Deriving the arc and sector formulae from the fraction of a circle

Both formulae come from one idea: a sector is the same fraction of its circle as its angle is of a full turn. Seeing that fraction is more useful than memorising two formulae, because the same reasoning works when a question changes the circle or the angle.

Arc length as a fraction of the circumference

The full circumference is 2πr, and a full turn is 2π radians. A sector of angle θ takes the fraction θ/(2π) of the circle, so s = (θ/2π) × 2πr = rθ. The π cancels, which is why radians make the arc formula so short.

Sector area as a fraction of the disc

The whole disc has area πr². The sector takes the same fraction, so A = (θ/2π) × πr² = ½r²θ. Check it with θ = 2π: ½r²(2π) = πr², the whole disc.

What goes wrong if the angle is in degrees

In degrees a full turn is 360, not 2π, so the fraction becomes θ/360 and the arc is (θ/360) × 2πr. Putting a degree value straight into rθ gives an answer about 57.3 times too large, because one radian is 180/π degrees.

The area formula from integration

Adding thin sectors of area ½r² dθ from 0 to θ gives ∫₀^θ ½r² dθ = ½r²θ. This is the same result reached by integration, and it is the method behind the formula rather than a separate rule.

Recovering the radius and angle from the arc and area

Dividing the area by the arc gives A/s = ½r, so r = 2A/s, and then θ = s/r. A sector with arc 15 cm and area 75 cm² has r = 2 × 75 / 15 = 10 cm and θ = 15/10 = 1.5 rad.

Checking the units of the answer

An arc is a length, so its unit is the radius unit. A sector's area has square units. An area with no square unit usually means the arc formula was used by mistake.

Converting angles and keeping exact values

Most lost marks on this topic are not hard mathematics. They come from an angle left in the wrong unit, or from a decimal where the question wanted π. These habits prevent both.

Degrees to radians, exactly

Multiply degrees by π/180. For example 150° × π/180 = 5π/6. When the question asks for an exact value, keep π in the answer and evaluate it only at the end.

Radians to degrees

Multiply radians by 180/π. For example 1.2 rad × 180/π = 68.75°. As a check, 1 rad is about 57.3°, so 1.2 rad must be a little more than 60°.

Multiples of π in an answer

A sector with r = 6 cm and θ = π/3 has arc length 6 × π/3 = 2π cm, which is about 6.28 cm. Give the exact form 2π cm when the question asks for it, and the decimal only when it asks for a decimal.

Estimating the size of a radian

π/2 ≈ 1.57 is a right angle and π ≈ 3.14 is a straight line. Since 1 rad is about 57°, an angle of 0.5 rad is roughly 29°. A quick estimate like this catches a wrong calculator mode before the answer is written.

Setting the calculator to radians

Check the mode before every trigonometric step. In RAD mode sin(π/6) = 0.5. In DEG mode, sin 0.5236 gives 0.0091, which shows the calculator was not in radians.

Mixed units in one question

A question may give the radius in metres and the angle in degrees. Convert the angle first, find the arc in the radius unit, and then state the answer in the unit the question asks for.

title: Circular Measure — Study Notes
content:
Circular Measure

Radians

One radian is the angle subtending an arc equal in length to the radius. π radians = 180°.

  • Degrees → radians: multiply by π/180.
  • Radians → degrees: multiply by 180/π.

Common angles: 30° = π/6, 45° = π/4, 60° = π/3, 90° = π/2, 180° = π, 360° = 2π.

Arc Length

s = rθ (θ in radians).

Example: r = 6, θ = π/3 gives s = 2π.

Sector Area

A = ½r²θ.

Example: r = 5, θ = 1.2 gives A = ½ × 25 × 1.2 = 15.

Segment Area

A = ½r²(θ − sin θ). For r = 2, θ = π/2: A = 2(π/2 − 1) = π − 2.

Rearranging

  • θ = s/r (must be radians)
  • θ = 2A/r²

Exam tips: never mix degrees into s = rθ; convert first. Sketch the sector and mark r and θ before computing, and check whether a question asks for the major or minor sector.

title: Pressure & Density — Study Notes
content:
Pressure & Density

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): pressure & pressure differences in fluids, density review (Extended pressure-depth).

1. Pressure basics

p = F/A (Pa = N/m²). Increase F or decrease A to raise pressure; explain applications (snowshoes, knives, hydraulic press).

2. Liquids

  • Pressure increases with depth: p = ρgh (Extended).
  • Same level, same liquid ⇒ same pressure (hydrostatic paradox).
  • Hydraulic systems transmit pressure — force multiplier: F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂.

3. Atmospheric pressure

~10⁵ Pa at sea level; demonstrated by collapsing can, mercury barometer 760 mmHg; decreases with altitude.

4. Density revisited

ρ = m/V; floating condition; upthrust = weight of displaced fluid (qualitative).

5. Gas pressure (particle model)

Particles collide with walls → force per area. Volume ↓ at same T ⇒ pressure ↑ (more frequent collisions). Temperature ↑ ⇒ faster particles ⇒ more frequent, harder impacts.

Density in more depth

Density is mass per unit volume, ρ = m/V. Its SI unit is kg/m³, and 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³. An object of a given density will float in a fluid only if the fluid has a higher density. To find the density of an irregular solid, measure its mass on a balance and its volume by displacement of water in a measuring cylinder.

Pressure and depth

Pressure is force per unit area, p = F/A, with unit the pascal (Pa = N/m²). In a liquid, the pressure increases with depth, p = hρg, and acts equally in all directions at a given depth. Atmospheric pressure at sea level is about 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa.

Exam tip: convert the area to m² before you calculate pressure, and use the density in kg/m³ in p = hρg.

Worked method for pressure questions

Step 1: write down the force in newtons and the area in m². Step 2: divide, p = F/A. Step 3: if the question is about a liquid, use p = hρg with h in metres, ρ in kg/m³ and g = 10 N/kg, and remember that the pressure is the same at equal depths in the same liquid. Atmospheric pressure is added to the liquid pressure when a question asks for total pressure at depth.

title: A Level Mathematics: Differentiation II
content:
A Level Mathematics: Differentiation II

A2 differentiation adds the rules for products, quotients and functions of functions, then applies them to implicit equations, parametric curves and rates of change. Every rule in this note is stated with the condition for using it and derived where the derivation is short, because the exam tests recognition as much as execution.

The chain rule

if y = f(g(x)) then dy/dx = f'(g(x)) g'(x)

or with u: dy/dx = dy/du x du/dx

Worked example 1. Differentiate y = (3x + 2)⁵.

dy/dx = 5(3x + 2)⁴ × 3 = 15(3x + 2)⁴

Worked example 2 (trigonometric). Differentiate y = sin(2x).

dy/dx = 2 cos(2x)

Worked example 3 (exponential). Differentiate y = e^(x²).

dy/dx = 2x e^(x²)

Worked example 4 (power of a trig function). Differentiate y = cos³x.

treat as (cos x)³: dy/dx = 3(cos x)² x (-sin x) = -3 sin x cos² x

The product rule

d(uv)/dx = u dv/dx + v du/dx

"first times derivative of second plus second times derivative of first"

Worked example 1. Differentiate y = x² sin x.

dy/dx = 2x sin x + x² cos x

Worked example 2. Differentiate y = x ln x.

dy/dx = ln x + x(1/x) = ln x + 1

Worked example 3. Differentiate y = x²e^(3x).

dy/dx = 2x e^(3x) + 3x² e^(3x) = x e^(3x)(2 + 3x)

Factorising the answer is not cosmetic: stationary points need the factorised form to be solved.

The quotient rule

d(u/v)/dx = (v du/dx - u dv/dx)/v²

the numerator's order matters: v times derivative of u minus u times
derivative of v

Worked example 1. Differentiate y = sin x/x.

dy/dx = (x cos x - sin x)/x²

Worked example 2 (a common form). Differentiate y = (2x + 1)/(x − 3).

dy/dx = [(x - 3)(2) - (2x + 1)(1)]/(x - 3)²
      = (2x - 6 - 2x - 1)/(x - 3)² = -7/(x - 3)²

Worked example 3 (exponential quotient). Differentiate y = e^x/ln x.

dy/dx = [ln x e^x - e^x(1/x)]/(ln x)²

Implicit differentiation

differentiate both sides with respect to x, treating y as a function
of x: each y term contributes its derivative times dy/dx

then solve for dy/dx

Worked example 1. Find dy/dx for x² + y² = 25.

2x + 2y dy/dx = 0
 dy/dx = -x/y

Worked example 2 (product inside). Find dy/dx for xy + y² = 6.

differentiate: y + x dy/dx + 2y dy/dx = 0
dy/dx (x + 2y) = -y
dy/dx = -y/(x + 2y)

Worked example 3 (tangent). Find the tangent to x² + xy = 6 at the point (2, 1).

2x + y + x dy/dx = 0
at (2, 1): 4 + 1 + 2 dy/dx = 0  →  dy/dx = -2.5
tangent: y - 1 = -2.5(x - 2)  →  5x + 2y = 12

Parametric differentiation

if x = f(t) and y = g(t): dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt)

Worked example. For x = t², y = t³ − t, find dy/dx in terms of t.

dx/dt = 2t;  dy/dt = 3t² - 1
dy/dx = (3t² - 1)/(2t)

Worked example 2 (tangent). Find the tangent at t = 2.

point: x = 4, y = 6
gradient: (12 - 1)/4 = 2.75
tangent: y - 6 = 2.75(x - 4)  →  y = 2.75x - 5

Worked example 3 (second derivative). Find d²y/dx² in terms of t for the same curve.

d/dx(dy/dx) = [d/dt(dy/dx)] / (dx/dt)
d/dt[(3t² - 1)/(2t)] = (6t x 2t - (3t² - 1)2)/(4t²) = (6t² + 2)/(4t²)
divide by 2t: (6t² + 2)/(8t³)

Stationary points with the new rules

Worked example. Find and classify the stationary point of y = x e^(−x²).

dy/dx = e^(-x²) + x(-2x)e^(-x²) = e^(-x²)(1 - 2x²)
stationary at x = +/- 1/sqrt 2 = +/- 0.707
at x = 0.707: y = 0.707 e^(-0.5) = 0.429  →  maximum
by symmetry x = -0.707 is a minimum with y = -0.429

Worked example 2 (product inside a log). Show y = x ln x has a minimum at x = e^(−1).

dy/dx = ln x + 1 = 0  →  x = e⁻¹ = 0.368
y = e⁻¹ ln(e⁻¹) = -e⁻¹ = -0.368
second derivative = 1/x > 0 at this point, so minimum

Connected rates of change

chain rule in rate form: dV/dt = dV/dr x dr/dt
strategy: write the quantity as a function of one variable, differentiate,
link the rates, substitute

Worked example. A spherical balloon is inflated so that its volume increases at 100 cm³/s. Find dr/dt when r = 5 cm.

V = (4/3) π r³  →  dV/dr = 4 π r²
at r = 5: dV/dr = 100 π = 314.2
dr/dt = (dV/dt)/(dV/dr) = 100/314.2 = 0.318 cm/s

Worked example 2 (area). A circular ripple's radius grows at 2 cm/s. How fast is the area growing when r = 10 cm?

A = π r²  →  dA/dr = 2 π r = 62.83
dA/dt = 62.83 × 2 = 125.7 cm²/s

Exponentials and logarithms to other bases

Every exponential can be rewritten with base e, because a = e^(ln a). That one identity turns an unfamiliar derivative into something the chain rule already handles, and it explains why base e is the natural choice: the conversion factor disappears.

y = a^x = e^(x ln a)
dy/dx = ln a x e^(x ln a) = a^x ln a

y = log_a(x);  write x = a^y and differentiate implicitly:
1 = a^y ln a dy/dx   →   dy/dx = 1/(x ln a)

special cases: d/dx(e^x) = e^x;  d/dx(ln x) = 1/x

The factor ln a is what students leave out. For a = e it equals 1, which is exactly why base-e derivatives come out clean and every other base drags a constant along.

Worked example. Differentiate y = 3^x.

y = e^(x ln 3)
dy/dx = ln 3 x e^(x ln 3) = 3^x ln 3 = 1.0986 × 3^x

Worked example 2 (chain rule inside the exponent). Differentiate y = 2^(x²).

y = e^(x² ln 2)
dy/dx = e^(x² ln 2) x (2x ln 2) = 2x ln 2 × 2^(x²) = 1.386 × 2^(x²)

Worked example 3 (logarithm of a linear function). Differentiate y = ln(3x + 2) and state where the derivative is valid.

inner u = 3x + 2, du/dx = 3
dy/dx = (1/u) × 3 = 3/(3x + 2)
valid for 3x + 2 > 0, i.e. x > -2/3

The second derivative test and curve sketching

At a stationary point the first derivative vanishes, so it cannot distinguish a peak from a trough. The second derivative does: it measures how the gradient itself is changing, which is the curvature of the graph at that point.

Condition at a stationary pointShape of the curveConclusion
d²y/dx² < 0concave down (∩)local maximum
d²y/dx² > 0concave up (∪)local minimum
d²y/dx² = 0test inconclusivecheck the sign of dy/dx either side

Worked example. Find and classify the stationary points of y = x³ − 3x, then sketch the curve.

dy/dx = 3x² - 3 = 3(x - 1)(x + 1)
stationary at x = 1 and x = -1
at x = 1:  y = 1 - 3 = -2;  y'' = 6x = 6 > 0  →  minimum (1, -2)
at x = -1: y = -1 + 3 = 2;  y'' = -6 < 0      →  maximum (-1, 2)
y intercept: x = 0, y = 0 (also a root)
end behaviour: x -> +inf gives y -> +inf; x -> -inf gives y -> -inf

Worked example 2 (where the test fails). Classify the stationary point of y = x⁴.

dy/dx = 4x³ = 0 only at x = 0, where y = 0
y'' = 12x² = 0 at x = 0, so the test is inconclusive
look at dy/dx: negative for x < 0, positive for x > 0
so the curve falls then rises: (0, 0) is a minimum

The failed case is examinable: y = x³ has no sign change in dy/dx at the origin, so it is a point of inflection, not an extremum. Reporting "stationary point" for x³ without that check loses the mark.

Kinematics with calculus

When displacement is given as a function of time, velocity is its derivative and acceleration the derivative of velocity. Those two definitions replace the constant-acceleration formulas the moment the motion stops being uniform, which is the whole point of the calculus treatment.

s(t) displacement;  v = ds/dt;  a = dv/dt = d²s/dt²
reverse: s = integral of v dt;  v = integral of a dt
maximum displacement occurs where v = 0
distance travelled = integral of |v| dt, split where v changes sign

Worked example. A particle moves with s = t³ − 6t² + 9t metres. Find when it is instantaneously at rest and its acceleration at those instants.

v = 3t² - 12t + 9 = 3(t - 1)(t - 3)
at rest: t = 1 and t = 3
a = 6t - 12   →   a(1) = -6 m/s²;  a(3) = 6 m/s²
s(1) = 4 m;  s(3) = 0 m

Worked example 2 (total distance versus displacement). For the same motion, find the distance travelled in 0 ≤ t ≤ 3.

v is positive on (0, 1) and negative on (1, 3)
distance = [s(1) - s(0)] + [s(1) - s(3)] = (4 - 0) + (4 - 0) = 8 m
note the displacement s(3) - s(0) = 0, so displacement alone would report 0

That last result is the standard trap: a question asking for distance needs the sign changes found first, or the positive and negative parts cancel and the answer is nonsense.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Chain) Differentiate (2x − 1)⁴. Answer: 8(2x − 1)³.
  2. (Product) Differentiate x³e^x. Answer: x²e^x(3 + x).
  3. (Quotient) Differentiate (x + 1)/(x − 1). Answer: −2/(x − 1)².
  4. (Implicit) x² + y² = 16: find dy/dx. Answer: −x/y.
  5. (Implicit tangent) Same circle at (2, √12): gradient? Answer: −2/3.46 = −0.577.
  6. (Parametric) x = t², y = 2t + 1: find dy/dx. Answer: 2/(2t) = 1/t.
  7. (Rates) V = s³, ds/dt = 1.5, s = 4. Find dV/dt. Answer: 3s² × 1.5 = 72.
  8. (Stationary) y = x²e^x: find the stationary points. Answer: e^x(x² + 2x) = 0 → x = 0 (min), x = −2 (max).

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Chain rule forgotten: differentiating sin 2x as 2 cos 2x, not cos 2x — the inner derivative is compulsory.
  • Quotient rule order reversed: v du − u dv, not u dv − v du; the sign flips if you swap.
  • Implicit y terms: each differentiated y term needs a dy/dx factor, including products like xy.
  • Parametric dy/dx inverted: it is (dy/dt)/(dx/dt), not the reciprocal.
  • Second derivative by differentiating dy/dx with respect to t: must divide by dx/dt, or the answer is d/dt, not d/dx.
  • Rates linked backwards: dV/dt = dV/dr × dr/dt; inverting gives an answer in the wrong units.
  • Stationary points unfactorised: equations like x e^x(2 + x) = 0 are solved only when factorised.
  • Domain of ln: differentiating ln x is valid only for x > 0; for negative arguments use ln|x|.

title: IGCSE Chemistry: Atoms, Elements and Compounds
content:
IGCSE Chemistry: Atoms, Elements and Compounds

Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry 0620 (2026–2028), Extended route, Topic 2 Atoms, elements and compounds: statements 2.1 Elements, compounds and mixtures, 2.2 Atomic structure and the Periodic Table, 2.3 Isotopes, 2.4 Ions and ionic bonds, 2.5 Simple molecules and covalent bonds, 2.6 Giant covalent structures, and 2.7 Metallic bonding. This is the foundation everything else stands on: what atoms are made of, why they bond, and how the four bonding types dictate every physical property you will ever be asked to explain. Every electron configuration and isotope calculation is worked digit by digit.

Elements, compounds and mixtures

An element is one kind of atom only (iron, oxygen gas) — it cannot be broken down chemically. A compound is two or more elements chemically joined in fixed proportions, with new properties (water: hydrogen and oxygen, but nothing like either). A mixture is substances physically together, unchanged, separable by physical means. The test-paper distinction: compounds need chemical change to separate (electrolysis); mixtures separate physically (distillation, chromatography, filtration).

Inside the atom

Picture the atom as a sports stadium: the nucleus is a marble at the centre of the pitch, and the electrons are specks of dust whizzing around the stands. Almost all the mass sits in that tiny nucleus; almost all the volume is empty space.

ParticleRelative chargeRelative massLocation
Proton+11Nucleus
Neutron01Nucleus
Electron−11/1836 (negligible)Electron shells around the nucleus

Definitions the exam demands verbatim: the proton (atomic) number is the number of protons in an atom and fixes the element; the mass (nucleon) number is the total of protons plus neutrons. Atoms are neutral because protons = electrons; an ion forms when electrons are lost or gained.

Reading the symbol notation, line by line:  ²³⁵₉₂U

  mass number (top)     = 235 = protons + neutrons
  proton number (bottom)= 92  = protons
  therefore:
    protons   = 92
    electrons = 92 (neutral atom)
    neutrons  = 235 - 92 = 143

Same arithmetic for any species:
  ⁴⁰₂₀Ca²⁺:  protons 20, neutrons 40 - 20 = 20,
             electrons 20 - 2 = 18 (the 2+ charge means 2 electrons LOST)

Electron arrangement, 1 to 20

Electrons occupy shells that fill in a fixed order — first shell 2, second 8, third 8 (for the first twenty elements), then 2. The arrangement is written as comma-separated numbers: sodium (11 electrons) is 2,8,1.

Building every configuration from hydrogen to calcium, step by step:

  H  1        He 2         [first shell full at 2]
  Li 2,1      Be 2,2       B 2,3        C²,4
  N²,5       O 2,6        F²,7        Ne 2,8     [second shell full at 8]
  Na 2,8,1    Mg 2,8,2     Al 2,8,3     Si 2,8,4
  P 2,8,5     S 2,8,6      Cl 2,8,7     Ar 2,8,8   [third shell full at 8]
  K²,8,8,1   Ca 2,8,8,2   [fourth shell starts after 8 in the third]

Two rules worth a mark each:
  outer-shell electron count = GROUP number  (Cl: 7 outer → Group VII)
  number of occupied shells = PERIOD number (Cl: 3 shells → Period 3)
A full outer shell (2 or 8) means the atom is unreactive - the noble gases.

Isotopes and relative atomic mass

Isotopes are atoms of the same element (same proton number) with different numbers of neutrons. They have identical chemical properties — chemistry lives in the electron arrangement, which isotopes share — but different masses. The relative atomic mass is the weighted average of the isotopic masses.

Worked: chlorine exists as ³⁵Cl (75%) and ³⁷Cl (25%). Calculate its Aᵣ.

  Aᵣ = (isotope 1 mass x its fraction) + (isotope 2 mass x its fraction)
     = (35 × 0.75) + (37 × 0.25)
     = 26.25 + 9.25
     = 35.5

Percentages can be used directly with the same arithmetic:
  Aᵣ = (35 × 75 + 37 × 25) / 10⁰ = (2625 + 925) / 10⁰ = 35.5 ✓

If the question gives abundances as 3:1 instead of 75:25, the fractions are
3/4 = 0.75 and 1/4 = 0.25 - convert counts to fractions first.

Ions and ionic bonding

Metals lose electrons, non-metals gain them, and the resulting oppositely charged ions attract — an ionic bond is the electrostatic attraction between cations and anions. The product is a giant ionic lattice: a regular, repeating grid of alternating ions, not individual molecules.

Deduction of ionic formulae by charge balance - worked three times:

  Na (2,8,1) loses 1 electron → Na⁺       Cl (2,8,7) gains 1 → Cl⁻
    charges +1 and -1 balance 1:1  →  NaCl

  Mg (2,8,2) loses 2 → Mg²⁺               O (2,6) gains 2 → O²⁻
    charges +2 and -2 balance 1:1  →  MgO

  Ca (2,8,8,2) loses 2 → Ca²⁺             Cl (2,8,7) gains 1 → Cl⁻
    one 2+ needs TWO 1-  →  CaCl₂

General rule: swap the charge NUMBERS to get the subscripts, then simplify
(Ca²⁺ and O²⁻ → Ca₂O₂ → CaO).

Properties follow from structure — the reasoning chain examiners want: ionic compounds have high melting and boiling points because the strong electrostatic forces in the giant lattice take lots of energy to overcome; they conduct electricity when molten or aqueous (ions free to move) but not when solid (ions locked in place); they are often soluble in water (polar water molecules pull ions from the lattice).

Covalent bonds and simple molecules

A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons holding two non-metal atoms together. Each shared pair is one bond; atoms bond until their outer shells are full. Dot-and-cross diagrams draw only the outer-shell electrons, with crosses from one atom and dots from the other.

Dot-and-cross logic for four standard molecules (describe, then draw):

  H₂   each H brings 1 electron; one shared pair fills both 1-electron
       shells → H-H
  H₂O  O (2,6) needs 2 electrons; each H shares 1 → two shared pairs,
       two lone pairs on oxygen → bent shape
  CH₄  C (2,4) needs 4; four H atoms each share 1 → four shared pairs,
       four lone pairs total on the hydrogens → tetrahedral
  NH₃  N (2,5) needs 3; three H atoms share → three shared pairs and ONE
       lone pair on nitrogen → pyramidal
  HCl  one shared pair between H and Cl (Cl keeps 3 lone pairs)

Simple molecular substances: LOW melting/boiling points - the covalent bonds
INSIDE molecules are strong, but the forces BETWEEN molecules are weak and
need little energy to break. They do not conduct: no free ions or electrons.

The distinction students most often miss: melting a molecular substance breaks intermolecular forces, not covalent bonds. Breaking covalent bonds is a chemical change.

Giant covalent structures

StructureBondingProperties and uses
DiamondEach C bonded to 4 others; giant 3D lattice of strong covalent bondsHardest natural substance; cutting tools, drill bits — no free electrons, so does not conduct
GraphiteEach C bonded to 3 others in flat hexagonal layers; delocalised electrons between layersLayers slide easily — lubricant; conducts electricity — electrodes; soft
Silicon(IV) oxideLike diamond: each Si bonded to 4 O in a giant latticeVery hard, very high melting point; similar to diamond in structure-property terms

The property question is always the same shape: name the structure → name the strong bonds → explain why that gives the property (and where relevant why the other structure differs: graphite's weakly bonded layers slide; its delocalised electrons conduct).

Metallic bonding

Metal atoms pack into a giant lattice of positive ions surrounded by a "sea" of delocalised electrons — electrons detached from their atoms and free to move. The metallic bond is the attraction between the positive ions and that delocalised sea.

  • Electrical and thermal conductivity: the delocalised electrons carry charge (and energy) through the structure.
  • Malleability and ductility: layers of identical ions can slide over each other without breaking the bonding — the electron sea simply re-forms around them (unlike ionic lattices, which shatter when layers shift and like charges align).
  • High melting points: strong attraction throughout the giant lattice (tungsten very high; mercury low because its bonding is weaker).

Worked example: the four bonding types compared on one property set

Question: explain why sodium chloride melts at 801 °C, but methane melts at
-182 °C - even though both contain strong covalent/ionic interactions.

  NaCl: ionic. Giant lattice of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ held by strong electrostatic
        forces throughout. Melting means overcoming these forces everywhere
        at once → lots of energy → high temperature.
  Methane (CH₄): simple molecular. Strong covalent bonds INSIDE each molecule
        stay intact on melting; only the weak intermolecular forces BETWEEN
        molecules are overcome → little energy → very low temperature.

The structure sentence earns the mark; "because it is ionic" alone does not.
Same shape of answer: diamond vs CO₂ (giant covalent vs simple molecular),
iron vs sodium (both metallic - compare bond strength and ion size).

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Swapping proton number and mass number in symbol notation; the bottom number is always the proton number.
  • Computing neutrons as mass number (it is mass number minus proton number).
  • Writing ion charges as counts (Ca⁺² instead of Ca²⁺) — charge goes top-right after the symbol.
  • Claiming isotopes differ chemically; only physical properties (mass-dependent behaviour like diffusion) differ.
  • Saying ionic compounds conduct when solid — only when molten or in solution, when ions can move.
  • Explaining low melting points of molecular substances by "weak covalent bonds" — the covalent bonds are strong; it is the intermolecular forces that are weak.
  • Forgetting lone pairs in dot-and-cross diagrams (ammonia's and water's lone pairs are marks).
  • Confusing graphite's conductivity (delocalised electrons within layers) with diamond's insulation (all four electrons locked in bonds).
  • Explaining malleability of metals by "layers slide" without mentioning the electron sea re-forming — the bonding must stay intact.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 4, 3 marks). An atom has 16 protons, 16 neutrons and 16 electrons. State the element, its mass number, and the electron arrangement.

Answer: Proton number 16 is sulfur. Mass number = 16 + 16 = 32. Electron arrangement 2,8,6.

Question 2 (Paper 4, 3 marks). Explain why isotopes of an element have the same chemical properties but different physical properties.

Answer: Chemical properties depend on electron arrangement (especially outer-shell electrons), and isotopes have identical electron arrangements since proton number fixes electron count. Physical properties that depend on mass — such as rate of diffusion — differ because isotopes have different numbers of neutrons and therefore different masses.

Question 3 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Describe the bonding in magnesium oxide and explain why it has a high melting point.

Answer: Magnesium atoms (2,8,2) each lose two electrons to become Mg²⁺; oxygen atoms (2,6) each gain two to become O²⁻. The oppositely charged ions form a giant ionic lattice in which each ion is electrostatically attracted to all its neighbours. The strong electrostatic forces throughout the lattice require large amounts of energy to overcome, so the melting point is high (2852 °C).

Question 4 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Explain why graphite conducts electricity but diamond does not, and why graphite is used as a lubricant.

Answer: In graphite each carbon bonds to three others, leaving one delocalised electron per atom free to move within the layers — these carry charge. In diamond every carbon bonds to four others with all electrons locked in bonds, so none are free. As a lubricant: graphite's layers are held only weakly and slide over each other easily while retaining bonding, reducing friction.

Question 5 (Paper 4, 3 marks). Substance A melts at 801 °C and conducts electricity only when molten. Substance B melts at 1610 °C and never conducts. Identify each structure type and explain.

Answer: A is ionic (giant ionic lattice, e.g. sodium chloride): its high melting point reflects strong electrostatic forces between ions, and it conducts only when molten because the ions are then free to move while they are locked in place when solid. B is giant covalent (e.g. silicon(IV) oxide): its higher melting point reflects extensive strong covalent bonds, and it never conducts because there are no free ions or delocalised electrons in any state.

Question 6 (Paper 4, 3 marks). Explain, in terms of structure, why metals are malleable while ionic compounds are brittle.

Answer: In metals, layers of identical positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons can slide without breaking metallic bonding — the electron sea re-forms around the displaced ions. In ionic lattices, shifting a layer brings like charges next to each other; the repulsion splits the crystal — so ionic solids shatter rather than bend.

With the particles and their bonds understood, the next foundations are the states those particles move through and the energy changes when they react.

title: Trigonometry — Sine and Cosine Rules — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Trigonometry — Sine and Cosine Rules

Mathematics — OL. area formula, sine rule, cosine rule, multi-step bearing and 3-D problems (Extended).

  • 1. Area of a triangle
  • 2. Sine rule
  • 3. Cosine rule
  • 4. Bearing problems
  • 5. 3-D trigonometry

Formulas to learn

  • Area of a triangle: one half of a b sin C.
  • Sine rule: a / sin A = b / sin B = c / sin C.
  • Cosine rule: a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc cos A, and cos A = (b^2 + c^2 - a^2) / (2bc).

Worked example

In a triangle with sides 7 and 9 and included angle 40 degrees, the area is one half of 7 x 9 x sin 40, about 20.2. The angle opposite the side 9 is then found by the sine rule, so check the answer against the cosine rule before you finish.

Formulas to learn

  • Area of a triangle: one half of a b sin C.
  • Sine rule: a / sin A = b / sin B = c / sin C.
  • Cosine rule: a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc cos A, and cos A = (b^2 + c^2 - a^2) / (2bc).

Worked example

In a triangle with sides 7 and 9 and included angle 40 degrees, the area is one half of 7 x 9 x sin 40, about 20.2. The angle opposite the side 9 is then found by the sine rule, so check the answer against the cosine rule before you finish.

How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

title: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Right-Angled Trigonometry
content:
Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Right-Angled Trigonometry

Right-angled triangles are the most useful triangles in mathematics: Pythagoras relates the three sides, and the sine, cosine and tangent ratios relate sides to angles. Between them they solve every distance and angle problem the IGCSE sets, from ladders against walls to angles of elevation and three-figure bearings. This note builds the topic from zero: Pythagoras with its converse and 3D use, the SOHCAHTOA ratios with the selection method, exact values derived rather than memorised, and the multi-step problems that combine Pythagoras with trigonometry.

Pythagoras' theorem

in a right-angled triangle: a² + b² = c²
where c is the hypotenuse (the side opposite the right angle)

The theorem is a statement about areas: the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides. The converse identifies right angles: if a² + b² = c² for the longest side c, the triangle is right-angled — the standard test for 3-4-5 and 5-12-13 triangles.

Worked example 1. A right-angled triangle has legs 6 cm and 8 cm. Find the hypotenuse.

c² = 6² + 8² = 36 + 64 = 100
c = 10 cm

Worked example 2 (finding a leg). The hypotenuse is 13 cm and one leg is 5 cm. Find the other leg.

a² = 13² - 5² = 169 - 25 = 144
a = 12 cm

Worked example 3 (converse). Is a triangle with sides 7, 24, 25 right-angled?

7² + 24² = 49 + 576 = 625 = 25²
yes - right-angled, with the right angle opposite the 25 side

Pythagoras in three dimensions

In a cuboid, the space diagonal uses Pythagoras twice: first across the base, then up the height.

space diagonal = √(l² + w² + h²)

Worked example. A cuboid is 3 cm by 4 cm by 12 cm. Find the length of the space diagonal.

d = √(9 + 16 + 144) = √(169) = 13 cm

The three ratios: SOHCAHTOA

sin(θ) = opposite/hypotenuse      (SOH)
cos(θ) = adjacent/hypotenuse      (CAH)
tan(θ) = opposite/adjacent       (TOA)

Label the sides relative to the angle in question: the hypotenuse is always opposite the right angle; the opposite is across from the angle; the adjacent is the remaining side touching the angle. The selection method: mark the known side and the wanted side, then ask which ratio contains both.

Worked example 1 (finding a side). In a right-angled triangle, the angle is 35° and the hypotenuse is 12 cm. Find the opposite side.

known: hypotenuse; want: opposite  →  sine
sin(35) = opposite/12
opposite = 12 sin(35) = 12 × 0.574 = 6.88 cm

Worked example 2 (finding a side with cosine). Angle 40°, hypotenuse 20 cm; find the adjacent side.

cos(40) = adjacent/20
adjacent = 20 cos(40) = 20 × 0.766 = 15.3 cm

Worked example 3 (finding an angle). Opposite 5 cm, adjacent 9 cm. Find the angle.

tan(θ) = 5/9 = 0.5556
θ = tan-1(0.5556) = 29.1 °

For angles, use the inverse functions (sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹, tan⁻¹) and check the calculator is in degree mode — a radian-mode calculator turns 90° into 1.57 and ruins the paper.

Exact trigonometric values

Three angles have exact values worth knowing, derived from two special triangles:

Anglesincostan
30°1/2√3/21/√3
45°1/√21/√21
60°√3/21/2√3

Derivation: a 45-45-90 triangle with legs 1 has hypotenuse √2 (Pythagoras), giving sin 45 = 1/√2. An equilateral triangle of side 2 split in half gives a 30-60-90 triangle with sides 1, √3, 2, giving all six values. Deriving them once beats memorising them badly.

Two sanity checks keep the table honest: sine increases from 0 to 1 as the angle grows from 0° to 90°, so sin 30 must be smaller than sin 60; and cosine runs the other way, so cos 30 must be larger than cos 60. If an exact value breaks either ordering, the table has been misremembered.

Worked example. Find the exact value of sin 60° × tan 30°.

sin 60 = √(3)/2;  tan 30 = 1/√(3)
product = (√(3)/2) x (1/√(3)) = 1/2

Angles of elevation and depression

An angle of elevation is measured upward from the horizontal to an object; an angle of depression is measured downward. Both are measured from the observer's eye line, and the angle of depression from A to B equals the angle of elevation from B to A (alternate angles).

Worked example. From a point 40 m from the base of a tower, the angle of elevation to the top is 32°. Find the tower's height.

tan(32) = height/40
height = 40 tan(32) = 40 × 0.625 = 25.0 m

Worked example 2 (depression). A cliff is 60 m high; the angle of depression to a boat is 25°. Find the horizontal distance to the boat.

the angle at the boat is also 25 ° (alternate)
tan(25) = 60/d  →  d = 60/tan(25) = 60/0.466 = 128.7 m

Choosing the method: a decision routine

Most lost trigonometry marks come from choosing the wrong tool, not from arithmetic. The routine below takes ten seconds and removes the guesswork:

  1. Is there a right angle? If not, the question needs the sine or cosine rule (a different topic) — do not force SOHCAHTOA onto a triangle without a right angle.
  2. What do you know — two sides, or a side and an angle? Two sides with no angle means Pythagoras. A side and an angle means trigonometry.
  3. Which ratio? Mark the known side and the target relative to the given angle, then pick the ratio containing both: sin uses opposite and hypotenuse, cos uses adjacent and hypotenuse, tan uses opposite and adjacent.
  4. What is the unknown — a side or an angle? A side comes from multiplying; an angle needs the inverse function.

Worked example. A roof rafter is 4.5 m long and meets the horizontal at 38°. Find the vertical rise and the horizontal run.

rise: sin(38) = rise/4.5  →  rise = 4.5 sin(38) = 2.77 m
run:  cos(38) = run/4.5   →  run = 4.5 cos(38) = 3.55 m
check: 2.77² + 3.55² = 7.67 + 12.60 = 20.27 ~ 4.5²

Worked example 2 (finding the angle of a ladder). A 6 m ladder reaches 5.2 m up a wall. Find the angle it makes with the ground.

sin(θ) = 5.2/6 = 0.867  →  θ = 60.1 °

Multi-step problems: Pythagoras and trigonometry together

Many questions need both tools: Pythagoras to find a side in one triangle, trigonometry to use it in another. The method: draw and label every triangle, find the shared side first, then proceed.

Worked example. A ladder 5 m long leans against a wall, with its foot 2 m from the wall. Find the height reached and the angle the ladder makes with the ground.

height: h² = 5² - 2² = 25 - 4 = 21  →  h = 4.58 m
angle: cos(θ) = 2/5 = 0.4  →  θ = 66.4 °

Worked example 2 (two triangles). From a point P, the angle of elevation to the top of a building is 30°; from a point Q, 20 m closer, it is 45°. Find the height.

let h be the height and x the distance from Q to the base.
tan(45) = h/x  →  h = x
tan(30) = h/(x + 20)
h = (x + 20) tan(30) = (h + 20)(1/√(3))
h √(3) = h + 20  →  h(√(3) - 1) = 20
h = 20/(1.732 - 1) = 20/0.732 = 27.3 m

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Pythagoras) A right-angled triangle has legs 9 and 12. Find the hypotenuse. Answer: √(81 + 144) = √225 = 15.
  2. (Leg) Hypotenuse 17, one leg 8. Find the other. Answer: √(289 − 64) = 15.
  3. (Ratio) Angle 28°, adjacent 15 cm. Find the opposite side. Answer: tan 28 = o/15 → o = 15 × 0.532 = 7.98 cm.
  4. (Angle) Opposite 7, hypotenuse 10. Find the angle. Answer: sin θ = 0.7 → θ = 44.4°.
  5. (Exact) Find cos 30° exactly. Answer: √3/2.
  6. (Elevation) From 25 m away, the angle of elevation to a tree top is 40°. Find the height. Answer: 25 tan 40 = 25 × 0.839 = 21.0 m.
  7. (3D) A cuboid is 2 cm by 3 cm by 6 cm. Find its space diagonal. Answer: √(4 + 9 + 36) = √49 = 7 cm.
  8. (Combined) A ship sails 30 km east then 40 km north. Find its distance from the start and the bearing of its final position. Answer: distance = 50 km; tan θ = 40/30 → θ = 53.1°, bearing 053°.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Calculator mode: check DEG, not RAD or GRAD, before any trigonometric calculation. A radian answer is usually obviously wrong (tiny or huge), but only if you check.
  • Wrong ratio: label the sides relative to the angle before choosing SOH, CAH or TOA; picking by habit is the commonest trigonometry error.
  • Hypotenuse identification: the hypotenuse is opposite the right angle, not necessarily the longest-looking side on the diagram.
  • Pythagoras with the hypotenuse as a leg: c² = a² + b² only when c is the hypotenuse; finding a leg requires subtraction.
  • Rounding early: keep full calculator accuracy until the final answer; round to 3 s.f. (or 1 d.p. for angles unless told otherwise).
  • Angle of depression drawn from the wrong line: it is measured from the horizontal, not from the cliff face; the alternate-angle equality fixes the geometry.
  • Exact values with decimals: "exact" means surds and fractions, not 0.866; leaving √3/2 is required.
  • Missing units and labels: state cm, m, km and degrees; name the side or angle found, especially in multi-step problems.

Label the triangle before you reach for a ratio

Right-angled trigonometry is not three formulas to memorise; it is one decision made three times: which side am I given, which do I want, and which ratio connects them. Every error in this topic is a labelling error made before any calculation starts.

Only the hypotenuse is fixed. It is the side opposite the right angle, and it is always the longest. "Opposite" and "adjacent" are relative to the angle you are working with: in the figure, the side BC is opposite θ and AB is adjacent to it. Put the angle at C instead and those two swap. Annotate the diagram with O, A and H in pencil before choosing anything.

The ratios are ratios, which is why they work at any size. Similar triangles taught that corresponding sides scale together — double every side and the ratio stays the same. That is precisely why sin 30° is ½ for a triangle of any size:

sin θ = opposite / hypotenuse Key: θ = the angle inside the triangle; opposite = the side across from θ; hypotenuse = the side opposite the right angle.
cos θ = adjacent / hypotenuse Key: adjacent = the side next to θ that is not the hypotenuse.
tan θ = opposite / adjacent Key: the only ratio that does not use the hypotenuse.

Choosing in one step. Given an angle and one side, mark on the diagram which two sides the question involves, then read off: two sides with the hypotenuse means sine or cosine; two sides without it means tangent. Use the inverse function when the angle is the unknown.

Worked example. A ladder 5.0 m long leans against a wall, making 68° with the ground. How far up the wall does it reach, and how far is its foot from the wall?

height is opposite the 68° angle, ladder is the hypotenuse:

sin 68° = h / 5.0, so h = 5.0 × sin 68° = 5.0 × 0.9272 = 4.6 m

distance from the wall is adjacent:

cos 68° = d / 5.0, so d = 5.0 × cos 68° = 5.0 × 0.3746 = 1.9 m

Check with Pythagoras: 4.6² + 1.9² = 21.2 + 3.6 = 24.8 ≈ 25 = 5.0². That thirty-second check catches a swapped ratio every time, and the two answers being 4.6 and 1.9 rather than a plausible pair like 4.6 and 4.4 is exactly what the check is for.

The special angles come from two triangles. A 45-45-90 triangle with legs 1 gives sin 45° = 1/√2. Half of an equilateral triangle of side 2 gives sides 1, √3 and 2, hence sin 30° = ½, cos 30° = √3/2 and tan 60° = √3. These are worth deriving once so they are not three more things to memorise.

Where marks are lost. The calculator in radians or grads — check the mode before the first question, not after. Using the adjacent side when the question needs the opposite, because the labels were never written on the diagram. And rounding at 4.6 m then using 4.6 in Pythagoras: keep the full value and round only the answer.

Pythagoras' theorem in more depth

Pythagoras' theorem states that in a right-angled triangle the square of the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides, so c² = a² + b², where c is the hypotenuse. The theorem is used in two directions: to find a missing side when the triangle is known to be right-angled, and to test whether a triangle is right-angled at all. The subsections below cover both directions, the common number patterns, and the errors that cost marks.

Finding the hypotenuse

When the two shorter sides are known, add their squares and take the square root. For a triangle with shorter sides 5 cm and 12 cm, the hypotenuse is √(5² + 12²) = √(25 + 144) = √169 = 13 cm. The hypotenuse is always the longest side and always opposite the right angle, so it is the side that is added, not subtracted, in the calculation.

Finding a shorter side

When the hypotenuse and one shorter side are known, subtract the square of the known shorter side from the square of the hypotenuse, then take the square root. For a hypotenuse of 13 cm and a side of 5 cm, the missing side is √(13² − 5²) = √(169 − 25) = √144 = 12 cm. Write the subtraction out in full, because the most common error in this type of question is to add the squares by mistake.

Testing whether a triangle is right-angled

The converse of Pythagoras' theorem says that if the square of the longest side equals the sum of the squares of the other two, the triangle is right-angled. For sides 6, 8 and 10, the check is 6² + 8² = 36 + 64 = 100 = 10², so the triangle is right-angled. For sides 7, 8 and 10, the check is 49 + 64 = 113, which is greater than 100, so the triangle is acute and not right-angled. Always compare the squares of the longest side with the others.

Pythagorean triples

A Pythagorean triple is a set of three whole numbers that satisfy a² + b² = c². The most used are 3, 4, 5; 5, 12, 13; 8, 15, 17; and 7, 24, 25. Any multiple of a triple is also a triple, so 6, 8, 10 and 9, 12, 15 are triples. Recognising a triple lets you give an exact answer with no square root, which is often what the question wants when the sides are whole numbers.

Pythagoras in a problem with several triangles

Some questions need the theorem twice, because the first right-angled triangle gives a side that is needed in the second. For example, a rectangle 9 cm by 12 cm has a diagonal of √(9² + 12²) = 15 cm. If a second triangle uses that diagonal as one of its sides, the same method applies again. Mark the sides you have found on the diagram before starting the next step, so each calculation has its numbers ready.

Real-world problems with Pythagoras

A ladder leaning against a wall, a diagonal across a field and the straight-line distance between two towns are all Pythagoras problems once the right angle is identified. Draw the triangle, label the hypotenuse as the longest side, and state which right angle the theorem is being used at. A question that describes a route going east then north is a right-angled triangle formed by the two legs and the straight line between the ends.

Rounding and giving the answer

Leave square roots exact if the question asks for an exact answer, and give a decimal to the accuracy the question states. A calculation that gives √50 can be left as 5√2 for an exact answer, or written as 7.07 to 3 significant figures for a decimal answer. Do the rounding only at the last step, because rounding an intermediate square root and then squaring it can change the final answer.

Common errors with Pythagoras

The errors that lose marks are forgetting the square root at the end, adding when the question needs a subtraction, and applying the theorem to a triangle that is not right-angled. Check the answer by reversing the calculation: square the two shorter sides, add them, and confirm the result equals the square of the hypotenuse. A quick reversal catches most slips.

Trigonometric ratios in more depth

The sine, cosine and tangent ratios connect an angle in a right-angled triangle to the ratio of two sides. They are defined by sin θ = opposite ÷ hypotenuse, cos θ = adjacent ÷ hypotenuse and tan θ = opposite ÷ adjacent, and the calculator supplies the values. The subsections below cover naming the sides, the two directions of use (finding a side and finding an angle), and why the ratios depend only on the angle.

Naming the sides from the angle

The three sides are named from the point of view of the angle θ you are using. The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle and is always the longest. The opposite side is the one across from θ, and the adjacent side is the one next to θ that is not the hypotenuse. The same side is the opposite side for one angle and the adjacent side for the other acute angle, so name the sides again for each angle rather than once for the whole triangle.

Finding a side when an angle is known

Choose the ratio that uses the side you know and the side you want. If the hypotenuse is 10 cm and the angle is 30°, and you want the opposite side, use sin 30° = opposite ÷ 10, so the opposite side is 10 × sin 30° = 10 × 0.5 = 5 cm. Writing the ratio first, with the unknown alone on one side, is the step that keeps the working correct.

Finding an angle from a ratio

When two sides are known, find the ratio and use the inverse function on the calculator. For opposite 7 and adjacent 24, tan θ = 7 ÷ 24 = 0.2917, so θ = tan⁻¹(0.2917) = 16.3° to 1 decimal place. Use sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹ or tan⁻¹ according to the pair of sides, and never take the inverse of a ratio that you have not first worked out.

Setting the calculator to degrees

Every trigonometry question in this note uses degrees, so the calculator must be in degree mode before any value is found. A calculator in radian mode gives sin 30 = −0.988, which is a wrong answer that looks like a real value. Check the mode at the start of each exam and again if an answer looks unreasonable. A quick test is that sin 30 should return 0.5 in degree mode.

Why the ratios depend only on the angle

Two right-angled triangles with the same angle are similar, so the ratio of opposite to hypotenuse is the same in both. A triangle with a hypotenuse of 10 and opposite of 5 has the same sin θ as one with hypotenuse 20 and opposite 10. This is why a table of sine values works for every triangle, and it is the reason the ratios can be used to find unknown sides.

Complementary angles

In a right-angled triangle the two acute angles add to 90°, so each is the complement of the other. This gives sin θ = cos (90° − θ) and cos θ = sin (90° − θ). For example, sin 30° = cos 60° = 0.5. The relationship is useful for checking a value, and it explains why sine and cosine are the same curve shifted by 90°.

Tangent as sine over cosine

The tangent ratio is the sine divided by the cosine, because tan θ = (opposite ÷ hypotenuse) ÷ (adjacent ÷ hypotenuse) = opposite ÷ adjacent. This is the form to use when a question gives the tangent of an angle and asks for a side, and it also explains why tangent is undefined at 90°, where the adjacent side would have length zero.

title: IGCSE Biology: Characteristics and Classification
content:
IGCSE Biology: Characteristics and Classification of Living Organisms

Biology is the study of life, and the first job of any scientist is to decide what counts as alive and how to organise the millions of species that do. This note sets out the seven life processes that define living things, walks through the hierarchical classification system from kingdom down to species using the modern five-kingdom scheme and the binomial naming system, and shows how organisms are grouped by their observable and internal features — from the vertebrae in your backbone to the molecular evidence that modern biologists now prefer. Every definition is given in the exact form mark schemes reward, and the worked examples show how to name an organism from a table of features.

The characteristics of living organisms

Living organisms all carry out seven processes, conveniently remembered as MRS GREN: Movement (changing position or moving parts), Respiration (chemical reactions releasing energy from food — not the same as breathing), Sensitivity (detecting and responding to changes in the environment), Growth (permanent increase in size and dry mass), Reproduction (making new organisms of the same kind), Excretion (removing the waste products of metabolism), and Nutrition (taking in materials for energy, growth and development). Any object doing all seven is alive; a crystal grows but does not respire; a robot moves but does not reproduce. The common exam trap is that respiration goes on in every cell all the time, while breathing merely supplies the oxygen for it.

Why we classify: the uses of classification systems

Classification sorts living things into groups based on shared features. Its uses are practical: naming organisms unambiguously so scientists worldwide mean the same thing, showing evolutionary relationships (which species share a recent ancestor), identifying unknown organisms (a doctor identifying a bacterium chooses the right antibiotic), and organising the study of biodiversity so conservation can target whole lineages. Modern classification is based on evolutionary relationships derived from DNA and protein comparisons — organisms with more similar base sequences are more closely related — while older schemes used only visible features such as body shape and number of legs.

The hierarchy of classification

Classification is a nested hierarchy: each level contains the one below it. From largest to smallest: kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species. A useful memory is "King Philip Came Over For Good Spaghetti". A species is defined as a group of organisms with similar features that can interbreed to produce fertile offspring. Each organism gets a two-part scientific name (binomial nomenclature, invented by Carolus Linnaeus): the first word is the genus (capitalised), the second is the species (lower case), both underlined or italicised in writing — for example, humans are Homo sapiens and the house cat is Felis catus. Two organisms in the same genus are closely related but not the same species; two in the same family are more distantly related, and so on up the hierarchy.

The five kingdoms

The five-kingdom scheme organises all life by cell structure and mode of nutrition. Prokaryotae: bacteria — no nucleus, no membrane-bound organelles, cell wall of murein, mostly decomposers or pathogens. Protoctista: mostly single-celled with a nucleus (Amoeba, Plasmodium, seaweeds like Chlorella) — no true tissues. Fungi: eukaryotic, cell walls of chitin, feed saprotrophically by extracellular digestion (secrete enzymes, absorb soluble products), body made of hyphae forming a mycelium (yeast is single-celled). Plantae: multicellular eukaryotes with cellulose cell walls, chloroplasts and photosynthetic autotrophic nutrition. Animalia: multicellular eukaryotes, no cell walls, no chloroplasts, heterotrophic (ingestive) nutrition, usually able to move and with nervous coordination. Learn one named example per kingdom — Penicillium (fungi), Plasmodium (protoctista), Escherichia coli (prokaryotae) — because questions often demand an example.

The five kingdoms compared

KingdomCell typeCell wallNutritionExample
ProkaryotaeProkaryote (no nucleus)MureinVaried: saprotrophic, parasiticEscherichia coli
ProtoctistaEukaryote, mostly unicellularSome (cellulose in algae)Photosynthetic or ingestiveAmoeba, Plasmodium
FungiEukaryote (yeast unicellular)ChitinSaprotrophic (extracellular digestion)Penicillium, yeast
PlantaeEukaryote, multicellularCelluloseAutotrophic (photosynthesis)Maize, moss
AnimaliaEukaryote, multicellularNoneHeterotrophic (ingestive)Human, earthworm

Vertebrates: the five classes of phylum Chordata

Vertebrates (animals with a backbone) form five classes, each with distinguishing features you must know. Fish: scales, gills, fins, lay eggs in water, cold-blooded (ectothermic). Amphibians: moist skin, lay shell-less eggs in water, larvae (tadpoles) have gills and metamorphose, cold-blooded. Reptiles: dry scaly skin, lay leathery eggs on land, lungs, cold-blooded. Birds: feathers, beaks, wings, lay hard-shelled eggs, warm-blooded (endothermic), high metabolic rate. Mammals: hair or fur, mammary glands producing milk, mostly placental (give birth to live young), warm-blooded, four-chambered heart.
