The distinction warm-blooded versus cold-blooded matters: endotherms maintain a constant body temperature using metabolic heat; ectotherms rely on external heat sources.

Invertebrates and the features used to group them

Arthropods share jointed legs, an exoskeleton of chitin that is moulted for growth, and segmented bodies; the four classes are insects (three body parts, six legs, often wings), arachnids (two parts, eight legs), crustaceans (ten or more legs, gills, aquatic) and myriapods (many legs, segmented). Molluscs have a soft body, usually a muscular foot and a shell (snail, octopus, mussel). Annelids are segmented worms (earthworm, leech). Nematodes are unsegmented roundworms. Cnidarians have stinging tentacles (jellyfish, hydra). Platyhelminthes are flatworms (tapeworm, planarian). Echinoderms are spiny-skinned with a water-vascular system (starfish, sea urchin). Dichotomous keys — a branching series of paired choices based on observable features — are built from exactly these distinctions and are a standard Paper 2 and Paper 6 question.

How features decide a group: worked classification

Table of observable and internal features used at each level: cellular organisation (prokaryote or eukaryote) decides the kingdom; cell wall composition (murein, chitin, cellulose) separates bacteria, fungi and plants; mode of nutrition (photosynthetic, saprotrophic, ingestive) separates plants, fungi and animals; presence of a vertebral column separates vertebrates from invertebrates; body covering (scales, feathers, hair) and reproduction (eggs, live young) separate the vertebrate classes. Modern classification adds molecular evidence: DNA-DNA hybridisation, ribosomal RNA sequences and immunological comparisons of blood proteins. Two species with 98 % similarity in a particular gene are more closely related than two with 70 %, and the resulting family trees (phylogenetic trees) can be drawn from the data — a skill worth practising, because drawing a tree from a table of differences is now common in Paper 4.

Worked example: building a dichotomous key

Organisms to key out: a spider, a woodlouse, a butterfly, a centipede. Step 1: list the distinguishing features — number of legs (6, 8, 10, many), wings (present or absent), number of body segments. Step 2: split first on the most obvious feature: "has wings — butterfly; no wings — continue". Step 3: split the remainder by leg number: "8 legs — spider; more than 8 legs — continue". Step 4: final pair: "10 legs and 2 body parts — woodlouse (a crustacean); many legs and many segments — centipede". Step 5: write each pair as numbered statements in the standard format: 1a has wings ... butterfly; 1b has no wings ... go to 2; and so on. The exam rewards keys written in matched pairs (a/b) where every organism is named exactly once. Binomial naming: write the spider as Araneus diadematus — genus capitalised, species lower case, both italicised (or underlined).

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Confusing genus and species in the scientific name: the first word is the genus (capital letter), the second the species (small letter).
  • Writing "breathing" for respiration: respiration is the chemical release of energy in every cell; breathing is the mechanical ventilation of the lungs or gills.
  • Describing a fungus as a plant: fungi have chitin walls and saprotrophic nutrition — no chloroplasts.
  • Leaving out "fertile" when defining species: "can interbreed and produce fertile offspring" is the required wording (mules are the classic counterexample).
  • Saying mammals "have live birth" absolutely — monotremes (platypus) lay eggs, and the mark scheme wants "mostly placental, produce milk".
  • Forgetting to name an example when asked for one with the kingdom.
  • In Paper 6 key construction, writing single-choice lines instead of matched pairs (a/b), or giving a character (like "has legs") that separates nothing.
  • Using observable features only when the question specifies molecular evidence; DNA base sequence comparisons are the modern basis of classification.

Exam-style questions and answers

Q1. List the seven characteristics of living organisms. (3 marks) Answer: any three of movement, respiration, sensitivity, growth, reproduction, excretion, nutrition — one mark for three correct, full marks for all seven in context.

Q2. Explain two ways in which a fungus differs from a plant. (2 marks) Answer: fungal cell walls contain chitin not cellulose (1); fungi feed saprotrophically by extracellular digestion and have no chloroplasts (1).

Q3. Write the scientific name of the lion (Panthera leo) correctly and explain the rules you used. (2 marks) Answer: Panthera leo — genus capitalised and species lower case (1); both words italicised or underlined (1).

Q4. Describe how modern classification differs from the system used by Linnaeus. (2 marks) Answer: modern classification uses evolutionary relationships from DNA/protein base sequence comparisons (1); Linnaeus used observable features such as body structure only (1).

Q5. Explain why classification systems are useful to scientists. (3 marks) Answer: standardised naming so scientists worldwide understand which organism is meant (1); identification of unknown organisms for medicine or agriculture (1); showing evolutionary relationships for conservation and research (1).

title: Algebra — Graphs — Study Notes
content:
Algebra — Graphs

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): straight lines (gradient, intercept), key curves (quadratic, cubic, reciprocal, exponential), tangents, kinematic reading.

1. Straight lines

  • Gradient m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁).
  • y = mx + c; parallel ⇒ equal m; perpendicular ⇒ m₁m₂ = −1.

Example: through (2, −1) parallel to y = 3x + 1: y + 1 = 3(x − 2) ⇒ y = 3x − 7.

2. Drawing curves

Table of values, plot, smooth curve. Parabola symmetry axis x = −b/2a. Recognise reciprocal y = 1/x (two branches) and exponential y = aˣ (through (0,1)).

3. Interpreting

  • Roots = x-intercepts; y-intercept from x = 0.
  • Turning points of quadratics by completing the square.

4. Tangents and rates

Gradient of tangent at a point = instantaneous rate: draw a large triangle, rise/run. Area under a speed–time graph = distance (trapezium estimate).

5. Graphical solutions

Simultaneous: intersection points. Quadratic = line: intersections give roots. Read off carefully to the accuracy allowed.

Exam tips: quote gradients as fractions where exact; when estimating a tangent gradient, use a triangle spanning at least 4 grid squares.

Plotting and reading straight-line graphs

A table of values is set up from the equation, points are plotted and joined with a ruler. For y = mx + c, m is the gradient and c the y-intercept. The gradient is the change in y divided by the change in x, measured on a large triangle drawn on the line, not between two points read from a table.

Quadratic and cubic curves

Curves are drawn freehand as smooth curves through plotted points. Turning points, roots (where the curve cuts the x-axis) and the y-intercept are read directly from the graph. A quadratic has one turning point; a cubic can have up to two.

Using graphs to solve equations

To solve f(x) = k, draw the line y = k and read the x-coordinates where it meets the curve. Intersections of two graphs give simultaneous solutions. Always state the solutions to the accuracy the question asks for.

Worked example: gradient and equation of a line

A line passes through (1, 3) and (4, −3). The gradient is (−3 − 3)/(4 − 1) = −6/3 = −2. Substituting into y = mx + c with the point (1, 3) gives 3 = −2 + c, so c = 5 and the equation is y = −2x + 5.

A parallel line has the same gradient, so a line through (0, 1) parallel to this one is y = −2x + 1. A perpendicular line has gradient 1/2.

Turning points of a quadratic

For y = x² − 6x + 5, complete the square: y = (x − 3)² − 4. The minimum turning point is (3, −4), and the curve crosses the x-axis where (x − 3)² = 4, that is at x = 1 and x = 5. Sketch the curve through these points and label the turning point.

Gradient of a curve at a point

Between two points on a curve, the average rate of change is the gradient of the chord. To estimate the gradient at a point, draw a tangent by eye and find its gradient from two clearly read points on the tangent, using a large triangle. The answer will only be as accurate as your tangent.

Reading a graph in context

A distance–time graph has gradient equal to speed, so a horizontal section means the object is stationary. A speed–time graph has gradient equal to acceleration, and the area under it equals the distance travelled. Always state the units of the gradient, for example m/s or m/s².

  • Plot points carefully and join curves with a smooth line, not straight segments.
  • When a question asks you to use a graph to solve an equation, draw the line y = (the right-hand side) and read off the x-values where the curve crosses it.

title: A2 Level Chemistry: Organic Chemistry: Carbonyls, Carboxylic Acids and Chirality
content:
Organic Chemistry: Carbonyls, Carboxylic Acids and Chirality

Edexcel International A Level Chemistry — Unit 4 (WCH14), Topic 15, covers the concepts of carbonyl compounds, carboxylic acids, and chirality. This topic includes the reactions and tests of aldehydes and ketones, the properties and reactions of carboxylic acids, and the concept of optical isomerism and chirality.

Introduction to Carbonyl Compounds

Carbonyl compounds contain the carbonyl group, C=O. Aldehydes have the C=O group at the end of a chain (RCHO), while ketones have it inside the chain (RCOR). The carbon of C=O is slightly positive, making it susceptible to nucleophilic attack.

  • Aldehydes: RCHO
  • Ketones: RCOR

Reactions of Carbonyl Compounds

Carbonyl compounds undergo nucleophilic addition reactions. The products of these reactions can be carboxylic acids, alcohols, or molecules with a chiral centre.

  • Hydrogen cyanide adds across C=O: RCHO + HCN → RCN
  • Sodium tetrahydridoborate(III) (NaBH4) reduces aldehydes to primary alcohols and ketones to secondary alcohols
  • 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine (2,4-DNPH) gives an orange or yellow precipitate with any carbonyl compound
  • Tollens' reagent gives a silver mirror with aldehydes but not with ketones
  • The iodoform test gives a yellow precipitate of triiodomethane with compounds containing CH3CO– or CH3CH(OH)– groups

Carboxylic Acids

Carboxylic acids contain –COOH and are weak acids. They are more acidic than alcohols because the carboxylate ion is stabilised by delocalisation.

  • Carboxylic acids react with alcohols in the presence of concentrated sulfuric acid to form esters
  • Primary alcohols are oxidised to carboxylic acids by heating with acidified potassium dichromate(VI) under reflux

Chirality and Optical Isomerism

A chiral carbon atom has four different groups attached. Molecules with a chiral centre exist as a pair of enantiomers. Enantiomers have identical physical properties except their effect on plane-polarised light.

  • A chiral carbon atom has four different groups attached
  • Enantiomers have identical physical properties except their effect on plane-polarised light
  • An equimolar mixture of the two enantiomers is a racemic mixture, which is optically inactive

Optical Activity

Optical activity is the ability of a single optical isomer to rotate the plane of polarisation of plane-polarised monochromatic light.

  • Optical activity is measured using a polarimeter
  • The specific rotation of a compound is a characteristic property

Nomenclature of Aldehydes and Ketones

Aldehydes and ketones are named based on the longest continuous chain containing the carbonyl group.

  • Aldehydes: RCHO
  • Ketones: RCOR

Nomenclature of Carboxylic Acids

Carboxylic acids are named based on the longest continuous chain containing the carboxyl group.

  • Carboxylic acids: RCOOH

Nomenclature of Acyl Chlorides and Esters

Acyl chlorides and esters are named based on the longest continuous chain containing the acyl group.

  • Acyl chlorides: RCOCl
  • Esters: RCOOR

Reactions of Acyl Chlorides

Acyl chlorides undergo nucleophilic substitution reactions.

  • Acyl chlorides react with water to form carboxylic acids
  • Acyl chlorides react with alcohols to form esters
  • Acyl chlorides react with concentrated ammonia to form amides
  • Acyl chlorides react with amines to form amides

Hydrolysis of Esters

Esters undergo hydrolysis reactions in acidic and alkaline solutions.

  • Esters react with water in the presence of an acid catalyst to form carboxylic acids and alcohols
  • Esters react with water in the presence of a base to form carboxylic acids and alcohols

Condensation Polymerisation

Polyesters are formed by condensation polymerisation reactions.

  • Polyesters are formed by the reaction of carboxylic acids and alcohols

Mass Spectra

Mass spectra provide information about the molecular mass of a compound.

  • The molecular ion is the ion with the highest mass-to-charge ratio
  • The base peak is the ion with the highest intensity

13C NMR Spectroscopy

13C NMR spectroscopy provides information about the environments of carbon atoms in a molecule.

  • The chemical shift of a carbon atom is a characteristic property
  • The number of peaks in a 13C NMR spectrum is equal to the number of different environments of carbon atoms

Proton NMR Spectroscopy

Proton NMR spectroscopy provides information about the environments of hydrogen atoms in a molecule.

  • The chemical shift of a hydrogen atom is a characteristic property
  • The number of peaks in a proton NMR spectrum is equal to the number of different environments of hydrogen atoms
  • The intensity of a peak is proportional to the number of hydrogen atoms in that environment

Chromatography

Chromatography is a technique used to separate the components of a mixture.

  • Chromatography separates components based on their affinity for a stationary phase and a mobile phase
  • The Rf value is a measure of the distance traveled by a component relative to the distance traveled by the solvent front

Typical Mistakes

  • Confusing the reactions of aldehydes and ketones
  • Forgetting to show the nucleophile attacking the carbon of C=O in nucleophilic addition reactions
  • Not understanding the concept of optical isomerism and chirality

Exam-Style Questions

  1. What is the difference between an aldehyde and a ketone? Answer: An aldehyde has the C=O group at the end of a chain, while a ketone has it inside the chain.
  2. What is the reaction of hydrogen cyanide with an aldehyde? Answer: Hydrogen cyanide adds across C=O to form a cyanohydrin.
  3. What is the specific rotation of a compound? Answer: The specific rotation of a compound is a characteristic property that is measured using a polarimeter.

To revise this topic, make sure to understand the reactions and tests of aldehydes and ketones, the properties and reactions of carboxylic acids, and the concept of optical isomerism and chirality. Practice drawing the structures of aldehydes, ketones, and carboxylic acids, and practice solving problems involving the reactions of these compounds. Also, make sure to understand the concepts of 13C NMR spectroscopy, proton NMR spectroscopy, and chromatography, and practice solving problems involving these techniques. Finally, practice answering exam-style questions to test your understanding of the topic.

Detailed Mechanisms of Nucleophilic Addition: HCN and KCN

The addition of hydrogen cyanide to carbonyl compounds is a classic Edexcel A2 mechanism. Because HCN is a weak acid and provides a very low concentration of cyanide ions, potassium cyanide (KCN) is added to provide a higher concentration of the active nucleophile, CN−. The mechanism proceeds via nucleophilic addition:

  • Step 1: The lone pair on the carbon atom of the cyanide ion (CN−) attacks the slightly positive carbon atom of the carbonyl group (C=O). A curly arrow goes from the lone pair on carbon to the carbonyl carbon.
  • Step 2: Simultaneously, the π bond of the carbonyl group breaks, with both electrons moving entirely to the oxygen atom. This forms a negatively charged intermediate (an alkoxide ion) and shows a curly arrow from the C=O bond to the oxygen.
  • Step 3: The intermediate accepts a proton (H+) from HCN or from the acidic aqueous environment to form a hydroxy-nitrile (cyanohydrin).

Stereochemical Evidence from Carbonyl Addition to Unsymmetrical Ketones

When an unsymmetrical aldehyde or ketone reacts with hydrogen cyanide, the planar nature of the carbonyl group allows the nucleophile (CN−) to attack from either above or below the plane with equal probability. If the product molecule contains a single chiral centre (i.e., four different groups attached to the central carbon), a racemic mixture of two optical isomers (enantiomers) is formed in equal amounts. This proves that the intermediate is planar around the original carbonyl carbon and provides crucial mechanistic evidence for the reaction pathway.

Physical Properties of Carbonyl Compounds and Carboxylic Acids

Understanding intermolecular forces explains the differing boiling temperatures and water solubilities:

  • Aldehydes and ketones cannot form hydrogen bonds with themselves because they lack a hydrogen atom bonded directly to a strongly electronegative oxygen or nitrogen atom. Their molecules are held together by permanent dipole-dipole attractions and London forces, resulting in lower boiling temperatures than corresponding alcohols or carboxylic acids of similar relative molecular mass.
  • Aldehydes, ketones, and carboxylic acids can form hydrogen bonds with water molecules through their lone pairs on the carbonyl or hydroxyl oxygens, which explains why smaller members of these homologous series are completely soluble in water.
  • Carboxylic acids can form stable hydrogen-bonded dimers with each other in the liquid and vapour phases. This effectively doubles their relative molecular mass during vaporisation, leading to significantly higher boiling temperatures than alcohols of comparable molecular mass.

Comprehensive Analysis of Spectroscopic Data

Examiners frequently test the ability to combine mass spectrometry, carbon-13 NMR, and proton NMR data to deduce molecular structures:

  • Mass Spectrometry: High-resolution mass spectrometry provides accurate relative molecular masses to four decimal places, allowing chemists to distinguish between molecules with the same nominal integer mass (e.g., CO, N2, and C2H4 all have a nominal mass of 28, but accurate masses separate them precisely). Fragmentation patterns reveal structural fragments, such as the loss of 15 (CH3), 17 (OH), or 45 (COOH).
  • Carbon-13 NMR: Each peak in a 13C NMR spectrum corresponds to a carbon atom in a distinct chemical environment. The chemical shift value (measured in ppm) gives information about the types of adjacent atoms or functional groups (e.g., carbon in a C=O group appears around 160 to 220 ppm, while aliphatic sp3 carbons appear between 0 and 50 ppm).
  • Proton (1H) NMR: The number of distinct peaks indicates the number of different hydrogen environments. The relative peak areas (integration traces) show the ratio of hydrogen atoms in each environment. The splitting pattern of each peak is determined by the number of adjacent non-equivalent protons using the (n + 1) rule, where n is the number of protons on adjacent carbon atoms. TMS (tetramethylsilane) is used as an internal reference standard because it produces a single sharp peak at 0 ppm, is inert, volatile, and non-toxic.

Advanced Chromatography Techniques

In addition to basic thin-layer chromatography (TLC) and paper chromatography where Rf values are calculated as the distance travelled by the solute divided by the distance travelled by the solvent front, modern analytical separation relies on column-based methods:

  • High-Performance Liquid Chromatography (HPLC): Uses a liquid mobile phase pumped under high pressure through a tightly packed column containing a solid stationary phase. Components separate based on their differing partition coefficients between the two phases.
  • Gas Chromatography (GC): Uses an inert carrier gas (such as helium or neon) as the mobile phase passing through a column containing a high-boiling liquid stationary phase coated on a solid support. Retention time is the time taken for a component to pass through the column from injection to detection.
  • Coupled Techniques: Both HPLC and GC can be directly coupled with mass spectrometry (HPLC-MS or GC-MS). This allows the chromatographic separation of complex mixtures followed immediately by mass spectral identification of each separated component, widely applied in forensic science, drug testing in sport, and environmental monitoring.

Worked Examples

  1. Worked Example: Calculating Rf Values
    Question: In a TLC experiment, the solvent front travels 8.4 cm from the baseline. A specific organic component travels 3.5 cm from the baseline. Calculate the Rf value for this component.
    Method: Use the formula Rf = (distance travelled by spot) ÷ (distance travelled by solvent front).
    Answer: Rf = 3.5 ÷ 8.4 = 0.42 (no units).
  2. Worked Example: Predicting 1H NMR Splitting
    Question: Predict the splitting pattern for the protons in the CH2 group of ethanol (CH3CH2OH), assuming standard high-resolution conditions.
    Method: Identify the number of non-equivalent protons (n) on the adjacent carbon atom. The adjacent carbon is the CH3 group, which has 3 protons. Apply the (n + 1) rule: 3 + 1 = 4.
    Answer: A quartet.

Common Student Mistakes and Corrections

  • Mistake: Confusing the action of Tollens reagent with Fehling solution on aliphatic aldehydes and aromatic aldehydes.
    Correction: Both Tollens reagent and Fehling solution give positive tests with aliphatic aldehydes (silver mirror and red precipitate respectively). However, aromatic aldehydes like benzaldehyde reduce Tollens reagent to form a silver mirror, but they do NOT reduce Fehling solution.
  • Mistake: Forgetting that carboxylic acids react with carbonates to release carbon dioxide gas, whereas alcohols do not.
    Correction: Always use sodium carbonate or sodium hydrogencarbonate solution to distinguish carboxylic acids from alcohols or phenols, as only carboxylic acids are strong enough acids to liberate carbon dioxide gas with effervescence.
  • Mistake: Misinterpreting peak splitting in proton NMR by counting protons on both sides indiscriminately.
    Correction: The (n + 1) rule only applies to protons on directly adjacent, non-equivalent carbon atoms. Protons separated by oxygen atoms or multiple bonds do not couple.

Exam-Style Questions and Answers

  1. Question: State why 1,1-dichloroethane and 1,2-dichloroethane have different numbers of peaks in their carbon-13 NMR spectra.
    Answer: 1,1-dichloroethane has two carbon environments (the CH3 carbon and the CHCl2 carbon), so it shows 2 peaks in its 13C NMR spectrum. 1,2-dichloroethane has only one carbon environment due to molecular symmetry (both carbons are bonded to a chlorine and a hydrogen and feel the same electronic environment), so it shows only 1 peak.
    Credit Point: Awarded for correctly identifying the carbon environments and linking them directly to the number of observed peaks.
  2. Question: Write an equation for the reaction of propanoyl chloride with concentrated ammonia, and name the organic product.
    Answer: CH3CH2COCl + 2NH3 → CH3CH2CONH2 + NH4Cl. The organic product is propanamide.
    Credit Point: Awarded for correct balanced stoichiometry (including the 2 moles of ammonia to react with the formed HCl) and correct naming of the amide.
  3. Question: Explain why a racemic mixture shows no optical activity when analysed in a polarimeter.
    Answer: A racemic mixture contains equal amounts of two enantiomers. Each enantiomer rotates the plane of plane-polarised light by an equal angle in opposite directions, resulting in the rotations cancelling each other out entirely.
    Credit Point: Awarded for mentioning equal amounts of enantiomers and the equal and opposite rotation of plane-polarised light.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Nucleophilic addition, applied to propanone with HCN and KCN: the cyanide ion attacks the δ+ carbon of the C=O, forming an alkoxide that picks up H⁺. The product is 2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanenitrile. Show the curly arrow from the C=O π bond to the oxygen.
  • Racemic product: the carbonyl carbon is planar, so the cyanide can attack from either face with equal likelihood. Propanal gives a racemic mixture of two enantiomers, and the product has no net optical activity. A chiral centre is one with four different groups attached.
  • Chirality, applied to 2-bromobutane: the second carbon carries H, Br, CH₃ and CH₂CH₃, four different groups, so the molecule is chiral and has two enantiomers that rotate plane-polarised light in opposite directions.
  • Tests: 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine gives an orange precipitate with any carbonyl. Tollens' reagent gives a silver mirror only with aldehydes, and acidified dichromate turns from orange to green with aldehydes. Name the test and the observation together.

Equations and symbols

The addition reaction, the two analytical relations that this topic is examined on, and the rule that predicts splitting. Mechanisms are drawn, not written, but these lines carry the marks that are typed.

RCHO + HCN → RCN Key: R = the rest of the chain; CHO = the aldehyde carbonyl group; HCN = hydrogen cyanide, the nucleophile source (KCN is added to raise the cyanide concentration); RCN = the cyanohydrin product, which has a new C–C bond and a new chiral centre. Ketones react the same way but give a product with two different R groups.

Rf = (distance travelled by spot) ÷ (distance travelled by solvent front) Key: Rf = retention factor, a ratio between 0 and 1 with no units; both distances measured from the same baseline, in the same units (cm or mm). A ratio cannot exceed 1, so an answer above 1 means the distances were measured from different origins.

Rf = 3.5 ÷ 8.4 = 0.42 Key: 3.5 cm = distance moved by the spot; 8.4 cm = distance moved by the solvent front; 0.42 is the Rf, quoted to two significant figures because the ruler reads to a millimetre. Rf is characteristic of a compound in a given solvent, which is how chromatography identifies it.

3 + 1 = 4 Key: the (n + 1) rule: n = number of non-equivalent protons on the adjacent carbon (here the CH₃ of ethanol, so 3); the answer 4 is the number of peaks in the multiplet, a quartet. Protons on the same carbon do not split each other, and OH protons usually exchange too fast to split at all.

title:
Molecules, Transport and Health — AS Level Biology

This revision note belongs to the Edexcel International Advanced Subsidiary (IAS) Biology specification, WBI12 Unit 1, Topic 1 Molecules, Transport and Health. It covers water as a solvent and its structure, carbohydrates and lipids, proteins and their structure and function, gas exchange surfaces and Fick's law, the mammalian circulatory system and the cardiac cycle, haemoglobin and the oxygen dissociation curve, atherosclerosis and blood clotting, the risk factors for cardiovascular disease, diet, cholesterol and antioxidants, how people use scientific knowledge to reduce risk, the benefits and risks of treatments, and data analysis and evaluation in health studies — plus the gas exchange surfaces and enzyme practical work that support the topic. Every statement the topic is responsible for is covered in its own section or paragraph.

1. Water: structure, properties and why it is the solvent of life

Water is a small molecule with two hydrogen atoms covalently bonded to one oxygen atom; because the oxygen atom is much more electronegative than hydrogen, the shared electrons spend more time near the oxygen, so the molecule is polar — the oxygen end is slightly negative and the hydrogen end slightly positive. This polarity lets water molecules form hydrogen bonds with each other, which gives water its high specific heat capacity, its high latent heat of vaporisation, its cohesion (important for the transpiration stream in plants) and its solvent powers. Water is an excellent solvent because its polarity lets it surround and dissolve ions and polar molecules; ions become hydrated with water molecules around them, and polar molecules such as glucose dissolve readily. In transport, water's solvent nature lets it carry dissolved substances in blood and in plant tissue fluid and sap, and its dipole nature explains why it can do that — the partial charges interact with the charges of ions and the polar groups of molecules like glucose and amino acids.

2. Carbohydrates: monosaccharides, disaccharides and polysaccharides

Carbohydrates are made of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, with hydrogen and oxygen in the same ratio as in water (2:1). Monosaccharides are the simplest carbohydrates and are the building blocks — glucose, fructose and galactose are hexose monosaccharides with the formula C6H12O6. Disaccharides form when two monosaccharides join by a condensation reaction, losing a water molecule and forming a glycosidic bond; the common ones are maltose (glucose + glucose), sucrose (glucose + fructose) and lactose (glucose + galactose). Polysaccharides are long chains of monosaccharides; starch in plants is made of two polymers — amylose, a long unbranched helix of glucose, which is compact for storage, and amylopectin, which is branched so that glucose can be added or removed quickly from the ends. Glycogen is similar to amylopectin but more branched, and it is the storage carbohydrate in animals, mainly in liver and muscle cells. Cellulose is a structural polysaccharide of beta-glucose chains forming long, straight fibres that cross-link by hydrogen bonds into strong microfibrils; it forms plant cell walls. Carbohydrates provide and store energy: starch and glycogen store glucose in a compact, insoluble, osmotically inert form, so they do not affect the cell's water potential, and they can be hydrolysed back to glucose when needed for respiration.

3. Core Practical 1 — semi-quantitative tests for reducing sugars and starch

Use Benedict's reagent to estimate the concentration of reducing sugars and iodine solution to estimate the concentration of starch, using colour standards. Benedict's reagent (copper(II) sulfate, sodium carbonate and sodium citrate) turns from blue to green, then yellow, then orange, then brick-red as reducing sugars are heated with it — the colour depends on the concentration of reducing sugar. For a semi-quantitative estimate, prepare a range of known reducing sugar concentrations (for example glucose solutions), heat each with Benedict's, compare the colour with a colour standard chart, and record the colour or its code for each; then use the standards to estimate the concentration in an unknown. For starch, add iodine solution (iodine in potassium iodide) to the sample; a blue-black colour shows starch, and the intensity of the colour relates to the concentration — compare with colour standards to estimate. State the variables: the independent variable is the sugar or starch concentration, the dependent variable is the colour or colour standard, and controlled variables include the volume, temperature and time of heating.

4. Glycosidic bonds: condensation and hydrolysis

Monosaccharides join by condensation reactions to form disaccharides and polysaccharides, with a glycosidic bond formed between them and a water molecule lost each time. Conversely, polysaccharides and disaccharides can be hydrolysed — split by the addition of water — into their monomers; hydrolysis breaks the glycosidic bond and needs a water molecule for each bond broken. Glucose, fructose and galactose join to make maltose (glucose + glucose), sucrose (glucose + fructose) and lactose (glucose + galactose). Amylose and amylopectin are formed from alpha-glucose units; cellulose is formed from beta-glucose units, and because beta-glucose has a different orientation the chain is straight rather than coiled, so the hydrogen bonds between adjacent chains form strong microfibrils. Hydrolysis of starch gives maltose then glucose; hydrolysis of sucrose gives glucose and fructose; hydrolysis of lactose gives glucose and galactose. This matters in the body: dietary starch is hydrolysed to glucose in the gut by enzymes, and that glucose is used in respiration or stored as glycogen; lactose intolerance is caused by a deficiency of lactase, the enzyme that hydrolyses lactose, so lactose stays in the gut and causes problems.

5. Triglycerides: structure and saturated and unsaturated lipids

A triglyceride is made from one glycerol molecule and three fatty acids, joined by three ester bonds formed in condensation reactions; it is insoluble in water (hydrophobic). Fatty acids have a carboxyl group at one end and a hydrocarbon chain that may be saturated — no double bonds in the chain, so the molecule is straight and packs tightly, and saturated fats (and the triglycerides made from them) are usually solid at room temperature — or unsaturated, with one or more double bonds that kink the chain and prevent tight packing, so unsaturated fats are usually liquid at room temperature (oils). Lipids have several roles: they store energy in a compact, insoluble form (1 g of fat stores more energy than 1 g of carbohydrate), they form the phospholipid bilayer of all cell membranes, they form the myelin sheath around nerve fibres, they form a protective waterproof layer in the skin (subcutaneous fat), and they form steroid hormones. In membranes the phospholipid bilayer controls what enters and leaves the cell; the membrane also has proteins, cholesterol and glycoproteins.

6. Why animals need a heart and circulation

Many animals need a heart and a circulatory system because as an organism grows, diffusion alone is too slow to supply its cells with oxygen and nutrients and to remove waste — the surface area to volume ratio falls as size increases, and diffusion is only effective over short distances. A mass transport system (heart, blood vessels and blood) moves substances rapidly around the body, overcoming the limitations of diffusion. Blood carries oxygen, nutrients, hormones, waste products and defence cells and molecules. In simple organisms (small ones, or those with a large surface area to volume ratio or a thin body wall) exchange can happen directly by diffusion with the environment; larger or more active animals need a specialised exchange surface and a circulation system to move materials there and back.

7. The structure of arteries, veins and capillaries

Blood vessels relate their structure to their function. Arteries carry blood away from the heart at high pressure; they have thick, muscular, elastic walls to withstand and smooth the pressure and to help push the blood on, and a narrow lumen relative to wall thickness; they have no valves (except at the heart). Veins carry blood back to the heart at low pressure; they have thinner walls (less muscle and elastic tissue) and a wide lumen, and they have valves to prevent backflow, helping return blood when pressure is low. Capillaries are the exchange vessels; they have walls only one cell thick, a very narrow lumen just wide enough for red blood cells to pass in single file, slowing the blood and maximising the surface area for the exchange of substances. The structure of each vessel matches the pressure and role it plays.

8. The cardiac cycle and the structure of the mammalian heart

The mammalian heart is a muscular pump with four chambers — two atria (thin-walled, receiving chambers) and two ventricles (thick-walled, pumping chambers), with the left side pumping oxygenated blood to the body and the right side pumping deoxygenated blood to the lungs. The cardiac cycle is the sequence of events in a heartbeat: atrial systole (the atria contract, pushing blood into the ventricles), ventricular systole (the ventricles contract, pushing blood out into the pulmonary artery and aorta, and the atrioventricular valves close to prevent backflow, making the first heart sound), and diastole (the heart relaxes, the ventricles fill, the semilunar valves close, making the second heart sound). The valves ensure one-way flow: the atrioventricular valves (between atria and ventricles) and the semilunar valves (in the aorta and pulmonary artery). The left ventricle has a much thicker wall than the right because it must pump blood at high pressure around the whole body, whereas the right ventricle pumps only to the nearby lungs. The structure of the heart and its operation are shown by dissection (a recommended additional practical), and the heart's own rhythm is myogenic, starting at the sinoatrial node, though details of that are not needed at IAS.

9. Haemoglobin, oxygen transport and the oxygen dissociation curve

Haemoglobin transports oxygen in red blood cells. Each haemoglobin molecule has four polypeptide chains, each with a haem group that contains an iron ion that can combine with one oxygen molecule, so one haemoglobin can carry four oxygen molecules. The oxygen dissociation curve shows how much oxygen haemoglobin takes up at different oxygen tensions: at high oxygen tension (in the lungs) it becomes almost fully saturated, and at low oxygen tension (in respiring tissues) it releases oxygen; the shape of the curve means a small drop in oxygen tension in the tissues releases a lot of oxygen — this is important. The Bohr effect: as carbon dioxide concentration rises and pH falls, haemoglobin's affinity for oxygen falls and it releases oxygen more readily — so where respiration is high and CO2 is produced, haemoglobin unloads oxygen. Adult haemoglobin has a lower oxygen affinity than fetal haemoglobin, which has a higher affinity — this lets the fetus pick up oxygen from the mother's blood across the placenta, because fetal haemoglobin can take oxygen from adult haemoglobin. Carbaminohaemoglobin carries some carbon dioxide as well, so haemoglobin transports both oxygen and carbon dioxide.

10. Atherosclerosis: how it develops and why it matters

Atherosclerosis is the narrowing and hardening of arteries by plaques. The process begins with endothelial dysfunction — damage to the lining of the artery, by high blood pressure, by smoking chemicals, or by immune responses — then an inflammatory response follows, white blood cells (including phagocytes) move into the artery wall, LDL cholesterol is taken up and oxidised, smooth muscle cells multiply and fibrous tissue forms, and a plaque builds up (a fibrous cap over a lipid core). As the plaque grows it narrows the artery, raising blood pressure further and reducing flow; eventually a plaque may rupture, triggering blood clotting and a thrombus, which can block a coronary artery and cause a myocardial infarction (heart attack). The main risk factors — genetics, diet, age, gender, high blood pressure, smoking and inactivity — act through these mechanisms, and the disease shows why passive transport and diffusion alone cannot supply the larger, more active human body and why the heart and blood vessels are needed.

11. Blood clotting and its role in cardiovascular disease

Blood clotting forms a network of insoluble fibrin threads that traps platelets and red blood cells to form a clot and seal a wound. The process: damage to a blood vessel exposes platelets to the collagen in the wall, and they are activated and release thromboplastin; thromboplastin, in the presence of calcium ions, converts prothrombin (an inactive plasma protein) to thrombin; thrombin then catalyses the conversion of soluble fibrinogen to insoluble fibrin, which forms a mesh that traps platelets and red blood cells into a clot. Clotting is needed to prevent blood loss and to stop pathogens entering, but in cardiovascular disease a clot formed on a ruptured plaque can block a coronary artery and cause a myocardial infarction, or travel to block a cerebral artery and cause a stroke. Treatments to reduce clotting include platelet inhibitors such as aspirin, and anticoagulants such as warfarin, which slow the clotting cascade.

12. Risk factors for cardiovascular disease

Many factors increase the risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD), and most act through the mechanisms above. Diet high in saturated fats and cholesterol raises LDL levels and contributes to plaques; high blood pressure damages the endothelium and raises the risk of both atherosclerosis and clotting; age increases risk because damage accumulates and repair is less efficient; males are at higher risk at younger ages than females; smoking introduces chemicals that damage the endothelium and raise blood pressure and heart rate and reduce oxygen carried by haemoglobin; inactivity contributes to high blood pressure, obesity and high cholesterol; and genetics/family history affects a person's baseline risk. Risk is often the result of several factors combined, and reducing one can help even if others remain. People's perception of risk is often different from the actual risk — they may underestimate or overestimate the risk from diet and other lifestyle factors, and scientists work to clarify the real risks through studies.

13. Diet, cholesterol and antioxidants and the evidence for them

Dietary antioxidants (such as vitamins C and E from fruits and vegetables) may reduce the risk of CVD by preventing the oxidation of LDL cholesterol — oxidised LDL is taken up more readily by artery walls and contributes to plaque formation. Blood cholesterol level is an important indicator: total cholesterol and LDL cholesterol are linked to CVD, and HDL cholesterol helps remove cholesterol from the artery wall, so high HDL is protective. The evidence that cholesterol causes CVD comes from studies showing a causal relationship between blood cholesterol levels and cardiovascular disease, and from trials of the statins, which lower cholesterol and reduce CVD events. People use scientific knowledge about diet, body mass index (BMI = mass (kg) / height (m) squared) and waist-to-hip ratio (a measure of central obesity), exercise and smoking to reduce their risk of coronary heart disease — and they should distinguish between correlation and causation when interpreting the data, because two things occurring together does not by itself prove one causes the other.

14. Data analysis in health studies: correlation, causation and study design

Health studies use quantitative data on illness and mortality rates to determine health risks. Two things can be correlated without one causing the other — a third factor may cause both, or the relationship may be coincidental — so a key skill is distinguishing correlation from causation. A causal relationship for cholesterol and CVD is supported by mechanistic evidence (the biology above) plus the results of trials. When evaluating the design of studies used to determine health risk factors, consider the sample selection (is it representative, or biased, as in a sample of only one type of person or only volunteers) and the sample size (small samples are less reliable and more easily swayed by chance). Conflicting evidence exists because studies differ in design, in the populations studied, and in the measures used, and scientific decisions draw on the whole body of evidence, not one study.

15. Perceived and actual risk and why people's views differ

People's perception of risks is often different from the actual risks — they may underestimate risks due to diet and lifestyle because those risks feel distant and small, or overestimate them because of vivid or recent examples, or because of personal experience, cultural beliefs or poor understanding of the probabilities. Scientific knowledge can clarify the actual risk: for example, many people underestimate the risk from diet and inactivity for coronary heart disease even though the evidence is strong, and the gap between perception and reality is itself a reason to communicate the science clearly. Understanding that perception and reality can diverge is part of evaluating the use of scientific knowledge in making decisions about health, and it explains why public health messages must be carefully designed and evidence-based.

16. Treatments for cardiovascular disease: benefits and risks

Several treatments are used for CVD. Antihypertensives lower blood pressure, reducing the risk of endothelial damage and of heart strain. Statins lower blood cholesterol, reducing plaque formation and the risk of atherosclerosis. Anticoagulants (such as warfarin) and platelet inhibitors (such as aspirin) reduce clot formation, lowering the risk of a clot on a ruptured plaque causing a heart attack or stroke. Each has benefits and risks: antihypertensives can cause dizziness, fatigue or kidney effects and may over-lower pressure; statins can cause muscle pain, digestive upset and, rarely, liver effects; aspirin can cause bleeding, especially in the gut, and is not suitable for everyone. Decisions about treatment balance the degree of risk against the benefit, take the person's overall risk factors into account, and should be supported by the evidence — and by the science behind the disease, so that treatment targets the actual risk factors.

17. Core Practical 2 — vitamin C content of food and drink

Investigate the vitamin C content of food and drink, using DCPIP (2,6-dichlorophenolindophenol), which is blue when oxidised and colourless when reduced. Ascorbic acid (vitamin C) reduces DCPIP, so as vitamin C is added from a food or drink sample, the blue colour fades; the volume of a known concentration of vitamin C solution needed to decolorise a fixed volume of DCPIP gives a calibration, and the volume of the food or drink needed to decolorise the same DCPIP lets you estimate its vitamin C concentration by comparison. Carry out the test for several drinks (for example fruit juices, boiled and unboiled samples) to compare vitamin C content, and note that heat (boiling) destroys vitamin C, so boiled samples contain much less. Record volumes, identify the independent (volume of sample) and dependent (volume needed to decolorise DCPIP) variables, and control temperature, DCPIP volume and end-point judgement.

18. Proteins: amino acids, peptide bonds and the levels of structure

Amino acids are the monomers of proteins; the basic structure is an amino group, a carboxyl group and a variable R group attached to a central carbon. There are around 20 amino acids, differing in their R group, and the sequence of amino acids in a protein (primary structure) determines its folding and function. Amino acids join by condensation reactions to form peptide bonds, making dipeptides and polypeptides. Secondary structure is local folding into alpha-helices and beta-pleated sheets, held by hydrogen bonds between peptide bonds. Tertiary structure is the overall three-dimensional shape, held by hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, disulfide bonds and hydrophobic interactions; it determines the protein's function. Haemoglobin is a globular protein with four chains and four haem groups each carrying one oxygen; collagen is a fibrous protein of three polypeptide chains in a triple helix, strong for tendons and skin. Biuret reagent (copper(II) sulfate and sodium hydroxide) turns purple in the presence of peptide bonds, and a semi-quantitative method using it and colour standards can estimate protein concentration — that is a recommended additional practical.

19. Gas exchange surfaces and Fick's law

An effective gas exchange surface has a large surface area to volume ratio, a thin surface (short diffusion distance) and a difference in concentration between the two sides — the three properties that make diffusion rapid. The rate of diffusion is described by Fick's law: rate of diffusion = (surface area × concentration difference) / thickness of the surface, so increasing surface area or concentration difference, or decreasing thickness, increases the rate. The mammalian lung is adapted for rapid gaseous exchange: the alveoli provide a huge total surface area (about 70–90 m² in an adult), they are thin-walled (one cell thick, with a shared basement membrane) so the diffusion distance is very short, the air in the alveoli is highly oxygenated while the blood arriving is deoxygenated, so there is a steep concentration gradient, and the constant ventilation and blood flow maintain that gradient. Fick's law explains why these adaptations matter quantitatively.

20. Enzymes: specificity, catalysing reactions and factors that affect rate

Enzymes are biological catalysts that speed up reactions by lowering the activation energy needed. Their mechanism of action is explained by their three-dimensional structure: the active site has a specific shape that fits the substrate (the lock-and-key model) or changes shape to fit it (the induced-fit model), and specificity comes from the exact shape of the active site — each enzyme works on one or a few substrates. Enzymes are proteins, and heat, pH and the concentrations of enzyme and substrate affect their rate: each enzyme has an optimum temperature and pH; above or below the optimum the rate falls, and extremes denature the enzyme (irreversibly changing the shape of the active site, so it no longer works). Enzyme concentration increases the rate when substrate is in excess, and substrate concentration increases the rate up to a point, after which the enzyme's active sites are saturated and the rate levels off (maximum rate, Vmax). These effects are investigated in Core Practical 4.

21. Core Practical 4 — factors affecting enzyme rate

Investigate the effect of temperature, pH, enzyme concentration and substrate concentration on the initial rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction. For each factor, choose a suitable enzyme and substrate (for example amylase and starch, or catalase and hydrogen peroxide) and measure the initial rate — the rate in the first part of the reaction, before the substrate is used up or the enzyme denatures. Change the factor being tested in steps, keep the other factors constant (control variables), take several measurements, and calculate the initial rate from the slope of the graph of product formed (or substrate used) against time. For temperature, the rate rises with temperature to an optimum, then falls as the enzyme denatures; for pH, rate is highest at the enzyme's optimum pH; for enzyme concentration, rate rises linearly with concentration; for substrate concentration, rate rises and then levels off at Vmax. Plot graphs and explain the patterns in terms of collisions, activation energy and denaturation.

22. How to use this note and what to revise next

Use these notes section by section, checking that you can state the structure of a water molecule and explain its polarity, draw the structures of alpha-glucose and beta-glucose and state the difference, carry out the Benedict's and iodine semi-quantitative tests and explain the variables and the colour standards, draw a triglyceride and distinguish saturated from unsaturated, state the structure and function of arteries, veins and capillaries, describe the cardiac cycle and the structure of the heart, sketch the oxygen dissociation curve and explain the Bohr effect and fetal haemoglobin, describe the stages of atherosclerosis and blood clotting, list the risk factors for CVD and state how each acts, carry out the DCPIP and biuret practicals, describe the properties of a gas exchange surface and apply Fick's law, and explain enzyme specificity and the effects of temperature, pH and concentrations. Molecules, Transport and Health — AS Level Biology

This revision note belongs to the Edexcel International Advanced Subsidiary (IAS) Biology specification, WBI12 Unit 1, Topic 1 Molecules, Transport and Health. It covers water as a solvent and its structure, carbohydrates and lipids, proteins and their structure and function, gas exchange surfaces and Fick''s law, the mammalian circulatory system and the cardiac cycle, haemoglobin and the oxygen dissociation curve, atherosclerosis and blood clotting, the risk factors for cardiovascular disease, diet, cholesterol and antioxidants, how people use scientific knowledge to reduce risk, the benefits and risks of treatments, and data analysis and evaluation in health studies — plus the gas exchange surfaces and enzyme practical work that support the topic. Every statement the topic is responsible for is covered in its own section or paragraph.

1. Water: structure, properties and why it is the solvent of life

Water is a small molecule with two hydrogen atoms covalently bonded to one oxygen atom; because the oxygen atom is much more electronegative than hydrogen, the shared electrons spend more time near the oxygen, so the molecule is polar — the oxygen end is slightly negative and the hydrogen end slightly positive. This polarity lets water molecules form hydrogen bonds with each other, which gives water its high specific heat capacity, its high latent heat of vaporisation, its cohesion (important for the transpiration stream in plants) and its solvent powers. Water is an excellent solvent because its polarity lets it surround and dissolve ions and polar molecules; ions become hydrated with water molecules around them, and polar molecules such as glucose dissolve readily. In transport, water''s solvent nature lets it carry dissolved substances in blood and in plant tissue fluid and sap, and its dipole nature explains why it can do that — the partial charges interact with the charges of ions and the polar groups of molecules like glucose and amino acids.

2. Carbohydrates: monosaccharides, disaccharides and polysaccharides

Carbohydrates are made of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, with hydrogen and oxygen in the same ratio as in water (2:1). Monosaccharides are the simplest carbohydrates and are the building blocks — glucose, fructose and galactose are hexose monosaccharides with the formula C6H12O6. Disaccharides form when two monosaccharides join by a condensation reaction, losing a water molecule and forming a glycosidic bond; the common ones are maltose (glucose + glucose), sucrose (glucose + fructose) and lactose (glucose + galactose). Polysaccharides are long chains of monosaccharides; starch in plants is made of two polymers — amylose, a long unbranched helix of glucose, which is compact for storage, and amylopectin, which is branched so that glucose can be added or removed quickly from the ends. Glycogen is similar to amylopectin but more branched, and it is the storage carbohydrate in animals, mainly in liver and muscle cells. Cellulose is a structural polysaccharide of beta-glucose chains forming long, straight fibres that cross-link by hydrogen bonds into strong microfibrils; it forms plant cell walls. Carbohydrates provide and store energy: starch and glycogen store glucose in a compact, insoluble, osmotically inert form, so they do not affect the cell''s water potential, and they can be hydrolysed back to glucose when needed for respiration.

3. Core Practical 1 — semi-quantitative tests for reducing sugars and starch

Use Benedict''s reagent to estimate the concentration of reducing sugars and iodine solution to estimate the concentration of starch, using colour standards. Benedict''s reagent (copper(II) sulfate, sodium carbonate and sodium citrate) turns from blue to green, then yellow, then orange, then brick-red as reducing sugars are heated with it — the colour depends on the concentration of reducing sugar. For a semi-quantitative estimate, prepare a range of known reducing sugar concentrations (for example glucose solutions), heat each with Benedict''s, compare the colour with a colour standard chart, and record the colour or its code for each; then use the standards to estimate the concentration in an unknown. For starch, add iodine solution (iodine in potassium iodide) to the sample; a blue-black colour shows starch, and the intensity of the colour relates to the concentration — compare with colour standards to estimate. State the variables: the independent variable is the sugar or starch concentration, the dependent variable is the colour or colour standard, and controlled variables include the volume, temperature and time of heating.

4. Glycosidic bonds: condensation and hydrolysis

Monosaccharides join by condensation reactions to form disaccharides and polysaccharides, with a glycosidic bond formed between them and a water molecule lost each time. Conversely, polysaccharides and disaccharides can be hydrolysed — split by the addition of water — into their monomers; hydrolysis breaks the glycosidic bond and needs a water molecule for each bond broken. Glucose, fructose and galactose join to make maltose (glucose + glucose), sucrose (glucose + fructose) and lactose (glucose + galactose). Amylose and amylopectin are formed from alpha-glucose units; cellulose is formed from beta-glucose units, and because beta-glucose has a different orientation the chain is straight rather than coiled, so the hydrogen bonds between adjacent chains form strong microfibrils. Hydrolysis of starch gives maltose then glucose; hydrolysis of sucrose gives glucose and fructose; hydrolysis of lactose gives glucose and galactose. This matters in the body: dietary starch is hydrolysed to glucose in the gut by enzymes, and that glucose is used in respiration or stored as glycogen; lactose intolerance is caused by a deficiency of lactase, the enzyme that hydrolyses lactose, so lactose stays in the gut and causes problems.

5. Triglycerides: structure and saturated and unsaturated lipids

A triglyceride is made from one glycerol molecule and three fatty acids, joined by three ester bonds formed in condensation reactions; it is insoluble in water (hydrophobic). Fatty acids have a carboxyl group at one end and a hydrocarbon chain that may be saturated — no double bonds in the chain, so the molecule is straight and packs tightly, and saturated fats (and the triglycerides made from them) are usually solid at room temperature — or unsaturated, with one or more double bonds that kink the chain and prevent tight packing, so unsaturated fats are usually liquid at room temperature (oils). Lipids have several roles: they store energy in a compact, insoluble form (1 g of fat stores more energy than 1 g of carbohydrate), they form the phospholipid bilayer of all cell membranes, they form the myelin sheath around nerve fibres, they form a protective waterproof layer in the skin (subcutaneous fat), and they form steroid hormones. In membranes the phospholipid bilayer controls what enters and leaves the cell; the membrane also has proteins, cholesterol and glycoproteins.

6. Why animals need a heart and circulation

Many animals need a heart and a circulatory system because as an organism grows, diffusion alone is too slow to supply its cells with oxygen and nutrients and to remove waste — the surface area to volume ratio falls as size increases, and diffusion is only effective over short distances. A mass transport system (heart, blood vessels and blood) moves substances rapidly around the body, overcoming the limitations of diffusion. Blood carries oxygen, nutrients, hormones, waste products and defence cells and molecules. In simple organisms (small ones, or those with a large surface area to volume ratio or a thin body wall) exchange can happen directly by diffusion with the environment; larger or more active animals need a specialised exchange surface and a circulation system to move materials there and back.

7. The structure of arteries, veins and capillaries

Blood vessels relate their structure to their function. Arteries carry blood away from the heart at high pressure; they have thick, muscular, elastic walls to withstand and smooth the pressure and to help push the blood on, and a narrow lumen relative to wall thickness; they have no valves (except at the heart). Veins carry blood back to the heart at low pressure; they have thinner walls (less muscle and elastic tissue) and a wide lumen, and they have valves to prevent backflow, helping return blood when pressure is low. Capillaries are the exchange vessels; they have walls only one cell thick, a very narrow lumen just wide enough for red blood cells to pass in single file, slowing the blood and maximising the surface area for the exchange of substances. The structure of each vessel matches the pressure and role it plays.

8. The cardiac cycle and the structure of the mammalian heart

The mammalian heart is a muscular pump with four chambers — two atria (thin-walled, receiving chambers) and two ventricles (thick-walled, pumping chambers), with the left side pumping oxygenated blood to the body and the right side pumping deoxygenated blood to the lungs. The cardiac cycle is the sequence of events in a heartbeat: atrial systole (the atria contract, pushing blood into the ventricles), ventricular systole (the ventricles contract, pushing blood out into the pulmonary artery and aorta, and the atrioventricular valves close to prevent backflow, making the first heart sound), and diastole (the heart relaxes, the ventricles fill, the semilunar valves close, making the second heart sound). The valves ensure one-way flow: the atrioventricular valves (between atria and ventricles) and the semilunar valves (in the aorta and pulmonary artery). The left ventricle has a much thicker wall than the right because it must pump blood at high pressure around the whole body, whereas the right ventricle pumps only to the nearby lungs. The structure of the heart and its operation are shown by dissection (a recommended additional practical), and the heart''s own rhythm is myogenic, starting at the sinoatrial node, though details of that are not needed at IAS.

9. Haemoglobin, oxygen transport and the oxygen dissociation curve

Haemoglobin transports oxygen in red blood cells. Each haemoglobin molecule has four polypeptide chains, each with a haem group that contains an iron ion that can combine with one oxygen molecule, so one haemoglobin can carry four oxygen molecules. The oxygen dissociation curve shows how much oxygen haemoglobin takes up at different oxygen tensions: at high oxygen tension (in the lungs) it becomes almost fully saturated, and at low oxygen tension (in respiring tissues) it releases oxygen; the shape of the curve means a small drop in oxygen tension in the tissues releases a lot of oxygen — this is important. The Bohr effect: as carbon dioxide concentration rises and pH falls, haemoglobin''s affinity for oxygen falls and it releases oxygen more readily — so where respiration is high and CO2 is produced, haemoglobin unloads oxygen. Adult haemoglobin has a lower oxygen affinity than fetal haemoglobin, which has a higher affinity — this lets the fetus pick up oxygen from the mother''s blood across the placenta, because fetal haemoglobin can take oxygen from adult haemoglobin. Carbaminohaemoglobin carries some carbon dioxide as well, so haemoglobin transports both oxygen and carbon dioxide.

10. Atherosclerosis: how it develops and why it matters

Atherosclerosis is the narrowing and hardening of arteries by plaques. The process begins with endothelial dysfunction — damage to the lining of the artery, by high blood pressure, by smoking chemicals, or by immune responses — then an inflammatory response follows, white blood cells (including phagocytes) move into the artery wall, LDL cholesterol is taken up and oxidised, smooth muscle cells multiply and fibrous tissue forms, and a plaque builds up (a fibrous cap over a lipid core). As the plaque grows it narrows the artery, raising blood pressure further and reducing flow; eventually a plaque may rupture, triggering blood clotting and a thrombus, which can block a coronary artery and cause a myocardial infarction (heart attack). The main risk factors — genetics, diet, age, gender, high blood pressure, smoking and inactivity — act through these mechanisms, and the disease shows why passive transport and diffusion alone cannot supply the larger, more active human body and why the heart and blood vessels are needed.

11. Blood clotting and its role in cardiovascular disease

Blood clotting forms a network of insoluble fibrin threads that traps platelets and red blood cells to form a clot and seal a wound. The process: damage to a blood vessel exposes platelets to the collagen in the wall, and they are activated and release thromboplastin; thromboplastin, in the presence of calcium ions, converts prothrombin (an inactive plasma protein) to thrombin; thrombin then catalyses the conversion of soluble fibrinogen to insoluble fibrin, which forms a mesh that traps platelets and red blood cells into a clot. Clotting is needed to prevent blood loss and to stop pathogens entering, but in cardiovascular disease a clot formed on a ruptured plaque can block a coronary artery and cause a myocardial infarction, or travel to block a cerebral artery and cause a stroke. Treatments to reduce clotting include platelet inhibitors such as aspirin, and anticoagulants such as warfarin, which slow the clotting cascade.

12. Risk factors for cardiovascular disease

Many factors increase the risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD), and most act through the mechanisms above. Diet high in saturated fats and cholesterol raises LDL levels and contributes to plaques; high blood pressure damages the endothelium and raises the risk of both atherosclerosis and clotting; age increases risk because damage accumulates and repair is less efficient; males are at higher risk at younger ages than females; smoking introduces chemicals that damage the endothelium and raise blood pressure and heart rate and reduce oxygen carried by haemoglobin; inactivity contributes to high blood pressure, obesity and high cholesterol; and genetics/family history affects a person''s baseline risk. Risk is often the result of several factors combined, and reducing one can help even if others remain. People''s perception of risk is often different from the actual risk — they may underestimate or overestimate the risk from diet and other lifestyle factors, and scientists work to clarify the real risks through studies.

13. Diet, cholesterol and antioxidants and the evidence for them

Dietary antioxidants (such as vitamins C and E from fruits and vegetables) may reduce the risk of CVD by preventing the oxidation of LDL cholesterol — oxidised LDL is taken up more readily by artery walls and contributes to plaque formation. Blood cholesterol level is an important indicator: total cholesterol and LDL cholesterol are linked to CVD, and HDL cholesterol helps remove cholesterol from the artery wall, so high HDL is protective. The evidence that cholesterol causes CVD comes from studies showing a causal relationship between blood cholesterol levels and cardiovascular disease, and from trials of the statins, which lower cholesterol and reduce CVD events. People use scientific knowledge about diet, body mass index (BMI = mass (kg) / height (m) squared) and waist-to-hip ratio (a measure of central obesity), exercise and smoking to reduce their risk of coronary heart disease — and they should distinguish between correlation and causation when interpreting the data, because two things occurring together does not by itself prove one causes the other.

14. Data analysis in health studies: correlation, causation and study design

Health studies use quantitative data on illness and mortality rates to determine health risks. Two things can be correlated without one causing the other — a third factor may cause both, or the relationship may be coincidental — so a key skill is distinguishing correlation from causation. A causal relationship for cholesterol and CVD is supported by mechanistic evidence (the biology above) plus the results of trials. When evaluating the design of studies used to determine health risk factors, consider the sample selection (is it representative, or biased, as in a sample of only one type of person or only volunteers) and the sample size (small samples are less reliable and more easily swayed by chance). Conflicting evidence exists because studies differ in design, in the populations studied, and in the measures used, and scientific decisions draw on the whole body of evidence, not one study.

title: Exam technique: Nuclear Physics (A2)
content:
### What earns the marks
For energy, mass defect times c squared with units earns both marks. For decay, ln2 over half-life quoted earns the method mark; activity as lambda N earns the second. For radii, the cube-root rule applied to ratios earns the mark.
### Traps
Error: half-life used as the decay constant. Correction: divide ln2 by it. Error: fission named for the Sun. Correction: fusion powers stars. Error: radius scaled linearly with A. Correction: cube root of nucleon number.
### Worked example
A nucleus has a half-life of 8 days. The decay constant is lambda = ln 2 / 8, which is about 0.087 per day. If the sample holds N = 2.0 x 10^10 nuclei, the activity is A = lambda N, about 1.7 x 10^9 decays per day. Quote the unit with the answer, because the mark depends on it.
### Check yourself
A nucleus with A = 64 has radius r = 1.2 x 64^(1/3) = 4.8 fm. State why doubling A does not double the radius. The radius grows with the cube root of A, so doubling A multiplies r by 2^(1/3), about 1.26.

title:
Energy Flow, Ecosystems and the Environment — Edexcel International A2 Level Biology

This revision note belongs to the Edexcel International A2 Level Biology specification and covers the topics that connect the biochemistry of photosynthesis to the way energy moves through ecosystems, the way ecologists measure populations and communities, the evidence for and the causes of climate change, and the biological ideas that tie the whole topic together in metabolism and evolution. It is written to be complete enough to revise from and to check yourself against the specification, so each numbered section is built around one or more specification statements rather than around a loose theme. The note deliberately stays at exam depth: it explains the reasoning behind each idea, gives the typical worked examples and comparisons that examiners look for, and lists the common mistakes that lose marks in this topic.

1. The overall photosynthesis reaction and the role of light energy in splitting water

Photosynthesis is the process that captures light energy and stores it in chemical form by using that energy to split water, combine the hydrogen with carbon dioxide, and release oxygen. The overall equation is the shorthand, carbon dioxide and water, with light, yield glucose and oxygen, but the important point is what the light energy is actually doing: it is splitting the strong bonds in water molecules, releasing oxygen gas into the atmosphere and storing hydrogen in glucose by combining it with carbon dioxide. This is the entry point for energy into ecosystems and the source of the atmospheric oxygen that most organisms use.

The significance of the water-splitting step is that it is what makes photosynthesis more than just a rearrangement of carbon. The energy from light is used to break the bonds in water, and the hydrogen that results is what ends up in glucose, while the oxygen from water is what is released to the atmosphere. If you remember that, you can explain why the equation is written the way it is and why light is necessary: without light, water is not split, hydrogen is not made available, and glucose cannot be formed from carbon dioxide. The overall reaction is therefore not just a summary but a statement of where the energy comes in and where the oxygen comes from.

A good answer says that light energy splits the strong bonds in water, that the hydrogen is stored in glucose by combining with carbon dioxide, and that oxygen is released. It does not merely repeat the equation; it explains what the light is for. That is the difference between a mark-scoring answer and one that simply copies the equation without understanding it. The equation is the starting point, not the answer.

2. Photophosphorylation and the role of ATP as an immediate energy supply

The immediate energy currency in cells is ATP, and photosynthesis makes it by photophosphorylation, the use of light energy to phosphorylate ADP to ATP. ATP is then used as a fast, small packet of energy for endergonic processes, and its hydrolysis provides an immediate supply of energy that can be used where and when it is needed. The link between the light-dependent and light-independent reactions is therefore not a direct transfer of glucose but a transfer of ATP and reduced NADP, which are the energy and reducing power needed to fix carbon in the Calvin cycle.

Photophosphorylation happens in the light-dependent reactions on the thylakoid membranes. Light energy excites electrons in chlorophyll, and the energy from those electrons is used to make ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate. The ATP is then available for the Calvin cycle and for other cellular processes, and its hydrolysis provides a quick source of energy for endergonic processes, which are processes that would not otherwise occur because they require an input of energy. The important conceptual point is that ATP is the link between the energy captured in the light and the work done by the cell, and that the light-dependent reactions exist largely to make the ATP and reduced NADP that the Calvin cycle needs.

A good answer says that photophosphorylation converts ADP and inorganic phosphate into ATP using light energy, that ATP hydrolysis provides an immediate supply of energy for biological processes, and that the ATP made in the light-dependent reactions is used in the Calvin cycle. It does not say that the light reactions make glucose; they make ATP and reduced NADP, and glucose comes later. That distinction is one of the most common mark-losers in this topic, so it is worth keeping it clear.

3. The light-dependent reactions: cyclic and non-cyclic photophosphorylation and the role of photolysis

The light-dependent reactions take place on the thylakoid membranes and are where light energy is converted into chemical energy in the form of ATP and reduced NADP, with oxygen released from the splitting of water. Light excites electrons in chlorophyll, and those electrons are passed along an electron transport chain, releasing energy that is used to make ATP and to reduce NADP to reduced NADP. Water is split by photolysis, releasing oxygen, protons and replacement electrons, so that the chlorophyll can lose electrons to the electron transport chain without running out of them. The two forms of photophosphorylation are cyclic and non-cyclic, and they are not the same thing, which is why the comparison matters.

Non-cyclic photophosphorylation produces ATP, reduced NADP and oxygen. Electrons from photosystem II are passed along the electron transport chain to photosystem I, and the energy released is used to make ATP. The electrons are then re-excited in photosystem I and used to reduce NADP to reduced NADP. Water is split in photosystem II to replace the electrons lost, releasing oxygen in the process. The overall result is that light energy drives the making of ATP and reduced NADP and the release of oxygen from water. This is the photophosphorylation that is linked to the Calvin cycle, because both ATP and reduced NADP are needed for carbon fixation.

Cyclic photophosphorylation produces ATP only. Electrons from photosystem I are passed back to the electron transport chain and return to photosystem I, rather than being used to reduce NADP. The energy released is used to make ATP, but no reduced NADP is made and no oxygen is produced from water splitting in the same way as in non-cyclic photophosphorylation. Cyclic photophosphorylation therefore makes extra ATP when the Calvin cycle needs more ATP than reduced NADP, balancing the ATP and reduced NADP supply to match the needs of the Calvin cycle.

A good answer says that non-cyclic photophosphorylation makes ATP, reduced NADP and oxygen, and that cyclic photophosphorylation makes ATP only. It explains that water is split in photolysis to replace electrons in non-cyclic photophosphorylation, releasing oxygen. It does not say that cyclic photophosphorylation makes oxygen or reduced NADP, and it does not say that non-cyclic photophosphorylation makes only ATP. The distinction between the two forms is one of the things examiners look for, because it shows that the student understands that the light reactions can adjust their outputs to the needs of the Calvin cycle.

4. The light-independent reactions: the Calvin cycle, RuBP, GP, GALP and RuBisCO

The light-independent reactions, the Calvin cycle, take place in the stroma of the chloroplast and use the ATP and reduced NADP from the light-dependent reactions to fix carbon dioxide into organic molecules. The key enzyme is RuBisCO, which fixes carbon dioxide onto ribulose bisphosphate, RuBP, forming glycerate 3-phosphate, GP. GP is then reduced using ATP and reduced NADP to glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate, GALP. Some GALP leaves the cycle to make glucose and other products; some is used to regenerate RuBP so the cycle can continue.

The cycle is a cycle because RuBP is regenerated, so carbon dioxide can continue to be fixed. The ATP provides the energy for the reduction of GP to GALP, and the reduced NADP provides the reducing power, the hydrogen and electrons, for that reduction. The glucose and other products made from GALP are then used in respiration and in the synthesis of new biological molecules, including polysaccharides, amino acids, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids. The point is that photosynthesis does not just make glucose; it makes the raw materials for the rest of the organism’s biochemistry.

A good answer says that the Calvin cycle occurs in the stroma, that RuBisCO fixes carbon dioxide onto RuBP, that GP is reduced to GALP using ATP and reduced NADP, that some GALP leaves the cycle to make glucose and other products and some regenerates RuBP, and that the products are used in respiration and in the synthesis of polysaccharides, amino acids, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids. It does not say that the Calvin cycle does not need the light reactions; it needs ATP and reduced NADP from them, which is why the light-independent reactions are not independent of light in the long run. The name “light-independent” means they do not directly use light, not that they can continue indefinitely without the products of the light reactions.

5. Chloroplast structure and function: thylakoids, stroma, envelope and pigments

The chloroplast is built so that its structure matches its function. The thylakoids provide a large surface area for light absorption and for the pigment arrays and electron transport chain, and they are where the light-dependent reactions happen. The stroma contains the enzymes of the Calvin cycle, including RuBisCO, and is where the light-independent reactions happen. The double membrane envelope keeps the internal conditions separated from the cytoplasm and isolates the biochemical machinery of the chloroplast.

The structure is not just a set of facts to memorise; each part exists for a reason. The thylakoids are stacked and membrane-bound because that gives a large surface area for the pigments and the electron transport chain, and the stroma is the fluid around the thylakoids because that is where the enzymes of the Calvin cycle are.
