The carbon cycle is the set of processes that move carbon between the atmosphere, living organisms, soils and the oceans. Photosynthesis removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and fixes it in biomass; respiration and decomposition return it; and the burning of fossil fuels adds carbon dioxide that had been stored for geological time. The methods for reducing atmospheric CO2 all work by affecting one of these fluxes: growing more plants increases the removal, protecting peatlands keeps carbon in the soil, reducing fossil fuel combustion reduces the addition, and carbon capture and storage keeps some of the carbon from reaching the atmosphere. A good answer says that the methods are applications of the carbon cycle, and that each has limitations.

A good answer does not say that planting trees is a complete solution, because it is not: trees take time to grow, can be lost to fire or disease, and can compete with other land uses. It does not say that carbon capture and storage is available everywhere at low cost, because it is not yet. The point is to apply the carbon cycle idea to the mitigation methods and to recognise their limitations, not to pretend that any one method is a complete answer. If you can do that, you are answering at the right level.

17. Extrapolation and the limitations of climate models

Data can be extrapolated to make predictions, and models of future climate change are built from such extrapolations and from our understanding of the system. Models are useful precisely because they let us explore the consequences of different scenarios. They are not crystal balls; they are tools for working out what might happen under different assumptions, and their value is in that exploration, not in certainty.

The limitations of models include complex feedback loops that are hard to quantify, such as cloud cover and ice albedo, incomplete historical data, and the unpredictability of future human behaviour, including policy, technology and emissions. A good answer says that models are the best tool available, not that they are perfect, and explains the nature of the uncertainty. It does not say that models are unreliable in the sense of being useless, because they are not; it says that they have limitations and that the limitations matter for how the results should be interpreted.

The distinction between a model and a prediction is useful here. A model is a representation of the system; a prediction is what the model says might happen under a particular scenario. The uncertainty in the prediction comes from both the model and the scenario, and a good answer recognises both. If you can say that, you can answer the question without either dismissing models or treating them as certain. The examiners are after the balanced answer, not the extreme one.

18. The effects of climate change on plants, animals and development

The effects of climate change include changing rainfall patterns and changes in seasonal cycles, which affect the distribution of species, their development and life cycles. Temperature affects enzyme activity, so it can affect metabolism and development directly as well as shifting the ranges of species. Phenological changes, the timing of flowering, breeding, migration and other seasonal events, are evidence of these effects. The point is that climate change is not just a temperature story; it is a biology story because organisms are sensitive to the conditions.

A good answer says that the effects of climate change include changing rainfall patterns and seasonal cycles, that these affect species distribution, development and life cycles, and that temperature affects enzyme activity and can affect metabolism and development. It also mentions phenological changes as evidence that the timing of biological events is being affected. The biological link is the important part, because it shows that the climate change is not only an atmospheric phenomenon but a biological one too. If you can say that, you have the effects in a form that scores marks.

A common mistake is to describe the effects of climate change only as weather events, such as storms or floods, without connecting them to the organisms affected. The biology is what matters here, because the question is from a biology specification. A good answer therefore connects the climatic change to the biological effect, such as the shift in distribution or the change in timing, and does not stay only at the level of the weather. If you can do that, you are answering the question the specification is actually asking.

19. Enzyme activity and temperature, and the Q10 temperature coefficient

Temperature affects enzyme activity up to an optimum, and beyond the optimum enzymes denature because their tertiary and quaternary structures are disrupted by the breakage of hydrogen and ionic bonds. The primary structure is not broken; peptide bonds remain intact. The Q10 temperature coefficient is a measure of how much the rate of a reaction changes with a 10 degree Celsius rise: Q10 equals the rate at T plus 10 degrees Celsius divided by the rate at T. It is not a universal constant; it is a measure that applies to a particular reaction under particular conditions.

A common mistake is to say that high temperature breaks peptide bonds or destroys the primary structure of an enzyme. It does not; it disrupts the higher-order structure that holds the active site in shape. The primary structure remains intact, and that is an important precision. Another frequent mistake is to treat Q10 as a constant for all reactions, when it is actually a measure of the thermal sensitivity of a particular reaction. If you can say that, you can answer the question correctly and avoid the trap.

Worked example: if a reaction rate is 4.0 units at 20 degrees Celsius and 8.0 units at 30 degrees Celsius, Q10 is 8.0 divided by 4.0, which is 2.0. The interpretation is that the rate doubles for a 10 degree Celsius rise in this case. The method is the same whichever numbers are given: state the formula, substitute, calculate. If the temperatures are not 10 degrees apart, the answer should note that the simple Q10 formula applies to a 10 degree rise, and that a different calculation is needed if the temperature interval is different. The point is to use the formula correctly and to know what Q10 is measuring, not just to crunch numbers.

20. Core Practical 12: the effect of temperature on organism development

Core Practical 12 investigates the effect of temperature on the development of organisms, for example seedling growth rate or brine shrimp hatch rate, while taking into account the ethical use of organisms. The practical point is to measure a rate or a development outcome at different temperatures and to relate it to the effect of temperature on enzyme activity, while using the organisms ethically. A good answer describes how the development outcome is measured, how temperature is varied, what the control variables are, and how the ethical use of organisms is handled.

The link to enzyme activity is the reason the practical matters biologically. Development is enzyme-controlled, and enzyme activity depends on temperature, so the effect of temperature on development is a biological effect, not just a physical one. A good answer says that the practical investigates how temperature affects development, that development is enzyme-controlled, and that the ethical use of organisms is part of the design. It does not say that temperature only has a physical effect; it says that the biological effect is through enzymes, and that is the deeper point.

A frequent exam point is to ask for the control variables and the ethical considerations. The control variables are the things that must be kept constant so that temperature is the only thing changing, such as the size and source of the organisms, the medium, the light and the time of observation. The ethical use of organisms means using the minimum number needed, avoiding suffering where possible, and using organisms in a way that is appropriate to the experiment. If you can say that, you have the practical in a form that scores marks.

21. Evolution as a change in allele frequency, mutation and natural selection

Evolution is a change in allele frequency in a gene pool over time, brought about by gene mutation creating new alleles and natural selection increasing the frequency of advantageous ones. The important definition is the allele-frequency one: evolution is not an individual changing during its life, it is a change in the genetic composition of a population across generations. Mutation provides the variation; selection changes the frequencies.

Mutation is the ultimate source of new alleles, but most mutations are neutral or harmful; a few are advantageous in a particular environment. Natural selection increases the frequency of alleles that improve survival or reproduction in the current environment, and this happens over generations, not in a single individual. A good answer says that evolution is a change in allele frequency in a gene pool over time, that mutation creates new alleles, and that natural selection increases the frequency of advantageous alleles. It does not say that an individual evolves during its lifetime, or that mutation is directed toward a need. The randomness of mutation and the non-randomness of selection are the key contrast, and they are the reason the process works the way it does.

A common mistake is to say that organisms evolve because they need to, as if the need causes the mutation. It does not; the mutation is random, and selection acts on the variation that happens to arise. Another mistake is to say that evolution is the same as a change in phenotype during an individual’s life, when it is a change in allele frequency across generations. If you can keep those two points clear, you can avoid the most common errors on this part of the topic. The Hardy-Weinberg idea is a useful way to think about allele frequencies, but the core definition is the change in allele frequency over time by mutation and selection.

22. Allopatric and sympatric speciation and the role of isolation

Isolation reduces gene flow between populations, allowing them to diverge genetically. Allopatric speciation happens when a physical barrier separates populations so that gene flow stops; sympatric speciation happens in the same habitat without a physical barrier, through reproductive isolation such as differences in timing, behaviour or genetics that prevent interbreeding. In both cases, the outcome is that populations become so different that they can no longer produce fertile offspring, and they are then distinct species.

The key difference between allopatric and sympatric speciation is the role of a physical barrier. Allopatric speciation needs one; sympatric does not. A good answer says that allopatric speciation is caused by geographical isolation, while sympatric speciation occurs in the same area through reproductive isolation, and that in both cases the result is reproductive isolation and the formation of new species. It does not say that sympatric speciation requires a physical barrier, because it does not. That is the mistake to avoid.

A good answer also says that isolation reduces gene flow, because gene flow between populations homogenises them and slows divergence, so reducing gene flow is what allows the populations to become different. The mechanism is that the populations accumulate different mutations and experience different selection pressures, and over time they diverge until they can no longer interbreed successfully. If you can say that, you have the speciation idea in a form that scores marks. The distinction between allopatric and sympatric is one of the most common exam questions on this topic, so it is worth keeping clear.

23. Scientific conclusions on controversial issues and the influence of who reaches them

Scientific conclusions about controversial issues can be influenced by who is reaching them, because funding, political agendas and stakeholder motives can affect what conclusions are emphasised or how evidence is interpreted. This is not a claim that science is arbitrary; it is a reason to look at the evidence, the method and the possible biases, and to distinguish a conclusion that follows from the data from one that is shaped by interests.

A good answer says that scientific conclusions can be shaped by the interests and biases of the people or organisations involved, and that this is why it is important to examine the evidence, the method and the possible conflicts of interest. It does not say that all science is biased or that no conclusions can be trusted, because that would be an overstatement. The point is that awareness of possible bias makes the evaluation of evidence more careful, not less. If you can say that, you have the idea in a form that scores marks and avoids the trap of dismissing science altogether.

The context in this topic is climate change and similar issues, where the scientific evidence is strong but the social and political stakes are high. A good answer therefore treats the science and the social influences as separate but related: the science is what it is, and the influences affect how it is used and presented. The ability to make that distinction is what the examiners are after.

24. Reforestation and sustainable resources as management of the human-conservation conflict

Reforestation and the use of sustainable resources, such as biofuels derived from fast-growing plants, are examples of managing the conflict between human needs and conservation. They try to meet human needs while limiting harm to the environment, and they are practical applications of the ideas in the topic, that ecosystems provide services, that carbon can be kept out of the atmosphere by vegetation and soil, and that trade-offs matter. The point is that conservation is not only about protecting species; it is also about managing the relationship between people and the environment.

A good answer says that reforestation increases the removal of carbon dioxide by photosynthesis and stores carbon in biomass and soil, and that sustainable resources such as biofuels can reduce the use of fossil fuels. It also recognises that there are trade-offs, because biofuel crops can compete with food production or land for nature, and that the choice of biofuel matters. If you can say that, you have the idea in a form that scores marks. The point is not that biofuels are automatically good, but that they are one way of managing the conflict, and that the details matter.

A common mistake is to present reforestation or biofuels as a complete solution without recognising the trade-offs. The specification point is that these are examples of management, not that they are perfect. A good answer therefore recognises the benefits and the limitations, and does not overclaim. If you can balance the two, you are answering at the right level.

25. How the pieces fit together: energy, ecosystems, climate and evolution

The topic is really about two movements of energy: into ecosystems through photosynthesis and then up through the trophic levels with losses at each step, and the parallel movement of carbon through the carbon cycle. The ecology part places organisms in their populations, communities and environments and explains why they are where they are. The climate change part uses the same system idea, flows, stores, feedbacks, to ask what happens when the energy balance of the planet changes, and what we might do about it. The final part, metabolism and evolution, is the reminder that organisms are constrained by their biochemistry and by their genetics, and that both constraints shape how they respond to the environment.

A good answer can trace the energy path: light captured by the pigments of the chloroplast, used to make ATP and reduced NADP, used to fix carbon in the Calvin cycle, ending as sugars that feed respiration and biosynthesis. It can then trace the energy transfer: GPP to NPP to the next trophic level, with an efficiency calculation that explains why chains are short. It can then go to the ecology: populations and communities, biotic and abiotic factors, niche and succession, and the fieldwork methods used to measure them. It can then go to the change: the evidence for climate change, the greenhouse mechanism, the carbon-cycle methods for mitigation, the limits of models, and the biological effects of a warmer, more variable climate. It can end with the basics that apply everywhere: temperature affects enzyme activity and development, Q10 measures the thermal sensitivity, and evolution is a change in allele frequency driven by mutation and selection, with isolation enabling speciation.

The ability to connect these parts is what the topic is for. Photosynthesis is the energy source for the ecosystem; the efficiency of transfer explains the structure of the food chains; the ecology explains the organisms’ distribution and abundance; the climate change part asks what happens when the system’s energy balance shifts; and the metabolism and evolution part explains the biological constraints on the organisms themselves. If you can see the connections, you can answer the questions that span more than one part of the topic, which is often where the higher marks are.

The note is long because the topic is broad, and the length is deliberate: the specification lists many separate ideas, from the photosynthesis compartments through the energy transfer and ecology, from the climate evidence and greenhouse mechanism through the models and effects, and from the enzyme and Q10 work through the evolution and speciation, and a revision note has to cover each one in enough detail to be useful. If you study it section by section and check yourself against the specification statements, you should be able to answer the typical questions on this topic without having to hold the whole thing in memory at once.

Typical mistakes

  • Saying the light-dependent reactions make glucose: they make ATP, reduced NADP and oxygen; glucose comes from the Calvin cycle.
  • Confusing absorption spectrum and action spectrum: one is about what the pigment absorbs, the other about the rate of photosynthesis at each wavelength.
  • Using the wrong Rf formula: Rf equals distance moved by pigment divided by distance moved by solvent front; a common variant is to invert it.
  • Treating GPP and NPP as the same thing: NPP is GPP minus respiration, and it is the energy available to consumers.
  • Forgetting to say that transfer efficiency is a percentage and giving the raw fraction alone.
  • Saying that evolution is an individual changing during its lifetime rather than a change in allele frequency in a population.
  • Saying that sympatric speciation needs a physical barrier: it does not; that is allopatric speciation.
  • Saying high temperature breaks peptide bonds or destroys the primary structure of an enzyme: it disrupts the higher-order structure, not the primary sequence.
  • Treating correlation as causation in climate evidence without saying so, or without mentioning the mechanism.
  • Using a single climate indicator as if it proved everything: the evidence is multiple and each line has limitations.
  • Saying that planting trees or biofuels are a complete solution without recognising the limitations and trade-offs.
  • Confusing the niche with just what a species eats: the niche is the whole role, including conditions, resources and interactions.
  • Forgetting that the light-independent reactions depend on ATP and reduced NADP from the light reactions, so they are not independent of light in the long run.

Exam-style questions

  1. Describe the roles of the light-dependent and light-independent reactions of photosynthesis and state where each occurs. Answer: The light-dependent reactions occur on the thylakoid membranes; they use light energy to excite electrons, make ATP and reduced NADP by non-cyclic photophosphorylation, and split water to release oxygen. The light-independent reactions occur in the stroma; they use ATP and reduced NADP to reduce carbon dioxide in the Calvin cycle, producing triose phosphate that can be used to synthesise glucose and other organic molecules, with RuBP regenerated so the cycle can continue. (5 marks)
  2. Explain how gross primary productivity and net primary productivity are related and why net primary productivity is the more important figure for consumers. Answer: GPP is the total energy fixed by photosynthesis; plant respiration uses some of it; NPP is GPP minus respiration, so NPP equals GPP minus R. NPP is the energy available to the next trophic level because it is what remains after the plant has covered its own respiration, so consumers depend on NPP, not GPP. (4 marks)
  3. Calculate the efficiency of energy transfer if a producer trophic level contains 12000 kJ m−2 year−1 and the primary consumer level contains 1500 kJ m−2 year−1. Answer: Efficiency equals (1500 divided by 12000) times 100, which is 12.5 percent. (2 marks)
  4. Describe how you would investigate the effect of light intensity on the rate of photosynthesis using an aquatic plant, and state one control variable. Answer: Place the aquatic plant in water at a fixed temperature and carbon dioxide concentration; vary the light intensity; count the bubbles of oxygen released per minute or measure the volume of gas collected in a fixed time; keep temperature, carbon dioxide concentration and plant species constant as control variables. (5 marks)
  5. Explain the difference between allopatric and sympatric speciation. Answer: Allopatric speciation occurs when a physical barrier separates populations so gene flow stops and they diverge; sympatric speciation occurs in the same area without a physical barrier, with reproductive isolation such as differences in breeding time or behaviour preventing interbreeding. In both cases the result is that populations become reproductively isolated and form new species. (4 marks)
  6. Describe the evidence for climate change and explain why correlation between two variables is not proof of causation. Answer: Evidence includes rising atmospheric carbon dioxide records, rising temperature records, pollen in peat bogs showing past vegetation, and tree rings. Correlation alone does not prove causation because the two variables could both be affected by a third factor, or the trend could be coincidental; to show causation you need a plausible mechanism and evidence that linking the variables is not better explained by something else. (5 marks)
  7. Explain the effect of temperature on enzyme activity up to and beyond the optimum, and define the Q10 temperature coefficient. Answer: Enzyme activity increases with temperature up to the optimum because molecules have more kinetic energy, but beyond the optimum the enzyme denatures as hydrogen and ionic bonds break and the active site is lost; the primary structure remains intact. Q10 is the factor by which the rate increases when the temperature rises by ten degrees Celsius, calculated as rate at T plus ten degrees Celsius divided by rate at T. (5 marks)
  8. Describe how reforestation can reduce atmospheric carbon dioxide and state one limitation of this approach. Answer: Trees take up carbon dioxide by photosynthesis and store the carbon in their biomass and in the soil, so planting trees increases the removal of CO2 from the atmosphere and holds it there. Limitation: newly planted trees take time to grow and store significant carbon, forests can be lost to fire or disease, and the land may compete with other uses. (4 marks)
  9. Define evolution and explain the roles of mutation and natural selection. Answer: Evolution is a change in allele frequency in a gene pool over time. Mutation creates new alleles randomly; natural selection increases the frequency of alleles that improve survival or reproduction in the current environment over generations. The process is not directed toward a need; mutation is random and selection acts on the variation that arises. (5 marks)
  10. Describe what is meant by the niche of a species and explain competitive exclusion. Answer: The niche is the role of a species in its ecosystem, including the conditions it tolerates, the resources it uses and the interactions it has. Two species cannot indefinitely occupy exactly the same niche, because one will outcompete the other, competitive exclusion, so species tend to partition resources and communities can be diverse. (4 marks)

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Carbon fixation in the Calvin cycle: each CO₂ joins a molecule of RuBP (5C) in a reaction catalysed by RuBisCO, which gives two molecules of GP (3C) per CO₂. Six CO₂ give twelve GP, which become twelve GALP. Two GALP leave the cycle to make one glucose, and ten regenerate RuBP. Count carbon atoms at each stage to check the working.
  • Energy transfer between trophic levels, applied to a plant store of 1000 kJ: about 10% passes to the herbivore, so 100 kJ, and about 10 kJ reaches the carnivore. The rest is lost as heat in respiration, in faeces and in uneaten material. Calculate the efficiency as energy passed on ÷ energy taken in × 100.
  • Percentage efficiency of photosynthesis: energy stored in the products ÷ energy of light absorbed × 100. The figure is low, typically around 1–2% for a whole crop, because most light is reflected, transmitted or lost as heat. Name the largest loss, not just the fact that loss happens.
  • Mark-scheme phrasing: energy is not recycled through an ecosystem, but nutrients are. Write that energy flows through in one direction, while nutrients such as carbon and nitrogen are cycled between the biotic and abiotic components.

title: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Transformations and Vectors
content:
Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Transformations and Vectors

Transformations move shapes on a grid, and vectors describe those moves with numbers. The exam asks two things: perform a transformation and, more often, describe one completely — with its centre, angle, direction, line or scale factor. This note builds the topic from zero: the four transformations and the full-description checklist for each, enlargement and its effect on area, vector notation with the house column-vector form (x; y), vector arithmetic, and the vector-geometry proofs that show lines are parallel or points are collinear.

The four transformations

TransformationWhat changesWhat must be stated in a description
Translationposition only, no rotation or resizethe column vector of the move
Reflectionmirror imagethe line of reflection (e.g. x = 2, y = x)
Rotationturns about a pointcentre, angle, and direction (clockwise or anticlockwise)
Enlargementresizes about a pointcentre and scale factor

The complete description is the mark: "rotation" alone scores nothing; "rotation 90° anticlockwise about (2, 1)" scores fully.

Translation

A translation moves every point by the same vector. In column form (x; y), x is the horizontal move and y the vertical move; right and up are positive.

Worked example. Triangle A has vertices (1, 1), (3, 1), (1, 4). Translate by (4; −2) and give the image coordinates.

(1, 1) → (5, -1)
(3, 1) → (7, -1)
(1, 4) → (5, 2)

The shape is congruent to the original (same size and shape), and the orientation is unchanged.

Reflection

A reflection flips a shape across a line; the line is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining each point to its image. Common lines: x = a (vertical), y = b (horizontal), y = x, y = −x.

Worked example. Reflect the point (3, 5) in the line y = x.

reflection in y = x swaps the coordinates: (3, 5) → (5, 3)

Worked example 2. Reflect (2, 4) in the line x = 1.

the line x = 1 is vertical; the distance of x = 2 from it is 1,
so the image is 1 unit on the other side: (0, 4)

To find the mirror line from a shape and its image, join a point to its image and draw the perpendicular bisector of that segment.

Rotation

A rotation turns a shape about a fixed centre through a given angle. The four standard angles are 90° and 180° in either direction; 90° clockwise equals 270° anticlockwise.

Worked example. Rotate the point (3, 1) 90° clockwise about the origin.

90 ° clockwise about O: (x, y) → (y, -x)
(3, 1) → (1, -3)

Worked example 2. Rotate (2, 5) 180° about the origin.

180 °: (x, y) → (-x, -y)
(2, 5) → (-2, -5)

For a centre other than the origin, translate the centre to the origin, rotate, then translate back — or count the grid squares from the centre.

Enlargement

An enlargement with centre C and scale factor k maps every point so that its distance from C is multiplied by k. Negative scale factors put the image on the far side of the centre; fractional factors between 0 and 1 shrink the shape.

image distance from centre = k x object distance from centre
area of image = k² x area of object

Worked example. Enlarge the point (2, 3) by scale factor 3 about the origin.

(2, 3) → (6, 9)

Worked example 2 (area). A triangle of area 12 cm² is enlarged by scale factor 2.5. Find the image area.

area factor = k² = 6.25
new area = 12 × 6.25 = 75 cm²

Enlargement is the only transformation that changes area (unless k = 1 or −1); translations, reflections and rotations preserve both shape and size.

Vectors: notation and magnitude

A vector has magnitude and direction. In this course it is written as a column vector (x; y): x is the horizontal component, y the vertical. The same vector can be written as a bold letter a with an arrow above it.

column vector (x; y)
magnitude = √(x² + y²)
direction angle to the horizontal: tan(θ) = y/x
equal vectors have the same components; opposite vectors
negate both components

Worked example. Find the magnitude and direction of the vector (3; 4).

magnitude = √(9 + 16) = 5
tan(θ) = 4/3  →  θ = 53.1 ° above the horizontal

Vector arithmetic and geometry

addition: (a; b) + (c; d) = (a + c; b + d)
subtraction: (a; b) - (c; d) = (a - c; b - d)
scalar multiple: k(a; b) = (ka; kb)

position vector of A relative to O: OA
AB = OB - OA
midpoint of AB: (OA + OB)/2

Worked example. OA = (2; 1), OB = (7; 5). Find AB and the midpoint of AB.

AB = OB - OA = (7 - 2; 5 - 1) = (5; 4)
midpoint = ((2 + 7)/2; (1 + 5)/2) = (4.5; 3)

Worked example 2 (parallel). Show that AB is parallel to CD given A(1, 2), B(5, 8), C(0, 1), D(6, 10).

AB = (5 - 1; 8 - 2) = (4; 6)
CD = (6 - 0; 10 - 1) = (6; 9)
(6; 9) = 1.5 x (4; 6), so CD = 1.5 AB: parallel (and longer)

Parallel vectors are scalar multiples of each other; collinear points occur when AB and AC (or AB and BC) are parallel and share a point.

Combining transformations and invariant points

Two transformations applied in sequence are not the same as the reverse order: a reflection followed by a rotation generally differs from the rotation followed by the reflection. When a question asks for the single transformation equivalent to two, apply both to a convenient point (the origin or a vertex) and to a second point, then identify the transformation that maps the original to the final image. Invariant points are points that do not move: every point on a mirror line is invariant under a reflection, the centre of a rotation is invariant, and no point is invariant under a translation.

Worked example. A shape is reflected in the x-axis and then translated by (0; 3). Find the image of (2, 1) and identify any invariant points.

reflection in the x-axis: (2, 1) → (2, -1)
translation by (0; 3): (2, -1) → (2, 2)
No invariant points: the reflection moved every point off the
axis, and the translation then moved everything upward.

Worked example 2 (invariant line). State the invariant points of a reflection in the line y = 2.

Every point with y-coordinate 2 lies on the mirror line and does
not move: the whole line y = 2 is invariant.

Vectors in context: displacement and velocity

Column vectors describe any quantity with magnitude and direction in two dimensions: displacement (a move from one point to another), velocity (displacement per second) and force (a push in a direction). The arithmetic is identical; only the interpretation changes.

  • Displacement: AB is the vector from A to B; a round trip returns to the start, so the sum of the vectors around a closed polygon is zero.
  • Velocity: a velocity vector (3; −2) means 3 units per second right and 2 units per second down; position after t seconds is the starting position plus t × velocity.
  • Resultant: the sum of two vectors; a vector and its negative cancel.

Worked example. A particle starts at (1, 2) and moves with velocity (3; −1) for 4 seconds. Find its final position.

displacement = 4 x (3; -1) = (12; -4)
final position = (1 + 12; 2 - 4) = (13; -2)

Worked examples: vector proofs

Worked example. In triangle OAB, P is the midpoint of OA and Q is the midpoint of OB. Prove PQ is parallel to AB.

OP = (1/2) OA, OQ = (1/2) OB
PQ = OQ - OP = (1/2)(OB - OA) = (1/2) AB
PQ is a scalar multiple of AB, so PQ is parallel to AB
(and half its length).

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Translation) Translate (2, 3) by (−1; 4). Answer: add the translation vector: (2, 3) + (−1, 4) = (2 − 1, 3 + 4) = (1, 7).
  2. (Reflection) Reflect (4, 1) in the x-axis. Answer: reflection in the x-axis negates the y-coordinate: x′ = x = 4 and y′ = −y = −1, so the image is (4, −1).
  3. (Rotation) Rotate (5, 2) 90° anticlockwise about the origin. Answer: a 90° anticlockwise turn about the origin maps (x, y) → (−y, x): x′ = −y = −2 and y′ = x = 5, so the image is (−2, 5).
  4. (Enlargement) Enlarge (1, 2) by factor −2 about the origin. Answer: enlargement about the origin maps (x, y) → k(x, y) with k = −2, so (1, 2) becomes (−2, −4); the negative factor puts the image on the opposite side of the centre.
  5. (Description) Describe fully the transformation mapping (1, 1) to (3, 5). Answer: translation vector = image − object = (3 − 1; 5 − 1) = (2; 4), so translation by (2; 4) — one of many correct complete descriptions.
  6. (Magnitude) Find the magnitude of (6; 8). Answer: |v| = √(x² + y²) = √(6² + 8²) = √(36 + 64) = √100 = 10.
  7. (Position vectors) OA = (1; 4), OB = (5; 2). Find AB. Answer: AB = OB − OA = (5; 2) − (1; 4) = (5 − 1; 2 − 4) = (4; −2).
  8. (Collinear) Show A(1, 1), B(3, 4), C(7, 10) are collinear. Answer: AB = (2; 3), AC = (6; 9) = 3 AB — parallel and share A, so collinear.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Incomplete descriptions: "enlargement by 2" omits the centre and loses marks; "reflection" omits the line. State every attribute.
  • Direction of rotation: clockwise and anticlockwise are different transformations; a 90° rotation clockwise is not the same as anticlockwise.
  • Area under enlargement: area scales by k², not k. Doubling the sides quadruples the area.
  • Vector direction: AB = OB − OA, not OA − OB. Reversing the subtraction negates the vector.
  • Column order: (x; y) is horizontal then vertical. Swapping produces a reflection in y = x, not the intended vector.
  • Parallelogram assumptions: equal magnitudes do not imply equal vectors — direction matters too.
  • Negative scale factors: the image lies on the opposite side of the centre; it is not simply "smaller".
  • Collinearity proof: showing parallel is not enough — the segments must also share a point. State it.

Equations and symbols

Every transformation is a coordinate map, and every vector is a column pair. Learn the four rotation maps and the two vector rules, and the topic is arithmetic.

90 ° clockwise about O: (x, y) → (y, -x) Key: (x, y) = the original coordinates; the arrow points to the image's coordinates; O = the origin, the fixed centre. Anticlockwise is the same map with the signs reversed — write the centre down, because a rotation about any other point is not this formula.

180 °: (x, y) → (-x, -y) Key: both coordinates change sign; a half-turn is the only rotation that is also a translation-free "point reflection" in the origin. Check with a point on an axis, where one coordinate stays zero.

reflection in y = x swaps the coordinates: (3, 5) → (5, 3) Key: the line y = x is the mirror; swapping means the image of (x, y) is (y, x). The line is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining each point to its image, which is the definition to quote.

(1, 1) → (5, -1) Key: left = a vertex of the object; right = the matching vertex of the image. Subtract to read off the translation: 5 − 1 = 4 across and −1 − 1 = −2 down, so the column vector is (4; −2).

(3, 1) → (1, -3) Key: this is a 90° clockwise turn about the origin applied to a second vertex — the same map, different numbers. With two vertices mapped you can describe the transformation fully rather than guessing from one.

title: A Level Mathematics: Integration II
content:
A Level Mathematics: Integration II

A2 integration extends the AS power rule to trigonometric and exponential functions, then adds the two general techniques — substitution and integration by parts — plus partial fractions, definite integrals with the new functions, areas, and differential equations. Each technique is presented with its recognition cue: which integrand signals which method is the skill the exam rewards.

Standard integrals to know

integral of sin(ax) dx = -(1/a) cos(ax) + c
integral of cos(ax) dx = (1/a) sin(ax) + c
integral of sec^2(ax) dx = (1/a) tan(ax) + c
integral of e^(ax) dx = (1/a) e^(ax) + c
integral of (1/x) dx = ln|x| + c
integral of (1/(ax + b)) dx = (1/a) ln|ax + b| + c

Worked example. Find ∫ (3 sin 2x + 4e^(−x)) dx.

= -(3/2) cos 2x - 4e^(-x) + c

Worked example 2. Find ∫ (1/(3x + 1)) dx.

= (1/3) ln|3x + 1| + c

Trigonometric identities before integrating

Products and even powers of sine and cosine do not integrate directly; use an identity first.

sin^2 x = (1 - cos 2x)/2
cos^2 x = (1 + cos 2x)/2
sin A cos B = (1/2)[sin(A + B) + sin(A - B)]

Worked example. Find ∫ sin²x dx.

= integral of (1 - cos 2x)/2 dx = x/2 - (sin 2x)/4 + c

Worked example 2. Find ∫ sin 3x cos x dx.

sin 3x cos x = (1/2)[sin 4x + sin 2x]
integral = -(1/8) cos 4x - (1/4) cos 2x + c

Integration by substitution

let u = g(x), du = g'(x) dx; rewrite the whole integral in u
for definite integrals, change the limits too

Worked example 1. Find ∫ 2x(x² + 1)⁵ dx.

u = x^2 + 1, du = 2x dx
integral becomes ∫ u^5 du = u^6/6 + c = (x^2 + 1)^6/6 + c

Worked example 2 (definite). Find ∫ from 0 to 1 of x e^(x²) dx.

u = x^2, du = 2x dx, so x dx = du/2
limits: x = 0 -> u = 0;  x = 1 -> u = 1
= (1/2) ∫ from 0 to 1 e^u du = (1/2)(e - 1) = 0.859

Worked example 3 (trigonometric). Find ∫ cos x sin³x dx.

u = sin x, du = cos x dx
∫ u^3 du = sin^4 x/4 + c

Integration by parts

∫ u dv = uv - ∫ v du

choose u to be the part that simplifies when differentiated
(LIATE: logs, inverse trig, algebra, trig, exponential)

Worked example 1. Find ∫ x e^x dx.

u = x, dv = e^x dx  ->  du = dx, v = e^x
= x e^x - ∫ e^x dx = x e^x - e^x + c = e^x(x - 1) + c

Worked example 2. Find ∫ x cos x dx.

u = x, dv = cos x dx  ->  du = dx, v = sin x
= x sin x - ∫ sin x dx = x sin x + cos x + c

Worked example 3 (logarithm). Find ∫ ln x dx.

u = ln x, dv = dx  ->  du = dx/x, v = x
= x ln x - ∫ 1 dx = x ln x - x + c

Worked example 4 (twice). Find ∫ x² e^x dx.

first: u = x^2, dv = e^x dx  ->  x^2 e^x - 2∫ x e^x dx
second: ∫ x e^x = e^x(x - 1)
result: e^x(x^2 - 2x + 2) + c

Partial fractions in integration

(px + q)/[(x - a)(x - b)]  ->  A/(x - a) + B/(x - b)
integrates to A ln|x - a| + B ln|x - b|

Worked example. Find ∫ 5/[(x − 1)(x + 4)] dx.

partial fractions: 1/(x - 1) - 1/(x + 4)
integral: ln|x - 1| - ln|x + 4| + c = ln|(x - 1)/(x + 4)| + c

Worked example 2 (repeated factor). Find ∫ 3/[(x + 1)²] dx.

= 3 ∫ (x + 1)^-2 dx = -3(x + 1)^-1 + c = -3/(x + 1) + c

Areas and volumes

area between curve and x-axis: definite integral (split at crossings)
volume of revolution about the x-axis: V = pi ∫ y^2 dx

Worked example 1. Find the area under y = sin x from 0 to π.

[-cos x] from 0 to pi = -(-1) - (-1) = 2 square units

Worked example 2 (volume). The region under y = x from 0 to 2 is rotated about the x-axis. Find the volume.

V = pi ∫ from 0 to 2 of x^2 dx = pi [x^3/3] = 8 pi/3 = 8.38 cubic units

The π multiplies the whole integral; forgetting it is the classic error.

Differential equations

separable: dy/dx = f(x) g(y)  ->  ∫ dy/g(y) = ∫ f(x) dx

apply the boundary condition to find the constant

Worked example. Solve dy/dx = xy with y = 3 when x = 0.

∫ dy/y = ∫ x dx
ln|y| = x^2/2 + c
y = A e^(x^2/2);  at x = 0, y = 3  ->  A = 3
y = 3e^(x^2/2)

Worked example 2 (rate of cooling). dT/dt = −k(T − 20), T = 90 when t = 0, T = 60 when t = 10. Find T at t = 25.

∫ dT/(T - 20) = -k ∫ dt  ->  ln(T - 20) = -kt + c
T - 20 = A e^(-kt);  at t = 0, A = 70
at t = 10: 40 = 70 e^(-10k)  ->  k = 0.0560
at t = 25: T = 20 + 70e^(-1.4) = 37.3 deg C

Choosing a method: the recognition cues

A2 integration is not a list of tricks to try at random; each integrand shape points at one method. Reading the shape before writing anything is the skill the exam actually tests.

Shape of the integrandMethodWhy
a function times its own derivativesubstitutionthe derivative becomes du
product of two unrelated functionsintegration by partsone factor is integrated, the other differentiated
a rational function with factorable denominatorpartial fractionseach part integrates to a logarithm
even powers of sin and cosdouble-angle identitylowers the power to a single wave
no elementary antiderivative (e.g. e^(−x²))numerical methodthe trapezium rule approximates it

Worked example (cue check). Name the method for each: ∫ 2x(x² + 1)⁵ dx, ∫ x e^x dx, ∫ (3x + 1)/(x² + x) dx.

first: 2x is the derivative of x^2 + 1  ->  substitution u = x^2 + 1
second: x and e^x are unrelated  ->  by parts with u = x
third: denominator factors x(x + 1)  ->  partial fractions

Definite integrals with substitution

When a definite integral is evaluated by substitution, the limits belong to the old variable and must be converted to the new one. Forgetting this is the most common single error in the whole topic, and it is invisible if the answer happens to be close.

integral from x = a to x = b of f(x) dx
with u = g(x):  limits become u = g(a) and u = g(b)
then integrate in u with no conversion back

Worked example. Evaluate ∫ from 0 to 2 of x(x² + 1)³ dx.

u = x^2 + 1, du = 2x dx  ->  x dx = du/2
limits: x = 0 -> u = 1;  x = 2 -> u = 5
integral = (1/2) ∫ from 1 to 5 of u^3 du = (1/2)[u^4/4] from 1 to 5
= (1/8)(625 - 1) = 78

Worked example 2 (by parts, definite). Evaluate ∫ from 0 to 1 of x e^(2x) dx.

u = x, dv = e^(2x) dx  ->  du = dx, v = e^(2x)/2
= [x e^(2x)/2] from 0 to 1 - ∫ from 0 to 1 of e^(2x)/2 dx
= e^2/2 - 0 - [e^(2x)/4] from 0 to 1
= e^2/2 - (e^2/4 - 1/4) = (e^2 + 1)/4 = 2.097

The trapezium rule

When no antiderivative exists in elementary terms, the area is estimated by joining the sampled heights with straight lines. Each strip is a trapezium, so the rule is exact for straight lines and underestimates for curves that bend upwards.

h = (b - a)/n  (width of each strip)
area = (h/2)[y0 + 2(y1 + y2 + ... + y(n-1)) + yn]
first and last heights counted once, all interior heights twice

Worked example. Use the trapezium rule with 4 strips to estimate ∫ from 0 to 1 of e^(−x²) dx.

h = 0.25;  heights at x = 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1
1, 0.9394, 0.7788, 0.5698, 0.3679
sum = 1 + 2(0.9394 + 0.7788 + 0.5698) + 0.3679 = 1 + 4.5760 + 0.3679 = 5.9439
area = (0.25/2)(5.9439) = 0.7430

Worked example 2 (error direction). The curve e^(−x²) is concave down on this interval. State whether the estimate is an over- or underestimate and how to improve it.

Tabulating the heights is worth the thirty seconds it costs. A single transcription error in one of five heights changes the answer but leaves the working looking correct, so the mark scheme cannot help you; writing the sample points in a column and summing them twice is the check that catches it. Mark schemes also accept the rule written in the equivalent form (h/2)(y0 + 2Σ interior + yn), which is often easier to key into a calculator without dropping a term.

chords lie below a concave-down curve, so the rule underestimates
halving h (doubling n) roughly quarters the error
an overestimate would need the curve concave up

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Standard) ∫ cos 3x dx. Answer: (1/3) sin 3x + c.
  2. (Identity) ∫ cos²x dx. Answer: x/2 + (sin 2x)/4 + c.
  3. (Substitution) ∫ 3x²(x³ + 1)⁴ dx. Answer: u = x³ + 1 → (x³ + 1)⁵/5 + c.
  4. (By parts) ∫ x sin x dx. Answer: −x cos x + sin x + c.
  5. (By parts log) ∫ x ln x dx. Answer: (x²/2)ln x − x²/4 + c.
  6. (Partial fractions) ∫ 4/[(x + 1)(x − 1)] dx. Answer: 2 ln|x − 1| − 2 ln|x + 1| + c.
  7. (Volume) y = x² rotated about x-axis from 0 to 1. Answer: π/5.
  8. (Differential equation) dy/dx = 2y, y = 5 at x = 0. Answer: y = 5e^(2x).

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Missing the reciprocal factor: ∫ cos 3x is (1/3)sin 3x, not sin 3x.
  • Integrating products directly: sin x cos x is not sin²x/2 by guesswork — use the identity.
  • Substitution without changing limits: definite integrals must convert the limits to the new variable, or convert back.
  • Wrong choice for u in by parts: choose the part that simplifies when differentiated; x and ln x are the standard picks.
  • Sign errors in by parts: the formula is uv − ∫v du; slipping the minus reverses the answer.
  • Forgetting the modulus in log integrals: ln|x| covers both signs.
  • Volume without π: the π multiplies the entire definite integral of y².
  • Differential equation constants: find the constant from the boundary condition and state the particular solution.

title: Exam technique: Networking & Communication
content:
### What earns the marks
For full marks on 2.1, explain why serial transmission is reliable over distance and describe the benefits of packet switching, including robustness and shared lines. For 2.2, state the purpose of checksums and explain how they detect errors. For 2.3, describe the process of encryption and justify its importance in secure data transmission. For 3.4, describe the functions of network hardware components, including routers, switches, and gateways.
### Traps
Error: confusing MAC and IP addresses. Correction: MAC addresses are burned-in and used for layer 2 communication, while IP addresses are assigned and used for layer 3 communication. Error: assuming parallel transmission is always faster. Correction: parallel transmission is faster over short distances, but serial transmission is more reliable over long distances. Error: thinking that HTTPS is a protocol. Correction: HTTPS is HTTP over TLS, a secure protocol for data transmission.
### Memory hooks
Use the mnemonic 'Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away' to remember the layers of the TCP/IP stack: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Application. To compare MAC and IP addresses, use a table to highlight their differences. To remember the functions of network hardware components, associate each component with its function, such as routers 'routing' traffic between networks.
### Timing
This topic typically accounts for 20-30% of the paper, and students should budget around 30-40 minutes to answer questions on networking and communication. Make sure to allocate time to read the questions carefully and plan your answers before starting to write.

title: Communication and Networking — Study Notes
content:
`# Communication and Networking

Transmission

  • Serial: one bit at a time — cheaper, reliable over distance
  • Parallel: multiple bits simultaneously — fast but suffers skew and crosstalk over long runs
  • Direction: simplex (one way), half-duplex (alternating), full-duplex (both ways)

Packets and Protocols

Data splits into packets with header (addresses, sequence) and trailer (checksum). A protocol is an agreed rule set — without one, devices cannot interpret signals.

  • TCP/IP stack: application → transport → network → link
  • HTTP/HTTPS: web transfer; HTTPS encrypts with TLS
  • FTP: file transfer; SMTP/POP3/IMAP: email

Network Types

  • LAN: small site, privately owned; WAN: large geographic scale (the internet)
  • Topologies: bus, star, mesh (star is most common — central switch)

Hardware

Routers join networks by IP; switches forward frames by MAC within a LAN; gateways translate protocols.

Client-Server vs Peer-to-Peer

Client-server: central services, easy administration, single point of failure. P2P: every node shares files directly — cheap, hard to manage (torrents, blockchain).

Exam tips: explain packet switching with header/trailer details; justify protocol choice per application (email vs streaming).

title: The Normal Distribution — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: The Normal Distribution

Mathematics — A2. A continuous distribution with the familiar bell shape, symmetric about the mean, described by two parameters: X ~ N(μ, σ²). The curve is fully determined by μ (centre) and σ (width). Total probability is 1, and because X is continuous, P(X = a) = 0 for any single point — inequalities do not need strictness.

Key areas to revise

  • The Model
  • Standardising
  • Backwards Problems
  • Symmetry Shortcuts
  • Normal Approximation to the Binomial

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

### Worked example X follows a normal distribution with mean μ and variance σ². Standardise with Z = (X − μ)/σ and read the probability from tables. For Z < 1.5, the table gives 0.9332. The curve is symmetric about the mean, so P(X < μ) = 0.5, and about 68% of values lie within one standard deviation of the mean and about 95% within two. ### Worked example X follows a normal distribution with mean μ and variance σ². Standardise with Z = (X − μ)/σ and read the probability from tables. For Z < 1.5, the table gives 0.9332. The curve is symmetric about the mean, so P(X < μ) = 0.5, and about 68% of values lie within one standard deviation of the mean and about 95% within two.

title: Edexcel IAL Computer Science: Database Definition, DDL/DML and Normalisation
content:
Edexcel IAL Computer Science: Database Definition, DDL/DML and Normalisation

Pearson Edexcel International Advanced Level in Computer Science, Unit 4 The Computing Practical Project (with Unit 2/3 foundations): data definition and data manipulation languages, and the normalisation that produces a defensible schema. The AS database note built the concepts; this one builds the artefacts a project needs — a schema written in DDL, queries written in DML, and a normalisation walk-through of the kind a project's design chapter must contain. Every statement is parsed clause by clause.

DDL: defining the structure

Data definition language (DDL) creates and alters the database's structure — tables, keys, constraints — while data manipulation language (DML) operates on the data inside (SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE). The DBMS stores the resulting schema in its data dictionary and enforces every declared rule on all clients — the reason DDL is written once but protects the data forever.

DDL worked: the clinic schema, each statement's effect named.

  CREATE TABLE patient (
      patientID   CHAR(5)      PRIMARY KEY,      -- unique, not null by rule
      name        VARCHAR(60)  NOT NULL,
      dob         DATE         NOT NULL,
      phone       VARCHAR(15),
      postcode    VARCHAR(8)
  );
  -- effect: table created; patientID is the entity key; name and dob may not
  -- be empty; phone may be unknown (nullable) - a design decision.

  CREATE TABLE appointment (
      apptID      INTEGER      PRIMARY KEY,
      patientID   CHAR(5)      NOT NULL,
      doctorID    CHAR(5)      NOT NULL,
      apptDate    DATE         NOT NULL,
      slot        TIME         NOT NULL,
      CONSTRAINT fk_appt_patient FOREIGN KEY (patientID)
          REFERENCES patient(patientID),
      CONSTRAINT uq_doctor_slot UNIQUE (doctorID, apptDate, slot)
  );
  -- effect: referential integrity (no appointment without a real patient),
  -- and a composite UNIQUE that makes double-booking impossible.

  ALTER TABLE patient ADD email VARCHAR(80);
  DROP TABLE old_backup;                        -- destructive; guarded
  CREATE INDEX idx_patient_name ON patient(name); -- speeds name lookups

Constraints the DBMS now enforces regardless of application code: PRIMARY KEY
(uniqueness + non-null), FOREIGN KEY (referential integrity, with ON DELETE
CASCADE / RESTRICT / SET NULL choices), UNIQUE, NOT NULL, CHECK (range):

  ALTER TABLE appointment ADD CONSTRAINT chk_slot
      CHECK (slot BETWEEN '08:00' AND '18:00');

DDL and DML command summary

CommandFamilyEffect
CREATE TABLE / INDEX / VIEWDDLAdds a structure the DBMS will enforce
ALTER TABLEDDLAdds, drops or modifies columns and constraints
DROP TABLEDDLRemoves a structure and its data — destructive
SELECTDML (query)Reads rows, filtered, grouped and sorted
INSERTDMLAdds a row; refused if any constraint would break
UPDATEDMLModifies rows matching a WHERE predicate
DELETEDMLRemoves rows matching a WHERE predicate
GRANT / REVOKEDCLAssigns or removes role permissions (least privilege)

A third family completes the picture: transaction control (TCL) — BEGIN, COMMIT and ROLLBACK group DML into atomic units, so a failure mid-transaction leaves the database exactly as it was. Every batch job and multi-step update in a project should be wrapped in one.

DML: manipulating the data

DML worked on the clinic tables, each query's execution order stated:

  INSERT INTO patient (patientID, name, dob, phone)
  VALUES ('P010', 'Chen', '2008-04-12', '07700 900123');
  -- the row must satisfy every constraint or the insert fails atomically.

  UPDATE patient SET phone = '07700 900456' WHERE patientID = 'P010';
  -- without WHERE this would touch every row - the classic destructive slip.

  DELETE FROM appointment WHERE apptDate < '2026-01-01';
  -- a FK referencing patient would RESTRICT or CASCADE here - state which.

  SELECT p.name, COUNT(a.apptID) AS visits
  FROM patient p
  LEFT JOIN appointment a ON p.patientID = a.patientID
  GROUP BY p.patientID, p.name
  HAVING COUNT(a.apptID) = 0
  ORDER BY p.name;
  -- Execution: FROM → JOIN → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER
  -- BY. LEFT JOIN keeps patients with no appointments (count 0); HAVING
  -- filters the GROUPS (WHERE could not - it runs before aggregation).

JOIN types to name: INNER (matching rows only), LEFT (all left rows, nulls
where unmatched), RIGHT (mirror), FULL (all rows both sides), and self-join
(table related to itself - staff/supervisor).

Normalisation, end to end

Normalisation restructures data to remove redundancy and the anomalies it causes. Full procedure with the reason each step matters:

Unnormalised: one row per (student, subject) with a repeating group:

  StudentID | Name  | Class | ClassTeacher | Subjects (repeating)
  S1        | Chen  | 11A   | Mr Hall      | Maths, Physics

1NF - eliminate repeating groups (each field single-valued):
  StudentID | Name | Class | ClassTeacher | Subject
  S1 | Chen | 11A | Mr Hall | Maths
  S1 | Chen | 11A | Mr Hall | Physics      <- duplication begins

2NF - 1NF and no partial dependency on a composite key
  (key here is (StudentID, Subject); Name, Class, ClassTeacher depend only
  on StudentID - part of the key):
  STUDENT(StudentID [PK], Name, Class, ClassTeacher)
  RESULT(StudentID [PK, FK], Subject [PK], Mark)

3NF - 2NF and no transitive dependency
  (in STUDENT, ClassTeacher depends on Class, not directly on StudentID):
  STUDENT(StudentID [PK], Name, Class [FK])
  CLASS(Class [PK], ClassTeacher)
  RESULT(StudentID [PK, FK], Subject [PK], Mark)

Anomalies removed at each step:
  1NF removes the multi-valued field (searching "who takes Physics" became
  impossible); 2NF removes the teacher's name repeating per subject;
  3NF means one class has ONE teacher stored ONCE - change Mr Hall in one row
  and every student of 11A sees it.

Denormalisation exists as a deliberate counter-move: merging tables back for read-heavy reporting trades integrity risk for fewer joins — valid when the project's non-functional requirements demand it and the trade is documented.

The design artefacts a project needs

  • Entity-relationship diagram — entities, attributes, cardinality (1:1, 1:M, M:N resolved with junction tables).
  • Data dictionary — every field: type, length, range, key role, validation rules.
  • Normalisation narrative — the unnormalised table and each step to 3NF with the dependency named at each split (the trace above is the model).
  • DDL script — the schema with all constraints, version-controlled.
  • Validation and security plan — input checks at the application plus DBMS-level constraints; roles and least-privilege grants.
Worked: GRANT statements for the clinic's two roles.

  CREATE ROLE reception;
  GRANT SELECT, INSERT ON appointment TO reception;
  GRANT SELECT ON patient TO reception;
  CREATE ROLE doctor;
  GRANT SELECT ON appointment, patient, prescription TO doctor;

  -- reception cannot read prescriptions; doctors cannot delete appointments.
  Least privilege means each role receives exactly what its work needs - and
  the project's security section records these decisions.

Normalisation worked example: the dependency proof

The one question format that catches people out is proving which normal form a table violates. The method: write the functional dependencies, then test each in turn.

Table: ENROLMENT(studentID, studentName, courseID, courseFee, lecturerID, lecturerName)
Dependencies: studentID → studentName; courseID → courseFee, lecturerID;
              lecturerID → lecturerName. Key: (studentID, courseID).

1NF? Every field single-valued - yes (assume no repeating groups).
2NF? studentName depends on only part of the key (studentID) - partial
     dependency - VIOLATED.
3NF? lecturerName depends on lecturerID which is not a key - transitive
     dependency - VIOLATED (and 2NF must hold first anyway).

Split for 2NF (remove partials):
  STUDENT(studentID, studentName)
  ENROL(studentID, courseID, courseFee, lecturerID, lecturerName)
Split for 3NF (remove transitives):
  COURSE(courseID, courseFee, lecturerID)
  LECTURER(lecturerID, lecturerName)

Every non-key attribute now depends on the key, the whole key, and nothing
but the key - the sentence markers look for.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Writing DML when DDL is asked: CREATE/ALTER/DROP define; SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE manipulate.
  • UPDATE or DELETE without a WHERE clause — the answer must state the predicate.
  • Stopping normalisation at "no repeating groups"; 2NF needs the partial-dependency split and 3NF the transitive one.
  • Declaring a foreign key without an ON DELETE choice in a design answer; cascade/restrict/set-null is a decision with consequences.
  • Using WHERE on aggregate results (needs HAVING), or grouping by fewer columns than selected (SQL strictness).
  • Confusing LEFT JOIN with INNER JOIN in "list all X even if no Y" questions — the unmatched rows are the point.
  • Denormalising without recording the trade-off; the exam rewards the conscious reversal, not the accident.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Unit 4, 4 marks). Explain the difference between DDL and DML with examples.

Answer: DDL defines and alters the database structure and is executed rarely by administrators — CREATE TABLE patient, ALTER TABLE add a column, CREATE INDEX. DML operates on the data within that structure and runs constantly — SELECT lists, INSERT adds, UPDATE modifies, DELETE removes. DDL changes the schema the DBMS enforces; DML changes rows subject to those constraints.

Question 2 (Unit 4, 5 marks). Normalise the table ORDER(orderID, customerName, customerPhone, productID, productName, quantity) to 3NF, naming the dependencies.

Answer: Key is orderID (assume one product per order row). customerName and customerPhone depend on the customer (transitive via a customerID that is missing) and productName on productID — non-key determinants. 2NF: none partial (single-column key), so split the transitive dependencies: ORDER(orderID, customerID, productID, quantity), CUSTOMER(customerID, customerName, customerPhone), PRODUCT(productID, productName). 3NF holds: every non-key field depends on its key, the whole key, and nothing but the key. Each customer and product is stored once.

Question 3 (Unit 4, 4 marks). Write DDL to create a student table with a primary key and a marks range constraint.

Answer: CREATE TABLE student (studentID CHAR(5) PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(60) NOT NULL, mark INTEGER CHECK (mark BETWEEN 0 AND 100)); — the PRIMARY KEY enforces unique identity, NOT NULL rejects empty names, and the CHECK makes out-of-range marks impossible at the database level.

Question 4 (Unit 4, 4 marks). Explain what happens when a row is deleted from a table referenced by foreign keys.

Answer: The DBMS enforces referential integrity according to the declared rule: ON DELETE RESTRICT refuses the delete while child rows exist (protective default); ON DELETE CASCADE deletes the dependent rows too (fast, but destructive); ON DELETE SET NULL keeps child rows with the key nulled (only if nullable). The choice is documented in the design because each has different consequences for data retention.

Question 5 (Unit 4, 4 marks). Write a query listing customers with no orders, and explain why HAVING is used.

Answer: SELECT c.customerID, c.name FROM customer c LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.customerID = o.customerID GROUP BY c.customerID, c.name HAVING COUNT(o.orderID) = 0. The LEFT JOIN keeps all customers, the count measures their orders per group, and HAVING filters groups after aggregation — WHERE cannot, because it runs before the groups exist.

Question 6 (Unit 4, 3 marks). Explain when denormalisation is justified.

Answer: In read-heavy reporting where join costs dominate query time, merging tables (e.g. storing the product name on the order row) removes joins and speeds reads. It is justified only when the redundancy is controlled (updated through one path, or refreshed from the normalised source) and the gain is documented — otherwise it reintroduces the update anomalies normalisation removed.

Data definitions shape the project's core; the network layer shapes how its users reach it.

title: AS Level Biology: Molecules, Transport and Health
content:
Molecules, Transport and Health — AS Level Biology

This revision note belongs to the Edexcel International Advanced Subsidiary (IAS) Biology specification, WBI11 Unit 1, Topic 1 Molecules, Transport and Health. It covers water as a solvent and its structure, carbohydrates and lipids, proteins and their structure and function, gas exchange surfaces and Fick’s law, the mammalian circulatory system and the cardiac cycle, haemoglobin and the oxygen dissociation curve, atherosclerosis and blood clotting, the risk factors for cardiovascular disease, diet, cholesterol and antioxidants, how people use scientific knowledge to reduce risk, the benefits and risks of treatments, and data analysis and evaluation in health studies — plus the gas exchange surfaces and enzyme practical work that support the topic. Every statement the topic is responsible for is covered in its own section or paragraph.

1. Water: structure, properties and why it is the solvent of life

Water is a small molecule with two hydrogen atoms covalently bonded to one oxygen atom; because the oxygen atom is much more electronegative than hydrogen, the shared electrons spend more time near the oxygen, so the molecule is polar — the oxygen end is slightly negative and the hydrogen end slightly positive. This polarity lets water molecules form hydrogen bonds with each other, which gives water its high specific heat capacity, its high latent heat of vaporisation, its cohesion (important for the transpiration stream in plants) and its solvent powers. Water is an excellent solvent because its polarity lets it surround and dissolve ions and polar molecules; ions become hydrated with water molecules around them, and polar molecules such as glucose dissolve readily. In transport, water’s solvent nature lets it carry dissolved substances in blood and in plant tissue fluid and sap, and its dipole nature explains why it can do that — the partial charges interact with the charges of ions and the polar groups of molecules like glucose and amino acids.

2. Carbohydrates: monosaccharides, disaccharides and polysaccharides

Carbohydrates are made of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, with hydrogen and oxygen in the same ratio as in water (2:1). Monosaccharides are the simplest carbohydrates and are the building blocks — glucose, fructose and galactose are hexose monosaccharides with the formula C6H12O6. Disaccharides form when two monosaccharides join by a condensation reaction, losing a water molecule and forming a glycosidic bond; the common ones are maltose (glucose + glucose), sucrose (glucose + fructose) and lactose (glucose + galactose). Polysaccharides are long chains of monosaccharides; starch in plants is made of two polymers — amylose, a long unbranched helix of glucose, which is compact for storage, and amylopectin, which is branched so that glucose can be added or removed quickly from the ends. Glycogen is similar to amylopectin but more branched, and it is the storage carbohydrate in animals, mainly in liver and muscle cells. Cellulose is a structural polysaccharide of beta-glucose chains forming long, straight fibres that cross-link by hydrogen bonds into strong microfibrils; it forms plant cell walls. Carbohydrates provide and store energy: starch and glycogen store glucose in a compact, insoluble, osmotically inert form, so they do not affect the cell’s water potential, and they can be hydrolysed back to glucose when needed for respiration.

3. Core Practical 1 — semi-quantitative tests for reducing sugars and starch

Use Benedict’s reagent to estimate the concentration of reducing sugars and iodine solution to estimate the concentration of starch, using colour standards. Benedict’s reagent (copper(II) sulfate, sodium carbonate and sodium citrate) turns from blue to green, then yellow, then orange, then brick-red as reducing sugars are heated with it — the colour depends on the concentration of reducing sugar. For a semi-quantitative estimate, prepare a range of known reducing sugar concentrations (for example glucose solutions), heat each with Benedict’s, compare the colour with a colour standard chart, and record the colour or its code for each; then use the standards to estimate the concentration in an unknown. For starch, add iodine solution (iodine in potassium iodide) to the sample; a blue-black colour shows starch, and the intensity of the colour relates to the concentration — compare with colour standards to estimate. State the variables: the independent variable is the sugar or starch concentration, the dependent variable is the colour or colour standard, and controlled variables include the volume, temperature and time of heating.

4. Glycosidic bonds: condensation and hydrolysis

Monosaccharides join by condensation reactions to form disaccharides and polysaccharides, with a glycosidic bond formed between them and a water molecule lost each time. Conversely, polysaccharides and disaccharides can be hydrolysed — split by the addition of water — into their monomers; hydrolysis breaks the glycosidic bond and needs a water molecule for each bond broken. Glucose, fructose and galactose join to make maltose (glucose + glucose), sucrose (glucose + fructose) and lactose (glucose + galactose). Amylose and amylopectin are formed from alpha-glucose units; cellulose is formed from beta-glucose units, and because beta-glucose has a different orientation the chain is straight rather than coiled, so the hydrogen bonds between adjacent chains form strong microfibrils. Hydrolysis of starch gives maltose then glucose; hydrolysis of sucrose gives glucose and fructose; hydrolysis of lactose gives glucose and galactose. This matters in the body: dietary starch is hydrolysed to glucose in the gut by enzymes, and that glucose is used in respiration or stored as glycogen; lactose intolerance is caused by a deficiency of lactase, the enzyme that hydrolyses lactose, so lactose stays in the gut and causes problems.

5. Triglycerides: structure and saturated and unsaturated lipids

A triglyceride is made from one glycerol molecule and three fatty acids, joined by three ester bonds formed in condensation reactions; it is insoluble in water (hydrophobic). Fatty acids have a carboxyl group at one end and a hydrocarbon chain that may be saturated — no double bonds in the chain, so the molecule is straight and packs tightly, and saturated fats (and the triglycerides made from them) are usually solid at room temperature — or unsaturated, with one or more double bonds that kink the chain and prevent tight packing, so unsaturated fats are usually liquid at room temperature (oils). Lipids have several roles: they store energy in a compact, insoluble form (1 g of fat stores more energy than 1 g of carbohydrate), they form the phospholipid bilayer of all cell membranes, they form the myelin sheath around nerve fibres, they form a protective waterproof layer in the skin (subcutaneous fat), and they form steroid hormones. In membranes the phospholipid bilayer controls what enters and leaves the cell; the membrane also has proteins, cholesterol and glycoproteins.

6. Why animals need a heart and circulation

Many animals need a heart and a circulatory system because as an organism grows, diffusion alone is too slow to supply its cells with oxygen and nutrients and to remove waste — the surface area to volume ratio falls as size increases, and diffusion is only effective over short distances. A mass transport system (heart, blood vessels and blood) moves substances rapidly around the body, overcoming the limitations of diffusion. Blood carries oxygen, nutrients, hormones, waste products and defence cells and molecules. In simple organisms (small ones, or those with a large surface area to volume ratio or a thin body wall) exchange can happen directly by diffusion with the environment; larger or more active animals need a specialised exchange surface and a circulation system to move materials there and back.

7. The structure of arteries, veins and capillaries

Blood vessels relate their structure to their function. Arteries carry blood away from the heart at high pressure; they have thick, muscular, elastic walls to withstand and smooth the pressure and to help push the blood on, and a narrow lumen relative to wall thickness; they have no valves (except at the heart). Veins carry blood back to the heart at low pressure; they have thinner walls (less muscle and elastic tissue) and a wide lumen, and they have valves to prevent backflow, helping return blood when pressure is low. Capillaries are the exchange vessels; they have walls only one cell thick, a very narrow lumen just wide enough for red blood cells to pass in single file, slowing the blood and maximising the surface area for the exchange of substances. The structure of each vessel matches the pressure and role it plays.

8. The cardiac cycle and the structure of the mammalian heart

The mammalian heart is a muscular pump with four chambers — two atria (thin-walled, receiving chambers) and two ventricles (thick-walled, pumping chambers), with the left side pumping oxygenated blood to the body and the right side pumping deoxygenated blood to the lungs. The cardiac cycle is the sequence of events in a heartbeat: atrial systole (the atria contract, pushing blood into the ventricles), ventricular systole (the ventricles contract, pushing blood out into the pulmonary artery and aorta, and the atrioventricular valves close to prevent backflow, making the first heart sound), and diastole (the heart relaxes, the ventricles fill, the semilunar valves close, making the second heart sound). The valves ensure one-way flow: the atrioventricular valves (between atria and ventricles) and the semilunar valves (in the aorta and pulmonary artery). The left ventricle has a much thicker wall than the right because it must pump blood at high pressure around the whole body, whereas the right ventricle pumps only to the nearby lungs. The structure of the heart and its operation are shown by dissection (a recommended additional practical), and the heart’s own rhythm is myogenic, starting at the sinoatrial node, though details of that are not needed at IAS.

9. Haemoglobin, oxygen transport and the oxygen dissociation curve

Haemoglobin transports oxygen in red blood cells. Each haemoglobin molecule has four polypeptide chains, each with a haem group that contains an iron ion that can combine with one oxygen molecule, so one haemoglobin can carry four oxygen molecules. The oxygen dissociation curve shows how much oxygen haemoglobin takes up at different oxygen tensions: at high oxygen tension (in the lungs) it becomes almost fully saturated, and at low oxygen tension (in respiring tissues) it releases oxygen; the shape of the curve means a small drop in oxygen tension in the tissues releases a lot of oxygen — this is important. The Bohr effect: as carbon dioxide concentration rises and pH falls, haemoglobin’s affinity for oxygen falls and it releases oxygen more readily — so where respiration is high and CO2 is produced, haemoglobin unloads oxygen. Adult haemoglobin has a lower oxygen affinity than fetal haemoglobin, which has a higher affinity — this lets the fetus pick up oxygen from the mother’s blood across the placenta, because fetal haemoglobin can take oxygen from adult haemoglobin. Carbaminohaemoglobin carries some carbon dioxide as well, so haemoglobin transports both oxygen and carbon dioxide.

10. Atherosclerosis: how it develops and why it matters

Atherosclerosis is the narrowing and hardening of arteries by plaques. The process begins with endothelial dysfunction — damage to the lining of the artery, by high blood pressure, by smoking chemicals, or by immune responses — then an inflammatory response follows, white blood cells (including phagocytes) move into the artery wall, LDL cholesterol is taken up and oxidised, smooth muscle cells multiply and fibrous tissue forms, and a plaque builds up (a fibrous cap over a lipid core). As the plaque grows it narrows the artery, raising blood pressure further and reducing flow; eventually a plaque may rupture, triggering blood clotting and a thrombus, which can block a coronary artery and cause a myocardial infarction (heart attack). The main risk factors — genetics, diet, age, gender, high blood pressure, smoking and inactivity — act through these mechanisms, and the disease shows why passive transport and diffusion alone cannot supply the larger, more active human body and why the heart and blood vessels are needed.

11. Blood clotting and its role in cardiovascular disease

Blood clotting forms a network of insoluble fibrin threads that traps platelets and red blood cells to form a clot and seal a wound. The process: damage to a blood vessel exposes platelets to the collagen in the wall, and they are activated and release thromboplastin; thromboplastin, in the presence of calcium ions, converts prothrombin (an inactive plasma protein) to thrombin; thrombin then catalyses the conversion of soluble fibrinogen to insoluble fibrin, which forms a mesh that traps platelets and red blood cells into a clot. Clotting is needed to prevent blood loss and to stop pathogens entering, but in cardiovascular disease a clot formed on a ruptured plaque can block a coronary artery and cause a myocardial infarction, or travel to block a cerebral artery and cause a stroke. Treatments to reduce clotting include platelet inhibitors such as aspirin, and anticoagulants such as warfarin, which slow the clotting cascade.

12. Risk factors for cardiovascular disease

Many factors increase the risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD), and most act through the mechanisms above. Diet high in saturated fats and cholesterol raises LDL levels and contributes to plaques; high blood pressure damages the endothelium and raises the risk of both atherosclerosis and clotting; age increases risk because damage accumulates and repair is less efficient; males are at higher risk at younger ages than females; smoking introduces chemicals that damage the endothelium and raise blood pressure and heart rate and reduce oxygen carried by haemoglobin; inactivity contributes to high blood pressure, obesity and high cholesterol; and genetics/family history affects a person’s baseline risk. Risk is often the result of several factors combined, and reducing one can help even if others remain. People’s perception of risk is often different from the actual risk — they may underestimate or overestimate the risk from diet and other lifestyle factors, and scientists work to clarify the real risks through studies.

13. Diet, cholesterol and antioxidants and the evidence for them

Dietary antioxidants (such as vitamins C and E from fruits and vegetables) may reduce the risk of CVD by preventing the oxidation of LDL cholesterol — oxidised LDL is taken up more readily by artery walls and contributes to plaque formation. Blood cholesterol level is an important indicator: total cholesterol and LDL cholesterol are linked to CVD, and HDL cholesterol helps remove cholesterol from the artery wall, so high HDL is protective. The evidence that cholesterol causes CVD comes from studies showing a causal relationship between blood cholesterol levels and cardiovascular disease, and from trials of the statins, which lower cholesterol and reduce CVD events. People use scientific knowledge about diet, body mass index (BMI = mass (kg) / height (m) squared) and waist-to-hip ratio (a measure of central obesity), exercise and smoking to reduce their risk of coronary heart disease — and they should distinguish between correlation and causation when interpreting the data, because two things occurring together does not by itself prove one causes the other.

14. Data analysis in health studies: correlation, causation and study design

Health studies use quantitative data on illness and mortality rates to determine health risks. Two things can be correlated without one causing the other — a third factor may cause both, or the relationship may be coincidental — so a key skill is distinguishing correlation from causation. A causal relationship for cholesterol and CVD is supported by mechanistic evidence (the biology above) plus the results of trials. When evaluating the design of studies used to determine health risk factors, consider the sample selection (is it representative, or biased, as in a sample of only one type of person or only volunteers) and the sample size (small samples are less reliable and more easily swayed by chance). Conflicting evidence exists because studies differ in design, in the populations studied, and in the measures used, and scientific decisions draw on the whole body of evidence, not one study.

15. Perceived and actual risk and why people’s views differ

People’s perception of risks is often different from the actual risks — they may underestimate risks due to diet and lifestyle because those risks feel distant and small, or overestimate them because of vivid or recent examples, or because of personal experience, cultural beliefs or poor understanding of the probabilities.
