Scientific knowledge can clarify the actual risk: for example, many people underestimate the risk from diet and inactivity for coronary heart disease even though the evidence is strong, and the gap between perception and reality is itself a reason to communicate the science clearly. Understanding that perception and reality can diverge is part of evaluating the use of scientific knowledge in making decisions about health, and it explains why public health messages must be carefully designed and evidence-based.

16. Treatments for cardiovascular disease: benefits and risks

Several treatments are used for CVD. Antihypertensives lower blood pressure, reducing the risk of endothelial damage and of heart strain. Statins lower blood cholesterol, reducing plaque formation and the risk of atherosclerosis. Anticoagulants (such as warfarin) and platelet inhibitors (such as aspirin) reduce clot formation, lowering the risk of a clot on a ruptured plaque causing a heart attack or stroke. Each has benefits and risks: antihypertensives can cause dizziness, fatigue or kidney effects and may over-lower pressure; statins can cause muscle pain, digestive upset and, rarely, liver effects; aspirin can cause bleeding, especially in the gut, and is not suitable for everyone. Decisions about treatment balance the degree of risk against the benefit, take the person’s overall risk factors into account, and should be supported by the evidence — and by the science behind the disease, so that treatment targets the actual risk factors.

17. Core Practical 2 — vitamin C content of food and drink

Investigate the vitamin C content of food and drink, using DCPIP (2,6-dichlorophenolindophenol), which is blue when oxidised and colourless when reduced. Ascorbic acid (vitamin C) reduces DCPIP, so as vitamin C is added from a food or drink sample, the blue colour fades; the volume of a known concentration of vitamin C solution needed to decolorise a fixed volume of DCPIP gives a calibration, and the volume of the food or drink needed to decolorise the same DCPIP lets you estimate its vitamin C concentration by comparison. Carry out the test for several drinks (for example fruit juices, boiled and unboiled samples) to compare vitamin C content, and note that heat (boiling) destroys vitamin C, so boiled samples contain much less. Record volumes, identify the independent (volume of sample) and dependent (volume needed to decolorise DCPIP) variables, and control temperature, DCPIP volume and end-point judgement.

18. Proteins: amino acids, peptide bonds and the levels of structure

Amino acids are the monomers of proteins; the basic structure is an amino group, a carboxyl group and a variable R group attached to a central carbon. There are around 20 amino acids, differing in their R group, and the sequence of amino acids in a protein (primary structure) determines its folding and function. Amino acids join by condensation reactions to form peptide bonds, making dipeptides and polypeptides. Secondary structure is local folding into alpha-helices and beta-pleated sheets, held by hydrogen bonds between peptide bonds. Tertiary structure is the overall three-dimensional shape, held by hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, disulfide bonds and hydrophobic interactions; it determines the protein’s function. Haemoglobin is a globular protein with four chains and four haem groups each carrying one oxygen; collagen is a fibrous protein of three polypeptide chains in a triple helix, strong for tendons and skin. Biuret reagent (copper(II) sulfate and sodium hydroxide) turns purple in the presence of peptide bonds, and a semi-quantitative method using it and colour standards can estimate protein concentration — that is a recommended additional practical.

19. Gas exchange surfaces and Fick’s law

An effective gas exchange surface has a large surface area to volume ratio, a thin surface (short diffusion distance) and a difference in concentration between the two sides — the three properties that make diffusion rapid. The rate of diffusion is described by Fick’s law: rate of diffusion = (surface area × concentration difference) / thickness of the surface, so increasing surface area or concentration difference, or decreasing thickness, increases the rate. The mammalian lung is adapted for rapid gaseous exchange: the alveoli provide a huge total surface area (about 70–90 m² in an adult), they are thin-walled (one cell thick, with a shared basement membrane) so the diffusion distance is very short, the air in the alveoli is highly oxygenated while the blood arriving is deoxygenated, so there is a steep concentration gradient, and the constant ventilation and blood flow maintain that gradient. Fick’s law explains why these adaptations matter quantitatively.

20. Enzymes: specificity, catalysing reactions and factors that affect rate

Enzymes are biological catalysts that speed up reactions by lowering the activation energy needed. Their mechanism of action is explained by their three-dimensional structure: the active site has a specific shape that fits the substrate (the lock-and-key model) or changes shape to fit it (the induced-fit model), and specificity comes from the exact shape of the active site — each enzyme works on one or a few substrates. Enzymes are proteins, and heat, pH and the concentrations of enzyme and substrate affect their rate: each enzyme has an optimum temperature and pH; above or below the optimum the rate falls, and extremes denature the enzyme (irreversibly changing the shape of the active site, so it no longer works). Enzyme concentration increases the rate when substrate is in excess, and substrate concentration increases the rate up to a point, after which the enzyme’s active sites are saturated and the rate levels off (maximum rate, Vmax). These effects are investigated in Core Practical 4.

21. Core Practical 4 — factors affecting enzyme rate

Investigate the effect of temperature, pH, enzyme concentration and substrate concentration on the initial rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction. For each factor, choose a suitable enzyme and substrate (for example amylase and starch, or catalase and hydrogen peroxide) and measure the initial rate — the rate in the first part of the reaction, before the substrate is used up or the enzyme denatures. Change the factor being tested in steps, keep the other factors constant (control variables), take several measurements, and calculate the initial rate from the slope of the graph of product formed (or substrate used) against time. For temperature, the rate rises with temperature to an optimum, then falls as the enzyme denatures; for pH, rate is highest at the enzyme’s optimum pH; for enzyme concentration, rate rises linearly with concentration; for substrate concentration, rate rises and then levels off at Vmax. Plot graphs and explain the patterns in terms of collisions, activation energy and denaturation.

22. How to use this note and what to revise next

Use these notes section by section, checking that you can state the structure of a water molecule and explain its polarity, draw the structures of alpha-glucose and beta-glucose and state the difference, carry out the Benedict’s and iodine semi-quantitative tests and explain the variables and the colour standards, draw a triglyceride and distinguish saturated from unsaturated, state the structure and function of arteries, veins and capillaries, describe the cardiac cycle and the structure of the heart, sketch the oxygen dissociation curve and explain the Bohr effect and fetal haemoglobin, describe the stages of atherosclerosis and blood clotting, list the risk factors for CVD and state how each acts, carry out the DCPIP and biuret practicals, describe the properties of a gas exchange surface and apply Fick’s law, and explain enzyme specificity and the effects of temperature, pH and concentrations. After this topic, revise Topic 2 Membranes, proteins, DNA and gene expression, and Topic 3 Cell structure, reproduction and development — the transport and exchange ideas here underpin the circulatory and gas exchange systems in later topics.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Cardiac output, applied to a resting heart: cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume. With a heart rate of 70 beats min⁻¹ and a stroke volume of 70 cm³, the output is 4900 cm³ min⁻¹, or about 4.9 dm³ min⁻¹. Convert the units before you multiply, and state the units of the answer.
  • Glycosidic bonds: condensation forms a glycosidic bond between two monosaccharides and releases one water molecule. Hydrolysis adds a water molecule and breaks the bond. A disaccharide such as maltose from two glucose units therefore has the formula C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁, not two copies of glucose's formula.
  • Triglycerides: one glycerol and three fatty acids form three ester bonds, and three water molecules are released. Saturated fatty acids have no C=C double bonds and pack tightly, so they are solid at room temperature. Unsaturated fatty acids have one or more C=C double bonds, which bend the chain and keep it liquid.
  • Artery, vein and capillary structure: arteries have thick elastic and muscle walls to withstand high pressure, veins have valves and a thinner wall, and capillaries are one cell thick to allow diffusion. Relate each structural feature to its function in the answer, because the mark is for the link.

The tests in Core Practicals 1, 2 and 4, compared

TestDetectsPositive resultWhat makes it semi-quantitative
Benedict's reagent, heatedReducing sugarsBlue to green, yellow, orange or brick-red precipitateComparing the colour with a set of standards made from known concentrations
Iodine solutionStarchOrange-brown to blue-blackJudging the depth of colour against standards
Biuret reagentPeptide bonds, so proteinBlue to purple or lilacColour standards for known protein concentrations
DCPIPVitamin CBlue to colourlessVolume of sample needed to decolourise a fixed volume of DCPIP
Emulsion testLipidMilky white emulsion after adding water to an ethanol extractNone: it is a qualitative test

Typical mistakes

  • Explaining water's properties from polarity alone. Polarity matters because it allows hydrogen bonds, and it is the hydrogen bonds that give water its high specific heat capacity, its high latent heat of vaporisation and its cohesion.
  • Confusing condensation with hydrolysis. Condensation joins monomers and releases water; hydrolysis adds water and splits the bond. State which one is happening before you name the bond.
  • Describing unsaturated fatty acids as "less healthy" instead of describing their structure. Unsaturated chains contain one or more carbon-carbon double bonds, so the chain kinks, the molecules cannot pack closely, and the substance is liquid at room temperature.
  • Giving the artery wall as "thick" without saying why. The elastic and muscle tissue withstands and smooths high pressure from the ventricles. Capillaries are one cell thick to shorten the diffusion distance, and veins have valves to prevent backflow.
  • Reading the oxygen dissociation curve backwards. A curve shifted to the right shows a lower affinity for oxygen, so haemoglobin unloads oxygen more readily to respiring tissue. That is the Bohr effect, and it is caused by a higher carbon dioxide concentration and lower pH.
  • Treating correlation as causation. A study that finds a statistical association has not shown that one factor causes the other; confounding variables, sample size and study design all have to be evaluated first.
  • Mixing up the treatments for cardiovascular disease. Statins lower blood cholesterol, antihypertensives lower blood pressure, anticoagulants reduce clotting, and platelet inhibitors reduce platelet aggregation. Name the effect, not just the drug.
  • Forgetting the control variables in an enzyme practical. When temperature is the independent variable, pH, enzyme concentration and substrate concentration must be held constant, and the initial rate is measured from the steepest part of the graph, before substrate is used up.

Exam-style questions

  1. Explain why water is an effective solvent for transport in organisms. Answer: the water molecule is a dipole, with a partial negative charge on the oxygen and partial positive charges on the hydrogens, so it attracts ions and polar molecules and surrounds them; this keeps them dissolved and able to move in the bloodstream or in xylem.
  2. A heart beats 75 times a minute with a stroke volume of 70 cm cubed. Calculate the cardiac output in dm cubed per minute. Answer: cardiac output = heart rate times stroke volume = 75 times 70 = 5 250 cm cubed per minute, which is 5.25 dm cubed per minute.
  3. An alveolus has a surface area of 0.02 m squared, a wall thickness of 0.0005 mm and an oxygen concentration difference of 40 units. Use Fick's law to explain what happens to the rate of diffusion if the wall thickens. Answer: rate is proportional to surface area times concentration difference divided by thickness. Thickening the wall increases the diffusion distance, so the rate falls in proportion. Rate = (0.02 times 40) / thickness, so doubling the thickness halves the rate.
  4. Describe the sequence of events that leads to atherosclerosis. Answer: the endothelium is damaged (for example by high blood pressure or smoking); an inflammatory response attracts white blood cells and lipids into the wall; fatty deposits form a plaque (atheroma); the plaque narrows the artery and stiffens it, raising blood pressure; if the plaque ruptures, a clot forms and can block the artery, causing a heart attack or stroke.
  5. Explain the role of haemoglobin in oxygen transport and how the Bohr effect helps a exercising muscle. Answer: haemoglobin binds oxygen in the lungs, where the partial pressure of oxygen is high, and releases it in tissues where it is low. Respiring muscle raises carbon dioxide and lowers pH, which shifts the dissociation curve to the right, lowering the affinity for oxygen so that more oxygen is unloaded where it is needed.
  6. A student tests four solutions with Benedict's reagent and records the time taken to reach a brick-red colour. Explain how this design could be made semi-quantitative and reliable. Answer: fix the volume of solution, the volume of reagent, the temperature of the water bath and the time, then compare each result with a set of standards made from known concentrations. Repeat each measurement and take a mean, and use the same observer or a colorimeter to judge the end point.
  7. Explain why a diet high in saturated fat and low in fruit and vegetables increases the risk of cardiovascular disease. Answer: saturated fat raises low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, which is deposited in artery walls and contributes to plaque formation; fruit and vegetables supply antioxidants that reduce the oxidation of LDL cholesterol, so a low intake removes part of that protection. Both act alongside other risk factors such as smoking, age and inactivity.
  8. Explain the difference between a channel protein and a carrier protein in a membrane. Answer: a channel protein forms a pore through which specific ions or small polar molecules pass down their gradient; a carrier protein binds the substance and changes shape to move it across, which is how active transport can move substances against a gradient using ATP.

title: Quantum Physics — Study Notes
content:
Quantum Physics

Photons

E = hf = hc/λ, h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s.

Example: green light 550 nm: E ≈ 3.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J ≈ 2.3 eV.

The Photoelectric Effect

Light above a threshold frequency ejects electrons instantly; intensity alone does nothing below f₀.

  • Einstein: hf = φ + KE_max (φ = work function)
  • KE_max = eV_s (stopping potential)

Example: sodium φ = 2.3 eV needs λ < 540 nm; 400 nm light gives KE_max = 3.1 − 2.3 = 0.8 eV.

Wave–Particle Duality

de Broglie: λ = h/p = h/(mv). Electrons diffract like waves — electron microscopes exploit short electron wavelengths.

Example: an electron at 10⁶ m s⁻¹: λ ≈ 0.7 nm.

Energy Levels and Line Spectra

Atoms absorb/emit photons matching level gaps: hf = E₁ − E₂. Emission lines are bright; absorption dark.

Example: the Hα line: 3 → 2 transition, 656 nm.

Exam tips: one photon interacts with one electron — that is why intensity cannot release electrons below threshold; convert eV ↔ J with 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹.

title: A Level Physics: Astronomy and Cosmology
content:
A Level Physics: Astronomy and Cosmology

Astronomy is physics at the largest scale: measuring the distance to a star by its brightness, its size by its temperature, and the age of the universe by how fast galaxies recede. This note builds the toolkit from zero: luminosity and the inverse-square law, standard candles (Cepheid variables and Type Ia supernovae) and the distance ladder, stellar radii from Stefan's law, Hubble's law and redshift, and the evidence for the Big Bang. Every calculation is worked in full, because the papers test exactly these three or four formulas.

Brightness, luminosity and the inverse-square law

A star's luminosity L is the total power it radiates (watts). What a telescope receives is intensity (or flux) I — power per unit area at the observer's distance:

I = L/(4 π d²)

I in W m⁻², L in W, d in m
doubling the distance quarters the intensity

The analogy: a light bulb's power is fixed, but the same light spreads over a sphere of radius d — four times the area at twice the distance, so a quarter of the brightness per square metre. This one law underlies every distance measurement in astronomy.

Worked example. A star has luminosity 4.0 × 10²⁶ W. Find its intensity at 10 parsecs (1 pc = 3.09 × 10¹⁶ m).

d = 10 × 3.09 × 10¹⁶ = 3.09 × 10¹⁷ m
I = L/(4 π d²) = 4.0 × 10²⁶/(4 × 3.14 x (3.09 × 10¹⁷)²)
  = 4.0 × 10²⁶/(1.20 × 10³⁶) = 3.3 × 10⁻¹⁰ W m⁻²

Standard candles and the distance ladder

A standard candle is an object whose luminosity is known, so its observed intensity gives its distance by rearranging the inverse-square law. Two are examinable:

  • Cepheid variables: pulsating stars whose period of variation is tightly related to their luminosity (longer period, more luminous). Measuring the period gives L; measuring I gives d. Cepheids calibrated the first rungs of the cosmic distance ladder.
  • Type Ia supernovae: exploding white dwarfs that reach a consistent peak luminosity, bright enough to be seen in distant galaxies; they extended the ladder to cosmological distances and revealed the accelerating expansion.
distance from a standard candle:
d = √(L/(4 π I))

Worked example. A Cepheid has luminosity 1.0 × 10²⁹ W and observed intensity 2.5 × 10⁻¹² W m⁻². Find its distance in parsecs.

d = √(L/(4 π I)) = √(1.0 × 10²⁹/(4 × 3.14 × 2.5 × 10⁻¹²))
  = √(1.0 × 10²⁹/3.14 × 10⁻¹¹) = √(3.18 × 10³⁹)
  = 5.64 × 10¹⁹ m
in parsecs: 5.64 × 10¹⁹/3.09 × 10¹⁶ = 1825 pc
          = 1.8 kpc (2 s.f.)

Stellar radii and Stefan's law

A star radiates approximately as a black body. Stefan's law relates its luminosity to its surface area and absolute temperature:

L = 4 π r² σ T⁴

σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴ (Stefan-Boltzmann constant)
r = stellar radius (m), T = surface temperature (K)

so r = √(L/(4 π σ T⁴))

The fourth power is the headline: doubling a star's temperature multiplies its radiated power per square metre by 16. That is why hot blue stars are vastly more luminous than cooler red ones of similar size — and why a red giant can outshine the Sun despite its low temperature, because its radius is enormous.

Worked example. The Sun has L = 3.8 × 10²⁶ W and T = 5800 K. Find its radius.

r = √(L/(4 π σ T⁴))
T⁴ = (5800)⁴ = 1.13 × 10¹⁵
4 π σ T⁴ = 4 × 3.14 × 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ x 1.13 × 10¹⁵
              = 8.05 × 10⁸
r = √(3.8 × 10²⁶/8.05 × 10⁸) = √(4.72 × 10¹⁷)
  = 6.87 × 10⁸ m  (about 7 × 10⁸ m; the accepted value is 6.96 × 10⁸ m)

Worked example 2 (comparison). A star has the same temperature as the Sun but 100 times its luminosity. Find its radius in solar radii.

L = 4 π r² σ T⁴, same T and σ:
r² proportional to L  →  r = 10 R_sun

Redshift and Hubble's law

Light from distant galaxies is shifted toward longer wavelengths — redshift — because the galaxies are receding. For speeds much less than c:

z = Δλ/λ = v/c     (v << c)

Hubble's law: v = H0 d

H0 = Hubble constant (about 70 km s⁻¹ Mpc-1)
d = distance (Mpc)

Worked example 1. A galaxy's spectral line at 656 nm is observed at 689 nm. Find its recession speed.

Δλ = 689 - 656 = 33 nm
z = 33/656 = 0.0503
v = z c = 0.0503 × 3.0 × 10⁸ = 1.51 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹
  = 1.5 × 10⁴ km s⁻¹

Worked example 2. A galaxy at 100 Mpc recedes at 7000 km s⁻¹. Find H₀ and the Hubble time.

H0 = v/d = 7000/100 = 70 km s⁻¹ Mpc-1
Hubble time = 1/H0:
70 km s⁻¹ Mpc-1 = 70 000/(3.09 × 10²²) s⁻¹ = 2.27 × 10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹
t = 1/H0 = 4.4 × 10¹⁷ s = 1.4 × 10¹⁰ years = 14 billion years

The Big Bang and its evidence

Hubble's law implies that galaxies were once much closer together — the universe expanded from a hot, dense state. Three pieces of evidence are examinable:

  • Redshift of galaxies: nearly all galaxies recede, and recession speed increases with distance — expansion from a common origin.
  • Cosmic microwave background (CMB): a uniform 2.7 K radiation filling the sky — the cooled remnant of the hot early universe, predicted before it was found.
  • Abundance of light elements: the observed ratios of hydrogen, helium and lithium match predictions of Big Bang nucleosynthesis.

The expanding universe has no centre: space itself stretches, so every observer sees distant galaxies receding in all directions. The age estimate 1/H₀ assumes constant expansion; accelerating expansion (dark energy) modifies it, and the measured value is about 13.8 billion years.

The theory makes a further testable claim: the CMB should be an almost perfect black-body spectrum with tiny temperature ripples, and it is — the ripples themselves are the seeds of galaxy formation, and their pattern matches the theory's predictions for the mix of ordinary matter, dark matter and dark energy. That agreement across independent observations is why the Big Bang is accepted as the standard cosmological model rather than a single unexplained measurement.

Worked examples: the standard exam types

Worked example. Two stars have the same radius; star A is twice as hot as star B. Find the ratio of their luminosities.

L = 4 π r² σ T⁴; same r and σ
L_A/L_B = (T_A/T_B)⁴ = 2⁴ = 16
Star A is 16 times more luminous.

Worked example 2. A star's luminosity is 4.0 × 10³⁰ W and its surface temperature 10 000 K. Find its radius and compare it with the Sun's (7.0 × 10⁸ m).

T⁴ = (10⁴)⁴ = 1.0 × 10¹⁶
4 π σ T⁴ = 4 × 3.14 × 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ x 1.0 × 10¹⁶ = 7.12 × 10⁹
r = √(4.0 × 10³⁰/7.12 × 10⁹) = √(5.62 × 10²⁰)
  = 2.37 × 10¹⁰ m
r/R_sun = 2.37 × 10¹⁰/7.0 × 10⁸ = 34 solar radii

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Inverse square) A star at 20 pc has intensity I. What is its intensity at 60 pc? Answer: Three times the distance gives 1/9 of the intensity: I/9.
  2. (Luminosity) Define luminosity and state its unit. Answer: The total power radiated by a star across all wavelengths, measured in watts (W).
  3. (Standard candle) Explain how a Cepheid variable is used to find distance. Answer: Its pulsation period determines its luminosity from the period–luminosity relation; comparing that luminosity with the observed intensity gives d = √(L/4πI).
  4. (Stefan) A star has twice the Sun's radius and half its temperature. Compare luminosities. Answer: L ∝ r²T⁴ → (2)² × (1/2)⁴ = 4 × 1/16 = 1/4: the star is a quarter as luminous.
  5. (Redshift) A line at 500 nm appears at 505 nm. Find v. Answer: z = 5/500 = 0.010; v = 0.010 × 3.0 × 10⁸ = 3.0 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹.
  6. (Hubble) A galaxy at 50 Mpc recedes at 3500 km s⁻¹. Find H₀. Answer: H₀ = 3500/50 = 70 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹.
  7. (Age) Estimate the age of the universe from H₀ = 70 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹. Answer: t = 1/H₀ ≈ 14 billion years (with unit conversions: 70 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹ = 2.27 × 10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹).
  8. (Big Bang evidence) State two observations supporting the Big Bang. Answer: The redshift–distance relation (Hubble's law) and the cosmic microwave background; the light-element abundances are a third.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Parsecs versus metres: convert before substituting; 1 pc = 3.09 × 10¹⁶ m, 1 Mpc = 3.09 × 10²² m, 1 AU = 1.50 × 10¹¹ m.
  • Luminosity versus intensity: L is the star's total power; I is what arrives per square metre. The inverse-square law connects them and d must be in metres.
  • T⁴ not T: Stefan's law is a fourth power — doubling temperature multiplies luminosity by 16, not 2. Most arithmetic errors here are exponent slips.
  • Kelvin: surface temperatures in Stefan's law must be absolute; a temperature given in °C needs +273 first.
  • Redshift approximation: z = v/c holds for v ≪ c; at large redshifts the relativistic formula is needed. State the assumption.
  • H₀ units: km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹ — mismatched units in 1/H₀ give absurd ages. Convert km to m and Mpc to m.
  • Hubble time is an estimate: 1/H₀ assumes constant expansion; note the acceleration caveat when discussing the age.
  • Centre of the universe: the Big Bang happened everywhere — there is no centre or edge; expansion stretches space between galaxies.
  • Precision: 2 or 3 s.f. with units (W, W m⁻², m, km s⁻¹, years); the data sheet supplies σ, c and H₀.

title: Trigonometry — Right-Angled Triangles — Study Notes
content:
Trigonometry — Right-Angled Triangles

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): SOH CAH TOA, exact values, angles of elevation/depression.

1. The ratios

Label sides first (opposite, adjacent, hypotenuse) with respect to the marked angle, then choose:

  • sin θ = opp/hyp; cos θ = adj/hyp; tan θ = opp/adj.

Example: hyp 10, angle 35°, find opposite: x = 10 sin 35° = 5.74 (3 s.f.).

2. Finding angles

Use inverse keys: θ = sin⁻¹(opp/hyp). tan θ = 3/4 ⇒ θ = 36.9° (1 d.p.).

3. Exact values (Extended)

θsincostan
30°1/2√3/2√3/3
45°√2/2√2/21
60°√3/21/2√3

4. Elevation and depression

Elevation: angle up from horizontal; depression: down. Both measured from the horizontal line at the observer.

Example: tower 20 m, elevation to top 42° → horizontal distance = 20/tan 42° = 22.2 m.

5. Pythagoras combinations

Find a missing side with Pythagoras before applying a ratio when two sides are known instead of an angle.

Exam tips: never round mid-calculation (keep full calculator accuracy); 3 s.f. for lengths, 1 d.p. for angles unless stated.

SOH CAH TOA

In a right-angled triangle with angle θ: sin θ = opposite ÷ hypotenuse, cos θ = adjacent ÷ hypotenuse and tan θ = opposite ÷ adjacent. Label the sides relative to the angle you are using before choosing the ratio. Use Pythagoras to find a missing side first if needed.

Finding angles

To find an angle, use the inverse function, sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹ or tan⁻¹, on the calculator. Set the calculator to degree mode and check that the answer is sensible for the triangle drawn.

Bearings and angles of elevation

An angle of elevation is measured up from the horizontal, and an angle of depression down from it. Draw a clear right-angled triangle from the description to choose the correct ratio. Round the answer to the accuracy in the question, and keep full accuracy in intermediate steps.

title: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Angles and Polygons
content:
Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Angles and Polygons

Angles are the simplest measurements in geometry and the most frequently examined: almost every Paper 2 and Paper 4 geometry question ends with a reason written next to a number, and the reason earns as many marks as the calculation. This note builds the whole angle toolkit from zero: the vocabulary of points, lines and angles; the parallel-line rules; the angle sums of triangles, quadrilaterals and polygons; and the full set of circle theorems with the standard reasons examiners accept. Every worked example writes the reason line, because that is how the marks are earned.

Geometrical terms

Geometry has a precise vocabulary, and Paper 2 questions often begin by asking you to use it:

  • Point: a position with no size; named with a capital letter.
  • Line segment: the straight path between two points; a line extends without end.
  • Ray: a line starting at a point and extending in one direction.
  • Parallel lines: always the same distance apart, never meeting (marked with arrows).
  • Perpendicular lines: meeting at 90°.
  • Vertex: a corner where two or more lines meet; vertices in the plural.
  • Polygon: a closed shape with straight sides; regular means all sides equal and all angles equal.

Angle vocabulary: acute (less than 90°), right (90°), obtuse (between 90° and 180°), straight (180°), reflex (between 180° and 360°). Angles on a straight line sum to 180°; angles around a point sum to 360°; vertically opposite angles are equal.

Parallel lines: the three rules

A transversal line crossing two parallel lines creates eight angles, and three relationships do all the work:

RelationshipWhat they look likeRule
Corresponding (F-shape)same position at each intersectionequal
Alternate (Z-shape)opposite sides of the transversal, between the parallelsequal
Co-interior (C-shape)same side of the transversal, between the parallelssum to 180°

Worked example. Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. One angle is 115°. Find the angle in the alternate position and the co-interior angle on the other side.

alternate angle = 115 °            (alternate angles are equal)
co-interior angle = 180 - 115 = 65 ° (co-interior angles sum to 180)

Always write the reason next to each answer: "alternate angles" or "co-interior angles sum to 180°". Paper 2 awards the reason mark explicitly.

Triangles and quadrilaterals

The angle sum of any triangle is 180° (proof: draw a line through one vertex parallel to the opposite side and use alternate angles). Consequences you must know:

  • Exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles.
  • Isosceles triangle: base angles are equal; the angle bisector from the apex is also the perpendicular bisector of the base.
  • Equilateral triangle: all angles 60°.
  • Quadrilateral: interior angles sum to 360° (split into two triangles).

Worked example. A quadrilateral has angles 85°, 95° and 110°. Find the fourth angle.

sum = 360 °
fourth = 360 - (85 + 95 + 110) = 360 - 290 = 70 °

Worked example 2 (exterior angle). In a triangle, an exterior angle is 125° and one opposite interior angle is 48°. Find the other opposite interior angle.

exterior = sum of opposite interiors
125 = 48 + x  →  x = 77 °

Angles in polygons

Any n-sided polygon can be split into (n − 2) triangles from one vertex, so:

interior angle sum = (n - 2) × 180 °

regular polygon: each interior angle = (n - 2) × 180/n
exterior angles of any convex polygon sum to 360 °
regular polygon: each exterior angle = 360/n
interior + exterior = 180 ° at each vertex

Worked example 1. Find the interior angle sum of a decagon (10 sides) and each interior angle of a regular decagon.

sum = (10 - 2) × 180 = 1440 °
each = 1440/10 = 144 °
check with exterior: 360/10 = 36; 180 - 36 = 144 °

Worked example 2 (working backwards). A regular polygon has each interior angle 150°. Find the number of sides.

exterior angle = 180 - 150 = 30 °
n = 360/30 = 12 sides  (a regular dodecagon)

Worked example 3 (exterior angles). A pentagon has exterior angles 70°, 80°, 60°, 90°. Find the fifth.

exterior angles sum to 360 °
fifth = 360 - (70 + 80 + 60 + 90) = 360 - 300 = 60 °

Circle theorems: the full set

Circle theorems are examined every session, and each answer needs its theorem named. Learn them as pictures with their standard reasons:

TheoremStatementReason to write
Angle at the centrethe angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference subtended by the same arcangle at centre = 2 × angle at circumference
Angle in a semicirclethe angle in a semicircle (subtended by a diameter) is 90°angle in a semicircle is 90°
Same segmentangles subtended by the same arc in the same segment are equalangles in the same segment are equal
Cyclic quadrilateralopposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180°opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180°
Tangent–radiusa tangent meets the radius at the point of contact at 90°tangent is perpendicular to the radius
Two tangentstangents from an external point are equal in lengthtangents from an external point are equal
Alternate segmentthe angle between a tangent and a chord equals the angle in the alternate segmentalternate segment theorem

Worked example 1 (centre). The angle at the centre subtended by an arc is 130°. Find the angle at the circumference subtended by the same arc.

angle at circumference = 130/2 = 65 °
(reason: angle at centre = 2 x angle at circumference)

Worked example 2 (cyclic quadrilateral). In a cyclic quadrilateral, one pair of opposite angles is 105° and 75°, and the other pair is 4x and 2x. Find x.

opposite angles sum to 180 °
4x + 2x = 180
6x = 180  →  x = 30
check the first pair: 105 + 75 = 180, consistent

Two disciplines make this safe: pair the angles that sit opposite each other (a diagonal between them), and verify both pairs satisfy the 180° rule before writing the answer.

Worked example 3 (tangent). A tangent touches a circle of radius 5 cm at T; O is the centre and P is a point on the tangent 12 cm from T. Find OP.

The radius OT is perpendicular to the tangent, so triangle OTP
is right-angled at T.
OP² = 5² + 12² = 25 + 144 = 169
OP = 13 cm

Worked example 4 (alternate segment). A tangent and a chord form an angle of 62° at the point of contact. Find the angle in the alternate segment.

alternate segment theorem: the tangent-chord angle equals the
angle in the alternate segment
answer = 62 °

Circle theorems: multi-step problems

Paper 4 circle problems chain two or three theorems. The method: mark every angle you can find with its reason, then use each new angle to unlock the next.

Worked example. O is the centre; A, B, C lie on the circle; angle BAC = 35°. Find angle BOC and angle OBC.

angle BOC = 2 × 35 = 70 °
  (angle at centre = 2 x angle at circumference)
triangle OBC is isosceles (OB = OC = radii)
base angles OBC and OCB are equal:
OBC = (180 - 70)/2 = 55 °

Worked example 2 (semicircle + cyclic). AB is a diameter; C and D lie on the circle; angle ABC = 40°. Find angle ADC.

angle ACB = 90 ° (angle in a semicircle)
angle BAC = 180 - 90 - 40 = 50 °
ABCD is cyclic, so angle ADC = 180 - angle ABC? No - opposite
pairs: A with C, B with D. Angle ADC is opposite angle ABC?
The vertices in order are A, B, C, D, so opposite pairs are
(A, C) and (B, D). Angle ADC is at D, opposite angle ABC at B:
angle ADC = 180 - 40 = 140 °.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Parallel lines) Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal; one co-interior angle is 72°. Find the other. Answer: 108°, because co-interior angles sum to 180°.
  2. (Polygon) Find the interior angle sum of a 15-sided polygon. Answer: (15 − 2) × 180 = 2340°.
  3. (Regular polygon) Each exterior angle of a regular polygon is 24°. Find the number of sides and each interior angle. Answer: n = 360/24 = 15; interior = 180 − 24 = 156°.
  4. (Circle — centre) An angle at the circumference is 28°. Find the angle at the centre subtended by the same arc. Answer: 56°.
  5. (Circle — semicircle) A triangle is inscribed in a semicircle with the diameter as one side; one base angle is 33°. Find the other. Answer: 90° at the circumference, so the other angle is 180 − 90 − 33 = 57°.
  6. (Circle — cyclic) A cyclic quadrilateral has one angle 118°. Find the opposite angle. Answer: 62° (180 − 118).
  7. (Tangent) Two tangents from P touch the circle at A and B; PA = 9 cm. Find PB and explain. Answer: 9 cm — tangents from an external point are equal.
  8. (Multi-step) In a circle, angle ABD = 42° and angle ACD = 42°. What does this tell you about A, B, C, D? Answer: They are concyclic — equal angles subtended by the same chord AD at B and C mean the points lie on the same circle (angles in the same segment).

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Missing reasons: Paper 2 geometry marks include the reason. "x = 65° (angles on a straight line)" scores; a bare "65°" may not.
  • Wrong pairing in cyclic quadrilaterals: opposite angles are the ones separated by a diagonal (A and C, B and D), not adjacent ones. Check both pairs sum to 180°.
  • Alternate versus corresponding: alternate angles form a Z, corresponding an F. Identifying the wrong pattern gives the wrong equality.
  • Interior formula mix-up: interior sum is (n − 2) × 180; each exterior is 360/n. Do not use 360/n for the interior of a regular polygon.
  • Reflex angles: the angle at the centre may be reflex; if the diagram shows an obtuse angle but the geometry demands a reflex one, use 360° − the drawn angle.
  • Assuming radii are parallel or equal to chords: radii are equal to each other, not to chords. Isosceles triangles in circles come from two radii.
  • Tangent–chord angle: the alternate segment theorem requires the angle between the tangent and the chord at the point of contact, not any angle involving the tangent.
  • Diagram not to scale: never measure an angle with a protractor in an exam diagram; the geometry must be calculated. "Diagram not accurately drawn" is a warning, not decoration.

Equations and symbols

Every relation this topic is examined on, written with its real notation and followed by a key naming each symbol, its unit and what it means. The sections above explain why each one is true; this sheet is the version to revise from, where the answer depends on reproducing the exact form and substituting into it without losing a unit.

Angle facts and parallel lines

angles at a point sum to 360°; angles on a straight line sum to 180°; vertically opposite angles are equal
Key: the angle in each case is measured in degrees at the named vertex. These three are the reason every angle chase starts by marking what is already known, not by guessing; a missing step is nearly always one of them.

alternate angles are equal, corresponding angles are equal, co-interior angles sum to 180°
Key: the pairs are formed where a transversal crosses two parallel lines; alternate angles lie on opposite sides in a Z-shape, corresponding angles are in matching positions, co-interior are on the same side inside the parallel lines. Naming the reason is worth a mark on its own, so write it beside the number.

triangle interior angles sum to 180°; exterior angle = sum of the two interior opposite angles
Key: interior angles are inside the triangle at each vertex; the exterior angle is formed by extending one side, and equals the sum of the two angles it does not touch. Quadrilaterals split into two triangles, so their angles sum to 360°.

Polygons

interior angle sum = (n − 2) × 180°
Key: n = the number of sides of the polygon; the result is in degrees. The (n − 2) counts the triangles a polygon can be split into from one vertex, which is the derivation rather than a fact to memorise.

exterior angles of any convex polygon sum to 360°, and for a regular polygon each exterior angle = 360°/n
Key: n = the number of sides; an exterior angle is the turn made at each vertex, so walking round once is a full revolution. Regularity is what makes every exterior angle equal — without it only the total is fixed.

regular polygon: each interior angle = (n − 2) × 180°/n, and interior + exterior = 180° at each vertex
Key: n = the number of sides; the two angles at a vertex lie on a straight line, which is why they add to 180°. The pair gives a fast check: an interior angle of 150° means an exterior of 30°, hence n = 360/30 = 12.

Circle theorems

angle at the centre = 2 × angle at the circumference, standing on the same arc
Key: both angles subtend the same chord; the centre angle is measured at the centre of the circle, the circumference angle at any point on the remaining arc. This is the theorem most others are proved from, so quote it by name.

angle in a semicircle = 90°
Key: the angle is subtended by a diameter at any point on the circumference; it is the centre-angle theorem with the centre angle at 180°. Its converse is how a question proves that a triangle's longest side is a diameter.

angles in the same segment are equal; opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180°
Key: a cyclic quadrilateral has all four vertices on one circle; the segment angles stand on the same chord from the same side. The 180° result is the single most useful one in multi-step problems, because it turns a known angle into the one opposite it.

tangent ⟂ radius at the point of contact; tangents from an external point are equal in length
Key: the tangent touches the circle at exactly one point; the radius is drawn to that point and meets it at 90°, which is what makes Pythagoras available. The equal tangents fact creates the two congruent right triangles that most tangent proofs rely on.

alternate segment theorem: the angle between a tangent and a chord equals the angle in the alternate segment
Key: the chord divides the circle into two segments; the angle is measured between the tangent and the chord at the point of contact, and equals the angle subtended by that chord at any point in the opposite segment. Quote the theorem by name — the reason carries marks.

title: Exam technique: Data Types and File Organisation
content:
### What earns the marks
For records, the mixed-type justification earns the mark: arrays hold one type only. For file access, the task matched to the method earns each mark: full runs suit sequential scans, single lookups suit indexed jumps. For floating point, the bias arithmetic shown earns the exponent mark.
### Traps
Error: plain arrays for heterogeneous records. Correction: composite types exist for exactly this. Error: sequential scan for one lookup. Correction: jump via the index. Error: bias forgotten in exponent. Correction: add the bias every time.

title: Biological Molecules
content:
Biological Molecules

Cambridge IGCSE Biology 0610, Extended route, topic 4 (statement 4.1). The building blocks and roles of carbohydrates, proteins and lipids, plus the four food tests and their expected results.

4.1 Biological molecules

  • Carbohydrates are built from monosaccharides (glucose, fructose, galactose) joined by condensation into disaccharides (maltose, sucrose, lactose) and polysaccharides (starch, glycogen, cellulose). Starch stores energy in plants; glycogen in animals; cellulose builds plant cell walls.
  • Proteins are built from about 20 amino acids joined by peptide bonds in condensation reactions. The sequence of amino acids determines the protein's shape and function; denaturation by heat or extreme pH changes that shape permanently.
  • Lipids (fats and oils) are glycerol plus three fatty acids joined into ester bonds. Fats store more energy per gram than carbohydrates, provide insulation and protection; oils are liquid because of unsaturated fatty acid chains.
  • Food tests: starch + iodine solution → blue-black. Reducing sugar + Benedict's solution, heat → brick-red precipitate. Protein + biuret reagent → purple. Lipid + ethanol then water → white emulsion.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Bond reasoning, applied to forming one triglyceride: three ester bonds form, and three molecules of water are released — one per bond. Condensation joins and releases water; hydrolysis breaks and requires water. State the numbers, not just the names.
  • Test interpretation, applied to a food sample that gives a brick-red precipitate with Benedict's but no colour change with biuret: it contains a reducing sugar and no protein. Write the conclusion as "contains X and not Y" — half-credit answers that identify the positive result only.
  • Structure-to-function reasoning, applied to why haemoglobin is a protein not a carbohydrate: its function of carrying oxygen requires a specific three-dimensional shape with haem groups, which only the amino acid sequence of a protein can provide. Function drives the answer — always name the specific function.
  • Denaturation reasoning, applied to enzyme protein denatured at high temperature: the bonds maintaining the tertiary structure break, so the active site changes shape and the substrate no longer fits. Reversible versus irreversible should be stated: at very high temperatures the change is permanent.

Common errors

  • Forgetting to heat the Benedict's test — no heat, no reaction.
  • Saying starch is a protein because it is "organic". Name the monomer and the test.
  • Confusing the emulsion test order: ethanol first to dissolve the lipid, then water to make the emulsion visible.

title: Intermolecular Forces — Study Notes
content:
Intermolecular Forces

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH12, Topic 7. Intermolecular forces are the attractions between molecules, not the bonds inside them. They determine boiling points, solubility and how molecules pack together.

Types of intermolecular force

  • London (instantaneous dipole–induced dipole) forces exist in all molecules. They grow with the number of electrons, so larger molecules have higher boiling points.
  • Permanent dipole–dipole forces occur between polar molecules, where the partial positive and negative charges attract one another.
  • Hydrogen bonding is a strong dipole–dipole attraction. It occurs when H is bonded to N, O or F and attracts a lone pair on another N, O or F.

Effect on physical properties

  • Boiling point depends on the strength of intermolecular forces: more energy is needed to separate molecules that attract strongly.
  • Water boils at a much higher temperature than hydrogen sulfide because hydrogen bonding is much stronger than the dipole forces between H2S molecules.
  • Branched alkanes have lower boiling points than straight-chain isomers because they have a smaller surface area for London forces.

Solubility

  • Substances dissolve when the new attractions between solute and solvent replace the attractions within each.
  • Polar solvents such as water dissolve ionic and polar solutes; non-polar solvents dissolve non-polar solutes.
  • Ethanol is miscible with water because its –OH group forms hydrogen bonds with water.

Ideal and real gases

  • A real gas deviates from ideal behaviour at high pressure and low temperature, because molecules have volume and attract one another.

Exam tip: when comparing boiling points, name the type of intermolecular force, state whether it is stronger or weaker, and say how much energy is needed to overcome it. Do not say that "bonds break" when a liquid boils.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Boiling point, applied to the alkanes: longer chains have more London forces, so boiling point rises with chain length. Branching makes the molecule more compact and lowers the surface contact, so a branched isomer boils at a lower temperature than the straight-chain isomer.
  • Hydrogen bonding, applied to water and H₂S: water boils at 100 °C while H₂S boils at about −60 °C, because water forms hydrogen bonds and H₂S does not. Name the hydrogen bond between a lone pair on O or N and an H attached to O, N or F.
  • Solubility, applied to ethanol and hexane in water: ethanol dissolves because it forms hydrogen bonds with water. Hexane does not, because it has only London forces and cannot replace the hydrogen bonds between water molecules. Use the phrase like dissolves like with the reason attached.
  • Ideal gas assumptions: no intermolecular forces and negligible molecular volume. Real gases deviate at high pressure, where molecules are close, and at low temperature, where attractions matter. State the conditions under which the deviation is largest.

title: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Area, Perimeter and Volume
content:
Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Area, Perimeter and Volume

Measurement questions are the most reliable marks on the paper — provided you convert units correctly and choose the right formula. This note builds the mensuration toolkit from zero: the unit system and its tricky area and volume conversions, the area formulas for every plane shape with derivations, circles, arcs and sectors, the volume and surface area of every solid in the syllabus, and compound shapes — how to add and subtract the pieces. Every worked example shows the substitution and the units, because units and premature rounding are where the marks disappear.

Units of measure

Length, area and volume units are linked by powers of the linear conversion factor:

ConversionLengthAreaVolume
1 m = 100 cm× 100× 100² = 10 000× 100³ = 1 000 000
1 cm = 10 mm× 10× 100× 1000
1 km = 1000 m× 1000× 10⁶× 10⁹

Capacity: 1 litre = 1000 cm³ = 1000 ml; 1 m³ = 1000 litres. The classic trap is converting area with a length factor — 1 m² is 10 000 cm², not 100 cm².

Worked example. Convert 3.5 m² to cm² and 2500 cm³ to litres.

3.5 m2 = 3.5 x 10 000 = 35 000 cm2
2500 cm3 = 2500/1000 = 2.5 litres

Area and perimeter of plane shapes

ShapePerimeterArea
Rectangle2(l + w)l × w
Trianglesum of sides½ × base × perpendicular height
Parallelogram2(a + b)base × perpendicular height
Trapeziumsum of sides½(a + b) × h (parallel sides a, b)
Circle2πrπr²

The triangle and parallelogram formulas both need the perpendicular height — not a slanted side. That single word accounts for more lost marks than any other in mensuration.

Worked example. Find the area of a trapezium with parallel sides 7 cm and 11 cm and height 5 cm.

A = (1/2)(a + b) h = 0.5 x (7 + 11) x 5
  = 0.5 x 18 x 5 = 45 cm2

Worked example 2 (triangle). A triangle has sides 6 cm, 8 cm, 10 cm. Is it right-angled, and what is its area?

6^2 + 8^2 = 36 + 64 = 100 = 10^2, so yes - right-angled
at the 6-8 corner. Area = (1/2) x 6 x 8 = 24 cm2.

Circles, arcs and sectors

An arc is a fraction of the circumference; a sector is the same fraction of the area. The fraction is the angle over a full turn:

circumference = 2 pi r;  area = pi r^2

arc length  = (theta/360) x 2 pi r
sector area = (theta/360) x pi r^2
perimeter of a sector = arc length + 2r
segment area = sector area - triangle area

Worked example. A sector has radius 9 cm and angle 140°. Find its arc length, sector area and perimeter (π = 3.142).

arc = (140/360) x 2 x 3.142 x 9 = 0.3889 x 56.56 = 21.99 cm
area = (140/360) x 3.142 x 81 = 0.3889 x 254.5 = 98.97 cm2
perimeter = 21.99 + 18 = 39.99 cm = 40.0 cm (3 s.f.)

The perimeter of a sector includes the two radii — students routinely answer only the arc length.

Worked example 2 (segment). Find the area of the segment cut off by a chord in a circle of radius 6 cm when the sector angle is 90°.

sector area = (90/360) x 3.142 x 36 = 28.28 cm2
triangle area = (1/2) x 6 x 6 = 18 cm2 (right angle at centre)
segment = 28.28 - 18 = 10.28 cm2

Surface area and volume of solids

SolidVolumeSurface area
Cuboidl × w × h2(lw + lh + wh)
Prism (any cross-section)area of cross-section × length2 × cross-section + perimeter × length
Cylinderπr²h2πr² + 2πrh
Cone⅓πr²hπr² + πrl (l = slant height)
Sphere⁴⁄₃πr³4πr²
Pyramid⅓ × base area × heightsum of face areas

Slant height versus vertical height is the cone trap: volume uses the perpendicular height h, surface area uses the slant height l, and l² = r² + h² connects them.

Worked example 1 (cylinder). A cylinder has radius 4 cm and height 10 cm. Find its volume and total surface area.

V = pi r^2 h = 3.142 x 16 x 10 = 502.7 cm3
SA = 2 pi r^2 + 2 pi r h = 2 x 3.142 x 16 + 2 x 3.142 x 4 x 10
   = 100.5 + 251.4 = 351.9 cm2  (352 cm2, 3 s.f.)

Worked example 2 (cone). A cone has radius 5 cm and vertical height 12 cm. Find its volume and slant height.

V = (1/3) pi r^2 h = (1/3) x 3.142 x 25 x 12 = 314.2 cm3
l = sqrt(5^2 + 12^2) = sqrt(169) = 13 cm

Worked example 3 (sphere). Find the volume of a sphere of radius 6 cm.

V = (4/3) pi r^3 = (4/3) x 3.142 x 216 = 904.8 cm3

Compound shapes: add and subtract

Compound figures are split into standard shapes (add) or standard shapes with a piece removed (subtract). The discipline: draw the split lines, label each sub-shape's dimensions, compute each area separately, then combine.

Worked example. An L-shape is made from a 10 cm × 8 cm rectangle with a 4 cm × 3 cm rectangle removed from one corner. Find its area and perimeter.

area = 10 x 8 - 4 x 3 = 80 - 12 = 68 cm2
perimeter: trace the outline:
10 + 8 + 6 + 5 + 4 + 3 = 36 cm
(6 = 10 - 4 along the removed edge; 5 = 8 - 3)

Worked example 2 (semicircle on a rectangle). A running track is a 60 m by 30 m rectangle with a semicircle of diameter 30 m at each end. Find its area.

rectangle = 60 x 30 = 1800 m2
two semicircles = one full circle of radius 15:
  pi x 225 = 706.9 m2
total = 1800 + 706.9 = 2507 m2  (2510 m2, 3 s.f.)

Worked examples: composite solids

Composite solids combine the standard formulas: a silo is a cylinder with a hemisphere on top; a pencil is a cylinder with a cone; a capsule is a cylinder with two hemispheres. The method: split the solid, compute each volume, add; for surface area, add only the faces that are actually exposed (the join is hidden).

Worked example. A capsule is a cylinder of radius 3 cm and length 10 cm with a hemisphere at each end. Find its total volume and surface area.

cylinder volume = pi r^2 h = 3.142 x 9 x 10 = 282.8 cm3
two hemispheres = one sphere: (4/3) pi r^3 = (4/3) x 3.142 x 27
               = 113.1 cm3
total volume = 282.8 + 113.1 = 395.9 cm3

surface area: cylinder curved surface 2 pi r h = 188.5 cm2
plus one full sphere 4 pi r^2 = 113.1 cm2
total = 301.6 cm2  (the circular joins are internal, not exposed)

Worked example 2 (frustum-free method). A cone of radius 6 cm and height 9 cm has its top 3 cm cut off parallel to the base. Find the volume removed.

the removed cone is similar to the whole cone, scale k = 3/9 = 1/3
volume of whole cone = (1/3) pi x 36 x 9 = 339.3 cm3
removed volume = k^3 x whole = (1/27) x 339.3 = 12.6 cm3
(the same as computing directly with radius 2 cm and height 3 cm)

Worked examples: reverse problems and density

Worked example. A cylindrical tank of radius 1.5 m holds 20 m³ of water. Find the depth.

V = pi r^2 h  ->  h = V/(pi r^2) = 20/(3.142 x 2.25)
h = 20/7.07 = 2.83 m

Worked example 2 (density). A metal cuboid 5 cm × 4 cm × 2 cm has mass 312 g. Find its density in g cm⁻³ and kg m⁻³.

volume = 5 x 4 x 2 = 40 cm3
density = 312/40 = 7.8 g cm-3
in kg m-3: 7.8 x 1000 = 7800 kg m-3

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Units) Convert 2.4 m² to cm² and 0.75 litres to cm³. Answer: 24 000 cm²; 750 cm³.
  2. (Trapezium) Parallel sides 12 cm and 8 cm, height 6 cm. Find the area. Answer: ½(12 + 8) × 6 = 60 cm².
  3. (Sector) Radius 7 cm, angle 72°. Find arc length and sector area. Answer: arc = (72/360) × 2π × 7 = 8.80 cm; area = (72/360) × π × 49 = 61.6 cm².
  4. (Cylinder) Radius 3 cm, height 12 cm. Find the volume. Answer: π × 9 × 12 = 339 cm³ (3 s.f.).
  5. (Cone) Radius 8 cm, height 15 cm. Find the volume and slant height. Answer: V = ⅓π × 64 × 15 = 1005 cm³; l = √(64 + 225) = 17 cm.
  6. (Sphere) Diameter 10 cm. Find the surface area. Answer: r = 5; SA = 4π × 25 = 314 cm².
  7. (Compound) A rectangle 14 m × 6 m has a semicircle of diameter 6 m removed from one end. Find the area. Answer: 84 − ½π × 9 = 84 − 14.14 = 69.9 m².
  8. (Reverse) A sphere has volume 288 cm³. Find its radius. Answer: 288 = ⁴⁄₃πr³ → r³ = 288 × 3/(4π) = 68.75 → r = 4.10 cm.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Slant versus perpendicular height: triangle/parallelogram areas use perpendicular height; cone surface area uses slant height; cone volume uses perpendicular height.
  • Area unit conversion: 1 m² = 10 000 cm² and 1 cm² = 100 mm². Multiplying by 100 instead of 10 000 is the single most common mensuration error.
  • Sector perimeter: add the two radii to the arc length. The question asks for the perimeter of the sector, not the arc.
  • Using the diameter as radius: halve the diameter first; every circle formula uses r.
  • π precision: use 3.142 or the calculator's π; rounding π to 3 loses accuracy on multi-step questions. Round only the final answer (usually 3 s.f. or as stated).
  • Compound shape subtraction: remove the correct region and keep the outline consistent — recompute the perimeter from the actual boundary, not the sum of the sub-shapes' perimeters.
  • Volume of a prism: cross-section area × length, where the length is perpendicular to the cross-section (a slanted prism uses the perpendicular distance).
  • Units in the answer: cm² for area, cm³ for volume, and capacity conversions (1000 cm³ = 1 litre). A correct number with the wrong unit loses marks on Paper 2.

title: Exam technique: Information Representation
content:
### What earns the marks
For two complement, inversion plus one stated earns the method mark before the value. For floating point, mantissa plus exponent roles stated earn one mark each. For normalisation, the leading-bit rule quoted earns the precision mark.
### Traps
Error: sign bit ignored in range. Correction: an n-bit signed range tops at 2^(n-1) - 1. Error: larger exponent read as more precision. Correction: exponent sets range, mantissa sets precision. Error: normalised form guessed. Correction: mantissa starts with 0.1 or 1.0 pattern per the scheme.

title: Further Algebra — Study Notes
content:
Further Algebra

Edexcel International A Level Mathematics: partial fractions are Pure Mathematics 4 (WMA14, A2); the polynomial-division and modulus sections recap Pure 2 (WMA12, AS).

Polynomial Division and the Remainder Theorem

Divide to rewrite p(x) = (x − a)q(x) + r. The remainder when dividing by (x − a) equals p(a).

Example: p(x) = x³ − 2x² + 5. p(2) = 8 − 8 + 5 = 5, so dividing by (x − 2) leaves remainder 5.

If p(a) = 0, then (x − a) is a factor — that is the factor theorem. Divide out fully to reduce a cubic to a quadratic and factorise completely.

The Modulus Function

|x| measures distance from zero: |x| = x for x ≥ 0, −x for x < 0. Its graph is V-shaped.

Solving |2x − 1| = 5: split into 2x − 1 = 5 or 2x − 1 = −5, giving x = 3 or −2.

Inequalities: |2x − 1| < 5 becomes −5 < 2x − 1 < 5, so −2 < x < 3.

Partial Fractions

Reverse of combining fractions — needed before binomial expansion of rational functions.

  • Repeated linear: (4x + 1)/(x + 1)² = A/(x + 1) + B/(x + 1)²
  • Distinct linear: (7x + 4)/(x + 1)(x + 2) = A/(x + 1) + B/(x + 2)

Example: cover the (x + 1) factor with x = −1: B = 3; then compare coefficients for A = 4.

Exam tips: for |ax + b| > c, remember two separate regions; check factor-theorem roots by substitution before long division.

Exam method: partial fractions

Partial fractions split a rational function into simpler fractions whose sum equals the original. Before splitting, check the degrees: if the numerator has degree at least that of the denominator, divide first to get a polynomial plus a proper fraction.

For distinct linear factors (x − p)(x − q), write the expression as A/(x − p) + B/(x − q). Multiply through by the denominator and compare coefficients, or substitute x = p and x = q to find A and B directly. This substitution is the cover-up method and is the fastest route when the factors are linear and distinct.

A repeated factor (x − p)² needs two terms, A/(x − p) + B/(x − p)². An irreducible quadratic factor such as x² + 1 needs a linear numerator over it, (Ax + B)/(x² + 1).

Partial fractions are used to integrate rational functions, so the split is often followed by a logarithmic integral. Check the answer by recombining the fractions at one simple value of x.

Exam cue: State the form of the partial fractions before finding the constants, because the form is credited separately from the values.

Worked example: remainder theorem

Find the remainder when f(x) = x³ − 2x² + 3x − 4 is divided by (x − 2). By the remainder theorem, the remainder equals f(2) = 8 − 8 + 6 − 4 = 2. The same test checks for a factor: if the remainder is zero, then (x − 2) is a factor. Here f(1) = −2 ≠ 0, so (x − 1) is not a factor of f(x).

Exam method: long division with a missing term

When a polynomial is missing a term, write that term with a coefficient of zero before dividing, for example x⁴ + 3x² − 1 becomes x⁴ + 0x³ + 3x² + 0x − 1. Leaving out the placeholder is the usual cause of an incorrect quotient. Check the answer by multiplying the quotient by the divisor and adding the remainder; the result should give back the original polynomial.

title: A Level Mathematics: Complex Numbers
content:
A Level Mathematics: Complex Numbers

Complex numbers exist because the real number line is not big enough to solve every quadratic. The equation x² + 1 = 0 has no real solution, and rather than declaring it unsolvable mathematicians invented a number whose square is −1 and then discovered that the resulting system is not a curiosity but the natural home of rotation, oscillation and alternating current. This note builds the arithmetic from that single definition, then shows the two representations — Cartesian a + bi and modulus-argument — and why switching between them turns multiplication into something you can do in your head.

Why the number system needed extending

The real numbers are ordered: given any two, one is bigger. That ordering is exactly what a complex number gives up, and it is why complex numbers cannot be drawn on a line but can be drawn on a plane. The analogy that makes the extension feel inevitable is the one that produced negative numbers: subtracting a larger number from a smaller one was once impossible, so the integers were invented to close the gap. Square-rooting a negative number closes the next gap in the same way.

i is defined by  i^2 = -1
a complex number is z = a + bi, where a and b are real
a = Re(z)  the real part;  b = Im(z)  the imaginary part
two complex numbers are equal only when both parts match:
a + bi = c + di  means  a = c and b = d

The last line is not a triviality — it is the standard method for finding unknown constants in complex equations, because one equation in complex numbers carries two real equations inside it.

Arithmetic in Cartesian form

Addition and subtraction work component by component, exactly like vectors. Multiplication works by expanding the brackets and then replacing i² with −1; nothing else is needed.

(3 + 2i) + (1 - 5i) = 4 - 3i
(3 + 2i)(1 - 5i) = 3 - 15i + 2i - 10i^2 = 3 - 13i + 10 = 13 - 13i

Worked example. Expand (2 + 3i)².

(2 + 3i)(2 + 3i) = 4 + 6i + 6i + 9i^2
= 4 + 12i - 9
= -5 + 12i

Worked example 2 (a product that comes out real). Expand (4 + 3i)(4 − 3i).

= 16 - 12i + 12i - 9i^2 = 16 + 9 = 25

That result is not a coincidence: it is the complex analogue of the difference of two squares, and it is the engine of division.

Powers of i cycle with period four, which saves a great deal of work:

PowerValueReason
i¹idefinition
i²−1definition
i³−ii² × i
i⁴1(i²)² = 1

So i^99 = i^(96+3) = (i⁴)^24 × i³ = −i, because 99 divided by 4 leaves remainder 3.

Complex conjugates and division

Division is made possible by the conjugate: the number with the imaginary part negated, written with a bar over the z. Multiplying a number by its own conjugate always gives a real, non-negative result, which is what allows the i to be cleared from a denominator.

conjugate of z = a + bi is z-bar = a - bi
z x z-bar = a^2 + b^2  (always real, always >= 0)
to divide: multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator

Worked example. Write (3 + 4i)/(1 − 2i) in the form a + bi.

multiply by (1 + 2i)/(1 + 2i):
numerator: (3 + 4i)(1 + 2i) = 3 + 6i + 4i + 8i^2 = 3 + 10i - 8 = -5 + 10i
denominator: (1 - 2i)(1 + 2i) = 1 + 4 = 5
result: (-5 + 10i)/5 = -1 + 2i

Worked example 2 (solving an equation). Find real x and y such that (x + iy)(2 − i) = 5 + i.

expand: 2x - xi + 2yi - i^2 y = (2x + y) + (2y - x)i
match parts:  2x + y = 5  and  2y - x = 1
from the second: x = 2y - 1
substitute: 2(2y - 1) + y = 5  ->  5y = 7  ->  y = 1.4, x = 1.8

The Argand diagram and modulus-argument form

A complex number is a point, and the plane it lives in is the Argand diagram: real part across, imaginary part up. That picture immediately supplies two other ways to describe the same point — how far it is from the origin and at what angle — and those are the coordinates that make multiplication behave.

modulus |z| = sqrt(a^2 + b^2)     (distance from the origin)
argument arg z = theta, the angle from the positive real axis
principal argument: -180 < theta <= 180 degrees (or -pi < theta <= pi)

tan theta = b/a, but the quadrant decides the actual angle

Worked example. Find the modulus and argument of z = −1 + √3 i.

|z| = sqrt(1 + 3) = 2
the point is in the second quadrant (a negative, b positive)
reference angle: tan^-1(sqrt3/1) = 60 degrees
argument = 180 - 60 = 120 degrees
so z = 2(cos 120 + i sin 120)

Worked example 2 (fourth quadrant). Find the argument of z = 3 − 3i.

|z| = sqrt(9 + 9) = 4.243
tan^-1(-3/3) = -45 degrees, and the point is in the fourth quadrant
so the principal argument is -45 degrees (equivalently 315 degrees)

Multiplying and dividing in modulus-argument form

In Cartesian form multiplication is a bracket expansion; in modulus-argument form it is two separate, simple operations. That is the whole reason the form exists.

z1 z2:  multiply the moduli, add the arguments
z1/z2:  divide the moduli, subtract the arguments
z^n:    modulus^n, argument x n     (de Moivre's theorem)

Worked example. z1 = 2(cos 30° + i sin 30°) and z2 = 3(cos 80° + i sin 80°). Find z1z2 and z1/z2.

z1 z2 = 6(cos 110 + i sin 110)
z1/z2 = (2/3)(cos(-50) + i sin(-50)) = 0.667(cos 50 - i sin 50)

Worked example 2 (de Moivre). Find (1 + i)⁸.

|1 + i| = sqrt 2, arg = 45 degrees
(1 + i)^8 = (sqrt2)^8 (cos 360 + i sin 360) = 16(1 + 0i) = 16

Worked example 3 (geometric reading). Describe what multiplying by i does to a point on the Argand diagram.

i has modulus 1 and argument 90 degrees
so multiplying by i keeps the distance from the origin and adds 90 degrees
that is a quarter turn anticlockwise - multiplication as rotation

Roots of polynomial equations

Real-coefficient polynomials have complex roots in conjugate pairs. That single fact lets you go from one known root to two, halve the degree by dividing out a quadratic factor, and often finish the job with ordinary factorisation.

if a + bi is a root of a polynomial with real coefficients, then a - bi is too
the pair supplies the quadratic factor (z - (a+bi))(z - (a-bi)) = z^2 - 2az + (a^2 + b^2)

Worked example. 2 + i is a root of z³ − 5z² + 9z − 5. Find all three roots.

conjugate pair: 2 + i and 2 - i
quadratic factor: z^2 - 4z + 5
divide: (z^3 - 5z^2 + 9z - 5) / (z^2 - 4z + 5) = z - 1
roots: 2 + i, 2 - i, 1

Worked example 2 (forming an equation). Find the quadratic with roots 3 ± 2i.

sum = 6, product = 9 + 4 = 13
z^2 - 6z + 13 = 0

Loci on the Argand diagram

A locus question asks for the set of points satisfying a condition on a complex number, and every standard condition has a shape you should recognise without algebra.

ConditionShapeWhy
|z − a| = rcircle, centre a, radius rconstant distance from a point
|z − a| = |z − b|perpendicular bisector of abequidistant from two points
arg(z − a) = θhalf-line from a at angle θconstant direction, one-way
|z − a| ≤ rclosed discthe inequality includes the boundary

Worked example. Sketch the locus of |z − 3 − 4i| = 5 and state its centre and radius.

rewrite: |z - (3 + 4i)| = 5
circle, centre 3 + 4i, radius 5
it passes through the origin because |0 - 3 - 4i| = 5

Worked example 2 (inequality region). Describe the region |z − 1| < 2 and arg z > 45°.

inside the circle centre 1 radius 2 (not the boundary)
AND above the half-line from the origin at 45 degrees
the answer is the part of the disc lying above that ray

Exponential form and Euler's relation

The modulus-argument form is usually written more compactly as re^(iθ), using Euler's relation. That notation is not decoration: it makes the multiplication rules obvious, because exponentials multiply by adding their powers.

Euler: e^(i theta) = cos theta + i sin theta
so z = r e^(i theta)
z1 z2 = r1 r2 e^(i(theta1 + theta2))
z^n = r^n e^(i n theta)
z-bar = r e^(-i theta)

Worked example. Write z = 1 + i in exponential form and hence find z⁶.

r = sqrt 2, theta = pi/4  ->  z = sqrt2 e^(i pi/4)
z^6 = (sqrt2)^6 e^(i 6 pi/4) = 8 e^(i 3pi/2) = 8(cos 270 + i sin 270) = -8i

Worked example 2 (cos and sin from exponentials). Use Euler's relation to express cos θ in terms of exponentials.

e^(i theta) = cos theta + i sin theta
e^(-i theta) = cos theta - i sin theta
adding: 2 cos theta = e^(i theta) + e^(-i theta)
cos theta = (e^(i theta) + e^(-i theta))/2

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Powers) Simplify i^35. Answer: 35 = 4 × 8 + 3, so i^35 = i³ = −i.
  2. (Arithmetic) Write (5 − 2i)(3 + 4i) in the form a + bi. Answer: 15 + 20i − 6i − 8i² = 23 + 14i.
  3. (Division) Write (2 + i)/(3 − i) in the form a + bi. Answer: multiply by (3 + i): (5 + 5i)/10 = 0.5 + 0.5i.
  4. (Modulus) Find |4 − 3i|. Answer: √(16 + 9) = 5.
  5. (Argument) Find arg(−2 − 2i) in the principal range. Answer: third quadrant, so −135°.
  6. (De Moivre) Find (√3 + i)⁴. Answer: r = 2, θ = 30°, so 16(cos 120 + i sin 120) = −8 + 8√3 i.
  7. (Roots) 1 − 2i is a root of z² − 2z + 5 = 0. State the other root. Answer: 1 + 2i.
  8. (Locus) Describe |z + 2| = 3. Answer: circle centre −2, radius 3.
  9. (Locus) Describe arg(z − 1) = π/3. Answer: half-line from 1 at 60°, excluding the point itself.
  10. (Exponential) Write 2 − 2i as re^(iθ). Answer: r = 2√2, θ = −45°, so 2√2 e^(−iπ/4).

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Squaring the imaginary part only: (2i)² = −4, not 4i² left uncollected, and (a + bi)² has a middle term 2abi that is easy to drop.
  • Conjugate applied to the numerator: divide by multiplying both parts by the conjugate of the denominator only.
  • Argument in the wrong quadrant: tan⁻¹(b/a) returns a first-quadrant angle; add or subtract 180° to place it correctly.
  • Principal range ignored: an argument of 300° is written −60°, not 300°, when the question asks for the principal value.
  • Modulus of a sum: |z1 + z2| is not |z1| + |z2|; only products and quotients distribute over modulus.
  • Conjugate pairs assumed for complex coefficients: the pairing holds for real coefficients, which is the case in every exam question — but say so when justifying.
  • Locus with the wrong centre: |z − a| is a circle centred at a, not at −a; the sign inside the modulus flips the centre.
  • deg/rad mode: de Moivre in radians while the question is in degrees gives a phase that is wrong by a factor of 57.3.

title: A Level Mathematics: The Binomial Distribution
content:
A Level Mathematics: The Binomial Distribution

A binomial distribution counts successes in a fixed number of independent trials, each with the same probability of success. Coins, multiple-choice guesses, defective items in a sample and free throws all fit the same template, and once a problem is recognised as binomial the calculation is a formula plus a cumulative table. This note builds the distribution from its four conditions, derives the formula from counting, and then uses it for the two things exams actually ask: probabilities and hypothesis tests.

The four conditions

Before writing X ~ B(n, p) you must be able to name the conditions, because most exam questions include a part asking whether the model is appropriate. The conditions are not red tape: drop any one and the formula is simply wrong.

1. a fixed number of trials n
2. each trial has exactly two outcomes (success / failure)
3. the probability of success p is constant for every trial
4. the trials are independent
then X = number of successes has X ~ B(n, p)

Worked example (checking the model). A bag holds 5 red and 15 blue counters. Four counters are taken without replacement. Is the number of red counters binomial?

n = 4 is fixed and each draw is red or not red
but p changes: 5/20, then 5/19 if a red was taken, ...
the trials are not independent, so NOT binomial (it is hypergeometric)

Taking with replacement would fix it: p stays 0.25 on every draw.

The formula, and where it comes from

The probability of a particular sequence of r successes and n − r failures is p^r (1−p)^(n−r), because independence lets you multiply. The number of such sequences is the number of ways to choose which r trials succeed, which is nCr. Multiplying gives the formula.

P(X = r) = nCr p^r (1 - p)^(n - r)
the nCr counts arrangements; the powers give the probability of one arrangement

Worked example. X ~ B(10, 0.3). Find P(X = 3).

P = 10C3 (0.3)³ (0.7)⁷
= 120 × 0.027 × 0.08235
= 120 × 0.002223 = 0.2668

Worked example 2 (a single trial count). A fair die is rolled 8 times. Find the probability of exactly two sixes.

X ~ B(8, 1/6)
P(X = 2) = 8C2 (1/6)² (5/6)⁶ = 28 × 0.02778 × 0.3349 = 0.2605

Worked example 3 (why nCr appears). For n = 3 and r = 1, list the sequences and confirm the coefficient.

sequences: SFF, FSF, FFS - three of them
each has probability p(1-p)²
so P(X = 1) = 3p(1-p)², and 3C1 = 3

Cumulative probabilities

Questions almost always ask for a range, not a single value, and the cumulative distribution is what the calculator or the tables supply. The skill is rewriting the question into the form the table gives you.

P(X <= r) is tabulated directly
P(X >= r) = 1 - P(X <= r - 1)
P(X < r)  = P(X <= r - 1)
P(a <= X <= b) = P(X <= b) - P(X <= a - 1)
P(X = r) = P(X <= r) - P(X <= r - 1)

Worked example. X ~ B(20, 0.4). Find P(X ≥ 8).

P(X >= 8) = 1 - P(X <= 7)
= 1 - 0.4159
= 0.5841

Worked example 2 (between). For the same X, find P(5 ≤ X ≤ 10).

= P(X <= 10) - P(X <= 4)
= 0.8725 - 0.0510
= 0.8215

Worked example 3 (the strict inequality trap). For the same X, find P(X > 6).

P(X > 6) = 1 - P(X <= 6) = 1 - 0.2500 = 0.7500
note this is different from P(X >= 6) = 1 - P(X <= 5) = 0.8746

Mean and variance

The binomial has the simplest mean and variance in the syllabus, and they are worth knowing both forwards and backwards: a question can give the mean and variance and ask for n and p.

E(X) = np
Var(X) = np(1 - p)
standard deviation = √(np(1-p))

Worked example. X ~ B(50, 0.2). Find the mean and standard deviation.

mean = 50 × 0.2 = 10
variance = 10 × 0.8 = 8
sd = 2.828

Worked example 2 (backwards). A binomial variable has mean 12 and variance 9. Find n and p.

np = 12;  np(1-p) = 9
divide: 1 - p = 9/12 = 0.75  →  p = 0.25
then n = 12/0.25 = 48

Hypothesis testing with the binomial

A one-tailed test asks whether p has increased or decreased; the test statistic is the observed count, and the p-value is the probability of a result at least as extreme in the direction of the alternative.

H0: p = p0      H1: p > p0 (or p < p0)
X ~ B(n, p0) under H0
p-value = P(X >= observed) or P(X <= observed)
compare with the significance level; reject H0 if p-value <= alpha

Worked example. A coin is tossed 20 times and lands heads 15 times. Test at the 5% level whether the coin is biased towards heads.

H0: p = 0.5;  H1: p > 0.5
X ~ B(20, 0.5)
P(X >= 15) = 1 - P(X <= 14) = 1 - 0.9793 = 0.0207
0.0207 < 0.05, so reject H0
there is evidence at the 5% level that the coin favours heads

Worked example 2 (two-tailed). The same data tested two-tailed.

double the smaller tail: 2 × 0.0207 = 0.0414
0.0414 < 0.05, so still reject H0 at the 5% level

Worked example 3 (critical region). For X ~ B(20, 0.5), find the critical region for a 5% one-tailed test of p > 0.5.

P(X >= 14) = 0.0577 (above 0.05)
P(X >= 15) = 0.0207 (below 0.05)
critical region: X >= 15

Note that the critical region is chosen so the probability of a Type I error is at most 5%, which is why 14 is excluded even though it is close.

When the model breaks down

Examiners like the question that asks why a binomial model is only an approximation. The usual culprits are dependence, a varying probability, or a fixed sample drawn without replacement from a small population.

SituationProblemEffect
sampling without replacementtrials not independentp drifts; use the hypergeometric instead
clustered data (pupils in classes)responses correlatedvariance underestimated
probability varies between trialsp not constantformula invalid
large n, p near 0.5computation heavynormal approximation is reasonable

Worked example (normal approximation). X ~ B(200, 0.4). Use a normal approximation to estimate P(X ≤ 70).

mean = 80;  variance = 200 × 0.4 × 0.6 = 48;  sd = 6.928
continuity correction: X <= 70 becomes X < 70.5
z = (70.5 - 80)/6.928 = -1.371
P(Z < -1.371) = 0.0852

The continuity correction is compulsory: a discrete count needs a half-unit boundary before it can be treated as continuous.

Expected frequencies and the shape of the distribution

A binomial distribution is not symmetric unless p = 0.5, and that shape decides which tail an exam question is fishing in. The most likely value — the mode — is the integer near (n + 1)p, and expected frequency multiplies the probability by the number of samples taken. Both are quick marks that are frequently missed because students jump straight to the formula.

mode is near (n + 1)p, checked by comparing consecutive probabilities
expected number in a sample of size N = N x P(X = r)

Worked example. X ~ B(12, 0.3). Find the most likely value of X and the expected number of 3s in 500 independent observations.

(n + 1)p = 13 × 0.3 = 3.9, so check r = 3 and r = 4
P(X = 3) = 220 × 0.027 × 0.1176 = 0.2397
P(X = 4) = 495 × 0.0081 × 0.1681 = 0.2311
mode = 3
expected number of 3s = 500 × 0.2397 = 120 (to the nearest whole)

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Model) State the distribution for the number of sixes in 12 rolls of a fair die. Answer: X ~ B(n, p) with n = 12 rolls and p = 1/6 the chance of a six on each, so X ~ B(12, 1/6).
  2. (Single value) X ~ B(8, 0.25): find P(X = 2). Answer: P(X = 2) = ⁸C₂ (0.25)² (0.75)⁶ = 28 × 0.0625 × 0.1780 = 0.3115.
  3. (Cumulative) X ~ B(15, 0.3): find P(X ≤ 4). Answer: P(X ≤ 4) = Σₖ₌₀⁴ ¹⁵Cₖ (0.3)ᵏ (0.7)¹⁵⁻ᵏ = 0.5155 from cumulative binomial tables.
  4. (Complement) Same X: find P(X ≥ 3). Answer: P(X ≥ 3) = 1 − P(X ≤ 2) = 1 − 0.2969 = 0.7031 — the complement, because the tables give the lower tail only.
  5. (Mean) X ~ B(40, 0.35): find E(X) and Var(X). Answer: 14 and 9.1.
  6. (Backwards) Mean 18, variance 12: find n and p. Answer: mean np = 18 and variance np(1 − p) = 12; dividing, 1 − p = 12/18 = 2/3, so p = 1/3 and n = 18 ÷ (1/3) = 54.
  7. (Test) 12 of 20 seeds germinate; test p = 0.5 against p < 0.5 at 5%. Answer: H₀: p = 0.5 against H₁: p < 0.5; under H₀, X ~ B(20, 0.5) and P(X ≤ 12) = 0.8684, which is far above 0.05, so there is no evidence to reject H₀.
  8. (Critical region) X ~ B(10, 0.2): find the 5% critical region for p < 0.2. Answer: the smallest possible tail is P(X ≤ 0) = (0.8)¹⁰ = 0.1074, which already exceeds 0.05, so no critical region exists at the 5% level for this n.
  9. (Approximation) X ~ B(100, 0.5): approximate P(X ≥ 60). Answer: μ = np = 50 and σ = √(np(1 − p)) = √25 = 5; with the continuity correction z = (59.5 − 50)/5 = 1.9, so P(X ≥ 60) ≈ P(Z > 1.9) = 0.0287.
  10. (Assumption) Give one reason a binomial model may fail for defects in boxes of 20. Answer: defects may cluster, so trials are not independent.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Forgetting nCr: the coefficient counts arrangements; without it the answer is the probability of one specific sequence.
  • nCr on the wrong factor: it is p^r (1−p)^(n−r), with the success probability raised to the number of successes.
  • Inequality direction: P(X ≥ 8) uses 1 − P(X ≤ 7), not 1 − P(X ≤ 8).
  • Variance confused with standard deviation: np(1−p) is the variance; the test and the normal approximation need the square root.
  • Continuity correction omitted: any normal approximation to a discrete count needs the half-unit adjustment.
