  • One-tailed evidence read as two: halving or doubling the tail without checking the alternative direction is a silent error.
  • Independence asserted, not checked: sampling without replacement from a small population breaks the model, and the question usually invites you to say so.
  • p-value compared with the wrong threshold: the significance level is given as a percentage; 5% means 0.05, not 5.

Recognising a binomial situation in context

Most binomial marks are lost before any arithmetic starts, because the question was not identified as binomial. The subsections below give a checklist for reading a question and writing the model in the standard form X ~ B(n, p) before you calculate anything.

Writing the model in the form X ~ B(n, p)

Once you decide a situation is binomial, state the model in full: X ~ B(n, p), where X is the number of successes, n is the number of trials and p is the probability of a success on each trial. Define X in words in your answer, for example “X is the number of defective bulbs in a box of 20”. A model with no definition of X loses the communication mark even when the probabilities are right.

Identifying the number of trials, n

The value of n is the fixed number of times the experiment is repeated: the number of bulbs tested, the number of patients treated, or the number of games played. Read the question for the phrase that fixes it, such as “of 20 bulbs chosen at random”. If the question keeps going until a result occurs, the number of trials is not fixed and the binomial model does not apply directly.

Identifying the probability of success, p

The value of p is the probability of the outcome you have chosen to call a success on one trial. It must stay the same for every trial. A fair coin gives p = 0.5, and a bag where 15% of items are faulty gives p = 0.15 for each item drawn with replacement. If the question gives a percentage, convert it to a decimal before you use it in any formula.

Checking for fixed trials

The number of trials must be decided before the experiment starts. Counting the number of successes in a fixed sample is binomial, whereas recording how many trials it takes to get the first success is not. A question about the number of heads in ten tosses is binomial; a question about how many tosses are needed for the first head is a different model. Make the fixed-n check before any other check.

Checking for independent trials

Each trial must not affect the next. Independence is what allows you to multiply the probabilities of several outcomes together, and it is the assumption most often ignored. Drawing items with replacement keeps p constant, and that is what the model needs. Drawing without replacement changes p after each draw, so the binomial model is only an approximation when the sample is small compared with the population.

Worked identification

A survey finds that 30% of adults own a bicycle. Twelve adults are chosen at random from a large town and asked whether they own one. Let X be the number who own a bicycle. Here n = 12, p = 0.3 and the answer is X ~ B(12, 0.3). The population is large, so the probability for each adult stays close to 0.3 and the model is a reasonable one to use. State that assumption, because a marker looks for it.

Probabilities of at least one, and of more than r

Questions that ask for “at least” or “more than” are the ones where the complement saves the most time. The subsections set out the choice between a direct sum and the complement, and the checks that stop an off-by-one error.

Probability of at least one success

“At least one” is the complement of “none”, so P(X ≥ 1) = 1 − P(X = 0) = 1 − qⁿ, where q = 1 − p. For X ~ B(5, 0.2), P(X ≥ 1) = 1 − 0.8⁵ = 1 − 0.32768 = 0.672 to 3 significant figures. Adding the probabilities of X = 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 gives the same answer but takes five calculations instead of one.

Probability of more than r successes

“More than 3” means 4 or more, so P(X > 3) = 1 − P(X ≤ 3). For X ~ B(10, 0.3), P(X ≤ 3) = 0.6496 to 4 decimal places, so P(X > 3) = 0.3504. The number 3 is included in the part you subtract from 1; forgetting that is the typical error on “more than” questions.

Choosing between a direct sum and the complement

Use the complement when the part you do not want is short: “at least one”, “at most one but not zero” and similar phrases. Use a direct sum when the wanted region has only a few terms, such as P(X = 2) + P(X = 3). With a calculator table of cumulative probabilities, most “at most” and “at least” questions reduce to one lookup and one subtraction.

Probability of exactly r on a calculator

For X ~ B(n, p), P(X = r) = ⁿCᵣ pʳ qⁿ⁻ʳ. The combination ⁿCᵣ counts the ways the r successes can be arranged among n trials. For X ~ B(10, 0.3), P(X = 3) = 120 × 0.3³ × 0.7⁷ = 120 × 0.027 × 0.0823543 = 0.2668 to 4 decimal places. Enter the combination with the nCr key so the arrangement count is not mistyped.

The most likely number of successes (the mode)

The most likely value of X is the mode. For a binomial distribution it is the whole number part of (n + 1)p, and if (n + 1)p is itself a whole number there are two modes, (n + 1)p − 1 and (n + 1)p. For X ~ B(10, 0.3), (n + 1)p = 3.3, so the mode is 3. Check against the probabilities: P(X = 3) = 0.2668 is larger than P(X = 2) = 0.2335 and P(X = 4) = 0.2001.

Equations and symbols

The distribution, its conditions and the four tail identities. Every question on this topic is one of these lines plus a calculator.

P(X = r) = nCr p^r (1 - p)^(n - r) Key: n = number of trials, fixed in advance; p = probability of success in one trial, constant; r = the number of successes asked for; nCr = n!/(r!(n − r)!), the number of orders the successes can occur in. The (1 − p) term is the failures, and its power must be n − r.

X ~ B(n, p) Key: X = the count of successes; the tilde means "is distributed as"; n and p as above. Write this line before calculating — it is often a mark on its own, and it fixes which parameters go into the calculator.

P = 10C3 (0.3)³ (0.7)⁷ Key: n = 10, p = 0.3, r = 3, so the failures are 7 and their probability is 0.7. The coefficient 10C3 = 120 accounts for the order of the three successes among the ten trials.

P(X >= r) = 1 - P(X <= r - 1) Key: a complement, so the two probabilities add to 1; the boundary moves by one because the binomial is discrete. Using 1 − P(X ≤ r) instead is the classic off-by-one error.

P(a <= X <= b) = P(X <= b) - P(X <= a - 1) Key: subtract the part below the interval; again the "− 1" is there because P(X ≤ a − 1) is everything before a. Check with a small case you can list by hand before trusting the calculator.

title: Exam technique: Poisson Distribution
content:
### What earns the marks
For lambda scaling, the rate times the interval stated earns the first mark. For probabilities, e^-lambda lambda^x / x! with values earns the method mark. For approximations, the condition named (n large, p small, lambda = np) earns credit.
### Traps
Error: unscaled lambda over a new interval. Correction: scale first. Error: binomial coefficients inside Poisson work. Correction: Poisson formula only. Error: mean and variance treated as different. Correction: both equal lambda.
### Worked example
Calls arrive at a rate of 3 per minute, so over 2 minutes λ = 6. The probability of exactly 2 calls is P(X = 2) = e⁻⁶ × 6² / 2! = 18e⁻⁶ ≈ 0.0446. The mean and the variance both equal λ, so the mean number in 2 minutes is 6.
### Check yourself
Explain why the rate must be scaled before you use the formula. The rate is given per minute, but the interval is 2 minutes, so λ must be the rate multiplied by the interval, giving 6 and not 3.

title: Nuclear Physics — Study Notes
content:
Nuclear Physics

The nucleus

The nucleus holds protons and neutrons, collectively nucleons. Nuclide notation ᴬZX gives Z protons and A nucleons, so N = A − Z neutrons. Isotopes share Z and differ in N. Nuclear densities are about 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³, so nearly all the mass of an atom sits in a tiny volume.

Mass defect and binding energy (23.1)

The mass of a nucleus is less than the sum of the masses of its separate nucleons. This difference is the mass defect Δm. Energy equivalent to Δm, given by E = Δmc², is the binding energy: the energy released when the nucleus is assembled from separate nucleons, and the energy needed to separate it. In nuclear work, 1 u = 931 MeV.

Example: a mass defect of 0.0300 u corresponds to E = 0.0300 × 931 ≈ 27.9 MeV.

The binding energy per nucleon peaks near iron-56, the most tightly bound nucleus. Energy is released when the nucleons move toward this peak, by fission of heavy nuclei or by fusion of light ones.

Radioactive decay (23.2)

Decay is random and spontaneous. The effect of each type on the nucleus and its penetration are:

TypeWhat changesStopped by
alphaZ − 2, A − 4paper
beta-minusZ + 1, A unchangeda few mm of aluminium
gammano change to Z or Athick lead

The activity A = λN is the rate of decay, in becquerel (Bq). The decay constant λ and the half-life t½ are related by λ = ln 2 / t½. The number of nuclei left after time t is N = N₀e^(−λt).

Example: a sample with t½ = 10 days has 1/8 of its original activity after 30 days, since three half-lives have passed.

Example: with t½ = 5.0 h = 1.8 × 10⁴ s, λ = 0.693 / 1.8 × 10⁴ ≈ 3.9 × 10⁻⁵ s⁻¹.

Fission and fusion

Heavy nuclei split (fission) into lighter nuclei of greater binding energy per nucleon, which releases energy in reactors. Light nuclei merge (fusion), which releases energy in stars.

Exam tips: balance Z and A on both sides of every decay equation. Convert the half-life to seconds before finding λ. Use A = λN, not guesswork with halves, when the number of nuclei is needed.

title: Networks and the Internet — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Networks and the Internet

Computer Science — A2. Four layers: Application (HTTP, FTP, SMTP, DNS), Transport (TCP reliable, connection-oriented with sequence numbers and acknowledgements; UDP fast, connectionless), Internet (IP addressing and routing), Link (physical delivery on the local network). Layering separates concerns so each layer can change independently.

Key areas to revise

  • The TCP/IP Stack
  • Switching
  • Addressing and Subnetting
  • Models and Protection

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

### Worked example The internet is a network of networks. Data travels as packets, and each packet carries a destination IP address. IPv4 addresses are 32 bits, giving 2³² possible addresses, and IPv6 addresses are 128 bits. DNS translates a domain name into an IP address. TCP checks that packets arrive and reassembles them in order, while HTTPS encrypts the data in transit. ### Check yourself Describe the role of DNS when you open a website by name. DNS looks up the domain name and returns the IP address, and the browser then sends its request to that address. Explain why packets may take different routes but still reach the destination.

title: Probability and Statistics I
content:
Probability and Statistics I

Permutations and Combinations

  • Permutations (order matters): ⁿPᵣ = n!/(n − r)!
  • Combinations (order irrelevant): ⁿCᵣ = n!/(r!(n − r)!)

Example: choosing a committee of 3 from 8 people: C(8,3) = 56. Arranging 3 of 8 books on a shelf: P(8,3) = 336.

Probability Rules

  • P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B)
  • Independent events: P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B)
  • Complement: P(A′) = 1 − P(A)

Conditional Probability

P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B). Tree diagrams multiply along branches and add across outcomes.

Example: P(two reds without replacement from 5 red + 3 blue) = (5/8)(4/7) = 5/14.

Discrete Random Variables

E(X) = Σ x P(X = x); Var(X) = E(X²) − [E(X)]².

Example: die: E(X) = 3.5; E(X²) = 91/6, so Var(X) ≈ 2.92.

Exam tips: decide permutation vs combination by testing whether swapping two items changes the outcome; always verify tree-branch probabilities sum to 1.

title: IGCSE Chemistry: Experimental Techniques and Analysis
content:
IGCSE Chemistry: Experimental Techniques and Analysis

Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry 0620 (2026–2028), Extended route, Topic 12 Experimental techniques and chemical analysis: statements 12.1 Experimental design, 12.2 Acid–base titrations, 12.3 Chromatography, 12.4 Separation and purification, and 12.5 Identification of ions and gases. This is the Paper 6 blueprint — the written practical paper — and it rewards precise procedure language: apparatus named, steps ordered, errors identified with improvements. Every technique below is described as a step-by-step method plus its accuracy reasoning.

Experimental design and apparatus

QuantityApparatusAccuracy notes
Volume (large)Measuring cylinderRead at the bottom of the meniscus at eye level
Volume (precise)Burette (titration), volumetric pipetteBurette reads to 0.05 cm³; pipette delivers one fixed volume accurately
MassBalance (±0.01 g)Zero the balance; subtract container mass
TimeStopwatchHuman reaction time ≈ 0.2 s — significant for fast reactions
TemperatureThermometer (or probe)Stir for even readings; do not rest the bulb on the vessel
Gas volumeGas syringe (or inverted burette)Check for leaks; read dead-on at eye level

Design variables: the independent variable (what you change), the dependent (what you measure), and control variables (what you keep fixed for a fair test). Range and number of values: at least 5–6 values across a sensible span, with repeats for averages and anomalous results.

Titration technique

Titration of sodium hydroxide with hydrochloric acid - full method:

  1. Rinse the burette with the acid; fill above the zero and run out to
     remove the air bubble below the tap (a trapped bubble corrupts every
     reading).
  2. Rinse the pipette with the alkali; pipette exactly 25.0 cm³ of NaOH
     into a conical flask.
  3. Add 2-3 drops of a suitable indicator (phenolphthalein or methyl
     orange - choose one that changes at the endpoint).
  4. Run acid in from the burette with constant swirling until the indicator
     CHANGES COLOUR permanently (the endpoint).
  5. Record the titre (final - initial reading). REPEAT to obtain CONCORDANT
     titres within 0.10 cm³; average only the concordant ones.

  Sources of error and their improvements:
   - misjudging the endpoint -> add the last cm³ dropwise, swirl;
   - bubble in the burette -> run the tap briefly before starting;
   - reading the meniscus at an angle (parallax) -> read at eye level;
   - overswirling spilling -> controlled swirling against a white tile.

  Titration calculation (linked to the stoichiometry note):
   moles = c x V ; use the balanced equation's ratio ; c = moles / V.

Chromatography

Paper chromatography separates soluble coloured mixtures: a spot of the mixture is placed on the baseline near the bottom of the paper, the paper stands in a solvent (the baseline must be ABOVE the solvent level, or the spot washes away), and the solvent rises carrying components at different rates.

Reading a chromatogram - the Rf calculation:

  Rf = distance travelled by the substance
       / distance travelled by the solvent front

  Worked: a component moves 4.2 cm; the solvent front moves 6.0 cm.
    Rf = 4.2 / 6.0 = 0.70

  Rf is always less than 1 (substances cannot outrun the solvent) and has
  no units. Measure from the CENTRE of the spot to the line, both distances
  from the same baseline.

  Colourless mixtures: run the chromatography, then use a LOCATING AGENT
  (spray with ninhydrin for amino acids, or view under UV) to reveal spots.
  Purity assessment: a pure substance gives ONE spot; mixtures give several.
  Identification: compare Rf values with known standards run on the same
  paper (same solvent, same conditions).

Separation and purification

  • Filtration — separates an insoluble solid from a liquid (filter paper/funnel; the residue stays, the filtrate passes).
  • Crystallisation — evaporate solvent to the point of crystallisation, then cool; used for soluble salts from solution.
  • Simple distillation — separates a solvent from a solution (water from salt solution): boil, condense the vapour in a Liebig condenser, collect the distillate.
  • Fractional distillation — separates miscible liquids with different boiling points (ethanol/water; petroleum fractions) using a fractionating column.
  • Purity checks — pure substances melt/boil at sharp, fixed temperatures; impure samples over a range and displaced (impure melts lower, boils higher).
Simple vs fractional distillation - the difference that earns marks:

  SIMPLE:  mixture heated; vapour goes straight to the condenser.
           Used when ONE component is needed (pure water from brine).
  FRACTIONAL: a fractionating column sits between flask and condenser;
           vapour condenses and re-evaporates up the column, so fractions
           with different boiling points separate at different heights.
           Used to separate several components (petroleum, air).

  Apparatus detail: the thermometer bulb sits level with the side arm of the
  still head - it must measure the VAPOR, not the liquid.

Qualitative analysis: ions and gases

TestReagent / methodPositive observation
CarbonateAdd dilute acidEffervescence; gas turns limewater milky (CO₂)
ChlorideDilute nitric acid + silver nitrateWhite precipitate
BromideAs chlorideCream precipitate
IodideAs chlorideYellow precipitate
SulfateDilute hydrochloric acid + barium chlorideWhite precipitate
NitrateAdd NaOH + aluminium foil, warmAmmonia gas (turns damp red litmus blue)
HydrogenBurning splint at the mouthSqueaky pop
OxygenGlowing splintRelights
Carbon dioxideBubble through limewaterTurns milky/cloudy
AmmoniaDamp red litmusTurns blue
ChlorineDamp litmusBleaches white

Flame tests: Li⁺ red, Na⁺ yellow, K⁺ lilac, Ca²⁺ orange-red, Ba²⁺ light green, Cu²⁺ blue-green — the wire is dipped in acid and cleaned between tests. Cation tests with NaOH(aq): Cu²⁺ light blue precipitate, Fe²⁺ green, Fe³⁺ red-brown, Zn²⁺ white (dissolves in excess), Al³⁺ white (dissolves in excess), NH₄⁺ gives ammonia on warming; with ammonia solution, copper gives a deep blue solution in excess.

Worked example: a full Paper 6 problem

Question: a student finds a white solid that could be sodium carbonate or
sodium chloride. Plan a test.

  1. SOLUBILITY/FUNCTIONAL: dissolve a sample in water; add dilute
     hydrochloric acid to a portion.
       Effervescence -> carbonate present (CO₂: limewater test confirms).
       No change -> chloride likely.
  2. CONFIRM CHLORIDE: acidify with dilute nitric acid, add silver nitrate.
       White precipitate of AgCl confirms chloride.
  3. FLAME TEST for sodium (yellow flame) confirms the cation either way.

  Error analysis the question may add: "the limewater was already milky
  before the test" -> use fresh limewater and a control; "no precipitate
  formed but chloride was claimed" -> the acid must be nitric (hydrochloric
  acid adds chloride itself - a classic trap).

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Hydrochloric acid in the sulfate or chloride test — it introduces the very ions being tested for; use nitric acid for halide tests, HCl + BaCl₂ only for sulfate.
  • Placing the baseline below the solvent level in chromatography (spot dissolves away).
  • Rf values greater than 1 or calculated without the solvent-front measurement from the same baseline.
  • Titration: forgetting to remove the burette bubble or averaging non-concordant titres.
  • Describing distillation apparatus without the thermometer position at the side arm.
  • Listing qualitative tests without the exact observation wording (precipitate colours, gas tests) — the observation is the mark.
  • Not naming control variables in design questions; a "fair test" answer must say what is kept constant and why.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 6, 4 marks). Describe how to obtain pure water from salt water and name the technique.

Answer: Simple distillation: heat the salt solution in a flask; water evaporates and the vapour passes into a Liebig condenser (cold water jacket) where it condenses; collect the distillate in a receiver. The salt remains in the flask. The thermometer bulb is placed at the side arm to confirm pure water distilling at 100 °C.

Question 2 (Paper 6, 4 marks). A chromatogram of a food dye gives a spot 5.0 cm from the baseline with a solvent front of 8.0 cm. Calculate Rf and explain how the mixture's components are identified.

Answer: Rf = 5.0 ÷ 8.0 = 0.625. Each component moves a characteristic distance; identification is by comparing Rf values with known standards run in the same solvent under the same conditions. A pure substance gives one spot; several spots show a mixture.

Question 3 (Paper 6, 5 marks). Describe a titration to find the concentration of hydrochloric acid using standard sodium hydroxide, including precautions.

Answer: Rinse and fill the burette with acid (remove the air bubble); pipette 25.0 cm³ of the sodium hydroxide into a conical flask; add 2–3 drops of indicator; run in acid with swirling until the colour changes permanently; record the titre; repeat to concordant titres within 0.10 cm³ and average. Precautions: read the meniscus at eye level; add the last cm³ dropwise; swirl continuously.

Question 4 (Paper 6, 3 marks). State the tests and results for carbon dioxide, oxygen and ammonia gases.

Answer: Carbon dioxide: bubble through limewater — turns milky/cloudy. Oxygen: insert a glowing splint — it relights. Ammonia: hold damp red litmus paper at the mouth — it turns blue.

Question 5 (Paper 6, 4 marks). A student must separate a mixture of sand and salt. Describe the method and how to recover solid salt.

Answer: Add water and stir to dissolve the salt; filter through filter paper and funnel — sand stays as the residue, salt solution is the filtrate. Evaporate the filtrate (gentle heating to the point of crystallisation) to recover solid salt crystals; the water can be distilled off for reuse. Check purity by melting-point determination.

Question 6 (Paper 6, 3 marks). Identify a white solid: it effervesces with acid and the gas turns limewater milky; the flame test is lilac. Name the compound and justify.

Answer: Effervescence with limewater-milky gas confirms carbonate (CO₃²⁻); the lilac flame confirms potassium. The solid is potassium carbonate, K₂CO₃.

With the full 0620 content in place, the IGCSE chemistry estate is complete — the A Level course builds directly on these foundations.

title: Complex Numbers — Study Notes
content:
Complex Numbers

Basics

i² = −1. A complex number z = a + bi has real part a and imaginary part b. Two numbers are equal iff both parts match.

Arithmetic: add/subtract parts; multiply with brackets and replace i² with −1.

Example: (2 + 3i)(1 − i) = 2 − 2i + 3i − 3i² = 5 + i.

Conjugates

z̄ = a − bi. zz̄ = a² + b² (real). Dividing: multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate.

Example: 1/(3 − i) × (3 + i)/(3 + i) = (3 + i)/10.

Argand Diagram

Plot z as the point (a, b). |z| = √(a² + b²) is the modulus (distance from origin); arg z = tan⁻¹(b/a) is the argument (angle). Multiply two numbers: moduli multiply, arguments add.

Modulus–Argument Form

z = r(cos θ + i sin θ), r = |z|, θ = arg z. Useful for powers and roots.

de Moivre and Roots

[r(cos θ + i sin θ)]ⁿ = rⁿ(cos nθ + i sin nθ).

Example: (1 + i)⁸: |1 + i| = √2, arg = π/4, so z⁸ = (√2)⁸ cis 2π = 16.

An nth root gives n evenly spaced solutions, 2π/n apart on a circle of radius r^(1/n).

Exam tips: always give arguments in the required interval; when solving equations, remember complex roots come in conjugate pairs for real polynomials.

title: Edexcel IAL AS Biology: Molecules, Transport and Health Revision Notes
content:
Quick revision: Molecules, Transport and Health

Biology — AS. Edexcel IAL Biology WBI11, Topic 1. Living things are built from a small set of biological molecules. Their structure decides how they are used, how substances move in and out of cells, and how diet affects health.

Key areas to revise

  • Carbohydrates
  • Lipids and proteins
  • Enzymes
  • Transport
  • Health

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Core Biological Molecules & Water

Water is an important solvent for transport due to its dipole nature, forming hydrogen bonds. Carbohydrates consist of monosaccharides, disaccharides, and polysaccharides, including glycogen and starch (amylose and amylopectin), relating their structures to energy roles. Monosaccharides such as glucose, fructose, and galactose join via condensation reactions forming glycosidic bonds to create disaccharides like maltose, sucrose, and lactose, and polysaccharides, which split via hydrolysis. Core Practical 1 uses semi-quantitative Benedict's reagent for reducing sugars and iodine solution for starch with colour standards. Triglycerides form via condensation between glycerol and three fatty acids creating ester bonds, differing from saturated lipids lacking double bonds and unsaturated lipids containing carbon-carbon double bonds. Amino acids possess a basic structure with an amine group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen, and an R group, linking via condensation into peptide bonds forming polypeptides. Primary structure determines secondary structure (alpha-helices and beta-pleated sheets via hydrogen bonding) and three-dimensional tertiary/quaternary structure, categorised into globular proteins (like haemoglobin) and fibrous proteins (like collagen) stabilised by hydrogen, ionic, and disulfide bonds. Core Practical uses biuret reagent and colour standards to estimate protein concentration.

Enzymes & Gas Exchange

Enzymes act as biological catalysts inside cells (intracellular) or outside (extracellular), reducing activation energy. Their three-dimensional active site provides high specificity for substrates, explained by the lock and key and induced fit models. Core Practical 4 investigates the effect of temperature, pH, enzyme concentration, and substrate concentration on initial reaction rates. Gas exchange surfaces require a large surface area to volume ratio, short diffusion distance (thinness), and a steep concentration gradient. Fick's Law calculates the rate of diffusion as proportional to (surface area × concentration difference) / thickness. Mammalian lungs adapt via millions of alveoli, a rich capillary network, and thin squamous epithelium for rapid gas exchange.

Transport & The Cardiovascular System

Mass transport in a mammalian heart and circulation overcomes the limitations of diffusion in meeting organism requirements. Blood vessels have distinct structures: arteries possess thick walls with elastic tissue and smooth muscle to withstand high pressure; veins have wider lumens, valves, and thinner walls; capillaries consist of a single layer of endothelial cells for rapid exchange. The cardiac cycle comprises atrial systole, ventricular systole, and cardiac diastole, operating via valves and pressure gradients driven by the mammalian heart and major blood vessels (aorta, vena cava, pulmonary artery, pulmonary vein), excluding myogenic stimulation details at IAS. Recommended additional practical involves dissection of a mammalian heart. Haemoglobin transports oxygen and carbon dioxide, showing an oxygen dissociation curve with cooperative binding, the Bohr effect where high carbon dioxide partial pressure shifts the curve right, and fetal haemoglobin exhibiting higher oxygen affinity than adult haemoglobin.

Cardiovascular Disease (CVD), Health & Risk Factors

Atherosclerosis begins with endothelial dysfunction, leading to an inflammatory response, white blood cell accumulation, plaque (atheroma) formation, and raised blood pressure. The blood clotting process involves thromboplastin release, converting prothrombin into thrombin, which then converts soluble fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin threads, creating a mesh that traps blood cells and can trigger CVD. Risk factors for CVD include genetics, diet, age, gender, high blood pressure, smoking, and physical inactivity. Dietary antioxidants reduce CVD risk. Core Practical 2 investigates vitamin C content in food and drink. Illness and mortality data analysis requires distinguishing between correlation and causation, recognising conflicting evidence, and evaluating study designs for sample selection and sample size validity and reliability. People often misperceive health risks, underestimating or overestimating lifestyle risks like diet. Blood cholesterol levels, high-density lipoproteins (HDLs), and low-density lipoproteins (LDLs) provide causal evidence linking high LDL and total cholesterol to CVD. Public health measures utilise body mass index (BMI) and waist-to-hip ratio as obesity indicators alongside diet, exercise, and smoking cessation to reduce coronary heart disease risk. CVD medical treatments carry both benefits and risks, including antihypertensives, statins, anticoagulants, and platelet inhibitors.

Worked example

Calculate the rate of diffusion using Fick's Law if the surface area is 200 mm squared, the concentration difference is 50 arbitrary units, and the membrane thickness is 0.05 mm. Step 1: Multiply surface area by concentration difference (200 × 50 = 10000). Step 2: Divide by thickness (10000 ÷ 0.05 = 200000). Answer: 200000 arbitrary units per second.

Key points to remember

Students often confuse condensation with hydrolysis; remember condensation releases water and forms bonds (glycosidic, ester, peptide), whilst hydrolysis breaks bonds using water. When discussing Fick's Law, always state that rate is directly proportional to surface area and concentration gradient, and inversely proportional to thickness.

In data analysis questions regarding health risks, never state correlation proves causation unless a clear mechanism is explained and confounding variables are controlled. Ensure you can differentiate between the protective role of HDLs carrying cholesterol to the liver and the harmful accumulation of LDLs forming plaques.

How to use this: read the full notes for any weak areas and complete the topic quiz.

title: Nuclear Physics — Study Notes
content:
Nuclear Physics

The Nucleus

Protons + neutrons (nucleons). Nuclide notation: ᴬZX — Z protons, A nucleons. Isotopes share Z, differ in N.

Nuclear densities are enormous (~10¹⁷ kg m⁻³) — nearly all mass in a tiny volume.

Radioactive Decay

Random and spontaneous:

TypeWhat changesStopped by
alphaZ − 2, A − 4paper
beta-minusZ + 1, A samemm of aluminium
gammanothingthick lead

Half-life: time for half the nuclei to decay. N = N₀ e^(−λt), λ = ln 2 / t½.

Example: a sample with t½ = 10 days: after 30 days, 1/8 of the original activity remains.

Mass–Energy

E = mc². Mass difference Δm in nuclear reactions becomes energy; binding energy = energy released assembling the nucleus. 1 u ≈ 931 MeV.

Fission and Fusion

Both release energy by moving toward iron (peak binding energy per nucleon): heavy nuclei split (fission, reactors), light nuclei merge (fusion, stars).

Exam tips: balance Z and A on both sides of every equation; activity questions use A = λN, not guesswork with halves.

title: Probability Distributions — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Probability Distributions

Mathematics — A2. A discrete random variable X takes values xᵢ with probabilities pᵢ where each pᵢ ≥ 0 and Σpᵢ = 1. A probability distribution can be given as a table, a formula, or a function. Any missing probability is found by subtraction.

Key areas to revise

  • Probability Distributions
  • Expectation
  • Variance
  • Linear Transforms
  • Independent Variables

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Key points to remember

For a discrete random variable X, the probabilities in the distribution table must add to 1. The expected value is E(X) = Σx P(X = x), and the variance is Var(X) = E(X²) − [E(X)]². Calculate E(X²) by squaring each value of x before you multiply by its probability.

For a linear transformation, E(aX + b) = aE(X) + b and Var(aX + b) = a² Var(X). The constant b shifts the mean but does not change the variance. Check your answer for the variance is never negative, which catches a sign error in the formula.

title: AS Level Mathematics: Proof
content:
AS Level Mathematics: Proof

Proof is the difference between "it works for these numbers" and "it must work for all". AS proof covers four methods — direct proof, proof by exhaustion, proof by counter-example (disproof) and proof by deduction from definitions — plus the algebra of odd, even and consecutive numbers, and completing the square as a tool for inequalities. This note builds each method from zero with templates, full worked examples and the precise wording examiners expect, because proof marks are awarded for structure as much as for algebra.

The language of proof

TermMeaning
ConjectureA statement believed true but not yet proved
TheoremA statement that has been proved
ProofA logical argument from known facts to the conclusion
DisproofOne counter-example that makes the statement false
ExhaustionChecking every possible case

A single counter-example disproves a "for all" statement; no number of examples proves one. That asymmetry is the heart of the topic and the first thing examiners test.

Odd, even and consecutive numbers

even: 2n           (n integer)
odd:  2n + 1       (or 2n - 1)
consecutive integers: n, n + 1, n + 2
consecutive even: 2n, 2n + 2
consecutive odd: 2n + 1, 2n + 3

These forms are not optional decoration: a proof about parity must start from them, because "let the number be x" proves nothing about oddness.

Worked example 1. Prove that the sum of two consecutive odd numbers is a multiple of 4.

let the numbers be 2n + 1 and 2n + 3
sum = 4n + 4 = 4(n + 1)
which is a multiple of 4 for every integer n

Worked example 2. Prove that the product of two odd numbers is odd.

let them be 2m + 1 and 2n + 1
product = 4mn + 2m + 2n + 1 = 2(2mn + m + n) + 1
of the form 2k + 1 with k = 2mn + m + n, an integer
so the product is odd

Worked example 3. Prove that the difference between the squares of consecutive integers is the sum of the integers.

(n + 1)^2 - n^2 = n^2 + 2n + 1 - n^2 = 2n + 1 = n + (n + 1)

Direct proof

Start from the definitions, manipulate algebraically, and arrive at the required form. Write the conclusion explicitly ("hence ... as required") so the argument is closed.

Worked example. Prove that if x is odd then x² is odd.

let x = 2n + 1
x^2 = 4n^2 + 4n + 1 = 2(2n^2 + 2n) + 1
which is 2k + 1, hence odd

Worked example 2. Prove that the sum of any three consecutive integers is divisible by 3.

n + (n + 1) + (n + 2) = 3n + 3 = 3(n + 1)
which is divisible by 3

Proof by exhaustion

When the domain is small enough to list, check every case. The proof is only complete if the list is genuinely exhaustive — state why nothing is missed.

Worked example. Prove that every prime between 20 and 30 is the sum of two square numbers or state otherwise.

primes in the range: 23, 29
23 = 9 + 14 (not two squares); 25 + (-2)? no
23 = 4 + 19? no; squares below 23: 1, 4, 9, 16
1 + 16 = 17; 4 + 16 = 20; 9 + 16 = 25; 4 + 9 = 13
so 23 is not a sum of two squares; 29: 4 + 25 = 29  yes
conclusion: the conjecture fails for 23; the true statement is
"29 is the only prime between 20 and 30 expressible as a sum of two squares"

Worked example 2. Prove that n² + n is even for all integers n by exhaustion of the two parity cases.

case 1: n even, n = 2k -> n^2 + n = 4k^2 + 2k = 2(2k^2 + k), even
case 2: n odd, n = 2k + 1 -> 4k^2 + 4k + 1 + 2k + 1 = 4k^2 + 6k + 2
        = 2(2k^2 + 3k + 1), even
both cases covered, so the statement holds for all integers

The two-case parity split is exhaustion in its most common exam form: every integer is even or odd, so the cases exhaust the domain.

Disproof by counter-example

To disprove a "for all" claim, produce one case where it fails and show the arithmetic. One is enough; a hundred confirming cases prove nothing.

Worked example. Disprove: "if n² is a multiple of 4 then n is a multiple of 4."

try n = 6: n^2 = 36, a multiple of 4? 36/4 = 9, yes
but 6 is not a multiple of 4
so n = 6 is a counter-example and the statement is false

Worked example 2. Disprove: "n² − n + 11 is prime for all positive integers n."

n = 11: 121 - 11 + 11 = 121 = 11^2, not prime
counter-example n = 11 disproves the conjecture

Proof by completing the square

Inequalities about quadratics are proved by completing the square: a squared term is never negative, so the expression's minimum (or maximum) is visible.

x^2 + bx + c = (x + b/2)^2 + c - b^2/4
since (x + b/2)^2 >= 0, the minimum value is c - b^2/4

Worked example 1. Prove that x² + 4x + 7 > 0 for all real x.

x^2 + 4x + 7 = (x + 2)^2 + 3
(x + 2)^2 >= 0, so the expression is at least 3 > 0

Worked example 2. Prove that 2x − x² ≤ 1 for all real x.

2x - x^2 = -(x^2 - 2x) = -[(x - 1)^2 - 1] = 1 - (x - 1)^2
since (x - 1)^2 >= 0, this is at most 1

Worked example 3. Find the values of k for which x² + kx + 9 > 0 for all x.

completing the square: (x + k/2)^2 + 9 - k^2/4 > 0 for all x
requires the constant term positive: 9 - k^2/4 > 0
k^2 < 36  ->  -6 < k < 6

That last question is the discriminant argument in disguise: "always positive" means no real roots, so b² − 4ac < 0. Either method earns the marks; the completing-the-square route often reads more clearly.

Divisibility and multiples

A statement of the form "is a multiple of k" is proved by putting the expression in the shape k times an integer. Do the algebra first, then identify the factor; never assume the factor exists.

Worked example. Prove that for any integer n, n(n + 1)(n + 2) is a multiple of 6.

among any three consecutive integers there is at least one even
number and exactly one multiple of 3
so the product contains a factor 2 and a factor 3
since 2 and 3 are coprime, the product is divisible by 6

Worked example 2. Prove that 3^(2n) - 1 is a multiple of 8 for positive integers n.

3^(2n) - 1 = 9^n - 1 = (9 - 1)(9^(n-1) + ... + 1)
= 8 x (a positive integer), so divisible by 8

Worked example 3. Prove that the sum of five consecutive integers is always divisible by 5.

n + (n+1) + (n+2) + (n+3) + (n+4) = 5n + 10 = 5(n + 2)

Proof by contradiction: the irrationality of root 2

Contradiction assumes the statement is false, derives an impossibility, and concludes the statement is true. The classic example is examinable and worth knowing in full.

assume sqrt(2) is rational: sqrt(2) = p/q in lowest terms, p, q integers
square: 2 = p^2/q^2  ->  p^2 = 2q^2
so p^2 is even  ->  p is even (a square is even only if its root is)
write p = 2k: 4k^2 = 2q^2  ->  q^2 = 2k^2
so q^2 is even  ->  q is even
but p and q cannot both be even if p/q is in lowest terms
contradiction  ->  sqrt(2) is irrational

The two logical hinges are that an even square implies an even root, and that "lowest terms" forbids a common factor of 2. State both; the marks live in them.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Parity) Prove that the sum of an odd and an even number is odd. Answer: (2m + 1) + 2n = 2(m + n) + 1, which is odd.
  2. (Consecutive) Prove that the product of two consecutive integers is even. Answer: n(n + 1): one of n, n + 1 is even, so the product is even.
  3. (Direct) Prove that (3n + 1)² − 1 is a multiple of 3. Answer: 9n² + 6n = 3(3n² + 2n).
  4. (Counter-example) Disprove "all primes are odd". Answer: 2 is prime and even.
  5. (Counter-example) Disprove "n² + 1 is prime for all n". Answer: n = 3 gives 10, not prime.
  6. (Completing the square) Prove x² − 6x + 10 > 0. Answer: (x − 3)² + 1 ≥ 1 > 0.
  7. (Exhaustion) Prove that n³ − n is divisible by 6 for n = 1, 2, 3, 4. Answer: 0, 6, 24, 60 — each divisible by 6 (a finite check is exhaustion).
  8. (Discriminant) Find k so that x² + 2kx + 4 = 0 has no real roots. Answer: 4k² − 16 < 0 → k² < 4 → −2 < k < 2.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Proving by example: two or three numbers never prove a "for all" statement; the argument must use algebra with a general n.
  • Not defining the variable: "let n be an integer" and "let n be odd, so n = 2k + 1" are required openings; an undefined x cannot carry a parity argument.
  • Assuming what you must prove: working backwards from the result to a true statement does not prove the original unless every step is reversible — say so if it is.
  • Counter-example not checked: show the arithmetic that makes the case fail; asserting "n = 6 fails" without the calculation loses the mark.
  • Incomplete exhaustion: if the domain has cases you did not cover (e.g. negatives, zero), the proof is incomplete — state the cases and why they exhaust.
  • Completing the square sign: a negative leading coefficient flips the inequality; factor out the minus first.
  • Conclusion missing: close with "hence ... as required"; an unclosed argument reads as unfinished.
  • Notation: write ≡ for identities and ⇒ for implications correctly; mixing them muddles the logic examiners follow.

title: Exam technique: Sine and Cosine Rules
content:
### What earns the marks
For the sine rule, the matched pairs written (b / sin 65 = 7 / sin 40) earn the method mark. For the cosine rule, the full substitution with cos evaluated earns the mark: write a squared = 25 + 64 - 2 x 5 x 8 x 0.5. For the largest angle, identifying the longest side first earns credit. For area, half a b sin C quoted earns the mark on its own.
### Traps
Error: sides paired with wrong angles in the sine rule. Correction: each side faces its angle. Error: 49 given as side a. Correction: root the cosine-rule result. Error: calculator-only acute angle for an obtuse ambiguous case. Correction: subtract from 180 by hand. Error: half a b without sine for a non-right triangle. Correction: area needs the sine factor unless the angle is 90 degrees.
### Worked example
Two sides are 7 cm and 9 cm, with an included angle of 40 degrees. The cosine rule gives x^2 = 7^2 + 9^2 - 2 x 7 x 9 x cos 40 = 130 - 126 x 0.766 = 33.5, so x is about 5.79 cm. Use the cosine rule when you have two sides and the angle between them.
### Check yourself
A right-angled triangle has legs 6 and 8. Compute the area as one half of 6 x 8 x sin 90 degrees, and the hypotenuse with the cosine rule. The area is 24, and the hypotenuse is sqrt(36 + 64) = 10, because cos 90 degrees is zero.

title:
Membranes, Proteins, DNA and Gene Expression — Quick Revision Summary

Biology — AS Edexcel IAL, WBI12 Unit 1 Topic 2. Membrane structure and the fluid mosaic model, Core Practical 3 on membrane permeability, osmosis and water potential and the different kinds of transport, protein structure from amino acid to tertiary and quaternary, DNA structure and the evidence for semi-conservative replication from Meselson and Stahl, the genetic code and how genes work, transcription and translation and alternative splicing, mutation types and their effects, patterns of inheritance including sex linkage, cystic fibrosis as a gene-mutation disorder, and genetic screening and its ethical and social issues.

  • 2.2 Membrane structure (fluid mosaic model): a phospholipid bilayer with hydrophilic heads out and hydrophobic tails in, proteins (channel, carrier, receptor, recognition) embedded or attached, cholesterol moderating fluidity in animal cells; the membrane is fluid and mosaic, an interpretation of the evidence.
  • 2.3 Core Practical 3: beetroot cylinders in water at different temperatures or in different alcohol concentrations; colourimeter measures the pigment leaked as membranes are damaged — permeability rises with temperature and alcohol as proteins denature and the bilayer is disrupted.
  • 2.4 Osmosis and water potential: osmosis is the net movement of free water through a partially permeable membrane down a water potential gradient; solute lowers water potential; pure water has the highest (zero) water potential; animal cells swell and may haemolyse or crenate; plant cells become turgid (supported) or plasmolysed.
  • 2.5 Passive and active transport: diffusion of small non-polar molecules through the bilayer; facilitated diffusion of ions and large polar molecules through channel and carrier proteins down their gradient; active transport against the gradient using ATP; endocytosis and exocytosis for bulk materials in vesicles.
  • 2.9 Mononucleotides and DNA/RNA structure: a mononucleotide is deoxyribose (or ribose) + phosphate + base (A, C, G, T in DNA; A, C, G, U in RNA); nucleotides join by phosphodiester bonds; two complementary strands hydrogen-bond A–T (two bonds) and C–G (three bonds) in an antiparallel double helix.
  • 2.10 DNA replication (semi-conservative): double helix unzips, each strand is a template, DNA polymerase joins free nucleotides; Meselson and Stahl's 15N/14N experiment gave a single hybrid band in generation 1 and hybrid + light bands later — exactly what semi-conservative replication predicts and ruling out the conservative and dispersive alternatives.
  • 2.11 Genetic code: triplet, non-overlapping and degenerate — three bases code for one amino acid and several codons can code for the same amino acid; a stop codon signals the end.
  • 2.12 Gene: a sequence of bases on DNA that codes for a sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide.
  • 2.13 Protein synthesis: transcription by RNA polymerase makes mRNA from the template (antisense) strand; mRNA goes to ribosomes; tRNA brings amino acids with anticodons that pair with mRNA codons, building the polypeptide in the order of the codons until a stop codon.
  • 2.14 Mutations: substitution may change one amino acid or none; insertion/deletion (not in threes) causes a frameshift, changing all later amino acids and usually destroying function; some mutations cause cancer or genetic disorders, many do nothing.
  • 2.15 Inheritance: gene, allele, genotype, phenotype, dominant, recessive, codominance, homozygote, heterozygote; monohybrid crosses with ratios; sex linkage on the X chromosome (red-green colour blindness, haemophilia — more common in males); pedigree diagram interpretation.
  • 2.16 Cystic fibrosis: a mutation in a chloride-channel gene (often a three-base deletion removing one amino acid) — chloride and water transport fails, mucus is thick; affects gaseous exchange (blocked airways, infections), digestion (blocked pancreatic duct, poor digestion, malnutrition) and reproduction (absent or blocked vas deferens, male infertility).
  • 2.17 Genetic screening: identifies carriers; prenatal testing (amniocentesis at 15–17 wks, CVS at 8–12 wks); PGD used with IVF to test embryos before implantation — testing for genetic disorders before pregnancy.
  • 2.18 Ethical and social issues: safety and reliability of the test, miscarriage risk with invasive tests, right to know or not to know, what counts as a disorder, choice to terminate, anxiety, access and cost, and the risk of moving from preventing disease to selecting non-medical traits.

Worked example

Monohybrid cross between two heterozygotes (Aa × Aa): Punnett gives AA (¼), Aa (½), aa (¼); phenotype ratio 3 : 1 if A is completely dominant; genotype ratio 1 : 2 : 1. Sex linkage: a carrier female (XᴮXᵇ) and a normal male (XᴮY): sons ½ colour-blind (XᵇY) and ½ normal (XᴮY); daughters ½ carriers (XᴮXᵇ) and ½ normal (XᴮXᴮ), none colour-blind (unless the father is colour-blind). Heterozygosity index: in a population of 20 individuals at one locus, 8 are heterozygotes → H = 8/20 = 0.40.

Key points to remember

Membranes: temperature and alcohol disrupt proteins and the bilayer — permeability rises. Osmosis: water moves from high to low water potential; the direction and whether a cell bursts, crenates, becomes turgid or plasmolysed depends on the water potential of the solution compared with the cell. Transport: diffusion and facilitated diffusion are passive; active transport uses ATP and goes against the gradient; endocytosis and exocytosis use vesicles and ATP. Protein structure: peptide bond from condensation; primary = sequence; secondary = alpha-helix and beta-sheet (hydrogen bonds); tertiary = overall 3D folding with hydrogen, ionic, disulfide and hydrophobic bonds; quaternary = several polypeptides together (haemoglobin). DNA: antiparallel, A–T (2 H-bonds), C–G (3 H-bonds); semi-conservative replication shown by Meselson and Stahl. Protein synthesis: transcription → mRNA; translation on ribosomes with tRNA anticodons; alternative splicing means one gene can make more than one protein. Mutation types: substitution, insertion, deletion (frameshift). Cystic fibrosis: faulty chloride channel → thick mucus → lung, digestion, reproduction problems. Screening: carriers, PGD, amniocentesis, CVS; weigh benefits against ethical and social issues.

How to use this

Read the summary list, then open the full revision notes for any point that feels weak, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself. Revise next by: drawing a cell membrane and labelling the bilayer, proteins and cholesterol; carrying out the beetroot permeability practical and explaining the trend and control variables; drawing DNA, showing base pairing and antiparallel strands, and explaining semi-conservative replication and the Meselson and Stahl evidence; drawing protein synthesis (transcription and translation) with mRNA, tRNA and the ribosome; and working through a monohybrid cross, a sex-linked cross and a pedigree to explain each ratio.

title: Exam technique: Programming Concepts
content:
### What earns the marks
For loops, the counted loop for known repeats versus conditional for unknown earns the choice mark. For procedures versus functions, parameters in plus value returned out earns each mark. For arrays, the index range declared earns the method mark.
### Traps
Error: WHILE used for fixed repeats. Correction: FOR loops count known iterations. Error: function with no return described. Correction: functions return a value; procedures do not. Error: array indices started at 0 in pseudocode. Correction: pseudocode arrays usually start at 1.

title: IGCSE Mathematics: Sequences and Functions
content:
IGCSE Mathematics: Sequences and Functions

Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580 (2025–2027), section 2 Algebra and graphs: statement 2.7 Sequences and statement 2.13 Functions (Extended). A sequence is a list of numbers generated by a rule; a function is the rule itself. This note builds nth-term rules from scratch — showing why the formula works, not just what it is — then function notation, composite functions and inverse functions, including the domain restrictions that decide whether an inverse exists.

What a sequence is; term-to-term rules

A sequence is an ordered list of numbers. The term-to-term rule gets from one term to the next: add 4, multiply by 2, subtract 1 then double. It tells you what happens step by step but not what the hundredth term is. The position-to-term rule (the nth term) gives any term directly from its position n, and that is the more powerful description.

Sequence: 3, 7, 11, 15, 19, ...

Term-to-term: add 4 each time.
Position-to-term: the terms are 4 less than 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, ..., so the nth term is 4n - 1.

Check: n = 1 gives 4(1) - 1 = 3 ✓;  n = 5 gives 4(5) - 1 = 19 ✓

Linear sequences and the nth term

A linear (arithmetic) sequence has a constant difference d between terms. Its nth term is dn + b, and b is chosen to make the first term correct.

Find the nth term of 5, 8, 11, 14, ...

Constant difference d = 3, so the nth term starts as 3n.
Compare with the sequence: 3, 6, 9, 12, ... is three times the table of 3;
the real sequence is 2 more each time, so b = 2.
nth term:  3n + 2

Check every term: n = 1: 5 ✓   n = 2: 8 ✓   n = 3: 11 ✓
The 50th term is 3(50) + 2 = 152.

Why dn + b always works. Adding d each time from a starting value a means the nth term is a + (n − 1)d, since term n has had (n − 1) additions of d. Expanding gives a + nd − d = nd + (a − d), which is exactly dn + b with b = a − d. Both forms are the same rule; examiners accept either.

Quadratic and special sequences

When the first difference changes but the second difference is constant, the rule is quadratic: an² + bn + c. The method: build the n² sequence, subtract it from the sequence, and finish the linear remainder.

Find the nth term of 2, 5, 10, 17, 26, ...

First differences: 3, 5, 7, 9;  second differences: 2, 2 (constant) -> quadratic.
The n^2 sequence is 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, ...
Subtract: (2-1), (5-4), (10-9), (17-16), (26-25) = 1, 1, 1, 1, 1
So the sequence is n^2 + 1.

Check: n = 3 gives 9 + 1 = 10 ✓

Other sequences to recognise on sight: the triangular numbers n(n + 1)/2 (1, 3, 6, 10, ...), the square numbers n², the Fibonacci sequence (each term is the sum of the two before it, and it has no simple nth term), and geometric sequences that multiply by a fixed ratio r — their nth term is arⁿ⁻¹ where a is the first term.

Geometric example: 3, 6, 12, 24, ... has a = 3 and r = 2, so the nth term is 3 x 2^(n-1).
The 6th term is 3 x 2^5 = 96.
Sequence typeExampleRule
Linear (arithmetic)5, 8, 11, 14Constant difference d; nth term dn + b
Quadratic2, 5, 10, 17Constant second difference; nth term an² + bn + c
Geometric3, 6, 12, 24Constant ratio r; nth term arⁿ⁻¹
Triangular numbers1, 3, 6, 10n(n + 1)/2
Square numbers1, 4, 9, 16n²
Fibonacci1, 1, 2, 3, 5Add the two previous terms (no simple nth term)

Choosing the right description is half the battle: check the first differences, then the second, then the ratio, before assuming any rule. Once a candidate rule is found, verify it against every given term — a sequence that matches only the first three terms is not proven.

Function notation

A function is a machine with an input and exactly one output for each input. The notation f(x) = 2x + 3 names the machine f and says what it does to x: multiply by 2, then add 3. Evaluating is substitution: f(4) = 2(4) + 3 = 11. The machine picture matters: one input never gives two outputs, though two inputs may share an output.

  • The domain is the set of allowed inputs; the range is the set of outputs the function actually produces.
  • For f(x) = x² with domain all real numbers, the range is y ⩾ 0, because squares are never negative.
  • For f(x) = 2x + 3 with domain 0 ⩽ x ⩽ 5, the range is 3 ⩽ f(x) ⩽ 13 — substitute the endpoints, since linear functions stretch ranges proportionally.

Questions ask for the range in terms of y or f(x); find the outputs at the domain boundaries and, for quadratics, at the turning point.

Composite functions

A composite function runs one machine after the other. fg(x) means apply g first, then f to the result — the notation reads right to left, like f(g(x)).

Given f(x) = 2x + 1 and g(x) = x^2, find fg(3), gf(x) and fg(x).

fg(3):  g(3) = 9, then f(9) = 2(9) + 1 = 19.
gf(x):  apply f first:  g(f(x)) = (2x + 1)^2 = 4x^2 + 4x + 1.
fg(x):  apply g first:  f(g(x)) = 2x^2 + 1.

Note fg(x) ≠ gf(x): order matters.

Every line is written out because the most common error is applying the functions in the wrong order — and the composite is not commutative.

Inverse functions

The inverse f⁻¹ undoes f: if f turns 4 into 11, f⁻¹ turns 11 back into 4. Inverse functions exist only for one-to-one functions — ones where different inputs always give different outputs. The graph of y = x² is not one-to-one over all real numbers (both 3 and −3 give 9), so it has no inverse unless the domain is restricted to x ⩾ 0.

Find the inverse of f(x) = (3x - 2)/5:

Write y = (3x - 2)/5 and make x the subject:
5y = 3x - 2          [multiply by 5]
5y + 2 = 3x          [add 2]
x = (5y + 2)/3       [divide by 3]

Swap x and y:  f^-1(x) = (5x + 2)/3

Check by composing: f^-1(f(x)) = [5((3x - 2)/5) + 2]/3 = [(3x - 2) + 2]/3 = 3x/3 = x  ✓
  • f⁻¹(x) is a single symbol meaning the inverse function; the −1 is not a power and f⁻¹(x) does not mean 1/f(x).
  • The domain of f⁻¹ is the range of f, and the range of f⁻¹ is the domain of f — they swap, exactly as the inputs and outputs swap roles.
  • Graphically, y = f⁻¹(x) is the reflection of y = f(x) in the line y = x.

Worked example: a full function question

Let f(x) = x² + 3 for x ⩾ 0, and g(x) = 4x − 5.

(a) Find f(2):  f(2) = 4 + 3 = 7.

(b) Find fg(x):  f(g(x)) = (4x - 5)^2 + 3 = 16x^2 - 40x + 25 + 3 = 16x^2 - 40x + 28.

(c) Find f^-1(x):  y = x^2 + 3, so x^2 = y - 3 and x = √(y - 3) (positive root, since x ⩾ 0).
Swap: f^-1(x) = √(x - 3).
Domain of f^-1: x ⩾ 3, which is exactly the range of f.

(d) Solve f(x) = 30 for x ⩾ 0:
x^2 + 3 = 30
x^2 = 27
x = √27 = 3√3 ≈ 5.20        [only the positive root is in the domain]

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Reading fg(x) as f then g. It is g first, then f — the notation runs right to left.
  • Assuming fg = gf; only special cases agree.
  • Treating f⁻¹(x) as 1/f(x). The inverse undoes the function; it is not a reciprocal.
  • Ignoring domain restrictions: with x ⩾ 0 on f(x) = x² + 3, the inverse takes the positive root only, and a negative root answer is wrong.
  • Claiming y = x² has an inverse over all real numbers; it is two-to-one and needs a restricted domain.
  • Building the nth term from the first difference alone without checking every term; a single wrong check sends a whole answer wrong.
  • Writing a geometric nth term as arⁿ instead of arⁿ⁻¹; the first term must be a itself.
  • Stating a range that ignores the turning point of a quadratic: the range of y = (x − 2)² + 1 is y ⩾ 1, not y ⩾ 0.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 2, 3 marks). Find the nth term of 7, 11, 15, 19, ...

Answer: Constant difference 4, so 4n + b; the first term 7 = 4 + b gives b = 3. The nth term is 4n + 3. The 20th term is 83.

Question 2 (Paper 2, 3 marks). A sequence has nth term 5n − 2. Write down the first four terms and the 100th.

Answer: n = 1, 2, 3, 4 give 3, 8, 13, 18; the 100th term is 5(100) − 2 = 498.

Question 3 (Paper 4, 4 marks). f(x) = 3x − 1 and g(x) = x² + 2. Find fg(x), gf(2) and f⁻¹(x).

Answer: fg(x) = 3(x² + 2) − 1 = 3x² + 5. gf(2): f(2) = 5, so g(5) = 27. Inverse: y = 3x − 1 gives x = (y + 1)/3, so f⁻¹(x) = (x + 1)/3.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 4 marks). The second differences of a sequence are constant at 4, and its first two terms are 2 and 7. Find the nth term.

Answer: Constant second difference 4 means the n² coefficient is 4/2 = 2, so the rule starts 2n². The n² sequence gives 2, 8, ... while the sequence is 2, 7, ..., so the remainder is 0, −1, ... a linear part with difference −1: −n + 1. Check: 2n² − n + 1 gives n = 1: 2 ✓ and n = 2: 8 − 2 + 1 = 7 ✓. The nth term is 2n² − n + 1.

Question 5 (Paper 4, 5 marks). f(x) = (x + 4)/(x − 2) for x ≠ 2. Find f⁻¹(x) and the value of x for which f(x) is undefined.

Answer: y = (x + 4)/(x − 2) gives y(x − 2) = x + 4, so yx − 2y = x + 4, yx − x = 2y + 4, x(y − 1) = 2y + 4 and x = (2y + 4)/(y − 1). Swapping: f⁻¹(x) = (2x + 4)/(x − 1). The function itself is undefined at x = 2, where the denominator vanishes; its inverse is undefined at x = 1.

Question 6 (Paper 2, 3 marks). The first three terms of a geometric sequence are 5, 15, 45. Find the 8th term.

Answer: Common ratio r = 15/5 = 3, so the nth term is 5 × 3ⁿ⁻¹ and the 8th term is 5 × 3⁷ = 5 × 2187 = 10 935.

From variables and patterns, the course now turns to the number system itself.

title: IGCSE Biology: Coordination and Response
content:
IGCSE Biology: Coordination and Response

Your body must detect change and react — fast when you touch something hot, slowly when a hormone regulates your blood sugar, and directionally when a plant bends towards the light. Coordination is that detection-and-response problem, solved by two systems (nervous and hormonal) and, in plants, by growth responses. This note builds the reflex arc synapse by synapse, traces an action potential down a neurone, works through the eye's adaptation, writes out the hormone loops for blood glucose and the menstrual cycle, defines homeostasis with its feedback logic, and shows how tropisms orient plants — with every mechanism stated in the order markschemes reward.

The two coordination systems compared

FeatureNervous systemHormonal (endocrine) system
SignalElectrical impulses along neuronesChemical messengers (hormones) in the blood
SpeedVery fast (milliseconds)Slow (seconds to hours)
TargetSpecific muscles or glands (precise)Widespread — any cell with receptors
DurationShort, brief effectLong-lasting effect
ExampleHand pulled from a flameAdrenaline in stress, insulin after a meal

Receptors detect stimuli (light, pressure, chemicals, temperature); effectors (muscles and glands) carry out the response; the nervous system coordinates via electrical impulses, the endocrine system via hormones secreted by glands into the blood. Both are coordinated by the brain and (for internal conditions) the hypothalamus.

The reflex arc, step by step

A reflex is a rapid, automatic, protective response that does not involve the conscious brain — and it is examined as a labelled sequence. Step 1: a stimulus (heat) is detected by receptors in the skin. Step 2: a sensory neurone carries impulses from the receptor to the central nervous system (spinal cord). Step 3: in the spinal cord, a relay neurone (intermediate neurone) links sensory to motor neurone; synapses connect the neurones. Step 4: a motor neurone carries impulses from the CNS to the effector. Step 5: the effector (a muscle) contracts and the hand is pulled away. Trace the arc: receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone → motor neurone → effector. This is faster than a conscious reaction because it is a short, hard-wired route with fewer synapses (each synapse adds a delay).

Synaptic transmission

A synapse is the junction between two neurones. When an impulse arrives, vesicles of a neurotransmitter (such as acetylcholine) fuse with the presynaptic membrane and release the chemical into the synaptic cleft; it diffuses across (a few tens of nanometres, so it is fast) and binds receptors on the postsynaptic membrane, triggering a new impulse in the next neurone; enzymes then break the transmitter down so the signal stops. Synapses ensure one-way transmission (vesicles only on the presynaptic side) and allow summation and filtering. Most drugs and poisons act here: acetylcholinesterase inhibitors prolong the signal; curare blocks receptors; nicotine mimics acetylcholine.

The neurone and the response speed

Three neurone types: sensory (from receptor to CNS, with a cell body in the middle), relay (short, inside the CNS), motor (from CNS to effector). Myelinated neurones have a fatty myelin sheath that insulates the axon so impulses jump between the nodes of Ranvier (saltatory conduction) — much faster than unmyelinated fibres. Reflex speed is maximised by: myelination, few synapses, and direct hard-wired arcs. In Paper 4, when asked why reflexes are fast, name these factors explicitly rather than saying "because they are reflexes".

Sense organs and the eye

Sense organs are groups of receptors: eye (light), ear (sound and balance), skin (touch, pressure, temperature, pain), tongue (taste), nose (smell). The eye: light enters through the cornea (refracts it), the pupil (amount controlled by the iris), the lens (fine focus by the ciliary muscles changing its shape — accommodation), and is focused onto the retina, which is packed with photoreceptors. Rod cells: sensitive to dim light, detect black-and-white, more numerous at the edges of the retina; cone cells: detect colour (three types, red-green-blue) and function best in bright light, concentrated in the fovea. Focusing: for distant objects the ciliary muscles relax, suspensory ligaments tighten, and the lens becomes thin; for near objects the ciliary muscles contract, suspensory ligaments slacken, and the lens becomes thicker and more rounded (elastic lens returns the shape). The pupil reflex (iris reflex) protects the retina: in bright light circular muscles contract (pupil constricts) to reduce entry; in dim light radial muscles contract (pupil dilates) to admit more light. Photoreceptors trigger impulses in the optic nerve to the brain's visual centre. Two reflexes examiners ask about in the eye: the pupil reflex (brain-mediated, protective) and accommodation (lens shape).

Hormones and homeostasis

Homeostasis is the maintenance of a constant internal environment within restricted limits (temperature, blood glucose, water potential), so enzymes and cells function normally. It works by negative feedback: any deviation from the set point triggers a response that reverses the deviation. Blood glucose control: after a carbohydrate-rich meal, blood glucose rises; the pancreas detects this and secretes insulin; insulin causes liver and muscle cells to take up glucose and convert it to glycogen (glycogenesis); glucose falls back to normal. When glucose drops (between meals or during exercise), the pancreas secretes glucagon; it causes the liver to convert glycogen back to glucose (glycogenolysis) and to make glucose from non-carbohydrate sources (gluconeogenesis); glucose rises back to normal. Adrenaline (from the adrenal glands, in stress) also raises blood glucose by accelerating glycogen breakdown. The negative loop structure to write: change detected → receptor (pancreas) → hormone released → effector action (liver) → change reversed → hormone secretion stops. Diabetes mellitus: type 1 (insulin-dependent, autoimmune destruction of pancreas cells in youth) treated with insulin injections; type 2 (non-insensitive, linked to obesity and diet in later life) controlled by diet, exercise and sometimes medication.

Temperature control, water balance and the menstrual cycle

Temperature: maintained near 37 °C because enzymes denature above ~40 °C and work slowly when cold. In cold: arterioles to the skin constrict (vasoconstriction), reducing blood flow and heat loss; erector pili muscles contract raising hairs to trap an insulating air layer; shivering generates heat from muscle contraction; metabolism (and appetite) rise. In heat: arterioles dilate (vasodilation), sweating increases (evaporation removes latent heat), hairs lie flat, behaviour changes (seeking shade). The hypothalamus is the temperature receptor and coordinator. Water balance: controlled by the kidney under ADH (antidiuretic hormone) from the pituitary; when the blood is too concentrated (dehydration), the hypothalamus triggers ADH release, the kidney reabsorbs more water, producing small volumes of concentrated urine, and thirst is stimulated; when overhydrated, ADH falls and dilute urine is produced. The menstrual cycle: FSH (follicle-stimulating hormone) matures a follicle in the ovary and stimulates oestrogen secretion; oestrogen repairs and thickens the uterus lining (endometrium) and, at high levels, triggers a surge of LH (luteinising hormone) causing ovulation around day 14; after ovulation the empty follicle forms the corpus luteum secreting progesterone, which maintains the endometrium; if no fertilisation, progesterone and oestrogen fall, the corpus luteum degenerates, the lining breaks down (menstruation) and FSH rises again to start the next cycle. Hormonal contraception (the pill) works by raising oestrogen/progesterone levels to suppress FSH and therefore ovulation.

Tropic responses in plants

Plants respond by growth (tropisms), directed by plant hormones called auxins. Phototropism: auxin is produced at the tip and diffuses down; in unilateral (one-sided) light, auxin moves to the shaded side of the shoot, making those cells elongate faster than the lit side, so the shoot bends towards the light (positive phototropism) — maximizing light for photosynthesis; roots show negative phototropism. Gravitropism (geotropism): auxin accumulates on the lower side of a horizontal stem; in shoots, high auxin concentration promotes elongation so the shoot grows up (negative gravitropism); in roots, high auxin inhibits elongation so the lower cells grow more slowly and the root grows down (positive gravitropism) — anchoring the plant and reaching water. The response to grow towards or away from a stimulus is adaptive: light for photosynthesis, gravity for anchorage and water. Auxin is also the basis of selective weedkillers (synthetic auxins overstimulate broadleaf weeds) and rooting powder for cuttings. The experiment to know: shoot tips on agar blocks placed centrally vs offset in unilateral light, showing the diffusible chemical (auxin) is responsible.

Worked example: blood glucose negative feedback traced

A student eats a sugary snack: blood glucose rises from 4.5 to 7.0 mmol/dm³ within 30 minutes. Step 1: receptors in the pancreas (beta cells) detect the rise. Step 2: they secrete insulin into the blood. Step 3: insulin binds receptors on liver and muscle cells, increasing glucose uptake and conversion to glycogen (and fat if glycogen stores are full). Step 4: blood glucose falls back towards 4.5 mmol/dm³, so insulin secretion decreases — the negative feedback. Two hours later the student runs a race: glucose falls to 3.5 mmol/dm³. Step 1: pancreatic alpha cells detect the fall. Step 2: glucagon is secreted. Step 3: liver glycogen is broken down to glucose and released into the blood. Step 4: glucose returns to normal, glucagon secretion stops. Examination answer writing: label the changes (rise/fall), name the receptor (pancreas), the hormone, the effector (liver/muscle), the action (glycogenesis or glycogenolysis), and the return to normal — each label is a separate mark.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Calling hormones "nerve impulses" or mixing the two systems: hormones travel in blood (slow, widespread), impulses along neurones (fast, targeted).
  • Writing that insulin "gives energy" — insulin lowers blood glucose by promoting uptake and glycogen storage; glucagon raises it.
  • Reversing iris muscles: in bright light the circular muscles contract (pupil gets smaller); in dim light the radial muscles contract (pupil gets larger).
  • Confusing rods and cones: rods — dim light, no colour; cones — bright light, colour.
  • Describing auxin as making cells "grow faster" without specifying the effect differs: in shoots auxin promotes elongation, in roots high concentration inhibits it.
  • Writing a tropism as "the plant moves towards light": it is differential growth (elongation), not movement.
  • Leaving "negative feedback" out of any homeostasis answer — the phrase itself earns marks.
  • Writing that menstruation is caused by "the egg dying" — it is caused by falling progesterone and oestrogen levels after the corpus luteum degenerates.
  • In reflex questions, forgetting the relay neurone or writing the arc backwards.

Exam-style questions and answers

Q1. Describe the pathway of a reflex arc when you touch a hot object. (5 marks) Answer: heat detected by receptors in the skin (1); sensory neurone carries impulses to the spinal cord (1); relay neurone crosses the synapse (1); motor neurone carries impulses to the effector muscle (1); muscle contracts pulling the hand away (1).

Q2. Explain how insulin and glucagon control blood glucose concentration. (4 marks) Answer: high glucose detected by pancreas which secretes insulin (1); liver and muscle take up glucose and convert it to glycogen (1); low glucose triggers glucagon from the pancreas (1); liver converts glycogen back to glucose and releases it (1).

Q3. Describe the changes in the eye when focusing on a near object. (3 marks) Answer: ciliary muscles contract (1); suspensory ligaments slacken (1); lens becomes thicker and more rounded to refract strongly (1).

Q4. Explain how auxin causes a shoot to bend towards a light source. (3 marks) Answer: auxin moves to the shaded side of the shoot (1); higher auxin concentration makes cells on the shaded side elongate more (1); the shoot therefore bends towards the light (1).

Q5. Compare nervous and hormonal coordination. (4 marks) Answer: nervous is electrical impulses in neurones, hormonal is chemicals in blood (1); nervous is fast, hormonal slow (1); nervous targets specific effectors, hormonal acts widely (1); nervous effect short-lived, hormonal long-lasting (1).

title: Descriptive Writing — Study Notes
content:
Descriptive writing succeeds when the reader can see, hear, smell or feel the scene. It is built from precise detail, controlled sentence rhythm and a clear sense of focus.

Sensory detail

Use all five senses where they fit, not only sight. Specific nouns and verbs do more work than general adjectives.

Precision

  • Replace weak words such as "nice" or "went" with exact ones: "gleaming", "stumbled".
  • Use concrete nouns: "rust-flecked railings" rather than "old fence".
  • Choose one striking image and develop it, rather than listing many.

Show, do not tell

Show a feeling through action and detail rather than naming it. "She was furious" tells the reader. "Her jaw tightened and she slammed the cupboard door" shows it.

Sentence variety

Varying sentence length controls pace. Long sentences can build a scene slowly, and short ones can cut the mood or create a jolt. Vary your openings too, rather than starting every sentence with the subject.

Structure

Organise the piece around a clear focus. Options include:

  • A close-up that moves outward, from a detail to the wider scene.
  • A changing viewpoint, following a person through a place.
  • A fixed point in time that shows change, such as dawn to dusk.

End with an image or a reflection that returns to your focus. Avoid ending on a plain statement of fact.

title: Electricity & Circuits — Study Notes
content:
Electricity & Circuits

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2023–2025): simple circuits, current, p.d., resistance, series/parallel, electrical safety, practical electricity.

1. Circuit symbols & current

Conventional current: + → − (electron flow opposite). I = Q/t. Ammeter in series; voltmeter in parallel.

2. Current, p.d., e.m.f.

  • Current: rate of charge flow; same everywhere in series.
  • p.d.: energy per coulomb across a component; e.m.f.: electrical energy per coulomb given by the source.

3. Resistance

  • R = V/I. Ohmic conductor: V ∝ I at constant temperature.
  • Series: R = R₁ + R₂ + …; same current; p.d. shares in proportion to R.
  • Parallel: 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂; same p.d.; current splits (inverse-R share).
  • Resistance ∝ length, ∝ 1/area (wires).

4. Components

Fixed/variable resistors, LDR (light ↑ R ↓), thermistor (T ↑ R ↓), diode/LED (one-way), relay, filament lamp (R grows as T rises — V–I curve flattens).

5. Power and energy

P = VI = I²R = V²/R; E = VIt. Fuse rating just above normal current; earth wire, double insulation, circuit breakers (trip quickly, resettable).

Example: 230 V, 2 A heater: P = 460 W; correct fuse 3 A or 5 A.

6. Digital electronics basics (syllabus 4.5 context)

Analogue vs digital; logic gates drive outputs from inputs (see CS link); sensors feed comparator-style circuits.

Exam tips: series: current same; parallel: p.d. same — say which before calculating; always compute total resistance first in mixed circuits.

title: Networking & Communication — Study Notes
content:
Networking & Communication

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): transmission modes, serial/parallel, packet switching, protocols, LAN/WAN, hardware, security layers.

1. Transmission basics

  • Serial: one bit at a time — reliable over distance, cheaper cable.
  • Parallel: several bits at once — faster over short runs; skew/crosstalk limit distance.
  • Simplex / half-duplex / full-duplex direction; bandwidth (bits/s) vs bit rate.

2. Packets

Header (sender/receiver addresses, sequence number) + payload + trailer (checksum). Packet switching: routes vary, packets reassembled at destination; checksum failure → re-request. Benefits: robustness, shared lines; delays/reassembly overhead.

3. Protocols

TCP/IP stack layers (application, transport, network, link). HTTP/HTTPS (TLS encryption), FTP (with login + commands), email: SMTP send, POP3/IMAP retrieve. Bluetooth/Wi-Fi for WPAN/WLAN.

4. Network types & hardware

LAN (site) vs WAN (internet). Router (joins networks, IP), switch (MAC frames within LAN), gateway (protocol translation), NIC, WAP. MAC address (burned-in, layer 2) vs IP address (assigned, layer 3).

5. Security in transmission

Encryption scrambles plaintext → ciphertext (key needed); HTTPS = HTTP over TLS; firewall packet filtering by port/IP; authentication (user+pass, 2FA); access levels.

Exam tips: explain why skew limits parallel over distance; compare MAC vs IP in a table; protocol questions want "rules for communication", not acronyms alone.

Packet switching and protocols

In packet switching, a message is divided into packets. Each packet carries a header with its source and destination addresses and a sequence number, so it can travel by any available route. The packets are reassembled in the correct order at the destination. Packet switching makes efficient use of the network, because no dedicated connection is held open for the whole transmission.

A protocol is an agreed set of rules that devices follow to communicate. TCP/IP is the set of protocols used on the internet. TCP splits data into packets and checks that they arrive, while IP handles addressing and routing between networks.

Exam tip: explain a protocol as a set of rules, and give one example of what it governs, such as addressing or error checking.
