title: A Level Physics: Magnetic Fields and Electromagnetism
content:
A Level Physics: Magnetic Fields and Electromagnetism

Magnetism and electricity are one phenomenon seen from two sides: every current makes a magnetic field, and every changing magnetic field makes a current. This note builds the subject from zero: what a magnetic field is and how flux density measures it, the forces on currents and on moving charges with their right-hand rules, the fields produced by wires and solenoids, electromagnetic induction through Faraday's and Lenz's laws, and the alternating-current ideas — rms values, rectification and smoothing — that connect the physics to the mains supply. Every calculation type is worked in full.

The magnetic field and flux density

A magnetic field is a region where a magnetic force acts on moving charges, currents and magnetic materials. Field lines run from north to south outside a magnet and never cross; their density indicates strength. The strength of the field is measured by the magnetic flux density B, in tesla (T): one tesla is one newton per ampere-metre of conductor, or one weber per square metre. Magnetic flux Φ through an area is the field passing through it:

Φ = B A cos(θ)        weber (Wb)

θ = angle between the field and the NORMAL to the area
flux linkage = N Φ        (N turns of a coil)

Force on a current-carrying conductor

F = B I L sin(θ)

B in T, I in A, L = length of conductor in the field (m)
θ = angle between the current and the field

The force is maximum when the current is perpendicular to the field (sin 90° = 1) and zero when parallel. Its direction comes from Fleming's left-hand rule: first finger = field, second finger = current, thumb = force (all mutually perpendicular). The analogy: think of the wire as a sail in a river of field lines — the force is perpendicular to both the flow and the sail.

Worked example. A 0.20 m wire carrying 3.0 A sits perpendicular to a 0.50 T field. Find the force.

F = B I L = 0.50 × 3.0 × 0.20 = 0.30 N

Force on a moving charge

F = B Q v sin(θ)

for a charge moving perpendicular to the field:
F = B Q v, and this force is centripetal:
B Q v = m v²/r  →  r = m v/(B Q)

A charged particle moving perpendicular to a uniform field follows a circular path; the radius grows with momentum and shrinks with field strength and charge. This is the working principle of the mass spectrometer (ions of different mass follow different radii) and the cyclotron.

Worked example. An electron moves at 2.0 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ perpendicular to a 0.10 T field. Find the force and the radius of its path.

F = B e v = 0.10 × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ x 2.0 × 10⁶ = 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁴ N
r = m v/(B e) = (9.11 × 10⁻³¹ x 2.0 × 10⁶)/(0.10 × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹)
  = 1.82 × 10⁻²⁴/1.6 × 10⁻²⁰ = 1.14 × 10⁻⁴ m  (0.11 mm)

Magnetic fields due to currents

  • Straight wire: concentric circular field lines around the wire; the right-hand grip rule (thumb along current, fingers curl with the field) gives direction; strength falls with distance, B = μ₀I/(2πr).
  • Solenoid: a uniform field inside, like a bar magnet, with the field direction set by the right-hand grip rule; adding an iron core concentrates the field (an electromagnet).
  • Parallel wires: currents in the same direction attract, opposite directions repel — a direct consequence of each wire's field acting on the other's current.

Worked example. Find the flux density 0.050 m from a long straight wire carrying 10 A (μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹).

B = μ₀ I/(2 π r) = (4 π x 10⁻⁷ x 10)/(2 π x 0.050)
  = (2 × 10⁻⁶)/0.050 = 4.0 × 10⁻⁵ T

Electromagnetic induction

Faraday's law: the induced e.m.f. is proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux linkage. Lenz's law: the induced current opposes the change producing it (a statement of energy conservation — the induced current's field pushes back).

ε = - N dPhi/dt

moving a rod of length L at speed v perpendicular to B:
ε = B L v

rotating coil (peak e.m.f.): ε₀ = N B A ω

Worked example. A 0.50 m rod moves at 4.0 m s⁻¹ perpendicular to a 0.20 T field. Find the induced e.m.f.

ε = B L v = 0.20 × 0.50 × 4.0 = 0.40 V

Worked example (flux change). A 200-turn coil of area 0.010 m² sits in a 0.50 T field; the field is reversed in 0.10 s. Find the average e.m.f.

initial flux linkage: N B A = 200 × 0.50 × 0.010 = 1.0 Wb-turn
field reversed: change = 2 × 1.0 = 2.0 Wb-turn
ε = change/time = 2.0/0.10 = 20 V

Alternating current: peak and rms values

Mains electricity is sinusoidal: the voltage and current reverse direction periodically. The average of a sine wave is zero, so power calculations use the root-mean-square value, which is the steady d.c. value that would deliver the same power:

V_rms = V_0/√(2) = 0.707 V_0
I_rms = I_0/√(2)

average power: P = V_rms I_rms = I_rms² R = V_rms²/R

Worked example. A 230 V rms mains supply feeds a 2.0 kW heater. Find the peak voltage and the rms current.

V_0 = 230 x √(2) = 325 V
I_rms = P/V_rms = 2000/230 = 8.7 A

Rectification and smoothing

A diode allows current in one direction only, so a single diode halves the a.c. wave (half-wave rectification); a bridge of four diodes produces full-wave rectification — the output always has the same polarity. A capacitor in parallel with the load then smooths the output: it charges at the peaks and discharges through the load between them, reducing the ripple. Larger capacitance and larger load resistance give less ripple (τ = RC longer relative to the cycle).

  • Half-wave: one diode; half the wave is missing; more ripple.
  • Full-wave: bridge of four diodes; both halves used; easier to smooth.
  • Smoothing: capacitor across the load; ripple reduced as C and R increase.

Worked examples: combined electromagnetism

Worked example. A generator coil of 50 turns and area 0.020 m² rotates at 60 rad s⁻¹ in a 0.40 T field. Find the peak e.m.f. and the rms e.m.f.

ε₀ = N B A ω = 50 × 0.40 × 0.020 × 60
         = 24 V
epsilon_rms = 24/√(2) = 17 V

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Force on wire) A 0.30 m wire carrying 2.0 A is perpendicular to a 0.80 T field. Find the force. Answer: F = BIL = 0.80 × 2.0 × 0.30 = 0.48 N.
  2. (Direction) State Fleming's left-hand rule. Answer: With the first finger along the field and the second along the current, the thumb points along the force — used for motors (the left hand gives the force on the conductor).
  3. (Charge) Explain why a moving charge in a uniform magnetic field moves in a circle. Answer: The magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work and changes only direction; a constant perpendicular force produces circular motion with r = mv/(BQ).
  4. (Solenoid) Describe the magnetic field inside a current-carrying solenoid. Answer: Strong, uniform, and directed along the axis; outside it resembles a bar magnet's field, with the end determined by the right-hand grip rule.
  5. (Faraday) State Faraday's law and Lenz's law. Answer: The induced e.m.f. is proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux linkage; the induced current opposes the change that produces it.
  6. (Lenz) Explain why Lenz's law is a consequence of energy conservation. Answer: If the induced current aided the change, it would generate energy from nothing; opposing it means work must be done to produce the change, and that work becomes electrical energy.
  7. (rms) An a.c. supply has peak voltage 340 V. Find the rms voltage. Answer: V_rms = 340/√2 = 240 V.
  8. (Smoothing) Explain how a capacitor smooths a rectified output. Answer: The capacitor charges as the rectified voltage rises to its peak and discharges through the load as the voltage falls, filling the gaps between peaks and reducing the ripple.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Angle in F = BIL sin θ: θ is between the current and the field; perpendicular means sin θ = 1. A wire parallel to the field feels no force.
  • Left hand versus right hand: use the left-hand rule for the force on a current (motor effect) and the right-hand grip rule for the field around a current. Mixing them reverses the answer.
  • Flux versus flux density: Φ = BA (weber), B is tesla; flux linkage multiplies by N turns. Do not call B flux.
  • Change of flux sign: reversing a field doubles the change (from +BA to −BA), a factor candidates often forget.
  • rms factor: peak over √2; the peak is rms × √2. Power uses rms values, not peak.
  • Induced e.m.f. needs change: a stationary coil in a steady field induces nothing; there must be a changing flux linkage (movement, rotation, or a changing current).
  • Lenz direction questions: state the opposing field direction and then the current direction; the reasoning chain is the mark.
  • Rectification understanding: diodes conduct one way only; a bridge gives full-wave, a single diode half-wave — do not claim a single diode gives full-wave output.
  • Precision and units: tesla, weber, volt; 2 or 3 s.f.; μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹ from the data sheet.

title: Mensuration — Bearings and Loci — Study Notes
content:
Mensuration — Bearings and Loci

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): compass bearings, scale drawings, constructions (perpendicular/angle bisectors), loci regions.

1. Bearings

  • Measured clockwise from north; three figures: 065°, 128°, 300°.
  • Back bearing = front bearing ± 180°.
  • Draw a north line at both points; north lines are parallel, giving Z-angles.

Example: B is on bearing 070° from A → A is on bearing 250° from B.

2. Scale drawings

1 cm : 500 m style scales; measure, convert, and quote distances/bearings from your drawing to the accuracy allowed.

3. Constructions

  • Perpendicular bisector of a segment: equal arcs from both ends, join the crossings.
  • Angle bisector: equal arcs from the vertex arms.
  • 60° and 90° constructions with compasses; leave all arcs visible.

4. Loci

Fixed distance from a point = circle; from a line = parallel lines with rounded ends; equidistant from two points = perpendicular bisector; from two lines = angle bisector.

Example: a goat tied by a 5 m rope to a corner of a 4 m × 6 m shed: the reachable region is ¾ circle radius 5 m + two ¼ circles radius 1 m where the rope wraps.

Exam tips: state "clockwise from north" in bearing definitions; shade/label locus regions clearly; use a ruler for construction lines too.

Three-figure bearings

A bearing is measured clockwise from north and written with three figures, so 045° is north-east and 250° is south-west. To find the back bearing, add or subtract 180°. Draw a north line at the starting point and measure the angle carefully with a protractor.

Scale drawings and distance

Use the scale given to convert a map distance to a real distance, and convert back when drawing. Scale 1:50 000 means 1 cm on the map represents 50 000 cm, or 0.5 km. Use Pythagoras or trigonometry to find distances where a direct measurement is not possible.

Loci

The locus of points at a fixed distance from a point is a circle. Points equidistant from two points lie on the perpendicular bisector of the line joining them. Points equidistant from two lines lie on an angle bisector. Shade a region by combining the loci and stating the condition clearly.

Worked example: the back bearing

An aircraft flies from A to B on a bearing of 118°. To find the bearing of A from B, add 180° because the north line at B is parallel to the north line at A: 118° + 180° = 298°. If the sum is greater than 360°, subtract 360°. Draw the north line at the point from which the angle is measured, because the marks depend on the angle being taken from the correct point.

Exam method: loci and constructions

The locus of points at a fixed distance from one point is a circle. The locus of points equidistant from two points is the perpendicular bisector of the line joining them. The locus of points equidistant from two lines is an angle bisector. Show every construction arc, because the marks are given for the arcs as well as the final line, and do not erase them.

title: IGCSE Physics: Waves and Sound
content:
IGCSE Physics: Waves and Sound

Cambridge IGCSE Physics 0625 (2026–2028), Topic 3 Waves: statements 3.1 General properties of waves, 3.2 Light, 3.3 Electromagnetic spectrum and 3.4 Sound. Waves are how energy travels from place to place without moving matter along with it, and everything from a ripple on a pond to a gamma ray obeys the same few rules. This note builds the general wave behaviour first, then light (reflection, refraction, lenses, colour), then the electromagnetic spectrum and finally sound, with the calculations and the ray constructions that Paper 4 and Paper 6 reward.

General properties of waves

A wave transfers energy without transferring matter. Drop a cork into a ripple tank and the ripples pass under it while the cork only bobs: the water moves up and down, not outward. Every wave is described by the same vocabulary:

TermMeaningUnit
AmplitudeMaximum displacement from the rest position; relates to energy (loudness for sound, brightness for light)metre (m)
Wavelength (λ)Distance between two equivalent points on neighbouring waves, e.g. crest to crestmetre (m)
FrequencyNumber of complete waves passing a point per second; equals the source's number of oscillations per secondhertz (Hz)
PeriodTime for one complete wave to pass a pointsecond (s)
Wave speedDistance a wave crest travels per secondmetre per second (m s⁻¹)
wave speed = frequency x wavelength        v = fλ
period = 1 / frequency        T = 1 / f
  • v: wave speed in metres per second (m s⁻¹); f: frequency in hertz (Hz, = s⁻¹); λ: wavelength in metres (m). All scalars, so there are no signs to worry about — but all three quantities must be in SI units before multiplying.

Transverse waves have the vibration perpendicular to the direction of travel: water waves, light and all electromagnetic waves, waves on a shaken rope. Longitudinal waves have the vibration parallel to the direction of travel: sound in air, the push-pull of a slinky. Longitudinal waves show compressions (where particles are pushed together) and rarefactions (where they are spread apart).

Three behaviours describe what happens when waves meet things. Reflection is bouncing off a surface; the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, measured from the normal. Refraction is the change of direction when a wave passes into a different medium at an angle, because its speed changes; moving into a slower medium bends the ray towards the normal and the wavelength shortens while the frequency stays constant. Diffraction is the spreading of waves through a gap or around an obstacle, and it is most pronounced when the gap width is comparable to the wavelength. Ripple tanks demonstrate all three: straight barriers give reflection, shallow regions give refraction, and narrow gaps give circular wavefronts after diffraction (Supplement: wider gaps give less spreading, and an edge produces noticeable diffraction only for longer wavelengths).

Reflection of light

Light travels in straight lines and reflects from smooth surfaces with the law of reflection: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, both measured between the ray and the normal (an imaginary line perpendicular to the surface at the point of incidence). A plane-mirror image is upright, the same size as the object, laterally inverted (left and right swapped), and as far behind the mirror as the object is in front.

Supplement: the ray construction. To locate the image, draw a ray from the object to the mirror, continue it behind the mirror at the same angle, and drop a perpendicular from the image position to the mirror; repeat with a second ray. Where the reflected rays appear to come from behind the mirror is where the image sits. Drawing the construction to scale with a protractor gives the image position exactly.

Refraction of light

When light passes from air into glass at an angle it slows and bends towards the normal; passing back out it speeds up and bends away from the normal. The amount of bending is fixed by the material's refractive index:

refractive index = sin(angle of incidence in vacuum or air) / sin(angle of refraction)        n = sin i / sin r
critical angle:        sin c = 1 / n
  • n: refractive index, a scalar with no unit, always greater than 1 for a material like glass or water.
  • i and r: angles in degrees measured from the normal, not from the surface.
  • c: critical angle in degrees, defined for a ray passing from the material into air.

Total internal reflection happens when a ray inside a material hits the boundary at an angle greater than the critical angle: none of it escapes and all reflects. Two applications are examinable: optical fibres, where light bounces along the core with total internal reflection and carries data over long distances with little loss, and prisms in periscopes and binoculars, where a 45° prism turns light through 90° or 180° by total internal reflection with almost no energy loss compared with a mirror.

Thin lenses and vision

A converging lens brings parallel rays to a focus at its principal focus; a diverging lens spreads them out as if they came from a focus on the near side. Three standard rays build any image on a converging lens:

  • A ray parallel to the axis refracts through the principal focus on the far side.
  • A ray through the centre of the lens passes straight through undeviated.
  • A ray through the near-side principal focus emerges parallel to the axis.

Where two refracted rays cross, a real image forms — it can be shown on a screen. Where they only appear to diverge from a point behind the lens, a virtual image forms — it cannot be caught on a screen and is seen only by looking through the lens. An object beyond twice the focal length gives a smaller inverted real image (a camera); an object between the focus and the lens gives a larger upright virtual image (a magnifying glass, Supplement). Short sight (myopia) is corrected with a diverging lens, long sight (hyperopia) with a converging lens (Supplement).

Dispersion and the electromagnetic spectrum

White light passing through a prism disperses into a spectrum from red to violet because different colours refract by different amounts: red light is refracted least (it travels fastest in glass) and violet most. Light of a single colour is monochromatic (Supplement). The visible spectrum sits inside a much larger family — the electromagnetic spectrum, all waves travelling at 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ in a vacuum, all transverse, arranged by increasing frequency (and decreasing wavelength) as: radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays.

RegionWavelength scaleUsesHazards
Radio wavesmetres to hundreds of metresRadio and TV broadcasting, communicationsLittle evidence of harm at normal levels
Microwavesmillimetres to centimetresMobile phones, satellite communications, microwave ovens, radarHeating of body tissue; dangerous at high intensity
InfraredmicrometresHeating, night-vision cameras, remote controls, optical fibresBurns and skin heating at high intensity
Visible light400–700 nmVision, photography, fibre-optic dataDazzle; eye damage from lasers and the Sun
Ultraviolet10–400 nmFluorescent lamps, sterilisation, security markingSunburn, skin ageing and skin cancer, eye damage
X-rays0.01–10 nmMedical imaging, airport security, detecting cracks in metalIonising: cell damage and cancer risk; dose kept low
Gamma raysbelow 0.01 nmSterilising equipment, cancer radiotherapy, food irradiationIonising: severe cell damage; shielded with lead and concrete

Supplement: signals and communication. An analogue signal varies continuously with the quantity it carries; a digital signal is a stream of on/off pulses. Digital signals are preferred because they can be regenerated without amplifying noise, can be compressed to carry more information, can be encrypted, and can carry text, sound and images in the same stream. Satellite links work by beaming a microwave signal to an orbiting satellite, which amplifies and retransmits it back to a distant ground station.

Sound

Sound is a longitudinal wave produced by vibrating objects and travelling through a medium — air at about 340 m s⁻¹ at room temperature, faster in liquids and fastest in solids, because the particles are closer together and pass the vibration on more quickly. Sound cannot travel through a vacuum. The frequency of a sound sets its pitch (high frequency, high pitch), and the amplitude sets its loudness. The human range of hearing is roughly 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz.

Echoes and distance measurement. Sound reflects from hard surfaces, giving echoes. The depth of the sea under a ship is found by sending a pulse and timing its return:

distance to the surface = (speed of sound x total time) / 2        s = v t / 2

The halving is essential — the pulse travels down and back — and forgetting it is the classic error in this topic. Measuring the time between two microphones a known distance apart gives the speed of sound directly: v = distance/time.

Ultrasound is sound above the human hearing range (above 20 kHz). Its short wavelength means it reflects well from small internal boundaries, which makes it useful for prenatal scanning (reflection at tissue boundaries builds an image), cleaning delicate items (high-energy vibrations dislodge dirt), flaw detection in metal castings (an internal crack reflects the pulse), and sonar depth sounding. All uses share the same principle: send a pulse, time the echo, calculate the distance with s = vt/2.

Worked example: wave calculation and echo depth

A ship's sonar sends ultrasound of frequency 50 kHz. The echo returns from the seabed after 0.12 s. The speed of sound in seawater is 1500 m s⁻¹.

total distance travelled = v t = 1500 × 0.12 = 180 m
depth of the sea = 180 / 2 = 90 m

Second calculation: a ripple tank wave has a wavelength of 0.040 m and the dippers oscillate 25 times per second. The wave speed is v = f λ = 25 × 0.040 = 1.0 m s⁻¹. The frequency of the wave equals the frequency of the source, and it stays unchanged when the wave passes into deeper water — only the speed and the wavelength change there.

Common mistakes

  • Measuring a wavelength from crest to trough; that is half a wavelength. Measure between two equivalent points on neighbouring waves.
  • Forgetting that frequency never changes on refraction. The speed and wavelength change; the frequency is set by the source and stays constant.
  • Mixing up the angle of incidence with its complement: all angles in reflection and refraction are measured from the normal.
  • Using v = fλ with mismatched units: hertz times centimetres gives cm s⁻¹, not m s⁻¹. Convert the wavelength to metres first.
  • Forgetting to halve the total distance in an echo calculation.
  • Drawing a converging lens ray diagram without the two special rays, or putting the image on the wrong side: real images form on the far side where rays actually cross, virtual images on the same side as the object.
  • Claiming light travels slower in a vacuum than in glass; it is fastest in a vacuum and slower in denser media, which is what causes refraction.
  • Describing a digital signal as continuously varying; it is discrete pulses, which is precisely why it resists noise.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 4, 3 marks). A water wave has a frequency of 4.0 Hz and a wavelength of 0.25 m. Calculate its speed and its period.

Answer: v = fλ = 4.0 × 0.25 = 1.0 m s⁻¹. Period T = 1/f = 1/4.0 = 0.25 s.

Question 2 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Explain why sound cannot be heard on the Moon but sunlight still reaches it.

Answer: Sound is a longitudinal wave that needs a medium, because it travels by particles passing vibrations to their neighbours. The Moon is surrounded by a vacuum, with no particles to carry the vibration, so sound cannot travel there. Light is an electromagnetic transverse wave that carries energy without needing a medium, so it crosses the vacuum of space easily.

Question 3 (Paper 2 style). Light passes from air into glass at an angle. Which quantity does not change? A speed; B wavelength; C frequency; D direction. Answer: C. The frequency is set by the source and is unchanged; speed and wavelength both fall in glass and the ray bends.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Ultrasound of speed 1500 m s⁻¹ is used to find the depth of the sea. The echo returns in 0.40 s. Calculate the depth and explain why ultrasound is used rather than audible sound.

Answer: Depth = v t / 2 = 1500 × 0.40 / 2 = 300 m. Ultrasound has a very short wavelength, so it reflects well from small boundaries and gives a clear echo pattern without diffracting uselessly around small features; it also does not interfere with ordinary sound and is harmless at the intensities used.

Question 5 (Paper 6 style). Describe how to measure the speed of sound in air using two microphones and a data logger.

Answer: Place two microphones a measured distance apart in a straight line from a sound source (a clapping board or signal generator and loudspeaker). Trigger the data logger with the sound at each microphone and record the time interval between the arrivals, or display both pulses on an oscilloscope and measure the time from the trace. Speed is the distance between the microphones divided by the time interval. Repeat at several separations and find the speed from the gradient of a distance–time graph, which averages out the reaction error.

Question 6 (Paper 4, 3 marks). State two differences between a transverse and a longitudinal wave, and give one example of each.

Answer: In a transverse wave the vibrations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer; in a longitudinal wave they are parallel to it. Transverse waves have crests and troughs; longitudinal waves have compressions and rarefactions. Examples: light (transverse) and sound in air (longitudinal).

Waves carry energy without matter; the next topic is the energy that drives circuits: Electricity and Circuits.

Drawing a wave to scale: what each label measures

Two quantities decide everything a wave does, and both are measured on the same drawing — which is exactly why they get confused. The wavelength is how long one repeat of the wave is; the amplitude is how far the medium is displaced from where it would sit if the wave were not there. Get those two straight and the wave equation, the energy argument and the "describe what you see" question all follow from the same picture.

Wavelength λ is a distance between identical points. Crest to crest works, trough to trough works, and so does any point to the next point doing exactly the same thing — a point on the way up to the next point on the way up, one full cycle later. What does not work is crest to trough: that is half a wavelength, and it is the single most common wrong answer on a wave diagram. In metres, λ is a length; the symbol is the Greek letter lambda.

Amplitude A is measured from the middle, not from the bottom. The dashed line in the figure is the equilibrium position — where the rope or the air would be with no wave. Amplitude is the distance from that line to a crest, and it is the same distance from the line down to a trough. Trough-to-crest is twice the amplitude. The amplitude tells you how much energy the wave carries: doubling the amplitude quadruples the energy, which is why a loud sound at a concert can damage hearing far more than its extra loudness suggests.

Frequency is the other half of the story. Frequency f is how many complete waves pass a point each second, measured in hertz (Hz), and it is set by the source, not by the medium. The period T is the time for one complete wave, so the two are reciprocals:

f = 1 / T Key: f = frequency (Hz); T = period (s). A wave with a period of 0.004 s has a frequency of 1 ÷ 0.004 = 250 Hz.

Put the distance of one wave and the time for one wave together and you get the wave equation:

v = f λ Key: v = wave speed (m s⁻¹); f = frequency (Hz); λ = wavelength (m). Multiplying "waves per second" by "metres per wave" leaves metres per second.

Worked example. A tuning fork of frequency 512 Hz sends a sound through air in which the wavelength is 0.66 m. Find the speed of the sound.

v = f λ = 512 × 0.66 = 338 m s⁻¹

The answer is close to the accepted 340 m s⁻¹, which is the check to make in your head: if a sound speed comes out as 34 or 3,400, a power of ten has slipped, usually because a wavelength was left in centimetres.

Which graph am I looking at? The same wave can be drawn against distance or against time, and the axis is the clue. A displacement–distance graph shows the wave frozen at one instant, so λ is read straight off the horizontal axis. A displacement–time graph shows one point of the medium as the wave passes, so the horizontal width of one cycle is the period T, not the wavelength. Students who read λ off a time graph get a number in seconds and a speed that is wrong by a factor of f — and the mark scheme gives nothing for the right arithmetic on the wrong quantity.

Where marks are lost. Crest-to-trough as the wavelength. Trough-to-crest as the amplitude. Reading λ from a displacement–time graph. And forgetting that frequency does not change when a wave crosses into a new medium while its speed and wavelength do — that is exactly how refraction is explained.

Equations and symbols

One equation, v = fλ, carries the whole of wave physics; the rest of this topic is refraction, the lens and the echo. Frequency and period are reciprocals, so a question that gives one and asks for the other is testing whether you inverted it correctly.

The wave equation

v = fλ
Key: v = wave speed (m/s); f = frequency (Hz, waves per second); λ (λ) = wavelength (m). The speed is set by the medium, so when a wave crosses into a new medium f stays the same and λ changes.

f = 1 / T
Key: f = frequency (Hz); T = period, the time for one complete oscillation (s). A 0.004 s period is 250 Hz.

T = 1 / f
Key: the same relation rearranged; T in seconds, f in hertz.

d = vt
Key: d = distance travelled by the wave (m); v = wave speed (m/s); t = time (s). For an echo the sound travels to the surface and back, so the distance to the surface is half of vt.

s = vt / 2
Key: s = distance to the reflecting surface (m); v = speed of sound in the medium (m/s); t = total time between the pulse and its echo (s). The factor of 2 is the most frequently dropped mark in echo questions.

v(sound in air) ≈ 340 m/s and v(light in vacuum) = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s
Key: the two speeds that explain thunder arriving after lightning; light is nearly a million times faster, so the flash is seen almost instantly.

audible range for a human = 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz
Key: f below 20 Hz is infrasound and above 20 kHz is ultrasound; both are outside human hearing but ultrasound is used in medical scanning and sonar.

Refraction

n = sin i / sin r
Key: n = refractive index of the material (no unit); i = angle of incidence in the less dense medium, measured from the normal (°); r = angle of refraction in the material (°). Both angles are always measured from the normal, never from the surface.

n = 1 / sin c
Key: c = critical angle (°), the angle of incidence in the denser medium for which the refracted ray runs along the surface. A larger n means a smaller critical angle.

n = c / v
Key: c = speed of light in a vacuum (3.0 × 10⁸ m/s); v = speed of light in the material (m/s). Light slows on entering a denser medium, which is what bends it towards the normal.

total internal reflection when i > c
Key: i = angle of incidence inside the denser medium (°); c = critical angle (°). Beyond c no light escapes, which is the rule behind optical fibres and reflecting prisms.

Lenses and images

m = h(image) / h(object)
Key: m = magnification (no unit); h(image) = image height (m or cm); h(object) = object height in the same unit. m greater than 1 means enlarged, less than 1 means diminished.

real image: formed where rays actually meet, and can be projected on a screen
Key: a converging lens gives a real image when the object is beyond the focal length; the image is inverted. A virtual image is where rays only appear to come from, and cannot be projected.

title: IGCSE Mathematics: Indices and Standard Form
content:
IGCSE Mathematics: Indices and Standard Form

Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580 (2025–2027), section 1 Number: statement 1.3 Powers and roots, 1.7 Indices I (with Extended fractional indices), 1.8 Standard form, E1.18 Surds, and section 2 statement E2.4 Indices II (algebraic indices). Indices are shorthand for repeated multiplication, and their laws are the shortcuts that make large and small numbers manageable. This note derives each law from what it counts, covers standard form arithmetic in full, and finishes with surds and rationalising — an Extended favourite that separates the top grades.

Powers, roots and the vocabulary

In 5³ the base is 5 and the index (plural: indices) is 3; it means 5 × 5 × 5 = 125. A square root reverses a square: √25 = 5 because 5² = 25. A cube root reverses a cube: ³√64 = 4 because 4³ = 64.

  • √16 = 4, the principal (positive) square root, as printed on a calculator. But the equation x² = 16 has two solutions, x = 4 or x = −4, because (−4)² = 16 as well. The question decides which is wanted: a length is positive; a solution of an equation may be negative.
  • Notation: a² is read a squared, a³ a cubed, and aⁿ a to the power n. a² ≠ 2a — a² = a × a while 2a = a + a.

The index laws

Each law is a statement about counting multiplications, so each can be checked by writing the multiplications out.

Law 1:  a^m x a^n = a^(m+n)
Why: a^3 x a^2 = (a x a x a) x (a x a) = a^5, and 3 + 2 = 5.
Example: 2^3 x 2^5 = 2^8 = 256; check: 8 x 32 = 256 ✓

Law 2:  a^m ÷ a^n = a^(m-n)
Why: a^5 ÷ a^2 = (a x a x a x a x a)/(a x a) = a x a x a = a^3, and 5 - 2 = 3.
Example: 5^7 ÷ 5^4 = 5^3 = 125

Law 3:  (a^m)^n = a^(m n)
Why: (a^2)^3 = a^2 x a^2 x a^2 = a^6, and 2 x 3 = 6.
Example: (2x^3)^2 = 2^2 x (x^3)^2 = 4x^6        [the power applies to every factor]

Law 4:  a^0 = 1  (a not zero)
Why: a^3 ÷ a^3 = a^(3-3) = a^0, and any number divided by itself is 1.
Example: 7^0 = 1

Law 5:  a^(-n) = 1/(a^n)
Why: a^(-2) = a^(0-2) = a^0 ÷ a^2 = 1/a^2.
Example: 5^(-2) = 1/25 = 0.04

Fractional indices (Extended). A fractional index is a root: the denominator of the fraction is the root, the numerator is the power.

a^(1/n) = nth root of a        a^(m/n) = (nth root of a)^m

16^(1/2) = √16 = 4
27^(2/3) = (cube root of 27)^2 = 3^2 = 9
Check the second: 27^(2/3) squared three times over should give 27^2 = 729; 9^3 = 729 ✓

Indices in algebra (Extended)

The same laws apply when the base is a letter, and every factor in a bracket carries the power:

Simplify:  (2x^3)^2 x^4 ÷ x^5

(2x^3)^2 = 4x^6        [square the 2 and double the index]
4x^6 x x^4 = 4x^10     [Law 1: add indices]
4x^10 ÷ x^5 = 4x^5     [Law 2: subtract indices]
Solve:  2^x = 32

Write both sides with base 2:  32 = 2^5
2^x = 2^5, so x = 5        [matching bases means matching indices]

When the bases differ, rewrite one as a power of the other: 8 = 2³, so 8^x = 2^(3x). Equations like 3^(x+1) = 27^(x−1) become 3^(x+1) = 3^(3x−3), so x + 1 = 3x − 3, giving x = 2.

LawStatementWorked line
Multiplyingaᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ2³ × 2⁵ = 2⁸ = 256
Dividingaᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ5⁷ ÷ 5⁴ = 5³ = 125
Power of a power(aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ(2x³)² = 4x⁶
Zero indexa⁰ = 1 (a not zero)7⁰ = 1
Negative indexa⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ5⁻² = 1/25
Fractional indexa^(m/n) = (ⁿ√a)ᵐ27^(2/3) = 9

Two edge cases deserve care. The zero index says nothing about 0⁰: 0⁰ is undefined, because the pattern a⁰ = 1 holds for every non-zero base while the pattern 0ⁿ = 0 holds for every positive power, and the two patterns collide at the origin. And a negative index never makes a value negative: 2⁻³ = 1/8 is positive, because the minus sign belongs to the position of the power, not to the number itself. Finally, every root can be written as a power — √x = x^(1/2), ³√x = x^(1/3) — which is how a calculator evaluates them and how algebraic roots are simplified in one notation.

Standard form

Standard form writes a number as a × 10ⁿ where 1 ⩽ a < 10 and n is an integer. It handles very large and very small quantities without long strings of zeros.

Write in standard form:

47 382 = 4.7382 x 10^4        [the decimal point moves 4 places left]
0.0056 = 5.6 x 10^(-3)        [the decimal point moves 3 places right, so n = -3]

Arithmetic in standard form. Multiply or divide the numbers first, then the powers of ten, and adjust back into standard form if needed:

(3 x 10^5) x (4 x 10^(-2))
= (3 x 4) x (10^5 x 10^(-2))     [regrouped]
= 12 x 10^3
= 1.2 x 10^4                     [12 is not between 1 and 10, so adjust]

(6 x 10^8) ÷ (2 x 10^3)
= (6 ÷ 2) x 10^(8-3) = 3 x 10^5

Addition and subtraction need matching powers first: 3 × 10⁵ + 4 × 10⁴ = 30 × 10⁴ + 4 × 10⁴ = 34 × 10⁴ = 3.4 × 10⁵. Real-world uses: the speed of light is 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, the size of an atom is about 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m, and masses, distances and populations in physics and chemistry questions are always quoted this way. A calculator's ×10ˣ key enters the power directly; the answer should be given in the form the question asks, often to 3 s.f.

Surds (Extended)

A surd is a root that cannot be written exactly as a fraction — √2, √3, 3√5. Exact answers in surds are often required on Paper 2, where a calculator cannot help. The laws:

√a x √b = √(ab)        √a ÷ √b = √(a/b)        (√a)^2 = a

Simplifying. Take out the largest square factor:

√50 = √(25 x 2) = √25 x √2 = 5√2
√72 = √(36 x 2) = 6√2
√(9/16) = √9 / √16 = 3/4

Adding like surds. Only like surds combine, exactly like algebraic terms:

√18 + √8 = 3√2 + 2√2 = 5√2        [simplify first]
2√3 + √5 cannot be combined: they are unlike surds.

Rationalising the denominator. A fraction with a surd underneath is tidied by multiplying top and bottom by the same surd (or its conjugate):

6/√3 = (6 x √3)/(√3 x √3) = 6√3/3 = 2√3

1/(3 + √2): multiply top and bottom by the conjugate (3 - √2):
= (3 - √2)/[(3 + √2)(3 - √2)]
= (3 - √2)/(9 - 2)          [difference of two squares below]
= (3 - √2)/7

The conjugate works because (a + b)(a − b) = a² − b² removes the square root entirely. Expanding surd brackets uses the same identity: (2 + √3)(2 − √3) = 4 − 3 = 1.

Worked example: a combined index calculation

Simplify (2³ × 2⁵) ÷ 2⁴ and check it two ways.

Method 1 (indices): 2^3 x 2^5 = 2^8, then 2^8 ÷ 2^4 = 2^4 = 16
Method 2 (arithmetic): 2^3 x 2^5 = 8 x 32 = 256;  256 ÷ 16 = 16
Both routes give 16 ✓

Second example: write (3√2)² − √8 in the form k√2.

(3√2)^2 = 9 x 2 = 18        [square both the 3 and the √2]
√8 = 2√2
18 - 2√2 is already simple; it cannot be written as k√2 because 18 is rational,
so the answer stays 18 - 2√2.

Standard form in a calculation. A red blood cell is 7 × 10⁻⁶ m across and a vein is 2.4 × 10⁻³ m wide. How many cells fit side by side?

2.4 x 10^(-3) ÷ 7 x 10^(-6)
= (2.4 ÷ 7) x 10^(-3 - (-6))        [divide the numbers, subtract the indices]
= 0.342857 x 10^3
= 3.43 x 10^2 (3 s.f.)  ≈ 343 cells

The index arithmetic is the whole question: subtracting −6 gives +3, and a sense-check on the powers alone (10⁻³ ÷ 10⁻⁶ = 10³) says the answer must be in the hundreds — which catches sign slips before they cost the final mark.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Multiplying the base by the index: 2³ is 8, not 6; (2³)² = 2⁶ = 64, not 2⁵.
  • Forgetting to square the coefficient: (2x³)² = 4x⁶, not 2x⁶.
  • Treating a⁻ⁿ as negative rather than reciprocal: 2⁻³ = 1/8.
  • Writing 0.00047 as 4.7 × 10⁻³; it is 4.7 × 10⁻⁴ — count the places the point moves.
  • Leaving a standard-form answer as 12 × 10³; the front number must be between 1 and 10.
  • Giving √16 = ±4 in a simplification; the square root symbol means the principal root, while x² = 16 has both solutions.
  • Rationalising only the surd and not its conjugate partner: 1/(3 + √2) needs (3 − √2) top and bottom.
  • Combining unlike surds: 2√3 + √5 is final; only matching surd parts can be added.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 2, 3 marks). Simplify (3x²)³ ÷ x⁴.

Answer: (3x²)³ = 27x⁶; 27x⁶ ÷ x⁴ = 27x².

Question 2 (Paper 2, 3 marks). Evaluate 8^(2/3).

Answer: ³√8 = 2, and 2² = 4. So 8^(2/3) = 4.

Question 3 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Write 0.000 42 and 63 000 in standard form, then find their product.

Answer: 4.2 × 10⁻⁴ and 6.3 × 10⁴. Product = (4.2 × 6.3) × 10⁰ = 26.46 = 2.646 × 10¹.

Question 4 (Paper 2, 4 marks). Simplify √48 + 3√12.

Answer: √48 = √(16 × 3) = 4√3; 3√12 = 3 × 2√3 = 6√3; total = 10√3.

Question 5 (Paper 2, 4 marks). Rationalise the denominator of 5/(2 + √3).

Answer: Multiply by the conjugate: 5(2 − √3)/[(2 + √3)(2 − √3)] = 5(2 − √3)/(4 − 3) = 5(2 − √3) = 10 − 5√3.

Question 6 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Solve 9^x = 27.

Answer: Write both as powers of 3: 3^(2x) = 3³, so 2x = 3 and x = 3/2. Check: 9^(3/2) = (√9)³ = 3³ = 27 ✓.

From the numbers themselves, the course turns to comparing and sharing them: ratio, rate and proportion.

title: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Statistics and Data Handling
content:
Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Statistics and Data Handling

Statistics is the art of describing a pile of numbers with a few well-chosen ones: an average to say where the middle lies, a spread to say how tightly the data cluster, and a chart to make the shape visible. The IGCSE questions test exactly that pipeline — classify the data, compute the averages and spread, draw or read the chart, and compare two distributions. This note builds the whole subject from zero: the data types, every average and measure of spread with the frequency-table method, the standard charts, cumulative frequency curves, and histograms with unequal class widths.

Classifying statistical data

TypeMeaningExamples
Qualitative (categorical)describes a quality, not a numberfavourite colour, blood group
Quantitativemeasured or counted as a numberheight, number of siblings
Discretecountable, separate values (usually integers)number of children, shoe size
Continuouscan take any value in a range (measured)height, time, mass

The classification decides which charts and averages are legal: a mode for categorical data, a median for ordered data, class intervals for continuous data. Discrete data are plotted as bar charts with gaps; continuous data as histograms with no gaps (and frequency density on the vertical axis).

Averages and range

mean = sum of values / number of values
median = middle value when ordered (mean of the two middle
         values for an even count)
mode = most frequent value (or class); none if no repeats
range = largest - smallest

quartiles: Q1 = lower quartile (25%), Q3 = upper quartile (75%)
interquartile range (IQR) = Q3 - Q1  (spread of the middle 50%)

The mean uses every value (sensitive to outliers); the median ignores extreme values (robust); the mode is the only average available for categorical data. When comparing two data sets, quote an average and a spread: "school A has a higher median but a larger IQR, so its results are higher on average but less consistent."

Worked example. Find the mean, median, mode and range of: 4, 7, 7, 9, 12, 15, 18.

mean = (4+7+7+9+12+15+18)/7 = 72/7 = 10.3 (3 s.f.)
median = 4th value = 9
mode = 7 (appears twice)
range = 18 - 4 = 14

Worked example 2 (even count). Find the median of 3, 5, 8, 10, 12, 15.

even count: average the 3rd and 4th values
median = (8 + 10)/2 = 9

Averages from frequency tables

mean = sum of (value x frequency) / sum of frequencies
median = the value at position (n + 1)/2 in cumulative order
mode = the value with the highest frequency

Worked example. The table shows goals scored: 0 (5 players), 1 (8), 2 (6), 3 (2). Find the mean and the median.

total players = 5 + 8 + 6 + 2 = 21
total goals = 0 × 5 + 1 × 8 + 2 × 6 + 3 × 2 = 0 + 8 + 12 + 6 = 26
mean = 26/21 = 1.24 (3 s.f.)
median position = (21 + 1)/2 = 11th value
cumulative: 5 (0 goals), 13 (1 goal) - the 11th value is 1
median = 1

For grouped data, use midpoints: the mean = Σ(midpoint × frequency)/Σfrequency, and the median comes from the cumulative frequency curve (below). The grouped mean is an estimate because the midpoint stands in for every value in the class.

Charts and diagrams

  • Bar chart: bars with gaps for categorical or discrete data; height = frequency.
  • Pie chart: angle = (frequency/total) × 360°; label the sectors with the category.
  • Pictogram: a symbol represents a fixed number; a half symbol represents half that number.
  • Stem-and-leaf: a sorted display that keeps the actual values; the key explains the split (e.g. 3|4 means 34).
  • Frequency polygon: plot frequency against the midpoint of each class and join with straight lines.

Worked example (pie chart). 40 students choose a sport: football 16, tennis 10, swimming 8, other 6. Find the angle for football.

angle = (16/40) × 360 = 144 °

Worked example 2 (pie chart reverse). A sector of 72° represents 9 students. How many students in total?

72 ° represents 9  →  360 ° represents 9 × 360/72 = 45 students

Cumulative frequency diagrams

A cumulative frequency table adds frequencies as you move up the classes. Plot cumulative frequency against the upper class boundary and join with a smooth curve; then read positions:

median at n/2
lower quartile at n/4
upper quartile at 3n/4
IQR = Q3 - Q1

Worked example. A cumulative frequency curve for 60 students' marks: Q1 = 42, median = 55, Q3 = 68. Find the IQR and interpret it.

IQR = 68 - 42 = 26 marks
The middle 50% of students scored within 26 marks of each other;

Always read across to the curve and then down to the horizontal axis — and use the class boundaries, not the midpoints, for the plot positions.

Histograms and frequency density

When class widths differ, the height of a bar cannot be the frequency — a wide class would dominate unfairly. Instead, the area of each bar is proportional to the frequency:

frequency density = frequency / class width
frequency = frequency density x class width (area of the bar)

Worked example. Class 0–10 has frequency 20; 10–20 has frequency 30; 20–40 has frequency 40. Find the frequency densities.

0-10: 20/10 = 2.0
10-20: 30/10 = 3.0
20-40: 40/20 = 2.0

Reading a histogram backwards is the standard question: measure a bar's width and height, multiply to get the frequency, and read the class from the horizontal axis. Remember that the axes often use class boundaries, so a bar from 20 to 40 covers width 20.

Stem-and-leaf diagrams and frequency polygons

A stem-and-leaf diagram sorts data while keeping every value visible: the stem is the leading digit and the leaf the final digit, with a key such as 3|4 meaning 34. Interpreting one means reading the ordered leaves to find the median, the quartiles and the shape: the median is the middle leaf, Q1 and Q3 sit at the quarter and three-quarter positions, and the distribution's skew shows in where the leaves bunch.

A frequency polygon plots frequency against the midpoint of each class and joins the points with straight lines; it is the grouped-data equivalent of a line graph and makes comparisons between two distributions easy (plot both polygons on the same axes).

Worked example. The leaves for stem 4 are 1, 3, 3, 6, 8 and for stem 5 are 0, 2, 5. List the data in order and find the median.

values: 41, 43, 43, 46, 48, 50, 52, 55
n = 8, so the median is the mean of the 4th and 5th values:
(46 + 48)/2 = 47

Worked example 2 (interpreting). Explain what a long right-hand tail of leaves in a stem-and-leaf diagram indicates.

A long right tail means a few unusually high values: the data
are positively skewed, and the mean will be greater than the
median because the high values pull it upward.

Comparing distributions

Comparison questions want two statements: one about the average (which is higher) and one about the spread (which is more consistent). Use median and IQR together — they are robust to outliers — or mean and standard deviation when the data are symmetric and the syllabus supplies it.

Worked example. Class A: median 62, IQR 18. Class B: median 58, IQR 9. Compare.

Class A has the higher typical score (median 62 vs 58), but its
results are more spread out (IQR 18 vs 9), so Class B is more
consistent even though its middle score is lower.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Averages) Find the mean and range of 12, 15, 11, 19, 13. Answer: mean = 70/5 = 14; range = 19 − 11 = 8.
  2. (Frequency table) Values 1, 2, 3 with frequencies 4, 7, 9. Find the mean. Answer: (4 + 14 + 27)/20 = 45/20 = 2.25.
  3. (Median) Find the median of 2, 4, 4, 6, 9, 10. Answer: (4 + 6)/2 = 5.
  4. (Pie chart) A sector of 90° represents 15 people. Find the total. Answer: 15 × 360/90 = 60.
  5. (Cumulative frequency) For 80 values, where do you read the median? Answer: At cumulative frequency 40, reading across to the curve and down to the axis.
  6. (Histogram) A bar of width 5 has frequency density 4. Find its frequency. Answer: 5 × 4 = 20.
  7. (Frequency density) Class 30–50 has frequency 24. Find the frequency density. Answer: 24/20 = 1.2.
  8. (Compare) Two runners' times: A median 42 s, IQR 3 s; B median 40 s, IQR 8 s. Compare. Answer: B is faster typically (lower median) but less consistent (larger IQR); A is more reliable.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Median without ordering: the median is the middle of the ordered list. Forgetting to sort is the commonest data-handling error.
  • Even-count median: average the two middle values; do not pick one of them.
  • Grouped mean: use midpoints and label the answer an estimate — the midpoint is not the actual mean of the class.
  • Histogram heights: the vertical axis is frequency density, not frequency; area is the frequency. Reading the height as the frequency is the classic histogram error.
  • Cumulative frequency positions: plot against upper class boundaries and read the median at n/2 (not (n+1)/2 on the graph).
  • Pie chart arithmetic: check that the angles sum to 360° before answering the next part.
  • IQR direction: IQR = upper − lower quartile; a negative IQR means the quartiles are swapped.
  • Comparison claims: quote actual values ("median 62 vs 58"), not "better" without evidence.

Equations and symbols

Seven formulas cover the whole paper: the three averages with their range and interquartile range, the two histogram relations, and the pie-chart angle. Every one carries the same mark-scheme requirement — substitute, then state the answer in the units of the data, not as a bare number.

mean = sum of values / number of values Key: mean = the arithmetic average, in the same units as the data; sum of values = the total of every reading; number of values = how many readings there are. Uses every value, so one outlier moves it.

median = the value at position (n + 1)/2 in cumulative order Key: n = the number of values; the position is a count through the ordered list, not a value. For an even n the position falls between two values, so average them — picking one of the two is the commonest lost mark.

mode = the value with the highest frequency Key: mode = the most frequent value, in the same units as the data; for grouped data it is the modal class. The only average available for categorical data.

range = largest - smallest Key: largest and smallest = the extreme values of the data set; the range is their difference, in the data's units. It uses only two values, so a single outlier destroys it.

IQR = Q3 - Q1 Key: IQR = interquartile range, the spread of the middle 50% of the data (same units); Q3 = upper quartile at the 75% position; Q1 = lower quartile at the 25% position. A negative IQR means the quartiles have been swapped.

IQR = 68 - 42 = 26 marks Key: 68 = Q3, the mark at the 75% position; 42 = Q1, the mark at the 25% position; 26 marks = the IQR. Interpret it in words: the middle half of the students scored within 26 marks of each other.

frequency density = frequency / class width Key: frequency density = the height of the bar (no units, since it is a count divided by a width); frequency = the number of readings in the class; class width = upper boundary minus lower boundary (in the data's units). Use it only when the class widths differ — with equal widths the height may be the frequency.

frequency = frequency density x class width (area of the bar) Key: the same relation rearranged; reading a histogram backwards means measuring a bar's width and height and multiplying. In a histogram it is the area, never the height, that represents the frequency.

angle = (frequency/total) × 360° Key: frequency = the count in the sector; total = the total count for the whole chart; angle in degrees, and the sectors must sum to 360°. To go the other way, total = frequency × 360/angle.

mean = sum of (value x frequency) / sum of frequencies Key: value = each reading, or the midpoint of a class for grouped data (same units); frequency = how many times it occurs. With midpoints the answer is labelled an estimate, because the midpoint stands in for every value in the class.

title: A Level Physics: Electric Fields and Capacitance
content:
A Level Physics: Electric Fields and Capacitance

Electric fields are the invisible architecture around every charge: the reason a balloon sticks to a wall, the reason a capacitor can store energy in a camera flash, the reason lightning finds a path. This note builds the topic from zero: what a field is and how field lines encode it, uniform and radial fields with their formulas, Coulomb's law and electric potential, and then capacitance — what it means to store charge, where the energy lives, and how a capacitor discharges exponentially. Every formula is derived or justified, and every calculation type is worked in full.

Electric fields and field lines

A field is a region where a force acts on a suitable object: an electric field exerts a force on a charge. Field lines are the map, drawn with three rules: they point in the direction of the force on a positive charge; their density indicates field strength (closer lines, stronger field); and they never cross. A positive point charge has lines radiating outward; a negative charge has them pointing inward; between two parallel plates the lines are equally spaced and parallel — a uniform field.

  • Uniform field: same magnitude and direction everywhere (between charged plates).
  • Radial field: strength falls with distance, direction along the radius (around a point charge or sphere).

Uniform electric fields

Between parallel plates separated by distance d with potential difference V, the field strength is constant:

E = V/d        (V m⁻¹ or N C⁻¹)

force on a charge in the field: F = Q E
so the acceleration of a particle of mass m: a = QE/m

The analogy: the field is a slope; a charge is a ball. Between parallel plates the slope is uniform, so the ball accelerates steadily — exactly like projectile motion with gravity replaced by QE, which is why electron beams deflect in parabolic arcs between deflection plates.

Worked example. Two plates 4.0 cm apart have a p.d. of 200 V. An electron enters the field.

E = V/d = 200/0.040 = 5000 V m⁻¹
force: F = eE = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 5000 = 8.0 × 10⁻¹⁶ N
acceleration: a = F/m_e = 8.0 × 10⁻¹⁶/9.11 × 10⁻³¹
            = 8.8 × 10¹⁴ m s⁻²  (toward the positive plate)

Coulomb's law: force between point charges

F = Q1 Q2 / (4 π ε₀ r²)

ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹ (permittivity of free space)
1/(4 π ε₀) = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²
r = separation between the charges (m)

The law is an inverse-square law like gravitation, but with two crucial differences: the force can attract or repel (like charges repel), and the constant is enormously larger. The 10³⁶ ratio between electric and gravitational forces between two protons is why gravity dominates the cosmos while electricity dominates chemistry.

Worked example. Two charges of +3.0 μC and −2.0 μC are 0.15 m apart in air. Find the force.

F = k Q1 Q2/r² = 8.99 × 10⁹ x (3.0 × 10⁻⁶ × 2.0 × 10⁻⁶)/0.15²
  = 8.99 × 10⁹ × 6.0 × 10⁻¹²/0.0225
  = 0.0539/0.0225 = 2.4 N  (attractive)

Electric field of a point charge

From Coulomb's law, the field strength at distance r from a point charge Q is the force per unit charge:

E = Q / (4 π ε₀ r²)        (N C⁻¹)

Compare with gravitational field strength g = GM/r²: same inverse-square shape, different constant and source. Field strength is a vector (direction is the force on a positive charge); field lines are denser near the charge, matching the 1/r² fall.

Worked example. Find the field strength 0.20 m from a +5.0 nC charge.

E = k Q/r² = 8.99 × 10⁹ × 5.0 × 10⁻⁹/0.040
  = 44.95/0.040 = 1.1 × 10³ N C⁻¹ (away from the charge)

Electric potential

Potential is the potential energy per unit charge at a point in a field, measured relative to infinity:

V = Q / (4 π ε₀ r)        (volts, J C⁻¹)

work done moving a charge: W = Q ΔV
relation to field strength: E = - dV/dr  (field is the
potential gradient; the minus sign means E points toward
decreasing potential)

The potential around a positive charge is positive and falls with distance; around a negative charge it is negative and rises toward zero at infinity. Equipotential surfaces are perpendicular to field lines — no work is done moving a charge along one.

Worked example. Find the potential 0.50 m from a −4.0 nC charge and the work needed to move a +2.0 nC charge there from infinity.

V = k Q/r = 8.99 × 10⁹ x (-4.0 × 10⁻⁹)/0.50 = -71.9 V
W = Q ΔV = 2.0 × 10⁻⁹ x (-71.9 - 0) = -1.4 × 10⁻⁷ J
The negative work means the field does the work - the charges attract.

Capacitors and capacitance

A capacitor stores charge on two conductors separated by an insulator. Its capacitance is the charge stored per volt:

C = Q/V        farad (F); 1 F = 1 C V⁻¹

parallel plates: C = ε₀ epsilon_r A/d

epsilon_r = relative permittivity of the dielectric,
A = plate area (m²), d = plate separation (m)

The analogy: a capacitor is a tank for charge, and capacitance is the tank's width — a wide tank (large C) holds more charge for the same pressure (voltage). The dielectric matters: inserting a material with ε_r > 1 (typically 2–10) multiplies the capacitance because the molecules polarise and reduce the effective field between the plates.

Worked example. A parallel-plate capacitor has plates of area 0.020 m² separated by 0.10 mm of air. Find C.

C = ε₀ A/d = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² × 0.020/1.0 × 10⁻⁴
  = 1.77 × 10⁻¹³/1.0 × 10⁻⁴ = 1.77 × 10⁻⁹ F = 1.8 nF

Combining capacitors reverses the resistor rules: capacitors in parallel add (C = C₁ + C₂ — bigger plates), while in series the reciprocals add (1/C = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂).

Worked example (series). Find the total capacitance of 4.0 μF and 12.0 μF in series.

1/C = 1/4.0 + 1/12.0 = 0.25 + 0.0833 = 0.333
C = 3.0 uF   (always smaller than the smallest capacitor)

Energy stored in a capacitor

Charging a capacitor means pushing charge onto a conductor that already repels it — the voltage rises as charge accumulates, so the work done is the area under the Q–V graph, a triangle:

W = (1/2) Q V = (1/2) C V² = Q²/(2C)

The energy is stored in the electric field between the plates. The Q–V graph is a straight line through the origin for a fixed capacitor; the stored energy is the triangular area beneath it — which is why the factor is ½ and not 1.

Worked example. A 100 μF capacitor is charged to 12 V. Find the energy stored and the charge.

Q = C V = 100 × 10⁻⁶ × 12 = 1.2 × 10⁻³ C
W = (1/2) C V² = 0.5 × 100 × 10⁻⁶ × 144 = 7.2 × 10⁻³ J
  = 7.2 mJ

Discharging a capacitor

A capacitor discharging through a resistor follows an exponential decay, like radioactive decay:

Q = Q0 e^(-t/RC)        V = V⁰ e^(-t/RC)        I = I0 e^(-t/RC)

time constant tau = RC   (seconds)
after one tau: about 37% of the starting value remains
after five tau: under 1% remains (effectively discharged)

Worked example. A 470 μF capacitor charged to 9.0 V discharges through 2.2 kΩ. Find the time constant and the voltage after 2.0 s.

tau = R C = 2200 × 470 × 10⁻⁶ = 1.03 s
V = 9.0 x e^(-2.0/1.03) = 9.0 x e^(-1.94)
  = 9.0 × 0.144 = 1.29 V  (1.3 V, 2 s.f.)

The discharge graph questions are standard: plot ln V against t and the gradient is −1/(RC); the area under a current–time graph is the charge that left the capacitor.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Field strength) Two plates 2.0 cm apart have a p.d. of 100 V. Find E. Answer: E = V/d = 100/0.020 = 5000 V m⁻¹.
  2. (Coulomb) Two +2.0 μC charges are 0.10 m apart. Find the force between them. Answer: F = 8.99 × 10⁹ × (2.0 × 10⁻⁶)²/(0.10)² = 8.99 × 10⁹ × 4.0 × 10⁻¹²/0.010 = 3.6 N, repulsive.
  3. (Potential) Explain why electric potential, unlike field strength, is a scalar. Answer: Potential is energy per unit charge, and energy is a scalar; it has sign (positive near positive charge) but no direction. Field strength is a vector because force has direction.
  4. (Capacitance) A capacitor stores 5.0 mC at 25 V. Find its capacitance. Answer: C = Q/V = 5.0 × 10⁻³/25 = 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ F = 200 μF.
  5. (Dielectric) Explain why inserting a dielectric increases capacitance. Answer: The dielectric's molecules polarise, creating an opposing field that reduces the net field for the same charge; since V = Ed falls while Q stays, C = Q/V rises (multiplied by ε_r).
  6. (Energy) A 2.0 μF capacitor is charged to 50 V. Find the energy stored. Answer: W = ½CV² = ½ × 2.0 × 10⁻⁶ × 2500 = 2.5 × 10⁻³ J = 2.5 mJ.
  7. (Discharge) A 2.0 kΩ resistor discharges a 100 μF capacitor. Find the time constant and the percentage remaining after 0.60 s. Answer: τ = RC = 2000 × 100 × 10⁻⁶ = 0.20 s; after 0.60 s = 3τ, remaining fraction = e⁻³ = 0.050, so 5.0%.
  8. (Graph) State how the gradient of a ln V against t graph relates to the time constant. Answer: ln V = ln V₀ − t/RC, so the gradient is −1/(RC) = −1/τ.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • V/d in centimetres: d must be in metres; 4.0 cm is 0.040 m, and the classic factor-of-100 error follows.
  • Charge units: μC = 10⁻⁶ C, nC = 10⁻⁹ C. Substituting μC as C inflates answers by a million.
  • Sign conventions: field strength is defined by the force on a positive charge; around a negative charge the lines point inward. State directions explicitly.
  • E = V/d only in uniform fields: between plates yes; around a point charge use E = kQ/r².
  • Series/parallel reversal: capacitors behave oppositely to resistors — series gives the reciprocals, parallel simply adds.
  • Energy factor ½: W = ½QV, not QV — the voltage rises during charging, so averaging matters. Forgetting the ½ doubles the answer.
  • Time-constant confusion: τ = RC in seconds means R in Ω and C in farads; the pair must be SI.
  • Discharge graph linearisation: a plot of V against t is a curve; only ln V against t is a straight line whose gradient gives −1/τ.
  • Precision: 2 or 3 s.f. with units (N, V m⁻¹, F, J, s); use ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹ from the data sheet.

title: AS Level Computer Science: Hardware, Logic Gates and Boolean Algebra
content:
Hardware, Logic Gates and Boolean Algebra

Cambridge International AS & A Level Computer Science 9618 (2026): this note follows syllabus statements 3.1, 3.2 and 15.2. It covers computer components and systems, gate functions and representations, Boolean algebra, adders, SR/JK flip-flops and Karnaugh maps. CPU architecture and the fetch-execute cycle are treated separately under statement 4.1.

1. Computer systems and embedded devices (3.1)

A computer system receives data, processes it, stores data or instructions, and produces output. Input devices convert user actions or measured physical quantities into usable data. A microphone converts sound into an electrical signal; a touchscreen both detects touch input and displays visual output. Output devices present processed results: speakers convert electrical signals into sound, while a laser printer forms a page image and fixes toner to paper. A 3D printer builds an object layer by layer from a digital model. A virtual-reality headset presents a close stereoscopic display and may sense head movement so the scene can respond.

Secondary storage keeps programs and files when power is removed. A magnetic hard disk stores data magnetically on rotating platters and uses moving heads; it offers high capacity but is vulnerable to mechanical shock. Solid-state flash storage stores charge in memory cells and has no moving parts, so it is fast and shock-resistant, though capacity costs more and cells have finite write endurance. An optical reader/writer uses a laser to read or record a disc. Primary memory is directly available to the processor while programs run; it is not a substitute for persistent secondary storage.

An embedded system is a computer built into a larger product to perform a specific or limited set of functions, often for monitoring or control. Benefits include compact size, low power use, reliable repeated operation and lower cost than a general-purpose computer. Limitations include less flexibility, difficulty upgrading or repairing it, and the risk that a failure affects the whole device. Suitability depends on the product and the consequences of failure.

2. Primary memory and buffers (3.1)

RAM is volatile read/write primary memory: its contents are lost when power is removed. It holds programs and data currently in use. ROM is non-volatile and holds instructions that must remain available, such as start-up firmware. Do not confuse ROM with secondary storage: ROM is primary memory with a persistent purpose.

  • PROM can be programmed once after manufacture; it cannot then be erased and rewritten.
  • EPROM can be erased using ultraviolet light and programmed again; conventionally the chip must be removed from its circuit for erasure.
  • EEPROM can be erased and reprogrammed electrically, often while installed. Flash memory is a widely used form of electrically erasable non-volatile memory.

SRAM stores each bit using a bistable circuit and does not need periodic refresh while power is present. It is fast but uses more circuit area per bit, so it is comparatively expensive and lower-density; it is used where speed matters, such as cache. DRAM stores each bit as charge in a capacitor. Charge leaks, so it must be refreshed periodically. DRAM is slower than SRAM but simpler per bit, cheaper and higher-density, making it suitable for main memory. Both SRAM and DRAM are volatile.

A buffer is a temporary memory area holding data during transfer between devices or processes that operate at different rates or transfer different-sized blocks. A printer buffer queues output while the printer works more slowly than the processor can send data. Buffering smooths transfer and lets the sending process continue; it is not permanent storage and does not itself make the receiving device faster.

3. Monitoring, control, sensors and feedback (3.1)

A monitoring system samples sensor readings and records, displays or reports them. It observes a process but does not automatically change it. A control system uses sensor input, compares the measured state with a required condition, and can send an output to an actuator. A temperature sensor may measure a greenhouse; a heater is an actuator. Pressure, infrared and sound sensors are further examples named in the syllabus.

In a feedback control loop, the system measures the result of its action and uses that new measurement to decide what to do next. For a thermostat, the target temperature is compared with the measured temperature: if the room is too cool, the controller switches the heater on; once the target is reached, it switches it off. Feedback helps the controller respond to changing conditions. A one-way system that acts without measuring the result is open-loop, not feedback control.

4. Logic gates and representations (3.2)

A logic gate maps binary input value(s) to a binary output. A NOT gate has one input; the other gates in this syllabus have two inputs. AND is 1 only when both inputs are 1; OR is 1 when at least one input is 1; XOR (EOR) is 1 when exactly one input is 1, so it is 0 when inputs match. NAND is NOT(AND), and NOR is NOT(OR). The prime mark means NOT and parentheses show which operation is complemented.

ABNOT AANDORNANDNORXOR
00100110
01101101
10001101
11011000

The same logic can be represented as a problem, Boolean expression, circuit diagram or truth table. Translate carefully: identify inputs, write the operation and parentheses, then evaluate every input combination. For Y=(A OR B) AND NOT C, evaluate the OR and NOT sub-expressions before the final AND. A circuit must preserve this grouping; a truth table must include all 2ⁿ rows for n inputs and show the output for each row.

5. Boolean algebra and De Morgan's laws (15.2)

Boolean algebra works with values 0 and 1. Here A·B means A AND B, A+B means A OR B, and A' means NOT A. These symbols are not ordinary arithmetic: 1+1=1 because 1 OR 1 is 1. Useful identities include A+0=A, A·1=A, A+A=A, A·A=A, A+A'=1 and A·A'=0. Use identities to simplify a circuit without changing its output for any input.

De Morgan's laws are (A·B)' = A' + B' and (A+B)' = A'·B'. To complement a bracketed expression, complement each input and change AND to OR or OR to AND. Example: (A·(B+C))' = A' + (B'·C'). Check the scope of the complement: A·B' is not the same as (A·B)'. Absorption identities include A+A·B=A and A·(A+B)=A. A truth-table check can confirm a proposed simplification.

6. Adders: half adder and full adder (15.2)

A half adder adds two one-bit inputs A and B. Its Sum output is S=A XOR B; its Carry output is C=A AND B. Thus 0+0 gives S=0,C=0; 0+1 and 1+0 give S=1,C=0; 1+1 gives S=0,C=1. The carry is passed into the next binary column. A half adder has no carry-in input.

A full adder also accepts carry-in Cin. Sum is 1 when an odd number of A, B and Cin are 1: S=A XOR B XOR Cin. Carry-out is 1 when at least two of the three inputs are 1: Cout=(A·B)+(A·Cin)+(B·Cin). For example, 1+1+1 has binary total 3, so S=1 and Cout=1. Keep Sum and Carry as separate outputs; exchanging their gate functions is a common error.

7. Flip-flops and data storage (15.2)

A flip-flop is a bistable circuit: it retains one of two states and therefore stores one bit. The state is retained until an input causes a change. The syllabus includes SR and JK flip-flops. State the circuit convention when interpreting an SR truth table: for a common active-high SR latch made from NOR gates, S=1 sets Q to 1, R=1 resets Q to 0, and S=R=0 holds the previous state. S=R=1 is forbidden for this implementation because it forces both NOR outputs low and violates the complementary-output condition. Other gate implementations may use different active levels; check the diagram before applying this table.

A JK flip-flop removes the SR latch's forbidden input combination: J=0,K=0 holds the current state; J=1,K=0 sets Q=1; J=0,K=1 resets Q=0; J=1,K=1 toggles Q to its complement. Flip-flops provide storage elements in sequential circuits. Distinguish stored state, which depends on previous state, from a combinational gate output, which depends only on current inputs.

8. Karnaugh maps (K-maps) (15.2)

A Karnaugh map is a visual way to simplify a Boolean function from its truth table. Place output values in cells labelled by input combinations. Arrange row and column labels in Gray-code order, for example 00, 01, 11, 10, so neighbouring cells differ in exactly one variable. Groups may wrap across opposite edges because those cells are adjacent; diagonal cells are not adjacent.

Group adjacent 1s in rectangles containing a power of two cells (1, 2, 4, 8, and so on). Use the largest useful groups, and overlap groups if that reduces the expression. Each group gives a product term containing only variables that stay constant throughout the group; variables that change are eliminated. OR the terms together. Every 1 must be covered, and do not include a 0 unless the question explicitly provides a don't-care condition. In a three-input map, minterms 1, 3, 5 and 7 are exactly the rows where C=1; they form a group of four and simplify to C. A K-map can make a multi-variable pattern easier to see than repeated algebra, but the final expression must still match every specified row.

Exam method and common checks

  1. Write input labels and output(s) before filling a truth table; for three inputs list all eight combinations exactly once.
  2. For a circuit, follow wires gate by gate and record intermediate outputs where useful.
  3. For Boolean simplification, preserve parentheses and complement scope; test the result on a truth table when uncertain.
  4. For an adder, calculate the binary total and report Sum and Carry separately.
  5. For a K-map, use Gray-code order, group adjacent 1s in powers of two, and eliminate only variables that change within a group.
  6. For a control-system scenario, name the sensor input, controller decision, actuator output and (if present) feedback measurement.

Syllabus basis: Cambridge International AS & A Level Computer Science 9618 syllabus for 2026, statements 3.1, 3.2 and 15.2; topic boundaries are stated at the start of this note.

Worked example: simplifying a function and checking the answer

Simplify F = A'BC + AB'C + ABC' + ABC. Start by grouping terms that differ in one variable. A'BC + ABC differ only in A, so they reduce to BC. AB'C + ABC reduce to AC, and ABC' + ABC reduce to AB. The function is therefore F = BC + AC + AB, the majority function: the output is 1 when at least two of the three inputs are 1. Check that on the original expression: the rows that should give 1 are 011, 101, 110 and 111, which match BC, AC, AB and all three together.

Now check a simplification made with De Morgan's laws rather than a K-map. Simplify Y = ((A + B) multiplied by C)'. Complement the whole expression: the complement of an AND is an OR of the complements, so Y = (A + B)' + C'. Then complement the bracket: (A + B)' = A' multiplied by B'. The result is Y = A'B' + C'. Test one row to be sure: with A = 1, B = 0, C = 0, the original gives (1 multiplied by 0)' = 1, and the simplification gives (0 multiplied by 1) + 1 = 1. A single check row does not prove the simplification, but it catches the common errors of dropping a complement or changing the wrong operator.

Typical mistakes

  • Treating XOR as OR. OR is 1 when at least one input is 1; XOR is 1 only when the inputs differ, so it is 0 for 1 and 1. Read the gate symbol, not just the name.
  • Losing the bracket scope in a complement. A multiplied by B' is not the same as (A multiplied by B)'. Write out the grouping before applying De Morgan, and complement the whole bracketed expression, not one term of it.
  • Swapping Sum and Carry in an adder. Sum is the XOR of the inputs; Carry is the AND, or for a full adder the majority of A, B and carry-in. For 1 plus 1 the Sum is 0 and the Carry is 1, which is the opposite of what a careless answer gives.
  • Breaking the Gray-code order in a K-map. Row and column labels run 00, 01, 11, 10 so that neighbouring cells differ by one variable. Placing labels in binary order groups cells that are not adjacent, and the simplified expression is then wrong.
  • Grouping diagonal cells or a non-power-of-two rectangle. Groups must be 1, 2, 4, 8 and so on adjacent cells, and groups may wrap around the edges. Each group contributes a term containing only the variables that stay constant.
  • Forgetting that S = R = 1 is forbidden in an SR latch. Both outputs would go low, which breaks the complementary-output condition. The JK flip-flop removes this state by toggling when J = K = 1.

Exam-style questions

  1. Simplify F = A + A'B. Answer: F = A + B. Either factor out the terms as (A + A')(A + B) using the distributive law, since A + A' = 1, or note that when A = 0 the expression is B and when A = 1 it is 1, which is exactly A + B.
  2. Use a K-map to simplify F(A, B, C) = the sum of minterms 0, 2, 4 and 6. Answer: the rows 000, 010, 100 and 110 all have C = 0 and the other two variables vary, so the four cells form one group and the only constant is C = 0. F = C'.
  3. State the Sum and Carry-out of a full adder when A = 1, B = 1 and carry-in = 1. Answer: the total is 3, which is 11 in binary, so Sum = 1 and Carry-out = 1.
  4. Write the truth table for Y = (A multiplied by B) + C' and give the output when A = 1, B = 0, C = 1. Answer: the expression is 1 when both A and B are 1, or when C is 0. With A = 1, B = 0, C = 1, the AND term is 0 and C' is 0, so Y = 0.
  5. Explain how a JK flip-flop differs from an SR latch. Answer: a JK flip-flop removes the forbidden input combination: with J = 1 and K = 1 the output toggles to its complement instead of forcing both outputs low. With J = 1, K = 0 it sets, with J = 0, K = 1 it resets, and with J = 0, K = 0 it holds its state, so it stores one bit until clocked again.
  6. A greenhouse heater is switched by a control system. Identify the sensor, actuator and feedback, and explain why the system is closed loop. Answer: the sensor is a temperature sensor, the actuator is the heater, and the feedback is the measured temperature compared with the target. It is closed loop because the system measures the result of its own action and changes its output accordingly, unlike a monitoring system that only records readings.

title: Coordinate Geometry — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Coordinate Geometry

Mathematics — AS (9709). Gradient m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁). From ax + by + c = 0, the gradient is −a/b.

Key areas to revise

  • Gradients and Equations of Lines
  • Parallel and Perpendicular
  • Midpoint and Distance
  • Intersections and Bisectors

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

### Worked example For A(1, 2) and B(5, 10), the gradient is (10 − 2)/(5 − 1) = 2. The midpoint is ((1 + 5)/2, (2 + 10)/2) = (3, 6). The length AB = √(4² + 8²) = √80 = 4√5 ≈ 8.94. The line through A with gradient 2 is y − 2 = 2(x − 1), which simplifies to y = 2x and passes through B.

Key points to remember

Gradient m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁). Parallel lines have equal gradients, and perpendicular lines satisfy m₁ × m₂ = −1. The midpoint of AB is found by averaging the coordinates, and the length of AB comes from Pythagoras applied to the differences in x and y.

Write a line as y = mx + c, or use y − y₁ = m(x − x₁) when you have a point. For a circle in the form (x − a)² + (y − b)² = r², the centre is (a, b) and the radius is r; complete the square to put a general equation into this form. A tangent meets the radius at right angles, so find the radius gradient first and take its negative reciprocal.
