title: Permutations and Combinations — Study Notes
content:
Permutations and Combinations

The Multiplication Principle

If a task is done in successive stages with m, n, ... choices at each stage, the total is the product of the choices. This underpins every counting problem: a menu with 4 starters and 6 mains gives 24 meals.

Permutations — Order Matters

The number of ways of arranging r objects from n distinct objects is

  • ⁿPᵣ = n!/(n − r)!

The number of arrangements of n distinct objects is n!. Five books on a shelf: 5! = 120 ways.

Combinations — Order Irrelevant

The number of ways of choosing r objects from n is

  • ⁿCᵣ = n!/(r!(n − r)!)

Choosing a committee of 3 from 8 people: ⁸C₃ = 56. Choosing is not arranging — a committee has no internal order, so we divide by r!.

Restricted Permutations

  • No two specified people adjacent: arrange everyone else, then slot the restricted people into gaps. For n people with 2 who must be separated: arrange the other n − 2 (ways), then place 2 people in distinct gaps between them.
  • Specified people together: bundle them as one item, arrange the bundle, then multiply by the internal arrangements of the bundle.
  • Words with repeated letters: divide by the factorials of each repeat count. ARRANGE has 7 letters with A appearing twice and R twice, so 7!/(2!·2!) = 1260.

Combinations with Constraints

  • At least / at most: split into cases and add. A team of 5 from 6 boys and 5 girls with at least 3 girls is ⁵C₃⁶C₂ + ⁵C₄⁶C₁ + ⁵C₅⁶C₀.
  • "Must include" pairs: choose the required items first, then choose freely from the remainder.

Exam tips: state whether a scenario is a permutation or combination before computing anything. Most lost marks come from counting an arrangement where order does not actually matter. Check every answer against a small case you can enumerate by hand.

Exam method: arrangements and selections

The number of arrangements of r objects from n distinct objects is nPr = n!/(n − r)!. The number of ways to select r objects from n, where order does not matter, is nCr = n!/(r!(n − r)!). Ask first whether order matters, because that decides which formula to use.

Arrangements with restrictions are solved by treating a block as one object or by placing the restricted items first. For example, if two people must sit together, treat them as one unit and multiply by 2 for their internal order.

Use the identity nCr = nC(n − r) to check answers, and remember that nC0 = nCn = 1. Pascal's identity nCr = (n−1)C(r−1) + (n−1)Cr links the two formulae.

When a question has several groups with separate conditions, count each part on its own and multiply the results, provided the parts are independent.

Exam cue: Write the formula with the numbers substituted before simplifying, since method marks are given for the correct expression.

title: Exam technique: Integration
content:
### What earns the marks
For indefinite integrals, each term raised correctly plus the constant earns full marks. For definite integrals, the antiderivative quoted earns one mark and the correct upper-minus-lower evaluation earns the next. For area and curve-finding, the limits or the given point used earns the final mark.
### Traps
Error: constant of integration omitted. Correction: +c always for indefinite. Error: limits subtracted backwards. Correction: upper minus lower. Error: power rule inverted on roots. Correction: root x is x to the half, integral goes up.
### Worked example
Find the integral of 6x² − 4x⁻³. Raise each power by one and divide by the new power: 6x² becomes 2x³, and −4x⁻³ becomes 2x⁻² because (−4)/(−2) = 2. Add the constant: 2x³ + 2x⁻² + c. Check by differentiating: 6x² + (−4)x⁻³, which matches the original.
### Check yourself
Evaluate the definite integral of 2x + 1 from 1 to 3. The antiderivative is x² + x, giving (9 + 3) − (1 + 1) = 10. Write both the antiderivative and the subtraction on the paper, because the method mark depends on them.

title: Integration — Study Notes
content:
Integration

Edexcel International A Level Mathematics — Pure Mathematics 1 (WMA11), sat at AS. Integration reverses differentiation. Questions want a general antiderivative, a specific curve through a point, a definite integral, or an area. Most lost marks come from the constant of integration, the limits, and the sign of a region below the axis.

Start from a question

A curve passes through (1, 1) and has dy/dx = 3√x − 2/x² for x > 0.

  1. Find y in terms of x.
  2. Evaluate the integral of (3√x − 2/x²) from x = 1 to x = 4.
  3. Find the area between the curve y = x² − 4 and the x-axis, from x = 0 to x = 3.

Part 1. Integrate term by term: 3x^(1/2) gives 2x^(3/2), and −2x⁻² gives 2x⁻¹. So y = 2x^(3/2) + 2/x + c. Substituting (1, 1) gives 2 + 2 + c = 1, so c = −3 and y = 2x^(3/2) + 2/x − 3.

Part 2. The antiderivative at 4 is 16 + ½ = 33/2. At 1 it is 4 = 8/2. The definite integral is 33/2 − 8/2 = 25/2. No +c is needed.

Part 3. The curve y = x² − 4 crosses the x-axis at x = 2. Between 0 and 2 it lies below the axis, so that part of the integral is negative. The area is |∫ from 0 to 2| + ∫ from 2 to 3. The first integral is [x³/3 − 4x] from 0 to 2 = −16/3, so its area is 16/3. The second is [x³/3 − 4x] from 2 to 3 = −3 − (−16/3) = 7/3. The total is 23/3. Taking the integral from 0 to 3 directly gives −3, which is the wrong answer for an area.

Indefinite integrals

∫axⁿ dx = a xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + c, for n ≠ −1. Add one to the power, divide by the new power, and write +c. Multiply out brackets and rewrite roots as powers first. Example: ∫(x − 2)(x + 4) dx = ∫(x² + 2x − 8) dx = x³/3 + x² − 8x + c.

Area between two curves

Find where the curves meet, then integrate the upper curve minus the lower curve between those x-values. Example: y = 2x and y = x² meet at x = 0 and x = 2. Between them 2x ≥ x², so the area is ∫ from 0 to 2 of (2x − x²) dx = [x² − x³/3] from 0 to 2 = 4/3.

Trapezium rule

With strips of width h and ordinates y₀, y₁, …, yₙ, the estimate is (h/2)[y₀ + 2(y₁ + … + yₙ₋₁) + yₙ]. Example: ∫ from 0 to 2 of (x² + 1) dx with h = 1. The ordinates are 1, 2 and 5, so the estimate is ½(1 + 4 + 5) = 5. The exact value is 14/3. The curve bends upwards, so the estimate is too large.

Traps that cost marks

  • Integrating a product term by term without expanding the brackets first.
  • Writing +c in a definite integral, or forgetting it in an indefinite one.
  • Subtracting the limits in the wrong order.
  • Quoting a negative answer for an area that lies below the x-axis.

Worked example: a definite integral

Evaluate the integral of (2x + 1) from x = 1 to x = 3. The indefinite integral is x² + x, so the value is [x² + x] between 1 and 3, which is (9 + 3) − (1 + 1) = 12 − 2 = 10. The constant of integration cancels when the limits are substituted, so it is not written in a definite integral. Substitute the upper limit first and subtract the lower limit, and do not evaluate the two ends separately and then add them.

Worked example: integrating a linear bracket

The integral of (2x + 1)³ with respect to x is (2x + 1)⁴ ÷ 8 + c. You can check this by differentiating: the chain rule gives 4 × 2 × (2x + 1)³ ÷ 8, which equals (2x + 1)³. Dividing by the derivative of the inside, here 2, is the reverse of the chain rule and is the quick method to use in the exam.

title: Communication and Networking — Study Notes
content:
`# Communication and Networking

Transmission

  • Serial: one bit at a time — cheaper, reliable over distance
  • Parallel: multiple bits simultaneously — fast but suffers skew and crosstalk over long runs
  • Direction: simplex (one way), half-duplex (alternating), full-duplex (both ways)

Packets and Protocols

Data splits into packets with header (addresses, sequence) and trailer (checksum). A protocol is an agreed rule set — without one, devices cannot interpret signals.

  • TCP/IP stack: application → transport → network → link
  • HTTP/HTTPS: web transfer; HTTPS encrypts with TLS
  • FTP: file transfer; SMTP/POP3/IMAP: email

Network Types

  • LAN: small site, privately owned; WAN: large geographic scale (the internet)
  • Topologies: bus, star, mesh (star is most common — central switch)

Hardware

Routers join networks by IP; switches forward frames by MAC within a LAN; gateways translate protocols.

Client-Server vs Peer-to-Peer

Client-server: central services, easy administration, single point of failure. P2P: every node shares files directly — cheap, hard to manage (torrents, blockchain).

Exam tips: explain packet switching with header/trailer details; justify protocol choice per application (email vs streaming).

Network topologies and hardware

In a star topology every device connects to a central switch. If one cable or device fails, the others keep working, but if the central switch fails the whole network stops. In a bus topology all devices share one cable, which is cheap but means a break in the cable disables the network.

A switch connects devices within a local area network (LAN) and sends each frame only to the device it is addressed to, using MAC addresses. A router connects separate networks together and forwards packets using IP addresses. A wireless access point lets wireless devices join a wired LAN.

Exam tip: when comparing topologies, state what happens when one device fails and when the central device fails. Those two cases are the usual differentiators.

title: Acid-base Equilibria A2 Level Chemistry Revision Notes
content:
Acid-base Equilibria A2 Level Chemistry

Edexcel International A Level Chemistry WCH14 Topic 14 Acid-base Equilibria builds upon GCSE and AS concepts by exploring proton transfer, the quantitative treatment of strong and weak acids and bases, pH scales, buffer solutions, titration curves, and acid dissociation constants.

Bronsed-Lowry Theory and Conjugate Pairs

Acid-base reactions involve the transfer of protons. A Brnsted-Lowry acid is defined as a proton donor, and a Brnsted-Lowry base is defined as a proton acceptor. When an acid donates a proton, it forms its conjugate base. When a base accepts a proton, it forms its conjugate acid. These species form conjugate acid-base pairs that differ by a single proton (H+).

  • Brnsted-Lowry acid: a proton (H+) donor.
  • Brnsted-Lowry base: a proton (H+) acceptor.
  • Conjugate acid-base pair: two species related by the gain or loss of a single proton, written as acid / conjugate base or base / conjugate acid.
  • In the reaction between ethanoic acid and water, CH3COOH and CH3COO- form one pair, while H3O+ and H2O form the other pair.

pH Scale and Calculations

The term pH is defined as the negative logarithm to the base 10 of the hydrogen ion concentration in aqueous solution, expressed mathematically. A ten-fold change in hydrogen ion concentration causes a change of one pH unit.

  • pH definition: pH = −log10[H+]
  • Hydrogen ion concentration from pH: [H+] = 10^(−pH)
  • Ionic product of water, Kw, is defined as Kw = [H+][OH−] with a value of 1.0 × 10^(−14) mol2 dm−6 at 298 K.
  • pKa is defined as −log10(Ka) and pKw is defined as −log10(Kw).
  • For strong bases, calculate pOH = −log10[OH−] and use pH = 14.00 − pOH at 298 K, or use [H+] = Kw / [OH−] before finding the pH.

Worked Example: Calculate the pH of 0.050 mol dm−3 sodium hydroxide at 298 K.

  • Step 1: Identify [OH−] = 0.050 mol dm−3 because NaOH is a strong base and dissociates completely.
  • Step 2: Calculate pOH = −log10(0.050) = 1.30.
  • Step 3: Calculate pH = 14.00 − 1.30 = 12.70.

Strong and Weak Acids and Experimental Analysis

A strong acid dissociates completely in water, meaning the concentration of hydrogen ions equals the concentration of the acid. A weak acid dissociates only partly in water, establishing an equilibrium. The degree of dissociation is much lower for weak acids than for strong acids.

  • Strong acid: dissociates completely, so [H+] = [acid]. For 0.010 mol dm−3 HCl, [H+] = 0.010 mol dm−3 and pH = 2.00.
  • Weak acid: dissociates partially, represented by HA ⇌ H+ + A−.
  • Acid dissociation constant expression: Ka = [H+][A−] / [HA].
  • Experimental analysis involves measuring the pH of a variety of substances, including equimolar solutions of strong and weak acids, strong and weak bases, and salts. Strong acids have much lower pH values than weak acids of the same concentration.
  • Comparing the pH of a strong acid and a weak acid after dilution 10, 100, and 1000 times shows that diluting a strong acid by a factor of 10 increases its pH by 1 unit, whereas diluting a weak acid by a factor of 10 increases its pH by less than 1 unit due to partial re-dissociation of the weak acid.

Worked Example: Calculate the pH of 0.100 mol dm−3 propanoic acid, CH3CH2COOH, given that Ka = 1.35 × 10^(−5) mol dm−3.

  • Step 1: Write the expression Ka = [H+]2 / [HA], assuming [H+] = [A−] and [HA]equilibrium equals initial [HA] because dissociation is very small.
  • Step 2: Rearrange to [H+] = √(Ka × [HA]) = √(1.35 × 10^(−5) × 0.100) = √(1.35 × 10^(−6)) = 1.16 × 10^(−3) mol dm−3.
  • Step 3: Calculate pH = −log10(1.16 × 10^(−3)) = 2.93.

Core Practical 11 and Determining Ka from Experimental Data

Core Practical 11 involves finding the Ka value for a weak acid by measuring the pH of solutions of known concentration, or by using titration methods and half-equivalence points.

  • To calculate Ka for a weak acid from experimental data given the pH of a solution containing a known mass of acid, first calculate the concentration of the acid in mol dm−3.
  • Use [H+] = 10^(−pH) to find the hydrogen ion concentration.
  • Substitute [H+], [OH−] approximations, and remaining undissociated acid concentration into Ka = [H+]2 / [HA].
  • In weak acid-strong base or strong acid-weak base titrations, at the exact point where half the acid is neutralised, [HA] = [A−], which simplifies the buffer equation to pH = pKa, allowing Ka to be determined directly from the pH reading at that volume.

Titration Curves and Indicators

Titration curves plot pH against volume of titrant added. They cover all combinations of strong and weak monoprotic and diprotic acids with bases.

  • Strong acid and strong base curve starts low, has a steep vertical section from pH 3 to 11 at the equivalence point of pH 7.
  • Weak acid and strong base curve starts higher (around pH 3), has a buffer region, and a steep vertical section from pH 7 to 11 with an equivalence point above pH 7.
  • Strong acid and weak base curve has a steep vertical section from pH 3 to 7 with an equivalence point below pH 7.
  • Weak acid and weak base curves show no sharp vertical pH change, making titrations difficult without a pH meter.
  • Diprotic acids show two distinct equivalence points corresponding to the donation of two protons per molecule.
  • Indicator selection: choose an indicator whose pH range falls entirely within the steep vertical section of the titration curve. Phenolphthalein (pH range 8.3 to 10.0) is suitable for weak acid-strong base titrations. Methyl orange (pH range 3.1 to 4.4) is suitable for strong acid-weak base titrations.

Buffer Solutions

A buffer solution is a system that minimises changes in pH when small amounts of acid or alkali are added. An acidic buffer consists of a weak acid and its salt (providing the conjugate base), such as ethanoic acid and sodium ethanoate.

  • Buffer action: when H+ is added, it reacts with the conjugate base (A−) to form undissociated weak acid (HA), removing excess H+. When OH− is added, it reacts with H+ ions (or HA directly) to form water, pulling the equilibrium to the right to replace the H+ ions.
  • Buffer pH calculation formula: pH = pKa + log([A−] / [HA]).
  • To calculate concentrations required to prepare a buffer solution of a given pH, rearrange the buffer formula using target pH, known Ka, and ratio of salt to acid.
  • Biological importance: buffers in cells and in blood, specifically the carbonic acid-hydrogencarbonate system (H2CO3 / HCO3−), maintain blood pH strictly between 7.35 and 7.45.
  • Importance in foods: buffers and acidulants prevent deterioration due to pH changes caused by bacterial or fungal activity, preserving texture and safety.

Typical mistakes

  • Mistake: Assuming weak acids dissociate completely. Correction: Always use Ka expressions and make the standard weak acid approximation [HA]start equals [HA]equilibrium.
  • Mistake: Forgetting that Kw varies with temperature and treating 1.0 × 10^(−14) as universal at all temperatures. Correction: Use 1.0 × 10^(−14) mol2 dm−6 strictly for 298 K unless specified otherwise.
  • Mistake: Selecting methyl orange for a weak acid-strong base titration. Correction: Methyl orange changes colour below pH 7, whereas the equivalence point of a weak acid-strong base titration is above pH 7; use phenolphthalein instead.
  • Mistake: Confusing conjugate acid-base pairs by omitting charges or hydrogen atoms. Correction: Check that pairs differ by exactly one H+ ion.

Exam-style questions

  1. Question: Define a Brnsted-Lowry acid. Answer: A proton donor. Step: State the definition clearly for credit.
  2. Question: Calculate the pH of 0.0200 mol dm−3 hydrochloric acid. Answer: [H+] = 0.0200 mol dm−3, so pH = −log10(0.0200) = 1.70. Step: Recognise complete dissociation of strong acid and apply pH formula.
  3. Question: Write the expression for the acid dissociation constant, Ka, for propanoic acid. Answer: Ka = [H+][CH3CH2COO−] / [CH3CH2COOH]. Step: Include all equilibrium concentrations correctly.
  4. Question: Explain why the pH of a weak acid changes less than that of a strong acid upon 10-fold dilution. Answer: Diluting a weak acid shifts the equilibrium to the right, causing further dissociation which partially compensates for the added water volume. Step: Mention equilibrium shift and partial dissociation.
  5. Question: State the buffer pair present in blood plasma. Answer: H2CO3 and HCO3−. Step: Name carbonic acid and hydrogencarbonate ions.

Use these notes alongside past paper practice questions for Edexcel IAL Chemistry Topic 14. Ensure all formula manipulations for Ka and buffer calculations are practiced thoroughly before moving on to Topic 15 Energetics II.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Weak acid pH, applied to 0.100 mol dm⁻³ ethanoic acid with Ka = 1.74 × 10⁻⁵: [H⁺] = √(Ka × c) = √(1.74 × 10⁻⁶) = 1.32 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³, so pH = 2.88. The square-root shortcut is valid only when dissociation is under about 5%; check that before you use it.
  • Buffer pH, applied to an equimolar ethanoic acid and sodium ethanoate buffer: pH = pKa + log([A⁻] ÷ [HA]). With equal concentrations, pH = pKa = 4.76. Doubling the base raises the pH by log 2, about 0.30 units. Say which ratio you have used.
  • Indicator choice: a strong acid with a strong base needs an indicator that changes within the steep part of the curve, such as methyl orange or phenolphthalein. A weak acid with a strong base ends above pH 7, so phenolphthalein is the usual choice. Methyl orange changes too early for that titration.
  • Mark-scheme phrasing: a weak acid is only partly dissociated, so [H⁺] is much less than the stated acid concentration. State that the dissociation is small before you simplify the expression.

title: Circular Motion and SHM — Study Notes
content:
Circular Motion and SHM

Uniform circular motion

A particle moving in a circle of radius r at constant speed has a constantly changing velocity, because its direction changes. Angular speed ω is the rate of change of angle in radians per second: ω = 2π/T = 2πf. The linear speed is v = ωr.

Centripetal acceleration and force

The acceleration is directed towards the centre: a = v²/r = ω²r. The resultant force providing it is F = mv²/r = mω²r, also towards the centre. This force does no work, because it is always perpendicular to the velocity, so the kinetic energy stays constant.

Example: a particle on a 0.40 m radius with T = 2.0 s has ω = π rad s⁻¹, v = 1.26 m s⁻¹ and a = π² × 0.40 ≈ 3.9 m s⁻².

Simple harmonic motion as projected circular motion

The displacement of a point moving on a circle, projected onto a diameter, is x = x₀ sin ωt (or cos ωt). Its acceleration is a = −ω²x, always opposite to the displacement, so the defining condition for SHM is that acceleration is proportional to and opposite to displacement.

Solutions: x = x₀ sin ωt starts at the centre; x = x₀ cos ωt starts at an extreme. Time period T = 2π/ω.

Velocity and acceleration:

  • v = ±ω√(x₀² − x²); v_max = ωx₀ at the centre
  • a_max = ω²x₀ at the extremes; a = 0 at the centre

Example: a pendulum with x₀ = 0.02 m and f = 0.5 Hz has a_max = (2π × 0.5)² × 0.02 ≈ 0.20 m s⁻².

Energy in SHM

The total energy is E = ½mω²x₀², constant. It is exchanged between kinetic energy (maximum at the centre) and potential energy (maximum at the extremes). Kinetic energy is at a maximum when displacement is zero, not when acceleration is largest.

Damping and resonance

Damping removes energy from the oscillator. Light damping gives slow decay of amplitude; critical damping returns the system to equilibrium in the shortest time without oscillating; heavy damping is slower still. A system driven at its natural frequency resonates, giving maximum amplitude (playground swings, microwave ovens, bridges that must avoid the wind frequency).

Exam tips: quote a = −ω²x as the defining condition in SHM questions. Time-period questions often need only T = 2π/ω. State which energy is at a maximum and where.

Worked example: a mass on a string

A 0.50 kg mass on a string of length 0.80 m moves in a horizontal circle at 4.0 m/s. The tension supplies the centripetal force, so T = mv²/r = 0.50 × 4.0² / 0.80 = 10 N. If the same mass is swung in a vertical circle, the tension is least at the top. The minimum speed at the top occurs when the tension falls to zero, giving v = √(gr). Here that is √(9.8 × 0.80) ≈ 2.8 m/s. Below this speed the string goes slack and the mass no longer follows the circle.

Exam method: SHM equations

Use x = A sin(ωt) or x = A cos(ωt), depending on the point at which timing starts. The maximum speed is v₀ = Aω and the maximum acceleration is a₀ = Aω². Use ω = 2π/T, and convert any frequency in hertz by multiplying by 2π before you substitute, because ω is in radians per second. For a simple pendulum at small angles, the period is T = 2π√(L/g) and does not depend on the amplitude.

title: Information Representation
content:
`# Information Representation

Number Systems and Ranges

Unsigned binary with n bits stores 0 to 2ⁿ − 1. Two's complement represents negatives: the MSB has value −2ⁿ⁻¹.

Example: 8-bit two's complement of −5: 11111011 (−128 + 64 + 32 + 16 + 8 + 2 + 1).

SystemBaseDigits
Binary20–1
Hexadecimal160–9, A–F
BCD—4 bits per decimal digit

Binary Arithmetic

Add: 0+0=0, 0+1=1, 1+1=0 carry 1, 1+1+1=1 carry 1. Overflow happens when a result exceeds the word size.

Subtraction uses two's complement addition (A − B = A + (−B)).

Text

  • ASCII: 7 bits, 128 characters, English only
  • Unicode: universal scripts; UTF-8 is variable-width (1–4 bytes)

Images and Sound

  • Bitmap: pixels with colour depth (bits per pixel). File size = width × height × depth. Key: width and height are counts of pixels; depth = bits used for each pixel; the product is in bits, so divide by 8 for bytes.
  • Sound: sampling rate (Hz) × bit depth × duration × channels.
  • Resolution trade-off: fidelity vs size.

Compression

  • Lossless (ZIP, run-length encoding): exact reconstruction — required for text/code
  • Lossy (JPEG, MP3): discards perceptually minor data — smaller files

Example: RLE of AAABBBCC → 3A3B2C.

Exam tips: show working for two's complement conversions; state why compression type suits the data (text must be lossless).

title: Ethics and Ownership
content:
Ethics and Ownership

Cambridge International AS & A Level Computer Science 9618: section 7 (Ethics and ownership), examined in AS Paper 1.

Professional Bodies

ACM/IEEE-CS and BCS codes: public interest, competence, integrity, avoid harm, respect privacy. Violations cost trust and employment.

Ethical Scenarios

  • Collecting more personal data than needed (privacy)
  • Releasing software with known bugs that risks safety (competence/honesty)
  • Automated decisions without human review (accountability)

Laws: data protection (GDPR-style), computer misuse (unauthorised access is a crime regardless of intent).

Exam tips: structure ethics answers as: identify the principle → apply to the scenario → give consequences for stakeholders.

Ownership and licensing

Copyright gives the creator legal protection over how their software and other original work is copied, distributed and changed. Copying software without permission is a breach of copyright and can be illegal. Open source software is released under licences that allow others to use, study and modify it, often on the condition that changes are shared in the same way.

Exam tip: link each ethical point to a consequence for a real user, such as a person losing a job or a loan being refused unfairly.

Ownership and licensing questions

  • Software written by an employee in the course of their job is normally owned by the employer, while software written by a freelancer is usually owned by the freelancer unless a contract says otherwise.
  • An open-source licence sets the conditions for using, changing and sharing code. Using open-source code in a commercial product still requires following its licence terms.

title: AS Level Chemistry: Redox Chemistry and Groups 1, 2 and 7
content:
Redox Chemistry and Groups 1, 2 and 7

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH12, Topic 8. Every statement 8.1 to 8.28 is covered below, with its code in the heading. Three ideas run through the whole topic: oxidation numbers track electron transfer, the Group 1 and 2 trends follow from atomic size and nuclear charge, and the Group 7 trends are the same ideas applied to halogens.

8.1 to 8.4: Oxidation numbers

  • Rules: an element is 0; a monatomic ion equals its charge; the sum of oxidation numbers equals the overall charge. Oxygen is usually −2 (but −1 in peroxides such as H₂O₂), hydrogen is usually +1 (but −1 in metal hydrides such as NaH), fluorine is always −1, Group 1 is +1 and Group 2 is +2.
  • 8.2: in MnO₄⁻, manganese must be +7, because four oxygens contribute −8 and the ion has a charge of −1.
  • 8.3: write the oxidation number as a Roman numeral in the name: manganese(VII), iron(III), copper(II).
  • 8.4: work backwards from oxidation numbers to a formula. Iron(III) sulfate is Fe₂(SO₄)₃, because Fe³⁺ must balance SO₄²⁻ in a 2:3 ratio.

8.5 to 8.9: Oxidation, reduction and disproportionation

  • 8.5: oxidation is loss of electrons, and it appears as an increase in oxidation number. Reduction is gain of electrons, a decrease in oxidation number. In 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl, sodium is oxidised (0 to +1) and chlorine is reduced (0 to −1). The same idea covers reactions of s-block metals and p-block non-metals.
  • 8.6: an oxidising agent gains electrons and is itself reduced. A reducing agent loses electrons and is itself oxidised.
  • 8.7: disproportionation is when one element in a single species is both oxidised and reduced at the same time. Chlorine in water is the standard example: Cl₂ → Cl⁻ (0 to −1) and HClO (0 to +1).
  • 8.8: oxidation numbers classify reactions. A reaction is redox if any oxidation number changes, and it is a disproportionation if the same element goes both up and down.
  • 8.9: metals form positive ions by losing electrons, so their oxidation number increases. Non-metals form negative ions by gaining electrons, so their oxidation number decreases.

8.10: Half-equations and full ionic equations

  • Write the oxidation and the reduction separately, balance atoms, then balance charge with electrons. For magnesium with chlorine: Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻ and Cl₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻.
  • Add the half-equations so the electrons cancel, then cancel any spectator ions to give the full ionic equation.

8.11 to 8.13: Group 1 and Group 2 trends and reactions

  • 8.11: ionisation energy falls down Groups 1 and 2. The outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded by inner shells, so less energy is needed to remove it.
  • 8.12: reactivity rises down Group 1 (Li to K) and Group 2 (Mg to Ba), for the same reason: the outer electron is removed more easily.
  • 8.13: Group 1 metals burn in oxygen and react vigorously with chlorine and water. Group 2 metals react with oxygen and chlorine to form oxides and chlorides. Magnesium reacts slowly with cold water and readily with steam, while calcium reacts steadily with cold water to form Ca(OH)₂ and hydrogen.

8.14: Reactions of oxides and hydroxides

  • Group 1 oxides dissolve in water to give alkaline hydroxides. Group 2 oxides react less vigorously, and CaO gives a limewater-type solution, Ca(OH)₂.
  • Oxides react with dilute acid to form a salt and water, for example MgO + 2H⁺ → Mg²⁺ + H₂O.
  • Hydroxides neutralise dilute acids: Ca(OH)₂ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + 2H₂O.

8.15: Solubility trends of Group 2 hydroxides and sulfates

  • Hydroxides: solubility increases down the group. Magnesium hydroxide is almost insoluble, calcium hydroxide is slightly soluble, barium hydroxide is quite soluble.
  • Sulfates: solubility decreases down the group. Magnesium sulfate is soluble, barium sulfate is insoluble, which is why acidified barium chloride gives a white precipitate in the sulfate test.

8.16: Thermal stability of nitrates and carbonates

  • Stability increases down each group. A larger cation has a lower charge density, so it polarises the carbonate or nitrate ion less, and the anion breaks down less easily.
  • Carbonates: MCO₃ → MO + CO₂. Group 2 nitrates: 2M(NO₃)₂ → 2MO + 4NO₂ + O₂. Group 1 nitrates (other than lithium) give the nitrite and oxygen: 2NaNO₃ → 2NaNO₂ + O₂.
  • Lithium is the exception: its nitrate decomposes like a Group 2 nitrate, because the small Li⁺ ion polarises the nitrate strongly.

8.17: Flame colours

  • Heat excites outer electrons to higher energy levels. When they fall back, they emit light of a specific wavelength. Lithium is crimson, sodium is yellow-orange, potassium is lilac, calcium is brick red, strontium is red and barium is green.

8.18: Experiments on thermal decomposition

  • Heat a small sample of nitrate or carbonate in a test tube and test the gas. Brown NO₂ shows a nitrate; a glowing splint relit by O₂ shows oxygen. A carbonate gives CO₂, which turns limewater milky.
  • Compare the temperatures needed for decomposition down a group to show the trend in 8.16.

8.19: Identifying ions

  • Carbonate (CO₃²⁻) or hydrogencarbonate (HCO₃⁻): add dilute acid. CO₂ is released and turns limewater milky. Ionic equation: CO₃²⁻ + 2H⁺ → H₂O + CO₂.
  • Sulfate (SO₄²⁻): add acidified barium chloride. A white precipitate of BaSO₄ forms: Ba²⁺ + SO₄²⁻ → BaSO₄. The acid stops carbonate and sulfite interfering.
  • Ammonium (NH₄⁺): add sodium hydroxide and warm. Ammonia is released, turns damp red litmus blue, and gives white fumes with HCl.

8.20 to 8.23: Concentrations, titrations and uncertainty

  • 8.20: concentration in mol dm⁻³ = moles ÷ volume in dm³. To convert to g dm⁻³, multiply by the molar mass.
  • Indicators: methyl orange changes from red to yellow at about pH 3–4, suited to strong acid against weak base. Phenolphthalein changes from colourless to pink at about pH 8–10, suited to weak acid against strong base.
  • 8.21 (core practical 3): titrate hydrochloric acid against a standard alkali, record the titre and use the balanced equation to find the acid's concentration.
  • 8.22: reduce uncertainty by rinsing the pipette and burette, reading the meniscus at eye level, and repeating until two titres agree within 0.10 cm³. A burette reading has an uncertainty of ±0.05 cm³, so a titre has ±0.10 cm³. Calculate the percentage uncertainty as uncertainty ÷ reading × 100.
  • 8.23 (core practical 4): weigh a solid acid such as hydrated ethanedioic acid accurately, dissolve it, make it up to 250 cm³ in a volumetric flask, and use it as a standard solution to find the concentration of sodium hydroxide.

8.24: Trends in Group 7

  • Melting and boiling points rise down the group, because the molecules are larger and have stronger London forces. Fluorine and chlorine are gases, bromine is a liquid, iodine is a solid.
  • Electronegativity falls down the group, because the bonding pair sits further from the nucleus and is shielded more.
  • Reactivity (oxidising power) falls down the group, because the atoms are larger and gain an electron less readily.

8.25: Displacement reactions and colours

  • A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive halide: Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂, and Cl₂ or Br₂ + 2I⁻ → I₂ + halide.
  • Colours: in water, chlorine is pale green-yellow, bromine is orange and iodine is brown. In a non-polar organic solvent such as cyclohexane, bromine stays orange and iodine turns violet.

8.26: Reactions of the halogens, including disproportionation

  • (i) Halogens oxidise Group 1 and 2 metals to halides, for example 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl.
  • (ii) Chlorine with water is a disproportionation: Cl₂ + H₂O ⇌ HCl + HClO. The HClO is the basis of chlorine water treatment.
  • (iii) Chlorine with cold, dilute NaOH gives bleach: Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaClO + H₂O.
  • (iv) With hot concentrated alkali, chlorine disproportionates to chlorate: 3Cl₂ + 6NaOH → 5NaCl + NaClO₃ + 3H₂O.
  • (v) Bromine behaves in the same way with cold alkali. Use the oxidation number of each chlorine to check each product.

8.27: Reactions of halides and hydrogen halides

  • (i) Solid halides with concentrated H₂SO₄ show the reducing trend. NaCl gives HCl only. NaBr is oxidised further to Br₂ and SO₂. NaI is oxidised to I₂ and H₂S. The reducing ability is HI > HBr > HCl.
  • (ii) Silver nitrate with the halide ions in nitric acid: AgCl is white, AgBr is cream, AgI is yellow. AgCl dissolves in dilute aqueous ammonia, AgBr only in concentrated ammonia, and AgI does not dissolve.
  • (iii) Hydrogen halides with ammonia give ammonium halides (NH₃ + HCl → NH₄Cl). With water they give acids.

8.28: Predicting fluorine and astatine

  • Fluorine is the most electronegative element and the strongest oxidising agent in the group. It reacts violently with water, displacing oxygen from it.
  • Astatine is at the bottom of the group, so by the trends it should be a dark, solid, less reactive halogen than iodine, with a lower electronegativity. It is radioactive, so its chemistry is hard to study directly, and predictions come from the trends.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Half-equations in acid, 8.10 applied: dichromate(VI) reduced by iron(II). Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6e⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O, and Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + e⁻ (multiply by 6). Adding gives Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 6Fe²⁺ + 14H⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + 6Fe³⁺ + 7H₂O. Check atoms, then charge: both sides total +24.
  • Titration calculation, 8.20 and 8.22 applied: 25.0 cm³ of an iron(II) solution needs 18.0 cm³ of 0.0200 mol dm⁻³ K₂Cr₂O₇. Moles of dichromate = 0.0200 × 0.0180 = 3.60 × 10⁻⁴ mol. Each dichromate needs six Fe²⁺, so Fe²⁺ = 2.16 × 10⁻³ mol. Concentration = 2.16 × 10⁻³ ÷ 0.0250 = 0.0864 mol dm⁻³. An A* answer shows the ratio from the balanced equation before any arithmetic.
  • Disproportionation, 8.7 and 8.26 applied: chlorine with cold dilute NaOH gives Cl⁻ (0 to −1, reduction) and ClO⁻ (0 to +1, oxidation) in one reaction. Name both oxidation numbers when explaining why a reaction is disproportionation.
  • Group 2 hydroxide solubility, 8.15 applied: solubility rises down the group because hydration enthalpy falls more steeply than lattice enthalpy as the cation grows. Lattice enthalpy depends on the ion sizes and charges; hydration enthalpy depends on how strongly water molecules bind the cation. Both are needed for full marks.
  • Thermal stability, 8.16 applied: a small, highly charged cation such as Mg²⁺ polarises a carbonate ion strongly, which weakens its C–O bonds, so MgCO₃ decomposes at a lower temperature than BaCO₃. Use the word polarisation, not just "smaller ions decompose more easily".
  • Halogen displacement and redox direction, 8.25 and 8.27 applied: chlorine oxidises bromide and iodide, bromine oxidises iodide, but iodine oxidises neither. Read the direction from the reducing trend: iodide is the strongest reducing agent among the halides, which is why concentrated sulfuric acid reduces HI to H₂S.

Common errors that lose marks

  • Using the wrong oxidation number for oxygen in a peroxide or hydrogen in a metal hydride.
  • Confusing reducing ability with reactivity for the halogens: reactivity falls down Group 7, but the reducing ability of the halide ions rises.
  • Writing the test for sulfate without acid. Without acid, carbonate would also give a white precipitate.

Exam-style questions

  1. Calculate the oxidation number of chromium in K2Cr2O7. Answer: potassium is +1 and oxygen is −2. Let chromium be x: 2(+1) + 2x + 7(−2) = 0, so 2x = 12 and x = +6.
  2. Chlorine reacts with cold, dilute aqueous sodium hydroxide to form sodium chloride and sodium chlorate(I). Explain why this is a disproportionation reaction. Answer: chlorine is oxidised from 0 in Cl2 to +1 in ClO− and reduced from 0 to −1 in Cl−, so the same element is simultaneously oxidised and reduced.
  3. Explain why the thermal stability of the Group 2 carbonates decreases down the group. Answer: the carbonate ion is polarised by the cation. Down the group the cation becomes larger, so its charge density falls and it polarises the carbonate ion less; less distortion of the carbonate ion means less energy is needed to break it down, so decomposition occurs at a lower temperature.
  4. Describe the test for sulfate ions and explain why the solution must be acidified. Answer: add dilute hydrochloric acid, then barium chloride solution; a white precipitate of barium sulfate confirms sulfate. The acid removes carbonate ions, which would otherwise also give a white precipitate of barium carbonate and give a false positive.
  5. Predict how astatine would behave with aqueous potassium chloride. Answer: astatine is below iodine in Group 7, so it is a weaker oxidising agent than chlorine and cannot displace chloride ions; no reaction occurs.

title: Electricity: D.C. Circuits — Study Notes
content:
Electricity: D.C. circuits

Current and charge

  • Current I = charge Q ÷ time t, so Q = It. Unit: ampere (A), where 1 A = 1 C s⁻¹.
  • Electron drift velocity is very small, but the electric field propagates through the circuit almost at the speed of light.

Potential difference and power

  • Potential difference V = energy transferred ÷ charge. Unit: volt (V), where 1 V = 1 J C⁻¹.
  • Power P = VI = I²R = V²/R. Unit: watt (W).

Resistance and resistivity

R = V/I (Ohm's law for an ohmic conductor, at constant temperature). For a wire of length L and cross-sectional area A, R = ρL/A, where ρ is the resistivity in Ω m. Resistance rises with length and falls with area.

Practical circuits

An ammeter is connected in series with the component it measures. A voltmeter is connected in parallel with the component. An ideal ammeter has zero resistance; an ideal voltmeter has infinite resistance.

Kirchhoff's laws

  • First law: at a junction, the total current entering equals the total current leaving (conservation of charge).
  • Second law: around any closed loop, the sum of the emfs equals the sum of the potential differences (conservation of energy).

Potential dividers

For two resistors R1 and R2 in series across a supply V, the potential difference across R2 is V × R2/(R1 + R2).

Worked example: a 100 Ω and a 300 Ω resistor are in series across 12 V. The current is 12/400 = 0.030 A, and the voltage across the 300 Ω resistor is 0.030 × 300 = 9.0 V.

Exam tips: draw the meter in the correct place, in series or in parallel. Apply Kirchhoff's first law to currents and the second law to loops, with consistent signs. Check that units are converted (e.g. mm² to m²) before using ρL/A.

Resistivity and temperature

For a metallic conductor at constant temperature, resistance is proportional to length and inversely proportional to cross-sectional area. Resistivity, ρ = RA/L, is a property of the material. As temperature rises, the ions in a metal vibrate more and impede the flow of electrons, so resistivity increases. A thermistor behaves differently: its resistance falls as temperature rises, because more charge carriers are released.

Exam tip: when asked to explain a resistance change, relate it to charge carriers and collisions, not just to the formula.

Worked example: resistors in series and in parallel

Two resistors of 4 Ω and 6 Ω in series have a combined resistance of 10 Ω, and the same current flows through each. In parallel, the same two resistors have a combined resistance found from 1/R = 1/4 + 1/6 = 5/12, so R = 2.4 Ω. The combined resistance in parallel is always less than the smallest individual resistance, and adding a branch to a parallel circuit always reduces the total resistance.

Worked example: EMF and internal resistance

A cell with EMF 1.5 V and internal resistance 0.5 Ω supplies a current of 2 A. The terminal potential difference is V = E − Ir = 1.5 − (2 × 0.5) = 0.5 V. Writing V = E − Ir before substituting shows that the energy lost inside the cell is the difference between the EMF and the terminal voltage. A cell with a larger current supplied has a smaller terminal voltage.

The potential divider

Two resistors in series across a supply give an output voltage across one of them that depends on the ratio of the resistances. For a supply of 12 V with resistors of 2 kΩ and 4 kΩ in series, the voltage across the 4 kΩ resistor is 12 × 4 ÷ 6 = 8 V. A thermistor or light-dependent resistor in place of one of the resistors makes this arrangement a sensor, because the output voltage changes with temperature or light level.

title: Integration — Study Notes
content:
Integration

Indefinite Integrals

Reverse the power rule and add a constant: ∫ xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n+1) + c (n ≠ −1).

Examples: ∫ x³ dx = x⁴/4 + c; ∫ 1/x dx = ln|x| + c; ∫ sin x dx = −cos x + c; ∫ e^x dx = e^x + c.

Definite Integrals

∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = [F(x)]ₐᵇ = F(b) − F(a). Constants of integration cancel.

Example: ∫₀¹ 6x² dx = [2x³]₀¹ = 2.

Areas Under Curves

Area between a curve and the x-axis = ∫ₐᵇ y dx, where y ≥ 0. If the curve dips below the axis, split the integral at the roots and add the absolute values.

Example: area between y = x² − 4 and the x-axis: roots ±2, and the area is |∫₋₂² (x² − 4) dx| = 32/3.

Trapezium Rule

A ≈ h/2 [y₀ + 2(y₁ + … + yₙ₋₁) + yₙ], h = (b − a)/n. More strips → better estimate; always an over-estimate for convex curves.

Exam tips: never forget +c on indefinite integrals; for areas with negative regions, sketch first and split.

title: Trigonometry — Right-Angled Triangles — Study Notes
content:
Trigonometry — Right-Angled Triangles

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): SOH CAH TOA, exact values, angles of elevation/depression.

1. The ratios

Label sides first (opposite, adjacent, hypotenuse) with respect to the marked angle, then choose:

  • sin θ = opp/hyp; cos θ = adj/hyp; tan θ = opp/adj.

Example: hyp 10, angle 35°, find opposite: x = 10 sin 35° = 5.74 (3 s.f.).

2. Finding angles

Use inverse keys: θ = sin⁻¹(opp/hyp). tan θ = 3/4 ⇒ θ = 36.9° (1 d.p.).

3. Exact values (Extended)

θsincostan
30°1/2√3/2√3/3
45°√2/2√2/21
60°√3/21/2√3

4. Elevation and depression

Elevation: angle up from horizontal; depression: down. Both measured from the horizontal line at the observer.

Example: tower 20 m, elevation to top 42° → horizontal distance = 20/tan 42° = 22.2 m.

5. Pythagoras combinations

Find a missing side with Pythagoras before applying a ratio when two sides are known instead of an angle.

Exam tips: never round mid-calculation (keep full calculator accuracy); 3 s.f. for lengths, 1 d.p. for angles unless stated.

SOH CAH TOA

In a right-angled triangle with angle θ: sin θ = opposite ÷ hypotenuse, cos θ = adjacent ÷ hypotenuse and tan θ = opposite ÷ adjacent. Label the sides relative to the angle you are using before choosing the ratio. Use Pythagoras to find a missing side first if needed.

Finding angles

To find an angle, use the inverse function, sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹ or tan⁻¹, on the calculator. Set the calculator to degree mode and check that the answer is sensible for the triangle drawn.

Bearings and angles of elevation

An angle of elevation is measured up from the horizontal, and an angle of depression down from it. Draw a clear right-angled triangle from the description to choose the correct ratio. Round the answer to the accuracy in the question, and keep full accuracy in intermediate steps.

Worked example: finding a side

In a right-angled triangle the hypotenuse is 10 cm and angle θ is 35°. The side opposite θ is found with sine: opposite = 10 × sin 35° = 10 × 0.5736 = 5.74 cm (to 2 decimal places). The side adjacent to θ uses cosine: adjacent = 10 × cos 35° = 10 × 0.8192 = 8.19 cm.

Worked example: finding an angle

In a right-angled triangle the opposite side is 6 cm and the adjacent side is 9 cm. Use tan: tan θ = 6 ÷ 9 = 0.6667, so θ = tan⁻¹(0.6667) = 33.7° (to 1 decimal place). Check the answer: an angle less than 45° means the opposite side should be shorter than the adjacent side, which it is.

Choosing the ratio

  • Label the sides as opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse relative to the angle you are given, not the angle at the right-angle corner.
  • Use the ratio that contains the two sides you know, or the side you want and one you know.
  • Keep the calculator in degree mode, and do not round until the final step.

Exam point: a bearing is measured clockwise from north, so draw the north line first and then mark the angle before using the triangle.
