title: Membranes, Proteins, DNA and Gene Expression
content:
Quick revision: Membranes, Proteins, DNA and Gene Expression

Biology — AS. Edexcel IAL Biology WBI11, Topic 2. DNA holds the code for proteins. Gene expression copies that code into mRNA and then builds the protein. Cell membranes control what enters and leaves the cell.

Key areas to revise

  • Cell membranes
  • DNA structure and replication
  • Protein synthesis
  • Mutations

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Worked example

Calculate the percentage change in mass of plant tissue in an osmosis experiment where initial mass is 2.50 g and final mass is 2.85 g. Step 1: Change in mass = Final − Initial = 2.85 − 2.50 = 0.35 g. Step 2: Percentage change = (Change ÷ Initial) × 100 = (0.35 ÷ 2.50) × 100 = 14.0%. Answer: +14.0%.

Key points to remember

For 2.2 (i) and (ii), the fluid mosaic model describes phospholipids, cholesterol, glycoproteins and glycolipids floating in a flexible bilayer; scientific models are interpretations of data like freeze-fracture electron microscopy. For 2.3 Core Practical 3, increasing temperature above 40 °C denatures membrane proteins and melts the phospholipid bilayer, increasing permeability, while alcohol dissolves lipids, leaking betalain pigment from beetroot. For 2.4, osmosis is the net movement of free water molecules through a partially permeable membrane down a water potential gradient from high to low water potential. For 2.5 (i) and (ii), passive transport (diffusion and facilitated diffusion) requires no ATP, active transport uses ATP via carrier proteins to move substances against a gradient, and bulk transport uses endocytosis and exocytosis. For 2.9 (i) and (ii), mononucleotides consist of pentose sugar (ribose or deoxyribose), phosphate group and a nitrogenous base (A, T, C, G, U), joined by phosphodiester bonds formed in condensation reactions, with complementary base pairing (A-T with 2 hydrogen bonds, C-G with 3 hydrogen bonds) forming the DNA double helix. For 2.10 (i) and (ii), semi-conservative DNA replication relies on DNA polymerase adding free nucleotides to the template strand, and Meselson and Stahl proved this using 14N and 15N nitrogen isotopes in E. coli DNA centrifugation. For 2.11 and 2.12, the genetic code is a triplet code (3 bases per amino acid), non-overlapping, and degenerate (multiple codons code for the same amino acid), where a gene is a sequence of bases coding for a polypeptide. For 2.13 (i) and (ii), transcription uses RNA polymerase to copy the antisense DNA strand into mRNA in the nucleus, and translation uses ribosomes, tRNA with specific anticodons, start codons and stop codons to assemble amino acids. For 2.14 (i) and (ii), mutations include base substitution, insertion and deletion, which can cause genetic disorders or cancer, though many are silent. For 2.15 (i), (ii) and (iii), key genetics terms include gene, allele, genotype, phenotype, recessive, dominant, codominance, homozygote and heterozygote, alongside monotypical pedigrees and X-linked recessive conditions like red-green colour blindness. For 2.16, the CFTR gene mutation in cystic fibrosis produces thick, sticky mucus impairing the gaseous exchange, digestive and reproductive systems. For 2.17 (i) and (ii) and 2.18, genetic screening includes carrier identification, PGD, amniocentesis and chorionic villus sampling, carrying social, moral and religious ethical implications regarding abortion and designer babies.

How to use this: read these concise summaries alongside your core practical notes, ensure definitions for water potential and transcription are precise, and apply your knowledge to pedigree and genetics problem questions.

title: Exam technique: Circular Measure
content:
### What earns the marks
For arc and sector work, the formula quoted with radians stated earns the method mark: s = r theta and A = half r squared theta. For conversions, the factor (pi/180 or 180/pi) shown earns the mark with exact multiples of pi simplified. For sector perimeter, the two radii added explicitly earn the final mark.
### Traps
Error: degrees used directly in arc formulas. Correction: convert to radians first. Error: arc-only answer for perimeter. Correction: add both radii. Error: decimal approximations for exact-multiple answers. Correction: simplify the pi fraction.

title: Thermal Physics — Study Notes
content:
Thermal Physics

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): kinetic particle model; thermal expansion; specific heat capacity; melting/boiling; conduction, convection, radiation.

1. Kinetic model

Solid: fixed positions, vibrate — fixed shape/volume. Liquid: move around, touching — fixed volume, flows. Gas: far apart, fast random motion — fills container. Brownian motion evidences random molecular motion.

2. Gas pressure and temperature

Pressure from wall collisions. Heating at fixed volume → faster particles → more frequent, harder collisions → higher pressure.

3. Thermal expansion

Heating → particles vibrate more → solids expand slightly (gases expand most). Applications: bimetallic strip (fire alarm/thermostat), gaps in bridges/rails; the liquid-in-glass thermometer.

4. Specific heat capacity

c = ΔE/(mΔθ). Heating: ΔE = mcΔθ.

Example: 2 kg water (c = 4200), 20→80 °C: ΔE = 2×4200×60 = 504 kJ.

High c of water → coolant; temperature rise measured with known heater power P in time t: c = Pt/(mΔθ).

5. State changes

Melting/boiling at fixed temperature despite heating (energy breaks bonds, not temperature). Condensation/ freezing release energy. Impurities raise melting point of mixtures/lower freezing; boiling needs nucleation.

6. Transfer: conduction, convection, radiation

  • Conduction: mainly metals (delocalised electrons + lattice vibration); non-metals poor; insulators trap air.
  • Convection: hot fluid expands, density falls, rises; denser cool fluid sinks — currents.
  • Radiation: infrared EM waves; no medium; matte black best absorber/emitter, shiny silver worst.

Applications: vacuum flask, house insulation, car radiators, solar heating panels.

Heat transfer and heat capacity

Energy transfer by conduction happens through a solid when particles vibrate and pass energy to their neighbours, with free electrons carrying energy in metals. Convection in fluids occurs because hotter, less dense fluid rises and is replaced by cooler, denser fluid. Black, matt surfaces are good absorbers and emitters of infrared radiation.

The energy needed to change the temperature of a substance is Q = mcΔT, where c is the specific heat capacity. Latent heat is the energy absorbed or released during a change of state with no change in temperature.

Worked example: heating a substance

A 2 kg block of aluminium with specific heat capacity 900 J/(kg °C) is heated from 20 °C to 70 °C. The energy supplied is Q = mcΔθ = 2 × 900 × 50 = 90 000 J, which is 90 kJ. The specific heat capacity is the energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of the substance by 1 °C, so the same calculation with a different material gives a different energy for the same mass and temperature rise.

Worked example: melting ice

The specific latent heat of fusion of ice is the energy needed to change 1 kg of ice at 0 °C into water at 0 °C without any change in temperature. For 0.5 kg of ice with latent heat 334 000 J/kg, the energy needed is Q = mL = 0.5 × 334 000 = 167 000 J. During melting the temperature stays constant, so the energy goes into breaking the bonds between molecules rather than raising the temperature.

Conduction, convection and radiation

Conduction transfers thermal energy through a solid by particles passing on kinetic energy to their neighbours, and metals conduct well because of their free electrons. Convection transfers energy through a fluid, because warmer, less dense fluid rises and cooler fluid sinks. Radiation transfers energy as infrared waves, which need no medium, and a dark matt surface is both the best absorber and the best emitter of radiation. Name the process in the question and link it to the property of the material that controls it.

title: IGCSE Computer Science: Automated Systems, Robotics and AI
content:
IGCSE Computer Science: Automated Systems, Robotics and AI

Cambridge IGCSE Computer Science 0478 (2026–2028), Paper 1 Computer Systems, Topic 6 Automated and emerging technologies: statement 6.1 Automated systems, 6.2 Robotics, and 6.3 Artificial intelligence. This is where the machine stops waiting for instructions and acts on its own — sensing, deciding and moving. Every feedback loop below is traced step by step, and the AI section separates what the syllabus actually expects (machine learning, natural language processing, robotics) from the hype, because examiners reward precise terminology over vague claims.

What makes a system automated

An automated system measures and controls a process with little or no human intervention. The architecture is always the same loop, and once you see it you can analyse any example the exam gives:

  • Input (sensors) — measure the real world: temperature, light, pressure, humidity, proximity, pH.
  • Processing — a microprocessor compares each measurement against a target (the set point) and decides what to do.
  • Output (actuators) — change the real world: motors, heaters, pumps, valves, lights, robotic arms.
  • Feedback — the sensors keep measuring the effect of the actuators, closing the loop so the system corrects itself.
Worked trace: a greenhouse temperature control system.

Set point: 22 degrees C. The sensor reads the air every 10 seconds.

1. 09:00:00  reading 18 C - below the set point.
   Processing: heating required. Actuators: heater ON, roof vent CLOSED.
2. 09:00:30  reading 21 C - still below (within the 2 C dead zone margin).
   Processing: continue heating.
3. 09:01:10  reading 23 C - above the set point.
   Processing: heater OFF (switching now, not at 22, avoids rapid cycling),
   roof vent OPEN to cool.
4. 09:03:00  reading 22 C - within the dead zone between 21 and 23.
   Processing: change nothing - the dead zone prevents constant switching,
   which would wear the heater out.

The loop repeats indefinitely. The set point is the target, the dead zone is
the tolerance band that stops the actuators chattering, and the feedback is the
sensor readings that drive each decision.

Closed-loop systems use feedback (as above); open-loop systems act without measuring the result — a toaster runs for a fixed time regardless of how brown the bread is. The exam asks you to say which a system is and justify it: if the output feeds back into the next decision, it is closed-loop.

Transducers: where physical change becomes data

Sensors and actuators are both transducers — devices that convert one form of energy into another — and knowing which way the conversion runs is the cleanest way to keep them straight. A sensor converts a physical quantity into an electrical signal the processor can read (temperature into resistance, light into voltage, sound into a varying current). An actuator does the reverse: it converts the processor's electrical signal into physical action (voltage into motion in a motor, into heat in a heater, into light in an LED).

Conversion direction, always:

  physical quantity --> electrical signal     SENSOR (input)
  electrical signal --> physical action       ACTUATOR (output)

Examples worked through:
  A thermistor in a greenhouse: temperature rises -> resistance falls -> the
  analogue voltage changes -> an analogue-to-digital converter (ADC) turns it
  into a binary number the processor compares with the set point.

  A motor on a roof vent: the processor outputs a digital command -> a digital-
  to-analogue converter (DAC) and driver circuit produce a varying current ->
  the motor turns the vent.

Many real devices are both at once in different roles: a microphone is a sensor
(sound -> electricity) and a speaker is an actuator (electricity -> sound).

Where automation is used

DomainExampleSensorsActuators
ManufacturingRobotic assembly linePosition, proximity, visionRobot arms, conveyors, welders
AgricultureAutomatic irrigationSoil moisture, rain, temperaturePumps, valves
HomeCentral heatingThermostat, timerBoiler, radiator valves
TrafficAdaptive traffic lightsInductive loop detectors, camerasSignal lamps
MedicineInsulin pumpGlucose sensorPump actuator

Benefits: consistent quality, output in dangerous or monotonous conditions, 24-hour working, long-run cost per unit falls, and precise control improves yield. Costs: high capital outlay, jobs lost or changed, expensive and disruptive breakdowns, and loss of human judgement when the unexpected happens — a self-driving vehicle's edge cases are the modern form of that risk.

Robotics

A robot is a programmable machine that can sense, process and act on its environment to carry out tasks, often autonomously. The syllabus separates the types: fixed robots (a welding arm bolted to a factory floor — precise and strong, one workspace), mobile robots (warehouse robots, rovers — move themselves, need navigation), and autonomous robots (self-driving cars, drones — make decisions without continuous human control).

Inside any robot, the same loop as any automated system: sensors (cameras, LiDAR, ultrasonic, gyroscopes, encoders on the motors), a processor running control software, and actuators (motors, servos, grippers) — plus a power supply (battery) and a communication link for supervision.

  • Industrial uses: welding, painting and assembly (consistent quality, no fatigue, hazardous-environment work); picking and packing; bomb disposal and deep-sea or space exploration where humans cannot go.
  • Domestic and service uses: vacuum cleaners, lawn mowers, surgical robots, warehouse logistics, companionship and care.
  • Advantages: repeatable precision, tireless, work in danger, cheaper than labour at volume.
  • Disadvantages: very expensive to design and install, rigid when the task changes, maintenance needs skilled engineers, and they displace workers — the social consequence earns its own marks.

Artificial intelligence and machine learning

Artificial intelligence (AI) is software that appears to make intelligent decisions — solving problems and carrying out tasks in ways we would call clever if a human did them. Machine learning (ML) is the subset the syllabus emphasises: instead of being explicitly programmed with rules, the system is given data and learns patterns from it, improving with experience.

An analogy before the mechanics: teaching a child to recognise cats does not mean listing ear shapes and whisker counts. Show the child thousands of labelled pictures and the rules form themselves inside their head. Machine learning does exactly that with numbers.

How a machine learning model is trained, step by step:

1. Collect data: thousands of emails labelled "spam" or "not spam" by humans.
2. Choose features: word frequencies, sender reputation, link count, subject
   line patterns - measurable properties of each email.
3. Split the data: most for training, some held back for testing.
4. TRAINING: the algorithm adjusts its internal weights to fit the training
   data. It predicts each email's label; each wrong prediction nudges the
   weights; repeat over the dataset many times. The weights ARE the learned
   model - no human wrote the rules.
5. TESTING: run the trained model on the held-back data it has never seen and
   measure accuracy (correct predictions / total predictions). High training
   accuracy but low test accuracy means overfitting - it memorised the
   examples rather than learning the pattern.
6. DEPLOYMENT: new emails are classified by the model; correct and incorrect
   feedback can be fed back in so it keeps improving.

The three kinds of learning the syllabus names: supervised learning trains on labelled data (the spam example; predicting house prices from past sales); unsupervised learning finds structure in unlabelled data (customer segmentation — "these shoppers behave alike"); reinforcement learning learns by trial and reward (a game-playing program gets points for winning and adjusts its strategy).

Other AI applications in the syllabus: natural language processing (NLP) — understanding and generating human language: translation, voice assistants, chatbots, spam filtering; speech recognition — turning spoken audio into text (dictation, voice control); expert systems — a knowledge base of facts plus an inference engine applying rules to reach a conclusion (medical diagnosis support, fault finding); computer vision — interpreting images (face recognition, self-driving perception, medical imaging); autonomous vehicles — combining sensors, vision and decision-making to navigate.

Advantages of AI systemsDisadvantages of AI systems
Fast decisions over huge data volumesTraining needs vast data and computing power
Consistent, no fatigue or emotionNo common sense; fails on cases unlike its training data
Handles dangerous or dull workJob displacement across many industries
Improves with more dataBiased training data produces biased decisions — and they are hard to challenge
Available 24/7Cannot explain its reasoning well; accountability is unclear

Worked example: applying the loop to an autonomous vehicle

Approaching a pedestrian crossing:

1. SENSORS: cameras, radar and LiDAR continuously measure distance to the
   crossing, the pedestrian's position and speed, and the car's own speed.
2. PROCESSING: the AI classifies the objects (camera vision: "pedestrian at
   kerb"), predicts likely movement from the training data, and compares this
   with safety rules - minimum stopping distance for current speed and grip.
3. DECISION: predicted conflict - begin braking now, at 4 m/s^2, and warn.
4. ACTUATORS: brake and steering systems carry out the decision.
5. FEEDBACK: sensors keep measuring; if the pedestrian steps back, the plan
   updates; if the road is wet, the sensors' distance readings lengthen the
   braking margin.

Every one of these five stages can be a separate exam answer.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Calling any machine with a motor a "robot"; the syllabus sense is a programmable machine that senses, processes and acts — and "autonomous" requires decisions without continuous human control.
  • Describing open-loop systems as using feedback; if the output is not measured to adjust the next action, the loop is open (a toaster), regardless of how clever it looks.
  • Confusing the sensor and the actuator in a scenario: sensors measure (input), actuators move or heat (output) — thermostats sense, heaters act.
  • Saying machine learning "is programmed with rules"; the whole point is that the rules are learned from data — the trained weights are the program.
  • Skipping the training/testing split when explaining ML; measuring on unseen data is what distinguishes learning from memorising.
  • Equating AI with robots (or robots with AI): AI is software that can run without a robot, and many robots run purely on fixed programs with no learning.
  • Listing advantages only; the disadvantages (job losses, bias, data hunger, no common sense) carry equal marks.
  • Forgetting the feedback loop when describing any control system — "the sensor keeps measuring the effect" is the sentence examiners look for.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 1, 4 marks). Describe the input, process and output stages of an automatic door.

Answer: Input: a motion or proximity sensor detects a person approaching (and a pressure sensor may detect someone standing on the mat). Processing: the microprocessor compares the sensor reading with its trigger condition and checks safety sensors before acting. Output: an actuator (an electric motor) slides the door open; a timer or sensor then closes it. Feedback: the sensors keep monitoring so the door stays open while the beam is broken.

Question 2 (Paper 1, 3 marks). Explain the difference between a closed-loop and an open-loop system, giving one example of each.

Answer: A closed-loop system measures its output and feeds that back to adjust its actions — a central heating system measures room temperature and switches the boiler accordingly. An open-loop system acts without measuring the result — a toaster runs for a fixed time regardless of how brown the toast is.

Question 3 (Paper 1, 4 marks). Describe how a machine learning system is trained to detect fraudulent bank transactions.

Answer: Collect a large dataset of past transactions each labelled fraudulent or genuine by humans. Choose features such as amount, location, time and spending pattern. The algorithm trains on most of the data, adjusting its internal weights each time its prediction is wrong, until the predictions fit. The model is then tested on held-back transactions it has never seen to measure accuracy, before being used to score new transactions — with feedback from confirmed cases improving it over time.

Question 4 (Paper 1, 4 marks). Discuss the impact of introducing robots into a car factory.

Answer: For the firm: consistent weld quality, output day and night without fatigue, safer handling of painting fumes and heavy parts, and lower unit costs at volume — offset by very high installation costs, expensive breakdowns and rigidity when the product changes. For workers: dangerous and repetitive jobs are replaced, but assembly jobs are lost and remaining roles demand higher skills, so retraining is needed and communities dependent on the plant can suffer.

Question 5 (Paper 1, 3 marks). State three differences between a robot and an AI system.

Answer: A robot is hardware that physically senses and acts in the world; AI is software that makes decisions and may never have a physical form. Robots follow explicit programs; AI systems (especially machine learning) derive behaviour from data. A robot can run with no AI at all (a fixed assembly arm), and AI can exist with no robot (a spam filter).

The counterpart to systems that act on their own is the people who attack them: cyber security.

title: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Angles and Polygons
content:
Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Angles and Polygons

Angles are the simplest measurements in geometry and the most frequently examined: almost every Paper 2 and Paper 4 geometry question ends with a reason written next to a number, and the reason earns as many marks as the calculation. This note builds the whole angle toolkit from zero: the vocabulary of points, lines and angles; the parallel-line rules; the angle sums of triangles, quadrilaterals and polygons; and the full set of circle theorems with the standard reasons examiners accept. Every worked example writes the reason line, because that is how the marks are earned.

Geometrical terms

Geometry has a precise vocabulary, and Paper 2 questions often begin by asking you to use it:

  • Point: a position with no size; named with a capital letter.
  • Line segment: the straight path between two points; a line extends without end.
  • Ray: a line starting at a point and extending in one direction.
  • Parallel lines: always the same distance apart, never meeting (marked with arrows).
  • Perpendicular lines: meeting at 90°.
  • Vertex: a corner where two or more lines meet; vertices in the plural.
  • Polygon: a closed shape with straight sides; regular means all sides equal and all angles equal.

Angle vocabulary: acute (less than 90°), right (90°), obtuse (between 90° and 180°), straight (180°), reflex (between 180° and 360°). Angles on a straight line sum to 180°; angles around a point sum to 360°; vertically opposite angles are equal.

Parallel lines: the three rules

A transversal line crossing two parallel lines creates eight angles, and three relationships do all the work:

RelationshipWhat they look likeRule
Corresponding (F-shape)same position at each intersectionequal
Alternate (Z-shape)opposite sides of the transversal, between the parallelsequal
Co-interior (C-shape)same side of the transversal, between the parallelssum to 180°

Worked example. Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. One angle is 115°. Find the angle in the alternate position and the co-interior angle on the other side.

alternate angle = 115 °            (alternate angles are equal)
co-interior angle = 180 - 115 = 65 ° (co-interior angles sum to 180)

Always write the reason next to each answer: "alternate angles" or "co-interior angles sum to 180°". Paper 2 awards the reason mark explicitly.

Triangles and quadrilaterals

The angle sum of any triangle is 180° (proof: draw a line through one vertex parallel to the opposite side and use alternate angles). Consequences you must know:

  • Exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles.
  • Isosceles triangle: base angles are equal; the angle bisector from the apex is also the perpendicular bisector of the base.
  • Equilateral triangle: all angles 60°.
  • Quadrilateral: interior angles sum to 360° (split into two triangles).

Worked example. A quadrilateral has angles 85°, 95° and 110°. Find the fourth angle.

sum = 360 °
fourth = 360 - (85 + 95 + 110) = 360 - 290 = 70 °

Worked example 2 (exterior angle). In a triangle, an exterior angle is 125° and one opposite interior angle is 48°. Find the other opposite interior angle.

exterior = sum of opposite interiors
125 = 48 + x  →  x = 77 °

Angles in polygons

Any n-sided polygon can be split into (n − 2) triangles from one vertex, so:

interior angle sum = (n - 2) × 180 °

regular polygon: each interior angle = (n - 2) × 180/n
exterior angles of any convex polygon sum to 360 °
regular polygon: each exterior angle = 360/n
interior + exterior = 180 ° at each vertex

Worked example 1. Find the interior angle sum of a decagon (10 sides) and each interior angle of a regular decagon.

sum = (10 - 2) × 180 = 1440 °
each = 1440/10 = 144 °
check with exterior: 360/10 = 36; 180 - 36 = 144 °

Worked example 2 (working backwards). A regular polygon has each interior angle 150°. Find the number of sides.

exterior angle = 180 - 150 = 30 °
n = 360/30 = 12 sides  (a regular dodecagon)

Worked example 3 (exterior angles). A pentagon has exterior angles 70°, 80°, 60°, 90°. Find the fifth.

exterior angles sum to 360 °
fifth = 360 - (70 + 80 + 60 + 90) = 360 - 300 = 60 °

Circle theorems: the full set

Circle theorems are examined every session, and each answer needs its theorem named. Learn them as pictures with their standard reasons:

TheoremStatementReason to write
Angle at the centrethe angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference subtended by the same arcangle at centre = 2 × angle at circumference
Angle in a semicirclethe angle in a semicircle (subtended by a diameter) is 90°angle in a semicircle is 90°
Same segmentangles subtended by the same arc in the same segment are equalangles in the same segment are equal
Cyclic quadrilateralopposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180°opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180°
Tangent–radiusa tangent meets the radius at the point of contact at 90°tangent is perpendicular to the radius
Two tangentstangents from an external point are equal in lengthtangents from an external point are equal
Alternate segmentthe angle between a tangent and a chord equals the angle in the alternate segmentalternate segment theorem

Worked example 1 (centre). The angle at the centre subtended by an arc is 130°. Find the angle at the circumference subtended by the same arc.

angle at circumference = 130/2 = 65 °
(reason: angle at centre = 2 x angle at circumference)

Worked example 2 (cyclic quadrilateral). In a cyclic quadrilateral, one pair of opposite angles is 105° and 75°, and the other pair is 4x and 2x. Find x.

opposite angles sum to 180 °
4x + 2x = 180
6x = 180  →  x = 30
check the first pair: 10⁵ + 75 = 180, consistent

Two disciplines make this safe: pair the angles that sit opposite each other (a diagonal between them), and verify both pairs satisfy the 180° rule before writing the answer.

Worked example 3 (tangent). A tangent touches a circle of radius 5 cm at T; O is the centre and P is a point on the tangent 12 cm from T. Find OP.

The radius OT is perpendicular to the tangent, so triangle OTP
is right-angled at T.
OP² = 5² + 12² = 25 + 144 = 169
OP = 13 cm

Worked example 4 (alternate segment). A tangent and a chord form an angle of 62° at the point of contact. Find the angle in the alternate segment.

alternate segment theorem: the tangent-chord angle equals the
angle in the alternate segment
answer = 62 °

Circle theorems: multi-step problems

Paper 4 circle problems chain two or three theorems. The method: mark every angle you can find with its reason, then use each new angle to unlock the next.

Worked example. O is the centre; A, B, C lie on the circle; angle BAC = 35°. Find angle BOC and angle OBC.

angle BOC = 2 × 35 = 70 °
  (angle at centre = 2 x angle at circumference)
triangle OBC is isosceles (OB = OC = radii)
base angles OBC and OCB are equal:
OBC = (180 - 70)/2 = 55 °

Worked example 2 (semicircle + cyclic). AB is a diameter; C and D lie on the circle; angle ABC = 40°. Find angle ADC.

angle ACB = 90 ° (angle in a semicircle)
angle BAC = 180 - 90 - 40 = 50 °
ABCD is cyclic, so angle ADC = 180 - angle ABC? No - opposite
pairs: A with C, B with D. Angle ADC is opposite angle ABC?
The vertices in order are A, B, C, D, so opposite pairs are
(A, C) and (B, D). Angle ADC is at D, opposite angle ABC at B:
angle ADC = 180 - 40 = 140 °.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Parallel lines) Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal; one co-interior angle is 72°. Find the other. Answer: 108°, because co-interior angles sum to 180°.
  2. (Polygon) Find the interior angle sum of a 15-sided polygon. Answer: (15 − 2) × 180 = 2340°.
  3. (Regular polygon) Each exterior angle of a regular polygon is 24°. Find the number of sides and each interior angle. Answer: n = 360/24 = 15; interior = 180 − 24 = 156°.
  4. (Circle — centre) An angle at the circumference is 28°. Find the angle at the centre subtended by the same arc. Answer: 56°.
  5. (Circle — semicircle) A triangle is inscribed in a semicircle with the diameter as one side; one base angle is 33°. Find the other. Answer: 90° at the circumference, so the other angle is 180 − 90 − 33 = 57°.
  6. (Circle — cyclic) A cyclic quadrilateral has one angle 118°. Find the opposite angle. Answer: 62° (180 − 118).
  7. (Tangent) Two tangents from P touch the circle at A and B; PA = 9 cm. Find PB and explain. Answer: 9 cm — tangents from an external point are equal.
  8. (Multi-step) In a circle, angle ABD = 42° and angle ACD = 42°. What does this tell you about A, B, C, D? Answer: They are concyclic — equal angles subtended by the same chord AD at B and C mean the points lie on the same circle (angles in the same segment).

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Missing reasons: Paper 2 geometry marks include the reason. "x = 65° (angles on a straight line)" scores; a bare "65°" may not.
  • Wrong pairing in cyclic quadrilaterals: opposite angles are the ones separated by a diagonal (A and C, B and D), not adjacent ones. Check both pairs sum to 180°.
  • Alternate versus corresponding: alternate angles form a Z, corresponding an F. Identifying the wrong pattern gives the wrong equality.
  • Interior formula mix-up: interior sum is (n − 2) × 180; each exterior is 360/n. Do not use 360/n for the interior of a regular polygon.
  • Reflex angles: the angle at the centre may be reflex; if the diagram shows an obtuse angle but the geometry demands a reflex one, use 360° − the drawn angle.
  • Assuming radii are parallel or equal to chords: radii are equal to each other, not to chords. Isosceles triangles in circles come from two radii.
  • Tangent–chord angle: the alternate segment theorem requires the angle between the tangent and the chord at the point of contact, not any angle involving the tangent.
  • Diagram not to scale: never measure an angle with a protractor in an exam diagram; the geometry must be calculated. "Diagram not accurately drawn" is a warning, not decoration.

title: System Software and Security — Study Notes
content:
`# System Software and Security

Operating System Roles

  • Manage memory (paging/segmentation, virtual memory to disk)
  • Schedule processes (round robin, priorities)
  • Handle I/O via device drivers and spooling
  • Provide the UI, file systems, and security (users, permissions)

Translators

  • Assembler: assembly → machine code (1:1)
  • Compiler: whole source → machine code, reports all errors, produces standalone executables
  • Interpreter: line-by-line execution, stops at first error, needs the interpreter present

Bytecode + VM (e.g. Java) combines both: compile once, run anywhere the VM exists.

Linkers and Loaders

Static linking copies library code into the executable; dynamic linking binds at runtime (smaller files, shared libraries). The loader places the program in memory, relocating addresses.

IDEs

Editors with syntax highlighting, autocompletion, debugger (breakpoints, stepping, variable watch), and integrated compilation.

Malware and Defences

Viruses, worms, trojans, spyware, phishing. Defences: antivirus (signature + heuristic scanning), firewalls (packet filtering by port/IP), sandboxing, user education, patches.

Exam tips: compare compiler vs interpreter with concrete error-handling differences; explain firewall rules using ports and addresses.

Malware types and prevention

A virus attaches itself to a file or program and needs a host to spread. A worm spreads across a network without a host file. A trojan looks like useful software but carries a hidden harmful payload. Phishing uses fake emails or websites to trick a user into revealing login details or other personal data.

A firewall monitors incoming and outgoing network traffic and blocks traffic that does not meet its rules. Anti-malware software scans for and removes known threats. Regular software updates close security weaknesses, and regular backups allow data to be restored after an attack.

Exam tip: match each threat to how it spreads, and each prevention method to the threat it stops. Do not confuse a virus with a worm.

Worked example: tracing a program through the toolchain

A programmer writes the source code for a calculator in a high-level language. A compiler translates the whole program into machine code before it runs, and reports syntax errors as a list. A linker then joins this object code with the library routines it calls, producing one executable file. A loader copies that executable into main memory and starts it. If the same program were run by an interpreter, each statement would be translated and executed in turn, so an error in line 40 would only appear when the program reached line 40.

Comparing translators

  • Compiler: translates everything first, produces a fast executable and a separate file for the output, and is harder to debug while running.
  • Interpreter: translates line by line, starts quickly and eases debugging, but runs more slowly because it translates again each time.
  • Assembler: converts assembly language, which uses mnemonics such as ADD and MOV, into machine code, with a one-to-one correspondence between each instruction and its binary form.

Why the operating system loads the program

The loader is part of the operating system's work of managing memory. It reserves space, places the instructions and data in that space and sets the starting address. Without this step the processor would not know where the program begins or which memory it may use.

Exam point: name the translator for each stage in the question, and state one advantage and one disadvantage of the translator the question describes.

title: IGCSE Physics: Energy, Work and Power
content:
IGCSE Physics: Energy, Work and Power

Cambridge IGCSE Physics 0625 (2026–2028), Topic 1 Motion, forces and energy, statement 1.7 Energy, work and power. Energy is the currency of every physical process: it is never created or destroyed, only moved between stores and converted between forms. This note builds the whole idea from scratch — stores, transfers, the two energy equations, work, power, the world's energy resources and efficiency — because Paper 4 rewards candidates who can both calculate an energy change and explain where the energy went.

Energy stores and transfers

Think of energy as money held in different bank accounts. It can sit in a store, and it can move between stores along a transfer pathway, but the total across all accounts never changes. The examined stores and transfers are:

Energy storeWhat it meansExample
KineticEnergy of a moving object; more mass or more speed means moreA moving lorry
Gravitational potentialEnergy stored by virtue of height in a gravitational fieldA book on a shelf
Elastic potentialEnergy stored by stretching, compressing or twistingA drawn bow, a compressed spring
Thermal (internal)Energy of the random motion of particles in a substanceHot water in a kettle
ChemicalEnergy stored in chemical bondsFood, fuel, a battery
NuclearEnergy stored in the nucleus of an atomUranium fuel

The four transfer pathways are mechanical work (a force acting over a distance), heating (energy transferred by a temperature difference), radiation (energy carried by waves, mainly infrared and light) and electrical work (charge moving through a potential difference). When a ball is thrown upwards, chemical energy in the muscles does mechanical work on the ball, and that energy becomes kinetic; as the ball rises, kinetic becomes gravitational potential; as it falls back, gravitational potential becomes kinetic again; on impact the kinetic spreads into the thermal stores of the ball, the ground and the air, and some is radiated as sound.

Conservation of energy and Sankey diagrams

The law of conservation of energy states that energy cannot be created or destroyed, and the total energy in a closed system stays constant. This is the most powerful statement in the syllabus: whenever a question says a machine loses energy, it means the energy has been transferred to less useful stores, not destroyed. A Sankey diagram draws the total energy input as one wide arrow, splits it into useful output and wasted arrows, and is drawn so the arrow widths are proportional to the energies.

Useful energy is the energy transferred to the store the device was designed to fill; wasted energy is transferred to stores that were not the goal, usually thermal energy of the surroundings, and it is eventually transferred to the environment, often by radiation. Wasted energy is not destroyed — it has simply become too spread out to be harnessed easily.

Kinetic and gravitational potential energy

Both equations are Supplement statements, and both appear constantly in Paper 4 calculations.

kinetic energy = 1/2 x mass x speed squared        EK = 1/2 m v^2
gravitational potential energy = mass x gravitational field strength x height        EP = m g h
  • EK: kinetic energy in joules (J); m: mass in kilograms (kg); v: speed in metres per second (m s⁻¹). Energy is a scalar, so the speed is squared and the direction of travel does not matter.
  • EP: gravitational potential energy in joules (J); g: gravitational field strength in newtons per kilogram (N kg⁻¹, use the value given in the question); h: vertical height in metres (m), measured between the two positions being compared.

Only the difference in height matters. Lifting a 2 kg book from a table to a shelf 0.50 m above it raises EP by 2 × 9.81 × 0.50 = 9.8 J, whatever the height of the room. The sign convention is simple: EP increases as an object rises and decreases as it falls, and the change is ΔEP = m g Δh.

Energy methods are often faster than forces and equations of motion. For a falling object with no air resistance, m g h = ½ m v², and the mass cancels: every object falls at the same rate in a vacuum. For a roller coaster of mass 500 kg dropping 20 m from rest, v = √(2 g h) = √(2 × 9.81 × 20) = 19.8 m s⁻¹.

Work done

Work is done when a force moves an object. It is energy transferred by mechanical work, and it is measured in joules:

work done = force x distance moved in the direction of the force        W = F s
  • W: work done in joules (J). One joule is the work done when a force of 1 newton moves its point of application 1 metre in the direction of the force.
  • F: force in newtons (N); s: distance moved in metres (m), measured in the direction of the force.

Work is a scalar, but the two quantities must line up: carrying a box horizontally at constant height does no work against gravity, because the motion is perpendicular to the weight. Pushing a trolley with 50 N against 20 N of friction over 4 m does 200 J of work in total, of which 80 J goes to heating the bearings and floor through friction and 120 J remains as kinetic energy. If you carry shopping upstairs, the work done against gravity is your weight multiplied by the vertical height gained, not the length of the staircase.

Power

Power measures how fast energy is transferred — the rate of doing work. A car engine that lifts the same load in half the time is twice as powerful.

power = work done / time taken = energy transferred / time taken        P = W / t = E / t
  • P: power in watts (W). One watt is one joule per second (1 W = 1 J s⁻¹). A kilowatt is 1000 W.
  • W: work done in joules (J); E: energy transferred in joules (J); t: time taken in seconds (s).

Power is a scalar. For a vehicle moving at constant speed against a constant force, the same idea gives P = F v (Supplement), with F in newtons and v in metres per second, giving watts directly. Doubling the speed of a car at constant driving force doubles the power needed; a car climbing a hill at constant speed needs power P = mgv sin θ to raise its weight.

Energy resources and electricity generation

Most electrical energy is generated the same way: a fuel heats water, the steam spins a turbine, and the turbine spins a generator that converts the kinetic energy of rotation into electrical energy. What differs is the energy store the heat comes from.

ResourceStore usedAdvantagesDisadvantages
Coal, oil, gas (fossil fuels)Chemical, burned to give heatReliable, cheap to run, existing infrastructureFinite supply; carbon dioxide and pollutants released; contributes to climate change and acid rain
BiofuelChemical, from plant or animal materialRenewable; carbon dioxide released was recently absorbed by the plantsLand and water needed to grow crops; energy cost of farming and transport
HydroelectricGravitational potential of stored waterRenewable, reliable, no fuel cost, no emissions in useDams flood valleys and disrupt habitats; high construction cost; depends on rainfall
GeothermalThermal energy inside the EarthRenewable, reliable, small land useOnly practical near volcanic regions; drilling cost; possible release of underground gases
Nuclear fuelNuclear, released by fissionVery large energy per kilogram; no carbon dioxide in operationRadioactive waste that must be stored safely for centuries; high decommissioning cost; accident risk
Solar cellsLight radiation converted directly to electricityRenewable, silent, no emissions in use, low maintenanceOutput varies with light and season; expensive to manufacture; large area needed for high output
Solar panels (heating)Light radiation heating water directlyRenewable and cheap to runOnly heats water; ineffective at night and in cloudy climates

Non-renewable resources exist in finite stock and are used faster than they form; renewable resources are replenished as they are used. Supplement statements add the deep connection: the Sun is the principal source for almost all of these resources. Sunlight drives the water cycle behind hydroelectric power and biofuels, heats the ground behind wind and geothermal gradients, and fossil fuels are the remains of organisms that grew in sunlight. The Sun releases energy by nuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium, and research into fusion on Earth aims to provide a fuel that is abundant and produces no long-lived radioactive waste, though sustained fusion power is still experimental.

Efficiency

Efficiency compares what a device delivers with what it is given:

efficiency = useful energy output / total energy input
efficiency = useful power output / total power input

Efficiency has no unit; multiply by 100 for a percentage. No real device is 100 per cent efficient, because some energy is always transferred to thermal stores of the surroundings by friction, resistance and radiation. A filament lamp is about 5 per cent efficient (most energy becomes heat, not light); an electric motor might reach 80 per cent. The most efficient heating device is a simple heater, because its useful output is thermal energy — the same store as its waste. A Sankey diagram makes this visible at a glance, and the arrows must sum to the total input.

Worked example: lifting and efficiency

A crane lifts a 500 kg load through 12 m at constant speed in 20 s. Take g = 9.81 N kg⁻¹.

weight = m g = 500 x 9.81 = 4905 N
useful work = force x distance = 4905 x 12 = 58 860 J
useful power = work / time = 58 860 / 20 = 2943 W (about 2.9 kW)

The motor takes 150 000 J of electrical energy to do this lift. Its efficiency is 58 860 / 150 000 = 0.39, or 39 per cent. The remaining 91 140 J is not destroyed: it warms the motor windings, the cables and the surrounding air.

Second stage, using energy conservation: if the load is dropped from rest through the same 12 m with negligible air resistance, m g h = ½ m v² gives v = √(2 × 9.81 × 12) = 15.3 m s⁻¹. The mass cancels, so any object dropped through 12 m reaches the same speed.

Common mistakes

  • Saying energy is used up or lost; energy is transferred to other stores, and the total is conserved. Examiners award the mark for transferred, not lost.
  • Putting speed rather than speed squared into EK = ½mv², and forgetting the ½.
  • Measuring h in EP = mgh along a slope or a staircase; h is the vertical height difference.
  • Using the wrong mass in W = mg: the mass in kilograms, multiplied by g, never the weight in newtons multiplied by g again.
  • Confusing work done with power: joules measure energy, watts measure the rate of energy transfer.
  • Calculating efficiency as total in over useful out; the useful output goes on top, so efficiency is always less than 1.
  • Forgetting that a percentage efficiency needs multiplying by 100, and leaving the answer as 0.39 when 39 per cent is asked for.
  • Mixing units: power in watts needs energy in joules and time in seconds, so kilowatts and minutes must be converted first.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 4, 3 marks). A ball of mass 0.15 kg is moving at 10 m s⁻¹. Calculate its kinetic energy and the height through which it would need to be raised to store the same energy. Take g = 9.81 N kg⁻¹.

Answer: EK = ½mv² = ½ × 0.15 × 10² = 7.5 J. Setting mgh = 7.5 gives h = 7.5 / (0.15 × 9.81) = 5.1 m.

Question 2 (Paper 4, 4 marks). A 60 kg student runs up a flight of stairs of vertical height 3.0 m in 4.0 s. Calculate the useful power developed. Take g = 10 N kg⁻¹.

Answer: work = mgh = 60 × 10 × 3.0 = 1800 J. Power = 1800 / 4.0 = 450 W. (Real power is higher, because the student also gains kinetic energy and warms their muscles.)

Question 3 (Paper 2 style). A machine takes in 2000 J and delivers 1500 J of useful work. Its efficiency is: A 25 per cent; B 75 per cent; C 133 per cent; D 175 per cent. Answer: B. 1500/2000 = 0.75 = 75 per cent. Option C comes from putting input over output — the classic trap.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 6 marks). Explain why a solar cell is described as renewable, and discuss whether it is a good replacement for a coal-fired power station.

Answer: A solar cell converts light energy directly into electrical energy and consumes no fuel, so its energy source, sunlight, is replenished continuously and it is renewable. It produces no carbon dioxide or pollutants in operation. Against that, output depends on light intensity and falls at night and in cloudy weather, so storage or backup generation is needed; manufacturing the cells is energy-intensive, and a large area is required for high output. Coal is reliable and dispatchable but burns a finite resource, releasing carbon dioxide that drives climate change plus sulfur dioxide and particulates. A balanced conclusion weighs reliability and land use against emissions and fuel sustainability.

Question 5 (Paper 4, 3 marks). A car engine produces a driving force of 2000 N while travelling at 30 m s⁻¹. Calculate the useful power output.

Answer: P = F v = 2000 × 30 = 60 000 W = 60 kW.

Question 6 (Paper 6 style). Suggest how you would determine experimentally the efficiency of an electric motor lifting a small mass.

Answer: Measure the mass with a balance and the height lifted with a ruler, and record the time with a stopwatch. The useful output is mgh, calculated from the measured mass and vertical height. Measure the electrical energy input with a joule meter, or with an ammeter and voltmeter readings and E = V I t. Efficiency is mgh divided by V I t. Repeat for several masses and quote an average, keeping the input voltage constant.

With energy accounted for, the next question is what happens when forces are spread over area and depth: pressure and density.

Equations and symbols

Statement 1.7 is a small set of equations used in a large number of combinations. The two rules that carry most of the marks are that work needs a force along the displacement, and that power is a rate, so every time must be in seconds before dividing.

Work and the energy stores

W = Fd
Key: W = work done (J); F = force in the direction of motion (N); d = distance moved along that direction (m). A force at right angles to the motion does no work.

KE = ½mv²
Key: KE = kinetic energy (J); m = mass (kg); v = speed (m/s). The speed is squared, so doubling the speed quadruples the energy — the reason braking distance rises so steeply.

GPE = mgh
Key: GPE = gravitational potential energy (J); m = mass (kg); g = gravitational field strength (9.8 N/kg); h = height gained (m). A fall is a loss of GPE, so state the sign or the word.

KE lost = GPE gained (no friction)
Key: the conservation statement used to link the two stores. With friction or air resistance, part of the energy is transferred to the thermal store of the surroundings and the equality becomes an inequality.

v = √(2gh)
Key: v = speed at the bottom of a frictionless fall (m/s); g = 9.8 m/s²; h = height fallen (m). It comes from ½mv² = mgh, and the mass cancels — which is why a feather and a hammer match on the Moon.

Power

P = E / t = W / t
Key: P = power (W); E or W = energy transferred or work done (J); t = time taken (s). One watt is one joule per second.

E = Pt
Key: E = energy transferred (J); P = power (W); t = time (s). With P in kilowatts and t in hours the energy comes out in kilowatt-hours, which is what a meter measures.

P = Fv
Key: P = useful power output (W); F = driving force (N); v = constant speed (m/s). For a car at steady speed the driving force equals the total resistive force.

1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J
Key: one kilowatt-hour is the energy of a 1000 W appliance running for one hour; 1 kW × 3600 s = 3.6 MJ.

Efficiency

efficiency = (useful energy output / total energy input) × 100%
Key: both energies in joules (or both powers in watts, since the time cancels); the result is a percentage and can never exceed 100. A figure above 100 means the wrong quantity was used as the input.

wasted energy = input − useful output
Key: the remainder is transferred by friction, air resistance or sound to the thermal store of the surroundings. Energy is not destroyed, so the widths of a Sankey diagram must balance.

useful power of a lifting motor = mgh / t
Key: m = load mass (kg); g = 9.8 N/kg; h = height lifted (m); t = time taken (s). Comparing this with the electrical input VI gives the motor's efficiency.

title: Edexcel IAL Computer Science: Data Representation and Data Types
content:
Edexcel IAL Computer Science: Data Representation and Data Types

Pearson Edexcel International Advanced Level in Computer Science, Unit 1 Principles of Computer Science: data representation — number systems, binary arithmetic, fixed- and floating-point numbers, text, images, sound and compression — together with the data types that programs declare over that raw binary. Everything below is derived or traced digit by digit: every conversion, every normalisation step and every rounding is shown in full, because at A Level the examiner asks not just for the result but for the mechanism. If the IGCSE course taught you that computers store bits, this note explains exactly how those bits stand for every value a program can hold.

Place value and number systems

Any number system is a place-value system: a digit's value depends on where it sits, and each column is a power of the base. Denary uses base 10 (columns 1, 10, 100…); binary uses base 2 (columns 1, 2, 4, 8…); hexadecimal uses base 16 (columns 1, 16, 256…, with digits 0–9 and A–F for 10–15). The only thing that changes between bases is which powers the columns represent.

Denary 347, read as place value:
  3 × 10² + 4 × 10¹ + 7 × 10⁰ = 300 + 40 + 7 = 347

Binary 1010 1101, read the same way:
  1 × 128 + 0 × 64 + 1 × 32 + 0 × 16 + 1 × 8 + 1 × 4 + 0 × 2 + 1 × 1
  = 128 + 32 + 8 + 4 + 1 = 173

Hex AD, read as place value:
  A x 16 + D x 1 = 10 × 16 + 13 × 1 = 173        [same value, three notations]
Denary to binary by repeated division (the general method for any base):

  173 / 2 = 86  remainder 1   <- least significant bit (bottom of the column)
   86 / 2 = 43  remainder 0
   43 / 2 = 21  remainder 1
   21 / 2 = 10  remainder 1
   10 / 2 =  5  remainder 0
    5 / 2 =  2  remainder 1
    2 / 2 =  1  remainder 0
    1 / 2 =  0  remainder 1   <- most significant bit

  Read the remainders bottom to top: 1010 1101 = 173.

Denary to hex uses base 16 the same way:
  173 / 16 = 10 remainder 13   (10 = A, 13 = D)
  10 / 16 =  0 remainder 10
  Read bottom to top: AD.

Hexadecimal matters for humans, not machines: one hex digit maps exactly to four bits (a nibble), so memory dumps, error codes and colour values (#FF8800) can be transcribed without bit-counting errors.

Binary arithmetic

Addition - the four rules of a single column:
  0 + 0 = 0
  0 + 1 = 1
  1 + 1 = 10   (write 0, carry 1)
  1 + 1 + 1 (with carry) = 11   (write 1, carry 1)

Worked: 1011 0110 (= 182) + 0110 1001 (= 105), column by column:

  bit 0: 0 + 1       = 1
  bit 1: 1 + 0       = 1
  bit 2: 1 + 0       = 1
  bit 3: 0 + 1       = 1
  bit 4: 1 + 0       = 1
  bit 5: 0 + 1       = 1
  bit 6: 1 + 1       = 0, carry 1
  bit 7: 1 + 0 + 1(c)= 0, carry 1

  Result with the final carry: 1 0011 1111 = 287.
  Check: 182 + 105 = 287 ✓

  The carry out of bit 7 is a 9th bit that 8 bits cannot hold: in 8-bit
  storage the answer would read 0011 1111 = 63, which is wrong - that is
  overflow, and exam questions deliberately set it.

Two's complement subtraction uses addition with a negated operand, so one adder circuit does both jobs — see below. Multiplication is repeated addition (or shift-and-add: multiplying by 2 is a left shift); division is repeated subtraction or a right shift.

Two's complement: signed integers

Storing negative numbers needs a convention. In two's complement the most significant bit carries a negative weight (for 8 bits: −128, 64, 32, …, 1), giving a range of −128 to +127. The construction rule (invert all bits, then add 1) comes from the requirement that negation must be its own inverse and that zero must have exactly one representation.

Write -53 in 8-bit two's complement, every step:

  +53 in binary:        0 0 1 1 0 1 0 1
  invert every bit:     1 1 0 0 1 0 1 0
  add 1:                1 1 0 0 1 0 1 1   = -53

Check with the column weights:
  -128 + 64 + 0 + 0 + 8 + 0 + 2 + 1 = -53 ✓

Subtraction as addition: 37 - 53
  37  = 0 0 1 0 0 1 0 1
 -53  = 1 1 0 0 1 0 1 1
 add:  (1) 1 1 1 1 0 0 0 0
  The carry out of bit 7 is DISCARDED in two's complement arithmetic.
  1111 0000 = -128 + 64 + 32 + 16 = -16. And 37 - 53 = -16 ✓
  • Range of n-bit two's complement: −2ⁿ⁻¹ to 2ⁿ⁻¹ − 1. The asymmetry (no +128) exists because zero takes the pattern that would otherwise be "negative zero".
  • Overflow test: signed overflow occurs when adding two positives gives a negative, or two negatives gives a positive — the sign bit is the witness. Unsigned overflow is a carry out of the MSB.
  • Arithmetic shift right preserves the sign bit (copies it into the vacated position), dividing a negative number by 2 correctly; a logical shift fills with zeros and would corrupt negatives.

Fixed-point and floating-point numbers

Real numbers cannot all be stored exactly in finite bits, so a convention is needed. Fixed point reserves a fixed number of bits for the integer part and the fraction (a hidden binary point, like writing money as pence). It is fast and exact within its range but rigid: 8.4 fixed point cannot represent very large and very small numbers at once.

Floating point is binary scientific notation: value = mantissa × 2^(exponent − bias), stored in three fields — sign, exponent (biased), mantissa (normalised).

Store 5.75 in an 8-bit float with 4-bit exponent (bias 7) and 4-bit mantissa.

1. Convert to binary:  5.75 = 101.11   [4 + 1 + 0.5 + 0.25]
2. Normalise: 101.11 = 1.0111 × 2²   [leading digit before the point is 1]
3. Mantissa: store the fraction after the point: 0111 (the leading 1 is
   implicit - "hidden bit" - saving one bit).
4. Exponent: 2 + bias 7 = 9 = 1001.
5. Sign: 0 (positive).

  0 | 1001 | 0111
  s   exp    mantissa

Decode the same way: exponent 1001 = 9 - 7 = 2; mantissa 1.0111;
1.0111 × 2² = 101.11 = 5.75 ✓

Normalisation maximises precision by forcing the leading mantissa bit to be 1 (for two's-complement mantissas, 0.1… for positives, 1.0… for negatives — the pattern chosen so no precision is wasted). An unnormalised float wastes mantissa bits on leading zeros.

Denormalisation / underflow and overflow: a number too small for the exponent field underflows to zero (or a denormal); too large overflows to "infinity". Rounding errors are inherent: 0.1 has no finite binary expansion, so (0.1 + 0.2 = 0.30000000000000004 in most languages). Quantisation error (rounding to the nearest representable value) is why money is stored in integer pence, not floats — an exam favourite.

Arithmetic with the 5.75 float encoding: add 2.5.

  2.5 = 10.1 = 1.01 × 2¹ → exponent 1 + 7 = 8 = 1000, mantissa 0100
  To add, align exponents: shift the smaller mantissa right by (2-1)=1.
      1.0111 × 2²
    + 0.1010 × 2²      (1.010 × 2¹ shifted)
    ----------------
      10.0001 × 2²
  Renormalise: 1.00001 × 2³ → mantissa 0000 (only 4 bits kept!), exponent 10.
  Answer: 1000.0 = 8. The true sum 5.75 + 2.5 = 8.25 - the lost fractional
  bits are precision loss, and questions ask you to name it.

Text, characters and codes

Characters are stored as agreed numeric codes. ASCII (7-bit, 128 codes: A = 65, a = 97, 0 = 48) covers Latin text and control codes; extended ASCII adds 128 more with 8 bits. Unicode (up to 21 bits per code point, over 140 000 characters) covers world scripts and emoji; UTF-8 stores common characters in 1 byte and rare ones in up to 4 — variable width, backwards compatible with ASCII, dominant on the web. Errors in text data are detected with parity bits or checksums at transmission level.

Images and sound at A Level depth

Multimedia data — graphics, images, sound and video — is where the representation choices become visible trade-offs between quality and size. Every format below is a different answer to the same question: which parts of the signal are worth keeping?

MediaRepresentationKey size factorsFormats
Graphics (bitmap)Grid of pixelsWidth × height × colour depthBMP, PNG, JPEG
Graphics (vector)Shape equations and coordinatesNumber of shapes and curvesSVG, PDF, CAD files
SoundSamples of amplitudeSample rate × bit depth × duration × channelsWAV, FLAC, MP3
VideoFrames of images plus sampled audioFrame size × colour depth × frame rate × durationMP4, MKV

Bitmap images: file size in bits = width × height × colour depth, plus metadata (dimensions, depth, DPI). 24-bit colour stores 8 bits each of red, green and blue (0–255 per channel); 1-bit is monochrome; palette modes (4-bit, 8-bit) index a colour table. Resolution (pixels) versus DPI (print density) are different ideas — the classic confusion. Vector graphics store shape equations (points, lines, Bézier curves, fills) and render at any resolution — smaller for logos and CAD, resolution-independent, but expensive for photorealistic images.

Sound is sampled: sample rate (Hz) × bit depth × duration × channels. Quantisation error (rounding each sample to the nearest level) and aliasing (insufficient sample rate; fixed by sampling at more than twice the highest frequency — Nyquist) are the A Level additions over IGCSE.

Worked: 60 seconds of stereo, 44.1 kHz, 16-bit, then compressed 4:1.

  bits = 60 × 44 100 × 16 × 2 = 84 672 000 bits
  bytes = 84 672 000 / 8 = 10 584 000 bytes
  MB (binary) = 10 584 000 / 1 048 576 = 10.09 MB
  compressed = 10.09 / 4 = 2.52 MB

Compression

Lossless methods remove statistical redundancy and restore the original exactly: run-length encoding (store runs as counts — great for large flat areas), dictionary compression (LZW-style: replace repeated strings with references to a dictionary — ZIP, PNG, GIF), and Huffman-style frequency coding (short codes for frequent symbols). Lossy methods discard perceptually minor detail: JPEG (frequency-domain discard), MP3 (psychoacoustic masking), used where the eye or ear cannot detect the loss. Choosing: documents and code demand lossless; photographs and music accept lossy.

Data types and abstraction

A data type defines a set of values and the valid operations on them: INTEGER (whole numbers, arithmetic), REAL (decimals, arithmetic with rounding), CHAR (single symbol), STRING (sequences of chars), BOOLEAN (true/false), DATE/TIME, plus user-defined types. Abstract data types (covered fully in the A2 notes) separate what a structure does from how it is stored. Casting between types has rules: integer to real is exact; real to integer truncates or rounds — 7.9 becomes 7 (truncate) or 8 (round); char to int gives its character code ('A' → 65).

Worked example: one value, three representations

The character 'K', the number -20, and the fraction 0.125 in the same memory:

'K'  : ASCII 75 = 0100 1011 (1 byte)
-20  : two's complement 8-bit: invert 0001 0100 → 1110 1011, add 1 →
       1110 1100. Check: -128 + 64 + 32 + 8 + 4 = -20 ✓
0.125: 0.001 binary exactly (2⁻³). In the 4-bit-mantissa float: 1.0 × 2⁻³;
       exponent -3 + 7 = 4 = 0100; mantissa 0000; value 0 | 0100 | 0000.
       Decode: 1.0000 × 2⁻³ = 0.125 ✓

Same bytes, three meanings - the type system decides the interpretation.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Reading division remainders top-down instead of bottom-up in base conversion.
  • Grouping bits from the wrong end when converting binary to hex.
  • Treating the MSB of two's complement as +128 instead of −128, and applying unsigned overflow rules to signed arithmetic (or vice versa).
  • Forgetting the "+1" when negating, or negating twice without checking.
  • Omitting the normalisation step in floating-point questions (value = 1.mantissa × 2^(exp−bias)), or dropping the hidden bit when decoding.
  • Confusing resolution with DPI, or bits with bytes in size calculations (×8 / ÷8).
  • Claiming floats store money safely: quantisation error makes integer minor units the correct choice.
  • Choosing lossy compression for data that must restore exactly (text, executables, medical images).

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Unit 1, 4 marks). Convert 0.375 to 8-bit binary fixed point (4 integer, 4 fraction bits) and to normalised floating-point form.

Answer: 0.375 = 0.011₂ (0.25 + 0.125). Fixed point 4.4: 0000.0110. Floating point: 1.1 × 2⁻² (normalised), mantissa 1000 (after the hidden 1), exponent −2 + bias.

Question 2 (Unit 1, 4 marks). Show how −29 is stored in 8-bit two's complement and verify it.

Answer: +29 = 0001 1101; invert = 1110 0010; add 1 = 1110 0011. Verification: −128 + 64 + 32 + 2 + 1 = −29 ✓.

Question 3 (Unit 1, 5 marks). Explain normalisation and why a floating-point number is stored normalised.

Answer: Normalisation rewrites the mantissa so the first significant bit is directly before the binary point (1.m × 2^e), by shifting the point and adjusting the exponent. This maximises the precision of the stored mantissa: with a fixed number of mantissa bits, leading zeros would waste bits carrying no information. The leading 1 can then be implied (hidden bit), extending precision by one bit, and every value has exactly one encoding, so equality comparisons work.

Question 4 (Unit 1, 4 marks). Calculate the size in MB of an uncompressed 1600 × 1200 image at 8-bit colour, and state its size after 5:1 lossless compression.

Answer: 1600 × 1200 × 8 = 15 360 000 bits; ÷ 8 = 1 920 000 bytes; ÷ 1 048 576 = 1.83 MB. At 5:1 compression: 1.83 ÷ 5 = 0.366 MB, with the original exactly recoverable.

Question 5 (Unit 1, 3 marks). Explain why (0.1 + 0.2) ≠ 0.3 in floating-point arithmetic.

Answer: 0.1 and 0.2 have no finite binary expansions, so each is rounded to the nearest representable floating-point value when stored; the tiny rounding errors carry into the sum, giving 0.30000000000000004. Floating-point arithmetic is therefore approximate — which is why financial calculations use integer pence.

Question 6 (Unit 1, 4 marks). Compare vector and bitmap graphics for a company logo.

Answer: A logo must scale from a favicon to a billboard. Vector graphics store shape definitions (points, curves, fills), so they scale without pixelation, have small file sizes for simple art and are easily recoloured. Bitmaps store a fixed pixel grid: enlarging one pixelates and inflates the file. Vector is therefore correct for logos; bitmap suits photographs.

From the raw bits, the next step up is the machine that manipulates them: the processor.

title: Logic Gates & Boolean Logic — Study Notes
content:
Logic Gates & Boolean Logic

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): six gates, truth tables, building/describing circuits, problem-to-logic mapping.

1. The six gates

ABANDORNANDNORXOR
0000110
0101101
1001101
1111000

NOT inverts. NAND = AND + invert; NOR = OR + invert; XOR = 1 when inputs differ.

2. Truth tables

2 inputs → 4 rows; 3 inputs → 8 rows. Work gate by gate, adding intermediate columns for sub-circuit outputs.

3. Logic expressions

A Boolean expression describes a circuit in logic: X = A AND NOT B, or X = (A OR B) AND C. Brackets fix the order — work out bracketed parts first, then AND, then OR.

  • Circuit → expression: label the output of every gate (P, Q, …), write one expression per gate in order, then combine them at the final gate.
  • Truth table → expression: mark the rows where the output is 1; for each such row write a term that is true only in that row (write NOT for an input that is 0, AND between the inputs); join the terms with OR. For XOR: X = (NOT A AND B) OR (A AND NOT B).
  • Expression → truth table: add an intermediate column for each sub-expression before the output column.
  • Rules used to simplify: A AND 1 = A; A AND 0 = 0; A OR 1 = 1; A OR 0 = A; A AND A = A; A AND NOT A = 0; A OR NOT A = 1; NOT(NOT A) = A; X OR (X AND Y) = X. (AS extension, 9618: De Morgan's laws — NOT(A AND B) = NOT A OR NOT B and NOT(A OR B) = NOT A AND NOT B.)

Example: a light X is on only when switch A is on and switch B is off → X = A AND NOT B, so X = 1 in exactly one row of its truth table (A = 1, B = 0).

4. Problem → logic

Define inputs/outputs first. Alarm rings (X=1) if sensor P triggered AND (door D OR window W): X = P AND (D OR W). Then draw the circuit: OR first, then AND.

5. Describing circuits

Write the expression from a diagram gate by gate; annotate output of each gate (X, Y) before combining.

Exam tips: check your truth table row count before writing; in problem questions, state "input P = 1 means sensor triggered" — definitions earn marks.

Worked example: building an expression from a circuit

A circuit gives Q = (A AND B) OR NOT C. Build it in stages: first the AND gate on A and B, then a NOT gate on C, then an OR gate combining the two outputs. A truth table with columns A, B, C, then the intermediate AND output, NOT C and finally Q, has eight rows for three inputs. Set out every row in order so that no combination is missed.

Simplifying with Boolean laws

Laws such as De Morgan's theorem let you rewrite NOT (A AND B) as NOT A OR NOT B. Use them to reduce a gate count before drawing a circuit. Always check a simplified expression against the original truth table, because a single misapplied law changes the output for some inputs.

title: Exam technique: DC Circuits
content:
### What earns the marks
For junctions, Kirchhoff current sums stated earn the mark. For combinations, the parallel reciprocal form quoted earns the method mark. For terminal p.d., E minus Ir earns both marks with the lost volts identified.
### Traps
Error: series rules applied to parallel branches. Correction: voltage is the shared quantity in parallel. Error: emf quoted as terminal voltage. Correction: subtract the Ir drop. Error: resistivity factors muddled. Correction: R scales with L over A.

title: Exam technique: Fractions, Decimals and Percentages
content:
### What earns the marks
For percentages of amounts, the 10-percent building blocks shown earn method marks without a calculator. For reverse percentages, state what the given amount represents (64 dollars = 80 percent) before dividing: that line earns the mark. For compound interest, each year on its own line earns credit. For Steel-type growth and decay, the multiplier (1/2 cubed) stated earns the method mark.
### Traps
Error: adding 20 percent to the sale price for the original. Correction: the sale price is the base of nothing; divide by 0.8. Error: simple interest applied twice for compound growth. Correction: grow each year from the new total. Error: decimal-point slips in 3/8 to percent. Correction: decimal first (0.375), then times 100.

title: International GCSE English as a Second Language: Writing Tasks and Themes
content:
International GCSE English as a Second Language: Writing Tasks and Themes

OxfordAQA International GCSE English as a Second Language (9280) assesses writing in a paper of its own (Paper 2 in the current official numbering — some older revision materials list the writing component first, so always check the code on your question paper). This note builds the whole writing skill set from zero: how to read the task, how to choose register, how to plan in five minutes, and how to write each task type — functional and transactional writing, short-form responses, extended discursive writing and narrative writing — across the three exam themes. Every task on this paper is a communication problem, not a grammar test, and the marks follow from solving that problem in the right tone.

What the Writing paper asks of you

The writing component carries 60 marks, is 1 hour 15 minutes long, and counts for 30% of the qualification. Its tasks are progressive: shorter functional writing first, then short-form responses, then one or two extended pieces that may be discursive or narrative. The exact task list and word limits are printed on your paper, so this note teaches the task types rather than guessing a fixed layout — and the word limit given in the question is always binding.

FeatureWhat it means for you
Duration and marks1 hour 15 minutes, 60 marks, 30% of the grade. Roughly one minute of planning per ten minutes of writing.
Task progressionShort functional tasks first (emails, notes, forms), then extended discursive or narrative writing. The later tasks carry more marks — save time for them.
The themesEverything you write sits under one of three theme areas, so vocabulary preparation is finite and examinable.
What earns marksTask fulfilment (did you do what was asked?), register (is the tone right for the reader?), organisation (is it structured?), and linguistic range and accuracy.

The three themes and their topic banks

Every question is drawn from the three OxfordAQA theme areas. You cannot predict the exact topic, but you can prepare vocabulary, examples and opinions for each theme bank, and that preparation is the single highest-return revision you can do for this paper.

ThemeTypical topicsVocabulary to prepare
Identity and cultureFamily life, traditions and festivals, food, personal identity, hobbies, music and film, cultural differencesdescribing habits and routines, comparing traditions, giving opinions about culture, describing people and places from your own experience
Local, national, international and global areas of interestYour town and region, travel and tourism, the environment, technology, news and current events, sportdescribing places, cause and effect language for problems (pollution, congestion), proposing solutions, comparing locations
Current and future study and employmentSchool subjects, exams, ambitions, jobs and careers, work experience, skills, further studydescribing plans and ambitions, talking about ability and skills, justifying choices, writing about the future with will, going to, would like to

The efficient way to revise: for each theme, prepare ten nouns, ten verbs, five adjectives, two personal examples and one opinion with a reason. That is a working vocabulary of about eighty items, and it covers almost anything the paper can ask.

The APF framework: Audience, Purpose, Form

Before writing a single sentence, three decisions control everything else. The exam rewards candidates who make these decisions visibly, because the marker can see that the writing is shaped rather than dumped.

  1. Audience — who reads this? A friend, a teacher, a stranger, an employer, a newspaper reader. This decides formality, pronouns (I and you versus one and people), abbreviations (don't versus do not), and how much you explain.
  2. Purpose — why am I writing? To persuade, inform, request, describe, entertain, complain, advise, or apply. Purpose decides the opening move and the content order: a complaint states the problem then the desired fix; a persuasive piece states the position then the reasons.
  3. Form — what shape does this text have? Email, letter, article, review, report, story. Form decides the layout features the marker looks for: greeting and sign-off on an email, headline and opening hook on an article, a clear introduction and conclusion on an essay.

Worked example of the APF decision: the task says, "Your school is thinking about banning mobile phones. Write an article for the school magazine giving your views." Audience: your classmates and teachers (semi-formal, first person plural we). Purpose: persuade with reasons and examples. Form: article, so you need a headline, a hook opening, paragraphs with linking, and a closing line that lands the point. Once those three answers exist, the plan writes itself.

Register and tone: the formal–informal continuum

Register is the difference between "Hiya, can't come, sorry!" and "Dear Mr Ahmed, I am writing to apologise for my absence." Neither is wrong in itself; each is wrong for the wrong reader. Markers describe the top band as a consistent register suited to audience and purpose — the key word is consistent. One slang phrase in an otherwise formal letter breaks that consistency and costs marks.

FeatureInformal (friend, peer)Formal (teacher, employer, institution)
OpeningHi ..., How are you?Dear Mr/Ms ..., I am writing to ...
Contractionsdon't, I'm, can'tdo not, I am, cannot
QuestionsDirect and chatty: What do you think?Polite forms: I would be grateful if you could ...
OpinionI reckon ..., To be honest ...In my opinion ..., It seems to me that ...
ClosingSee you soon! Best wishesYours sincerely / Yours faithfully

One rule of thumb saves many marks: match the formality of the task, and never mix the two columns inside one text.

Functional and transactional writing: format skeletons

Functional tasks (emails, letters, notes, messages, short articles) are marked for doing the job: covering every content point in the prompt, using the right form, and keeping the register right. A skeleton for each form means your brain can spend its energy on language instead of layout.

  • Email to a friend: greeting → reaction to their news → answers to their questions (one per bullet in the prompt) → your news/questions → closing line.
  • Formal letter or email: Dear ... → why you are writing (one sentence) → the content points in logical order, one paragraph each → what you want to happen → Yours sincerely, name.
  • Article: headline → hook (a question, a surprising fact, a short scene) → two or three paragraphs each making one point → closing line that echoes the hook.
  • Review: what it is → description → evaluation with reasons → recommendation and who it suits.
  • Report: title → introduction stating the scope → findings under clear headings → recommendation.

For every content point in the prompt, write one developed sentence or more. Under-developed content is the most common reason a competent writer scores mid-band: the marker counts content points and how fully each is covered.

Short-form responses: from notes to sentences

Short-form tasks give you information in notes, a table, or a picture and ask for connected sentences. The skill is expansion: each note must become real grammar, not a list with a capital letter.

  • Step 1 — read every note and mark the content points; one sentence minimum per point.
  • Step 2 — add the missing grammar: articles (a, the), pronouns to avoid repetition, a verb in the right tense, connectors (because, so, although, however).
  • Step 3 — check the target reader: if the task says "write to your English-speaking friend", contractions and questions are welcome; if it says "write to the school principal", they are not.

Worked example. The task: "Your friend wants to know about your new school. Use these notes to write a message: new school / big / near home / walk 10 minutes / favourite subject science / teacher good / start football club next month." A weak answer copies the notes. A top-band answer expands every point with grammar and personality: "My new school is really big — there are about a thousand students! The best part is that it's near home, so I only walk ten minutes every morning. My favourite subject is science because the teacher explains everything clearly and lets us do experiments. I've also started a football club — well, it opens next month, and I can't wait." Every note became a sentence; the register is friendly; the message reads like a message.

Extended discursive writing: the argument engine

Discursive tasks (an essay, an opinion article, a for-and-against discussion) reward organisation above fancy vocabulary. The marker needs to find your position, your reasons and your ending without hunting. Build the piece from modules:

  1. Introduction (2-3 sentences): restate the topic in your own words and give your position or the question you will explore. Never copy the prompt wording.
  2. Body paragraph 1: strongest reason. Topic sentence (the point) → explanation (why it is true) → example (a specific case, ideally personal or local) → link back to the position.
  3. Body paragraph 2: second reason, same four-beat shape.
