Forgetting the two radii in a perimeter. And using ½r²θ for a segment — the segment is the sector minus the triangle, and the triangle's area is ½r² sin θ.

title: IGCSE Chemistry: Acids, Bases and Salts
content:
IGCSE Chemistry: Acids, Bases and Salts

Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry 0620 (2026–2028), Extended route, Topic 7 Acids, bases and salts: statement 7.1 The characteristic properties of acids and bases, 7.2 Oxides, and 7.3 Preparation of salts. This note builds from what an acid physically is (a proton donor) through every reaction type worth marks, to the four salt-preparation methods with their procedures — and it is those procedures that carry Paper 6 as well as Paper 4. Every equation is balanced and every calculation line is explicit.

What acids and bases are

The everyday definition: acids taste sour, turn litmus red and react with metals and carbonates; bases are metal oxides or hydroxides that neutralise acids; alkalis are soluble bases (they dissolve to give hydroxide ions). The Extended definition that earns the extra mark: an acid is a proton (H⁺) donor and a base is a proton acceptor — in water an acid donates H⁺ to the solvent, forming H₃O⁺ but conventionally written as H⁺(aq).

Dissociation of acids in water - the strong/weak distinction:

  STRONG acid - fully dissociated (every molecule releases its proton):
    HCl(aq) -> H⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq)          [single arrow]
    HNO₃(aq) -> H⁺(aq) + NO₃⁻(aq)
    H₂SO₄(aq) -> 2H⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq)

  WEAK acid - only partially dissociated (an equilibrium):
    CH₃COOH(aq) ⇌ H⁺(aq) + CH₃COO⁻(aq)   [equilibrium arrow]
    H₂CO₃(aq) ⇌ H⁺(aq) + HCO₃⁻(aq)

Strong vs weak is about the DISOCIATION, not the concentration:
  dilute HCl is strong but dilute; concentrated ethanoic acid is weak but
  concentrated. Strong acids attack metals and carbonates faster (more H⁺
  ions per volume); weak acids are safer (vinegar, lemon juice).

Reactions of acids: the four types

Reacts withProductsWorked equation
MetalsSalt + hydrogenMg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g)
Bases (metal oxides/hydroxides)Salt + waterCuO(s) + H₂SO₄(aq) → CuSO₄(aq) + H₂O(l)
CarbonatesSalt + water + carbon dioxideCaCO₃(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl₂(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g)
Ammonia (alkali)Ammonium saltNH₃(g) + HCl(aq) → NH₄Cl(aq)

Neutralisation is acid + base → salt + water; the ionic essence is H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O. Indicators: litmus (red in acid, blue in alkali), thymolphthalein (colourless in acid, blue in alkali), methyl orange (red in acid, yellow in alkali), universal indicator for a pH estimate. pH measures acidity: pH 7 neutral, below 7 acidic, above 7 alkaline; each unit is a tenfold change in H⁺ concentration.

Oxides: the four classes

  • Basic oxides — metal oxides (CuO, CaO) that react with acids to give salt and water.
  • Acidic oxides — non-metal oxides (SO₂, CO₂, NO₂) that react with alkalis to give salt and water.
  • Amphoteric oxides — react with both acids and alkalis (Al₂O₃, ZnO) — the Extended favourite.
  • Neutral oxides — neither (CO, NO, H₂O).
Amphoteric behaviour worked, both directions:

  Al₂O₃ + 6HCl -> 2AlCl₃ + 3H₂O         [acts as a base, with acid]
  Al₂O₃ + 2NaOH -> 2NaAlO₂ + H₂O        [acts as an acid, with alkali]

The oxide's character tracks the element's position: metallic oxides basic,
non-metallic oxides acidic, and the metal/metalloid border (Al, Zn) gives
amphoteric behaviour.

Preparation of salts: four methods

The method is chosen by the salt's solubility and the acid type — a decision tree the exam expects you to reason through, not recite.

Decision tree:

  Soluble salt?
  |-- YES -> use an ACID + excess INSOLUBLE base/metal/carbonate, then
  |          filter off the excess and crystallise.
  |-- NO  -> precipitation: mix two solutions of soluble salts, filter,
             wash and dry the precipitate.

Worked procedure 1 - soluble salt from an insoluble base:
  copper(II) sulfate from copper(II) oxide + dilute sulfuric acid.
  1. Warm dilute H₂SO₄ in a beaker.
  2. Add CuO powder a little at a time with stirring - it reacts and
     dissolves: CuO + H₂SO₄ -> CuSO₄ + H₂O
  3. Keep adding until NO MORE DISSOLVES (the excess solid remains) -
     this guarantees all the acid is used up.
  4. FILTER off the excess CuO (the filtrate is pure copper(II) sulfate
     solution).
  5. Heat the filtrate to the point of crystallisation, leave to cool and
     crystallise; dry the crystals between filter papers.

  The excess-solid trick is the key exam point: a pure salt needs either
  reagent fully consumed, and only an insoluble excess can be filtered off.

Worked procedure 2 - insoluble salt by precipitation:
  barium sulfate from barium chloride + sodium sulfate solutions.
  BaCl₂(aq) + Na₂SO₄(aq) -> BaSO₄(s) + 2NaCl(aq)
  Mix solutions, filter the precipitate, wash with distilled water, dry.

Worked procedure 3 - titration (soluble salt from acid + soluble alkali):
  sodium chloride from hydrochloric acid + sodium hydroxide.
  Both are solutions, so there is no excess solid to filter - use EXACT
  volumes from a titration (see the techniques note), then evaporate.

Worked procedure 4 - acid + excess metal (hydrogen given off):
  zinc sulfate from zinc + dilute sulfuric acid; filter excess zinc.

Water of crystallisation

Many salts crystallise with water locked into their lattice — hydrated salts (CuSO₄·5H₂O blue; CoCl₂·6H₂O pink). Heating drives the water off as anhydrous salt (white CuSO₄), and the change is reversible — the water test from the environment topic. In calculations the water counts in the formula mass: Mᵣ of CuSO₄·5H₂O = 160 + 5 × 18 = 250, not 160.

Worked example: a full salt-preparation calculation

10.0 g of calcium carbonate reacts with excess hydrochloric acid:
  CaCO₃ + 2HCl -> CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂

(a) moles CaCO₃ = 10.0 / 100 = 0.100 mol
(b) ratio 1:1 -> moles CaCl₂ = 0.100 mol
(c) mass CaCl₂ (Mᵣ = 111) = 0.100 x 111 = 11.1 g   [theoretical yield]
(d) if 9.4 g of dry salt is collected:
    percentage yield = 9.4 / 11.1 x 100 = 84.7%

Where the mass is lost: crystals left in solution, spills, incomplete
reaction, or wet product if not dried - the usual evaluation question.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Confusing acid strength with concentration — strong = fully dissociated; concentrated = lots of acid per volume. The two are independent axes.
  • Writing weak acid dissociation with a single arrow; weak acids are equilibria.
  • Salt formula errors from ion charges: Al³⁺ + Cl⁻ → AlCl₃, not AlCl — check charge balance.
  • Forgetting carbon dioxide in acid + carbonate answers (three products, not two).
  • Adding excess soluble alkali in salt prep (then the salt is contaminated and cannot be filtered) — only insoluble reagents can be used in excess.
  • Leaving water of crystallisation out of formula mass or percentage-composition calculations.
  • Describing neutralisation as "acid + metal" — that is a separate reaction type; neutralisation is acid + base.
  • In precipitation questions, not washing the precipitate (residual soluble ions contaminate it).

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 4, 3 marks). Explain the difference between a strong acid and a concentrated acid.

Answer: A strong acid dissociates completely in water, releasing all its protons (e.g. hydrochloric acid); a concentrated acid contains a large amount of acid per unit volume of solution. A dilute solution of a strong acid is strong but dilute; a concentrated solution of a weak acid (ethanoic) is concentrated but weak.

Question 2 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Write equations for sulfuric acid reacting with (i) magnesium (ii) copper(II) oxide (iii) sodium carbonate.

Answer: (i) Mg + H₂SO₄ → MgSO₄ + H₂. (ii) CuO + H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + H₂O. (iii) Na₂CO₃ + H₂SO₄ → Na₂SO₄ + H₂O + CO₂.

Question 3 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Describe how pure crystals of copper(II) sulfate are prepared from copper(II) oxide and dilute sulfuric acid.

Answer: Warm the dilute acid; add copper(II) oxide with stirring until it no longer dissolves (excess solid ensures all acid reacts); filter off the excess copper(II) oxide; heat the filtrate to the point of crystallisation; leave the solution to cool and crystallise; filter and dry the crystals between filter papers.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 3 marks). Explain why aluminium oxide is described as amphoteric.

Answer: Aluminium oxide reacts with acids to form a salt and water (acting as a base), e.g. Al₂O₃ + 6HCl → 2AlCl₃ + 3H₂O, and also reacts with alkalis to form a salt and water (acting as an acid), e.g. Al₂O₃ + 2NaOH → 2NaAlO₂ + H₂O. Oxides with both behaviours are amphoteric.

Question 5 (Paper 4, 5 marks). Calculate the mass of anhydrous sodium sulfate formed when 21.2 g of sodium carbonate is neutralised by excess sulfuric acid. (Mᵣ: Na₂CO₃ = 106, Na₂SO₄ = 142)

Answer: Na₂CO₃ + H₂SO₄ → Na₂SO₄ + H₂O + CO₂. Moles Na₂CO₃ = 21.2 ÷ 106 = 0.200 mol. Ratio 1:1 → 0.200 mol Na₂SO₄. Mass = 0.200 × 142 = 28.4 g.

Question 6 (Paper 6, 3 marks). A student prepares lead(II) iodide by precipitation. State the reagents and describe the steps after mixing.

Answer: Mix solutions of lead(II) nitrate and potassium iodide. Filter to collect the yellow precipitate; wash it with distilled water to remove soluble nitrate/iodide ions; dry it between filter papers or in a warm oven.

Acids and salts live in the wider map of the elements — the Periodic Table's groups and their trends.

title: Transition Metals and their Chemistry Quick Revision
content:
Quick revision: Transition Metals and their Chemistry

Chemistry — A2. Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH15, Topic 17. Transition metals form coloured complex ions, show variable oxidation states and act as catalysts. These properties come from partly filled d orbitals.

Key areas to revise

  • Complex ions and ligands
  • Colour
  • Ligand substitution and isomerism
  • Catalysis

Worked example

Deduce the electronic configuration of the Fe2+ ion given atomic number Z = 26. Step 1: Write the neutral atom configuration, which is 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d6. Step 2: Remove electrons from the outermost principal quantum shell first, meaning the two 4s electrons are removed. Answer: 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 3d6.

Key points to remember

Transition metals are d-block elements forming one or more stable ions with incompletely-filled d-orbitals. Scandium and zinc are d-block elements but not transition metals because Sc3+ has an empty d-orbital (3d0) and Zn2+ has a full d-orbital (3d10). Variable oxidation numbers occur because the 4s and 3d sub-shells are very close in energy, requiring similar amounts of energy for successive ionization. A ligand is a species with a lone pair of electrons that can form a dative coordinate bond with a central metal ion to form a complex ion, which consists of a central metal ion surrounded by ligands. Aqueous transition metal ions are coloured due to d-orbital splitting caused by the electrostatic field of surrounding ligands, where light is absorbed promoting an electron between split d-orbitals. Lack of colour in ions like Sc3+ (3d0) or Zn2+ (3d10) arises because d-orbitals are empty or completely full, so no d-to-d electron transitions can occur. Coordination number is the total number of coordinate bonds formed between ligands and the central metal ion.

Colour changes in transition metal ions arise from changes in the oxidation number of the ion, changes in the ligand, or changes in the coordination number of the complex. Water (H2O), hydroxide (OH−) and ammonia (NH3) act as monodentate ligands forming six-coordinate octahedral complexes. Chloride ions (Cl−) are relatively large, so fewer can fit around a central metal ion, forming four-coordinate tetrahedral complexes. Square planar complexes are formed by certain metal ions such as Pt(II); cis-platin is a square planar platinum(II) complex used as an anticancer drug, supplied as a single cis isomer because the trans isomer is inactive. Bidentate ligands like ethane-1,2-diamine (NH2CH2CH2NH2) donate two lone pairs, and hexadentate ligands like EDTA4− donate six lone pairs. Haemoglobin is an iron(II) complex containing a polydentate macrocyclic ligand, where oxygen bound to haemoglobin undergoes ligand exchange and is replaced by carbon monoxide due to stronger binding affinity.

Vanadium exhibits four oxidation states in aqueous solution with distinct colours: +5 is yellow (VO2+), +4 is blue (VO2+), +3 is green (V3+), and +2 is violet (V2+). These can be interconverted using zinc in acidic conditions, where Eo values dictate the reduction steps. Dichromate(VI) ions (Cr2O7 2−) can be reduced to Cr3+ and Cr2+ using zinc in acidic conditions, or produced from Cr3+ by oxidation with hydrogen peroxide in alkaline conditions followed by acidification. Dichromate(VI) ions exist in equilibrium with chromate(VI) ions: Cr2O7 2− + H2O = 2CrO4 2− + 2H+. Transition metal ions like Cr3+, Mn2+, Fe2+, Fe3+, Co2+, Ni2+, Cu2+, and Zn2+ react with aqueous sodium hydroxide and aqueous ammonia to form characteristic precipitates, some of which dissolve in excess alkali or ammonia due to amphoteric behaviour, deprotonation, or ligand exchange. Notable ligand exchanges include forming [Cu(NH3)4(H2O)2]2+ from [Cu(H2O)6]2+ via Cu(OH)2(H2O)4, forming [CuCl4]2− from [Cu(H2O)6]2+, and forming [CoCl4]2− from [Co(H2O)6]2+. Substituting monodentate ligands with bidentate or hexadentate ligands increases entropy (positive ΔSsystem), driving the chelate effect and yielding a more stable complex ion.

Catalysis by transition metals is split into heterogeneous and homogeneous types. Heterogeneous catalysts are in a different phase from reactants, with reactions occurring on the active sites of the catalyst surface, as seen with V2O5 acting via oxidation state changes in the contact process (SO2 to SO3), and catalytic converters adsorbing CO and NO, weakening bonds, reacting to form CO2 and N2, and desorbing the products. Homogeneous catalysts are in the same phase as reactants and proceed via intermediate species, such as Fe2+ ions catalysing the reaction between I− and S2O8 2− ions, and Mn2+ ions autocatalysing the reaction between MnO4− and C2O4 2− ions. Core Practical 14 involves the laboratory preparation of a transition metal complex such as copper(II) sulfate crystals or potassium tris(oxalato)ferrate(III).

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

title: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Scatter Diagrams and Correlation
content:
Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Scatter Diagrams and Correlation

A scatter diagram plots two measurements for each person or object, one on each axis, and reveals whether they move together. The IGCSE questions ask you to describe that relationship — correlation — draw a line of best fit, and use it to estimate. The arithmetic is light; the marks come from precise language and from the discipline of drawing and reading the line correctly. This note builds the topic from zero: what correlation means and how to describe it, how to draw a line of best fit that earns the marks, how to use it for interpolation and extrapolation, and why correlation is not causation.

What a scatter diagram shows

Each point represents one individual: its horizontal coordinate is one variable (say, hours of revision) and its vertical coordinate the other (say, test score). The pattern of points — the scatter — is the data's message. Bivariate data means two variables measured on the same individuals; the diagram is the quickest way to see whether a relationship exists.

  • Positive correlation: as one variable increases, the other tends to increase (revision time and score).
  • Negative correlation: as one increases, the other tends to decrease (car age and value).
  • No correlation: no pattern — the points form a cloud (shoe size and score).
  • Strength: strong correlation means the points lie close to a line; weak means they are widely scattered around it.

Describing correlation precisely

The mark scheme wants three things in a description: direction (positive or negative), strength (strong, moderate or weak), and the variables named. "There is a strong positive correlation between hours of revision and test score" earns the mark; "the graph goes up" does not.

Worked example. A scatter diagram of 30 cars shows points tightly clustered around a line falling from top-left to bottom-right. Describe the correlation and interpret it.

Strong negative correlation between age and value:
older cars tend to be worth less. The tightness of the
cluster means the relationship is consistent, but individual
cars can still deviate (condition, mileage).

Drawing the line of best fit

A line of best fit summarises the trend. The marks are awarded for a straight line that:

  1. Passes through the middle of the cloud — roughly equal numbers of points above and below.
  2. Follows the trend direction (rising for positive, falling for negative correlation).
  3. Is drawn with a ruler and extends across the plotted range.

A useful anchor: the line should pass close to the mean point (the mean of the x-values, mean of the y-values). It does not have to pass through the origin, and it should not be forced through any single point.

Worked example. Points cluster with mean x = 12 and mean y = 60, trending upward. Describe where the line of best fit should pass and how to check it.

The line should pass through (12, 60) and follow the upward
trend; check by counting points above and below - roughly equal
numbers on each side, with the line through the middle of the
vertical spread at each x.

Using the line: interpolation and extrapolation

Once the line is drawn, estimates are read from it — not from individual points:

  • Interpolation: estimating within the range of the data. Reliable, because the trend is supported by nearby points.
  • Extrapolation: estimating beyond the plotted range. Risky, because nothing guarantees the relationship continues — a straight line cannot describe a curve that turns.

Worked example. A line of best fit passes through (4, 30) and (10, 54). Estimate y when x = 7, and comment on estimating y when x = 30.

gradient = (54 - 30)/(10 - 4) = 24/6 = 4
equation: y = 4x + c; using (4, 30): 30 = 16 + c → c = 14
y = 4x + 14
at x = 7: y = 28 + 14 = 42  (interpolation - reliable)
at x = 30: y = 134 (extrapolation - unreliable; the trend may
not continue that far)

Worked example: from table to diagram to estimate

Data: hours studied (x): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6; marks (y): 35, 42, 50, 55, 63, 70.

Step 1: plot each pair as a point (x horizontal, y vertical).
Step 2: describe - strong positive correlation.
Step 3: draw the line through the middle: the points rise
        about 7 marks per hour; a line from (1, 35) to (6, 70)
        passes through the centre of the cloud.
Step 4: estimate the mark for 3.5 hours: read up from x = 3.5
        to the line, then across: about 53 marks.
Step 5: estimate the hours for 60 marks: read across from y = 60
        to the line, then down: about 4.6 hours.

Note the wording in answers: "from the line of best fit, approximately 53 marks" — the word approximately signals that it is an estimate, which the mark scheme expects.

Correlation and causation

Correlation does not prove cause. Two variables can move together because a third factor drives both (ice-cream sales and drowning rates both rise in summer — heat causes both), or by coincidence in a small sample. Exam questions reward this caution explicitly: state that the correlation shows an association, not that one variable causes the other, unless the data come from a controlled experiment.

Worked example. A study finds a strong positive correlation between the number of books in a home and children's reading scores. Does buying books raise scores?

Not necessarily: households with more books may also have more
educated parents, more time for reading, or higher income - all
of which could raise scores. The correlation is real, but the
causal claim is unsupported by this evidence alone.

A second discipline follows: when a question asks you to comment on a study, name the possible confounding variable rather than simply denying causation. In the books example, income, parental education and available time are all plausible common causes; naming one shows the examiner you understand what a confounding factor is. The same reasoning explains why a strong correlation from a small sample deserves caution: with only a handful of points, a pattern can appear by chance, and a single outlier can create or destroy the apparent trend.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Describe) Points on a scatter diagram trend downward and are tightly clustered. Describe the correlation. Answer: Strong negative correlation — as one variable increases, the other tends to decrease consistently.
  2. (No correlation) Describe a scatter diagram whose points form a random cloud. Answer: No correlation — there is no clear trend between the variables.
  3. (Line) State two features of a correctly drawn line of best fit. Answer: A straight line through the middle of the points with roughly equal numbers above and below, following the trend and drawn with a ruler.
  4. (Estimate) A line of best fit passes through (2, 10) and (6, 26). Estimate y at x = 4. Answer: gradient 4; y = 4x + 2; at x = 4, y = 18.
  5. (Interpolation) Explain why an estimate inside the data range is more reliable than one outside it. Answer: Inside the range the trend is supported by nearby data points (interpolation); outside it (extrapolation) there is no evidence that the relationship continues in the same way.
  6. (Causation) A shop finds that sales of umbrellas and sales of coats rise together. Explain the correlation without claiming that umbrellas cause coat sales. Answer: Both are driven by a third variable — rainy weather — which increases demand for both; the correlation is association, not causation.
  7. (Outlier) One point sits far from the trend. What should you do with it when drawing the line? Answer: Note it as an outlier and draw the line through the main body of points; do not let one point pull the line away from the trend.
  8. (Strength) Two scatter diagrams both show positive correlation; in one the points are close to the line. Compare them. Answer: The tighter diagram shows stronger positive correlation; the looser one shows weaker positive correlation.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Joining the dots: a line of best fit is a single straight line through the trend, never a zigzag connecting points.
  • Forcing through the origin: the line passes through the middle of the cloud; there is no reason for it to start at (0, 0).
  • Reading a point instead of the line: estimates come from the line of best fit, not from the nearest plotted point.
  • Ignoring outliers: one extreme point should not swing the line; note it and fit the main cluster.
  • Weak description: "positive" alone is incomplete — direction and strength, with variables named.
  • Causal language: "revision causes higher scores" overclaims from observational data; write "is associated with" and mention confounding factors.
  • Extrapolating confidently: beyond the data range, state the estimate is unreliable.
  • Axes: plot the explanatory variable on the horizontal axis and the response on the vertical, label both with units, and use the given scales exactly.

Plotting the points: axes, scales and accuracy

A scatter diagram shows two variables plotted against each other, one point for each pair of values. Most of the marks for a plotting question come from setting the axes up correctly and placing each point accurately, so the subsections below take the process one step at a time.

Choosing which variable goes on which axis

The variable that is being explained or predicted goes on the vertical axis, and the variable that does the explaining goes on the horizontal axis. If a question gives a table of hours of revision and test scores, hours go on the x-axis and scores on the y-axis. Check the wording of the question, because an examiner may ask you to read a value from one axis to predict a value on the other.

Choosing a sensible scale

The scale on each axis should spread the data over at least half of the grid in both directions. Use equal steps of 1, 2, 5 or 10 units, and do not start an axis at a value that wastes most of the grid. If the values run from 42 to 58, the axis can start at 40 rather than at 0, provided the axis is labelled clearly so the reader sees that it does not start at zero.

Labelling the axes with name and unit

Each axis needs the name of the quantity and its unit, for example "Mass (kg)" or "Time (minutes)". A diagram without labels or units loses the presentation mark even when every point is correct. Write the scale numbers evenly spaced and make the labels readable, because an unreadable scale makes an estimate from the graph unreliable.

Plotting each point accurately

Plot each pair (x, y) by moving across to x and then up to y, and mark the point with a small neat cross or dot. A point plotted at (3, 7) must sit three units along the horizontal axis and seven units up, not one unit off in either direction. Check the table again after plotting, because a single misread value shows up as a point far away from the rest of the cloud.

Checking the number of points

Count the points on the diagram and compare with the number of rows in the table. A missing point is the most common error, and a diagram with one point missing can still look like a correct pattern. Tick each row of the table as you plot it, which takes a few seconds and protects the mark.

Spotting an outlier before you draw the line

An outlier is a point that lies well away from the general pattern of the others. Identify any outlier before you decide on the trend, because a single extreme point can pull a line of best fit away from where most of the data lies. An outlier is not always an error: note it and say whether it affects the conclusion.

Using a table to check the diagram

Once the diagram is drawn, read two or three points back from the graph and check them against the table. If the graph reads 6 at a point the table lists as 9, there is a plotting mistake that would cost every later estimate. This habit is quick and it turns a plausible but wrong diagram into a checked one.

Equations and symbols

The arithmetic of a scatter diagram is the equation of the line of best fit, read in both directions: from the line to an estimate, and from two points back to the line. Keep the meaning of each letter in view, because the exam asks you to interpret the gradient rather than just compute it.

gradient = (54 - 30)/(10 - 4) = 24/6 = 4 Key: 54 and 30 are the y-values of two points on the line; 10 and 4 the matching x-values; the gradient is the change in the vertical variable per unit of the horizontal one, so here the response rises 4 for every 1 of the explanatory variable.

y = 4x + c Key: y = the predicted value on the vertical axis; x = the explanatory variable on the horizontal axis; 4 = the gradient just calculated; c = the intercept, still unknown. Substitute one point to find c.

30 = 16 + c → c = 14 Key: substituting the point (4, 30) into y = 4x + c gives 16 + c = 30, so c = 14. The intercept is where the line would cross x = 0 — meaningful only if x = 0 is inside the data.

y = 4x + 14 Key: the finished line of best fit; use it for every estimate, never the plotted points themselves. From the line, x = 7 gives y = 42 — an interpolation, inside the data range, so reliable.

y = 28 + 14 = 42 Key: the same estimate written out; 28 = 4 × 7 and 14 is the intercept. Showing this line earns the method mark even if the earlier gradient was wrong.

y = 134 Key: the prediction at x = 30, far outside the plotted range. It is an extrapolation: the arithmetic is right and the estimate is unreliable, which is exactly what the question wants you to say.

The language that earns the marks. Name the direction and the strength and the two variables — "strong positive correlation between hours of revision and test score" — and say "approximately" for any value read from the line. Correlation is association, not causation: name the third variable that could drive both.

title: Organic Nitrogen Compounds: Amines, Amides, Amino Acids and Proteins Revision Notes
content:
Organic Nitrogen Compounds: Amines, Amides, Amino Acids and Proteins A2 Level Chemistry

These revision notes cover Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH15 Topic 19, focusing on the structures, preparations, reactions, and physical properties of amines, amides, amino acids, and polymers including polyamides and addition polymers, alongside Core Practical 15.

Nomenclature and Formulae of Nitrogen Compounds

Students must be able to name and draw structural, displayed, and skeletal formulae for amides, primary amines, and amino acids according to IUPAC rules.

  • Primary aliphatic amines are named by adding the suffix -amine to the alkyl chain, such as butylamine (CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂NH₂).
  • Aromatic amines feature an amino group directly attached to a benzene ring, such as phenylamine (C₆H₅NH₂).
  • Amides are named based on the corresponding carboxylic acid chain with the suffix -amide, such as ethanamide (CH₃CONH₂).
  • Amino acids contain both an amine group and a carboxylic acid group, typically on the same carbon, such as 2-aminopropanoic acid (CH₃CH(NH₂)COOH).
  • Structural formulae show every atom and bond clearly in displayed formulae, while skeletal formulae omit carbon and hydrogen labels from carbon chains for simplicity.

Reactions and Basicity of Amines

Amines act as bases due to the lone pair of electrons on the nitrogen atom, which can accept a proton.

  • Primary aliphatic amines like butylamine are miscible with water due to hydrogen bonding between the nitrogen and hydrogen atoms of water and the amine.
  • Basicity varies: ammonia has a base dissociation constant dependent on its lone pair availability; primary aliphatic amines are stronger bases than ammonia because alkyl groups push electron density onto the nitrogen via the positive inductive effect, increasing lone pair availability.
  • Primary aromatic amines like phenylamine are weaker bases than ammonia because the nitrogen lone pair delocalises into the delocalised pi-system of the benzene ring, decreasing its availability to accept protons.
  • Reaction with water: primary aliphatic amines dissolve to form alkaline solutions containing hydroxide ions, for example CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂NH₂ + H₂O gives CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂NH₃⁺ + OH⁻.
  • Reaction with acids: amines react with mineral acids like hydrochloric acid to form soluble alkylammonium salts, such as CH₃NH₂ + HCl gives CH₃NH₃⁺Cl⁻.
  • Reaction with halogenoalkanes: primary amines react with halogenoalkanes via nucleophilic substitution to produce secondary and tertiary amines.
  • Reaction with acyl chlorides: primary amines react with ethanoyl chloride to form N-substituted amides, releasing misty fumes of hydrogen chloride.
  • Reaction with copper(II) ions: dropwise addition of aqueous copper(II) sulfate to an excess of an aliphatic amine like butylamine forms a pale blue precipitate that dissolves in excess amine to form a deep blue complex ion, [Cu(CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂NH₂)₄(H₂O)²]²⁺.

Preparation of Aliphatic and Aromatic Amines

Different synthetic routes are required to produce aliphatic versus aromatic amines.

  • Preparation of primary aliphatic amines from halogenoalkanes: heating a haloalkane with excess ethanolic ammonia in a sealed tube via nucleophilic substitution; excess ammonia is essential to prevent further substitution leading to secondary and tertiary amines.
  • Preparation of primary aliphatic amines from nitriles: reduction of a nitrile using lithium aluminium hydride in dry ether followed by dilute acid, or catalytic hydrogenation using hydrogen and a nickel catalyst.
  • Preparation of aromatic amines: reduction of an aromatic nitro-compound, such as nitrobenzene, using tin and concentrated hydrochloric acid heated under reflux, followed by the addition of sodium hydroxide to release the free phenylamine base.

Azo Dyes and Diazonium Salts

Aromatic amines undergo specific reactions involving nitrous acid to form useful colorants.

  • Reaction of aromatic amines with nitrous acid: phenylamine reacts with nitrous acid (formed in situ from sodium nitrite and hydrochloric acid) at temperatures below 5°C to form a benzenediazonium ion (C₆H₅N₂⁺Cl⁻).
  • Coupling reaction: the benzenediazonium ion undergoes an electrophilic substitution coupling reaction with alkaline phenol at low temperatures to form a brightly coloured azo dye, such as 4-hydroxyphenylazobenzene.

Preparation and Properties of Amides

Amides are carboxylic acid derivatives containing the carbonyl-nitrogen bond.

  • Preparation: amides are prepared from acyl chlorides by reacting them with ammonia or a primary amine at room temperature, for example ethanoyl chloride with ammonia gives ethanamide and hydrogen chloride.
  • Hydrolysis: amides undergo acid hydrolysis when heated with dilute hydrochloric acid to yield a carboxylic acid and an ammonium salt, or alkaline hydrolysis with sodium hydroxide to yield a carboxylate salt and ammonia gas.

Polymers: Polyamides and Addition Polymers

Polymerisation processes link small monomer units into large macromolecules.

  • Condensation polymerisation: involves the reaction of monomers with two functional groups, releasing a small molecule such as water or hydrogen chloride; polyamides like nylon-6,6 are formed from hexane-1,6-diamine and hexanedioic acid.
  • Proteins are natural polyamides formed from amino acid monomers linked by peptide bonds.
  • Addition polymerisation: involves unsaturated monomers opening their double bonds without eliminating small molecules; examples include poly(propenamide) and poly(ethenol).
  • Structural formulae: students must be able to draw repeat units of nylon, proteins, poly(propenamide), and poly(ethenol) enclosed in square brackets with an extension bond outside the brackets.
  • Physical properties of polyamides: strong intermolecular hydrogen bonds form between the polar carbonyl and N-H groups of adjacent polymer chains, resulting in high tensile strength and high melting points.
  • Solubility of poly(ethenol): despite being an addition polymer, poly(ethenol) is soluble in water because its numerous pendant alcohol (-OH) groups form extensive hydrogen bonds with water molecules, making it ideal for soluble laundry bags and liquid-detergent capsules (liquitabs).

Amino Acids, Zwitterions, and Peptides

Amino acids exhibit amphoteric properties and form complex structural hierarchies in proteins.

  • Zwitterions: in the solid state and near neutral pH, amino acids exist as dipolar ions called zwitterions, ⁺H₃NCH(R)COO⁻, carrying no net overall charge due to internal proton transfer from the carboxylic acid group to the amine group.
  • Acidity and basicity: at the isoelectric point, the zwitterion has a net charge of zero. In strong acid solutions, the amino group accepts a proton to form a positive cation; in strong alkali solutions, the carboxylic acid group loses a proton to form a negative anion.
  • Optical activity: aqueous solutions of standard amino acids contain chiral carbon atoms (except glycine) and rotate plane-polarised monochromatic light because they are optically active.
  • Peptide bond formation: a peptide link (-CONH-) forms when the carboxylic acid group of one amino acid condenses with the amine group of another, eliminating a molecule of water via condensation polymerisation.
  • Protein structure: proteins possess primary structure (amino acid sequence), secondary structure (alpha-helices and beta-pleated sheets held by hydrogen bonds between C=O and N-H groups), and tertiary structure (3D folding stabilized by ionic bonds, hydrogen bonds, and disulfide bridges). Complete hydrolysis of proteins with hot concentrated hydrochloric acid yields a mixture of constituent amino acids.

Core Practical 15: Analysis of Unknowns

Practical analysis involves systematic chemical tests to identify functional groups in organic and inorganic unknowns.

  • Testing for amines: use universal indicator to confirm an alkaline pH, or react with ethanoyl chloride to observe misty fumes of hydrogen chloride.
  • Testing for amino acids: use paper chromatography followed by locating agents like ninhydrin to reveal purple spots.
  • Testing for amides: warm with sodium hydroxide and test evolved ammonia gas with damp red litmus paper, which turns blue.

Typical mistakes

  • Mistake: stating that alkyl groups attract electron density in amines. Correction: alkyl groups push electron density onto the nitrogen atom via a positive inductive effect.
  • Mistake: drawing the zwitterion structure with a neutral carboxylic acid and amine group at neutral pH. Correction: draw the zwitterion with a protonated amine (⁺H₃N-) and deprotonated carboxylate (-COO⁻).
  • Mistake: omitting the repeat brackets or extension bonds when drawing polymer repeat units. Correction: always enclose repeat units in square brackets with bonds extending outside the brackets.
  • Mistake: confusing addition polymerisation with condensation polymerisation. Correction: addition polymerisation involves unsaturated monomers with no eliminated small molecules, whereas condensation polymerisation eliminates small molecules like water.

Exam-style questions

  2. Explain why phenylamine is a weaker base than butylamine. Answer: Phenylamine's nitrogen lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring, decreasing proton acceptance ability, whereas butylamine's alkyl group pushes electron density onto nitrogen via a positive inductive effect, increasing lone pair availability.
  5. Describe the reagents and conditions needed to prepare phenylamine from nitrobenzene. Answer: Heat nitrobenzene under reflux with tin (Sn) and concentrated hydrochloric acid, followed by addition of sodium hydroxide.
  8. Draw the structural repeat unit of nylon-6,6. Answer: [−NH−(CH₂)₆−NH−CO−(CH₂)₄−CO−].
  11. Explain why poly(ethenol) dissolves in water while poly(ethene) does not. Answer: Poly(ethenol) has pendant −OH groups that form hydrogen bonds with water molecules, whereas poly(ethene) is non-polar and cannot form hydrogen bonds.
  14. Write the ionic equation for the reaction of butylamine with hydrochloric acid. Answer: CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂NH₂ + H⁺ gives CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂NH₃⁺.

Use these notes alongside past paper practice questions to test your knowledge of reaction conditions and mechanisms. Revise aromatic chemistry and polymer chemistry next to consolidate your understanding of WCH15.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Basicity, applied to amines: alkyl groups donate electron density to the nitrogen, so CH₃NH₂ is more basic than NH₃. Phenylamine is less basic than NH₃, because the lone pair on nitrogen delocalises into the benzene ring. Give that delocalisation as the reason, not just the fact.
  • Diazonium coupling, applied to benzenediazonium chloride with phenol: the reaction is carried out at 0–5 °C in alkaline conditions, and it gives an azo dye through electrophilic attack by the diazonium ion on the phenoxide ring. The –N=N– group links the two aromatic rings.
  • Amide formation, applied to ethanoyl chloride and ammonia: the nitrogen lone pair attacks the carbonyl carbon, and HCl is lost. Use two equivalents of ammonia, one to react and one to neutralise the HCl formed.
  • Amino acids: at the isoelectric point, the amino acid exists as a zwitterion with both NH₃⁺ and COO⁻. Its net charge is zero and it does not move in an electric field. Give the zwitterion structure when asked about the form of the amino acid in solution.

title: Exam technique: Information Representation
content:
### What earns the marks
For two complement, inversion plus one stated earns the method mark before the value. For floating point, mantissa plus exponent roles stated earn one mark each. For normalisation, the leading-bit rule quoted earns the precision mark.
### Traps
Error: sign bit ignored in range. Correction: an n-bit signed range tops at 2^(n-1) - 1. Error: larger exponent read as more precision. Correction: exponent sets range, mantissa sets precision. Error: normalised form guessed. Correction: mantissa starts with 0.1 or 1.0 pattern per the scheme.
### Worked example
Write -45 in 8-bit two's complement. First write 45 in binary: 00101101. Invert every bit to get 11010010, then add 1 to get 11010011. Check: the sign bit has weight -128, so the value is -128 + 64 + 16 + 2 + 1 = -45, which matches.
### Check yourself
State the range of an 8-bit two's complement integer, and say which bit sets the sign. The range is -128 to +127, and the leftmost bit is the sign bit with weight -128.

### Worked example
Write -45 in 8-bit two's complement. First write 45 in binary: 00101101. Invert every bit to get 11010010, then add 1 to get 11010011. Check: the sign bit has weight -128, so the value is -128 + 64 + 16 + 2 + 1 = -45, which matches.

title: Exam technique: Arithmetic and Place Value
content:
### What earns the marks
For HCF and LCM, the prime factorisation of each number earns the method mark; state highest powers for LCM and lowest for HCF. For bounds, half-the-precision stated (0.05 for 1 d.p.) earns the method mark before the bound. For estimation, the rounded line (50 x 20 / 10) must be shown: a bare calculator value scores nothing. For time and money, each conversion step shown earns its mark.
### Traps
Error: 16:80 as a time. Correction: 60 minutes carry. Error: largest rounded value confused with the upper bound (6.34 vs 6.35). Correction: the bound is the first value that rounds away. Error: HCF powers used for LCM. Correction: LCM takes the highest of each prime.
### Worked example
In 4 706 325 the digit 7 is in the hundred-thousands place, so its value is 700 000. For order of operations, 3 + 4 × (10 − 6)² is worked out as 3 + 4 × 4² = 3 + 4 × 16 = 3 + 64 = 67. Brackets and powers come before multiplication, and addition comes last.
### Check yourself
State the value of the digit 6 in 4 706 325, then calculate 20 − 2 × (3 + 4)². The 6 is worth 6000. The second is 20 − 2 × 49 = 20 − 98 = −78, which shows why the brackets must be done first.

title: IGCSE Mathematics: Indices and Standard Form
content:
IGCSE Mathematics: Indices and Standard Form

Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580 (2025–2027), section 1 Number: statement 1.3 Powers and roots, 1.7 Indices I (with Extended fractional indices), 1.8 Standard form, E1.18 Surds, and section 2 statement E2.4 Indices II (algebraic indices). Indices are shorthand for repeated multiplication, and their laws are the shortcuts that make large and small numbers manageable. This note derives each law from what it counts, covers standard form arithmetic in full, and finishes with surds and rationalising — an Extended favourite that separates the top grades.

Powers, roots and the vocabulary

In 5³ the base is 5 and the index (plural: indices) is 3; it means 5 × 5 × 5 = 125. A square root reverses a square: √25 = 5 because 5² = 25. A cube root reverses a cube: ³√64 = 4 because 4³ = 64.

  • √16 = 4, the principal (positive) square root, as printed on a calculator. But the equation x² = 16 has two solutions, x = 4 or x = −4, because (−4)² = 16 as well. The question decides which is wanted: a length is positive; a solution of an equation may be negative.
  • Notation: a² is read a squared, a³ a cubed, and aⁿ a to the power n. a² ≠ 2a — a² = a × a while 2a = a + a.

The index laws

Each law is a statement about counting multiplications, so each can be checked by writing the multiplications out.

Law 1:  a^m x a^n = a^(m+n)
Why: a³ x a² = (a x a x a) x (a x a) = a⁵, and 3 + 2 = 5.
Example: 2³ × 2⁵ = 2⁸ = 256; check: 8 × 32 = 256 ✓

Law 2:  a^m ÷ a^n = a^(m-n)
Why: a⁵ ÷ a² = (a x a x a x a x a)/(a x a) = a x a x a = a³, and 5 - 2 = 3.
Example: 5⁷ ÷ 5⁴ = 5³ = 125

Law 3:  (a^m)^n = a^(m n)
Why: (a²)³ = a² x a² x a² = a⁶, and 2 × 3 = 6.
Example: (2x³)² = 2² x (x³)² = 4x⁶        [the power applies to every factor]

Law 4:  a⁰ = 1  (a not zero)
Why: a³ ÷ a³ = a^(3-3) = a⁰, and any number divided by itself is 1.
Example: 7⁰ = 1

Law 5:  a^(-n) = 1/(a^n)
Why: a^(-2) = a^(0-2) = a⁰ ÷ a² = 1/a².
Example: 5^(-2) = 1/25 = 0.04

Fractional indices (Extended). A fractional index is a root: the denominator of the fraction is the root, the numerator is the power.

a^(1/n) = nth root of a        a^(m/n) = (nth root of a)^m

16^(1/2) = √16 = 4
27^(2/3) = (cube root of 27)² = 3² = 9
Check the second: 27^(2/3) squared three times over should give 27² = 729; 9³ = 729 ✓

Indices in algebra (Extended)

The same laws apply when the base is a letter, and every factor in a bracket carries the power:

Simplify:  (2x³)² x⁴ ÷ x⁵

(2x³)² = 4x⁶        [square the 2 and double the index]
4x⁶ x x⁴ = 4x¹⁰     [Law 1: add indices]
4x¹⁰ ÷ x⁵ = 4x⁵     [Law 2: subtract indices]
Solve:  2^x = 32

Write both sides with base 2:  32 = 2⁵
2^x = 2⁵, so x = 5        [matching bases means matching indices]

When the bases differ, rewrite one as a power of the other: 8 = 2³, so 8^x = 2^(3x). Equations like 3^(x+1) = 27^(x−1) become 3^(x+1) = 3^(3x−3), so x + 1 = 3x − 3, giving x = 2.

LawStatementWorked line
Multiplyingaᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ2³ × 2⁵ = 2⁸ = 256
Dividingaᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ5⁷ ÷ 5⁴ = 5³ = 125
Power of a power(aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ(2x³)² = 4x⁶
Zero indexa⁰ = 1 (a not zero)7⁰ = 1
Negative indexa⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ5⁻² = 1/25
Fractional indexa^(m/n) = (ⁿ√a)ᵐ27^(2/3) = 9

Two edge cases deserve care. The zero index says nothing about 0⁰: 0⁰ is undefined, because the pattern a⁰ = 1 holds for every non-zero base while the pattern 0ⁿ = 0 holds for every positive power, and the two patterns collide at the origin. And a negative index never makes a value negative: 2⁻³ = 1/8 is positive, because the minus sign belongs to the position of the power, not to the number itself. Finally, every root can be written as a power — √x = x^(1/2), ³√x = x^(1/3) — which is how a calculator evaluates them and how algebraic roots are simplified in one notation.

Standard form

Standard form writes a number as a × 10ⁿ where 1 ⩽ a < 10 and n is an integer. It handles very large and very small quantities without long strings of zeros.

Write in standard form:

47 382 = 4.7382 × 10⁴        [the decimal point moves 4 places left]
0.0056 = 5.6 × 10^(-3)        [the decimal point moves 3 places right, so n = -3]

Arithmetic in standard form. Multiply or divide the numbers first, then the powers of ten, and adjust back into standard form if needed:

(3 × 10⁵) x (4 × 10^(-2))
= (3 × 4) x (10⁵ × 10^(-2))     [regrouped]
= 12 × 10³
= 1.2 × 10⁴                     [12 is not between 1 and 10, so adjust]

(6 × 10⁸) ÷ (2 × 10³)
= (6 ÷ 2) × 10^(8-3) = 3 × 10⁵

Addition and subtraction need matching powers first: 3 × 10⁵ + 4 × 10⁴ = 30 × 10⁴ + 4 × 10⁴ = 34 × 10⁴ = 3.4 × 10⁵. Real-world uses: the speed of light is 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, the size of an atom is about 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m, and masses, distances and populations in physics and chemistry questions are always quoted this way. A calculator's ×10ˣ key enters the power directly; the answer should be given in the form the question asks, often to 3 s.f.

Surds (Extended)

A surd is a root that cannot be written exactly as a fraction — √2, √3, 3√5. Exact answers in surds are often required on Paper 2, where a calculator cannot help. The laws:

√a x √b = √(ab)        √a ÷ √b = √(a/b)        (√a)² = a

Simplifying. Take out the largest square factor:

√50 = √(25 × 2) = √25 x √2 = 5√2
√72 = √(36 × 2) = 6√2
√(9/16) = √9 / √16 = 3/4

Adding like surds. Only like surds combine, exactly like algebraic terms:

√18 + √8 = 3√2 + 2√2 = 5√2        [simplify first]
2√3 + √5 cannot be combined: they are unlike surds.

Rationalising the denominator. A fraction with a surd underneath is tidied by multiplying top and bottom by the same surd (or its conjugate):

6/√3 = (6 x √3)/(√3 x √3) = 6√3/3 = 2√3

1/(3 + √2): multiply top and bottom by the conjugate (3 - √2):
= (3 - √2)/[(3 + √2)(3 - √2)]
= (3 - √2)/(9 - 2)          [difference of two squares below]
= (3 - √2)/7

The conjugate works because (a + b)(a − b) = a² − b² removes the square root entirely. Expanding surd brackets uses the same identity: (2 + √3)(2 − √3) = 4 − 3 = 1.

Worked example: a combined index calculation

Simplify (2³ × 2⁵) ÷ 2⁴ and check it two ways.

Method 1 (indices): 2³ × 2⁵ = 2⁸, then 2⁸ ÷ 2⁴ = 2⁴ = 16
Method 2 (arithmetic): 2³ × 2⁵ = 8 × 32 = 256;  256 ÷ 16 = 16
Both routes give 16 ✓

Second example: write (3√2)² − √8 in the form k√2.

(3√2)² = 9 × 2 = 18        [square both the 3 and the √2]
√8 = 2√2
18 - 2√2 is already simple; it cannot be written as k√2 because 18 is rational,
so the answer stays 18 - 2√2.

Standard form in a calculation. A red blood cell is 7 × 10⁻⁶ m across and a vein is 2.4 × 10⁻³ m wide. How many cells fit side by side?

2.4 × 10^(-3) ÷ 7 × 10^(-6)
= (2.4 ÷ 7) × 10^(-3 - (-6))        [divide the numbers, subtract the indices]
= 0.342857 × 10³
= 3.43 × 10² (3 s.f.)  ≈ 343 cells

The index arithmetic is the whole question: subtracting −6 gives +3, and a sense-check on the powers alone (10⁻³ ÷ 10⁻⁶ = 10³) says the answer must be in the hundreds — which catches sign slips before they cost the final mark.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Multiplying the base by the index: 2³ is 8, not 6; (2³)² = 2⁶ = 64, not 2⁵.
  • Forgetting to square the coefficient: (2x³)² = 4x⁶, not 2x⁶.
  • Treating a⁻ⁿ as negative rather than reciprocal: 2⁻³ = 1/8.
  • Writing 0.00047 as 4.7 × 10⁻³; it is 4.7 × 10⁻⁴ — count the places the point moves.
  • Leaving a standard-form answer as 12 × 10³; the front number must be between 1 and 10.
  • Giving √16 = ±4 in a simplification; the square root symbol means the principal root, while x² = 16 has both solutions.
  • Rationalising only the surd and not its conjugate partner: 1/(3 + √2) needs (3 − √2) top and bottom.
  • Combining unlike surds: 2√3 + √5 is final; only matching surd parts can be added.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 2, 3 marks). Simplify (3x²)³ ÷ x⁴.

Answer: (3x²)³ = 27x⁶; 27x⁶ ÷ x⁴ = 27x².

Question 2 (Paper 2, 3 marks). Evaluate 8^(2/3).

Answer: ³√8 = 2, and 2² = 4. So 8^(2/3) = 4.

Question 3 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Write 0.000 42 and 63 000 in standard form, then find their product.

Answer: 4.2 × 10⁻⁴ and 6.3 × 10⁴. Product = (4.2 × 6.3) × 10⁰ = 26.46 = 2.646 × 10¹.

Question 4 (Paper 2, 4 marks). Simplify √48 + 3√12.

Answer: √48 = √(16 × 3) = 4√3; 3√12 = 3 × 2√3 = 6√3; total = 10√3.

Question 5 (Paper 2, 4 marks). Rationalise the denominator of 5/(2 + √3).

Answer: Multiply by the conjugate: 5(2 − √3)/[(2 + √3)(2 − √3)] = 5(2 − √3)/(4 − 3) = 5(2 − √3) = 10 − 5√3.

Question 6 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Solve 9^x = 27.

Answer: Write both as powers of 3: 3^(2x) = 3³, so 2x = 3 and x = 3/2. Check: 9^(3/2) = (√9)³ = 3³ = 27 ✓.

From the numbers themselves, the course turns to comparing and sharing them: ratio, rate and proportion.

The powers-of-ten ladder: seeing standard form instead of memorising it

Indices look like a rule to memorise and are really a picture to read. Every quantity in the course sits somewhere on one ladder of powers of ten, and multiplying, dividing and converting all move you up or down that ladder by whole rungs.

One rung, one index. Moving up a rung multiplies by 10, and that is exactly what adding 1 to the index does: 10³ × 10 = 10⁴. Moving down divides by 10 and subtracts 1. Every index law is that sentence applied twice:

aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ Key: a = the base; m and n = the indices (powers). Multiplying adds the indices because each factor contributes its own rungs.
aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ Key: dividing subtracts, because dividing by aⁿ is multiplying by a⁻ⁿ.
(aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ Key: a bracket applied n times multiplies the rungs by n.
a⁰ = 1 and a⁻ⁿ = 1 / aⁿ Key: both follow from the subtraction law: a³ ÷ a³ = a⁰ must be 1, and a² ÷ a⁵ = a⁻³ must be 1/a³.

Standard form is a position on the ladder. A number is in standard form when it is written as

N = A × 10ⁿ Key: A = a number with 1 ≤ A < 10 (one non-zero digit before the point); n = a whole number, positive for large values and negative for small ones. 4.2 × 10³ means four decimal places' worth of rungs above 1: 4,200.

Converting is counting rungs, not guessing the sign. To write 47,500 in standard form, move the point left until one digit remains in front: 4.75, which is three moves, so the index is +3 and the value is 4.75 × 10⁴. To write 0.00062, move the point right until one digit remains in front: 6.2, which is four moves, so the index is −4 and the value is 6.2 × 10⁻⁴. Left is positive, right is negative — the point moving right on a small number gives a negative index, which is the sign students most often flip.

Worked example. A red blood cell has diameter 0.0000072 m and a virus 1.2 × 10⁻⁷ m. Write the cell in standard form and find how many times longer it is.

cell: 0.0000072 = 7.2 × 10⁻⁶ m (six moves right)
ratio: (7.2 × 10⁻⁶) ÷ (1.2 × 10⁻⁷) = (7.2 ÷ 1.2) × 10⁻⁶⁻⁽⁻⁷⁾ = 6.0 × 10¹ = 60

The division law did the work: subtracting a negative index adds. Doing that sum as −6 − 7 = −13 is the error that turns 60 into 0.0000000000006.

Estimating with the ladder. A calculation like (4.9 × 10⁵) × (2.1 × 10³) is roughly 5 × 2 = 10 times 10⁵⁺³ = 10⁸, so about 1.0 × 10⁹ before any calculator. This is how you catch a wrong power of ten — the most common way a correct method still loses the answer mark.

Where marks are lost. Writing 0.42 × 10⁴ or 42 × 10² and calling it standard form: A must be at least 1 and less than 10. Flipping the sign of the index on a small number. And adding indices when multiplying different bases — 2³ × 3² is 8 × 9 = 72, not 6⁵.

Negative and zero indices in depth

A negative index tells you to take a reciprocal, and a zero index gives the value 1. These two rules follow from the index laws, not from memory, so the working below shows how each one is forced. The subsections cover the reasons, the calculator entry, and the common slips that turn a negative power into a negative number.

Why a zero index gives one

Take a number and divide it by itself. Using the division law, a⁵ ÷ a⁵ = a⁰, and the same quotient is 1 because any number divided by itself is 1. So a⁰ = 1 for any non-zero a. The rule is therefore a consequence of the laws already in use, and it is why 5⁰ = 1, 100⁰ = 1 and (−3)⁰ = 1.

Why a negative index is a reciprocal

Divide a power by a larger power of the same base: a² ÷ a⁵ = a^(2−5) = a⁻³. Writing the same quotient as 1/a³ shows that a⁻³ = 1/a³. So a negative index moves the base to the denominator and changes the sign of the index. The value 2⁻³ is 1/2³ = 1/8, which is positive, because a negative index does not make the answer negative.

Negative indices with fractions

The reciprocal rule also works on fractions, where it flips the fraction. (2/3)⁻² = (3/2)² = 9/4. Invert the fraction first, then apply the positive index. A common error is to change only the index and leave the fraction alone, which gives (2/3)⁻² = 4/9 and loses the mark.

Entering negative and fractional powers on a calculator

Use the power key, and enter the negative index in brackets so the calculator reads the whole index as a negative number. For 5⁻², enter 5, the power key and (−2), giving 0.04. A fractional power such as 8^(1/3) is entered with brackets around the fraction, and the calculator returns 2. Check the result by reversing the operation: 2³ = 8 confirms the cube root.

Simplifying expressions with negative powers

To simplify 3x⁻² × 6x⁵, multiply the numbers and add the indices: 18x^(−2+5) = 18x³. To write the answer with only positive indices, move any negative power to the denominator. For example, 4y⁻³ becomes 4/y³. Collect the coefficients first, then deal with the indices, so the final form is easy to check.

Mistakes with negative and zero indices

The commonest errors are treating 2⁻³ as −8, writing a⁰ as 0, and reading (−2)⁻² as −1/4 when the correct value is 1/4. The bracket in (−2)⁻² is what makes the base negative, and an even power of a negative number is positive. Write the bracket in the working so the sign is clear before the reciprocal is taken.

Fractional indices and roots

A fractional index is a root combined with a power, so a^(1/n) is the nth root of a, and a^(m/n) is the nth root of a raised to the mth power. The index laws extend to fractions without any new rule. The subsections below explain the notation, how to evaluate by hand and on a calculator, and how fractional indices appear in equations.

The meaning of a^(1/n)

The index law (a^(1/2))² = a^(1/2 × 2) = a¹ = a shows that a^(1/2) must be the square root of a. In the same way a^(1/3) is the cube root and a^(1/4) is the fourth root. So 16^(1/2) = 4, 27^(1/3) = 3 and 81^(1/4) = 3. The index is the reciprocal of the root.

Evaluating a^(m/n)

Take the root first, then the power, because the root is usually the smaller number. For 8^(2/3), the cube root of 8 is 2, and 2² = 4. Taking the power first gives 8² = 64, and the cube root of 64 is also 4, so the order does not change the answer, but the root first keeps the numbers small and is less error-prone.

Negative fractional indices

A negative fractional index takes a reciprocal of the root. For 16^(−3/4), the fourth root of 16 is 2, so 2³ = 8 and the reciprocal gives 16^(−3/4) = 1/8. Apply the reciprocal last, after the root and power have been found, and write the answer as a fraction if the question asks for an exact value.

Solving an equation with a fractional index

To solve x^(2/3) = 4, raise both sides to the power 3/2, which undoes the 2/3. Then x = 4^(3/2) = (√4)³ = 2³ = 8. Raising both sides to the reciprocal of the index is the step to remember, and the result should be checked by substituting back: 8^(2/3) = 4.

Fractional indices on the calculator

Enter the base, press the power key, and enter the fraction in brackets. For 125^(2/3), the calculator gives 25. Enter the bracket around the index to avoid reading 2 ÷ 3 as a separate step, and check a simple value first, such as 9^(1/2) = 3, so a mis-entered index is spotted.

Why fractional indices matter

Fractional indices let a root be treated with the same index laws as a power. Once a root is written as an index, multiplying and dividing it follows the usual rules. This is why the Extended content treats roots as powers, and it is also the link to surds, which are the roots that are left unevaluated.

Standard form in calculations

Standard form writes a number as a × 10ⁿ, where 1 ≤ a < 10 and n is a whole number. It is used to write very large and very small numbers compactly, and it allows multiplication and division to be done by applying the index laws to the powers of ten. The subsections cover converting, multiplying and dividing, adding, and the calculator display.

Converting to and from standard form

To write 47 000 in standard form, move the decimal point until one non-zero digit is in front of it: 4.7. The point moved 4 places left, so the power is 10⁴, giving 4.7 × 10⁴. For 0.00052, the point moves 4 places right to give 5.2, so the power is −4 and the answer is 5.2 × 10⁻⁴. Count the places moved, and remember that a move to the left is a positive power.

Multiplying numbers in standard form

Multiply the number parts and add the powers of ten. (3 × 10⁵) × (2 × 10³) = 6 × 10⁸. If the product of the number parts is 10 or more, rewrite it in standard form and adjust the power. For (4 × 10⁶) × (5 × 10⁴) = 20 × 10¹⁰, which is 2 × 10¹¹ in standard form.

Dividing numbers in standard form

Divide the number parts and subtract the powers of ten. (8 × 10⁹) ÷ (2 × 10³) = 4 × 10⁶. If the number part is not between 1 and 10, adjust it. For (9 × 10⁴) ÷ (3 × 10⁶) = 3 × 10⁻², which is 0.03.

Adding and subtracting in standard form

Write both numbers with the same power of ten before adding or subtracting the number parts. To add 3 × 10⁴ and 5 × 10³, write the first as 30 × 10³, so the sum is (30 + 5) × 10³ = 35 × 10³ = 3.5 × 10⁴. Rewriting the answer in standard form is the step that loses marks when it is left out.

Standard form on the calculator

A calculator shows a standard form answer as a number with E or as a small power-of-ten display, such as 6.0E8, which means 6.0 × 10⁸. Enter a number in standard form with the EXP or ×10ˣ key, not by typing ×10 and the power separately, because the calculator then multiplies the brackets in the wrong order. Convert the display to the written form for the final answer.

Real-world uses of standard form

Standard form is used for distances in space, the mass of atoms and the population of large countries. The Earth is about 1.5 × 10⁸ km from the Sun, and a hydrogen atom has a mass of about 1.7 × 10⁻²⁷ kg. Comparing two such numbers is easy in standard form, because the larger power of ten is the larger number when the number parts are similar.

title: A Level Mathematics: Permutations and Combinations
content:
A Level Mathematics: Permutations and Combinations

Counting is the part of probability that requires no formula to start with, only a decision: does the order matter? Every question in this topic is answered by that one question. If order matters the count is a permutation; if it does not the count is a combination. Everything else — repetitions, restrictions, arrangements around a circle — is a variation on the same counting principle, and this note sets out each variation with the reasoning behind it.

The multiplication principle

If a choice can be made in a ways and, independently, a second choice in b ways, the pair can be made in a × b ways. That is the whole foundation; the formulas are shortcuts for repeated applications of it.

arrangements of n distinct objects in a row: n! = n x (n-1) x ... x 2 × 1
0! = 1 by convention, so that formulas stay consistent
choosing r from n with order: nPr = n!/(n - r)!
choosing r from n without order: nCr = n!/(r!(n - r)!)

Worked example. A password is 4 distinct letters from the 26-letter alphabet. How many passwords are possible?

order matters, so 26P4 = 26 × 25 × 24 × 23 = 358,800

Worked example 2 (no order). How many ways can 4 students be chosen from 26?

order does not matter, so 26C4 = 14,950

Worked example 3 (a leading zero is not allowed). A code uses four distinct digits from 0 to 9 and cannot begin with zero. How many codes?

first digit: 9 choices (1 to 9)
remaining three: 9P3 = 9 × 8 × 7 = 504
total = 9 × 504 = 4536

Worked example 4 (the link). Explain why nPr = nCr × r!.

every unordered selection of r objects can be arranged in r! orders
so counting ordered selections = counting unordered ones then arranging them

Deciding whether order matters

The decision is not about the words "choose" or "arrange" in the question — those are hints, not rules. The safe test is to imagine two selections differing only by swapping two items: if that counts as a different outcome, order matters.

SituationOrder?Count
finishing order of a raceyesnPr
a committee of 3nonCr
a 4-digit PINyespermutation, with repetition allowed
a hand of cardsnonCr
seating 5 people in a rowyes5!

Worked example. A team of 11 is chosen from 16 players, and one of the 11 is captain. Count the possibilities.

choose the 11: 16C11 = 4368
choose the captain from them: 11 ways
total = 4368 × 11 = 48,048

The multiplication principle is doing the work here: two independent choices, multiplied.

Repetition and identical items

When some objects are identical, arranging them as if all were distinct overcounts by the number of ways the identical ones can be swapped. Dividing by those factorials corrects it.

arrangements of n items with groups of identical items:
n!/(a! b! c! ...) where a, b, c are the group sizes
with repetition allowed, choosing r from n: n^r

Worked example. How many distinct arrangements of the letters in BANANA?

6 letters: B once, A three times, N twice
6!/(1! 3! 2!) = 720/12 = 60

Worked example 2 (repetition allowed). A 3-digit code uses digits 0-9, repeats allowed. How many codes?

10 × 10 × 10 = 1000
if repeats were not allowed: 10 × 9 × 8 = 720

Worked example 3 (identical plus restriction). How many arrangements of the letters of LEVEL begin with L?

fix L at the front; remaining letters E, V, E, L
that is 4 letters with E twice: 4!/2! = 12
but the leading L is one of the two Ls, so there is only one choice for the front
answer 12

Restrictions: the "glue" method

When certain items must be together, treat the group as a single object, arrange the objects, then arrange within the group. When certain items must not be together, count the total and subtract the "together" case.

together: glue the group, arrange the objects, multiply by the internal arrangements
not together: total arrangements minus the together arrangements
specific positions: fix those items first, then arrange the rest

Worked example. Five books, two of which must stand together, are arranged on a shelf. How many orders?

glue the pair: now 4 objects, arranged in 4! = 24 ways
the pair interchange in 2! = 2 ways
total = 48

Worked example 2 (not together). The same five books with the pair not together.

total arrangements = 5! = 120
together = 48
not together = 120 - 48 = 72

Worked example 3 (fixed positions). Four men and three women sit in a row of seven. How many arrangements have all three women together?

glue the women into one block: now 5 objects (4 men + block), 5! = 120
internal arrangements of the women: 3! = 6
total = 720

Circular arrangements

Around a circle, rotations of the same arrangement are not distinguishable, so fixing one item removes the rotational symmetry and the count drops by a factor of n.

n distinct items around a circle: (n - 1)!
a necklace (where reflection also counts as the same): (n - 1)!/2

Worked example. In how many ways can 6 people sit around a round table?

(6 - 1)! = 5! = 120

Worked example 2 (with a fixed seat). How many ways if one particular person must sit in a specified chair?

fix that person, arrange the other 5 around: 5! = 120
the specified chair removes the rotational freedom entirely, so the answer is unchanged here

Worked example 3 (two people together at a round table). Six people, two of whom must sit together.

glue the pair: 5 objects around a circle = 4! = 24
internal order of the pair: 2
total = 48

Combinations with conditions

Committee questions combine cases: choose so many from one group and so many from another, then add the disjoint alternatives. The discipline is to make the cases genuinely disjoint, or the same selection gets counted twice.

choose a from group A and b from group B: C(a-group, a) x C(b-group, b)
several allowed compositions: add the separate cases
at least one: total minus none

Worked example. From 6 men and 5 women, how many committees of 4 contain exactly 2 women?

choose 2 women from 5: 10
choose 2 men from 6: 15
total = 150

Worked example 2 (at least one). How many committees of 4 contain at least one woman?

total committees: 11C4 = 330
none: 6C4 = 15
at least one = 330 - 15 = 315

Worked example 3 (cases added). How many committees of 3 contain more women than men?

3 women: 5C3 = 10
2 women and 1 man: 5C2 × 6C1 = 10 × 6 = 60
total = 70

Counting inside probability

Combinations are usually the denominator of a probability question: count the favourable selections, count all selections, divide. Doing the counting separately from the probability keeps both parts clean and makes partial credit possible.

Worked example. A bag holds 5 red and 7 blue counters. Four are drawn at random. Find the probability of exactly 2 red.

total selections: 12C4 = 495
favourable: 5C2 × 7C2 = 10 × 21 = 210
probability = 210/495 = 0.4242

Worked example 2 (at least one). For the same bag, find the probability of at least one red.

complement: no red means all four blue
7C4 = 35
P(no red) = 35/495 = 0.0707
P(at least one red) = 1 - 0.0707 = 0.9293

Worked example 3 (order matters in the numerator). Three cards are drawn from a standard deck without replacement. Find the probability they are drawn in increasing order of value.

every set of three distinct cards has exactly one increasing order out of 3! orders
so the probability is 1/6, independent of the deck

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Factorial) Evaluate 7!. Answer: 7! = 7 × 6 × 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 5040.
  2. (Permutation) In how many orders can 5 runners finish? Answer: 5P5 = 5! = 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 120.
  3. (Combination) Evaluate 10C3. Answer: 10C3 = 10!/(3! × 7!) = (10 × 9 × 8)/(3 × 2 × 1) = 720/6 = 120.
  4. (Choice) From 8 books, how many ways to choose 3? Answer: 8C3 = 8!/(3! × 5!) = (8 × 7 × 6)/(3 × 2 × 1) = 336/6 = 56.
  5. (Arrangement) How many arrangements of the letters of STATISTICS? Answer: 10!/(3! × 3! × 2!) = 3 628 800/(6 × 6 × 2) = 3 628 800/72 = 50,400.
  6. (Glue) 6 people in a row with two together: Answer: glue the pair: 5! × 2! = 120 × 2 = 240.
  7. (Not together) Same 6, not together: Answer: total − together = 6! − 5! × 2! = 720 − 240 = 480.
  8. (Circle) 7 people around a table: Answer: (n − 1)! = 6! = 720.
  9. (Committee) 3 from 5 men and 4 women, exactly 2 men: Answer: 5C2 × 4C1 = 10 × 4 = 40.
  10. (At least) 4 from the same 9 with at least one woman: Answer: all − none = 9C4 − 5C4 = 126 − 5 = 121.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Using nPr where order does not matter: a committee is unordered; using permutations overcounts by r!.
  • Forgetting to divide by repeated factorials: identical letters need the divisor or the count is inflated.
  • Glue method without the internal factor: the block also has an internal arrangement, and dropping the 2! halves the answer.
  • Circular arrangements with n! instead of (n − 1)!: rotations are the same seating.
  • Adding what should be multiplied: independent stages multiply; alternative cases add.
  • Overlapping cases: cases must be disjoint, or selections are counted twice.
  • "At least one" counted directly: the complement is almost always faster and safer.
  • Restrictions applied after the count: fix the restricted positions first, then count what remains.

title: Forces & Motion — Study Notes
content:
Forces & Motion

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2023–2025): motion (speed, acceleration, graphs); mass & weight; density link; force basics (F = ma, resultant); momentum (Extended); turning effects; equilibrium.

1. Kinematics

  • Speed = distance/time; average speed = (u + v)/2 for uniform acceleration.
  • Acceleration a = (v − u)/t.
  • SUVAT (uniform a): v = u + at; s = ut + ½at²; v² = u² + 2as.

2. Motion graphs

  • Distance–time: gradient = speed.
  • Speed–time: gradient = acceleration; area = distance. Negative gradient = deceleration.
  • Free fall 1: g ≈ 9.8 m/s² (use 10) — v = gt from rest.

3. Mass, weight, density

W = mg (g ≈ 10 N/kg). Weight acts at the centre of mass; mass is invariant. Density ρ = m/V.

4. Newton's laws and resultant force

  • Resultant: colinear addition/subtraction; perpendicular by Pythagoras.
  • F = ma. Terminal velocity: drag grows with speed until it balances weight.
  • Third law pairs: equal magnitude, opposite direction, different bodies.

5. Momentum (Extended)

p = mv; impulse Ft = Δ(mv); conservation: Σpbefore = Σpafter (explosions, collisions).

Example: 2 kg at 3 m/s hits 1 kg at rest, combined 1 m/s: 6 = 3v ⇒ v = 2 m/s.

6. Moments and equilibrium

  • Moment = F × perpendicular distance from pivot.
  • Principle of moments: Σclockwise = Σanticlockwise.
  • Equilibrium: resultant force = 0 and resultant moment = 0.

Example: 100 N at 0.3 m balances F at 0.5 m: F = 60 N.

title: Edexcel IAL Computer Science: Database Concepts and DBMS
content:
Edexcel IAL Computer Science: Database Concepts and DBMS

Pearson Edexcel International Advanced Level in Computer Science, Unit 2 Practical Programming and Problem Solving (with Unit 4 design depth): database concepts — the relational model, keys and relationships — and the functions of a database management system. SQL querying and normalisation appear at Unit 4 depth; this note builds the conceptual foundation every later question assumes. Each design rule is demonstrated on a worked table where breaking it visibly corrupts the data.

From files to databases

Flat files per department lead to classic failures: duplication (the same customer stored in sales and delivery files), inconsistency (one copy updated, one stale), no cross-file querying without bespoke code, weak security (each file its own controls), and concurrent-update hazards (two users editing copies that later overwrite each other). A database stores integrated data once under shared rules; a DBMS manages it — and the comparison question wants those failure modes named.

The relational model

Data lives in tables (relations): rows are records (tuples), columns are fields (attributes) of one type. The model's rules: each field holds one value (no repeating groups), each row is unique, and rows have no order (a table is a set — ordering comes from queries). The design vocabulary: a primary key uniquely identifies each row (never null, never duplicated); a foreign key is a field whose values must match a primary key in another table, creating the relationship and enforcing referential integrity.

Worked tables and their keys:

STUDENT (studentID [PK], name, class)
  S1  Chen   11A
  S2  Ali    11B
  S3  Banda  11A

GRADE (resultID [PK], studentID [FK → STUDENT], subject, mark)
  R1  S1  Maths    72
  R2  S1  Physics  65
  R3  S2  Maths    58

Relationships: STUDENT to GRADE is one-to-many (one student, many grades).
Referential integrity: a GRADE row with studentID S9 would be rejected -
no such student. Deleting S2 must handle their grade R3 (restrict, cascade
or set null) - the delete rule is a design decision the exam probes.

Relationship types: one-to-one (student ↔ locker), one-to-many (student ↔ grades), many-to-many (students ↔ subjects) — resolved with a linking/junction table (ENROLMENT: studentID, subject) so every relationship is physically one-to-many.

DBMS functions

  • Data dictionary / metadata management — stores the schema (tables, types, keys, constraints) that defines valid data.
  • Storage and retrieval — efficient physical management and indexing.
  • Security — accounts, authentication, permissions per user/role, and audit trails.
  • Integrity — enforcing constraints: type, range (CHECK), entity (primary key uniqueness), referential (foreign keys), so bad data cannot be stored regardless of the client.
  • Concurrency control — locking and transaction isolation so simultaneous users cannot corrupt data (lost updates prevented).
  • Recovery / backup — transaction logs and restore after failure.
  • Query facilities — a query language (SQL) and report generation.
Concurrency worked: two clerks updating the same stock level (10⁰).

Without control:                          With locking:
  Clerk A reads 10⁰                        Clerk A reads 10⁰ (row locked)
  Clerk B reads 10⁰                        Clerk B's update WAITS
  Clerk A writes 10⁰ - 10 = 90             Clerk A writes 90 (lock released)
  Clerk B writes 10⁰ - 25 = 75             Clerk B reads 90, writes 65
  Result 75: A's sale LOST - wrong.        Result 65: both sales counted.

Transactions are ACID: Atomic (all-or-nothing), Consistent (rules hold
afterwards), Isolated (concurrent transactions do not interfere), Durable
(committed data survives failure) - the four initials are directly
examinable.

Schema design and normalisation (foundation)

Normalisation removes duplication and the anomalies it causes. 1NF: no repeating groups; every field single-valued. 2NF: 1NF and no partial dependency on part of a composite key. 3NF: 2NF and no transitive dependency (non-key fields must not determine each other). Full treatment with worked conversions sits in the A2 database-design note; the foundation idea here is single fact, single place.

Anomaly worked on an unnormalised order table:
  (orderID, customerName, customerPhone, product, price)

Update anomaly:  customer changes phone - every order row must be updated.
Insert anomaly:  a new customer with no orders cannot be stored.
Delete anomaly:  deleting their only order deletes the customer's details.

Normalised:
  CUSTOMER (customerID [PK], name, phone)
  PRODUCT  (productID [PK], price)
  ORDER    (orderID [PK], customerID [FK], productID [FK], quantity)

Each fact now lives once; the anomalies vanish.

Reading and writing data: the SQL shape

Though examined formally at Unit 4, the query shape appears already at Unit 2: SELECT (columns) FROM (table) WHERE (row filter) ORDER BY (sort), with aggregates COUNT/SUM/AVG/MIN/MAX and GROUP BY. Declarative: state the result wanted, not the procedure. The DBMS's query optimiser chooses the access path — an index turns a table scan into a lookup.

Worked queries on GRADE above:

  "Average mark per subject, highest first":
    SELECT subject, AVG(mark)
    FROM GRADE
    GROUP BY subject
    ORDER BY AVG(mark) DESC;
    → Maths 65, Physics 65   [(72+58)/2 = 65; 65]

  "Students with a mark above 60":
    SELECT studentID, subject, mark
    FROM GRADE
    WHERE mark > 60
    ORDER BY mark DESC;
    → (S1, Maths, 72), (S1, Physics, 65)

Execution order to remember: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING →
SELECT → ORDER BY.
ConceptDefinitionWorked check on the clinic database
EntityA thing about which data is heldPATIENT, DOCTOR, APPOINTMENT
AttributeA property of an entitypatient name, appointment date
Primary keyUnique, non-null identifier of a rowpatientID — no two patients share it
Foreign keyReference to another table's primary keyAPPOINTMENT.patientID must exist in PATIENT
RelationshipAssociation between entitiesPATIENT -< APPOINTMENT >- DOCTOR
ConstraintRule the DBMS enforcesdoctorID + slot UNIQUE stops double booking

Worked example: a database for a small clinic

Requirements: patients, doctors, appointments; one patient sees one doctor
per appointment; track prescriptions.

Design steps:
1. Entities: PATIENT, DOCTOR, APPOINTMENT, PRESCRIPTION.
2. Keys: each gets a surrogate primary key (patientID, doctorID...);
   APPOINTMENT carries patientID and doctorID as foreign keys;
   PRESCRIPTION carries appointmentID.
3. Relationships: PATIENT -< APPOINTMENT >- DOCTOR (many-to-many resolved by
   APPOINTMENT); APPOINTMENT -< PRESCRIPTION (one-to-many).
4. Constraints: appointment date not null; time slot unique per doctor
   (composite unique: doctorID + slot) - double booking becomes impossible at
   the schema level.
5. Security: receptionists insert/read appointments; only doctors read
   prescriptions; audit log for access.

Testing the design: try the three anomalies above on it - each is now
impossible, which is the design's proof.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Calling any column with an ID a "primary key"; the key must be unique and non-null — and chosen deliberately (surrogate vs natural).
  • Explaining foreign keys as "links" without referential integrity: every FK value must exist in the referenced PK.
  • Missing the many-to-many linking table answer; junction tables are the standard resolution.
  • Listing DBMS features without effect — "security" means accounts, permissions and audit; "integrity" means constraints the DBMS enforces.
  • Confusing a database with a DBMS (the data versus the software managing it).
  • Assuming tables have an order; ORDER BY exists precisely because rows are unordered sets.
  • Skipping the delete rule (cascade/restrict/set null) in relationship questions.

Exam-style questions and answers
