Question 1 (Unit 2, 4 marks). Explain two problems of storing the same data in separate department files.

Answer: Duplication leads to inconsistency — when a customer's address changes, each file must be updated separately and stale copies persist, so different departments act on different data. Updates and deletions create anomalies — deleting the last order record may erase the only copy of a customer's details (deletion anomaly), and a new customer cannot be recorded before they order (insertion anomaly).

Question 2 (Unit 2, 4 marks). Explain the roles of primary keys and foreign keys in a relational database.

Answer: A primary key uniquely and non-null identifies each record in its table, enabling reliable retrieval and preventing duplicates. A foreign key in another table references that primary key, creating a relationship and enforcing referential integrity — the DBMS rejects any value with no matching record, and can cascade or restrict deletions so relationships never dangle.

Question 3 (Unit 2, 4 marks). Describe how a DBMS handles two users updating the same record simultaneously.

Answer: Concurrency control locks the record (or uses versioning) when the first transaction begins, so the second waits or operates on a prior version. Isolation ensures one transaction's uncommitted changes are invisible to the other; commit releases the lock and logs the change, so the update is atomic and durable. Without this, interleaved updates produce lost updates.

Question 4 (Unit 2, 3 marks). State what ACID stands for and why it matters.

Answer: Atomic — a transaction completes fully or not at all; Consistent — it leaves the database satisfying all constraints; Isolated — concurrent transactions do not interfere; Durable — committed changes survive failure. Together they guarantee correctness of shared data despite crashes and concurrent users.

Question 5 (Unit 2, 4 marks). A library stores (loanID, memberName, memberPhone, bookTitle, dueDate). Explain one anomaly and how normalisation fixes it.

Answer: MemberPhone depends on the member, not the loan — so a member's phone is duplicated across every loan row; changing it requires many updates and one miss leaves it inconsistent (update anomaly). Splitting into MEMBER(memberID, name, phone) and LOAN(loanID, memberID, bookTitle, dueDate) stores the phone once, with the loan referencing it by key.

Question 6 (Unit 2, 3 marks). Explain the difference between a database and a DBMS.

Answer: The database is the organised collection of integrated data itself — tables of records and their relationships. The DBMS is the software that manages it: creating and enforcing schema rules, handling security, concurrency, backup and query processing. Application programs request data through the DBMS rather than reading files directly.

Unit 2 is complete. A2 builds directly on these foundations — starting with the advanced data structures that generalise arrays and records.

title: Transition Metals and their Chemistry - A2 Chemistry
content:
Transition Metals and their Chemistry - A2 Level

This topic belongs to the Edexcel International Advanced Level (IAL) Chemistry specification, Unit 5 (WCH15), and covers the electronic configurations, variable oxidation states, complex ion formation, ligand exchange, colour changes, standard electrode potentials of vanadium and chromium systems, catalysis, and practical preparations associated with d-block transition elements of Period 4 from scandium to zinc.

Definition and Electronic Configurations of Transition Metals

Transition metals are defined as d-block elements that form one or more stable ions with incompletely-filled d-orbitals. Scandium and zinc are in the d-block but are not true transition metals because Sc3+ has an empty d-orbital (3d0) and Zn2+ has a completely filled d-orbital (3d10). To deduce electronic configurations of Period 4 atoms and ions from Sc to Zn, remember that the 4s orbital fills before 3d, but when positive ions are formed, electrons are always removed from the 4s orbital before the 3d orbitals.

  • Transition metals are d-block elements forming stable ions with incompletely-filled d-orbitals (17.1).
  • Electronic configuration rules: fill 4s then 3d, empty 4s before 3d when forming ions (17.2).
  • Example atom Ti (atomic number 22): 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d2 (17.2).
  • Example ion Fe2+ (atomic number 26): 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 3d6, with the two 4s electrons removed (17.2).
  • Example ion Cu+ (atomic number 29): 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 3d10 (17.2).
  • Variable oxidation numbers occur because the 4s and 3d sub-shells have very similar energies, allowing different numbers of electrons to be lost or involved in bonding with minimal energy penalty (17.3).

Complex Ions, Ligands, and Coordination Numbers

A complex ion consists of a central metal ion surrounded by species called ligands. A ligand is a species containing at least one lone pair of electrons that forms a dative covalent (coordinate) bond to the central metal ion. The coordination number is the total number of coordinate bonds formed to the central metal ion. The nature and size of ligands determine the spatial arrangement and geometry of the resulting complex ion.

  • Ligand definition: a species with a lone pair that forms a dative covalent bond to a metal ion (17.4, 17.5).
  • Complex ion definition: a central metal ion surrounded by ligands (17.6).
  • Coordination number: the number of coordinate bonds to the central metal ion (17.10).
  • Monodentate ligands donate one pair of electrons; H2O, OH− and NH3 act as monodentate ligands (17.12).
  • Six-fold coordination complexes have an octahedral shape, such as [M(H2O)6]n+, [M(OH)6]n−, and [M(NH3)6]n+ (17.13).
  • Tetrahedral complexes form with relatively large ligands such as Cl−, for example [CuCl4]2− and [CoCl4]2−, due to steric hindrance preventing six chloride ions from packing around the small metal centre (17.14).
  • Square planar complexes are also formed by transition metal ions; cis-platin, [Pt(NH3)2Cl2], is a square planar complex used in cancer treatment supplied as a single active cis isomer rather than a mixture with the inactive trans form (17.15).
  • Bidentate ligands have two donor atoms donating two lone pairs, such as ethane-1,2-diamine (NH2CH2CH2NH2). Hexadentate ligands have six donor atoms, such as EDTA4− (17.16).
  • Haemoglobin is an iron(II) complex containing a polydentate porphyrin ring ligand; ligand exchange occurs when an oxygen molecule bound to haemoglobin in the lungs is replaced by a carbon monoxide molecule in the body tissues (17.17).

Colour and d-Orbital Splitting

Aqueous solutions of transition metal ions are usually coloured because the presence of surrounding ligands causes the five degenerate d-orbitals to split into two different energy levels. When white light passes through the solution, electrons absorb specific frequencies of visible light to jump from the lower d-orbitals to the higher d-orbitals. The colour observed is due to the remaining unabsorbed wavelengths transmitted or reflected. A lack of colour in some aqueous ions or complex ions, such as Sc3+ (3d0) or Zn2+ (3d10), occurs because their d-orbitals are either completely empty or completely full, so d-d electronic transitions are impossible.

  • Aqueous solutions of transition metal ions are usually coloured (17.7).
  • Colour arises from the splitting of the energy levels of d-orbitals by the electrostatic field of surrounding ligands (17.8).
  • Lack of colour in ions like Sc3+ (3d0) and Zn2+ (3d10) is due to empty or full d-orbitals preventing d-d electron transitions (17.9).
  • Colour changes in transition metal ions arise from changes in oxidation number, changes in ligand, or changes in the coordination number of the complex (17.11).

Vanadium and Chromium Redox Chemistry

Vanadium exhibits four stable oxidation states in aqueous solution, each with a characteristic colour: +5 (yellow, VO2+), +4 (blue, VO2+), +3 (green, V3+), and +2 (violet, V2+). These oxidation states can be interconverted via redox reactions using zinc metal in acidic conditions as a reducing agent, driven by standard electrode potential (Eo) values. Similarly, chromium chemistry involves the interconversion of Cr3+ and dichromate(VI) ions, Cr2O7 2−. Dichromate(VI) ions can be reduced using zinc in acid and produced by oxidising Cr3+ with hydrogen peroxide in alkaline conditions followed by acidification. In aqueous solution, dichromate(VI) ions exist in a pH-dependent equilibrium with chromate(VI) ions.

  • Vanadium oxidation states and colours: +5 is yellow (VO2+), +4 is blue (VO2+), +3 is green (V3+), and +2 is violet (V2+) (17.18).
  • Redox interconversion of vanadium oxidation states is achieved using zinc in acidic solution, evaluated through relevant Eo values where Zn/Zn2+ is sufficiently negative to reduce V5+ down to V2+ (17.19).
  • Dchromate(VI) ions (Cr2O7 2−) can be reduced to Cr3+ and further to Cr2+ using zinc in acidic conditions (17.20i).
  • Dichromate(VI) ions can be produced by the oxidation of Cr3+ ions using hydrogen peroxide in alkaline conditions, followed by subsequent acidification (17.20ii).
  • Dichromate(VI) ion equilibrium with chromate(VI): Cr2O7 2− + H2O <-> 2CrO4 2− + 2H+ (17.21). Adding acid shifts this equilibrium left towards orange dichromate; adding alkali shifts it right towards yellow chromate.

Reactions of Aqueous Transition Metal Ions with Hydroxide and Ammonia

Aqueous metal ions react with sodium hydroxide and aqueous ammonia to produce precipitates, which may show amphoteric behaviour or dissolve in excess reagent due to ligand exchange. You must know the exact observations and write balanced ionic equations for Cr3+(aq), Mn2+(aq), Fe2+(aq), Fe3+(aq), Co2+(aq), Ni2+(aq), Cu2+(aq), and Zn2+(aq).

  • Cr3+(aq) + 3OH−(aq) -> Cr(OH)3(H2O)3(s) (grey-green precipitate). Excess OH− gives [Cr(OH)6]3− (dark green solution) demonstrating amphoteric behaviour (17.22, 17.23).
  • Cr3+(aq) with NH3(aq): grey-green precipitate of Cr(OH)3(H2O)3, insoluble in excess ammonia (17.22).
  • Mn2+(aq) + 2OH−(aq) -> Mn(OH)2(s) (off-white precipitate, turns brown on standing in air due to oxidation). Insoluble in excess OH− and excess NH3 (17.22).
  • Fe2+(aq) + 2OH−(aq) -> Fe(OH)2(s) (green precipitate, turns brown on surface in air). Insoluble in excess OH− and excess NH3 (17.22).
  • Fe3+(aq) + 3OH−(aq) -> Fe(OH)3(s) (rusty-brown precipitate). Insoluble in excess OH− and excess NH3 (17.22).
  • Co2+(aq) + 2OH−(aq) -> Co(OH)2(s) (blue precipitate, turns pink on standing). Insoluble in excess OH−. With excess NH3, forms [Co(NH3)6]2+ (pale yellow solution turning brown) via ligand exchange (17.22, 17.23, 17.24).
  • Ni2+(aq) + 2OH−(aq) -> Ni(OH)2(s) (green precipitate). Insoluble in excess OH−. With excess NH3, dissolves to form [Ni(NH3)6]2+ (blue solution) (17.22, 17.23).
  • Cu2+(aq) + 2OH−(aq) -> Cu(OH)2(s) (pale blue precipitate). Insoluble in excess OH−. With excess NH3, dissolves to form [Cu(NH3)4(H2O)2]2+ (deep blue solution) (17.22, 17.23, 17.24).
  • Zn2+(aq) + 2OH−(aq) -> Zn(OH)2(s) (white precipitate). Dissolves in excess OH− to form [Zn(OH)4]2− (colourless solution) demonstrating amphoteric behaviour (17.22, 17.23).
  • Zn2+(aq) with excess NH3(aq): white precipitate dissolves to form [Zn(NH3)4]2+ (colourless solution) (17.22, 17.23).
  • Deprotonation reactions involve aqueous metal ions losing protons from coordinated water molecules to form neutral hydroxide precipitates (17.23).

Specific Ligand Exchange Reactions and Entropy

Ligand exchange occurs when one ligand in a complex is replaced by another, accompanied by a distinct colour change and often a change in coordination number. The thermodynamic stability of complex ions is significantly enhanced when monodentate ligands are replaced by bidentate or hexadentate ligands, known as the chelate effect. This can be understood in terms of the positive increase in entropy (Ssystem) because there are more free moles of product species than reactant species in solution.

  • Formation of [Cu(NH3)4(H2O)2]2+ (deep blue) from [Cu(H2O)6]2+ (pale blue) proceeds via an intermediate Cu(OH)2(H2O)4 precipitate upon adding ammonia, which then redissolves in excess ammonia (17.24i).
  • Formation of [CuCl4]2− (yellow-green) from [Cu(H2O)6]2+ (blue) occurs upon adding concentrated hydrochloric acid, resulting in a change in coordination number from 6 to 4 and a shape change from octahedral to tetrahedral (17.24ii).
  • Formation of [CoCl4]2− (blue) from [Co(H2O)6]2+ (pink) occurs on adding concentrated hydrochloric acid, changing coordination number from 6 to 4 and shape from octahedral to tetrahedral (17.24iii).
  • Substitution of monodentate ligands by bidentate or hexadentate ligands leads to a more stable complex ion due to a positive increase in system entropy (Ssystem), as the number of independent particles in solution increases (17.25).

Catalysis by Transition Metals

Transition metals and their compounds are exceptionally effective catalysts, operating as either heterogeneous catalysts (in a different phase from reactants, with reactions occurring on the catalyst surface) or homogeneous catalysts (in the same phase as reactants, proceeding via intermediate species). V2O5 acts as a heterogeneous catalyst in the Contact process for manufacturing sulfur trioxide. Catalytic converters in vehicles use solid platinum/rhodium heterogeneous catalysts to remove carbon monoxide and nitrogen monoxide emissions via adsorption, bond weakening, reaction, and desorption. Homogeneous catalysis is exemplified by Fe2+ catalysing the reaction between iodide and peroxydisulfate ions, and Mn2+ autocatalysing the reaction between manganate(VII) and ethanedioate ions.

  • Heterogeneous catalyst: in a different phase from reactants; reaction occurs at the active sites on the surface of the catalyst (17.26, 17.27).
  • V2O5 acts as a heterogeneous catalyst in the Contact process by being reduced from V(V) to V(IV) by SO2, then reoxidised back to V(V) by O2: SO2 + V2O5 -> SO3 + V2O4, followed by V2O4 + 0.5O2 -> V2O5 (17.28).
  • Catalytic converter mechanism: 1. Adsorption of CO and NO molecules onto the metal surface, weakening covalent bonds. 2. Chemical reaction between adsorbed species to form CO2 and N2. 3. Desorption of product molecules from the surface (17.29).
  • Homogeneous catalyst: in the same phase as reactants, proceeding through distinct intermediate species (17.30).
  • Role of Fe2+ in catalysing reaction between I− and S2O8 2−: Fe2+ reduces S2O8 2− to SO4 2− forming Fe3+ intermediate (S2O8 2− + 2Fe2+ -> 2SO4 2− + 2Fe3+), then Fe3+ oxidises I− back to I2 regenerating Fe2+ (2Fe3+ + 2I− -> 2Fe2+ + I2) (17.31).
  • Role of Mn2+ in autocatalysing reaction between MnO4 − and C2O4 2−: reaction starts very slowly, but the Mn2+ product acts as a catalyst, speeding up the reaction as its concentration increases (autocatalysis) (17.32).
  • Core Practical 14: The preparation of a transition metal complex, such as potassium tris(oxalato)ferrate(III) trihydrate, involving ligand substitution, precipitation, recrystallisation, and percentage yield calculation (17.33).

Typical mistakes

  • Mistake: Removing electrons from 3d orbitals before 4s orbitals when writing ion configurations. Correction: Always fill 4s before 3d, but remove electrons from the 4s orbital first when forming positive ions.
  • Mistake: Stating that Sc3+ or Zn2+ solutions are coloured. Correction: They are colourless because they do not have incompletely-filled d-orbitals to permit d-d electron transitions.
  • Mistake: Confusing coordination number with the number of ligands. Correction: Coordination number is the total number of coordinate bonds, which equals the number of monodentate ligands, but is double the number of bidentate ligands.
  • Mistake: Omitting phase or charge when writing complex ion formulas. Correction: Always enclose the complex in square brackets with the overall charge outside, e.g., [Cu(NH3)4(H2O)2]2+.
  • Mistake: Forgetting that cis-platin must be supplied as a single isomer. Correction: Cis-platin is supplied specifically as the cis isomer because only this form binds to DNA to inhibit cancer cell replication.

Exam-style questions

  1. Deduce the ground state electronic configuration of a cobalt(II) atom (atomic number 27) and a cobalt(III) ion. (2 marks)

    Answer: Co atom is 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d7 (1 mark). Co3+ ion is 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 3d6, with electrons removed from 4s first (1 mark).

  2. Explain why aqueous copper(II) sulfate is blue, whereas aqueous scandium(III) chloride is colourless. (3 marks)

    Answer: Cu2+ has an incompletely-filled 3d9 configuration; d-orbitals split in the ligand field, allowing d-d electron transitions which absorb specific frequencies of visible light (2 marks). Sc3+ has a 3d0 configuration with no d-electrons, so no d-d transitions are possible, making it colourless (1 mark).

  3. Describe what you would observe when excess aqueous ammonia is added dropwise to an aqueous solution containing copper(II) ions. Write ionic equations for the reactions that occur. (4 marks)

    Answer: Observations: pale blue solution forms a pale blue precipitate of Cu(OH)2, which then dissolves in excess ammonia to form a deep blue solution (2 marks). Equations: Cu2+(aq) + 2OH−(aq) -> Cu(OH)2(s) followed by Cu(OH)2(s) + 4NH3(aq) + 2H2O(l) -> [Cu(NH3)4(H2O)2]2+(aq) + 2OH−(aq) (2 marks).

  4. Explain why the substitution of six monodentate water ligands by three bidentate ethane-1,2-diamine ligands in a complex ion is thermodynamically favoured by entropy. (2 marks)

    Answer: There is an increase in the total number of independent particles/molecules in solution from 4 reactants to 7 products (1 mark), leading to a positive entropy change (Ssystem > 0) making the complex more stable (1 mark).

  5. Outline how V2O5 acts as a heterogeneous catalyst in the Contact process, including chemical equations. (3 marks)

    Answer: V2O5 is in a different phase (solid) from the gaseous reactants (1 mark). It oxidises SO2 to SO3, being reduced itself: SO2 + V2O5 -> SO3 + V2O4 (1 mark). The V2O4 is then reoxidised by oxygen back to V2O5: V2O4 + 0.5O2 -> V2O5 (1 mark).

Use these revision notes alongside active recall of colour changes, precipitation reactions, and equation writing. Practise balancing redox equations for vanadium and chromium, and ensure you can explain the chelate effect using entropy arguments before moving on to past paper practice.

title: A2 Level Biology: Coordination, Response and Gene Technology
content:
Coordination, Response and Gene Technology — A2 Level Biology

This revision note belongs to the Edexcel International A2 Biology specification, WBI15 Unit 5, Topic 8 Coordination, Response and Gene Technology. It covers the nervous system — sensory, relay and motor neurones, myelination and saltatory conduction, the action potential and its conduction along the axon, the spinal reflex arc, synapses and the role of neurotransmitters, how the pupil dilates and contracts, how drugs influence nerve impulse transmission (nicotine, lidocaine, cobra venom alpha toxin, L-DOPA and Parkinson’s disease, MDMA), how the retina detects light and forms action potentials in the optic neurones, habituation, the central and peripheral nervous systems, hormonal and nervous coordination, the structure and function of the brain (cerebral hemispheres, hypothalamus, pituitary gland, cerebellum, medulla oblongata), how MRI, fMRI, PET and CT are used in diagnosis and investigation of brain structure and function, how imbalances in brain chemicals contribute to ill health (dopamine in Parkinson’s disease, serotonin in depression) and to the development of new drugs, how drugs can be produced using genetically modified organisms, how recombinant DNA is produced and inserted into other cells, how microarrays identify active genes, what bioinformatics is, and the risks and benefits of genetically modified organisms. Every statement the topic is responsible for is covered in its own section or paragraph, with the material set so that a student can revise from it and check themselves against the specification.

1. Sensory, relay and motor neurones, Schwann cells and myelination

The nervous system has three main types of neurone, each with a structure suited to its function. Sensory neurones carry impulses from receptors to the central nervous system; their cell body is off to one side of the axon, halfway along it, and they have a long dendron that carries the impulse from the receptor to the cell body and a long axon that carries it into the CNS. Relay neurones connect sensory and motor neurones within the CNS; their cell body is in the centre of the neurone, and they have many short dendrites and a short axon. Motor neurones carry impulses from the CNS to effectors (muscles or glands); their cell body is in the CNS, and they have a long axon with many short dendrites. All neurones have a cell body containing the nucleus and many mitochondria (to supply ATP), dendrites that carry impulses towards the cell body, and an axon that carries impulses away from the cell body. Many axons are wrapped in Schwann cells, which wrap tightly around the axon in a fatty myelin sheath; the myelin sheath insulates the axon and speeds conduction. The gaps in the myelin sheath are called nodes of Ranvier. The structure of each neurone type reflects what it does — sensory neurones bring information in, relay neurones process it inside the CNS, and motor neurones carry the response out to effectors.

2. The nervous system and how it makes effectors respond to a stimulus

A stimulus is a change in the environment (internal or external) that is detected by a receptor. The receptor converts the stimulus into an electrical signal (a generator potential, then if it reaches threshold an action potential) in a sensory neurone. The impulse travels along the sensory neurone to the CNS, where it is passed to a relay neurone; the relay neurone may synapse with other relay neurones and process the information, then pass the impulse to a motor neurone, which carries it to an effector. The effector — a muscle or a gland — responds: a muscle contracts, or a gland secretes its product. This is the general pathway: stimulus → receptor → sensory neurone → CNS (relay neurone) → motor neurone → effector → response. The response is specific to the stimulus and to the circuitry involved, and rapid because electrical impulses travel fast along neurones.

3. The spinal reflex arc: grey matter, white matter and the withdrawal reflex

A reflex arc is the pathway of neurones that produces a rapid, involuntary response to a stimulus, without involving conscious control. In the spinal reflex arc, a sensory neurone from a receptor (for example in the skin) synapses with a relay neurone in the spinal cord, which in turn synapses with a motor neurone that runs to an effector (for example a muscle). The grey matter of the spinal cord is the inner, butterfly-shaped region where the cell bodies of relay and motor neurones and the synapses between them are found; the white matter is the outer region, made up of myelinated axons that carry impulses up and down the cord, to and from the brain. In the withdrawal reflex, for example touching a hot object, a pain receptor in the skin sends an impulse via a sensory neurone to a relay neurone in the spinal cord, which excites a motor neurone that makes the arm flex (biceps contracts, triceps relaxes) and withdraws from the stimulus. The response is rapid and automatic, and happens before the brain is even aware of the stimulus, because the arc involves only the spinal cord; this protects the body from harm.

4. The action potential: how an impulse is conducted along an axon

An action potential is the nerve impulse — a rapid, transient change in the membrane potential of a neurone, from about −70 mV (resting potential) up to about +40 mV and back, caused by the opening and closing of voltage-gated sodium and potassium ion channels. At rest the inside of the axon is negatively charged relative to the outside (the resting potential), mainly because sodium ions are pumped out and potassium ions are pumped in by the sodium–potassium pump, and the membrane is more permeable to potassium ions than to sodium ions at rest. When a stimulus depolarises the membrane to the threshold, voltage-gated sodium ion channels open, sodium ions flood in, the inside becomes positively charged (depolarisation, up to +40 mV). At about the peak, the sodium channels close and voltage-gated potassium channels open, potassium ions flood out, and the inside returns towards resting (repolarisation); it rises a little too far (hyperpolarisation) before returning to resting. The sodium–potassium pump then restores the resting ion distribution. The all-or-nothing principle applies: once threshold is reached, the action potential fires at full size; a stronger stimulus does not produce a bigger action potential, it produces more of them (greater frequency). During the absolute refractory period, the sodium channels are inactivated and no new action potential can be started, which ensures impulses travel one way and sets a maximum frequency.

5. Myelination and saltatory conduction: why some axons are faster

Myelination speeds up conduction of the action potential. In a myelinated axon the myelin sheath insulates the axon so that ions cannot cross the membrane where it is covered; the action potential can only be generated at the nodes of Ranvier, where the axon is bare. The impulse therefore jumps from node to node — saltatory conduction — and this is much faster than the continuous conduction along an unmyelinated axon, because the impulse does not have to depolarise every part of the membrane. The speed of conduction also depends on the diameter of the axon (larger axons conduct faster because there is less resistance to the flow of ions inside) and on the number of sodium channels and the extent of myelination; the fastest axons in the body are large and heavily myelinated.

6. Synapses: structure, transmission, acetylcholine, and the pupillary reflex

A synapse is the junction between two neurones (or between a neurone and an effector cell) across which the impulse is passed by a chemical neurotransmitter. At a cholinergic synapse, an action potential arriving at the presynaptic neurone opens voltage-gated calcium ion channels; calcium ions enter the presynaptic terminal, causing synaptic vesicles containing the neurotransmitter acetylcholine to fuse with the presynaptic membrane and release their contents by exocytosis into the synaptic cleft. Acetylcholine diffuses across the cleft and binds to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane, opening sodium ion channels so sodium ions enter and depolarise the postsynaptic membrane (this may start an action potential if the threshold is reached). Acetylcholinesterase in the cleft breaks down acetylcholine to stop the signal and recycle the choline. Drugs and toxins can affect the synapse: nicotine mimics acetylcholine and stimulates the postsynaptic receptor; lidocaine blocks voltage-gated sodium channels and stops impulse transmission (used as a local anaesthetic); cobra venom alpha toxin blocks acetylcholine receptors so the muscle cannot be stimulated (paralysis). Meanwhile, the pupil is controlled by two sets of muscles in the iris: circular muscles and radial muscles. In bright light, the parasympathetic nervous system makes the circular muscles of the iris contract, which constricts (makes smaller) the pupil, reducing the light entering the eye; in dim light, the radial muscles contract, dilating (widening) the pupil so more light enters.

7. Drugs and nerve impulse transmission: nicotine, lidocaine, cobra venom alpha toxin, L-DOPA, and MDMA

Many drugs act on the nervous system by influencing nerve impulse transmission. Nicotine stimulates nicotinic acetylcholine receptors in the brain, producing a temporary feeling of alertness and pleasure, and it is addictive because repeated use changes the brain’s reward pathways; it also raises blood pressure and heart rate, and is a carcinogen. Lidocaine is a local anaesthetic that blocks voltage-gated sodium ion channels in sensory neurones, preventing the formation and conduction of action potentials, so pain signals are not sent to the brain — it is used to numb a local area. Cobra venom alpha toxin binds to acetylcholine receptors on the muscle and blocks acetylcholine from binding, so the muscle cannot be stimulated and paralysis results, which can be fatal if the respiratory muscles are paralysed. L-DOPA is used to treat Parkinson’s disease; Parkinson’s is caused by a loss of dopamine-producing neurones in a part of the brain (the substantia nigra), so the level of dopamine falls and movement becomes impaired (tremor, stiffness, slow movement); L-DOPA is a precursor that can cross the blood–brain barrier and is converted to dopamine in the brain, restoring the level and easing the symptoms, at least for a time. MDMA (ecstasy) causes a large release of serotonin from presynaptic neurones and blocks its reuptake, so serotonin levels in the synapse rise sharply, producing a feeling of wellbeing and empathy, but the subsequent depletion of serotonin and damage to serotonin neurones can cause depression and memory problems, and repeated use is harmful.

8. Detecting light: the rod cell, rhodopsin, and how an action potential is generated in the optic neurone

Rods in the retina of mammals detect light and allow us to see in dim light. A rod cell contains the pigment rhodopsin, which is made of a protein (opsin) and a light-absorbing molecule (retinal, a derivative of vitamin A). When light hits rhodopsin, the retinal changes shape (from 11-cis to all-trans retinal), which changes the opsin and causes the rod cell to hyperpolarise — it becomes more negative inside. This hyperpolarisation closes sodium ion channels that are normally open in the dark, so sodium ion entry is reduced and the rod cell hyperpolarises; this in turn reduces the release of the neurotransmitter (glutamate) from the rod cell’s synaptic terminal. The change in transmitter release affects the bipolar neurone, which in turn affects the neurone that runs to the brain (the optic neurone); so the rod cell’s hyperpolarisation to light ultimately leads to action potentials in the optic neurone, which travel to the brain and are interpreted as vision. This is a relatively fine point — light does not itself produce the action potential in the rod, it changes the rod’s membrane potential, and that change is passed on through the retinal circuit to generate action potentials in the optic neurone. Cone cells work similarly but are responsible for colour vision and detail in bright light.

9. Habituation: what it is and how it is investigated

Habituation is a simple form of learning in which a response to a repeated, harmless stimulus decreases over time; the organism learns to ignore the stimulus because it has learned it is not important. For example, a snail initially withdraws into its shell when its shell is tapped, but with repeated tapping the withdrawal response becomes slower and eventually disappears — the snail has habituated to the tap. Habituation is not fatigue of the muscle (if a new stimulus, such as a poke to the body, still produces a strong response, the withdrawal machinery is fine) and not sensory adaptation (the receptor still responds to the stimulus), but a decrease in the synaptic transmission at the synapse between the sensory neurone and the motor neurone that produces the withdrawal. A recommended additional practical is to investigate habituation to a stimulus — for example using the snail withdrawal response, tapping the snail and recording the time to emerge or the frequency of withdrawal, and showing that with repeated harmless taps the response declines and that the decline is not due to muscle fatigue.

10. The central and peripheral nervous systems

The mammalian nervous system consists of the central nervous system (CNS) and the peripheral nervous system (PNS). The CNS is the brain and spinal cord; it integrates information and coordinates responses. The PNS is the network of nerves that connect the CNS to the rest of the body — to receptors and to effectors; it includes the sensory neurones that bring information to the CNS and the motor neurones that carry commands to effectors. The motor part of the PNS can be divided into the voluntary (somatic) nervous system, which controls skeletal muscles consciously, and the autonomic nervous system, which controls involuntary functions such as heart rate, gut movement and the pupils, and which is further divided into the sympathetic (which prepares the body for action — fight or flight) and parasympathetic (which promotes rest and digestion) nervous systems; these two often have opposite effects on the same organ.

11. Coordination in animals: nervous and hormonal control together

Animals coordinate their bodies by both nervous and hormonal control, and the two work together. The nervous system uses electrical impulses that travel fast along neurones and chemical signals (neurotransmitters) across synapses, giving rapid, short-lived responses targeted at specific effectors — good for rapid movements and reflexes. The hormonal system uses hormones carried in the blood, which travel more slowly and affect many cells at once, producing slower, longer-lasting, more widespread responses — good for things like growth, metabolism, reproduction and responding to stress over a longer time. In many situations they act together: for example, in the fight-or-flight response, the sympathetic nervous system acts quickly to increase heart rate, while the hormone adrenaline from the adrenal glands sustains and amplifies the response; in the control of blood glucose, hormones (insulin and glucagon) act more slowly and over longer periods than nervous control would allow. Plants coordinate only by hormones (plant growth substances such as auxin, gibberellin and phytochrome), because they have no nervous system.

12. The human brain: cerebral hemispheres, hypothalamus, pituitary gland, cerebellum, medulla oblongata

The brain controls and coordinates the activities of the body and is the seat of thought, memory and emotion. The cerebral hemispheres are the large, folded upper parts of the brain; they are responsible for higher functions — thought, memory, reasoning, conscious actions, language and sensation — and each hemisphere controls the opposite side of the body. The hypothalamus links the nervous and endocrine systems; it controls the pituitary gland, regulates body temperature, water balance, hunger and thirst, and the sleep cycle, and it plays a central role in homeostasis. The pituitary gland, under the influence of the hypothalamus, releases several hormones that control other endocrine glands and body functions — for example growth hormone, ADH and the hormones that regulate reproduction. The cerebellum is responsible for coordination of movement and balance — it makes sure movements are smooth and coordinated and posture is maintained. The medulla oblongata controls unconscious and automatic functions essential to life — breathing rate, heart rate and the reflex centres for coughing, sneezing and swallowing — and it is where the cardiovascular control centre and the ventilation (breathing) centre are located. Damage to different parts of the brain produces different deficits, and knowing the location and main functions makes it possible to link symptoms to brain regions.

13. Brain imaging: MRI, fMRI, PET and CT — what they show and how they are used

Different imaging techniques give different kinds of information about the brain. Computed tomography (CT) uses X-rays from many angles to produce a cross-sectional image of the brain’s structure; it is good at showing bone, bleeding and structural abnormalities, and it is quick and widely available, but it uses ionising radiation and gives limited soft-tissue contrast. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) uses a strong magnetic field and radio waves to give detailed images of soft tissue; it shows brain structure without ionising radiation and is excellent for detecting tumours, inflammation, demyelination and injury, but it takes longer and is noisy and claustrophobic for the patient. Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) is MRI adapted to show brain function — it detects changes in blood flow and oxygen use that accompany neural activity, so it can show which parts of the brain are active during a task; it has good spatial resolution but poor time resolution because the blood flow change lags the neural activity. Positron emission tomography (PET) uses a radioactive tracer (for example, a labelled glucose) injected into the patient; the tracer accumulates in active tissues and its radioactivity is detected, so PET can show brain activity and metabolism, and it can show neurotransmitter receptors and help in diagnosing and studying disorders such as Alzheimer’s and cancer, but it uses ionising radiation and is expensive. These techniques are used in medical diagnosis (for example to locate a tumour, or to investigate a stroke or a degenerative disease) and in research into brain structure and function — for example to see which areas are involved in a particular task or how activity differs in a disorder.

14. Brain chemicals and disease: dopamine in Parkinson’s disease, serotonin in depression, and new drugs

Imbalances in certain naturally-occurring brain chemicals can contribute to ill health, and understanding these has driven the development of new drugs. Parkinson’s disease is caused by the loss of neurones in the substantia nigra that produce dopamine, a neurotransmitter involved in controlling movement; the resulting dopamine deficiency causes tremor, stiffness, slowness of movement and balance problems. Treatment with L-DOPA (a precursor that crosses the blood–brain barrier and is converted to dopamine) can relieve symptoms, at least for a time, and other drugs may mimic dopamine or prevent its breakdown. Depression is associated with lower levels of the neurotransmitter serotonin (and also noradrenaline) in the brain; selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) block the reuptake of serotonin into the presynaptic neurone, so more serotonin stays in the synapse and helps improve mood, and they are widely used to treat depression and anxiety. New drugs can be developed using this understanding of the role of brain chemicals — for example by targeting the receptors or the synthesis or breakdown of a neurotransmitter — and knowledge of the cause of a disease (such as the dopamine deficiency in Parkinson’s) is what makes targeted treatment possible.

15. Producing drugs using genetically modified organisms

Drugs can be produced using genetically modified organisms (GMOs) — plants, animals and microorganisms. The best-known example is human insulin: the human gene for insulin is inserted into bacteria (usually E. coli) using a plasmid, and the bacteria are grown in large fermenters to produce human insulin, which is then extracted and purified. Human insulin made this way is identical to the insulin made in the human body, so it does not cause the immune reactions that some people had to the animal insulin formerly used. Other products made from GMOs include human growth hormone, clotting factor for haemophiliacs, and enzymes for washing powders; and modified plants and animals are being explored to produce vaccines and other pharmaceuticals. Using GMOs to produce drugs has advantages: the product can be made in large quantities, it can be made more cheaply than by extraction from animals or people, and it can be made identical to the human version. There are concerns, however — about the containment of the GMOs, the possibility of unintended effects, and the ethical questions of modifying organisms in this way.

16. Recombinant DNA: how it is produced (restriction enzymes and DNA ligase) and inserted into other cells

Recombinant DNA is DNA made by joining together pieces of DNA from different sources. Restriction endonucleases (restriction enzymes) cut DNA at specific base sequences, making cuts that can leave complementary ‘sticky ends’ — short single-stranded overhangs that can base-pair with each other — and these sticky ends allow a gene of interest to be joined to a vector (such as a plasmid) cut with the same enzyme. DNA ligase then seals the backbone of the sugar–phosphate chain, joining the gene to the vector to make recombinant DNA. To insert recombinant DNA into other cells, the vector (carrying the gene) is introduced into host cells: bacterial cells can take up plasmids in a process called transformation (which can be helped by making the bacteria competent — for example by calcium chloride treatment and a heat shock); viral vectors can be engineered to carry the gene into the cells they infect, using the virus’s natural ability to enter cells; and other methods such as microinjection or gene guns can put DNA directly into cells. Once inside, the host cell’s machinery may read and express the gene, making the protein it codes for (for example insulin), and if the vector also carries a gene for resistance to an antibiotic, only the cells that took up the vector will survive on antibiotic-containing medium — giving a way to select the transformed cells.

17. Microarrays: how they identify active genes

A microarray (DNA microarray) is a small slide or chip carrying thousands of known DNA sequences (probes), each in a known position. Messenger RNA is extracted from two samples (for example, a diseased tissue and a healthy tissue, or cells treated with a drug and untreated cells), converted to cDNA, and labelled with different coloured fluorescent tags (for example green for one sample and red for the other). The labelled cDNA is mixed and allowed to hybridise to the probes on the microarray: if a gene is active (expressed) in a sample, its cDNA will bind (hybridise) to the complementary probe on the chip. By scanning the chip, the colours and intensities can be read: a green spot means the gene is more active in the green-labelled sample, a red spot means more active in the red-labelled sample, yellow means similar activity in both, and the intensity reflects how active the gene is. By looking at all the spots, researchers can see which genes are active (turned on) or inactive (turned off) in a sample and compare activity between samples — for example to see which genes are active in a cancer cell that are not in a normal cell, or to see how a drug changes gene activity. This makes it possible to identify active genes and to use gene activity patterns for diagnosis and to understand disease and drug action.

18. Bioinformatics: what it is and what it is used for

Bioinformatics is the use of computer technology to collect, store, analyse and interpret biological data, especially large datasets such as DNA and protein sequences, gene expression data from microarrays, and protein structures. It depends on the availability of sequence data — the DNA sequences of genomes and the sequences of proteins — and on databases that store and organise these sequences so they can be compared and searched. Bioinformatics is used to compare sequences to find similarities and differences, to identify genes and their functions (for example by comparing a new sequence with known ones to suggest what it does), to study evolutionary relationships (by building phylogenetic trees from sequence comparisons), to predict the structure and function of proteins from their amino acid sequence, and to analyse gene expression patterns from microarrays. It depends on the work of the Human Genome Project and other sequencing projects, and on the computational tools that turn raw sequence data into useful biological knowledge. Bioinformatics is now part of nearly every area of biology — from identifying a gene, to understanding what it does, to finding targets for drugs, to tracing the evolution of a pathogen.

19. Risks and benefits of genetically modified organisms

Genetically modified organisms (GMOs) — plants, animals and microorganisms — have both benefits and risks. Benefits include: in agriculture, crops can be modified to resist pests (for example Bt crops that produce a bacterial toxin harmful to insect pests but not to people) or herbicides, to tolerate drought or salinity, to improve nutrition (for example golden rice producing beta-carotene, a vitamin A precursor), and to increase yield — which can support food security; in medicine, GM bacteria produce human insulin and other proteins for therapy; in research, GM animals and plants are used to study gene function and disease. Risks and concerns include: the possibility that the modified gene could spread to wild relatives or other organisms (gene flow) and have unintended effects; the potential harm to non-target organisms (for example whether Bt crops affect beneficial insects); the development of resistant pests or weeds; the concentration of control of food and seed in a few companies, and the effect on farmers and on traditional varieties; the long-term effects on ecosystems, which are not fully known; and the ethical questions about modifying organisms, especially animals, and about food that has been genetically modified. These must be weighed case by case: the benefits and risks of each GMO depend on what it is, how it is used, and how it is regulated. The scientific evidence about each GMO is needed to evaluate it properly, and the public has a legitimate role in the decisions because the issues are not only scientific — they include values, economics and the environment.

20. Plant responses: phytochrome, auxin, gibberellins and Core Practical 18

Plants coordinate responses without a nervous system, using pigments and hormones that change gene expression. Phytochrome is a pigment that exists in two interconvertible forms. Red light at about 660 nm converts the inactive form, Pr, into the active form, Pfr; far-red light at about 730 nm converts Pfr back to Pr, and in darkness Pfr slowly reverts. Because daylight is rich in red light, Pfr accumulates during the day, so the ratio of Pfr to Pr tells the plant whether it is in light or shade and how long the night is. Pfr acts as a transcription factor: it enters the nucleus and switches on genes, for example for germination in lettuce seeds or for flowering in long-day plants. A brief flash of red light is enough to trigger germination, and a flash of far-red light immediately afterwards cancels it, which is the classic experimental evidence that phytochrome is the receptor.

Auxin, principally indoleacetic acid or IAA, is made in the shoot tip and moves down the stem. It is transported polarly, from cell to cell, and it accumulates on the shaded side of a shoot in phototropism and on the lower side of a root or shoot in gravitropism. In the shoot, a higher auxin concentration stimulates cell elongation, so the shaded side grows faster and the shoot bends towards the light. In the root the same concentration inhibits elongation, which is why a root bends downwards. Auxin works by binding a receptor that triggers the destruction of repressor proteins, so transcription factors are released and genes for wall-loosening enzymes are transcribed, allowing the cell wall to stretch.

Gibberellins promote stem elongation, seed germination and the transition to flowering. In a germinating cereal grain the embryo releases gibberellin, which diffuses to the aleurone layer and switches on transcription of the gene for amylase. The amylase is secreted into the endosperm, where it hydrolyses starch to maltose, which the embryo respires. Core Practical 18 investigates exactly this: sterilise and soak cereal grains, place them on starch agar with and without gibberellin, leave them to incubate, then flood the plate with iodine solution. Clear zones around the treated grains show that amylase has broken down the starch, and measuring or comparing the zones shows that gibberellin has induced the enzyme.

21. How to use this note and what to revise next

Use these notes by working through each section and checking that you can: describe the structure of sensory, relay and motor neurones; describe the spinal reflex arc, including the roles of grey and white matter; explain how the action potential is generated, including depolarisation, repolarisation, hyperpolarisation, the role of sodium and potassium ions and the sodium–potassium pump, and the all-or-nothing principle; explain how myelination allows saltatory conduction and speeds it up; describe the cholinergic synapse and the roles of calcium, acetylcholine, receptors, acetylcholinesterase; explain the pupillary reflex (circular muscles constrict in bright light, radial muscles dilate in dim); describe how nicotine, lidocaine, cobra venom alpha toxin, L-DOPA and MDMA affect nerve impulse transmission, including examples; describe how rod cells detect light, the role of rhodopsin, opsin, retinal, sodium channels and hyperpolarisation, and how this leads to action potentials in the optic neurone; describe habituation and the evidence for it (the snail withdrawal practical); describe the central and peripheral nervous systems and the sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions; locate and state the functions of the cerebral hemispheres, hypothalamus, pituitary gland, cerebellum and medulla oblongata; explain how MRI, fMRI, PET and CT work and what they are used for; explain the role of dopamine in Parkinson’s disease and serotonin in depression and how the drugs work; describe the production of drugs using GMOs (human insulin as the example); describe how recombinant DNA is made with restriction enzymes and DNA ligase and inserted into cells; describe how microarrays work and what they show; define bioinformatics; and discuss the risks and benefits of GMOs. After this topic, revise the rest of this unit and the related practicals, and the Biology practicals (Core Practicals 14–18) which reinforce these topics.

Worked example: reading an action potential trace

Two electrodes on a giant axon are 30 mm apart. The trace shows an action potential arriving at the first electrode, and the same potential arriving at the second 1.5 ms later. Conduction velocity is distance divided by time, so the answer is 0.030 m divided by 0.0015 s = 20 m per second. Convert millimetres to metres and milliseconds to seconds before dividing, and give the unit, because the mark is for the calculation and the unit together. Written as a relation: v = d / t = 0.030 m / 0.0015 s = 20 m s⁻¹ Key: v = conduction velocity (m s⁻¹); d = distance between the two electrodes (m); t = time between the two arrivals (s).

The same trace gives information about the refractory period. If the axon cannot fire again for 5 ms after each impulse, the maximum frequency is 1 divided by 0.005 s = 200 impulses per second. That limit, not the size of the stimulus, is why a stronger stimulus cannot raise the frequency indefinitely: the all-or-nothing law means a bigger stimulus does not make a bigger impulse, it can only make more impulses or recruit more axons. Written as a relation: f = 1 / T = 1 / 0.005 s = 200 Hz Key: f = maximum frequency of impulses (Hz, impulses per second); T = refractory period (s), the shortest gap the axon can manage between impulses; 1/T = the reciprocal of that gap, which is the frequency.

Drugs and nerve transmission, compared

SubstanceSite of actionEffect
NicotineBinds nicotinic acetylcholine receptors on the postsynaptic membraneMimics acetylcholine, so the postsynaptic membrane depolarises; prolonged exposure desensitises the receptor
LidocaineBlocks voltage-gated sodium channels in the axon membraneNo sodium influx means no depolarisation, so no impulse is generated and the area is anaesthetised
Cobra venom alpha toxinBinds nicotinic acetylcholine receptors and blocks themAcetylcholine cannot bind, the postsynaptic membrane is not depolarised, and paralysis follows
L-DOPACrosses the blood-brain barrier and is converted to dopamineReplaces the dopamine that is missing in Parkinson's disease, improving movement control
MDMAIncreases the release of serotonin and blocks its reuptake at synapses in the brainProlongs serotonin signalling, altering mood and perception and raising body temperature

Typical mistakes

  • Making the action potential bigger with a bigger stimulus. The impulse is all-or-nothing; a stronger stimulus increases the frequency of impulses or the number of neurones firing, not the amplitude.
  • Describing depolarisation as potassium leaving the axon. Depolarisation is sodium ions entering through voltage-gated sodium channels. Repolarisation is potassium ions leaving, and the sodium-potassium pump restores the resting distribution afterwards.
  • Saying saltatory conduction is faster because the impulse jumps "through" the myelin. The myelin is an insulator, so the local circuits skip from one node of Ranvier to the next, where the channels are, which is why the impulse travels faster in a myelinated axon.
  • Treating habituation as fatigue. Habituation is a learned decrease in response to a repeated harmless stimulus, as in the snail withdrawal response; the sensory and motor pathways still work, which is why a novel stimulus still produces a response.
  • Using "MRI" for everything. MRI shows structure from the behaviour of hydrogen nuclei in a magnetic field; fMRI shows activity through changes in blood oxygenation; PET shows metabolic activity using a radioactive tracer such as labelled glucose; CT uses X-rays and shows dense tissue such as bone.
  • Explaining a drug's effect without naming the protein or the ion. Say whether it mimics or blocks a receptor, or blocks a channel, and then say what that does to the postsynaptic membrane potential.
  • Confusing nervous and hormonal coordination. Nervous control is electrical along neurones and chemical across synapses, so it is fast, short-lived and targeted. Hormonal control travels in the blood, so it is slower, longer-lasting and widespread.

Exam-style questions

  1. Explain how the myelin sheath increases the speed of conduction. Answer: myelin is a lipid insulator wrapped by Schwann cells, so the membrane cannot depolarise where it is covered. The local circuit current therefore travels from one node of Ranvier to the next, where voltage-gated sodium channels are concentrated, and the impulse is regenerated at each node rather than continuously. This saltatory conduction is faster than conduction in an unmyelinated axon of the same diameter.
  2. Describe the sequence of events at a cholinergic synapse. Answer: the arrival of an action potential depolarises the presynaptic membrane, which opens calcium channels; calcium ions enter and cause vesicles to fuse with the presynaptic membrane and release acetylcholine into the cleft; acetylcholine binds receptors on the postsynaptic membrane, which opens sodium channels and depolarises it; acetylcholinesterase then hydrolyses acetylcholine so the signal ends and the synapse can transmit again.
  3. Explain how a rod cell signals the presence of light. Answer: light is absorbed by rhodopsin, which is retinal bound to opsin. The retinal changes shape, opsin is activated and triggers a cascade that breaks down a messenger molecule, so sodium channels close. Sodium ions stop entering, the cell hyperpolarises, and less neurotransmitter is released, which alters the rate of action potentials in the optic neurone. Rod cells therefore signal light by switching off rather than switching on.
  4. Explain how L-DOPA relieves the symptoms of Parkinson's disease but dopamine itself does not. Answer: dopamine cannot cross the blood-brain barrier, so taken as a drug it does not reach the brain. L-DOPA is its precursor, crosses the barrier using amino acid transporters, and is converted to dopamine by enzymes in the brain, replacing the dopamine that the substantia nigra no longer supplies.
  5. Explain how recombinant DNA is made and inserted into a bacterium. Answer: a restriction endonuclease cuts the gene out of the donor DNA at specific recognition sites, leaving sticky ends; the same enzyme cuts a plasmid vector, giving complementary sticky ends; DNA ligase joins the gene into the plasmid by forming phosphodiester bonds; the recombinant plasmid is inserted into a bacterium, for example by heat shock or electroporation, and the bacterium is selected, often with an antibiotic resistance marker, then grown to produce the protein.
  6. Explain what a microarray shows and why it is useful. Answer: a microarray carries many known DNA probes fixed in a grid. Labelled cDNA made from the mRNA of a sample hybridises to the probes it matches, and the pattern and intensity of the signal show which genes are being transcribed. It therefore compares gene expression between samples, such as healthy and tumour tissue, without testing genes one at a time.
  7. Give two benefits and two risks of using genetically modified organisms, and explain why the answer depends on the GMO. Answer: benefits could include higher yield or reduced pesticide use, and production of human insulin without the risk of animal-derived contamination. Risks could include genes spreading to wild relatives and long-term effects on ecosystems. Each assessment depends on which organism is modified, which gene is inserted and how it is regulated, because a crop modified for drought tolerance is not the same case as a modified animal.

The refractory period and why impulses travel one way

An action potential is a brief reversal of the membrane potential. At rest the inside of the axon is about −70 mV, maintained by the sodium–potassium pump, which moves three sodium ions out for every two potassium ions moved in. A stimulus that brings the membrane to threshold opens voltage-gated sodium channels, and the potential rises to about +40 mV before the channels close and potassium channels open to restore it.

Key: membrane potential is measured in millivolts (mV); time is in milliseconds (ms); threshold is the potential at which the all-or-nothing response is triggered.

The all-or-nothing response

Below threshold nothing happens. Once threshold is reached, the full action potential follows, whatever the size of the stimulus. A stronger stimulus does not make a bigger impulse; it makes more neurones fire, or fires them more often, which is how the nervous system codes the intensity of a stimulus.

The refractory period

After the peak, the sodium channels are inactivated and cannot be opened again until the membrane has returned close to its resting potential. During this refractory period no second action potential can start in that region of the axon. Because the region just behind the impulse is refractory, the impulse cannot travel backwards, and it moves in one direction along the axon.

Why the refractory period matters

The refractory period limits how often a neurone can fire, which sets its maximum frequency, and it ensures that each impulse is separate from the one before. In an answer, link the one-way movement to the refractory region behind the impulse, and do not describe it as the membrane being unable to "rest".

title: Exam technique: Differentiation
content:
### What earns the marks
For differentiation, every term handled earns credit: show each power lowered. For stationary points, setting dy/dx = 0 earns one mark and the second-derivative (or sign) test earns the next. For always-increasing proofs, the discriminant shown negative with positive leading coefficient earns both marks.
### Traps
Error: constants surviving differentiation. Correction: constants vanish. Error: tangent gradient used for normals. Correction: negative reciprocal first. Error: claiming increase without the discriminant. Correction: no roots plus positive shape proves it.

title: Circular Motion and SHM
content:
Circular Motion and SHM

Circular Motion Recap

Angular speed ω = 2π/T; v = ωr; a = ω²r = v²/r; F = mv²/r toward the centre.

Simple Harmonic Motion

Acceleration is proportional to displacement and opposite: a = −ω²x.

Solutions: x = x₀ sin ωt (start at centre) or x = x₀ cos ωt (start at extreme), with ω = 2πf.

Velocity and acceleration:

  • v_max = ωx₀ at the centre
  • a_max = ω²x₀ at the extremes

Example: a pendulum with x₀ = 0.02 m, f = 0.5 Hz has a_max = (2π × 0.5)² × 0.02 ≈ 0.20 m s⁻².

Energy in SHM

E = ½mω²x₀² total (constant), exchanged between KE (max at centre) and PE (max at extremes).

Damping and Resonance

Damping removes energy: light damping → slow decay; critical → fastest return without oscillation. Resonance: driving at the natural frequency gives maximum amplitude (microwave ovens, swing pushing, bridge disasters).

Exam tips: quote a = −ω²x as the defining condition; time period questions often need only T = 2π/ω.

title: Earth & Space — Study Notes
content:
Earth & Space

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2023–2025): Earth & Solar System; stars & the Universe (Extended).

1. Earth, Moon, Sun

Earth rotates 24 h (day/night), orbits 365¼ d (year + leap). Moon orbits Earth ~27.3 d; phases from viewing angle; lunar/solar eclipses when aligned. Seasons from axial tilt (23.5°), not distance.

2. Solar system

Planets (Mercury → Neptune), dwarf planets (Pluto), moons, asteroids, comets (eccentric orbits, tails away from Sun), natural satellites. Gravity keeps orbits; orbital speed & radius relate to the central mass.

3. Orbital motion

Orbital speed v = 2πr/T. T grows with r (Kepler trend). Comets speed up near the Sun (ellipse, Sun at focus).

4. Stars (Extended)

Star formation: nebula → protostar (gravity, KE→thermal) → main sequence (hydrogen fusion: H→He, radiation pressure balances gravity) → red giant → white dwarf (Sun-mass) or supergiant → supernova → neutron star/black hole (massive stars). Elements heavier than iron form in supernovae.

5. Universe (Extended)

The Sun is one star in the Milky Way; the Milky Way is one of billions of galaxies. Redshift: receding galaxies show stretched wavelengths → the Universe is expanding → Big Bang model; CMB is the afterglow. Hubble: farther ⇒ faster recession.

6. Scales

light-year = distance light travels in a year (9.5 × 10¹⁵ m); astronomical unit = Earth–Sun distance (1.5 × 10¹¹ m).

Quick revision: Number — Indices and Standard Form

Mathematics — OL. index laws, negative and fractional indices, standard form arithmetic, surds.

  • 1. Index laws
