  • 4. Solving index equations
  • 5. Surds

How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

Key points to remember

The index laws let you combine powers: multiply by adding indices, divide by subtracting them, and raise a power to another power by multiplying. A zero index gives 1, and a negative index means the reciprocal. A fractional index such as one half means the square root.

Standard form writes a number as A times 10 to the power n, where A is at least 1 and less than 10. A large number has a positive power and a small number a negative one. Count how far the decimal point moves to find n, and check that A lies between 1 and 10 before you finish.

title: Programming Paradigms and Low-Level — Study Notes
content:
Programming Paradigms and Low-Level

Paradigms

  • Procedural: programs as sequences of instructions in procedures — good for straightforward algorithms.
  • Object-oriented: classes encapsulate state (attributes) and behaviour (methods); supports encapsulation, inheritance and polymorphism.
  • Declarative: state what is required, not how (SQL queries, logic programming).
  • Low-level: assembly maps closely to machine code; used where hardware control or timing precision is needed.

Assembly Essentials

The opcode names the operation (LDM load, STR store, ADD, CMP compare, JMP branch, IN/OUT for I/O). The operand names the data. The assembler translates mnemonics to machine code one-to-one; two-pass assemblers resolve forward references via the symbol table.

Addressing Modes

  • Immediate: operand is the constant itself, ADD #5.
  • Direct: operand is the memory address of the data.
  • Indirect: operand is the address OF the address; one extra memory read.
  • Indexed: effective address = base + index register; ideal for arrays.
  • Relative: address given as an offset from the program counter; enables position-independent code.

Fetch-Execute

Fetch: PC gives address, instruction loads into the CIR, PC increments. Decode: control unit interprets the opcode. Execute: the operation runs, possibly updating registers or memory. Interrupts are checked at cycle boundaries.

Exam tips: trace short assembly programs register by register; compute effective addresses for each addressing mode; state one advantage of OOP for large systems.

Programming paradigms

An imperative paradigm describes how to do a task as a sequence of statements that change state. An object-oriented paradigm groups data and the methods that act on it into classes. A declarative paradigm states the result wanted and leaves the method to the system, as in SQL.

Exception handling

An exception is a run-time error such as a missing file or a division by zero. A try block runs the risky code, and a catch (or except) block handles the exception so the program can recover rather than crash.

Exam tip: name the paradigm and give one feature that shows it, such as classes for object-oriented programming.

title: IGCSE Biology: Transport in Animals
content:
IGCSE Biology: Transport in Animals

Your body contains about 5 litres of blood travelling through roughly 100 000 km of vessels, driven by a pump the size of your fist that beats around 100 000 times a day. This note builds the circulatory system from first principles: why large animals need a double circulation, how the heart is wired (with every chamber, valve and vessel named and the blood path traced through it), how arteries, veins and capillaries are each built for their job, what blood is made of and what each component does, and how coronary heart disease develops and is prevented. The heart-cycle sequence is expanded beat by beat so you can follow the pressure changes rather than memorise a diagram.

Single and double circulations

Small organisms rely on diffusion alone; larger animals need a mass-transport system. A single circulation (fish): blood passes through the heart once per circuit — heart → gills → body → heart. Gas exchange at the gills drops the pressure, so flow to the body is slow; a double circulation solves this. A double circulation (mammals, birds): blood passes through the heart twice per full circuit. The right side pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs (pulmonary circulation); oxygenated blood returns to the left side, which pumps it at high pressure around the body (systemic circulation). Advantage: blood pressure is restored after the lungs, so oxygen reaches tissues fast; and the two circuits can operate at different pressures (low in the delicate lungs, high for the body). An open circulation (insects) bathes organs directly in haemolymph; a closed circulation keeps blood in vessels at all times — the mammalian system is closed.

Heart structure and the double circulation

The heart has four chambers: two thin-walled atria (singular: atrium) that receive blood, and two thick-walled ventricles that pump it out. The right atrium receives deoxygenated blood from the vena cava; the right ventricle pumps it to the lungs via the pulmonary artery. The left atrium receives oxygenated blood from the pulmonary veins; the left ventricle pumps it to the whole body via the aorta — its wall is thickest because it generates the highest pressure. Four valves ensure one-way flow: the atrioventricular valves (tricuspid on the right, bicuspid/mitral on the left) between atria and ventricles, and the semilunar valves at the base of the pulmonary artery and aorta. Valves open when pressure behind them exceeds pressure ahead, and close to prevent backflow — the "lub" of the heartbeat is the atrioventricular valves closing; the "dub" is the semilunar valves closing. Coronary arteries wrap over the heart muscle itself and deliver oxygenated blood to the cardiac muscle, which cannot absorb oxygen from the blood inside its chambers.

The cardiac cycle, step by step

Step 1 — atrial systole: the atria contract, pushing the last of the blood into the ventricles (atrioventricular valves open; semilunar valves closed). Step 2 — ventricular systole: the ventricles contract, pressure rises above the atria (atrioventricular valves slam shut — "lub"), blood is ejected into the pulmonary artery and aorta (semilunar valves forced open). Step 3 — diastole: the ventricles relax, pressure drops below that in the arteries (semilunar valves snap shut — "dub"), blood fills the atria again from the veins, and the cycle repeats. Duration: about 0.8 s at rest (0.1 s atrial systole, 0.3 s ventricular systole, 0.4 s diastole). During exercise the cycle shortens (more beats per minute) and stroke volume rises, so cardiac output (heart rate × stroke volume) increases to deliver more oxygen.

Blood vessels: structure fits function

VesselWallLumenSpecial featuresFunction
ArteryThick, muscular, elasticNarrowElastic recoil smooths pressure pulsesCarries blood at high pressure away from the heart
ArterioleMuscularNarrowSmooth muscle contracts/relaxes to control flowDiverts blood to active organs
CapillaryOne cell thick (endothelium)Very narrow (one cell wide)Huge total surface area, slow flowExchange of gases, nutrients and wastes with tissue fluid
VeinThin, less muscle/elasticWideValves prevent backflowReturns blood at low pressure to the heart

Artery walls are thick and elastic to withstand and smooth the pulsing pressure (elastic recoil maintains flow between beats); veins have valves and rely on skeletal muscle contraction to squeeze blood back against gravity. Capillaries are exactly one cell thick so the diffusion distance is minimal, and their slow flow gives time for exchange — structure and function matched at every level.

Blood: plasma, cells and their roles

Plasma is the straw-coloured liquid: about 55 % of blood volume; it carries water, dissolved glucose, amino acids, fatty acids, glycerol, hormones, carbon dioxide (as hydrogencarbonate ions), urea, plasma proteins (fibrinogen for clotting, albumin for osmotic balance), and antibodies. Red blood cells (erythrocytes): biconcave discs with no nucleus and packed haemoglobin; haemoglobin binds oxygen at high partial pressure in the lungs and releases it at low partial pressure in the tissues (oxyhaemoglobin ↔ haemoglobin + oxygen). White blood cells (leucocytes): part of immunity — phagocytes engulf pathogens; lymphocytes produce antibodies and antitoxins. Platelets (cell fragments): clotting — they stick to a wound, trap red cells and activate fibrinogen → fibrin threads, forming a scab that seals the vessel and blocks pathogen entry. Tissue fluid: plasma minus large proteins, formed at the arteriole end of capillaries where pressure forces it out; most is reabsorbed at the venule end; excess drains into the lymphatic system.

Coronary heart disease

The coronary arteries supply the heart muscle itself. Coronary heart disease develops when fatty deposits (atheroma/cholesterol plaques) build up in the artery walls, narrowing the lumen and restricting blood flow; the muscle is starved of oxygen and glucose, causing angina (chest pain on exertion) and, if a coronary artery blocks completely (a thrombus/clot), a myocardial infarction — heart attack — and muscle death. Risk factors: diet high in saturated fat and salt, smoking (carbon monoxide reduces oxygen-carrying capacity; nicotine raises heart rate and constricts vessels), obesity, stress, lack of exercise, alcohol, age, and inherited family history. Prevention and treatment: a balanced diet low in saturated fat, regular exercise, not smoking, statins (lower cholesterol), anticoagulants (aspirin/warfarin), angioplasty (balloon to widen the artery, often with a stent), and coronary bypass surgery (grafting a vessel to detour the blockage). The exam wants risk factor linked to mechanism — not just a list.

Worked example: cardiac output calculation and reading a heart diagram

At rest a person has a heart rate of 70 beats per minute and a stroke volume of 70 cm³. Step 1: cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume = 70 × 70 = 4900 cm³ per minute = 4.9 dm³/min ≈ the whole blood volume circulated each minute. Step 2: during exercise, rate rises to 150 and stroke volume to 110: output = 150 × 110 = 16 500 cm³/min — 3.4 times the resting output. Step 3: explain the benefit: more oxygen and glucose delivered to muscles per minute, more carbon dioxide removed, so respiration rate can stay high. Diagram-reading practice: trace one drop of blood — vena cava → right atrium → (tricuspid valve) → right ventricle → (semilunar valve) → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary veins → left atrium → (bicuspid valve) → left ventricle → (semilunar valve) → aorta → body. Name the valves in order and you answer almost any "trace the path" question for full marks.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Saying arteries "carry oxygenated blood": the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood; arteries carry blood away from the heart, whatever its oxygen content.
  • Confusing atrium and ventricle roles: atria receive; ventricles pump.
  • Explaining the left ventricle's thick wall as "it is bigger" — the answer is higher pressure needed for the systemic circulation.
  • Forgetting the coronary arteries in a heart-structure question — they are often the last mark.
  • Describing blood flow in veins as due to "suction" or gravity alone; mention valves and skeletal muscle contraction.
  • Writing that platelets "carry oxygen": they clot blood; red blood cells carry oxygen.
  • Listing heart-disease risk factors without explaining the mechanism (e.g. saturated fat raises blood cholesterol which deposits in artery walls).
  • In valve questions, writing "valves stop the blood going back" without the pressure context: they open forward when pressure behind them is higher and close to prevent backflow.

Exam-style questions and answers

Q1. Describe the route of blood through the heart, naming the chambers and vessels. (4 marks) Answer: vena cava to right atrium (1); to right ventricle and out via the pulmonary artery to the lungs (1); pulmonary veins to left atrium (1); to left ventricle and out via the aorta to the body (1).

Q2. Explain why the wall of the left ventricle is thicker than that of the right. (2 marks) Answer: it pumps blood at higher pressure to the whole body (1), while the right ventricle only pumps to the nearby lungs at lower pressure (1).

Q3. Compare the structure of an artery and a vein. (4 marks) Answer: artery has thicker muscular/elastic wall, vein thinner (1); artery narrower lumen, vein wider (1); veins have valves, arteries generally do not (1); arteries carry blood under high pressure from the heart, veins return it at low pressure (1).

Q4. Explain how a diet high in saturated fat can lead to a heart attack. (3 marks) Answer: raises blood cholesterol (1); fatty deposits build up in coronary artery walls narrowing the lumen (1); a clot can block the vessel completely, starving the muscle of oxygen (1).

Q5. Describe the role of platelets and plasma in blood clotting. (3 marks) Answer: platelets stick to the damaged vessel wall and release clotting factors (1); fibrinogen is converted to fibrin threads (1); the mesh traps red blood cells forming a scab; plasma carries the fibrinogen and other clotting proteins (1).

title: Geometry — Angles and Polygons — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Geometry — Angles and Polygons

Mathematics — OL. angle facts, parallel lines, polygon angles, circle theorems (Extended).

  • 1. Core angle facts
  • 2. Polygons
  • 3. Circle theorems (Extended)
  • 4. Algebra with angles

How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

Worked example

The interior angle sum of a polygon with n sides is (n − 2) × 180°. For a regular octagon, n = 8, so the sum is 6 × 180° = 1080°. Each interior angle is 1080 ÷ 8 = 135°, and each exterior angle is 360 ÷ 8 = 45°. Exterior angles of any convex polygon always add up to 360°.

Common mistakes

  • Using 360° for the interior sum instead of (n − 2) × 180°.
  • Confusing the angle at the centre with the angle at the circumference. The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference when both subtend the same arc.
  • Writing a reason without naming the theorem. Name it, for example "angles in the same segment" or "opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180°".

Worked example

The interior angle sum of a polygon with n sides is (n − 2) × 180°. For a regular octagon, n = 8, so the sum is 6 × 180° = 1080°. Each interior angle is 1080 ÷ 8 = 135°, and each exterior angle is 360 ÷ 8 = 45°. Exterior angles of any convex polygon always add up to 360°.

Common mistakes

  • Using 360° for the interior sum instead of (n − 2) × 180°.
  • Confusing the angle at the centre with the angle at the circumference. The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference when both subtend the same arc.
  • Writing a reason without naming the theorem. Name it, for example "angles in the same segment" or "opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180°".

title: System Software and Security
content:
`# System Software and Security

Operating System Roles

  • Manage memory (paging/segmentation, virtual memory to disk)
  • Schedule processes (round robin, priorities)
  • Handle I/O via device drivers and spooling
  • Provide the UI, file systems, and security (users, permissions)

Translators

  • Assembler: assembly → machine code (1:1)
  • Compiler: whole source → machine code, reports all errors, produces standalone executables
  • Interpreter: line-by-line execution, stops at first error, needs the interpreter present

Bytecode + VM (e.g. Java) combines both: compile once, run anywhere the VM exists.

Linkers and Loaders

Static linking copies library code into the executable; dynamic linking binds at runtime (smaller files, shared libraries). The loader places the program in memory, relocating addresses.

IDEs

Editors with syntax highlighting, autocompletion, debugger (breakpoints, stepping, variable watch), and integrated compilation.

Malware and Defences

Viruses, worms, trojans, spyware, phishing. Defences: antivirus (signature + heuristic scanning), firewalls (packet filtering by port/IP), sandboxing, user education, patches.

Exam tips: compare compiler vs interpreter with concrete error-handling differences; explain firewall rules using ports and addresses.

title: A Level Physics: Further Mechanics
content:
A Level Physics: Further Mechanics

Newton's cradle is the whole topic in one toy: a ball arrives, a ball leaves at the same speed, and something invisible has been conserved through the collision. That something is momentum — mass times velocity — and with impulse and energy it lets you analyse every collision, explosion and crash the papers can invent. This note builds the mechanics from zero: the momentum vector and its conservation, impulse as the area under a force–time graph and the physics of why cars crumple, elastic and inelastic collisions with full energy bookkeeping, and the standard problem types solved line by line.

Momentum and its conservation

momentum p = m v        (kg m s⁻¹; a vector)

conservation: in the absence of external forces, the total
momentum of a system stays constant:
  m¹ u1 + m² u2 = m¹ v1 + m² v2

Velocity is a vector, so momentum carries direction: assign positive and negative directions before writing any equation. The conservation law follows from Newton's third law — the forces two bodies exert on each other are equal and opposite for equal times, so the impulses are equal and opposite, so the momentum changes cancel.

Worked example. A 2.0 kg trolley moving at 3.0 m s⁻¹ collides with a stationary 1.0 kg trolley; they stick together. Find the common velocity.

before: 2.0 × 3.0 + 1.0 × 0 = 6.0 kg m s⁻¹
after:  (2.0 + 1.0) v = 3.0 v
3.0 v = 6.0  →  v = 2.0 m s⁻¹ (same direction)

Impulse

impulse = force x time = change in momentum
J = F Δt = Δp = m v - m u

on a force-time graph: impulse = area under the graph

The analogy: catching a ball. A hard catch (short time) means a huge force; moving your hands back (longer time) spreads the same momentum change over more time and reduces the force. That is the entire physics of crumple zones, airbags, seatbelts, helmets, landing mats and bending your knees when you jump down.

Worked example. A 0.16 kg cricket ball arrives at 30 m s⁻¹ and is struck back at 45 m s⁻¹; contact lasts 12 ms. Find the impulse and the average force.

take the incoming direction as negative:
u = -30, v = +45
Δp = m(v - u) = 0.16 x (45 - (-30)) = 0.16 × 75
        = 12 kg m s⁻¹
F = Δp/Δt = 12/0.012 = 10⁰⁰ N = 1.0 kN

Worked example (graph). A force-time graph shows a triangular pulse rising to 800 N over 0.050 s and falling to zero over the next 0.050 s. Find the impulse and the speed change of a 2.0 kg object.

area = (1/2) x base x height = 0.5 × 0.10 × 800 = 40 N s
Δp = 40 kg m s⁻¹  →  Δv = 40/2.0 = 20 m s⁻¹

Elastic and inelastic collisions

Momentum is conserved in every collision (absent external forces); kinetic energy is conserved only in elastic ones:

ElasticInelastic
Momentumconservedconserved
Kinetic energyconservednot conserved — some becomes heat, sound, deformation
Typical examplegas molecules, billiard-ball idealisationcars sticking together, clay, crumple zones

Explosions run the same conservation law backwards: total momentum before is zero, so the fragments' momenta must cancel.

Worked example (explosion). A 0.50 kg firework at rest explodes into two pieces; the 0.30 kg piece flies at 12 m s⁻¹. Find the velocity of the other piece.

0 = 0.30 × 12 + 0.20 v
0.20 v = -3.6  →  v = -18 m s⁻¹
The 0.20 kg piece moves at 18 m s⁻¹ in the opposite direction.

Worked examples: the full audit

Worked example. A 1500 kg car at 20 m s⁻¹ crashes into a stationary 1000 kg car; they lock together. Find the velocity after impact, the kinetic energy lost, and explain where it went.

momentum: 1500 × 20 = 2500 v  →  v = 12 m s⁻¹
KE before = (1/2) × 1500 × 400 = 300 000 J
KE after  = (1/2) × 2500 × 144 = 180 000 J
lost = 120 000 J = 120 kJ
The energy goes to deformation of the bodies, heat, and sound.

Worked example 2 (elastic check). Two identical trolleys approach each other at 2.0 m s⁻¹ and bounce back at 2.0 m s⁻¹ each. Show the collision is elastic.

momentum before: m(2) + m(-2) = 0; after: m(-2) + m(2) = 0
KE before = (1/2)m(4) + (1/2)m(4) = 4m
KE after  = 4m  - unchanged, so elastic.

Momentum in two dimensions

Momentum is conserved separately in each perpendicular direction. For a collision that is not head-on, resolve the momenta into x and y components before and after, and set up two conservation equations. The geometry is where the marks are: a ball striking a wall at an angle rebounds with its perpendicular component reversed and its parallel component unchanged (for a smooth wall), which is why the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence in the ideal case.

before: p_x = m u cos(θ),  p_y = m u sin(θ)
after a smooth-wall bounce:
  p_x = -m v cos(θ)  (normal component reversed)
  p_y = +m v sin(θ)  (parallel component unchanged)
  |Δp| = 2 m v cos(θ)

Worked example. A 0.20 kg ball hits a smooth wall at 12 m s⁻¹ at 30° to the normal and rebounds elastically at the same speed and angle. Find the impulse on the ball.

Δp = 2 m v cos(θ) = 2 × 0.20 × 12 x cos(30)
        = 4.8 × 0.866 = 4.2 kg m s⁻¹
(directed away from the wall)

Explosions, recoil and rockets

An explosion is a collision reversed: total momentum stays at its initial value (usually zero), so the fragments' momenta must cancel. Recoil problems — a gun, a skateboarder pushing off, an astronaut throwing a tool — are all this one equation. A rocket is the continuous version: it expels gas backward at high speed and gains forward momentum, and it works in a vacuum precisely because it pushes against its own exhaust, not against the air.

recoil: 0 = m¹ v1 + m² v2   →   v2 = -(m¹/m²) v1
rocket thrust: F = (rate of change of momentum of the exhaust)
             = (mass per second) x (exhaust speed)

Worked example. A 4.0 kg rifle fires a 0.020 kg bullet at 400 m s⁻¹. Find the rifle's recoil speed.

0 = 0.020 × 400 + 4.0 v
4.0 v = -8.0  →  v = -2.0 m s⁻¹
The rifle recoils at 2.0 m s⁻¹ opposite to the bullet.

Forces, momentum and safety engineering

Questions about safety devices are impulse questions in disguise: the momentum change is fixed by the crash, so the only variable is time. A seatbelt extends the stopping time, so F = Δp/Δt falls; a crumple zone does the same by deforming; an airbag spreads the force over area as well. When asked to evaluate a design, quantify: if the stopping time triples, the average force falls to a third.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Momentum) Define momentum and state its unit. Answer: Momentum is the product of mass and velocity, p = mv, a vector; unit kg m s⁻¹ (equivalently N s).
  2. (Conservation) A 3.0 kg block at 4.0 m s⁻¹ hits a stationary 1.0 kg block and they move together. Find the final speed. Answer: 3.0 × 4.0 = 4.0v → v = 3.0 m s⁻¹.
  3. (Impulse) A 0.50 kg ball hits a wall at 8.0 m s⁻¹ and rebounds at 6.0 m s⁻¹; contact time 0.020 s. Find the average force. Answer: Δp = 0.50 × (6.0 + 8.0) = 7.0 kg m s⁻¹; F = 7.0/0.020 = 350 N.
  4. (Graph) Explain how to find impulse from a force–time graph. Answer: Impulse is the area under the graph; for a curve, count squares or integrate.
  5. (Elasticity) A collision conserves momentum but not kinetic energy. Classify it and name a real example. Answer: Inelastic; a car crash or two lumps of clay sticking together.
  6. (Explosion) A 60 kg astronaut pushes off a 400 kg spacecraft, moving at 0.50 m s⁻¹ relative to it. Find the spacecraft's recoil speed. Answer: 60 × 0.50 = 400 × v → v = 0.075 m s⁻¹ (opposite direction).
  7. (Safety) Explain how a crumple zone reduces injury. Answer: It deforms, increasing the collision time for a given momentum change; since F = Δp/Δt, the average force falls, reducing injury.
  8. (Energy) In an inelastic collision, where does the lost kinetic energy go? Answer: Into thermal energy, sound and permanent deformation of the materials — energy is conserved overall, but not as kinetic energy.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Dropping signs: momentum is a vector; a rebound reverses sign. The classic error is Δp = m(v − u) with both speeds positive, halving the true impulse.
  • Adding speeds wrongly: for a rebound, the change is v + u in magnitude (with signs, v − (−u)).
  • Assuming KE is conserved: check the type; "they stick together" is always inelastic. Compute KE before and after when asked.
  • External forces: conservation needs no net external force — a collision on a rough surface during a long interval is not the same as an instantaneous impact.
  • Unit of impulse: N s or kg m s⁻¹ are equivalent; force alone (N) is not.
  • Force–time areas: triangles and trapeziums need the correct geometric factors (½ for a triangle), not base × height.
  • Mass in grams: convert to kg before momentum calculations; a factor of 1000 error is common in cricket-ball questions.
  • Precision: 2 or 3 s.f. with units; keep direction words (opposite, same direction) in the answer.

title: Magnetism & Electromagnetism — Study Notes
content:
Magnetism & Electromagnetism

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): magnets & fields; magnetic effect of a current; force on a current-carrying conductor; motor effect; electromagnetic induction (Extended); transformers (Extended).

1. Magnets and fields

Iron/steel/cobalt/nickel; like poles repel. Field lines exit N, enter S; compass plotting; plotting compass aligns with field. Induced magnetism: iron (temporary) vs steel (permanent).

2. Electromagnets

Solenoid field like a bar magnet; strength ↑ with current, turns, iron core. Uses: relays, scrapyard crane, electric bell, speaker. Hard/soft magnetic materials choose permanent vs core use.

3. Force on a current-carrying conductor

F = BIL, direction by Fleming's left hand (fIeld, current, force). Reversing current or field reverses force. D.C. motor: coil, commutator reverses current each half-turn for continuous rotation; speed/torque ↑ with current, field strength, turns/area.

4. Electromagnetic induction (Extended)

Induced e.m.f. when a conductor cuts field lines or flux changes. Fleming's right hand (generator). Factors: speed, field strength, turns. A.C. generator: slip rings; dynamo effect; Lenz's law opposes change (direction of induced current).

5. Transformers (Extended)

Vp/Vs = Np/Ns; Pin ≈ Pout (100% assumed): IpVp = IsVs. Step-up raises V, lowers I → lower I²R transmission losses; a.c. required (changing flux).

title: The Normal Distribution — Study Notes
content:
The Normal Distribution

The Model

A continuous distribution with the familiar bell shape, symmetric about the mean, described by two parameters: X ~ N(μ, σ²). The curve is fully determined by μ (centre) and σ (width). Total probability is 1, and because X is continuous, P(X = a) = 0 for any single point — inequalities do not need strictness.

Standardising

Convert any normal variable to the standard normal Z ~ N(0, 1) with

  • Z = (X − μ)/σ

Then read probabilities from the normal table. For X ~ N(50, 4²): P(X > 56) = P(Z > 1.5) = 1 − 0.9332 = 0.0668.

Backwards Problems

Given a probability, find μ or σ. Convert the target percentile to a z-value from the table, then solve (x − μ)/σ = z.

Example: P(X < 30) = 0.15 with unknown σ. From tables z = −1.036, so (30 − μ)/σ = −1.036 — one equation per unknown; use a second condition if both are missing.

Symmetry Shortcuts

P(X > μ) = 0.5. P(X < a) for a above the mean uses the complement. Tables usually give Φ(z) for z ≥ 0 only; use Φ(−z) = 1 − Φ(z).

Normal Approximation to the Binomial

For large n with p near ½, X ~ B(n, p) ≈ N(np, np(1 − p)). The condition usually quoted at this level is np > 5 and n(1 − p) > 5. Apply a continuity correction: to approximate P(X ≥ 12) for a binomial, compute P(Y > 11.5) for the normal Y.

Example: B(100, 0.5) ≈ N(50, 25). P(X ≥ 55) ≈ P(Y > 54.5) = P(Z > 0.9) = 0.1841.

Exam tips: always sketch and shade — the picture prevents complement errors. State the standardisation step explicitly; marks sit in the working. Check whether a question says "mean and standard deviation" (σ) or "variance" (σ²) before standardising.

Exam method: standardising and symmetry

For X ~ N(μ, σ²) the standard score is z = (x − μ)/σ, and Z ~ N(0, 1). Note that the second parameter is the variance, so take the square root to get σ before standardising. Many errors come from using 25 instead of 5 when the variance is 25.

Probabilities are found from the standard normal table or calculator using Φ(z) = P(Z ≤ z). Because the curve is symmetric about 0, Φ(−z) = 1 − Φ(z), and P(Z > z) = 1 − Φ(z).

For a probability between two values, P(a < X < b) = Φ(z_b) − Φ(z_a). Standardise each limit separately and subtract.

To find a value from a probability, read the z-value from the table with the required area, and then rearrange z = (x − μ)/σ to find x.

Exam cue: Sketch the curve and shade the area asked for, then match it to the table value, since the sketch catches sign errors.

title: IGCSE Physics: Measurement and Units
content:
IGCSE Physics: Measurement and Units

Cambridge IGCSE Physics 0625 (2026–2028), Topic 1 Motion, forces and energy, statement 1.1 Physical quantities and measurement techniques — plus the experimental skills that Paper 6, Alternative to Practical, examines directly. Every physics result rests on a measurement, and every measurement is uncertain. This note builds the vocabulary of quantities and units, the practical techniques for length, volume and time, and then the full Paper 6 method: variables, safety, tables, graph plotting, gradients and intercepts, conclusions and error analysis. Paper 2 and Paper 4 carry the theory marks; Paper 6 carries these skills as a written exam of their own.

Physical quantities and SI units

A physical quantity is a property that can be measured, and every measurement needs a number and a unit. Physics uses the SI system, whose base units include the metre (m) for length, the kilogram (kg) for mass, the second (s) for time, the ampere (A) for electric current, the kelvin (K) for temperature and the mole (mol) for amount of substance. All other units are derived from these: speed in metres per second (m s⁻¹) is a base unit divided by a base unit, and force in newtons is defined so that 1 N = 1 kg m s⁻².

QuantitySymbolSI unitHow the unit is built
Lengths or lmetre (m)base unit
Massmkilogram (kg)base unit
Timetsecond (s)base unit
VolumeVcubic metre (m³)m³; litres and cm³ are everyday alternatives (1 litre = 0.001 m³)
Speedvmetre per second (m s⁻¹)m ÷ s
Frequencyfhertz (Hz)1 Hz = 1 cycle per second (s⁻¹)
ForceFnewton (N)kg m s⁻²
EnergyEjoule (J)N m = kg m² s⁻²
Pressureppascal (Pa)N m⁻²

Large and small quantities use standard prefixes or standard form: kilo (×1000), centi (÷100), milli (÷1000), micro (÷10⁶). Standard form writes a quantity as a number between 1 and 10 multiplied by a power of ten, so the speed of light is 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. Units obey ordinary algebra: dividing metres by seconds gives m s⁻¹, and a unit written as m/s and one written as m s⁻¹ are the same thing.

Measuring length, area and volume

Length is measured with a ruler or a tape. The three rules of good practice are fixed: place the scale edge along the line being measured, start from the zero mark rather than the worn end of the ruler, and take the reading at eye level directly above the point to avoid parallax error. A ruler reading should be quoted to the nearest half millimetre with an uncertainty of about ±0.5 mm; a vernier caliper or a micrometer screw gauge reads to 0.01 mm and is used when the length is small.

Areas and volumes are calculated from measured lengths. The area of a rectangle is length × width; the volume of a rectangular block is length × width × height; the volume of a cylinder is π r² l. For an irregular solid, the volume is found by displacement: water is poured into a measuring cylinder, the starting volume is read, the object is lowered in, and the rise in level is the object's volume. Read the bottom of the curved meniscus at eye level. The technique fails for objects that float (use a sinker), objects that absorb water or dissolve (use sand or oil), and objects that splash water out on entry (lower them gently on a thread).

Area scales with the square of a length and volume with the cube, so a small length error is amplified: a 2 per cent error in each of the three dimensions of a cube gives about a 6 per cent error in its volume. This is exactly the kind of reasoning Paper 6 rewards in its evaluation questions.

Measuring time intervals

Short times are measured with a stopwatch, and human reaction time of about 0.2 s dominates a single reading. Two standard techniques control it. First, repeat and average: time several oscillations of a pendulum and divide by the number of swings, because the reaction error is then spread over many periods. Second, use a larger quantity: time 20 trolley passes rather than one, or measure the time for 50 dots from a 50 Hz ticker timer, where consecutive dots are 0.02 s apart. Timing devices built into the apparatus — light gates, data loggers and ticker timers — remove reaction time entirely and are the expected answer when a question asks how to improve a timing measurement.

Errors, precision and percentage uncertainty

Every measurement carries an uncertainty, usually taken as the range of the scale: ±0.5 mm on a ruler, ±0.5 s on a stopwatch read to seconds, ±0.5 of the smallest scale division on a measuring cylinder. Two kinds of error behave differently. A random error scatters readings in both directions and is reduced by repeating and averaging; a systematic error shifts every reading the same way — a zero error on a balance, a bent ruler, parallax — and is removed by correcting the instrument, never by averaging. An anomaly is a result that does not fit the pattern; it is discarded only with a stated reason, never because it is inconvenient.

The size of an uncertainty is compared using percentage uncertainty, a technique Paper 6 tests whenever results are combined:

percentage uncertainty in one reading = (uncertainty / reading) × 100
percentage uncertainty in a sum or difference = (largest absolute uncertainty / answer) × 100
percentage uncertainty in a product or quotient = sum of the individual percentage uncertainties

Worked example: a cube of side 2.0 ± 0.05 cm has a mass of 24.0 ± 0.1 g. The side's percentage uncertainty is 0.05/2.0 × 100 = 2.5 per cent, so the volume (a product of three lengths) carries 3 × 2.5 = 7.5 per cent. The mass carries 0.1/24.0 × 100 = 0.4 per cent. The density = mass/volume carries 7.5 + 0.4 = 7.9 per cent, so ρ = 24.0/8.0 = 3.0 g cm⁻³ ± 0.2 g cm⁻³. The volume term dominates: improving the ruler improves the result far more than improving the balance.

Scalars and vectors (Supplement)

A scalar has size only: distance, speed, mass, energy, temperature, pressure. A vector has size and direction: displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, momentum, weight. Vectors are added by direction: two forces in a line add or subtract; two forces at right angles combine by Pythagoras, with the direction found from an angle. If a boat is pushed 3.0 m north and 4.0 m east, its resultant displacement is 5.0 m on a bearing of about 53° from north. Drawing the vector triangle to scale is a complete method on Paper 4 whenever the angle is not 90°.

Paper 6: how the practical exam is written

Paper 6 is a written exam about practical physics; you handle no apparatus but you must think like an experimenter. The question types repeat, and each has a method.

  • Choosing apparatus. Match the instrument to the quantity and its size: a ruler for lengths of centimetres, a micrometer for wires, a measuring cylinder for volumes, a balance for masses. State the range and the precision you expect.
  • Variables. Name the independent variable (what you change), the dependent variable (what you measure) and the control variables (what you keep fixed). A fair test changes one thing only, and every control earns a mark: same material, same temperature, same apparatus, same operator.
  • Safety. Link each hazard to a control: hot water and burners — use tongs and keep hands clear; masses and clamps — secure the clamp to the bench and stand clear of falling masses; lasers and ultrasound — never look into the beam; electricity — low voltages only, and switch off between readings.
  • Tables. Draw a box with a column per quantity and a heading of quantity divided by unit, e.g. length / cm. Numbers sit in the cells without units. Give each column enough rows for repeats, quote consistent significant figures, and record raw readings before any calculated column.
  • Graphs. The independent variable goes on the horizontal axis. Choose a scale that fills at least half the sheet, label both axes with quantity and unit, plot points with a fine cross, and draw a single smooth line of best fit — a thin ruled line for a linear relationship, a smooth curve otherwise. Never join dots dot to dot.
  • Gradient and intercept. The gradient = (change in vertical quantity) / (change in horizontal quantity), taken between two distant points on the line, not between plotted points. For a straight line through the origin the two variables are directly proportional; a non-zero intercept has physical meaning — on a speed–time graph it is the initial speed, on a cooling curve the ambient temperature — and the equation of the line is written as vertical quantity = gradient × horizontal quantity + intercept.
  • Conclusions. State the relationship the graph shows in words and symbols, quote the gradient with its unit, and relate the result to the physics (for example, a load–extension graph through the origin shows extension proportional to load, and its gradient is the spring constant).
  • Evaluation. Name the largest source of uncertainty with a reason, say which way it pushes the answer, and propose a specific improvement — more repeats, a longer measurement interval, a sensor or data logger, a wider range of values — not a vague plea for more care.

Worked example: reading a graph and its gradient

A student measures the speed of a trolley pulled down a runway, plotting speed on the vertical axis against time on the horizontal axis. The plotted points lie close to a straight line crossing the vertical axis at 0.10 m s⁻¹ and passing through (2.0 s, 1.30 m s⁻¹) and (6.0 s, 3.30 m s⁻¹).

gradient = (3.30 - 1.30) / (6.0 - 2.0) = 2.00 / 4.0 = 0.50 m s⁻²
intercept = 0.10 m s⁻¹
equation: speed = 0.50 x time + 0.10

The gradient is the trolley's acceleration, 0.50 m s⁻², and the intercept is its initial speed, 0.10 m s⁻¹. A conclusion that says only speed increases with time earns no mark; the mark is for the number, its unit and its physical meaning.

Common mistakes

  • Writing a number without its unit, or putting units into the cells of a results table whose heading already carries the unit.
  • Starting a ruler scale from the broken zero end, or reading at an angle and introducing parallax error.
  • Joining plotted points with a zig-zag line instead of drawing one smooth line of best fit, which hides anomalies rather than revealing them.
  • Calculating a gradient between two neighbouring plotted points; use two distant points on the line to shrink the reading error.
  • Reducing a systematic error by repeating readings; averaging shrinks random error only, and a zero error must be corrected at the instrument.
  • Keeping an anomaly with no comment, or discarding one without a stated physical reason.
  • Confusing scalar and vector: adding a speed to a velocity, or giving a direction for energy.
  • Reporting a percentage uncertainty but never saying which measurement dominates the final result.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 6, 3 marks). Describe how you would measure the average speed of a trolley on a runway.

Answer: Mark a fixed distance along the runway and measure it with a metre ruler. Release the trolley from the same point each time and time its passage over the marked distance with light gates and a data logger (or a stopwatch, repeated and averaged to reduce reaction error). Average speed is the distance divided by the time. Repeat for several distances or heights and record results in a table.

Question 2 (Paper 6, 3 marks). A student measures the period of a pendulum once and gets 1.3 s. Suggest two improvements to the method.

Answer: Time 20 complete oscillations and divide by 20, so reaction time error becomes a small fraction of the total; repeat the whole measurement several times and take a mean. Keep the pendulum length fixed and time from the release point to avoid a variable starting condition.

Question 3 (Paper 4, 2 marks). A length is recorded as 2.50 cm. State the instrument used and its uncertainty.

Answer: A ruler reading to 0.1 cm (or a vernier caliper if the precision demands it), with an uncertainty of ±0.05 cm, half the smallest scale division.

Question 4 (Paper 6, 4 marks). The volume of a small stone is found from 30 cm³ to 45 cm³ in a measuring cylinder and its mass is 36 g. Calculate the density and its percentage uncertainty if each volume reading is uncertain by ±0.5 cm³.

Answer: Volume = 15 cm³. The uncertainty in the difference is 0.5 + 0.5 = 1.0 cm³ (worst case for a difference), so the percentage uncertainty is 1.0/15 × 100 = 6.7 per cent. Density = 36/15 = 2.4 g cm⁻³, so the answer is 2.4 g cm⁻³ ± 0.2 g cm³ (about ±7 per cent). Using a larger volume difference would shrink the percentage uncertainty.

Question 5 (Paper 2 style). Which quantity is a vector? A energy; B temperature; C momentum; D pressure. Answer: C. Momentum has size and direction; the rest are scalars.

With measurements trustworthy, the next topic is what heat does to matter: thermal physics.

Equations and symbols

Measurement is the one topic whose equations are mostly about the arithmetic of uncertainty rather than a physical law. Paper 6 marks the method, the significant figures and the uncertainty, so each relation below is given with the symbols it uses and the unit each symbol carries.

Averages and rates

x̄ = (x₁ + x₂ + … + xₙ) / n
Key: x̄ = mean value (same unit as the readings); x₁ … xₙ = individual readings, all in the same unit; n = number of readings (no unit). Anomalous readings are discarded before averaging, never included and then blamed on the mean.

v = d / t
Key: v = average speed (m/s); d = total distance travelled (m); t = total time taken (s). On a two-leg journey this is total distance over total time, not the mean of the two speeds.

T = t / N
Key: T = period of one oscillation (s); t = total time for N oscillations (s); N = number of oscillations counted (no unit). Timing twenty swings and dividing moves the reaction-time error from each swing to the whole interval.

Uncertainty

percentage uncertainty = (Δx / x) × 100%
Key: Δx = absolute uncertainty of the reading, taken as ± half the smallest division for a single reading (same unit as x); x = the reading itself; the result is a percentage (no unit).

percentage uncertainty of a product or quotient = %A + %B
Key: %A, %B = the percentage uncertainties of the measured quantities being multiplied or divided. Adding the percentages is the rule whenever the quantities are combined by × or ÷.

percentage uncertainty of a power = n × (%x)
Key: n = the power to which the quantity is raised (2 for an area, 3 for a volume); %x = the percentage uncertainty in the measured length. This is why a 5% uncertainty in a diameter becomes 15% in a volume.

Geometry needed to find a volume

V = πr²h
Key: V = volume of a cylinder (m³ or cm³); r = radius, half the diameter (m or cm); h = height (m or cm); π = 3.14 (no unit).

V = (4/3)πr³
Key: V = volume of a sphere (m³ or cm³); r = radius (m or cm). The cube is what makes the percentage uncertainty three times the radius's.

A = πr²
Key: A = area of a circle (m² or cm²); r = radius (m or cm).

V = V₂ − V₁
Key: V = volume of an irregular solid (cm³); V₂ = cylinder reading with the solid submerged (cm³); V₁ = cylinder reading before it was added (cm³).

Converting units before substituting

1 km/h = 1000 m / 3600 s = 0.278 m/s
Key: divide a speed in km/h by 3.6 to get m/s. Converting after substituting is the commonest arithmetic error on Paper 2.

1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³
Key: multiply a density in g/cm³ by 1000 to use it with masses in kg and volumes in m³.

1 cm² = 1 × 10⁻⁴ m² and 1 cm³ = 1 × 10⁻⁶ m³
Key: areas scale with the square of the length conversion and volumes with the cube, which is why 100 cm² is 0.01 m², not 1 m².

The one derived quantity this topic measures

ρ = m / V
Key: ρ (ρ) = density (kg/m³ or g/cm³); m = mass (kg or g); V = volume (m³ or cm³). The units must match before dividing: 250 g in 30 cm³ is 8.3 g/cm³, which is 8300 kg/m³.

title: Transport in Animals
content:
Transport in Animals

Cambridge IGCSE Biology 0610, Extended route, topic 9 (statements 9.1–9.4). Why mammals need a double circulatory system, heart structure and the cardiac cycle, blood vessels, and the composition and roles of blood.

9.1 to 9.2 Circulatory systems and the heart

  • Mammals have a double circulation: blood passes through the heart twice per complete circuit. This keeps blood pressure high to the lungs and restores it to a suitable level for the body, so oxygen delivery is efficient.
  • Heart structure: four chambers, two atria and two ventricles. The right side pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs; the left side, with the thicker muscular wall, pumps oxygenated blood to the whole body. Valves ensure one-way flow.
  • The cardiac cycle: atria contract (atrial systole), pushing blood through the atrioventricular valves; then the ventricles contract (ventricular systole), closing the atrioventricular valves and opening the semilunar valves; then all chambers relax (diastole) and refill.
  • Coronary heart disease: narrowed coronary arteries reduce blood supply to the heart muscle, causing angina or a heart attack. Risk factors: smoking, a diet high in saturated fat and salt, stress and lack of exercise.

9.3 Blood vessels

  • Arteries carry blood away from the heart at high pressure, with thick muscular walls and elastic tissue; veins return it at low pressure, with thin walls and valves; capillaries are one cell thick for efficient exchange.

9.4 Blood

  • Plasma carries dissolved nutrients, urea, hormones and antibodies; red blood cells carry oxygen bound to haemoglobin; white blood cells fight infection; platelets help clotting.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Cardiac output calculation, applied to a heart rate of 72 beats per minute with a stroke volume of 70 cm³: cardiac output = 72 × 70 = 5040 cm³ per minute, about 5 dm³. During exercise both heart rate and stroke volume rise, and the answer should name which factor changes more in a trained athlete — stroke volume.
  • Structure reasoning, applied to why the left ventricle wall is thicker than the right: it pumps blood the whole distance around the body against greater resistance, so it needs the stronger muscle. Compare the two sides explicitly; the comparison is the mark.
  • Valve reasoning, applied to which valves are heard as heart sounds: the atrioventricular valves close at the start of ventricular systole and the semilunar valves close at the end, so both sounds come from valves slamming shut under pressure. Name the events, not just the valves.

Common errors

  • Calling the double circulation "two hearts". It is one heart, two circuits.
  • Saying arteries always carry oxygenated blood. Pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood — vessels are named by direction, not content.
  • Claiming valves in veins are powered by the heart. Vein valves work with skeletal muscle contractions.

title: Exam technique: Functions
content:
### What earns the marks
For range, the domain endpoints evaluated earn the first mark with monotonicity justifying the interval. For composites, the inner value written down earns a mark before the outer application. For inverses, the swap-and-solve shown earns the method mark; domain restriction discussed earns the reasoning mark.
### Traps
Error: gf computed as fg. Correction: start from the rightmost letter. Error: inverse claimed on many-one functions. Correction: restrict the domain first. Error: full reals claimed despite a bounded domain. Correction: map the endpoints.

title: A Level Mathematics: Further Trigonometry
content:
A Level Mathematics: Further Trigonometry

A2 trigonometry covers the reciprocal functions, the compound and double-angle identities, the harmonic form R sin(θ + α) that turns a sum into a single wave, inverse functions with their domains, and equations with multiple or transformed angles. This note builds every identity from the compound-angle results, so the whole set is reconstructable rather than memorised.

The reciprocal functions

sec x = 1/cos x;  cosec x = 1/sin x;  cot x = 1/tan x = cos x/sin x

identities: 1 + tan^2 x = sec^2 x;  1 + cot^2 x = cosec^2 x

Worked example. Solve sec x = 2 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 360°.

cos x = 1/2  ->  x = 60 or 300

Worked example 2 (identity). Prove that sec²x − tan²x = 1.

sec^2 - tan^2 = 1/cos^2 - sin^2/cos^2 = (1 - sin^2)/cos^2 = cos^2/cos^2 = 1

Worked example 3 (solve). Solve 2 cosec²x = 5 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 360°.

cosec^2 x = 2.5  ->  sin^2 x = 0.4  ->  sin x = +/- 0.6325
x = 39.2, 140.8, 219.2, 320.8

Reciprocal functions blow up where the denominator vanishes: sec and tan at 90°, cosec and cot at 0°. Sketching is the safest way to see the asymptotes.

Compound-angle identities

sin(A + B) = sin A cos B + cos A sin B
sin(A - B) = sin A cos B - cos A sin B
cos(A + B) = cos A cos B - sin A sin B
cos(A - B) = cos A cos B + sin A sin B
tan(A + B) = (tan A + tan B)/(1 - tan A tan B)

Worked example 1 (exact value). Find sin 75° exactly.

sin(45 + 30) = sin45 cos30 + cos45 sin30
= (sqrt2/2)(sqrt3/2) + (sqrt2/2)(1/2) = (sqrt6 + sqrt2)/4

Worked example 2 (prove). Prove that sin(A + B) + sin(A − B) = 2 sin A cos B.

add the two expansions: the cos A sin B terms cancel
leaving 2 sin A cos B

Worked example 3 (solve). Solve sin(x + 30°) = cos x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 360°.

sin x cos30 + cos x sin30 = cos x
0.866 sin x + 0.5 cos x = cos x
0.866 sin x = 0.5 cos x  ->  tan x = 0.577  ->  x = 30 or 210

Double-angle identities

sin 2A = 2 sin A cos A
cos 2A = cos^2 A - sin^2 A = 2cos^2 A - 1 = 1 - 2 sin^2 A
tan 2A = 2 tan A/(1 - tan^2 A)

Worked example. Given sin A = 3/5 with A acute, find sin 2A and cos 2A.

cos A = 4/5
sin 2A = 2(3/5)(4/5) = 24/25
cos 2A = 1 - 2(9/25) = 7/25

Worked example 2 (solve). Solve cos 2x = sin x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 360°.

1 - 2 sin^2 x = sin x  ->  2 sin^2 x + sin x - 1 = 0
(2 sin x - 1)(sin x + 1) = 0
sin x = 1/2  ->  x = 30, 150;  sin x = -1  ->  x = 270

The choice of cos 2A form matters: pick the one that leaves a single trigonometric function in the resulting equation.

The harmonic form

a sin x + b cos x = R sin(x + alpha)
R = sqrt(a^2 + b^2);  tan alpha = b/a

always expand back to check the sign of alpha

Worked example. Express 3 sin x + 4 cos x in the form R sin(x + α).

R = 5; tan alpha = 4/3  ->  alpha = 53.13 deg
3 sin x + 4 cos x = 5 sin(x + 53.13 deg)
check: 5[sin x cos53.13 + cos x sin53.13] = 3 sin x + 4 cos x

Worked example 2 (maximum). Hence find the maximum value of 3 sin x + 4 cos x and the x at which it occurs.

maximum = 5, when sin(x + 53.13) = 1
x + 53.13 = 90  ->  x = 36.87 deg

Worked example 3 (solve). Solve 3 sin x + 4 cos x = 2 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 360°.

5 sin(x + 53.13) = 2  ->  sin(x + 53.13) = 0.4
x + 53.13 = 23.58 or 156.42
x = -29.5 (reject, or add 360: 330.5) or 103.3

Adjusting the interval for the phase shift is compulsory: the angle x + α runs over a different range from x.

Inverse trigonometric functions

arcsin: domain [-1, 1], range [-90, 90] degrees
arccos: domain [-1, 1], range [0, 180]
arctan: all reals, range (-90, 90)

The restricted ranges are what make the inverses functions. That is why arcsin(sin 150°) = 30°, not 150°.

Worked example. Evaluate arcsin(sin 200°).

sin 200 = -0.342
arcsin(-0.342) = -20 deg, which lies in the principal range

Worked example 2 (equation). Solve tan⁻¹(2x) = 45°.

2x = tan 45 = 1  ->  x = 0.5

Worked example 3 (derivative link). Differentiate y = arcsin x.

dy/dx = 1/sqrt(1 - x^2), valid for |x| < 1

Equations with transformed angles

for sin(kx + c) = value over a range of x:
  1. find the range of the argument kx + c
  2. solve for the argument
  3. convert back to x and keep only values in the x-range

Worked example. Solve sin(2x − 30°) = 0.5 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 180°.

argument range: -30 <= 2x - 30 <= 330
2x - 30 = 30, 150, 390 (out of range)
2x = 60 or 180  ->  x = 30 or 90

Worked example 2. Solve cos(3x) = −0.5 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 180°.

argument range 0 <= 3x <= 540
3x = 120, 240, 480  ->  x = 40, 80, 160

Solving equations in a given range

The single most reliable routine in A2 trigonometry is a fixed order of operations, because the marks are lost in the bookkeeping, never in the trigonometry.

step 1  reduce to ONE trigonometric function (identity if needed)
step 2  solve for the function value, keeping every sign
step 3  find the principal solution
step 4  use symmetry to find all solutions in the argument's range
step 5  convert back to x, and discard anything outside the stated range

Worked example. Solve 2 sin²x + 3 cos x = 3 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 360°.

sin^2 = 1 - cos^2  ->  2(1 - cos^2 x) + 3 cos x = 3
2 - 2cos^2 x + 3 cos x - 3 = 0
2cos^2 x - 3 cos x + 1 = 0   ->  (2cos x - 1)(cos x - 1) = 0
cos x = 1/2  ->  x = 60, 300
cos x = 1    ->  x = 0, 360
solutions: 0, 60, 300, 360 degrees

Worked example 2 (quadratic in tan). Solve 3 tan²x − tan x − 2 = 0 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 360°.

(3 tan x + 2)(tan x - 1) = 0
tan x = 1  ->  x = 45, 225
tan x = -2/3  ->  x = 180 - 33.7 = 146.3;  and 326.3
tangent repeats every 180 degrees, so each root gives exactly two solutions here

Note the period: sin and cos repeat every 360°, tan every 180°. Getting the period wrong either loses half the solutions or invents ones outside the range.

Proving identities

An identity is proved by transforming one side into the other, never by moving terms across the equals sign as if it were an equation. The safe strategy is to start on the side that looks worse and simplify towards the other.

allowed moves: rewrite sec/cosec/cot as sin and cos; apply Pythagoras;
               expand compound angles; use a double-angle form
not allowed:   multiplying both sides by something, unless every step is reversible
               and the result is still an identity

Worked example. Prove that (1 + sin x)/(cos x) = cos x/(1 − sin x).

start from the left; multiply numerator and denominator by (1 - sin x):
(1 + sin x)(1 - sin x) / [cos x (1 - sin x)]
= (1 - sin^2 x) / [cos x (1 - sin x)]
= cos^2 x / [cos x (1 - sin x)]
= cos x / (1 - sin x)

Worked example 2 (double angle). Prove that (sin 2x)/(1 + cos 2x) = tan x.

sin 2x = 2 sin x cos x;  1 + cos 2x = 1 + (2cos^2 x - 1) = 2cos^2 x
ratio = 2 sin x cos x / 2cos^2 x = sin x/cos x = tan x

The choice of cos 2A form is not taste: pick the version that cancels against the rest of the expression. Here 2cos²x − 1 was right because the denominator needed a cosine.

Modelling with the harmonic form

The R-formula is not only an algebraic trick; it is the reason oscillating physical quantities are written as a single wave. Tidal height, temperature, alternating current and the height of a point on a rotating wheel are all of the form a sin θ + b cos θ, and every question about their maximum, minimum or first occurrence is answered by the amplitude and phase.

h = 12 + 5 sin(30t) + 12 cos(30t)  (t in hours)
R = sqrt(25 + 144) = 13;  tan alpha = 12/5  ->  alpha = 67.38 degrees
h = 12 + 13 sin(30t + 67.38)
maximum depth = 12 + 13 = 25;  minimum = 12 - 13 = -1 (below the datum)

Worked example. For that model, find the first time after t = 0 at which the height is a maximum.

sin(30t + 67.38) = 1  ->  30t + 67.38 = 90
30t = 22.62  ->  t = 0.754 hours = 45.2 minutes

Worked example 2 (period and interpretation). State the period of the model and what it represents.

argument 30t has period 360 degrees in t:  360/30 = 12 hours
the tide repeats every 12 hours, twice a day

Worked example 3 (minimum as a phrase). Find the time of the first minimum.

sin(30t + 67.38) = -1  ->  30t + 67.38 = 270
30t = 202.62  ->  t = 6.75 hours

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Reciprocal) Solve cosec x = 2 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 360°. Answer: sin x = ½ → 30°, 150°.
  2. (Identity) Simplify (1 − cos²x)/sin x. Answer: sin x.
  3. (Compound) Find cos 15° exactly. Answer: (√6 + √2)/4.
  4. (Double) Given cos A = 5/13, find sin 2A. Answer: 2(12/13)(5/13) = 120/169.
  5. (Double solve) Solve sin 2x = cos x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 180°. Answer: cos x(2 sin x − 1) = 0 → x = 90°, 30°, 150°.
  6. (Harmonic) Express 5 sin x − 12 cos x as R sin(x − α). Answer: 13 sin(x − 67.4°).
  7. (Maximum) Max of 5 sin x − 12 cos x? Answer: 13.
  8. (Inverse) Solve arccos(2x) = 60°. Answer: 2x = ½ → x = ¼.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Losing solutions: quadratics in sin or cos give two values, each with its own solutions in the range.
  • Wrong cos 2A form: choose the version that leaves one function; otherwise the equation becomes unsolvable.
  • Harmonic sign: R sin(x − α) versus R sin(x + α) depends on the signs of a and b; expand to check.
  • Interval not adjusted: transformed angles need the argument's range computed before solving.
  • Inverse range ignored: arcsin returns only the principal value; other solutions come from the symmetries.
  • sec/cosec confused: sec = 1/cos, cosec = 1/sin — the reverse is a silent disaster.
  • Degrees and radians: the R-formula's α follows the mode; mixing them gives a phase error.
  • Identity proofs without a direction: start from the more complicated side and transform towards the simpler; do not work on both sides at once unless every step is reversible.

title: IGCSE Physics: Earth and Space
content:
IGCSE Physics: Earth and Space

Cambridge IGCSE Physics 0625 (2026–2028), Topic 6 Space physics: statements 6.1 The Earth and the Solar System and 6.2 Stars and the Universe. This final topic scales the mechanics and nuclear physics of the rest of the course up to the largest objects there are. Gravity holds planets in orbit and holds stars together; fusion powers stars; the light from distant galaxies tells us the Universe is expanding. Paper 4 usually has one structured question here, and the calculations are orbital mechanics and redshift.

The Earth: rotation, orbit and seasons

The Earth spins on its axis once every 24 hours, which gives day and night, and it orbits the Sun once every 365.25 days, which gives the year. The Earth's axis is tilted at about 23.5° to the plane of its orbit, and that tilt — not the changing distance from the Sun — causes the seasons: when a hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun its rays strike more directly and the days are longer, so it is summer.

The Moon orbits the Earth in about 27 days. It shines by reflected sunlight, and because we see different fractions of its lit half as it orbits, it shows phases: new moon, crescent, half, gibbous, full. A lunar eclipse occurs when the Earth's shadow falls on the Moon; a solar eclipse when the Moon's shadow falls on the Earth.

Supplement: orbital speed. For a circular orbit of radius r completed in period T:

orbital speed = 2πr / T        v = 2πr / T
  • v: orbital speed in metres per second (m s⁻¹); r: orbital radius in metres (m); T: orbital period in seconds (s). Convert days and years to seconds first.

The Solar System

The Solar System is the Sun and the bodies bound to it by gravity: eight planets (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune), their moons, dwarf planets, asteroids and comets. The four inner planets are small and rocky with few or no moons; the four outer planets are gas giants — large, low density, with many moons and ring systems. Asteroids orbit mainly between Mars and Jupiter; comets have highly elliptical orbits and grow bright tails of gas and dust when near the Sun.

Gravity provides the centripetal force that keeps every planet, moon and satellite in orbit. A planet's orbital speed falls with distance from the Sun (Kepler's laws), and the planets' orbits are ellipses with the Sun at one focus (Supplement: conservation of energy means a planet speeds up at perihelion and slows at aphelion, trading kinetic for gravitational potential energy).

Supplement: light-travel time. Light from the Sun takes about 8 minutes to reach Earth; from the nearest star, about 4.2 years. The light-year is the distance light travels in one year, about 9.5 × 10¹⁵ m, so looking at distant objects is literally looking into the past.

The Sun as a star

The Sun is an ordinary main-sequence star: a sphere of hot gas, about three-quarters hydrogen and one-quarter helium by mass, with a core at roughly 15 million degrees Celsius. Its energy comes from nuclear fusion in the core, where hydrogen nuclei fuse into helium nuclei, and a small loss of mass becomes the radiated energy. That radiation powers the whole Solar System: it drives the water cycle behind hydroelectric power and biofuels, heats the Earth's surface, and — over geological time — built the fossil fuels (Supplement: solar energy is the principal source behind almost every renewable resource on Earth).

The Sun is a medium-sized star about 4.6 billion years old, with enough hydrogen for roughly another 5 billion years of fusion before it swells into a red giant.

Stars and galaxies

A galaxy is a vast collection of stars, gas and dust held together by gravity. The Sun is one of roughly 200 billion stars in the Milky Way, a spiral galaxy, and galaxies themselves are grouped into clusters. The nearest large galaxy to us is Andromeda, about 2.5 million light-years away.

Stars have life cycles set by their mass:

  • Nebula: a huge cloud of gas and dust, pulled inward by gravity.
  • Protostar: the contracting, heating core of the cloud.
  • Main sequence star: when the core is hot enough for hydrogen fusion to start, the outward radiation pressure balances gravity and the star is stable — the Sun's current stage.
  • Red giant or supergiant: when core hydrogen runs low, fusion moves outwards and the star swells and cools at the surface.
  • End state: a star like the Sun sheds its outer layers as a planetary nebula and leaves a white dwarf. A massive star explodes as a supernova and leaves a neutron star, or, for the most massive, a black hole — an object whose gravity is so strong that not even light escapes.

Supernovae matter beyond astrophysics: they create and scatter the elements heavier than helium, so the carbon, oxygen and iron in your body were forged inside stars.

The Universe: redshift, expansion and the Big Bang

Light from distant galaxies is shifted towards the red end of the spectrum: the spectral lines appear at longer wavelengths than the same lines produced in a laboratory. This redshift is a Doppler effect — the galaxies are moving away from us. Crucially, almost every galaxy shows redshift, and the more distant the galaxy, the greater the redshift and the faster it is receding. The conclusion is that the Universe is expanding.

Running the expansion backwards implies that everything was once at one place — the Big Bang, roughly 13.8 billion years ago. Two further pieces of evidence support it: the cosmic microwave background (CMB), faint microwave radiation coming from every direction, which is the cooled remnant of the hot early Universe, and the abundance of light elements (hydrogen and helium) matching the predictions of Big Bang nucleosynthesis.

Supplement: Hubble's law and the age of the Universe. The recession speed of a galaxy is proportional to its distance:

recession speed = Hubble constant x distance        v = H d
  • v: recession speed in metres per second (m s⁻¹); d: distance in metres (m) (often megaparsecs, but convert); H: the Hubble constant in s⁻¹ (quoted as km s⁻¹ per megaparsec).
  • The age of the Universe follows as roughly 1/H: run the expansion back at the present rate.

Worked example: orbital speed and Hubble's law

The Earth orbits the Sun at a radius of 1.5 × 10¹¹ m with a period of 365 days.

T = 365 x 24 x 3600 = 3.15 × 10⁷ s
v = 2πr / T = 2 × 3.14 × 1.5 × 10¹¹ / 3.15 × 10⁷ = 3.0 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹ (about 30 km s⁻¹)

Second calculation: a galaxy is 200 megaparsecs away and Hubble's constant is 70 km s⁻¹ per megaparsec. Its recession speed is v = Hd = 70 × 200 = 14 000 km s⁻¹. The age estimate is 1/H: one megaparsec is 3.1 × 10¹⁹ km, so 1/H = 3.1 × 10¹⁹/70 = 4.4 × 10¹⁷ s ≈ 14 billion years — consistent with the accepted value.

Common mistakes

  • Blaming the seasons on the Earth–Sun distance; it is the axial tilt. The Earth is actually closest to the Sun in January.
  • Confusing the Moon's phases with eclipses: phases are the normal monthly cycle of the lit fraction; eclipses are shadows, and are rare because the Moon's orbit is tilted.
  • Using kilometres and seconds in v = 2πr/T without one consistent unit system; convert the period to seconds and the radius to metres.
  • Calling a light-year a unit of time; it is a distance — the distance light travels in one year.
  • Saying redshift means the galaxies are moving through space away from us; the accepted interpretation is that space itself is expanding, stretching the light.
  • Mixing up redshift and blueshift: receding sources shift to longer (redder) wavelengths; approaching sources shift shorter (bluer) — nearby Andromeda is blueshifted.
  • Placing the Sun at the centre of the Solar System as an absolute; the Sun is the centre of the Solar System, but the Solar System is an ordinary part of the Milky Way.
  • Forgetting that the fusion in stars is hydrogen to helium, which is not the same as the fission of uranium in power stations.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 4, 3 marks). Calculate the orbital speed of a satellite orbiting 7.0 × 10⁶ m from the Earth's centre every 5900 s.

Answer: v = 2πr/T = 2 × 3.14 × 7.0 × 10⁶ / 5900 = 7.5 × 10³ m s⁻¹ (7.5 km s⁻¹).

Question 2 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Explain the evidence from redshift that the Universe is expanding.

Answer: The spectral lines from distant galaxies are shifted towards longer wavelengths than laboratory lines, which by the Doppler effect means the sources are receding. The more distant the galaxy, the greater the redshift and the faster it recedes, so the whole Universe is expanding with every distance growing over time. Reversing that expansion implies all matter was once concentrated at one point — the Big Bang.

Question 3 (Paper 2 style). The seasons on Earth are caused by: A the changing Earth–Sun distance; B the tilt of the Earth's axis; C the Moon's gravity; D the Sun's rotation. Answer: B. The tilt changes the angle of the sunlight and the length of day through the year.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 6 marks). Describe the life cycle of a star like the Sun.

Answer: It begins as a nebula, a cloud of gas and dust. Gravity contracts the cloud and the core heats into a protostar. When the core temperature reaches about 15 million degrees, hydrogen fusion begins and the star joins the main sequence, where radiation pressure from fusion balances gravity and it is stable for billions of years. As core hydrogen depletes, fusion moves outwards, the outer layers expand and cool and the star becomes a red giant. Finally the outer layers are expelled as a planetary nebula, leaving a white dwarf that slowly cools — no fusion, supported by electron degeneracy pressure.

Question 5 (Paper 4, 3 marks). State two pieces of evidence for the Big Bang theory besides the redshift of galaxies.

Answer: The cosmic microwave background radiation — faint microwave radiation arriving from every direction, the cooled afterglow of the hot early Universe. The observed abundances of the light elements, especially hydrogen and helium, match the amounts predicted to have formed in the first minutes after the Big Bang.

Question 6 (Paper 4, 3 marks). Explain why nuclear fusion in the Sun releases energy.

Answer: In fusion, light hydrogen nuclei combine to form a heavier helium nucleus. The product nucleus has slightly less mass than the four protons that formed it; that lost mass is converted into energy in accordance with mass–energy equivalence, and the energy is radiated from the Sun's core. Fusion releases energy for light elements up to iron, which is why it powers stars.

That completes the Cambridge IGCSE 0625 course: the AS notes begin with Edexcel IAL Unit 1 and Kinematics.

Equations and symbols

Earth and space is mostly descriptive, but three quantitative ideas carry the marks: orbital speed, weight on another world, and the distance units that make astronomy's numbers manageable. The cosmological relations are marked as extensions, because 0625 examines the redshift qualitatively.

Orbits

v = 2πr / T
Key: v = orbital speed (m/s); r = orbital radius, measured from the centre of the body being orbited (m); T = orbital period, the time for one complete orbit (s). The 2πr is the circumference of the orbit, so the equation is just speed = distance ÷ time applied to a circle.

a larger orbital radius gives a smaller orbital speed for the same central body
Key: the rule behind a satellite's period rising steeply with height; a geostationary satellite must sit at about 36 000 km above the equator to take exactly 24 hours.

gravitational force provides the centripetal force
Key: the single force keeping a planet or satellite in orbit points towards the centre of the orbit; without it the body would travel in a straight line.

Weight elsewhere

W = mg
Key: W = weight (N); m = mass (kg), unchanged by location; g = gravitational field strength of that body (N/kg). On the Moon g is about 1.6 N/kg, so a 60 kg astronaut weighs about 96 N there and 588 N on Earth.

g(Earth) = 9.8 N/kg and g(Moon) = 1.6 N/kg
Key: the two values used in 0625 questions; weight changes with g while mass does not, which is the whole point of the distinction.

Astronomical distances

1 light year = 9.46 × 10¹⁵ m
Key: the distance light travels in one year, from d = vt with v = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s and t = 3.15 × 10⁷ s. A light year is a distance, not a time.

1 astronomical unit (AU) = 1.5 × 10¹¹ m
Key: the mean Earth–Sun distance, used for distances inside the Solar System; a light year is about 63 000 AU.

orbital period of the planets: T² ∝ r³ (extension)
Key: T = orbital period (s or years); r = orbital radius (m or AU). Kepler's third law, which is why the outer planets take far longer to complete an orbit.

Redshift and the expanding Universe

z = Δλ / λ
Key: z = redshift (no unit); Δλ (delta lambda) = increase in wavelength (m); λ = wavelength emitted in the laboratory (m). A larger z means the galaxy is receding faster.

v = H₀ d (extension)
Key: v = recession speed of a galaxy (km/s); H₀ = the Hubble constant (about 70 km/s per Mpc); d = distance to the galaxy (Mpc). Plotting v against d and taking the gradient gives H₀, and 1/H₀ estimates the age of the Universe.

redshift means the source is receding; blueshift means it is approaching
Key: the observed wavelength is stretched when the source moves away and compressed when it moves towards the observer — the same Doppler effect as a passing siren.

title: Hardware & Architecture — Study Notes
content:
Hardware & Architecture

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): von Neumann model, FDE cycle, registers, buses, RAM/ROM, secondary storage, embedded systems.

1. Von Neumann model

CPU (ALU, control unit, registers) + memory + I/O on shared buses; instructions stored as data (stored program concept).

2. Registers

RegisterRole
PCaddress of next instruction
MARaddress being read/written
MDRdata/instruction in transit
ACCALU results accumulator

3. FDE cycle

Fetch: PC → MAR; memory → MDR → CIR; PC + 1. Decode: control unit interprets opcode. Execute: ALU/registers act. Interrupts can pause between cycles.

4. Buses and performance

Address bus (one-way, width ⇒ addressable memory), data bus (two-way, width ⇒ bits per transfer), control bus. Performance factors: clock speed, cache size, core count — explain the effect, not just the name.

5. RAM vs ROM

RAM: volatile, read/write, holds running programs + data. ROM: non-volatile, read-only, bootstrap/firmware. Embedded systems: dedicated microprocessors inside devices (washing machines, engines) — one function, low cost, hard to update.

6. Secondary storage

  • Magnetic (HDD): platters, read/write heads; high capacity, cheap per GB, moving parts (shock-sensitive).
  • Optical (CD/DVD/Blu-ray): laser pits/lands; cheap, portable, slow, small capacity.
  • Solid state (SSD/flash): NAND cells; fast, silent, robust, no moving parts, more expensive per GB, finite write cycles.

Choose by use case: video editing (SSD), archive (optical/magnetic), tablets (flash).

Exam tips: trace FDE with register values; compare storage on capacity, speed, cost, durability, portability; always tie a performance factor to its effect.

Worked example: clock speed and throughput

A processor runs at 2.0 GHz, which is 2.0 × 10⁹ clock cycles per second. If each instruction takes four cycles on average, the processor completes 2.0 × 10⁹ / 4 = 5.0 × 10⁸ instructions per second. Clock speed alone does not decide performance: a faster clock with more cycles per instruction can still be slower overall.

Cache memory

Cache is small, fast memory between the CPU and main memory. It holds copies of recently or frequently used data and instructions. A cache hit avoids a slow RAM access; a cache miss forces one. Cache is faster than RAM but much smaller, which is why it holds only the data most likely to be needed next.

The ALU and the control unit

The ALU performs arithmetic and logic operations. The control unit fetches and decodes instructions and sends control signals around the system. A comparison such as A > B is evaluated in the ALU, while the decision about which instruction runs next is made by the control unit.

  • Pipelining overlaps the fetch, decode and execute stages of successive instructions to raise throughput.
  • Multi-core processors run several fetch-decode-execute cycles at once, but one program gains speed only if its work can be split into parallel tasks.
  • A 16-bit address bus can address 2¹⁶ = 65 536 locations.

title: Superposition
content:
Superposition

The Principle of Superposition

When waves meet, displacements add. In phase → constructive (big amplitude); antiphase → destructive (cancellation).

Coherence and Path Difference

Two sources are coherent if they share frequency and constant phase difference. Maxima occur where path difference = nλ; minima where it = (n + ½)λ.

Double-Slit (Young)

Fringe spacing x = λD/a (D = slit–screen distance, a = slit separation).

Example: λ = 600 nm, D = 2 m, a = 0.5 mm: x = 2.4 mm.

Red light gives wider fringes than blue; smaller slit separation also widens fringes.

Diffraction Grating

d sin θ = nθth order maximum. More slits → sharper, brighter maxima. The number of visible orders is the largest n with sin θ ≤ 1.

Example: 600 lines/mm → d = 1.67 μm; for 500 nm light, n_max = 3.

Stationary Waves

Two identical waves travelling opposite directions (e.g. wave + reflection) create nodes (no movement) and antinodes (max movement), spaced λ/2 apart. Strings and closed pipes resonate at f₁ = v/2L (fundamental) and harmonics.

Exam tips: always compute d from 'lines per mm' first; state 'path difference = nλ' explicitly in explain-the-fringe questions.

Quick revision: Communication and Networking

Computer Science — AS. `# Communication and Networking

  • Transmission

  • Network Types
  • Hardware
  • Client-Server vs Peer-to-Peer

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

### Worked example A parity bit makes the total number of 1s even (even parity) or odd. For the 7-bit pattern 1011001 there are four 1s, so the even-parity bit is 0. If the receiver counts an odd number of 1s, it knows an error occurred. Packet switching divides data into packets that can take different routes, and each packet is checked before reassembly. ### Check yourself Find the even-parity bit for 1100111. It has five 1s, so the parity bit is 1. Explain why parity detects a single flipped bit but cannot always correct it.

title: Exam technique: Differentiation II
content:
### What earns the marks
For chain rule, outer derivative times inner derivative stated earns both marks. For products and quotients, the full rule quoted earns the method mark before substitution. For parametric and implicit work, dy/dt over dx/dt (or -Fx/Fy structure) earns the method mark.
### Traps
Error: inner derivative forgotten. Correction: multiply by it always. Error: product rule halved. Correction: both halves required. Error: dy/dx inverted for parametrics. Correction: y-derivative over x-derivative.

title: AS Level Mathematics: Exponentials and Logarithms
content:
AS Level Mathematics: Exponentials and Logarithms

Exponentials describe growth and decay — populations, investments, radioactive isotopes, cooling cups of tea — where the change is proportional to the amount present. Logarithms are their inverses: they turn multiplication into addition and, crucially, let you solve equations where the unknown sits in the exponent. This note builds the topic from zero: the meaning of a logarithm, the three laws with derivations, solving exponential and logarithmic equations including quadratics in disguise, the graph properties and transformations, and the applied growth/decay models.

What a logarithm is

log_a(x) = n  means  a^n = x

common log: log x = log_10 x
natural log: ln x = log_e x,  e = 2.71828...

The logarithm answers "to what power must I raise the base to get this number?" So log₂8 = 3 because 2³ = 8, and log₅(1/25) = −2 because 5⁻² = 1/25. Two identities follow immediately and are always true:

log_a(a) = 1
log_a(1) = 0
a^(log_a x) = x   and   log_a(a^x) = x

Worked example. Evaluate log₃81, log₂(1/8) and ln 1.

3⁴ = 81  →  log_3 81 = 4
2⁻³ = 1/8  →  log_2(1/8) = -3
anything to the power 0 is 1  →  ln 1 = 0

The three laws of logarithms

product:   log(xy) = log x + log y
quotient:  log(x/y) = log x - log y
power:     log(x^n) = n log x

consequences: log(1/x) = -log x;  log(sqrt x) = (1/2)log x

Why they work. Write x = a^m and y = a^n, so log x = m and log y = n. Then xy = a^(m+n), so log(xy) = m + n = log x + log y. The quotient law follows from a^(m−n) and the power law from (a^m)^n = a^(mn). Each law is a restatement of an index law, which is why logarithms convert products into sums.

Worked example 1 (combine). Write 2 log 3 + log 4 − log 6 as a single logarithm.

2 log 3 = log 9
log 9 + log 4 = log 36
log 36 - log 6 = log 6

Worked example 2 (split). Express log(x³y/√z) in terms of log x, log y and log z.

= 3 log x + log y - (1/2) log z

Worked example 3 (solve). Solve log₂x + log₂(x − 2) = 3.

combine: log_2[x(x - 2)] = 3
x(x - 2) = 2³ = 8
x² - 2x - 8 = 0  →  (x - 4)(x + 2) = 0
x = 4 or x = -2;  reject x = -2 because log of a negative is undefined
x = 4
