Rejecting invalid roots is compulsory: a logarithm only accepts a positive argument, so always check each answer against the original equation.

Solving exponential equations

When the unknown is in the exponent, take logs of both sides and use the power law to bring it down.

Worked example 1. Solve 3^x = 20.

take logs: x log 3 = log 20
x = log 20 / log 3 = 1.301/0.4771 = 2.73

Worked example 2 (different bases). Solve 5^(2x−1) = 7^(x+1).

(2x - 1) log 5 = (x + 1) log 7
2x log 5 - log 5 = x log 7 + log 7
x(2 log 5 - log 7) = log 7 + log 5
x = (log 7 + log 5)/(2 log 5 - log 7)
  = (0.845 + 0.699)/(1.398 - 0.845) = 1.544/0.553 = 2.79

Worked example 3 (quadratic in disguise). Solve 2^(2x) − 5(2^x) + 4 = 0.

let y = 2^x:  y² - 5y + 4 = 0  →  (y - 1)(y - 4) = 0
y = 1  →  2^x = 1  →  x = 0
y = 4  →  2^x = 4  →  x = 2

The substitution trick is the standard route for any equation where one power is double another: put y = a^x and solve the quadratic, then convert back.

Graphs of exponential and logarithmic functions

FunctionDomainRangeKey points
y = e^xall real xy > 0(0, 1); always increasing; asymptote y = 0
y = e^(−x)all real xy > 0(0, 1); always decreasing; decay
y = ln xx > 0all real y(1, 0); increasing; asymptote x = 0

y = ln x is the reflection of y = e^x in the line y = x, because they are inverse functions. That reflection explains the domain and range swap and the asymptote turning from horizontal to vertical.

Worked example. Sketch y = e^(x−2) + 1, stating the asymptote and intercepts.

translation 2 right, 1 up
asymptote y = 1 (was y = 0)
y-intercept: e⁻² + 1 = 0.135 + 1 = 1.135
no x-intercept (the curve stays above y = 1)

Growth and decay models

exponential model: N = N_0 e^(kt)
  k > 0 growth;  k < 0 decay
half-life: time for N to halve = ln 2 / |k| (decay)
doubling time = ln 2 / k (growth)

Worked example (decay). A radioactive sample decays as N = 500e^(−0.02t) with t in years. Find the initial amount, the amount after 50 years, and the half-life.

t = 0: N = 500
at t = 50: 500e⁻¹ = 500 × 0.3679 = 184
half-life: 500e^(-0.02t) = 250  →  e^(-0.02t) = 0.5
-0.02t = ln 0.5 = -0.693  →  t = 34.7 years

Worked example 2 (growth). Bacteria grow as N = 200e^(0.15t), t in hours. When does the population reach 1000?

200e^(0.15t) = 1000  →  e^(0.15t) = 5
0.15t = ln 5 = 1.609  →  t = 10.7 hours

Logarithmic scales in context

Some quantities span so many orders of magnitude that a logarithmic scale is used: pH for acidity, the Richter scale for earthquakes, decibels for sound. A change of 1 on the Richter scale means 10 times the amplitude, so an increase of 3 means 10³ = 1000 times.

Worked example. Two earthquakes differ by 2.4 on the Richter scale. How many times larger is the amplitude of the stronger?

difference 2.4 in log_10  →  10².4 = 251 times

Change of base and log-linearisation

Calculators offer base 10 and base e only, so any other base is converted with the change-of-base formula. The same formula turns a power law into a straight line, which is how experimental data is tested for exponential behaviour.

change of base: log_a(x) = log_b(x)/log_b(a)
so log_2(7) = ln 7 / ln 2 = log 7 / log 2 = 2.807

if y = a x^n then log y = log a + n log x  (straight line in log-log)
if y = a b^x then log y = log a + x log b  (straight line in log-x)

Worked example 1. Evaluate log_5(30).

log 30 / log 5 = 1.477/0.699 = 2.113

Worked example 2 (log-linearisation). Data gives a straight line when log y is plotted against x, with gradient 0.3 and intercept 1.4. Find the model connecting y and x.

log y = 1.4 + 0.3x
so y = 10¹.4 × 10^(0.3x) = 25.1 × 2.00^x
an exponential growth model with a = 25.1 and b = 2.0

Worked example 3 (inequality). Solve 2^x < 100.

take logs (base 2 is increasing, so the inequality is preserved)
x < log_2 100 = log 100/log 2 = 6.64

Taking logs of both sides is safe for any base greater than 1 because the log function is increasing; a base between 0 and 1 would reverse the inequality, which never arises in these models.

Rewriting any exponential in base e

Any exponential a^x can be written as e^(kx), because a = e^(ln a). This is why every growth model in the syllabus uses e: the base is absorbed into the constant.

a^x = e^(x ln a)
so 2^x = e^(0.693x);  5^x = e^(1.609x);  0.8^x = e^(-0.223x)

Worked example. Express y = 300(1.04)^t in the form y = 300e^(kt), and state the annual percentage rate it represents.

1.04 = e^k  →  k = ln 1.04 = 0.0392
y = 300e^(0.0392t)
the rate is 3.92 per year in continuous-compounding form, while the
annual multiplier is still 1.04 (4 per cent per year)

Worked example 2. A model is N = 80e^(0.25t). Rewrite it as N = 80b^t and find the percentage growth per unit time.

b = e⁰.25 = 1.284
N = 80(1.284)^t, so growth is 28.4 per cent per unit time

The two forms describe the same curve; the e-form is convenient for calculus, the b-form for reading off a percentage rate. Converting between them is a standard exam demand.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Evaluate) Find log₄64. Answer: 3, since 4³ = 64.
  2. (Laws) Simplify log 8 + log 5 − log 2. Answer: log(40/2) = log 20.
  3. (Solve log) Solve log₃x = 2. Answer: x = 3² = 9.
  4. (Solve exponential) Solve 2^x = 50. Answer: x = log 50/log 2 = 1.699/0.301 = 5.64.
  5. (Quadratic) Solve e^(2x) − 3e^x + 2 = 0. Answer: y = e^x → y² − 3y + 2 = 0 → y = 1 or 2 → x = 0 or ln 2 = 0.693.
  6. (Combine) Write 3 ln 2 − ln 4 as a single logarithm. Answer: ln 8 − ln 4 = ln 2.
  7. (Inverse) Find the inverse of f(x) = e^(3x). Answer: y = e^(3x) → ln y = 3x → f⁻¹(x) = (ln x)/3.
  8. (Model) A car's value is V = 15000e^(−0.2t). Find its value after 4 years. Answer: 15000e^(−0.8) = 15000 × 0.4493 = 6740 pounds.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • log(x + y) is not log x + log y: the product law applies to products only; there is no law for the log of a sum.
  • Forgetting the domain: logs need a positive argument. Roots that make an argument negative or zero are rejected, explicitly.
  • Dividing by log: log 20/log 3 is not log(20/3); the quotient law is for two logs, not a quotient of logs.
  • Base consistency: mixing log₁₀ and ln inside one equation is an error; convert first (ln x = log x / log e).
  • Power law misuse: (log x)² is not 2 log x. Only log(x²) = 2 log x.
  • Quadratic substitution: after solving for y, the answer is x — convert back and solve the exponential equation.
  • Half-life sign: with a decay model k is negative, so half-life = ln 2/|k|; dropping the modulus gives a negative time.
  • Sketch asymptotes: state the asymptote after transformations; e^x + c has asymptote y = c, not y = 0.

title: Coordinate Geometry — Study Notes
content:
Coordinate Geometry

Cambridge International AS & A Level Mathematics 9709, Paper 1. Every question in this topic gives you some information about points and lines and asks you to turn it into an equation or a length. Decide which kind of information you have, then use the matching method below.

Which method to use

  • Two points given: find the distance, midpoint or gradient between them, or the perpendicular bisector.
  • A point and a direction given: build the line from the point and a gradient.
  • Two lines given: find where they meet, or check whether they are parallel or perpendicular.
  • A circle given: read off its centre and radius, or test a point against it.

Distance, midpoint and the perpendicular bisector

For A(x₁, y₁) and B(x₂, y₂): AB = √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²), the midpoint is ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2) and the gradient is (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁). The perpendicular bisector of AB passes through the midpoint and has the negative reciprocal of the gradient of AB.

Worked case: P(−2, 6) and Q(4, −2). PQ = √(36 + 64) = 10. The midpoint is (1, 2). The gradient of PQ is −8/6 = −4/3, so the bisector has gradient 3/4. Then y − 2 = 3/4(x − 1), which gives 3x − 4y + 5 = 0.

A line from a point and a direction

A straight line is fixed by one point on it and its gradient. Parallel lines share a gradient. Perpendicular lines have gradients whose product is −1. Once you have both, substitute into y − y₁ = m(x − x₁) and rearrange into the form the question asks for.

Parallel case: the line through (−3, 1) parallel to 5x − 2y + 4 = 0. Rearranging gives y = 5/2 x + 2, so m = 5/2. Then y − 1 = 5/2(x + 3), which rearranges to 5x − 2y + 17 = 0.

Perpendicular case: the line through (6, −1) perpendicular to 2x + 7y = 3. The given gradient is −2/7, so the required gradient is 7/2. Then y + 1 = 7/2(x − 6), which gives 7x − 2y − 44 = 0.

Where two lines meet

A common point satisfies both equations, so solve them simultaneously. If the gradients differ, the lines meet exactly once. If the gradients are equal, the lines are parallel: substitution then gives a false statement (no meeting point) or an identity (the same line).

Example: 3x + y = 7 and x − 2y = −4. The second equation gives x = 2y − 4. Substituting gives 7y − 12 = 7, so y = 19/7 and x = 10/7. The lines meet at (10/7, 19/7).

Where a line meets a circle

Substitute the line into the circle's equation. The result is a quadratic, and its discriminant tells you whether there are two intersection points, one (a tangent), or none. Solve the quadratic only when you need the coordinates.

Example: y = x + 1 and x² + y² = 13. Substituting gives 2x² + 2x − 12 = 0, so x² + x − 6 = 0 and (x + 3)(x − 2) = 0. The points are (−3, −2) and (2, 3).

Circles

The centre–radius form is (x − a)² + (y − b)² = r², with centre (a, b). For the general form x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0, complete the square in x and in y: the centre is (−g, −f) and r² = g² + f² − c. To test a point, substitute it into the left-hand side of the centre–radius form and compare with r². A smaller value means inside the circle, equal means on it, and larger means outside.

Example: x² + y² − 8x + 2y − 8 = 0 becomes (x − 4)² + (y + 1)² = 25, so the centre is (4, −1) and the radius is 5. The point (1, 2) gives 9 + 9 = 18, which is less than 25, so it lies inside.

Tangents and normals

A tangent touches the circle at one point and is perpendicular to the radius at that point. A normal is the line through the point and the centre. Find the gradient of the radius, then take the negative reciprocal for the tangent.

Example: the point (8, 2) lies on the circle above, since 4² + 3² = 25. The radius has gradient 3/4, so the tangent has gradient −4/3 and equation 4x + 3y − 38 = 0. The normal has gradient 3/4 and equation 3x − 4y − 16 = 0, which passes through the centre (4, −1).

Exam technique

  • Draw a rough diagram first. It shows whether a point should lie inside or outside a circle before any algebra is done.
  • With a "show that" instruction, finish with the exact expression that was asked for.
  • To check a tangent, confirm that the distance from the centre to the line equals the radius.
  • Keep fractions exact until the final line; rounding early is the most common cause of a lost mark.

title: Electricity & Circuits — Study Notes
content:
Electricity & Circuits

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): simple circuits, current, p.d., resistance, series/parallel, electrical safety, practical electricity.

1. Circuit symbols & current

Conventional current: + → − (electron flow opposite). I = Q/t. Ammeter in series; voltmeter in parallel.

2. Current, p.d., e.m.f.

  • Current: rate of charge flow; same everywhere in series.
  • p.d.: energy per coulomb across a component; e.m.f.: electrical energy per coulomb given by the source.

3. Resistance

  • R = V/I. Ohmic conductor: V ∝ I at constant temperature.
  • Series: R = R₁ + R₂ + …; same current; p.d. shares in proportion to R.
  • Parallel: 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂; same p.d.; current splits (inverse-R share).
  • Resistance ∝ length, ∝ 1/area (wires).

4. Components

Fixed/variable resistors, LDR (light ↑ R ↓), thermistor (T ↑ R ↓), diode/LED (one-way), relay, filament lamp (R grows as T rises — V–I curve flattens).

5. Power and energy

P = VI = I²R = V²/R; E = VIt. Fuse rating just above normal current; earth wire, double insulation, circuit breakers (trip quickly, resettable).

Example: 230 V, 2 A heater: P = 460 W; correct fuse 3 A or 5 A.

6. Digital electronics basics (syllabus 4.5 context)

Analogue vs digital; logic gates drive outputs from inputs (see CS link); sensors feed comparator-style circuits.

Exam tips: series: current same; parallel: p.d. same — say which before calculating; always compute total resistance first in mixed circuits.

title: IGCSE Physics: Thermal Physics
content:
IGCSE Physics: Thermal Physics

Cambridge IGCSE Physics 0625 (2026–2028), Topic 2 Thermal physics: statements 2.1 Kinetic particle model of matter, 2.2 Thermal properties and temperature, and 2.3 Transfer of thermal energy. Heat is the traffic of energy between hot and cold objects, and the particle model explains every thermal phenomenon in the syllabus: expansion, pressure, changes of state, conduction, convection and radiation. Paper 4 loves the particle explanations as much as the calculations, so both are built here from the same model.

States of matter and changes of state

All matter is made of tiny particles in constant motion, and the three states differ in how those particles are arranged and how they move.

StateArrangementMotionShape and volume
SolidClose-packed regular rows, touchingVibrate about fixed positionsFixed shape and fixed volume
LiquidClose together but disorderedSlide over each otherTakes the shape of the container; fixed volume
GasFar apart, random, filling the containerFast, random, straight-line between collisionsNo fixed shape or volume

When a substance is heated, energy is transferred to its thermal store and the particles move faster. On a heating curve the temperature rises until a change of state begins; during melting or boiling the temperature stays constant while the energy goes into breaking the forces between particles rather than into speed. The names of the changes are: melting (solid to liquid), freezing (liquid to solid), boiling or vaporisation (liquid to gas), condensation (gas to liquid), sublimation (solid straight to gas, as with dry ice).

The particle model of pressure and Brownian motion

Gas pressure arises because particles collide with the walls of their container: each collision gives a tiny push, and billions of pushes per second produce a steady pressure. Squeezing the same particles into a smaller volume raises the collision rate per unit area and so raises the pressure; heating a gas at fixed volume makes the particles move faster and collide harder and more often, again raising the pressure.

Brownian motion is the random jiggling of smoke particles seen under a microscope. The smoke particles are bombarded unevenly by fast-moving invisible air molecules, and the bigger the imbalance of hits at any instant, the bigger the lurch. It is direct evidence that gas particles move randomly and continuously (Supplement: the uneven collisions and their random distribution are the explanation demanded).

The gas laws and the absolute scale of temperature

For a fixed mass of gas, three qualitative rules are examined at Core level: heating a gas at constant pressure makes it expand (and cooling makes it contract); compressing a gas at constant temperature raises its pressure; and the relationships are summarised by the particle model above. The Celsius scale is everyday but its zero is arbitrary; the kelvin scale starts at absolute zero, the temperature at which particles have the minimum possible energy.

temperature in kelvin = temperature in degrees Celsius + 273        T (K) = θ (°C) + 273

Supplement: Boyle's law. For a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature, pressure and volume are inversely proportional:

p V = constant        p1 V1 = p2 V2
  • p: pressure in pascals (Pa), positive; V: volume in cubic metres (m³) or any consistent unit. Both are scalars.
  • The product pV stays constant only while the temperature and the amount of gas are fixed.

Doubling the pressure halves the volume; a graph of p against V is a curve (inverse proportion), while a graph of p against 1/V is a straight line through the origin — a standard Paper 4 graph question.

Thermal expansion of solids, liquids and gases

Almost everything expands when heated: the particles move faster and push further apart. Everyday consequences include gaps between railway rails and bridge sections, expansion loops in power cables, the bimetallic strip in a thermostat (two metals expand by different amounts, so the strip bends and breaks a circuit), and the difficulty of undoing a metal jar lid, which can be loosened by running hot water over it so the metal lid expands more than the glass. Liquids expand more than solids for the same temperature rise, and gases expand most of all.

The particle explanation is a Supplement statement: heating increases the average separation of the particles because their increased energy makes them swing wider about their positions in a solid, slide further apart in a liquid, and occupy a larger volume in a gas at the same pressure. Thermometers work because liquids expand predictably with temperature: the liquid column rises in a narrow capillary, making a small volume change visible as a large length change.

Specific heat capacity

Equal masses of different substances need different amounts of energy to warm by the same temperature: water resists temperature change far more than sand, which is why coastal towns have mild climates and why water makes an excellent coolant in car engines and central heating. That property is the specific heat capacity:

energy transferred = mass x specific heat capacity x temperature change        E = m c Δθ
  • E: energy transferred in joules (J); m: mass in kilograms (kg).
  • c: specific heat capacity in joules per kilogram per degree Celsius (J kg⁻¹ °C⁻¹, numerically the same as J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹). A scalar.
  • Δθ: temperature change in degrees Celsius (°C) or kelvin (K). Temperature rises give a positive energy input; falls give energy out.

Supplement: measuring c experimentally. An electrical heater warms a well-lagged block of the substance; an ammeter and voltmeter give the electrical energy E = V I t, and a thermometer gives the temperature rise. Plot temperature against time; the gradient gives the rate of heating, and c = V I t / (m Δθ). Lagging reduces heat loss to the surroundings, the stirrer evens out hot spots, and the same method compares two materials by heating equal masses with the same heater for the same time.

Melting, boiling and evaporation

Melting and boiling happen at fixed temperatures for a pure substance at fixed pressure: 0 °C and 100 °C for pure water at one atmosphere. On a heating curve, plateaus mark the changes of state, and the energy supplied during a plateau is the latent heat: the energy needed to change the state of 1 kg without any temperature change (latent heat of fusion for melting, of vaporisation for boiling). The plateau exists because the energy breaks intermolecular attractions rather than increasing particle speed.

Evaporation is different from boiling and happens at any temperature. Particles at the liquid surface occasionally escape with above-average energy, so the average energy of those left falls and the liquid cools. Evaporation is faster when the temperature is higher, the surface area is larger, and a draught carries vapour away — the three factors Paper 4 expects in an evaporation-and-cooling explanation. Boiling happens throughout the liquid at a fixed temperature, with bubbles of vapour forming internally; evaporation happens only at the surface, at all temperatures, and cools the liquid left behind. Wet skin cools you because the water evaporates and takes the highest-energy particles with it.

Conduction

Conduction is the transfer of energy through a substance without the substance itself moving. In metals, the free electrons carry energy quickly from the hot end to the cold end, which is why metals are good conductors; in non-metals the energy passes only as vibrations handed along the vibrating particles, which is much slower. In gases and most liquids, conduction is poor because the particles are too far apart to pass on vibrations efficiently — hence insulating materials trap air in fibres or foam.

The core practical comparison: rods of different materials are coated with wax at one end and held over a heat source; the wax falls first from the best conductor. Metals come out in order (copper and aluminium good, steel poorer), while wood, plastic and glass barely conduct at all.

Convection

Convection is the transfer of energy by the movement of a fluid itself. Heating a fluid lowers its density: the warm parcel rises, cooler fluid sinks to take its place, and a convection current sets up. This is how radiators heat a room (hot air rises from the radiator, cools at the ceiling and returns down the far wall), how a kettle boils from the bottom, how sea breezes blow from sea to land by day, and how the element of a domestic water heater sits at the bottom so the whole tank warms. Convection requires a fluid — it cannot occur in a solid, and in a vacuum there is no medium at all.

Radiation

Radiation is the transfer of energy by electromagnetic waves, mainly infrared. It needs no medium, so it is the only way energy crosses the vacuum of space — which is why the Sun's heat reaches the Earth. The rate of emission and absorption depends on surface colour and texture: dull black surfaces are the best emitters and the best absorbers; shiny white or silvered surfaces are the poorest and reflect most radiation.

ApplicationSurface choice and reason
House radiatorMatte dark paint: emits radiation well
Hot-water tank and pipesSilvered foil: reduces radiation loss
Thermos flaskSilvered glass walls on both sides: minimises radiated loss in and out
Ice box / cool boxShiny white outside: reflects incoming radiation
Desert survival bagShiny side outwards in hot sun: reflects the Sun's radiation

Supplement: the Earth's energy balance. The Earth absorbs short-wavelength radiation from the Sun and radiates longer-wavelength infrared back to space. At equilibrium the two rates match and the average temperature is steady; greenhouse gases absorb some outgoing infrared and re-radiate it downwards, raising the equilibrium temperature. More greenhouse gas shifts the balance and warms the surface — the physics behind climate change.

Worked example: heating water

A 2.0 kg kettle of water is heated from 15 °C to 100 °C. The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J kg⁻¹ °C⁻¹. The kettle's heater supplies 2400 W.

energy needed = m c Δθ = 2.0 x 4200 x (100 - 15) = 714 000 J
time = energy / power = 714 000 / 2400 = 298 s (about 5.0 minutes)

Real kettles take longer, because some energy warms the kettle body and is lost to the air — which is exactly why the efficiency of a kettle is less than 100 per cent. To boil the water away would need far more energy again, because of the latent heat of vaporisation.

Second calculation: a 0.50 kg block of aluminium (c = 900 J kg⁻¹ °C⁻¹) cools from 80 °C to 25 °C. Energy released = 0.50 × 900 × 55 = 24 750 J ≈ 25 kJ. Cooling gives out the same energy that heating took in; only the sign of the temperature change differs.

Common mistakes

  • Saying heat rises. Heat is energy, not a substance; it is the warm fluid that rises because it is less dense.
  • Confusing temperature with internal energy: temperature measures the average energy per particle, while internal energy is the total energy of all particles.
  • Forgetting that during melting or boiling the temperature stays constant even though energy is still being supplied.
  • Mixing up conduction (through a substance), convection (by a moving fluid) and radiation (by waves, no medium). A vacuum flask blocks all three: silvered walls (radiation), vacuum gap (conduction and convection), foam or stopper (conduction).
  • Using degrees Celsius where kelvin are required in a gas-law calculation; always convert with T = θ + 273 before using pV = constant relationships.
  • Putting mass in grams into E = mcΔθ; the unit J kg⁻¹ °C⁻¹ demands kilograms.
  • Describing evaporation as boiling; evaporation occurs at any temperature, only at the surface, and cools the remaining liquid.
  • Claiming particles expand; it is the average separation between the particles that increases.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 4, 3 marks). A 500 g block of copper (c = 390 J kg⁻¹ °C⁻¹) is heated from 20 °C to 120 °C. Calculate the energy transferred.

Answer: E = mcΔθ = 0.50 × 390 × 100 = 19 500 J = 19.5 kJ.

Question 2 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Explain, using the particle model, why a metal lid on a glass jar loosens under hot water.

Answer: The hot water heats both the lid and the jar. The particles in the metal gain energy and vibrate with greater amplitude, so their average separation increases more than that of the glass particles, because metals expand more than glass for the same temperature rise. The metal lid therefore becomes slightly larger in diameter than the neck of the jar and turns more easily.

Question 3 (Paper 2 style). Which change does not occur at a fixed temperature? A ice melting at 0 °C; B water boiling at 100 °C; C water evaporating from a puddle; D steam condensing at 100 °C. Answer: C. Evaporation occurs at any temperature and is not a fixed-temperature change of state.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 6 marks). Explain how a vacuum flask keeps a drink hot, referring to all three methods of thermal energy transfer.

Answer: The double-walled glass vessel has a vacuum between the walls, and a vacuum contains no particles, so energy cannot be transferred across the gap by conduction or convection. Both walls are silvered to reduce radiation: the shiny surfaces are poor emitters and poor absorbers, so little infrared escapes. The plastic stopper and foam supports are poor conductors and block convection in the air above the liquid. Together these keep energy in the drink for hours.

Question 5 (Paper 6 style). Describe an experiment to compare how well different materials conduct heat.

Answer: Fix rods of equal length and thickness made from the different materials, each coated at the far end with an equal blob of wax, over identical heat sources. Start together and record the time for each wax blob to fall. The shortest time identifies the best conductor. Keep the source, rod dimensions, coating thickness and starting temperature identical so the comparison is fair, and repeat to check the ranking.

Question 6 (Paper 4, 3 marks). A gas is trapped in a sealed syringe at 100 cm³ and 20 °C. It is heated to 87 °C at constant pressure. Find its new volume.

Answer: Convert first: 20 °C = 293 K, 87 °C = 360 K. At constant pressure V/T is constant, so V₂ = 100 × 360/293 = 123 cm³. (For a Core-level answer, the gas expands when heated at constant pressure, and the volume rises by roughly a quarter.)

From heat to the transfer of energy by waves: the next topic is Waves and Sound.

Equations and symbols

Thermal physics at 0625 is built on two energy equations — one for a change of temperature, one for a change of state — plus the power relation that turns either into a rate. The specific heat capacity and specific latent heat values are given in the exam, so the marks are in choosing the right equation and the right mass.

Heating and cooling

E = mcΔθ
Key: E = energy transferred to or from the substance (J); m = mass (kg); c = specific heat capacity (J/(kg °C)); Δθ (delta theta) = temperature change (°C). Use mcΔθ when the temperature changes but the state does not.

c(water) = 4200 J/(kg °C)
Key: the energy needed to raise 1 kg of water by 1 °C. Water's high value is why it is used as a coolant and why coastal climates are mild.

E = mL
Key: E = energy needed to change state (J); m = mass changing state (kg); L = specific latent heat (J/kg). Use it at a melting or boiling point, where the temperature stays constant while the state changes.

L(fusion, water) = 3.34 × 10⁵ J/kg and L(vaporisation, water) = 2.26 × 10⁶ J/kg
Key: L(fusion) melts or freezes 1 kg without changing temperature; L(vaporisation) boils or condenses it. Boiling takes far more energy than melting, which is why steam burns are worse than boiling-water burns at the same temperature.

E(total) = mcΔθ + mL
Key: the two stages of heating ice from below 0 °C to steam above 100 °C, added in sequence: warm the ice, melt it, warm the water, boil it, warm the steam. Each stage uses the equation that matches what is happening.

Rate of energy transfer

P = E / t
Key: P = power of the heater or the rate of energy transfer (W); E = energy transferred (J); t = time (s). Combined with mcΔθ this gives P = mcΔθ / t, the standard heater calculation.

efficiency = (energy gained by the substance / energy supplied) × 100%
Key: the useful gain is mcΔθ (J); the supplied energy is Pt (J). Heat lost to the surroundings is why a measured specific heat capacity often comes out higher than the data-book value.

Temperature and the gas laws

T(K) = θ(°C) + 273
Key: T = thermodynamic temperature (K); θ (theta) = Celsius temperature (°C). Gas-law ratios need kelvin: doubling 20 °C to 40 °C is not a doubling in kelvin.

p / T = constant (volume fixed)
Key: p = gas pressure (Pa); T = temperature (K). Heating a sealed container raises the pressure because the particles move faster and hit the walls harder and more often.

p₁V₁ = p₂V₂ (temperature fixed)
Key: p₁, V₁ = pressure and volume before (Pa, m³); p₂, V₂ = after. Compressing a gas at constant temperature raises its pressure in inverse proportion.

p₁V₁ / T₁ = p₂V₂ / T₂
Key: the combined form, with temperatures in kelvin. Any one of pressure, volume or temperature can be found if the other two change and the third is fixed.

The particle model as a rule set

pressure ∝ rate of collision × momentum change per collision
Key: the qualitative gas model behind every explanation mark: more particles per unit volume, or faster particles, means more forceful collisions with the container walls, hence a higher pressure.

title: IGCSE Mathematics: Simplifying and Expanding
content:
IGCSE Mathematics: Simplifying and Expanding

Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580 (2025–2027), section 2 Algebra and graphs: statements 2.1 Introduction to algebra, 2.2 Algebraic manipulation and 2.3 Algebraic fractions (Extended). Algebra is the language the rest of the course is written in, and this note is its grammar: what letters mean, how expressions are simplified and expanded, how they are factorised, and how algebraic fractions are handled. Every manipulation below is written out line by line, because on Paper 2 (non-calculator) the method marks are the marks — and on Paper 4 an unexplained jump is where sign errors hide.

What a letter means: an introduction to algebra

A letter in algebra is a placeholder for a number whose value can change (a variable) or for a number that is fixed but unknown (a constant). The expression 3x + 2 says: take a number, multiply it by 3, then add 2. Substitution is the reverse: if x = 5, then 3x + 2 = 3 × 5 + 2 = 15 + 2 = 17. Work in the given order — multiplication before addition — because the conventions of algebra are just the conventions of arithmetic with letters standing in for numbers.

  • 3x means 3 × x. Writing 3 × x with a multiplication sign is unnecessary, but writing 3x as 3 + x is a serious error.
  • x² means x × x, and 2x² means 2 × x × x — the index applies only to the x, not to the 2.
  • xy means x × y, and x(y + 2) means x multiplied by the whole bracket.
  • A term is a product of numbers and letters, such as 3x²; terms are separated by + and − signs.
  • Like terms have exactly the same letter part: 3x² and −7x² are like terms; 3x² and 3x are not.

Why letters work at all. A rule like a(b + c) = ab + ac is not a trick to memorise — it is the distributive property of arithmetic, true for every number, so writing it once with letters proves it for all cases at once instead of checking each one. That is the whole power of algebra: one line of symbols replaces a million examples.

Simplifying: collecting like terms

To simplify, gather the like terms and add their coefficients (the numbers in front). Work one letter part at a time and keep every sign with its term.

Simplify:  5x + 3y - 2x + 7 - y + 4

Group the x terms, then the y terms, then the numbers:
= 5x - 2x + 3y - y + 7 + 4        [terms rearranged; each sign travels with its term]
= (5 - 2)x + (3 - 1)y + (7 + 4)   [coefficients collected]
= 3x + 2y + 11

For expressions with powers, only identical letter parts can join:

Simplify:  4x² + 3x - x² + 2x - 9

= 4x² - x² + 3x + 2x - 9
= (4 - 1)x² + (3 + 2)x - 9
= 3x² + 5x - 9

The x² and x terms never combine: x² counts squares while x counts lengths, and they are different kinds of quantity — exactly why the index must match before terms are collected.

Expanding brackets

Expanding uses the distributive law: every term outside the bracket multiplies every term inside. The golden rule of signs is that a minus sign in front of a bracket changes the sign of everything inside.

Expand:  3(2x - 5)

= 3 × 2x + 3 x (-5)        [each term inside multiplied by 3]
= 6x - 15
Expand:  -(4x - 7)

= -1 × 4x + (-1) x (-7)    [a bracket with no number means x (-1)]
= -4x + 7

Two brackets multiply every term of the first by every term of the second. Writing each product on its own line prevents the classic dropped-term error:

Expand and simplify:  (2x + 3)(x - 5)

= 2x x x + 2x x (-5) + 3 x x + 3 x (-5)     [four products: each term x each term]
= 2x² - 10x + 3x - 15
= 2x² - 7x - 15

The pattern is sometimes called FOIL (First, Outer, Inner, Last), but the safe habit is the one above: systematic, complete, and it scales to three brackets:

Expand:  (x + 1)(x - 2)(x + 3)

First expand the first two brackets:
(x + 1)(x - 2) = x x x + x x (-2) + 1 x x + 1 x (-2) = x² - 2x + x - 2 = x² - x - 2
Now multiply by the third bracket, term by term:
(x² - x - 2)(x + 3) = x² x x + x² × 3 + (-x) x x + (-x) × 3 + (-2) x x + (-2) × 3
= x³ + 3x² - x² - 3x - 2x - 6
= x³ + 2x² - 5x - 6

Perfect squares deserve instant recognition: (x + 5)² = (x + 5)(x + 5) = x² + 10x + 25. The middle term is 2 × 5 × x = 10x, so (x + a)² = x² + 2ax + a². Writing (x + 5)² as x² + 25 is the single most common error in the whole of algebra.

Factorising

Factorising is expanding in reverse: writing a sum as a product. Every factorisation can be checked by expanding again, and on an exam that check costs seconds.

Common factors. Take out the highest factor of every term:

Factorise:  12x³ - 8x²

Highest common factor of 12x³ and 8x² is 4x²:
= 4x²(3x) + 4x²(-2)        [showing the division of each term]
= 4x²(3x - 2)

Factorising quadratics of the form x² + bx + c. Find two numbers that multiply to c and add to b:

Factorise:  x² + 7x + 12

Two numbers with product +12 and sum +7: 3 and 4 (both positive, since c and b are positive)
Check: 3 × 4 = 12 and 3 + 4 = 7
= (x + 3)(x + 4)

Expand to verify: (x + 3)(x + 4) = x² + 4x + 3x + 12 = x² + 7x + 12  ✓

Signs follow from the product and sum: for x² − 2x − 15 the product is −15 and the sum is −2, so the numbers are −5 and +3 (the larger number carries the sign of the sum), giving (x − 5)(x + 3).

Factorising ax² + bx + c. When the coefficient of x² is not 1, multiply a × c and split the middle term:

Factorise:  6x² + 11x - 10

a x c = 6 x (-10) = -60; find two numbers with product -60 and sum +11: +15 and -4
Split the middle term:  6x² + 15x - 4x - 10
Factorise in pairs:     3x(2x + 5) - 2(2x + 5)        [first pair gives 3x, second gives -2]
Take out (2x + 5):      (2x + 5)(3x - 2)

Expand to verify: 6x² - 4x + 15x - 10 = 6x² + 11x - 10  ✓

Difference of two squares. Whenever an expression is two squares subtracted, x² − a² = (x + a)(x − a), because the middle terms cancel when expanded: (x + a)(x − a) = x² − ax + ax − a² = x² − a². So 9x² − 25 = (3x + 5)(3x − 5).

Completing the square (Extended). Rewrite x² + bx as a square minus a correction:

Write x² + 6x - 7 in the form (x + p)² + q

x² + 6x - 7 = (x + 3)² - 3² - 7        [half of 6 is 3; (x+3)² introduces +9, so subtract 9]
= (x + 3)² - 9 - 7
= (x + 3)² - 16

This form reads off the turning point at once: the minimum value is −16, at x = −3. For 2x² + 8x − 5, take the 2 out first: 2(x² + 4x) − 5 = 2[(x + 2)² − 4] − 5 = 2(x + 2)² − 13.

ExpressionFactorisationHow to spot it
ax² + bxx(ax + b)Common factor: every term shares an x
x² + bx + c(x + p)(x + q) with pq = c, p + q = bFind the number pair with product c and sum b
ax² + bx + c(px + q)(rx + s)Split the middle term using a × c, then factorise in pairs
x² − a²(x + a)(x − a)Difference of two squares: a subtraction of two square terms
x² + 2ax + a²(x + a)²Perfect square: first and last terms are squares and the middle is twice their product

The order matters: take out a common factor before looking for any pattern, and check every factorisation by re-expanding. A table like this is worth copying into revision cards, because recognising the shape is faster in the exam than deriving it.

Algebraic fractions (Extended)

Algebraic fractions obey exactly the same rules as ordinary fractions — and it is worth knowing why those rules are what they are. Multiplication multiplies tops and bottoms because a fraction is a product. Division asks how many of one fraction fit into another, and the answer is the reciprocal: 3/4 ÷ 1/2 asks how many halves fit into three quarters, and the answer is 1½, which is 3/4 × 2/1 = 3/2. Dividing by a fraction is the same as multiplying by its reciprocal — the rule is not arbitrary; it is what division means.

Simplify:  (x² - 9) / (x² + 5x + 6)

Factorise top and bottom completely first:
= (x + 3)(x - 3) / [(x + 3)(x + 2)]
Cancel the common factor (x + 3):
= (x - 3) / (x + 2)        valid except where x + 3 = 0

Cancellation divides top and bottom by the same thing, which is legitimate; cancelling individual terms across a sum (writing (x + 3)/(x + 2) as 3/2) is not, because the top is not a product.

Express as a single fraction:  2/(x - 1) - 3/(x + 2)

The lowest common denominator is (x - 1)(x + 2):
= 2(x + 2) / [(x - 1)(x + 2)] - 3(x - 1) / [(x - 1)(x + 2)]     [each fraction multiplied by the missing factor]
= [2(x + 2) - 3(x - 1)] / [(x - 1)(x + 2)]                       [single denominator; brackets protect the signs]
= [2x + 4 - 3x + 3] / [(x - 1)(x + 2)]                           [expanding: -3 x -1 = +3]
= (7 - x) / [(x - 1)(x + 2)]
Multiply and divide:  (x² - 4)/(x + 5)  x  (x + 5)/(x + 2)

= [(x + 2)(x - 2)(x + 5)] / [(x + 5)(x + 2)]     [factorise, then multiply tops and bottoms]
= x - 2

Worked example: a full simplification

Simplify and factorise completely: 3(x + 2)² − 2(x + 2)(x − 1) − 5x.

Expand (x + 2)² first:   (x + 2)(x + 2) = x² + 2x + 2x + 4 = x² + 4x + 4
So 3(x + 2)² = 3x² + 12x + 12

Expand (x + 2)(x - 1):    x x x + x x (-1) + 2 x x + 2 x (-1) = x² - x + 2x - 2 = x² + x - 2
So -2(x + 2)(x - 1) = -2x² - 2x + 4

Put everything together:
3x² + 12x + 12 - 2x² - 2x + 4 - 5x
= 3x² - 2x² + 12x - 2x - 5x + 12 + 4
= x² + 5x + 16

The expression x² + 5x + 16 does not factorise over the integers (no pair multiplies to 16 and adds to 5),
so the simplified form is the final answer.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Writing (x + 5)² as x² + 25. Squaring a bracket gives a middle term: x² + 10x + 25.
  • Dropping a minus sign when expanding a bracket with a minus in front: −(3x − 4) = −3x + 4, not −3x − 4.
  • Cancelling a single term across a sum: (x + 3)/(x + 2) cannot be simplified by cancelling x.
  • Collecting unlike terms: 3x² + 5x is already simplified; nothing more can join.
  • Losing the sign of a term when rearranging: 5 − 2x written as 2x − 5 flips the expression.
  • Forgetting to divide every term when taking out a common factor: 12x³ − 8x² = 4x²(3x − 2), and the −2 must be checked by re-expanding.
  • On Paper 2, leaving a decimal where an exact fraction or surd is required — without a calculator, exact answers are the point.
  • Assuming x² + bx + c always factorises; when no integer pair works (or the discriminant is negative), the expression is already final.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 2, 3 marks). Simplify fully: 4(2x − 3) − 3(x − 5).

Answer: 8x − 12 − 3x + 15 = 5x + 3. (Distribute the −3 correctly: −3 × −5 = +15.)

Question 2 (Paper 2, 4 marks). Factorise completely: 3x² − 27.

Answer: Take out the common factor 3: 3(x² − 9). Recognise the difference of two squares inside: 3(x + 3)(x − 3). Taking only one factor loses the second mark.

Question 3 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Expand and simplify (2x − 1)(x + 4).

Answer: 2x × x + 2x × 4 + (−1) × x + (−1) × 4 = 2x² + 8x − x − 4 = 2x² + 7x − 4.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Write (2x − 3)/(x + 1) − 2/(x − 2) as a single fraction in its simplest form.

Answer: Common denominator (x + 1)(x − 2): [(2x − 3)(x − 2) − 2(x + 1)] / [(x + 1)(x − 2)] = [2x² − 4x − 3x + 6 − 2x − 2] / [(x + 1)(x − 2)] = (2x² − 9x + 4) / [(x + 1)(x − 2)], which factorises to (2x − 1)(x − 4)/[(x + 1)(x − 2)] and no longer cancels.

Question 5 (Paper 2, 3 marks). Express 2x² + 12x − 7 in the form 2(x + a)² + b.

Answer: 2(x² + 6x) − 7 = 2[(x + 3)² − 9] − 7 = 2(x + 3)² − 18 − 7 = 2(x + 3)² − 25. So a = 3, b = −25.

Question 6 (Paper 4, 3 marks). Given f(x) = (x² − 4)/(x² + x − 2), simplify f(x) and state the value of x for which it is undefined.

Answer: f(x) = (x + 2)(x − 2)/[(x + 2)(x − 1)] = (x − 2)/(x − 1). It is undefined where the original denominator is zero: x² + x − 2 = (x + 2)(x − 1) = 0, so x = −2 or x = 1.

Once expressions are in hand, equations solve for the unknowns they contain.

title: Respiration, Muscles and the Internal Environment Revision Notes
content:
Respiration, Muscles and the Internal Environment A2 Level Biology

Edexcel IAL Biology WBI15, Topic 7. Respiration releases energy as ATP for muscle contraction. Homeostasis keeps the internal environment stable, and the kidney is central to this. The topic links biochemistry to physiology.

Aerobic Respiration Mechanics and Steps

Aerobic respiration is the overall reaction of splitting the respiratory substrate to release carbon dioxide as a waste product and reuniting hydrogen with atmospheric oxygen with the release of large amounts of energy. Respiration is a stepped process, with each step controlled and catalysed by a specific intracellular enzyme, though names of specific enzymes are not required. Glycolysis takes place in the cytoplasm, where glucose is phosphorylated using ATP and split into two pyruvate molecules, yielding a net gain of ATP produced by substrate-level phosphorylation, reduced coenzyme (reduced NAD), and pyruvate. The link reaction takes place in the mitochondrial matrix, converting pyruvate to acetyl coenzyme A via decarboxylation and dehydrogenation, producing carbon dioxide and reduced NAD. The Krebs cycle takes place in the matrix, involving a series of oxidation-reduction reactions that completely oxidise glucose derivatives, releasing carbon dioxide by decarboxylation, producing ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation, and generating reduced NAD and reduced FAD by dehydrogenation. Oxidative phosphorylation takes place on the inner mitochondrial membrane, associated with the electron transport chain in mitochondria, where electrons passed along carriers release energy to pump protons into the intermembrane space, establishing a proton gradient for chemiosmosis where protons flow back through ATP synthase to synthesise ATP, with oxygen acting as the final electron acceptor.

  • Overall reaction: C6H12O6 + 6O2 yields 6CO2 + 6H2O + large amount of ATP.
  • Glycolysis: cytoplasm, phosphorylation of hexoses, substrate-level phosphorylation, production of pyruvate, reduced NAD, and ATP.
  • Link reaction and Krebs cycle: mitochondrial matrix, complete oxidation, decarboxylation producing CO2, substrate-level phosphorylation producing ATP, dehydrogenation producing reduced NAD and reduced FAD.
  • Oxidative phosphorylation: inner mitochondrial membrane, electron transport chain, chemiosmosis, ATP synthase.

Anaerobic Respiration and Lactate Metabolism

In the absence of oxygen, anaerobic respiration relies solely on glycolysis. In mammalian cells, pyruvate accepts hydrogen from reduced NAD to form lactate, catalysed by lactate dehydrogenase, which regenerates oxidised NAD so that glycolysis can continue to produce a small net amount of ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation. After a period of anaerobic respiration in animals, the accumulated lactate is removed by being transported in the blood to the liver, where a proportion is oxidised back to pyruvate and then converted into glucose or glycogen, or respired aerobically, requiring an extra volume of oxygen known as the oxygen debt.

  • Role of glycolysis: phosphorylation of hexoses, production of ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation, reduced coenzyme, pyruvate and lactate.
  • Fate of lactate: transported to the liver, oxidised to pyruvate, converted to glucose or glycogen, or respired.

Worked Example: Calculate the volume of carbon dioxide produced if an organism consumes 20 cm³ of oxygen and has an RQ of 0.85.

  • Step 1: State the formula for respiratory quotient: RQ = volume of CO2 produced ÷ volume of O2 consumed.
  • Step 2: Rearrange the formula to solve for volume of CO2: volume of CO2 = RQ × volume of O2 consumed.
  • Step 3: Substitute the given values: volume of CO2 = 0.85 × 20 cm³.
  • Step 4: Calculate the final answer: volume of CO2 = 17 cm³.

Respiratory Quotient and Core Practical Measurements

The respiratory quotient (RQ) is defined as the ratio of the volume of carbon dioxide produced to the volume of oxygen consumed over a given period. Core Practical 15 involves using an artificial hydrogen carrier, such as methylene blue or DCPIP as a redox indicator, to investigate respiration in yeast by timing how long it takes for the indicator to change colour as it accepts hydrogen ions released during respiratory pathways. Core Practical 16 involves using a simple respirometer to determine the rate of respiration and RQ of a suitable material, such as germinating seeds or small invertebrates, by measuring the movement of a coloured drop in a capillary tube with and without carbon dioxide absorbents like soda lime.

  • RQ formula: RQ = volume of CO2 produced ÷ volume of O2 consumed.
  • Carbohydrate RQ is approximately 1.0, lipid RQ is approximately 0.7, protein RQ is approximately 0.9.
  • Core Practical 15: artificial hydrogen carrier redox indicator, yeast respiration rate.
  • Core Practical 16: simple respirometer, germinating seeds or small invertebrates, soda lime to absorb CO2.

Skeletal Muscles and Contraction Mechanism

Skeletal muscles, tendons, the skeleton, and ligaments interact to enable movement, operating via antagonistic muscle pairs where one muscle contracts (agonist) to pull a bone while the opposing muscle relaxes, consisting of extensors that straighten a limb and flexors that bend it. Mammalian skeletal muscle fibres are multinucleate cells containing myofibrils made of repeating units called sarcomeres, delineated by Z lines. Structurally and physiologically, slow twitch muscle fibres are adapted for endurance with high myoglobin content, numerous mitochondria, and a dense capillary network relying on aerobic respiration, whereas fast twitch muscle fibres are adapted for short, intense bursts of speed with fewer mitochondria, less myoglobin, a rich supply of glycogen, and reliance on anaerobic glycolysis. The process of contraction of skeletal muscle is explained by the sliding filament theory, where calcium ions (Ca2+) released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum bind to troponin, causing tropomyosin to shift and expose binding sites on actin. Myosin heads bind to these sites to form cross-bridges, hydrolysing ATP via ATPase to execute the power stroke, pulling actin filaments towards the centre of the sarcomere and shortening it without changing the lengths of the myofilaments themselves, with fresh ATP binding to myosin to break the cross-bridge.

  • Interactions: antagonistic muscle pairs, extensors, flexors, tendons attach muscle to bone, ligaments attach bone to bone.
  • Muscle fibre structure: sarcolemma, sarcoplasmic reticulum, transverse tubules, myofibrils, sarcomeres with actin and myosin.
  • Slow vs fast twitch: myoglobin, mitochondria, capillary density, respiration type, speed of contraction, fatigue resistance.
  • Sliding filament theory: actin, myosin, troponin, tropomyosin, calcium ions, ATP, ATPase.

Cardiac Muscle, ECGs, and Control of Circulation

Cardiac muscle is myogenic, meaning it initiates its own contraction without external nervous stimulation. The normal electrical activity of the heart coordinates the heartbeat: the sinoatrial node (SAN) acts as the pacemaker sending waves of electrical excitation across the atria, the atrioventricular node (AVN) delays the impulse before passing it down the bundle of His, and Purkyne fibres conduct the excitation rapidly up through the walls of the ventricles from the apex, causing coordinated ventricular contraction. Electrocardiograms (ECGs) record the electrical activity of the heart, showing P waves (atrial depolarisation), QRS complexes (ventricular depolarisation), and T waves (ventricular repolarisation), which aid in the diagnosis of abnormal heart rhythms such as tachycardia, bradycardia, or fibrillation. Cardiac output is calculated as heart rate multiplied by stroke volume. Variations in ventilation and cardiac output enable rapid delivery of oxygen to tissues and the removal of carbon dioxide from them, controlled by the cardiovascular control centre and the ventilation centre located in the medulla oblongata, which respond to changes in blood pH, carbon dioxide concentration, and blood pressure detected by chemoreceptors and baroreceptors.

  • Myogenic nature: intrinsic rhythmicity of cardiac muscle cells.
  • Conduction pathway: SAN to atria, AVN with delay, bundle of His, Purkyne fibres to ventricles.
  • ECG interpretation: P wave, QRS complex, T wave, diagnosing arrhythmias.
  • Cardiac output formula: Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume.
  • Medulla oblongata: cardiovascular control centre and ventilation centre regulating heart rate and breathing rate.

Fight or Flight Response and Spirometer Traces

The role of adrenaline in the fight or flight response includes binding to specific receptors on target cells, activating second messenger systems that prepare the body for intense physical activity by increasing heart rate, dilating bronchioles, and redirecting blood flow away from non-essential organs towards skeletal muscles. Core Practical 17 involves investigating the effects of exercise on tidal volume, breathing rate, respiratory minute ventilation, and oxygen consumption using data from spirometer traces, allowing precise calculation of lung volumes and metabolic rates.

  • Adrenaline: hormone secreted by adrenal glands, binds to surface receptors, triggers intracellular cascade via cyclic AMP.
  • Spirometer parameters: tidal volume, breathing rate, respiratory minute ventilation (tidal volume × breathing rate), oxygen consumption.

Worked Example: Calculate the respiratory minute ventilation for a person with a tidal volume of 0.5 dm³ and a breathing rate of 14 breaths per minute.

  • Step 1: State the formula: respiratory minute ventilation = tidal volume × breathing rate.
  • Step 2: Substitute the values: respiratory minute ventilation = 0.5 dm³ × 14 breaths per minute.
  • Step 3: Calculate the product: respiratory minute ventilation = 7.0 dm³ min−1.

Homeostasis, Negative Feedback, and Thermoregulation

Negative feedback is a control mechanism where a change in a variable from its set point triggers a response that opposes the change, bringing the system back within narrow limits to maintain dynamic equilibrium, whereas positive feedback amplifies the initial change away from the set point. Homeostasis is the maintenance of a constant internal environment despite external fluctuations. During exercise, dynamic equilibrium is maintained, and the hypothalamus acts as the body's thermoregulation centre, monitoring core blood temperature via internal thermoreceptors and coordinating effector responses such as vasodilation, vasoconstriction, sweating, shivering, and behavioural changes to maintain optimal body temperature.

  • Negative feedback: sensor, coordinator, effector, corrective response reducing deviation from set point.
  • Positive feedback: deviation amplified, e.g., action potentials in neurones or oxytocin during birth.
  • Homeostasis: dynamic equilibrium, stability of internal environment.
  • Hypothalamus: thermoregulation control centre.

Kidney Structure and Osmoregulation

The gross and microscopic structure of the mammalian kidney includes the outer cortex, inner medulla, pelvis, ureter, and functional units called nephrons consisting of the Bowman's capsule, proximal convoluted tubule, loop of Henle, distal convoluted tubule, and collecting duct. Urea is produced in the liver from excess amino acids via deamination (details of the ornithine cycle are not required), and it is removed from the bloodstream along with water, ions, and glucose by ultrafiltration in the Bowman's capsule under high hydrostatic pressure created by the difference in diameter between the afferent and efferent arterioles. In the proximal tubule, essential solutes such as glucose, amino acids, and mineral ions are selectively reabsorbed into the blood capillaries by active transport and cotransport mechanisms. The loop of Henle acts as a countercurrent multiplier to establish a steep sodium ion concentration gradient in the medulla, which maximises the reabsorption of water from the collecting duct. Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus monitor blood water potential; when blood water potential drops, the posterior pituitary gland releases antidiuretic hormone (ADH), which travels to the kidneys and increases the permeability of the collecting duct cells to water via aquaporins, bringing about negative feedback control of mammalian plasma concentration and blood volume.

  • Gross structure: cortex, medulla, pelvis, ureter, renal artery, renal vein.
  • Urea production: deamination of excess amino acids in the liver.
  • Ultrafiltration: high hydrostatic pressure in glomerulus, basement membrane acting as a filter.
  • Proximal tubule reabsorption: active transport, cotransport, microvilli.
  • Loop of Henle: countercurrent multiplier, descending limb permeable to water, ascending limb impermeable to water and actively pumping sodium ions.
  • Osmoregulation loop: osmoreceptors in hypothalamus, posterior pituitary gland, ADH release, collecting duct permeability, negative feedback.

Exam tip: when you describe the link between ADH and water reabsorption, follow the steps in order: osmoreceptors detect water potential, posterior pituitary releases ADH, collecting duct walls become more permeable, water is reabsorbed into blood by osmosis.

Gene Control via Transcription Factors

Genes can be switched on and off by DNA transcription factors, which are proteins that bind to specific base sequences on DNA either promoting or blocking RNA polymerase binding. Peptide hormones act extracellularly by binding to cell surface membrane receptors and activating second messenger systems that trigger intracellular cascades involving transcription factors. In contrast, steroid hormones, being lipid-soluble, pass directly through the phospholipid bilayer of the cell membrane, bind to intracellular receptors in the cytoplasm or nucleus, and the hormone-receptor complex acts directly as a transcription factor to switch specific genes on or off.

  • Transcription factors: proteins regulating transcription by binding to promoter regions.
  • Peptide hormones: hydrophilic, bind to surface receptors, use second messengers.
  • Steroid hormones: hydrophobic, cross cell membrane, bind to intracellular receptors, act directly on DNA.

Typical mistakes

  • Confusing substrate-level phosphorylation in glycolysis and the Krebs cycle with oxidative phosphorylation at the electron transport chain. Correction: remember substrate-level phosphorylation involves direct transfer of a phosphate group to ADP from a reactive intermediate, whereas oxidative phosphorylation uses a proton gradient driven by electron transport.
  • Stating that the filaments shorten during muscle contraction in the sliding filament theory. Correction: actin and myosin filaments remain the same length; the sarcomere shortens because the filaments slide past each other, increasing the overlap.
  • Forgetting the exact sequence of osmoregulation. Correction: always start with blood water potential dropping, detected by osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus, leading to ADH release from the posterior pituitary, increasing collecting duct permeability.
  • Confusing the mechanism of peptide and steroid hormones. Correction: peptide hormones bind to extracellular surface receptors because they cannot cross the membrane, whereas steroid hormones cross membranes to bind intracellular receptors.

Exam-style questions

  1. Explain how chemiosmosis leads to the synthesis of ATP during oxidative phosphorylation in mitochondria. (Answer: electrons move along the electron transport chain releasing energy; this energy pumps protons from the matrix into the intermembrane space creating a proton gradient; protons flow down their electrochemical gradient back into the matrix through ATP synthase channels, driving the phosphorylation of ADP to ATP.)
  2. Describe the role of calcium ions in the contraction of skeletal muscle. (Answer: calcium ions are released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum into the sarcoplasm; they bind to troponin molecules; this causes tropomyosin to change shape and move away from the binding sites on actin, allowing myosin heads to form cross-bridges.)
  3. Explain how the loop of Henle acts as a countercurrent multiplier to enable the production of concentrated urine. (Answer: sodium and chloride ions are actively pumped out of the ascending limb into the medulla; this lowers the water potential of the tissue fluid in the medulla; water moves out of the descending limb by osmosis; the hairpin countercurrent arrangement multiplies the concentration gradient down to the tip of the loop, facilitating maximum water reabsorption in the collecting duct.)
  4. Explain how negative feedback maintains blood glucose or plasma concentration within narrow limits. (Answer: a deviation from the set point is detected by sensory receptors; this sends a signal to a coordination centre; effectors are stimulated to bring about a corrective response that opposes the original change, returning the variable back to the set point.)
  5. Compare the action of peptide and steroid hormones in controlling gene transcription. (Answer: peptide hormones are water-soluble and bind to cell surface receptors, activating second messenger cascades that indirectly affect transcription factors; steroid hormones are lipid-soluble, diffuse through the cell membrane, bind to intracellular receptors, and the complex acts directly as a transcription factor to initiate or inhibit transcription of target genes.)

Use these notes alongside past paper practice questions to test your application of biochemical pathways and physiological feedback loops. Next, revise Topic 8: Genetics, Populations, Evolution and Ecosystems.

title: Data Types and File Organisation
content:
Data Types and File Organisation

User-Defined Types

A user-defined type is derived from existing types. An enumerated type lists named values in order: TYPE Months = (Jan, Feb, Mar ...). Internally each value is an integer index starting at 0. Pointer types store a memory address; the dereference operator returns the value at that address, which is how linked structures reference their nodes. Set types store unordered collections of distinct values from an ordinal base type, supporting union, intersection and difference.

Records

A record groups related fields of different types under one identifier, for example a Student record with name : STRING and mark : INTEGER. Arrays of records are the standard structure for storing a table of items in memory.

File Organisation

  • Serial: records in insertion order; searching checks every record. Simple but slow.
  • Sequential: records kept in key order; binary search possible, but insertion needs rewriting.
  • Random (direct): a hashing function converts the key into a storage address, giving near-instant access. A poor hash causes collisions — two keys hashing to the same address — resolved by chaining or overflow areas.

Hashing

A common method is division hashing: Address = Key MOD TableSize. A good hash distributes keys evenly; load factor above roughly 70 percent degrades performance.

Exam tips: state the internal integer representation of enumerated values; define a collision before describing its resolution; compare the three file organisations in terms of search and insert cost.

title: Exam technique: Ethics, Security & Impact
content:
### What earns the marks
To earn full marks on this topic, students need to precisely name the threat and provide the matched defence. For example, when asked to explain a security threat, students should state the threat, such as pharming, and then describe the defence, such as keeping DNS servers and hosts files secure and checking HTTPS certificates. Command words like explain, describe, and justify are commonly used in this topic's questions. Students should also be able to apply ethical principles to scenarios, as outlined in the ACM/IEEE-CS/BCS codes, and show how they affect stakeholders and consequences.
### Traps
A common mistake is confusing phishing and pharming. Another error is not providing a matched defence for a given threat. Students should also avoid giving opinions instead of principle-based answers in ethics questions.
### Memory hooks
To remember the types of malware, students can use the mnemonic VIRUS: V for virus, I for intercept, R for ransomware, U for unsecured, and S for spyware. Another hook is to associate each type of threat with its corresponding defence. For example, malware is defended against with anti-malware software. Students can also use a diagram to illustrate the blockchain concept and its components.
### Timing
This topic typically accounts for 10-15% of the paper, and students should budget around 10-12 minutes to answer the questions. Students should allocate their time according to the marks available for each question and make sure to read the questions carefully to avoid common traps.

title: A Level Physics: Astronomy and Cosmology
content:
A Level Physics: Astronomy and Cosmology

Astronomy is physics at the largest scale: measuring the distance to a star by its brightness, its size by its temperature, and the age of the universe by how fast galaxies recede. This note builds the toolkit from zero: luminosity and the inverse-square law, standard candles (Cepheid variables and Type Ia supernovae) and the distance ladder, stellar radii from Stefan's law, Hubble's law and redshift, and the evidence for the Big Bang. Every calculation is worked in full, because the papers test exactly these three or four formulas.

Brightness, luminosity and the inverse-square law

A star's luminosity L is the total power it radiates (watts). What a telescope receives is intensity (or flux) I — power per unit area at the observer's distance:

I = L/(4 pi d^2)

I in W m-2, L in W, d in m
doubling the distance quarters the intensity

The analogy: a light bulb's power is fixed, but the same light spreads over a sphere of radius d — four times the area at twice the distance, so a quarter of the brightness per square metre. This one law underlies every distance measurement in astronomy.

Worked example. A star has luminosity 4.0 × 10²⁶ W. Find its intensity at 10 parsecs (1 pc = 3.09 × 10¹⁶ m).

d = 10 x 3.09 x 10^16 = 3.09 x 10^17 m
I = L/(4 pi d^2) = 4.0 x 10^26/(4 x 3.14 x (3.09 x 10^17)^2)
  = 4.0 x 10^26/(1.20 x 10^36) = 3.3 x 10^-10 W m-2

Standard candles and the distance ladder

A standard candle is an object whose luminosity is known, so its observed intensity gives its distance by rearranging the inverse-square law. Two are examinable:

  • Cepheid variables: pulsating stars whose period of variation is tightly related to their luminosity (longer period, more luminous). Measuring the period gives L; measuring I gives d. Cepheids calibrated the first rungs of the cosmic distance ladder.
  • Type Ia supernovae: exploding white dwarfs that reach a consistent peak luminosity, bright enough to be seen in distant galaxies; they extended the ladder to cosmological distances and revealed the accelerating expansion.
distance from a standard candle:
d = sqrt(L/(4 pi I))

Worked example. A Cepheid has luminosity 1.0 × 10²⁹ W and observed intensity 2.5 × 10⁻¹² W m⁻². Find its distance in parsecs.

d = sqrt(L/(4 pi I)) = sqrt(1.0 x 10^29/(4 x 3.14 x 2.5 x 10^-12))
  = sqrt(1.0 x 10^29/3.14 x 10^-11) = sqrt(3.18 x 10^39)
  = 5.64 x 10^19 m
in parsecs: 5.64 x 10^19/3.09 x 10^16 = 1825 pc
          = 1.8 kpc (2 s.f.)

Stellar radii and Stefan's law

A star radiates approximately as a black body. Stefan's law relates its luminosity to its surface area and absolute temperature:

L = 4 pi r^2 sigma T^4

sigma = 5.67 x 10-8 W m-2 K-4 (Stefan-Boltzmann constant)
r = stellar radius (m), T = surface temperature (K)

so r = sqrt(L/(4 pi sigma T^4))

The fourth power is the headline: doubling a star's temperature multiplies its radiated power per square metre by 16. That is why hot blue stars are vastly more luminous than cooler red ones of similar size — and why a red giant can outshine the Sun despite its low temperature, because its radius is enormous.

Worked example. The Sun has L = 3.8 × 10²⁶ W and T = 5800 K. Find its radius.

r = sqrt(L/(4 pi sigma T^4))
T^4 = (5800)^4 = 1.13 x 10^15
4 pi sigma T^4 = 4 x 3.14 x 5.67 x 10^-8 x 1.13 x 10^15
              = 8.05 x 10^8
r = sqrt(3.8 x 10^26/8.05 x 10^8) = sqrt(4.72 x 10^17)
  = 6.87 x 10^8 m  (about 7 x 10^8 m; the accepted value is 6.96 x 10^8 m)

Worked example 2 (comparison). A star has the same temperature as the Sun but 100 times its luminosity. Find its radius in solar radii.

L = 4 pi r^2 sigma T^4, same T and sigma:
r^2 proportional to L  ->  r = 10 R_sun

Redshift and Hubble's law

Light from distant galaxies is shifted toward longer wavelengths — redshift — because the galaxies are receding. For speeds much less than c:

z = Delta lambda/lambda = v/c     (v << c)

Hubble's law: v = H0 d

H0 = Hubble constant (about 70 km s-1 Mpc-1)
d = distance (Mpc)

Worked example 1. A galaxy's spectral line at 656 nm is observed at 689 nm. Find its recession speed.

Delta lambda = 689 - 656 = 33 nm
z = 33/656 = 0.0503
v = z c = 0.0503 x 3.0 x 10^8 = 1.51 x 10^7 m s-1
  = 1.5 x 10^4 km s-1

Worked example 2. A galaxy at 100 Mpc recedes at 7000 km s⁻¹. Find H₀ and the Hubble time.

H0 = v/d = 7000/100 = 70 km s-1 Mpc-1
Hubble time = 1/H0:
70 km s-1 Mpc-1 = 70 000/(3.09 x 10^22) s-1 = 2.27 x 10^-18 s-1
t = 1/H0 = 4.4 x 10^17 s = 1.4 x 10^10 years = 14 billion years

The Big Bang and its evidence

Hubble's law implies that galaxies were once much closer together — the universe expanded from a hot, dense state. Three pieces of evidence are examinable:

  • Redshift of galaxies: nearly all galaxies recede, and recession speed increases with distance — expansion from a common origin.
  • Cosmic microwave background (CMB): a uniform 2.7 K radiation filling the sky — the cooled remnant of the hot early universe, predicted before it was found.
  • Abundance of light elements: the observed ratios of hydrogen, helium and lithium match predictions of Big Bang nucleosynthesis.

The expanding universe has no centre: space itself stretches, so every observer sees distant galaxies receding in all directions. The age estimate 1/H₀ assumes constant expansion; accelerating expansion (dark energy) modifies it, and the measured value is about 13.8 billion years.

The theory makes a further testable claim: the CMB should be an almost perfect black-body spectrum with tiny temperature ripples, and it is — the ripples themselves are the seeds of galaxy formation, and their pattern matches the theory's predictions for the mix of ordinary matter, dark matter and dark energy. That agreement across independent observations is why the Big Bang is accepted as the standard cosmological model rather than a single unexplained measurement.

Worked examples: the standard exam types

Worked example. Two stars have the same radius; star A is twice as hot as star B. Find the ratio of their luminosities.

L = 4 pi r^2 sigma T^4; same r and sigma
L_A/L_B = (T_A/T_B)^4 = 2^4 = 16
Star A is 16 times more luminous.

Worked example 2. A star's luminosity is 4.0 × 10³⁰ W and its surface temperature 10 000 K. Find its radius and compare it with the Sun's (7.0 × 10⁸ m).

T^4 = (10^4)^4 = 1.0 x 10^16
4 pi sigma T^4 = 4 x 3.14 x 5.67 x 10^-8 x 1.0 x 10^16 = 7.12 x 10^9
r = sqrt(4.0 x 10^30/7.12 x 10^9) = sqrt(5.62 x 10^20)
  = 2.37 x 10^10 m
r/R_sun = 2.37 x 10^10/7.0 x 10^8 = 34 solar radii

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Inverse square) A star at 20 pc has intensity I. What is its intensity at 60 pc? Answer: Three times the distance gives 1/9 of the intensity: I/9.
  2. (Luminosity) Define luminosity and state its unit. Answer: The total power radiated by a star across all wavelengths, measured in watts (W).
  3. (Standard candle) Explain how a Cepheid variable is used to find distance. Answer: Its pulsation period determines its luminosity from the period–luminosity relation; comparing that luminosity with the observed intensity gives d = √(L/4πI).
  4. (Stefan) A star has twice the Sun's radius and half its temperature. Compare luminosities. Answer: L ∝ r²T⁴ → (2)² × (1/2)⁴ = 4 × 1/16 = 1/4: the star is a quarter as luminous.
  5. (Redshift) A line at 500 nm appears at 505 nm. Find v. Answer: z = 5/500 = 0.010; v = 0.010 × 3.0 × 10⁸ = 3.0 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹.
  6. (Hubble) A galaxy at 50 Mpc recedes at 3500 km s⁻¹. Find H₀. Answer: H₀ = 3500/50 = 70 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹.
  7. (Age) Estimate the age of the universe from H₀ = 70 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹. Answer: t = 1/H₀ ≈ 14 billion years (with unit conversions: 70 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹ = 2.27 × 10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹).
  8. (Big Bang evidence) State two observations supporting the Big Bang. Answer: The redshift–distance relation (Hubble's law) and the cosmic microwave background; the light-element abundances are a third.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Parsecs versus metres: convert before substituting; 1 pc = 3.09 × 10¹⁶ m, 1 Mpc = 3.09 × 10²² m, 1 AU = 1.50 × 10¹¹ m.
  • Luminosity versus intensity: L is the star's total power; I is what arrives per square metre. The inverse-square law connects them and d must be in metres.
  • T⁴ not T: Stefan's law is a fourth power — doubling temperature multiplies luminosity by 16, not 2. Most arithmetic errors here are exponent slips.
  • Kelvin: surface temperatures in Stefan's law must be absolute; a temperature given in °C needs +273 first.
  • Redshift approximation: z = v/c holds for v ≪ c; at large redshifts the relativistic formula is needed. State the assumption.
  • H₀ units: km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹ — mismatched units in 1/H₀ give absurd ages. Convert km to m and Mpc to m.
  • Hubble time is an estimate: 1/H₀ assumes constant expansion; note the acceleration caveat when discussing the age.
  • Centre of the universe: the Big Bang happened everywhere — there is no centre or edge; expansion stretches space between galaxies.
  • Precision: 2 or 3 s.f. with units (W, W m⁻², m, km s⁻¹, years); the data sheet supplies σ, c and H₀.

title: Exam technique: Integration
content:
### What earns the marks
For indefinite integrals, each term raised correctly plus the constant earns full marks. For definite integrals, the antiderivative quoted earns one mark and the correct upper-minus-lower evaluation earns the next. For area and curve-finding, the limits or the given point used earns the final mark.
### Traps
Error: constant of integration omitted. Correction: +c always for indefinite. Error: limits subtracted backwards. Correction: upper minus lower. Error: power rule inverted on roots. Correction: root x is x to the half, integral goes up.
### Worked example
Find the integral of 6x² − 4x⁻³. Raise each power by one and divide by the new power: 6x² becomes 2x³, and −4x⁻³ becomes 2x⁻² because (−4)/(−2) = 2. Add the constant: 2x³ + 2x⁻² + c. Check by differentiating: 6x² + (−4)x⁻³, which matches the original.
### Check yourself
Evaluate the definite integral of 2x + 1 from 1 to 3. The antiderivative is x² + x, giving (9 + 3) − (1 + 1) = 10. Write both the antiderivative and the subtraction on the paper, because the method mark depends on them.

### Worked example
Find the integral of 6x² − 4x⁻³. Raise each power by one and divide by the new power: 6x² becomes 2x³, and −4x⁻³ becomes 2x⁻² because (−4)/(−2) = 2. Add the constant: 2x³ + 2x⁻² + c. Check by differentiating: 6x² + (−4)x⁻³, which matches the original.

title: Algebra — Graphs — Study Notes
content:
Graphs

Key features of a curve

Find the y-intercept by setting x = 0, the x-intercepts by setting y = 0, and any turning point by completing the square or differentiating. A quadratic y = a(x − p)(x − q) crosses the x-axis at p and q.

Example: y = x² − 4x + 3 = (x − 1)(x − 3). The x-intercepts are 1 and 3, the y-intercept is 3, and completing the square gives the turning point (2, −1).

Transformations

  • y = f(x) + a translates the graph by a units up (down if a is negative).
  • y = f(x + a) translates the graph by a units to the left.
  • y = af(x) stretches the graph vertically by scale factor a, parallel to the y-axis.
  • y = f(ax) stretches the graph horizontally by scale factor 1/a, parallel to the x-axis.

Intersections of graphs

The points where two graphs meet are found by equating their equations. The resulting equation is solved for x, and the y-values are found by substituting back into either equation.

Exam technique

  • Label every intercept and turning point with its coordinates.
  • Check the sign of the leading coefficient to decide whether a quadratic has a minimum or a maximum.

title: AS Level Mathematics: Coordinate Geometry
content:
AS Level Mathematics: Coordinate Geometry

Coordinate geometry turns shapes into algebra: every line is an equation, every intersection is a simultaneous equation, and every circle is a completed square waiting to happen. This note builds the whole AS toolkit from zero: distance and midpoint, gradients with the parallel and perpendicular rules, the three forms of a line's equation, intersections and perpendicular bisectors, circles in both centre-radius and expanded form, and tangents and normals to circles. Every worked example writes the formula line first, because that is where the method marks are.

Distance and midpoint

distance between (x1, y1) and (x2, y2):
d = √((x2 - x1)² + (y2 - y1)²)

midpoint: ((x1 + x2)/2, (y1 + y2)/2)

The distance formula is Pythagoras in disguise: the horizontal and vertical gaps are the legs of a right triangle, and the distance is the hypotenuse.

Worked example. Find the distance and midpoint of A(1, 2) and B(7, 10).

d = √(6² + 8²) = √(10⁰) = 10
midpoint = ((1 + 7)/2, (2 + 10)/2) = (4, 6)

Gradient and the parallel/perpendicular rules

gradient m = (y2 - y1)/(x2 - x1)   (rise over run)

parallel lines: m¹ = m²
perpendicular lines: m¹ x m² = -1   (m² = -1/m¹)

Worked example. Find the gradient of AB for A(1, 2), B(5, 10), and the gradient of a line perpendicular to it.

m = (10 - 2)/(5 - 1) = 8/4 = 2
perpendicular gradient = -1/2

Worked example 2 (collinearity). Show A(1, 1), B(3, 5), C(5, 9) are collinear.

m(AB) = 4/2 = 2;  m(BC) = 4/2 = 2
equal gradients and a shared point B, so collinear

Equations of straight lines

Three forms, each useful in its own situation:

  • y = mx + c: gradient m, y-intercept c. Use when you know both.
  • y − y₁ = m(x − x₁): point-slope form. Use when you know a point and the gradient.
  • ax + by + c = 0: general form. Rearrange to find m and c when needed.

Worked example 1. Find the equation of the line through (2, 5) with gradient 3.

y - 5 = 3(x - 2)
y = 3x - 6 + 5
y = 3x - 1

Worked example 2 (two points). Find the equation of the line through (1, 4) and (4, 13).

m = (13 - 4)/(4 - 1) = 9/3 = 3
using (1, 4): y - 4 = 3(x - 1)  →  y = 3x + 1

Worked example 3 (perpendicular). Find the line through (2, 1) perpendicular to y = 2x + 3.

perpendicular gradient = -1/2
y - 1 = -1/2 (x - 2)
y = -x/2 + 1 + 1 = -x/2 + 2

Intersections and the perpendicular bisector

Two lines meet where their equations are simultaneously true: set them equal and solve. The perpendicular bisector of AB passes through the midpoint of AB with gradient −1/m(AB).

Worked example. Find where y = 3x − 1 meets y = −x + 7.

3x - 1 = -x + 7
4x = 8  →  x = 2;  y = 3(2) - 1 = 5
intersection: (2, 5)

Worked example 2 (perpendicular bisector). Find the perpendicular bisector of A(1, 2) and B(5, 10).

midpoint = (3, 6)
m(AB) = 8/4 = 2  →  perpendicular gradient = -1/2
y - 6 = -1/2 (x - 3)
y = -x/2 + 3/2 + 6 = -x/2 + 7.5

Circles: centre-radius form

(x - a)² + (y - b)² = r²
centre (a, b), radius r

expanded form x² + y² + 2fx + 2gy + c = 0:
complete the square in x and y to recover the centre and radius

Worked example 1. State the centre and radius of (x − 3)² + (y + 2)² = 25.

centre (3, -2); radius = 5

Worked example 2 (completing the square). Find the centre and radius of x² + y² − 6x + 8y − 11 = 0.

(x² - 6x) + (y² + 8y) = 11
(x - 3)² - 9 + (y + 4)² - 16 = 11
(x - 3)² + (y + 4)² = 36
centre (3, -4), radius 6

Worked example 3 (circle from diameter). AB is a diameter with A(1, 2) and B(7, 10). Find the circle's equation.

centre = midpoint = (4, 6)
radius = half the distance = 10/2 = 5
(x - 4)² + (y - 6)² = 25

Tangents and normals to circles

A tangent to a circle is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact. The method: find the gradient of the radius from the centre to the point, take the negative reciprocal for the tangent, then use the point-slope form.

Worked example. Find the tangent to the circle centre (2, 3) at the point (5, 7).

radius gradient = (7 - 3)/(5 - 2) = 4/3
tangent gradient = -3/4
y - 7 = -3/4 (x - 5)
4y - 28 = -3x + 15
3x + 4y = 43

Worked example 2 (tangent length). From the point P(8, 3), find the length of the tangent to the circle (x − 2)² + (y − 1)² = 13.

centre C(2, 1), radius √(13)
distance PC = √(6² + 2²) = √(40)
tangent² = PC² - r² = 40 - 13 = 27
tangent length = √(27) = 3 √(3) = 5.20

The right angle between radius and tangent makes every tangent-length question a Pythagoras problem in disguise; drawing the radius to the contact point is the step that unlocks it.

Worked example 2 (normal). The normal at a point on a circle is the radius line extended. Find the normal at the same point.

normal gradient = radius gradient = 4/3
y - 7 = 4/3 (x - 5)  →  4x - 3y + 1 = 0 (rearranged)

Circles and lines: intersection problems

Where a line meets a circle, substitute the line into the circle's equation and solve the resulting quadratic. The discriminant then classifies the geometry: two roots mean a secant (two intersection points), one root means a tangent, none means the line misses the circle.

substitute y = mx + c into (x - a)² + (y - b)² = r²
solve for x; each x gives a y from the line
