  • Change of flux sign: reversing a field doubles the change (from +BA to −BA), a factor candidates often forget.
  • rms factor: peak over √2; the peak is rms × √2. Power uses rms values, not peak.
  • Induced e.m.f. needs change: a stationary coil in a steady field induces nothing; there must be a changing flux linkage (movement, rotation, or a changing current).
  • Lenz direction questions: state the opposing field direction and then the current direction; the reasoning chain is the mark.
  • Rectification understanding: diodes conduct one way only; a bridge gives full-wave, a single diode half-wave — do not claim a single diode gives full-wave output.
  • Precision and units: tesla, weber, volt; 2 or 3 s.f.; μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹ from the data sheet.

Equations and symbols

Eleven relations run this topic and they come in four groups: flux, force, field from a current, and induction — plus the three a.c. results that connect any of it to the mains. In every one the angle is measured between the field and something else, and getting that angle wrong is worth more marks than any arithmetic.

Φ = B A cos(θ) Key: Φ = magnetic flux (Wb); B = magnetic flux density (T); A = area of the surface (m²); θ = angle between the field and the normal to the area, not between the field and the surface. Flux is maximum when the field is perpendicular to the surface, because then θ = 0 and cos θ = 1.

flux linkage = N Φ Key: N = number of turns in the coil (no units); Φ = flux through one turn (Wb); the product is measured in weber-turns (Wb-turn). Induction depends on the rate of change of this quantity, so a 200-turn coil multiplies the effect of a single loop two hundredfold.

F = B I L sin(θ) Key: F = force on the conductor (N); B = flux density (T); I = current (A); L = length of conductor in the field (m); θ = angle between the current and the field. Maximum at θ = 90°, zero when the wire lies along the field.

F = B Q v sin(θ) Key: Q = charge on the particle (C); v = its speed (m s⁻¹); the other symbols as above. For a charge moving perpendicular to the field this becomes F = B Q v, and that force is centripetal.

B Q v = m v²/r → r = m v/(B Q) Key: m = mass of the particle (kg); r = radius of the circular path (m); the other symbols as above. The radius grows with momentum and shrinks with field strength and charge — which is exactly how a mass spectrometer separates ions of different mass.

B = μ₀I/(2πr) Key: B = flux density at distance r from a long straight wire (T); μ₀ = permeability of free space, 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹; I = current (A); r = perpendicular distance from the wire (m). The field falls as 1/r, so doubling the distance halves it.

ε = - N dPhi/dt Key: ε = induced e.m.f. (V); N = number of turns; dPhi/dt = rate of change of flux through one turn (Wb s⁻¹). This is Faraday's law, and the minus sign is Lenz's law: the induced e.m.f. opposes the change that produced it.

ε = B L v Key: the special case of a rod of length L (m) moving at speed v (m s⁻¹) perpendicular to a field B (T); ε in volts. A rod moving along the field induces nothing, because no flux is being cut.

ε₀ = N B A ω Key: ε₀ = peak (maximum) e.m.f. from a rotating coil (V); N = turns; B = flux density (T); A = area of the coil (m²); ω = angular velocity of the rotation (rad s⁻¹). The sinusoidal output then has rms value ε₀/√2.

V_rms = V_0/√(2) = 0.707 V_0 Key: V_rms = the root-mean-square voltage (V), the steady d.c. value delivering the same power; V_0 = the peak voltage (V). Use it whenever a power is asked for, because the average of a sine wave is zero and the average power is not.

P = V_rms I_rms = I_rms² R = V_rms²/R Key: P = average power (W); I_rms = root-mean-square current (A), equal to I_0/√2; R = resistance (Ω). All three forms are the same statement, and all three need rms values — substituting peak values overstates the power by a factor of two.

τ = RC Key: τ = the time constant of the smoothing circuit (s); R = load resistance (Ω); C = capacitance (F). A larger τ relative to the period of the supply means the capacitor discharges less between peaks, so the ripple is smaller — the sentence that answers every smoothing question.

F = BIL = 0.80 × 2.0 × 0.30 = 0.48 N Key: a worked instance with B = 0.80 T, I = 2.0 A, L = 0.30 m perpendicular to the field. Quote the formula first, then substitute, then give the unit — a bare number loses the method mark.

SymbolQuantityUnit
Bmagnetic flux densityT (tesla = N A⁻¹ m⁻¹ = Wb m⁻²)
Φmagnetic fluxWb
μ₀permeability of free space4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹
ωangular velocity of a rotating coilrad s⁻¹

title: Waves — Study Notes
content:
Waves

Progressive waves

  • A progressive wave transfers energy without transferring matter. Its speed is v = fλ, where f is the frequency and λ the wavelength. Period T = 1/f.
  • Phase difference: two points separated by one wavelength are in phase. Points separated by half a wavelength are in antiphase.

Transverse and longitudinal waves

  • Transverse: the oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer (e.g. light, waves on a string).
  • Longitudinal: the oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer (e.g. sound in air, compressions and rarefactions).

Doppler effect for sound

When a source moves towards an observer, the observed frequency is higher and the wavelength is shorter. When it moves away, the observed frequency is lower and the wavelength is longer. The speed of sound in the medium does not change.

Electromagnetic spectrum

All electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum. In order of increasing wavelength: gamma rays, X-rays, ultraviolet, visible light, infrared, microwaves, radio waves. Frequency increases in the reverse order.

Polarisation

Only transverse waves can be polarised. Polarisation restricts the oscillations to a single plane. Longitudinal waves such as sound cannot be polarised.

Worked example: a wave has frequency 50 Hz and wavelength 6.0 m. Its speed is v = fλ = 50 × 6.0 = 300 m s⁻¹.

Exam tips: learn the spectrum order in terms of wavelength, not frequency. For the Doppler effect, state which way the source moves relative to the observer. Only transverse waves can show polarisation.

Polarisation and the Doppler effect

Only transverse waves can be polarised, because their oscillations can be restricted to one plane. A polariser passes only the component of the oscillation along its transmission axis. Light from a sky or a reflection is partly polarised, which is why polarising filters reduce glare. The Doppler effect for a moving source gives an observed frequency f' = f v/(v ± vs), where the upper sign applies when the source moves away from the observer and the lower sign when it approaches.

Exam tip: longitudinal waves such as sound cannot be polarised, so say so explicitly if a question asks about it.

Worked example: wave speed from frequency and wavelength

A sound wave has frequency 680 Hz and wavelength 0.50 m. Using v = fλ, the speed is 680 × 0.50 = 340 m/s, close to the speed of sound in air. For an electromagnetic wave in a vacuum the same relation applies, with v = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s. Take the wavelength from a displacement–distance graph and the period from a displacement–time graph, then use f = 1/T before substituting.

Exam method: reading wave graphs

On a displacement–distance graph, the wavelength is the distance between two adjacent points in phase, such as two successive crests, not the distance between a crest and a trough. On a displacement–time graph, the period is the time for one complete oscillation at a fixed point. Mark the values on the axes carefully, because many lost marks come from reading half a wavelength or half a period.

title: IGCSE Physics: Energy, Work and Power
content:
IGCSE Physics: Energy, Work and Power

Cambridge IGCSE Physics 0625 (2026–2028), Topic 1 Motion, forces and energy, statement 1.7 Energy, work and power. Energy is the currency of every physical process: it is never created or destroyed, only moved between stores and converted between forms. This note builds the whole idea from scratch — stores, transfers, the two energy equations, work, power, the world's energy resources and efficiency — because Paper 4 rewards candidates who can both calculate an energy change and explain where the energy went.

Energy stores and transfers

Think of energy as money held in different bank accounts. It can sit in a store, and it can move between stores along a transfer pathway, but the total across all accounts never changes. The examined stores and transfers are:

Energy storeWhat it meansExample
KineticEnergy of a moving object; more mass or more speed means moreA moving lorry
Gravitational potentialEnergy stored by virtue of height in a gravitational fieldA book on a shelf
Elastic potentialEnergy stored by stretching, compressing or twistingA drawn bow, a compressed spring
Thermal (internal)Energy of the random motion of particles in a substanceHot water in a kettle
ChemicalEnergy stored in chemical bondsFood, fuel, a battery
NuclearEnergy stored in the nucleus of an atomUranium fuel

The four transfer pathways are mechanical work (a force acting over a distance), heating (energy transferred by a temperature difference), radiation (energy carried by waves, mainly infrared and light) and electrical work (charge moving through a potential difference). When a ball is thrown upwards, chemical energy in the muscles does mechanical work on the ball, and that energy becomes kinetic; as the ball rises, kinetic becomes gravitational potential; as it falls back, gravitational potential becomes kinetic again; on impact the kinetic spreads into the thermal stores of the ball, the ground and the air, and some is radiated as sound.

Conservation of energy and Sankey diagrams

The law of conservation of energy states that energy cannot be created or destroyed, and the total energy in a closed system stays constant. This is the most powerful statement in the syllabus: whenever a question says a machine loses energy, it means the energy has been transferred to less useful stores, not destroyed. A Sankey diagram draws the total energy input as one wide arrow, splits it into useful output and wasted arrows, and is drawn so the arrow widths are proportional to the energies.

Useful energy is the energy transferred to the store the device was designed to fill; wasted energy is transferred to stores that were not the goal, usually thermal energy of the surroundings, and it is eventually transferred to the environment, often by radiation. Wasted energy is not destroyed — it has simply become too spread out to be harnessed easily.

Kinetic and gravitational potential energy

Both equations are Supplement statements, and both appear constantly in Paper 4 calculations.

kinetic energy = 1/2 x mass x speed squared        EK = 1/2 m v^2
gravitational potential energy = mass x gravitational field strength x height        EP = m g h
  • EK: kinetic energy in joules (J); m: mass in kilograms (kg); v: speed in metres per second (m s⁻¹). Energy is a scalar, so the speed is squared and the direction of travel does not matter.
  • EP: gravitational potential energy in joules (J); g: gravitational field strength in newtons per kilogram (N kg⁻¹, use the value given in the question); h: vertical height in metres (m), measured between the two positions being compared.

Only the difference in height matters. Lifting a 2 kg book from a table to a shelf 0.50 m above it raises EP by 2 × 9.81 × 0.50 = 9.8 J, whatever the height of the room. The sign convention is simple: EP increases as an object rises and decreases as it falls, and the change is ΔEP = m g Δh.

Energy methods are often faster than forces and equations of motion. For a falling object with no air resistance, m g h = ½ m v², and the mass cancels: every object falls at the same rate in a vacuum. For a roller coaster of mass 500 kg dropping 20 m from rest, v = √(2 g h) = √(2 × 9.81 × 20) = 19.8 m s⁻¹.

Work done

Work is done when a force moves an object. It is energy transferred by mechanical work, and it is measured in joules:

work done = force x distance moved in the direction of the force        W = F s
  • W: work done in joules (J). One joule is the work done when a force of 1 newton moves its point of application 1 metre in the direction of the force.
  • F: force in newtons (N); s: distance moved in metres (m), measured in the direction of the force.

Work is a scalar, but the two quantities must line up: carrying a box horizontally at constant height does no work against gravity, because the motion is perpendicular to the weight. Pushing a trolley with 50 N against 20 N of friction over 4 m does 200 J of work in total, of which 80 J goes to heating the bearings and floor through friction and 120 J remains as kinetic energy. If you carry shopping upstairs, the work done against gravity is your weight multiplied by the vertical height gained, not the length of the staircase.

Power

Power measures how fast energy is transferred — the rate of doing work. A car engine that lifts the same load in half the time is twice as powerful.

power = work done / time taken = energy transferred / time taken        P = W / t = E / t
  • P: power in watts (W). One watt is one joule per second (1 W = 1 J s⁻¹). A kilowatt is 1000 W.
  • W: work done in joules (J); E: energy transferred in joules (J); t: time taken in seconds (s).

Power is a scalar. For a vehicle moving at constant speed against a constant force, the same idea gives P = F v (Supplement), with F in newtons and v in metres per second, giving watts directly. Doubling the speed of a car at constant driving force doubles the power needed; a car climbing a hill at constant speed needs power P = mgv sin θ to raise its weight.

Energy resources and electricity generation

Most electrical energy is generated the same way: a fuel heats water, the steam spins a turbine, and the turbine spins a generator that converts the kinetic energy of rotation into electrical energy. What differs is the energy store the heat comes from.

ResourceStore usedAdvantagesDisadvantages
Coal, oil, gas (fossil fuels)Chemical, burned to give heatReliable, cheap to run, existing infrastructureFinite supply; carbon dioxide and pollutants released; contributes to climate change and acid rain
BiofuelChemical, from plant or animal materialRenewable; carbon dioxide released was recently absorbed by the plantsLand and water needed to grow crops; energy cost of farming and transport
HydroelectricGravitational potential of stored waterRenewable, reliable, no fuel cost, no emissions in useDams flood valleys and disrupt habitats; high construction cost; depends on rainfall
GeothermalThermal energy inside the EarthRenewable, reliable, small land useOnly practical near volcanic regions; drilling cost; possible release of underground gases
Nuclear fuelNuclear, released by fissionVery large energy per kilogram; no carbon dioxide in operationRadioactive waste that must be stored safely for centuries; high decommissioning cost; accident risk
Solar cellsLight radiation converted directly to electricityRenewable, silent, no emissions in use, low maintenanceOutput varies with light and season; expensive to manufacture; large area needed for high output
Solar panels (heating)Light radiation heating water directlyRenewable and cheap to runOnly heats water; ineffective at night and in cloudy climates

Non-renewable resources exist in finite stock and are used faster than they form; renewable resources are replenished as they are used. Supplement statements add the deep connection: the Sun is the principal source for almost all of these resources. Sunlight drives the water cycle behind hydroelectric power and biofuels, heats the ground behind wind and geothermal gradients, and fossil fuels are the remains of organisms that grew in sunlight. The Sun releases energy by nuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium, and research into fusion on Earth aims to provide a fuel that is abundant and produces no long-lived radioactive waste, though sustained fusion power is still experimental.

Efficiency

Efficiency compares what a device delivers with what it is given:

efficiency = useful energy output / total energy input
efficiency = useful power output / total power input

Efficiency has no unit; multiply by 100 for a percentage. No real device is 100 per cent efficient, because some energy is always transferred to thermal stores of the surroundings by friction, resistance and radiation. A filament lamp is about 5 per cent efficient (most energy becomes heat, not light); an electric motor might reach 80 per cent. The most efficient heating device is a simple heater, because its useful output is thermal energy — the same store as its waste. A Sankey diagram makes this visible at a glance, and the arrows must sum to the total input.

Worked example: lifting and efficiency

A crane lifts a 500 kg load through 12 m at constant speed in 20 s. Take g = 9.81 N kg⁻¹.

weight = m g = 500 x 9.81 = 4905 N
useful work = force x distance = 4905 x 12 = 58 860 J
useful power = work / time = 58 860 / 20 = 2943 W (about 2.9 kW)

The motor takes 150 000 J of electrical energy to do this lift. Its efficiency is 58 860 / 150 000 = 0.39, or 39 per cent. The remaining 91 140 J is not destroyed: it warms the motor windings, the cables and the surrounding air.

Second stage, using energy conservation: if the load is dropped from rest through the same 12 m with negligible air resistance, m g h = ½ m v² gives v = √(2 × 9.81 × 12) = 15.3 m s⁻¹. The mass cancels, so any object dropped through 12 m reaches the same speed.

Common mistakes

  • Saying energy is used up or lost; energy is transferred to other stores, and the total is conserved. Examiners award the mark for transferred, not lost.
  • Putting speed rather than speed squared into EK = ½mv², and forgetting the ½.
  • Measuring h in EP = mgh along a slope or a staircase; h is the vertical height difference.
  • Using the wrong mass in W = mg: the mass in kilograms, multiplied by g, never the weight in newtons multiplied by g again.
  • Confusing work done with power: joules measure energy, watts measure the rate of energy transfer.
  • Calculating efficiency as total in over useful out; the useful output goes on top, so efficiency is always less than 1.
  • Forgetting that a percentage efficiency needs multiplying by 100, and leaving the answer as 0.39 when 39 per cent is asked for.
  • Mixing units: power in watts needs energy in joules and time in seconds, so kilowatts and minutes must be converted first.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 4, 3 marks). A ball of mass 0.15 kg is moving at 10 m s⁻¹. Calculate its kinetic energy and the height through which it would need to be raised to store the same energy. Take g = 9.81 N kg⁻¹.

Answer: EK = ½mv² = ½ × 0.15 × 10² = 7.5 J. Setting mgh = 7.5 gives h = 7.5 / (0.15 × 9.81) = 5.1 m.

Question 2 (Paper 4, 4 marks). A 60 kg student runs up a flight of stairs of vertical height 3.0 m in 4.0 s. Calculate the useful power developed. Take g = 10 N kg⁻¹.

Answer: work = mgh = 60 × 10 × 3.0 = 1800 J. Power = 1800 / 4.0 = 450 W. (Real power is higher, because the student also gains kinetic energy and warms their muscles.)

Question 3 (Paper 2 style). A machine takes in 2000 J and delivers 1500 J of useful work. Its efficiency is: A 25 per cent; B 75 per cent; C 133 per cent; D 175 per cent. Answer: B. 1500/2000 = 0.75 = 75 per cent. Option C comes from putting input over output — the classic trap.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 6 marks). Explain why a solar cell is described as renewable, and discuss whether it is a good replacement for a coal-fired power station.

Answer: A solar cell converts light energy directly into electrical energy and consumes no fuel, so its energy source, sunlight, is replenished continuously and it is renewable. It produces no carbon dioxide or pollutants in operation. Against that, output depends on light intensity and falls at night and in cloudy weather, so storage or backup generation is needed; manufacturing the cells is energy-intensive, and a large area is required for high output. Coal is reliable and dispatchable but burns a finite resource, releasing carbon dioxide that drives climate change plus sulfur dioxide and particulates. A balanced conclusion weighs reliability and land use against emissions and fuel sustainability.

Question 5 (Paper 4, 3 marks). A car engine produces a driving force of 2000 N while travelling at 30 m s⁻¹. Calculate the useful power output.

Answer: P = F v = 2000 × 30 = 60 000 W = 60 kW.

Question 6 (Paper 6 style). Suggest how you would determine experimentally the efficiency of an electric motor lifting a small mass.

Answer: Measure the mass with a balance and the height lifted with a ruler, and record the time with a stopwatch. The useful output is mgh, calculated from the measured mass and vertical height. Measure the electrical energy input with a joule meter, or with an ammeter and voltmeter readings and E = V I t. Efficiency is mgh divided by V I t. Repeat for several masses and quote an average, keeping the input voltage constant.

With energy accounted for, the next question is what happens when forces are spread over area and depth: pressure and density.

title: Thermal Physics — Study Notes
content:
Thermal Physics

Temperature and scales

Thermodynamic temperature is measured in kelvin. The kelvin and Celsius scales have the same size of degree, with T/K = θ/°C + 273. Absolute zero (0 K) is the lowest possible temperature, at which the particles of an ideal gas have minimum kinetic energy.

Example: 25 °C = 298 K.

Specific heat capacity and latent heat

Specific heat capacity c is the energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 K: Q = mcΔθ. Latent heat is the energy needed to change the state of 1 kg without a change in temperature: Q = mL. Melting and boiling absorb energy without a temperature rise, because the energy goes into breaking intermolecular bonds, not into kinetic energy.

Example: warming 2.0 kg of water (c = 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) by 10 K needs 84 kJ. Melting 0.20 kg of ice (L = 334 kJ kg⁻¹) needs 67 kJ.

The mole and Avogadro constant

One mole contains N_A = 6.02 × 10²³ particles. The number of particles is N = nN_A, where n is the amount in moles. Molar mass is the mass of one mole, in kg mol⁻¹ in SI units.

Equation of state for an ideal gas

pV = nRT, where R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ and T must be absolute. Equivalently pV = NkT, with k = R/N_A = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹.

Example: 0.10 mol at 300 K in 2.0 × 10⁻³ m³ has p = nRT/V ≈ 1.2 × 10⁵ Pa.

Kinetic theory

The pressure of an ideal gas comes from molecules colliding with the container walls. The mean kinetic energy of a molecule is ⟨Ek⟩ = 3kT/2, so it depends only on the absolute temperature. At 300 K it is about 6.2 × 10⁻²¹ J.

Internal energy and the first law

The internal energy of an ideal gas is the sum of the kinetic and potential energies of its molecules. For an ideal gas there are no intermolecular forces, so internal energy depends only on temperature. The first law of thermodynamics is ΔU = Q + W, where Q is heat added to the system and W is work done on the system. Heat lost by a system is therefore negative.

Example: a gas has 500 J of work done on it and loses 200 J of heat. ΔU = −200 + 500 = +300 J.

Exam tips: convert to kelvin before using pV = nRT or the kinetic-energy formula. Check the sign convention for W in the question. Use latent heat only when the temperature is constant.

Worked example: pressure of a fixed amount of gas

A sample of 0.50 mol of ideal gas is at 300 K in a container of volume 2.0 × 10⁻³ m³. Using pV = nRT with R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, the pressure is p = (0.50 × 8.31 × 300) ÷ (2.0 × 10⁻³) ≈ 6.2 × 10⁵ Pa. If the same gas is heated to 600 K in a rigid container, the pressure doubles, because for a fixed amount of gas at constant volume p is proportional to T in kelvin. Converting temperatures to kelvin before multiplying is the step examiners check first.

Exam method: units and conversions

Convert cm³ to m³ by dividing by 1 000 000, and convert °C to K by adding 273 (or 273.15). Mass in grams must be turned into kilograms for kinetic energy calculations, and into moles using the molar mass. A quick unit check helps: pressure in pascals multiplied by volume in cubic metres gives joules, the unit of energy.

title: Exam technique: Magnetism and Electromagnetism
content:
### What earns the marks
For electromagnets, turns plus current plus soft iron core earns each mark. For transformers, the turns ratio equation quoted earns the method mark. For induction, rate of change of flux linked to emf size earns the explanation mark.
### Traps
Error: steel chosen for electromagnet cores. Correction: soft iron; steel suits permanent magnets. Error: Fleming hands swapped. Correction: left for motor, right for generator. Error: step-up confused with step-down. Correction: more secondary turns means step-up.

title: Hypothesis Testing
content:
Hypothesis Testing

The Framework

The null hypothesis H₀ is the default claim (no change, p = p₀). The alternative H₁ is what a suspicious observation suggests (p > p₀, p < p₀, or p ≠ p₀). The significance level α is the probability of rejecting a true H₀ — the false-alarm rate, usually 5% or 1%.

Test for a Binomial Proportion

With X ~ B(n, p₀) under H₀, compute the probability of results at least as extreme as the observed count in the direction of H₁.

Example: H₀: p = 0.3 against H₁: p > 0.3, observed 10 successes in n = 20. Compute P(X ≥ 10) under B(20, 0.3). If that tail probability is below α, reject H₀.

One-Tailed vs Two-Tailed

One-tailed tests take the whole α in one direction. Two-tailed tests split α across both tails: compare against α/2 on each side, or equivalently check whether the observation falls in the extreme 2.5% (for α = 5%). Choose the tails from the wording of H₁, not from the data.

Critical Regions

The critical region is the set of values of the test statistic that would lead to rejection. Its boundary is the critical value. For B(20, 0.3) at the 5% level with H₁: p > 0.3, find the smallest k with P(X ≥ k) < 0.05 — that k opens the critical region.

Conclusions in Context

Never just say "reject H₀". Conclude in the language of the problem: "there is sufficient evidence at the 5% level that the proportion has increased". State the significance level, the direction, and the real-world quantity.

Exam tips: define H₀ and H₁ with symbols AND words. Verify which tail the observation sits in before computing. If the observed value lies in the critical region, evidence supports H₁; otherwise there is insufficient evidence — never "prove H₀ true".

title: Oscillations and Waves II
content:
Oscillations and Waves II

Progressive vs Stationary

Progressive waves transfer energy; stationary waves store it in loops. Stationary patterns arise from two identical waves travelling in opposite directions (reflections on strings, air columns).

PropertyProgressiveStationary
Amplitudesame for all pointsvaries: nodes zero, antinodes max
Phasevaries along wavesame within a loop, π flip across nodes
Energytransferredtrapped

Harmonics

A string fixed at both ends: f₁ = v/2L, then 2f₁, 3f₁… Closed pipes resonate at odd multiples; open pipes at all multiples.

Superposition Applications

  • Young's double slit: x = λD/a — evidence light is a wave
  • Diffraction grating: d sin θ = nλ — resolution of spectra
  • Noise-cancelling headphones: destructive interference of antiphase sound

Polarization Applications

Polaroid sunglasses cut glare from horizontal surfaces; stress analysis in plastics; LCD screens control light with twisted polarizers. Malus' law I = I₀cos²θ.

Exam tips: 'explain' marks want the physics: path difference, phase, node/antinode conditions — not just formula substitution.

title: Exam technique: Bearings and Loci
content:
### What earns the marks
For bearings, measure earns marks for the angle taken clockwise from north with three figures in the final answer: add leading zeros (075, 008). For back bearings, the 180-degree adjustment stated earns the method mark. For scale drawings, the scale multiplication shown earns a mark independent of arithmetic. For loci, construct earns marks for the correct locus type (circle, bisector, parallel pair) drawn and labelled.
### Traps
Error: measuring anticlockwise or from the wrong datum. Correction: north line up, clockwise. Error: dropping leading zeros. Correction: three figures always. Error: one angle bisector instead of the pair for intersecting lines. Correction: two lines cross, so two bisectors. Error: dividing by the scale instead of multiplying. Correction: real distances exceed map distances.

title: AS Level Physics: Waves
content:
AS Level Physics: Waves

Waves are how energy moves without matter moving with it — a statement that sounds abstract until you watch a crowd do the Mexican wave: the people stay in their seats while the disturbance travels the stadium. This note builds the full wave toolkit from zero: the vocabulary of progressive waves and the two graphs that encode them, the wave equation and its arithmetic, the difference between transverse and longitudinal waves, the Doppler effect for sound, the electromagnetic spectrum, and polarisation. Every quantity here is defined by how it is measured, and every calculation reduces to v = fλ applied carefully.

What a wave is: the rope and the stadium

Shake one end of a long rope: a crest travels to the far end, but the rope itself only moves up and down. That separation is the whole idea — a wave is a propagating disturbance that transfers energy and, in some cases, information, while the medium oscillates about fixed positions. Two families of wave carry the syllabus: mechanical waves (sound, water, waves on ropes — they need a medium) and electromagnetic waves (light, radio, X-rays — they need no medium and travel at c in vacuum).

Progressive waves: the vocabulary

A progressive wave transfers energy from place to place. Its quantities are defined on two graphs, and learning to read both is half the topic:

  • Displacement–distance graph (a snapshot, like a photograph of the rope): the horizontal axis is position along the wave, the vertical axis is displacement from equilibrium.
  • Displacement–time graph (one point's diary): the horizontal axis is time, the vertical axis is the displacement of a single particle.
QuantitySymbolDefinitionRead from which graph
Displacementx (m)distance of a particle from equilibrium, with directionvertical axis of both
AmplitudeA (m)maximum displacement from equilibriumpeak height (both)
Wavelengthλ (m)distance between two consecutive points in phase (crest to crest)distance graph: crest-to-crest
PeriodT (s)time for one complete oscillation of one particletime graph: one full cycle
Frequencyf (Hz)number of complete oscillations per second, f = 1/Tcalculated from T
Phase differenceφ (rad)fraction of a cycle between two points, in radians (2π per cycle)horizontal shift as a fraction of λ or T
Speedv (m s⁻¹)distance the disturbance travels per secondcalculated from v = fλ

Phase is worth an explicit definition because marks live there: two points are in phase when they are one or more whole wavelengths (or periods) apart — same displacement, moving in the same direction. They are in antiphase when separated by half a wavelength (π radians, 180°). A quarter wavelength is π/2 radians. The exam expects radians here.

The wave equation and its arithmetic

One speed, three expressions: in one period T a wave travels exactly one wavelength λ, so λ = vT and therefore

v = f λ        f = 1/T        λ = vT

Units discipline: v in m s⁻¹, f in Hz, λ in m. Convert before substituting: 3.4 cm = 0.034 m; 450 kHz = 4.5 × 10⁵ Hz.

Worked example 1. A wave on a rope has frequency 2.5 Hz and wavelength 1.20 m. Find its speed and period.

v = f λ = 2.5 × 1.20 = 3.0 m s⁻¹
T = 1/f = 1/2.5 = 0.40 s

Worked example 2. A sound wave travels at 340 m s⁻¹ and has frequency 2.0 kHz. Find the wavelength in centimetres.

f = 2.0 kHz = 2000 Hz
λ = v/f = 340/2000 = 0.17 m
       = 17 cm

Worked example 3 (reading the graphs). On a displacement–distance graph, consecutive crests sit at 0.20 m and 0.65 m. A particle completes one oscillation in 0.020 s. Find v.

λ = 0.65 - 0.20 = 0.45 m
T = 0.020 s  →  f = 1/0.020 = 50 Hz
v = f λ = 50 × 0.45 = 22.5 m s⁻¹

Note the exam habit that prevents the commonest error: write the wavelength and period extractions as their own lines before any multiplication.

Intensity: how the energy spreads

Intensity is power per unit area, I = P/A, measured in W m⁻². For a wave spreading from a point source uniformly in three dimensions, the same power spreads over the surface of a sphere, so I = P/(4πr²) and intensity falls with the inverse square of distance. Amplitude matters too: intensity is proportional to the square of the amplitude, I ∝ A² — double the amplitude, quadruple the intensity.

Worked example. A small source emits 4.0 W uniformly. Find the intensity 2.0 m away.

I = P/(4 π r²) = 4.0/(4 × 3.14 × 2.0²) = 4.0/50.3
  = 0.080 W m⁻²

Transverse and longitudinal waves

The distinction is the angle between the oscillation and the travel direction:

TransverseLongitudinal
Particle vibrationperpendicular to the direction of energy transferparallel to the direction of energy transfer
Featurescrests and troughs; can be polarisedcompressions and rarefactions; cannot be polarised
Exampleslight and all EM waves, waves on strings, S-wavessound in air, ultrasound in tissue, P-waves, spring coils

A key exam consequence: because electromagnetic waves are transverse, they can be polarised; sound in air is longitudinal, so it cannot. The oscillation of the electric field vector in a light wave can be confined to one plane by a polarising filter — that is polarisation, and it is a property only transverse waves possess.

The Doppler effect for sound

When a source of sound moves relative to an observer, the observed frequency shifts: the wavefronts bunch up ahead of the source (higher pitch) and stretch out behind (lower pitch). Ambulances are the standard demonstration. For sound with source speed vₛ along the line joining source and observer, and sound speed v:

source approaching observer:   f' = f v/(v - v_s)
source receding from observer: f' = f v/(v + v_s)

The general form taught for exams: f' = f v/(v ∓ vₛ) with the minus sign for approach and the plus sign for recession; for a moving observer the roles swap (approaching observer: f' = f (v + v_o)/v). Learn the sign logic, not a mnemonic: less distance between wavefronts means higher frequency.

Worked example. A car horn emits 400 Hz. The car approaches a stationary pedestrian at 25 m s⁻¹. Take the speed of sound as 340 m s⁻¹.

approaching: f' = f v/(v - v_s) = 400 × 340/(340 - 25)
           = 136 000/315 = 432 Hz
receding:    f' = 400 × 340/(340 + 25) = 136 000/365 = 373 Hz

The classic two-part question: the observer hears 432 Hz as the car arrives and 373 Hz as it leaves. The perceived shift is about 59 Hz in total — the difference of the two answers, not one answer.

Limitation to know: the formula above assumes the motion is along the line of source and observer, and it fails when vₛ approaches v (the denominator collapses) — at the speed of sound the wavefronts pile into a shock wave, the sonic boom.

The electromagnetic spectrum

All electromagnetic waves travel at c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ in vacuum; they differ in frequency and wavelength, and their properties follow in an unbroken spectrum. The order is examinable in both directions:

Region (increasing frequency)Wavelength scaleTypical uses and effects
Radio10³–10⁻¹ mbroadcasting, communications, MRI signals
Microwave10⁻¹–10⁻³ msatellite links, mobile phones, ovens (water rotation)
Infrared10⁻³–7 × 10⁻⁷ mthermal imaging, remote controls, heating
Visible7 × 10⁻⁷–4 × 10⁻⁷ mvision, photography, fibre optics
Ultraviolet4 × 10⁻⁷–10⁻⁸ msterilisation, fluorescence, vitamin D; sunburn risk
X-rays10⁻⁸–10⁻¹¹ mmedical imaging, security scanning; ionising
Gammabelow 10⁻¹¹ msterilising equipment, cancer radiotherapy; ionising

Shared properties: all transverse, all travel at c in vacuum, all obey v = fλ, all can be polarised. The property that changes down the table is photon energy — which is why the short-wavelength end (UV, X-ray, gamma) is ionising and dangerous to tissue.

Polarisation in depth

Unpolarised light has its electric field vector oscillating in every direction perpendicular to travel. A polarising filter passes only the component aligned with its axis — so a second filter (the analyser) at 90° to the first extinguishes the beam entirely. Intermediate angles pass a fraction of the intensity. Practical applications are examinable: Polaroid sunglasses cut glare (glare from roads and water is partially polarised by reflection), and radio aerials must be aligned with the polarisation of the signal.

Worked example. Unpolarised light of intensity I₀ passes one polariser. What fraction emerges, and what happens if a second polariser is added at 30° to the first?

after 1st polariser: I1 = I0/2
2nd polariser at 30 °: I2 = I1 cos²(30) = (I0/2)(0.75)
                       = 0.375 I0

The first filter halves unpolarised light; subsequent filters follow the cos²θ rule (an A-level standard result worth knowing for multiple-choice items).

Worked examples: exam-style calculations

Worked example 1 (graph + equation). A student measures a wave: 5 full waves occupy 2.0 m, and 20 oscillations take 3.0 s. Find the wave speed.

5 wavelengths in 2.0 m → λ = 2.0/5 = 0.40 m
20 oscillations in 3.0 s → T = 3.0/20 = 0.15 s
f = 1/0.15 = 6.67 Hz
v = f λ = 6.67 × 0.40 = 2.67 m s⁻¹  (2 s.f.: 2.7 m s⁻¹)

Worked example 2 (Doppler with unknown speed). A stationary observer hears 500 Hz from an approaching source and 420 Hz as it recedes. If v = 340 m s⁻¹, find the source speed.

approach: 500 = f x 340/(340 - v_s)   ... (1)
recede:   420 = f x 340/(340 + v_s)   ... (2)
divide (1) by (2): 500/420 = (340 + v_s)/(340 - v_s)
1.190(340 - v_s) = 340 + v_s
404.6 - 1.190 v_s = 340 + v_s
64.6 = 2.190 v_s  →  v_s = 29.5 m s⁻¹  (2 s.f.: 30 m s⁻¹)

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Definitions) Define wavelength and phase difference. Answer: Wavelength: the distance between consecutive points in phase, e.g. crest to crest. Phase difference: the fraction of an oscillation cycle between two oscillating points, expressed in radians (2π per complete cycle).
  2. (Wave equation) A radio wave has frequency 1.5 MHz. Find its wavelength (c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹). Answer: λ = c/f = 3.0 × 10⁸ / 1.5 × 10⁶ = 200 m.
  3. (Graphs) On a displacement–time graph for one particle, successive peaks occur at 0.10 s and 0.35 s. State the period and frequency. Answer: T = 0.25 s; f = 1/T = 4.0 Hz.
  4. (Transverse/longitudinal) Explain, in terms of particle motion, why sound cannot be polarised. Answer: In a longitudinal wave the oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer, so there is no perpendicular vibration to restrict to one plane; polarisation requires transverse oscillations.
  5. (Doppler) An ambulance emitting 700 Hz moves away from a cyclist at 20 m s⁻¹ (sound 340 m s⁻¹). Find the frequency heard. Answer: f' = 700 × 340/(340 + 20) = 238 000/360 = 661 Hz.
  6. (EM spectrum) Arrange in order of increasing frequency: infrared, gamma, radio, visible. Name one use of ultraviolet. Answer: radio, infrared, visible, gamma. Uses of UV include sterilising equipment, detecting forged notes (fluorescence) and sunbeds; also responsible for sunburn and vitamin D production.
  7. (Polarisation) Two polarising filters are placed in a beam of light with their axes at 90°. State and explain the observation. Answer: No light passes: the first filter polarises the light along its axis, and the second (analyser) blocks all vibration parallel to that axis because its own axis is perpendicular.
  8. (Intensity) The amplitude of a wave is doubled. State the effect on intensity. Answer: Intensity increases by a factor of 4, because I ∝ A².

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Graph confusion: reading wavelength from a displacement–time graph (it gives period) or period from a distance graph (it gives wavelength). Label the axes first, always.
  • Unit conversions: kHz and MHz to Hz, cm to m, before substitution. Losing a factor of 1000 in the Doppler denominator is the classic arithmetic loss.
  • Phase in degrees: phase difference is demanded in radians (π, 2π). 180° is π; a quarter cycle is π/2.
  • Doppler signs: approach is minus in the denominator — do not memorise blindly; sketch the bunched and stretched wavefronts and derive the sign each time.
  • f versus T: f = 1/T, and f = 50 Hz means T = 0.02 s, not 50 s. Inverting too quickly under pressure is common.
  • Spectrum order and properties: candidates memorise the order but forget that all EM waves travel at c and are transverse — the shared-properties questions catch them.
  • Polarisation of sound: stating that sound can be polarised is an immediate mark loss; sound is longitudinal.
  • Precision and units: this paper wants answers to 2 or 3 significant figures with units; unrounded 7-digit answers and unitless numbers cost marks.
  • Method marks: write v = fλ and substitute in separate lines — the formula line earns credit even when the arithmetic fails.

title: Exam technique: Networks and the Internet
content:
### What earns the marks
For protocol choice, the requirement matched earns each mark: delay-sensitive goes UDP, accuracy-critical goes TCP. For devices, the layer and key stated (MAC for bridges, IP for routers) earn the pair. For topologies, the failure scope described earns the resilience mark.
### Traps
Error: one protocol for both voice and files. Correction: optimise per requirement. Error: hubs credited with MAC forwarding. Correction: hubs broadcast; switches target. Error: star failure claimed total. Correction: only the spoke drops.

title: Integration — Study Notes
content:
Integration

Cambridge International AS & A Level Mathematics 9709, Paper 1. Integration reverses differentiation, so each method here is a differentiation rule read backwards. Two things cost most marks: the constant of integration, and the way limits are applied to a definite integral.

Indefinite integrals

∫axⁿ dx = a x^(n+1)/(n + 1) + c, for n ≠ −1. Add one to the power, divide by the new power, and always write +c. Multiply out brackets and rewrite roots as powers before you integrate.

Example: ∫(6x² − 4√x) dx = 2x³ − (8/3)x^(3/2) + c.

Example: ∫(x − 2)(x + 4) dx = ∫(x² + 2x − 8) dx = x³/3 + x² − 8x + c.

Finding a specific curve

The integral gives a family of curves, all differing by the constant c. A point the curve passes through fixes c. Integrate dy/dx, then substitute the coordinates of the point to find c.

Example: dy/dx = 3x² − 2x + 1, and the curve passes through (−1, 4). Integrating gives y = x³ − x² + x + c. Substituting x = −1 and y = 4 gives c = 7, so y = x³ − x² + x + 7.

Definite integrals

Evaluate the antiderivative at the upper limit and subtract its value at the lower limit. No +c is needed, because it cancels. A negative result is normal when the region lies below the x-axis.

Example: ∫ from −1 to 2 of (3x² − 4) dx = [x³ − 4x] from −1 to 2 = (8 − 8) − (−1 + 4) = −3.

Area under a curve

Find where the curve crosses the x-axis, then integrate between those points. Any part below the axis gives a negative integral, so take its sign off before adding the areas together.

Example: y = 4x − x² crosses the x-axis at 0 and 4, and lies above it between them. The area is ∫ from 0 to 4 of (4x − x²) dx = [2x² − x³/3] from 0 to 4 = 32/3 square units.

Area between two curves

Find the intersection points, then integrate the upper curve minus the lower curve between them. To check which curve is on top, test a value between the two points.

Example: y = x² and y = x + 2 meet where x² = x + 2, so x = −1 and x = 2. The area is ∫ from −1 to 2 of (x + 2 − x²) dx = 9/2 square units.

Trapezium rule

With strips of width h and ordinates y₀, y₁, …, yₙ, the estimate is (h/2)[y₀ + 2(y₁ + … + yₙ₋₁) + yₙ]. For a curve that bends upwards, the estimate is an overestimate.

Example: ∫ from 0 to 2 of (x² + 1) dx with two strips (h = 1). The ordinates are 1, 2 and 5, so the estimate is (1/2)(1 + 4 + 5) = 5. The exact value is 14/3, so the estimate is larger, as expected for a curve bending upwards.

Common errors

  • Integrating a product term by term without expanding the brackets first.
  • Writing +c in a definite integral, or forgetting it in an indefinite one.
  • Subtracting the limits the wrong way round.
  • Quoting a negative area for a region that sits below the axis.

title: Probability — Study Notes
content:
Probability

Basic Rules

For an event A with P(A) = p: 0 ≤ p ≤ 1, and P(A′) = 1 − P(A). For mutually exclusive events, probabilities add: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B). For events that can occur together, subtract the overlap:

  • P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B)

Venn Diagrams

Draw the universe first, then the events. Fill from the intersection outwards: if P(A) = 0.6, P(B) = 0.5 and P(A ∩ B) = 0.25, then only-A = 0.35, only-B = 0.25, neither = 0.15. Every region must sum to 1.

Tree Diagrams

Branch probabilities multiply along a path; outcomes at the end of complete paths add. Draw one branch set per stage of the experiment. For two draws without replacement from a bag of 5 red and 3 blue: P(RR) = (5/8)(4/7) = 20/56.

Conditional Probability

P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B) — the probability of A given that B has occurred. The condition shrinks the sample space.

Example: P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.4, P(A ∩ B) = 0.2. Then P(A | B) = 0.2/0.4 = 0.5, so A and B are independent since P(A | B) = P(A).

Independence

A and B are independent exactly when P(A ∩ B) = P(A)·P(B). Do not confuse independent (no influence on probabilities) with mutually exclusive (cannot co-occur). Mutually exclusive events with non-zero probabilities are never independent.

Exam tips: convert every "given that" into a conditional. With trees, label the second-stage branches with conditional probabilities; they are usually different from the first stage when drawing without replacement.

title: IGCSE Computer Science: Networking and Data Transmission
content:
IGCSE Computer Science: Networking and Data Transmission

Cambridge IGCSE Computer Science 0478 (2026–2028), Paper 1 Computer Systems: statement 2.1 Types and methods of data transmission, 2.2 Methods of error detection, 2.3 Encryption, and 3.4 Network hardware. This note explains how data travels between machines — the modes and media it moves over, how errors in transit are spotted and fixed, how it is kept secret from eavesdroppers, and the hardware that carries it. Every parity bit and checksum below is worked line by line, because Paper 1 asks you to produce the check bits, not just name the method.

Why network computers at all

Networking lets machines share resources and communicate: shared files, printers and internet connections; centralised backup and security; email and messaging; and collaboration on the same data. The three sizes you must distinguish: a LAN (local area network) covers one site — a school or office — over its own cabling; a WLAN is a LAN using wireless links; a WAN (wide area network) spans many sites over public infrastructure such as telephone lines and fibre, with the internet the largest WAN of all.

Two ways to organise a LAN. In a client–server network, dedicated servers hold shared files, user accounts and backups, and clients request services from them: central control, easy backups, better security, but expensive hardware and an administrator is required — a server failure can stop everyone. In a peer-to-peer network every computer is equal and shares its own resources: cheap and simple, but no central control, each machine backed up separately, and security is harder to enforce.

Serial and parallel transmission

Serial sends one bit at a time down a single wire (or channel). It needs fewer wires, so it is cheaper and works over long distances without the signals interfering with each other; modern systems use serial links for almost everything outside the chip (USB, Ethernet, SATA). Parallel sends several bits at once — one per wire. It looks faster, and is over very short distances such as the paths inside a computer, but over long cables the wires pick up each other's signals (crosstalk) and the pulses arrive at slightly different times (skew), so the receiving end misreads them. Memory buses and internal data paths stay parallel; anything long-distance is serial.

Simplex, half-duplex and full-duplex

ModeDirectionExample
SimplexOne direction onlyKeyboard to computer; a TV broadcast
Half-duplexBoth directions, but one way at a timeWalkie-talkie; older Ethernet hubs
Full-duplexBoth directions simultaneouslyTelephone call; modern switched Ethernet

Two more distinctions the syllabus names. Synchronous transmission sends a continuous stream of data with a shared clock signal synchronising sender and receiver — fast and efficient for large transfers. Asynchronous transmission sends one character at a time wrapped in a start bit and stop bit (with a parity bit), so no shared clock is needed; it is slower because of the overhead but simple and cheap for bursty traffic such as a keyboard. Baseband means the whole medium carries a single digital signal (ordinary Ethernet); broadband splits the medium into several frequency channels so different signals travel at once (the cable TV and ADSL line into a house).

Transmission media

MediumHow it carries dataStrengthsWeaknesses
Twisted pair (Ethernet cable)Electrical pulses in paired copper wiresCheap, easy to install, fine for LANsLimited distance and speed; electrical interference
Coaxial cableElectrical pulses in a shielded copper coreBetter shielding than twisted pair; TV and cable networksThicker, dearer, still limited bandwidth compared with fibre
Fibre opticPulses of laser light down glass fibresHuge bandwidth, very long distances, immune to electrical interference, hard to tapExpensive; needs specialist skills to join and repair
Wireless (radio, microwave, infrared)Electromagnetic waves through the airMobility; no cabling costInterference and obstacles; slower; eavesdropping risk; coverage limits

Bandwidth is the maximum data rate of a link, in bits per second (bps, kbps, Mbps, Gbps) — the width of the pipe. Latency is the delay before data arrives. High bandwidth with high latency still feels sluggish: size of pipe versus distance the water travels. Time to send a file is roughly file size in bits divided by bandwidth:

Worked example: how long to send a 45 MB file over an 8 Mbps link?

45 MB = 45 × 8 = 360 megabits                [bytes to bits: multiply by 8]
360 / 8 = 45 seconds

Note the two eights doing different jobs: one converts bytes to bits,
the other is the 8 Mbps bandwidth. Confusing them is the classic error.

Error detection: parity

Signals degrade in transit — crosstalk, interference, dirty connectors — so receiving systems must check whether what arrived is what was sent. The simplest method, parity checking, appends one extra bit (the parity bit) to each byte so that the number of 1-bits in the group is always odd (odd parity) or always even (even parity). The sender works the bit out; the receiver recounts.

Send 0110 10¹¹ with EVEN parity.

Count the 1-bits: 0+1+1+0+1+0+1+1 = 5 ones (odd).
For the group to have an even number of ones, the parity bit must be 1.
Transmitted byte (with parity bit at the front): 1 0110 10¹¹

Now suppose one bit is flipped in transit: 1 0010 10¹¹.
The receiver counts the ones: 1+0+0+1+0+1+0+1+1 = 5 (odd), but even parity was
agreed, so an error is detected and the byte is retransmitted.

With ODD parity for the same byte, the parity bit would be 0 (already 5 ones),
and the receiver expects an odd total.

Parity catches any single bit flip (the total changes parity), but two flips cancel out and pass unnoticed — a limitation worth a mark on its own.

Error detection: checksums

A checksum covers a whole block of data rather than one byte. The sender adds the data values together and sends the sum (or its complement) with the block; the receiver repeats the addition and compares. A corrupted value gives a different total.

Send the block 25, 47, 12 with a checksum.

Sender: 25 + 47 + 12 = 84. Transmit 25, 47, 12, 84.
Suppose 47 is corrupted to 48.
Receiver: 25 + 48 + 12 = 85, which does not match the received checksum 84:
error detected, request retransmission.

A plain sum can miss compensating errors (25 up by 1 and 12 down by 1), so real
systems use the one's complement of the sum, which catches more patterns.

Checksums detect most multi-bit errors in a block but not all; they are used together with retransmission (below), not instead of it.

Error correction and ARQ

Automatic repeat request (ARQ) is the protocol that turns detection into recovery. The receiver acknowledges each correctly received packet with an ACK; a corrupted packet gets a NAK (negative acknowledgement), and the sender resends it. If the packet or its ACK is lost entirely, the sender's timeout expires and it resends anyway. Sequence numbers on packets let the receiver spot duplicates caused by those resends and discard them. Stop-and-wait ARQ sends one packet and waits for its ACK before the next; continuous ARQ keeps a window of packets flowing and retransmits only the missing ones — faster on long links.

Error-correcting codes go further: extra bits are added so the receiver can repair a single-bit error without retransmission (vital where no return channel exists, such as on CDs). The trade-off in every method: more check bits means more reliability and less room for data.

Encryption

Anything crossing a network can be intercepted, so sensitive data is encrypted: the readable plain text is scrambled by an algorithm (a cipher) using a key into unreadable cipher text; the receiver uses a key to decrypt it back. The algorithm is public — the security lives in the key, like a lock whose design everyone knows but whose key you alone hold.

Symmetric encryptionAsymmetric encryption
KeysOne shared secret key for both encrypting and decryptingA matched pair: a public key (encrypts) and a private key (decrypts)
SpeedFast, suited to bulk dataSlow, suited to short messages and key exchange
ProblemGetting the shared key to the other party securely in the first placeNothing is secret to distribute, but the private key must be kept safe
ExamplesAES, DESRSA

Real systems combine them: HTTPS uses the asymmetric pair to agree a symmetric session key, then encrypts the whole conversation with the fast cipher. Hashing is a third tool — a one-way function producing a fixed-length value (the hash) from any input; it cannot be reversed, so passwords are stored as hashes (with a salt against rainbow tables) and any change to a message changes its hash, proving integrity. Digital certificates issued by certificate authorities bind a public key to a real identity, so a browser knows it is talking to the genuine bank and not an impostor.

Network hardware (statement 3.4)

  • Network interface card (NIC) — gives a device a network connection and a MAC address; it frames data onto the medium.
  • Switch — connects devices within a LAN and forwards each frame only to the port holding the destination MAC address; filters traffic and reduces collisions.
  • Router — connects different networks (your LAN to the internet) and forwards packets between them by choosing the best path using IP addresses.
  • Wireless access point — lets Wi-Fi devices join the wired LAN.
  • Hub — an older, simple repeater broadcasting every frame to all ports; largely replaced by switches.

Two addresses appear in exam answers and they belong to different layers: the MAC address is the permanent hardware identifier of a NIC used within a LAN, while the IP address is the logical address of a device on a network, used by routers to deliver packets across networks. Domains and DNS sit on top of that (see the internet note).

Worked example: a school LAN sends a file from room 1 to a server.

The file is split into numbered packets. Each packet is given the server's IP
address. The sending switch looks up the server's MAC address and forwards the
frame within the LAN. Along the way each packet may take a different route;
the server uses the sequence numbers to reassemble the file in order, and ACKs
any packet that fails its checksum so the sender retransmits only that packet.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Saying parity "corrects" errors; parity detects most single-bit errors — correction needs error-correcting codes or retransmission.
  • Getting the parity bit backwards: count the existing ones first; even parity needs the total to be even, so an odd count means the parity bit is 1.
  • Claiming two flipped bits are detected by parity; they change the count by two, which parity cannot see.
  • Confusing bandwidth with latency, or forgetting to convert bytes to bits (×8) before dividing by a bits-per-second rate.
  • Describing a router's job as "connects computers in a LAN" — that is the switch; the router connects networks and routes packets by IP address.
  • Swapping MAC and IP: MAC is fixed hardware identity on a LAN; IP is logical and can change, and is what routing uses.
  • Saying symmetric encryption is more secure than asymmetric (or vice versa); they are secure in different ways — the exam wants the key-distribution and speed trade-off.
  • Forgetting the timeout case in ARQ questions: a lost packet or lost ACK is recovered by the sender's timer, not by a NAK.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 1, 4 marks). Describe the difference between serial and parallel transmission and state one use for each.

Answer: Serial transmission sends the bits of a byte one after another down a single channel, so it is cheaper, immune to crosstalk between wires and reliable over long distances — used for USB, Ethernet and all long-distance links. Parallel transmission sends several bits simultaneously down multiple channels, which is faster over short distances but suffers skew and crosstalk over long cables — used for data buses inside a computer.

Question 2 (Paper 1, 3 marks). The byte 1011 0010 is to be sent using odd parity. State the parity bit and the transmitted group.

Answer: The byte contains five 1-bits (odd). Odd parity requires an odd total, so the parity bit is 0 and the transmitted group is 0 1011 0010 (parity bit shown first).

Question 3 (Paper 1, 4 marks). Explain how ARQ recovers from (i) a corrupted packet and (ii) a lost packet.

Answer: (i) The receiver's checksum test fails, so it returns a NAK; the sender retransmits that packet. (ii) No packet arrives, so no ACK is returned; the sender's timeout expires and it retransmits. In both cases the packet carries a sequence number so the receiver can discard duplicates and reassemble the data in order.

Question 4 (Paper 1, 4 marks). Explain why a bank uses asymmetric encryption to start a secure connection but symmetric encryption to transfer the data.

Answer: Asymmetric encryption (a public/private key pair) needs no shared secret to be distributed, so the bank can safely agree a session key with any customer who encrypts with the bank's published public key — only the bank's private key decrypts it. That process is slow, so once the session key is agreed both sides switch to fast symmetric encryption for the bulk of the transaction, which is efficient for large amounts of data.

Question 5 (Paper 1, 2 marks). Calculate the time to send a 12 MB file over a 4 Mbps link.

Answer: 12 MB = 96 megabits (12 × 8), and 96 ÷ 4 = 24 seconds.

Question 6 (Paper 1, 4 marks). Compare a switch and a router in a school network.

Answer: A switch connects devices within the LAN and forwards each frame only to the port of the destination MAC address, keeping local traffic off the rest of the network. A router connects the school LAN to other networks such as the internet and forwards packets between them, choosing routes using IP addresses. A switch works within one network; a router works between networks.

With the data safely moved, the next question is what runs on the machines: the software and the operating system that manages everything.

title: A Level Physics: Oscillations and Waves II
content:
A Level Physics: Oscillations and Waves II

Simple harmonic motion is the master oscillation: the movement of a pendulum, a mass on a spring, a guitar string, a child on a swing — every system that accelerates back toward an equilibrium position with a restoring force proportional to displacement. This note builds SHM from zero: the defining condition and its equations, the displacement, velocity and acceleration graphs and their calculus links, the energy bookkeeping within a cycle, and the real-world finishing topics — damping and resonance — with the applications and disasters that make them examinable.

What simple harmonic motion is

A body performs simple harmonic motion (SHM) when its acceleration is proportional to its displacement from a fixed equilibrium point and always directed toward that point:

a = - omega^2 x

a = acceleration (m s-2), x = displacement from equilibrium (m)
omega = angular frequency (rad s-1); the minus sign means the
acceleration always points back toward equilibrium

The analogy: a ball in a bowl. Push the ball up the side (displacement) and gravity pulls it back with a force proportional to how far up the slope it is — push twice as far, and the restoring force doubles. That proportionality is the whole defining feature; friction-less mass-spring systems and small-angle pendulums obey it.

QuantitySymbolRelation
Displacementxx = A sin(ωt) (from equilibrium at t = 0)
AmplitudeAmaximum displacement
PeriodTT = 2π/ω; mass on a spring: T = 2π√(m/k); pendulum: T = 2π√(L/g)
Frequencyff = 1/T = ω/(2π)
Angular frequencyωω = 2πf = √(k/m) (spring), √(g/L) (pendulum)

SHM equations and graphs

Starting from equilibrium at t = 0, the kinematics follows by differentiation (or by reading the graphs):

displacement:  x = A sin(omega t)
velocity:      v = A omega cos(omega t)
acceleration:  a = - A omega^2 sin(omega t) = - omega^2 x

velocity-displacement relation:
v = omega sqrt(A^2 - x^2)

Graph discipline is a mark source in its own right: displacement is a sine wave; velocity leads displacement by a quarter cycle (cosine); acceleration is the inverted displacement (anti-phase, scaled by ω²). At the extremes (x = ±A): velocity is zero and acceleration is maximum; at equilibrium (x = 0): velocity is maximum and acceleration is zero. Learn the four positions (centre, both extremes, mid-point) as a table of states.

Worked example. A mass oscillates with amplitude 0.10 m and frequency 2.0 Hz. Find ω, the maximum speed, and the maximum acceleration.

omega = 2 pi f = 2 x 3.14 x 2.0 = 12.6 rad s-1
v_max = A omega = 0.10 x 12.6 = 1.26 m s-1
a_max = A omega^2 = 0.10 x 158 = 15.8 m s-2

Worked example 2 (using v = ω√(A² − x²)). With the same oscillation, find the speed at x = 0.06 m.

v = omega sqrt(A^2 - x^2) = 12.6 x sqrt(0.010 - 0.0036)
  = 12.6 x sqrt(0.0064) = 12.6 x 0.08 = 1.01 m s-1

Worked example 3 (pendulum). Find the period of a 0.90 m pendulum (g = 9.81 m s⁻²).

T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g) = 2 x 3.14 x sqrt(0.90/9.81)
  = 6.28 x sqrt(0.0917) = 6.28 x 0.303 = 1.90 s

Energy in simple harmonic motion

Energy shuttles between kinetic and potential stores while the total stays constant (undamped SHM):

total energy:  E = (1/2) m omega^2 A^2 = (1/2) k A^2
kinetic:       KE = (1/2) m omega^2 (A^2 - x^2)
potential:     PE = (1/2) m omega^2 x^2   (spring: (1/2) k x^2)

The energy curves are examinable as graphs: total energy is a horizontal line over x; KE is an inverted parabola peaking at equilibrium; PE is an upright parabola peaking at the extremes; against time both are sine-squared curves oscillating at twice the frequency of x. Doubling the amplitude quadruples the total energy (E ∝ A²) — a favourite multiple-choice item.

Worked example. A 0.50 kg mass on a spring (k = 200 N m⁻¹) oscillates with amplitude 0.08 m. Find the total energy and the kinetic energy at x = 0.04 m.

E = (1/2) k A^2 = 0.5 x 200 x 0.0064 = 0.64 J
PE at x = 0.04: (1/2) k x^2 = 0.5 x 200 x 0.0016 = 0.16 J
KE = E - PE = 0.64 - 0.16 = 0.48 J

Damping

Real oscillations lose energy to drag and friction — damping. The three regimes matter:

  • Light damping: amplitude decays exponentially while the system keeps oscillating at almost the natural frequency (a child's swing gradually slowing).
  • Critical damping: the system returns to equilibrium in the minimum time without overshooting — deliberately engineered for car suspension, door closers and moving-coil meters.
  • Heavy (over) damping: a slow, sluggish return without oscillation.

The energy lost per cycle is the exam phrasing: light damping reduces amplitude gradually because each cycle transfers energy to the surroundings; the total energy falls exponentially with time even though the frequency barely changes.

Resonance

A driven oscillation responds most strongly when the driving frequency matches the system's natural frequency — resonance. The amplitude–frequency curve shows a peak at resonance; sharper peaks mean lighter damping. The mechanism: at resonance the driving force is in phase with the velocity, so energy is transferred most efficiently each cycle.

ApplicationUse or effect
Musical instrumentsair columns and strings resonate at their natural frequencies to amplify sound
Radio tuningan LC circuit selects the broadcast frequency that resonates with it
Microwave ovensdrive water molecules near their resonant absorption frequency
Car suspensiondesigned so road-frequency inputs never match the car's natural frequency; damping controls the peak
Tacoma Narrows (1940)wind-driven resonance (with aeroelastic flutter) destroyed the bridge — the cautionary case study
Bridges and buildingsseismic design detunes natural frequencies from earthquake oscillations

Worked example. Explain why soldiers break step crossing a bridge. Answer: Marching produces a periodic driving force at the step frequency; if it matched the bridge's natural frequency, resonance would build large-amplitude oscillations and structural damage; breaking step makes the driving frequency irregular and removes the coherent input.

Worked examples: combined SHM problems

Worked example. A 0.25 kg mass on a spring completes 20 oscillations in 8.0 s. Find the spring constant k.

T = 8.0/20 = 0.40 s
T = 2 pi sqrt(m/k)  ->  k = m (2 pi/T)^2
k = 0.25 x (6.28/0.40)^2 = 0.25 x 246.4 = 61.6 N m-1
  = 62 N m-1 (2 s.f.)

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Definition) State the defining condition for SHM. Answer: The acceleration is proportional to the displacement from equilibrium and directed toward it: a = −ω²x.
  2. (Graphs) Sketch or describe the velocity–time graph of an oscillating mass starting at maximum displacement. Answer: Velocity is a cosine-like curve starting at zero, reaching extremes of ±v_max as the mass passes equilibrium, one quarter cycle ahead of the displacement.
  3. (Calculations) An oscillator has amplitude 0.12 m and ω = 8.0 rad s⁻¹. Find the maximum acceleration. Answer: a_max = Aω² = 0.12 × 64 = 7.68 m s⁻² ≈ 7.7 m s⁻².
  4. (Energy) State how the total energy of an SHM system depends on amplitude and explain the effect of doubling it. Answer: E = ½kA², so energy is proportional to A²; doubling the amplitude quadruples the total energy.
  5. (Pendulum) Explain why a pendulum clock keeps worse time on a warm day. Answer: Warmth lengthens the pendulum L, and T = 2π√(L/g), so the period increases and the clock runs slow.
  6. (Damping) Distinguish light and critical damping. Answer: Light damping: oscillations continue with amplitude decaying exponentially; critical damping: the system returns to equilibrium in the shortest time without oscillating.
  7. (Resonance) Sketch qualitatively the amplitude–frequency response for a lightly and a heavily damped driven system, and state one use of resonance. Answer: Both peak at the natural frequency; the lightly damped peak is tall and sharp, the heavily damped one short and broad. Use: radio tuning circuits selecting a station's frequency.
  8. (Practical) Describe how you would determine g using a simple pendulum. Answer: Measure pendulum length L from pivot to bob centre; time N complete oscillations with a stopwatch and find T = t/N; repeat for several L values; plot T² against L — the gradient is 4π²/g, so g = 4π²/gradient.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • ω versus f: ω = 2πf. In a = −ω²x the ω is angular frequency; using f directly misses a factor of 4π².
  • Phase of the graphs: at maximum displacement, speed is zero and acceleration is maximum — candidates often invert this. Anchor on the extremes first: nothing moves at the turning points.
  • Energy ∝ A²: doubling amplitude quadruples energy; the amplitude of displacement does not scale energy linearly.
  • Pendulum validity: T = 2π√(L/g) assumes small angles (under about 10°) and a point mass; large angles lengthen the period.
  • Period independence: a pendulum's period is independent of bob mass and amplitude (small angle) — the classic conceptual question.
  • Damping and frequency: damping reduces amplitude and slightly shifts the peak frequency; in light damping the frequency is almost unchanged — do not claim the oscillation stops instantly.
  • Resonance condition: resonance requires the driving frequency to match the natural frequency; merely being "vibrated" does not guarantee it.
  • Spring constant from period: rearrange algebraically first (k = m(2π/T)²) and write the formula line — the rearrangement itself carries marks.
  • Precision: 2 or 3 s.f. with units (rad s⁻¹, m s⁻², N m⁻¹, J); keep π in the working until the final step.

title: Energy, Work & Power — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Energy, Work & Power

Physics — OL. stores and transfers, KE/PE, work, energy sources, power, efficiency.

  • 1. Energy stores & transfers
  • 2. Formulas
  • 3. Energy sources
  • 4. Efficiency
  • 5. Energy-chain problems

How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

Key relationships

  • Work done W = force × distance moved in the direction of the force.
  • Power P = energy transferred / time, and efficiency = useful energy output / total energy input × 100%.
  • Kinetic energy = ½mv² and gravitational potential energy = mgh.
  • Energy is conserved, so the total energy after a transfer equals the total before it.

Common errors

Do not confuse work with power, or energy with power. Efficiency can never be more than 100%, so a larger answer means an error in the calculation.

title: Variation and Selection
content:
Variation and Selection

Cambridge IGCSE Biology 0610, Extended route, topic 18 (statements 18.1–18.3). Types of variation, adaptive features, and natural selection including antibiotic resistance as the standard application.

18.1 Variation

  • Continuous variation shows a range of values (height, mass); discontinuous variation falls into distinct categories (blood group, tongue rolling). Variation has genetic causes (alleles) and environmental causes (diet, climate); most characteristics show both.

18.2 Adaptive features

  • Adaptive features are structural (shape, camouflage), behavioural (migration, nocturnal activity) or physiological ( venom production, heat generation) and they improve survival and reproduction in a specific environment.

18.3 Selection

  • Natural selection: organisms vary, those best adapted survive and reproduce, and they pass their advantageous alleles to offspring. Over generations the population changes. Darwin's theory, supported by evidence including selective breeding, fossils and antibiotic resistance.
  • Selective breeding (artificial selection) chooses parents with desired traits — higher crop yield, docile behaviour in livestock — over many generations.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Selection chain, applied to bacteria and antibiotics: the population already contains a few resistant individuals by random mutation; the antibiotic kills the non-resistant, so the survivors reproduce without competition and the resistant alleles increase in frequency. Name random mutation first — the ordering of the chain is what earns the marks.
  • Variation classification, applied to a data set of leaf lengths: continuous, and likely controlled by many genes plus environment. If the question gives discrete categories, it is discontinuous with a simpler genetic control. Justify from the data, not from a memorised list.
  • Evaluation reasoning, applied to whether evolution is "progress": argue that selection favours fit in the current environment, not perfection, and that a change in environment can reverse which variant is favoured. That nuance is what separates top-band answers.

Common errors

  • Saying organisms "try to adapt" or "develop resistance". Variation is random; selection is not.
  • Claiming acquired characteristics are inherited (Lamarck's error).
  • Confusing selective breeding with genetic modification — selective breeding uses existing variation.

title: A Level Mathematics: Numerical Methods
content:
A Level Mathematics: Numerical Methods

Some equations cannot be solved exactly: x = cos x, x³ − x − 1 = 0, e^x = 4x. Numerical methods find the solutions to any required accuracy by iteration and refinement. This note builds the four techniques A2 requires — locating a root by sign change, fixed-point iteration and its convergence, the Newton-Raphson formula with its derivation, and the trapezium rule for integrals that have no elementary antiderivative — together with the failure modes examiners test.

Locating a root: change of sign

if f(a) and f(b) have opposite signs and f is continuous on [a, b],
there is at least one root in (a, b)

Worked example. Show that x³ − x − 1 = 0 has a root between 1 and 2.

f(1) = 1 - 1 - 1 = -1
f(2) = 8 - 2 - 1 = 5
sign change and the cubic is continuous  →  a root in (1, 2)

The two conditions are both required: continuity rules out a jump, and the sign change forces a crossing. The theorem guarantees at least one root, not exactly one — say "at least" in the answer.

Worked example 2 (narrowing). Show the root lies between 1.3 and 1.4.

f(1.3) = 2.197 - 1.3 - 1 = -0.103
f(1.4) = 2.744 - 1.4 - 1 = 0.344
so the root lies in (1.3, 1.4)

Fixed-point iteration

rearrange f(x) = 0 into x = g(x), then iterate x_(n+1) = g(x_n)

the iteration converges when |g'(x)| < 1 near the root

Worked example. Use x_(n+1) = (x_n + 1)^(1/3) with x₁ = 1.3 to find the root of x³ − x − 1 = 0 to 4 d.p.

x2 = (2.3)^(1/3) = 1.3200 × 3 = (2.32)^(1/3) = 1.3238 × 4 = 1.3245;  x5 = 1.3246;  x6 = 1.3247
the sequence settles: root = 1.3247 (4 d.p.)

Worked example 2 (testing convergence). For g(x) = (x + 1)^(1/3), show the iteration converges near 1.32.

g'(x) = (1/3)(x + 1)^(-2/3)
at x = 1.32: g' = (1/3)(2.32)^(-2/3) = 0.19 < 1
so the iteration converges

If |g′| > 1 near the root the iteration diverges, and a different rearrangement is needed. The same equation usually has several rearrangements, only some of which converge — that is exactly what the |g′| test decides.

Failure modes of iteration

divergence: |g'| > 1 near the root
oscillation: the sequence jumps between two values
slow convergence: |g'| close to 1

Worked example. The rearrangement x = x³ − 1 for x³ − x − 1 = 0 gives g′(x) = 3x², which is about 5.3 near the root: the iteration diverges rapidly. That is why the cube-root rearrangement, with g′ ≈ 0.19, is used instead.

Newton-Raphson

x_(n+1) = x_n - f(x_n)/f'(x_n)

the tangent at the current point is followed to the x-axis;
the intercept becomes the next estimate

Derivation. The tangent at x_n has equation y − f(x_n) = f′(x_n)(x − x_n). Setting y = 0 gives x = x_n − f(x_n)/f′(x_n), which is the formula.

Worked example. Use Newton-Raphson on f(x) = x³ − x − 1 with x₁ = 1.3.

f'(x) = 3x² - 1 × 2 = 1.3 - (-0.103)/(4.07) = 1.3 + 0.0253 = 1.3253 × 3 = 1.3253 - (0.00053)/(4.2637) = 1.3252
root = 1.3252 (4 d.p.) in two steps, against six for the iteration

Worked example 2 (failure). Explain why x₁ = 0.5 fails for f(x) = x³ − x − 1.

f'(0.5) = -0.25, so x2 = 0.5 - (-1.375)/(-0.25) = 0.5 - 5.5 = -5.0
the tangent is nearly horizontal, so the step overshoots wildly;
the method can diverge when f' is small near the initial guess

State the failure condition explicitly: Newton-Raphson needs f′(x_n) ≠ 0 and a good starting value close to the root.

The trapezium rule

integral from a to b of f(x) dx ~ (h/2)[y_0 + 2(y_1 + ... + y_(n-1)) + y_n]
where h = (b - a)/n and y_i = f(a + ih)

the error: a larger n reduces it; the rule overestimates for a
concave-up curve and underestimates for concave-down

Worked example. Use the trapezium rule with 4 strips to estimate ∫ from 0 to 2 of e^(x²) dx.

h = 0.5; x: 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2
y: 1, 1.2840, 2.7183, 6.4760, 54.5982
I ~ (0.5/2)[1 + 2(1.2840 + 2.7183 + 6.4760) + 54.5982]
  = 0.25[1 + 20.9566 + 54.5982] = 0.25 × 76.5548 = 19.14

Worked example 2 (over or under). Is the estimate above or below the true value here?

e^(x²) is concave up (its gradient is increasing), so each chord lies
above the curve and the trapezium rule overestimates

Accuracy and error

the error of a trapezium estimate is roughly proportional to h²
halving h roughly quarters the error

rounding to k decimal places requires the estimate to be stable at
the next place

Worked example. An estimate with h = 0.5 gives 19.14; with h = 0.25 the estimate is 18.92. Estimate the answer to 1 d.p.

the two agree to 1 d.p. at 18.9; quoting 18.9 is defensible, and the
difference indicates the scale of the remaining error

Comparing two step sizes is the standard way to justify an accuracy claim; a single estimate cannot.

Setting up an iteration properly

An iteration question usually hands you the rearrangement; the marks are for using it correctly, showing the iterates, and judging convergence. Three habits cover it:

  • Write the recurrence exactly as given and substitute the stated starting value.
  • Record each iterate to one more decimal place than required.
  • Show two consecutive iterates agreeing at the required accuracy before quoting the root.

Worked example. f(x) = x³ + 2x − 5 has a root near 1.3. Show that x = (5 − 2x)^(1/3) is a valid rearrangement and iterate twice.

from x³ + 2x - 5 = 0: x³ = 5 - 2x  →  x = (5 - 2x)^(1/3) × 2 = (5 - 2.6)^(1/3) = (2.4)^(1/3) = 1.3389 × 3 = (5 - 2.6777)^(1/3) = (2.3223)^(1/3) = 1.3241
converging towards about 1.328

Worked example 2 (convergence check). Test |g′| for g(x) = (5 − 2x)^(1/3) near 1.33.

g'(x) = (1/3)(5 - 2x)^(-2/3) x (-2) = -0.667(5 - 2x)^(-2/3)
|g'(1.33)| = 0.667 x (2.34)^(-2/3) = 0.667 × 0.534 = 0.356 < 1
so the iteration converges

Newton-Raphson on other functions

The formula is universal; what changes is the derivative and the care needed with trigonometry and logs.

Worked example. Use Newton-Raphson to solve cos x = x starting from x₁ = 0.7.

f(x) = cos x - x;  f'(x) = -sin x - 1 × 2 = 0.7 - (0.7648 - 0.7)/(-0.6442 - 1) = 0.7 + 0.0648/1.6442 = 0.7394 × 3 = 0.7394 - (0.7391 - 0.7394)/(-0.6735 - 1) = 0.7391
root = 0.7391 (4 d.p.)
