Worked example 2 (log equation). Solve x ln x = 1 from x₁ = 1.5.

f(x) = x ln x - 1;  f'(x) = ln x + 1 × 2 = 1.5 - (0.6082 - 1)/(0.4055 + 1) = 1.5 + 0.2788 = 1.7788 × 3 = 1.7788 - 0.0423/1.5755 = 1.7519 × 4 = 1.7632;  converging to 1.7632

Radians are compulsory in any Newton-Raphson question involving trigonometry; degrees give a value of f′ scaled by π/180 and destroy convergence.

Choosing a starting value

Both iteration and Newton-Raphson need a starting value near the root, and a sketch is the reliable way to find one. Plot or sketch y = left-hand side and y = right-hand side of the rearranged equation; the intersections are the roots, and their approximate positions are the starting values.

Worked example. e^x = 4x has two roots. Sketch and estimate them.

sketch y = e^x and y = 4x: they cross once near x = 0.3 and again
near x = 2.2
checking: e^0.3 = 1.35 against 1.2; e^2.2 = 9.03 against 8.8
so start Newton-Raphson from 0.4 and from 2.2 separately

Two roots require two separate runs; a single guess finds only the root it is near. That is the most common lost mark in equations with several roots.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Sign change) Show x³ + x − 3 = 0 has a root in (1, 2). Answer: f(1) = −1, f(2) = 7; continuous; sign change.
  2. (Iteration) x_(n+1) = (3 − x_n)^(1/3), x₁ = 1. Find x₃. Answer: 1.2599, 1.2020.
  3. (Convergence) g(x) = (3 − x)^(1/3): show |g′| < 1 near 1.21. Answer: |g′| = (1/3)(3 − x)^(−2/3) ≈ 0.21 < 1.
  4. (Newton) f(x) = x² − 5, x₁ = 2. Find x₂. Answer: 2 − (−1)/4 = 2.25.
  5. (Newton again) Find x₃ for the same. Answer: 2.25 − 0.0625/4.5 = 2.2361.
  6. (Newton failure) f(x) = x³, x₁ = −1. What happens? Answer: x₂ = −1 − (−1)/3 = −0.667, converging slowly towards 0; the root is a stationary point, so convergence is linear.
  7. (Trapezium) Estimate ∫₀² x² dx with 2 strips. Answer: h = 1; (1/2)[0 + 2(1) + 4] = 3.
  8. (Error) Is that estimate over or under? Answer: over, since x² is concave up; the true value is 8/3 = 2.667.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Claiming exactly one root: the sign change proves at least one; uniqueness needs monotonicity or a sketch.
  • Iterating too few times: the answer must be stable at the required number of decimal places — show consecutive values agreeing.
  • Calculator in the wrong mode: iteration on a reset calculator silently uses the last answer; store x_n in a variable.
  • Newton with a small derivative: the step overshoots; state the failure rather than ploughing on.
  • Wrong h: h = (b − a)/n, not the number of ordinates; counting strips and counting points are different.
  • Trapezium brackets: the first and last ordinates are counted once, the interior ones twice; a factor-of-two error here is the classic slip.
  • Error direction guessed: justify over/under estimate from the concavity, not from the size of the answer.
  • Accuracy unqualified: "the answer is 1.32" without evidence that later iterations agree is not a numerical-methods answer.

Equations and symbols

Four relations cover the paper: the sign-change test that locates a root, the iteration and Newton–Raphson formulas that refine it, and the trapezium rule for an integral with no closed form. Each has a failure mode the examiner asks you to name, so the conditions matter as much as the algebra.

x_(n+1) = g(x_n) Key: x_n = the current estimate of the root (in the variable's units); x_(n+1) = the next estimate; g = the rearranged equation, obtained by making x the subject of f(x) = 0. The same equation has several rearrangements and only some of them converge.

the iteration converges when |g'(x)| < 1 near the root Key: g′(x) = the derivative of the rearrangement (no units); a value smaller than 1 in size pulls successive estimates together, larger than 1 pushes them apart. This single test decides which rearrangement to use, and a question that says "show that this rearrangement converges" wants exactly this line.

x_(n+1) = x_n - f(x_n)/f'(x_n) Key: f(x_n) = the value of the function at the current estimate; f′(x_n) = its derivative there; the quotient is the horizontal distance from x_n to where the tangent meets the axis. Geometrically the method follows the tangent down to the x-axis, which is why it converges far faster than plain iteration.

f(1) = 1 - 1 - 1 = -1 and f(2) = 8 - 2 - 1 = 5 Key: for f(x) = x³ − x − 1; the two values have opposite signs and a cubic is continuous, so there is at least one root in (1, 2). Say "at least" — the sign change never proves uniqueness.

g'(x) = (1/3)(x + 1)^(-2/3) Key: the derivative of g(x) = (x + 1)^(1/3), the rearrangement that converges for x³ − x − 1 = 0; at x = 1.32 it is about 0.19, well under 1. The other rearrangement, x = x³ − 1, has g′ ≈ 5.3 there and diverges — the comparison is the answer to "why this rearrangement".

h = (b - a)/n Key: h = the width of one strip (in the units of x); b and a = the upper and lower limits of the integral; n = the number of strips, so there are n + 1 ordinates. Counting strips and counting points are different, and mixing them halves or doubles h.

h = 0.5; x: 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2 Key: for the integral of e^(x²) from 0 to 2 with four strips: h = (2 − 0)/4 = 0.5, and the ordinates sit at x = 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2. Tabulate the ordinates before substituting, because the bracket is where the factor-of-two errors happen.

y: 1, 1.2840, 2.7183, 6.4760, 54.5982 Key: the five values of e^(x²) at those ordinates; in the trapezium rule the first and last are counted once and the interior values twice, giving 0.25[1 + 20.9566 + 54.5982] = 19.14. The rule overestimates here because e^(x²) is concave up, and halving h roughly quarters the error.

x2 = 0.5 - (-1.375)/(-0.25) = 0.5 - 5.5 = -5.0 Key: Newton–Raphson failing: f(0.5) = −1.375 and f′(0.5) = −0.25, a nearly horizontal tangent, so the step overshoots wildly. The method needs f′ ≠ 0 and a starting value near the root; state that condition rather than continuing the arithmetic.

SymbolQuantityUnit
f(x)the function whose root or integral is wantedwhatever the function returns (no units if dimensionless)
x_nthe nth estimate of the rootsame units as x
hstrip widthsame units as x

title: Forces & Motion — Study Notes
content:
Forces & Motion

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): motion (speed, acceleration, graphs); mass & weight; density link; force basics (F = ma, resultant); momentum (Extended); turning effects; equilibrium.

1. Kinematics

  • Speed = distance/time; average speed = (u + v)/2 for uniform acceleration.
  • Acceleration a = (v − u)/t.
  • SUVAT (uniform a): v = u + at; s = ut + ½at²; v² = u² + 2as.

2. Motion graphs

  • Distance–time: gradient = speed.
  • Speed–time: gradient = acceleration; area = distance. Negative gradient = deceleration.
  • Free fall 1: g ≈ 9.8 m/s² (use 10) — v = gt from rest.

3. Mass, weight, density

W = mg (g ≈ 10 N/kg). Weight acts at the centre of mass; mass is invariant. Density ρ = m/V.

4. Newton's laws and resultant force

  • Resultant: colinear addition/subtraction; perpendicular by Pythagoras.
  • F = ma. Terminal velocity: drag grows with speed until it balances weight.
  • Third law pairs: equal magnitude, opposite direction, different bodies.

5. Momentum (Extended)

p = mv; impulse Ft = Δ(mv); conservation: Σpbefore = Σpafter (explosions, collisions).

Example: 2 kg at 3 m/s hits 1 kg at rest, combined 1 m/s: 6 = 3v ⇒ v = 2 m/s.

6. Moments and equilibrium

  • Moment = F × perpendicular distance from pivot.
  • Principle of moments: Σclockwise = Σanticlockwise.
  • Equilibrium: resultant force = 0 and resultant moment = 0.

Example: 100 N at 0.3 m balances F at 0.5 m: F = 60 N.

title: Vectors
content:
Vectors

Components and Arithmetic

A vector a = 3i + 4j has magnitude |a| = √(3² + 4²) = 5. Parallel vectors are scalar multiples; unit vector = a/|a|.

Position and Direction

The line through point A with direction d: r = a + t d. Two lines are parallel if their directions are multiples.

Example: r = (1, 2) + t(3, −1).

Scalar (Dot) Product

a · b = |a||b| cos θ = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂.

Perpendicular ⇔ a · b = 0. Parallel ⇔ cross-multiplied components are equal (in 2D: a₁b₂ − a₂b₁ = 0).

Example: (2, 3) · (−6, 4) = −12 + 12 = 0, so they are perpendicular.

Angle Between Vectors

cos θ = (a · b)/(|a||b|).

Example: between (1, 0) and (1, 1): cos θ = 1/(1 × √2), θ = 45°.

Lines and Points

Foot of perpendicular from P to a line, intersection of two lines, and shortest distances all come from dot products and parameter t.

Exam tips: write column vectors cleanly; check answers by substituting the found t back into both position vectors; keep exact surd magnitudes rather than decimals.

title: Redox Chemistry and Groups 1, 2 and 7 — Study Notes
content:
Redox Chemistry and Groups 1, 2 and 7

Edexcel IAL Chemistry 9CH0 AS, topic 8. Every statement 8.1 to 8.28 is covered below, with its code in the heading. Three ideas run through the whole topic: oxidation numbers track electron transfer, the Group 1 and 2 trends follow from atomic size and nuclear charge, and the Group 7 trends are the same ideas applied to halogens.

8.1 to 8.4: Oxidation numbers

  • Rules: an element is 0; a monatomic ion equals its charge; the sum of oxidation numbers equals the overall charge. Oxygen is usually −2 (but −1 in peroxides such as H₂O₂), hydrogen is usually +1 (but −1 in metal hydrides such as NaH), fluorine is always −1, Group 1 is +1 and Group 2 is +2.
  • 8.2: in MnO₄⁻, manganese must be +7, because four oxygens contribute −8 and the ion has a charge of −1.
  • 8.3: write the oxidation number as a Roman numeral in the name: manganese(VII), iron(III), copper(II).
  • 8.4: work backwards from oxidation numbers to a formula. Iron(III) sulfate is Fe₂(SO₄)₃, because Fe³⁺ must balance SO₄²⁻ in a 2:3 ratio.

8.5 to 8.9: Oxidation, reduction and disproportionation

  • 8.5: oxidation is loss of electrons, and it appears as an increase in oxidation number. Reduction is gain of electrons, a decrease in oxidation number. In 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl, sodium is oxidised (0 to +1) and chlorine is reduced (0 to −1). The same idea covers reactions of s-block metals and p-block non-metals.
  • 8.6: an oxidising agent gains electrons and is itself reduced. A reducing agent loses electrons and is itself oxidised.
  • 8.7: disproportionation is when one element in a single species is both oxidised and reduced at the same time. Chlorine in water is the standard example: Cl₂ → Cl⁻ (0 to −1) and HClO (0 to +1).
  • 8.8: oxidation numbers classify reactions. A reaction is redox if any oxidation number changes, and it is a disproportionation if the same element goes both up and down.
  • 8.9: metals form positive ions by losing electrons, so their oxidation number increases. Non-metals form negative ions by gaining electrons, so their oxidation number decreases.

8.10: Half-equations and full ionic equations

  • Write the oxidation and the reduction separately, balance atoms, then balance charge with electrons. For magnesium with chlorine: Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻ and Cl₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻.
  • Add the half-equations so the electrons cancel, then cancel any spectator ions to give the full ionic equation.

8.11 to 8.13: Group 1 and Group 2 trends and reactions

  • 8.11: ionisation energy falls down Groups 1 and 2. The outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded by inner shells, so less energy is needed to remove it.
  • 8.12: reactivity rises down Group 1 (Li to K) and Group 2 (Mg to Ba), for the same reason: the outer electron is removed more easily.
  • 8.13: Group 1 metals burn in oxygen and react vigorously with chlorine and water. Group 2 metals react with oxygen and chlorine to form oxides and chlorides. Magnesium reacts slowly with cold water and readily with steam, while calcium reacts steadily with cold water to form Ca(OH)₂ and hydrogen.

8.14: Reactions of oxides and hydroxides

  • Group 1 oxides dissolve in water to give alkaline hydroxides. Group 2 oxides react less vigorously, and CaO gives a limewater-type solution, Ca(OH)₂.
  • Oxides react with dilute acid to form a salt and water, for example MgO + 2H⁺ → Mg²⁺ + H₂O.
  • Hydroxides neutralise dilute acids: Ca(OH)₂ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + 2H₂O.

8.15: Solubility trends of Group 2 hydroxides and sulfates

  • Hydroxides: solubility increases down the group. Magnesium hydroxide is almost insoluble, calcium hydroxide is slightly soluble, barium hydroxide is quite soluble.
  • Sulfates: solubility decreases down the group. Magnesium sulfate is soluble, barium sulfate is insoluble, which is why acidified barium chloride gives a white precipitate in the sulfate test.

8.16: Thermal stability of nitrates and carbonates

  • Stability increases down each group. A larger cation has a lower charge density, so it polarises the carbonate or nitrate ion less, and the anion breaks down less easily.
  • Carbonates: MCO₃ → MO + CO₂. Group 2 nitrates: 2M(NO₃)₂ → 2MO + 4NO₂ + O₂. Group 1 nitrates (other than lithium) give the nitrite and oxygen: 2NaNO₃ → 2NaNO₂ + O₂.
  • Lithium is the exception: its nitrate decomposes like a Group 2 nitrate, because the small Li⁺ ion polarises the nitrate strongly.

8.17: Flame colours

  • Heat excites outer electrons to higher energy levels. When they fall back, they emit light of a specific wavelength. Lithium is crimson, sodium is yellow-orange, potassium is lilac, calcium is brick red, strontium is red and barium is green.

8.18: Experiments on thermal decomposition

  • Heat a small sample of nitrate or carbonate in a test tube and test the gas. Brown NO₂ shows a nitrate; a glowing splint relit by O₂ shows oxygen. A carbonate gives CO₂, which turns limewater milky.
  • Compare the temperatures needed for decomposition down a group to show the trend in 8.16.

8.19: Identifying ions

  • Carbonate (CO₃²⁻) or hydrogencarbonate (HCO₃⁻): add dilute acid. CO₂ is released and turns limewater milky. Ionic equation: CO₃²⁻ + 2H⁺ → H₂O + CO₂.
  • Sulfate (SO₄²⁻): add acidified barium chloride. A white precipitate of BaSO₄ forms: Ba²⁺ + SO₄²⁻ → BaSO₄. The acid stops carbonate and sulfite interfering.
  • Ammonium (NH₄⁺): add sodium hydroxide and warm. Ammonia is released, turns damp red litmus blue, and gives white fumes with HCl.

8.20 to 8.23: Concentrations, titrations and uncertainty

  • 8.20: concentration in mol dm⁻³ = moles ÷ volume in dm³. To convert to g dm⁻³, multiply by the molar mass.
  • Indicators: methyl orange changes from red to yellow at about pH 3–4, suited to strong acid against weak base. Phenolphthalein changes from colourless to pink at about pH 8–10, suited to weak acid against strong base.
  • 8.21 (core practical 3): titrate hydrochloric acid against a standard alkali, record the titre and use the balanced equation to find the acid's concentration.
  • 8.22: reduce uncertainty by rinsing the pipette and burette, reading the meniscus at eye level, and repeating until two titres agree within 0.10 cm³. A burette reading has an uncertainty of ±0.05 cm³, so a titre has ±0.10 cm³. Calculate the percentage uncertainty as uncertainty ÷ reading × 100.
  • 8.23 (core practical 4): weigh a solid acid such as hydrated ethanedioic acid accurately, dissolve it, make it up to 250 cm³ in a volumetric flask, and use it as a standard solution to find the concentration of sodium hydroxide.

8.24: Trends in Group 7

  • Melting and boiling points rise down the group, because the molecules are larger and have stronger London forces. Fluorine and chlorine are gases, bromine is a liquid, iodine is a solid.
  • Electronegativity falls down the group, because the bonding pair sits further from the nucleus and is shielded more.
  • Reactivity (oxidising power) falls down the group, because the atoms are larger and gain an electron less readily.

8.25: Displacement reactions and colours

  • A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive halide: Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂, and Cl₂ or Br₂ + 2I⁻ → I₂ + halide.
  • Colours: in water, chlorine is pale green-yellow, bromine is orange and iodine is brown. In a non-polar organic solvent such as cyclohexane, bromine stays orange and iodine turns violet.

8.26: Reactions of the halogens, including disproportionation

  • (i) Halogens oxidise Group 1 and 2 metals to halides, for example 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl.
  • (ii) Chlorine with water is a disproportionation: Cl₂ + H₂O ⇌ HCl + HClO. The HClO is the basis of chlorine water treatment.
  • (iii) Chlorine with cold, dilute NaOH gives bleach: Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaClO + H₂O.
  • (iv) With hot concentrated alkali, chlorine disproportionates to chlorate: 3Cl₂ + 6NaOH → 5NaCl + NaClO₃ + 3H₂O.
  • (v) Bromine behaves in the same way with cold alkali. Use the oxidation number of each chlorine to check each product.

8.27: Reactions of halides and hydrogen halides

  • (i) Solid halides with concentrated H₂SO₄ show the reducing trend. NaCl gives HCl only. NaBr is oxidised further to Br₂ and SO₂. NaI is oxidised to I₂ and H₂S. The reducing ability is HI > HBr > HCl.
  • (ii) Silver nitrate with the halide ions in nitric acid: AgCl is white, AgBr is cream, AgI is yellow. AgCl dissolves in dilute aqueous ammonia, AgBr only in concentrated ammonia, and AgI does not dissolve.
  • (iii) Hydrogen halides with ammonia give ammonium halides (NH₃ + HCl → NH₄Cl). With water they give acids.

8.28: Predicting fluorine and astatine

  • Fluorine is the most electronegative element and the strongest oxidising agent in the group. It reacts violently with water, displacing oxygen from it.
  • Astatine is at the bottom of the group, so by the trends it should be a dark, solid, less reactive halogen than iodine, with a lower electronegativity. It is radioactive, so its chemistry is hard to study directly, and predictions come from the trends.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Half-equations in acid, 8.10 applied: dichromate(VI) reduced by iron(II). Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6e⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O, and Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + e⁻ (multiply by 6). Adding gives Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 6Fe²⁺ + 14H⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + 6Fe³⁺ + 7H₂O. Check atoms, then charge: both sides total +24.
  • Titration calculation, 8.20 and 8.22 applied: 25.0 cm³ of an iron(II) solution needs 18.0 cm³ of 0.0200 mol dm⁻³ K₂Cr₂O₇. Moles of dichromate = 0.0200 × 0.0180 = 3.60 × 10⁻⁴ mol. Each dichromate needs six Fe²⁺, so Fe²⁺ = 2.16 × 10⁻³ mol. Concentration = 2.16 × 10⁻³ ÷ 0.0250 = 0.0864 mol dm⁻³. An A* answer shows the ratio from the balanced equation before any arithmetic.
  • Disproportionation, 8.7 and 8.26 applied: chlorine with cold dilute NaOH gives Cl⁻ (0 to −1, reduction) and ClO⁻ (0 to +1, oxidation) in one reaction. Name both oxidation numbers when explaining why a reaction is disproportionation.
  • Group 2 hydroxide solubility, 8.15 applied: solubility rises down the group because hydration enthalpy falls more steeply than lattice enthalpy as the cation grows. Lattice enthalpy depends on the ion sizes and charges; hydration enthalpy depends on how strongly water molecules bind the cation. Both are needed for full marks.
  • Thermal stability, 8.16 applied: a small, highly charged cation such as Mg²⁺ polarises a carbonate ion strongly, which weakens its C–O bonds, so MgCO₃ decomposes at a lower temperature than BaCO₃. Use the word polarisation, not just "smaller ions decompose more easily".
  • Halogen displacement and redox direction, 8.25 and 8.27 applied: chlorine oxidises bromide and iodide, bromine oxidises iodide, but iodine oxidises neither. Read the direction from the reducing trend: iodide is the strongest reducing agent among the halides, which is why concentrated sulfuric acid reduces HI to H₂S.

Common errors that lose marks

  • Using the wrong oxidation number for oxygen in a peroxide or hydrogen in a metal hydride.
  • Confusing reducing ability with reactivity for the halogens: reactivity falls down Group 7, but the reducing ability of the halide ions rises.
  • Writing the test for sulfate without acid. Without acid, carbonate would also give a white precipitate.

title: IGCSE Physics: Energy, Work and Power
content:
IGCSE Physics: Energy, Work and Power

Cambridge IGCSE Physics 0625 (2026–2028), Topic 1 Motion, forces and energy, statement 1.7 Energy, work and power. Energy is the currency of every physical process: it is never created or destroyed, only moved between stores and converted between forms. This note builds the whole idea from scratch — stores, transfers, the two energy equations, work, power, the world's energy resources and efficiency — because Paper 4 rewards candidates who can both calculate an energy change and explain where the energy went.

Energy stores and transfers

Think of energy as money held in different bank accounts. It can sit in a store, and it can move between stores along a transfer pathway, but the total across all accounts never changes. The examined stores and transfers are:

Energy storeWhat it meansExample
KineticEnergy of a moving object; more mass or more speed means moreA moving lorry
Gravitational potentialEnergy stored by virtue of height in a gravitational fieldA book on a shelf
Elastic potentialEnergy stored by stretching, compressing or twistingA drawn bow, a compressed spring
Thermal (internal)Energy of the random motion of particles in a substanceHot water in a kettle
ChemicalEnergy stored in chemical bondsFood, fuel, a battery
NuclearEnergy stored in the nucleus of an atomUranium fuel

The four transfer pathways are mechanical work (a force acting over a distance), heating (energy transferred by a temperature difference), radiation (energy carried by waves, mainly infrared and light) and electrical work (charge moving through a potential difference). When a ball is thrown upwards, chemical energy in the muscles does mechanical work on the ball, and that energy becomes kinetic; as the ball rises, kinetic becomes gravitational potential; as it falls back, gravitational potential becomes kinetic again; on impact the kinetic spreads into the thermal stores of the ball, the ground and the air, and some is radiated as sound.

Conservation of energy and Sankey diagrams

The law of conservation of energy states that energy cannot be created or destroyed, and the total energy in a closed system stays constant. This is the most powerful statement in the syllabus: whenever a question says a machine loses energy, it means the energy has been transferred to less useful stores, not destroyed. A Sankey diagram draws the total energy input as one wide arrow, splits it into useful output and wasted arrows, and is drawn so the arrow widths are proportional to the energies.

Useful energy is the energy transferred to the store the device was designed to fill; wasted energy is transferred to stores that were not the goal, usually thermal energy of the surroundings, and it is eventually transferred to the environment, often by radiation. Wasted energy is not destroyed — it has simply become too spread out to be harnessed easily.

Kinetic and gravitational potential energy

Both equations are Supplement statements, and both appear constantly in Paper 4 calculations.

kinetic energy = 1/2 x mass x speed squared        EK = 1/2 m v²
gravitational potential energy = mass x gravitational field strength x height        EP = m g h
  • EK: kinetic energy in joules (J); m: mass in kilograms (kg); v: speed in metres per second (m s⁻¹). Energy is a scalar, so the speed is squared and the direction of travel does not matter.
  • EP: gravitational potential energy in joules (J); g: gravitational field strength in newtons per kilogram (N kg⁻¹, use the value given in the question); h: vertical height in metres (m), measured between the two positions being compared.

Only the difference in height matters. Lifting a 2 kg book from a table to a shelf 0.50 m above it raises EP by 2 × 9.81 × 0.50 = 9.8 J, whatever the height of the room. The sign convention is simple: EP increases as an object rises and decreases as it falls, and the change is ΔEP = m g Δh.

Energy methods are often faster than forces and equations of motion. For a falling object with no air resistance, m g h = ½ m v², and the mass cancels: every object falls at the same rate in a vacuum. For a roller coaster of mass 500 kg dropping 20 m from rest, v = √(2 g h) = √(2 × 9.81 × 20) = 19.8 m s⁻¹.

Work done

Work is done when a force moves an object. It is energy transferred by mechanical work, and it is measured in joules:

work done = force x distance moved in the direction of the force        W = F s
  • W: work done in joules (J). One joule is the work done when a force of 1 newton moves its point of application 1 metre in the direction of the force.
  • F: force in newtons (N); s: distance moved in metres (m), measured in the direction of the force.

Work is a scalar, but the two quantities must line up: carrying a box horizontally at constant height does no work against gravity, because the motion is perpendicular to the weight. Pushing a trolley with 50 N against 20 N of friction over 4 m does 200 J of work in total, of which 80 J goes to heating the bearings and floor through friction and 120 J remains as kinetic energy. If you carry shopping upstairs, the work done against gravity is your weight multiplied by the vertical height gained, not the length of the staircase.

Power

Power measures how fast energy is transferred — the rate of doing work. A car engine that lifts the same load in half the time is twice as powerful.

power = work done / time taken = energy transferred / time taken        P = W / t = E / t
  • P: power in watts (W). One watt is one joule per second (1 W = 1 J s⁻¹). A kilowatt is 1000 W.
  • W: work done in joules (J); E: energy transferred in joules (J); t: time taken in seconds (s).

Power is a scalar. For a vehicle moving at constant speed against a constant force, the same idea gives P = F v (Supplement), with F in newtons and v in metres per second, giving watts directly. Doubling the speed of a car at constant driving force doubles the power needed; a car climbing a hill at constant speed needs power P = mgv sin θ to raise its weight.

Energy resources and electricity generation

Most electrical energy is generated the same way: a fuel heats water, the steam spins a turbine, and the turbine spins a generator that converts the kinetic energy of rotation into electrical energy. What differs is the energy store the heat comes from.

ResourceStore usedAdvantagesDisadvantages
Coal, oil, gas (fossil fuels)Chemical, burned to give heatReliable, cheap to run, existing infrastructureFinite supply; carbon dioxide and pollutants released; contributes to climate change and acid rain
BiofuelChemical, from plant or animal materialRenewable; carbon dioxide released was recently absorbed by the plantsLand and water needed to grow crops; energy cost of farming and transport
HydroelectricGravitational potential of stored waterRenewable, reliable, no fuel cost, no emissions in useDams flood valleys and disrupt habitats; high construction cost; depends on rainfall
GeothermalThermal energy inside the EarthRenewable, reliable, small land useOnly practical near volcanic regions; drilling cost; possible release of underground gases
Nuclear fuelNuclear, released by fissionVery large energy per kilogram; no carbon dioxide in operationRadioactive waste that must be stored safely for centuries; high decommissioning cost; accident risk
Solar cellsLight radiation converted directly to electricityRenewable, silent, no emissions in use, low maintenanceOutput varies with light and season; expensive to manufacture; large area needed for high output
Solar panels (heating)Light radiation heating water directlyRenewable and cheap to runOnly heats water; ineffective at night and in cloudy climates

Non-renewable resources exist in finite stock and are used faster than they form; renewable resources are replenished as they are used. Supplement statements add the deep connection: the Sun is the principal source for almost all of these resources. Sunlight drives the water cycle behind hydroelectric power and biofuels, heats the ground behind wind and geothermal gradients, and fossil fuels are the remains of organisms that grew in sunlight. The Sun releases energy by nuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium, and research into fusion on Earth aims to provide a fuel that is abundant and produces no long-lived radioactive waste, though sustained fusion power is still experimental.

Efficiency

Efficiency compares what a device delivers with what it is given:

efficiency = useful energy output / total energy input
efficiency = useful power output / total power input

Efficiency has no unit; multiply by 100 for a percentage. No real device is 100 per cent efficient, because some energy is always transferred to thermal stores of the surroundings by friction, resistance and radiation. A filament lamp is about 5 per cent efficient (most energy becomes heat, not light); an electric motor might reach 80 per cent. The most efficient heating device is a simple heater, because its useful output is thermal energy — the same store as its waste. A Sankey diagram makes this visible at a glance, and the arrows must sum to the total input.

Worked example: lifting and efficiency

A crane lifts a 500 kg load through 12 m at constant speed in 20 s. Take g = 9.81 N kg⁻¹.

weight = m g = 500 × 9.81 = 4905 N
useful work = force x distance = 4905 × 12 = 58 860 J
useful power = work / time = 58 860 / 20 = 2943 W (about 2.9 kW)

The motor takes 150 000 J of electrical energy to do this lift. Its efficiency is 58 860 / 150 000 = 0.39, or 39 per cent. The remaining 91 140 J is not destroyed: it warms the motor windings, the cables and the surrounding air.

Second stage, using energy conservation: if the load is dropped from rest through the same 12 m with negligible air resistance, m g h = ½ m v² gives v = √(2 × 9.81 × 12) = 15.3 m s⁻¹. The mass cancels, so any object dropped through 12 m reaches the same speed.

Common mistakes

  • Saying energy is used up or lost; energy is transferred to other stores, and the total is conserved. Examiners award the mark for transferred, not lost.
  • Putting speed rather than speed squared into EK = ½mv², and forgetting the ½.
  • Measuring h in EP = mgh along a slope or a staircase; h is the vertical height difference.
  • Using the wrong mass in W = mg: the mass in kilograms, multiplied by g, never the weight in newtons multiplied by g again.
  • Confusing work done with power: joules measure energy, watts measure the rate of energy transfer.
  • Calculating efficiency as total in over useful out; the useful output goes on top, so efficiency is always less than 1.
  • Forgetting that a percentage efficiency needs multiplying by 100, and leaving the answer as 0.39 when 39 per cent is asked for.
  • Mixing units: power in watts needs energy in joules and time in seconds, so kilowatts and minutes must be converted first.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 4, 3 marks). A ball of mass 0.15 kg is moving at 10 m s⁻¹. Calculate its kinetic energy and the height through which it would need to be raised to store the same energy. Take g = 9.81 N kg⁻¹.

Answer: EK = ½mv² = ½ × 0.15 × 10² = 7.5 J. Setting mgh = 7.5 gives h = 7.5 / (0.15 × 9.81) = 5.1 m.

Question 2 (Paper 4, 4 marks). A 60 kg student runs up a flight of stairs of vertical height 3.0 m in 4.0 s. Calculate the useful power developed. Take g = 10 N kg⁻¹.

Answer: work = mgh = 60 × 10 × 3.0 = 1800 J. Power = 1800 / 4.0 = 450 W. (Real power is higher, because the student also gains kinetic energy and warms their muscles.)

Question 3 (Paper 2 style). A machine takes in 2000 J and delivers 1500 J of useful work. Its efficiency is: A 25 per cent; B 75 per cent; C 133 per cent; D 175 per cent. Answer: B. 1500/2000 = 0.75 = 75 per cent. Option C comes from putting input over output — the classic trap.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 6 marks). Explain why a solar cell is described as renewable, and discuss whether it is a good replacement for a coal-fired power station.

Answer: A solar cell converts light energy directly into electrical energy and consumes no fuel, so its energy source, sunlight, is replenished continuously and it is renewable. It produces no carbon dioxide or pollutants in operation. Against that, output depends on light intensity and falls at night and in cloudy weather, so storage or backup generation is needed; manufacturing the cells is energy-intensive, and a large area is required for high output. Coal is reliable and dispatchable but burns a finite resource, releasing carbon dioxide that drives climate change plus sulfur dioxide and particulates. A balanced conclusion weighs reliability and land use against emissions and fuel sustainability.

Question 5 (Paper 4, 3 marks). A car engine produces a driving force of 2000 N while travelling at 30 m s⁻¹. Calculate the useful power output.

Answer: P = F v = 2000 × 30 = 60 000 W = 60 kW.

Question 6 (Paper 6 style). Suggest how you would determine experimentally the efficiency of an electric motor lifting a small mass.

Answer: Measure the mass with a balance and the height lifted with a ruler, and record the time with a stopwatch. The useful output is mgh, calculated from the measured mass and vertical height. Measure the electrical energy input with a joule meter, or with an ammeter and voltmeter readings and E = V I t. Efficiency is mgh divided by V I t. Repeat for several masses and quote an average, keeping the input voltage constant.

With energy accounted for, the next question is what happens when forces are spread over area and depth: pressure and density.

Reading a Sankey diagram — and why its widths are the physics

A Sankey diagram looks like decoration and is actually an equation. The width of each band is the amount of energy in that transfer, which means conservation of energy is visible as a shape: whatever goes in on the left comes out on the right, split into useful and wasted. Once you read the widths as numbers, efficiency stops being a formula to memorise and becomes a comparison of two lengths.

Why the bands widen and narrow. Energy is never created or destroyed, only transferred between stores. A machine takes energy in one store, moves some of it to the store you wanted, and the rest to a store you did not — usually the thermal store of the surroundings. In the motor above, 200 J of electrical energy becomes 150 J of kinetic energy and 50 J of heating: 150 + 50 = 200, and the diagram cannot be drawn any other way.

Efficiency = useful output ÷ total input Key: efficiency = the fraction of the energy supplied that ends up in the useful store (no unit, or %); useful output = energy in the store you wanted (J); total input = energy supplied (J).

Worked example. For the motor above, find the efficiency and the energy wasted each second if it is supplied with 200 J every second.

efficiency = useful ÷ total = 150 ÷ 200 = 0.75 = 75%
wasted per second = 200 J − 150 J = 50 J

The same number read as power: the motor is supplied with 200 W and delivers 150 W of useful mechanical power, so 50 W is transferred to the surroundings by heating. Efficiency is the same whether you use energy or power, because both sides are divided by the same time.

The word the examiner wants for "wasted". Energy that does not reach the useful store is dissipated — spread out into the surroundings, usually by heating, at a slightly higher temperature. It has not disappeared, and writing "lost" invites the follow-up "where did it go?". Writing "dissipated to the surroundings by heating" earns it in one phrase.

Chained efficiency: the reason a lamp is worse than it looks. Machines are usually in series, and efficiencies multiply. A power station converts fuel at about 40%, transmission through the grid keeps about 95%, and a filament lamp turns about 5% of what reaches it into light. The overall figure is
0.40 × 0.95 × 0.05 = 0.019
so roughly 2% of the chemical energy in the fuel leaves the lamp as light. Multiplying fractions that are all less than one gives an answer smaller than any of them, which is the arithmetic behind every "why is this so inefficient?" question.

Where marks are lost. Drawing a Sankey whose output bands do not add up to the input band — it is a conservation diagram, and the mark scheme checks the widths. Quoting efficiency as a fraction when the question asks for a percentage, or the other way round. And describing the wasted arrow as "energy lost", which is both wrong and, in an exam, a marked error.

Equations and symbols

Statement 1.7 is a small set of equations used in a large number of combinations. The two rules that carry most of the marks are that work needs a force along the displacement, and that power is a rate, so every time must be in seconds before dividing.

Work and the energy stores

W = Fd
Key: W = work done (J); F = force in the direction of motion (N); d = distance moved along that direction (m). A force at right angles to the motion does no work.

KE = ½mv²
Key: KE = kinetic energy (J); m = mass (kg); v = speed (m/s). The speed is squared, so doubling the speed quadruples the energy — the reason braking distance rises so steeply.

GPE = mgh
Key: GPE = gravitational potential energy (J); m = mass (kg); g = gravitational field strength (9.8 N/kg); h = height gained (m). A fall is a loss of GPE, so state the sign or the word.

KE lost = GPE gained (no friction)
Key: the conservation statement used to link the two stores. With friction or air resistance, part of the energy is transferred to the thermal store of the surroundings and the equality becomes an inequality.

v = √(2gh)
Key: v = speed at the bottom of a frictionless fall (m/s); g = 9.8 m/s²; h = height fallen (m). It comes from ½mv² = mgh, and the mass cancels — which is why a feather and a hammer match on the Moon.

Power

P = E / t = W / t
Key: P = power (W); E or W = energy transferred or work done (J); t = time taken (s). One watt is one joule per second.

E = Pt
Key: E = energy transferred (J); P = power (W); t = time (s). With P in kilowatts and t in hours the energy comes out in kilowatt-hours, which is what a meter measures.

P = Fv
Key: P = useful power output (W); F = driving force (N); v = constant speed (m/s). For a car at steady speed the driving force equals the total resistive force.

1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J
Key: one kilowatt-hour is the energy of a 1000 W appliance running for one hour; 1 kW × 3600 s = 3.6 MJ.

Efficiency

efficiency = (useful energy output / total energy input) × 100%
Key: both energies in joules (or both powers in watts, since the time cancels); the result is a percentage and can never exceed 100. A figure above 100 means the wrong quantity was used as the input.

wasted energy = input − useful output
Key: the remainder is transferred by friction, air resistance or sound to the thermal store of the surroundings. Energy is not destroyed, so the widths of a Sankey diagram must balance.

useful power of a lifting motor = mgh / t
Key: m = load mass (kg); g = 9.8 N/kg; h = height lifted (m); t = time taken (s). Comparing this with the electrical input VI gives the motor's efficiency.

title: AS Level Chemistry: Intermolecular Forces
content:
AS Level Chemistry: Intermolecular Forces

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH12, Topic 7 explains the forces that hold molecules to one another, as distinct from the covalent bonds inside them. These forces are far weaker than covalent bonds, yet they decide boiling temperature, volatility, solubility and the anomalous behaviour of water, and they are the reason a molecule with polar bonds is not necessarily a polar molecule. Examiners test the explanation rather than the label, so every answer should name the force, say what causes it, and relate it to the property asked about.

Three types of intermolecular force

All intermolecular forces are electrostatic: they arise from the attraction between regions of opposite charge. They differ in what creates those regions.

ForceOriginTypical strength
London forces (instantaneous dipole–induced dipole)Fluctuating electron density in one molecule induces a dipole in a neighbourVery weak, but increases with the number of electrons
Permanent dipole–permanent dipolePermanently polar bonds and an asymmetric shape leave one end of the molecule slightly positive and the other slightly negativeWeak, roughly 5–20 kJ mol⁻¹
Hydrogen bondingA hydrogen atom bonded to N, O or F is attracted to a lone pair on N, O or F in another moleculeStrongest of the three, up to about 40 kJ mol⁻¹

London forces

Electrons are in constant motion, so at any instant the electron distribution in a molecule may be uneven. That creates an instantaneous dipole, which in turn distorts the electron cloud of a neighbouring molecule and induces a dipole in it. The two dipoles then attract. The effect is present in every substance, including the noble gases and non-polar molecules such as methane, and it is the only intermolecular force in a non-polar substance.

The strength of London forces depends on how easily the electron cloud can be distorted, which is called polarisability. Two factors control it:

  • Number of electrons: more electrons means a larger, more polarisable cloud. Iodine (I₂) is a solid and chlorine (Cl₂) a gas at room temperature for this reason.
  • Surface area and shape: a long unbranched chain has more surface contact between neighbouring molecules than a compact branched isomer with the same formula, so it has stronger London forces.

London forces are also the reason why a noble gas such as argon can be liquefied at low temperature, even though its atoms have no permanent dipole and no bonds to break.

Permanent dipole–dipole interactions

A bond between atoms of different electronegativity is polar: the more electronegative atom carries a partial negative charge, δ−, and the less electronegative atom carries δ+. If the molecule is not symmetrical, the individual bond dipoles do not cancel, and the molecule as a whole has a permanent dipole. Neighbouring molecules then line up with opposite ends together, and the attraction is a permanent dipole–permanent dipole interaction.

Hydrogen chloride, HCl, is polar and its molecules attract this way. Carbon dioxide has two polar C=O bonds, but the molecule is linear and symmetrical, so the dipoles cancel exactly and CO₂ has no permanent dipole; its molecules are held only by London forces. Tetrachloromethane, CCl₄, is also symmetrical and non-polar for the same reason, while trichloromethane, CHCl₃, is polar because the fourth substituent is hydrogen rather than chlorine and the symmetry is broken. Whether a molecule is polar therefore needs two checks: are the bonds polar, and is the shape symmetrical?

Hydrogen bonding

Hydrogen bonding is a particularly strong form of permanent dipole attraction. It occurs only when two conditions are satisfied:

  • A hydrogen atom is covalently bonded to a highly electronegative atom, limited to nitrogen, oxygen or fluorine.
  • A lone pair is available on an N, O or F atom in a neighbouring molecule, which the δ+ hydrogen can approach.

The result is a strong attraction between the δ+ hydrogen and the lone pair, often drawn as a dotted line: O–H···O. The bond is directional, which is why hydrogen bonding produces specific structures rather than a random arrangement.

Water, ammonia and hydrogen fluoride all hydrogen bond:

SubstanceHydrogen-bonding unitNumber of hydrogen bonds per molecule in the liquid
H₂OO–H···OTwo hydrogen atoms and two lone pairs allow an extensive network
NH₃N–H···NThree hydrogen atoms but only one lone pair, so fewer bonds than water
HFF–H···FOne hydrogen atom and three lone pairs; chains of HF molecules

Hydrogen bonding is not the same as a covalent bond to hydrogen. It is an intermolecular attraction, so it is broken when a substance melts or boils, while the O–H covalent bond stays intact. That distinction is worth stating explicitly in an answer.

The anomalous properties of water

Water's properties do not follow the pattern of similar molecules, and hydrogen bonding is the explanation.

High melting and boiling temperatures. Compared with hydrogen sulfide, H₂S, which has a similar formula, water boils about 160 °C higher. The molecules of H₂S are held only by London forces and weak dipole–dipole attractions, whereas each water molecule can hydrogen bond to several neighbours. Breaking those attractions needs far more energy, so the melting and boiling temperatures are unusually high, and water is a liquid at room temperature while H₂S is a gas.

Ice is less dense than liquid water. In ice, each water molecule hydrogen bonds to four neighbours in a regular tetrahedral arrangement, which holds the molecules further apart than in the liquid and leaves open hexagonal spaces. When ice melts, much of that open framework collapses and the molecules pack more closely, so liquid water is denser than ice. This is why ice floats, and why a lake freezes from the top, insulating the water beneath and allowing aquatic life to survive.

Hydrogen bonding also gives water a high surface tension, a high specific heat capacity and a high enthalpy of vaporisation, all of which follow from the energy needed to overcome the network of hydrogen bonds.

Predicting hydrogen bonding

To decide whether a molecule can hydrogen bond, look for an O–H, N–H or F–H group and for a lone pair on O, N or F. Ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH, can hydrogen bond because of its O–H group; ethanal, CH₃CHO, has a C=O bond with lone pairs but no hydrogen attached to an electronegative atom, so it cannot donate a hydrogen bond, although its oxygen can accept one. A molecule such as CH₃F has no H–F bond, so it does not hydrogen bond. Methanol and water mix in all proportions because both can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds, whereas methane, with only C–H bonds, cannot.

Intermolecular forces and physical properties

Boiling temperature is a measure of the energy needed to separate molecules, so it reports the strength of the intermolecular forces, not the strength of the covalent bonds. Four trends are examined.

Boiling temperature of alkanes increases with chain length. Each additional CH₂ group adds electrons and surface area, so the London forces between the molecules become stronger and more energy is needed to separate them. Methane boils at −162 °C, ethane at −89 °C and decane at 174 °C.

Branching lowers the boiling temperature. Pentane and 2,2-dimethylpropane have the same molecular formula, but the branched molecule is more compact. Its molecules have less surface contact, so its London forces are weaker and it boils at 9.5 °C compared with 36 °C for pentane. The same reasoning explains why branched isomers have lower boiling temperatures throughout the alkanes.

Alcohols have higher boiling temperatures than alkanes of similar electron count. Ethanol (46 electrons) boils at 78 °C while propane (26 electrons) boils at −42 °C. The comparison is not quite like for like, but the key point is that ethanol molecules hydrogen bond through the O–H group, while propane molecules have only London forces. The hydrogen bonding more than compensates for the smaller number of electrons.

Boiling temperatures of the hydrogen halides are not a simple trend. HF is the highest because of hydrogen bonding. From HCl to HBr to HI, London forces grow as the number of electrons increases, so the boiling temperatures rise in that order: HCl −85 °C, HBr −67 °C, HI −35 °C. HF, at 20 °C, sits far above the smooth trend, and that outlier is the evidence for hydrogen bonding.

Choosing a solvent

Dissolving depends on the solute particles being separated and surrounded by solvent particles, so the solute–solvent attractions must be comparable to the forces they replace. In practice, like dissolves like.

  • Water dissolves ionic compounds because the polar water molecules attract the ions: the partially negative oxygen surrounds a cation and the partially positive hydrogens surround an anion. This is hydration, and it releases hydration enthalpy that helps to compensate for the lattice enthalpy that must be overcome.
  • Water dissolves simple alcohols such as methanol and ethanol, because the alcohol's O–H group can both donate a hydrogen bond to water and accept one from it. As the hydrocarbon chain grows, the non-polar part becomes a larger fraction of the molecule and solubility falls: ethanol mixes with water in all proportions, but hexan-1-ol is only slightly soluble.
  • Water is a poor solvent for halogenoalkanes and other polar organic molecules such as chloroethane. The molecule has a dipole, so it is attracted to water to some extent, but it has no O–H group and cannot hydrogen bond with water, and its hydrocarbon part cannot interact favourably with the water network. The solute–solvent attractions are too weak to overcome the hydrogen bonding between water molecules.
  • Non-aqueous solvents are used when the solute's intermolecular forces resemble the solvent's. Iodine, a non-polar molecule held by London forces, dissolves in hexane, which is also non-polar; bromine dissolves in cyclohexane for the same reason. Propanone is a useful intermediate case, dissolving both polar and many non-polar substances because it has a polar C=O group and a hydrocarbon part.

A good answer states the force between solvent molecules, the force between solute and solvent, and whether the second is strong enough to replace the first.

Typical mistakes

  • Saying a substance has hydrogen bonds when the hydrogen is bonded to carbon; only N–H, O–H and F–H count.
  • Describing hydrogen bonding as a covalent bond, or claiming that boiling water breaks O–H bonds.
  • Assuming that a molecule with polar bonds must be polar, without checking whether the shape cancels the dipoles.
  • Attributing the trend in alkane boiling temperatures to stronger covalent bonds rather than to stronger London forces.
  • Explaining branching by saying the molecule has fewer electrons; the number of electrons is the same, the surface contact is not.
  • Explaining the lower density of ice as an expansion on freezing without mentioning the open hydrogen-bonded lattice.
  • Describing London forces as "weak covalent forces" or as attractions between permanent dipoles.

Exam-style questions

  1. Explain why the boiling temperature of iodine is higher than that of chlorine. Answer: iodine has more electrons and a larger, more polarisable electron cloud, so the London forces between its molecules are stronger; more energy is needed to separate the molecules.
  2. Explain why 2-methylbutane has a lower boiling temperature than pentane. Answer: both have the molecular formula C5H12 and the same number of electrons. 2-methylbutane is more branched and more compact, so its molecules have less surface area in contact, the London forces between them are weaker, and less energy is needed to separate them.
  3. Explain, in terms of intermolecular forces, why ethanol is soluble in water but chloroethane is not. Answer: ethanol has an O–H group and can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds with water, so the solute–solvent attractions are strong enough to replace the hydrogen bonds between water molecules. Chloroethane is polar but has no O–H group, so it cannot hydrogen bond with water; its attractions to water are too weak to compensate for breaking the water–water hydrogen bonds.
  4. Explain why ice is less dense than liquid water. Answer: in ice each water molecule forms hydrogen bonds to four neighbours in a tetrahedral arrangement, producing an open lattice with spaces between the molecules. When ice melts the lattice collapses and the molecules pack more closely, so the liquid is denser.
  5. Identify the strongest intermolecular force in each of the following and justify your answer: (a) HCl, (b) CH₃OH, (c) CCl₄. Answer: (a) permanent dipole–permanent dipole, because the molecule is polar and has no O–H, N–H or F–H group; (b) hydrogen bonding, because of the O–H group; (c) London forces, because the molecule is symmetrical and the bond dipoles cancel, so it is non-polar.

When revising, practise the three-part answer: name the force, explain what causes it in these molecules, then link it to the property in the question. Move on to Introduction to Kinetics and Equilibria next, where the same molecular picture explains why reactions need collisions with sufficient energy.

Worked example: hydrogen bonding and the energy to boil water

Calculate the energy needed to heat 100 g of water from 25 °C to 100 °C and then to convert it to steam at 100 °C. The specific heat capacity of water is 4.18 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹ and the enthalpy of vaporisation is 40.7 kJ mol⁻¹.

Step 1, heating: q = mcΔT = 100 × 4.18 × 75 = 31 350 J = 31.4 kJ
Step 2, boiling: n(H2O) = 100 / 18.0 = 5.56 mol
                 energy = 5.56 × 40.7 = 226 kJ
Total = 31.4 + 226 = 257 kJ, of which 226 kJ (88 %) is used to separate molecules

The result is the quantitative version of the argument in the text. Almost nine tenths of the energy goes into overcoming intermolecular forces rather than into raising the temperature, and for water those forces are hydrogen bonds. Compare hydrogen sulfide, whose enthalpy of vaporisation is about 18.7 kJ mol⁻¹: the same 5.56 mol would need only 104 kJ to vaporise, which is why water boils 160 °C higher.

Two exam conclusions follow from the same numbers. Steam at 100 °C causes worse burns than water at 100 °C because condensing it releases 40.7 kJ mol⁻¹, and sweating cools the body effectively because each gram of water that evaporates carries away about 2.3 kJ.

title: Dynamics — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Dynamics

Physics — AS. Dynamics links forces to the motion they cause. Example: a 2 kg mass with a 10 N resultant force accelerates at a = F/m = 10/2 = 5 m s⁻².

Key areas to revise

  • Newton's laws: a body stays at rest or in uniform motion unless a resultant force acts; F = ma gives the acceleration; every action has an equal and opposite reaction.
  • Weight and mass: weight is W = mg, a force measured in newtons, while mass is the amount of matter, measured in kilograms.
  • Momentum: p = mv. The impulse of a force equals the change in momentum, Ft = Δp.
  • Friction and connected bodies: friction F = μR opposes motion, and in connected bodies the tension is the same throughout a light string over a smooth pulley.

Core facts to recall

  • Draw a free-body diagram first, and show every force with its direction.
  • Resolve forces into components along and perpendicular to a slope before you apply F = ma.
  • Check units at each step: newtons, kilograms and metres per second squared must agree.

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

title: A Level Mathematics: The Binomial Distribution
content:
A Level Mathematics: The Binomial Distribution

A binomial distribution counts successes in a fixed number of independent trials, each with the same probability of success. Coins, multiple-choice guesses, defective items in a sample and free throws all fit the same template, and once a problem is recognised as binomial the calculation is a formula plus a cumulative table. This note builds the distribution from its four conditions, derives the formula from counting, and then uses it for the two things exams actually ask: probabilities and hypothesis tests.

The four conditions

Before writing X ~ B(n, p) you must be able to name the conditions, because most exam questions include a part asking whether the model is appropriate. The conditions are not red tape: drop any one and the formula is simply wrong.

1. a fixed number of trials n
2. each trial has exactly two outcomes (success / failure)
3. the probability of success p is constant for every trial
4. the trials are independent
then X = number of successes has X ~ B(n, p)

Worked example (checking the model). A bag holds 5 red and 15 blue counters. Four counters are taken without replacement. Is the number of red counters binomial?

n = 4 is fixed and each draw is red or not red
but p changes: 5/20, then 5/19 if a red was taken, ...
the trials are not independent, so NOT binomial (it is hypergeometric)

Taking with replacement would fix it: p stays 0.25 on every draw.

The formula, and where it comes from

The probability of a particular sequence of r successes and n − r failures is p^r (1−p)^(n−r), because independence lets you multiply. The number of such sequences is the number of ways to choose which r trials succeed, which is nCr. Multiplying gives the formula.

P(X = r) = nCr p^r (1 - p)^(n - r)
the nCr counts arrangements; the powers give the probability of one arrangement

Worked example. X ~ B(10, 0.3). Find P(X = 3).

P = 10C3 (0.3)³ (0.7)⁷
= 120 × 0.027 × 0.08235
= 120 × 0.002223 = 0.2668

Worked example 2 (a single trial count). A fair die is rolled 8 times. Find the probability of exactly two sixes.

X ~ B(8, 1/6)
P(X = 2) = 8C2 (1/6)² (5/6)⁶ = 28 × 0.02778 × 0.3349 = 0.2605

Worked example 3 (why nCr appears). For n = 3 and r = 1, list the sequences and confirm the coefficient.

sequences: SFF, FSF, FFS - three of them
each has probability p(1-p)²
so P(X = 1) = 3p(1-p)², and 3C1 = 3

Cumulative probabilities

Questions almost always ask for a range, not a single value, and the cumulative distribution is what the calculator or the tables supply. The skill is rewriting the question into the form the table gives you.

P(X <= r) is tabulated directly
P(X >= r) = 1 - P(X <= r - 1)
P(X < r)  = P(X <= r - 1)
P(a <= X <= b) = P(X <= b) - P(X <= a - 1)
P(X = r) = P(X <= r) - P(X <= r - 1)

Worked example. X ~ B(20, 0.4). Find P(X ≥ 8).

P(X >= 8) = 1 - P(X <= 7)
= 1 - 0.4159
= 0.5841

Worked example 2 (between). For the same X, find P(5 ≤ X ≤ 10).

= P(X <= 10) - P(X <= 4)
= 0.8725 - 0.0510
= 0.8215

Worked example 3 (the strict inequality trap). For the same X, find P(X > 6).

P(X > 6) = 1 - P(X <= 6) = 1 - 0.2500 = 0.7500
note this is different from P(X >= 6) = 1 - P(X <= 5) = 0.8746

Mean and variance

The binomial has the simplest mean and variance in the syllabus, and they are worth knowing both forwards and backwards: a question can give the mean and variance and ask for n and p.

E(X) = np
Var(X) = np(1 - p)
standard deviation = √(np(1-p))

Worked example. X ~ B(50, 0.2). Find the mean and standard deviation.

mean = 50 × 0.2 = 10
variance = 10 × 0.8 = 8
sd = 2.828

Worked example 2 (backwards). A binomial variable has mean 12 and variance 9. Find n and p.

np = 12;  np(1-p) = 9
divide: 1 - p = 9/12 = 0.75  →  p = 0.25
then n = 12/0.25 = 48

Hypothesis testing with the binomial

A one-tailed test asks whether p has increased or decreased; the test statistic is the observed count, and the p-value is the probability of a result at least as extreme in the direction of the alternative.

H0: p = p0      H1: p > p0 (or p < p0)
X ~ B(n, p0) under H0
p-value = P(X >= observed) or P(X <= observed)
compare with the significance level; reject H0 if p-value <= alpha

Worked example. A coin is tossed 20 times and lands heads 15 times. Test at the 5% level whether the coin is biased towards heads.

H0: p = 0.5;  H1: p > 0.5
X ~ B(20, 0.5)
P(X >= 15) = 1 - P(X <= 14) = 1 - 0.9793 = 0.0207
0.0207 < 0.05, so reject H0
there is evidence at the 5% level that the coin favours heads

Worked example 2 (two-tailed). The same data tested two-tailed.

double the smaller tail: 2 × 0.0207 = 0.0414
0.0414 < 0.05, so still reject H0 at the 5% level

Worked example 3 (critical region). For X ~ B(20, 0.5), find the critical region for a 5% one-tailed test of p > 0.5.

P(X >= 14) = 0.0577 (above 0.05)
P(X >= 15) = 0.0207 (below 0.05)
critical region: X >= 15

Note that the critical region is chosen so the probability of a Type I error is at most 5%, which is why 14 is excluded even though it is close.

When the model breaks down

Examiners like the question that asks why a binomial model is only an approximation. The usual culprits are dependence, a varying probability, or a fixed sample drawn without replacement from a small population.

SituationProblemEffect
sampling without replacementtrials not independentp drifts; use the hypergeometric instead
clustered data (pupils in classes)responses correlatedvariance underestimated
probability varies between trialsp not constantformula invalid
large n, p near 0.5computation heavynormal approximation is reasonable

Worked example (normal approximation). X ~ B(200, 0.4). Use a normal approximation to estimate P(X ≤ 70).

mean = 80;  variance = 200 × 0.4 × 0.6 = 48;  sd = 6.928
continuity correction: X <= 70 becomes X < 70.5
z = (70.5 - 80)/6.928 = -1.371
P(Z < -1.371) = 0.0852

The continuity correction is compulsory: a discrete count needs a half-unit boundary before it can be treated as continuous.

Expected frequencies and the shape of the distribution

A binomial distribution is not symmetric unless p = 0.5, and that shape decides which tail an exam question is fishing in. The most likely value — the mode — is the integer near (n + 1)p, and expected frequency multiplies the probability by the number of samples taken. Both are quick marks that are frequently missed because students jump straight to the formula.

mode is near (n + 1)p, checked by comparing consecutive probabilities
expected number in a sample of size N = N x P(X = r)

Worked example. X ~ B(12, 0.3). Find the most likely value of X and the expected number of 3s in 500 independent observations.

(n + 1)p = 13 × 0.3 = 3.9, so check r = 3 and r = 4
P(X = 3) = 220 × 0.027 × 0.1176 = 0.2397
P(X = 4) = 495 × 0.0081 × 0.1681 = 0.2311
mode = 3
expected number of 3s = 500 × 0.2397 = 120 (to the nearest whole)

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Model) State the distribution for the number of sixes in 12 rolls of a fair die. Answer: X ~ B(n, p) with n = 12 rolls and p = 1/6 the chance of a six on each, so X ~ B(12, 1/6).
  2. (Single value) X ~ B(8, 0.25): find P(X = 2). Answer: P(X = 2) = ⁸C₂ (0.25)² (0.75)⁶ = 28 × 0.0625 × 0.1780 = 0.3115.
  3. (Cumulative) X ~ B(15, 0.3): find P(X ≤ 4). Answer: P(X ≤ 4) = Σₖ₌₀⁴ ¹⁵Cₖ (0.3)ᵏ (0.7)¹⁵⁻ᵏ = 0.5155 from cumulative binomial tables.
  4. (Complement) Same X: find P(X ≥ 3). Answer: P(X ≥ 3) = 1 − P(X ≤ 2) = 1 − 0.2969 = 0.7031 — the complement, because the tables give the lower tail only.
  5. (Mean) X ~ B(40, 0.35): find E(X) and Var(X). Answer: 14 and 9.1.
  6. (Backwards) Mean 18, variance 12: find n and p. Answer: mean np = 18 and variance np(1 − p) = 12; dividing, 1 − p = 12/18 = 2/3, so p = 1/3 and n = 18 ÷ (1/3) = 54.
  7. (Test) 12 of 20 seeds germinate; test p = 0.5 against p < 0.5 at 5%. Answer: H₀: p = 0.5 against H₁: p < 0.5; under H₀, X ~ B(20, 0.5) and P(X ≤ 12) = 0.8684, which is far above 0.05, so there is no evidence to reject H₀.
  8. (Critical region) X ~ B(10, 0.2): find the 5% critical region for p < 0.2. Answer: the smallest possible tail is P(X ≤ 0) = (0.8)¹⁰ = 0.1074, which already exceeds 0.05, so no critical region exists at the 5% level for this n.
  9. (Approximation) X ~ B(100, 0.5): approximate P(X ≥ 60). Answer: μ = np = 50 and σ = √(np(1 − p)) = √25 = 5; with the continuity correction z = (59.5 − 50)/5 = 1.9, so P(X ≥ 60) ≈ P(Z > 1.9) = 0.0287.
  10. (Assumption) Give one reason a binomial model may fail for defects in boxes of 20. Answer: defects may cluster, so trials are not independent.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Forgetting nCr: the coefficient counts arrangements; without it the answer is the probability of one specific sequence.
  • nCr on the wrong factor: it is p^r (1−p)^(n−r), with the success probability raised to the number of successes.
  • Inequality direction: P(X ≥ 8) uses 1 − P(X ≤ 7), not 1 − P(X ≤ 8).
  • Variance confused with standard deviation: np(1−p) is the variance; the test and the normal approximation need the square root.
  • Continuity correction omitted: any normal approximation to a discrete count needs the half-unit adjustment.
  • One-tailed evidence read as two: halving or doubling the tail without checking the alternative direction is a silent error.
  • Independence asserted, not checked: sampling without replacement from a small population breaks the model, and the question usually invites you to say so.
  • p-value compared with the wrong threshold: the significance level is given as a percentage; 5% means 0.05, not 5.

Recognising a binomial situation in context

Most binomial marks are lost before any arithmetic starts, because the question was not identified as binomial. The subsections below give a checklist for reading a question and writing the model in the standard form X ~ B(n, p) before you calculate anything.

Writing the model in the form X ~ B(n, p)

Once you decide a situation is binomial, state the model in full: X ~ B(n, p), where X is the number of successes, n is the number of trials and p is the probability of a success on each trial. Define X in words in your answer, for example “X is the number of defective bulbs in a box of 20”. A model with no definition of X loses the communication mark even when the probabilities are right.

Identifying the number of trials, n

The value of n is the fixed number of times the experiment is repeated: the number of bulbs tested, the number of patients treated, or the number of games played. Read the question for the phrase that fixes it, such as “of 20 bulbs chosen at random”. If the question keeps going until a result occurs, the number of trials is not fixed and the binomial model does not apply directly.

Identifying the probability of success, p

The value of p is the probability of the outcome you have chosen to call a success on one trial. It must stay the same for every trial. A fair coin gives p = 0.5, and a bag where 15% of items are faulty gives p = 0.15 for each item drawn with replacement. If the question gives a percentage, convert it to a decimal before you use it in any formula.

Checking for fixed trials

The number of trials must be decided before the experiment starts. Counting the number of successes in a fixed sample is binomial, whereas recording how many trials it takes to get the first success is not. A question about the number of heads in ten tosses is binomial; a question about how many tosses are needed for the first head is a different model. Make the fixed-n check before any other check.

Checking for independent trials

Each trial must not affect the next. Independence is what allows you to multiply the probabilities of several outcomes together, and it is the assumption most often ignored. Drawing items with replacement keeps p constant, and that is what the model needs. Drawing without replacement changes p after each draw, so the binomial model is only an approximation when the sample is small compared with the population.

Worked identification

A survey finds that 30% of adults own a bicycle. Twelve adults are chosen at random from a large town and asked whether they own one. Let X be the number who own a bicycle. Here n = 12, p = 0.3 and the answer is X ~ B(12, 0.3). The population is large, so the probability for each adult stays close to 0.3 and the model is a reasonable one to use. State that assumption, because a marker looks for it.

Probabilities of at least one, and of more than r

Questions that ask for “at least” or “more than” are the ones where the complement saves the most time. The subsections set out the choice between a direct sum and the complement, and the checks that stop an off-by-one error.

Probability of at least one success

“At least one” is the complement of “none”, so P(X ≥ 1) = 1 − P(X = 0) = 1 − qⁿ, where q = 1 − p. For X ~ B(5, 0.2), P(X ≥ 1) = 1 − 0.8⁵ = 1 − 0.32768 = 0.672 to 3 significant figures. Adding the probabilities of X = 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 gives the same answer but takes five calculations instead of one.

Probability of more than r successes

“More than 3” means 4 or more, so P(X > 3) = 1 − P(X ≤ 3). For X ~ B(10, 0.3), P(X ≤ 3) = 0.6496 to 4 decimal places, so P(X > 3) = 0.3504. The number 3 is included in the part you subtract from 1; forgetting that is the typical error on “more than” questions.

Choosing between a direct sum and the complement

Use the complement when the part you do not want is short: “at least one”, “at most one but not zero” and similar phrases. Use a direct sum when the wanted region has only a few terms, such as P(X = 2) + P(X = 3). With a calculator table of cumulative probabilities, most “at most” and “at least” questions reduce to one lookup and one subtraction.

Probability of exactly r on a calculator

For X ~ B(n, p), P(X = r) = ⁿCᵣ pʳ qⁿ⁻ʳ. The combination ⁿCᵣ counts the ways the r successes can be arranged among n trials. For X ~ B(10, 0.3), P(X = 3) = 120 × 0.3³ × 0.7⁷ = 120 × 0.027 × 0.0823543 = 0.2668 to 4 decimal places. Enter the combination with the nCr key so the arrangement count is not mistyped.

The most likely number of successes (the mode)

The most likely value of X is the mode. For a binomial distribution it is the whole number part of (n + 1)p, and if (n + 1)p is itself a whole number there are two modes, (n + 1)p − 1 and (n + 1)p. For X ~ B(10, 0.3), (n + 1)p = 3.3, so the mode is 3. Check against the probabilities: P(X = 3) = 0.2668 is larger than P(X = 2) = 0.2335 and P(X = 4) = 0.2001.

Checking that the probabilities add to 1

A complete check is that P(X = 0) + P(X = 1) + … + P(X = n) = 1. You rarely add every term in an exam, but the check is useful when you build a table of probabilities for a whole distribution. If a column does not total 1 to the rounding used, one of the terms was calculated with the wrong value of q or the wrong combination count.

Adding independent binomial variables

A question can combine two or more binomial counts, for example the total number of faults from two machines. The result is binomial only under particular conditions, and the subsections below say what those conditions are and how to check them.

Same probability, different numbers of trials

If X ~ B(n, p) and Y ~ B(m, p) are independent, and both use the same probability of success p, then X + Y ~ B(n + m, p). Two batches tested for the same fault, with the same chance of that fault on each item, combine into one larger binomial. The shared p is the key condition: the trials must all be a success or failure with the same chance.

The rule for X + Y

Write the result as X + Y ~ B(n + m, p). For example, X ~ B(4, 0.5) and Y ~ B(6, 0.5), independent, give X + Y ~ B(10, 0.5). Add the trial counts, not the probabilities. The probability of success stays the same because each trial still has the same chance of success.

When the probabilities differ

If X ~ B(n, p) and Y ~ B(m, q) with p ≠ q, the sum is not binomial, and you cannot use the rule above. The number of successes comes from trials that have different chances, so no single p describes all of them. A question that asks for the distribution in this case expects a table of values, not a single binomial statement.

Worked example: two batches

Batch A has 8 items and batch B has 12 items. Each item in either batch is defective with probability 0.05, and the items are independent. Let T be the total number of defective items. Then T ~ B(20, 0.05), because both batches share p = 0.05. The probability of no defective items at all is P(T = 0) = 0.95²⁰ = 0.358 to 3 significant figures.

Why the mean and variance add

The mean of a sum is always the sum of the means, whether or not the variables are independent. The variance of a sum is the sum of the variances only when the variables are independent. For the batch example, E(T) = 20 × 0.05 = 1 and Var(T) = 20 × 0.05 × 0.95 = 0.95, which is the same as adding the separate variances 8 × 0.0475 and 12 × 0.0475.

Contrast with a normal approximation

For a large n, a binomial count is often approximated by a normal distribution with the same mean np and variance npq. The approximation is weak when np or nq is small, as in the batch example where np = 1. In that case use the exact binomial probabilities, and quote the normal approximation only when the question asks for it or when n is large enough for both np and nq to be well above 5.

A one-tailed hypothesis test, step by step

A binomial hypothesis test asks whether an observed count is too unlikely for the claimed probability to be true. The method has the same steps every time, and each step earns its own mark, so write them in order.

State H₀ and H₁ in terms of the parameter

H₀ states the claimed value of p, and H₁ states the direction of the alternative. For a claim that a coin or process produces fewer successes than stated, write H₀: p = 0.4 and H₁: p < 0.4 in your working, with the symbols defined. The hypotheses are always about p, never about X, and H₀ always contains the equals sign.

Find the tail the alternative points to

The direction of H₁ tells you which tail of the distribution is critical. A “less than” alternative uses the lower tail, which contains small values of X. A “greater than” alternative uses the upper tail. Decide the tail before you look at the observed value, because choosing it afterwards invalidates the test.

Compute the probability of the observed value or more extreme

For a lower-tail test, find P(X ≤ x), where x is the observed count, assuming H₀ is true. Suppose X ~ B(12, 0.4) and 1 success is observed. Then P(X ≤ 1) = 0.6¹² + 12 × 0.4 × 0.6¹¹ = 0.00218 + 0.01741 = 0.0196 to 3 significant figures. The working must show both terms, because a single number with no method earns only a fraction of the method marks.

Compare the probability with the significance level

If the probability is less than or equal to the significance level, reject H₀. Here 0.0196 is less than 0.05, so the result is significant at the 5% level and H₀ is rejected. If the question gives a 1% level, the same probability would not be significant, because 0.0196 is greater than 0.01. Always compare with the level the question states.

Write the conclusion in the context of the question

A complete conclusion states what the result means for the claim, not just whether H₀ was rejected. For example: “There is evidence at the 5% level that the proportion of successes is less than 0.4.” Use the word “evidence” and refer to the proportion, because a test gives evidence about a population, not a proof about it.

Find the critical region and the actual significance level

The critical region is the set of values of X that lead to rejection. For B(12, 0.4), P(X ≤ 1) = 0.0196 is at most 0.05 but P(X ≤ 2) = 0.0196 + 66 × 0.16 × 0.6¹⁰ = 0.0835 is more than 0.05, so the critical region at the 5% level is {0, 1}. The actual significance level is 0.0196, which is 1.96%, because the discrete distribution cannot be cut at exactly 5%.

Two-tailed tests and the split significance level

A two-tailed test asks whether p has changed in either direction. The main difference from a one-tailed test is how the significance level is shared between the two tails, and that is where most marks are lost.

Why the significance level is split

A two-tailed test rejects H₀ for a very small or a very large count, so the total probability of rejection must stay at the stated level. The level is split equally, with half in each tail. At the 5% level each tail is allowed a probability of at most 0.025. Using 0.05 in each tail would double the chance of a false rejection and is an error.

Setting up two-tailed hypotheses

A two-tailed alternative is written H₁: p ≠ 0.5, with H₀: p = 0.5. The alternative does not say which direction the change will be, so both tails are critical. Use a two-tailed test only when the question asks whether the probability has changed, without saying it has increased or decreased.

Find the critical region from both tails

For X ~ B(20, 0.5) at the 5% level, find the largest lower value with P(X ≤ k) ≤ 0.025. Here P(X ≤ 5) = 0.0207, so the lower critical region is X ≤ 5. By symmetry, P(X ≥ 15) = 0.0207, so the upper critical region is X ≥ 15. The combined region {0 to 5} ∪ {15 to 20} has probability 0.0414, which is no more than 0.05.

Worked two-tailed example

A coin is tested by tossing it 20 times and getting 4 heads. Test H₀: p = 0.5 against H₁: p ≠ 0.5 at the 5% level. Since 4 is in the lower critical region {0 to 5}, reject H₀. The probability needed is P(X ≤ 4) = 0.0059. The one-tailed value would be smaller, and the shared level makes the test twice as demanding in each tail.

Reject, or fail to reject: never accept H₀

If the observed count is outside the critical region, the correct conclusion is that there is not enough evidence to reject H₀. It is not correct to say that H₀ is accepted or that p is 0.5. A test shows only whether the data are inconsistent with H₀ at the chosen level, and a non-significant result is consistent with many values of p.

Avoiding the common sign error

The most common error is to compare the observed count with the critical region for the wrong tail. For a high observed count such as 17 out of 20, the test uses the upper tail, P(X ≥ 17), and the probability is (1140 + 190 + 20 + 1)/2²⁰ = 1351/1048576 = 0.0013. Writing the tail you used in words, before the number, makes the error easy to spot when you check your work.

Equations and symbols

The distribution, its conditions and the four tail identities. Every question on this topic is one of these lines plus a calculator.

P(X = r) = nCr p^r (1 - p)^(n - r) Key: n = number of trials, fixed in advance; p = probability of success in one trial, constant; r = the number of successes asked for; nCr = n!/(r!(n − r)!), the number of orders the successes can occur in. The (1 − p) term is the failures, and its power must be n − r.

X ~ B(n, p) Key: X = the count of successes; the tilde means "is distributed as"; n and p as above. Write this line before calculating — it is often a mark on its own, and it fixes which parameters go into the calculator.

P = 10C3 (0.3)³ (0.7)⁷ Key: n = 10, p = 0.3, r = 3, so the failures are 7 and their probability is 0.7. The coefficient 10C3 = 120 accounts for the order of the three successes among the ten trials.

P(X >= r) = 1 - P(X <= r - 1) Key: a complement, so the two probabilities add to 1; the boundary moves by one because the binomial is discrete. Using 1 − P(X ≤ r) instead is the classic off-by-one error.

P(a <= X <= b) = P(X <= b) - P(X <= a - 1) Key: subtract the part below the interval; again the "− 1" is there because P(X ≤ a − 1) is everything before a. Check with a small case you can list by hand before trusting the calculator.

title:
Energy Flow, Ecosystems and the Environment — Edexcel International A2 Level Biology

This revision note belongs to the Edexcel International A2 Level Biology specification and covers the topics that connect the biochemistry of photosynthesis to the way energy moves through ecosystems, the way ecologists measure populations and communities, the evidence for and the causes of climate change, and the biological ideas that tie the whole topic together in metabolism and evolution. It is written to be complete enough to revise from and to check yourself against the specification, so each numbered section is built around one or more specification statements rather than around a loose theme. The note deliberately stays at exam depth: it explains the reasoning behind each idea, gives the typical worked examples and comparisons that examiners look for, and lists the common mistakes that lose marks in this topic.

1. The overall photosynthesis reaction and the role of light energy in splitting water
