title: Nuclear Physics — Study Notes
content:
Nuclear Physics

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): nuclear model, radioactivity, decay types, half-life, safety, fission/fusion (Extended).

1. The nuclear model

Nucleus (protons +, neutrons 0) with orbiting electrons (−). Nuclide notation ᴬ_Z X. Isotopes: same Z, different A. Rutherford scattering established the nuclear model; proton number Z, nucleon number A.

2. Radiation types

TypeNatureRange (air)Stopped by
alpha αhelium nucleus (2p2n)few cmpaper
beta β⁻fast electron~20–30 cmfew mm aluminium
gamma γEM wavevery farthick lead/concrete

Deflection in fields: α/β opposite, γ none. Ionising: α > β > γ. Background radiation: radon, cosmic, rocks, medical, fallout.

3. Decay equations

  • α: A −4, Z −2 (e.g. ²³⁸₉₂U → ²³⁴₉₀Th + α).
  • β⁻: neutron → proton; A same, Z +1 (e.g. ¹⁴₆C → ¹⁴₇N + β⁻).
  • γ: no change to A or Z.

Balance A and Z on both sides — that is the check.

4. Half-life

Time for half the unstable nuclei to decay (random process). Read from a decay curve or count halves: 80 → 40 → 20 over two half-lives.

Example: 800 Bq, half-life 2 h → 200 Bq after 4 h.

5. Safety and uses

Uses: medical tracers (β/γ), sterilisation, thickness gauge (β), dating (C-14), smoke alarms (α). Safety: distance, time, shielding, wear badges, store in lead. Handle with tongs; never point at people.

6. Fission and fusion (Extended)

Fission: heavy nucleus splits (U-235 + neutron), chain reaction controlled by moderators/control rods — power stations. Fusion: light nuclei join (stellar) — needs huge T/P; releases more energy per kg; no long-lived waste.

Nuclear decay and half-life

Alpha particles are helium nuclei with two protons and two neutrons, and they are strongly ionising but have low penetration. Beta-minus emission happens when a neutron changes into a proton and an electron is emitted. Gamma radiation is electromagnetic, carries no charge and no mass, and has high penetration. Background radiation must be subtracted from measured count rates before a half-life is calculated.

Worked example: half-life from a count rate

A radioactive sample gives a count rate of 800 counts per minute. After 30 minutes the count rate is 100 counts per minute. Each half-life halves the count rate: 800 to 400, then 200, then 100. That is three half-lives in 30 minutes, so the half-life is 30 / 3 = 10 minutes. When the ratio is a power of two you can count the halvings directly; use a logarithm or the decay equation only when it is not.

Exam method: background radiation

Background radiation comes from natural sources such as rocks and cosmic rays, and from man-made sources such as medical X-rays. A measured count must be corrected for background before you use it in a half-life calculation: subtract the background count from every reading. Forgetting this step is a common reason for a wrong answer, because background sets a floor that the sample's own count never falls below.

title: International GCSE English as a Second Language: Writing Tasks and Themes
content:
International GCSE English as a Second Language: Writing Tasks and Themes

OxfordAQA International GCSE English as a Second Language (9280) assesses writing in a paper of its own (Paper 2 in the current official numbering — some older revision materials list the writing component first, so always check the code on your question paper). This note builds the whole writing skill set from zero: how to read the task, how to choose register, how to plan in five minutes, and how to write each task type — functional and transactional writing, short-form responses, extended discursive writing and narrative writing — across the three exam themes. Every task on this paper is a communication problem, not a grammar test, and the marks follow from solving that problem in the right tone.

What the Writing paper asks of you

The writing component carries 60 marks, is 1 hour 15 minutes long, and counts for 30% of the qualification. Its tasks are progressive: shorter functional writing first, then short-form responses, then one or two extended pieces that may be discursive or narrative. The exact task list and word limits are printed on your paper, so this note teaches the task types rather than guessing a fixed layout — and the word limit given in the question is always binding.

FeatureWhat it means for you
Duration and marks1 hour 15 minutes, 60 marks, 30% of the grade. Roughly one minute of planning per ten minutes of writing.
Task progressionShort functional tasks first (emails, notes, forms), then extended discursive or narrative writing. The later tasks carry more marks — save time for them.
The themesEverything you write sits under one of three theme areas, so vocabulary preparation is finite and examinable.
What earns marksTask fulfilment (did you do what was asked?), register (is the tone right for the reader?), organisation (is it structured?), and linguistic range and accuracy.

The three themes and their topic banks

Every question is drawn from the three OxfordAQA theme areas. You cannot predict the exact topic, but you can prepare vocabulary, examples and opinions for each theme bank, and that preparation is the single highest-return revision you can do for this paper.

ThemeTypical topicsVocabulary to prepare
Identity and cultureFamily life, traditions and festivals, food, personal identity, hobbies, music and film, cultural differencesdescribing habits and routines, comparing traditions, giving opinions about culture, describing people and places from your own experience
Local, national, international and global areas of interestYour town and region, travel and tourism, the environment, technology, news and current events, sportdescribing places, cause and effect language for problems (pollution, congestion), proposing solutions, comparing locations
Current and future study and employmentSchool subjects, exams, ambitions, jobs and careers, work experience, skills, further studydescribing plans and ambitions, talking about ability and skills, justifying choices, writing about the future with will, going to, would like to

The efficient way to revise: for each theme, prepare ten nouns, ten verbs, five adjectives, two personal examples and one opinion with a reason. That is a working vocabulary of about eighty items, and it covers almost anything the paper can ask.

The APF framework: Audience, Purpose, Form

Before writing a single sentence, three decisions control everything else. The exam rewards candidates who make these decisions visibly, because the marker can see that the writing is shaped rather than dumped.

  1. Audience — who reads this? A friend, a teacher, a stranger, an employer, a newspaper reader. This decides formality, pronouns (I and you versus one and people), abbreviations (don't versus do not), and how much you explain.
  2. Purpose — why am I writing? To persuade, inform, request, describe, entertain, complain, advise, or apply. Purpose decides the opening move and the content order: a complaint states the problem then the desired fix; a persuasive piece states the position then the reasons.
  3. Form — what shape does this text have? Email, letter, article, review, report, story. Form decides the layout features the marker looks for: greeting and sign-off on an email, headline and opening hook on an article, a clear introduction and conclusion on an essay.

Worked example of the APF decision: the task says, "Your school is thinking about banning mobile phones. Write an article for the school magazine giving your views." Audience: your classmates and teachers (semi-formal, first person plural we). Purpose: persuade with reasons and examples. Form: article, so you need a headline, a hook opening, paragraphs with linking, and a closing line that lands the point. Once those three answers exist, the plan writes itself.

Register and tone: the formal–informal continuum

Register is the difference between "Hiya, can't come, sorry!" and "Dear Mr Ahmed, I am writing to apologise for my absence." Neither is wrong in itself; each is wrong for the wrong reader. Markers describe the top band as a consistent register suited to audience and purpose — the key word is consistent. One slang phrase in an otherwise formal letter breaks that consistency and costs marks.

FeatureInformal (friend, peer)Formal (teacher, employer, institution)
OpeningHi ..., How are you?Dear Mr/Ms ..., I am writing to ...
Contractionsdon't, I'm, can'tdo not, I am, cannot
QuestionsDirect and chatty: What do you think?Polite forms: I would be grateful if you could ...
OpinionI reckon ..., To be honest ...In my opinion ..., It seems to me that ...
ClosingSee you soon! Best wishesYours sincerely / Yours faithfully

One rule of thumb saves many marks: match the formality of the task, and never mix the two columns inside one text.

Functional and transactional writing: format skeletons

Functional tasks (emails, letters, notes, messages, short articles) are marked for doing the job: covering every content point in the prompt, using the right form, and keeping the register right. A skeleton for each form means your brain can spend its energy on language instead of layout.

  • Email to a friend: greeting → reaction to their news → answers to their questions (one per bullet in the prompt) → your news/questions → closing line.
  • Formal letter or email: Dear ... → why you are writing (one sentence) → the content points in logical order, one paragraph each → what you want to happen → Yours sincerely, name.
  • Article: headline → hook (a question, a surprising fact, a short scene) → two or three paragraphs each making one point → closing line that echoes the hook.
  • Review: what it is → description → evaluation with reasons → recommendation and who it suits.
  • Report: title → introduction stating the scope → findings under clear headings → recommendation.

For every content point in the prompt, write one developed sentence or more. Under-developed content is the most common reason a competent writer scores mid-band: the marker counts content points and how fully each is covered.

Short-form responses: from notes to sentences

Short-form tasks give you information in notes, a table, or a picture and ask for connected sentences. The skill is expansion: each note must become real grammar, not a list with a capital letter.

  • Step 1 — read every note and mark the content points; one sentence minimum per point.
  • Step 2 — add the missing grammar: articles (a, the), pronouns to avoid repetition, a verb in the right tense, connectors (because, so, although, however).
  • Step 3 — check the target reader: if the task says "write to your English-speaking friend", contractions and questions are welcome; if it says "write to the school principal", they are not.

Worked example. The task: "Your friend wants to know about your new school. Use these notes to write a message: new school / big / near home / walk 10 minutes / favourite subject science / teacher good / start football club next month." A weak answer copies the notes. A top-band answer expands every point with grammar and personality: "My new school is really big — there are about a thousand students! The best part is that it's near home, so I only walk ten minutes every morning. My favourite subject is science because the teacher explains everything clearly and lets us do experiments. I've also started a football club — well, it opens next month, and I can't wait." Every note became a sentence; the register is friendly; the message reads like a message.

Extended discursive writing: the argument engine

Discursive tasks (an essay, an opinion article, a for-and-against discussion) reward organisation above fancy vocabulary. The marker needs to find your position, your reasons and your ending without hunting. Build the piece from modules:

  1. Introduction (2-3 sentences): restate the topic in your own words and give your position or the question you will explore. Never copy the prompt wording.
  2. Body paragraph 1: strongest reason. Topic sentence (the point) → explanation (why it is true) → example (a specific case, ideally personal or local) → link back to the position.
  3. Body paragraph 2: second reason, same four-beat shape.
  4. Body paragraph 3 (optional): the other side of the argument, then why your position still wins. This concession move reads as sophisticated thinking.
  5. Conclusion (2-3 sentences): restate the position in fresh words and end with the consequence or a call to action.

Model paragraph with top-band breakdown: "Some people believe that homework should be abolished because it causes stress. In my view, however, homework teaches students to work independently, a skill they will need at university and at work. For example, when I prepared for my maths exam last term, the practice I did at home was what moved my grade from a C to an A. Therefore, rather than abolishing homework, schools should limit its quantity." Why it scores: the topic sentence names the counter-argument, the contrast word however marks the writer's position, the explanation states the reason in abstract terms (independence), the example grounds it in a specific personal case, and the final sentence turns the concession into a balanced recommendation. That is the whole engine: point, reason, example, link — used once per paragraph.

Narrative writing: story craft under time pressure

Narrative tasks ask for a story, and the marker rewards a controlled arc over an ambitious plot. Three moves separate top-band stories from mid-band ones: a clear structure, controlled tense, and concrete detail instead of abstract claims.

  • The arc: opening situation (who, where, when) → an incident that changes things → rising tension in two or three beats → a climax moment → a short resolution or closing image. Plan all five before writing.
  • Tense control: past simple for events (I opened the door), past continuous for background (The rain was falling), past perfect for earlier events (I had forgotten my keys). Choose one main past tense and stay there; tense drift is a classic accuracy loss.
  • Showing, not telling: instead of "I was nervous", write "My hands were shaking as I unfolded the paper." Concrete detail (hands, paper, rain) lets the reader feel the emotion the writer claims.
  • Sentence variation: mix short dramatic sentences ("The door opened.") with longer flowing ones. Sentence control is explicitly rewarded in the writing criteria.

Worked example of turning telling into showing. Weak: "The market was busy and colourful and I felt excited." Top-band: "The market was a wall of noise: vendors shouting prices, scooters threading between the stalls, the smell of grilled corn drifting over everything. I stood on my toes, grinning, trying to see everything at once." The second version names concrete sounds and smells, uses a colon and participles, and shows the excitement through behaviour (standing on toes, grinning) rather than the adjective excited.

The five-minute plan

Planning is not wasted time; it is where the marks are decided. For every extended task, spend five minutes on a grid: APF in one corner (who, why, what form), then five content beats (for discursive: position, reason 1, reason 2, other side, conclusion; for narrative: situation, incident, rising tension, climax, resolution). Under each beat, jot one keyword or example. The writing stage then becomes transcription with style — and the marker sees structure immediately.

Worked examples: task to top-band answer

Worked example 1 — functional task. "You have won a place on a summer course in another country. Write an email to the course organiser. Say why you chose the course, ask two questions about accommodation and food, and explain your travel arrangements."

APF:  Audience = adult organiser (formal, no slang)
      Purpose  = inform + request information (cover all three bullets)
      Form     = email: greeting, clear paragraphs, sign-off
Plan: 1 why chosen  2 question: accommodation  3 question: food
      4 travel arrangements  5 closing

Model answer: "Dear Ms Carter, I am writing to confirm my place on the International Summer Course in July and to say how delighted I am to have been accepted. I chose this course because I hope to study engineering at university, and the robotics module is exactly the experience I need. I would be grateful if you could tell me a little about the accommodation. Will students stay with host families or in a residence? I also have a question about food: will it be possible to provide vegetarian meals? As for my travel, I will fly from Kuala Lumpur on 2 July and expect to arrive at the airport at about three o'clock in the afternoon. Thank you for your help. Yours sincerely, Amir Rahman." Why it scores: every bullet is covered and developed (the reason is specific — robotics and engineering; the questions are polite and precise; the travel gives a date, a route and a time), the register is consistently formal (I am writing, I would be grateful, no contractions), and the form features (greeting, sign-off, clear paragraphing) are all present.

Worked example 2 — discursive task. "Some students think that school uniforms should be banned. Write an article for your school magazine giving your views."

Plan: position = keep uniforms (with a change: student input on design)
      P1 identity/equality argument + example of bullying over clothes
      P2 practical argument (cost, mornings) + example
      P3 concession: freedom matters — answer it with the design compromise
      Conclusion: keep, but reform

Model opening and body paragraph: "Should we all dress the same? Every September the uniform debate returns to our school, and this year I think we can answer it honestly: uniforms should stay, but they should change. The strongest reason is equality. When everyone wears the same clothes, nobody is judged for what their parents can afford. At my old school, a classmate was mocked for wearing the same jacket every day; with a uniform, that cruelty simply had no surface to attach to." Why it scores: the headline question hooks, the opening states a nuanced position (stay, but change), and the first body paragraph runs the point–reason–example–link engine with a concrete story instead of a vague claim.

Exam-style questions and answers

Practise each of these in timed conditions, planning with APF first.

  1. (Functional, 12 marks worth of practice) Your English-speaking friend has invited you to a festival in their country. Write an email: thank them, ask about what to wear and what to bring, explain why you are looking forward to it. Answer outline: informal register, three developed paragraphs, two clear questions, contractions and a warm closing.
  2. (Short-form) Notes: library / opens 8am / new computers / free wifi / quiet room upstairs. Write four sentences for the school website. Answer outline: expand each note with articles, linking and a positive recommendation sentence.
  3. (Discursive) "Public transport should be free for everyone." Write an article giving your views. Answer outline: position (free for students and the elderly at least), reasons (cost of living, pollution, congestion), concession (who pays — taxation), conclusion (phased scheme).
  4. (Narrative) Write a story that begins: "The letter had been sitting on the table for three days." Answer outline: five-beat arc, past-tense control, showing detail in the climax, closing image.
  5. (Review) A travel website wants reviews of places in your area. Write a review of a place visitors should see. Answer outline: identify the place, describe it, evaluate with reasons, recommend to a named type of visitor.
  6. (Formal letter) You want a part-time job at a local café. Write a letter explaining why you are suitable and asking for an interview. Answer outline: formal opening, two skill examples with evidence, polite request, Yours sincerely.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Register drift: starting formally ("Dear Sir") and ending informally ("See ya!"). Pick one register in the plan and check it at the end.
  • Bullet copying: answering a content-point prompt as a list. Every point needs a full, developed sentence — the marker looks for development, not mention.
  • Wrong form: writing an essay when the task asked for an email. The form features (greeting, sign-off, headline) are easy marks and easy to lose.
  • Ignoring the word limit: the limit on the paper is binding. Under-length answers cap your content marks; long answers eat the time later tasks need.
  • Memorised paragraphs: examiners read thousands of scripts; a pasted "global warming is one of the biggest problems" paragraph without task-specific detail reads as filler and cannot reach the top band.
  • Time management: spending 30 minutes on the short task and 10 on the extended one inverts the mark distribution. Budget roughly 15 minutes for short tasks and the remainder for extended writing, with 5 minutes to check.
  • Theme blindness: not preparing vocabulary for the three themes leaves you translating in the exam. Translation costs accuracy, range and time at once.
  • Final check failure: the last three minutes should hunt only for verb tenses, subject–verb agreement, articles and spelling of your most-used theme words.

Structures the mark scheme rewards

The writing paper is marked on content, organisation and language, so each structure below is one that wins marks in one of those. Every part is explained — check a draft against them and the part you have left out is the mark you are about to lose.

Answer structures

developed point — point + detail + example or consequence
point means the claim in one sentence; detail means the specifics (who, when, how much); example or consequence means what follows from it. A list of undeveloped points scores in the lowest content band however long it is.

paragraph — topic sentence + support + link
topic sentence means the paragraph's one idea, stated first; support means two or three sentences of detail; link means a connective that carries the reader to the next paragraph. Organisation marks are given for exactly this shape, visible at a glance.

formal email or letter — salutation + purpose + details + closing
salutation means Dear Mr/Ms + surname, or Dear Sir/Madam if unknown; purpose means why you are writing, in the first line; details means the numbered points from the task; closing means Yours sincerely (named) or Yours faithfully (unnamed). Wrong closing with the wrong salutation costs a register mark.

review — summary + evaluation + recommendation
summary means what the thing is; evaluation means what worked and what did not, with reasons; recommendation means who should try it and why. A review that only describes has not reviewed.

article — headline + hook + development + conclusion
headline means short and specific; hook means a question, a statistic or a striking detail that makes the reader continue; development means two or three paragraphs each making one point; conclusion means a closing thought, not a summary of what has just been said.

Language control

tense frame: narrative — past simple; discursive — present simple; future plans — will or going to
the dominant tense of each task type. Choose it in the plan and keep it: tense drift mid-paragraph is the single most common language-band limiter in this paper.

connective ladder — addition (moreover) → contrast (however) → cause (therefore) → example (for instance) → conclusion (in conclusion)
the five functions a linking word can perform. Using the right function with the wrong word ("although" for "therefore") reads as a content error as well as a language one.

word budget: plan 10%, write 80%, check 10% of the time allowed
the split that keeps a candidate inside the word limit without losing the checking pass. Under-length answers lose content marks; over-length answers lose accuracy marks to unchecked errors.

range — simple + compound + complex sentence in every paragraph
simple means one clause; compound means two main clauses joined by and/but/so; complex means a main clause plus a subordinate clause (because, although, which). The language band rewards variety, and variety is countable — one of each per paragraph is the target.

title: Exam technique: Robotics & AI
content:
### What earns the marks
For expert systems, knowledge base plus inference engine plus explanation system earns each mark. For machine learning, training on data stated earns the method mark. For robotics, the named sensor matched to its reading earns the mark.
### Traps
Error: AI claimed to understand like a human. Correction: it matches patterns from training. Error: inference engine confused with interface. Correction: inference reasons, interface talks to users. Error: automation effects one-sided. Correction: weigh jobs lost against jobs created.

title: A Level Mathematics: The Poisson Distribution
content:
A Level Mathematics: The Poisson Distribution

The Poisson distribution models the number of events that happen in a fixed interval of time, length, area or volume when those events occur randomly and independently at a constant average rate. Where the binomial counts successes in a fixed number of trials, the Poisson counts arrivals in a continuous window: calls reaching a switchboard in an hour, defects along a length of cable, radioactive decays in a minute. This note derives the formula from the binomial, sets out the two conditions that must hold, and then uses the distribution for the probability and hypothesis-test questions the exam sets.

Where the formula comes from

Imagine slicing the interval into a very large number of tiny sub-intervals. In each slice the chance of an event is tiny but the number of slices is enormous, so the count is binomial with n huge and p tiny. Taking that limit turns nCr p^r (1−p)^(n−r) into the Poisson formula, with the mean λ = np surviving as the only parameter.

X ~ Po(λ):  P(X = r) = e^(-λ) λ^r / r!
mean E(X) = λ
variance Var(X) = λ
so the mean and variance are equal - a diagnostic test for the model

The equality of mean and variance is not a coincidence to memorise; it is the fingerprint of the limit, and it is why an exam question can give you a sample mean and variance and ask whether a Poisson model is plausible.

The three conditions

A Poisson model needs randomness, independence and a constant rate. Naming them is worth marks, and each failure has a characteristic symptom.

1. events occur singly (not in pairs or batches)
2. events occur at random, independently of each other
3. the average rate λ is constant over the interval
then the count in that interval is Poisson

Worked example (checking the model). A shop counts customers arriving per hour. Explain why a Poisson model may be unsuitable.

the arrival rate is not constant: it peaks at lunchtime and is near zero at night
so condition 3 fails and the mean over a whole day is not a single rate
a better model splits the day into periods of roughly constant rate

Calculating probabilities

The formula handles a single value; the cumulative sum handles a range. Because the Poisson has no upper limit, every "at least" question becomes a complement.

P(X = r) = e^(-λ) λ^r / r!
P(X <= r) sums from 0 to r (tables or calculator)
P(X >= r) = 1 - P(X <= r - 1)
P(X < r)  = P(X <= r - 1)

Worked example. X ~ Po(3). Find P(X = 2).

P = e^(-3) × 3² / 2!
= 0.049787 × 9 / 2
= 0.2240

Worked example 2 (at least). For the same X, find P(X ≥ 4).

P(X >= 4) = 1 - P(X <= 3)
P(X <= 3) = 0.049787(1 + 3 + 4.5 + 4.5) = 0.6472
so P(X >= 4) = 0.3528

Worked example 3 (scale change). Calls arrive at 4 per minute. Find the probability of 10 or more calls in two minutes.

the rate scales with the interval: λ = 8 for two minutes
P(X >= 10) = 1 - P(X <= 9) = 1 - 0.7170 = 0.2830

Scaling is the most common source of avoidable error: the parameter must be expressed for the interval the question actually asks about.

Adding independent Poisson variables

If two independent counts each follow a Poisson distribution, their sum does too, and the parameters add. This is why the distribution is so usable: a total across separate sources needs no convolution.

X ~ Po(l1), Y ~ Po(l2), independent
X + Y ~ Po(l1 + l2)
but X - Y is NOT Poisson

Worked example. A website gets 5 hits per minute from Europe and 3 per minute from Asia, independently. Find the probability of more than 10 hits in a minute in total.

total ~ Po(8)
P(X > 10) = 1 - P(X <= 10) = 1 - 0.8159 = 0.1841

The Poisson as an approximation to the binomial

When n is large and p is small, the binomial is well approximated by a Poisson with λ = np. The rule of thumb used in this course is n > 50 and p < 0.05, or np < 5.

X ~ B(n, p) with n large, p small  →  X is approximately Po(np)

Worked example. A factory produces items with a 2% defect rate. In a batch of 200, use a Poisson approximation to find the probability of at most 2 defects.

λ = 200 × 0.02 = 4
P(X <= 2) = e^(-4)(1 + 4 + 8) = 0.018316 × 13 = 0.2381
the exact binomial gives 0.2351, so the approximation is close

Worked example 2 (justifying the approximation). State why the approximation is reasonable here.

n = 200 is large and p = 0.02 is small, with np = 4
so the rare-event limit conditions hold

Hypothesis testing with the Poisson

The structure is identical to the binomial test: state hypotheses, assume the null rate, compute the tail probability, compare with the significance level. The only new step is that the rate may need scaling to the observed interval.

H0: λ = lambda0    H1: λ > lambda0 (or <)
observed count x in the interval
p-value = P(X >= x) or P(X <= x) under Po(lambda0)
reject H0 if the p-value <= the significance level

Worked example. A call centre historically receives 6 calls per hour. In a new hour it receives 12. Test at the 5% level whether the rate has increased.

H0: λ = 6;  H1: λ > 6
X ~ Po(6) under H0
P(X >= 12) = 1 - P(X <= 11) = 1 - 0.9799 = 0.0201
0.0201 < 0.05, so reject H0
there is evidence the rate has increased

Worked example 2 (critical region). For Po(6), find the 5% one-tailed critical region for an increase.

P(X >= 11) = 0.0426 (below 0.05)
P(X >= 10) = 0.0839 (above 0.05)
critical region: X >= 11

Worked example 3 (two intervals). The same centre observes 16 calls over two hours. Test for an increase at 5%.

expected over two hours under H0 = 12, so X ~ Po(12)
P(X >= 16) = 1 - P(X <= 15) = 1 - 0.8444 = 0.1556
0.1556 > 0.05, so do not reject H0

Compare the two: twelve calls in one hour was significant, sixteen in two hours is not, because the expected count doubled. The rate, not the raw count, is what is being tested.

Reading the distribution's shape

The Poisson is skewed to the right when λ is small and becomes almost symmetric as λ grows, which is why small-rate questions usually live in the lower tail and why the normal approximation becomes usable once λ passes about 20. Knowing the shape tells you at a glance whether an answer is plausible: a probability of 0.4 for "more than 10" when λ = 3 should feel wrong before any arithmetic is checked.

A useful sanity check is that the standard deviation is the square root of the mean. For Po(9) the mean is 9 and the standard deviation 3, so counts between 6 and 12 are ordinary and a count of 20 is roughly three and a half standard deviations out — surprising enough to prompt a hypothesis test. That comparison is what turns a bare probability into an interpretation, and interpretation marks are the easiest ones to lose.

Finally, note that the model is about a count in an interval, so the interval has to be defined in the answer. "Three calls per hour" and "three calls per minute" describe different distributions, and a rate quoted per unit time without its unit is not a λ at all.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Definition) State two conditions for a Poisson model. Answer: events occur singly at random, independently, at a constant rate.
  2. (Single value) X ~ Po(2.5): find P(X = 3). Answer: P(X = 3) = e^(−λ)λ³/3! = e^(−2.5) × 15.625/6 = 0.0821 × 2.604 = 0.2138.
  3. (Cumulative) X ~ Po(4): find P(X ≤ 2). Answer: P(X ≤ 2) = e^(−4)(1 + 4 + 8) = 0.0183 × 13 = 0.2381.
  4. (Complement) X ~ Po(5): find P(X ≥ 3). Answer: P(X ≥ 3) = 1 − P(X ≤ 2) = 1 − e^(−5)(1 + 5 + 12.5) = 1 − 0.1247 = 0.8753.
  5. (Scaling) Rate 3 per hour: find P(X = 0) in 20 minutes. Answer: the rate scales with the interval: λ = 3 × 20/60 = 1, so P(X = 0) = e^(−1) = 0.3679.
  6. (Sum) Independent Po(2) and Po(3): find P(total = 4). Answer: independent Poisson variables add, so T ~ Po(2 + 3) = Po(5) and P(T = 4) = e^(−5)5⁴/4! = 0.1755.
  7. (Approximation) B(500, 0.01): approximate P(X = 0). Answer: n is large and p small, so use Po(λ = np = 5): P(X = 0) ≈ e^(−5) = 0.00674.
  8. (Mean/variance) A sample has mean 4.2 and variance 9.1. Comment on the Poisson fit. Answer: variance far exceeds the mean, so the model is doubtful (over-dispersed).
  9. (Test) 9 events observed where 4 expected; test for an increase at 5%. Answer: under H₀, X ~ Po(4); P(X ≥ 9) = 1 − P(X ≤ 8) = 0.0214 < 0.05, so reject H₀ — the observed rate is significantly higher.
  10. (Critical region) Po(3), 5% upper tail: find the critical region. Answer: P(X ≥ 6) = 0.0839 and P(X ≥ 7) = 0.0335; the largest region still at or below 5% starts at 7, so the critical region is X ≥ 7.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Using the wrong interval: λ must match the window asked about; doubling a time doubles the rate.
  • Complement off by one: P(X ≥ 4) = 1 − P(X ≤ 3); subtracting P(X ≤ 4) is the classic error.
  • Treating a difference as Poisson: sums of independent Poisson variables are Poisson, differences are not.
  • Approximation outside its range: np must be small; with np large the Poisson is a poor fit to the binomial.
  • Variance assumed equal to the mean without checking: the test mean = variance is a diagnostic, not a guarantee.
  • Ignoring clustering: events that arrive in bursts break the single-event condition and inflate the variance.
  • r! miscomputed: 0! = 1 and 1! = 1, and a missing factorial term changes the answer entirely.
  • p-value direction: a one-tailed test uses one tail only; doubling it makes a borderline result look significant.

Equations and symbols

One formula does the arithmetic, and one identity checks the model: for a Poisson variable the mean and the variance are the same number λ. Every exam error on this topic is either a λ expressed for the wrong interval or a complement taken one term too far.

P(X = r) = e^(-λ) λ^r / r! Key: X = the number of events counted in the fixed interval (a count, no units); r = the particular count asked about; λ = the mean number of events in that same interval (no units — it is a count, not a rate per second, unless the interval is one second); e = 2.71828…; r! = factorial of r, with 0! = 1.

mean E(X) = λ Key: E(X) = the expected count in the interval; λ = the mean. Read it with the line below: the equality of mean and variance is the fingerprint of the model, and a sample whose variance far exceeds its mean is not Poisson.

variance Var(X) = λ Key: Var(X) = the variance of the count; λ = the same mean. So the standard deviation is √λ, which is the quickest sanity check on an observed count: for λ = 9, counts between 6 and 12 are ordinary.

P(X >= r) = 1 - P(X <= r - 1) Key: the complement rule, because the Poisson has no upper limit; r = the smallest count that counts as "at least". Subtracting P(X ≤ r) instead of P(X ≤ r − 1) is the classic off-by-one and throws the whole tail away.

P = e^(-3) × 3² / 2! Key: λ = 3 for this interval; r = 2; 3² = λ^r; 2! = 2. The arithmetic is 0.049787 × 9 / 2 = 0.2240 — quote four decimal places unless told otherwise.

λ = 200 × 0.02 = 4 Key: 200 = n, the number of trials; 0.02 = p, the probability of the event in one trial; λ = np = 4, the mean of the approximating Poisson. The approximation is used when n is large and p small — n > 50 and p < 0.05, or np < 5.

P(X <= 2) = e^(-4)(1 + 4 + 8) = 0.018316 × 13 = 0.2381 Key: the bracket is λ^r/r! summed for r = 0, 1, 2: 1, 4 and 8 (since 4²/2! = 8); e^(−4) = 0.018316. The exact binomial gives 0.2351, so the approximation is close — say so when a question asks you to comment.

X + Y ~ Po(l1 + l2) Key: X and Y = two independent Poisson counts; l1, l2 = their means; the total count is Poisson with the means added. A difference of two Poisson variables is not Poisson — only sums combine.

X ~ B(n, p) with n large, p small → X is approximately Po(np) Key: B(n, p) = the binomial with n trials and success probability p; np = the Poisson mean that replaces them. State both conditions before using it, because the approximation fails when np is large.

SymbolQuantityUnit
λmean number of events in the stated intervala count (no units) — quote the interval with it
rthe observed or asked-about counta count (no units)
H₀null hypothesis, λ = λ₀a stated mean count for the interval

Scaling is the other half of the topic and it is not a formula but a substitution: a rate of 4 per minute is λ = 8 for a two-minute window, and 12 calls in one hour must be tested against 24 expected in two hours, not against 12. Write the interval beside the λ every time.

title: Hypothesis Testing — Quick Revision Summary

Quick revision: Hypothesis Testing

Mathematics — A2. The null hypothesis H₀ is the default claim (no change, p = p₀). The alternative H₁ is what a suspicious observation suggests (p > p₀, p < p₀, or p ≠ p₀). The significance level α is the probability of rejecting a true H₀ — the false-alarm rate, usually 5% or 1%.

Key areas to revise

  • The Framework
  • Test for a Binomial Proportion
  • One-Tailed vs Two-Tailed
  • Critical Regions
  • Conclusions in Context

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

title: Cell Structure, Reproduction and Development — Study Notes
content:
Cell Structure, Reproduction and Development

Edexcel IAL Biology WBI12, Topic 3. Cells are the basic units of life. Their structure reflects their function, and cell division produces the new cells needed for growth, repair and reproduction.

Cell structure

  • Prokaryotic cells have no nucleus; their DNA is a circular loop in the cytoplasm, and their ribosomes are 70S. Eukaryotic cells have a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.
  • The nucleus holds DNA. Mitochondria carry out aerobic respiration. Chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis in plant cells. Rough endoplasmic reticulum has ribosomes and makes proteins; the Golgi apparatus modifies and packages them.
  • Electron microscopes have higher resolution than light microscopes because electrons have a much shorter wavelength than visible light.
  • Magnification = image size ÷ actual size. For an image 40 mm across at a magnification of ×400, the actual size is 0.1 mm.

Cell division

  • The cell cycle has interphase (G1, S and G2) and mitotic division. DNA replicates in the S phase.
  • Mitosis produces two genetically identical diploid daughter cells. It is used for growth and repair.
  • Meiosis has two divisions and produces four genetically different haploid gametes. Crossing over happens in prophase I, and independent assortment happens when homologous pairs line up at metaphase I.

Stem cells and development

  • A totipotent cell can form any cell type, including the cells of the placenta. Embryonic stem cells are pluripotent: they can form any cell type of the body. Adult stem cells are multipotent.
  • Differentiation switches on particular genes so that a cell becomes specialised.

Cancer

  • Cancer results from mutations that disrupt the control of the cell cycle. The cells divide in an uncontrolled way and can form a tumour.

Exam tip: when you compare mitosis and meiosis, name the number of divisions, the number of daughter cells, their ploidy and whether they are genetically identical.

title:
Cell Structure, Reproduction and Development — Quick Revision Summary

Biology — AS Edexcel IAL, WBI12 Unit 1 Topic 3. The cell as the unit of life, eukaryotic and prokaryotic ultrastructure, light and electron microscopy and measurement, mitosis and the cell cycle, meiosis and variation, gametes and fertilisation in mammals and flowering plants, stem cells and their uses, and genetic control through gene expression, epigenetics and inheritance patterns.

  • 3.1 Common features of all cells: a plasma membrane, cytoplasm and ribosomes are shared by every cell; differences such as a nucleus, cell wall and organelles explain cell function.
  • 3.2 Levels of organisation: cells form tissues, tissues form organs, organs form organ systems; each level carries out a particular function and shapes the level above it.
  • 3.3 Eukaryotic ultrastructure: nucleus with nuclear envelope and nucleolus, ribosomes (80S) on rER and free, rER (protein synthesis and transport), sER (lipid synthesis), mitochondria (double membrane, cristae, matrix, aerobic respiration), centrioles (spindle organisation), lysosomes (digestive enzymes), Golgi (modifies, sorts and packages proteins, forms extracellular enzymes).
  • 3.4 rER and Golgi: the rER makes proteins and passes them to the Golgi in vesicles; the Golgi modifies, sorts and packages them, and is involved in forming extracellular enzymes.
  • 3.5 Prokaryotic ultrastructure: no membrane-bound nucleus — a single circular DNA free in the cytoplasm; cell wall of peptidoglycan; capsule; plasmids (small rings of DNA, often carrying resistance genes); flagella (rotate for motility); pili (attachment and conjugation); 70S ribosomes — smaller than eukaryotic 80S.
  • 3.6 EM recognition: in EM images, recognise nucleus, nucleolus, ribosomes, rER, sER, mitochondria, centrioles, lysosomes, Golgi and — in prokaryotes — the cell wall, capsule, circular DNA, 70S ribosomes, flagella and pili.
  • 3.7 Microscopy and staining: light microscopes use visible light and have low resolution (~0.2 µm, ~×1500 max); electron microscopes (TEM for internal ultrastructure, SEM for surface detail) give far higher resolution and magnification. Staining with methylene blue (animal cells) or iodine (starch, cell walls) makes transparent structures visible; a graticule calibrated with a stage micrometer lets you measure real sizes.

Worked example

Calibrate a graticule: one eyepiece division at ×400 equals 2.5 µm (calibrated against a stage micrometer). A cell spans 20 divisions, so its real length = 20 × 2.5 µm = 50 µm. To find real size from image size, real size = image size ÷ magnification, so a cell drawn 50 mm long at ×2000 is 50 mm ÷ 2000 = 0.025 mm = 25 µm.

Key points to remember

  • Magnification ≠ resolution; resolution is the ability to distinguish two close points and sets the useful limit of detail.
  • In a light microscope total magnification = eyepiece × objective; always calibrate the graticule at each objective before measuring.
  • A stain makes transparent structures visible — methylene blue shows nuclei in animal cells, iodine shows starch grains and cell walls.
  • Staining matters in electron microscopy too: heavy-metal stains increase contrast in TEM and SEM images.
  • The plasma membrane is an active, protein-studded barrier; without it the cell cannot control what enters and leaves.
  • The nucleus holds the DNA and nucleolus; the nucleolus makes ribosomes, which then leave the nucleus.
  • Ribosomes are the same fundamental structure in all living things (though smaller in prokaryotes: 70S), and that is part of the evidence for common ancestry.
  • Mitochondria have a double membrane and cristae that increase surface area for aerobic respiration — the energy for cell activities.
  • The Golgi modifies and packages proteins; extracellular enzymes (such as digestive enzymes) are secreted by exocytosis after Golgi packaging.
  • Endocytosis and exocytosis move materials in vesicles, and both need ATP — another place ATP is used beyond respiration.

Key points to remember

Know the cell cycle: interphase (G1, S, G2 — growth and DNA replication) then mitosis (prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase) then cytokinesis; mitosis makes genetically identical cells for growth and asexual reproduction. Meiosis makes genetically non-identical gametes and is the source of variation, through independent assortment in metaphase I and crossing over in prophase I. A locus is the position of a gene on a chromosome; linked genes do not assort independently. Sperm are specialised: small, motile, with an acrosome of digestive enzymes, mitochondria for energy and a haploid nucleus; eggs are large with food reserves and the zona pellucida. Fertilisation in mammals: acrosome reaction digests the zona pellucida, cortical reaction blocks further sperm, nuclei fuse to form the zygote. In flowering plants: pollen tube grows to the embryo sac, double fertilisation — one male nucleus fertilises the egg (zygote → embryo), one fuses with the two polar nuclei to form triploid endosperm. Mitotic index = number of cells dividing ÷ total cells; used in Core Practical 6 root tip squash to count mitotic stages. Totipotent cells (zygote, early embryo, plant meristems) can form a whole organism; pluripotent cells (blastocyst cells) can form many but not all cell types. Stem cells are used in bone marrow transplants, and their use raises ethical and social questions.

Key points to remember

Cells become specialised by differential gene expression — different genes switched on or off produce different proteins; one gene can give several proteins through alternative splicing of mRNA. Transcription factors switch genes on or off. Epigenetic modification — DNA methylation and histone modification — changes gene activity without changing the DNA sequence, and the modification can be passed on after cell division. Phenotype is genotype plus environment: multiple alleles (ABO blood groups), polygenic inheritance (height — continuous variation) and environment all contribute. Mutations are changes in DNA base sequence: substitution may change one amino acid or none, insertion/deletion may cause a frameshift. Mutations are the source of new alleles and can cause cancer or genetic disorders such as cystic fibrosis (faulty chloride channel — lung, gut and reproductive problems). Pedigree diagrams show inheritance patterns; sex linkage (red-green colour blindness, haemophilia) is carried on the X and is more common in males. Genetic screening can identify carriers and test embryos (PGD) or a fetus (amniocentesis, CVS); this raises ethical and social questions — consent, the right to know, what counts as a disorder, the choice to terminate, access and cost, and the risk of selecting for non-medical traits.

How to use this

Read the summary list first, then open the full revision notes for any point that feels weak, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself. Revise next by: drawing and labelling a plant cell and an animal cell from memory with each organelle's function; carrying out the graticule calibration and mitotic index calculations; and working through a monohybrid cross, a sex-linked cross and a pedigree to explain the ratios and the logic for each.
