  • Endocytosis and exocytosis move materials in vesicles, and both need ATP — another place ATP is used beyond respiration.

Key points to remember

Know the cell cycle: interphase (G1, S, G2 — growth and DNA replication) then mitosis (prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase) then cytokinesis; mitosis makes genetically identical cells for growth and asexual reproduction. Meiosis makes genetically non-identical gametes and is the source of variation, through independent assortment in metaphase I and crossing over in prophase I. A locus is the position of a gene on a chromosome; linked genes do not assort independently. Sperm are specialised: small, motile, with an acrosome of digestive enzymes, mitochondria for energy and a haploid nucleus; eggs are large with food reserves and the zona pellucida. Fertilisation in mammals: acrosome reaction digests the zona pellucida, cortical reaction blocks further sperm, nuclei fuse to form the zygote. In flowering plants: pollen tube grows to the embryo sac, double fertilisation — one male nucleus fertilises the egg (zygote → embryo), one fuses with the two polar nuclei to form triploid endosperm. Mitotic index = number of cells dividing ÷ total cells; used in Core Practical 6 root tip squash to count mitotic stages. Totipotent cells (zygote, early embryo, plant meristems) can form a whole organism; pluripotent cells (blastocyst cells) can form many but not all cell types. Stem cells are used in bone marrow transplants, and their use raises ethical and social questions.

Key points to remember

Cells become specialised by differential gene expression — different genes switched on or off produce different proteins; one gene can give several proteins through alternative splicing of mRNA. Transcription factors switch genes on or off. Epigenetic modification — DNA methylation and histone modification — changes gene activity without changing the DNA sequence, and the modification can be passed on after cell division. Phenotype is genotype plus environment: multiple alleles (ABO blood groups), polygenic inheritance (height — continuous variation) and environment all contribute. Mutations are changes in DNA base sequence: substitution may change one amino acid or none, insertion/deletion may cause a frameshift. Mutations are the source of new alleles and can cause cancer or genetic disorders such as cystic fibrosis (faulty chloride channel — lung, gut and reproductive problems). Pedigree diagrams show inheritance patterns; sex linkage (red-green colour blindness, haemophilia) is carried on the X and is more common in males. Genetic screening can identify carriers and test embryos (PGD) or a fetus (amniocentesis, CVS); this raises ethical and social questions — consent, the right to know, what counts as a disorder, the choice to terminate, access and cost, and the risk of selecting for non-medical traits.

How to use this

Read the summary list first, then open the full revision notes for any point that feels weak, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself. Revise next by: drawing and labelling a plant cell and an animal cell from memory with each organelle''s function; carrying out the graticule calibration and mitotic index calculations; and working through a monohybrid cross, a sex-linked cross and a pedigree to explain the ratios and the logic for each.

title: Geometry — Congruence and Similarity — Study Notes
content:
Geometry — Congruence and Similarity

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): congruence criteria, similar shapes, scale factors for length/area/volume, symmetry.

1. Congruence

Criteria: SSS, SAS, ASA (AAS), RHS. State the criterion used when proving triangles congruent, then transfer matching sides/angles.

2. Similarity

Equal angles + sides in proportion. Scale factor k = corresponding new ÷ old.

Example: triangles with sides 4, 6, 8 and 6, 9, 12: k = 1.5.

3. Length, area, volume factors

Length ×k; area ×k²; volume ×k³ — including reverse problems.

Example: volumes 250 cm³ and 2000 cm³: k³ = 8 ⇒ k = 2 ⇒ areas ×4.

4. Area/volume calculations from similarity

Find k from a matching length pair, then apply the right power. Watch hidden pairs (radii, heights, slants).

5. Symmetry

Line symmetry (reflect) and rotational symmetry order — for 2-D shapes and 3-D solids (prisms, cubes, pyramids).

Exam tips: write the matching-vertex order in similarity statements (△ABC ~ △DEF); choose which k-power applies before calculating.

title: Electric Fields and Capacitance — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Electric Fields and Capacitance

Physics — A2. F = q₁q₂/(4πε₀r²). Field strength E = F/q (N C⁻¹); for a point charge E = q/(4πε₀r²).

Key areas to revise

  • Coulomb's Law
  • Uniform Fields
  • Potential
  • Capacitance
  • Charging and Discharging

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Key relationships

  • Coulomb's law: F = Q q / (4 π ε₀ r²) for point charges, and E = F / Q.
  • Radial field strength E = Q / (4 π ε₀ r²), and potential V = Q / (4 π ε₀ r).
  • Capacitance C = Q / V, and energy stored = ½ Q V = ½ C V².
  • Capacitors in series: 1/C = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂; in parallel: C = C₁ + C₂.

Common errors

Capacitors in series are added as reciprocals, which is the reverse of resistors in parallel. Field strength is a vector and potential is a scalar, so do not add field strengths as if they were energies.

title: AS Level Physics: Kinematics
content:
AS Level Physics: Kinematics

Edexcel International A Level Physics, Unit 1 (WPH11) Mechanics and Materials — motion in a straight line and in a plane, and the measurement skills the companion Unit 3 paper (WPH13, Practical Skills in Physics I) examines. Everything in mechanics starts here: quantities with units and directions, the equations of motion, free fall, projectiles and the graphs that describe them. The unit also demands real data-handling skill — uncertainties, error bars, gradients and intercepts — because WPH13 is a written paper that marks your experimental thinking, not your hands.

Quantities, units, scalars and vectors

A physical quantity is a number with a unit, and every unit in mechanics is built from four SI base units: the metre (m), kilogram (kg), second (s) and ampere (A). Speed in m s⁻¹ and force in newtons (1 N = 1 kg m s⁻²) are derived from them. A scalar has size only — distance, speed, mass, time, energy, power. A vector has size and direction — displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, momentum. The distinction is operational, not decorative: vectors add by direction, and every mechanics question that mentions direction is testing it.

  • Two vectors in a line: add if in the same direction, subtract if opposite, and state the direction of the resultant.
  • Two vectors at right angles: the resultant is the hypotenuse, R = √(A² + B²), at an angle θ = tan⁻¹(B/A) to A.
  • Any two vectors: resolve each into perpendicular components with A cos θ and A sin θ, add the components separately, then recombine.

Resolution is the workhorse of A-level mechanics. A force F at angle θ to the horizontal has a horizontal component F cos θ along the motion and a vertical component F sin θ across it; only the component along the motion changes the motion. Sign convention is chosen, not given: for vertical motion taking up as positive makes g = −9.81 m s⁻²; for slopes, taking down the slope as positive is usually simplest.

Motion in a straight line

Uniform motion means constant velocity; accelerated motion means changing velocity. The five quantities in every equation of motion are: displacement s (m), initial velocity u (m s⁻¹), final velocity v (m s⁻¹), acceleration a (m s⁻²), and time t (s). Average velocity is (u + v)/2 only when the acceleration is constant.

QuantityDefinitionUnitScalar or vector
DisplacementDistance from a start point in a stated directionmVector
VelocityRate of change of displacementm s⁻¹Vector
AccelerationRate of change of velocitym s⁻²Vector
SpeedDistance travelled per unit timem s⁻¹Scalar

The equations of motion

For motion with constant acceleration, four equations connect the five quantities. They are valid only while a is constant, and they are all vector equations, so the sign convention must be applied to u, v, a and s consistently.

v = u + a t
s = u t + 1/2 a t²
v² = u² + 2 a s
s = 1/2 (u + v) t
  • Each equation omits one quantity: pick the equation that does not contain the unknown you do not need.
  • Units must be SI before substituting: kilometres to metres, minutes to seconds, km h⁻¹ to m s⁻¹ (divide by 3.6).
  • Direction convention: write one down before touching the algebra — for example, upward positive means a falling object has a = −9.81 m s⁻² and a downward displacement is negative.

Free fall and projectile motion

Free fall is motion under gravity alone. Near the Earth's surface the acceleration is g = 9.81 m s⁻² downwards and is constant (air resistance neglected), so the equations of motion apply directly. An object thrown straight up decelerates at 9.81 m s⁻², stops instantaneously at the top, and falls back with the same acceleration; the time up equals the time down from the same height.

A projectile is any object moving under gravity alone once launched. The key insight is independence of components: the horizontal motion has zero acceleration and constant velocity, while the vertical motion has constant acceleration g. Resolve the launch velocity into u cos θ horizontally and u sin θ vertically, treat the two motions separately with the equations of motion, and combine at the end. At the highest point the vertical velocity is zero but the horizontal velocity is unchanged — the projectile is never at rest. The trajectory is a parabola.

Motion graphs

GraphGradient givesArea gives
Displacement–timeVelocityNot used
Velocity–timeAccelerationChange in displacement
Acceleration–timeNot usedChange in velocity

The equation s = ½(u + v)t is the area of a trapezium under a velocity–time graph, and v² = u² + 2as is what falls out of that geometry — which is why the equations and the graphs never disagree. Curved velocity–time graphs mean changing acceleration; the gradient at a point is found from a tangent drawn with a ruler and evaluated between two distant points on the tangent.

Non-uniform motion: drag and terminal velocity

When a real object falls, air resistance (drag) acts opposite to the motion and grows with speed. The resultant force is weight minus drag, so the acceleration is greatest at the start and falls as speed rises. When drag equals the weight the resultant force is zero and the object continues at terminal velocity. A skydiver reaches terminal velocity in free fall, opens the parachute (which raises drag enormously), and decelerates to a much lower terminal velocity before landing. The same physics sets the thinking and braking distances of a vehicle: thinking distance grows with reaction time and speed; braking distance grows with the square of the speed, because the work the brakes must do is ½mv².

Unit 3 skills: measurement, data and uncertainty

WPH13 examines the practical skills of Units 1 and 2 in writing, using unfamiliar contexts. The marks come from method and analysis, and the analysis rules are fixed.

  • Absolute uncertainty is the precision of the instrument: ±0.5 of the smallest scale division for an analogue scale, ± the smallest reading for a digital one. A length of 24.5 mm on a ruler carries ±0.5 mm.
  • Percentage uncertainty = (absolute uncertainty ÷ measured value) × 100. A small quantity measured with the same instrument carries the biggest percentage uncertainty — which is why measuring a short wire's extension with a ruler is poor method.
  • Combining uncertainties: for a sum or difference, add the absolute uncertainties; for a product or quotient (including powers), add the percentage uncertainties, and for a quantity raised to the power n, multiply its percentage uncertainty by n.
  • Repeat readings reduce random error; the mean is quoted with the uncertainty taken as half the range or the instrument precision, whichever is larger. Systematic errors (zero errors, calibration faults) are corrected at the instrument, never by averaging.
  • Graphs and error bars: plot every point with error bars in both directions where both quantities are uncertain, draw the line of best fit and also the worst acceptable steepest and shallowest lines within the error bars; the gradient's uncertainty comes from their spread.
  • Gradient and intercept: gradient = Δy/Δx taken between two distant points on the line; state it with its unit. The intercept is physical only if the theory predicts one — on a velocity–time graph the intercept is the initial velocity; on a load–extension graph a non-zero intercept suggests the spring was already stretched.
  • Calibration: a known input is applied to an instrument and its output recorded, giving a calibration graph against which unknown readings are converted.
  • Control of variables and safety: identify the independent, dependent and control variables; keep controls fixed and name them; risk assessment links each hazard to a control (falling masses — clamp the stand; long wires under tension — eye protection).

Worked example: equations of motion and uncertainty

A ball is dropped from rest and falls 1.50 m. Neglecting air resistance, take g = 9.81 m s⁻².

v² = u² + 2 a s = 0 + 2 × 9.81 × 1.50 = 29.4, so v = 5.42 m s⁻¹
time: s = u t + 1/2 a t² gives 1.50 = 4.905 t², so t = 0.553 s

Now the uncertainty: if the height is measured as 1.50 ± 0.01 m, its percentage uncertainty is 0.01/1.50 × 100 = 0.67 per cent. Since v = √(2gs), the percentage uncertainty in v is half of that in s, so v = 5.42 ± 0.04 m s⁻¹. Treating powers correctly is the difference between a right and a wrong uncertainty.

Common mistakes

  • Applying the equations of motion when the acceleration is not constant (for example once drag becomes significant).
  • Ignoring sign convention: mixing upward-positive displacements with downward-positive g gives nonsense answers.
  • Forgetting that at the top of a projectile's flight the vertical velocity is zero but the acceleration is still 9.81 m s⁻² downwards.
  • Adding percentage uncertainties for a sum instead of absolute uncertainties, or halving the percentage uncertainty of a square-rooted quantity incorrectly.
  • Joining plotted points with straight lines instead of drawing a smooth line of best fit, or ignoring error bars when asked for uncertainty.
  • Taking the gradient between two plotted points rather than two distant points on the best-fit line.
  • Confusing distance with displacement and speed with velocity in questions that mention direction.
  • Using km h⁻¹ directly in the equations: divide by 3.6 to convert to m s⁻¹ first.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (WPH11, 3 marks). A car accelerates uniformly from 5.0 m s⁻¹ to 15 m s⁻¹ in 6.0 s. Find the acceleration and the distance travelled.

Answer: a = (v − u)/t = (15 − 5.0)/6.0 = 1.7 m s⁻². s = ½(u + v)t = ½(5.0 + 15)(6.0) = 60 m.

Question 2 (WPH11, 4 marks). A stone is thrown vertically upwards at 20 m s⁻¹. Calculate the maximum height and the total time of flight. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².

Answer: At the top v = 0, so v² = u² + 2as gives 0 = 400 − 2(9.81)h, so h = 20.4 m. Time up: v = u + at gives 0 = 20 − 9.81t, so t = 2.04 s; total flight = 2 × 2.04 = 4.08 s (the motion is symmetric when the landing height equals the launch height).

Question 3 (WPH13, 4 marks). A student measures the period of a pendulum as T = 1.98 ± 0.02 s and the length as L = 98.0 ± 0.5 cm. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in g if g = 4π²L/T².

Answer: Percentage uncertainty in L = 0.5/98.0 × 100 = 0.51 per cent. In T = 0.02/1.98 × 100 = 1.01 per cent, doubled for T² = 2.02 per cent. Total for g = 0.51 + 2.02 = 2.5 per cent. The period dominates, so timing more oscillations would improve the result most.

Question 4 (WPH11, 3 marks). A projectile is launched at 30 m s⁻¹ at 30° above the horizontal. Find its initial horizontal and vertical velocity components.

Answer: Horizontal = 30 cos 30° = 26 m s⁻¹; vertical = 30 sin 30° = 15 m s⁻¹. The horizontal component stays constant (no air resistance); the vertical component decreases at 9.81 m s⁻².

Question 5 (WPH13, 3 marks). A graph of extension against load does not pass through the origin. Suggest a reason and an improvement.

Answer: The spring may already have been loaded (its own weight or an unstated mass), or the initial length was measured incorrectly. Measure the spring's original length hanging vertically with no added load, allow it to settle, and take that as the true zero extension; repeat readings at each load and plot a best-fit line.

Question 6 (WPH11, 3 marks). Explain, in terms of forces, why a skydiver reaches a terminal velocity before opening the parachute.

Answer: On leaving the aircraft, weight exceeds drag, so there is a downward resultant force and she accelerates. As speed increases, drag increases, reducing the resultant force and the acceleration. When drag equals the weight the resultant force is zero, so the acceleration is zero and she continues at constant terminal velocity.

Motion is caused by forces — the subject of Dynamics.

Equations and symbols

Four equations cover every constant-acceleration problem, and each one is missing exactly one quantity — which is how you choose between them. They are vector equations, so the sign convention written down before the substitution is part of the method, not a preliminary.

v = u + a t Key: u = initial velocity (m s⁻¹); v = final velocity (m s⁻¹); a = acceleration (m s⁻²); t = time (s). Omits s — use it when displacement is neither given nor wanted.

s = u t + 1/2 a t² Key: s = displacement (m); u = initial velocity (m s⁻¹); a = acceleration (m s⁻²); t = time (s). Omits v, and it is the one to use when the time is the unknown.

v² = u² + 2 a s Key: v, u = final and initial velocity (m s⁻¹); a = acceleration (m s⁻²); s = displacement (m). Omits t, which is why it is the fastest route whenever time is neither given nor asked for.

s = 1/2 (u + v) t Key: s = displacement (m); u, v = initial and final velocity (m s⁻¹); t = time (s). This is the area of the trapezium under a velocity–time graph, which is why the equations and the graphs always agree.

R = √(A² + B²) Key: R = the resultant of two perpendicular vectors (units of A and B); A, B = the magnitudes of the two vectors. At an angle to A the direction is θ = tan⁻¹(B/A) — magnitude alone is incomplete for a vector quantity.

1 N = 1 kg m s⁻² Key: the definition of the newton in SI base units, which is how every derived unit in mechanics resolves: check a calculation's units by substituting these and the answer's unit follows.

a = (v − u)/t = (15 − 5.0)/6.0 = 1.7 m s⁻² Key: the worked case — 15 and 5.0 m s⁻¹ are the final and initial velocities, 6.0 s the time, and the answer is positive because the car speeds up in the chosen direction. A negative result would mean deceleration, not an error.

s = ½(u + v)t = ½(5.0 + 15)(6.0) = 60 m Key: the same journey's displacement — the mean velocity 10 m s⁻¹ for 6.0 s. This form is the quickest when both velocities and the time are known.

Quantities, units and the scalar–vector split

QuantityUnitScalar or vector
DisplacementmVector
Velocitym s⁻¹Vector
Accelerationm s⁻²Vector
Speedm s⁻¹Scalar
TimesScalar

Traps specific to the equations

  • Using them while the acceleration is changing — after drag becomes significant they no longer apply.
  • Mixing sign conventions: upward positive with g = +9.81 gives nonsense.
  • Reading "at the top" as "at rest": so long as the flight continues, a is 9.81 m s⁻² downwards even where v_y is momentarily zero.
  • Feeding km h⁻¹ straight in; divide by 3.6 first.
  • Adding percentage uncertainties for a sum, where absolute uncertainties add.

title: Algebra — Equations — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Algebra — Equations

Mathematics — OL. linear equations, simultaneous equations, quadratic formula, completing the square, forming equations from words.

  • 1. Linear equations
  • 2. Forming equations
  • 3. Simultaneous equations
  • 4. Quadratics by formula
  • 5. Completing the square

How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

### Worked example Solve 3(x − 2) = 2x + 5. Expand to 3x − 6 = 2x + 5, then subtract 2x and add 6 to get x = 11. Check by substitution: 3(11 − 2) = 27 and 2(11) + 5 = 27. For rearranging, make t the subject of v = u + at by subtracting u and dividing by a, giving t = (v − u)/a.

Key points to remember

Solve a linear equation by doing the same operation to both sides until the unknown stands alone. Do the inverse operations in reverse order of BIDMAS, so undo addition or subtraction before multiplication or division. For an equation with the unknown on both sides, collect the terms with the unknown on one side first.

Check every answer by substituting it back into the original equation. When an equation has brackets or fractions, expand or clear the fractions before you start rearranging, and show each line of working so that a method mark can be awarded even if the final answer is wrong.

title: Exam technique: Ethics, Security & Impact
content:
### What earns the marks
For definitions, each term stated precisely earns its mark (hacking is unauthorised access, not every attack). For discuss questions, one benefit plus one drawback plus a reasoned conclusion earns full marks. For security, the named threat matched to its countermeasure earns each mark.
### Traps
Error: one-sided discuss answers. Correction: both sides plus a verdict. Error: virus named for every malware. Correction: worms, spyware and trojans differ. Error: copyright confused with plagiarism. Correction: copyright is the legal right.

title: Exam technique: Measurement and Units
content:
### What earns the marks
For instrument choice, the micrometer for small diameters earns the mark with its 0.01 mm precision. For density, mass over volume with correct units earns both marks. For readings, meniscus bottom at eye level earns the method mark.
### Traps
Error: parallax ignored in cylinders. Correction: eye level with the meniscus. Error: newton expanded wrongly. Correction: kg m/s squared from F = ma. Error: volume of a box miscalculated. Correction: multiply all three sides.

title: Circular Measure — Study Notes
content:
Circular Measure

Cambridge International AS & A Level Mathematics 9709, Paper 1: radian measure, arc length, and the areas and perimeters of sectors and segments. Every formula here takes its angle in radians — that is the single fact most marks hinge on.

Radians

One radian is the angle at the centre of a circle subtended by an arc whose length equals the radius. The full circumference is 2πr, so a full turn is 2π radians and π radians = 180°.

  • Degrees → radians: multiply by π/180. Example: 150° = 150π/180 = 5π/6 ≈ 2.618 rad.
  • Radians → degrees: multiply by 180/π. Example: 1.5 rad = 1.5 × 180/π ≈ 85.9°.

Learn the common values: 30° = π/6, 45° = π/4, 60° = π/3, 90° = π/2, 180° = π, 360° = 2π. Leave answers in terms of π unless the question asks for a decimal — and when it does, give three significant figures.

Arc Length

s = rθ (θ in radians).

Example: r = 6, θ = π/3 gives s = 6 × π/3 = 2π.

A chord splits the circumference into a minor arc and a major arc, and their lengths add to 2πr. If a question gives the major angle, use θ_major = 2π − θ_minor before substituting.

Sector Area

A = ½r²θ.

Example: r = 5, θ = 1.2 gives A = ½ × 25 × 1.2 = 15.

Minor and major sector areas add to πr². The perimeter of a sector is P = 2r + s = 2r + rθ — the two straight edges count, so an arc length alone is not a perimeter.

Segment Area

A = ½r²(θ − sin θ). For r = 2, θ = π/2: A = 2(π/2 − 1) = π − 2.

The segment is the sector minus the triangle ½r²sin θ — that subtraction is where the formula comes from, and writing it down earns method marks even if the arithmetic slips. Its perimeter is the arc plus the chord, with chord length 2r sin(θ/2).

Putting It Together

Worked example: a sector has radius 8 cm and angle 1.1 rad. Arc length s = 8 × 1.1 = 8.8 cm. Area A = ½ × 64 × 1.1 = 35.2 cm². Perimeter P = 2 × 8 + 8.8 = 24.8 cm.

Rearranging

  • θ = s/r (must be radians)
  • θ = 2A/r²
  • r = s/θ, and r = √(2A/θ) — isolate the squared term first, then take the positive root only, since a radius is a length.

Exam traps: never mix degrees into s = rθ or A = ½r²θ — convert first, and check the calculator is in radian mode. Sketch the sector and mark r and θ before computing. Read whether the question asks for the major or the minor arc, sector, or segment, and confirm area answers carry squared units while arcs and perimeters are plain lengths.

Worked example: arc length and sector area

A sector has radius 5 cm and angle 0.8 radians. The arc length is rθ = 5 × 0.8 = 4 cm. The sector area is ½r²θ = ½ × 25 × 0.8 = 10 cm².

Both formulas need the angle in radians. If the question gives degrees, convert first: 60° = π/3 radians, and 1 radian is about 57.3°. Writing a degree value into rθ is one of the most common lost marks in this topic.

Exact answers with π

For radius 6 cm and angle π/3, the arc length is 6 × π/3 = 2π cm, and the sector area is ½ × 36 × π/3 = 6π cm². Leave answers in terms of π when the question asks for an exact value, and give a decimal only if it asks for one.

Segment area

A segment is the region between a chord and an arc. Its area is the sector area minus the area of the triangle formed by the two radii and the chord, so segment = ½r²(θ − sin θ).

Example: with r = 5 and θ = 0.8, sin 0.8 is about 0.7174, so the segment area is ½ × 25 × (0.8 − 0.7174) = 1.03 cm² to 2 decimal places. Keep sin θ in your calculator, not rounded, until the final line.

Finding an angle or radius from a perimeter or arc

If an arc has length 12 cm on a circle of radius 4 cm, the angle is θ = 12/4 = 3 radians. If the perimeter of a sector is given, the perimeter is 2r + rθ, so set that expression equal to the known value and solve for the unknown.

  • Check that the answer is reasonable: an angle of 3 radians is less than π, so the sector must be less than a half-disc.
  • Sketch the sector and label the radii and the angle before you substitute.
  • When a question combines two sectors or a sector with a triangle, find each area separately and then add or subtract, stating which operation you used.

title: Differentiation — Study Notes
content:
Differentiation

Cambridge International AS & A Level Mathematics 9709, Paper 1. Differentiation finds how fast y changes with x. Most questions ask for one of three things: a gradient at a point, a tangent or normal, or the nature of a stationary point.

Start from a question

The curve C has equation y = 2x³ − 9x² + 12x − 1.

  1. Find dy/dx.
  2. Find the coordinates of the stationary points and state their nature.
  3. Find the equation of the normal to C at x = 3.

Part 1. dy/dx = 6x² − 18x + 12 = 6(x − 1)(x − 2).

Part 2. dy/dx = 0 at x = 1 and x = 2. When x = 1, y = 4, and when x = 2, y = 3. Next, d²y/dx² = 12x − 18. At (1, 4) this is −6, so the point is a maximum. At (2, 3) it is 6, so the point is a minimum.

Part 3. At x = 3, dy/dx = 6(2)(1) = 12, so the normal has gradient −1/12. Also y = 54 − 81 + 36 − 1 = 8, so the point is (3, 8). The normal is y − 8 = −(x − 3)/12, which gives x + 12y − 99 = 0.

The power rule

If y = axⁿ, then dy/dx = naxⁿ⁻¹, for any rational n. A constant differentiates to zero. Rewrite roots and reciprocals as powers first: 4√x − 6/x² = 4x^(1/2) − 6x⁻², so dy/dx = 2/√x + 12/x³.

Expand before you differentiate

Differentiation works term by term, so multiply out any brackets first. Example: y = (x + 2)(x − 5) = x² − 3x − 10, so dy/dx = 2x − 3.

A zero gradient is not always a turning point

Use the second derivative when it is non-zero at the point. If it is zero, test the sign of dy/dx on each side. Example: y = x⁴ − 4x³ gives dy/dx = 4x²(x − 3). At x = 0 the gradient is negative on both sides, so the curve keeps falling and (0, 0) is not a maximum or minimum. At x = 3 the gradient changes from negative to positive, so (3, −27) is a minimum.

Tangents and normals

Substitute x into the original equation to find y, and into dy/dx to find the gradient. The tangent uses that gradient, and the normal uses its negative reciprocal. Write both as y − y₁ = m(x − x₁) and simplify.

Traps that cost marks

  • Differentiating a product factor by factor instead of expanding it first.
  • Giving the normal the same gradient as the tangent, rather than the negative reciprocal.
  • Giving only the x-value of a stationary point, rather than its coordinates (x, y).
  • Calling a point a maximum or minimum from dy/dx = 0 alone, without checking the nature.

Worked example: the chain rule

Differentiate y = (3x − 2)⁵. Treat this as an outer power of an inner linear function. The derivative of the outer function, with the inside kept as a single unit, is 5(3x − 2)⁴. Multiply by the derivative of the inside, which is 3. So dy/dx = 15(3x − 2)⁴. Forgetting the factor 3 from the inside is the most frequent error on this type of question, and it loses the accuracy mark even when the power rule has been applied correctly.

Worked example: the product rule

For y = x² sin x, let u = x² and v = sin x. Then dy/dx = u dv/dx + v du/dx = x² cos x + 2x sin x. Write the two products out separately and then collect like terms. If the question asks for the gradient at a particular point, substitute only after the derivative has been simplified, because substituting first makes it harder to spot an algebra slip.

title: Algebra — Sequences and Functions — Study Notes
content:
Algebra — Sequences and Functions

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): nth term (linear & quadratic), special sequences, function notation, composites, inverses.

1. Linear sequences

nth term = a + (n − 1)d. 5, 8, 11, … → 3n + 2. Check n = 1, 2, 3.

2. Quadratic sequences

Second difference = 2a → an² + bn + c. 3, 8, 15, 24 … has second difference 2 → n² + bn + c; subtract n² → 2, 4, 6, 8 → 2n; so nth term = n² + 2n.

3. Special sequences

Even/odd, triangular (½n(n+1)), squares, cubes, Fibonacci-type (each term = sum of previous two), geometric (×r).

4. Function notation

f(x) = 2x − 5: f(3) = 1. Solve f(x) = 11 → x = 8.

5. Composite functions

fg(x) = f(g(x)) — g first. f(x) = 2x − 5, g(x) = x²: gf(2) = g(1) = 1; fg(3) = f(9) = 13.

6. Inverse functions

Swap x and y, rearrange. f(x) = 2x − 5 ⇒ f⁻¹(x) = (x + 5)/2. Domain of inverse = range of original. Verify: f⁻¹(f(x)) = x.

Exam tips: write the bracket order explicitly in composites; show the "swap and rearrange" line for inverses — answer-only scores little.

Finding the nth term of a linear sequence

For a sequence with a constant difference d, the nth term is dn + (a − d), where a is the first term. Check the rule by substituting n = 1, 2 and 3 before using it. Given a term value, set the nth term equal to it and solve for n to test whether it belongs to the sequence.

Functions as machines

A function takes an input and gives exactly one output. Composite functions are applied right to left: fg(x) means apply g first, then f. The inverse f⁻¹ reverses each step, found by writing y = f(x), swapping x and y, and rearranging for y.

Domain and range

The domain is the set of allowed inputs; the range is the set of outputs produced. Restrictions usually come from division by zero or from taking square roots of negative numbers. State both when asked to describe a function fully.

title: Exam technique: Scatter Diagrams
content:
### What earns the marks
For correlation, direction (rising or falling) and strength (tight or spread) each earn a mark: comment on both. For lines of best fit, the mean point plotted first earns the method mark. For estimation questions, naming interpolation versus extrapolation earns a mark before any value, with the reliability comment credited separately.
### Traps
Error: claiming correlation proves causation. Correction: name the confounder (hot weather drives both). Error: trusting extrapolation like interpolation. Correction: outside the range is always less reliable. Error: forcing the line through the origin. Correction: anchor at (mean x, mean y). Error: calling curved association zero correlation. Correction: zero means no pattern at all.

title: Data Types and File Organisation — Study Notes
content:
Data Types and File Organisation

User-Defined Types

A user-defined type is derived from existing types. An enumerated type lists named values in order: TYPE Months = (Jan, Feb, Mar ...). Internally each value is an integer index starting at 0. Pointer types store a memory address; the dereference operator returns the value at that address, which is how linked structures reference their nodes. Set types store unordered collections of distinct values from an ordinal base type, supporting union, intersection and difference.

Records

A record groups related fields of different types under one identifier, for example a Student record with name : STRING and mark : INTEGER. Arrays of records are the standard structure for storing a table of items in memory.

File Organisation

  • Serial: records in insertion order; searching checks every record. Simple but slow.
  • Sequential: records kept in key order; binary search possible, but insertion needs rewriting.
  • Random (direct): a hashing function converts the key into a storage address, giving near-instant access. A poor hash causes collisions — two keys hashing to the same address — resolved by chaining or overflow areas.

Hashing

A common method is division hashing: Address = Key MOD TableSize. A good hash distributes keys evenly; load factor above roughly 70 percent degrades performance.

Exam tips: state the internal integer representation of enumerated values; define a collision before describing its resolution; compare the three file organisations in terms of search and insert cost.

File organisation and access

Serial files store records in the order they are written and suit sequential processing. Sequential files store records in key order, so a search can stop early. Random (direct) access files calculate a record's address from its key, using a hashing function, so any record can be reached quickly.

Exam tip: state the trade-off: sequential access is simple but slow for searching; direct access is fast but needs a hashing function and can produce collisions.

title: Organic Synthesis Revision Notes A2 Level Chemistry
content:
Organic Synthesis A2 Level Chemistry

These revision notes belong to Edexcel International A Level Chemistry WCH15, Topic 20, and cover structural elucidation, carbon chain extension via Grignard reagents, advanced problem solving, the preparation of aspirin, and practical purification techniques.

Deducing Formulae and Structure from Analytical Data

You must be able to deduce empirical formulae, molecular formulae, and structural formulae from data drawn from combustion analysis, element percentage composition, characteristic reactions of functional groups, infrared spectra, mass spectra, and both 13C and proton NMR spectra.

  • Combustion analysis and elemental percentage composition give the empirical formula by finding the simplest whole-number ratio of moles of atoms.
  • Mass spectrometry provides the molecular ion peak (m/z value) giving the relative molecular mass, alongside fragmentation patterns indicating specific structural units.
  • Infrared spectroscopy identifies functional groups from characteristic absorption wavenumbers, such as O-H stretching in alcohols or C=O stretching in carbonyl compounds.
  • 13C NMR spectroscopy reveals the number of chemically distinct carbon environments and the types of carbon environments present from chemical shift values.
  • Proton NMR spectroscopy shows the number of hydrogen environments, the relative peak areas (integration traces) representing the ratio of protons, and splitting patterns (using the n+1 rule) showing adjacent protons.

Increasing Carbon Chain Length and Grignard Reagents

You must understand methods of increasing the length of the carbon chain in a molecule by the use of magnesium to form Grignard reagents and the reactions of the latter with carbon dioxide and with carbonyl compounds in dry ether.

  • Grignard reagents are formed by reacting a haloalkane with magnesium metal in dry ether. The general formula is RMgX, where X is Cl, Br, or I. Dry ether is essential as water destroys the Grignard reagent.
  • Reaction of a Grignard reagent with carbon dioxide, followed by dilute acid hydrolysis, forms a carboxylic acid with a carbon chain length increased by one. RMgX + CO2 yields RCOOMgX, which upon acidification yields RCOOH.
  • Reaction of a Grignard reagent with methanal (formaldehyde) yields a primary alcohol with an extended chain.
  • Reaction of a Grignard reagent with other aldehydes yields secondary alcohols.
  • Reaction of a Grignard reagent with ketones yields tertiary alcohols. All carbonyl additions require dry ether followed by dilute acid hydrolysis.
  • Carbon chain length can also be increased with KCN, which turns a haloalkane into a nitrile. The nitrile can then be hydrolysed to a carboxylic acid or reduced to an amine.

Problem Solving and Planning Reaction Schemes

You must be able to use knowledge of organic chemistry contained in the specification to solve problems, including predicting properties of unfamiliar functional groups, planning multi-step synthesis routes, selecting suitable practical procedures, and identifying appropriate control measures to reduce risk based on hazard data.

  • Predicting properties of unfamiliar compounds requires applying known chemical behaviors of familiar functional groups to novel molecular structures.
  • Planning reaction schemes of up to four steps involves recalling familiar reactions and using unfamiliar reactions given sufficient information, keeping track of functional groups, reagents, and conditions.
  • Selecting suitable practical procedures involves choosing appropriate apparatus for operations such as reflux, distillation, and separation.
  • Identifying appropriate control measures to reduce risk requires interpreting hazard data such as flammability, toxicity, and corrosiveness, ensuring safe handling of volatile or corrosive chemicals.

Core Practical 16: The Preparation of Aspirin

You must understand Core Practical 16, which covers the preparation of aspirin (2-acetyloxybenzoic acid).

  • Equation: 2-hydroxybenzoic acid + ethanoic anhydride yields 2-acetyloxybenzoic acid + ethanoic acid. A little concentrated phosphoric acid or sulfuric acid is added as a catalyst.
  • Method: Mix 2.0 g of 2-hydroxybenzoic acid with 4.0 cm3 of ethanoic anhydride and 5 drops of concentrated phosphoric acid in a pear-shaped flask. Warm the mixture on a water bath for about 10 minutes.
  • Purification: Allow to cool, then add cold water to precipitate the impure aspirin crystals. Filter under reduced pressure using a Buchner funnel. Recrystallise the crude aspirin from a minimum volume of hot ethanol-water mixture. Filter again and dry the solid.
  • Yield and Purity: Determine the melting temperature to check purity; pure aspirin melts sharply at approximately 135 °C. Calculate percentage yield using actual mass divided by theoretical mass multiplied by 100.

Preparation and Purification Techniques

You must understand specific techniques used in the preparation and purification of organic compounds.

  • Refluxing heats a reaction mixture with a vertical condenser so volatile vapours condense and drip back into the flask without escaping, allowing complete reaction without losing reactants.
  • Purification by washing, including with water and sodium carbonate solution, removes soluble impurities such as unreacted acid or acid catalysts. Sodium carbonate neutralises acidic impurities, releasing carbon dioxide gas.
  • Solvent extraction transfers a solute from one solvent to another based on differing partition coefficients, using a separating funnel to isolate the organic layer.
  • Recrystallisation purifies impure solid products by dissolving them in a minimum volume of hot solvent, hot filtering to remove insoluble impurities, cooling to recrystallise, filtering under reduced pressure, and drying.
  • Drying removes trace water from an organic liquid using an anhydrous inorganic salt such as anhydrous sodium sulfate, magnesium sulfate, or calcium chloride.
  • Distillation separates liquids with different boiling temperatures. Primary alcohol to aldehyde uses distillation with acidified dichromate(VI), so the aldehyde is removed before it oxidises further. Primary alcohol to carboxylic acid uses reflux with excess acidified dichromate(VI). Aldehyde or ketone to alcohol uses NaBH4 (or LiAlH4 for carboxylic acids and nitriles). Alkene to haloalkane uses addition of HBr. Alkene to alcohol uses steam with an acid catalyst. Nitrobenzene to phenylamine uses reduction with Sn and concentrated HCl. Nitration of benzene is the first step of a route to phenylamine.
  • Steam distillation extracts organic compounds that are immiscible with water and decompose near their normal boiling points, distilling them at a lower temperature.
  • Melting temperature determination assesses purity; a sharp melting point close to the true value indicates a pure substance, whereas a broad range starting lower indicates impurities.
  • Boiling temperature determination identifies a liquid and tests its purity by checking if it boils within a narrow, specific temperature range.

Key Interconversions and Yield Calculations

Exam tip: state the reagent, the condition (reflux, distillation, heat under pressure) and the product of each step. Marks are often given for the condition, not just the reagent.

  • Percentage yield = actual mass divided by theoretical mass multiplied by 100.
  • Overall yield for a multi-step route is the product of the individual step yields. Two steps at 80% and 70% give 0.80 multiplied by 0.70 = 0.56, or 56% overall.
  • Atom economy measures the proportion of reactant atoms that end up in the desired product: (molar mass of desired product divided by sum of molar masses of all products) multiplied by 100.

Typical Mistakes

  • Mistake: Forgetting that Grignard reagents react violently with water. Correction: Ensure all apparatus and solvents (dry ether) are strictly anhydrous.
  • Mistake: Confusing distillation and reflux conditions when converting primary alcohols. Correction: Use distillation to isolate aldehydes and reflux to make carboxylic acids.
  • Mistake: Assuming melting point ranges for impure substances are sharp. Correction: Remember that impurities lower and broaden the melting temperature range.
  • Mistake: Omitting the acid hydrolysis step after reacting a Grignard reagent with a carbonyl compound. Correction: Always include dilute acid as a second step to protonate the intermediate alkoxide.

Exam-style Questions

  1. Question: Outline a two-step synthesis of propanoic acid starting from bromoethane. Answer: Step 1: Heat bromoethane with aqueous potassium cyanide under reflux to form propannenitrile. Step 2: Heat propannenitrile under reflux with dilute hydrochloric acid followed by distillation to form propanoic acid.
  2. Question: Describe how to purify a crude solid product of aspirin. Answer: Dissolve the solid in a minimum volume of hot solvent, filter hot, cool to recrystallise, filter under reduced pressure using a Buchner funnel, and dry in a desiccator.
  3. Question: State the reagents and conditions needed to convert bromobenzene into benzoic acid using a Grignard method. Answer: React bromobenzene with magnesium in dry ether to form phenylmagnesium bromide, then react this with carbon dioxide, followed by dilute acid hydrolysis.
  4. Question: Explain why sodium carbonate solution is used during the washing stage of organic liquid purification. Answer: It neutralises any unreacted acid impurities or acidic catalysts present in the organic layer, releasing carbon dioxide gas which is vented.
  5. Question: Calculate the overall percentage yield of a three-step reaction where individual yields are 80 percent, 75 percent, and 90 percent. Answer: Multiply the decimal yields together: 0.80 multiplied by 0.75 multiplied by 0.90 equals 0.54, which is 54 percent overall yield.

Use these notes alongside active recall of reaction mechanisms and practical procedures, then practice multi-step synthesis and spectral interpretation questions next.

title: A Level Physics: Circular Motion and SHM
content:
A Level Physics: Circular Motion and SHM

Circular motion is motion at constant speed but changing velocity — because velocity is a vector, turning is accelerating. This note builds the kinematics of uniform circular motion from zero: angular displacement and angular velocity, the relation v = ωr, centripetal acceleration and the force that causes it, and then the beautiful connection to simple harmonic motion — SHM is literally the shadow of circular motion. Every formula is derived from the geometry, and the standard calculation types (car cornering, vertical circles, conical pendulums, satellite orbits) are worked in full.

Kinematics of uniform circular motion

An object moving in a circle at constant speed has a continuously changing direction, so its velocity changes continuously — it is accelerating. Two measures describe the motion:

angular displacement: theta (radians); one revolution = 2 pi rad
angular velocity: omega = theta/t = 2 pi/T = 2 pi f   (rad s-1)
linear speed: v = omega r        (m s-1)

period T = 2 pi/omega; frequency f = 1/T

The analogy: a point on a record's edge and a point near its centre complete a revolution in the same time, but the edge point travels further — hence v = ωr. Angular velocity is shared; linear speed depends on radius.

Worked example. A wheel of radius 0.30 m spins at 20 revolutions per minute. Find ω and the speed of a point on its rim.

f = 20/60 = 0.333 Hz  ->  omega = 2 pi f = 2.09 rad s-1
v = omega r = 2.09 x 0.30 = 0.63 m s-1

Centripetal acceleration

The acceleration of circular motion points toward the centre — it changes the direction of velocity, not its magnitude. From the geometry of a small angular displacement, the change in velocity points inward with magnitude v²/r:

a = v^2/r = omega^2 r        (directed toward the centre)

centripetal force: F = m a = m v^2/r = m omega^2 r

Derivation sketch worth reproducing in an exam: as the object turns through a small angle θ, the velocity triangle has a small change Δv perpendicular to v, and Δv/v = Δs/r (similar triangles), so Δv/Δt = (v/r)(Δs/Δt) = v²/r. The direction of Δv is toward the centre — hence centripetal.

Worked example. A 1200 kg car rounds a bend of radius 50 m at 15 m s⁻¹. Find the centripetal force.

F = m v^2/r = 1200 x 225/50 = 1200 x 4.5 = 5400 N
The force is provided by friction between tyres and road.

Where the centripetal force comes from

Centripetal force is not a new kind of force — it is the name for whatever real force points toward the centre:

SituationForce providing the centripetal effect
Car on a flat bendstatic friction between tyres and road
Car on a banked trackcomponent of the normal reaction
Satellite in orbitgravitational attraction
Ball on a stringtension in the string
Electron in a magnetic fieldmagnetic force (qvB)
Conical pendulumhorizontal component of tension

The exam favourite is the vertical circle: at the top of a loop, gravity and any normal force both point down and together provide mv²/r; the minimum speed to stay in contact is when the normal force falls to zero, so mg = mv²/r and v_min = √(gr).

Worked example (vertical circle). A ball on a string of length 0.80 m is swung in a vertical circle. Find the minimum speed at the top for the string to stay taut.

at the top: mg + T = mv^2/r; minimum when T = 0
v_min = sqrt(g r) = sqrt(9.81 x 0.80) = sqrt(7.85)
      = 2.8 m s-1

Worked example (banked track). A track is banked at angle θ with no friction. Show that the design speed satisfies tan θ = v²/(rg).

vertical: N cos(theta) = mg
horizontal (centripetal): N sin(theta) = mv^2/r
divide: tan(theta) = v^2/(r g)

Circular motion and SHM: the projection connection

Watch a point moving uniformly around a circle from the side: its shadow on a diameter moves back and forth with simple harmonic motion. This is not an analogy — it is an identity, and it lets you derive every SHM equation from circular motion:

if a particle moves on a circle of radius A with angular
velocity omega, its projection on a diameter has
displacement x = A cos(omega t)  (or A sin, depending on start)
velocity v = -A omega sin(omega t)
acceleration a = -omega^2 A cos(omega t) = -omega^2 x

maximum speed at the centre: v_max = A omega
maximum acceleration at the extremes: a_max = A omega^2

So the SHM angular frequency ω is exactly the angular velocity of the reference circle, and the period T = 2π/ω. The geometry also explains the phase relationships: velocity leads displacement by a quarter turn (90°), acceleration is anti-phase with displacement (180°).

Worked example. A point moves on a circle of radius 0.050 m at 3.0 rad s⁻¹. Find the amplitude, period and maximum speed of its projection.

amplitude A = 0.050 m
T = 2 pi/omega = 6.28/3.0 = 2.1 s
v_max = A omega = 0.050 x 3.0 = 0.15 m s-1

Applications: centrifuges and looping tracks

Circular motion is engineered into everyday machines. A centrifuge spins samples so that the required centripetal force — provided by the container walls — vastly exceeds gravity; denser components need a larger force at the same radius, so they settle outward and separate. The same logic sizes a washing machine's spin cycle (water leaves through the drum holes when the required force exceeds what surface tension can supply) and a car's brake discs (ventilation handles the frictional heat).

A looping track is the vertical-circle problem made physical: at the top of the loop the riders' weight and the track's normal reaction both point inward, providing mv²/r; the design speed is set just above v = √(gr) so the normal reaction never falls to zero and contact is maintained. Rollercoaster designers use the excess above that minimum to create the sensation of lightness without losing the car.

Worked examples: the standard exam types

Worked example 1 (conical pendulum). A 0.20 kg mass on a 1.0 m string moves in a horizontal circle, the string at 30° to the vertical. Find the tension and the period.

vertical: T cos(30) = mg  ->  T = 0.20 x 9.81/0.866 = 2.27 N
radius: r = L sin(30) = 0.50 m
horizontal: T sin(30) = m v^2/r
2.27 x 0.5 = 0.20 x v^2/0.50  ->  v^2 = 2.84  ->  v = 1.69 m s-1
T_period = 2 pi r/v = 6.28 x 0.50/1.69 = 1.86 s

Worked example 2 (satellite). Find the orbital speed of a satellite at radius 7.0 × 10⁶ m around Earth (M = 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg).

GMm/r^2 = mv^2/r  ->  v = sqrt(GM/r)
v = sqrt(6.67 x 10^-11 x 5.97 x 10^24/7.0 x 10^6)
  = sqrt(5.69 x 10^7) = 7.54 x 10^3 m s-1

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Angular velocity) A cyclist's wheel of radius 0.35 m turns at 2.0 revolutions per second. Find the speed of the rim. Answer: ω = 2π × 2.0 = 12.6 rad s⁻¹; v = ωr = 12.6 × 0.35 = 4.4 m s⁻¹.
  2. (Acceleration) State the direction of centripetal acceleration and explain why speed stays constant. Answer: It points toward the centre, perpendicular to the velocity; because the acceleration has no component along the velocity, it changes direction only, not speed.
  3. (Force) A 0.15 kg ball on a 0.60 m string moves at 4.0 m s⁻¹ in a horizontal circle. Find the tension. Answer: T = mv²/r = 0.15 × 16/0.60 = 4.0 N.
  4. (Vertical circle) Explain why a bucket of water can be swung overhead without spilling. Answer: At the top, the water's weight provides the centripetal force; if v ≥ √(gr) the water stays in contact with the bucket base, so it does not fall out.
  5. (Banking) A bend of radius 80 m is banked for 20 m s⁻¹. Find the angle. Answer: tan θ = v²/(rg) = 400/(80 × 9.81) = 0.510; θ = 27°.
  6. (SHM link) Explain how simple harmonic motion can be modelled by the projection of circular motion. Answer: A point moving uniformly on a circle of radius A projects onto a diameter as x = A cos ωt; differentiating gives v and a with a = −ω²x, the defining SHM condition.
  7. (Satellite) Show that the period of a satellite is proportional to r^(3/2). Answer: v = √(GM/r) and T = 2πr/v, so T = 2πr/√(GM/r) = 2π√(r³/GM), hence T ∝ r^(3/2).
  8. (Misconception) A student says a car turning at constant speed has no acceleration. Correct the statement. Answer: Velocity is a vector; its direction changes continuously in a turn, so the car accelerates centripetally toward the centre of the turn even though the speedometer reading is constant.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • The centrifugal fiction: there is no outward force in the inertial frame; the "centrifugal force" felt in a turning car is the inertia of your body, not a force on the car. Never put it on a free-body diagram.
  • v²/r with the wrong r: radius from the centre of the circular path — for a conical pendulum r = L sin θ, not the string length.
  • ω versus v: v = ωr; forgetting the radius converts angular to linear incorrectly. And ω in rad s⁻¹ means revolutions per second × 2π.
  • Units of angle: radians, not degrees, in ω = 2π/T and in the projection equations.
  • Centripetal force is not extra: it is the resultant of the real forces (tension, friction, weight component) — do not add it alongside them.
  • Vertical circles: tension and weight are collinear at top and bottom but not at the sides; resolve properly rather than assuming T = mv²/r everywhere.
  • Period direction: T = 2πr/v uses the circumference; mixing in angular velocity without converting gives factor-of-2π errors.
  • SHM phase: the projection can be sine or cosine depending on the starting point; state your choice and stay consistent.
  • Precision: 2 or 3 s.f. with units (rad s⁻¹, m s⁻¹, N, s); keep π symbolic until the end to avoid rounding drift.

title: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Sets and Venn Diagrams
content:
Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Sets and Venn Diagrams

Set notation is the language of sorting: it describes which elements belong together, which belong to both groups, and which belong to neither. The IGCSE questions are almost always Venn-diagram problems in disguise — a survey of students, a group of numbers, a club membership — and the marks come from filling every region correctly. This note builds the topic from zero: the notation and symbols, the two-set and three-set Venn diagrams and how to shade them, the counting formulas, and the word-problem method that never misses a region.

Set notation and vocabulary

SymbolMeaningExample
∈is an element of3 ∈ {1, 2, 3}
∉is not an element of5 ∉ {1, 2, 3}
ξ (or U)the universal set — everything under discussionξ = {1, 2, ..., 12}
∅the empty setodd multiples of 2 = ∅
A′the complement of A — everything in ξ not in AA′ = ξ A
A ∪ Bunion — in A or B or both{1,2} ∪ {2,3} = {1,2,3}
A ∩ Bintersection — in both{1,2} ∩ {2,3} = {2}
n(A)the number of elements of An({2, 4, 6}) = 3

Two rules follow directly: A ∩ A′ = ∅ (nothing is both in and out), and A ∪ A′ = ξ (everything is one or the other). Subsets: A ⊂ B means every element of A is also in B. The empty set has no elements, so n(∅) = 0, and it is a subset of every set — a fact worth stating explicitly when a question asks whether ∅ ⊂ A is true.

Two-set Venn diagrams

A two-set diagram divides the universal set into four regions: only A, only B, both, and neither. Filling them from the inside out is the reliable method:

  1. Write the number in the intersection (both) first.
  2. Work outward: only A = n(A) − both; only B = n(B) − both.
  3. Neither = total − (only A + only B + both).

Worked example. In a class of 32, 18 study French, 15 study Spanish, and 7 study both. Find the number studying only French, only Spanish, and neither.

both = 7
only French = 18 - 7 = 11
only Spanish = 15 - 7 = 8
neither = 32 - (11 + 8 + 7) = 32 - 26 = 6

Worked example 2 (reverse). In a group, 20 like tea, 14 like coffee and 5 like neither. Everyone likes at least one of the two? Then find n(tea ∩ coffee).

n(T union C) = 20 + 14 - both
total = 20 + 14 - both + 5 = 39 - both
If the group has 30 people: 30 = 39 - both → both = 9

The inclusion–exclusion formula

n(A union B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A intersection B)

for three sets:
n(A u B u C) = n(A) + n(B) + n(C)
             - n(A n B) - n(A n C) - n(B n C)
             + n(A n B n C)

The subtraction corrects double counting; the final addition corrects the triple-counted centre. Knowing the formula lets you answer "how many in total" questions without a full diagram, but a diagram is still the safer route for word problems.

Worked example. A survey of 50 people: 30 read newspapers, 25 read magazines, 12 read both. How many read at least one?

n(N union M) = 30 + 25 - 12 = 43
neither = 50 - 43 = 7

Three-set Venn diagrams

The three-set diagram has eight regions (counting "none of the three"). The fill order that never fails:

  1. Start with the triple intersection (all three).
  2. Find the "exactly two" regions by subtracting the triple from each pair.
  3. Find the "only one" regions by subtracting the pair and triple totals from each set total.
  4. Find "none" from the grand total.

Worked example. 40 students choose subjects: 20 take Maths, 18 take Physics, 15 take Chemistry; 8 take Maths and Physics, 6 take Maths and Chemistry, 5 take Physics and Chemistry; 3 take all three. Find how many take exactly one subject and how many take none.

triple = 3
exactly M and P = 8 - 3 = 5
exactly M and C = 6 - 3 = 3
exactly P and C = 5 - 3 = 2
only M = 20 - (5 + 3 + 3) = 9
only P = 18 - (5 + 2 + 3) = 8
only C = 15 - (3 + 2 + 3) = 7
exactly one = 9 + 8 + 7 = 24
total counted = 24 + 5 + 3 + 2 + 3 = 37
none = 40 - 37 = 3

Sets of numbers and shading

Questions often use number sets inside the universal set: ξ = {1, 2, ..., 20}, A = multiples of 3, B = multiples of 4. List them, then use the same four regions:

A = {3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18}
B = {4, 8, 12, 16, 20}
A n B = {12}
A u B = {3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 12, 15, 16, 18, 20}
neither = {1, 2, 5, 7, 10, 11, 13, 14, 17, 19}

Shading questions ask for a region described in symbols. Translate the symbols into words first: A′ ∩ B means "not in A, but in B" — the part of B outside A. A ∪ B′ means "in A, or outside B" — everything except the part of B that is not in A.

Listing sets and set-builder notation

Sets can be written in three ways, and questions move between them. The roster method lists the elements: A = {2, 4, 6, 8}. The description method states the rule in words: A is the set of even numbers from 2 to 8. Set-builder notation states the rule symbolically: A = {x : x is an even number, 2 ≤ x ≤ 8} — read as "the set of all x such that x is even and between 2 and 8".

  • Roster for finite sets: list every element once, in braces, separated by commas; order does not matter and repeats are not counted twice.
  • Description for patterns: "multiples of 3 less than 30" is clearer than listing ten numbers.
  • Set-builder for precision: the colon means "such that"; the condition after it does the work.

Worked example. Write the set of odd numbers between 1 and 11 in roster and set-builder form, and find its size.

roster: {3, 5, 7, 9}  (strictly between, so 1 and 11 excluded)
set-builder: {x : x odd, 1 < x < 11}
n(A) = 4

Reading the inequalities is the trap: "between" usually excludes the endpoints, "from ... to ..." usually includes them, and the question's wording decides. When in doubt, list both interpretations and choose the one consistent with the other numbers in the question.

Worked examples: word problems

Worked example. In a hostel of 60 students, 35 play football, 28 play basketball, and 12 play both. How many play neither?

at least one = 35 + 28 - 12 = 51
neither = 60 - 51 = 9

Worked example 2 (with a variable). In a group of 25, x people like both tea and coffee, 12 like tea only and 8 like coffee only. Find x if everyone likes at least one.

12 + 8 + x = 25  →  x = 5

Worked example 3 (conditional language). Of 40 students, 24 study History, 18 study Geography and 6 study neither. How many study both?

at least one = 40 - 6 = 34
34 = 24 + 18 - both  →  both = 42 - 34 = 8

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Notation) ξ = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8}; A = {2, 4, 6, 8}; B = {1, 3, 5, 7}. Find A ∩ B and A ∪ B. Answer: A ∩ B = ∅; A ∪ B = ξ.
  2. (Complement) With A = {2, 4, 6, 8} in ξ above, list A′. Answer: {1, 3, 5, 7}.
  3. (Two sets) n(A) = 14, n(B) = 9, n(A ∩ B) = 4. Find n(A ∪ B). Answer: 14 + 9 − 4 = 19.
  4. (Neither) In a class of 30, 17 like cricket, 12 like tennis and 5 like both. Find the number who like neither. Answer: at least one = 24; neither = 6.
  5. (Three sets) 30 students: 15 like Maths, 12 like Physics, 10 like Chemistry; 5 like Maths and Physics, 4 like Maths and Chemistry, 3 like Physics and Chemistry, 2 like all three. Find the number who like exactly one. Answer: only M = 15 − (3 + 2 + 2) = 8; only P = 12 − (3 + 1 + 2) = 6; only C = 10 − (2 + 1 + 2) = 5; total = 19 (with exactly-two counts 3, 2, 1 and triple 2).
  6. (Shading) Describe the region A′ ∩ B in words. Answer: Elements in B but not in A — the part of B outside A.
  7. (Numbers) ξ = {1, ..., 20}; A = even numbers; B = multiples of 5. Find n(A ∩ B). Answer: multiples of 10 in the set = {10, 20}, so 2.
  8. (Reasoning) Explain why n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) is wrong when A and B overlap. Answer: The elements in both sets are counted twice in n(A) + n(B), so the intersection must be subtracted once: n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B).

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Filling the intersection last: start at the centre. Adding both set totals and forgetting the overlap counts shared elements twice.
  • Forgetting the "neither" region: the universal set includes elements outside all named sets; if the question gives a total, subtract to find them.
  • Confusing ∪ and ∩: union is "or" (everything), intersection is "and" (only the middle). A quick mnemonic: ∪ looks like a cup that holds everything.
  • Shading the wrong side for A′: the complement is everything outside A, including parts of other sets and the region outside them all.
  • Triple intersection double subtraction: when subtracting pairs, remember each pair already includes the triple; subtract the triple from each pair before using them.
  • Reading "only": "only A" means A and nothing else — exclude the overlaps. The word only is a region instruction, not decoration.
  • Notation in answers: list elements with braces and commas; do not write 1, 2, 3 as an unbraced list when the answer is a set.
  • Assuming everyone likes something: unless stated, some may be outside both sets — check whether the total equals the sum of the regions.

title: Exam technique: Hardware & Architecture
content:
### What earns the marks
To earn full marks on this topic, students need to demonstrate a clear understanding of the concepts. For 3.1, explain the von Neumann model and the FDE cycle, showing how instructions are stored as data. For 3.2, describe input and output devices, and for 3.3, compare different storage types, justifying their use cases. Command words like explain, describe, and justify require working and a reason to be shown.
### Traps
Common mistakes include confusing the roles of the PC and MAR registers, and not understanding the difference between RAM and ROM. Another error is not considering the effects of performance factors like clock speed and cache size. Correction: review the FDE cycle and the characteristics of each storage type.
### Memory hooks
To remember the FDE cycle, use the mnemonic Fetch-Decode-Execute. For the types of buses, think address-data-control. To compare storage types, consider the acronym CAPD: capacity, access time, portability, and durability. Finally, to sanity-check an answer, ask whether it aligns with the stored program concept.
### Timing
This topic typically accounts for 20-30% of the paper, so budget around 30-40 minutes for it. Make sure to leave time to review and check your work.
