title: Exam technique: Fractions, Decimals and Percentages
content:
### What earns the marks
For percentages of amounts, the 10-percent building blocks shown earn method marks without a calculator. For reverse percentages, state what the given amount represents (64 dollars = 80 percent) before dividing: that line earns the mark. For compound interest, each year on its own line earns credit. For Steel-type growth and decay, the multiplier (1/2 cubed) stated earns the method mark.
### Traps
Error: adding 20 percent to the sale price for the original. Correction: the sale price is the base of nothing; divide by 0.8. Error: simple interest applied twice for compound growth. Correction: grow each year from the new total. Error: decimal-point slips in 3/8 to percent. Correction: decimal first (0.375), then times 100.
### Worked example
Find 35% of 240: 0.35 × 240 = 84. A value increases by 20% to reach 180. The original is 180 ÷ 1.2 = 150, because you divide by the multiplier rather than taking 20% of 180. Check: 150 × 1.2 = 180. For fractions, 3/4 + 2/5 = 15/20 + 8/20 = 23/20 = 1 3/20.
### Check yourself
A price falls from £80 to £68. Find the percentage decrease. The decrease is £12, so the percentage is 12/80 × 100 = 15%. Show the divisor is the original price and not the new one.

### Worked example
Find 35% of 240: 0.35 × 240 = 84. A value increases by 20% to reach 180. The original is 180 ÷ 1.2 = 150, because you divide by the multiplier rather than taking 20% of 180. Check: 150 × 1.2 = 180. For fractions, 3/4 + 2/5 = 15/20 + 8/20 = 23/20 = 1 3/20.

title: A Level Physics: Motion in a Circle and Gravity
content:
A Level Physics: Motion in a Circle and Gravity

Gravity is the weakest of the four fundamental forces and yet it shapes galaxies — because it never cancels: mass has only one sign, so every particle attracts every other. This note builds the gravitational toolkit from zero: the field concept and field lines, Newton's law of gravitation, field strength and potential for a point mass, and then the applications that fill the papers — satellite orbits, escape velocity and the energy bookkeeping of lifting a mass to infinity. Every formula is derived from the inverse-square law, and every calculation type is worked in full.

The gravitational field

A gravitational field is a region in which a mass experiences a force. Field lines point toward the mass creating the field (gravity is always attractive), and their density shows strength — close to a planet the lines are dense (strong field), far away they are sparse. Two field shapes are examinable:

  • Radial field: around a point mass or a spherical planet outside its surface; strength falls with distance.
  • Uniform field: near a planet's surface over small height changes; strength g is effectively constant (the approximation behind mgh).

Newton's law of gravitation

F = G M m / r^2

G = 6.67 x 10-11 N m2 kg-2 (gravitational constant)
M, m = the two masses (kg)
r = separation between their centres (m)

The analogy that makes the law intuitive: the force weakens like light spreading from a lamp — doubling the distance spreads the same influence over four times the area, so the force quarters. The law is universal: the same G applies to an apple and the Earth as to two galaxies.

Worked example. Find the gravitational force between two 1000 kg masses 2.0 m apart.

F = G M m/r^2 = 6.67 x 10^-11 x 1000 x 1000/4.0
  = 6.67 x 10^-5/4.0 = 1.7 x 10^-5 N

Note how tiny it is — gravity only matters when one mass is astronomical, which is why the electric force dominates at particle scales.

Gravitational field strength

Field strength g is force per unit mass (N kg⁻¹), and for a point mass or a spherical body:

g = G M / r^2

at a planet's surface: g = G M / R^2  (R = planet radius)
variation with height: g falls as 1/r^2 from the centre

Worked example. Find g at the surface of Mars (M = 6.4 × 10²³ kg, R = 3.4 × 10⁶ m).

g = G M/R^2 = 6.67 x 10^-11 x 6.4 x 10^23/(3.4 x 10^6)^2
  = 4.27 x 10^13/1.156 x 10^13 = 3.7 N kg-1

Worked example 2 (height). At what height above Earth's surface does g fall to half its surface value? (R = 6.4 × 10⁶ m.)

g_surface = GM/R^2; half -> GM/r^2 = (1/2) GM/R^2
r^2 = 2 R^2 -> r = R sqrt(2) = 9.05 x 10^6 m
height = r - R = 2.65 x 10^6 m  (about 2650 km)

Gravitational potential

Potential is the work done per unit mass in bringing a mass from infinity to that point (zero at infinity by definition). Because gravity attracts, the work is done by the field on the way in, so potential is negative everywhere:

V = - G M / r        (J kg-1)

potential energy of a mass m: U = m V = - G M m / r
work to move between potentials: W = m (V2 - V1)

The negative sign is not a detail — it is the physical statement that masses are bound. The potential well around a planet is a dip; escape means climbing out of it to V = 0 at infinity.

Worked example. Find the potential at Earth's surface (M = 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg, R = 6.37 × 10⁶ m).

V = -GM/R = -(6.67 x 10^-11 x 5.97 x 10^24)/6.37 x 10^6
  = -3.98 x 10^14/6.37 x 10^6 = -6.25 x 10^7 J kg-1

Escape velocity

To escape a planet's gravity, a body needs enough kinetic energy to climb from the surface potential to zero:

(1/2) m v^2 = G M m / R  ->  v_escape = sqrt(2 G M / R)

Earth: v = sqrt(2 x 6.67 x 10^-11 x 5.97 x 10^24/6.37 x 10^6)
     = sqrt(1.25 x 10^8) = 1.12 x 10^4 m s-1 = 11.2 km s-1

The derivation is worth learning as a pattern: set kinetic energy equal to the depth of the potential well, cancel m, solve for v. Escape speed is independent of the escaping body's mass — a rocket and a molecule need the same speed (though not the same fuel).

The potential well picture explains the sign conventions in one image: near a planet the potential is deeply negative (the bottom of a dip), and moving outward means climbing toward zero. A body with total energy (kinetic plus potential) below zero is bound — it will fall back; a body with total energy at or above zero can coast to infinity. That single inequality, kinetic energy compared with the depth of the well, decides every escape and orbit question, and it is the most reliable way to check an answer's sign and size.

Orbits

A satellite in a circular orbit has gravity as its centripetal force:

G M m / r^2 = m v^2 / r   ->   v = sqrt(G M / r)

period: T = 2 pi r / v = 2 pi sqrt(r^3/(G M))
(Kepler's third law: T^2 proportional to r^3)

The counter-intuitive exam favourite: a lower orbit means a faster satellite. Since v = √(GM/r), smaller r gives larger v and shorter periods — which is why the International Space Station orbits in about 90 minutes while the Moon takes 27 days.

Worked example. Find the speed and period of a satellite 400 km above Earth's surface.

r = 6.37 x 10^6 + 4.0 x 10^5 = 6.77 x 10^6 m
v = sqrt(GM/r) = sqrt(6.67 x 10^-11 x 5.97 x 10^24/6.77 x 10^6)
  = sqrt(5.88 x 10^7) = 7.67 x 10^3 m s-1
T = 2 pi r/v = 2 x 3.14 x 6.77 x 10^6/7.67 x 10^3
  = 4.25 x 10^7/7.67 x 10^3 = 5.5 x 10^3 s  (about 92 minutes)

Geostationary orbits are the applied case: r ≈ 4.2 × 10⁷ m gives T = 24 hours, the satellite sits above one point on the equator, and it must orbit west-to-east in the equatorial plane.

Worked examples: combined gravity problems

Worked example. Compare the gravitational potential energy of a 500 kg satellite at 400 km altitude with its value at infinity, and find the energy needed to escape from that orbit.

r = 6.77 x 10^6 m
U_orbit = -GMm/r = -(6.67 x 10^-11 x 5.97 x 10^24 x 500)/6.77 x 10^6
        = -1.99 x 10^17/6.77 x 10^6 = -2.94 x 10^10 J
U_infinity = 0
energy to escape = 0 - (-2.94 x 10^10) = 2.9 x 10^10 J

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Law) State Newton's law of gravitation. Answer: The gravitational force between two point masses is proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centres: F = GMm/r².
  2. (Field strength) Define gravitational field strength. Answer: The force per unit mass on a small test mass at that point, g = F/m, measured in N kg⁻¹.
  3. (Inverse square) State how g changes when the distance from a planet's centre is tripled. Answer: g = GM/r², so tripling r divides g by 9.
  4. (Potential) Explain why gravitational potential is negative. Answer: Potential is defined as zero at infinity; gravity attracts, so the field does work on a mass brought in from infinity, meaning its potential energy — and therefore potential — decreases below zero.
  5. (Escape) Calculate the escape velocity from the Moon (M = 7.35 × 10²² kg, R = 1.74 × 10⁶ m). Answer: v = √(2GM/R) = √(2 × 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 7.35 × 10²²/1.74 × 10⁶) = √(5.63 × 10⁶) = 2.37 × 10³ m s⁻¹ ≈ 2.4 km s⁻¹.
  6. (Orbit) Explain why a satellite in a lower orbit moves faster. Answer: Gravity provides the centripetal force: GMm/r² = mv²/r, so v = √(GM/r); a smaller r gives a larger speed and a shorter period.
  7. (Geostationary) State two conditions for a geostationary orbit. Answer: The period must be 24 hours, the orbit must be equatorial and the satellite must orbit in the same direction as Earth's rotation (west to east) — all three are usually wanted.
  8. (Energy) Explain why the energy needed to move a satellite from a low orbit to a higher one is not simply mgh. Answer: Over large distances g is not constant; the correct treatment uses the change in gravitational potential energy, U = −GMm/r, evaluated at both radii.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • r measured from the centre: the separation is centre-to-centre, so a satellite's r includes the planet's radius. Using altitude alone underestimates r and inflates g and v.
  • Mass cancellation: in orbital and escape calculations m cancels — do not carry a satellite's mass through and then wonder why the answer is huge.
  • Negative potentials: V and U are negative; a "larger" potential energy at a higher orbit is less negative, not more. Work done = m(V₂ − V₁), keeping the signs.
  • g versus G: g = GM/r² is field strength (N kg⁻¹); G is the universal constant (N m² kg⁻²). Confusing the symbols loses marks and factors of mass.
  • Surface approximation: mgh applies only for small heights; over planetary distances use the potential formula.
  • Orbit direction: geostationary requires equatorial, west-to-east, 24 hours — a polar orbit is not geostationary however high it is.
  • Units of G and distances: G in N m² kg⁻², masses in kg, distances in metres — km into m, and planet masses given in scientific notation handled carefully.
  • Precision: 2 or 3 s.f. with units; the data sheet supplies G, Earth's mass and radius — quote them rather than relying on memory.
  • Method marks: write F = GMm/r² or v = √(GM/r) before substituting; formulae earn credit independently of arithmetic.

title: IGCSE Chemistry (OxfordAQA): Structure, Bonding and the Properties of Matter
content:
Structure, Bonding and the Properties of Matter

This is the topic where chemistry stops being a list of facts and becomes an explanation. Once you can say what holds the particles together in a substance, you can predict its melting point, whether it conducts electricity, whether it dissolves and why it behaves differently from something that looks similar. The OxfordAQA 9202 specification divides the topic into four parts — chemical bonds (ionic, covalent and metallic), the link between bonding and properties, the structures of carbon, and nanoparticles — and the exam regularly asks you to explain a property by naming the bond and the force that has to be overcome. This note covers all four statements, with the explanations phrased the way the mark scheme expects.

1. Why atoms bond at all

Atoms bond because the arrangement of a full outer shell is more stable than the arrangement they start with. There are three routes to it, and they lead to three different kinds of structure:

  • Electron transfer — a metal loses electrons and a non-metal gains them, producing oppositely charged ions held by electrostatic attraction: ionic bonding.
  • Electron sharing — two non-metals share pairs of electrons, producing molecules or a giant network: covalent bonding.
  • Delocalisation — metal atoms release their outer electrons into a shared "sea" while the positive ions stay in a lattice: metallic bonding.

The structure that results is at least as important as the bond. Sodium chloride and hydrogen chloride both contain strong bonds, but one is a giant lattice with a melting point of 801 °C and the other is a simple molecule that is a gas at room temperature. The difference is the structure, not the strength of the bond inside it.

2. Ionic bonding

An ionic bond is the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions. In sodium chloride, sodium (2,8,1) loses one electron to become Na⁺ with the arrangement 2,8, and chlorine (2,8,7) gains one to become Cl⁻ with 2,8,8. The ions are arranged in a regular giant ionic lattice in which each ion is surrounded by ions of the opposite charge, and the formula NaCl records the ratio of ions rather than a molecule — there is no such thing as one "NaCl particle".

The charge on the formula comes from balancing the ions: Mg²⁺ with Cl⁻ needs two chloride ions, so magnesium chloride is MgCl₂; Al³⁺ with O²⁻ needs two aluminium ions and three oxide ions, so aluminium oxide is Al₂O₃; Ca²⁺ with PO₄³⁻ needs three calcium ions and two phosphate ions, so calcium phosphate is Ca₃(PO₄)₂.

Three properties follow directly from a giant lattice of strong attractions:

  • High melting and boiling points, because melting means breaking many strong electrostatic attractions, not just the bond between one pair of ions.
  • Conducts electricity when molten or dissolved, but not when solid, because the ions are fixed in place in the solid lattice and only become free to move when the lattice is broken.
  • Brittle, because shifting one layer brings ions of the same charge alongside each other, and the repulsion splits the crystal.

3. Covalent bonding

A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons between two non-metal atoms, and each atom contributes one electron to the pair. In a water molecule the oxygen atom shares two pairs, one with each hydrogen atom; in carbon dioxide the carbon shares two pairs with each oxygen; in nitrogen the two atoms share three pairs. The atoms are held together strongly inside the molecule, but the molecules themselves are held to each other only by weak intermolecular forces.

That distinction explains the properties of simple molecular substances:

  • Low melting and boiling points, because only the weak forces between molecules have to be overcome, not the covalent bonds inside them. Iodine, carbon dioxide and water are all examples.
  • Never conduct electricity, because there are no ions and no free electrons — the molecules are neutral and the electrons are locked into bonds.
  • Often insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents, because a molecule that is not charged has nothing to attract it to water molecules.

4. Metallic bonding

In a metal the outer electrons are not attached to any one atom. Metal atoms are packed in a regular lattice, and their outer electrons form a sea of delocalised electrons that is shared across the whole structure. The bonding is the attraction between the positive ions and this sea of negative electrons.

The properties of metals follow from it: they conduct electricity because the delocalised electrons can move through the structure and carry charge; they conduct heat because those electrons carry kinetic energy; they are malleable and ductile because the layers of ions can slide over one another without breaking the attraction to the electron sea; and their melting points are generally high, but vary a great deal — mercury is a liquid at room temperature while tungsten melts near 3,400 °C, because the strength of the attraction depends on the size of the ion and the number of electrons contributed.

5. Giant covalent structures and the many faces of carbon

Carbon is the clearest example of the rule that structure decides properties, because the same element appears in four very different forms:

  • Diamond — each carbon atom is covalently bonded to four others in a rigid three-dimensional network, so diamond is the hardest natural substance, has a very high melting point, and does not conduct electricity because there are no free electrons.
  • Graphite — each carbon atom is bonded to three others in flat layers of hexagons, with the fourth electron delocalised between the layers. The weak forces between layers let them slide, which is why graphite is soft and is used as a lubricant and in pencils; the delocalised electrons make graphite a conductor.
  • Graphene — a single layer one atom thick taken from graphite, extremely strong and an excellent conductor, which is why it is used in composites and electronics.
  • Fullerenes — closed cage structures of carbon such as C₆₀, a football-shaped molecule of 60 atoms. Their hollow shape has been used to deliver drugs and as catalysts, and carbon nanotubes are related structures with very high strength.

Silicon dioxide, the main component of sand, is a giant covalent structure like diamond and shares diamond's hardness and high melting point. That is why sand does not melt in a Bunsen flame.

6. Comparing the four structures

StructureParticles and attractionMelting pointConducts?Example
Giant ionic latticeIons held by strong electrostatic attractionHighOnly when molten or dissolvedSodium chloride
Simple molecularMolecules held by weak intermolecular forcesLowNoCarbon dioxide
Giant covalentAtoms held by many strong covalent bondsVery highOnly graphite and grapheneDiamond, sand
MetallicPositive ions in a sea of delocalised electronsVaries, generally highYesCopper

An exam answer that names the structure and the attraction it must overcome can explain almost any property question, and it works for substances you have never seen.

7. Nanoparticles

A nanoparticle is a particle with at least one dimension between about 1 and 100 nanometres. A nanometre is 10⁻⁹ m, so a nanoparticle is roughly a thousand times smaller than a red blood cell. Because they are so small, a given mass of nanoparticles has an enormous surface area compared with the same mass of a bulk material, and most of their atoms are on the surface rather than buried inside.

surface area : volume = 6a² ÷ a³ = 6 ÷ a → Key: a = side length of the particle (m); the ratio has units of 1/m. The relation shows the point: as a falls, the ratio rises, so a 10 nm cube exposes six times the relative surface of a 60 nm cube.

  • Uses: catalysts (a larger surface area means more collisions per second), sunscreens that block ultraviolet light while appearing transparent, silver nanoparticles as antibacterial coatings, and drug delivery in medicine.
  • Risks: their small size lets them enter the body more easily than bulk materials, and their long-term effect on health and the environment is not yet fully understood.

8. Worked examples

Worked example 1 — why molten sodium chloride conducts but the solid does not. In the solid the ions are held in fixed positions by the lattice, so there is no movement of charge; when molten the lattice is broken and the ions are free to move to the electrodes, so the melt conducts. The answer needs both halves: "ions free to move" and "only when molten".

Worked example 2 — formula from the ions. Aluminium forms Al³⁺ and oxygen forms O²⁻. The lowest common multiple of the charges is 6, so two Al³⁺ give +6 and three O²⁻ give −6, and the formula is Al₂O₃. Always check the charges add to zero before writing it down.

Worked example 3 — why graphite conducts but diamond does not. In graphite each carbon is bonded to three others, leaving one delocalised electron per atom that can move along the layer; in diamond all four outer electrons are used in bonds, so there is no free electron and no conduction. Naming the electron is the mark.

Worked example 4 — surface area to volume. For a cube of side 10 nm, surface area : volume = 6 ÷ a = 6 ÷ 10 = 0.6 nm⁻¹; for a cube of side 60 nm it is 6 ÷ 60 = 0.1 nm⁻¹. The small particle is six times greater in relative surface, which is why it is the better catalyst.

9. Exam-style questions

  1. Explain why magnesium oxide has a much higher melting point than hydrogen chloride. Answer: magnesium oxide is a giant ionic lattice, so melting needs many strong electrostatic attractions broken; hydrogen chloride is a simple molecular substance, so melting only needs the weak intermolecular forces overcome, not the covalent bonds.
  2. Explain why a crystal of sodium chloride shatters when struck. Answer: the layers shift so that ions of like charge are alongside each other; the resulting repulsion splits the lattice, which is why ionic crystals are brittle.
  3. Deduce the formula of calcium phosphate, given Ca²⁺ and PO₄³⁻. Answer: lowest common multiple of 2 and 3 is 6, so 3 × Ca²⁺ = +6 and 2 × PO₄³⁻ = −6; formula = Ca₃(PO₄)₂.
  4. Describe how the structure of graphite allows it to act as a lubricant and as a conductor. Answer: graphite has layers of hexagons held together by weak forces, so the layers slide over one another and it is slippery; each carbon has one delocalised electron, so charge can pass along the layers.
  5. Explain why a nanoparticle catalyst is more effective than the same mass of the bulk metal. Answer: surface area : volume = 6 ÷ a, so the smaller particle has a much larger surface area for the same mass; reactants collide with the exposed surface, so more collisions happen per second and the rate increases.
  6. State two properties of simple molecular substances and explain them in terms of their structure. Answer: low melting point, because only the weak intermolecular forces are overcome on melting; no electrical conductivity, because the molecules are neutral and there are no free electrons or ions.

10. Common mistakes

  • Saying that covalent bonds break when a simple molecular substance melts. They do not — the molecules separate intact; only the intermolecular forces are overcome.
  • Writing "graphite has free electrons" without saying where they come from: it is the fourth electron per carbon atom that is not used in a bond.
  • Explaining conductivity of solid sodium chloride. The ions exist, but they are not free to move until the lattice is molten or dissolved.
  • Treating the formula of an ionic compound as a molecule. NaCl is a ratio of ions in a lattice.
  • Confusing nano with micro. A nanoparticle is 1 to 100 nm, so it is far smaller than a microscope can resolve.
  • Answering "it has strong bonds" without naming the type. The mark is for naming the bond or the force that is overcome.

11. Exam technique for this topic

  • Every "explain the property" answer takes the same three steps: name the structure, name the attraction, say how much energy is needed to overcome it.
  • For conduction, always say whether ions or electrons are moving, and whether they can move in that state.
  • For a formula from ions, write the charges first, find the lowest common multiple, then the ratio — that is a mark scheme's own working.
  • Compare questions need a comparison word: "higher", "stronger", "more energy", not just a description of each substance.
  • If the question names an unfamiliar substance, decide whether it is ionic, simple molecular, giant covalent or metallic first; the property answer follows from that choice.

title: A Level Physics: Motion in a Circle and Gravity
content:
A Level Physics: Motion in a Circle and Gravity

F = G M m/r² = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ x 10⁰⁰ × 10⁰⁰/4.0
  = 6.67 × 10⁻⁵/4.0 = 1.7 × 10⁻⁵ N
