Field strength g is force per unit mass (N kg⁻¹), and for a point mass or a spherical body:

g = G M / r²

at a planet's surface: g = G M / R²  (R = planet radius)
variation with height: g falls as 1/r² from the centre

Worked example. Find g at the surface of Mars (M = 6.4 × 10²³ kg, R = 3.4 × 10⁶ m).

g = G M/R² = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ x 6.4 × 10²³/(3.4 × 10⁶)²
  = 4.27 × 10¹³/1.156 × 10¹³ = 3.7 N kg⁻¹

Worked example 2 (height). At what height above Earth's surface does g fall to half its surface value? (R = 6.4 × 10⁶ m.)

g_surface = GM/R²; half → GM/r² = (1/2) GM/R²
r² = 2 R² → r = R √(2) = 9.05 × 10⁶ m
height = r - R = 2.65 × 10⁶ m  (about 2650 km)

Gravitational potential

Potential is the work done per unit mass in bringing a mass from infinity to that point (zero at infinity by definition). Because gravity attracts, the work is done by the field on the way in, so potential is negative everywhere:

V = - G M / r        (J kg⁻¹)

potential energy of a mass m: U = m V = - G M m / r
work to move between potentials: W = m (V² - V¹)

The negative sign is not a detail — it is the physical statement that masses are bound. The potential well around a planet is a dip; escape means climbing out of it to V = 0 at infinity.

Worked example. Find the potential at Earth's surface (M = 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg, R = 6.37 × 10⁶ m).

V = -GM/R = -(6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ x 5.97 × 10²⁴)/6.37 × 10⁶
  = -3.98 × 10¹⁴/6.37 × 10⁶ = -6.25 × 10⁷ J kg⁻¹

Escape velocity

To escape a planet's gravity, a body needs enough kinetic energy to climb from the surface potential to zero:

(1/2) m v² = G M m / R  →  v_escape = √(2 G M / R)

Earth: v = √(2 × 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ x 5.97 × 10²⁴/6.37 × 10⁶)
     = √(1.25 × 10⁸) = 1.12 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹ = 11.2 km s⁻¹

The derivation is worth learning as a pattern: set kinetic energy equal to the depth of the potential well, cancel m, solve for v. Escape speed is independent of the escaping body's mass — a rocket and a molecule need the same speed (though not the same fuel).

The potential well picture explains the sign conventions in one image: near a planet the potential is deeply negative (the bottom of a dip), and moving outward means climbing toward zero. A body with total energy (kinetic plus potential) below zero is bound — it will fall back; a body with total energy at or above zero can coast to infinity. That single inequality, kinetic energy compared with the depth of the well, decides every escape and orbit question, and it is the most reliable way to check an answer's sign and size.

Orbits

A satellite in a circular orbit has gravity as its centripetal force:

G M m / r² = m v² / r   →   v = √(G M / r)

period: T = 2 π r / v = 2 π √(r³/(G M))
(Kepler's third law: T² proportional to r³)

The counter-intuitive exam favourite: a lower orbit means a faster satellite. Since v = √(GM/r), smaller r gives larger v and shorter periods — which is why the International Space Station orbits in about 90 minutes while the Moon takes 27 days.

Worked example. Find the speed and period of a satellite 400 km above Earth's surface.

r = 6.37 × 10⁶ + 4.0 × 10⁵ = 6.77 × 10⁶ m
v = √(GM/r) = √(6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ x 5.97 × 10²⁴/6.77 × 10⁶)
  = √(5.88 × 10⁷) = 7.67 × 10³ m s⁻¹
T = 2 π r/v = 2 × 3.14 × 6.77 × 10⁶/7.67 × 10³
  = 4.25 × 10⁷/7.67 × 10³ = 5.5 × 10³ s  (about 92 minutes)

Geostationary orbits are the applied case: r ≈ 4.2 × 10⁷ m gives T = 24 hours, the satellite sits above one point on the equator, and it must orbit west-to-east in the equatorial plane.

Worked examples: combined gravity problems

Worked example. Compare the gravitational potential energy of a 500 kg satellite at 400 km altitude with its value at infinity, and find the energy needed to escape from that orbit.

r = 6.77 × 10⁶ m
U_orbit = -GMm/r = -(6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ x 5.97 × 10²⁴ x 500)/6.77 × 10⁶
        = -1.99 × 10¹⁷/6.77 × 10⁶ = -2.94 × 10¹⁰ J
U_infinity = 0
energy to escape = 0 - (-2.94 × 10¹⁰) = 2.9 × 10¹⁰ J

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Law) State Newton's law of gravitation. Answer: The gravitational force between two point masses is proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centres: F = GMm/r².
  2. (Field strength) Define gravitational field strength. Answer: The force per unit mass on a small test mass at that point, g = F/m, measured in N kg⁻¹.
  3. (Inverse square) State how g changes when the distance from a planet's centre is tripled. Answer: g = GM/r², so tripling r divides g by 9.
  4. (Potential) Explain why gravitational potential is negative. Answer: Potential is defined as zero at infinity; gravity attracts, so the field does work on a mass brought in from infinity, meaning its potential energy — and therefore potential — decreases below zero.
  5. (Escape) Calculate the escape velocity from the Moon (M = 7.35 × 10²² kg, R = 1.74 × 10⁶ m). Answer: v = √(2GM/R) = √(2 × 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 7.35 × 10²²/1.74 × 10⁶) = √(5.63 × 10⁶) = 2.37 × 10³ m s⁻¹ ≈ 2.4 km s⁻¹.
  6. (Orbit) Explain why a satellite in a lower orbit moves faster. Answer: Gravity provides the centripetal force: GMm/r² = mv²/r, so v = √(GM/r); a smaller r gives a larger speed and a shorter period.
  7. (Geostationary) State two conditions for a geostationary orbit. Answer: The period must be 24 hours, the orbit must be equatorial and the satellite must orbit in the same direction as Earth's rotation (west to east) — all three are usually wanted.
  8. (Energy) Explain why the energy needed to move a satellite from a low orbit to a higher one is not simply mgh. Answer: Over large distances g is not constant; the correct treatment uses the change in gravitational potential energy, U = −GMm/r, evaluated at both radii.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • r measured from the centre: the separation is centre-to-centre, so a satellite's r includes the planet's radius. Using altitude alone underestimates r and inflates g and v.
  • Mass cancellation: in orbital and escape calculations m cancels — do not carry a satellite's mass through and then wonder why the answer is huge.
  • Negative potentials: V and U are negative; a "larger" potential energy at a higher orbit is less negative, not more. Work done = m(V₂ − V₁), keeping the signs.
  • g versus G: g = GM/r² is field strength (N kg⁻¹); G is the universal constant (N m² kg⁻²). Confusing the symbols loses marks and factors of mass.
  • Surface approximation: mgh applies only for small heights; over planetary distances use the potential formula.
  • Orbit direction: geostationary requires equatorial, west-to-east, 24 hours — a polar orbit is not geostationary however high it is.
  • Units of G and distances: G in N m² kg⁻², masses in kg, distances in metres — km into m, and planet masses given in scientific notation handled carefully.
  • Precision: 2 or 3 s.f. with units; the data sheet supplies G, Earth's mass and radius — quote them rather than relying on memory.
  • Method marks: write F = GMm/r² or v = √(GM/r) before substituting; formulae earn credit independently of arithmetic.

title: AS Level Physics: Quantum Physics
content:
AS Level Physics: Quantum Physics

Quantum physics begins with a failure: classical physics could not explain why hot objects glow the way they do, why light sometimes knocks electrons out of metal, or why atoms emit sharp lines rather than continuous rainbows. The answers — photons, the photoelectric effect, wave–particle duality and quantised energy levels — rebuilt physics in the twentieth century. This note builds the quantum toolkit from zero: the photon model and its arithmetic, Einstein's photoelectric equation with its graphs, de Broglie's matter waves, and the energy-level picture of the atom that explains every spectrum you will meet.

Why classical physics failed

Classical theory treated light as a continuous wave and predicted that any frequency should eject electrons from a metal if you wait long enough. Experiment said otherwise: below a threshold frequency, no electrons appear however intense the light; above it, electrons appear instantly however faint the light. Similarly, classical theory predicted that hot objects should radiate infinite energy at high frequencies (the ultraviolet catastrophe) — absurd. Planck's and Einstein's fix: energy is exchanged in discrete packets, quanta, each carrying E = hf. The packet idea is the whole foundation.

Photons: energy and momentum

A photon is a quantum of electromagnetic radiation. Its energy is set by its frequency alone:

E = h f = h c / lambda

h = 6.63 x 10-34 J s  (Planck constant)
f = frequency (Hz)
c = 3.0 x 108 m s-1
lambda = wavelength (m)

Photons also carry momentum, p = h/λ — a particle property that waves do not have in classical theory, and the bridge to matter waves later.

Worked example 1. Find the energy of a photon of 500 nm light.

E = hc/lambda = (6.63 x 10-34 x 3.0 x 108)/(5.0 x 10-7)
  = 1.989 x 10-25/5.0 x 10-7 = 3.98 x 10-19 J

Worked example 2 (electronvolts). Convert to electronvolts (1 eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J) and find the photon momentum.

E = 3.98 x 10-19/1.60 x 10-19 = 2.49 eV
p = h/lambda = 6.63 x 10-34/5.0 x 10-7 = 1.33 x 10-27 kg m s-1

Exam conversions deserve care: keV and MeV appear in nuclear contexts, and the eV↔J conversion (multiply or divide by 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹) is a mark waiting to be lost.

The photoelectric effect

Light on a clean metal surface ejects electrons — but only according to rules that demand the photon model:

  • Threshold frequency f₀: below it, no emission at all, whatever the intensity. The photon's energy must exceed the metal's work function φ (the minimum energy to free an electron from the surface).
  • Instantaneity: above f₀, emission begins immediately — one photon transfers all its energy to one electron in one interaction.
  • Intensity effect: above threshold, doubling the intensity doubles the number of photons and hence the photoelectric current (more electrons per second) but does not change their maximum kinetic energy.
  • Frequency effect: raising the frequency above f₀ increases the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons linearly.

Einstein's equation ties the numbers together:

h f = phi + KE_max

phi = work function of the metal (J or eV)
KE_max = maximum kinetic energy of an emitted electron
f0 = threshold frequency: h f0 = phi

Worked example. Sodium has work function 2.3 eV. Light of wavelength 450 nm falls on it. Find whether emission occurs and the maximum kinetic energy.

photon energy: E = hc/lambda = (6.63 x 10-34 x 3.0 x 108)/(4.5 x 10-7)
               = 4.42 x 10-19 J = 2.76 eV
compare: 2.76 eV > 2.3 eV  ->  emission occurs
KE_max = 2.76 - 2.3 = 0.46 eV
       = 0.46 x 1.6 x 10-19 = 7.4 x 10-20 J

Worked example (threshold). Find the threshold wavelength for sodium (φ = 2.3 eV).

h f0 = phi -> f0 = phi/h = (2.3 x 1.6 x 10-19)/6.63 x 10-34
     = 5.55 x 1014 Hz
lambda0 = c/f0 = 3.0 x 108/5.55 x 1014 = 5.4 x 10-7 m = 540 nm

Below 540 nm (higher frequency) sodium emits; above it, nothing. Note the inverse relationship: threshold wavelength corresponds to threshold frequency.

The graphs the papers love

Two plots encode the photoelectric effect and both are examinable:

  • KEₘₐₓ against frequency: a straight line with gradient h, crossing the frequency axis at f₀ and the KE axis at −φ. The gradient is the same for every metal — the metal only moves the intercepts.
  • Stopping potential against frequency: the same shape, since eVₛ = KEₘₐₓ.
  • Current against intensity: linear above threshold (more photons, more electrons).

Worked example. A plot of KEₘₐₓ against frequency has gradient 6.5 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and crosses the axis at 5.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz. Identify Planck's constant and the work function.

gradient = h = 6.5 x 10-34 J s (close to 6.63 x 10-34,
           the difference being experimental error)
phi = h f0 = 6.5 x 10-34 x 5.0 x 1014 = 3.25 x 10-19 J
    = 2.0 eV

Wave–particle duality

The quantum world refuses the wave/particle distinction: light, treated for centuries as a wave, arrives in photon packets; electrons, treated as particles, can diffract. Electron diffraction — beams of electrons producing interference patterns when scattered by crystals — is the evidence that convinced the profession. De Broglie unified the picture: every particle of momentum p has an associated wavelength

lambda = h / p = h / (m v)

Worked example. Find the de Broglie wavelength of an electron accelerated through 100 V.

KE = eV = 1.60 x 10-19 x 100 = 1.60 x 10-17 J
KE = (1/2) m v^2 -> p = sqrt(2 m KE)
p = sqrt(2 x 9.11 x 10-31 x 1.60 x 10-17)
  = sqrt(2.915 x 10-47) = 5.40 x 10-24 kg m s-1
lambda = h/p = 6.63 x 10-34/5.40 x 10-24 = 1.23 x 10-10 m
       = 0.123 nm   (comparable to atomic spacing: electrons
         diffract through crystals)

Why electrons diffract through crystals but footballs do not: the wavelength is only noticeable when it is comparable to the gap it passes through — the same rule as diffraction for waves. A macroscopic ball has such a large momentum that its de Broglie wavelength is immeasurably small.

Energy levels in atoms and line spectra

Electrons in atoms occupy quantised energy levels — only specific energies are allowed. Transitions between them absorb or emit a photon whose energy exactly equals the level difference:

Delta E = E_upper - E_lower = h f = h c / lambda
  • Emission spectrum: an excited atom drops to a lower level and emits a photon; a hot gas produces bright lines at specific wavelengths — a line spectrum.
  • Absorption spectrum: cold gas absorbs those same wavelengths from white light, leaving dark lines at identical positions.
  • Fluorescence: a photon is absorbed (UV, say), some energy is lost as heat, and a lower-energy (visible) photon is emitted — which is why white shirts glow blue under UV light.

The energy-level diagram is the standard question: a vertical scale in eV or J, arrows drawn downward for emission and upward for absorption, each arrow labelled with its transition energy.

Worked example 1. A hydrogen electron falls from level −0.54 eV to −1.51 eV. Find the photon's wavelength.

Delta E = -0.54 - (-1.51) = 0.97 eV
in joules: 0.97 x 1.60 x 10-19 = 1.552 x 10-19 J
lambda = hc/Delta E = (6.63 x 10-34 x 3.0 x 108)/1.552 x 10-19
       = 1.28 x 10-6 m = 1280 nm  (infrared)

Worked example 2. Explain why the spectral lines of an element are sharp rather than continuous.

Electrons occupy quantised levels, so only specific differences
Delta E exist between them; only photons with energy exactly equal
to a difference are emitted or absorbed; since f = Delta E/h, only
specific frequencies appear - sharp lines, not a continuum.

Worked examples: combined quantum calculations

Worked example. A metal has threshold frequency 7.5 × 10¹⁴ Hz. Light of wavelength 300 nm shines on it. Find the work function and the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons.

phi = h f0 = 6.63 x 10-34 x 7.5 x 1014 = 4.97 x 10-19 J
    = 3.1 eV
photon energy: E = hc/lambda = (6.63 x 10-34 x 3.0 x 108)/(3.0 x 10-7)
               = 6.63 x 10-19 J = 4.14 eV
KE_max = E - phi = 6.63 x 10-19 - 4.97 x 10-19 = 1.66 x 10-19 J
       = 1.04 eV

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Photon energy) Calculate the energy of a photon of frequency 5.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz. Answer: E = hf = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 5.0 × 10¹⁴ = 3.3 × 10⁻¹⁹ J (≈ 2.1 eV).
  2. (Photoelectric rules) Explain why red light cannot eject electrons from a given metal however intense it is, while faint blue light can. Answer: Emission requires individual photons above the threshold frequency f₀; red photons have lower frequency and energy below the work function, so no single red photon can free an electron regardless of photon number; blue photons exceed the energy requirement, so each can eject an electron on its own.
  3. (Graph reading) State what the gradient and x-intercept of a KEₘₐₓ against frequency graph represent. Answer: The gradient is Planck's constant h; the x-intercept is the threshold frequency f₀.
  4. (Intensity) The intensity of light above the threshold frequency is doubled. State the effect on (a) the photoelectric current, (b) the maximum kinetic energy. Answer: (a) The current doubles — twice the photons, twice the electrons. (b) The maximum kinetic energy is unchanged — it depends only on frequency and the work function.
  5. (De Broglie) Explain why electrons can be diffracted by crystals but tennis balls cannot. Answer: Diffraction is noticeable when the de Broglie wavelength λ = h/(mv) is comparable to the gap size; electrons have very small momentum and wavelengths of atomic scale, while a tennis ball's momentum makes its wavelength negligibly small.
  6. (Energy levels) An atom transitions between two levels 3.0 eV apart. Find the frequency of the emitted photon. Answer: ΔE = 3.0 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 4.8 × 10⁻¹⁹ J; f = ΔE/h = 4.8 × 10⁻¹⁹/6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ = 7.2 × 10¹⁴ Hz.
  7. (Spectra) Distinguish between an emission and an absorption spectrum. Answer: An emission spectrum shows bright lines on black where excited atoms drop to lower levels; an absorption spectrum shows dark lines on a continuous spectrum where cooler gas absorbs the same wavelengths — the line positions match.
  8. (Explanation) Explain, using photon theory, why photoelectric emission is instantaneous. Answer: One photon transfers all its energy to one electron in a single interaction; there is no gradual accumulation, so emission happens immediately once the photon energy exceeds the work function.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Intensity/frequency confusion: intensity changes the electron count, not their energy; frequency changes their energy. The two-sentence distinction above is worth marks every year.
  • eV/J conversions: 1 eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Work function in eV with photon energy in joules is a guaranteed arithmetic failure — convert before subtracting.
  • Threshold frequency vs threshold wavelength: they are inversely related (f₀ = φ/h, λ₀ = c/f₀); a short threshold wavelength means a high threshold frequency. Do not mix the inequalities.
  • h units: Planck's constant is 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s (or 4.14 × 10⁻¹⁵ eV s); using the wrong pair with the wrong energy unit fails the calculation.
  • Sign errors in ΔE: emission means the electron falls, so ΔE = E_upper − E_lower is positive for the photon. Sketch the level diagram and draw the arrow before calculating.
  • De Broglie with v = fλ confusion: for matter waves λ = h/(mv); substituting the wave speed of sound or light for the electron's speed is a common error.
  • Graph axes: KEₘₐₓ against f has gradient h — but KE against intensity is flat (above threshold, no change). Label what is plotted before reading anything off.
  • Photons of light and electrons are different things: photon energy E = hf for radiation; electron kinetic energy uses ½mv² (non-relativistic). Mixing the two formulas in one question is frequent under pressure.
  • Precision: give answers to 2 or 3 significant figures with units; quote h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s from the data sheet rather than from memory.

Equations and symbols

The whole of this topic as equations, each written with its real symbols and each followed by a key naming every symbol and its unit. Where a law has more than one useful form both are given, because which one is quickest depends on which quantities the question hands you. Learn the form here and the algebraic rearrangement becomes mechanical in the exam.

22.1 Energy and momentum of a photon

E = h f
Key: E = energy of one photon (J); h = Planck constant, 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s; f = frequency of the radiation (Hz). The energy is carried in discrete packets, so a dim beam of high-frequency light delivers more energy per photon than a bright beam of low-frequency light.

f = c / λ
Key: f = frequency (Hz); c = speed of light in a vacuum, 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹; λ = wavelength (m). In a medium the speed falls but the frequency — and therefore the photon energy — is unchanged.

E = h c / λ
Key: E = photon energy (J); h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s; c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹; λ = wavelength (m). The working form, since wavelengths are what a spectrum gives you.

p = h / λ
Key: p = momentum of the photon (kg m s⁻¹ = N s); h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s; λ = wavelength (m). A photon has no mass but does have momentum, which is how radiation pressure and Compton scattering arise.

E = p c
Key: E = photon energy (J); p = photon momentum (kg m s⁻¹); c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. The massless-particle energy relation, and a quick check on the two equations above.

N = P / (h f)
Key: N = number of photons emitted per second (s⁻¹); P = power of the source (W); h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s; f = frequency (Hz). Dividing the beam power by the energy of one photon counts the photons.

22.2 The photoelectric effect

h f = Φ + KE_max
Key: h f = energy of the incident photon (J); Φ = work function, the minimum energy needed to remove an electron from the metal surface (J); KE_max = maximum kinetic energy of an emitted photoelectron (J). Einstein's equation: one photon interacts with one electron, and whatever is left after the escape cost becomes kinetic energy.

Φ = h f₀ = h c / λ₀
Key: Φ = work function (J); f₀ = threshold frequency, below which no emission occurs whatever the intensity (Hz); λ₀ = threshold wavelength (m); h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s; c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. The threshold exists because a single photon must carry the whole escape energy — intensity cannot make up the deficit, which is the observation classical wave theory cannot explain.

KE_max = e V_s
Key: KE_max = maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons (J); e = elementary charge, 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C; V_s = stopping potential, the reverse p.d. that just stops the photocurrent (V). The stopping potential measures the fastest electrons directly, which is how KE_max is found in the experiment.

KE_max = h (f − f₀)
Key: KE_max = maximum kinetic energy (J); h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s; f = incident frequency (Hz); f₀ = threshold frequency (Hz). The linear graph: KE_max against f is a straight line of gradient h, intercept −Φ on the energy axis and f₀ on the frequency axis.

gradient = h, y-intercept = −Φ
Key: on a graph of KE_max (J) against frequency f (Hz); gradient = Planck constant (J s); y-intercept = minus the work function (−J). This is the standard "use the graph" question, and it works for any metal — only the intercept moves.

1 eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J
Key: eV = electronvolt, the energy gained by one electron accelerated through 1 V. Convert before substituting into h f = Φ + KE_max unless every term is in eV.

22.3 Wave–particle duality

λ = h / p
Key: λ = de Broglie wavelength of the particle (m); h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s; p = momentum of the particle (kg m s⁻¹). Every particle has a wavelength; it is immeasurably small for a cricket ball and comparable to atomic spacing for an electron.

λ = h / (m v)
Key: λ = de Broglie wavelength (m); m = mass of the particle (kg); v = its speed (m s⁻¹); h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s. The non-relativistic form, valid while v ≪ c.

p = √(2 m KE)
Key: p = momentum (kg m s⁻¹); m = mass (kg); KE = kinetic energy (J). From KE = ½ m v² and p = m v, eliminating v.

λ = h / √(2 m KE)
Key: λ = de Broglie wavelength (m); m = mass of the particle (kg); KE = its kinetic energy (J); h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s. The form to use when the energy is given rather than the speed.

e V = ½ m v², so λ = h / √(2 m e V)
Key: e = elementary charge, 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C; V = accelerating potential difference (V); m = mass of the electron, 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg; v = its speed (m s⁻¹); λ = de Broglie wavelength (m); h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s. An electron accelerated through 100 V has a wavelength of about 0.12 nm — the same order as atomic spacing, which is why electron diffraction works and electron microscopes resolve what light cannot.

22.4 Energy levels in atoms and line spectra

ΔE = E_upper − E_lower = h f = h c / λ
Key: ΔE = energy difference between two levels (J); E_upper, E_lower = energies of the levels involved (J); h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s; f = frequency of the emitted or absorbed photon (Hz); c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹; λ = its wavelength (m). Emission when an electron falls, absorption when one is raised.

λ = h c / ΔE
Key: λ = wavelength of the line (m); h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s; c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹; ΔE = level separation (J). Rearranged for the wavelength question; convert ΔE from eV to joules first.

E_n = −13.6 / n² eV (hydrogen)
Key: E_n = energy of the nth level of the hydrogen atom (eV); n = principal quantum number, 1, 2, 3 …; the negative sign means the electron is bound, with zero energy at infinite separation. The spacing between levels shrinks as n grows, which is why the spectral lines bunch together towards a series limit.

ionisation energy = 0 − E₁ = 13.6 eV (hydrogen)
Key: E₁ = energy of the ground state (eV). The energy needed to remove an electron completely from the ground state; for any other level it is 0 − E_n, which is smaller.

line spectra: ΔE fixed, so λ fixed
Key: because only discrete level differences exist, only photons of those exact energies can be emitted or absorbed, so a spectrum shows sharp lines rather than a continuous band. Each element has its own set of levels and therefore its own signature lines — the basis of spectroscopic identification.

title: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Statistics and Data Handling
content:
Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Statistics and Data Handling

Statistics is the art of describing a pile of numbers with a few well-chosen ones: an average to say where the middle lies, a spread to say how tightly the data cluster, and a chart to make the shape visible. The IGCSE questions test exactly that pipeline — classify the data, compute the averages and spread, draw or read the chart, and compare two distributions. This note builds the whole subject from zero: the data types, every average and measure of spread with the frequency-table method, the standard charts, cumulative frequency curves, and histograms with unequal class widths.

Classifying statistical data

TypeMeaningExamples
Qualitative (categorical)describes a quality, not a numberfavourite colour, blood group
Quantitativemeasured or counted as a numberheight, number of siblings
Discretecountable, separate values (usually integers)number of children, shoe size
Continuouscan take any value in a range (measured)height, time, mass

The classification decides which charts and averages are legal: a mode for categorical data, a median for ordered data, class intervals for continuous data. Discrete data are plotted as bar charts with gaps; continuous data as histograms with no gaps (and frequency density on the vertical axis).

Averages and range

mean = sum of values / number of values
median = middle value when ordered (mean of the two middle
         values for an even count)
mode = most frequent value (or class); none if no repeats
range = largest - smallest

quartiles: Q1 = lower quartile (25%), Q3 = upper quartile (75%)
interquartile range (IQR) = Q3 - Q1  (spread of the middle 50%)

The mean uses every value (sensitive to outliers); the median ignores extreme values (robust); the mode is the only average available for categorical data. When comparing two data sets, quote an average and a spread: "school A has a higher median but a larger IQR, so its results are higher on average but less consistent."

Worked example. Find the mean, median, mode and range of: 4, 7, 7, 9, 12, 15, 18.

mean = (4+7+7+9+12+15+18)/7 = 72/7 = 10.3 (3 s.f.)
median = 4th value = 9
mode = 7 (appears twice)
range = 18 - 4 = 14

Worked example 2 (even count). Find the median of 3, 5, 8, 10, 12, 15.

even count: average the 3rd and 4th values
median = (8 + 10)/2 = 9

Averages from frequency tables

mean = sum of (value x frequency) / sum of frequencies
median = the value at position (n + 1)/2 in cumulative order
mode = the value with the highest frequency

Worked example. The table shows goals scored: 0 (5 players), 1 (8), 2 (6), 3 (2). Find the mean and the median.

total players = 5 + 8 + 6 + 2 = 21
total goals = 0 × 5 + 1 × 8 + 2 × 6 + 3 × 2 = 0 + 8 + 12 + 6 = 26
mean = 26/21 = 1.24 (3 s.f.)
median position = (21 + 1)/2 = 11th value
cumulative: 5 (0 goals), 13 (1 goal) - the 11th value is 1
median = 1

For grouped data, use midpoints: the mean = Σ(midpoint × frequency)/Σfrequency, and the median comes from the cumulative frequency curve (below). The grouped mean is an estimate because the midpoint stands in for every value in the class.

Charts and diagrams

  • Bar chart: bars with gaps for categorical or discrete data; height = frequency.
  • Pie chart: angle = (frequency/total) × 360°; label the sectors with the category.
  • Pictogram: a symbol represents a fixed number; a half symbol represents half that number.
  • Stem-and-leaf: a sorted display that keeps the actual values; the key explains the split (e.g. 3|4 means 34).
  • Frequency polygon: plot frequency against the midpoint of each class and join with straight lines.

Worked example (pie chart). 40 students choose a sport: football 16, tennis 10, swimming 8, other 6. Find the angle for football.

angle = (16/40) × 360 = 144 °

Worked example 2 (pie chart reverse). A sector of 72° represents 9 students. How many students in total?

72 ° represents 9  →  360 ° represents 9 × 360/72 = 45 students

Cumulative frequency diagrams

A cumulative frequency table adds frequencies as you move up the classes. Plot cumulative frequency against the upper class boundary and join with a smooth curve; then read positions:

median at n/2
lower quartile at n/4
upper quartile at 3n/4
IQR = Q3 - Q1

Worked example. A cumulative frequency curve for 60 students' marks: Q1 = 42, median = 55, Q3 = 68. Find the IQR and interpret it.

IQR = 68 - 42 = 26 marks
The middle 50% of students scored within 26 marks of each other;

Always read across to the curve and then down to the horizontal axis — and use the class boundaries, not the midpoints, for the plot positions.

Histograms and frequency density

When class widths differ, the height of a bar cannot be the frequency — a wide class would dominate unfairly. Instead, the area of each bar is proportional to the frequency:

frequency density = frequency / class width
frequency = frequency density x class width (area of the bar)

Worked example. Class 0–10 has frequency 20; 10–20 has frequency 30; 20–40 has frequency 40. Find the frequency densities.

0-10: 20/10 = 2.0
10-20: 30/10 = 3.0
20-40: 40/20 = 2.0

Reading a histogram backwards is the standard question: measure a bar's width and height, multiply to get the frequency, and read the class from the horizontal axis. Remember that the axes often use class boundaries, so a bar from 20 to 40 covers width 20.

Stem-and-leaf diagrams and frequency polygons

A stem-and-leaf diagram sorts data while keeping every value visible: the stem is the leading digit and the leaf the final digit, with a key such as 3|4 meaning 34. Interpreting one means reading the ordered leaves to find the median, the quartiles and the shape: the median is the middle leaf, Q1 and Q3 sit at the quarter and three-quarter positions, and the distribution's skew shows in where the leaves bunch.

A frequency polygon plots frequency against the midpoint of each class and joins the points with straight lines; it is the grouped-data equivalent of a line graph and makes comparisons between two distributions easy (plot both polygons on the same axes).

Worked example. The leaves for stem 4 are 1, 3, 3, 6, 8 and for stem 5 are 0, 2, 5. List the data in order and find the median.

values: 41, 43, 43, 46, 48, 50, 52, 55
n = 8, so the median is the mean of the 4th and 5th values:
(46 + 48)/2 = 47

Worked example 2 (interpreting). Explain what a long right-hand tail of leaves in a stem-and-leaf diagram indicates.

A long right tail means a few unusually high values: the data
are positively skewed, and the mean will be greater than the
median because the high values pull it upward.

Comparing distributions

Comparison questions want two statements: one about the average (which is higher) and one about the spread (which is more consistent). Use median and IQR together — they are robust to outliers — or mean and standard deviation when the data are symmetric and the syllabus supplies it.

Worked example. Class A: median 62, IQR 18. Class B: median 58, IQR 9. Compare.

Class A has the higher typical score (median 62 vs 58), but its
results are more spread out (IQR 18 vs 9), so Class B is more
consistent even though its middle score is lower.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Averages) Find the mean and range of 12, 15, 11, 19, 13. Answer: mean = (12 + 15 + 11 + 19 + 13)/5 = 70/5 = 14; range = largest − smallest = 19 − 11 = 8.
  2. (Frequency table) Values 1, 2, 3 with frequencies 4, 7, 9. Find the mean. Answer: mean = Σfx/Σf = (1 × 4 + 2 × 7 + 3 × 9)/(4 + 7 + 9) = (4 + 14 + 27)/20 = 45/20 = 2.25.
  3. (Median) Find the median of 2, 4, 4, 6, 9, 10. Answer: there are six values, so the median is the mean of the 3rd and 4th: (4 + 6)/2 = 5.
  4. (Pie chart) A sector of 90° represents 15 people. Find the total. Answer: 90° is 90/360 = ¼ of the circle, so the total is 15 ÷ ¼ = 15 × 4 = 60 people.
  5. (Cumulative frequency) For 80 values, where do you read the median? Answer: At cumulative frequency 40, reading across to the curve and down to the axis.
  6. (Histogram) A bar of width 5 has frequency density 4. Find its frequency. Answer: frequency = frequency density × class width = 4 × 5 = 20.
  7. (Frequency density) Class 30–50 has frequency 24. Find the frequency density. Answer: class width = 50 − 30 = 20, so frequency density = frequency/width = 24/20 = 1.2.
  8. (Compare) Two runners' times: A median 42 s, IQR 3 s; B median 40 s, IQR 8 s. Compare. Answer: B is faster typically (lower median) but less consistent (larger IQR); A is more reliable.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Median without ordering: the median is the middle of the ordered list. Forgetting to sort is the commonest data-handling error.
  • Even-count median: average the two middle values; do not pick one of them.
  • Grouped mean: use midpoints and label the answer an estimate — the midpoint is not the actual mean of the class.
  • Histogram heights: the vertical axis is frequency density, not frequency; area is the frequency. Reading the height as the frequency is the classic histogram error.
  • Cumulative frequency positions: plot against upper class boundaries and read the median at n/2 (not (n+1)/2 on the graph).
  • Pie chart arithmetic: check that the angles sum to 360° before answering the next part.
  • IQR direction: IQR = upper − lower quartile; a negative IQR means the quartiles are swapped.
  • Comparison claims: quote actual values ("median 62 vs 58"), not "better" without evidence.

Equations and symbols

Seven formulas cover the whole paper: the three averages with their range and interquartile range, the two histogram relations, and the pie-chart angle. Every one carries the same mark-scheme requirement — substitute, then state the answer in the units of the data, not as a bare number.

mean = sum of values / number of values Key: mean = the arithmetic average, in the same units as the data; sum of values = the total of every reading; number of values = how many readings there are. Uses every value, so one outlier moves it.

median = the value at position (n + 1)/2 in cumulative order Key: n = the number of values; the position is a count through the ordered list, not a value. For an even n the position falls between two values, so average them — picking one of the two is the commonest lost mark.

mode = the value with the highest frequency Key: mode = the most frequent value, in the same units as the data; for grouped data it is the modal class. The only average available for categorical data.

range = largest - smallest Key: largest and smallest = the extreme values of the data set; the range is their difference, in the data's units. It uses only two values, so a single outlier destroys it.

IQR = Q3 - Q1 Key: IQR = interquartile range, the spread of the middle 50% of the data (same units); Q3 = upper quartile at the 75% position; Q1 = lower quartile at the 25% position. A negative IQR means the quartiles have been swapped.

IQR = 68 - 42 = 26 marks Key: 68 = Q3, the mark at the 75% position; 42 = Q1, the mark at the 25% position; 26 marks = the IQR. Interpret it in words: the middle half of the students scored within 26 marks of each other.

frequency density = frequency / class width Key: frequency density = the height of the bar (no units, since it is a count divided by a width); frequency = the number of readings in the class; class width = upper boundary minus lower boundary (in the data's units). Use it only when the class widths differ — with equal widths the height may be the frequency.

frequency = frequency density x class width (area of the bar) Key: the same relation rearranged; reading a histogram backwards means measuring a bar's width and height and multiplying. In a histogram it is the area, never the height, that represents the frequency.

angle = (frequency/total) × 360° Key: frequency = the count in the sector; total = the total count for the whole chart; angle in degrees, and the sectors must sum to 360°. To go the other way, total = frequency × 360/angle.

mean = sum of (value x frequency) / sum of frequencies Key: value = each reading, or the midpoint of a class for grouped data (same units); frequency = how many times it occurs. With midpoints the answer is labelled an estimate, because the midpoint stands in for every value in the class.

title: A Level Mathematics: The Binomial Distribution
content:
A Level Mathematics: The Binomial Distribution

A binomial distribution counts successes in a fixed number of independent trials, each with the same probability of success. Coins, multiple-choice guesses, defective items in a sample and free throws all fit the same template, and once a problem is recognised as binomial the calculation is a formula plus a cumulative table. This note builds the distribution from its four conditions, derives the formula from counting, and then uses it for the two things exams actually ask: probabilities and hypothesis tests.

The four conditions

Before writing X ~ B(n, p) you must be able to name the conditions, because most exam questions include a part asking whether the model is appropriate. The conditions are not red tape: drop any one and the formula is simply wrong.

1. a fixed number of trials n
2. each trial has exactly two outcomes (success / failure)
3. the probability of success p is constant for every trial
4. the trials are independent
then X = number of successes has X ~ B(n, p)

Worked example (checking the model). A bag holds 5 red and 15 blue counters. Four counters are taken without replacement. Is the number of red counters binomial?

n = 4 is fixed and each draw is red or not red
but p changes: 5/20, then 5/19 if a red was taken, ...
the trials are not independent, so NOT binomial (it is hypergeometric)

Taking with replacement would fix it: p stays 0.25 on every draw.

The formula, and where it comes from

The probability of a particular sequence of r successes and n − r failures is p^r (1−p)^(n−r), because independence lets you multiply. The number of such sequences is the number of ways to choose which r trials succeed, which is nCr. Multiplying gives the formula.

P(X = r) = nCr p^r (1 - p)^(n - r)
the nCr counts arrangements; the powers give the probability of one arrangement

Worked example. X ~ B(10, 0.3). Find P(X = 3).

P = 10C3 (0.3)³ (0.7)⁷
= 120 × 0.027 × 0.08235
= 120 × 0.002223 = 0.2668

Worked example 2 (a single trial count). A fair die is rolled 8 times. Find the probability of exactly two sixes.

X ~ B(8, 1/6)
P(X = 2) = 8C2 (1/6)² (5/6)⁶ = 28 × 0.02778 × 0.3349 = 0.2605

Worked example 3 (why nCr appears). For n = 3 and r = 1, list the sequences and confirm the coefficient.

sequences: SFF, FSF, FFS - three of them
each has probability p(1-p)²
so P(X = 1) = 3p(1-p)², and 3C1 = 3

Cumulative probabilities

Questions almost always ask for a range, not a single value, and the cumulative distribution is what the calculator or the tables supply. The skill is rewriting the question into the form the table gives you.

P(X <= r) is tabulated directly
P(X >= r) = 1 - P(X <= r - 1)
P(X < r)  = P(X <= r - 1)
P(a <= X <= b) = P(X <= b) - P(X <= a - 1)
P(X = r) = P(X <= r) - P(X <= r - 1)

Worked example. X ~ B(20, 0.4). Find P(X ≥ 8).

P(X >= 8) = 1 - P(X <= 7)
= 1 - 0.4159
= 0.5841

Worked example 2 (between). For the same X, find P(5 ≤ X ≤ 10).

= P(X <= 10) - P(X <= 4)
= 0.8725 - 0.0510
= 0.8215

Worked example 3 (the strict inequality trap). For the same X, find P(X > 6).

P(X > 6) = 1 - P(X <= 6) = 1 - 0.2500 = 0.7500
note this is different from P(X >= 6) = 1 - P(X <= 5) = 0.8746

Mean and variance

The binomial has the simplest mean and variance in the syllabus, and they are worth knowing both forwards and backwards: a question can give the mean and variance and ask for n and p.

E(X) = np
Var(X) = np(1 - p)
standard deviation = √(np(1-p))

Worked example. X ~ B(50, 0.2). Find the mean and standard deviation.

mean = 50 × 0.2 = 10
variance = 10 × 0.8 = 8
sd = 2.828

Worked example 2 (backwards). A binomial variable has mean 12 and variance 9. Find n and p.

np = 12;  np(1-p) = 9
divide: 1 - p = 9/12 = 0.75  →  p = 0.25
then n = 12/0.25 = 48

Hypothesis testing with the binomial

A one-tailed test asks whether p has increased or decreased; the test statistic is the observed count, and the p-value is the probability of a result at least as extreme in the direction of the alternative.

H0: p = p0      H1: p > p0 (or p < p0)
X ~ B(n, p0) under H0
p-value = P(X >= observed) or P(X <= observed)
compare with the significance level; reject H0 if p-value <= alpha

Worked example. A coin is tossed 20 times and lands heads 15 times. Test at the 5% level whether the coin is biased towards heads.

H0: p = 0.5;  H1: p > 0.5
X ~ B(20, 0.5)
P(X >= 15) = 1 - P(X <= 14) = 1 - 0.9793 = 0.0207
0.0207 < 0.05, so reject H0
there is evidence at the 5% level that the coin favours heads

Worked example 2 (two-tailed). The same data tested two-tailed.

double the smaller tail: 2 × 0.0207 = 0.0414
0.0414 < 0.05, so still reject H0 at the 5% level

Worked example 3 (critical region). For X ~ B(20, 0.5), find the critical region for a 5% one-tailed test of p > 0.5.

P(X >= 14) = 0.0577 (above 0.05)
P(X >= 15) = 0.0207 (below 0.05)
critical region: X >= 15

Note that the critical region is chosen so the probability of a Type I error is at most 5%, which is why 14 is excluded even though it is close.

When the model breaks down

Examiners like the question that asks why a binomial model is only an approximation. The usual culprits are dependence, a varying probability, or a fixed sample drawn without replacement from a small population.

SituationProblemEffect
sampling without replacementtrials not independentp drifts; use the hypergeometric instead
clustered data (pupils in classes)responses correlatedvariance underestimated
probability varies between trialsp not constantformula invalid
large n, p near 0.5computation heavynormal approximation is reasonable

Worked example (normal approximation). X ~ B(200, 0.4). Use a normal approximation to estimate P(X ≤ 70).

mean = 80;  variance = 200 × 0.4 × 0.6 = 48;  sd = 6.928
continuity correction: X <= 70 becomes X < 70.5
z = (70.5 - 80)/6.928 = -1.371
P(Z < -1.371) = 0.0852

The continuity correction is compulsory: a discrete count needs a half-unit boundary before it can be treated as continuous.

Expected frequencies and the shape of the distribution

A binomial distribution is not symmetric unless p = 0.5, and that shape decides which tail an exam question is fishing in. The most likely value — the mode — is the integer near (n + 1)p, and expected frequency multiplies the probability by the number of samples taken. Both are quick marks that are frequently missed because students jump straight to the formula.

mode is near (n + 1)p, checked by comparing consecutive probabilities
expected number in a sample of size N = N x P(X = r)

Worked example. X ~ B(12, 0.3). Find the most likely value of X and the expected number of 3s in 500 independent observations.

(n + 1)p = 13 × 0.3 = 3.9, so check r = 3 and r = 4
P(X = 3) = 220 × 0.027 × 0.1176 = 0.2397
P(X = 4) = 495 × 0.0081 × 0.1681 = 0.2311
mode = 3
expected number of 3s = 500 × 0.2397 = 120 (to the nearest whole)

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Model) State the distribution for the number of sixes in 12 rolls of a fair die. Answer: X ~ B(n, p) with n = 12 rolls and p = 1/6 the chance of a six on each, so X ~ B(12, 1/6).
  2. (Single value) X ~ B(8, 0.25): find P(X = 2). Answer: P(X = 2) = ⁸C₂ (0.25)² (0.75)⁶ = 28 × 0.0625 × 0.1780 = 0.3115.
  3. (Cumulative) X ~ B(15, 0.3): find P(X ≤ 4). Answer: P(X ≤ 4) = Σₖ₌₀⁴ ¹⁵Cₖ (0.3)ᵏ (0.7)¹⁵⁻ᵏ = 0.5155 from cumulative binomial tables.
  4. (Complement) Same X: find P(X ≥ 3). Answer: P(X ≥ 3) = 1 − P(X ≤ 2) = 1 − 0.2969 = 0.7031 — the complement, because the tables give the lower tail only.
  5. (Mean) X ~ B(40, 0.35): find E(X) and Var(X). Answer: 14 and 9.1.
  6. (Backwards) Mean 18, variance 12: find n and p. Answer: mean np = 18 and variance np(1 − p) = 12; dividing, 1 − p = 12/18 = 2/3, so p = 1/3 and n = 18 ÷ (1/3) = 54.
  7. (Test) 12 of 20 seeds germinate; test p = 0.5 against p < 0.5 at 5%. Answer: H₀: p = 0.5 against H₁: p < 0.5; under H₀, X ~ B(20, 0.5) and P(X ≤ 12) = 0.8684, which is far above 0.05, so there is no evidence to reject H₀.
  8. (Critical region) X ~ B(10, 0.2): find the 5% critical region for p < 0.2. Answer: the smallest possible tail is P(X ≤ 0) = (0.8)¹⁰ = 0.1074, which already exceeds 0.05, so no critical region exists at the 5% level for this n.
  9. (Approximation) X ~ B(100, 0.5): approximate P(X ≥ 60). Answer: μ = np = 50 and σ = √(np(1 − p)) = √25 = 5; with the continuity correction z = (59.5 − 50)/5 = 1.9, so P(X ≥ 60) ≈ P(Z > 1.9) = 0.0287.
  10. (Assumption) Give one reason a binomial model may fail for defects in boxes of 20. Answer: defects may cluster, so trials are not independent.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Forgetting nCr: the coefficient counts arrangements; without it the answer is the probability of one specific sequence.
  • nCr on the wrong factor: it is p^r (1−p)^(n−r), with the success probability raised to the number of successes.
  • Inequality direction: P(X ≥ 8) uses 1 − P(X ≤ 7), not 1 − P(X ≤ 8).
  • Variance confused with standard deviation: np(1−p) is the variance; the test and the normal approximation need the square root.
  • Continuity correction omitted: any normal approximation to a discrete count needs the half-unit adjustment.
  • One-tailed evidence read as two: halving or doubling the tail without checking the alternative direction is a silent error.
  • Independence asserted, not checked: sampling without replacement from a small population breaks the model, and the question usually invites you to say so.
  • p-value compared with the wrong threshold: the significance level is given as a percentage; 5% means 0.05, not 5.

Recognising a binomial situation in context

Most binomial marks are lost before any arithmetic starts, because the question was not identified as binomial. The subsections below give a checklist for reading a question and writing the model in the standard form X ~ B(n, p) before you calculate anything.

Writing the model in the form X ~ B(n, p)

Once you decide a situation is binomial, state the model in full: X ~ B(n, p), where X is the number of successes, n is the number of trials and p is the probability of a success on each trial. Define X in words in your answer, for example “X is the number of defective bulbs in a box of 20”. A model with no definition of X loses the communication mark even when the probabilities are right.

Identifying the number of trials, n

The value of n is the fixed number of times the experiment is repeated: the number of bulbs tested, the number of patients treated, or the number of games played. Read the question for the phrase that fixes it, such as “of 20 bulbs chosen at random”. If the question keeps going until a result occurs, the number of trials is not fixed and the binomial model does not apply directly.

Identifying the probability of success, p

The value of p is the probability of the outcome you have chosen to call a success on one trial. It must stay the same for every trial. A fair coin gives p = 0.5, and a bag where 15% of items are faulty gives p = 0.15 for each item drawn with replacement. If the question gives a percentage, convert it to a decimal before you use it in any formula.

Checking for fixed trials

The number of trials must be decided before the experiment starts. Counting the number of successes in a fixed sample is binomial, whereas recording how many trials it takes to get the first success is not. A question about the number of heads in ten tosses is binomial; a question about how many tosses are needed for the first head is a different model. Make the fixed-n check before any other check.

Checking for independent trials

Each trial must not affect the next. Independence is what allows you to multiply the probabilities of several outcomes together, and it is the assumption most often ignored. Drawing items with replacement keeps p constant, and that is what the model needs. Drawing without replacement changes p after each draw, so the binomial model is only an approximation when the sample is small compared with the population.

Worked identification

A survey finds that 30% of adults own a bicycle. Twelve adults are chosen at random from a large town and asked whether they own one. Let X be the number who own a bicycle. Here n = 12, p = 0.3 and the answer is X ~ B(12, 0.3). The population is large, so the probability for each adult stays close to 0.3 and the model is a reasonable one to use. State that assumption, because a marker looks for it.

Probabilities of at least one, and of more than r

Questions that ask for “at least” or “more than” are the ones where the complement saves the most time. The subsections set out the choice between a direct sum and the complement, and the checks that stop an off-by-one error.

Probability of at least one success

“At least one” is the complement of “none”, so P(X ≥ 1) = 1 − P(X = 0) = 1 − qⁿ, where q = 1 − p. For X ~ B(5, 0.2), P(X ≥ 1) = 1 − 0.8⁵ = 1 − 0.32768 = 0.672 to 3 significant figures. Adding the probabilities of X = 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 gives the same answer but takes five calculations instead of one.

Probability of more than r successes

“More than 3” means 4 or more, so P(X > 3) = 1 − P(X ≤ 3). For X ~ B(10, 0.3), P(X ≤ 3) = 0.6496 to 4 decimal places, so P(X > 3) = 0.3504. The number 3 is included in the part you subtract from 1; forgetting that is the typical error on “more than” questions.

Choosing between a direct sum and the complement

Use the complement when the part you do not want is short: “at least one”, “at most one but not zero” and similar phrases. Use a direct sum when the wanted region has only a few terms, such as P(X = 2) + P(X = 3). With a calculator table of cumulative probabilities, most “at most” and “at least” questions reduce to one lookup and one subtraction.

Probability of exactly r on a calculator

For X ~ B(n, p), P(X = r) = ⁿCᵣ pʳ qⁿ⁻ʳ. The combination ⁿCᵣ counts the ways the r successes can be arranged among n trials. For X ~ B(10, 0.3), P(X = 3) = 120 × 0.3³ × 0.7⁷ = 120 × 0.027 × 0.0823543 = 0.2668 to 4 decimal places. Enter the combination with the nCr key so the arrangement count is not mistyped.

The most likely number of successes (the mode)

The most likely value of X is the mode. For a binomial distribution it is the whole number part of (n + 1)p, and if (n + 1)p is itself a whole number there are two modes, (n + 1)p − 1 and (n + 1)p. For X ~ B(10, 0.3), (n + 1)p = 3.3, so the mode is 3. Check against the probabilities: P(X = 3) = 0.2668 is larger than P(X = 2) = 0.2335 and P(X = 4) = 0.2001.

Checking that the probabilities add to 1

A complete check is that P(X = 0) + P(X = 1) + … + P(X = n) = 1. You rarely add every term in an exam, but the check is useful when you build a table of probabilities for a whole distribution. If a column does not total 1 to the rounding used, one of the terms was calculated with the wrong value of q or the wrong combination count.

Adding independent binomial variables

A question can combine two or more binomial counts, for example the total number of faults from two machines. The result is binomial only under particular conditions, and the subsections below say what those conditions are and how to check them.

Same probability, different numbers of trials

If X ~ B(n, p) and Y ~ B(m, p) are independent, and both use the same probability of success p, then X + Y ~ B(n + m, p). Two batches tested for the same fault, with the same chance of that fault on each item, combine into one larger binomial. The shared p is the key condition: the trials must all be a success or failure with the same chance.

The rule for X + Y

Write the result as X + Y ~ B(n + m, p). For example, X ~ B(4, 0.5) and Y ~ B(6, 0.5), independent, give X + Y ~ B(10, 0.5). Add the trial counts, not the probabilities. The probability of success stays the same because each trial still has the same chance of success.

When the probabilities differ

If X ~ B(n, p) and Y ~ B(m, q) with p ≠ q, the sum is not binomial, and you cannot use the rule above. The number of successes comes from trials that have different chances, so no single p describes all of them. A question that asks for the distribution in this case expects a table of values, not a single binomial statement.

Worked example: two batches

Batch A has 8 items and batch B has 12 items. Each item in either batch is defective with probability 0.05, and the items are independent. Let T be the total number of defective items. Then T ~ B(20, 0.05), because both batches share p = 0.05. The probability of no defective items at all is P(T = 0) = 0.95²⁰ = 0.358 to 3 significant figures.

Why the mean and variance add

The mean of a sum is always the sum of the means, whether or not the variables are independent. The variance of a sum is the sum of the variances only when the variables are independent. For the batch example, E(T) = 20 × 0.05 = 1 and Var(T) = 20 × 0.05 × 0.95 = 0.95, which is the same as adding the separate variances 8 × 0.0475 and 12 × 0.0475.

Contrast with a normal approximation

For a large n, a binomial count is often approximated by a normal distribution with the same mean np and variance npq. The approximation is weak when np or nq is small, as in the batch example where np = 1. In that case use the exact binomial probabilities, and quote the normal approximation only when the question asks for it or when n is large enough for both np and nq to be well above 5.

Equations and symbols

The distribution, its conditions and the four tail identities. Every question on this topic is one of these lines plus a calculator.

P(X = r) = nCr p^r (1 - p)^(n - r) Key: n = number of trials, fixed in advance; p = probability of success in one trial, constant; r = the number of successes asked for; nCr = n!/(r!(n − r)!), the number of orders the successes can occur in. The (1 − p) term is the failures, and its power must be n − r.

X ~ B(n, p) Key: X = the count of successes; the tilde means "is distributed as"; n and p as above. Write this line before calculating — it is often a mark on its own, and it fixes which parameters go into the calculator.

P = 10C3 (0.3)³ (0.7)⁷ Key: n = 10, p = 0.3, r = 3, so the failures are 7 and their probability is 0.7. The coefficient 10C3 = 120 accounts for the order of the three successes among the ten trials.

P(X >= r) = 1 - P(X <= r - 1) Key: a complement, so the two probabilities add to 1; the boundary moves by one because the binomial is discrete. Using 1 − P(X ≤ r) instead is the classic off-by-one error.

P(a <= X <= b) = P(X <= b) - P(X <= a - 1) Key: subtract the part below the interval; again the "− 1" is there because P(X ≤ a − 1) is everything before a. Check with a small case you can list by hand before trusting the calculator.
