title: AS Level Mathematics: Statistics S1 — Correlation and Regression
content:
AS Level Mathematics: Statistics S1 — Correlation and Regression

Statistics S1 turns data into claims about relationships. Two variables measured together can be displayed on a scatter diagram; the strength of any straight-line relationship is measured by the product-moment correlation coefficient; and the line of best fit — the regression line — predicts one variable from the other. This note builds the unit from zero: bivariate data and scatter diagrams, the correlation coefficient with its calculation and interpretation, regression lines and their equations, and the assumptions that make prediction honest.

Bivariate data and scatter diagrams

each observation gives a pair (x, y)
plot y against x; look for direction, strength and shape
PatternMeaning
Points rise left to rightPositive correlation
Points fall left to rightNegative correlation
No patternLittle or no linear correlation
Curved patternA relationship, but not linear

An outlier is a point far from the pattern. It can dominate both the correlation coefficient and the regression line, so it should be identified and its effect discussed, not silently deleted.

The product-moment correlation coefficient

r = Sxy / sqrt(Sxx Syy)

Sxx = sum x^2 - (sum x)^2/n
Syy = sum y^2 - (sum y)^2/n
Sxy = sum xy - (sum x)(sum y)/n

-1 <= r <= 1

Worked example (full calculation). Five pairs give sum x = 20, sum y = 30, sum x² = 90, sum y² = 220, sum xy = 140, n = 5. Find r.

Sxx = 90 - 400/5 = 10
Syy = 220 - 900/5 = 40
Sxy = 140 - 600/5 = 20
r = 20/sqrt(10 x 40) = 20/20 = 1.0  (perfect positive)

Worked example 2. With sum x = 15, sum y = 24, sum x² = 55, sum y² = 130, sum xy = 60, n = 5.

Sxx = 55 - 45 = 10;  Syy = 130 - 115.2 = 14.8
Sxy = 60 - 72 = -12
r = -12/sqrt(148) = -12/12.166 = -0.986

Interpretation is a required sentence, not a number: r = 0.986 means a strong positive linear relationship; r = 0.2 means a weak positive one. Also state that r measures only linear association — a strong curve can give r near zero.

The regression line

y on x:  y = a + bx  with b = Sxy/Sxx and a = ybar - b xbar

x on y (the other regression): x = c + dy with d = Sxy/Syy

There are two regression lines because minimising vertical distances is not the same as minimising horizontal distances. The line of y on x is the one used to predict y from x, and its gradient is always steeper (for |r| < 1) than the x-on-y line.

Worked example. Using the second data set above, find the regression line of y on x.

xbar = 3, ybar = 4.8
b = -12/10 = -1.2
a = 4.8 - (-1.2)(3) = 8.4
y = 8.4 - 1.2x

Worked example 2 (prediction). Use that line to predict y when x = 4, and comment on a prediction at x = 20.

at x = 4: y = 8.4 - 4.8 = 3.6
at x = 20: y = 8.4 - 24 = -15.6, and 20 lies far outside the data
range (1 to 5), so this is extrapolation and unreliable

Interpolation is prediction inside the observed range; extrapolation is outside it. Extrapolation assumes the straight-line pattern continues, which the data cannot support — say so.

Interpreting the gradient and intercept

In context, b is the change in y per unit increase in x, and a is the predicted y when x = 0 (often meaningless: no one weighs 0 kg at 0 cm).

Worked example. A regression of exam mark (y) on hours studied (x) gives y = 30 + 5x. Interpret.

each extra hour of study is associated with 5 more marks
(b is an association, not proof of causation)
the intercept 30 is the predicted mark with no study, but x = 0
may lie outside the data range, so treat it cautiously

Correlation, causation and reliability

A strong correlation never establishes causation. Two variables can move together because a third drives both (ice-cream sales and drowning both rise with temperature), or by coincidence in a small sample.

r measures linear association only
r is unaffected by changing units or swapping x and y
r is sensitive to outliers
r = 0 does not mean no relationship: a symmetric curve can give r = 0

Worked example. A study finds r = 0.85 between shoe size and reading age in children. Explain why this does not mean bigger feet cause better reading.

both increase with age; age is a lurking variable
the correlation is real but confounded, so a causal claim needs a
controlled comparison at a fixed age

Choosing the right summary

S1 questions ask you to select and justify the statistic. The decision table is worth memorising:

SituationBest choiceReason
Outliers presentMedian, IQRRobust to extremes
All values should countMean, sdUses every observation
Two variables, linear patternr and the regression lineMeasures strength and predicts
Curved patternTransform, or do not use rr assumes linearity

Worked example. A data set of salaries has one director earning ten times the rest. Which average and spread should summarise it, and why?

median and IQR: the director's salary drags the mean upward and
inflates the sd, so neither represents a typical employee

Where the least-squares coefficients come from

The regression line is chosen to minimise the sum of squared vertical distances from the points. That criterion produces the formulas already quoted, and knowing why makes them far easier to recall.

minimise sum (y - a - bx)^2 over a and b
differentiate with respect to a: -2 sum (y - a - bx) = 0
  ->  ybar = a + b xbar   (the line passes through the mean point)
differentiate with respect to b: -2 sum x(y - a - bx) = 0
  ->  Sxy = b Sxx  ->  b = Sxy/Sxx

Two consequences worth stating in an exam: the line always passes through (x̄, ȳ), and if Sxy is zero the gradient is zero — no linear trend, so r = 0 and prediction by the line is useless.

Worked example. Show that the line passes through the mean point for y = 8.4 − 1.2x with x̄ = 3.

y at x = 3: 8.4 - 3.6 = 4.8 = ybar, as the derivation requires

Answering S1 questions the way mark schemes reward

The statistics marks are split between calculation and commentary, and the commentary is where candidates lose most. Four habits cover almost every question:

  • State the statistic with its units and three significant figures.
  • Interpret in context, naming the variables rather than x and y.
  • Qualify every causal claim as an association.
  • For a prediction, say whether it is interpolation or extrapolation.

Worked example. A regression of height y (cm) on age x (years) for 8- to 12-year-olds gives y = 90 + 6x, r = 0.96. Write a full interpretation.

strong positive linear correlation (r = 0.96) between age and height
in this sample; on average each additional year of age is associated
with 6 cm more height; the line explains the data well within the
8-12 range, and a prediction at age 20 would be extrapolation and
unreliable because growth does not continue linearly

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (r meaning) r = −0.9. Interpret. Answer: strong negative linear correlation; as x increases y tends to decrease.
  2. (r range) Can r = 1.2? Answer: no; r lies between −1 and 1.
  3. (Calculation) Sxx = 20, Syy = 45, Sxy = 27. Find r. Answer: r = 27/√900 = 0.9.
  4. (Gradient) Sxy = 27, Sxx = 20. Find b. Answer: 1.35.
  5. (Intercept) b = 1.35, x̄ = 5, ȳ = 10. Find a. Answer: a = 10 − 6.75 = 3.25.
  6. (Prediction) y = 3.25 + 1.35x. Predict y at x = 8. Answer: 14.05.
  7. (Extrapolation) Data covers x = 1 to 10. Is a prediction at x = 50 reliable? Answer: no; extrapolation beyond the data range.
  8. (Causation) r = 0.95 between umbrella sales and rainfall. Does buying umbrellas cause rain? Answer: no; rainfall drives sales, so the correlation is not causal in that direction.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Using the wrong regression line: predict y from x with the y-on-x line, not the x-on-y line.
  • Confusing b and r: the gradient is a rate of change; r is a unitless strength between −1 and 1.
  • Claiming causation: always qualify — "associated with" rather than "causes".
  • Ignoring the outlier: one extreme point can lift or destroy r; comment on its effect.
  • Extrapolating silently: state when a prediction lies outside the data range and that it is unreliable.
  • Rounding r: quote three significant figures and keep full accuracy in Sxy, Sxx, Syy.
  • Swapping Sxy and Syy: the y-on-x gradient divides by Sxx; the x-on-y gradient divides by Syy.
  • Forgetting units in interpretation: "5 more marks per hour" reads as a real claim; "y increases by 5" does not.

Formula summary

Sxx = sum x^2 - (sum x)^2/n;  Syy = sum y^2 - (sum y)^2/n
Sxy = sum xy - (sum x)(sum y)/n
r = Sxy/sqrt(Sxx Syy)
y on x: b = Sxy/Sxx,  a = ybar - b xbar

Compute Sxx, Syy and Sxy first and keep them to four significant figures; every later statistic is a combination of those three, so an early rounding error propagates into r, the gradient and the prediction alike.

title: AS Level Physics: Quantum Physics
content:
AS Level Physics: Quantum Physics

Quantum physics begins with a failure: classical physics could not explain why hot objects glow the way they do, why light sometimes knocks electrons out of metal, or why atoms emit sharp lines rather than continuous rainbows. The answers — photons, the photoelectric effect, wave–particle duality and quantised energy levels — rebuilt physics in the twentieth century. This note builds the quantum toolkit from zero: the photon model and its arithmetic, Einstein's photoelectric equation with its graphs, de Broglie's matter waves, and the energy-level picture of the atom that explains every spectrum you will meet.

Why classical physics failed

Classical theory treated light as a continuous wave and predicted that any frequency should eject electrons from a metal if you wait long enough. Experiment said otherwise: below a threshold frequency, no electrons appear however intense the light; above it, electrons appear instantly however faint the light. Similarly, classical theory predicted that hot objects should radiate infinite energy at high frequencies (the ultraviolet catastrophe) — absurd. Planck's and Einstein's fix: energy is exchanged in discrete packets, quanta, each carrying E = hf. The packet idea is the whole foundation.

Photons: energy and momentum

A photon is a quantum of electromagnetic radiation. Its energy is set by its frequency alone:

E = h f = h c / λ

h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s  (Planck constant)
f = frequency (Hz)
c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹
λ = wavelength (m)

Photons also carry momentum, p = h/λ — a particle property that waves do not have in classical theory, and the bridge to matter waves later.

Worked example 1. Find the energy of a photon of 500 nm light.

E = hc/λ = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ x 3.0 × 10⁸)/(5.0 × 10⁻⁷)
  = 1.989 × 10⁻²⁵/5.0 × 10⁻⁷ = 3.98 × 10⁻¹⁹ J

Worked example 2 (electronvolts). Convert to electronvolts (1 eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J) and find the photon momentum.

E = 3.98 × 10⁻¹⁹/1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 2.49 eV
p = h/λ = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴/5.0 × 10⁻⁷ = 1.33 × 10⁻²⁷ kg m s⁻¹

Exam conversions deserve care: keV and MeV appear in nuclear contexts, and the eV↔J conversion (multiply or divide by 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹) is a mark waiting to be lost.

The photoelectric effect

Light on a clean metal surface ejects electrons — but only according to rules that demand the photon model:

  • Threshold frequency f₀: below it, no emission at all, whatever the intensity. The photon's energy must exceed the metal's work function φ (the minimum energy to free an electron from the surface).
  • Instantaneity: above f₀, emission begins immediately — one photon transfers all its energy to one electron in one interaction.
  • Intensity effect: above threshold, doubling the intensity doubles the number of photons and hence the photoelectric current (more electrons per second) but does not change their maximum kinetic energy.
  • Frequency effect: raising the frequency above f₀ increases the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons linearly.

Einstein's equation ties the numbers together:

h f = Φ + KE_max

Φ = work function of the metal (J or eV)
KE_max = maximum kinetic energy of an emitted electron
f0 = threshold frequency: h f0 = Φ

Worked example. Sodium has work function 2.3 eV. Light of wavelength 450 nm falls on it. Find whether emission occurs and the maximum kinetic energy.

photon energy: E = hc/λ = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ x 3.0 × 10⁸)/(4.5 × 10⁻⁷)
               = 4.42 × 10⁻¹⁹ J = 2.76 eV
compare: 2.76 eV > 2.3 eV  →  emission occurs
KE_max = 2.76 - 2.3 = 0.46 eV
       = 0.46 × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 7.4 × 10⁻²⁰ J

Worked example (threshold). Find the threshold wavelength for sodium (φ = 2.3 eV).

h f0 = Φ → f0 = Φ/h = (2.3 × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹)/6.63 × 10⁻³⁴
     = 5.55 × 10¹⁴ Hz
lambda0 = c/f0 = 3.0 × 10⁸/5.55 × 10¹⁴ = 5.4 × 10⁻⁷ m = 540 nm

Below 540 nm (higher frequency) sodium emits; above it, nothing. Note the inverse relationship: threshold wavelength corresponds to threshold frequency.

The graphs the papers love

Two plots encode the photoelectric effect and both are examinable:

  • KEₘₐₓ against frequency: a straight line with gradient h, crossing the frequency axis at f₀ and the KE axis at −φ. The gradient is the same for every metal — the metal only moves the intercepts.
  • Stopping potential against frequency: the same shape, since eVₛ = KEₘₐₓ.
  • Current against intensity: linear above threshold (more photons, more electrons).

Worked example. A plot of KEₘₐₓ against frequency has gradient 6.5 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and crosses the axis at 5.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz. Identify Planck's constant and the work function.

gradient = h = 6.5 × 10⁻³⁴ J s (close to 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴,
           the difference being experimental error)
Φ = h f0 = 6.5 × 10⁻³⁴ x 5.0 × 10¹⁴ = 3.25 × 10⁻¹⁹ J
    = 2.0 eV

Wave–particle duality

The quantum world refuses the wave/particle distinction: light, treated for centuries as a wave, arrives in photon packets; electrons, treated as particles, can diffract. Electron diffraction — beams of electrons producing interference patterns when scattered by crystals — is the evidence that convinced the profession. De Broglie unified the picture: every particle of momentum p has an associated wavelength

λ = h / p = h / (m v)

Worked example. Find the de Broglie wavelength of an electron accelerated through 100 V.

KE = eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ x 10⁰ = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁷ J
KE = (1/2) m v² → p = √(2 m KE)
p = √(2 × 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ x 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁷)
  = √(2.915 × 10⁻⁴⁷) = 5.40 × 10⁻²⁴ kg m s⁻¹
λ = h/p = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴/5.40 × 10⁻²⁴ = 1.23 × 10⁻¹⁰ m
       = 0.123 nm   (comparable to atomic spacing: electrons
         diffract through crystals)

Why electrons diffract through crystals but footballs do not: the wavelength is only noticeable when it is comparable to the gap it passes through — the same rule as diffraction for waves. A macroscopic ball has such a large momentum that its de Broglie wavelength is immeasurably small.

Energy levels in atoms and line spectra

Electrons in atoms occupy quantised energy levels — only specific energies are allowed. Transitions between them absorb or emit a photon whose energy exactly equals the level difference:

ΔE = E_upper - E_lower = h f = h c / λ
  • Emission spectrum: an excited atom drops to a lower level and emits a photon; a hot gas produces bright lines at specific wavelengths — a line spectrum.
  • Absorption spectrum: cold gas absorbs those same wavelengths from white light, leaving dark lines at identical positions.
  • Fluorescence: a photon is absorbed (UV, say), some energy is lost as heat, and a lower-energy (visible) photon is emitted — which is why white shirts glow blue under UV light.

The energy-level diagram is the standard question: a vertical scale in eV or J, arrows drawn downward for emission and upward for absorption, each arrow labelled with its transition energy.

Worked example 1. A hydrogen electron falls from level −0.54 eV to −1.51 eV. Find the photon's wavelength.

ΔE = -0.54 - (-1.51) = 0.97 eV
in joules: 0.97 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 1.552 × 10⁻¹⁹ J
λ = hc/ΔE = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ x 3.0 × 10⁸)/1.552 × 10⁻¹⁹
       = 1.28 × 10⁻⁶ m = 1280 nm  (infrared)

Worked example 2. Explain why the spectral lines of an element are sharp rather than continuous.

Electrons occupy quantised levels, so only specific differences
ΔE exist between them; only photons with energy exactly equal
to a difference are emitted or absorbed; since f = ΔE/h, only
specific frequencies appear - sharp lines, not a continuum.

Worked examples: combined quantum calculations

Worked example. A metal has threshold frequency 7.5 × 10¹⁴ Hz. Light of wavelength 300 nm shines on it. Find the work function and the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons.

Φ = h f0 = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ x 7.5 × 10¹⁴ = 4.97 × 10⁻¹⁹ J
    = 3.1 eV
photon energy: E = hc/λ = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ x 3.0 × 10⁸)/(3.0 × 10⁻⁷)
               = 6.63 × 10⁻¹⁹ J = 4.14 eV
KE_max = E - Φ = 6.63 × 10⁻¹⁹ - 4.97 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 1.66 × 10⁻¹⁹ J
       = 1.04 eV

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Photon energy) Calculate the energy of a photon of frequency 5.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz. Answer: E = hf = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 5.0 × 10¹⁴ = 3.3 × 10⁻¹⁹ J (≈ 2.1 eV).
  2. (Photoelectric rules) Explain why red light cannot eject electrons from a given metal however intense it is, while faint blue light can. Answer: Emission requires individual photons above the threshold frequency f₀; red photons have lower frequency and energy below the work function, so no single red photon can free an electron regardless of photon number; blue photons exceed the energy requirement, so each can eject an electron on its own.
  3. (Graph reading) State what the gradient and x-intercept of a KEₘₐₓ against frequency graph represent. Answer: The gradient is Planck's constant h; the x-intercept is the threshold frequency f₀.
  4. (Intensity) The intensity of light above the threshold frequency is doubled. State the effect on (a) the photoelectric current, (b) the maximum kinetic energy. Answer: (a) The current doubles — twice the photons, twice the electrons. (b) The maximum kinetic energy is unchanged — it depends only on frequency and the work function.
  5. (De Broglie) Explain why electrons can be diffracted by crystals but tennis balls cannot. Answer: Diffraction is noticeable when the de Broglie wavelength λ = h/(mv) is comparable to the gap size; electrons have very small momentum and wavelengths of atomic scale, while a tennis ball's momentum makes its wavelength negligibly small.
  6. (Energy levels) An atom transitions between two levels 3.0 eV apart. Find the frequency of the emitted photon. Answer: ΔE = 3.0 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 4.8 × 10⁻¹⁹ J; f = ΔE/h = 4.8 × 10⁻¹⁹/6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ = 7.2 × 10¹⁴ Hz.
  7. (Spectra) Distinguish between an emission and an absorption spectrum. Answer: An emission spectrum shows bright lines on black where excited atoms drop to lower levels; an absorption spectrum shows dark lines on a continuous spectrum where cooler gas absorbs the same wavelengths — the line positions match.
  8. (Explanation) Explain, using photon theory, why photoelectric emission is instantaneous. Answer: One photon transfers all its energy to one electron in a single interaction; there is no gradual accumulation, so emission happens immediately once the photon energy exceeds the work function.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Intensity/frequency confusion: intensity changes the electron count, not their energy; frequency changes their energy. The two-sentence distinction above is worth marks every year.
  • eV/J conversions: 1 eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Work function in eV with photon energy in joules is a guaranteed arithmetic failure — convert before subtracting.
  • Threshold frequency vs threshold wavelength: they are inversely related (f₀ = φ/h, λ₀ = c/f₀); a short threshold wavelength means a high threshold frequency. Do not mix the inequalities.
  • h units: Planck's constant is 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s (or 4.14 × 10⁻¹⁵ eV s); using the wrong pair with the wrong energy unit fails the calculation.
  • Sign errors in ΔE: emission means the electron falls, so ΔE = E_upper − E_lower is positive for the photon. Sketch the level diagram and draw the arrow before calculating.
  • De Broglie with v = fλ confusion: for matter waves λ = h/(mv); substituting the wave speed of sound or light for the electron's speed is a common error.
  • Graph axes: KEₘₐₓ against f has gradient h — but KE against intensity is flat (above threshold, no change). Label what is plotted before reading anything off.
  • Photons of light and electrons are different things: photon energy E = hf for radiation; electron kinetic energy uses ½mv² (non-relativistic). Mixing the two formulas in one question is frequent under pressure.
  • Precision: give answers to 2 or 3 significant figures with units; quote h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s from the data sheet rather than from memory.

Equations and symbols

The whole of this topic as equations, each written with its real symbols and each followed by a key naming every symbol and its unit. Where a law has more than one useful form both are given, because which one is quickest depends on which quantities the question hands you. Learn the form here and the algebraic rearrangement becomes mechanical in the exam.

22.1 Energy and momentum of a photon

E = h f
Key: E = energy of one photon (J); h = Planck constant, 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s; f = frequency of the radiation (Hz). The energy is carried in discrete packets, so a dim beam of high-frequency light delivers more energy per photon than a bright beam of low-frequency light.

f = c / λ
Key: f = frequency (Hz); c = speed of light in a vacuum, 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹; λ = wavelength (m). In a medium the speed falls but the frequency — and therefore the photon energy — is unchanged.

E = h c / λ
Key: E = photon energy (J); h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s; c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹; λ = wavelength (m). The working form, since wavelengths are what a spectrum gives you.

p = h / λ
Key: p = momentum of the photon (kg m s⁻¹ = N s); h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s; λ = wavelength (m). A photon has no mass but does have momentum, which is how radiation pressure and Compton scattering arise.

E = p c
Key: E = photon energy (J); p = photon momentum (kg m s⁻¹); c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. The massless-particle energy relation, and a quick check on the two equations above.

N = P / (h f)
Key: N = number of photons emitted per second (s⁻¹); P = power of the source (W); h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s; f = frequency (Hz). Dividing the beam power by the energy of one photon counts the photons.

22.2 The photoelectric effect

h f = Φ + KE_max
Key: h f = energy of the incident photon (J); Φ = work function, the minimum energy needed to remove an electron from the metal surface (J); KE_max = maximum kinetic energy of an emitted photoelectron (J). Einstein's equation: one photon interacts with one electron, and whatever is left after the escape cost becomes kinetic energy.

Φ = h f₀ = h c / λ₀
Key: Φ = work function (J); f₀ = threshold frequency, below which no emission occurs whatever the intensity (Hz); λ₀ = threshold wavelength (m); h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s; c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. The threshold exists because a single photon must carry the whole escape energy — intensity cannot make up the deficit, which is the observation classical wave theory cannot explain.

KE_max = e V_s
Key: KE_max = maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons (J); e = elementary charge, 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C; V_s = stopping potential, the reverse p.d. that just stops the photocurrent (V). The stopping potential measures the fastest electrons directly, which is how KE_max is found in the experiment.

KE_max = h (f − f₀)
Key: KE_max = maximum kinetic energy (J); h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s; f = incident frequency (Hz); f₀ = threshold frequency (Hz). The linear graph: KE_max against f is a straight line of gradient h, intercept −Φ on the energy axis and f₀ on the frequency axis.

gradient = h, y-intercept = −Φ
Key: on a graph of KE_max (J) against frequency f (Hz); gradient = Planck constant (J s); y-intercept = minus the work function (−J). This is the standard "use the graph" question, and it works for any metal — only the intercept moves.

1 eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J
Key: eV = electronvolt, the energy gained by one electron accelerated through 1 V. Convert before substituting into h f = Φ + KE_max unless every term is in eV.

22.3 Wave–particle duality

λ = h / p
Key: λ = de Broglie wavelength of the particle (m); h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s; p = momentum of the particle (kg m s⁻¹). Every particle has a wavelength; it is immeasurably small for a cricket ball and comparable to atomic spacing for an electron.

λ = h / (m v)
Key: λ = de Broglie wavelength (m); m = mass of the particle (kg); v = its speed (m s⁻¹); h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s. The non-relativistic form, valid while v ≪ c.

p = √(2 m KE)
Key: p = momentum (kg m s⁻¹); m = mass (kg); KE = kinetic energy (J). From KE = ½ m v² and p = m v, eliminating v.

λ = h / √(2 m KE)
Key: λ = de Broglie wavelength (m); m = mass of the particle (kg); KE = its kinetic energy (J); h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s. The form to use when the energy is given rather than the speed.

e V = ½ m v², so λ = h / √(2 m e V)
Key: e = elementary charge, 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C; V = accelerating potential difference (V); m = mass of the electron, 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg; v = its speed (m s⁻¹); λ = de Broglie wavelength (m); h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s. An electron accelerated through 100 V has a wavelength of about 0.12 nm — the same order as atomic spacing, which is why electron diffraction works and electron microscopes resolve what light cannot.

22.4 Energy levels in atoms and line spectra

ΔE = E_upper − E_lower = h f = h c / λ
Key: ΔE = energy difference between two levels (J); E_upper, E_lower = energies of the levels involved (J); h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s; f = frequency of the emitted or absorbed photon (Hz); c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹; λ = its wavelength (m). Emission when an electron falls, absorption when one is raised.

λ = h c / ΔE
Key: λ = wavelength of the line (m); h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s; c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹; ΔE = level separation (J). Rearranged for the wavelength question; convert ΔE from eV to joules first.

E_n = −13.6 / n² eV (hydrogen)
Key: E_n = energy of the nth level of the hydrogen atom (eV); n = principal quantum number, 1, 2, 3 …; the negative sign means the electron is bound, with zero energy at infinite separation. The spacing between levels shrinks as n grows, which is why the spectral lines bunch together towards a series limit.

ionisation energy = 0 − E₁ = 13.6 eV (hydrogen)
Key: E₁ = energy of the ground state (eV). The energy needed to remove an electron completely from the ground state; for any other level it is 0 − E_n, which is smaller.

line spectra: ΔE fixed, so λ fixed
Key: because only discrete level differences exist, only photons of those exact energies can be emitted or absorbed, so a spectrum shows sharp lines rather than a continuous band. Each element has its own set of levels and therefore its own signature lines — the basis of spectroscopic identification.

title: IGCSE English as a Second Language: Writing Tasks and Themes
Further Algebra — Study Notes
content:
Further Algebra

Polynomial Division and the Remainder Theorem

Divide to rewrite p(x) = (x − a)q(x) + r. The remainder when dividing by (x − a) equals p(a).

Example: p(x) = x³ − 2x² + 5. p(2) = 8 − 8 + 5 = 5, so dividing by (x − 2) leaves remainder 5.

If p(a) = 0, then (x − a) is a factor — that is the factor theorem. Divide out fully to reduce a cubic to a quadratic and factorise completely.

The Modulus Function

|x| measures distance from zero: |x| = x for x ≥ 0, −x for x < 0. Its graph is V-shaped.

Solving |2x − 1| = 5: split into 2x − 1 = 5 or 2x − 1 = −5, giving x = 3 or −2.

Inequalities: |2x − 1| < 5 becomes −5 < 2x − 1 < 5, so −2 < x < 3.

Partial Fractions

Reverse of combining fractions — needed before binomial expansion of rational functions.

  • Repeated linear: (4x + 1)/(x + 1)² = A/(x + 1) + B/(x + 1)²
  • Distinct linear: (7x + 4)/(x + 1)(x + 2) = A/(x + 1) + B/(x + 2)

Example: cover the (x + 1) factor with x = −1: B = 3; then compare coefficients for A = 4.

Exam tips: for |ax + b| > c, remember two separate regions; check factor-theorem roots by substitution before long division.

Exam method: partial fractions

Partial fractions split a rational function into simpler fractions whose sum equals the original. Before splitting, check the degrees: if the numerator has degree at least that of the denominator, divide first to get a polynomial plus a proper fraction.

For distinct linear factors (x − p)(x − q), write the expression as A/(x − p) + B/(x − q). Multiply through by the denominator and compare coefficients, or substitute x = p and x = q to find A and B directly. This substitution is the cover-up method and is the fastest route when the factors are linear and distinct.

A repeated factor (x − p)² needs two terms, A/(x − p) + B/(x − p)². An irreducible quadratic factor such as x² + 1 needs a linear numerator over it, (Ax + B)/(x² + 1).

Partial fractions are used to integrate rational functions, so the split is often followed by a logarithmic integral. Check the answer by recombining the fractions at one simple value of x.

Exam cue: State the form of the partial fractions before finding the constants, because the form is credited separately from the values.

title: Edexcel IAL Computer Science: File Organisation, Data Types and Floating Point
content:
Edexcel IAL Computer Science: File Organisation, Data Types and Floating Point

Pearson Edexcel International Advanced Level in Computer Science, Unit 3 Advanced Computer Science: files and their organisation and access, user-defined data types, and floating-point representation and manipulation. This note goes beneath the arrays and records of AS into how data physically lives on backing storage and how real numbers are stored and computed — the two topics where exam questions demand mechanism, not definitions. Every pointer movement and every normalisation step is traced on a diagram.

File concepts and access methods

A file is a named collection of records on secondary storage; a record is a collection of fields describing one entity; records may be fixed-length (each record the same size — simple addressing, wasted space for short records) or variable-length (space-efficient, but locating records needs length markers or delimiters). A key field identifies each record uniquely and drives access.

Access methodMechanismStrengthsWeaknesses
SequentialRecords read/written in key order, one after anotherEfficient for batch processing and tape/streamed media; simpleSlow for random queries (average half the file scanned); updates need rewriting
Direct (random)Record located by key → address (hashing or an index)Immediate single-record retrieval regardless of file sizeNeeds hashing/index infrastructure; may leave unused slots
Indexed sequential (ISAM)Sequential file plus an index of keys → addressesBoth fast random lookup and ordered sequential processingIndex maintenance cost; index itself can fragment
Sequential access worked: pay run over a 1000-record file.

  Open file; read record 1, process, write to output; read record 2...;
  one pass, one read per record - O(n) with tiny constants: ideal for batch.

Direct access worked: find one customer account.

  Hash the account number to a slot: address = hash(key); read once at that
  address - O(1). But finding "all accounts in London" needs scanning or a
  secondary index - the query pattern decides the method.

Record address arithmetic (fixed-length):
  record i's byte address = start + i x recordSize
  With 32-byte records starting at byte 100: record 5 = 100 + 5x32 = 260.
  Variable-length records break this arithmetic - a pointer table or length
  prefix is needed instead.

File organisation in commercial systems: heap files (unordered, append anywhere), sorted files (binary-searchable, expensive insertion), hashed files (O(1) by key, poor at ranges), clustered files (records grouped by a related key — e.g. all of a customer's orders physically together). The exam wants the choice justified by the workload: point lookup, range scan, or ordered processing.

File maintenance operations: serial update (new transaction file + old master → new master, one pass), random update (locate and rewrite one record), and the failure handling around them (transaction logs keep a recovery trail — the link to the DBMS recovery work in the database note).

File organisation in database systems

Relational tables are files underneath, and the same organisation choices appear as storage-engine decisions. Heap storage appends rows cheaply (good for bulk loads, poor for key lookup); sorted storage supports binary search but rewrites on insertion; hashed storage gives O(1) key access but no ordering; clustered storage groups rows by a related key (all a customer's orders together), making that join a sequential read. Secondary indexes are files of (key, pointer) pairs that restore fast lookup on non-key fields, at the cost of maintaining them on every write. The exam's design question wants the workload named first — point lookup, range scan, ordered report — and the organisation chosen for it.

Worked example: index selection for a query workload

A library table book(ISBN [PK], title, author, year, copies) serves three queries:

  Q1 find by ISBN           -> the primary key index already answers this
  Q2 find by author         -> secondary index on author (point lookup by name)
  Q3 list all books of a year, in title order -> composite index (year, title)
                                so the range scan returns rows already sorted

Writing cost: each additional index slows INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE (every index
must be maintained) and costs storage - so index the read paths the workload
actually uses, not every column. The rule of thumb earns the mark: indexes
serve queries, constraints serve correctness.

User-defined data types

Primitive types cannot express domain structure, so languages offer composition. A record (struct) groups named fields of differing types; enumerated types name a finite set of legal values (DAY = {Mon…Sun}); arrays/sequences group like values; union/variant types hold one of several shapes; and classes bundle records with behaviour (see the OOP note).

Worked: a payroll record type and its use.

  TYPE Employee = RECORD
      empID     : STRING
      name      : STRING
      payGrade  : (A, B, C)          // enumerated: illegal values impossible
      hours     : REAL
      rate      : REAL
  END RECORD

  VAR e : Employee
  e.empID <- "E104"; e.rate <- 12.50; e.hours <- 37.5

  pay <- e.hours * e.rate   // 37.5 x 12.50 = 468.75

Benefits visible here: typed fields prevent "hours = "Tues"" at the type
level; the enum prevents payGrade = "Z"; and grouping means one array element
holds the whole employee - ARRAY[1:500] OF Employee is a payroll file in
memory. Records of records (nested) express containment: a Department record
holds an array of Employee sub-records.

Static versus dynamic typing is the exam's comparison: static types (Pascal, Java) check at compile time, catching whole classes of errors before run and enabling optimisation; dynamic types (Python) defer checks to run time, gaining flexibility at the cost of late error discovery. User-defined types sit on the static side: they make invalid states unrepresentable.

Floating point: representation and manipulation

Recalling the AS construction (value = mantissa × 2^(exponent−bias), normalised with a hidden leading 1), this note adds the manipulation rules and their pitfalls.

Addition in floating point, step by step with rounding:

  x = 1.1011 x 2^2   (mantissa 1011, exponent 2)
  y = 1.0110 x 2^0   (mantissa 0110, exponent 0)

  1. ALIGN: shift the smaller mantissa right by the exponent difference (2),
     truncating bits shifted off the end (this is where precision is lost):
     y' = 0.0101(10...) x 2^2   (dropped bits rounded: 10 -> round up here)
  2. ADD the mantissas:
     1.1011 + 0.0101 = 10.0000 x 2^2
  3. RENORMALISE: 10.0000 x 2^2 = 1.0000 x 2^3
  4. ROUND to the available mantissa bits (here exact), check exponent range.

Multiplication differs: multiply mantissas, ADD exponents, normalise once -
no alignment step, so no alignment truncation:
  (1.1011 x 2^2) x (1.0110 x 2^0):
  mantissas: 1.1011 x 1.0110 = 10.0110(01...) -> 1.0011(0) x 2^1 after
  normalise; exponents: 2 + 0 = 1. Result ≈ 1.0011 x 2^1 = 2.375.

Division: divide mantissas, subtract exponents, normalise.

Errors and their names: rounding error (values between representable numbers are rounded — 0.1 is not exactly representable), absorption/cancellation (adding a large and small float loses the small one's digits; subtracting nearly equal values loses significant figures), underflow (result too small for the exponent field → zero or denormal), overflow (too large → infinity). Standards: IEEE 754 defines single (32-bit: 1+8+23) and double (64-bit: 1+11+52) formats, special values (±0, ±∞, NaN), and rounding modes.

Cancellation worked:

  x = 1.0000001 x 2^7 = 128.000128
  y = 1.0000000 x 2^7 = 128.000000
  x - y = 0.000128 - exact in this case, but if the mantissa held only 6
  significant bits, x and y would round to the SAME stored value and the
  difference would be 0.000000. "Why is (x + y) - x not always y?" is
  exactly this: the alignment step of x + y may have rounded y away.

Money in floats (again, now with the mechanism): 0.1 + 0.2 in IEEE 754
double = 0.30000000000000004, because 0.1 is stored as 0.1000000000000000055...
and 0.2 as 0.2000000000000000111...; the sum's alignment and rounding leave
the residue. Integer pence avoid the whole class of error.

Worked example: choosing storage for three problems

1. Payroll processed every Friday for 800 employees (all records, in ID
   order): sequential access over a sorted file - one pass, O(n), no index
   maintenance needed.

2. A cashier pulling one account by number on demand: direct access - hash
   the key to an address, O(1) retrieval; the query is always by unique key.

3. A clinic system that takes appointments by patient and occasionally
   lists all patients alphabetically: indexed sequential - the index makes
   the point lookup fast while the ordered scan serves the listing; or a
   database (with the same indexing ideas) if concurrent updates matter.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Saying direct access "reads the record directly from the key" — the key is hashed or looked up in an index to get an address; something must translate one to the other.
  • Quoting record-address arithmetic on variable-length files; it needs a pointer table or length prefix.
  • Forgetting alignment in floating-point addition questions — the exponent difference dictates the right shift, and shifted-off bits are where error enters.
  • Confusing overflow/underflow with rounding error: range failures versus precision loss.
  • Claiming (x + y) − x = y always; cancellation and absorption make float algebra non-associative.
  • Choosing variable-length records when the exam's workload is fixed-size batch processing (or vice versa) without reasoning.
  • Describing enums as "shorthand for numbers"; their point is restricting a field to legal values.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Unit 3, 4 marks). Compare sequential and direct file access.

Answer: Sequential access reads records in order from the start — one pass, efficient for batch processing of whole files (payroll), but finding one record scans on average half the file. Direct access computes a record's location from its key (hashing or index) and reads it immediately — O(1) retrieval for single-record queries (cashier lookups), but it needs the hashing/index infrastructure and suits random rather than ordered workloads.

Question 2 (Unit 3, 4 marks). Explain two differences between fixed-length and variable-length records.

Answer: Fixed-length records reserve the same space for each record, so any record's address is arithmetic (start + i × size) and access is fast, but short records waste space and field sizes are capped. Variable-length records store only what each needs, saving space and allowing long fields, but locating records requires length prefixes or a pointer table and processing is more complex.

Question 3 (Unit 3, 4 marks). Describe how two floating-point numbers are added and where precision can be lost.

Answer: Align the exponents by shifting the smaller mantissa right by their difference (bits shifted off are truncated/rounded), add the mantissas, renormalise the result, and round to the available mantissa bits. Precision is lost during alignment (truncated bits) and the final rounding; if the exponent difference is large, the small number's contribution may vanish entirely (absorption).

Question 4 (Unit 3, 3 marks). Explain why floating-point arithmetic can give (0.1 + 0.2) ≠ 0.3.

Answer: 0.1 and 0.2 have no exact binary representation, so each is stored as the nearest representable mantissa × power of two; their tiny errors propagate through the alignment and addition, and the sum rounds to a value slightly above 0.3 (0.30000000000000004). Float algebra is approximate — a reason to use integer minor units or decimal types for money.

Question 5 (Unit 3, 4 marks). Explain the purpose of user-defined data types and give two examples.

Answer: User-defined types express domain structure that primitives cannot, making invalid data impossible to represent. A record (struct) groups named fields of different types describing one entity (employee: string ID, real rate); an enumerated type names the complete legal value set (payGrade ∈ {A, B, C}), so any other value is rejected at compile time. Both improve readability and safety over loose collections of primitives.

Question 6 (Unit 3, 3 marks). State what overflow and underflow mean in floating-point arithmetic.

Answer: Overflow is a result too large in magnitude for the exponent field to represent — it becomes infinity (or an error). Underflow is a result too small in magnitude for the smallest normal exponent — it becomes zero or a denormal number. Both are range failures of the format, distinct from rounding error, which affects precision within the representable range.

Files store data; databases govern it — the next note is the design and language layer on top.

title: Organic Nitrogen Compounds: Amines, Amides, Amino Acids and Proteins Revision Notes
content:
Organic Nitrogen Compounds: Amines, Amides, Amino Acids and Proteins A2 Level Chemistry

These revision notes cover Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH15 Topic 19, focusing on the structures, preparations, reactions, and physical properties of amines, amides, amino acids, and polymers including polyamides and addition polymers, alongside Core Practical 15.

Nomenclature and Formulae of Nitrogen Compounds

Students must be able to name and draw structural, displayed, and skeletal formulae for amides, primary amines, and amino acids according to IUPAC rules.

  • Primary aliphatic amines are named by adding the suffix -amine to the alkyl chain, such as butylamine (CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂NH₂).
  • Aromatic amines feature an amino group directly attached to a benzene ring, such as phenylamine (C₆H₅NH₂).
  • Amides are named based on the corresponding carboxylic acid chain with the suffix -amide, such as ethanamide (CH₃CONH₂).
  • Amino acids contain both an amine group and a carboxylic acid group, typically on the same carbon, such as 2-aminopropanoic acid (CH₃CH(NH₂)COOH).
  • Structural formulae show every atom and bond clearly in displayed formulae, while skeletal formulae omit carbon and hydrogen labels from carbon chains for simplicity.

Reactions and Basicity of Amines

Amines act as bases due to the lone pair of electrons on the nitrogen atom, which can accept a proton.

  • Primary aliphatic amines like butylamine are miscible with water due to hydrogen bonding between the nitrogen and hydrogen atoms of water and the amine.
  • Basicity varies: ammonia has a base dissociation constant dependent on its lone pair availability; primary aliphatic amines are stronger bases than ammonia because alkyl groups push electron density onto the nitrogen via the positive inductive effect, increasing lone pair availability.
  • Primary aromatic amines like phenylamine are weaker bases than ammonia because the nitrogen lone pair delocalises into the delocalised π-system of the benzene ring, decreasing its availability to accept protons.
  • Reaction with water: primary aliphatic amines dissolve to form alkaline solutions containing hydroxide ions, for example CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂NH₂ + H₂O gives CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂NH₃⁺ + OH⁻.
  • Reaction with acids: amines react with mineral acids like hydrochloric acid to form soluble alkylammonium salts, such as CH₃NH₂ + HCl gives CH₃NH₃⁺Cl⁻.
  • Reaction with halogenoalkanes: primary amines react with halogenoalkanes via nucleophilic substitution to produce secondary and tertiary amines.
  • Reaction with acyl chlorides: primary amines react with ethanoyl chloride to form N-substituted amides, releasing misty fumes of hydrogen chloride.
  • Reaction with copper(II) ions: dropwise addition of aqueous copper(II) sulfate to an excess of an aliphatic amine like butylamine forms a pale blue precipitate that dissolves in excess amine to form a deep blue complex ion, [Cu(CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂NH₂)₄(H₂O)²]²⁺.

Preparation of Aliphatic and Aromatic Amines

Different synthetic routes are required to produce aliphatic versus aromatic amines.

  • Preparation of primary aliphatic amines from halogenoalkanes: heating a haloalkane with excess ethanolic ammonia in a sealed tube via nucleophilic substitution; excess ammonia is essential to prevent further substitution leading to secondary and tertiary amines.
  • Preparation of primary aliphatic amines from nitriles: reduction of a nitrile using lithium aluminium hydride in dry ether followed by dilute acid, or catalytic hydrogenation using hydrogen and a nickel catalyst.
  • Preparation of aromatic amines: reduction of an aromatic nitro-compound, such as nitrobenzene, using tin and concentrated hydrochloric acid heated under reflux, followed by the addition of sodium hydroxide to release the free phenylamine base.

Azo Dyes and Diazonium Salts

Aromatic amines undergo specific reactions involving nitrous acid to form useful colorants.

  • Reaction of aromatic amines with nitrous acid: phenylamine reacts with nitrous acid (formed in situ from sodium nitrite and hydrochloric acid) at temperatures below 5°C to form a benzenediazonium ion (C₆H₅N₂⁺Cl⁻).
  • Coupling reaction: the benzenediazonium ion undergoes an electrophilic substitution coupling reaction with alkaline phenol at low temperatures to form a brightly coloured azo dye, such as 4-hydroxyphenylazobenzene.

Preparation and Properties of Amides

Amides are carboxylic acid derivatives containing the carbonyl-nitrogen bond.

  • Preparation: amides are prepared from acyl chlorides by reacting them with ammonia or a primary amine at room temperature, for example ethanoyl chloride with ammonia gives ethanamide and hydrogen chloride.
  • Hydrolysis: amides undergo acid hydrolysis when heated with dilute hydrochloric acid to yield a carboxylic acid and an ammonium salt, or alkaline hydrolysis with sodium hydroxide to yield a carboxylate salt and ammonia gas.

Polymers: Polyamides and Addition Polymers

Polymerisation processes link small monomer units into large macromolecules.

  • Condensation polymerisation: involves the reaction of monomers with two functional groups, releasing a small molecule such as water or hydrogen chloride; polyamides like nylon-6,6 are formed from hexane-1,6-diamine and hexanedioic acid.
  • Proteins are natural polyamides formed from amino acid monomers linked by peptide bonds.
  • Addition polymerisation: involves unsaturated monomers opening their double bonds without eliminating small molecules; examples include poly(propenamide) and poly(ethenol).
  • Structural formulae: students must be able to draw repeat units of nylon, proteins, poly(propenamide), and poly(ethenol) enclosed in square brackets with an extension bond outside the brackets.
  • Physical properties of polyamides: strong intermolecular hydrogen bonds form between the polar carbonyl and N-H groups of adjacent polymer chains, resulting in high tensile strength and high melting points.
  • Solubility of poly(ethenol): despite being an addition polymer, poly(ethenol) is soluble in water because its numerous pendant alcohol (-OH) groups form extensive hydrogen bonds with water molecules, making it ideal for soluble laundry bags and liquid-detergent capsules (liquitabs).

Amino Acids, Zwitterions, and Peptides

Amino acids exhibit amphoteric properties and form complex structural hierarchies in proteins.

  • Zwitterions: in the solid state and near neutral pH, amino acids exist as dipolar ions called zwitterions, ⁺H₃NCH(R)COO⁻, carrying no net overall charge due to internal proton transfer from the carboxylic acid group to the amine group.
  • Acidity and basicity: at the isoelectric point, the zwitterion has a net charge of zero. In strong acid solutions, the amino group accepts a proton to form a positive cation; in strong alkali solutions, the carboxylic acid group loses a proton to form a negative anion.
  • Optical activity: aqueous solutions of standard amino acids contain chiral carbon atoms (except glycine) and rotate plane-polarised monochromatic light because they are optically active.
  • Peptide bond formation: a peptide link (-CONH-) forms when the carboxylic acid group of one amino acid condenses with the amine group of another, eliminating a molecule of water via condensation polymerisation.
  • Protein structure: proteins possess primary structure (amino acid sequence), secondary structure (alpha-helices and beta-pleated sheets held by hydrogen bonds between C=O and N-H groups), and tertiary structure (3D folding stabilized by ionic bonds, hydrogen bonds, and disulfide bridges). Complete hydrolysis of proteins with hot concentrated hydrochloric acid yields a mixture of constituent amino acids.

Core Practical 15: Analysis of Unknowns

Practical analysis involves systematic chemical tests to identify functional groups in organic and inorganic unknowns.

  • Testing for amines: use universal indicator to confirm an alkaline pH, or react with ethanoyl chloride to observe misty fumes of hydrogen chloride.
  • Testing for amino acids: use paper chromatography followed by locating agents like ninhydrin to reveal purple spots.
  • Testing for amides: warm with sodium hydroxide and test evolved ammonia gas with damp red litmus paper, which turns blue.

Typical mistakes

  • Mistake: stating that alkyl groups attract electron density in amines. Correction: alkyl groups push electron density onto the nitrogen atom via a positive inductive effect.
  • Mistake: drawing the zwitterion structure with a neutral carboxylic acid and amine group at neutral pH. Correction: draw the zwitterion with a protonated amine (⁺H₃N-) and deprotonated carboxylate (-COO⁻).
  • Mistake: omitting the repeat brackets or extension bonds when drawing polymer repeat units. Correction: always enclose repeat units in square brackets with bonds extending outside the brackets.
  • Mistake: confusing addition polymerisation with condensation polymerisation. Correction: addition polymerisation involves unsaturated monomers with no eliminated small molecules, whereas condensation polymerisation eliminates small molecules like water.

Exam-style questions

  2. Explain why phenylamine is a weaker base than butylamine. Answer: Phenylamine's nitrogen lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring, decreasing proton acceptance ability, whereas butylamine's alkyl group pushes electron density onto nitrogen via a positive inductive effect, increasing lone pair availability.
  5. Describe the reagents and conditions needed to prepare phenylamine from nitrobenzene. Answer: Heat nitrobenzene under reflux with tin (Sn) and concentrated hydrochloric acid, followed by addition of sodium hydroxide.
  8. Draw the structural repeat unit of nylon-6,6. Answer: [−NH−(CH₂)₆−NH−CO−(CH₂)₄−CO−].
  11. Explain why poly(ethenol) dissolves in water while poly(ethene) does not. Answer: Poly(ethenol) has pendant −OH groups that form hydrogen bonds with water molecules, whereas poly(ethene) is non-polar and cannot form hydrogen bonds.
  14. Write the ionic equation for the reaction of butylamine with hydrochloric acid. Answer: CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂NH₂ + H⁺ gives CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂NH₃⁺.

Use these notes alongside past paper practice questions to test your knowledge of reaction conditions and mechanisms. Revise aromatic chemistry and polymer chemistry next to consolidate your understanding of WCH15.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Basicity, applied to amines: alkyl groups donate electron density to the nitrogen, so CH₃NH₂ is more basic than NH₃. Phenylamine is less basic than NH₃, because the lone pair on nitrogen delocalises into the benzene ring. Give that delocalisation as the reason, not just the fact.
  • Diazonium coupling, applied to benzenediazonium chloride with phenol: the reaction is carried out at 0–5 °C in alkaline conditions, and it gives an azo dye through electrophilic attack by the diazonium ion on the phenoxide ring. The –N=N– group links the two aromatic rings.
  • Amide formation, applied to ethanoyl chloride and ammonia: the nitrogen lone pair attacks the carbonyl carbon, and HCl is lost. Use two equivalents of ammonia, one to react and one to neutralise the HCl formed.
  • Amino acids: at the isoelectric point, the amino acid exists as a zwitterion with both NH₃⁺ and COO⁻. Its net charge is zero and it does not move in an electric field. Give the zwitterion structure when asked about the form of the amino acid in solution.

title: Computational Thinking and Problem-Solving — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Computational Thinking and Problem-Solving

Computer Science — A2. A recursive routine calls itself with a smaller input and a base case that stops the recursion. Elegant for trees and divide-and-conquer, but each call consumes stack space — deep recursion can overflow. Any recursion can be rewritten with a loop and explicit stack.

Key areas to revise

  • Thinking Ahead, Abstractly, Systematically
  • Recursion
  • Searching and Sorting
  • Testing

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

title: Waves — Study Notes
content:
Waves

Progressive waves

  • A progressive wave transfers energy without transferring matter. Its speed is v = fλ, where f is the frequency and λ the wavelength. Period T = 1/f.
  • Phase difference: two points separated by one wavelength are in phase. Points separated by half a wavelength are in antiphase.

Transverse and longitudinal waves

  • Transverse: the oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer (e.g. light, waves on a string).
  • Longitudinal: the oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer (e.g. sound in air, compressions and rarefactions).

Doppler effect for sound

When a source moves towards an observer, the observed frequency is higher and the wavelength is shorter. When it moves away, the observed frequency is lower and the wavelength is longer. The speed of sound in the medium does not change.

Electromagnetic spectrum

All electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum. In order of increasing wavelength: gamma rays, X-rays, ultraviolet, visible light, infrared, microwaves, radio waves. Frequency increases in the reverse order.

Polarisation

Only transverse waves can be polarised. Polarisation restricts the oscillations to a single plane. Longitudinal waves such as sound cannot be polarised.

Worked example: a wave has frequency 50 Hz and wavelength 6.0 m. Its speed is v = fλ = 50 × 6.0 = 300 m s⁻¹.

Exam tips: learn the spectrum order in terms of wavelength, not frequency. For the Doppler effect, state which way the source moves relative to the observer. Only transverse waves can show polarisation.

title: Materials: Deformation — Study Notes
content:
Materials: deformation

Stress and strain

  • Stress = F ÷ A, where A is the cross-sectional area perpendicular to the force. Unit: pascal (Pa), where 1 Pa = 1 N m⁻².
  • Strain = extension ÷ original length. It has no unit.

Young modulus

Young modulus E = stress ÷ strain, measured in the region where stress is proportional to strain. Unit: Pa.

Force–extension behaviour

  • Up to the limit of proportionality, extension is proportional to force (Hooke's law), and the graph is a straight line through the origin.
  • Up to the elastic limit, the material returns to its original length when unloaded. This is elastic deformation.
  • Beyond the elastic limit, the material is plastically deformed and does not return to its original length. The graph curves, and the energy in the extension is not recovered.

Energy stored

The elastic energy stored in a stretched material equals the area under its force–extension graph up to the point of interest. For a spring obeying Hooke's law, E = ½Fx = ½kx².

Worked example: a wire of cross-sectional area 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ m² is pulled by 500 N. Stress = 500 ÷ (2.0 × 10⁻⁴) = 2.5 × 10⁶ Pa. If it extends by 1.0 mm from an original length of 2.0 m, strain = 0.001 ÷ 2.0 = 5.0 × 10⁻⁴, so E = 2.5 × 10⁶ ÷ 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ = 5.0 × 10⁹ Pa.

Exam tips: convert the area to m² and the extension to m before calculating. Strain has no unit, so do not write a unit for it. Say "the limit of proportionality" and "the elastic limit" as separate ideas.

Stored elastic energy and Hooke's law

Within the limit of proportionality, extension is proportional to force, F = kx, and the stiffness k depends on the material and its dimensions. The elastic strain energy stored in a stretched wire is equal to the area under the force-extension graph, E = ½Fx. For a material, the Young modulus E = stress / strain. Beyond the elastic limit the material deforms plastically and does not return to its original length.

Exam tip: state the limit of proportionality on the graph, because the energy formula only applies while the material obeys Hooke's law.

Worked example: a stretched wire with a load

A steel wire 1.5 m long and 0.80 mm in diameter is loaded with a 20 kg mass. The cross-sectional area is π(0.40 × 10⁻³)² ≈ 5.03 × 10⁻⁷ m². The force is F = mg = 20 × 9.81 = 196 N, so the stress is 196 ÷ (5.03 × 10⁻⁷) ≈ 3.9 × 10⁸ Pa.

If the wire stretches by 1.1 mm, the strain is 0.0011 ÷ 1.5 ≈ 7.3 × 10⁻⁴, and E = stress ÷ strain = 3.9 × 10⁸ ÷ 7.3 × 10⁻⁴ ≈ 5.3 × 10¹¹ Pa. Quote the Young modulus with its unit and to two significant figures, and check that the value is in the range expected for the material: steel is roughly 2 × 10¹¹ Pa, so a result far from that points to an area or unit error.

Comparing materials

  • A stiff material has a large Young modulus: for a given stress, it produces a small strain.
  • A brittle material fractures soon after the elastic limit, with little or no plastic deformation, so its graph stops abruptly.
  • A ductile material, such as copper, undergoes large plastic deformation before it breaks, so its graph shows a long curved section after the elastic limit.

Area under the graph

For a non-linear force–extension graph, the energy stored is still the area under the curve. Count the squares, or split the region into a triangle and a rectangle, and convert the result to joules using the scale factors. Only the energy up to the elastic limit can be recovered when the load is removed; the rest is dissipated as heat.

Hysteresis and loading cycles

When a material is loaded and then unloaded, the unloading curve may not retrace the loading curve. The region enclosed between the two curves is energy dissipated per cycle, often as heat. Rubber bands and car tyres show this, which is why they warm up when repeatedly deformed.

  • Strain is extension divided by the original length, so do not use the stretched length.
  • Young modulus has the unit of pascal, the same as stress, because strain is dimensionless.
  • Only a sample loaded within its elastic region returns to the same length; a permanent set after unloading means plastic deformation has occurred.

Common errors that lose marks

  • Using the diameter as the radius in the area formula, which quadruples the area.
  • Calling the gradient of the stress-strain graph the "stiffness". Stiffness belongs to the force-extension graph; the gradient of stress against strain gives E.
  • Quoting Hooke's law as valid beyond the limit of proportionality, where extension is no longer proportional to force.

title: Algebra — Inequalities — Study Notes
content:
Algebra — Inequalities

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): solving linear inequalities, integer solution sets, shading regions on graphs (linear programming context).

1. Solving

Like equations, but reverse the sign when multiplying/dividing by a negative: −2x ≥ 6 ⇒ x ≤ −3.

Example: 3x − 5 < 2x + 1 ⇒ x < 6.

2. Integer solutions

−1 ≤ x < 4 ⇒ x ∈ {−1, 0, 1, 2, 3}. Closed endpoint for ≤/≥, open for </>.

3. Double inequalities

Handle both sides: −3 < 2x + 1 ≤ 7 → −4 < 2x ≤ 6 → −2 < x ≤ 3.

4. Shading regions

  • Draw the boundary line: dashed for </>, solid for ≤/≥.
  • Test a point (usually (0,0)) to pick the wanted side; shade the unwanted side or label the wanted region.
  • Feasible region satisfies all constraints simultaneously.

Example: y ≤ 2x + 1: solid line, test (0,0): 0 ≤ 1 ✓ → region containing origin.

Exam tips: never divide by an unknown sign — move x terms first; list integer solutions inside curly brackets; state which region you shade.

title: A Level Mathematics: Sampling and Estimation
content:
A Level Mathematics: Sampling and Estimation

Statistics works by measuring a sample and reasoning about a population that was never fully measured. That inference is only as good as the sample: a biased sample cannot be rescued by a larger one. This note covers how samples are drawn, what the sampling distribution of the mean is, why the central limit theorem makes normal methods work for almost any population, and how to build and interpret a confidence interval.

Populations, samples and parameters

A parameter describes the population and is usually unknown; a statistic describes the sample and is known. The whole of estimation is the attempt to learn a parameter from a statistic, and naming the two correctly is the first mark in many questions.

parameter: mu (population mean), σ (population sd), p (proportion)
statistic: x-bar (sample mean), s (sample sd), p-hat (sample proportion)
an estimator is unbiased if its expected value equals the parameter

Worked example. A sample of 40 light bulbs has mean life 1,020 hours. Identify the parameter and the statistic.

statistic: x-bar = 1020 hours (known, from the sample)
parameter: mu, the mean life of all bulbs produced (unknown)
the estimate of mu is 1020 hours, with an uncertainty to be quantified

Sampling methods and bias

The method determines whether the sample can speak for the population at all. Every named method is a compromise between practicality and representativeness, and the exam asks you to identify which compromise a described survey has made.

MethodHow it worksWeakness
simple randomevery member equally likely, chosen by numberneeds a complete list
systematicevery k-th member from a random startperiodic patterns can bias it
stratifiedsample each subgroup in proportionneeds known subgroup sizes
quotafill fixed categories by interviewer choiceinterviewer bias, not random
opportunitywhoever is availablestrongly unrepresentative

Worked example. A surveyor interviews shoppers in a town centre on a weekday morning about working hours. Identify the bias.

people free on a weekday morning are systematically different from the
population: the employed, the housebound and shift workers are under-represented
this is an opportunity sample with selection bias, and no sample size fixes it

The sampling distribution of the mean

Take many samples of size n, compute each mean, and plot them: the result is the sampling distribution, and its spread is smaller than the population's by a factor of √n.

if X has mean mu and variance σ², then x-bar has
mean = mu
variance = σ²/n
standard error = σ/sqrt n

Worked example. A population has mean 50 and standard deviation 12. For samples of 36, find the mean and standard error of the sample mean.

mean of x-bar = 50
standard error = 12/6 = 2

Worked example 2 (effect of quadrupling n). What happens to the standard error if the sample size is quadrupled?

standard error = σ/√(4n) = (σ/sqrt n)/2
it halves; quadrupling the sample buys a factor of two in precision

That square-root relationship is why doubling precision costs four times the data, and it is a standard exam comment.

The central limit theorem

Whatever shape the population has, the distribution of the sample mean becomes approximately normal as n grows. That is what licenses normal methods for non-normal populations, and it is the single most important result in the topic.

for large n (in practice n >= 30), x-bar is approximately N(mu, σ²/n)
the population itself need not be normal
if the population is already normal, the result is exact for any n

Worked example. A population is strongly skewed with mean 20 and standard deviation 10. Describe the distribution of the mean of samples of 50.

by the central limit theorem, approximately normal
mean 20, standard error 10/sqrt 50 = 1.414
so x-bar is approximately N(20, 2.0)

Confidence intervals for a mean

A confidence interval gives a range of plausible values for the parameter, with a stated long-run success rate. It is not a probability that the parameter lies in this particular interval — the parameter is fixed, the interval is random.

95% interval for mu: x-bar +/- 1.96 (σ/sqrt n)
99% interval: x-bar +/- 2.5758 (σ/sqrt n)
with s estimated from the sample, replace σ by s (large n)
wider interval: more confidence, less precision

Worked example. A sample of 64 measurements has mean 25.4 and known standard deviation 4. Find a 95% confidence interval for the population mean.

standard error = 4/8 = 0.5
margin = 1.96 × 0.5 = 0.98
interval: 25.4 +/- 0.98 = (24.42, 26.38)

Worked example 2 (99%). The same data at 99%.

margin = 2.5758 × 0.5 = 1.288
interval: (24.11, 26.69), wider as expected

Worked example 3 (required sample size). How large a sample is needed for the 95% margin to be at most 0.2?

1.96 × 4/sqrt n <= 0.2
sqrt n >= 39.2
n >= 1537, so the sample must be at least 1537

Confidence intervals for a proportion

The sample proportion is a mean in disguise: each observation is a 0 or 1, so the same machinery applies with p in place of μ.

p-hat = r/n;  standard error = √(p-hat(1 - p-hat)/n)
95% interval: p-hat +/- 1.96 x standard error
valid when n p-hat and n(1 - p-hat) are both at least 5

Worked example. In a sample of 200 voters, 84 support a candidate. Find a 95% confidence interval for the support.

p-hat = 0.42
standard error = √(0.42 × 0.58/200) = √(0.001218) = 0.0349
margin = 1.96 × 0.0349 = 0.0684
interval: (0.352, 0.488)

Worked example 2 (interpretation). A rival claims support is 50%. Does the interval support that claim?

0.5 lies outside (0.352, 0.488)
so at the 95% level the data are not consistent with 50% support

Estimators and their properties

Two properties decide whether an estimator is worth using: unbiasedness (correct on average) and low variance (consistent from sample to sample). The sample mean is unbiased for μ; the sample variance with divisor n is biased, which is why the divisor n − 1 appears.

E(x-bar) = mu  (unbiased)
E(s²) with divisor n underestimates σ² by a factor (n-1)/n
divisor n - 1 corrects the bias

Worked example. Explain why the divisor n − 1 is used in the sample variance.

deviations are measured from the sample mean, which is itself fitted to the data
that fitting uses up one degree of freedom, so the sum of squares is
systematically too small; dividing by n - 1 instead of n corrects it

Why the standard error is the whole story

Every formula in this topic contains σ/√n somewhere, and the reason is that estimating a mean averages away noise: independent errors partly cancel, and they cancel in proportion to the square root of how many there are. That is why precision is expensive — halving the standard error needs four times the data — and why a very precise interval from a biased sample is worse than useless, since it states a wrong answer with confidence.

The habitual check before trusting any interval is therefore two questions, not one: is the sample random, and is the sample large enough for the approximation used? An interval built from a quota sample answers a question about that quota, not about the population, however narrow it looks.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Parameter) Distinguish a parameter from a statistic. Answer: a parameter describes the population and is unknown; a statistic comes from the sample.
  2. (Method) Name a method that guarantees every member is equally likely. Answer: simple random sampling.
  3. (Bias) Give one weakness of a quota sample. Answer: the interviewer chooses who fills each quota, so selection bias remains.
  4. (Standard error) σ = 15, n = 25: find the standard error. Answer: SE = σ/√n = 15/√25 = 15/5 = 3.
  5. (Effect) n increases from 25 to 100: what happens to the standard error? Answer: SE = σ/√n, so quadrupling n multiplies √n by 2: 15/√25 = 3 becomes 15/√100 = 1.5, so the standard error halves.
  6. (CLT) State the central limit theorem. Answer: for large n the sample mean is approximately normal whatever the population shape.
  7. (CI) x̄ = 40, σ = 6, n = 36: 95% interval. Answer: CI = x̄ ± z σ/√n = 40 ± 1.96 × 6/√36 = 40 ± 1.96 × 1 = 40 ± 1.96 = (38.04, 41.96).
  8. (Width) How can the interval be made narrower? Answer: increase n, or lower the confidence level.
  9. (Proportion) 60 of 400: 95% interval. Answer: p̂ ± z √(p̂(1 − p̂)/n) = 0.15 ± 1.96 √(0.15 × 0.85/400) = 0.15 ± 1.96 × 0.01785 = (0.115, 0.185).
  10. (Estimator) Why divide by n − 1? Answer: to correct the bias caused by measuring deviations from the sample mean.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Dividing by n instead of √n: the standard error is σ/√n; using σ/n makes intervals far too narrow.
  • Reading a CI as a probability: the parameter is fixed; the 95% refers to the long-run performance of the method.
  • Assuming normality of the data: it is the sample mean that is approximately normal, by the central limit theorem, not the population.
  • Bias described as variance: a biased sample is wrong however large; a variable one is merely imprecise.
  • Stratified confused with quota: stratified is random within known groups; quota is interviewer-selected.
  • Wrong z for 99%: it is 2.5758, not 2.33 (that is the one-tailed 1% value).
  • Confidence level and sample size traded silently: a narrower interval at the same confidence costs a larger sample.
  • Proportion interval outside [0, 1]: check the validity conditions and truncate, or report that the normal approximation is unsuitable.

title: International GCSE English as a Second Language: Prepositions and Collocations
content:
International GCSE English as a Second Language: Prepositions and Collocations

Prepositions — at, on, in, by, for, of, with — are the smallest words that cause the biggest problems, because English chooses them by habit rather than by logic. That habit has a name: collocation, the tendency of words to appear together (depend on, good at, by accident). This note builds the full system from zero: the core spatial and temporal prepositions with their reasoning, the adjective, verb and noun collocation tables an exam candidate must know, phrasal verbs for everyday exam topics, and the collocational errors that most often cost accuracy marks in the 9280 writing and speaking papers.

What collocation is: the knife-and-fork analogy

Some words in English come in pairs the way knives and forks do. A native speaker says make a decision, not do a decision, and heavy rain, not strong rain — not because logic demands it, but because that is the established pairing. You cannot compute collocations; you learn them as units, the way you learned football and homework as single items of vocabulary. The good news for exam candidates: the testable collocation set is finite, and the exam repeats the same few hundred pairs every session.

The core three: at, on and in

The most-tested prepositions follow a containment logic: at is a point (a point in space or time), on is a surface or line, in is an enclosed space or a bounded period.

PrepositionTimePlace
atat 7 o'clock, at night, at noon, at the moment, at the weekendat the bus stop, at the door, at school, at home, at work
onon Monday, on 3 May, on my birthday, on Friday morningon the table, on the wall, on the bus (as a passenger), on the second floor
inin May, in 2026, in the morning, in the holidays, in two hoursin the room, in London, in a car (as a passenger), in the garden

The exceptions earn their own marks: at night but in the morning (the day parts take in, night takes at); at the weekend (British) / on the weekend (American); on a bus but in a car; in time (before the deadline) versus on time (exactly at the scheduled moment).

Worked example. "The meeting is ___ Monday ___ 9 am ___ the morning ___ May." Step 1: day → on Monday. Step 2: clock time → at 9 am. Step 3: part of the day → in the morning. Step 4: month → in May. Answers: on / at / in / in. Method visible: decide whether each target is a point (at), a surface/day (on), or an enclosed period (in).

Prepositions of movement and position

  • to / into / onto: to = direction (go to school), into = entering (walk into the room), onto = onto a surface (jump onto the wall).
  • at / to after verbs of position: arrive at (a place), arrive in (a city or country), get to.
  • above / over / under / below: over and under imply vertical opposition (the bridge over the river); above and below are relative levels (the temperature fell below zero).
  • between / among: between two or more distinct things (between the shops), among a group (among the crowd).

Adjective + preposition collocations

This table is the highest-yield collocation list for the exam; learn each adjective with its preposition as one chunk.

AdjectivePrepositionExample
afraid, frightened, scaredofafraid of the dark
good, bad, excellent, betteratgood at mathematics
interestedininterested in history
proudofproud of my sister
responsibleforresponsible for the project
famousforfamous for its beaches
keenonkeen on football
fed up, boredwithfed up with the noise
angry, annoyedwith (a person) / about (a thing)angry with my brother about the mess
marriedtomarried to a teacher
usedtoused to the climate
differentfromdifferent from the others
similartosimilar to mine
polite, kind, rude, generoustokind to animals

Verb + preposition collocations

VerbPrepositionExample
depend, relyonIt depends on the weather.
listentolisten to the radio
applyfor (a job) / to (an institution)apply for the job, apply to university
belongtobelong to my brother
consistofconsist of three parts
arriveat / inarrive at the station, arrive in Spain
explain, suggest, describe, discuss(no to with an object: explain something to someone)explain the problem to me — never "explain me the problem"
succeedinsucceed in passing the exam
apologisefor (something) / to (someone)apologise for being late, apologise to my teacher
pay, wait, ask, thankforpay for the tickets, wait for the bus
thinkabout (consider) / of (have an opinion)think about the offer, think of a better idea

The explain/suggest family is the single most common first-language interference error: these verbs never take a personal indirect object without to. "Explain me the rule" is wrong; "explain the rule to me" is right. Likewise "suggest me a book" is wrong; "suggest a book to me" or "recommend a book to me" is right.

Noun + preposition collocations

  • reason for, cause of, solution to, answer to, invitation to, damage to, effect on, advantage/disadvantage of, increase/decrease in, demand for, opportunity for, experience of/in, attitude to/towards.
  • Prepositional phrases of manner and circumstance: by accident, on purpose, by mistake, at least, at last, in fact, in spite of, due to, because of, according to.

Worked example. Correct the sentence: "She explained me the reason of the delay and asked an apology." Step 1: explain + object + to: "She explained the reason for the delay to me." (reason for, not reason of.) Step 2: ask for an apology — but the meaning is she apologised; the writer wanted "apologised for the delay". Cleanest correction: "She explained the reason for the delay to me and apologised." Two errors in one sentence: verb pattern and noun collocation.

Phrasal verbs for exam topics

Phrasal verbs are verb + particle units whose meaning is not predictable from the parts. The exam themes repeat a manageable set:

Phrasal verbMeaningTheme
look aftercare forfamily, children
grow upbecome an adultidentity, biography
get on withhave a good relationship withpeople, colleagues
find outdiscover informationstudy, research
sign up forenrol incourses, jobs
carry oncontinueany theme
give upstop trying / quithabits, work
cut down onreducehealth, environment
run out ofexhaust the supplyresources, money
take part inparticipateevents, sport
come up withthink of (an idea)study, projects
deal withhandleproblems, stress

Worked examples: collocation decisions

Worked example 1 — gap fill with reasoning. "I am very keen ___ tennis, but I am not very good ___ it. My coach says I need to concentrate ___ my serve and stop worrying ___ losing." Step 1: keen on (adjective collocation) → on. Step 2: good at → at. Step 3: concentrate on → on. Step 4: worry about → about. Answers: on / at / on / about. Every answer is a memorised pair; the reasoning is retrieval, not translation.

Worked example 2 — prepositions of time in a real task. "My course starts ___ September and finishes ___ the end of June. I have exams ___ the first week ___ June, and results come ___ August." Step 1: month → in September. Step 2: fixed phrase → at the end of June. Step 3: a bounded week inside June → in the first week of June (note the second of: week of June). Step 4: in August. Answers: in / at / in / in ... of ... in.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. Fill with at / on / in: "The flight leaves ___ 6:30 ___ Tuesday ___ the morning." Answer: at / on / in.
  2. Fill with adjective collocations: "She is afraid ___ speaking ___ large audiences but is very good ___ writing speeches." Answer: of / to / at. (speak to an audience; good at writing.)
  3. Correct the errors: "He explained me the problem and suggested me to wait." Answer: "He explained the problem to me and suggested that I wait." Why: explain and suggest never take a bare personal object.
  4. Choose: "The solution ___ the problem is a change ___ the law." (of / to / for / in / of) Answer: solution to the problem, change in the law.
  5. Choose the phrasal verb: "If you want to ___ smoking, try to ___ it ___ gradually." Answer: give up ... cut down on ... (give up smoking; cut down on it gradually).
  6. Fill: "We arrived ___ the airport late ___ night ___ the end of the holiday." Answer: at / at / of. (arrive at a point; at night; at the end of.)

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Translating the preposition: "depends of", "married with", "interested on" — the L1 preposition is not the English one. Learn the pairs as chunks and test yourself with gap fills, not translation.
