  • explain me / suggest me: the classic transfer error; both verbs need to + person or no person at all.
  • discuss about: discuss takes no preposition ("we discussed the plan"), and "answer to the question" is wrong for the verb ("answer the question" — answer to exists only as a noun: the answer to).
  • Preposition stranding avoided wrongly: "Who did you talk to?" is correct English; "To whom did you talk?" is correct but overly formal for most tasks. Match the register.
  • Time/at-on-in slips: at night / in the morning / on Monday morning — the part-of-day rule (in) and the day-surface rule (on) combine.
  • Strong vs heavy: collocation again — heavy rain, strong wind, big mistake (not strong mistake). Quantifier adjectives are memorised pairs.
  • Phrasal-verb register: "give up the job" is informal; formal writing prefers resign from the post. Choose phrasal verbs for informal tasks and their single-word equivalents for formal ones.
  • Double prepositions: "Where are you going to?" with a destination already stated, or "discuss about" — check each verb's pattern once in the final proofread.

The mapping rules, one page

Each rule below is a mapping: a type of time or place on the left, the preposition it takes on the right. Learn the mapping, not the translation — the same four rules answer every gap-fill.

day → on Monday left means the category the target belongs to (a named day or date); right means the preposition that category always takes. Collocation, not logic: there is no reason "on" belongs to a day, only that English fixed it that way.

clock time → at 9 am left means a point in time, including at noon, at night, at the weekend (BrE); right means the preposition for points. Change the category and the preposition changes, which is why the decision comes before the word.

part of the day → in the morning left means an enclosed period (morning, afternoon, evening, month, year, season); right means "in". The exception worth memorising is "at night", the one part of the day that behaves like a point.

month → in May left means a month or year; right means "in", because the period encloses the event. Compare "in May" with "on 3 May", where naming the day moves the target into the day category.

keen on (adjective collocation) → on left means the adjective and the preposition it is fixed to (keen on, good at, interested in, worried about); right means the preposition to retrieve. The word after the gap is what tells you which pair you are in — read it before you choose.

title: Exam technique: Information Representation
content:
### What earns the marks
For 1.1 Data Representation, calculate earns marks for correct binary arithmetic and two's complement conversions, showing working. Explain earns marks for describing number systems and their ranges. For 1.2 Multimedia Graphics, describe earns marks for outlining bitmap and sound representation. For 1.3 Compression, justify earns marks for stating why a compression type suits the data, with reasons.
### Traps
Error: incorrect two's complement conversion, Correction: remember the MSB has value -2^(n-1). Error: confusing lossless and lossy compression, Correction: lossless is required for text and code. Error: incorrect calculation of file size, Correction: check the formula, e.g. width x height x depth for bitmap images.
### Memory hooks
To remember binary arithmetic rules, use the mnemonic '0+0=0, 0+1=1, 1+1=0 carry 1'. For two's complement, recall 'invert and add 1'. To check the number of bits required for a number, use the formula 2^n - 1. For compression, associate lossless with text and lossy with images and sound.
### Timing
Information Representation is around 20-25% of the paper, budget 30-40 minutes for these questions.

title: Kinematics — Study Notes
content:
Kinematics

This note covers motion in a straight line and projectile motion for Cambridge AS & A Level Physics 9702 (Mechanics). Kinematics describes how position, velocity and acceleration change with time, without asking what causes the motion. Most exam marks come from choosing the right tool, setting a sign convention, and reading graphs correctly.

Definitions

  • Distance and speed are scalars: they have magnitude only.
  • Displacement s and velocity v are vectors: they have magnitude and direction. Displacement is the change in position, measured from a fixed origin.
  • Velocity is the rate of change of displacement: v = ds/dt.
  • Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity: a = dv/dt. An object moving at constant speed around a circle is accelerating, because its direction is changing.

Speed is the magnitude of velocity. An object that travels 60 m in one direction and then 20 m back has a distance of 80 m and a displacement of 40 m.

Interpreting graphs

  • On a displacement–time graph, the gradient is the velocity. A horizontal line means the object is at rest, and a steeper line means a higher speed.
  • On a velocity–time graph, the gradient is the acceleration. A straight line with constant gradient means uniform acceleration. A horizontal line means constant velocity.
  • The area under a velocity–time graph equals the displacement. Area below the time axis counts as negative, so a return journey partly cancels out.
  • On an acceleration–time graph, the area under the line equals the change in velocity.

Worked example. A velocity–time graph rises from 0 to 12 m s⁻¹ in 4 s, stays at 12 m s⁻¹ for 6 s, then falls to 0 in 3 s. The area of the triangle is ½ × 4 × 12 = 24 m, the rectangle is 6 × 12 = 72 m, and the final triangle is ½ × 3 × 12 = 18 m. The total displacement is 114 m. The accelerations are 3 m s⁻² for the first 4 s and −4 m s⁻² for the last 3 s.

SUVAT equations (uniform acceleration only)

SUVAT stands for displacement s, initial velocity u, final velocity v, acceleration a and time t. The four equations below apply only when acceleration is constant.

EquationQuantity not involved
v = u + ats
s = ut + ½at²v
v² = u² + 2ast
s = ½(u + v)ta

Choose the equation that omits the quantity you were not given and do not need. Writing down the list of known and unknown quantities first prevents most errors. Pick a sign convention at the start, normally taking the direction of motion, or up, as positive. For a body falling freely under gravity with up as positive, a = −9.81 m s⁻² (or −9.8 m s⁻² if the question uses g = 9.8).

Worked example. A car accelerates from 5 m s⁻¹ to 25 m s⁻¹ at 2 m s⁻². The time is found from v = u + at: 25 = 5 + 2t, so t = 10 s. The distance follows from v² = u² + 2as: 625 = 25 + 4s, so s = 150 m. Check with s = ½(u + v)t = ½ × 30 × 10 = 150 m.

Non-uniform motion

  • When acceleration is not constant, SUVAT cannot be used. Work from the graphs, or from a displacement function such as s = 3t² − t³, differentiating for velocity and acceleration.
  • Average speed is total distance divided by total time. Average velocity is total displacement divided by total time. These differ whenever the object changes direction.
  • The gradient at a point on a curved graph is the gradient of the tangent at that point. Estimate it by drawing the tangent carefully, and state which point you used.

Projectile motion

A projectile moves under gravity alone, with air resistance ignored. Resolve the launch velocity into two independent components:

  • Horizontal: uₓ = u cos θ. There is no acceleration, so the horizontal velocity stays constant and s = uₓt.
  • Vertical: u_y = u sin θ. The acceleration is g downwards, so SUVAT applies to this component alone.

The two motions share only the time t. At the highest point the vertical velocity is zero, so the time to reach the top is u_y/g. If the object lands at the same height it was launched from, the time of flight is 2u_y/g.

Worked example. A ball is launched at 20 m s⁻¹ at 30° above the horizontal from level ground. uₓ = 20 cos 30° ≈ 17.3 m s⁻¹ and u_y = 20 sin 30° = 10 m s⁻¹. The time of flight is 2 × 10 / 9.81 ≈ 2.04 s. The horizontal range is 17.3 × 2.04 ≈ 35 m. The maximum height is u_y²/(2g) = 100 / 19.62 ≈ 5.1 m.

Exam tips

  • Write the sign convention at the top of your working. Many lost marks come from a sign error in a vertical question.
  • Check whether the question asks for speed or velocity, and distance or displacement. The words decide which quantity to give.
  • Treat the horizontal and vertical motions of a projectile as two one-dimensional problems linked only by time.
  • When a graph is given, say which feature (gradient or area) gives the quantity you want before you calculate it.

title: AS Level Mathematics: Numerical Measures of Central Tendency
content:
AS Level Mathematics: Numerical Measures of Central Tendency

Statistics begins with describing data: where its centre lies and how it is spread. This note covers representation of data — tables, histograms, cumulative frequency curves and box plots — and the three averages with their strengths, plus the quartiles and interquartile range that measure spread robustly. The emphasis throughout is on choosing the right representation for the data type and reading values off a graph with the precision the marks require.

Types of data and the right representation

Data typeMeaningUseful displays
QualitativeCategories, no orderBar chart, pie chart
DiscreteCountable valuesBar chart, stem-and-leaf, histogram of counts
ContinuousAny value in a rangeHistogram, cumulative frequency, box plot

A histogram is the display for continuous data grouped into classes; unlike a bar chart, the bars touch because the variable is continuous. For unequal class widths the frequency density is plotted, not the frequency:

frequency density = frequency / class width
area of a bar = frequency (so areas are comparable)

Worked example. A class of width 10 contains 25 items; another of width 20 contains 30. Find the frequency densities.

25/10 = 2.5;  30/20 = 1.5
The narrower class is denser even though it holds fewer items.

The three averages

AverageHow to findStrengthWeakness
MeanSum ÷ countUses every valueDragged by outliers
MedianMiddle of ordered dataResistant to outliersIgnores exact values at the ends
ModeMost frequent valueWorks for categoriesMay not exist or be unique

Worked example. Find all three averages of 4, 7, 7, 9, 13.

mean = 40/5 = 8
median = 7 (third of five ordered values)
mode = 7

Worked example 2 (grouped mean). Estimate the mean of the grouped data: 0–10 (4), 10–20 (9), 20–30 (7).

use midpoints 5, 15, 25
sum = 4(5) + 9(15) + 7(25) = 20 + 135 + 175 = 330
total frequency = 20
estimated mean = 330/20 = 16.5

Grouped means are estimates: the midpoint stands in for every value in its class, so the answer is only as good as the grouping.

Median, quartiles and the interquartile range

median position (n data values) = (n + 1)/2
lower quartile Q1 at position (n + 1)/4
upper quartile Q3 at position 3(n + 1)/4
interquartile range IQR = Q3 - Q1

Worked example. Find the median and IQR of 3, 5, 7, 8, 10, 12, 15, 18.

n = 8; median position 4.5 → average of 4th and 5th = (8 + 10)/2 = 9
Q1 position 2.25 → 5 + 0.25(7 - 5) = 5.5
Q3 position 6.75 → 12 + 0.75(15 - 12) = 14.25
IQR = 14.25 - 5.5 = 8.75

The IQR is the robust measure of spread: it discards the extreme quarter at each end, so one outlier cannot inflate it the way it inflates the range.

Cumulative frequency and box plots

A cumulative frequency curve plots the running total against the upper class boundary. The median, quartiles and any percentile are read off at the corresponding cumulative frequencies.

read the median at n/2, Q1 at n/4, Q3 at 3n/4
(from a cumulative frequency curve, interpolate on the curve)

Worked example. A cumulative frequency curve for 80 students gives Q1 = 42 marks, median = 55, Q3 = 66. Describe the distribution.

IQR = 66 - 42 = 24 marks
the median sits closer to Q1 than Q3? 55 - 42 = 13; 66 - 55 = 11
so the middle half is roughly symmetric, slightly longer tail below
the upper whisker reaches the maximum; compare its length with the
lower whisker to judge skew

Box plot construction. A box from Q1 to Q3 with a line at the median, whiskers to the smallest and largest values that are not outliers. Outliers (beyond 1.5 × IQR from the quartiles) are plotted as separate points.

lower fence = Q1 - 1.5 IQR;  upper fence = Q3 + 1.5 IQR
values outside the fences are outliers

Comparing distributions

A comparison answer needs two parts: a measure of location (median or mean) and a measure of spread (IQR or standard deviation), each with a sentence of interpretation. "School A's median is higher, so its typical student scored more; its IQR is smaller, so its results are more consistent."

Worked example. A: median 62, IQR 18. B: median 58, IQR 9. Compare.

A has the higher typical mark (+4 on the median)
B is more consistent (IQR 9 vs 18)
A's spread suggests a wider mix of abilities; B's results cluster

Choosing and justifying an average

Exam questions ask which average best represents a data set — the answer is a reasoned choice, not a preference:

  • Skewed data or outliers: the median, because it is not dragged by extremes.
  • Categorical data: the mode, because a mean of categories is meaningless.
  • Data where every value should count (e.g. total rainfall per month): the mean.

Worked example. House prices in a street are 180k, 190k, 195k, 200k and 1.2m. Which average represents a typical price?

mean = 393k (dragged up by the 1.2m house)
median = 195k (the middle price)
the median is the honest summary; the mean misrepresents the street

Coding and combined means

Coding simplifies arithmetic without changing the shape of the data. If every value is transformed by y = (x - a)/b, the mean and standard deviation transform the same way, which is why coded means can be decoded exactly.

coded values: y = (x - a)/b
mean(x) = b mean(y) + a
median(x) = b median(y) + a
IQR(x) = b IQR(y)   (spread scales but does not shift)

Worked example. The coded values y = (x - 50)/10 have mean 2.4 and IQR 1.5. Find the mean and IQR of x.

mean x = 10(2.4) + 50 = 74
IQR x = 10(1.5) = 15

Worked example 2 (combined groups). Class A has 20 students with mean mark 60; class B has 30 with mean 70. Find the combined mean.

total marks = 20(60) + 30(70) = 1200 + 2100 = 3300
combined mean = 3300/50 = 66
not the average of 60 and 70, because the groups differ in size

The combined-mean formula is the weighted average: the group sizes are the weights. Averaging two means without weighting is one of the most common arithmetic errors in statistics questions.

Stem-and-leaf diagrams

A stem-and-leaf diagram keeps every value visible while ordering the data, which makes it the quickest route to the median and quartiles without arithmetic. The stem is the leading digit, the leaf the final digit, and a key must be stated.

example key: 3 | 4 means 34

3 | 4 7 9
4 | 1 2 2 5 8
5 | 0 3 6
6 | 1

Reading it: the data are 34, 37, 39, 41, 42, 42, 45, 48, 50, 53, 56, 61. With n = 12, the median sits between the 6th and 7th values, the lower quartile at position 3.25 and the upper at 9.75.

Worked example. Find the median and IQR of the data above.

median = (42 + 45)/2 = 43.5
Q1 = 37 + 0.25(39 - 37) = 37.5
Q3 = 50 + 0.75(53 - 50) = 52.25
IQR = 14.75

Back-to-back stems compare two groups: leaves for one group run left of the stem and for the other to the right, sharing the same stems so the shapes line up. Comparison answers then read off both a location and a spread for each group, exactly as with box plots.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Mean) Find the mean of 12, 15, 9, 18, 16. Answer: 70/5 = 14.
  2. (Median) Find the median of 4, 9, 2, 7, 11, 6. Answer: ordered 2, 4, 6, 7, 9, 11; median (6 + 7)/2 = 6.5.
  3. (Mode) Find the mode of 3, 5, 5, 7, 9, 9, 9. Answer: 9.
  4. (Grouped) Estimate the mean of 0–20 (5), 20–40 (10), 40–60 (5). Answer: (5×10 + 10×30 + 5×50)/20 = 600/20 = 30.
  5. (Quartiles) Find the IQR of 2, 5, 6, 8, 9, 12, 14, 15. Answer: Q1 = 5.5, Q3 = 13.5, IQR = 8.
  6. (Histogram) A bar of height 3 has class width 5. What frequency does it represent? Answer: 3 × 5 = 15.
  7. (Comparison) Two classes: median 55, IQR 10 and median 55, IQR 20. Compare. Answer: same typical mark; the first is more consistent.
  8. (Choice) Which average suits shoe sizes? Answer: the mode, because sizes are categorical/ordinal and the most common size is what a shop stocks.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Not ordering first: the median requires sorted data; taking the middle of the raw list is wrong whenever the data is unsorted.
  • Position versus value: (n + 1)/2 gives the position, not the median; count to that place.
  • Midpoint error: the midpoint of 10–20 is 15, not 10 or 20; open-ended classes make a grouped mean impossible without an assumption, which must be stated.
  • Histogram heights: plot frequency density, not frequency, when class widths differ; areas, not heights, compare.
  • Reading the curve: cumulative frequency is read against the upper boundary; using the lower boundary shifts every quartile.
  • IQR arithmetic: Q3 − Q1, never Q1 − Q3, and never the range.
  • Comparison without spread: a comparison that mentions only the median is half an answer.
  • Mean of grouped data called exact: call it an estimate and say why.

Equations and symbols

Every definition and relation these topics are examined on, gathered into one reference sheet, each written with its real notation and followed by a key naming each symbol and what it stands for. The sections above derive them; this is the sheet you revise from when a question has to be turned into algebra quickly and the marks depend on using the right formula, not a nearly-right one.

The three averages

mean x̄ = Σx/n and, for a frequency table, x̄ = Σfx/Σf
Key: x̄ = the arithmetic mean, in the unit of the data; x = each observation, or the midpoint of a class; f = its frequency; n = Σf = the number of observations. It uses every value, which makes it the most informative average and the one an outlier distorts most.

median: the ((n + 1)/2)th value in order for n odd; the average of the (n/2)th and (n/2 + 1)th for n even
Key: n = the number of observations; the data must be sorted first, ascending or descending. The median is the value with half the data on each side, so it is unaffected by how extreme the extremes are — the reason it is preferred for incomes, house prices and any skewed data.

mode = the most frequent value; modal class = the class with the highest frequency
Key: mode applies to the raw values (it can be non-numeric, such as the most common colour); the modal class is the grouped equivalent and reports the interval, not a single number. A data set can have no mode or several, and both are acceptable answers when stated.

weighted mean = Σwx/Σw
Key: w = the weight of each value (a frequency, a credit rating, a number of items); x = the value; the denominator is the sum of the weights. It is the general form of the frequency-table mean, and it is what a "mean mark across classes of different sizes" question is asking for.

Quartiles and the spread that goes with them

Q₁ position = (n + 1)/4, Q₃ position = 3(n + 1)/4
Key: n = the number of observations; the positions count from the smallest value upwards, and with n not a multiple of four the position falls between two values, so interpolate between them. Q₁ and Q₃ are in the unit of the data; the interquartile range is Q₃ − Q₁.

grouped quartiles: value = L + ((n/4 − cumulative before)/frequency of class) × class width
Key: L = the lower boundary of the quartile's class; n = the total frequency; the cumulative-before count is the total frequency below that class; the class width is the interval's size. The same linear-interpolation shape gives any percentile, with n/4 replaced by the relevant fraction of n.

Representations: histograms, cumulative frequency and box plots

frequency density = frequency/class width
Key: frequency = the number of observations in the class; class width = the size of the interval (in the variable's unit); frequency density is in observations per unit of the variable, which is what the vertical axis of an unequal-width histogram carries. Area, not height, represents frequency: area = frequency density × class width = frequency.

cumulative frequency at an upper boundary = the running total of all classes up to and including it
Key: the axes are the variable (x) and the cumulative count (n); the curve never decreases and reaches the total frequency at the top boundary. The median is read where the curve crosses n/2, the quartiles where it crosses n/4 and 3n/4, and the readings are interpolated horizontally to the required precision.

box plot: whiskers to the minimum and maximum, box from Q₁ to Q₃, line at the median
Key: Q₁, median, Q₃ = the three summary values, all in the data's unit; the box length is the IQR and each whisker the relevant quarter of the range. Two box plots side by side compare location (median line) and spread (box length) in one glance — the comparison sentence a question always wants.

Choosing an average, and how the shape decides

mean > median > mode for positive skew; mean < median < mode for negative skew; all three equal for a symmetric distribution
Key: the three averages, in the unit of the data; skew is the direction of the long tail, not the side where the bulk of the data sits. The mean is dragged towards the tail, so it sits furthest out; that ordering is the quickest read of a histogram and the answer to "which average best represents the data".

adding a constant a to every value adds a to the mean and median and leaves the mode shifted equally: no change in spread
Key: a = the constant added, in the data's unit; the mean, median and mode all move by a, while the range, IQR and standard deviation are unchanged. Multiplying every value by b multiplies each average and every measure of spread by |b| — the reason a unit conversion never changes the shape of a distribution.

title: Formulae, Equations and Amount of Substance
content:
Formulae, Equations and Amount of Substance

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH11, Topic 1. The mole is the bridge between the mass you can weigh and the number of particles a reaction actually uses, so every quantitative question in the course depends on it.

Relative masses and the mole

  • Relative atomic mass (Ar) and relative molecular mass (Mr) are based on the carbon-12 scale.
  • One mole contains the Avogadro constant, 6.02 × 10²³ particles, and the molar mass in g mol⁻¹ equals Mr numerically.
  • Moles: n = m / M. Rearrange to find mass (m = n × M) or molar mass (M = m / n).

Empirical and molecular formulae

  • Convert percentage (or mass) composition to moles, divide by the smallest value and multiply until the ratios are whole numbers.
  • The molecular formula is a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula: n = Mr / Mr(empirical formula).

Equations and reacting masses

  • Balance equations by conserving each element, then use the coefficients as mole ratios.
  • Limiting reagent: work out the moles each reactant could give, then take the smallest.
  • Percentage yield = actual yield / theoretical yield × 100.

Solutions and gases

  • Concentration c = n / V, with V in dm³ (cm³ ÷ 1000). Titration data follow the same route.
  • At room temperature and pressure one mole of gas occupies 24 dm³, so n = V / 24.

Exam tip: write the unit on every line of working, and check that your final answer has the same number of significant figures as the least precise data given.

title: Work, Energy and Power — Study Notes
content:
Work, Energy and Power

Work

W = Fs cos θ — force × displacement in the force's direction. Unit: joule (J).

Example: 100 N over 5 m in the same direction: W = 500 J. At 60°: 100 × 5 × cos 60° = 250 J.

Energy Forms

  • Kinetic energy: Ek = ½mv²
  • Gravitational PE: Ep = mgh
  • Elastic PE: ½kx² (spring, Hooke's law region)

Conservation of Energy

Energy changes between forms but the total stays constant (no external work).

Falling from height h: mgh = ½mv², so v = √(2gh) — independent of mass.

Example: a 0.5 kg ball dropped from 4 m hits at v = √(2 × 9.81 × 4) ≈ 8.9 m s⁻¹.

Power

P = W/t = Fv. Unit: watt (W = J s⁻¹).

Example: a 750 N runner at 6 m s⁻¹ outputs P = 4500 W.

Efficiency

Efficiency = useful output / total input × 100%.

Exam tips: energy questions are solved with energy, not kinematics, when forces vary; always ask 'where did the missing energy go?' — usually heat or sound.

title: IGCSE Computer Science: The Internet and Digital Currency
content:
IGCSE Computer Science: The Internet and Digital Currency

Cambridge IGCSE Computer Science 0478 (2026–2028), Paper 1 Computer Systems, Topic 5: statement 5.1 The internet and the world wide web, and 5.2 Digital currency. This note explains how a request typed into a browser becomes a page on screen (traced step by step through DNS and HTTP), what the internet's protocols each do, and how digital money — from card payments to cryptocurrency — actually works, including what a blockchain is under the hood.

The internet and the World Wide Web are not the same thing

The internet is the global infrastructure: the physical network of cables, switches, routers and satellites connecting millions of computers, plus the protocols that let them communicate. The World Wide Web is one service that runs over the internet: the collection of web pages and resources, linked by hyperlinks and accessed with a browser through HTTP. Analogy: the internet is the road network; the web is the shops and signs along it. Email, file transfer and online gaming also use the internet without being part of the web — a distinction worth a mark almost every year.

Access is through an ISP (internet service provider), which supplies the connection and often email and hosting. The web is a client–server system: your browser (client) requests resources from web servers, which return them.

How a web page loads, step by step

You type www.example.com/page.html and press Enter.

1. The browser checks its cache for the address; if not found it asks DNS.
2. DNS (domain name system) is the internet's phone book: the browser queries a
   DNS server, which returns the IP address of the domain name
   (www.example.com → 93.184.216.34).
3. The browser opens a TCP connection to that IP address on port 80 (HTTP) or
   443 (HTTPS). TCP handles reliable, ordered delivery of the data.
4. The browser sends an HTTP request message:
       GET /page.html HTTP/1.1
       Host: www.example.com
5. The web server locates the file and replies with an HTTP response:
   a status line (200 OK), headers (content type, cookies), and the HTML body.
6. The browser parses the HTML and requests any further files it references -
   images, CSS, JavaScript - each time performing steps 2-5 as needed.
7. The page is rendered on screen.

If the server cannot find the page it returns 404 Not Found; a secure site uses
HTTPS, where the exchange is encrypted after a certificate check.

Domain names exist because people cannot memorise IP addresses. Names read from right to left in levels: in www.bbc.co.uk, uk is the top-level country code, co the second level (commercial), bbc the organisation's name, and www the host machine. Generic top-level domains include .com, .org, .edu; registrars sell domain names to organisations, and each domain's records live in DNS.

Internet protocols

A protocol is an agreed set of rules every device follows so that communication works whoever built the hardware. The TCP/IP model layers the job: application protocols handle the user's task, TCP breaks data into packets and reassembles them reliably in order, IP addresses and routes the packets, and the hardware layer carries the signals.

ProtocolJobWhere you meet it
TCPSplits data into packets, numbers them, reassembles in order, resends lost onesUnderneath most internet traffic (with IP: TCP/IP)
IPAddresses packets and routes them between networksEvery internet connection
HTTPRequests and delivers web pages (unencrypted)Browsing ordinary websites
HTTPSHTTP over TLS encryptionBanking, shopping, logins
FTPTransfers whole files between client and serverUploading a website to a host
SMTPSends email from a client to a mail server and between serversSending mail
POP3 / IMAPCollects email from a mail server (POP3 downloads and usually deletes; IMAP synchronises across devices)Reading mail

When a message is sent it is broken into packets, each labelled with its sequence number and the source and destination IP addresses. Packets from one message may travel different routes; the receiving TCP layer reorders them and requests retransmission of any that fail checksums. Packet switching shares the network efficiently among many conversations — the alternative, a dedicated line per conversation, would waste capacity.

Email in one pass

The client composes the message and hands it to SMTP, which delivers it to the sender's mail server; that server looks up the recipient's domain in DNS and forwards it to the recipient's mail server, where it waits in a mailbox. The recipient's client then fetches it with POP3 (download and delete from server) or IMAP (keep on server, synchronise across phone and laptop). Attachments are encoded into text by MIME and travel inside the message — which is why a 5 MB attachment becomes about 6.7 MB in transit.

Cookies, caching and search engines

  • Cookies are small text files a website stores on the client: they keep you logged in, remember basket contents and preferences, and enable site analytics. They raise privacy concerns (tracking across sites), so laws require consent and browsers offer blocking.
  • Caching stores copies of frequently used pages or files on the client or on proxy servers, so repeat visits load faster and network traffic falls — the freshness trade-off is that cached copies can be out of date.
  • Search engines use automated crawlers (spiders) to fetch pages and build an index; when you search, the engine matches your terms against that index and ranks results by relevance measures such as links pointing at a page. Paying for placement is advertising, not relevance — a distinction exam questions probe.

Digital currency (statement 5.2)

Digital money is money that exists only as data. Everyday forms are online card payments, mobile wallets (Apple Pay, Google Pay) and online banking transfers: these move conventional currency through trusted intermediaries — banks and card networks — protected by encryption, two-factor authentication and regulated by law. Cryptocurrency (Bitcoin, Ethereum) is different: it is a purely digital currency with no central bank, secured by cryptography and recorded on a distributed ledger.

Blockchain under the hood — the anatomy of the idea:

  • Transactions are grouped into a block and broadcast to a peer-to-peer network of computers (nodes).
  • Nodes check each transaction against the ledger (has the sender got the funds? is the signature valid?)
  • Proof-of-work nodes (miners) compete to solve a hard computational puzzle; the winner adds the block and earns new coins plus fees — this is mining.
  • Each block contains the hash of the previous block, chaining them together; altering an old block would change its hash and break every later link, so the history is tamper-evident and practically immutable.
  • Every node keeps a full copy of the ledger, so there is no single point of failure and no central authority.

Wallets and keys: a wallet holds your keys, not coins. The public key is your address (like an account number, safe to publish); the private key signs transactions to prove ownership. Lose the private key and the funds are unrecoverable — there is no bank to appeal to.

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Fast, direct transfers anywhere in the world without banksValue is extremely volatile — huge gains and losses in days
Lower fees for international transfersUsed for illegal transactions because identity is pseudonymous
No central authority, so no bank failure or political control affects itMining consumes enormous electricity; environmental concerns
Transparent, tamper-evident ledgerNo consumer protection: lost keys and fraud are irreversible
Financial access for the unbankedLegal status varies by country; regulation is uncertain

Worked example: one Bitcoin payment

Amina pays 0.05 BTC to a shop.

1. Amina's wallet creates a transaction record: amount, shop's public key
   (address), and her public key.
2. It signs the transaction with her PRIVATE key - anyone can verify the
   signature against her public key, but nobody can forge it.
3. The transaction is broadcast to the Bitcoin network.
4. Nodes verify she has 0.05 BTC (checking the ledger's history) and that the
   signature is valid.
5. A miner includes the transaction in a new block and races the proof-of-work
   puzzle.
6. The winning block is broadcast; nodes accept it and append it to their copy
   of the chain, referencing the previous block's hash.
7. After further blocks are added (confirmations), the payment is considered
   final; the shop sees the funds and Amina cannot reverse it.

Contrast with a card payment: the card network can reverse or refund; a
blockchain payment cannot, which is both its strength (no chargeback fraud)
and its weakness (no recourse).

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Saying "the internet and the web are the same"; the web runs over the internet alongside email, FTP and gaming.
  • Describing DNS as translating IP addresses into domain names; DNS resolves domain names to IP addresses.
  • Skipping the TCP layer in "how is a file transferred" answers — packets, sequence numbers, reassembly and checksum retransmission are the marks.
  • Claiming packets all take the same route or arrive in order; they may not, and reordering at the receiving end is the point of sequence numbers.
  • Writing that HTTPS encrypts only the password; the whole session is encrypted after the certificate handshake.
  • Confusing cookies with cache: cookies store user state and preferences; cache stores copies of content for speed.
  • Saying blockchain is "a database that hackers cannot touch"; it is a distributed, chained ledger that is tamper-evident — precise wording earns marks.
  • Forgetting the private key in cryptocurrency answers: transactions are signed with it and losing it loses the funds permanently.
  • Mixing up SMTP and POP3/IMAP: sending versus receiving.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 1, 3 marks). Explain the difference between the internet and the World Wide Web.

Answer: The internet is the global physical network of cables, routers and computers plus the protocols (TCP/IP) that connect them. The web is a service running over that network: the collection of hyperlinked web pages delivered by HTTP and viewed in a browser. Email and file transfer also use the internet but are not part of the web.

Question 2 (Paper 1, 5 marks). Describe what happens when a user requests a web page from a server they have not visited before.

Answer: The browser queries a DNS server to resolve the domain name into an IP address. A TCP connection opens to the server at that address. The browser sends an HTTP GET request for the page. The server responds with the HTML (plus a status code such as 200 OK). The browser parses the HTML and requests any linked resources (images, CSS), then renders the page.

Question 3 (Paper 1, 4 marks). Explain the purpose of TCP and IP in transferring a large file over the internet.

Answer: IP handles addressing and routing: it stamps each packet with the source and destination IP addresses and forwards it between networks. TCP handles reliability: it splits the file into packets, numbers them with sequence numbers, reassembles them in order at the destination, and uses checksums, ACKs and retransmission to ensure nothing is lost or duplicated. Together they make unreliable networks deliver files correctly.

Question 4 (Paper 1, 4 marks). Explain two privacy concerns with cookies and how users are protected.

Answer: Cookies can track a user's activity across multiple sites, building a profile of their behaviour and interests without their full awareness — used for targeted advertising. They can also store personal details that expose the user if the device is shared. Protection comes from data-protection laws requiring sites to obtain informed consent before setting non-essential cookies, and from browser controls that block or delete them.

Question 5 (Paper 1, 6 marks). Describe how a cryptocurrency transaction is recorded on a blockchain and state two disadvantages of cryptocurrency.

Answer: The payer's wallet creates and signs the transaction with the payer's private key. It is broadcast to the peer-to-peer network, where nodes verify the signature and that the funds exist. A miner groups it into a block and competes to solve the proof-of-work puzzle; the winning block references the previous block's hash and is appended to every node's copy of the ledger, making the record tamper-evident. Disadvantages: values are extremely volatile, mining uses vast amounts of electricity, transactions are irreversible (lost keys mean lost funds), and the pseudonymous design attracts illegal use.

Question 6 (Paper 1, 2 marks). Explain why a shop might prefer card payments to cryptocurrency.

Answer: Card payments come with consumer protection, refunds and chargebacks, and prices stay stable because the currency is regulated; cryptocurrency values can swing dramatically between sale and settlement and payments cannot be reversed if something goes wrong.

Paper 1 closes with the systems that act on their own — automated systems, robotics and artificial intelligence.

title: Edexcel IAL Computer Science: Operating Systems, Translators and Data Security
content:
Edexcel IAL Computer Science: Operating Systems, Translators and Data Security

Pearson Edexcel International Advanced Level in Computer Science, Unit 1 Principles of Computer Science: operating systems and their purposes, language translators, and data security and integrity. This note goes below the GUI: what an operating system actually allocates and protects, how source code becomes machine instructions, and how data is kept correct and confidential — with the security section structured as threat → mechanism → defence, the shape examiners mark against.

The operating system as resource manager

An operating system is the system software that manages the hardware and provides services to applications. Two complementary views: the resource manager (allocating CPU time, memory, storage and peripherals fairly and efficiently) and the extended machine (hiding hardware complexity behind clean interfaces so applications never program the disk controller directly).

  • Processor management — scheduling processes onto the CPU; time slicing and priorities give multitasking; a process moves between ready, running and blocked states.
  • Memory management — allocating RAM to processes, protecting one process's space from another, and using virtual memory (paging to backing store) when RAM is exhausted.
  • File management — directories, file naming, access permissions, and tracking free space.
  • Device management — device drivers translate OS requests into device-specific commands; a buffer smooths speed differences between CPU and peripherals; interrupts and spooling coordinate them.
  • User interface — GUI (intuitive, direct manipulation) or CLI (scriptable, low overhead, precise).
  • Security — authentication, access rights, audit logs.

Interrupts underpin responsiveness: a device raises an interrupt; the CPU completes its current instruction, saves state, runs the interrupt service routine (ISR), restores state and resumes. Priorities arbitrate simultaneous interrupts. Polling (asking devices in turn) wastes cycles; interrupts let devices signal need.

Utility software

Utilities maintain and protect the system: antivirus (signature and heuristic scanning), defragmentation (recontiguating scattered files on magnetic disks — pointless on SSDs), backup (full vs incremental; the 3-2-1 rule: three copies, two media, one off-site), compression, file management, firewalls and disk partitioning tools. The exam wants each utility's function stated as an effect on performance, security or reliability.

Language translators

TranslatorMechanismOutputConsequence
CompilerWhole-program translation before executionStandalone machine-code executableFast execution; errors reported across the whole program at compile time; recompilation needed per change
InterpreterLine-by-line translation and immediate executionNone saved (translator needed each run)Slower; errors surface exactly at the failing line; ideal for development and portability
AssemblerOne mnemonic to one machine instructionMachine code for that processorFull hardware control; tied to the instruction set
Same program, two translation paths:

  source:  total = 0
           for i in 1..5: total = total + i
           print(total)

Compiler:  scans the whole file -> syntax check all lines -> optimises ->
           emits executable -> the executable runs at machine speed. The
           compiled file runs again and again with no translator present.

Interpreter: takes line 1, translates and runs it (total = 0 in memory);
           takes line 2's loop, translating and running each iteration; then
           line 3 prints 15. Every rerun repeats the translation.

Intermediate languages (bytecode for the JVM) sit between: compiled once,
interpreted or JIT-compiled at run time - portable without source exposure.

Choosing a translator: worked factors

Exam questions ask which translation approach suits a given project; the answer weighs four factors. Execution speed: compiled code runs at machine speed — pick it for number-crunching or embedded targets. Development cycle: interpreters give immediate feedback and pinpointed errors — pick them for prototyping and teaching. Portability: an interpreter or bytecode VM runs anywhere the runtime exists; native executables need rebuilding per platform. Intellectual property: distributing an executable or bytecode keeps source private; distributing interpreted source exposes it. Hybrid systems (Java's compile-to-bytecode then JIT, or Python's compiled .pyc cache) mix the trade-offs — mention them when the question allows.

Data security and integrity

Security protects confidentiality, integrity and availability of data; integrity means data is accurate, complete and unaltered — maintained by validation at input, verification, access control and transaction controls. The two ideas interlock: a security breach often destroys integrity (tampering), and integrity measures (checksums, audit trails) also reveal breaches.

ThreatMechanismDefence
Malware (virus/worm/trojan/ransomware)Malicious code: attaches and replicates / spreads over networks / disguises itself / encrypts for ransomAntivirus, patching, firewalls, least privilege, offline backups
Phishing / social engineeringManipulating people into revealing credentialsTraining, verification procedures, spam filters, 2FA
Brute force / dictionary attacksAutomated password guessingLong complex passwords, lockouts, rate limiting, hashing with salt
Interception / sniffingEavesdropping on trafficEncryption (TLS, VPNs), secure protocols
DoS / DDoSOverwhelming a service with trafficTraffic filtering, rate limiting, redundancy
SQL injectionHostile input executed as codeParameterised queries, input validation
Insider misuseAuthorised users exceeding needLeast privilege, auditing, separation of duties

Access-control mechanisms: authentication (knowledge, possession, inherence — and two-factor combinations), authorisation (rights matrices and role-based access), encryption (symmetric AES for bulk; asymmetric RSA for key exchange and signatures; hashing for password storage and integrity), and physical security. Passwords are stored as salted hashes so a database leak does not yield usable passwords.

Worked: protecting a payroll database, defence in depth.

Layer 1 physical: locked server room, encrypted backups off-site.
Layer 2 network: firewall rules; payroll VLAN; TLS for all access.
Layer 3 host: patched OS; antivirus; full-disk encryption.
Layer 4 application: parameterised queries (SQL injection), session timeouts.
Layer 5 data: least-privilege roles (clerk sees one department; only the
              payroll officer sees salaries); all changes audit-logged.
Layer 6 people: security training, two-factor admin logins, separation of
              duties (the person who adds employees is not the one who
              approves pay changes).

An attacker must beat every layer; a defender must hold each one - asymmetry
the answer should name.

Integrity in databases: validation (type, range, length, presence, check digits), verification (double entry, visual checks), and access-controlled updates. Recovery: backups, transaction logs, journaling — restoring to the last consistent state after failure.

Worked example: analysing a breach

Incident: an admin's credentials are phished; an attacker copies the customer
table overnight; data appears on a leak site.

Analysis against the layers:
  phishing succeeded -> no 2FA on admin accounts (authentication gap);
  overnight copy unnoticed -> no anomaly alerting on bulk reads (monitoring);
  full table visible -> excessive rights; data not encrypted at rest;
  customer impact -> notification obligations triggered.

Remediation: enforce 2FA on all admin access; alert on bulk export; encrypt
the table at rest; reduce each account to least privilege; staff refresher on
phishing; restore confidence with a published incident report.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Describing the OS as "the software you click on"; frame it as resource management and services — scheduling, memory, files, devices.
  • Saying virtual memory makes a computer faster; it prevents crashes when RAM is full at the cost of speed.
  • Confusing compilation with interpretation in a comparison; the deliverable (executable versus nothing saved) is the decisive point.
  • Claiming compiled code can never be interpreted or vice versa — hybrid systems (JVM) exist; the question wants the primary mechanism.
  • Answering security questions with antivirus alone; map each threat to its mechanism and defence.
  • Storing passwords encrypted rather than hashed (reversible storage is a vulnerability), or hashing without a salt (rainbow tables).
  • Conflating validation with verification: validation checks plausibility of the value; verification checks it matches the source.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Unit 1, 4 marks). Describe two operating system functions and why each matters.

Answer: Memory management allocates RAM to each running process and protects one process's memory from another, so programs cannot corrupt each other and available RAM is used fully; virtual memory lets processes exceed physical RAM. Processor scheduling allocates CPU time among processes (time slicing, priorities), so several programs appear to run at once and urgent tasks are not starved.

Question 2 (Unit 1, 4 marks). Explain how an interrupt improves the efficiency of I/O.

Answer: Instead of the CPU repeatedly polling each device (wasting cycles on idle devices), a device raises an interrupt when it needs service. The CPU finishes its current instruction, saves the program counter, runs the device's ISR, and resumes exactly where it left off — so the CPU does useful work until attention is genuinely required.

Question 3 (Unit 1, 4 marks). Compare compiled and interpreted approaches for a cross-platform scientific application.

Answer: A compiled version runs at full machine speed — critical for heavy computation — but needs a separate build per platform and a recompile for each change. An interpreter runs unchanged anywhere the interpreter exists, simplifying distribution and debugging, but executes more slowly because translation repeats at run time. For number-crunching, compile; for portability and rapid iteration, interpret — or compile to portable bytecode.

Question 4 (Unit 1, 4 marks). Explain how hashing protects stored passwords.

Answer: Passwords are never stored in plain text; a one-way hash function maps each password to a fixed-length digest that cannot be reversed. A random salt per user defeats rainbow-table and precomputed-dictionary attacks, and equal passwords then hash differently. At login the submitted password is hashed with the stored salt and compared. Even a database leak yields only digests, which must be cracked one guess at a time.

Question 5 (Unit 1, 5 marks). Describe how a company can protect data against both external attack and internal misuse.

Answer: External: firewalls and patched systems block and contain attacks; TLS/VPNs stop interception; 2FA and strong password policies defeat credential theft; tested off-site backups defeat ransomware. Internal: least-privilege roles ensure staff access only what their job needs; audit logs and anomaly alerts deter and detect misuse; separation of duties prevents any one person completing a sensitive action alone; training builds a reporting culture. Together these give defence in depth across technology and people.

Question 6 (Unit 1, 3 marks). Explain the difference between validation and verification with examples.

Answer: Validation checks that data is plausible before storage — a range check rejects a mark of 250, a type check rejects "abc" as an integer. Verification checks the data captured matches the source — double-entering a new bank account number, or visually checking a scanned form against the record. Validation enforces integrity of values; verification enforces accuracy of capture.

The last Unit 1 domain steps back from mechanisms to consequences: who owns data, what is fair use, and what AI changes.

title: A Level Mathematics: Hypothesis Testing
content:
A Level Mathematics: Hypothesis Testing

A hypothesis test is a formal way of deciding whether data are surprising enough to overturn an assumption. The logic is legal rather than mathematical in spirit: assume the claim is true, compute how unlikely the observed evidence would be under that assumption, and reject the claim only if the evidence is unlikely enough. This note sets out the machinery — null and alternative hypotheses, significance levels, tails, critical regions — and then applies it to the binomial and normal cases the exam uses.

The logic of a test

The null hypothesis H0 is the assumption of no change, no effect, no bias: the status quo. The alternative H1 is what you would conclude if the data are too extreme. The significance level α is the risk of rejecting a true H0 that you are willing to accept.

H0: the parameter equals its old value
H1: the parameter is greater, less, or simply different
alpha: the maximum acceptable probability of a Type I error (often 0.05 or 0.01)
test statistic: the observed value computed from the sample
p-value: probability of a result at least as extreme, assuming H0

The analogy that makes the asymmetry clear: a criminal trial presumes innocence. The presumption is not a belief, it is the default that evidence must overcome. Failing to reject H0 is not proof of H0 — it is a verdict of "not proven".

One-tailed and two-tailed tests

The alternative decides the tail. A one-tailed test is used when the direction of the change is specified in advance; a two-tailed test when any change would matter.

AlternativeTest typep-value
p > p0one-tailed, upperP(X ≥ observed)
p < p0one-tailed, lowerP(X ≤ observed)
p ≠ p0two-tailed2 × the smaller tail

Worked example (choosing the alternative). A coin is suspected of favouring heads. Which alternative applies?

the suspicion has a direction, so H1: p > 0.5, a one-tailed upper test
a two-tailed test would be right only if any bias mattered

Errors and their consequences

Every test can go wrong in two ways, and the significance level controls only one of them. Understanding which is which is a frequent exam question and a genuine conceptual point.

Type I error: reject H0 when it is true  (probability alpha)
Type II error: fail to reject H0 when it is false
reducing alpha reduces Type I errors but increases Type II errors
increasing the sample size reduces both

Worked example. A test at the 5% level concludes a die is biased when it is fair. Which error is this?

H0 (fair) was true and was rejected
that is a Type I error, with probability at most 5%

Worked example 2 (effect of sample size). Explain why the same observed proportion can be significant in a large sample and not in a small one.

a larger sample reduces the standard error, so the same deviation
becomes more standard errors away from the null value
the evidence is measured in standard errors, not in raw counts

Testing a binomial proportion

The test statistic is the observed number of successes, the null distribution is binomial, and the p-value is a cumulative binomial probability.

H0: p = p0;  X ~ B(n, p0)
upper tail p-value = P(X >= x)
lower tail p-value = P(X <= x)
reject H0 if p-value <= alpha

Worked example. A manufacturer claims 90% of components are fault-free. In a sample of 20, only 15 are fault-free. Test at the 5% level whether the claim is too high.

H0: p = 0.9;  H1: p < 0.9
X ~ B(20, 0.9)
P(X <= 15) = 0.0432
0.0432 < 0.05, so reject H0
there is evidence the fault-free rate is below 90%

Worked example 2 (critical region). Find the 5% critical region for that test.

P(X <= 15) = 0.0432 (below 0.05)
P(X <= 16) = 0.1330 (above 0.05)
critical region: X <= 15

Worked example 3 (actual significance level). State the actual significance level of that test.

the probability of a Type I error is P(X <= 15) under H0 = 0.0432
so the actual level is 4.32%, just inside the 5% requirement

Testing a normal mean

When the variable is continuous and the population is normal — or the sample is large — the test statistic is standardised with a z-score and compared with critical values.

test statistic z = (x-bar - mu)/(σ/sqrt n)   (σ known)
or z = (x-bar - mu)/(s/sqrt n)                  (σ estimated, large n)
critical values at 5% one-tailed: 1.6449;  two-tailed: 1.96
at 1% one-tailed: 2.3263;  two-tailed: 2.5758

Worked example. A machine fills bags with a mean of 500 g and standard deviation 8 g. A sample of 16 bags has mean 496 g. Test at the 5% level whether the mean has fallen.

H0: mu = 500;  H1: mu < 500
standard error = 8/sqrt 16 = 2
z = (496 - 500)/2 = -2
critical value at 5% one-tailed is -1.6449
-2 < -1.6449, so reject H0: the mean has fallen

Worked example 2 (two-tailed). Same data, tested two-tailed at 5%.

critical values are +/-1.96
|-2| > 1.96, so still reject H0
the evidence is that the mean is not 500, in either direction

Worked example 3 (interpreting a p-value). A test gives z = 1.72 for H1: μ > μ0. Find the p-value and conclude at 5%.

p-value = P(Z > 1.72) = 0.0427
0.0427 < 0.05, so reject H0
the result is significant at the 5% level but not at 1%

Choosing the right test

The exam does not label the test; the shape of the data decides it. Getting the distribution wrong makes every later mark unreachable, so the decision is worth making explicitly.

count of successes in n trials with constant p  →  binomial test
count of events in an interval at a constant rate  →  Poisson test
mean of a continuous measurement  →  normal test (z)
correlation between two variables  →  product-moment test

Worked example. A nurse records the number of patients arriving in an hour on 30 separate days. Which test?

counts of arrivals in equal intervals at a roughly constant rate
use a Poisson test on the mean count, not a binomial test
a normal test on the mean of the 30 counts is also defensible for large n

Writing a conclusion that earns the marks

The final mark of a hypothesis test is for the conclusion, and it has three components: a decision about H0, a reference to the significance level, and the finding stated in the context of the question. Dropping any one of them costs a mark even when the arithmetic is perfect.

Compare these two endings. "0.0201 < 0.05, so reject H0" scores the comparison. "There is sufficient evidence at the 5% level that the call rate has increased" scores the comparison and the interpretation. "The rate has increased" scores neither, because it reports a certainty the test cannot deliver.

The opposite case is often mishandled too. When the p-value is above the level the correct wording is that there is insufficient evidence to reject H0 — never that H0 is true, and never that nothing has happened. A non-significant result from a small sample is weak evidence either way, and saying so is better than overclaiming in either direction.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Hypotheses) A coin might be biased against heads. State H0 and H1. Answer: H0: p = 0.5; H1: p < 0.5.
  2. (Error) Define a Type II error. Answer: failing to reject H0 when it is false.
  3. (Binomial) 8 of 20 seeds germinate; test p = 0.6 against p < 0.6 at 5%. Answer: X ~ B(20, 0.6), so P(X ≤ 8) = 0.0565; since 0.0565 > 0.05 there is insufficient evidence to reject H0.
  4. (Critical region) X ~ B(15, 0.4): 5% lower critical region. Answer: test P(X ≤ c) ≤ 0.05: P(X ≤ 2) = 0.0271 ≤ 0.05, but P(X ≤ 3) = 0.0905 > 0.05, so the critical region is X ≤ 2.
  5. (Actual level) For that region, state the actual significance level. Answer: actual significance level = P(X ≤ 2) = 0.0271 = 2.71%.
  6. (Normal) μ0 = 20, σ = 4, n = 25, mean 21.5: test at 5% one-tailed. Answer: z = (x̄ − μ0)/(σ/√n) = (21.5 − 20)/(4/√25) = 1.5/0.8 = 1.875, and 1.875 > 1.6449, so reject H0.
  7. (Two-tailed) Same data two-tailed: Answer: z = (21.5 − 20)/(4/√25) = 1.875, and 1.875 < 1.96, so do not reject H0.
  8. (p-value) z = 2.4, H1: μ > μ0. Find the p-value. Answer: p-value = P(Z > 2.4) = 1 − 0.9918 = 0.0082.
  9. (Sample size) Why can a larger sample turn a non-significant result significant? Answer: the standard error shrinks, so the same deviation is more standard errors away.
  10. (Conclusion wording) Write a valid conclusion for a rejected H0. Answer: there is sufficient evidence at the 5% level that the mean has fallen.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Concluding H0 is true: failing to reject means the evidence is insufficient; it is never proof of the null.
  • Wrong tail: compute P(X ≥ x) for an increase and P(X ≤ x) for a decrease; using the other tail inverts the conclusion.
  • Doubling without a two-tailed alternative: the p-value is doubled only when H1 is "not equal".
  • p-value compared with the wrong threshold: 5% is 0.05; comparing 0.043 with 5 instead of 0.05 reverses the verdict.
  • Standard error omitted: the z-score divides by σ/√n, not by σ.
  • Critical value for the wrong tail: the 5% one-tailed value is 1.6449, the two-tailed is 1.96; the sign matters too.
  • Type I and Type II swapped: Type I is rejecting a true null — the error the significance level controls.
  • Conclusion beyond the data: a rejected H0 says the parameter has changed, not why, and never that the change is important.

Setting up the hypotheses before any calculation

Hypotheses are the first lines a marker reads, and a wrong direction or a sample statistic written where a parameter belongs loses marks before any arithmetic is checked. The subsections set out how to define the parameter, write H₀ as a single value and read H₁ from the wording of the question.

Defining the parameter in words first

Before writing any symbol, say what the parameter measures. Let p be the proportion of seeds that germinate, or let μ be the mean mass of a bag in grams. The parameter belongs to the population the claim is about, not to the sample you were given. The definition is the line that makes the rest of the working easy to follow, so write it first.

Writing H₀ as a single value

H₀ names one value for the parameter with an equals sign, such as H₀: p = 0.6 or H₀: μ = 50. It is the value the test assumes is true when it calculates the probability of the data. The probability can only be worked out at one specific value, so the test is always carried out at the value stated in H₀, and the working should say so.

Reading the direction of H₁ from the wording

Words map to symbols in a fixed way. “Greater than”, “more than”, “has increased” and “above” give >. “Less than”, “fewer”, “has decreased” and “below” give <. “Different from”, “has changed” and “is not equal to” give ≠. A question that asks whether a proportion has changed, without saying which way, needs H₁: p ≠ p₀, and that choice fixes a two-tailed test.

Hypotheses for a mean from a normal model

When X is normal with a known standard deviation, the hypotheses concern μ, and the variance belongs to the model: X ~ N(μ, σ²). Write the assumption that the population is normal with known σ, or that the sample is large enough for the central limit theorem to apply. The hypotheses for a sample mean are the same as for the population mean, because the test is about μ.

Hypotheses set before the data are used

The direction of H₁ must come from the claim in the question, not from the sample. If the sample mean is 49 and the claim is μ = 50, it is tempting to choose H₁: μ < 50 after looking at the data. That choice invalidates the test, because it lets the data pick the tail. Settle the direction from the wording, and show it in the working before the test statistic.

Critical regions and the significance level

A critical region is the set of outcomes that leads to rejecting H₀. For a discrete distribution it is a set of whole numbers, and for a normal test it is a range of z-values. The subsections show how each is built from the significance level, and where the sign and boundary errors come from.

Building a critical region from tail probabilities

For a lower-tail test at level α, find the largest value k with P(X ≤ k) ≤ α, assuming H₀. The critical region is then {0, 1, …, k}. For X ~ B(10, 0.5) at the 5% level, P(X ≤ 1) = 11/1024 = 0.0107 and P(X ≤ 2) = 56/1024 = 0.0547. The second value is greater than 0.05, so k = 1 and the critical region is {0, 1}.

The actual significance level is rarely the stated level

Because X takes only whole-number values, the probability in the critical region is usually below the stated level. Here it is 0.0107, about 1.07%, not 5%. Say so in the working, using the phrase “actual significance level”. A discrete test that falls short of 5% is correct; a candidate who claims the level is exactly 5% makes a false statement.

Critical values for a normal test

For a normal test with known σ, a critical value of z replaces the critical count. The standard values are 1.645 for a one-tailed test at 5%, 2.326 for one-tailed at 1%, 1.96 for two-tailed at 5% and 2.576 for two-tailed at 1%. A lower-tailed test rejects when z ≤ −1.645; an upper-tailed test rejects when z ≥ 1.645. The normal distribution is continuous, so the actual level equals the stated level exactly.

Two-tailed critical regions for a discrete test

For a two-tailed test at 5%, each tail may carry probability at most 0.025. For X ~ B(10, 0.5), P(X ≤ 1) = 0.0107 is at most 0.025, while P(X ≤ 2) = 0.0547 is not. The lower critical region is {0, 1}, and by symmetry the upper one is {9, 10}. The combined probability is 0.0215, which is below 0.05, so the test can reject for 0, 1, 9 or 10 successes.

Checking the boundary and the sign

A common slip is to put the boundary in the wrong region or to use the wrong sign. For a lower-tailed normal test at 5%, the boundary z = −1.645 is itself in the critical region, because the test rejects when z ≤ −1.645. A critical value of +1.645 on a lower-tailed test is the commonest sign error. Write the inequality with the boundary included, then check that its sign matches the tail named in H₁.

p-values, step by step

A p-value gives the same decision as a critical region, but it reports how unlikely the data are on the assumption that H₀ is true, rather than only whether they fall inside a region. Many A2 questions ask for a p-value directly, and some ask for a comparison with the level in a single sentence.

What a p-value is and is not

The p-value is the probability, assuming H₀ is true, of a result at least as extreme as the one observed, in the direction stated in H₁. It is not the probability that H₀ is true, and it is not the probability that the result happened by chance. A p-value of 0.03 means that a result this extreme would occur 3% of the time if H₀ were true.

A p-value for a lower-tailed binomial test

For X ~ B(10, 0.5) with H₁: p < 0.5, suppose 2 successes are observed. The p-value is P(X ≤ 2) = 56/1024 = 0.0547. That is greater than 0.05, so the result is not significant at the 5% level. At the 10% level, 0.0547 is less than 0.10, so H₀ is rejected. The same observation gives different decisions at different levels, which is why the level must always be stated.

A p-value for a two-tailed binomial test

For the same observation with H₁: p ≠ 0.5, the p-value is twice the smaller tail probability: 2 × 0.0547 = 0.1094. A two-tailed p-value is never the value of one tail alone, and it is capped at 1 if doubling would exceed 1. Here 0.1094 is greater than 0.05, so the result is not significant at 5%. A two-tailed p-value is always at least as large as the one-tailed value, which is why a two-tailed test is the harder one to pass.

A p-value for a normal test

Suppose z = −2.1 is found for a lower-tailed normal test. The p-value is Φ(−2.1) = 1 − Φ(2.1) = 1 − 0.9821 = 0.0179. For a two-tailed test the p-value would be 2 × 0.0179 = 0.0357. Use the symmetry of the normal curve, and show the Φ step so that the table lookup can be checked.

Comparing a p-value with the significance level

If the p-value is less than or equal to the significance level, reject H₀. Write the comparison as a statement with both numbers, for example 0.0547 > 0.05, so do not reject H₀. Then give the decision in words, in the context of the question. The comparison in numbers is what the working shows, and the sentence is what the conclusion mark asks for.

Equations and symbols

A hypothesis test is a decision rule, and these are its moving parts: the test statistic, the standard error, the tail probability and the comparison that produces the verdict.

The decision

reject H0 if p-value <= alpha Key: H0 = the null hypothesis, the assumption of no change; p-value = the probability of a result at least as extreme, assuming H0 is true; alpha = the significance level, the acceptable risk of rejecting a true H0 (often 0.05 or 0.01). Failing to reject is not proof that H0 is true — it means the evidence was insufficient.

P(X <= 15) = 0.0432 Key: X = number of fault-free components in a sample of 20; 0.0432 = the lower-tail probability under H0: p = 0.9. Because 0.0432 < 0.05 the null is rejected, and the same figure is the actual significance level of the test.

The normal test

standard error = 8/sqrt 16 = 2 Key: 8 = population standard deviation σ (g); 16 = sample size n (bags); 2 = the standard error of the mean (g). The standard error, not σ, is the denominator of the test statistic — omitting the √n is the classic lost mark.

z = (496 - 500)/2 = -2 Key: z = the test statistic, in standard errors; 496 = sample mean (g); 500 = hypothesised mean μ (g); 2 = the standard error (g). Compare |z| with the critical value: 1.6449 one-tailed at 5%, 1.96 two-tailed at 5%.

p-value = P(Z > 1.72) = 0.0427 Key: Z = the standard normal variable; 1.72 = the observed test statistic; 0.0427 = the area beyond it, for an upper-tail alternative. Significant at 5% but not at 1% — say which level you are concluding at.

Errors

A Type I error rejects a true H0 and has probability alpha; a Type II error fails to reject a false H0. Lowering alpha reduces Type I errors and increases Type II; a larger sample reduces both, because it shrinks the standard error so the same deviation counts as more standard errors.

The slip worth naming

Comparing a p-value with 5 instead of 0.05, or doubling the tail without a two-sided alternative. Both reverse a correct conclusion, which is exactly the mark the question is testing.

title: International GCSE English as a Second Language: Writing Tasks and Themes
content:
International GCSE English as a Second Language: Writing Tasks and Themes

OxfordAQA International GCSE English as a Second Language (9280) assesses writing in a paper of its own (Paper 2 in the current official numbering — some older revision materials list the writing component first, so always check the code on your question paper). This note builds the whole writing skill set from zero: how to read the task, how to choose register, how to plan in five minutes, and how to write each task type — functional and transactional writing, short-form responses, extended discursive writing and narrative writing — across the three exam themes. Every task on this paper is a communication problem, not a grammar test, and the marks follow from solving that problem in the right tone.

What the Writing paper asks of you

The writing component carries 60 marks, is 1 hour 15 minutes long, and counts for 30% of the qualification. Its tasks are progressive: shorter functional writing first, then short-form responses, then one or two extended pieces that may be discursive or narrative. The exact task list and word limits are printed on your paper, so this note teaches the task types rather than guessing a fixed layout — and the word limit given in the question is always binding.

FeatureWhat it means for you
Duration and marks1 hour 15 minutes, 60 marks, 30% of the grade. Roughly one minute of planning per ten minutes of writing.
Task progressionShort functional tasks first (emails, notes, forms), then extended discursive or narrative writing. The later tasks carry more marks — save time for them.
The themesEverything you write sits under one of three theme areas, so vocabulary preparation is finite and examinable.
What earns marksTask fulfilment (did you do what was asked?), register (is the tone right for the reader?), organisation (is it structured?), and linguistic range and accuracy.

The three themes and their topic banks

Every question is drawn from the three OxfordAQA theme areas. You cannot predict the exact topic, but you can prepare vocabulary, examples and opinions for each theme bank, and that preparation is the single highest-return revision you can do for this paper.

ThemeTypical topicsVocabulary to prepare
Identity and cultureFamily life, traditions and festivals, food, personal identity, hobbies, music and film, cultural differencesdescribing habits and routines, comparing traditions, giving opinions about culture, describing people and places from your own experience
Local, national, international and global areas of interestYour town and region, travel and tourism, the environment, technology, news and current events, sportdescribing places, cause and effect language for problems (pollution, congestion), proposing solutions, comparing locations
Current and future study and employmentSchool subjects, exams, ambitions, jobs and careers, work experience, skills, further studydescribing plans and ambitions, talking about ability and skills, justifying choices, writing about the future with will, going to, would like to

The efficient way to revise: for each theme, prepare ten nouns, ten verbs, five adjectives, two personal examples and one opinion with a reason. That is a working vocabulary of about eighty items, and it covers almost anything the paper can ask.

The APF framework: Audience, Purpose, Form

Before writing a single sentence, three decisions control everything else. The exam rewards candidates who make these decisions visibly, because the marker can see that the writing is shaped rather than dumped.

  1. Audience — who reads this? A friend, a teacher, a stranger, an employer, a newspaper reader. This decides formality, pronouns (I and you versus one and people), abbreviations (don't versus do not), and how much you explain.
  2. Purpose — why am I writing? To persuade, inform, request, describe, entertain, complain, advise, or apply. Purpose decides the opening move and the content order: a complaint states the problem then the desired fix; a persuasive piece states the position then the reasons.
  3. Form — what shape does this text have? Email, letter, article, review, report, story. Form decides the layout features the marker looks for: greeting and sign-off on an email, headline and opening hook on an article, a clear introduction and conclusion on an essay.

Worked example of the APF decision: the task says, "Your school is thinking about banning mobile phones. Write an article for the school magazine giving your views." Audience: your classmates and teachers (semi-formal, first person plural we). Purpose: persuade with reasons and examples. Form: article, so you need a headline, a hook opening, paragraphs with linking, and a closing line that lands the point. Once those three answers exist, the plan writes itself.

Register and tone: the formal–informal continuum

Register is the difference between "Hiya, can't come, sorry!" and "Dear Mr Ahmed, I am writing to apologise for my absence." Neither is wrong in itself; each is wrong for the wrong reader. Markers describe the top band as a consistent register suited to audience and purpose — the key word is consistent. One slang phrase in an otherwise formal letter breaks that consistency and costs marks.

FeatureInformal (friend, peer)Formal (teacher, employer, institution)
OpeningHi ..., How are you?Dear Mr/Ms ..., I am writing to ...
Contractionsdon't, I'm, can'tdo not, I am, cannot
QuestionsDirect and chatty: What do you think?Polite forms: I would be grateful if you could ...
OpinionI reckon ..., To be honest ...In my opinion ..., It seems to me that ...
ClosingSee you soon! Best wishesYours sincerely / Yours faithfully

One rule of thumb saves many marks: match the formality of the task, and never mix the two columns inside one text.

Functional and transactional writing: format skeletons

Functional tasks (emails, letters, notes, messages, short articles) are marked for doing the job: covering every content point in the prompt, using the right form, and keeping the register right. A skeleton for each form means your brain can spend its energy on language instead of layout.

  • Email to a friend: greeting → reaction to their news → answers to their questions (one per bullet in the prompt) → your news/questions → closing line.
  • Formal letter or email: Dear ... → why you are writing (one sentence) → the content points in logical order, one paragraph each → what you want to happen → Yours sincerely, name.
  • Article: headline → hook (a question, a surprising fact, a short scene) → two or three paragraphs each making one point → closing line that echoes the hook.
  • Review: what it is → description → evaluation with reasons → recommendation and who it suits.
  • Report: title → introduction stating the scope → findings under clear headings → recommendation.

For every content point in the prompt, write one developed sentence or more. Under-developed content is the most common reason a competent writer scores mid-band: the marker counts content points and how fully each is covered.

Short-form responses: from notes to sentences

Short-form tasks give you information in notes, a table, or a picture and ask for connected sentences. The skill is expansion: each note must become real grammar, not a list with a capital letter.

  • Step 1 — read every note and mark the content points; one sentence minimum per point.
  • Step 2 — add the missing grammar: articles (a, the), pronouns to avoid repetition, a verb in the right tense, connectors (because, so, although, however).
  • Step 3 — check the target reader: if the task says "write to your English-speaking friend", contractions and questions are welcome; if it says "write to the school principal", they are not.

Worked example. The task: "Your friend wants to know about your new school. Use these notes to write a message: new school / big / near home / walk 10 minutes / favourite subject science / teacher good / start football club next month." A weak answer copies the notes. A top-band answer expands every point with grammar and personality: "My new school is really big — there are about a thousand students! The best part is that it's near home, so I only walk ten minutes every morning. My favourite subject is science because the teacher explains everything clearly and lets us do experiments. I've also started a football club — well, it opens next month, and I can't wait." Every note became a sentence; the register is friendly; the message reads like a message.

Extended discursive writing: the argument engine

Discursive tasks (an essay, an opinion article, a for-and-against discussion) reward organisation above fancy vocabulary. The marker needs to find your position, your reasons and your ending without hunting. Build the piece from modules:

  1. Introduction (2-3 sentences): restate the topic in your own words and give your position or the question you will explore. Never copy the prompt wording.
  2. Body paragraph 1: strongest reason. Topic sentence (the point) → explanation (why it is true) → example (a specific case, ideally personal or local) → link back to the position.
  3. Body paragraph 2: second reason, same four-beat shape.
  4. Body paragraph 3 (optional): the other side of the argument, then why your position still wins. This concession move reads as sophisticated thinking.
  5. Conclusion (2-3 sentences): restate the position in fresh words and end with the consequence or a call to action.

Model paragraph with top-band breakdown: "Some people believe that homework should be abolished because it causes stress. In my view, however, homework teaches students to work independently, a skill they will need at university and at work. For example, when I prepared for my maths exam last term, the practice I did at home was what moved my grade from a C to an A. Therefore, rather than abolishing homework, schools should limit its quantity." Why it scores: the topic sentence names the counter-argument, the contrast word however marks the writer's position, the explanation states the reason in abstract terms (independence), the example grounds it in a specific personal case, and the final sentence turns the concession into a balanced recommendation. That is the whole engine: point, reason, example, link — used once per paragraph.

Narrative writing: story craft under time pressure

Narrative tasks ask for a story, and the marker rewards a controlled arc over an ambitious plot. Three moves separate top-band stories from mid-band ones: a clear structure, controlled tense, and concrete detail instead of abstract claims.

  • The arc: opening situation (who, where, when) → an incident that changes things → rising tension in two or three beats → a climax moment → a short resolution or closing image. Plan all five before writing.
  • Tense control: past simple for events (I opened the door), past continuous for background (The rain was falling), past perfect for earlier events (I had forgotten my keys). Choose one main past tense and stay there; tense drift is a classic accuracy loss.
  • Showing, not telling: instead of "I was nervous", write "My hands were shaking as I unfolded the paper." Concrete detail (hands, paper, rain) lets the reader feel the emotion the writer claims.
