  • Sentence variation: mix short dramatic sentences ("The door opened.") with longer flowing ones. Sentence control is explicitly rewarded in the writing criteria.

Worked example of turning telling into showing. Weak: "The market was busy and colourful and I felt excited." Top-band: "The market was a wall of noise: vendors shouting prices, scooters threading between the stalls, the smell of grilled corn drifting over everything. I stood on my toes, grinning, trying to see everything at once." The second version names concrete sounds and smells, uses a colon and participles, and shows the excitement through behaviour (standing on toes, grinning) rather than the adjective excited.

The five-minute plan

Planning is not wasted time; it is where the marks are decided. For every extended task, spend five minutes on a grid: APF in one corner (who, why, what form), then five content beats (for discursive: position, reason 1, reason 2, other side, conclusion; for narrative: situation, incident, rising tension, climax, resolution). Under each beat, jot one keyword or example. The writing stage then becomes transcription with style — and the marker sees structure immediately.

Worked examples: task to top-band answer

Worked example 1 — functional task. "You have won a place on a summer course in another country. Write an email to the course organiser. Say why you chose the course, ask two questions about accommodation and food, and explain your travel arrangements."

APF:  Audience = adult organiser (formal, no slang)
      Purpose  = inform + request information (cover all three bullets)
      Form     = email: greeting, clear paragraphs, sign-off
Plan: 1 why chosen  2 question: accommodation  3 question: food
      4 travel arrangements  5 closing

Model answer: "Dear Ms Carter, I am writing to confirm my place on the International Summer Course in July and to say how delighted I am to have been accepted. I chose this course because I hope to study engineering at university, and the robotics module is exactly the experience I need. I would be grateful if you could tell me a little about the accommodation. Will students stay with host families or in a residence? I also have a question about food: will it be possible to provide vegetarian meals? As for my travel, I will fly from Kuala Lumpur on 2 July and expect to arrive at the airport at about three o'clock in the afternoon. Thank you for your help. Yours sincerely, Amir Rahman." Why it scores: every bullet is covered and developed (the reason is specific — robotics and engineering; the questions are polite and precise; the travel gives a date, a route and a time), the register is consistently formal (I am writing, I would be grateful, no contractions), and the form features (greeting, sign-off, clear paragraphing) are all present.

Worked example 2 — discursive task. "Some students think that school uniforms should be banned. Write an article for your school magazine giving your views."

Plan: position = keep uniforms (with a change: student input on design)
      P1 identity/equality argument + example of bullying over clothes
      P2 practical argument (cost, mornings) + example
      P3 concession: freedom matters — answer it with the design compromise
      Conclusion: keep, but reform

Model opening and body paragraph: "Should we all dress the same? Every September the uniform debate returns to our school, and this year I think we can answer it honestly: uniforms should stay, but they should change. The strongest reason is equality. When everyone wears the same clothes, nobody is judged for what their parents can afford. At my old school, a classmate was mocked for wearing the same jacket every day; with a uniform, that cruelty simply had no surface to attach to." Why it scores: the headline question hooks, the opening states a nuanced position (stay, but change), and the first body paragraph runs the point–reason–example–link engine with a concrete story instead of a vague claim.

Exam-style questions and answers

Practise each of these in timed conditions, planning with APF first.

  1. (Functional, 12 marks worth of practice) Your English-speaking friend has invited you to a festival in their country. Write an email: thank them, ask about what to wear and what to bring, explain why you are looking forward to it. Answer outline: informal register, three developed paragraphs, two clear questions, contractions and a warm closing.
  2. (Short-form) Notes: library / opens 8am / new computers / free wifi / quiet room upstairs. Write four sentences for the school website. Answer outline: expand each note with articles, linking and a positive recommendation sentence.
  3. (Discursive) "Public transport should be free for everyone." Write an article giving your views. Answer outline: position (free for students and the elderly at least), reasons (cost of living, pollution, congestion), concession (who pays — taxation), conclusion (phased scheme).
  4. (Narrative) Write a story that begins: "The letter had been sitting on the table for three days." Answer outline: five-beat arc, past-tense control, showing detail in the climax, closing image.
  5. (Review) A travel website wants reviews of places in your area. Write a review of a place visitors should see. Answer outline: identify the place, describe it, evaluate with reasons, recommend to a named type of visitor.
  6. (Formal letter) You want a part-time job at a local café. Write a letter explaining why you are suitable and asking for an interview. Answer outline: formal opening, two skill examples with evidence, polite request, Yours sincerely.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Register drift: starting formally ("Dear Sir") and ending informally ("See ya!"). Pick one register in the plan and check it at the end.
  • Bullet copying: answering a content-point prompt as a list. Every point needs a full, developed sentence — the marker looks for development, not mention.
  • Wrong form: writing an essay when the task asked for an email. The form features (greeting, sign-off, headline) are easy marks and easy to lose.
  • Ignoring the word limit: the limit on the paper is binding. Under-length answers cap your content marks; long answers eat the time later tasks need.
  • Memorised paragraphs: examiners read thousands of scripts; a pasted "global warming is one of the biggest problems" paragraph without task-specific detail reads as filler and cannot reach the top band.
  • Time management: spending 30 minutes on the short task and 10 on the extended one inverts the mark distribution. Budget roughly 15 minutes for short tasks and the remainder for extended writing, with 5 minutes to check.
  • Theme blindness: not preparing vocabulary for the three themes leaves you translating in the exam. Translation costs accuracy, range and time at once.
  • Final check failure: the last three minutes should hunt only for verb tenses, subject–verb agreement, articles and spelling of your most-used theme words.

title: Simplifying, Expanding and Factorising
content:
Algebra — Simplifying and Expanding

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): substitution, collecting like terms, expanding brackets, factorising (common factor, quadratics, difference of two squares), algebraic fractions.

1. Substitution

a = 3, b = −2: 2a² − b = 2(9) + 2 = 20. Always bracket substituted negatives.

2. Collecting like terms

5x + 3y − 2x + y = 3x + 4y. Terms need identical letter parts (x² and x are not like terms).

3. Expanding

  • Single: 3(2x − 5) = 6x − 15.
  • Double: (x + 3)(x − 4) = x² − x − 12 (grid or FOIL).
  • Cubic products: (x+2)³ = x³ + 6x² + 12x + 8.

4. Factorising

  • Common factor: 6x²y − 9xy² = 3xy(2x − 3y).
  • Quadratics: x² − 5x + 6 = (x − 2)(x − 3) (two numbers ×6, sum −5).
  • Harder: 6x² + 7x + 2 = (3x + 2)(2x + 1) — split the middle term.
  • Difference of two squares: 9x² − 25 = (3x − 5)(3x + 5).

5. Algebraic fractions

Factorise top and bottom fully, then cancel: (x² − 9)/(x + 3) = (x − 3). To add, use a common denominator: 1/(x+1) + 2/(x−1) = (3x + 1)/((x+1)(x−1)).

Exam tips: always factorise out the highest common factor including the number; check expansion by substituting x = 1 into both forms.

title: Algebra — Simplifying and Expanding — Study Notes
content:
Algebra — Simplifying and Expanding

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): substitution, collecting like terms, expanding brackets, factorising (common factor, quadratics, difference of two squares), algebraic fractions.

1. Substitution

a = 3, b = −2: 2a² − b = 2(9) + 2 = 20. Always bracket substituted negatives.

2. Collecting like terms

5x + 3y − 2x + y = 3x + 4y. Terms need identical letter parts (x² and x are not like terms).

3. Expanding

  • Single: 3(2x − 5) = 6x − 15.
  • Double: (x + 3)(x − 4) = x² − x − 12 (grid or FOIL).
  • Cubic products: (x+2)³ = x³ + 6x² + 12x + 8.

4. Factorising

  • Common factor: 6x²y − 9xy² = 3xy(2x − 3y).
  • Quadratics: x² − 5x + 6 = (x − 2)(x − 3) (two numbers ×6, sum −5).
  • Harder: 6x² + 7x + 2 = (3x + 2)(2x + 1) — split the middle term.
  • Difference of two squares: 9x² − 25 = (3x − 5)(3x + 5).

5. Algebraic fractions

Factorise top and bottom fully, then cancel: (x² − 9)/(x + 3) = (x − 3). To add, use a common denominator: 1/(x+1) + 2/(x−1) = (3x + 1)/((x+1)(x−1)).

Exam tips: always factorise out the highest common factor including the number; check expansion by substituting x = 1 into both forms.

Expanding brackets

Each term outside a bracket multiplies every term inside it. For a double bracket, multiply each term in the first by each term in the second, then collect like terms. Expanding (x + 3)(x − 5) gives x² − 2x − 15. Keep track of signs carefully, since most lost marks come from negative terms.

Factorising

Take out the highest common factor first, then look for a pair of brackets. For a quadratic x² + bx + c, find two numbers that multiply to c and add to b. For the difference of two squares, a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b). Check by expanding your answer.

Algebraic fractions

Simplify by factorising the numerator and denominator and cancelling common factors. Add or subtract fractions by writing them over a common denominator. Never cancel terms that are added, only factors that multiply.

Worked example: expanding and collecting terms

Expand (2x + 3)(x − 4). Multiply each term in the first bracket by each term in the second: 2x × x = 2x², 2x × (−4) = −8x, 3 × x = 3x, 3 × (−4) = −12. Collect the like terms: 2x² − 5x − 12.

A quick check is to substitute x = 1: (5)(−3) = −15, and 2 − 5 − 12 = −15. The two agree.

Factorising quadratics and the difference of two squares

Factorise x² + x − 12. Find two numbers that multiply to −12 and add to +1: +4 and −3. So x² + x − 12 = (x + 4)(x − 3).

The difference of two squares gives 4x² − 9 = (2x − 3)(2x + 3). Recognise it whenever there is no middle term and both terms are squares with a minus sign between them.

Simplifying algebraic fractions

Simplify (x² − 9)/(x² + x − 6). Factorise the numerator as (x − 3)(x + 3) and the denominator as (x + 3)(x − 2). Cancel the common factor (x + 3) to get (x − 3)/(x − 2), with the restriction x ≠ −3 stated because the original expression is undefined there.

Common errors that lose marks

  • Writing (a + b)² = a² + b², which drops the middle term 2ab.
  • Cancelling a term rather than a factor, for example simplifying (x + 3)/(x + 2) to 3/2.
  • Expanding a negative bracket without changing the signs inside it: −(x − 4) = −x + 4.

title: Complex Numbers
content:
Complex Numbers

Basics

i² = −1. A complex number z = a + bi has real part a and imaginary part b. Two numbers are equal iff both parts match.

Arithmetic: add/subtract parts; multiply with brackets and replace i² with −1.

Example: (2 + 3i)(1 − i) = 2 − 2i + 3i − 3i² = 5 + i.

Conjugates

z̄ = a − bi. zz̄ = a² + b² (real). Dividing: multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate.

Example: 1/(3 − i) × (3 + i)/(3 + i) = (3 + i)/10.

Argand Diagram

Plot z as the point (a, b). |z| = √(a² + b²) is the modulus (distance from origin); arg z = tan⁻¹(b/a) is the argument (angle). Multiply two numbers: moduli multiply, arguments add.

Modulus–Argument Form

z = r(cos θ + i sin θ), r = |z|, θ = arg z. Useful for powers and roots.

de Moivre and Roots

[r(cos θ + i sin θ)]ⁿ = rⁿ(cos nθ + i sin nθ).

Example: (1 + i)⁸: |1 + i| = √2, arg = π/4, so z⁸ = (√2)⁸ cis 2π = 16.

An nth root gives n evenly spaced solutions, 2π/n apart on a circle of radius r^(1/n).

Exam tips: always give arguments in the required interval; when solving equations, remember complex roots come in conjugate pairs for real polynomials.

title: Organic Chemistry: Arenes (Edexcel IAL A2 Chemistry)
content:
Organic Chemistry: Arenes - Edexcel IAL A2 Chemistry

This topic belongs to Edexcel International A-Level Chemistry WCH15, Topic 18, and covers the structure, stability, and characteristic reactions of arenes, specifically benzene, alongside activating and directing effects including phenol.

Structure and Evidence for Benzene

Benzene is an arene with the molecular formula C6H6, possessing a planar ring structure supported by multiple lines of physical and chemical evidence.

  • Thermochemical evidence: The measured enthalpy of hydrogenation of benzene is approximately −208 kJ mol−1, which is significantly less exothermic than the theoretical value of −360 kJ mol−1 calculated for a hypothetical cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene with three isolated double bonds. The difference of about 150 kJ mol−1 is the stabilisation energy, also known as the delocalisation energy, proving benzene is much more stable than the classical Kekule structure.
  • X-ray diffraction data: X-ray crystallography shows that all six carbon-carbon bond lengths in benzene are identical at 0.139 nm, a value intermediate between a typical carbon-carbon single bond (0.154 nm) and a carbon-carbon double bond (0.134 nm).
  • Infrared spectroscopy: IR data shows characteristic carbon-carbon aromatic ring stretching absorptions and aromatic carbon-hydrogen stretching bands.
  • Delocalised model: The delocalised model for the structure of benzene involves the sideways overlap of unhybridised p-orbitals on each of the six carbon atoms, forming a continuous ring of π-bonds above and below the plane of the carbon ring. Students may represent the structure of benzene as a ring inside a hexagon or as alternating double and single bonds as appropriate in equations and mechanisms.

Resistance to Bromination and Comparison with Alkenes

Benzene displays very different chemical reactivity compared to alkenes due to the nature of its bonding.

  • Resistance to bromination: Benzene is resistant to bromination compared to alkenes because of the delocalisation of π-bonds in benzene, which spreads the electron density over the whole ring, making it a stable region. In contrast, alkenes possess a localised electron density in their π-bond situated between two carbon atoms, which polarises approaching electrophiles much more readily.
  • Reactivity consequence: Alkenes undergo electrophilic addition reactions readily at room temperature without a catalyst, whereas benzene undergoes electrophilic substitution reactions and requires a halogen carrier catalyst to polarise non-polar molecules like bromine.

Reactions of Benzene

Benzene undergoes a variety of chemical reactions under specific conditions.

  • Combustion: Benzene burns in oxygen in air with a smoky flame due to its high carbon-to-hydrogen ratio, indicating unburnt carbon particles.
  • Halogenation: Benzene reacts with bromine in the presence of a catalyst such as iron(III) bromide or aluminium bromide.
  • Nitration: Benzene reacts with a mixture of concentrated nitric acid and concentrated sulfuric acids heated to about 50 degrees Celsius.
  • Sulfonation: Benzene reacts with fuming sulfuric acid (sulfuric(VI) acid containing dissolved sulfur trioxide).
  • Friedel-Crafts reactions: Benzene reacts with halogenoalkanes (alkylation) and acyl chlorides (acylation) with anhydrous aluminium chloride as a catalyst.

Mechanisms of Electrophilic Substitution

Electrophilic substitution in benzene proceeds through the generation of an electrophile followed by attack and proton loss.

  • Generation of electrophiles: For nitration, concentrated nitric acid and concentrated sulfuric acid generate the nitronium ion electrophile: HNO3 + 2H2SO4 yields NO2+ + 2HSO4− + H3O+. For halogenation, bromine reacts with an aluminium halide catalyst to generate the Br+ or polarised Br-Br-AlCl3 electrophilic species. For Friedel-Crafts alkylation and acylation, the halogenoalkane or acyl chloride reacts with aluminium chloride, acting as a Lewis acid, to generate a carbocation or acylium ion electrophile: RCl + AlCl3 yields R+ + AlCl4−.
  • Substitution mechanism: The electron-rich π system of the benzene ring acts as a nucleophile and donates a pair of electrons to the electrophile, forming an unstable arenium intermediate where the positive charge is delocalised over the remaining five carbon atoms of the ring. A base removes a hydrogen ion from the substituted carbon, restoring the stable delocalised π system of the benzene ring and regenerating the catalyst.

Reactivity of Phenol

Phenol contains a hydroxyl group attached directly to an aromatic ring, significantly altering its reactivity compared to benzene.

  • Reaction with bromine water: Phenol reacts readily with bromine water at room temperature without any halogen carrier catalyst, instantly decolorising the orange bromine water and giving a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol, accompanied by steamy fumes of hydrogen bromide.
  • Reasons for relative ease: The lone pair of electrons on the oxygen atom of the −OH group in phenol overlaps with the π system of the benzene ring. This partially delocalises the lone pair into the ring, significantly increasing the electron density of the ring compared to benzene. As a result, the benzene ring in phenol is strongly activated, polarizing incoming electrophiles like bromine much more effectively and attracting them faster than benzene can.

Side-Chain Oxidation and Directing Effects

Substituents on the benzene ring affect both the position of further substitution and the reactivity of side chains.

  • Directing effects: Alkyl groups, such as the methyl group in methylbenzene, and activating groups direct a second incoming substituent primarily to the 2- and 4- positions (ortho and para). A nitro group is a deactivating group and directs incoming electrophiles to the 3- (meta) position. Hydroxyl and amino groups are strongly activating.
  • Side-chain oxidation: Hot, acidified potassium manganate(VII) solution oxidises any alkyl side chain on a benzene ring directly to a carboxylic acid group, regardless of the length of the alkyl chain, provided there is at least one benzylic hydrogen atom. For example, methylbenzene is oxidised to benzoic acid.

Typical mistakes

  • Mistake: Stating that benzene undergoes electrophilic addition because it has double bonds. Correction: Benzene undergoes electrophilic substitution to preserve the stable delocalised π electron system.
  • Mistake: Omitting the catalyst in Friedel-Crafts equations or halogenation. Correction: Always include anhydrous aluminium chloride or iron(III) bromide as catalysts.
  • Mistake: Drawing the positive charge inside the intermediate horseshoe incorrectly. Correction: Ensure the incomplete horseshoe representing the positive charge in the arenium intermediate extends over five carbon atoms and does not touch the carbon bonded to the incoming electrophile and leaving hydrogen.
  • Mistake: Confusing the conditions for phenol bromination with benzene bromination. Correction: Phenol reacts with aqueous bromine without a catalyst at room temperature, whereas benzene requires liquid bromine and a halogen carrier catalyst.

Exam-style questions

  1. Question: State the thermochemical evidence that supports the delocalised model of benzene over the Kekule structure of cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene. Answer: The measured enthalpy of hydrogenation of benzene is approximately −208 kJ mol−1, whereas the theoretical value for cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene is −360 kJ mol−1. The difference of about 150 kJ mol−1 is the delocalisation energy, proving benzene is thermodynamically more stable. (Earns credit by stating both values, their difference, and naming delocalisation energy).
  2. Question: Explain why benzene is resistant to bromination compared to cyclohexene. Answer: Benzene has a delocalised ring of π-electrons which spreads electron density, whereas cyclohexene has a localised π-bond between two carbons. The localised electron density in cyclohexene polarises bromine molecules much more readily than the stable delocalised ring of benzene. (Earns credit for contrasting delocalised and localised electron density).
  3. Question: Write the equation for the generation of the electrophile in the nitration of benzene using concentrated nitric and sulfuric acids. Answer: HNO3 + 2H2SO4 yields NO2+ + 2HSO4− + H3O+. (Earns credit for correct reactants, products, and stoichiometry).
  4. Question: Outline the mechanism for the alkylation of benzene with chloromethane in the presence of aluminium chloride. Include curly arrows and the intermediate. Answer: CH3Cl + AlCl3 yields CH3+ + AlCl4−. The benzene ring π electrons attack the CH3+ electrophile to form the arenium intermediate with a positive charge spread over five carbons, followed by loss of H+ to form methylbenzene and regenerate AlCl3 alongside HCl. (Earns credit for electrophile generation, curly arrows from the ring, correct arenium intermediate structure, and loss of H+).
  5. Question: Explain why phenol reacts with bromine water much more readily than benzene does. Answer: The oxygen atom in the −OH group of phenol has a lone pair of electrons that overlaps with the π system of the benzene ring. This increases the electron density of the ring, activating it and allowing it to polarise bromine molecules without a catalyst. (Earns credit for mentioning lone pair overlap, increased electron density, and ring activation).

Use these notes alongside active recall of mechanisms, reagent-condition pairs, and thermochemical definitions. Revise next the chemistry of carbonyl compounds, carboxylic acids, and esters to complete your organic chemistry mastery for WCH15.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Evidence for delocalisation, applied to hydrogenation: cyclohexene releases about −120 kJ mol⁻¹, so three double bonds would release about −360 kJ mol⁻¹. Benzene releases only about −208 kJ mol⁻¹, a difference of about 152 kJ mol⁻¹ that is the extra stability from delocalisation.
  • Nitration, applied to benzene: concentrated HNO₃ and H₂SO₄ generate the NO₂⁺ electrophile. The sulfuric acid is a catalyst and dehydrates the nitric acid. Show the electrophile first, then the arrow from the ring to it, then the loss of H⁺ to restore the aromatic ring.
  • Phenol versus benzene, applied to bromination: the lone pair on oxygen donates into the ring, so phenol reacts with aqueous bromine at room temperature without a catalyst and forms 2,4,6-tribromophenol as a white precipitate. Benzene does not react under the same conditions.
  • Directing effects: an electron-donating group such as –OH or –CH₃ directs an incoming electrophile to positions 2, 4 and 6 (ortho and para). A nitro group directs to the meta position and deactivates the ring. Name the group and its effect in the answer.

title: Exam technique: Hypothesis Testing
content:
### What earns the marks
For hypotheses, H0 and H1 in words or symbols earn the first mark. For the test statistic, its value compared against the critical value earns the method mark. For conclusions, contextual wording (evidence of change, not proof) earns the final mark.
### Traps
Error: significant claimed equals proven. Correction: evidence only. Error: wrong tail direction. Correction: H1 fixes the tail. Error: H0 restated in the conclusion without context. Correction: answer about the situation.

title: A Level Mathematics: The Binomial Distribution
content:
A Level Mathematics: The Binomial Distribution

A binomial distribution counts successes in a fixed number of independent trials, each with the same probability of success. Coins, multiple-choice guesses, defective items in a sample and free throws all fit the same template, and once a problem is recognised as binomial the calculation is a formula plus a cumulative table. This note builds the distribution from its four conditions, derives the formula from counting, and then uses it for the two things exams actually ask: probabilities and hypothesis tests.

The four conditions

Before writing X ~ B(n, p) you must be able to name the conditions, because most exam questions include a part asking whether the model is appropriate. The conditions are not red tape: drop any one and the formula is simply wrong.

1. a fixed number of trials n
2. each trial has exactly two outcomes (success / failure)
3. the probability of success p is constant for every trial
4. the trials are independent
then X = number of successes has X ~ B(n, p)

Worked example (checking the model). A bag holds 5 red and 15 blue counters. Four counters are taken without replacement. Is the number of red counters binomial?

n = 4 is fixed and each draw is red or not red
but p changes: 5/20, then 5/19 if a red was taken, ...
the trials are not independent, so NOT binomial (it is hypergeometric)

Taking with replacement would fix it: p stays 0.25 on every draw.

The formula, and where it comes from

The probability of a particular sequence of r successes and n − r failures is p^r (1−p)^(n−r), because independence lets you multiply. The number of such sequences is the number of ways to choose which r trials succeed, which is nCr. Multiplying gives the formula.

P(X = r) = nCr p^r (1 - p)^(n - r)
the nCr counts arrangements; the powers give the probability of one arrangement

Worked example. X ~ B(10, 0.3). Find P(X = 3).

P = 10C3 (0.3)^3 (0.7)^7
= 120 x 0.027 x 0.08235
= 120 x 0.002223 = 0.2668

Worked example 2 (a single trial count). A fair die is rolled 8 times. Find the probability of exactly two sixes.

X ~ B(8, 1/6)
P(X = 2) = 8C2 (1/6)^2 (5/6)^6 = 28 x 0.02778 x 0.3349 = 0.2605

Worked example 3 (why nCr appears). For n = 3 and r = 1, list the sequences and confirm the coefficient.

sequences: SFF, FSF, FFS - three of them
each has probability p(1-p)^2
so P(X = 1) = 3p(1-p)^2, and 3C1 = 3

Cumulative probabilities

Questions almost always ask for a range, not a single value, and the cumulative distribution is what the calculator or the tables supply. The skill is rewriting the question into the form the table gives you.

P(X <= r) is tabulated directly
P(X >= r) = 1 - P(X <= r - 1)
P(X < r)  = P(X <= r - 1)
P(a <= X <= b) = P(X <= b) - P(X <= a - 1)
P(X = r) = P(X <= r) - P(X <= r - 1)

Worked example. X ~ B(20, 0.4). Find P(X ≥ 8).

P(X >= 8) = 1 - P(X <= 7)
= 1 - 0.4159
= 0.5841

Worked example 2 (between). For the same X, find P(5 ≤ X ≤ 10).

= P(X <= 10) - P(X <= 4)
= 0.8725 - 0.0510
= 0.8215

Worked example 3 (the strict inequality trap). For the same X, find P(X > 6).

P(X > 6) = 1 - P(X <= 6) = 1 - 0.2500 = 0.7500
note this is different from P(X >= 6) = 1 - P(X <= 5) = 0.8746

Mean and variance

The binomial has the simplest mean and variance in the syllabus, and they are worth knowing both forwards and backwards: a question can give the mean and variance and ask for n and p.

E(X) = np
Var(X) = np(1 - p)
standard deviation = sqrt(np(1-p))

Worked example. X ~ B(50, 0.2). Find the mean and standard deviation.

mean = 50 x 0.2 = 10
variance = 10 x 0.8 = 8
sd = 2.828

Worked example 2 (backwards). A binomial variable has mean 12 and variance 9. Find n and p.

np = 12;  np(1-p) = 9
divide: 1 - p = 9/12 = 0.75  ->  p = 0.25
then n = 12/0.25 = 48

Hypothesis testing with the binomial

A one-tailed test asks whether p has increased or decreased; the test statistic is the observed count, and the p-value is the probability of a result at least as extreme in the direction of the alternative.

H0: p = p0      H1: p > p0 (or p < p0)
X ~ B(n, p0) under H0
p-value = P(X >= observed) or P(X <= observed)
compare with the significance level; reject H0 if p-value <= alpha

Worked example. A coin is tossed 20 times and lands heads 15 times. Test at the 5% level whether the coin is biased towards heads.

H0: p = 0.5;  H1: p > 0.5
X ~ B(20, 0.5)
P(X >= 15) = 1 - P(X <= 14) = 1 - 0.9793 = 0.0207
0.0207 < 0.05, so reject H0
there is evidence at the 5% level that the coin favours heads

Worked example 2 (two-tailed). The same data tested two-tailed.

double the smaller tail: 2 x 0.0207 = 0.0414
0.0414 < 0.05, so still reject H0 at the 5% level

Worked example 3 (critical region). For X ~ B(20, 0.5), find the critical region for a 5% one-tailed test of p > 0.5.

P(X >= 14) = 0.0577 (above 0.05)
P(X >= 15) = 0.0207 (below 0.05)
critical region: X >= 15

Note that the critical region is chosen so the probability of a Type I error is at most 5%, which is why 14 is excluded even though it is close.

When the model breaks down

Examiners like the question that asks why a binomial model is only an approximation. The usual culprits are dependence, a varying probability, or a fixed sample drawn without replacement from a small population.

SituationProblemEffect
sampling without replacementtrials not independentp drifts; use the hypergeometric instead
clustered data (pupils in classes)responses correlatedvariance underestimated
probability varies between trialsp not constantformula invalid
large n, p near 0.5computation heavynormal approximation is reasonable

Worked example (normal approximation). X ~ B(200, 0.4). Use a normal approximation to estimate P(X ≤ 70).

mean = 80;  variance = 200 x 0.4 x 0.6 = 48;  sd = 6.928
continuity correction: X <= 70 becomes X < 70.5
z = (70.5 - 80)/6.928 = -1.371
P(Z < -1.371) = 0.0852

The continuity correction is compulsory: a discrete count needs a half-unit boundary before it can be treated as continuous.

Expected frequencies and the shape of the distribution

A binomial distribution is not symmetric unless p = 0.5, and that shape decides which tail an exam question is fishing in. The most likely value — the mode — is the integer near (n + 1)p, and expected frequency multiplies the probability by the number of samples taken. Both are quick marks that are frequently missed because students jump straight to the formula.

mode is near (n + 1)p, checked by comparing consecutive probabilities
expected number in a sample of size N = N x P(X = r)

Worked example. X ~ B(12, 0.3). Find the most likely value of X and the expected number of 3s in 500 independent observations.

(n + 1)p = 13 x 0.3 = 3.9, so check r = 3 and r = 4
P(X = 3) = 220 x 0.027 x 0.1176 = 0.2397
P(X = 4) = 495 x 0.0081 x 0.1681 = 0.2311
mode = 3
expected number of 3s = 500 x 0.2397 = 120 (to the nearest whole)

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Model) State the distribution for the number of sixes in 12 rolls of a fair die. Answer: X ~ B(12, 1/6).
  2. (Single value) X ~ B(8, 0.25): find P(X = 2). Answer: 28 × 0.0625 × 0.1780 = 0.3115.
  3. (Cumulative) X ~ B(15, 0.3): find P(X ≤ 4). Answer: 0.5155 from tables.
  4. (Complement) Same X: find P(X ≥ 3). Answer: 1 − 0.2969 = 0.7031.
  5. (Mean) X ~ B(40, 0.35): find E(X) and Var(X). Answer: 14 and 9.1.
  6. (Backwards) Mean 18, variance 12: find n and p. Answer: p = 1/3, n = 54.
  7. (Test) 12 of 20 seeds germinate; test p = 0.5 against p < 0.5 at 5%. Answer: P(X ≤ 12) = 0.8684, no evidence to reject.
  8. (Critical region) X ~ B(10, 0.2): find the 5% critical region for p < 0.2. Answer: P(X ≤ 0) = 0.1074 > 0.05, so no region exists at 5%.
  9. (Approximation) X ~ B(100, 0.5): approximate P(X ≥ 60). Answer: μ = 50, σ = 5, z = 1.9, P = 0.0287.
  10. (Assumption) Give one reason a binomial model may fail for defects in boxes of 20. Answer: defects may cluster, so trials are not independent.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Forgetting nCr: the coefficient counts arrangements; without it the answer is the probability of one specific sequence.
  • nCr on the wrong factor: it is p^r (1−p)^(n−r), with the success probability raised to the number of successes.
  • Inequality direction: P(X ≥ 8) uses 1 − P(X ≤ 7), not 1 − P(X ≤ 8).
  • Variance confused with standard deviation: np(1−p) is the variance; the test and the normal approximation need the square root.
  • Continuity correction omitted: any normal approximation to a discrete count needs the half-unit adjustment.
  • One-tailed evidence read as two: halving or doubling the tail without checking the alternative direction is a silent error.
  • Independence asserted, not checked: sampling without replacement from a small population breaks the model, and the question usually invites you to say so.
  • p-value compared with the wrong threshold: the significance level is given as a percentage; 5% means 0.05, not 5.

title: AS Level Physics: Forces and Equilibrium
content:
AS Level Physics: Forces and Equilibrium

Equilibrium is the physics of things that stay put — or move steadily — because everything acting on them cancels. The two conditions it obeys (no resultant force, no resultant moment) turn architecture, cranes and ladders into solvable puzzles. This note builds the toolkit from zero: what a moment is and why doors have handles at their edges, couples and torque, the centre of gravity, and the two equilibrium conditions applied to beams and multi-force systems, with every worked example solved in full.

Moment: the turning effect of a force

A force that does not act through a pivot makes a body turn. The measure of that turning effect is the moment:

moment of a force = force x perpendicular distance from the pivot
M = F d          (unit: newton metre, N m)

The analogy: a door. Push at the handle (far from the hinges) and it swings easily; push near the hinges and the same force barely turns it. The perpendicular is the load-bearing word: the distance must be measured along the line perpendicular to the force's line of action. If a force acts at an angle, resolve it first and use the perpendicular component.

Worked example. A door handle is 0.80 m from the hinges. A student pushes with 30 N at 40° to the door's surface. Find the moment about the hinges.

component perpendicular to the door: F_perp = 30 sin(40) = 19.3 N
(the angle is measured from the door itself, so the perpendicular
 component carries the sine)
M = F_perp d = 19.3 × 0.80 = 15.4 N m  (2 s.f.: 15 N m)

Direction matters in sign conventions: anticlockwise moments are usually taken as positive, clockwise as negative (or vice versa — consistency is what the marker checks).

Couples and torque

A couple is a pair of equal and opposite forces whose lines of action do not coincide: it produces pure rotation with no resultant force. The moment of a couple (its torque) is one force times the perpendicular distance between the two forces:

torque of a couple = F x d_between        (or 2 x F x (d/2))
unit: N m

Everyday couples: turning a steering wheel (both hands push oppositely), winding a clock key, the compass needle between two poles. The commonest exam error is halving or doubling the separation — measure between the two forces, full stop.

Centre of gravity

The centre of gravity is the point where the entire weight of a body may be taken to act. For uniform regular shapes it sits at the geometric centre; for irregular shapes it can be found experimentally (plumb-line method: hang the shape freely from two different points; the verticals from the suspension points meet at the centre of gravity). Stability questions follow from its position: an object topples when its line of action of weight falls outside its base — wide bases and low centres of gravity give stability (racing cars, furniture anti-tip brackets).

Worked example. Explain why a double-decker bus is more likely to topple on a sharp bend when fully loaded on the upper deck. Answer: Loading the upper deck raises the combined centre of gravity; on the bend, the turning effect of the weight about the outer wheels increases with the perpendicular distance to the pivot; if the weight's line of action passes beyond the outer wheels, the net moment topples the bus.

Equilibrium of forces: the two conditions

A body is in equilibrium when both conditions hold:

  1. Translational equilibrium: the vector sum of forces is zero — ΣF = 0 in every direction.
  2. Rotational equilibrium: the sum of moments about any pivot is zero — ΣM = 0 (total anticlockwise = total clockwise).

The practical routine for any beam problem: (1) draw the diagram and mark every force; (2) take moments about a chosen pivot — choosing one where an unknown force acts eliminates it; (3) write ΣM = 0 and solve; (4) use ΣF = 0 to find the remaining unknowns.

Worked examples: beam problems in full

Worked example 1. A uniform beam of weight 40 N and length 2.0 m rests on two supports, one at each end. A 20 N load sits 0.50 m from the left support. Find the reaction forces.

Let the reactions be R_L (left) and R_R (right).
Take moments about the left support (eliminates R_L):
anticlockwise = clockwise
R_R x 2.0 = (40 × 1.0) + (20 × 0.50)
R_R x 2.0 = 40 + 10 = 50
R_R = 25 N
Vertical equilibrium: R_L + R_R = 40 + 20 = 60 N
R_L = 60 - 25 = 35 N
Check: moments about the right support:
35 × 2.0 = 70 clockwise, and (40 × 1.0) + (20 × 1.5) = 70
anticlockwise. Balanced.

Worked example 2 (non-uniform). A 3.0 m plank of weight 60 N rests with one end on a pivot and the other on a scale. Its centre of gravity is 1.2 m from the pivot end. Find the scale reading.

Take moments about the pivot:
R_scale x 3.0 = 60 × 1.2 = 72
R_scale = 72/3.0 = 24 N
(and the pivot takes the remaining 60 - 24 = 36 N)

Worked example 3 (angled force). A horizontal beam is held by a rope at 30° to the beam at its far end; the beam's weight W acts at its centre. Find the rope tension T in terms of W.

Moments about the beam end at the wall:
anticlockwise (rope): T sin(30) x L
clockwise (weight):  W x L/2
T sin(30) x L = W L/2
T x 0.5 = W/2  →  T = W

The habit that prevents errors: cancel the common factor (L) only after writing both moment lines fully.

Multi-force equilibrium: triangles and resolution

When three non-parallel forces hold a body in equilibrium, they can be arranged tip-to-tail into a closed triangle — a graphical method with marks attached. For more forces, resolve into perpendicular components (usually horizontal and vertical) and set each sum to zero:

sum of horizontal components = 0
sum of vertical components   = 0

Worked example. A 100 N weight hangs from two ropes, one at 30° and one at 60° to the horizontal. Find the tensions.

Let tensions be A (30 ° rope) and B (60 ° rope).
Horizontal: A cos(30) = B cos(60)
            0.866 A = 0.5 B  →  B = 1.732 A
Vertical:   A sin(30) + B sin(60) = 100
            0.5 A + 0.866 × 1.732 A = 100
            0.5 A + 1.5 A = 100 → 2.0 A = 100
A = 50 N,  B = 1.732 × 50 = 86.6 N

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Moment) A spanner grips a nut 0.25 m from its pivot end; a mechanic pushes at 60° to the spanner with 80 N. Find the moment. Answer: perpendicular component = 80 sin 60 = 69.3 N; M = 69.3 × 0.25 = 17.3 N m ≈ 17 N m.
  2. (Definition) Define centre of gravity. Answer: The point at which the whole weight of a body may be taken to act.
  3. (Couple) Two opposite 15 N forces act 0.40 m apart on a wheel rim. Find the torque. Answer: τ = Fd = 15 × 0.40 = 6.0 N m.
  4. (Beam) A uniform 4.0 m beam (weight 100 N) rests on supports 0.50 m from each end. A 50 N load sits at the midpoint. Find the reactions. Answer: By symmetry each reaction = (100 + 50)/2 = 75 N.
  5. (Stability) Explain why a racing car is built low and wide. Answer: A low centre of gravity and wide base increase stability: the weight's line of action must move further before it falls outside the base, so larger moments are needed to topple it.
  6. (Equilibrium conditions) State the two conditions for a rigid body to be in equilibrium. Answer: The resultant force on the body is zero (ΣF = 0), and the resultant moment about any point is zero (ΣM = 0).
  7. (Resolution) A single rope holds a 20 N weight stationary, the rope making 40° with the horizontal. Find the tension. Answer: Vertical equilibrium: T sin 40 = 20, so T = 20/0.643 = 31.1 N ≈ 31 N. (For a picture hung on a cord fixed at both ends, resolve both halves' tensions instead.)
  8. (Practical) Describe how to find the centre of gravity of an irregular lamina. Answer: Hang the lamina freely from a pin through a hole near its edge; hang a plumb line from the same pin and draw the vertical line; repeat from a second hole; the intersection of the two vertical lines is the centre of gravity.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Perpendicular distance: the moment is Fd with d perpendicular to F. Using the slant distance when a force acts at an angle is the commonest error — resolve the force or find the true perpendicular first.
  • Couple geometry: d in Fd for a couple is the full separation of the two forces, not the radius. Turning a steering wheel with hands 0.60 m apart: τ = F × 0.60.
  • Pivot choice: take moments about a point where an unknown force acts to eliminate it; taking them about the wrong point creates simultaneous equations unnecessarily.
  • Uniform assumption: a uniform beam's weight acts at its midpoint; a non-uniform one's does not — read which the question gives.
  • Reaction direction: assume upward reactions; a negative result simply means the force acts downward (a tether, not a support). Do not panic at minus signs.
  • Forces without directions: ΣF = 0 is a vector statement — write horizontal and vertical sums separately rather than one jumble.
  • Three-force triangle conditions: the forces must be coplanar and non-parallel for the triangle method; parallel forces need the moment approach.
  • Units and precision: moments in N m (not J — even though the units are dimensionally identical, the mark requires the moment unit), forces in N, 2 or 3 s.f.
  • Method marks: state "taking moments about the pivot" and write ΣM = 0 explicitly before substituting numbers.

title: Measurement & Units — Study Notes
content:
Measurement & Units

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): 1.1 lengths & volumes; 1.2 density; 1.3 forces & motion context (measurements) — plus measurement techniques, SI units, scalars/vectors.

1. Measuring

  • Length: ruler (mm), vernier calipers (0.1 mm / 0.01 cm), micrometer screw gauge (0.01 mm).
  • Volume: measuring cylinder read at the meniscus bottom; regular solids by calculation; irregular by displacement (eureka can).
  • Time: stopwatch — human reaction time ±0.2 s; measure many oscillations and divide (e.g. 20 T).
  • Pendulum: T = time/oscillations; f = 1/T.

2. SI units and prefixes

QuantityUnitSymbol
lengthmetrem
masskilogramkg
timeseconds
currentampereA
temperaturekelvin (°C used)K

kilo 10³; centi 10⁻²; milli 10⁻³; micro 10⁻⁶; nano 10⁻⁹.

3. Scalars and vectors

Scalars: distance, speed, mass, energy, time. Vectors: displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, weight, momentum. Vector addition by scale diagram (tip-to-tail) or by components.

4. Density

ρ = m/V (kg/m³ or g/cm³; 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³). Determining: mass on balance; volume by displacement. Floating: ρobject < ρfluid.

5. Accuracy and improvements

Avoid parallax (eye level with reading), zero errors (subtract the zero reading), measure multiple laps for small times. Suggest improvements by naming the error and the fix.

title: A2 Level Chemistry: Kinetics and Rate Equations
content:
Kinetics: Edexcel International A Level Chemistry A2 Revision Notes

This topic belongs to Edexcel International A Level Chemistry WCH14 Topic 11 Kinetics. It covers the quantitative study of reaction speeds, the factors affecting them, experimental techniques, rate equations, order of reaction, reaction mechanisms including halogenoalkane hydrolysis, catalysts, core practicals, and the Arrhenius equation to calculate activation energy.

Definitions and Key Terms

To master kinetics, you must learn precise definitions for key terminology used in exam marking points.

  • Rate of reaction is the change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit time, with units mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹.
  • Rate equation is an expression showing how the rate of reaction depends on the concentrations of reactants, given in the form rate = k[A]m[B]n where m and n are the orders with respect to specific substances and are 0, 1 or 2.
  • Order with respect to a substance is the power to which the concentration of that reactant is raised in the rate equation.
  • Overall order of a reaction is the sum of all the individual orders of the reactants in the rate equation (m + n + ...).
  • Rate constant (k) is the proportionality constant that links the rate of reaction to the concentrations in the rate equation at a fixed temperature.
  • Half-life (t1/2) is the time taken for the concentration of a reactant to decrease to half of its initial value.
  • Rate-determining step is the slowest step in a multi-step reaction mechanism, which controls the overall rate of the reaction.
  • Activation energy (Ea) is the minimum kinetic energy that colliding particles must possess for a successful reaction to occur.
  • Heterogeneous catalyst is a catalyst in a different physical state or phase from the reactants, typically providing a solid surface for gas-phase reactions.
  • Homogeneous catalyst is a catalyst in the same physical state or phase as the reactants.

Experimental Techniques and Monitoring Methods

Choosing and justifying the correct experimental technique to obtain rate data is essential for both practical endorsements and written papers.

  • Titration involves quenching reaction aliquots at timed intervals and titrating against a standard solution, suitable for slow reactions like the acid-catalysed iodination of propanone.
  • Colorimetry measures the absorbance of light by a coloured species over time, ideal for reactions involving iodine or transition metal ions.
  • Mass change uses a sensitive balance to track mass loss over time as a gas evolves, suitable for reactions producing carbon dioxide.
  • Volume of gas evolved uses a gas syringe or inverted measuring cylinder over water to measure gas collected per unit time.
  • Initial-rate method involves carrying out separate experiments where different initial concentrations of one reagent are used while others are kept constant, measuring only the initial rate to avoid complications from reactant depletion.
  • Clock reaction is a convenient approximation of the initial-rate method where a single measurement is taken of the time taken for a specific visual change (such as a sudden colour change) to occur, assuming initial rate is proportional to 1 / t provided less than 15 percent of the reaction occurs.
  • Continuous monitoring method generates data over the entire course of a single reaction run to enable concentration-time or volume-time graphs to be plotted.

Deducing Reaction Orders and Calculations

You must be able to deduce the order with respect to a substance using different graphical and numerical representations.

  • Concentration-time graphs show how reactant concentration changes over time. A straight-line downward slope indicates a zero-order reaction with a constant rate. A downward curve with a constant half-life indicates a first-order reaction. A downward curve where the half-life increases as concentration decreases indicates a second-order reaction.
  • Rate-concentration graphs plot rate on the y-axis against concentration on the x-axis. A horizontal straight line parallel to the x-axis indicates zero order (rate is independent of concentration). A straight line passing through the origin indicates first order (rate is directly proportional to concentration). A curve with an increasing gradient (parabola) passing through the origin indicates second order (rate is proportional to concentration squared).
  • Initial-rate calculations compare how changes in initial concentration affect initial rate to find integer orders of 0, 1 or 2.
  • Half-life calculations use data from concentration-time graphs. Identifying a constant half-life is definitive proof that a reaction is first order with respect to that reactant.

Mechanisms and Rate-Determining Steps

The rate equation provides direct evidence for the composition of the rate-determining step and helps deduce reaction pathways.

  • Deducing rate-determining step from a rate equation means any species appearing in the rate equation with a non-zero order must be involved in the rate-determining step or in preceding fast steps that equilibrate before it. Stoichiometric coefficients of reactants in the rate-determining step match their orders in the rate equation.
  • Deducing reaction mechanism uses the rate equation alongside the overall stoichiometric equation. Fast steps before the rate-determining step introduce intermediate concentrations that can be substituted using equilibrium expressions.
  • Hydrolysis of halogenoalkanes provides classic evidence for mechanisms. Primary halogenoalkanes undergo SN2 hydrolysis, which is second-order overall (rate = k[halogenoalkane][OH−]), involving a single concerted step with a transition state. Tertiary halogenoalkanes undergo SN1 hydrolysis, which is first-order overall (rate = k[halogenoalkane]), where the slow rate-determining step is the heterolytic fission of the carbon-halogen bond to form a carbocation intermediate before rapid attack by the nucleophile.
  • Acid-catalysed iodination of propanone involves obtaining data to calculate the order with respect to propanone, hydrogen ions, and iodine. Iodine is found to be zero-order, while propanone and hydrogen ions are first-order. This data proves that neither iodine nor the second step is in the rate-determining step, leading to a mechanism featuring a slow, acid-catalysed tautomerization step forming an enol, followed by rapid reaction with iodine.

Heterogeneous Catalysis in Industry

Solid catalysts function by physical and chemical adsorption of gas-phase reactants.

  • Solid heterogeneous catalysts provide an active surface where reactant molecules are adsorbed.
  • Adsorption weakens internal covalent bonds within the reactant molecules, lowering the activation energy.
  • Reacted species subsequently desorb from the surface, freeing active sites for further catalytic cycles. Examples include iron in the Haber process and platinum, palladium, and rhodium in catalytic converters.

Core Practicals and Activation Energy

Experimental determination of activation energy links rate constants at different temperatures.

  • Core Practical 9a involves following the rate of the iodine-propanone reaction by a titrimetric method, quenching reaction samples with sodium hydrogencarbonate at timed intervals and titrating remaining iodine with standard sodium thiosulfate solution.
  • Core Practical 9b involves investigating a clock reaction, such as the Harcourt-Esson hydrogen peroxide-iodide reaction or the iodine clock, measuring time t for a colour change to appear using varying initial volumes of reagents.
  • Core Practical 10 involves finding the activation energy of a reaction by measuring reaction rates at different temperatures, calculating rate constants k, and applying the Arrhenius equation.
  • Arrhenius equation is given as k = A e^(−Ea / RT), where R is the ideal gas constant (8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹) and T is temperature in Kelvin.
  • Taking natural logarithms yields ln k = (−Ea / R) × (1 / T) + ln A.
  • Plotting ln k on the y-axis against 1 / T on the x-axis produces a straight line with gradient equal to −Ea / R, allowing Ea to be calculated from gradient × (−R).

Typical mistakes

  • Mistake: Assuming the orders in a rate equation match the stoichiometric coefficients in the overall balanced equation. Correction: Remember that rate equations must be determined experimentally, as overall equations show only reactants and products, not the step-by-step mechanism.
  • Mistake: Stating that the rate constant k changes when reactant concentrations are altered. Correction: The rate constant k is only affected by changes in temperature and the addition of a catalyst. Changing concentration alters the rate, not k.
  • Mistake: Forgetting temperature must be in Kelvin when using the Arrhenius equation. Correction: Always convert Celsius to Kelvin by adding 273.15 before calculating 1 / T or using ln k.
  • Mistake: Confusing the units of k for different overall orders. Correction: Derive the units dynamically by rearranging the rate equation: units of k = (units of rate) / (units of concentration) raised to the power of the overall order.

Exam-style questions

  1. Question: The reaction between nitrogen monoxide and hydrogen has the rate equation rate = k[NO]²[H₂]. State the order with respect to NO, the order with respect to H₂, and the overall order of the reaction. Answer: Order with respect to NO is 2; order with respect to H₂ is 1; overall order is 3 (obtained by summing 2 + 1).
  2. Question: Deduce the units of the rate constant k for a third-order overall reaction where rate is measured in mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹ and concentration in mol dm⁻³. Answer: Rearranging gives k = rate / [concentration]³. Units = (mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹) / (mol dm⁻³)³ = s⁻¹ mol⁻² dm⁶.
  3. Question: In an experiment, a student plots a concentration-time graph for a reactant and finds that successive half-lives are constant at 45 seconds. Deduce the order of the reaction with respect to this reactant. Answer: A constant half-life is the defining characteristic of a first-order reaction.
  4. Question: Explain why tertiary halogenoalkanes undergo hydrolysis via an SN1 mechanism whereas primary halogenoalkanes undergo an SN2 mechanism. Answer: Tertiary halogenoalkanes form a relatively stable tertiary carbocation intermediate due to the electron-releasing inductive effect of three alkyl groups, favouring SN1. Primary halogenoalkanes cannot form stable carbocations, so the attack by the nucleophile must occur simultaneously in a concerted SN2 transition state.
  5. Question: A graph of ln k against 1 / T for a reaction gives a straight line with a gradient of −12400 K. Calculate the activation energy Ea in kJ mol⁻¹. Use R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. Answer: Gradient = −Ea / R, so Ea = −(gradient) × R = −(−12400) × 8.31 = 103044 J mol⁻¹ = 103 kJ mol⁻¹ to 3 significant figures.

Use these notes alongside active recall of definitions, rigorous practice of initial-rate data tables, and past paper calculations on the Arrhenius equation. Next, revise Equilibria (Topic 12) to connect reaction kinetics with thermodynamic and dynamic stability.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Order from initial rates, applied to data showing the rate quadruples when [A] doubles with [B] constant: the order with respect to A is 2, because 2² = 4. Read the orders from the experiments, not from the coefficients in the equation, because the orders are found experimentally.
  • Rate constant units, applied to rate = k[A]²: rate is in mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹ and [A]² is in mol² dm⁻⁶, so k is in mol⁻¹ dm³ s⁻¹. If rate = 2.4 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹ at [A] = 0.20 mol dm⁻³, then k = 2.4 × 10⁻³ ÷ 0.040 = 0.060 mol⁻¹ dm³ s⁻¹.
  • Rate-determining step: the slowest step sets the rate, so the orders in the rate equation contain only the species up to and including that step. Catalysts appear in the rate equation if they take part in the rate-determining step.
  • Activation energy from Arrhenius data: a plot of ln k against 1/T gives a straight line with gradient −Ea ÷ R. Use the gradient, and convert the temperature to kelvin before you plot.

title: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Ratio, Rate and Proportion
content:
Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Ratio, Rate and Proportion

Ratio, rate and proportion are the mathematics of comparison: how two quantities share a whole, how fast one changes with another, and what happens when one stays on the same path to infinity. They appear in nearly every Paper 2, usually as multi-step word problems where the arithmetic is easy and the interpretation is not. This note builds the topic from zero: simplifying and dividing in ratios, the unitary method for direct and inverse proportion, the algebra forms y = kx and y = k/x, and rates — speed, density, flow — with their unit conversions.

Ratio fundamentals

A ratio compares quantities of the same kind. The notation a : b means "a for every b". Equivalent ratios are made by multiplying or dividing all parts by the same number; the simplified ratio has no common factor (other than 1) and, for measurements, the same units.

  • Simplify: 24 : 36 = 2 : 3 (divide both by 12).
  • Three-part: 2 : 3 : 5 means five shares in total; each share is total ÷ 10.
  • Units first: 500 g : 1.5 kg = 500 : 1500 = 1 : 3. Convert before simplifying, never after.

Worked example. Share £84 in the ratio 3 : 4.

total parts = 3 + 4 = 7
one part = 84/7 = 12
shares = 3 × 12 = 36 and 4 × 12 = 48
check: 36 + 48 = 84

Worked example 2 (three parts). A sum of $240 is divided among A, B and C in the ratio 2 : 3 : 5. Find each share.

parts = 2 + 3 + 5 = 10
one part = 240/10 = 24
A = 2 × 24 = 48, B = 3 × 24 = 72, C = 5 × 24 = 120

Combining ratios and ratio changes

Two ratios sharing a middle term can be combined by making that term common:

A : B = 2 : 3 and B : C = 4 : 5
LCM of the B terms (3 and 4) is 12:
A : B = 8 : 12 and B : C = 12 : 15
so A : B : C = 8 : 12 : 15

Worked example (change). A bag contains red and blue counters in the ratio 5 : 3. After 6 red counters are removed, the ratio becomes 1 : 1. Find the original numbers.

let red = 5x, blue = 3x
(5x - 6)/3x = 1  →  5x - 6 = 3x  →  2x = 6  →  x = 3
original: red = 15, blue = 9
check: after removing 6 red, 9 : 9 = 1 : 1

Direct proportion

Two quantities are in direct proportion when one is a constant multiple of the other: double one, double the other. The algebra form is y = kx, a straight line through the origin.

y = k x        k = y/x (the constant of proportionality)
unitary method: find the value of one unit, then multiply

Worked example. 5 pens cost $3.25. Find the cost of 12 pens.

one pen = 3.25/5 = $0.65
12 pens = 12 × 0.65 = $7.80

Worked example 2 (algebra form). y is directly proportional to x, and y = 18 when x = 6. Find y when x = 11.

y = kx  →  18 = 6k  →  k = 3
y = 3 × 11 = 33

Worked example 3 (proportion with powers). The mass of a sphere is proportional to the cube of its radius; a sphere of radius 2 cm has mass 40 g. Find the mass of a sphere of radius 3 cm.

m = k r³  →  40 = k x 8  →  k = 5
m = 5 × 27 = 135 g

Inverse proportion

Inverse proportion means one quantity falls as the other rises: double one, halve the other. The algebra form is y = k/x (the product xy is constant).

y = k/x        x y = k
unitary method: find the total "work" (product), then divide

Worked example. Six workers build a wall in 8 days. How long will 4 workers take (same rate)?

total work = 6 × 8 = 48 worker-days
time for 4 = 48/4 = 12 days

Worked example 2 (algebra). y is inversely proportional to x; y = 5 when x = 4. Find y when x = 10.

xy = k  →  4 × 5 = 20  →  y = 20/10 = 2

The shape on a graph distinguishes the two: direct proportion is a straight line through the origin; inverse proportion is a curve that never touches either axis (a hyperbola).

Rates

A rate compares quantities with different units: speed (distance per time), density (mass per volume), pressure (force per area), flow rate (volume per time). Each is a division, and each can be rearranged.

speed = distance/time        density = mass/volume
pressure = force/area        flow rate = volume/time

average speed over a journey = total distance/total time
(not the average of the speeds, unless the times are equal)

Worked example 1 (speed). A car travels 150 km in 2 hours 30 minutes. Find its average speed in km/h and m/s.

time = 2.5 h
speed = 150/2.5 = 60 km/h
in m/s: 60 × 10⁰⁰/3600 = 16.7 m/s

Worked example 2 (density). A block of volume 250 cm³ has mass 675 g. Find its density, and the mass of 400 cm³ of the same material.

density = 675/250 = 2.7 g/cm³
mass = 2.7 × 400 = 1080 g = 1.08 kg

Worked example 3 (average speed trap). A cyclist rides 20 km at 20 km/h, then 20 km at 10 km/h. Find the average speed for the whole journey.

time 1 = 20/20 = 1 h;  time 2 = 20/10 = 2 h
total distance = 40 km; total time = 3 h
average speed = 40/3 = 13.3 km/h (not 15!)

Flow rates and filling problems

Flow-rate questions combine a rate with a volume: a tap fills at 4 litres per minute, a pump empties at 6 litres per minute, a pipe delivers water at 2.5 m s⁻¹ through a cross-section. The method is the same division, but the units demand attention — litres per minute into litres and minutes, cubic metres per second into m³ and s, with 1 m³ = 1000 litres and 1 minute = 60 s.

Worked example. A bath holds 180 litres. A tap fills it at 9 litres per minute, but the plug leaks 1.5 litres per minute. How long does the bath take to fill?

net rate = 9 - 1.5 = 7.5 litres per minute
time = 180/7.5 = 24 minutes

Best buys and multi-step comparisons

Ratio reasoning powers the practical comparison questions: which packet is better value, which journey is faster per kilometre, which contract costs less per month. The method is always to reduce both options to the same unit before comparing, and to compare like with like (price per 100 g, cost per km, cost per month).

Worked example. A 750 g box of cereal costs $3.60 and a 1.2 kg box costs $5.28. Which is better value?

large: 5.28/1.2 = $4.40 per kg
small: 3.60/0.75 = $4.80 per kg
better value: the 1.2 kg box (lower cost per kg)

Worked example 2 (multi-step). Two phone contracts: A charges $12 per month plus $0.10 per GB; B charges $20 per month with 15 GB included. For someone using 20 GB per month, which is cheaper over a year?

A: 12 + 0.10 × 20 = $14 per month; yearly = 168
B: $20 per month; yearly = 240
A is cheaper for a 20 GB user by $72 per year.
(check the crossover: 12 + 0.1g = 20 → g = 80 GB, so B
only wins for very heavy users)

The crossover point is a favourite extension: set the two cost expressions equal and solve, then interpret which side of the crossing each customer sits on.

Worked examples: mixed problems

Worked example. A recipe for 4 people uses 300 g of rice. How much is needed for 10 people, and how many people can be served with 2.1 kg?

per person = 300/4 = 75 g
for 10: 750 g
2100 g / 75 = 28 people

Worked example 2 (currency). An exchange rate is £1 = $1.25. Convert £240 to dollars and $500 to pounds.

240 × 1.25 = $300
500/1.25 = £400

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Divide) Share 360 in the ratio 5 : 7. Answer: parts 12; one part 30; shares 150 and 210.
  2. (Simplify with units) Simplify 40 minutes : 2 hours. Answer: 40 : 120 = 1 : 3.
  3. (Direct) 8 m of cloth costs $52. Find the cost of 13 m. Answer: per metre $6.50; 13 × 6.50 = $84.50.
  4. (Inverse) 4 taps fill a tank in 45 minutes. How long for 6 taps? Answer: total = 4 × 45 = 180 tap-minutes; 180/6 = 30 minutes.
  5. (Algebra) y ∝ x² and y = 50 when x = 5. Find y when x = 8. Answer: 50 = k × 25 → k = 2; y = 2 × 64 = 128.
  6. (Rate) A train covers 210 km in 2 h 20 min. Find its average speed. Answer: 2⅓ h; 210 ÷ 7/3 = 90 km/h.
  7. (Density) 150 cm³ of a liquid has mass 120 g. Find the mass of 1 litre. Answer: density 0.8 g/cm³; 1000 cm³ × 0.8 = 800 g.
  8. (Reverse) A map scale is 1 : 50 000. Two points are 7 cm apart on the map. Find the real distance in km. Answer: 7 × 50 000 = 350 000 cm = 3.5 km.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Averaging speeds: average speed is total distance over total time, never the mean of the two speeds unless the times are equal. The classic 20/10 km/h trap answers 15 instead of 13.3.
  • Ratio direction: dividing 84 in 3 : 4 is not 84 × 3/4 for both shares; identify which share is which before writing the answer.
  • Units in ratios: 500 g : 1.5 kg simplifies only after conversion to 500 : 1500 = 1 : 3. Mixing units gives 1 : 0.003.
  • Direct versus inverse: ask "if one doubles, what happens to the other?" Doubling both means direct; one doubling while the other halves means inverse.
  • Proportional to a power: for y ∝ x², doubling x multiplies y by 4; for y ∝ √x it multiplies by √2. Find k from the given pair first.
  • Currency direction: multiplying by the rate converts one way; the reverse needs division. Check with a rough estimate.
  • Time units: 2 h 30 min is 2.5 h, not 2.3 h. Convert minutes to a decimal fraction of an hour before dividing.
  • Rounding mid-calculation: keep full accuracy until the final answer, then round to 3 s.f. or as instructed; money answers usually need 2 decimal places.
