title: IGCSE Physics (OxfordAQA): Nuclear Physics
content:
Nuclear Physics

Almost all of the mass of an atom sits in a nucleus a hundred thousand times smaller than the atom itself, and almost all of the energy released in a power station or a star comes from rearranging that nucleus. This topic follows the story in four steps: what the nucleus contains, what it emits when it is unstable, what happens when a heavy nucleus splits, and what happens when light nuclei join. Every equation in it is a conservation statement — the mass numbers and the atomic numbers on both sides of a decay must balance — so the arithmetic and the physics are the same thing.

3.7.1 Atomic structure

An atom consists of a nucleus of protons and neutrons, surrounded by electrons arranged in shells. A proton has a relative mass of 1 and a charge of +1, a neutron has a relative mass of 1 and no charge, and an electron has negligible mass and a charge of −1. Nearly all the mass is in the nucleus, while nearly all the volume is the electron cloud.

QuantitySymbolWhat it counts
Atomic (proton) numberZThe number of protons; it identifies the element
Mass (nucleon) numberAProtons plus neutrons
Neutron numberNA minus Z
Charge on the nucleus+ZOne positive unit per proton

An atom is neutral because the number of electrons equals the number of protons. An ion is formed when electrons are gained or lost, which changes the charge but never the element: a chloride ion still has seventeen protons, whatever its charge.

A = Z + N

Key: A = mass number, the number of nucleons; Z = atomic number, the number of protons; N = the number of neutrons; the equation is used rearranged as N = A - Z.

Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. Carbon-12 and carbon-14 both have six protons, so both are carbon, but carbon-14 has eight neutrons rather than six. Isotopes have almost identical chemical properties because chemistry depends on electrons, and different nuclear properties: carbon-14 is radioactive while carbon-12 is not.

3.7.2 Ionizing radiation from the nucleus

An unstable nucleus emits radiation to become more stable. The three types are alpha, beta and gamma, and they differ in what they are, how far they travel and how strongly they ionise.

RadiationWhat it isRange in airStopped byIonising power
AlphaTwo protons and two neutrons (a helium nucleus)A few centimetresA sheet of paper or the dead layer of skinStrongest, because it is large and charged
BetaA fast electron emitted when a neutron turns into a protonA few metresA few millimetres of aluminiumModerate
GammaAn electromagnetic wave of very short wavelengthEffectively unlimited; intensity falls with distanceThick lead or concrete, and only partlyWeakest

Alpha and beta are deflected in electric and magnetic fields in opposite directions, because one is positive and the other negative, while gamma is undeflected because it has no charge. The deflection of alpha is smaller than that of beta because an alpha particle is far more massive.

Every decay changes the nucleus in a way that can be written down and checked. In alpha decay the mass number falls by four and the atomic number by two. In beta decay the mass number is unchanged and the atomic number rises by one, because a neutron has become a proton. Gamma emission changes neither number; it simply carries away energy.

  • Alpha decay of radon-222: the nucleus loses two protons and two neutrons, so mass number 222 - 4 = 218 and atomic number 86 - 2 = 84, giving polonium-218.
  • Beta decay of carbon-14: mass number stays 14, atomic number rises from 6 to 7, giving nitrogen-14.
  • Gamma emission leaves the element unchanged and is written with the same mass and atomic numbers on both sides.

Half-life is the time taken for half of the unstable nuclei in a sample to decay, or for the count rate from it to halve. Nothing about an individual nucleus can be predicted; the half-life is a statement about a very large number of them. Activity is measured in becquerels, one decay per second, and background radiation from rocks, cosmic rays, food and medical sources must be subtracted from a measured count rate before a half-life is calculated.

3.7.3 Nuclear fission

Fission is the splitting of a large nucleus into two smaller ones, releasing energy. It happens when a nucleus such as uranium-235 absorbs a neutron and becomes unstable. The products are two smaller nuclei, two or three further neutrons, and a large amount of energy, which appears as kinetic energy of the fragments.

  • The neutrons released can be absorbed by other uranium nuclei, so the process can sustain a chain reaction.
  • In a nuclear reactor the chain reaction is controlled: control rods made of boron or cadmium absorb surplus neutrons, and a moderator such as graphite or water slows the neutrons so they are more likely to be captured.
  • The energy released heats a coolant, which turns water into steam and drives a turbine, exactly as in a fossil-fuel station.
  • The waste is radioactive for thousands of years, which is why it must be stored and shielded for a very long time.

The mass of the products is slightly less than the mass of the original nucleus plus the neutron, and the difference appears as energy. That is the most important sentence in the topic: the energy released by fission is not created from nothing but converted from mass, in a proportion set by the speed of light squared.

3.7.4 Nuclear fusion

Fusion is the joining together of two light nuclei to form a heavier one, releasing energy. It is the reaction that powers every star, including the Sun, where hydrogen nuclei fuse to form helium at extremely high temperature and pressure.

  • Fusion needs very high temperatures because the nuclei are positively charged and repel each other, so they must be moving fast enough to get close enough for the strong nuclear force to act.
  • It needs very high pressure and density to keep the nuclei close together for long enough to react.
  • The energy released per kilogramme of fuel is much larger than for fission, and the fuel is abundant in seawater.
  • It produces far less long-lived radioactive waste than fission, which is why it is the long-term goal.
  • The difficulty is containment: no material can touch a gas at those temperatures, so magnetic or inertial confinement is required, and no reactor yet produces more energy than it consumes.

Fusion in the Sun and fission in a reactor are opposite ends of the same binding-energy curve: light nuclei release energy when they join, and heavy ones release energy when they split. In both cases the energy comes from the small change in mass.

Worked example: particles in an atom and an ion

Write down the number of protons, neutrons and electrons in a neutral atom of uranium-235, and in the ion U-235 with a charge of 3+.

Neutral atom: protons = 92 (the atomic number of uranium), neutrons = 235 - 92 = 143, electrons = 92. For the 3+ ion, electrons = 92 - 3 = 89, with protons and neutrons unchanged.

Key: 92 = atomic number Z (protons); 235 = mass number A (nucleons); 143 = neutrons, found from N = A - Z; 3 = the charge, which removes three electrons because each electron is -1.

An ion is never a different element: the proton count is what defines the element, and it has not changed. That is why a 3+ uranium ion is still uranium.

Worked example: completing a decay equation

Polonium-210 decays by alpha emission. Write the balanced equation and identify the new element. Its atomic number is 84.

The alpha particle is a helium nucleus, with mass number 4 and atomic number 2. So the daughter has mass number 210 - 4 = 206 and atomic number 84 - 2 = 82. Atomic number 82 is lead, so the equation is Po-210 → Pb-206 + alpha, with 210 = 206 + 4 and 84 = 82 + 2 on the two sides.

Key: 210 and 84 = mass and atomic numbers of the parent; 4 and 2 = mass and atomic numbers of the alpha particle; 206 and 82 = the mass and atomic numbers of the daughter; both totals must match on each side.

Both conservation rules must be checked. An answer that balances the mass numbers but not the atomic numbers has either forgotten that the alpha carries two protons or miscounted the element.

Worked example: half-life

A source has a count rate of 640 counts per minute. After 24 days the count rate is 80 per minute. Calculate the half-life and state the count rate after a further 12 days.

640 halves to 320, then 160, then 80: that is three half-lives, so each is 24 ÷ 3 = 8 days. After a further 12 days, one and a half more half-lives pass, so the rate goes 80 → 40 → 20 in the last half-life, giving 20 counts per minute.

Key: 640 and 80 = count rates (counts per minute); 3 = the number of halvings; 24 days = total time (days); 8 days = one half-life.

Halving is multiplicative, not linear, so the count rate never reaches zero in a finite time. A rate of 0 would be a wrong answer for that reason alone.

Worked example: choosing shielding

A source emits alpha, beta and gamma radiation. Describe the count rate recorded by a detector placed behind paper, then behind aluminium, then behind thick lead.

Behind paper the detector records beta and gamma, because the alpha is stopped: the count falls to about two thirds of the unshielded value if the three are equally intense. Behind aluminium the beta is also stopped, so only gamma is recorded. Behind thick lead the gamma is greatly reduced but not eliminated, so the count falls further but rarely to zero.

Key: paper = the shielding for alpha; aluminium = the shielding for beta; lead = the shielding for gamma; the residual count with lead in place shows that gamma is only attenuated, not absorbed completely.

Typical mistakes

  • Saying an ion is a different element. The proton number is unchanged, so the element is unchanged.
  • Writing the mass number of an alpha particle as 2. It is 4, because it contains two protons and two neutrons.
  • Forgetting that beta decay raises the atomic number by one, because a neutron becomes a proton.
  • Changing the mass number during gamma emission, which changes neither number.
  • Treating half-life as a linear decrease, or predicting that the activity will reach zero.
  • Confusing fission with fusion: heavy nuclei split in fission, light nuclei join in fusion.
  • Claiming fusion needs no energy to start. It needs extremely high temperature because the nuclei repel.
  • Forgetting to subtract background radiation before calculating a half-life from measured counts.

Exam-style questions

  1. State the number of protons, neutrons and electrons in a neutral atom of carbon-14. Answer: Six protons, eight neutrons (14 - 6) and six electrons.
  2. Explain why alpha particles are more ionising than gamma rays but travel a shorter distance. Answer: An alpha particle is large, doubly charged and slow, so it interacts strongly with atoms along its path and ionises many of them, losing its energy quickly. Gamma is uncharged and interacts weakly, so it penetrates much further before being absorbed.
  3. Write the equation for the beta decay of carbon-14 and name the daughter element. Answer: Carbon-14 → nitrogen-14 + beta, with mass number 14 unchanged and atomic number rising from 6 to 7.
  4. A sample's activity falls from 800 Bq to 100 Bq in 45 hours. Calculate the half-life. Answer: 800 → 400 → 200 → 100 is three half-lives, so each is 15 hours.
  5. Describe what happens in a controlled chain reaction in a nuclear reactor. Answer: A neutron splits a uranium-235 nucleus, releasing two or three more neutrons, which split further nuclei. Control rods absorb surplus neutrons so that on average one neutron from each fission causes another, keeping the rate steady.
  6. Explain why nuclear fusion requires very high temperatures. Answer: The nuclei are positively charged and repel each other. At very high temperatures they move fast enough to overcome that repulsion and get close enough for the strong nuclear force to bind them.
  7. State one similarity and one difference between fission and fusion. Answer: Both release energy from a change in nuclear mass. Fission splits a heavy nucleus and is used in reactors; fusion joins light nuclei, powers stars and is not yet a practical power source.
  8. A detector near a source records 300 counts per minute; the background is 20. After 6 days the reading is 90 counts per minute. Calculate the corrected count rate and the half-life. Answer: Corrected rates are 280 and 70, which is two halvings, so the half-life is 3 days.

Revision checklist

  • I can give the mass and charge of each subatomic particle and calculate proton, neutron and electron numbers.
  • I can define isotope and explain why isotopes differ in nuclear but not chemical behaviour.
  • I can compare alpha, beta and gamma in nature, range, penetration and ionising power.
  • I can complete alpha and beta decay equations and check both conservation rules.
  • I can define half-life and calculate it from count-rate data, subtracting background.
  • I can describe fission, a chain reaction and the roles of control rods and moderator.
  • I can describe fusion, the conditions it needs and why it is hard to sustain.
  • I can explain that both fission and fusion release energy from a change in mass.

title: IGCSE Physics: Electricity and Circuits
content:
IGCSE Physics: Electricity and Circuits

Cambridge IGCSE Physics 0625 (2026–2028), Topic 4 Electricity and magnetism: statements 4.2 Electrical quantities, 4.3 Electric circuits and 4.4 Electrical safety. Electric circuits are the most calculation-dense part of the Paper 4 paper, and every result in them flows from one picture: a battery pushes charge round a circuit, the charge pays a price (p.d.) to get through each component, and the rate of flow is the current. This note builds charge, current, e.m.f., p.d., resistance, energy and power from scratch, then builds real circuits from them and finishes with the mains safety that saves lives.

Electric charge and the electron model

There are two kinds of charge, positive and negative, and the rule is simple: like charges repel, unlike charges attract. Rubbing a polythene rod with a cloth transfers electrons from the cloth to the rod, so the rod becomes negatively charged and the cloth positive; nothing is created — charge is transferred. A conductor (metal, graphite, the human body, tap water) lets charge move through it because it contains free electrons; an insulator (plastic, rubber, dry air, glass) does not. Charging by friction works only when the object is isolated on an insulating support, or the charge leaks away instantly.

Supplement adds the two deeper ideas. Charge is measured in coulombs (C); one coulomb is the charge that flows when a current of 1 ampere passes for 1 second, and the charge on one electron is 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. A charged object also creates an electric field in the space around it — a region where other charges experience a force — and the field of a point charge is drawn as radial lines pointing away from a positive charge and towards a negative one.

Electric current

Electric current is the rate of flow of charge. In metals the charge carriers are free electrons drifting slowly around the circuit while the electric field travels almost at the speed of light, which is why a lamp lights the instant a switch is closed.

current = charge / time        I = Q / t
  • I: current in amperes (A); Q: charge in coulombs (C); t: time in seconds (s). Current is treated as a scalar in circuit calculations.
  • Conventional current flows from the positive terminal, round the circuit, to the negative terminal; electrons drift the opposite way. Both descriptions are accepted, but conventional current is the one used in circuit diagrams.

An ammeter measures current and is connected in series, so the whole current passes through it. Direct current (d.c.) flows in one direction only, as from a battery; alternating current (a.c.) reverses direction repeatedly, as from the mains, which in the UK completes 50 cycles per second at 230 V.

Electromotive force and potential difference

The electromotive force (e.m.f.) of a source is the energy transferred from other forms to electrical energy per unit charge driven round the whole circuit; the potential difference (p.d.) across a component is the energy transferred from electrical to other forms per unit charge passing through that component. Both are measured in volts, and a voltmeter is connected in parallel with the component being measured.

potential difference = energy transferred / charge        V = W / Q
electromotive force = energy transferred from other forms / charge driven
  • V: potential difference in volts (V); W: energy in joules (J); Q: charge in coulombs (C). One volt is one joule per coulomb (1 V = 1 J C⁻¹).

The distinction that earns marks: e.m.f. is about energy supplied to the circuit (a battery's rating, 1.5 V for a dry cell), while p.d. is about energy delivered to a component. In a series circuit the p.d.s across the components add up to the supply e.m.f., because each coulomb spends its energy bit by bit around the loop.

Resistance

Resistance is how much a component opposes current. It is measured in Ω (Ω): a 12 Ω resistor passes less current than a 4 Ω resistor at the same p.d.

resistance = potential difference / current        R = V / I
  • R: resistance in Ω (Ω); V: p.d. across the component in volts (V); I: current through it in amperes (A). Resistance is a scalar.

Resistance is measured by setting up a circuit with the unknown resistor, an ammeter in series and a voltmeter across it, then changing the supply with a variable resistor and taking several pairs of readings. The resistance is found from the gradient of a graph of V against I, which averages the whole data set.

The wire's dimensions matter. A longer wire has greater resistance (resistance is proportional to length); a thicker wire has less (resistance is inversely proportional to cross-sectional area); and the material matters because of how many free electrons it provides. Nichrome wire is used for heating elements because it has a high resistance and resists oxidation when hot.

Supplement: current–voltage graphs. A metallic conductor at constant temperature gives a straight line through the origin — ohmic. A filament lamp curves over: as it heats, its resistance rises, so the graph flattens. A diode conducts in one direction only, giving almost zero current in reverse; a light-dependent resistor falls in resistance as light intensity rises; a thermistor falls in resistance as temperature rises. All three are basis-of-operation questions for sensors.

Electrical energy and power

Every component turns electrical energy into something else — heat in a resistor, light and heat in a lamp, kinetic energy in a motor. The rate of that transfer is electrical power:

electrical power = potential difference x current        P = V I
electrical energy = power x time = V I t        E = V I t
  • P: power in watts (W); V: volts (V); I: amperes (A); E: energy in joules (J); t: time in seconds (s).
  • Combined with R = V/I this gives P = I²R and P = V²/R, useful when the resistance is known instead of the p.d.

The kilowatt-hour is the domestic unit of energy: one kWh is the energy used by a 1000 W device running for one hour (3.6 × 10⁶ J). Electricity bills charge cost = number of kWh × price per kWh, and a Paper 4 question usually asks for the cost of running a named appliance for a stated time.

Circuit components and circuit rules

Circuit diagrams use standard symbols: cell, battery, lamp, resistor, variable resistor, thermistor, LDR, diode, LED, ammeter, voltmeter, switch, motor. The two rules for series and parallel circuits are the spine of every calculation:

SeriesParallel
CurrentThe same through every componentShared between the branches; the branch currents add up to the total
Potential differenceShared between the components; the p.d.s add up to the supplyThe same across every branch
ResistanceR(total) = R1 + R2 + ...1/R(total) = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + ... (Supplement); two equal resistors in parallel give half the resistance of one

Adding lamps in series makes all of them dimmer, because the total resistance rises and the current falls; adding lamps in parallel leaves each at full brightness (each has the full p.d. across it) but draws more current from the supply. A variable resistor in series with a lamp dims it by reducing the current; a potential divider (Supplement) is two resistors in series with the output tapped between them:

output voltage = supply voltage x R2 / (R1 + R2)

A potential divider feeding a sensor gives an output voltage that changes with light or temperature, which is the basis of automatic night lights and thermostats.

Electrical safety

The domestic mains in the UK is 230 V a.c., enough to kill. The three wires in a three-core cable are colour-coded: live (brown) carries the alternating p.d. at about 230 V; neutral (blue) completes the circuit and is held near 0 V; earth (green and yellow) is a safety wire connected to the metal case of the appliance and to the ground.

  • Fuse: a thin wire in the live path that melts and breaks the circuit if the current exceeds its rating, protecting against overheating and fire. Choose a rating just above the normal working current.
  • Circuit breaker: a magnetic or electronic switch that trips and can be reset; faster and reusable, doing the same job as a fuse.
  • Earthing: if a fault connects the live wire to a metal case, the earth wire carries a large current that blows the fuse instead of giving the user a shock.
  • Double insulation: appliances with plastic cases need no earth wire, because no fault can make the case live.

Everyday hazards to name in an exam: frayed cables, damaged plugs, wet hands, water near electrical equipment, overloaded adapters, and touching a live conductor. The physics of the danger is current through the body: even a few tens of milliamperes through the heart can be fatal, and wet skin lowers body resistance and raises that current.

Worked example: a mixed circuit

Two resistors, 6.0 Ω and 3.0 Ω, are connected in parallel across a 12 V supply.

1 / R(total) = 1/6.0 + 1/3.0 = 0.167 + 0.333 = 0.500, so R(total) = 2.0 Ω
total current = V / R = 12 / 2.0 = 6.0 A
current in the 6.0 Ω resistor = 12 / 6.0 = 2.0 A
current in the 3.0 Ω resistor = 12 / 3.0 = 4.0 A   (branch currents add to 6.0 A)
power in the circuit = V I = 12 × 6.0 = 72 W
energy in 5 minutes = P t = 72 × 300 = 21 600 J

Each resistor has the full 12 V across it, as the parallel rule demands. If the two were instead in series, the total resistance would be 9.0 Ω, the current 1.33 A, and each p.d. would add to 12 V — a useful check before trusting any circuit answer.

Common mistakes

  • Putting an ammeter in parallel or a voltmeter in series; ammeters join in series, voltmeters across the component.
  • Using the supply voltage as the p.d. across one component in a series circuit; the supply is shared.
  • Adding resistances in parallel by simple addition; the reciprocals add, so the total is always less than the smallest branch.
  • Confusing current direction with electron drift, or saying charge is used up; the current is the same everywhere in a series circuit, and energy is transferred, not the charge.
  • Using watts and minutes in E = VIt; power in watts needs energy in joules and time in seconds (convert kWh and hours carefully in cost questions).
  • Forgetting that a filament lamp's resistance rises as it heats, so its I–V graph is a curve, not a straight line.
  • Choosing a fuse rating far above the working current for safety; too high a rating defeats the protection.
  • Mixing e.m.f. and p.d.: the battery has an e.m.f.; each component has a p.d. across it.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 4, 3 marks). A lamp is marked 24 W, 12 V. Calculate the current it takes and its resistance.

Answer: P = VI gives I = 24/12 = 2.0 A. R = V/I = 12/2.0 = 6.0 Ω.

Question 2 (Paper 4, 3 marks). A charge of 360 C passes through a lamp in 3.0 minutes. Calculate the current.

Answer: I = Q/t = 360/180 = 2.0 A. (Convert minutes to seconds first.)

Question 3 (Paper 2 style). In a series circuit of two resistors, which statement is true? A the current is largest through the smaller resistor; B the p.d. across each is the same as the supply; C the current is the same in both; D the total resistance is less than either. Answer: C. Current is the same everywhere in series; the p.d. is shared and the total resistance is the sum.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 4 marks). A 3.0 kW kettle runs for 4.0 minutes from 230 V. Find the charge that flows and the energy transferred.

Answer: I = P/V = 3000/230 = 13 A. Q = It = 13 × 240 = 3120 C. Energy = Pt = 3000 × 240 = 720 000 J (0.20 kWh).

Question 5 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Explain why a metal-cased washing machine has an earth wire but a plastic hairdryer does not.

Answer: The metal case is a conductor; if a fault brings the live wire into contact with it, the case would become live at 230 V and anyone touching it would receive a shock. The earth wire connects the case to the ground, so a large fault current flows to earth and melts the fuse, isolating the supply. The hairdryer has a plastic (double-insulated) case which cannot conduct, so no fault can make the outside live and no earth wire is needed.

Question 6 (Paper 6 style). Describe how you would determine the resistance of a coil of wire.

Answer: Connect the coil in series with an ammeter, a cell and a variable resistor, with a voltmeter across the coil. Vary the current and record several pairs of current and p.d. readings. Plot p.d. against current; the gradient is the resistance of the coil. Taking several readings and using the graph removes the effect of random errors and of the coil warming up (which would otherwise change its resistance).

Where charge flows, fields follow: next is Magnetism and Electromagnetism.

Equations and symbols

Statements 4.2 to 4.4 rest on five equations and three circuit rules. Charge, current, voltage and resistance are defined by the first three; the power relations all follow from them, so a question that gives two quantities can almost always be finished without memorising a fourth formula.

Charge, current and voltage

Q = It
Key: Q = charge flowing (C); I = current (A); t = time (s). One coulomb is one ampere for one second.

I = Q / t
Key: I = current (A); Q = charge passing a point (C); t = time (s). Current is a rate of charge flow, not a quantity of charge.

V = W / Q
Key: V = potential difference (V); W = work done or energy transferred (J); Q = charge moved (C). One volt is one joule per coulomb, which is the definition the mark scheme wants.

E = QV
Key: E = energy transferred by the charge (J); Q = charge (C); V = potential difference (V).

Q = Ne
Key: Q = total charge (C); N = number of electrons (no unit); e = elementary charge, 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. Used when a question asks how many electrons carry a given charge.

Resistance and Ohm's law

V = IR
Key: V = potential difference across the component (V); I = current through it (A); R = resistance (Ω). Ohm's law holds only when temperature is constant, which is why a filament lamp's I–V graph curves.

R = V / I
Key: R = resistance (Ω); V = potential difference (V); I = current (A). For a curved I–V graph, R is still V/I at the chosen point, not the gradient.

1 Ω = 1 V / 1 A
Key: the definition of the Ω; a component has 1 Ω when 1 V drives 1 A through it.

Power and energy in a circuit

P = VI
Key: P = power (W); V = potential difference (V); I = current (A).

P = I²R
Key: P = power dissipated as heat (W); I = current (A); R = resistance (Ω). This is the form that explains why transmission cables carry a low current at high voltage.

P = V² / R
Key: P = power (W); V = potential difference (V); R = resistance (Ω). Use it when the current is not given.

E = Pt = VIt
Key: E = energy transferred (J); P = power (W); t = time (s); V = potential difference (V); I = current (A).

cost = P(kW) × t(h) × price per kWh
Key: P in kilowatts (W ÷ 1000); t in hours; the price is per kilowatt-hour. A 2000 W heater for 3 hours uses 6 kWh.

fuse rating: I = P / V
Key: I = normal operating current (A); P = appliance power (W); V = supply voltage (V). Choose the next standard fuse above this value, never below it.

The three circuit rules

series: R(total) = R₁ + R₂ + …
Key: resistances in Ω (Ω); the current is the same everywhere in the series path and the supply voltage divides between the components.

parallel: 1 / R(total) = 1 / R₁ + 1 / R₂ + …
Key: resistances in Ω (Ω); the potential difference is the same across each branch and the current divides. Two 6 Ω resistors in parallel give 3 Ω, which is less than either — a parallel combination always has a lower resistance.

V(total) = V₁ + V₂ (series) and I(total) = I₁ + I₂ (parallel)
Key: the voltage rule for series and the current rule for parallel, both in the units of the quantity. The companion rules — voltage equal in parallel, current equal in series — follow from charge and energy conservation.

title: Edexcel IAL Computer Science: Algorithms, Recursion and Graph Traversal
content:
Edexcel IAL Computer Science: Algorithms, Recursion and Graph Traversal

Pearson Edexcel International Advanced Level in Computer Science, Unit 3 Advanced Computer Science: algorithms — sorting and searching — recursion, and graph traversal. Every algorithm below is traced on the same small dataset so the mechanisms are comparable, and every complexity claim is derived from the trace rather than asserted. At A Level the examiner wants the pass-by-pass state and the reason for the complexity, not just the name.

Searching: linear and binary

Dataset (10 values): [12, 19, 24, 31, 38, 44, 52, 67, 71, 89]

Linear search for 52: scan from the left - 12, 19, 24, 31, 38, 44, 52 (7
comparisons). Worst case n comparisons (value absent or last): O(n).
Requires nothing of the data.

Binary search for 52 (data must be sorted): compare with the MIDDLE element.
  low=0 high=9 mid=4 → [38]  52 > 38 → search right half
  low=5 high=9 mid=7 → [67]  52 < 67 → search left half
  low=5 high=6 mid=5 → [44]  52 > 44 → search right half
  low=6 high=6 mid=6 → [52]  found at index 6 - 4 comparisons for 10 items.

Halving the range each step: O(log n). Every "why is binary faster" answer
must name the halving and the sorted-data precondition.

Sorting algorithms compared

Before the traces, the comparison the exam wants in one place. Each algorithm's mechanism dictates its complexity and its niche; the traces below then show why each number is what it is.

SortBestAverageWorstSpaceStableBest niche
BubbleO(n)O(n²)O(n²)O(1)YesTeaching; tiny nearly-sorted sets (early-exit pass)
InsertionO(n)O(n²)O(n²)O(1)YesNearly-sorted or small data
SelectionO(n²)O(n²)O(n²)O(1)NoFew writes available (n swaps total)
MergeO(n log n)O(n log n)O(n log n)O(n)YesGuaranteed performance; linked lists; external sorting

Sorting: bubble, insertion, selection, merge

Data: [24, 12, 31, 19] - sort ascending with each algorithm's mechanism.

BUBBLE SORT - swap adjacent out-of-order pairs, pass by pass:
  pass 1: [24,12] swap → [12,24,31,19]; [24,31] ok; [31,19] swap →
          [12,24,19,31]  (largest value 31 has "bubbled" to the end)
  pass 2: [12,24] ok; [24,19] swap → [12,19,24,31]; end is sorted
  pass 3: [12,19] ok; [19,24] ok → sorted, no swaps means done.
  Worst case O(n²): reverse-ordered data swaps at every comparison.

INSERTION SORT - build a sorted left portion, insert each next value:
  start [24 | 12 31 19]        (left portion [24])
  insert 12: 12 < 24 → shift → [12 24 | 31 19]
  insert 31: 31 >= 24 → place  → [12 24 31 | 19]
  insert 19: 19 < 31, 19 < 24, 19 > 12 → [12 19 24 31]
  Fast on nearly-sorted data (few shifts); worst case O(n²).

SELECTION SORT - find the minimum of the unsorted part, swap to its front:
  [24 12 31 19] min=12 → swap with 24 → [12 | 24 31 19]
  [24 31 19]   min=19 → swap with 24 → [12 19 | 31 24]
  [31 24]      min=24 → swap with 31 → [12 19 24 31]
  Always O(n²) comparisons, but only n swaps - good when writes are costly.

MERGE SORT - divide in half recursively, then merge sorted halves:
  [24 12 31 19] → [24 12] [31 19] → [24] [12] [31] [19]
  merge → [12 24] [19 31] → merge → [12 19 24 31]
  Every level merges n items, and there are log n levels: O(n log n) always,
  at the cost of O(n) extra memory.

Choosing: small or nearly-sorted data → insertion; minimal memory and small n → selection; guaranteed performance and memory available → merge; tiny arrays with expensive swaps → bubble (mostly pedagogical). The exam asks for the comparison and a reason.

Recursion

A recursive function calls itself on a smaller instance, with a base case ending the recursion. Every recursion is equivalent to iteration plus an explicit stack (the call stack does the pushing). Two rules for correctness: each call must move toward the base case, and the base case must be reachable.

Recursive factorial, traced through the call stack:

  def factorial(n):
      if n <= 1: return 1        # base case
      return n * factorial(n-1)  # recursive case

  factorial(4):
    4 * factorial(3)
        3 * factorial(2)
            2 * factorial(1)
                1                 # base case reached; returns start
            2 * 1 = 2
        3 * 2 = 6
    4 * 6 = 24

Stack depth is n (each call waits for the return below it). A missing base
case never terminates - and deep recursion on large n overflows the stack,
which is why iterative solutions are preferred for deep, simple loops.

Trace table alternative for factorial(4): n=4 → 24, n=3 → 6, n=2 → 2,
n=1 → 1 (returns), then the multiplications unwind: 2, 6, 24.
Recursive binary search on [12, 19, 24, 31, 38, 44, 52, 67, 71, 89]:

  def bsearch(lo, hi, target):
      if lo > hi: return -1          # base case: empty range
      mid = (lo + hi) // 2
      if data[mid] == target: return mid
      if data[mid] > target: return bsearch(lo, mid-1, target)   # left
      return bsearch(mid+1, hi, target)                          # right

  Search for 31: mid=4 (38) → 31 < 38 → recurse left [0..3];
  mid=1 (19) → 31 > 19 → recurse right [2..3]; mid=2 (24) → right [3..3];
  mid=3 (31) → found. Four recursive calls, each halving the range.

Graphs and traversal

A graph is nodes (vertices) joined by edges — modelling networks, maps, dependencies. Terminology: undirected/directed, weighted (edges carry costs), path, cycle, connected. Storage: adjacency matrix (n×n grid — O(1) edge check, O(n²) space) versus adjacency list (list of neighbours per node — O(V+E) space, faster to iterate edges).

Graph: A connected to B, C; B to D; C to D; D to E.  Start at A.

BREADTH-FIRST SEARCH (queue; visit level by level):
  queue [A]; visit A → neighbours B, C → queue [B, C]
  visit B → neighbour D → queue [C, D]
  visit C → neighbour D (already queued/visited) → queue [D]
  visit D → neighbour E → queue [E]
  visit E → queue []
  Order: A, B, C, D, E. Finds SHORTEST PATH in unweighted graphs (level order).

DEPTH-FIRST SEARCH (stack or recursion; dive to the end, then backtrack):
  visit A → B (first neighbour)
  visit B → D
  visit D → E
  visit E → backtrack to D → backtrack to B → backtrack to A
  visit C → D already visited → backtrack
  Order: A, B, D, E, C. Detects CYCLES and solves maze-like problems.

Both mark nodes visited - without that, cycles make them loop forever.
Complexity: O(V + E) with adjacency lists - every vertex and edge processed
once.

Dijkstra's algorithm (weighted shortest path) extends BFS with a priority queue: keep tentative distances from the source, always settle the nearest unsettled node, and relax (shorten) its neighbours' distances; O((V+E) log V) with a heap. The trace question walks one node's relaxation exactly this way.

Worked example: algorithm choice for three problems

1. Find a name in an unsorted phone book (data streams in):
   linear search - no ordering to exploit; O(n).

2. Find a name in a sorted directory of 10⁶ entries:
   binary search - O(log n) is about 20 comparisons; sorting once with
   merge sort (O(n log n)) then searching many times amortises quickly.

3. Find the shortest route between two towns on a weighted map:
   Dijkstra - BFS ignores the road distances; a greedy relaxation over a
   priority queue computes the true shortest path; complexity
   O((V+E) log V).

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Applying binary search to unsorted data; the sorted precondition is part of the answer.
  • Complexity claims without the mechanism ("bubble sort is O(n²)" needs nested loops and the swap rule).
  • Confusing best/average/worst case; quote worst unless asked.
  • Recursion without a reachable base case, or not moving toward it.
  • Forgetting the call stack's cost: recursion uses O(n) stack space even when the algorithm is O(1) in its own memory.
  • BFS versus DFS purpose swap: BFS = shortest unweighted path; DFS = cycles, connectivity, exhaustive paths.
  • Unmarked visited sets in graph traversal — infinite loops on cycles.
  • Merge sort's memory cost omitted; it is O(n) extra space, the standard trade against in-place O(n²) sorts.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Unit 3, 4 marks). Trace bubble sort on [5, 3, 4, 1] for one pass and describe what the pass achieves.

Answer: Compare 5 and 3 → swap [3, 5, 4, 1]; 5 and 4 → swap [3, 4, 5, 1]; 5 and 1 → swap [3, 4, 1, 5]. The largest value (5) has bubbled to its final position; each pass places one more element, so n−1 passes complete the sort — O(n²).

Question 2 (Unit 3, 4 marks). Explain why binary search is O(log n) and state its precondition.

Answer: Each comparison discards half the remaining range (compare against the middle, keep one half), so the number of comparisons grows with the number of halvings needed to reach one element — log₂n: a million items need at most 20. Precondition: the data must be sorted by the searched key.

Question 3 (Unit 3, 5 marks). Write a recursive algorithm to compute the sum of an array and explain its base case.

Answer: FUNCTION sum(a, n): IF n = 0 THEN RETURN 0; ELSE RETURN a[n] + sum(a, n−1); ENDIF. The base case n = 0 returns 0 (empty array sums to zero), guaranteeing termination; each recursive call shrinks n by one toward it. Recursion depth is n, so iterative summation avoids stack growth for huge arrays.

Question 4 (Unit 3, 5 marks). Compare BFS and DFS on an undirected graph.

Answer: BFS uses a queue and explores level by level, visiting all neighbours before descending — giving the shortest path in unweighted graphs and O(V+E) time, at the cost of queue memory. DFS uses a stack (or recursion) and dives along one path to its end before backtracking — suiting cycle detection, topological ordering and exhaustive search, with memory proportional to the deepest path. Both must mark visited vertices to terminate on cycles.

Question 5 (Unit 3, 4 marks). Compare adjacency matrices and adjacency lists.

Answer: An adjacency matrix is a V×V grid giving O(1) edge-existence checks but O(V²) space — wasteful for sparse graphs. An adjacency list stores each vertex's neighbours, using O(V+E) space and fast edge iteration, but checking one edge takes O(degree). Dense graphs with frequent edge queries favour matrices; sparse graphs favour lists.

Question 6 (Unit 3, 3 marks). Explain how Dijkstra's algorithm finds a shortest path and state its limitation.

Answer: It maintains tentative distances from the source, repeatedly settling the unvisited node with the smallest distance and relaxing its edges (updating neighbour distances when the new route is shorter). Once a node is settled its distance is final. Limitation: it requires non-negative edge weights — negative weights break the greedy finality, needing Bellman-Ford instead.

Algorithms need code to run on; the next note covers how programming paradigms structure that code.

Quick revision: Hardware and Logic Gates

Computer Science — AS. `# Hardware and Logic Gates

Key areas to revise

  • Logic Gates
  • Boolean Algebra Laws
  • Constructing Circuits
  • Flip-Flops (Bistables)
  • Von Neumann Model

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Key points to remember

Logic gates are the building blocks of the processor and memory. AND, OR and NOT are the basic gates; NAND and NOR are universal, so any circuit can be built from either alone. A logic circuit takes binary inputs and produces an output that depends only on the current inputs.

Write a Boolean expression for a circuit by reading each gate from the inputs to the output, using a dot for AND, a plus for OR and a bar for NOT. Build the truth table from the expression, then check that the output column matches the circuit for every row. Show each column, because marks are awarded for the intermediate values as well as the final output.

title: Permutations and Combinations — Study Notes
content:
Permutations and Combinations

Board note: permutations and combinations are not examined in the Edexcel International A Level main specification; Cambridge examines them at A2 (9709). This note serves both boards.

The Multiplication Principle

If a task is done in successive stages with m, n, ... choices at each stage, the total is the product of the choices. This underpins every counting problem: a menu with 4 starters and 6 mains gives 24 meals.

Permutations — Order Matters

The number of ways of arranging r objects from n distinct objects is

  • ⁿPᵣ = n!/(n − r)!

The number of arrangements of n distinct objects is n!. Five books on a shelf: 5! = 120 ways.

Combinations — Order Irrelevant

The number of ways of choosing r objects from n is

  • ⁿCᵣ = n!/(r!(n − r)!)

Choosing a committee of 3 from 8 people: ⁸C₃ = 56. Choosing is not arranging — a committee has no internal order, so we divide by r!.

Restricted Permutations

  • No two specified people adjacent: arrange everyone else, then slot the restricted people into gaps. For n people with 2 who must be separated: arrange the other n − 2 (ways), then place 2 people in distinct gaps between them.
  • Specified people together: bundle them as one item, arrange the bundle, then multiply by the internal arrangements of the bundle.
  • Words with repeated letters: divide by the factorials of each repeat count. ARRANGE has 7 letters with A appearing twice and R twice, so 7!/(2!·2!) = 1260.

Combinations with Constraints

  • At least / at most: split into cases and add. A team of 5 from 6 boys and 5 girls with at least 3 girls is ⁵C₃⁶C₂ + ⁵C₄⁶C₁ + ⁵C₅⁶C₀.
  • "Must include" pairs: choose the required items first, then choose freely from the remainder.

Exam tips: state whether a scenario is a permutation or combination before computing anything. Most lost marks come from counting an arrangement where order does not actually matter. Check every answer against a small case you can enumerate by hand.

Exam method: arrangements and selections

The number of arrangements of r objects from n distinct objects is nPr = n!/(n − r)!. The number of ways to select r objects from n, where order does not matter, is nCr = n!/(r!(n − r)!). Ask first whether order matters, because that decides which formula to use.

Arrangements with restrictions are solved by treating a block as one object or by placing the restricted items first. For example, if two people must sit together, treat them as one unit and multiply by 2 for their internal order.

Use the identity nCr = nC(n − r) to check answers, and remember that nC0 = nCn = 1. Pascal's identity nCr = (n−1)C(r−1) + (n−1)Cr links the two formulae.

When a question has several groups with separate conditions, count each part on its own and multiply the results, provided the parts are independent.

Exam cue: Write the formula with the numbers substituted before simplifying, since method marks are given for the correct expression.

title: AS Level Mathematics: Integration
content:
AS Level Mathematics: Integration

Integration is differentiation in reverse: it recovers a function from its gradient, and it accumulates a rate into a total — the area under a curve, the distance from a velocity, the cost from a marginal. This note builds the topic from zero: the indefinite integral and the constant of integration, the power rule, definite integrals and the fundamental theorem, areas above and below the axis, the area between two curves, and kinematics. Every worked example shows the antiderivative line before any substitution of limits.

The indefinite integral

if dy/dx = x^n then y = x^(n+1)/(n+1) + c   (n not -1)

integral of x^n dx = x^(n+1)/(n+1) + c
integral of k f(x) dx = k integral of f(x) dx
integral of a sum = sum of integrals

The +c is mandatory for indefinite integrals: every antiderivative differs by a constant, and the constant is fixed by a boundary condition (a point on the curve).

Worked example 1. Find ∫(6x² − 4x + 3) dx.

= 6x³/3 - 4x²/2 + 3x + c
= 2x³ - 2x² + 3x + c

Worked example 2 (negative and fractional powers). Find ∫(1/x² + √x) dx.

rewrite: integral of (x⁻² + x^(1/2)) dx
= -x⁻¹ + (2/3)x^(3/2) + c
= -1/x + (2/3)x^(3/2) + c

Worked example 3 (finding c). dy/dx = 3x² + 2 and the curve passes through (1, 5). Find y.

y = x³ + 2x + c
5 = 1 + 2 + c  →  c = 2
y = x³ + 2x + 2

Definite integrals and area

integral from a to b of f(x) dx = F(b) - F(a)

area under the curve between x = a and x = b (above the axis)
= definite integral; a negative value means the region is
below the x-axis, and the area is the magnitude

Worked example. Evaluate ∫ from 1 to 3 of (2x + 1) dx.

antiderivative: x² + x
F(3) = 9 + 3 = 12;  F(1) = 1 + 1 = 2
value = 12 - 2 = 10

Worked example 2 (area under a curve). Find the area under y = x² between x = 0 and x = 3.

integral: x³/3
from 0 to 3: 27/3 - 0 = 9 square units

Worked example 3 (below the axis). Find the area between y = x² − 4 and the x-axis from x = 0 to x = 2.

integral: x³/3 - 4x
from 0 to 2: 8/3 - 8 = -16/3
the value is negative because the region is below the axis;
area = 16/3 = 5.33 square units

Areas crossing the axis

When a curve crosses the x-axis inside the interval, integrate each piece separately and add the magnitudes — a single integral would cancel positive and negative areas.

Worked example. Find the total area between y = x² − 1 and the x-axis from x = −2 to x = 2.

crossings at x = -1 and x = 1
piece 1 (-2 to -1): F = x³/3 - x; F(-1) - F(-2) = (2/3) - (-2/3) = 4/3
piece 2 (-1 to 1): F(1) - F(-1) = (-2/3) - (2/3) = -4/3 → magnitude 4/3
piece 3 (1 to 2): F(2) - F(1) = (2/3) - (-2/3) = 4/3
total area = 4/3 + 4/3 + 4/3 = 4 square units

Area between two curves

area between y = f(x) and y = g(x) from a to b
= integral of (f(x) - g(x)) dx from a to b
where f is the upper curve and g the lower

Worked example. Find the area between y = x² and y = x from x = 0 to x = 1.

upper curve on this interval is y = x
integral of (x - x²) dx = x²/2 - x³/3
from 0 to 1: 1/2 - 1/3 = 1/6 square units

Worked example 2 (intersections). Find the area enclosed by y = x² and y = 2x.

intersections: x² = 2x → x(x - 2) = 0 → x = 0, 2
upper on (0, 2) is y = 2x
integral of (2x - x²) dx = x² - x³/3
from 0 to 2: 4 - 8/3 = 4/3 square units

Kinematics with integration

velocity v = ds/dt  →  displacement s = integral of v dt
acceleration a = dv/dt  →  velocity v = integral of a dt

definite integral of v from t1 to t2 = displacement
integral of |v| = distance travelled

Worked example. A particle has velocity v = 3t² − 6t (m/s). Find its displacement from t = 0 to t = 3 and its distance travelled.

s = integral of (3t² - 6t) dt = t³ - 3t²
from 0 to 3: 27 - 27 = 0  →  net displacement zero
sign of v: 3t(t - 2), negative between 0 and 2, positive after
distance = |integral 0 to 2| + integral 2 to 3
= |8 - 12| + (27 - 27) - (8 - 12) = 4 + 4 = 8 m

The distinction between displacement and distance is examinable: displacement is the signed integral, distance is the sum of the absolute pieces.

Worked examples: mixed integration

Worked example. The curve y = f(x) has f'(x) = 6x − 4 and passes through (2, 3). Find f(x) and the area under the curve from x = 1 to x = 2.

f(x) = 3x² - 4x + c;  3 = 12 - 8 + c → c = -1
f(x) = 3x² - 4x - 1
area = integral 1 to 2: x³ - 2x² - x
F(2) = 8 - 8 - 2 = -2; F(1) = 1 - 2 - 1 = -2
area = -2 - (-2) = 0  (the curve is below the axis and the
signed areas cancel); the geometric area needs the crossing
checked - a useful reminder to sketch first

Integrating expressions that need rearranging

Integration has no product or quotient rule at AS level, so expressions must first be written as sums of powers. Two standard rearrangements cover almost every case:

product: expand, then integrate term by term
quotient with a single term denominator: divide through first

(x + 2)(x - 5) = x² - 3x - 10
(3x² + 4x)/x = 3x + 4
√(x)(x + 1) = x^(3/2) + x^(1/2)

Worked example. Find ∫ (x + 3)(x − 1) dx.

expand: x² + 2x - 3
integrate: x³/3 + x² - 3x + c

Worked example 2. Find ∫ (4x³ + 2x)/x dx.

divide: 4x² + 2
integrate: (4/3)x³ + 2x + c

Two boundary conditions

When the second derivative is given, integrate twice and use two pieces of information to fix both constants. The order matters: the first integration produces the gradient function and its constant, the second the curve and its constant.

Worked example. d²y/dx² = 6x, dy/dx = 2 when x = 1, and y = 5 when x = 1. Find y.

first: dy/dx = 3x² + c;  2 = 3 + c  →  c = -1, so dy/dx = 3x² - 1
second: y = x³ - x + k;  5 = 1 - 1 + k  →  k = 5
y = x³ - x + 5

Finding limits and constants from area information

Area questions are often inverted: the area is given and a limit or coefficient must be found. Set up the definite integral with the unknown, evaluate, and solve the resulting equation — rejecting any root outside the geometric context.

Worked example. The area under y = kx² from x = 0 to x = 3 is 36. Find k.

integral: kx³/3
from 0 to 3: 27k/3 = 9k
9k = 36  →  k = 4

Worked example 2 (unknown upper limit). The area under y = 2x from x = 0 to x = a is 25. Find a.

integral: x²;  from 0 to a: a² = 25
a = 5  (the negative root is rejected: a is an x-coordinate to
the right of the origin in this setup)

Kinematics: recovering velocity from acceleration

Worked example. A particle starts from rest with acceleration a = 6t − 4 (m/s²). Find its velocity at t = 3 and the distance travelled in the first 3 seconds.

v = integral of (6t - 4) dt = 3t² - 4t + c
at rest at t = 0: c = 0  →  v = 3t² - 4t
v(3) = 27 - 12 = 15 m/s
distance = integral of |v| from 0 to 3
v = 0 at t = 0 and t = 4/3; v is negative on (0, 4/3)
piece 1: [t³ - 2t²] from 0 to 4/3 = 64/27 - 32/9 = -32/27 → 32/27
piece 2: [t³ - 2t²] from 4/3 to 3 = (27 - 18) - (-32/27) = 9 + 32/27
distance = 32/27 + 9 + 32/27 = 9 + 64/27 = 11.4 m

The sign analysis is the whole question: sketch v against t, mark where it crosses zero, and integrate each piece with its sign removed.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Indefinite) Find ∫(4x³ − 2) dx. Answer: x⁴ − 2x + c.
  2. (Negative power) Find ∫x⁻² dx. Answer: −x⁻¹ + c = −1/x + c.
  3. (Definite) Evaluate ∫ from 0 to 2 of 3x² dx. Answer: [x³] = 8.
  4. (Area) Find the area under y = x + 2 from x = 0 to x = 3. Answer: [x²/2 + 2x] = 4.5 + 6 = 10.5.
  5. (Below axis) Find the area between y = x − 3 and the x-axis from x = 0 to x = 2. Answer: integral = [x²/2 − 3x] = 2 − 6 = −4; area 4.
  6. (Between curves) Find the area between y = x² and y = x³ from 0 to 1. Answer: upper is x²; ∫(x² − x³) = 1/3 − 1/4 = 1/12.
  7. (Constant) dy/dx = 4x and y = 7 when x = 1. Find y. Answer: y = 2x² + c → 7 = 2 + c → c = 5 → y = 2x² + 5.
  8. (Kinematics) v = 2t + 1. Find the displacement from t = 0 to t = 4. Answer: [t² + t] = 16 + 4 = 20 m.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Forgetting +c: an indefinite integral without the constant loses a mark; with a boundary condition, the constant is required for the answer.
  • Power rule reversal: integrate xⁿ to x^(n+1)/(n+1); adding one and dividing is the opposite of differentiating, and mixing them up produces nonsense.
  • Limits order: F(b) − F(a), never the reverse. A negative area often means the limits were swapped.
  • Ignoring crossings: a definite integral over a region that crosses the axis gives the signed area; split at the crossings and add magnitudes for the geometric area.
  • Wrong upper curve: subtract lower from upper; sketching between the intersection points avoids the sign error.
  • Distance versus displacement: displacement is the signed integral; distance sums the absolute pieces. Read which is asked.
  • Expanding before integrating: products must be expanded or divided first; there is no product rule for integration at AS level.
  • Units: areas are square units, displacements in metres; attach and interpret units in applied questions.

title: A Level Mathematics: Proof
content:
A Level Mathematics: Proof

Proof at A2 extends the AS methods with contradiction, disproof by counter-example in unfamiliar settings, and algebraic arguments about divisibility, parity and inequalities. The examinable skills are choosing a method, setting up general notation, and closing the argument — not spotting a clever trick. This note works through each method with complete examples and the wording mark schemes expect.

The four methods and when to use them

MethodUse whenShape of the argument
DirectThe statement is algebraicStart from definitions, manipulate to the target form
ExhaustionThe domain splits into a few casesCheck each case
Counter-exampleThe statement claims "for all" and looks falseProduce one failing case with arithmetic
ContradictionThe statement is negative or about irrationality/infinityAssume the opposite, derive an impossibility

Choosing badly wastes time: a "prove that there is no largest prime" question cannot be done directly, and a parity statement cannot be done by example.

Proof by contradiction

assume the negation, derive a contradiction with a known truth,
conclude the original statement

Worked example 1 (irrationality of √2). The classic, examinable in full.

assume √(2) = p/q in lowest terms, p and q integers
2q² = p², so p² is even, so p is even: p = 2k
4k² = 2q²  →  q² = 2k², so q is even
p and q both even contradicts "lowest terms"
hence √(2) is irrational

Worked example 2 (no largest prime). Prove there are infinitely many primes.

assume finitely many: p1, p2, ..., pn
consider N = p1 p2 ... pn + 1
N leaves remainder 1 when divided by any π, so no π divides N
so N has a prime factor not in the list: contradiction
hence there are infinitely many primes

Worked example 3 (no rational solution). Prove that x² = 6 has no rational root.

assume x = p/q in lowest terms: p² = 6q²
so 3 divides p², hence 3 divides p: p = 3k
9k² = 6q²  →  3k² = 2q², so 3 divides q², hence q
both divisible by 3 contradicts lowest terms

Disproof by counter-example

Worked example 1. Disprove "if a > b then a² > b²".

take a = 1, b = -3: 1 > -3 but 1 < 9
counter-example disproves the statement

Worked example 2. Disprove "n² + n + 41 is prime for all positive integers n".

n = 41: 1681 + 41 + 41 = 1763 = 41 × 43, not prime

Worked example 3. Disprove "every odd number is prime".

9 is odd and 9 = 3 × 3, not prime

Each disproof is complete with one case; the arithmetic must be shown, not asserted.

Algebraic proof with parity and divisibility

even: 2n;  odd: 2n + 1
"is a multiple of k" means the expression equals k times an integer

Worked example 1. Prove that the difference of the squares of two consecutive odd numbers is a multiple of 8.

(2n + 3)² - (2n + 1)² = (4n² + 12n + 9) - (4n² + 4n + 1) = 8n + 8
= 8(n + 1), a multiple of 8

Worked example 2. Prove that n³ − n is divisible by 6 for all integers n.

n³ - n = n(n - 1)(n + 1), three consecutive integers
one is even, one is a multiple of 3; since 2 and 3 are coprime,
the product is divisible by 6

Worked example 3. Prove that the product of two consecutive even numbers is a multiple of 8.

2n(2n + 2) = 4n(n + 1); n(n + 1) is even, so the product is 8k

Inequalities by completing the square

a squared term is never negative; complete the square to expose a
minimum, then conclude the inequality

Worked example 1. Prove that x² − 4x + 7 > 0 for all real x.

= (x - 2)² + 3 >= 3 > 0

Worked example 2. Prove that 4x − x² − 5 < 0 for all x.

= -(x² - 4x + 5) = -[(x - 2)² + 1] = -(x - 2)² - 1 <= -1 < 0

Worked example 3 (unknown constant). Find the values of k for which x² + kx + k > 0 for all x.

(x + k/2)² + k - k²/4 > 0 requires k - k²/4 > 0
k(1 - k/4) > 0  →  0 < k < 4

The discriminant route gives the same answer (k² − 4k < 0); the completing-the-square route states the minimum explicitly, which is usually clearer in a proof.

Proof by exhaustion

Worked example. Prove that every integer from 1 to 10 is either prime, a square, or the sum of two primes.

1 (square); 2 (prime); 3 (prime); 4 (square); 5 (prime);
6 = 3 + 3; 7 (prime); 8 = 3 + 5; 9 (square); 10 = 3 + 7
all ten cases checked  →  statement proved for this finite domain

Exhaustion is only valid for a finite domain, and the proof is incomplete unless every case is listed. State the domain explicitly.

Setting out a proof for full marks

  • Define every variable with its domain ("let n be an integer").
  • State which method you are using when it is not obvious.
  • Write the algebra in connected steps, each justified.
  • Finish with a sentence tying the result to the claim ("hence ... as required").
  • For contradiction, state the assumption and where the contradiction lies.

Worked example (full structure). Prove that if n is odd then n² + 1 is even.

let n be an odd integer, so n = 2k + 1 for some integer k   [definition]
n² + 1 = 4k² + 4k + 1 + 1 = 4k² + 4k + 2              [algebra]
        = 2(2k² + 2k + 1)                              [target form]
which is even, hence n² + 1 is even whenever n is odd      [conclusion]

Inequalities with the discriminant

"Always positive" or "always negative" quadratics are proved with the discriminant, which is the algebraic form of the completing-the-square argument.

ax² + bx + c > 0 for all x  (a > 0)  <=>  b² - 4ac < 0
ax² + bx + c < 0 for all x  (a < 0)  <=>  b² - 4ac < 0

Worked example. Prove that 2x² − 3x + 4 > 0 for all real x.

a = 2 > 0;  discriminant = 9 - 32 = -23 < 0
no real roots and the parabola opens upward, so it never touches the
x-axis and is positive throughout

Worked example 2 (find the range). Find p such that x² + (p + 1)x + 4 > 0 for all x.

(p + 1)² - 16 < 0  →  -4 < p + 1 < 4  →  -5 < p < 3

Worked example 3 (negative leading coefficient). Prove that −x² + 2x − 5 < 0 for all x.

a = -1 < 0;  discriminant = 4 - 20 = -16 < 0
no real roots and the parabola opens downward, so it stays below the axis

Proving statements about sums and sequences

Closed-form statements about sums are proved by deriving the formula or by induction on the pattern; the derivation is always acceptable and often shorter.

Worked example 1. Prove that the sum of the first n odd numbers is n².

S = 1 + 3 + 5 + ... + (2n - 1), an arithmetic series
a = 1, d = 2: S = (n/2)[2 + 2(n - 1)] = (n/2)(2n) = n²

Worked example 2. Prove that the sum of the first n terms of 2 + 4 + 8 + ... is 2^(n+1) − 2.

geometric with a = 2, r = 2: S = 2(2^n - 1)/(2 - 1) = 2^(n+1) - 2

Worked example 3 (difference of squares). Prove that every odd number greater than 1 is the difference of two squares.

let the odd number be 2n + 1 = (n + 1)² - n²
since (n + 1)² - n² = 2n + 1, the representation always exists

Statements about the roots of a quadratic

Relations between roots and coefficients are provable from the quadratic formula and are a favourite A2 proof.

for ax² + bx + c = 0 with roots alpha and beta:
alpha + beta = -b/a;  alpha beta = c/a

Worked example. Prove that the sum of the roots of x² + px + q = 0 is −p.

roots: (-p +/- √(p² - 4q))/2
sum: [-p + √(...) - p - √(...)]/2 = -2p/2 = -p

Worked example 2. Prove that if one root of x² + bx + c = 0 is twice the other, then 2b² = 9c.

roots k and 2k: sum 3k = -b, product 2k² = c
k = -b/3, so 2b²/9 = c  →  2b² = 9c

Worked example 3 (discriminant). Prove that x² + 2x + 2 = 0 has no real roots.

discriminant = 4 - 8 = -4 < 0, so no real solutions
(equivalently (x + 1)² + 1 = 0 has no real solution)

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Contradiction) Prove √3 is irrational. Answer: assume p/q lowest terms, 3q² = p², 3 | p, then 3 | q — contradiction.
  2. (Counter-example) Disprove "n² − n + 1 is prime for all n". Answer: n = 4 gives 13 (prime) — try n = 5: 21 = 3 × 7, not prime.
  3. (Parity) Prove the sum of two odd numbers is even. Answer: (2m + 1) + (2n + 1) = 2(m + n + 1).
  4. (Divisibility) Prove 5n² + 5n is a multiple of 10. Answer: 5n(n + 1); n(n + 1) is even, so 5 × even = 10k.
  5. (Inequality) Prove x² + 2x + 2 > 0. Answer: (x + 1)² + 1 ≥ 1.
  6. (Constant) Find k so that x² + 2kx + 9 > 0 always. Answer: 4k² < 36 → −3 < k < 3.
  7. (Exhaustion) Prove n² + n is even by cases. Answer: n even → 4k² + 2k; n odd → 4k² + 6k + 2; both even.
  8. (Contradiction) Prove there is no greatest even integer. Answer: if N were greatest, N + 2 is even and larger — contradiction.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Examples offered as proof: only a general algebraic argument proves a universal claim.
  • Undefined variables: "let x be odd" without x = 2k + 1 leaves nothing to manipulate.
  • Contradiction not closed: name the contradiction explicitly — "this contradicts lowest terms".
  • Assuming the conclusion: starting from the statement to be proved and deriving a truth proves nothing unless every step is reversible.
  • Divisibility without coprimality: "divisible by 2 and by 3 hence by 6" needs 2 and 3 coprime; it is true here, but state it.
  • Exhaustion on an infinite domain: cases must cover every possibility; a finite sample is not exhaustion.
  • Counter-example unchecked: show the arithmetic that breaks the claim.
  • Conclusion missing: finish with a sentence; an algebraic derivation alone reads as unfinished.

How a proof is marked: the four lines that earn the marks

At A level the algebra is rarely the hard part — the marking is. A proof is read for four things, in order, and a script that has all the algebra but none of the signposting loses marks that were never in doubt.

Line 1: state what you are working with. Introduce every variable and say what kind of object it is: "let n be an integer", "let x and y be real numbers with x < y". Every mark that depends on parity or divisibility hangs off this line, because without it the algebra could be about anything.

Line 2: the algebra, one implication at a time. Each step must follow from the previous one, and the connector says which way the logic runs. "⇒" means the next line follows; a proof needs that direction, not its converse. Writing = between two expressions that are merely equal in value at the end is not the same as showing one implies the other.

Line 3: name the conclusion. "Therefore n² + n is always even, for every integer n." A proof that stops at the algebra leaves the marker to infer the point, and that inference is the mark.

Line 4: say what the conclusion shows about the original statement. In a contradiction this is the sentence that names what was contradicted; in exhaustion it is "these cases are exhaustive, so the result holds in all cases"; in direct proof it is "as required".

Worked example. Prove that x² + 4x + 7 > 0 for all real x.

Complete the square:
x² + 4x + 7 = (x + 2)² − 4 + 7 = (x + 2)² + 3

Now argue from a fact about squares: (x + 2)² ≥ 0 for every real x, so (x + 2)² + 3 ≥ 3 > 0. Hence x² + 4x + 7 > 0 for all real x.

The line (x + 2)² ≥ 0 is not decoration: it is the only reason the conclusion holds, and the mark scheme wants it written. The same argument answers "show this quadratic has no real roots" — the completed-square form shows the minimum value, and a minimum above zero cannot touch the axis.

The three ways this goes wrong. Assuming the result and working towards something true — that proves nothing, because a false statement can imply a true one. Using "if and only if" when only one direction was proved. And proving the converse: "if n is even then n² is even" is a different statement from "if n² is even then n is even", and only the second needs contradiction.

Reading the question's verbs. "Show that" wants a derivation from given facts. "Prove" wants the argument with its assumptions stated. "Disprove" wants one counter-example and no more. "Determine whether" wants a decision plus its justification — and the mark is for the decision being argued, not merely stated.

Equations and symbols

The chain of a contradiction proof and the two algebraic identities that close most A2 proofs. Each arrow is a step whose justification is a sentence of your answer.

2q² = p², so p² is even, so p is even: p = 2k Key: p, q = integers with no common factor, assumed at the start; q² = the square of the denominator; k = an integer, so 2k is the definition of even. The last implication uses the fact that only an even number has an even square — quote it, because it is a step.

4k² = 2q² → q² = 2k², so q is even Key: substituting p = 2k into p² = 2q²; dividing by 2 gives the second equation; q even contradicts "no common factor", which is the finish. Without the contradiction sentence the proof is incomplete.

assume √(2) = p/q in lowest terms, p and q integers Key: the assumption being negated; "lowest terms" is what makes the contradiction bite, so it must be written. For x² = 6 the divisor argument runs the same way with 3 in place of 2.

n³ - n = n(n - 1)(n + 1), three consecutive integers Key: n = any integer; the product of three consecutive integers always contains a multiple of 2 and a multiple of 3, so it is divisible by 6. The factorisation is the proof; testing n = 1, 2, 3 is not.

(2n + 3)² - (2n + 1)² = (4n² + 12n + 9) - (4n² + 4n + 1) = 8n + 8 Key: n = integer; 2n + 1 and 2n + 3 are consecutive odd numbers; 8n + 8 = 8(n + 1) proves the difference is always a multiple of 8. Expanding both squares and subtracting is faster and safer than the difference-of-squares identity here.

2n(2n + 2) = 4n(n + 1); n(n + 1) is even, so the product is 8k Key: the product of two consecutive even numbers; the 4 outside times the even n(n + 1) gives 4 × 2k = 8k. The proof is the observation that one of any two consecutive integers is even.
