title: Forces and Equilibrium
content:
Forces and Equilibrium

Free-Body Diagrams

Draw every force on one body: weight (down), normal reactions (perpendicular to surfaces), tension (along strings), friction (opposing motion).

Resolving Forces

Any force F at angle θ splits into F cos θ (along) and F sin θ (perpendicular).

Example: a 50 N pull at 30° above horizontal drags with 50 cos 30° ≈ 43.3 N horizontally.

An object on a slope of angle θ has components mg sin θ down the slope and mg cos θ into it.

Equilibrium

A body is in equilibrium when the resultant force is zero in every direction and the resultant moment is zero.

Moments and the Principle of Moments

Moment = force × perpendicular distance from the pivot.

For equilibrium: Σ clockwise moments = Σ anticlockwise moments.

Example: a 600 N child 2 m from a pivot balances an adult 1.2 m away: 600 × 2 = W × 1.2, so W = 1000 N.

Centre of Gravity

The point where the weight appears to act. For stable equilibrium the line of action must pass through the base.

Exam tips: take moments about the point with the most unknown forces; include the normal reaction and friction of any support, and check units of perpendicular distance.

title: AS Level Physics: Work, Energy and Power
content:
AS Level Physics: Work, Energy and Power

Energy is the currency of physics: it is never created or destroyed, only changed in form and moved from place to place, and every calculation in mechanics is really an accounting exercise in that currency. This note builds the energy toolkit from zero: what work actually is (a transfer, not a thing), the conservation principle that governs every process, the two energy formulas you will use daily — kinetic and gravitational potential — and power, the rate at which the currency is spent. Every worked example is a full energy audit with each line shown.

Work: energy in transit

Work is done when a force moves its point of application: energy is transferred from one store to another. The definition that earns the mark:

work done = force x distance moved in the direction of the force
W = F s cos(θ)

W in joules (J), F in newtons (N), s in metres (m)
θ = angle between the force and the displacement

The analogy: pushing a shopping trolley. Push along the direction of travel (θ = 0, cos θ = 1) and all your effort does work; push sideways (θ = 90°, cos θ = 0) and you do no work on its forward motion — you merely warm your arms. One joule is the work done when a force of one newton moves its point of application one metre: 1 J = 1 N m.

Worked example. A woman pushes a trolley with 80 N along 15 m of horizontal floor, the force angled 30° above the horizontal. Find the work done.

W = F s cos(θ) = 80 × 15 x cos(30)
  = 80 × 15 × 0.866 = 10³⁹ J  (2 s.f.: 1.0 kJ)

If instead the question were a box pushed horizontally with 80 N over 15 m, the answer is simply 80 × 15 = 1200 J. Read whether an angle is given; the cos θ line is where method marks live.

Conservation of energy

Energy cannot be created or destroyed; the total energy of a closed system is constant. Energy transfers between stores — kinetic, gravitational potential, elastic potential, thermal, internal — and every real transfer leaks some energy to thermal stores of the surroundings through friction. The exam phrasing: "energy is transferred usefully to X and dissipated to the surroundings as heat" — learn the transfer vocabulary (transferred, dissipated, stored) because the mark schemes use it deliberately.

StoreChange that fills itExample
Kinetican object speeds upa falling stone
Gravitational potentialan object is lifteda book on a shelf
Elastic potentiala spring is stretched or compresseda drawn bow
Thermal (internal)friction, or heatingbrake pads after a descent

Kinetic energy and gravitational potential energy

kinetic energy:  KE = (1/2) m v²
gravitational potential energy (near a planet's surface):
                 GPE = m g h     (change in GPE = m g Δh)

m in kg, v in m s⁻¹, g = 9.81 m s⁻² (or the value given),
h = vertical height change in metres

Two traps live in the definitions. First, h is vertical: moving a box 10 m along a shelf adds no gravitational potential energy however far it slides. Second, GPE is defined as a change — only differences matter, so the question's reference level (where h = 0) is yours to choose; pick the lowest point and every height stays positive.

Worked example 1 (falling object). A 0.50 kg ball is dropped from 20 m. Find its speed just before impact (ignore air resistance).

energy at top:   GPE = m g h = 0.50 × 9.81 × 20 = 98.1 J
energy at bottom: KE = (1/2) m v², and KE = GPE
(1/2)(0.50) v² = 98.1
0.25 v² = 98.1 → v² = 392.4 → v = 19.8 m s⁻¹

Worked example 2 (with friction). A 2.0 kg trolley starts at the top of a 5.0 m slope at 30° and reaches the bottom at 3.0 m s⁻¹. Find the energy dissipated by friction.

vertical height: h = 5.0 sin(30) = 2.5 m
initial GPE = m g h = 2.0 × 9.81 × 2.5 = 49.05 J
final KE = (1/2)(2.0)(3.0)² = 9.0 J
energy lost to friction = 49.05 - 9.0 = 40.05 J
                        = 40 J (2 s.f.)

Note the structure of every friction question: start energy minus end energy is the dissipation. Nothing is destroyed — it went to thermal stores.

Bringing things to rest: work done by braking

A whole family of questions asks how far a vehicle takes to stop, or what force stops it. The engine of the calculation is always the same: the kinetic energy the vehicle loses becomes work done by the braking force.

KE lost = work done by braking
(1/2) m v² = F s        (F = average braking force, s = stopping distance)

Worked example. A 1200 kg car travelling at 20 m s⁻¹ brakes to a halt over 40 m. Find the average braking force.

initial KE = (1/2) m v² = 0.5 × 1200 × 20² = 240 000 J
(1/2) m v² = F s  →  240 000 = F x 40
F = 240 000/40 = 6000 N = 6.0 kN

The same equation rearranged answers the safety version: since KE grows with v², doubling the speed quadruples the energy the brakes must absorb and hence the stopping distance at constant force. That single statement is a full mark in most questions about speed limits.

Power: the rate of transfer

power = work done / time = energy transferred / time
P = W/t          (watts, W; 1 W = 1 J s⁻¹)

also, for a force moving at constant speed:
P = F v          (derivable: W/t = F s/t = F v)

Worked example 1. A motor lifts a 200 kg crate through 8.0 m in 12 s at constant speed. Find its useful power output (g = 9.81 m s⁻²).

useful work = gain in GPE = m g h = 200 × 9.81 × 8.0 = 15 696 J
P = W/t = 15 696/12 = 1308 W = 1.3 kW (2 s.f.)

Worked example 2 (P = Fv). A car engine provides 20 kN of thrust at a steady 30 m s⁻¹. Find the power developed.

P = F v = 20 000 × 30 = 6.0 × 10⁵ W = 600 kW

Efficiency closes the topic: efficiency = useful energy output / total energy input, always a fraction (or ×100%). Real machines are between 0 and 1 — an efficiency of 1.2 is a red flag in your own answer.

Worked example 3 (efficiency). A lift uses 40 kJ of electrical energy to raise a 500 kg load through 6.0 m. Find its efficiency.

useful output = m g h = 500 × 9.81 × 6.0 = 29 430 J
input = 40 kJ = 40 000 J
efficiency = 29 430/40 000 = 0.74  (74%)

Worked examples: the mixed audit

Worked example. A 1.5 kg trolley is pushed by a 6.0 N force along a 4.0 m horizontal track. It starts from rest and ends at 3.0 m s⁻¹. Account for the energy.

work input from the push: W = F s = 6.0 × 4.0 = 24 J
final KE = (1/2)(1.5)(3.0)² = 6.75 J
energy to friction/thermal = 24 - 6.75 = 17.25 J = 17 J (2 s.f.)
comment: most of the push became heat - the track is rough.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Work) A 40 N force acts at 60° to the horizontal, moving a box 5.0 m horizontally. Find the work done. Answer: W = Fs cos θ = 40 × 5.0 × cos 60 = 40 × 5.0 × 0.5 = 100 J.
  2. (Conservation) A cyclist freewheels down a hill. Describe the energy transfers. Answer: Gravitational potential energy is transferred to kinetic energy as the cyclist descends; some energy is dissipated to the thermal stores of the brakes, tyres and air through friction and drag, so the final kinetic energy is slightly less than the initial GPE.
  3. (GPE/KE) A 0.20 kg ball is thrown up at 15 m s⁻¹. Find the maximum height reached (no air resistance). Answer: ½mv² = mgh → h = v²/(2g) = 225/(2 × 9.81) = 11.5 m.
  4. (Power) A crane lifts 800 kg through 12 m at constant speed in 20 s. Find the useful power (g = 9.81). Answer: W = mgh = 800 × 9.81 × 12 = 94 176 J; P = W/t = 4709 W = 4.7 kW.
  5. (Efficiency) A generator takes in 50 kJ and delivers 38 kJ of electrical energy. Find the efficiency and state where the rest goes. Answer: 38/50 = 0.76 (76%); the remaining 12 kJ is dissipated as heat to the surroundings (thermal stores) through friction and electrical resistance.
  6. (P = Fv) A car moves at constant speed against a total drag of 500 N. Find the engine power at 25 m s⁻¹. Answer: P = Fv = 500 × 25 = 12 500 W = 12.5 kW.
  7. (Vertical height) A 3.0 kg suitcase is carried 4.0 m horizontally across a room. Find the change in its GPE. Answer: Zero — the vertical height did not change, and GPE depends only on vertical displacement.
  8. (Full audit) A 1.0 kg block slides 2.0 m down a 25° slope and reaches 2.5 m s⁻¹. Find the energy dissipated. Answer: h = 2.0 sin 25 = 0.845 m; GPE lost = 1.0 × 9.81 × 0.845 = 8.29 J; KE gained = ½ × 1.0 × 6.25 = 3.13 J; dissipated = 8.29 − 3.13 = 5.2 J.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • h is vertical: sliding along a level floor changes no GPE. Convert slope distance to vertical height with sin θ before mgh.
  • Speed squared: KE = ½mv² — doubling v quadruples KE. Candidates who double the energy on doubling speed lose marks in multi-step questions.
  • W = Fs versus W = mgh: the work done by a lifting force equals the gain in GPE only at constant speed; if the load accelerates, some work also becomes KE.
  • Forgetting the energy audit structure: friction questions want input energy minus output energy as a stated subtraction — show both energies first.
  • Power units: kW into W before dividing by seconds (1 kW = 1000 W). 1300 W is 1.3 kW, not 13.
  • Efficiency as a percentage over 100: impossible; check the ratio direction (output over input, never the reverse).
  • g value: use 9.81 m s⁻² unless the paper supplies another value; a question giving g = 10 expects 10.
  • Significant figures and units: answers to 2 or 3 s.f. with units (J, W, m s⁻¹) — unrounded calculator output costs marks.
  • Method visibility: write the formula (W = Fs cos θ, P = W/t) as its own line before substitution; formulae earn credit independently of arithmetic.

title: Statistics — Probability — Study Notes
content:
Statistics — Probability

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): probability scale, combined events, tree diagrams, conditional probability, relative frequency.

1. Basics

P(event) = favourable/total; 0 ≤ P ≤ 1; P(not A) = 1 − P(A). Probabilities of a complete set sum to 1 — use to find a missing probability.

2. Combined events

  • Independent: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).
  • Mutually exclusive: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B).
  • With replacement ⇒ independent; without replacement ⇒ denominators shrink.

Example: bag 4 red, 6 blue; two draws without replacement: P(both red) = 4/10 × 3/9 = 2/15.

3. Tree diagrams

Multiply along branches; add between outcome paths. Label end products like 4/10 × 6/9 = 4/15.

4. Conditional probability

P(A|B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B). From tree diagrams it is the "given the first branch happened" re-weighting.

5. Relative frequency (experimental)

Relative frequency = successes ÷ trials. More trials → closer to theoretical probability; compare with expected counts (n × P).

Exam tips: always reduce fractions for final answers; in tree diagrams write the multiplication line before the product — that is where the marks are.

Probability scale and notation

Probabilities lie between 0 (impossible) and 1 (certain), and may be written as fractions, decimals or percentages. The probabilities of all outcomes in a sample space add up to 1, so the probability of an event not happening is 1 minus the probability it happens.

Combined events and tree diagrams

For independent events, multiply the probabilities along the branches. For events without replacement, the second probabilities change, so recalculate the denominators on the second set of branches. Add the probabilities of separate routes that give the required outcome.

Expected frequency

Expected frequency is the probability multiplied by the number of trials. For example, if a coin is tossed 200 times the expected number of heads is 200 × 0.5 = 100.

Worked example: drawing without replacement

A bag holds 3 red and 2 blue counters. Two counters are taken without replacement. P(red, red) = 3/5 × 2/4 = 3/10. P(blue, blue) = 2/5 × 1/4 = 1/10. P(one of each) = 1 − 3/10 − 1/10 = 6/10 = 3/5. The probabilities of all the outcomes must add up to 1, so use this as a check.

With replacement and at least one

If the first counter is replaced, the second draw has the same probabilities. P(at least one red) is quicker through the complement: 1 − P(no red) = 1 − (2/5 × 2/5) = 21/25. Use the complement whenever the phrase "at least one" appears.

Mutually exclusive and independent events

  • Mutually exclusive events cannot both happen, so P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B).
  • Independent events do not affect each other, so P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B). Test independence by checking whether P(A and B) equals this product.
  • Probabilities always lie between 0 and 1 inclusive. An answer outside this range signals an error.

Exam point: give probabilities as exact fractions unless the question asks for a decimal, and round only the final answer, to the accuracy the question requests.

title: Coordinate Geometry — Study Notes
content:
Coordinate Geometry

Gradients and Equations of Lines

Gradient m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁). From ax + by + c = 0, the gradient is −a/b.

Point-slope form: y − y₁ = m(x − x₁).

Example: through (4, 3) with m = −1/2: y − 3 = −(x − 4)/2, i.e. y = −x/2 + 5.

Parallel and Perpendicular

  • Parallel lines: equal gradients.
  • Perpendicular lines: m₁m₂ = −1 (gradients are negative reciprocals).

Example: perpendicular to y = 2x + 1 has gradient −1/2.

Midpoint and Distance

Midpoint of (x₁, y₁), (x₂, y₂): ((x₁+x₂)/2, (y₁+y₂)/2).

Distance: √((x₂−x₁)² + (y₂−y₁)²). The line from (0,0) to (3,4) has length 5 — recognise 3-4-5 triangles.

Intersections and Bisectors

Intersections: solve the equations simultaneously. The perpendicular bisector of AB passes through the midpoint of AB with gradient −1/m(AB) — equate distances PA = PB for the locus method.

Exam tips: rationalise gradients as fractions; check perpendicularity by multiplying gradients to get −1.

Key results and exam method

Distance between (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂) is √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²). The midpoint is ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2). The gradient is (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁); a vertical line has no gradient and a horizontal line has gradient 0.

Parallel lines have equal gradients. Perpendicular lines have gradients m₁ and m₂ with m₁m₂ = −1, so a line perpendicular to gradient 3/4 has gradient −4/3. The perpendicular bisector of a chord passes through the midpoint of the chord, is perpendicular to it, and always passes through the centre of the circle.

A circle with centre (a, b) and radius r has equation (x − a)² + (y − b)² = r². Expand and compare with x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 to read the centre (−g, −f) and the radius √(g² + f² − c). To test whether a line meets a circle, substitute the line into the circle equation and examine the discriminant.

Exam cue: Sketch the situation first. Many marks are for stating which point is the midpoint, which gradient is perpendicular, and which radius is used.

title: Edexcel IAL Computer Science: Data Types, Records and Arrays
content:
Edexcel IAL Computer Science: Data Types, Records and Arrays

Pearson Edexcel International Advanced Level in Computer Science, Unit 2 Practical Programming and Problem Solving: data types and records, and arrays. Choosing how data is represented decides what code can do with it — so this note follows each structure from declaration through memory layout to the algorithms that use it, with every index and pointer traced on a drawn memory diagram.

Primitive data types

TypeValuesOperationsWatch for
INTEGERWhole numbers in a fixed rangeArithmetic, comparisonOverflow at range limits
REAL/FLOATApproximate decimalsArithmeticRounding error; equality tests unreliable
CHAROne symbolComparison by code'A' ≠ 'a' in ASCII
STRINGSequences of charactersConcatenation, slicing, length, searchImmutable in Python; indexing from 0
BOOLEANTRUE / FALSEAND, OR, NOTTruthiness of 0 and ""
DATE/TIMECalendar valuesComparison, differenceTime zones and formats

Type casting: int→float widening is exact; float→int truncates (7.9 → 7) unless rounded; string→number raises errors on bad input (hence validation first); char→int yields the character code. Python's dynamic typing assigns without declaration, but the underlying values still have types — the difference between language convenience and data semantics is examinable.

Records

An array groups values of one type; a record groups values of different types describing one entity. A student record: {studentID: STRING, name: STRING, mark: INTEGER, isEnrolled: BOOLEAN}. Records give structure and meaning; fields are accessed by name, eliminating the "which index was the mark?" problem.

Memory view of one student record:

  +-----------+--------+------+------------+
  | studentID | name   | mark | isEnrolled |
  +-----------+--------+------+------------+
  | "S1024"   | "Chen" |  72  |    TRUE    |
  +-----------+--------+------+------------+

A file of records is the same shape repeated: each line/record one student -
the bridge between in-memory structures and file organisation (covered in
depth at A2).

Python dictionaries play the record role:
  student = {"studentID": "S1024", "name": "Chen", "mark": 72}
  student["mark"] = 75         # field update by name
  if student["mark"] >= 70: ...

Strings as character arrays

A string is conceptually an array of characters, so every array operation has a string analogue: indexing (name[0] is the first character), traversal (examining each character), searching (finding a substring), and length. String-specific operations the exam expects: concatenation, slicing, case conversion, and comparison by character code. Python immutability matters here — methods like upper() return new strings rather than modifying the original — and off-by-one errors appear in slicing (s[2:5] gives characters at indices 2, 3 and 4, not 5). Converting between characters and their codes (ord('A') = 65, chr(66) = 'B') links this note back to the representation work in Unit 1.

Array algorithms in full

Four operations cover most exam questions, and each has a cost worth stating. Traverse: visit every slot once — O(n), one loop. Search: linear search compares each slot until a match (O(n)); on sorted arrays, binary search halves the remaining range each comparison (O(log n)) — examined fully at A2. Sort: ordering an array (bubble, insertion, selection) so search and output are possible. Aggregate: count, sum, min, max, mean — one pass with a running value. Each pattern is a loop with a purpose; the trace table is the proof.

Arrays: declaration, indexing and processing

An array reserves a contiguous block, one slot per index, accessed in constant time. Declaration fixes the size and element type; index conventions matter (pseudocode often 0..n−1 or 1..n — always state which). Standard patterns: traverse, search, insert, delete, and compute aggregates.

Array of 6 marks, 0-based, after filling:

  index:  0    1    2    3    4    5
  value: 55   72   41   68   90   55

Linear search for 68 - every step:
  i=0: marks[0]=55, not 68
  i=1: marks[1]=72, not 68
  i=2: marks[2]=41, not 68
  i=3: marks[3]=68 - found; return index 3 (and stop)

  Worst case: searching for a value not present walks all 6 slots - n
  comparisons for n items: O(n). (Complexity is examined fully at A2.)

Counting above the pass mark - aggregate pattern:
  count = 0
  for i in range(6):
      if marks[i] >= 50:
          count += 1
  # trace: i=0:55 yes (1); i=1:72 yes (2); i=2:41 no; i=3:68 yes (3);
  #        i=4:90 yes (4); i=5:55 yes (5) -> count = 5

Insert shifting (insert 60 at position 2): shift elements right from the end -
  [55, 72, 41, 68, 90] -> [55, 72, 60, 41, 68] with 90 dropped if full.
  Deleting at position 1 shifts left: [55, 60, 41, 68] - O(n) moves either way.

Bounds and traps: marks[6] on the array above is out of range (undefined behaviour in many languages; Python raises IndexError); an array is fixed size in classic languages (overflow/underflow on insert/delete), while Python lists are dynamic. Two-dimensional arrays are grids: declaration ARRAY[0:3, 0:2] gives 4 rows × 3 columns; a value needs both indices — board[row][col] — and traversal nests a loop within a loop.

2D array worked: seating plan 3 rows x 4 columns, mark every empty seat.

  seats = [[0, 1, 0, 0],
           [1, 1, 0, 1],
           [0, 0, 0, 0]]

  empty = 0
  for row in range(3):
      for col in range(4):
          if seats[row][col] == 0:
              empty += 1
  # row 0: 3 empty; row 1: 1 empty; row 2: 4 empty -> empty = 8

Memory is linear (row-major: row 0's four cells, then row 1's...), which is
why nested loops traverse row by row.

Static versus dynamic structures

Static arrays: fixed size set at declaration, contiguous, fast indexed access, wasted or insufficient space decided in advance. Dynamic structures (Python lists, linked lists at A2) grow as needed with allocation overhead. Choosing: known fixed bounds and heavy indexing → static array; unpredictable growth and frequent inserts → dynamic. The exam wants the reason in terms of allocation and access cost.

Worked example: choosing a structure for three jobs.

1. Storing 30 daily temperatures with heavy day-by-day access:
   static array of 30 REALs - known size, constant-time indexed reads.

2. A task queue where items arrive and leave unpredictably:
   a dynamic structure (list or queue) - a fixed array would overflow.

3. Storing 200 employee records keyed by staff number:
   an array/FILE of records, or a dictionary - records give typed fields,
   a dictionary gives name-based access; sequential arrays suit batch
   processing, dictionaries suit lookups.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Off-by-one indices: an array declared [0:5] has six slots; a loop for i in range(6) covers exactly those.
  • Assuming the language's array bounds are checked; pseudocode questions want you to state the guard, not assume one.
  • Using float for money (rounding error) or equality tests on floats (use a tolerance).
  • Confusing records with arrays: uniform typed slots versus named mixed fields of one entity.
  • 2D indexing order: seats[row][col], and nested loops must match that order.
  • Forgetting that insertion/deletion in arrays shifts elements (O(n)) — cost statements earn marks.
  • Declaring a fixed array for data of unpredictable size without discussing the overflow risk.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Unit 2, 3 marks). Explain the difference between a record and an array.

Answer: An array stores multiple values of the same data type under one name, accessed by index — suited to lists of like values. A record groups fields of different types describing one entity (a student: string name, integer mark, boolean status), accessed by field name. Arrays suit collections; records suit entities.

Question 2 (Unit 2, 4 marks). An array holds 5 values at indices 1–5. Describe what happens when a value is inserted at index 2.

Answer: To make room, elements at indices 5 down to 2 are each shifted one position up (5→6 slot if space, else the last is lost in fixed arrays); the new value is written at index 2. The operation takes O(n) moves, and a bounds check must confirm the array is not full before shifting.

Question 3 (Unit 2, 4 marks). Write pseudocode to find the smallest value in an array of 100 numbers and explain the role of the first element.

Answer: smallest <- numbers[1]; FOR i <- 2 TO 100; IF numbers[i] < smallest THEN; smallest <- numbers[i]; ENDIF; NEXT i; OUTPUT smallest. Initialising smallest with the first element guarantees a real value from the array is the starting benchmark (initialising with 0 would fail for all-negative data).

Question 4 (Unit 2, 3 marks). Explain two differences between static and dynamic data structures.

Answer: A static structure's size is fixed at declaration — memory is reserved once, giving fast indexed access but overflow risk or wasted space. A dynamic structure grows and shrinks during execution by allocating memory as needed — flexible for unpredictable data volumes, at the cost of allocation overhead and (for linked structures) slower indexed access.

Question 5 (Unit 2, 4 marks). Describe how a 2D array could represent a noughts-and-crosses board and how a win is checked.

Answer: A 3×3 array stores each cell's state (empty, X, O), addressed board[row][col]. A win check tests the eight lines: three rows (board[0][0]=board[0][1]=board[0][2], etc.), three columns, and two diagonals — each test comparing three cells for equality and not-empty.

Question 6 (Unit 2, 3 marks). Explain why money should not be stored in a float variable.

Answer: Binary floating point cannot represent many decimal fractions exactly (0.1 has no finite binary expansion), so repeated arithmetic accumulates rounding error and balance checks drift out. Money is stored as integer minor units (pence) or a decimal type, with rounding rules applied explicitly at defined points.

Records in files are the raw material of information systems; the next note shows how databases organise them at scale.

title: Energy, Work & Power — Study Notes
content:
Energy, Work & Power

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): stores and transfers, KE/PE, work, energy sources, power, efficiency.

1. Energy stores & transfers

Stores: kinetic, gravitational, elastic, chemical, nuclear, thermal. Transfer mechanisms: mechanically, electrically, heating, waves. Energy is conserved overall; transfers via work done.

2. Formulas

  • KE = ½mv²; PE = mgh.
  • Work W = Fd (force along displacement, joules).
  • Power P = W/t = E/t; P = Fv for constant speed.

Example: 0.5 kg at 4 m/s: KE = 4 J. Lift 2 kg by 3 m: PE = 60 J (g = 10).

3. Energy sources

Renewable: solar, wind, hydro, geothermal, biofuel, tidal — replenished. Non-renewable: fossil fuels, nuclear — finite. Discuss reliability, cost, pollution for "evaluate" questions.

4. Efficiency

Efficiency = useful output ÷ total input (×100%). Sankey diagrams show losses.

Example: motor: 150 J useful from 600 J → 25%.

5. Energy-chain problems

Equating KE loss to PE gain: v = √(2gh) for frictionless drop; braking distance grows with v².

Exam tips: define work as "force × distance moved in the direction of the force"; use g = 10 unless told otherwise; efficiency is a ratio — no units.

Work, power and energy transfer

Work is done when a force moves an object through a distance in the direction of the force, W = Fd, measured in joules. Power is the rate of doing work, P = W/t, measured in watts. Energy is conserved: it is transferred from one store to another, and the total stays the same. The efficiency of a device is the useful energy output as a percentage of the total energy input, and it is always less than 100 percent.

Kinetic energy is ½mv², and gravitational potential energy is mgh, which is the energy a mass gains when it is raised through height h near the Earth's surface.

Exam tip: show the energy store changes in order, for example chemical to kinetic to thermal, when a question asks you to describe energy transfer.

title: Exam technique: Data Structures
content:
### What earns the marks
For structure choice, justify earns marks for matching the type mix to the structure: mixed fields need records, many same-type values need arrays. For stacks and queues, the operation order stated (LIFO vs FIFO) earns the method mark before any trace. For 2D arrays, the inclusive bounds multiplied earn the count mark.
### Traps
Error: plain arrays for name-plus-score records. Correction: one data type per array; mix needs composite type. Error: dequeuing from the rear. Correction: queues leave from the front. Error: counting Array[1:8] as nine per dimension. Correction: inclusive bounds give eight.

title: IGCSE Mathematics: Trig Graphs, Sine and Cosine Rules
content:
IGCSE Mathematics: Trig Graphs, Sine and Cosine Rules

Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580 (2025–2027), section 6 Trigonometry, Extended statements E6.4 Trigonometric functions (the graphs of sine, cosine and tangent over 0° to 360°, and solving trigonometric equations) and E6.5 Non-right-angled triangles (the sine rule, the cosine rule and the area formula ½ab sin C). The right-angled toolkit SOH CAH TOA only works when a right angle is present; these are the tools that work for every triangle. The note also covers the bearing and three-dimensional applications that appear in Paper 4, with every worked example fully recalculated.

From right-angled ratios to any angle

In a right-angled triangle, sin θ = opposite/hypotenuse, cos θ = adjacent/hypotenuse and tan θ = opposite/adjacent. The graphs in this note extend those definitions to every angle from 0° to 360°, which is what makes them useful for waves, rotating objects and periodic motion later in the course. The exact values to know by heart:

Anglesincostan
0°010
30°1/2√3/21/√3
45°√2/2√2/21
60°√3/21/2√3
90°10undefined

These come from two triangles worth knowing: the half-equilateral (30°–60°–90° with sides 1, √3, 2) and the isosceles right triangle (45°–45°–90° with sides 1, 1, √2).

The trigonometric graphs, 0° to 360°

  • y = sin x starts at 0, rises to 1 at 90°, falls through 0 at 180°, to −1 at 270°, and back to 0 at 360°. It is a wave, maximum 1 and minimum −1.
  • y = cos x is the sine wave shifted: it starts at 1, falls through 0 at 90°, to −1 at 180°, through 0 at 270°, back to 1 at 360°.
  • y = tan x is 0 at 0° and 180° and 360°, rises steeply towards +∞ just before 90°, and comes from −∞ just after 90°; it has vertical asymptotes at 90° and 270° because cos x = 0 there and tan = sin/cos.

The symmetries behind solving equations:

sin x = sin (180° - x)        e.g. sin 40° = sin 140°
cos x = -cos (180° - x)       e.g. cos 60° = -cos 120°
cos x = cos (360° - x)        e.g. cos 40° = cos 320°

Solving trigonometric equations. Find the first solution from the calculator or the exact-value table, then use the symmetry to find the others in 0° ⩽ x ⩽ 360°:

Solve sin x = 0.5 for 0° ⩽ x ⩽ 360°:

First solution: x = 30° (from the exact values)
Sine is positive in the first and second quadrants, so the second solution is
x = 180° - 30° = 150°
Answers: x = 30° and x = 150°
Solve 2 cos x + 1 = 0 for 0° ⩽ x ⩽ 360°:

2 cos x = -1
cos x = -1/2
First solution: x = 120° (cosine is negative in the second quadrant; cos 60° = 1/2)
Cosine is also negative in the third quadrant: x = 360° - 120° = 240°
Answers: x = 120° and x = 240°

A sketch of the graph before solving is the safest habit: it shows how many answers to expect, which is exactly what examiners check for.

Area of a triangle: ½ab sin C

The familiar area formula is ½ × base × height. For a triangle with sides a and b and included angle C, the height above base b is a sin C (from SOH in the right-angled triangle formed by the height), so:

area = 1/2 x a x b x sin C
  • a, b: the two known sides, in any units as long as both match; C: the angle between those two sides, in degrees; area: in the square of the side units.
Worked example: a = 8 cm, b = 5 cm, C = 48°:

area = 1/2 x 8 x 5 x sin 48°
     = 20 x 0.7431        [sin 48° = 0.7431 to 4 d.p.]
     = 14.86 cm^2  ≈ 14.9 cm^2 (3 s.f.)

The angle must be the included one; using a non-included angle gives a different (wrong) triangle.

The sine rule

For any triangle with sides a, b, c opposite angles A, B, C:

a / sin A = b / sin B = c / sin C

or, when looking for an angle:  sin A / a = sin B / b = sin C / c

Use it when you know a matching side–angle pair (a side and the angle opposite it) plus one other item. It generalises SOH CAH TOA to triangles without a right angle.

Worked example: A = 40°, a = 7 cm, B = 65°. Find b.

a / sin A = b / sin B
7 / sin 40° = b / sin 65°
b = 7 x sin 65° / sin 40°
  = 7 x 0.9063 / 0.6428      [4 d.p. values]
  = 6.3441 / 0.6428
  = 9.87 cm (3 s.f.)

The ambiguous case. When you know two sides and an angle that is not between them (SSA), the triangle may not be unique: if the given angle is acute and the opposite side is shorter than the other side but longer than the perpendicular distance, there are two possible triangles. Since sin θ = sin (180° − θ), the calculator's answer θ may need supplementing with 180° − θ. Check both candidates against the angle sum of 180° before accepting them.

The cosine rule

For any triangle with sides a, b, c and angle A opposite side a:

a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2 b c cos A
rearranged for an angle:  cos A = (b^2 + c^2 - a^2) / (2 b c)

Use it when you know SAS (two sides and the included angle) or SSS (all three sides). It is the general form of Pythagoras: with A = 90°, cos 90° = 0 and the formula collapses to a² = b² + c².

Worked example (SAS): b = 7 cm, c = 5 cm, A = 52°. Find a.

a^2 = 7^2 + 5^2 - 2 x 7 x 5 x cos 52°
    = 49 + 25 - 70 x 0.6157        [cos 52° = 0.6157 to 4 d.p.]
    = 74 - 43.10
    = 30.90
a = √30.90 = 5.56 cm (3 s.f.)
Worked example (SSS): a = 8 cm, b = 5 cm, c = 7 cm. Find angle B.

cos B = (a^2 + c^2 - b^2) / (2 a c)
      = (64 + 49 - 25) / (2 x 8 x 7)
      = 88 / 112
      = 0.7857
B = cos^(-1)(0.7857) = 38.2° (3 s.f.)

The rule never fails for a valid triangle, and the angle found is always the one opposite the side that appears alone with the minus sign.

Bearings and multi-step problems

A bearing is measured clockwise from north, written as three figures (070°, 150°). The method: draw both north lines (they are parallel), transfer angles using parallel-line facts (alternate angles are equal), then choose the sine or cosine rule for the triangle formed.

Worked example: from a port Q, a ship sails 60 km on a bearing of 070° to P,
then 45 km on a bearing of 150° to R. Find the distance PR.

Both legs start at Q, so the angle at Q between them is the difference of the
bearings: angle PQR = 150° - 070° = 80° (draw the north line at Q and measure
clockwise to each leg; the angle inside the triangle is the gap between them).
PR^2 = 60^2 + 45^2 - 2 x 60 x 45 x cos 80°        [cosine rule at angle Q]
     = 3600 + 2025 - 5400 x 0.1736
     = 5625 - 937.7
     = 4687.3
PR = 68.5 km (3 s.f.)

The 3-D extension uses the same toolkit: a space diagonal has length d = √(x² + y² + z²), and the angle between a line and a plane is found by projecting the line onto the plane and solving the right-angled triangle that remains. Sketch the relevant 2-D triangle separately — that is the step most answers skip and most marks follow.

Worked example: choosing the right rule

In triangle PQR, PQ = 5 cm, PR = 8 cm and angle QPR = 60°. Find QR and the area.

QR is opposite the known angle 60° with the two other sides known (SAS):
QR^2 = 8^2 + 5^2 - 2 x 8 x 5 x cos 60°
     = 64 + 25 - 80 x 0.5        [cos 60° = 0.5]
     = 89 - 40
     = 49
QR = 7 cm exactly.

Area = 1/2 x 8 x 5 x sin 60° = 20 x 0.8660 = 17.3 cm^2 (3 s.f.)

Note the exact answer: when the numbers conspire, the square root is whole and leaving it as √49 would be an incomplete answer. Now find angle PQR with the sine rule: sin Q / 8 = sin 60° / 7 gives sin Q = 8 × 0.8660/7 = 0.9897, so Q = 81.8° or 98.2° (ambiguous case); the cosine rule resolves it: cos Q = (25 + 49 − 64)/(2 × 5 × 7) = 10/70 = 0.1429, so Q = 81.8°.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Using the sine rule without a matched pair: you need a side and the angle opposite it; otherwise use the cosine rule.
  • Forgetting the ambiguous case: two triangles may satisfy the data when two sides and a non-included angle are given — check both.
  • Mixing degrees and calculator mode: the calculator must be in degrees mode, and answers should be given to 3 s.f. unless told otherwise.
  • Losing a minus sign in the cosine rule: a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A; for an obtuse angle cos A is negative, which makes the side longer, and an answer that contradicts that is a sign slip.
  • Using ½ab sin C with a non-included angle; C must be the angle between a and b.
  • Writing bearings without three figures (070°, not 70°) or measuring anticlockwise.
  • Rounding intermediate values too early; keep 4+ d.p. through the working and round only the final answer.
  • Reading sin⁻¹ as 1/sin; it is the inverse function giving an angle from a ratio.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 2, 4 marks). Solve cos x = 0.6 for 0° ⩽ x ⩽ 360°.

Answer: First solution x = 53.1° (3 s.f.). Cosine is positive in the first and fourth quadrants, so the second is x = 360° − 53.1° = 306.9°. Answers: 53.1° and 306.9°.

Question 2 (Paper 2, 3 marks). Sketch y = sin x for 0° ⩽ x ⩽ 360° and state its maximum and minimum.

Answer: A wave starting at (0, 0), peaking at (90°, 1), crossing (180°, 0), bottoming at (270°, −1), ending at (360°, 0). Maximum 1, minimum −1.

Question 3 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Triangle ABC has AB = 9 cm, AC = 7 cm and angle BAC = 50°. Find BC.

Answer: Cosine rule: BC² = 9² + 7² − 2 × 9 × 7 × cos 50° = 81 + 49 − 126 × 0.6428 = 130 − 81.0 = 49.0, so BC = 7.0 cm (3 s.f.).

Question 4 (Paper 4, 4 marks). In triangle PQR, angle P = 30°, angle Q = 105° and PR = 12 cm. Find QR.

Answer: Angle R = 45°. By the sine rule, QR/sin 30° = 12/sin 45°, so QR = 12 × 0.5/0.7071 = 8.49 cm (3 s.f.).

Question 5 (Paper 4, 4 marks). A triangle has sides 6 cm, 8 cm and 11 cm. Find its area.

Answer: Find the angle between two known sides first. cos C = (36 + 64 − 121)/(2 × 6 × 8) = −21/96 = −0.2188, so C = 102.6°. Area = ½ × 6 × 8 × sin 102.6° = 24 × 0.9763 = 23.4 cm² (3 s.f.).

Question 6 (Paper 4, 5 marks). A boat sails 2.8 km due south from a point A to a point B. A lighthouse L is 4.2 km from A on a bearing of 120°. Find the distance BL and the bearing of the lighthouse from B.

Answer: At A the due-south direction is bearing 180°, so angle BAL = 180° − 120° = 60°. Cosine rule: BL² = 2.8² + 4.2² − 2 × 2.8 × 4.2 × cos 60° = 7.84 + 17.64 − 11.76 = 13.72, so BL = 3.70 km (3 s.f.). For the bearing, find angle ABL: cos B = (2.8² + 13.72 − 17.64)/(2 × 2.8 × 3.704) = 3.92/20.74 = 0.1890, so B = 79.1°. Since B is due south of A, the direction from B to A is due north, and the lighthouse lies east of that line, so its bearing from B is 079° (3 s.f.).

Angles and sides are the language of shape; the next note measures those shapes — area, volume and mensuration.

title: IGCSE Computer Science: Hardware and Architecture
content:
IGCSE Computer Science: Hardware and Architecture

Cambridge IGCSE Computer Science 0478 (2026–2028), Paper 1 Computer Systems, Topic 3 Hardware: statement 3.1 Computer architecture, 3.2 Input and output devices, and 3.3 Data storage. This is where the physical machine is opened up: what a CPU actually does with machine code, how instructions and data travel around the system, and how storage technologies differ. Every fetch–execute cycle below is traced register by register, because Paper 1 routinely asks you to follow the cycle through a memory dump — and that question is free marks once you have traced it a dozen times.

Hardware, firmware and software: the layers

Before the parts, the big picture — and the analogy that makes the whole topic click. A computer system is a factory. The hardware is the building and machines (physical, touchable). The software is the list of orders the factory must carry out (instructions, intangible). Firmware is software permanently etched into a chip — like the safety rules bolted to the wall: it survives a power cut and tells the hardware how to start. The operating system is the factory manager, deciding which order runs when and which machine each order may use.

The stored-program concept and Von Neumann architecture

Early machines had to be rewired for every new task. The breakthrough of the stored-program concept is that both the instructions and the data they work on live in the same memory, and the CPU reads instructions from memory and obeys them — no rewiring. In the chef analogy: the recipe (program) and the ingredients (data) sit on the same kitchen shelf; the chef fetches a recipe line, does what it says to the ingredients, and moves to the next line.

Von Neumann architecture is the standard layout built on that idea:

  • CPU — the processor, containing the control unit (CU), the arithmetic logic unit (ALU) and registers.
  • Main memory — RAM (and ROM), holding both program instructions and data.
  • Input and output devices — the system's contact with the outside world.
  • Buses — the cables connecting them: address, data and control.

Its famous weakness is the Von Neumann bottleneck: instructions and data share one memory and one set of buses, so the CPU can fetch only one thing at a time and spends much of its cycle waiting. Caches, pipelining and multiple cores exist largely to hide that bottleneck.

Inside the CPU

The control unit fetches and decodes instructions and orchestrates the rest of the machine; it is the foreman. The ALU performs arithmetic (add, subtract, multiply, divide) and logic (comparisons, AND/OR/NOT); it is the workbench. Registers are tiny, extremely fast storage locations inside the CPU — the foreman's desk, where the handful of items being worked on right now are kept.

RegisterFull nameWhat it holds
PCProgram counterThe memory address of the next instruction to fetch
MARMemory address registerThe address currently being read from or written to
MDRMemory data register (also called MBR)The data or instruction just fetched, or about to be written
CIRCurrent instruction registerThe instruction being decoded and executed
ACCAccumulatorThe result of the last ALU calculation

The clock paces the CPU: each tick synchronises one step, and the clock speed (measured in GHz) is the number of ticks per second. Cache is small, very fast memory inside or beside the CPU holding copies of recently used data and instructions — a cache hit saves a slow trip to RAM. Cores are independent processing units; more cores mean more instructions can be completed simultaneously, provided the software is written to use them.

The buses

BusDirectionCarriesWidth matters because
Address busCPU to memory/peripherals (one-way)Memory addressesMore address lines mean more memory can be addressed (n lines address 2ⁿ locations)
Data busBoth waysInstructions and dataMore lines mean more bits per transfer, so wider = faster
Control busBoth waysSignals: read, write, clock, interrupt, resetCoordinates who does what and when

The fetch–decode–execute cycle

Every program is a list of instructions in memory, and the CPU runs them one at a time in a repeating three-stage cycle. Fetch: get the instruction. Decode: work out what it means. Execute: do it. Then the cycle repeats — millions of times per second.

Memory holds addresses like a street of numbered houses. Suppose memory looks like this before the program runs:

Address   Contents   Meaning
  5       0010 1000  LOAD 8        (copy the value at address 8 into the ACC)
  6       0011 1001  ADD 9         (add the value at address 9 to the ACC)
  7       0100 1010  STORE 10      (copy the ACC into address 10)
  8       0000 0101  the value 5
  9       0000 0011  the value 3
 10       0000 0000  (empty)

Trace the whole run, register by register. The first two bits of each instruction are the opcode (the operation) and the remaining six bits are the operand (the address to work on).

Cycle 1 - FETCH of LOAD 8:
  PC = 5. The PC's value is copied to the MAR: MAR = 5.
  The control bus sends a READ signal; memory returns the contents of address 5.
  The instruction arrives in the MDR: MDR = 0010 1000.
  The MDR's value is copied to the CIR: CIR = 0010 1000. PC is incremented: PC = 6.
Cycle 1 - DECODE:
  The control unit reads the opcode 00 = LOAD: copy the value at the operand address to the ACC.
Cycle 1 - EXECUTE:
  The operand is 01 1000 = address 8. MAR = 8; READ; MDR = 0000 0101 (the value 5).
  ACC = 5.

Cycle 2 - FETCH of ADD 9:
  PC = 6 -> MAR = 6; READ; MDR = 0011 1001; CIR = 0011 1001; PC = 7.
Cycle 2 - DECODE:
  Opcode 01 = ADD: add the value at the operand address to the ACC.
Cycle 2 - EXECUTE:
  Operand 01 1001 = address 9. MAR = 9; READ; MDR = 0000 0011 (the value 3).
  ALU computes ACC + MDR = 5 + 3 = 8. ACC = 8.

Cycle 3 - FETCH of STORE 10:
  PC = 7 -> MAR = 7; READ; MDR = 0100 1010; CIR = 0100 1010; PC = 8.
Cycle 3 - DECODE:
  Opcode 10 = STORE: copy the ACC into the operand address.
Cycle 3 - EXECUTE:
  Operand 01 1010 = address 10. MAR = 10; MDR = 8 (from the ACC); a WRITE signal
  stores it. Address 10 now holds 0000 1000. The program stops (STOP instruction).

Notice the pattern examiners look for: PC → MAR → (READ) → MDR → CIR for the fetch, PC incremented after the fetch, and the execute stage differing per opcode. An interrupt (a signal from a device demanding attention, like a keypress or timer) pauses the cycle between instructions: the CPU finishes the current instruction, saves the PC, jumps to an interrupt service routine, then returns.

What makes a processor faster

  • More clock cycles per second (GHz) — each instruction is paced by the clock; more ticks per second means more instructions per second, other things equal.
  • More cores — several CPUs on one chip work on different tasks simultaneously.
  • Larger cache — more of the working data sits close to the CPU, so fewer slow RAM accesses.
  • Wider data bus — more bits move per transfer.
  • Instruction set — the set of operations a CPU understands. RISC processors use few simple instructions, each executed in one clock cycle; CISC processors have many complex instructions, each taking several cycles but needing fewer instructions per task. Say what the difference does: fewer cycles per instruction versus fewer instructions per task.
Worked example: a processor runs at 2.0 GHz and each instruction takes 4 cycles.

2.0 GHz = 2.0 x 10^9 cycles per second
instructions per second = 2.0 x 10^9 / 4 = 5.0 x 10^8

So 500 million instructions per second. Clock speed alone is not the whole story:
a 2.0 GHz CPU needing 4 cycles per instruction matches a 4.0 GHz CPU needing 8.

Embedded systems

An embedded system is a processor built into a device to run one dedicated task — the microcontroller in a washing machine, engine management unit, microwave, traffic light or digital camera. Characteristics: single function, small and cheap, low power, often real-time (must respond within a deadline), and rarely updated. Advantages: low cost, compact, reliable, energy-efficient. Disadvantages: inflexible, hard to upgrade or repair, and a bug affects the whole appliance. The exam wants the trade-off stated, not just a list of examples.

Input and output devices

DeviceTypeTypical use and why it suits it
KeyboardInputEntering text and commands quickly and accurately
Mouse / touchscreenInputDirect graphical manipulation; touchscreens suit kiosks where space or hygiene matters
Scanner / cameraInputDigitising documents and images; OCR software then reads the text
Sensors (temperature, light, pressure, moisture)InputAutomatic measurement in control systems — greenhouses, weather stations, car engines
MicrophoneInputSound capture for recording and voice input
Monitor / projectorOutputVisual display; projectors for audiences, monitors for detail
Printer / plotterOutputHard copy; plotters for large-scale technical drawings
Speakers / headphonesOutputSound reproduction
Actuators (motors, heaters, valves, robotic arms)OutputPhysical action in control systems — the hands of an automated system

The sensor–processor–actuator loop is the heart of every automated system: a sensor measures the world, the microprocessor compares the reading with a target, and the actuator changes the world. Choosing a device is always justified by accuracy, speed, cost and environment.

Primary storage: RAM and ROM

RAMROM
VolatilityVolatile — contents lost on power offNon-volatile — contents survive power off
Read/writeBoth, constantlyRead only (written at manufacture or by special processes)
HoldsThe running OS, open programs and their dataBootstrap/firmware: the start-up instructions that load the OS
Speed/sizeFast, measured in GBFast, but small (MB)

Virtual memory extends RAM by reserving space on the secondary storage device: when RAM fills, less-active pages are swapped to disk. It prevents crashes but is slow, because secondary storage is far slower than RAM — thrashing (constant swapping) can make a machine crawl.

Secondary storage: magnetic, optical and solid state

MediumHow it storesStrengthsWeaknesses
Magnetic (HDD, tape)Magnetised regions on spinning platters or tape, read by headsVery cheap per GB, huge capacityMoving parts: slower, noisy, shock-sensitive; tape is sequential access only
Optical (CD, DVD, Blu-ray)Pits and lands burned by laser, read by reflected lightCheap, portable, long shelf life, good for archiving and distributionLow capacity, slower write speeds, easily scratched
Solid state (SSD, USB flash, memory cards)Electrical charges in NAND flash cellsVery fast, silent, robust (no moving parts), low powerMore expensive per GB, finite number of write cycles

Compare on the four axes examiners name: capacity, speed (access and transfer), cost per GB, durability and portability. Choose by use case — an SSD for video editing, an HDD for a media archive, flash for a phone, optical for distributing software.

Cloud storage keeps data on remote servers reached over a network: accessible anywhere, easy to back up and share, with storage that scales without new hardware. Against that: it needs a connection, costs ongoing fees, gives slower access than local storage, and raises privacy and security concerns because data leaves your control. Local storage is fast and offline but vulnerable to loss or theft and limited by device capacity — most systems use both.

Worked example: choosing storage and reading a memory dump

A school records 200 hours of video per year at 1 GB per hour and wants 5 years of archive with daily access, plus backups.

Capacity needed: 200 x 1 x 5 = 1000 GB (about 1 TB), plus backup = 2 TB.

HDD: about £45 per TB, random access for daily retrieval, but a mechanical drive
     is the weak point - keep the backup on a second drive or in the cloud.
SSD: faster and more robust but roughly three times the cost per TB.
Optical: about 25 GB per disc - 80 discs for the archive, sequential retrieval
     only - impractical for daily access.
Cloud: no hardware to fail and off-site backup included, but 2 TB of storage
     for 5 years is an ongoing subscription and every retrieval needs the network.

Choice: working copies on an SSD, archive on one or two HDDs, plus cloud backup.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Saying the fetch stage "executes" the instruction. Fetch retrieves; decode interprets; execute acts — and the PC is incremented during the fetch stage, not the execute stage.
  • Confusing the MAR and the MDR: the MAR holds the address being accessed; the MDR holds the data travelling to or from it.
  • Claiming RAM is permanent because the computer "remembers" files; files live on secondary storage — RAM is volatile.
  • Describing the address bus as two-way; only the data bus is two-way.
  • Listing performance factors without effects: "it has cache" earns nothing; "a larger cache means more data is found without slow RAM access" earns the mark.
  • Calling a sensor an output device; sensors input data, actuators output action.
  • Writing that virtual memory "increases RAM"; it borrows secondary storage and is slower — it prevents out-of-memory failures, not slowness.
  • Forgetting units in capacity calculations (GB vs TB) or mixing up bytes and bits — the classic file-size question trap.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 1, 3 marks). State the purpose of the program counter and the memory address register in the fetch–execute cycle.

Answer: The program counter holds the address of the next instruction to be fetched, so the CPU knows where to look in memory; it is incremented after the fetch. The memory address register holds the address currently being accessed (read from or written to) during the cycle.

Question 2 (Paper 1, 4 marks). Describe what happens to the MDR and CIR during the fetch stage.

Answer: The address in the MAR is sent down the address bus with a READ control signal; memory returns the instruction or data at that address into the memory data register (MDR). The MDR's contents are then copied into the current instruction register (CIR), where the control unit decodes them.

Question 3 (Paper 1, 6 marks). Compare magnetic and solid-state secondary storage for a laptop used for field research.

Answer: Solid state has no moving parts, so it is far more resistant to shock and drops (vital in the field), silent, lighter and much faster, and uses less battery. Against that it costs more per gigabyte and wears out after many write cycles. Magnetic drives offer far more capacity per pound but their spinning platters and heads are damaged by knocks, they are slower and heavier. For field research, robustness and battery life dominate, so solid state is the better choice.

Question 4 (Paper 1, 4 marks). Explain what an embedded system is and give two advantages of using one in a washing machine.

Answer: An embedded system is a processor built into a device to perform one dedicated task, running firmware rather than a general-purpose OS. In a washing machine it is cheap to mass-produce, small enough to fit inside the appliance, low-power, and reliable because there is no general-purpose software to fail — the machine does its one job well and quickly boots each time.

Question 5 (Paper 1, 5 marks). A CPU runs at 3.0 GHz and averages 5 cycles per instruction. Calculate its instruction rate and explain why a 2.0 GHz CPU with 2 cycles per instruction could be faster.

Answer: 3.0 × 10⁹ cycles/second ÷ 5 = 6.0 × 10⁸ instructions per second. The 2.0 GHz CPU gives 2.0 × 10⁹ ÷ 2 = 1.0 × 10⁹ instructions per second — higher despite the lower clock, because instructions per second depends on both clock speed and cycles per instruction, not clock speed alone.

Question 6 (Paper 1, 3 marks). Explain the purpose of virtual memory and one disadvantage of using it.

Answer: When RAM is full, the operating system moves less-active programs and data to a reserved area of secondary storage (the swap file), freeing RAM so programs keep running instead of crashing. Disadvantage: secondary storage is far slower than RAM, so swapping causes noticeable slowdowns — especially thrashing, where the system spends its time swapping rather than working.

With the machine understood at the hardware level, the next question is how it represents everything it knows: data representation.

title:
Coordination, Response and Gene Technology — Quick Revision Summary

Biology — Edexcel IAL A2, WBI14 Unit 4 Topic 8. Nervous system structure and function (sensory, relay and motor neurones, myelination and saltatory conduction, the action potential, the spinal reflex arc and grey/white matter, synapses and acetylcholine, the pupillary reflex); drugs and nerve transmission (nicotine, lidocaine, cobra venom alpha toxin, L-DOPA and Parkinson’s disease, MDMA); light detection by rod cells (rhodopsin, opsin, retinal, sodium channels, hyperpolarisation, action potentials in the optic neurone); habituation (animal model, the evidence, the synapse involved); the central and peripheral nervous systems; hormonal and nervous coordination compared; the brain (cerebral hemispheres, hypothalamus, pituitary gland, cerebellum, medulla oblongata) and its functions and imaging (MRI, fMRI, PET, CT); the role of dopamine in Parkinson’s disease and serotonin in depression and the drugs used; producing drugs from genetically modified organisms (human insulin from bacteria as the example); recombinant DNA — how it is made with restriction enzymes and DNA ligase and inserted into cells; microarrays for identifying active genes; what bioinformatics is; the risks and benefits of genetically modified organisms.

  • Neurones and myelination: sensory neurone — long dendron and long axon, cell body off to one side; relay neurone — short dendrites, cell body central; motor neurone — long axon, cell body in CNS, many short dendrites; Schwann cells wrap myelin around the axon; nodes of Ranvier are gaps; myelin speeds conduction.
  • Action potential: at threshold, voltage-gated sodium channels open, Na⁺ floods in — depolarisation to about +40 mV; then Na⁺ channels close and K⁺ channels open, K⁺ floods out — repolarisation; hyperpolarisation; the Na⁺/K⁺ pump restores resting potential; all-or-nothing; refractory period ensures one-way conduction and limits frequency.
  • Synapse (cholinergic): action potential opens Ca²⁺ channels in presynaptic terminal, Ca²⁺ enters, vesicles with acetylcholine (ACh) fuse and release ACh by exocytosis, ACh diffuses across cleft, binds to postsynaptic receptors, Na⁺ channels open, Na⁺ enters and depolarises; acetylcholinesterase breaks down ACh.
  • Pupil reflex: bright light — circular iris muscles contract, radial relax — pupil constricts; dim light — radial iris muscles contract, circular relax — pupil dilates.
  • Drugs on transmission: nicotine mimics ACh at nicotinic receptors (alertness, addictive, raises BP and HR); lidocaine blocks voltage-gated Na⁺ channels — local anaesthetic, no pain signal; cobra venom alpha toxin blocks ACh receptors — muscle paralysis; L-DOPA (Parkinson’s) crosses blood–brain barrier, converted to dopamine — eases tremor/stiffness/slowness; MDMA causes massive serotonin release and blocks reuptake — wellbeing/empathy then serotonin depletion and damage (depression, memory).
  • Rod cell and light detection: rhodopsin = opsin + retinal (vitamin A derivative); light → retinal changes shape (11-cis to all-trans) → opsin changes → rod cell hyperpolarises (more negative); this closes Na⁺ channels that are open in the dark, reduces neurotransmitter (glutamate) release; bipolar cell then optic neurone — action potentials generated in the optic neurone, sent to brain as vision; rods = dim light, cones = colour/detail in bright light.
  • Habituation: a decrease in response to a repeated harmless stimulus; snail withdrawal reflex to a tap — response slows and stops; not muscle fatigue (a new stimulus still produces a strong response) and not sensory adaptation; decrease is at the synapse between sensory and motor neurone; Core Practical 18 investigate production of amylase in germinating cereal grains.
  • CNS and PNS: CNS = brain + spinal cord (integration and coordination); PNS = nerves connecting CNS to receptors and effectors; motor part = voluntary (somatic) + autonomic (sympathetic fight or flight, parasympathetic rest and digest — often opposite effects on the same organ).
  • Brain structure and function: cerebral hemispheres — higher functions: thought, memory, reasoning, language, sensation, voluntary movement — each hemisphere controls the opposite side; hypothalamus — links nervous and endocrine systems, controls pituitary, regulates temperature, water balance, hunger, thirst, sleep; pituitary gland — releases many hormones controlling other glands (growth hormone, ADH, reproduction hormones); cerebellum — coordination of movement and balance, smooth coordinated movement and posture; medulla oblongata — involuntary automatic functions: breathing rate, heart rate, cough/sneeze/swallow centres, cardiovascular and ventilation centres.
  • Brain imaging: CT — X-rays, cross-sectional structure, good for bone, bleeding, quick, ionising radiation, limited soft-tissue contrast; MRI — strong magnetic field and radio waves, detailed soft tissue, no ionising radiation, detects tumour/inflammation/demyelination/injury, takes longer, noisy; fMRI — MRI showing function via blood flow/oxygenation change with neural activity, good spatial but poor time resolution; PET — radioactive tracer (e.g. labelled glucose) shows activity/metabolism and receptor distribution, used for Alzheimer’s, cancer, e.g., ionising radiation, expensive.
  • Brain chemicals and disease: Parkinson’s disease — loss of dopamine-producing neurones in substantia nigra, tremor/stiffness/slowness/balance; L-DOPA is a dopamine precursor that crosses blood–brain barrier and is converted to dopamine; serotonin deficiency in depression; SSRIs block serotonin reuptake, more serotonin in synapse, helps mood.
  • Drugs from GMOs: human insulin — human insulin gene inserted into bacteria (E. coli) in a plasmid, bacteria grown in fermenters, insulin extracted and purified — identical to human insulin, fewer immune reactions, cheaper to produce in bulk; also growth hormone, clotting factor, enzymes for washing powders; modified plants/animals explored for vaccines and other proteins.
  • Recombinant DNA: cut gene of interest and plasmid vector with same restriction enzyme → complementary sticky ends; join with DNA ligase to make recombinant DNA; insert into host cells (bacterial transformation with CaCl₂ and heat shock, viral vectors, microinjection, gene gun); select transformed cells using antibiotic resistance marker on the vector; host cell then expresses the gene (e.g. makes insulin).
  • Microarrays: a chip with many DNA probes; mRNA from two samples converted to cDNA and labelled with different fluorescent tags (e.g. green vs red); mixture hybridises to probes; scan: green = more active in green sample, red = more active in red sample, yellow = similar activity, intensity = level of activity — used to compare gene activity (e.g. cancer vs normal, drug effect) and to identify active genes and diagnose/understand disease.
  • Bioinformatics: using computers to collect, store, analyse and interpret large biological datasets — DNA/protein sequences, gene expression (microarray), structures; used to compare sequences (find similarities/differences, infer function, build phylogenetic trees), predict protein structure from amino acid sequence, analyse gene expression; depends on genome projects and databases; used across biology — gene identification, function, drug targets, pathogen evolution.
  • Risks and benefits of GMOs: benefits — agriculture: pest resistance (Bt crops), herbicide tolerance, drought/salinity tolerance, improved nutrition (golden rice — beta-carotene/vitamin A), higher yield, food security; medicine: GM bacteria make human insulin, growth hormone, clotting factor, enzymes; research: study gene function and disease. Risks/concerns — gene flow to wild relatives or other organisms, unintended effects on non-target organisms (e.g. beneficial insects and Bt crops), resistant pests/weeds, corporate control of food/seed and effects on farmers and traditional varieties, unknown long-term ecosystem effects, ethical questions (especially animals, GM food); weigh case by case with scientific evidence and regulation, not only science — values, economics, environment.

Worked examples

Action potential frequency: a weak stimulus above threshold may produce 10 action potentials per second; a strong stimulus above threshold may produce 100 per second — same size each, but more frequent. Refractory period limits the maximum frequency (absolute ~1–2 ms), so the maximum is about 500–1000 per second.

Microarray interpretation: a spot is green — the gene is more active in the green-labelled sample; red — more active in the red-labelled sample; yellow — similar activity in both; dark — neither sample has much of that mRNA; the brightness shows how active. Example: a cancer sample labelled green and a normal sample labelled red — a gene whose spot is bright green is more active in the cancer (possible oncogene or marker); a bright red spot is more active in the normal (possible tumour suppressor).

Recombinant DNA insulin: cut the human insulin gene and a plasmid with the same restriction enzyme (complementary sticky ends); mix and add DNA ligase to join the gene into the plasmid (recombinant DNA); introduce the plasmid into E. coli (transformation with CaCl₂ and heat shock); grow on agar with an antibiotic — only bacteria that took up the plasmid (with its antibiotic-resistance gene) survive; among these, those expressing the insulin gene make human insulin, which is harvested and purified.

How to use this

Read the summary list, then open the full revision notes for any point that feels weak, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself. Revise next by: drawing a neurone and labelling sensory/relay/motor forms, myelin and nodes of Ranvier; drawing the action potential graph and labelling resting potential, depolarisation, repolarisation, hyperpolarisation, threshold, and stating what happens to Na⁺ and K⁺ channels at each stage; drawing a cholinergic synapse and labelling the events; drawing the iris and pupillary reflex; drawing the responses to drugs (nicotine, lidocaine, cobra venom, L-DOPA, MDMA) and stating the mechanism and effect; describing rod cell light detection step by step; describing habituation and the practical; describing CNS/PNS and sympathetic/parasympathetic; locating and stating the functions of each brain region; comparing MRI/fMRI/PET/CT; explaining Parkinson’s and serotonin/depression and the drugs; describing recombinant DNA and the insulin example (restriction enzymes, ligase, transformation, selection); describing microarrays; defining bioinformatics and giving its uses; and discussing the risks and benefits of GMOs. After this topic, revise the related A2 topics (physiology, energy, evolution) and the core practicals for this unit.

Biology — Edexcel IAL A2, WBI14 Unit 4 Topic 8.   • Neurones and myelination: sensory neurone — long dendron and long axon, cell body off to one side; relay neurone — short dendrites, cell body central; motor neurone — long axon, cell body in CNS, many short dendrites; Schwann cells wrap myelin around the axon; nodes of Ranvier are gaps; myelin speeds conduction.
  • Action potential: at threshold, voltage-gated sodium channels open, Na⁺ floods in — depolarisation to about +40 mV; then Na⁺ channels close and K⁺ channels open, K⁺ floods out — repolarisation; hyperpolarisation; the Na⁺/K⁺ pump restores resting potential; all-or-nothing; refractory period ensures one-way conduction and limits frequency.
  • Synapse (cholinergic): action potential opens Ca²⁺ channels in presynaptic terminal, Ca²⁺ enters, vesicles with acetylcholine (ACh) fuse and release ACh by exocytosis, ACh diffuses across cleft, binds to postsynaptic receptors, Na⁺ channels open, Na⁺ enters and depolarises; acetylcholinesterase breaks down ACh.
  • Pupil reflex: bright light — circular iris muscles contract, radial relax — pupil constricts; dim light — radial iris muscles contract, circular relax — pupil dilates.
  • Drugs on transmission: nicotine mimics ACh at nicotinic receptors (alertness, addictive, raises BP and HR); lidocaine blocks voltage-gated Na⁺ channels — local anaesthetic, no pain signal; cobra venom alpha toxin blocks ACh receptors — muscle paralysis; L-DOPA (Parkinson’s) crosses blood–brain barrier, converted to dopamine — eases tremor/stiffness/slowness; MDMA causes massive serotonin release and blocks reuptake — wellbeing/empathy then serotonin depletion and damage (depression, memory).
  • Rod cell and light detection: rhodopsin = opsin + retinal (vitamin A derivative); light → retinal changes shape (11-cis to all-trans) → opsin changes → rod cell hyperpolarises (more negative); this closes Na⁺ channels that are open in the dark, reduces neurotransmitter (glutamate) release; bipolar cell then optic neurone — action potentials generated in the optic neurone, sent to brain as vision; rods = dim light, cones = colour/detail in bright light.
  • Habituation: a decrease in response to a repeated harmless stimulus; snail withdrawal reflex to a tap — response slows and stops; not muscle fatigue (a new stimulus still produces a strong response) and not sensory adaptation; decrease is at the synapse between sensory and motor neurone; Core Practical 18 investigate production of amylase in germinating cereal grains.
  • CNS and PNS: CNS = brain + spinal cord (integration and coordination); PNS = nerves connecting CNS to receptors and effectors; motor part = voluntary (somatic) + autonomic (sympathetic fight or flight, parasympathetic rest and digest — often opposite effects on the same organ).
  • Brain structure and function: cerebral hemispheres — higher functions: thought, memory, reasoning, language, sensation, voluntary movement — each hemisphere controls the opposite side; hypothalamus — links nervous and endocrine systems, controls pituitary, regulates temperature, water balance, hunger, thirst, sleep; pituitary gland — releases many hormones controlling other glands (growth hormone, ADH, reproduction hormones); cerebellum — coordination of movement and balance, smooth coordinated movement and posture; medulla oblongata — involuntary automatic functions: breathing rate, heart rate, cough/sneeze/swallow centres, cardiovascular and ventilation centres.

  • Brain chemicals and disease: Parkinson’s disease — loss of dopamine-producing neurones in substantia nigra, tremor/stiffness/slowness/balance; L-DOPA is a dopamine precursor that crosses blood–brain barrier and is converted to dopamine; serotonin deficiency in depression; SSRIs block serotonin reuptake, more serotonin in synapse, helps mood.
  • Drugs from GMOs: human insulin — human insulin gene inserted into bacteria (E. coli) in a plasmid, bacteria grown in fermenters, insulin extracted and purified — identical to human insulin, fewer immune reactions, cheaper to produce in bulk; also growth hormone, clotting factor, enzymes for washing powders; modified plants/animals explored for vaccines and other proteins.

  • Bioinformatics: using computers to collect, store, analyse and interpret large biological datasets — DNA/protein sequences, gene expression (microarray), structures; used to compare sequences (find similarities/differences, infer function, build phylogenetic trees), predict protein structure from amino acid sequence, analyse gene expression; depends on genome projects and databases; used across biology — gene identification, function, drug targets, pathogen evolution.

title: Integration — Study Notes
content:
Integration

Indefinite Integrals

Reverse the power rule and add a constant: ∫ xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n+1) + c (n ≠ −1).

Examples: ∫ x³ dx = x⁴/4 + c; ∫ 1/x dx = ln|x| + c; ∫ sin x dx = −cos x + c; ∫ e^x dx = e^x + c.

Definite Integrals

∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = [F(x)]ₐᵇ = F(b) − F(a). Constants of integration cancel.

Example: ∫₀¹ 6x² dx = [2x³]₀¹ = 2.

Areas Under Curves

Area between a curve and the x-axis = ∫ₐᵇ y dx, where y ≥ 0. If the curve dips below the axis, split the integral at the roots and add the absolute values.

Example: area between y = x² − 4 and the x-axis: roots ±2, and the area is |∫₋₂² (x² − 4) dx| = 32/3.

Trapezium Rule

A ≈ h/2 [y₀ + 2(y₁ + … + yₙ₋₁) + yₙ], h = (b − a)/n. More strips → better estimate; always an over-estimate for convex curves.

Exam tips: never forget +c on indefinite integrals; for areas with negative regions, sketch first and split.

Rules and exam method

For xⁿ with n ≠ −1, ∫xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + c. Integrate term by term. The special case is ∫(1/x) dx = ln|x| + c. An indefinite integral needs + c; a definite integral does not.

For a definite integral, ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a), where F is any antiderivative. Write the limits as [F(x)] between a and b, and substitute carefully: a negative limit raised to a power needs brackets.

The area between a curve and the x-axis is ∫ y dx when y ≥ 0 over the interval. If the curve lies below the axis the integral is negative, so take the modulus. If the curve crosses the axis, find the root and integrate each part separately, adding the moduli of the parts.

The area between two curves is the integral of (upper − lower) between their intersection points, found by solving the equations simultaneously.

Exam cue: Show the expanded antiderivative before substituting limits; method marks are given for a correct integration even when the arithmetic later slips.

Worked examples: indefinite and definite integrals

Example 1. Find ∫(3x² + 2x − 5) dx. Integrate term by term and add a constant: x³ + x² − 5x + c. Always include + c for an indefinite integral; examiners remove the mark when it is missing.

Example 2. Evaluate ∫13 x² dx = [x³/3] from 1 to 3 = (27/3) − (1/3) = 9 − 1/3 = 26/3. Substitute the upper limit, then subtract the value at the lower limit; the constant of integration cancels and is not written.

Reverse chain rule

∫(2x + 1)⁵ dx = (2x + 1)⁶ / (6 × 2) + c = (2x + 1)⁶/12 + c. Check by differentiating: the chain rule gives 6(2x + 1)⁵ × 2 / 12 = (2x + 1)⁵. The divisor is the new power multiplied by the coefficient of x inside the bracket.

Area between a curve and the x-axis

A definite integral gives a signed area. If the curve crosses the x-axis between the limits, the integral from a to b can be smaller than the true area, because the part below the axis counts negatively. Split the integral at each crossing and take the modulus of each part: area = |∫ from a to c| + |∫ from c to b|. Sketch the curve before integrating; it is the quickest way to see where the crossings are.

Area between two curves

For y = f(x) above y = g(x) between x = a and x = b, the area is ∫ab [f(x) − g(x)] dx. Find the intersection points by solving f(x) = g(x), since they give the limits. A common error is subtracting in the wrong order, which gives a negative answer; the area is always positive.

Trapezium rule

With n strips of equal width h, the trapezium rule gives ∫ab y dx ≈ (h/2)[y₀ + 2(y₁ + … + yn−1) + yn]. Where the curve is concave down the estimate is an underestimate, and where it is concave up it is an overestimate. Give the answer to the accuracy the question asks for and show the y-values in a table to earn the method marks.

Common errors

  • Forgetting + c on an indefinite integral, or writing + c on a definite one.
  • Dividing by the power before the coefficient in a reverse chain rule question.
  • Reporting a negative area from a definite integral without splitting at the x-axis crossings.
  • Using the trapezium rule with the wrong number of ordinates: n strips need n + 1 y-values.

title: Earth & Space — Study Notes
content:
Earth & Space

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): Earth & Solar System; stars & the Universe (Extended).

1. Earth, Moon, Sun

Earth rotates 24 h (day/night), orbits 365¼ d (year + leap). Moon orbits Earth ~27.3 d; phases from viewing angle; lunar/solar eclipses when aligned. Seasons from axial tilt (23.5°), not distance.

2. Solar system

Planets (Mercury → Neptune), dwarf planets (Pluto), moons, asteroids, comets (eccentric orbits, tails away from Sun), natural satellites. Gravity keeps orbits; orbital speed & radius relate to the central mass.

3. Orbital motion

Orbital speed v = 2πr/T. T grows with r (Kepler trend). Comets speed up near the Sun (ellipse, Sun at focus).

4. Stars (Extended)

Star formation: nebula → protostar (gravity, KE→thermal) → main sequence (hydrogen fusion: H→He, radiation pressure balances gravity) → red giant → white dwarf (Sun-mass) or supergiant → supernova → neutron star/black hole (massive stars). Elements heavier than iron form in supernovae.

5. Universe (Extended)

The Sun is one star in the Milky Way; the Milky Way is one of billions of galaxies. Redshift: receding galaxies show stretched wavelengths → the Universe is expanding → Big Bang model; CMB is the afterglow. Hubble: farther ⇒ faster recession.

6. Scales

light-year = distance light travels in a year (9.5 × 10¹⁵ m); astronomical unit = Earth–Sun distance (1.5 × 10¹¹ m).

title: Numerical Measures of Central Tendency — Study Notes
content:
Central Tendency: Mean, Median and Mode

The Mean

For data x₁, ..., xₙ the mean is

  • x̄ = Σx/n

For a frequency table with midpoints x and frequencies f: x̄ = Σfx/Σf. The mean uses every value, so a single extreme value drags it — that is its main weakness.

The Median

The median is the middle value: position (n + 1)/2 for ordered raw data. With n even, average the two middle values. The median ignores the size of extreme values, so it describes skewed data more honestly. For grouped data, estimate the median by linear interpolation within the median class.

The Mode

The most frequent value. A dataset may have no mode or several. For grouped data the modal class is the one with the highest frequency density (frequency ÷ class width), not the highest frequency.

Effects of Data Changes

Adding a constant a to every value adds a to the mean and median (the mode too) but leaves the spread untouched. Multiplying every value by b multiplies mean and median by b.

Coding

Subtract a constant and divide by a convenient width: y = (x − a)/b. Then x̄ = b·ȳ + a. Coding simplifies arithmetic and always preserves the relationship — the coded mean decodes exactly.

Example: data 2, 4, 4, 10: mean = 5, median = 4, mode = 4. Change 10 to 100: mean = 27.5, median and mode unchanged — the mean chased the outlier.

Exam tips: always state which average you used and why. When asked to compare two distributions, pair a central measure with a spread measure; a mean without a spread is only half an answer.

Exam method: mean, median and mode

For ungrouped data, the mean is the sum of the values divided by the number of values. The median is the middle value of the ordered list, at position (n + 1)/2, and the mode is the value that occurs most often. Always order the data before finding the median.

For grouped data, the mean is Σfx/Σf using the class midpoints. The modal class is the class with the highest frequency, and the median class is the one containing the (n + 1)/2 th value.

Each average suits different data. The mean uses every value, so an outlier pulls it away from the centre, while the median is unaffected by extreme values. Say which average is more representative when the question asks you to comment.

Changing one value changes the mean but may not change the median, which is useful to check a calculation.

Exam cue: When the question gives a mean and asks for a missing value, form the equation Σx = n × mean and solve for the unknown.

Worked example: the mean of grouped data

A frequency table gives class intervals, not individual values, so each class is represented by its midpoint. For the classes 0 to 10 with frequency 4, 10 to 20 with frequency 9 and 20 to 30 with frequency 7, the midpoints are 5, 15 and 25. The estimated total is 4 × 5 + 9 × 15 + 7 × 25 = 20 + 135 + 175 = 330, and the total frequency is 20, so the estimated mean is 330 ÷ 20 = 16.5. Because the midpoints replace the true values, this is an estimate, and the answer should be stated as approximately 16.5.

Worked example: the median from a cumulative frequency table

With n = 20 the median is the value of the 10.5th item.
