Read the cumulative frequency up to the class that contains the 10.5th item, which is the class 10 to 20 here, and interpolate within that class using the proportion of its frequency that lies before the median. The median is the lower boundary of the class plus the class width multiplied by (10.5 − 4) ÷ 9. Here that is 10 + 10 × 6.5 ÷ 9, which gives a median of approximately 17.2.

Choosing a measure

The mean uses every value, so one extreme value moves it. The median is unaffected by extreme values and is the better choice for skewed data such as house prices. The mode is the most common value and is the only measure that can be used for categorical data. A question that asks which average is most representative should be answered by giving a reason tied to the shape of the data.

title: IGCSE Biology: Organisation of the Organism
content:
IGCSE Biology: Organisation of the Organism

Every living thing you will ever meet — from a single bacterium to a blue whale — is built from cells, and this note starts where all biology starts: at the microscope. We begin with the idea that the cell is the smallest unit that can still be called alive, then map the structures inside animal and plant cells, explain what each one actually does, and finish with the specimen-size calculations that Paper 6 loves. Nothing here assumes prior knowledge; each structure is introduced with a physical analogy before the formal term, and every calculation is expanded line by line so you can follow it with no chemistry or maths background at all.

What a cell is, and why it is the unit of life

A cell is the smallest structure that carries out all seven life processes: movement, respiration, sensitivity, growth, reproduction, excretion and nutrition (the mnemonic MRS GREN). A brick is not alive; a single white blood cell is, because it does all seven. Two organisational levels follow. Unicellular organisms (bacteria, Amoeba, yeast) are one cell doing everything. Multicellular organisms (you, an oak tree) are communities of cells that specialise, so the body shows three levels of organisation: cells group into tissues (one job, like muscle tissue), tissues into organs (the stomach), and organs into organ systems (the digestive system).

Cell specialisation means a cell's structure fits its function like a tool fits a job. A red blood cell is a flat biconcave disc with no nucleus, leaving maximum room for haemoglobin. A sperm cell carries a long tail (flagellum) and a packed mitochondria cluster for swimming. A root hair cell pushes out one long extension to maximise surface area for absorption. A palisade cell packs its top half with chloroplasts to catch light. When asked to explain a specialised cell, always write it as: feature, then what the feature does, then why the job needs it.

Animal cell structure

Think of a cell as a factory. The cell membrane is the security door: a thin, selectively permeable layer of lipid and protein that decides what enters and leaves. The cytoplasm is the factory floor: a jelly-like solution of water, salts and enzymes where most reactions happen. The nucleus is the manager's office: it contains genetic material (DNA) and controls the cell's activities by regulating which proteins are made. Mitochondria are the power stations: rod-shaped organelles where aerobic respiration releases energy from glucose. Ribosomes are the assembly lines: tiny structures where proteins are assembled from amino acids. The cytoplasm and cell membrane together carry out most of the life processes; the nucleus stores and passes on genetic information.

Plant cell structure — the three additions

A plant cell has everything an animal cell has, plus three structures an exam will always want named. The cell wall is a rigid layer of cellulose outside the membrane: it gives mechanical strength and stops the cell bursting when water enters. Chloroplasts are the solar panels: they contain the green pigment chlorophyll and are the site of photosynthesis. The permanent vacuole is a storage tank: a large sac of cell sap (dilute sugars, salts and acids) that keeps the cell turgid, pressing the cytoplasm against the wall so leaves stay firm. Learn the comparison as a table — it is the single most reliable three-mark question in Paper 4.

StructureAnimal cellPlant cellJob
Cell membranePresentPresentControls what enters and leaves
Cell wallAbsentPresent (cellulose)Strength and support; prevents bursting
ChloroplastsAbsentPresent (palisade, spongy mesophyll)Photosynthesis in chlorophyll
Permanent vacuoleSmall, temporaryLarge, permanent, cell sapTurgor, storage
NucleusPresentPresentControls activities; stores DNA
MitochondriaPresentPresentAerobic respiration, releases energy
RibosomesPresentPresentProtein synthesis

Bacterial cells: the prokaryote difference

Bacteria are prokaryotes — cells with no nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles. Their DNA is a single circular chromosome free in the cytoplasm, often with small extra rings called plasmids. They have a cell wall (not cellulose — it is murein), a cell membrane, cytoplasm and ribosomes (smaller than eukaryotic ones), and many have a flagellum for swimming and a capsule for protection. The exam answer to "give two differences between a bacterium and a plant cell" is: no nucleus in the bacterium (DNA free in cytoplasm) and no chloroplasts or mitochondria (respiration at the membrane).

Microscopy and magnification

An optical (light) microscope uses glass lenses and visible light; specimens can be living or dead and are often stained (methyl blue for nuclei, iodine for starch) to add contrast. An electron microscope uses a beam of electrons, giving far higher magnification and resolution so organelles such as mitochondria, ribosomes, lysosomes and the endoplasmic reticulum can be seen — but specimens must be dead and in a vacuum. Magnification is how many times larger the image is than the real object; resolution is the minimum distance between two points still seen as separate — a blurry zoomed image has magnification without resolution. The three calculations you must know are written below, and the worked example expands each one.

Size of specimens — the three equations

Equation 1, magnification: magnification = size of image divided by size of real object. Equation 2, real size: real size = image size divided by magnification. Equation 3, image size: image size = real size × magnification. The golden rule of units: convert everything to the same unit before dividing. 1 millimetre (mm) = 1000 micrometres (µm); 1 µm = 1000 nanometres (nm). A common exam device is a scale bar drawn under an image: measure the bar in millimetres with a ruler, note the length it claims to represent in µm, and the magnification is bar length (in µm) ÷ claimed length (in µm). Drawing magnification for Paper 6 is measured the same way: magnification = drawing width (mm) ÷ real width (mm), with the real width first converted from µm by dividing by 1000.

Worked example: specimen size from first principles

An image of a plant cell is 40 mm long in a textbook, and the real cell is 80 µm long. Calculate the magnification. Step 1: write the equation: magnification = image size ÷ real size. Step 2: list what you have: image = 40 mm, real = 80 µm. Step 3: convert to one unit — 40 mm = 40 × 1000 = 40 000 µm. Step 4: divide: 40 000 ÷ 80 = 500. Step 5: write the answer with its × symbol: magnification = ×500. Now the reverse direction. A cell is 12 µm wide and you draw it at ×1500. Step 1: image size = real size × magnification. Step 2: 12 µm × 1500 = 18 000 µm. Step 3: convert to a workable unit: 18 000 ÷ 1000 = 18 mm. Your drawing must be 18 mm wide — measure it with a ruler in the practical. Finally, a bacterium appears 35 mm long in a micrograph at ×20 000. Step 1: real size = 35 mm ÷ 20 000 = 0.00175 mm. Step 2: convert: 0.00175 mm × 1000 = 1.75 µm. Step 3: state the answer: 1.75 µm, which is a sensible bacterium size.

Exam technique: command words and drawing rules

"State" wants one short fact; "describe" wants what you see in a diagram or graph (no reasons); "explain" wants the mechanism with because. For drawings: use clean, unbroken pencil lines with no shading; the drawing should be at least 6 cm wide for a decent magnification; label lines are straight, horizontal, do not cross, and touch the structure named; labels name the structure (write "mitochondrion", not "the power station"). When asked for differences between two diagrams (typical Paper 6), compare like with like: "the plant cell has a cell wall, the animal cell does not" is two marks in one line.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Calling the cell wall "membrane": the membrane is inside the wall; mixing them loses the mark.
  • Writing "chloroplast" on an animal cell diagram — animals have mitochondria, never chloroplasts.
  • Forgetting units after converting: 40 mm ÷ 80 µm is wrong until both are µm; always show the conversion line.
  • Saying magnification and resolution are the same thing; they are different, and Paper 4 has asked for the distinction outright.
  • Shading a drawing or using a ruler-free squiggle: both are explicitly penalised in Paper 6 mark schemes.
  • Label lines crossing each other or drawn as arrows; a line that does not touch the structure scores zero.
  • Writing "cytoplasm" when you mean "cytosol" or vice versa is safe at IGCSE — use "cytoplasm" — but never write "cell sap" for cytoplasm; cell sap is only inside the vacuole.

Exam-style questions and answers

Q1. State two structures found in a plant cell but not in an animal cell. (2 marks) Answer: cell wall (cellulose) and chloroplasts — one mark each; the permanent vacuole is also accepted but do not list more than the question asks.

Q2. A cell is drawn 60 mm wide. The real cell is 150 µm wide. Calculate the magnification and show your working. (3 marks) Answer: 60 mm = 60 000 µm (1); magnification = 60 000 ÷ 150 (1); = ×400 (1).

Q3. Explain why root hair cells are specialised for absorption. (2 marks) Answer: they have a long extension that increases surface area (1), so more water and mineral ions can be absorbed per unit time by diffusion and active transport (1).

Q4. Describe how you would prepare a slide of onion cells for viewing. (4 marks) Answer: peel a thin transparent layer of epidermis (1); place it flat in a drop of water on a slide (1); add a coverslip at an angle without trapping air bubbles (1); view at low power then focus with the fine adjustment (1).

Q5. Explain why the electron microscope was needed to discover ribosomes. (2 marks) Answer: ribosomes are very small (around 20 nm) so need much higher resolution than the light microscope provides (1); the electron microscope's shorter wavelength of electrons gives that resolution (1).

Organisation of the Organism: the cell in detail

Cell structure questions look like recall and are really about function. A mark scheme rarely asks what a mitochondrion is; it asks why a cell that secretes a lot of enzyme has many of them, or why a root hair cell has no chloroplasts. This section gives the organelle functions in enough detail to answer those, then does the arithmetic of magnification properly, because that is where most marks are lost.

Organelles and what each one is for

StructureWhat it isFunction, and the clue it leaves in a cellPlantAnimal
NucleusChromatin (DNA and protein) inside a double membrane with poresControls the cell and holds the genetic code; the pores let messenger RNA out. Large and dark in a cell making lots of proteinYesYes
MitochondrionDouble membrane, inner one folded into cristae; own small amount of DNASite of aerobic respiration; cristae increase the area for the reactions. Numerous in muscle, sperm midpiece and active transport cellsYesYes
RibosomeTwo subunits of RNA and protein, about 20 nmProtein synthesis; free in the cytoplasm or attached to the rough ER. Never visible with a light microscopeYesYes
Rough ERMembranes studded with ribosomesFolds and transports proteins made on its ribosomes; abundant in cells that secrete enzymes or antibodiesYesYes
Smooth ERMembrane tubules, no ribosomesMakes lipids and steroids, and detoxifies drugs; abundant in liver cellsYesYes
Golgi apparatusStack of flattened sacsModifies proteins (for example by adding carbohydrate), packages them into vesicles for secretionYesYes
LysosomeVesicle containing hydrolytic enzymesDigests worn-out organelles and material taken in by phagocytosis; abundant in phagocytesRareYes
ChloroplastDouble membrane, stacks of thylakoid discs (grana) in a stroma, containing chlorophyllPhotosynthesis: light absorbed in the grana, carbon fixation in the stroma; contains starch grains. Only in photosynthetic cellsYesNo
VacuoleFluid-filled sac bounded by the tonoplastStores water, sugars and salts and provides turgor; the large permanent vacuole is what keeps a plant cell firmLarge, permanentSmall, temporary
Cell wallCellulose microfibrilsStrength and support; freely permeable, so it does not control what entersYesNo
Cell membranePhospholipid bilayer with proteinsPartially permeable boundary controlling exchange; the site of osmosis, diffusion and active transportYesYes

Two exam traps sit in that table. The cell wall is freely permeable, so it plays no part in osmosis — the membrane does. And a plant cell has mitochondria as well as chloroplasts, because it respires at night and in its roots; a plant cell is not a photosynthetic cell by default.

Prokaryote and eukaryote, in the terms that get marked

A prokaryote has no nucleus: its DNA is a single circular molecule lying free in the cytoplasm, often with additional small circles called plasmids. It has no membrane-bound organelles, so no mitochondria, no chloroplasts and no Golgi; its ribosomes are smaller. Many have a cell wall of peptidoglycan (murein), a capsule for protection, and one or more flagella for movement. A eukaryote has a nucleus, membrane-bound organelles and larger ribosomes, and may be unicellular or multicellular. Sizes overlap at the edges, but as a rule a prokaryote is 1–5 µm and a eukaryotic cell 10–100 µm (Figure 1).

The practical consequence of the size difference is what a microscope can show. With a light microscope, resolution is limited to about 0.2 µm by the wavelength of visible light, so you can see a nucleus, a vacuole and a chloroplast, but not a ribosome, a membrane or the cristae of a mitochondrion. An electron microscope uses electrons with a far shorter wavelength, so it resolves to a fraction of a nanometre and reveals those structures — but the specimen must be dead, because the preparation requires a vacuum. Magnification and resolution are different things: magnification enlarges the image, resolution determines how much detail survives the enlargement.

Specialised cells: structure written as function

CellStructural featureFunction it serves
Red blood cellNo nucleus, biconcave disc, haemoglobinMore room for haemoglobin; large surface area for oxygen uptake; flexible enough to pass capillaries
Sperm cellMany mitochondria in the midpiece, a tail, an acrosome of enzymesEnergy for swimming, propulsion, and enzymes to penetrate the egg
Ciliated epithelial cellCilia on the free surface, many mitochondriaBeats mucus and trapped particles away from the lungs; ATP for the beating
Root hair cellLong thin extension, no cuticle, large vacuole, many mitochondriaLarge surface area for water uptake; concentrated sap maintains the osmotic gradient; ATP for ion uptake
Palisade mesophyll cellMany chloroplasts, near the upper surface, cylindricalMaximum light absorption where light is strongest
Nerve cell (neurone)Long axon, branched endings, myelin sheathRapid conduction over distance; many connections
Muscle cellElongated, packed with protein filaments and mitochondriaContraction and the ATP to power it
Xylem vesselDead, hollow, no end walls, lignifiedContinuous low-resistance column for water under tension
Guard cellThicker inner wall, chloroplasts, can change shapeOpens and closes the stoma by turgor change

From cell to organism

A tissue is a group of similar cells working together for one function: muscular tissue, epithelial tissue, xylem, phloem, palisade mesophyll. An organ is several tissues working together: the stomach contains muscular tissue to churn, epithelial tissue to secrete, and glandular tissue to make acid. An organ system is several organs with a common function, such as the digestive system or the circulatory system, and the organism is the sum of its systems. The same hierarchy applies to plants, with the leaf as an organ and the transport system as the plant's equivalent of a system.

Questions that ask "why is a leaf an organ?" want the answer "because it contains several tissues — epidermis, palisade mesophyll, spongy mesophyll, xylem and phloem — working together for photosynthesis". Naming two tissues is the evidence; the word "organ" alone is not.

Magnification and actual size, done without slips

Three quantities are related by one equation, and every version of the question is that equation rearranged:

magnification = image size ÷ actual size; actual size = image size ÷ magnification; image size = actual size × magnification.

Work in one unit and convert at the end. A cell drawn 40 mm across at a magnification of ×2,000 has an actual size of 40 ÷ 2,000 = 0.02 mm, which is 20 µm. A chloroplast 5 µm long viewed at ×4,000 appears 5 × 4,000 = 20,000 µm = 20 mm. The conversion is the step that loses marks: 1 mm = 1,000 µm, and 1 µm = 1,000 nm, so 0.02 mm = 20 µm = 20,000 nm.

When the question gives you a scale bar instead of a magnification, measure the bar, work out how many micrometres it represents, and use that as your conversion — do not try to calculate a magnification from the print size, because the print size is not the specimen. And when you are asked to draw a cell, use a sharp pencil, unbroken lines, no shading, and label with straight lines that touch the structure; the drawing rules are worth marks on their own.

Equations and symbols

The magnification triangle in words, the unit ladder, and the two direction-of-use forms. Paper 6 gives you two of the three quantities and marks the conversion line as much as the arithmetic.

magnification = size of image divided by size of real object Key: magnification = how many times larger the image is (×, no unit); size of image = length measured on the drawing or micrograph (mm); size of real object = the true length of the specimen (µm). Both lengths must be in the same unit before dividing.

real size = image size divided by magnification Key: real size = the specimen's true length (µm or mm, whichever the question asks for); image size = the measured length on the page; magnification = the × value printed on the micrograph. This is the rearrangement used when the micrograph gives ×20 000 and you must name the organelle.

image size = real size × magnification Key: image size = the length your drawing must be (convert to mm for a ruler); real size = the specimen's true length; magnification = the required drawing magnification. A draw-at-×1500 instruction is this line and a conversion, nothing more.

magnification = drawing width (mm) ÷ real width (mm) Key: drawing width = your own pencil drawing, measured with a ruler (mm); real width = the specimen's true width (mm, so divide a µm value by 1000 first). This is the form that earns the "calculate the magnification of your drawing" mark.

1 millimetre (mm) = 1000 micrometres (µm) Key: the first step of the unit ladder; multiply by 1000 to go down, divide by 1000 to go up. A 40 mm image is 40 × 1000 = 40 000 µm, and only then may it be divided by a real size in µm.

1 µm = 1000 nanometres (nm) Key: the second rung, used for organelles: a ribosome at 20 nm is 0.02 µm, which is why a light microscope cannot resolve it. Writing a bacterium's size in nm when the question asked for µm is the commonest unit slip on this topic.

title: Organic Chemistry: Halogenoalkanes, Alcohols and Spectra
content:
Organic Chemistry: Halogenoalkanes, Alcohols and Spectra

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH12, Topic 10. Halogenoalkanes and alcohols are the first families where a functional group changes the reactivity of the molecule. Spectra are the tools that identify those groups in an unknown compound.

Halogenoalkanes

  • A halogenoalkane has a halogen atom bonded to a carbon atom. The C–X bond is polar because the halogen is more electronegative, so the carbon is slightly positive.
  • Reactivity rises down the group because the C–X bond gets weaker (C–I is weakest), so the iodoalkane reacts fastest.
  • Nucleophilic substitution with aqueous hydroxide ions gives an alcohol. The nucleophile donates a pair of electrons to the carbon atom.
  • Halogenoalkanes can be tested by warming with aqueous silver nitrate in ethanol: the precipitate forms at different rates, and iodoalkanes react fastest.

Alcohols

  • Alcohols contain the –OH group. Primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols depend on how many other carbons are attached to the carbon bearing the –OH.
  • Oxidation of primary alcohols with acidified potassium dichromate(VI) gives aldehydes, which can be oxidised further to carboxylic acids; excess oxidant and heat give the acid.
  • Secondary alcohols oxidise to ketones; tertiary alcohols are not oxidised under these conditions.
  • Dehydration with hot concentrated sulfuric acid or aluminium oxide forms an alkene.

Mass spectrometry

  • The molecular ion peak gives the relative molecular mass. Fragmentation patterns reveal structural features.
  • Peaks at m/z 15 and 29 can indicate CH3 and C2H5 fragments.

Infrared spectroscopy

  • Bonds absorb infrared radiation at characteristic wavenumbers. A broad absorption near 3200–3550 cm⁻¹ indicates an O–H group in an alcohol. A strong absorption near 1700 cm⁻¹ indicates a C=O group.
  • Use tables of characteristic absorptions with the spectrum, rather than memorised single values.

NMR (introduced)

  • The number of peaks in a proton NMR spectrum gives the number of environments of hydrogen atoms; the relative areas give the ratio of hydrogens.

Exam tip: when identifying an unknown, combine evidence: the molecular formula from mass spectrometry, the functional groups from infrared, and the environments from NMR.

title: Coordinate Geometry — Study Notes
content:
Coordinate Geometry

Cambridge International AS & A Level Mathematics 9709, Paper 1. Most questions in this topic reduce to one habit: turn each geometric fact into an equation, solve the system, then check the answer against a sketch.

Lengths, midpoints and gradients

For points (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂):

  • Length: √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²)
  • Midpoint: ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2)
  • Gradient: (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁). A vertical line has no gradient; a horizontal line has gradient zero.

Two lines are parallel when their gradients are equal. They are perpendicular when the product of their gradients is −1, so one gradient is the negative reciprocal of the other.

Example: A(−1, 4) and B(5, −4). AB = √(6² + 8²) = 10. The midpoint is (2, 0) and the gradient of AB is −8/6 = −4/3. The perpendicular bisector has gradient 3/4 and passes through (2, 0), so its equation is 3x − 4y − 6 = 0.

Finding a line from given information

Every line question needs two facts: a point on the line and its gradient. Find whichever one is missing. The gradient can come from a second point, from a parallel line (which shares its gradient), or from a perpendicular line (take the negative reciprocal). Substitute into y − y₁ = m(x − x₁), then rearrange into the form the question asks for: usually y = mx + c, or ax + by + c = 0 with integer coefficients.

Example: the line through (−2, 5) perpendicular to 3x − 4y = 1. The given line has gradient 3/4, so the required gradient is −4/3. Then y − 5 = −4/3(x + 2), which rearranges to 4x + 3y − 7 = 0.

Where lines meet lines and curves

A common point satisfies both equations, so substitute one into the other and solve. Two lines with different gradients meet exactly once. Parallel lines with different intercepts never meet, and the substitution leaves a statement that cannot be true. For a line and a curve, the resulting quadratic has two distinct roots, one repeated root, or no real roots, and the discriminant b² − 4ac tells you which before you solve it.

Example: y = 2x − 1 meets x² + y² = 10. Substituting gives 5x² − 4x − 9 = 0, so (5x − 9)(x + 1) = 0. The points are (9/5, 13/5) and (−1, −3).

Circles

The centre–radius form is (x − a)² + (y − b)² = r². If the equation is given in general form, x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0, complete the square in x and in y. The centre is then (−g, −f) and the radius is √(g² + f² − c). To test a point, substitute its coordinates into the left-hand side and compare with r²: a smaller value means inside the circle, equal means on it, and larger means outside.

Example: x² + y² − 6x + 4y − 12 = 0 becomes (x − 3)² + (y + 2)² = 25, so the centre is (3, −2) and the radius is 5.

Tangents and normals

A tangent touches the circle at one point and is perpendicular to the radius through that point. Find the gradient of the radius from the centre, take the negative reciprocal for the tangent, then use the point–gradient form. The normal is the radius itself, so it passes through the centre.

Example: the tangent to (x − 3)² + (y + 2)² = 25 at (7, 1). The radius has gradient 3/4, so the tangent has gradient −4/3, and its equation is 4x + 3y − 31 = 0.

Exam technique

  • Draw a rough diagram first. It shows whether a point should lie inside or outside a circle before any algebra is done.
  • With a "show that" instruction, finish with the exact expression that was asked for.
  • To check a tangent, confirm that the distance from the centre to the line equals the radius.
  • Keep fractions exact until the final line; rounding early is the most common cause of a lost mark.

title: System Software and Security — Study Notes
content:
`# System Software and Security

Operating System Roles

  • Manage memory (paging/segmentation, virtual memory to disk)
  • Schedule processes (round robin, priorities)
  • Handle I/O via device drivers and spooling
  • Provide the UI, file systems, and security (users, permissions)

Translators

  • Assembler: assembly → machine code (1:1)
  • Compiler: whole source → machine code, reports all errors, produces standalone executables
  • Interpreter: line-by-line execution, stops at first error, needs the interpreter present

Bytecode + VM (e.g. Java) combines both: compile once, run anywhere the VM exists.

Linkers and Loaders

Static linking copies library code into the executable; dynamic linking binds at runtime (smaller files, shared libraries). The loader places the program in memory, relocating addresses.

IDEs

Editors with syntax highlighting, autocompletion, debugger (breakpoints, stepping, variable watch), and integrated compilation.

Malware and Defences

Viruses, worms, trojans, spyware, phishing. Defences: antivirus (signature + heuristic scanning), firewalls (packet filtering by port/IP), sandboxing, user education, patches.

Exam tips: compare compiler vs interpreter with concrete error-handling differences; explain firewall rules using ports and addresses.

Malware types and prevention

A virus attaches itself to a file or program and needs a host to spread. A worm spreads across a network without a host file. A trojan looks like useful software but carries a hidden harmful payload. Phishing uses fake emails or websites to trick a user into revealing login details or other personal data.

A firewall monitors incoming and outgoing network traffic and blocks traffic that does not meet its rules. Anti-malware software scans for and removes known threats. Regular software updates close security weaknesses, and regular backups allow data to be restored after an attack.

Exam tip: match each threat to how it spreads, and each prevention method to the threat it stops. Do not confuse a virus with a worm.

title: Transition Metals and their Chemistry — Study Notes
content:
Transition Metals and their Chemistry

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH15, Topic 17. Transition metals form coloured complex ions, show variable oxidation states and act as catalysts. These properties come from partly filled d orbitals.

Complex ions and ligands

  • A ligand is a species with a lone pair that forms a dative bond to a metal ion. Water, ammonia and chloride are monodentate ligands.
  • Ethane-1,2-diamine is bidentate because it has two donor atoms. EDTA⁴⁻ is hexadentate.
  • The coordination number is the number of coordinate bonds to the central metal ion. Common shapes are octahedral (6), tetrahedral (4), square planar (4) and linear (2, e.g. [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺).

Colour

  • In a ligand field the five d orbitals split into two energy levels. Electrons absorb light to jump between them, and the colour seen is complementary to the colour absorbed.
  • The d-orbital splitting depends on the metal, its oxidation state and the ligands. Ligand exchange changes the colour.

Ligand substitution and isomerism

  • Concentrated HCl converts [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ (blue) into [CuCl₄]²⁻ (yellow-green, tetrahedral).
  • Excess aqueous ammonia converts Cu²⁺ into [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺, a deep blue complex.
  • Square planar [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂] shows cis-trans isomerism. The cis form is the anticancer drug cisplatin.

Catalysis

  • Heterogeneous catalysts (iron in the Haber process) work on a surface. Homogeneous catalysts such as Fe²⁺ in the iodide–peroxydisulfate reaction are in the same phase as the reactants.
  • In the MnO₄⁻ and ethanedioate reaction, Mn²⁺ is the product and catalyses the reaction, so the rate increases as it forms: this is autocatalysis.

Exam tip: when a ligand exchange is asked for, name both the shape and the colour change, and write the complex formula with its charge.

title: Movement into and out of Cells
content:
Movement into and out of Cells

Cambridge IGCSE Biology 0610, Extended route, topic 3 (statements 3.1–3.3). Diffusion, osmosis and active transport, with the water-potential reasoning that separates the top grades.

3.1 Diffusion

  • Diffusion is the net movement of particles down a concentration gradient until evenly spread. It is passive: no energy is needed. Oxygen moves into cells and carbon dioxide out by diffusion.

3.2 Osmosis

  • Osmosis is the net movement of water molecules from a dilute solution to a concentrated solution, through a partially permeable membrane, down a water potential gradient. Pure water has a water potential of zero; all solutions have negative water potential, and more negative means more concentrated.
  • Animal cells in pure water gain water and burst (lyse); in concentrated solution they lose water and shrink (crenate). Plant cells in pure water become turgid — the wall resists further entry; in concentrated solution they become plasmolysed, the membrane pulls away from the wall.

3.3 Active transport

  • Active transport moves substances against a concentration gradient, from dilute to concentrated, using energy from respiration. Root hair cells absorb mineral ions this way; the small intestine absorbs amino acids and glucose when concentrations are lower inside than outside.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Explanation chain, applied to why root hair cells take in water by osmosis but mineral ions by active transport: water moves down its gradient automatically because the cell sap is more concentrated; minerals must be moved from dilute soil solution into a more concentrated cell, which needs energy from respiration. Name both gradient directions — that contrast is the mark.
  • Practical interpretation, applied to potato cylinders left in a series of sucrose solutions and plotted as percentage change in mass: the solution where the line crosses zero change is isotonic with the tissue. Explain the shape: below that concentration cells gain water by osmosis, above it they lose it.
  • Experimental control, applied to a diffusion investigation: the independent variable is the distance or concentration, and the control variables include temperature and the particle size of the agar. Naming temperature as controlled shows you know diffusion rate depends on it.

Common errors

  • Omitting "partially permeable membrane" from the osmosis definition — it is a required phrase.
  • Saying water moves to the "salty side". Use dilute to concentrated solution and water potential.
  • Claiming active transport needs a concentration gradient to be followed. It works against the gradient.

title: Number — Indices and Standard Form — Study Notes
content:
Number — Indices and Standard Form

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): index laws, negative and fractional indices, standard form arithmetic, surds and rationalising denominators.

1. Index laws

  • aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ; aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ; (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ
  • a⁰ = 1; a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ; a^(1/n) = ⁿ√a; a^(m/n) = (ⁿ√a)ᵐ

Examples: 27^(2/3) = (³√27)² = 9; 5⁻² = 1/25; (2x³)² = 4x⁶.

2. Standard form

a × 10ⁿ with 1 ≤ a < 10.

  • 47 382 = 4.7382 × 10⁴; 0.0056 = 5.6 × 10⁻³
  • Multiplication: multiply a's, add powers. Division: divide a's, subtract powers.

Example: (3 × 10⁵) × (4 × 10⁻²) = 12 × 10³ = 1.2 × 10⁴.

3. Calculator use

Use the ×10ˣ key, not 10 ^; keep working in standard form and convert at the end. Give final answers in the form asked (often 3 s.f. standard form).

4. Solving index equations

Match bases: 2ˣ = 32 ⇒ 2ˣ = 2⁵ ⇒ x = 5. With different bases, rewrite (8 = 2³).

5. Surds

A surd is a root that cannot be written as a rational number: √2, √3, 3√5.

  • Rules: √a × √b = √(ab); √a ÷ √b = √(a/b); (√a)² = a.
  • Simplify by taking out the largest square factor: √50 = √25 × √2 = 5√2; √72 = 6√2; √(9/16) = 3/4.
  • Add and subtract like surds: √18 + √8 = 3√2 + 2√2 = 5√2. Unlike surds cannot be combined: 2√3 + √5 stays as it is.
  • Rationalise the denominator so no root is left below the line: 6/√3 = 6√3/3 = 2√3; 1/(3 + √2) = (3 − √2) / ((3 + √2)(3 − √2)) = (3 − √2)/7 — multiply top and bottom by the conjugate.
  • Expanding: (2 + √3)(2 − √3) = 4 − 3 = 1; difference of two squares clears the surd.

Example: write √12 + √75 in the form k√3 → 2√3 + 5√3 = 7√3.

Exam tips: check a is in [1, 10) before writing standard form; in "multiply out" questions apply the power to every factor including coefficients.

Worked example: a combined index calculation

Simplify (2³ × 2⁵) ÷ 2⁴. Add the indices in the numerator to get 2⁸ ÷ 2⁴, then subtract the indices to get 2⁴ = 16. Check by a second method: 2³ × 2⁵ = 8 × 32 = 256, and 256 ÷ 16 = 16. Both routes agree.

Fractional and negative powers

A negative index means a reciprocal: 5⁻² = 1/5² = 1/25. A fractional index with denominator n means an nth root: 16^(1/2) = 4, and 27^(2/3) = (27^(1/3))² = 3² = 9. Taking the root first and then raising the result to the power keeps the arithmetic small.

  • Any non-zero number to the power 0 equals 1, so 7⁰ = 1.
  • Do not multiply the base by the index: (2³)² = 2⁶, not 2⁵ and not 6.
  • Standard form for a number between 0 and 1 uses a negative index: 0.00047 = 4.7 × 10⁻⁴.

Worked example: converting to and from standard form

Write 0.00046 in standard form by moving the decimal point four places to the right, giving 4.6 × 10⁻⁴. The number 3.2 × 10⁵ is 320 000. To multiply, multiply the coefficients and add the powers: (2 × 10⁶) × (4 × 10³) = 8 × 10⁹. To divide, divide the coefficients and subtract the powers: (6 × 10⁸) ÷ (2 × 10³) = 3 × 10⁵. The coefficient must lie between 1 and 10, so 12 × 10⁴ must be rewritten as 1.2 × 10⁵.

Exam method: checking the size of an answer

A large number should have a positive power of ten and a small number a negative one, so check the sign of the index after every conversion. If a question asks for an answer in standard form to 3 significant figures, round only at the end and keep all the digits your calculator gives while working. Rounding at each step can change the third figure and cost the accuracy mark.

title: Exam technique: Magnetism and Electromagnetism
content:
### What earns the marks
For electromagnets, turns plus current plus soft iron core earns each mark. For transformers, the turns ratio equation quoted earns the method mark. For induction, rate of change of flux linked to emf size earns the explanation mark.
### Traps
Error: steel chosen for electromagnet cores. Correction: soft iron; steel suits permanent magnets. Error: Fleming hands swapped. Correction: left for motor, right for generator. Error: step-up confused with step-down. Correction: more secondary turns means step-up.
### Worked example
A transformer has 2000 primary turns and 100 secondary turns. The primary is supplied at 240 V. The turns ratio gives Vs = Vp × Ns / Np = 240 × 100 / 2000 = 12 V. More secondary turns than primary turns means a step-up transformer, so the output voltage rises.
### Check yourself
An ideal transformer has 12 V at its secondary and a current of 4.0 A there. Find the primary current when the primary is at 240 V. Power in equals power out, so Ip = (12 × 4.0) / 240 = 0.20 A.

### Worked example
A transformer has 2000 primary turns and 100 secondary turns. The primary is supplied at 240 V. The turns ratio gives Vs = Vp × Ns / Np = 240 × 100 / 2000 = 12 V. More secondary turns than primary turns means a step-up transformer, so the output voltage rises.
### Check yourself
An ideal transformer has 12 V at its secondary and a current of 4.0 A there. Find the primary current when the primary is at 240 V. Power in equals power out, so Ip = (12 × 4.0) / 240 = 0.20 A.

title: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Right-Angled Trigonometry
content:
Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Right-Angled Trigonometry

Right-angled triangles are the most useful triangles in mathematics: Pythagoras relates the three sides, and the sine, cosine and tangent ratios relate sides to angles. Between them they solve every distance and angle problem the IGCSE sets, from ladders against walls to angles of elevation and three-figure bearings. This note builds the topic from zero: Pythagoras with its converse and 3D use, the SOHCAHTOA ratios with the selection method, exact values derived rather than memorised, and the multi-step problems that combine Pythagoras with trigonometry.

Pythagoras' theorem

in a right-angled triangle: a² + b² = c²
where c is the hypotenuse (the side opposite the right angle)

The theorem is a statement about areas: the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides. The converse identifies right angles: if a² + b² = c² for the longest side c, the triangle is right-angled — the standard test for 3-4-5 and 5-12-13 triangles.

Worked example 1. A right-angled triangle has legs 6 cm and 8 cm. Find the hypotenuse.

c² = 6² + 8² = 36 + 64 = 100
c = 10 cm

Worked example 2 (finding a leg). The hypotenuse is 13 cm and one leg is 5 cm. Find the other leg.

a² = 13² - 5² = 169 - 25 = 144
a = 12 cm

Worked example 3 (converse). Is a triangle with sides 7, 24, 25 right-angled?

7² + 24² = 49 + 576 = 625 = 25²
yes - right-angled, with the right angle opposite the 25 side

Pythagoras in three dimensions

In a cuboid, the space diagonal uses Pythagoras twice: first across the base, then up the height.

space diagonal = √(l² + w² + h²)

Worked example. A cuboid is 3 cm by 4 cm by 12 cm. Find the length of the space diagonal.

d = √(9 + 16 + 144) = √(169) = 13 cm

The three ratios: SOHCAHTOA

sin(θ) = opposite/hypotenuse      (SOH)
cos(θ) = adjacent/hypotenuse      (CAH)
tan(θ) = opposite/adjacent       (TOA)

Label the sides relative to the angle in question: the hypotenuse is always opposite the right angle; the opposite is across from the angle; the adjacent is the remaining side touching the angle. The selection method: mark the known side and the wanted side, then ask which ratio contains both.

Worked example 1 (finding a side). In a right-angled triangle, the angle is 35° and the hypotenuse is 12 cm. Find the opposite side.

known: hypotenuse; want: opposite  →  sine
sin(35) = opposite/12
opposite = 12 sin(35) = 12 × 0.574 = 6.88 cm

Worked example 2 (finding a side with cosine). Angle 40°, hypotenuse 20 cm; find the adjacent side.

cos(40) = adjacent/20
adjacent = 20 cos(40) = 20 × 0.766 = 15.3 cm

Worked example 3 (finding an angle). Opposite 5 cm, adjacent 9 cm. Find the angle.

tan(θ) = 5/9 = 0.5556
θ = tan-1(0.5556) = 29.1 °

For angles, use the inverse functions (sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹, tan⁻¹) and check the calculator is in degree mode — a radian-mode calculator turns 90° into 1.57 and ruins the paper.

Exact trigonometric values

Three angles have exact values worth knowing, derived from two special triangles:

Anglesincostan
30°1/2√3/21/√3
45°1/√21/√21
60°√3/21/2√3

Derivation: a 45-45-90 triangle with legs 1 has hypotenuse √2 (Pythagoras), giving sin 45 = 1/√2. An equilateral triangle of side 2 split in half gives a 30-60-90 triangle with sides 1, √3, 2, giving all six values. Deriving them once beats memorising them badly.

Two sanity checks keep the table honest: sine increases from 0 to 1 as the angle grows from 0° to 90°, so sin 30 must be smaller than sin 60; and cosine runs the other way, so cos 30 must be larger than cos 60. If an exact value breaks either ordering, the table has been misremembered.

Worked example. Find the exact value of sin 60° × tan 30°.

sin 60 = √(3)/2;  tan 30 = 1/√(3)
product = (√(3)/2) x (1/√(3)) = 1/2

Angles of elevation and depression

An angle of elevation is measured upward from the horizontal to an object; an angle of depression is measured downward. Both are measured from the observer's eye line, and the angle of depression from A to B equals the angle of elevation from B to A (alternate angles).

Worked example. From a point 40 m from the base of a tower, the angle of elevation to the top is 32°. Find the tower's height.

tan(32) = height/40
height = 40 tan(32) = 40 × 0.625 = 25.0 m

Worked example 2 (depression). A cliff is 60 m high; the angle of depression to a boat is 25°. Find the horizontal distance to the boat.

the angle at the boat is also 25 ° (alternate)
tan(25) = 60/d  →  d = 60/tan(25) = 60/0.466 = 128.7 m

Choosing the method: a decision routine

Most lost trigonometry marks come from choosing the wrong tool, not from arithmetic. The routine below takes ten seconds and removes the guesswork:

  1. Is there a right angle? If not, the question needs the sine or cosine rule (a different topic) — do not force SOHCAHTOA onto a triangle without a right angle.
  2. What do you know — two sides, or a side and an angle? Two sides with no angle means Pythagoras. A side and an angle means trigonometry.
  3. Which ratio? Mark the known side and the target relative to the given angle, then pick the ratio containing both: sin uses opposite and hypotenuse, cos uses adjacent and hypotenuse, tan uses opposite and adjacent.
  4. What is the unknown — a side or an angle? A side comes from multiplying; an angle needs the inverse function.

Worked example. A roof rafter is 4.5 m long and meets the horizontal at 38°. Find the vertical rise and the horizontal run.

rise: sin(38) = rise/4.5  →  rise = 4.5 sin(38) = 2.77 m
run:  cos(38) = run/4.5   →  run = 4.5 cos(38) = 3.55 m
check: 2.77² + 3.55² = 7.67 + 12.60 = 20.27 ~ 4.5²

Worked example 2 (finding the angle of a ladder). A 6 m ladder reaches 5.2 m up a wall. Find the angle it makes with the ground.

sin(θ) = 5.2/6 = 0.867  →  θ = 60.1 °

Multi-step problems: Pythagoras and trigonometry together

Many questions need both tools: Pythagoras to find a side in one triangle, trigonometry to use it in another. The method: draw and label every triangle, find the shared side first, then proceed.

Worked example. A ladder 5 m long leans against a wall, with its foot 2 m from the wall. Find the height reached and the angle the ladder makes with the ground.

height: h² = 5² - 2² = 25 - 4 = 21  →  h = 4.58 m
angle: cos(θ) = 2/5 = 0.4  →  θ = 66.4 °

Worked example 2 (two triangles). From a point P, the angle of elevation to the top of a building is 30°; from a point Q, 20 m closer, it is 45°. Find the height.

let h be the height and x the distance from Q to the base.
tan(45) = h/x  →  h = x
tan(30) = h/(x + 20)
h = (x + 20) tan(30) = (h + 20)(1/√(3))
h √(3) = h + 20  →  h(√(3) - 1) = 20
h = 20/(1.732 - 1) = 20/0.732 = 27.3 m

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Pythagoras) A right-angled triangle has legs 9 and 12. Find the hypotenuse. Answer: √(81 + 144) = √225 = 15.
  2. (Leg) Hypotenuse 17, one leg 8. Find the other. Answer: √(289 − 64) = 15.
  3. (Ratio) Angle 28°, adjacent 15 cm. Find the opposite side. Answer: tan 28 = o/15 → o = 15 × 0.532 = 7.98 cm.
  4. (Angle) Opposite 7, hypotenuse 10. Find the angle. Answer: sin θ = 0.7 → θ = 44.4°.
  5. (Exact) Find cos 30° exactly. Answer: √3/2.
  6. (Elevation) From 25 m away, the angle of elevation to a tree top is 40°. Find the height. Answer: 25 tan 40 = 25 × 0.839 = 21.0 m.
  7. (3D) A cuboid is 2 cm by 3 cm by 6 cm. Find its space diagonal. Answer: √(4 + 9 + 36) = √49 = 7 cm.
  8. (Combined) A ship sails 30 km east then 40 km north. Find its distance from the start and the bearing of its final position. Answer: distance = 50 km; tan θ = 40/30 → θ = 53.1°, bearing 053°.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Calculator mode: check DEG, not RAD or GRAD, before any trigonometric calculation. A radian answer is usually obviously wrong (tiny or huge), but only if you check.
  • Wrong ratio: label the sides relative to the angle before choosing SOH, CAH or TOA; picking by habit is the commonest trigonometry error.
  • Hypotenuse identification: the hypotenuse is opposite the right angle, not necessarily the longest-looking side on the diagram.
  • Pythagoras with the hypotenuse as a leg: c² = a² + b² only when c is the hypotenuse; finding a leg requires subtraction.
  • Rounding early: keep full calculator accuracy until the final answer; round to 3 s.f. (or 1 d.p. for angles unless told otherwise).
  • Angle of depression drawn from the wrong line: it is measured from the horizontal, not from the cliff face; the alternate-angle equality fixes the geometry.
  • Exact values with decimals: "exact" means surds and fractions, not 0.866; leaving √3/2 is required.
  • Missing units and labels: state cm, m, km and degrees; name the side or angle found, especially in multi-step problems.

Label the triangle before you reach for a ratio

Right-angled trigonometry is not three formulas to memorise; it is one decision made three times: which side am I given, which do I want, and which ratio connects them. Every error in this topic is a labelling error made before any calculation starts.

Only the hypotenuse is fixed. It is the side opposite the right angle, and it is always the longest. "Opposite" and "adjacent" are relative to the angle you are working with: in the figure, the side BC is opposite θ and AB is adjacent to it. Put the angle at C instead and those two swap. Annotate the diagram with O, A and H in pencil before choosing anything.

The ratios are ratios, which is why they work at any size. Similar triangles taught that corresponding sides scale together — double every side and the ratio stays the same. That is precisely why sin 30° is ½ for a triangle of any size:

sin θ = opposite / hypotenuse Key: θ = the angle inside the triangle; opposite = the side across from θ; hypotenuse = the side opposite the right angle.
cos θ = adjacent / hypotenuse Key: adjacent = the side next to θ that is not the hypotenuse.
tan θ = opposite / adjacent Key: the only ratio that does not use the hypotenuse.

Choosing in one step. Given an angle and one side, mark on the diagram which two sides the question involves, then read off: two sides with the hypotenuse means sine or cosine; two sides without it means tangent. Use the inverse function when the angle is the unknown.

Worked example. A ladder 5.0 m long leans against a wall, making 68° with the ground. How far up the wall does it reach, and how far is its foot from the wall?

height is opposite the 68° angle, ladder is the hypotenuse:

sin 68° = h / 5.0, so h = 5.0 × sin 68° = 5.0 × 0.9272 = 4.6 m

distance from the wall is adjacent:

cos 68° = d / 5.0, so d = 5.0 × cos 68° = 5.0 × 0.3746 = 1.9 m

Check with Pythagoras: 4.6² + 1.9² = 21.2 + 3.6 = 24.8 ≈ 25 = 5.0². That thirty-second check catches a swapped ratio every time, and the two answers being 4.6 and 1.9 rather than a plausible pair like 4.6 and 4.4 is exactly what the check is for.

The special angles come from two triangles. A 45-45-90 triangle with legs 1 gives sin 45° = 1/√2. Half of an equilateral triangle of side 2 gives sides 1, √3 and 2, hence sin 30° = ½, cos 30° = √3/2 and tan 60° = √3. These are worth deriving once so they are not three more things to memorise.

Where marks are lost. The calculator in radians or grads — check the mode before the first question, not after. Using the adjacent side when the question needs the opposite, because the labels were never written on the diagram. And rounding at 4.6 m then using 4.6 in Pythagoras: keep the full value and round only the answer.

Pythagoras' theorem in more depth

Pythagoras' theorem states that in a right-angled triangle the square of the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides, so c² = a² + b², where c is the hypotenuse. The theorem is used in two directions: to find a missing side when the triangle is known to be right-angled, and to test whether a triangle is right-angled at all. The subsections below cover both directions, the common number patterns, and the errors that cost marks.

Finding the hypotenuse

When the two shorter sides are known, add their squares and take the square root. For a triangle with shorter sides 5 cm and 12 cm, the hypotenuse is √(5² + 12²) = √(25 + 144) = √169 = 13 cm. The hypotenuse is always the longest side and always opposite the right angle, so it is the side that is added, not subtracted, in the calculation.

Finding a shorter side

When the hypotenuse and one shorter side are known, subtract the square of the known shorter side from the square of the hypotenuse, then take the square root. For a hypotenuse of 13 cm and a side of 5 cm, the missing side is √(13² − 5²) = √(169 − 25) = √144 = 12 cm. Write the subtraction out in full, because the most common error in this type of question is to add the squares by mistake.

Testing whether a triangle is right-angled

The converse of Pythagoras' theorem says that if the square of the longest side equals the sum of the squares of the other two, the triangle is right-angled. For sides 6, 8 and 10, the check is 6² + 8² = 36 + 64 = 100 = 10², so the triangle is right-angled. For sides 7, 8 and 10, the check is 49 + 64 = 113, which is greater than 100, so the triangle is acute and not right-angled. Always compare the squares of the longest side with the others.

Pythagorean triples

A Pythagorean triple is a set of three whole numbers that satisfy a² + b² = c². The most used are 3, 4, 5; 5, 12, 13; 8, 15, 17; and 7, 24, 25. Any multiple of a triple is also a triple, so 6, 8, 10 and 9, 12, 15 are triples. Recognising a triple lets you give an exact answer with no square root, which is often what the question wants when the sides are whole numbers.

Pythagoras in a problem with several triangles

Some questions need the theorem twice, because the first right-angled triangle gives a side that is needed in the second. For example, a rectangle 9 cm by 12 cm has a diagonal of √(9² + 12²) = 15 cm. If a second triangle uses that diagonal as one of its sides, the same method applies again. Mark the sides you have found on the diagram before starting the next step, so each calculation has its numbers ready.

Real-world problems with Pythagoras

A ladder leaning against a wall, a diagonal across a field and the straight-line distance between two towns are all Pythagoras problems once the right angle is identified. Draw the triangle, label the hypotenuse as the longest side, and state which right angle the theorem is being used at. A question that describes a route going east then north is a right-angled triangle formed by the two legs and the straight line between the ends.

Rounding and giving the answer

Leave square roots exact if the question asks for an exact answer, and give a decimal to the accuracy the question states. A calculation that gives √50 can be left as 5√2 for an exact answer, or written as 7.07 to 3 significant figures for a decimal answer. Do the rounding only at the last step, because rounding an intermediate square root and then squaring it can change the final answer.

Common errors with Pythagoras

The errors that lose marks are forgetting the square root at the end, adding when the question needs a subtraction, and applying the theorem to a triangle that is not right-angled. Check the answer by reversing the calculation: square the two shorter sides, add them, and confirm the result equals the square of the hypotenuse. A quick reversal catches most slips.

Trigonometric ratios in more depth

The sine, cosine and tangent ratios connect an angle in a right-angled triangle to the ratio of two sides. They are defined by sin θ = opposite ÷ hypotenuse, cos θ = adjacent ÷ hypotenuse and tan θ = opposite ÷ adjacent, and the calculator supplies the values. The subsections below cover naming the sides, the two directions of use (finding a side and finding an angle), and why the ratios depend only on the angle.

Naming the sides from the angle

The three sides are named from the point of view of the angle θ you are using. The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle and is always the longest. The opposite side is the one across from θ, and the adjacent side is the one next to θ that is not the hypotenuse. The same side is the opposite side for one angle and the adjacent side for the other acute angle, so name the sides again for each angle rather than once for the whole triangle.

Finding a side when an angle is known

Choose the ratio that uses the side you know and the side you want. If the hypotenuse is 10 cm and the angle is 30°, and you want the opposite side, use sin 30° = opposite ÷ 10, so the opposite side is 10 × sin 30° = 10 × 0.5 = 5 cm. Writing the ratio first, with the unknown alone on one side, is the step that keeps the working correct.

Finding an angle from a ratio

When two sides are known, find the ratio and use the inverse function on the calculator. For opposite 7 and adjacent 24, tan θ = 7 ÷ 24 = 0.2917, so θ = tan⁻¹(0.2917) = 16.3° to 1 decimal place. Use sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹ or tan⁻¹ according to the pair of sides, and never take the inverse of a ratio that you have not first worked out.

Setting the calculator to degrees

Every trigonometry question in this note uses degrees, so the calculator must be in degree mode before any value is found. A calculator in radian mode gives sin 30 = −0.988, which is a wrong answer that looks like a real value. Check the mode at the start of each exam and again if an answer looks unreasonable. A quick test is that sin 30 should return 0.5 in degree mode.

Why the ratios depend only on the angle

Two right-angled triangles with the same angle are similar, so the ratio of opposite to hypotenuse is the same in both. A triangle with a hypotenuse of 10 and opposite of 5 has the same sin θ as one with hypotenuse 20 and opposite 10. This is why a table of sine values works for every triangle, and it is the reason the ratios can be used to find unknown sides.

Complementary angles

In a right-angled triangle the two acute angles add to 90°, so each is the complement of the other. This gives sin θ = cos (90° − θ) and cos θ = sin (90° − θ). For example, sin 30° = cos 60° = 0.5. The relationship is useful for checking a value, and it explains why sine and cosine are the same curve shifted by 90°.

Tangent as sine over cosine

The tangent ratio is the sine divided by the cosine, because tan θ = (opposite ÷ hypotenuse) ÷ (adjacent ÷ hypotenuse) = opposite ÷ adjacent. This is the form to use when a question gives the tangent of an angle and asks for a side, and it also explains why tangent is undefined at 90°, where the adjacent side would have length zero.

Trigonometry in three dimensions

Many three-dimensional questions are answered by finding a right-angled triangle inside a solid and then using the methods already covered. The skill is to see the triangle, not to learn a new rule. The subsections below cover the angle between a line and a plane, the diagonal of a solid, and the choice of triangle in a pyramid or cone.

Finding a right-angled triangle inside a solid

In a cuboid, a cone or a pyramid, pick the triangle that contains both the length you want and a length you know. The triangle must have a right angle, and that right angle is often at a vertex where an edge meets the base or where the height meets the base. Draw the triangle on its own, separate from the solid, with the known lengths marked on it. This makes the method the same as the two-dimensional case.

The diagonal of a cuboid

A cuboid with sides 3 cm, 4 cm and 12 cm has a base diagonal of √(3² + 4²) = 5 cm. The space diagonal is then found using the base diagonal and the vertical edge: √(5² + 12²) = √169 = 13 cm. Two applications of Pythagoras give the answer, and the first triangle lies flat on the base while the second stands on its edge.

The angle between a line and the base

To find the angle a space diagonal makes with the base, first find the base diagonal, then use the triangle formed by the vertical height, the base diagonal and the space diagonal. For a box with a base diagonal of 10 cm and a vertical height of 12 cm, the angle is tan θ = 12 ÷ 10 = 1.2, so θ = tan⁻¹(1.2) = 50.2°. The angle is measured between the line and the base, not the vertical.

Heights in pyramids and cones

The vertical height of a pyramid or cone meets the base at a right angle, so it forms a right-angled triangle with a line from the centre of the base to a corner or to the edge. For a square-based pyramid with base side 10 cm, the distance from the centre of the base to a corner is √(5² + 5²) = √50 = 7.07 cm to 2 decimal places. The slant edge then uses that distance and the vertical height.

Choosing the triangle that contains the answer

Ask what you need to find, then identify the triangle whose sides include it. If the question asks for an angle in a plane through the solid, use the triangle in that plane. If it asks for a length along a diagonal of the base, use the triangle in the base. Writing down the triangle you have chosen before any calculation prevents the common error of using lengths from two different triangles in one step.

Sketching a three-dimensional figure

A clear sketch is worth marks, because it shows the examiner which triangle you are using. Draw the solid as a simple outline, use dashed lines for hidden edges, and mark the right angle with a small square. Label the lengths you know and the one you want. A sketch that is a neat outline with the triangle shaded is enough, and it does not need to be drawn to scale.

Checking the three-dimensional answer

A space diagonal must be longer than any edge of the solid, and an angle with the base must lie between 0° and 90°. In the cuboid example, 13 cm is longer than the 12 cm edge, which confirms the calculation. An answer that is shorter than an edge, or an angle above 90° for a line to the base, shows a wrong triangle or a swapped length.

Accuracy, units and reporting answers

A correct method can still lose the final mark through rounding too early, leaving out a unit or giving the wrong degree of accuracy. The syllabus asks for answers to a stated accuracy, and the examiner checks the final line against the question. The subsections below give the rules for rounding, units and presentation that apply to every right-angled trigonometry question.

Working with the calculator's full value

Keep the full calculator value in memory and round only the final answer, or round to at least one more significant figure than the answer requires. If a side is found as 7.0711… and then used in a second calculation, the rounded 7.07 can give a final answer that is one unit out. Use the stored value where the calculator allows it, or write intermediate answers to four significant figures at least.

Significant figures and decimal places

Read the question carefully for the accuracy it requires. "Give your answer to 3 significant figures" means the first three non-zero digits, so 16.2849 becomes 16.3 and 0.0034567 becomes 0.00346. "Give your answer to 1 decimal place" means one digit after the point, so 16.2849 becomes 16.3. The two rules differ for numbers below 1 and for numbers that are whole.

Giving exact answers

When an answer is a surd or uses an exact trigonometric value, give it exactly if the question asks for an exact value. A hypotenuse of √50 simplifies to 5√2, and sin 30° is exactly 1/2. If the question asks for a decimal, round the exact value at the end. An exact answer is always acceptable where the question says "exact", and a decimal is not.

Units in the final answer

Every length answer needs a unit, and the unit must match the question. If the sides are in centimetres, the answer is in centimetres, and an area is in square centimetres. A common error is to convert the unit partway through a calculation and forget to convert the final answer, so state the unit next to the number at every step and check it at the end.

Angles and the form of the answer

An angle answer is given in degrees to the accuracy asked for, with the degree sign. For bearings, the answer has three figures and is measured clockwise from north, as covered in the mensuration note. An angle of elevation or depression is given as a single angle from the horizontal, so check that the question asks for the angle from the horizontal and not from the vertical.

Estimating before calculating

Estimate the answer before using the calculator, so a wrong value is obvious. A side opposite a 30° angle in a triangle with hypotenuse 10 must be less than half the hypotenuse, so the answer cannot be 8. Estimating takes seconds and is the simplest protection against a wrong mode, a swapped ratio or a misplaced decimal point.

Checking the answer against the diagram

Compare the answer with the diagram once it is found. The longest side must be the hypotenuse, an angle opposite a longer side must be larger, and a side in a triangle with a 60° angle must not be shorter than one opposite a 30° angle. A result that contradicts the diagram means the wrong ratio or the wrong side was used, and the calculation should be repeated before the answer is written.

Presenting the working for method marks

Write each step on its own line: the formula or ratio, the substitution, the calculation, and the result with its unit. The method marks are given for the ratio and the substitution, even if the final number is wrong, so a clear working is worth marks in its own right. A bare final answer, even when it is correct, can earn only the marks for the answer.

title: Exam technique: Representation via Numerical Measures
content:
### What earns the marks
For skewness direction, mean vs median comparison stated earns the mark. For box plots, all five values labelled earn one mark and the skew comment earns the second. For outlier checks, the fence calculation shown earns the method mark.
### Traps
Error: skew direction flipped. Correction: tail side names the skew. Error: quartiles mislabeled on plots. Correction: order min, Q1, median, Q3, max. Error: max value called an outlier by eye. Correction: test against the fence.

title: Oscillations and Waves II — Study Notes
content:
Oscillations and Waves II

Edexcel International A Level Physics — Unit 5 (WPH15), sat at A2: oscillations and SHM. The superposition recap at the end is AS Unit 2 (WPH12) revision.

Simple harmonic motion (17.1)

A body oscillates with simple harmonic motion when its acceleration is proportional to its displacement x and directed towards the equilibrium position: a = −ω²x. The angular frequency is ω = 2πf, and the displacement is x = x₀ sin ωt, where x₀ is the amplitude.

The velocity is v = ±ω√(x₀² − x²), and the maximum acceleration is a₀ = ω²x₀. Velocity is zero at the extremes and maximum at equilibrium. Acceleration is maximum at the extremes and zero at equilibrium.

Example: amplitude 0.030 m and frequency 2.0 Hz give a₀ = (2π × 2.0)² × 0.030 ≈ 4.7 m s⁻².

Energy in SHM (17.2)

Kinetic energy is greatest at the equilibrium position, where speed is greatest. Potential energy is greatest at the extremes. The total energy is constant: E = ½mω²x₀², and it is shared between kinetic and potential energy as the body oscillates.

Example: a 0.20 kg mass with ω = 10 rad s⁻¹ and x₀ = 0.050 m has E = ½ × 0.20 × 10² × 0.050² = 0.025 J.

Damping, forced oscillations and resonance (17.3)

Damping removes energy from an oscillator. Light damping gives decaying oscillations. Critical damping returns the system to equilibrium in the shortest time without oscillating. Heavy damping is also non-oscillatory but slower.

A forced oscillator is driven by a periodic force. When the driving frequency equals the natural frequency, the amplitude is at its maximum, which is resonance. Greater damping lowers the peak and broadens the resonance curve.

Exam tips: state which quantity is maximum or zero at each point of the cycle. For resonance, always name the driving frequency relative to the natural frequency.

Waves: the superposition ideas

Progressive vs Stationary

Progressive waves transfer energy; stationary waves store it in loops. Stationary patterns arise from two identical waves travelling in opposite directions (reflections on strings, air columns).

PropertyProgressiveStationary
Amplitudesame for all pointsvaries: nodes zero, antinodes max
Phasevaries along wavesame within a loop, π flip across nodes
Energytransferredtrapped

Harmonics

A string fixed at both ends: f₁ = v/2L, then 2f₁, 3f₁… Closed pipes resonate at odd multiples; open pipes at all multiples.

Superposition Applications

  • Young's double slit: x = λD/a — evidence light is a wave
  • Diffraction grating: d sin θ = nλ — resolution of spectra
  • Noise-cancelling headphones: destructive interference of antiphase sound

Polarization Applications

Polaroid sunglasses cut glare from horizontal surfaces; stress analysis in plastics; LCD screens control light with twisted polarizers. Malus' law I = I₀cos²θ.

Exam tips: 'explain' marks want the physics: path difference, phase, node/antinode conditions — not just formula substitution.

title: Exam technique: Data Handling
content:
### What earns the marks
For averages, the total shown earns a mark before any division. For even-count medians, the two middle values identified earn the method mark. For grouped data, the modal class stated as an interval earns full credit; single numbers score nothing. For cumulative frequency, the position formula (n + 1) / 2 quoted earns the method mark before reading off.
### Traps
Error: total given as the mean. Correction: divide by the count last. Error: 3rd value picked as median of six values. Correction: average the 3rd and 4th. Error: 40th value read for the median of 80. Correction: position 40.5. Error: quartiles read for median and vice versa. Correction: 20th/60th are quartiles at n = 80.
### Worked example
Four values are 2, 3, 3, 5, 8, 9 (six values in total). The median is the average of the 3rd and 4th values: (3 + 5) / 2 = 4. For a mean of 9 from four values, the total must be 36: write the sum first, then divide by 4. Both steps earn their own marks.
### Check yourself
Eighty values are ordered. Which values are the quartiles? Using the n/4 and 3n/4 positions gives the 20th and 60th values, so the 20th is the lower quartile and the 60th is the upper quartile. Quote the position before reading the value.

title: Databases — Study Notes
content:
`# Databases

Relational Basics

Tables (relations) of records with fields. Keys:

  • Primary key: unique identifier
  • Foreign key: references another table's PK — creates relationships
  • Candidate/secondary keys: other unique identifiers

Normalisation

  • 1NF: atomic values, no repeating groups
  • 2NF: 1NF + no partial dependency on a composite key
  • 3NF: 2NF + no transitive dependencies (non-key → non-key)

Example: (StudentID, Course, CourseFee) has CourseFee depending on Course, not StudentID — move course data to its own table (3NF).

SQL

SELECT name, grade FROM students
  WHERE grade >= 'A' ORDER BY name;
INSERT INTO students VALUES (...);
UPDATE students SET grade = 'B' WHERE id = 5;
DELETE FROM students WHERE id = 5;

Joins combine tables: FROM students s JOIN enrolments e ON s.id = e.sid.

Transactions

ACID: Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (rules hold), Isolation (no interference), Durability (committed = permanent). Record locking prevents conflicting simultaneous edits.

Exam tips: justify each normal form step with the dependency removed; write SQL with correct WHERE clauses to avoid accidental full-table updates.

title: Programming and Algorithms — Study Notes
content:
`# Programming and Algorithms

Design Approaches

  • Top-down (stepwise refinement): decompose into modules — planned structure
  • Object-oriented: classes encapsulating state + behaviour — reusability
  • WAD (write all down): rapid prototyping — evolves during coding

Pseudocode Conventions

DECLARE x : INTEGER
IF x > 10 THEN ... ELSE ... ENDIF
WHILE ... ENDWHILE
FOR i ← 1 TO n ... NEXT i
FUNCTION f(a) RETURNS INTEGER

Searching

  • Linear: check each item, O(n), works unsorted
  • Binary: halve a sorted list each step, O(log n)

Example: 1,000,000 items: binary search needs ≤ 20 comparisons.

Sorting

AlgorithmBestAverageIdea
BubbleO(n)O(n²)swap neighbours
InsertionO(n)O(n²)insert into sorted prefix
MergeO(n log n)O(n log n)divide and merge

Merge sort example: [5,2,9,1] → [5,2][9,1] → [2,5][1,9] → [1,2,5,9].

Recursion

A function calling itself with a base case. Factorial: f(0)=1, f(n)=n·f(n−1). Stack frames handle state.

Exam tips: state the Big-O and justify it; for traces, tabulate variable changes per iteration.

Testing with normal, boundary and erroneous data

Normal test data is typical valid input that the program should accept and process correctly. Boundary (extreme) test data sits at the edges of the valid range, such as the lowest and highest permitted values, because errors often occur there. Erroneous test data is invalid input that the program should reject, such as text entered where a number is required.

A trace table records the value of each variable at each step of an algorithm. Tracing a algorithm by hand with test data shows where it departs from the intended result, and it is a common exam task.

Exam tip: a complete test plan includes all three kinds of data, with the expected output written beside each test value.

Worked example: tracing a binary search

Search for 23 in the sorted list 2, 5, 8, 12, 16, 23, 38, 56, 72, 91. The first middle position is (0 + 9) ÷ 2 = 4 (rounded down), which holds 16. Since 23 is greater than 16, the lower bound becomes 5. The next middle is (5 + 9) ÷ 2 = 7, which holds 56. Since 23 is less than 56, the upper bound becomes 6. The next middle is (5 + 6) ÷ 2 = 5, which holds 23, so the item is found after 3 comparisons. A linear search of the same list would need 6 comparisons.

Worked example: bubble sort passes

Sort 5, 1, 4, 2, 8 into ascending order. In the first pass the algorithm compares adjacent pairs and swaps them when they are out of order, giving 1, 4, 2, 5, 8. The second pass gives 1, 2, 4, 5, 8. A third pass makes no swaps, which shows the list is sorted. Stopping early when a pass has no swaps is a common improvement and is worth stating in an answer.

Worked example: recursion

The factorial function is defined as factorial(n) = n × factorial(n − 1), with the base case factorial(0) = 1. Then factorial(4) = 4 × factorial(3) = 4 × 3 × factorial(2) and so on until the base case is reached, giving 24. A recursive routine must always have a base case, otherwise it never stops and the stack overflows.

Exam point: a trace table with one column per variable is the clearest way to show an algorithm's steps, and it earns method marks even when the final answer is wrong.

title: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Probability
content:
Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Probability

Probability measures how likely an event is on a scale from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). The IGCSE questions build from single events to combined ones — two dice, two draws without replacement, "at least one" — and the toolkit is small but must be used precisely: the complement rule, the addition rule for mutually exclusive events, the multiplication rule for independent ones, and tree diagrams for everything with stages. This note builds the topic from zero with every rule justified and every standard question type worked.

The probability scale and notation

P(event) = number of favourable outcomes / total outcomes
         (when outcomes are equally likely)

0 <= P(A) <= 1
P(not A) = 1 - P(A)        (the complement rule)

Probabilities are written as fractions, decimals or percentages — but keep one form within a question. The complement rule is the most powerful single line in the topic: "at least one" is almost always easier as 1 − P(none).

Worked example. A bag has 5 red, 3 blue and 2 green counters. Find P(red) and P(not red).

total = 10
P(red) = 5/10 = 1/2
P(not red) = 1 - 1/2 = 1/2  (check: 3 + 2 = 5 of 10)

Relative frequency and expected frequency

relative frequency = number of times the event occurred
                     / total number of trials

expected number = probability x number of trials

Relative frequency estimates probability from experiment; it approaches the theoretical value as trials increase (the law of large numbers). Questions ask you to compare an experimental relative frequency with a theoretical probability and comment on the discrepancy — small samples fluctuate, large samples converge.

Worked example. A biased die is rolled 200 times; a six appears 50 times. Estimate P(six) and predict the number of sixes in 500 rolls.

relative frequency = 50/200 = 0.25
expected in 500 = 0.25 x 500 = 125

Combined events: the two rules

RuleWhen to use itFormula
Addition (OR)mutually exclusive events — cannot both happenP(A or B) = P(A) + P(B)
Multiplication (AND)independent events — one does not affect the otherP(A and B) = P(A) × P(B)

The words "or" and "and" map onto add and multiply, but the conditions matter: if events are not mutually exclusive, subtract the overlap; if they are not independent, the second probability changes (see trees below).

Worked example 1. A fair die is rolled once. Find P(3 or 4).

mutually exclusive: 1/6 + 1/6 = 2/6 = 1/3

Worked example 2. Two fair coins are tossed. Find P(both heads).

independent: 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/4

Worked example 3 (not mutually exclusive). From a standard pack, find P(a heart or a king).

P(heart) = 13/52, P(king) = 4/52, P(heart and king) = 1/52
P(heart or king) = 13/52 + 4/52 - 1/52 = 16/52 = 4/13

Tree diagrams

Trees handle multi-stage experiments, especially without replacement. Multiply along the branches for a sequence, add between branches for alternative ways to get the same outcome.

Worked example 1 (with replacement). A bag has 3 red and 2 blue counters. Two are drawn with replacement. Find P(two red) and P(one of each).

P(RR) = 3/5 x 3/5 = 9/25
P(RB) = 3/5 x 2/5 = 6/25;  P(BR) = 2/5 x 3/5 = 6/25
P(one of each) = 6/25 + 6/25 = 12/25

Worked example 2 (without replacement). Same bag, two counters drawn without replacement. Find P(two red) and P(one of each).

P(RR) = 3/5 x 2/4 = 6/20 = 3/10
P(RB) = 3/5 x 2/4 = 6/20;  P(BR) = 2/5 x 3/4 = 6/20
P(one of each) = 12/20 = 3/5

The denominators drop by one on the second draw without replacement — that is the entire difference, and forgetting it is the standard error.

Sample space diagrams

A sample space diagram lists every possible outcome, so probabilities can be counted rather than guessed. For two dice, a two-way grid of 36 cells shows each pair; shading the cells that satisfy an event turns the question into counting squares. The method protects against the commonest combined-event error — treating non-equally-likely outcomes as equally likely.

Worked example. Two fair dice are rolled. Find P(total = 7).

total outcomes = 6 x 6 = 36
totals of 7: (1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2), (6,1) = 6 outcomes
P(total 7) = 6/36 = 1/6

Worked example 2 (sums). From the same grid, find P(total is more than 10).

totals 11 or 12: (5,6), (6,5), (6,6) = 3 outcomes
P = 3/36 = 1/12

The grid also answers difference and product questions: mark the cells whose difference is 2, or whose product is even, and count. Writing the grid out takes a minute and removes the guesswork from every part of the question.

Two-way tables and Venn diagrams

A two-way table classifies individuals by two attributes at once — boys and girls against glasses and no glasses — with totals in the margins. Reading probabilities from it is a matter of restricting attention to the right row, column or cell:

  • P(A and B): the cell where the row and column meet, over the grand total.
  • P(A or B): the sum of the cells in A plus the cells in B minus the overlap, over the grand total.
  • P(A | B): the A-cell inside B's row (or column) over B's total.

Venn diagrams do the same job for sets: the intersection is "and" (multiply along a branch or read the overlap), the union is "or" (add the regions). Choosing between the two representations is a matter of what the question gives; both are equally valid, and the arithmetic is identical once the numbers sit in the right places.

Conditional probability

Conditional probability asks for the chance of A given that B has happened:

P(A | B) = P(A and B) / P(B)

Two-way tables are the friendliest setting: restrict attention to the row or column named by the condition, then divide by that row or column's total.

Worked example. 60 students: 25 study French, 35 study Spanish, 15 study both. Find P(studies French | studies Spanish).

given Spanish: restrict to the 35 Spanish students
of those, 15 also study French
P(French | Spanish) = 15/35 = 3/7

Worked example 2 (two-way table). A table shows 40 boys (12 play chess) and 30 girls (18 play chess). Find P(plays chess | girl).

restrict to girls: 30; chess players among them: 18
P = 18/30 = 3/5

Independent events and the multiplication rule

Two events are independent when the outcome of one does not change the probability of the other. The test is arithmetic: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B) exactly when they are independent. Questions often give the separate probabilities and ask you to check independence, or give P(A), P(B) and P(A and B) and ask whether the events are independent.

if P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B)  ->  independent
if not                        ->  not independent (associated)

Worked example. P(rain) = 0.3, P(late) = 0.2, P(rain and late) = 0.06. Are the events independent?

P(rain) x P(late) = 0.3 x 0.2 = 0.06
0.06 = 0.06, so the events are independent.

"At least one" problems

The complement trick: P(at least one) = 1 − P(none).

Worked example. A die is rolled twice. Find P(at least one six).

P(no six) = (5/6) x (5/6) = 25/36
P(at least one six) = 1 - 25/36 = 11/36

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Complement) P(A) = 0.35. Find P(not A). Answer: 0.65.
  2. (Single event) A bag has 4 green and 6 yellow balls. Find P(green). Answer: 4/10 = 2/5.
