title: IGCSE Chemistry: The Periodic Table
content:
IGCSE Chemistry: The Periodic Table

Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry 0620 (2026–2028), Extended route, Topic 8 The Periodic Table: statement 8.1 Arrangement of elements, 8.2 Group I properties, 8.3 Group VII properties, 8.4 Transition elements, and 8.5 Noble gases. The Periodic Table is chemistry's master chart — position predicts behaviour — and this note derives every trend from electron structure rather than asking you to memorise it. Each group's properties are traced down the group with the particle-level reason, because Paper 4 asks "explain the trend", never "state the trend".

Arrangement: periods, groups and the prediction power

Elements are arranged in order of increasing proton number in rows (periods) and columns (groups). Two structural facts run everything: elements in the same group have the same number of outer-shell electrons (hence similar chemistry), and the period number equals the number of occupied shells. Across a period, the character changes from metallic (left) to non-metallic (right); group number gives the ion charge (Group I → +1, Group VII → −1 for monatomic ions).

Group I: the alkali metals

Trend down Group IPatternWhy (electron structure)
ReactivityIncreases (Li < Na < K)The outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded, so it is lost more easily
Melting/boiling pointDecreasesThe metallic bond weakens as ions get larger and the delocalised electrons are further from the nuclei
DensityIncreases (they float or sink accordingly)Mass grows faster than atomic radius
Reactions of Group I with water - the pattern, worked:

  2Li + 2H₂O -> 2LiOH + H₂       lithium: steady fizz, floats
  2Na + 2H₂O -> 2NaOH + H₂       sodium: vigorous, melts into a ball
  2K  + 2H₂O -> 2KOH  + H₂       potassium: lilac flame, skitters

  The products are the group's hydroxide (an alkali, so the name) and
  hydrogen. Down the group the fizzing gets more vigorous - the outer
  electron is lost more easily, so the reaction with water speeds up.

  Burning in oxygen: lithium oxide Li₂O, sodium peroxide Na₂O₂,
  potassium superoxide KO₂ - the pattern of increasing reactivity also
  shows in the oxide formed.

Group VII: the halogens

Trend down Group VIIPatternWhy
ReactivityDecreases (F > Cl > Br > I)The outer shell is further from the nucleus, so an incoming electron is attracted less strongly
ColourDarkens: pale yellow-green gas → red-brown liquid → black solidMolecular size and polarisability increase
Boiling pointIncreasesLarger molecules → stronger intermolecular forces → more energy needed
Displacement reactions - the reactivity rule, worked:

  A more reactive halogen DISPLACES a less reactive halide from solution.

  Cl₂(aq) + 2KBr(aq) -> 2KCl(aq) + Br₂(aq)
    chlorine displaces bromine: the solution turns orange-brown.
  Cl₂(aq) + 2KI(aq)  -> 2KCl(aq) + I₂(aq)
    iodine formed: with hexane/hexane layer it shows violet.
  Br₂(aq) + 2KI(aq)  -> 2KBr(aq) + I₂(aq)
  Br₂(aq) + 2KCl(aq) -> no reaction (bromine is less reactive than chlorine)

  Rule: the higher element in the group displaces the lower one's ions.
  Exam answers quote the observation, not just the equation - name the
  colour change.

Group VIII: the noble gases

The noble gases (He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn) are monatomic gases with full outer shells — hence almost completely unreactive. Their existence and inertness are the proof that a full outer shell confers stability — the electron-configuration explanation that underpins all of bonding.

Transition elements

  • Physical: high density, high melting point, strong metallic bonding (partly from their delocalised electrons).
  • Chemical: form coloured compounds (Cu²⁺ blue, Fe²⁺ pale green, Fe³⁺ yellow), show variable oxidation numbers (iron(II) and iron(III)), and act as catalysts (iron in the Haber process, V₂O₅ in the Contact process, nickel in hydrogenation).
Variable oxidation numbers - worked:

  Iron(II) chloride FeCl₂  -> iron is +2
  Iron(III) chloride FeCl₃ -> iron is +3
  Copper(II) sulfate CuSO₄ -> +2 ; copper(I) oxide Cu₂O -> +1

  Roman numeral in the NAME = oxidation number. The same element in two
  oxidation states means two families of compounds - a transition-metal
  signature. Colour changes in redox titrations (e.g. MnO₄⁻ purple to
  Mn²⁺ colourless) exploit these states.

The electron-configuration link is worth stating as a rule of its own, because nearly every explanation in this topic reduces to it. The number of outer electrons equals the group number (Group II elements have two outer electrons and form 2+ ions), and the number of occupied shells equals the period number. Similarity within a group is not a coincidence of mass — it is a consequence of identical outer-shell electron arrangements, which is why lithium and potassium, thousands of mass units apart in behaviour terms, give hydroxides of the same formula type and both release hydrogen from water. Across a period, proton number rises while shells stay the same, so the nucleus pulls electrons in more tightly, the atom shrinks, and metallic character gives way to non-metallic — which is why Period 3 runs from sodium's vigorous water chemistry to chlorine's and argon's total inertness.

Worked example: predicting from position

Question: predict the properties of astatine (At, below iodine in Group VII).

  From the trends down the group:
  - state: solid at room temperature (darker than iodine - black),
  - melting point: higher than iodine's,
  - reactivity: LOWER than iodine (outer electron furthest from nucleus),
  - displacement: iodine would displace astatide from solution, and At
    would NOT displace Cl/Br/I.
  - reaction with hydrogen: At₂ + H₂ -> 2HAt, less readily than iodine's.

Every prediction cites the trend AND the electron-structure reason - that
pair is the mark scheme.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Explaining Group I reactivity with "gets bigger" alone — the mark is outer electron distance/shielding and ease of loss.
  • Confusing Group I and Group VII trends: Group I reactivity increases down; Group VII decreases — keep the electron argument (lose vs gain) straight.
  • Forgetting the colour observations in displacement answers — the visible change is half the marks.
  • Saying noble gases "have full outer shells so they are stable" without connecting to why that stops bonding.
  • Listing transition-metal properties without examples (coloured compounds: name the ion and its colour).
  • Confusing period number (shells) with group number (outer electrons).
  • Claiming Group I metals float or sink universally — density increases down the group, and lithium floats while others sink in water/oil.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Explain why the reactivity of Group I metals increases down the group.

Answer: Each element down the group has one more occupied shell, so the outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded by inner shells. The electrostatic attraction holding the outer electron weakens, so it is lost more readily in reactions — the metal is more reactive.

Question 2 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Explain why the reactivity of Group VII elements decreases down the group.

Answer: Halogens react by gaining an electron into the outer shell. Down the group the outer shell is further from the nucleus and more shielded, so the attraction for an incoming electron is weaker and it is gained less readily — reactivity falls.

Question 3 (Paper 4, 3 marks). Describe what happens when chlorine is added to potassium iodide solution and name the reaction type.

Answer: The solution turns brown as iodine is displaced: Cl₂ + 2KI → 2KCl + I₂. This is a displacement (redox) reaction — chlorine is more reactive and displaces iodine from its salt.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 3 marks). State three characteristic properties of transition elements and give an example of each.

Answer: Form coloured compounds (copper(II) sulfate is blue); show variable oxidation states (iron(II) and iron(III) compounds); act as catalysts (iron in the Haber process).

Question 5 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Explain why noble gases are unreactive.

Answer: Noble gases have full outer electron shells (2 for helium, 8 for the rest). A full outer shell is energetically stable, so the atoms neither lose, gain nor share electrons — there is no bonding advantage — and they exist as monatomic gases.

Question 6 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Compare the melting points of Group I metals and Group VII elements down each group, explaining both trends.

Answer: Group I metals: melting points decrease down the group — atoms grow larger, the metallic bond between positive ions and delocalised electrons weakens. Group VII elements: melting points increase — molecules get larger (Cl₂ → Br₂ → I₂) and the intermolecular forces between molecules strengthen, so more energy is needed to separate them.

The table's metals deserve their own machinery — extraction, corrosion and the reactivity series.

title: IGCSE Chemistry: Organic Chemistry
content:
IGCSE Chemistry: Organic Chemistry

Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry 0620 (2026–2028), Extended route, Topic 11 Organic chemistry: statements 11.1 Formulae, functional groups and terminology, 11.2 Naming organic compounds, 11.3 Fuels, 11.4 Alkanes, 11.5 Alkenes, 11.6 Alcohols, 11.7 Carboxylic acids, and 11.8 Polymers. Organic chemistry is a system, not a list — one structural logic generates every name, formula and reaction in this note. Each homologous series is derived from its general formula, and every reaction shows the functional-group change explicitly.

The organic framework: homologous series and functional groups

A homologous series is a family of similar compounds with the same functional group and general formula, differing by CH₂ units, showing gradual physical-property trends and similar chemistry. A functional group is the atom or group of atoms responsible for the characteristic reactions (C=C for alkenes, –OH for alcohols, –COOH for acids).

SeriesGeneral formulaFunctional groupSuffix
AlkanesCₙH₂ₙ₊₂None (single bonds)-ane
AlkenesCₙH₂ₙC=C-ene
AlcoholsCₙH₂ₙ₊₁OH–OH-ol
Carboxylic acidsCₙH₂ₙ₊₁COOH–COOH-oic acid

Saturated = all single C–C bonds (alkanes); unsaturated = at least one C=C (alkenes). Structural isomers share the molecular formula but have different structural formulae (butane and methylpropane, both C₄H₁₀) — the reason displayed formula alone is not enough. Naming: count the carbons (meth- 1, eth- 2, prop- 3, but- 4), add the suffix for the functional group.

Fuels and fractional distillation

Petroleum = a mixture of hydrocarbons, separated by FRACTIONAL DISTILLATION.

  The crude oil is vaporised and fed into the column:
   - hot at the bottom, cooler at the top;
   - each fraction condenses at the height where its boiling range matches
     the temperature.

  Fractions (lightest at top): refinery gas (C¹-C⁴, bottled gas),
  gasoline/petrol (C⁵-C10, car fuel), naphtha (chemical feedstock),
  kerosene/paraffin (jet fuel), diesel oil (lorry fuel), fuel oil (ships),
  lubricating fraction (oils, waxes), bitumen (road surfaces).

  Trend up the column (towards longer chains):
   - BOILING POINT RISES (bigger molecules, stronger intermolecular forces);
   - VISCOSITY INCREASES (thicker, flows less easily);
   - VOLATILITY FALLS (evaporates less readily);
   - COMBUSTION gets less clean (more soot/carbon).

Fractional cracking breaks long alkane chains into shorter, more useful ones (alkanes + alkenes): C₁₀H₂₂ → C₈H₁₈ + C₂H₄ — driven by the need for petrol and alkene feedstock.

Alkanes: substitution

Alkanes are generally unreactive (strong, non-polar C–C and C–H bonds) but burn (combustion) and undergo substitution with halogens in UV light.

Complete combustion (all hydrocarbons):
  CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O
Incomplete combustion (limited O₂):
  2CH₄ + 3O₂ → 2CO + 4H₂O   (carbon monoxide - toxic)
  or soot (C) forms - a visible flame with yellow tips.

Chlorination of methane (photochemical substitution):
  CH₄ + Cl₂  →  CH₃Cl + HCl (UV light)
  One H is REPLACED by Cl - the definition of substitution. The UV light
  provides the activation energy to split the Cl-Cl bond into radicals.
  Further substitution gives CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃, CCl₄ - the products are a
  mixture, which is why the reaction is poor for synthesis.

Alkenes: addition

Alkenes react via the C=C double bond in addition reactions — two reactants join to give one product (nothing is lost).

Addition to ethene - each with its conditions:

  + bromine (test for unsaturation):
    C₂H₄ + Br₂ → C₂H₄Br₂        (1,2-dibromoethane)
    OBSERVATION: orange bromine water is DECOLOURISED - the test that
    distinguishes alkenes from alkanes.

  + hydrogen (nickel catalyst, heat):
    C₂H₄ + H₂ → C₂H₆            (ethane; hydrogenation - margarine making)

  + steam (phosphoric acid catalyst, heat + pressure):
    C₂H₄ + H₂O → C₂H₅OH         (ethanol)

In every case the double bond opens to single bonds and the atoms add on -
draw the product by "opening" the C=C and attaching one atom to each carbon.

Alcohols

Two production routes for ethanol, with the trade-off the exam always asks:

1. FERMENTATION of glucose (yeast, no oxygen, 25-35 °C):
     C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂
   Advantages: renewable feedstock (sugar/corn), low energy conditions,
   batch process.
   Disadvantages: slow (days), dilute product (needs distilling), depends on
   crop supply and weather.

2. CATALYTIC HYDRATION of ethene (H₃PO₄ catalyst, 300 °C, 60 atm):
     C₂H₄ + H₂O → C₂H₅OH
   Advantages: fast, continuous, high purity and yield.
   Disadvantages: ethene comes from crude oil (finite), high energy/pressure
   costs.

Ethanol itself: burns cleanly (C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O) as a fuel;
a solvent (perfumes, paints); in alcoholic drinks.

Carboxylic acids and esters

Carboxylic acids are weak acids: they react with metals (salt + hydrogen), bases (salt + water) and carbonates (salt + water + carbon dioxide — the fizz test that identifies an acid).

Oxidation of ethanol to ethanoic acid:
  ethanol + [O] → ethanoic acid     e.g. by acidified potassium
  manganate(VII), or by bacterial action in vinegar production (air + 
  Acetobacter).

Esterification (acid + alcohol, concentrated H₂SO₄ catalyst):
  ethanoic acid + ethanol → ethyl ethanoate + water
  CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O

  Naming esters: the FIRST word comes from the ALCOHOL (ethyl, from ethanol),
  the second from the ACID (ethanoate, from ethanoic acid).
  Propyl methanoate = propanol + methanoic acid.

  Esters: sweet smells (fruits, perfumes), solvents, plasticisers.

Polymers

A monomer is the small molecule that repeats; a polymer is the very long chain of joined monomers. Addition polymerisation joins many alkene molecules by opening the double bonds — nothing else is produced.

Deducing the repeat unit - the master method:

  Monomer: propene, CH₂=CH-CH₃
  1. Open the double bond: -CH₂-CH(CH₃)-
  2. Extend the "bonds" at both ends to show the chain continuing:
     [ -CH₂-CH(CH₃)- ]ₙ

  Reverse (monomer from repeat unit): find the two backbone carbons of one
  unit, restore the double bond between them, and cap the ends with the
  substituents that were drawn.

  poly(ethene):  n CH₂=CH₂ → [ -CH₂-CH₂- ]ₙ
  poly(propene): n CH₂=CHCH₃ → [ -CH₂-CH(CH₃)- ]ₙ
  poly(chloroethene) (PVC): n CH₂=CHCl → [ -CH₂-CHCl- ]ₙ

Condensation polymerisation (two different bifunctional monomers):
  a small molecule (usually water) is LOST at each link.
  Nylon (a polyamide): diamine + dicarboxylic acid → nylon + water.
  PET (a polyester): diol + dicarboxylic acid → PET + water.
  Proteins are natural polyamides from amino-acid monomers.

Disposal: plastics are non-biodegradable — landfill accumulates, plastics in the ocean harm wildlife, burning releases toxic gases (HCl from PVC, CO from incomplete combustion). Options: recycling (sorted by type), depolymerisation (PET can be broken back to monomers and re-polymerised), and biodegradable alternatives.

Worked example: one route map, every reaction type

From ethane to ethyl ethanoate:

  ethane --(cracking/heat)-→ ethene      [thermal decomposition]
  ethene + steam --(H₃PO₄, 300 °C)-→ ethanol   [addition / hydration]
  ethanol + [O] --(bacterial)-→ ethanoic acid  [oxidation]
  ethanol + ethanoic acid --(conc. H₂SO₄)-→ ethyl ethanoate [esterification]

  Each arrow names its type, conditions and the functional-group change:
  alkane → alkene (C-C to C=C), alkene → alcohol (C=C to C-OH),
  alcohol → acid (-OH to -COOH), acid + alcohol → ester (-COOH/-OH to
  -COO-). Tracking the functional group through a route map is the skill
  the exam tests.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Forgetting that addition reactions need the C=C — alkanes substitute, alkenes add; mixing them up loses every mark on the question.
  • Bromine water: decolourised by alkenes (addition) but NOT by alkanes — the observation sentence must name the colour loss.
  • Counting general formula wrong for the first members (methane CH₄ fits CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ with n = 1).
  • Writing polymers without the extending bonds at both ends of the repeat unit (it must show continuation).
  • In ester naming, swapping which part comes from the acid and which from the alcohol.
  • Leaving reaction conditions off (UV for substitution, Ni/heat for hydrogenation, concentrated H₂SO₄ for esterification) — conditions are marks.
  • Claiming fermentation is fast/pure — the comparison with catalytic hydration needs both sides.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 4, 3 marks). Define a homologous series and state three general characteristics.

Answer: A homologous series is a family of similar compounds with the same functional group and general formula, each member differing from the next by a CH₂ unit. Characteristics: similar chemical properties; gradual trend in physical properties (boiling point rises with chain length); can be made by similar methods.

Question 2 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Describe the test that distinguishes ethene from ethane, with equations.

Answer: Add aqueous bromine and shake. Ethene decolourises the orange bromine (addition: C₂H₄ + Br₂ → C₂H₄Br₂); ethane shows no change (no reaction in the dark at room temperature). The C=C double bond is responsible for the addition.

Question 3 (Paper 4, 5 marks). Compare fermentation and catalytic hydration as routes to ethanol.

Answer: Fermentation (C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂, yeast, 25–35 °C) uses renewable sugar crops and mild conditions, but is slow, gives dilute ethanol needing distillation, and varies with crop supply. Catalytic hydration (C₂H₄ + H₂O → C₂H₅OH, H₃PO₄, 300 °C, 60 atm) is fast, continuous and high-yield, but depends on crude-oil-derived ethene and costly high-pressure conditions.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Draw the repeat unit of poly(propene) and name the polymerisation type.

Answer: Monomer propene CH₂=CHCH₃ opens at the double bond giving repeat unit [–CH₂–CH(CH₃)–]ₙ, with the chain bonds extending at both ends. This is addition polymerisation — many monomers join with no other product.

Question 5 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Describe how ethyl ethanoate is made and state its uses.

Answer: Warm ethanol with ethanoic acid in the presence of concentrated sulfuric acid catalyst (esterification): CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O. The ester is distilled off. Ethyl ethanoate is used as a solvent (nail-varnish remover), in perfumes and flavourings (sweet smell).

Question 6 (Paper 4, 3 marks). Explain why burning PVC can be more harmful than burning poly(ethene).

Answer: PVC contains chlorine; burning it releases hydrogen chloride gas, which is toxic and forms acidic fumes, plus carbon monoxide from incomplete combustion. Poly(ethene) contains only carbon and hydrogen and burns to CO₂ and water if complete — less acutely toxic though still a CO₂ source.

Organic molecules can be burned as fuels — the next topic is what happens when electrons move instead: electrochemistry.

title: Astronomy and Cosmology — Study Notes
content:
Astronomy and Cosmology

Edexcel International A Level Physics — Unit 5 (WPH15), sat at A2.

Luminosity and Intensity

Luminosity L is total power radiated (W). Intensity at distance d: I = L/(4πd²) — the key to distances.

Standard candles (Cepheid variables, Type Ia supernovae) have known L, so measuring I gives d.

Example: the Sun: I = 1370 W m⁻² at d = 1.5 × 10¹¹ m gives L ≈ 3.9 × 10²⁶ W.

Stellar radii (25.2)

A star radiates as a black body of surface temperature T, so L = 4πR²σT⁴. Rearranged, R = √(L / 4πσT⁴). Luminosity therefore depends on both radius and temperature.

Example: with L = 3.9 × 10²⁶ W and T = 5800 K, R = √(3.9 × 10²⁶ / (4π × 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ × 5800⁴)) ≈ 7.0 × 10⁸ m.

Doubling the temperature at fixed radius multiplies L by 2⁴ = 16. A cool red giant can be far more luminous than the Sun because its radius is very large.

Wien and Stefan–Boltzmann

  • Wien: λ_max T = 2.9 × 10⁻³ m K — hotter stars are bluer
  • Stefan: L = σAT⁴, σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸

Hubble's Law

Galaxies recede with v = Hd, H₀ ≈ 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹. Redshift z = Δλ/λ ≈ v/c for small z.

Example: a galaxy at 100 Mpc recedes at v = 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ × 100 × 3.09 × 10²² ≈ 6800 km s⁻¹.

The Big Bang

Evidence: Hubble expansion, cosmic microwave background (2.7 K), hydrogen/helium abundance. Age estimate: t ≈ 1/H₀ ≈ 14 billion years. The fate question: critical density, Ω.

Exam tips: convert Mpc to metres (×3.09 × 10²²) before Hubble arithmetic; distinguish redshift of light from distance ladder methods.

Standard candles and the cosmic distance ladder

A standard candle is an object whose luminosity is known, such as a Type Ia supernova or a Cepheid variable star. Comparing its known luminosity with its observed brightness gives its distance, using the inverse-square law. Stellar radii can be found in the same way: the luminosity L = 4πR2σT4 links radius, surface temperature and output power.

Exam tip: state which assumption you are making, such as that the star radiates as a black body, before you calculate the radius.

Worked example: distance from parallax

A star has a parallax angle of 0.25 arcseconds when observed from opposite sides of the Earth's orbit. The distance in parsecs is d = 1/p = 1/0.25 = 4.0 pc. One parsec is about 3.26 light-years, so the star is roughly 13 light-years away. Parallax is the most direct distance method, and it works only for nearby stars.

Inverse-square law for brightness

The apparent brightness of a star falls as the inverse square of its distance. A star that is four times as far away appears 4² = 16 times fainter, for the same luminosity. This is why luminosity, which is intrinsic, must be distinguished from apparent brightness, which depends on distance.

Hubble's law and the expanding universe

  • Hubble's law states that v = H₀d, where v is the recession speed and d is the distance.
  • With H₀ ≈ 70 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹, a galaxy 100 Mpc away recedes at about 7000 km s⁻¹.
  • Redshift shows that most galaxies are moving away from us, which is evidence that the universe is expanding.

Exam point: the Big Bang model gives an age for the universe of about 13.8 billion years, consistent with the cosmic microwave background, which is the faint, nearly uniform radiation left from the early universe.

title: A Level Mathematics: Continuous Random Variables
content:
A Level Mathematics: Continuous Random Variables

A continuous random variable can take any value in an interval, so the probability of one exact value is zero and probabilities are found by integrating over a range. The probability density function replaces the probability table: area under the curve, not height, is probability. This note builds the density function, the cumulative distribution, the mean, the variance and the median from that single idea, and shows the standard exam moves — normalising a density, finding a constant, and reading probabilities off a piecewise curve.

Why density, not probability

If a random variable is a measurement — a length, a waiting time, a mass — there are infinitely many possible values, and giving each a positive probability is impossible because they would have to sum to one. So probability lives in intervals, and the density describes how concentrated it is.

P(a <= X <= b) = integral from a to b of f(x) dx
P(X = c) = 0 for any single value c
f(x) >= 0 everywhere (it is a density, so non-negative)
the total area is 1: integral of f over the whole range = 1

Notice that a density may exceed 1 without contradicting anything: on a narrow support the curve must be tall for its area to reach 1, and no rule forbids that. Only the area is constrained.

The analogy that makes this concrete: the density is like the height of a landscape, and probability is the volume of soil above a patch of ground. A mathematically exact point has no width, so no soil — that is why P(X = c) = 0 even at the peak.

Finding the constant in a density

Most first parts of a question give a density with an unknown constant and require the total area to be one. That single condition fixes the constant and is worth a mark on its own.

set the integral of f over its support equal to 1, solve for k
then check f(x) >= 0 on the support

Worked example. f(x) = kx for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2, and 0 otherwise. Find k.

integral from 0 to 2 of kx dx = k x^2/2 evaluated = k(4/2) = 2k
2k = 1  ->  k = 0.5

Worked example 2 (quadratic density). f(x) = kx² for 0 ≤ x ≤ 3. Find k and then P(X ≤ 1).

integral = k x^3/3 from 0 to 3 = k(27/3) = 9k = 1  ->  k = 1/9
P(X <= 1) = (1/9) x^3/3 from 0 to 1 = (1/9)(1/3) = 0.0370

Worked example 3 (piecewise). f(x) = kx for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1 and k(2 − x) for 1 < x ≤ 2. Find k.

first part: k/2
second part: k[2x - x^2/2] from 1 to 2 = k[(4 - 2) - (2 - 0.5)] = k(0.5)
total: k/2 + k/2 = k = 1  ->  k = 1

The cumulative distribution function

The cumulative distribution F(x) is the integral of the density up to x, and it answers every "less than" question directly. Differentiating it recovers the density, which is why the two are always presented together.

F(x) = P(X <= x) = integral from the lower limit to x of f(t) dt
F is non-decreasing, F(lower) = 0, F(upper) = 1
f(x) = F'(x) where F is differentiable

Worked example. For f(x) = x/2 on 0 ≤ x ≤ 2, find F(x) and hence P(X ≤ 1.5).

F(x) = integral of t/2 from 0 to x = x^2/4
P(X <= 1.5) = 2.25/4 = 0.5625
check: F(2) = 1

Worked example 2 (from F back to f). Given F(x) = x²/9 on 0 ≤ x ≤ 3, find f(x) and P(1 ≤ X ≤ 2).

f(x) = F'(x) = 2x/9
P(1 <= X <= 2) = F(2) - F(1) = 4/9 - 1/9 = 1/3

The mean and variance

For a continuous variable the sums of the discrete case become integrals, with the same structure: mean is the first moment, variance is the second moment minus the square of the mean.

E(X) = integral of x f(x) dx over the support
E(X^2) = integral of x^2 f(x) dx
Var(X) = E(X^2) - [E(X)]^2

Worked example. f(x) = x/2 on 0 ≤ x ≤ 2. Find E(X) and Var(X).

E(X) = integral of x(x/2) = x^3/6 from 0 to 2 = 8/6 = 1.333
E(X^2) = integral of x^2(x/2) = x^4/8 from 0 to 2 = 16/8 = 2
Var(X) = 2 - (1.333)^2 = 2 - 1.778 = 0.222

Worked example 2 (uniform special case). For X uniform on [a, b], show E(X) = (a + b)/2.

f(x) = 1/(b - a)
E(X) = (1/(b-a)) integral of x from a to b = (1/(b-a))(b^2 - a^2)/2 = (a + b)/2

The uniform result is worth remembering: the mean is the midpoint and the variance is (b − a)²/12, so a question about a uniform variable can be answered without any integration.

The median and quartiles

The median is the value m with F(m) = 0.5, the lower quartile has F = 0.25 and the upper 0.75. Because a continuous distribution has no lumpy probabilities, these are always found by solving an equation.

median m: F(m) = 0.5
lower quartile: F(q1) = 0.25
upper quartile: F(q3) = 0.75
interquartile range = q3 - q1

Worked example. Find the median of the distribution with f(x) = x/2 on 0 ≤ x ≤ 2.

F(m) = m^2/4 = 0.5
m^2 = 2  ->  m = 1.414

Worked example 2 (quartiles). Find the quartiles of the same distribution.

q1^2/4 = 0.25  ->  q1 = 1
q3^2/4 = 0.75  ->  q3 = sqrt 3 = 1.732
IQR = 0.732

Worked example 3 (median of a uniform). X is uniform on [2, 10]. State the median and the IQR.

median = 6;  q1 = 4;  q3 = 8;  IQR = 4
for a uniform, the quartiles split the interval into four equal parts

The mode and the shape

The mode of a continuous distribution is where the density is largest — the peak of the curve. It is found by differentiating and setting the derivative to zero, or by inspection when the density is increasing or decreasing throughout.

mode: maximise f(x) on the support
compare f(peak) with the endpoint values, because a density can be largest at an endpoint

Worked example. Find the mode of f(x) = 6x(1 − x) on 0 ≤ x ≤ 1.

f(x) = 6x - 6x^2
f'(x) = 6 - 12x = 0  ->  x = 0.5
f(0.5) = 1.5, larger than f(0) = f(1) = 0, so the mode is 0.5

Worked example 2 (no stationary point). Find the mode of f(x) = 2x on 0 ≤ x ≤ 1.

f increases throughout the support, so there is no interior maximum
the mode is at the endpoint x = 1

Working backwards from a probability

A frequent final part gives a probability and asks for the value of x that produces it. The method is to set F(k) equal to that probability and solve for k, remembering that the result is a position on the axis, not a probability, so it should carry the units of the variable.

Worked example. For f(x) = x/2 on 0 ≤ x ≤ 2, find the value of k with P(X ≤ k) = 0.8.

F(k) = k^2/4 = 0.8
k^2 = 3.2  ->  k = 1.789

Worked example 2 (two-sided). For the same distribution, find the interquartile range directly from the density rather than a table.

q1: q1^2/4 = 0.25  ->  q1 = 1
q3: q3^2/4 = 0.75  ->  q3 = 1.732
IQR = 0.732

Percentile questions are the same calculation with a different probability, and a question that says "the 90th percentile" is asking for k with F(k) = 0.9. Reading the wording as a cumulative condition is the whole skill.

One more variant deserves attention: the density may be defined in two pieces, and then P(X ≤ k) depends on which piece k sits in. The routine is to evaluate F at the join first — if the probability asked for is larger than the value at the join, the answer lies in the second piece and the integral starts from the join, carrying the accumulated probability forward. Getting the join wrong is the one error in this topic that produces a plausible but completely wrong number.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Constant) f(x) = k on [0, 5]: find k. Answer: 5k = 1, k = 0.2.
  2. (Probability) For that f, find P(1 ≤ X ≤ 3). Answer: 0.2 × 2 = 0.4.
  3. (Constant) f(x) = kx² on [0, 2]: find k. Answer: 8k/3 = 1, k = 0.375.
  4. (CDF) F(x) = x³/8 on [0, 2]: find f(x). Answer: 3x²/8.
  5. (Mean) f(x) = 0.5 on [0, 2]: find E(X). Answer: 1.
  6. (Variance) Uniform on [0, 4]: find Var(X). Answer: 16/12 = 1.333.
  7. (Median) F(x) = x²/16 on [0, 4]: find the median. Answer: m² = 8, m = 2.828.
  8. (Quartiles) Same F: find the IQR. Answer: q1 = 2, q3 = 3.464, IQR = 1.464.
  9. (Mode) f(x) = 12x²(1 − x) on [0, 1]: find the mode. Answer: f' = 24x − 36x², x = 2/3.
  10. (Interpretation) Explain why P(X = 1.5) = 0 for a continuous variable. Answer: probability is area, and a single point has zero width.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Reading probability off the height: f(x) is a density; only the area is a probability, and f(x) can exceed 1.
  • Integration limits ignored: outside the support the density is zero, so an integral that strays outside must be split.
  • Forgetting the normalising condition: the first mark of a constant question is the integral equal to one.
  • Variance formula misremembered: it is E(X²) − [E(X)]², not E(X²) − E(X) or E(X²) + [E(X)]².
  • Median found by averaging: for a continuous distribution the median solves F(m) = 0.5; it is not the midpoint unless the distribution is uniform.
  • Mode at a stationary point assumed: check the endpoints, because a monotone density peaks at the boundary.
  • F and f confused: F is cumulative (a probability), f is the density; F is the integral of f, not the other way round.
  • Piecewise densities integrated as one piece: a density defined in two parts needs two integrals, one per part.

title: Geometry — Angles and Polygons — Study Notes
content:
Geometry — Angles and Polygons

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): angle facts, parallel lines, polygon angles, circle theorems (Extended).

1. Core angle facts

  • Line 180°; point 360°; vertically opposite equal.
  • Parallel lines: corresponding (F), alternate (Z), co-interior (C, sum 180°).
  • Triangle 180°; isosceles/equilateral properties; exterior angle = sum of two remote interior angles.

2. Polygons

Interior angle sum = (n − 2) × 180°. Regular polygon: exterior = 360° ÷ n; interior = 180° − exterior.

Example: regular octagon: exterior 45°, interior 135°.

3. Circle theorems (Extended)

  1. Angle at centre = 2 × angle at circumference (same arc).
  2. Angle in a semicircle = 90°.
  3. Angles in the same segment are equal.
  4. Cyclic quadrilateral: opposite angles sum to 180°.
  5. Tangent ⊥ radius; two tangents from an external point are equal.
  6. Alternate segment theorem.

Quote the reason in brackets every time: "∠ACB = 62° (angles in same segment)".

4. Algebra with angles

Set up equations from the theorem: cyclic quad (2x + 10) + (3x − 5) = 180 ⇒ x = 35.

Exam tips: mark every found angle on the diagram immediately; use radii to create isosceles triangles; never leave a theorem unquoted.

Angle facts you must know

Angles on a straight line sum to 180°; angles at a point sum to 360°; vertically opposite angles are equal. Parallel lines give equal alternate and corresponding angles and supplementary co-interior angles. Give a reason with every step, naming the rule (for example, alternate angles).

Interior and exterior angles of polygons

The interior angles of a polygon with n sides sum to (n − 2) × 180°. For a regular polygon each interior angle is that sum divided by n, and each exterior angle is 360° divided by n. The exterior angles of any convex polygon always sum to 360°.

Triangles and quadrilaterals

Angles in a triangle sum to 180°, and an exterior angle equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles. Angles in a quadrilateral sum to 360°. Use the properties of isosceles, equilateral and special quadrilaterals to find unknown angles.

title: Computational Thinking and Problem-Solving — Study Notes
content:
Computational Thinking and Problem-Solving

Cambridge International AS & A Level Computer Science 9618: section 19 (Computational thinking and problem-solving), examined in Papers 3 and 4.

Thinking Ahead, Abstractly, Systematically

  • Abstraction: keep essential features, drop detail — a metro map ignores street geometry.
  • Decomposition: split the problem into sub-problems solved independently.
  • Thinking ahead: pre-plan inputs, outputs and reusable components; pre-calculate tables where possible.

Recursion

A recursive routine calls itself with a smaller input and a base case that stops the recursion. Elegant for trees and divide-and-conquer, but each call consumes stack space — deep recursion can overflow. Any recursion can be rewritten with a loop and explicit stack.

Searching and Sorting

  • Linear search: O(n), works unsorted.
  • Binary search: O(log n), needs sorted data.
  • Bubble sort: O(n²) average; simple; detects a sorted pass.
  • Insertion sort: O(n²) average; fast on nearly-sorted data.
  • Merge sort: O(n log n) always; needs extra memory.

Testing

White-box tests trace internal paths; black-box tests check specification behaviour. Choose normal, boundary and erroneous data. Dry runs use trace tables recording variables line by line; a trace of recursion should log each call and its return.

Exam tips: write the base case before the recursive call in pseudocode; give the Big-O with a one-line justification; construct a trace table for a small loop or recursive call.

Recursion

A recursive routine calls itself on a smaller version of the problem. It needs a base case that stops the calls and a recursive case that moves towards the base case. Without a base case the routine never terminates and the call stack overflows.

Example: factorial(n) = 1 if n = 0, otherwise n × factorial(n − 1).

Recursion and iteration can solve the same problems. Recursion is often clearer for tree-shaped problems; iteration uses less memory because it does not build up stack frames.

Worked example: binary search on sixteen items

A sorted list has 16 items. Each comparison with the middle item halves the search range: 16 to 8, 8 to 4, 4 to 2, 2 to 1. At most ⌈log₂16⌉ = 4 comparisons are needed to find the item or confirm it is absent. A linear search on the same list may need 16 comparisons, so binary search is much faster, but only when the list is sorted.

Recursion: factorial

A recursive function calls itself on a smaller problem. For factorial, fact(n) returns 1 when n is 0 (the base case), and otherwise returns n × fact(n − 1). Each call waits for the next one to return, so the calls build up on the call stack. Without a base case the recursion never ends.

Testing a solution

  • Normal test data checks the typical case.
  • Boundary test data checks the limits, such as the first item, the last item and an empty list.
  • Erroneous test data checks that invalid input is rejected, for example a letter typed where a number is expected.

Exam point: a test plan lists the input, the expected output and the reason for each test, so that the result can be checked against the design.

title: Exam technique: Indices and Standard Form
content:
### What earns the marks
For index laws, each law applied on its own line earns credit: subtract for division, multiply for powers of powers. For fractional powers, the root-first order (cube root, then square) stated earns the method mark. For standard form, the coefficient between 1 and 10 with the power justified by the point shift earns both marks. For surds, the split into square factor times prime remainder earns the method mark, and rationalising must finish simplified.
### Traps
Error: (x to the 5th / x squared) cubed answered x to the 6th. Correction: inner subtraction first, then multiply powers. Error: 27 x 2/3 for 27 to the 2/3. Correction: root, then power. Error: unsimplified 6 root 3 / 3 accepted as final. Correction: always cancel to 2 root 3. Error: non-standard-form coefficients (45 x 10 to the -5). Correction: one non-zero digit, then fix the power.
### Worked example
Write 0.00042 in standard form. Move the decimal point until one non-zero digit is in front: 4.2. The point moved 4 places to the right, so the power is −4, giving 4.2 × 10⁻⁴. Now work out (3 × 10⁵)(2 × 10⁴). Multiply the numbers to get 6 and add the powers to get 10⁹, so the answer is 6 × 10⁹.
### Check yourself
Evaluate 8^(2/3) and 2⁻³ without a calculator. Take the cube root of 8 first to get 2, then square it to get 4. For 2⁻³, write 1/2³ to get 1/8. Write one line of working for each step, because the method marks depend on it.

title: Differentiation
content:
Differentiation

Basic Rules

  • d/dx (xⁿ) = n xⁿ⁻¹
  • d/dx (k) = 0, d/dx (kx) = k

Example: y = 5x² − 3x gives dy/dx = 10x − 3.

Chain Rule

dy/dx = dy/du × du/dx.

Example: y = (3x − 1)⁵: dy/dx = 5(3x − 1)⁴ × 3 = 15(3x − 1)⁴.

Tangents and Normals

The tangent gradient at a point is dy/dx there; the normal gradient is −1/(dy/dx).

Example: y = x² at (2, 4): tangent y = 4x − 4; normal has gradient −1/4.

Stationary Points

Set dy/dx = 0, then classify with the second derivative:

  • d²y/dx² > 0 → minimum
  • d²y/dx² < 0 → maximum
  • d²y/dx² = 0 → test either side

Example: y = x³ − 3x: dy/dx = 3x² − 3 = 0 at x = ±1; d²y/dx² = 6x, so a maximum at x = −1 and a minimum at x = 1.

Rates of Change

dy/dx is a rate: if V = 4/3 πr³, then dV/dr = 4πr² links volume change to radius change.

Exam tips: always restart gradients from the derivative at the exact point, and answer rate questions with units.

title: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Right-Angled Trigonometry
content:
Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Right-Angled Trigonometry

Right-angled triangles are the most useful triangles in mathematics: Pythagoras relates the three sides, and the sine, cosine and tangent ratios relate sides to angles. Between them they solve every distance and angle problem the IGCSE sets, from ladders against walls to angles of elevation and three-figure bearings. This note builds the topic from zero: Pythagoras with its converse and 3D use, the SOHCAHTOA ratios with the selection method, exact values derived rather than memorised, and the multi-step problems that combine Pythagoras with trigonometry.

Pythagoras' theorem

in a right-angled triangle: a² + b² = c²
where c is the hypotenuse (the side opposite the right angle)

The theorem is a statement about areas: the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides. The converse identifies right angles: if a² + b² = c² for the longest side c, the triangle is right-angled — the standard test for 3-4-5 and 5-12-13 triangles.

Worked example 1. A right-angled triangle has legs 6 cm and 8 cm. Find the hypotenuse.

c² = 6² + 8² = 36 + 64 = 10⁰
c = 10 cm

Worked example 2 (finding a leg). The hypotenuse is 13 cm and one leg is 5 cm. Find the other leg.

a² = 13² - 5² = 169 - 25 = 144
a = 12 cm

Worked example 3 (converse). Is a triangle with sides 7, 24, 25 right-angled?

7² + 24² = 49 + 576 = 625 = 25²
yes - right-angled, with the right angle opposite the 25 side

Pythagoras in three dimensions

In a cuboid, the space diagonal uses Pythagoras twice: first across the base, then up the height.

space diagonal = √(l² + w² + h²)

Worked example. A cuboid is 3 cm by 4 cm by 12 cm. Find the length of the space diagonal.

d = √(9 + 16 + 144) = √(169) = 13 cm

The three ratios: SOHCAHTOA

sin(θ) = opposite/hypotenuse      (SOH)
cos(θ) = adjacent/hypotenuse      (CAH)
tan(θ) = opposite/adjacent       (TOA)

Label the sides relative to the angle in question: the hypotenuse is always opposite the right angle; the opposite is across from the angle; the adjacent is the remaining side touching the angle. The selection method: mark the known side and the wanted side, then ask which ratio contains both.

Worked example 1 (finding a side). In a right-angled triangle, the angle is 35° and the hypotenuse is 12 cm. Find the opposite side.

known: hypotenuse; want: opposite  →  sine
sin(35) = opposite/12
opposite = 12 sin(35) = 12 × 0.574 = 6.88 cm

Worked example 2 (finding a side with cosine). Angle 40°, hypotenuse 20 cm; find the adjacent side.

cos(40) = adjacent/20
adjacent = 20 cos(40) = 20 × 0.766 = 15.3 cm

Worked example 3 (finding an angle). Opposite 5 cm, adjacent 9 cm. Find the angle.

tan(θ) = 5/9 = 0.5556
θ = tan-1(0.5556) = 29.1 °

For angles, use the inverse functions (sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹, tan⁻¹) and check the calculator is in degree mode — a radian-mode calculator turns 90° into 1.57 and ruins the paper.

Exact trigonometric values

Three angles have exact values worth knowing, derived from two special triangles:

Anglesincostan
30°1/2√3/21/√3
45°1/√21/√21
60°√3/21/2√3

Derivation: a 45-45-90 triangle with legs 1 has hypotenuse √2 (Pythagoras), giving sin 45 = 1/√2. An equilateral triangle of side 2 split in half gives a 30-60-90 triangle with sides 1, √3, 2, giving all six values. Deriving them once beats memorising them badly.

Two sanity checks keep the table honest: sine increases from 0 to 1 as the angle grows from 0° to 90°, so sin 30 must be smaller than sin 60; and cosine runs the other way, so cos 30 must be larger than cos 60. If an exact value breaks either ordering, the table has been misremembered.

Worked example. Find the exact value of sin 60° × tan 30°.

sin 60 = √(3)/2;  tan 30 = 1/√(3)
product = (√(3)/2) x (1/√(3)) = 1/2

Angles of elevation and depression

An angle of elevation is measured upward from the horizontal to an object; an angle of depression is measured downward. Both are measured from the observer's eye line, and the angle of depression from A to B equals the angle of elevation from B to A (alternate angles).

Worked example. From a point 40 m from the base of a tower, the angle of elevation to the top is 32°. Find the tower's height.

tan(32) = height/40
height = 40 tan(32) = 40 × 0.625 = 25.0 m

Worked example 2 (depression). A cliff is 60 m high; the angle of depression to a boat is 25°. Find the horizontal distance to the boat.

the angle at the boat is also 25 ° (alternate)
tan(25) = 60/d  →  d = 60/tan(25) = 60/0.466 = 128.7 m

Choosing the method: a decision routine

Most lost trigonometry marks come from choosing the wrong tool, not from arithmetic. The routine below takes ten seconds and removes the guesswork:

  1. Is there a right angle? If not, the question needs the sine or cosine rule (a different topic) — do not force SOHCAHTOA onto a triangle without a right angle.
  2. What do you know — two sides, or a side and an angle? Two sides with no angle means Pythagoras. A side and an angle means trigonometry.
  3. Which ratio? Mark the known side and the target relative to the given angle, then pick the ratio containing both: sin uses opposite and hypotenuse, cos uses adjacent and hypotenuse, tan uses opposite and adjacent.
  4. What is the unknown — a side or an angle? A side comes from multiplying; an angle needs the inverse function.

Worked example. A roof rafter is 4.5 m long and meets the horizontal at 38°. Find the vertical rise and the horizontal run.

rise: sin(38) = rise/4.5  →  rise = 4.5 sin(38) = 2.77 m
run:  cos(38) = run/4.5   →  run = 4.5 cos(38) = 3.55 m
check: 2.77² + 3.55² = 7.67 + 12.60 = 20.27 ~ 4.5²

Worked example 2 (finding the angle of a ladder). A 6 m ladder reaches 5.2 m up a wall. Find the angle it makes with the ground.

sin(θ) = 5.2/6 = 0.867  →  θ = 60.1 °

Multi-step problems: Pythagoras and trigonometry together

Many questions need both tools: Pythagoras to find a side in one triangle, trigonometry to use it in another. The method: draw and label every triangle, find the shared side first, then proceed.

Worked example. A ladder 5 m long leans against a wall, with its foot 2 m from the wall. Find the height reached and the angle the ladder makes with the ground.

height: h² = 5² - 2² = 25 - 4 = 21  →  h = 4.58 m
angle: cos(θ) = 2/5 = 0.4  →  θ = 66.4 °

Worked example 2 (two triangles). From a point P, the angle of elevation to the top of a building is 30°; from a point Q, 20 m closer, it is 45°. Find the height.

let h be the height and x the distance from Q to the base.
tan(45) = h/x  →  h = x
tan(30) = h/(x + 20)
h = (x + 20) tan(30) = (h + 20)(1/√(3))
h √(3) = h + 20  →  h(√(3) - 1) = 20
h = 20/(1.732 - 1) = 20/0.732 = 27.3 m

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Pythagoras) A right-angled triangle has legs 9 and 12. Find the hypotenuse. Answer: √(81 + 144) = √225 = 15.
  2. (Leg) Hypotenuse 17, one leg 8. Find the other. Answer: √(289 − 64) = 15.
  3. (Ratio) Angle 28°, adjacent 15 cm. Find the opposite side. Answer: tan 28 = o/15 → o = 15 × 0.532 = 7.98 cm.
  4. (Angle) Opposite 7, hypotenuse 10. Find the angle. Answer: sin θ = 0.7 → θ = 44.4°.
  5. (Exact) Find cos 30° exactly. Answer: √3/2.
  6. (Elevation) From 25 m away, the angle of elevation to a tree top is 40°. Find the height. Answer: 25 tan 40 = 25 × 0.839 = 21.0 m.
  7. (3D) A cuboid is 2 cm by 3 cm by 6 cm. Find its space diagonal. Answer: √(4 + 9 + 36) = √49 = 7 cm.
  8. (Combined) A ship sails 30 km east then 40 km north. Find its distance from the start and the bearing of its final position. Answer: distance = 50 km; tan θ = 40/30 → θ = 53.1°, bearing 053°.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Calculator mode: check DEG, not RAD or GRAD, before any trigonometric calculation. A radian answer is usually obviously wrong (tiny or huge), but only if you check.
  • Wrong ratio: label the sides relative to the angle before choosing SOH, CAH or TOA; picking by habit is the commonest trigonometry error.
  • Hypotenuse identification: the hypotenuse is opposite the right angle, not necessarily the longest-looking side on the diagram.
  • Pythagoras with the hypotenuse as a leg: c² = a² + b² only when c is the hypotenuse; finding a leg requires subtraction.
  • Rounding early: keep full calculator accuracy until the final answer; round to 3 s.f. (or 1 d.p. for angles unless told otherwise).
  • Angle of depression drawn from the wrong line: it is measured from the horizontal, not from the cliff face; the alternate-angle equality fixes the geometry.
  • Exact values with decimals: "exact" means surds and fractions, not 0.866; leaving √3/2 is required.
  • Missing units and labels: state cm, m, km and degrees; name the side or angle found, especially in multi-step problems.

title: Robotics & AI — Study Notes
content:
Robotics & AI

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): AI characteristics, machine learning basics, robotics/simulation contexts, automated systems.

1. AI characteristics

Systems exhibiting: planning, learning, reasoning, problem-solving, perception, knowledge representation. Narrow (task-specific) vs general AI distinction for discussion answers.

2. Machine learning

Supervised (labelled data — spam filters), unsupervised (clusters — segmentation), reinforcement (rewards — game agents). Training/evaluation loop: train on a set, test on unseen data; overfitting = memorising rather than generalising.

3. Robotics

Components: sensors (input), processors (decision), actuators/motors (output), power. Examples: manufacturing arms, delivery drones, autonomous vehicles (LIDAR + vision). Benefits: precision, 24/7 operation, dangerous jobs; concerns: job displacement, safety, cost.

4. Automated systems & simulation

Sensors → processor → actuators loops (greenhouses, traffic lights, self-checkouts). Simulation models real systems cheaply and safely (flight training, weather, crash tests) — limitations: model quality, missing variables.

5. Ethics of AI

Bias from unrepresentative training data; opacity of decisions; accountability for errors; privacy of training data; effect on employment.

Exam tips: for "describe how AI could be used in X" — tie each AI characteristic to a concrete step in the scenario; for evaluations, give both sides then a justified conclusion.

Sensors, actuators and feedback

A sensor converts a physical quantity, such as light, temperature or pressure, into an electrical signal. An actuator does the opposite: it converts an electrical signal into physical movement, for example by turning a motor. A robot or automated system uses sensors to read its environment, a processor to decide what to do, and actuators to act.

A feedback loop compares the measured value with the required value and adjusts the output to close the gap. A thermostat is a simple example: it switches the heater off when the room reaches the set temperature. Feedback allows a system to correct itself, but a poorly set loop can overshoot or oscillate.

Exam tip: name a sensor and an actuator in any automated system you describe, and explain what the feedback corrects.

Worked example: a sensor-driven robot

A robot moves forward while an ultrasonic sensor reports distances greater than 20 cm. When the reading falls to 20 cm or less, the robot stops and turns right, then resumes. Describe this as input (distance reading), process (compare the reading with the threshold) and output (motor commands). Mark schemes reward naming each part of the control loop: sensing, decision and actuation.

Sensors, actuators and feedback

  • A sensor converts a physical quantity such as light, temperature or distance into a signal. An actuator converts an electrical signal into motion, such as a motor or servo.
  • Feedback means the output is measured and used to correct the next action. Without feedback a robot cannot adjust when conditions change, such as a wheel slipping on a wet floor.

title: AS Level Biology: Membranes, Proteins, DNA and Gene Expression
content:
Membranes, Proteins, DNA and Gene Expression — AS Level Biology

This revision note belongs to the Edexcel International Advanced Subsidiary (IAS) Biology specification, WBI11 Unit 1, Topic 2 Membranes, Proteins, DNA and Gene Expression. It covers membrane structure and properties, osmosis and the different kinds of membrane transport, the structure of proteins and how they are built from amino acids, the structure of DNA and RNA and how DNA replicates, the genetic code and how genes work, transcription and translation, mutations and their effects, patterns of inheritance including sex linkage, cystic fibrosis as an example of a gene mutation in humans, and genetic screening and its ethical and social issues. Every statement the topic is responsible for is covered in its own section or paragraph.

1. Cell membranes and the fluid mosaic model

The cell surface membrane (plasma membrane) is a phospholipid bilayer; each phospholipid has a hydrophilic head and two hydrophobic tails, and the heads face out and in while the tails face each other, making a barrier to charged and water-soluble substances. The fluid mosaic model is the accepted interpretation: the membrane is fluid — the phospholipids and proteins can move laterally in the layer — and mosaic because it contains a variety of proteins embedded in or attached to the bilayer, including channel proteins and carrier proteins for transport, receptor proteins for signalling, and proteins for cell recognition. The model is an interpretation of data — it was built from evidence such as electron micrographs and the ability of membranes to fuse and to self-seal — and it explains the structure and properties of cell membranes and how they control what enters and leaves the cell. Cholesterol in the membrane reduces fluidity at high temperatures and prevents the membrane from becoming too rigid at low temperatures.

2. Core Practical 3 — investigating membrane properties

Investigate membrane properties including the effect of alcohol and of temperature on membrane permeability. A typical method uses beetroot cylinders, which contain the red pigment betalain in their vacuoles; as the membrane is damaged, pigment leaks out and the colour of the surrounding solution deepens. Cut cylinders to the same length, wash off surface pigment in distilled water, then place them in water at a range of temperatures or in different concentrations of alcohol for a fixed time, remove the tissue and measure the concentration of pigment in the solution with a colorimeter. As temperature rises or alcohol concentration rises, the membrane proteins denature and the lipid bilayer is disrupted, so permeability increases and more pigment leaks out; a control at room temperature or in distilled water shows the baseline. Record the colorimeter reading for each tube, plot a graph of permeability against temperature or against alcohol concentration, and explain the trend in terms of the effect on membrane proteins and lipids.

3. Osmosis and how water moves across membranes

Osmosis is the net movement of free water molecules through a partially permeable membrane, down a water potential gradient — from higher water potential to lower water potential. Water potential is the tendency of water to move; adding a solute lowers it, so a concentrated solution has a more negative water potential than a dilute one, and pure water has the highest (zero) water potential. If a cell is placed in a solution of higher water potential than its contents, water enters by osmosis and the cell swells; if it is an animal cell it may burst (haemolysis); if it is a plant cell the cell wall prevents bursting and the cell becomes turgid, which supports the plant. In a solution of lower water potential, water leaves and the cell shrinks — animal cells crenate and plant cells become plasmolysed, with the membrane pulling away from the wall. A recommended additional practical is to investigate tissue water potentials using plant tissue (for example potato or onion epidermis) and graded concentrations of a solute: place tissue in solutions of different molarity, note the change in length or mass, and find the concentration at which there is no change — that concentration has the same water potential as the tissue.

4. Passive transport, active transport, endocytosis and exocytosis

Passive transport needs no energy input because substances move down their concentration gradient. Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to one of lower concentration; small, non-polar molecules such as oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse directly through the phospholipid bilayer, while ions and large polar molecules cannot. Facilitated diffusion is the movement of specific particles down their concentration gradient through channel proteins or carrier proteins — channel proteins form water-filled pores for ions, and carrier proteins change shape to carry molecules across. Active transport moves substances against their concentration gradient (from low to high concentration) and needs energy directly from ATP; carrier proteins use ATP to pump substances across, as in the sodium–potassium pump. Endocytosis is the bulk movement of material into the cell inside a vesicle formed from the plasma membrane; phagocytosis takes in solid material and pinocytosis takes in fluid. Exocytosis is the reverse — material is moved out of the cell in a vesicle that fuses with the plasma membrane, as in the secretion of proteins and neurotransmitters. Carrier and channel proteins are involved in facilitated diffusion and active transport; the key difference is that active transport needs ATP and moves substances against their gradient.

5. Protein structure: from amino acid to three-dimensional shape

Amino acids are the monomers of proteins; the basic structure of an amino acid is an amino group, a carboxyl group and a variable R group all attached to a central carbon, with a hydrogen on the remaining bond. There are around 20 amino acids found in proteins, differing only in their R group, and the sequence of amino acids in a protein is its primary structure. Amino acids join by condensation reactions to form peptide bonds, making dipeptides and then polypeptides; a polypeptide chain is a protein’s primary structure and it determines everything about the protein. The secondary structure is the local folding of the chain into alpha-helices and beta-pleated sheets, held by hydrogen bonds between the peptide bonds. The tertiary structure is the overall three-dimensional folding of the whole polypeptide, held by hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, disulfide bonds and hydrophobic interactions; it gives the protein its specific shape and therefore its function. Globular proteins are roughly spherical and usually soluble and active — haemoglobin is the classic example, with four polypeptide chains and a haem group each carrying one oxygen molecule, and it shows quaternary structure (several polypeptides together) plus the importance of the three-dimensional shape for its oxygen-carrying function. Fibrous proteins are long, insoluble and structural — collagen is the example, made of three polypeptide chains wound into a rope-like triple helix, giving strength for tendons, ligaments and skin. The shape of a protein determines its function, so a change to the primary structure can alter the folding and disable the protein.

6. DNA structure and replication

A DNA molecule is made of two nucleotide strands twisted into a double helix. Each nucleotide is made of a deoxyribose sugar, a phosphate group and a base — either adenine (A), cytosine (C), guanine (G) or thymine (T). The two strands run antiparallel and are linked by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases — A pairs with T (two hydrogen bonds) and C pairs with G (three hydrogen bonds). RNA is similar but has ribose instead of deoxyribose, uracil instead of thymine, and is usually single-stranded. The two strands are complementary, so knowing one strand tells you the other, and the two strands separate at replication. DNA replication is semi-conservative: the double helix unzips, each strand acts as a template, and free nucleotides pair with their complementary bases; DNA polymerase joins the nucleotides into a new strand. The result is two identical DNA molecules, each with one old strand and one new strand. Meselson and Stahl’s experiment supported this: they grew bacteria in a medium with a heavy isotope of nitrogen (15N), then moved them to a 14N medium and examined the DNA by centrifugation; the first generation was a single hybrid band (not one heavy and one light, which would be conservative replication), and later generations showed a mixture of hybrid and light bands — exactly what semi-conservative replication predicts and ruling out the conservative and dispersive alternatives.

7. The genetic code and how it works

The genetic code is the set of rules translating the base sequence of mRNA into the amino acid sequence of a protein. It is a triplet code — three bases (a base triplet on DNA, a codon on mRNA) code for one amino acid; it is non-overlapping — each base is read once in order; and it is degenerate — more than one codon can code for the same amino acid, which is why many mutations change a base but not the amino acid. Part of the code is a stop codon that signals the end of translation; there is no amino acid for it. A gene is a sequence of bases on a DNA molecule that codes for a sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide chain. In transcription, the gene is copied into a complementary mRNA molecule by the enzyme RNA polymerase, using the DNA template (antisense) strand; the mRNA is complementary to the template strand and the same as the coding (sense) strand except with uracil in place of thymine. mRNA leaves the nucleus and attaches to ribosomes in the cytoplasm; transfer RNA (tRNA) molecules carry amino acids to the ribosome, each with a three-base anticodon that pairs with the mRNA codon, so the ribosome joins the amino acids into a polypeptide chain in the order of the codons until a stop codon is reached.

8. Mutations: the changes and their effects

A mutation is a change in the DNA base sequence. A substitution replaces one base with another — it may do nothing, change one amino acid, or, rarely, create a stop codon that shortens the protein. An insertion adds one or more bases and a deletion removes one or more; because the code is read in triplets, an insertion or deletion not in a multiple of three causes a frameshift, changing every amino acid after the mutation and usually destroying the protein’s function. Mutations are the only source of new alleles, and most have no observable effect — they may be in non-coding DNA, or a degenerate codon and amino acid may stay the same, or the changed protein still folds and works. Some mutations give rise to cancer (if they affect control of the cell cycle) or to genetic disorders. Ionising radiation such as X-rays and ultraviolet light, and some chemicals such as those in tobacco smoke, can increase the rate of mutation by damaging DNA.

9. Patterns of inheritance: monohybrid crosses, pedigree diagrams and sex linkage

A gene can have different alleles; the genotype is the alleles an organism has, the phenotype is the observable feature. Dominant alleles show in the phenotype even when heterozygous; recessive alleles only show when homozygous. A monohybrid cross is the inheritance of one gene with two alleles; the typical ratios are a 3:1 phenotype ratio in the F2 of a monohybrid cross between two heterozygotes, but only if the alleles are completely dominant and the gene is autosomal. Sex linkage is the inheritance of a gene on the X chromosome — because males have only one X, a recessive allele on it shows in their phenotype even though they are effectively hemizygous; red-green colour blindness and haemophilia are human X-linked conditions that are more common in males. Pedigree diagrams record which family members show a trait and are used to work out whether a trait is dominant or recessive and whether it is autosomal or sex-linked. Codominance is when both alleles are expressed in the heterozygote, as in the ABO blood group system where IA and IB are codominant and i is recessive, giving the four blood groups A, B, AB and O.

10. Cystic fibrosis: a mutation that affects three systems

Cystic fibrosis is caused by a mutation in a gene that codes for a chloride ion channel protein; in the most common form a deletion of three bases removes a single amino acid from the protein, so the channel does not work properly. As a result, chloride ions and water cannot move properly across cell membranes, and the mucus and other secretions become abnormally thick. In the gaseous exchange system the thick mucus blocks the airways and makes it hard to breathe and to clear infections; in the digestive system the pancreatic duct is blocked so digestive enzymes from the pancreas cannot reach the gut, so food is not digested and absorbed properly, and the person may be malnourished; in the reproductive system the vas deferens is often absent or blocked in males, causing infertility. Treatments include physiotherapy and antibiotics for the lungs, and enzyme supplements with meals for digestion, and newer treatments aim to correct the underlying defect.

11. Genetic screening: what it can do and the issues it raises

Genetic screening can identify carriers of recessive alleles (people who have one normal allele and one faulty allele and are unaffected but could pass the allele on), and prenatal testing can check a fetus: amniocentesis takes a sample of amniotic fluid at around 15–17 weeks, and chorionic villus sampling takes a sample of placental tissue at 8–12 weeks. Pre-implantation genetic diagnosis is used with IVF to test embryos before implantation and select unaffected ones. Each raises ethical and social questions — the safety and reliability of the test, the risks of miscarriage with invasive prenatal testing, the right to know or not to know, who decides which conditions to test for, the possible choice to terminate a pregnancy, anxiety and guilt, and the risk that screening could be used to select non-medical traits. Students should be able to identify and discuss these from religious, moral and social viewpoints and to evaluate the implications of prenatal genetic screening.

12. How to use this note and what to revise next

Use these notes by working through each section and checking that you can draw a cell membrane from the fluid mosaic model and label the phospholipid bilayer, the proteins, cholesterol and glycoproteins; state the difference between diffusion, facilitated diffusion and active transport, and give an example of each; outline the steps of DNA extraction (a simple practical with strawberries or onions is useful to remember); and carry out a genetic cross with a Punnett square and interpret the ratios. Revise by drawing protein structure from amino acid to tertiary, then drawing the DNA double helix and explaining semi-conservative replication and the Meselson–Stahl evidence. After this topic, revise Topic 3 Cell structure, reproduction and development, because the same DNA and protein-synthesis processes control cell differentiation and the cell cycle.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Osmosis, applied to a potato cylinder placed in a sugar solution: water moves from the higher water potential to the lower one, down a gradient, through a partially permeable membrane. A cylinder that loses mass has been placed in a solution of lower water potential than its cells. Give the direction of water movement and the reason in the same sentence.
  • Monohybrid cross, applied to two heterozygotes (Aa × Aa): the offspring are 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa, so the phenotypic ratio is 3 : 1. Write the parental genotypes, the gametes and the Punnett square, then state the ratio. A ratio alone earns less than the full working. Key: AA = homozygous dominant; Aa = heterozygote; aa = homozygous recessive; the numbers 1 : 2 : 1 are the expected proportions of those genotypes among the offspring, not counts unless the family is large.
  • Sex linkage, applied to X-linked haemophilia: a carrier mother (XᴴXʰ) and a normal father (XᴴY) have a 50% chance of a son with haemophilia, but a daughter cannot be affected unless her father is affected. Use the X and Y chromosomes explicitly in the genotypes.
  • Mutation effects: a substitution may have no effect because the genetic code is degenerate, while a frameshift changes every codon after the mutation. Name the type of mutation and state whether the change alters the amino acid sequence.

How substances cross a membrane, compared

RouteDirectionProtein neededATP usedExample
Simple diffusionDown the concentration gradientNoNoOxygen into a cell
Facilitated diffusionDown the concentration gradientChannel or carrierNoGlucose into a red blood cell through a carrier
OsmosisDown a water potential gradientNo (partially permeable membrane)NoWater into a root hair cell
Active transportAgainst the concentration gradientCarrier that changes shapeYes, ATP hydrolysedIons reabsorbed in the kidney
Endocytosis and exocytosisInto or out of the cell in a vesicleNo, membrane fusionYesPhagocytosis of a bacterium; secretion of an enzyme

Typical mistakes

  • Writing that active transport "uses energy" and stopping there. The mark is for ATP being hydrolysed to change the shape of the carrier protein, which moves the substance against its gradient.
  • Confusing water potential with solute concentration. Pure water at atmospheric pressure has a water potential of zero, and every solution has a negative value. Water moves from the less negative (higher) water potential to the more negative one.
  • Swapping codon and anticodon. The codon is the triplet on messenger RNA; the anticodon is the triplet on transfer RNA that pairs with it.
  • Saying DNA polymerase unzips the helix. Helicase breaks the hydrogen bonds between the strands; DNA polymerase then adds free nucleotides to the exposed template, always in the 5-prime to 3-prime direction.
  • Claiming the Meselson and Stahl experiment showed dispersive replication. After one generation in nitrogen-15 there was a single hybrid band, and after two generations there were hybrid and light bands. A dispersive model would have given a single intermediate band throughout.
  • Assuming a dominant allele is the more common one. Dominance describes expression in the heterozygote, not frequency in the population.
  • Confusing amniocentesis with chorionic villus sampling. Amniocentesis samples amniotic fluid at about 15 to 17 weeks; chorionic villus sampling takes placental tissue at about 8 to 12 weeks, earlier but with a higher risk of miscarriage.
  • Explaining cystic fibrosis without a mechanism. The mutation changes the chloride channel, so chloride and water cannot cross normally, secretions become thick, and the airways, pancreatic duct and vas deferens are affected. Name the ion, the effect on the secretion and the effect on the organ.

Exam-style questions

  1. Explain why the fluid mosaic model was modified as new evidence appeared. Answer: the model is an interpretation of data, not a direct observation. Freeze-fracture electron micrographs showed proteins embedded within the bilayer rather than coating it, and experiments on membrane fusion showed that proteins move within the membrane, so the model was revised to show a fluid bilayer with proteins partly or wholly embedded.
  2. A potato cylinder loses mass after 30 minutes in 0.6 mol per dm cubed sucrose solution. Explain the loss in terms of water potential. Answer: the sucrose solution has a lower (more negative) water potential than the vacuole contents, so water leaves the cells by osmosis down a water potential gradient through the partially permeable membranes, the cells lose turgor, and the cylinder shrinks.
  3. Distinguish facilitated diffusion from active transport. Answer: both use membrane proteins, but facilitated diffusion moves substances down their concentration gradient through channels or carriers and needs no ATP, while active transport moves them against the gradient using a carrier whose shape is changed by ATP hydrolysis.
  4. Describe the evidence that DNA replication is semi-conservative. Answer: bacteria were grown in nitrogen-15 so that all DNA was heavy, then transferred to nitrogen-14. After one generation all DNA was of intermediate density, which rules out conservative replication; after two generations half the DNA was intermediate and half light, which fits each new molecule keeping one parental strand.
  5. Give the role of the template strand, the codon and the anticodon in protein synthesis. Answer: the template (antisense) strand is the DNA strand that RNA polymerase copies; the codon is the triplet of bases on mRNA that specifies one amino acid; the anticodon on tRNA is complementary to the codon and pairs with it at the ribosome so that the correct amino acid is added.
  6. Explain how a substitution and a deletion affect the polypeptide differently. Answer: a substitution changes one base, so at most one codon changes and, because the code is degenerate, the amino acid sequence may not change at all. A deletion shifts the reading frame, so every codon after the mutation is different and the protein is usually non-functional.
  7. A carrier mother and an unaffected father are expecting a child. Explain the probability that a son is colour blind. Answer: the mother is heterozygous, with one affected X chromosome and one normal X chromosome. A son inherits one of her X chromosomes with equal probability, so half the sons are colour blind. Daughters receive the father's normal X, so none is colour blind, although half are carriers.
  8. Explain how the mutation that causes cystic fibrosis impairs three body systems. Answer: the three-base deletion removes one amino acid from the chloride channel protein, so chloride transport is faulty and water follows less readily. Mucus in the airways becomes thick and blocks gas exchange; the pancreatic duct blocks so digestive enzymes do not reach the gut; the vas deferens is absent or blocked, reducing male fertility.

Key areas to revise

  • Sector Area

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

### Worked example An arc of a circle of radius r and angle θ in radians has length s = rθ. The sector area is ½r²θ. With r = 5 cm and θ = 0.6 rad, s = 3 cm and the area is 0.5 × 25 × 0.6 = 7.5 cm². To convert, 180° = π radians, so 60° = π/3 ≈ 1.047 radians. ### Check yourself Convert 150° into radians and find the arc length for r = 4 cm. 150° = 5π/6 ≈ 2.618 radians, and the arc length is 4 × 2.618 ≈ 10.47 cm. Explain why the radian measure is needed for the formula.

title: Complex Numbers — Study Notes
content:
Complex Numbers

Basics

i² = −1. A complex number z = a + bi has real part a and imaginary part b. Two numbers are equal iff both parts match.

Arithmetic: add/subtract parts; multiply with brackets and replace i² with −1.

Example: (2 + 3i)(1 − i) = 2 − 2i + 3i − 3i² = 5 + i.

Conjugates

z̄ = a − bi. zz̄ = a² + b² (real). Dividing: multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate.

Example: 1/(3 − i) × (3 + i)/(3 + i) = (3 + i)/10.

Argand Diagram

Plot z as the point (a, b). |z| = √(a² + b²) is the modulus (distance from origin); arg z = tan⁻¹(b/a) is the argument (angle). Multiply two numbers: moduli multiply, arguments add.

Modulus–Argument Form

z = r(cos θ + i sin θ), r = |z|, θ = arg z. Useful for powers and roots.

de Moivre and Roots

[r(cos θ + i sin θ)]ⁿ = rⁿ(cos nθ + i sin nθ).

Example: (1 + i)⁸: |1 + i| = √2, arg = π/4, so z⁸ = (√2)⁸ cis 2π = 16.

An nth root gives n evenly spaced solutions, 2π/n apart on a circle of radius r^(1/n).

Exam tips: always give arguments in the required interval; when solving equations, remember complex roots come in conjugate pairs for real polynomials.

Exam method: arithmetic and modulus

Treat i as a symbol with i² = −1 and collect real and imaginary parts separately. When multiplying complex numbers expand like brackets, then replace i² by −1. To divide, multiply the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator, which turns the denominator into a real number.

For z = a + bi the modulus is |z| = √(a² + b²) and the argument is the angle θ in the Argand diagram with tan θ = b/a, placed in the correct quadrant. The conjugate z* = a − bi reverses the sign of the imaginary part, and z z* = a² + b², which is always real.

Equal complex numbers have equal real parts and equal imaginary parts. Use this to solve for unknown real values, comparing coefficients on both sides of an equation.

Exam cue: State the final answer in the form a + bi, and check the sign of the imaginary part after every multiplication.

title: Probability Distributions — Study Notes
content:
Discrete Random Variables

Edexcel International A Level Mathematics — Statistics 1 (WST01), sat at AS.

Probability Distributions

A discrete random variable X takes values xᵢ with probabilities pᵢ where each pᵢ ≥ 0 and Σpᵢ = 1. A probability distribution can be given as a table, a formula, or a function. Any missing probability is found by subtraction.

Example: X = number of heads in 2 fair tosses: P(0) = 1/4, P(1) = 1/2, P(2) = 1/4.

Expectation

The mean of X is

  • E(X) = Σxᵢpᵢ

It is a weighted average — the long-run average value over many repetitions. E(X) need not equal any value X can actually take.

Variance

  • Var(X) = E(X²) − (E(X))²

where E(X²) = Σxᵢ²pᵢ — square the values before multiplying by probabilities. The standard deviation is √Var(X).

Linear Transforms

For constants a and b:

  • E(aX + b) = a·E(X) + b and Var(aX + b) = a²·Var(X)

Adding a constant shifts but does not spread; multiplying scales the spread by |a|.

Independent Variables

If X and Y are independent: E(X + Y) = E(X) + E(Y) and Var(X + Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y). The addition rule for expectation always holds; the variance addition needs independence. The same applies to differences: Var(X − Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) — the subtraction does not cancel spread.

Exam tips: first verify Σp = 1 in any given table. Write E(X²) and (E(X))² separately; merging them is the most common exam error. In games of chance, set the expected profit to zero to find a fair entry fee.

Exam method: discrete distributions

A discrete probability distribution gives P(X = x) for each value x. Each probability lies between 0 and 1, and the probabilities sum to 1. Use the sum to find an unknown constant before calculating any other probability.

The expected value is E(X) = Σ x P(X = x), and E(X²) = Σ x² P(X = x). The variance is Var(X) = E(X²) − [E(X)]². Set out the values, probabilities and products in a table to keep the working clear.

For a function of X, such as Y = 2X + 3, the expected value is E(Y) = 2E(X) + 3. The variance changes as Var(2X + 3) = 4 Var(X), because adding a constant does not change the spread.

When a question asks for P(X ≤ x) or P(X ≥ x), add the probabilities for the values in the range.

Exam cue: Check that the probabilities sum to 1 before reporting any expected value, because a missing or wrong probability makes the rest of the answer wrong.

Worked example: expectation and variance of a discrete variable

Let X take the values 0, 1, 2 and 3 with probabilities 0.1, 0.4, 0.3 and 0.2. The expectation is E(X) = 0(0.1) + 1(0.4) + 2(0.3) + 3(0.2) = 0 + 0.4 + 0.6 + 0.6 = 1.6.
