To find the variance, first find E(X²) = 0 + 0.4 + 1.2 + 1.8 = 3.4, then Var(X) = E(X²) − [E(X)]² = 3.4 − 2.56 = 0.84. Calculating E(X²) directly and subtracting the square of the mean is quicker than summing squared deviations, and it is the method to use when the probabilities are given as a table.

Checking a probability distribution

Every probability must lie between 0 and 1 inclusive, and the probabilities must sum to 1. If a question gives an unknown probability, use the sum to find it before calculating any expectation. Writing the check on the page shows the examiner that the distribution is valid, and it protects you from losing the later method marks when a slip appears in the first line.

The binomial distribution

If X is the number of successes in n independent trials, each with success probability p, then X follows a binomial distribution. Its mean is np and its variance is np(1 − p). The probability of exactly r successes is the binomial coefficient multiplied by p to the power r and by (1 − p) to the power n − r. State the conditions of independence and constant probability when you use this model.

title: Databases
content:
`# Databases

Relational Basics

Tables (relations) of records with fields. Keys:

  • Primary key: unique identifier
  • Foreign key: references another table's PK — creates relationships
  • Candidate/secondary keys: other unique identifiers

Normalisation

  • 1NF: atomic values, no repeating groups
  • 2NF: 1NF + no partial dependency on a composite key
  • 3NF: 2NF + no transitive dependencies (non-key → non-key)

Example: (StudentID, Course, CourseFee) has CourseFee depending on Course, not StudentID — move course data to its own table (3NF).

SQL

SELECT name, grade FROM students
  WHERE grade >= 'A' ORDER BY name;
INSERT INTO students VALUES (...);
UPDATE students SET grade = 'B' WHERE id = 5;
DELETE FROM students WHERE id = 5;

Joins combine tables: FROM students s JOIN enrolments e ON s.id = e.sid.

Transactions

ACID: Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (rules hold), Isolation (no interference), Durability (committed = permanent). Record locking prevents conflicting simultaneous edits.

Exam tips: justify each normal form step with the dependency removed; write SQL with correct WHERE clauses to avoid accidental full-table updates.

title: Exam technique: Algebra Inequalities
content:
### What earns the marks
For solving, calculate earns marks for each correct rearrangement step with the inequality sign carried through, and the final solution as an inequality or integer list as demanded. For integer-solution questions, list earns marks only for the complete correct set: show the solved inequality first, then enumerate. For combined inequalities, handle each side separately and intersect at the end.
### Traps
Error: forgetting to reverse the sign when dividing by a negative. Correction: circle every division by a negative and flip immediately. Error: answering x < 9 with 9 for the largest integer. Correction: step down one for strict inequalities. Error: including -1 in -1 < n <= 3. Correction: strict ends exclude, slack ends include.
### Worked example
Solve −2x > 6. Divide both sides by −2 and reverse the sign, giving x < −3. For a quadratic x² − 4 < 0, factorise to (x − 2)(x + 2) < 0. The product is negative between the roots, so −2 < x < 2.
### Check yourself
Solve 5 − 3x ≤ 17 and show the solution on a number line. Subtract 5 to get −3x ≤ 12, then divide by −3 and reverse the sign to get x ≥ −4. Draw a closed circle at −4 with an arrow to the right.

title: IGCSE Physics: Earth and Space
content:
IGCSE Physics: Earth and Space

Cambridge IGCSE Physics 0625 (2026–2028), Topic 6 Space physics: statements 6.1 The Earth and the Solar System and 6.2 Stars and the Universe. This final topic scales the mechanics and nuclear physics of the rest of the course up to the largest objects there are. Gravity holds planets in orbit and holds stars together; fusion powers stars; the light from distant galaxies tells us the Universe is expanding. Paper 4 usually has one structured question here, and the calculations are orbital mechanics and redshift.

The Earth: rotation, orbit and seasons

The Earth spins on its axis once every 24 hours, which gives day and night, and it orbits the Sun once every 365.25 days, which gives the year. The Earth's axis is tilted at about 23.5° to the plane of its orbit, and that tilt — not the changing distance from the Sun — causes the seasons: when a hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun its rays strike more directly and the days are longer, so it is summer.

The Moon orbits the Earth in about 27 days. It shines by reflected sunlight, and because we see different fractions of its lit half as it orbits, it shows phases: new moon, crescent, half, gibbous, full. A lunar eclipse occurs when the Earth's shadow falls on the Moon; a solar eclipse when the Moon's shadow falls on the Earth.

Supplement: orbital speed. For a circular orbit of radius r completed in period T:

orbital speed = (2 pi r) / T        v = 2 pi r / T
  • v: orbital speed in metres per second (m s⁻¹); r: orbital radius in metres (m); T: orbital period in seconds (s). Convert days and years to seconds first.

The Solar System

The Solar System is the Sun and the bodies bound to it by gravity: eight planets (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune), their moons, dwarf planets, asteroids and comets. The four inner planets are small and rocky with few or no moons; the four outer planets are gas giants — large, low density, with many moons and ring systems. Asteroids orbit mainly between Mars and Jupiter; comets have highly elliptical orbits and grow bright tails of gas and dust when near the Sun.

Gravity provides the centripetal force that keeps every planet, moon and satellite in orbit. A planet's orbital speed falls with distance from the Sun (Kepler's laws), and the planets' orbits are ellipses with the Sun at one focus (Supplement: conservation of energy means a planet speeds up at perihelion and slows at aphelion, trading kinetic for gravitational potential energy).

Supplement: light-travel time. Light from the Sun takes about 8 minutes to reach Earth; from the nearest star, about 4.2 years. The light-year is the distance light travels in one year, about 9.5 × 10¹⁵ m, so looking at distant objects is literally looking into the past.

The Sun as a star

The Sun is an ordinary main-sequence star: a sphere of hot gas, about three-quarters hydrogen and one-quarter helium by mass, with a core at roughly 15 million degrees Celsius. Its energy comes from nuclear fusion in the core, where hydrogen nuclei fuse into helium nuclei, and a small loss of mass becomes the radiated energy. That radiation powers the whole Solar System: it drives the water cycle behind hydroelectric power and biofuels, heats the Earth's surface, and — over geological time — built the fossil fuels (Supplement: solar energy is the principal source behind almost every renewable resource on Earth).

The Sun is a medium-sized star about 4.6 billion years old, with enough hydrogen for roughly another 5 billion years of fusion before it swells into a red giant.

Stars and galaxies

A galaxy is a vast collection of stars, gas and dust held together by gravity. The Sun is one of roughly 200 billion stars in the Milky Way, a spiral galaxy, and galaxies themselves are grouped into clusters. The nearest large galaxy to us is Andromeda, about 2.5 million light-years away.

Stars have life cycles set by their mass:

  • Nebula: a huge cloud of gas and dust, pulled inward by gravity.
  • Protostar: the contracting, heating core of the cloud.
  • Main sequence star: when the core is hot enough for hydrogen fusion to start, the outward radiation pressure balances gravity and the star is stable — the Sun's current stage.
  • Red giant or supergiant: when core hydrogen runs low, fusion moves outwards and the star swells and cools at the surface.
  • End state: a star like the Sun sheds its outer layers as a planetary nebula and leaves a white dwarf. A massive star explodes as a supernova and leaves a neutron star, or, for the most massive, a black hole — an object whose gravity is so strong that not even light escapes.

Supernovae matter beyond astrophysics: they create and scatter the elements heavier than helium, so the carbon, oxygen and iron in your body were forged inside stars.

The Universe: redshift, expansion and the Big Bang

Light from distant galaxies is shifted towards the red end of the spectrum: the spectral lines appear at longer wavelengths than the same lines produced in a laboratory. This redshift is a Doppler effect — the galaxies are moving away from us. Crucially, almost every galaxy shows redshift, and the more distant the galaxy, the greater the redshift and the faster it is receding. The conclusion is that the Universe is expanding.

Running the expansion backwards implies that everything was once at one place — the Big Bang, roughly 13.8 billion years ago. Two further pieces of evidence support it: the cosmic microwave background (CMB), faint microwave radiation coming from every direction, which is the cooled remnant of the hot early Universe, and the abundance of light elements (hydrogen and helium) matching the predictions of Big Bang nucleosynthesis.

Supplement: Hubble's law and the age of the Universe. The recession speed of a galaxy is proportional to its distance:

recession speed = Hubble constant x distance        v = H d
  • v: recession speed in metres per second (m s⁻¹); d: distance in metres (m) (often megaparsecs, but convert); H: the Hubble constant in s⁻¹ (quoted as km s⁻¹ per megaparsec).
  • The age of the Universe follows as roughly 1/H: run the expansion back at the present rate.

Worked example: orbital speed and Hubble's law

The Earth orbits the Sun at a radius of 1.5 × 10¹¹ m with a period of 365 days.

T = 365 x 24 x 3600 = 3.15 × 10⁷ s
v = 2 pi r / T = 2 × 3.14 × 1.5 × 10¹¹ / 3.15 × 10⁷ = 3.0 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹ (about 30 km s⁻¹)

Second calculation: a galaxy is 200 megaparsecs away and Hubble's constant is 70 km s⁻¹ per megaparsec. Its recession speed is v = Hd = 70 × 200 = 14 000 km s⁻¹. The age estimate is 1/H: one megaparsec is 3.1 × 10¹⁹ km, so 1/H = 3.1 × 10¹⁹/70 = 4.4 × 10¹⁷ s ≈ 14 billion years — consistent with the accepted value.

Common mistakes

  • Blaming the seasons on the Earth–Sun distance; it is the axial tilt. The Earth is actually closest to the Sun in January.
  • Confusing the Moon's phases with eclipses: phases are the normal monthly cycle of the lit fraction; eclipses are shadows, and are rare because the Moon's orbit is tilted.
  • Using kilometres and seconds in v = 2πr/T without one consistent unit system; convert the period to seconds and the radius to metres.
  • Calling a light-year a unit of time; it is a distance — the distance light travels in one year.
  • Saying redshift means the galaxies are moving through space away from us; the accepted interpretation is that space itself is expanding, stretching the light.
  • Mixing up redshift and blueshift: receding sources shift to longer (redder) wavelengths; approaching sources shift shorter (bluer) — nearby Andromeda is blueshifted.
  • Placing the Sun at the centre of the Solar System as an absolute; the Sun is the centre of the Solar System, but the Solar System is an ordinary part of the Milky Way.
  • Forgetting that the fusion in stars is hydrogen to helium, which is not the same as the fission of uranium in power stations.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 4, 3 marks). Calculate the orbital speed of a satellite orbiting 7.0 × 10⁶ m from the Earth's centre every 5900 s.

Answer: v = 2πr/T = 2 × 3.14 × 7.0 × 10⁶ / 5900 = 7.5 × 10³ m s⁻¹ (7.5 km s⁻¹).

Question 2 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Explain the evidence from redshift that the Universe is expanding.

Answer: The spectral lines from distant galaxies are shifted towards longer wavelengths than laboratory lines, which by the Doppler effect means the sources are receding. The more distant the galaxy, the greater the redshift and the faster it recedes, so the whole Universe is expanding with every distance growing over time. Reversing that expansion implies all matter was once concentrated at one point — the Big Bang.

Question 3 (Paper 2 style). The seasons on Earth are caused by: A the changing Earth–Sun distance; B the tilt of the Earth's axis; C the Moon's gravity; D the Sun's rotation. Answer: B. The tilt changes the angle of the sunlight and the length of day through the year.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 6 marks). Describe the life cycle of a star like the Sun.

Answer: It begins as a nebula, a cloud of gas and dust. Gravity contracts the cloud and the core heats into a protostar. When the core temperature reaches about 15 million degrees, hydrogen fusion begins and the star joins the main sequence, where radiation pressure from fusion balances gravity and it is stable for billions of years. As core hydrogen depletes, fusion moves outwards, the outer layers expand and cool and the star becomes a red giant. Finally the outer layers are expelled as a planetary nebula, leaving a white dwarf that slowly cools — no fusion, supported by electron degeneracy pressure.

Question 5 (Paper 4, 3 marks). State two pieces of evidence for the Big Bang theory besides the redshift of galaxies.

Answer: The cosmic microwave background radiation — faint microwave radiation arriving from every direction, the cooled afterglow of the hot early Universe. The observed abundances of the light elements, especially hydrogen and helium, match the amounts predicted to have formed in the first minutes after the Big Bang.

Question 6 (Paper 4, 3 marks). Explain why nuclear fusion in the Sun releases energy.

Answer: In fusion, light hydrogen nuclei combine to form a heavier helium nucleus. The product nucleus has slightly less mass than the four protons that formed it; that lost mass is converted into energy in accordance with mass–energy equivalence, and the energy is radiated from the Sun's core. Fusion releases energy for light elements up to iron, which is why it powers stars.

That completes the Cambridge IGCSE 0625 course: the AS notes begin with Edexcel IAL Unit 1 and Kinematics.

Equations and symbols

Earth and space is mostly descriptive, but three quantitative ideas carry the marks: orbital speed, weight on another world, and the distance units that make astronomy's numbers manageable. The cosmological relations are marked as extensions, because 0625 examines the redshift qualitatively.

Orbits

v = 2πr / T
Key: v = orbital speed (m/s); r = orbital radius, measured from the centre of the body being orbited (m); T = orbital period, the time for one complete orbit (s). The 2πr is the circumference of the orbit, so the equation is just speed = distance ÷ time applied to a circle.

a larger orbital radius gives a smaller orbital speed for the same central body
Key: the rule behind a satellite's period rising steeply with height; a geostationary satellite must sit at about 36 000 km above the equator to take exactly 24 hours.

gravitational force provides the centripetal force
Key: the single force keeping a planet or satellite in orbit points towards the centre of the orbit; without it the body would travel in a straight line.

Weight elsewhere

W = mg
Key: W = weight (N); m = mass (kg), unchanged by location; g = gravitational field strength of that body (N/kg). On the Moon g is about 1.6 N/kg, so a 60 kg astronaut weighs about 96 N there and 588 N on Earth.

g(Earth) = 9.8 N/kg and g(Moon) = 1.6 N/kg
Key: the two values used in 0625 questions; weight changes with g while mass does not, which is the whole point of the distinction.

Astronomical distances

1 light year = 9.46 × 10¹⁵ m
Key: the distance light travels in one year, from d = vt with v = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s and t = 3.15 × 10⁷ s. A light year is a distance, not a time.

1 astronomical unit (AU) = 1.5 × 10¹¹ m
Key: the mean Earth–Sun distance, used for distances inside the Solar System; a light year is about 63 000 AU.

orbital period of the planets: T² ∝ r³ (extension)
Key: T = orbital period (s or years); r = orbital radius (m or AU). Kepler's third law, which is why the outer planets take far longer to complete an orbit.

Redshift and the expanding Universe

z = Δλ / λ
Key: z = redshift (no unit); Δλ (delta lambda) = increase in wavelength (m); λ = wavelength emitted in the laboratory (m). A larger z means the galaxy is receding faster.

v = H₀ d (extension)
Key: v = recession speed of a galaxy (km/s); H₀ = the Hubble constant (about 70 km/s per Mpc); d = distance to the galaxy (Mpc). Plotting v against d and taking the gradient gives H₀, and 1/H₀ estimates the age of the Universe.

redshift means the source is receding; blueshift means it is approaching
Key: the observed wavelength is stretched when the source moves away and compressed when it moves towards the observer — the same Doppler effect as a passing siren.

title: A Level Physics: Further Mechanics
content:
A Level Physics: Further Mechanics

Newton's cradle is the whole topic in one toy: a ball arrives, a ball leaves at the same speed, and something invisible has been conserved through the collision. That something is momentum — mass times velocity — and with impulse and energy it lets you analyse every collision, explosion and crash the papers can invent. This note builds the mechanics from zero: the momentum vector and its conservation, impulse as the area under a force–time graph and the physics of why cars crumple, elastic and inelastic collisions with full energy bookkeeping, and the standard problem types solved line by line.

Momentum and its conservation

momentum p = m v        (kg m s-1; a vector)

conservation: in the absence of external forces, the total
momentum of a system stays constant:
  m1 u1 + m2 u2 = m1 v1 + m2 v2

Velocity is a vector, so momentum carries direction: assign positive and negative directions before writing any equation. The conservation law follows from Newton's third law — the forces two bodies exert on each other are equal and opposite for equal times, so the impulses are equal and opposite, so the momentum changes cancel.

Worked example. A 2.0 kg trolley moving at 3.0 m s⁻¹ collides with a stationary 1.0 kg trolley; they stick together. Find the common velocity.

before: 2.0 x 3.0 + 1.0 x 0 = 6.0 kg m s-1
after:  (2.0 + 1.0) v = 3.0 v
3.0 v = 6.0  ->  v = 2.0 m s-1 (same direction)

Impulse

impulse = force x time = change in momentum
J = F Delta t = Delta p = m v - m u

on a force-time graph: impulse = area under the graph

The analogy: catching a ball. A hard catch (short time) means a huge force; moving your hands back (longer time) spreads the same momentum change over more time and reduces the force. That is the entire physics of crumple zones, airbags, seatbelts, helmets, landing mats and bending your knees when you jump down.

Worked example. A 0.16 kg cricket ball arrives at 30 m s⁻¹ and is struck back at 45 m s⁻¹; contact lasts 12 ms. Find the impulse and the average force.

take the incoming direction as negative:
u = -30, v = +45
Delta p = m(v - u) = 0.16 x (45 - (-30)) = 0.16 x 75
        = 12 kg m s-1
F = Delta p/Delta t = 12/0.012 = 1000 N = 1.0 kN

Worked example (graph). A force-time graph shows a triangular pulse rising to 800 N over 0.050 s and falling to zero over the next 0.050 s. Find the impulse and the speed change of a 2.0 kg object.

area = (1/2) x base x height = 0.5 x 0.10 x 800 = 40 N s
Delta p = 40 kg m s-1  ->  Delta v = 40/2.0 = 20 m s-1

Elastic and inelastic collisions

Momentum is conserved in every collision (absent external forces); kinetic energy is conserved only in elastic ones:

ElasticInelastic
Momentumconservedconserved
Kinetic energyconservednot conserved — some becomes heat, sound, deformation
Typical examplegas molecules, billiard-ball idealisationcars sticking together, clay, crumple zones

Explosions run the same conservation law backwards: total momentum before is zero, so the fragments' momenta must cancel.

Worked example (explosion). A 0.50 kg firework at rest explodes into two pieces; the 0.30 kg piece flies at 12 m s⁻¹. Find the velocity of the other piece.

0 = 0.30 x 12 + 0.20 v
0.20 v = -3.6  ->  v = -18 m s-1
The 0.20 kg piece moves at 18 m s-1 in the opposite direction.

Worked examples: the full audit

Worked example. A 1500 kg car at 20 m s⁻¹ crashes into a stationary 1000 kg car; they lock together. Find the velocity after impact, the kinetic energy lost, and explain where it went.

momentum: 1500 x 20 = 2500 v  ->  v = 12 m s-1
KE before = (1/2) x 1500 x 400 = 300 000 J
KE after  = (1/2) x 2500 x 144 = 180 000 J
lost = 120 000 J = 120 kJ
The energy goes to deformation of the bodies, heat, and sound.

Worked example 2 (elastic check). Two identical trolleys approach each other at 2.0 m s⁻¹ and bounce back at 2.0 m s⁻¹ each. Show the collision is elastic.

momentum before: m(2) + m(-2) = 0; after: m(-2) + m(2) = 0
KE before = (1/2)m(4) + (1/2)m(4) = 4m
KE after  = 4m  - unchanged, so elastic.

Momentum in two dimensions

Momentum is conserved separately in each perpendicular direction. For a collision that is not head-on, resolve the momenta into x and y components before and after, and set up two conservation equations. The geometry is where the marks are: a ball striking a wall at an angle rebounds with its perpendicular component reversed and its parallel component unchanged (for a smooth wall), which is why the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence in the ideal case.

before: p_x = m u cos(theta),  p_y = m u sin(theta)
after a smooth-wall bounce:
  p_x = -m v cos(theta)  (normal component reversed)
  p_y = +m v sin(theta)  (parallel component unchanged)
  |Delta p| = 2 m v cos(theta)

Worked example. A 0.20 kg ball hits a smooth wall at 12 m s⁻¹ at 30° to the normal and rebounds elastically at the same speed and angle. Find the impulse on the ball.

Delta p = 2 m v cos(theta) = 2 x 0.20 x 12 x cos(30)
        = 4.8 x 0.866 = 4.2 kg m s-1
(directed away from the wall)

Explosions, recoil and rockets

An explosion is a collision reversed: total momentum stays at its initial value (usually zero), so the fragments' momenta must cancel. Recoil problems — a gun, a skateboarder pushing off, an astronaut throwing a tool — are all this one equation. A rocket is the continuous version: it expels gas backward at high speed and gains forward momentum, and it works in a vacuum precisely because it pushes against its own exhaust, not against the air.

recoil: 0 = m1 v1 + m2 v2   ->   v2 = -(m1/m2) v1
rocket thrust: F = (rate of change of momentum of the exhaust)
             = (mass per second) x (exhaust speed)

Worked example. A 4.0 kg rifle fires a 0.020 kg bullet at 400 m s⁻¹. Find the rifle's recoil speed.

0 = 0.020 x 400 + 4.0 v
4.0 v = -8.0  ->  v = -2.0 m s-1
The rifle recoils at 2.0 m s-1 opposite to the bullet.

Forces, momentum and safety engineering

Questions about safety devices are impulse questions in disguise: the momentum change is fixed by the crash, so the only variable is time. A seatbelt extends the stopping time, so F = Δp/Δt falls; a crumple zone does the same by deforming; an airbag spreads the force over area as well. When asked to evaluate a design, quantify: if the stopping time triples, the average force falls to a third.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Momentum) Define momentum and state its unit. Answer: Momentum is the product of mass and velocity, p = mv, a vector; unit kg m s⁻¹ (equivalently N s).
  2. (Conservation) A 3.0 kg block at 4.0 m s⁻¹ hits a stationary 1.0 kg block and they move together. Find the final speed. Answer: 3.0 × 4.0 = 4.0v → v = 3.0 m s⁻¹.
  3. (Impulse) A 0.50 kg ball hits a wall at 8.0 m s⁻¹ and rebounds at 6.0 m s⁻¹; contact time 0.020 s. Find the average force. Answer: Δp = 0.50 × (6.0 + 8.0) = 7.0 kg m s⁻¹; F = 7.0/0.020 = 350 N.
  4. (Graph) Explain how to find impulse from a force–time graph. Answer: Impulse is the area under the graph; for a curve, count squares or integrate.
  5. (Elasticity) A collision conserves momentum but not kinetic energy. Classify it and name a real example. Answer: Inelastic; a car crash or two lumps of clay sticking together.
  6. (Explosion) A 60 kg astronaut pushes off a 400 kg spacecraft, moving at 0.50 m s⁻¹ relative to it. Find the spacecraft's recoil speed. Answer: 60 × 0.50 = 400 × v → v = 0.075 m s⁻¹ (opposite direction).
  7. (Safety) Explain how a crumple zone reduces injury. Answer: It deforms, increasing the collision time for a given momentum change; since F = Δp/Δt, the average force falls, reducing injury.
  8. (Energy) In an inelastic collision, where does the lost kinetic energy go? Answer: Into thermal energy, sound and permanent deformation of the materials — energy is conserved overall, but not as kinetic energy.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Dropping signs: momentum is a vector; a rebound reverses sign. The classic error is Δp = m(v − u) with both speeds positive, halving the true impulse.
  • Adding speeds wrongly: for a rebound, the change is v + u in magnitude (with signs, v − (−u)).
  • Assuming KE is conserved: check the type; "they stick together" is always inelastic. Compute KE before and after when asked.
  • External forces: conservation needs no net external force — a collision on a rough surface during a long interval is not the same as an instantaneous impact.
  • Unit of impulse: N s or kg m s⁻¹ are equivalent; force alone (N) is not.
  • Force–time areas: triangles and trapeziums need the correct geometric factors (½ for a triangle), not base × height.
  • Mass in grams: convert to kg before momentum calculations; a factor of 1000 error is common in cricket-ball questions.
  • Precision: 2 or 3 s.f. with units; keep direction words (opposite, same direction) in the answer.

title: Exam technique: Arithmetic and Place Value
content:
### What earns the marks
For HCF and LCM, the prime factorisation of each number earns the method mark; state highest powers for LCM and lowest for HCF. For bounds, half-the-precision stated (0.05 for 1 d.p.) earns the method mark before the bound. For estimation, the rounded line (50 x 20 / 10) must be shown: a bare calculator value scores nothing. For time and money, each conversion step shown earns its mark.
### Traps
Error: 16:80 as a time. Correction: 60 minutes carry. Error: largest rounded value confused with the upper bound (6.34 vs 6.35). Correction: the bound is the first value that rounds away. Error: HCF powers used for LCM. Correction: LCM takes the highest of each prime.
### Worked example
In 4 706 325 the digit 7 is in the hundred-thousands place, so its value is 700 000. For order of operations, 3 + 4 × (10 − 6)² is worked out as 3 + 4 × 4² = 3 + 4 × 16 = 3 + 64 = 67. Brackets and powers come before multiplication, and addition comes last.
### Check yourself
State the value of the digit 6 in 4 706 325, then calculate 20 − 2 × (3 + 4)². The 6 is worth 6000. The second is 20 − 2 × 49 = 20 − 98 = −78, which shows why the brackets must be done first.

### Worked example
In 4 706 325 the digit 7 is in the hundred-thousands place, so its value is 700 000. For order of operations, 3 + 4 × (10 − 6)² is worked out as 3 + 4 × 4² = 3 + 4 × 16 = 3 + 64 = 67. Brackets and powers come before multiplication, and addition comes last.

title: AS Level Biology: Membranes, Proteins, DNA and Gene Expression
content:
Membranes, Proteins, DNA and Gene Expression — AS Level Biology

This revision note belongs to the Edexcel International Advanced Subsidiary (IAS) Biology specification, WBI11 Unit 1, Topic 2 Membranes, Proteins, DNA and Gene Expression. It covers membrane structure and properties, osmosis and the different kinds of membrane transport, the structure of proteins and how they are built from amino acids, the structure of DNA and RNA and how DNA replicates, the genetic code and how genes work, transcription and translation, mutations and their effects, patterns of inheritance including sex linkage, cystic fibrosis as an example of a gene mutation in humans, and genetic screening and its ethical and social issues. Every statement the topic is responsible for is covered in its own section or paragraph.

1. Cell membranes and the fluid mosaic model

The cell surface membrane (plasma membrane) is a phospholipid bilayer; each phospholipid has a hydrophilic head and two hydrophobic tails, and the heads face out and in while the tails face each other, making a barrier to charged and water-soluble substances. The fluid mosaic model is the accepted interpretation: the membrane is fluid — the phospholipids and proteins can move laterally in the layer — and mosaic because it contains a variety of proteins embedded in or attached to the bilayer, including channel proteins and carrier proteins for transport, receptor proteins for signalling, and proteins for cell recognition. The model is an interpretation of data — it was built from evidence such as electron micrographs and the ability of membranes to fuse and to self-seal — and it explains the structure and properties of cell membranes and how they control what enters and leaves the cell. Cholesterol in the membrane reduces fluidity at high temperatures and prevents the membrane from becoming too rigid at low temperatures.

2. Core Practical 3 — investigating membrane properties

Investigate membrane properties including the effect of alcohol and of temperature on membrane permeability. A typical method uses beetroot cylinders, which contain the red pigment betalain in their vacuoles; as the membrane is damaged, pigment leaks out and the colour of the surrounding solution deepens. Cut cylinders to the same length, wash off surface pigment in distilled water, then place them in water at a range of temperatures or in different concentrations of alcohol for a fixed time, remove the tissue and measure the concentration of pigment in the solution with a colorimeter. As temperature rises or alcohol concentration rises, the membrane proteins denature and the lipid bilayer is disrupted, so permeability increases and more pigment leaks out; a control at room temperature or in distilled water shows the baseline. Record the colorimeter reading for each tube, plot a graph of permeability against temperature or against alcohol concentration, and explain the trend in terms of the effect on membrane proteins and lipids.

3. Osmosis and how water moves across membranes

Osmosis is the net movement of free water molecules through a partially permeable membrane, down a water potential gradient — from higher water potential to lower water potential. Water potential is the tendency of water to move; adding a solute lowers it, so a concentrated solution has a more negative water potential than a dilute one, and pure water has the highest (zero) water potential. If a cell is placed in a solution of higher water potential than its contents, water enters by osmosis and the cell swells; if it is an animal cell it may burst (haemolysis); if it is a plant cell the cell wall prevents bursting and the cell becomes turgid, which supports the plant. In a solution of lower water potential, water leaves and the cell shrinks — animal cells crenate and plant cells become plasmolysed, with the membrane pulling away from the wall. A recommended additional practical is to investigate tissue water potentials using plant tissue (for example potato or onion epidermis) and graded concentrations of a solute: place tissue in solutions of different molarity, note the change in length or mass, and find the concentration at which there is no change — that concentration has the same water potential as the tissue.

4. Passive transport, active transport, endocytosis and exocytosis

Passive transport needs no energy input because substances move down their concentration gradient. Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to one of lower concentration; small, non-polar molecules such as oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse directly through the phospholipid bilayer, while ions and large polar molecules cannot. Facilitated diffusion is the movement of specific particles down their concentration gradient through channel proteins or carrier proteins — channel proteins form water-filled pores for ions, and carrier proteins change shape to carry molecules across. Active transport moves substances against their concentration gradient (from low to high concentration) and needs energy directly from ATP; carrier proteins use ATP to pump substances across, as in the sodium–potassium pump. Endocytosis is the bulk movement of material into the cell inside a vesicle formed from the plasma membrane; phagocytosis takes in solid material and pinocytosis takes in fluid. Exocytosis is the reverse — material is moved out of the cell in a vesicle that fuses with the plasma membrane, as in the secretion of proteins and neurotransmitters. Carrier and channel proteins are involved in facilitated diffusion and active transport; the key difference is that active transport needs ATP and moves substances against their gradient.

5. Protein structure: from amino acid to three-dimensional shape

Amino acids are the monomers of proteins; the basic structure of an amino acid is an amino group, a carboxyl group and a variable R group all attached to a central carbon, with a hydrogen on the remaining bond. There are around 20 amino acids found in proteins, differing only in their R group, and the sequence of amino acids in a protein is its primary structure. Amino acids join by condensation reactions to form peptide bonds, making dipeptides and then polypeptides; a polypeptide chain is a protein''s primary structure and it determines everything about the protein. The secondary structure is the local folding of the chain into alpha-helices and beta-pleated sheets, held by hydrogen bonds between the peptide bonds. The tertiary structure is the overall three-dimensional folding of the whole polypeptide, held by hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, disulfide bonds and hydrophobic interactions; it gives the protein its specific shape and therefore its function. Globular proteins are roughly spherical and usually soluble and active — haemoglobin is the classic example, with four polypeptide chains and a haem group each carrying one oxygen molecule, and it shows quaternary structure (several polypeptides together) plus the importance of the three-dimensional shape for its oxygen-carrying function. Fibrous proteins are long, insoluble and structural — collagen is the example, made of three polypeptide chains wound into a rope-like triple helix, giving strength for tendons, ligaments and skin. The shape of a protein determines its function, so a change to the primary structure can alter the folding and disable the protein.

6. DNA structure and replication

A DNA molecule is made of two nucleotide strands twisted into a double helix. Each nucleotide is made of a deoxyribose sugar, a phosphate group and a base — either adenine (A), cytosine (C), guanine (G) or thymine (T). The two strands run antiparallel and are linked by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases — A pairs with T (two hydrogen bonds) and C pairs with G (three hydrogen bonds). RNA is similar but has ribose instead of deoxyribose, uracil instead of thymine, and is usually single-stranded. The two strands are complementary, so knowing one strand tells you the other, and the two strands separate at replication. DNA replication is semi-conservative: the double helix unzips, each strand acts as a template, and free nucleotides pair with their complementary bases; DNA polymerase joins the nucleotides into a new strand. The result is two identical DNA molecules, each with one old strand and one new strand. Meselson and Stahl''s experiment supported this: they grew bacteria in a medium with a heavy isotope of nitrogen (15N), then moved them to a 14N medium and examined the DNA by centrifugation; the first generation was a single hybrid band (not one heavy and one light, which would be conservative replication), and later generations showed a mixture of hybrid and light bands — exactly what semi-conservative replication predicts and ruling out the conservative and dispersive alternatives.

7. The genetic code and how it works

The genetic code is the set of rules translating the base sequence of mRNA into the amino acid sequence of a protein. It is a triplet code — three bases (a base triplet on DNA, a codon on mRNA) code for one amino acid; it is non-overlapping — each base is read once in order; and it is degenerate — more than one codon can code for the same amino acid, which is why many mutations change a base but not the amino acid. Part of the code is a stop codon that signals the end of translation; there is no amino acid for it. A gene is a sequence of bases on a DNA molecule that codes for a sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide chain. In transcription, the gene is copied into a complementary mRNA molecule by the enzyme RNA polymerase, using the DNA template (antisense) strand; the mRNA is complementary to the template strand and the same as the coding (sense) strand except with uracil in place of thymine. mRNA leaves the nucleus and attaches to ribosomes in the cytoplasm; transfer RNA (tRNA) molecules carry amino acids to the ribosome, each with a three-base anticodon that pairs with the mRNA codon, so the ribosome joins the amino acids into a polypeptide chain in the order of the codons until a stop codon is reached.

8. Mutations: the changes and their effects

A mutation is a change in the DNA base sequence. A substitution replaces one base with another — it may do nothing, change one amino acid, or, rarely, create a stop codon that shortens the protein. An insertion adds one or more bases and a deletion removes one or more; because the code is read in triplets, an insertion or deletion not in a multiple of three causes a frameshift, changing every amino acid after the mutation and usually destroying the protein''s function. Mutations are the only source of new alleles, and most have no observable effect — they may be in non-coding DNA, or a degenerate codon and amino acid may stay the same, or the changed protein still folds and works. Some mutations give rise to cancer (if they affect control of the cell cycle) or to genetic disorders. Ionising radiation such as X-rays and ultraviolet light, and some chemicals such as those in tobacco smoke, can increase the rate of mutation by damaging DNA.

9. Patterns of inheritance: monohybrid crosses, pedigree diagrams and sex linkage

A gene can have different alleles; the genotype is the alleles an organism has, the phenotype is the observable feature. Dominant alleles show in the phenotype even when heterozygous; recessive alleles only show when homozygous. A monohybrid cross is the inheritance of one gene with two alleles; the typical ratios are a 3:1 phenotype ratio in the F2 of a monohybrid cross between two heterozygotes, but only if the alleles are completely dominant and the gene is autosomal. Sex linkage is the inheritance of a gene on the X chromosome — because males have only one X, a recessive allele on it shows in their phenotype even though they are effectively hemizygous; red-green colour blindness and haemophilia are human X-linked conditions that are more common in males. Pedigree diagrams record which family members show a trait and are used to work out whether a trait is dominant or recessive and whether it is autosomal or sex-linked. Codominance is when both alleles are expressed in the heterozygote, as in the ABO blood group system where IA and IB are codominant and i is recessive, giving the four blood groups A, B, AB and O.

10. Cystic fibrosis: a mutation that affects three systems

Cystic fibrosis is caused by a mutation in a gene that codes for a chloride ion channel protein; in the most common form a deletion of three bases removes a single amino acid from the protein, so the channel does not work properly. As a result, chloride ions and water cannot move properly across cell membranes, and the mucus and other secretions become abnormally thick. In the gaseous exchange system the thick mucus blocks the airways and makes it hard to breathe and to clear infections; in the digestive system the pancreatic duct is blocked so digestive enzymes from the pancreas cannot reach the gut, so food is not digested and absorbed properly, and the person may be malnourished; in the reproductive system the vas deferens is often absent or blocked in males, causing infertility. Treatments include physiotherapy and antibiotics for the lungs, and enzyme supplements with meals for digestion, and newer treatments aim to correct the underlying defect.

11. Genetic screening: what it can do and the issues it raises

Genetic screening can identify carriers of recessive alleles (people who have one normal allele and one faulty allele and are unaffected but could pass the allele on), and prenatal testing can check a fetus: amniocentesis takes a sample of amniotic fluid at around 15–17 weeks, and chorionic villus sampling takes a sample of placental tissue at 8–12 weeks. Pre-implantation genetic diagnosis is used with IVF to test embryos before implantation and select unaffected ones. Each raises ethical and social questions — the safety and reliability of the test, the risks of miscarriage with invasive prenatal testing, the right to know or not to know, who decides which conditions to test for, the possible choice to terminate a pregnancy, anxiety and guilt, and the risk that screening could be used to select non-medical traits. Students should be able to identify and discuss these from religious, moral and social viewpoints and to evaluate the implications of prenatal genetic screening.

12. How to use this note and what to revise next

Use these notes by working through each section and checking that you can draw a cell membrane from the fluid mosaic model and label the phospholipid bilayer, the proteins, cholesterol and glycoproteins; state the difference between diffusion, facilitated diffusion and active transport, and give an example of each; outline the steps of DNA extraction (a simple practical with strawberries or onions is useful to remember); and carry out a genetic cross with a Punnett square and interpret the ratios. Revise by drawing protein structure from amino acid to tertiary, then drawing the DNA double helix and explaining semi-conservative replication and the Meselson–Stahl evidence. After this topic, revise Topic 3 Cell structure, reproduction and development, because the same DNA and protein-synthesis processes control cell differentiation and the cell cycle.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Osmosis, applied to a potato cylinder placed in a sugar solution: water moves from the higher water potential to the lower one, down a gradient, through a partially permeable membrane. A cylinder that loses mass has been placed in a solution of lower water potential than its cells. Give the direction of water movement and the reason in the same sentence.
  • Monohybrid cross, applied to two heterozygotes (Aa × Aa): the offspring are 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa, so the phenotypic ratio is 3 : 1. Write the parental genotypes, the gametes and the Punnett square, then state the ratio. A ratio alone earns less than the full working.
  • Sex linkage, applied to X-linked haemophilia: a carrier mother (XᴴXʰ) and a normal father (XᴴY) have a 50% chance of a son with haemophilia, but a daughter cannot be affected unless her father is affected. Use the X and Y chromosomes explicitly in the genotypes.
  • Mutation effects: a substitution may have no effect because the genetic code is degenerate, while a frameshift changes every codon after the mutation. Name the type of mutation and state whether the change alters the amino acid sequence.

How substances cross a membrane, compared

RouteDirectionProtein neededATP usedExample
Simple diffusionDown the concentration gradientNoNoOxygen into a cell
Facilitated diffusionDown the concentration gradientChannel or carrierNoGlucose into a red blood cell through a carrier
OsmosisDown a water potential gradientNo (partially permeable membrane)NoWater into a root hair cell
Active transportAgainst the concentration gradientCarrier that changes shapeYes, ATP hydrolysedIons reabsorbed in the kidney
Endocytosis and exocytosisInto or out of the cell in a vesicleNo, membrane fusionYesPhagocytosis of a bacterium; secretion of an enzyme

Typical mistakes

  • Writing that active transport "uses energy" and stopping there. The mark is for ATP being hydrolysed to change the shape of the carrier protein, which moves the substance against its gradient.
  • Confusing water potential with solute concentration. Pure water at atmospheric pressure has a water potential of zero, and every solution has a negative value. Water moves from the less negative (higher) water potential to the more negative one.
  • Swapping codon and anticodon. The codon is the triplet on messenger RNA; the anticodon is the triplet on transfer RNA that pairs with it.
  • Saying DNA polymerase unzips the helix. Helicase breaks the hydrogen bonds between the strands; DNA polymerase then adds free nucleotides to the exposed template, always in the 5-prime to 3-prime direction.
  • Claiming the Meselson and Stahl experiment showed dispersive replication. After one generation in nitrogen-15 there was a single hybrid band, and after two generations there were hybrid and light bands. A dispersive model would have given a single intermediate band throughout.
  • Assuming a dominant allele is the more common one. Dominance describes expression in the heterozygote, not frequency in the population.
  • Confusing amniocentesis with chorionic villus sampling. Amniocentesis samples amniotic fluid at about 15 to 17 weeks; chorionic villus sampling takes placental tissue at about 8 to 12 weeks, earlier but with a higher risk of miscarriage.
  • Explaining cystic fibrosis without a mechanism. The mutation changes the chloride channel, so chloride and water cannot cross normally, secretions become thick, and the airways, pancreatic duct and vas deferens are affected. Name the ion, the effect on the secretion and the effect on the organ.

Exam-style questions

  1. Explain why the fluid mosaic model was modified as new evidence appeared. Answer: the model is an interpretation of data, not a direct observation. Freeze-fracture electron micrographs showed proteins embedded within the bilayer rather than coating it, and experiments on membrane fusion showed that proteins move within the membrane, so the model was revised to show a fluid bilayer with proteins partly or wholly embedded.
  2. A potato cylinder loses mass after 30 minutes in 0.6 mol per dm cubed sucrose solution. Explain the loss in terms of water potential. Answer: the sucrose solution has a lower (more negative) water potential than the vacuole contents, so water leaves the cells by osmosis down a water potential gradient through the partially permeable membranes, the cells lose turgor, and the cylinder shrinks.
  3. Distinguish facilitated diffusion from active transport. Answer: both use membrane proteins, but facilitated diffusion moves substances down their concentration gradient through channels or carriers and needs no ATP, while active transport moves them against the gradient using a carrier whose shape is changed by ATP hydrolysis.
  4. Describe the evidence that DNA replication is semi-conservative. Answer: bacteria were grown in nitrogen-15 so that all DNA was heavy, then transferred to nitrogen-14. After one generation all DNA was of intermediate density, which rules out conservative replication; after two generations half the DNA was intermediate and half light, which fits each new molecule keeping one parental strand.
  5. Give the role of the template strand, the codon and the anticodon in protein synthesis. Answer: the template (antisense) strand is the DNA strand that RNA polymerase copies; the codon is the triplet of bases on mRNA that specifies one amino acid; the anticodon on tRNA is complementary to the codon and pairs with it at the ribosome so that the correct amino acid is added.
  6. Explain how a substitution and a deletion affect the polypeptide differently. Answer: a substitution changes one base, so at most one codon changes and, because the code is degenerate, the amino acid sequence may not change at all. A deletion shifts the reading frame, so every codon after the mutation is different and the protein is usually non-functional.
  7. A carrier mother and an unaffected father are expecting a child. Explain the probability that a son is colour blind. Answer: the mother is heterozygous, with one affected X chromosome and one normal X chromosome. A son inherits one of her X chromosomes with equal probability, so half the sons are colour blind. Daughters receive the father's normal X, so none is colour blind, although half are carriers.
  8. Explain how the mutation that causes cystic fibrosis impairs three body systems. Answer: the three-base deletion removes one amino acid from the chloride channel protein, so chloride transport is faulty and water follows less readily. Mucus in the airways becomes thick and blocks gas exchange; the pancreatic duct blocks so digestive enzymes do not reach the gut; the vas deferens is absent or blocked, reducing male fertility.

title: AS Level Mathematics: Quadratics
content:
AS Level Mathematics: Quadratics

A quadratic is a curve you already know from everyday life: the path of a thrown ball, the profit curve of a business, the shape of a satellite dish. Algebraically it is any expression ax² + bx + c with a ≠ 0, and this note builds every technique the AS papers test: solving by factorising, completing the square and the formula; using the discriminant to count roots without solving; reading the vertex and intercepts off a sketch; and solving simultaneous and inequality problems where the quadratic meets a line. Every step is shown line by line, because the method marks live in the middle.

The three forms of a quadratic

FormExpressionWhat it reveals
Standardax² + bx + cthe y-intercept is c
Factoriseda(x − p)(x − q)roots at x = p and x = q
Completed squarea(x + h)² + kvertex at (−h, k); minimum or maximum k

The sign of a decides the shape: a > 0 opens upward (a minimum), a < 0 opens downward (a maximum). The axis of symmetry runs through the vertex, halfway between the roots.

Solving by factorising

Look for two numbers that multiply to ac and add to b, then split the middle term and factorise in pairs.

Worked example. Solve 2x² + 7x + 3 = 0.

ac = 6, b = 7: numbers 6 and 1
2x^2 + 6x + x + 3 = 0
2x(x + 3) + 1(x + 3) = 0
(2x + 1)(x + 3) = 0
x = -1/2 or x = -3

Worked example 2 (difference of squares). Solve 9x² − 25 = 0.

(3x - 5)(3x + 5) = 0
x = 5/3 or x = -5/3

Completing the square

Write x² + bx + c as (x + b/2)² − (b/2)² + c. The method: halve the coefficient of x, square the bracket, subtract the square of that half.

Worked example. Write x² − 6x + 11 in completed-square form and state the vertex.

x^2 - 6x + 11 = (x - 3)^2 - 9 + 11
              = (x - 3)^2 + 2
vertex: (3, 2); minimum value 2 at x = 3

Worked example 2 (leading coefficient not 1). Write 2x² + 8x + 5 in completed-square form.

factor out 2: 2(x^2 + 4x) + 5
complete inside: 2[(x + 2)^2 - 4] + 5
= 2(x + 2)^2 - 8 + 5 = 2(x + 2)^2 - 3
vertex: (-2, -3); minimum -3

Worked example 3 (solving by completing the square). Solve x² + 4x − 1 = 0, giving exact answers.

(x + 2)^2 - 4 - 1 = 0
(x + 2)^2 = 5
x + 2 = +/- sqrt(5)
x = -2 +/- sqrt(5)

The quadratic formula and the discriminant

x = (-b +/- sqrt(b^2 - 4ac)) / (2a)

discriminant D = b^2 - 4ac
D > 0: two distinct real roots
D = 0: one repeated root (the curve touches the x-axis)
D < 0: no real roots (the curve misses the x-axis)

Worked example. Solve 3x² − 5x − 2 = 0 using the formula.

a = 3, b = -5, c = -2
D = 25 + 24 = 49
x = (5 +/- 7)/6
x = 12/6 = 2 or x = -2/6 = -1/3

Worked example 2 (discriminant). Find the values of k for which x² + kx + 9 = 0 has equal roots.

equal roots: D = 0
k^2 - 36 = 0
k = 6 or k = -6

Sketching a quadratic

A sketch needs four features: the shape (up or down from the sign of a), the y-intercept (c), the roots (from factorising or the formula) and the vertex (from completing the square or the midpoint of the roots). Mark them, then draw a smooth curve through them.

Worked example. Sketch y = x² − 4x + 3.

a = 1 > 0: opens upward
y-intercept: (0, 3)
roots: x^2 - 4x + 3 = (x - 1)(x - 3) -> x = 1, 3
vertex: (x - 2)^2 - 1 -> (2, -1)
axis of symmetry: x = 2

Simultaneous equations: a line and a curve

The method: make one variable the subject in the line, substitute into the curve, solve the resulting quadratic, then find the partner values. Two solutions mean the line cuts the curve twice; one means it is a tangent; none means it misses.

Worked example. Solve y = x² − 1 and y = 3x − 3.

x^2 - 1 = 3x - 3
x^2 - 3x + 2 = 0
(x - 1)(x - 2) = 0  ->  x = 1 or x = 2
y = 3(1) - 3 = 0  and  y = 3(2) - 3 = 3
solutions: (1, 0) and (2, 3)

Worked example 2 (tangency condition). Find k such that y = 2x + k is tangent to y = x² + 3.

x^2 + 3 = 2x + k  ->  x^2 - 2x + (3 - k) = 0
tangent: D = 0  ->  4 - 4(3 - k) = 0
4 - 12 + 4k = 0  ->  4k = 8  ->  k = 2

Quadratic inequalities

Solve the corresponding equation first, sketch the parabola, then read which x-values satisfy the inequality.

Worked example. Solve x² − x − 6 < 0.

roots: (x - 3)(x + 2) = 0  ->  x = 3, x = -2
the parabola opens upward, so it is below the axis between
the roots:  -2 < x < 3

Worked example 2 (outside). Solve x² − 4 ≥ 0.

roots x = +/-2; upward parabola is above the axis outside:
x <= -2 or x >= 2

Disguised quadratics

Many equations are quadratic in disguise: a substitution turns them into the standard form. The signal is a repeated expression appearing with two different powers — x⁴ and x², or 2^x and 2^(2x), or a trigonometric term squared and unsquared.

Worked example 1. Solve x⁴ − 5x² + 4 = 0.

let u = x^2:  u^2 - 5u + 4 = 0
(u - 1)(u - 4) = 0  ->  u = 1 or u = 4
back-substitute:
x^2 = 1  ->  x = +/-1
x^2 = 4  ->  x = +/-2
four solutions: x = 1, -1, 2, -2

Worked example 2 (exponential). Solve 2^(2x) − 5(2^x) + 4 = 0.

let u = 2^x:  u^2 - 5u + 4 = 0  ->  u = 1 or 4
2^x = 1  ->  x = 0
2^x = 4  ->  x = 2

The discipline is to return to the original variable at the end and to check that each candidate is valid in the original domain (a negative u cannot equal 2^x).

Modelling with quadratics

Applied questions give a context and expect you to build the quadratic, then use completing the square or the formula for a maximum or minimum.

Worked example (area). A rectangular garden is to be fenced with 40 m of fencing against a wall (so only three sides need fencing). Find the maximum area.

let the two equal sides be x; the third side is 40 - 2x
area A = x(40 - 2x) = 40x - 2x^2
complete the square: A = -2(x^2 - 20x) = -2[(x - 10)^2 - 100]
                    = -2(x - 10)^2 + 200
maximum area = 200 m2 when x = 10
(dimensions 10 m by 20 m)

Worked example 2 (profit). A stall sells n items at price (20 − 0.5n) pounds each. Find the number that maximises revenue.

revenue R = n(20 - 0.5n) = 20n - 0.5n^2
R = -0.5(n^2 - 40n) = -0.5[(n - 20)^2 - 400]
  = -0.5(n - 20)^2 + 200
maximum revenue 200 pounds at n = 20 items

Both examples share the signature: a product of two linear expressions in the same variable, completed to reveal a maximum. Negative leading coefficient means maximum; positive means minimum.

Worked example 3 (sum and product of roots). For 2x² − 7x + 3 = 0, find the sum and product of the roots without solving.

sum of roots = -b/a = 7/2
product of roots = c/a = 3/2
check by solving: (2x - 1)(x - 3) = 0 -> roots 1/2 and 3;
sum 3.5, product 1.5 - consistent

These two relations are useful for forming equations from given roots and for checking a factorisation. If a question says the roots are p and q, the quadratic is x² − (p + q)x + pq = 0 (up to a constant factor). They also settle symmetric questions such as "find p² + q² given the equation": p² + q² = (p + q)² − 2pq, computed straight from the coefficients without finding the roots themselves.

A shortcut worth knowing for sketch questions: the vertex of y = ax² + bx + c sits at x = −b/(2a), and its y-coordinate comes from substituting that x back into the equation. This is the same result as completing the square, reached faster when only the turning point is needed and the exact form is not requested.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Factorise) Solve x² + x − 12 = 0. Answer: (x + 4)(x − 3) = 0 → x = −4 or 3.
  2. (Complete the square) Write x² + 8x + 10 in the form (x + p)² + q. Answer: (x + 4)² − 6.
  3. (Vertex) State the minimum point of y = (x − 5)² + 7. Answer: (5, 7).
  4. (Formula) Solve 2x² + 5x − 3 = 0. Answer: D = 25 + 24 = 49; x = (−5 ± 7)/4 = ½ or −3.
  5. (Discriminant) Show that x² + 2x + 5 = 0 has no real roots. Answer: D = 4 − 20 = −16 < 0.
  6. (Simultaneous) Solve y = x² and y = x + 2. Answer: x² = x + 2 → x² − x − 2 = 0 → x = 2 or −1; points (2, 4) and (−1, 1).
  7. (Inequality) Solve x² + 3x − 10 < 0. Answer: (x + 5)(x − 2) < 0 → −5 < x < 2.
  8. (Tangent) Find k so that y = kx + 1 touches y = x² − 2x + 3. Answer: x² − (2 + k)x + 2 = 0; D = 0 → (2 + k)² = 8 → k = −2 ± 2√2.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Sign inside the completed square: x² − 6x completes to (x − 3)², not (x + 3)². The sign inside is half the coefficient's sign.
  • Forgetting to subtract the square: (x + 4)² is x² + 8x + 16, so x² + 8x needs −16. The correction term is mandatory.
  • Formula sign errors: x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac))/2a — both terms negate b, and the whole numerator divides by 2a (not just the root).
  • Discriminant conclusions: D > 0 means two roots, D = 0 one repeated, D < 0 none; "two roots" does not mean two positive roots.
  • Inequality direction: for "< 0" the solution lies between the roots when a > 0; for "> 0" outside them. Sketching prevents reversal.
  • Not using the original equation: when solving simultaneous equations, substitute back into the line (simpler) and state both coordinates.
  • Dividing by x: x² = 4x gives x = 0 or x = 4; dividing by x loses the root x = 0.
  • Sketch versus plot: a sketch needs shape, intercepts and turning point marked; a plot needs plotted points. Answer the question asked.

title: Ethics, Security & Impact — Study Notes
content:
Ethics, Security & Impact

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): ethics & professional codes, security threats, malware, online safety, environmental/employment impact.

1. Ethics and codes

ACM/IEEE-CS/BCS codes: public interest, competence, integrity, privacy. Applying: identify the principle → apply to scenario → stakeholders affected → consequences.

2. Threats

  • Malware: virus (attaches, replicates via host), worm (self-spreads), trojan (disguised), spyware, ransomware.
  • Social: phishing (fake emails/sites), pharming (DNS/hosts redirect), shoulder surfing, brute force.
  • Technical: interception (packet sniffing), SQL injection (malicious input into queries), DoS (flooding services).

3. Cyber security

Cyber security protects data, systems and users from attack. A vulnerability is a weakness an attack can use; a threat is what exploits it.

  • Vulnerabilities: default or weak passwords, unpatched software, misconfigured access rights, unsecured or public Wi-Fi, removable media (memory sticks), insider threat, unencrypted data in transit.
  • Malware: virus (needs a host file and replicates when that file runs), worm (self-spreads across a network), trojan (disguised as useful software), spyware (records activity), ransomware (encrypts files and demands payment), adware.
  • Social engineering: phishing (fake email or site asks for details), pharming (malicious redirect via DNS or the hosts file), blagging (invented story), shoulder surfing, brute-force and dictionary attacks.
  • Technical attacks: interception / packet sniffing on an unsecured network, SQL injection (malicious input typed into a query field), denial of service and DDoS (flooding a service so it cannot respond), session hijacking.

Protection: strong unique passwords plus 2FA; biometric authentication (fingerprint, face); encryption so intercepted data is unreadable (plaintext is turned into ciphertext with a key — HTTPS/TLS does this on websites); firewalls filtering traffic by IP address and port; anti-malware that scans, blocks and quarantines; patching and updates; user access levels so staff reach only what they need; regular backups; user training; penetration testing to find holes first.

Answer shape: name the threat precisely (pharming is not phishing), then give the matched defence — pharming → keep DNS servers and hosts files secure and check HTTPS certificates.

4. Digital currency

A digital currency exists only in electronic form. A cryptocurrency (for example Bitcoin) is a decentralised digital currency secured by cryptography and recorded on a blockchain.

  • Blockchain: a distributed ledger — every node holds a copy. Transactions are grouped into blocks, and each block stores the hash of the previous block, so altering an old record breaks the chain and is rejected by the network.
  • Keys and wallets: the owner holds a public key (the address others pay to) and a private key (proves ownership and signs a payment). A wallet stores these keys — lose the private key and the money is gone.
  • Transactions: broadcast to the network, checked by nodes and added to a block; the verifier (miner) is rewarded. No bank or central authority is involved.

Advantages: quick international transfers, low transaction fees, no central authority to fail or censor, a transparent ledger, and coins cannot be counterfeited. Disadvantages: the value is very volatile, payments are irreversible, mining uses large amounts of energy, it appeals to criminals and ransomware demands, it needs internet access and technical care, and there is little consumer protection if a wallet is lost or stolen.

5. Defences

Antivirus/antispyware (scan, quarantine), firewalls (port/IP filtering), 2FA + biometrics, strong passwords + managers, encryption (HTTPS, VPN), access levels, patches/updates, user training.

6. Online behaviour

Digital footprint, cyberbullying, fake news, privacy settings, verification of sources.

7. Wider impact

Employment: automation displaces roles but creates IT jobs. Environment: e-waste, energy use vs paperless efficiency. Monitoring: workplace tracking, CCTV — balance with privacy laws (GDPR-style).

Exam tips: name the threat precisely (pharming ≠ phishing), then the matched defence; ethics answers need principle + application, not opinion.

title: Hardware & Architecture — Study Notes
content:
Hardware & Architecture

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): von Neumann model, FDE cycle, registers, buses, RAM/ROM, secondary storage, embedded systems.

1. Von Neumann model

CPU (ALU, control unit, registers) + memory + I/O on shared buses; instructions stored as data (stored program concept).

2. Registers

RegisterRole
PCaddress of next instruction
MARaddress being read/written
MDRdata/instruction in transit
ACCALU results accumulator

3. FDE cycle

Fetch: PC → MAR; memory → MDR → CIR; PC + 1. Decode: control unit interprets opcode. Execute: ALU/registers act. Interrupts can pause between cycles.

4. Buses and performance

Address bus (one-way, width ⇒ addressable memory), data bus (two-way, width ⇒ bits per transfer), control bus. Performance factors: clock speed, cache size, core count — explain the effect, not just the name.

5. RAM vs ROM

RAM: volatile, read/write, holds running programs + data. ROM: non-volatile, read-only, bootstrap/firmware. Embedded systems: dedicated microprocessors inside devices (washing machines, engines) — one function, low cost, hard to update.

6. Secondary storage

  • Magnetic (HDD): platters, read/write heads; high capacity, cheap per GB, moving parts (shock-sensitive).
  • Optical (CD/DVD/Blu-ray): laser pits/lands; cheap, portable, slow, small capacity.
  • Solid state (SSD/flash): NAND cells; fast, silent, robust, no moving parts, more expensive per GB, finite write cycles.

Choose by use case: video editing (SSD), archive (optical/magnetic), tablets (flash).

Exam tips: trace FDE with register values; compare storage on capacity, speed, cost, durability, portability; always tie a performance factor to its effect.

title: IGCSE Mathematics: Graphs and Coordinate Geometry
content:
IGCSE Mathematics: Graphs and Coordinate Geometry

Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580 (2025–2027), section 2 statements 2.9 Graphs in practical situations, 2.10 Graphs of functions, 2.11 Sketching curves, 2.12 Differentiation (Extended), and section 3 statements 3.1 to 3.7 Coordinate geometry. Graphs turn algebra into pictures and pictures into algebra, and the coordinate geometry of straight lines is the most examined machinery in both papers. This note builds coordinates, gradient, the equation of a line, length and midpoint from scratch, then practical graphs, curves and the first steps of differentiation — with every formula derived rather than asserted.

Coordinates and the Cartesian plane

A point's position is given by an ordered pair (x, y): the x-coordinate says how far right (positive) or left (negative) of the origin, and the y-coordinate says how far up (positive) or down (negative). Order matters: (3, 5) is a different point from (5, 3). The plane is cut into four quadrants by the x-axis and y-axis, and a point on an axis has one coordinate equal to zero. Plotting accurately means counting in the scale given on the axes, marking with a small cross, and labelling the point.

The gradient of a straight line

Gradient measures steepness: how far the line rises or falls for each unit it runs to the right. The word to remember is vertical over horizontal.

gradient = (change in y) / (change in x) = (y2 - y1) / (x2 - x1)
  • Gradient m is a number with no unit: 2 means the line rises 2 units for every 1 unit right.
  • Uphill lines have positive gradient, downhill lines negative; a horizontal line has gradient 0 and a vertical line has undefined gradient (zero run).
  • The gradient between two points is the same wherever the points are taken on a straight line — that constancy is what makes the line straight.

Why the formula works. Take points (1, 2) and (4, 10). Walking from the first to the second you go up 10 − 2 = 8 units and right 4 − 1 = 3 units, so the steepness is 8/3. The formula just records that walk for any two points.

Find the gradient of the line through (-2, 5) and (3, -7):

m = (-7 - 5) / (3 - (-2)) = -12 / 5 = -2.4        [negative: the line falls to the right]

The equation of a straight line

Every straight-line graph can be written as y = mx + c, where m is the gradient and c is the y-intercept (where the line crosses the y-axis). The formula calculates the y-value for any x, and it is the algebraic twin of the drawing.

Find the equation of the line with gradient 2 passing through (1, 5):

y = mx + c gives 5 = 2(1) + c        [substitute the point and the gradient]
5 = 2 + c
c = 3
y = 2x + 3

Given two points instead, find the gradient first, then use one point to find c. Given the intercept and a point, substitute. The form ax + by + d = 0 is the same line rearranged, and gradient-intercept form can always be recovered by solving for y.

Parallel lines never meet, so they have equal gradients: m₁ = m₂. Perpendicular lines meet at right angles, and their gradients multiply to −1:

m¹ x m² = -1        so the perpendicular gradient is  m² = -1 / m¹

Why −1. Rotating a right-angled triangle through 90° swaps its two legs and reverses one direction, turning a rise/run of m into a run/rise of −1/m. If one line has gradient 2, a line at right angles to it has gradient −1/2; if a line has gradient 0 (horizontal), the perpendicular line is vertical with undefined gradient.

Find the equation of the line perpendicular to y = 3x - 4 passing through (3, 0):

perpendicular gradient = -1/3
y = (-1/3)x + c
0 = (-1/3)(3) + c = -1 + c,  so c = 1
y = -x/3 + 1

Length and midpoint of a line segment (Extended)

The distance between two points is Pythagoras applied to the horizontal and vertical gaps; the midpoint is the average of the coordinates.

length = √[(x2 - x1)² + (y2 - y1)²]
midpoint = ((x1 + x2)/2, (y1 + y2)/2)

Why. The horizontal gap is (x₂ − x₁) and the vertical gap is (y₂ − y₁); these are the two shorter sides of a right-angled triangle whose hypotenuse is the distance, so Pythagoras gives the length at once. The midpoint formula is just the average of the two x-values and of the two y-values.

Find the length and midpoint of the segment joining A(-1, 2) and B(5, 8):

horizontal gap = 5 - (-1) = 6;  vertical gap = 8 - 2 = 6
length = √(6² + 6²) = √72 = 6√2 ≈ 8.49
midpoint = ((-1 + 5)/2, (2 + 8)/2) = (2, 5)

Graphs in practical situations

Real data is plotted on axes carrying units, and the shape of the graph tells the story. The skills are reading values, finding gradients and interpreting what sections mean.

GraphVertical axisGradient meansArea means
Distance–timeDistance (m or km)SpeedNot used
Speed–timeSpeed (m s⁻¹)AccelerationDistance travelled
Temperature–timeTemperature (°C)Rate of heating or coolingNot used
Conversion graphsOne unit (e.g. °F)The conversion rateNot used

A horizontal section means the quantity is constant; a steep section means fast change; a curved section means the rate itself is changing. Interpolation reads values inside the plotted range; extrapolation reads beyond it and is unreliable — a distinction the questions like to test. On a distance–time graph for a journey, a stop is flat, a return journey heads down, and the steepest section is the fastest.

Graphs of functions and sketching curves

A function is a machine turning x into y; its graph is all the (x, y) pairs it produces. To sketch, plot a short table of values and recognise the shape:

FunctionShapeKey features
y = mx + cStraight lineGradient m, crossing the y-axis at c
y = ax² + bx + cParabola (U-shape, or ∩ if a is negative)Crosses the x-axis at the roots; turning point on the axis of symmetry midway between the roots
y = x³S-shaped cubicFlattening at the origin; grows steeply both ways
y = k/xHyperbolaTwo branches; the axes are asymptotes the curve approaches but never touches
y = aˣExponential growthPasses through (0, 1); rises ever faster; never touches the x-axis

Quadratics deserve particular care. The graph of y = ax² + bx + c has its turning point where x = −b/(2a), and the y-coordinate follows by substitution. Factorising y = (x − p)(x − q) shows the roots p and q at once, and the axis of symmetry is exactly halfway: x = (p + q)/2.

Solving equations graphically. The roots of f(x) = 0 are where the curve crosses the x-axis. To solve f(x) = g(x), draw both graphs and read the x-coordinates of the intersection points. A rearrangement like x³ − 2x − 5 = 0 becomes y = x³ − 2x and y = 5: where they meet, the equation holds. Answers read from a graph are approximate, so always state them to the accuracy the graph supports.

Gradients of curves and differentiation (Extended)

A curve's gradient changes from point to point, so the straight-line formula does not apply directly. The fix is a limit: take two points on the curve closer and closer together, and the chord between them settles towards the tangent — the line that just touches the curve at that point. Its gradient is the instantaneous rate of change of y with respect to x: how fast y is changing at that exact moment, like a speedometer reading rather than an average speed.

For y = x^n, the gradient function is:  dy/dx = n x^(n-1)
  • dy/dx: the gradient function, meaning the gradient at any value of x; it is read dy by dx.
  • n: the power of x in the term. Multiply by the power, then reduce the power by one: y = x³ gives dy/dx = 3x².
  • A constant term differentiates to zero (its graph is flat), and a constant multiple survives: y = 5x² gives dy/dx = 10x.

Why the rule works. Expand (x + h)ⁿ for a tiny step h, subtract y = xⁿ, and divide by h. For y = x²: [(x + h)² − x²]/h = [x² + 2xh + h² − x²]/h = (2xh + h²)/h = 2x + h. As h shrinks to nothing, this approaches 2x — exactly the rule. The same argument gives nxⁿ⁻¹ for every whole power.

Stationary points are where the gradient is zero — the tops of hills and bottoms of valleys. Solve dy/dx = 0 for x, substitute back for y, then decide which by looking at the curve or the gradient either side: a maximum has positive gradient before and negative after; a minimum the reverse. Maximum and minimum questions are the standard Paper 4 use of differentiation.

Worked example: tangent, stationary point and a practical graph

For the curve y = x² − 4x + 3:

dy/dx = 2x - 4
Stationary point: 2x - 4 = 0, so x = 2;  y = 4 - 8 + 3 = -1. The turning point is (2, -1).
Since the x² term is positive the parabola opens upwards, so (2, -1) is a minimum.
Roots: x² - 4x + 3 = (x - 1)(x - 3) = 0, so the curve crosses the x-axis at 1 and 3.
Gradient at x = 4: dy/dx = 2(4) - 4 = 4.
Tangent at x = 4: the point is (4, 3), and the tangent has gradient 4:
y - 3 = 4(x - 4), so y = 4x - 13.

The axis of symmetry, x = 2, sits midway between the roots 1 and 3 — everything is consistent, and cross-checking like this catches slips before they cost marks.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Dividing the gradient the wrong way round: it is always (change in y) over (change in x), with the coordinates subtracted in the same order in both.
  • Reading c from where the line crosses the x-axis; the y-intercept is on the y-axis.
  • Assuming parallel and perpendicular lines share a rule: parallel gradients are equal, perpendicular gradients multiply to −1.
  • Forgetting to halve the step in a midpoint, or using the Pythagoras formula without squaring both gaps.
  • Confusing the x-intercepts with the turning point on a quadratic sketch, or sketching y = (x − 2)² as crossing the x-axis at −2 (the root is +2).
  • Treating the asymptote of y = k/x as part of the curve; the curve approaches the axes and never crosses them.
  • Quoting an average speed from a speed–time graph's gradient at one point; the gradient there is acceleration.
  • Differentiating x³ as 3x² and then claiming the gradient of y = x³ is 3 at x = 1 — correct value, but the method mark is for writing dy/dx = 3x² and substituting x = 1.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 2, 3 marks). Find the gradient of the line through (2, 3) and (6, 11).

Answer: m = (11 − 3)/(6 − 2) = 8/4 = 2.

Question 2 (Paper 2, 4 marks). Find the equation of the line with gradient −3 passing through (4, −2).

Answer: y = mx + c gives −2 = −3(4) + c, so c = 10 and the equation is y = −3x + 10.

Question 3 (Paper 4, 4 marks). A line L passes through (1, 2) and (5, 10). Find the equation of the line perpendicular to L through the origin.

Answer: Gradient of L is (10 − 2)/(5 − 1) = 2, so the perpendicular gradient is −1/2. Through the origin c = 0, so y = −x/2.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 5 marks). A car travels at 20 m s⁻¹ for 30 s, then decelerates uniformly to rest in 10 s. Sketch the speed–time graph and find the total distance.

Answer: The graph is a horizontal line at 20 from t = 0 to t = 30, then a straight fall from (30, 20) to (40, 0). Distance = area = rectangle 30 × 20 = 600 m plus triangle ½ × 10 × 20 = 100 m, total 700 m.

Question 5 (Paper 4, 5 marks). For y = x² − 6x + 5, find the coordinates of the turning point and the roots, and sketch the curve.

Answer: dy/dx = 2x − 6 = 0 gives x = 3, y = 9 − 18 + 5 = −4, so the minimum is (3, −4). Roots: (x − 1)(x − 5) = 0 gives x = 1 and x = 5. The parabola opens upward through (1, 0) and (5, 0) with its minimum at (3, −4), crossing the y-axis at (0, 5).

Question 6 (Paper 4, 4 marks). The points A(−2, 1), B(4, 7) and C(10, 1) form a triangle. Show that AB = BC and find the midpoint of AC.

Answer: AB = √[(4 − (−2))² + (7 − 1)²] = √(36 + 36) = √72 = 6√2. BC = √[(10 − 4)² + (1 − 7)²] = √(36 + 36) = √72 = 6√2. The two sides are equal, so the triangle is isosceles. Midpoint of AC = ((−2 + 10)/2, (1 + 1)/2) = (4, 1).

Graphs describe change; sequences describe discrete patterns, and functions describe the machines behind both.

title: Edexcel IAL Computer Science: Protocols, Circuit and Packet Switching
content:
Edexcel IAL Computer Science: Protocols, Circuit and Packet Switching

Pearson Edexcel International Advanced Level in Computer Science, Unit 3 Advanced Computer Science: protocols, and circuit switching versus packet switching. The AS networking note traced data across a LAN and the internet; this note goes deeper into the rules themselves — what a protocol specification contains, how the layers compose, and why the telephone model and the packet model make opposite trades. The switching comparison is traced end to end on both models.

What a protocol is

A protocol is an agreed specification governing communication between systems: message format and syntax, semantics (what each field means), timing and sequencing (who speaks when, timeouts, rate), and error handling (detection, correction, retransmission). Without a shared protocol, hardware interoperation is impossible — the exam's "why protocols are needed" question wants those four components, not just "so devices understand each other".

Layering exists so each level can evolve independently and vendors can implement one layer against a stable interface. The TCP/IP model: application (HTTP, SMTP, FTP, DNS), transport (TCP, UDP), internet (IP, ICMP, ARP), network access (Ethernet, Wi-Fi, PPP). The OSI reference model's seven layers (Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application) are the vocabulary examiners use when asking for names — know both, map TCP/IP onto OSI, and explain encapsulation: each layer wraps the one above's data in its own header (and trailer at the data-link layer), and the receiver unwraps in reverse.

Encapsulation traced for sending "Hi" over HTTP:

  Application   : HTTP request headers + "Hi"
  Transport     : TCP header (ports, sequence no.) + HTTP data  = segment
  Internet      : IP header (src/dst addresses) + segment       = packet
  Network access: Ethernet header + trailer (FCS) + packet      = frame

  Receiver unwraps in order: frame -> packet -> segment -> HTTP data.
  Each layer reads only ITS header - the modularity is the point.

ARP bridging the layers: an IP packet needs the destination MAC address on
the LAN; ARP broadcasts "who has 192.168.1.5?" and the owner replies with its
MAC - the address-resolution seam between internet and network-access layers.

The protocol families in depth

ProtocolLayerGuaranteesCostUsed for
TCPTransportReliable, ordered, flow-controlled, connection-oriented (3-way handshake)Round-trips and header overheadHTTP, email, file transfer
UDPTransportNone — best-effort, connectionlessMinimal delayDNS, streaming, gaming, VoIP
IP (v4/v6)InternetBest-effort addressing and routing; fragmentationNo delivery guarantee (IP alone)Everything routed
ICMPInternetError/query messages (ping, TTL exceeded)—Diagnostics
TLSSession/PresentationEncryption, integrity, authentication (certificates)Handshake latency, CPUHTTPS, secure email
The TCP three-way handshake, packet by packet:

  Client                          Server
    | ---- SYN (seq=x) ------------->|    "I want to connect"
