    | <--- SYN-ACK (seq=y, ack=x+1) -|    "acknowledged; my sequence is y"
    | ---- ACK (ack=y+1) ----------->|    "confirmed"
  connection ESTABLISHED; data flows with sequence/ack numbers.

Why three steps: each side learns the other's initial sequence number and
both agree the connection exists - a two-way exchange could leave the server
believing in a connection the client never confirmed. Teardown mirrors it
(FIN/ACK), and timeouts recover lost packets - the reliability story.

Circuit switching

In circuit switching, a dedicated physical path is established end to end for the whole conversation and released at the end — the telephone network model. Three phases: circuit establishment (signalling reserves each link), data transfer (the path is exclusive), circuit teardown.

  • Strengths: guaranteed constant bandwidth and latency for the call's duration; no congestion mid-call once established; simple in-call ordering (one path).
  • Weaknesses: the reserved path is wasted during silence (speech is ~40% silence); setup delay before any data flows; a failed link breaks the call with no rerouting; capacity is fixed per circuit.

Packet switching

In packet switching, messages are split into packets, each carrying source/destination addresses and a sequence number; packets travel independently (possibly different routes — datagram approach) or along a pre-agreed virtual circuit, sharing links with other conversations' packets. The receiving end reassembles by sequence number.

One message, both models, traced:

  Message: 1.2 Mbit, links of 1.2 Mbps each.

  CIRCUIT: establish path (say 200 ms signalling), then the message flows on
  its exclusive path: 1.2 Mbit / 1.2 Mbps = 1 s, then teardown. Total ≈ 1.2 s.
  During the transfer no other call can use those links.

  PACKET (1500-byte packets, ~800 packets): packets interleave with other
  traffic. Each hop queues and forwards (store-and-forward: each router
  receives the whole packet, checks it, sends on). If a link is busy, packets
  queue (variable latency - jitter); if a router drops one, only THAT packet
  is retransmitted (TCP). No setup delay; total time depends on congestion.
  A failed route just changes the next hop for later packets.

  Store-and-forward delay per hop = packetSize / linkRate; the end-to-end sum
  plus queueing is the latency - the number a "why is video call laggy?"
  answer quotes.
Circuit switchingPacket switching
PathDedicated, reserved per callShared, per-packet routes
SetupRequired before dataNone (datagram) / light (virtual circuit)
BandwidthGuaranteed constantStatistical; can vary (jitter)
Failure handlingCall drops; no reroutingPackets reroute; lost packets retransmitted
EfficiencyLow during silence/idleHigh — links shared statistically
FitsVoice telephony, constant-rate streamsData networks, the internet, bursty traffic

Modern note the exam appreciates: voice over the internet (VoIP) is packet switching engineered to imitate circuit guarantees — priority queues and reserved capacity give latency-sensitive packets the reserved feel of a circuit.

Worked example: designing a link for a school

Requirement: 40 classrooms, each streaming 2 Mbps video lessons at peak, plus
email/web traffic.

  Peak video demand: 40 x 2 = 80 Mbps, before overheads (add ~20% for
  headers/retransmission): ≈ 96 Mbps.
  Packet switching with a 100 Mbps backbone just fits; a 1 Gbps link gives
  headroom. Circuit switching would reserve 2 Mbps per room regardless of use
  (40 x 2 = 80 Mbps permanently committed) and no room could burst above its
  allocation - wasteful for bursty web traffic.

Choice: packet switching with QoS priority for the video VLAN; the answer
names the burstiness argument (statistical multiplexing) and the QoS trade.

Quality of service on packet networks

Because packet switching offers no inherent guarantee, engineered guarantees are added on top: QoS marks latency-sensitive packets (voice, video) for priority queuing; traffic shaping smooths bursts so links are not overwhelmed; reservation (RSVP-style) holds capacity for a flow; and MPLS gives labelled paths that behave like fast virtual circuits. Each mechanism trades simplicity for predictability — the exam's "how does VoIP work reliably?" answer is exactly this list with priority queuing first.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Describing circuit switching as "faster" universally; it is predictable (guaranteed rate), while packet switching is efficient and burst-friendly — match the claim to the traffic.
  • Forgetting store-and-forward when computing latency: each hop holds the packet, and links serialise it.
  • Saying packets arrive in order; the sequence numbers and reassembly exist because they may not.
  • Listing OSI layers without their function or mis-ordering them (Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application).
  • Confusing IP (best-effort delivery) with TCP (reliability); neither alone is "the internet" — the pairing is.
  • Claiming UDP is unreliable so it is useless; its speed is exactly why real-time services choose it.
  • Leaving handshake/timing out of protocol answers; sequencing and synchronisation are part of what a protocol defines.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Unit 3, 4 marks). Describe the features a protocol must specify.

Answer: Message format/syntax (bit patterns, header fields); semantics (what each field and code means, what actions follow); timing and sequencing (who transmits when, synchronisation, timeouts, rate control); and error handling (detection via checksums, correction or retransmission rules). These four allow independent implementations to interoperate exactly.

Question 2 (Unit 3, 5 marks). Explain encapsulation using the TCP/IP layers.

Answer: Each layer adds its own header to the data from the layer above: the application data gets a TCP header (ports, sequence numbers) forming a segment; the segment gets an IP header (addresses) forming a packet; the packet gets a network-access header and trailer (MAC addresses, checksum) forming a frame. The receiver reverses the process, each layer reading only its own header and passing the payload upward — layering isolates responsibilities so protocols can change independently.

Question 3 (Unit 3, 5 marks). Compare circuit switching and packet switching for a national voice network.

Answer: Circuit switching reserves an exclusive path per call: guaranteed constant bandwidth and latency once established and simple ordering, but setup delay before speech, wasted capacity during silence, and a failed link drops the call. Packet switching shares links statistically: no setup, high efficiency and rerouting around failures, but variable latency (jitter) that voice dislikes unless QoS prioritises it. Traditional telephony chose circuits; modern VoIP chooses packets with engineered priority — the efficiency of sharing wins once jitter can be controlled.

Question 4 (Unit 3, 4 marks). Describe the TCP three-way handshake and explain its purpose.

Answer: The client sends SYN with its initial sequence number; the server replies SYN-ACK acknowledging it and supplying its own sequence number; the client confirms with ACK. Purpose: both sides learn each other's sequence numbers (needed for ordered reassembly), agree the connection exists, and agree parameters — avoiding the half-open connections a two-message exchange would permit.

Question 5 (Unit 3, 4 marks). Explain why the internet uses packet switching rather than circuit switching.

Answer: Internet traffic is bursty — web pages, email and files arrive in irregular bursts with idle gaps. Packet switching shares links statistically, so all conversations use whatever capacity is free at each instant (high utilisation), packets reroute around failures (resilience), and each packet need not hold capacity when silent. Circuit switching would reserve bandwidth through idle periods and block bursts above the reservation. Real-time needs are met with QoS on top rather than dedicated circuits.

Question 6 (Unit 3, 3 marks). Calculate the store-and-forward delay for a 1500-byte packet over three 10 Mbps hops.

Answer: Packet = 1500 × 8 = 12 000 bits. Per hop: 12 000 ÷ 10⁷ = 1.2 ms. Three hops store-and-forward the packet serially (each waits for the whole packet before sending): 3 × 1.2 = 3.6 ms transmission delay, plus any propagation and queueing delay at each router.

The protocols above carry encrypted traffic as often as plain; the security layer on top is the next note's subject.

title: Binomial Distribution
content:
The Binomial Distribution

When Binomial Applies

X ~ B(n, p) counts successes in n independent trials when:

  • a fixed number n of identical trials,
  • each trial ends in success or failure,
  • constant success probability p,
  • trials are independent.

Check all four before using the model — "justifying a binomial model" is a real exam question.

The Formula

P(X = r) = ⁿCᵣ pʳ(1 − p)ⁿ⁻ʳ for r = 0, 1, ..., n. The ⁿCᵣ counts which r of the n trials were the successes.

Example: X ~ B(5, 0.3). P(X = 2) = ¹⁰C₂? No — ⁵C₂ × 0.3² × 0.7³ = 10 × 0.09 × 0.343 = 0.3087.

Cumulative Probabilities

P(X ≤ 2) = P(0) + P(1) + P(2). "At least" questions convert by the complement: P(X ≥ 2) = 1 − P(X ≤ 1). Keep one extra decimal place in intermediate steps to avoid rounding drift.

Expectation and Variance

  • E(X) = np and Var(X) = np(1 − p)

For X ~ B(20, 0.4): E(X) = 8 and Var(X) = 4.8.

Modelling Decisions

If trials are dependent (drawing without replacement from a small population) binomial is not appropriate. If p changes between trials it is not binomial. When n is large and p small, the binomial is approximately Poisson — but at A2 you usually stay exact.

Exam tips: identify n and p in words before touching the calculator. For P(X ≥ k) always rewrite as 1 − P(X ≤ k − 1). Tables give cumulative values — use them rather than summing by hand.

title: Electricity & Circuits — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Electricity & Circuits

Physics — OL. simple circuits, current, p.d., resistance, series/parallel, electrical safety, practical electricity.

  • 1. Circuit symbols & current
  • 2. Current, p.d., e.m.f.
  • 3. Resistance
  • 4. Components
  • 5. Power and energy
  • 6. Digital electronics basics (syllabus 4.5 context)

How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

Key relationships

  • Current I = charge Q / time t, and voltage V = energy E / charge Q.
  • Resistance R = V / I. Components in series share the voltage, and parallel branches share the current.
  • Power P = I × V, and energy transferred E = P × t.

Common errors

Resistors in parallel are not added directly; the combined resistance is less than the smallest single resistor. Current is not used up as it passes through a component.

title: AS Level Mathematics: Integration
content:
AS Level Mathematics: Integration

Integration is differentiation in reverse: it recovers a function from its gradient, and it accumulates a rate into a total — the area under a curve, the distance from a velocity, the cost from a marginal. This note builds the topic from zero: the indefinite integral and the constant of integration, the power rule, definite integrals and the fundamental theorem, areas above and below the axis, the area between two curves, and kinematics. Every worked example shows the antiderivative line before any substitution of limits.

The indefinite integral

if dy/dx = x^n then y = x^(n+1)/(n+1) + c   (n not -1)

integral of x^n dx = x^(n+1)/(n+1) + c
integral of k f(x) dx = k integral of f(x) dx
integral of a sum = sum of integrals

The +c is mandatory for indefinite integrals: every antiderivative differs by a constant, and the constant is fixed by a boundary condition (a point on the curve).

Worked example 1. Find ∫(6x² − 4x + 3) dx.

= 6x³/3 - 4x²/2 + 3x + c
= 2x³ - 2x² + 3x + c

Worked example 2 (negative and fractional powers). Find ∫(1/x² + √x) dx.

rewrite: integral of (x⁻² + x^(1/2)) dx
= -x⁻¹ + (2/3)x^(3/2) + c
= -1/x + (2/3)x^(3/2) + c

Worked example 3 (finding c). dy/dx = 3x² + 2 and the curve passes through (1, 5). Find y.

y = x³ + 2x + c
5 = 1 + 2 + c  →  c = 2
y = x³ + 2x + 2

Definite integrals and area

integral from a to b of f(x) dx = F(b) - F(a)

area under the curve between x = a and x = b (above the axis)
= definite integral; a negative value means the region is
below the x-axis, and the area is the magnitude

Worked example. Evaluate ∫ from 1 to 3 of (2x + 1) dx.

antiderivative: x² + x
F(3) = 9 + 3 = 12;  F(1) = 1 + 1 = 2
value = 12 - 2 = 10

Worked example 2 (area under a curve). Find the area under y = x² between x = 0 and x = 3.

integral: x³/3
from 0 to 3: 27/3 - 0 = 9 square units

Worked example 3 (below the axis). Find the area between y = x² − 4 and the x-axis from x = 0 to x = 2.

integral: x³/3 - 4x
from 0 to 2: 8/3 - 8 = -16/3
the value is negative because the region is below the axis;
area = 16/3 = 5.33 square units

Areas crossing the axis

When a curve crosses the x-axis inside the interval, integrate each piece separately and add the magnitudes — a single integral would cancel positive and negative areas.

Worked example. Find the total area between y = x² − 1 and the x-axis from x = −2 to x = 2.

crossings at x = -1 and x = 1
piece 1 (-2 to -1): F = x³/3 - x; F(-1) - F(-2) = (2/3) - (-2/3) = 4/3
piece 2 (-1 to 1): F(1) - F(-1) = (-2/3) - (2/3) = -4/3 → magnitude 4/3
piece 3 (1 to 2): F(2) - F(1) = (2/3) - (-2/3) = 4/3
total area = 4/3 + 4/3 + 4/3 = 4 square units

Area between two curves

area between y = f(x) and y = g(x) from a to b
= integral of (f(x) - g(x)) dx from a to b
where f is the upper curve and g the lower

Worked example. Find the area between y = x² and y = x from x = 0 to x = 1.

upper curve on this interval is y = x
integral of (x - x²) dx = x²/2 - x³/3
from 0 to 1: 1/2 - 1/3 = 1/6 square units

Worked example 2 (intersections). Find the area enclosed by y = x² and y = 2x.

intersections: x² = 2x → x(x - 2) = 0 → x = 0, 2
upper on (0, 2) is y = 2x
integral of (2x - x²) dx = x² - x³/3
from 0 to 2: 4 - 8/3 = 4/3 square units

Kinematics with integration

velocity v = ds/dt  →  displacement s = integral of v dt
acceleration a = dv/dt  →  velocity v = integral of a dt

definite integral of v from t1 to t2 = displacement
integral of |v| = distance travelled

Worked example. A particle has velocity v = 3t² − 6t (m/s). Find its displacement from t = 0 to t = 3 and its distance travelled.

s = integral of (3t² - 6t) dt = t³ - 3t²
from 0 to 3: 27 - 27 = 0  →  net displacement zero
sign of v: 3t(t - 2), negative between 0 and 2, positive after
distance = |integral 0 to 2| + integral 2 to 3
= |8 - 12| + (27 - 27) - (8 - 12) = 4 + 4 = 8 m

The distinction between displacement and distance is examinable: displacement is the signed integral, distance is the sum of the absolute pieces.

Worked examples: mixed integration

Worked example. The curve y = f(x) has f'(x) = 6x − 4 and passes through (2, 3). Find f(x) and the area under the curve from x = 1 to x = 2.

f(x) = 3x² - 4x + c;  3 = 12 - 8 + c → c = -1
f(x) = 3x² - 4x - 1
area = integral 1 to 2: x³ - 2x² - x
F(2) = 8 - 8 - 2 = -2; F(1) = 1 - 2 - 1 = -2
area = -2 - (-2) = 0  (the curve is below the axis and the
signed areas cancel); the geometric area needs the crossing
checked - a useful reminder to sketch first

Integrating expressions that need rearranging

Integration has no product or quotient rule at AS level, so expressions must first be written as sums of powers. Two standard rearrangements cover almost every case:

product: expand, then integrate term by term
quotient with a single term denominator: divide through first

(x + 2)(x - 5) = x² - 3x - 10
(3x² + 4x)/x = 3x + 4
√(x)(x + 1) = x^(3/2) + x^(1/2)

Worked example. Find ∫ (x + 3)(x − 1) dx.

expand: x² + 2x - 3
integrate: x³/3 + x² - 3x + c

Worked example 2. Find ∫ (4x³ + 2x)/x dx.

divide: 4x² + 2
integrate: (4/3)x³ + 2x + c

Two boundary conditions

When the second derivative is given, integrate twice and use two pieces of information to fix both constants. The order matters: the first integration produces the gradient function and its constant, the second the curve and its constant.

Worked example. d²y/dx² = 6x, dy/dx = 2 when x = 1, and y = 5 when x = 1. Find y.

first: dy/dx = 3x² + c;  2 = 3 + c  →  c = -1, so dy/dx = 3x² - 1
second: y = x³ - x + k;  5 = 1 - 1 + k  →  k = 5
y = x³ - x + 5

Finding limits and constants from area information

Area questions are often inverted: the area is given and a limit or coefficient must be found. Set up the definite integral with the unknown, evaluate, and solve the resulting equation — rejecting any root outside the geometric context.

Worked example. The area under y = kx² from x = 0 to x = 3 is 36. Find k.

integral: kx³/3
from 0 to 3: 27k/3 = 9k
9k = 36  →  k = 4

Worked example 2 (unknown upper limit). The area under y = 2x from x = 0 to x = a is 25. Find a.

integral: x²;  from 0 to a: a² = 25
a = 5  (the negative root is rejected: a is an x-coordinate to
the right of the origin in this setup)

Kinematics: recovering velocity from acceleration

Worked example. A particle starts from rest with acceleration a = 6t − 4 (m/s²). Find its velocity at t = 3 and the distance travelled in the first 3 seconds.

v = integral of (6t - 4) dt = 3t² - 4t + c
at rest at t = 0: c = 0  →  v = 3t² - 4t
v(3) = 27 - 12 = 15 m/s
distance = integral of |v| from 0 to 3
v = 0 at t = 0 and t = 4/3; v is negative on (0, 4/3)
piece 1: [t³ - 2t²] from 0 to 4/3 = 64/27 - 32/9 = -32/27 → 32/27
piece 2: [t³ - 2t²] from 4/3 to 3 = (27 - 18) - (-32/27) = 9 + 32/27
distance = 32/27 + 9 + 32/27 = 9 + 64/27 = 11.4 m

The sign analysis is the whole question: sketch v against t, mark where it crosses zero, and integrate each piece with its sign removed.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Indefinite) Find ∫(4x³ − 2) dx. Answer: x⁴ − 2x + c.
  2. (Negative power) Find ∫x⁻² dx. Answer: −x⁻¹ + c = −1/x + c.
  3. (Definite) Evaluate ∫ from 0 to 2 of 3x² dx. Answer: [x³] = 8.
  4. (Area) Find the area under y = x + 2 from x = 0 to x = 3. Answer: [x²/2 + 2x] = 4.5 + 6 = 10.5.
  5. (Below axis) Find the area between y = x − 3 and the x-axis from x = 0 to x = 2. Answer: integral = [x²/2 − 3x] = 2 − 6 = −4; area 4.
  6. (Between curves) Find the area between y = x² and y = x³ from 0 to 1. Answer: upper is x²; ∫(x² − x³) = 1/3 − 1/4 = 1/12.
  7. (Constant) dy/dx = 4x and y = 7 when x = 1. Find y. Answer: y = 2x² + c → 7 = 2 + c → c = 5 → y = 2x² + 5.
  8. (Kinematics) v = 2t + 1. Find the displacement from t = 0 to t = 4. Answer: [t² + t] = 16 + 4 = 20 m.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Forgetting +c: an indefinite integral without the constant loses a mark; with a boundary condition, the constant is required for the answer.
  • Power rule reversal: integrate xⁿ to x^(n+1)/(n+1); adding one and dividing is the opposite of differentiating, and mixing them up produces nonsense.
  • Limits order: F(b) − F(a), never the reverse. A negative area often means the limits were swapped.
  • Ignoring crossings: a definite integral over a region that crosses the axis gives the signed area; split at the crossings and add magnitudes for the geometric area.
  • Wrong upper curve: subtract lower from upper; sketching between the intersection points avoids the sign error.
  • Distance versus displacement: displacement is the signed integral; distance sums the absolute pieces. Read which is asked.
  • Expanding before integrating: products must be expanded or divided first; there is no product rule for integration at AS level.
  • Units: areas are square units, displacements in metres; attach and interpret units in applied questions.

Equations and symbols

Integration is four formulas and two decisions: which power rule, and whether the answer is signed. Learn the rule with its condition attached — the exception at n = −1 is the mark most often lost.

integral of x^n dx = x^(n+1)/(n+1) + c Key: x = the variable of integration (no units for a pure function); n = the power, any real number except −1; c = the constant of integration, fixed by a boundary condition. Raise the power by one, then divide by the new power — the reverse of differentiating, and n = −1 is excluded because it would divide by zero.

if dy/dx = x^n then y = x^(n+1)/(n+1) + c (n not -1) Key: dy/dx = the gradient function; y = the function recovered from it; n = the power; c = the constant. The same statement read from the other end: differentiating the answer returns the question.

integral of k f(x) dx = k integral of f(x) dx Key: k = a constant multiplier (no units); f(x) = the function being integrated. Constants pass through the integral sign, which is why a polynomial is integrated term by term.

integral from a to b of f(x) dx = F(b) - F(a) Key: a = the lower limit; b = the upper limit; f(x) = the integrand; F(x) = any antiderivative of f(x). Upper value minus lower value, never the reverse — a negative area usually means the limits were swapped.

velocity v = ds/dt Key: v = velocity (m s⁻¹); s = displacement (m); t = time (s). The gradient form; integrate it in reverse to recover displacement.

displacement s = integral of v dt Key: s = displacement (m); v = velocity (m s⁻¹); t = time (s). The signed integral, so motion backwards subtracts from the total.

acceleration a = dv/dt Key: a = acceleration (m s⁻²); v = velocity (m s⁻¹); t = time (s). The link that lets a question give acceleration and ask for velocity or displacement.

velocity v = integral of a dt Key: v = velocity (m s⁻¹); a = acceleration (m s⁻²); t = time (s). Integrate, then use "starts from rest" or a stated value to fix the constant.

integral of |v| = distance travelled Key: |v| = the magnitude of the velocity, so every piece counts positive (m s⁻¹); the integral gives distance (m), not displacement. Split the integral wherever v = 0, because that is where the sign changes.

9k = 36 → k = 4 Key: 9k = the definite integral of kx² from 0 to 3, written with the unknown constant k; 36 = the given area (square units); k = 4 (no units). The inverted-area question: set the integral equal to the stated area and solve, rather than integrating a known function.

title: The Normal Distribution — Study Notes
content:
The Normal Distribution

The Model

A continuous distribution with the familiar bell shape, symmetric about the mean, described by two parameters: X ~ N(μ, σ²). The curve is fully determined by μ (centre) and σ (width). Total probability is 1, and because X is continuous, P(X = a) = 0 for any single point — inequalities do not need strictness.

Standardising

Convert any normal variable to the standard normal Z ~ N(0, 1) with

  • Z = (X − μ)/σ

Then read probabilities from the normal table. For X ~ N(50, 4²): P(X > 56) = P(Z > 1.5) = 1 − 0.9332 = 0.0668.

Backwards Problems

Given a probability, find μ or σ. Convert the target percentile to a z-value from the table, then solve (x − μ)/σ = z.

Example: P(X < 30) = 0.15 with unknown σ. From tables z = −1.036, so (30 − μ)/σ = −1.036 — one equation per unknown; use a second condition if both are missing.

Symmetry Shortcuts

P(X > μ) = 0.5. P(X < a) for a above the mean uses the complement. Tables usually give Φ(z) for z ≥ 0 only; use Φ(−z) = 1 − Φ(z).

Normal Approximation to the Binomial

For large n with p near ½, X ~ B(n, p) ≈ N(np, np(1 − p)). The condition usually quoted at this level is np > 5 and n(1 − p) > 5. Apply a continuity correction: to approximate P(X ≥ 12) for a binomial, compute P(Y > 11.5) for the normal Y.

Example: B(100, 0.5) ≈ N(50, 25). P(X ≥ 55) ≈ P(Y > 54.5) = P(Z > 0.9) = 0.1841.

Exam tips: always sketch and shade — the picture prevents complement errors. State the standardisation step explicitly; marks sit in the working. Check whether a question says "mean and standard deviation" (σ) or "variance" (σ²) before standardising.

Exam method: standardising and symmetry

For X ~ N(μ, σ²) the standard score is z = (x − μ)/σ, and Z ~ N(0, 1). Note that the second parameter is the variance, so take the square root to get σ before standardising. Many errors come from using 25 instead of 5 when the variance is 25.

Probabilities are found from the standard normal table or calculator using Φ(z) = P(Z ≤ z). Because the curve is symmetric about 0, Φ(−z) = 1 − Φ(z), and P(Z > z) = 1 − Φ(z).

For a probability between two values, P(a < X < b) = Φ(z_b) − Φ(z_a). Standardise each limit separately and subtract.

To find a value from a probability, read the z-value from the table with the required area, and then rearrange z = (x − μ)/σ to find x.

Exam cue: Sketch the curve and shade the area asked for, then match it to the table value, since the sketch catches sign errors.

Standardising a normal variable

If X follows a normal distribution with mean μ and standard deviation σ, then Z = (X − μ) ÷ σ follows the standard normal distribution with mean 0 and standard deviation 1. Standardising allows any normal probability to be read from the standard normal table. For example, if X is normal with mean 50 and standard deviation 4, then P(X > 54) = P(Z > 1), which the table gives as about 0.1587.

Worked example: finding a value from a probability

Suppose P(X < k) = 0.9 for a normal variable with mean 20 and standard deviation 3. The table gives the z-value 1.2816 for a probability of 0.9, so k = 20 + 1.2816 × 3 = 23.85. When the probability is less than 0.5, the z-value is negative, so take care with the sign. Sketch the normal curve and shade the area you need before you use the table, because the sketch shows whether the answer should be above or below the mean.

Symmetry and the 68-95-99 rule

The normal curve is symmetric about the mean, so P(Z < −a) = P(Z > a). Roughly 68% of values lie within one standard deviation of the mean, 95% within two and 99.7% within three. These approximate figures are useful for checking whether a calculated probability is reasonable.

title: A Level Physics: Nuclear Physics
content:
A Level Physics: Nuclear Physics

Nuclear physics studies the dense heart of the atom: what the nucleus contains, why some nuclei fly apart, and how the mass of a nucleus is less than the sum of its parts — the most famous equation in physics. This note builds the subject from zero: nuclear composition and notation, the three kinds of radiation and their detection, mass defect and binding energy with the binding-energy curve, and radioactive decay as an exponential process with its own vocabulary (activity, decay constant, half-life). Every calculation type is worked line by line.

Atoms, nuclei and radiation

An atom is a tiny nucleus surrounded by electrons. The nucleus contains protons (positive) and neutrons (neutral); the notation uses X with atomic number Z (protons) above and mass number A (nucleons: protons + neutrons) below. Isotopes share Z but differ in N; they are chemically identical (same electron configuration) but physically different (different mass and nuclear stability).

Three kinds of emission come from unstable nuclei:

PropertyAlpha (α)Beta-minus (β⁻)Gamma (γ)
What it ishelium nucleus (2 protons + 2 neutrons)fast electron from the nucleushigh-energy photon
Notation⁴₂He⁰₋₁e⁰₀γ
Charge+2e−1e0
Speedup to ~0.05cup to ~0.99cc
Range in aira few cma few metreshundreds of metres
Ionisingstrongly (double charge, slow)moderatelyweakly
Deflectionslight, in magnetic/electric fieldsgreater, opposite direction to αnone
Stopped bypaperthin aluminiumlead or thick concrete

Nuclear equations balance on two counts: nucleon number A and proton number Z both conserved. In beta-minus decay a neutron turns into a proton plus an electron plus an antineutrino (n → p + e⁻ + ν̄), which is why A stays the same while Z rises by one.

Worked example. Complete: ²³⁸₉₂U → ²³⁴₉₀Th + ? Answer: the missing particle has A = 238 − 234 = 4 and Z = 92 − 90 = 2 → an alpha particle ⁴₂He. For ¹⁴₆C → ¹⁴₇N + ?: A = 0, Z = −1 → beta-minus ⁰₋₁e (plus an antineutrino).

Mass defect and nuclear binding energy

Every nucleus weighs less than its separated nucleons — the mass defect Δm. That missing mass is the energy released when the nucleus assembled, by Einstein's mass–energy equivalence:

E = Δm c²        c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹

binding energy = energy needed to separate a nucleus into
                 its individual nucleons
binding energy per nucleon = binding energy / A

The atomic mass unit, u, is defined so that 1 u = 1.661 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, equivalent to 931.5 MeV of energy. The binding-energy-per-nucleon curve is the map of nuclear energy: it rises steeply to a maximum near iron-56 (about 8.8 MeV per nucleon) and falls slowly for heavier nuclei. Consequences, both examinable:

  • Fission: a heavy nucleus (uranium) splitting toward the middle of the curve releases energy — each fragment is more tightly bound.
  • Fusion: light nuclei (hydrogen isotopes) joining toward the peak also release energy — this powers stars.

Worked example 1. Find the binding energy of a helium-4 nucleus (mass 4.0026 u) given proton mass 1.0073 u and neutron mass 1.0087 u.

separate nucleons: 2(1.0073) + 2(1.0087) = 4.0320 u
nucleus: 4.0026 u
mass defect: Δm = 4.0320 - 4.0026 = 0.0294 u
binding energy = 0.0294 × 931.5 = 27.4 MeV
per nucleon = 27.4/4 = 6.85 MeV

Worked example 2 (joules). Convert the mass defect 0.0294 u to joules.

Δm = 0.0294 × 1.661 × 10⁻²⁷ = 4.88 × 10⁻²⁹ kg
E = Δm c² = 4.88 × 10⁻²⁹ x (3.0 × 10⁸)²
  = 4.88 × 10⁻²⁹ × 9.0 × 10¹⁶ = 4.39 × 10⁻¹² J

Radioactive decay

Radioactive decay is spontaneous and random: no external condition (temperature, pressure, chemistry) changes when a given nucleus decays. What is predictable is the behaviour of huge numbers of nuclei — an exponential law:

N = N⁰ e^(-λ t)

N = number of undecayed nuclei; N⁰ at t = 0
λ = decay constant (s⁻¹)

activity A = λ N    (becquerel, Bq; 1 Bq = 1 decay per second)
A = A⁰ e^(-λ t)

half-life t_half = ln(2)/λ = 0.693/λ

The decay constant is the probability per unit time that any one nucleus decays. The half-life is the time for half the present nuclei to decay — a fixed fraction, not a fixed number. On a graph of N against t, read the half-life directly as the time to fall from any value to half of it; the gradient of ln N against t is −λ.

Worked example 1. A sample has activity 8000 Bq. After 6.0 hours the activity is 1000 Bq. Find the half-life.

8000 → 1000 is three halvings (8 → 4 → 2 → 1)
three half-lives = 6.0 hours  →  t_half = 2.0 hours

Worked example 2 (decay constant). Find λ and the number of nuclei in a 1000 Bq sample with that half-life.

λ = 0.693/t_half = 0.693/(2.0 × 3600) = 9.6 × 10⁻⁵ s⁻¹
A = λ N → N = A/λ = 1000/9.6 × 10⁻⁵ = 1.04 × 10⁷ nuclei

Worked example 3 (exponential). A sample of 4.0 × 10¹⁰ nuclei has λ = 2.0 × 10⁻⁶ s⁻¹. How many remain after one hour?

N = N⁰ e^(-λ t) = 4.0 × 10¹⁰ x e^(-2.0 × 10⁻⁶ × 3600)
  = 4.0 × 10¹⁰ x e^(-0.0072) = 4.0 × 10¹⁰ × 0.9928
  = 3.97 × 10¹⁰  (only 0.7% decayed - short times barely dent N)

Worked examples: interpreting decay data

Worked example. A student measures count rate against time and finds it falls from 640 counts per minute to 40 in 30 minutes. Explain why count rate is used instead of activity directly, and find the half-life.

640 → 320 → 160 → 80 → 40 : four halvings in 30 min
t_half = 30/4 = 7.5 minutes
why counts: a detector records only the fraction of decays that
reach it (geometric efficiency), so the count rate is proportional
to activity but not equal to it - proportional, so halvings work.

Fission, fusion and the binding-energy curve

The curve of binding energy per nucleon against nucleon number is the energy map of the nucleus. It rises steeply through the light nuclei, peaks near iron-56 at about 8.8 MeV per nucleon, and falls slowly for the heaviest nuclei. Any process that moves nucleons toward the peak releases energy: splitting a heavy nucleus (fission) and joining light nuclei (fusion) both climb toward iron. The energy released is the difference in total binding energy between the starting nucleus and the products.

energy released = (binding energy of products)
                - (binding energy of reactants)

for fission of one U-235 nucleus: about 200 MeV is released;
it appears as the kinetic energy of the two fragments
(and some neutrons) plus gamma radiation

Worked example. Estimate the energy released when one uranium-235 nucleus fissions into fragments whose binding energy per nucleon averages 8.5 MeV, given U-235 has about 7.6 MeV per nucleon.

change per nucleon = 8.5 - 7.6 = 0.9 MeV
235 nucleons take part (approximately)
energy = 235 × 0.9 = 211 MeV
       = 211 × 10⁶ × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 3.4 × 10⁻¹¹ J

Fusion in the Sun is the same arithmetic in reverse: four protons combine through a chain of reactions into helium-4, releasing about 26.7 MeV per nucleus formed — small per nucleus but astronomical in total because the Sun fuses about 600 million tonnes of hydrogen every second.

Detecting radiation and handling it safely

Radiation is detected by its ionising effect: a Geiger-Muller tube counts individual particles or photons (each gives a click or count), a cloud chamber shows tracks as condensed droplets along ionisation paths, and a photographic film badge darkens cumulatively with dose. Every measurement must subtract background radiation — the constant low level from cosmic rays, rocks, radon gas and medical sources — recorded with no source present.

  • Alpha: dangerous only if inhaled or swallowed (it is stopped by skin but deposits all its energy in a small volume of tissue); handled with gloves and no eating in the lab.
  • Beta: stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium or by thick clothing; eye protection and distance matter.
  • Gamma: penetrates deeply; lead shielding, distance and limiting exposure time are the protections (dose falls with the inverse square of distance).
  • General rules: minimise time near a source, maximise distance, use shielding, and never point a source at anyone. Tracers in medicine use short-half-life isotopes (technetium-99m, t½ = 6 hours) so activity falls quickly after use.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Structure) Define isotope and state one pair of isotopes. Answer: Isotopes are nuclei of the same element (same proton number Z) with different numbers of neutrons (different mass number A) — e.g. carbon-12 and carbon-14.
  2. (Radiation) Explain why alpha radiation is more ionising than gamma. Answer: An alpha particle has double charge and moves slowly, so it exerts strong Coulomb forces on nearby electrons over a longer interaction time, stripping many electrons; gamma photons interact only occasionally.
  3. (Equations) Complete: ²¹⁰₈₄Po → ²⁰⁶₈₂Pb + X. Answer: X has A = 4, Z = 2 → ⁴₂He (alpha).
  4. (Binding energy) Explain, in terms of binding energy per nucleon, why fusion releases energy. Answer: Light nuclei have low binding energy per nucleon; fusing them moves products toward the peak of the curve near iron, where each nucleon is more tightly bound; the difference in total binding energy is released.
  5. (Mass defect) State what mass defect represents. Answer: The difference between the mass of a nucleus and the total mass of its separate nucleons; it equals the energy released when the nucleus formed (E = Δmc²), and also the energy required to disassemble it.
  6. (Decay law) Define activity and the decay constant. Answer: Activity is the rate of decay of a sample (decays per second, Bq); the decay constant is the probability per unit time that a given nucleus decays, with A = λN.
  7. (Half-life) A sample's activity drops from 2000 Bq to 250 Bq in 12 days. Find the half-life. Answer: 2000 → 250 is three halvings; t½ = 12/3 = 4 days.
  8. (Randomness) Explain why radioactive decay is described as random yet its rate is predictable. Answer: Each nucleus decays spontaneously with no known trigger, so no individual decay can be predicted; but for a large population the probability per unit time (λ) is constant, so the number decaying per second — the activity — follows A = λN predictably.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Conservation bookkeeping: A and Z both balance in nuclear equations; beta decay keeps A constant while Z changes — write both numbers at every arrow.
  • u to joules: 1 u = 1.661 × 10⁻²⁷ kg; 1 u = 931.5 MeV. Use one route consistently; mixing MeV and joules mid-question fails.
  • Binding energy direction: energy is released when a tightly bound nucleus forms and required to split it; the sign of ΔE follows the arrow.
  • Half-life arithmetic: it is the time to halve the current amount, not to reach zero; count the halvings (80 → 20 is two halvings).
  • ln 2 versus base-2: N = N₀(½)^(t/t½) and N = N₀e^(−λt) are the same law; λ = 0.693/t½ converts between them. Do not apply e-folding time as a half-life.
  • Activity vs count rate: count rate is proportional to activity but reduced by detector geometry and absorption; background radiation must be subtracted before analysis.
  • Decay units: λ in s⁻¹ (or per the time unit given), A in Bq; hours and minutes into seconds when mixing with s⁻¹.
  • Ignoring neutrinos: beta decay equations in modern syllabuses include the antineutrino; omitting it is an accuracy loss where the paper's data sheet includes it.
  • Precision: 2 or 3 s.f. with units; quote c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ and Nₐ = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ from the data sheet.

title: Exam technique: Abstract Data Types
content:
### What earns the marks
For ADT choice, the access pattern stated earns the mark: LIFO for stacks, FIFO for queues, keyed jumps for BSTs. For traversals, the visit order written (root-left-right for preorder) earns each mark. For linked structures, pointer relinking described earns the insertion mark without any shifting claim.
### Traps
Error: queues for undo. Correction: undo is LIFO, so stack. Error: inorder claimed as root-first. Correction: preorder is root-first. Error: arrays claimed best for mid-list churn. Correction: shifting costs every insert.
### Worked example
Trace a stack. Push A, push B, push C, then pop, then push D, then pop. After the three pushes the top is C, so the first pop returns C. Pushing D leaves the stack as A, B, D, so the second pop returns D and B is left on top. A stack is last in, first out, so the top item always leaves first.
### Check yourself
State which structure a printer queue uses and why, in one sentence that names the order of service. A print queue serves the first job submitted first, so it is first in, first out.

### Worked example
Trace a stack. Push A, push B, push C, then pop, then push D, then pop. After the three pushes the top is C, so the first pop returns C. Pushing D leaves the stack as A, B, D, so the second pop returns D and B is left on top. A stack is last in, first out, so the top item always leaves first.

title: Exam technique: Work Energy and Power
content:
### What earns the marks
For work, force times distance along the force earns both marks. For energy, mgh and half m v squared quoted earn one mark each. For efficiency, useful over total earns the method mark with waste named.
### Traps
Error: g taken as 10 without comment at AS. Correction: use 9.81 for energy work. Error: efficiency above 100 percent. Correction: impossible; check the ratio. Error: power and energy units swapped. Correction: watts are joules per second.

content:

title: Redox Equilibria — Study Notes
content:
Redox Equilibria

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH15, Topic 16. Redox reactions transfer electrons. Standard electrode potentials let you predict whether a reaction is feasible and quantify the reducing and oxidising power of species.

Oxidation and reduction

  • Oxidation is loss of electrons and an increase in oxidation state. Reduction is gain of electrons and a decrease in oxidation state.
  • The reducing agent is oxidised; the oxidising agent is reduced.

Standard electrode potentials

  • Each half-cell has a standard electrode potential, E⁰, measured under standard conditions: 298 K, 1.0 mol dm⁻³ solutions and 100 kPa for gases.
  • E⁰ is measured against the standard hydrogen electrode, which is defined as 0 V.
  • A more positive E⁰ means a stronger oxidising agent on the left of the half-equation. A more negative E⁰ means a stronger reducing agent.

Predicting feasibility

  • E⁰cell = E⁰(reduction) − E⁰(oxidation). A positive E⁰cell means the reaction is feasible under standard conditions.
  • ΔG = −nFE. A negative ΔG (positive E⁰cell) means the reaction is spontaneous.

Redox titrations

  • Manganate(VII) is its own indicator: it is purple in solution and becomes colourless at the end point when Mn²⁺ forms.
  • Acidified dichromate(VI) turns from orange to green as Cr³⁺ forms. Iodine and thiosulfate use starch, which turns blue-black with iodine and loses that colour at the end point.

Exam tip: write the ion-electron half-equations first, balance the electrons, then combine them. The ratio of electrons sets the mole ratio in titration calculations.

title: Exam technique: Fractions, Decimals and Percentages
content:
### What earns the marks
For percentages of amounts, the 10-percent building blocks shown earn method marks without a calculator. For reverse percentages, state what the given amount represents (64 dollars = 80 percent) before dividing: that line earns the mark. For compound interest, each year on its own line earns credit. For Steel-type growth and decay, the multiplier (1/2 cubed) stated earns the method mark.
### Traps
Error: adding 20 percent to the sale price for the original. Correction: the sale price is the base of nothing; divide by 0.8. Error: simple interest applied twice for compound growth. Correction: grow each year from the new total. Error: decimal-point slips in 3/8 to percent. Correction: decimal first (0.375), then times 100.
### Worked example
Find 35% of 240: 0.35 × 240 = 84. A value increases by 20% to reach 180. The original is 180 ÷ 1.2 = 150, because you divide by the multiplier rather than taking 20% of 180. Check: 150 × 1.2 = 180. For fractions, 3/4 + 2/5 = 15/20 + 8/20 = 23/20 = 1 3/20.
### Check yourself
A price falls from £80 to £68. Find the percentage decrease. The decrease is £12, so the percentage is 12/80 × 100 = 15%. Show the divisor is the original price and not the new one.

title: IGCSE Physics: Earth and Space
content:
IGCSE Physics: Earth and Space

Cambridge IGCSE Physics 0625 (2026–2028), Topic 6 Space physics: statements 6.1 The Earth and the Solar System and 6.2 Stars and the Universe. This final topic scales the mechanics and nuclear physics of the rest of the course up to the largest objects there are. Gravity holds planets in orbit and holds stars together; fusion powers stars; the light from distant galaxies tells us the Universe is expanding. Paper 4 usually has one structured question here, and the calculations are orbital mechanics and redshift.

The Earth: rotation, orbit and seasons

The Earth spins on its axis once every 24 hours, which gives day and night, and it orbits the Sun once every 365.25 days, which gives the year. The Earth's axis is tilted at about 23.5° to the plane of its orbit, and that tilt — not the changing distance from the Sun — causes the seasons: when a hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun its rays strike more directly and the days are longer, so it is summer.

The Moon orbits the Earth in about 27 days. It shines by reflected sunlight, and because we see different fractions of its lit half as it orbits, it shows phases: new moon, crescent, half, gibbous, full. A lunar eclipse occurs when the Earth's shadow falls on the Moon; a solar eclipse when the Moon's shadow falls on the Earth.

Supplement: orbital speed. For a circular orbit of radius r completed in period T:

orbital speed = (2 pi r) / T        v = 2 pi r / T
  • v: orbital speed in metres per second (m s⁻¹); r: orbital radius in metres (m); T: orbital period in seconds (s). Convert days and years to seconds first.

The Solar System

The Solar System is the Sun and the bodies bound to it by gravity: eight planets (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune), their moons, dwarf planets, asteroids and comets. The four inner planets are small and rocky with few or no moons; the four outer planets are gas giants — large, low density, with many moons and ring systems. Asteroids orbit mainly between Mars and Jupiter; comets have highly elliptical orbits and grow bright tails of gas and dust when near the Sun.

Gravity provides the centripetal force that keeps every planet, moon and satellite in orbit. A planet's orbital speed falls with distance from the Sun (Kepler's laws), and the planets' orbits are ellipses with the Sun at one focus (Supplement: conservation of energy means a planet speeds up at perihelion and slows at aphelion, trading kinetic for gravitational potential energy).

Supplement: light-travel time. Light from the Sun takes about 8 minutes to reach Earth; from the nearest star, about 4.2 years. The light-year is the distance light travels in one year, about 9.5 × 10¹⁵ m, so looking at distant objects is literally looking into the past.

The Sun as a star

The Sun is an ordinary main-sequence star: a sphere of hot gas, about three-quarters hydrogen and one-quarter helium by mass, with a core at roughly 15 million degrees Celsius. Its energy comes from nuclear fusion in the core, where hydrogen nuclei fuse into helium nuclei, and a small loss of mass becomes the radiated energy. That radiation powers the whole Solar System: it drives the water cycle behind hydroelectric power and biofuels, heats the Earth's surface, and — over geological time — built the fossil fuels (Supplement: solar energy is the principal source behind almost every renewable resource on Earth).

The Sun is a medium-sized star about 4.6 billion years old, with enough hydrogen for roughly another 5 billion years of fusion before it swells into a red giant.

Stars and galaxies

A galaxy is a vast collection of stars, gas and dust held together by gravity. The Sun is one of roughly 200 billion stars in the Milky Way, a spiral galaxy, and galaxies themselves are grouped into clusters. The nearest large galaxy to us is Andromeda, about 2.5 million light-years away.

Stars have life cycles set by their mass:

  • Nebula: a huge cloud of gas and dust, pulled inward by gravity.
  • Protostar: the contracting, heating core of the cloud.
  • Main sequence star: when the core is hot enough for hydrogen fusion to start, the outward radiation pressure balances gravity and the star is stable — the Sun's current stage.
  • Red giant or supergiant: when core hydrogen runs low, fusion moves outwards and the star swells and cools at the surface.
  • End state: a star like the Sun sheds its outer layers as a planetary nebula and leaves a white dwarf. A massive star explodes as a supernova and leaves a neutron star, or, for the most massive, a black hole — an object whose gravity is so strong that not even light escapes.

Supernovae matter beyond astrophysics: they create and scatter the elements heavier than helium, so the carbon, oxygen and iron in your body were forged inside stars.

The Universe: redshift, expansion and the Big Bang

Light from distant galaxies is shifted towards the red end of the spectrum: the spectral lines appear at longer wavelengths than the same lines produced in a laboratory. This redshift is a Doppler effect — the galaxies are moving away from us. Crucially, almost every galaxy shows redshift, and the more distant the galaxy, the greater the redshift and the faster it is receding. The conclusion is that the Universe is expanding.

Running the expansion backwards implies that everything was once at one place — the Big Bang, roughly 13.8 billion years ago. Two further pieces of evidence support it: the cosmic microwave background (CMB), faint microwave radiation coming from every direction, which is the cooled remnant of the hot early Universe, and the abundance of light elements (hydrogen and helium) matching the predictions of Big Bang nucleosynthesis.

Supplement: Hubble's law and the age of the Universe. The recession speed of a galaxy is proportional to its distance:

recession speed = Hubble constant x distance        v = H d
  • v: recession speed in metres per second (m s⁻¹); d: distance in metres (m) (often megaparsecs, but convert); H: the Hubble constant in s⁻¹ (quoted as km s⁻¹ per megaparsec).
  • The age of the Universe follows as roughly 1/H: run the expansion back at the present rate.

Worked example: orbital speed and Hubble's law

The Earth orbits the Sun at a radius of 1.5 × 10¹¹ m with a period of 365 days.

T = 365 x 24 x 3600 = 3.15 × 10⁷ s
v = 2 pi r / T = 2 × 3.14 × 1.5 × 10¹¹ / 3.15 × 10⁷ = 3.0 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹ (about 30 km s⁻¹)

Second calculation: a galaxy is 200 megaparsecs away and Hubble's constant is 70 km s⁻¹ per megaparsec. Its recession speed is v = Hd = 70 × 200 = 14 000 km s⁻¹. The age estimate is 1/H: one megaparsec is 3.1 × 10¹⁹ km, so 1/H = 3.1 × 10¹⁹/70 = 4.4 × 10¹⁷ s ≈ 14 billion years — consistent with the accepted value.

Common mistakes

  • Blaming the seasons on the Earth–Sun distance; it is the axial tilt. The Earth is actually closest to the Sun in January.
  • Confusing the Moon's phases with eclipses: phases are the normal monthly cycle of the lit fraction; eclipses are shadows, and are rare because the Moon's orbit is tilted.
  • Using kilometres and seconds in v = 2πr/T without one consistent unit system; convert the period to seconds and the radius to metres.
  • Calling a light-year a unit of time; it is a distance — the distance light travels in one year.
  • Saying redshift means the galaxies are moving through space away from us; the accepted interpretation is that space itself is expanding, stretching the light.
  • Mixing up redshift and blueshift: receding sources shift to longer (redder) wavelengths; approaching sources shift shorter (bluer) — nearby Andromeda is blueshifted.
  • Placing the Sun at the centre of the Solar System as an absolute; the Sun is the centre of the Solar System, but the Solar System is an ordinary part of the Milky Way.
  • Forgetting that the fusion in stars is hydrogen to helium, which is not the same as the fission of uranium in power stations.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 4, 3 marks). Calculate the orbital speed of a satellite orbiting 7.0 × 10⁶ m from the Earth's centre every 5900 s.

Answer: v = 2πr/T = 2 × 3.14 × 7.0 × 10⁶ / 5900 = 7.5 × 10³ m s⁻¹ (7.5 km s⁻¹).

Question 2 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Explain the evidence from redshift that the Universe is expanding.

Answer: The spectral lines from distant galaxies are shifted towards longer wavelengths than laboratory lines, which by the Doppler effect means the sources are receding. The more distant the galaxy, the greater the redshift and the faster it recedes, so the whole Universe is expanding with every distance growing over time. Reversing that expansion implies all matter was once concentrated at one point — the Big Bang.

Question 3 (Paper 2 style). The seasons on Earth are caused by: A the changing Earth–Sun distance; B the tilt of the Earth's axis; C the Moon's gravity; D the Sun's rotation. Answer: B. The tilt changes the angle of the sunlight and the length of day through the year.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 6 marks). Describe the life cycle of a star like the Sun.

Answer: It begins as a nebula, a cloud of gas and dust. Gravity contracts the cloud and the core heats into a protostar. When the core temperature reaches about 15 million degrees, hydrogen fusion begins and the star joins the main sequence, where radiation pressure from fusion balances gravity and it is stable for billions of years. As core hydrogen depletes, fusion moves outwards, the outer layers expand and cool and the star becomes a red giant. Finally the outer layers are expelled as a planetary nebula, leaving a white dwarf that slowly cools — no fusion, supported by electron degeneracy pressure.

Question 5 (Paper 4, 3 marks). State two pieces of evidence for the Big Bang theory besides the redshift of galaxies.

Answer: The cosmic microwave background radiation — faint microwave radiation arriving from every direction, the cooled afterglow of the hot early Universe. The observed abundances of the light elements, especially hydrogen and helium, match the amounts predicted to have formed in the first minutes after the Big Bang.

Question 6 (Paper 4, 3 marks). Explain why nuclear fusion in the Sun releases energy.

Answer: In fusion, light hydrogen nuclei combine to form a heavier helium nucleus. The product nucleus has slightly less mass than the four protons that formed it; that lost mass is converted into energy in accordance with mass–energy equivalence, and the energy is radiated from the Sun's core. Fusion releases energy for light elements up to iron, which is why it powers stars.

That completes the Cambridge IGCSE 0625 course: the AS notes begin with Edexcel IAL Unit 1 and Kinematics.

title: Indices and Standard Form
content:
Number — Indices and Standard Form

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): index laws, negative and fractional indices, standard form arithmetic.

1. Index laws

  • aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ; aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ; (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ
  • a⁰ = 1; a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ; a^(1/n) = ⁿ√a; a^(m/n) = (ⁿ√a)ᵐ

Examples: 27^(2/3) = (³√27)² = 9; 5⁻² = 1/25; (2x³)² = 4x⁶.

2. Standard form

a × 10ⁿ with 1 ≤ a < 10.

  • 47 382 = 4.7382 × 10⁴; 0.0056 = 5.6 × 10⁻³
  • Multiplication: multiply a's, add powers. Division: divide a's, subtract powers.

Example: (3 × 10⁵) × (4 × 10⁻²) = 12 × 10³ = 1.2 × 10⁴.

3. Calculator use

Use the ×10ˣ key, not 10 ^; keep working in standard form and convert at the end. Give final answers in the form asked (often 3 s.f. standard form).

4. Solving index equations

Match bases: 2ˣ = 32 ⇒ 2ˣ = 2⁵ ⇒ x = 5. With different bases, rewrite (8 = 2³).

Exam tips: check a is in [1, 10) before writing standard form; in "multiply out" questions apply the power to every factor including coefficients.
