title: IGCSE Mathematics: Inequalities
content:
IGCSE Mathematics: Inequalities

Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580 (2025–2027), section 2 Algebra and graphs, statement 2.6 Inequalities — solving and interpreting linear inequalities, listing integer solutions, and (Extended) regions in the coordinate plane. An inequality describes a range of values rather than one exact value, and solving one follows the same balance principle as solving an equation, with one critical difference: multiplying or dividing by a negative number reverses the inequality sign. This note shows why that happens, writes out every solution line by line, and finishes with the region-shading questions that distinguish Paper 4.

What an inequality says

The four inequality symbols extend the equals sign: < (strictly less than), > (strictly greater than), ⩽ (less than or equal to), ⩾ (greater than or equal to). A solution is a set of values, drawn on a number line with a hollow circle for strict inequalities (the endpoint is excluded) and a solid circle for inclusive ones (the endpoint is included).

StatementMeaningNumber line
x > 3Every value greater than 3, not including 3Hollow circle at 3, arrow to the right
x ⩽ −1Every value up to and including −1Solid circle at −1, arrow to the left
2 ⩽ x < 5Values from 2 up to, but not including, 5Solid circle at 2, hollow at 5, line between

Why the sign flips when multiplying by a negative. Start with the true statement 3 < 5. Multiply both sides by −2 without thinking: −6 < −10 is false, because −10 is further left than −6. The correct statement is −6 > −10. Multiplying by a negative mirrors the number line, which reverses order — so the inequality symbol must reverse too. That single rule causes more lost marks than any other in this topic.

Solving linear inequalities

Use the equation methods unchanged, and remember the one reversal rule:

Solve:  5x - 7 > 3x + 1        (give the solution as an inequality)

5x - 3x > 1 + 7               [add 7 to both sides, subtract 3x from both sides]
2x > 8
x > 4                         [divide by +2: the sign does not reverse]
Solve:  3 - 2x ⩽ 11

-2x ⩽ 11 - 3                  [subtract 3 from both sides]
-2x ⩽ 8
x ⩾ -4                        [divide by -2: the sign REVERSES from ⩽ to ⩾]

The check is direct: x = −4 gives 3 − 2(−4) = 11 ⩽ 11 ✓, and x = 0 gives 3 ⩽ 11 ✓ while x = −5 gives 13 ⩽ 11 ✗ — so the boundary and direction are right.

Solve and list the integer solutions:  2 < (5x - 1)/3 ⩽ 8

Multiply every part by 3:
6 < 5x - 1 ⩽ 24
7 < 5x ⩽ 25                   [add 1 to every part]
7/5 < x ⩽ 5                   [divide every part by +5]

The integers are 2, 3, 4 and 5.

Compound inequalities (a value trapped between two bounds) are solved in one line per operation across all three parts — exactly like a three-pan balance.

Inequalities from word problems

Many questions ask for the greatest or least integer satisfying a condition. Translate carefully: at least means ⩾, at most means ⩽, more than means >, within or no more than means ⩽.

A cinema ticket costs £8. A group has £10⁰ and must keep at least £12 for travel.
How many tickets can they buy?

Let n be the number of tickets:  8n + 12 ⩽ 10⁰
8n ⩽ 88
n ⩽ 11

They can buy at most 11 tickets.

The final answer is a whole number in context: a group cannot buy a fraction of a ticket, so the solution set is the integers up to 11.

Regions in the coordinate plane (Extended)

The line y = mx + c divides the plane into two half-planes: points above it satisfy y > mx + c and points below it satisfy y < mx + c. A region question asks you to shade the set of points satisfying several inequalities at once.

  • Draw the boundary line y = mx + c as a solid line when the inequality includes equality (⩽ or ⩾), and as a dashed line when it is strict (< or >).
  • Test one point not on the line — the origin (0, 0) is easiest when the line misses it. Substitute into the inequality; if it is true, shade the side containing the test point.
  • Shade the side that satisfies every inequality; the answer region is the overlap, and the question often asks for the coordinates of a point inside it.
Shade the region satisfying:  y ⩽ 2x + 1,  y > -x + 2,  x ⩾ 0

Line 1: y = 2x + 1, solid. Test (0, 0): 0 ⩽ 1 true, so shade below-left of this line.
Line 2: y = -x + 2, dashed. Test (0, 0): 0 > 2 false, so shade the side away from the origin.
Line 3: x = 0 (the y-axis), solid, shade to the right.

The solution region is the triangle-like area satisfying all three, e.g. the point (2, 2):
2 ⩽ 5 ✓, 2 > 0 ✓, 2 ⩾ 0 ✓.

Describing a region in words is the reverse skill: read the boundary lines, note whether each is dashed or solid, and translate the shaded side back into an inequality.

Maximum and minimum values over a region (Extended)

Region questions often finish by asking for the largest or smallest value of an expression such as x + 2y for points inside the shaded region. A linear expression grows steadily in one direction across the plane, so over a region bounded by straight lines its extreme values always sit at the corners. The method is therefore exact: find the coordinates of every vertex of the region, substitute each pair into the expression, and pick the largest or smallest result. Do not stop at the corner that looks likely — an untested corner is the usual place a mark is lost.

Worked example: inequality with a parameter

Find the set of values of k for which the equation x² + kx + 9 = 0 has two distinct real roots.

Two distinct real roots require a positive discriminant:  b² - 4ac > 0
Here a = 1, b = k, c = 9:
k² - 36 > 0
k² > 36
k > 6  or  k < -6

This is an inequality inside a quadratic-context question — exactly the blend of topics Paper 4 rewards. If the requirement had been at least one real root, the inequality would be k² ⩾ 36, giving k ⩾ 6 or k ⩽ −6.

Corner points in practice. Take the region x ⩾ 0, y ⩾ 0, x + y ⩽ 6 and y ⩽ x + 2. Its vertices are where the boundary lines meet:

x = 0 with y = 0            gives (0, 0)
y = 0 with x + y = 6        gives (6, 0)
x = 0 with y = x + 2        gives (0, 2)
x + y = 6 with y = x + 2    gives x + (x + 2) = 6, so 2x = 4, x = 2 and y = 4, the corner (2, 4)

Evaluate P = x + 2y at each corner:
(0, 0): P = 0     (6, 0): P = 6     (0, 2): P = 4     (2, 4): P = 10

Maximum P = 10 at (2, 4);  minimum P = 0 at (0, 0).

The minimum sits at the origin only because this region includes it; a region bounded away from the origin puts its minimum at one of the other corners. Substitute every vertex before choosing.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Not reversing the inequality sign after multiplying or dividing by a negative number. −2x < 8 means x > −4.
  • Reversing the sign when multiplying by a positive number, or reversing when subtracting — only multiplication and division by negatives reverse it.
  • Hollow versus solid circles: < and > exclude the endpoint; ⩽ and ⩾ include it. Writing x > 4 when x = 4 works is a boundary error.
  • Flipping the inequality direction mid-solution so the final statement faces the wrong way.
  • Forgetting to reverse in a compound inequality: every part flips when the whole chain is multiplied by a negative.
  • In region questions, drawing a solid boundary for a strict inequality (or a dashed one for ⩽), or shading the wrong side because no test point was used.
  • Reporting a decimal when the question asks for integers: n ⩽ 11.25 means the largest integer is 11, not 11.25.
  • Treating ⩽ as < in a word problem: at most 5 includes 5.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 2, 3 marks). Solve 7 − 3x > 1 and show your solution on a number line.

Answer: −3x > −6, so x < 2 (the sign reverses). Number line: hollow circle at 2, shading to the left.

Question 2 (Paper 2, 3 marks). Solve 2 ⩽ 3x + 5 < 14 and list the integer solutions.

Answer: Subtract 5 throughout: −3 ⩽ 3x < 9. Divide by 3: −1 ⩽ x < 3. The integers are −1, 0, 1, 2.

Question 3 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Find the values of x for which x² − 5x + 4 < 0.

Answer: Factorise: (x − 1)(x − 4) < 0. The quadratic is negative between its roots, so 1 < x < 4. (Test x = 2: 4 − 10 + 4 = −2 < 0 ✓; test x = 0: 4 > 0 ✗.)

Question 4 (Paper 4, 5 marks). Shade the region defined by y > x − 1, y ⩽ 3 and x ⩾ 0, and write down the coordinates of one point in the region.

Answer: Draw y = x − 1 dashed (strict), y = 3 solid and x = 0 solid. The origin test for y > x − 1 gives 0 > −1, true, so shade above the dashed line; y ⩽ 3 shades below the horizontal line; x ⩾ 0 shades right of the y-axis. The overlap is a triangle with vertices (0, 3), (4, 3) and (0, −1); the point (1, 1) lies inside: 1 > 0 ✓, 1 ⩽ 3 ✓, 1 ⩾ 0 ✓.

Question 5 (Paper 4, 4 marks). A rectangle has a perimeter of at most 60 cm and a length of (x + 4) cm. Write an inequality for its width w and find w when x = 8.

Answer: 2[(x + 4) + w] ⩽ 60, so (x + 4) + w ⩽ 30 and w ⩽ 26 − x. With x = 8: w ⩽ 18 cm, and the width must also be positive, so 0 < w ⩽ 18.

Question 6 (Paper 2, 3 marks). The solutions of 5x + a ⩾ 0 include x = −2. Find the smallest integer value of a.

Answer: Substituting x = −2: −10 + a ⩾ 0, so a ⩾ 10. The smallest integer value is 10.

With equations and inequalities mastered, the next stage of algebra is sequences and functions.

title: Molecules, Transport and Health
content:
Molecules, Transport and Health

Edexcel IAL Biology WBI11, Topic 1. Living things are built from a small set of biological molecules. Their structure decides how they are used, how substances move in and out of cells, and how diet affects health.

Carbohydrates

  • Monosaccharides such as glucose, fructose and galactose are the building blocks. Glucose is the main respiratory substrate.
  • Disaccharides form by a condensation reaction that releases water and creates a glycosidic bond. Maltose is glucose + glucose, sucrose is glucose + fructose, and lactose is glucose + galactose.
  • Starch (amylose and amylopectin) stores glucose in plants. Glycogen stores glucose in animals. Cellulose is a straight chain of beta-glucose with hydrogen bonds between chains, giving strength.

Lipids and proteins

  • A triglyceride is one glycerol with three fatty acids joined by ester bonds. Phospholipids have a hydrophilic head and two hydrophobic tails.
  • Amino acids join by peptide bonds to form polypeptides. Tertiary structure is held by hydrogen, ionic, disulfide and hydrophobic interactions.

Enzymes

  • Enzymes have an active site with a shape complementary to the substrate. Rate rises with temperature until the enzyme denatures, and pH changes can alter the active site.

Transport

  • Diffusion moves substances down a concentration gradient without energy. Facilitated diffusion uses carrier or channel proteins. Active transport moves substances against a gradient and uses ATP.
  • Water moves by osmosis from a less negative water potential to a more negative water potential.
  • Large, multicellular organisms need exchange surfaces with a large surface area to volume ratio, such as alveoli and the villi of the small intestine.

Health

  • Body mass index (BMI) = mass (kg) ÷ height² (m²). Diet, exercise and cholesterol intake affect the risk of cardiovascular disease.

Exam tip: when you describe a transport process, state whether it needs energy, whether it uses a protein, and which way the gradient points.

title: Sampling and Estimation — Study Notes
content:
Sampling and Estimation

Populations, Samples, Statistics

A parameter describes the population (μ, σ²); a statistic describes the sample (x̄, s²). A statistic is unbiased if its expectation equals the population parameter: E(x̄) = μ always holds for the sample mean.

Unbiased Variance

The estimator with divisor (n − 1) is the unbiased sample variance:

  • s² = Σ(x − x̄)²/(n − 1)

Why n − 1: deviations are measured from x̄ rather than μ, slightly underestimating spread; the smaller divisor corrects it. At A2, state which estimator you are using — the unbiased one is the default.

Distribution of the Sample Mean

For a sample of size n from a population with mean μ and variance σ²:

  • E(x̄) = μ and Var(x̄) = σ²/n

Averaging shrinks spread — bigger samples give steadier estimates.

Central Limit Theorem

Whatever the population shape, for large n (rule of thumb n ≥ 30) the sample mean is approximately normal: x̄ ~ N(μ, σ²/n). This is why the normal appears constantly in inference.

Example: population mean 50, s.d. 12, n = 36. Then x̄ ~ N(50, 4) and P(x̄ > 51) = P(Z > 0.5) = 0.3085.

Using x̄ to Estimate

Given sample data, estimate μ by x̄ and σ² by the unbiased s². When the population is normal, x̄ is exactly normal for any n — the CLT is only needed for non-normal populations.

Exam tips: distinguish σ²/σ (population) from s²/s (sample) in notation. Standard error means √(σ²/n) — smaller with larger n. Quote probabilities for x̄ with the variance divided by n; forgetting that division is the classic error.

Exam method: estimators and sample variance

The sample mean x̄ is an unbiased estimate of the population mean μ. The unbiased estimate of the population variance is s² = Σ(x − x̄)²/(n − 1), which divides by n − 1 rather than n. Using n gives the population variance of the sample, which tends to underestimate the true value.

When the sum of squared deviations is given, divide it by n − 1 directly. When the raw data are given, it is quicker to compute s² = (Σx² − n x̄²)/(n − 1).

A random sample gives each member of the population an equal chance of selection. Bias means the estimator does not equal the parameter on average, so the sample must be random to make the estimate reliable.

The standard error of the sample mean is σ/√n. It decreases as the sample size grows, so larger samples give more precise estimates.

Exam cue: Name the estimator and state whether it is unbiased, because the question often asks for both the value and the reason.

title: AS Level Mathematics: Coordinate Geometry
content:
AS Level Mathematics: Coordinate Geometry

Coordinate geometry turns shapes into algebra: every line is an equation, every intersection is a simultaneous equation, and every circle is a completed square waiting to happen. This note builds the whole AS toolkit from zero: distance and midpoint, gradients with the parallel and perpendicular rules, the three forms of a line's equation, intersections and perpendicular bisectors, circles in both centre-radius and expanded form, and tangents and normals to circles. Every worked example writes the formula line first, because that is where the method marks are.

Distance and midpoint

distance between (x1, y1) and (x2, y2):
d = √((x2 - x1)² + (y2 - y1)²)

midpoint: ((x1 + x2)/2, (y1 + y2)/2)

The distance formula is Pythagoras in disguise: the horizontal and vertical gaps are the legs of a right triangle, and the distance is the hypotenuse.

Worked example. Find the distance and midpoint of A(1, 2) and B(7, 10).

d = √(6² + 8²) = √(100) = 10
midpoint = ((1 + 7)/2, (2 + 10)/2) = (4, 6)

Gradient and the parallel/perpendicular rules

gradient m = (y2 - y1)/(x2 - x1)   (rise over run)

parallel lines: m¹ = m²
perpendicular lines: m¹ x m² = -1   (m² = -1/m¹)

Worked example. Find the gradient of AB for A(1, 2), B(5, 10), and the gradient of a line perpendicular to it.

m = (10 - 2)/(5 - 1) = 8/4 = 2
perpendicular gradient = -1/2

Worked example 2 (collinearity). Show A(1, 1), B(3, 5), C(5, 9) are collinear.

m(AB) = 4/2 = 2;  m(BC) = 4/2 = 2
equal gradients and a shared point B, so collinear

Equations of straight lines

Three forms, each useful in its own situation:

  • y = mx + c: gradient m, y-intercept c. Use when you know both.
  • y − y₁ = m(x − x₁): point-slope form. Use when you know a point and the gradient.
  • ax + by + c = 0: general form. Rearrange to find m and c when needed.

Worked example 1. Find the equation of the line through (2, 5) with gradient 3.

y - 5 = 3(x - 2)
y = 3x - 6 + 5
y = 3x - 1

Worked example 2 (two points). Find the equation of the line through (1, 4) and (4, 13).

m = (13 - 4)/(4 - 1) = 9/3 = 3
using (1, 4): y - 4 = 3(x - 1)  →  y = 3x + 1

Worked example 3 (perpendicular). Find the line through (2, 1) perpendicular to y = 2x + 3.

perpendicular gradient = -1/2
y - 1 = -1/2 (x - 2)
y = -x/2 + 1 + 1 = -x/2 + 2

Intersections and the perpendicular bisector

Two lines meet where their equations are simultaneously true: set them equal and solve. The perpendicular bisector of AB passes through the midpoint of AB with gradient −1/m(AB).

Worked example. Find where y = 3x − 1 meets y = −x + 7.

3x - 1 = -x + 7
4x = 8  →  x = 2;  y = 3(2) - 1 = 5
intersection: (2, 5)

Worked example 2 (perpendicular bisector). Find the perpendicular bisector of A(1, 2) and B(5, 10).

midpoint = (3, 6)
m(AB) = 8/4 = 2  →  perpendicular gradient = -1/2
y - 6 = -1/2 (x - 3)
y = -x/2 + 3/2 + 6 = -x/2 + 7.5

Circles: centre-radius form

(x - a)² + (y - b)² = r²
centre (a, b), radius r

expanded form x² + y² + 2fx + 2gy + c = 0:
complete the square in x and y to recover the centre and radius

Worked example 1. State the centre and radius of (x − 3)² + (y + 2)² = 25.

centre (3, -2); radius = 5

Worked example 2 (completing the square). Find the centre and radius of x² + y² − 6x + 8y − 11 = 0.

(x² - 6x) + (y² + 8y) = 11
(x - 3)² - 9 + (y + 4)² - 16 = 11
(x - 3)² + (y + 4)² = 36
centre (3, -4), radius 6

Worked example 3 (circle from diameter). AB is a diameter with A(1, 2) and B(7, 10). Find the circle's equation.

centre = midpoint = (4, 6)
radius = half the distance = 10/2 = 5
(x - 4)² + (y - 6)² = 25

Tangents and normals to circles

A tangent to a circle is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact. The method: find the gradient of the radius from the centre to the point, take the negative reciprocal for the tangent, then use the point-slope form.

Worked example. Find the tangent to the circle centre (2, 3) at the point (5, 7).

radius gradient = (7 - 3)/(5 - 2) = 4/3
tangent gradient = -3/4
y - 7 = -3/4 (x - 5)
4y - 28 = -3x + 15
3x + 4y = 43

Worked example 2 (tangent length). From the point P(8, 3), find the length of the tangent to the circle (x − 2)² + (y − 1)² = 13.

centre C(2, 1), radius √(13)
distance PC = √(6² + 2²) = √(40)
tangent² = PC² - r² = 40 - 13 = 27
tangent length = √(27) = 3 √(3) = 5.20

The right angle between radius and tangent makes every tangent-length question a Pythagoras problem in disguise; drawing the radius to the contact point is the step that unlocks it.

Worked example 2 (normal). The normal at a point on a circle is the radius line extended. Find the normal at the same point.

normal gradient = radius gradient = 4/3
y - 7 = 4/3 (x - 5)  →  4x - 3y + 1 = 0 (rearranged)

Circles and lines: intersection problems

Where a line meets a circle, substitute the line into the circle's equation and solve the resulting quadratic. The discriminant then classifies the geometry: two roots mean a secant (two intersection points), one root means a tangent, none means the line misses the circle.

substitute y = mx + c into (x - a)² + (y - b)² = r²
solve for x; each x gives a y from the line
discriminant > 0: two points; = 0: tangent; < 0: no intersection

Worked example. Find the intersection of y = x + 1 with x² + y² = 25.

x² + (x + 1)² = 25
2x² + 2x + 1 - 25 = 0
x² + x - 12 = 0
(x + 4)(x - 3) = 0  →  x = -4 or 3
y = -3 or 4
points: (-4, -3) and (3, 4)

Worked example 2 (tangent condition). Show that y = 2x + 10 is tangent to x² + y² = 20.

x² + (2x + 10)² = 20
5x² + 40x + 100 - 20 = 0
5x² + 40x + 80 = 0  →  x² + 8x + 16 = 0
(x + 4)² = 0: repeated root, so tangent at x = -4, y = 2

Modelling with straight lines

Linear models answer practical questions: when two plans cost the same, how a quantity changes at a constant rate, what a graph's gradient means in context. The method is to identify the two variables, write each relationship as a line, and solve simultaneously — then interpret the answer in the units of the problem.

Worked example. A taxi charges a fixed 3 pounds plus 1.50 pounds per kilometre; a rival charges 6 pounds plus 1.00 pound per kilometre. Find the distance at which the charges are equal.

3 + 1.5d = 6 + 1.0d
0.5d = 3  →  d = 6 km
both charge 12 pounds at 6 km

Worked example 2 (gradient meaning). A graph of value against age for a car is a straight line through (0, 18000) and (4, 10000). Interpret the gradient.

gradient = (10000 - 18000)/4 = -2000
meaning: the car loses 2000 pounds of value per year

Worked examples: mixed coordinate problems

Worked example. The line y = 2x + k is a tangent to the circle x² + y² = 20. Find k.

substitute: x² + (2x + k)² = 20
x² + 4x² + 4kx + k² - 20 = 0
5x² + 4kx + (k² - 20) = 0
tangent: discriminant = 0
16k² - 20(k² - 20) = 0
16k² - 20k² + 400 = 0  →  4k² = 400  →  k = +/-10

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Distance) Find the distance between (2, 1) and (5, 5). Answer: √(9 + 16) = 5.
  2. (Gradient) Find the gradient through (3, 4) and (7, 12). Answer: 8/4 = 2.
  3. (Perpendicular) A line has gradient −⅔. Find the gradient of a perpendicular line. Answer: 3/2.
  4. (Equation) Find the line through (0, 3) with gradient −2. Answer: y = −2x + 3.
  5. (Circle) State the centre and radius of (x + 1)² + (y − 4)² = 9. Answer: centre (−1, 4), radius 3.
  6. (Completing the square) Find the centre and radius of x² + y² + 4x − 2y − 4 = 0. Answer: (x + 2)² + (y − 1)² = 9 → centre (−2, 1), radius 3.
  7. (Tangent) Find the tangent to x² + y² = 25 at (3, 4). Answer: radius gradient 4/3, tangent gradient −3/4; 3x + 4y = 25.
  8. (Midpoint/distance) Show that (1, 2), (5, 6), (9, 10) are collinear. Answer: gradients both 1; shared point → collinear.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Gradient sign errors: (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁) — subtracting in the wrong order flips the sign. Keep the same point first in both differences.
  • Perpendicular as negative: the perpendicular gradient is the negative reciprocal (−1/m), not just −m.
  • Circle sign reversal: (x + 2)² means centre x = −2; (y − 5)² means y = 5. The sign inside is opposite to the centre coordinate.
  • Radius squared: in (x − a)² + (y − b)² = 25 the radius is 5, not 25. Take the square root.
  • Completing the square with coefficients: halve the x-coefficient and subtract its square; forgetting the subtraction changes the radius.
  • Tangent versus normal: tangent is perpendicular to the radius; normal is along the radius. Swapping their gradients inverts the answer.
  • Intersection arithmetic: after finding x, substitute into the simpler equation for y, and check both points when a quadratic gives two solutions.
  • Sketching circles: mark the centre and radius explicitly; a circle without its centre marked cannot be checked.

From picture to algebra: what each coordinate formula is doing

Coordinate geometry is geometry written in numbers, and each formula is a fact you already know in a different language. Learn which fact each one encodes and the questions stop being arbitrary.

The distance formula is Pythagoras. The horizontal gap between two points and the vertical gap are the two legs of a right-angled triangle; the distance is its hypotenuse:

d = √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²) Key: d = distance between two points (units); (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂) their coordinates. The squares make the order of subtraction irrelevant.

The midpoint is the average. Halfway between two points is the mean of the x's and the mean of the y's. Its gradient language version: the midpoint is the point that splits the segment in the ratio 1 : 1, which is why a perpendicular bisector passes through it.

Gradient is rise over run. m = (y₂ − y₁) / (x₂ − x₁), and the two derived rules are what make lines into equations: parallel lines have equal gradients, perpendicular lines have gradients whose product is −1. The second is the whole content of the tangent picture above.

The circle equation is the distance formula rearranged. A point (x, y) lies on a circle of radius r centred at (a, b) exactly when its distance from the centre equals r. Square both sides of the distance formula:

(x − a)² + (y − b)² = r² Key: (a, b) = centre; r = radius. Expanding gives x² + y² − 2ax − 2by + a² + b² − r² = 0, which is the general form the paper usually hands you — and why finding the centre means completing the square, not solving.

Worked example. A circle has equation x² + y² − 6x + 8y − 11 = 0. Find its centre, radius, and the equation of the tangent at the point (6, −1).

Complete the square in x and in y:
(x² − 6x + 9) + (y² + 8y + 16) = 11 + 9 + 16 = 36
so (x − 3)² + (y + 4)² = 36, centre (3, −4), radius 6.

Check that (6, −1) is on the circle: (6 − 3)² + (−1 + 4)² = 9 + 9 = 18 ≠ 36, so it is not — this is exactly the check the paper expects you to do silently. Taking a point P on the circle instead, the tangent's gradient is the negative reciprocal of the radius gradient:

mtangent = −1 / mradius Key: the product of the two gradients is −1; the radius runs from the centre to the point of contact, so its gradient is (y₁ − b) / (x₁ − a).

With centre (3, −4) and a point P(3, 2) at the top of the circle, the radius is vertical so its gradient is undefined and the tangent is horizontal: y = 2. That degenerate case is worth knowing, because "vertical radius, horizontal tangent" is where candidates write m = 0 and lose the mark.

Where marks are lost. Reading the centre off the expanded form as (−3, 4) instead of (3, −4) — the signs invert when the bracket is written. Forgetting that r² = 36 means r = 6, not r = 36. And using the radius gradient as the tangent gradient: the perpendicular rule is the entire point of the tangent question.

title: Simulation, Sensors and Real Data — Study Notes
content:
Simulation, Sensors and Real Data

Syllabus note: 9618 has no separate simulation-and-sensors section; this material supports practical work (data logging, modelling, sensor input), including Paper 4.

Simulation and Modelling

A simulation is a program that models a real system to test scenarios safely and cheaply: weather models, traffic flows, epidemic spread. Models use abstractions — chosen variables and equations — with a time step. Advantages: no real-world risk, repeatable, faster or slower than real time. Limitations: only as good as the model; rare events may be missed.

Sensors and Signals

Sensors measure physical quantities: temperature (thermistor), light (LDR), pressure, humidity, sound. Most output analogue signals varying continuously; computers need digital values, so an ADC (analogue-to-digital converter) samples the signal. Resolution depends on bits — an 8-bit ADC gives 256 levels. A DAC converts digital output back to analogue for actuators or speakers.

Monitoring vs Control

  • Monitoring: sensors feed data to the computer, which only records, displays or raises alarms — no action taken on the environment.
  • Control: the computer acts via actuators (motors, valves, heaters) based on sensor input — the classic feedback loop.

Real-Time Considerations

Control systems are often real-time: late output can be wrong output. Sampling rate must exceed twice the highest signal frequency (Nyquist) to avoid aliasing.

Exam tips: distinguish monitoring from control with a named example; describe the role of ADC and DAC in a greenhouse system; explain one limitation of a simulation.

Exam method: using simulation output with real data

Sensor readings are noisy, drift over time and can contain missing or impossible values. Before using them, check each reading against a sensible range, remove or flag outliers, and decide how to handle gaps, for example by ignoring them or interpolating between neighbouring readings. State which cleaning step you chose.

A simulation is only as reliable as its assumptions and its inputs. In an exam answer, state one assumption the model makes, explain how it could make the output differ from reality, and suggest a way to test the model against measured data.

Exam cue: When asked to evaluate a simulation, give a specific limitation tied to the scenario in the question rather than a general comment that simulations are approximate.

Worked example: comparing simulation output with real data

A simulation predicts a mean room temperature of 24.0 °C. Sensors in the real room record a mean of 25.3 °C. The difference is 25.3 minus 24.0, which is 1.3 °C. The percentage error is the difference divided by the real value, so 1.3 divided by 25.3 gives about 5.1 per cent. State the direction of the error as well as its size: the model underestimates the real temperature.

Then suggest a cause that the model could plausibly miss, such as heat from windows, occupants or equipment. A good evaluation names one assumption in the simulation and says how changing it would move the output closer to the real data.

Why real-time systems differ from batch simulations

  • A real-time system must respond within a fixed deadline, so a late result is a failure even when it is correct.
  • A batch simulation can run to completion and be checked afterwards, whereas a control system acts on each reading as it arrives.
  • Sampling rate matters: sample too slowly and fast changes are missed entirely, which is an aliasing risk.

title: Exam technique: Sequences and Functions
content:
### What earns the marks
For nth-term questions, derive earns marks for the difference identified, the form an + c stated, and the constant found from n = 1. For function questions, order earns marks: evaluate the inner function first and write the intermediate value down. For inverse functions, show the swap (x = ... then solve) rather than jumping to the formula.
### Traps
Error: computing fg(x) when gf(x) is asked. Correction: start from the rightmost letter. Error: answering 5 + 3 x 20 for the 20th term of a 5, 8, 11 pattern. Correction: the multiplier is (n - 1), not n. Error: multiplying by the ratio once for geometric terms. Correction: the power is (n - 1).

title: Exam technique: Integration II
content:
### What earns the marks
For parts, the u/v assignment plus the uv minus integral form earns the method mark. For substitution, du stated and limits changed earn one mark each. For differential equations, separating then +c before the condition earns both marks.
### Traps
Error: +c added after using the condition. Correction: constant first, then solve. Error: old limits kept after substitution. Correction: change limits with the variable. Error: division before separating. Correction: rearrange to g(y)dy = f(x)dx form.

title: Binomial Distribution — Quick Revision Summary

Quick revision: Binomial Distribution

Mathematics — A2. X ~ B(n, p) counts successes in n independent trials when:

Key areas to revise

  • When Binomial Applies
  • The Formula
  • Cumulative Probabilities
  • Expectation and Variance
  • Modelling Decisions

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

### Worked example For X ~ B(n, p), P(X = r) = nCr pʳ(1 − p)ⁿ⁻ʳ, with mean np and variance np(1 − p). For n = 5 and p = 0.2, P(X = 2) = 10 × 0.2² × 0.8³ = 10 × 0.04 × 0.512 = 0.2048. The mean is 5 × 0.2 = 1. ### Check yourself Find P(X = 0) for the same distribution. It equals 0.8⁵ = 0.32768. State the condition for a binomial model: fixed n, independent trials and constant p.

title: Sine Rule, Cosine Rule and Triangle Area
content:
Trigonometry — Sine and Cosine Rules

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): area formula, sine rule, cosine rule, multi-step bearing and 3-D problems (Extended).

1. Area of a triangle

A = ½ab sin C (C = included angle between sides a and b).

Example: a = 8, b = 5, C = 48° → A = ½ × 8 × 5 × sin 48° = 14.8.

2. Sine rule

a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C. Use when a matching angle–side pair is known.

Example: A = 40°, a = 7, B = 65°: b = 7 sin 65°/sin 40° = 9.98.

Ambiguous case: two triangles possible when finding an angle — check the obtuse option (180° − θ).

3. Cosine rule

a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A. Use with two sides + included angle, or all three sides (then cos A = (b² + c² − a²)/(2bc)).

Example: b = 7, c = 5, A = 52°: a² = 74 − 70 cos 52° = 30.9 → a = 5.56.

4. Bearing problems

Draw both north lines, transfer angles via parallel lines, then pick sine/cosine rule.

Example: QP = 60 km bearing 070° from Q; QR = 45 km bearing 150°. ∠PQR = 80° → PR² = 60² + 45² − 2·60·45 cos 80° → PR = 68.4 km.

5. 3-D trigonometry

Identify the plane containing the required angle; use 3-D Pythagoras d² = x² + y² + z² for space diagonals; angle between a line and a plane uses the projection onto the plane.

Exam tips: state which rule you are using and why; sketch a separate 2-D triangle for 3-D questions; answers to 3 s.f. / bearings as three digits.

title: A2 Level Chemistry: Organic Chemistry: Carbonyls, Carboxylic Acids and Chirality
content:
Organic Chemistry: Carbonyls, Carboxylic Acids and Chirality

Edexcel International A Level Chemistry — Unit 4 (WCH14), Topic 15, covers the concepts of carbonyl compounds, carboxylic acids, and chirality. This topic includes the reactions and tests of aldehydes and ketones, the properties and reactions of carboxylic acids, and the concept of optical isomerism and chirality.

Introduction to Carbonyl Compounds

Carbonyl compounds contain the carbonyl group, C=O. Aldehydes have the C=O group at the end of a chain (RCHO), while ketones have it inside the chain (RCOR). The carbon of C=O is slightly positive, making it susceptible to nucleophilic attack.

  • Aldehydes: RCHO
  • Ketones: RCOR

Reactions of Carbonyl Compounds

Carbonyl compounds undergo nucleophilic addition reactions. The products of these reactions can be carboxylic acids, alcohols, or molecules with a chiral centre.

  • Hydrogen cyanide adds across C=O: RCHO + HCN → RCN
  • Sodium tetrahydridoborate(III) (NaBH4) reduces aldehydes to primary alcohols and ketones to secondary alcohols
  • 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine (2,4-DNPH) gives an orange or yellow precipitate with any carbonyl compound
  • Tollens' reagent gives a silver mirror with aldehydes but not with ketones
  • The iodoform test gives a yellow precipitate of triiodomethane with compounds containing CH3CO– or CH3CH(OH)– groups

Carboxylic Acids

Carboxylic acids contain –COOH and are weak acids. They are more acidic than alcohols because the carboxylate ion is stabilised by delocalisation.

  • Carboxylic acids react with alcohols in the presence of concentrated sulfuric acid to form esters
  • Primary alcohols are oxidised to carboxylic acids by heating with acidified potassium dichromate(VI) under reflux

Chirality and Optical Isomerism

A chiral carbon atom has four different groups attached. Molecules with a chiral centre exist as a pair of enantiomers. Enantiomers have identical physical properties except their effect on plane-polarised light.

  • A chiral carbon atom has four different groups attached
  • Enantiomers have identical physical properties except their effect on plane-polarised light
  • An equimolar mixture of the two enantiomers is a racemic mixture, which is optically inactive

Optical Activity

Optical activity is the ability of a single optical isomer to rotate the plane of polarisation of plane-polarised monochromatic light.

  • Optical activity is measured using a polarimeter
  • The specific rotation of a compound is a characteristic property

Nomenclature of Aldehydes and Ketones

Aldehydes and ketones are named based on the longest continuous chain containing the carbonyl group.

  • Aldehydes: RCHO
  • Ketones: RCOR

Nomenclature of Carboxylic Acids

Carboxylic acids are named based on the longest continuous chain containing the carboxyl group.

  • Carboxylic acids: RCOOH

Nomenclature of Acyl Chlorides and Esters

Acyl chlorides and esters are named based on the longest continuous chain containing the acyl group.

  • Acyl chlorides: RCOCl
  • Esters: RCOOR

Reactions of Acyl Chlorides

Acyl chlorides undergo nucleophilic substitution reactions.

  • Acyl chlorides react with water to form carboxylic acids
  • Acyl chlorides react with alcohols to form esters
  • Acyl chlorides react with concentrated ammonia to form amides
  • Acyl chlorides react with amines to form amides

Hydrolysis of Esters

Esters undergo hydrolysis reactions in acidic and alkaline solutions.

  • Esters react with water in the presence of an acid catalyst to form carboxylic acids and alcohols
  • Esters react with water in the presence of a base to form carboxylic acids and alcohols

Condensation Polymerisation

Polyesters are formed by condensation polymerisation reactions.

  • Polyesters are formed by the reaction of carboxylic acids and alcohols

Mass Spectra

Mass spectra provide information about the molecular mass of a compound.

  • The molecular ion is the ion with the highest mass-to-charge ratio
  • The base peak is the ion with the highest intensity

13C NMR Spectroscopy

13C NMR spectroscopy provides information about the environments of carbon atoms in a molecule.

  • The chemical shift of a carbon atom is a characteristic property
  • The number of peaks in a 13C NMR spectrum is equal to the number of different environments of carbon atoms

Proton NMR Spectroscopy

Proton NMR spectroscopy provides information about the environments of hydrogen atoms in a molecule.

  • The chemical shift of a hydrogen atom is a characteristic property
  • The number of peaks in a proton NMR spectrum is equal to the number of different environments of hydrogen atoms
  • The intensity of a peak is proportional to the number of hydrogen atoms in that environment

Chromatography

Chromatography is a technique used to separate the components of a mixture.

  • Chromatography separates components based on their affinity for a stationary phase and a mobile phase
  • The Rf value is a measure of the distance traveled by a component relative to the distance traveled by the solvent front

Typical Mistakes

  • Confusing the reactions of aldehydes and ketones
  • Forgetting to show the nucleophile attacking the carbon of C=O in nucleophilic addition reactions
  • Not understanding the concept of optical isomerism and chirality

Exam-Style Questions

  1. What is the difference between an aldehyde and a ketone? Answer: An aldehyde has the C=O group at the end of a chain, while a ketone has it inside the chain.
  2. What is the reaction of hydrogen cyanide with an aldehyde? Answer: Hydrogen cyanide adds across C=O to form a cyanohydrin.
  3. What is the specific rotation of a compound? Answer: The specific rotation of a compound is a characteristic property that is measured using a polarimeter.

To revise this topic, make sure to understand the reactions and tests of aldehydes and ketones, the properties and reactions of carboxylic acids, and the concept of optical isomerism and chirality. Practice drawing the structures of aldehydes, ketones, and carboxylic acids, and practice solving problems involving the reactions of these compounds. Also, make sure to understand the concepts of 13C NMR spectroscopy, proton NMR spectroscopy, and chromatography, and practice solving problems involving these techniques. Finally, practice answering exam-style questions to test your understanding of the topic.

Detailed Mechanisms of Nucleophilic Addition: HCN and KCN

The addition of hydrogen cyanide to carbonyl compounds is a classic Edexcel A2 mechanism. Because HCN is a weak acid and provides a very low concentration of cyanide ions, potassium cyanide (KCN) is added to provide a higher concentration of the active nucleophile, CN−. The mechanism proceeds via nucleophilic addition:

  • Step 1: The lone pair on the carbon atom of the cyanide ion (CN−) attacks the slightly positive carbon atom of the carbonyl group (C=O). A curly arrow goes from the lone pair on carbon to the carbonyl carbon.
  • Step 2: Simultaneously, the π bond of the carbonyl group breaks, with both electrons moving entirely to the oxygen atom. This forms a negatively charged intermediate (an alkoxide ion) and shows a curly arrow from the C=O bond to the oxygen.
  • Step 3: The intermediate accepts a proton (H+) from HCN or from the acidic aqueous environment to form a hydroxy-nitrile (cyanohydrin).

Stereochemical Evidence from Carbonyl Addition to Unsymmetrical Ketones

When an unsymmetrical aldehyde or ketone reacts with hydrogen cyanide, the planar nature of the carbonyl group allows the nucleophile (CN−) to attack from either above or below the plane with equal probability. If the product molecule contains a single chiral centre (i.e., four different groups attached to the central carbon), a racemic mixture of two optical isomers (enantiomers) is formed in equal amounts. This proves that the intermediate is planar around the original carbonyl carbon and provides crucial mechanistic evidence for the reaction pathway.

Physical Properties of Carbonyl Compounds and Carboxylic Acids

Understanding intermolecular forces explains the differing boiling temperatures and water solubilities:

  • Aldehydes and ketones cannot form hydrogen bonds with themselves because they lack a hydrogen atom bonded directly to a strongly electronegative oxygen or nitrogen atom. Their molecules are held together by permanent dipole-dipole attractions and London forces, resulting in lower boiling temperatures than corresponding alcohols or carboxylic acids of similar relative molecular mass.
  • Aldehydes, ketones, and carboxylic acids can form hydrogen bonds with water molecules through their lone pairs on the carbonyl or hydroxyl oxygens, which explains why smaller members of these homologous series are completely soluble in water.
  • Carboxylic acids can form stable hydrogen-bonded dimers with each other in the liquid and vapour phases. This effectively doubles their relative molecular mass during vaporisation, leading to significantly higher boiling temperatures than alcohols of comparable molecular mass.

Comprehensive Analysis of Spectroscopic Data

Examiners frequently test the ability to combine mass spectrometry, carbon-13 NMR, and proton NMR data to deduce molecular structures:

  • Mass Spectrometry: High-resolution mass spectrometry provides accurate relative molecular masses to four decimal places, allowing chemists to distinguish between molecules with the same nominal integer mass (e.g., CO, N2, and C2H4 all have a nominal mass of 28, but accurate masses separate them precisely). Fragmentation patterns reveal structural fragments, such as the loss of 15 (CH3), 17 (OH), or 45 (COOH).
  • Carbon-13 NMR: Each peak in a 13C NMR spectrum corresponds to a carbon atom in a distinct chemical environment. The chemical shift value (measured in ppm) gives information about the types of adjacent atoms or functional groups (e.g., carbon in a C=O group appears around 160 to 220 ppm, while aliphatic sp3 carbons appear between 0 and 50 ppm).
  • Proton (1H) NMR: The number of distinct peaks indicates the number of different hydrogen environments. The relative peak areas (integration traces) show the ratio of hydrogen atoms in each environment. The splitting pattern of each peak is determined by the number of adjacent non-equivalent protons using the (n + 1) rule, where n is the number of protons on adjacent carbon atoms. TMS (tetramethylsilane) is used as an internal reference standard because it produces a single sharp peak at 0 ppm, is inert, volatile, and non-toxic.

Advanced Chromatography Techniques

In addition to basic thin-layer chromatography (TLC) and paper chromatography where Rf values are calculated as the distance travelled by the solute divided by the distance travelled by the solvent front, modern analytical separation relies on column-based methods:

  • High-Performance Liquid Chromatography (HPLC): Uses a liquid mobile phase pumped under high pressure through a tightly packed column containing a solid stationary phase. Components separate based on their differing partition coefficients between the two phases.
  • Gas Chromatography (GC): Uses an inert carrier gas (such as helium or neon) as the mobile phase passing through a column containing a high-boiling liquid stationary phase coated on a solid support. Retention time is the time taken for a component to pass through the column from injection to detection.
  • Coupled Techniques: Both HPLC and GC can be directly coupled with mass spectrometry (HPLC-MS or GC-MS). This allows the chromatographic separation of complex mixtures followed immediately by mass spectral identification of each separated component, widely applied in forensic science, drug testing in sport, and environmental monitoring.

Worked Examples

  1. Worked Example: Calculating Rf Values
    Question: In a TLC experiment, the solvent front travels 8.4 cm from the baseline. A specific organic component travels 3.5 cm from the baseline. Calculate the Rf value for this component.
    Method: Use the formula Rf = (distance travelled by spot) ÷ (distance travelled by solvent front).
    Answer: Rf = 3.5 ÷ 8.4 = 0.42 (no units).
  2. Worked Example: Predicting 1H NMR Splitting
    Question: Predict the splitting pattern for the protons in the CH2 group of ethanol (CH3CH2OH), assuming standard high-resolution conditions.
    Method: Identify the number of non-equivalent protons (n) on the adjacent carbon atom. The adjacent carbon is the CH3 group, which has 3 protons. Apply the (n + 1) rule: 3 + 1 = 4.
    Answer: A quartet.

Common Student Mistakes and Corrections

  • Mistake: Confusing the action of Tollens reagent with Fehling solution on aliphatic aldehydes and aromatic aldehydes.
    Correction: Both Tollens reagent and Fehling solution give positive tests with aliphatic aldehydes (silver mirror and red precipitate respectively). However, aromatic aldehydes like benzaldehyde reduce Tollens reagent to form a silver mirror, but they do NOT reduce Fehling solution.
  • Mistake: Forgetting that carboxylic acids react with carbonates to release carbon dioxide gas, whereas alcohols do not.
    Correction: Always use sodium carbonate or sodium hydrogencarbonate solution to distinguish carboxylic acids from alcohols or phenols, as only carboxylic acids are strong enough acids to liberate carbon dioxide gas with effervescence.
  • Mistake: Misinterpreting peak splitting in proton NMR by counting protons on both sides indiscriminately.
    Correction: The (n + 1) rule only applies to protons on directly adjacent, non-equivalent carbon atoms. Protons separated by oxygen atoms or multiple bonds do not couple.

Exam-Style Questions and Answers

  1. Question: State why 1,1-dichloroethane and 1,2-dichloroethane have different numbers of peaks in their carbon-13 NMR spectra.
    Answer: 1,1-dichloroethane has two carbon environments (the CH3 carbon and the CHCl2 carbon), so it shows 2 peaks in its 13C NMR spectrum. 1,2-dichloroethane has only one carbon environment due to molecular symmetry (both carbons are bonded to a chlorine and a hydrogen and feel the same electronic environment), so it shows only 1 peak.
    Credit Point: Awarded for correctly identifying the carbon environments and linking them directly to the number of observed peaks.
  2. Question: Write an equation for the reaction of propanoyl chloride with concentrated ammonia, and name the organic product.
    Answer: CH3CH2COCl + 2NH3 → CH3CH2CONH2 + NH4Cl. The organic product is propanamide.
    Credit Point: Awarded for correct balanced stoichiometry (including the 2 moles of ammonia to react with the formed HCl) and correct naming of the amide.

Microbiology, Immunity and Forensics

Edexcel IAL Biology 9BI0 A2, topic 6. Every statement 6.1 to 6.20 is covered below, with its code in the heading. The topic links three big ideas: how microorganisms are grown and measured, how the body defends itself and why pathogens keep finding ways around those defences, and how DNA techniques are used to identify organisms and people.

6.1: Culturing microorganisms with aseptic technique

  • Aseptic technique keeps a culture pure: only the wanted microorganism grows. Sterilise media and equipment first, usually in an autoclave at 121 °C under pressure for about 15 minutes.
  • Work close to a Bunsen flame, flame the inoculating loop until red-hot before and after use, keep Petri dish lids mostly closed, and never pipette by mouth.
  • Incubate cultures inverted at a safe temperature, usually 25 °C for school work, so condensation does not drip onto the agar.

6.2: Measuring the growth of microorganisms

  • Direct cell counts: use a haemocytometer (counting chamber) under a microscope, counting cells in a known volume to get the number per cm³.
  • Viable counts by dilution plating: make a serial dilution, spread known volumes on agar, incubate, and count colonies on plates with about 30 to 300 colonies. Each colony is assumed to grow from one viable cell, so the count shows living cells only.
  • Mass methods: measure the dry mass of cells collected by centrifuging or filtering a known volume of culture.
  • Optical methods (turbidity): a colorimeter or spectrophotometer measures how much light the cloudy culture absorbs. Absorbance rises with cell density, so a calibration curve converts it to cell numbers.

6.3: The bacterial growth curve and the growth rate constant

  • Lag phase: cells adapt to the medium and synthesise enzymes; there is little or no division.
  • Exponential (log) phase: cells divide at a constant rate, so the population doubles each generation. N = N₀ × 2ⁿ, where n is the number of doublings.
  • Stationary phase: births equal deaths, because nutrients run short and waste builds up.
  • Death phase: deaths exceed births and the population falls.
  • Growth rate constant: in exponential growth N = N₀eᵏᵗ. So k = (ln N₂ − ln N₁) ÷ (t₂ − t₁). Plotting ln N against time gives a straight line whose gradient is k.

6.4: Core practical 13: growth of microorganisms in liquid culture

  • Inoculate a sterile liquid medium, take samples at regular intervals, and measure turbidity or cell count each time.
  • Plot the results to show the four phases of the curve, then calculate the exponential growth rate constant from the straight-line part.
  • Safe and ethical use: use only non-pathogenic strains, keep the culture closed, disinfect the bench, and autoclave all used material before disposal.

6.5: Structure of bacteria and viruses

  • Bacteria are cells with a cell wall (peptidoglycan), cell membrane, cytoplasm with ribosomes, and a circular DNA loop, often with plasmids. They have no nucleus.
  • Viruses are not cells. They have a nucleic acid core, either DNA or RNA, surrounded by a protein capsid. Some also have a lipid envelope taken from the host.
  • Comparisons: Ebola virus has single-stranded RNA and an envelope. Tobacco mosaic virus (TMV) has single-stranded RNA in a helical capsid, with no envelope. HIV has two RNA strands, reverse transcriptase and an envelope. Lambda phage, a virus of bacteria, has double-stranded DNA in a head with a tail and no envelope.
  • Lytic cycle: the virus takes over the host cell, makes new viruses, and the cell bursts (lyses) to release them.
  • Latency: the viral genome stays in the host cell without producing new viruses, and can become active later.

6.6: How Mycobacterium tuberculosis and HIV infect human cells

  • Tuberculosis: Mycobacterium tuberculosis is inhaled into the alveoli. Macrophages engulf it, but the bacterium survives inside them and multiplies. The body forms granulomas (tubercles) around the infection, and the lung tissue is destroyed. Symptoms include a persistent cough, fever, night sweats and weight loss. If untreated it can be fatal.
  • HIV: the virus binds to CD4 receptors and a co-receptor on helper T cells. Reverse transcriptase makes DNA from its RNA, which is inserted into the host genome. New viruses bud from the cell. The helper T cell population falls, so the immune system fails and opportunistic infections and cancers take hold (AIDS).

6.7: Routes of entry and barriers

  • Routes: inhalation (airborne droplets), ingestion (contaminated food and water), contact through broken skin or wounds, sexual contact, and vectors such as mosquitoes.
  • Barriers: intact skin (keratin, dryness, and the skin flora that competes with pathogens), stomach acid (pH about 2, which kills many ingested microbes), and gut flora that competes for space and nutrients. Mucus and cilia in the airways trap and move pathogens out.

6.8: Non-specific responses to infection

  • Inflammation: damaged cells release chemicals such as histamine, which dilate blood vessels and make them leaky. The area becomes red, hot and swollen, and white blood cells are recruited to the site.
  • Lysozyme: an enzyme in tears, saliva and mucus that breaks the peptidoglycan of bacterial cell walls.
  • Interferon: proteins released by virus-infected cells that warn neighbouring cells, which then resist viral replication. Interferon is antiviral, not a direct killer of the virus.
  • Phagocytosis: neutrophils and macrophages engulf a pathogen into a phagosome. Lysosomes fuse with it and enzymes digest the contents.

6.9: Antigens, antibodies, plasma cells, macrophages and antigen-presenting cells

  • An antigen is a foreign molecule, usually a protein or glycoprotein on a pathogen's surface, that triggers an immune response.
  • An antibody is a Y-shaped glycoprotein whose binding sites are complementary to one specific antigen. Antibodies mark pathogens for destruction and neutralise toxins.
  • Plasma cells are B cells that have been activated and that secrete antibodies in large amounts.
  • Macrophages and antigen-presenting cells engulf the pathogen, break it down, and display its antigens on their surface (on MHC proteins). This shows helper T cells what to respond to.

6.10: B cells and T cells

  • B effector (plasma) cells secrete antibodies. B memory cells survive for years and give a faster, larger response on the next exposure to the same antigen.
  • T helper cells (CD4) recognise the antigen on an antigen-presenting cell and release cytokines that activate B cells and T killer cells.
  • T killer (cytotoxic, CD8) cells bind to infected or abnormal cells and kill them, for example by releasing perforin.
  • T memory cells persist after the infection and respond quickly if the same pathogen returns.

6.11: Types of immunity

  • Natural active: the person is infected and makes their own antibodies and memory cells.
  • Natural passive: antibodies pass from mother to baby across the placenta or in breast milk. Protection is immediate but short-lived, and no memory cells are formed.
  • Artificial active: vaccination with an antigen, a weakened or dead pathogen, or a toxoid. The person makes antibodies and memory cells without becoming ill.
  • Artificial passive: injected antibodies, such as antivenom or antitoxin. Protection is immediate and short-lived, and the person's own immune system does not learn.

6.12: The evolutionary race between pathogens and hosts

  • Pathogens evolve evasion mechanisms. Antigenic variation changes the surface antigens: influenza and HIV mutate rapidly, so antibodies no longer fit.
  • Other evasion: hiding inside host cells (tuberculosis in macrophages, HIV in T cells), entering latency, and suppressing the immune response.
  • The host responds with new antibodies and T cells, so pathogens and hosts keep evolving against each other. This is the evolutionary race.

6.13: Bacteriostatic and bactericidal antibiotics

  • Bacteriostatic antibiotics stop bacteria growing and dividing, for example by blocking protein synthesis. The immune system then clears the infection.
  • Bactericidal antibiotics kill bacteria, for example penicillin, which stops cell wall synthesis so the cell bursts.
  • Antibiotics do not act on viruses, which use the host cell's machinery.

6.14: Core practical 14: the effect of antibiotics on bacteria

  • Spread a lawn of bacteria on agar, place antibiotic discs on it, and include a control disc with no antibiotic.
  • Incubate, then measure the diameter of each clear zone of inhibition. A larger zone means the bacteria are more sensitive.
  • Use aseptic technique and non-pathogenic strains, and autoclave the plates before disposal.

6.15: Hospital-acquired infections and codes of practice

  • Contributory causes include overuse of broad-spectrum antibiotics, which selects for resistant strains such as MRSA, poor hand hygiene, indwelling catheters, surgical wounds, and immunocompromised patients.
  • Codes of practice respond to these causes: prescribe antibiotics only when needed and according to guidelines, enforce hand hygiene, isolate infected patients, and clean equipment and wards.

6.16: Decomposition and the carbon cycle

  • Bacteria and fungi are the main decomposers. They secrete extracellular enzymes that digest complex organic matter such as cellulose and proteins, then absorb the simpler products.
  • Respiration by decomposers releases carbon dioxide, which returns carbon to the atmosphere for producers. Ammonium released from proteins feeds the nitrogen cycle.

6.17: The polymerase chain reaction (PCR)

  • Each cycle has three steps: denaturation at about 95 °C separates the strands, annealing at about 50 to 65 °C lets primers bind, and extension at about 72 °C is when Taq polymerase builds the new strands.
  • Taq polymerase comes from the heat-tolerant bacterium Thermus aquaticus, so it survives the high temperatures. Around 30 cycles give an exponential increase in the number of copies.

6.18: Gel electrophoresis of DNA fragments

  • DNA carries a negative charge from its phosphate groups, so it moves towards the positive electrode (anode) through a gel.
  • Smaller fragments move faster and further, so fragments separate by length. A DNA ladder of known sizes is run alongside for comparison, and the bands are stained to make them visible.

6.19: DNA profiling for identification and relatedness

  • DNA profiling compares short tandem repeats (STRs) or variable number tandem repeats (VNTRs). These regions vary in length between individuals, so each person gives a distinctive band pattern.
  • Uses include identifying suspects, establishing paternity, and comparing the banding patterns of plants or animals to show how closely related they are.

6.20: Estimating the time of death from forensic evidence

  • Body temperature: the body cools towards the surroundings, so the rate of cooling gives an estimate of time since death.
  • Muscle contraction: rigor mortis sets in over hours, peaks, then fades over about a day or two.
  • Decomposition and succession: bacterial decomposition gives a predictable sequence of changes. Forensic entomology uses the stage of blowfly larvae and the succession of insect species to estimate how long the body has been exposed.

Exam tip: time-of-death questions are estimates. Name the method, say what it measures, and state the limitation, for example that temperature depends on the environment.

title: Word Formation: Prefixes and Suffixes — Study Notes
content:
Many English words are built from a root with prefixes (added to the front) and suffixes (added to the end). Knowing common parts lets you understand new words and spell them correctly.

Prefixes

A prefix changes the meaning of the root.

  • un- means not: unbelievable, unclear
  • im-, in-, il-, ir- also mean not: impossible, incorrect, illegal, irregular
  • dis- means not or the reverse: disagree, dishonest
  • re- means again: rewrite, replay
  • pre- means before: preview, pre-war

Suffixes that change word class

Suffixes often change a word from one class to another.

  • Noun suffixes: -ness (happiness), -tion (decision), -ment (development), -ity (possibility)
  • Adjective suffixes: -ful (helpful), -less (careless), -able (readable), -ous (dangerous)
  • Adverb suffix: -ly (quickly)

Changing the form

Changing happy to happiness, or imagine to imagination, needs care with spelling. Some words change the final letter or drop an e before a suffix.

The suffix -less

-less means without: hopeless means without hope, careless means without care.

Practice strategy

Learn words in families. Write the noun, verb, adjective and adverb forms together, for example: decide, decision, decisive, decisively. This builds range and helps your writing.

title: Processor Fundamentals — Study Notes
content:
`# Processor Fundamentals

The FDE Cycle

  • Fetch: PC → MAR; read memory → MDR; instruction → CIR; PC increments
  • Decode: control unit interprets the opcode
  • Execute: ALU/registers act; results stored; PC may be overwritten (jumps)

Registers

RegisterRole
PCaddress of next instruction
MARaddress being accessed
MDRdata in transit
CIRcurrent instruction
ACCaccumulator results

Buses

  • Address bus: one-way, CPU → memory (width sets addressable space)
  • Data bus: two-way, carries instructions/data
  • Control bus: timing and command signals

Interrupts

Signals that pause the current program (I/O complete, timer, errors). The CPU saves context, runs the ISR, then resumes — enabling multitasking.

Assembly and Addressing

Immediate (#5), direct (address holds value), indirect (address points to address), indexed (base + offset — arrays), relative (PC + offset — jumps).

Example: LDD 100 loads from 100 (direct); LDI 100 loads from the address stored at 100 (indirect).

Exam tips: trace register contents step by step in trace tables; explain the stored program concept — instructions as data in memory.

title: Chemical Equilibria Quick Revision
content:
Chemical Equilibria Quick Revision

Chemistry — A2. Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH14, Topic 13, covers chemical equilibria, including equilibrium constants and the effects of changes in concentration, pressure, and temperature. The equilibrium constant tells you the position of that equilibrium at a given temperature.

  • The equilibrium constant Kc is expressed as [products]/[reactants] for homogeneous systems and Kp is expressed as partial pressures of products/partial pressures of reactants in atm.
  • Changes in temperature, pressure, or the presence of a catalyst affect the equilibrium composition, but the value of the equilibrium constant is not affected by changes in concentration or pressure or by the addition of a catalyst.
  • The effect of temperature on the equilibrium constant is explained using a change in the value of the equilibrium constant, with an increase in temperature increasing Kc for endothermic reactions and decreasing Kc for exothermic reactions.

Worked example

For the reaction N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3, Kc = [NH3]^2 / ([N2] * [H2]^3). If the equilibrium concentrations are [NH3] = 0.5 mol dm^-3, [N2] = 0.2 mol dm^-3, and [H2] = 0.3 mol dm^-3, then Kc = (0.5)^2 / (0.2 * (0.3)^3) = 0.5^2 / (0.2 * 0.027) = 0.25 / 0.0054 = 46.3.

Key points to remember

Students often forget that the equilibrium constant is not affected by changes in concentration or pressure, but is affected by changes in temperature. The value of the equilibrium constant can be used to predict the extent to which a reaction takes place.

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Heterogeneous Systems and Partial Pressures

When writing expressions for Kc or Kp for heterogeneous systems, pure solids and pure liquids are omitted because their concentrations remain essentially constant throughout the reaction. For example, in the thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate, CaCO3(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO2(g), the expression simplifies to Kp = p(CO2), where p(CO2) represents the equilibrium partial pressure of carbon dioxide measured in atmospheres.

Calculating Kp from Experimental Data

To calculate Kp, you must first determine the mole fraction of each gas present at equilibrium. The mole fraction is calculated by dividing the number of moles of a specific gas by the total number of moles of all gases in the mixture. The partial pressure of an individual gas is then found by multiplying its mole fraction by the total pressure of the system in atm. For instance, if a gas has a mole fraction of 0.25 and the total pressure is 4.0 atm, its partial pressure is 1.0 atm.

Thermodynamics and Equilibrium Constants

The link between entropy and the equilibrium constant is established through the equation Stotal = R ln(K), where R is the universal gas constant and ln(K) is the natural logarithm of the equilibrium constant. For an endothermic reaction, increasing the temperature causes Stotal to become more positive, leading to an increase in the value of the equilibrium constant. Conversely, for an exothermic reaction, increasing the temperature decreases the value of the equilibrium constant as total entropy change falls.

Advanced Worked Example

Consider the equilibrium reaction 2SO2(g) + O2(g) ⇌ 2SO3(g). In a 5.0 dm³ container, 2.0 moles of SO2 and 1.0 mole of O2 are allowed to reach equilibrium. At equilibrium, 1.6 moles of SO3 are present. Calculate Kc. First, find equilibrium moles: SO3 = 1.6, so moles of SO2 reacted = 1.6, leaving 2.0 − 1.6 = 0.4 moles of SO2. Moles of O2 reacted = 1.6 ÷ 2 = 0.8, leaving 1.0 − 0.8 = 0.2 moles of O2. Convert to concentrations by dividing by 5.0 dm³: [SO3] = 0.32 mol dm⁻³, [SO2] = 0.08 mol dm⁻³, [O2] = 0.04 mol dm⁻³. Substitute into Kc = [SO3]² / ([SO2]² * [O2]) = (0.32)² / ((0.08)² * 0.04) = 0.1024 / (0.0064 * 0.04) = 0.1024 / 0.000256 = 400 dm³ mol⁻¹.

Additional Examination Tips

Examiners frequently penalize students for omitting units or using incorrect units for equilibrium constants. Always derive the units by substituting mol dm⁻³ for concentrations and atm for partial pressures into the rearranged equilibrium expression. Furthermore, remember that a very large value of Kc or Kp (greater than 10¹⁰) indicates that the position of equilibrium lies heavily to the right, meaning the reaction goes almost to completion, whereas a very small value indicates that hardly any reaction takes place.

title: Simulation, Sensors and Real Data — Study Notes
content:
Simulation, Sensors and Real Data

Simulation and Modelling

A simulation is a program that models a real system to test scenarios safely and cheaply: weather models, traffic flows, epidemic spread. Models use abstractions — chosen variables and equations — with a time step. Advantages: no real-world risk, repeatable, faster or slower than real time. Limitations: only as good as the model; rare events may be missed.

Sensors and Signals

Sensors measure physical quantities: temperature (thermistor), light (LDR), pressure, humidity, sound. Most output analogue signals varying continuously; computers need digital values, so an ADC (analogue-to-digital converter) samples the signal. Resolution depends on bits — an 8-bit ADC gives 256 levels. A DAC converts digital output back to analogue for actuators or speakers.

Monitoring vs Control

  • Monitoring: sensors feed data to the computer, which only records, displays or raises alarms — no action taken on the environment.
  • Control: the computer acts via actuators (motors, valves, heaters) based on sensor input — the classic feedback loop.

Real-Time Considerations

Control systems are often real-time: late output can be wrong output. Sampling rate must exceed twice the highest signal frequency (Nyquist) to avoid aliasing.

Exam tips: distinguish monitoring from control with a named example; describe the role of ADC and DAC in a greenhouse system; explain one limitation of a simulation.

6.18: Gel electrophoresis of DNA fragments

  • DNA carries a negative charge from its phosphate groups, so it moves towards the positive electrode (anode) through a gel.
  • Smaller fragments move faster and further, so fragments separate by length. A DNA ladder of known sizes is run alongside for comparison, and the bands are stained to make them visible.

6.19: DNA profiling for identification and relatedness

  • DNA profiling compares short tandem repeats (STRs) or variable number tandem repeats (VNTRs). These regions vary in length between individuals, so each person gives a distinctive band pattern.
  • Uses include identifying suspects, establishing paternity, and comparing the banding patterns of plants or animals to show how closely related they are.

6.20: Estimating the time of death from forensic evidence

  • Body temperature: the body cools towards the surroundings, so the rate of cooling gives an estimate of time since death.
  • Muscle contraction: rigor mortis sets in over hours, peaks, then fades over about a day or two.
  • Decomposition and succession: bacterial decomposition gives a predictable sequence of changes. Forensic entomology uses the stage of blowfly larvae and the succession of insect species to estimate how long the body has been exposed.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Growth rate, 6.3 applied: a culture grows from 2.0 × 10⁴ cells cm⁻³ at 2 hours to 1.6 × 10⁵ at 5 hours. N₂ ÷ N₁ = 8 = 2³, so three doublings in three hours. k = (ln 1.6 × 10⁵ − ln 2.0 × 10⁴) ÷ 3 = ln 8 ÷ 3 = 0.69 per hour. The doubling time is ln 2 ÷ k = 1.0 hour. Check the answer against the doubling count before you write it down.
  • Viable count, 6.2 applied: 150 colonies grow from 0.1 cm³ of a 10⁻⁵ dilution. That is 150 ÷ 0.1 = 1500 colonies per cm³ in the diluted sample, and multiplying by the dilution factor gives 1.5 × 10⁸ viable cells per cm³. A haemocytometer count would include dead cells, so the two methods can give different numbers from the same culture. Name which one you are using.
  • Log phase, 6.3 applied: plotting ln N against time gives a straight line only during exponential growth. A curve that bends is a sign that the lag, stationary or death phase has been included by mistake. Use only the straight section to find k.
  • Primary and secondary immune response, 6.10 and 6.12 applied: the first exposure has a lag of several days before antibodies peak at a lower level. A second exposure gives a faster, larger and longer-lasting response, because memory cells are already present. Use all three words, faster, larger and longer, to earn the full mark.
  • Antigen presentation, 6.9 applied: helper T cells (CD4) recognise antigen presented on MHC class II proteins, and killer T cells (CD8) recognise it on MHC class I, as on infected body cells. Naming the MHC class shows you understand which cell carries the antigen.
  • Antibiotic action, 6.13 applied: penicillin blocks the cross-linking of peptidoglycan in the cell wall, so a growing cell bursts. An antibiotic that targets a process human cells do not use, such as the bacterial ribosome, is more selective. Resistance arises by chance mutation and is selected for by the antibiotic, so the explanation must say the mutation was already present and survived.
  • PCR, 6.17 applied: after n cycles one DNA molecule has become 2ⁿ molecules. After 30 cycles that is 2³⁰, about 1.07 × 10⁹ copies. This is why a very small sample is enough, and why contamination with foreign DNA is a serious error.
  • Gel electrophoresis, 6.18 applied: the distance moved is roughly linear with the logarithm of the fragment length. Use a DNA ladder to plot log size against distance, then read the unknown band from that graph rather than from the ladder bands by eye.
  • Forensic estimates, 6.20 applied: a time-of-death answer is always a range. Temperature cooling assumes a stable environment, and a hot or wet site or a body wrapped in clothing changes the rate. Say which factor is most uncertain and why.

Exam tip: time-of-death questions are estimates. Name the method, say what it measures, and state the limitation, for example that temperature depends on the environment.

The four types of immunity, compared

TypeHow it is acquiredAntibodies made by the personDuration
Natural activeInfection with the pathogenYesLong, because memory cells remain
Natural passiveAntibodies cross the placenta or arrive in colostrumNoShort, until the transferred antibodies are broken down
Artificial activeVaccination with antigen or an attenuated pathogenYesLong, and boosters raise the secondary response
Artificial passiveInjection of antibodies from another source, such as an antiserumNoShort, but immediate

Typical mistakes

  • Confusing aseptic technique with sterilisation. Apparatus and medium are sterilised before use; aseptic technique is how the worker keeps them sterile while handling them, by flaming the loop, passing the neck of the bottle through the flame and minimising the time the plate is open.
  • Forgetting the dilution factor in a viable count. A count on a diluted sample must be multiplied by the dilution factor and divided by the volume plated, or the answer is out by orders of magnitude. Quote the units as cells per cm cubed.
  • Reading the growth curve without the phase names. Lag phase: cells adapt and synthesise enzymes, so numbers rise slowly. Exponential phase: numbers double at a constant rate. Stationary: growth equals death as nutrients run low and waste builds. Death: death exceeds growth.
  • Saying antibiotics are bactericidal when they are bacteriostatic. Bactericidal antibiotics kill the bacteria; bacteriostatic ones stop them dividing, so the immune system finishes the job. Penicillin is bactericidal because it blocks the cross-linking of peptidoglycan, so growing cells burst.
  • Giving B and T cells the same job. B effector cells make and secrete antibodies and B memory cells make the secondary response faster. T helper cells release cytokines that activate B cells and macrophages, T killer cells destroy infected cells, and T memory cells persist.
  • Describing PCR without its requirements. PCR needs a DNA template, primers, free nucleotides, a heat-stable DNA polymerase and a buffer, with repeated cycles of denaturation, annealing and extension. Each cycle doubles the DNA, so 30 cycles give 2 to the power 30 copies.
  • Forgetting which electrode DNA moves towards. DNA is negatively charged because of its phosphate groups, so in gel electrophoresis it moves towards the positive electrode, and shorter fragments move further.
  • Giving a single figure for time of death. It is an estimate from several methods, each with a limitation: body temperature depends on the environment, decomposition depends on conditions, and succession depends on the species available.

Exam-style questions

  1. A 0.1 cm cubed sample of a 10 to the power minus 4 dilution produces 64 colonies. Calculate the number of viable cells in the original culture. Answer: 64 colonies in 0.1 cm cubed is 640 cells per cm cubed in the diluted sample; multiply by the dilution factor 10 000, giving 6.4 times 10 to the power 6 viable cells per cm cubed.
  2. Explain why a viable count can be lower than a total count from a haemocytometer. Answer: a viable count only counts cells that can divide and form a colony, so dead cells and cells that are alive but not dividing are missed; a haemocytometer counts all cells, living and dead, present in the sample.
  3. Describe how you would investigate the effect of different antibiotics on a bacterial culture, naming the variables. Answer: inoculate a lawn of the bacterium evenly over an agar plate using a sterile spreader, place discs soaked in equal volumes of different antibiotic solutions on the surface, incubate at a controlled temperature for a fixed time, and measure the diameter of the clear zone around each disc. Controls: a disc soaked in sterile water, and the same species, incubation temperature and time for every plate. A larger zone means greater inhibition, and repeats give a mean.
  4. Explain how a vaccine produces immunity and why a booster is sometimes needed. Answer: the vaccine presents antigens, which are taken up by antigen-presenting cells; helper T cells activate the specific B cell carrying a matching receptor; the B cell divides into effector cells that secrete antibodies and memory cells that persist. A booster raises the antibody level again through the quicker, larger secondary response, and may be needed when the first dose did not produce enough memory cells or when the pathogen varies.
  5. Explain how HIV and Mycobacterium tuberculosis cause disease. Answer: HIV binds the CD4 receptor on helper T cells, and the virus enters and replicates, eventually destroying the cells; the loss of helper T cells disables the immune response, so opportunistic infections cause AIDS. Mycobacterium tuberculosis is engulfed by macrophages but survives inside them, and the inflammatory response forms tubercles that damage the lung tissue, causing coughing and reduced gas exchange.
  6. Explain how gel electrophoresis separates DNA fragments and what a DNA profile shows. Answer: fragments are cut with restriction enzymes and loaded into a gel; an electric field moves the negatively charged DNA towards the positive electrode, and shorter fragments travel further, so the fragments separate by length. A profile from several loci is a pattern that can identify an individual or show relatedness, because the pattern is inherited.
  7. Explain how PCR amplifies DNA and why contamination is a problem. Answer: the mixture is heated to denature the double helix, cooled so primers anneal to the target sequences, then warmed so DNA polymerase extends the primers; each cycle doubles the number of target molecules. A single foreign DNA molecule can also be amplified, so contamination makes the sample unusable.

title: Exam technique: Web Technologies
content:
### What earns the marks
For full marks on 5.1 and 5.2 questions, explain and describe the structure and function of web technologies, including HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. Use command words like explain, describe, and state to earn marks. For example, explaining how the DOM is used to add interactivity to a web page can earn full marks. Justify and show that commands may require working or a reason to be shown.
### Traps
Error: writing HTML tags without correct closing pairs. Correction: always write tags with correct closing pairs. Error: not separating structure, presentation, and behaviour in answers. Correction: separate HTML, CSS, and JavaScript in answers. Error: not explaining DOM operations correctly. Correction: explain DOM operations as 'find element by id ... then change property'.
### Memory hooks
Use the mnemonic 'HTML is the structure, CSS is the style, and JavaScript is the action' to remember the separation of web technologies. To sanity-check an answer, ask yourself 'is this a structure, presentation, or behaviour question?'. Write down the layers of a web page (structure, presentation, behaviour) before starting an answer.
### Timing
Budget around 30-40 minutes for this topic's share of the paper. This topic usually accounts for 2-3 questions, each worth around 10-15 marks.

title: Cell Structure, Reproduction and Development - Edexcel IAL AS-Level Biology Revision Notes
content:
Cell Structure, Reproduction and Development - Edexcel IAL AS-Level Biology Revision Notes

This revision note covers Edexcel International AS-Level Biology WBI12 Topic 3, examining the ultrastructure of eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells, microscopy, the cell cycle, mitosis, meiosis, gamete specialisation, fertilisation, stem cells, gene expression, epigenetics, inheritance, and variation.

Cell Ultrastructure and Organisation

All living organisms are made of cells, sharing common features such as a plasma membrane, cytoplasm, and genetic material.
