This note shows why that happens, writes out every solution line by line, and finishes with the region-shading questions that distinguish Paper 4.

What an inequality says

The four inequality symbols extend the equals sign: < (strictly less than), > (strictly greater than), ⩽ (less than or equal to), ⩾ (greater than or equal to). A solution is a set of values, drawn on a number line with a hollow circle for strict inequalities (the endpoint is excluded) and a solid circle for inclusive ones (the endpoint is included).

StatementMeaningNumber line
x > 3Every value greater than 3, not including 3Hollow circle at 3, arrow to the right
x ⩽ −1Every value up to and including −1Solid circle at −1, arrow to the left
2 ⩽ x < 5Values from 2 up to, but not including, 5Solid circle at 2, hollow at 5, line between

Why the sign flips when multiplying by a negative. Start with the true statement 3 < 5. Multiply both sides by −2 without thinking: −6 < −10 is false, because −10 is further left than −6. The correct statement is −6 > −10. Multiplying by a negative mirrors the number line, which reverses order — so the inequality symbol must reverse too. That single rule causes more lost marks than any other in this topic.

Solving linear inequalities

Use the equation methods unchanged, and remember the one reversal rule:

Solve:  5x - 7 > 3x + 1        (give the solution as an inequality)

5x - 3x > 1 + 7               [add 7 to both sides, subtract 3x from both sides]
2x > 8
x > 4                         [divide by +2: the sign does not reverse]
Solve:  3 - 2x ⩽ 11

-2x ⩽ 11 - 3                  [subtract 3 from both sides]
-2x ⩽ 8
x ⩾ -4                        [divide by -2: the sign REVERSES from ⩽ to ⩾]

The check is direct: x = −4 gives 3 − 2(−4) = 11 ⩽ 11 ✓, and x = 0 gives 3 ⩽ 11 ✓ while x = −5 gives 13 ⩽ 11 ✗ — so the boundary and direction are right.

Solve and list the integer solutions:  2 < (5x - 1)/3 ⩽ 8

Multiply every part by 3:
6 < 5x - 1 ⩽ 24
7 < 5x ⩽ 25                   [add 1 to every part]
7/5 < x ⩽ 5                   [divide every part by +5]

The integers are 2, 3, 4 and 5.

Compound inequalities (a value trapped between two bounds) are solved in one line per operation across all three parts — exactly like a three-pan balance.

Inequalities from word problems

Many questions ask for the greatest or least integer satisfying a condition. Translate carefully: at least means ⩾, at most means ⩽, more than means >, within or no more than means ⩽.

A cinema ticket costs £8. A group has £100 and must keep at least £12 for travel.
How many tickets can they buy?

Let n be the number of tickets:  8n + 12 ⩽ 100
8n ⩽ 88
n ⩽ 11

They can buy at most 11 tickets.

The final answer is a whole number in context: a group cannot buy a fraction of a ticket, so the solution set is the integers up to 11.

Regions in the coordinate plane (Extended)

The line y = mx + c divides the plane into two half-planes: points above it satisfy y > mx + c and points below it satisfy y < mx + c. A region question asks you to shade the set of points satisfying several inequalities at once.

  • Draw the boundary line y = mx + c as a solid line when the inequality includes equality (⩽ or ⩾), and as a dashed line when it is strict (< or >).
  • Test one point not on the line — the origin (0, 0) is easiest when the line misses it. Substitute into the inequality; if it is true, shade the side containing the test point.
  • Shade the side that satisfies every inequality; the answer region is the overlap, and the question often asks for the coordinates of a point inside it.
Shade the region satisfying:  y ⩽ 2x + 1,  y > -x + 2,  x ⩾ 0

Line 1: y = 2x + 1, solid. Test (0, 0): 0 ⩽ 1 true, so shade below-left of this line.
Line 2: y = -x + 2, dashed. Test (0, 0): 0 > 2 false, so shade the side away from the origin.
Line 3: x = 0 (the y-axis), solid, shade to the right.

The solution region is the triangle-like area satisfying all three, e.g. the point (2, 2):
2 ⩽ 5 ✓, 2 > 0 ✓, 2 ⩾ 0 ✓.

Describing a region in words is the reverse skill: read the boundary lines, note whether each is dashed or solid, and translate the shaded side back into an inequality.

Maximum and minimum values over a region (Extended)

Region questions often finish by asking for the largest or smallest value of an expression such as x + 2y for points inside the shaded region. A linear expression grows steadily in one direction across the plane, so over a region bounded by straight lines its extreme values always sit at the corners. The method is therefore exact: find the coordinates of every vertex of the region, substitute each pair into the expression, and pick the largest or smallest result. Do not stop at the corner that looks likely — an untested corner is the usual place a mark is lost.

Worked example: inequality with a parameter

Find the set of values of k for which the equation x² + kx + 9 = 0 has two distinct real roots.

Two distinct real roots require a positive discriminant:  b² - 4ac > 0
Here a = 1, b = k, c = 9:
k² - 36 > 0
k² > 36
k > 6  or  k < -6

This is an inequality inside a quadratic-context question — exactly the blend of topics Paper 4 rewards. If the requirement had been at least one real root, the inequality would be k² ⩾ 36, giving k ⩾ 6 or k ⩽ −6.

Corner points in practice. Take the region x ⩾ 0, y ⩾ 0, x + y ⩽ 6 and y ⩽ x + 2. Its vertices are where the boundary lines meet:

x = 0 with y = 0            gives (0, 0)
y = 0 with x + y = 6        gives (6, 0)
x = 0 with y = x + 2        gives (0, 2)
x + y = 6 with y = x + 2    gives x + (x + 2) = 6, so 2x = 4, x = 2 and y = 4, the corner (2, 4)

Evaluate P = x + 2y at each corner:
(0, 0): P = 0     (6, 0): P = 6     (0, 2): P = 4     (2, 4): P = 10

Maximum P = 10 at (2, 4);  minimum P = 0 at (0, 0).

The minimum sits at the origin only because this region includes it; a region bounded away from the origin puts its minimum at one of the other corners. Substitute every vertex before choosing.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Not reversing the inequality sign after multiplying or dividing by a negative number. −2x < 8 means x > −4.
  • Reversing the sign when multiplying by a positive number, or reversing when subtracting — only multiplication and division by negatives reverse it.
  • Hollow versus solid circles: < and > exclude the endpoint; ⩽ and ⩾ include it. Writing x > 4 when x = 4 works is a boundary error.
  • Flipping the inequality direction mid-solution so the final statement faces the wrong way.
  • Forgetting to reverse in a compound inequality: every part flips when the whole chain is multiplied by a negative.
  • In region questions, drawing a solid boundary for a strict inequality (or a dashed one for ⩽), or shading the wrong side because no test point was used.
  • Reporting a decimal when the question asks for integers: n ⩽ 11.25 means the largest integer is 11, not 11.25.
  • Treating ⩽ as < in a word problem: at most 5 includes 5.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 2, 3 marks). Solve 7 − 3x > 1 and show your solution on a number line.

Answer: −3x > −6, so x < 2 (the sign reverses). Number line: hollow circle at 2, shading to the left.

Question 2 (Paper 2, 3 marks). Solve 2 ⩽ 3x + 5 < 14 and list the integer solutions.

Answer: Subtract 5 throughout: −3 ⩽ 3x < 9. Divide by 3: −1 ⩽ x < 3. The integers are −1, 0, 1, 2.

Question 3 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Find the values of x for which x² − 5x + 4 < 0.

Answer: Factorise: (x − 1)(x − 4) < 0. The quadratic is negative between its roots, so 1 < x < 4. (Test x = 2: 4 − 10 + 4 = −2 < 0 ✓; test x = 0: 4 > 0 ✗.)

Question 4 (Paper 4, 5 marks). Shade the region defined by y > x − 1, y ⩽ 3 and x ⩾ 0, and write down the coordinates of one point in the region.

Answer: Draw y = x − 1 dashed (strict), y = 3 solid and x = 0 solid. The origin test for y > x − 1 gives 0 > −1, true, so shade above the dashed line; y ⩽ 3 shades below the horizontal line; x ⩾ 0 shades right of the y-axis. The overlap is a triangle with vertices (0, 3), (4, 3) and (0, −1); the point (1, 1) lies inside: 1 > 0 ✓, 1 ⩽ 3 ✓, 1 ⩾ 0 ✓.

Question 5 (Paper 4, 4 marks). A rectangle has a perimeter of at most 60 cm and a length of (x + 4) cm. Write an inequality for its width w and find w when x = 8.

Answer: 2[(x + 4) + w] ⩽ 60, so (x + 4) + w ⩽ 30 and w ⩽ 26 − x. With x = 8: w ⩽ 18 cm, and the width must also be positive, so 0 < w ⩽ 18.

Question 6 (Paper 2, 3 marks). The solutions of 5x + a ⩾ 0 include x = −2. Find the smallest integer value of a.

Answer: Substituting x = −2: −10 + a ⩾ 0, so a ⩾ 10. The smallest integer value is 10.

With equations and inequalities mastered, the next stage of algebra is sequences and functions.

Equations and symbols

An inequality is solved like an equation with one extra rule, and the region questions are all the same line tested against a point. This sheet is the boundary lines and the sign rule — the two places marks are lost.

y = mx + c Key: y and x = the coordinates of a point on the plane (no units); m = the gradient; c = the y-intercept. Drawn solid when the inequality includes equality (⩽ or ⩾) and dashed when it is strict (< or >) — the line style is the first mark of a region question.

y = 2x + 1 Key: the boundary line of y ⩽ 2x + 1, drawn solid because equality is included. Test the origin (0, 0): 0 ⩽ 1 is true, so shade the side containing the origin — testing, never guessing, is what earns the shading mark.

y = -x + 2 Key: the boundary line of y > −x + 2, drawn dashed because the inequality is strict, so points on the line are excluded. Here (0, 0) gives 0 > 2, false, so the region is the side away from the origin.

x = 0 (the y-axis) Key: the boundary of x ⩾ 0; a vertical line has no gradient to quote, which is why the general form breaks down and the line is named instead. Shade to the right of it.

x + y = 6 Key: a boundary written in implicit form; the intercepts are (6, 0) and (0, 6). With y = x + 2 it meets at x + (x + 2) = 6, so x = 2 and y = 4 — corner (2, 4), where the maximum of a linear expression over that region always sits.

x² + kx + 9 = 0 Key: x = the variable; k = the unknown coefficient; the condition "two distinct real roots" becomes b² − 4ac > 0 with a = 1, b = k, c = 9, so k² > 36 and k > 6 or k < −6. The result is a pair of rays, not an interval between them — writing 6 < k < −6 is the standard wrong answer.

The sign rule, in one table

OperationEffect on the sign
Add or subtract the same valueUnchanged
Multiply or divide by a positive numberUnchanged
Multiply or divide by a negative numberReverses: < becomes >, ⩽ becomes ⩾
Reverse the two sidesReverses: 3 < 5 is the same statement as 5 > 3

Traps specific to the algebra

  • Forgetting to reverse when dividing by a negative: −2x ⩽ 8 gives x ⩾ −4.
  • Reversing when subtracting, which is not a reversal at all.
  • Hollow versus solid endpoints: x = 4 does not satisfy x > 4.
  • Reporting 11.25 when the question asks for the greatest integer, which is 11.
  • Shading every inequality's own side instead of their overlap.

### What earns the marks
For phase, path difference converted to degrees earns the method mark. For patterns, constructive versus destructive located earns each mark. For stationary waves, nodes and antinodes described earn the explanation marks.
### Traps
Error: half lambda called in phase. Correction: half lambda is antiphase. Error: nodes credited with motion. Correction: nodes stay at zero. Error: diffraction condition forgotten. Correction: gap near lambda spreads most.

title:
Cell Structure, Reproduction and Development — AS Level Biology

This revision note belongs to the Edexcel International Advanced Subsidiary (IAS) Biology specification, WBI12 Unit 1, Topic 3 Cell Structure, Reproduction and Development. It covers the cell as the unit of life, eukaryotic and prokaryotic ultrastructure, microscopy and measurement, the cell cycle and mitosis, meiosis and genetic variation, gametes and fertilisation in mammals and flowering plants, stem cells, and the genetic control of development through gene expression, epigenetics and inheritance. Every statement below the topic owns is covered in its own section or paragraph.

1. Cells as the units of life and the levels of organisation

All living organisms are made of cells, and all cells share some common features: a plasma membrane (cell surface membrane) enclosing the cell, cytoplasm in which most chemical reactions occur, and ribosomes for protein synthesis. Differences between cell types are explained from these common features — for example the presence or absence of a cell wall, a nucleus, or membrane-bound organelles decides what a cell can do. In multicellular organisms, cells are organised into tissues, tissues into organs, and organs into organ systems, each level carrying out a particular function. A tissue is a group of similar cells working together; an organ is made of several tissues with a combined function; an organ system is a group of organs whose functions are linked, such as the digestive system. Understanding this hierarchy matters because a structure at one level is shaped by the level below it — the properties of a tissue follow from the cells it contains.

2. Eukaryotic cell ultrastructure and the functions of the organelles

Eukaryotic cells have a membrane-bound nucleus that contains the chromosomes, and a range of membrane-bound organelles, each with a distinct function. The plasma membrane (cell surface membrane) is a phospholipid bilayer with proteins embedded in it, controlling what enters and leaves the cell. The nucleus is surrounded by a double nuclear envelope with nuclear pores, and contains the cell's DNA; the nucleolus inside the nucleus is the site of ribosome assembly. Ribosomes, made of a large and a small subunit, are the sites of protein synthesis and occur free in the cytoplasm or attached to the rough endoplasmic reticulum. The rough endoplasmic reticulum (rER) is a stack of membrane-bound sacs studded with ribosomes; it synthesises proteins and passes them on in vesicles. The smooth endoplasmic reticulum (sER) lacks ribosomes and synthesises lipids and carbohydrates. Mitochondria have a double membrane, the inner one folded into cristae to increase surface area, and a matrix that contains the enzymes for aerobic respiration; they supply ATP. Centrioles are paired microtubule cylinders that organise the spindle fibres during nuclear division. Lysosomes are membrane-bound sacs containing hydrolytic enzymes that digest worn-out cell components and pathogens. The Golgi apparatus modifies, sorts and packages proteins into vesicles for secretion or for delivery to other parts of the cell; it is also involved in the formation of extracellular enzymes. The cytoskeleton of microtubules and microfilaments maintains cell shape, holds organelles in place and enables movement within the cell.

3. Prokaryotic cell ultrastructure and how to tell the two apart

Prokaryotic cells are much smaller than eukaryotic cells and lack a membrane-bound nucleus. Their genetic material is a single, circular DNA molecule that lies free in the cytoplasm, not associated with histones. The cell wall is made of peptidoglycan and gives rigidity and shape. Many prokaryotes have a protective capsule outside the cell wall. Plasmids are small circles of DNA separate from the main chromosome; they can be transferred between cells and often carry genes for antibiotic resistance. Flagella — rigid helical tails that rotate — give motility in some prokaryotes, and pili help cells attach to surfaces and to each other and mediate conjugation. Prokaryotic ribosomes are 70S, smaller than the 80S ribosomes of eukaryotes. A bacterium therefore shows, in EM images: cell wall, capsule, plasma membrane, circular DNA free in the cytoplasm, 70S ribosomes, plasmids, and, where present, flagella and pili — and none of the membrane-bound organelles found in a eukaryotic cell.

4. Seeing the ultrastructure: light and electron microscopy

A light microscope uses visible light passed through a specimen; its maximum useful magnification is around ×1500 and its resolution is about 0.2 µm, limited by the wavelength of light. An electron microscope uses a beam of electrons, giving far higher resolution and magnification; transmission electron microscopes (TEM) show the internal ultrastructure of thin sections, and scanning electron microscopes (SEM) show the surface detail of a specimen. Staining is essential in light microscopy because most cells are transparent — stains such as methylene blue for animal cells or iodine solution for starch make structures visible and show up nuclei, starch grains and cell walls. The electron microscope can show the organelles listed in 3.3 — nucleus, nucleolus, ribosomes, rER, sER, mitochondria, centrioles, lysosomes, Golgi apparatus — and, in prokaryotes, the cell wall, capsule, plasma membrane, circular DNA, 70S ribosomes, flagella and pili, so that students can recognise the organelles from electron micrographs. In a light microscope the total magnification equals eyepiece magnification × objective magnification; a graticule (eye-piece graticule) fitted with a stage micrometer lets you calibrate it so real sizes can be measured, and specimens can be drawn to scale from the microscope.

5. Core Practical 5 — observing and drawing animal cells

Use a light microscope to make observations and labelled drawings of suitable animal cells, for example cheek epithelial cells. The steps are: sterilise by wiping the mouth, smear a thin layer of cells onto a slide, stain with methylene blue, lower a coverslip at an angle to avoid air bubbles, and observe under the microscope. Draw what you see with the correct relative sizes of nucleus, cytoplasm and cell membrane, label the parts, and add a title and magnification. Core Practical 5 also develops the skill of using a graticule with a microscope to make measurements and understand the concept of scale — the graticule is calibrated against a stage micrometer at each objective, so the real size of a cell or organelle can be calculated from the number of graticule divisions it spans.

6. Cell division: mitosis, the cell cycle and genetic variation by meiosis

Mitosis produces genetically identical daughter cells for growth and asexual reproduction and is one part of the cell cycle, which is the regular sequence of events in a dividing cell: interphase (during which the cell grows, and DNA is replicated — G1, S and G2), mitosis and cytokinesis. Mitosis itself has stages — prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase — in which the copied chromosomes line up on the equator, separate and move to opposite poles, and new nuclei form, followed by division of the cytoplasm. A useful calculation is the mitotic index, the proportion of cells in a sample that are dividing: mitotic index = number of cells undergoing mitosis ÷ total number of cells in the field of view. This is used in Core Practical 6, the root tip squash, to see and count the stages of mitosis. Meiosis, by contrast, produces genetically non-identical gametes and is the source of variation: in metaphase I the homologous chromosomes line up as pairs and assort independently (independent assortment), and in prophase I crossing over exchanges alleles between the chromatids of a homologous pair, so that gametes carry new combinations of alleles. A locus is the fixed position of a gene on a chromosome; genes on the same chromosome are linked and tend to be inherited together, so linked genes do not assort independently.

7. Gametes, fertilisation in mammals and fertilisation in flowering plants

Mammalian gametes are specialised for their function. Sperm are small and motile, with a haploid nucleus, a lot of mitochondria to power the flagellum, and an acrosome at the head containing enzymes that digest a path through the egg's outer layers. Egg cells are larger, with cytoplasm containing food reserves; the zona pellucida is a glycoprotein layer around the egg that sperm must penetrate. Fertilisation in mammals begins when the acrosome reaction releases enzymes that digest the zona pellucida, then the cortical reaction releases cortical granules into the space around the egg, hardening the zona pellucida and preventing more than one sperm from entering; finally the sperm and egg nuclei fuse, restoring the diploid number. In flowering plants, fertilisation begins with pollination and the growth of a pollen tube from the pollen grain down through the style to the embryo sac; two male nuclei travel down the tube, one fertilising the egg to form the zygote (which develops into the embryo) and one fusing with the two polar nuclei to form the triploid endosperm that will feed the developing seed — double fertilisation, unique to flowering plants.

8. Stem cells and what society does with them

A stem cell is an undifferentiated cell that can divide to produce more stem cells and differentiated cells. Totipotent stem cells can develop into any cell type and form a complete organism; the zygote and the cells of the early embryo up to the 16-cell morula are totipotent. Pluripotent stem cells can give rise to many, but not all, cell types; cells of the blastocyst are pluripotent, and in plants many meristem cells are totipotent, which is why a whole plant can be grown from a single cell or tissue. Stem cells are used medically — for example in bone marrow transplants for leukaemia — and their use raises ethical and social questions: the source of embryonic stem cells, the balance of benefit against risk, and decisions made by individuals, committees and governments all draw on scientific knowledge but also on values. Students should be able to discuss these issues from a range of ethical viewpoints.

9. Gene expression: how one gene makes more than one protein and how proteins control cells

Cells become specialised through differential gene expression — different genes are switched on or off in different cells, producing active mRNA and then proteins that control cell processes or determine cell structure. One gene can give rise to more than one protein through post-transcriptional changes to messenger RNA (mRNA) such as alternative splicing, in which the same primary transcript is spliced in different ways to make different mRNAs and therefore different polypeptides. Transcription factors switch genes on or off by binding to DNA and promoting or blocking transcription, so they control which proteins a cell makes. Epigenetic modification — including DNA methylation and histone modification — alters the activation of certain genes without changing the DNA sequence itself, and these modifications can be passed on following cell division, so that a cell's gene activity can be inherited by its daughter cells and, in some cases, across generations.

10. Inheritance: alleles, genotypes, phenotypes and how they vary

A gene is a sequence of bases on a DNA molecule that codes for a sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide. The allele is one of the different forms of a gene; the genotype is the alleles an organism has; the phenotype is the observable feature that results from the genotype and the environment. Recessive alleles only show in the phenotype when homozygous; dominant alleles show even in the heterozygous state; codominance is when both alleles in the heterozygote contribute to the phenotype. Sex linkage is the inheritance of a gene carried on the X chromosome, such as red-green colour blindness in humans, which appears more often in males because they have only one X chromosome and so express a recessive allele on it. Some phenotypes are affected by multiple alleles for the same gene, and others by polygenic inheritance, where many genes each contribute a small effect, giving rise to continuous variation in the phenotype — height in humans is a classic example. The environment can also affect phenotype, so that a feature is the result of an interaction between genotype and environment rather than genotype alone.

11. Mutations: how they arise and what they can do

Errors in DNA replication can give rise to mutations — changes to the base sequence of DNA. A substitution replaces one base with another and may change one amino acid or none (because the code is degenerate); an insertion adds one or more bases, and a deletion removes one or more, and these can cause a frameshift that changes every amino acid after the mutation and often produces a non-functional protein. Mutations are the source of new alleles, and some mutations give rise to cancer or genetic disorders, while many have no observable effect. Cystic fibrosis is a genetic disorder caused by a recessive allele; the faulty allele affects chloride ion channels, so the functioning of the gaseous exchange, digestive and reproductive systems is impaired — thick mucus blocks the airways, the pancreas duct is blocked so digestion is affected, and fertility in males is reduced because the vas deferens is absent or blocked.

12. Genetic screening and the questions it raises

Genetic screening can identify carriers of a recessive allele, and prenatal testing — including amniocentesis (sampling the fluid around the embryo) and chorionic villus sampling (taking a sample of placental tissue) — can check an embryo or fetus for genetic disorders. Pre-implantation genetic diagnosis (PGD) is used during IVF to test embryos before implantation so that only unaffected embryos are used. These techniques raise ethical and social questions: the reliability and risk of the test, the right to know or not to know, who decides what is a disorder worth preventing, the cost and access to treatment, and the risk of starting down a path toward selecting traits rather than preventing disease. Students should be able to identify and discuss these issues from religious, moral and social viewpoints.

13. How to use this note and what to revise next

Use these notes by working section by section through the topic, checking that you can name every organelle, state its function, and recognise it in an electron micrograph. Practise the calculations — magnification, real size from image size and magnification, mitotic index, and the index of diversity and the calculations that appear in the genetics sections. Revise by drawing and labelling an animal cell and a plant cell from memory, annotating each organelle with its function, then testing yourself on meiosis and on how variation arises. After this topic, revise Topic 4 Plant structure, biodiversity and conservation, and Topic 5 Energy flow, ecosystems and the environment, because the genetics here underpins inheritance in those later topics.

6. Cell division: mitosis, the cell cycle and genetic variation by meiosis

Mitosis produces genetically identical daughter cells for growth and asexual reproduction and is one part of the cell cycle, which is the regular sequence of events in a dividing cell: interphase (during which the cell grows, and DNA is replicated — G1, S and G2), mitosis and cytokinesis. Mitosis itself has stages — prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase — in which the copied chromosomes line up on the equator, separate and move to opposite poles, and new nuclei form, followed by division of the cytoplasm. A useful calculation is the mitotic index, the proportion of cells in a sample that are dividing: mitotic index = number of cells undergoing mitosis ÷ total number of cells in the field of view. This is used in Core Practical 6, the root tip squash, to see and count the stages of mitosis. Meiosis, by contrast, produces genetically non-identical gametes and is the source of variation: in metaphase I the homologous chromosomes line up as pairs and assort independently (independent assortment), and in prophase I crossing over exchanges alleles between the chromatids of a homologous pair, so that gametes carry new combinations of alleles. A locus is the fixed position of a gene on a chromosome; genes on the same chromosome are linked and tend to be inherited together, so linked genes do not assort independently.

7. Gametes, fertilisation in mammals and fertilisation in flowering plants

Mammalian gametes are specialised for their function. Sperm are small and motile, with a haploid nucleus, a lot of mitochondria to power the flagellum, and an acrosome at the head containing enzymes that digest a path through the egg''s outer layers. Egg cells are larger, with cytoplasm containing food reserves; the zona pellucida is a glycoprotein layer around the egg that sperm must penetrate. Fertilisation in mammals begins when the acrosome reaction releases enzymes that digest the zona pellucida, then the cortical reaction releases cortical granules into the space around the egg, hardening the zona pellucida and preventing more than one sperm from entering; finally the sperm and egg nuclei fuse, restoring the diploid number. In flowering plants, fertilisation begins with pollination and the growth of a pollen tube from the pollen grain down through the style to the embryo sac; two male nuclei travel down the tube, one fertilising the egg to form the zygote (which develops into the embryo) and one fusing with the two polar nuclei to form the triploid endosperm that will feed the developing seed — double fertilisation, unique to flowering plants.

8. Stem cells and what society does with them

A stem cell is an undifferentiated cell that can divide to produce more stem cells and differentiated cells. Totipotent stem cells can develop into any cell type and form a complete organism; the zygote and the cells of the early embryo up to the 16-cell morula are totipotent. Pluripotent stem cells can give rise to many, but not all, cell types; cells of the blastocyst are pluripotent, and in plants many meristem cells are totipotent, which is why a whole plant can be grown from a single cell or tissue. Stem cells are used medically — for example in bone marrow transplants for leukaemia — and their use raises ethical and social questions: the source of embryonic stem cells, the balance of benefit against risk, and decisions made by individuals, committees and governments all draw on scientific knowledge but also on values. Students should be able to discuss these issues from a range of ethical viewpoints.

9. Gene expression: how one gene makes more than one protein and how proteins control cells

Cells become specialised through differential gene expression — different genes are switched on or off in different cells, producing active mRNA and then proteins that control cell processes or determine cell structure. One gene can give rise to more than one protein through post-transcriptional changes to messenger RNA (mRNA) such as alternative splicing, in which the same primary transcript is spliced in different ways to make different mRNAs and therefore different polypeptides. Transcription factors switch genes on or off by binding to DNA and promoting or blocking transcription, so they control which proteins a cell makes. Epigenetic modification — including DNA methylation and histone modification — alters the activation of certain genes without changing the DNA sequence itself, and these modifications can be passed on following cell division, so that a cell''s gene activity can be inherited by its daughter cells and, in some cases, across generations.

10. Inheritance: alleles, genotypes, phenotypes and how they vary

A gene is a sequence of bases on a DNA molecule that codes for a sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide. The allele is one of the different forms of a gene; the genotype is the alleles an organism has; the phenotype is the observable feature that results from the genotype and the environment. Recessive alleles only show in the phenotype when homozygous; dominant alleles show even in the heterozygous state; codominance is when both alleles in the heterozygote contribute to the phenotype. Sex linkage is the inheritance of a gene carried on the X chromosome, such as red-green colour blindness in humans, which appears more often in males because they have only one X chromosome and so express a recessive allele on it. Some phenotypes are affected by multiple alleles for the same gene, and others by polygenic inheritance, where many genes each contribute a small effect, giving rise to continuous variation in the phenotype — height in humans is a classic example. The environment can also affect phenotype, so that a feature is the result of an interaction between genotype and environment rather than genotype alone.

11. Mutations: how they arise and what they can do

Errors in DNA replication can give rise to mutations — changes to the base sequence of DNA. A substitution replaces one base with another and may change one amino acid or none (because the code is degenerate); an insertion adds one or more bases, and a deletion removes one or more, and these can cause a frameshift that changes every amino acid after the mutation and often produces a non-functional protein. Mutations are the source of new alleles, and some mutations give rise to cancer or genetic disorders, while many have no observable effect. Cystic fibrosis is a genetic disorder caused by a recessive allele; the faulty allele affects chloride ion channels, so the functioning of the gaseous exchange, digestive and reproductive systems is impaired — thick mucus blocks the airways, the pancreas duct is blocked so digestion is affected, and fertility in males is reduced because the vas deferens is absent or blocked.

12. Genetic screening and the questions it raises

Genetic screening can identify carriers of a recessive allele, and prenatal testing — including amniocentesis (sampling the fluid around the embryo) and chorionic villus sampling (taking a sample of placental tissue) — can check an embryo or fetus for genetic disorders. Pre-implantation genetic diagnosis (PGD) is used during IVF to test embryos before implantation so that only unaffected embryos are used. These techniques raise ethical and social questions: the reliability and risk of the test, the right to know or not to know, who decides what is a disorder worth preventing, the cost and access to treatment, and the risk of starting down a path toward selecting traits rather than preventing disease. Students should be able to identify and discuss these issues from religious, moral and social viewpoints.

13. How to use this note and what to revise next

Use these notes by working section by section through the topic, checking that you can name every organelle, state its function, and recognise it in an electron micrograph. Practise the calculations — magnification, real size from image size and magnification, mitotic index, and the index of diversity and the calculations that appear in the genetics sections. Revise by drawing and labelling an animal cell and a plant cell from memory, annotating each organelle with its function, then testing yourself on meiosis and on how variation arises. After this topic, revise Topic 4 Plant structure, biodiversity and conservation, and Topic 5 Energy flow, ecosystems and the environment, because the genetics here underpins inheritance in those later topics.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Magnification, applied to a mitochondrion measuring 4.2 cm on a micrograph at ×20 000: actual size = image size ÷ magnification. 4.2 cm = 42 000 µm, so the real length is 42 000 ÷ 20 000 = 2.1 µm. Convert every unit to µm before you divide, and write the magnification formula out.
  • Prokaryote or eukaryote: a eukaryote has a nucleus, membrane-bound organelles and 80S ribosomes. A prokaryote has a circular DNA loop, no nucleus and 70S ribosomes. Name at least two of these features; a single feature such as the cell wall is not enough because plants and some prokaryotes both have one.
  • Mitosis versus meiosis: mitosis gives two genetically identical diploid cells. Meiosis gives four haploid cells, and genetic variation comes from crossing over in prophase I and independent assortment at metaphase I. Mark schemes award these two sources separately.
  • Mammalian fertilisation: a sperm and an egg fuse to form a diploid zygote, which restores the diploid number. Name the haploid gametes explicitly, because the mark depends on the stage of meiosis that produces them.

title: AS Level Chemistry: Formulae, Equations and Amount of Substance
content:
AS Level Chemistry: Formulae, Equations and Amount of Substance

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH11, Topic 1 is the quantitative foundation of the whole course: every later topic, from titrations to equilibria to organic mechanisms, is marked using the ideas here. This topic covers the vocabulary of formulae, relative masses and the mole, balanced and ionic equations with state symbols, concentration in mol dm⁻³ and ppm, empirical and molecular formulae from experimental data, reacting masses, gas volumes including pV = nRT, percentage yield and atom economy, and the two core practicals that turn these ideas into measurements.

The language of formulae

Chemistry names substances at three levels: the particle, the formula and the amount. The vocabulary is examined directly, so learn the definitions precisely.

  • Atom: the smallest particle of an element that can take part in a chemical reaction.
  • Element: a substance containing only one type of atom; it cannot be broken down chemically into anything simpler.
  • Ion: a particle with a charge produced when an atom or group of atoms loses or gains electrons.
  • Molecule: two or more atoms joined by covalent bonds; it is the smallest particle of a covalent substance that can exist independently.
  • Compound: a substance containing two or more elements chemically combined in fixed proportions.
  • Empirical formula: the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound.
  • Molecular formula: the actual number of atoms of each element in one molecule of a compound.

A molecular formula is a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula. Hydrogen peroxide has the empirical formula HO and the molecular formula H₂O₂; ethanoic acid has the empirical formula CH₂O and the molecular formula C₂H₄O₂. Compounds with giant structures, such as sodium chloride or silicon dioxide, have no molecules, so they are described by their empirical formula alone.

Relative masses and the mole

Relative atomic mass, Aᵣ, is the weighted mean mass of the atoms of an element compared with one twelfth of the mass of an atom of carbon-12. Because it is a mean, it takes account of the natural abundances of the isotopes, which is why chlorine has Aᵣ = 35.5 rather than a whole number.

Relative molecular mass, Mᵣ, is the sum of the relative atomic masses in a molecule. For compounds with giant structures, use the term relative formula mass instead: NaCl has a relative formula mass of 23.0 + 35.5 = 58.5. Molar mass, M, is the mass per mole of a substance in g mol⁻¹, and it is numerically equal to Mᵣ or the relative formula mass.

The mole is the unit for amount of substance. One mole contains the Avogadro number of particles, L = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹. Three relationships do nearly all the work in this topic:

RelationshipUse it for
n = m / Mconverting a mass in grams to moles, and back
N = n × Lconverting moles to a number of particles
n = c × V / 1000moles from concentration in mol dm⁻³ and volume in cm³

Worked example. How many molecules are in 4.40 g of carbon dioxide? M(CO₂) = 12.0 + 2(16.0) = 44.0 g mol⁻¹, so n = 4.40 / 44.0 = 0.100 mol. Then N = 0.100 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 6.02 × 10²² molecules. The number of oxygen atoms is twice that, 1.20 × 10²³, because each molecule holds two oxygen atoms.

Balanced equations, state symbols and ionic equations

A balanced equation has the same number of atoms of each element on both sides, and the total charge must balance too. State symbols (s), (l), (g) and (aq) are part of the answer, not decoration: they are how you show that, for example, a reaction produces hydrogen gas rather than hydrogen atoms. Never change a formula to balance an equation; change only the coefficients. Balance the elements that appear once first, leave hydrogen and oxygen until the end, and check by counting a polyatomic ion such as sulfate or nitrate as one unit.

Ionic equations show only the species that change. To construct one, write the full equation, split every soluble ionic compound into its ions, then cancel the ions that appear unchanged on both sides. Those unchanged ions are spectator ions.

Worked example. Silver nitrate solution added to sodium chloride solution:

AgNO3(aq) + NaCl(aq) → AgCl(s) + NaNO3(aq)
Ag+(aq) + NO3−(aq) + Na+(aq) + Cl−(aq) → AgCl(s) + Na+(aq) + NO3−(aq)
Ag+(aq) + Cl−(aq) → AgCl(s)

Sodium and nitrate ions appear on both sides unchanged, so they are spectators. The ionic equation shows the actual change: hydrated silver ions meeting chloride ions to form a white precipitate.

You must be able to link equations to test-tube observations. Displacement reactions, typical acid reactions and precipitation reactions all follow this pattern: the observation is a change in appearance, and the equation explains it.

ObservationIonic equation
Magnesium added to dilute hydrochloric acid: fizzing, metal dissolves, gas pops with a lighted splintMg(s) + 2H+(aq) → Mg2+(aq) + H2(g)
Zinc added to copper(II) sulfate solution: blue colour fades, red-brown solid formsZn(s) + Cu2+(aq) → Zn2+(aq) + Cu(s)
Barium chloride solution added to sodium sulfate solution: white precipitateBa2+(aq) + SO42−(aq) → BaSO4(s)
Calcium carbonate added to nitric acid: fizzing, solid dissolves, gas turns limewater milkyCaCO3(s) + 2H+(aq) → Ca2+(aq) + H2O(l) + CO2(g)

Concentration, dilution and ppm

Concentration is the amount of solute per unit volume of solution. Two units are used and both are examinable:

  • mol dm⁻³ (molarity): moles of solute per cubic decimetre of solution. 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³.
  • g dm⁻³: mass of solute per cubic decimetre of solution.

The bridge between them is molar mass: g dm⁻³ = mol dm⁻³ × M. So 0.250 mol dm⁻³ sodium hydroxide contains 0.250 × 40.0 = 10.0 g dm⁻³.

Worked example. 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ sodium hydroxide is diluted to 250 cm³. The moles of solute do not change: n = 0.100 × 25.0 / 1000 = 2.50 × 10⁻³ mol. The new concentration is 2.50 × 10⁻³ / 0.250 = 0.0100 mol dm⁻³. Diluting tenfold divides the concentration by ten.

Parts per million, ppm, expresses very small proportions and is used for trace gases in the atmosphere and impurities in water. One ppm means one part in a million by mass or by volume, depending on the context:

ppm = (mass of component / mass of sample) × 10^6

If the atmosphere contains 410 ppm of carbon dioxide and the total pressure is 100 kPa, the partial pressure of carbon dioxide is 410 / 10⁶ × 100 kPa = 0.0410 kPa. The same number treated as a volume fraction gives 0.041 % by volume.

Empirical and molecular formulae from experiment

Experimental data is converted into a formula in four steps: mass, moles, simplify, then scale using the molar mass.

Worked example. A compound contains 40.0 % carbon, 6.7 % hydrogen and 53.3 % oxygen by mass, and its molar mass is 180 g mol⁻¹.

ElementMass in 100 gDivide by AᵣDivide by smallest
C40.040.0 / 12.0 = 3.331
H6.76.7 / 1.0 = 6.672
O53.353.3 / 16.0 = 3.331

The empirical formula is CH₂O, with empirical formula mass 30.0. The molecular formula is (CH₂O)n where n = 180 / 30.0 = 6, so the molecular formula is C6H12O6. Always check that a ratio such as 1 : 1.5 is multiplied through to 2 : 3 before writing a formula.

Two related experiments are examined. In a magnesium oxide determination, a known mass of magnesium is burned in a crucible, the lid is lifted periodically to let air in, and the mass of the white powder is found; the increase in mass is the mass of oxygen that combined. In a water-of-crystallisation determination, a hydrated salt is heated to constant mass and the loss in mass is the water driven off, giving the value of x in a formula such as CuSO4·xH2O. In both cases heating to constant mass is essential, and in both the evaluation should name the errors: some magnesium oxide may escape as smoke, magnesium may react with nitrogen in the air to form a nitride, or the heating may not have removed all the water.

Reacting masses

A reacting-mass calculation follows the same route every time: balance the equation, convert the known mass to moles, use the mole ratio, convert back to a mass.

Worked example. What mass of iron is produced when 8.00 g of iron(III) oxide is reduced by carbon monoxide?

Fe2O3 + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO2

M(Fe₂O₃) = 2(55.8) + 3(16.0) = 159.6 g mol⁻¹, so n(Fe₂O₃) = 8.00 / 159.6 = 0.0501 mol. The ratio is 1 : 2, so n(Fe) = 0.100 mol and m(Fe) = 0.100 × 55.8 = 5.59 g. Notice that the mass of the solid fell: the oxygen was removed as carbon dioxide, and mass is conserved because the carbon dioxide carries it away.

Where two reactant amounts are given, one will be limiting. Calculate the moles of each, divide by the coefficient in the balanced equation, and the smaller quotient is the limiting reactant. The other is in excess and does not take part fully. All product calculations use the limiting reactant.

Gas volumes, molar volume and pV = nRT

One mole of any gas occupies the same volume at the same temperature and pressure. At room temperature and pressure, this molar volume is approximately 24 dm³ mol⁻¹, so 0.0500 mol of any gas occupies 1.20 dm³. Use this only when the conditions are stated as room temperature and pressure.

When conditions differ, use the ideal gas equation:

pV = nRT

In this equation p is in pascals, V in m³, n in moles, T in kelvin and R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Unit conversion causes most lost marks: 1 kPa = 1000 Pa, 1 dm³ = 1 × 10⁻³ m³, and T = θ + 273.

Worked example. A 0.250 g sample of a volatile liquid is vaporised in a syringe at 100 °C and 100 kPa, and occupies 97 cm³. Find its molar mass.

p = 100 000 Pa, V = 97 × 10⁻⁶ m³, T = 373 K. Then n = pV / RT = (100000 × 97 × 10⁻⁶) / (8.31 × 373) = 9.7 / 3099 = 3.13 × 10⁻³ mol. M = m / n = 0.250 / 3.13 × 10⁻³ = 79.9 g mol⁻¹, so the liquid is likely a small molecule such as benzene (Mᵣ = 78).

Percentage yield and atom economy

Percentage yield compares what you actually obtained with the maximum the equation allows:

percentage yield = (actual yield / theoretical yield) × 100

Reasons for a yield below 100 % include incomplete reaction, reversible reactions, loss during transfer or filtration, side reactions producing other products, and impurities in the reactants.

Atom economy asks a different question: how much of the mass of all the reactants ends up in the product you want?

atom economy = (molar mass of desired product / sum of molar masses of all products) × 100

Worked example. Ethene is hydrated to ethanol: C2H4 + H2O → C2H5OH. The only product is ethanol, so the atom economy is 100 %, even though the yield may be well below that because the reaction is reversible. Compare the synthesis of bromoethane from ethene and hydrogen bromide: C2H4 + HBr → C2H5Br also has 100 % atom economy. In a reaction such as CH4 + Cl2 → CH3Cl + HCl, the desired product has Mᵣ = 50.5 and the products total 50.5 + 36.5 = 87.0, so the atom economy is 58.0 %. The HCl is a co-product with little value, which is why industry prefers addition reactions to substitutions.

Core Practical 1: measurement of the molar volume of a gas

A known mass of magnesium ribbon reacts with excess dilute hydrochloric acid and the hydrogen is collected in a gas syringe. The apparatus is assembled and checked for leaks, the acid is added, and the final syringe reading is taken once the reaction has finished and the apparatus has cooled to room temperature.

Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl2(aq) + H2(g)

Calculation. If 0.024 g of magnesium gives 24.0 cm³ of hydrogen, n(Mg) = 0.024 / 24.3 = 9.88 × 10⁻⁴ mol, and the ratio is 1 : 1, so n(H₂) is the same. The molar volume is 24.0 / 9.88 × 10⁻⁴ = 24 300 cm³ mol⁻¹ = 24.3 dm³ mol⁻¹, close to the accepted 24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹ at room temperature and pressure.

Evaluation. The main sources of error are gas escaping before the bung is replaced, a syringe that sticks or leaks, the temperature not being room temperature when the reading is taken, and the small mass of magnesium producing a large percentage uncertainty in mass. Using a larger mass of magnesium reduces the percentage uncertainty but needs a larger syringe.

Typical mistakes

  • Using the mass of a solution rather than the mass of solute, or forgetting to divide by 1000 when converting cm³ to dm³.
  • Rounding an empirical formula ratio such as 1 : 2.5 to 1 : 3 instead of doubling it to 2 : 5.
  • Changing a subscript to balance an equation instead of the coefficient in front of the formula.
  • Leaving state symbols out of an equation when the question asks for a full equation, or including spectator ions in an ionic equation.
  • Forgetting to convert temperature to kelvin, or pressure to pascals, in pV = nRT.
  • Using the actual yield as the theoretical yield in a percentage-yield calculation.
  • Calculating atom economy from the reactants rather than from the products.

Exam-style questions

  1. Define the terms empirical formula and molecular formula, using a compound of your choice to show the difference. Answer: the empirical formula is the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element; the molecular formula is the actual number of atoms of each element in a molecule. Ethanoic acid has the empirical formula CH2O and the molecular formula C2H4O2.
  2. 0.500 g of a hydrated salt, MgSO4·xH2O, is heated to constant mass and 0.244 g of anhydrous magnesium sulfate remains. Find x. Answer: mass of water lost = 0.500 − 0.244 = 0.256 g. n(MgSO4) = 0.244 / 120.4 = 2.03 × 10⁻³ mol; n(H2O) = 0.256 / 18.0 = 1.42 × 10⁻² mol. The ratio is 1.42 × 10⁻² / 2.03 × 10⁻³ = 7.0, so x = 7 and the formula is MgSO4·7H2O.
  3. Write the ionic equation, with state symbols, for the reaction between aqueous sodium carbonate and dilute hydrochloric acid, and state one observation. Answer: CO32−(aq) + 2H+(aq) → CO2(g) + H2O(l); effervescence, and the gas turns limewater milky.
  4. 25.0 cm³ of 0.150 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid is neutralised by 0.100 mol dm⁻³ sodium hydroxide. Calculate the volume of alkali required. Answer: n(HCl) = 0.150 × 25.0 / 1000 = 3.75 × 10⁻³ mol. HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H2O, so n(NaOH) = 3.75 × 10⁻³ mol and V = n / c = 3.75 × 10⁻³ / 0.100 = 0.0375 dm³ = 37.5 cm³.
  5. Explain why the percentage yield of a reaction can be less than 100 %, and why a reaction with a high percentage yield can still have a low atom economy. Answer: the yield is reduced by incomplete reaction, side reactions, losses in transfer and purification, or by the reaction being reversible. Atom economy depends only on the balanced equation, so a reaction can convert nearly all the limiting reactant into products while most of the product mass is an unwanted co-product.

Revise this topic by practising calculations with the units written at every step, because each mark scheme rewards the mole ratio and the correct final unit as much as the numerical answer. Next, move to Atomic Structure and the Periodic Table, where the mole is used again for relative atomic mass and mass spectra.

title: Networks and the Internet — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Networks and the Internet

Computer Science — A2. Four layers: Application (HTTP, FTP, SMTP, DNS), Transport (TCP reliable, connection-oriented with sequence numbers and acknowledgements; UDP fast, connectionless), Internet (IP addressing and routing), Link (physical delivery on the local network). Layering separates concerns so each layer can change independently.

Key areas to revise

  • The TCP/IP Stack
  • Switching
  • Addressing and Subnetting
  • Models and Protection

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

### Worked example The internet is a network of networks. Data travels as packets, and each packet carries a destination IP address. IPv4 addresses are 32 bits, giving 2³² possible addresses, and IPv6 addresses are 128 bits. DNS translates a domain name into an IP address. TCP checks that packets arrive and reassembles them in order, while HTTPS encrypts the data in transit. ### Check yourself Describe the role of DNS when you open a website by name. DNS looks up the domain name and returns the IP address, and the browser then sends its request to that address. Explain why packets may take different routes but still reach the destination. ### Worked example The internet is a network of networks. Data travels as packets, and each packet carries a destination IP address. IPv4 addresses are 32 bits, giving 2³² possible addresses, and IPv6 addresses are 128 bits. DNS translates a domain name into an IP address. TCP checks that packets arrive and reassembles them in order, while HTTPS encrypts the data in transit.

title: Sequences and Series — Study Notes
content:
Sequences and Series

Edexcel International A Level Mathematics — Pure Mathematics 2 (WMA12), sat at AS.

Arithmetic Progressions (AP)

Terms increase by a common difference d.

  • nth term: uₙ = a + (n − 1)d
  • Sum: Sₙ = n/2 [2a + (n − 1)d]

Example: AP 5, 8, 11: the 20th term is 5 + 19 × 3 = 62.

Geometric Progressions (GP)

Terms multiply by a common ratio r.

  • nth term: uₙ = arⁿ⁻¹
  • Sum: Sₙ = a(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r)
  • Sum to infinity (|r| < 1 only): S∞ = a/(1 − r)

Example: a = 8, r = 1/2 gives S∞ = 8/(1/2) = 16.

Binomial Expansion

(1 + x)ⁿ = 1 + nx + n(n − 1)/2! x² + n(n − 1)(n − 2)/3! x³ + …, valid for |x| < 1.

For positive integer n, coefficients come from Pascal's triangle: (1 + 2x)⁴ = 1 + 8x + 24x² + 32x³ + 16x⁴.

Exam tips: identify a, d or r first; for "sum to infinity" questions check |r| < 1 explicitly, and for binomial expansions give terms up to the power asked (usually x² or x³).

Formulae and exam method

Arithmetic progression: the nth term is Tₙ = a + (n − 1)d, where a is the first term and d the common difference. The sum of the first n terms is Sₙ = n/2 [2a + (n − 1)d], or Sₙ = n/2 (a + l) when the last term l is known.

Geometric progression: Tₙ = arⁿ⁻¹, and Sₙ = a(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r) for r ≠ 1. The sum to infinity exists only when |r| < 1, and then S∞ = a/(1 − r).

To find the number of terms, substitute the known sum or term and solve for n. When n sits in an exponent, take logarithms. Check that n is a positive integer.

Sigma notation: Σ from r = 1 to n of (ar + b) is evaluated with the standard sums, but write out the first few terms when the pattern is unclear.

Exam cue: Identify whether the question is AP or GP before choosing a formula, and state the value of r when using the sum to infinity.

Exam method: arithmetic and geometric sums

For an arithmetic sequence with first term a and common difference d, the nth term is a + (n − 1)d and the sum of the first n terms is S_n = n/2 (2a + (n − 1)d). For a geometric sequence with ratio r, the nth term is ar^(n − 1) and S_n = a(1 − r^n)/(1 − r) for r ≠ 1.

The sum to infinity exists only when |r| < 1, and then S∞ = a/(1 − r). If |r| ≥ 1, say so explicitly rather than applying the formula.

Exam cue: Identify whether the sequence is arithmetic or geometric from the common difference or ratio before choosing a formula. Check the number of terms n carefully when you set up the equation.

Worked example: arithmetic progression

The sequence 3, 7, 11, … has first term a = 3 and common difference d = 4. The 20th term is a + 19d = 3 + 76 = 79. The sum of the first 20 terms is Sₙ = n/2 (2a + (n − 1)d) = 10 × (6 + 76) = 820.

Check with the average method: the first and last terms average (3 + 79)/2 = 41, and 41 × 20 = 820.

Worked example: geometric progression

The sequence 5, 10, 20, … has r = 2. The 8th term is 5 × 2⁷ = 640. The sum of the first six terms is 5(2⁶ − 1)/(2 − 1) = 315. Adding them directly gives 5 + 10 + 20 + 40 + 80 + 160 = 315, which confirms the formula.

Sum to infinity

A geometric series has a sum to infinity only when |r| < 1, and then S∞ = a/(1 − r). For 81, 27, 9, … the ratio is 1/3, so S∞ = 81/(2/3) = 121.5. If |r| ≥ 1 the terms do not shrink and the sum does not converge, so say so rather than quoting a formula.

Binomial expansion

For (1 + 2x)⁵, the first terms are 1 + 5(2x) + 10(2x)² + … The coefficient of x² is C(5, 2) × 2² = 10 × 4 = 40. The expansion is valid for |2x| < 1, so the range of x must be stated when the question asks for it.

Common errors that lose marks

  • Using n instead of n − 1 in the n-th term formula, which shifts every term.
  • Confusing the nth term with the sum of the first n terms, a very common error on exam questions that ask for both.
  • Dividing a/(1 − r) when the series starts at a term other than the first, so check the index on the first term before using the formula.
  • Forgetting that the binomial expansion of (a + b)ⁿ has a coefficient C(n, r) on each term, and that the powers of a and b add to n.

title: A Level Physics: Thermal Physics
content:
A Level Physics: Thermal Physics

Thermal physics is the accountancy of heat: what temperature really measures, how much energy it takes to change a substance's state, and how the invisible motion of billions of particles produces the pressure in a balloon. This note builds the whole subject from zero: thermal equilibrium and the temperature scales, specific heat capacity and specific latent heat with full calorimetry arithmetic, the mole and the equation of state, the kinetic theory that justifies it, and the first law of thermodynamics — the energy bookkeeping rule that governs engines, fridges and stars alike.

Thermal equilibrium

Heat flows from hotter to cooler bodies until no further net transfer occurs — that final state is thermal equilibrium, when both bodies are at the same temperature. The zeroth law of thermodynamics makes the logic precise: if A is in thermal equilibrium with B, and B with C, then A is in equilibrium with C — which is exactly why thermometers work (they reach equilibrium with the thing measured, and the reading transfers). The distinction examiners demand: temperature measures the average random kinetic energy per particle; heat is energy in transit because of a temperature difference. Objects do not contain heat — they contain internal energy.

Temperature scales

The Celsius scale is defined by two fixed points: the melting point of pure ice (0 °C) and the boiling point of pure water (100 °C) at standard pressure. The thermodynamic (Kelvin) scale starts at absolute zero — the temperature at which particles have minimum kinetic energy, −273.15 °C — and its unit, the kelvin, is the same size as the degree Celsius:

T (K) = θ (°C) + 273        (273.15 exact; 273 usual in exams)
temperature change: ΔT in K = Δθ in °C

Every gas-law and kinetic-theory calculation demands kelvin; forgetting the conversion is the single commonest thermal error. A temperature change of 10 °C is a change of 10 K — only absolute values need converting.

Specific heat capacity

Heating a body raises its temperature; the energy needed depends on the substance's own reluctance to change temperature:

E = m c Δθ        (or E = C Δθ for a whole body)

E in J, m in kg, c in J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ (specific heat capacity)
Δθ in °C or K (the same size)
C = m c = heat capacity of the object (J K⁻¹)

The electrical method of measuring c is examinable as a practical: a heater of known power runs for a known time (E = Pt), the temperature rise is recorded, and losses are reduced with insulation and a lid; the graph of temperature against time is extrapolated back to the start to correct for losses during heating.

Worked example 1. A 2.0 kg aluminium block (c = 900 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) is heated from 20 °C to 80 °C by a 500 W heater. Find the energy needed and the minimum heating time.

E = m c Δθ = 2.0 × 900 × 60 = 10⁸ 000 J = 10⁸ kJ
t = E/P = 10⁸ 000/500 = 216 s = 3.6 minutes

Worked example 2 (mixing). 0.50 kg of water at 90 °C is mixed with 0.50 kg of water at 10 °C. Find the final temperature (no losses).

heat lost = heat gained
m c (90 - T) = m c (T - 10)   (same m and c cancel)
90 - T = T - 10 → 10⁰ = 2T → T = 50 °C

The mixing equation is worth learning as a shape: Σ(heat lost) = Σ(heat gained), with each term mcΔθ evaluated from its own temperature difference to the final T.

Specific latent heat

During a change of state, energy goes into breaking intermolecular bonds rather than raising temperature — the heating curve flatlines at the melting or boiling point. The energy for the change:

E = m L        L = specific latent heat (J kg⁻¹)

L_fusion for melting/freezing; L_vaporisation for boiling/condensing

Worked example. A 3.0 kW kettle boils 1.5 kg of water already at 100 °C. How long to boil it dry (L_vap = 2.26 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹)?

E = m L = 1.5 × 2.26 × 10⁶ = 3.39 × 10⁶ J
t = E/P = 3.39 × 10⁶/3000 = 1130 s = 18.8 minutes

Reading a heating curve is a standard question: sloped sections are temperature rise (mcΔθ applies), flat sections are change of state (mL applies), and the flat at 0 °C is melting while the flat at 100 °C is boiling.

The mole

The mole counts particles the way a dozen counts eggs: one mole contains exactly Nₐ = 6.02 × 10²³ particles (Avogadro's constant). The molar mass M is the mass of one mole (numerically the relative atomic mass in grams; in kg mol⁻¹ for calculations).

n = m / M        N = n N_A

n in mol, m in kg (or g consistently with M), M in kg mol⁻¹

Worked example. Find the number of molecules in 8.0 g of oxygen (O₂, M = 0.032 kg mol⁻¹).

n = m/M = 0.008/0.032 = 0.25 mol
N = n N_A = 0.25 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 1.505 × 10²³ molecules
  = 1.5 × 10²³ (2 s.f.)

The equation of state

For a fixed mass of an ideal gas, pressure, volume and temperature obey one master equation:

p V = n R T        (also p V = N k T)

p in pascals (Pa), V in m³, T in kelvin (K)
R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹  (molar gas constant)
k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹ (Boltzmann constant), N = number of molecules

Unit discipline: 1 atm = 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa; 1 cm³ = 10⁻⁶ m³; 1 litre = 10⁻³ m³. The ideal-gas assumptions are examinable: molecules are point particles with negligible volume, intermolecular forces are negligible except during collisions, and collisions are perfectly elastic.

Worked example. 0.40 mol of gas occupies 2.0 × 10⁻³ m³ at 27 °C. Find the pressure.

T = 27 + 273 = 300 K
p = nRT/V = (0.40 × 8.31 × 300)/(2.0 × 10⁻³)
  = 997.2/2.0 × 10⁻³ = 4.99 × 10⁵ Pa = 5.0 × 10⁵ Pa (2 s.f.)

Boyle's, Charles's and the pressure law are all slices of this one equation — if a question gives a change at constant moles, either hold one variable fixed to get the simple law, or write p₁V₁/T₁ = p₂V₂/T₂ for the general case.

Kinetic theory

The kinetic model explains pressure: gas molecules collide elastically with container walls, and each collision transfers momentum; billions per second give a steady average force per unit area — pressure. The model's assumptions (large number of molecules, random motion, elastic collisions, negligible molecular volume, forces only during collisions) justify the ideal-gas behaviour, and the theory links the microscopic to the macroscopic:

p V = (1/3) N m c²        c = root-mean-square speed

mean kinetic energy per molecule = (3/2) k T
so (1/2) m c² = (3/2) k T  →  c = √(3 k T / m)

The rms speed rises with the square root of absolute temperature and falls with molecular mass — hydrogen molecules move faster than oxygen molecules at the same temperature.

Worked example. Find the rms speed of helium atoms (m = 6.6 × 10⁻²⁷ kg) at 300 K.

c = √(3 k T/m) = √(3 × 1.38 × 10⁻²³ x 300/6.6 × 10⁻²⁷)
  = √(1.242 × 10⁻²⁰/6.6 × 10⁻²⁷) = √(1.88 × 10⁶)
  = 1372 m s⁻¹  (2 s.f.: 1.4 × 10³ m s⁻¹)

Internal energy

The internal energy of a substance is the sum of the random kinetic energies of its particles plus the potential energies of their interactions. For an ideal gas (no intermolecular forces) internal energy is purely kinetic and proportional to absolute temperature; for real substances, melting and boiling raise internal energy because potential energy increases as bonds stretch and break. State the split precisely in definitions: internal energy = total random kinetic energy + total intermolecular potential energy.

The first law of thermodynamics

Energy is conserved: the change in a system's internal energy equals the heat added to it plus the work done on it.

ΔU = Q + W

ΔU = change in internal energy (J)
Q = heat energy transferred to the system (J), negative if lost
W = work done ON the system (J), negative if the system does work
    (for a gas: W = -p ΔV under the convention W = work done
     on the system; expanding gas does work, so W is negative)

The sign convention must match your course's — state it in words when you apply the law. Applications the papers love: compressing a gas quickly (W positive, little Q, so ΔU and temperature rise); a gas expanding slowly at constant temperature (ΔU = 0 for an ideal gas, so Q = −W — heat flows in to supply the work done); and refrigerators (work is done to move heat against its natural flow).

Worked example. A gas is compressed so that 500 J of work is done on it while 200 J of heat flows out. Find ΔU and state the temperature change.

W = +500 J (done on the system), Q = -200 J (lost)
ΔU = Q + W = -200 + 500 = +300 J
internal energy rises → temperature rises (for an ideal gas)

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Definitions) Distinguish between temperature and internal energy. Answer: Temperature is proportional to the mean random kinetic energy per molecule; internal energy is the total random kinetic energy plus the intermolecular potential energy of all the particles.
  2. (Kelvin) Convert 27 °C to kelvin and state absolute zero in °C. Answer: T = 27 + 273 = 300 K; absolute zero = −273 °C (−273.15 °C exactly).
  3. (Specific heat) 0.15 kg of a metal at 100 °C is dropped into 0.25 kg of water at 15 °C; the final temperature is 22 °C. Find the metal's specific heat capacity (c_water = 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹). Answer: heat gained by water = 0.25 × 4200 × 7 = 7350 J; metal lost = 0.15 × c × 78 = 7350 → c = 7350/(0.15 × 78) = 628 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ ≈ 630 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.
  4. (Latent heat) Explain why the temperature of boiling water stays constant. Answer: The energy supplied breaks intermolecular bonds during the change of state instead of raising the average kinetic energy of the molecules, so the temperature is unchanged until all the liquid has vaporised.
  5. (Equation of state) 2.0 g of helium (M = 4.0 g mol⁻¹) occupies 0.012 m³ at 300 K. Find the pressure. Answer: n = 2.0/4.0 = 0.50 mol; p = nRT/V = (0.50 × 8.31 × 300)/0.012 = 103 875 Pa ≈ 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa.
  6. (Kinetic theory) State two assumptions of the kinetic model and explain why doubling absolute temperature changes rms speed the way it does. Answer: Molecules are point particles with negligible volume; collisions are perfectly elastic; intermolecular forces are negligible except during collisions (any two). Since c = √(3kT/m), doubling T multiplies c by √2 — speed depends on the square root of absolute temperature.
  7. (First law) A gas expands, doing 300 J of work, while 100 J of heat is supplied. Find ΔU. Answer: W = −300 J (work done by the system), Q = +100 J; ΔU = 100 − 300 = −200 J — internal energy falls and the gas cools.
  8. (Practical) Describe how to determine the specific heat capacity of a metal block electrically. Answer: Place a known-power heater in the block, insulate it, record temperature against time as the heater runs; energy input E = Pt; plot temperature vs time and use the gradient (with m and the extrapolated zero-time temperature) to find c from E = mcΔθ; extrapolating back corrects for heat lost during the experiment.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Celsius in gas laws: pV = nRT demands kelvin. A gas-law calculation with 300 °C is wrong by 273 K at the first step.
  • Δθ in specific heat: E = mcΔθ uses a temperature change; questions giving start and end temperatures need the difference, not a raw value.
  • Latent vs specific heat: during a change of state use mL, not mcΔθ; on a heating curve the flat sections are where Δθ = 0.
  • Molar mass units: grams versus kilograms must match the mass unit in n = m/M; the equation of state with R = 8.31 needs moles and SI units throughout.
  • Pressure units: kPa and atm into Pa, cm³ into m³, before substitution.
  • Internal energy wording: it includes potential energy for real substances; defining it as kinetic only is wrong outside ideal gases.
  • First-law signs: pick a convention and state it — work done on the system is positive in ΔU = Q + W; expanding gas does work on the surroundings (negative W).
  • rms speed vs mean speed: the c in pV = ⅓Nmc² is the root-mean-square speed; it is not the average of speeds (which is smaller).
  • Precision and method: 2 or 3 s.f. with units (J, Pa, K, mol, m s⁻¹); write the formula line before numbers — the physics formulae are credit in their own right.

Equations and symbols

Every relation this topic can be examined on, in the form the mark scheme expects, with a key naming each symbol and its unit. The derivations in the sections above end here: if you can write these from memory and say what each symbol means, the algebra in the exam is bookkeeping.

14.1-14.2 Thermal equilibrium and temperature scales

T(K) = θ(°C) + 273.15
Key: T = thermodynamic temperature (K); θ = Celsius temperature (°C); 273.15 = the offset between the ice point and absolute zero (K). Exams accept 273, and a temperature given as 27 °C becomes 300 K.

ΔT (in K) = Δθ (in °C)
Key: ΔT = temperature change in kelvin (K); Δθ = the same change in degrees Celsius (°C). A change of one kelvin is a change of one degree Celsius, because the scales differ only by their zero — which is why a specific heat capacity in J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ can be used with a temperature difference measured in °C.

thermal equilibrium: no net heat flow between bodies in contact
Key: two bodies are in thermal equilibrium when they are at the same temperature, so no net energy transfers between them; the thermometer reads the same as the body only once this state is reached. The zeroth law in one line: equilibrium is transitive, which is what makes a thermometer possible.

14.3 Specific heat capacity and specific latent heat

E = m c Δθ
Key: E = energy supplied to raise the temperature (J); m = mass of the substance (kg); c = specific heat capacity, the energy needed to raise 1 kg by 1 K (J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹); Δθ = temperature rise (°C or K, the same number). No phase change is allowed during the heating, or some of E goes into breaking bonds instead.

c = E / (m Δθ)
Key: c = specific heat capacity (J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹); E = energy supplied (J); m = mass (kg); Δθ = temperature rise (K). The measuring form, used with an electrical heater where E = V I t.

C = m c
Key: C = heat capacity of the whole object (J K⁻¹); m = its mass (kg); c = specific heat capacity of its material (J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹). Then E = C Δθ for the object as a whole; two objects of the same material have heat capacities in the ratio of their masses.

E = m L
Key: E = energy transferred during a change of state (J); m = mass changing state (kg); L = specific latent heat, the energy per kilogram to change state at constant temperature (J kg⁻¹). Use L_fusion for melting and freezing, L_vaporisation for boiling and condensing; the temperature does not rise while this energy is supplied.

E_total = m c Δθ (heating to the change) + m L (the change itself) + m c Δθ (heating beyond it)
Key: each term is the energy for one stage (J); the symbols are as above. The shape of a heating curve: sloped where a single phase is warming, flat where it changes state.

heat lost = heat gained
Key: in an insulated system, the energy leaving the hotter body (J) equals that entering the colder one, so m₁ c₁ (θ_hot − θ_mix) = m₂ c₂ (θ_mix − θ_cold). The method of mixtures: the only unknown is usually the final temperature, or a specific heat capacity once it is measured.

15.1 The mole

n = m / M
Key: n = amount of substance (mol); m = mass of the sample (kg or g); M = molar mass, the mass of one mole (kg mol⁻¹ or g mol⁻¹). Keep m and M in the same unit — grams with g mol⁻¹, kilograms with kg mol⁻¹.

N = n N_A
Key: N = number of particles (dimensionless); n = amount of substance (mol); N_A = Avogadro constant, 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹. One mole of any substance contains the same number of particles, which is why molar masses compare masses of equal particle counts.

N_A = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹
Key: Avogadro constant: the number of particles in one mole. In this specification it is defined as the number of atoms in 0.012 kg of carbon-12.

15.2 The equation of state

p V = n R T
Key: p = pressure (Pa = N m⁻²); V = volume (m³); n = amount of gas (mol); R = molar gas constant, 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; T = thermodynamic temperature (K). The molar form — use it when the amount is known in moles.

p V = N k T
Key: p = pressure (Pa); V = volume (m³); N = number of molecules; k = Boltzmann constant, 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹; T = temperature (K). The molecular form — use it when the question counts molecules rather than moles.

R = N_A k
Key: R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; N_A = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹; k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹. The bridge between the two forms of the equation of state: dividing pV = NkT by n gives pV = (N/n) kT = N_A k T.

p V / T = constant (for a fixed mass of gas)
Key: p = pressure (Pa); V = volume (m³); T = temperature (K). The combined gas law: states 1 and 2 of the same sample satisfy p₁V₁/T₁ = p₂V₂/T₂, which covers Boyle's, Charles' and the pressure law as special cases.

p = ρ R T / M
Key: p = pressure (Pa); ρ = density of the gas (kg m⁻³); R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; T = temperature (K); M = molar mass (kg mol⁻¹). Since ρ = m/V and n = m/M, the equation of state written in terms of density — the form for "why is hot air less dense".

15.3 Kinetic theory of gases

p V = ⅓ N m ⟨c²⟩
Key: p = pressure (Pa); V = volume (m³); N = number of molecules; m = mass of one molecule (kg); ⟨c²⟩ = mean square speed of the molecules (m² s⁻²). The pressure comes from molecular collisions with the walls: momentum change per collision times collision rate per unit area.

½ m ⟨c²⟩ = (3/2) k T
Key: ½ m ⟨c²⟩ = mean translational kinetic energy of one molecule (J); m = molecular mass (kg); ⟨c²⟩ = mean square speed (m² s⁻²); k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹; T = temperature (K). The mean kinetic energy depends only on temperature, and is the same for every gas at that temperature — heavier molecules simply move more slowly.

⟨c²⟩ = 3 k T / m = 3 p / ρ
Key: ⟨c²⟩ = mean square speed (m² s⁻²); k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹; T = temperature (K); m = mass of one molecule (kg); p = pressure (Pa); ρ = density (kg m⁻³). The second form needs no molecular data at all.

c_rms = √(3 k T / m) = √(3 p / ρ)
Key: c_rms = root-mean-square speed (m s⁻¹); k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹; T = temperature (K); m = mass of one molecule (kg); p = pressure (Pa); ρ = density (kg m⁻³). Take the rms speed rather than the mean speed: the mean of the squared speeds carries the energy.

n = N / V = p / (k T)
Key: n = number density of molecules (m⁻³); N = number of molecules; V = volume (m³); p = pressure (Pa); k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹; T = temperature (K). At s.t.p. this gives about 2.7 × 10²⁵ m⁻³, the number worth remembering for order-of-magnitude checks.

16.1 Internal energy

U = Σ KE + Σ PE of the molecules
Key: U = internal energy of the body (J); Σ KE = total random kinetic energy of its molecules (J); Σ PE = total potential energy from the intermolecular forces (J). For an ideal gas the potential term is negligible, so U depends only on temperature; for a real solid or liquid the potential term dominates the latent heat.

U = (3/2) N k T (ideal monatomic gas)
Key: U = internal energy (J); N = number of molecules; k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹; T = temperature (K). Follows from ½ m ⟨c²⟩ = (3/2) k T multiplied by N molecules — no potential energy to add.

16.2 The first law of thermodynamics

ΔU = q + w
Key: ΔU = increase in internal energy of the system (J); q = heat supplied to the system (J); w = work done on the system (J). The sign convention used throughout this specification — energy in is positive. Get the convention wrong and every answer is out by a sign, so state it in the working.

w = − p ΔV
Key: w = work done on the gas (J); p = pressure (Pa); ΔV = change in volume (m³); the minus sign says that a gas expanding (ΔV positive) does work on its surroundings, so work is done on it negatively. For a constant-pressure process this is the area under a p–V graph.

ΔU = q − p ΔV
Key: ΔU = change in internal energy (J); q = heat supplied to the gas (J); p = pressure (Pa); ΔV = volume change (m³). The expanded first law: heat in, minus the work the gas does by expanding.

q = 0 ⇒ ΔU = w (adiabatic); ΔV = 0 ⇒ ΔU = q (isochoric); ΔT = 0 ⇒ ΔU = 0 (isothermal, ideal gas)
Key: the three named processes as special cases; q = heat exchanged (J); w = work done on the system (J); ΔU = internal energy change (J); ΔV = volume change (m³); ΔT = temperature change (K). An adiabatic change is fast enough, or insulated enough, that no heat flows — a sudden compression, or a gas expanding into a vacuum.

C_p − C_v = R
Key: C_p = molar heat capacity at constant pressure (J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹); C_v = molar heat capacity at constant volume (J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹); R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. At constant pressure some of the heat goes into work of expansion, so more is needed for the same temperature rise — the difference is exactly R per mole.

title: Mensuration — Area and Volume — Study Notes
content:
Mensuration — Area and Volume

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): units, perimeter/area (incl. sectors), surface area, volume of standard solids, composite shapes.

1. Units

1 m² = 10 000 cm²; 1 m³ = 1 000 000 cm³; 1 litre = 1000 cm³. Convert area/volume factors carefully (square/cube the length factor).

2. Area

  • Triangle ½bh; trapezium ½(a + b)h; parallelogram bh.
  • Circle A = πr²; sector area = (θ/360)πr²; arc = (θ/360) × 2πr.
  • Composites: split, calculate, add/subtract.

3. Volume and surface area

  • Cuboid V = lbh; prism V = cross-section × length.
  • Cylinder V = πr²h; SA = 2πr² + 2πrh.
  • Pyramid V = ⅓ × base area × h.
  • Cone V = ⅓πr²h; SA = πr² + πrl, with l² = r² + h².
  • Sphere V = (4/3)πr³; SA = 4πr².

4. Problem solving

Flow/filling: volume ÷ rate = time. Packing: divide volumes (check edge alignment). Nets for surface area: label every face before adding.

Exam tips: keep π on the calculator until the final answer; for sector problems ask "fraction of the full circle?"; quote units in every answer.

Area formulae

Rectangle: length × width. Triangle: ½ × base × perpendicular height. Parallelogram: base × perpendicular height. Trapezium: ½(a + b)h, where a and b are the parallel sides. Circle: πr², and circumference 2πr. Leave answers in terms of π when asked, or round to the accuracy stated.

Volume and surface area

Prism volume is cross-sectional area × length. Cylinder volume is πr²h. Cone volume is ⅓πr²h and sphere volume is ⁴⁄₃πr³. Surface area of a cylinder is 2πr² + 2πrh. Sketch the solid and label radii and heights before you substitute.

Units and compound measures

Convert units before calculating: 1 m² = 10 000 cm² and 1 m³ = 1 000 000 cm³. Density is mass ÷ volume, and speed is distance ÷ time. Keep the units with the answer.

title: Exam technique: Ratio, Rate and Proportion
content:
### What earns the marks
For sharing in a ratio, total parts and value of one part each earn a mark: write 5 parts = 600 before splitting.
