Correlation is association, not causation: name the third variable that could drive both.

title: Exam technique: Thermal Physics
content:
### What earns the marks
For conduction, free electrons named earn the explanation mark. For convection, rise of hot less-dense fluid earns the mark. For radiation, matt black as best emitter and absorber earns the mark; Q = mcT quoted earns the calculation marks.
### Traps
Error: convection claimed in solids. Correction: conduction only in solids. Error: shiny surfaces called best emitters. Correction: matt black emits and absorbs best. Error: evaporation cooling unexplained. Correction: fastest molecules escape.

title: A Level Mathematics: The Poisson Distribution
content:
A Level Mathematics: The Poisson Distribution

The Poisson distribution models the number of events that happen in a fixed interval of time, length, area or volume when those events occur randomly and independently at a constant average rate. Where the binomial counts successes in a fixed number of trials, the Poisson counts arrivals in a continuous window: calls reaching a switchboard in an hour, defects along a length of cable, radioactive decays in a minute. This note derives the formula from the binomial, sets out the two conditions that must hold, and then uses the distribution for the probability and hypothesis-test questions the exam sets.

Where the formula comes from

Imagine slicing the interval into a very large number of tiny sub-intervals. In each slice the chance of an event is tiny but the number of slices is enormous, so the count is binomial with n huge and p tiny. Taking that limit turns nCr p^r (1−p)^(n−r) into the Poisson formula, with the mean λ = np surviving as the only parameter.

X ~ Po(λ):  P(X = r) = e^(-λ) λ^r / r!
mean E(X) = λ
variance Var(X) = λ
so the mean and variance are equal - a diagnostic test for the model

The equality of mean and variance is not a coincidence to memorise; it is the fingerprint of the limit, and it is why an exam question can give you a sample mean and variance and ask whether a Poisson model is plausible.

The three conditions

A Poisson model needs randomness, independence and a constant rate. Naming them is worth marks, and each failure has a characteristic symptom.

1. events occur singly (not in pairs or batches)
2. events occur at random, independently of each other
3. the average rate λ is constant over the interval
then the count in that interval is Poisson

Worked example (checking the model). A shop counts customers arriving per hour. Explain why a Poisson model may be unsuitable.

the arrival rate is not constant: it peaks at lunchtime and is near zero at night
so condition 3 fails and the mean over a whole day is not a single rate
a better model splits the day into periods of roughly constant rate

Calculating probabilities

The formula handles a single value; the cumulative sum handles a range. Because the Poisson has no upper limit, every "at least" question becomes a complement.

P(X = r) = e^(-λ) λ^r / r!
P(X <= r) sums from 0 to r (tables or calculator)
P(X >= r) = 1 - P(X <= r - 1)
P(X < r)  = P(X <= r - 1)

Worked example. X ~ Po(3). Find P(X = 2).

P = e^(-3) × 3² / 2!
= 0.049787 × 9 / 2
= 0.2240

Worked example 2 (at least). For the same X, find P(X ≥ 4).

P(X >= 4) = 1 - P(X <= 3)
P(X <= 3) = 0.049787(1 + 3 + 4.5 + 4.5) = 0.6472
so P(X >= 4) = 0.3528

Worked example 3 (scale change). Calls arrive at 4 per minute. Find the probability of 10 or more calls in two minutes.

the rate scales with the interval: λ = 8 for two minutes
P(X >= 10) = 1 - P(X <= 9) = 1 - 0.7170 = 0.2830

Scaling is the most common source of avoidable error: the parameter must be expressed for the interval the question actually asks about.

Adding independent Poisson variables

If two independent counts each follow a Poisson distribution, their sum does too, and the parameters add. This is why the distribution is so usable: a total across separate sources needs no convolution.

X ~ Po(l1), Y ~ Po(l2), independent
X + Y ~ Po(l1 + l2)
but X - Y is NOT Poisson

Worked example. A website gets 5 hits per minute from Europe and 3 per minute from Asia, independently. Find the probability of more than 10 hits in a minute in total.

total ~ Po(8)
P(X > 10) = 1 - P(X <= 10) = 1 - 0.8159 = 0.1841

The Poisson as an approximation to the binomial

When n is large and p is small, the binomial is well approximated by a Poisson with λ = np. The rule of thumb used in this course is n > 50 and p < 0.05, or np < 5.

X ~ B(n, p) with n large, p small  →  X is approximately Po(np)

Worked example. A factory produces items with a 2% defect rate. In a batch of 200, use a Poisson approximation to find the probability of at most 2 defects.

λ = 200 × 0.02 = 4
P(X <= 2) = e^(-4)(1 + 4 + 8) = 0.018316 × 13 = 0.2381
the exact binomial gives 0.2351, so the approximation is close

Worked example 2 (justifying the approximation). State why the approximation is reasonable here.

n = 200 is large and p = 0.02 is small, with np = 4
so the rare-event limit conditions hold

Hypothesis testing with the Poisson

The structure is identical to the binomial test: state hypotheses, assume the null rate, compute the tail probability, compare with the significance level. The only new step is that the rate may need scaling to the observed interval.

H0: λ = lambda0    H1: λ > lambda0 (or <)
observed count x in the interval
p-value = P(X >= x) or P(X <= x) under Po(lambda0)
reject H0 if the p-value <= the significance level

Worked example. A call centre historically receives 6 calls per hour. In a new hour it receives 12. Test at the 5% level whether the rate has increased.

H0: λ = 6;  H1: λ > 6
X ~ Po(6) under H0
P(X >= 12) = 1 - P(X <= 11) = 1 - 0.9799 = 0.0201
0.0201 < 0.05, so reject H0
there is evidence the rate has increased

Worked example 2 (critical region). For Po(6), find the 5% one-tailed critical region for an increase.

P(X >= 11) = 0.0426 (below 0.05)
P(X >= 10) = 0.0839 (above 0.05)
critical region: X >= 11

Worked example 3 (two intervals). The same centre observes 16 calls over two hours. Test for an increase at 5%.

expected over two hours under H0 = 12, so X ~ Po(12)
P(X >= 16) = 1 - P(X <= 15) = 1 - 0.8444 = 0.1556
0.1556 > 0.05, so do not reject H0

Compare the two: twelve calls in one hour was significant, sixteen in two hours is not, because the expected count doubled. The rate, not the raw count, is what is being tested.

Reading the distribution's shape

The Poisson is skewed to the right when λ is small and becomes almost symmetric as λ grows, which is why small-rate questions usually live in the lower tail and why the normal approximation becomes usable once λ passes about 20. Knowing the shape tells you at a glance whether an answer is plausible: a probability of 0.4 for "more than 10" when λ = 3 should feel wrong before any arithmetic is checked.

A useful sanity check is that the standard deviation is the square root of the mean. For Po(9) the mean is 9 and the standard deviation 3, so counts between 6 and 12 are ordinary and a count of 20 is roughly three and a half standard deviations out — surprising enough to prompt a hypothesis test. That comparison is what turns a bare probability into an interpretation, and interpretation marks are the easiest ones to lose.

Finally, note that the model is about a count in an interval, so the interval has to be defined in the answer. "Three calls per hour" and "three calls per minute" describe different distributions, and a rate quoted per unit time without its unit is not a λ at all.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Definition) State two conditions for a Poisson model. Answer: events occur singly at random, independently, at a constant rate.
  2. (Single value) X ~ Po(2.5): find P(X = 3). Answer: P(X = 3) = e^(−λ)λ³/3! = e^(−2.5) × 15.625/6 = 0.0821 × 2.604 = 0.2138.
  3. (Cumulative) X ~ Po(4): find P(X ≤ 2). Answer: P(X ≤ 2) = e^(−4)(1 + 4 + 8) = 0.0183 × 13 = 0.2381.
  4. (Complement) X ~ Po(5): find P(X ≥ 3). Answer: P(X ≥ 3) = 1 − P(X ≤ 2) = 1 − e^(−5)(1 + 5 + 12.5) = 1 − 0.1247 = 0.8753.
  5. (Scaling) Rate 3 per hour: find P(X = 0) in 20 minutes. Answer: the rate scales with the interval: λ = 3 × 20/60 = 1, so P(X = 0) = e^(−1) = 0.3679.
  6. (Sum) Independent Po(2) and Po(3): find P(total = 4). Answer: independent Poisson variables add, so T ~ Po(2 + 3) = Po(5) and P(T = 4) = e^(−5)5⁴/4! = 0.1755.
  7. (Approximation) B(500, 0.01): approximate P(X = 0). Answer: n is large and p small, so use Po(λ = np = 5): P(X = 0) ≈ e^(−5) = 0.00674.
  8. (Mean/variance) A sample has mean 4.2 and variance 9.1. Comment on the Poisson fit. Answer: variance far exceeds the mean, so the model is doubtful (over-dispersed).
  9. (Test) 9 events observed where 4 expected; test for an increase at 5%. Answer: under H₀, X ~ Po(4); P(X ≥ 9) = 1 − P(X ≤ 8) = 0.0214 < 0.05, so reject H₀ — the observed rate is significantly higher.
  10. (Critical region) Po(3), 5% upper tail: find the critical region. Answer: P(X ≥ 6) = 0.0839 and P(X ≥ 7) = 0.0335; the largest region still at or below 5% starts at 7, so the critical region is X ≥ 7.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Using the wrong interval: λ must match the window asked about; doubling a time doubles the rate.
  • Complement off by one: P(X ≥ 4) = 1 − P(X ≤ 3); subtracting P(X ≤ 4) is the classic error.
  • Treating a difference as Poisson: sums of independent Poisson variables are Poisson, differences are not.
  • Approximation outside its range: np must be small; with np large the Poisson is a poor fit to the binomial.
  • Variance assumed equal to the mean without checking: the test mean = variance is a diagnostic, not a guarantee.
  • Ignoring clustering: events that arrive in bursts break the single-event condition and inflate the variance.
  • r! miscomputed: 0! = 1 and 1! = 1, and a missing factorial term changes the answer entirely.
  • p-value direction: a one-tailed test uses one tail only; doubling it makes a borderline result look significant.

Choosing between a Poisson and a binomial model

Both models count things, and both are discrete, so the choice is a common source of lost marks. The question is always what is fixed: a number of trials, or a length of time, area or volume.

Fixed trials or a continuous window

A binomial model counts successes among a fixed number n of trials, such as 20 items inspected or 12 people surveyed. A Poisson model counts events in a continuous interval, such as calls in an hour or flaws along a metre of wire, where there is no fixed number of trials to count out.

Using the wording of the question

Phrases such as “out of 40” or “of 15 chosen at random” point to a binomial. Phrases such as “in a period of”, “per kilometre” or “per square metre” point to a Poisson. When the wording is unclear, ask whether you could list the trials in advance; if you could, the model is binomial.

Variance as a clue

The binomial variance is np(1 − p), which is smaller than its mean np by the factor 1 − p. The Poisson variance equals its mean. So when p is not small, a Poisson model overstates the spread, and the binomial is the better fit.

A worked choice: binomial

A quality checker tests 40 bolts from a line, and each bolt is faulty independently with probability 0.08. The number of bolts is fixed at 40, so X ~ B(40, 0.08). A Poisson with the same mean would have variance 3.2 instead of 2.944, which is close here, but the binomial is the model the question describes.

A worked choice: Poisson

Bacteria colonies appear on a plate at random, and the average number per square centimetre is known. The area of the plate is not a number of trials, so the count is a Poisson variable with λ proportional to the area of the region counted. Nothing about the plate fixes how many colonies there will be.

Stating the choice in the answer

Write the model as the first line of the solution, with its reason: “X ~ B(40, 0.08), because the sample size is fixed at 40”. A marker can only credit a choice that is written down, and the reason is often worth a mark on its own.

Setting λ for the interval in the question

λ is the mean count for the interval the question asks about, and that interval is often not the one in which the rate is given. Most wrong answers on Poisson questions come from using a rate for the wrong length of time or distance.

The rate and the interval

If events occur at a rate r per unit of time and the question concerns an interval of length t in the same unit, then λ = rt. The rate and the interval must use the same unit before you multiply.

Scaling down to a shorter interval

Calls arrive at 6 per hour. For a 10-minute interval, the time is one sixth of an hour, so λ = 6 × 10/60 = 1. The probability of no calls in those 10 minutes is then e⁻¹ = 0.3679, not e⁻⁶.

Scaling up to a longer interval

Defects occur at 1.5 per kilometre of cable. For a 8 km stretch, λ = 1.5 × 8 = 12. Doubling the length doubles the mean, and the variance doubles with it, so a longer stretch is more spread out as well as higher.

Rates per area or volume

Flaws appear at 3 per square metre on a sheet. For a region of 4.5 m², λ = 3 × 4.5 = 13.5. The same method works for volume, provided the rate is given per unit of volume and the region is measured in the same units.

Keeping λ and the interval together

λ has no unit of its own because it is a count, but it always refers to a named interval. Writing “λ = 3 for 15 minutes” keeps the reference; writing a bare “λ = 3” invites the wrong interval to be used later in the same question.

A worked example

Emails arrive at a server at 12 per hour, at random and independently. Find the probability of exactly 2 arrivals in a 15-minute period. The interval is 0.25 hours, so λ = 12 × 0.25 = 3. Then P(X = 2) = e⁻³ × 3²/2! = 0.2240, which matches the value a student gets by scaling the rate first, not by using 12 directly.

Equations and symbols

One formula does the arithmetic, and one identity checks the model: for a Poisson variable the mean and the variance are the same number λ. Every exam error on this topic is either a λ expressed for the wrong interval or a complement taken one term too far.

P(X = r) = e^(-λ) λ^r / r! Key: X = the number of events counted in the fixed interval (a count, no units); r = the particular count asked about; λ = the mean number of events in that same interval (no units — it is a count, not a rate per second, unless the interval is one second); e = 2.71828…; r! = factorial of r, with 0! = 1.

mean E(X) = λ Key: E(X) = the expected count in the interval; λ = the mean. Read it with the line below: the equality of mean and variance is the fingerprint of the model, and a sample whose variance far exceeds its mean is not Poisson.

variance Var(X) = λ Key: Var(X) = the variance of the count; λ = the same mean. So the standard deviation is √λ, which is the quickest sanity check on an observed count: for λ = 9, counts between 6 and 12 are ordinary.

P(X >= r) = 1 - P(X <= r - 1) Key: the complement rule, because the Poisson has no upper limit; r = the smallest count that counts as "at least". Subtracting P(X ≤ r) instead of P(X ≤ r − 1) is the classic off-by-one and throws the whole tail away.

P = e^(-3) × 3² / 2! Key: λ = 3 for this interval; r = 2; 3² = λ^r; 2! = 2. The arithmetic is 0.049787 × 9 / 2 = 0.2240 — quote four decimal places unless told otherwise.

λ = 200 × 0.02 = 4 Key: 200 = n, the number of trials; 0.02 = p, the probability of the event in one trial; λ = np = 4, the mean of the approximating Poisson. The approximation is used when n is large and p small — n > 50 and p < 0.05, or np < 5.

P(X <= 2) = e^(-4)(1 + 4 + 8) = 0.018316 × 13 = 0.2381 Key: the bracket is λ^r/r! summed for r = 0, 1, 2: 1, 4 and 8 (since 4²/2! = 8); e^(−4) = 0.018316. The exact binomial gives 0.2351, so the approximation is close — say so when a question asks you to comment.

X + Y ~ Po(l1 + l2) Key: X and Y = two independent Poisson counts; l1, l2 = their means; the total count is Poisson with the means added. A difference of two Poisson variables is not Poisson — only sums combine.

X ~ B(n, p) with n large, p small → X is approximately Po(np) Key: B(n, p) = the binomial with n trials and success probability p; np = the Poisson mean that replaces them. State both conditions before using it, because the approximation fails when np is large.

SymbolQuantityUnit
λmean number of events in the stated intervala count (no units) — quote the interval with it
rthe observed or asked-about counta count (no units)
H₀null hypothesis, λ = λ₀a stated mean count for the interval

Scaling is the other half of the topic and it is not a formula but a substitution: a rate of 4 per minute is λ = 8 for a two-minute window, and 12 calls in one hour must be tested against 24 expected in two hours, not against 12. Write the interval beside the λ every time.

title: Reading for Information and Inference — Study Notes
content:
Reading questions reward two different skills: finding information that is stated, and working out what is implied. Keep them apart when you plan an answer.

Information: what the text says

Information questions ask for facts the writer states directly. Locate the key words in the question, scan the text for matching ideas, and copy only the words you need. Do not add personal comment unless the question asks for it.

Scanning for key words

  • Underline the nouns and verbs in the question.
  • Look for synonyms, because the text rarely repeats the question's exact words.
  • Check the line reference if one is given, then read a sentence either side to confirm the context.

Inference: what the text suggests

An inference is a conclusion supported by evidence. The writer does not state it, so you must show how the evidence points to it.

Building a strong inference

  • Choose a precise quotation or a short phrase.
  • Explain what the word or phrase suggests, using a verb such as suggests, implies or hints.
  • Link the suggestion back to the character, mood or idea the question asks about.

Common mistakes

  • Retelling the plot instead of explaining the evidence.
  • Quoting a long passage with no comment.
  • Stating a fact when the question asks for a feeling or an opinion.

Exam approach

Answer the information questions quickly and accurately, because they are worth marks for precision. Spend the most time on inference questions: one well-explained quotation usually earns more than three vague ones.

title: Data Structures — Study Notes
content:
`# Data Structures

Arrays and Lists

Contiguous, indexed, O(1) access; fixed size. 2D arrays: element (i, j) — rows × columns.

Stack (LIFO)

push/pop/peek at one end. Uses: call stacks, undo, expression evaluation, DFS.

Example: evaluating 3 4 + : push 3, push 4, pop both, push 7.

Queue (FIFO)

enqueue at rear, dequeue at front. Uses: print queues, schedulers, BFS. A circular queue reuses vacated slots with head/tail pointers modulo capacity.

Linked List

Nodes with data + pointer. Insert/delete O(1) at a known node; search O(n). Traversal follows next pointers until null.

Hash Table

Hash function maps keys → index. Collisions resolved by chaining or open addressing. Average O(1) lookup, worst O(n).

Complexity

OperationArrayLinked ListHash
Access by indexO(1)O(n)—
SearchO(n)O(n)O(1) avg
Insert/deleteO(n)O(1)O(1) avg

Exam tips: trace pointers carefully in linked-list diagrams; for circular queues, show head/tail movement and overflow/underflow checks.

Two-dimensional arrays and records

A two-dimensional array stores values in rows and columns, and each element is found with two indexes, usually written A[row, column]. A table of marks for five students in three subjects is a 5 by 3 array. Indexes normally start at 0, so the last element of an array with 8 elements has index 7.

A record groups fields of different data types under one name. A student record might hold a name as a string, an age as an integer and a pass flag as a Boolean. An array of records lets a program store a whole list of students, each with several fields, in one structure.

Exam tip: an array holds one data type throughout, while a record can mix types. Say this when asked to compare them.

Worked example: a stack trace

Start with an empty stack. Push A, push B and push C, so the stack holds A, B, C with C on top. Pop returns C, and a second pop returns B. Push D, and the stack now holds A and D. A trace table with one row per operation is the method examiners expect in a trace question.

Choosing a structure

  • Use a queue for tasks processed in arrival order, such as a print queue.
  • Use a stack for reversing data, undo operations and backtracking, because the last item added is the first removed.
  • Use a hash table for fast lookup by key. A good hash gives average-case constant-time access, but collisions must be handled, usually by chaining or open addressing.

Linked list pointers

Each node holds a data item and a pointer to the next node. Inserting or deleting a node means changing pointers rather than moving elements, so the change is quick once the position is known. Finding a node by its position still means following pointers from the start of the list, which is a linear search.

Exam point: state the behaviour precisely. Describing a queue as first in, last out loses the mark; the correct description is first in, first out (FIFO).

title: Organic Chemistry: Arenes
content:
Quick revision: Organic Chemistry: Arenes

Chemistry — A2 Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH15 Topic 18. This topic covers the structure and stability of arenes, electrophilic substitution mechanisms, and the reactivity differences between benzene, alkenes, and phenol.

  • Structure and stability: thermochemical, X-ray diffraction and infrared data prove benzene is a planar regular hexagon with intermediate carbon-carbon bond lengths, supported by the delocalised model involving side-on overlap of p-orbitals to form pi-bonds.
  • Reactivity difference: benzene is resistant to bromination compared to alkenes due to the delocalised ring of six pi electrons having lower electron density than the localised pi-bond in alkenes, preventing electrophilic addition.
  • Reactions of benzene: combustion with oxygen in air forming a smoky flame; halogenation with bromine in the presence of a catalyst; nitration using a mixture of concentrated nitric and sulfuric acids; sulfonation using fuming sulfuric acid; Friedel-Crafts alkylation and acylation using halogenoalkanes and acyl chlorides with aluminium chloride as a catalyst.
  • Electrophilic substitution mechanisms: halogenation, nitration, and Friedel-Crafts reactions proceed via electrophilic substitution, which includes the vital step of generating the electrophile using a catalyst.
  • Phenol reactivity: phenol reacts readily with bromine water at room temperature without a catalyst, producing 2,4,6-tribromophenol, due to the overlapping of a lone pair of electrons from the oxygen atom into the pi system, increasing electron density on the ring.

Worked example

Describe the generation of the electrophile and the mechanism for the nitration of benzene. Step 1: React concentrated nitric acid with concentrated sulfuric acid to generate the nitronium ion electrophile: HNO3 + 2H2SO4 yields NO2(+) + 2HSO4(−) + H3O(+). Step 2: The pi electrons of benzene attack the electrophile to form an unstable intermediate. Step 3: A hydrogen ion is lost to restore the stable delocalised ring, yielding nitrobenzene and regenerating the sulfuric acid catalyst.

Key points to remember

Students often forget that benzene undergoes substitution rather than addition because addition destroys the stable delocalised pi system, whereas substitution preserves it.

Always state the catalyst explicitly in Friedel-Crafts and halogenation reactions, noting that aluminium chloride acts as a Lewis acid catalyst to generate strong electrophiles.

Remember that phenol is far more reactive than benzene towards electrophilic attack because the oxygen lone pair is partially delocalised into the pi system, activating the ring.

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

title: IGCSE Chemistry: Electrochemistry
content:
IGCSE Chemistry: Electrochemistry

Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry 0620 (2026–2028), Extended route, Topic 4 Electrochemistry: statement 4.1 Electrolysis and 4.2 Hydrogen–oxygen fuel cells. Electrolysis is chemistry driven by electricity — forced electron movement — and every question asks three things: what is the electrolyte, what forms at each electrode, and why. The product rules below are derived from ion behaviour, not memorised lists, and every half-equation is balanced for atoms and charge.

What electrolysis is

Electrolysis is the breakdown of an ionic compound (molten or aqueous) by passing electricity through it. Vocabulary: the electrolyte is the ionic compound that conducts when molten or in solution (ions free to move); the cathode is the negative electrode (reduction: cations are attracted to it); the anode is the positive electrode (oxidation: anions are attracted to it). Electrons flow through the wires; ions carry the charge through the liquid.

The electron bookkeeping, spelled out:

  CATHODE (negative): positive ions (cations) drift here.
    Each cation GAINS electrons → reduction:  Mⁿ⁺ + n e⁻ → M
  ANODE (positive): negative ions (anions) drift here.
    Each anion LOSES electrons → oxidation:  X⁻ → X + e⁻

  Mnemonic that never fails: OIL RIG
    Oxidation Is Loss (of electrons) - at the ANODE
    Reduction Is Gain - at the CATHODE

  And the electrode names:
    PANC - Positive Anode, Negative Cathode.

Molten electrolysis

Case study: molten lead(II) bromide, PbBr₂ (electrolysis of the melt)

  Ions present: Pb²⁺ and Br⁻

  CATHODE: Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb(l)    [lead metal, grey liquid]
    OBSERVATION: grey molten lead collects.
  ANODE:   2Br⁻ → Br₂(g) + 2e⁻    [bromine vapour]
    OBSERVATION: orange-brown vapour with choking smell.

  Overall: PbBr₂ → Pb + Br₂  (electrons supplied by the circuit)

General molten-binary rule: the METAL forms at the cathode (reduced);
the NON-METAL forms at the anode (oxidised).

Aqueous electrolysis: the competition

In solution, water provides H⁺ and OH⁻ alongside the salt's ions, so both electrodes have competing species. The rules, applied in order:

  • Cathode: the less reactive ion is discharged (e.g. copper over hydrogen in copper sulfate); if the metal is above hydrogen (Na, K, Ca, Mg, Al), hydrogen is discharged from water.
  • Anode: concentrated halide solutions give halogen (Cl₂ from concentrated NaCl); otherwise (sulfate, nitrate, dilute solutions) hydroxide/oxygen is discharged from water.
Three standard aqueous cases, worked:

1. Concentrated sodium chloride solution (brine):
   CATHODE: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂(g)         [hydrogen - sodium is too reactive]
   ANODE:   2Cl⁻ → Cl₂(g) + 2e⁻        [chlorine - concentrated halide]
   Left in solution: NaOH (sodium hydroxide) - a useful by-product.
   Uses: chlorine (water treatment, plastics), hydrogen (ammonia), NaOH.

2. Dilute sulfuric acid (electrolysis of water):
   CATHODE: 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂
   ANODE:   2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻  (or 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻)
   Volume ratio H₂ : O₂ = 2 : 1 (the classic exam volume question).

3. Aqueous copper(II) sulfate with INERT (platinum/graphite) electrodes:
   CATHODE: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu(s)        [copper coats the electrode]
   ANODE:   4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻    [oxygen bubbles; solution goes
                                         acidic as Cu²⁺ removed and H⁺
                                         remains from water]

   With COPPER electrodes (electroplating setup):
   CATHODE: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu          [object being plated gains copper]
   ANODE:   Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻          [copper anode dissolves, refilling
                                        the solution - the classic
                                        electroplating arrangement]

Ionic half-equation discipline: atoms balanced first, then charges balanced
with electrons on the correct side (right for oxidation, left for reduction).
ElectrolyteElectrodesCathode productAnode product
Molten PbBr₂InertLead (Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb)Bromine (2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻)
Conc. NaCl(aq)InertHydrogen (2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂)Chlorine (2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻)
Dilute H₂SO₄(aq)InertHydrogenOxygen (2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻)
CuSO₄(aq)InertCopper (Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu)Oxygen (from OH⁻)
CuSO₄(aq)Copper anodeCopperNone — anode dissolves (Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻)

Electroplating

Electroplating coats an object with a thin layer of another metal (cutlery with chromium, jewellery with silver, cans with tin) — for appearance, corrosion resistance and reduced cost. The object is the cathode; the plating metal is the anode; the electrolyte contains the plating metal's ions. Its purpose in the syllabus: protection, looks and cost.

Hydrogen–oxygen fuel cells

The fuel cell reaction, both half-equations:

  At the anode (hydrogen side):  2H₂ → 4H⁺ + 4e⁻
  At the cathode (oxygen side):  O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O
  Overall:  2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O     (electrical energy + heat - a redox
                                   reaction whose electrons travel through
                                   an external circuit instead of direct
                                   contact)

  Key point: the ONLY product is WATER - no CO₂ at the point of use.

Comparison with petrol engines (the "advantages and disadvantages" question):
  + no pollutants at point of use (only water),
  + more efficient than combustion engines (no thermal cycle limits),
  + refuel in minutes (unlike battery charging).
  - hydrogen storage is hard (high pressure/low temperature; bulky tanks),
  - hydrogen is usually made from natural gas (so CO₂ is emitted at the
    production stage) unless made by electrolysis with renewables,
  - fuel cells and hydrogen infrastructure are expensive.

Worked example: predicting products systematically

Question: predict all products of electrolysis of aqueous copper(II) sulfate
with copper electrodes, and write the equations.

Step 1 - ions in solution: Cu²⁺, SO₄²⁻, and from water H⁺, OH⁻.
Step 2 - cathode (reduction): competing Cu²⁺ and H⁺; copper is BELOW
  hydrogen in the reactivity series, so Cu²⁺ is discharged:
    Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu
Step 3 - anode (oxidation): sulfate is not discharged; OH⁻ from water would
  give O₂ - BUT the anode is copper, and the copper anode OXIDISES first:
    Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻
Step 4 - overall: copper is transferred from anode to cathode (electroplating
  geometry). The solution concentration stays constant (Cu²⁺ lost at the
  cathode is replaced from the anode).
Observations: cathode gains mass (reddish coating); anode loses mass.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Swapping electrodes: cathode is negative (reduction of cations); anode is positive (oxidation of anions) — PANC and OIL RIG together prevent this.
  • Putting electrons on the wrong side of half-equations (reduction gains them — left; oxidation loses — right) or leaving charge unbalanced.
  • Ignoring the "concentrated" in brine questions: dilute NaCl gives oxygen at the anode, not chlorine.
  • Discharging the reactive metal (Na) instead of hydrogen at the cathode in aqueous solutions.
  • Forgetting the electrodes' material in aqueous cases: copper anodes dissolve rather than producing oxygen.
  • Claiming fuel cells produce "no products" — water is the product; and ignoring that hydrogen production may still emit CO₂.
  • Misreading gas volumes: electrolysis of dilute acid gives H₂:O₂ = 2:1 by volume (twice as much hydrogen).

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 4, 3 marks). Define electrolysis and name the electrode where reduction occurs.

Answer: Electrolysis is the decomposition of an ionic compound (molten or aqueous) by passing an electric current through it. Reduction occurs at the cathode (the negative electrode), where cations gain electrons.

Question 2 (Paper 4, 5 marks). Write the half-equations and observations for the electrolysis of molten lead(II) bromide.

Answer: Cathode: Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb — grey molten lead collects. Anode: 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻ — orange-brown bromine vapour forms. The melt conducts because its ions are free to move; lead forms because Pb²⁺ ions are reduced at the negative electrode.

Question 3 (Paper 4, 5 marks). Predict the products of electrolysis of concentrated aqueous sodium chloride and explain each choice.

Answer: Cathode: hydrogen (2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂) — sodium is more reactive than hydrogen, so H⁺ from water is discharged. Anode: chlorine (2Cl⁻ → Cl₂) — the solution is concentrated in chloride, which is discharged in preference to hydroxide. Sodium hydroxide remains in solution. Both gases are industrially useful.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 3 marks). Describe the electrolysis of aqueous copper(II) sulfate with copper electrodes.

Answer: The copper anode dissolves (Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻) and copper is deposited on the cathode (Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu), transferring copper from anode to object — the electroplating arrangement. The blue colour of the solution stays constant because Cu²⁺ is replenished at the anode.

Question 5 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Write the electrode reactions in a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell and state one advantage and one disadvantage versus petrol.

Answer: Anode: 2H₂ → 4H⁺ + 4e⁻. Cathode: O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O. Overall 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. Advantage: the only product is water, so no pollutants at the point of use. Disadvantage: hydrogen is hard to store safely and is currently mostly produced from natural gas, which generates CO₂.

Question 6 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Explain why a copper coating is applied to a steel object and how the setup is arranged.

Answer: The copper coating improves appearance and protects the steel from corrosion at lower cost than solid copper. The steel object is made the cathode, a copper anode is used, and the electrolyte is aqueous copper(II) sulfate (or acidified copper sulfate): Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu deposits on the object while the anode dissolves, keeping the ion concentration constant.

The final pillar of the course is the laboratory itself — the techniques and analyses that Paper 6 tests in writing.

title: Number — Indices and Standard Form — Study Notes
content:
Number — Indices and Standard Form

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): index laws, negative and fractional indices, standard form arithmetic, surds and rationalising denominators.

1. Index laws

  • aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ; aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ; (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ
  • a⁰ = 1; a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ; a^(1/n) = ⁿ√a; a^(m/n) = (ⁿ√a)ᵐ

Examples: 27^(2/3) = (³√27)² = 9; 5⁻² = 1/25; (2x³)² = 4x⁶.

2. Standard form

a × 10ⁿ with 1 ≤ a < 10.

  • 47 382 = 4.7382 × 10⁴; 0.0056 = 5.6 × 10⁻³
  • Multiplication: multiply a's, add powers. Division: divide a's, subtract powers.

Example: (3 × 10⁵) × (4 × 10⁻²) = 12 × 10³ = 1.2 × 10⁴.

3. Calculator use

Use the ×10ˣ key, not 10 ^; keep working in standard form and convert at the end. Give final answers in the form asked (often 3 s.f. standard form).

4. Solving index equations

Match bases: 2ˣ = 32 ⇒ 2ˣ = 2⁵ ⇒ x = 5. With different bases, rewrite (8 = 2³).

5. Surds

A surd is a root that cannot be written as a rational number: √2, √3, 3√5.

  • Rules: √a × √b = √(ab); √a ÷ √b = √(a/b); (√a)² = a.
  • Simplify by taking out the largest square factor: √50 = √25 × √2 = 5√2; √72 = 6√2; √(9/16) = 3/4.
  • Add and subtract like surds: √18 + √8 = 3√2 + 2√2 = 5√2. Unlike surds cannot be combined: 2√3 + √5 stays as it is.
  • Rationalise the denominator so no root is left below the line: 6/√3 = 6√3/3 = 2√3; 1/(3 + √2) = (3 − √2) / ((3 + √2)(3 − √2)) = (3 − √2)/7 — multiply top and bottom by the conjugate.
  • Expanding: (2 + √3)(2 − √3) = 4 − 3 = 1; difference of two squares clears the surd.

Example: write √12 + √75 in the form k√3 → 2√3 + 5√3 = 7√3.

Exam tips: check a is in [1, 10) before writing standard form; in "multiply out" questions apply the power to every factor including coefficients.

title: Astronomy and Cosmology — Study Notes
content:
Astronomy and Cosmology

Luminosity and Intensity

Luminosity L is total power radiated (W). Intensity at distance d: I = L/(4πd²) — the key to distances.

Standard candles (Cepheid variables, Type Ia supernovae) have known L, so measuring I gives d.

Example: the Sun: I = 1370 W m⁻² at d = 1.5 × 10¹¹ m gives L ≈ 3.9 × 10²⁶ W.

Stellar radii (25.2)

A star radiates as a black body of surface temperature T, so L = 4πR²σT⁴. Rearranged, R = √(L / 4πσT⁴). Luminosity therefore depends on both radius and temperature.

Example: with L = 3.9 × 10²⁶ W and T = 5800 K, R = √(3.9 × 10²⁶ / (4π × 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ × 5800⁴)) ≈ 7.0 × 10⁸ m.

Doubling the temperature at fixed radius multiplies L by 2⁴ = 16. A cool red giant can be far more luminous than the Sun because its radius is very large.

Wien and Stefan–Boltzmann

  • Wien: λ_max T = 2.9 × 10⁻³ m K — hotter stars are bluer
  • Stefan: L = σAT⁴, σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸

Hubble's Law

Galaxies recede with v = Hd, H₀ ≈ 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹. Redshift z = Δλ/λ ≈ v/c for small z.

Example: a galaxy at 100 Mpc recedes at v = 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ × 100 × 3.09 × 10²² ≈ 6800 km s⁻¹.

The Big Bang

Evidence: Hubble expansion, cosmic microwave background (2.7 K), hydrogen/helium abundance. Age estimate: t ≈ 1/H₀ ≈ 14 billion years. The fate question: critical density, Ω.

Exam tips: convert Mpc to metres (×3.09 × 10²²) before Hubble arithmetic; distinguish redshift of light from distance ladder methods.

Standard candles and the cosmic distance ladder

A standard candle is an object whose luminosity is known, such as a Type Ia supernova or a Cepheid variable star. Comparing its known luminosity with its observed brightness gives its distance, using the inverse-square law. Stellar radii can be found in the same way: the luminosity L = 4πR2σT4 links radius, surface temperature and output power.

Exam tip: state which assumption you are making, such as that the star radiates as a black body, before you calculate the radius.

title: IGCSE Computer Science: Algorithm Design and Problem-Solving
content:
IGCSE Computer Science: Algorithm Design and Problem-Solving

Cambridge IGCSE Computer Science 0478 (2026–2028), Paper 2 Algorithms, Programming and Logic, statement 7 Algorithm design and problem-solving. Writing code is the last 20% of the job; this note is the other 80% — decomposition, abstraction, stepwise refinement, algorithm design and representation, and the testing that proves it works. Every refinement below is shown stage by stage, and the trace tables demonstrate the dry-run technique examiners expect you to produce under time pressure.

The problem-solving cycle

  • 1. Analyse the problem — state precisely what is wanted: the inputs, the required outputs, and any constraints (data ranges, time limits, the algorithm's likely size).
  • 2. Design — decompose into subtasks and design each algorithm (structure charts, pseudocode, flowcharts).
  • 3. Refine — develop each subtask stepwise until every step is a statement a coder could translate directly.
  • 4. Write the code — translate the refined design into a programming language.
  • 5. Test — run normal, boundary, erroneous and extreme data; compare results with expectations.
  • 6. Maintain — fix discovered bugs, adapt to new requirements, improve performance.

Skipping to step 4 is the failure mode this statement exists to cure: code written without a design is where logic errors breed.

Abstraction and decomposition

Decomposition breaks a big problem into smaller, independently solvable subproblems — planning a school trip becomes booking transport, booking accommodation, collecting money, producing a register. Each subtask is solved on its own and recombined. Abstraction is deliberately ignoring detail that does not matter to the task: a seat-booking system models seat numbers and states but not the fabric colour of the seats. Together they keep designs comprehensible — the exam wants a structure chart with named subtasks, not just prose.

Decomposition worked example: a school sports-day results system.

Level 0 (whole problem): record events, score house points, print winners.
Level 1 subtasks:
  1. Input event results (validation included)
  2. Convert places to house points
  3. Accumulate house totals
  4. Determine and print the winning house

Each level-1 subtask decomposes again - refinement of subtask 2:
  2.1  read the event's placing (1st, 2nd, 3rd)
  2.2  look up the points for that placing (5, 3, 1)
  2.3  add the points to the correct house total
  2.4  repeat for each event

At the end of refinement every leaf step is a single statement - that is the
stopping rule for stepwise refinement.

Stepwise refinement

Refinement turns an outline into detail in stages, keeping each stage reviewable. Start with one line; expand the hardest or vaguest part into steps; expand those; stop when each step is trivially translatable. The trace at each stage catches errors while they are cheap.

Refinement stages: "find the mean of a set of numbers".

Stage 0 (outline):     get the numbers, compute the mean, print it.

Stage 1:
  initialise total and count
  get the numbers, adding each to the total and counting it
  compute mean <- total / count
  print mean

Stage 2 (final pseudocode):
  1  total <- 0
  2  count <- 0
  3  INPUT num
  4  WHILE num <> -1              [-1 as a sentinel value meaning "no more"]
  5      total <- total + num
  6      count <- count + 1
  7      INPUT num
  8  ENDWHILE
  9  IF count > 0 THEN
 10      mean <- total / count
 11      OUTPUT mean
 12  ELSE
 13      OUTPUT "no data entered"
 14  ENDIF

Note what refinement surfaced: the empty-input case (line 9). Division by zero
would have been a runtime failure - refinement finds these before coding.

The sentinel (-1) is one way to end input; alternatives are a known count (read exactly n values) or an end-of-file test. State which you use and make sure the sentinel can never be legitimate data.

Representing algorithms

FormWhat it showsBest for
Structure chartWhole problem decomposed into named subtasks and their data linksThe overview; planning who does what
PseudocodeThe logic in structured, language-independent statementsPrecise design and exam answers
FlowchartFlow of control visually: oval start/stop, parallelogram I/O, rectangle process, diamond decisionShowing branches and loops at a glance
Trace tableVariable values statement by statement for given inputsProving correctness before coding
The same algorithm as a flowchart text sketch: reading marks until -1 and
counting passes (mark >= 40).

  (start) → [passes <- 0] → [INPUT mark] → <mark = -1?>
      | no                         | yes
      v                            v
  <mark >= 40?> --yes-→ [passes <- passes + 1] --+
      | no                                       |
      +------------------------------------------+
                                                 v
                                    [INPUT mark] → loop back to <mark = -1?>
  (stop) <- [OUTPUT passes]

Note the two diamonds in sequence: the loop test runs first on every value,
including the very first, and the sentinel is tested BEFORE the pass test so
-1 is never counted as a fail.

Trace tables and dry running

A trace table proves the design with real data before any code runs. One column per variable; one row per statement executed (loops repeat rows); outputs recorded as they happen. Always test at least: normal data, boundary data, and erroneous data.

Trace: count how many of 5 numbers exceed their predecessor.

  1  count <- 0
  2  INPUT previous
  3  FOR i <- 2 TO 5
  4      INPUT current
  5      IF current > previous THEN
  6          count <- count + 1
  7      ENDIF
  8      previous <- current
  9  NEXT i
 10  OUTPUT count

Inputs: 10, 15, 15, 9, 20

Step    i   previous  current  count   comment
1                             0
2             10⁰
3       2      10⁰
4       2      10¹⁵     0
5       2      10¹⁵     0   15 > 10 TRUE
6       2      10¹⁵     1
8       2      15      15     1   previous tracks the latest
3       3      15             1
4       3      15      15     1
5       3      15      15     1   15 > 15 FALSE (equal is not greater)
8       3      15      15     1
3       4      15             1
4       4      15       9     1
5       4      15       9     1   9 > 15 FALSE
8       4       9       9     1
3       5       9             1
4       5       9      20     1
5       5       9      20     1   20 > 9 TRUE
6       5       9      20     2
8       5      20      20     2
10                        output 2

Boundary check: equal neighbours (15, 15) must NOT count - that row is the one
markers look for.

Testing

  • Normal (valid) data — typical values that should work; checks the happy path.
  • Boundary (extreme) data — values at the edges of validity (0 and 100 for marks, exactly at a threshold); most bugs live here.
  • Erroneous (invalid) data — values the program should reject (negative marks, letters where numbers are expected); checks validation and error handling.

Test data should be chosen deliberately with an expected result stated for each test before running it — otherwise you are checking what the program does, not what it should do. For the mean example above: normal (2, 4, 6 → mean 4), boundary (one value only → the value itself), erroneous (sentinel entered first → "no data entered", not a division by zero).

Iterative (agile) development is examined here too: develop in small iterations, each designing, coding and testing one subtask, then review with the client before the next. Advantages: working software early, changing requirements absorbed cheaply, frequent feedback and testing built in; disadvantages: unclear final scope and budget, and endless change without discipline. Against waterfall (one linear design→build→test→release pass): clear milestones and documentation, but late testing and expensive changes once built.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Jumping straight to code: marks are for analysis, decomposition and refinement stages — show them.
  • Decomposition that is too shallow: subtasks must reach single-statement steps ("input the numbers" is a subtask, not a refinement).
  • Test data without expected outputs; and boundary values are worth as many marks as the normal case.
  • Forgetting the empty-input and division-by-zero case in averages — the most-missed validation mark in Paper 2.
  • Sentinel values that collide with real data (using -1 to stop, when -1 is a valid score).
  • Trace tables that skip loop repetitions or show only the final value; markers want the statement-by-statement rows.
  • Confusing validation (is the data in range?) with verification (is the data the right data — e.g. double entry).
  • Listing agile benefits alone; the question usually wants the comparison against a linear model stated explicitly.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 2, 4 marks). Explain what is meant by decomposition and abstraction, giving an example of each.

Answer: Decomposition splits a problem into smaller subproblems that can be solved separately — an online shop system breaks into stock control, basket, payment and delivery subsystems. Abstraction ignores details irrelevant to the problem — the basket subsystem models items and quantities but not the warehouse's shelf colours, so the design stays manageable.

Question 2 (Paper 2, 4 marks). Refine the step "process the order" into structured pseudocode.

Answer: READ order lines from the file; FOR each line: check the item is in stock; IF in stock THEN add the line total (price × quantity) to orderTotal and reduce stock; ELSE record the item as out of stock; NEXT; apply any discount to orderTotal; OUTPUT orderTotal and the out-of-stock list.

Question 3 (Paper 2, 3 marks). State three types of test data and give one example of each for a program accepting a mark between 0 and 100.

Answer: Normal data — a typical in-range value such as 65. Boundary data — the edge values 0 and 100 (and just outside, 101). Erroneous data — an invalid value such as -5 or the letter "A".

Question 4 (Paper 2, 4 marks). Explain why a trace table is produced before code is written.

Answer: A trace table executes the algorithm step by step on paper, recording each variable's value after every statement, so logic errors — infinite loops, wrong branch conditions, off-by-one errors — are found while the design is still cheap to change. It also provides the expected outputs used later as test data, so the coded program can be checked against a proven result.

Question 5 (Paper 2, 4 marks). Compare iterative development with a waterfall approach.

Answer: Iterative development builds in small cycles with client review after each, delivering working software early and absorbing requirement changes cheaply, at the cost of a less predictable final scope and budget. Waterfall completes each stage before the next, giving fixed milestones, clear documentation and easy planning, but testing happens late and changes after coding are expensive.

Question 6 (Paper 2, 5 marks). Write pseudocode that reads numbers until the user enters 0, then outputs the largest number entered (0 not counted).

Answer: largest <- 0; INPUT num; WHILE num <> 0; IF num > largest THEN; largest <- num; ENDIF; INPUT num; ENDWHILE; OUTPUT largest. (Assumes positive input; a full solution might flag if no positive number was entered.)

These design skills now apply to the two remaining Paper 2 domains: databases and Boolean logic.

title: Materials: Deformation — Study Notes
content:
Materials: deformation

Stress and strain

  • Stress = F ÷ A, where A is the cross-sectional area perpendicular to the force. Unit: pascal (Pa), where 1 Pa = 1 N m⁻².
  • Strain = extension ÷ original length. It has no unit.

Young modulus

Young modulus E = stress ÷ strain, measured in the region where stress is proportional to strain. Unit: Pa.

Force–extension behaviour

  • Up to the limit of proportionality, extension is proportional to force (Hooke's law), and the graph is a straight line through the origin.
  • Up to the elastic limit, the material returns to its original length when unloaded. This is elastic deformation.
  • Beyond the elastic limit, the material is plastically deformed and does not return to its original length. The graph curves, and the energy in the extension is not recovered.

Energy stored

The elastic energy stored in a stretched material equals the area under its force–extension graph up to the point of interest. For a spring obeying Hooke's law, E = ½Fx = ½kx².

Worked example: a wire of cross-sectional area 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ m² is pulled by 500 N. Stress = 500 ÷ (2.0 × 10⁻⁴) = 2.5 × 10⁶ Pa. If it extends by 1.0 mm from an original length of 2.0 m, strain = 0.001 ÷ 2.0 = 5.0 × 10⁻⁴, so E = 2.5 × 10⁶ ÷ 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ = 5.0 × 10⁹ Pa.

Exam tips: convert the area to m² and the extension to m before calculating. Strain has no unit, so do not write a unit for it. Say "the limit of proportionality" and "the elastic limit" as separate ideas.

Stored elastic energy and Hooke's law

Within the limit of proportionality, extension is proportional to force, F = kx, and the stiffness k depends on the material and its dimensions. The elastic strain energy stored in a stretched wire is equal to the area under the force-extension graph, E = ½Fx. For a material, the Young modulus E = stress / strain. Beyond the elastic limit the material deforms plastically and does not return to its original length.

Exam tip: state the limit of proportionality on the graph, because the energy formula only applies while the material obeys Hooke's law.

title: AS Level Physics: Waves
content:
AS Level Physics: Waves

Waves are how energy moves without matter moving with it — a statement that sounds abstract until you watch a crowd do the Mexican wave: the people stay in their seats while the disturbance travels the stadium. This note builds the full wave toolkit from zero: the vocabulary of progressive waves and the two graphs that encode them, the wave equation and its arithmetic, the difference between transverse and longitudinal waves, the Doppler effect for sound, the electromagnetic spectrum, and polarisation. Every quantity here is defined by how it is measured, and every calculation reduces to v = fλ applied carefully.

What a wave is: the rope and the stadium

Shake one end of a long rope: a crest travels to the far end, but the rope itself only moves up and down. That separation is the whole idea — a wave is a propagating disturbance that transfers energy and, in some cases, information, while the medium oscillates about fixed positions. Two families of wave carry the syllabus: mechanical waves (sound, water, waves on ropes — they need a medium) and electromagnetic waves (light, radio, X-rays — they need no medium and travel at c in vacuum).

Progressive waves: the vocabulary

A progressive wave transfers energy from place to place. Its quantities are defined on two graphs, and learning to read both is half the topic:

  • Displacement–distance graph (a snapshot, like a photograph of the rope): the horizontal axis is position along the wave, the vertical axis is displacement from equilibrium.
  • Displacement–time graph (one point's diary): the horizontal axis is time, the vertical axis is the displacement of a single particle.
QuantitySymbolDefinitionRead from which graph
Displacementx (m)distance of a particle from equilibrium, with directionvertical axis of both
AmplitudeA (m)maximum displacement from equilibriumpeak height (both)
Wavelengthλ (m)distance between two consecutive points in phase (crest to crest)distance graph: crest-to-crest
PeriodT (s)time for one complete oscillation of one particletime graph: one full cycle
Frequencyf (Hz)number of complete oscillations per second, f = 1/Tcalculated from T
Phase differenceφ (rad)fraction of a cycle between two points, in radians (2π per cycle)horizontal shift as a fraction of λ or T
Speedv (m s⁻¹)distance the disturbance travels per secondcalculated from v = fλ

Phase is worth an explicit definition because marks live there: two points are in phase when they are one or more whole wavelengths (or periods) apart — same displacement, moving in the same direction. They are in antiphase when separated by half a wavelength (π radians, 180°). A quarter wavelength is π/2 radians. The exam expects radians here.

The wave equation and its arithmetic

One speed, three expressions: in one period T a wave travels exactly one wavelength λ, so λ = vT and therefore

v = f λ        f = 1/T        λ = vT

Units discipline: v in m s⁻¹, f in Hz, λ in m. Convert before substituting: 3.4 cm = 0.034 m; 450 kHz = 4.5 × 10⁵ Hz.

Worked example 1. A wave on a rope has frequency 2.5 Hz and wavelength 1.20 m. Find its speed and period.

v = f λ = 2.5 x 1.20 = 3.0 m s-1
T = 1/f = 1/2.5 = 0.40 s

Worked example 2. A sound wave travels at 340 m s⁻¹ and has frequency 2.0 kHz. Find the wavelength in centimetres.

f = 2.0 kHz = 2000 Hz
lambda = v/f = 340/2000 = 0.17 m
       = 17 cm

Worked example 3 (reading the graphs). On a displacement–distance graph, consecutive crests sit at 0.20 m and 0.65 m. A particle completes one oscillation in 0.020 s. Find v.

lambda = 0.65 - 0.20 = 0.45 m
T = 0.020 s  ->  f = 1/0.020 = 50 Hz
v = f lambda = 50 x 0.45 = 22.5 m s-1

Note the exam habit that prevents the commonest error: write the wavelength and period extractions as their own lines before any multiplication.

Intensity: how the energy spreads

Intensity is power per unit area, I = P/A, measured in W m⁻². For a wave spreading from a point source uniformly in three dimensions, the same power spreads over the surface of a sphere, so I = P/(4πr²) and intensity falls with the inverse square of distance. Amplitude matters too: intensity is proportional to the square of the amplitude, I ∝ A² — double the amplitude, quadruple the intensity.

Worked example. A small source emits 4.0 W uniformly. Find the intensity 2.0 m away.

I = P/(4 pi r^2) = 4.0/(4 x 3.14 x 2.0^2) = 4.0/50.3
  = 0.080 W m-2

Transverse and longitudinal waves

The distinction is the angle between the oscillation and the travel direction:

TransverseLongitudinal
Particle vibrationperpendicular to the direction of energy transferparallel to the direction of energy transfer
Featurescrests and troughs; can be polarisedcompressions and rarefactions; cannot be polarised
Exampleslight and all EM waves, waves on strings, S-wavessound in air, ultrasound in tissue, P-waves, spring coils

A key exam consequence: because electromagnetic waves are transverse, they can be polarised; sound in air is longitudinal, so it cannot. The oscillation of the electric field vector in a light wave can be confined to one plane by a polarising filter — that is polarisation, and it is a property only transverse waves possess.

The Doppler effect for sound

When a source of sound moves relative to an observer, the observed frequency shifts: the wavefronts bunch up ahead of the source (higher pitch) and stretch out behind (lower pitch). Ambulances are the standard demonstration. For sound with source speed vₛ along the line joining source and observer, and sound speed v:

source approaching observer:   f' = f v/(v - v_s)
source receding from observer: f' = f v/(v + v_s)

The general form taught for exams: f' = f v/(v ∓ vₛ) with the minus sign for approach and the plus sign for recession; for a moving observer the roles swap (approaching observer: f' = f (v + v_o)/v). Learn the sign logic, not a mnemonic: less distance between wavefronts means higher frequency.

Worked example. A car horn emits 400 Hz. The car approaches a stationary pedestrian at 25 m s⁻¹. Take the speed of sound as 340 m s⁻¹.

approaching: f' = f v/(v - v_s) = 400 x 340/(340 - 25)
           = 136 000/315 = 432 Hz
receding:    f' = 400 x 340/(340 + 25) = 136 000/365 = 373 Hz

The classic two-part question: the observer hears 432 Hz as the car arrives and 373 Hz as it leaves. The perceived shift is about 59 Hz in total — the difference of the two answers, not one answer.

Limitation to know: the formula above assumes the motion is along the line of source and observer, and it fails when vₛ approaches v (the denominator collapses) — at the speed of sound the wavefronts pile into a shock wave, the sonic boom.

The electromagnetic spectrum

All electromagnetic waves travel at c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ in vacuum; they differ in frequency and wavelength, and their properties follow in an unbroken spectrum. The order is examinable in both directions:

Region (increasing frequency)Wavelength scaleTypical uses and effects
Radio10³–10⁻¹ mbroadcasting, communications, MRI signals
Microwave10⁻¹–10⁻³ msatellite links, mobile phones, ovens (water rotation)
Infrared10⁻³–7 × 10⁻⁷ mthermal imaging, remote controls, heating
Visible7 × 10⁻⁷–4 × 10⁻⁷ mvision, photography, fibre optics
Ultraviolet4 × 10⁻⁷–10⁻⁸ msterilisation, fluorescence, vitamin D; sunburn risk
X-rays10⁻⁸–10⁻¹¹ mmedical imaging, security scanning; ionising
Gammabelow 10⁻¹¹ msterilising equipment, cancer radiotherapy; ionising

Shared properties: all transverse, all travel at c in vacuum, all obey v = fλ, all can be polarised. The property that changes down the table is photon energy — which is why the short-wavelength end (UV, X-ray, gamma) is ionising and dangerous to tissue.

Polarisation in depth

Unpolarised light has its electric field vector oscillating in every direction perpendicular to travel. A polarising filter passes only the component aligned with its axis — so a second filter (the analyser) at 90° to the first extinguishes the beam entirely. Intermediate angles pass a fraction of the intensity. Practical applications are examinable: Polaroid sunglasses cut glare (glare from roads and water is partially polarised by reflection), and radio aerials must be aligned with the polarisation of the signal.

Worked example. Unpolarised light of intensity I₀ passes one polariser. What fraction emerges, and what happens if a second polariser is added at 30° to the first?

after 1st polariser: I1 = I0/2
2nd polariser at 30 deg: I2 = I1 cos^2(30) = (I0/2)(0.75)
                       = 0.375 I0

The first filter halves unpolarised light; subsequent filters follow the cos²θ rule (an A-level standard result worth knowing for multiple-choice items).

Worked examples: exam-style calculations

Worked example 1 (graph + equation). A student measures a wave: 5 full waves occupy 2.0 m, and 20 oscillations take 3.0 s. Find the wave speed.

5 wavelengths in 2.0 m -> lambda = 2.0/5 = 0.40 m
20 oscillations in 3.0 s -> T = 3.0/20 = 0.15 s
f = 1/0.15 = 6.67 Hz
v = f lambda = 6.67 x 0.40 = 2.67 m s-1  (2 s.f.: 2.7 m s-1)

Worked example 2 (Doppler with unknown speed). A stationary observer hears 500 Hz from an approaching source and 420 Hz as it recedes. If v = 340 m s⁻¹, find the source speed.

approach: 500 = f x 340/(340 - v_s)   ... (1)
recede:   420 = f x 340/(340 + v_s)   ... (2)
divide (1) by (2): 500/420 = (340 + v_s)/(340 - v_s)
1.190(340 - v_s) = 340 + v_s
404.6 - 1.190 v_s = 340 + v_s
64.6 = 2.190 v_s  ->  v_s = 29.5 m s-1  (2 s.f.: 30 m s-1)

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Definitions) Define wavelength and phase difference. Answer: Wavelength: the distance between consecutive points in phase, e.g. crest to crest. Phase difference: the fraction of an oscillation cycle between two oscillating points, expressed in radians (2π per complete cycle).
  2. (Wave equation) A radio wave has frequency 1.5 MHz. Find its wavelength (c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹). Answer: λ = c/f = 3.0 × 10⁸ / 1.5 × 10⁶ = 200 m.
  3. (Graphs) On a displacement–time graph for one particle, successive peaks occur at 0.10 s and 0.35 s. State the period and frequency. Answer: T = 0.25 s; f = 1/T = 4.0 Hz.
  4. (Transverse/longitudinal) Explain, in terms of particle motion, why sound cannot be polarised. Answer: In a longitudinal wave the oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer, so there is no perpendicular vibration to restrict to one plane; polarisation requires transverse oscillations.
  5. (Doppler) An ambulance emitting 700 Hz moves away from a cyclist at 20 m s⁻¹ (sound 340 m s⁻¹). Find the frequency heard. Answer: f' = 700 × 340/(340 + 20) = 238 000/360 = 661 Hz.
  6. (EM spectrum) Arrange in order of increasing frequency: infrared, gamma, radio, visible. Name one use of ultraviolet. Answer: radio, infrared, visible, gamma. Uses of UV include sterilising equipment, detecting forged notes (fluorescence) and sunbeds; also responsible for sunburn and vitamin D production.
  7. (Polarisation) Two polarising filters are placed in a beam of light with their axes at 90°. State and explain the observation. Answer: No light passes: the first filter polarises the light along its axis, and the second (analyser) blocks all vibration parallel to that axis because its own axis is perpendicular.
  8. (Intensity) The amplitude of a wave is doubled. State the effect on intensity. Answer: Intensity increases by a factor of 4, because I ∝ A².

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Graph confusion: reading wavelength from a displacement–time graph (it gives period) or period from a distance graph (it gives wavelength). Label the axes first, always.
  • Unit conversions: kHz and MHz to Hz, cm to m, before substitution. Losing a factor of 1000 in the Doppler denominator is the classic arithmetic loss.
  • Phase in degrees: phase difference is demanded in radians (π, 2π). 180° is π; a quarter cycle is π/2.
  • Doppler signs: approach is minus in the denominator — do not memorise blindly; sketch the bunched and stretched wavefronts and derive the sign each time.
  • f versus T: f = 1/T, and f = 50 Hz means T = 0.02 s, not 50 s. Inverting too quickly under pressure is common.
  • Spectrum order and properties: candidates memorise the order but forget that all EM waves travel at c and are transverse — the shared-properties questions catch them.
  • Polarisation of sound: stating that sound can be polarised is an immediate mark loss; sound is longitudinal.
  • Precision and units: this paper wants answers to 2 or 3 significant figures with units; unrounded 7-digit answers and unitless numbers cost marks.
  • Method marks: write v = fλ and substitute in separate lines — the formula line earns credit even when the arithmetic fails.

title: Plant Structure and Function, Biodiversity and Conservation Revision Notes
content:
Quick revision: Plant Structure and Function, Biodiversity and Conservation

Biology — AS. Edexcel IAL Biology WBI12, Topic 4. Plant tissues are arranged to transport water, move sugars and carry out photosynthesis. Biodiversity measures and conservation methods show how ecosystems are monitored and protected.

Key areas to revise

  • Plant tissues
  • Stomata and transpiration
  • Measuring biodiversity
  • Sampling
  • Conservation

Worked example

Calculate the index of diversity (D) for a habitat containing 5 species with individual counts of 10, 25, 5, 40 and 20. First find N, the total number of organisms: 10 + 25 + 5 + 40 + 20 = 100. Next, calculate n(n − 1) for each species: 10(9) = 90, 25(24) = 600, 5(4) = 20, 40(39) = 1560, 20(19) = 380. Sum these values to get the denominator: 90 + 600 + 20 + 1560 + 380 = 2650. Now calculate N(N − 1): 100 × 99 = 9900. Divide 9900 by 2650 to get D = 3.74.

Key points to remember

Plant cells possess a rigid cell wall made of cellulose microfibrils, chloroplasts for photosynthesis, amyloplasts for starch storage, a large permanent vacuole bounded by a tonoplast, plasmodesmata for cytoplasmic connection, pits, and a middle lamella acting as an adhesive layer. Animal cells lack cell walls, chloroplasts, amyloplasts, large vacuoles, tonoplasts, plasmodesmata, pits and middle lamellae.

Cellulose is a polymer of beta-glucose molecules joined by 1,4-glycosidic bonds, where alternate glucose monomers are inverted by 180 degrees. Hydrogen bonds form between adjacent chains, grouping together to form microfibrils, which bundle into macrofibrils with secondary thickening to give high tensile strength to xylem vessels and sclerenchyma fibres.

Xylem vessels provide structural support and transport water and mineral ions upwards. Sclerenchyma fibres provide mechanical support with thick lignified walls. Phloem sieve tubes transport organic solutes by translocation. Roots, stems and leaves show distinct tissue arrangements visible under light microscopes using stained transverse section sections.

Sustainable use of plant materials involves replacing oil-based plastics with plant-based starches and fibres. Plants require inorganic ions: nitrates for amino acids and proteins, calcium ions for calcium pectate in the middle lamella, and magnesium ions to form chlorophyll. Deficiencies in these ions cause characteristic symptoms in plant growth.

Bacterial growth requires an appropriate temperature, moisture, pH, oxygen availability, and nutrient supply. Plants produce antimicrobial substances tested using aseptic techniques. Drug testing protocols have evolved from William Withering's digitalis soup to modern clinical trials involving double-blind trials, placebos, and three distinct phases.

Biodiversity includes species richness and genetic diversity measured via the heterozygosity index (number of heterozygotes divided by total individuals). The index of diversity formula is D = N(N − 1) / sum of n(n − 1). The Hardy-Weinberg equation (p squared + 2pq + q squared = 1 and p + q = 1) tracks allele frequency changes driven by mutation, natural selection, and reproductive isolation leading to speciation. Conservation employs zoos and seed banks via scientific research, captive breeding, reintroduction, and education.

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

title: Logic Gates & Boolean Logic
content:
Logic Gates & Boolean Logic

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2023–2025): six gates, truth tables, building/describing circuits, problem-to-logic mapping.

1. The six gates

ABANDORNANDNORXOR
0000110
0101101
1001101
1111000

NOT inverts. NAND = AND + invert; NOR = OR + invert; XOR = 1 when inputs differ.

2. Truth tables

2 inputs → 4 rows; 3 inputs → 8 rows. Work gate by gate, adding intermediate columns for sub-circuit outputs.

3. Problem → logic

Define inputs/outputs first. Alarm rings (X=1) if sensor P triggered AND (door D OR window W): X = P AND (D OR W). Then draw the circuit: OR first, then AND.

4. Describing circuits

Write the expression from a diagram gate by gate; annotate output of each gate (X, Y) before combining.

Exam tips: check your truth table row count before writing; in problem questions, state "input P = 1 means sensor triggered" — definitions earn marks.

title: Organic Nitrogen Compounds: Amines, Amides, Amino Acids and Proteins Revision Notes
content:
Organic Nitrogen Compounds: Amines, Amides, Amino Acids and Proteins A2 Level Chemistry

These revision notes cover Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH15 Topic 19, focusing on the structures, preparations, reactions, and physical properties of amines, amides, amino acids, and polymers including polyamides and addition polymers, alongside Core Practical 15.

Nomenclature and Formulae of Nitrogen Compounds

Students must be able to name and draw structural, displayed, and skeletal formulae for amides, primary amines, and amino acids according to IUPAC rules.

  • Primary aliphatic amines are named by adding the suffix -amine to the alkyl chain, such as butylamine (CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂NH₂).
  • Aromatic amines feature an amino group directly attached to a benzene ring, such as phenylamine (C₆H₅NH₂).
  • Amides are named based on the corresponding carboxylic acid chain with the suffix -amide, such as ethanamide (CH₃CONH₂).
  • Amino acids contain both an amine group and a carboxylic acid group, typically on the same carbon, such as 2-aminopropanoic acid (CH₃CH(NH₂)COOH).
  • Structural formulae show every atom and bond clearly in displayed formulae, while skeletal formulae omit carbon and hydrogen labels from carbon chains for simplicity.

Reactions and Basicity of Amines

Amines act as bases due to the lone pair of electrons on the nitrogen atom, which can accept a proton.

  • Primary aliphatic amines like butylamine are miscible with water due to hydrogen bonding between the nitrogen and hydrogen atoms of water and the amine.
  • Basicity varies: ammonia has a base dissociation constant dependent on its lone pair availability; primary aliphatic amines are stronger bases than ammonia because alkyl groups push electron density onto the nitrogen via the positive inductive effect, increasing lone pair availability.
  • Primary aromatic amines like phenylamine are weaker bases than ammonia because the nitrogen lone pair delocalises into the delocalised pi-system of the benzene ring, decreasing its availability to accept protons.
  • Reaction with water: primary aliphatic amines dissolve to form alkaline solutions containing hydroxide ions, for example CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂NH₂ + H₂O gives CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂NH₃⁺ + OH⁻.
  • Reaction with acids: amines react with mineral acids like hydrochloric acid to form soluble alkylammonium salts, such as CH₃NH₂ + HCl gives CH₃NH₃⁺Cl⁻.
  • Reaction with halogenoalkanes: primary amines react with halogenoalkanes via nucleophilic substitution to produce secondary and tertiary amines.
  • Reaction with acyl chlorides: primary amines react with ethanoyl chloride to form N-substituted amides, releasing misty fumes of hydrogen chloride.
  • Reaction with copper(II) ions: dropwise addition of aqueous copper(II) sulfate to an excess of an aliphatic amine like butylamine forms a pale blue precipitate that dissolves in excess amine to form a deep blue complex ion, [Cu(CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂NH₂)₄(H₂O)²]²⁺.

Preparation of Aliphatic and Aromatic Amines

Different synthetic routes are required to produce aliphatic versus aromatic amines.

  • Preparation of primary aliphatic amines from halogenoalkanes: heating a haloalkane with excess ethanolic ammonia in a sealed tube via nucleophilic substitution; excess ammonia is essential to prevent further substitution leading to secondary and tertiary amines.
  • Preparation of primary aliphatic amines from nitriles: reduction of a nitrile using lithium aluminium hydride in dry ether followed by dilute acid, or catalytic hydrogenation using hydrogen and a nickel catalyst.
  • Preparation of aromatic amines: reduction of an aromatic nitro-compound, such as nitrobenzene, using tin and concentrated hydrochloric acid heated under reflux, followed by the addition of sodium hydroxide to release the free phenylamine base.

Azo Dyes and Diazonium Salts

Aromatic amines undergo specific reactions involving nitrous acid to form useful colorants.

  • Reaction of aromatic amines with nitrous acid: phenylamine reacts with nitrous acid (formed in situ from sodium nitrite and hydrochloric acid) at temperatures below 5°C to form a benzenediazonium ion (C₆H₅N₂⁺Cl⁻).
  • Coupling reaction: the benzenediazonium ion undergoes an electrophilic substitution coupling reaction with alkaline phenol at low temperatures to form a brightly coloured azo dye, such as 4-hydroxyphenylazobenzene.

Preparation and Properties of Amides

Amides are carboxylic acid derivatives containing the carbonyl-nitrogen bond.

  • Preparation: amides are prepared from acyl chlorides by reacting them with ammonia or a primary amine at room temperature, for example ethanoyl chloride with ammonia gives ethanamide and hydrogen chloride.
  • Hydrolysis: amides undergo acid hydrolysis when heated with dilute hydrochloric acid to yield a carboxylic acid and an ammonium salt, or alkaline hydrolysis with sodium hydroxide to yield a carboxylate salt and ammonia gas.

Polymers: Polyamides and Addition Polymers

Polymerisation processes link small monomer units into large macromolecules.

  • Condensation polymerisation: involves the reaction of monomers with two functional groups, releasing a small molecule such as water or hydrogen chloride; polyamides like nylon-6,6 are formed from hexane-1,6-diamine and hexanedioic acid.
  • Proteins are natural polyamides formed from amino acid monomers linked by peptide bonds.
  • Addition polymerisation: involves unsaturated monomers opening their double bonds without eliminating small molecules; examples include poly(propenamide) and poly(ethenol).
  • Structural formulae: students must be able to draw repeat units of nylon, proteins, poly(propenamide), and poly(ethenol) enclosed in square brackets with an extension bond outside the brackets.
  • Physical properties of polyamides: strong intermolecular hydrogen bonds form between the polar carbonyl and N-H groups of adjacent polymer chains, resulting in high tensile strength and high melting points.
  • Solubility of poly(ethenol): despite being an addition polymer, poly(ethenol) is soluble in water because its numerous pendant alcohol (-OH) groups form extensive hydrogen bonds with water molecules, making it ideal for soluble laundry bags and liquid-detergent capsules (liquitabs).

Amino Acids, Zwitterions, and Peptides

Amino acids exhibit amphoteric properties and form complex structural hierarchies in proteins.

  • Zwitterions: in the solid state and near neutral pH, amino acids exist as dipolar ions called zwitterions, ⁺H₃NCH(R)COO⁻, carrying no net overall charge due to internal proton transfer from the carboxylic acid group to the amine group.
  • Acidity and basicity: at the isoelectric point, the zwitterion has a net charge of zero. In strong acid solutions, the amino group accepts a proton to form a positive cation; in strong alkali solutions, the carboxylic acid group loses a proton to form a negative anion.
  • Optical activity: aqueous solutions of standard amino acids contain chiral carbon atoms (except glycine) and rotate plane-polarised monochromatic light because they are optically active.
  • Peptide bond formation: a peptide link (-CONH-) forms when the carboxylic acid group of one amino acid condenses with the amine group of another, eliminating a molecule of water via condensation polymerisation.
  • Protein structure: proteins possess primary structure (amino acid sequence), secondary structure (alpha-helices and beta-pleated sheets held by hydrogen bonds between C=O and N-H groups), and tertiary structure (3D folding stabilized by ionic bonds, hydrogen bonds, and disulfide bridges). Complete hydrolysis of proteins with hot concentrated hydrochloric acid yields a mixture of constituent amino acids.

Core Practical 15: Analysis of Unknowns

Practical analysis involves systematic chemical tests to identify functional groups in organic and inorganic unknowns.

  • Testing for amines: use universal indicator to confirm an alkaline pH, or react with ethanoyl chloride to observe misty fumes of hydrogen chloride.
  • Testing for amino acids: use paper chromatography followed by locating agents like ninhydrin to reveal purple spots.
  • Testing for amides: warm with sodium hydroxide and test evolved ammonia gas with damp red litmus paper, which turns blue.

Typical mistakes

  • Mistake: stating that alkyl groups attract electron density in amines. Correction: alkyl groups push electron density onto the nitrogen atom via a positive inductive effect.
  • Mistake: drawing the zwitterion structure with a neutral carboxylic acid and amine group at neutral pH. Correction: draw the zwitterion with a protonated amine (⁺H₃N-) and deprotonated carboxylate (-COO⁻).
  • Mistake: omitting the repeat brackets or extension bonds when drawing polymer repeat units. Correction: always enclose repeat units in square brackets with bonds extending outside the brackets.
  • Mistake: confusing addition polymerisation with condensation polymerisation. Correction: addition polymerisation involves unsaturated monomers with no eliminated small molecules, whereas condensation polymerisation eliminates small molecules like water.

Exam-style questions

  2. Explain why phenylamine is a weaker base than butylamine. Answer: Phenylamine's nitrogen lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring, decreasing proton acceptance ability, whereas butylamine's alkyl group pushes electron density onto nitrogen via a positive inductive effect, increasing lone pair availability.
  5. Describe the reagents and conditions needed to prepare phenylamine from nitrobenzene. Answer: Heat nitrobenzene under reflux with tin (Sn) and concentrated hydrochloric acid, followed by addition of sodium hydroxide.
  8. Draw the structural repeat unit of nylon-6,6. Answer: [−NH−(CH₂)₆−NH−CO−(CH₂)₄−CO−].
  11. Explain why poly(ethenol) dissolves in water while poly(ethene) does not. Answer: Poly(ethenol) has pendant −OH groups that form hydrogen bonds with water molecules, whereas poly(ethene) is non-polar and cannot form hydrogen bonds.
  14. Write the ionic equation for the reaction of butylamine with hydrochloric acid. Answer: CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂NH₂ + H⁺ gives CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂NH₃⁺.

Use these notes alongside past paper practice questions to test your knowledge of reaction conditions and mechanisms. Revise aromatic chemistry and polymer chemistry next to consolidate your understanding of WCH15.

title: Measurement & Units — Study Notes
content:
Measurement & Units

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2023–2025): 1.1 lengths & volumes; 1.2 density; 1.3 forces & motion context (measurements) — plus measurement techniques, SI units, scalars/vectors.

1. Measuring

  • Length: ruler (mm), vernier calipers (0.1 mm / 0.01 cm), micrometer screw gauge (0.01 mm).
