  5. (Stationary) Find the stationary point of y = x² − 6x + 5. Answer: 2x − 6 = 0 → x = 3; y = −4; minimum.
  6. (Second derivative) Classify the stationary point of y = x³ at x = 0. Answer: dy/dx = 3x², d²y/dx² = 6x = 0 at x = 0 — the test is inconclusive; the gradient is positive either side, so it is a point of inflection, not an extremum.
  7. (Increasing) Find where y = x² − 4x is decreasing. Answer: 2x − 4 < 0 → x < 2.
  8. (Kinematics) s = t³ − 6t² + 9t. Find the acceleration at t = 1. Answer: v = 3t² − 12t + 9; a = 6t − 12 → −6 m/s².

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Forgetting to rewrite powers: differentiate 1/x and √x only after rewriting as x⁻¹ and x^(1/2); the power rule does not apply to the original form.
  • Dropping the constant: the derivative of a constant is 0 — a leftover +7 in dy/dx is an error.
  • Tangent versus normal: the normal's gradient is −1/m, not −m; and it passes through the same point.
  • Second derivative sign: negative means maximum (the curve is concave down); positive means minimum. Reversing the classification is the classic slip.
  • d²y/dx² = 0: inconclusive, not automatically an inflection — check the gradient either side.
  • Stationary point coordinates: the question wants (x, y), so substitute the x back into the original curve, not the derivative.
  • Rates of change with units: attach units (m/s, m/s², units per item) and interpret the sign in context.
  • Method marks: write dy/dx = ... explicitly before substituting; the derivative itself is credit even if the later arithmetic slips.

title: A Level Mathematics: The Binomial Distribution
content:
A Level Mathematics: The Binomial Distribution

A binomial distribution counts successes in a fixed number of independent trials, each with the same probability of success. Coins, multiple-choice guesses, defective items in a sample and free throws all fit the same template, and once a problem is recognised as binomial the calculation is a formula plus a cumulative table. This note builds the distribution from its four conditions, derives the formula from counting, and then uses it for the two things exams actually ask: probabilities and hypothesis tests.

The four conditions

Before writing X ~ B(n, p) you must be able to name the conditions, because most exam questions include a part asking whether the model is appropriate. The conditions are not red tape: drop any one and the formula is simply wrong.

1. a fixed number of trials n
2. each trial has exactly two outcomes (success / failure)
3. the probability of success p is constant for every trial
4. the trials are independent
then X = number of successes has X ~ B(n, p)

Worked example (checking the model). A bag holds 5 red and 15 blue counters. Four counters are taken without replacement. Is the number of red counters binomial?

n = 4 is fixed and each draw is red or not red
but p changes: 5/20, then 5/19 if a red was taken, ...
the trials are not independent, so NOT binomial (it is hypergeometric)

Taking with replacement would fix it: p stays 0.25 on every draw.

The formula, and where it comes from

The probability of a particular sequence of r successes and n − r failures is p^r (1−p)^(n−r), because independence lets you multiply. The number of such sequences is the number of ways to choose which r trials succeed, which is nCr. Multiplying gives the formula.

P(X = r) = nCr p^r (1 - p)^(n - r)
the nCr counts arrangements; the powers give the probability of one arrangement

Worked example. X ~ B(10, 0.3). Find P(X = 3).

P = 10C3 (0.3)³ (0.7)⁷
= 120 × 0.027 × 0.08235
= 120 × 0.002223 = 0.2668

Worked example 2 (a single trial count). A fair die is rolled 8 times. Find the probability of exactly two sixes.

X ~ B(8, 1/6)
P(X = 2) = 8C2 (1/6)² (5/6)⁶ = 28 × 0.02778 × 0.3349 = 0.2605

Worked example 3 (why nCr appears). For n = 3 and r = 1, list the sequences and confirm the coefficient.

sequences: SFF, FSF, FFS - three of them
each has probability p(1-p)²
so P(X = 1) = 3p(1-p)², and 3C1 = 3

Cumulative probabilities

Questions almost always ask for a range, not a single value, and the cumulative distribution is what the calculator or the tables supply. The skill is rewriting the question into the form the table gives you.

P(X <= r) is tabulated directly
P(X >= r) = 1 - P(X <= r - 1)
P(X < r)  = P(X <= r - 1)
P(a <= X <= b) = P(X <= b) - P(X <= a - 1)
P(X = r) = P(X <= r) - P(X <= r - 1)

Worked example. X ~ B(20, 0.4). Find P(X ≥ 8).

P(X >= 8) = 1 - P(X <= 7)
= 1 - 0.4159
= 0.5841

Worked example 2 (between). For the same X, find P(5 ≤ X ≤ 10).

= P(X <= 10) - P(X <= 4)
= 0.8725 - 0.0510
= 0.8215

Worked example 3 (the strict inequality trap). For the same X, find P(X > 6).

P(X > 6) = 1 - P(X <= 6) = 1 - 0.2500 = 0.7500
note this is different from P(X >= 6) = 1 - P(X <= 5) = 0.8746

Mean and variance

The binomial has the simplest mean and variance in the syllabus, and they are worth knowing both forwards and backwards: a question can give the mean and variance and ask for n and p.

E(X) = np
Var(X) = np(1 - p)
standard deviation = √(np(1-p))

Worked example. X ~ B(50, 0.2). Find the mean and standard deviation.

mean = 50 × 0.2 = 10
variance = 10 × 0.8 = 8
sd = 2.828

Worked example 2 (backwards). A binomial variable has mean 12 and variance 9. Find n and p.

np = 12;  np(1-p) = 9
divide: 1 - p = 9/12 = 0.75  →  p = 0.25
then n = 12/0.25 = 48

Hypothesis testing with the binomial

A one-tailed test asks whether p has increased or decreased; the test statistic is the observed count, and the p-value is the probability of a result at least as extreme in the direction of the alternative.

H0: p = p0      H1: p > p0 (or p < p0)
X ~ B(n, p0) under H0
p-value = P(X >= observed) or P(X <= observed)
compare with the significance level; reject H0 if p-value <= alpha

Worked example. A coin is tossed 20 times and lands heads 15 times. Test at the 5% level whether the coin is biased towards heads.

H0: p = 0.5;  H1: p > 0.5
X ~ B(20, 0.5)
P(X >= 15) = 1 - P(X <= 14) = 1 - 0.9793 = 0.0207
0.0207 < 0.05, so reject H0
there is evidence at the 5% level that the coin favours heads

Worked example 2 (two-tailed). The same data tested two-tailed.

double the smaller tail: 2 × 0.0207 = 0.0414
0.0414 < 0.05, so still reject H0 at the 5% level

Worked example 3 (critical region). For X ~ B(20, 0.5), find the critical region for a 5% one-tailed test of p > 0.5.

P(X >= 14) = 0.0577 (above 0.05)
P(X >= 15) = 0.0207 (below 0.05)
critical region: X >= 15

Note that the critical region is chosen so the probability of a Type I error is at most 5%, which is why 14 is excluded even though it is close.

When the model breaks down

Examiners like the question that asks why a binomial model is only an approximation. The usual culprits are dependence, a varying probability, or a fixed sample drawn without replacement from a small population.

SituationProblemEffect
sampling without replacementtrials not independentp drifts; use the hypergeometric instead
clustered data (pupils in classes)responses correlatedvariance underestimated
probability varies between trialsp not constantformula invalid
large n, p near 0.5computation heavynormal approximation is reasonable

Worked example (normal approximation). X ~ B(200, 0.4). Use a normal approximation to estimate P(X ≤ 70).

mean = 80;  variance = 200 × 0.4 × 0.6 = 48;  sd = 6.928
continuity correction: X <= 70 becomes X < 70.5
z = (70.5 - 80)/6.928 = -1.371
P(Z < -1.371) = 0.0852

The continuity correction is compulsory: a discrete count needs a half-unit boundary before it can be treated as continuous.

Expected frequencies and the shape of the distribution

A binomial distribution is not symmetric unless p = 0.5, and that shape decides which tail an exam question is fishing in. The most likely value — the mode — is the integer near (n + 1)p, and expected frequency multiplies the probability by the number of samples taken. Both are quick marks that are frequently missed because students jump straight to the formula.

mode is near (n + 1)p, checked by comparing consecutive probabilities
expected number in a sample of size N = N x P(X = r)

Worked example. X ~ B(12, 0.3). Find the most likely value of X and the expected number of 3s in 500 independent observations.

(n + 1)p = 13 × 0.3 = 3.9, so check r = 3 and r = 4
P(X = 3) = 220 × 0.027 × 0.1176 = 0.2397
P(X = 4) = 495 × 0.0081 × 0.1681 = 0.2311
mode = 3
expected number of 3s = 500 × 0.2397 = 120 (to the nearest whole)

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Model) State the distribution for the number of sixes in 12 rolls of a fair die. Answer: X ~ B(12, 1/6).
  2. (Single value) X ~ B(8, 0.25): find P(X = 2). Answer: 28 × 0.0625 × 0.1780 = 0.3115.
  3. (Cumulative) X ~ B(15, 0.3): find P(X ≤ 4). Answer: 0.5155 from tables.
  4. (Complement) Same X: find P(X ≥ 3). Answer: 1 − 0.2969 = 0.7031.
  5. (Mean) X ~ B(40, 0.35): find E(X) and Var(X). Answer: 14 and 9.1.
  6. (Backwards) Mean 18, variance 12: find n and p. Answer: p = 1/3, n = 54.
  7. (Test) 12 of 20 seeds germinate; test p = 0.5 against p < 0.5 at 5%. Answer: P(X ≤ 12) = 0.8684, no evidence to reject.
  8. (Critical region) X ~ B(10, 0.2): find the 5% critical region for p < 0.2. Answer: P(X ≤ 0) = 0.1074 > 0.05, so no region exists at 5%.
  9. (Approximation) X ~ B(100, 0.5): approximate P(X ≥ 60). Answer: μ = 50, σ = 5, z = 1.9, P = 0.0287.
  10. (Assumption) Give one reason a binomial model may fail for defects in boxes of 20. Answer: defects may cluster, so trials are not independent.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Forgetting nCr: the coefficient counts arrangements; without it the answer is the probability of one specific sequence.
  • nCr on the wrong factor: it is p^r (1−p)^(n−r), with the success probability raised to the number of successes.
  • Inequality direction: P(X ≥ 8) uses 1 − P(X ≤ 7), not 1 − P(X ≤ 8).
  • Variance confused with standard deviation: np(1−p) is the variance; the test and the normal approximation need the square root.
  • Continuity correction omitted: any normal approximation to a discrete count needs the half-unit adjustment.
  • One-tailed evidence read as two: halving or doubling the tail without checking the alternative direction is a silent error.
  • Independence asserted, not checked: sampling without replacement from a small population breaks the model, and the question usually invites you to say so.
  • p-value compared with the wrong threshold: the significance level is given as a percentage; 5% means 0.05, not 5.

title: Continuous Random Variables — Study Notes
content:
Continuous Random Variables

Probability Density Functions

A continuous variable X is described by a density f(x) with f(x) ≥ 0 and ∫f(x)dx = 1 over all x. Probabilities are areas:

  • P(a ≤ X ≤ b) = ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx

Single points have zero probability, so strict or loose inequalities make no difference: P(X < 2) = P(X ≤ 2).

Finding Unknown Constants

Piecewise densities carry an unknown k: impose that the total area is 1 (and continuity at joins where required). One equation, one unknown.

Example: f(x) = kx on 0 ≤ x ≤ 2. Total area: k·(2²/2) = 2k = 1, so k = ½.

Expectation and Variance

  • E(X) = ∫x·f(x) dx
  • E(X²) = ∫x²·f(x) dx
  • Var(X) = E(X²) − (E(X))²

The mean is the balancing point of the area under the density. For symmetric densities the mean sits at the symmetry point — worth spotting before integrating.

The Median and Mode

The median m solves ∫₋∞ᵐ f(x) dx = 0.5 (left half of the area). The mode is the x maximising f(x). For uniform densities the median is the midpoint.

Uniform Distribution

If f(x) = 1/(b − a) on [a, b], every point is equally likely. Then E(X) = (a + b)/2 and Var(X) = (b − a)²/12 — memorise both; they are quick exam marks.

Exam tips: always verify ∫f = 1 before computing anything else. Sketch the density — area intuitions catch algebra slips. Median questions are integration-to-0.5 questions; set them up before calculating.

title: Probability — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Probability

Mathematics — A2. For an event A with P(A) = p: 0 ≤ p ≤ 1, and P(A′) = 1 − P(A). For mutually exclusive events, probabilities add: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B). For events that can occur together, subtract the overlap:

Key areas to revise

  • Basic Rules
  • Venn Diagrams
  • Tree Diagrams
  • Conditional Probability
  • Independence

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Key points to remember

For any two events, P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B). Conditional probability is P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B). Events A and B are independent only when P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B), so test this before you multiply probabilities.

Use a Venn diagram or a tree diagram to organise the information. On a tree diagram, multiply along each branch and add the branches that give the outcome you want. Mutually exclusive events cannot both happen, so P(A ∩ B) = 0 for them, and this is a different idea from independence.

title: Data Representation
content:
Data Representation

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2023–2025): binary/hex, two's complement, BCD, text/image/sound encoding, file sizes, compression.

1. Number systems

  • Binary place values 128…1; hex digits 0–9, A–F; one hex digit = one nibble (4 bits).
  • Conversions: binary ↔ decimal ↔ hex. 0101 1010 → 5A; FF = 255.
  • BCD: 4 bits per decimal digit — 0029 → 0000 0000 0010 1001. Used in clocks/calculators; easier digit conversions, more bits than pure binary.

2. Two's complement (signed)

MSB is negative: −128 64 32 16 8 4 2 1. −5 = 1111 1011. Range 8-bit: −128…+127.

Negating: invert bits, add 1. Subtraction: add the negated number — 7 − 5 = 7 + (−5) = 0000 0111 + 1111 1011 = 0000 0010.

3. Text

ASCII 7-bit (128 chars) → extended sets; Unicode for all scripts (UTF-8 variable width). Character sets map codes to glyphs; uppercase/lowercase codes differ by one bit.

4. Images and sound

  • Bitmap: pixels; colour depth = bits per pixel. File size (bits) = W × H × depth. Metadata (width, height, depth) stores dimensions.
  • Sound: sample rate (Hz), resolution (bits per sample), track duration × channels. Higher rate/depth = better fidelity, larger files.

5. Compression

  • Lossless (RLE, ZIP): exact restore — text/code must use it. RLE example: AAABBBCC → 3A3B2C; effective with runs.
  • Lossy (JPEG, MP3): discards perceptually minor data — photos/music OK, text never.

Exam tips: show full working in conversions; for size questions write the formula first with units; state the reason a compression type suits the file.

title: A Level Physics: Motion in a Circle and Gravity
content:
A Level Physics: Motion in a Circle and Gravity

Gravity is the weakest of the four fundamental forces and yet it shapes galaxies — because it never cancels: mass has only one sign, so every particle attracts every other. This note builds the gravitational toolkit from zero: the field concept and field lines, Newton's law of gravitation, field strength and potential for a point mass, and then the applications that fill the papers — satellite orbits, escape velocity and the energy bookkeeping of lifting a mass to infinity. Every formula is derived from the inverse-square law, and every calculation type is worked in full.

The gravitational field

A gravitational field is a region in which a mass experiences a force. Field lines point toward the mass creating the field (gravity is always attractive), and their density shows strength — close to a planet the lines are dense (strong field), far away they are sparse. Two field shapes are examinable:

  • Radial field: around a point mass or a spherical planet outside its surface; strength falls with distance.
  • Uniform field: near a planet's surface over small height changes; strength g is effectively constant (the approximation behind mgh).

Newton's law of gravitation

F = G M m / r²

G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻² (gravitational constant)
M, m = the two masses (kg)
r = separation between their centres (m)

The analogy that makes the law intuitive: the force weakens like light spreading from a lamp — doubling the distance spreads the same influence over four times the area, so the force quarters. The law is universal: the same G applies to an apple and the Earth as to two galaxies.

Worked example. Find the gravitational force between two 1000 kg masses 2.0 m apart.

F = G M m/r² = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ x 1000 × 10⁰⁰/4.0
  = 6.67 × 10⁻⁵/4.0 = 1.7 × 10⁻⁵ N

Note how tiny it is — gravity only matters when one mass is astronomical, which is why the electric force dominates at particle scales.

Gravitational field strength

Field strength g is force per unit mass (N kg⁻¹), and for a point mass or a spherical body:

g = G M / r²

at a planet's surface: g = G M / R²  (R = planet radius)
variation with height: g falls as 1/r² from the centre

Worked example. Find g at the surface of Mars (M = 6.4 × 10²³ kg, R = 3.4 × 10⁶ m).

g = G M/R² = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ x 6.4 × 10²³/(3.4 × 10⁶)²
  = 4.27 × 10¹³/1.156 × 10¹³ = 3.7 N kg⁻¹

Worked example 2 (height). At what height above Earth's surface does g fall to half its surface value? (R = 6.4 × 10⁶ m.)

g_surface = GM/R²; half → GM/r² = (1/2) GM/R²
r² = 2 R² → r = R √(2) = 9.05 × 10⁶ m
height = r - R = 2.65 × 10⁶ m  (about 2650 km)

Gravitational potential

Potential is the work done per unit mass in bringing a mass from infinity to that point (zero at infinity by definition). Because gravity attracts, the work is done by the field on the way in, so potential is negative everywhere:

V = - G M / r        (J kg⁻¹)

potential energy of a mass m: U = m V = - G M m / r
work to move between potentials: W = m (V² - V¹)

The negative sign is not a detail — it is the physical statement that masses are bound. The potential well around a planet is a dip; escape means climbing out of it to V = 0 at infinity.

Worked example. Find the potential at Earth's surface (M = 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg, R = 6.37 × 10⁶ m).

V = -GM/R = -(6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ x 5.97 × 10²⁴)/6.37 × 10⁶
  = -3.98 × 10¹⁴/6.37 × 10⁶ = -6.25 × 10⁷ J kg⁻¹

Escape velocity

To escape a planet's gravity, a body needs enough kinetic energy to climb from the surface potential to zero:

(1/2) m v² = G M m / R  →  v_escape = √(2 G M / R)

Earth: v = √(2 × 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ x 5.97 × 10²⁴/6.37 × 10⁶)
     = √(1.25 × 10⁸) = 1.12 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹ = 11.2 km s⁻¹

The derivation is worth learning as a pattern: set kinetic energy equal to the depth of the potential well, cancel m, solve for v. Escape speed is independent of the escaping body's mass — a rocket and a molecule need the same speed (though not the same fuel).

The potential well picture explains the sign conventions in one image: near a planet the potential is deeply negative (the bottom of a dip), and moving outward means climbing toward zero. A body with total energy (kinetic plus potential) below zero is bound — it will fall back; a body with total energy at or above zero can coast to infinity. That single inequality, kinetic energy compared with the depth of the well, decides every escape and orbit question, and it is the most reliable way to check an answer's sign and size.

Orbits

A satellite in a circular orbit has gravity as its centripetal force:

G M m / r² = m v² / r   →   v = √(G M / r)

period: T = 2 π r / v = 2 π √(r³/(G M))
(Kepler's third law: T² proportional to r³)

The counter-intuitive exam favourite: a lower orbit means a faster satellite. Since v = √(GM/r), smaller r gives larger v and shorter periods — which is why the International Space Station orbits in about 90 minutes while the Moon takes 27 days.

Worked example. Find the speed and period of a satellite 400 km above Earth's surface.

r = 6.37 × 10⁶ + 4.0 × 10⁵ = 6.77 × 10⁶ m
v = √(GM/r) = √(6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ x 5.97 × 10²⁴/6.77 × 10⁶)
  = √(5.88 × 10⁷) = 7.67 × 10³ m s⁻¹
T = 2 π r/v = 2 × 3.14 × 6.77 × 10⁶/7.67 × 10³
  = 4.25 × 10⁷/7.67 × 10³ = 5.5 × 10³ s  (about 92 minutes)

Geostationary orbits are the applied case: r ≈ 4.2 × 10⁷ m gives T = 24 hours, the satellite sits above one point on the equator, and it must orbit west-to-east in the equatorial plane.

Worked examples: combined gravity problems

Worked example. Compare the gravitational potential energy of a 500 kg satellite at 400 km altitude with its value at infinity, and find the energy needed to escape from that orbit.

r = 6.77 × 10⁶ m
U_orbit = -GMm/r = -(6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ x 5.97 × 10²⁴ x 500)/6.77 × 10⁶
        = -1.99 × 10¹⁷/6.77 × 10⁶ = -2.94 × 10¹⁰ J
U_infinity = 0
energy to escape = 0 - (-2.94 × 10¹⁰) = 2.9 × 10¹⁰ J

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Law) State Newton's law of gravitation. Answer: The gravitational force between two point masses is proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centres: F = GMm/r².
  2. (Field strength) Define gravitational field strength. Answer: The force per unit mass on a small test mass at that point, g = F/m, measured in N kg⁻¹.
  3. (Inverse square) State how g changes when the distance from a planet's centre is tripled. Answer: g = GM/r², so tripling r divides g by 9.
  4. (Potential) Explain why gravitational potential is negative. Answer: Potential is defined as zero at infinity; gravity attracts, so the field does work on a mass brought in from infinity, meaning its potential energy — and therefore potential — decreases below zero.
  5. (Escape) Calculate the escape velocity from the Moon (M = 7.35 × 10²² kg, R = 1.74 × 10⁶ m). Answer: v = √(2GM/R) = √(2 × 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 7.35 × 10²²/1.74 × 10⁶) = √(5.63 × 10⁶) = 2.37 × 10³ m s⁻¹ ≈ 2.4 km s⁻¹.
  6. (Orbit) Explain why a satellite in a lower orbit moves faster. Answer: Gravity provides the centripetal force: GMm/r² = mv²/r, so v = √(GM/r); a smaller r gives a larger speed and a shorter period.
  7. (Geostationary) State two conditions for a geostationary orbit. Answer: The period must be 24 hours, the orbit must be equatorial and the satellite must orbit in the same direction as Earth's rotation (west to east) — all three are usually wanted.
  8. (Energy) Explain why the energy needed to move a satellite from a low orbit to a higher one is not simply mgh. Answer: Over large distances g is not constant; the correct treatment uses the change in gravitational potential energy, U = −GMm/r, evaluated at both radii.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • r measured from the centre: the separation is centre-to-centre, so a satellite's r includes the planet's radius. Using altitude alone underestimates r and inflates g and v.
  • Mass cancellation: in orbital and escape calculations m cancels — do not carry a satellite's mass through and then wonder why the answer is huge.
  • Negative potentials: V and U are negative; a "larger" potential energy at a higher orbit is less negative, not more. Work done = m(V₂ − V₁), keeping the signs.
  • g versus G: g = GM/r² is field strength (N kg⁻¹); G is the universal constant (N m² kg⁻²). Confusing the symbols loses marks and factors of mass.
  • Surface approximation: mgh applies only for small heights; over planetary distances use the potential formula.
  • Orbit direction: geostationary requires equatorial, west-to-east, 24 hours — a polar orbit is not geostationary however high it is.
  • Units of G and distances: G in N m² kg⁻², masses in kg, distances in metres — km into m, and planet masses given in scientific notation handled carefully.
  • Precision: 2 or 3 s.f. with units; the data sheet supplies G, Earth's mass and radius — quote them rather than relying on memory.
  • Method marks: write F = GMm/r² or v = √(GM/r) before substituting; formulae earn credit independently of arithmetic.

title: Exam technique: Astronomy and Cosmology
content:
### What earns the marks
For parallax, 1 over p in arcseconds earns the method mark with parsecs stated. For Hubble, v = H0 d quoted earns both marks. For evidence, CMB and redshift each linked to the model earn the explanation marks.
### Traps
Error: parallax inverted. Correction: distance is 1 over angle. Error: standard candle reasoning skipped. Correction: period gives luminosity, brightness gives distance. Error: fusion claimed for white dwarfs. Correction: degeneracy pressure supports them.

title: Exam technique: Database Systems
content:
### What earns the marks
For keys, primary identified as unique plus foreign as the link earns one mark each. For SQL, SELECT plus FROM plus WHERE in order earns each mark. For flat versus relational, one concrete drawback of duplication earns the discussion mark.
### Traps
Error: SELECT * claimed as precise. Correction: name the fields asked for. Error: primary key assigned to a non-unique field. Correction: keys must be unique. Error: flat file praised for large data. Correction: duplication corrupts it.

title: Organic Synthesis
content:
Organic Synthesis

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH15, Topic 20. Organic synthesis plans a route from a starting material to a target molecule. You need to choose reagents and conditions, track functional groups and calculate the overall yield.

Planning a route

  • Retrosynthesis works backwards from the target: identify the functional group, then find a precursor that converts into it in one step.
  • Each step should be a known functional group interconversion with suitable reagents and conditions.
  • Carbon chain length can be increased with KCN, which turns a haloalkane into a nitrile. The nitrile can then be hydrolysed to a carboxylic acid or reduced to an amine.

Key interconversions

  • Primary alcohol to aldehyde: distillation with acidified dichromate(VI), so the aldehyde is removed before it oxidises further.
  • Primary alcohol to carboxylic acid: reflux with excess acidified dichromate(VI).
  • Aldehyde or ketone to alcohol: NaBH₄ (or LiAlH₄ for carboxylic acids and nitriles).
  • Alkene to haloalkane: addition of HBr. Alkene to alcohol: steam with an acid catalyst.
  • Nitrobenzene to phenylamine: reduction with Sn and concentrated HCl. Nitration of benzene is the first step of a route to phenylamine.

Yield calculations

  • Percentage yield = actual mass ÷ theoretical mass × 100.
  • Overall yield for a multi-step route is the product of the individual step yields. Two steps at 80% and 70% give 0.80 × 0.70 = 0.56, or 56% overall.
  • Atom economy measures the proportion of reactant atoms that end up in the desired product: (molar mass of desired product ÷ sum of molar masses of all products) × 100.

Exam tip: state the reagent, the condition (reflux, distillation, heat under pressure) and the product of each step. Marks are often given for the condition, not just the reagent.

title: Thermal Physics — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Thermal Physics

Physics — OL. kinetic particle model; thermal expansion; specific heat capacity; melting/boiling; conduction, convection, radiation.

  • 1. Kinetic model
  • 2. Gas pressure and temperature
  • 3. Thermal expansion
  • 4. Specific heat capacity
  • 5. State changes
  • 6. Transfer: conduction, convection, radiation

How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

Key relationships

  • Thermal energy moves by conduction in solids, convection in fluids, and radiation, which can pass through a vacuum.
  • Dark, matt surfaces are good absorbers and good emitters of infrared radiation.
  • Energy for a temperature change: Q = m c Δθ. Energy for a change of state: Q = m L.
  • The temperature stays constant during a change of state because the energy is used to break bonds between particles.

Common errors

Convection needs a fluid to flow, so it cannot occur in a solid. Do not say that heat is stored in a substance; it is thermal energy that is transferred.

title: IGCSE Biology: Movement Into and Out of Cells
content:
IGCSE Biology: Movement Into and Out of Cells

Nothing in a cell can work unless molecules can get in and waste can get out. Three mechanisms do all of that transport, and they differ in one thing: how much energy the cell must spend. Diffusion is free movement down a concentration gradient; osmosis is the special case of water crossing a partially permeable membrane; active transport is the paid, uphill service that pushes molecules against their gradient using energy from respiration. This note builds each one from a physical analogy first, then gives the formal definition you must memorise, the factors examiners ask about, and the calculations (water potential and percentage change) fully expanded line by line.

Diffusion: the crowd analogy

Imagine a packed crowd pouring through a wide gate into an empty field: particles spread out until they are evenly shared, with no instruction and no energy spent. That is diffusion — the net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration, down a concentration gradient, as a result of their random movement. It is passive: no energy from respiration is used. It is also vital: oxygen diffusing from alveoli into blood, carbon dioxide diffusing out of cells into the plasma, and urea diffusing out of cells into the blood for excretion.

Three factors control the rate. A steeper concentration gradient speeds it (more difference, faster net flow). A higher temperature speeds it (particles carry more kinetic energy and move faster). A larger surface area speeds it (more room for particles to cross). For single cells, a large surface-area-to-volume ratio keeps diffusion effective; as a cube grows, volume rises faster than area (area scales as length², volume as length³), which is why large organisms need specialised exchange surfaces (alveoli, villi, root hairs) and transport systems (blood, xylem). Membrane thickness matters too: a thinner diffusion path means faster exchange — flattened red blood cells and thin alveolar walls are both built for exactly that.

Osmosis: water crossing a membrane

Picture a nightclub with a rope that lets small people through but blocks large ones: over time the small people spread evenly on both sides. A partially permeable membrane does this to water. Osmosis is the net movement of water molecules from a region of higher water potential to a region of lower water potential, through a partially permeable membrane. Water potential (symbol ψ, measured in kilopascals, kPa) measures the tendency of water to leave a solution: pure water is 0 kPa, and dissolving anything lowers the water potential, making it more negative. A dilute solution has a higher water potential than a concentrated one — remember: more solute means less free water, so lower water potential.

Osmosis in animal cells: an animal cell in pure water takes water in, swells and may burst (lysis) because it has no wall. In a concentrated solution it loses water and shrivels (crenation). In an isotonic solution (same water potential) it keeps its normal shape. Osmosis in plant cells: in pure water a plant cell becomes turgid — the vacuole fills, the cytoplasm presses against the cellulose wall, and the wall stops it bursting. In a concentrated solution it loses water and the membrane pulls away from the wall: this is plasmolysis, and the cell is plasmolysed. At intermediate water potentials the cell is flaccid. Percentage change in mass is the standard Paper 4 calculation: percentage change = (final mass − initial mass) ÷ initial mass × 100.

Worked example: the osmosis calculation from scratch

A potato cylinder starts at 2.40 g and, after 30 minutes in a 0.4 mol/dm³ sucrose solution, weighs 2.10 g. Calculate the percentage change in mass. Step 1: write the equation: percentage change = (final − initial) ÷ initial × 100. Step 2: substitute: (2.10 − 2.40) ÷ 2.40 × 100. Step 3: the top line first: 2.10 − 2.40 = −0.30 g — the minus sign matters, it shows water left the tissue. Step 4: divide: −0.30 ÷ 2.40 = −0.125. Step 5: multiply by 100: −0.125 × 100 = −12.5 %. The mass decreased by 12.5 %. Interpretation, which the examiner often wants next: the solution had a lower water potential than the cell sap, so water left the cells by osmosis. Plotting percentage change against concentration gives a curve through zero at the concentration where there is no net movement — the point where the external solution matches the tissue's water potential. Always plot percentage change (not raw mass change) so that differently sized samples compare fairly.

Active transport: the paid pump

Imagine pushing a boulder uphill: it will never roll there on its own, so you must spend energy. Active transport is the movement of particles through a cell membrane from a lower concentration to a higher concentration (against the gradient) using energy released by respiration. Carrier proteins in the membrane bind the specific molecule, change shape, and release it on the other side; each cycle burns ATP made in the mitochondria. It is essential where the gradient runs the wrong way: mineral ions into root hair cells from dilute soil, glucose from the gut into epithelial cells after absorption has lowered the lumen concentration, and glucose into muscle cells during exercise.

Diffusion, osmosis and active transport compared

FeatureDiffusionOsmosisActive transport
What movesAny solute particlesWater onlySpecific molecules or ions
DirectionDown the gradient (high to low)Higher to lower water potentialAgainst the gradient (low to high)
EnergyNone (passive)None (passive)Energy from respiration (ATP)
Membrane rolePassage through or between lipidsPartially permeable membrane requiredCarrier proteins required
Example in the bodyOxygen from alveolus into bloodWater in the kidney tubuleGlucose from the gut into the blood

The surface-area-to-volume problem

Work through the cube model numerically and the biology becomes obvious. A 1 cm cube has a surface area of 6 cm² and a volume of 1 cm³ — a ratio of 6:1. An 8 cm cube has a surface area of 6 × 8² = 384 cm² and a volume of 8³ = 512 cm³ — a ratio of 0.75:1. The big cube has relatively less surface per unit volume, so diffusion alone would starve its centre. Cells stay small to keep the ratio high; large organisms flatten exchange surfaces (alveoli, villi), fold them, or thin them to a single layer of cells, and then add a mass-transport system (the heart) to carry molecules the rest of the distance.

Adaptations for exchange — applied to whole organisms

  • Root hair cells: a long extension greatly increases surface area and the thin wall gives a short diffusion path for water and ions.
  • Alveoli in the lung: thousands of spherical sacs give a huge combined surface area; each wall is one cell thick; rich blood supply and constant ventilation maintain steep gradients.
  • Villi in the small intestine: finger-like projections with one-cell-thick walls and a dense capillary network, absorbing digested food rapidly.
  • Capillary walls: a single endothelial cell thick, so gases exchange fast between plasma and tissue fluid.
  • Flat shape of red blood cells: short diffusion path for oxygen to reach haemoglobin.

Worked example: comparing rates and designing a fair test

An investigation puts potato discs in five sucrose concentrations (0.0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8 mol/dm³) for 30 minutes. Identify the variables. Independent variable (the one you change): sucrose concentration. Dependent variable (the one you measure): percentage change in mass. Control variables (the ones you keep the same): temperature (affects rate of osmosis), time in solution, volume of solution, same potato variety and same disc dimensions (surface area to volume ratio), same blotting technique before weighing (surface liquid adds mass). Repeat for each concentration and calculate a mean to spot anomalous results. The gradient of the plotted curve is steepest where the concentration is closest to the tissue's own water potential — outside that range almost all water potential difference is already exploited.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Defining osmosis without the words "partially permeable membrane" — that phrase is a mark on its own.
  • Writing "water moves from weak to strong solution" — acceptable in some mark schemes, but "high water potential to low water potential" is the guaranteed-accurate wording.
  • Forgetting the minus sign in percentage change: negative means a loss of mass and the interpretation follows from it.
  • Saying active transport "uses energy" without saying where it comes from: respiration (mitochondria) — a favourite one-mark probe.
  • Confusing turgid (plant cell, full of water, firm) with plasmolysed (plant cell, lost water, membrane pulled from wall).
  • Describing water as "moving through the membrane holes" — membranes are not sieves; they are lipid bilayers with protein channels.
  • In Paper 6, failing to state repeats and a mean, or listing the independent and dependent variables the wrong way round.
  • Answering "describe" with reasons or "explain" with only a description: describe = what happens, explain = why it happens.

Exam-style questions and answers

Q1. Define osmosis. (2 marks) Answer: net movement of water molecules from a region of higher water potential to a region of lower water potential (1) through a partially permeable membrane (1).

Q2. Explain why a cell placed in pure water may burst if it is an animal cell but not if it is a plant cell. (3 marks) Answer: water enters both cells by osmosis down the water potential gradient (1); the animal cell has no cell wall so swells and lyses (1); the plant cell's cellulose wall resists the pressure so the cell becomes turgid instead (1).

Q3. A potato core loses 0.24 g from a starting mass of 3.00 g. Calculate the percentage change. (2 marks) Answer: (−0.24 ÷ 3.00) × 100 (1); = −8 % (1).

Q4. Explain why active transport is needed to absorb mineral ions from the soil into a root hair cell when diffusion cannot do the job. (3 marks) Answer: ions are at higher concentration inside the root hair than in the soil (1), so the gradient runs against entry (1); active transport uses energy from respiration to move them in by carrier proteins (1).

Q5. Describe two ways the small intestine is adapted for absorption. (2 marks) Answer: villi/ microvilli increase surface area (1); walls one cell thick and rich capillary supply maintain steep gradients and short diffusion paths (1).

Equations and symbols

This topic is examined on two calculations and one ratio: the percentage change that every osmosis practical reports, the arithmetic that turns raw masses into comparable data, and the surface-area-to-volume comparison that explains why exchange surfaces exist. There is no formula for diffusion itself — the marks there are for the definition and the three factors.

percentage change = (final mass − initial mass) ÷ initial mass × 100 Key: final mass and initial mass are the two weighings of the same sample (g); percentage change is the result (%). Report it as a percentage, not as a raw mass change, so samples of different starting sizes compare fairly.

−0.30 ÷ 2.40 = −0.125 Key: −0.30 = change in mass, final minus initial (g) — the minus sign means water left the tissue; 2.40 = initial mass (g); −0.125 = the proportional change (no units), which is then multiplied by 100.

−0.125 × 100 = −12.5 % Key: −0.125 = proportional change (no units); −12.5 % = the answer. Losing the minus sign is the commonest lost mark on this calculation, because the sign is the evidence that water moved out by osmosis.

6 × 8² = 384 cm² Key: 6 = the number of faces of a cube (no units); 8 = the side length (cm); 384 cm² = the total surface area. Surface area scales with the square of the length.

8³ = 512 cm³ Key: 8 = the side length (cm); 512 cm³ = the volume. Volume scales with the cube of the length, which is why the larger cube's surface-area-to-volume ratio (384 : 512, about 0.75:1) is far worse than the 1 cm cube's 6:1 — and why large organisms need exchange surfaces and a transport system.

SymbolQuantityUnit
ψwater potentialkPa (pure water = 0 kPa; solutes make it negative)
SA : Vsurface-area-to-volume rationo units (area ÷ volume)
%percentage change in mass%

title: Robotics & AI — Study Notes
content:
Robotics & AI

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): AI characteristics, machine learning basics, robotics/simulation contexts, automated systems.

1. AI characteristics

Systems exhibiting: planning, learning, reasoning, problem-solving, perception, knowledge representation. Narrow (task-specific) vs general AI distinction for discussion answers.

2. Machine learning

Supervised (labelled data — spam filters), unsupervised (clusters — segmentation), reinforcement (rewards — game agents). Training/evaluation loop: train on a set, test on unseen data; overfitting = memorising rather than generalising.

3. Robotics

Components: sensors (input), processors (decision), actuators/motors (output), power. Examples: manufacturing arms, delivery drones, autonomous vehicles (LIDAR + vision). Benefits: precision, 24/7 operation, dangerous jobs; concerns: job displacement, safety, cost.

4. Automated systems & simulation

Sensors → processor → actuators loops (greenhouses, traffic lights, self-checkouts). Simulation models real systems cheaply and safely (flight training, weather, crash tests) — limitations: model quality, missing variables.

5. Ethics of AI

Bias from unrepresentative training data; opacity of decisions; accountability for errors; privacy of training data; effect on employment.

Exam tips: for "describe how AI could be used in X" — tie each AI characteristic to a concrete step in the scenario; for evaluations, give both sides then a justified conclusion.

title: Abstract Data Types — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Abstract Data Types

Computer Science — A2. An abstract data type is a logical description of a collection of data plus the operations on it, independent of implementation. Stacks, queues, linked lists, binary trees and hash tables are all ADTs; in A Level you must show how they are built from arrays or records with pointers.

Key areas to revise

  • What is an ADT?
  • Linked Lists
  • Stacks and Queues
  • Binary Search Trees
  • Hash Tables

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

### Worked example An abstract data type defines the data and operations without fixing the implementation. A stack is last-in-first-out: push adds an item to the top and pop removes the top item. If you push 3, then 7, then pop twice, the first pop returns 7 and the second returns 3. A queue is first-in-first-out, so enqueue and dequeue return 3 then 7 in the same sequence. ### Check yourself Trace a queue after enqueue(A), enqueue(B), dequeue(). State which item is returned and what remains. The result is A, and the queue now holds B.

title: Exam technique: Pressure and Density
content:
### What earns the marks
For solids, p = F/A with substitution earns both marks. For liquids, proportionality with depth stated earns the explanation mark. For hydraulics, pressure equated across pistons earns the method mark.
### Traps
Error: force and pressure interchanged. Correction: pressure divides by area. Error: depth effect inverted. Correction: deeper means greater pressure. Error: atmospheric pressure guessed at 10 Pa. Correction: about 100 kPa at sea level.
### Method marks
Pressure = force ÷ area, and the area must be in m² for the answer in pascals. Density = mass ÷ volume. For an irregular solid, find the volume from the displacement of water.
### Explain, do not just name
Pressure in a liquid increases with depth because the weight of the column above increases. Write p = hρg and name each symbol in the explanation.
### Traps
Using cm² without converting: 1 cm² = 10^-4 m². Forgetting that the pressure in a fluid at a given depth acts equally in all directions.

title: Atomic Structure and the Periodic Table
content:
Atomic Structure and the Periodic Table

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH11, Topic 2. The periodic table is not a list to memorise: its rows and columns follow directly from how electrons fill shells and sub-shells.

Atoms, isotopes and mass spectrometry

  • Protons and neutrons make up the nucleus; the mass number is protons plus neutrons, and the atomic number is the number of protons.
  • Isotopes have the same number of protons and different numbers of neutrons, so the same chemistry but a different mass.
  • Relative atomic mass is the weighted mean of isotopic masses. In a mass spectrum, abundance is read from the peak heights.

Electron configuration

  • Electrons fill orbitals in order of energy: 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d and so on, each orbital holding at most two electrons with opposite spins.
  • Write configurations such as 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ for neon; for transition metals the 4s electrons are lost before the 3d electrons when forming ions.

Periodic trends

  • Ionisation energy increases across a period because nuclear charge rises with similar shielding, and falls down a group as the outer electrons sit further from the nucleus.
  • Atomic radius falls across a period and rises down a group.
  • Successive ionisation energies reveal the group of an element: a large jump appears after the outer-shell electrons are removed.

Electron arrangement and the table

  • Period number = highest principal quantum number in use; group number relates to the number of outer electrons.
  • Blocks: s-block (groups 1-2), p-block (groups 13-18), d-block (transition metals).

Exam tip: when explaining an ionisation energy trend, name the factor (nuclear charge, shielding, distance) and say which way it changes.

title: Data Representation — Study Notes
content:
Data Representation

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): binary/hex, two's complement, BCD, text/image/sound encoding, file sizes, compression.

1. Number systems

  • Binary place values 128…1; hex digits 0–9, A–F; one hex digit = one nibble (4 bits).
  • Conversions: binary ↔ decimal ↔ hex. 0101 1010 → 5A; FF = 255.
  • BCD: 4 bits per decimal digit — 0029 → 0000 0000 0010 1001. Used in clocks/calculators; easier digit conversions, more bits than pure binary.

2. Two's complement (signed)

MSB is negative: −128 64 32 16 8 4 2 1. −5 = 1111 1011. Range 8-bit: −128…+127.

Negating: invert bits, add 1. Subtraction: add the negated number — 7 − 5 = 7 + (−5) = 0000 0111 + 1111 1011 = 0000 0010.

3. Text

ASCII 7-bit (128 chars) → extended sets; Unicode for all scripts (UTF-8 variable width). Character sets map codes to glyphs; uppercase/lowercase codes differ by one bit.

4. Images and sound

  • Bitmap: pixels; colour depth = bits per pixel. File size (bits) = W × H × depth. Metadata (width, height, depth) stores dimensions.
  • Sound: sample rate (Hz), resolution (bits per sample), track duration × channels. Higher rate/depth = better fidelity, larger files.

5. Compression

  • Lossless (RLE, ZIP): exact restore — text/code must use it. RLE example: AAABBBCC → 3A3B2C; effective with runs.
  • Lossy (JPEG, MP3): discards perceptually minor data — photos/music OK, text never.

Exam tips: show full working in conversions; for size questions write the formula first with units; state the reason a compression type suits the file.

Binary addition and overflow

Binary addition follows the same carry rule as denary, except that 1 + 1 = 10 (0 carry 1). For example, 0110 + 0111 = 1101. A register or storage location has a fixed number of bits, so a result that needs more bits than are available overflows and gives a wrong answer. Programmers and examiners look for an overflow error when the carry out of the leftmost bit is set.

Exam tip: state the number of bits used. Overflow depends on that width, not on the value of the numbers alone.

Worked example: converting between number systems

The binary number 1011 0110 can be written as the hexadecimal number B6. Split the binary digits into groups of four from the right, then convert each group: 1011 is B (11) and 0110 is 6. The decimal value is 128 + 32 + 16 + 4 + 2 = 182, and B6 in hexadecimal is 11 × 16 + 6 = 182, which confirms the conversion.

Worked example: two's complement

To represent −45 in 8-bit two's complement, start with 45 = 0010 1101. Invert every bit to get 1101 0010, then add 1 to get 1101 0011. As an unsigned number this is 211, and 211 − 256 = −45, which confirms the value. The leading bit is 1, so the number is negative, as expected.

Worked example: file size of an image

An image of 800 × 600 pixels with 24-bit colour needs 800 × 600 × 24 = 11 520 000 bits. Dividing by 8 gives 1 440 000 bytes, which is about 1.44 MB. Halving the colour depth to 12 bits halves the file size, which shows the trade-off between quality and storage.

Run-length encoding

Run-length encoding replaces each run of the same symbol by the count and the symbol. The string AAAABBBCCD is encoded as 4A3B2C1D, which is shorter. The method works best on data with long runs, and it can make a file larger if the data has few repeats, so it is a lossless method suited to simple graphics.

Exam point: state the number of bits used and show the working when calculating file sizes, because method marks are awarded for the calculation even if the arithmetic slips.

title: IGCSE Mathematics: Equations
content:
IGCSE Mathematics: Equations

Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580 (2025–2027), section 2 Algebra and graphs, statement 2.5 Equations — linear equations, changing the subject, simultaneous equations and quadratic equations, with the Extended additions of fractional equations and simultaneous linear–non-linear pairs. Solving an equation is finding the value of an unknown that makes a statement true, and every technique in this note is one idea applied repeatedly: do the same to both sides. The worked lines below are written out in full, because the method marks on both Paper 2 and Paper 4 are earned line by line.

What solving means: the balance principle

An equation is a balance. The equals sign says the left and right sides hold the same value, so any operation — add, subtract, multiply, divide — is legal only if it is applied to both sides. Solving then uses inverse operations to peel away everything around the unknown: addition undoes subtraction, multiplication undoes division, and a square root undoes a square. The golden rule of order: undo addition and subtraction first, then multiplication and division, then powers and roots.

Solve:  3x + 7 = 22

3x + 7 - 7 = 22 - 7        [subtract 7 from both sides]
3x = 15
3x / 3 = 15 / 3            [divide both sides by 3]
x = 5

Check in the original: 3 x 5 + 7 = 15 + 7 = 22  ✓

The check is not optional decoration: it costs five seconds and catches sign errors, which are the most common mark lost on Paper 2.

If the equation contains...First moveWhy
BracketsExpand every bracketSeparate terms can then be collected
FractionsMultiply every term by the lowest common denominatorOne step clears all fractions
Unknowns on both sidesCollect unknowns on one side, numbers on the otherThe equation must end as x = number
Powers of the unknownBring to one side as a quadratic and factorise or use the formulaLinear methods cannot isolate x inside x²

Linear equations with brackets, fractions and unknowns on both sides

The strategy is always the same: expand, collect, solve. Write one step per line and keep the equation balanced.

Solve:  5(2x - 3) = 3x + 11

10x - 15 = 3x + 11        [expand the bracket]
10x - 3x = 11 + 15        [subtract 3x from both sides, add 15 to both sides]
7x = 26
x = 26/7 = 3 5/7          [exact fraction, not a rounded decimal]
Solve:  (x + 4)/3 - 2 = x/5

Multiply every term by 15, the lowest common denominator of 3 and 5:
15 x (x + 4)/3 - 15 x 2 = 15 x x/5
5(x + 4) - 30 = 3x
5x + 20 - 30 = 3x        [expand]
5x - 10 = 3x             [collect constants]
5x - 3x = 10
2x = 10
x = 5

Check in the original: (5 + 4)/3 - 2 = 3 - 2 = 1 and 5/5 = 1  ✓

Multiplying by the common denominator clears fractions in one step — a technique worth using deliberately, since working with fractions line by line is where slips happen.

Changing the subject of a formula

Making x the subject means rearranging until the formula reads x = ... . Unwrap x the same way: undo additions, then multiplications, and if x appears in more than one place, collect all x-terms on one side first and factorise.

Make x the subject:  y = (2x + 3)/(x - 1)

Multiply both sides by (x - 1):
y(x - 1) = 2x + 3
yx - y = 2x + 3          [expand the left side]
yx - 2x = y + 3          [bring x terms left, others right]
x(y - 2) = y + 3         [factorise: x taken out of both terms]
x = (y + 3)/(y - 2)

Every line is a legitimate balanced move, and the final answer is a formula valid for any y except y = 2. Formula rearrangement is a Paper 4 staple — often disguised as a physics or mensuration problem.

Simultaneous equations

Two unknowns need two equations. There are two standard methods, and both produce both unknowns.

Elimination — make one unknown's coefficients match and subtract:

Solve:  3x + 2y = 16   and   5x - 2y = 8

The y coefficients already match (+2 and -2), so add the equations:
(3x + 2y) + (5x - 2y) = 16 + 8
8x = 24
x = 3

Substitute x = 3 into the first equation:
3(3) + 2y = 16
9 + 2y = 16
2y = 7
y = 3.5

Check in the second equation: 5(3) - 2(3.5) = 15 - 7 = 8  ✓

Substitution — make one unknown the subject of one equation:

Solve:  x + y = 10   and   y = x^2 - 4        [one linear, one non-linear: Extended]

From the first equation: y = 10 - x
Substitute into the second:
10 - x = x^2 - 4
0 = x^2 + x - 14        [rearranged: x^2 - 4 + x - 10 = x^2 + x - 14]
x = [-1 ± √(1 + 56)]/2 = [-1 ± √57]/2       [quadratic formula]

Numerically x ≈ 3.275 or x ≈ -4.275, with the matching y values y = 10 - x ≈ 6.725 and 14.275.

For a pair of straight lines there is exactly one solution unless the lines are parallel (no solution) or identical (infinitely many) — a common Paper 2 short question.

Quadratic equations

A quadratic has the form ax² + bx + c = 0 and may have two solutions, one, or none. Three methods are examinable.

1. Factorising.

Solve:  x^2 - 5x + 6 = 0

(x - 2)(x - 3) = 0        [factors of +6 that sum to -5]
A product is zero only when a factor is zero:
x - 2 = 0  or  x - 3 = 0
x = 2  or  x = 3

2. Completing the square.

Solve:  x^2 + 6x + 2 = 0

(x + 3)^2 - 9 + 2 = 0        [(x+3)^2 = x^2 + 6x + 9, so subtract 9 to keep equality]
(x + 3)^2 - 7 = 0
(x + 3)^2 = 7
x + 3 = ±√7                  [both roots, positive and negative]
x = -3 ± √7
x ≈ -0.354  or  x ≈ -5.65

3. The quadratic formula. It is completing the square, done once and for all. Starting from ax² + bx + c = 0 and dividing by a:

x^2 + (b/a)x + c/a = 0
x^2 + (b/a)x = -c/a
x^2 + (b/a)x + (b/2a)^2 = -c/a + (b/2a)^2        [add the completing-the-square term]
(x + b/2a)^2 = (b^2 - 4ac)/(4a^2)
x + b/2a = ±√(b^2 - 4ac)/(2a)
x = [-b ± √(b^2 - 4ac)] / (2a)

The discriminant b² − 4ac decides how many solutions there are before any solving: if it is positive there are two distinct roots, if it is zero there is one repeated root, and if it is negative there are no real roots.

Solve:  2x^2 - 3x - 5 = 0

a = 2, b = -3, c = -5;  b^2 - 4ac = 9 + 40 = 49, so two roots
x = [3 ± √49] / 4 = [3 ± 7]/4
x = (3 + 7)/4 = 2.5    or    x = (3 - 7)/4 = -1

Fractional equations (Extended)

An equation with x in a denominator is cleared the same way as any fraction equation — multiply through by the denominator — but the solutions must be checked against it, because a value that makes the denominator zero is not a solution at all.

Solve:  3/(x - 1) + 2 = 5/(x + 2)

Multiply every term by (x - 1)(x + 2):
3(x + 2) + 2(x - 1)(x + 2) = 5(x - 1)
3x + 6 + 2(x^2 + x - 2) = 5x - 5
3x + 6 + 2x^2 + 2x - 4 = 5x - 5
2x^2 + 5x + 2 = 5x - 5
2x^2 + 7 = 0
x^2 = -7/2

No real solutions. (Had a value like x = 1 appeared, it would be rejected as it makes x - 1 = 0.)

Worked example: an exam-style multi-step equation

A rectangle has length (2x + 1) cm and width (x − 3) cm. Its area is 30 cm². Find x and the dimensions.

(2x + 1)(x - 3) = 30
2x^2 - 6x + x - 3 = 30        [expand]
2x^2 - 5x - 3 = 30
2x^2 - 5x - 33 = 0            [subtract 30 from both sides]
(x - 3.5)(2x + 11) ... check by formula instead:
Factorise the quadratic: we need two numbers with product 2 x (-33) = -66 and sum -5.
The pair -11 and +6 works: (-11) x 6 = -66 and -11 + 6 = -5.
Split the middle term:  2x^2 + 6x - 11x - 33 = 0
Factorise in pairs:     2x(x + 3) - 11(x + 3) = 0
(x + 3)(2x - 11) = 0
x = -3  or  x = 11/2 = 5.5
x = 22/4 = 5.5   or   x = -12/4 = -3

The negative answer is rejected: a length of x − 3 with x = −3 gives −6 cm, which is impossible. So x = 5.5, the length is 12 cm and the width is 2.5 cm. Checking the area: 12 × 2.5 = 30 ✓. Interpreting the solutions in context is a mark in its own right.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Applying an operation to one side only. The single most common algebraic error; the equation must stay balanced.
  • Sign errors when expanding: −3(x − 4) = −3x + 12, not −3x − 12.
  • Forgetting the ± when taking a square root: x² = 9 gives x = 3 or x = −3.
  • Rejecting or accepting context solutions carelessly: lengths, counts and times must be positive, and the rejected root should be stated as rejected with a reason.
  • Leaving a fractional answer as a rounded decimal on Paper 2, where exact fractions are expected.
  • Ignoring the discriminant's role: if b² − 4ac is negative the quadratic has no real roots — say so rather than hunting for errors.
  • Missing a denominator restriction in a fractional equation and quoting x = 1 as a solution of 1/(x − 1) = ... .
  • Rounding too early: keep exact values (fractions, surds) until the final line of a multi-step question.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 2, 3 marks). Solve 4x − 7 = 2x + 9.

Answer: 4x − 2x = 9 + 7, so 2x = 16 and x = 8. Check: 32 − 7 = 25 and 16 + 9 = 25 ✓.

Question 2 (Paper 2, 4 marks). Solve x² + 2x − 15 = 0.

Answer: (x + 5)(x − 3) = 0, so x = −5 or x = 3. (Factor pairs of −15 summing to +2: +5 and −3.)

Question 3 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Solve the simultaneous equations 2x + 3y = 12 and 4x − y = 5.

Answer: Multiply the second equation by 3: 12x − 3y = 15. Add to the first: 14x = 27, so x = 27/14. Substitute: 2(27/14) + 3y = 12 gives 27/7 + 3y = 12, so 3y = 12 − 27/7 = 57/7 and y = 19/7.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Solve 2x² − 8x + 3 = 0, giving answers to 2 decimal places.

Answer: b² − 4ac = 64 − 24 = 40. x = [8 ± √40]/4 = [8 ± 6.325]/4, so x ≈ 3.58 or x ≈ 0.42.

Question 5 (Paper 4, 5 marks). Make r the subject of V = (1/3)πr²h.

Answer: 3V = πr²h (multiply by 3); 3V/(πh) = r² (divide by πh); r = √[3V/(πh)] (take the positive square root, since a radius is positive).

Question 6 (Paper 4, 5 marks). The length of a rectangle is 3 cm more than twice its width. Its perimeter is 54 cm. Find its area.

Answer: Let the width be w; the length is 2w + 3. Perimeter: 2[w + (2w + 3)] = 54, so 2(3w + 3) = 54, 3w + 3 = 27, 3w = 24 and w = 8. The length is 19 cm and the area is 8 × 19 = 152 cm².

Inequalities generalise equations from exact equality to a range of permitted values.

title: IGCSE Physics: Magnetism and Electromagnetism
content:
IGCSE Physics: Magnetism and Electromagnetism

Cambridge IGCSE Physics 0625 (2026–2028), Topic 4 Electricity and magnetism: statements 4.1 Simple phenomena of magnetism and 4.5 Electromagnetic effects. Magnetism and electricity are two faces of one interaction: moving charge makes magnetic fields, and changing magnetic fields make currents. That single loop of cause and effect explains generators, motors, transformers and every device that turns movement into electricity or electricity into movement.

Magnets and magnetic fields

A magnet has two poles, north and south. Like poles repel; unlike poles attract; and a magnet freely suspended turns to line up with the Earth's magnetic field, which is why a compass points north. Magnetic materials (iron, steel, nickel, cobalt) are attracted to magnets; non-magnetic materials are not. Induced magnetism is what happens when a magnetic material near a magnet becomes a magnet itself: a paper clip picked up by a magnet can pick up a second clip. Soft iron makes temporary magnets (it magnetises and demagnetises easily — good for electromagnets and relays); steel makes permanent magnets (hard to demagnetise — good for compass needles).

A magnetic field is the region around a magnet where another magnet experiences a force. Its direction is the direction a north pole would move — out of a north pole and into a south pole. Field lines never cross, and their spacing shows the field strength: close together for a strong field, spread out for a weak one (Supplement: the field is the region of influence, and its strength is represented by the line density). Plotting fields is done with a small plotting compass on a sheet of paper over the magnet; the compass needle traces the lines from pole to pole.

Electromagnetic induction

Move a magnet into a coil of wire and a voltage appears across the coil: this is electromagnetic induction, discovered by Faraday. The induced e.m.f. (and the current it drives if the circuit is closed) is bigger when:

  • the magnet or coil moves faster;
  • the magnet is stronger;
  • the coil has more turns;
  • the coil's core is soft iron (which concentrates the magnetic field).

It is the change in the field that induces a voltage — a stationary magnet inside a coil does nothing. Supplement: Lenz's law. The induced current always flows in a direction that opposes the change producing it: push a north pole in and the coil's near face becomes north to push back; pull it out and the coil becomes south to hold it. Energy conservation demands this — the mechanical work done pushing against the opposition is exactly the electrical energy induced.

The a.c. generator

A generator turns kinetic energy into electrical energy by spinning a coil in a magnetic field (or a magnet inside a coil). As the coil rotates, the amount of magnetic field passing through it changes continuously, so an e.m.f. is induced that rises, falls and reverses, producing alternating current.

  • The coil ends are joined to two slip rings, each touching a brush (a carbon block) that carries the current to the external circuit.
  • Supplement: the e.m.f.–time graph is a sine wave; it is zero when the coil is vertical (moving parallel to the field) and maximum when the coil is horizontal (cutting the field fastest).

A power station generator is the same machine scaled up: steam, water or wind spins the coil, and the faster it spins or the stronger the field, the greater the peak e.m.f.

The magnetic effect of a current

A current in a wire produces a magnetic field around it — the discovery that links electricity and magnetism. The field lines are concentric circles centred on the wire, and the field is stronger closer to the wire. The right-hand grip rule gives the direction: point the thumb along the conventional current and the curled fingers show the direction of the field lines.

Winding the wire into a solenoid (coil) concentrates the field into a pattern just like a bar magnet's: strong and uniform inside the coil, out of one end and into the other. The field is stronger with more turns and a larger current, and an iron core inside the coil makes an electromagnet — a magnet that can be switched on and off, made stronger at will, and loses its magnetism when the current stops.

  • Relay: a small current in an electromagnet's coil attracts a soft-iron armature that closes a second, high-current circuit. It lets a low-voltage circuit switch a dangerous mains circuit safely.
  • Loudspeaker: alternating current in a coil in the field of a permanent magnet makes the coil (attached to the cone) vibrate with the frequency of the current, producing sound waves. The loudspeaker turns electrical energy into sound energy; a microphone does the reverse.

Force on a current-carrying conductor

A wire carrying a current in a magnetic field experiences a force — the principle of the motor and of the moving-coil loudspeaker. The force is largest when the wire is perpendicular to the field and zero when it runs parallel to it.

force on a conductor = magnetic flux density x current x length        F = B I L
  • F: force in newtons (N); B: magnetic flux density in tesla (T); I: current in amperes (A); L: length of wire in the field in metres (m). The force direction is given by Fleming's left-hand rule and is a vector: swap any two of field, current and force and the force reverses.

Fleming's left-hand rule: first finger Field, seCond finger Current, thuMb Motion. The three fingers held mutually at right angles give all three directions. The force can be increased by raising the current, using a stronger magnet, or making the wire longer in the field (more turns on the coil). Supplement: a charged particle moving through a magnetic field is deflected for the same reason, which is how a beam of electrons can be bent on a screen.

The d.c. motor

A coil carrying current in a magnetic field experiences opposite forces on its two sides, producing a turning effect (a couple) that rotates the coil. A simple d.c. motor has the coil, a commutator (a split-ring), brushes, and a permanent-magnet field. The split-ring commutator is the clever part: every half turn it reverses the current in the coil, so the forces always push the same way and the rotation continues instead of stalling at the vertical position.

  • The rotation speeds up with a larger current, a stronger field or more turns on the coil.
  • Energy conversion: electrical energy in, kinetic energy out (plus heat from the coil's resistance).
  • Running the motor in reverse — driving the coil instead of feeding it — turns it into a generator, which is how a bicycle dynamo works.

The transformer

A transformer changes the size of an alternating voltage using electromagnetic induction. It has two coils wound on the same soft-iron core: the alternating current in the primary coil makes an alternating magnetic field in the core, which induces an alternating e.m.f. in the secondary coil.

secondary voltage / primary voltage = secondary turns / primary turns        Vs / Vp = Ns / Np
  • Vp and Vs: voltages in volts (V); Np and Ns: numbers of turns on each coil. A step-up transformer has more turns on the secondary; a step-down has fewer.
  • Supplement: for an ideal transformer, power in = power out, so Vp Ip = Vs Is; stepping the voltage up steps the current down, and vice versa.

Transformers are why the National Grid transmits at 11 000 V or more. For the same power, P = IV means a high voltage needs a small current, and the energy wasted heating the cables is I²R — squaring a small current makes the waste tiny. Power stations therefore step up for transmission and step down again at substations and on poles for safe domestic use. An ideal transformer has no energy losses; real ones lose a little to heating in the coils, to eddy currents in the core (reduced by a laminated core) and to magnetising the core, giving efficiencies of 95 per cent or better.

Worked example: transmission losses

A power station sends 20 MW at 250 V along cables of total resistance 0.10 Ω, and again at 25 000 V.

current at 250 V = P / V = 20 000 000 / 250 = 80 000 A
power wasted = I² R = 80 000² × 0.10 = 640 MW   (impossible in practice - the cable would melt)
current at 25 000 V = 20 000 000 / 25 000 = 800 A
power wasted = 800² × 0.10 = 64 000 W = 64 kW

Stepping the voltage up one hundredfold cuts the current one hundredfold and the wasted power ten thousandfold — 64 kW instead of 640 MW. That is the entire reason the grid uses transformers.

Common mistakes

  • Using Fleming's left-hand rule for generators; the left hand is for motors (force on a current), while generators and induction use the idea that the induced current opposes the change (Lenz's law).
  • Saying a stationary magnet in a coil induces a current; only a changing field does.
  • Forgetting to square the current in the cable-loss equation, or using the transmission voltage instead of the current in I²R.
  • Drawing transformer field lines that do not link both coils; the coils share one core and one magnetic field.
  • Assuming transformers work on d.c.; a steady d.c. produces no changing field and no induced e.m.f. in the secondary.
  • Reversing the turns ratio: step-up means more turns on the secondary, so Vs is bigger than Vp.
  • Mixing up where the force points: current along the second finger, field along the first, motion along the thumb, and all three at right angles.
  • Forgetting that the commutator reverses the current every half turn; without it the coil would stop at the vertical.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 4, 3 marks). A transformer has 500 primary turns and 2000 secondary turns with a 230 V input. Calculate the output voltage and state the transformer type.

Answer: Vs = Vp × Ns/Np = 230 × 2000/500 = 920 V. It is a step-up transformer because the secondary has more turns.

Question 2 (Paper 4, 3 marks). A straight wire carries 4.0 A perpendicular to a 0.25 T field. Find the force on 0.30 m of wire.

Answer: F = BIL = 0.25 × 4.0 × 0.30 = 0.30 N, in the direction given by Fleming's left-hand rule.

Question 3 (Paper 2 style). Which change increases the e.m.f. induced in a coil? A holding the magnet still inside it; B moving the magnet faster; C using fewer turns; D using a weaker magnet. Answer: B. Faster motion means a faster change of field through the coil.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 6 marks). Explain how a transformer works and why the grid transmits power at high voltage.

Answer: The a.c. in the primary coil produces an alternating magnetic field in the soft-iron core. That changing field passes through the secondary coil and induces an alternating e.m.f. in it by electromagnetic induction. The size of the output voltage depends on the turns ratio: Vs/Vp = Ns/Np. For transmission, P = IV, so the same power can be sent at high voltage and low current. The energy wasted heating the cables is I²R, so a smaller current greatly reduces the wasted energy; the voltage is then stepped down with transformers for safe domestic use.

Question 5 (Paper 4, 3 marks). State two ways to increase the turning effect on the coil of a d.c. motor.

Answer: Increase the current, use a stronger magnetic field (or increase the flux density), or wind more turns on the coil. Any two, with the reasoning that the force on each side of the coil is F = BIL, so bigger B or I or L gives a bigger force.

Question 6 (Paper 6 style). Describe an experiment to show the pattern of the magnetic field around a bar magnet.

Answer: Place the bar magnet on a sheet of paper and sprinkle iron filings (or use a small plotting compass). Tap the paper gently; the filings line up along the field. The compass needle is placed at several points and its direction marked with an arrow pointing away from the north pole; the marks are joined into smooth field lines from north to south, close together near the poles where the field is strongest.

Fields move charges and magnets; inside the atom, a different kind of energy is stored: Nuclear Physics next.

title: Exam technique: Congruence and Similarity
content:
### What earns the marks
For similarity lengths, calculate earns marks for the scale factor stated (larger over smaller, matched pairs) and then applied. For area and volume, the squared and cubed factors stated earn the method mark before any multiplication: write k squared or k cubed explicitly. For symmetry, count earns marks per correct count with the reasoning (vertices, rotation step 360 / n). For congruence, name earns the test (SSS, SAS, ASA, RHS) with the matching parts listed.
### Traps
Error: adding the length difference instead of scaling. Correction: similarity always multiplies. Error: using k instead of k squared for area or k cubed for volume. Correction: write the power first. Error: equal angles claimed as congruence. Correction: angles alone prove similarity; a matching side upgrades it.
### Worked example
Two triangles have sides 3 cm, 4 cm and 5 cm, and a second triangle has sides 6 cm, 8 cm and 10 cm. The second triangle is an enlargement with scale factor 2. Each length is multiplied by 2, so each area is multiplied by 2² = 4. If the lengths are scaled by 2.5, the areas are scaled by 6.25.
### Check yourself
Two triangles have all three angles equal. Are they similar, congruent, or neither? They are similar, because equal angles give equal shape but not necessarily equal size. They are congruent only if the side lengths also match, which you check using SSS, SAS, ASA or RHS.

title: Sampling and Estimation — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Sampling and Estimation

Mathematics — A2. A parameter describes the population (μ, σ²); a statistic describes the sample (x̄, s²). A statistic is unbiased if its expectation equals the population parameter: E(x̄) = μ always holds for the sample mean.

Key areas to revise

  • Populations, Samples, Statistics
  • Unbiased Variance
  • Distribution of the Sample Mean
  • Central Limit Theorem
  • Using x̄ to Estimate

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.
