title:
Molecules, Transport and Health — Quick Revision Summary

Biology — AS Edexcel IAL, WBI12 Unit 1 Topic 1. Water as a polar solvent and its role in transport, carbohydrates (monosaccharides, disaccharides, polysaccharides including starch, glycogen and cellulose) and their structure and role in energy storage and structure, lipids (triglycerides, saturated and unsaturated) and their roles, proteins and their structure from amino acid to tertiary and quaternary, gas exchange surfaces and Fick's law and the mammalian lung adaptations, the mammalian heart and circulatory system and the cardiac cycle, haemoglobin and the oxygen dissociation curve and the Bohr effect and fetal haemoglobin, atherosclerosis and blood clotting, risk factors for CVD (diet, blood pressure, smoking, age, gender, inactivity, cholesterol, obesity) and how each acts, diet and antioxidants and cholesterol and the evidence, people using scientific knowledge to reduce risk, the benefits and risks of treatments (antihypertensives, statins, anticoagulants, platelet inhibitors), and the data analysis skills of distinguishing correlation from causation and evaluating study design and sample size — plus the two core practicals (Benedict's and iodine semi-quantitative tests, DCPIP vitamin C, biuret protein, enzyme factors).

  • 1.1 Water: a dipole — oxygen slightly negative, hydrogen slightly positive — so it forms hydrogen bonds, has high specific heat capacity and high latent heat of vaporisation, is cohesive, and is an excellent solvent for ions and polar molecules (because the partial charges surround and dissolve them); in transport it carries dissolved substances.
  • 1.2 Carbohydrates: monosaccharides (glucose, fructose, galactose — hexoses, C₆H₁₂O₆); disaccharides by condensation forming glycosidic bonds (maltose = glucose+glucose, sucrose = glucose+fructose, lactose = glucose+galactose); polysaccharides: starch (amylose helical and amylopectin branched — glucose storage in plants, compact and insoluble), glycogen (more branched storage in animals, mainly liver and muscle), cellulose (beta-glucose straight chains, hydrogen-bonded into microfibrils — structural).
  • 1.3 Core Practical 1: Benedict's reagent turns blue → green → yellow → orange → brick-red as reducing sugar concentration increases (heat with the sample, compare with a colour standard chart to estimate); iodine solution turns blue-black with starch — compare intensity with a colour standard to estimate.
  • 1.4 Glycosidic bonds: monosaccharides join by condensation (losing water, forming a glycosidic bond) to make disaccharides and polysaccharides; hydrolysis (adding water) breaks the bond — starch → maltose → glucose; sucrose → glucose + fructose; lactose → glucose + galactose.
  • 1.5 Triglycerides: one glycerol + three fatty acids, joined by ester bonds; saturated fatty acids have no double bonds (straight, pack tight — solid fats), unsaturated have double bonds (kinks, loose packing — liquid oils); roles: energy storage (more energy per gram than carbohydrate), phospholipid bilayer, myelin sheath, waterproof skin layer (subcutaneous fat), steroid hormones.
  • 1.6 Why animals need a heart and circulation: as organisms grow, diffusion alone becomes too slow to supply cells deep inside the body — surface area to volume ratio falls with size, so a mass transport system (heart, blood vessels, blood) moves materials fast.
  • 1.7 Blood vessels: arteries carry blood away from the heart at high pressure — thick muscular, elastic walls, narrow lumen, no valves; veins carry blood to the heart at low pressure — thinner walls, wide lumen, valves to prevent backflow; capillaries are one cell thick with the smallest lumen — thin walls and large total surface area for exchange.
  • 1.8 Cardiac cycle: atrial systole (atria contract, blood into ventricles), ventricular systole (ventricles contract, blood into aorta and pulmonary artery, AV valves close → first heart sound), diastole (heart relaxes, ventricles fill, semilunar valves close → second heart sound); valves ensure one-way flow; left ventricle has a much thicker wall than the right because it pumps to the whole body at higher pressure; the heart is myogenic.
  • 1.9 Haemoglobin and oxygen transport: haemoglobin has four polypeptide chains each with a haem group carrying one O₂ molecule, so one haemoglobin carries four O₂; the oxygen dissociation curve shows saturation rising steeply then levelling; the Bohr effect: higher CO₂ and lower pH lower haemoglobin's oxygen affinity, so it unloads more O₂ in respiring tissues; fetal haemoglobin has a higher oxygen affinity than adult haemoglobin, so it can take oxygen from adult haemoglobin across the placenta.
  • 1.10 Atherosclerosis: endothelial dysfunction (damage from high blood pressure, smoking chemicals or immune responses) → inflammatory response, white blood cells enter the wall, LDL oxidised and taken up, smooth muscle and fibrous tissue build up → plaque (fibrous cap over a lipid core); the plaque narrows the artery, raises pressure, and can rupture → clot (thrombus) → blocked artery → myocardial infarction (heart attack) or stroke.
  • 1.11 Blood clotting: vessel damage exposes collagen, platelets activate and release thromboplastin, thromboplastin + Ca²⁺ converts prothrombin → thrombin, thrombin converts soluble fibrinogen → insoluble fibrin threads that form a mesh trapping platelets and red blood cells → a clot; clotting prevents blood loss and pathogen entry, but a clot on a ruptured plaque can block a coronary artery and cause a myocardial infarction or a cerebral artery and cause a stroke.

Worked example

Risk calculation from data: a study finds that smokers have a 15% chance of a heart attack by age 70, and non-smokers 4% — the relative risk for smokers = 15/4 = 3.75, so smokers are about 3.75 times as likely to have a heart attack by 70; but this is a correlation — part of the risk is caused by smoking itself (mechanistically, the chemicals damage the endothelium, raise blood pressure and reduce oxygen carried by haemoglobin), and it may also be that smokers differ in other ways (diet, exercise); still, smoking is a causal risk factor, so the relative risk is used as evidence, not proof, and decisions use the whole body of evidence. To evaluate the study, check the sample (is it representative, and large enough, and free from bias in selection or loss of participants) and the method (were the groups comparable, and were confounding factors such as diet and exercise accounted for).

Key points to remember

Risk factors for CVD and how they act: high blood pressure damages endothelium and raises heart strain and atherosclerosis risk; high saturated fat and cholesterol raise LDL and contribute to plaques; smoking introduces chemicals that damage endothelium, raise blood pressure and heart rate and reduce oxygen carried by haemoglobin (carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin); age increases risk as damage accumulates and repair is less efficient; males are at higher risk than females at younger ages; inactivity contributes to blood pressure, obesity and cholesterol; genetics/family history affects baseline risk; obesity (BMI = mass (kg)/height (m)², and waist-to-hip ratio) is a risk factor; high cholesterol (total and LDL) is linked to CVD and HDL is protective. Diet and antioxidants: vitamin C and E (from fruit and vegetables) may reduce risk by preventing oxidation of LDL; evidence for cholesterol causing CVD comes from the biology and from the results of statin trials, which lower cholesterol and reduce events. People use this knowledge — BMI, waist-to-hip ratio, exercise, smoking, diet — to reduce their risk. Benefits and risks of treatments: antihypertensives lower blood pressure (dizziness, fatigue, kidney effects, over-lowering); statins lower cholesterol (muscle pain, digestive upset, rarely liver effects); anticoagulants (warfarin) and platelet inhibitors (aspirin) reduce clotting (bleeding risk, gut bleeding, not for everyone). Distinguish correlation from causation and evaluate study design — sample selection (representative or biased), sample size (small samples less reliable, more chance variation), and whether confounding factors were controlled.

How to use this

Read the summary list, then open the full revision notes for any point that feels weak, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself. Revise next by: drawing a triglyceride and distinguishing saturated and unsaturated; drawing a cholesterol molecule and stating how saturated and unsaturated fats differ; carrying out the Benedict's, iodine and DCPIP practicals and explaining the variables, the colour standards and the control variables; describing the cardiac cycle and drawing the pressure/volume changes through a heartbeat; sketching the oxygen dissociation curve of haemoglobin, showing the Bohr effect and the fetal haemoglobin curve to the left; describing the stages of atherosclerosis and blood clotting and the enzymes and factors in clotting; listing the risk factors for CVD and stating how each acts; and working through a risk calculation from study data and evaluating the study design.

title: Databases and Data Definition — Study Notes
content:
Databases and Data Definition

Relational Concepts

A table (relation) stores rows (tuples) and columns (attributes). The primary key uniquely identifies each row; a foreign key references a primary key in another table, creating the relationship. A composite key uses two or more columns together.

Normalisation

  • 1NF: atomic values, no repeating groups.
  • 2NF: 1NF plus every non-key attribute depends on the whole key (kills partial dependency in composite keys).
  • 3NF: 2NF plus no transitive dependency — non-key attributes must not depend on other non-key attributes.

Normalisation reduces redundancy and prevents update, insert and delete anomalies.

DDL and DML

DDL defines structure: CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE, DROP. DML manipulates data: SELECT ... FROM ... WHERE, INSERT INTO, UPDATE, DELETE. Joins combine related tables: FROM Student s JOIN Enrolment e ON s.id = e.StudentID. Aggregates: COUNT, SUM, AVG with GROUP BY and HAVING.

Transactions and Concurrency

A transaction is a unit of work obeying ACID: Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (rules preserved), Isolation (concurrent transactions do not interfere), Durability (committed data survives crashes). Record locking blocks conflicting simultaneous edits; a deadlock occurs when two transactions each hold a lock the other needs.

Exam tips: normalise a small table through 1NF, 2NF, 3NF naming the dependency removed at each step; write a two-table SELECT with JOIN; state which ACID property a scenario breaks.

title: Electricity: D.C. Circuits — Study Notes
content:
Electricity: D.C. Circuits

Current and Charge

I = Q/t — charge per second, in amperes. Conventional current flows + to − (electrons drift the other way).

I = nAvq links microscopic drift to macroscopic current (n = carrier density).

Voltage and Power

  • V = W/Q (joules per coulomb)
  • P = VI = I²R = V²/R

Resistance and Resistivity

R = V/I; R = ρL/A. Resistivity ρ is a material property (Ω m). Metals' resistance rises with temperature; thermistors' falls (NTC).

Example: a wire 2 m long, 0.5 mm² cross-section, ρ = 5 × 10⁻⁷: R = 2 Ω.

Series and Parallel

  • Series: same current, R_total = R₁ + R₂ + …
  • Parallel: same voltage, 1/R_total = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + …

EMF and Internal Resistance

ε = I(R + r) — some voltage is 'lost' inside the battery. Terminal voltage V = ε − Ir drops as load current rises.

Potential Dividers

V_out = V_in × R₂/(R₁ + R₂). Used with LDRs/thermistors to make sensor circuits.

Exam tips: redraw messy networks with clean junctions; always account for internal resistance in 'maximum power' questions.

title: Organic Chemistry: Arenes (Edexcel IAL A2 Chemistry)
content:
Organic Chemistry: Arenes - Edexcel IAL A2 Chemistry

This topic belongs to Edexcel International A-Level Chemistry WCH15, Topic 18, and covers the structure, stability, and characteristic reactions of arenes, specifically benzene, alongside activating and directing effects including phenol.

Structure and Evidence for Benzene

Benzene is an arene with the molecular formula C6H6, possessing a planar ring structure supported by multiple lines of physical and chemical evidence.

  • Thermochemical evidence: The measured enthalpy of hydrogenation of benzene is approximately −208 kJ mol−1, which is significantly less exothermic than the theoretical value of −360 kJ mol−1 calculated for a hypothetical cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene with three isolated double bonds. The difference of about 150 kJ mol−1 is the stabilisation energy, also known as the delocalisation energy, proving benzene is much more stable than the classical Kekule structure.
  • X-ray diffraction data: X-ray crystallography shows that all six carbon-carbon bond lengths in benzene are identical at 0.139 nm, a value intermediate between a typical carbon-carbon single bond (0.154 nm) and a carbon-carbon double bond (0.134 nm).
  • Infrared spectroscopy: IR data shows characteristic carbon-carbon aromatic ring stretching absorptions and aromatic carbon-hydrogen stretching bands.
  • Delocalised model: The delocalised model for the structure of benzene involves the sideways overlap of unhybridised p-orbitals on each of the six carbon atoms, forming a continuous ring of pi-bonds above and below the plane of the carbon ring. Students may represent the structure of benzene as a ring inside a hexagon or as alternating double and single bonds as appropriate in equations and mechanisms.

Resistance to Bromination and Comparison with Alkenes

Benzene displays very different chemical reactivity compared to alkenes due to the nature of its bonding.

  • Resistance to bromination: Benzene is resistant to bromination compared to alkenes because of the delocalisation of pi-bonds in benzene, which spreads the electron density over the whole ring, making it a stable region. In contrast, alkenes possess a localised electron density in their pi-bond situated between two carbon atoms, which polarises approaching electrophiles much more readily.
  • Reactivity consequence: Alkenes undergo electrophilic addition reactions readily at room temperature without a catalyst, whereas benzene undergoes electrophilic substitution reactions and requires a halogen carrier catalyst to polarise non-polar molecules like bromine.

Reactions of Benzene

Benzene undergoes a variety of chemical reactions under specific conditions.

  • Combustion: Benzene burns in oxygen in air with a smoky flame due to its high carbon-to-hydrogen ratio, indicating unburnt carbon particles.
  • Halogenation: Benzene reacts with bromine in the presence of a catalyst such as iron(III) bromide or aluminium bromide.
  • Nitration: Benzene reacts with a mixture of concentrated nitric acid and concentrated sulfuric acids heated to about 50 degrees Celsius.
  • Sulfonation: Benzene reacts with fuming sulfuric acid (sulfuric(VI) acid containing dissolved sulfur trioxide).
  • Friedel-Crafts reactions: Benzene reacts with halogenoalkanes (alkylation) and acyl chlorides (acylation) with anhydrous aluminium chloride as a catalyst.

Mechanisms of Electrophilic Substitution

Electrophilic substitution in benzene proceeds through the generation of an electrophile followed by attack and proton loss.

  • Generation of electrophiles: For nitration, concentrated nitric acid and concentrated sulfuric acid generate the nitronium ion electrophile: HNO3 + 2H2SO4 yields NO2+ + 2HSO4− + H3O+. For halogenation, bromine reacts with an aluminium halide catalyst to generate the Br+ or polarised Br-Br-AlCl3 electrophilic species. For Friedel-Crafts alkylation and acylation, the halogenoalkane or acyl chloride reacts with aluminium chloride, acting as a Lewis acid, to generate a carbocation or acylium ion electrophile: RCl + AlCl3 yields R+ + AlCl4−.
  • Substitution mechanism: The electron-rich pi system of the benzene ring acts as a nucleophile and donates a pair of electrons to the electrophile, forming an unstable arenium intermediate where the positive charge is delocalised over the remaining five carbon atoms of the ring. A base removes a hydrogen ion from the substituted carbon, restoring the stable delocalised pi system of the benzene ring and regenerating the catalyst.

Reactivity of Phenol

Phenol contains a hydroxyl group attached directly to an aromatic ring, significantly altering its reactivity compared to benzene.

  • Reaction with bromine water: Phenol reacts readily with bromine water at room temperature without any halogen carrier catalyst, instantly decolorising the orange bromine water and giving a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol, accompanied by steamy fumes of hydrogen bromide.
  • Reasons for relative ease: The lone pair of electrons on the oxygen atom of the −OH group in phenol overlaps with the pi system of the benzene ring. This partially delocalises the lone pair into the ring, significantly increasing the electron density of the ring compared to benzene. As a result, the benzene ring in phenol is strongly activated, polarizing incoming electrophiles like bromine much more effectively and attracting them faster than benzene can.

Side-Chain Oxidation and Directing Effects

Substituents on the benzene ring affect both the position of further substitution and the reactivity of side chains.

  • Directing effects: Alkyl groups, such as the methyl group in methylbenzene, and activating groups direct a second incoming substituent primarily to the 2- and 4- positions (ortho and para). A nitro group is a deactivating group and directs incoming electrophiles to the 3- (meta) position. Hydroxyl and amino groups are strongly activating.
  • Side-chain oxidation: Hot, acidified potassium manganate(VII) solution oxidises any alkyl side chain on a benzene ring directly to a carboxylic acid group, regardless of the length of the alkyl chain, provided there is at least one benzylic hydrogen atom. For example, methylbenzene is oxidised to benzoic acid.

Typical mistakes

  • Mistake: Stating that benzene undergoes electrophilic addition because it has double bonds. Correction: Benzene undergoes electrophilic substitution to preserve the stable delocalised pi electron system.
  • Mistake: Omitting the catalyst in Friedel-Crafts equations or halogenation. Correction: Always include anhydrous aluminium chloride or iron(III) bromide as catalysts.
  • Mistake: Drawing the positive charge inside the intermediate horseshoe incorrectly. Correction: Ensure the incomplete horseshoe representing the positive charge in the arenium intermediate extends over five carbon atoms and does not touch the carbon bonded to the incoming electrophile and leaving hydrogen.
  • Mistake: Confusing the conditions for phenol bromination with benzene bromination. Correction: Phenol reacts with aqueous bromine without a catalyst at room temperature, whereas benzene requires liquid bromine and a halogen carrier catalyst.

Exam-style questions

  1. Question: State the thermochemical evidence that supports the delocalised model of benzene over the Kekule structure of cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene. Answer: The measured enthalpy of hydrogenation of benzene is approximately −208 kJ mol−1, whereas the theoretical value for cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene is −360 kJ mol−1. The difference of about 150 kJ mol−1 is the delocalisation energy, proving benzene is thermodynamically more stable. (Earns credit by stating both values, their difference, and naming delocalisation energy).
  2. Question: Explain why benzene is resistant to bromination compared to cyclohexene. Answer: Benzene has a delocalised ring of pi-electrons which spreads electron density, whereas cyclohexene has a localised pi-bond between two carbons. The localised electron density in cyclohexene polarises bromine molecules much more readily than the stable delocalised ring of benzene. (Earns credit for contrasting delocalised and localised electron density).
  3. Question: Write the equation for the generation of the electrophile in the nitration of benzene using concentrated nitric and sulfuric acids. Answer: HNO3 + 2H2SO4 yields NO2+ + 2HSO4− + H3O+. (Earns credit for correct reactants, products, and stoichiometry).
  4. Question: Outline the mechanism for the alkylation of benzene with chloromethane in the presence of aluminium chloride. Include curly arrows and the intermediate. Answer: CH3Cl + AlCl3 yields CH3+ + AlCl4−. The benzene ring pi electrons attack the CH3+ electrophile to form the arenium intermediate with a positive charge spread over five carbons, followed by loss of H+ to form methylbenzene and regenerate AlCl3 alongside HCl. (Earns credit for electrophile generation, curly arrows from the ring, correct arenium intermediate structure, and loss of H+).
  5. Question: Explain why phenol reacts with bromine water much more readily than benzene does. Answer: The oxygen atom in the −OH group of phenol has a lone pair of electrons that overlaps with the pi system of the benzene ring. This increases the electron density of the ring, activating it and allowing it to polarise bromine molecules without a catalyst. (Earns credit for mentioning lone pair overlap, increased electron density, and ring activation).

Use these notes alongside active recall of mechanisms, reagent-condition pairs, and thermochemical definitions. Revise next the chemistry of carbonyl compounds, carboxylic acids, and esters to complete your organic chemistry mastery for WCH15.

title: IGCSE Mathematics: Fractions, Decimals and Percentages
content:
IGCSE Mathematics: Fractions, Decimals and Percentages

Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580 (2025–2027), section 1 Number: statement 1.4 Fractions, decimals and percentages (equivalence and conversion), 1.13 Percentages (including Extended reverse percentages) and E1.17 Exponential growth and decay. These three representations describe the same quantities, and fluent movement between them is one of the biggest sources of marks in both papers. The note explains why the conversion methods work before showing them, then builds percentages as multipliers — the technique behind most Paper 4 percentage problems.

What a fraction really is

A fraction is a division: 3/4 means 3 divided by 4, or three quarters of a whole. The top (numerator) counts the parts; the bottom (denominator) says how many equal parts the whole is cut into. A proper fraction has a smaller numerator (3/4); an improper fraction has a larger one (7/4); a mixed number combines a whole number with a proper fraction (1 3/4).

Convert 2 3/5 to an improper fraction:

2 wholes = 10 fifths, and 3 more fifths gives 13 fifths:
2 3/5 = (2 × 5 + 3)/5 = 13/5

Equivalent fractions are the same quantity written differently: 3/4 = 6/8 = 15/20, because multiplying top and bottom by the same number is multiplying by 1 (a form of 1, such as 3/3), which changes the look but not the value. Cancelling is the reverse: dividing top and bottom by a common factor. Only factors of the whole numerator and denominator can be cancelled — (x + 3)/(x + 2) cannot be simplified by cancelling the x's, because the top is a sum, not a product.

Converting between fractions, decimals and percentages

Fraction to decimal: divide.  3/8 = 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375
Decimal to fraction: read the place value.  0.47 = 47/100
Fraction to percentage: divide, then multiply by 100.  3/8 = 0.375 = 37.5%
Percentage to fraction: write over 100 and simplify.  45% = 45/100 = 9/20

Recurring decimals. A fraction always produces either a terminating decimal or a recurring one, and every recurring decimal converts back to a fraction by the algebra method:

Write 0.444... (4 recurring) as a fraction:

Let x = 0.444...
Then 10x = 4.444...        [shift the decimal one place]
Subtract:  10x - x = 4.444... - 0.444...
9x = 4
x = 4/9
Write 0.273636... (36 recurring) as a fraction:

Let x = 0.273636...
Two digits repeat, so shift two places:  100x = 27.363636...
100x - x = 27.3636... - 0.2736... = 27.09
99x = 27.09  →  x = 27.09/99 = 301/1100 after multiplying top and bottom by 100 and simplifying

Knowing the common conversions by heart saves time: 1/2 = 0.5 = 50%, 1/4 = 0.25 = 25%, 3/4 = 0.75, 1/5 = 0.2 = 20%, 1/8 = 0.125, 1/3 = 0.333... = 33 1/3%.

FractionDecimalPercentage
1/20.550%
1/40.2525%
3/40.7575%
1/50.220%
1/80.12512.5%
1/30.333...33 1/3%
2/30.666...66 2/3%

These seven values answer a surprising share of Paper 2 questions by inspection, and they anchor every conversion done the long way.

Percentages: the multiplier method

A percentage is a fraction out of 100 — literally per cent, per hundred. Every percentage problem is a multiplication, and the fastest method converts straight to a multiplier.

Find 35% of 240:

35% = 35/100 = 0.35, so  0.35 × 240 = 84

Increase 240 by 35%:
the new value is 135% of the old, so multiply by 1.35:  1.35 × 240 = 324

Decrease 240 by 35%:
the new value is 65% of the old, so multiply by 0.65:   0.65 × 240 = 156

Why the multiplier works. Increasing by 35% means keeping the original 100% and adding 35%, so the result is 135% of the original, which is 1.35 times it. Decreasing by 35% leaves 65%, which is 0.65 times. The multiplier also chains: successive changes multiply, which is why two discounts of 20% are not one discount of 40% (0.8 × 0.8 = 0.64, a 36% total reduction).

One quantity as a percentage of another:  18 out of 60

18/60 × 100 = 30%

Reverse percentages (Extended). Working backwards from a final value needs division:

A price after a 20% increase is £72. Find the original price.

The original is 100%, the new price is 120% of it, so the multiplier is 1.2:
original = 72 / 1.2 = £60

Check: 60 × 1.2 = 72 ✓

The common error is finding 20% of 72 and subtracting; the percentage must be taken from the original 100%, not the final amount.

Percentage change and comparisons

A coat falls from £80 to £56. Find the percentage decrease.

change = 80 - 56 = 24
percentage change = change / original x 100 = 24/80 × 100 = 30%

Percentage change always uses the original value as the denominator. Comparing quantities with different sizes — prices per 100 g, speeds, wages per hour — is done by putting both over a common quantity before comparing.

Exponential growth and decay (Extended)

When a quantity changes by the same percentage each period, it is multiplied by a fixed factor each time, and the result is exponential growth or decay. The multiplier is 1 + r for growth and 1 − r for decay, where r is the rate as a decimal.

After n periods at rate r:
growth:    final = original x (1 + r)^n
decay:     final = original x (1 - r)^n

Why the power. Each period multiplies by the same factor, so n periods multiply n times: an investment of £500 growing 3% a year becomes 500 × 1.03 after one year, 500 × 1.03 × 1.03 after two, and 500 × 1.03ⁿ after n years. The power counts the multiplications.

£500 is invested at 3% compound interest per year for 4 years.

500 × 1.03⁴ = 500 × 1.12550881 = £562.75 (2 d.p.)

Year by year check: 515.00 → 530.45 → 546.36 → 562.75 ✓
A car worth £18 000 depreciates 15% per year. Value after 3 years:

18 000 × 0.85³ = 18 000 × 0.614125 = £11 054.25

Exponential growth graphs climb ever faster and never touch zero; exponential decay graphs fall steeply at first and then level off towards — but never reach — zero (a horizontal asymptote). Doubling and halving questions are solved by logs or trial multiplication: for how many years does £500 at 3% exceed £600? Solve 500 × 1.03ⁿ > 600 by testing values of n, since 1.03ⁿ > 1.2 needs n ⩾ 7 years.

Worked example: a full percentage question

A shop sells a jacket for £84 after a 20% reduction. A further 10% discount is offered for cash.

Original price before the 20% reduction:
84 = original x 0.80
original = 84 / 0.80 = £105

Cash price after the extra 10%:
84 × 0.90 = £75.60

Total percentage saving against the original:
saving = 105 - 75.60 = 29.40
percentage saving = 29.40/105 × 100 = 28%

Check with multipliers: 0.80 × 0.90 = 0.72, so the cash price is 72% of the
original and the saving is 28% ✓

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Finding a percentage of the wrong amount: increase/decrease percentages apply to the original; reverse percentages divide by the multiplier.
  • Adding percentage changes: two 20% discounts give 0.8 × 0.8 = 0.64, a 36% reduction, not 40%.
  • Writing a recurring decimal as a fraction by eye; use the shift-and-subtract method and show it.
  • Cancelling across a sum: 3/4 is not 3 quarters of the top and bottom separately.
  • Using 365 days or 12 months inconsistently in compound problems: the power n counts compounding periods, so match it to the rate.
  • Forgetting that 15% decrease means multiplying by 0.85, not by −0.15 or 0.15.
  • Confusing 33% with 1/3 exactly: 1/3 = 33 1/3%, and the difference matters in exact answers.
  • Deciding an exponential decay value reaches zero; it falls below £1 or 0.001 but never reaches zero.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 2, 3 marks). Express 0.45 as a fraction in its lowest terms.

Answer: 0.45 = 45/100 = 9/20.

Question 2 (Paper 2, 3 marks). Write 0.27 with the 27 recurring as a fraction.

Answer: Let x = 0.272727...; then 100x = 27.2727...; subtracting gives 99x = 27, so x = 27/99 = 3/11.

Question 3 (Paper 4, 4 marks). In a sale, a bike is reduced by 15% to £255. Find the original price.

Answer: £255 represents 85% of the original, so the multiplier is 0.85 and the original price is 255/0.85 = £300. Check: 300 × 0.85 = 255 ✓.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 4 marks). A bacteria culture starts with 2000 and increases by 8% each hour. Find the size after 5 hours.

Answer: 2000 × 1.08⁵ = 2000 × 1.4693280768 = 2938.7 ≈ 2939 bacteria.

Question 5 (Paper 4, 3 marks). A town's population falls from 45 000 to 36 000 over a year. Find the percentage decrease.

Answer: Change = 9000; percentage = 9000/45 000 × 100 = 20%.

Question 6 (Paper 4, 5 marks). A car is bought for £12 000 and depreciates 18% in the first year and 12% in the second. Find its value after two years and the overall percentage loss.

Answer: 12 000 × 0.82 × 0.88 = 12 000 × 0.7216 = £8659.20. Overall loss = £3340.80, which is 3340.80/12 000 × 100 = 27.84% ≈ 27.8%. (Note 0.82 × 0.88 = 0.7216, a 27.84% total fall — not 30%.)

Fractions describe parts; powers and roots describe repeated multiplication — the next topic.

Fractions in practice: simplifying, adding and dividing

Most lost marks on fraction questions come from skipping one small step. Simplify early, find a common denominator before adding, and turn a division into a multiplication by the reciprocal. Each subsection below gives one rule and one fully worked number.

Simplifying by the highest common factor

To simplify a fraction, divide the numerator and the denominator by their highest common factor. For example, 6/8 has a highest common factor of 2, so 6/8 = 3/4. A fraction is fully simplified when the numerator and denominator share no factor except 1. Check this before you give a final answer, because an unsimplified fraction usually loses the accuracy mark.

Adding and subtracting fractions

Fractions can only be added or subtracted once they share a denominator. Write each over the lowest common multiple of the denominators. For 2/3 + 3/4, the common denominator is 12, so the sum is 8/12 + 9/12 = 17/12. Leave an improper fraction as a mixed number if the question asks for one: 17/12 = 1 5/12.

Multiplying fractions

Multiply the numerators together and the denominators together. Cancel common factors first, because it keeps the numbers small. For 2/3 × 3/5, the 3 on the top and the 3 on the bottom cancel, leaving 2/5. Do not add the denominators when multiplying, which is a common error.

Dividing fractions: keep, change, flip

To divide by a fraction, multiply by its reciprocal. Keep the first fraction, change the division to multiplication, and flip the second fraction. For 3/4 ÷ 2/5, write 3/4 × 5/2 = 15/8 = 1 7/8. A whole number divided by a fraction works the same way once the whole number is written over 1.

Converting between mixed numbers and improper fractions

To write a mixed number as an improper fraction, multiply the whole number by the denominator, add the numerator, and keep the denominator. So 2 3/5 = (2 × 5 + 3)/5 = 13/5. To go the other way, divide the numerator by the denominator: 13 ÷ 5 gives 2 remainder 3, so 13/5 = 2 3/5. Use whichever form the question's wording suggests.

Finding a fraction of an amount

To find a fraction of a quantity, divide by the denominator and then multiply by the numerator. Three eighths of 240 is 240 ÷ 8 = 30, then 30 × 3 = 90. Writing the fraction as a single multiplication, 3/8 × 240 = 90, gives the same answer and is quicker on a calculator.

Fractions in word problems

When a question says "two fifths of the class walk to school", the phrase "of" means multiply. Identify the whole first, because the fraction applies to that whole. If a quantity is left after a fraction is taken, subtract the fraction from 1 before you multiply. For example, if 3/8 of the money is spent, 1 − 3/8 = 5/8 is left.

Equations and symbols

The conversion cycle in one place: fraction ↔ decimal ↔ percentage, the multiplier that handles every percentage change, and the mixed-number rule. Non-calculator Paper 2 lives on these.

Fraction to decimal: divide. 3/8 = 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375 Key: the line means "a fraction is a division"; the numerator is divided by the denominator. Terminating here because 8 has only 2 as a prime factor; a denominator with any other prime gives a recurring decimal.

Fraction to percentage: divide, then multiply by 100. 3/8 = 0.375 = 37.5% Key: the decimal comes first, then ×100 moves the point two places; the % sign replaces the "per hundred" you multiplied by. Reversing it, divide by 100 and simplify.

Percentage to fraction: write over 100 and simplify. 45% = 45/100 = 9/20 Key: percent means "per hundred", so the denominator is 100 before simplifying; cancel by the highest common factor, 5 here. Leaving 45/100 is a lost mark in a "give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form" question.

2 3/5 = (2 × 5 + 3)/5 = 13/5 Key: the whole-number part (2) is multiplied by the denominator (5), the numerator (3) is added, and the result goes over the same denominator. This is the step needed before multiplying or dividing mixed numbers.

the new value is 135% of the old, so multiply by 1.35: 1.35 × 240 = 324 Key: 1.35 is the multiplier for an increase of 35% (100% + 35%, as a decimal); 240 is the original. The multiplier chains: 0.8 × 0.8 = 0.64 is not a 40% discount but a 36% one, which is the trap this line exists to close.

18/60 × 100 = 30% Key: 18 = the part; 60 = the whole; ×100 turns the fraction into a percentage. "18 out of 60" and "18 as a percentage of 60" are the same question, and the fraction is always part ÷ whole.

title: Exam technique: Hardware & Architecture
content:
### What earns the marks
For the fetch-execute cycle, each stage in order earns stepwise credit. For CPU parts, control unit versus ALU roles stated earn one mark each. For sensors, the named sensor matched to its use earns the mark.
### Traps
Error: RAM and ROM roles swapped. Correction: RAM is working memory, ROM holds boot code. Error: control unit claimed to compute. Correction: the ALU computes, the CU coordinates. Error: stages given out of order. Correction: fetch, decode, execute, store.

title: Exam technique: Databases and Data Definition
content:
### What earns the marks
For DDL vs DML, purpose decides: structure changes are DDL, row changes are DML. For transactions, atomicity (all-or-nothing rollback) and durability (surviving crashes) each earn a mark when tied to the failure. For concurrency, the lost-update mechanism described earns the mark before locking is prescribed.
### Traps
Error: SELECT classed as DDL. Correction: queries read rows, so DML. Error: half-applied transfers accepted. Correction: atomicity rolls them back. Error: views claimed as backups. Correction: views are access windows, not copies.

title: Exam technique: Angles and Polygons
content:
### What earns the marks
For angle-chasing, justify earns marks for each reason stated alongside the value: angles on a straight line, vertically opposite, alternate, corresponding, and the circle theorems by name. For cyclic quadrilaterals, quote earns the theorem (opposite angles sum to 180) before the equation. For polygons, the formula (n - 2) x 180 stated earns the method mark.
### Traps
Error: using adjacent instead of opposite angles in a cyclic quadrilateral. Correction: mark the diagram first. Error: answering each interior angle when the sum is asked. Correction: only divide at the very end. Error: treating any triangle in a circle as right-angled. Correction: the right angle needs the diameter as hypotenuse.

title: IGCSE Mathematics: Sequences and Functions
content:
IGCSE Mathematics: Sequences and Functions

Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580 (2025–2027), section 2 Algebra and graphs: statement 2.7 Sequences and statement 2.13 Functions (Extended). A sequence is a list of numbers generated by a rule; a function is the rule itself. This note builds nth-term rules from scratch — showing why the formula works, not just what it is — then function notation, composite functions and inverse functions, including the domain restrictions that decide whether an inverse exists.

What a sequence is; term-to-term rules

A sequence is an ordered list of numbers. The term-to-term rule gets from one term to the next: add 4, multiply by 2, subtract 1 then double. It tells you what happens step by step but not what the hundredth term is. The position-to-term rule (the nth term) gives any term directly from its position n, and that is the more powerful description.

Sequence: 3, 7, 11, 15, 19, ...

Term-to-term: add 4 each time.
Position-to-term: the terms are 4 less than 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, ..., so the nth term is 4n - 1.

Check: n = 1 gives 4(1) - 1 = 3 ✓;  n = 5 gives 4(5) - 1 = 19 ✓

Linear sequences and the nth term

A linear (arithmetic) sequence has a constant difference d between terms. Its nth term is dn + b, and b is chosen to make the first term correct.

Find the nth term of 5, 8, 11, 14, ...

Constant difference d = 3, so the nth term starts as 3n.
Compare with the sequence: 3, 6, 9, 12, ... is three times the table of 3;
the real sequence is 2 more each time, so b = 2.
nth term:  3n + 2

Check every term: n = 1: 5 ✓   n = 2: 8 ✓   n = 3: 11 ✓
The 50th term is 3(50) + 2 = 152.

Why dn + b always works. Adding d each time from a starting value a means the nth term is a + (n − 1)d, since term n has had (n − 1) additions of d. Expanding gives a + nd − d = nd + (a − d), which is exactly dn + b with b = a − d. Both forms are the same rule; examiners accept either.

Quadratic and special sequences

When the first difference changes but the second difference is constant, the rule is quadratic: an² + bn + c. The method: build the n² sequence, subtract it from the sequence, and finish the linear remainder.

Find the nth term of 2, 5, 10, 17, 26, ...

First differences: 3, 5, 7, 9;  second differences: 2, 2 (constant) → quadratic.
The n² sequence is 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, ...
Subtract: (2-1), (5-4), (10-9), (17-16), (26-25) = 1, 1, 1, 1, 1
So the sequence is n² + 1.

Check: n = 3 gives 9 + 1 = 10 ✓

Other sequences to recognise on sight: the triangular numbers n(n + 1)/2 (1, 3, 6, 10, ...), the square numbers n², the Fibonacci sequence (each term is the sum of the two before it, and it has no simple nth term), and geometric sequences that multiply by a fixed ratio r — their nth term is arⁿ⁻¹ where a is the first term.

Geometric example: 3, 6, 12, 24, ... has a = 3 and r = 2, so the nth term is 3 × 2^(n-1).
The 6th term is 3 × 2⁵ = 96.
Sequence typeExampleRule
Linear (arithmetic)5, 8, 11, 14Constant difference d; nth term dn + b
Quadratic2, 5, 10, 17Constant second difference; nth term an² + bn + c
Geometric3, 6, 12, 24Constant ratio r; nth term arⁿ⁻¹
Triangular numbers1, 3, 6, 10n(n + 1)/2
Square numbers1, 4, 9, 16n²
Fibonacci1, 1, 2, 3, 5Add the two previous terms (no simple nth term)

Choosing the right description is half the battle: check the first differences, then the second, then the ratio, before assuming any rule. Once a candidate rule is found, verify it against every given term — a sequence that matches only the first three terms is not proven.

Function notation

A function is a machine with an input and exactly one output for each input. The notation f(x) = 2x + 3 names the machine f and says what it does to x: multiply by 2, then add 3. Evaluating is substitution: f(4) = 2(4) + 3 = 11. The machine picture matters: one input never gives two outputs, though two inputs may share an output.

  • The domain is the set of allowed inputs; the range is the set of outputs the function actually produces.
  • For f(x) = x² with domain all real numbers, the range is y ⩾ 0, because squares are never negative.
  • For f(x) = 2x + 3 with domain 0 ⩽ x ⩽ 5, the range is 3 ⩽ f(x) ⩽ 13 — substitute the endpoints, since linear functions stretch ranges proportionally.

Questions ask for the range in terms of y or f(x); find the outputs at the domain boundaries and, for quadratics, at the turning point.

Composite functions

A composite function runs one machine after the other. fg(x) means apply g first, then f to the result — the notation reads right to left, like f(g(x)).

Given f(x) = 2x + 1 and g(x) = x², find fg(3), gf(x) and fg(x).

fg(3):  g(3) = 9, then f(9) = 2(9) + 1 = 19.
gf(x):  apply f first:  g(f(x)) = (2x + 1)² = 4x² + 4x + 1.
fg(x):  apply g first:  f(g(x)) = 2x² + 1.

Note fg(x) ≠ gf(x): order matters.

Every line is written out because the most common error is applying the functions in the wrong order — and the composite is not commutative.

Inverse functions

The inverse f⁻¹ undoes f: if f turns 4 into 11, f⁻¹ turns 11 back into 4. Inverse functions exist only for one-to-one functions — ones where different inputs always give different outputs. The graph of y = x² is not one-to-one over all real numbers (both 3 and −3 give 9), so it has no inverse unless the domain is restricted to x ⩾ 0.

Find the inverse of f(x) = (3x - 2)/5:

Write y = (3x - 2)/5 and make x the subject:
5y = 3x - 2          [multiply by 5]
5y + 2 = 3x          [add 2]
x = (5y + 2)/3       [divide by 3]

Swap x and y:  f⁻¹(x) = (5x + 2)/3

Check by composing: f⁻¹(f(x)) = [5((3x - 2)/5) + 2]/3 = [(3x - 2) + 2]/3 = 3x/3 = x  ✓
  • f⁻¹(x) is a single symbol meaning the inverse function; the −1 is not a power and f⁻¹(x) does not mean 1/f(x).
  • The domain of f⁻¹ is the range of f, and the range of f⁻¹ is the domain of f — they swap, exactly as the inputs and outputs swap roles.
  • Graphically, y = f⁻¹(x) is the reflection of y = f(x) in the line y = x.

Worked example: a full function question

Let f(x) = x² + 3 for x ⩾ 0, and g(x) = 4x − 5.

(a) Find f(2):  f(2) = 4 + 3 = 7.

(b) Find fg(x):  f(g(x)) = (4x - 5)² + 3 = 16x² - 40x + 25 + 3 = 16x² - 40x + 28.

(c) Find f⁻¹(x):  y = x² + 3, so x² = y - 3 and x = √(y - 3) (positive root, since x ⩾ 0).
Swap: f⁻¹(x) = √(x - 3).
Domain of f⁻¹: x ⩾ 3, which is exactly the range of f.

(d) Solve f(x) = 30 for x ⩾ 0:
x² + 3 = 30
x² = 27
x = √27 = 3√3 ≈ 5.20        [only the positive root is in the domain]

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Reading fg(x) as f then g. It is g first, then f — the notation runs right to left.
  • Assuming fg = gf; only special cases agree.
  • Treating f⁻¹(x) as 1/f(x). The inverse undoes the function; it is not a reciprocal.
  • Ignoring domain restrictions: with x ⩾ 0 on f(x) = x² + 3, the inverse takes the positive root only, and a negative root answer is wrong.
  • Claiming y = x² has an inverse over all real numbers; it is two-to-one and needs a restricted domain.
  • Building the nth term from the first difference alone without checking every term; a single wrong check sends a whole answer wrong.
  • Writing a geometric nth term as arⁿ instead of arⁿ⁻¹; the first term must be a itself.
  • Stating a range that ignores the turning point of a quadratic: the range of y = (x − 2)² + 1 is y ⩾ 1, not y ⩾ 0.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 2, 3 marks). Find the nth term of 7, 11, 15, 19, ...

Answer: Constant difference 4, so 4n + b; the first term 7 = 4 + b gives b = 3. The nth term is 4n + 3. The 20th term is 83.

Question 2 (Paper 2, 3 marks). A sequence has nth term 5n − 2. Write down the first four terms and the 100th.

Answer: n = 1, 2, 3, 4 give 3, 8, 13, 18; the 100th term is 5(100) − 2 = 498.

Question 3 (Paper 4, 4 marks). f(x) = 3x − 1 and g(x) = x² + 2. Find fg(x), gf(2) and f⁻¹(x).

Answer: fg(x) = 3(x² + 2) − 1 = 3x² + 5. gf(2): f(2) = 5, so g(5) = 27. Inverse: y = 3x − 1 gives x = (y + 1)/3, so f⁻¹(x) = (x + 1)/3.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 4 marks). The second differences of a sequence are constant at 4, and its first two terms are 2 and 7. Find the nth term.

Answer: Constant second difference 4 means the n² coefficient is 4/2 = 2, so the rule starts 2n². The n² sequence gives 2, 8, ... while the sequence is 2, 7, ..., so the remainder is 0, −1, ... a linear part with difference −1: −n + 1. Check: 2n² − n + 1 gives n = 1: 2 ✓ and n = 2: 8 − 2 + 1 = 7 ✓. The nth term is 2n² − n + 1.

Question 5 (Paper 4, 5 marks). f(x) = (x + 4)/(x − 2) for x ≠ 2. Find f⁻¹(x) and the value of x for which f(x) is undefined.

Answer: y = (x + 4)/(x − 2) gives y(x − 2) = x + 4, so yx − 2y = x + 4, yx − x = 2y + 4, x(y − 1) = 2y + 4 and x = (2y + 4)/(y − 1). Swapping: f⁻¹(x) = (2x + 4)/(x − 1). The function itself is undefined at x = 2, where the denominator vanishes; its inverse is undefined at x = 1.

Question 6 (Paper 2, 3 marks). The first three terms of a geometric sequence are 5, 15, 45. Find the 8th term.

Answer: Common ratio r = 15/5 = 3, so the nth term is 5 × 3ⁿ⁻¹ and the 8th term is 5 × 3⁷ = 5 × 2187 = 10 935.

From variables and patterns, the course now turns to the number system itself.

title: IGCSE Chemistry: Organic Chemistry
content:
IGCSE Chemistry: Organic Chemistry

Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry 0620 (2026–2028), Extended route, Topic 11 Organic chemistry: statements 11.1 Formulae, functional groups and terminology, 11.2 Naming organic compounds, 11.3 Fuels, 11.4 Alkanes, 11.5 Alkenes, 11.6 Alcohols, 11.7 Carboxylic acids, and 11.8 Polymers. Organic chemistry is a system, not a list — one structural logic generates every name, formula and reaction in this note. Each homologous series is derived from its general formula, and every reaction shows the functional-group change explicitly.

The organic framework: homologous series and functional groups

A homologous series is a family of similar compounds with the same functional group and general formula, differing by CH₂ units, showing gradual physical-property trends and similar chemistry. A functional group is the atom or group of atoms responsible for the characteristic reactions (C=C for alkenes, –OH for alcohols, –COOH for acids).

SeriesGeneral formulaFunctional groupSuffix
AlkanesCₙH₂ₙ₊₂None (single bonds)-ane
AlkenesCₙH₂ₙC=C-ene
AlcoholsCₙH₂ₙ₊₁OH–OH-ol
Carboxylic acidsCₙH₂ₙ₊₁COOH–COOH-oic acid

Saturated = all single C–C bonds (alkanes); unsaturated = at least one C=C (alkenes). Structural isomers share the molecular formula but have different structural formulae (butane and methylpropane, both C₄H₁₀) — the reason displayed formula alone is not enough. Naming: count the carbons (meth- 1, eth- 2, prop- 3, but- 4), add the suffix for the functional group.

Fuels and fractional distillation

Petroleum = a mixture of hydrocarbons, separated by FRACTIONAL DISTILLATION.

  The crude oil is vaporised and fed into the column:
   - hot at the bottom, cooler at the top;
   - each fraction condenses at the height where its boiling range matches
     the temperature.

  Fractions (lightest at top): refinery gas (C¹-C⁴, bottled gas),
  gasoline/petrol (C⁵-C10, car fuel), naphtha (chemical feedstock),
  kerosene/paraffin (jet fuel), diesel oil (lorry fuel), fuel oil (ships),
  lubricating fraction (oils, waxes), bitumen (road surfaces).

  Trend up the column (towards longer chains):
   - BOILING POINT RISES (bigger molecules, stronger intermolecular forces);
   - VISCOSITY INCREASES (thicker, flows less easily);
   - VOLATILITY FALLS (evaporates less readily);
   - COMBUSTION gets less clean (more soot/carbon).

Fractional cracking breaks long alkane chains into shorter, more useful ones (alkanes + alkenes): C₁₀H₂₂ → C₈H₁₈ + C₂H₄ — driven by the need for petrol and alkene feedstock.

Alkanes: substitution

Alkanes are generally unreactive (strong, non-polar C–C and C–H bonds) but burn (combustion) and undergo substitution with halogens in UV light.

Complete combustion (all hydrocarbons):
  CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O
Incomplete combustion (limited O₂):
  2CH₄ + 3O₂ → 2CO + 4H₂O   (carbon monoxide - toxic)
  or soot (C) forms - a visible flame with yellow tips.

Chlorination of methane (photochemical substitution):
  CH₄ + Cl₂  →  CH₃Cl + HCl (UV light)
  One H is REPLACED by Cl - the definition of substitution. The UV light
  provides the activation energy to split the Cl-Cl bond into radicals.
  Further substitution gives CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃, CCl₄ - the products are a
  mixture, which is why the reaction is poor for synthesis.

Alkenes: addition

Alkenes react via the C=C double bond in addition reactions — two reactants join to give one product (nothing is lost).

Addition to ethene - each with its conditions:

  + bromine (test for unsaturation):
    C₂H₄ + Br₂ → C₂H₄Br₂        (1,2-dibromoethane)
    OBSERVATION: orange bromine water is DECOLOURISED - the test that
    distinguishes alkenes from alkanes.

  + hydrogen (nickel catalyst, heat):
    C₂H₄ + H₂ → C₂H₆            (ethane; hydrogenation - margarine making)

  + steam (phosphoric acid catalyst, heat + pressure):
    C₂H₄ + H₂O → C₂H₅OH         (ethanol)

In every case the double bond opens to single bonds and the atoms add on -
draw the product by "opening" the C=C and attaching one atom to each carbon.

Alcohols

Two production routes for ethanol, with the trade-off the exam always asks:

1. FERMENTATION of glucose (yeast, no oxygen, 25-35 °C):
     C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂
   Advantages: renewable feedstock (sugar/corn), low energy conditions,
   batch process.
   Disadvantages: slow (days), dilute product (needs distilling), depends on
   crop supply and weather.

2. CATALYTIC HYDRATION of ethene (H₃PO₄ catalyst, 300 °C, 60 atm):
     C₂H₄ + H₂O → C₂H₅OH
   Advantages: fast, continuous, high purity and yield.
   Disadvantages: ethene comes from crude oil (finite), high energy/pressure
   costs.

Ethanol itself: burns cleanly (C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O) as a fuel;
a solvent (perfumes, paints); in alcoholic drinks.

Carboxylic acids and esters

Carboxylic acids are weak acids: they react with metals (salt + hydrogen), bases (salt + water) and carbonates (salt + water + carbon dioxide — the fizz test that identifies an acid).

Oxidation of ethanol to ethanoic acid:
  ethanol + [O] → ethanoic acid     e.g. by acidified potassium
  manganate(VII), or by bacterial action in vinegar production (air + 
  Acetobacter).

Esterification (acid + alcohol, concentrated H₂SO₄ catalyst):
  ethanoic acid + ethanol → ethyl ethanoate + water
  CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O

  Naming esters: the FIRST word comes from the ALCOHOL (ethyl, from ethanol),
  the second from the ACID (ethanoate, from ethanoic acid).
  Propyl methanoate = propanol + methanoic acid.

  Esters: sweet smells (fruits, perfumes), solvents, plasticisers.

Polymers

A monomer is the small molecule that repeats; a polymer is the very long chain of joined monomers. Addition polymerisation joins many alkene molecules by opening the double bonds — nothing else is produced.

Deducing the repeat unit - the master method:

  Monomer: propene, CH₂=CH-CH₃
  1. Open the double bond: -CH₂-CH(CH₃)-
  2. Extend the "bonds" at both ends to show the chain continuing:
     [ -CH₂-CH(CH₃)- ]ₙ

  Reverse (monomer from repeat unit): find the two backbone carbons of one
  unit, restore the double bond between them, and cap the ends with the
  substituents that were drawn.

  poly(ethene):  n CH₂=CH₂ → [ -CH₂-CH₂- ]ₙ
  poly(propene): n CH₂=CHCH₃ → [ -CH₂-CH(CH₃)- ]ₙ
  poly(chloroethene) (PVC): n CH₂=CHCl → [ -CH₂-CHCl- ]ₙ

Condensation polymerisation (two different bifunctional monomers):
  a small molecule (usually water) is LOST at each link.
  Nylon (a polyamide): diamine + dicarboxylic acid → nylon + water.
  PET (a polyester): diol + dicarboxylic acid → PET + water.
  Proteins are natural polyamides from amino-acid monomers.

Disposal: plastics are non-biodegradable — landfill accumulates, plastics in the ocean harm wildlife, burning releases toxic gases (HCl from PVC, CO from incomplete combustion). Options: recycling (sorted by type), depolymerisation (PET can be broken back to monomers and re-polymerised), and biodegradable alternatives.

Worked example: one route map, every reaction type

From ethane to ethyl ethanoate:

  ethane --(cracking/heat)-→ ethene      [thermal decomposition]
  ethene + steam --(H₃PO₄, 300 °C)-→ ethanol   [addition / hydration]
  ethanol + [O] --(bacterial)-→ ethanoic acid  [oxidation]
  ethanol + ethanoic acid --(conc. H₂SO₄)-→ ethyl ethanoate [esterification]

  Each arrow names its type, conditions and the functional-group change:
  alkane → alkene (C-C to C=C), alkene → alcohol (C=C to C-OH),
  alcohol → acid (-OH to -COOH), acid + alcohol → ester (-COOH/-OH to
  -COO-). Tracking the functional group through a route map is the skill
  the exam tests.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Forgetting that addition reactions need the C=C — alkanes substitute, alkenes add; mixing them up loses every mark on the question.
  • Bromine water: decolourised by alkenes (addition) but NOT by alkanes — the observation sentence must name the colour loss.
  • Counting general formula wrong for the first members (methane CH₄ fits CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ with n = 1).
  • Writing polymers without the extending bonds at both ends of the repeat unit (it must show continuation).
  • In ester naming, swapping which part comes from the acid and which from the alcohol.
  • Leaving reaction conditions off (UV for substitution, Ni/heat for hydrogenation, concentrated H₂SO₄ for esterification) — conditions are marks.
  • Claiming fermentation is fast/pure — the comparison with catalytic hydration needs both sides.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 4, 3 marks). Define a homologous series and state three general characteristics.

Answer: A homologous series is a family of similar compounds with the same functional group and general formula, each member differing from the next by a CH₂ unit. Characteristics: similar chemical properties; gradual trend in physical properties (boiling point rises with chain length); can be made by similar methods.

Question 2 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Describe the test that distinguishes ethene from ethane, with equations.

Answer: Add aqueous bromine and shake. Ethene decolourises the orange bromine (addition: C₂H₄ + Br₂ → C₂H₄Br₂); ethane shows no change (no reaction in the dark at room temperature). The C=C double bond is responsible for the addition.

Question 3 (Paper 4, 5 marks). Compare fermentation and catalytic hydration as routes to ethanol.

Answer: Fermentation (C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂, yeast, 25–35 °C) uses renewable sugar crops and mild conditions, but is slow, gives dilute ethanol needing distillation, and varies with crop supply. Catalytic hydration (C₂H₄ + H₂O → C₂H₅OH, H₃PO₄, 300 °C, 60 atm) is fast, continuous and high-yield, but depends on crude-oil-derived ethene and costly high-pressure conditions.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Draw the repeat unit of poly(propene) and name the polymerisation type.

Answer: Monomer propene CH₂=CHCH₃ opens at the double bond giving repeat unit [–CH₂–CH(CH₃)–]ₙ, with the chain bonds extending at both ends. This is addition polymerisation — many monomers join with no other product.

Question 5 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Describe how ethyl ethanoate is made and state its uses.

Answer: Warm ethanol with ethanoic acid in the presence of concentrated sulfuric acid catalyst (esterification): CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O. The ester is distilled off. Ethyl ethanoate is used as a solvent (nail-varnish remover), in perfumes and flavourings (sweet smell).

Question 6 (Paper 4, 3 marks). Explain why burning PVC can be more harmful than burning poly(ethene).

Answer: PVC contains chlorine; burning it releases hydrogen chloride gas, which is toxic and forms acidic fumes, plus carbon monoxide from incomplete combustion. Poly(ethene) contains only carbon and hydrogen and burns to CO₂ and water if complete — less acutely toxic though still a CO₂ source.

Organic molecules can be burned as fuels — the next topic is what happens when electrons move instead: electrochemistry.

Equations and symbols

Organic chemistry is examined as equations plus conditions: the formula alone is half the mark, and the reagent, catalyst and temperature are the other half. Every equation below is a reaction type you must be able to name as well as balance.

C₁₀H₂₂ → C₈H₁₈ + C₂H₄ Key: the numbers are the carbon counts of the alkane feedstock and its two products — one long alkane cracked into a shorter alkane plus an alkene. Cracking is thermal decomposition: heat, no air.

CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O Key: complete combustion of methane; enough oxygen oxidises every carbon to CO₂, which is the clean flame. Balance carbon, then hydrogen, then oxygen last.

2CH₄ + 3O₂ → 2CO + 4H₂O Key: incomplete combustion in limited oxygen; carbon monoxide is produced instead of carbon dioxide, and it is toxic because it binds haemoglobin irreversibly.

CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl Key: substitution in ultraviolet light — one hydrogen is replaced by one chlorine, and HCl is the second product. The UV supplies the activation energy that splits Cl₂ into radicals; without it, nothing happens in the dark.

C₂H₄ + Br₂ → C₂H₄Br₂ Key: addition across the C=C; the orange bromine water is decolourised, which is the test that distinguishes an alkene from an alkane.

C₂H₄ + H₂ → C₂H₆ Key: hydrogenation over a nickel catalyst with heat; the double bond opens and the product is the saturated alkane. This is how margarine is hardened.

C₂H₄ + H₂O → C₂H₅OH Key: hydration of ethene with phosphoric acid catalyst, high temperature and pressure; the industrial route to ethanol, fast and continuous but dependent on crude oil.

C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂ Key: fermentation of glucose by yeast at 25–35 °C with no oxygen; renewable and low-energy, but slow and dilute, so the ethanol must be distilled.

C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O Key: complete combustion of ethanol as a fuel; count the oxygens on the right (4 + 3 = 7), subtract the one in the ethanol, and 6 remain, so 3O₂.

CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O Key: esterification, catalysed by concentrated sulfuric acid and warmed; the ⇌ marks it as reversible, so the ester is distilled off to drive it forward. The first word of the ester name comes from the alcohol, the second from the acid.

Where the marks go. Name the type (substitution, addition, oxidation, esterification, polymerisation) before writing the equation, and never write an alkene reaction without the C=C on the left — an addition that starts from an alkane is a contradiction.

title: Exam technique: Arithmetic and Place Value
content:
### What earns the marks
For HCF and LCM, the prime factorisation of each number earns the method mark; state highest powers for LCM and lowest for HCF. For bounds, half-the-precision stated (0.05 for 1 d.p.) earns the method mark before the bound. For estimation, the rounded line (50 x 20 / 10) must be shown: a bare calculator value scores nothing. For time and money, each conversion step shown earns its mark.
### Traps
Error: 16:80 as a time. Correction: 60 minutes carry. Error: largest rounded value confused with the upper bound (6.34 vs 6.35). Correction: the bound is the first value that rounds away. Error: HCF powers used for LCM. Correction: LCM takes the highest of each prime.

title: Work, Energy and Power — Study Notes
content:
Work, energy and power

Edexcel International A Level Physics — Unit 1 (WPH11), sat at AS.

Work

  • Work done = force × displacement in the direction of the force, W = Fs cos θ. Unit: joule (J), where 1 J = 1 N m.
  • No work is done by a force that acts perpendicular to the displacement, such as the normal contact force on a body moving along a horizontal surface.

Energy stores and transfers

Gravitational potential energy, kinetic energy, elastic potential energy, chemical energy and thermal energy are energy stores. Work done transfers energy from one store to another.

Conservation of energy

Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred. Where only conservative forces such as gravity act, the total mechanical energy is constant. Where non-conservative forces such as friction or air resistance act, the energy they dissipate appears as thermal energy.

Kinetic and gravitational potential energy

  • Kinetic energy: Ek = ½mv².
  • Gravitational potential energy change near the Earth's surface: ΔEp = mgΔh.

Power and efficiency

  • Power = work done ÷ time = energy transferred ÷ time. Unit: watt (W), where 1 W = 1 J s⁻¹.
  • Efficiency = useful energy output ÷ total energy input × 100%. It is always less than 100%.

Worked example: a 2.0 kg object falls freely from rest through 5.0 m. Its speed at the bottom, from energy conservation: ½mv² = mgh, so v = √(2gh) = √(2 × 9.81 × 5.0) ≈ 9.9 m s⁻¹.

Exam tips: check whether the question says air resistance is negligible before using conservation of energy. Always convert minutes to seconds in power calculations. Give efficiency as a percentage.

Power, efficiency and energy transfer

Power is the rate at which work is done or energy is transferred, P = W/t = Fv for a force moving at constant velocity. Efficiency is the useful energy output divided by the total energy input, and it is always less than 1 because some energy is dissipated, usually as thermal energy from friction. When a body is raised, its gain in gravitational potential energy is mgh, and a kinetic energy change is ½m(v2 - u2). Both can be used to find the work done against resistive forces.

Exam tip: state the percentage efficiency with units, and check that it is below 100 percent.

Worked example: lifting a load

A 40 kg load is lifted through 5.0 m at a steady speed. The work done against gravity is W = mgh = 40 × 9.8 × 5.0 = 1960 J, or about 2.0 kJ. If the lifting motor is 60% efficient, the electrical energy supplied is 1960 / 0.60 ≈ 3270 J, and the rest is wasted as thermal energy. Efficiency is the useful energy output divided by the total energy input, and it can never exceed 100%.

Exam method: power and energy

Power is the rate of energy transfer: P = E/t. When a constant force moves an object at speed v, the power is P = Fv. Convert every time to seconds and every energy to joules before you substitute. Questions that give power in kilowatts sometimes ask for energy in kilowatt-hours, so check which unit the answer should use.

title: Further Algebra — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Further Algebra

Mathematics — A2 (9709). Divide to rewrite p(x) = (x − a)q(x) + r. The remainder when dividing by (x − a) equals p(a).

Key areas to revise

  • Polynomial Division and the Remainder Theorem
  • The Modulus Function
  • Partial Fractions

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Key points to remember

Partial fractions split a rational function into simpler fractions that are easier to integrate or expand. Factorise the denominator first. A linear factor (x − a) gives a term A/(x − a), and a repeated factor (x − a)² needs both A/(x − a) and B/(x − a)². If the degree of the numerator is not less than that of the denominator, divide first.

To find the constants, substitute values of x that make the factors zero, or compare coefficients after multiplying through by the denominator. Modulus equations and inequalities are solved by considering both the positive and negative cases, and each solution is checked against the original condition.

title: IGCSE Chemistry: Chemistry of the Environment
content:
IGCSE Chemistry: Chemistry of the Environment

Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry 0620 (2026–2028), Extended route, Topic 10 Chemistry of the environment: statement 10.1 Water, 10.2 Fertilisers, and 10.3 Air quality and climate. This is applied chemistry at its most exam-visible: the greenhouse mechanism, pollutant chemistry and water treatment are all regular Paper 4 questions that demand particle-level and chemical explanations, not lists. Every reaction below is written in the form the mark scheme expects.

Water: testing, purity and treatment

The test for water is anhydrous copper(II) sulfate (white → blue) or anhydrous cobalt(II) chloride (blue → pink) — the hydrated colour change from the salts topic. Purity is judged by melting/boiling point: pure water boils sharply at 100 °C; an impure sample boils over a range and above 100 °C (boiling-point elevation). Practical chemistry uses distilled water because tap water's dissolved ions interfere with reactions and leave residues.

Domestic water treatment, stage by stage:

  1. SEDIMENTATION: water stands in settling tanks; insoluble particles
     sink (sometimes a flocculant like aluminium sulfate is added to bind
     small particles).
  2. FILTRATION: through gravel and sand beds - removes remaining solids.
  3. CARBON FILTRATION: activated carbon adsorbs dissolved organic
     substances, taste and odour compounds.
  4. CHLORINATION: chlorine kills bacteria and viruses (dose ~1 ppm);
     it stays in the supply to guard against recontamination.

  Natural waters may contain: dissolved oxygen (essential for aquatic
  life), metal compounds (toxic - e.g. lead from old pipes), nitrates and
  phosphates (from fertiliser run-off - cause eutrophication: algal bloom,
  blocked light, decay deoxygenates the water, fish die), sewage and
  microbes (disease), plastics (physical harm, microplastics).

Fertilisers

Fertilisers supply the three nutrients NPK: nitrogen (leaf growth), phosphorus (roots), potassium (flowers/fruit). Ammonium salts (e.g. ammonium nitrate, NH₄NO₃) and nitrates are the main nitrogen sources. Manufacture is the Haber–Bosch chain: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, then NH₃ + HNO₃ → NH₄NO₃. Fertilisers boost yields but cause water pollution when washed off — the trade-off earns marks in environment questions.

Air quality and climate

PollutantSourceEffectCountermeasure
COIncomplete combustion of fuelsToxic (binds haemoglobin)Catalytic converters; efficient engines
SO₂Combustion of sulfur-containing fossil fuelsAcid rain (damages buildings, lakes, trees)Flue-gas desulfurisation (CaO/CaCO₃ scrubbing); low-sulfur fuels
NO/NO₂High-temperature combustion in enginesAcid rain; photochemical smogCatalytic converters (2CO + 2NO → 2CO₂ + N₂)
CO₂Combustion of all carbon fuelsGreenhouse gas — enhanced global warmingRenewables, efficiency, carbon capture
ParticulatesDiesel engines, industryRespiratory diseaseFilters
The greenhouse effect explained mechanistically - the Extended wording:

  1. Solar radiation arrives mostly as short-wavelength (visible/UV) light,
     which passes through the atmosphere and warms the Earth's surface.
  2. The warm Earth re-radiates energy as longer-wavelength INFRA-RED.
  3. Greenhouse gases (CO₂, CH₄, H₂O vapour) ABSORB this infra-red and
     re-emit it in all directions - some back toward the surface.
  4. Less energy escapes to space than arrived, so the lower atmosphere and
     surface warm further.

  Sources of the enhanced effect: burning fossil fuels (CO₂), agriculture
  and landfill (CH₄), deforestation (less CO₂ absorbed).
  Why methane matters: each CH₄ molecule absorbs MORE infra-red per molecule
  than CO₂, though it is shorter-lived in the atmosphere.

Nitrogen oxides in engines: N₂ + O₂ -> 2NO at high temperature inside the
engine (the heat of combustion breaks the very strong N≡N and O=O bonds);
2NO + O₂ -> 2NO₂ in the air. Catalytic converters reduce them back:
  2CO + 2NO -> 2CO₂ + N₂   (both pollutants converted to less harmful gases)

Photosynthesis:  6CO₂ + 6H₂O -> C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂   (light, chlorophyll)

The atmosphere and climate change evidence

Clean dry air is approximately 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, 1% noble gases and about 0.04% carbon dioxide — a composition worth stating in source-and-effect answers because the gases that matter climatically are the trace ones. Climate evidence the syllabus expects candidates to interpret: rising global mean temperatures, retreating glaciers and ice sheets, rising sea levels from thermal expansion and melting ice, and changing weather patterns. Mitigation strategies split into two families: adaptation (building flood defences, developing drought-resistant crops) and mitigation (renewable energy, efficiency, reforestation, international agreements to cut emissions). Chemistry contributes both the diagnosis — isotopic analysis of atmospheric CO₂ traces its source to fossil fuels — and the solutions: catalytic converters, flue-gas scrubbing, carbon capture and hydrogen fuel technology.

Worked example: evaluating an environmental scenario

A coal power plant adds a desulfurisation unit. Evaluate.

  Problem: SO₂ from sulfur impurities in coal causes acid rain:
    SO₂ + H₂O -> H₂SO₃ (and further oxidation to H₂SO₄).
  Countermeasure: CaCO₃ or CaO in the flue:
    CaCO₃ -> CaO + CO₂ ;  CaO + SO₂ -> CaSO₃ ;
    2CaSO₃ + O₂ -> 2CaSO₄ (gypsum - sold for plasterboard).
  Trade-offs: removes >90% of SO₂ and turns waste into a product, but costs
  energy and money, adds CO₂ from the calcination step, and the slurry waste
  must be handled. Net: acid rain reduced substantially; the CO₂ problem
  (global warming) remains - pollution problems are separate.

Water purity and the oxygen cycle

Aquatic chemistry ties the water and air topics together. Dissolved oxygen sustains fish and is replenished at the surface by diffusion and by photosynthesis; organic pollution (sewage, fertiliser run-off) upsets the balance because bacteria consuming the waste also consume the dissolved oxygen — biochemical oxygen demand (BOD) rises and aquatic life suffocates. Heavy-metal compounds (mercury, lead) are toxic because they bind to enzymes and accumulate up the food chain. Microplastics and pathogens add physical and disease hazards. The treatment train in the first section targets exactly these: filtration removes particulates and the organisms sheltering in them, carbon adsorption removes organics, and chlorination kills the pathogens — while distillation in the laboratory removes everything dissolved, which is why distilled water is the chemist's standard.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Describing the greenhouse effect as "the ozone layer" or "the sun getting hotter" — it is infra-red absorption by specific gases.
  • Confusing global warming (CO₂/CH₄, climate) with acid rain (SO₂/NOₓ) and with ozone depletion (CFCs) — three distinct problems.
  • Writing acid rain as sulfuric acid only from SO₂ without the water/oxidation steps.
  • Saying chlorination removes impurities — it kills microbes; sedimentation/filtration removes solids; carbon removes taste/odour.
  • Forgetting dissolved oxygen in water-quality answers (its absence is the harm in eutrophication).
  • Claiming fertilisers are simply "pollution" — the balanced answer names yield benefits and run-off costs.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Describe how carbon dioxide causes global warming.

Answer: Solar radiation warms the Earth's surface, which re-radiates energy as infra-red. CO₂ absorbs this outgoing infra-red and re-emits it in all directions, including back to the surface, so less energy escapes to space. Burning fossil fuels increases atmospheric CO₂, enhancing this natural effect and raising average temperatures.

Question 2 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Explain how sulfur dioxide causes acid rain and one method of reducing it.

Answer: Sulfur impurities in fuels burn to sulfur dioxide: S + O₂ → SO₂. In the atmosphere it dissolves in rainwater and oxidises to sulfuric acid: SO₂ + H₂O → H₂SO₃, then further oxidation gives H₂SO₄. Reduction: flue-gas desulfurisation using calcium oxide/carbonate, which reacts with SO₂ to give calcium sulfate; or use low-sulfur fuels.

Question 3 (Paper 4, 3 marks). Describe the stages of domestic water treatment.

Answer: Sedimentation (solids settle, sometimes with a flocculant), filtration through gravel/sand (removes remaining insoluble particles), activated-carbon adsorption (removes taste, odour, dissolved organics), and chlorination (kills bacteria and viruses and protects the supply).

Question 4 (Paper 4, 3 marks). Explain the test for water and how boiling-point data shows purity.

Answer: Anhydrous copper(II) sulfate turns from white to blue (or cobalt(II) chloride from blue to pink) when water is added. Pure water boils sharply at exactly 100 °C at standard pressure; an impure sample boils over a range of temperatures and above 100 °C.

Question 5 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Explain the environmental problems caused by fertiliser run-off.

Answer: Nitrates and phosphates wash into rivers and lakes, causing eutrophication: algae grow explosively and block light, so aquatic plants die; the decay of this material by bacteria consumes dissolved oxygen, suffocating fish and other organisms. Excess nitrate in drinking water is also a health risk (it affects blood oxygen transport).

Question 6 (Paper 4, 3 marks). Write an equation for the catalytic conversion of nitrogen monoxide and carbon monoxide and name the products.

Answer: 2CO + 2NO → 2CO₂ + N₂. The products are carbon dioxide and nitrogen — both far less harmful than the reactants.

The environment is shaped by carbon chemistry too — the organic family tree comes next.

title: IGCSE Chemistry: Acids, Bases and Salts
content:
IGCSE Chemistry: Acids, Bases and Salts

Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry 0620 (2026–2028), Extended route, Topic 7 Acids, bases and salts: statement 7.1 The characteristic properties of acids and bases, 7.2 Oxides, and 7.3 Preparation of salts. This note builds from what an acid physically is (a proton donor) through every reaction type worth marks, to the four salt-preparation methods with their procedures — and it is those procedures that carry Paper 6 as well as Paper 4. Every equation is balanced and every calculation line is explicit.

What acids and bases are

The everyday definition: acids taste sour, turn litmus red and react with metals and carbonates; bases are metal oxides or hydroxides that neutralise acids; alkalis are soluble bases (they dissolve to give hydroxide ions). The Extended definition that earns the extra mark: an acid is a proton (H⁺) donor and a base is a proton acceptor — in water an acid donates H⁺ to the solvent, forming H₃O⁺ but conventionally written as H⁺(aq).

Dissociation of acids in water - the strong/weak distinction:

  STRONG acid - fully dissociated (every molecule releases its proton):
    HCl(aq) → H⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq)          [single arrow]
    HNO₃(aq) → H⁺(aq) + NO₃⁻(aq)
    H₂SO₄(aq) → 2H⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq)

  WEAK acid - only partially dissociated (an equilibrium):
    CH₃COOH(aq) ⇌ H⁺(aq) + CH₃COO⁻(aq)   [equilibrium arrow]
    H₂CO₃(aq) ⇌ H⁺(aq) + HCO₃⁻(aq)

Strong vs weak is about the DISOCIATION, not the concentration:
  dilute HCl is strong but dilute; concentrated ethanoic acid is weak but
  concentrated. Strong acids attack metals and carbonates faster (more H⁺
  ions per volume); weak acids are safer (vinegar, lemon juice).

Reactions of acids: the four types

Reacts withProductsWorked equation
MetalsSalt + hydrogenMg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g)
Bases (metal oxides/hydroxides)Salt + waterCuO(s) + H₂SO₄(aq) → CuSO₄(aq) + H₂O(l)
CarbonatesSalt + water + carbon dioxideCaCO₃(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl₂(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g)
Ammonia (alkali)Ammonium saltNH₃(g) + HCl(aq) → NH₄Cl(aq)

Neutralisation is acid + base → salt + water; the ionic essence is H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O. Indicators: litmus (red in acid, blue in alkali), thymolphthalein (colourless in acid, blue in alkali), methyl orange (red in acid, yellow in alkali), universal indicator for a pH estimate. pH measures acidity: pH 7 neutral, below 7 acidic, above 7 alkaline; each unit is a tenfold change in H⁺ concentration.

Oxides: the four classes

  • Basic oxides — metal oxides (CuO, CaO) that react with acids to give salt and water.
  • Acidic oxides — non-metal oxides (SO₂, CO₂, NO₂) that react with alkalis to give salt and water.
  • Amphoteric oxides — react with both acids and alkalis (Al₂O₃, ZnO) — the Extended favourite.
  • Neutral oxides — neither (CO, NO, H₂O).
Amphoteric behaviour worked, both directions:

  Al₂O₃ + 6HCl → 2AlCl₃ + 3H₂O         [acts as a base, with acid]
  Al₂O₃ + 2NaOH → 2NaAlO₂ + H₂O        [acts as an acid, with alkali]

The oxide's character tracks the element's position: metallic oxides basic,
non-metallic oxides acidic, and the metal/metalloid border (Al, Zn) gives
amphoteric behaviour.

Preparation of salts: four methods

The method is chosen by the salt's solubility and the acid type — a decision tree the exam expects you to reason through, not recite.

Decision tree:

  Soluble salt?
  |-- YES → use an ACID + excess INSOLUBLE base/metal/carbonate, then
  |          filter off the excess and crystallise.
  |-- NO  → precipitation: mix two solutions of soluble salts, filter,
             wash and dry the precipitate.

Worked procedure 1 - soluble salt from an insoluble base:
  copper(II) sulfate from copper(II) oxide + dilute sulfuric acid.
  1. Warm dilute H₂SO₄ in a beaker.
  2. Add CuO powder a little at a time with stirring - it reacts and
     dissolves: CuO + H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + H₂O
  3. Keep adding until NO MORE DISSOLVES (the excess solid remains) -
     this guarantees all the acid is used up.
  4. FILTER off the excess CuO (the filtrate is pure copper(II) sulfate
     solution).
  5. Heat the filtrate to the point of crystallisation, leave to cool and
     crystallise; dry the crystals between filter papers.

  The excess-solid trick is the key exam point: a pure salt needs either
  reagent fully consumed, and only an insoluble excess can be filtered off.

Worked procedure 2 - insoluble salt by precipitation:
  barium sulfate from barium chloride + sodium sulfate solutions.
  BaCl₂(aq) + Na₂SO₄(aq) → BaSO₄(s) + 2NaCl(aq)
  Mix solutions, filter the precipitate, wash with distilled water, dry.

Worked procedure 3 - titration (soluble salt from acid + soluble alkali):
  sodium chloride from hydrochloric acid + sodium hydroxide.
  Both are solutions, so there is no excess solid to filter - use EXACT
  volumes from a titration (see the techniques note), then evaporate.

Worked procedure 4 - acid + excess metal (hydrogen given off):
  zinc sulfate from zinc + dilute sulfuric acid; filter excess zinc.

Water of crystallisation

Many salts crystallise with water locked into their lattice — hydrated salts (CuSO₄·5H₂O blue; CoCl₂·6H₂O pink). Heating drives the water off as anhydrous salt (white CuSO₄), and the change is reversible — the water test from the environment topic. In calculations the water counts in the formula mass: Mᵣ of CuSO₄·5H₂O = 160 + 5 × 18 = 250, not 160.
