Worked example: a full salt-preparation calculation

10.0 g of calcium carbonate reacts with excess hydrochloric acid:
  CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂

(a) moles CaCO₃ = 10.0 / 10⁰ = 0.100 mol
(b) ratio 1:1 → moles CaCl₂ = 0.100 mol
(c) mass CaCl₂ (Mᵣ = 111) = 0.100 × 111 = 11.1 g   [theoretical yield]
(d) if 9.4 g of dry salt is collected:
    percentage yield = 9.4 / 11.1 × 10⁰ = 84.7%

Where the mass is lost: crystals left in solution, spills, incomplete
reaction, or wet product if not dried - the usual evaluation question.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Confusing acid strength with concentration — strong = fully dissociated; concentrated = lots of acid per volume. The two are independent axes.
  • Writing weak acid dissociation with a single arrow; weak acids are equilibria.
  • Salt formula errors from ion charges: Al³⁺ + Cl⁻ → AlCl₃, not AlCl — check charge balance.
  • Forgetting carbon dioxide in acid + carbonate answers (three products, not two).
  • Adding excess soluble alkali in salt prep (then the salt is contaminated and cannot be filtered) — only insoluble reagents can be used in excess.
  • Leaving water of crystallisation out of formula mass or percentage-composition calculations.
  • Describing neutralisation as "acid + metal" — that is a separate reaction type; neutralisation is acid + base.
  • In precipitation questions, not washing the precipitate (residual soluble ions contaminate it).

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 4, 3 marks). Explain the difference between a strong acid and a concentrated acid.

Answer: A strong acid dissociates completely in water, releasing all its protons (e.g. hydrochloric acid); a concentrated acid contains a large amount of acid per unit volume of solution. A dilute solution of a strong acid is strong but dilute; a concentrated solution of a weak acid (ethanoic) is concentrated but weak.

Question 2 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Write equations for sulfuric acid reacting with (i) magnesium (ii) copper(II) oxide (iii) sodium carbonate.

Answer: (i) Mg + H₂SO₄ → MgSO₄ + H₂. (ii) CuO + H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + H₂O. (iii) Na₂CO₃ + H₂SO₄ → Na₂SO₄ + H₂O + CO₂.

Question 3 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Describe how pure crystals of copper(II) sulfate are prepared from copper(II) oxide and dilute sulfuric acid.

Answer: Warm the dilute acid; add copper(II) oxide with stirring until it no longer dissolves (excess solid ensures all acid reacts); filter off the excess copper(II) oxide; heat the filtrate to the point of crystallisation; leave the solution to cool and crystallise; filter and dry the crystals between filter papers.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 3 marks). Explain why aluminium oxide is described as amphoteric.

Answer: Aluminium oxide reacts with acids to form a salt and water (acting as a base), e.g. Al₂O₃ + 6HCl → 2AlCl₃ + 3H₂O, and also reacts with alkalis to form a salt and water (acting as an acid), e.g. Al₂O₃ + 2NaOH → 2NaAlO₂ + H₂O. Oxides with both behaviours are amphoteric.

Question 5 (Paper 4, 5 marks). Calculate the mass of anhydrous sodium sulfate formed when 21.2 g of sodium carbonate is neutralised by excess sulfuric acid. (Mᵣ: Na₂CO₃ = 106, Na₂SO₄ = 142)

Answer: Na₂CO₃ + H₂SO₄ → Na₂SO₄ + H₂O + CO₂. Moles Na₂CO₃ = 21.2 ÷ 106 = 0.200 mol. Ratio 1:1 → 0.200 mol Na₂SO₄. Mass = 0.200 × 142 = 28.4 g.

Question 6 (Paper 6, 3 marks). A student prepares lead(II) iodide by precipitation. State the reagents and describe the steps after mixing.

Answer: Mix solutions of lead(II) nitrate and potassium iodide. Filter to collect the yellow precipitate; wash it with distilled water to remove soluble nitrate/iodide ions; dry it between filter papers or in a warm oven.

Acids and salts live in the wider map of the elements — the Periodic Table's groups and their trends.

title: Exam technique: Materials and Deformation
content:
### What earns the marks
For stress and strain, each definition quoted with units or unitless noted earns a mark. For Young modulus, stress over strain earns the method mark with a steel-scale answer. For graphs, area read as stored energy earns the mark.
### Traps
Error: strain given units. Correction: strain is a pure ratio. Error: force-extension gradient called energy. Correction: gradient is stiffness; area is energy. Error: plastic region called elastic. Correction: only the straight line obeys Hooke.

title: IGCSE Mathematics: Fractions, Decimals and Percentages
content:
IGCSE Mathematics: Fractions, Decimals and Percentages

Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580 (2025–2027), section 1 Number: statement 1.4 Fractions, decimals and percentages (equivalence and conversion), 1.13 Percentages (including Extended reverse percentages) and E1.17 Exponential growth and decay. These three representations describe the same quantities, and fluent movement between them is one of the biggest sources of marks in both papers. The note explains why the conversion methods work before showing them, then builds percentages as multipliers — the technique behind most Paper 4 percentage problems.

What a fraction really is

A fraction is a division: 3/4 means 3 divided by 4, or three quarters of a whole. The top (numerator) counts the parts; the bottom (denominator) says how many equal parts the whole is cut into. A proper fraction has a smaller numerator (3/4); an improper fraction has a larger one (7/4); a mixed number combines a whole number with a proper fraction (1 3/4).

Convert 2 3/5 to an improper fraction:

2 wholes = 10 fifths, and 3 more fifths gives 13 fifths:
2 3/5 = (2 × 5 + 3)/5 = 13/5

Equivalent fractions are the same quantity written differently: 3/4 = 6/8 = 15/20, because multiplying top and bottom by the same number is multiplying by 1 (a form of 1, such as 3/3), which changes the look but not the value. Cancelling is the reverse: dividing top and bottom by a common factor. Only factors of the whole numerator and denominator can be cancelled — (x + 3)/(x + 2) cannot be simplified by cancelling the x's, because the top is a sum, not a product.

Converting between fractions, decimals and percentages

Fraction to decimal: divide.  3/8 = 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375
Decimal to fraction: read the place value.  0.47 = 47/10⁰
Fraction to percentage: divide, then multiply by 10⁰.  3/8 = 0.375 = 37.5%
Percentage to fraction: write over 10⁰ and simplify.  45% = 45/10⁰ = 9/20

Recurring decimals. A fraction always produces either a terminating decimal or a recurring one, and every recurring decimal converts back to a fraction by the algebra method:

Write 0.444... (4 recurring) as a fraction:

Let x = 0.444...
Then 10x = 4.444...        [shift the decimal one place]
Subtract:  10x - x = 4.444... - 0.444...
9x = 4
x = 4/9
Write 0.273636... (36 recurring) as a fraction:

Let x = 0.273636...
Two digits repeat, so shift two places:  100x = 27.363636...
100x - x = 27.3636... - 0.2736... = 27.09
99x = 27.09  →  x = 27.09/99 = 301/1100 after multiplying top and bottom by 10⁰ and simplifying

Knowing the common conversions by heart saves time: 1/2 = 0.5 = 50%, 1/4 = 0.25 = 25%, 3/4 = 0.75, 1/5 = 0.2 = 20%, 1/8 = 0.125, 1/3 = 0.333... = 33 1/3%.

FractionDecimalPercentage
1/20.550%
1/40.2525%
3/40.7575%
1/50.220%
1/80.12512.5%
1/30.333...33 1/3%
2/30.666...66 2/3%

These seven values answer a surprising share of Paper 2 questions by inspection, and they anchor every conversion done the long way.

Percentages: the multiplier method

A percentage is a fraction out of 100 — literally per cent, per hundred. Every percentage problem is a multiplication, and the fastest method converts straight to a multiplier.

Find 35% of 240:

35% = 35/10⁰ = 0.35, so  0.35 × 240 = 84

Increase 240 by 35%:
the new value is 135% of the old, so multiply by 1.35:  1.35 × 240 = 324

Decrease 240 by 35%:
the new value is 65% of the old, so multiply by 0.65:   0.65 × 240 = 156

Why the multiplier works. Increasing by 35% means keeping the original 100% and adding 35%, so the result is 135% of the original, which is 1.35 times it. Decreasing by 35% leaves 65%, which is 0.65 times. The multiplier also chains: successive changes multiply, which is why two discounts of 20% are not one discount of 40% (0.8 × 0.8 = 0.64, a 36% total reduction).

One quantity as a percentage of another:  18 out of 60

18/60 × 10⁰ = 30%

Reverse percentages (Extended). Working backwards from a final value needs division:

A price after a 20% increase is £72. Find the original price.

The original is 10⁰%, the new price is 120% of it, so the multiplier is 1.2:
original = 72 / 1.2 = £60

Check: 60 × 1.2 = 72 ✓

The common error is finding 20% of 72 and subtracting; the percentage must be taken from the original 100%, not the final amount.

Percentage change and comparisons

A coat falls from £80 to £56. Find the percentage decrease.

change = 80 - 56 = 24
percentage change = change / original x 10⁰ = 24/80 × 10⁰ = 30%

Percentage change always uses the original value as the denominator. Comparing quantities with different sizes — prices per 100 g, speeds, wages per hour — is done by putting both over a common quantity before comparing.

Exponential growth and decay (Extended)

When a quantity changes by the same percentage each period, it is multiplied by a fixed factor each time, and the result is exponential growth or decay. The multiplier is 1 + r for growth and 1 − r for decay, where r is the rate as a decimal.

After n periods at rate r:
growth:    final = original x (1 + r)^n
decay:     final = original x (1 - r)^n

Why the power. Each period multiplies by the same factor, so n periods multiply n times: an investment of £500 growing 3% a year becomes 500 × 1.03 after one year, 500 × 1.03 × 1.03 after two, and 500 × 1.03ⁿ after n years. The power counts the multiplications.

£500 is invested at 3% compound interest per year for 4 years.

500 × 1.03⁴ = 500 × 1.12550881 = £562.75 (2 d.p.)

Year by year check: 515.00 → 530.45 → 546.36 → 562.75 ✓
A car worth £18 000 depreciates 15% per year. Value after 3 years:

18 000 × 0.85³ = 18 000 × 0.614125 = £11 054.25

Exponential growth graphs climb ever faster and never touch zero; exponential decay graphs fall steeply at first and then level off towards — but never reach — zero (a horizontal asymptote). Doubling and halving questions are solved by logs or trial multiplication: for how many years does £500 at 3% exceed £600? Solve 500 × 1.03ⁿ > 600 by testing values of n, since 1.03ⁿ > 1.2 needs n ⩾ 7 years.

Worked example: a full percentage question

A shop sells a jacket for £84 after a 20% reduction. A further 10% discount is offered for cash.

Original price before the 20% reduction:
84 = original x 0.80
original = 84 / 0.80 = £10⁵

Cash price after the extra 10%:
84 × 0.90 = £75.60

Total percentage saving against the original:
saving = 10⁵ - 75.60 = 29.40
percentage saving = 29.40/10⁵ × 10⁰ = 28%

Check with multipliers: 0.80 × 0.90 = 0.72, so the cash price is 72% of the
original and the saving is 28% ✓

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Finding a percentage of the wrong amount: increase/decrease percentages apply to the original; reverse percentages divide by the multiplier.
  • Adding percentage changes: two 20% discounts give 0.8 × 0.8 = 0.64, a 36% reduction, not 40%.
  • Writing a recurring decimal as a fraction by eye; use the shift-and-subtract method and show it.
  • Cancelling across a sum: 3/4 is not 3 quarters of the top and bottom separately.
  • Using 365 days or 12 months inconsistently in compound problems: the power n counts compounding periods, so match it to the rate.
  • Forgetting that 15% decrease means multiplying by 0.85, not by −0.15 or 0.15.
  • Confusing 33% with 1/3 exactly: 1/3 = 33 1/3%, and the difference matters in exact answers.
  • Deciding an exponential decay value reaches zero; it falls below £1 or 0.001 but never reaches zero.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 2, 3 marks). Express 0.45 as a fraction in its lowest terms.

Answer: 0.45 = 45/100 = 9/20.

Question 2 (Paper 2, 3 marks). Write 0.27 with the 27 recurring as a fraction.

Answer: Let x = 0.272727...; then 100x = 27.2727...; subtracting gives 99x = 27, so x = 27/99 = 3/11.

Question 3 (Paper 4, 4 marks). In a sale, a bike is reduced by 15% to £255. Find the original price.

Answer: £255 represents 85% of the original, so the multiplier is 0.85 and the original price is 255/0.85 = £300. Check: 300 × 0.85 = 255 ✓.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 4 marks). A bacteria culture starts with 2000 and increases by 8% each hour. Find the size after 5 hours.

Answer: 2000 × 1.08⁵ = 2000 × 1.4693280768 = 2938.7 ≈ 2939 bacteria.

Question 5 (Paper 4, 3 marks). A town's population falls from 45 000 to 36 000 over a year. Find the percentage decrease.

Answer: Change = 9000; percentage = 9000/45 000 × 100 = 20%.

Question 6 (Paper 4, 5 marks). A car is bought for £12 000 and depreciates 18% in the first year and 12% in the second. Find its value after two years and the overall percentage loss.

Answer: 12 000 × 0.82 × 0.88 = 12 000 × 0.7216 = £8659.20. Overall loss = £3340.80, which is 3340.80/12 000 × 100 = 27.84% ≈ 27.8%. (Note 0.82 × 0.88 = 0.7216, a 27.84% total fall — not 30%.)

Fractions describe parts; powers and roots describe repeated multiplication — the next topic.

title: Exam technique: Bearings and Loci
content:
### What earns the marks
For bearings, measure earns marks for the angle taken clockwise from north with three figures in the final answer: add leading zeros (075, 008). For back bearings, the 180-degree adjustment stated earns the method mark. For scale drawings, the scale multiplication shown earns a mark independent of arithmetic. For loci, construct earns marks for the correct locus type (circle, bisector, parallel pair) drawn and labelled.
### Traps
Error: measuring anticlockwise or from the wrong datum. Correction: north line up, clockwise. Error: dropping leading zeros. Correction: three figures always. Error: one angle bisector instead of the pair for intersecting lines. Correction: two lines cross, so two bisectors. Error: dividing by the scale instead of multiplying. Correction: real distances exceed map distances.
### Worked example
A boat sails from A on a bearing of 065° and reaches B. Its back bearing from B to A is 065 + 180 = 245°. Draw the north line at both points, because the angles at the two north lines are alternate and the back bearing follows from that.
### Check yourself
Describe the locus of points exactly 3 cm from a fixed point P, and the locus of points equidistant from two points A and B. The first is a circle of radius 3 cm centred on P. The second is the perpendicular bisector of the line AB. State both in words and draw them with compasses and a ruler.

title: Operating Systems — Study Notes
content:
Operating Systems

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): OS roles, memory/process management, hardware–software layer, interrupts, buffers, utility software.

1. What an OS does

Manages memory, processes/files, I/O via drivers, security (users, permissions), and provides the UI (CLI/GUI) between user, applications and hardware.

2. Memory and process management

  • Paging/segmentation move programs in/out; virtual memory extends RAM to disk when RAM is full.
  • Multitasking: scheduler gives each process time slices; context switching saves/restores state.

3. Interrupts and buffers

Interrupts signal events (I/O complete, timer); CPU saves context, services via ISR, resumes. Buffers hold data in transit (printing) so slow devices don't block the CPU; spooling queues jobs.

4. Utility software

Disk formatter, defragmenter (reduces head movement on HDDs; unnecessary for SSD), backup scheduler, compression, antivirus, file compression.

5. UI and drivers

CLI: precise, scriptable, low overhead. GUI: icons/windows, discoverable, more resources. Device drivers translate OS calls to hardware specifics — each device needs its own.

Exam tips: "manage" verbs earn marks: manages memory, manages processes, manages peripherals; explain virtual memory by RAM-full scenario, not definition alone.

Interrupts and scheduling

An interrupt is a signal that tells the processor to stop its current task and deal with an event, such as a key press, a timer ending or an error. The processor saves the state of the current task, runs the interrupt service routine, and then resumes the task it was doing. Interrupts let the processor respond to devices without checking them constantly.

The operating system manages several programs at once through scheduling. Each program receives processor time in turn, which gives the impression that they run at the same time. Memory management keeps each program's data separate, and the operating system provides a user interface and manages files and devices.

Exam tip: describe the steps of an interrupt in order: save state, run the routine, restore state.

Worked example: round-robin scheduling

Three processes arrive together at time 0: A needs 5 ms, B needs 3 ms and C needs 1 ms. The time quantum is 2 ms. The timeline is A (0 to 2), B (2 to 4), C (4 to 5, finished), A (5 to 7), B (7 to 8, finished), A (8 to 9, finished). The completion times are A = 9 ms, B = 8 ms and C = 5 ms. The processor is shared fairly, but a short job such as C still waits for the earlier turns of the others.

Virtual memory and paging

The operating system divides a program into fixed-size pages and keeps only the pages in use in main memory. When a page that is needed is not in RAM, a page fault occurs and the operating system loads it from secondary storage. This allows programs larger than the physical memory to run, at the cost of slower access when faults are frequent.

Batch processing and multiprogramming

  • Batch processing runs a set of jobs one after another with no user interaction, which suits payroll runs.
  • Multiprogramming keeps several jobs in memory at once and switches between them, so the processor is not idle while one job waits for input or output.
  • Real-time systems guarantee a response within a fixed deadline, which matters in control systems such as a car's braking system.

Exam point: when a question asks why an operating system is needed, link each function to the hardware problem it solves, for example scheduling because there is one processor and many processes.

title: IGCSE Physics: Forces and Motion
content:
IGCSE Physics: Forces and Motion

Cambridge IGCSE Physics 0625 (2026–2028), Topic 1 Motion, forces and energy: statements 1.2 Motion, 1.3 Mass and weight, 1.5 Forces and 1.6 Momentum. This is the mechanics spine of the whole course, and it is where the Paper 4 structured calculation marks are won and lost. Almost every mechanics question begins the same way: label the velocities, find the resultant force, then choose the equation. The ideas below are built from absolute zero, but the definitions are examinable word for word, so learn them exactly as stated.

Speed, velocity and acceleration

Start with an analogy. A car's speedometer tells you how fast the car is covering ground; it says nothing about which way the car points. That everyday reading is speed. Add a compass direction to it and you have velocity. Speed is a scalar (size only); velocity is a vector (size and direction), and that single distinction runs through the entire course.

QuantityDefinitionSymbol and unitScalar or vector
DistanceTotal length of the path travelleds, metre (m)Scalar
DisplacementDistance in a stated straight-line direction from a start points, metre (m)Vector
SpeedDistance travelled per unit timev, metre per second (m s⁻¹)Scalar
VelocityRate of change of displacement, i.e. speed in a stated directionv, metre per second (m s⁻¹)Vector
AccelerationRate of change of velocitya, metre per second squared (m s⁻²)Vector

The two equations every question uses are:

average speed = total distance travelled / total time taken        v = s / t
acceleration = (final velocity - initial velocity) / time taken    a = (v - u) / t

Here u is the initial velocity, v is the final velocity, and t is the time taken. The SI units must be metres, seconds and metres per second before the equations are used; convert kilometres to metres and minutes to seconds first. The sign convention is the student's choice but must be stated: pick one direction as positive (upwards or forwards is usual), then velocities and accelerations in the opposite direction are negative. A negative acceleration that slows an object is often called a deceleration. An object thrown upwards has g = 9.81 m s⁻² downwards throughout its flight, so if up is positive its acceleration is −9.81 m s⁻² at every point, including the instant it stops at the top.

Average speed over a whole journey is not the average of the speeds. It is total distance divided by total time, so a car that covers 100 km at 50 km h⁻¹ and the next 100 km at 100 km h⁻¹ has an average speed of 200 km in 3 hours, which is 67 km h⁻¹, not 75 km h⁻¹.

Describing motion with graphs

Graphs are the language of this topic, and Paper 4 nearly always carries one. Two kinds do all the work.

FeatureDistance–time graphSpeed–time graph
GradientSpeed (or velocity)Acceleration
Area under the graphNot meaningfulDistance travelled
Horizontal lineObject at restConstant speed, zero acceleration
Straight sloping lineConstant speedConstant acceleration
CurveChanging speed (draw a tangent to find the speed at a point)Changing acceleration

On a distance–time graph the gradient is the distance moved divided by the time taken, which is the speed. On a speed–time graph the gradient is the change in speed divided by the time taken, which is the acceleration, and the area under the graph is made of rectangles (speed × time = distance) and triangles (½ × base × height), so it gives the total distance travelled. Drawing a tangent to a curve at a point is a Paper 6 skill: place the ruler so it just touches the curve, extend the line well past the curve on both sides, and take two distant points on the tangent to work out its gradient.

Paper 6 link. A trolley pulled by a falling mass leaves dots on ticker tape from a 50 Hz timer, so consecutive dots are 0.02 s apart. The distance between successive dots gives the speed over that interval, and a speed–time graph of those speeds has a gradient equal to the trolley's acceleration. Measuring a short distance with a ruler and dividing by 0.02 s is exactly the averaging technique in statement 1.1.

Mass, weight and gravitational field strength

Mass is the amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms with a balance. It does not change wherever the object is taken: the mass of an astronaut is the same on the Moon as on Earth. Weight is the force of gravity on that mass, measured in newtons with a spring balance, and it is a vector because gravity always pulls towards the centre of the attracting body. The astronaut's weight on the Moon is about one sixth of that on Earth because the Moon's gravitational field is weaker.

weight = mass x gravitational field strength        W = m g
  • W: weight in newtons (N). Weight is a vector, and its direction is straight down towards the centre of the Earth.
  • m: mass in kilograms (kg). Mass is a scalar.
  • g: gravitational field strength in newtons per kilogram (N kg⁻¹); on Earth g ≈ 9.81 N kg⁻¹, which is numerically the same as the free-fall acceleration 9.81 m s⁻².

Examination questions give the value of g to use, and many IGCSE papers round it to 10 N kg⁻¹ to keep the arithmetic simple. Always use the value printed in the question, and quote it in your answer when you substitute. Never confuse the two instruments: a balance compares masses and would give the same reading on the Moon, while a newton meter compares weights and would not.

Forces and their effects

A force is a push or a pull, measured in newtons, and it is a vector: direction matters. Forces can change an object's speed, change its direction of travel, or change its shape. Newton's first law states that an object remains at rest, or continues at constant velocity in a straight line, unless a resultant (net) force acts on it. Motion only changes when forces are unbalanced; a book resting on a table has weight and an equal upward normal contact force acting on it, so its resultant force is zero and it does not accelerate.

The resultant force is the single force that has the same effect as all the real forces combined. Two people pushing a trolley the same way add; pushing opposite ways subtract; forces at right angles combine by Pythagoras on the diagonal (Supplement). Newton's second law, in the form examined at IGCSE, is a Supplement statement:

resultant force = mass x acceleration        F = m a
  • F: resultant force in newtons (N), positive in the chosen positive direction.
  • m: mass in kilograms (kg).
  • a: acceleration in metres per second squared (m s⁻²), in the same direction as F.

The equation only works with the resultant force and only in SI units. If a car's engine produces 3000 N while drag is 1000 N, the resultant is 2000 N, and it is that 2000 N that goes into F = ma.

Friction and drag. Friction acts where surfaces touch and always opposes the motion or the tendency to move. Drag (air resistance or water resistance) opposes motion through a fluid and grows as the speed grows. A falling object released from rest therefore accelerates at first, because weight exceeds drag; as speed rises, drag rises until it equals the weight. From that moment the resultant force is zero, the acceleration is zero, and the object falls at terminal velocity. This is a Supplement explanation and it is a regular Paper 4 six-mark question: describe the motion in stages and use the words resultant force, drag and terminal velocity.

Springs and extension. A load hung on a spring stretches it. The relationship is summarised on a load–extension graph: a straight line through the origin shows extension proportional to load, up to the limit of proportionality. The stiffness of the spring is its spring constant:

force = spring constant x extension        F = k x
  • F: force applied to the spring in newtons (N).
  • k: spring constant in newtons per metre (N m⁻¹); larger k means a stiffer spring.
  • x: extension in metres (m). Extension = stretched length − original length, so it is a scalar in practice.

Beyond the limit of proportionality the line curves: the spring is permanently deformed and does not return to its original length when the load is removed. Doubling the load doubles the extension only while the graph is still a straight line. Two identical springs in series share the load and stretch twice as far; in parallel they share the load and stretch half as far (Supplement).

Turning effects of forces: moments

A force that does not act through a pivot makes an object turn. The size of that turning effect is the moment of the force:

moment of a force = force x perpendicular distance from the pivot        M = F d
  • M: moment in newton metres (N m). A moment is a vector in the sense that it turns clockwise or anticlockwise, and that sense must be carried through the calculation as a sign.
  • F: force in newtons (N).
  • d: perpendicular distance from the line of action of the force to the pivot in metres (m).

The word perpendicular is the whole mark. If a 10 N force acts at 30° to a spanner handle, the moment uses the perpendicular component of the force, or equivalently the perpendicular distance. For an object in equilibrium the principle of moments applies: the sum of the clockwise moments about any pivot equals the sum of the anticlockwise moments, and the resultant force is zero. A see-saw balances when the anticlockwise moment of the near child equals the clockwise moment of the far child; moving either child outwards increases that child's moment without changing their weight. Two equal and opposite forces whose lines of action do not coincide form a couple, which produces rotation without translation, as when a steering wheel is turned with both hands.

Centre of gravity and stability

The centre of gravity of an object is the single point through which its entire weight may be taken to act. For a uniform object it is the geometric centre; for a lamina (a flat sheet) it can be found experimentally by the plumb-line method, which is a classic Paper 6 task: hang the lamina freely from one hole, hang a plumb line from the same pin, and mark the line; repeat from a second hole; the lines cross at the centre of gravity.

Stability depends on where that point sits relative to the base. An object topples when the line of action of its weight falls outside its base, because the weight then produces a resultant moment that overturns it. Wide bases and low centres of gravity make objects stable (racing cars carry ballast low; tall trucks are loaded low), and top-heavy objects with narrow bases topple easily.

Momentum and impulse

Momentum is the quantity of motion a moving object carries: a lorry at 20 m s⁻¹ is far harder to stop than a bicycle at the same speed. Momentum is a Supplement statement for 0625 and is a favourite for Paper 4 calculation questions.

momentum = mass x velocity        p = m v
impulse = change in momentum = resultant force x time        F t = m v - m u
  • p: momentum in kilogram metres per second (kg m s⁻¹). Momentum is a vector, in the same direction as the velocity, so the sign convention chosen at the start must be applied to every velocity.
  • m: mass in kilograms (kg); v and u: final and initial velocity in metres per second (m s⁻¹), positive in the chosen positive direction.
  • Impulse: newton seconds (N s), equal to the change in momentum.

The principle of conservation of momentum: in a closed system, where no external resultant force acts, the total momentum before an event equals the total momentum after it. Total means the vector sum: momenta in opposite directions carry opposite signs. This one statement solves collisions, explosions and recoil problems. Newton's second law in its full form is implied here: the resultant force equals the rate of change of momentum, F = (mv − mu)/t, which is why increasing the time of impact reduces the force for the same change in momentum — that is how airbags, crash barriers and landing on a bent knee work.

Worked example: collision and impact force

Collision. A 1200 kg car travelling at 15 m s⁻¹ runs into a stationary 800 kg car and the two lock together. Find their common velocity. Take the first car's direction as positive.

total momentum before = 1200 × 15 + 800 × 0 = 18 000 kg m s⁻¹
total momentum after = (1200 + 800) v = 2000 v
2000 v = 18 000, so v = 9 m s⁻¹, in the original direction

The combined cars move at 9 m s⁻¹ in the direction the first car was travelling. Note that kinetic energy is not conserved in this collision — most of it is lost to sound and deformation — but momentum is always conserved.

Impact force. A 0.50 kg ball travelling at 12 m s⁻¹ hits a wall and rebounds at 8 m s⁻¹ in the opposite direction. The contact lasts 0.050 s. Find the average force on the ball. Take the initial direction as positive, so the rebound velocity is −8 m s⁻¹.

change in momentum = m v - m u = 0.50 x (-8) - 0.50 × 12 = -4.0 - 6.0 = -10 kg m s⁻¹
average force = change in momentum / time = -10 / 0.050 = -200 N

The minus sign shows the force acts opposite to the ball's initial motion, which is what a wall does. The magnitude is 200 N. Getting the sign of the rebound velocity wrong is the single most common error in this topic, and it doubles the answer.

Common mistakes

  • Confusing mass and weight: mass is in kilograms and never changes; weight is in newtons and equals mg. A mass of 5 kg has a weight of about 50 N, not 5 kg.
  • Using the average of speeds for the average speed of a journey; it is always total distance over total time.
  • Reading the wrong quantity from a graph: gradient on a distance–time graph is speed, gradient on a speed–time graph is acceleration, and only the speed–time graph has a meaningful area.
  • Putting any force into F = ma. Only the resultant force gives the acceleration, so add and subtract the forces first.
  • Using a slanted distance in a moment calculation; d is measured perpendicular to the line of action of the force.
  • Losing the sign of a velocity in a momentum calculation. Reversal of direction is a sign change, and the total momentum is a vector sum, not a sum of sizes.
  • Using g = 9.81 when the question says take g = 10 N kg⁻¹, and forgetting to state which value was used.
  • Adding a force in newtons to a momentum in kg m s⁻¹; if the units do not match, the physics does not either.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 4, 3 marks). A cyclist starts from rest and reaches 8.0 m s⁻¹ in 5.0 s. Calculate the average acceleration and the distance travelled.

Answer: a = (v − u)/t = (8.0 − 0)/5.0 = 1.6 m s⁻². Distance = average speed × time = ½(0 + 8.0) × 5.0 = 20 m. (A speed–time graph of the motion is a triangle of area ½ × 5.0 × 8.0 = 20 m.)

Question 2 (Paper 4, 4 marks). A skydiver of mass 80 kg falls. Explain, using forces, why she reaches a terminal velocity, and state the size of the drag force at that moment.

Answer: Weight W = mg = 80 × 9.8 = 784 N downwards (≈ 800 N if g = 10 is taken). At first weight exceeds drag, so there is a downward resultant force and she accelerates. As speed increases, drag increases. When drag equals the weight the resultant force is zero, acceleration is zero, and she falls at constant terminal velocity. The drag force is then 784 N (or 800 N) upwards.

Question 3 (Paper 2 style). Which statement about a ball thrown straight up is correct? A: its acceleration at the top is zero; B: its velocity at the top is zero; C: its momentum at the top is maximum; D: its weight is zero at the top. Answer: B. The velocity is instantaneously zero at the top, but g still acts there, so the acceleration is 9.81 m s⁻² downwards and the weight is unchanged. Paper 2 setters rely on this confusion between velocity and acceleration.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 4 marks). A 1500 kg car travelling at 20 m s⁻¹ brakes to a stop in 4.0 s. Calculate the braking force.

Answer: change in momentum = mv − mu = 1500 × 0 − 1500 × 20 = −30 000 kg m s⁻¹. Force = change in momentum / time = −30 000 / 4.0 = −7500 N. The braking force is 7500 N opposite to the motion.

Question 5 (Paper 6 style). Describe how you would find the centre of gravity of an irregular lamina.

Answer: Hang the lamina from a pin through a hole near its edge so it swings freely. Hang a plumb line from the same pin and, when everything is at rest, mark the plumb-line position on the lamina. Repeat with the lamina hung from a second hole. The point where the two marked lines cross is the centre of gravity. The plumb line marks the vertical through the pivot, and the centre of gravity lies on it in both cases.

Question 6 (Paper 4, 3 marks). A 0.20 kg ball moving at 6.0 m s⁻¹ collides with an identical ball at rest and stops dead. Find the velocity of the second ball after the impact.

Answer: total momentum before = 0.20 × 6.0 = 1.2 kg m s⁻¹. After the impact the first ball has zero momentum, so 0.20 × v = 1.2 and v = 6.0 m s⁻¹ in the original direction.

Momentum, moments and Newton's laws are the tools; the next step is what those forces actually do to energy.

Equations and symbols

Every equation 0625 uses across statements 1.2, 1.3, 1.5 and 1.6, in the form the mark scheme expects. Motion equations assume constant acceleration in a straight line; the force equations are vector equations, so direction is part of the answer.

Motion

v = Δs / Δt
Key: v = speed or velocity (m/s); Δs = change in displacement (m); Δt = time interval (s). Velocity is a vector, so a change of direction is a change of velocity even at constant speed.

a = Δv / Δt = (v − u) / t
Key: a = acceleration (m/s²); v = final velocity (m/s); u = initial velocity (m/s); t = time taken (s). A negative a means deceleration.

v² = u² + 2as
Key: v = final velocity (m/s); u = initial velocity (m/s); a = constant acceleration (m/s²); s = displacement (m). Use it whenever time is neither given nor asked for.

s = ut + ½at²
Key: s = displacement (m); u = initial velocity (m/s); t = time (s); a = acceleration (m/s²). For a body released from rest, u = 0 and the distance is ½at².

s = ½(u + v)t
Key: s = displacement (m); u, v = initial and final velocity (m/s); t = time (s). This is the area under a velocity–time graph for constant acceleration, which is why the area is always a valid route to distance.

g = 9.8 N/kg (9.8 m/s²)
Key: g = gravitational field strength near the Earth's surface; numerically equal to free-fall acceleration, so a dropped body gains 9.8 m/s of speed each second in the absence of air resistance.

Mass, weight and force

W = mg
Key: W = weight (N); m = mass (kg); g = gravitational field strength (N/kg), 9.8 on Earth and about 1.6 on the Moon. Mass stays in kilograms and does not change with location; weight is the force and does.

F = ma
Key: F = resultant force (N); m = mass (kg); a = acceleration (m/s²). F is the resultant after friction and air resistance are subtracted, which is the single most common lost mark in this topic.

R = √(F₁² + F₂²)
Key: R = magnitude of the resultant (N); F₁, F₂ = two perpendicular forces (N). For forces along one line, add them when they point the same way and subtract when they oppose.

Balanced forces: ΣF = 0 implies a = 0
Key: ΣF = the vector sum of all forces (N); a = acceleration (m/s²). Zero resultant means at rest or at constant velocity — never "no forces acting".

Moments and springs

M = F × d
Key: M = moment of the force (N m); F = the force (N); d = the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force (m). A distance measured along a slant gives the wrong moment.

Σ clockwise moments = Σ anticlockwise moments
Key: the principle of moments, for a body in equilibrium. Each term is a force times its perpendicular distance (N m).

F = kx
Key: F = load or tension (N); k = spring constant (N/m or N/cm); x = extension beyond the natural length (m or cm). Valid only up to the limit of proportionality; beyond it the graph curves and the equation stops applying.

k = F / x
Key: k = spring constant (N/m); found as the gradient of the straight part of a force–extension graph, not from a single point beyond the limit.

Momentum

p = mv
Key: p = momentum (kg m/s); m = mass (kg); v = velocity (m/s). Momentum is a vector: opposite directions need opposite signs.

F = Δp / Δt
Key: F = average force acting (N); Δp = change in momentum (kg m/s); Δt = time over which it acts (s). This is the form that explains crumple zones and seatbelts: the same Δp spread over a longer Δt gives a smaller F.

m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂
Key: m₁, m₂ = masses (kg); u₁, u₂ = velocities before the collision (m/s); v₁, v₂ = velocities after (m/s). Total momentum is conserved when no external resultant force acts; kinetic energy is not necessarily conserved.

title: Exam technique: Materials and Deformation
content:
### What earns the marks
For stress and strain, each definition quoted with units or unitless noted earns a mark. For Young modulus, stress over strain earns the method mark with a steel-scale answer. For graphs, area read as stored energy earns the mark.
### Traps
Error: strain given units. Correction: strain is a pure ratio. Error: force-extension gradient called energy. Correction: gradient is stiffness; area is energy. Error: plastic region called elastic. Correction: only the straight line obeys Hooke.
### Worked example
Under a rotation of 90° anticlockwise about the origin, the point (3, 1) maps to (−1, 3). Each point's x and y change places with one sign reversed. Under a reflection in the line y = x, the same point maps to (1, 3), so the coordinates swap. For a translation by vector (2; −3), the point (3, 1) maps to (5, −2).

title: Edexcel IAL Computer Science: Encryption, Protocols and Digital Certificates
content:
Edexcel IAL Computer Science: Encryption, Protocols and Digital Certificates

Pearson Edexcel International Advanced Level in Computer Science, Unit 3 Advanced Computer Science: encryption, encryption protocols and digital certificates. The AS security note covered threats and defence-in-depth; this note goes into the cryptography itself — how symmetric and asymmetric systems work under the hood, how protocols like TLS compose them into secure channels, and how certificates bind keys to identities. Every exchange below is traced message by message, because the marks sit in the sequence.

The goals of cryptography

Cryptography serves four properties, and each technique below should be read against them: confidentiality (only the intended reader), integrity (detect any change), authentication (prove who sent it), and non-repudiation (the sender cannot deny it). A plain lock (encryption) gives only the first; the rest need hashes, signatures and certificates.

Symmetric encryption under the hood

One shared secret key encrypts and decrypts. Modern ciphers (AES) work by substitution–permutation networks: repeated rounds that substitute bytes (confusion) and shuffle positions (diffusion), each round keyed from the original key by a key schedule — so a single flipped plaintext bit changes roughly half the ciphertext bits after a few rounds. Block ciphers process fixed blocks (AES: 128 bits) in a mode (CBC chains blocks by XOR-ing each plaintext block with the previous ciphertext block, requiring an initialisation vector; ECB — the naive mode — leaks patterns and is unsafe; CTR turns the block cipher into a stream).

One AES-style round, conceptually:

  plaintext block (128 bits)
    → AddRoundKey (XOR with round key)
    → SubBytes (substitution table: confusion)
    → ShiftRows (permute: diffusion)
    → MixColumns (mix within columns: more diffusion)
  ... 10-14 rounds (key size dependent) ...
  → ciphertext block

Property worth the mark: encryption itself is deterministic without the IV/mode,
so identical plaintext blocks would give identical ciphertext - the pattern
leak ECB suffers. CBC's XOR of the previous ciphertext block (and a random IV)
breaks that regularity.

The symmetric strengths and weaknesses: very fast (bulk data), strong with adequate key lengths (AES-256); the weakness is the key distribution problem — every pair of communicators needs a shared secret, and every new pair multiplies the keys (n(n−1)/2 pairs) — plus key revocation and rotation logistics.

Asymmetric encryption under the hood

A mathematically related key pair: the public key encrypts (or verifies), the private key decrypts (or signs). RSA's mechanism rests on the trapdoor: multiplying two large primes is easy; factoring their product is computationally infeasible at key sizes of 2048+ bits. Elliptic-curve systems (ECC) give equivalent strength with far smaller keys, suiting mobile and TLS today.

RSA, the shape of the maths (numbers exaggerated for clarity):

  1. Choose primes p = 61, q = 53.  n = p x q = 3233   (public modulus)
  2. Φ(n) = (p-1)(q-1) = 3120.
  3. Choose public exponent e = 17 (coprime to 3120).
  4. Compute private exponent d: d x e = 1 mod 3120 → d = 2753.
  5. Encrypt message m = 65:  c = m^e mod n = 65¹⁷ mod 3233 = 2790.
  6. Decrypt:  m = c^d mod n = 2790²⁷⁵³ mod 3233 = 65.  ✓

Security: publishing (n = 3233, e = 17) reveals nothing useful WITHOUT
factoring n; with real 2048-bit n, factoring is the infeasible step. Signing
runs the other way: the signer applies d, anyone verifies with e.

Asymmetric strengths: no shared secret to distribute (the public key can be published), enabling signatures and non-repudiation; weakness: orders of magnitude slower than symmetric, so it is used for key exchange and signatures, not bulk data — the hybrid pattern below.

Signatures and hashing, traced:

  Signing a message:
    hash = SHA-256(message)                 (fixed 256-bit digest)
    signature = RSA-encrypt(hash) with the SIGNER'S PRIVATE key
    send (message, signature)

  Verifying:
    compute hash1 = SHA-256(message)
    hash2 = RSA-decrypt(signature) with the signer's PUBLIC key
    match → the message is unaltered AND only the private-key holder signed
             it (authentication AND non-repudiation).

A hash is one-way and collision-resistant: any edit changes the digest
completely (avalanche), so tampering is detectable even in large documents.
SymmetricAsymmetric
KeysOne shared secretPublic/private pair
SpeedFast (AES)Slow (RSA, ECC) — 100–1000× for bulk
UseBulk data encryptionKey exchange, signatures, certificates
Key distributionHard problem (n(n−1)/2 keys)Public key can be published freely
Non-repudiationNo (either holder could have made the ciphertext)Yes — signatures bind the private key

Hybrid systems and encryption protocols

Real protocols combine the two families: use asymmetric cryptography to authenticate and agree a fresh symmetric session key, then encrypt the conversation symmetrically for speed. The session key is ephemeral — compromising it later decrypts nothing else.

TLS handshake (HTTPS), message by message:

  Client                                    Server
    | --- ClientHello (ciphers, random) ---→|
    | <--- ServerHello (cipher chosen) ------|
    | <--- Certificate (server's public key) |
    | <--- ServerHelloDone ------------------|
    |    [client verifies the CERTIFICATE chain to a trusted CA]
    | --- KeyExchange (pre-master secret     |
    |     encrypted with server's public key)|
    | --- ChangeCipherSpec + Finished -----→|
    | <--- ChangeCipherSpec + Finished ------|
    Both now hold the same symmetric session key (derived from the secret).
    | <========== encrypted application data ==========> |

Why each step matters: Hello negotiates the cipher suite; the certificate
authenticates the server; the key exchange gives confidentiality (only the
private-key holder reads the pre-master secret); Finished confirms both sides
derived the same keys, defeating downgrade tampering.

Related protocols: SSH (encrypted remote shell and transfer, authenticating hosts by keys), IPsec/VPNs (encrypting whole IP tunnels between sites), PGP/GPG (email signing/encryption with a web-of-trust model), WPA2/WPA3 (Wi-Fi link encryption). Each solves the same composition problem for a different layer.

Digital certificates and trust

A digital certificate binds an identity to a public key, issued and signed by a certificate authority (CA) whose own key is trusted by the client's operating system/browser (the trust store). Contents: subject (domain), subject's public key, issuer, validity period, serial number, and the CA's signature. Verification walks the chain from the site's certificate up through intermediates to a trusted root.

  • Issuance: the applicant generates a key pair, sends a CSR (with proof of control over the domain), the CA validates (DV by email/DNS; EV with organisation checks) and signs.
  • Revocation: compromised keys must die early — CRLs (revocation lists) and OCSP (live status queries); browsers check before trusting.
  • Self-signed certificates: usable for testing only; no chain to a trusted root, so browsers warn — the mechanism, not mere "untrustworthiness", is the mark.
  • Trust model weaknesses worth naming: a compromised CA can sign falsely; the system is only as strong as its least careful CA (notable incidents: DigiNotar).
Worked: verifying a certificate chain in a browser, step by step.

1. The server sends its certificate (leaf) plus intermediates.
2. The browser checks the leaf's validity period (not expired/not future).
3. It verifies the CA signature on the leaf using the intermediate's key.
4. It follows intermediates up to a root already in its trust store.
5. It checks the hostname matches the certificate's subject (SAN field).
6. It checks revocation status (OCSP/CRL) for the leaf and intermediates.

Any failure breaks the padlock: expired date (step 2), unknown issuer
(step 4 - self-signed), wrong domain (step 5 - another site's certificate),
or revoked key (step 6 - the compromised-key case).

Worked example: securing a web application end to end

Requirements: users log in, place orders, view invoices.

1. Transport: HTTPS everywhere (TLS 1.3), HSTS so plain HTTP never negotiates -
   protects credentials and cookies in transit.
2. Certificates: a CA-signed certificate with auto-renewal (certbot-style);
   monitor expiry - the classic outage is a lapsed certificate.
3. Passwords: stored as salted bcrypt/argon2 hashes (never reversible
   encryption); 2FA at login for account takeover resistance.
4. Sessions: random session IDs, Secure/HttpOnly/SameSite cookies, short
   expiry; CSRF tokens on state-changing requests.
5. Data at rest: card details tokenised (never stored raw); database backups
   encrypted with keys held separately.
6. Integrity: signed software releases (code-signing certificates) so the
   deployed application is provably what the team built.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Saying asymmetric encryption "is more secure"; it solves key distribution and signatures — security depends on key sizes and protocol design, not the family.
  • Forgetting that hashing alone proves integrity but not authorship; a shared hash proves nothing about who sent it — signatures add the private-key step.
  • Describing certificates as "encryption files"; a certificate is a signed binding of identity to public key.
  • Tracing TLS without the verification steps: the CA chain check and hostname match are the authentication marks.
  • Confusing CRL with OCSP (list pulled periodically vs live per-lookup) or missing revocation entirely.
  • Reusing session keys or calling them permanent; ephemerality limits the blast radius of compromise.
  • Claiming a padlock proves a site is honest; TLS proves the connection is private and the domain is authenticated — not the merchant's intent.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Unit 3, 4 marks). Explain how symmetric and asymmetric encryption are combined in HTTPS.

Answer: Asymmetric encryption authenticates the server (its certificate carries a public key signed by a trusted CA) and encrypts a pre-master secret the client generates, so only the server's private key can read it. Both sides then derive the same ephemeral symmetric session key and encrypt the actual data with a fast symmetric cipher. This gets asymmetric's safe key agreement and symmetric's speed where the bulk flows.

Question 2 (Unit 3, 4 marks). Describe how a digital signature provides authentication and non-repudiation.

Answer: The signer hashes the message and encrypts the digest with their private key; the signature travels with the message. A verifier decrypts the signature with the signer's public key and compares it with their own hash of the message. A match proves the message is unaltered (integrity) and that only the holder of the private key could have signed it (authentication), so the signer cannot later deny it (non-repudiation).

Question 3 (Unit 3, 5 marks). Explain the role of certificate authorities in establishing trust.

Answer: A CA binds an identity to a public key by signing a certificate containing the subject, key, validity period and issuer. Clients hold trusted root CA keys in their trust store, so verifying the chain from the site's certificate up to a root proves the key belongs to that domain. CAs validate applicants (DV/EV), and revocation (CRL/OCSP) ends trust early if keys leak. The model's weakness is that any compromised CA can sign falsely — trust is only as strong as its weakest CA.

Question 4 (Unit 3, 4 marks). Explain the key distribution problem and how it is addressed.

Answer: Symmetric encryption needs every communicating pair to share a secret key in advance; with n users that is n(n−1)/2 keys, and any interception of a distributed key compromises the channel. It is addressed by asymmetric key exchange (publishing a public key lets any party agree a session key securely), key distribution centres/protocols, and hybrid systems where asymmetric agreement hands over an ephemeral symmetric key.

Question 5 (Unit 3, 3 marks). Explain why TLS uses a new session key for each connection.

Answer: Ephemeral keys limit exposure: if a session key is later compromised, only that one session's traffic is decryptable, not past or future ones. Fresh keys also resist replay attacks (old captured traffic under a different key reads as noise) and shrink the value of any single key theft.

Question 6 (Unit 3, 4 marks). A browser warns that a certificate is invalid. Explain three possible causes.

Answer: The certificate has expired (outside its validity period); the chain cannot be verified to a trusted root (self-signed or an untrusted intermediate); the hostname does not match the certificate's subject/SAN (the certificate belongs to another domain); or the certificate has been revoked following key compromise. Each failure corresponds to one check of the verification process.

Cryptography protects channels between machines; the next note covers the software that increasingly acts within them — artificial intelligence.

title: Electricity: D.C. Circuits — Study Notes
content:
Electricity: D.C. circuits

Current and charge

  • Current I = charge Q ÷ time t, so Q = It. Unit: ampere (A), where 1 A = 1 C s⁻¹.
  • Electron drift velocity is very small, but the electric field propagates through the circuit almost at the speed of light.

Potential difference and power

  • Potential difference V = energy transferred ÷ charge. Unit: volt (V), where 1 V = 1 J C⁻¹.
  • Power P = VI = I²R = V²/R. Unit: watt (W).

Resistance and resistivity

R = V/I (Ohm's law for an ohmic conductor, at constant temperature). For a wire of length L and cross-sectional area A, R = ρL/A, where ρ is the resistivity in Ω m. Resistance rises with length and falls with area.

Practical circuits

An ammeter is connected in series with the component it measures. A voltmeter is connected in parallel with the component. An ideal ammeter has zero resistance; an ideal voltmeter has infinite resistance.

Kirchhoff's laws

  • First law: at a junction, the total current entering equals the total current leaving (conservation of charge).
  • Second law: around any closed loop, the sum of the emfs equals the sum of the potential differences (conservation of energy).

Potential dividers

For two resistors R1 and R2 in series across a supply V, the potential difference across R2 is V × R2/(R1 + R2).

Worked example: a 100 Ω and a 300 Ω resistor are in series across 12 V. The current is 12/400 = 0.030 A, and the voltage across the 300 Ω resistor is 0.030 × 300 = 9.0 V.

Exam tips: draw the meter in the correct place, in series or in parallel. Apply Kirchhoff's first law to currents and the second law to loops, with consistent signs. Check that units are converted (e.g. mm² to m²) before using ρL/A.

Resistivity and temperature

For a metallic conductor at constant temperature, resistance is proportional to length and inversely proportional to cross-sectional area. Resistivity, ρ = RA/L, is a property of the material. As temperature rises, the ions in a metal vibrate more and impede the flow of electrons, so resistivity increases. A thermistor behaves differently: its resistance falls as temperature rises, because more charge carriers are released.

Exam tip: when asked to explain a resistance change, relate it to charge carriers and collisions, not just to the formula.

title: Permutations and Combinations — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Permutations and Combinations

Mathematics — A2. If a task is done in successive stages with m, n, ... choices at each stage, the total is the product of the choices. This underpins every counting problem: a menu with 4 starters and 6 mains gives 24 meals.

Key areas to revise

  • The Multiplication Principle
  • Permutations — Order Matters
  • Combinations — Order Irrelevant
  • Restricted Permutations
  • Combinations with Constraints

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

### Worked example A permutation is an ordered arrangement, so nPr = n! ÷ (n − r)!. A combination ignores order, so nCr = n! ÷ (r!(n − r)!). Five people in a line can be arranged in 5! = 120 ways. Choosing a committee of 3 from 8 people gives 8C3 = 56, while choosing a ranked top 2 from 5 gives 5P2 = 20. ### Worked example A permutation is an ordered arrangement, so nPr = n! ÷ (n − r)!. A combination ignores order, so nCr = n! ÷ (r!(n − r)!). Five people in a line can be arranged in 5! = 120 ways. Choosing a committee of 3 from 8 people gives 8C3 = 56, while choosing a ranked top 2 from 5 gives 5P2 = 20.

title: Algebra — Equations — Study Notes
content:
Algebra — Equations

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): linear equations, simultaneous equations, quadratic formula, completing the square, forming equations from words.

1. Linear equations

3(x − 2) = x + 4 → 3x − 6 = x + 4 → 2x = 10 → x = 5. With fractions, multiply through by the LCD first.

2. Forming equations

Translate shapes/situations: "rectangle length 3 cm more than width, perimeter 34" → 2w + 2(w + 3) = 34 → w = 7.

3. Simultaneous equations

  • Elimination: 2x + y = 7 and x − y = 2 → add → 3x = 9 → x = 3, y = 1.
  • Substitution for linear–quadratic: substitute y = 2x into x² + y² = 20 → 5x² = 20 → x = ±2.

4. Quadratics by formula

x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / 2a.

Example: 2x² − 4x − 3 = 0 → x = (4 ± √(16 + 24))/4 = 2.58 or −0.58 (2 d.p.).

5. Completing the square

x² + bx + c = (x + b/2)² − (b/2)² + c. x² − 6x + 5 = (x − 3)² − 4 → minimum at (3, −4). Use for turning points and for solving when factorising fails.

Exam tips: substitute answers back to verify; in word problems define the unknown clearly ("let w = width in cm"); give quadratic solutions to the accuracy demanded.

Solving linear equations step by step

Collect the unknown on one side and the numbers on the other, undoing operations in the reverse order to BODMAS. Whatever you do to one side you must do to the other. When brackets are present, expand first, then collect like terms. Fractions are cleared by multiplying every term by the lowest common denominator.

Simultaneous equations

Two linear equations in x and y can be solved by elimination (make the coefficient of one unknown equal and opposite, then add or subtract) or by substitution (rearrange one equation for one unknown and put it into the other). Check the answer in both original equations. Examiners award method marks for a correct, clearly shown elimination even when arithmetic slips later.

Rearranging formulae

Treat the subject letter as the unknown and apply inverse operations. Where the subject appears twice, gather every term containing it, factorise, then divide. Square roots or squares are undone with a square and a root, applied to both sides.

title: Integration II — Study Notes
content:
Integration II

Standard Integrals

  • ∫ sin x dx = −cos x + c
  • ∫ cos x dx = sin x + c
  • ∫ e^x dx = e^x + c
  • ∫ 1/x dx = ln|x| + c
  • ∫ sec²x dx = tan x + c

With linear arguments: ∫ e^(3x) dx = e^(3x)/3 + c; ∫ cos 2x dx = sin 2x/2 + c.

Substitution

Reverse of the chain rule. For ∫ 2x e^(x²) dx, let u = x²: du = 2x dx, so the integral is ∫ e^u du = e^(x²) + c.

Integration by Parts

∫ u (dv/dx) dx = uv − ∫ v (du/dx) dx. Choose u to be the part that simplifies when differentiated (LIATE: logs, inverse trig, algebraic, trig, exponential).

Example: ∫ x e^x dx = x e^x − ∫ e^x dx = x e^x − e^x + c.

Partial Fractions

Break rational functions into pieces like ∫ 1/(x+1) dx = ln|x + 1| + c.

Example: ∫ 4x/(x² − 1) dx = ∫ [2/(x − 1) + 2/(x + 1)] dx = 2 ln|x − 1| + 2 ln|x + 1| + c.

Exam tips: definite integrals: substitute limits into the transformed variable directly; for by-parts integrals like ∫ ln x dx, take u = ln x, dv/dx = 1.

title: Data Types and File Organisation — Study Notes
content:
Data Types and File Organisation

Cambridge International AS & A Level Computer Science 9618: section 13 (Data representation), examined in Paper 3.

User-Defined Types

A user-defined type is derived from existing types. An enumerated type lists named values in order: TYPE Months = (Jan, Feb, Mar ...). Internally each value is an integer index starting at 0. Pointer types store a memory address; the dereference operator returns the value at that address, which is how linked structures reference their nodes. Set types store unordered collections of distinct values from an ordinal base type, supporting union, intersection and difference.

Records

A record groups related fields of different types under one identifier, for example a Student record with name : STRING and mark : INTEGER. Arrays of records are the standard structure for storing a table of items in memory.

File Organisation

  • Serial: records in insertion order; searching checks every record. Simple but slow.
  • Sequential: records kept in key order; binary search possible, but insertion needs rewriting.
  • Random (direct): a hashing function converts the key into a storage address, giving near-instant access. A poor hash causes collisions — two keys hashing to the same address — resolved by chaining or overflow areas.

Hashing

A common method is division hashing: Address = Key MOD TableSize. A good hash distributes keys evenly; load factor above roughly 70 percent degrades performance.

Exam tips: state the internal integer representation of enumerated values; define a collision before describing its resolution; compare the three file organisations in terms of search and insert cost.

File organisation and access

Serial files store records in the order they are written and suit sequential processing. Sequential files store records in key order, so a search can stop early. Random (direct) access files calculate a record's address from its key, using a hashing function, so any record can be reached quickly.

Exam tip: state the trade-off: sequential access is simple but slow for searching; direct access is fast but needs a hashing function and can produce collisions.

Worked example: a record definition

A record groups fields of different data types under one name. A record called Book might have Title (string), Pages (integer), Price (real) and InStock (Boolean). Each field is then referred to by the record name and the field name, for example Book.Pages. Records let a program keep related data together and pass it to a procedure as one item.

Worked example: hashing with linear probing

A hash table has 5 slots numbered 0 to 4, and the hash function is h(k) = k mod 5. Insert the keys 12, 27 and 8 in that order. The key 12 gives 12 mod 5 = 2, so it is stored in slot 2. The key 27 also gives 2, which is already occupied, so the next slot 3 is used. The key 8 gives 3, which is occupied, so it moves on to slot 4. A collision happens whenever two keys hash to the same slot, and the probing method determines where the second key is placed.

Comparing file access methods

  • Serial files store records one after another in the order they arrive, so finding one record means reading from the start.
  • Sequential files store records in key order, so a search can stop once it passes the place where the record should be.
  • Random (direct) files use a hash function to calculate the address of a record directly, which gives the fastest access for a single record.

Exam point: when asked to choose a file organisation, state the access pattern the question describes, such as frequent single-record look-ups or regular batch reads in order, and justify the choice from that pattern.

title: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Right-Angled Trigonometry
content:
Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Right-Angled Trigonometry

Right-angled triangles are the most useful triangles in mathematics: Pythagoras relates the three sides, and the sine, cosine and tangent ratios relate sides to angles. Between them they solve every distance and angle problem the IGCSE sets, from ladders against walls to angles of elevation and three-figure bearings. This note builds the topic from zero: Pythagoras with its converse and 3D use, the SOHCAHTOA ratios with the selection method, exact values derived rather than memorised, and the multi-step problems that combine Pythagoras with trigonometry.

Pythagoras' theorem

in a right-angled triangle: a² + b² = c²
where c is the hypotenuse (the side opposite the right angle)

The theorem is a statement about areas: the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides. The converse identifies right angles: if a² + b² = c² for the longest side c, the triangle is right-angled — the standard test for 3-4-5 and 5-12-13 triangles.

Worked example 1. A right-angled triangle has legs 6 cm and 8 cm. Find the hypotenuse.

c² = 6² + 8² = 36 + 64 = 100
c = 10 cm

Worked example 2 (finding a leg). The hypotenuse is 13 cm and one leg is 5 cm. Find the other leg.

a² = 13² - 5² = 169 - 25 = 144
a = 12 cm

Worked example 3 (converse). Is a triangle with sides 7, 24, 25 right-angled?

7² + 24² = 49 + 576 = 625 = 25²
yes - right-angled, with the right angle opposite the 25 side

Pythagoras in three dimensions

In a cuboid, the space diagonal uses Pythagoras twice: first across the base, then up the height.

space diagonal = √(l² + w² + h²)

Worked example. A cuboid is 3 cm by 4 cm by 12 cm. Find the length of the space diagonal.

d = √(9 + 16 + 144) = √(169) = 13 cm

The three ratios: SOHCAHTOA

sin(θ) = opposite/hypotenuse      (SOH)
cos(θ) = adjacent/hypotenuse      (CAH)
tan(θ) = opposite/adjacent       (TOA)

Label the sides relative to the angle in question: the hypotenuse is always opposite the right angle; the opposite is across from the angle; the adjacent is the remaining side touching the angle. The selection method: mark the known side and the wanted side, then ask which ratio contains both.

Worked example 1 (finding a side). In a right-angled triangle, the angle is 35° and the hypotenuse is 12 cm. Find the opposite side.

known: hypotenuse; want: opposite  →  sine
sin(35) = opposite/12
opposite = 12 sin(35) = 12 × 0.574 = 6.88 cm

Worked example 2 (finding a side with cosine). Angle 40°, hypotenuse 20 cm; find the adjacent side.

cos(40) = adjacent/20
adjacent = 20 cos(40) = 20 × 0.766 = 15.3 cm

Worked example 3 (finding an angle). Opposite 5 cm, adjacent 9 cm. Find the angle.

tan(θ) = 5/9 = 0.5556
θ = tan-1(0.5556) = 29.1 °

For angles, use the inverse functions (sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹, tan⁻¹) and check the calculator is in degree mode — a radian-mode calculator turns 90° into 1.57 and ruins the paper.

Exact trigonometric values

Three angles have exact values worth knowing, derived from two special triangles:

Anglesincostan
30°1/2√3/21/√3
45°1/√21/√21
60°√3/21/2√3

Derivation: a 45-45-90 triangle with legs 1 has hypotenuse √2 (Pythagoras), giving sin 45 = 1/√2. An equilateral triangle of side 2 split in half gives a 30-60-90 triangle with sides 1, √3, 2, giving all six values. Deriving them once beats memorising them badly.

Two sanity checks keep the table honest: sine increases from 0 to 1 as the angle grows from 0° to 90°, so sin 30 must be smaller than sin 60; and cosine runs the other way, so cos 30 must be larger than cos 60. If an exact value breaks either ordering, the table has been misremembered.

Worked example. Find the exact value of sin 60° × tan 30°.

sin 60 = √(3)/2;  tan 30 = 1/√(3)
product = (√(3)/2) x (1/√(3)) = 1/2

Angles of elevation and depression

An angle of elevation is measured upward from the horizontal to an object; an angle of depression is measured downward. Both are measured from the observer's eye line, and the angle of depression from A to B equals the angle of elevation from B to A (alternate angles).

Worked example. From a point 40 m from the base of a tower, the angle of elevation to the top is 32°. Find the tower's height.

tan(32) = height/40
height = 40 tan(32) = 40 × 0.625 = 25.0 m

Worked example 2 (depression). A cliff is 60 m high; the angle of depression to a boat is 25°. Find the horizontal distance to the boat.

the angle at the boat is also 25 ° (alternate)
tan(25) = 60/d  →  d = 60/tan(25) = 60/0.466 = 128.7 m

Choosing the method: a decision routine

Most lost trigonometry marks come from choosing the wrong tool, not from arithmetic. The routine below takes ten seconds and removes the guesswork:

  1. Is there a right angle? If not, the question needs the sine or cosine rule (a different topic) — do not force SOHCAHTOA onto a triangle without a right angle.
  2. What do you know — two sides, or a side and an angle? Two sides with no angle means Pythagoras. A side and an angle means trigonometry.
  3. Which ratio? Mark the known side and the target relative to the given angle, then pick the ratio containing both: sin uses opposite and hypotenuse, cos uses adjacent and hypotenuse, tan uses opposite and adjacent.
  4. What is the unknown — a side or an angle? A side comes from multiplying; an angle needs the inverse function.

Worked example. A roof rafter is 4.5 m long and meets the horizontal at 38°. Find the vertical rise and the horizontal run.

rise: sin(38) = rise/4.5  →  rise = 4.5 sin(38) = 2.77 m
run:  cos(38) = run/4.5   →  run = 4.5 cos(38) = 3.55 m
check: 2.77² + 3.55² = 7.67 + 12.60 = 20.27 ~ 4.5²

Worked example 2 (finding the angle of a ladder). A 6 m ladder reaches 5.2 m up a wall. Find the angle it makes with the ground.

sin(θ) = 5.2/6 = 0.867  →  θ = 60.1 °

Multi-step problems: Pythagoras and trigonometry together

Many questions need both tools: Pythagoras to find a side in one triangle, trigonometry to use it in another. The method: draw and label every triangle, find the shared side first, then proceed.

Worked example. A ladder 5 m long leans against a wall, with its foot 2 m from the wall. Find the height reached and the angle the ladder makes with the ground.

height: h² = 5² - 2² = 25 - 4 = 21  →  h = 4.58 m
angle: cos(θ) = 2/5 = 0.4  →  θ = 66.4 °

Worked example 2 (two triangles). From a point P, the angle of elevation to the top of a building is 30°; from a point Q, 20 m closer, it is 45°. Find the height.

let h be the height and x the distance from Q to the base.
tan(45) = h/x  →  h = x
tan(30) = h/(x + 20)
h = (x + 20) tan(30) = (h + 20)(1/√(3))
h √(3) = h + 20  →  h(√(3) - 1) = 20
h = 20/(1.732 - 1) = 20/0.732 = 27.3 m

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Pythagoras) A right-angled triangle has legs 9 and 12. Find the hypotenuse. Answer: √(81 + 144) = √225 = 15.
  2. (Leg) Hypotenuse 17, one leg 8. Find the other. Answer: √(289 − 64) = 15.
  3. (Ratio) Angle 28°, adjacent 15 cm. Find the opposite side. Answer: tan 28 = o/15 → o = 15 × 0.532 = 7.98 cm.
  4. (Angle) Opposite 7, hypotenuse 10. Find the angle. Answer: sin θ = 0.7 → θ = 44.4°.
  5. (Exact) Find cos 30° exactly. Answer: √3/2.
  6. (Elevation) From 25 m away, the angle of elevation to a tree top is 40°. Find the height. Answer: 25 tan 40 = 25 × 0.839 = 21.0 m.
  7. (3D) A cuboid is 2 cm by 3 cm by 6 cm. Find its space diagonal. Answer: √(4 + 9 + 36) = √49 = 7 cm.
  8. (Combined) A ship sails 30 km east then 40 km north. Find its distance from the start and the bearing of its final position. Answer: distance = 50 km; tan θ = 40/30 → θ = 53.1°, bearing 053°.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Calculator mode: check DEG, not RAD or GRAD, before any trigonometric calculation. A radian answer is usually obviously wrong (tiny or huge), but only if you check.
  • Wrong ratio: label the sides relative to the angle before choosing SOH, CAH or TOA; picking by habit is the commonest trigonometry error.
  • Hypotenuse identification: the hypotenuse is opposite the right angle, not necessarily the longest-looking side on the diagram.
  • Pythagoras with the hypotenuse as a leg: c² = a² + b² only when c is the hypotenuse; finding a leg requires subtraction.
  • Rounding early: keep full calculator accuracy until the final answer; round to 3 s.f. (or 1 d.p. for angles unless told otherwise).
  • Angle of depression drawn from the wrong line: it is measured from the horizontal, not from the cliff face; the alternate-angle equality fixes the geometry.
  • Exact values with decimals: "exact" means surds and fractions, not 0.866; leaving √3/2 is required.
  • Missing units and labels: state cm, m, km and degrees; name the side or angle found, especially in multi-step problems.

title: Integration II — Study Notes
content:
Integration II

Edexcel International A Level Mathematics — Pure Mathematics 4 (WMA14), sat at A2.

Standard Integrals

  • ∫ sin x dx = −cos x + c
  • ∫ cos x dx = sin x + c
  • ∫ e^x dx = e^x + c
  • ∫ 1/x dx = ln|x| + c
  • ∫ sec²x dx = tan x + c

With linear arguments: ∫ e^(3x) dx = e^(3x)/3 + c; ∫ cos 2x dx = sin 2x/2 + c.

Substitution

Reverse of the chain rule. For ∫ 2x e^(x²) dx, let u = x²: du = 2x dx, so the integral is ∫ e^u du = e^(x²) + c.

Integration by Parts

∫ u (dv/dx) dx = uv − ∫ v (du/dx) dx. Choose u to be the part that simplifies when differentiated (LIATE: logs, inverse trig, algebraic, trig, exponential).

Example: ∫ x e^x dx = x e^x − ∫ e^x dx = x e^x − e^x + c.

Partial Fractions

Break rational functions into pieces like ∫ 1/(x+1) dx = ln|x + 1| + c.

Example: ∫ 4x/(x² − 1) dx = ∫ [2/(x − 1) + 2/(x + 1)] dx = 2 ln|x − 1| + 2 ln|x + 1| + c.

Exam tips: definite integrals: substitute limits into the transformed variable directly; for by-parts integrals like ∫ ln x dx, take u = ln x, dv/dx = 1.

Exam method: exponential and reciprocal integrals

The integral of e^(kx) is (1/k) e^(kx) + c, and the integral of e^x is e^x + c. The integral of 1/(ax + b) is (1/a) ln|ax + b| + c. Dividing by the coefficient of x is the step most often missed, so check it by differentiating your answer.

For a definite integral, evaluate the antiderivative at the upper limit, subtract its value at the lower limit, and write the bracket with its limits, such as [e^(2x)/2] from 0 to 1.

When the integrand is a product, integration by parts gives ∫u dv = uv − ∫v du. Choose u to be the part that becomes simpler when differentiated, such as x in x eˣ.

Substitution changes the limits as well as the variable. Either change the limits to the new variable or substitute back before using the original limits; do not mix the two.

Exam cue: Give the answer as an exact value, such as (e² − 1)/2, unless the question asks for a decimal.

Worked example: integration by parts

Find the integral of x e^x with respect to x. Let u = x and dv/dx = e^x, so du/dx = 1 and v = e^x. Then the integral equals x e^x minus the integral of e^x, which is x e^x − e^x + c = (x − 1) e^x + c. Differentiate the answer to check that it returns the integrand.

Definite integrals and area

For a region above the x-axis, the definite integral between the limits gives its area. If part of the curve lies below the axis, that part contributes a negative value to the integral, so the total area is the sum of the absolute values of each part. Sketch the curve first. Integrating across a point where the curve crosses the axis gives the signed net value, not the area.

Checking your answer

  • After integrating, differentiate the answer and confirm that it reproduces the original function.
  • Include the constant of integration on indefinite integrals, and never write it on a definite integral.
  • When a substitution changes the variable, change the limits too, or convert back to x before substituting the original limits.

The integration topic of the Cambridge AS and A Level Mathematics 9709 syllabus expects these methods to be applied to standard forms and to exam-style problems, with the method stated clearly at each step.

title: Algorithms & Programming — Study Notes
content:
Algorithms & Programming

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): pseudocode, flowcharts, standard algorithms (linear/bubble), trace tables, validation & verification.

1. Pseudocode

OUTPUT "Enter n"
INPUT n
IF n MOD 2 = 0 THEN
  OUTPUT "even"
ELSE
  OUTPUT "odd"
ENDIF

FOR i ← 1 TO 10
  total ← total + i
NEXT i

WHILE total < 100
  total ← total + n
ENDWHILE

FUNCTION square(x : INTEGER) RETURNS INTEGER
  RETURN x * x
ENDFUNCTION

Assignment ←, comparison =, MOD/DIV for remainders/quotients.

2. Flowchart symbols

Terminator (oval), process (rectangle), decision (diamond), input/output (parallelogram), flow lines with arrows.

3. Standard algorithms

  • Linear search: check each item until found/end — works unsorted.
  • Bubble sort: repeated adjacent swaps; largest bubbles to the end each pass; n−1 passes max; early exit when no swaps.
  • Counting/totaling patterns; max/min with a running best value.

4. Trace tables

One column per variable; log every assignment in order; watch loop counters and reassignments.

x ← 1; total ← 0
WHILE x <= 4
  total ← total + x * 2
  x ← x + 1
ENDWHILE  // total = 20

5. Validation vs verification

  • Validation: automatic checks on data — range (exam mark 0–100), length (password ≥ 8), type, format (postcode pattern), presence (field not empty), check digit (barcode).
  • Verification: data matches the source — double entry, visual/proof reading.

6. Testing

Normal (typical), abnormal (rejects invalid), boundary (extremes just inside/outside). Test data tables list input → expected output.

Exam tips: write pseudocode with ENDIF/NEXT/ENDWHILE terminators; in trace tables record the condition result too; boundary choices need "just above/below/at" values.

Algorithm design in practice

A good algorithm is correct, efficient and easy to follow. Designers begin by breaking the problem into smaller parts, a method called decomposition. Each part is then written as a step, and the steps are tested with sample data, including data at the limits of the input range.

Pseudocode is a way of writing an algorithm in plain structured English before it is coded in a specific language. It makes the logic clear, so it can be checked and changed without worrying about syntax. Flowcharts show the same logic with symbols for input, process, decision and output.

Exam tip: trace the algorithm step by step with a table of values to show that it produces the expected output.

Worked example: tracing a linear search

Take the list 14, 7, 22, 9, 31 and search for 22. Start at index 0 and compare: 14 is not 22, so move on. Index 1 holds 7, not a match. Index 2 holds 22, which matches, so the algorithm returns index 2 and stops. If the target were 40, every element would be compared and the algorithm would report that the value is absent after checking all five. A trace table with columns for index, value compared and result makes this easy to show in an exam answer.

Common mistakes in algorithm questions

  • Stopping a loop one element too early or too late. Check the start value, the end condition and whether the upper bound is inclusive.
  • Confusing a counter with the value being tested. Trace both variables separately.
  • Writing pseudocode without a clear output. Always state what the algorithm returns or prints.

title: IGCSE Chemistry (OxfordAQA): Atomic Structure and the Periodic Table
content:
Atomic Structure and the Periodic Table

Everything in chemistry comes back to this topic. The particle model explains why ice melts and why perfume crosses a room; the model of the atom explains why sodium loses an electron and chlorine gains one; and the periodic table turns those two ideas into predictions you can make for an element you have never seen.
