In the OxfordAQA 9202 papers this material is not a single question — it is the language the rest of the paper is written in, so a shaky answer here shows up in bonding, electrolysis, quantitative chemistry and organic chemistry too. This note covers specification statements 3.1.1, 3.1.2 and 3.1.3, works through the calculations the examiner actually sets, and ends with exam-style questions with full working.

1. The three states of matter

Matter is classified into three states by how its particles are arranged and how freely they move. The particles themselves do not change when a substance changes state — only their arrangement and their energy do. That is why melting ice is a physical change and not a chemical one: H₂O is still H₂O.

PropertySolidLiquidGas
ArrangementRegular lattice, particles touchingIrregular, particles still touchingFar apart, random
MovementVibrate about fixed positionsSlide past one anotherMove quickly in straight lines
ShapeFixedTakes the shape of the containerFills the container
VolumeFixedFixed (almost)Fills the container
CompressibilityAlmost noneAlmost noneEasily compressed

The state a substance is in at room temperature depends on the balance between the forces holding its particles together and the kinetic energy they have. Strong forces and low energy give a solid; weak forces and high energy give a gas. Heating raises the average kinetic energy of the particles, so it is always the route from solid to liquid to gas.

2. Changing state, and the energy it costs

Each change of state has its own name, and the examiner expects the exact word rather than "it turns into":

  • melting — solid to liquid; freezing — liquid to solid
  • boiling or evaporating — liquid to gas; condensing — gas to liquid
  • subliming — solid straight to gas (dry ice and iodine both do this); depositing — gas straight to solid

During a change of state the temperature does not rise even though energy is being supplied. The energy is being used to overcome the forces between particles rather than to speed them up. On a heating curve this appears as a flat section: the first flat section is melting, the second is boiling, and the boiling one is longer because vaporisation needs more energy than melting.

The energy needed to change the state of a mass without changing its temperature is given by the specific latent heat: E = m L → Key: E = energy (J); m = mass (kg); L = specific latent heat (J/kg). For boiling the value used is the specific latent heat of vaporisation, and for melting the specific latent heat of fusion.

3. Diffusion and the evidence for particles

Diffusion is the spreading of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration because of their random motion. It is the simplest evidence that particles exist and that they move:

  • bromine vapour in air — the brown colour spreads through the gas jar without stirring
  • ammonia and hydrogen chloride at opposite ends of a tube — a white ring of ammonium chloride forms nearer the hydrogen chloride end, because ammonia particles are lighter and travel faster
  • potassium manganate(VII) in water — the purple colour spreads slowly through the liquid

Diffusion is faster at a higher temperature, because the particles have more kinetic energy, and faster for a lighter particle at the same temperature. In a liquid it is much slower than in a gas, because the particles are close together and collide constantly. The kinetic energy of a particle is Eₖ = ½ m v² → Key: Eₖ = kinetic energy (J); m = mass (kg); v = speed (m/s). Two particles at the same temperature have the same average kinetic energy, so the lighter one must have the greater speed — which is exactly why the ammonia particles reach the middle of the tube first.

4. A simple model of the atom

An atom is the smallest part of an element that can exist. An element contains only one kind of atom; a compound contains atoms of two or more elements chemically combined in fixed proportions; a mixture contains substances that are not chemically combined. The atom itself is built from three subatomic particles.

ParticleRelative massRelative chargeWhere it is
Proton1+1Nucleus
Neutron10Nucleus
Electron1/1836 (negligible)−1Shells around the nucleus

Two numbers describe any atom. The atomic number (Z) is the number of protons, and it is what makes the element what it is — every carbon atom has six protons and no other element does. The mass number (A) is the number of protons plus the number of neutrons, because the electron's mass is negligible. In an ion the protons never change; only the electrons do.

neutrons = A − Z → Key: neutrons = number of neutrons in the nucleus; A = mass number (protons + neutrons); Z = atomic number (protons). For a neutral atom electrons = Z; for an ion of charge q, electrons = Z − q, where q is the charge as a number with its sign.

Electrons occupy shells, filled from the inside out. The first shell holds 2, the second 8, the third 8, and the fourth fills after the third has eight (potassium and calcium are the two you meet at this level). The configuration of an element is written as a list of shell occupancies, for example sodium is 2,8,1 and calcium is 2,8,8,2. The number of electrons in the outer shell is the same as the group number for the main-group elements, and the number of shells is the same as the period number.

5. Isotopes and relative atomic mass

Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. Carbon-12 and carbon-14 both have six protons, but carbon-14 has eight neutrons instead of six. Isotopes have identical chemical properties, because chemistry is decided by the electrons, and slightly different physical properties, because mass affects how fast particles move and diffuse.

Because a sample of an element usually contains a mixture of isotopes, the mass quoted in the periodic table is a weighted mean called the relative atomic mass: Aᵣ = (mass₁ × abundance₁ + mass₂ × abundance₂ + …) ÷ 100 → Key: Aᵣ = relative atomic mass (no units); mass = mass number of each isotope; abundance = percentage of that isotope in the sample. That is why chlorine's relative atomic mass is 35.5 and not a whole number.

6. Ions, and why atoms form them

Atoms react to reach the stable electron arrangement of a noble gas. Metals lose electrons and become positively charged ions; non-metals gain electrons and become negatively charged ions. Sodium (2,8,1) loses its outer electron to become Na⁺ with the arrangement 2,8; chlorine (2,8,7) gains one to become Cl⁻ with 2,8,8; magnesium (2,8,2) loses two to become Mg²⁺; oxygen (2,6) gains two to become O²⁻.

The charge on an ion tells you the ratio in which ions combine, because the total charge in a compound must be zero: Na⁺ with Cl⁻ gives NaCl; Mg²⁺ with O²⁻ gives MgO; Al³⁺ with O²⁻ needs two aluminium ions and three oxide ions, giving Al₂O₃.

7. The Periodic Table

Mendeleev arranged the elements in order of atomic weight but left gaps for elements that had not been discovered, and predicted their properties from their neighbours — and the predictions turned out to be right, which is why his table became the basis of the modern one. The modern table arranges elements in order of atomic number, which removes the few places where Mendeleev had to break his own weight order.

A group is a vertical column and contains elements with the same number of outer electrons, so they react in similar ways. A period is a horizontal row, and going across a period the atoms gain a proton and an electron and the elements change from metals to non-metals.

  • Group 1, the alkali metals (lithium, sodium, potassium): one outer electron, so they are very reactive; reactivity increases down the group because the outer electron is further from the nucleus and lost more easily; they are soft, low density, and react with water to give a hydroxide and hydrogen: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂
  • Group 7, the halogens (fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine): seven outer electrons, so they gain one; reactivity decreases down the group; a more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive one from its salt: Cl₂ + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br₂
  • Group 0, the noble gases (helium, neon, argon): full outer shells, so they are unreactive; used where a non-reactive atmosphere is needed, such as argon in a filament lamp
  • Transition metals (the block between groups 2 and 3): hard, dense, high melting points, coloured compounds, variable oxidation states and useful catalysts — iron in the Haber process is the example the paper uses

The table is a prediction machine: an element's group tells you its outer electrons and therefore its ion, and its position tells you whether it is a metal or a non-metal. That is how the properties of an unfamiliar element are answered without memorising it.

8. Worked examples

Worked example 1 — counting the particles in an ion. Give the number of protons, neutrons and electrons in ²⁴Mg²⁺. The mass number is 24 and the atomic number of magnesium is 12. Protons = Z = 12; neutrons = A − Z = 24 − 12 = 12; electrons = Z − charge = 12 − 2 = 10. The ion has 10 electrons and the arrangement 2,8, the same as neon.

Worked example 2 — relative atomic mass from abundances. A sample of chlorine contains 75% ³⁵Cl and 25% ³⁷Cl. Aᵣ = (35 × 75 + 37 × 25) ÷ 100 = (2625 + 925) ÷ 100 = 3550 ÷ 100 = 35.5. The answer is not rounded to a whole number, because a relative atomic mass is a weighted mean and chlorine really is a mixture.

Worked example 3 — electron configuration. Calcium has atomic number 20, so it has 20 electrons: 2 in the first shell, 8 in the second, 8 in the third, and the remaining 2 in the fourth, giving 2,8,8,2. The Ca²⁺ ion has lost the two outer electrons, so its configuration is 2,8,8 and it is isoelectronic with argon.

Worked example 4 — energy to boil a liquid. How much energy is needed to boil 0.50 kg of water if its specific latent heat of vaporisation is 2.3 × 10⁶ J/kg? Using E = m L: E = 0.50 × 2.3 × 10⁶ = 1.15 × 10⁶ J. Show the substitution — the mark scheme pays for the numbers being put into the relation, not for the final value alone.

9. Exam-style questions

  1. An atom of an element has 17 protons and 18 neutrons. State its mass number, its number of electrons, and the charge on the ion it forms. Answer: mass number = protons + neutrons = 17 + 18 = 35; electrons = Z = 17; the atom has seven outer electrons, so it gains one and forms a 1− ion.
  2. Explain why the melting point of sodium is lower than the melting point of magnesium. Answer: both are metals, but magnesium contributes two delocalised electrons per atom and has a smaller ion, so the electrostatic attraction between the ions and the delocalised electrons is stronger, so more energy is needed to break the lattice.
  3. Bromine exists as ⁷⁹Br and ⁸¹Br in a 1:1 ratio. Calculate its relative atomic mass. Answer: Aᵣ = (mass₁ × abundance₁ + mass₂ × abundance₂) ÷ 100 = (79 × 50 + 81 × 50) ÷ 100 = (3950 + 4050) ÷ 100 = 8000 ÷ 100 = 80.0.
  4. Describe what happens to the particles of a solid as it is heated to its melting point and then melted. Answer: the particles vibrate more vigorously as the temperature rises, until the vibrations are strong enough to overcome the forces holding them in the lattice; at the melting point the temperature stays constant while the energy supplied breaks those forces, and the particles can then slide over one another.
  5. Chlorine water is added to potassium bromide solution. State what is observed and write the equation. Answer: the solution turns orange-brown because bromine is displaced; Cl₂ + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br₂; because chlorine is above bromine in group 7, it is the more reactive halogen and takes the bromide ion's electron.
  6. Explain why argon is used as the atmosphere inside a filament lamp. Answer: argon has a full outer shell so it is unreactive, and it will not react with the hot filament; it also stops the filament oxidising, which would shorten its life.

10. Common mistakes

  • Writing "the particles get bigger" when a substance is heated. They do not — they move faster.
  • Giving the number of electrons in an ion as the atomic number. In a positive ion the electron count is lower than Z.
  • Confusing mass number with relative atomic mass: the first belongs to one atom, the second is a weighted mean for the element.
  • Saying reactivity increases down group 7. It decreases; the halogen nearer the top of the group displaces the one below.
  • Explaining a flat section on a heating curve as "the substance is not being heated". Energy is still being supplied; it is being used to change state.
  • Giving a relative atomic mass with units. Aᵣ has no units, because it is a comparison with carbon-12.

11. Exam technique for this topic

  • When asked to explain a trend, name the force and say what happens to it: "the attraction between the ions and the delocalised electrons is stronger, so more energy is needed".
  • For "describe the arrangement and movement", answer both parts — examiners award a mark for arrangement and a separate one for movement.
  • In a calculation question, write the relation, then the substitution, then the result with its unit. A bare answer can score zero even when the number is right.
  • For an unfamiliar element, use its group number for outer electrons and its period for shells instead of trying to recall it.
  • If a question says "explain", a statement of fact is not enough: link the observation to the particle-level reason.

title: Magnetism & Electromagnetism
content:
Magnetism & Electromagnetism

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2023–2025): magnets & fields; magnetic effect of a current; force on a current-carrying conductor; motor effect; electromagnetic induction (Extended); transformers (Extended).

1. Magnets and fields

Iron/steel/cobalt/nickel; like poles repel. Field lines exit N, enter S; compass plotting; plotting compass aligns with field. Induced magnetism: iron (temporary) vs steel (permanent).

2. Electromagnets

Solenoid field like a bar magnet; strength ↑ with current, turns, iron core. Uses: relays, scrapyard crane, electric bell, speaker. Hard/soft magnetic materials choose permanent vs core use.

3. Force on a current-carrying conductor

F = BIL, direction by Fleming's left hand (fIeld, current, force). Reversing current or field reverses force. D.C. motor: coil, commutator reverses current each half-turn for continuous rotation; speed/torque ↑ with current, field strength, turns/area.

4. Electromagnetic induction (Extended)

Induced e.m.f. when a conductor cuts field lines or flux changes. Fleming's right hand (generator). Factors: speed, field strength, turns. A.C. generator: slip rings; dynamo effect; Lenz's law opposes change (direction of induced current).

5. Transformers (Extended)

Vp/Vs = Np/Ns; Pin ≈ Pout (100% assumed): IpVp = IsVs. Step-up raises V, lowers I → lower I²R transmission losses; a.c. required (changing flux).

title: Exam technique: Nuclear Physics (A2)
content:
### What earns the marks
For energy, mass defect times c squared with units earns both marks. For decay, ln2 over half-life quoted earns the method mark; activity as lambda N earns the second. For radii, the cube-root rule applied to ratios earns the mark.
### Traps
Error: half-life used as the decay constant. Correction: divide ln2 by it. Error: fission named for the Sun. Correction: fusion powers stars. Error: radius scaled linearly with A. Correction: cube root of nucleon number.

title: Edexcel IAL Computer Science: Abstract Data Types and Complexity
content:
Edexcel IAL Computer Science: Abstract Data Types and Complexity

Pearson Edexcel International Advanced Level in Computer Science, Unit 3 Advanced Computer Science: abstract data types — stacks, queues, linked lists, trees and hash tables — and the algorithmic complexity that decides which one to choose. An abstract data type (ADT) defines behaviour, not implementation: what operations exist and what they guarantee, leaving storage open. That separation is the whole idea — "a queue is FIFO" says nothing about arrays or linked lists — and this note traces every structure operation step by step on drawn memory diagrams.

Complexity: measuring before choosing

Big-O notation describes how an algorithm's time (or space) grows with input size n, ignoring constants and lower-order terms — how it scales, not how fast it is on one machine. Common classes: O(1) constant (array index), O(log n) logarithmic (binary search), O(n) linear (linear search), O(n log n) (merge sort), O(n²) quadratic (bubble sort), O(2ⁿ) exponential (naive recursive fib). Best/average/worst case may differ; the worst case is quoted unless stated.

Deriving complexity from code, step by step:

  for i in range(n):          # n iterations
      print(i)                # O(1) work
  -> O(n)

  for i in range(n):          # n iterations
      for j in range(n):      # n iterations EACH
          print(i, j)         # O(1) work
  -> n x n = O(n^2)

  i = 1
  while i < n:                # doubles each pass
      i = i * 2
  -> passes: 1, 2, 4, 8, ... 2^k < n  => k = log2(n)  -> O(log n)

Doubling-and-halving loops are logarithmic because the value spans powers of
two; counting down by one is linear. Reading the update rule is the skill.
StructureAccessInsertDeleteTypical use
ArrayO(1) by indexO(n) shiftO(n) shiftFixed collections, heavy indexing
Linked listO(n) sequentialO(1) at known nodeO(1) at known nodeFrequent inserts/deletes, unknown size
Stack (LIFO)O(1) top onlyO(1) pushO(1) popUndo, call stack, expression parsing
Queue (FIFO)O(1) front onlyO(1) enqueueO(1) dequeuePrint jobs, scheduling, BFS
BSTO(log n) balancedO(log n)O(log n)Sorted data with dynamic updates
Hash tableO(1) averageO(1) averageO(1) averageKey-value lookup, no ordering

Stacks: LIFO

A stack is last-in, first-out: push adds to the top, pop removes from the top, peek reads it. It models nesting: function calls (the call stack), undo history, expression evaluation, browser back buttons, and recursion (below). Implementations: array with a top index, or linked list with pushes/pops at the head — both O(1) for push/pop.

Trace: evaluate the postfix expression 3 4 + 2 * 7 -   [ (3+4)*2 - 7 ]

Read left to right; numbers push; operators pop two, compute, push.

  token 3:  push 3                      stack [3]
  token 4:  push 4                      stack [3, 4]
  token +:  pop 4, pop 3 -> 3+4 = 7
            push 7                      stack [7]
  token 2:  push 2                      stack [7, 2]
  token *:  pop 2, pop 7 -> 7*2 = 14
            push 14                     stack [14]
  token 7:  push 7                      stack [14, 7]
  token -:  pop 7, pop 14 -> 14-7 = 7
            push 7                      stack [7]

Result: 7. Order matters: the SECOND pop is the left operand - getting that
backwards is the classic stack error (14-7 vs 7-14).

Bracket matching, same mechanism: push every opening bracket; on a closing
bracket, pop and check the pair matches; at the end the stack must be empty.

Queues: FIFO

A queue is first-in, first-out: enqueue at the rear, dequeue from the front. It models waiting lines: print jobs, keyboard buffers, breadth-first search, task scheduling. Variants: circular queue (fixed array with front/rear wrapping — avoids shifting), priority queue (dequeue serves the highest priority first), deque (insert/remove at both ends).

Trace: queue of print jobs with a circular array of size 4.

  enqueue "A"        [A, -, -, -]   front=0 rear=1
  enqueue "B"        [A, B, -, -]   front=0 rear=2
  dequeue -> "A"     [-, B, -, -]   front=1 rear=2
  enqueue "C"        [-, B, C, -]   front=1 rear=3
  enqueue "D"        [-, B, C, D]   front=1 rear=0 (wraps around)
  dequeue -> "B"     [-, -, C, D]   front=2 rear=0

Full or empty? With front = rear after a dequeue the queue is empty; after an
enqueue it is full - so implementations track a count or leave one slot spare
to disambiguate. That disambiguation is exactly the exam's hard question.

Linked lists

A linked list stores elements in nodes: data plus a pointer (reference) to the next node; the list holds a head pointer. Insertion and deletion are O(1) once the node is located — re-point two pointers, no shifting — versus the array's O(n); but access is O(n) sequential (no indexing), and each node costs extra memory for its pointer. Variants: doubly linked (pointers both ways — O(1) deletion from a known node), circular (last node points back to head).

Insert 7 between nodes holding 5 and 9, step by step:

  before:  head -> [5 | *] -> [9 | *] -> [3 | /]

  1. new node: [7 | *]  (its next currently unset)
  2. new.next <- node9          -> [7 | *] -> [9 | *] -> ...
  3. node5.next <- new          -> [5 | *] -> [7 | *] -> [9 | *] -> [3 | /]

  after:   head -> [5] -> [7] -> [9] -> [3] -> None

Order of steps is load-bearing: if step 3 ran first, the link to node 9 would
be lost - the list could not reach 9 or 3 at all. Deleting node 9:
  node7.next <- node9.next (= node3). The unlinked node is garbage collected.

Trees

A tree is a hierarchical node structure: one root, each node having zero or more children; leaves have none; the depth/level of a node is its distance from the root; a binary tree has at most two children per node. A binary search tree (BST) keeps every left subtree's values below the node's and every right subtree's above, giving O(log n) search/insert on a balanced tree (degenerating to O(n) if built badly — the balancing motivation behind AVL/red-black trees).

Insert 8, 3, 10, 1, 6, 14, 4, 7 into a BST, one at a time:

  8 is root. 3 < 8 -> left. 10 > 8 -> right. 1 < 8 -> left; 1 < 3 -> left.
  6 < 8 -> left; 6 > 3 -> right. 14 > 8 -> right; 14 > 10 -> right.
  4 < 8 -> left; 4 > 3 -> right; 4 < 6 -> left.

              8
           /               3       10
         /                1   6       14
           /
          4

In-order traversal (left, node, right) visits values in order:
  1, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10, 14 - the property that makes BSTs useful.

Search for 4: 4 < 8 go left -> 4 > 3 go right -> 4 < 6 go left -> found.
Three comparisons for seven nodes - the O(log n) promise.

Traversals to know by mechanism: pre-order (node, left, right — copies a tree), in-order (left, node, right — sorted order from a BST), post-order (left, right, node — deletes/frees a tree safely), breadth-first/level-order (level by level, via a queue).

Hash tables

A hash table maps keys to array slots through a hash function, giving O(1) average lookup. The design questions are the exam: a good hash function spreads keys evenly and computes quickly; collisions (two keys hashing to one slot) are inevitable and resolved by chaining (each slot holds a list) or open addressing (probe for the next free slot — linear probing, quadratic probing, double hashing).

Worked: hash(key) = key mod 7, inserting 15, 22, 8, 3, 29 with chaining.

  15 mod 7 = 1   slot 1: [15]
  22 mod 7 = 1   slot 1: [15, 22]      <- collision, chained
   8 mod 7 = 1   slot 1: [15, 22, 8]   <- third collision: a bad function
                                         for this data, or unlucky keys
   3 mod 7 = 3   slot 3: [3]
  29 mod 7 = 1   slot 1: [15, 22, 8, 29]

  Look-up of 29: hash -> slot 1 -> scan the chain 15, 22, 8, 29 -> found.

With open addressing (linear probing) instead:
  15 -> slot 1. 22 -> slot 1 taken, probe 2 -> [_, 15, 22, ...]. 8 -> probe
  1, 2 taken -> slot 3. 3 -> hash 3 taken -> probe 4. 29 -> probe 1,2,3,4
  taken -> slot 5. Look-up probes the same sequence.

Clustering (long chains / long probe runs) degrades toward O(n); a load
factor kept below ~0.75 and a rehash when exceeded is the standard remedy.
Deleting with open addressing needs tombstones so probe chains do not break.

Worked example: choosing a structure

Three requirements, three choices with reasons:

1. "Undo feature in an editor" - stack. Actions nest in reverse order of
   doing; undo must pop the most recent first (LIFO), and redo is a second
   stack.

2. "Printer jobs in arrival order" - queue. The job that arrived first must
   print first (FIFO); a stack would starve the oldest job forever.

3. "Fast lookup of student records by ID" - hash table. IDs are unique keys
   with no ordering requirement; hashing gives O(1) average retrieval versus
   O(n) search or O(log n) tree. If range queries ("all students with marks
   60-70") matter, a BST wins instead - the query pattern decides.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Quoting Big-O for the wrong case, or counting constants ("O(2n)"); simplify to the dominant term.
  • Subtraction and division order in stack evaluation: the second pop is the left operand.
  • Saying a linked list has random access; only arrays do — lists are sequential.
  • Forgetting the update-order trap when relinking list nodes (the lost-pointer bug).
  • Claiming BST operations are always O(log n); only when reasonably balanced — worst case O(n).
  • Confusing in-order (sorted) with pre-order (copy) traversal purposes.
  • Ignoring collision handling in hash answers; the function guarantees nothing without a resolution strategy.
  • Deleting from a linear-probing table by simply clearing the slot — probe chains must survive (tombstones).

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Unit 3, 4 marks). Explain what is meant by an abstract data type and why it is useful.

Answer: An ADT defines a data structure purely by its behaviour — the operations it supports (push/pop for a stack) and their guarantees — without specifying storage. This separates interface from implementation, so the structure can be reimplemented (array to linked list) without changing client code, and the same behaviour can be implemented differently per performance need.

Question 2 (Unit 3, 5 marks). Trace the stack while evaluating postfix 5 2 + 3 * and give the result.

Answer: Push 5 → [5]; push 2 → [5, 2]; '+': pop 2 and 5, push 7 → [7]; push 3 → [7, 3]; '*': pop 3 and 7, push 21 → [21]. Result 21 = (5 + 2) × 3.

Question 3 (Unit 3, 4 marks). Compare arrays and linked lists for implementing a dynamic list.

Answer: Arrays give O(1) indexed access and compact storage, but insertion/deletion shifts elements (O(n)) and resizing is disruptive. Linked lists insert and delete in O(1) given a node reference and grow dynamically, but access is sequential O(n) and each node pays pointer overhead. Heavy indexing → array; frequent inserts/deletes at known positions → linked list.

Question 4 (Unit 3, 5 marks). Explain how a hash table handles collisions and why the hash function matters.

Answer: When two keys hash to one slot, chaining stores a list per slot (lookup scans the short chain) or open addressing probes for the next free slot (linear, quadratic or double hashing). The hash function decides performance: an even spread keeps chains/probes short for O(1) average lookup; a poor function clusters keys, degenerating to O(n). The load factor is monitored and the table rehashed when it grows too full.

Question 5 (Unit 3, 4 marks). Give the in-order, pre-order and post-order traversals of a BST and state one use of each.

Answer: In-order (left, node, right) visits values sorted — used to output ordered data. Pre-order (node, left, right) preserves structure — used to copy or serialise a tree. Post-order (left, right, node) visits children first — used to delete or free a tree safely.

Question 6 (Unit 3, 3 marks). Determine the complexity of binary search and explain why.

Answer: O(log n). Each comparison halves the remaining search space (compare with the middle element, discard one half), so after k comparisons at most 2^k items could have been covered; n items need log₂(n) halvings — 1 000 000 items in at most 20 comparisons.

The structures above are only as good as the algorithms that run on them — the next note is those algorithms.

title: Hardware & Architecture — Study Notes
content:
Hardware & Architecture

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2023–2025): von Neumann model, FDE cycle, registers, buses, RAM/ROM, secondary storage, embedded systems.

1. Von Neumann model

CPU (ALU, control unit, registers) + memory + I/O on shared buses; instructions stored as data (stored program concept).

2. Registers

RegisterRole
PCaddress of next instruction
MARaddress being read/written
MDRdata/instruction in transit
ACCALU results accumulator

3. FDE cycle

Fetch: PC → MAR; memory → MDR → CIR; PC + 1. Decode: control unit interprets opcode. Execute: ALU/registers act. Interrupts can pause between cycles.

4. Buses and performance

Address bus (one-way, width ⇒ addressable memory), data bus (two-way, width ⇒ bits per transfer), control bus. Performance factors: clock speed, cache size, core count — explain the effect, not just the name.

5. RAM vs ROM

RAM: volatile, read/write, holds running programs + data. ROM: non-volatile, read-only, bootstrap/firmware. Embedded systems: dedicated microprocessors inside devices (washing machines, engines) — one function, low cost, hard to update.

6. Secondary storage

  • Magnetic (HDD): platters, read/write heads; high capacity, cheap per GB, moving parts (shock-sensitive).
  • Optical (CD/DVD/Blu-ray): laser pits/lands; cheap, portable, slow, small capacity.
  • Solid state (SSD/flash): NAND cells; fast, silent, robust, no moving parts, more expensive per GB, finite write cycles.

Choose by use case: video editing (SSD), archive (optical/magnetic), tablets (flash).

Exam tips: trace FDE with register values; compare storage on capacity, speed, cost, durability, portability; always tie a performance factor to its effect.

### Worked example Solve 3(x − 2) = 2x + 5. Expand to 3x − 6 = 2x + 5, then subtract 2x and add 6 to get x = 11. Check by substitution: 3(11 − 2) = 27 and 2(11) + 5 = 27. For rearranging, make t the subject of v = u + at by subtracting u and dividing by a, giving t = (v − u)/a. ### Check yourself Solve 5(y + 1) = 2y + 13 and verify your answer. Expand to 5y + 5 = 2y + 13, so 3y = 8 and y = 8/3. Check: 5(8/3 + 1) = 5 × 11/3 = 55/3, and 2 × 8/3 + 13 = 16/3 + 39/3 = 55/3.

title: Dynamics — Study Notes
content:
Dynamics

Momentum

  • Momentum p = mv. It is a vector, with unit kg m s⁻¹, and it has the same direction as the velocity.
  • Momentum and kinetic energy are different. Momentum is a vector and changes sign with direction. Kinetic energy is a scalar.

Newton's laws of motion

  • First law: a body stays at rest or keeps moving at constant velocity unless a resultant (net) force acts on it.
  • Second law: the resultant force equals the rate of change of momentum, F = ma for constant mass. The acceleration is in the direction of the resultant force.
  • Third law: when body A exerts a force on body B, B exerts an equal and opposite force on A. The two forces are the same type and act on different bodies, so they never cancel.

Weight and mass

Mass is the amount of matter (scalar, kg). Weight is the gravitational force on it, W = mg (vector, N). Mass is the same everywhere; weight changes with the value of g.

Impulse

Impulse = FΔt = Δp = m(v − u). The area under a force–time graph equals the impulse. A longer contact time for the same change in momentum means a smaller average force, which is why airbags and crumple zones work.

Conservation of linear momentum

For a system with no resultant external force, the total momentum before an event equals the total momentum after. In an elastic collision momentum and kinetic energy are both conserved. In an inelastic collision only momentum is conserved. In a collision where the bodies stick together, the kinetic energy lost is greatest.

Worked example: a 0.5 kg trolley moving at 4 m s⁻¹ hits a stationary 1.0 kg trolley and they stick together. Total momentum before = 0.5 × 4 = 2.0 kg m s⁻¹. Common velocity = 2.0 / 1.5 ≈ 1.3 m s⁻¹.

Exam tips: choose a positive direction and keep signs consistent in every momentum term. State that the system is isolated before applying conservation. For a recoil question, the two momenta are equal and opposite.

title: A Level Mathematics: Further Trigonometry
content:
A Level Mathematics: Further Trigonometry

A2 trigonometry covers the reciprocal functions, the compound and double-angle identities, the harmonic form R sin(θ + α) that turns a sum into a single wave, inverse functions with their domains, and equations with multiple or transformed angles. This note builds every identity from the compound-angle results, so the whole set is reconstructable rather than memorised.

The reciprocal functions

sec x = 1/cos x;  cosec x = 1/sin x;  cot x = 1/tan x = cos x/sin x

identities: 1 + tan² x = sec² x;  1 + cot² x = cosec² x

Worked example. Solve sec x = 2 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 360°.

cos x = 1/2  →  x = 60 or 300

Worked example 2 (identity). Prove that sec²x − tan²x = 1.

sec² - tan² = 1/cos² - sin²/cos² = (1 - sin²)/cos² = cos²/cos² = 1

Worked example 3 (solve). Solve 2 cosec²x = 5 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 360°.

cosec² x = 2.5  →  sin² x = 0.4  →  sin x = +/- 0.6325
x = 39.2, 140.8, 219.2, 320.8

Reciprocal functions blow up where the denominator vanishes: sec and tan at 90°, cosec and cot at 0°. Sketching is the safest way to see the asymptotes.

Compound-angle identities

sin(A + B) = sin A cos B + cos A sin B
sin(A - B) = sin A cos B - cos A sin B
cos(A + B) = cos A cos B - sin A sin B
cos(A - B) = cos A cos B + sin A sin B
tan(A + B) = (tan A + tan B)/(1 - tan A tan B)

Worked example 1 (exact value). Find sin 75° exactly.

sin(45 + 30) = sin45 cos30 + cos45 sin30
= (sqrt2/2)(sqrt3/2) + (sqrt2/2)(1/2) = (sqrt6 + sqrt2)/4

Worked example 2 (prove). Prove that sin(A + B) + sin(A − B) = 2 sin A cos B.

add the two expansions: the cos A sin B terms cancel
leaving 2 sin A cos B

Worked example 3 (solve). Solve sin(x + 30°) = cos x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 360°.

sin x cos30 + cos x sin30 = cos x
0.866 sin x + 0.5 cos x = cos x
0.866 sin x = 0.5 cos x  →  tan x = 0.577  →  x = 30 or 210

Double-angle identities

sin 2A = 2 sin A cos A
cos 2A = cos² A - sin² A = 2cos² A - 1 = 1 - 2 sin² A
tan 2A = 2 tan A/(1 - tan² A)

Worked example. Given sin A = 3/5 with A acute, find sin 2A and cos 2A.

cos A = 4/5
sin 2A = 2(3/5)(4/5) = 24/25
cos 2A = 1 - 2(9/25) = 7/25

Worked example 2 (solve). Solve cos 2x = sin x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 360°.

1 - 2 sin² x = sin x  →  2 sin² x + sin x - 1 = 0
(2 sin x - 1)(sin x + 1) = 0
sin x = 1/2  →  x = 30, 150;  sin x = -1  →  x = 270

The choice of cos 2A form matters: pick the one that leaves a single trigonometric function in the resulting equation.

The harmonic form

a sin x + b cos x = R sin(x + alpha)
R = √(a² + b²);  tan alpha = b/a

always expand back to check the sign of alpha

Worked example. Express 3 sin x + 4 cos x in the form R sin(x + α).

R = 5; tan alpha = 4/3  →  alpha = 53.13 °
3 sin x + 4 cos x = 5 sin(x + 53.13 °)
check: 5[sin x cos53.13 + cos x sin53.13] = 3 sin x + 4 cos x

Worked example 2 (maximum). Hence find the maximum value of 3 sin x + 4 cos x and the x at which it occurs.

maximum = 5, when sin(x + 53.13) = 1
x + 53.13 = 90  →  x = 36.87 °

Worked example 3 (solve). Solve 3 sin x + 4 cos x = 2 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 360°.

5 sin(x + 53.13) = 2  →  sin(x + 53.13) = 0.4
x + 53.13 = 23.58 or 156.42
x = -29.5 (reject, or add 360: 330.5) or 103.3

Adjusting the interval for the phase shift is compulsory: the angle x + α runs over a different range from x.

Inverse trigonometric functions

arcsin: domain [-1, 1], range [-90, 90] degrees
arccos: domain [-1, 1], range [0, 180]
arctan: all reals, range (-90, 90)

The restricted ranges are what make the inverses functions. That is why arcsin(sin 150°) = 30°, not 150°.

Worked example. Evaluate arcsin(sin 200°).

sin 200 = -0.342
arcsin(-0.342) = -20 °, which lies in the principal range

Worked example 2 (equation). Solve tan⁻¹(2x) = 45°.

2x = tan 45 = 1  →  x = 0.5

Worked example 3 (derivative link). Differentiate y = arcsin x.

dy/dx = 1/√(1 - x²), valid for |x| < 1

Equations with transformed angles

for sin(kx + c) = value over a range of x:
  1. find the range of the argument kx + c
  2. solve for the argument
  3. convert back to x and keep only values in the x-range

Worked example. Solve sin(2x − 30°) = 0.5 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 180°.

argument range: -30 <= 2x - 30 <= 330
2x - 30 = 30, 150, 390 (out of range)
2x = 60 or 180  →  x = 30 or 90

Worked example 2. Solve cos(3x) = −0.5 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 180°.

argument range 0 <= 3x <= 540
3x = 120, 240, 480  →  x = 40, 80, 160

Solving equations in a given range

The single most reliable routine in A2 trigonometry is a fixed order of operations, because the marks are lost in the bookkeeping, never in the trigonometry.

step 1  reduce to ONE trigonometric function (identity if needed)
step 2  solve for the function value, keeping every sign
step 3  find the principal solution
step 4  use symmetry to find all solutions in the argument's range
step 5  convert back to x, and discard anything outside the stated range

Worked example. Solve 2 sin²x + 3 cos x = 3 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 360°.

sin² = 1 - cos²  →  2(1 - cos² x) + 3 cos x = 3
2 - 2cos² x + 3 cos x - 3 = 0
2cos² x - 3 cos x + 1 = 0   →  (2cos x - 1)(cos x - 1) = 0
cos x = 1/2  →  x = 60, 300
cos x = 1    →  x = 0, 360
solutions: 0, 60, 300, 360 degrees

Worked example 2 (quadratic in tan). Solve 3 tan²x − tan x − 2 = 0 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 360°.

(3 tan x + 2)(tan x - 1) = 0
tan x = 1  →  x = 45, 225
tan x = -2/3  →  x = 180 - 33.7 = 146.3;  and 326.3
tangent repeats every 180 degrees, so each root gives exactly two solutions here

Note the period: sin and cos repeat every 360°, tan every 180°. Getting the period wrong either loses half the solutions or invents ones outside the range.

Proving identities

An identity is proved by transforming one side into the other, never by moving terms across the equals sign as if it were an equation. The safe strategy is to start on the side that looks worse and simplify towards the other.

allowed moves: rewrite sec/cosec/cot as sin and cos; apply Pythagoras;
               expand compound angles; use a double-angle form
not allowed:   multiplying both sides by something, unless every step is reversible
               and the result is still an identity

Worked example. Prove that (1 + sin x)/(cos x) = cos x/(1 − sin x).

start from the left; multiply numerator and denominator by (1 - sin x):
(1 + sin x)(1 - sin x) / [cos x (1 - sin x)]
= (1 - sin² x) / [cos x (1 - sin x)]
= cos² x / [cos x (1 - sin x)]
= cos x / (1 - sin x)

Worked example 2 (double angle). Prove that (sin 2x)/(1 + cos 2x) = tan x.

sin 2x = 2 sin x cos x;  1 + cos 2x = 1 + (2cos² x - 1) = 2cos² x
ratio = 2 sin x cos x / 2cos² x = sin x/cos x = tan x

The choice of cos 2A form is not taste: pick the version that cancels against the rest of the expression. Here 2cos²x − 1 was right because the denominator needed a cosine.

Modelling with the harmonic form

The R-formula is not only an algebraic trick; it is the reason oscillating physical quantities are written as a single wave. Tidal height, temperature, alternating current and the height of a point on a rotating wheel are all of the form a sin θ + b cos θ, and every question about their maximum, minimum or first occurrence is answered by the amplitude and phase.

h = 12 + 5 sin(30t) + 12 cos(30t)  (t in hours)
R = √(25 + 144) = 13;  tan alpha = 12/5  →  alpha = 67.38 degrees
h = 12 + 13 sin(30t + 67.38)
maximum depth = 12 + 13 = 25;  minimum = 12 - 13 = -1 (below the datum)

Worked example. For that model, find the first time after t = 0 at which the height is a maximum.

sin(30t + 67.38) = 1  →  30t + 67.38 = 90
30t = 22.62  →  t = 0.754 hours = 45.2 minutes

Worked example 2 (period and interpretation). State the period of the model and what it represents.

argument 30t has period 360 degrees in t:  360/30 = 12 hours
the tide repeats every 12 hours, twice a day

Worked example 3 (minimum as a phrase). Find the time of the first minimum.

sin(30t + 67.38) = -1  →  30t + 67.38 = 270
30t = 202.62  →  t = 6.75 hours

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Reciprocal) Solve cosec x = 2 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 360°. Answer: sin x = ½ → 30°, 150°.
  2. (Identity) Simplify (1 − cos²x)/sin x. Answer: sin x.
  3. (Compound) Find cos 15° exactly. Answer: (√6 + √2)/4.
  4. (Double) Given cos A = 5/13, find sin 2A. Answer: 2(12/13)(5/13) = 120/169.
  5. (Double solve) Solve sin 2x = cos x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 180°. Answer: cos x(2 sin x − 1) = 0 → x = 90°, 30°, 150°.
  6. (Harmonic) Express 5 sin x − 12 cos x as R sin(x − α). Answer: 13 sin(x − 67.4°).
  7. (Maximum) Max of 5 sin x − 12 cos x? Answer: 13.
  8. (Inverse) Solve arccos(2x) = 60°. Answer: 2x = ½ → x = ¼.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Losing solutions: quadratics in sin or cos give two values, each with its own solutions in the range.
  • Wrong cos 2A form: choose the version that leaves one function; otherwise the equation becomes unsolvable.
  • Harmonic sign: R sin(x − α) versus R sin(x + α) depends on the signs of a and b; expand to check.
  • Interval not adjusted: transformed angles need the argument's range computed before solving.
  • Inverse range ignored: arcsin returns only the principal value; other solutions come from the symmetries.
  • sec/cosec confused: sec = 1/cos, cosec = 1/sin — the reverse is a silent disaster.
  • Degrees and radians: the R-formula's α follows the mode; mixing them gives a phase error.
  • Identity proofs without a direction: start from the more complicated side and transform towards the simpler; do not work on both sides at once unless every step is reversible.

title: Algebra — Sequences and Functions — Study Notes
content:
Algebra — Sequences and Functions

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): nth term (linear & quadratic), special sequences, function notation, composites, inverses.

1. Linear sequences

nth term = a + (n − 1)d. 5, 8, 11, … → 3n + 2. Check n = 1, 2, 3.

2. Quadratic sequences

Second difference = 2a → an² + bn + c. 3, 8, 15, 24 … has second difference 2 → n² + bn + c; subtract n² → 2, 4, 6, 8 → 2n; so nth term = n² + 2n.

3. Special sequences

Even/odd, triangular (½n(n+1)), squares, cubes, Fibonacci-type (each term = sum of previous two), geometric (×r).

4. Function notation

f(x) = 2x − 5: f(3) = 1. Solve f(x) = 11 → x = 8.

5. Composite functions

fg(x) = f(g(x)) — g first. f(x) = 2x − 5, g(x) = x²: gf(2) = g(1) = 1; fg(3) = f(9) = 13.

6. Inverse functions

Swap x and y, rearrange. f(x) = 2x − 5 ⇒ f⁻¹(x) = (x + 5)/2. Domain of inverse = range of original. Verify: f⁻¹(f(x)) = x.

Exam tips: write the bracket order explicitly in composites; show the "swap and rearrange" line for inverses — answer-only scores little.

Finding the nth term of a linear sequence

For a sequence with a constant difference d, the nth term is dn + (a − d), where a is the first term. Check the rule by substituting n = 1, 2 and 3 before using it. Given a term value, set the nth term equal to it and solve for n to test whether it belongs to the sequence.

Functions as machines

A function takes an input and gives exactly one output. Composite functions are applied right to left: fg(x) means apply g first, then f. The inverse f⁻¹ reverses each step, found by writing y = f(x), swapping x and y, and rearranging for y.

Domain and range

The domain is the set of allowed inputs; the range is the set of outputs produced. Restrictions usually come from division by zero or from taking square roots of negative numbers. State both when asked to describe a function fully.

Worked examples: sequences

Linear. The sequence 5, 9, 13, 17 has a common difference of 4. The nth term is 4n + 1, since the nth term of a linear sequence is dn + (first term − d). Check the 10th term: 4 × 10 + 1 = 41.

Quadratic. For 2, 6, 12, 20, the first differences are 4, 6, 8 and the second difference is 2. The coefficient of n² is half the second difference, so it is 1. Subtract n² from each term: 1, 2, 3, 4, which is linear with nth term n. So the nth term is n² + n. Check n = 3: 9 + 3 = 12 ✓.

Function notation with composites

Let f(x) = 2x + 3 and g(x) = x − 1. Then fg(x) means f(g(x)) = f(x − 1) = 2(x − 1) + 3 = 2x + 1. Note that gf(x) = g(2x + 3) = 2x + 2, which is different. Composition is not commutative, and questions often ask for both to test whether you apply the inner function first.

Inverse functions

To find f⁻¹(x) for f(x) = 2x + 3: write y = 2x + 3, swap to x = 2y + 3 and solve, giving y = (x − 3)/2. So f⁻¹(x) = (x − 3)/2. Check by substituting: f(f⁻¹(x)) = 2(x − 3)/2 + 3 = x ✓. The graph of f⁻¹ is the reflection of f in the line y = x.

Domain and range

For f(x) = √(x − 2), the expression under the root must be non-negative, so the domain is x ≥ 2. The output of a square root is never negative, so the range is f(x) ≥ 0. For a rational function such as 1/(x − 4), the domain excludes x = 4, and the range excludes y = 0, since the value 0 is never reached.

Common errors

  • Taking the nth term of a quadratic sequence from the first term alone; the second difference must be used.
  • Reversing the order of composition: fg(x) and gf(x) are not the same.
  • Writing the domain as x > 2 when the question allows equality, or stating the range with an inequality in the wrong direction.
  • Forgetting to swap x and y before solving for the inverse.

title: Alkenes
content:
Alkenes

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH11, Topic 5. Alkenes contain a carbon–carbon double bond, which makes them far more reactive than alkanes. Their addition reactions are a central part of organic synthesis.

Structure and bonding

  • A C=C double bond consists of one σ bond and one π bond. The π bond is an electron cloud above and below the plane of the atoms, and it is the reactive part.
  • The carbons of a C=C bond are planar, with bond angles of about 120°.

Addition reactions

  • Hydrogen adds across the double bond in the presence of a nickel catalyst to form an alkane.
  • Halogens (for example bromine water) add across the double bond: a colour change from orange to colourless is the test for an alkene.
  • Steam adds across the double bond in the presence of phosphoric acid to form an alcohol.
  • Hydrogen halides add to give halogenoalkanes; with unsymmetrical alkenes the Markovnikov rule predicts the major product.

Polymerisation

  • Addition polymers form when many alkene monomers join together. Poly(ethene) and poly(chloroethene) are examples.
  • The repeat unit is drawn with the double bond opened and the bonds extended through brackets.

Isomerism

  • Restricted rotation about the C=C bond allows E/Z isomers when each carbon carries two different groups.

Exam tip: when drawing a polymer, show the repeat unit with the bonds extending outwards, and do not leave a dangling double bond.

title: A Level Mathematics: Permutations and Combinations
content:
A Level Mathematics: Permutations and Combinations

Counting is the part of probability that requires no formula to start with, only a decision: does the order matter? Every question in this topic is answered by that one question. If order matters the count is a permutation; if it does not the count is a combination. Everything else — repetitions, restrictions, arrangements around a circle — is a variation on the same counting principle, and this note sets out each variation with the reasoning behind it.

The multiplication principle

If a choice can be made in a ways and, independently, a second choice in b ways, the pair can be made in a × b ways. That is the whole foundation; the formulas are shortcuts for repeated applications of it.

arrangements of n distinct objects in a row: n! = n x (n-1) x ... x 2 × 1
0! = 1 by convention, so that formulas stay consistent
choosing r from n with order: nPr = n!/(n - r)!
choosing r from n without order: nCr = n!/(r!(n - r)!)

Worked example. A password is 4 distinct letters from the 26-letter alphabet. How many passwords are possible?

order matters, so 26P4 = 26 × 25 × 24 × 23 = 358,800

Worked example 2 (no order). How many ways can 4 students be chosen from 26?

order does not matter, so 26C4 = 14,950

Worked example 3 (a leading zero is not allowed). A code uses four distinct digits from 0 to 9 and cannot begin with zero. How many codes?

first digit: 9 choices (1 to 9)
remaining three: 9P3 = 9 × 8 × 7 = 504
total = 9 × 504 = 4536

Worked example 4 (the link). Explain why nPr = nCr × r!.

every unordered selection of r objects can be arranged in r! orders
so counting ordered selections = counting unordered ones then arranging them

Deciding whether order matters

The decision is not about the words "choose" or "arrange" in the question — those are hints, not rules. The safe test is to imagine two selections differing only by swapping two items: if that counts as a different outcome, order matters.

SituationOrder?Count
finishing order of a raceyesnPr
a committee of 3nonCr
a 4-digit PINyespermutation, with repetition allowed
a hand of cardsnonCr
seating 5 people in a rowyes5!

Worked example. A team of 11 is chosen from 16 players, and one of the 11 is captain. Count the possibilities.

choose the 11: 16C11 = 4368
choose the captain from them: 11 ways
total = 4368 × 11 = 48,048

The multiplication principle is doing the work here: two independent choices, multiplied.

Repetition and identical items

When some objects are identical, arranging them as if all were distinct overcounts by the number of ways the identical ones can be swapped. Dividing by those factorials corrects it.

arrangements of n items with groups of identical items:
n!/(a! b! c! ...) where a, b, c are the group sizes
with repetition allowed, choosing r from n: n^r

Worked example. How many distinct arrangements of the letters in BANANA?

6 letters: B once, A three times, N twice
6!/(1! 3! 2!) = 720/12 = 60

Worked example 2 (repetition allowed). A 3-digit code uses digits 0-9, repeats allowed. How many codes?

10 × 10 × 10 = 1000
if repeats were not allowed: 10 × 9 × 8 = 720

Worked example 3 (identical plus restriction). How many arrangements of the letters of LEVEL begin with L?

fix L at the front; remaining letters E, V, E, L
that is 4 letters with E twice: 4!/2! = 12
but the leading L is one of the two Ls, so there is only one choice for the front
answer 12

Restrictions: the "glue" method

When certain items must be together, treat the group as a single object, arrange the objects, then arrange within the group. When certain items must not be together, count the total and subtract the "together" case.

together: glue the group, arrange the objects, multiply by the internal arrangements
not together: total arrangements minus the together arrangements
specific positions: fix those items first, then arrange the rest

Worked example. Five books, two of which must stand together, are arranged on a shelf. How many orders?

glue the pair: now 4 objects, arranged in 4! = 24 ways
the pair interchange in 2! = 2 ways
total = 48

Worked example 2 (not together). The same five books with the pair not together.

total arrangements = 5! = 120
together = 48
not together = 120 - 48 = 72

Worked example 3 (fixed positions). Four men and three women sit in a row of seven. How many arrangements have all three women together?

glue the women into one block: now 5 objects (4 men + block), 5! = 120
internal arrangements of the women: 3! = 6
total = 720

Circular arrangements

Around a circle, rotations of the same arrangement are not distinguishable, so fixing one item removes the rotational symmetry and the count drops by a factor of n.

n distinct items around a circle: (n - 1)!
a necklace (where reflection also counts as the same): (n - 1)!/2

Worked example. In how many ways can 6 people sit around a round table?

(6 - 1)! = 5! = 120

Worked example 2 (with a fixed seat). How many ways if one particular person must sit in a specified chair?

fix that person, arrange the other 5 around: 5! = 120
the specified chair removes the rotational freedom entirely, so the answer is unchanged here

Worked example 3 (two people together at a round table). Six people, two of whom must sit together.

glue the pair: 5 objects around a circle = 4! = 24
internal order of the pair: 2
total = 48

Combinations with conditions

Committee questions combine cases: choose so many from one group and so many from another, then add the disjoint alternatives. The discipline is to make the cases genuinely disjoint, or the same selection gets counted twice.

choose a from group A and b from group B: C(a-group, a) x C(b-group, b)
several allowed compositions: add the separate cases
at least one: total minus none

Worked example. From 6 men and 5 women, how many committees of 4 contain exactly 2 women?

choose 2 women from 5: 10
choose 2 men from 6: 15
total = 150

Worked example 2 (at least one). How many committees of 4 contain at least one woman?

total committees: 11C4 = 330
none: 6C4 = 15
at least one = 330 - 15 = 315

Worked example 3 (cases added). How many committees of 3 contain more women than men?

3 women: 5C3 = 10
2 women and 1 man: 5C2 × 6C1 = 10 × 6 = 60
total = 70

Counting inside probability

Combinations are usually the denominator of a probability question: count the favourable selections, count all selections, divide. Doing the counting separately from the probability keeps both parts clean and makes partial credit possible.

Worked example. A bag holds 5 red and 7 blue counters. Four are drawn at random. Find the probability of exactly 2 red.

total selections: 12C4 = 495
favourable: 5C2 × 7C2 = 10 × 21 = 210
probability = 210/495 = 0.4242

Worked example 2 (at least one). For the same bag, find the probability of at least one red.

complement: no red means all four blue
7C4 = 35
P(no red) = 35/495 = 0.0707
P(at least one red) = 1 - 0.0707 = 0.9293

Worked example 3 (order matters in the numerator). Three cards are drawn from a standard deck without replacement. Find the probability they are drawn in increasing order of value.

every set of three distinct cards has exactly one increasing order out of 3! orders
so the probability is 1/6, independent of the deck

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Factorial) Evaluate 7!. Answer: 7! = 7 × 6 × 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 5040.
  2. (Permutation) In how many orders can 5 runners finish? Answer: 5P5 = 5! = 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 120.
  3. (Combination) Evaluate 10C3. Answer: 10C3 = 10!/(3! × 7!) = (10 × 9 × 8)/(3 × 2 × 1) = 720/6 = 120.
  4. (Choice) From 8 books, how many ways to choose 3? Answer: 8C3 = 8!/(3! × 5!) = (8 × 7 × 6)/(3 × 2 × 1) = 336/6 = 56.
  5. (Arrangement) How many arrangements of the letters of STATISTICS? Answer: 10!/(3! × 3! × 2!) = 3 628 800/(6 × 6 × 2) = 3 628 800/72 = 50,400.
  6. (Glue) 6 people in a row with two together: Answer: glue the pair: 5! × 2! = 120 × 2 = 240.
  7. (Not together) Same 6, not together: Answer: total − together = 6! − 5! × 2! = 720 − 240 = 480.
  8. (Circle) 7 people around a table: Answer: (n − 1)! = 6! = 720.
  9. (Committee) 3 from 5 men and 4 women, exactly 2 men: Answer: 5C2 × 4C1 = 10 × 4 = 40.
  10. (At least) 4 from the same 9 with at least one woman: Answer: all − none = 9C4 − 5C4 = 126 − 5 = 121.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Using nPr where order does not matter: a committee is unordered; using permutations overcounts by r!.
  • Forgetting to divide by repeated factorials: identical letters need the divisor or the count is inflated.
  • Glue method without the internal factor: the block also has an internal arrangement, and dropping the 2! halves the answer.
  • Circular arrangements with n! instead of (n − 1)!: rotations are the same seating.
  • Adding what should be multiplied: independent stages multiply; alternative cases add.
  • Overlapping cases: cases must be disjoint, or selections are counted twice.
  • "At least one" counted directly: the complement is almost always faster and safer.
  • Restrictions applied after the count: fix the restricted positions first, then count what remains.

Choosing between nPr, nCr and a plain product

Most lost marks in this topic come from using the right formula for the wrong question. Before any calculation, decide whether you are selecting, arranging or doing both, and whether the answer depends on the order. The subsections below set out the decision in the order a careful candidate works through it.

Selecting without arranging: nCr

If you only need to choose a group and the order inside the group does not matter, use ⁿCᵣ = n! / (r!(n − r)!). Choosing a committee of 4 from 10 people gives ¹⁰C₄ = 210. The result counts groups, so two committees with the same members in a different order are the same committee.

Selecting and arranging: nPr

If the chosen items are then placed in distinct positions, the order matters and you use ⁿPᵣ = n! / (n − r)!. Choosing a chair, a vice-chair and a secretary from 10 people gives ¹⁰P₃ = 720. Each committee of 3 from the previous example can be arranged in 3! = 6 ways, so 720 = 120 × 6, which is a useful check.

A plain product for independent choices

When each decision is made separately and the number of options for one does not depend on the others, multiply. Three shirts and four trousers give 3 × 4 = 12 outfits. Do not reach for a combination formula here: nothing is being chosen from a single pool of identical kinds of object.

Checking the order question

Ask whether swapping two chosen items changes the outcome. A password changes if its letters are swapped, so it is an arrangement. A team does not change when two members swap places, so it is a selection. If the words in the question say “the first, second and third” or “positions”, the order matters.

Worked decision

Seven runners compete for gold, silver and bronze. The medals are different, so the order matters and the count is ⁷P₃ = 7 × 6 × 5 = 210. If the question asked for three runners to go through to a final with no ranking, the count would be ⁷C₃ = 35. The same seven people give 210 or 35 depending only on whether the medal order is asked for, so state which one you have chosen before you write the number.

Common error: dividing when you should not

Students often divide by a factorial out of habit. Divide only when items are truly identical or the outcome groups are truly unordered. Dividing ⁷P₃ by 3! to get the medal count gives 35 and throws away the difference between gold and silver, which the question asked you to keep.

Keeping items apart and placing them together

Restriction questions usually ask that certain people or letters are together, or that they are not. Two methods work, and the complement is often shorter. Choose the method from the wording before you start counting.

Together: treat the pair as one object

If two items must sit together, glue them into one block. Arrange the block with the others, then multiply by the number of internal orders of the block. Seven people in a row with two particular people side by side give 6! × 2! = 720 × 2 = 1440 arrangements. Omitting the 2! halves the answer.

Not together: subtract the together cases

For the same seven people with the two not allowed together, the total is 7! = 5040. Subtract the 1440 arrangements in which they are together, giving 5040 − 1440 = 3600. This is usually quicker than building the arrangements directly, because the gaps between people are hard to count without listing them.

Not together: place people in the gaps

An alternative for the same question is to arrange the other five people first, which gives 5! = 120 orders. There are six gaps, including the two ends, and the two special people must go into different gaps. Choose 2 of the 6 gaps in order, 6P2 = 30 ways, and this gives 120 × 30 = 3600. Both methods agree, and showing the second one earns the method marks even if the first has an error.

Letters that must not be adjacent

For the word HEART with the vowels E and A not next to each other, count the arrangements with the vowels together (4! × 2! = 48) and subtract from 5! = 120, giving 72. The same subtraction pattern applies to any pair that must be kept apart.

Position restrictions

If one person must stand at one end, fix that person first and arrange the rest. A person fixed at one end leaves 6 people for 6 places, giving 6! = 720. Fixing the restricted item before counting the free ones avoids double counting, which is the usual cause of an answer that is too large.

Interpreting “together” and “next to”

“Side by side” and “next to each other” mean adjacent in the order given. They do not mean the same chair or a shared seat. Read the wording carefully, because a question about two people sitting “with one seat between them” needs a different count altogether.

Equations and symbols

Every formula here is a shortcut for the multiplication principle, and each one carries a condition that decides whether it applies. The condition is the mark: "order matters" and "items are identical" change the count by a factorial.

n! = n x (n-1) x ... x 2 × 1 Key: n = the number of distinct objects (a count, no units); n! = the number of orders they can be arranged in (a count). The falling product stops at 1, and 0! = 1 by convention so the formulas stay consistent.

nPr = n!/(n - r)! Key: n = how many objects are available; r = how many are being chosen; nPr = the number of ordered selections (a count). Read it as "start at n and write down r factors": 26P4 = 26 × 25 × 24 × 23.

nCr = n!/(r!(n - r)!) Key: n = objects available; r = objects chosen; nCr = the number of unordered selections (a count). The extra r! in the denominator is exactly what removes the orderings — which is the whole difference between a permutation and a combination.

nPr = nCr × r! Key: nPr = ordered selections; nCr = unordered selections; r! = the ways to order each selection. The identity explains both formulas at once: count the sets, then arrange each one.

26P4 = 26 × 25 × 24 × 23 = 358,800 Key: 26 = letters available; 4 = letters chosen without replacement; 358,800 = ordered passwords (a count). The factors fall because each letter is used once — repetition allowed would give 26⁴ instead.

26C4 = 14,950 Key: 26 = students available; 4 = students chosen; 14,950 = unordered groups (a count). The same numbers as the password question, 24 times smaller, because a group of four has 4! orderings that all count as one group.

n!/(a! b! c! ...) Key: n = total items; a, b, c = the sizes of the groups of identical items. Dividing by the factorials of the repeats removes the arrangements that look identical — 6!/(1! 3! 2!) = 60 arrangements of BANANA, not 720.

6!/(1! 3! 2!) = 720/12 = 60 Key: 6 = letters in BANANA; 1! = the single B; 3! = the three As; 2! = the two Ns; 60 = distinct arrangements (a count). Every repeated letter needs its own factorial in the denominator, or the count is inflated.

n^r Key: n = choices available at each stage; r = number of stages; the result counts selections with repetition allowed (a count). It is the multiplication principle applied r times — three digits from 0 to 9 with repeats gives 10³ = 1000.

(n - 1)! Key: n = people or objects around a circle; the result counts distinct circular arrangements (a count), because rotating a seating does not create a new one. For a necklace, where a reflection is also the same, divide once more: (n - 1)!/2.

5! × 2! = 120 × 2 = 240 Key: 5! = the arrangements of four single items plus the glued pair as one object; 2! = the internal orders of the pair; 240 = total arrangements (a count). Gluing without the internal factor halves the answer, which is the classic lost mark in this topic.

title: Molecules, Transport and Health Revision Notes
content:
Molecules, Transport and Health AS Level Biology

This revision note belongs to the Edexcel International AS Level Biology specification, covering biological molecules, transport mechanisms, gas exchange, and cardiovascular health.

Water and Its Biological Importance

Water is essential for life due to its chemical properties. It acts as an important solvent in transport because of its dipole nature, where the oxygen atom has a partial negative charge and hydrogen atoms have partial positive charges. This allows polar molecules and ionic substances to dissolve and be transported easily in blood and plant sap.

  • Dipole nature: polar molecule with uneven charge distribution.
  • Solvent properties: allows chemical reactions and transport of dissolved ions and molecules.

Carbohydrates and Sugars

Carbohydrates exist as monosaccharides, disaccharides, and polysaccharides. Monosaccharides include glucose, fructose, and galactose. They join via condensation reactions, forming glycosidic bonds and releasing water molecules, creating disaccharides such as maltose (glucose + glucose), sucrose (glucose + fructose), and lactose (glucose + galactose), and polysaccharides such as glycogen, amylose, and amylopectin. Glycosidic bonds can be split through hydrolysis reactions using water molecules. Amylose has a helical structure formed by 1,4-glycosidic bonds, while amylopectin is branched with 1,4 and 1,6-glycosidic bonds, making both suited for energy storage in plants. Glycogen is highly branched with many 1,4 and 1,6-glycosidic bonds for rapid hydrolysis to release glucose in animals.

  • Monosaccharides: single sugar units like glucose, fructose, galactose.
  • Disaccharides: two monosaccharides joined by a glycosidic bond via condensation.
  • Polysaccharides: long chains of monosaccharides acting as energy stores (starch, glycogen).
  • Hydrolysis: breaks glycosidic bonds using water.

Core Practical 1: Estimating Sugar and Starch Concentrations

Semi-quantitative methods use colour standards to estimate concentrations. For reducing sugars, add Benedict's reagent to the sample, heat in a water bath, and observe the colour change from blue to green, yellow, orange, or brick-red. Compare against standard known concentrations. For starch, add iodine dissolved in potassium iodide solution and observe the colour change from browny-orange to blue-black, comparing with standard concentrations.

  • Reducing sugars test: Benedict's reagent, heat, observe colour change from blue to brick-red.
  • Starch test: iodine solution, observe colour change from orange-brown to blue-black.
  • Colour standards: compare unknowns against solutions of known concentrations.

Lipids and Triglyceride Synthesis

Triglycerides are synthesised by condensation reactions between one glycerol molecule and three fatty acids, forming ester bonds. Saturated lipids contain only single carbon-carbon bonds in their hydrocarbon chains, whereas unsaturated lipids contain one or more carbon-carbon double bonds, causing kinks that prevent tight packing.

  • Triglyceride: 1 glycerol + 3 fatty acids linked by 3 ester bonds.
  • Saturated fatty acids: no carbon-carbon double bonds, solid at room temperature.
  • Unsaturated fatty acids: contain carbon-carbon double bonds, liquid at room temperature.

Proteins and Amino Acids

Proteins are polymers made of amino acid monomers. An amino acid consists of a central carbon atom bonded to an amine group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen atom, and a variable R group. Amino acids join by peptide bonds formed in condensation reactions to create polypeptides. The primary structure is the sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide chain. This determines the secondary structure (alpha-helices and beta-pleated sheets held by hydrogen bonds), which further folds into the three-dimensional tertiary structure held by hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, disulfide bridges, and hydrophobic interactions. Globular proteins, such as haemoglobin, are folded into spherical, soluble shapes with hydrophilic groups on the outside, and function in metabolic roles. Fibrous proteins, such as collagen, form long, strong, insoluble fibres made of triple helices with cross-linking, providing structural strength.

  • Amino acid structure: central carbon, amine group, carboxyl group, hydrogen, R group.
  • Peptide bond: formed between amine and carboxyl groups via condensation.
  • Primary structure: amino acid sequence.
  • Secondary structure: alpha-helix or beta-pleated sheet formed by hydrogen bonding.
  • Tertiary structure: 3D folding stabilised by hydrogen, ionic, disulfide, and hydrophobic interactions.
  • Globular vs Fibrous: globular is soluble and spherical (haemoglobin); fibrous is structural and insoluble (collagen).

Enzymes and Biological Catalysts

Enzymes are biological catalysts that speed up metabolic reactions by lowering the activation energy without being used up. They are globular proteins with a specific active site whose three-dimensional shape is complementary to a specific substrate. Intracellular enzymes catalyse reactions inside cells, while extracellular enzymes are secreted to catalyse reactions outside cells. Enzyme action depends on temperature, pH, enzyme concentration, and substrate concentration.

  • Mechanism: substrate binds to active site to form an enzyme-substrate complex.
  • Activation energy: lowered by enzymes, increasing the rate of reaction.
  • Specificity: determined by the precise 3D shape of the active site.

Core Practical 4: Investigating Enzyme-Catalysed Reactions

To investigate the effect of temperature, pH, enzyme concentration, or substrate concentration on the initial rate of reaction, measure the formation of products or disappearance of substrate over time using continuous or initial rate sampling.

  • Independent variables: temperature, pH, enzyme concentration, substrate concentration.
  • Dependent variable: initial rate of reaction, calculated from the linear steepest part of a product against time graph.
  • Control variables: keep all non-tested variables constant.

Mass Transport and Circulation

Many animals have a heart and circulation because mass transport is necessary to overcome the limitations of diffusion in meeting the metabolic requirements of large, multicellular organisms with small surface area to volume ratios. Blood vessels have specific adaptations: arteries have thick walls with elastic tissue and smooth muscle to withstand high pressure from the heart; veins have thinner walls, wider lumens, and valves to prevent backflow of blood under low pressure; capillaries have walls that are one cell thick to provide a short diffusion distance for exchanging substances with tissues.

  • Diffusion limits: inadequate for deep body tissues in large organisms.
  • Arteries: thick muscular and elastic walls to withstand high pulse pressure.
  • Veins: thin walls, large lumen, valves to prevent backflow.
  • Capillaries: single endothelial cell layer for rapid exchange.

The Mammalian Heart and Cardiac Cycle

The mammalian heart pumps blood through a double circulatory system. The cardiac cycle consists of three stages: atrial systole, where the atria contract and push blood into the ventricles through open atrioventricular valves; ventricular systole, where the ventricles contract, increasing pressure and closing atrioventricular valves while forcing semilunar valves open to push blood into the aorta and pulmonary artery; and cardiac diastole, where all chambers relax, and blood passively fills the atria and ventricles. Major blood vessels include the vena cava, pulmonary artery, pulmonary vein, and aorta. Dissection of a mammalian heart allows the identification of atria, ventricles, valves, and thick-walled muscular left ventricles compared to thin-walled right ventricles.

  • Atrial systole: atria contract, ventricles relax, atrioventricular valves open.
  • Ventricular systole: ventricles contract, atrioventricular valves close, semilunar valves open.
  • Cardiac diastole: heart chambers relax, blood flows into atria and ventricles.

Gas Exchange and Fick's Law

Gas exchange surfaces have a large surface area to volume ratio, a short diffusion distance due to being thin, and a steep concentration gradient maintained by ventilation and blood flow. The rate of diffusion depends on these properties and is calculated using Fick's Law of Diffusion: Rate is proportional to (surface area × concentration difference) ÷ thickness of membrane. The mammalian lung is adapted for rapid gaseous exchange through millions of alveoli providing a massive surface area, capillary walls that are one cell thick, and a constant supply of blood to maintain the concentration gradient.

  • Fick's Law: Rate proportional to Area × Concentration Difference ÷ Thickness.
  • Alveoli adaptations: thin squamous epithelium, extensive capillary network, moist lining.

Haemoglobin and Oxygen Transport

Haemoglobin is a globular protein with four polypeptide chains, each containing a haem group with an iron ion. It transports oxygen by forming oxyhaemoglobin. The oxygen dissociation curve shows the relationship between percentage saturation of haemoglobin and partial pressure of oxygen. The sigmoidal curve occurs because the binding of the first oxygen molecule alters the protein's tertiary structure, making it easier for subsequent oxygen molecules to bind (positive cooperativity). The Bohr effect describes how an increase in carbon dioxide partial pressure decreases haemoglobin's affinity for oxygen, shifting the curve to the right and unloading more oxygen in respiring tissues. Fetal haemoglobin has a higher affinity for oxygen than adult haemoglobin, shifting its dissociation curve to the left, allowing it to extract oxygen from maternal blood across the placenta.

  • Haemoglobin structure: 4 polypeptide subunits, each with an iron-containing haem group.
  • Oxygen dissociation curve: sigmoidal shape due to cooperative binding.
  • Bohr effect: high carbon dioxide concentration shifts curve right, increasing oxygen unloading.
  • Fetal haemoglobin: higher oxygen affinity, curve shifts left compared to adult.

Cardiovascular Disease (CVD) and Risk Factors

Cardiovascular disease often begins with endothelial dysfunction, where damage to the arterial lining leads to an inflammatory response. White blood cells accumulate, absorbing cholesterol to form fatty streaks, which develop into atheromas or plaques. Plaque formation narrows arteries and raises blood pressure. The blood clotting process is triggered when damage exposes tissue factor; thromboplastin is released, catalysing the conversion of prothrombin into the active enzyme thrombin. Thrombin then catalyses the soluble protein fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin fibres, which mesh with platelets to form a blood clot, potentially blocking coronary arteries and causing myocardial infarction.

  • Atherosclerosis sequence: endothelial damage, inflammatory response, plaque/atheroma formation, raised blood pressure.
  • Blood clotting cascade: thromboplastin released, prothrombin converted to thrombin, fibrinogen converted to fibrin.
  • Risk factors: genetics, high-fat/salt diet, age, gender, high blood pressure, smoking, physical inactivity.

Health Studies and Risk Evaluation

Epidemiological data on illness and mortality rates help determine health risks. It is vital to distinguish between correlation and causation and to recognise conflicting evidence. When evaluating the design of studies used to determine health risk factors, consider sample selection, sample size, and whether the data collected is both valid and reliable. People's perception of risks often differs from actual risks due to underestimating or overestimating lifestyle factors. Body mass index (BMI) is calculated as mass (kg) divided by height squared (m squared), and waist-to-hip ratio are obesity indicators used alongside diet, exercise, and smoking cessation to reduce coronary heart disease risk.

  • BMI formula: mass (kg) ÷ height squared (m squared).
  • Correlation vs causation: correlation does not prove one variable causes another.
  • Study design evaluation: check for representative sample size, control of variables, validity, and reliability.

Treatments for Cardiovascular Disease (CVD)

Treatments for cardiovascular disease carry both benefits and risks. Antihypertensives lower blood pressure but can cause dizziness and fatigue. Statins lower blood cholesterol by inhibiting liver enzymes but may cause muscle pain and liver damage. Anticoagulants and platelet inhibitors reduce blood clotting but increase the risk of uncontrolled bleeding from injuries.

  • Antihypertensives: reduce blood pressure; risk of dizziness and nausea.
  • Statins: lower blood cholesterol; risk of muscle damage and liver inflammation.
  • Anticoagulants and platelet inhibitors: reduce clotting risk; risk of haemorrhage.

Worked Examples

Calculating BMI: A person has a mass of 70 kg and a height of 1.75 m.

  • Square the height: 1.75 × 1.75 = 3.0625.
  • Divide mass by squared height: 70 ÷ 3.0625 = 22.86.
  • State the unit: 22.86 kg per m squared.

Typical mistakes

  • Confusing condensation and hydrolysis: condensation joins molecules and releases water; hydrolysis splits molecules using water.
  • Stating correlation is proof of causation: correlation only shows a relationship, not a causal mechanism.
  • Forgetting the units in Fick's Law or BMI calculations: always include correct units in answers.
  • Confusing adult and fetal haemoglobin curves: fetal curve is to the left of the adult curve, indicating higher oxygen affinity at lower partial pressures.

Exam-style questions

  1. Describe how the structure of an artery is related to its function. Answer: Arteries have thick walls containing collagen for strength, elastic tissue to stretch and recoil under high pressure, and smooth muscle to constrict and dilate the lumen.
  2. Explain why high levels of LDL cholesterol increase the risk of cardiovascular disease. Answer: LDLs transport cholesterol to tissues where they can deposit it in artery walls, leading to atheroma formation, narrowing of arteries, and increased blood pressure.
  3. Explain the significance of the Bohr effect in actively respiring tissues. Answer: Respiring tissues produce high levels of carbon dioxide, which lowers pH, causing haemoglobin to release more oxygen more readily.
  4. Explain how glycogen's structure relates to its function as an energy storage molecule in animals. Answer: Glycogen is branched, allowing rapid hydrolysis to release glucose monomers, and is insoluble so it does not affect water potential.
  5. State the role of thromboplastin in blood clotting. Answer: Thromboplastin is released from damaged tissue and catalyses the conversion of prothrombin into thrombin.

Use these notes alongside active recall and past paper practice questions. Revise enzymes, gas exchange, and transport mechanisms next.

title: Operating Systems — Study Notes
content:
Operating Systems

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): OS roles, memory/process management, hardware–software layer, interrupts, buffers, utility software.

1. What an OS does

Manages memory, processes/files, I/O via drivers, security (users, permissions), and provides the UI (CLI/GUI) between user, applications and hardware.

2. Memory and process management

  • Paging/segmentation move programs in/out; virtual memory extends RAM to disk when RAM is full.
  • Multitasking: scheduler gives each process time slices; context switching saves/restores state.

3. Interrupts and buffers

Interrupts signal events (I/O complete, timer); CPU saves context, services via ISR, resumes. Buffers hold data in transit (printing) so slow devices don't block the CPU; spooling queues jobs.

4. Utility software

Disk formatter, defragmenter (reduces head movement on HDDs; unnecessary for SSD), backup scheduler, compression, antivirus, file compression.

5. UI and drivers
