CLI: precise, scriptable, low overhead. GUI: icons/windows, discoverable, more resources. Device drivers translate OS calls to hardware specifics — each device needs its own.

Exam tips: "manage" verbs earn marks: manages memory, manages processes, manages peripherals; explain virtual memory by RAM-full scenario, not definition alone.

title: Sampling and Estimation — Study Notes
content:
Sampling and Estimation

Populations, Samples, Statistics

A parameter describes the population (μ, σ²); a statistic describes the sample (x̄, s²). A statistic is unbiased if its expectation equals the population parameter: E(x̄) = μ always holds for the sample mean.

Unbiased Variance

The estimator with divisor (n − 1) is the unbiased sample variance:

  • s² = Σ(x − x̄)²/(n − 1)

Why n − 1: deviations are measured from x̄ rather than μ, slightly underestimating spread; the smaller divisor corrects it. At A2, state which estimator you are using — the unbiased one is the default.

Distribution of the Sample Mean

For a sample of size n from a population with mean μ and variance σ²:

  • E(x̄) = μ and Var(x̄) = σ²/n

Averaging shrinks spread — bigger samples give steadier estimates.

Central Limit Theorem

Whatever the population shape, for large n (rule of thumb n ≥ 30) the sample mean is approximately normal: x̄ ~ N(μ, σ²/n). This is why the normal appears constantly in inference.

Example: population mean 50, s.d. 12, n = 36. Then x̄ ~ N(50, 4) and P(x̄ > 51) = P(Z > 0.5) = 0.3085.

Using x̄ to Estimate

Given sample data, estimate μ by x̄ and σ² by the unbiased s². When the population is normal, x̄ is exactly normal for any n — the CLT is only needed for non-normal populations.

Exam tips: distinguish σ²/σ (population) from s²/s (sample) in notation. Standard error means √(σ²/n) — smaller with larger n. Quote probabilities for x̄ with the variance divided by n; forgetting that division is the classic error.

Exam method: estimators and sample variance

The sample mean x̄ is an unbiased estimate of the population mean μ. The unbiased estimate of the population variance is s² = Σ(x − x̄)²/(n − 1), which divides by n − 1 rather than n. Using n gives the population variance of the sample, which tends to underestimate the true value.

When the sum of squared deviations is given, divide it by n − 1 directly. When the raw data are given, it is quicker to compute s² = (Σx² − n x̄²)/(n − 1).

A random sample gives each member of the population an equal chance of selection. Bias means the estimator does not equal the parameter on average, so the sample must be random to make the estimate reliable.

The standard error of the sample mean is σ/√n. It decreases as the sample size grows, so larger samples give more precise estimates.

Exam cue: Name the estimator and state whether it is unbiased, because the question often asks for both the value and the reason.

Population and sample

A population is the complete set of items being studied, and a sample is the subset that is actually measured. A sample is used because measuring the whole population is too slow or too costly. A random sample gives every member an equal chance of selection, and a sample that is not random may be biased. A sample statistic, such as the sample mean, is used to estimate a population parameter, such as the population mean.

Worked example: an unbiased estimate of the population variance

A sample of size 5 has values 4, 6, 7, 8 and 10. The sample mean is 35 ÷ 5 = 7. The sum of squared deviations from the mean is 9 + 1 + 0 + 1 + 9 = 20. Dividing by n gives 4, but the unbiased estimate of the population variance divides by n − 1, which gives s² = 20 ÷ 4 = 5. The divisor n − 1 is used because the sample mean is itself estimated from the data, and it corrects the tendency of the divisor n to underestimate the population variance.

Confidence intervals for a mean

For a large sample from a population with known standard deviation σ, a 95% confidence interval for the population mean is the sample mean plus or minus 1.96 multiplied by σ divided by the square root of n. The quantity σ divided by the square root of n is the standard error. A wider interval means less precision, and increasing the sample size narrows the interval. Give the interval as two values and state the confidence level in the conclusion.

title: Proof — Study Notes
content:
Proof

Edexcel International A Level Mathematics — Pure Mathematics 2 (WMA12), sat at AS.

Proof is a logical argument that shows a statement is true in every case in its domain. At AS level you must know the four proof techniques, choose the right one for a given statement, and produce or critique a short algebraic argument.

Direct proof

Start from known facts and deduce the result by valid steps. Most algebraic identities are proved this way: expand, factorise or substitute until the required form appears.

  • To prove "the sum of two even numbers is even": write the numbers as 2a and 2b, so their sum is 2(a + b), which is even by definition.
  • To prove "the sum of two consecutive integers is odd": write them as n and n + 1, so the sum is 2n + 1, which is odd.

Proof by exhaustion

Check every case one by one. Only valid when the number of cases is finite and small, for example proving a statement about the factors of 12 by listing 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12.

Disproof by counter-example

A single case where the statement fails disproves a universal claim. This is the fastest way to kill a false statement: for "n^2 + n + 17 is prime for all n", the case n = 16 gives 289 = 17 x 17, so the claim is false.

Proof by contradiction

Assume the statement is false, then deduce something impossible. The classic is proving that the square root of 2 is irrational: assume sqrt(2) = p/q in lowest terms, derive that both p and q must be even, contradicting the lowest-terms assumption.

Common algebraic forms

  • Even: 2n. Odd: 2n + 1. Consecutive integers: n, n + 1, n + 2.
  • Consecutive even numbers: 2n, 2n + 2, 2n + 4.
  • A square number is n^2; the difference of two squares is (a - b)(a + b).
  • Divisibility: show the expression can be written as the required factor times an integer.

title: Kinetics
content:
Kinetics Revision Notes

Edexcel IAL Chemistry A2 Unit 4 Topic 11. This topic covers the quantitative study of reaction rates, rate equations, reaction mechanisms, catalysis, and the Arrhenius equation.

  • Rate of reaction is the change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit time, while rate equation is expressed as rate = k[A]m[B]n where m and n are orders 0, 1 or 2.
  • Order with respect to a substance is the power to which its concentration term is raised in the rate equation, and overall order is the sum of all individual orders.
  • Rate constant k is constant for a given temperature, half-life t1/2 is the time taken for the concentration of a reactant to halve, and rate-determining step is the slowest step in a multi-step mechanism.
  • Activation energy Ea is the minimum energy colliding particles must possess to react, heterogeneous catalyst is in a different phase from reactants, and homogeneous catalyst is in the same phase.
  • First-order reactions have a constant half-life independent of concentration, calculated from concentration-time graphs.
  • Experimental techniques to monitor rates include titration, colorimetry, mass change, volume of gas evolved, and other methods such as conductivity or pH measurement.
  • Initial-rate methods use separate experiments with different initial concentrations, and continuous monitoring tracks a single reaction over time to plot concentration-time or volume-time graphs.
  • Orders 0, 1 or 2 can be deduced from concentration-time graphs, rate-concentration graphs, or initial-rate method data.
  • Acid-catalysed iodination of propanone uses titrimetric methods to find orders with respect to propanone, iodine, and hydrogen ions to deduce the rate-determining step and mechanism.
  • Rate-determining step dictates the rate equation, and a reaction mechanism must agree with the stoichiometric equation and the rate equation.
  • Hydrolysis of halogenoalkanes provides evidence for SN1 (unimolecular, tertiary) and SN2 (bimolecular, primary) mechanisms based on rate equations involving hydroxide ions.
  • Activation energy can be calculated using graphical methods from experimental rate constant data at various temperatures using the Arrhenius equation.
  • Solid heterogeneous catalysts provide an active surface for gas-phase industrial reactions by adsorbing reactants, weakening bonds, and desorbing products.
  • Core Practical 9a and 9b involve following the rate of the iodine-propanone reaction by titrimetry and investigating clock reactions like the Harcourt-Esson or iodine clock.
  • Core Practical 10 involves finding the activation energy of a reaction using titrimetric or colorimetric methods at different temperatures.

Worked example

For a reaction with rate equation rate = k[A][B]2, if the initial concentration of A is doubled and B is halved, the new rate becomes rate = k(2[A])(0.5[B])2 = k × 2[A] × 0.25[B]2 = 0.5 × k[A][B]2, meaning the rate halves.

Key points to remember

Students often forget that rate equations must be determined experimentally, never from the stoichiometric balancing numbers in the overall equation unless the step is elementary. When calculating activation energy from the Arrhenius equation, remember to convert temperatures from Celsius to Kelvin and ensure units of k match the overall order of the reaction. For heterogeneous catalysts, always mention adsorption onto the active surface, reaction, and desorption of products.

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

title: AS Level Mathematics: Integration
content:
AS Level Mathematics: Integration

Integration is differentiation in reverse: it recovers a function from its gradient, and it accumulates a rate into a total — the area under a curve, the distance from a velocity, the cost from a marginal. This note builds the topic from zero: the indefinite integral and the constant of integration, the power rule, definite integrals and the fundamental theorem, areas above and below the axis, the area between two curves, and kinematics. Every worked example shows the antiderivative line before any substitution of limits.

The indefinite integral

if dy/dx = x^n then y = x^(n+1)/(n+1) + c   (n not -1)

integral of x^n dx = x^(n+1)/(n+1) + c
integral of k f(x) dx = k integral of f(x) dx
integral of a sum = sum of integrals

The +c is mandatory for indefinite integrals: every antiderivative differs by a constant, and the constant is fixed by a boundary condition (a point on the curve).

Worked example 1. Find ∫(6x² − 4x + 3) dx.

= 6x³/3 - 4x²/2 + 3x + c
= 2x³ - 2x² + 3x + c

Worked example 2 (negative and fractional powers). Find ∫(1/x² + √x) dx.

rewrite: integral of (x⁻² + x^(1/2)) dx
= -x⁻¹ + (2/3)x^(3/2) + c
= -1/x + (2/3)x^(3/2) + c

Worked example 3 (finding c). dy/dx = 3x² + 2 and the curve passes through (1, 5). Find y.

y = x³ + 2x + c
5 = 1 + 2 + c  →  c = 2
y = x³ + 2x + 2

Definite integrals and area

integral from a to b of f(x) dx = F(b) - F(a)

area under the curve between x = a and x = b (above the axis)
= definite integral; a negative value means the region is
below the x-axis, and the area is the magnitude

Worked example. Evaluate ∫ from 1 to 3 of (2x + 1) dx.

antiderivative: x² + x
F(3) = 9 + 3 = 12;  F(1) = 1 + 1 = 2
value = 12 - 2 = 10

Worked example 2 (area under a curve). Find the area under y = x² between x = 0 and x = 3.

integral: x³/3
from 0 to 3: 27/3 - 0 = 9 square units

Worked example 3 (below the axis). Find the area between y = x² − 4 and the x-axis from x = 0 to x = 2.

integral: x³/3 - 4x
from 0 to 2: 8/3 - 8 = -16/3
the value is negative because the region is below the axis;
area = 16/3 = 5.33 square units

Areas crossing the axis

When a curve crosses the x-axis inside the interval, integrate each piece separately and add the magnitudes — a single integral would cancel positive and negative areas.

Worked example. Find the total area between y = x² − 1 and the x-axis from x = −2 to x = 2.

crossings at x = -1 and x = 1
piece 1 (-2 to -1): F = x³/3 - x; F(-1) - F(-2) = (2/3) - (-2/3) = 4/3
piece 2 (-1 to 1): F(1) - F(-1) = (-2/3) - (2/3) = -4/3 → magnitude 4/3
piece 3 (1 to 2): F(2) - F(1) = (2/3) - (-2/3) = 4/3
total area = 4/3 + 4/3 + 4/3 = 4 square units

Area between two curves

area between y = f(x) and y = g(x) from a to b
= integral of (f(x) - g(x)) dx from a to b
where f is the upper curve and g the lower

Worked example. Find the area between y = x² and y = x from x = 0 to x = 1.

upper curve on this interval is y = x
integral of (x - x²) dx = x²/2 - x³/3
from 0 to 1: 1/2 - 1/3 = 1/6 square units

Worked example 2 (intersections). Find the area enclosed by y = x² and y = 2x.

intersections: x² = 2x → x(x - 2) = 0 → x = 0, 2
upper on (0, 2) is y = 2x
integral of (2x - x²) dx = x² - x³/3
from 0 to 2: 4 - 8/3 = 4/3 square units

Kinematics with integration

velocity v = ds/dt  →  displacement s = integral of v dt
acceleration a = dv/dt  →  velocity v = integral of a dt

definite integral of v from t1 to t2 = displacement
integral of |v| = distance travelled

Worked example. A particle has velocity v = 3t² − 6t (m/s). Find its displacement from t = 0 to t = 3 and its distance travelled.

s = integral of (3t² - 6t) dt = t³ - 3t²
from 0 to 3: 27 - 27 = 0  →  net displacement zero
sign of v: 3t(t - 2), negative between 0 and 2, positive after
distance = |integral 0 to 2| + integral 2 to 3
= |8 - 12| + (27 - 27) - (8 - 12) = 4 + 4 = 8 m

The distinction between displacement and distance is examinable: displacement is the signed integral, distance is the sum of the absolute pieces.

Worked examples: mixed integration

Worked example. The curve y = f(x) has f'(x) = 6x − 4 and passes through (2, 3). Find f(x) and the area under the curve from x = 1 to x = 2.

f(x) = 3x² - 4x + c;  3 = 12 - 8 + c → c = -1
f(x) = 3x² - 4x - 1
area = integral 1 to 2: x³ - 2x² - x
F(2) = 8 - 8 - 2 = -2; F(1) = 1 - 2 - 1 = -2
area = -2 - (-2) = 0  (the curve is below the axis and the
signed areas cancel); the geometric area needs the crossing
checked - a useful reminder to sketch first

Integrating expressions that need rearranging

Integration has no product or quotient rule at AS level, so expressions must first be written as sums of powers. Two standard rearrangements cover almost every case:

product: expand, then integrate term by term
quotient with a single term denominator: divide through first

(x + 2)(x - 5) = x² - 3x - 10
(3x² + 4x)/x = 3x + 4
√(x)(x + 1) = x^(3/2) + x^(1/2)

Worked example. Find ∫ (x + 3)(x − 1) dx.

expand: x² + 2x - 3
integrate: x³/3 + x² - 3x + c

Worked example 2. Find ∫ (4x³ + 2x)/x dx.

divide: 4x² + 2
integrate: (4/3)x³ + 2x + c

Two boundary conditions

When the second derivative is given, integrate twice and use two pieces of information to fix both constants. The order matters: the first integration produces the gradient function and its constant, the second the curve and its constant.

Worked example. d²y/dx² = 6x, dy/dx = 2 when x = 1, and y = 5 when x = 1. Find y.

first: dy/dx = 3x² + c;  2 = 3 + c  →  c = -1, so dy/dx = 3x² - 1
second: y = x³ - x + k;  5 = 1 - 1 + k  →  k = 5
y = x³ - x + 5

Finding limits and constants from area information

Area questions are often inverted: the area is given and a limit or coefficient must be found. Set up the definite integral with the unknown, evaluate, and solve the resulting equation — rejecting any root outside the geometric context.

Worked example. The area under y = kx² from x = 0 to x = 3 is 36. Find k.

integral: kx³/3
from 0 to 3: 27k/3 = 9k
9k = 36  →  k = 4

Worked example 2 (unknown upper limit). The area under y = 2x from x = 0 to x = a is 25. Find a.

integral: x²;  from 0 to a: a² = 25
a = 5  (the negative root is rejected: a is an x-coordinate to
the right of the origin in this setup)

Kinematics: recovering velocity from acceleration

Worked example. A particle starts from rest with acceleration a = 6t − 4 (m/s²). Find its velocity at t = 3 and the distance travelled in the first 3 seconds.

v = integral of (6t - 4) dt = 3t² - 4t + c
at rest at t = 0: c = 0  →  v = 3t² - 4t
v(3) = 27 - 12 = 15 m/s
distance = integral of |v| from 0 to 3
v = 0 at t = 0 and t = 4/3; v is negative on (0, 4/3)
piece 1: [t³ - 2t²] from 0 to 4/3 = 64/27 - 32/9 = -32/27 → 32/27
piece 2: [t³ - 2t²] from 4/3 to 3 = (27 - 18) - (-32/27) = 9 + 32/27
distance = 32/27 + 9 + 32/27 = 9 + 64/27 = 11.4 m

The sign analysis is the whole question: sketch v against t, mark where it crosses zero, and integrate each piece with its sign removed.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Indefinite) Find ∫(4x³ − 2) dx. Answer: integrate term by term and add the constant: ∫4x³ dx = x⁴ and ∫2 dx = 2x, so the result is x⁴ − 2x + c.
  2. (Negative power) Find ∫x⁻² dx. Answer: raise the power by one and divide by the new power: ∫x⁻² dx = x⁻¹/(−1) + c = −1/x + c.
  3. (Definite) Evaluate ∫ from 0 to 2 of 3x² dx. Answer: integrate, then substitute the limits: ∫₀² 3x² dx = [x³]₀² = 2³ − 0³ = 8.
  4. (Area) Find the area under y = x + 2 from x = 0 to x = 3. Answer: [x²/2 + 2x] = 4.5 + 6 = 10.5.
  5. (Below axis) Find the area between y = x − 3 and the x-axis from x = 0 to x = 2. Answer: integral = [x²/2 − 3x] = 2 − 6 = −4; area 4.
  6. (Between curves) Find the area between y = x² and y = x³ from 0 to 1. Answer: upper is x²; ∫(x² − x³) = 1/3 − 1/4 = 1/12.
  7. (Constant) dy/dx = 4x and y = 7 when x = 1. Find y. Answer: y = 2x² + c → 7 = 2 + c → c = 5 → y = 2x² + 5.
  8. (Kinematics) v = 2t + 1. Find the displacement from t = 0 to t = 4. Answer: [t² + t] = 16 + 4 = 20 m.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Forgetting +c: an indefinite integral without the constant loses a mark; with a boundary condition, the constant is required for the answer.
  • Power rule reversal: integrate xⁿ to x^(n+1)/(n+1); adding one and dividing is the opposite of differentiating, and mixing them up produces nonsense.
  • Limits order: F(b) − F(a), never the reverse. A negative area often means the limits were swapped.
  • Ignoring crossings: a definite integral over a region that crosses the axis gives the signed area; split at the crossings and add magnitudes for the geometric area.
  • Wrong upper curve: subtract lower from upper; sketching between the intersection points avoids the sign error.
  • Distance versus displacement: displacement is the signed integral; distance sums the absolute pieces. Read which is asked.
  • Expanding before integrating: products must be expanded or divided first; there is no product rule for integration at AS level.
  • Units: areas are square units, displacements in metres; attach and interpret units in applied questions.

Reverse differentiation and the constant of integration

Integration undoes differentiation. Every indefinite integral is found by asking which function differentiates to the one given, and every answer carries a constant of integration, because a constant disappears when a function is differentiated.

Integrating powers of x

For any power other than −1, ∫xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + c. Raise the power by one and divide by the new power. For example ∫x³ dx = x⁴/4 + c, and ∫x⁻² dx = x⁻¹/(−1) + c = −1/x + c. Students often forget to add one to the power, which gives a result that does not differentiate back to the start.

Integrating a sum and a constant multiple

Integrate term by term and keep constant multipliers outside. ∫(3x² − 4x + 5) dx = x³ − 2x² + 5x + c. Check it by differentiating: 3x² − 4x + 5 is returned exactly, which is the test that the answer is correct.

Why the constant of integration is needed

The derivative of x³ + 7 is the same as the derivative of x³ − 2, so the integral of 3x² must be x³ plus some unknown constant. Writing +c records that the answer is a whole family of curves, one for each value of c. A question that gives one point on the curve fixes c, and that step is worth marks in its own right.

Integrating (ax + b)ⁿ

When the bracket is linear, the chain rule runs backwards and needs one extra division by a. ∫(2x + 3)⁴ dx = (2x + 3)⁵/(2 × 5) + c = (2x + 3)⁵/10 + c. Differentiating (2x + 3)⁵/10 gives 5 × 2 × (2x + 3)⁴/10, which is (2x + 3)⁴, so the answer is confirmed.

Integrating expressions that need rearranging

Expand brackets and split fractions before integrating, because the power rule works only on single powers. (x + 1)² is x² + 2x + 1 before integration, so ∫(x + 1)² dx = x³/3 + x² + x + c. Writing (x + 1)² as a power of a bracket and applying the linear rule gives the same answer, but expanding is the safer route when the bracket is not linear.

Checking an integral by differentiating

Differentiate the answer and compare it with the integrand. If the two do not match, the error is in the power, the division or a missing coefficient. This check takes a few seconds and catches most sign and division slips before they reach the final line.

Definite integrals: meaning and evaluation

A definite integral has limits and gives a number. It is the signed area between the curve and the x-axis between those limits, and it is evaluated by substituting the upper limit, substituting the lower limit and subtracting. The constant of integration cancels in that subtraction, so it is not written for a definite integral.

Evaluating between limits

Write the result in square brackets with the limits at the top and bottom, then substitute. ∫₁³ (2x + 1) dx = [x² + x]₁³ = (9 + 3) − (1 + 1) = 12 − 2 = 10. Put the subtraction in brackets when the limit is negative, so that the sign is not lost.

Reversing the limits

Swapping the limits changes the sign of the answer: ∫₃¹ f(x) dx = −∫₁³ f(x) dx. This is useful when the limits are given in the wrong order, and it is also a common source of a wrong sign when a question asks for an area, because an area is always positive.

Integrals over an interval of zero width

If the two limits are equal, the integral is zero, because the interval has no width. ∫₂² f(x) dx = 0 for any function f. The rule is used as a quick check: an answer that is not zero for equal limits has a mistake in the evaluation.

Using the fundamental theorem

The definite integral equals F(b) − F(a), where F is any antiderivative of f. The choice of antiderivative does not matter, because adding a constant to F adds the same constant to both values and cancels. This is why the constant can be left out of definite integrals.

Finding a constant from a definite integral

If ∫₀² (kx) dx = 4, then [kx²/2]₀² = 2k = 4, so k = 2. Set up the integral with the unknown inside it, evaluate it in terms of the unknown, and then solve the resulting equation as a normal linear or quadratic equation.

Area as a definite integral from a graph

When a question asks for the area between a curve and the x-axis, first sketch the curve to see whether it is above or below the axis on the interval. Only then write the integral. A region above the axis gives a positive integral, and a region below gives a negative one, so the area is the absolute value.

Equations and symbols

Integration is four formulas and two decisions: which power rule, and whether the answer is signed. Learn the rule with its condition attached — the exception at n = −1 is the mark most often lost.

integral of x^n dx = x^(n+1)/(n+1) + c Key: x = the variable of integration (no units for a pure function); n = the power, any real number except −1; c = the constant of integration, fixed by a boundary condition. Raise the power by one, then divide by the new power — the reverse of differentiating, and n = −1 is excluded because it would divide by zero.

if dy/dx = x^n then y = x^(n+1)/(n+1) + c (n not -1) Key: dy/dx = the gradient function; y = the function recovered from it; n = the power; c = the constant. The same statement read from the other end: differentiating the answer returns the question.

integral of k f(x) dx = k integral of f(x) dx Key: k = a constant multiplier (no units); f(x) = the function being integrated. Constants pass through the integral sign, which is why a polynomial is integrated term by term.

integral from a to b of f(x) dx = F(b) - F(a) Key: a = the lower limit; b = the upper limit; f(x) = the integrand; F(x) = any antiderivative of f(x). Upper value minus lower value, never the reverse — a negative area usually means the limits were swapped.

velocity v = ds/dt Key: v = velocity (m s⁻¹); s = displacement (m); t = time (s). The gradient form; integrate it in reverse to recover displacement.

displacement s = integral of v dt Key: s = displacement (m); v = velocity (m s⁻¹); t = time (s). The signed integral, so motion backwards subtracts from the total.

acceleration a = dv/dt Key: a = acceleration (m s⁻²); v = velocity (m s⁻¹); t = time (s). The link that lets a question give acceleration and ask for velocity or displacement.

velocity v = integral of a dt Key: v = velocity (m s⁻¹); a = acceleration (m s⁻²); t = time (s). Integrate, then use "starts from rest" or a stated value to fix the constant.

integral of |v| = distance travelled Key: |v| = the magnitude of the velocity, so every piece counts positive (m s⁻¹); the integral gives distance (m), not displacement. Split the integral wherever v = 0, because that is where the sign changes.

9k = 36 → k = 4 Key: 9k = the definite integral of kx² from 0 to 3, written with the unknown constant k; 36 = the given area (square units); k = 4 (no units). The inverted-area question: set the integral equal to the stated area and solve, rather than integrating a known function.

title: Tenses in Context — Study Notes
content:
Why tenses are harder than they look

Tense choice depends on time, but time is only the start. Two sentences about the same event can use different tenses and mean different things. A student who picks the right tense for a single gap usually gets the harder questions wrong because they have learned the form, not the use. These notes build from the form to the use, and then to the situations where examiners ask you to choose.

The tense families

It is easier to think in families than in a list of twelve forms. Each family groups tenses that share one central idea. Learn the idea first; the exact form comes from the time you are talking about.

Present family

The present family covers what is true now, what happens regularly, and what is happening at this moment.

  • Present simple: facts, general truths, routines, states. Water boils at 100 C. The bus leaves at seven. She works in a bank.
  • Present continuous: actions happening now, temporary situations, fixed future arrangements. I am studying for my exams this week. They are meeting the principal tomorrow.
  • Present perfect: a past action connected to now, with since, for, ever, never, just, already, yet. I have lived here since 2019. Have you ever been to Paris?

The common mistake is using the present perfect with a finished time word. Write "I have lived here since 2019", not "I have lived here in 2019". "Ago" forces the past simple: "I lived here two years ago".

Past family

The past family covers finished actions and states, whether the time is stated or simply understood.

  • Past simple: a completed action at a definite past time. She went to the cinema yesterday. We moved to Leeds in 2015.
  • Past continuous: an action in progress at a past moment, often as background to a shorter action. When the phone rang, I was taking a shower.
  • Past perfect: an action completed before another past time. By the time we arrived, the film had started. She had already left when I called.

Students often use the past simple where the past perfect is needed because both refer to the past. The difference is order: the past perfect happened first. If two past events appear, the earlier one takes the past perfect.

Future family

English has several future forms, and the choice depends on how certain the future event is and how it is viewed.

  • Will: spontaneous decisions, predictions without present evidence, offers, promises. I will help you with that. It will rain tomorrow.
  • Going to: predictions with present evidence, plans and intentions. Look at those clouds - it is going to rain. She is going to study medicine.
  • Present continuous for future: fixed arrangements with a time and place. I am meeting her at six. We are flying to Madrid next week.
  • Future continuous: an action in progress at a future time. This time next week, we will be lying on the beach.
  • Future perfect: an action completed before a future time. By next year, she will have graduated. By the time you arrive, they will have finished.

The most common error is using "will" when present evidence is clear. "Look at those clouds - it will rain" is weaker than "it is going to rain" because the evidence is present now.

Perfect family

The perfect forms connect two times. The auxiliaries have/has/had + past participle always carry that connection.

  • Present perfect: past to now. I have lost my keys (and I still cannot get in).
  • Past perfect: earlier past to later past. When I got home, she had cooked dinner.
  • Future perfect: now to a future point. By 2030, the bridge will have been built.

The perfect is not about the action itself but about the link it makes. "I lost my keys" tells you the action; "I have lost my keys" tells you the action and its present result.

Continuous family

The continuous forms carry the idea of duration or interruption rather than completion.

  • Past continuous: background action interrupted by a shorter past action.
  • Present continuous: action around now, or a temporary state.
  • Future continuous: action in progress at a future point.

A continuous form is right when the focus is on the activity in progress, not on the fact that it is finished.

Passive voice

The passive puts the receiver first: the subject receives the action. It is common in formal and scientific writing, and in exam questions where the actor is unknown or unimportant.

  • The report was written by the team.
  • The bridge is being built this year.
  • The results have been published.

Form: be + past participle. Keep the tense of "be" correct - the passive of the present simple is "is/are + past participle", the passive of the past simple is "was/were + past participle", the passive of the present perfect is "has/have been + past participle".

Do not overuse the passive. Use it when the receiver matters more than the actor, or when the actor is unknown.

Conditionals

Conditionals describe what happens if a condition is met. The four main types are:

  • Zero conditional: general truth. If you heat ice, it melts. Present simple in both parts.
  • First conditional: real future possibility. If it rains, I will stay home. If + present simple, will + infinitive.
  • Second conditional: unreal present. If I had more time, I would learn the piano. If + past simple, would + infinitive.
  • Third conditional: unreal past. If I had studied harder, I would have passed. If + past perfect, would have + past participle.

The most common errors are mixing the types (e.g. "If I would have known, I would tell you") and using "was" instead of "were" in the second conditional ("If I were you"). After verbs of suggestion (suggest, recommend, insist), the base form is standard: "She suggested that he leave early".

Common errors that lose marks

  • Using the past simple with since/for: "I lived here since 2019" should be "I have lived here since 2019".
  • Using "will" where present evidence makes "going to" better: "Look at those clouds - it will rain" should be "it is going to rain".
  • Using "ago" in the present perfect: "I have seen him ago" should be "I saw him a week ago".
  • Using the past perfect without a later past event to compare with.
  • Confusing "used to" (past habit, no longer true) with "would" (repeated past action): "When I was young, I used to swim every day" and "When I was young, I would swim every day" are both correct, but "used to" emphasises that the habit has ended.
  • Writing "I am knowing" - stative verbs such as know, believe, want, like, belong usually do not take the continuous form.

How to choose in an exam question

When a gap-fill or multiple-choice question asks for a tense, work through these checks in order:

  1. Is there a time word? "Yesterday", "in 2015", "ago" leads to past simple. "Since", "for", "ever", "never" leads to present perfect. "By the time", "before" with another past event leads to past perfect.
  2. Is the action finished or still connected to now? Finished and no present link leads to past simple. Finished but with a present result leads to present perfect.
  3. Is one action in progress when another happens? The longer action leads to continuous. The shorter, interrupting action leads to simple.
  4. Is the future event a fixed arrangement, a plan, or a spontaneous decision? Fixed arrangement leads to present continuous. Plan or intention with evidence leads to going to. Spontaneous decision leads to will.
  5. Is there a condition? Identify the type (real future, unreal present, unreal past) and match the form.

Most exam tense questions can be solved by finding the time word or the relationship between the events, then matching the family.

Examples that teach the rule

A tense is easier to remember when you see the contrast. These pairs show how the meaning changes with the tense:

  • Present simple vs present continuous: "She teaches maths" (permanent job) vs "She is teaching maths this term" (temporary).
  • Past simple vs present perfect: "I lived in London in 2019" (finished) vs "I have lived in London since 2019" (continues now).
  • Past simple vs past perfect: "When I arrived, she cooked dinner" (she cooked after I arrived, or at about the same time) vs "When I arrived, she had cooked dinner" (the dinner was ready when I arrived).
  • Will vs going to: "I think it will rain tomorrow" (prediction) vs "Look at those clouds - it is going to rain" (present evidence).
  • First vs second conditional: "If I have time, I will help" (possible) vs "If I had time, I would help" (impossible now).
  • Active vs passive: "The team wrote the report" (actor important) vs "The report was written by the team" (receiver important) vs "The report was written" (actor unknown or unimportant).

Quick reference

Present simple: facts, routines, states. Present continuous: happening now, temporary, fixed future arrangement. Present perfect: past action connected to now, with since, for, ever, never, just, already, yet. Past simple: finished past action, with yesterday, last week, in 2015, ago. Past continuous: action in progress at a past moment, often as background. Past perfect: action before another past event, with by the time, before, after a past reference. Future will: prediction, decision, offer, promise. Future going to: plan, intention, prediction with present evidence. Future continuous: action in progress at a future time. Future perfect: action completed before a future point, with by next year, by 2030, by the time. Passive: receiver first, actor unknown or unimportant. First conditional: real future possibility. Second conditional: unreal present. Third conditional: unreal past.

Use this as a check, not as a substitute for understanding the families. If you can explain why a tense fits a situation, you can choose correctly in any exam question.

title: Forces and Equilibrium — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Forces and Equilibrium

Physics — AS. Draw every force on one body: weight (down), normal reactions (perpendicular to surfaces), tension (along strings), friction (opposing motion).

Key areas to revise

  • Free-Body Diagrams
  • Resolving Forces
  • Equilibrium
  • Moments and the Principle of Moments
  • Centre of Gravity

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Key relationships

  • Moment of a force = force × perpendicular distance from the pivot.
  • Principle of moments: for an object in rotational equilibrium, the sum of clockwise moments equals the sum of anticlockwise moments.
  • For translational equilibrium, the resultant force in each direction is zero.
  • A couple is two equal and opposite forces that produce a turning effect with no net force; its moment is F × d.

Common errors

The distance used in a moment must be the perpendicular distance from the line of action to the pivot. Using the length of a lever arm at an angle gives a wrong answer.

title: Web Technologies — Study Notes
content:
Web Technologies

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): HTML structure/tags, CSS styling, JS interactivity, the DOM, microprocessors/controllers in web context.

1. HTML

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head><title>Page</title></head>
<body>
  <h1>Heading</h1>
  <p>Paragraph with <strong>bold</strong> text</p>
  <img src="pic.jpg" alt="description">
  <a href="https://example.com">Link</a>
  <table><tr><td>cell</td></tr></table>
</body>
</html>

Head holds metadata/title; body holds visible content; hypertext links via <a href>.

2. CSS

p { color: red; font-size: 14px; }
.highlight { background-color: yellow; }
#header { text-align: center; }

Element, class (.) and id (#) selectors; inline vs external stylesheets; separation of content (HTML) from presentation (CSS).

3. JavaScript and the DOM

document.getElementById("demo").innerHTML = "Hello";
document.getElementsByClassName("item")[0].style.color = "blue";

DOM = the browser's object model of the page; JS reads/changes it for interactivity (validation, sliders, dynamic text). Events (click, submit) trigger functions.

4. How pages load

URL → DNS lookup → server request → HTML parsed → assets fetched → DOM built → render. Layers: structure (HTML) → presentation (CSS) → behaviour (JS).

Exam tips: write tags with correct closing pairs; explain DOM operations as "find element by id … then change property"; separate structure/presentation/behaviour in answers.

HTML, CSS and the client-server model

HTML defines the structure and content of a web page using tags, such as headings and paragraphs. CSS controls how that content looks, including colour, layout and font size. Keeping structure and style separate means one stylesheet can change the appearance of many pages.

In the client-server model, a client such as a browser sends a request, and a server returns the requested resources. When a web page is requested, the browser uses the domain name to look up the server's IP address through the Domain Name System (DNS), then sends the request over HTTP or HTTPS.

Exam tip: describe a web request as a sequence: DNS lookup, request, server response, rendering in the browser.

title: Pressure & Density
content:
Pressure & Density

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2023–2025): pressure & pressure differences in fluids, density review (Extended pressure-depth).

1. Pressure basics

p = F/A (Pa = N/m²). Increase F or decrease A to raise pressure; explain applications (snowshoes, knives, hydraulic press).

2. Liquids

  • Pressure increases with depth: p = ρgh (Extended).
  • Same level, same liquid ⇒ same pressure (hydrostatic paradox).
  • Hydraulic systems transmit pressure — force multiplier: F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂.

3. Atmospheric pressure

~10⁵ Pa at sea level; demonstrated by collapsing can, mercury barometer 760 mmHg; decreases with altitude.

4. Density revisited

ρ = m/V; floating condition; upthrust = weight of displaced fluid (qualitative).

5. Gas pressure (particle model)

Particles collide with walls → force per area. Volume ↓ at same T ⇒ pressure ↑ (more frequent collisions). Temperature ↑ ⇒ faster particles ⇒ more frequent, harder impacts.

title: IGCSE Biology: Variation and Selection
content:
IGCSE Biology: Variation and Selection

No two humans are identical (except identical twins), and that variation is the raw material of evolution. This note separates the two kinds of variation and their causes, explains how adaptation arises through natural selection step by step, works through antibiotic and pesticide resistance as the exam's favourite modern example, describes artificial selection and selective breeding, and closes with classification-by-DNA and the evidence for evolution. The mechanism of natural selection is written as a five-step sequence — the order examiners mark.

Types of variation

Continuous variation shows a full range of intermediate phenotypes with no distinct classes: height, mass, hand-span, skin colour — plotted, they give a bell-shaped normal distribution curve (most individuals near the mean, few at the extremes), shaped by many genes plus the environment. Discontinuous variation falls into distinct categories with no intermediates: blood group (A, B, AB, O), tongue rolling (yes/no), eye colour categories, sex — each phenotype is clear-cut, usually controlled by one or a few genes with little environmental influence. Causes: genetic (the alleles inherited from parents), environmental (temperature, nutrition, light, exercise — e.g. plant height in different soils), and most often a combination of both (genes set a potential, the environment determines how much of it is realised). Mutations — random changes in DNA — create brand-new alleles and are the ultimate source of genetic variation.

Continuous and discontinuous variation compared

FeatureContinuousDiscontinuous
PatternFull range of intermediatesDistinct categories
GraphBell-shaped normal distributionSeparate bars
Genetic controlMany genes (polygenic)Usually one gene
Environmental influenceStrong (e.g. diet, exercise)Little
ExamplesHeight, mass, hand-spanBlood group, tongue rolling, sex

Natural selection: the five-step mechanism

Darwin's mechanism works on any reproducing population. Step 1: variation exists in the population (from mutation, meiosis and sexual reproduction). Step 2: a change in the environment creates a struggle for survival (resources, predators, disease, climate) — more offspring are produced than can survive. Step 3: individuals with characteristics better suited to the new environment (the adaptive features) survive and reproduce more successfully — "survival of the fittest", where fitness means reproductive success, not strength. Step 4: the advantageous alleles are passed to offspring, so their frequency increases in the population over generations. Step 5: over many generations, the population becomes adapted to its environment; if populations become isolated and diverge enough, new species may form (speciation). Antibiotic resistance is the textbook application: in any bacterial population, random mutation produces some resistant bacteria; when the antibiotic is applied, non-resistant bacteria die while resistant ones survive and reproduce with the drug present, passing the resistance gene on (including by plasmid transfer); the population becomes resistant. Pesticide resistance in insects and herbicide resistance in weeds follow the identical five steps — the exam often gives one of these instead of bacteria and expects the same logic.

Adaptive features

An adaptive feature is any inherited characteristic that increases an organism's chance of survival and reproduction in its environment. Examples worth memorising: polar bear — white fur (camouflage), thick blubber and fur (insulation), large paws (weight distribution on ice, swimming); cactus — spines instead of leaves (reduced water loss, defence), thick fleshy stem (water storage), shallow roots (rapid absorption); deep-sea fish — large eyes (dim light), bioluminescence (communication), no swim bladder (pressure); desert fox — large ears (heat loss); bacteria — rapid reproduction and plasmid exchange (resistance spread). Adaptations are always relative to an environment: an adaptation in one habitat can be a liability in another (a polar bear in the desert).

Artificial selection (selective breeding)

Humans drive artificial selection by choosing organisms with desired features to breed together, generation after generation, until the trait is fixed in the population. Examples: crops bred for higher yield, disease resistance or uniform ripening (modern wheat from wild grasses); domestic animals bred for milk yield, muscle mass, temperament or appearance (dogs from wolves — the enormous variety of breeds from one species); ornamental plants for flower colour and size. The method: identify parents with the desired phenotype → cross them → select offspring showing the trait → repeat over many generations; use inbreeding to fix the trait (homozygosity) — but inbreeding also concentrates harmful recessive alleles and reduces variation (inbreeding depression), so new genetic material must periodically be introduced. Selective breeding is slow (many generations) and depends on the trait being heritable.

Evidence for evolution and speciation

Direct evidence: antibiotic-resistant bacteria, pesticide-resistant insects, beak size changes in Galápagos finches observed over decades. Fossil evidence: the sequence of forms in rock strata shows change over time (horse evolution, Archaeopteryx linking reptiles and birds) — though the fossil record is incomplete. Molecular evidence: comparison of DNA base sequences and proteins; the more similar the sequences of a given gene, the more closely related the species — this underpins modern classification. Comparative anatomy: homologous structures (the pentadactyl limb — same bone pattern in human arm, whale flipper, bat wing, horse leg — indicating common ancestry) versus analogous structures (wings of insects and birds: similar function, different origin). Biogeography: island species resemble those of the nearest mainland (Darwin's finches). Speciation occurs when populations of the same species become isolated (geographically — a mountain range or river; or behaviourally) and face different selection pressures; over many generations, allele frequencies diverge until they can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring — then they are separate species.

Worked example: natural selection applied to a new scenario

Scenario: a moth population lives on tree trunks; most are pale, some carry a dark allele. Industrial soot darkens the trunks. Step 1: state the variation — pale and dark morphs exist from genetic variation. Step 2: state the selection pressure — dark trunks make pale moths conspicuous to birds. Step 3: differential survival — pale moths are eaten more; dark moths survive and reproduce. Step 4: inheritance — the dark allele is passed on, its frequency rises. Step 5: prediction — over generations the population becomes mostly dark (and the reverse when pollution falls, as recorded in the peppered moth). Calculation practice from population data: if the frequency of the recessive phenotype (bb) is 0.09 (9 %), then q² = 0.09, q = 0.3, p = 0.7, so carriers (2pq) = 2 × 0.7 × 0.3 = 0.42 = 42 % — at IGCSE the arithmetic of phenotype percentages from a data table is common even where Hardy-Weinberg is not named.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Writing that organisms "develop resistance because they need it": variation must pre-exist — selection acts on existing mutation-driven variation. This Lamarckian phrasing is a classic lost mark.
  • Describing natural selection as "the strongest survive": fitness means reproductive success of better-adapted individuals, not physical strength.
  • Confusing continuous (bell curve, many genes) and discontinuous (distinct categories, one gene) variation in a graph question.
  • Leaving "heritable/variation passed to offspring" out of the natural-selection sequence — without inheritance there is no evolution.
  • Saying artificial selection produces "new genes": it selects from existing variation; only mutation creates new alleles.
  • Explaining antibiotic resistance as caused "by the antibiotic": the antibiotic selects resistant mutants that already exist; it does not create them.
  • In data questions, quoting percentages without converting between fractions and percentages when asked.
  • Calling analogous structures evidence of common ancestry: only homologous structures (same origin) are.

Exam-style questions and answers

Q1. Describe how bacteria become resistant to antibiotics. (4 marks) Answer: random mutation produces resistant bacteria in the population (1); antibiotics kill non-resistant bacteria, leaving resistant ones (1); resistant bacteria survive and reproduce, passing on the resistance gene (1); frequency of resistant bacteria in the population increases (1).

Q2. Explain the difference between continuous and discontinuous variation with an example of each. (4 marks) Answer: continuous shows a range of intermediates (1) e.g. height (1); discontinuous falls into distinct categories (1) e.g. blood group (1).

Q3. Describe how a farmer might use selective breeding to increase milk yield in cattle. (3 marks) Answer: select cows and bulls with the highest milk yield (1); breed them together (1); select offspring with the highest yield and repeat over generations (1).

Q4. Explain how the fossil record provides evidence for evolution. (3 marks) Answer: fossils in older rock layers are simpler than those above (1); transitional forms such as Archaeopteryx link groups (1); shows change in species over millions of years (1).

Q5. Explain why the peppered moth population became darker during the Industrial Revolution. (4 marks) Answer: variation in colour already existed (1); soot darkened tree trunks so pale moths were predated more (1); dark moths survived and reproduced (1); dark allele frequency increased over generations (1).

title: A Level Mathematics: Further Algebra
content:
A Level Mathematics: Further Algebra

A2 algebra is about rewriting expressions so that they can be handled: splitting a fraction into partial fractions before integrating it, dividing polynomials to expose factors, and using the remainder and factor theorems to find unknowns. This note builds each technique from zero, with the long division written out term by term, because the algebra is the part candidates rush and lose marks on.

Polynomial division

Dividing a polynomial by a linear factor works like numerical long division: divide the leading term, multiply back, subtract, bring down, repeat until the degree of the remainder is lower than the divisor.

Worked example. Divide 2x³ − 5x² + 4x − 7 by (x − 2).

2x² into x - 2: 2x²(x - 2) = 2x³ - 4x²;  subtract: -x² + 4x - 7
-x into x - 2: -x(x - 2) = -x² + 2x;  subtract: 2x - 7
+2 into x - 2: 2(x - 2) = 2x - 4;  subtract: -3
quotient 2x² - x + 2 with remainder -3
so 2x³ - 5x² + 4x - 7 = (x - 2)(2x² - x + 2) - 3

Worked example 2 (missing terms). Divide x³ + 1 by (x + 1).

write as x³ + 0x² + 0x + 1 to keep the columns aligned
quotient x², subtract x³ + x² → -x² + 1
quotient -x, subtract -x² - x → x + 1
quotient +1, subtract x + 1 → 0
x³ + 1 = (x + 1)(x² - x + 1)

Leaving gaps in the descending powers is the commonest slip; write the zeros in explicitly.

The factor and remainder theorems

remainder theorem: dividing f(x) by (x - a) leaves remainder f(a)
factor theorem: (x - a) is a factor exactly when f(a) = 0
for (ax - b): remainder is f(b/a)

Worked example 1. Find the remainder when f(x) = x³ − 4x + 5 is divided by (x + 2).

f(-2) = -8 + 8 + 5 = 5

Worked example 2 (find a factor). Show that (x − 3) is a factor of x³ − 4x² − 3x + 18.

f(3) = 27 - 36 - 9 + 18 = 0, so (x - 3) is a factor
then divide: x³ - 4x² - 3x + 18 = (x - 3)(x² - x - 6)
                                     = (x - 3)(x - 3)(x + 2)

Worked example 3 (unknown constant). f(x) = 2x³ + ax² − 5x + 6 has (x + 2) as a factor. Find a.

f(-2) = -16 + 4a + 10 + 6 = 0
4a = 0  →  a = 0
check: 2x³ - 5x + 6 divided by (x + 2) gives 2x² - 4x + 3 with no remainder

Partial fractions: distinct linear factors

(px + q)/[(x - a)(x - b)] = A/(x - a) + B/(x - b)

multiply through by the denominator and substitute x = a, x = b
in turn (the cover-up method)

Worked example. Express (5x + 1)/[(x − 1)(x + 2)] in partial fractions.

5x + 1 = A(x + 2) + B(x - 1)
x = 1: 6 = 3A  →  A = 2
x = -2: -9 = -3B  →  B = 3
(5x + 1)/[(x - 1)(x + 2)] = 2/(x - 1) + 3/(x + 2)

Worked example 2 (three factors). Express 2/[(x)(x + 1)(x − 2)] in partial fractions.

2 = A(x + 1)(x - 2) + Bx(x - 2) + Cx(x + 1)
x = 0: 2 = -2A  →  A = -1
x = -1: 2 = 3B  →  B = 2/3
x = 2: 2 = 6C  →  C = 1/3
so 2/[...] = -1/x + (2/3)/(x + 1) + (1/3)/(x - 2)

Partial fractions: repeated and improper cases

repeated factor: (px + q)/[(x - a)²] = A/(x - a) + B/(x - a)²
improper (degree of numerator >= degree of denominator): divide first

Worked example 1 (repeated). Express (3x + 5)/(x − 1)² in partial fractions.

3x + 5 = A(x - 1) + B
x = 1: 8 = B
compare coefficients of x: 3 = A
so 3/(x - 1) + 8/(x - 1)²

Worked example 2 (improper). Express (x² + 3x + 2)/(x − 1) in partial fractions.

divide first: (x² + 3x + 2)/(x - 1) = x + 4 + 6/(x - 1)
check by multiplying back: (x + 4)(x - 1) + 6 = x² + 3x + 2

The division step must come first: writing A + B/(x − 1) for an improper fraction gives the wrong form and cannot be solved consistently.

Inequalities and modulus

|x - a| < b  means  a - b < x < a + b
|x - a| > b  means  x < a - b or x > a + b

rational inequalities: move everything to one side, combine over a
common denominator, then use a sign diagram

Worked example. Solve |2x − 3| < 7.

-7 < 2x - 3 < 7
-4 < 2x < 10⁻² < x < 5

Worked example 2 (rational). Solve (x + 1)/(x − 3) > 2.

(x + 1)/(x - 3) - 2 > 0
(x + 1 - 2x + 6)/(x - 3) > 0
(7 - x)/(x - 3) > 0
critical values x = 3 (undefined) and x = 7
sign test: x = 4 gives 3/1 > 0 true; x = 8 gives -1/5 < 0 false
so 3 < x < 7

Never multiply a rational inequality by the denominator without knowing its sign: multiplying by a negative reverses the inequality, which is why the sign-diagram method is used instead.

Solving cubic equations completely

Once one factor is found by the factor theorem, polynomial division reduces the cubic to a quadratic, and the quadratic gives the remaining roots. The routine never varies:

  1. Try small integer values (±1, ±2, ±3) in f(x) until one gives zero.
  2. Divide by the corresponding linear factor.
  3. Factorise or use the quadratic formula on the quotient.
  4. State every root, including repeats.

Worked example. Solve x³ − 2x² − 5x + 6 = 0.

f(1) = 1 - 2 - 5 + 6 = 0, so (x - 1) is a factor
divide: x³ - 2x² - 5x + 6 = (x - 1)(x² - x - 6)
                            = (x - 1)(x - 3)(x + 2)
roots: x = 1, 3, -2

Worked example 2 (repeated root). Solve x³ − 3x + 2 = 0.

f(1) = 0  →  (x - 1) is a factor
divide: (x - 1)(x² + x - 2) = (x - 1)(x + 2)(x - 1)
roots: x = 1 (repeated) and x = -2; the curve touches the axis at x = 1

A repeated root is a tangency, which is why a cubic can have two distinct roots but three real ones counted with multiplicity.

Partial fractions with an irreducible quadratic

for a factor (x² + px + q) with no real roots:
(ax + b)/[(x - c)(x² + px + q)] = A/(x - c) + (Bx + C)/(x² + px + q)

Worked example. Express (3x + 1)/[x(x² + 1)] in partial fractions.

3x + 1 = A(x² + 1) + (Bx + C)x
x = 0: 1 = A
compare x²: 0 = A + B  →  B = -1
compare x: 3 = C
so 1/x + (-x + 3)/(x² + 1)

The numerator over a quadratic factor must be linear (Bx + C); a constant alone cannot satisfy the coefficients in general.

One linear and one quadratic equation

Simultaneous equations where one is a circle or parabola are solved by substitution, producing a quadratic whose roots give the intersection points.

Worked example. Solve y = x + 1 and x² + y² = 25.

substitute: x² + (x + 1)² = 25
2x² + 2x + 1 = 25  →  x² + x - 12 = 0
(x + 4)(x - 3) = 0  →  x = -4 or 3
points: (-4, -3) and (3, 4)

A line and a curve meet in 0, 1 or 2 points; the discriminant of the substituted quadratic tells you which, without solving — a standard link to the next section.

Surds and rationalising

rationalise 1/(a + sqrt b) by multiplying by (a - sqrt b)/(a - sqrt b)
denominator becomes a² - b, which is rational

Worked example. Simplify 3/(2 + √5).

multiply by (2 - sqrt 5)/(2 - sqrt 5):
3(2 - sqrt 5)/(4 - 5) = 3(2 - sqrt 5)/(-1) = 3 sqrt 5 - 6

Worked example 2. Solve x² − 6x + 2 = 0, giving answers in surd form.

x = [6 +/- √(36 - 8)]/2 = (6 +/- sqrt 28)/2 = 3 +/- sqrt 7

Surd answers should be simplified (√28 = 2√7) and, where the question asks, rationalised.

Algebraic fractions and cancelling

Simplifying an algebraic fraction requires factorising both parts first; cancelling terms before factorising is invalid because a sum is not a product.

Worked example. Simplify (x² − 9)/(x² + x − 6).

factorise: (x - 3)(x + 3)/[(x + 3)(x - 2)]
cancel (x + 3): (x - 3)/(x - 2), valid for x not 3 or -2

Worked example 2 (addition). Write 1/(x − 1) + 2/(x + 2) as a single fraction.

common denominator: [(x + 2) + 2(x - 1)]/[(x - 1)(x + 2)]
= (3x)/[(x - 1)(x + 2)]

The excluded values belong in the answer: a cancelled factor leaves a hole in the domain, which the equation's original form still cannot accept.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Remainder) Find the remainder when x³ + 2x − 4 is divided by (x − 1). Answer: 1 + 2 − 4 = −1.
  2. (Factor) Is (x + 3) a factor of x³ + 2x² − 5x + 6? Answer: f(−3) = −27 + 18 + 15 + 6 = 12 ≠ 0, no.
  3. (Unknown) f(x) = x³ + kx − 6 has (x − 2) as a factor. Find k. Answer: 8 + 2k − 6 = 0 → k = −1.
  4. (Partial fractions) Express 7/[(x − 1)(x + 6)]. Answer: 1/(x − 1) − 1/(x + 6).
  5. (Repeated) Express (2x + 1)/(x + 1)². Answer: 2/(x + 1) − 1/(x + 1)².
  6. (Improper) Express (x² + 1)/(x + 1). Answer: x − 1 + 2/(x + 1).
  7. (Modulus) Solve |x − 4| ≥ 3. Answer: x ≤ 1 or x ≥ 7.
  8. (Rational) Solve (x − 2)/(x + 1) < 1. Answer: (x − 2 − x − 1)/(x + 1) < 0 → −3/(x + 1) < 0 → x > −1.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Partial fractions for an improper fraction: divide first; the polynomial part is part of the answer.
  • Repeated factors written once: (x − a)² needs both A/(x − a) and B/(x − a)².
  • Cover-up used on repeating factors: the cover-up method substitutes only for distinct linear factors; for repeats, compare coefficients as well.
  • Sign of the remainder: f(a) gives the remainder when dividing by (x − a); for (x + a) substitute −a.
  • Missing powers in division: write 0x², 0x placeholders so the columns line up.
  • Multiplying inequalities by a variable: the sign may be negative; use a sign diagram instead.
  • Not excluding undefined values: a denominator's zero is never in the solution set; mark it as excluded.
  • Not checking: multiply the partial fractions back, or substitute one value, to confirm the decomposition.

title: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Sets and Venn Diagrams
content:
Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Sets and Venn Diagrams

Set notation is the language of sorting: it describes which elements belong together, which belong to both groups, and which belong to neither. The IGCSE questions are almost always Venn-diagram problems in disguise — a survey of students, a group of numbers, a club membership — and the marks come from filling every region correctly. This note builds the topic from zero: the notation and symbols, the two-set and three-set Venn diagrams and how to shade them, the counting formulas, and the word-problem method that never misses a region.

Set notation and vocabulary

SymbolMeaningExample
∈is an element of3 ∈ {1, 2, 3}
∉is not an element of5 ∉ {1, 2, 3}
ξ (or U)the universal set — everything under discussionξ = {1, 2, ..., 12}
∅the empty setodd multiples of 2 = ∅
A′the complement of A — everything in ξ not in AA′ = ξ A
A ∪ Bunion — in A or B or both{1,2} ∪ {2,3} = {1,2,3}
A ∩ Bintersection — in both{1,2} ∩ {2,3} = {2}
n(A)the number of elements of An({2, 4, 6}) = 3

Two rules follow directly: A ∩ A′ = ∅ (nothing is both in and out), and A ∪ A′ = ξ (everything is one or the other). Subsets: A ⊂ B means every element of A is also in B. The empty set has no elements, so n(∅) = 0, and it is a subset of every set — a fact worth stating explicitly when a question asks whether ∅ ⊂ A is true.

Two-set Venn diagrams

A two-set diagram divides the universal set into four regions: only A, only B, both, and neither. Filling them from the inside out is the reliable method:

  1. Write the number in the intersection (both) first.
  2. Work outward: only A = n(A) − both; only B = n(B) − both.
  3. Neither = total − (only A + only B + both).

Worked example. In a class of 32, 18 study French, 15 study Spanish, and 7 study both. Find the number studying only French, only Spanish, and neither.

both = 7
only French = 18 - 7 = 11
only Spanish = 15 - 7 = 8
neither = 32 - (11 + 8 + 7) = 32 - 26 = 6

Worked example 2 (reverse). In a group, 20 like tea, 14 like coffee and 5 like neither. Everyone likes at least one of the two? Then find n(tea ∩ coffee).

n(T union C) = 20 + 14 - both
total = 20 + 14 - both + 5 = 39 - both
If the group has 30 people: 30 = 39 - both → both = 9

The inclusion–exclusion formula

n(A union B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A intersection B)

for three sets:
n(A u B u C) = n(A) + n(B) + n(C)
             - n(A n B) - n(A n C) - n(B n C)
             + n(A n B n C)

The subtraction corrects double counting; the final addition corrects the triple-counted centre. Knowing the formula lets you answer "how many in total" questions without a full diagram, but a diagram is still the safer route for word problems.

Worked example. A survey of 50 people: 30 read newspapers, 25 read magazines, 12 read both. How many read at least one?

n(N union M) = 30 + 25 - 12 = 43
neither = 50 - 43 = 7

Three-set Venn diagrams

The three-set diagram has eight regions (counting "none of the three"). The fill order that never fails:

  1. Start with the triple intersection (all three).
  2. Find the "exactly two" regions by subtracting the triple from each pair.
  3. Find the "only one" regions by subtracting the pair and triple totals from each set total.
  4. Find "none" from the grand total.

Worked example. 40 students choose subjects: 20 take Maths, 18 take Physics, 15 take Chemistry; 8 take Maths and Physics, 6 take Maths and Chemistry, 5 take Physics and Chemistry; 3 take all three. Find how many take exactly one subject and how many take none.

triple = 3
exactly M and P = 8 - 3 = 5
exactly M and C = 6 - 3 = 3
exactly P and C = 5 - 3 = 2
only M = 20 - (5 + 3 + 3) = 9
only P = 18 - (5 + 2 + 3) = 8
only C = 15 - (3 + 2 + 3) = 7
exactly one = 9 + 8 + 7 = 24
total counted = 24 + 5 + 3 + 2 + 3 = 37
none = 40 - 37 = 3

Sets of numbers and shading

Questions often use number sets inside the universal set: ξ = {1, 2, ..., 20}, A = multiples of 3, B = multiples of 4. List them, then use the same four regions:

A = {3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18}
B = {4, 8, 12, 16, 20}
A n B = {12}
A u B = {3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 12, 15, 16, 18, 20}
neither = {1, 2, 5, 7, 10, 11, 13, 14, 17, 19}

Shading questions ask for a region described in symbols. Translate the symbols into words first: A′ ∩ B means "not in A, but in B" — the part of B outside A. A ∪ B′ means "in A, or outside B" — everything except the part of B that is not in A.

Listing sets and set-builder notation

Sets can be written in three ways, and questions move between them. The roster method lists the elements: A = {2, 4, 6, 8}. The description method states the rule in words: A is the set of even numbers from 2 to 8. Set-builder notation states the rule symbolically: A = {x : x is an even number, 2 ≤ x ≤ 8} — read as "the set of all x such that x is even and between 2 and 8".

  • Roster for finite sets: list every element once, in braces, separated by commas; order does not matter and repeats are not counted twice.
  • Description for patterns: "multiples of 3 less than 30" is clearer than listing ten numbers.
  • Set-builder for precision: the colon means "such that"; the condition after it does the work.

Worked example. Write the set of odd numbers between 1 and 11 in roster and set-builder form, and find its size.

roster: {3, 5, 7, 9}  (strictly between, so 1 and 11 excluded)
set-builder: {x : x odd, 1 < x < 11}
n(A) = 4

Reading the inequalities is the trap: "between" usually excludes the endpoints, "from ... to ..." usually includes them, and the question's wording decides. When in doubt, list both interpretations and choose the one consistent with the other numbers in the question.

Worked examples: word problems

Worked example. In a hostel of 60 students, 35 play football, 28 play basketball, and 12 play both. How many play neither?

at least one = 35 + 28 - 12 = 51
neither = 60 - 51 = 9

Worked example 2 (with a variable). In a group of 25, x people like both tea and coffee, 12 like tea only and 8 like coffee only. Find x if everyone likes at least one.

12 + 8 + x = 25  →  x = 5

Worked example 3 (conditional language). Of 40 students, 24 study History, 18 study Geography and 6 study neither. How many study both?

at least one = 40 - 6 = 34
34 = 24 + 18 - both  →  both = 42 - 34 = 8

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Notation) ξ = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8}; A = {2, 4, 6, 8}; B = {1, 3, 5, 7}. Find A ∩ B and A ∪ B. Answer: A ∩ B = ∅; A ∪ B = ξ.
  2. (Complement) With A = {2, 4, 6, 8} in ξ above, list A′. Answer: A′ is everything in ξ that is not in A: ξ = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8} and A = {2, 4, 6, 8}, so A′ = {1, 3, 5, 7}.
  3. (Two sets) n(A) = 14, n(B) = 9, n(A ∩ B) = 4. Find n(A ∪ B). Answer: the overlap is counted twice when the sizes are added, so take it off once: n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B) = 14 + 9 − 4 = 19.
  4. (Neither) In a class of 30, 17 like cricket, 12 like tennis and 5 like both. Find the number who like neither. Answer: at least one = 24; neither = 6.
  5. (Three sets) 30 students: 15 like Maths, 12 like Physics, 10 like Chemistry; 5 like Maths and Physics, 4 like Maths and Chemistry, 3 like Physics and Chemistry, 2 like all three. Find the number who like exactly one. Answer: only M = 15 − (3 + 2 + 2) = 8; only P = 12 − (3 + 1 + 2) = 6; only C = 10 − (2 + 1 + 2) = 5; total = 19 (with exactly-two counts 3, 2, 1 and triple 2).
  6. (Shading) Describe the region A′ ∩ B in words. Answer: Elements in B but not in A — the part of B outside A.
  7. (Numbers) ξ = {1, ..., 20}; A = even numbers; B = multiples of 5. Find n(A ∩ B). Answer: A ∩ B holds the numbers that are both even and a multiple of 5, i.e. multiples of 10; up to 20 those are 10 and 20, so n(A ∩ B) = 2.
  8. (Reasoning) Explain why n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) is wrong when A and B overlap. Answer: The elements in both sets are counted twice in n(A) + n(B), so the intersection must be subtracted once: n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B).

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Filling the intersection last: start at the centre. Adding both set totals and forgetting the overlap counts shared elements twice.
  • Forgetting the "neither" region: the universal set includes elements outside all named sets; if the question gives a total, subtract to find them.
  • Confusing ∪ and ∩: union is "or" (everything), intersection is "and" (only the middle). A quick mnemonic: ∪ looks like a cup that holds everything.
  • Shading the wrong side for A′: the complement is everything outside A, including parts of other sets and the region outside them all.
  • Triple intersection double subtraction: when subtracting pairs, remember each pair already includes the triple; subtract the triple from each pair before using them.
  • Reading "only": "only A" means A and nothing else — exclude the overlaps. The word only is a region instruction, not decoration.
  • Notation in answers: list elements with braces and commas; do not write 1, 2, 3 as an unbraced list when the answer is a set.
  • Assuming everyone likes something: unless stated, some may be outside both sets — check whether the total equals the sum of the regions.

The four regions: reading a Venn diagram as a counting grid

A two-set Venn diagram is not a picture of two sets. It is a grid with four cells, and every question about it is answered by putting a number in each cell and adding.

Name the four cells before you write anything. For sets A and B inside a universal set ξ, every element is in exactly one of: only A, both, only B, neither. In the figure that is 7, 5, 9 and 4. The moment all four numbers are on the page, every part of the question is a sum:

n(A) = 7 + 5 = 12 Key: n(A) counts everything inside circle A, including the overlap.
n(A ∩ B) = 5 Key: the intersection — the region inside both circles.
n(A ∪ B) = 7 + 5 + 9 = 21 Key: the union — everything inside at least one circle.
n(ξ) = 21 + 4 = 25 Key: the universal set also counts what is in neither set.

Why the formula has a minus sign. Adding n(A) and n(B) counts the overlap twice — once with each circle — so it has to come back off:

n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B) Key: n(A ∪ B) = elements in at least one set; n(A ∩ B) = elements in both. In the figure, 12 + 14 − 5 = 21, which is exactly the sum of the three inner cells. The subtraction is not a rule to remember; it is the double count being removed.

Worked example. In a class of 30, 18 study French, 15 study Spanish and 6 study both. How many study neither?

French only = 18 − 6 = 12
Spanish only = 15 − 6 = 9
at least one = 12 + 6 + 9 = 27
neither = 30 − 27 = 3

Going the other way — "9 study neither" — is the same arithmetic in reverse, and it is the version that appears when the examiner wants an unknown: if the total is 30 and 9 study neither, then 21 study at least one, and 18 + 15 − x = 21 gives x = 12 studying both. Filling the grid from the overlap outwards always works, because the overlap is the only cell that belongs to both circles.

Where marks are lost. Treating "18 study French" as 18 in the French-only region, which double-counts 6. Forgetting the neither region, so the four numbers do not add to the total. And shading the wrong side for A′ ∩ B: the complement of A is everything outside A, so A′ ∩ B is the B-only region, not the overlap.

Sets: the building blocks of counting

A set is a well-defined collection of objects, called its elements or members. In IGCSE Mathematics, sets are used to organise numbers and to count how many items share or avoid a property. Questions on this statement test three things: reading and writing set notation, drawing and filling Venn diagrams, and using counting rules without double-counting. The subsections below take these one at a time.

What counts as a set

A set is defined by a rule that tells you, for any object, whether it is in the set or not. "The even numbers less than 10" is a set because every number either is or is not an even number less than 10. A list such as "some tall students" is not a set, because two people might disagree about who is tall. Exam questions always use clear rules, so the first step is to write each set as a list or a rule before counting anything.

Writing a set in roster form

Roster form lists every element between curly brackets, separated by commas. The set of prime numbers less than 12 is {2, 3, 5, 7, 11}. The order of the elements does not matter, and an element is never written twice. Roster form is quickest for small sets, and it is the form the examiner usually expects when a question says "list the elements".

The element and not-element symbols

The symbol ∈ means "is an element of", and ∉ means "is not an element of". So 4 ∈ {1, 2, 3, 4} is true, and 5 ∉ {1, 2, 3, 4} is also true. These symbols are used in statements about membership, and they should be read aloud as whole sentences when you check an answer, because a reversed symbol reverses the meaning of the statement.

The empty set

The empty set, written ∅ or { }, contains no elements at all. The set of whole numbers that are both odd and even is the empty set, because no number has both properties. The empty set is a subset of every set, and in a Venn diagram it is shown by a region with no number in it. Do not confuse ∅ with the set containing zero, {0}, which has one element.

Subsets and the subset symbol

A set A is a subset of a set B when every element of A is also an element of B, and this is written A ⊂ B. For example, {1, 2} ⊂ {1, 2, 3, 4} because both 1 and 2 are in the larger set. Every set is a subset of itself, and the empty set is a subset of every set. A question asking whether one set is a subset of another can be answered by checking each element of the first set in turn.

Equal sets

Two sets are equal when they contain exactly the same elements, whatever order they are listed in. So {3, 1, 2} and {1, 2, 3} are equal, because both contain the numbers 1, 2 and 3 and no others. A repeated element does not make a set bigger, so {1, 1, 2} is the same set as {1, 2}. This is why counting the elements of a set means counting distinct members.

The number of elements in a set

The number of elements in a set A is written n(A). For A = {2, 4, 6, 8}, n(A) = 4. The notation is used in every counting formula in the Venn diagram work later in this note, so write it carefully. A common slip is to count the brackets, the commas or the repeated entries rather than the distinct elements.

Union, intersection and complement

Three operations combine or select sets, and every Venn diagram question uses at least one of them. The union collects everything in either set, the intersection keeps only what is common to both, and the complement takes everything outside a set. The subsections below define each operation, show how it is written, and give a method for working with them.

The universal set

Most set questions give a universal set, written ξ, which contains every element under discussion. The complement of a set is always taken relative to the universal set. If ξ is the set of integers from 1 to 10, then the complement of the even numbers is the odd numbers within those ten integers. Always state the universal set before you find any complement, because the same set has a different complement in a different universe.

Union: everything in either set

The union of A and B, written A ∪ B, is the set of all elements that are in A, or in B, or in both. For A = {1, 2, 3} and B = {3, 4}, the union is A ∪ B = {1, 2, 3, 4}. The element 3 appears once in the answer, even though it is in both sets. The word "or" in mathematics includes the case where both are true, so the union is never smaller than either set on its own.

Intersection: what the two sets share

The intersection of A and B, written A ∩ B, is the set of elements that are in both A and B. For the same sets, A ∩ B = {3}. If two sets have no elements in common, their intersection is the empty set, and the sets are called disjoint. The word "and" in a question such as "students who play both hockey and tennis" points to an intersection.

Complement: everything not in the set

The complement of A, written A′ (read as "A dash"), is the set of all elements of the universal set that are not in A. With ξ = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} and A = {1, 2, 3}, the complement is A′ = {4, 5}. Every element of ξ is in exactly one of A and A′, so the two together account for the whole universal set. This is a useful check when you list a complement by hand.

Combining operations in one expression

Expressions such as (A ∪ B)′ or A ∩ B′ contain more than one operation. Work inside the brackets first, and then apply the outer operation. For A = {1, 2, 3}, B = {3, 4} and ξ = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}, the union A ∪ B is {1, 2, 3, 4}, so its complement is {5}. Writing each stage on a separate line makes the working easy to mark.

Reading the notation in words

Translating between symbols and words is a skill in its own right. A ∪ B is "A or B", A ∩ B is "A and B", and A′ is "not A". A question that asks for "students who do not study French" describes the complement of the French set. Write the set in symbols first, then check your answer against the words of the question before you count.

Identifying the sets from a list

Given a list of properties, the sets are found by reading each property as a rule. For instance, "the multiples of 3 from 1 to 20" is {3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18}. Construct each set from its rule separately, then apply the operation the question asks for. This prevents mixing up the elements of the two sets when the question involves several properties at once.

Checking an answer with the universal set

When a result is a union or an intersection, check that every element is inside the universal set, and that no element of A or B is missing. When a result is a complement, check that it and the original set together make up the universal set with no overlap. These two checks take a few seconds and catch most of the errors made with set operations.

title: Plant Nutrition
content:
Plant Nutrition

Cambridge IGCSE Biology 0610, Extended route, topic 6 (statements 6.1–6.2). The photosynthesis equation, limiting factors, uses of glucose, mineral requirements and leaf structure as adaptations.

6.1 Photosynthesis

  • Carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen, in the presence of light and chlorophyll. Balanced: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂.
  • Glucose is used for: respiration, making cellulose for cell walls, making starch for storage, making amino acids when combined with mineral ions, and making oils. Mineral ions needed include nitrate (for amino acids and proteins), magnesium (for chlorophyll) and phosphate.
  • A limiting factor is the variable in shortest supply — light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration or temperature — which caps the rate. Raising a limiting factor raises the rate until another factor becomes limiting.

6.2 Leaf structure

  • Upper epidermis, palisade mesophyll (packed with chloroplasts, at the top for maximum light), spongy mesophyll (large air spaces for gas exchange), lower epidermis with stomata (guard cells control opening), and veins carrying water in and sugars out.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Limiting factor analysis, applied to a graph of photosynthesis rate against light intensity at two CO₂ levels: the curve rises then plateaus; the plateau is set by CO₂ concentration or temperature. When asked which factor limits at a point, name the variable that, if increased, would raise the rate — that is the operational definition examiners want.
  • Mineral deficiency reasoning, applied to a plant with yellowing young leaves in magnesium-deficient soil: magnesium is the central ion in chlorophyll, so without it chlorophyll cannot be made and chlorosis appears. Nitrate deficiency gives poor growth overall because amino acids, and therefore proteins, cannot be synthesised.
  • Adaptation reasoning, applied to why palisade cells are column-shaped and stacked: the shape packs the maximum chloroplasts near the light, and vertical orientation lets light penetrate. Tie each structural feature to its function explicitly — each pairing is its own mark.
  • Equation writing, applied to a word-symbol answer: include the balanced symbol equation with the condition above the arrow, light and chlorophyll. An unbalanced equation loses the mark even when the chemistry is right.

Common errors

  • Writing water as a product instead of a reactant in the photosynthesis equation.
  • Saying stomata open "to let carbon dioxide in" as a complete answer — guard cell turgor caused by potassium ion movement is the mechanism.
  • Confusing magnesium (chlorophyll) with nitrate (amino acids) when explaining deficiencies.

title: Exam technique: Waves (AS)
content:
### What earns the marks
