For phase, one lambda equated to 360 degrees earns the mark. For refraction, n = c/v quoted earns the method mark. For TIR, both conditions stated earn one mark each with sin c = 1/n earning the calculation mark.
### Traps
Error: TIR claimed with one condition only. Correction: denser medium plus beyond critical angle. Error: spectrum order flipped. Correction: radio longest, gamma shortest. Error: phase from amplitude guessed. Correction: phase comes from path or time difference.

title: Programming and Algorithms — Study Notes
content:
`# Programming and Algorithms

Cambridge International AS & A Level Computer Science 9618: sections 9, 11 and 12 (Algorithm design; Programming; Software development), examined in AS Paper 2.

Design Approaches

  • Top-down (stepwise refinement): decompose into modules — planned structure
  • Object-oriented: classes encapsulating state + behaviour — reusability
  • WAD (write all down): rapid prototyping — evolves during coding

Pseudocode Conventions

DECLARE x : INTEGER
IF x > 10 THEN ... ELSE ... ENDIF
WHILE ... ENDWHILE
FOR i ← 1 TO n ... NEXT i
FUNCTION f(a) RETURNS INTEGER

Searching

  • Linear: check each item, O(n), works unsorted
  • Binary: halve a sorted list each step, O(log n)

Example: 1,000,000 items: binary search needs ≤ 20 comparisons.

Sorting

AlgorithmBestAverageIdea
BubbleO(n)O(n²)swap neighbours
InsertionO(n)O(n²)insert into sorted prefix
MergeO(n log n)O(n log n)divide and merge

Merge sort example: [5,2,9,1] → [5,2][9,1] → [2,5][1,9] → [1,2,5,9].

Recursion

A function calling itself with a base case. Factorial: f(0)=1, f(n)=n·f(n−1). Stack frames handle state.

Exam tips: state the Big-O and justify it; for traces, tabulate variable changes per iteration.

Testing with normal, boundary and erroneous data

Normal test data is typical valid input that the program should accept and process correctly. Boundary (extreme) test data sits at the edges of the valid range, such as the lowest and highest permitted values, because errors often occur there. Erroneous test data is invalid input that the program should reject, such as text entered where a number is required.

A trace table records the value of each variable at each step of an algorithm. Tracing a algorithm by hand with test data shows where it departs from the intended result, and it is a common exam task.

Exam tip: a complete test plan includes all three kinds of data, with the expected output written beside each test value.

Worked example: tracing a binary search

Search for 23 in the sorted list 2, 5, 8, 12, 16, 23, 38, 56, 72, 91. The first middle position is (0 + 9) ÷ 2 = 4 (rounded down), which holds 16. Since 23 is greater than 16, the lower bound becomes 5. The next middle is (5 + 9) ÷ 2 = 7, which holds 56. Since 23 is less than 56, the upper bound becomes 6. The next middle is (5 + 6) ÷ 2 = 5, which holds 23, so the item is found after 3 comparisons. A linear search of the same list would need 6 comparisons.

Worked example: bubble sort passes

Sort 5, 1, 4, 2, 8 into ascending order. In the first pass the algorithm compares adjacent pairs and swaps them when they are out of order, giving 1, 4, 2, 5, 8. The second pass gives 1, 2, 4, 5, 8. A third pass makes no swaps, which shows the list is sorted. Stopping early when a pass has no swaps is a common improvement and is worth stating in an answer.

Worked example: recursion

The factorial function is defined as factorial(n) = n × factorial(n − 1), with the base case factorial(0) = 1. Then factorial(4) = 4 × factorial(3) = 4 × 3 × factorial(2) and so on until the base case is reached, giving 24. A recursive routine must always have a base case, otherwise it never stops and the stack overflows.

Exam point: a trace table with one column per variable is the clearest way to show an algorithm's steps, and it earns method marks even when the final answer is wrong.

title: A Level Mathematics: Integration II
content:
A Level Mathematics: Integration II

A2 integration extends the AS power rule to trigonometric and exponential functions, then adds the two general techniques — substitution and integration by parts — plus partial fractions, definite integrals with the new functions, areas, and differential equations. Each technique is presented with its recognition cue: which integrand signals which method is the skill the exam rewards.

Standard integrals to know

integral of sin(ax) dx = -(1/a) cos(ax) + c
integral of cos(ax) dx = (1/a) sin(ax) + c
integral of sec²(ax) dx = (1/a) tan(ax) + c
integral of e^(ax) dx = (1/a) e^(ax) + c
integral of (1/x) dx = ln|x| + c
integral of (1/(ax + b)) dx = (1/a) ln|ax + b| + c

Worked example. Find ∫ (3 sin 2x + 4e^(−x)) dx.

= -(3/2) cos 2x - 4e^(-x) + c

Worked example 2. Find ∫ (1/(3x + 1)) dx.

= (1/3) ln|3x + 1| + c

Trigonometric identities before integrating

Products and even powers of sine and cosine do not integrate directly; use an identity first.

sin² x = (1 - cos 2x)/2
cos² x = (1 + cos 2x)/2
sin A cos B = (1/2)[sin(A + B) + sin(A - B)]

Worked example. Find ∫ sin²x dx.

= integral of (1 - cos 2x)/2 dx = x/2 - (sin 2x)/4 + c

Worked example 2. Find ∫ sin 3x cos x dx.

sin 3x cos x = (1/2)[sin 4x + sin 2x]
integral = -(1/8) cos 4x - (1/4) cos 2x + c

Integration by substitution

let u = g(x), du = g'(x) dx; rewrite the whole integral in u
for definite integrals, change the limits too

Worked example 1. Find ∫ 2x(x² + 1)⁵ dx.

u = x² + 1, du = 2x dx
integral becomes ∫ u⁵ du = u⁶/6 + c = (x² + 1)⁶/6 + c

Worked example 2 (definite). Find ∫ from 0 to 1 of x e^(x²) dx.

u = x², du = 2x dx, so x dx = du/2
limits: x = 0 → u = 0;  x = 1 → u = 1
= (1/2) ∫ from 0 to 1 e^u du = (1/2)(e - 1) = 0.859

Worked example 3 (trigonometric). Find ∫ cos x sin³x dx.

u = sin x, du = cos x dx
∫ u³ du = sin⁴ x/4 + c

Integration by parts

∫ u dv = uv - ∫ v du

choose u to be the part that simplifies when differentiated
(LIATE: logs, inverse trig, algebra, trig, exponential)

Worked example 1. Find ∫ x e^x dx.

u = x, dv = e^x dx  →  du = dx, v = e^x
= x e^x - ∫ e^x dx = x e^x - e^x + c = e^x(x - 1) + c

Worked example 2. Find ∫ x cos x dx.

u = x, dv = cos x dx  →  du = dx, v = sin x
= x sin x - ∫ sin x dx = x sin x + cos x + c

Worked example 3 (logarithm). Find ∫ ln x dx.

u = ln x, dv = dx  →  du = dx/x, v = x
= x ln x - ∫ 1 dx = x ln x - x + c

Worked example 4 (twice). Find ∫ x² e^x dx.

first: u = x², dv = e^x dx  →  x² e^x - 2∫ x e^x dx
second: ∫ x e^x = e^x(x - 1)
result: e^x(x² - 2x + 2) + c

Partial fractions in integration

(px + q)/[(x - a)(x - b)]  →  A/(x - a) + B/(x - b)
integrates to A ln|x - a| + B ln|x - b|

Worked example. Find ∫ 5/[(x − 1)(x + 4)] dx.

partial fractions: 1/(x - 1) - 1/(x + 4)
integral: ln|x - 1| - ln|x + 4| + c = ln|(x - 1)/(x + 4)| + c

Worked example 2 (repeated factor). Find ∫ 3/[(x + 1)²] dx.

= 3 ∫ (x + 1)⁻² dx = -3(x + 1)⁻¹ + c = -3/(x + 1) + c

Areas and volumes

area between curve and x-axis: definite integral (split at crossings)
volume of revolution about the x-axis: V = π ∫ y² dx

Worked example 1. Find the area under y = sin x from 0 to π.

[-cos x] from 0 to π = -(-1) - (-1) = 2 square units

Worked example 2 (volume). The region under y = x from 0 to 2 is rotated about the x-axis. Find the volume.

V = π ∫ from 0 to 2 of x² dx = π [x³/3] = 8 π/3 = 8.38 cubic units

The π multiplies the whole integral; forgetting it is the classic error.

Differential equations

separable: dy/dx = f(x) g(y)  →  ∫ dy/g(y) = ∫ f(x) dx

apply the boundary condition to find the constant

Worked example. Solve dy/dx = xy with y = 3 when x = 0.

∫ dy/y = ∫ x dx
ln|y| = x²/2 + c
y = A e^(x²/2);  at x = 0, y = 3  →  A = 3
y = 3e^(x²/2)

Worked example 2 (rate of cooling). dT/dt = −k(T − 20), T = 90 when t = 0, T = 60 when t = 10. Find T at t = 25.

∫ dT/(T - 20) = -k ∫ dt  →  ln(T - 20) = -kt + c
T - 20 = A e^(-kt);  at t = 0, A = 70
at t = 10: 40 = 70 e^(-10k)  →  k = 0.0560
at t = 25: T = 20 + 70e^(-1.4) = 37.3 °C

Choosing a method: the recognition cues

A2 integration is not a list of tricks to try at random; each integrand shape points at one method. Reading the shape before writing anything is the skill the exam actually tests.

Shape of the integrandMethodWhy
a function times its own derivativesubstitutionthe derivative becomes du
product of two unrelated functionsintegration by partsone factor is integrated, the other differentiated
a rational function with factorable denominatorpartial fractionseach part integrates to a logarithm
even powers of sin and cosdouble-angle identitylowers the power to a single wave
no elementary antiderivative (e.g. e^(−x²))numerical methodthe trapezium rule approximates it

Worked example (cue check). Name the method for each: ∫ 2x(x² + 1)⁵ dx, ∫ x e^x dx, ∫ (3x + 1)/(x² + x) dx.

first: 2x is the derivative of x² + 1  →  substitution u = x² + 1
second: x and e^x are unrelated  →  by parts with u = x
third: denominator factors x(x + 1)  →  partial fractions

Definite integrals with substitution

When a definite integral is evaluated by substitution, the limits belong to the old variable and must be converted to the new one. Forgetting this is the most common single error in the whole topic, and it is invisible if the answer happens to be close.

integral from x = a to x = b of f(x) dx
with u = g(x):  limits become u = g(a) and u = g(b)
then integrate in u with no conversion back

Worked example. Evaluate ∫ from 0 to 2 of x(x² + 1)³ dx.

u = x² + 1, du = 2x dx  →  x dx = du/2
limits: x = 0 → u = 1;  x = 2 → u = 5
integral = (1/2) ∫ from 1 to 5 of u³ du = (1/2)[u⁴/4] from 1 to 5
= (1/8)(625 - 1) = 78

Worked example 2 (by parts, definite). Evaluate ∫ from 0 to 1 of x e^(2x) dx.

u = x, dv = e^(2x) dx  →  du = dx, v = e^(2x)/2
= [x e^(2x)/2] from 0 to 1 - ∫ from 0 to 1 of e^(2x)/2 dx
= e²/2 - 0 - [e^(2x)/4] from 0 to 1
= e²/2 - (e²/4 - 1/4) = (e² + 1)/4 = 2.097

The trapezium rule

When no antiderivative exists in elementary terms, the area is estimated by joining the sampled heights with straight lines. Each strip is a trapezium, so the rule is exact for straight lines and underestimates for curves that bend upwards.

h = (b - a)/n  (width of each strip)
area = (h/2)[y0 + 2(y1 + y2 + ... + y(n-1)) + yn]
first and last heights counted once, all interior heights twice

Worked example. Use the trapezium rule with 4 strips to estimate ∫ from 0 to 1 of e^(−x²) dx.

h = 0.25;  heights at x = 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1
1, 0.9394, 0.7788, 0.5698, 0.3679
sum = 1 + 2(0.9394 + 0.7788 + 0.5698) + 0.3679 = 1 + 4.5760 + 0.3679 = 5.9439
area = (0.25/2)(5.9439) = 0.7430

Worked example 2 (error direction). The curve e^(−x²) is concave down on this interval. State whether the estimate is an over- or underestimate and how to improve it.

Tabulating the heights is worth the thirty seconds it costs. A single transcription error in one of five heights changes the answer but leaves the working looking correct, so the mark scheme cannot help you; writing the sample points in a column and summing them twice is the check that catches it. Mark schemes also accept the rule written in the equivalent form (h/2)(y0 + 2Σ interior + yn), which is often easier to key into a calculator without dropping a term.

chords lie below a concave-down curve, so the rule underestimates
halving h (doubling n) roughly quarters the error
an overestimate would need the curve concave up

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Standard) ∫ cos 3x dx. Answer: (1/3) sin 3x + c.
  2. (Identity) ∫ cos²x dx. Answer: x/2 + (sin 2x)/4 + c.
  3. (Substitution) ∫ 3x²(x³ + 1)⁴ dx. Answer: u = x³ + 1 → (x³ + 1)⁵/5 + c.
  4. (By parts) ∫ x sin x dx. Answer: −x cos x + sin x + c.
  5. (By parts log) ∫ x ln x dx. Answer: (x²/2)ln x − x²/4 + c.
  6. (Partial fractions) ∫ 4/[(x + 1)(x − 1)] dx. Answer: 2 ln|x − 1| − 2 ln|x + 1| + c.
  7. (Volume) y = x² rotated about x-axis from 0 to 1. Answer: π/5.
  8. (Differential equation) dy/dx = 2y, y = 5 at x = 0. Answer: y = 5e^(2x).

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Missing the reciprocal factor: ∫ cos 3x is (1/3)sin 3x, not sin 3x.
  • Integrating products directly: sin x cos x is not sin²x/2 by guesswork — use the identity.
  • Substitution without changing limits: definite integrals must convert the limits to the new variable, or convert back.
  • Wrong choice for u in by parts: choose the part that simplifies when differentiated; x and ln x are the standard picks.
  • Sign errors in by parts: the formula is uv − ∫v du; slipping the minus reverses the answer.
  • Forgetting the modulus in log integrals: ln|x| covers both signs.
  • Volume without π: the π multiplies the entire definite integral of y².
  • Differential equation constants: find the constant from the boundary condition and state the particular solution.

Equations and symbols

Every relation this topic is examined on, written with its real notation and followed by a key naming each symbol, its unit and what it means. Restaurant-bill questions, savings plans and areas under curves all reduce to one of these lines with numbers in it.

Standard integrals

∫ xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + c, n ≠ −1
Key: x = the variable; n = the power, any real except −1; c = the constant of integration. The power rule: raise the power by one and divide by the new power. The excluded case n = −1 is the logarithm below.

∫ (ax + b)ⁿ dx = (ax + b)ⁿ⁺¹/(a(n + 1)) + c, n ≠ −1
Key: a, b = constants with a ≠ 0; n = the power; c = constant. The extra 1/a is the chain rule undone — differentiating the answer brings it back.

∫ (1/x) dx = ln|x| + c and ∫ f′(x)/f(x) dx = ln|f(x)| + c
Key: x = the variable, x ≠ 0; f(x) = any differentiable function with f(x) ≠ 0; ln = natural logarithm; c = constant. The modulus is not decoration: it keeps the antiderivative valid where the function is negative but still defined.

∫ e^(ax) dx = (1/a)e^(ax) + c; ∫ sin(ax) dx = −(1/a)cos(ax) + c; ∫ cos(ax) dx = (1/a)sin(ax) + c; ∫ sec²(ax) dx = (1/a)tan(ax) + c
Key: a = constant frequency or rate, a ≠ 0; e = 2.71828…; c = constant. Each is its partner derivative run backwards, with the 1/a that the chain rule produced.

Substitution and parts

∫ f(g(x)) g′(x) dx = ∫ f(u) du, with u = g(x)
Key: u = the substitution; g′(x) = du/dx; f = the outer function. Valid when the integrand contains a function and (a multiple of) its derivative — the cue to look for a substitution at all. For a definite integral, change the limits to u-values rather than converting back.

∫ u (dv/dx) dx = uv − ∫ v (du/dx) dx
Key: u = the part differentiated; dv/dx = the part integrated; v = its integral. Choose u by the order that makes du/dx simpler — logarithm, then power, then exponential, then trigonometric. The formula transfers a hard integral into an easier one, so a wrong choice shows up as a worse integral, not as an error.

(px + q)/((x − a)(x − b)) = A/(x − a) + B/(x − b)
Key: p, q = the numerator's coefficients; a, b = the roots of the denominator; A, B = constants found by substituting x = a and x = b. Partial fractions turn a rational function into pieces that integrate to logarithms. A repeated factor (x − a)² needs an A/(x − a) term as well as B/(x − a)².

Definite integrals, areas and volumes

∫_{a}^{b} f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a)
Key: a, b = the lower and upper limits; f = the integrand; F = any antiderivative of f. The fundamental theorem: the definite integral is the antiderivative evaluated at the limits, and the constant c cancels.

area between y₁ and y₂ from x = a to x = b = ∫_{a}^{b} (y₁ − y₂) dx
Key: y₁ = the upper curve; y₂ = the lower curve; a, b = the x-values of the intersections. Subtract in the order upper minus lower; where the curves cross, split the interval, or the signed areas cancel.

V = π ∫_{a}^{b} y² dx
Key: V = the volume of the solid formed by rotating the curve about the x-axis; y = the curve's height; a, b = the limits along x; π = 3.14159…. Each thin slice is a disc of radius y, so the integrand is its area πy².

dy/dx = f(x)g(y) ⇒ ∫ (1/g(y)) dy = ∫ f(x) dx
Key: x = the independent variable; y = the dependent variable; f, g = given functions. Separating the variables is the whole method for a first-order differential equation; the constant of integration is fixed by the given condition, and the answer is usually left implicit.

∫_{a}^{b} f(x) dx ≈ (h/2)[y₀ + 2(y₁ + y₂ + … + yₙ₋₁) + yₙ], h = (b − a)/n
Key: h = the width of each strip; n = the number of strips; yᵢ = the function value at each ordinate; a, b = the limits. The trapezium rule: end ordinates once, interior ordinates twice. It overestimates for a curve that is concave up and underestimates for one that is concave down.

title: IGCSE Mathematics: Sequences and Functions
content:
IGCSE Mathematics: Sequences and Functions

Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580 (2025–2027), section 2 Algebra and graphs: statement 2.7 Sequences and statement 2.13 Functions (Extended). A sequence is a list of numbers generated by a rule; a function is the rule itself. This note builds nth-term rules from scratch — showing why the formula works, not just what it is — then function notation, composite functions and inverse functions, including the domain restrictions that decide whether an inverse exists.

What a sequence is; term-to-term rules

A sequence is an ordered list of numbers. The term-to-term rule gets from one term to the next: add 4, multiply by 2, subtract 1 then double. It tells you what happens step by step but not what the hundredth term is. The position-to-term rule (the nth term) gives any term directly from its position n, and that is the more powerful description.

Sequence: 3, 7, 11, 15, 19, ...

Term-to-term: add 4 each time.
Position-to-term: the terms are 4 less than 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, ..., so the nth term is 4n - 1.

Check: n = 1 gives 4(1) - 1 = 3 ✓;  n = 5 gives 4(5) - 1 = 19 ✓

Linear sequences and the nth term

A linear (arithmetic) sequence has a constant difference d between terms. Its nth term is dn + b, and b is chosen to make the first term correct.

Find the nth term of 5, 8, 11, 14, ...

Constant difference d = 3, so the nth term starts as 3n.
Compare with the sequence: 3, 6, 9, 12, ... is three times the table of 3;
the real sequence is 2 more each time, so b = 2.
nth term:  3n + 2

Check every term: n = 1: 5 ✓   n = 2: 8 ✓   n = 3: 11 ✓
The 50th term is 3(50) + 2 = 152.

Why dn + b always works. Adding d each time from a starting value a means the nth term is a + (n − 1)d, since term n has had (n − 1) additions of d. Expanding gives a + nd − d = nd + (a − d), which is exactly dn + b with b = a − d. Both forms are the same rule; examiners accept either.

Quadratic and special sequences

When the first difference changes but the second difference is constant, the rule is quadratic: an² + bn + c. The method: build the n² sequence, subtract it from the sequence, and finish the linear remainder.

Find the nth term of 2, 5, 10, 17, 26, ...

First differences: 3, 5, 7, 9;  second differences: 2, 2 (constant) → quadratic.
The n² sequence is 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, ...
Subtract: (2-1), (5-4), (10-9), (17-16), (26-25) = 1, 1, 1, 1, 1
So the sequence is n² + 1.

Check: n = 3 gives 9 + 1 = 10 ✓

Other sequences to recognise on sight: the triangular numbers n(n + 1)/2 (1, 3, 6, 10, ...), the square numbers n², the Fibonacci sequence (each term is the sum of the two before it, and it has no simple nth term), and geometric sequences that multiply by a fixed ratio r — their nth term is arⁿ⁻¹ where a is the first term.

Geometric example: 3, 6, 12, 24, ... has a = 3 and r = 2, so the nth term is 3 × 2^(n-1).
The 6th term is 3 × 2⁵ = 96.
Sequence typeExampleRule
Linear (arithmetic)5, 8, 11, 14Constant difference d; nth term dn + b
Quadratic2, 5, 10, 17Constant second difference; nth term an² + bn + c
Geometric3, 6, 12, 24Constant ratio r; nth term arⁿ⁻¹
Triangular numbers1, 3, 6, 10n(n + 1)/2
Square numbers1, 4, 9, 16n²
Fibonacci1, 1, 2, 3, 5Add the two previous terms (no simple nth term)

Choosing the right description is half the battle: check the first differences, then the second, then the ratio, before assuming any rule. Once a candidate rule is found, verify it against every given term — a sequence that matches only the first three terms is not proven.

Function notation

A function is a machine with an input and exactly one output for each input. The notation f(x) = 2x + 3 names the machine f and says what it does to x: multiply by 2, then add 3. Evaluating is substitution: f(4) = 2(4) + 3 = 11. The machine picture matters: one input never gives two outputs, though two inputs may share an output.

  • The domain is the set of allowed inputs; the range is the set of outputs the function actually produces.
  • For f(x) = x² with domain all real numbers, the range is y ⩾ 0, because squares are never negative.
  • For f(x) = 2x + 3 with domain 0 ⩽ x ⩽ 5, the range is 3 ⩽ f(x) ⩽ 13 — substitute the endpoints, since linear functions stretch ranges proportionally.

Questions ask for the range in terms of y or f(x); find the outputs at the domain boundaries and, for quadratics, at the turning point.

Composite functions

A composite function runs one machine after the other. fg(x) means apply g first, then f to the result — the notation reads right to left, like f(g(x)).

Given f(x) = 2x + 1 and g(x) = x², find fg(3), gf(x) and fg(x).

fg(3):  g(3) = 9, then f(9) = 2(9) + 1 = 19.
gf(x):  apply f first:  g(f(x)) = (2x + 1)² = 4x² + 4x + 1.
fg(x):  apply g first:  f(g(x)) = 2x² + 1.

Note fg(x) ≠ gf(x): order matters.

Every line is written out because the most common error is applying the functions in the wrong order — and the composite is not commutative.

Inverse functions

The inverse f⁻¹ undoes f: if f turns 4 into 11, f⁻¹ turns 11 back into 4. Inverse functions exist only for one-to-one functions — ones where different inputs always give different outputs. The graph of y = x² is not one-to-one over all real numbers (both 3 and −3 give 9), so it has no inverse unless the domain is restricted to x ⩾ 0.

Find the inverse of f(x) = (3x - 2)/5:

Write y = (3x - 2)/5 and make x the subject:
5y = 3x - 2          [multiply by 5]
5y + 2 = 3x          [add 2]
x = (5y + 2)/3       [divide by 3]

Swap x and y:  f⁻¹(x) = (5x + 2)/3

Check by composing: f⁻¹(f(x)) = [5((3x - 2)/5) + 2]/3 = [(3x - 2) + 2]/3 = 3x/3 = x  ✓
  • f⁻¹(x) is a single symbol meaning the inverse function; the −1 is not a power and f⁻¹(x) does not mean 1/f(x).
  • The domain of f⁻¹ is the range of f, and the range of f⁻¹ is the domain of f — they swap, exactly as the inputs and outputs swap roles.
  • Graphically, y = f⁻¹(x) is the reflection of y = f(x) in the line y = x.

Worked example: a full function question

Let f(x) = x² + 3 for x ⩾ 0, and g(x) = 4x − 5.

(a) Find f(2):  f(2) = 4 + 3 = 7.

(b) Find fg(x):  f(g(x)) = (4x - 5)² + 3 = 16x² - 40x + 25 + 3 = 16x² - 40x + 28.

(c) Find f⁻¹(x):  y = x² + 3, so x² = y - 3 and x = √(y - 3) (positive root, since x ⩾ 0).
Swap: f⁻¹(x) = √(x - 3).
Domain of f⁻¹: x ⩾ 3, which is exactly the range of f.

(d) Solve f(x) = 30 for x ⩾ 0:
x² + 3 = 30
x² = 27
x = √27 = 3√3 ≈ 5.20        [only the positive root is in the domain]

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Reading fg(x) as f then g. It is g first, then f — the notation runs right to left.
  • Assuming fg = gf; only special cases agree.
  • Treating f⁻¹(x) as 1/f(x). The inverse undoes the function; it is not a reciprocal.
  • Ignoring domain restrictions: with x ⩾ 0 on f(x) = x² + 3, the inverse takes the positive root only, and a negative root answer is wrong.
  • Claiming y = x² has an inverse over all real numbers; it is two-to-one and needs a restricted domain.
  • Building the nth term from the first difference alone without checking every term; a single wrong check sends a whole answer wrong.
  • Writing a geometric nth term as arⁿ instead of arⁿ⁻¹; the first term must be a itself.
  • Stating a range that ignores the turning point of a quadratic: the range of y = (x − 2)² + 1 is y ⩾ 1, not y ⩾ 0.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 2, 3 marks). Find the nth term of 7, 11, 15, 19, ...

Answer: Constant difference 4, so 4n + b; the first term 7 = 4 + b gives b = 3. The nth term is 4n + 3. The 20th term is 83.

Question 2 (Paper 2, 3 marks). A sequence has nth term 5n − 2. Write down the first four terms and the 100th.

Answer: n = 1, 2, 3, 4 give 3, 8, 13, 18; the 100th term is 5(100) − 2 = 498.

Question 3 (Paper 4, 4 marks). f(x) = 3x − 1 and g(x) = x² + 2. Find fg(x), gf(2) and f⁻¹(x).

Answer: fg(x) = 3(x² + 2) − 1 = 3x² + 5. gf(2): f(2) = 5, so g(5) = 27. Inverse: y = 3x − 1 gives x = (y + 1)/3, so f⁻¹(x) = (x + 1)/3.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 4 marks). The second differences of a sequence are constant at 4, and its first two terms are 2 and 7. Find the nth term.

Answer: Constant second difference 4 means the n² coefficient is 4/2 = 2, so the rule starts 2n². The n² sequence gives 2, 8, ... while the sequence is 2, 7, ..., so the remainder is 0, −1, ... a linear part with difference −1: −n + 1. Check: 2n² − n + 1 gives n = 1: 2 ✓ and n = 2: 8 − 2 + 1 = 7 ✓. The nth term is 2n² − n + 1.

Question 5 (Paper 4, 5 marks). f(x) = (x + 4)/(x − 2) for x ≠ 2. Find f⁻¹(x) and the value of x for which f(x) is undefined.

Answer: y = (x + 4)/(x − 2) gives y(x − 2) = x + 4, so yx − 2y = x + 4, yx − x = 2y + 4, x(y − 1) = 2y + 4 and x = (2y + 4)/(y − 1). Swapping: f⁻¹(x) = (2x + 4)/(x − 1). The function itself is undefined at x = 2, where the denominator vanishes; its inverse is undefined at x = 1.

Question 6 (Paper 2, 3 marks). The first three terms of a geometric sequence are 5, 15, 45. Find the 8th term.

Answer: Common ratio r = 15/5 = 3, so the nth term is 5 × 3ⁿ⁻¹ and the 8th term is 5 × 3⁷ = 5 × 2187 = 10 935.

From variables and patterns, the course now turns to the number system itself.

Sequences: terms, term-to-term rules and position rules

A sequence is an ordered list of numbers that follows a rule. Each number in the list is a term, and the position of a term in the list is its term number, written n. Exam questions give a sequence and ask for a missing term, a rule, or a check on whether a particular number belongs to the pattern. The subsections below cover the two kinds of rule and how to move between them.

Reading a sequence and naming its terms

Write the first term as the term with n = 1, the second as n = 2, and so on. In the sequence 5, 8, 11, 14, the first term is 5 and the fourth term is 14. Read the terms from left to right, and keep the positions fixed, because a term that is shifted by one place gives a wrong answer even when the arithmetic is correct.

Term-to-term rules

A term-to-term rule says how to get the next term from the one before it. "Add 3 each time" and "multiply by 2 each time" are term-to-term rules. To use one, start from a known term and apply the rule repeatedly. A term-to-term rule is quick to apply to a few terms, but it is slow to find a term far down the list, which is why the position rule is needed.

Position-to-term rules, or nth term

A position-to-term rule, often called the nth term, gives any term directly from its position n. For the sequence 5, 8, 11, 14, the nth term is 3n + 2. Check it by substitution: n = 1 gives 5, n = 2 gives 8, and n = 4 gives 14. The nth term is the more useful form in an exam, because it finds the 50th term without listing the first 49.

Finding a term from an nth term

Substitute the position into the rule. For the nth term 3n + 2, the 20th term is 3 × 20 + 2 = 62. Write the substitution in full, with the position inside brackets if it is negative or a fraction, and keep the working so that a method mark can be awarded even if the arithmetic slips.

Testing whether a number belongs to a sequence

To check whether a number such as 80 is in the sequence with nth term 3n + 2, set the rule equal to 80 and solve: 3n + 2 = 80, so 3n = 78 and n = 26. Because n is a whole number, 80 is a term, and it is the 26th term. If the solution for n is not a whole number, the number is not in the sequence.

Arithmetic sequences and the common difference

In an arithmetic sequence the difference between consecutive terms is the same every time. This fixed difference is the common difference, written d. For the sequence 5, 8, 11, 14, the common difference is 3. The nth term of any arithmetic sequence has the form dn + c, where d is the common difference and c is found by substituting the first term.

Geometric sequences and the common ratio

In a geometric sequence each term is found by multiplying the previous one by the same number, called the common ratio. The sequence 3, 6, 12, 24 has common ratio 2. A geometric sequence can grow very quickly, so check the ratio by dividing two consecutive terms rather than guessing it from the first two numbers.

Linear and quadratic sequences in depth

Most sequence questions at this level use a linear rule or a quadratic rule. A linear sequence has a constant first difference, and a quadratic sequence has a constant second difference. Recognising which kind a sequence is decides the method, and the subsections below show how to find the rule and how to confirm it.

Finding the nth term of a linear sequence

For a linear sequence, write the common difference as d and the term before the first as a. The nth term is then dn + (a − d). Take the sequence 7, 10, 13, 16. The common difference is 3 and the first term is 7, so the nth term is 3n + (7 − 3), which is 3n + 4. Check the answer against the second term: 3 × 2 + 4 = 10, which matches.

Checking a linear rule with the difference

A quick check on a linear rule is to compare the coefficient of n with the difference between consecutive terms. The coefficient of n must equal the common difference. If the rule is 3n + 4 and the terms increase by 3 each time, the rule is consistent. A mismatch between the coefficient and the difference means the rule is wrong, and the mistake is usually in the constant term.

Quadratic sequences and second differences

Find the first differences, which are the gaps between consecutive terms, and then find the differences between those. If the second differences are constant, the sequence is quadratic. For 4, 7, 12, 19, the first differences are 3, 5, 7, and the second differences are 2, 2. The constant second difference shows that the sequence is quadratic, and the coefficient of n² is half of 2, so it is 1.

Finding the nth term of a quadratic

Write the nth term as an n² + bn + c, where a is half the second difference. Subtract a n² from each term and look at what is left. For 4, 7, 12, 19, subtracting n² leaves 3 for every term, so the remainder is the constant 3 and the nth term is n² + 3. Check n = 2: 2² + 3 = 7, which is the second term.

Special sequences: squares, cubes and triangular numbers

Some sequences should be recognised on sight. The square numbers are 1, 4, 9, 16, with nth term n². The cube numbers are 1, 8, 27, 64, with nth term n³. Triangular numbers are 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, and their nth term is n(n + 1) / 2. A sequence that matches one of these, with a small change, is often a question about adjusting the standard pattern.

Recognising a sequence from its pattern

Some questions give a pattern made of shapes or matchsticks and ask for the number of items in a given step. Write down the number for the first three steps, find the difference or the second difference, and form the rule. For steps that add 4 matchsticks each time, starting from 4 matchsticks, the rule is 4n. Test the rule against a step that is not used to find it, so that a pattern that only fits the first two steps is caught.

Sequences in context

A context question describes a sequence in words, such as the number of tiles in a border or the total of a savings plan that adds the same amount each month. Identify whether the change is by a fixed amount or a fixed factor, write the nth term, and then answer the question in the words of the context. A reply that states "the 12th term is 40" should go on to say what the 40 represents, such as the number of tiles in the 12th border.

Functions: notation, evaluation, domain and range

A function takes an input, applies a rule, and gives exactly one output for each input. Functions are written in notation such as f(x), which is read as "f of x". The subsections below cover the notation, how to evaluate a function, and how to state the set of inputs and outputs that a function can have.

What a function does

Think of a function as a machine. Each input goes in, the rule is applied, and one output comes out. For the function f(x) = 2x + 1, the input 3 gives the output 7. A function cannot give two different outputs for the same input, which is why a rule such as "the square root of x" is only a function when the positive root is taken by convention.

Function notation f(x)

The letter in front of the bracket names the function, and the letter in the bracket is the input variable. The statement f(x) = x² − 4 says that the function called f squares its input and subtracts 4. Any letter can name a function, such as g or h, and the variable inside the bracket can be replaced by an expression, so the notation is used in the same way for every rule.

Evaluating f(x) for a given input

To find f(3) when f(x) = x² − 4, replace every x in the rule by 3 and calculate: f(3) = 3² − 4 = 9 − 4 = 5. Write the substitution in full, including the brackets around negative inputs, because f(−3) = (−3)² − 4 is different from −3² − 4 when the brackets are dropped.

Finding a function of an expression

The input can be an expression rather than a number. For f(x) = 2x + 1, the expression f(x + 2) replaces x by x + 2 everywhere in the rule, giving 2(x + 2) + 1, which expands to 2x + 5. Expand the brackets fully before you simplify, and keep the result as a single expression in x.

Solving f(x) = k

To find the input that gives a particular output, set the rule equal to that output and solve. For f(x) = 2x + 1, the input that gives 11 satisfies 2x + 1 = 11, so 2x = 10 and x = 5. Check the answer by evaluating f(5) = 11, which confirms the solution.

Domain: the inputs a function can take

The domain is the set of inputs for which the function is defined. For f(x) = 1 / (x − 2), the input 2 is not allowed because it makes the denominator zero, so the domain is every real number except 2. Write the domain as a statement, such as "all real numbers except 2", and not as a list of the values you tried.

Range: the outputs a function can give

The range is the set of outputs that the function actually produces for its domain. For f(x) = x² on all real numbers, the outputs are never negative, so the range is every number greater than or equal to 0. Work out the range from the rule and the domain together, and sketch the graph if the shape is not obvious from the algebra.

Equations and symbols

Two families of formula share this topic: the rules that generate a sequence, and the algebra of function notation. Both are asked as "find the rule", so the sheet is a list of rules with the letters they use.

4n - 1 Key: n = the position of the term in the sequence (1, 2, 3, …); the coefficient 4 is the common difference and −1 is the adjustment that makes n = 1 give the first term, 3. Substitute n to get any term directly; the 20th term here is 79.

3n + 2 Key: n = position; 3 = common difference of 5, 8, 11, 14; +2 makes the first term correct. Every linear sequence can be written dn + b, and b always equals the first term minus d.

n² + 1 Key: n = position; the n² term means the second difference is constant, which is what identifies a quadratic sequence. Build the n² sequence, subtract it, and finish the remaining linear part.

n(n + 1)/2 Key: n = position; the triangular numbers 1, 3, 6, 10, found by adding the integers 1 to n. Recognise the shape rather than deriving it under exam pressure.

arⁿ⁻¹ Key: a = first term; r = common ratio, found by dividing any term by the one before; n = position. The exponent is n − 1, not n: at n = 1 the term must be a itself, and r⁰ = 1 guarantees that.

f(x) = 2x + 3 Key: f = the function's name; x = the input, in the domain; the expression is the rule — multiply by 2, add 3. Evaluating is substitution: f(4) = 11.

fg(x) = 2x² + 1 Key: fg means apply g first (g(x) = x²), then f to the result; the notation reads right to left. fg(x) is not gf(x) — order matters, and swapping it is the standard error.

f⁻¹(x) = (5x + 2)/3 Key: f⁻¹ = the inverse function, the machine that undoes f; the −1 is not a power, and f⁻¹(x) is never 1/f(x). Found by writing y = f(x), making x the subject, then swapping the letters.

f⁻¹(x) = √(x - 3) Key: the inverse of f(x) = x² + 3 on the domain x ⩾ 0; the positive root alone is taken because the original domain excludes negatives. The domain of f⁻¹ is the range of f, here x ⩾ 3.

How the marks are given. Show the substitution, keep the composite order, and state any domain restriction. A range quoted without checking the turning point — y ⩾ 1 for (x − 2)² + 1, not y ⩾ 0 — is the quiet loss on this topic.

title: Databases and Data Definition — Study Notes
content:
Databases and Data Definition

Relational Concepts

A table (relation) stores rows (tuples) and columns (attributes). The primary key uniquely identifies each row; a foreign key references a primary key in another table, creating the relationship. A composite key uses two or more columns together.

Normalisation

  • 1NF: atomic values, no repeating groups.
  • 2NF: 1NF plus every non-key attribute depends on the whole key (kills partial dependency in composite keys).
  • 3NF: 2NF plus no transitive dependency — non-key attributes must not depend on other non-key attributes.

Normalisation reduces redundancy and prevents update, insert and delete anomalies.

DDL and DML

DDL defines structure: CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE, DROP. DML manipulates data: SELECT ... FROM ... WHERE, INSERT INTO, UPDATE, DELETE. Joins combine related tables: FROM Student s JOIN Enrolment e ON s.id = e.StudentID. Aggregates: COUNT, SUM, AVG with GROUP BY and HAVING.

Transactions and Concurrency

A transaction is a unit of work obeying ACID: Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (rules preserved), Isolation (concurrent transactions do not interfere), Durability (committed data survives crashes). Record locking blocks conflicting simultaneous edits; a deadlock occurs when two transactions each hold a lock the other needs.

Exam tips: normalise a small table through 1NF, 2NF, 3NF naming the dependency removed at each step; write a two-table SELECT with JOIN; state which ACID property a scenario breaks.

DDL and DML

Data Definition Language (DDL) creates and changes the structure of a database: CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE and DROP TABLE. Data Manipulation Language (DML) works with the data inside the structure: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE.

Example: CREATE TABLE Student (ID INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, Name VARCHAR(30)); is DDL; INSERT INTO Student VALUES (1, 'Ana'); is DML.

Exam tip: classify each statement by whether it changes structure or changes data.

title: Abstract Data Types — Study Notes
content:
Abstract Data Types

Syllabus note: 9618 introduces abstract data types at AS (section 10.4, AS Paper 2); this note is the extended treatment — trees and hash tables go beyond the AS introduction.

What is an ADT?

An abstract data type is a logical description of a collection of data plus the operations on it, independent of implementation. Stacks, queues, linked lists, binary trees and hash tables are all ADTs; in A Level you must show how they are built from arrays or records with pointers.

Linked Lists

Each node holds a value and a pointer to the next node; a start pointer marks the head and a null marks the end. Insertion rewires two pointers — no shifting — giving O(1) insertion at a known position, but access requires walking the list, O(n).

Stacks and Queues

A stack is LIFO (push and pop at the top); a queue is FIFO (enqueue at the rear, dequeue from the front). Both can be arrays with index pointers or linked lists. Stack uses include call stacks and expression evaluation; queue uses include print buffers and breadth-first search.

Binary Search Trees

Each node has up to two children; left subtree keys are smaller, right subtree keys larger. Search, insert and (average-case) delete are O(log n). An in-order traversal outputs keys in ascending order. A degenerate (linear) tree from sorted input degrades to O(n).

Hash Tables

Covered in file organisation, but as an ADT a hash table pairs a hash function with bucket storage for O(1) average access.

Exam tips: be able to draw a tree after a sequence of insertions and write its three traversals; state the pointer changes for a linked-list insertion; compare ADT operations with Big-O.

Abstract data types in practice

An abstract data type is defined by the operations it supports and their behaviour, not by how it is stored. A stack is defined by push, pop and isEmpty; the programmer using it does not need to know whether it is built from an array or a linked list.

Separating the interface from the implementation lets the implementation change without breaking the code that uses it, and makes each part easier to test.

Exam tip: when asked to define an ADT, name the operations and say what each does, not how it is stored.

Worked example: building a binary search tree

Insert 8, 3, 10, 1 and 6 in that order. The first value, 8, becomes the root. Since 3 is less than 8, it goes to the left; 10 goes to the right. The value 1 is less than 8 and less than 3, so it sits to the left of 3. The value 6 is less than 8 and greater than 3, so it sits to the right of 3. An in-order traversal (left, node, right) then lists the values in sorted order: 1, 3, 6, 8, 10.

Complexity of the main operations

  • Search, insert and delete in a balanced tree take O(log n) time, because each comparison discards about half the remaining nodes.
  • If the values are inserted in sorted order, the tree becomes a chain and the same operations degrade to O(n).
  • Hash table lookup takes O(1) on average but gives no ordering, so a hash table cannot list the data in sorted order.

Choosing between the structures

A stack, a queue and a linked list each store a collection, but they differ in how items are added and removed. A stack is last in, first out. A queue is first in, first out. A linked list allows insertion and deletion at a known position without shifting other items. The exam question usually asks you to justify the choice, so state the access pattern the data needs.

Exam method: tracing a stack and a queue

Write the contents after every operation. Start with an empty stack. Push 5, push 9, pop, then push 2. After the pop the stack holds 5 only, so the final push leaves 5 at the bottom and 2 at the top. The value returned by the pop is 9, because a stack returns the most recently added item.

A queue works in the opposite order. Enqueue 5, enqueue 9, then dequeue. The dequeue returns 5, the item that entered first, and 9 remains at the front. Marks are given for the returned value and for the final state, so show both.

Common errors

  • Describing a stack as first in, first out. That describes a queue; a stack is last in, first out.
  • Forgetting to check for an empty structure before a pop or dequeue. Good answers say what the program should do when the structure is empty.
  • Saying an array-based queue never needs wrapping. A fixed-size array queue can waste space at the front unless its pointers wrap round to the start.

title: IGCSE Chemistry: Rates, Equilibrium and Redox
content:
IGCSE Chemistry: Rates, Equilibrium and Redox

Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry 0620 (2026–2028), Extended route, Topic 6 Chemical reactions: statement 6.1 Physical and chemical changes, 6.2 Rate of reaction, 6.3 Reversible reactions and equilibrium, and 6.4 Redox. Three questions meet here: how fast a reaction goes, how far it goes, and what happens to the electrons. Each section below works from the particle model to the exam wording, with collision theory as the engine of every rate explanation and the Haber and Contact processes traced condition by condition.

Physical and chemical changes

A physical change alters form without changing the substance — no new material is made (melting, dissolving, evaporation), and it is usually reversible. A chemical change makes new substances with new properties — new bonds form and old ones break (burning, rusting, reacting acid with metal), is often harder to reverse, and usually involves an energy change. The decisive question: "has a new substance formed?"

Rate of reaction: the measurement

Rate is how fast a reaction happens: rate = change in quantity ÷ time. Measure it by how fast a reactant disappears or a product appears.

Three standard measurement methods, each with its apparatus:

  1. MASS CHANGE (balance + flask): a gas escapes, so mass falls.
     rate = loss of mass / time. Good for CO₂ from acid + carbonate.
     Limitation: only works when the gas escapes and is not toxic.
  2. GAS VOLUME (gas syringe): collect the gas; read volume at intervals.
     rate = volume of gas / time. Works for any gaseous product.
     Limitation: gas may leak past the plunger; syringe may stick.
  3. COLOUR CHANGE / TURBIDITY (colorimeter or cross-on-paper): for
     thiosulfate + acid (sulfur precipitate clouds the solution); time how
     long a marked cross disappears from view.
  4. TEMPERATURE CHANGE for neutralisation-type reactions (thermometer).

Reading rate from a graph: the rate at any moment is the GRADIENT of the
tangent to the curve. Steep = fast; the curve flattens as reactants are used
up and collisions become rarer.

Rate and collision theory

Particles react when they collide with enough energy (≥ the activation energy) in the right orientation. Anything that increases the frequency or energy of successful collisions increases the rate.

FactorParticle-level explanationEffect on graph
ConcentrationMore particles per volume → more frequent collisionsSteeper initial gradient, same final product
Pressure (gases)Same as concentration: particles closer togetherSteeper initial gradient
Surface areaPowder exposes more particles to collide at onceSteeper initial gradient, same final product
TemperatureParticles move faster (more frequent collisions) AND a bigger fraction exceed EₐSteeper initial gradient; often reaches the same final product
CatalystProvides an alternative route with LOWER activation energy; more particles can react on collision; unchanged at the endSteeper initial gradient, same final product

Enzymes are biological catalysts — same mechanism, protein shaped to fit the substrate; denatured by high temperature (shape changes, substrate no longer fits).

Rate worked example: marble chips + acid, measured by gas volume.

  50 cm³ of CO₂ collected: first 30 s -> 20 cm³; second 30 s -> 12 cm³;
  third 30 s -> 8 cm³; fourth -> 6 cm³; fifth -> 4 cm³ (total 50).

  rates (cm³/s): 20/30 = 0.67 ; 12/30 = 0.40 ; 8/30 = 0.27 ; 6/30 = 0.20 ;
                 4/30 = 0.13

  The rate falls because acid concentration drops as it is consumed - fewer
  collisions per second. Adding the same mass of powdered marble instead of
  chips would double the early rate (more surface) but the SAME 50 cm³ total
  appears - the amount of product depends on the limiting reactant, not the
  rate.

Reversible reactions and equilibrium

A reversible reaction (⇌) can go in both directions. In a closed system nothing escapes, so eventually the forward and reverse reactions proceed at the same rate and concentrations stay constant — dynamic equilibrium. "Dynamic" matters: both reactions continue; the observable amounts just stop changing.

Le Chatelier's principle - the exam's master rule:

  "If a condition is changed, the position of equilibrium shifts to
   OPPOSE the change."

Worked through each variable on the Haber process:
  N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g)   ΔH negative (exothermic forward)

  - Increase pressure: shift to the side with FEWER gas molecules to reduce
    it -> products (1 mole N₂ + 3 H₂ = 4 gas moles -> 2 NH₃) -> more NH₃.
  - Increase temperature: shift to ABSORB heat -> endothermic direction
    (reverse) -> LESS NH₃. (A real conflict: higher T speeds the rate but
    lowers the yield - compromise at 450 °C.)
  - Add more N₂: shift to use it up -> more NH₃.
  - Remove NH₃ as it forms: shift to replace it -> more NH₃.
  - Catalyst: NO shift - it speeds both directions equally, so equilibrium
    is reached sooner at the same position.

Why the Haber conditions (chosen, not optimal for yield alone):
  450 °C - a compromise: lower temperature gives better yield but too slow
  a rate; 450 gives an economic rate with acceptable yield.
  200 atm - high pressure favours the 4-gas-mole side and improves yield,
  but very high pressures cost too much in plant and energy.
  Iron catalyst - faster equilibrium attainment, cheaper than platinum.

Contact process: 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃ (exothermic) - same reasoning:
  450 °C, 1-2 atm, V₂O₅ catalyst.

The hydrated–anhydrous reversible pair is the syllabus's visual example: blue anhydrous copper(II) sulfate + water ⇌ blue hydrated crystals (and pink ⇌ blue for cobalt(II) chloride) — adding water drives it one way, heat drives it back.

Redox

Redox is a reaction involving simultaneous reduction and oxidation. The classic definitions: oxidation is gain of oxygen (or loss of electrons, or increase in oxidation number); reduction is loss of oxygen (or gain of electrons, or decrease in oxidation number). One process never happens without the other — if something is oxidised, something else has been reduced.

Three ways to spot redox - all on one reaction:

  CuO + H₂ -> Cu + H₂O

  1. Oxygen: CuO loses oxygen -> CuO is REDUCED; H₂ gains oxygen -> H₂ is
     OXIDISED.
  2. Electrons: Cu²⁺ gains 2 electrons to become Cu (reduction); H loses
     electrons to become H⁺ in water (oxidation).
  3. Oxidation numbers: Cu goes +2 -> 0 (decrease: reduction);
     H goes 0 -> +1 (increase: oxidation).

  Oxidation number rules:
    element alone = 0; simple ion = its charge; O in compounds = -2
    (except peroxides); H in compounds = +1; sum over a compound = 0.
    Roman numerals in names give the metal's number: iron(III) = Fe³⁺.

  Oxidising agent: ACCEPTS electrons and is itself reduced (CuO above).
  Reducing agent: DONATES electrons and is itself oxidised (H₂ above).
Half-equations - worked through two examples:

  Mg -> Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻            (oxidation: electrons on the right)
  Cl₂ + 2e⁻ -> 2Cl⁻           (reduction: electrons on the left)

  Check both the atoms AND the charge balance:
    left of the second: 0 charge + 2e⁻ = -2 total; right: 2 x -1 = -2 ✓

  Combining: Mg + Cl₂ -> MgCl₂ - electrons lost by Mg exactly equal those
  gained by Cl₂ (2 = 2 ✓). If they are not equal, multiply the half-
  equations so they are before adding.

Worked example: one scenario, all three topics

Hydrogen + iodine ⇌ hydrogen iodide (reversible, exothermic):

Rate side: raising temperature speeds both directions (more collisions
  exceed Eₐ); adding a catalyst reaches equilibrium faster without moving it.

Equilibrium side: heating shifts the equilibrium to oppose the change -
  the endothermic (reverse) direction - so less HI forms; increasing pressure
  has no effect here (2 gas moles each side).

Redox side: H goes 0 -> +1 (oxidised); I goes 0 -> -1 (reduced).
  Half-equations: H₂ -> 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ ; I₂ + 2e⁻ -> 2I⁻.
  I₂ is the oxidising agent (it gains the electrons).

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Sign errors in Le Chatelier wording: say which direction the equilibrium shifts and what the change does — "shifts to oppose the increase" is the credit-worthy phrasing.
  • Claiming a catalyst changes the yield or equilibrium position — it only changes how fast equilibrium is reached.
  • Confusing rate with yield: a steeper graph is speed; total product height is yield/amount, set by the limiting reactant.
  • Explaining temperature effects with collision frequency alone — the activation-energy fraction is the more important half at this level.
  • Redox: putting electrons on the wrong side of half-equations (oxidation loses electrons — they appear on the right) or leaving atoms/charge unbalanced.
  • Calling the reducing agent "the thing that gets reduced" — the agent does the reducing while being oxidised itself.
  • Forgetting closed-system conditions when defining equilibrium (open systems never reach it — reactants escape).
  • Reading tangent gradients as vertical heights on rate graphs.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Explain, using collision theory, why powdered calcium carbonate reacts faster with acid than large chips.

Answer: Powder has a much larger surface area than the same mass of chips, so more calcium carbonate particles are exposed to acid particles at any moment. Collisions therefore occur more frequently, the rate of successful collisions per second increases, and the reaction is faster.

Question 2 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Explain how increasing temperature affects the rate of a reaction in terms of collision theory.

Answer: Increasing temperature increases particles' average kinetic energy: they collide more often and, crucially, a much greater fraction of collisions have energy equal to or greater than the activation energy. The number of successful collisions per second rises sharply, so the rate increases.

Question 3 (Paper 4, 5 marks). For N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ (ΔH negative), explain the effect of (i) increasing pressure (ii) increasing temperature on the yield of ammonia.

Answer: (i) The forward reaction converts 4 moles of gas to 2, so higher pressure shifts the equilibrium to the side with fewer gas molecules — the products — to oppose the increase, raising the yield. (ii) The forward reaction is exothermic, so heating shifts the equilibrium in the endothermic (reverse) direction to oppose the temperature rise, lowering the yield — which is why a compromise temperature of about 450 °C is used.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 3 marks). Explain why adding a catalyst does not change the position of equilibrium.

Answer: A catalyst lowers the activation energy of both the forward and reverse reactions equally, so both rates increase by the same factor. Equilibrium is reached sooner, but the ratio of products to reactants at equilibrium is unchanged.

Question 5 (Paper 4, 4 marks). In the reaction CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O, identify what is oxidised and what is reduced, justifying with oxidation numbers.

Answer: In CuO, copper has oxidation number +2; it becomes Cu with oxidation number 0 — a decrease, so copper is reduced (CuO is the oxidising agent). Hydrogen goes from 0 in H₂ to +1 in H₂O — an increase, so hydrogen is oxidised (it is the reducing agent).

Question 6 (Paper 4, 3 marks). Write half-equations for the conversion of magnesium to magnesium ions and of chlorine to chloride ions, and name the type of each change.

Answer: Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻ (oxidation — electrons lost); Cl₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻ (reduction — electrons gained). The electrons lost by magnesium equal those gained by chlorine, so the combination Mg + Cl₂ → MgCl₂ is balanced in charge.

Rates and equilibrium describe reactions in general; the next topics give that machinery a home — the acids, salts and Periodic Table groups where it is applied.

title: AS Level Chemistry: Intermolecular Forces
content:
AS Level Chemistry: Intermolecular Forces

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH12, Topic 7 explains the forces that hold molecules to one another, as distinct from the covalent bonds inside them. These forces are far weaker than covalent bonds, yet they decide boiling temperature, volatility, solubility and the anomalous behaviour of water, and they are the reason a molecule with polar bonds is not necessarily a polar molecule. Examiners test the explanation rather than the label, so every answer should name the force, say what causes it, and relate it to the property asked about.

Three types of intermolecular force

All intermolecular forces are electrostatic: they arise from the attraction between regions of opposite charge. They differ in what creates those regions.

ForceOriginTypical strength
London forces (instantaneous dipole–induced dipole)Fluctuating electron density in one molecule induces a dipole in a neighbourVery weak, but increases with the number of electrons
Permanent dipole–permanent dipolePermanently polar bonds and an asymmetric shape leave one end of the molecule slightly positive and the other slightly negativeWeak, roughly 5–20 kJ mol⁻¹
Hydrogen bondingA hydrogen atom bonded to N, O or F is attracted to a lone pair on N, O or F in another moleculeStrongest of the three, up to about 40 kJ mol⁻¹

London forces

Electrons are in constant motion, so at any instant the electron distribution in a molecule may be uneven. That creates an instantaneous dipole, which in turn distorts the electron cloud of a neighbouring molecule and induces a dipole in it. The two dipoles then attract. The effect is present in every substance, including the noble gases and non-polar molecules such as methane, and it is the only intermolecular force in a non-polar substance.

The strength of London forces depends on how easily the electron cloud can be distorted, which is called polarisability. Two factors control it:

  • Number of electrons: more electrons means a larger, more polarisable cloud. Iodine (I₂) is a solid and chlorine (Cl₂) a gas at room temperature for this reason.
  • Surface area and shape: a long unbranched chain has more surface contact between neighbouring molecules than a compact branched isomer with the same formula, so it has stronger London forces.

London forces are also the reason why a noble gas such as argon can be liquefied at low temperature, even though its atoms have no permanent dipole and no bonds to break.

Permanent dipole–dipole interactions

A bond between atoms of different electronegativity is polar: the more electronegative atom carries a partial negative charge, δ−, and the less electronegative atom carries δ+. If the molecule is not symmetrical, the individual bond dipoles do not cancel, and the molecule as a whole has a permanent dipole. Neighbouring molecules then line up with opposite ends together, and the attraction is a permanent dipole–permanent dipole interaction.

Hydrogen chloride, HCl, is polar and its molecules attract this way. Carbon dioxide has two polar C=O bonds, but the molecule is linear and symmetrical, so the dipoles cancel exactly and CO₂ has no permanent dipole; its molecules are held only by London forces. Tetrachloromethane, CCl₄, is also symmetrical and non-polar for the same reason, while trichloromethane, CHCl₃, is polar because the fourth substituent is hydrogen rather than chlorine and the symmetry is broken. Whether a molecule is polar therefore needs two checks: are the bonds polar, and is the shape symmetrical?

Hydrogen bonding

Hydrogen bonding is a particularly strong form of permanent dipole attraction. It occurs only when two conditions are satisfied:

  • A hydrogen atom is covalently bonded to a highly electronegative atom, limited to nitrogen, oxygen or fluorine.
  • A lone pair is available on an N, O or F atom in a neighbouring molecule, which the δ+ hydrogen can approach.

The result is a strong attraction between the δ+ hydrogen and the lone pair, often drawn as a dotted line: O–H···O. The bond is directional, which is why hydrogen bonding produces specific structures rather than a random arrangement.

Water, ammonia and hydrogen fluoride all hydrogen bond:

SubstanceHydrogen-bonding unitNumber of hydrogen bonds per molecule in the liquid
H₂OO–H···OTwo hydrogen atoms and two lone pairs allow an extensive network
NH₃N–H···NThree hydrogen atoms but only one lone pair, so fewer bonds than water
HFF–H···FOne hydrogen atom and three lone pairs; chains of HF molecules

Hydrogen bonding is not the same as a covalent bond to hydrogen. It is an intermolecular attraction, so it is broken when a substance melts or boils, while the O–H covalent bond stays intact. That distinction is worth stating explicitly in an answer.

The anomalous properties of water

Water's properties do not follow the pattern of similar molecules, and hydrogen bonding is the explanation.

High melting and boiling temperatures. Compared with hydrogen sulfide, H₂S, which has a similar formula, water boils about 160 °C higher. The molecules of H₂S are held only by London forces and weak dipole–dipole attractions, whereas each water molecule can hydrogen bond to several neighbours. Breaking those attractions needs far more energy, so the melting and boiling temperatures are unusually high, and water is a liquid at room temperature while H₂S is a gas.

Ice is less dense than liquid water. In ice, each water molecule hydrogen bonds to four neighbours in a regular tetrahedral arrangement, which holds the molecules further apart than in the liquid and leaves open hexagonal spaces. When ice melts, much of that open framework collapses and the molecules pack more closely, so liquid water is denser than ice. This is why ice floats, and why a lake freezes from the top, insulating the water beneath and allowing aquatic life to survive.

Hydrogen bonding also gives water a high surface tension, a high specific heat capacity and a high enthalpy of vaporisation, all of which follow from the energy needed to overcome the network of hydrogen bonds.

Predicting hydrogen bonding

To decide whether a molecule can hydrogen bond, look for an O–H, N–H or F–H group and for a lone pair on O, N or F. Ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH, can hydrogen bond because of its O–H group; ethanal, CH₃CHO, has a C=O bond with lone pairs but no hydrogen attached to an electronegative atom, so it cannot donate a hydrogen bond, although its oxygen can accept one. A molecule such as CH₃F has no H–F bond, so it does not hydrogen bond. Methanol and water mix in all proportions because both can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds, whereas methane, with only C–H bonds, cannot.

Intermolecular forces and physical properties

Boiling temperature is a measure of the energy needed to separate molecules, so it reports the strength of the intermolecular forces, not the strength of the covalent bonds. Four trends are examined.

Boiling temperature of alkanes increases with chain length. Each additional CH₂ group adds electrons and surface area, so the London forces between the molecules become stronger and more energy is needed to separate them. Methane boils at −162 °C, ethane at −89 °C and decane at 174 °C.

Branching lowers the boiling temperature. Pentane and 2,2-dimethylpropane have the same molecular formula, but the branched molecule is more compact. Its molecules have less surface contact, so its London forces are weaker and it boils at 9.5 °C compared with 36 °C for pentane. The same reasoning explains why branched isomers have lower boiling temperatures throughout the alkanes.

Alcohols have higher boiling temperatures than alkanes of similar electron count. Ethanol (46 electrons) boils at 78 °C while propane (26 electrons) boils at −42 °C. The comparison is not quite like for like, but the key point is that ethanol molecules hydrogen bond through the O–H group, while propane molecules have only London forces. The hydrogen bonding more than compensates for the smaller number of electrons.

Boiling temperatures of the hydrogen halides are not a simple trend. HF is the highest because of hydrogen bonding. From HCl to HBr to HI, London forces grow as the number of electrons increases, so the boiling temperatures rise in that order: HCl −85 °C, HBr −67 °C, HI −35 °C. HF, at 20 °C, sits far above the smooth trend, and that outlier is the evidence for hydrogen bonding.

Choosing a solvent

Dissolving depends on the solute particles being separated and surrounded by solvent particles, so the solute–solvent attractions must be comparable to the forces they replace. In practice, like dissolves like.

  • Water dissolves ionic compounds because the polar water molecules attract the ions: the partially negative oxygen surrounds a cation and the partially positive hydrogens surround an anion. This is hydration, and it releases hydration enthalpy that helps to compensate for the lattice enthalpy that must be overcome.
  • Water dissolves simple alcohols such as methanol and ethanol, because the alcohol's O–H group can both donate a hydrogen bond to water and accept one from it. As the hydrocarbon chain grows, the non-polar part becomes a larger fraction of the molecule and solubility falls: ethanol mixes with water in all proportions, but hexan-1-ol is only slightly soluble.
  • Water is a poor solvent for halogenoalkanes and other polar organic molecules such as chloroethane. The molecule has a dipole, so it is attracted to water to some extent, but it has no O–H group and cannot hydrogen bond with water, and its hydrocarbon part cannot interact favourably with the water network. The solute–solvent attractions are too weak to overcome the hydrogen bonding between water molecules.
  • Non-aqueous solvents are used when the solute's intermolecular forces resemble the solvent's. Iodine, a non-polar molecule held by London forces, dissolves in hexane, which is also non-polar; bromine dissolves in cyclohexane for the same reason. Propanone is a useful intermediate case, dissolving both polar and many non-polar substances because it has a polar C=O group and a hydrocarbon part.

A good answer states the force between solvent molecules, the force between solute and solvent, and whether the second is strong enough to replace the first.

Typical mistakes

  • Saying a substance has hydrogen bonds when the hydrogen is bonded to carbon; only N–H, O–H and F–H count.
  • Describing hydrogen bonding as a covalent bond, or claiming that boiling water breaks O–H bonds.
  • Assuming that a molecule with polar bonds must be polar, without checking whether the shape cancels the dipoles.
  • Attributing the trend in alkane boiling temperatures to stronger covalent bonds rather than to stronger London forces.
  • Explaining branching by saying the molecule has fewer electrons; the number of electrons is the same, the surface contact is not.
  • Explaining the lower density of ice as an expansion on freezing without mentioning the open hydrogen-bonded lattice.
  • Describing London forces as "weak covalent forces" or as attractions between permanent dipoles.

Exam-style questions

  1. Explain why the boiling temperature of iodine is higher than that of chlorine. Answer: iodine has more electrons and a larger, more polarisable electron cloud, so the London forces between its molecules are stronger; more energy is needed to separate the molecules.
  2. Explain why 2-methylbutane has a lower boiling temperature than pentane. Answer: both have the molecular formula C5H12 and the same number of electrons. 2-methylbutane is more branched and more compact, so its molecules have less surface area in contact, the London forces between them are weaker, and less energy is needed to separate them.
  3. Explain, in terms of intermolecular forces, why ethanol is soluble in water but chloroethane is not. Answer: ethanol has an O–H group and can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds with water, so the solute–solvent attractions are strong enough to replace the hydrogen bonds between water molecules. Chloroethane is polar but has no O–H group, so it cannot hydrogen bond with water; its attractions to water are too weak to compensate for breaking the water–water hydrogen bonds.
  4. Explain why ice is less dense than liquid water. Answer: in ice each water molecule forms hydrogen bonds to four neighbours in a tetrahedral arrangement, producing an open lattice with spaces between the molecules. When ice melts the lattice collapses and the molecules pack more closely, so the liquid is denser.
  5. Identify the strongest intermolecular force in each of the following and justify your answer: (a) HCl, (b) CH₃OH, (c) CCl₄. Answer: (a) permanent dipole–permanent dipole, because the molecule is polar and has no O–H, N–H or F–H group; (b) hydrogen bonding, because of the O–H group; (c) London forces, because the molecule is symmetrical and the bond dipoles cancel, so it is non-polar.

When revising, practise the three-part answer: name the force, explain what causes it in these molecules, then link it to the property in the question. Move on to Introduction to Kinetics and Equilibria next, where the same molecular picture explains why reactions need collisions with sufficient energy.

Worked example: hydrogen bonding and the energy to boil water

Calculate the energy needed to heat 100 g of water from 25 °C to 100 °C and then to convert it to steam at 100 °C. The specific heat capacity of water is 4.18 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹ and the enthalpy of vaporisation is 40.7 kJ mol⁻¹.

Step 1, heating: q = mcΔT = 10⁰ × 4.18 × 75 = 31 350 J = 31.4 kJ
Step 2, boiling: n(H2O) = 10⁰ / 18.0 = 5.56 mol
                 energy = 5.56 × 40.7 = 226 kJ
Total = 31.4 + 226 = 257 kJ, of which 226 kJ (88 %) is used to separate molecules

The result is the quantitative version of the argument in the text. Almost nine tenths of the energy goes into overcoming intermolecular forces rather than into raising the temperature, and for water those forces are hydrogen bonds. Compare hydrogen sulfide, whose enthalpy of vaporisation is about 18.7 kJ mol⁻¹: the same 5.56 mol would need only 104 kJ to vaporise, which is why water boils 160 °C higher.

Two exam conclusions follow from the same numbers. Steam at 100 °C causes worse burns than water at 100 °C because condensing it releases 40.7 kJ mol⁻¹, and sweating cools the body effectively because each gram of water that evaporates carries away about 2.3 kJ.

title: Astronomy and Cosmology — Study Notes
content:
Astronomy and Cosmology

Luminosity and Intensity

Luminosity L is total power radiated (W). Intensity at distance d: I = L/(4πd²) — the key to distances.

Standard candles (Cepheid variables, Type Ia supernovae) have known L, so measuring I gives d.

Example: the Sun: I = 1370 W m⁻² at d = 1.5 × 10¹¹ m gives L ≈ 3.9 × 10²⁶ W.

Wien and Stefan–Boltzmann

  • Wien: λ_max T = 2.9 × 10⁻³ m K — hotter stars are bluer
  • Stefan: L = σAT⁴, σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸

Hubble's Law

Galaxies recede with v = Hd, H₀ ≈ 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹. Redshift z = Δλ/λ ≈ v/c for small z.

Example: a galaxy at 100 Mpc recedes at v = 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ × 100 × 3.09 × 10²² ≈ 6800 km s⁻¹.

The Big Bang

Evidence: Hubble expansion, cosmic microwave background (2.7 K), hydrogen/helium abundance. Age estimate: t ≈ 1/H₀ ≈ 14 billion years. The fate question: critical density, Ω.

Exam tips: convert Mpc to metres (×3.09 × 10²²) before Hubble arithmetic; distinguish redshift of light from distance ladder methods.

title: Waves — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Waves

Physics — AS. A wave transfers energy without net transfer of matter.

Key areas to revise

  • Basics
  • The Wave Equation
  • Intensity
  • Doppler Effect
  • EM Spectrum
  • Polarization

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Worked example

A wave on a rope has a frequency of 500 Hz and a wavelength of 0.68 m. Its speed is v = fλ = 500 × 0.68 = 340 m s⁻¹. The same equation applies to sound and light, but the speed of light in a vacuum is 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ and does not depend on the source. Intensity falls with the inverse square of distance from a point source, so doubling the distance cuts the intensity to one quarter.

Common mistakes

  • Mixing up frequency and wavelength in v = fλ, or leaving wavelength in centimetres while using metres per second.
  • Saying waves carry matter. A wave carries energy, and the particles of the medium oscillate about fixed positions.
  • Assuming polarisation applies to longitudinal waves. Only transverse waves can be polarised.

Worked example

The same equation applies to sound and light, but the speed of light in a vacuum is 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ and does not depend on the source. Intensity falls with the inverse square of distance from a point source, so doubling the distance cuts the intensity to one quarter.

  • Saying waves carry matter. A wave carries energy, and the particles of the medium oscillate about fixed positions.
  • Assuming polarisation applies to longitudinal waves. Only transverse waves can be polarised.

title: Abstract Data Types — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Abstract Data Types

Computer Science — A2. An abstract data type is a logical description of a collection of data plus the operations on it, independent of implementation. Stacks, queues, linked lists, binary trees and hash tables are all ADTs; in A Level you must show how they are built from arrays or records with pointers.

Key areas to revise

  • What is an ADT?
  • Linked Lists
  • Stacks and Queues
  • Binary Search Trees
  • Hash Tables

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

### Worked example An abstract data type defines the data and operations without fixing the implementation. A stack is last-in-first-out: push adds an item to the top and pop removes the top item. If you push 3, then 7, then pop twice, the first pop returns 7 and the second returns 3. A queue is first-in-first-out, so enqueue and dequeue return 3 then 7 in the same sequence. ### Check yourself Trace a queue after enqueue(A), enqueue(B), dequeue(). State which item is returned and what remains. The result is A, and the queue now holds B. ### Worked example An abstract data type defines the data and operations without fixing the implementation. title: Sequences and Series — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Sequences and Series

Mathematics — AS (9709). Terms increase by a common difference d.

Key areas to revise

  • Arithmetic Progressions (AP)
  • Geometric Progressions (GP)
  • Binomial Expansion

Formulas to learn

  • Arithmetic progression: nth term a + (n - 1)d; sum of n terms S_n = n/2 (2a + (n - 1)d).
  • Geometric progression: nth term ar^(n - 1); sum of n terms S_n = a(1 - r^n)/(1 - r) for r not equal to 1.
  • Sum to infinity: a/(1 - r), valid only when |r| is less than 1.

Worked example

An arithmetic sequence starts at 3 with common difference 4. The 10th term is 3 + 9 x 4 = 39, and the sum of the first 10 terms is 10/2 (6 + 36) = 210. Check the sum by pairing the first and last terms: 3 + 39 = 42, and five such pairs give 210.
