  • Magnification, applied to a mitochondrion measuring 4.2 cm on a micrograph at ×20 000: actual size = image size ÷ magnification. 4.2 cm = 42 000 µm, so the real length is 42 000 ÷ 20 000 = 2.1 µm. Convert every unit to µm before you divide, and write the magnification formula out.
  • Prokaryote or eukaryote: a eukaryote has a nucleus, membrane-bound organelles and 80S ribosomes. A prokaryote has a circular DNA loop, no nucleus and 70S ribosomes. Name at least two of these features; a single feature such as the cell wall is not enough because plants and some prokaryotes both have one.
  • Mitosis versus meiosis: mitosis gives two genetically identical diploid cells. Meiosis gives four haploid cells, and genetic variation comes from crossing over in prophase I and independent assortment at metaphase I. Mark schemes award these two sources separately.
  • Mammalian fertilisation: a sperm and an egg fuse to form a diploid zygote, which restores the diploid number. Name the haploid gametes explicitly, because the mark depends on the stage of meiosis that produces them.

title: AS Level Mathematics: Differentiation
content:
AS Level Mathematics: Differentiation

Differentiation measures how fast something changes: the gradient of a curve at a point, the speed of a moving object, the rate at which cost rises with output. It is the central tool of AS mathematics, and this note builds it from zero: the idea of a limit and the gradient function, the power rule with every algebraic case, tangents and normals, stationary points and their classification, increasing and decreasing intervals, and rates of change. Every worked example writes the derivative line before substituting, because the method marks live there.

Gradient as a limit

The gradient of a curve at a point is the gradient of the tangent there. Approximate it with a chord between two nearby points: as the points close up, the chord's gradient approaches the tangent's. That limiting process defines the derivative:

gradient of chord = [f(x + h) - f(x)]/h
derivative = limit as h → 0
notation: dy/dx, f'(x)

For y = x², the chord gradient simplifies to 2x + h, which tends to 2x as h → 0: the derivative of x² is 2x. That single calculation is the model for the general rule.

The power rule

if y = x^n then dy/dx = n x^(n - 1)

constant multiple: d/dx [k f(x)] = k f'(x)
sum: differentiate term by term
constant term: differentiates to 0

Worked example 1. Differentiate y = 4x³ − 2x² + 7x − 5.

dy/dx = 12x² - 4x + 7

Worked example 2 (negative and fractional powers). Differentiate y = 3/x² + √x.

rewrite: y = 3x⁻² + x^(1/2)
dy/dx = -6x⁻³ + (1/2)x^(-1/2)
      = -6/x³ + 1/(2 √(x))

Worked example 3 (expand first). Differentiate y = x²(2x + 1).

expand: y = 2x³ + x²
dy/dx = 6x² + 2x

Worked example 4 (gradient at a point). Find the gradient of y = x³ − 4x at x = 2.

dy/dx = 3x² - 4
at x = 2: 12 - 4 = 8

Tangents and normals

tangent at x = a: gradient m = f'(a), through (a, f(a))
normal: gradient -1/m (perpendicular to the tangent)
equation: y - y1 = m(x - x1)

Worked example. Find the tangent and normal to y = x² − 3x + 1 at x = 4.

point: y = 16 - 12 + 1 = 5  →  (4, 5)
dy/dx = 2x - 3  →  m = 5
tangent: y - 5 = 5(x - 4)  →  y = 5x - 15
normal: gradient -1/5
y - 5 = -1/5 (x - 4)  →  x + 5y = 29

Worked example 2 (tangent through a point). Find where the tangent to y = x³ at (2, 8) crosses the x-axis.

dy/dx = 3x²  →  m = 12
tangent: y - 8 = 12(x - 2)  →  y = 12x - 16
set y = 0: x = 16/12 = 4/3

Stationary points

stationary point: dy/dx = 0
classify with the second derivative:
  d2y/dx2 < 0: maximum
  d2y/dx2 > 0: minimum
  d2y/dx2 = 0: could be either - check the gradient either side

Worked example. Find and classify the stationary points of y = x³ − 3x² + 4.

dy/dx = 3x² - 6x = 3x(x - 2)
stationary at x = 0 and x = 2
points: (0, 4) and (2, 0)
d2y/dx2 = 6x - 6
at x = 0: -6 < 0  →  maximum
at x = 2: +6 > 0  →  minimum

Worked example 2 (unknown coefficient). The curve y = x³ + ax² + b has a stationary point at (2, 1). Find a and b.

point condition: 8 + 4a + b = 1
derivative condition: 3x² + 2ax = 0 at x = 2 → 12 + 4a = 0 → a = -3
substitute: 8 - 12 + b = 1  →  b = 5

Increasing and decreasing functions

increasing where dy/dx > 0
decreasing where dy/dx < 0

Worked example. Find the intervals where y = x³ − 6x² + 9x is increasing.

dy/dx = 3x² - 12x + 9 = 3(x - 1)(x - 3)
positive outside the roots: x < 1 or x > 3
increasing on x < 1 and x > 3; decreasing on 1 < x < 3

Rates of change and kinematics

if s(t) is displacement: velocity v = ds/dt; acceleration a = dv/dt
displacement from velocity: integrate (next topic)

Worked example. A particle's displacement is s = 2t³ − 9t² + 12t (metres, seconds). Find its velocity and acceleration at t = 2.

v = ds/dt = 6t² - 18t + 12
at t = 2: 24 - 36 + 12 = 0 m/s (momentarily at rest)
a = dv/dt = 12t - 18
at t = 2: 24 - 18 = 6 m/s²

Worked example 2 (maximum displacement). With the same s(t), find when the particle is at rest and classify each moment.

v = 0: 6t² - 18t + 12 = 0 → t² - 3t + 2 = 0 → t = 1, 2
a(1) = -6 < 0 → at t = 1 the displacement is a maximum
a(2) = +6 > 0 → at t = 2 the displacement is a minimum

Optimisation problems

Applied maximum/minimum questions follow a fixed routine: write the quantity to optimise as a function of one variable, differentiate, set to zero, solve, and classify (or argue from the context).

Worked example. A rectangular pen is to be made against a wall with 24 m of fencing (three sides). Find the maximum area.

let the two equal sides be x; the third is 24 - 2x
A = x(24 - 2x) = 24x - 2x²
dA/dx = 24 - 4x = 0  →  x = 6
A = 6(24 - 12) = 72 m² (maximum since d2A/dx2 = -4 < 0)

Differentiation from first principles

The definition is examinable and shows why the power rule works. The routine: form f(x + h), subtract f(x), divide by h, simplify, then let h → 0.

Worked example. Differentiate f(x) = x² + 3x from first principles.

f(x + h) = (x + h)² + 3(x + h) = x² + 2xh + h² + 3x + 3h
f(x + h) - f(x) = 2xh + h² + 3h
divide by h: 2x + h + 3
let h → 0: f'(x) = 2x + 3

Worked example 2. Differentiate f(x) = 5x² from first principles.

f(x + h) - f(x) = 5(x² + 2xh + h²) - 5x² = 10xh + 5h²
divide by h: 10x + 5h  →  limit 10x

Concavity and the second derivative

The second derivative describes how the gradient itself is changing. Where d²y/dx² > 0 the gradient is increasing and the curve is concave up (holds water); where it is negative the gradient is decreasing and the curve is concave down. That is exactly why the sign classifies stationary points, and it also answers direct questions about concavity:

d2y/dx2 > 0: concave up / minimum
d2y/dx2 < 0: concave down / maximum
d2y/dx2 = 0: possible point of inflection - test the gradient either side

Worked example. Find where y = x³ − 3x is concave up.

dy/dx = 3x² - 3;  d2y/dx2 = 6x
concave up where 6x > 0  →  x > 0

Sketching curves with calculus

Calculus turns a sketch from guesswork into a list of facts: intercepts, stationary points and their nature, behaviour at the ends, and any asymptotes. A reliable order:

  1. Set x = 0 for the y-intercept; solve y = 0 for the x-intercepts where factorisable.
  2. Differentiate, solve dy/dx = 0, and classify each stationary point.
  3. Use the second derivative sign to fix concavity between the points.
  4. Check the sign of y at the extremes of the sketch (a positive cubic rises to the right).

Worked example. Sketch y = x³ − 3x².

intercepts: y = 0 at x = 0 and x = 3 (x²(x - 3))
dy/dx = 3x² - 6x = 3x(x - 2)
stationary: (0, 0) and (2, -4)
d2y/dx2 = 6x - 6: at 0 negative → maximum; at 2 positive → minimum
The curve rises from the left, peaks at the origin, falls to (2, -4),
then rises, crossing the x-axis at x = 3.

Optimisation with a constraint

Most real optimisation questions give a constraint (fixed perimeter, fixed volume, fixed budget) that must be used to eliminate one variable before differentiating.

Worked example. A closed cylinder has volume 250 cm³. Find the radius that minimises its surface area.

V = π r² h = 250  →  h = 250/(π r²)
S = 2 π r² + 2 π r h = 2 π r² + 500/r
dS/dr = 4 π r - 500/r² = 0
4 π r³ = 500  →  r³ = 39.79  →  r = 3.41 cm
check: d2S/dr2 = 4 π + 10⁰⁰/r³ > 0  →  minimum

The pattern is always the same: one constraint equation, one quantity to optimise, substitute, differentiate, solve, justify the nature of the stationary point — and answer the question actually asked (here the radius, not the height).

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Differentiate) Differentiate y = 5x⁴ − 3x² + 2. Answer: 20x³ − 6x.
  2. (Negative power) Differentiate y = 4/x. Answer: y = 4x⁻¹ → −4x⁻² = −4/x².
  3. (Gradient) Find the gradient of y = x² + 2x at x = −1. Answer: 2x + 2 → 0.
  4. (Tangent) Find the tangent to y = x² at (3, 9). Answer: m = 6; y = 6x − 9.
  5. (Stationary) Find the stationary point of y = x² − 6x + 5. Answer: 2x − 6 = 0 → x = 3; y = −4; minimum.
  6. (Second derivative) Classify the stationary point of y = x³ at x = 0. Answer: dy/dx = 3x², d²y/dx² = 6x = 0 at x = 0 — the test is inconclusive; the gradient is positive either side, so it is a point of inflection, not an extremum.
  7. (Increasing) Find where y = x² − 4x is decreasing. Answer: 2x − 4 < 0 → x < 2.
  8. (Kinematics) s = t³ − 6t² + 9t. Find the acceleration at t = 1. Answer: v = 3t² − 12t + 9; a = 6t − 12 → −6 m/s².

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Forgetting to rewrite powers: differentiate 1/x and √x only after rewriting as x⁻¹ and x^(1/2); the power rule does not apply to the original form.
  • Dropping the constant: the derivative of a constant is 0 — a leftover +7 in dy/dx is an error.
  • Tangent versus normal: the normal's gradient is −1/m, not −m; and it passes through the same point.
  • Second derivative sign: negative means maximum (the curve is concave down); positive means minimum. Reversing the classification is the classic slip.
  • d²y/dx² = 0: inconclusive, not automatically an inflection — check the gradient either side.
  • Stationary point coordinates: the question wants (x, y), so substitute the x back into the original curve, not the derivative.
  • Rates of change with units: attach units (m/s, m/s², units per item) and interpret the sign in context.
  • Method marks: write dy/dx = ... explicitly before substituting; the derivative itself is credit even if the later arithmetic slips.

title: AS Level Mathematics: Quadratics
content:
AS Level Mathematics: Quadratics

A quadratic is a curve you already know from everyday life: the path of a thrown ball, the profit curve of a business, the shape of a satellite dish. Algebraically it is any expression ax² + bx + c with a ≠ 0, and this note builds every technique the AS papers test: solving by factorising, completing the square and the formula; using the discriminant to count roots without solving; reading the vertex and intercepts off a sketch; and solving simultaneous and inequality problems where the quadratic meets a line. Every step is shown line by line, because the method marks live in the middle.

The three forms of a quadratic

FormExpressionWhat it reveals
Standardax² + bx + cthe y-intercept is c
Factoriseda(x − p)(x − q)roots at x = p and x = q
Completed squarea(x + h)² + kvertex at (−h, k); minimum or maximum k

The sign of a decides the shape: a > 0 opens upward (a minimum), a < 0 opens downward (a maximum). The axis of symmetry runs through the vertex, halfway between the roots.

Solving by factorising

Look for two numbers that multiply to ac and add to b, then split the middle term and factorise in pairs.

Worked example. Solve 2x² + 7x + 3 = 0.

ac = 6, b = 7: numbers 6 and 1
2x² + 6x + x + 3 = 0
2x(x + 3) + 1(x + 3) = 0
(2x + 1)(x + 3) = 0
x = -1/2 or x = -3

Worked example 2 (difference of squares). Solve 9x² − 25 = 0.

(3x - 5)(3x + 5) = 0
x = 5/3 or x = -5/3

Completing the square

Write x² + bx + c as (x + b/2)² − (b/2)² + c. The method: halve the coefficient of x, square the bracket, subtract the square of that half.

Worked example. Write x² − 6x + 11 in completed-square form and state the vertex.

x² - 6x + 11 = (x - 3)² - 9 + 11
              = (x - 3)² + 2
vertex: (3, 2); minimum value 2 at x = 3

Worked example 2 (leading coefficient not 1). Write 2x² + 8x + 5 in completed-square form.

factor out 2: 2(x² + 4x) + 5
complete inside: 2[(x + 2)² - 4] + 5
= 2(x + 2)² - 8 + 5 = 2(x + 2)² - 3
vertex: (-2, -3); minimum -3

Worked example 3 (solving by completing the square). Solve x² + 4x − 1 = 0, giving exact answers.

(x + 2)² - 4 - 1 = 0
(x + 2)² = 5
x + 2 = +/- √(5)
x = -2 +/- √(5)

The quadratic formula and the discriminant

x = (-b +/- √(b² - 4ac)) / (2a)

discriminant D = b² - 4ac
D > 0: two distinct real roots
D = 0: one repeated root (the curve touches the x-axis)
D < 0: no real roots (the curve misses the x-axis)

Worked example. Solve 3x² − 5x − 2 = 0 using the formula.

a = 3, b = -5, c = -2
D = 25 + 24 = 49
x = (5 +/- 7)/6
x = 12/6 = 2 or x = -2/6 = -1/3

Worked example 2 (discriminant). Find the values of k for which x² + kx + 9 = 0 has equal roots.

equal roots: D = 0
k² - 36 = 0
k = 6 or k = -6

Sketching a quadratic

A sketch needs four features: the shape (up or down from the sign of a), the y-intercept (c), the roots (from factorising or the formula) and the vertex (from completing the square or the midpoint of the roots). Mark them, then draw a smooth curve through them.

Worked example. Sketch y = x² − 4x + 3.

a = 1 > 0: opens upward
y-intercept: (0, 3)
roots: x² - 4x + 3 = (x - 1)(x - 3) → x = 1, 3
vertex: (x - 2)² - 1 → (2, -1)
axis of symmetry: x = 2

Simultaneous equations: a line and a curve

The method: make one variable the subject in the line, substitute into the curve, solve the resulting quadratic, then find the partner values. Two solutions mean the line cuts the curve twice; one means it is a tangent; none means it misses.

Worked example. Solve y = x² − 1 and y = 3x − 3.

x² - 1 = 3x - 3
x² - 3x + 2 = 0
(x - 1)(x - 2) = 0  →  x = 1 or x = 2
y = 3(1) - 3 = 0  and  y = 3(2) - 3 = 3
solutions: (1, 0) and (2, 3)

Worked example 2 (tangency condition). Find k such that y = 2x + k is tangent to y = x² + 3.

x² + 3 = 2x + k  →  x² - 2x + (3 - k) = 0
tangent: D = 0  →  4 - 4(3 - k) = 0
4 - 12 + 4k = 0  →  4k = 8  →  k = 2

Quadratic inequalities

Solve the corresponding equation first, sketch the parabola, then read which x-values satisfy the inequality.

Worked example. Solve x² − x − 6 < 0.

roots: (x - 3)(x + 2) = 0  →  x = 3, x = -2
the parabola opens upward, so it is below the axis between
the roots:  -2 < x < 3

Worked example 2 (outside). Solve x² − 4 ≥ 0.

roots x = +/-2; upward parabola is above the axis outside:
x <= -2 or x >= 2

Disguised quadratics

Many equations are quadratic in disguise: a substitution turns them into the standard form. The signal is a repeated expression appearing with two different powers — x⁴ and x², or 2^x and 2^(2x), or a trigonometric term squared and unsquared.

Worked example 1. Solve x⁴ − 5x² + 4 = 0.

let u = x²:  u² - 5u + 4 = 0
(u - 1)(u - 4) = 0  →  u = 1 or u = 4
back-substitute:
x² = 1  →  x = +/-1
x² = 4  →  x = +/-2
four solutions: x = 1, -1, 2, -2

Worked example 2 (exponential). Solve 2^(2x) − 5(2^x) + 4 = 0.

let u = 2^x:  u² - 5u + 4 = 0  →  u = 1 or 4
2^x = 1  →  x = 0
2^x = 4  →  x = 2

The discipline is to return to the original variable at the end and to check that each candidate is valid in the original domain (a negative u cannot equal 2^x).

Modelling with quadratics

Applied questions give a context and expect you to build the quadratic, then use completing the square or the formula for a maximum or minimum.

Worked example (area). A rectangular garden is to be fenced with 40 m of fencing against a wall (so only three sides need fencing). Find the maximum area.

let the two equal sides be x; the third side is 40 - 2x
area A = x(40 - 2x) = 40x - 2x²
complete the square: A = -2(x² - 20x) = -2[(x - 10)² - 10⁰]
                    = -2(x - 10)² + 200
maximum area = 200 m² when x = 10
(dimensions 10 m by 20 m)

Worked example 2 (profit). A stall sells n items at price (20 − 0.5n) pounds each. Find the number that maximises revenue.

revenue R = n(20 - 0.5n) = 20n - 0.5n²
R = -0.5(n² - 40n) = -0.5[(n - 20)² - 400]
  = -0.5(n - 20)² + 200
maximum revenue 200 pounds at n = 20 items

Both examples share the signature: a product of two linear expressions in the same variable, completed to reveal a maximum. Negative leading coefficient means maximum; positive means minimum.

Worked example 3 (sum and product of roots). For 2x² − 7x + 3 = 0, find the sum and product of the roots without solving.

sum of roots = -b/a = 7/2
product of roots = c/a = 3/2
check by solving: (2x - 1)(x - 3) = 0 → roots 1/2 and 3;
sum 3.5, product 1.5 - consistent

These two relations are useful for forming equations from given roots and for checking a factorisation. If a question says the roots are p and q, the quadratic is x² − (p + q)x + pq = 0 (up to a constant factor). They also settle symmetric questions such as "find p² + q² given the equation": p² + q² = (p + q)² − 2pq, computed straight from the coefficients without finding the roots themselves.

A shortcut worth knowing for sketch questions: the vertex of y = ax² + bx + c sits at x = −b/(2a), and its y-coordinate comes from substituting that x back into the equation. This is the same result as completing the square, reached faster when only the turning point is needed and the exact form is not requested.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Factorise) Solve x² + x − 12 = 0. Answer: (x + 4)(x − 3) = 0 → x = −4 or 3.
  2. (Complete the square) Write x² + 8x + 10 in the form (x + p)² + q. Answer: (x + 4)² − 6.
  3. (Vertex) State the minimum point of y = (x − 5)² + 7. Answer: (5, 7).
  4. (Formula) Solve 2x² + 5x − 3 = 0. Answer: D = 25 + 24 = 49; x = (−5 ± 7)/4 = ½ or −3.
  5. (Discriminant) Show that x² + 2x + 5 = 0 has no real roots. Answer: D = 4 − 20 = −16 < 0.
  6. (Simultaneous) Solve y = x² and y = x + 2. Answer: x² = x + 2 → x² − x − 2 = 0 → x = 2 or −1; points (2, 4) and (−1, 1).
  7. (Inequality) Solve x² + 3x − 10 < 0. Answer: (x + 5)(x − 2) < 0 → −5 < x < 2.
  8. (Tangent) Find k so that y = kx + 1 touches y = x² − 2x + 3. Answer: x² − (2 + k)x + 2 = 0; D = 0 → (2 + k)² = 8 → k = −2 ± 2√2.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Sign inside the completed square: x² − 6x completes to (x − 3)², not (x + 3)². The sign inside is half the coefficient's sign.
  • Forgetting to subtract the square: (x + 4)² is x² + 8x + 16, so x² + 8x needs −16. The correction term is mandatory.
  • Formula sign errors: x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac))/2a — both terms negate b, and the whole numerator divides by 2a (not just the root).
  • Discriminant conclusions: D > 0 means two roots, D = 0 one repeated, D < 0 none; "two roots" does not mean two positive roots.
  • Inequality direction: for "< 0" the solution lies between the roots when a > 0; for "> 0" outside them. Sketching prevents reversal.
  • Not using the original equation: when solving simultaneous equations, substitute back into the line (simpler) and state both coordinates.
  • Dividing by x: x² = 4x gives x = 0 or x = 4; dividing by x loses the root x = 0.
  • Sketch versus plot: a sketch needs shape, intercepts and turning point marked; a plot needs plotted points. Answer the question asked.

title: Binomial Distribution — Study Notes
content:
The Binomial Distribution

Edexcel International A Level Mathematics — Statistics 2 (WST02), sat at A2.

When Binomial Applies

X ~ B(n, p) counts successes in n independent trials when:

  • a fixed number n of identical trials,
  • each trial ends in success or failure,
  • constant success probability p,
  • trials are independent.

Check all four before using the model — "justifying a binomial model" is a real exam question.

The Formula

P(X = r) = ⁿCᵣ pʳ(1 − p)ⁿ⁻ʳ for r = 0, 1, ..., n. The ⁿCᵣ counts which r of the n trials were the successes.

Example: X ~ B(5, 0.3). P(X = 2) = ¹⁰C₂? No — ⁵C₂ × 0.3² × 0.7³ = 10 × 0.09 × 0.343 = 0.3087.

Cumulative Probabilities

P(X ≤ 2) = P(0) + P(1) + P(2). "At least" questions convert by the complement: P(X ≥ 2) = 1 − P(X ≤ 1). Keep one extra decimal place in intermediate steps to avoid rounding drift.

Expectation and Variance

  • E(X) = np and Var(X) = np(1 − p)

For X ~ B(20, 0.4): E(X) = 8 and Var(X) = 4.8.

Modelling Decisions

If trials are dependent (drawing without replacement from a small population) binomial is not appropriate. If p changes between trials it is not binomial. When n is large and p small, the binomial is approximately Poisson — but at A2 you usually stay exact.

Exam tips: identify n and p in words before touching the calculator. For P(X ≥ k) always rewrite as 1 − P(X ≤ k − 1). Tables give cumulative values — use them rather than summing by hand.

Exam method: binomial probabilities

If X ~ B(n, p) then X counts successes in n independent trials, each with probability p. P(X = r) = nCr p^r (1 - p)^(n - r) for r = 0, 1, ..., n. The mean is np and the variance is np(1 - p).

Check the conditions first: a fixed number of trials, two outcomes, a constant p and independent trials. If any condition fails, the binomial model does not apply.

Exam cue: Always state n and p before calculating, and say which condition you are checking. For P(X ≥ r) or P(X > r), use the complement 1 − P(X ≤ r − 1), read from the cumulative table or calculator, and state the final probability to three significant figures.

Worked example: a binomial probability

A biased coin lands on heads with probability 0.3. Let X be the number of heads in 10 throws, so X ~ B(10, 0.3). The probability of exactly 3 heads is P(X = 3) = C(10, 3) × 0.3³ × 0.7⁷ = 120 × 0.027 × 0.08235 = 0.2668 (to 4 decimal places). The coefficient 120 counts the arrangements of the 3 heads among 10 throws, and it is needed because the heads may fall in any of those positions.

At least one success

For P(X ≥ 1), use the complement: P(X ≥ 1) = 1 − P(X = 0) = 1 − 0.7¹⁰ = 1 − 0.02825 = 0.9718. Examiners look for this shortcut, and writing the full sum from X = 1 to X = 10 is both slower and more error-prone.

Checking the mean and variance

  • Mean: E(X) = np = 10 × 0.3 = 3.
  • Variance: Var(X) = np(1 − p) = 10 × 0.3 × 0.7 = 2.1, so the standard deviation is √2.1 = 1.45 (to 2 decimal places).

Use these values to judge whether a stated answer is sensible: a mean of 3 with a standard deviation of 1.45 means most results fall between 1 and 5.

Exam point: a binomial model needs a fixed number of trials, independence, and the same probability of success on each trial. If the items are drawn without replacement from a small group, the probability changes after each draw and the binomial model is not valid.

title: Edexcel IAL Computer Science: Protocols, Circuit and Packet Switching
content:
Edexcel IAL Computer Science: Protocols, Circuit and Packet Switching

Pearson Edexcel International Advanced Level in Computer Science, Unit 3 Advanced Computer Science: protocols, and circuit switching versus packet switching. The AS networking note traced data across a LAN and the internet; this note goes deeper into the rules themselves — what a protocol specification contains, how the layers compose, and why the telephone model and the packet model make opposite trades. The switching comparison is traced end to end on both models.

What a protocol is

A protocol is an agreed specification governing communication between systems: message format and syntax, semantics (what each field means), timing and sequencing (who speaks when, timeouts, rate), and error handling (detection, correction, retransmission). Without a shared protocol, hardware interoperation is impossible — the exam's "why protocols are needed" question wants those four components, not just "so devices understand each other".

Layering exists so each level can evolve independently and vendors can implement one layer against a stable interface. The TCP/IP model: application (HTTP, SMTP, FTP, DNS), transport (TCP, UDP), internet (IP, ICMP, ARP), network access (Ethernet, Wi-Fi, PPP). The OSI reference model's seven layers (Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application) are the vocabulary examiners use when asking for names — know both, map TCP/IP onto OSI, and explain encapsulation: each layer wraps the one above's data in its own header (and trailer at the data-link layer), and the receiver unwraps in reverse.

Encapsulation traced for sending "Hi" over HTTP:

  Application   : HTTP request headers + "Hi"
  Transport     : TCP header (ports, sequence no.) + HTTP data  = segment
  Internet      : IP header (src/dst addresses) + segment       = packet
  Network access: Ethernet header + trailer (FCS) + packet      = frame

  Receiver unwraps in order: frame → packet → segment → HTTP data.
  Each layer reads only ITS header - the modularity is the point.

ARP bridging the layers: an IP packet needs the destination MAC address on
the LAN; ARP broadcasts "who has 192.168.1.5?" and the owner replies with its
MAC - the address-resolution seam between internet and network-access layers.

The protocol families in depth

ProtocolLayerGuaranteesCostUsed for
TCPTransportReliable, ordered, flow-controlled, connection-oriented (3-way handshake)Round-trips and header overheadHTTP, email, file transfer
UDPTransportNone — best-effort, connectionlessMinimal delayDNS, streaming, gaming, VoIP
IP (v4/v6)InternetBest-effort addressing and routing; fragmentationNo delivery guarantee (IP alone)Everything routed
ICMPInternetError/query messages (ping, TTL exceeded)—Diagnostics
TLSSession/PresentationEncryption, integrity, authentication (certificates)Handshake latency, CPUHTTPS, secure email
The TCP three-way handshake, packet by packet:

  Client                          Server
    | ---- SYN (seq=x) ------------→|    "I want to connect"
    | <--- SYN-ACK (seq=y, ack=x+1) -|    "acknowledged; my sequence is y"
    | ---- ACK (ack=y+1) ----------→|    "confirmed"
  connection ESTABLISHED; data flows with sequence/ack numbers.

Why three steps: each side learns the other's initial sequence number and
both agree the connection exists - a two-way exchange could leave the server
believing in a connection the client never confirmed. Teardown mirrors it
(FIN/ACK), and timeouts recover lost packets - the reliability story.

Circuit switching

In circuit switching, a dedicated physical path is established end to end for the whole conversation and released at the end — the telephone network model. Three phases: circuit establishment (signalling reserves each link), data transfer (the path is exclusive), circuit teardown.

  • Strengths: guaranteed constant bandwidth and latency for the call's duration; no congestion mid-call once established; simple in-call ordering (one path).
  • Weaknesses: the reserved path is wasted during silence (speech is ~40% silence); setup delay before any data flows; a failed link breaks the call with no rerouting; capacity is fixed per circuit.

Packet switching

In packet switching, messages are split into packets, each carrying source/destination addresses and a sequence number; packets travel independently (possibly different routes — datagram approach) or along a pre-agreed virtual circuit, sharing links with other conversations' packets. The receiving end reassembles by sequence number.

One message, both models, traced:

  Message: 1.2 Mbit, links of 1.2 Mbps each.

  CIRCUIT: establish path (say 200 ms signalling), then the message flows on
  its exclusive path: 1.2 Mbit / 1.2 Mbps = 1 s, then teardown. Total ≈ 1.2 s.
  During the transfer no other call can use those links.

  PACKET (1500-byte packets, ~800 packets): packets interleave with other
  traffic. Each hop queues and forwards (store-and-forward: each router
  receives the whole packet, checks it, sends on). If a link is busy, packets
  queue (variable latency - jitter); if a router drops one, only THAT packet
  is retransmitted (TCP). No setup delay; total time depends on congestion.
  A failed route just changes the next hop for later packets.

  Store-and-forward delay per hop = packetSize / linkRate; the end-to-end sum
  plus queueing is the latency - the number a "why is video call laggy?"
  answer quotes.
Circuit switchingPacket switching
PathDedicated, reserved per callShared, per-packet routes
SetupRequired before dataNone (datagram) / light (virtual circuit)
BandwidthGuaranteed constantStatistical; can vary (jitter)
Failure handlingCall drops; no reroutingPackets reroute; lost packets retransmitted
EfficiencyLow during silence/idleHigh — links shared statistically
FitsVoice telephony, constant-rate streamsData networks, the internet, bursty traffic

Modern note the exam appreciates: voice over the internet (VoIP) is packet switching engineered to imitate circuit guarantees — priority queues and reserved capacity give latency-sensitive packets the reserved feel of a circuit.

Worked example: designing a link for a school

Requirement: 40 classrooms, each streaming 2 Mbps video lessons at peak, plus
email/web traffic.

  Peak video demand: 40 × 2 = 80 Mbps, before overheads (add ~20% for
  headers/retransmission): ≈ 96 Mbps.
  Packet switching with a 10⁰ Mbps backbone just fits; a 1 Gbps link gives
  headroom. Circuit switching would reserve 2 Mbps per room regardless of use
  (40 × 2 = 80 Mbps permanently committed) and no room could burst above its
  allocation - wasteful for bursty web traffic.

Choice: packet switching with QoS priority for the video VLAN; the answer
names the burstiness argument (statistical multiplexing) and the QoS trade.

Quality of service on packet networks

Because packet switching offers no inherent guarantee, engineered guarantees are added on top: QoS marks latency-sensitive packets (voice, video) for priority queuing; traffic shaping smooths bursts so links are not overwhelmed; reservation (RSVP-style) holds capacity for a flow; and MPLS gives labelled paths that behave like fast virtual circuits. Each mechanism trades simplicity for predictability — the exam's "how does VoIP work reliably?" answer is exactly this list with priority queuing first.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Describing circuit switching as "faster" universally; it is predictable (guaranteed rate), while packet switching is efficient and burst-friendly — match the claim to the traffic.
  • Forgetting store-and-forward when computing latency: each hop holds the packet, and links serialise it.
  • Saying packets arrive in order; the sequence numbers and reassembly exist because they may not.
  • Listing OSI layers without their function or mis-ordering them (Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application).
  • Confusing IP (best-effort delivery) with TCP (reliability); neither alone is "the internet" — the pairing is.
  • Claiming UDP is unreliable so it is useless; its speed is exactly why real-time services choose it.
  • Leaving handshake/timing out of protocol answers; sequencing and synchronisation are part of what a protocol defines.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Unit 3, 4 marks). Describe the features a protocol must specify.

Answer: Message format/syntax (bit patterns, header fields); semantics (what each field and code means, what actions follow); timing and sequencing (who transmits when, synchronisation, timeouts, rate control); and error handling (detection via checksums, correction or retransmission rules). These four allow independent implementations to interoperate exactly.

Question 2 (Unit 3, 5 marks). Explain encapsulation using the TCP/IP layers.

Answer: Each layer adds its own header to the data from the layer above: the application data gets a TCP header (ports, sequence numbers) forming a segment; the segment gets an IP header (addresses) forming a packet; the packet gets a network-access header and trailer (MAC addresses, checksum) forming a frame. The receiver reverses the process, each layer reading only its own header and passing the payload upward — layering isolates responsibilities so protocols can change independently.

Question 3 (Unit 3, 5 marks). Compare circuit switching and packet switching for a national voice network.

Answer: Circuit switching reserves an exclusive path per call: guaranteed constant bandwidth and latency once established and simple ordering, but setup delay before speech, wasted capacity during silence, and a failed link drops the call. Packet switching shares links statistically: no setup, high efficiency and rerouting around failures, but variable latency (jitter) that voice dislikes unless QoS prioritises it. Traditional telephony chose circuits; modern VoIP chooses packets with engineered priority — the efficiency of sharing wins once jitter can be controlled.

Question 4 (Unit 3, 4 marks). Describe the TCP three-way handshake and explain its purpose.

Answer: The client sends SYN with its initial sequence number; the server replies SYN-ACK acknowledging it and supplying its own sequence number; the client confirms with ACK. Purpose: both sides learn each other's sequence numbers (needed for ordered reassembly), agree the connection exists, and agree parameters — avoiding the half-open connections a two-message exchange would permit.

Question 5 (Unit 3, 4 marks). Explain why the internet uses packet switching rather than circuit switching.

Answer: Internet traffic is bursty — web pages, email and files arrive in irregular bursts with idle gaps. Packet switching shares links statistically, so all conversations use whatever capacity is free at each instant (high utilisation), packets reroute around failures (resilience), and each packet need not hold capacity when silent. Circuit switching would reserve bandwidth through idle periods and block bursts above the reservation. Real-time needs are met with QoS on top rather than dedicated circuits.

Question 6 (Unit 3, 3 marks). Calculate the store-and-forward delay for a 1500-byte packet over three 10 Mbps hops.

Answer: Packet = 1500 × 8 = 12 000 bits. Per hop: 12 000 ÷ 10⁷ = 1.2 ms. Three hops store-and-forward the packet serially (each waits for the whole packet before sending): 3 × 1.2 = 3.6 ms transmission delay, plus any propagation and queueing delay at each router.

The protocols above carry encrypted traffic as often as plain; the security layer on top is the next note's subject.

title: Superposition — Study Notes
content:
Superposition

The Principle of Superposition

When waves meet, displacements add. In phase → constructive (big amplitude); antiphase → destructive (cancellation).

Coherence and Path Difference

Two sources are coherent if they share frequency and constant phase difference. Maxima occur where path difference = nλ; minima where it = (n + ½)λ.

Double-Slit (Young)

Fringe spacing x = λD/a (D = slit–screen distance, a = slit separation).

Example: λ = 600 nm, D = 2 m, a = 0.5 mm: x = 2.4 mm.

Red light gives wider fringes than blue; smaller slit separation also widens fringes.

Diffraction Grating

d sin θ = nθth order maximum. More slits → sharper, brighter maxima. The number of visible orders is the largest n with sin θ ≤ 1.

Example: 600 lines/mm → d = 1.67 μm; for 500 nm light, n_max = 3.

Stationary Waves

Two identical waves travelling opposite directions (e.g. wave + reflection) create nodes (no movement) and antinodes (max movement), spaced λ/2 apart. Strings and closed pipes resonate at f₁ = v/2L (fundamental) and harmonics.

Exam tips: always compute d from 'lines per mm' first; state 'path difference = nλ' explicitly in explain-the-fringe questions.

title: Exam technique: Algorithms & Programming
content:
### What earns the marks
For trace tables, every variable column updated stepwise earns the marks; the final OUTPUT row earns the last one. For validation versus verification, one named example of each earns one mark each. For test data, normal plus abnormal plus extreme or boundary stated earns full marks.
### Traps
Error: dry-running only the final values. Correction: fill every row of the table. Error: validation and verification swapped. Correction: validation checks input, verification checks transfer. Error: one test type only. Correction: name all three kinds.

title: Proof — Study Notes
content:
Proof

Proof is a logical argument that shows a statement is true in every case in its domain. At AS level you must know the four proof techniques, choose the right one for a given statement, and produce or critique a short algebraic argument.

Direct proof

Start from known facts and deduce the result by valid steps. Most algebraic identities are proved this way: expand, factorise or substitute until the required form appears.

  • To prove "the sum of two even numbers is even": write the numbers as 2a and 2b, so their sum is 2(a + b), which is even by definition.
  • To prove "the sum of two consecutive integers is odd": write them as n and n + 1, so the sum is 2n + 1, which is odd.

Proof by exhaustion

Check every case one by one. Only valid when the number of cases is finite and small, for example proving a statement about the factors of 12 by listing 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12.

Disproof by counter-example

A single case where the statement fails disproves a universal claim. This is the fastest way to kill a false statement: for "n^2 + n + 17 is prime for all n", the case n = 16 gives 289 = 17 x 17, so the claim is false.

Proof by contradiction

Assume the statement is false, then deduce something impossible. The classic is proving that the square root of 2 is irrational: assume sqrt(2) = p/q in lowest terms, derive that both p and q must be even, contradicting the lowest-terms assumption.

Common algebraic forms

  • Even: 2n. Odd: 2n + 1. Consecutive integers: n, n + 1, n + 2.
  • Consecutive even numbers: 2n, 2n + 2, 2n + 4.
  • A square number is n^2; the difference of two squares is (a - b)(a + b).
  • Divisibility: show the expression can be written as the required factor times an integer.

title: Programming Concepts — Study Notes
content:
Programming Concepts

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2023–2025): variables/constants, data types, selection/iteration, arrays, file handling, subroutines, scope, IDE tools.

1. Basics

Constants vs variables; types: INTEGER, REAL, CHAR, STRING, BOOLEAN, DATE; casting between them. Declaration with meaningful names.

2. Selection and iteration

IF score >= 50 THEN
  grade ← "pass"
ELSE
  grade ← "fail"
ENDIF

CASE OF grade
  "A" : OUTPUT "excellent"
  OTHERWISE : OUTPUT "keep going"
ENDCASE

REPEAT
  INPUT pin
UNTIL pin = storedPin

FOR i ← 1 TO 10 STEP 2 ... NEXT i

WHILE: condition first (may not run); REPEAT: runs at least once.

3. Arrays

Fixed size, indexed (0- or 1-based per spec); 2D arrays: row, column. Bounds errors when index leaves range. Traversal with FOR loops.

4. Files

OPENFILE "data.txt" FOR READ
READFILE "data.txt", line
CLOSEFILE "data.txt"

OPENFILE "log.txt" FOR APPEND
WRITEFILE "log.txt", record

Modes: READ, WRITE (overwrites), APPEND (adds).

5. Subroutines

Procedure (no return) vs function (returns value). Parameters by value (copy) vs reference (original). Local scope inside; global shared — declare deliberately, avoid overuse.

6. IDE tools

Syntax highlighting, autocompletion, breakpoints, single stepping, variable watch — name the tool and its debugging benefit.

Exam tips: use the exam pseudocode style exactly; for 2D arrays, loop rows outer/columns inner; choose WHILE vs REPEAT by "must it run once?"

title: Exponentials and Logarithms — Study Notes
content:
Exponentials and logarithms in calculus and modelling

The A2 work on e^x and ln x adds calculus and rates of change to the AS algebraic toolkit.

Differentiation and integration

  • d/dx (e^(kx)) = k e^(kx); so d/dx (e^x) = e^x.
  • d/dx (ln x) = 1/x; by the chain rule d/dx (ln(ax + b)) = a/(ax + b).
  • d/dx (ln(kx)) = 1/x for any constant k > 0.
  • The integral of e^(kx) is (1/k) e^(kx) + c; the integral of 1/x is ln x + c (x > 0).
  • Product rule with logs: d/dx (x ln x) = ln x + 1.

Solving equations

  • ln(x^2) = 4 gives x^2 = e^4, so x = e^2 or x = -e^2 (check the domain).
  • Log equations combine: ln a + ln b = ln(ab); always reject solutions outside the domain.
  • ln(x) = 1 + ln(3) gives ln x = ln(3e), so x = 3e.

Exponential growth and decay

  • If dN/dt = kN then N = N0 e^(kt): the rate of change is proportional to the quantity itself.
  • Examples: population growth, radioactive decay, cooling, compound interest.
  • Doubling time = ln 2 / k; half-life = ln(0.5) / k.

Graphs and limits

  • e^x grows without bound; e^(-x) tends to 0 as x increases (asymptote y = 0).
  • The gradient of e^x at x = 0 is 1.
  • ln x grows slowly; its graph crosses the x-axis at (1, 0).

title: IGCSE Chemistry (OxfordAQA): Acids, Bases and Salts
content:
Acids, Bases and Salts

Acids and bases are the most quoted chemistry in everyday life — vinegar, lemon juice, indigestion tablets, soap, bleach — and the exam asks about them in two quite different ways. The first is properties: what an acid does to an indicator, to a metal, to a carbonate, and why a strong acid is not the same thing as a concentrated one. The second is preparation: given a named salt, which method would you use to make it, and why would the other two methods fail. That second question is where most marks are lost, because it cannot be answered from memory of a recipe — it needs the solubility rules and the reason each step exists. Both are covered here, with the equations written to the state symbols the mark scheme asks for.

1. What an acid and a base actually are

An acid is a proton donor: it releases hydrogen ions, H⁺, when it is dissolved in water. A base is a proton acceptor: it takes those hydrogen ions. An alkali is simply a base that dissolves in water, and it is the alkali that supplies the hydroxide ions, OH⁻, that neutralise the acid.

  • Acids: hydrochloric acid, HCl; sulfuric acid, H₂SO₄; nitric acid, HNO₃; ethanoic acid (the acid in vinegar), CH₃COOH; citric acid in citrus fruit.
  • Alkalis: sodium hydroxide, NaOH; potassium hydroxide, KOH; ammonia solution, NH₃(aq); calcium hydroxide solution, Ca(OH)₂, which is limewater.
  • Bases that are not alkalis: copper(II) oxide, CuO; magnesium oxide, MgO; iron(III) oxide, Fe₂O₃. These accept protons but do not dissolve in water, which is why they are used as solids in salt preparation.

The distinction between an acid and an alkali is not about strength but about which ion is in excess. In acidic solution there are more H⁺ ions than OH⁻; in alkaline solution there are more OH⁻; in a neutral solution the two are equal, which is what pH 7 records. The reaction between them is neutralisation, and its ionic equation is the same for every acid-alkali pair: H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O.

2. Indicators and the pH scale

The pH scale runs from 0 to 14 and measures the concentration of hydrogen ions: the lower the pH, the more H⁺ ions are present. A change of one pH unit is a change by a factor of ten in that concentration, which is why pH 2 is a hundred times more acidic than pH 4, not twice.

pHUniversal indicator colourWhat it means
1–3Red to orangeStrong acid
4–6Orange to yellowWeak acid
7GreenNeutral
8–11Blue to blue-greenWeak alkali
12–14PurpleStrong alkali

Universal indicator gives an approximate pH from the colour. Two other indicators are used because they change sharply over a narrow range, which is what a titration needs: litmus is red in acid and blue in alkali; methyl orange is red in acid and yellow in alkali; phenolphthalein is colourless in acid and pink in alkali. Phenolphthalein is the usual choice when titrating an acid with an alkali, because the first permanent pink is easy to see and appears at the end point.

The most accurate measurement is a pH meter, which reads the pH as a number rather than a colour. That is the same point as the instrumental methods in chemical analysis: an instrument is more precise than a dye, at the cost of the equipment.

3. The four reactions of acids

Dilute acids react with four families of substance, and each produces a salt with something different:

  • Metal: acid + metal → salt + hydrogen. Only for metals above hydrogen in the reactivity series: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂.
  • Metal oxide or hydroxide (a base): acid + base → salt + water. CuO + H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + H₂O. This is neutralisation, and it is how most soluble salts are made.
  • Carbonate: acid + carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide. CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂. The fizzing is the carbon dioxide, which turns limewater milky.
  • Alkali: acid + alkali → salt + water. NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O, with the ionic equation H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O.

Every one of these produces a salt, and the salt is named from the two things that combined: the metal (or ammonium) from the base, and the acid's own ending. Hydrochloric acid gives chlorides, sulfuric acid gives sulfates, nitric acid gives nitrates, phosphoric acid gives phosphates, and ethanoic acid gives ethanoates. So copper(II) oxide with sulfuric acid gives copper(II) sulfate, and sodium hydroxide with nitric acid gives sodium nitrate.

Notice that the carbonate reaction fizzes while the oxide reaction does not. That difference is the reason an examiner can ask you to distinguish two white solids with one reagent: add dilute acid and only the carbonate effervesces.

4. Strong and weak, concentrated and dilute

These four words are examined together precisely because students mix them up. Strong and weak describe how completely an acid ionises in water. Concentrated and dilute describe how much acid there is per unit volume.

  • A strong acid is fully ionised: every HCl molecule becomes H⁺ and Cl⁻, so the solution is full of hydrogen ions.
  • A weak acid is only partly ionised: most ethanoic acid molecules stay intact, so there are few H⁺ ions even in a concentrated solution.
  • A concentrated solution has a large amount of acid dissolved in a given volume, whether it is strong or weak.
  • A dilute solution has little acid per unit volume, whether it is strong or weak.

The consequences are testable. A strong acid of a given concentration has a lower pH than a weak acid of the same concentration, conducts electricity better because there are more ions to carry the charge, and reacts faster with a metal for the same reason. But a concentrated weak acid can have a lower pH than a dilute strong acid, which is the trap: it is the concentration of H⁺ that sets the pH, and both strength and concentration affect it. Sulfuric acid is the awkward case worth knowing — it is strong and it is also dibasic, so one mole can supply two moles of H⁺.

5. Solubility rules, and why they decide the method

A salt can be prepared in three different ways, and the choice is forced by one question: is the salt soluble in water, and are the starting materials soluble?

Salt typeSolubility in water
Sodium, potassium and ammonium saltsAll soluble
NitratesAll soluble
ChloridesSoluble, except silver chloride and lead(II) chloride
SulfatesSoluble, except barium sulfate and lead(II) sulfate; calcium sulfate is only slightly soluble
CarbonatesInsoluble, except sodium, potassium and ammonium carbonates
HydroxidesInsoluble, except sodium and potassium hydroxides; calcium hydroxide is slightly soluble

Those rules give the three methods. A soluble salt of a metal other than sodium, potassium or ammonium is made from the acid and an insoluble base, oxide or carbonate, adding the solid in excess. A soluble salt of sodium, potassium or ammonium cannot be made that way, because every candidate base is soluble too and there is no excess solid to filter off — so it is made by titration. An insoluble salt is made by precipitation, mixing two solutions that each contain one of its ions.

Copper(II) sulfate and sodium chloride show the contrast perfectly. Copper(II) sulfate is soluble and its base, copper(II) oxide, is not, so the acid-plus-excess-oxide method works. Sodium chloride is soluble and every sodium base is soluble, so adding excess sodium hydroxide to hydrochloric acid would leave sodium hydroxide in the product — the titration is the only way to get the exact amount.

6. Preparing a soluble salt: acid plus excess insoluble base

The method is the same whether the base is an oxide, a hydroxide, a carbonate or a metal, with one difference: a metal also produces hydrogen. For copper(II) sulfate from copper(II) oxide and dilute sulfuric acid:

  1. Warm the acid gently and add copper(II) oxide a little at a time, stirring, until no more dissolves and some solid remains at the bottom. The excess is the point: it guarantees that all the acid has reacted, so the product cannot be contaminated with acid.
  2. Filter the mixture. The filtrate is the copper(II) sulfate solution; the residue is the unreacted copper(II) oxide.
  3. Heat the filtrate in an evaporating basin to concentrate it, stopping when crystals begin to appear at the edge — the crystallising point.
  4. Leave it to cool slowly so that large crystals form, then filter them off and dry them between sheets of filter paper.

Each step has a reason, and the reasons are what get marked. Warming the acid speeds the reaction up. Adding the solid in excess rather than measuring it means you do not need to know the concentration of the acid. Filtering removes the excess. Evaporating only to the crystallising point, rather than to dryness, matters because heating a salt solution to dryness drives off the water of crystallisation, gives a powder rather than crystals, and concentrates any soluble impurity into the product.

With a carbonate the same method applies but the mixture fizzes, because carbon dioxide is released: CuCO₃ + H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + H₂O + CO₂. The excess solid is still needed, and it is still removed by filtration.

7. Preparing a soluble salt of sodium, potassium or ammonium: titration

Both reactants are soluble, so there is no excess solid to remove and the amounts must be measured exactly. That is what a titration does:

  1. Pipette a measured volume of the acid (25.0 cm³ is standard) into a conical flask and add two or three drops of indicator.
  2. Fill a burette with the alkali, record the starting reading, and run it in until the indicator changes permanently. Record the final reading and subtract to get the volume added.
  3. Repeat until two readings agree to within 0.1 cm³ — concordant results — and take the average of those.
  4. Repeat the titration using the same volumes but no indicator, because the indicator would contaminate the salt. Evaporate the resulting solution to the crystallising point, cool and dry the crystals.

Every detail earns a mark. Reading the burette at the bottom of the meniscus, at eye level, prevents a systematic error. Rinsing the pipette with the solution it will deliver, but the conical flask with distilled water, prevents dilution errors. The indicator is left out of the final run because the whole point is a pure salt, and the reason two concordant titrations are needed is that one reading can be spoiled by a single extra drop.

8. Preparing an insoluble salt: precipitation

When the salt is insoluble, it can be made by mixing two solutions that each supply one of its ions, and it appears immediately as a solid. Barium sulfate, the "barium meal" used in hospital X-rays because it does not dissolve and so is not absorbed, is made this way: BaCl₂ + Na₂SO₄ → BaSO₄ + 2NaCl, with the ionic equation Ba²⁺ + SO₄²⁻ → BaSO₄.

The practical steps are short but each has a reason:

  • Mix the two solutions — the precipitate forms at once.
  • Filter to collect the solid on the filter paper.
  • Wash the residue with distilled water, to remove the soluble sodium chloride that would otherwise dry onto the crystals.
  • Dry it, usually in a warm oven or between filter papers.

A silver halide is made the same way, from silver nitrate and a solution of the halide: Ag⁺ + Cl⁻ → AgCl. The choice of solutions is constrained by solubility, not by preference — you need one solution that is soluble and contains the cation and another that is soluble and contains the anion, which is why sodium sulfate is used as the sulfate source rather than, say, lead(II) sulfate.

9. Water of crystallisation and hydrated salts

Many salts crystallise with a fixed number of water molecules built into the crystal, written after a dot: CuSO₄·5H₂O is hydrated copper(II) sulfate, blue, with five water molecules per formula unit. Heating drives the water off and leaves the anhydrous salt, which is white: CuSO₄·5H₂O → CuSO₄ + 5H₂O. Adding water reverses it, and the blue colour returns.

That colour change is the standard test for water: anhydrous copper(II) sulfate turns from white to blue, and cobalt chloride paper turns from blue to pink. Both are tests for water rather than for purity — they confirm that water is present, not that it is pure.

The dot matters in calculations. The relative formula mass of the hydrated salt includes the water, so 1 mol of CuSO₄·5H₂O is 250 g, not 160 g, and the water is 90 of those 250 g. A question that asks for the percentage of water in a hydrated salt is asking you to add the water in before dividing.

10. Worked examples

Example 1. Name the salt formed when magnesium oxide reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid, and write the balanced equation.

The metal is magnesium and the acid is hydrochloric, so the salt is magnesium chloride. The oxide is a base, so the products are a salt and water: MgO + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂O. The equation balances with two HCl because magnesium is 2+ and chloride is 1−, so two chloride ions are needed.

Example 2. Describe how you would prepare pure, dry crystals of copper(II) sulfate from copper(II) oxide and dilute sulfuric acid.

Warm the dilute sulfuric acid and add copper(II) oxide in excess, stirring until no more dissolves; filter off the excess oxide; evaporate the filtrate to the crystallising point; cool to crystallise; filter and dry the crystals between filter papers. The excess ensures the acid is fully used up, and stopping at the crystallising point rather than dryness keeps the water of crystallisation in the crystals.

Example 3. 25.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide solution is neutralised by 20.0 cm³ of hydrochloric acid of concentration 0.125 mol/dm³. Calculate the concentration of the sodium hydroxide.

The equation is NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O, so the ratio is 1 : 1. The amounts come from n = c × V → Key: n = amount of solute (mol); c = concentration (mol/dm³); V = volume of solution (dm³), so a volume in cm³ is divided by 1000 before it is used. Moles of acid: n = c × V = 0.125 × 0.0200 = 0.00250 mol. Moles of alkali = 0.00250 mol, and its volume is 25.0 ÷ 1000 = 0.0250 dm³. Then c = n ÷ V = 0.00250 ÷ 0.0250 = 0.100 mol/dm³.

Example 4. Explain why sodium chloride cannot be prepared by adding excess sodium hydroxide to hydrochloric acid.

Sodium hydroxide is soluble, so there would be no excess solid to filter off; any unreacted sodium hydroxide would stay in solution and contaminate the salt, and evaporating the solution would leave it in the product. The titration method is used instead, because it measures exactly the volume needed to neutralise the acid.

11. Exam-style questions

  1. State what is meant by a weak acid and explain why it has a higher pH than a strong acid of the same concentration. Answer: a weak acid is only partially ionised in water, so few of its molecules release H⁺ ions; the concentration of hydrogen ions is therefore lower than in a strong acid of the same concentration, and a lower H⁺ concentration means a higher pH.
  2. Describe the test that would distinguish a carbonate from a metal oxide, using one reagent. Answer: add dilute acid to each; the carbonate effervesces because carbon dioxide is released and the gas turns limewater milky, while the oxide dissolves without effervescence to give a salt solution.
  3. Write the ionic equation for the neutralisation of hydrochloric acid by sodium hydroxide. Answer: H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O. The sodium and chloride ions are spectators and are left out.
  4. Name the salt formed from calcium carbonate and nitric acid, and write the balanced equation. Answer: calcium nitrate; CaCO₃ + 2HNO₃ → Ca(NO₃)₂ + H₂O + CO₂.
  5. Explain why the excess solid must be filtered off before the salt solution is evaporated. Answer: the excess base did not react, so leaving it in would contaminate the crystals and make the product impure; filtration removes it while the salt stays in the filtrate.
  6. Explain why an indicator is used in the first titration but not in the final one. Answer: the indicator shows when neutralisation is complete, which is how the required volume is found; it is left out of the final run because it would dissolve in the solution and contaminate the salt being prepared.
  7. A white precipitate forms when solutions of barium chloride and sodium sulfate are mixed. Name the precipitate, write the ionic equation, and state why the precipitate is washed with distilled water. Answer: barium sulfate; Ba²⁺ + SO₄²⁻ → BaSO₄; washing removes the soluble sodium chloride that would otherwise dry onto the precipitate and contaminate it.
  8. Explain why anhydrous copper(II) sulfate cannot be used to show that a liquid is pure water. Answer: the test only shows that water is present, since any solution containing water would turn the solid blue; purity needs a boiling point measurement, because pure water boils sharply at 100 °C and a solution boils over a range.

12. Common mistakes

  • Treating "strong" and "concentrated" as the same word. Strong is about ionisation; concentrated is about how much is dissolved.
  • Calling copper(II) oxide an alkali. It is a base, but it does not dissolve, so it is not an alkali.
  • Writing that an acid plus a carbonate gives salt and water only. Carbon dioxide is the third product, and the mark scheme counts it.
  • Using the titration method for a salt of an insoluble base. If the base is insoluble, the excess-solid method is simpler and is what the question expects.
  • Forgetting to remove the indicator from the final titration, or using the average of non-concordant readings.
  • Evaporating the salt solution to dryness and calling the powder crystals. The water of crystallisation is lost and the product is not what was asked for.
  • Washing an insoluble precipitate with tap water rather than distilled water, which adds impurities instead of removing them.
  • Mixing up the indicator colours: methyl orange is red in acid and yellow in alkali; phenolphthalein is colourless in acid and pink in alkali.

13. Exam technique for this topic

  • When asked to "describe how you would prepare" a salt, give the steps in order and add a reason for the two steps that carry marks: the excess solid and the crystallising point.
  • Name the salt before writing the equation, then check the formula against the charges. Magnesium chloride is MgCl₂ and not MgCl because Mg is 2+.
  • For an "explain why" question about method, the answer is almost always solubility: which reagent dissolves, and therefore which method can remove what is left over.
  • Write state symbols whenever the question shows them in the equation stem, and keep them consistent.
  • If a titration volume is given in cm³, convert it to dm³ before any concentration calculation, and show that conversion — it is worth a mark on its own.
  • For indicator questions, quote the colour before and after the change, not just the final colour.

title: Programming and Algorithms
content:
`# Programming and Algorithms

Design Approaches

  • Top-down (stepwise refinement): decompose into modules — planned structure
  • Object-oriented: classes encapsulating state + behaviour — reusability
  • WAD (write all down): rapid prototyping — evolves during coding

Pseudocode Conventions

DECLARE x : INTEGER
IF x > 10 THEN ... ELSE ... ENDIF
WHILE ... ENDWHILE
FOR i ← 1 TO n ... NEXT i
FUNCTION f(a) RETURNS INTEGER

Searching

  • Linear: check each item, O(n), works unsorted
  • Binary: halve a sorted list each step, O(log n)

Example: 1,000,000 items: binary search needs ≤ 20 comparisons.

Sorting

AlgorithmBestAverageIdea
BubbleO(n)O(n²)swap neighbours
InsertionO(n)O(n²)insert into sorted prefix
MergeO(n log n)O(n log n)divide and merge

Merge sort example: [5,2,9,1] → [5,2][9,1] → [2,5][1,9] → [1,2,5,9].

Recursion

A function calling itself with a base case. Factorial: f(0)=1, f(n)=n·f(n−1). Stack frames handle state. Key: f(n) = n factorial, the product 1 × 2 × … × n (no units); n = a non-negative integer; the base case f(0) = 1 is what stops the recursion.

Exam tips: state the Big-O and justify it; for traces, tabulate variable changes per iteration.

title: Mechanics (M1) — Study Notes
content:
Mechanics 1: forces and motion

M1 models particles under constant acceleration and in equilibrium. The whole subject rests on three pillars: the SUVAT equations, Newton's laws, and the turning-effect (moments) of forces.

Kinematics (constant acceleration)

  • v = u + at
  • s = ut + (1/2)at^2
  • v^2 = u^2 + 2as
  • s = (u + v)t / 2
  • A displacement-time graph has gradient = velocity; a velocity-time graph has gradient = acceleration and area = displacement.
  • Free fall: a = g = 9.8 m/s^2 downwards; a ball thrown up decelerates at g on the way up.

Dynamics: Newton's laws

  • First law: a body stays at rest or constant velocity unless a resultant force acts.
  • Second law: F = ma, where F is the resultant force on the particle.
  • Third law: every action has an equal and opposite reaction, acting on DIFFERENT bodies.
  • Weight = mg, acting vertically downwards through the centre of mass.

Connected particles

Treat the system as one body first (F = total mass x a) to find the acceleration, then isolate one particle to find the connecting force (tension in a string, thrust in a tow bar).

Forces at angles

Resolve horizontally and vertically: a force F at angle theta to the horizontal has components F cos(theta) and F sin(theta). Equilibrium means the resultant force in each direction is zero.

Friction

  • F <= mu R, with limiting friction F = mu R when the body is on the point of slipping.
  • Friction opposes motion (or the tendency to motion) and acts along the surface.
  • On a rough inclined plane: R = mg cos(theta) and the component down the plane is mg sin(theta).

Moments

  • Moment of a force = force x perpendicular distance from the pivot.
  • A rigid body in equilibrium has zero resultant force AND zero total moment about any point.
  • Uniform beams have their weight acting at the mid-point.

title: Human Influences on Ecosystems
content:
Human Influences on Ecosystems

Cambridge IGCSE Biology 0610, Extended route, topic 20 (statements 20.1–20.4). Food supply, habitat destruction, pollution including eutrophication and greenhouse gases, and conservation.

20.1 to 20.4 Human influences

  • Food supply is increased by selective breeding, fertilisers, pesticides, controlled grazing and irrigation — each carrying trade-offs such as pollution, habitat loss or cost.
  • Habitat destruction through deforestation, urban development and intensive farming reduces biodiversity and removes carbon sinks, adding to atmospheric carbon dioxide.
  • Pollution: sewage and fertiliser runoff cause eutrophication; pesticides accumulate in food chains (bioaccumulation); air pollutants include carbon monoxide, sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen; greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide and methane enhance the greenhouse effect and warm the climate.
  • Conservation maintains biodiversity: protected areas, replanting, breeding programmes, reducing pollution, and sustainable harvesting. It is needed because species loss is irreversible and ecosystems provide services humans depend on.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Evaluation chain, applied to a proposal to build on a wetland: weigh the economic benefit against the loss of flood protection, water filtration, and habitat for migratory species. A top-band answer states a judgement and supports it with ecosystem services, not feelings.
  • Pollution reasoning, applied to DDT concentrating up a food chain: it is not excreted or broken down, so it accumulates in fat at each trophic level, reaching highest concentrations in top predators. Name bioaccumulation and biomagnification and give the consequence — thin eggshells in birds of prey.
  • Greenhouse reasoning, applied to why methane matters: it absorbs more infrared per molecule than carbon dioxide, so although there is less of it, its warming contribution is disproportionately large. Quantity and per-molecule effect both belong in the answer.

Common errors

  • Confusing the greenhouse effect with ozone depletion. They are different problems with different gases.
  • Saying pesticides "poison the food chain" without the concentration mechanism.
  • Claiming conservation means complete prohibition of use. Sustainable use is a core conservation strategy.

title: AS Level Mathematics: The Normal Distribution
content:
AS Level Mathematics: The Normal Distribution

Many measurements cluster symmetrically about a mean: heights, reaction times, measurement errors, the fill of a production line. The normal distribution is the mathematical shape of that clustering — a symmetric bell curve defined entirely by its mean and standard deviation. This note builds the topic from zero: the shape and its properties, standardising to the standard normal, reading probabilities from tables, working backwards from a probability to an unknown mean or standard deviation, and combining normal variables.

Properties of the normal distribution

X ~ N(mu, sigma^2)   (mean mu, variance sigma^2)

symmetric about the mean: P(X < mu) = P(X > mu) = 0.5
total area under the curve = 1
inflection points at mu +/- sigma
about 68 per cent within 1 sd, 95 per cent within 2, 99.7 within 3

The notation takes the variance, not the standard deviation: N(10, 4) means mean 10 and standard deviation 2. Writing N(10, 4) while treating 4 as the standard deviation is the single commonest error in the topic.

Worked example. X ~ N(20, 9). State the mean and standard deviation and find P(X < 20).

mu = 20, sigma = 3
P(X < 20) = 0.5 by symmetry

Standardising

z = (x - mu)/sigma

Z ~ N(0, 1), the standard normal, tabulated in most formula booklets
P(X < x) = P(Z < z) = Phi(z)

Standardising answers "how many standard deviations above the mean is this value?" Every normal probability question reduces to that one number.

Worked example. X ~ N(50, 16). Find P(X < 58).

sigma = 4;  z = (58 - 50)/4 = 2
P(Z < 2) = 0.9772

Worked example 2 (above). For the same X, find P(X > 45).

z = (45 - 50)/4 = -1.25
P(Z > -1.25) = P(Z < 1.25) = 0.8944

Between two values

P(a < X < b) = Phi(z_b) - Phi(z_a)

below a value, subtract from 1
between two values, subtract the smaller cumulative from the larger

Worked example. X ~ N(100, 225). Find P(85 < X < 115).

sigma = 15
z1 = (85 - 100)/15 = -1;  z2 = (115 - 100)/15 = 1
P = Phi(1) - Phi(-1) = 0.8413 - 0.1587 = 0.6826

Worked example 2 (both tails). X ~ N(30, 25). Find P(X < 25 or X > 38).

sigma = 5
z1 = -1  ->  Phi = 0.1587
z2 = 1.6  ->  Phi = 0.9452, so upper tail = 0.0548
total = 0.2135

Working backwards: finding x from a probability

given P(X < x) = p, find z from the inverse table, then
x = mu + z sigma

Worked example. X ~ N(40, 64). Find the value exceeded by 10 per cent of the distribution.

P(X > x) = 0.10  ->  P(X < x) = 0.90  ->  z = 1.2816
x = 40 + 1.2816(8) = 50.25

Worked example 2 (middle 80 per cent). X ~ N(50, 100). Find the range containing the middle 80 per cent.

tails of 10 per cent each: z = +/-1.2816
x = 50 +/- 1.2816(10)  ->  37.2 to 62.8

Finding the mean or standard deviation

When mu or sigma is unknown, each probability statement gives an equation in z, and two statements give simultaneous equations.

Worked example 1 (find sigma). X ~ N(20, sigma²) and P(X > 26) = 0.05. Find sigma.

P(X < 26) = 0.95  ->  z = 1.6449
(26 - 20)/sigma = 1.6449  ->  sigma = 6/1.6449 = 3.648

Worked example 2 (simultaneous). X ~ N(mu, sigma²) with P(X < 10) = 0.20 and P(X < 20) = 0.90. Find mu and sigma.

z values: -0.8416 and 1.2816
(mu - 0.8416 sigma) = 10
(mu + 1.2816 sigma) = 20
subtract: 2.1232 sigma = 10  ->  sigma = 4.71
mu = 10 + 0.8416(4.71) = 13.96

The signs matter: a value below the mean has a negative z, so 10 = mu − 0.8416 sigma. Setting both equations up with the same sign convention is what makes the simultaneous solve work.

Combining normal variables

if X ~ N(m1, s1^2) and Y ~ N(m2, s2^2) are independent:
X + Y ~ N(m1 + m2, s1^2 + s2^2)
X - Y ~ N(m1 - m2, s1^2 + s2^2)
aX + b ~ N(a m1 + b, a^2 s1^2)

The variance of a difference adds, exactly as in the probability-distributions topic: independent uncertainties compound in either direction.

Worked example. The masses of apples are N(120, 100) grams and of pears N(150, 144), independent. Find the probability that a random apple and pear together weigh more than 300 g.

T = A + P ~ N(270, 244)
sigma_T = 15.62
z = (300 - 270)/15.62 = 1.921
P(T > 300) = 1 - Phi(1.921) = 0.0274

Worked example 2 (difference). Two machines fill bottles: A ~ N(500, 25) ml, B ~ N(505, 36) ml, independent. Find P(A's fill exceeds B's).

D = A - B ~ N(-5, 61);  sigma = 7.81
P(D > 0):  z = (0 + 5)/7.81 = 0.640
P = 1 - 0.7389 = 0.261

Normal approximations and modelling assumptions

The normal model is used for continuous measurements that arise from many small independent influences. Before applying it, check the assumptions: the variable is continuous (or discrete with enough values to ignore the gaps), the distribution is roughly symmetric, and the mean and standard deviation are known or estimable.

Worked example (quality control). A machine produces rods of mean 25.0 mm and standard deviation 0.2 mm. Rods outside 24.7–25.3 mm are scrapped. Find the proportion scrapped.

z1 = (24.7 - 25.0)/0.2 = -1.5  ->  0.0668
z2 = (25.3 - 25.0)/0.2 = 1.5   ->  upper tail 0.0668
total scrapped = 0.1336, about 13.4 per cent

Interpretation matters: state the proportion and, where asked, the expected number in a batch — 13.4 per cent of 1000 rods is about 134 rods.

Reading the table and using symmetry

The standard normal table gives Phi(z) = P(Z < z) only for positive z. Two symmetries cover every other case:

Phi(-z) = 1 - Phi(z)
P(Z > z) = 1 - Phi(z)
P(-z < Z < z) = 2 Phi(z) - 1

Worked example. Find P(-1.5 < Z < 0.5).

Phi(0.5) = 0.6915;  Phi(-1.5) = 1 - 0.9332 = 0.0668
P = 0.6915 - 0.0668 = 0.6247

Worked example 2 (inverse with symmetry). Find z such that P(Z > z) = 0.75.

Phi(z) = 0.25, so z is negative
z = -0.6745  (the value with Phi = 0.6745 is 0.6745)
check: P(Z > -0.6745) = 1 - 0.25 = 0.75

A rough sketch of the bell with the required region shaded prevents sign errors; the area asked for must match the area you extract from the table.

Normal approximation to the binomial

For a large number of trials the binomial distribution becomes bell-shaped and can be approximated by a normal with the same mean and variance, with a continuity correction because the binomial is discrete.

X ~ B(n, p):  mu = np,  sigma^2 = np(1 - p)
use the normal when np > 5 and n(1 - p) > 5
continuity correction: X >= k becomes X > k - 0.5
                        X <= k becomes X < k + 0.5

Worked example. X ~ B(100, 0.3). Estimate P(X ≥ 35).

mu = 30, sigma^2 = 21, sigma = 4.583
with continuity: P(X > 34.5)
z = (34.5 - 30)/4.583 = 0.982
P = 1 - 0.8370 = 0.163

Without the 0.5 shift the estimate is noticeably worse, and the correction is explicitly credited in mark schemes. State both the approximation and the correction.

Is the normal model appropriate?

Before using the bell curve, check four things: the variable is continuous (or a discrete variable with many values); the distribution is roughly symmetric with a single peak; the mean and standard deviation are known or estimated from a large sample; and the values extend, in principle, in both directions. Heights and measurement errors satisfy these; incomes and waiting times do not, because they are skewed.

Worked example. A shop's daily sales figures have a mean of 400 pounds and an sd of 250 pounds, and the normal model gives P(sales < 0) = 0.055. Is the model appropriate?

the calculation implies a 5.5 per cent chance of negative sales,
which is impossible, so the normal model is a poor fit here
sales are right-skewed with a floor at zero; a model with a lower
bound, or a transformation, would be more honest

Recognising when a model fails is examinable: the arithmetic can be flawless and the modelling still wrong, and the marks for that judgement are separate.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Notation) X ~ N(12, 25). State the sd. Answer: 5.
  2. (Standardise) X ~ N(12, 25): find P(X < 17). Answer: z = 1; 0.8413.
  3. (Above) X ~ N(12, 25): find P(X > 9). Answer: z = −0.6; 0.7257.
  4. (Between) X ~ N(12, 25): find P(10 < X < 15). Answer: z = −0.4 and 0.6; 0.7257 − 0.3446 = 0.3811.
  5. (Inverse) X ~ N(12, 25): find the 90th percentile. Answer: z = 1.2816; x = 18.4.
  6. (Unknown sigma) X ~ N(50, s²), P(X > 60) = 0.10. Find s. Answer: z = 1.2816; s = 10/1.2816 = 7.80.
  7. (Combination) X ~ N(10, 4), Y ~ N(15, 9), independent. Find P(X + Y < 30). Answer: sum ~ N(25, 13), sd 3.606, z = 1.387, P = 0.917.
  8. (Difference) Same X, Y: find P(Y − X > 10). Answer: D ~ N(5, 13), z = (10 − 5)/3.606 = 1.387; P = 0.083.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Variance mistaken for sd: N(mu, sigma²) — square-root the second parameter before standardising.
  • Forgetting the tails: P(X > x) = 1 − Phi(z); the table gives "less than".
  • Wrong z sign: values below the mean have negative z; symmetrise using Phi(−z) = 1 − Phi(z).
  • Subtracting variances of a difference: Var(X − Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) when independent.
  • Not stating independence: combinations need it; without the assumption the variance rule does not hold.
  • Continuity: for a discrete variable approximated by the normal, use a continuity correction (P(X ≥ 5) becomes P(X > 4.5)) — required in A2, and stating it early avoids the habit.
  • Rounding z: use four decimal places from tables or the full calculator value; rounding z to 2 d.p. shifts the probability noticeably.
  • Answer without context: convert the probability into a proportion, a number of items or a percentage, as the question asks.

title: Exam technique: Poisson Distribution
content:
### What earns the marks
For lambda scaling, the rate times the interval stated earns the first mark. For probabilities, e^-lambda lambda^x / x! with values earns the method mark. For approximations, the condition named (n large, p small, lambda = np) earns credit.
### Traps
Error: unscaled lambda over a new interval. Correction: scale first. Error: binomial coefficients inside Poisson work. Correction: Poisson formula only. Error: mean and variance treated as different. Correction: both equal lambda.
### Worked example
Calls arrive at a rate of 3 per minute, so over 2 minutes λ = 6. The probability of exactly 2 calls is P(X = 2) = e⁻⁶ × 6² / 2! = 18e⁻⁶ ≈ 0.0446. The mean and the variance both equal λ, so the mean number in 2 minutes is 6.
### Check yourself
Explain why the rate must be scaled before you use the formula. The rate is given per minute, but the interval is 2 minutes, so λ must be the rate multiplied by the interval, giving 6 and not 3.

title: Electricity: D.C. Circuits
content:
Electricity: D.C. Circuits

Current and Charge

I = Q/t — charge per second, in amperes. Conventional current flows + to − (electrons drift the other way).

I = nAvq links microscopic drift to macroscopic current (n = carrier density).

Voltage and Power

  • V = W/Q (joules per coulomb)
  • P = VI = I²R = V²/R

Resistance and Resistivity

R = V/I; R = ρL/A. Resistivity ρ is a material property (Ω m). Metals' resistance rises with temperature; thermistors' falls (NTC).

Example: a wire 2 m long, 0.5 mm² cross-section, ρ = 5 × 10⁻⁷: R = 2 Ω.

Series and Parallel

  • Series: same current, R_total = R₁ + R₂ + …
  • Parallel: same voltage, 1/R_total = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + …

EMF and Internal Resistance

ε = I(R + r) — some voltage is 'lost' inside the battery. Terminal voltage V = ε − Ir drops as load current rises.

Potential Dividers

V_out = V_in × R₂/(R₁ + R₂). Used with LDRs/thermistors to make sensor circuits.

Exam tips: redraw messy networks with clean junctions; always account for internal resistance in 'maximum power' questions.

Core facts to recall

  • Reflection: state the mirror line. Under y = x the coordinates swap, so (a, b) maps to (b, a).
  • Rotation: state the centre, the angle and the direction. A 90° anticlockwise rotation about the origin maps (x, y) to (−y, x).
  • Translation: give a column vector (x; y). Every point moves by the same amount.
  • Enlargement: state the scale factor and the centre. A negative scale factor rotates the image 180° about the centre as well as scaling it.
  • Vectors: the magnitude of (x; y) is √(x² + y²). A resultant is found by adding the component vectors head to tail.
