  • Let the character misjudge a situation, so the reader worries.

Dialogue

Dialogue should reveal character and move the plot forward. Each speaker should sound distinct, and the reader should learn something from each exchange. Use punctuation correctly and begin a new line for each speaker.

Point of view

First person gives direct access to one mind, using I. Third person can be close to one character or wider in view. Choose one viewpoint and keep it consistent.

Ending

A satisfying ending resolves or meaningfully changes the central conflict. It can be open, but it should feel earned, not abandoned.

title: IGCSE Mathematics: Sequences and Functions
content:
IGCSE Mathematics: Sequences and Functions

Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580 (2025–2027), section 2 Algebra and graphs: statement 2.7 Sequences and statement 2.13 Functions (Extended). A sequence is a list of numbers generated by a rule; a function is the rule itself. This note builds nth-term rules from scratch — showing why the formula works, not just what it is — then function notation, composite functions and inverse functions, including the domain restrictions that decide whether an inverse exists.

What a sequence is; term-to-term rules

A sequence is an ordered list of numbers. The term-to-term rule gets from one term to the next: add 4, multiply by 2, subtract 1 then double. It tells you what happens step by step but not what the hundredth term is. The position-to-term rule (the nth term) gives any term directly from its position n, and that is the more powerful description.

Sequence: 3, 7, 11, 15, 19, ...

Term-to-term: add 4 each time.
Position-to-term: the terms are 4 less than 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, ..., so the nth term is 4n - 1.

Check: n = 1 gives 4(1) - 1 = 3 ✓;  n = 5 gives 4(5) - 1 = 19 ✓

Linear sequences and the nth term

A linear (arithmetic) sequence has a constant difference d between terms. Its nth term is dn + b, and b is chosen to make the first term correct.

Find the nth term of 5, 8, 11, 14, ...

Constant difference d = 3, so the nth term starts as 3n.
Compare with the sequence: 3, 6, 9, 12, ... is three times the table of 3;
the real sequence is 2 more each time, so b = 2.
nth term:  3n + 2

Check every term: n = 1: 5 ✓   n = 2: 8 ✓   n = 3: 11 ✓
The 50th term is 3(50) + 2 = 152.

Why dn + b always works. Adding d each time from a starting value a means the nth term is a + (n − 1)d, since term n has had (n − 1) additions of d. Expanding gives a + nd − d = nd + (a − d), which is exactly dn + b with b = a − d. Both forms are the same rule; examiners accept either.

Quadratic and special sequences

When the first difference changes but the second difference is constant, the rule is quadratic: an² + bn + c. The method: build the n² sequence, subtract it from the sequence, and finish the linear remainder.

Find the nth term of 2, 5, 10, 17, 26, ...

First differences: 3, 5, 7, 9;  second differences: 2, 2 (constant) → quadratic.
The n² sequence is 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, ...
Subtract: (2-1), (5-4), (10-9), (17-16), (26-25) = 1, 1, 1, 1, 1
So the sequence is n² + 1.

Check: n = 3 gives 9 + 1 = 10 ✓

Other sequences to recognise on sight: the triangular numbers n(n + 1)/2 (1, 3, 6, 10, ...), the square numbers n², the Fibonacci sequence (each term is the sum of the two before it, and it has no simple nth term), and geometric sequences that multiply by a fixed ratio r — their nth term is arⁿ⁻¹ where a is the first term.

Geometric example: 3, 6, 12, 24, ... has a = 3 and r = 2, so the nth term is 3 × 2^(n-1).
The 6th term is 3 × 2⁵ = 96.
Sequence typeExampleRule
Linear (arithmetic)5, 8, 11, 14Constant difference d; nth term dn + b
Quadratic2, 5, 10, 17Constant second difference; nth term an² + bn + c
Geometric3, 6, 12, 24Constant ratio r; nth term arⁿ⁻¹
Triangular numbers1, 3, 6, 10n(n + 1)/2
Square numbers1, 4, 9, 16n²
Fibonacci1, 1, 2, 3, 5Add the two previous terms (no simple nth term)

Choosing the right description is half the battle: check the first differences, then the second, then the ratio, before assuming any rule. Once a candidate rule is found, verify it against every given term — a sequence that matches only the first three terms is not proven.

Function notation

A function is a machine with an input and exactly one output for each input. The notation f(x) = 2x + 3 names the machine f and says what it does to x: multiply by 2, then add 3. Evaluating is substitution: f(4) = 2(4) + 3 = 11. The machine picture matters: one input never gives two outputs, though two inputs may share an output.

  • The domain is the set of allowed inputs; the range is the set of outputs the function actually produces.
  • For f(x) = x² with domain all real numbers, the range is y ⩾ 0, because squares are never negative.
  • For f(x) = 2x + 3 with domain 0 ⩽ x ⩽ 5, the range is 3 ⩽ f(x) ⩽ 13 — substitute the endpoints, since linear functions stretch ranges proportionally.

Questions ask for the range in terms of y or f(x); find the outputs at the domain boundaries and, for quadratics, at the turning point.

Composite functions

A composite function runs one machine after the other. fg(x) means apply g first, then f to the result — the notation reads right to left, like f(g(x)).

Given f(x) = 2x + 1 and g(x) = x², find fg(3), gf(x) and fg(x).

fg(3):  g(3) = 9, then f(9) = 2(9) + 1 = 19.
gf(x):  apply f first:  g(f(x)) = (2x + 1)² = 4x² + 4x + 1.
fg(x):  apply g first:  f(g(x)) = 2x² + 1.

Note fg(x) ≠ gf(x): order matters.

Every line is written out because the most common error is applying the functions in the wrong order — and the composite is not commutative.

Inverse functions

The inverse f⁻¹ undoes f: if f turns 4 into 11, f⁻¹ turns 11 back into 4. Inverse functions exist only for one-to-one functions — ones where different inputs always give different outputs. The graph of y = x² is not one-to-one over all real numbers (both 3 and −3 give 9), so it has no inverse unless the domain is restricted to x ⩾ 0.

Find the inverse of f(x) = (3x - 2)/5:

Write y = (3x - 2)/5 and make x the subject:
5y = 3x - 2          [multiply by 5]
5y + 2 = 3x          [add 2]
x = (5y + 2)/3       [divide by 3]

Swap x and y:  f⁻¹(x) = (5x + 2)/3

Check by composing: f⁻¹(f(x)) = [5((3x - 2)/5) + 2]/3 = [(3x - 2) + 2]/3 = 3x/3 = x  ✓
  • f⁻¹(x) is a single symbol meaning the inverse function; the −1 is not a power and f⁻¹(x) does not mean 1/f(x).
  • The domain of f⁻¹ is the range of f, and the range of f⁻¹ is the domain of f — they swap, exactly as the inputs and outputs swap roles.
  • Graphically, y = f⁻¹(x) is the reflection of y = f(x) in the line y = x.

Worked example: a full function question

Let f(x) = x² + 3 for x ⩾ 0, and g(x) = 4x − 5.

(a) Find f(2):  f(2) = 4 + 3 = 7.

(b) Find fg(x):  f(g(x)) = (4x - 5)² + 3 = 16x² - 40x + 25 + 3 = 16x² - 40x + 28.

(c) Find f⁻¹(x):  y = x² + 3, so x² = y - 3 and x = √(y - 3) (positive root, since x ⩾ 0).
Swap: f⁻¹(x) = √(x - 3).
Domain of f⁻¹: x ⩾ 3, which is exactly the range of f.

(d) Solve f(x) = 30 for x ⩾ 0:
x² + 3 = 30
x² = 27
x = √27 = 3√3 ≈ 5.20        [only the positive root is in the domain]

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Reading fg(x) as f then g. It is g first, then f — the notation runs right to left.
  • Assuming fg = gf; only special cases agree.
  • Treating f⁻¹(x) as 1/f(x). The inverse undoes the function; it is not a reciprocal.
  • Ignoring domain restrictions: with x ⩾ 0 on f(x) = x² + 3, the inverse takes the positive root only, and a negative root answer is wrong.
  • Claiming y = x² has an inverse over all real numbers; it is two-to-one and needs a restricted domain.
  • Building the nth term from the first difference alone without checking every term; a single wrong check sends a whole answer wrong.
  • Writing a geometric nth term as arⁿ instead of arⁿ⁻¹; the first term must be a itself.
  • Stating a range that ignores the turning point of a quadratic: the range of y = (x − 2)² + 1 is y ⩾ 1, not y ⩾ 0.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 2, 3 marks). Find the nth term of 7, 11, 15, 19, ...

Answer: Constant difference 4, so 4n + b; the first term 7 = 4 + b gives b = 3. The nth term is 4n + 3. The 20th term is 83.

Question 2 (Paper 2, 3 marks). A sequence has nth term 5n − 2. Write down the first four terms and the 100th.

Answer: n = 1, 2, 3, 4 give 3, 8, 13, 18; the 100th term is 5(100) − 2 = 498.

Question 3 (Paper 4, 4 marks). f(x) = 3x − 1 and g(x) = x² + 2. Find fg(x), gf(2) and f⁻¹(x).

Answer: fg(x) = 3(x² + 2) − 1 = 3x² + 5. gf(2): f(2) = 5, so g(5) = 27. Inverse: y = 3x − 1 gives x = (y + 1)/3, so f⁻¹(x) = (x + 1)/3.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 4 marks). The second differences of a sequence are constant at 4, and its first two terms are 2 and 7. Find the nth term.

Answer: Constant second difference 4 means the n² coefficient is 4/2 = 2, so the rule starts 2n². The n² sequence gives 2, 8, ... while the sequence is 2, 7, ..., so the remainder is 0, −1, ... a linear part with difference −1: −n + 1. Check: 2n² − n + 1 gives n = 1: 2 ✓ and n = 2: 8 − 2 + 1 = 7 ✓. The nth term is 2n² − n + 1.

Question 5 (Paper 4, 5 marks). f(x) = (x + 4)/(x − 2) for x ≠ 2. Find f⁻¹(x) and the value of x for which f(x) is undefined.

Answer: y = (x + 4)/(x − 2) gives y(x − 2) = x + 4, so yx − 2y = x + 4, yx − x = 2y + 4, x(y − 1) = 2y + 4 and x = (2y + 4)/(y − 1). Swapping: f⁻¹(x) = (2x + 4)/(x − 1). The function itself is undefined at x = 2, where the denominator vanishes; its inverse is undefined at x = 1.

Question 6 (Paper 2, 3 marks). The first three terms of a geometric sequence are 5, 15, 45. Find the 8th term.

Answer: Common ratio r = 15/5 = 3, so the nth term is 5 × 3ⁿ⁻¹ and the 8th term is 5 × 3⁷ = 5 × 2187 = 10 935.

From variables and patterns, the course now turns to the number system itself.

Sequences: terms, term-to-term rules and position rules

A sequence is an ordered list of numbers that follows a rule. Each number in the list is a term, and the position of a term in the list is its term number, written n. Exam questions give a sequence and ask for a missing term, a rule, or a check on whether a particular number belongs to the pattern. The subsections below cover the two kinds of rule and how to move between them.

Reading a sequence and naming its terms

Write the first term as the term with n = 1, the second as n = 2, and so on. In the sequence 5, 8, 11, 14, the first term is 5 and the fourth term is 14. Read the terms from left to right, and keep the positions fixed, because a term that is shifted by one place gives a wrong answer even when the arithmetic is correct.

Term-to-term rules

A term-to-term rule says how to get the next term from the one before it. "Add 3 each time" and "multiply by 2 each time" are term-to-term rules. To use one, start from a known term and apply the rule repeatedly. A term-to-term rule is quick to apply to a few terms, but it is slow to find a term far down the list, which is why the position rule is needed.

Position-to-term rules, or nth term

A position-to-term rule, often called the nth term, gives any term directly from its position n. For the sequence 5, 8, 11, 14, the nth term is 3n + 2. Check it by substitution: n = 1 gives 5, n = 2 gives 8, and n = 4 gives 14. The nth term is the more useful form in an exam, because it finds the 50th term without listing the first 49.

Finding a term from an nth term

Substitute the position into the rule. For the nth term 3n + 2, the 20th term is 3 × 20 + 2 = 62. Write the substitution in full, with the position inside brackets if it is negative or a fraction, and keep the working so that a method mark can be awarded even if the arithmetic slips.

Testing whether a number belongs to a sequence

To check whether a number such as 80 is in the sequence with nth term 3n + 2, set the rule equal to 80 and solve: 3n + 2 = 80, so 3n = 78 and n = 26. Because n is a whole number, 80 is a term, and it is the 26th term. If the solution for n is not a whole number, the number is not in the sequence.

Arithmetic sequences and the common difference

In an arithmetic sequence the difference between consecutive terms is the same every time. This fixed difference is the common difference, written d. For the sequence 5, 8, 11, 14, the common difference is 3. The nth term of any arithmetic sequence has the form dn + c, where d is the common difference and c is found by substituting the first term.

Geometric sequences and the common ratio

In a geometric sequence each term is found by multiplying the previous one by the same number, called the common ratio. The sequence 3, 6, 12, 24 has common ratio 2. A geometric sequence can grow very quickly, so check the ratio by dividing two consecutive terms rather than guessing it from the first two numbers.

Equations and symbols

Two families of formula share this topic: the rules that generate a sequence, and the algebra of function notation. Both are asked as "find the rule", so the sheet is a list of rules with the letters they use.

4n - 1 Key: n = the position of the term in the sequence (1, 2, 3, …); the coefficient 4 is the common difference and −1 is the adjustment that makes n = 1 give the first term, 3. Substitute n to get any term directly; the 20th term here is 79.

3n + 2 Key: n = position; 3 = common difference of 5, 8, 11, 14; +2 makes the first term correct. Every linear sequence can be written dn + b, and b always equals the first term minus d.

n² + 1 Key: n = position; the n² term means the second difference is constant, which is what identifies a quadratic sequence. Build the n² sequence, subtract it, and finish the remaining linear part.

n(n + 1)/2 Key: n = position; the triangular numbers 1, 3, 6, 10, found by adding the integers 1 to n. Recognise the shape rather than deriving it under exam pressure.

arⁿ⁻¹ Key: a = first term; r = common ratio, found by dividing any term by the one before; n = position. The exponent is n − 1, not n: at n = 1 the term must be a itself, and r⁰ = 1 guarantees that.

f(x) = 2x + 3 Key: f = the function's name; x = the input, in the domain; the expression is the rule — multiply by 2, add 3. Evaluating is substitution: f(4) = 11.

fg(x) = 2x² + 1 Key: fg means apply g first (g(x) = x²), then f to the result; the notation reads right to left. fg(x) is not gf(x) — order matters, and swapping it is the standard error.

f⁻¹(x) = (5x + 2)/3 Key: f⁻¹ = the inverse function, the machine that undoes f; the −1 is not a power, and f⁻¹(x) is never 1/f(x). Found by writing y = f(x), making x the subject, then swapping the letters.

f⁻¹(x) = √(x - 3) Key: the inverse of f(x) = x² + 3 on the domain x ⩾ 0; the positive root alone is taken because the original domain excludes negatives. The domain of f⁻¹ is the range of f, here x ⩾ 3.

How the marks are given. Show the substitution, keep the composite order, and state any domain restriction. A range quoted without checking the turning point — y ⩾ 1 for (x − 2)² + 1, not y ⩾ 0 — is the quiet loss on this topic.

title: IGCSE Biology: Respiration
content:
IGCSE Biology: Respiration

Respiration is the process that keeps every cell alive: the chemical release of energy from glucose inside cells. It is not breathing, it is not combustion, and it happens day and night in every organism. This note separates the definitions that examiners insist on, writes and balances both the aerobic and anaerobic equations from first principles, traces how energy from glucose is transferred to ATP for use in the cell, and covers oxygen debt, the oxygen debt calculation, and the practical methods for measuring respiration rate (the respirometer) that appear in Paper 6.

What respiration is — and what it is not

Respiration is the chemical reactions in cells that break down nutrient molecules (usually glucose) to release energy, which is transferred to ATP. It occurs in every living cell, all the time. Aerobic respiration requires oxygen and releases much more energy per glucose molecule; anaerobic respiration occurs without oxygen and releases much less. Important distinctions: breathing (ventilation) brings oxygen to the lungs and removes carbon dioxide, but respiration happens inside cells; combustion is burning outside the body; and the energy released is used for muscle contraction, active transport, protein synthesis, cell division and maintaining body temperature (mammals and birds are endothermic).

Aerobic respiration: the equation and its stages

Word equation: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy. Symbol equation: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O. Balance check: 6 carbons each side; 12 hydrogens each side (6 × 2 in water); oxygens: 6 + 12 = 18 on the left, 12 + 6 = 18 on the right. The full pathway at A Level and in the supplement: glycolysis (in the cytoplasm) splits glucose into two pyruvate molecules, releasing a small amount of ATP and reduced NAD; the link reaction and Krebs cycle (in the mitochondrial matrix) strip hydrogen and release carbon dioxide; oxidative phosphorylation (on the inner mitochondrial membrane) uses the hydrogen electrons in the electron transfer chain to make large amounts of ATP, with oxygen as the final electron acceptor forming water. The folded cristae of the inner membrane increase surface area for the ATP-generating enzymes — a favourite structure-function question.

Anaerobic respiration in animals and plants

When oxygen is short (sprinting, flooded roots), cells switch to anaerobic respiration. In animals: glucose → lactic acid (+ a little energy), equation C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₃H₆O₃. Only glycolysis runs, so the yield is 2 ATP per glucose versus about 30–32 aerobically. Lactic acid accumulates in muscles, causing fatigue and cramp, and must be broken down later. In plants and yeast: glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide + energy, equation C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂. Yeast fermentation is used industrially to make bread (carbon dioxide raises the dough) and alcoholic drinks (ethanol); both anaerobic equations must balance — check the atoms: C₆ → 2C₃ (animals) or 2C₂ + 2C (yeast, six carbons total), H₁₂ → 6 in two lactic acid molecules or 12 in two ethanol molecules, and the oxygens accordingly.

Oxygen debt

Oxygen debt (excess post-exercise oxygen consumption) is the extra oxygen the body takes in after exercise to restore itself: repaying the lactic acid (oxidising it back to carbon dioxide and water in the liver), resynthesising ATP and phosphocreatine stores, and returning heart rate, breathing rate and body temperature to resting levels. Measure it as the volume of oxygen consumed during recovery minus the resting requirement over the same period. The heavier the exercise, the larger the debt and the longer the recovery — which is exactly the shape of the oxygen-uptake graph before, during and after exercise.

Measuring respiration rate: the respirometer

A respirometer measures oxygen consumption: germinating seeds (actively respiring) are placed in a sealed tube with a small tube of sodium hydroxide solution (which absorbs the carbon dioxide produced, so any gas volume change is due to oxygen use). As oxygen is consumed, gas pressure drops and the coloured drop of liquid in the capillary tube moves towards the apparatus; the distance moved per minute is proportional to the rate of respiration. Control tube: same setup with dead seeds (no respiration) to correct for atmospheric pressure and temperature changes. Variables: independent = temperature or seed type; dependent = distance moved per minute (or volume of oxygen per gram per hour); controls = same mass of seeds, same volume of sodium hydroxide, same time, same apparatus. Use a water bath to set temperature. To calculate actual oxygen consumption, measure the distance moved and convert using the capillary tube's internal volume (volume = π × radius² × distance).

Aerobic and anaerobic compared

FeatureAerobic respirationAnaerobic respiration
OxygenRequiredAbsent or in short supply
SiteCytoplasm and mitochondriaCytoplasm only
Products (animals)Carbon dioxide and waterLactic acid
Products (yeast/plants)Carbon dioxide and waterEthanol and carbon dioxide
Energy per glucoseLarge amount (about 30-32 ATP)Small amount (2 ATP)
EquationC₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂OC₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₃H₆O₃ (animals)

The two pathways also differ in what happens to the hydrogen stripped from glucose. In aerobic respiration the hydrogen is carried by NAD to the inner mitochondrial membrane, where the electron transfer chain passes it to oxygen, forming water and driving the phosphorylation of ADP to ATP — this final step is where most of the ATP comes from. In anaerobic respiration there is no oxygen to accept the hydrogen, so pyruvate itself accepts it (forming lactic acid in animals) or loses carbon dioxide first (forming ethanol in yeast), and the electron transfer chain never runs. That single difference explains the enormous gap in ATP yield, and it is the mechanistic point A Level examiners probe when they ask why lactic acid forms at all.

Worked example: a full anaerobic comparison and the respirometer calculation

An athlete runs 400 m and produces 12 g of lactic acid. What mass of glucose was respired anaerobically? Step 1: the equation: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₃H₆O₃; relative formula masses: glucose 180, lactic acid 90 each, so 180 g of glucose gives 2 × 90 = 180 g of lactic acid. Step 2: ratio 180:180, that is 1:1. Step 3: 12 g lactic acid therefore came from 12 g of glucose. Now the respirometer: in 10 minutes at 25 °C the drop moved 12 mm; at 15 °C it moved 4 mm; dead-seed control moved 1 mm in both cases. Step 1: subtract the control (temperature effects on gas volume): 12 − 1 = 11 mm and 4 − 1 = 3 mm. Step 2: per minute: 11 ÷ 10 = 1.1 mm/min and 3 ÷ 10 = 0.3 mm/min. Step 3: compare: respiration at 25 °C is 1.1 ÷ 0.3 ≈ 3.7 times faster than at 15 °C. Step 4: explain: enzymes of respiration have more kinetic energy at the higher temperature, so more frequent successful collisions.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Defining respiration as "breathing" — it is a chemical process in cells; the distinction is worth a mark almost every year.
  • Writing "energy is released" without saying it is "transferred to ATP" — ATP is the usable energy currency, and the phrasing earns marks.
  • Unbalanced equations: aerobic has 6O₂ and 6H₂O — anything else loses marks.
  • Writing lactic acid as "lactate" only or giving the wrong formula; the symbol equation C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₃H₆O₃ is required at this level.
  • Claiming anaerobic respiration "releases no energy" — it releases less, not none.
  • Explaining oxygen debt as "paying back oxygen": it is the oxygen used to oxidise lactic acid and restore ATP, measured as extra uptake.
  • Forgetting the control (dead seeds) in a respirometer plan — a whole mark for "controls for atmospheric pressure/temperature".
  • Saying the mitochondrion is "where respiration happens" without noting glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm.

Exam-style questions and answers

Q1. Write the word equation for aerobic respiration. (2 marks) Answer: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + (energy transferred to ATP) — one mark for reactants, one for products.

Q2. Compare aerobic and anaerobic respiration in muscle cells. (4 marks) Answer: aerobic uses oxygen, anaerobic does not (1); aerobic in mitochondria and cytoplasm, anaerobic in cytoplasm only (1); aerobic produces carbon dioxide and water, anaerobic produces lactic acid (1); aerobic releases much more energy per glucose (1).

Q3. Explain what happens to lactic acid after exercise. (3 marks) Answer: it is transported to the liver (1); oxidised to carbon dioxide and water or converted back to glycogen (1); the oxygen used in this and in restoring ATP/heat is the oxygen debt (1).

Q4. Describe how you would use a respirometer to compare respiration rates in germinating and dead seeds. (4 marks) Answer: place equal masses in sealed tubes with sodium hydroxide to absorb carbon dioxide (1); record distance moved by the coloured drop per minute (1); run a dead-seed control to correct for pressure/temperature (1); keep temperature constant in a water bath and repeat for means (1).

Q5. Explain why the rate of respiration increases when temperature rises from 15 °C to 25 °C. (2 marks) Answer: enzymes gain kinetic energy (1); more frequent successful collisions, so respiration is faster (1).

Respiration: the chemistry under the equation

The equation for aerobic respiration balances, so it is easy to write and easy to misunderstand. It is not one reaction but a chain of them, and the chain explains the details mark schemes keep asking about: why oxygen is needed at all, why anaerobic respiration releases so little energy, why carbon dioxide appears in some organisms and not others, and where the oxygen debt goes. This section follows the chemistry far enough to answer those questions without going beyond what the specification expects.

ATP: the cell's currency, not its fuel

Glucose is the fuel; ATP is what the cell actually spends. Respiration transfers the energy released by oxidising glucose into the bonds of ATP, and a cell then hydrolyses ATP to ADP and inorganic phosphate wherever work is needed: active transport across a membrane, protein synthesis on a ribosome, contraction of a muscle fibre, movement of chromosomes in mitosis, and the maintenance of body temperature in endotherms. Each hydrolysis releases a small, usable packet of energy, roughly thirty kilojoules per mole, rather than the sudden large release that burning glucose would give.

ATP is not stored in quantity. A working muscle can use its entire ATP content in seconds, so it is continually remade, and this is the real reason respiration never stops. Even a resting cell respires continuously, and the rate rises with activity. If you are asked why a dead organism stops producing carbon dioxide, the answer is not "it has run out of glucose" but "its enzymes have denatured, so the reactions that regenerate ATP have stopped".

Glycolysis: the stage that needs no oxygen

The first stage takes place in the cytoplasm and needs no oxygen at all. A six-carbon glucose molecule is split into two three-carbon pyruvate molecules, and the process yields a net two ATP per glucose. Because this stage is anaerobic, it is the reason any respiration at all is possible without oxygen: anaerobic respiration is not a different pathway so much as a different ending to the same beginning.

This is also why the anaerobic equations are worth writing as a two-step story. Glucose goes to pyruvate first, in both cases; then pyruvate is converted either onward into the mitochondrion, when oxygen is available, or into lactate or ethanol, when it is not.

Aerobic: where the oxygen is actually spent

With oxygen present, pyruvate enters a mitochondrion. There it is broken down completely: the carbon atoms leave as carbon dioxide, and the hydrogen atoms are removed and carried to the inner membrane — the cristae — where they are passed along a chain of electron carriers. At the end of that chain, hydrogen combines with oxygen to form water. Oxygen's role is therefore not to "burn" glucose directly but to accept the hydrogen at the end of the chain: remove it and the carriers stay reduced, the chain stops, and the whole of aerobic respiration stops with it. That single sentence explains why breathing faster after exercise is not enough on its own — the oxygen has to reach the mitochondrion, which is why circulation and haemoglobin matter too.

The yield is about thirty to thirty-two ATP per glucose, against two for the anaerobic route. Do not write thirty-eight; modern counting gives a lower figure, and the mark scheme only needs "much more than anaerobic". Carbon dioxide is released in the mitochondrion, never in the cytoplasm, which is why a respiring plant cell releases carbon dioxide but a respiring human red blood cell — which has no mitochondria — does not.

Check the balance once by counting atoms. Glucose C₆H₁₂O₆ plus six O₂ gives six CO₂ and six H₂O: six carbons, twelve hydrogens and eighteen oxygens on each side. If a question gives you an unfamiliar fuel, this is how you write its equation.

Anaerobic: two different endings, two different equations

In animals, including your own muscles, pyruvate is converted to lactate. No carbon dioxide is released, and the yield is two ATP per glucose: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₃H₆O₃. In yeast and in plant cells, pyruvate is converted to ethanol and carbon dioxide, again with two ATP: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂. The difference matters in the exam: if a respiring tissue releases carbon dioxide without oxygen, it is not animal muscle.

Lactate is not a waste product in the way carbon dioxide is, because it still holds usable energy. It is carried in the blood to the liver, where it is oxidised back to pyruvate using oxygen supplied after exercise has stopped. That extra oxygen is the oxygen debt, and it is why breathing stays elevated for minutes afterwards. The lactate that accumulates in muscle lowers the pH slightly and is associated with the burning sensation and fatigue of sprinting; the older claim that lactate alone causes cramp is too strong, so write "associated with fatigue" and gain the mark without overstating the evidence.

Where each route happens in real organisms is examinable. Anaerobic respiration in animals occurs during vigorous exercise, when breathing and circulation cannot deliver oxygen fast enough. In plants it happens in roots in waterlogged soil, where air spaces fill with water and oxygen cannot diffuse in; this is one reason waterlogged fields damage crops. In microorganisms it is the basis of brewing and bread-making, where the carbon dioxide from yeast raises the dough, and of biogas production.

The respirometer: what the bubble is really showing

A respirometer seals a living organism in a tube with a carbon dioxide absorbent such as potassium hydroxide. The organism uses oxygen and releases carbon dioxide, but the alkali removes the carbon dioxide, so the only gas leaving the air in the tube is oxygen. The volume falls, the pressure falls, and the bubble at the end of the capillary moves towards the organism. The distance it travels is therefore a direct measure of oxygen consumption, not of total gas exchange — a distinction the exam likes.

Temperature must be held constant, and there is a specific reason: a rise of one degree Celsius expands a gas by about 0.3 %, and over ten minutes that expansion can equal the movement caused by a small organism's respiration. A control tube — the same apparatus with the same mass of dead organism, or with glass beads — is called a thermobarometer. It shows how far the bubble moves for reasons that are not respiration, and you subtract that movement from the reading.

Calculate in the order the mark scheme expects. Rate equals distance divided by time; divide by the mass of the organism to compare fairly; state the units. Two tubes at different temperatures give two rates (Figure 2), and the comparison is only valid if the masses, the species, the state of the organism and the time are the same. Good Paper 6 answers add repeats and a mean, and mention that the apparatus was sealed and left to equilibrate for a few minutes before the first reading.

Evidence: how we know what we know

Four demonstrations are worth having at your fingertips, because each isolates one claim. Yeast with glucose in a sealed tube, connected to limewater, turns the limewater milky: carbon dioxide is produced without oxygen, so anaerobic respiration occurs. Boiled yeast in the same apparatus produces nothing: the process needs intact enzymes, so it is biological, not a chemical decomposition. Germinating seeds in a respirometer take up oxygen faster than dry seeds: germination is energetically expensive and powered by aerobic respiration. And a person's oxygen consumption stays above resting rate for several minutes after hard exercise, while blood lactate falls: the extra oxygen is being used to clear the lactate, which is the oxygen debt made visible.

Anaerobic and aerobic compared, in the terms an examiner uses

FeatureAerobicAnaerobic (animal)Anaerobic (yeast)
OxygenRequiredNot requiredNot required
WhereCytoplasm, then mitochondriaCytoplasm onlyCytoplasm only
ProductsCarbon dioxide and waterLactateEthanol and carbon dioxide
ATP per glucoseAbout 3022
When it happensContinuously, in all living cellsVigorous exercise, oxygen shortfallWaterlogged roots, brewing, baking
RecoveryNone neededOxygen debt repaid in the liverEthanol accumulates and is toxic

One last precision point. Respiration is a series of enzyme-controlled reactions inside cells; breathing is the mechanical movement of air into and out of the lungs; gas exchange is diffusion across a surface. They are three different words for three different things, and a paper that asks for two of them usually has a mark for keeping them apart.

Equations and symbols

The three equations of respiration and the one calculation behind the respirometer. Arrow means "is converted into"; the state symbols are not required at IGCSE, but the balancing is.

C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O Key: C₆H₁₂O₆ = glucose, one molecule; O₂ = oxygen, six molecules; CO₂ = carbon dioxide; H₂O = water. Count the atoms before you write it: 6 carbon, 12 hydrogen and 18 oxygen on each side.

C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₃H₆O₃ Key: C₃H₆O₃ = lactic acid, two molecules from one glucose; no oxygen appears on either side, which is what makes this the anaerobic equation of muscle. The energy released is small and is not shown as a product — write "energy transferred to ATP" in words.

C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂ Key: C₂H₅OH = ethanol; CO₂ = carbon dioxide, which is what raises bread dough and shows as bubbles in yeast experiments. Plants and yeast use this route; animals never do, because they cannot excrete ethanol.

volume = π × radius² × distance Key: volume = oxygen taken up (cm³); π = 3.14; radius = internal radius of the capillary bore (cm, so 0.5 mm becomes 0.05 cm); distance = how far the coloured drop moved (cm). The area of the bore times the distance travelled is the volume, and dividing by the time gives a rate.

11 ÷ 10 = 1.1 mm/min and 3 ÷ 10 = 0.3 mm/min Key: 11 mm and 3 mm are the control-corrected distances the drop moved at 25 °C and at 15 °C; 10 is the time in minutes; the quotients are rates of oxygen uptake. Their ratio, 1.1 ÷ 0.3 ≈ 3.7, is the comparison the question wants, and the dead-seed control is what makes both numbers trustworthy.

title: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Scatter Diagrams and Correlation
content:
Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Scatter Diagrams and Correlation

A scatter diagram plots two measurements for each person or object, one on each axis, and reveals whether they move together. The IGCSE questions ask you to describe that relationship — correlation — draw a line of best fit, and use it to estimate. The arithmetic is light; the marks come from precise language and from the discipline of drawing and reading the line correctly. This note builds the topic from zero: what correlation means and how to describe it, how to draw a line of best fit that earns the marks, how to use it for interpolation and extrapolation, and why correlation is not causation.

What a scatter diagram shows

Each point represents one individual: its horizontal coordinate is one variable (say, hours of revision) and its vertical coordinate the other (say, test score). The pattern of points — the scatter — is the data's message. Bivariate data means two variables measured on the same individuals; the diagram is the quickest way to see whether a relationship exists.

  • Positive correlation: as one variable increases, the other tends to increase (revision time and score).
  • Negative correlation: as one increases, the other tends to decrease (car age and value).
  • No correlation: no pattern — the points form a cloud (shoe size and score).
  • Strength: strong correlation means the points lie close to a line; weak means they are widely scattered around it.

Describing correlation precisely

The mark scheme wants three things in a description: direction (positive or negative), strength (strong, moderate or weak), and the variables named. "There is a strong positive correlation between hours of revision and test score" earns the mark; "the graph goes up" does not.

Worked example. A scatter diagram of 30 cars shows points tightly clustered around a line falling from top-left to bottom-right. Describe the correlation and interpret it.

Strong negative correlation between age and value:
older cars tend to be worth less. The tightness of the
cluster means the relationship is consistent, but individual
cars can still deviate (condition, mileage).

Drawing the line of best fit

A line of best fit summarises the trend. The marks are awarded for a straight line that:

  1. Passes through the middle of the cloud — roughly equal numbers of points above and below.
  2. Follows the trend direction (rising for positive, falling for negative correlation).
  3. Is drawn with a ruler and extends across the plotted range.

A useful anchor: the line should pass close to the mean point (the mean of the x-values, mean of the y-values). It does not have to pass through the origin, and it should not be forced through any single point.

Worked example. Points cluster with mean x = 12 and mean y = 60, trending upward. Describe where the line of best fit should pass and how to check it.

The line should pass through (12, 60) and follow the upward
trend; check by counting points above and below - roughly equal
numbers on each side, with the line through the middle of the
vertical spread at each x.

Using the line: interpolation and extrapolation

Once the line is drawn, estimates are read from it — not from individual points:

  • Interpolation: estimating within the range of the data. Reliable, because the trend is supported by nearby points.
  • Extrapolation: estimating beyond the plotted range. Risky, because nothing guarantees the relationship continues — a straight line cannot describe a curve that turns.

Worked example. A line of best fit passes through (4, 30) and (10, 54). Estimate y when x = 7, and comment on estimating y when x = 30.

gradient = (54 - 30)/(10 - 4) = 24/6 = 4
equation: y = 4x + c; using (4, 30): 30 = 16 + c → c = 14
y = 4x + 14
at x = 7: y = 28 + 14 = 42  (interpolation - reliable)
at x = 30: y = 134 (extrapolation - unreliable; the trend may
not continue that far)

Worked example: from table to diagram to estimate

Data: hours studied (x): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6; marks (y): 35, 42, 50, 55, 63, 70.

Step 1: plot each pair as a point (x horizontal, y vertical).
Step 2: describe - strong positive correlation.
Step 3: draw the line through the middle: the points rise
        about 7 marks per hour; a line from (1, 35) to (6, 70)
        passes through the centre of the cloud.
Step 4: estimate the mark for 3.5 hours: read up from x = 3.5
        to the line, then across: about 53 marks.
Step 5: estimate the hours for 60 marks: read across from y = 60
        to the line, then down: about 4.6 hours.

Note the wording in answers: "from the line of best fit, approximately 53 marks" — the word approximately signals that it is an estimate, which the mark scheme expects.

Correlation and causation

Correlation does not prove cause. Two variables can move together because a third factor drives both (ice-cream sales and drowning rates both rise in summer — heat causes both), or by coincidence in a small sample. Exam questions reward this caution explicitly: state that the correlation shows an association, not that one variable causes the other, unless the data come from a controlled experiment.

Worked example. A study finds a strong positive correlation between the number of books in a home and children's reading scores. Does buying books raise scores?

Not necessarily: households with more books may also have more
educated parents, more time for reading, or higher income - all
of which could raise scores. The correlation is real, but the
causal claim is unsupported by this evidence alone.

A second discipline follows: when a question asks you to comment on a study, name the possible confounding variable rather than simply denying causation. In the books example, income, parental education and available time are all plausible common causes; naming one shows the examiner you understand what a confounding factor is. The same reasoning explains why a strong correlation from a small sample deserves caution: with only a handful of points, a pattern can appear by chance, and a single outlier can create or destroy the apparent trend.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Describe) Points on a scatter diagram trend downward and are tightly clustered. Describe the correlation. Answer: Strong negative correlation — as one variable increases, the other tends to decrease consistently.
  2. (No correlation) Describe a scatter diagram whose points form a random cloud. Answer: No correlation — there is no clear trend between the variables.
  3. (Line) State two features of a correctly drawn line of best fit. Answer: A straight line through the middle of the points with roughly equal numbers above and below, following the trend and drawn with a ruler.
  4. (Estimate) A line of best fit passes through (2, 10) and (6, 26). Estimate y at x = 4. Answer: gradient 4; y = 4x + 2; at x = 4, y = 18.
  5. (Interpolation) Explain why an estimate inside the data range is more reliable than one outside it. Answer: Inside the range the trend is supported by nearby data points (interpolation); outside it (extrapolation) there is no evidence that the relationship continues in the same way.
  6. (Causation) A shop finds that sales of umbrellas and sales of coats rise together. Explain the correlation without claiming that umbrellas cause coat sales. Answer: Both are driven by a third variable — rainy weather — which increases demand for both; the correlation is association, not causation.
  7. (Outlier) One point sits far from the trend. What should you do with it when drawing the line? Answer: Note it as an outlier and draw the line through the main body of points; do not let one point pull the line away from the trend.
  8. (Strength) Two scatter diagrams both show positive correlation; in one the points are close to the line. Compare them. Answer: The tighter diagram shows stronger positive correlation; the looser one shows weaker positive correlation.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Joining the dots: a line of best fit is a single straight line through the trend, never a zigzag connecting points.
  • Forcing through the origin: the line passes through the middle of the cloud; there is no reason for it to start at (0, 0).
  • Reading a point instead of the line: estimates come from the line of best fit, not from the nearest plotted point.
  • Ignoring outliers: one extreme point should not swing the line; note it and fit the main cluster.
  • Weak description: "positive" alone is incomplete — direction and strength, with variables named.
  • Causal language: "revision causes higher scores" overclaims from observational data; write "is associated with" and mention confounding factors.
  • Extrapolating confidently: beyond the data range, state the estimate is unreliable.
  • Axes: plot the explanatory variable on the horizontal axis and the response on the vertical, label both with units, and use the given scales exactly.

title: Number — Arithmetic and Place Value — Study Notes
content:
Number — Arithmetic and Place Value

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): 1.1 integers & place value; 1.2 fractions/decimals/percentages context; 1.3 powers & roots; HCF/LCM.

1. Types of number

  • Integers: … −2, −1, 0, 1, 2 … Primes: exactly two factors; 2 is the only even prime; 1 is not prime.
  • HCF = product of common prime factors (lowest powers); LCM = all prime factors (highest powers).

Example: 60 = 2²×3×5 and 84 = 2²×3×7 ⇒ HCF = 2²×3 = 12; LCM = 2²×3×5×7 = 420.

2. Place value

In 47 382 the digit 7 has value 7000. Rounding to significant figures: keep n digits, round using the next digit (≥5 up).

Estimation: round inputs to 1 s.f. first — 39.2 × 5.98 ≈ 40 × 6 = 240.

3. Order of operations

BIDMAS. 3 + 4 × 2² = 3 + 16 = 19. Insert brackets yourself when translating words: "3 added to the product of 4 and 2²" = 3 + (4 × 2²).

4. Negative numbers and calculators

Bracket negatives when substituting. Know the ×10ˣ, x², √, ˣ√ and fraction keys; give answers to 3 s.f. unless told otherwise.

5. Bounds (Extended)

Measured to nearest u: UB = +u/2, LB = −u/2. Division p/q: max = UBp ÷ LBq.

Example: 45 cm (nearest cm) in 6 s (nearest s): max speed = 45.5 ÷ 5.5 = 8.27 m/s (3 s.f.).

Exam tips: show prime-factor trees for HCF/LCM; always state rounding units (3 s.f., 1 d.p.); bounds answers quote both limits.

Place value and ordering

Each digit is worth ten times the digit to its right. To order decimals, compare digits from left to right, padding with zeros so every number has the same number of decimal places. Rounding to a given number of decimal places or significant figures looks at the next digit: 5 or more rounds up.

Written methods

Long multiplication and division are set out in columns with place value kept aligned. Estimate first by rounding each number to one significant figure; the estimate shows whether the exact answer is reasonable. Check using the inverse operation.

Order of operations

Brackets, then indices, then division and multiplication from left to right, then addition and subtraction from left to right. For example, 3 + 4 × 2² = 3 + 4 × 4 = 19. Use a calculator's brackets key to enter long expressions in one go.

Worked example: signs in multiplication and division

Two negatives multiply to a positive, so (−3) × (−4) = 12. A negative times a positive gives a negative, so −24 ÷ 6 = −4. Subtracting a negative is the same as adding, so 3 − (−5) = 8. Apply the order of operations first: in 2 + 3 × (−4), the multiplication gives 2 − 12 = −10, not (2 + 3) × (−4) = −20.

Exam method: estimating before calculating

Round each number to one significant figure to estimate the answer before you use a calculator. For 4.9 × 21.8, the estimate 5 × 20 = 100 tells you that an answer of 10.68 or 1068 is wrong and that the true value, 106.82, is sensible. Writing the estimate down also gives you a check when a key is pressed incorrectly. When a question asks you to show working, write each step on its own line so that method marks can be awarded.

title: A Level Physics: Thermal Physics
content:
A Level Physics: Thermal Physics

Thermal physics is the accountancy of heat: what temperature really measures, how much energy it takes to change a substance's state, and how the invisible motion of billions of particles produces the pressure in a balloon. This note builds the whole subject from zero: thermal equilibrium and the temperature scales, specific heat capacity and specific latent heat with full calorimetry arithmetic, the mole and the equation of state, the kinetic theory that justifies it, and the first law of thermodynamics — the energy bookkeeping rule that governs engines, fridges and stars alike.

Thermal equilibrium

Heat flows from hotter to cooler bodies until no further net transfer occurs — that final state is thermal equilibrium, when both bodies are at the same temperature. The zeroth law of thermodynamics makes the logic precise: if A is in thermal equilibrium with B, and B with C, then A is in equilibrium with C — which is exactly why thermometers work (they reach equilibrium with the thing measured, and the reading transfers). The distinction examiners demand: temperature measures the average random kinetic energy per particle; heat is energy in transit because of a temperature difference. Objects do not contain heat — they contain internal energy.

Temperature scales

The Celsius scale is defined by two fixed points: the melting point of pure ice (0 °C) and the boiling point of pure water (100 °C) at standard pressure. The thermodynamic (Kelvin) scale starts at absolute zero — the temperature at which particles have minimum kinetic energy, −273.15 °C — and its unit, the kelvin, is the same size as the degree Celsius:

T (K) = theta (deg C) + 273        (273.15 exact; 273 usual in exams)
temperature change: Delta T in K = Delta theta in deg C

Every gas-law and kinetic-theory calculation demands kelvin; forgetting the conversion is the single commonest thermal error. A temperature change of 10 °C is a change of 10 K — only absolute values need converting.

Specific heat capacity

Heating a body raises its temperature; the energy needed depends on the substance's own reluctance to change temperature:

E = m c Delta theta        (or E = C Delta theta for a whole body)

E in J, m in kg, c in J kg-1 K-1 (specific heat capacity)
Delta theta in deg C or K (the same size)
C = m c = heat capacity of the object (J K-1)

The electrical method of measuring c is examinable as a practical: a heater of known power runs for a known time (E = Pt), the temperature rise is recorded, and losses are reduced with insulation and a lid; the graph of temperature against time is extrapolated back to the start to correct for losses during heating.

Worked example 1. A 2.0 kg aluminium block (c = 900 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) is heated from 20 °C to 80 °C by a 500 W heater. Find the energy needed and the minimum heating time.

E = m c Delta theta = 2.0 x 900 x 60 = 108 000 J = 108 kJ
t = E/P = 108 000/500 = 216 s = 3.6 minutes

Worked example 2 (mixing). 0.50 kg of water at 90 °C is mixed with 0.50 kg of water at 10 °C. Find the final temperature (no losses).

heat lost = heat gained
m c (90 - T) = m c (T - 10)   (same m and c cancel)
90 - T = T - 10 -> 100 = 2T -> T = 50 deg C

The mixing equation is worth learning as a shape: Σ(heat lost) = Σ(heat gained), with each term mcΔθ evaluated from its own temperature difference to the final T.

Specific latent heat

During a change of state, energy goes into breaking intermolecular bonds rather than raising temperature — the heating curve flatlines at the melting or boiling point. The energy for the change:

E = m L        L = specific latent heat (J kg-1)

L_fusion for melting/freezing; L_vaporisation for boiling/condensing

Worked example. A 3.0 kW kettle boils 1.5 kg of water already at 100 °C. How long to boil it dry (L_vap = 2.26 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹)?

E = m L = 1.5 x 2.26 x 10^6 = 3.39 x 10^6 J
t = E/P = 3.39 x 10^6/3000 = 1130 s = 18.8 minutes

Reading a heating curve is a standard question: sloped sections are temperature rise (mcΔθ applies), flat sections are change of state (mL applies), and the flat at 0 °C is melting while the flat at 100 °C is boiling.

The mole

The mole counts particles the way a dozen counts eggs: one mole contains exactly Nₐ = 6.02 × 10²³ particles (Avogadro's constant). The molar mass M is the mass of one mole (numerically the relative atomic mass in grams; in kg mol⁻¹ for calculations).

n = m / M        N = n N_A

n in mol, m in kg (or g consistently with M), M in kg mol-1

Worked example. Find the number of molecules in 8.0 g of oxygen (O₂, M = 0.032 kg mol⁻¹).

n = m/M = 0.008/0.032 = 0.25 mol
N = n N_A = 0.25 x 6.02 x 10^23 = 1.505 x 10^23 molecules
  = 1.5 x 10^23 (2 s.f.)

The equation of state

For a fixed mass of an ideal gas, pressure, volume and temperature obey one master equation:

p V = n R T        (also p V = N k T)

p in pascals (Pa), V in m3, T in kelvin (K)
R = 8.31 J K-1 mol-1  (molar gas constant)
k = 1.38 x 10-23 J K-1 (Boltzmann constant), N = number of molecules

Unit discipline: 1 atm = 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa; 1 cm³ = 10⁻⁶ m³; 1 litre = 10⁻³ m³. The ideal-gas assumptions are examinable: molecules are point particles with negligible volume, intermolecular forces are negligible except during collisions, and collisions are perfectly elastic.

Worked example. 0.40 mol of gas occupies 2.0 × 10⁻³ m³ at 27 °C. Find the pressure.

T = 27 + 273 = 300 K
p = nRT/V = (0.40 x 8.31 x 300)/(2.0 x 10^-3)
  = 997.2/2.0 x 10^-3 = 4.99 x 10^5 Pa = 5.0 x 10^5 Pa (2 s.f.)

Boyle's, Charles's and the pressure law are all slices of this one equation — if a question gives a change at constant moles, either hold one variable fixed to get the simple law, or write p₁V₁/T₁ = p₂V₂/T₂ for the general case.

Kinetic theory

The kinetic model explains pressure: gas molecules collide elastically with container walls, and each collision transfers momentum; billions per second give a steady average force per unit area — pressure. The model's assumptions (large number of molecules, random motion, elastic collisions, negligible molecular volume, forces only during collisions) justify the ideal-gas behaviour, and the theory links the microscopic to the macroscopic:

p V = (1/3) N m c^2        c = root-mean-square speed

mean kinetic energy per molecule = (3/2) k T
so (1/2) m c^2 = (3/2) k T  ->  c = sqrt(3 k T / m)

The rms speed rises with the square root of absolute temperature and falls with molecular mass — hydrogen molecules move faster than oxygen molecules at the same temperature.

Worked example. Find the rms speed of helium atoms (m = 6.6 × 10⁻²⁷ kg) at 300 K.

c = sqrt(3 k T/m) = sqrt(3 x 1.38 x 10^-23 x 300/6.6 x 10^-27)
  = sqrt(1.242 x 10^-20/6.6 x 10^-27) = sqrt(1.88 x 10^6)
  = 1372 m s-1  (2 s.f.: 1.4 x 10^3 m s-1)

Internal energy

The internal energy of a substance is the sum of the random kinetic energies of its particles plus the potential energies of their interactions. For an ideal gas (no intermolecular forces) internal energy is purely kinetic and proportional to absolute temperature; for real substances, melting and boiling raise internal energy because potential energy increases as bonds stretch and break. State the split precisely in definitions: internal energy = total random kinetic energy + total intermolecular potential energy.

The first law of thermodynamics

Energy is conserved: the change in a system's internal energy equals the heat added to it plus the work done on it.

Delta U = Q + W

Delta U = change in internal energy (J)
Q = heat energy transferred to the system (J), negative if lost
W = work done ON the system (J), negative if the system does work
    (for a gas: W = -p Delta V under the convention W = work done
     on the system; expanding gas does work, so W is negative)

The sign convention must match your course's — state it in words when you apply the law. Applications the papers love: compressing a gas quickly (W positive, little Q, so ΔU and temperature rise); a gas expanding slowly at constant temperature (ΔU = 0 for an ideal gas, so Q = −W — heat flows in to supply the work done); and refrigerators (work is done to move heat against its natural flow).

Worked example. A gas is compressed so that 500 J of work is done on it while 200 J of heat flows out. Find ΔU and state the temperature change.

W = +500 J (done on the system), Q = -200 J (lost)
Delta U = Q + W = -200 + 500 = +300 J
internal energy rises -> temperature rises (for an ideal gas)

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Definitions) Distinguish between temperature and internal energy. Answer: Temperature is proportional to the mean random kinetic energy per molecule; internal energy is the total random kinetic energy plus the intermolecular potential energy of all the particles.
  2. (Kelvin) Convert 27 °C to kelvin and state absolute zero in °C. Answer: T = 27 + 273 = 300 K; absolute zero = −273 °C (−273.15 °C exactly).
  3. (Specific heat) 0.15 kg of a metal at 100 °C is dropped into 0.25 kg of water at 15 °C; the final temperature is 22 °C. Find the metal's specific heat capacity (c_water = 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹). Answer: heat gained by water = 0.25 × 4200 × 7 = 7350 J; metal lost = 0.15 × c × 78 = 7350 → c = 7350/(0.15 × 78) = 628 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ ≈ 630 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.
  4. (Latent heat) Explain why the temperature of boiling water stays constant. Answer: The energy supplied breaks intermolecular bonds during the change of state instead of raising the average kinetic energy of the molecules, so the temperature is unchanged until all the liquid has vaporised.
  5. (Equation of state) 2.0 g of helium (M = 4.0 g mol⁻¹) occupies 0.012 m³ at 300 K. Find the pressure. Answer: n = 2.0/4.0 = 0.50 mol; p = nRT/V = (0.50 × 8.31 × 300)/0.012 = 103 875 Pa ≈ 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa.
  6. (Kinetic theory) State two assumptions of the kinetic model and explain why doubling absolute temperature changes rms speed the way it does. Answer: Molecules are point particles with negligible volume; collisions are perfectly elastic; intermolecular forces are negligible except during collisions (any two). Since c = √(3kT/m), doubling T multiplies c by √2 — speed depends on the square root of absolute temperature.
  7. (First law) A gas expands, doing 300 J of work, while 100 J of heat is supplied. Find ΔU. Answer: W = −300 J (work done by the system), Q = +100 J; ΔU = 100 − 300 = −200 J — internal energy falls and the gas cools.
  8. (Practical) Describe how to determine the specific heat capacity of a metal block electrically. Answer: Place a known-power heater in the block, insulate it, record temperature against time as the heater runs; energy input E = Pt; plot temperature vs time and use the gradient (with m and the extrapolated zero-time temperature) to find c from E = mcΔθ; extrapolating back corrects for heat lost during the experiment.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Celsius in gas laws: pV = nRT demands kelvin. A gas-law calculation with 300 °C is wrong by 273 K at the first step.
  • Δθ in specific heat: E = mcΔθ uses a temperature change; questions giving start and end temperatures need the difference, not a raw value.
  • Latent vs specific heat: during a change of state use mL, not mcΔθ; on a heating curve the flat sections are where Δθ = 0.
  • Molar mass units: grams versus kilograms must match the mass unit in n = m/M; the equation of state with R = 8.31 needs moles and SI units throughout.
  • Pressure units: kPa and atm into Pa, cm³ into m³, before substitution.
  • Internal energy wording: it includes potential energy for real substances; defining it as kinetic only is wrong outside ideal gases.
  • First-law signs: pick a convention and state it — work done on the system is positive in ΔU = Q + W; expanding gas does work on the surroundings (negative W).
  • rms speed vs mean speed: the c in pV = ⅓Nmc² is the root-mean-square speed; it is not the average of speeds (which is smaller).
  • Precision and method: 2 or 3 s.f. with units (J, Pa, K, mol, m s⁻¹); write the formula line before numbers — the physics formulae are credit in their own right.

Equations and symbols

Every relation this topic can be examined on, in the form the mark scheme expects, with a key naming each symbol and its unit. The derivations in the sections above end here: if you can write these from memory and say what each symbol means, the algebra in the exam is bookkeeping.

14.1-14.2 Thermal equilibrium and temperature scales

T(K) = θ(°C) + 273.15
Key: T = thermodynamic temperature (K); θ = Celsius temperature (°C); 273.15 = the offset between the ice point and absolute zero (K). Exams accept 273, and a temperature given as 27 °C becomes 300 K.

ΔT (in K) = Δθ (in °C)
Key: ΔT = temperature change in kelvin (K); Δθ = the same change in degrees Celsius (°C). A change of one kelvin is a change of one degree Celsius, because the scales differ only by their zero — which is why a specific heat capacity in J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ can be used with a temperature difference measured in °C.

thermal equilibrium: no net heat flow between bodies in contact
Key: two bodies are in thermal equilibrium when they are at the same temperature, so no net energy transfers between them; the thermometer reads the same as the body only once this state is reached. The zeroth law in one line: equilibrium is transitive, which is what makes a thermometer possible.

14.3 Specific heat capacity and specific latent heat

E = m c Δθ
Key: E = energy supplied to raise the temperature (J); m = mass of the substance (kg); c = specific heat capacity, the energy needed to raise 1 kg by 1 K (J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹); Δθ = temperature rise (°C or K, the same number). No phase change is allowed during the heating, or some of E goes into breaking bonds instead.

c = E / (m Δθ)
Key: c = specific heat capacity (J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹); E = energy supplied (J); m = mass (kg); Δθ = temperature rise (K). The measuring form, used with an electrical heater where E = V I t.

C = m c
Key: C = heat capacity of the whole object (J K⁻¹); m = its mass (kg); c = specific heat capacity of its material (J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹). Then E = C Δθ for the object as a whole; two objects of the same material have heat capacities in the ratio of their masses.

E = m L
Key: E = energy transferred during a change of state (J); m = mass changing state (kg); L = specific latent heat, the energy per kilogram to change state at constant temperature (J kg⁻¹). Use L_fusion for melting and freezing, L_vaporisation for boiling and condensing; the temperature does not rise while this energy is supplied.

E_total = m c Δθ (heating to the change) + m L (the change itself) + m c Δθ (heating beyond it)
Key: each term is the energy for one stage (J); the symbols are as above. The shape of a heating curve: sloped where a single phase is warming, flat where it changes state.

heat lost = heat gained
Key: in an insulated system, the energy leaving the hotter body (J) equals that entering the colder one, so m₁ c₁ (θ_hot − θ_mix) = m₂ c₂ (θ_mix − θ_cold). The method of mixtures: the only unknown is usually the final temperature, or a specific heat capacity once it is measured.

15.1 The mole

n = m / M
Key: n = amount of substance (mol); m = mass of the sample (kg or g); M = molar mass, the mass of one mole (kg mol⁻¹ or g mol⁻¹). Keep m and M in the same unit — grams with g mol⁻¹, kilograms with kg mol⁻¹.

N = n N_A
Key: N = number of particles (dimensionless); n = amount of substance (mol); N_A = Avogadro constant, 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹. One mole of any substance contains the same number of particles, which is why molar masses compare masses of equal particle counts.

N_A = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹
Key: Avogadro constant: the number of particles in one mole. In this specification it is defined as the number of atoms in 0.012 kg of carbon-12.

15.2 The equation of state

p V = n R T
Key: p = pressure (Pa = N m⁻²); V = volume (m³); n = amount of gas (mol); R = molar gas constant, 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; T = thermodynamic temperature (K). The molar form — use it when the amount is known in moles.

p V = N k T
Key: p = pressure (Pa); V = volume (m³); N = number of molecules; k = Boltzmann constant, 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹; T = temperature (K). The molecular form — use it when the question counts molecules rather than moles.

R = N_A k
Key: R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; N_A = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹; k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹. The bridge between the two forms of the equation of state: dividing pV = NkT by n gives pV = (N/n) kT = N_A k T.

p V / T = constant (for a fixed mass of gas)
Key: p = pressure (Pa); V = volume (m³); T = temperature (K). The combined gas law: states 1 and 2 of the same sample satisfy p₁V₁/T₁ = p₂V₂/T₂, which covers Boyle's, Charles' and the pressure law as special cases.

p = ρ R T / M
Key: p = pressure (Pa); ρ = density of the gas (kg m⁻³); R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; T = temperature (K); M = molar mass (kg mol⁻¹). Since ρ = m/V and n = m/M, the equation of state written in terms of density — the form for "why is hot air less dense".

15.3 Kinetic theory of gases

p V = ⅓ N m ⟨c²⟩
Key: p = pressure (Pa); V = volume (m³); N = number of molecules; m = mass of one molecule (kg); ⟨c²⟩ = mean square speed of the molecules (m² s⁻²). The pressure comes from molecular collisions with the walls: momentum change per collision times collision rate per unit area.

½ m ⟨c²⟩ = (3/2) k T
Key: ½ m ⟨c²⟩ = mean translational kinetic energy of one molecule (J); m = molecular mass (kg); ⟨c²⟩ = mean square speed (m² s⁻²); k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹; T = temperature (K). The mean kinetic energy depends only on temperature, and is the same for every gas at that temperature — heavier molecules simply move more slowly.

⟨c²⟩ = 3 k T / m = 3 p / ρ
Key: ⟨c²⟩ = mean square speed (m² s⁻²); k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹; T = temperature (K); m = mass of one molecule (kg); p = pressure (Pa); ρ = density (kg m⁻³). The second form needs no molecular data at all.

c_rms = √(3 k T / m) = √(3 p / ρ)
Key: c_rms = root-mean-square speed (m s⁻¹); k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹; T = temperature (K); m = mass of one molecule (kg); p = pressure (Pa); ρ = density (kg m⁻³). Take the rms speed rather than the mean speed: the mean of the squared speeds carries the energy.

n = N / V = p / (k T)
Key: n = number density of molecules (m⁻³); N = number of molecules; V = volume (m³); p = pressure (Pa); k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹; T = temperature (K). At s.t.p. this gives about 2.7 × 10²⁵ m⁻³, the number worth remembering for order-of-magnitude checks.

16.1 Internal energy

U = Σ KE + Σ PE of the molecules
Key: U = internal energy of the body (J); Σ KE = total random kinetic energy of its molecules (J); Σ PE = total potential energy from the intermolecular forces (J). For an ideal gas the potential term is negligible, so U depends only on temperature; for a real solid or liquid the potential term dominates the latent heat.

U = (3/2) N k T (ideal monatomic gas)
Key: U = internal energy (J); N = number of molecules; k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹; T = temperature (K). Follows from ½ m ⟨c²⟩ = (3/2) k T multiplied by N molecules — no potential energy to add.

16.2 The first law of thermodynamics

ΔU = q + w
Key: ΔU = increase in internal energy of the system (J); q = heat supplied to the system (J); w = work done on the system (J). The sign convention used throughout this specification — energy in is positive. Get the convention wrong and every answer is out by a sign, so state it in the working.

w = − p ΔV
Key: w = work done on the gas (J); p = pressure (Pa); ΔV = change in volume (m³); the minus sign says that a gas expanding (ΔV positive) does work on its surroundings, so work is done on it negatively. For a constant-pressure process this is the area under a p–V graph.

ΔU = q − p ΔV
Key: ΔU = change in internal energy (J); q = heat supplied to the gas (J); p = pressure (Pa); ΔV = volume change (m³). The expanded first law: heat in, minus the work the gas does by expanding.

q = 0 ⇒ ΔU = w (adiabatic); ΔV = 0 ⇒ ΔU = q (isochoric); ΔT = 0 ⇒ ΔU = 0 (isothermal, ideal gas)
Key: the three named processes as special cases; q = heat exchanged (J); w = work done on the system (J); ΔU = internal energy change (J); ΔV = volume change (m³); ΔT = temperature change (K). An adiabatic change is fast enough, or insulated enough, that no heat flows — a sudden compression, or a gas expanding into a vacuum.

C_p − C_v = R
Key: C_p = molar heat capacity at constant pressure (J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹); C_v = molar heat capacity at constant volume (J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹); R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. At constant pressure some of the heat goes into work of expansion, so more is needed for the same temperature rise — the difference is exactly R per mole.

title: IGCSE Chemistry: Stoichiometry and the Mole
content:
IGCSE Chemistry: Stoichiometry and the Mole

Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry 0620 (2026–2028), Extended route, Topic 3 Stoichiometry: statement 3.1 Formulae, 3.2 Relative masses of atoms and molecules, and 3.3 The mole and the Avogadro constant. Stoichiometry is the accounting of chemistry — it answers "how much?" for every reaction — and it is the single highest-yield calculation topic on Paper 4. Every calculation below is expanded one line at a time with no skipped arithmetic, and each method is stated as a repeatable recipe before the numbers, because the marks sit in the working.

What a chemical formula tells you

Think of a formula as a recipe for one particle of a substance. H₂O says: every molecule of water contains exactly two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom. The small numbers are subscripts — they count atoms inside the particle, and changing them changes the substance entirely (H₂O is water; H₂O₂ is hydrogen peroxide).

  • Empirical formula: the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms in a compound. For glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆) the empirical formula is CH₂O — the ratio 6:12:6 divided by 6.
  • Molecular formula: the actual number of each atom in one molecule (C₆H₁₂O₆).
  • Formula of ionic compounds: the ratio that makes the charges balance. Ca²⁺ and Cl⁻ combine as CaCl₂ because one 2+ ion needs two 1− ions for neutrality.

State symbols appear on every equation and carry a mark: (s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas, (aq) aqueous (dissolved in water).

Equations: balancing and the conservation of mass

Atoms are never created or destroyed in a chemical reaction — mass is conserved. Balancing an equation is simply making the atom count of each element equal on both sides. The master method:

Balance: Al + O2 → Al2O3   (no state symbols until balanced)

1. List the elements and count each side:
     left:  Al 1, O 2      right: Al 2, O 3
2. Pick the element that appears in the most complex formula and balance it
   first - here Al: put 2 in front of Al:
     2Al + O2 → Al2O3      left: Al 2, O 2   right: Al 2, O 3
3. Balance O. Left has 2, right has 3. The lowest number both divide into
   is 6 - so aim for 6 O on each side:
     O2 needs 3 molecules (3 × 2 = 6); Al2O3 needs 2 formula units
     (2 × 3 = 6):
     2Al + 3O2 → 2Al2O3
4. Re-count Al: right now has 4 (2 × 2). Fix the left:
     4Al + 3O2 → 2Al2O3
5. Final check, every element:
     Al 4 = 4 ✓    O 6 = 6 ✓
6. Add state symbols from the facts you know:
     4Al(s) + 3O2(g) → 2Al2O3(s)

Rules that never fail: only change the BIG numbers in front (never the
subscripts), never invent atoms, and always re-count at the end.

Relative atomic mass and relative formula mass

You cannot weigh individual atoms, so chemistry compares masses against a standard: one-twelfth the mass of a carbon-12 atom. The relative atomic mass (Aᵣ) is the weighted average mass of an element's atoms on that scale. The relative molecular mass (Mᵣ) (or relative formula mass for ionic compounds) is the sum of the Aᵣ values in the formula.

Worked: find the Mᵣ of calcium carbonate, CaCO₃.

  Aᵣ values from the Periodic Table: Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16
  Mᵣ = 40 + 12 + (3 × 16)
     = 40 + 12 + 48
     = 100

Note the parenthesis: the subscript 3 multiplies ONLY the oxygen.
A common error is 40 + 12 + 16 = 68 - one mark lost to a bracket.

Mᵣ of sulfuric acid, H₂SO₄:
  Mᵣ = (2 × 1) + 32 + (4 × 16)
     = 2 + 32 + 64
     = 98

The mole and the Avogadro constant

A mole is the chemist's counting unit, like "a dozen" — but sized for atoms. One mole of any substance contains 6.02 × 10²³ particles (the Avogadro constant, L). The practical magic: one mole of any substance has a mass in grams equal to its Mᵣ, which turns unweighable atoms into weighable quantities.

The mole triangle - the three relationships and how to rearrange them:

        mass (g)
        /      \
       /        \
    moles x Mᵣ = mass        moles = mass / Mᵣ     Mᵣ = mass / moles

  particles = moles x 6.02 × 10²³

Worked: how many molecules are in 4.4 g of carbon dioxide, CO₂?

Step 1 - Mᵣ of CO₂ = 12 + (2 × 16) = 44
Step 2 - moles = mass / Mᵣ = 4.4 / 44 = 0.1 mol
Step 3 - molecules = 0.1 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 6.02 × 10²² molecules
Step 4 (if asked for ATOMS): each CO₂ has 3 atoms, so
        atoms = 6.02 × 10²² × 3 = 1.806 × 10²³ atoms

"Particles" can mean atoms, molecules or ions - read the question's word.
Question asks forWorking lineWorked number
Moles from massmoles = mass ÷ Mᵣ25 g CaCO₃ → 25 ÷ 100 = 0.25 mol
Mass from molesmass = moles × Mᵣ0.25 mol CO₂ → 0.25 × 44 = 11 g
Particles from molesparticles = moles × 6.02 × 10²³0.25 mol → 1.505 × 10²³ molecules
Gas volume at r.t.p.volume = moles × 24 dm³0.25 mol → 6 dm³
Solution molesmoles = c (mol/dm³) × V (dm³)0.1 × 0.025 = 0.0025 mol
Concentrationc = moles ÷ V (dm³)0.004 mol in 25 cm³ → 0.16 mol/dm³

Reacting masses

The balanced equation is a recipe in moles: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O says 2 moles of hydrogen react with 1 mole of oxygen to make 2 moles of water. Master method for every reacting-mass question: balance the equation → convert given mass to moles → use the equation's ratio → convert back to mass.

Worked: what mass of water forms when 10 g of hydrogen burns in 100 g of
oxygen? And which reactant limits the yield?

Step 1 - balance:  2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O
Step 2 - moles of each reactant:
   H₂:  Mᵣ = 2   →  moles = 10 / 2  = 5 mol
   O₂:  Mᵣ = 32  →  moles = 100 / 32 = 3.125 mol
Step 3 - the ratio needed is 2 : 1.
   5 mol H₂ would need 5 / 2 = 2.5 mol O₂.
   We have 3.125 mol O₂ - MORE than needed, so O₂ is in excess and
   H₂ is the LIMITING reactant. All calculations use the limiting one.
Step 4 - moles of water from the limiting reactant:
   ratio H₂ : H₂O = 2 : 2 = 1 : 1  →  water = 5 mol
Step 5 - mass of water:
   Mᵣ(H₂O) = 18  →  mass = 5 × 18 = 90 g

Sanity check: 10 + 100 = 110 g in; 90 g water + 10 g unreacted O₂ out
(3.125 - 2.5 = 0.625 mol O₂ left = 0.625 × 32 = 20 g... 
wait - recompute: 100 - 80 = 20 g O₂ left, and 90 + 20 = 110 g ✓)

Percentage yield = (actual mass ÷ theoretical mass) × 100. If the reaction above actually gave 72 g of water: percentage yield = 72 ÷ 90 × 100 = 80%. Percentage purity = (mass of pure product ÷ mass of impure sample) × 100 — a different question, and mixing the two up is a classic lost mark.

Gas volumes

At room temperature and pressure (r.t.p.), one mole of any gas occupies 24 dm³ (24 000 cm³). This connects gas volumes straight to moles.

Worked: what volume of carbon dioxide forms when 25 g of calcium carbonate
decomposes?  CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂

Step 1 - balance (already 1:1:1)
Step 2 - moles CaCO₃ = 25 / 100 = 0.25 mol
Step 3 - ratio 1 : 1  →  CO₂ = 0.25 mol
Step 4 - volume = moles x 24 = 0.25 × 24 = 6 dm³
        (in cm³: 6 × 1000 = 6000 cm³)

The reverse works identically: 480 cm³ of gas = 0.48 dm³
→ moles = 0.48 / 24 = 0.02 mol.

Solutions, concentration and titration

Concentration says how much solute sits in a given volume of solution, in g/dm³ or mol/dm³. The working equations: moles = concentration (mol/dm³) × volume (dm³), and cm³ ÷ 1000 = dm³.

Titration worked in full: 25.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide solution is neutralised
by 20.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ sulfuric acid. Find the NaOH concentration.

  2NaOH + H₂SO₄ → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O        [balanced first: ratio 2 : 1]

Step 1 - moles of acid used:
   volume = 20.0 cm³ = 20.0 / 1000 = 0.0200 dm³
   moles H₂SO₄ = 0.100 × 0.0200 = 0.00200 mol
Step 2 - ratio 2 : 1, so:
   moles NaOH = 0.00200 × 2 = 0.00400 mol
Step 3 - concentration of NaOH:
   volume = 25.0 cm³ = 0.0250 dm³
   conc = moles / volume = 0.00400 / 0.0250 = 0.160 mol/dm³

Three marks hide in three places: the balanced ratio (2:1), the cm³ to dm³
conversion, and the final division the right way up.

Titrration technique itself (burette, pipette, indicator, concordant titres) is Paper 6 material — see the experimental techniques note — but the calculation above is pure Paper 4.

Empirical and molecular formulae from data

Worked: a compound contains 40.0% carbon, 6.7% hydrogen and 53.3% oxygen
by mass. Its Mᵣ is 180. Find the empirical and molecular formulae.

Master method: assume 100 g → divide each percentage by Aᵣ → divide by the
smallest → scale to whole numbers.

Step 1 - assume 100 g: C 40.0 g, H 6.7 g, O 53.3 g
Step 2 - convert to moles (Aᵣ: C 12, H 1, O 16):
   C: 40.0 / 12 = 3.33 mol
   H:  6.7 /  1 = 6.70 mol
   O: 53.3 / 16 = 3.33 mol
Step 3 - divide by the smallest (3.33):
   C: 3.33 / 3.33 = 1
   H: 6.70 / 3.33 = 2.01 ≈ 2
   O: 3.33 / 3.33 = 1
Step 4 - empirical formula = CH₂O   (empirical Mᵣ = 12 + 2 + 16 = 30)
Step 5 - molecular formula: 180 / 30 = 6, so multiply by 6
   molecular formula = C₆H₁₂O₆

Check: 6 × 12 + 12 × 1 + 6 × 16 = 72 + 12 + 96 = 180 ✓

Worked example: one problem using every method

10.0 g of magnesium reacts with hydrochloric acid:
  Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂

(a) moles Mg = 10.0 / 24 = 0.4167 mol
(b) moles HCl needed = 0.4167 × 2 = 0.8333 mol
(c) if HCl is supplied as 2.00 mol/dm³, volume needed =
    0.8333 / 2.00 = 0.4167 dm³ = 416.7 cm³
(d) volume of H₂ at r.t.p. = 0.4167 × 24 = 10.0 dm³
(e) if only 8.4 dm³ of H₂ is collected, percentage yield =
    8.4 / 10.0 × 100 = 84%

One equation, five question shapes - mass, ratio, concentration, gas volume,
yield. The method never changes: moles first, ratio second, back to units.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Changing subscripts to "balance" an equation — that invents a different substance; only front numbers change.
  • Forgetting subscripts when calculating Mᵣ (Mᵣ of CaCO₃ is 100, not 68); bracket the multiplied terms.
  • Skipping the cm³ → dm³ conversion (divide by 1000) in concentration work — the most common single arithmetic slip on Paper 4.
  • Inverting the concentration rearrangement: moles = c × V, so c = moles ÷ V — state the triangle, don't improvise.
  • Using the excess reactant instead of the limiting one in reacting-mass questions; always compare moles ÷ coefficient first.
  • Confusing percentage yield with percentage purity — yield compares actual vs theoretical product; purity compares pure substance vs sample.
  • Dropping the ×10²³ or writing 6.02 × 10⁻²³; the Avogadro constant is positive-indexed and multiplied, not divided, for particle counts.
  • Quoting 24 dm³ without the conditions "at r.t.p."; the molar gas volume only holds there.
  • In empirical formula questions, not scaling 2.01 or 1.99 to whole numbers (2) — ratios are always whole numbers.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 4, 3 marks). Calculate the relative formula mass of ammonium nitrate, NH₄NO₃. (Aᵣ: N = 14, H = 1, O = 16)

Answer: Mᵣ = (2 × 14) + (4 × 1) + (3 × 16) = 28 + 4 + 48 = 80.

Question 2 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Calculate the mass of iron formed when 320 g of iron(III) oxide is reduced by carbon monoxide: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂. (Aᵣ: Fe = 56, O = 16)

Answer: Mᵣ(Fe₂O₃) = (2 × 56) + (3 × 16) = 160. Moles Fe₂O₃ = 320 ÷ 160 = 2 mol. Ratio Fe₂O₃ : Fe = 1 : 2, so Fe = 4 mol. Mass Fe = 4 × 56 = 224 g.

Question 3 (Paper 4, 5 marks). A student neutralises 25.0 cm³ of 0.200 mol/dm³ HNO₃ with Na₂CO₃ solution. Calculate the moles of acid and the mass of anhydrous Na₂CO₃ needed. (Mᵣ Na₂CO₃ = 106)

Answer: Moles HNO₃ = 0.200 × (25.0 ÷ 1000) = 0.200 × 0.025 = 0.00500 mol. Equation: Na₂CO₃ + 2HNO₃ → 2NaNO₃ + H₂O + CO₂, ratio 1 : 2, so moles Na₂CO₃ = 0.00500 ÷ 2 = 0.00250 mol. Mass = 0.00250 × 106 = 0.265 g.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 3 marks). Calculate the volume at r.t.p. of 8.8 g of carbon dioxide.

Answer: Mᵣ(CO₂) = 44; moles = 8.8 ÷ 44 = 0.2 mol; volume = 0.2 × 24 = 4.8 dm³.

Question 5 (Paper 4, 4 marks). An oxide of iron contains 69.9% iron by mass, the rest oxygen. Find its empirical formula. (Aᵣ: Fe = 56, O = 16)

Answer: Assume 100 g: Fe 69.9 g, O 30.1 g. Moles: Fe = 69.9 ÷ 56 = 1.248; O = 30.1 ÷ 16 = 1.881. Divide by the smallest (1.248): Fe 1, O 1.881 ÷ 1.248 = 1.51 ≈ 1.5. Multiply by 2 for whole numbers: Fe₂O₃. Check: (2 × 56) + (3 × 16) = 160; Fe fraction = 112 ÷ 160 = 69.9% ✓.

Question 6 (Paper 4, 3 marks). 0.24 g of magnesium gives 240 cm³ of hydrogen at r.t.p. Calculate the percentage yield if theory predicts 288 cm³.

Answer: Percentage yield = (240 ÷ 288) × 100 = 83.3%.

With the quantitative bookkeeping in place, the next question is what these particles actually are — atomic structure and bonding.

title: Introduction to Kinetics and Equilibria
content:
Introduction to Kinetics and Equilibria
