Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH12, Topic 9. Kinetics asks how fast a reaction goes, and equilibria asks how far it goes before the forward and backward reactions balance. Both depend on the same collision ideas.

Rates and collision theory

  • For a reaction to occur, particles must collide with enough energy (the activation energy, Ea) and in the correct orientation.
  • Increasing concentration or pressure increases the frequency of collisions. Increasing temperature raises the proportion of particles with energy above Ea, which has a larger effect than the increase in collision frequency.
  • A catalyst provides an alternative route with a lower Ea; it is not used up.

Measuring rates

  • Rates can be found from the gradient of a concentration–time graph at the start of the reaction (the initial rate).
  • Methods include measuring the volume of gas produced, the change in mass, or the time for a colour change to occur (1/time gives a relative rate).

Dynamic equilibrium

  • In a closed system, the forward and reverse rates become equal. Concentrations stop changing, but the reaction has not stopped.
  • Equilibrium constant Kc = [products]^n / [reactants]^m, with each concentration raised to the power of its coefficient. Kc is constant for a given temperature.

Le Chatelier's principle

  • If a system at equilibrium is disturbed, the position shifts to oppose the change.
  • Increasing temperature favours the endothermic direction. Increasing pressure favours the side with fewer gas molecules. Adding a reactant shifts the position towards products.
  • A catalyst speeds up both directions equally, so it changes the rate of reaching equilibrium but not the equilibrium position or Kc.

Exam tip: say which direction is favoured and why, using the principle. Do not claim that a catalyst increases the yield.

title: Thermal Physics — Study Notes
content:
Thermal Physics

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): kinetic particle model; thermal expansion; specific heat capacity; melting/boiling; conduction, convection, radiation.

1. Kinetic model

Solid: fixed positions, vibrate — fixed shape/volume. Liquid: move around, touching — fixed volume, flows. Gas: far apart, fast random motion — fills container. Brownian motion evidences random molecular motion.

2. Gas pressure and temperature

Pressure from wall collisions. Heating at fixed volume → faster particles → more frequent, harder collisions → higher pressure.

3. Thermal expansion

Heating → particles vibrate more → solids expand slightly (gases expand most). Applications: bimetallic strip (fire alarm/thermostat), gaps in bridges/rails; the liquid-in-glass thermometer.

4. Specific heat capacity

c = ΔE/(mΔθ). Heating: ΔE = mcΔθ.

Example: 2 kg water (c = 4200), 20→80 °C: ΔE = 2×4200×60 = 504 kJ.

High c of water → coolant; temperature rise measured with known heater power P in time t: c = Pt/(mΔθ).

5. State changes

Melting/boiling at fixed temperature despite heating (energy breaks bonds, not temperature). Condensation/ freezing release energy. Impurities raise melting point of mixtures/lower freezing; boiling needs nucleation.

6. Transfer: conduction, convection, radiation

  • Conduction: mainly metals (delocalised electrons + lattice vibration); non-metals poor; insulators trap air.
  • Convection: hot fluid expands, density falls, rises; denser cool fluid sinks — currents.
  • Radiation: infrared EM waves; no medium; matte black best absorber/emitter, shiny silver worst.

Applications: vacuum flask, house insulation, car radiators, solar heating panels.

Heat transfer and heat capacity

Energy transfer by conduction happens through a solid when particles vibrate and pass energy to their neighbours, with free electrons carrying energy in metals. Convection in fluids occurs because hotter, less dense fluid rises and is replaced by cooler, denser fluid. Black, matt surfaces are good absorbers and emitters of infrared radiation.

The energy needed to change the temperature of a substance is Q = mcΔT, where c is the specific heat capacity. Latent heat is the energy absorbed or released during a change of state with no change in temperature.

title: Web Technologies and Security — Study Notes
content:
Web Technologies and Security

The Three Layers

  • HTML gives structure and content: elements, attributes, forms for user input.
  • CSS gives presentation: selectors, properties, responsive layout.
  • JavaScript gives client-side behaviour: validation before submission, DOM updates without reload.

Server-side scripting (PHP) runs on the server: reads form fields ($_POST), queries the database, outputs HTML. The client never sees PHP source.

SQL Injection

An attack where crafted input changes the meaning of a query. If a login query concatenates the username directly, entering X OR 1=1 can match every row. Defences: parameterised queries (prepared statements) that separate code from data, validation, and least-privilege database accounts.

Encryption

  • Symmetric: one shared key (AES). Fast, but key distribution is the weak point.
  • Asymmetric: public/private key pair (RSA). Anyone encrypts with the public key; only the holder decrypts with the private key. Slower, so used to exchange a symmetric session key.
  • SSL/TLS combines both: certificates verify the server, asymmetric key exchange establishes a symmetric session key, then traffic is encrypted. HTTPS = HTTP over TLS on port 443.

Hashing vs Encryption

Hashing (e.g. SHA-256) is one-way: passwords should be stored hashed with a unique salt, never encrypted reversibly.

Exam tips: explain why parameterised queries stop injection; describe the TLS handshake in three steps; distinguish hashing from encryption with password storage as the example.

Symmetric and asymmetric encryption

Symmetric encryption uses one shared key to encrypt and decrypt. It is fast, but the key must be shared securely. Asymmetric encryption uses a public key to encrypt and a private key to decrypt. TLS uses asymmetric encryption to agree a shared symmetric key at the start of a session.

A digital certificate binds a public key to an organisation. A trusted certificate authority signs it so that a browser can check the site's identity.

Exam tip: explain the hybrid approach: asymmetric for the key exchange, symmetric for the bulk data.

title: AS Level Mathematics: Exponentials and Logarithms
content:
AS Level Mathematics: Exponentials and Logarithms

Exponentials describe growth and decay — populations, investments, radioactive isotopes, cooling cups of tea — where the change is proportional to the amount present. Logarithms are their inverses: they turn multiplication into addition and, crucially, let you solve equations where the unknown sits in the exponent. This note builds the topic from zero: the meaning of a logarithm, the three laws with derivations, solving exponential and logarithmic equations including quadratics in disguise, the graph properties and transformations, and the applied growth/decay models.

What a logarithm is

log_a(x) = n  means  a^n = x

common log: log x = log_10 x
natural log: ln x = log_e x,  e = 2.71828...

The logarithm answers "to what power must I raise the base to get this number?" So log₂8 = 3 because 2³ = 8, and log₅(1/25) = −2 because 5⁻² = 1/25. Two identities follow immediately and are always true:

log_a(a) = 1
log_a(1) = 0
a^(log_a x) = x   and   log_a(a^x) = x

Worked example. Evaluate log₃81, log₂(1/8) and ln 1.

3⁴ = 81  →  log_3 81 = 4
2⁻³ = 1/8  →  log_2(1/8) = -3
anything to the power 0 is 1  →  ln 1 = 0

The three laws of logarithms

product:   log(xy) = log x + log y
quotient:  log(x/y) = log x - log y
power:     log(x^n) = n log x

consequences: log(1/x) = -log x;  log(sqrt x) = (1/2)log x

Why they work. Write x = a^m and y = a^n, so log x = m and log y = n. Then xy = a^(m+n), so log(xy) = m + n = log x + log y. The quotient law follows from a^(m−n) and the power law from (a^m)^n = a^(mn). Each law is a restatement of an index law, which is why logarithms convert products into sums.

Worked example 1 (combine). Write 2 log 3 + log 4 − log 6 as a single logarithm.

2 log 3 = log 9
log 9 + log 4 = log 36
log 36 - log 6 = log 6

Worked example 2 (split). Express log(x³y/√z) in terms of log x, log y and log z.

= 3 log x + log y - (1/2) log z

Worked example 3 (solve). Solve log₂x + log₂(x − 2) = 3.

combine: log_2[x(x - 2)] = 3
x(x - 2) = 2³ = 8
x² - 2x - 8 = 0  →  (x - 4)(x + 2) = 0
x = 4 or x = -2;  reject x = -2 because log of a negative is undefined
x = 4

Rejecting invalid roots is compulsory: a logarithm only accepts a positive argument, so always check each answer against the original equation.

Solving exponential equations

When the unknown is in the exponent, take logs of both sides and use the power law to bring it down.

Worked example 1. Solve 3^x = 20.

take logs: x log 3 = log 20
x = log 20 / log 3 = 1.301/0.4771 = 2.73

Worked example 2 (different bases). Solve 5^(2x−1) = 7^(x+1).

(2x - 1) log 5 = (x + 1) log 7
2x log 5 - log 5 = x log 7 + log 7
x(2 log 5 - log 7) = log 7 + log 5
x = (log 7 + log 5)/(2 log 5 - log 7)
  = (0.845 + 0.699)/(1.398 - 0.845) = 1.544/0.553 = 2.79

Worked example 3 (quadratic in disguise). Solve 2^(2x) − 5(2^x) + 4 = 0.

let y = 2^x:  y² - 5y + 4 = 0  →  (y - 1)(y - 4) = 0
y = 1  →  2^x = 1  →  x = 0
y = 4  →  2^x = 4  →  x = 2

The substitution trick is the standard route for any equation where one power is double another: put y = a^x and solve the quadratic, then convert back.

Graphs of exponential and logarithmic functions

FunctionDomainRangeKey points
y = e^xall real xy > 0(0, 1); always increasing; asymptote y = 0
y = e^(−x)all real xy > 0(0, 1); always decreasing; decay
y = ln xx > 0all real y(1, 0); increasing; asymptote x = 0

y = ln x is the reflection of y = e^x in the line y = x, because they are inverse functions. That reflection explains the domain and range swap and the asymptote turning from horizontal to vertical.

Worked example. Sketch y = e^(x−2) + 1, stating the asymptote and intercepts.

translation 2 right, 1 up
asymptote y = 1 (was y = 0)
y-intercept: e⁻² + 1 = 0.135 + 1 = 1.135
no x-intercept (the curve stays above y = 1)

Growth and decay models

exponential model: N = N_0 e^(kt)
  k > 0 growth;  k < 0 decay
half-life: time for N to halve = ln 2 / |k| (decay)
doubling time = ln 2 / k (growth)

Worked example (decay). A radioactive sample decays as N = 500e^(−0.02t) with t in years. Find the initial amount, the amount after 50 years, and the half-life.

t = 0: N = 500
at t = 50: 500e⁻¹ = 500 × 0.3679 = 184
half-life: 500e^(-0.02t) = 250  →  e^(-0.02t) = 0.5
-0.02t = ln 0.5 = -0.693  →  t = 34.7 years

Worked example 2 (growth). Bacteria grow as N = 200e^(0.15t), t in hours. When does the population reach 1000?

200e^(0.15t) = 10⁰⁰  →  e^(0.15t) = 5
0.15t = ln 5 = 1.609  →  t = 10.7 hours

Logarithmic scales in context

Some quantities span so many orders of magnitude that a logarithmic scale is used: pH for acidity, the Richter scale for earthquakes, decibels for sound. A change of 1 on the Richter scale means 10 times the amplitude, so an increase of 3 means 10³ = 1000 times.

Worked example. Two earthquakes differ by 2.4 on the Richter scale. How many times larger is the amplitude of the stronger?

difference 2.4 in log_10  →  10².4 = 251 times

Change of base and log-linearisation

Calculators offer base 10 and base e only, so any other base is converted with the change-of-base formula. The same formula turns a power law into a straight line, which is how experimental data is tested for exponential behaviour.

change of base: log_a(x) = log_b(x)/log_b(a)
so log_2(7) = ln 7 / ln 2 = log 7 / log 2 = 2.807

if y = a x^n then log y = log a + n log x  (straight line in log-log)
if y = a b^x then log y = log a + x log b  (straight line in log-x)

Worked example 1. Evaluate log_5(30).

log 30 / log 5 = 1.477/0.699 = 2.113

Worked example 2 (log-linearisation). Data gives a straight line when log y is plotted against x, with gradient 0.3 and intercept 1.4. Find the model connecting y and x.

log y = 1.4 + 0.3x
so y = 10¹.4 × 10^(0.3x) = 25.1 × 2.00^x
an exponential growth model with a = 25.1 and b = 2.0

Worked example 3 (inequality). Solve 2^x < 100.

take logs (base 2 is increasing, so the inequality is preserved)
x < log_2 10⁰ = log 10⁰/log 2 = 6.64

Taking logs of both sides is safe for any base greater than 1 because the log function is increasing; a base between 0 and 1 would reverse the inequality, which never arises in these models.

Rewriting any exponential in base e

Any exponential a^x can be written as e^(kx), because a = e^(ln a). This is why every growth model in the syllabus uses e: the base is absorbed into the constant.

a^x = e^(x ln a)
so 2^x = e^(0.693x);  5^x = e^(1.609x);  0.8^x = e^(-0.223x)

Worked example. Express y = 300(1.04)^t in the form y = 300e^(kt), and state the annual percentage rate it represents.

1.04 = e^k  →  k = ln 1.04 = 0.0392
y = 300e^(0.0392t)
the rate is 3.92 per year in continuous-compounding form, while the
annual multiplier is still 1.04 (4 per cent per year)

Worked example 2. A model is N = 80e^(0.25t). Rewrite it as N = 80b^t and find the percentage growth per unit time.

b = e⁰.25 = 1.284
N = 80(1.284)^t, so growth is 28.4 per cent per unit time

The two forms describe the same curve; the e-form is convenient for calculus, the b-form for reading off a percentage rate. Converting between them is a standard exam demand.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Evaluate) Find log₄64. Answer: 3, since 4³ = 64.
  2. (Laws) Simplify log 8 + log 5 − log 2. Answer: log(40/2) = log 20.
  3. (Solve log) Solve log₃x = 2. Answer: x = 3² = 9.
  4. (Solve exponential) Solve 2^x = 50. Answer: x = log 50/log 2 = 1.699/0.301 = 5.64.
  5. (Quadratic) Solve e^(2x) − 3e^x + 2 = 0. Answer: y = e^x → y² − 3y + 2 = 0 → y = 1 or 2 → x = 0 or ln 2 = 0.693.
  6. (Combine) Write 3 ln 2 − ln 4 as a single logarithm. Answer: ln 8 − ln 4 = ln 2.
  7. (Inverse) Find the inverse of f(x) = e^(3x). Answer: y = e^(3x) → ln y = 3x → f⁻¹(x) = (ln x)/3.
  8. (Model) A car's value is V = 15000e^(−0.2t). Find its value after 4 years. Answer: 15000e^(−0.8) = 15000 × 0.4493 = 6740 pounds.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • log(x + y) is not log x + log y: the product law applies to products only; there is no law for the log of a sum.
  • Forgetting the domain: logs need a positive argument. Roots that make an argument negative or zero are rejected, explicitly.
  • Dividing by log: log 20/log 3 is not log(20/3); the quotient law is for two logs, not a quotient of logs.
  • Base consistency: mixing log₁₀ and ln inside one equation is an error; convert first (ln x = log x / log e).
  • Power law misuse: (log x)² is not 2 log x. Only log(x²) = 2 log x.
  • Quadratic substitution: after solving for y, the answer is x — convert back and solve the exponential equation.
  • Half-life sign: with a decay model k is negative, so half-life = ln 2/|k|; dropping the modulus gives a negative time.
  • Sketch asymptotes: state the asymptote after transformations; e^x + c has asymptote y = c, not y = 0.

title: Number — Sets — Study Notes
content:
Number — Sets

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): set notation, Venn diagrams, shading, universal set, subsets.

1. Notation

  • ∈ belongs to; ∉ not in; ∅ empty set; ξ (or U) universal set; n(A) = number of elements.
  • A ∩ B intersection (AND); A ∪ B union (OR); A′ complement (NOT A).
  • A ⊆ B: every element of A is in B.

2. Venn diagrams

Fill the intersection first, then work outwards. Two sets: only A, both, only B, neither.

Example: 30 students; 18 maths, 15 physics, 7 both ⇒ neither = 30 − (11 + 7 + 8) = 4.

3. Shading

For A ∩ B′ shade where A and outside-B overlap. (A ∪ B)′ = A′ ∩ B′ (De Morgan) — check every region.

4. Regions algebra

With region variables x, y, z: use the totals to form equations, e.g. n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B).

5. Probability links

P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B) — inclusion–exclusion from the diagram.

Exam tips: "neither" sits outside both circles — subtract from the universal set last; label regions with numbers, not expressions, as you fill.

The number sets

Natural numbers are 1, 2, 3 and so on; integers add zero and negatives; rational numbers can be written as a fraction p/q with q not zero; irrational numbers, such as π and √2, cannot. Terminating and recurring decimals are rational. Prime numbers have exactly two factors, 1 and themselves.

Prime factors and HCF/LCM

Write a number as a product of primes using a factor tree. The highest common factor uses the common primes at their lowest powers; the lowest common multiple uses every prime at its highest power. Venn diagrams sort numbers by properties such as even, square or prime.

Square roots and cube roots

The square root of a number is positive or negative: √16 = 4 but x² = 16 gives x = ±4. Check whether a root is exact or needs a calculator, and give a non-exact answer to the accuracy asked.

title: Functions — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Functions

Mathematics — AS (9709). A function maps each input in the domain to exactly one output in the range. Example: f(x) = x² + 1 for x ∈ ℝ has range f(x) ≥ 1, because x² is never negative.

Key areas to revise

  • Composite functions: fg(x) means f(g(x)), so g is applied first. The domain of fg must allow the output of g to be a valid input for f.
  • Inverse functions: f⁻¹ exists only when f is one-to-one. Its graph is the reflection of f in the line y = x, and f⁻¹(f(x)) = x.
  • Transformations: y = f(x) + a moves the graph up by a; y = f(x + a) moves it left by a; y = af(x) stretches it parallel to the y-axis by factor a; y = f(ax) stretches it parallel to the x-axis by factor 1/a.
  • Reflections: y = −f(x) reflects in the x-axis, and y = f(−x) reflects in the y-axis.

Core facts to recall

  • A many-to-one function has no inverse unless its domain is restricted to make it one-to-one.
  • When you sketch a transformed graph, follow one key point, such as the vertex or an intercept, through each step.
  • State the domain and range in set notation or interval notation, as the question asks.

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

title: Number — Fractions, Decimals and Percentages — Study Notes
content:
Number — Fractions, Decimals and Percentages

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): conversions between fractions, decimals and percentages; percentage change; reverse percentages; compound change.

1. Conversions

Fraction → decimal by division; decimal → percentage ×100. Recurring decimals: let x = 0.7̄, then 10x − x = 7 ⇒ x = 7/9.

Compare fractions by common denominator or by converting to decimals.

2. Operating on fractions

  • Add/subtract: common denominator. 2/3 + 1/4 = 8/12 + 3/12 = 11/12.
  • Multiply: top×top, bottom×bottom. Divide: flip and multiply — 2/3 ÷ 4/5 = 2/3 × 5/4 = 5/6.
  • Of: 3/5 of 45 = 27.

3. Percentage change

change ÷ original × 100. Increase $80 by 15%: 80 × 1.15 = $92.

4. Reverse percentages

Original = new ÷ multiplier. "After a 20% increase a coat is $72" → 72 ÷ 1.2 = $60. "After 12% discount a phone is $440" → 440 ÷ 0.88 = $500.

5. Compound change

Multiplierⁿ. Simple interest I = Prt/100 vs compound P(1 + r/100)ⁿ.

Example: $800 at 3% for 4 years → 800 × 1.03⁴ = $900.41. Successive +10% then −10% ⇒ ×0.99 (net 1% decrease).

Exam tips: identify "increase TO" vs "increase BY"; for reverse questions divide, never subtract the percentage; quote money to 2 d.p.

Equivalent fractions and simplifying

Multiply or divide the numerator and denominator by the same non-zero number. Simplify by dividing both by their highest common factor. Mixed numbers are converted to improper fractions before multiplying or dividing.

Adding and subtracting fractions

Find the lowest common denominator, rewrite each fraction over it, then add or subtract the numerators only. Multiplying fractions multiplies the numerators and the denominators; dividing multiplies by the reciprocal of the second fraction.

Percentages

To find a percentage of a quantity, multiply by the decimal equivalent: 15% of 240 is 0.15 × 240 = 36. Percentage change is the change divided by the original value, multiplied by 100. Repeated percentage change multiplies by one plus the multiplier each time, so 5% increase twice is × 1.05 × 1.05.

title: AS Level Mathematics: Circular Measure
content:
AS Level Mathematics: Circular Measure

Radians measure angles by the arc they cut: one radian is the angle subtended when the arc equals the radius. That definition makes every circle formula simpler — arc length becomes s = rθ and sector area becomes ½r²θ, with no 360 in sight. This note builds the topic from zero: the radian definition and conversions, arc length and sector area with derivations, the segment area formula, and the applied problems (belts, pendulums, cones) that combine circular measure with trigonometry. Every worked example keeps the calculator in radian mode, which is the first habit this topic demands.

Radians and conversion

one full turn = 2 π radians = 360 degrees
π radians = 180 degrees

degrees → radians: multiply by π/180
radians → degrees: multiply by 180/π

common values: 30 ° = π/6, 45 ° = π/4,
60 ° = π/3, 90 ° = π/2, 180 ° = π

Worked example. Convert 150° to radians and 2.4 radians to degrees.

150 x π/180 = 5 π/6 = 2.618 rad
2.4 × 180/π = 137.5 °

Why radians: the arc length formula s = rθ only works when θ is in radians. In degrees the same arc is (θ/360) × 2πr — the same quantity, but with the conversion built in.

Arc length and sector area

arc length: s = r θ
sector area: A = (1/2) r² θ
perimeter of a sector: s + 2r

(θ in radians, r in the same length unit as s)

Worked example 1. A sector has radius 8 cm and angle 1.5 radians. Find the arc length and area.

s = r θ = 8 × 1.5 = 12 cm
A = (1/2) r² θ = 0.5 × 64 × 1.5 = 48 cm²

Worked example 2 (perimeter). Find the perimeter of the same sector.

perimeter = arc + 2 radii = 12 + 16 = 28 cm

Worked example 3 (working backwards). A sector of radius 6 cm has area 27 cm². Find the angle in radians and degrees.

27 = (1/2)(36) θ  →  27 = 18 θ  →  θ = 1.5 rad
in degrees: 1.5 × 180/π = 85.9 °

Segment area

segment area = sector area - triangle area
             = (1/2) r² θ - (1/2) r² sin(θ)
             = (1/2) r² (θ - sin θ)

The triangle is formed by the two radii and the chord; its area uses ½r² sin θ (the sine rule area formula). The subtraction is always the same picture: the segment is the sector with the triangle removed.

Worked example. Find the area of the segment cut off by a chord in a circle of radius 10 cm when the angle at the centre is 1.2 radians.

sector area = (1/2)(100)(1.2) = 60 cm²
triangle area = (1/2)(100) sin(1.2) = 50 × 0.932 = 46.6 cm²
segment = 60 - 46.6 = 13.4 cm²

Worked examples: the standard exam types

Worked example 1 (belt around pulleys). Two pulleys of radius 0.20 m and 0.50 m have centres 1.5 m apart. Find the length of the belt around them (straight sections plus arcs).

straight sections: 2 × 1.5 = 3.0 m (approximately, for the
common external tangents when the radii differ the geometry
needs the tangent length, but the exam version usually gives
equal pulleys or the tangent length directly)
equal-pulley version: belt = 2d + 2 π r = 3.0 + 1.26 = 4.26 m

Worked example 2 (pendulum arc). A pendulum of length 0.80 m swings through 0.6 radians. Find the arc length travelled by the bob.

s = r θ = 0.80 × 0.6 = 0.48 m

Worked example 3 (cone sector). A sector of radius 12 cm and angle 2.0 radians is folded into a cone. Find the base radius.

arc length becomes the base circumference:
s = 12 × 2.0 = 24 cm² π r_base = 24  →  r_base = 24/(2 π) = 3.82 cm

Radian trigonometry and small angles

In radian mode, the trigonometric functions take radian inputs, and small-angle approximations become available: for small θ, sin θ ≈ θ and tan θ ≈ θ (with θ in radians), and cos θ ≈ 1 − θ²/2. These approximations underpin pendulum motion and lens theory later, and they appear in exam questions as "show that for small θ ...".

Worked example. Show that for small θ, the arc length and the chord length are approximately equal.

arc = r θ
chord = 2r sin(θ/2) ~ 2r (θ/2) = r θ  for small θ
so chord ~ arc, with the difference of order θ³

Composite shapes with sectors

Exam figures combine sectors with triangles, rectangles and semicircles. The method is always the same: shade the required region, split it into standard pieces, compute each piece with the radian formulas, then add or subtract. Perimeter questions require the boundary only — internal lines are not part of it.

Worked example. A shape is a rectangle 12 cm by 8 cm with a quarter-circle of radius 8 cm removed from one corner. Find the area and perimeter of the remaining shape.

rectangle area = 96 cm²
quarter circle = (1/4) π r² = (1/4)(3.142)(64) = 50.3 cm²
remaining area = 96 - 50.3 = 45.7 cm²

perimeter: straight edges 12 + 4 + 8 = 24 cm (the 4 cm is the
remaining part of the 8 cm side)
plus the arc: quarter circumference = (1/4)(2 π)(8) = 12.6 cm
total perimeter = 36.6 cm

Worked example 2 (two sectors). Two circles of radius 5 cm have centres 8 cm apart. Find the area common to both.

the overlap is two identical segments. In each circle the chord
subtends an angle θ where cos(θ/2) = 4/5, so θ/2 =
0.6435 and θ = 1.287 rad.
segment area = (1/2)(25)(1.287 - sin 1.287)
             = 12.5(1.287 - 0.960) = 4.09 cm²
common area = 2 × 4.09 = 8.18 cm²

Arc, chord and sector in practice

Three quantities are easy to confuse and each has its own formula. Keep them side by side:

QuantityFormula (θ in radians)What it measures
Arc lengths = r θthe curved boundary
Chord lengthc = 2r sin(θ/2)the straight line joining the arc's ends
Sector areaA = (1/2) r^2 θthe pie-slice region

Worked example. A sector has radius 10 cm and angle 1.0 rad. Find the arc length, chord length and the difference between them.

arc = 10 × 1.0 = 10.0 cm
chord = 2 × 10 x sin(0.5) = 20 × 0.4794 = 9.59 cm
difference = 0.41 cm (the arc bulges beyond the chord)

Worked example (angular speed). A wheel of radius 0.35 m turns at 12 rad s⁻¹. Find the linear speed of a point on its rim and the angle turned in 5 s.

v = r ω = 0.35 × 12 = 4.2 m s⁻¹
angle = ω t = 12 × 5 = 60 rad (about 9.5 full turns)

Angular speed links circular measure to mechanics: one radian per second means one radius of arc per second, so the rim speed is rω. Exam questions on rotating wheels, pulleys and centrifuges all reduce to this one relation, and it also explains why a point near the rim of a wheel moves faster than a point near the hub despite both completing a turn in the same time. The same relation converts between the two ways of measuring rotation: revolutions per minute to radians per second is a factor of 2π/60.

The difference is the sagitta-related gap that appears in lens and bridge questions; it grows as the angle grows, which is why the small-angle approximation fails for large sectors.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Convert) Convert 72° to radians. Answer: θ(rad) = θ(°) × π/180°, so 72 × π/180 = 72π/180 = 2π/5 ≈ 1.257 rad.
  2. (Arc) Radius 5 cm, θ = 2.0 rad. Find the arc length. Answer: arc length s = rθ = 5 × 2.0 = 10 cm.
  3. (Sector) Radius 4 cm, θ = 3.0 rad. Find the area. Answer: sector area A = ½r²θ = ½ × 4² × 3.0 = ½ × 16 × 3 = 24 cm².
  4. (Reverse) A sector of radius 9 cm has arc length 13.5 cm. Find θ in radians. Answer: θ = 13.5/9 = 1.5 rad.
  5. (Segment) Radius 6 cm, θ = π/3. Find the segment area. Answer: sector = ½ × 36 × π/3 = 6π ≈ 18.85; triangle = ½ × 36 × sin(π/3) = 18 × 0.866 = 15.59; segment ≈ 3.26 cm².
  6. (Perimeter) Find the perimeter of a sector of radius 7 cm and angle 0.8 rad. Answer: the perimeter is the arc plus two radii: rθ + 2r = 7(0.8) + 14 = 5.6 + 14 = 19.6 cm.
  7. (Cone) A sector of radius 10 cm and angle 1.8 rad forms a cone. Find the base radius and slant height. Answer: arc = 18 cm → base radius 18/(2π) = 2.86 cm; slant height = 10 cm.
  8. (Small angle) Use sin θ ≈ θ to estimate sin(0.10) and compare with the calculator value. Answer: in radians sin θ ≈ θ for small θ, so sin(0.10) ≈ 0.10 against the calculator's 0.0998 — an error of about 0.2%, small because 0.10 rad is small.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Degree mode: every radians formula requires the calculator in RAD mode. A sin of 1.2 in degree mode gives an entirely different number.
  • Mixing units: s = rθ silently assumes r in metres and s in metres; cm and m mixed in one calculation produces a factor-of-100 error.
  • Half forgotten: sector area is ½r²θ, not r²θ. The ½ comes from the triangle comparison.
  • Angle in degrees in the formula: θ must be radians; convert first, and only convert the final answer back if asked.
  • Perimeter includes the radii: the perimeter of a sector is arc + 2r; the arc alone is not the perimeter.
  • Segment triangle: use ½r² sin θ for the triangle, with θ the same central angle; a different angle changes the answer.
  • Exact versus decimal: when the question says "in terms of π", keep π symbolic; converting to 3.14 loses the required form.
  • Small-angle validity: sin θ ≈ θ is good only for small θ (roughly under 0.2 rad); do not apply it to 1.5 rad.

Reading a sector: the one drawing this topic is built on

Every formula in circular measure comes from a single picture, and nearly every mistake comes from mixing up the two curves in it. Draw the sector once, label the radius, the angle and the arc, and the rest is arithmetic on that drawing.

Why the radian exists. An angle in radians is defined as the arc it cuts off divided by the radius:

θ = s / r Key: θ = angle at the centre (rad); s = arc length (m); r = radius (m). The units cancel, so a radian is a pure ratio — one radius-length of arc per radius. That is why a full turn is 2π radians and not 360: the whole circumference is 2πr, so the angle it subtends is 2πr ÷ r = 2π.

Turn the definition around and you get the arc formula, which is the one you actually use:

s = r θ Key: s = arc length (m); r = radius (m); θ = angle at the centre in radians. Using degrees here gives an answer 57 times too large — the single most common error in the topic.

Where ½r²θ comes from. Cut the sector into many thin triangles, each with height r and a sliver of arc as its base. A triangle's area is ½ × base × height, so each sliver is ½ × (rΔθ) × r, and adding them all up gives ½r² × (total θ):

A = ½ r² θ Key: A = area of the sector (m²); r = radius (m); θ = angle at the centre (rad). Notice that the arc is in this formula too — A = ½ r × (rθ) = ½ r s, which is the "thin triangle" statement written algebraically.

Worked example. A sector has radius 9.0 cm and angle 1.2 rad. Find its arc length, its area, and the length of its chord.

arc: s = rθ = 9.0 × 1.2 = 10.8 cm
area: A = ½r²θ = ½ × 81 × 1.2 = 48.6 cm²
chord: the two radii and the chord form an isosceles triangle with sides 9.0, 9.0 and included angle 1.2 rad, so chord = 2 × 9.0 × sin(1.2/2) = 18 × 0.5646 = 10.2 cm

That last line is the step students skip, and it is the step the paper is testing: the chord is a straight line, so it needs trigonometry, not the arc formula. The segment area is then sector minus triangle, A = ½r²(θ − sin θ) = 48.6 − ½ × 81 × sin 1.2 = 48.6 − 37.7 = 10.9 cm².

The perimeter of a sector is three sides, not one. A sector's boundary is the arc plus the two radii: P = 2r + rθ. For the example above, P = 18.0 + 10.8 = 28.8 cm. Answering with 10.8 alone is the most frequently lost mark on this topic, because the word "perimeter" invites you to think of the curve only.

Where marks are lost. Degrees in an equation that needs radians (check the calculator is in RAD mode the moment a question says "radians"). Reading "arc" as "chord". Forgetting the two radii in a perimeter. And using ½r²θ for a segment — the segment is the sector minus the triangle, and the triangle's area is ½r² sin θ.

Deriving the arc and sector formulae from the fraction of a circle

Both formulae come from one idea: a sector is the same fraction of its circle as its angle is of a full turn. Seeing that fraction is more useful than memorising two formulae, because the same reasoning works when a question changes the circle or the angle.

Arc length as a fraction of the circumference

The full circumference is 2πr, and a full turn is 2π radians. A sector of angle θ takes the fraction θ/(2π) of the circle, so s = (θ/2π) × 2πr = rθ. The π cancels, which is why radians make the arc formula so short.

Sector area as a fraction of the disc

The whole disc has area πr². The sector takes the same fraction, so A = (θ/2π) × πr² = ½r²θ. Check it with θ = 2π: ½r²(2π) = πr², the whole disc.

What goes wrong if the angle is in degrees

In degrees a full turn is 360, not 2π, so the fraction becomes θ/360 and the arc is (θ/360) × 2πr. Putting a degree value straight into rθ gives an answer about 57.3 times too large, because one radian is 180/π degrees.

The area formula from integration

Adding thin sectors of area ½r² dθ from 0 to θ gives ∫₀^θ ½r² dθ = ½r²θ. This is the same result reached by integration, and it is the method behind the formula rather than a separate rule.

Recovering the radius and angle from the arc and area

Dividing the area by the arc gives A/s = ½r, so r = 2A/s, and then θ = s/r. A sector with arc 15 cm and area 75 cm² has r = 2 × 75 / 15 = 10 cm and θ = 15/10 = 1.5 rad.

Checking the units of the answer

An arc is a length, so its unit is the radius unit. A sector's area has square units. An area with no square unit usually means the arc formula was used by mistake.

Converting angles and keeping exact values

Most lost marks on this topic are not hard mathematics. They come from an angle left in the wrong unit, or from a decimal where the question wanted π. These habits prevent both.

Degrees to radians, exactly

Multiply degrees by π/180. For example 150° × π/180 = 5π/6. When the question asks for an exact value, keep π in the answer and evaluate it only at the end.

Radians to degrees

Multiply radians by 180/π. For example 1.2 rad × 180/π = 68.75°. As a check, 1 rad is about 57.3°, so 1.2 rad must be a little more than 60°.

Multiples of π in an answer

A sector with r = 6 cm and θ = π/3 has arc length 6 × π/3 = 2π cm, which is about 6.28 cm. Give the exact form 2π cm when the question asks for it, and the decimal only when it asks for a decimal.

Estimating the size of a radian

π/2 ≈ 1.57 is a right angle and π ≈ 3.14 is a straight line. Since 1 rad is about 57°, an angle of 0.5 rad is roughly 29°. A quick estimate like this catches a wrong calculator mode before the answer is written.

Setting the calculator to radians

Check the mode before every trigonometric step. In RAD mode sin(π/6) = 0.5. In DEG mode, sin 0.5236 gives 0.0091, which shows the calculator was not in radians.

Mixed units in one question

A question may give the radius in metres and the angle in degrees. Convert the angle first, find the arc in the radius unit, and then state the answer in the unit the question asks for.

The triangle and the segment inside a sector

A chord joins the two ends of the arc, which turns the sector into a triangle plus a segment. Most questions on this topic that look hard are one of these three shapes in disguise, so identify the shape before choosing a formula.

The triangle inside a sector

The two radii and the chord form an isosceles triangle with sides r, r and included angle θ. Its area is ½r² sin θ, and it is always smaller than the sector.

Segment area as sector minus triangle

The segment between the chord and the arc has area ½r²θ − ½r² sin θ = ½r²(θ − sin θ). With r = 10 cm and θ = 1.2 rad, sin 1.2 = 0.9320, so the segment is ½ × 100 × (1.2 − 0.9320) = 13.4 cm².

Chord length from the cosine rule

The chord satisfies c² = r² + r² − 2r² cos θ, which simplifies to c = 2r sin(θ/2). With r = 10 cm and θ = 1.2 rad, c = 20 sin 0.6 = 11.29 cm.

Choosing the sector, triangle or segment

Read the shaded region before choosing a formula. Bounded by the two radii and the arc, it is the sector. Bounded by the chord and the arc, it is the segment. Bounded by the two radii and the chord, it is the triangle. Choosing the wrong one is the most common cause of a lost method mark.

Angles in the isosceles triangle

The two base angles of the triangle are equal, and each is (π − θ)/2. Those angles are needed when a question asks for an angle at the chord rather than at the centre.

Reflex angles and the major segment

The segment formula ½r²(θ − sin θ) applies for θ less than π. For a reflex angle, find the minor segment using 2π − θ, and subtract it from the whole disc to get the major part.

Applied problems: pendulums, wheels and wipers

Context questions give the same arc and sector formulae inside a story. The skill is to see which length is the radius and which angle is in radians, and then apply the formula for the quantity asked.

A pendulum sweeping an arc

The bob of a pendulum moves on an arc whose radius is the string length. A string of length 0.8 m that swings through 0.5 rad traces an arc of length 0.8 × 0.5 = 0.4 m.

Distance covered by a wheel

A wheel of radius 0.35 m turns through 2π per revolution, so it rolls 2π × 0.35 = 2.20 m per turn. In 50 turns it covers about 110 m.

The area swept by a windscreen wiper

An arm of length 0.6 m sweeps 100°, which is θ = 100π/180 = 1.745 rad. The swept area is ½ × 0.6² × 1.745 = 0.314 m².

Working backwards from an arc length

A curved track has arc length 18 m and subtends 0.75 rad at the centre of its circle. The radius is r = s/θ = 18/0.75 = 24 m.

Perimeter of a shape with arcs and straight sides

Add the straight sides to the arc lengths. For a sector, the perimeter is the arc plus both radii, not the arc alone. For a shape that contains only a curved edge, use the arc alone.

Angular speed and the angle turned

An angular speed in rad s⁻¹ multiplied by a time gives the angle turned in radians. A wheel at 4 rad s⁻¹ turns through 4 × 2.5 = 10 rad in 2.5 s, and the arc it rolls is rθ.

title: Acid-base Equilibria A2 Level Chemistry Revision Notes
content:
Acid-base Equilibria A2 Level Chemistry

Edexcel International A Level Chemistry WCH14 Topic 14 Acid-base Equilibria builds upon GCSE and AS concepts by exploring proton transfer, the quantitative treatment of strong and weak acids and bases, pH scales, buffer solutions, titration curves, and acid dissociation constants.

Bronsed-Lowry Theory and Conjugate Pairs

Acid-base reactions involve the transfer of protons. A Brnsted-Lowry acid is defined as a proton donor, and a Brnsted-Lowry base is defined as a proton acceptor. When an acid donates a proton, it forms its conjugate base. When a base accepts a proton, it forms its conjugate acid. These species form conjugate acid-base pairs that differ by a single proton (H+).

  • Brnsted-Lowry acid: a proton (H+) donor.
  • Brnsted-Lowry base: a proton (H+) acceptor.
  • Conjugate acid-base pair: two species related by the gain or loss of a single proton, written as acid / conjugate base or base / conjugate acid.
  • In the reaction between ethanoic acid and water, CH3COOH and CH3COO- form one pair, while H3O+ and H2O form the other pair.

pH Scale and Calculations

The term pH is defined as the negative logarithm to the base 10 of the hydrogen ion concentration in aqueous solution, expressed mathematically. A ten-fold change in hydrogen ion concentration causes a change of one pH unit.

  • pH definition: pH = −log10[H+]
  • Hydrogen ion concentration from pH: [H+] = 10^(−pH)
  • Ionic product of water, Kw, is defined as Kw = [H+][OH−] with a value of 1.0 × 10^(−14) mol2 dm−6 at 298 K.
  • pKa is defined as −log10(Ka) and pKw is defined as −log10(Kw).
  • For strong bases, calculate pOH = −log10[OH−] and use pH = 14.00 − pOH at 298 K, or use [H+] = Kw / [OH−] before finding the pH.

Worked Example: Calculate the pH of 0.050 mol dm−3 sodium hydroxide at 298 K.

  • Step 1: Identify [OH−] = 0.050 mol dm−3 because NaOH is a strong base and dissociates completely.
  • Step 2: Calculate pOH = −log10(0.050) = 1.30.
  • Step 3: Calculate pH = 14.00 − 1.30 = 12.70.

Strong and Weak Acids and Experimental Analysis

A strong acid dissociates completely in water, meaning the concentration of hydrogen ions equals the concentration of the acid. A weak acid dissociates only partly in water, establishing an equilibrium. The degree of dissociation is much lower for weak acids than for strong acids.

  • Strong acid: dissociates completely, so [H+] = [acid]. For 0.010 mol dm−3 HCl, [H+] = 0.010 mol dm−3 and pH = 2.00.
  • Weak acid: dissociates partially, represented by HA ⇌ H+ + A−.
  • Acid dissociation constant expression: Ka = [H+][A−] / [HA].
  • Experimental analysis involves measuring the pH of a variety of substances, including equimolar solutions of strong and weak acids, strong and weak bases, and salts. Strong acids have much lower pH values than weak acids of the same concentration.
  • Comparing the pH of a strong acid and a weak acid after dilution 10, 100, and 1000 times shows that diluting a strong acid by a factor of 10 increases its pH by 1 unit, whereas diluting a weak acid by a factor of 10 increases its pH by less than 1 unit due to partial re-dissociation of the weak acid.

Worked Example: Calculate the pH of 0.100 mol dm−3 propanoic acid, CH3CH2COOH, given that Ka = 1.35 × 10^(−5) mol dm−3.

  • Step 1: Write the expression Ka = [H+]2 / [HA], assuming [H+] = [A−] and [HA]equilibrium equals initial [HA] because dissociation is very small.
  • Step 2: Rearrange to [H+] = √(Ka × [HA]) = √(1.35 × 10^(−5) × 0.100) = √(1.35 × 10^(−6)) = 1.16 × 10^(−3) mol dm−3.
  • Step 3: Calculate pH = −log10(1.16 × 10^(−3)) = 2.93.

Core Practical 11 and Determining Ka from Experimental Data

Core Practical 11 involves finding the Ka value for a weak acid by measuring the pH of solutions of known concentration, or by using titration methods and half-equivalence points.

  • To calculate Ka for a weak acid from experimental data given the pH of a solution containing a known mass of acid, first calculate the concentration of the acid in mol dm−3.
  • Use [H+] = 10^(−pH) to find the hydrogen ion concentration.
  • Substitute [H+], [OH−] approximations, and remaining undissociated acid concentration into Ka = [H+]2 / [HA].
  • In weak acid-strong base or strong acid-weak base titrations, at the exact point where half the acid is neutralised, [HA] = [A−], which simplifies the buffer equation to pH = pKa, allowing Ka to be determined directly from the pH reading at that volume.

Titration Curves and Indicators

Titration curves plot pH against volume of titrant added. They cover all combinations of strong and weak monoprotic and diprotic acids with bases.

  • Strong acid and strong base curve starts low, has a steep vertical section from pH 3 to 11 at the equivalence point of pH 7.
  • Weak acid and strong base curve starts higher (around pH 3), has a buffer region, and a steep vertical section from pH 7 to 11 with an equivalence point above pH 7.
  • Strong acid and weak base curve has a steep vertical section from pH 3 to 7 with an equivalence point below pH 7.
  • Weak acid and weak base curves show no sharp vertical pH change, making titrations difficult without a pH meter.
  • Diprotic acids show two distinct equivalence points corresponding to the donation of two protons per molecule.
  • Indicator selection: choose an indicator whose pH range falls entirely within the steep vertical section of the titration curve. Phenolphthalein (pH range 8.3 to 10.0) is suitable for weak acid-strong base titrations. Methyl orange (pH range 3.1 to 4.4) is suitable for strong acid-weak base titrations.

Buffer Solutions

A buffer solution is a system that minimises changes in pH when small amounts of acid or alkali are added. An acidic buffer consists of a weak acid and its salt (providing the conjugate base), such as ethanoic acid and sodium ethanoate.

  • Buffer action: when H+ is added, it reacts with the conjugate base (A−) to form undissociated weak acid (HA), removing excess H+. When OH− is added, it reacts with H+ ions (or HA directly) to form water, pulling the equilibrium to the right to replace the H+ ions.
  • Buffer pH calculation formula: pH = pKa + log([A−] / [HA]).
  • To calculate concentrations required to prepare a buffer solution of a given pH, rearrange the buffer formula using target pH, known Ka, and ratio of salt to acid.
  • Biological importance: buffers in cells and in blood, specifically the carbonic acid-hydrogencarbonate system (H2CO3 / HCO3−), maintain blood pH strictly between 7.35 and 7.45.
  • Importance in foods: buffers and acidulants prevent deterioration due to pH changes caused by bacterial or fungal activity, preserving texture and safety.

Typical mistakes

  • Mistake: Assuming weak acids dissociate completely. Correction: Always use Ka expressions and make the standard weak acid approximation [HA]start equals [HA]equilibrium.
  • Mistake: Forgetting that Kw varies with temperature and treating 1.0 × 10^(−14) as universal at all temperatures. Correction: Use 1.0 × 10^(−14) mol2 dm−6 strictly for 298 K unless specified otherwise.
  • Mistake: Selecting methyl orange for a weak acid-strong base titration. Correction: Methyl orange changes colour below pH 7, whereas the equivalence point of a weak acid-strong base titration is above pH 7; use phenolphthalein instead.
  • Mistake: Confusing conjugate acid-base pairs by omitting charges or hydrogen atoms. Correction: Check that pairs differ by exactly one H+ ion.

Exam-style questions

  1. Question: Define a Brnsted-Lowry acid. Answer: A proton donor. Step: State the definition clearly for credit.
  2. Question: Calculate the pH of 0.0200 mol dm−3 hydrochloric acid. Answer: [H+] = 0.0200 mol dm−3, so pH = −log10(0.0200) = 1.70. Step: Recognise complete dissociation of strong acid and apply pH formula.
  3. Question: Write the expression for the acid dissociation constant, Ka, for propanoic acid. Answer: Ka = [H+][CH3CH2COO−] / [CH3CH2COOH]. Step: Include all equilibrium concentrations correctly.
  4. Question: Explain why the pH of a weak acid changes less than that of a strong acid upon 10-fold dilution. Answer: Diluting a weak acid shifts the equilibrium to the right, causing further dissociation which partially compensates for the added water volume. Step: Mention equilibrium shift and partial dissociation.
  5. Question: State the buffer pair present in blood plasma. Answer: H2CO3 and HCO3−. Step: Name carbonic acid and hydrogencarbonate ions.

Use these notes alongside past paper practice questions for Edexcel IAL Chemistry Topic 14. Ensure all formula manipulations for Ka and buffer calculations are practiced thoroughly before moving on to Topic 15 Energetics II.

title: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Transformations and Vectors
content:
Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Transformations and Vectors

Transformations move shapes on a grid, and vectors describe those moves with numbers. The exam asks two things: perform a transformation and, more often, describe one completely — with its centre, angle, direction, line or scale factor. This note builds the topic from zero: the four transformations and the full-description checklist for each, enlargement and its effect on area, vector notation with the house column-vector form (x; y), vector arithmetic, and the vector-geometry proofs that show lines are parallel or points are collinear.

The four transformations

TransformationWhat changesWhat must be stated in a description
Translationposition only, no rotation or resizethe column vector of the move
Reflectionmirror imagethe line of reflection (e.g. x = 2, y = x)
Rotationturns about a pointcentre, angle, and direction (clockwise or anticlockwise)
Enlargementresizes about a pointcentre and scale factor

The complete description is the mark: "rotation" alone scores nothing; "rotation 90° anticlockwise about (2, 1)" scores fully.

Translation

A translation moves every point by the same vector. In column form (x; y), x is the horizontal move and y the vertical move; right and up are positive.

Worked example. Triangle A has vertices (1, 1), (3, 1), (1, 4). Translate by (4; −2) and give the image coordinates.

(1, 1) → (5, -1)
(3, 1) → (7, -1)
(1, 4) → (5, 2)

The shape is congruent to the original (same size and shape), and the orientation is unchanged.

Reflection

A reflection flips a shape across a line; the line is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining each point to its image. Common lines: x = a (vertical), y = b (horizontal), y = x, y = −x.

Worked example. Reflect the point (3, 5) in the line y = x.

reflection in y = x swaps the coordinates: (3, 5) → (5, 3)

Worked example 2. Reflect (2, 4) in the line x = 1.

the line x = 1 is vertical; the distance of x = 2 from it is 1,
so the image is 1 unit on the other side: (0, 4)

To find the mirror line from a shape and its image, join a point to its image and draw the perpendicular bisector of that segment.

Rotation

A rotation turns a shape about a fixed centre through a given angle. The four standard angles are 90° and 180° in either direction; 90° clockwise equals 270° anticlockwise.

Worked example. Rotate the point (3, 1) 90° clockwise about the origin.

90 ° clockwise about O: (x, y) → (y, -x)
(3, 1) → (1, -3)

Worked example 2. Rotate (2, 5) 180° about the origin.

180 °: (x, y) → (-x, -y)
(2, 5) → (-2, -5)

For a centre other than the origin, translate the centre to the origin, rotate, then translate back — or count the grid squares from the centre.

Enlargement

An enlargement with centre C and scale factor k maps every point so that its distance from C is multiplied by k. Negative scale factors put the image on the far side of the centre; fractional factors between 0 and 1 shrink the shape.

image distance from centre = k x object distance from centre
area of image = k² x area of object

Worked example. Enlarge the point (2, 3) by scale factor 3 about the origin.

(2, 3) → (6, 9)

Worked example 2 (area). A triangle of area 12 cm² is enlarged by scale factor 2.5. Find the image area.

area factor = k² = 6.25
new area = 12 × 6.25 = 75 cm²

Enlargement is the only transformation that changes area (unless k = 1 or −1); translations, reflections and rotations preserve both shape and size.

Vectors: notation and magnitude

A vector has magnitude and direction. In this course it is written as a column vector (x; y): x is the horizontal component, y the vertical. The same vector can be written as a bold letter a with an arrow above it.

column vector (x; y)
magnitude = √(x² + y²)
direction angle to the horizontal: tan(θ) = y/x
equal vectors have the same components; opposite vectors
negate both components

Worked example. Find the magnitude and direction of the vector (3; 4).

magnitude = √(9 + 16) = 5
tan(θ) = 4/3  →  θ = 53.1 ° above the horizontal

Vector arithmetic and geometry

addition: (a; b) + (c; d) = (a + c; b + d)
subtraction: (a; b) - (c; d) = (a - c; b - d)
scalar multiple: k(a; b) = (ka; kb)

position vector of A relative to O: OA
AB = OB - OA
midpoint of AB: (OA + OB)/2

Worked example. OA = (2; 1), OB = (7; 5). Find AB and the midpoint of AB.

AB = OB - OA = (7 - 2; 5 - 1) = (5; 4)
midpoint = ((2 + 7)/2; (1 + 5)/2) = (4.5; 3)

Worked example 2 (parallel). Show that AB is parallel to CD given A(1, 2), B(5, 8), C(0, 1), D(6, 10).

AB = (5 - 1; 8 - 2) = (4; 6)
CD = (6 - 0; 10 - 1) = (6; 9)
(6; 9) = 1.5 x (4; 6), so CD = 1.5 AB: parallel (and longer)

Parallel vectors are scalar multiples of each other; collinear points occur when AB and AC (or AB and BC) are parallel and share a point.

Combining transformations and invariant points

Two transformations applied in sequence are not the same as the reverse order: a reflection followed by a rotation generally differs from the rotation followed by the reflection. When a question asks for the single transformation equivalent to two, apply both to a convenient point (the origin or a vertex) and to a second point, then identify the transformation that maps the original to the final image. Invariant points are points that do not move: every point on a mirror line is invariant under a reflection, the centre of a rotation is invariant, and no point is invariant under a translation.

Worked example. A shape is reflected in the x-axis and then translated by (0; 3). Find the image of (2, 1) and identify any invariant points.

reflection in the x-axis: (2, 1) → (2, -1)
translation by (0; 3): (2, -1) → (2, 2)
No invariant points: the reflection moved every point off the
axis, and the translation then moved everything upward.

Worked example 2 (invariant line). State the invariant points of a reflection in the line y = 2.

Every point with y-coordinate 2 lies on the mirror line and does
not move: the whole line y = 2 is invariant.

Vectors in context: displacement and velocity

Column vectors describe any quantity with magnitude and direction in two dimensions: displacement (a move from one point to another), velocity (displacement per second) and force (a push in a direction). The arithmetic is identical; only the interpretation changes.

  • Displacement: AB is the vector from A to B; a round trip returns to the start, so the sum of the vectors around a closed polygon is zero.
  • Velocity: a velocity vector (3; −2) means 3 units per second right and 2 units per second down; position after t seconds is the starting position plus t × velocity.
  • Resultant: the sum of two vectors; a vector and its negative cancel.

Worked example. A particle starts at (1, 2) and moves with velocity (3; −1) for 4 seconds. Find its final position.

displacement = 4 x (3; -1) = (12; -4)
final position = (1 + 12; 2 - 4) = (13; -2)

Worked examples: vector proofs

Worked example. In triangle OAB, P is the midpoint of OA and Q is the midpoint of OB. Prove PQ is parallel to AB.

OP = (1/2) OA, OQ = (1/2) OB
PQ = OQ - OP = (1/2)(OB - OA) = (1/2) AB
PQ is a scalar multiple of AB, so PQ is parallel to AB
(and half its length).

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Translation) Translate (2, 3) by (−1; 4). Answer: (1, 7).
  2. (Reflection) Reflect (4, 1) in the x-axis. Answer: (4, −1).
  3. (Rotation) Rotate (5, 2) 90° anticlockwise about the origin. Answer: (−2, 5).
  4. (Enlargement) Enlarge (1, 2) by factor −2 about the origin. Answer: (−2, −4).
  5. (Description) Describe fully the transformation mapping (1, 1) to (3, 5). Answer: Translation by (2; 4) — one of many correct complete descriptions.
  6. (Magnitude) Find the magnitude of (6; 8). Answer: √(36 + 64) = 10.
  7. (Position vectors) OA = (1; 4), OB = (5; 2). Find AB. Answer: (4; −2).
  8. (Collinear) Show A(1, 1), B(3, 4), C(7, 10) are collinear. Answer: AB = (2; 3), AC = (6; 9) = 3 AB — parallel and share A, so collinear.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Incomplete descriptions: "enlargement by 2" omits the centre and loses marks; "reflection" omits the line. State every attribute.
  • Direction of rotation: clockwise and anticlockwise are different transformations; a 90° rotation clockwise is not the same as anticlockwise.
  • Area under enlargement: area scales by k², not k. Doubling the sides quadruples the area.
  • Vector direction: AB = OB − OA, not OA − OB. Reversing the subtraction negates the vector.
  • Column order: (x; y) is horizontal then vertical. Swapping produces a reflection in y = x, not the intended vector.
  • Parallelogram assumptions: equal magnitudes do not imply equal vectors — direction matters too.
  • Negative scale factors: the image lies on the opposite side of the centre; it is not simply "smaller".
  • Collinearity proof: showing parallel is not enough — the segments must also share a point. State it.

title: Exam technique: Robotics & AI
content:
### What earns the marks
For full marks on 6.1, 6.2 and 6.3, the examiner needs to see explanations, descriptions and justifications. For example, to answer a question on automated systems, a student must explain how sensors, processors and actuators work together, and describe how this relates to real-world applications. For AI characteristics, a student must justify how a particular characteristic, such as learning or problem-solving, is used in a given scenario.
### Traps
A common mistake is to confuse supervised and unsupervised machine learning. Correction: supervised learning uses labelled data, while unsupervised learning uses unlabelled data. Another mistake is to overlook the importance of ethics in AI development. Correction: students must consider the potential biases and consequences of AI systems. A third mistake is to fail to provide concrete examples when describing AI applications. Correction: students must tie each AI characteristic to a specific step in the scenario.
### Memory hooks
To remember the components of a robotic system, use the mnemonic SPAP: Sensors, Processors, Actuators and Power. To recall the types of machine learning, use the phrase SUR: Supervised, Unsupervised and Reinforcement. When evaluating the benefits and concerns of robotics, consider the acronym PJD: Precision, Job displacement and Danger.
### Timing
This topic typically accounts for 20-30% of the paper, and students should budget around 30-40 minutes to answer the relevant questions. Students should allocate their time based on the mark allocation for each question, and make sure to leave time for review and revision.

title: IGCSE Chemistry: Chemical Energetics
content:
IGCSE Chemistry: Chemical Energetics

Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry 0620 (2026–2028), Extended route, Topic 5 Chemical energetics, statement 5.1 Exothermic and endothermic reactions. This note covers the energy accounting of reactions: where the energy goes when bonds break and form, how to read and draw reaction pathway diagrams, and how to calculate enthalpy changes from bond energies. Every calculation is worked line by line, and the sign convention — where most marks are lost — is derived from the physics rather than memorised.

Exothermic and endothermic: the physical picture

Every chemical reaction involves breaking bonds in the reactants and making new bonds in the products. Breaking bonds takes energy in (you must pull atoms apart against their attraction); making bonds releases energy out (atoms fall into each other's attraction). The overall energy change is the balance between the two — like a bank account with deposits and withdrawals.

  • Exothermic reactions release more energy than they absorb — the products have lower energy than the reactants, the temperature of the surroundings rises. Examples: combustion, neutralisation, respiration.
  • Endothermic reactions absorb more than they release — products have higher energy, surroundings cool. Examples: thermal decomposition, photosynthesis, dissolving ammonium nitrate.

Definitions to write exactly: an enthalpy change (ΔH) is the heat energy change at constant pressure; ΔH is negative for exothermic reactions (the system loses energy to the surroundings) and positive for endothermic reactions (the system gains). The activation energy (Eₐ) is the minimum energy colliding particles need to react — the hill every reaction must climb first, even exothermic ones.

Reaction pathway diagrams

Exothermic profile (combustion of methane):

  energy
    |  *  <- reactants (CH₄ + 2O₂) at higher energy
    |   \
    |    \  Eₐ (activation energy: reactants to the peak)
    |     \_
    |       * <- transition state (the hill's peak)
    |        \
    |         \  ΔH negative (downhill overall)
    |          \
    |           *  <- products (CO₂ + 2H₂O) at lower energy
    +---------------- reaction path

Endothermic profile (thermal decomposition):

  energy
    |             *  <- products at HIGHER energy
    |            /   ΔH positive (uphill overall)
    |           /
    |       * <- transition state
    |      /
    |  *  <- reactants
    +---------------- reaction path

Drawing rules that earn marks:
  - label BOTH energy levels (reactants and products),
  - draw Eₐ from reactants up to the peak,
  - draw ΔH as the DIFFERENCE between reactant and product levels
    (arrow down for exothermic, up for endothermic),
  - label the axes (energy against reaction path).
BondBond energy (kJ/mol)BondBond energy (kJ/mol)
H-H436O-H464
Cl-Cl242C-H413
O=O498C=O (in CO₂)805
C-C348H-Cl431

These are average values for the bonds in many environments; an exam supplies the table it expects you to use, so always take numbers from the question. The arithmetic above stays identical whichever numbers arrive.

Calculating enthalpy changes from bond energies

Master method: ΔH = (energy needed to break all reactant bonds) − (energy released making all product bonds). Bond energies are always positive quantities; the sign of ΔH comes out of the subtraction.

Worked: calculate ΔH for the combustion of methane using bond energies.
  CH₄ + 2O₂ -> CO₂ + 2H₂O

  Bond energies (kJ/mol): C-H 413, O=O 498, C=O 805, O-H 464

Step 1 - count and list bonds BROKEN (reactants):
  4 x C-H  = 4 x 413 = 1652 kJ
  2 x O=O  = 2 x 498 =  996 kJ
  total in = 2648 kJ

Step 2 - count and list bonds MADE (products):
  2 x C=O  = 2 x 805 = 1610 kJ   (CO₂ has two C=O double bonds)
  4 x O-H  = 4 x 464 = 1856 kJ   (2 H₂O x two O-H each)
  total out = 3466 kJ

Step 3 - subtract:
  ΔH = 2648 - 3466 = -818 kJ per mole of CH₄

Step 4 - sign check: negative = energy released = exothermic ✓
  (combustion must be exothermic - a positive answer means a counting error)

Common counting errors flagged: CO₂ contains TWO C=O bonds (not one); each
water has TWO O-H bonds, and there are TWO waters (four O-H in total).

The master method for any energetics question

1. Write the BALANCED equation first (unbalanced = wrong bond counts).
2. Draw out or list every bond in reactants and products.
3. Multiply each bond energy by the number of those bonds.
4. ΔH = bonds broken − bonds made.
5. Check the sign matches the reaction type (combustion: negative).

Worked mini-example: H₂ + Cl₂ -> 2HCl
  broken: H-H 436 + Cl-Cl 242 = 678
  made:   2 x H-Cl 2 x 431 = 862
  ΔH = 678 - 862 = -184 kJ/mol  (exothermic ✓)

Worked example: an enthalpy cycle question from scratch

Enthalpy of combustion is measured in a calorimeter; the same data can be
reached through a cycle. Example: given
  (1) C(s) + O₂(g) -> CO₂(g)                ΔH = -394 kJ/mol
  (2) H₂(g) + 1/2 O₂(g) -> H₂O(l)           ΔH = -286 kJ/mol
  (3) C(s) + 2H₂(g) -> CH₄(g)               ΔH = -75 kJ/mol
find the enthalpy of combustion of methane.

Target: CH₄ + 2O₂ -> CO₂ + 2H₂O

Method: combine the given equations so they add to the target.
  Reverse (3): CH₄ -> C + 2H₂       ΔH = +75      (sign flips on reversal)
  Keep (1):    C + O₂ -> CO₂        ΔH = -394
  2 x (2):     2H₂ + O₂ -> 2H₂O    ΔH = 2 x -286 = -572
  ------------------------------------------------------------
  Add: CH₄ + 2O₂ -> CO₂ + 2H₂O
  ΔH = +75 - 394 - 572 = -891 kJ/mol

Sanity check: combustion must be exothermic - a negative answer is the
signature. The sign-flip-on-reversal rule and the multiply-everything rule
are where the marks live.

Everyday energy changes

Instant cold packs (ammonium nitrate dissolving in water — endothermic, the pack cools); self-heating cans (calcium oxide + water — exothermic); hand warmers (iron oxidation — exothermic); the energy value of fuels (calorimetry: energy = mass of water × 4.2 J/g°C × temperature rise). These applied questions always ask for the particle-level reason as well as the sign.

Calorimetry worked: burning 0.5 g of a fuel heats 100 g of water from
22.0 °C to 32.0 °C. Calculate the energy released per gram.

  energy = mass x specific heat x ΔT
         = 100 x 4.2 x (32.0 - 22.0)
         = 100 x 4.2 x 10
         = 4200 J = 4.2 kJ
  per gram: 4.2 kJ / 0.5 g = 8.4 kJ/g

Watch the units: 4.2 is J/g°C (so the answer starts in joules); the question
may want kJ - divide by 1000 and say so.

Calorimetry questions also probe assumptions: heat is lost to the surroundings and to the calorimeter itself, so measured temperature rises underestimate the true enthalpy change; insulation and a lid reduce that loss. Incomplete combustion (carbon monoxide or soot forming instead of carbon dioxide) releases less energy than the complete-combustion value, which is why experimental answers fall below data-book figures. Stating these two effects is often the last mark on a fuel-comparison question.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Getting ΔH's sign backwards: exothermic = negative (energy leaves the system); endothermic = positive. Bond energy method: broken − made, not the reverse.
  • Subtracting bond energies the wrong way round — the formula is energy in (broken) minus energy out (made).
  • Forgetting to multiply by the number of bonds (four C-H, not one).
  • Confusing activation energy with enthalpy change: Eₐ is the reactant-to-peak height (always positive); ΔH is reactant-to-product difference.
  • Drawing an exothermic profile with products above reactants (or forgetting to label levels/axes).
  • Claiming bond making absorbs energy — making bonds releases; breaking absorbs.
  • Mixing J and kJ in calorimetry (4.2 J/g°C × g × °C gives joules).

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 4, 3 marks). Define enthalpy change and state the sign of ΔH for (i) combustion (ii) thermal decomposition.

Answer: Enthalpy change is the heat energy change at constant pressure during a reaction. (i) Combustion is exothermic, so ΔH is negative. (ii) Thermal decomposition is endothermic, so ΔH is positive.

Question 2 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Explain, in terms of bonds, why combustion is exothermic.

Answer: Combustion breaks the bonds in the fuel and in oxygen (absorbing energy) and makes new bonds in carbon dioxide and water (releasing energy). The energy released forming the very strong C=O and O-H bonds in the products exceeds the energy absorbed breaking the reactant bonds, so net energy is released to the surroundings and ΔH is negative.

Question 3 (Paper 4, 5 marks). Calculate ΔH for 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O using bond energies: H-H 436, O=O 498, O-H 464 kJ/mol.

Answer: Broken: 2 × H-H = 872; 1 × O=O = 498; total = 1370 kJ. Made: 4 × O-H = 1856 kJ. ΔH = 1370 − 1856 = −486 kJ per mole of reaction as written (−243 kJ per mole of H₂).

Question 4 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Draw and label a reaction pathway diagram for an endothermic reaction, identifying activation energy and ΔH.

Answer: Axes: energy (y) against reaction path (x). Products are drawn above reactants. Eₐ is the vertical arrow from reactants up to the peak of the curve (positive, the energy needed to start the reaction). ΔH is the vertical arrow between reactant and product levels, pointing up (positive) since products have higher energy.

Question 5 (Paper 4, 3 marks). A student burns 1.0 g of ethanol and heats 200 g of water by 15.0 °C. Calculate the energy released and give it in kJ/g. (c = 4.2 J/g°C)

Answer: Energy = 200 × 4.2 × 15.0 = 12 600 J = 12.6 kJ. Per gram of ethanol: 12.6 ÷ 1.0 = 12.6 kJ/g.

Question 6 (Paper 2, 2 marks). Explain why an instant cold pack feels cold.

Answer: The pack dissolves an endothermic salt (ammonium nitrate): the dissolving process absorbs heat energy from the surroundings to break the solute's lattice, so the pack and hand lose thermal energy and feel cold.

Energy decides whether a reaction can happen at all; whether it actually does — and how fast — is the next topic.

title: A Level Mathematics: Further Trigonometry
content:
A Level Mathematics: Further Trigonometry

A2 trigonometry covers the reciprocal functions, the compound and double-angle identities, the harmonic form R sin(θ + α) that turns a sum into a single wave, inverse functions with their domains, and equations with multiple or transformed angles. This note builds every identity from the compound-angle results, so the whole set is reconstructable rather than memorised.

The reciprocal functions

sec x = 1/cos x;  cosec x = 1/sin x;  cot x = 1/tan x = cos x/sin x

identities: 1 + tan² x = sec² x;  1 + cot² x = cosec² x

Worked example. Solve sec x = 2 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 360°.

cos x = 1/2  →  x = 60 or 300

Worked example 2 (identity). Prove that sec²x − tan²x = 1.

sec² - tan² = 1/cos² - sin²/cos² = (1 - sin²)/cos² = cos²/cos² = 1

Worked example 3 (solve). Solve 2 cosec²x = 5 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 360°.

cosec² x = 2.5  →  sin² x = 0.4  →  sin x = +/- 0.6325
x = 39.2, 140.8, 219.2, 320.8

Reciprocal functions blow up where the denominator vanishes: sec and tan at 90°, cosec and cot at 0°. Sketching is the safest way to see the asymptotes.

Compound-angle identities

sin(A + B) = sin A cos B + cos A sin B
sin(A - B) = sin A cos B - cos A sin B
cos(A + B) = cos A cos B - sin A sin B
cos(A - B) = cos A cos B + sin A sin B
tan(A + B) = (tan A + tan B)/(1 - tan A tan B)

Worked example 1 (exact value). Find sin 75° exactly.

sin(45 + 30) = sin45 cos30 + cos45 sin30
= (sqrt2/2)(sqrt3/2) + (sqrt2/2)(1/2) = (sqrt6 + sqrt2)/4

Worked example 2 (prove). Prove that sin(A + B) + sin(A − B) = 2 sin A cos B.

add the two expansions: the cos A sin B terms cancel
leaving 2 sin A cos B

Worked example 3 (solve). Solve sin(x + 30°) = cos x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 360°.

sin x cos30 + cos x sin30 = cos x
0.866 sin x + 0.5 cos x = cos x
0.866 sin x = 0.5 cos x  →  tan x = 0.577  →  x = 30 or 210

Double-angle identities

sin 2A = 2 sin A cos A
cos 2A = cos² A - sin² A = 2cos² A - 1 = 1 - 2 sin² A
tan 2A = 2 tan A/(1 - tan² A)

Worked example. Given sin A = 3/5 with A acute, find sin 2A and cos 2A.

cos A = 4/5
sin 2A = 2(3/5)(4/5) = 24/25
cos 2A = 1 - 2(9/25) = 7/25

Worked example 2 (solve). Solve cos 2x = sin x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 360°.

1 - 2 sin² x = sin x  →  2 sin² x + sin x - 1 = 0
(2 sin x - 1)(sin x + 1) = 0
sin x = 1/2  →  x = 30, 150;  sin x = -1  →  x = 270

The choice of cos 2A form matters: pick the one that leaves a single trigonometric function in the resulting equation.

The harmonic form

a sin x + b cos x = R sin(x + alpha)
R = √(a² + b²);  tan alpha = b/a

always expand back to check the sign of alpha

Worked example. Express 3 sin x + 4 cos x in the form R sin(x + α).

R = 5; tan alpha = 4/3  →  alpha = 53.13 °
3 sin x + 4 cos x = 5 sin(x + 53.13 °)
check: 5[sin x cos53.13 + cos x sin53.13] = 3 sin x + 4 cos x

Worked example 2 (maximum). Hence find the maximum value of 3 sin x + 4 cos x and the x at which it occurs.

maximum = 5, when sin(x + 53.13) = 1
x + 53.13 = 90  →  x = 36.87 °

Worked example 3 (solve). Solve 3 sin x + 4 cos x = 2 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 360°.

5 sin(x + 53.13) = 2  →  sin(x + 53.13) = 0.4
x + 53.13 = 23.58 or 156.42
x = -29.5 (reject, or add 360: 330.5) or 103.3

Adjusting the interval for the phase shift is compulsory: the angle x + α runs over a different range from x.

Inverse trigonometric functions

arcsin: domain [-1, 1], range [-90, 90] degrees
arccos: domain [-1, 1], range [0, 180]
arctan: all reals, range (-90, 90)

The restricted ranges are what make the inverses functions. That is why arcsin(sin 150°) = 30°, not 150°.

Worked example. Evaluate arcsin(sin 200°).

sin 200 = -0.342
arcsin(-0.342) = -20 °, which lies in the principal range

Worked example 2 (equation). Solve tan⁻¹(2x) = 45°.

2x = tan 45 = 1  →  x = 0.5

Worked example 3 (derivative link). Differentiate y = arcsin x.

dy/dx = 1/√(1 - x²), valid for |x| < 1

Equations with transformed angles

for sin(kx + c) = value over a range of x:
  1. find the range of the argument kx + c
  2. solve for the argument
  3. convert back to x and keep only values in the x-range

Worked example. Solve sin(2x − 30°) = 0.5 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 180°.

argument range: -30 <= 2x - 30 <= 330
2x - 30 = 30, 150, 390 (out of range)
2x = 60 or 180  →  x = 30 or 90

Worked example 2. Solve cos(3x) = −0.5 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 180°.

argument range 0 <= 3x <= 540
3x = 120, 240, 480  →  x = 40, 80, 160

Solving equations in a given range

The single most reliable routine in A2 trigonometry is a fixed order of operations, because the marks are lost in the bookkeeping, never in the trigonometry.

step 1  reduce to ONE trigonometric function (identity if needed)
step 2  solve for the function value, keeping every sign
step 3  find the principal solution
step 4  use symmetry to find all solutions in the argument's range
step 5  convert back to x, and discard anything outside the stated range

Worked example. Solve 2 sin²x + 3 cos x = 3 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 360°.

sin² = 1 - cos²  →  2(1 - cos² x) + 3 cos x = 3
2 - 2cos² x + 3 cos x - 3 = 0
2cos² x - 3 cos x + 1 = 0   →  (2cos x - 1)(cos x - 1) = 0
cos x = 1/2  →  x = 60, 300
cos x = 1    →  x = 0, 360
solutions: 0, 60, 300, 360 degrees

Worked example 2 (quadratic in tan). Solve 3 tan²x − tan x − 2 = 0 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 360°.

(3 tan x + 2)(tan x - 1) = 0
tan x = 1  →  x = 45, 225
tan x = -2/3  →  x = 180 - 33.7 = 146.3;  and 326.3
tangent repeats every 180 degrees, so each root gives exactly two solutions here

Note the period: sin and cos repeat every 360°, tan every 180°. Getting the period wrong either loses half the solutions or invents ones outside the range.

Proving identities

An identity is proved by transforming one side into the other, never by moving terms across the equals sign as if it were an equation. The safe strategy is to start on the side that looks worse and simplify towards the other.

allowed moves: rewrite sec/cosec/cot as sin and cos; apply Pythagoras;
               expand compound angles; use a double-angle form
not allowed:   multiplying both sides by something, unless every step is reversible
               and the result is still an identity

Worked example. Prove that (1 + sin x)/(cos x) = cos x/(1 − sin x).

start from the left; multiply numerator and denominator by (1 - sin x):
(1 + sin x)(1 - sin x) / [cos x (1 - sin x)]
= (1 - sin² x) / [cos x (1 - sin x)]
= cos² x / [cos x (1 - sin x)]
= cos x / (1 - sin x)

Worked example 2 (double angle). Prove that (sin 2x)/(1 + cos 2x) = tan x.

sin 2x = 2 sin x cos x;  1 + cos 2x = 1 + (2cos² x - 1) = 2cos² x
ratio = 2 sin x cos x / 2cos² x = sin x/cos x = tan x

The choice of cos 2A form is not taste: pick the version that cancels against the rest of the expression. Here 2cos²x − 1 was right because the denominator needed a cosine.

Modelling with the harmonic form

The R-formula is not only an algebraic trick; it is the reason oscillating physical quantities are written as a single wave. Tidal height, temperature, alternating current and the height of a point on a rotating wheel are all of the form a sin θ + b cos θ, and every question about their maximum, minimum or first occurrence is answered by the amplitude and phase.

h = 12 + 5 sin(30t) + 12 cos(30t)  (t in hours)
R = √(25 + 144) = 13;  tan alpha = 12/5  →  alpha = 67.38 degrees
h = 12 + 13 sin(30t + 67.38)
maximum depth = 12 + 13 = 25;  minimum = 12 - 13 = -1 (below the datum)

Worked example. For that model, find the first time after t = 0 at which the height is a maximum.

sin(30t + 67.38) = 1  →  30t + 67.38 = 90
30t = 22.62  →  t = 0.754 hours = 45.2 minutes

Worked example 2 (period and interpretation). State the period of the model and what it represents.

argument 30t has period 360 degrees in t:  360/30 = 12 hours
the tide repeats every 12 hours, twice a day

Worked example 3 (minimum as a phrase). Find the time of the first minimum.

sin(30t + 67.38) = -1  →  30t + 67.38 = 270
30t = 202.62  →  t = 6.75 hours

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Reciprocal) Solve cosec x = 2 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 360°. Answer: sin x = ½ → 30°, 150°.
  2. (Identity) Simplify (1 − cos²x)/sin x. Answer: sin x.
  3. (Compound) Find cos 15° exactly. Answer: (√6 + √2)/4.
  4. (Double) Given cos A = 5/13, find sin 2A. Answer: 2(12/13)(5/13) = 120/169.
  5. (Double solve) Solve sin 2x = cos x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 180°. Answer: cos x(2 sin x − 1) = 0 → x = 90°, 30°, 150°.
  6. (Harmonic) Express 5 sin x − 12 cos x as R sin(x − α). Answer: 13 sin(x − 67.4°).
  7. (Maximum) Max of 5 sin x − 12 cos x? Answer: 13.
  8. (Inverse) Solve arccos(2x) = 60°. Answer: 2x = ½ → x = ¼.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Losing solutions: quadratics in sin or cos give two values, each with its own solutions in the range.
  • Wrong cos 2A form: choose the version that leaves one function; otherwise the equation becomes unsolvable.
  • Harmonic sign: R sin(x − α) versus R sin(x + α) depends on the signs of a and b; expand to check.
  • Interval not adjusted: transformed angles need the argument's range computed before solving.
  • Inverse range ignored: arcsin returns only the principal value; other solutions come from the symmetries.
  • sec/cosec confused: sec = 1/cos, cosec = 1/sin — the reverse is a silent disaster.
  • Degrees and radians: the R-formula's α follows the mode; mixing them gives a phase error.
  • Identity proofs without a direction: start from the more complicated side and transform towards the simpler; do not work on both sides at once unless every step is reversible.

Equations and symbols

Every relation this topic is examined on, written with its real notation and followed by a key naming each symbol, its unit and what it means. Where a statement has a second useful form both are given, so a rearrangement in the exam is mechanical rather than something to rediscover under time pressure.

Reciprocal functions and their identities

sec θ = 1/cos θ, cosec θ = 1/sin θ, cot θ = 1/tan θ = cos θ/sin θ
Key: θ = the angle, in degrees or radians; sec, cosec, cot = the reciprocals of cosine, sine and tangent. Each is undefined wherever its denominator is zero — sec and tan at 90°, cosec at 0° — and those exclusions are part of the domain.

1 + tan²θ = sec²θ
Key: θ = any angle where both sides are defined. Divide sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 by cos²θ; it is the identity that turns a quadratic in tan into one in sec, which is how many equations in this topic are solved.

1 + cot²θ = cosec²θ
Key: θ = any angle where both sides are defined. The same division by sin²θ instead of cos²θ. Knowing which of the two to use is decided by which function appears in the equation.

sin²θ + cos²θ = 1
Key: θ = any angle. The parent identity; both Pythagorean forms above come from it and every proof starts here.

Compound angles

sin(A ± B) = sin A cos B ± cos A sin B
Key: A, B = two angles. The signs match on both sides: a plus in the bracket gives a plus between the terms.

cos(A ± B) = cos A cos B ∓ sin A sin B
Key: A, B = two angles. The signs are opposite on the two sides — the one place the pattern breaks, and the reason cos(90° − θ) = sin θ rather than −sin θ.

tan(A ± B) = (tan A ± tan B)/(1 ∓ tan A tan B)
Key: A, B = two angles, with A + B ≠ 90° + 180°n. Derived from the sine and cosine forms by dividing through by cos A cos B.

Double angles and half angles

sin 2A = 2 sin A cos A
Key: A = the single angle; 2A = its double. Set B = A in the compound formula. It converts a product of sine and cosine into a single sine, which is what makes ∫sin A cos A dx tractable.

cos 2A = cos²A − sin²A = 2cos²A − 1 = 1 − 2sin²A
Key: A = the single angle. Three forms of one identity: the first from the compound formula, the other two by substituting sin²A = 1 − cos²A or cos²A = 1 − sin²A. Choose the form that leaves only the function already in the question.

tan 2A = 2 tan A/(1 − tan²A)
Key: A = the single angle, tan A ≠ ±1. The double-angle formula for tangent, undefined at the values that make the denominator zero.

sin²A = (1 − cos 2A)/2 and cos²A = (1 + cos 2A)/2
