Key: A = the single angle. The double-angle identity rearranged: the standard way to integrate an even power of sine or cosine, because it replaces the square with a cosine of the double angle.

Harmonic form and equations

a sin θ + b cos θ = R sin(θ + α), where R = √(a² + b²) and tan α = b/a
Key: a = coefficient of sin θ; b = coefficient of cos θ; R = the amplitude of the combined wave; α = the phase shift, chosen in the quadrant that matches the signs of a and b. Expand the right-hand side and compare coefficients to prove it: R cos α = a and R sin α = b.

−R ≤ a sin θ + b cos θ ≤ R, so the maximum is R and the minimum is −R
Key: R = √(a² + b²). A single sine wave cannot leave its amplitude, which is why "find the greatest value of 3 sin θ + 4 cos θ" is answered by 5 without differentiating anything.

sin θ = k ⇒ θ = (−1)ⁿ arcsin k + 180°n
Key: k = the given value, −1 ≤ k ≤ 1; n = any integer; arcsin = the principal value. The general solution, covering both the first-quadrant answer and its supplement. In radians replace 180°n with πn.

cos θ = k ⇒ θ = ±arccos k + 360°n; tan θ = k ⇒ θ = arctan k + 180°n
Key: k = the given value (|k| ≤ 1 for cosine, any real for tangent); n = any integer. Cosine repeats every 360° and is symmetric about 0°; tangent repeats every 180° with no symmetry, which is why its solution needs one line rather than two.

sin θ ≈ θ, tan θ ≈ θ, cos θ ≈ 1 − θ²/2 (θ in radians)
Key: θ = a small angle measured in radians. The small-angle approximations, valid because the curve and its tangent coincide near zero; the cosine form keeps the squared term because the linear term cancels, and that quadratic term is what a limits question needs.

title: IGCSE Biology: Plant Nutrition
content:
IGCSE Biology: Plant Nutrition

Every food chain on Earth begins with a plant capturing sunlight and turning it into sugar. This note covers photosynthesis from the raw materials to the limiting-factor graphs that decide crop yields, then works through the anatomy of a leaf with each structure tied to the job it performs, and finishes with the mineral requirements of plants and the deficiency symptoms that reveal what is missing. The word equations, the balanced symbol equation and the limiting-factor reasoning are all expanded step by step, because Paper 4 asks for all three almost every year.

The word and symbol equations for photosynthesis

Photosynthesis is the process by which plants make glucose from carbon dioxide and water using light energy trapped by chlorophyll. Word equation: carbon dioxide + water --(light energy, chlorophyll)-→ glucose + oxygen. Symbol equation: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O --(light)-→ C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂. Key: CO₂ = carbon dioxide; H₂O = water; C₆H₁₂O₆ = glucose; O₂ = oxygen; the coefficients give 6 C, 12 H and 18 O on each side, which is what balanced means. To balance it from scratch: count the carbons — 6 on the left means C₆ on the right; then the hydrogens — 12 on the left from 6H₂O means H₁₂ in glucose; then the oxygens — 12 on the left (6 × 2) plus 6 from water totals 18; the right side has 6 in glucose plus 6 × 2 = 12 in oxygen, giving 18. Carbon dioxide enters through stomata (pores in the leaf epidermis flanked by guard cells), water is drawn up through xylem in the veins, and the glucose produced is either used in respiration, converted to starch for storage, converted to sucrose for transport, used to make cellulose for cell walls, or used with nitrate ions to make amino acids and proteins.

Chloroplasts, chlorophyll and the role of each factor

Photosynthesis happens in chloroplasts, which are concentrated in the palisade mesophyll layer of the leaf. Chlorophyll is the green pigment that absorbs light energy (mainly in the red and blue wavelengths, reflecting green — which is why leaves look green). The energy is used to power the conversion of carbon dioxide and water into glucose; carbon dioxide is raw material, and water is the hydrogen donor (split in the light-dependent reactions). At IGCSE level, know the three requirements — light, chlorophyll, carbon dioxide — and where each comes from. A variegated leaf (with white non-chlorophyll patches) tested with iodine shows starch only in the green regions, proving chlorophyll is necessary; a destarched plant kept in the dark shows no starch, proving light is necessary.

Limiting factors

The rate of photosynthesis is limited by whichever factor is in shortest supply — the limiting factor. Three are examinable: light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and temperature. As light intensity rises, rate rises proportionally until another factor (usually carbon dioxide) becomes limiting and the graph plateaus. As carbon dioxide rises (from the 0.04 % of the atmosphere), rate rises until light or temperature limits it. Temperature follows the enzyme pattern: rising to an optimum (about 25–30 °C for tropical plants) then falling as enzymes denature. The logic of commercial greenhouses and polytunnels follows directly: add artificial light at night, enrich carbon dioxide to 0.1–0.2 %, and heat to the optimum — but each expense is only worthwhile while that factor is the one limiting. The standard graph questions give a rate-versus-one-factor curve with two or three lines at different levels of a second factor; explain each plateau by naming the new limiting factor.

Leaf structure: form fits function

A cross-section through a leaf reveals adaptations for photosynthesis and gas exchange: a broad flat shape gives maximum light absorption and surface area; a thin lamina keeps a short diffusion path; the upper epidermis is transparent and coated with cuticle (waxy, waterproof, reduces water loss); the palisade mesophyll is a column of tall cells packed with chloroplasts near the top where light is strongest; the spongy mesophyll has irregular cells with air spaces between them for gas circulation; veins contain xylem (water and minerals arriving) and phloem (sugars leaving); stomata on the lower epidermis let carbon dioxide in and oxygen out; guard cells open and close the stomata — opening in light (for photosynthesis) and closing in darkness or when the plant is short of water (to reduce transpiration). The structure-to-function questions reward this chain: feature, then effect on light, gas exchange or water loss.

Mineral requirements and deficiency symptoms

Plants need mineral ions absorbed from the soil solution by root hair cells (by diffusion and active transport). Nitrate ions: needed to make amino acids and therefore proteins and chlorophyll; deficiency causes stunted growth and yellow leaves (chlorosis). Magnesium ions: the central atom in every chlorophyll molecule; deficiency causes yellowing between the leaf veins. Phosphate ions: needed for DNA, RNA, ATP and cell membranes; deficiency causes poor root growth and purplish leaves. Potassium ions: needed for enzymes in respiration and for opening stomata; deficiency causes poor fruit and seed development. Plants grown in hydroponic culture (mineral solution without soil) show exactly these symptoms when one ion is omitted — a standard Paper 6 identification question.

Limiting factors in practice: crops and greenhouses

The same principles scale to agriculture. Growing crops densely shades lower leaves, so light becomes limiting and yields per plant fall even as yield per field rises. Glasshouses trap heat (raising temperature) and allow carbon dioxide enrichment; grow-lights extend the photoperiod. Water stress closes stomata, cutting carbon dioxide entry and thus photosynthesis — irrigation protects yield. But temperature above the optimum denatures the enzymes of the Calvin cycle, and excessive light can bleach chlorophyll (photoinhibition). The examiner's favourite commercial question: "a farmer adds carbon dioxide but yield does not rise — explain why" — the answer: another factor (light or temperature) is now limiting; identify which from the conditions given.

Mineral ions and deficiency at a glance

IonNeeded forDeficiency symptom
NitrateAmino acids, proteins, chlorophyllStunted growth, yellow leaves (chlorosis)
MagnesiumThe chlorophyll moleculeYellowing between the veins
PhosphateDNA, RNA, ATP, membranesPoor root growth, purplish leaves
PotassiumEnzymes of respiration, stomatal openingPoor fruit and seed development

Worked example: reading limiting-factor graphs

A graph shows the rate of photosynthesis versus light intensity at three carbon dioxide concentrations (0.05 %, 0.10 %, 0.20 %): all three lines rise together at low light, then the 0.05 % line plateaus first, followed by the 0.10 %, then the 0.20 %. Step 1: describe the trend in data terms: "rate increases with light intensity initially and then levels off". Step 2: explain the first region: light is limiting — more photons reach chlorophyll, so the light-dependent reactions supply energy faster. Step 3: explain each plateau: above the kink, carbon dioxide concentration is limiting because it is in shortest supply; the higher the carbon dioxide, the higher the plateau. Step 4: name the limiting factor for each line at maximum light: carbon dioxide concentration for all three. Step 5: apply to practice: at the plateau of the 0.05 % curve, adding more light changes nothing; enriching carbon dioxide raises the rate. A second calculation type: comparing rate as a percentage — if rate rises from 20 to 50 arbitrary units, the increase is (50 − 20) ÷ 20 × 100 = 150 %.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Writing the equation with oxygen on the left or forgetting to balance the hydrogens; check every atom before writing "done".
  • Saying plants photosynthesise "to make energy": plants make glucose (chemical energy store); the light energy is converted, not created.
  • Confusing the roles: carbon dioxide is the raw material, water supplies hydrogen, light is the energy source, chlorophyll is the trap.
  • Explaining a plateau without naming the new limiting factor — the word "limiting factor" itself is worth a mark.
  • Describing guard cells as "letting light in": stomata control gas exchange and water loss, not light.
  • Forgetting the cuticle when asked about water loss adaptations.
  • Writing deficiency symptoms without linking the ion to its molecule: magnesium → chlorophyll → yellow leaves; nitrate → protein → stunting.
  • Interpreting a rate graph against temperature without mentioning enzyme denaturation at the peak.

Exam-style questions and answers

Q1. Write the balanced symbol equation for photosynthesis. (2 marks) Answer: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ — one mark for reactants and products, one for correct balancing with light/chlorophyll over the arrow.

Q2. Explain why the rate of photosynthesis levels off as light intensity continues to increase. (2 marks) Answer: another factor becomes limiting (1) — carbon dioxide concentration or temperature in shortest supply (1).

Q3. Describe two ways in which a leaf is adapted for photosynthesis. (4 marks) Answer: broad flat shape for maximum light absorption (1); palisade mesophyll packed with chloroplasts near the upper surface (1); thin lamina for short diffusion path (1); veins bring water by xylem and carry sugars away by phloem (1).

Q4. A plant has yellow leaves with green veins. Identify the missing mineral ion and explain your answer. (2 marks) Answer: magnesium (1) because it is needed to make chlorophyll and its absence causes chlorosis (1).

Q5. Explain how a farmer could increase the rate of photosynthesis in a greenhouse in winter. (3 marks) Answer: add artificial light to raise light intensity (1); heat the greenhouse to the optimum temperature for the enzymes (1); enrich carbon dioxide concentration so it is no longer limiting (1).

title: Abstract Data Types — Study Notes
content:
Abstract Data Types

What is an ADT?

An abstract data type is a logical description of a collection of data plus the operations on it, independent of implementation. Stacks, queues, linked lists, binary trees and hash tables are all ADTs; in A Level you must show how they are built from arrays or records with pointers.

Linked Lists

Each node holds a value and a pointer to the next node; a start pointer marks the head and a null marks the end. Insertion rewires two pointers — no shifting — giving O(1) insertion at a known position, but access requires walking the list, O(n).

Stacks and Queues

A stack is LIFO (push and pop at the top); a queue is FIFO (enqueue at the rear, dequeue from the front). Both can be arrays with index pointers or linked lists. Stack uses include call stacks and expression evaluation; queue uses include print buffers and breadth-first search.

Binary Search Trees

Each node has up to two children; left subtree keys are smaller, right subtree keys larger. Search, insert and (average-case) delete are O(log n). An in-order traversal outputs keys in ascending order. A degenerate (linear) tree from sorted input degrades to O(n).

Hash Tables

Covered in file organisation, but as an ADT a hash table pairs a hash function with bucket storage for O(1) average access.

Exam tips: be able to draw a tree after a sequence of insertions and write its three traversals; state the pointer changes for a linked-list insertion; compare ADT operations with Big-O.

Abstract data types in practice

An abstract data type is defined by the operations it supports and their behaviour, not by how it is stored. A stack is defined by push, pop and isEmpty; the programmer using it does not need to know whether it is built from an array or a linked list.

Separating the interface from the implementation lets the implementation change without breaking the code that uses it, and makes each part easier to test.

Exam tip: when asked to define an ADT, name the operations and say what each does, not how it is stored.

Worked example: building a binary search tree

Insert 8, 3, 10, 1 and 6 in that order. The first value, 8, becomes the root. Since 3 is less than 8, it goes to the left; 10 goes to the right. The value 1 is less than 8 and less than 3, so it sits to the left of 3. The value 6 is less than 8 and greater than 3, so it sits to the right of 3. An in-order traversal (left, node, right) then lists the values in sorted order: 1, 3, 6, 8, 10.

Complexity of the main operations

  • Search, insert and delete in a balanced tree take O(log n) time, because each comparison discards about half the remaining nodes.
  • If the values are inserted in sorted order, the tree becomes a chain and the same operations degrade to O(n).
  • Hash table lookup takes O(1) on average but gives no ordering, so a hash table cannot list the data in sorted order.

Choosing between the structures

A stack, a queue and a linked list each store a collection, but they differ in how items are added and removed. A stack is last in, first out. A queue is first in, first out. A linked list allows insertion and deletion at a known position without shifting other items. The exam question usually asks you to justify the choice, so state the access pattern the data needs.

Exam method: tracing a stack and a queue

Write the contents after every operation. Start with an empty stack. Push 5, push 9, pop, then push 2. After the pop the stack holds 5 only, so the final push leaves 5 at the bottom and 2 at the top. The value returned by the pop is 9, because a stack returns the most recently added item.

A queue works in the opposite order. Enqueue 5, enqueue 9, then dequeue. The dequeue returns 5, the item that entered first, and 9 remains at the front. Marks are given for the returned value and for the final state, so show both.

Common errors

  • Describing a stack as first in, first out. That describes a queue; a stack is last in, first out.
  • Forgetting to check for an empty structure before a pop or dequeue. Good answers say what the program should do when the structure is empty.
  • Saying an array-based queue never needs wrapping. A fixed-size array queue can waste space at the front unless its pointers wrap round to the start.

title: Communication and Networking — Study Notes
content:
`# Communication and Networking

Cambridge International AS & A Level Computer Science 9618: section 2 (Communication), examined in AS Paper 1.

Transmission

  • Serial: one bit at a time — cheaper, reliable over distance
  • Parallel: multiple bits simultaneously — fast but suffers skew and crosstalk over long runs
  • Direction: simplex (one way), half-duplex (alternating), full-duplex (both ways)

Packets and Protocols

Data splits into packets with header (addresses, sequence) and trailer (checksum). A protocol is an agreed rule set — without one, devices cannot interpret signals.

  • TCP/IP stack: application → transport → network → link
  • HTTP/HTTPS: web transfer; HTTPS encrypts with TLS
  • FTP: file transfer; SMTP/POP3/IMAP: email

Network Types

  • LAN: small site, privately owned; WAN: large geographic scale (the internet)
  • Topologies: bus, star, mesh (star is most common — central switch)

Hardware

Routers join networks by IP; switches forward frames by MAC within a LAN; gateways translate protocols.

Client-Server vs Peer-to-Peer

Client-server: central services, easy administration, single point of failure. P2P: every node shares files directly — cheap, hard to manage (torrents, blockchain).

Exam tips: explain packet switching with header/trailer details; justify protocol choice per application (email vs streaming).

Network topologies and hardware

In a star topology every device connects to a central switch. If one cable or device fails, the others keep working, but if the central switch fails the whole network stops. In a bus topology all devices share one cable, which is cheap but means a break in the cable disables the network.

A switch connects devices within a local area network (LAN) and sends each frame only to the device it is addressed to, using MAC addresses. A router connects separate networks together and forwards packets using IP addresses. A wireless access point lets wireless devices join a wired LAN.

Exam tip: when comparing topologies, state what happens when one device fails and when the central device fails. Those two cases are the usual differentiators.

Worked example: transfer time and latency

A 2 Mbit file sent over a link of 1 Mbit per second takes 2 seconds to transfer, ignoring overheads. Latency is the delay before the first bit arrives, and it adds to the total time. If the latency is 0.2 seconds, the complete delivery takes about 2.2 seconds. Stating which quantity you are calculating, and the units, earns method marks even when the final figure is slightly off.

Bandwidth and the shared medium

  • Bandwidth is the maximum data rate of a link. Actual throughput is lower when many devices share the medium, because they take turns or collide.
  • Wired connections such as Ethernet usually give more stable speeds than wireless, which is affected by distance, walls and interference.

title: AS Level Mathematics: Exponentials and Logarithms
content:
AS Level Mathematics: Exponentials and Logarithms

Exponentials describe growth and decay — populations, investments, radioactive isotopes, cooling cups of tea — where the change is proportional to the amount present. Logarithms are their inverses: they turn multiplication into addition and, crucially, let you solve equations where the unknown sits in the exponent. This note builds the topic from zero: the meaning of a logarithm, the three laws with derivations, solving exponential and logarithmic equations including quadratics in disguise, the graph properties and transformations, and the applied growth/decay models.

What a logarithm is

log_a(x) = n  means  a^n = x

common log: log x = log_10 x
natural log: ln x = log_e x,  e = 2.71828...

The logarithm answers "to what power must I raise the base to get this number?" So log₂8 = 3 because 2³ = 8, and log₅(1/25) = −2 because 5⁻² = 1/25. Two identities follow immediately and are always true:

log_a(a) = 1
log_a(1) = 0
a^(log_a x) = x   and   log_a(a^x) = x

Worked example. Evaluate log₃81, log₂(1/8) and ln 1.

3⁴ = 81  →  log_3 81 = 4
2⁻³ = 1/8  →  log_2(1/8) = -3
anything to the power 0 is 1  →  ln 1 = 0

The three laws of logarithms

product:   log(xy) = log x + log y
quotient:  log(x/y) = log x - log y
power:     log(x^n) = n log x

consequences: log(1/x) = -log x;  log(sqrt x) = (1/2)log x

Why they work. Write x = a^m and y = a^n, so log x = m and log y = n. Then xy = a^(m+n), so log(xy) = m + n = log x + log y. The quotient law follows from a^(m−n) and the power law from (a^m)^n = a^(mn). Each law is a restatement of an index law, which is why logarithms convert products into sums.

Worked example 1 (combine). Write 2 log 3 + log 4 − log 6 as a single logarithm.

2 log 3 = log 9
log 9 + log 4 = log 36
log 36 - log 6 = log 6

Worked example 2 (split). Express log(x³y/√z) in terms of log x, log y and log z.

= 3 log x + log y - (1/2) log z

Worked example 3 (solve). Solve log₂x + log₂(x − 2) = 3.

combine: log_2[x(x - 2)] = 3
x(x - 2) = 2³ = 8
x² - 2x - 8 = 0  →  (x - 4)(x + 2) = 0
x = 4 or x = -2;  reject x = -2 because log of a negative is undefined
x = 4

Rejecting invalid roots is compulsory: a logarithm only accepts a positive argument, so always check each answer against the original equation.

Solving exponential equations

When the unknown is in the exponent, take logs of both sides and use the power law to bring it down.

Worked example 1. Solve 3^x = 20.

take logs: x log 3 = log 20
x = log 20 / log 3 = 1.301/0.4771 = 2.73

Worked example 2 (different bases). Solve 5^(2x−1) = 7^(x+1).

(2x - 1) log 5 = (x + 1) log 7
2x log 5 - log 5 = x log 7 + log 7
x(2 log 5 - log 7) = log 7 + log 5
x = (log 7 + log 5)/(2 log 5 - log 7)
  = (0.845 + 0.699)/(1.398 - 0.845) = 1.544/0.553 = 2.79

Worked example 3 (quadratic in disguise). Solve 2^(2x) − 5(2^x) + 4 = 0.

let y = 2^x:  y² - 5y + 4 = 0  →  (y - 1)(y - 4) = 0
y = 1  →  2^x = 1  →  x = 0
y = 4  →  2^x = 4  →  x = 2

The substitution trick is the standard route for any equation where one power is double another: put y = a^x and solve the quadratic, then convert back.

Graphs of exponential and logarithmic functions

FunctionDomainRangeKey points
y = e^xall real xy > 0(0, 1); always increasing; asymptote y = 0
y = e^(−x)all real xy > 0(0, 1); always decreasing; decay
y = ln xx > 0all real y(1, 0); increasing; asymptote x = 0

y = ln x is the reflection of y = e^x in the line y = x, because they are inverse functions. That reflection explains the domain and range swap and the asymptote turning from horizontal to vertical.

Worked example. Sketch y = e^(x−2) + 1, stating the asymptote and intercepts.

translation 2 right, 1 up
asymptote y = 1 (was y = 0)
y-intercept: e⁻² + 1 = 0.135 + 1 = 1.135
no x-intercept (the curve stays above y = 1)

Growth and decay models

exponential model: N = N_0 e^(kt)
  k > 0 growth;  k < 0 decay
half-life: time for N to halve = ln 2 / |k| (decay)
doubling time = ln 2 / k (growth)

Worked example (decay). A radioactive sample decays as N = 500e^(−0.02t) with t in years. Find the initial amount, the amount after 50 years, and the half-life.

t = 0: N = 500
at t = 50: 500e⁻¹ = 500 × 0.3679 = 184
half-life: 500e^(-0.02t) = 250  →  e^(-0.02t) = 0.5
-0.02t = ln 0.5 = -0.693  →  t = 34.7 years

Worked example 2 (growth). Bacteria grow as N = 200e^(0.15t), t in hours. When does the population reach 1000?

200e^(0.15t) = 1000  →  e^(0.15t) = 5
0.15t = ln 5 = 1.609  →  t = 10.7 hours

Logarithmic scales in context

Some quantities span so many orders of magnitude that a logarithmic scale is used: pH for acidity, the Richter scale for earthquakes, decibels for sound. A change of 1 on the Richter scale means 10 times the amplitude, so an increase of 3 means 10³ = 1000 times.

Worked example. Two earthquakes differ by 2.4 on the Richter scale. How many times larger is the amplitude of the stronger?

difference 2.4 in log_10  →  10^2.4 = 251 times

Change of base and log-linearisation

Calculators offer base 10 and base e only, so any other base is converted with the change-of-base formula. The same formula turns a power law into a straight line, which is how experimental data is tested for exponential behaviour.

change of base: log_a(x) = log_b(x)/log_b(a)
so log_2(7) = ln 7 / ln 2 = log 7 / log 2 = 2.807

if y = a x^n then log y = log a + n log x  (straight line in log-log)
if y = a b^x then log y = log a + x log b  (straight line in log-x)

Worked example 1. Evaluate log_5(30).

log 30 / log 5 = 1.477/0.699 = 2.113

Worked example 2 (log-linearisation). Data gives a straight line when log y is plotted against x, with gradient 0.3 and intercept 1.4. Find the model connecting y and x.

log y = 1.4 + 0.3x
so y = 10^1.4 × 10^(0.3x) = 25.1 × 2.00^x
an exponential growth model with a = 25.1 and b = 2.0

Worked example 3 (inequality). Solve 2^x < 100.

take logs (base 2 is increasing, so the inequality is preserved)
x < log_2 100 = log 100/log 2 = 6.64

Taking logs of both sides is safe for any base greater than 1 because the log function is increasing; a base between 0 and 1 would reverse the inequality, which never arises in these models.

Rewriting any exponential in base e

Any exponential a^x can be written as e^(kx), because a = e^(ln a). This is why every growth model in the syllabus uses e: the base is absorbed into the constant.

a^x = e^(x ln a)
so 2^x = e^(0.693x);  5^x = e^(1.609x);  0.8^x = e^(-0.223x)

Worked example. Express y = 300(1.04)^t in the form y = 300e^(kt), and state the annual percentage rate it represents.

1.04 = e^k  →  k = ln 1.04 = 0.0392
y = 300e^(0.0392t)
the rate is 3.92 per year in continuous-compounding form, while the
annual multiplier is still 1.04 (4 per cent per year)

Worked example 2. A model is N = 80e^(0.25t). Rewrite it as N = 80b^t and find the percentage growth per unit time.

b = e^0.25 = 1.284
N = 80(1.284)^t, so growth is 28.4 per cent per unit time

The two forms describe the same curve; the e-form is convenient for calculus, the b-form for reading off a percentage rate. Converting between them is a standard exam demand.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Evaluate) Find log₄64. Answer: 3, since 4³ = 64.
  2. (Laws) Simplify log 8 + log 5 − log 2. Answer: log(40/2) = log 20.
  3. (Solve log) Solve log₃x = 2. Answer: x = 3² = 9.
  4. (Solve exponential) Solve 2^x = 50. Answer: x = log 50/log 2 = 1.699/0.301 = 5.64.
  5. (Quadratic) Solve e^(2x) − 3e^x + 2 = 0. Answer: y = e^x → y² − 3y + 2 = 0 → y = 1 or 2 → x = 0 or ln 2 = 0.693.
  6. (Combine) Write 3 ln 2 − ln 4 as a single logarithm. Answer: ln 8 − ln 4 = ln 2.
  7. (Inverse) Find the inverse of f(x) = e^(3x). Answer: y = e^(3x) → ln y = 3x → f⁻¹(x) = (ln x)/3.
  8. (Model) A car's value is V = 15000e^(−0.2t). Find its value after 4 years. Answer: 15000e^(−0.8) = 15000 × 0.4493 = 6740 pounds.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • log(x + y) is not log x + log y: the product law applies to products only; there is no law for the log of a sum.
  • Forgetting the domain: logs need a positive argument. Roots that make an argument negative or zero are rejected, explicitly.
  • Dividing by log: log 20/log 3 is not log(20/3); the quotient law is for two logs, not a quotient of logs.
  • Base consistency: mixing log₁₀ and ln inside one equation is an error; convert first (ln x = log x / log e).
  • Power law misuse: (log x)² is not 2 log x. Only log(x²) = 2 log x.
  • Quadratic substitution: after solving for y, the answer is x — convert back and solve the exponential equation.
  • Half-life sign: with a decay model k is negative, so half-life = ln 2/|k|; dropping the modulus gives a negative time.
  • Sketch asymptotes: state the asymptote after transformations; e^x + c has asymptote y = c, not y = 0.

title: Bonding and Structure — Study Notes
content:
Bonding and Structure

Edexcel IAL Chemistry 9CH0 AS, topic 3. Every statement 3.1 to 3.22 is covered below, with its code in the heading so you can check your own gaps against the specification. The big idea: the type of bonding and the shape of a molecule explain almost every physical property a question can ask about, including melting point, conductivity, solubility and polarity.

3.1 to 3.2: Evidence for ions, and how they form

  • Evidence for ions: ionic compounds conduct electricity only when molten or dissolved, because the ions are then free to move. In electrolysis, a coloured ion such as manganate(VII), MnO₄⁻, migrates to the positive electrode (the anode), which is direct evidence that it carries a negative charge.
  • Electron density maps for ionic compounds show near-spherical regions of electron density around each ion, with a clear drop in density between them.
  • Formation by loss or gain of electrons: sodium loses one electron to form Na⁺ (2,8,1 becomes 2,8), while chlorine gains one to form Cl⁻ (2,8,7 becomes 2,8,8). A metal loses electrons to form a positive ion; a non-metal gains electrons to form a negative ion.

3.3: Dot-and-cross diagrams for ions

  • Show the outer electrons of each atom as dots or crosses. For a cation such as Mg²⁺, the outer shell is empty, so the symbol is written with square brackets and the charge: [Mg]²⁺.
  • For an anion such as O²⁻, the transferred electrons are added to the outer shell, which then holds eight electrons: [O]²⁻ with eight dots and crosses inside the brackets.
  • Always put the charge outside the brackets, and check that the total number of electrons transferred matches the charges.

3.4 to 3.5: Giant ionic lattices and the ionic bond

  • An ionic crystal is a giant lattice of alternating positive and negative ions, repeating in three dimensions. There are no discrete molecules, so the formula, such as NaCl, is only the simplest ratio of ions. In sodium chloride each Na⁺ is surrounded by six Cl⁻ ions and each Cl⁻ by six Na⁺ ions (6:6 coordination).
  • An ionic bond is the strong net electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions. "Net" matters: the attraction between a cation and an anion is partly cancelled by repulsion between like ions, but the attraction wins at the equilibrium distance.

3.6: Effect of ionic radius and ionic charge on bond strength

  • The electrostatic attraction grows with the charge on the ions and falls as the ions get larger, because the centres of charge are further apart.
  • Compare MgO (melting point about 2850 °C) with NaCl (about 800 °C). Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ carry double charges and are small, so their attraction is much stronger than that between the singly charged, larger Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions.

3.7: Trends in ionic radius

  • Down a group, ionic radius increases, because each ion has an additional electron shell. Li⁺ is smaller than Na⁺, which is smaller than K⁺.
  • Across a set of isoelectronic ions, all the species have the same number of electrons (ten, in the series N³⁻, O²⁻, F⁻, Na⁺, Mg²⁺, Al³⁺). The nuclear charge rises from 7 to 13 across the series, so the outer electrons are pulled in more strongly and the radius falls. N³⁻ is the largest and Al³⁺ the smallest.

3.8 to 3.9: Polarisation of ions

  • Polarisation is the distortion of the electron cloud of an anion by a nearby cation. The cation pulls the anion's electron density towards itself, so the bonding stops being purely ionic and gains covalent character.
  • The polarising power of a cation is greatest when it is small and highly charged. Al³⁺ > Mg²⁺ > Na⁺.
  • The polarisability of an anion is greatest when it is large and highly charged, because its outer electrons are held loosely. I⁻ is more polarisable than Br⁻, which is more polarisable than Cl⁻, which is more polarisable than F⁻.
  • Example: aluminium chloride has a low melting point and sublimes, far below what a purely ionic lattice would need. The small, highly charged Al³⁺ polarises the chloride ions strongly, so the bonding is largely covalent.

3.10: Covalent bonding and the evidence for it

  • A covalent bond is the strong electrostatic attraction between two nuclei (both positive) and the shared pair of electrons between them.
  • Evidence: giant atomic structures such as diamond and silicon(IV) oxide have very high melting points, which only strong covalent bonds can explain. Electron density maps for simple molecules such as hydrogen show a build-up of electron density between the two nuclei.

3.11: Dot-and-cross diagrams for covalent substances

  • Multiple bonds: in carbon dioxide, O=C=O, each double bond is two shared pairs. In nitrogen, N≡N, there are three shared pairs.
  • Dative (coordinate) bonds: both electrons in the shared pair come from one atom, the donor, which has a lone pair. The arrow points from donor to acceptor. In the ammonium ion, NH₄⁺, the nitrogen in NH₃ donates its lone pair to H⁺.
  • Aluminium chloride dimer, Al₂Cl₆: each aluminium has four chlorines. Two of the chlorines bridge the two aluminium atoms, and each bridging chlorine forms a dative bond from a chlorine lone pair into the empty orbital of the other aluminium.

3.12: Giant carbon structures: diamond, graphite and graphene

  • Diamond: each carbon forms four single covalent bonds in a tetrahedral giant lattice. It is very hard, has a very high melting point and does not conduct, because there are no free electrons. It is used in cutting and drilling tools.
  • Graphite: each carbon forms three bonds in flat hexagonal sheets. The fourth outer electron on each carbon is delocalised, so graphite conducts along the sheets. The sheets are held by weak forces and slide over each other, so graphite is soft and is used as a lubricant and as electrodes.
  • Graphene: a single sheet of graphite, one atom thick. It is very strong, conducts well and is light and flexible. Applications include electronics, sensors and composite materials.

3.13 to 3.14: Electronegativity and the bonding continuum

  • Electronegativity is the power of an atom to attract the bonding pair of electrons in a covalent bond. Fluorine is the most electronegative element (4.0 on the Pauling scale).
  • The bonding continuum: the bigger the electronegativity difference between two atoms, the more polar the bond. A very small difference gives a non-polar covalent bond, a moderate difference gives a polar covalent bond (as in HCl), and a very large difference gives essentially ionic bonding (as in NaCl). Ionic and covalent bonding are the two ends of this continuum, not separate categories.

3.15: Polar bonds and polar molecules

  • A polar bond has a permanent dipole. A molecule is polar only if its bond dipoles do not cancel, so polar bonds do not automatically make a polar molecule.
  • Carbon tetrachloride, CCl₄: the C–Cl bonds are polar, but the tetrahedral arrangement cancels them, so the molecule is non-polar.
  • Water, H₂O, is bent, so its dipoles add up and the molecule is polar. Carbon dioxide is linear, so its two C=O dipoles cancel and it is non-polar.

3.16 to 3.19: Electron-pair repulsion and molecular shapes

  • Electron-pair repulsion theory: bonding pairs and lone pairs around a central atom repel each other and arrange themselves to be as far apart as possible.
  • Lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs, so lone pairs compress bond angles. The order of repulsion is lone pair to lone pair, then lone pair to bonding pair, then bonding pair to bonding pair.
  • 3.17, bond length and bond angle: bond length is the distance between the nuclei of two bonded atoms. Bond angle is the angle between two bonds at the central atom. Triple bonds are shorter than double bonds, which are shorter than single bonds (C≡C shorter than C=C shorter than C–C).

3.18, the shapes and bond angles of the named species:

SpeciesElectron pairs on central atomShapeBond angle
BeCl₂2 bondingLinear180°
BCl₃3 bondingTrigonal planar120°
CH₄4 bondingTetrahedral109.5°
NH₃3 bonding, 1 loneTrigonal pyramidalabout 107°
NH₄⁺4 bondingTetrahedral109.5°
H₂O2 bonding, 2 loneBentabout 104.5°
CO₂2 bonding (double bonds)Linear180°
PCl₅ (gas)5 bondingTrigonal bipyramidal90° and 120°
SF₆6 bondingOctahedral90°
C₂H₄3 regions around each carbonPlanar around each carbonabout 120°

Applying the same rules to analogous species (3.19): SiH₄ is tetrahedral (109.5°), BF₃ is trigonal planar (120°), PH₃ is pyramidal (about 93°), H₂S is bent (about 92°), XeF₄ is square planar (90°, with two lone pairs), and ClF₃ is T-shaped. Count the electron pairs first, then decide how many are lone pairs.

3.20 to 3.22: Metallic bonding and the properties of metals

  • A metal is a giant lattice of positive metal ions in a sea of delocalised electrons, the outer electrons that are free to move through the whole structure.
  • 3.21, metallic bonding is the strong electrostatic attraction between the metal cations and the delocalised electrons. It is not a bond between two particular atoms.
  • Electrical conduction: the delocalised electrons carry charge through the metal when a voltage is applied.
  • High melting temperature: the attraction is strong and is non-directional, so a lot of energy is needed to overcome it. Magnesium melts at about 650 °C, far above sodium at about 98 °C, because Mg²⁺ carries a double charge and provides two delocalised electrons per atom.
  • Malleability: the layers of ions can slide over each other, and the delocalised electrons keep the ions attracted to each other as they move, so the metal does not shatter.

Common errors that lose marks

  • Saying covalent or metallic bonds are "between molecules" (they are within the structure; the forces between molecules are intermolecular forces).
  • Calling a polar bond a polar molecule. Always check the shape before you decide the molecule's polarity.
  • Saying ions "move" in solid ionic compounds. They vibrate in place; only molten or dissolved compounds conduct through ion movement.

title: Edexcel IAL Computer Science: Networks Including the Internet
content:
Edexcel IAL Computer Science: Networks Including the Internet

Pearson Edexcel International Advanced Level in Computer Science, Unit 1 Principles of Computer Science: networks including the internet. This note covers networking from the physical layer up — why networks exist, how bits travel over media and through hardware, how protocols layer to make communication reliable, and how the internet's addressing and routing deliver a packet across the world. Every packet flow is traced hop by hop, because the exam rewards answers that follow data's actual path rather than naming components.

Why build networks

Networking exists to share: files and data, peripherals such as printers and scanners, internet connections, and services such as email and cloud storage. Beyond sharing, networks enable communication and collaboration, centralised administration (accounts, security policies, backups) and remote working. The trade-offs are administration overhead, the security exposure of every connected machine, and dependence on connectivity.

Network classifications by scale: a LAN covers one site over privately owned cabling; a WLAN is a LAN using radio links; a WAN spans sites over leased or public infrastructure (the internet is the largest WAN). Architectures: client–server (dedicated servers manage accounts, files and security; centralised control and backup, but costly and a single point of failure) versus peer-to-peer (equal machines sharing resources; cheap and simple, but no central control or easy backup). Cloud computing extends client–server to on-demand rented infrastructure, trading capital cost and elasticity against data-privacy and connectivity dependence.

Transmission: modes and media

MediumCarriesBest pointsWeaknesses
Twisted pair (Cat5e/6)Electrical pulsesCheap, easy to install; up to ~100 m per runInterference, distance limited
CoaxialElectrical pulses, shieldedBetter shielding; TV/cable broadbandBulkier, lower bandwidth than fibre
Fibre opticLight pulsesEnormous bandwidth, very long runs, immune to electromagnetic interference, hard to tapExpensive; specialist installation
Wireless (Wi-Fi, microwave, satellite)Radio wavesMobility; no cablingInterference, obstacles, security risk, shared medium

Serial transmission (bits one after another down one channel) dominates long-distance and modern links — cheap cabling, no skew; parallel (bits simultaneously down several channels) is confined to short internal buses where skew and crosstalk are manageable. Direction modes: simplex (one way — broadcast), half-duplex (both ways, one at a time — walkie-talkie), full-duplex (both ways at once — switched Ethernet, phone). Synchronous transmission sends a clock-synchronised stream; asynchronous wraps each character in start/stop bits.

Performance vocabulary: bandwidth is the maximum data rate (bps); latency is delay. Transfer time ≈ file size in bits ÷ bandwidth — and converting bytes to bits (×8) is the classic slip.

Network hardware and addressing

  • NIC — the interface giving a device a connection and its hardware MAC address.
  • Switch — forwards frames within a LAN, learning which MAC address sits on which port; reduces collisions versus a hub (which broadcasts blindly).
  • Router — joins networks and forwards packets between them using IP addresses and a routing table; the boundary between LAN and internet.
  • Access point — bridges wireless clients to the wired LAN.
  • Modem / ONT — converts signals for transmission over the line (fibre, cable, phone) to the ISP.
  • Firewall — filters traffic by rules; often built into routers or hosts.

Addresses at different layers: MAC addresses identify the NIC within the local network (flat, hardware-assigned); IP addresses identify a device on internetworks (hierarchical, assigned by the network, enabling routing). IPv4's 32-bit addresses (dotted decimal, e.g. 192.168.1.10) are exhausted; IPv6's 128-bit addresses restore abundance and add built-in security and auto-configuration. A subnet mask separates the network portion of an address from the host portion.

Protocols and layering

A protocol is an agreed set of rules — message format, order, error handling — so any vendor's devices interoperate. Layering splits the job: the TCP/IP model has application (HTTP, SMTP, FTP), transport (TCP or UDP), internet (IP) and network-access (Ethernet, Wi-Fi) layers. TCP is connection-oriented and reliable: it numbers segments, acknowledges receipt, retransmits losses and reassembles in order. UDP is connectionless and fast, tolerating loss (streaming, gaming, DNS). IP handles addressing and routing. Encapsulation wraps each layer's data with that layer's header as the message descends the stack.

ProtocolLayer role
HTTP / HTTPSWeb page request and delivery (HTTPS adds TLS encryption)
FTP / SFTPFile transfer
SMTP, POP3, IMAPSend email / collect email (POP3 downloads-and-deletes; IMAP synchronises)
DNSResolves domain names to IP addresses
DHCPAssigns IP configuration to devices automatically
TCP / UDP / IPTransport and internetwork delivery

Worked example: the internet, end to end

Trace: a browser requests https://example.com/page.html from a home network.

1. The browser checks its cache and the OS DNS cache; not found, so a DNS
   query is needed.
2. DHCP gave this machine its IP, gateway and DNS server at boot; the DNS
   query goes to that server (possibly through several resolvers) and returns
   the IP address of example.com.
3. A TCP connection opens to the server's IP on port 443 (three-way SYN,
   SYN-ACK, ACK). For HTTPS, a TLS handshake follows: the server presents a
   certificate, the client verifies it with a trusted CA and derives a
   symmetric session key.
4. The client sends GET /page.html (over the encrypted channel).
5. The request is encapsulated: TCP segment → IP packet (source and
   destination addresses) → Ethernet frames on the LAN.
6. The home router performs NAT (its public IP stands in for private
   addresses) and routes the packet toward the server - possibly a dozen hops,
   each router reading the IP header and forwarding on its routing table.
   Packets of one message may take different routes.
7. The server responds 200 OK with the HTML; the client reassembles segments
   in order (TCP sequence numbers), decrypts (TLS), parses the HTML and
   requests its images and CSS the same way.
8. If any segment is corrupted (checksum) or lost, TCP retransmits; the
   browser renders progressively.

Public versus private addressing: private ranges (10.x, 192.168.x) are not routable on the internet and are mapped through NAT; firewalls and network security appliances guard the boundary; proxy servers cache content to save bandwidth.

Network performance and reliability

Explanations of slow networks combine the vocabulary: contention on shared media, insufficient bandwidth for the load, high latency on long or satellite links, and collision domains (shrunk by switches). Redundancy — extra links, multiple servers — improves availability; the cost is complexity. Fault tolerance and load balancing are the reliability side of the same story.

Worked: a 250 MB database backup goes over a 50 Mbps link.

  250 MB = 250 × 8 = 2000 megabits
  2000 / 50 = 40 seconds (ideal; protocol overheads add a little)

Same file over an 11 Mbps Wi-Fi link at 60% of rated throughput:
  effective rate = 6.6 Mbps → 2000 / 6.6 = 303 seconds = about 5 minutes.
Bandwidth of the weakest segment and contention from other users dominate
real transfer times.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Calling the switch a router: switches forward within a LAN by MAC address; routers forward between networks by IP address.
  • Saying DNS "converts IPs into names"; it resolves names to IP addresses (the reverse lookup is a special case).
  • Forgetting NAT when explaining how many private-addressed devices share one public IP.
  • Describing TCP as fast and UDP as reliable — it is the other way round: TCP reliable/connection-oriented, UDP fast/connectionless.
  • Ignoring the ×8 byte-to-bit conversion in transfer-time calculations.
  • Claiming packets always take the same route or arrive in order; TCP's sequence numbers exist precisely because they may not.
  • Listing cable types without their trade-off pairs (bandwidth/distance/cost/interference) — the comparison is the mark.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Unit 1, 4 marks). Describe the function of a router and a switch in a school network.

Answer: A switch connects devices within the LAN and forwards each frame only to the port where the destination MAC address was learned, keeping local traffic contained and reducing collisions. A router connects the school LAN to the internet and other networks, reading each packet's IP address and consulting its routing table to forward packets between networks, performing NAT for the school's private addresses.

Question 2 (Unit 1, 4 marks). Explain the purpose of TCP and IP in downloading a file.

Answer: IP addresses and routes packets: it stamps source and destination IP addresses on each packet and forwards them hop by hop between networks. TCP guarantees delivery: it splits the file into segments, numbers them, reassembles them in order at the destination, acknowledges receipt, retransmits lost or corrupt segments, and controls flow so the receiver is not overwhelmed.

Question 3 (Unit 1, 4 marks). Compare fibre optic and twisted-pair cabling for a campus backbone.

Answer: Fibre carries light, giving far higher bandwidth over much longer distances and immunity to electromagnetic interference and eavesdropping — ideal for a backbone linking buildings. Twisted pair is much cheaper and easier to install but limited to roughly 100 m per run and lower speeds, suiting horizontal runs to desks. A backbone carrying traffic for many buildings needs fibre's bandwidth and distance; twisted pair serves the final connection.

Question 4 (Unit 1, 5 marks). Describe what happens when a user types a URL into a browser.

Answer: The domain name is resolved to an IP address via DNS. A TCP connection opens to the web server at that address (port 80 or 443). For HTTPS, a TLS handshake authenticates the server with its certificate and negotiates a session key. The browser sends an HTTP GET request for the page; the server replies with the HTML and status code; the browser parses the HTML, fetches linked resources, and renders the page.

Question 5 (Unit 1, 3 marks). Explain two advantages of using DHCP.

Answer: Devices receive IP addresses, subnet mask, gateway and DNS automatically — so configuration is error-free and fast for every new device, addresses are reused when devices leave rather than wasted, and a change of network settings is made centrally rather than on every machine.

Question 6 (Unit 1, 3 marks). Explain why UDP might be chosen for video conferencing.

Answer: Real-time conversation prioritises low delay over perfect reliability: a lost packet is skipped rather than retransmitted, because a retransmitted late frame is worse than a missing one. UDP's minimal overhead and absence of acknowledgement round-trips keep latency low and support smooth playback.

Networks carry data between machines; the next note covers the software layer that manages each machine and protects that data.

title: Reproduction
content:
Reproduction

Cambridge IGCSE Biology 0610, Extended route, topic 16 (statements 16.1–16.6). Asexual and sexual reproduction, plant reproduction from flower to seed, human reproduction, sex hormones and sexually transmitted infections.

16.1 to 16.2 Asexual and sexual reproduction

  • Asexual reproduction involves one parent and mitosis, producing genetically identical offspring — binary fission in bacteria, budding in yeast, plant propagation by runners or cuttings. There is no variation.
  • Sexual reproduction involves two parents and the fusion of gametes, producing genetically varied offspring, which gives an advantage in changing environments.

16.3 Plant reproduction

  • Flower structure: anthers produce pollen, ovaries contain ovules. Pollination is the transfer of pollen from anther to stigma — self-pollination or cross-pollination (by insects or wind). Fertilisation is the fusion of male and female nuclei; the ovule develops into the seed and the ovary wall into the fruit.
  • Seed germination needs water, oxygen and a suitable temperature; the seed coat breaks, the radicle emerges first, and the seedling first uses stored food until it can photosynthesise.

16.4 to 16.6 Human reproduction

  • Testes produce sperm and testosterone; ovaries produce eggs and oestrogen and progesterone. Fertilisation occurs in the fallopian tube; the blastocyst implants in the uterus lining, and the placenta allows exchange of glucose, amino acids, oxygen, antibodies and wastes between mother and foetus, with the umbilical cord carrying blood.
  • Sexually transmitted infections including HIV are spread by unprotected sexual contact, shared needles or mother to child; prevention uses condoms, screening and education.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Comparison reasoning, applied to why sexual reproduction produces variation: meiosis creates new combinations of alleles through crossing over and independent assortment, and fertilisation combines two different parents' genes. Name the two mechanisms of meiosis — each is its own mark.
  • Placenta exchange reasoning, applied to why antibodies cross but large cells do not: antibodies are small proteins that diffuse across the placental barrier, protecting the foetus; pathogens generally do not cross, which is why some immunity is transferred rather than infection. Explain with size and diffusion, not just "they pass through".
  • Germination evaluation, applied to a seed experiment at different temperatures: the independent variable is temperature, and water and oxygen must be controlled in excess so temperature is the limiting factor. Name which factor would be limiting if water were scarce — that shows you understand limiting factors, not just procedure.

Common errors

  • Confusing pollination (pollen transfer) with fertilisation (nuclei fusion).
  • Saying the placenta is part of the foetus. It forms from uterine tissue and both mother and foetus contribute to it.
  • Claiming seeds need light to germinate. The required factors are water, oxygen and the right temperature.

title: Exam technique: Angles and Polygons
content:
### What earns the marks
For angle-chasing, justify earns marks for each reason stated alongside the value: angles on a straight line, vertically opposite, alternate, corresponding, and the circle theorems by name. For cyclic quadrilaterals, quote earns the theorem (opposite angles sum to 180) before the equation. For polygons, the formula (n - 2) x 180 stated earns the method mark.
### Traps
Error: using adjacent instead of opposite angles in a cyclic quadrilateral. Correction: mark the diagram first. Error: answering each interior angle when the sum is asked. Correction: only divide at the very end. Error: treating any triangle in a circle as right-angled. Correction: the right angle needs the diameter as hypotenuse.
### Worked example
The sum of the interior angles of an n-sided polygon is (n − 2) × 180°. For a regular octagon (n = 8), each interior angle is 6 × 180 ÷ 8 = 135°, so each exterior angle is 45°. The exterior angles of any polygon add up to 360°, which gives a quick check: 8 × 45 = 360.
### Check yourself
Find the interior angle of a regular hexagon. Use (6 − 2) × 180 ÷ 6 = 120°. Explain why the exterior angle is 60° and why this matches 360 ÷ 6.

### Worked example
The sum of the interior angles of an n-sided polygon is (n − 2) × 180°. For a regular octagon (n = 8), each interior angle is 6 × 180 ÷ 8 = 135°, so each exterior angle is 45°. The exterior angles of any polygon add up to 360°, which gives a quick check: 8 × 45 = 360.

title: Ethics, Security & Impact — Study Notes
content:
Ethics, Security & Impact

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): ethics & professional codes, cyber security threats and protection, malware, online safety, digital currency, environmental/employment impact.

1. Ethics and codes

ACM/IEEE-CS/BCS codes: public interest, competence, integrity, privacy. Applying: identify the principle → apply to scenario → stakeholders affected → consequences.

2. Threats

  • Malware: virus (attaches, replicates via host), worm (self-spreads), trojan (disguised), spyware, ransomware.
  • Social: phishing (fake emails/sites), pharming (DNS/hosts redirect), shoulder surfing, brute force.
  • Technical: interception (packet sniffing), SQL injection (malicious input into queries), DoS (flooding services).

3. Cyber security

Cyber security protects data, systems and users from attack. A vulnerability is a weakness an attack can use; a threat is what exploits it.

  • Vulnerabilities: default or weak passwords, unpatched software, misconfigured access rights, unsecured or public Wi-Fi, removable media (memory sticks), insider threat, unencrypted data in transit.
  • Malware: virus (needs a host file and replicates when that file runs), worm (self-spreads across a network), trojan (disguised as useful software), spyware (records activity), ransomware (encrypts files and demands payment), adware.
  • Social engineering: phishing (fake email or site asks for details), pharming (malicious redirect via DNS or the hosts file), blagging (invented story), shoulder surfing, brute-force and dictionary attacks.
  • Technical attacks: interception / packet sniffing on an unsecured network, SQL injection (malicious input typed into a query field), denial of service and DDoS (flooding a service so it cannot respond), session hijacking.

Protection: strong unique passwords plus 2FA; biometric authentication (fingerprint, face); encryption so intercepted data is unreadable (plaintext is turned into ciphertext with a key — HTTPS/TLS does this on websites); firewalls filtering traffic by IP address and port; anti-malware that scans, blocks and quarantines; patching and updates; user access levels so staff reach only what they need; regular backups; user training; penetration testing to find holes first.

Answer shape: name the threat precisely (pharming is not phishing), then give the matched defence — pharming → keep DNS servers and hosts files secure and check HTTPS certificates.

4. Digital currency

A digital currency exists only in electronic form. A cryptocurrency (for example Bitcoin) is a decentralised digital currency secured by cryptography and recorded on a blockchain.

  • Blockchain: a distributed ledger — every node holds a copy. Transactions are grouped into blocks, and each block stores the hash of the previous block, so altering an old record breaks the chain and is rejected by the network.
  • Keys and wallets: the owner holds a public key (the address others pay to) and a private key (proves ownership and signs a payment). A wallet stores these keys — lose the private key and the money is gone.
  • Transactions: broadcast to the network, checked by nodes and added to a block; the verifier (miner) is rewarded. No bank or central authority is involved.

Advantages: quick international transfers, low transaction fees, no central authority to fail or censor, a transparent ledger, and coins cannot be counterfeited. Disadvantages: the value is very volatile, payments are irreversible, mining uses large amounts of energy, it appeals to criminals and ransomware demands, it needs internet access and technical care, and there is little consumer protection if a wallet is lost or stolen.

5. Defences

Antivirus/antispyware (scan, quarantine), firewalls (port/IP filtering), 2FA + biometrics, strong passwords + managers, encryption (HTTPS, VPN), access levels, patches/updates, user training.

6. Online behaviour

Digital footprint, cyberbullying, fake news, privacy settings, verification of sources.

7. Wider impact

Employment: automation displaces roles but creates IT jobs. Environment: e-waste, energy use vs paperless efficiency. Monitoring: workplace tracking, CCTV — balance with privacy laws (GDPR-style).

Exam tips: name the threat precisely (pharming ≠ phishing), then the matched defence; ethics answers need principle + application, not opinion.

title: Vectors — Study Notes
content:
Vectors

Components and Arithmetic

A vector a = 3i + 4j has magnitude |a| = √(3² + 4²) = 5. Parallel vectors are scalar multiples; unit vector = a/|a|.

Position and Direction

The line through point A with direction d: r = a + t d. Two lines are parallel if their directions are multiples.

Example: r = (1, 2) + t(3, −1).

Scalar (Dot) Product

a · b = |a||b| cos θ = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂.

Perpendicular ⇔ a · b = 0. Parallel ⇔ cross-multiplied components are equal (in 2D: a₁b₂ − a₂b₁ = 0).

Example: (2, 3) · (−6, 4) = −12 + 12 = 0, so they are perpendicular.

Angle Between Vectors

cos θ = (a · b)/(|a||b|).

Example: between (1, 0) and (1, 1): cos θ = 1/(1 × √2), θ = 45°.

Lines and Points

Foot of perpendicular from P to a line, intersection of two lines, and shortest distances all come from dot products and parameter t.

Exam tips: write column vectors cleanly; check answers by substituting the found t back into both position vectors; keep exact surd magnitudes rather than decimals.

title: AS Level Mathematics: Circular Measure
content:
AS Level Mathematics: Circular Measure

Radians measure angles by the arc they cut: one radian is the angle subtended when the arc equals the radius. That definition makes every circle formula simpler — arc length becomes s = rθ and sector area becomes ½r²θ, with no 360 in sight. This note builds the topic from zero: the radian definition and conversions, arc length and sector area with derivations, the segment area formula, and the applied problems (belts, pendulums, cones) that combine circular measure with trigonometry. Every worked example keeps the calculator in radian mode, which is the first habit this topic demands.

Radians and conversion

one full turn = 2 π radians = 360 degrees
π radians = 180 degrees

degrees → radians: multiply by π/180
radians → degrees: multiply by 180/π

common values: 30 ° = π/6, 45 ° = π/4,
60 ° = π/3, 90 ° = π/2, 180 ° = π

Worked example. Convert 150° to radians and 2.4 radians to degrees.

150 x π/180 = 5 π/6 = 2.618 rad
2.4 × 180/π = 137.5 °

Why radians: the arc length formula s = rθ only works when θ is in radians. In degrees the same arc is (θ/360) × 2πr — the same quantity, but with the conversion built in.

Arc length and sector area

arc length: s = r θ
sector area: A = (1/2) r² θ
perimeter of a sector: s + 2r

(θ in radians, r in the same length unit as s)

Worked example 1. A sector has radius 8 cm and angle 1.5 radians. Find the arc length and area.

s = r θ = 8 × 1.5 = 12 cm
A = (1/2) r² θ = 0.5 × 64 × 1.5 = 48 cm²

Worked example 2 (perimeter). Find the perimeter of the same sector.

perimeter = arc + 2 radii = 12 + 16 = 28 cm

Worked example 3 (working backwards). A sector of radius 6 cm has area 27 cm². Find the angle in radians and degrees.

27 = (1/2)(36) θ  →  27 = 18 θ  →  θ = 1.5 rad
in degrees: 1.5 × 180/π = 85.9 °

Segment area

segment area = sector area - triangle area
             = (1/2) r² θ - (1/2) r² sin(θ)
             = (1/2) r² (θ - sin θ)

The triangle is formed by the two radii and the chord; its area uses ½r² sin θ (the sine rule area formula). The subtraction is always the same picture: the segment is the sector with the triangle removed.

Worked example. Find the area of the segment cut off by a chord in a circle of radius 10 cm when the angle at the centre is 1.2 radians.

sector area = (1/2)(100)(1.2) = 60 cm²
triangle area = (1/2)(100) sin(1.2) = 50 × 0.932 = 46.6 cm²
segment = 60 - 46.6 = 13.4 cm²

Worked examples: the standard exam types

Worked example 1 (belt around pulleys). Two pulleys of radius 0.20 m and 0.50 m have centres 1.5 m apart. Find the length of the belt around them (straight sections plus arcs).

straight sections: 2 × 1.5 = 3.0 m (approximately, for the
common external tangents when the radii differ the geometry
needs the tangent length, but the exam version usually gives
equal pulleys or the tangent length directly)
equal-pulley version: belt = 2d + 2 π r = 3.0 + 1.26 = 4.26 m

Worked example 2 (pendulum arc). A pendulum of length 0.80 m swings through 0.6 radians. Find the arc length travelled by the bob.

s = r θ = 0.80 × 0.6 = 0.48 m

Worked example 3 (cone sector). A sector of radius 12 cm and angle 2.0 radians is folded into a cone. Find the base radius.

arc length becomes the base circumference:
s = 12 × 2.0 = 24 cm² π r_base = 24  →  r_base = 24/(2 π) = 3.82 cm

Radian trigonometry and small angles

In radian mode, the trigonometric functions take radian inputs, and small-angle approximations become available: for small θ, sin θ ≈ θ and tan θ ≈ θ (with θ in radians), and cos θ ≈ 1 − θ²/2. These approximations underpin pendulum motion and lens theory later, and they appear in exam questions as "show that for small θ ...".

Worked example. Show that for small θ, the arc length and the chord length are approximately equal.

arc = r θ
chord = 2r sin(θ/2) ~ 2r (θ/2) = r θ  for small θ
so chord ~ arc, with the difference of order θ³

Composite shapes with sectors

Exam figures combine sectors with triangles, rectangles and semicircles. The method is always the same: shade the required region, split it into standard pieces, compute each piece with the radian formulas, then add or subtract. Perimeter questions require the boundary only — internal lines are not part of it.

Worked example. A shape is a rectangle 12 cm by 8 cm with a quarter-circle of radius 8 cm removed from one corner. Find the area and perimeter of the remaining shape.

rectangle area = 96 cm²
quarter circle = (1/4) π r² = (1/4)(3.142)(64) = 50.3 cm²
remaining area = 96 - 50.3 = 45.7 cm²

perimeter: straight edges 12 + 4 + 8 = 24 cm (the 4 cm is the
remaining part of the 8 cm side)
plus the arc: quarter circumference = (1/4)(2 π)(8) = 12.6 cm
total perimeter = 36.6 cm

Worked example 2 (two sectors). Two circles of radius 5 cm have centres 8 cm apart. Find the area common to both.

the overlap is two identical segments. In each circle the chord
subtends an angle θ where cos(θ/2) = 4/5, so θ/2 =
0.6435 and θ = 1.287 rad.
segment area = (1/2)(25)(1.287 - sin 1.287)
             = 12.5(1.287 - 0.960) = 4.09 cm²
common area = 2 × 4.09 = 8.18 cm²

Arc, chord and sector in practice

Three quantities are easy to confuse and each has its own formula. Keep them side by side:

QuantityFormula (θ in radians)What it measures
Arc lengths = r θthe curved boundary
Chord lengthc = 2r sin(θ/2)the straight line joining the arc's ends
Sector areaA = (1/2) r^2 θthe pie-slice region

Worked example. A sector has radius 10 cm and angle 1.0 rad. Find the arc length, chord length and the difference between them.

arc = 10 × 1.0 = 10.0 cm
chord = 2 × 10 x sin(0.5) = 20 × 0.4794 = 9.59 cm
difference = 0.41 cm (the arc bulges beyond the chord)

Worked example (angular speed). A wheel of radius 0.35 m turns at 12 rad s⁻¹. Find the linear speed of a point on its rim and the angle turned in 5 s.

v = r ω = 0.35 × 12 = 4.2 m s⁻¹
angle = ω t = 12 × 5 = 60 rad (about 9.5 full turns)

Angular speed links circular measure to mechanics: one radian per second means one radius of arc per second, so the rim speed is rω. Exam questions on rotating wheels, pulleys and centrifuges all reduce to this one relation, and it also explains why a point near the rim of a wheel moves faster than a point near the hub despite both completing a turn in the same time. The same relation converts between the two ways of measuring rotation: revolutions per minute to radians per second is a factor of 2π/60.

The difference is the sagitta-related gap that appears in lens and bridge questions; it grows as the angle grows, which is why the small-angle approximation fails for large sectors.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Convert) Convert 72° to radians. Answer: 72 × π/180 = 2π/5 ≈ 1.257 rad.
  2. (Arc) Radius 5 cm, θ = 2.0 rad. Find the arc length. Answer: 10 cm.
  3. (Sector) Radius 4 cm, θ = 3.0 rad. Find the area. Answer: ½ × 16 × 3 = 24 cm².
  4. (Reverse) A sector of radius 9 cm has arc length 13.5 cm. Find θ in radians. Answer: θ = 13.5/9 = 1.5 rad.
  5. (Segment) Radius 6 cm, θ = π/3. Find the segment area. Answer: sector = ½ × 36 × π/3 = 6π ≈ 18.85; triangle = ½ × 36 × sin(π/3) = 18 × 0.866 = 15.59; segment ≈ 3.26 cm².
  6. (Perimeter) Find the perimeter of a sector of radius 7 cm and angle 0.8 rad. Answer: arc 5.6 + 14 = 19.6 cm.
  7. (Cone) A sector of radius 10 cm and angle 1.8 rad forms a cone. Find the base radius and slant height. Answer: arc = 18 cm → base radius 18/(2π) = 2.86 cm; slant height = 10 cm.
  8. (Small angle) Use sin θ ≈ θ to estimate sin(0.10) and compare with the calculator value. Answer: ≈ 0.10; calculator 0.0998 — agreement to about 0.2%.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Degree mode: every radians formula requires the calculator in RAD mode. A sin of 1.2 in degree mode gives an entirely different number.
  • Mixing units: s = rθ silently assumes r in metres and s in metres; cm and m mixed in one calculation produces a factor-of-100 error.
  • Half forgotten: sector area is ½r²θ, not r²θ. The ½ comes from the triangle comparison.
  • Angle in degrees in the formula: θ must be radians; convert first, and only convert the final answer back if asked.
  • Perimeter includes the radii: the perimeter of a sector is arc + 2r; the arc alone is not the perimeter.
  • Segment triangle: use ½r² sin θ for the triangle, with θ the same central angle; a different angle changes the answer.
  • Exact versus decimal: when the question says "in terms of π", keep π symbolic; converting to 3.14 loses the required form.
  • Small-angle validity: sin θ ≈ θ is good only for small θ (roughly under 0.2 rad); do not apply it to 1.5 rad.

title: Exam technique: Poisson Distribution
content:
### What earns the marks
For lambda scaling, the rate times the interval stated earns the first mark. For probabilities, e^-lambda lambda^x / x! with values earns the method mark. For approximations, the condition named (n large, p small, lambda = np) earns credit.
### Traps
Error: unscaled lambda over a new interval. Correction: scale first. Error: binomial coefficients inside Poisson work. Correction: Poisson formula only. Error: mean and variance treated as different. Correction: both equal lambda.
### Worked example
Calls arrive at a rate of 3 per minute, so over 2 minutes λ = 6. The probability of exactly 2 calls is P(X = 2) = e⁻⁶ × 6² / 2! = 18e⁻⁶ ≈ 0.0446. The mean and the variance both equal λ, so the mean number in 2 minutes is 6.
### Worked example
Calls arrive at a rate of 3 per minute, so over 2 minutes λ = 6. The probability of exactly 2 calls is P(X = 2) = e⁻⁶ × 6² / 2! = 18e⁻⁶ ≈ 0.0446. The mean and the variance both equal λ, so the mean number in 2 minutes is 6.

title: IGCSE Chemistry: Chemistry of the Environment
content:
IGCSE Chemistry: Chemistry of the Environment

Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry 0620 (2026–2028), Extended route, Topic 10 Chemistry of the environment: statement 10.1 Water, 10.2 Fertilisers, and 10.3 Air quality and climate. This is applied chemistry at its most exam-visible: the greenhouse mechanism, pollutant chemistry and water treatment are all regular Paper 4 questions that demand particle-level and chemical explanations, not lists. Every reaction below is written in the form the mark scheme expects.

Water: testing, purity and treatment

The test for water is anhydrous copper(II) sulfate (white → blue) or anhydrous cobalt(II) chloride (blue → pink) — the hydrated colour change from the salts topic. Purity is judged by melting/boiling point: pure water boils sharply at 100 °C; an impure sample boils over a range and above 100 °C (boiling-point elevation). Practical chemistry uses distilled water because tap water's dissolved ions interfere with reactions and leave residues.

Domestic water treatment, stage by stage:

  1. SEDIMENTATION: water stands in settling tanks; insoluble particles
     sink (sometimes a flocculant like aluminium sulfate is added to bind
     small particles).
  2. FILTRATION: through gravel and sand beds - removes remaining solids.
  3. CARBON FILTRATION: activated carbon adsorbs dissolved organic
     substances, taste and odour compounds.
  4. CHLORINATION: chlorine kills bacteria and viruses (dose ~1 ppm);
     it stays in the supply to guard against recontamination.

  Natural waters may contain: dissolved oxygen (essential for aquatic
  life), metal compounds (toxic - e.g. lead from old pipes), nitrates and
  phosphates (from fertiliser run-off - cause eutrophication: algal bloom,
  blocked light, decay deoxygenates the water, fish die), sewage and
  microbes (disease), plastics (physical harm, microplastics).

Fertilisers

Fertilisers supply the three nutrients NPK: nitrogen (leaf growth), phosphorus (roots), potassium (flowers/fruit). Ammonium salts (e.g. ammonium nitrate, NH₄NO₃) and nitrates are the main nitrogen sources. Manufacture is the Haber–Bosch chain: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, then NH₃ + HNO₃ → NH₄NO₃. Fertilisers boost yields but cause water pollution when washed off — the trade-off earns marks in environment questions.

Air quality and climate

PollutantSourceEffectCountermeasure
COIncomplete combustion of fuelsToxic (binds haemoglobin)Catalytic converters; efficient engines
SO₂Combustion of sulfur-containing fossil fuelsAcid rain (damages buildings, lakes, trees)Flue-gas desulfurisation (CaO/CaCO₃ scrubbing); low-sulfur fuels
NO/NO₂High-temperature combustion in enginesAcid rain; photochemical smogCatalytic converters (2CO + 2NO → 2CO₂ + N₂)
CO₂Combustion of all carbon fuelsGreenhouse gas — enhanced global warmingRenewables, efficiency, carbon capture
ParticulatesDiesel engines, industryRespiratory diseaseFilters
The greenhouse effect explained mechanistically - the Extended wording:

  1. Solar radiation arrives mostly as short-wavelength (visible/UV) light,
     which passes through the atmosphere and warms the Earth's surface.
  2. The warm Earth re-radiates energy as longer-wavelength INFRA-RED.
  3. Greenhouse gases (CO₂, CH₄, H₂O vapour) ABSORB this infra-red and
     re-emit it in all directions - some back toward the surface.
  4. Less energy escapes to space than arrived, so the lower atmosphere and
     surface warm further.

  Sources of the enhanced effect: burning fossil fuels (CO₂), agriculture
  and landfill (CH₄), deforestation (less CO₂ absorbed).
  Why methane matters: each CH₄ molecule absorbs MORE infra-red per molecule
  than CO₂, though it is shorter-lived in the atmosphere.

Nitrogen oxides in engines: N₂ + O₂ → 2NO at high temperature inside the
engine (the heat of combustion breaks the very strong N≡N and O=O bonds);
2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂ in the air. Catalytic converters reduce them back:
  2CO + 2NO → 2CO₂ + N₂   (both pollutants converted to less harmful gases)

Photosynthesis:  6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂   (light, chlorophyll)

The atmosphere and climate change evidence

Clean dry air is approximately 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, 1% noble gases and about 0.04% carbon dioxide — a composition worth stating in source-and-effect answers because the gases that matter climatically are the trace ones. Climate evidence the syllabus expects candidates to interpret: rising global mean temperatures, retreating glaciers and ice sheets, rising sea levels from thermal expansion and melting ice, and changing weather patterns. Mitigation strategies split into two families: adaptation (building flood defences, developing drought-resistant crops) and mitigation (renewable energy, efficiency, reforestation, international agreements to cut emissions). Chemistry contributes both the diagnosis — isotopic analysis of atmospheric CO₂ traces its source to fossil fuels — and the solutions: catalytic converters, flue-gas scrubbing, carbon capture and hydrogen fuel technology.

Worked example: evaluating an environmental scenario

A coal power plant adds a desulfurisation unit. Evaluate.

  Problem: SO₂ from sulfur impurities in coal causes acid rain:
    SO₂ + H₂O → H₂SO₃ (and further oxidation to H₂SO₄).
  Countermeasure: CaCO₃ or CaO in the flue:
    CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ ;  CaO + SO₂ → CaSO₃ ;
    2CaSO₃ + O₂ → 2CaSO₄ (gypsum - sold for plasterboard).
  Trade-offs: removes >90% of SO₂ and turns waste into a product, but costs
  energy and money, adds CO₂ from the calcination step, and the slurry waste
  must be handled. Net: acid rain reduced substantially; the CO₂ problem
  (global warming) remains - pollution problems are separate.

Water purity and the oxygen cycle

Aquatic chemistry ties the water and air topics together. Dissolved oxygen sustains fish and is replenished at the surface by diffusion and by photosynthesis; organic pollution (sewage, fertiliser run-off) upsets the balance because bacteria consuming the waste also consume the dissolved oxygen — biochemical oxygen demand (BOD) rises and aquatic life suffocates. Heavy-metal compounds (mercury, lead) are toxic because they bind to enzymes and accumulate up the food chain. Microplastics and pathogens add physical and disease hazards. The treatment train in the first section targets exactly these: filtration removes particulates and the organisms sheltering in them, carbon adsorption removes organics, and chlorination kills the pathogens — while distillation in the laboratory removes everything dissolved, which is why distilled water is the chemist's standard.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Describing the greenhouse effect as "the ozone layer" or "the sun getting hotter" — it is infra-red absorption by specific gases.
  • Confusing global warming (CO₂/CH₄, climate) with acid rain (SO₂/NOₓ) and with ozone depletion (CFCs) — three distinct problems.
  • Writing acid rain as sulfuric acid only from SO₂ without the water/oxidation steps.
  • Saying chlorination removes impurities — it kills microbes; sedimentation/filtration removes solids; carbon removes taste/odour.
  • Forgetting dissolved oxygen in water-quality answers (its absence is the harm in eutrophication).
  • Claiming fertilisers are simply "pollution" — the balanced answer names yield benefits and run-off costs.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Describe how carbon dioxide causes global warming.

Answer: Solar radiation warms the Earth's surface, which re-radiates energy as infra-red. CO₂ absorbs this outgoing infra-red and re-emits it in all directions, including back to the surface, so less energy escapes to space. Burning fossil fuels increases atmospheric CO₂, enhancing this natural effect and raising average temperatures.

Question 2 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Explain how sulfur dioxide causes acid rain and one method of reducing it.

Answer: Sulfur impurities in fuels burn to sulfur dioxide: S + O₂ → SO₂. In the atmosphere it dissolves in rainwater and oxidises to sulfuric acid: SO₂ + H₂O → H₂SO₃, then further oxidation gives H₂SO₄. Reduction: flue-gas desulfurisation using calcium oxide/carbonate, which reacts with SO₂ to give calcium sulfate; or use low-sulfur fuels.

Question 3 (Paper 4, 3 marks). Describe the stages of domestic water treatment.

Answer: Sedimentation (solids settle, sometimes with a flocculant), filtration through gravel/sand (removes remaining insoluble particles), activated-carbon adsorption (removes taste, odour, dissolved organics), and chlorination (kills bacteria and viruses and protects the supply).

Question 4 (Paper 4, 3 marks). Explain the test for water and how boiling-point data shows purity.

Answer: Anhydrous copper(II) sulfate turns from white to blue (or cobalt(II) chloride from blue to pink) when water is added. Pure water boils sharply at exactly 100 °C at standard pressure; an impure sample boils over a range of temperatures and above 100 °C.

Question 5 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Explain the environmental problems caused by fertiliser run-off.

Answer: Nitrates and phosphates wash into rivers and lakes, causing eutrophication: algae grow explosively and block light, so aquatic plants die; the decay of this material by bacteria consumes dissolved oxygen, suffocating fish and other organisms. Excess nitrate in drinking water is also a health risk (it affects blood oxygen transport).

Question 6 (Paper 4, 3 marks). Write an equation for the catalytic conversion of nitrogen monoxide and carbon monoxide and name the products.

Answer: 2CO + 2NO → 2CO₂ + N₂. The products are carbon dioxide and nitrogen — both far less harmful than the reactants.

The environment is shaped by carbon chemistry too — the organic family tree comes next.

title: Edexcel IAL Computer Science: Database Definition, DDL/DML and Normalisation
content:
Edexcel IAL Computer Science: Database Definition, DDL/DML and Normalisation

Pearson Edexcel International Advanced Level in Computer Science, Unit 4 The Computing Practical Project (with Unit 2/3 foundations): data definition and data manipulation languages, and the normalisation that produces a defensible schema. The AS database note built the concepts; this one builds the artefacts a project needs — a schema written in DDL, queries written in DML, and a normalisation walk-through of the kind a project's design chapter must contain. Every statement is parsed clause by clause.

DDL: defining the structure

Data definition language (DDL) creates and alters the database's structure — tables, keys, constraints — while data manipulation language (DML) operates on the data inside (SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE).
