The DBMS stores the resulting schema in its data dictionary and enforces every declared rule on all clients — the reason DDL is written once but protects the data forever.

DDL worked: the clinic schema, each statement's effect named.

  CREATE TABLE patient (
      patientID   CHAR(5)      PRIMARY KEY,      -- unique, not null by rule
      name        VARCHAR(60)  NOT NULL,
      dob         DATE         NOT NULL,
      phone       VARCHAR(15),
      postcode    VARCHAR(8)
  );
  -- effect: table created; patientID is the entity key; name and dob may not
  -- be empty; phone may be unknown (nullable) - a design decision.

  CREATE TABLE appointment (
      apptID      INTEGER      PRIMARY KEY,
      patientID   CHAR(5)      NOT NULL,
      doctorID    CHAR(5)      NOT NULL,
      apptDate    DATE         NOT NULL,
      slot        TIME         NOT NULL,
      CONSTRAINT fk_appt_patient FOREIGN KEY (patientID)
          REFERENCES patient(patientID),
      CONSTRAINT uq_doctor_slot UNIQUE (doctorID, apptDate, slot)
  );
  -- effect: referential integrity (no appointment without a real patient),
  -- and a composite UNIQUE that makes double-booking impossible.

  ALTER TABLE patient ADD email VARCHAR(80);
  DROP TABLE old_backup;                        -- destructive; guarded
  CREATE INDEX idx_patient_name ON patient(name); -- speeds name lookups

Constraints the DBMS now enforces regardless of application code: PRIMARY KEY
(uniqueness + non-null), FOREIGN KEY (referential integrity, with ON DELETE
CASCADE / RESTRICT / SET NULL choices), UNIQUE, NOT NULL, CHECK (range):

  ALTER TABLE appointment ADD CONSTRAINT chk_slot
      CHECK (slot BETWEEN '08:00' AND '18:00');

DDL and DML command summary

CommandFamilyEffect
CREATE TABLE / INDEX / VIEWDDLAdds a structure the DBMS will enforce
ALTER TABLEDDLAdds, drops or modifies columns and constraints
DROP TABLEDDLRemoves a structure and its data — destructive
SELECTDML (query)Reads rows, filtered, grouped and sorted
INSERTDMLAdds a row; refused if any constraint would break
UPDATEDMLModifies rows matching a WHERE predicate
DELETEDMLRemoves rows matching a WHERE predicate
GRANT / REVOKEDCLAssigns or removes role permissions (least privilege)

A third family completes the picture: transaction control (TCL) — BEGIN, COMMIT and ROLLBACK group DML into atomic units, so a failure mid-transaction leaves the database exactly as it was. Every batch job and multi-step update in a project should be wrapped in one.

DML: manipulating the data

DML worked on the clinic tables, each query's execution order stated:

  INSERT INTO patient (patientID, name, dob, phone)
  VALUES ('P010', 'Chen', '2008-04-12', '07700 900123');
  -- the row must satisfy every constraint or the insert fails atomically.

  UPDATE patient SET phone = '07700 900456' WHERE patientID = 'P010';
  -- without WHERE this would touch every row - the classic destructive slip.

  DELETE FROM appointment WHERE apptDate < '2026-01-01';
  -- a FK referencing patient would RESTRICT or CASCADE here - state which.

  SELECT p.name, COUNT(a.apptID) AS visits
  FROM patient p
  LEFT JOIN appointment a ON p.patientID = a.patientID
  GROUP BY p.patientID, p.name
  HAVING COUNT(a.apptID) = 0
  ORDER BY p.name;
  -- Execution: FROM -> JOIN -> WHERE -> GROUP BY -> HAVING -> SELECT -> ORDER
  -- BY. LEFT JOIN keeps patients with no appointments (count 0); HAVING
  -- filters the GROUPS (WHERE could not - it runs before aggregation).

JOIN types to name: INNER (matching rows only), LEFT (all left rows, nulls
where unmatched), RIGHT (mirror), FULL (all rows both sides), and self-join
(table related to itself - staff/supervisor).

Normalisation, end to end

Normalisation restructures data to remove redundancy and the anomalies it causes. Full procedure with the reason each step matters:

Unnormalised: one row per (student, subject) with a repeating group:

  StudentID | Name  | Class | ClassTeacher | Subjects (repeating)
  S1        | Chen  | 11A   | Mr Hall      | Maths, Physics

1NF - eliminate repeating groups (each field single-valued):
  StudentID | Name | Class | ClassTeacher | Subject
  S1 | Chen | 11A | Mr Hall | Maths
  S1 | Chen | 11A | Mr Hall | Physics      <- duplication begins

2NF - 1NF and no partial dependency on a composite key
  (key here is (StudentID, Subject); Name, Class, ClassTeacher depend only
  on StudentID - part of the key):
  STUDENT(StudentID [PK], Name, Class, ClassTeacher)
  RESULT(StudentID [PK, FK], Subject [PK], Mark)

3NF - 2NF and no transitive dependency
  (in STUDENT, ClassTeacher depends on Class, not directly on StudentID):
  STUDENT(StudentID [PK], Name, Class [FK])
  CLASS(Class [PK], ClassTeacher)
  RESULT(StudentID [PK, FK], Subject [PK], Mark)

Anomalies removed at each step:
  1NF removes the multi-valued field (searching "who takes Physics" became
  impossible); 2NF removes the teacher's name repeating per subject;
  3NF means one class has ONE teacher stored ONCE - change Mr Hall in one row
  and every student of 11A sees it.

Denormalisation exists as a deliberate counter-move: merging tables back for read-heavy reporting trades integrity risk for fewer joins — valid when the project's non-functional requirements demand it and the trade is documented.

The design artefacts a project needs

  • Entity-relationship diagram — entities, attributes, cardinality (1:1, 1:M, M:N resolved with junction tables).
  • Data dictionary — every field: type, length, range, key role, validation rules.
  • Normalisation narrative — the unnormalised table and each step to 3NF with the dependency named at each split (the trace above is the model).
  • DDL script — the schema with all constraints, version-controlled.
  • Validation and security plan — input checks at the application plus DBMS-level constraints; roles and least-privilege grants.
Worked: GRANT statements for the clinic's two roles.

  CREATE ROLE reception;
  GRANT SELECT, INSERT ON appointment TO reception;
  GRANT SELECT ON patient TO reception;
  CREATE ROLE doctor;
  GRANT SELECT ON appointment, patient, prescription TO doctor;

  -- reception cannot read prescriptions; doctors cannot delete appointments.
  Least privilege means each role receives exactly what its work needs - and
  the project's security section records these decisions.

Normalisation worked example: the dependency proof

The one question format that catches people out is proving which normal form a table violates. The method: write the functional dependencies, then test each in turn.

Table: ENROLMENT(studentID, studentName, courseID, courseFee, lecturerID, lecturerName)
Dependencies: studentID -> studentName; courseID -> courseFee, lecturerID;
              lecturerID -> lecturerName. Key: (studentID, courseID).

1NF? Every field single-valued - yes (assume no repeating groups).
2NF? studentName depends on only part of the key (studentID) - partial
     dependency - VIOLATED.
3NF? lecturerName depends on lecturerID which is not a key - transitive
     dependency - VIOLATED (and 2NF must hold first anyway).

Split for 2NF (remove partials):
  STUDENT(studentID, studentName)
  ENROL(studentID, courseID, courseFee, lecturerID, lecturerName)
Split for 3NF (remove transitives):
  COURSE(courseID, courseFee, lecturerID)
  LECTURER(lecturerID, lecturerName)

Every non-key attribute now depends on the key, the whole key, and nothing
but the key - the sentence markers look for.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Writing DML when DDL is asked: CREATE/ALTER/DROP define; SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE manipulate.
  • UPDATE or DELETE without a WHERE clause — the answer must state the predicate.
  • Stopping normalisation at "no repeating groups"; 2NF needs the partial-dependency split and 3NF the transitive one.
  • Declaring a foreign key without an ON DELETE choice in a design answer; cascade/restrict/set-null is a decision with consequences.
  • Using WHERE on aggregate results (needs HAVING), or grouping by fewer columns than selected (SQL strictness).
  • Confusing LEFT JOIN with INNER JOIN in "list all X even if no Y" questions — the unmatched rows are the point.
  • Denormalising without recording the trade-off; the exam rewards the conscious reversal, not the accident.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Unit 4, 4 marks). Explain the difference between DDL and DML with examples.

Answer: DDL defines and alters the database structure and is executed rarely by administrators — CREATE TABLE patient, ALTER TABLE add a column, CREATE INDEX. DML operates on the data within that structure and runs constantly — SELECT lists, INSERT adds, UPDATE modifies, DELETE removes. DDL changes the schema the DBMS enforces; DML changes rows subject to those constraints.

Question 2 (Unit 4, 5 marks). Normalise the table ORDER(orderID, customerName, customerPhone, productID, productName, quantity) to 3NF, naming the dependencies.

Answer: Key is orderID (assume one product per order row). customerName and customerPhone depend on the customer (transitive via a customerID that is missing) and productName on productID — non-key determinants. 2NF: none partial (single-column key), so split the transitive dependencies: ORDER(orderID, customerID, productID, quantity), CUSTOMER(customerID, customerName, customerPhone), PRODUCT(productID, productName). 3NF holds: every non-key field depends on its key, the whole key, and nothing but the key. Each customer and product is stored once.

Question 3 (Unit 4, 4 marks). Write DDL to create a student table with a primary key and a marks range constraint.

Answer: CREATE TABLE student (studentID CHAR(5) PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(60) NOT NULL, mark INTEGER CHECK (mark BETWEEN 0 AND 100)); — the PRIMARY KEY enforces unique identity, NOT NULL rejects empty names, and the CHECK makes out-of-range marks impossible at the database level.

Question 4 (Unit 4, 4 marks). Explain what happens when a row is deleted from a table referenced by foreign keys.

Answer: The DBMS enforces referential integrity according to the declared rule: ON DELETE RESTRICT refuses the delete while child rows exist (protective default); ON DELETE CASCADE deletes the dependent rows too (fast, but destructive); ON DELETE SET NULL keeps child rows with the key nulled (only if nullable). The choice is documented in the design because each has different consequences for data retention.

Question 5 (Unit 4, 4 marks). Write a query listing customers with no orders, and explain why HAVING is used.

Answer: SELECT c.customerID, c.name FROM customer c LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.customerID = o.customerID GROUP BY c.customerID, c.name HAVING COUNT(o.orderID) = 0. The LEFT JOIN keeps all customers, the count measures their orders per group, and HAVING filters groups after aggregation — WHERE cannot, because it runs before the groups exist.

Question 6 (Unit 4, 3 marks). Explain when denormalisation is justified.

Answer: In read-heavy reporting where join costs dominate query time, merging tables (e.g. storing the product name on the order row) removes joins and speeds reads. It is justified only when the redundancy is controlled (updated through one path, or refreshed from the normalised source) and the gain is documented — otherwise it reintroduces the update anomalies normalisation removed.

Data definitions shape the project's core; the network layer shapes how its users reach it.

title: Edexcel IAL Computer Science: Programming Paradigms and Object-Oriented Programming
content:
Edexcel IAL Computer Science: Programming Paradigms and Object-Oriented Programming

Pearson Edexcel International Advanced Level in Computer Science, Unit 3 Advanced Computer Science: programming paradigms, object-oriented programming, file processing and exception handling. A paradigm is a style of organising programs — a different answer to "what is a program made of?" — and this note compares the major ones before building object-oriented systems in full: encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism and abstraction, each traced through concrete code.

The paradigms

ParadigmProgram is…StrengthsWeaknesses
Procedural/imperativeOrdered instructions updating stateDirect, efficient, easy to traceState sprawl; hard to reuse and reason about at scale
Object-orientedInteracting objects bundling data and behaviourModularity, reuse through inheritance, modelling real entitiesOverhead; deep hierarchies become brittle
Declarative (e.g. SQL, logic)A description of the desired resultConcise; the system chooses the methodLess control over the procedure; unfamiliar reasoning
FunctionalPure functions composing values, no mutable stateEasy to reason about and parallelise; no side-effect bugsLearning curve; awkward for stateful I/O

Event-driven programming (handlers reacting to user/system events) is a style layered over these — the paradigm of GUIs and games — worth naming whenever the question mentions interfaces.

Object-oriented programming: the four pillars

  • Encapsulation — bundle fields with the methods that operate on them, and hide internals behind an interface (private fields, public methods). A bank account's balance is private; deposit() and withdraw() are the only mutators — invalid states become unrepresentable.
  • Inheritance — a subclass reuses and extends a superclass (Dog extends Animal), expressing "is-a" relationships and factoring shared code upward.
  • Polymorphism — one interface, many implementations: a call like shape.area() dispatches to the correct class's method at run time (overriding), and overloading allows same-named methods with different parameter lists.
  • Abstraction — expose essential behaviour and hide detail; abstract classes/interfaces define contracts that implementations must fulfil.
Python 3 - all four pillars in one system, traced:

  class Shape:                       # abstraction: a contract
      def area(self):
          raise NotImplementedError

  class Rectangle(Shape):            # inheritance: Rectangle is-a Shape
      def __init__(self, w, h):
          self.__w = w               # encapsulation: name-mangled private
          self.__h = h
      def area(self):                # overriding: polymorphic method
          return self.__w * self.__h

  class Circle(Shape):
      def __init__(self, r):
          self.__r = r
      def area(self):
          return 3.14159 * self.__r ** 2

  shapes = [Rectangle(3, 4), Circle(2)]   # one list, two types
  for s in shapes:
      print(s.area())                # polymorphic dispatch

Trace:
  s = Rectangle(3,4): area() resolves to Rectangle.area -> 12
  s = Circle(2):      area() resolves to Circle.area     -> 12.56636
  The CALLER never branches on type - the object knows its own behaviour.
  print(shapes[0].__w) would fail outside the class: encapsulation holds.

Design vocabulary the exam expects: class (the blueprint), object (an instance), attributes (state), methods (behaviour), constructors (__init__ initialising valid state), message passing (objects collaborating via method calls), and delegation over deep inheritance ("has-a" composition is often better than "is-a" inheritance).

Procedural decomposition in code

Even inside paradigm debates, the exam wants to see structured code: one entry and exit per construct, no goto, clear naming, and subprograms with explicit interfaces. Decomposition maps a design's structure chart onto modules — a function per leaf — and the discipline of keeping functions short and side-effect-transparent is what makes later maintenance possible. Refactoring patterns name the moves: extracting a repeated block into a function, replacing a magic number with a named constant, and splitting a function that does two jobs into two that do one. Marks attach to showing the decomposition in the answer, not merely asserting that the code is structured.

Translation software

Recalling the AS foundation: compilers produce standalone executables (whole-program checks, fast execution), interpreters execute line by line (portable, immediate feedback), assemblers map mnemonics to machine code. A2 depth: multi-stage pipelines (source → lexer → parser → intermediate code → optimiser → code generator), the role of linkers (combining object files, resolving symbols) and loaders (placing code in memory), and virtual-machine targets (bytecode + JIT compiling hot paths at run time).

File processing and exception handling

File processing at A2 depth: sequential versus random-access files; text versus binary (binary is compact and exact for typed data but not human-readable); opening modes (read, write, append, read/write); and the exception model for the errors file work reliably produces.

Python 3 - robust file processing with exceptions, line by line:

  try:
      with open("stock.dat", "rb") as f:      # binary, auto-closed
          while True:
              record = f.read(24)             # fixed-size records
              if not record:                  # clean end of file
                  break
              process(record)
  except FileNotFoundError:
      log("stock file missing - restore from backup")
  except PermissionError:
      log("no access - escalate to administrator")
  except (ValueError, struct.error) as e:     # corrupt record
      log("bad record skipped: " + str(e))
  else:
      log("processing complete")
  finally:
      close_resources()                       # ALWAYS runs

Reading the structure: try wraps risky work; each except catches one failure
type and handles it SEPARATELY; else runs only if no exception; finally always
runs (cleanup). Catching bare Exception hides bugs - name the failures you
expect. A missing finally leaks file handles on the error path.

Exception philosophy: exceptions are for exceptional conditions (missing file, network failure, corrupt data), not ordinary control flow (end of loop is a condition, not an exception); propagate what you cannot handle meaningfully, handle at a layer that can; never swallow silently.

Worked example: designing a small OOP system

Requirement: a ticket booking system with standard and concession tickets;
concessions are 30% off; both print a description.

1. Identify classes: Booking, Ticket (abstract), StandardTicket,
   ConcessionTicket, Customer.
2. Factor: shared behaviour (description, price calculation interface) goes
   in Ticket; differences go in subclasses - the Liskov-friendly shape.
3. Attributes: Ticket holds event, seat, base price; ConcessionTicket adds
   eligibility proof (encapsulated - checked in __init__).
4. Polymorphism: checkout() calls ticket.price() without branching.
5. Composition: Booking HAS Tickets and a Customer - "has-a", not "is-a".

class Ticket:
    def price(self): raise NotImplementedError

class StandardTicket(Ticket):
    def __init__(self, event, seat, base):
        self.event, self.seat, self.base = event, seat, base
    def price(self): return self.base

class ConcessionTicket(Ticket):
    def __init__(self, event, seat, base):
        self.event, self.seat, self.base = event, seat, base
    def price(self): return self.base * 0.7

Adding a VIP ticket later needs one new subclass and no change to checkout -
the open/closed principle in practice.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Describing inheritance as code reuse only; its exam meaning is an is-a relationship with substitutability (Liskov).
  • Confusing overloading (compile-time, same name different parameters) with overriding (run-time, subclass redefinition).
  • Public fields everywhere; encapsulation marks demand private state and controlled access.
  • Using exceptions for normal flow (EOF is a loop condition; input() returning a sentinel), or catching bare Exception.
  • finally omitted from file-handling answers — cleanup on the error path is the point.
  • Calling SQL "procedural" — it is declarative; the question loves this contrast.
  • Claiming a paradigm is universally best; answers weigh trade-offs per project shape.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Unit 3, 4 marks). Explain encapsulation and why it improves software quality.

Answer: Encapsulation bundles an object's data with the methods operating on it and hides the data behind an interface (private attributes, public methods). It improves quality because invalid states become unrepresentable — all changes go through validated methods — internal representation can change without breaking clients, and bugs are localised to the class. A bank account exposing only deposit/withdraw cannot be given a negative balance by direct field pokes.

Question 2 (Unit 3, 4 marks). Explain polymorphism with an example.

Answer: Polymorphism lets one interface serve many implementations, resolved at run time. A drawing program holds a list of Shape objects; calling shape.area() invokes Rectangle.area, Circle.area or Triangle.area depending on each object's actual class, without the caller branching on type. New shapes extend the system without modifying the loop — code is open for extension, closed for modification.

Question 3 (Unit 3, 4 marks). Compare procedural and object-oriented paradigms.

Answer: Procedural programs are ordered procedures over shared data — straightforward to trace and efficient, but data and functions separate, so state bugs and reuse problems grow with size. OOP bundles state and behaviour into interacting objects, giving modularity, reuse via inheritance and natural modelling of real entities, at the cost of runtime overhead and the discipline needed to keep hierarchies shallow. Small scripting tasks suit procedural style; large evolving systems suit OOP.

Question 4 (Unit 3, 5 marks). Describe how exceptions improve error handling over return codes.

Answer: With return codes every caller must remember to check them, and errors are easily ignored or mistaken for valid data. Exceptions separate error handling from the main path: try wraps risky work, except blocks handle specific failures at a layer that can respond, finally guarantees cleanup, and an unhandled exception cannot pass silently — it propagates until something handles it or the program reports it. This forces explicit treatment of failure and prevents corrupted state continuing.

Question 5 (Unit 3, 4 marks). Explain the difference between a compiler and an interpreter and when each suits development.

Answer: A compiler translates the whole program to machine code ahead of execution, producing a fast standalone executable with whole-program diagnostics — suiting production release. An interpreter translates and runs statement by statement, giving immediate feedback and precise error locations but slower execution — suiting development and testing. Many modern systems combine both: compile to bytecode, then interpret or JIT-compile hot paths.

Question 6 (Unit 3, 3 marks). Describe a situation where composition is preferred over inheritance.

Answer: When a class needs behaviour it does not semantically "is-a": a Car has-an Engine rather than is-a Vehicle-part hierarchy. Composition (holding an Engine object and delegating to it) keeps hierarchies shallow, allows swapping implementations at run time, and avoids the fragile base class problem where a superclass change breaks distant subclasses.

Unit 3's paradigms and structures feed directly into Unit 4's practical project discipline — where design, data and testing become documented process.

title: Edexcel IAL Computer Science: Data Representation and Data Types
content:
Edexcel IAL Computer Science: Data Representation and Data Types

Pearson Edexcel International Advanced Level in Computer Science, Unit 1 Principles of Computer Science: data representation — number systems, binary arithmetic, fixed- and floating-point numbers, text, images, sound and compression — together with the data types that programs declare over that raw binary. Everything below is derived or traced digit by digit: every conversion, every normalisation step and every rounding is shown in full, because at A Level the examiner asks not just for the result but for the mechanism. If the IGCSE course taught you that computers store bits, this note explains exactly how those bits stand for every value a program can hold.

Place value and number systems

Any number system is a place-value system: a digit's value depends on where it sits, and each column is a power of the base. Denary uses base 10 (columns 1, 10, 100…); binary uses base 2 (columns 1, 2, 4, 8…); hexadecimal uses base 16 (columns 1, 16, 256…, with digits 0–9 and A–F for 10–15). The only thing that changes between bases is which powers the columns represent.

Denary 347, read as place value:
  3 x 10^2 + 4 x 10^1 + 7 x 10^0 = 300 + 40 + 7 = 347

Binary 1010 1101, read the same way:
  1x128 + 0x64 + 1x32 + 0x16 + 1x8 + 1x4 + 0x2 + 1x1
  = 128 + 32 + 8 + 4 + 1 = 173

Hex AD, read as place value:
  A x 16 + D x 1 = 10 x 16 + 13 x 1 = 173        [same value, three notations]
Denary to binary by repeated division (the general method for any base):

  173 / 2 = 86  remainder 1   <- least significant bit (bottom of the column)
   86 / 2 = 43  remainder 0
   43 / 2 = 21  remainder 1
   21 / 2 = 10  remainder 1
   10 / 2 =  5  remainder 0
    5 / 2 =  2  remainder 1
    2 / 2 =  1  remainder 0
    1 / 2 =  0  remainder 1   <- most significant bit

  Read the remainders bottom to top: 1010 1101 = 173.

Denary to hex uses base 16 the same way:
  173 / 16 = 10 remainder 13   (10 = A, 13 = D)
  10 / 16 =  0 remainder 10
  Read bottom to top: AD.

Hexadecimal matters for humans, not machines: one hex digit maps exactly to four bits (a nibble), so memory dumps, error codes and colour values (#FF8800) can be transcribed without bit-counting errors.

Binary arithmetic

Addition - the four rules of a single column:
  0 + 0 = 0
  0 + 1 = 1
  1 + 1 = 10   (write 0, carry 1)
  1 + 1 + 1 (with carry) = 11   (write 1, carry 1)

Worked: 1011 0110 (= 182) + 0110 1001 (= 105), column by column:

  bit 0: 0 + 1       = 1
  bit 1: 1 + 0       = 1
  bit 2: 1 + 0       = 1
  bit 3: 0 + 1       = 1
  bit 4: 1 + 0       = 1
  bit 5: 0 + 1       = 1
  bit 6: 1 + 1       = 0, carry 1
  bit 7: 1 + 0 + 1(c)= 0, carry 1

  Result with the final carry: 1 0011 1111 = 287.
  Check: 182 + 105 = 287 ✓

  The carry out of bit 7 is a 9th bit that 8 bits cannot hold: in 8-bit
  storage the answer would read 0011 1111 = 63, which is wrong - that is
  overflow, and exam questions deliberately set it.

Two's complement subtraction uses addition with a negated operand, so one adder circuit does both jobs — see below. Multiplication is repeated addition (or shift-and-add: multiplying by 2 is a left shift); division is repeated subtraction or a right shift.

Two's complement: signed integers

Storing negative numbers needs a convention. In two's complement the most significant bit carries a negative weight (for 8 bits: −128, 64, 32, …, 1), giving a range of −128 to +127. The construction rule (invert all bits, then add 1) comes from the requirement that negation must be its own inverse and that zero must have exactly one representation.

Write -53 in 8-bit two's complement, every step:

  +53 in binary:        0 0 1 1 0 1 0 1
  invert every bit:     1 1 0 0 1 0 1 0
  add 1:                1 1 0 0 1 0 1 1   = -53

Check with the column weights:
  -128 + 64 + 0 + 0 + 8 + 0 + 2 + 1 = -53 ✓

Subtraction as addition: 37 - 53
  37  = 0 0 1 0 0 1 0 1
 -53  = 1 1 0 0 1 0 1 1
 add:  (1) 1 1 1 1 0 0 0 0
  The carry out of bit 7 is DISCARDED in two's complement arithmetic.
  1111 0000 = -128 + 64 + 32 + 16 = -16. And 37 - 53 = -16 ✓
  • Range of n-bit two's complement: −2ⁿ⁻¹ to 2ⁿ⁻¹ − 1. The asymmetry (no +128) exists because zero takes the pattern that would otherwise be "negative zero".
  • Overflow test: signed overflow occurs when adding two positives gives a negative, or two negatives gives a positive — the sign bit is the witness. Unsigned overflow is a carry out of the MSB.
  • Arithmetic shift right preserves the sign bit (copies it into the vacated position), dividing a negative number by 2 correctly; a logical shift fills with zeros and would corrupt negatives.

Fixed-point and floating-point numbers

Real numbers cannot all be stored exactly in finite bits, so a convention is needed. Fixed point reserves a fixed number of bits for the integer part and the fraction (a hidden binary point, like writing money as pence). It is fast and exact within its range but rigid: 8.4 fixed point cannot represent very large and very small numbers at once.

Floating point is binary scientific notation: value = mantissa × 2^(exponent − bias), stored in three fields — sign, exponent (biased), mantissa (normalised).

Store 5.75 in an 8-bit float with 4-bit exponent (bias 7) and 4-bit mantissa.

1. Convert to binary:  5.75 = 101.11   [4 + 1 + 0.5 + 0.25]
2. Normalise: 101.11 = 1.0111 x 2^2   [leading digit before the point is 1]
3. Mantissa: store the fraction after the point: 0111 (the leading 1 is
   implicit - "hidden bit" - saving one bit).
4. Exponent: 2 + bias 7 = 9 = 1001.
5. Sign: 0 (positive).

  0 | 1001 | 0111
  s   exp    mantissa

Decode the same way: exponent 1001 = 9 - 7 = 2; mantissa 1.0111;
1.0111 x 2^2 = 101.11 = 5.75 ✓

Normalisation maximises precision by forcing the leading mantissa bit to be 1 (for two's-complement mantissas, 0.1… for positives, 1.0… for negatives — the pattern chosen so no precision is wasted). An unnormalised float wastes mantissa bits on leading zeros.

Denormalisation / underflow and overflow: a number too small for the exponent field underflows to zero (or a denormal); too large overflows to "infinity". Rounding errors are inherent: 0.1 has no finite binary expansion, so (0.1 + 0.2 = 0.30000000000000004 in most languages). Quantisation error (rounding to the nearest representable value) is why money is stored in integer pence, not floats — an exam favourite.

Arithmetic with the 5.75 float encoding: add 2.5.

  2.5 = 10.1 = 1.01 x 2^1 -> exponent 1 + 7 = 8 = 1000, mantissa 0100
  To add, align exponents: shift the smaller mantissa right by (2-1)=1.
      1.0111 x 2^2
    + 0.1010 x 2^2      (1.010 x 2^1 shifted)
    ----------------
      10.0001 x 2^2
  Renormalise: 1.00001 x 2^3 -> mantissa 0000 (only 4 bits kept!), exponent 10.
  Answer: 1000.0 = 8. The true sum 5.75 + 2.5 = 8.25 - the lost fractional
  bits are precision loss, and questions ask you to name it.

Text, characters and codes

Characters are stored as agreed numeric codes. ASCII (7-bit, 128 codes: A = 65, a = 97, 0 = 48) covers Latin text and control codes; extended ASCII adds 128 more with 8 bits. Unicode (up to 21 bits per code point, over 140 000 characters) covers world scripts and emoji; UTF-8 stores common characters in 1 byte and rare ones in up to 4 — variable width, backwards compatible with ASCII, dominant on the web. Errors in text data are detected with parity bits or checksums at transmission level.

Images and sound at A Level depth

Multimedia data — graphics, images, sound and video — is where the representation choices become visible trade-offs between quality and size. Every format below is a different answer to the same question: which parts of the signal are worth keeping?

MediaRepresentationKey size factorsFormats
Graphics (bitmap)Grid of pixelsWidth × height × colour depthBMP, PNG, JPEG
Graphics (vector)Shape equations and coordinatesNumber of shapes and curvesSVG, PDF, CAD files
SoundSamples of amplitudeSample rate × bit depth × duration × channelsWAV, FLAC, MP3
VideoFrames of images plus sampled audioFrame size × colour depth × frame rate × durationMP4, MKV

Bitmap images: file size in bits = width × height × colour depth, plus metadata (dimensions, depth, DPI). 24-bit colour stores 8 bits each of red, green and blue (0–255 per channel); 1-bit is monochrome; palette modes (4-bit, 8-bit) index a colour table. Resolution (pixels) versus DPI (print density) are different ideas — the classic confusion. Vector graphics store shape equations (points, lines, Bézier curves, fills) and render at any resolution — smaller for logos and CAD, resolution-independent, but expensive for photorealistic images.

Sound is sampled: sample rate (Hz) × bit depth × duration × channels. Quantisation error (rounding each sample to the nearest level) and aliasing (insufficient sample rate; fixed by sampling at more than twice the highest frequency — Nyquist) are the A Level additions over IGCSE.

Worked: 60 seconds of stereo, 44.1 kHz, 16-bit, then compressed 4:1.

  bits = 60 x 44 100 x 16 x 2 = 84 672 000 bits
  bytes = 84 672 000 / 8 = 10 584 000 bytes
  MB (binary) = 10 584 000 / 1 048 576 = 10.09 MB
  compressed = 10.09 / 4 = 2.52 MB

Compression

Lossless methods remove statistical redundancy and restore the original exactly: run-length encoding (store runs as counts — great for large flat areas), dictionary compression (LZW-style: replace repeated strings with references to a dictionary — ZIP, PNG, GIF), and Huffman-style frequency coding (short codes for frequent symbols). Lossy methods discard perceptually minor detail: JPEG (frequency-domain discard), MP3 (psychoacoustic masking), used where the eye or ear cannot detect the loss. Choosing: documents and code demand lossless; photographs and music accept lossy.

Data types and abstraction

A data type defines a set of values and the valid operations on them: INTEGER (whole numbers, arithmetic), REAL (decimals, arithmetic with rounding), CHAR (single symbol), STRING (sequences of chars), BOOLEAN (true/false), DATE/TIME, plus user-defined types. Abstract data types (covered fully in the A2 notes) separate what a structure does from how it is stored. Casting between types has rules: integer to real is exact; real to integer truncates or rounds — 7.9 becomes 7 (truncate) or 8 (round); char to int gives its character code ('A' → 65).

Worked example: one value, three representations

The character 'K', the number -20, and the fraction 0.125 in the same memory:

'K'  : ASCII 75 = 0100 1011 (1 byte)
-20  : two's complement 8-bit: invert 0001 0100 -> 1110 1011, add 1 ->
       1110 1100. Check: -128 + 64 + 32 + 8 + 4 = -20 ✓
0.125: 0.001 binary exactly (2^-3). In the 4-bit-mantissa float: 1.0 x 2^-3;
       exponent -3 + 7 = 4 = 0100; mantissa 0000; value 0 | 0100 | 0000.
       Decode: 1.0000 x 2^-3 = 0.125 ✓

Same bytes, three meanings - the type system decides the interpretation.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Reading division remainders top-down instead of bottom-up in base conversion.
  • Grouping bits from the wrong end when converting binary to hex.
  • Treating the MSB of two's complement as +128 instead of −128, and applying unsigned overflow rules to signed arithmetic (or vice versa).
  • Forgetting the "+1" when negating, or negating twice without checking.
  • Omitting the normalisation step in floating-point questions (value = 1.mantissa × 2^(exp−bias)), or dropping the hidden bit when decoding.
  • Confusing resolution with DPI, or bits with bytes in size calculations (×8 / ÷8).
  • Claiming floats store money safely: quantisation error makes integer minor units the correct choice.
  • Choosing lossy compression for data that must restore exactly (text, executables, medical images).

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Unit 1, 4 marks). Convert 0.375 to 8-bit binary fixed point (4 integer, 4 fraction bits) and to normalised floating-point form.

Answer: 0.375 = 0.011₂ (0.25 + 0.125). Fixed point 4.4: 0000.0110. Floating point: 1.1 × 2⁻² (normalised), mantissa 1000 (after the hidden 1), exponent −2 + bias.

Question 2 (Unit 1, 4 marks). Show how −29 is stored in 8-bit two's complement and verify it.

Answer: +29 = 0001 1101; invert = 1110 0010; add 1 = 1110 0011. Verification: −128 + 64 + 32 + 2 + 1 = −29 ✓.

Question 3 (Unit 1, 5 marks). Explain normalisation and why a floating-point number is stored normalised.

Answer: Normalisation rewrites the mantissa so the first significant bit is directly before the binary point (1.m × 2^e), by shifting the point and adjusting the exponent. This maximises the precision of the stored mantissa: with a fixed number of mantissa bits, leading zeros would waste bits carrying no information. The leading 1 can then be implied (hidden bit), extending precision by one bit, and every value has exactly one encoding, so equality comparisons work.

Question 4 (Unit 1, 4 marks). Calculate the size in MB of an uncompressed 1600 × 1200 image at 8-bit colour, and state its size after 5:1 lossless compression.

Answer: 1600 × 1200 × 8 = 15 360 000 bits; ÷ 8 = 1 920 000 bytes; ÷ 1 048 576 = 1.83 MB. At 5:1 compression: 1.83 ÷ 5 = 0.366 MB, with the original exactly recoverable.

Question 5 (Unit 1, 3 marks). Explain why (0.1 + 0.2) ≠ 0.3 in floating-point arithmetic.

Answer: 0.1 and 0.2 have no finite binary expansions, so each is rounded to the nearest representable floating-point value when stored; the tiny rounding errors carry into the sum, giving 0.30000000000000004. Floating-point arithmetic is therefore approximate — which is why financial calculations use integer pence.

Question 6 (Unit 1, 4 marks). Compare vector and bitmap graphics for a company logo.

Answer: A logo must scale from a favicon to a billboard. Vector graphics store shape definitions (points, curves, fills), so they scale without pixelation, have small file sizes for simple art and are easily recoloured. Bitmaps store a fixed pixel grid: enlarging one pixelates and inflates the file. Vector is therefore correct for logos; bitmap suits photographs.

From the raw bits, the next step up is the machine that manipulates them: the processor.

Molecules, Transport and Health — AS Level Biology

This revision note belongs to the Edexcel International Advanced Subsidiary (IAS) Biology specification, WBI12 Unit 1, Topic 1 Molecules, Transport and Health. It covers water as a solvent and its structure, carbohydrates and lipids, proteins and their structure and function, gas exchange surfaces and Fick's law, the mammalian circulatory system and the cardiac cycle, haemoglobin and the oxygen dissociation curve, atherosclerosis and blood clotting, the risk factors for cardiovascular disease, diet, cholesterol and antioxidants, how people use scientific knowledge to reduce risk, the benefits and risks of treatments, and data analysis and evaluation in health studies — plus the gas exchange surfaces and enzyme practical work that support the topic. Every statement the topic is responsible for is covered in its own section or paragraph.

1. Water: structure, properties and why it is the solvent of life

Water is a small molecule with two hydrogen atoms covalently bonded to one oxygen atom; because the oxygen atom is much more electronegative than hydrogen, the shared electrons spend more time near the oxygen, so the molecule is polar — the oxygen end is slightly negative and the hydrogen end slightly positive. This polarity lets water molecules form hydrogen bonds with each other, which gives water its high specific heat capacity, its high latent heat of vaporisation, its cohesion (important for the transpiration stream in plants) and its solvent powers. Water is an excellent solvent because its polarity lets it surround and dissolve ions and polar molecules; ions become hydrated with water molecules around them, and polar molecules such as glucose dissolve readily. In transport, water's solvent nature lets it carry dissolved substances in blood and in plant tissue fluid and sap, and its dipole nature explains why it can do that — the partial charges interact with the charges of ions and the polar groups of molecules like glucose and amino acids.

2. Carbohydrates: monosaccharides, disaccharides and polysaccharides

Carbohydrates are made of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, with hydrogen and oxygen in the same ratio as in water (2:1). Monosaccharides are the simplest carbohydrates and are the building blocks — glucose, fructose and galactose are hexose monosaccharides with the formula C6H12O6. Disaccharides form when two monosaccharides join by a condensation reaction, losing a water molecule and forming a glycosidic bond; the common ones are maltose (glucose + glucose), sucrose (glucose + fructose) and lactose (glucose + galactose). Polysaccharides are long chains of monosaccharides; starch in plants is made of two polymers — amylose, a long unbranched helix of glucose, which is compact for storage, and amylopectin, which is branched so that glucose can be added or removed quickly from the ends. Glycogen is similar to amylopectin but more branched, and it is the storage carbohydrate in animals, mainly in liver and muscle cells. Cellulose is a structural polysaccharide of beta-glucose chains forming long, straight fibres that cross-link by hydrogen bonds into strong microfibrils; it forms plant cell walls. Carbohydrates provide and store energy: starch and glycogen store glucose in a compact, insoluble, osmotically inert form, so they do not affect the cell's water potential, and they can be hydrolysed back to glucose when needed for respiration.

3. Core Practical 1 — semi-quantitative tests for reducing sugars and starch

Use Benedict's reagent to estimate the concentration of reducing sugars and iodine solution to estimate the concentration of starch, using colour standards. Benedict's reagent (copper(II) sulfate, sodium carbonate and sodium citrate) turns from blue to green, then yellow, then orange, then brick-red as reducing sugars are heated with it — the colour depends on the concentration of reducing sugar. For a semi-quantitative estimate, prepare a range of known reducing sugar concentrations (for example glucose solutions), heat each with Benedict's, compare the colour with a colour standard chart, and record the colour or its code for each; then use the standards to estimate the concentration in an unknown. For starch, add iodine solution (iodine in potassium iodide) to the sample; a blue-black colour shows starch, and the intensity of the colour relates to the concentration — compare with colour standards to estimate. State the variables: the independent variable is the sugar or starch concentration, the dependent variable is the colour or colour standard, and controlled variables include the volume, temperature and time of heating.

4. Glycosidic bonds: condensation and hydrolysis

Monosaccharides join by condensation reactions to form disaccharides and polysaccharides, with a glycosidic bond formed between them and a water molecule lost each time. Conversely, polysaccharides and disaccharides can be hydrolysed — split by the addition of water — into their monomers; hydrolysis breaks the glycosidic bond and needs a water molecule for each bond broken. Glucose, fructose and galactose join to make maltose (glucose + glucose), sucrose (glucose + fructose) and lactose (glucose + galactose). Amylose and amylopectin are formed from alpha-glucose units; cellulose is formed from beta-glucose units, and because beta-glucose has a different orientation the chain is straight rather than coiled, so the hydrogen bonds between adjacent chains form strong microfibrils. Hydrolysis of starch gives maltose then glucose; hydrolysis of sucrose gives glucose and fructose; hydrolysis of lactose gives glucose and galactose. This matters in the body: dietary starch is hydrolysed to glucose in the gut by enzymes, and that glucose is used in respiration or stored as glycogen; lactose intolerance is caused by a deficiency of lactase, the enzyme that hydrolyses lactose, so lactose stays in the gut and causes problems.

5. Triglycerides: structure and saturated and unsaturated lipids

A triglyceride is made from one glycerol molecule and three fatty acids, joined by three ester bonds formed in condensation reactions; it is insoluble in water (hydrophobic). Fatty acids have a carboxyl group at one end and a hydrocarbon chain that may be saturated — no double bonds in the chain, so the molecule is straight and packs tightly, and saturated fats (and the triglycerides made from them) are usually solid at room temperature — or unsaturated, with one or more double bonds that kink the chain and prevent tight packing, so unsaturated fats are usually liquid at room temperature (oils). Lipids have several roles: they store energy in a compact, insoluble form (1 g of fat stores more energy than 1 g of carbohydrate), they form the phospholipid bilayer of all cell membranes, they form the myelin sheath around nerve fibres, they form a protective waterproof layer in the skin (subcutaneous fat), and they form steroid hormones. In membranes the phospholipid bilayer controls what enters and leaves the cell; the membrane also has proteins, cholesterol and glycoproteins.

6. Why animals need a heart and circulation

Many animals need a heart and a circulatory system because as an organism grows, diffusion alone is too slow to supply its cells with oxygen and nutrients and to remove waste — the surface area to volume ratio falls as size increases, and diffusion is only effective over short distances. A mass transport system (heart, blood vessels and blood) moves substances rapidly around the body, overcoming the limitations of diffusion. Blood carries oxygen, nutrients, hormones, waste products and defence cells and molecules. In simple organisms (small ones, or those with a large surface area to volume ratio or a thin body wall) exchange can happen directly by diffusion with the environment; larger or more active animals need a specialised exchange surface and a circulation system to move materials there and back.

7. The structure of arteries, veins and capillaries

Blood vessels relate their structure to their function. Arteries carry blood away from the heart at high pressure; they have thick, muscular, elastic walls to withstand and smooth the pressure and to help push the blood on, and a narrow lumen relative to wall thickness; they have no valves (except at the heart). Veins carry blood back to the heart at low pressure; they have thinner walls (less muscle and elastic tissue) and a wide lumen, and they have valves to prevent backflow, helping return blood when pressure is low. Capillaries are the exchange vessels; they have walls only one cell thick, a very narrow lumen just wide enough for red blood cells to pass in single file, slowing the blood and maximising the surface area for the exchange of substances. The structure of each vessel matches the pressure and role it plays.

8. The cardiac cycle and the structure of the mammalian heart

The mammalian heart is a muscular pump with four chambers — two atria (thin-walled, receiving chambers) and two ventricles (thick-walled, pumping chambers), with the left side pumping oxygenated blood to the body and the right side pumping deoxygenated blood to the lungs. The cardiac cycle is the sequence of events in a heartbeat: atrial systole (the atria contract, pushing blood into the ventricles), ventricular systole (the ventricles contract, pushing blood out into the pulmonary artery and aorta, and the atrioventricular valves close to prevent backflow, making the first heart sound), and diastole (the heart relaxes, the ventricles fill, the semilunar valves close, making the second heart sound). The valves ensure one-way flow: the atrioventricular valves (between atria and ventricles) and the semilunar valves (in the aorta and pulmonary artery). The left ventricle has a much thicker wall than the right because it must pump blood at high pressure around the whole body, whereas the right ventricle pumps only to the nearby lungs. The structure of the heart and its operation are shown by dissection (a recommended additional practical), and the heart's own rhythm is myogenic, starting at the sinoatrial node, though details of that are not needed at IAS.

9. Haemoglobin, oxygen transport and the oxygen dissociation curve

Haemoglobin transports oxygen in red blood cells. Each haemoglobin molecule has four polypeptide chains, each with a haem group that contains an iron ion that can combine with one oxygen molecule, so one haemoglobin can carry four oxygen molecules. The oxygen dissociation curve shows how much oxygen haemoglobin takes up at different oxygen tensions: at high oxygen tension (in the lungs) it becomes almost fully saturated, and at low oxygen tension (in respiring tissues) it releases oxygen; the shape of the curve means a small drop in oxygen tension in the tissues releases a lot of oxygen — this is important. The Bohr effect: as carbon dioxide concentration rises and pH falls, haemoglobin's affinity for oxygen falls and it releases oxygen more readily — so where respiration is high and CO2 is produced, haemoglobin unloads oxygen. Adult haemoglobin has a lower oxygen affinity than fetal haemoglobin, which has a higher affinity — this lets the fetus pick up oxygen from the mother's blood across the placenta, because fetal haemoglobin can take oxygen from adult haemoglobin. Carbaminohaemoglobin carries some carbon dioxide as well, so haemoglobin transports both oxygen and carbon dioxide.

10. Atherosclerosis: how it develops and why it matters

Atherosclerosis is the narrowing and hardening of arteries by plaques. The process begins with endothelial dysfunction — damage to the lining of the artery, by high blood pressure, by smoking chemicals, or by immune responses — then an inflammatory response follows, white blood cells (including phagocytes) move into the artery wall, LDL cholesterol is taken up and oxidised, smooth muscle cells multiply and fibrous tissue forms, and a plaque builds up (a fibrous cap over a lipid core). As the plaque grows it narrows the artery, raising blood pressure further and reducing flow; eventually a plaque may rupture, triggering blood clotting and a thrombus, which can block a coronary artery and cause a myocardial infarction (heart attack). The main risk factors — genetics, diet, age, gender, high blood pressure, smoking and inactivity — act through these mechanisms, and the disease shows why passive transport and diffusion alone cannot supply the larger, more active human body and why the heart and blood vessels are needed.

11. Blood clotting and its role in cardiovascular disease

Blood clotting forms a network of insoluble fibrin threads that traps platelets and red blood cells to form a clot and seal a wound. The process: damage to a blood vessel exposes platelets to the collagen in the wall, and they are activated and release thromboplastin; thromboplastin, in the presence of calcium ions, converts prothrombin (an inactive plasma protein) to thrombin; thrombin then catalyses the conversion of soluble fibrinogen to insoluble fibrin, which forms a mesh that traps platelets and red blood cells into a clot. Clotting is needed to prevent blood loss and to stop pathogens entering, but in cardiovascular disease a clot formed on a ruptured plaque can block a coronary artery and cause a myocardial infarction, or travel to block a cerebral artery and cause a stroke. Treatments to reduce clotting include platelet inhibitors such as aspirin, and anticoagulants such as warfarin, which slow the clotting cascade.

12. Risk factors for cardiovascular disease

Many factors increase the risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD), and most act through the mechanisms above. Diet high in saturated fats and cholesterol raises LDL levels and contributes to plaques; high blood pressure damages the endothelium and raises the risk of both atherosclerosis and clotting; age increases risk because damage accumulates and repair is less efficient; males are at higher risk at younger ages than females; smoking introduces chemicals that damage the endothelium and raise blood pressure and heart rate and reduce oxygen carried by haemoglobin; inactivity contributes to high blood pressure, obesity and high cholesterol; and genetics/family history affects a person's baseline risk. Risk is often the result of several factors combined, and reducing one can help even if others remain. People's perception of risk is often different from the actual risk — they may underestimate or overestimate the risk from diet and other lifestyle factors, and scientists work to clarify the real risks through studies.

13. Diet, cholesterol and antioxidants and the evidence for them

Dietary antioxidants (such as vitamins C and E from fruits and vegetables) may reduce the risk of CVD by preventing the oxidation of LDL cholesterol — oxidised LDL is taken up more readily by artery walls and contributes to plaque formation. Blood cholesterol level is an important indicator: total cholesterol and LDL cholesterol are linked to CVD, and HDL cholesterol helps remove cholesterol from the artery wall, so high HDL is protective. The evidence that cholesterol causes CVD comes from studies showing a causal relationship between blood cholesterol levels and cardiovascular disease, and from trials of the statins, which lower cholesterol and reduce CVD events. People use scientific knowledge about diet, body mass index (BMI = mass (kg) / height (m) squared) and waist-to-hip ratio (a measure of central obesity), exercise and smoking to reduce their risk of coronary heart disease — and they should distinguish between correlation and causation when interpreting the data, because two things occurring together does not by itself prove one causes the other.

14. Data analysis in health studies: correlation, causation and study design

Health studies use quantitative data on illness and mortality rates to determine health risks. Two things can be correlated without one causing the other — a third factor may cause both, or the relationship may be coincidental — so a key skill is distinguishing correlation from causation. A causal relationship for cholesterol and CVD is supported by mechanistic evidence (the biology above) plus the results of trials. When evaluating the design of studies used to determine health risk factors, consider the sample selection (is it representative, or biased, as in a sample of only one type of person or only volunteers) and the sample size (small samples are less reliable and more easily swayed by chance). Conflicting evidence exists because studies differ in design, in the populations studied, and in the measures used, and scientific decisions draw on the whole body of evidence, not one study.

15. Perceived and actual risk and why people's views differ

People's perception of risks is often different from the actual risks — they may underestimate risks due to diet and lifestyle because those risks feel distant and small, or overestimate them because of vivid or recent examples, or because of personal experience, cultural beliefs or poor understanding of the probabilities. Scientific knowledge can clarify the actual risk: for example, many people underestimate the risk from diet and inactivity for coronary heart disease even though the evidence is strong, and the gap between perception and reality is itself a reason to communicate the science clearly. Understanding that perception and reality can diverge is part of evaluating the use of scientific knowledge in making decisions about health, and it explains why public health messages must be carefully designed and evidence-based.

16. Treatments for cardiovascular disease: benefits and risks

Several treatments are used for CVD. Antihypertensives lower blood pressure, reducing the risk of endothelial damage and of heart strain. Statins lower blood cholesterol, reducing plaque formation and the risk of atherosclerosis. Anticoagulants (such as warfarin) and platelet inhibitors (such as aspirin) reduce clot formation, lowering the risk of a clot on a ruptured plaque causing a heart attack or stroke. Each has benefits and risks: antihypertensives can cause dizziness, fatigue or kidney effects and may over-lower pressure; statins can cause muscle pain, digestive upset and, rarely, liver effects; aspirin can cause bleeding, especially in the gut, and is not suitable for everyone. Decisions about treatment balance the degree of risk against the benefit, take the person's overall risk factors into account, and should be supported by the evidence — and by the science behind the disease, so that treatment targets the actual risk factors.

17. Core Practical 2 — vitamin C content of food and drink

Investigate the vitamin C content of food and drink, using DCPIP (2,6-dichlorophenolindophenol), which is blue when oxidised and colourless when reduced. Ascorbic acid (vitamin C) reduces DCPIP, so as vitamin C is added from a food or drink sample, the blue colour fades; the volume of a known concentration of vitamin C solution needed to decolorise a fixed volume of DCPIP gives a calibration, and the volume of the food or drink needed to decolorise the same DCPIP lets you estimate its vitamin C concentration by comparison. Carry out the test for several drinks (for example fruit juices, boiled and unboiled samples) to compare vitamin C content, and note that heat (boiling) destroys vitamin C, so boiled samples contain much less. Record volumes, identify the independent (volume of sample) and dependent (volume needed to decolorise DCPIP) variables, and control temperature, DCPIP volume and end-point judgement.

18. Proteins: amino acids, peptide bonds and the levels of structure

Amino acids are the monomers of proteins; the basic structure is an amino group, a carboxyl group and a variable R group attached to a central carbon. There are around 20 amino acids, differing in their R group, and the sequence of amino acids in a protein (primary structure) determines its folding and function. Amino acids join by condensation reactions to form peptide bonds, making dipeptides and polypeptides. Secondary structure is local folding into alpha-helices and beta-pleated sheets, held by hydrogen bonds between peptide bonds. Tertiary structure is the overall three-dimensional shape, held by hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, disulfide bonds and hydrophobic interactions; it determines the protein's function. Haemoglobin is a globular protein with four chains and four haem groups each carrying one oxygen; collagen is a fibrous protein of three polypeptide chains in a triple helix, strong for tendons and skin. Biuret reagent (copper(II) sulfate and sodium hydroxide) turns purple in the presence of peptide bonds, and a semi-quantitative method using it and colour standards can estimate protein concentration — that is a recommended additional practical.

19. Gas exchange surfaces and Fick's law

An effective gas exchange surface has a large surface area to volume ratio, a thin surface (short diffusion distance) and a difference in concentration between the two sides — the three properties that make diffusion rapid. The rate of diffusion is described by Fick's law: rate of diffusion = (surface area × concentration difference) / thickness of the surface, so increasing surface area or concentration difference, or decreasing thickness, increases the rate. The mammalian lung is adapted for rapid gaseous exchange: the alveoli provide a huge total surface area (about 70–90 m² in an adult), they are thin-walled (one cell thick, with a shared basement membrane) so the diffusion distance is very short, the air in the alveoli is highly oxygenated while the blood arriving is deoxygenated, so there is a steep concentration gradient, and the constant ventilation and blood flow maintain that gradient. Fick's law explains why these adaptations matter quantitatively.

20. Enzymes: specificity, catalysing reactions and factors that affect rate

Enzymes are biological catalysts that speed up reactions by lowering the activation energy needed. Their mechanism of action is explained by their three-dimensional structure: the active site has a specific shape that fits the substrate (the lock-and-key model) or changes shape to fit it (the induced-fit model), and specificity comes from the exact shape of the active site — each enzyme works on one or a few substrates. Enzymes are proteins, and heat, pH and the concentrations of enzyme and substrate affect their rate: each enzyme has an optimum temperature and pH; above or below the optimum the rate falls, and extremes denature the enzyme (irreversibly changing the shape of the active site, so it no longer works). Enzyme concentration increases the rate when substrate is in excess, and substrate concentration increases the rate up to a point, after which the enzyme's active sites are saturated and the rate levels off (maximum rate, Vmax). These effects are investigated in Core Practical 4.

21. Core Practical 4 — factors affecting enzyme rate

Investigate the effect of temperature, pH, enzyme concentration and substrate concentration on the initial rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction. For each factor, choose a suitable enzyme and substrate (for example amylase and starch, or catalase and hydrogen peroxide) and measure the initial rate — the rate in the first part of the reaction, before the substrate is used up or the enzyme denatures. Change the factor being tested in steps, keep the other factors constant (control variables), take several measurements, and calculate the initial rate from the slope of the graph of product formed (or substrate used) against time. For temperature, the rate rises with temperature to an optimum, then falls as the enzyme denatures; for pH, rate is highest at the enzyme's optimum pH; for enzyme concentration, rate rises linearly with concentration; for substrate concentration, rate rises and then levels off at Vmax. Plot graphs and explain the patterns in terms of collisions, activation energy and denaturation.

22. How to use this note and what to revise next

Use these notes section by section, checking that you can state the structure of a water molecule and explain its polarity, draw the structures of alpha-glucose and beta-glucose and state the difference, carry out the Benedict's and iodine semi-quantitative tests and explain the variables and the colour standards, draw a triglyceride and distinguish saturated from unsaturated, state the structure and function of arteries, veins and capillaries, describe the cardiac cycle and the structure of the heart, sketch the oxygen dissociation curve and explain the Bohr effect and fetal haemoglobin, describe the stages of atherosclerosis and blood clotting, list the risk factors for CVD and state how each acts, carry out the DCPIP and biuret practicals, describe the properties of a gas exchange surface and apply Fick's law, and explain enzyme specificity and the effects of temperature, pH and concentrations. After this topic, revise Topic 2 Membranes, proteins, DNA and gene expression, and Topic 3 Cell structure, reproduction and development — the transport and exchange ideas here underpin the circulatory and gas exchange systems in later topics.
