Worked example 2 (fourth quadrant). Find the argument of z = 3 − 3i.

|z| = √(9 + 9) = 4.243
tan⁻¹(-3/3) = -45 degrees, and the point is in the fourth quadrant
so the principal argument is -45 degrees (equivalently 315 degrees)

Multiplying and dividing in modulus-argument form

In Cartesian form multiplication is a bracket expansion; in modulus-argument form it is two separate, simple operations. That is the whole reason the form exists.

z1 z2:  multiply the moduli, add the arguments
z1/z2:  divide the moduli, subtract the arguments
z^n:    modulus^n, argument x n     (de Moivre's theorem)

Worked example. z1 = 2(cos 30° + i sin 30°) and z2 = 3(cos 80° + i sin 80°). Find z1z2 and z1/z2.

z1 z2 = 6(cos 110 + i sin 110)
z1/z2 = (2/3)(cos(-50) + i sin(-50)) = 0.667(cos 50 - i sin 50)

Worked example 2 (de Moivre). Find (1 + i)⁸.

|1 + i| = sqrt 2, arg = 45 degrees
(1 + i)⁸ = (sqrt2)⁸ (cos 360 + i sin 360) = 16(1 + 0i) = 16

Worked example 3 (geometric reading). Describe what multiplying by i does to a point on the Argand diagram.

i has modulus 1 and argument 90 degrees
so multiplying by i keeps the distance from the origin and adds 90 degrees
that is a quarter turn anticlockwise - multiplication as rotation

Roots of polynomial equations

Real-coefficient polynomials have complex roots in conjugate pairs. That single fact lets you go from one known root to two, halve the degree by dividing out a quadratic factor, and often finish the job with ordinary factorisation.

if a + bi is a root of a polynomial with real coefficients, then a - bi is too
the pair supplies the quadratic factor (z - (a+bi))(z - (a-bi)) = z² - 2az + (a² + b²)

Worked example. 2 + i is a root of z³ − 5z² + 9z − 5. Find all three roots.

conjugate pair: 2 + i and 2 - i
quadratic factor: z² - 4z + 5
divide: (z³ - 5z² + 9z - 5) / (z² - 4z + 5) = z - 1
roots: 2 + i, 2 - i, 1

Worked example 2 (forming an equation). Find the quadratic with roots 3 ± 2i.

sum = 6, product = 9 + 4 = 13
z² - 6z + 13 = 0

Loci on the Argand diagram

A locus question asks for the set of points satisfying a condition on a complex number, and every standard condition has a shape you should recognise without algebra.

ConditionShapeWhy
|z − a| = rcircle, centre a, radius rconstant distance from a point
|z − a| = |z − b|perpendicular bisector of abequidistant from two points
arg(z − a) = θhalf-line from a at angle θconstant direction, one-way
|z − a| ≤ rclosed discthe inequality includes the boundary

Worked example. Sketch the locus of |z − 3 − 4i| = 5 and state its centre and radius.

rewrite: |z - (3 + 4i)| = 5
circle, centre 3 + 4i, radius 5
it passes through the origin because |0 - 3 - 4i| = 5

Worked example 2 (inequality region). Describe the region |z − 1| < 2 and arg z > 45°.

inside the circle centre 1 radius 2 (not the boundary)
AND above the half-line from the origin at 45 degrees
the answer is the part of the disc lying above that ray

Exponential form and Euler's relation

The modulus-argument form is usually written more compactly as re^(iθ), using Euler's relation. That notation is not decoration: it makes the multiplication rules obvious, because exponentials multiply by adding their powers.

Euler: e^(i θ) = cos θ + i sin θ
so z = r e^(i θ)
z1 z2 = r1 r2 e^(i(theta1 + theta2))
z^n = r^n e^(i n θ)
z-bar = r e^(-i θ)

Worked example. Write z = 1 + i in exponential form and hence find z⁶.

r = sqrt 2, θ = π/4  →  z = sqrt2 e^(i π/4)
z⁶ = (sqrt2)⁶ e^(i 6 π/4) = 8 e^(i 3pi/2) = 8(cos 270 + i sin 270) = -8i

Worked example 2 (cos and sin from exponentials). Use Euler's relation to express cos θ in terms of exponentials.

e^(i θ) = cos θ + i sin θ
e^(-i θ) = cos θ - i sin θ
adding: 2 cos θ = e^(i θ) + e^(-i θ)
cos θ = (e^(i θ) + e^(-i θ))/2

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Powers) Simplify i^35. Answer: 35 = 4 × 8 + 3, so i^35 = i³ = −i.
  2. (Arithmetic) Write (5 − 2i)(3 + 4i) in the form a + bi. Answer: 15 + 20i − 6i − 8i² = 23 + 14i.
  3. (Division) Write (2 + i)/(3 − i) in the form a + bi. Answer: multiply by (3 + i): (5 + 5i)/10 = 0.5 + 0.5i.
  4. (Modulus) Find |4 − 3i|. Answer: √(16 + 9) = 5.
  5. (Argument) Find arg(−2 − 2i) in the principal range. Answer: third quadrant, so −135°.
  6. (De Moivre) Find (√3 + i)⁴. Answer: r = 2, θ = 30°, so 16(cos 120 + i sin 120) = −8 + 8√3 i.
  7. (Roots) 1 − 2i is a root of z² − 2z + 5 = 0. State the other root. Answer: 1 + 2i.
  8. (Locus) Describe |z + 2| = 3. Answer: circle centre −2, radius 3.
  9. (Locus) Describe arg(z − 1) = π/3. Answer: half-line from 1 at 60°, excluding the point itself.
  10. (Exponential) Write 2 − 2i as re^(iθ). Answer: r = 2√2, θ = −45°, so 2√2 e^(−iπ/4).

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Squaring the imaginary part only: (2i)² = −4, not 4i² left uncollected, and (a + bi)² has a middle term 2abi that is easy to drop.
  • Conjugate applied to the numerator: divide by multiplying both parts by the conjugate of the denominator only.
  • Argument in the wrong quadrant: tan⁻¹(b/a) returns a first-quadrant angle; add or subtract 180° to place it correctly.
  • Principal range ignored: an argument of 300° is written −60°, not 300°, when the question asks for the principal value.
  • Modulus of a sum: |z1 + z2| is not |z1| + |z2|; only products and quotients distribute over modulus.
  • Conjugate pairs assumed for complex coefficients: the pairing holds for real coefficients, which is the case in every exam question — but say so when justifying.
  • Locus with the wrong centre: |z − a| is a circle centred at a, not at −a; the sign inside the modulus flips the centre.
  • °/rad mode: de Moivre in radians while the question is in degrees gives a phase that is wrong by a factor of 57.3.

title: Algebra — Graphs — Study Notes
content:
Algebra — Graphs

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): straight lines (gradient, intercept), key curves (quadratic, cubic, reciprocal, exponential), tangents, kinematic reading.

1. Straight lines

  • Gradient m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁).
  • y = mx + c; parallel ⇒ equal m; perpendicular ⇒ m₁m₂ = −1.

Example: through (2, −1) parallel to y = 3x + 1: y + 1 = 3(x − 2) ⇒ y = 3x − 7.

2. Drawing curves

Table of values, plot, smooth curve. Parabola symmetry axis x = −b/2a. Recognise reciprocal y = 1/x (two branches) and exponential y = aˣ (through (0,1)).

3. Interpreting

  • Roots = x-intercepts; y-intercept from x = 0.
  • Turning points of quadratics by completing the square.

4. Tangents and rates

Gradient of tangent at a point = instantaneous rate: draw a large triangle, rise/run. Area under a speed–time graph = distance (trapezium estimate).

5. Graphical solutions

Simultaneous: intersection points. Quadratic = line: intersections give roots. Read off carefully to the accuracy allowed.

Exam tips: quote gradients as fractions where exact; when estimating a tangent gradient, use a triangle spanning at least 4 grid squares.

Plotting and reading straight-line graphs

A table of values is set up from the equation, points are plotted and joined with a ruler. For y = mx + c, m is the gradient and c the y-intercept. The gradient is the change in y divided by the change in x, measured on a large triangle drawn on the line, not between two points read from a table.

Quadratic and cubic curves

Curves are drawn freehand as smooth curves through plotted points. Turning points, roots (where the curve cuts the x-axis) and the y-intercept are read directly from the graph. A quadratic has one turning point; a cubic can have up to two.

Using graphs to solve equations

To solve f(x) = k, draw the line y = k and read the x-coordinates where it meets the curve. Intersections of two graphs give simultaneous solutions. Always state the solutions to the accuracy the question asks for.

title: System Software and Security — Study Notes
content:
`# System Software and Security

Cambridge International AS & A Level Computer Science 9618: sections 5 and 6 (System software; Security, privacy and data integrity), examined in AS Paper 1.

Operating System Roles

  • Manage memory (paging/segmentation, virtual memory to disk)
  • Schedule processes (round robin, priorities)
  • Handle I/O via device drivers and spooling
  • Provide the UI, file systems, and security (users, permissions)

Translators

  • Assembler: assembly → machine code (1:1)
  • Compiler: whole source → machine code, reports all errors, produces standalone executables
  • Interpreter: line-by-line execution, stops at first error, needs the interpreter present

Bytecode + VM (e.g. Java) combines both: compile once, run anywhere the VM exists.

Linkers and Loaders

Static linking copies library code into the executable; dynamic linking binds at runtime (smaller files, shared libraries). The loader places the program in memory, relocating addresses.

IDEs

Editors with syntax highlighting, autocompletion, debugger (breakpoints, stepping, variable watch), and integrated compilation.

Malware and Defences

Viruses, worms, trojans, spyware, phishing. Defences: antivirus (signature + heuristic scanning), firewalls (packet filtering by port/IP), sandboxing, user education, patches.

Exam tips: compare compiler vs interpreter with concrete error-handling differences; explain firewall rules using ports and addresses.

Malware types and prevention

A virus attaches itself to a file or program and needs a host to spread. A worm spreads across a network without a host file. A trojan looks like useful software but carries a hidden harmful payload. Phishing uses fake emails or websites to trick a user into revealing login details or other personal data.

A firewall monitors incoming and outgoing network traffic and blocks traffic that does not meet its rules. Anti-malware software scans for and removes known threats. Regular software updates close security weaknesses, and regular backups allow data to be restored after an attack.

Exam tip: match each threat to how it spreads, and each prevention method to the threat it stops. Do not confuse a virus with a worm.

Worked example: tracing a program through the toolchain

A programmer writes the source code for a calculator in a high-level language. A compiler translates the whole program into machine code before it runs, and reports syntax errors as a list. A linker then joins this object code with the library routines it calls, producing one executable file. A loader copies that executable into main memory and starts it. If the same program were run by an interpreter, each statement would be translated and executed in turn, so an error in line 40 would only appear when the program reached line 40.

Comparing translators

  • Compiler: translates everything first, produces a fast executable and a separate file for the output, and is harder to debug while running.
  • Interpreter: translates line by line, starts quickly and eases debugging, but runs more slowly because it translates again each time.
  • Assembler: converts assembly language, which uses mnemonics such as ADD and MOV, into machine code, with a one-to-one correspondence between each instruction and its binary form.

Why the operating system loads the program

The loader is part of the operating system's work of managing memory. It reserves space, places the instructions and data in that space and sets the starting address. Without this step the processor would not know where the program begins or which memory it may use.

Exam point: name the translator for each stage in the question, and state one advantage and one disadvantage of the translator the question describes.

title: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Right-Angled Trigonometry
content:
Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Right-Angled Trigonometry

Right-angled triangles are the most useful triangles in mathematics: Pythagoras relates the three sides, and the sine, cosine and tangent ratios relate sides to angles. Between them they solve every distance and angle problem the IGCSE sets, from ladders against walls to angles of elevation and three-figure bearings. This note builds the topic from zero: Pythagoras with its converse and 3D use, the SOHCAHTOA ratios with the selection method, exact values derived rather than memorised, and the multi-step problems that combine Pythagoras with trigonometry.

Pythagoras' theorem

in a right-angled triangle: a² + b² = c²
where c is the hypotenuse (the side opposite the right angle)

The theorem is a statement about areas: the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides. The converse identifies right angles: if a² + b² = c² for the longest side c, the triangle is right-angled — the standard test for 3-4-5 and 5-12-13 triangles.

Worked example 1. A right-angled triangle has legs 6 cm and 8 cm. Find the hypotenuse.

c² = 6² + 8² = 36 + 64 = 100
c = 10 cm

Worked example 2 (finding a leg). The hypotenuse is 13 cm and one leg is 5 cm. Find the other leg.

a² = 13² - 5² = 169 - 25 = 144
a = 12 cm

Worked example 3 (converse). Is a triangle with sides 7, 24, 25 right-angled?

7² + 24² = 49 + 576 = 625 = 25²
yes - right-angled, with the right angle opposite the 25 side

Pythagoras in three dimensions

In a cuboid, the space diagonal uses Pythagoras twice: first across the base, then up the height.

space diagonal = √(l² + w² + h²)

Worked example. A cuboid is 3 cm by 4 cm by 12 cm. Find the length of the space diagonal.

d = √(9 + 16 + 144) = √(169) = 13 cm

The three ratios: SOHCAHTOA

sin(θ) = opposite/hypotenuse      (SOH)
cos(θ) = adjacent/hypotenuse      (CAH)
tan(θ) = opposite/adjacent       (TOA)

Label the sides relative to the angle in question: the hypotenuse is always opposite the right angle; the opposite is across from the angle; the adjacent is the remaining side touching the angle. The selection method: mark the known side and the wanted side, then ask which ratio contains both.

Worked example 1 (finding a side). In a right-angled triangle, the angle is 35° and the hypotenuse is 12 cm. Find the opposite side.

known: hypotenuse; want: opposite  →  sine
sin(35) = opposite/12
opposite = 12 sin(35) = 12 × 0.574 = 6.88 cm

Worked example 2 (finding a side with cosine). Angle 40°, hypotenuse 20 cm; find the adjacent side.

cos(40) = adjacent/20
adjacent = 20 cos(40) = 20 × 0.766 = 15.3 cm

Worked example 3 (finding an angle). Opposite 5 cm, adjacent 9 cm. Find the angle.

tan(θ) = 5/9 = 0.5556
θ = tan-1(0.5556) = 29.1 °

For angles, use the inverse functions (sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹, tan⁻¹) and check the calculator is in degree mode — a radian-mode calculator turns 90° into 1.57 and ruins the paper.

Exact trigonometric values

Three angles have exact values worth knowing, derived from two special triangles:

Anglesincostan
30°1/2√3/21/√3
45°1/√21/√21
60°√3/21/2√3

Derivation: a 45-45-90 triangle with legs 1 has hypotenuse √2 (Pythagoras), giving sin 45 = 1/√2. An equilateral triangle of side 2 split in half gives a 30-60-90 triangle with sides 1, √3, 2, giving all six values. Deriving them once beats memorising them badly.

Two sanity checks keep the table honest: sine increases from 0 to 1 as the angle grows from 0° to 90°, so sin 30 must be smaller than sin 60; and cosine runs the other way, so cos 30 must be larger than cos 60. If an exact value breaks either ordering, the table has been misremembered.

Worked example. Find the exact value of sin 60° × tan 30°.

sin 60 = √(3)/2;  tan 30 = 1/√(3)
product = (√(3)/2) x (1/√(3)) = 1/2

Angles of elevation and depression

An angle of elevation is measured upward from the horizontal to an object; an angle of depression is measured downward. Both are measured from the observer's eye line, and the angle of depression from A to B equals the angle of elevation from B to A (alternate angles).

Worked example. From a point 40 m from the base of a tower, the angle of elevation to the top is 32°. Find the tower's height.

tan(32) = height/40
height = 40 tan(32) = 40 × 0.625 = 25.0 m

Worked example 2 (depression). A cliff is 60 m high; the angle of depression to a boat is 25°. Find the horizontal distance to the boat.

the angle at the boat is also 25 ° (alternate)
tan(25) = 60/d  →  d = 60/tan(25) = 60/0.466 = 128.7 m

Choosing the method: a decision routine

Most lost trigonometry marks come from choosing the wrong tool, not from arithmetic. The routine below takes ten seconds and removes the guesswork:

  1. Is there a right angle? If not, the question needs the sine or cosine rule (a different topic) — do not force SOHCAHTOA onto a triangle without a right angle.
  2. What do you know — two sides, or a side and an angle? Two sides with no angle means Pythagoras. A side and an angle means trigonometry.
  3. Which ratio? Mark the known side and the target relative to the given angle, then pick the ratio containing both: sin uses opposite and hypotenuse, cos uses adjacent and hypotenuse, tan uses opposite and adjacent.
  4. What is the unknown — a side or an angle? A side comes from multiplying; an angle needs the inverse function.

Worked example. A roof rafter is 4.5 m long and meets the horizontal at 38°. Find the vertical rise and the horizontal run.

rise: sin(38) = rise/4.5  →  rise = 4.5 sin(38) = 2.77 m
run:  cos(38) = run/4.5   →  run = 4.5 cos(38) = 3.55 m
check: 2.77² + 3.55² = 7.67 + 12.60 = 20.27 ~ 4.5²

Worked example 2 (finding the angle of a ladder). A 6 m ladder reaches 5.2 m up a wall. Find the angle it makes with the ground.

sin(θ) = 5.2/6 = 0.867  →  θ = 60.1 °

Multi-step problems: Pythagoras and trigonometry together

Many questions need both tools: Pythagoras to find a side in one triangle, trigonometry to use it in another. The method: draw and label every triangle, find the shared side first, then proceed.

Worked example. A ladder 5 m long leans against a wall, with its foot 2 m from the wall. Find the height reached and the angle the ladder makes with the ground.

height: h² = 5² - 2² = 25 - 4 = 21  →  h = 4.58 m
angle: cos(θ) = 2/5 = 0.4  →  θ = 66.4 °

Worked example 2 (two triangles). From a point P, the angle of elevation to the top of a building is 30°; from a point Q, 20 m closer, it is 45°. Find the height.

let h be the height and x the distance from Q to the base.
tan(45) = h/x  →  h = x
tan(30) = h/(x + 20)
h = (x + 20) tan(30) = (h + 20)(1/√(3))
h √(3) = h + 20  →  h(√(3) - 1) = 20
h = 20/(1.732 - 1) = 20/0.732 = 27.3 m

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Pythagoras) A right-angled triangle has legs 9 and 12. Find the hypotenuse. Answer: √(81 + 144) = √225 = 15.
  2. (Leg) Hypotenuse 17, one leg 8. Find the other. Answer: √(289 − 64) = 15.
  3. (Ratio) Angle 28°, adjacent 15 cm. Find the opposite side. Answer: tan 28 = o/15 → o = 15 × 0.532 = 7.98 cm.
  4. (Angle) Opposite 7, hypotenuse 10. Find the angle. Answer: sin θ = 0.7 → θ = 44.4°.
  5. (Exact) Find cos 30° exactly. Answer: √3/2.
  6. (Elevation) From 25 m away, the angle of elevation to a tree top is 40°. Find the height. Answer: 25 tan 40 = 25 × 0.839 = 21.0 m.
  7. (3D) A cuboid is 2 cm by 3 cm by 6 cm. Find its space diagonal. Answer: √(4 + 9 + 36) = √49 = 7 cm.
  8. (Combined) A ship sails 30 km east then 40 km north. Find its distance from the start and the bearing of its final position. Answer: distance = 50 km; tan θ = 40/30 → θ = 53.1°, bearing 053°.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Calculator mode: check DEG, not RAD or GRAD, before any trigonometric calculation. A radian answer is usually obviously wrong (tiny or huge), but only if you check.
  • Wrong ratio: label the sides relative to the angle before choosing SOH, CAH or TOA; picking by habit is the commonest trigonometry error.
  • Hypotenuse identification: the hypotenuse is opposite the right angle, not necessarily the longest-looking side on the diagram.
  • Pythagoras with the hypotenuse as a leg: c² = a² + b² only when c is the hypotenuse; finding a leg requires subtraction.
  • Rounding early: keep full calculator accuracy until the final answer; round to 3 s.f. (or 1 d.p. for angles unless told otherwise).
  • Angle of depression drawn from the wrong line: it is measured from the horizontal, not from the cliff face; the alternate-angle equality fixes the geometry.
  • Exact values with decimals: "exact" means surds and fractions, not 0.866; leaving √3/2 is required.
  • Missing units and labels: state cm, m, km and degrees; name the side or angle found, especially in multi-step problems.

Label the triangle before you reach for a ratio

Right-angled trigonometry is not three formulas to memorise; it is one decision made three times: which side am I given, which do I want, and which ratio connects them. Every error in this topic is a labelling error made before any calculation starts.

Only the hypotenuse is fixed. It is the side opposite the right angle, and it is always the longest. "Opposite" and "adjacent" are relative to the angle you are working with: in the figure, the side BC is opposite θ and AB is adjacent to it. Put the angle at C instead and those two swap. Annotate the diagram with O, A and H in pencil before choosing anything.

The ratios are ratios, which is why they work at any size. Similar triangles taught that corresponding sides scale together — double every side and the ratio stays the same. That is precisely why sin 30° is ½ for a triangle of any size:

sin θ = opposite / hypotenuse Key: θ = the angle inside the triangle; opposite = the side across from θ; hypotenuse = the side opposite the right angle.
cos θ = adjacent / hypotenuse Key: adjacent = the side next to θ that is not the hypotenuse.
tan θ = opposite / adjacent Key: the only ratio that does not use the hypotenuse.

Choosing in one step. Given an angle and one side, mark on the diagram which two sides the question involves, then read off: two sides with the hypotenuse means sine or cosine; two sides without it means tangent. Use the inverse function when the angle is the unknown.

Worked example. A ladder 5.0 m long leans against a wall, making 68° with the ground. How far up the wall does it reach, and how far is its foot from the wall?

height is opposite the 68° angle, ladder is the hypotenuse:

sin 68° = h / 5.0, so h = 5.0 × sin 68° = 5.0 × 0.9272 = 4.6 m

distance from the wall is adjacent:

cos 68° = d / 5.0, so d = 5.0 × cos 68° = 5.0 × 0.3746 = 1.9 m

Check with Pythagoras: 4.6² + 1.9² = 21.2 + 3.6 = 24.8 ≈ 25 = 5.0². That thirty-second check catches a swapped ratio every time, and the two answers being 4.6 and 1.9 rather than a plausible pair like 4.6 and 4.4 is exactly what the check is for.

The special angles come from two triangles. A 45-45-90 triangle with legs 1 gives sin 45° = 1/√2. Half of an equilateral triangle of side 2 gives sides 1, √3 and 2, hence sin 30° = ½, cos 30° = √3/2 and tan 60° = √3. These are worth deriving once so they are not three more things to memorise.

Where marks are lost. The calculator in radians or grads — check the mode before the first question, not after. Using the adjacent side when the question needs the opposite, because the labels were never written on the diagram. And rounding at 4.6 m then using 4.6 in Pythagoras: keep the full value and round only the answer.

Pythagoras' theorem in more depth

Pythagoras' theorem states that in a right-angled triangle the square of the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides, so c² = a² + b², where c is the hypotenuse. The theorem is used in two directions: to find a missing side when the triangle is known to be right-angled, and to test whether a triangle is right-angled at all. The subsections below cover both directions, the common number patterns, and the errors that cost marks.

Finding the hypotenuse

When the two shorter sides are known, add their squares and take the square root. For a triangle with shorter sides 5 cm and 12 cm, the hypotenuse is √(5² + 12²) = √(25 + 144) = √169 = 13 cm. The hypotenuse is always the longest side and always opposite the right angle, so it is the side that is added, not subtracted, in the calculation.

Finding a shorter side

When the hypotenuse and one shorter side are known, subtract the square of the known shorter side from the square of the hypotenuse, then take the square root. For a hypotenuse of 13 cm and a side of 5 cm, the missing side is √(13² − 5²) = √(169 − 25) = √144 = 12 cm. Write the subtraction out in full, because the most common error in this type of question is to add the squares by mistake.

Pythagorean triples

A Pythagorean triple is a set of three whole numbers that satisfy a² + b² = c². The most used are 3, 4, 5; 5, 12, 13; 8, 15, 17; and 7, 24, 25. Any multiple of a triple is also a triple, so 6, 8, 10 and 9, 12, 15 are triples. Recognising a triple lets you give an exact answer with no square root, which is often what the question wants when the sides are whole numbers.

Pythagoras in a problem with several triangles

Some questions need the theorem twice, because the first right-angled triangle gives a side that is needed in the second. For example, a rectangle 9 cm by 12 cm has a diagonal of √(9² + 12²) = 15 cm. If a second triangle uses that diagonal as one of its sides, the same method applies again. Mark the sides you have found on the diagram before starting the next step, so each calculation has its numbers ready.

Real-world problems with Pythagoras

A ladder leaning against a wall, a diagonal across a field and the straight-line distance between two towns are all Pythagoras problems once the right angle is identified. Draw the triangle, label the hypotenuse as the longest side, and state which right angle the theorem is being used at. A question that describes a route going east then north is a right-angled triangle formed by the two legs and the straight line between the ends.

Rounding and giving the answer

Leave square roots exact if the question asks for an exact answer, and give a decimal to the accuracy the question states. A calculation that gives √50 can be left as 5√2 for an exact answer, or written as 7.07 to 3 significant figures for a decimal answer. Do the rounding only at the last step, because rounding an intermediate square root and then squaring it can change the final answer.

Trigonometric ratios in more depth

The sine, cosine and tangent ratios connect an angle in a right-angled triangle to the ratio of two sides. They are defined by sin θ = opposite ÷ hypotenuse, cos θ = adjacent ÷ hypotenuse and tan θ = opposite ÷ adjacent, and the calculator supplies the values. The subsections below cover naming the sides, the two directions of use (finding a side and finding an angle), and why the ratios depend only on the angle.

Naming the sides from the angle

The three sides are named from the point of view of the angle θ you are using. The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle and is always the longest. The opposite side is the one across from θ, and the adjacent side is the one next to θ that is not the hypotenuse. The same side is the opposite side for one angle and the adjacent side for the other acute angle, so name the sides again for each angle rather than once for the whole triangle.

Finding a side when an angle is known

Choose the ratio that uses the side you know and the side you want. If the hypotenuse is 10 cm and the angle is 30°, and you want the opposite side, use sin 30° = opposite ÷ 10, so the opposite side is 10 × sin 30° = 10 × 0.5 = 5 cm. Writing the ratio first, with the unknown alone on one side, is the step that keeps the working correct.

Finding an angle from a ratio

When two sides are known, find the ratio and use the inverse function on the calculator. For opposite 7 and adjacent 24, tan θ = 7 ÷ 24 = 0.2917, so θ = tan⁻¹(0.2917) = 16.3° to 1 decimal place. Use sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹ or tan⁻¹ according to the pair of sides, and never take the inverse of a ratio that you have not first worked out.

Setting the calculator to degrees

Every trigonometry question in this note uses degrees, so the calculator must be in degree mode before any value is found. A calculator in radian mode gives sin 30 = −0.988, which is a wrong answer that looks like a real value. Check the mode at the start of each exam and again if an answer looks unreasonable. A quick test is that sin 30 should return 0.5 in degree mode.

Why the ratios depend only on the angle

Two right-angled triangles with the same angle are similar, so the ratio of opposite to hypotenuse is the same in both. A triangle with a hypotenuse of 10 and opposite of 5 has the same sin θ as one with hypotenuse 20 and opposite 10. This is why a table of sine values works for every triangle, and it is the reason the ratios can be used to find unknown sides.

Complementary angles

In a right-angled triangle the two acute angles add to 90°, so each is the complement of the other. This gives sin θ = cos (90° − θ) and cos θ = sin (90° − θ). For example, sin 30° = cos 60° = 0.5. The relationship is useful for checking a value, and it explains why sine and cosine are the same curve shifted by 90°.

Tangent as sine over cosine

The tangent ratio is the sine divided by the cosine, because tan θ = (opposite ÷ hypotenuse) ÷ (adjacent ÷ hypotenuse) = opposite ÷ adjacent. This is the form to use when a question gives the tangent of an angle and asks for a side, and it also explains why tangent is undefined at 90°, where the adjacent side would have length zero.

Trigonometry in three dimensions

Many three-dimensional questions are answered by finding a right-angled triangle inside a solid and then using the methods already covered. The skill is to see the triangle, not to learn a new rule. The subsections below cover the angle between a line and a plane, the diagonal of a solid, and the choice of triangle in a pyramid or cone.

Finding a right-angled triangle inside a solid

In a cuboid, a cone or a pyramid, pick the triangle that contains both the length you want and a length you know. The triangle must have a right angle, and that right angle is often at a vertex where an edge meets the base or where the height meets the base. Draw the triangle on its own, separate from the solid, with the known lengths marked on it. This makes the method the same as the two-dimensional case.

The diagonal of a cuboid

A cuboid with sides 3 cm, 4 cm and 12 cm has a base diagonal of √(3² + 4²) = 5 cm. The space diagonal is then found using the base diagonal and the vertical edge: √(5² + 12²) = √169 = 13 cm. Two applications of Pythagoras give the answer, and the first triangle lies flat on the base while the second stands on its edge.

The angle between a line and the base

To find the angle a space diagonal makes with the base, first find the base diagonal, then use the triangle formed by the vertical height, the base diagonal and the space diagonal. For a box with a base diagonal of 10 cm and a vertical height of 12 cm, the angle is tan θ = 12 ÷ 10 = 1.2, so θ = tan⁻¹(1.2) = 50.2°. The angle is measured between the line and the base, not the vertical.

Heights in pyramids and cones

The vertical height of a pyramid or cone meets the base at a right angle, so it forms a right-angled triangle with a line from the centre of the base to a corner or to the edge. For a square-based pyramid with base side 10 cm, the distance from the centre of the base to a corner is √(5² + 5²) = √50 = 7.07 cm to 2 decimal places. The slant edge then uses that distance and the vertical height.

Choosing the triangle that contains the answer

Ask what you need to find, then identify the triangle whose sides include it. If the question asks for an angle in a plane through the solid, use the triangle in that plane. If it asks for a length along a diagonal of the base, use the triangle in the base. Writing down the triangle you have chosen before any calculation prevents the common error of using lengths from two different triangles in one step.

Sketching a three-dimensional figure

A clear sketch is worth marks, because it shows the examiner which triangle you are using. Draw the solid as a simple outline, use dashed lines for hidden edges, and mark the right angle with a small square. Label the lengths you know and the one you want. A sketch that is a neat outline with the triangle shaded is enough, and it does not need to be drawn to scale.

Accuracy, units and reporting answers

A correct method can still lose the final mark through rounding too early, leaving out a unit or giving the wrong degree of accuracy. The syllabus asks for answers to a stated accuracy, and the examiner checks the final line against the question. The subsections below give the rules for rounding, units and presentation that apply to every right-angled trigonometry question.

Working with the calculator's full value

Keep the full calculator value in memory and round only the final answer, or round to at least one more significant figure than the answer requires. If a side is found as 7.0711… and then used in a second calculation, the rounded 7.07 can give a final answer that is one unit out. Use the stored value where the calculator allows it, or write intermediate answers to four significant figures at least.

Significant figures and decimal places

Read the question carefully for the accuracy it requires. "Give your answer to 3 significant figures" means the first three non-zero digits, so 16.2849 becomes 16.3 and 0.0034567 becomes 0.00346. "Give your answer to 1 decimal place" means one digit after the point, so 16.2849 becomes 16.3. The two rules differ for numbers below 1 and for numbers that are whole.

Giving exact answers

When an answer is a surd or uses an exact trigonometric value, give it exactly if the question asks for an exact value. A hypotenuse of √50 simplifies to 5√2, and sin 30° is exactly 1/2. If the question asks for a decimal, round the exact value at the end. An exact answer is always acceptable where the question says "exact", and a decimal is not.

Units in the final answer

Every length answer needs a unit, and the unit must match the question. If the sides are in centimetres, the answer is in centimetres, and an area is in square centimetres. A common error is to convert the unit partway through a calculation and forget to convert the final answer, so state the unit next to the number at every step and check it at the end.

Angles and the form of the answer

An angle answer is given in degrees to the accuracy asked for, with the degree sign. For bearings, the answer has three figures and is measured clockwise from north, as covered in the mensuration note. An angle of elevation or depression is given as a single angle from the horizontal, so check that the question asks for the angle from the horizontal and not from the vertical.

Estimating before calculating

Estimate the answer before using the calculator, so a wrong value is obvious. A side opposite a 30° angle in a triangle with hypotenuse 10 must be less than half the hypotenuse, so the answer cannot be 8. Estimating takes seconds and is the simplest protection against a wrong mode, a swapped ratio or a misplaced decimal point.

Checking the answer against the diagram

Compare the answer with the diagram once it is found. The longest side must be the hypotenuse, an angle opposite a longer side must be larger, and a side in a triangle with a 60° angle must not be shorter than one opposite a 30° angle. A result that contradicts the diagram means the wrong ratio or the wrong side was used, and the calculation should be repeated before the answer is written.

Presenting the working for method marks

Write each step on its own line: the formula or ratio, the substitution, the calculation, and the result with its unit. The method marks are given for the ratio and the substitution, even if the final number is wrong, so a clear working is worth marks in its own right. A bare final answer, even when it is correct, can earn only the marks for the answer.

title: Exam technique: Energy Work and Power
content:
### What earns the marks
For stores, mgh and half m v squared quoted earn one mark each. For efficiency, useful over total stated earns the method mark. For power, work over time with units earns the final mark.
### Traps
Error: efficiency above 100 percent claimed. Correction: impossible; check the ratio direction. Error: mass in grams mixed with kg units. Correction: convert to kg first. Error: power and energy units swapped. Correction: watts are joules per second.

title: Hardware and Logic Gates
content:
`# Hardware and Logic Gates

Logic Gates

ABANDORNANDNORXOR
0000110
0101101
1001101
1111000

NOT inverts; NAND is 'AND then NOT'; XOR outputs 1 when inputs differ.

Boolean Algebra Laws

  • De Morgan: (A·B)′ = A′ + B′; (A + B)′ = A′ · B′
  • Distribution: A·(B + C) = A·B + A·C
  • Absorption: A + A·B = A

Example: simplify A + A′B = (A + A′)(A + B) = A + B.

Constructing Circuits

Truth table → Boolean expression → gates. A half adder: S = A XOR B, C = A AND B.

Flip-Flops (Bistables)

  • SR latch: set/reset, invalid state S=R=1
  • JK: like SR but J=K=1 toggles
  • Clock signals synchronise state changes

Von Neumann Model

CPU (ALU, control unit, registers: PC, MAR, MDR, ACC) + memory + I/O, sharing one bus system; instructions fetched–decoded–executed in cycles.

Exam tips: write truth tables fully; simplify before drawing circuits to save gates, and name the law you use.

title: Further Mechanics — Study Notes
content:
Further mechanics: momentum, impulse and circular motion

This unit unifies two big ideas: momentum (with its conservation law) and circular motion (with its centripetal requirement). Both are favourite sources of longer exam questions.

Momentum and impulse

  • Momentum p = mv, a vector measured in kg m/s.
  • Impulse = force x time = change of momentum: F t = m(v - u). Units N s (equivalently kg m/s).
  • Newton's second law in momentum form: F = rate of change of momentum = m(v - u)/t.
  • A force-time graph has area = impulse.

Conservation of momentum

  • In a closed system (no external resultant force) total momentum before = total after. This is a vector law: in two dimensions, resolve along two perpendicular axes.
  • It holds for all collisions, explosions and separations.

Collisions

  • Elastic: total kinetic energy is conserved as well as momentum (e.g. perfectly hard spheres).
  • Inelastic: kinetic energy is not conserved — it transforms into heat, sound and deformation.
  • Perfectly inelastic: the bodies stick together; this gives the maximum kinetic energy loss.
  • In one dimension use simultaneous momentum (and, if elastic, energy) equations.

Circular motion

  • Angular speed: omega = 2 pi / T = 2 pi f = v / r.
  • A body moving in a circle at constant speed still accelerates: centripetal acceleration a = v^2 / r = omega^2 r, directed towards the centre.
  • The centripetal force is the resultant force towards the centre: F = m v^2 / r = m omega^2 r. It is not a new type of force — tension, weight, friction or normal reaction can supply it.

Vertical circles and pendulums

  • For a body on a string in a vertical circle, the string stays taut at the top only if v >= sqrt(g r).
  • Conical pendulum: a mass on a string sweeps a horizontal circle; with string length L at angle theta to the vertical, tan(theta) = v^2/(r g) and the period is T = 2 pi sqrt(L cos(theta)/g).
  • Banked track with no friction: tan(theta) = v^2/(r g); the normal reaction supplies the centripetal force.

Exam technique

  • Momentum is a vector: fix a positive direction and keep signs consistent.
  • Energy is scalar and never negative; check whether the collision is elastic before conserving energy.
  • For circles, draw the force diagram at the point of interest first, then resolve towards the centre.

title: IGCSE Mathematics: Fractions, Decimals and Percentages
content:
IGCSE Mathematics: Fractions, Decimals and Percentages

Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580 (2025–2027), section 1 Number: statement 1.4 Fractions, decimals and percentages (equivalence and conversion), 1.13 Percentages (including Extended reverse percentages) and E1.17 Exponential growth and decay. These three representations describe the same quantities, and fluent movement between them is one of the biggest sources of marks in both papers. The note explains why the conversion methods work before showing them, then builds percentages as multipliers — the technique behind most Paper 4 percentage problems.

What a fraction really is

A fraction is a division: 3/4 means 3 divided by 4, or three quarters of a whole. The top (numerator) counts the parts; the bottom (denominator) says how many equal parts the whole is cut into. A proper fraction has a smaller numerator (3/4); an improper fraction has a larger one (7/4); a mixed number combines a whole number with a proper fraction (1 3/4).

Convert 2 3/5 to an improper fraction:

2 wholes = 10 fifths, and 3 more fifths gives 13 fifths:
2 3/5 = (2 × 5 + 3)/5 = 13/5

Equivalent fractions are the same quantity written differently: 3/4 = 6/8 = 15/20, because multiplying top and bottom by the same number is multiplying by 1 (a form of 1, such as 3/3), which changes the look but not the value. Cancelling is the reverse: dividing top and bottom by a common factor. Only factors of the whole numerator and denominator can be cancelled — (x + 3)/(x + 2) cannot be simplified by cancelling the x's, because the top is a sum, not a product.

Converting between fractions, decimals and percentages

Fraction to decimal: divide.  3/8 = 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375
Decimal to fraction: read the place value.  0.47 = 47/100
Fraction to percentage: divide, then multiply by 100.  3/8 = 0.375 = 37.5%
Percentage to fraction: write over 100 and simplify.  45% = 45/100 = 9/20

Recurring decimals. A fraction always produces either a terminating decimal or a recurring one, and every recurring decimal converts back to a fraction by the algebra method:

Write 0.444... (4 recurring) as a fraction:

Let x = 0.444...
Then 10x = 4.444...        [shift the decimal one place]
Subtract:  10x - x = 4.444... - 0.444...
9x = 4
x = 4/9
Write 0.273636... (36 recurring) as a fraction:

Let x = 0.273636...
Two digits repeat, so shift two places:  100x = 27.363636...
100x - x = 27.3636... - 0.2736... = 27.09
99x = 27.09  →  x = 27.09/99 = 301/1100 after multiplying top and bottom by 100 and simplifying

Knowing the common conversions by heart saves time: 1/2 = 0.5 = 50%, 1/4 = 0.25 = 25%, 3/4 = 0.75, 1/5 = 0.2 = 20%, 1/8 = 0.125, 1/3 = 0.333... = 33 1/3%.

FractionDecimalPercentage
1/20.550%
1/40.2525%
3/40.7575%
1/50.220%
1/80.12512.5%
1/30.333...33 1/3%
2/30.666...66 2/3%

These seven values answer a surprising share of Paper 2 questions by inspection, and they anchor every conversion done the long way.

Percentages: the multiplier method

A percentage is a fraction out of 100 — literally per cent, per hundred. Every percentage problem is a multiplication, and the fastest method converts straight to a multiplier.

Find 35% of 240:

35% = 35/100 = 0.35, so  0.35 × 240 = 84

Increase 240 by 35%:
the new value is 135% of the old, so multiply by 1.35:  1.35 × 240 = 324

Decrease 240 by 35%:
the new value is 65% of the old, so multiply by 0.65:   0.65 × 240 = 156

Why the multiplier works. Increasing by 35% means keeping the original 100% and adding 35%, so the result is 135% of the original, which is 1.35 times it. Decreasing by 35% leaves 65%, which is 0.65 times. The multiplier also chains: successive changes multiply, which is why two discounts of 20% are not one discount of 40% (0.8 × 0.8 = 0.64, a 36% total reduction).

One quantity as a percentage of another:  18 out of 60

18/60 × 100 = 30%

Reverse percentages (Extended). Working backwards from a final value needs division:

A price after a 20% increase is £72. Find the original price.

The original is 100%, the new price is 120% of it, so the multiplier is 1.2:
original = 72 / 1.2 = £60

Check: 60 × 1.2 = 72 ✓

The common error is finding 20% of 72 and subtracting; the percentage must be taken from the original 100%, not the final amount.

Percentage change and comparisons

A coat falls from £80 to £56. Find the percentage decrease.

change = 80 - 56 = 24
percentage change = change / original x 100 = 24/80 × 100 = 30%

Percentage change always uses the original value as the denominator. Comparing quantities with different sizes — prices per 100 g, speeds, wages per hour — is done by putting both over a common quantity before comparing.

Exponential growth and decay (Extended)

When a quantity changes by the same percentage each period, it is multiplied by a fixed factor each time, and the result is exponential growth or decay. The multiplier is 1 + r for growth and 1 − r for decay, where r is the rate as a decimal.

After n periods at rate r:
growth:    final = original x (1 + r)^n
decay:     final = original x (1 - r)^n

Why the power. Each period multiplies by the same factor, so n periods multiply n times: an investment of £500 growing 3% a year becomes 500 × 1.03 after one year, 500 × 1.03 × 1.03 after two, and 500 × 1.03ⁿ after n years. The power counts the multiplications.

£500 is invested at 3% compound interest per year for 4 years.

500 × 1.03⁴ = 500 × 1.12550881 = £562.75 (2 d.p.)

Year by year check: 515.00 → 530.45 → 546.36 → 562.75 ✓
A car worth £18 000 depreciates 15% per year. Value after 3 years:

18 000 × 0.85³ = 18 000 × 0.614125 = £11 054.25

Exponential growth graphs climb ever faster and never touch zero; exponential decay graphs fall steeply at first and then level off towards — but never reach — zero (a horizontal asymptote). Doubling and halving questions are solved by logs or trial multiplication: for how many years does £500 at 3% exceed £600? Solve 500 × 1.03ⁿ > 600 by testing values of n, since 1.03ⁿ > 1.2 needs n ⩾ 7 years.

Worked example: a full percentage question

A shop sells a jacket for £84 after a 20% reduction. A further 10% discount is offered for cash.

Original price before the 20% reduction:
84 = original x 0.80
original = 84 / 0.80 = £105

Cash price after the extra 10%:
84 × 0.90 = £75.60

Total percentage saving against the original:
saving = 105 - 75.60 = 29.40
percentage saving = 29.40/105 × 100 = 28%

Check with multipliers: 0.80 × 0.90 = 0.72, so the cash price is 72% of the
original and the saving is 28% ✓

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Finding a percentage of the wrong amount: increase/decrease percentages apply to the original; reverse percentages divide by the multiplier.
  • Adding percentage changes: two 20% discounts give 0.8 × 0.8 = 0.64, a 36% reduction, not 40%.
  • Writing a recurring decimal as a fraction by eye; use the shift-and-subtract method and show it.
  • Cancelling across a sum: 3/4 is not 3 quarters of the top and bottom separately.
  • Using 365 days or 12 months inconsistently in compound problems: the power n counts compounding periods, so match it to the rate.
  • Forgetting that 15% decrease means multiplying by 0.85, not by −0.15 or 0.15.
  • Confusing 33% with 1/3 exactly: 1/3 = 33 1/3%, and the difference matters in exact answers.
  • Deciding an exponential decay value reaches zero; it falls below £1 or 0.001 but never reaches zero.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 2, 3 marks). Express 0.45 as a fraction in its lowest terms.

Answer: 0.45 = 45/100 = 9/20.

Question 2 (Paper 2, 3 marks). Write 0.27 with the 27 recurring as a fraction.

Answer: Let x = 0.272727...; then 100x = 27.2727...; subtracting gives 99x = 27, so x = 27/99 = 3/11.

Question 3 (Paper 4, 4 marks). In a sale, a bike is reduced by 15% to £255. Find the original price.

Answer: £255 represents 85% of the original, so the multiplier is 0.85 and the original price is 255/0.85 = £300. Check: 300 × 0.85 = 255 ✓.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 4 marks). A bacteria culture starts with 2000 and increases by 8% each hour. Find the size after 5 hours.

Answer: 2000 × 1.08⁵ = 2000 × 1.4693280768 = 2938.7 ≈ 2939 bacteria.

Question 5 (Paper 4, 3 marks). A town's population falls from 45 000 to 36 000 over a year. Find the percentage decrease.

Answer: Change = 9000; percentage = 9000/45 000 × 100 = 20%.

Question 6 (Paper 4, 5 marks). A car is bought for £12 000 and depreciates 18% in the first year and 12% in the second. Find its value after two years and the overall percentage loss.

Answer: 12 000 × 0.82 × 0.88 = 12 000 × 0.7216 = £8659.20. Overall loss = £3340.80, which is 3340.80/12 000 × 100 = 27.84% ≈ 27.8%. (Note 0.82 × 0.88 = 0.7216, a 27.84% total fall — not 30%.)

Fractions describe parts; powers and roots describe repeated multiplication — the next topic.

Fractions in practice: simplifying, adding and dividing

Most lost marks on fraction questions come from skipping one small step. Simplify early, find a common denominator before adding, and turn a division into a multiplication by the reciprocal. Each subsection below gives one rule and one fully worked number.

Simplifying by the highest common factor

To simplify a fraction, divide the numerator and the denominator by their highest common factor. For example, 6/8 has a highest common factor of 2, so 6/8 = 3/4. A fraction is fully simplified when the numerator and denominator share no factor except 1. Check this before you give a final answer, because an unsimplified fraction usually loses the accuracy mark.

Adding and subtracting fractions

Fractions can only be added or subtracted once they share a denominator. Write each over the lowest common multiple of the denominators. For 2/3 + 3/4, the common denominator is 12, so the sum is 8/12 + 9/12 = 17/12. Leave an improper fraction as a mixed number if the question asks for one: 17/12 = 1 5/12.

Multiplying fractions

Multiply the numerators together and the denominators together. Cancel common factors first, because it keeps the numbers small. For 2/3 × 3/5, the 3 on the top and the 3 on the bottom cancel, leaving 2/5. Do not add the denominators when multiplying, which is a common error.

Dividing fractions: keep, change, flip

To divide by a fraction, multiply by its reciprocal. Keep the first fraction, change the division to multiplication, and flip the second fraction. For 3/4 ÷ 2/5, write 3/4 × 5/2 = 15/8 = 1 7/8. A whole number divided by a fraction works the same way once the whole number is written over 1.

Converting between mixed numbers and improper fractions

To write a mixed number as an improper fraction, multiply the whole number by the denominator, add the numerator, and keep the denominator. So 2 3/5 = (2 × 5 + 3)/5 = 13/5. To go the other way, divide the numerator by the denominator: 13 ÷ 5 gives 2 remainder 3, so 13/5 = 2 3/5. Use whichever form the question's wording suggests.

Finding a fraction of an amount

To find a fraction of a quantity, divide by the denominator and then multiply by the numerator. Three eighths of 240 is 240 ÷ 8 = 30, then 30 × 3 = 90. Writing the fraction as a single multiplication, 3/8 × 240 = 90, gives the same answer and is quicker on a calculator.

Fractions in word problems

When a question says "two fifths of the class walk to school", the phrase "of" means multiply. Identify the whole first, because the fraction applies to that whole. If a quantity is left after a fraction is taken, subtract the fraction from 1 before you multiply. For example, if 3/8 of the money is spent, 1 − 3/8 = 5/8 is left.

Decimals in practice: place value, rounding and estimating

Decimal questions test place value more than arithmetic. Know which digit is the tenths, the hundredths and the thousandths, and round only once you have the final value. The subsections below cover the rules that appear most often in papers.

Rounding to decimal places and significant figures

To round to a number of decimal places, look at the digit after the last one you keep. If it is 5 or more, round up. For example, 0.004 56 rounded to 3 decimal places is 0.005, while rounded to 2 significant figures it is 0.0046. Significant figures count from the first non-zero digit, so the leading zeros in 0.004 56 do not count.

Multiplying and dividing by powers of ten

Multiplying by 10 moves every digit one place to the left, so 3.27 × 100 = 327. Dividing by 10 moves the digits one place to the right, so 0.5 ÷ 10 = 0.05. Use this rule instead of long multiplication when the multiplier is a power of ten. It is also how you check that a decimal point is in a sensible position.

Terminating and recurring decimals

A fraction in its simplest form gives a terminating decimal if its denominator has no prime factors other than 2 and 5. So 1/4 = 0.25 terminates, while 1/3 = 0.333… recurs. Recurring decimals are written with a dot or a line over the repeating digits. Knowing which fractions terminate helps you decide whether a decimal answer is exact.

Converting a recurring decimal to a fraction (Extended)

Let x = 0.363636…. Multiply by 100 because two digits repeat, so 100x = 36.363636…. Subtract the first equation from the second: 99x = 36, so x = 36/99. Simplify by 9 to get x = 4/11. The method works because the repeating part cancels out exactly.

Ordering decimals

To order decimals, compare the digits place by place, starting from the left. Pad the numbers with zeros so they have the same number of decimal places. Writing 0.7, 0.07 and 0.707 as 0.700, 0.070 and 0.707 makes the order clear: 0.07 is smallest, then 0.7, then 0.707. A common mistake is to think 0.707 is smaller than 0.7 because it has more digits.

Decimals in money and measurement

Money is written to two decimal places, so £4.5 should be written as £4.50 when you give a final answer. Measurements in decimal form convert with a power of ten: 3.5 km = 3.5 × 1000 m = 3500 m. Check that the unit in your answer matches the unit the question asks for.

Estimating answers before calculating

To estimate, round each number to one significant figure and calculate the result. For 49.8 × 0.31, use 50 × 0.3 = 15, which tells you the true answer should be close to 15. An estimate is a check, not an answer. If your calculator gives a value far from the estimate, you have probably mistyped a number or put the decimal point in the wrong place.

Percentages in practice: finding, reversing and compounding

Percentage questions are often about the base: the original amount that the percentage refers to. Each subsection below asks you to identify the base first, then choose a method that uses it. The multiplier method is the reliable choice in most cases.

Finding a percentage of an amount

To find 17.5% of 260, write 17.5% as the decimal 0.175 and multiply: 0.175 × 260 = 45.5. A percentage is always a fraction of 100, so dividing by 100 and multiplying by the percentage gives the same result. Use the multiplier method rather than a separate division step, because it leaves fewer places to make a mistake.

Reversing a percentage change

If a price rises by 20% to £36, the new price is 120% of the original, so the original is found by dividing by 1.2: 36 ÷ 1.2 = £30. Taking 20% off £36 gives £28.80, which is not the original price. This is the most common percentage error in examinations.

Percentage increase and decrease with multipliers

A 35% decrease is a multiplier of 1 − 0.35 = 0.65, and a 6% increase is a multiplier of 1.06. Multiply the original amount by the multiplier once. A quantity increased by 35% and then decreased by 35% does not return to its original value, because the two changes apply to different bases.

Repeated percentage change (compound growth)

If £1000 is invested at 5% a year and left for three years, each year multiplies the amount by 1.05. After three years the value is 1000 × 1.05 × 1.05 × 1.05 = 1000 × 1.05³ = £1157.63 to the nearest penny. The power of the multiplier equals the number of years, so the calculation does not need a separate step for each year.

Simple interest

Simple interest is calculated on the original amount only. The formula is I = PRT/100, where P is the principal, R is the rate per cent and T is the time in years. For £500 at 4% for 3 years, I = 500 × 4 × 3 / 100 = £60. Simple interest grows in a straight line, while compound interest grows faster each year.

Profit and loss as a percentage

Profit as a percentage is always taken of the cost price, not the selling price. An item bought for £40 and sold for £52 gives a profit of £12, and 12 ÷ 40 × 100 = 30%. Using the selling price as the base gives 23.1%, which is wrong. Identify the cost price in the question before you divide.

Comparing proportions expressed as percentages

To compare two results, convert each to a percentage of its own total. If 18 out of 45 students passed one test and 25 out of 60 passed another, the first pass rate is 18/45 = 40% and the second is 25/60 = 41.7%, so the second test had the higher pass rate. Comparing the raw numbers, 18 and 25, would mislead because the groups are different sizes.

Equations and symbols

The conversion cycle in one place: fraction ↔ decimal ↔ percentage, the multiplier that handles every percentage change, and the mixed-number rule. Non-calculator Paper 2 lives on these.

Fraction to decimal: divide. 3/8 = 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375 Key: the line means "a fraction is a division"; the numerator is divided by the denominator. Terminating here because 8 has only 2 as a prime factor; a denominator with any other prime gives a recurring decimal.

Fraction to percentage: divide, then multiply by 100. 3/8 = 0.375 = 37.5% Key: the decimal comes first, then ×100 moves the point two places; the % sign replaces the "per hundred" you multiplied by. Reversing it, divide by 100 and simplify.

Percentage to fraction: write over 100 and simplify. 45% = 45/100 = 9/20 Key: percent means "per hundred", so the denominator is 100 before simplifying; cancel by the highest common factor, 5 here. Leaving 45/100 is a lost mark in a "give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form" question.

2 3/5 = (2 × 5 + 3)/5 = 13/5 Key: the whole-number part (2) is multiplied by the denominator (5), the numerator (3) is added, and the result goes over the same denominator. This is the step needed before multiplying or dividing mixed numbers.

the new value is 135% of the old, so multiply by 1.35: 1.35 × 240 = 324 Key: 1.35 is the multiplier for an increase of 35% (100% + 35%, as a decimal); 240 is the original. The multiplier chains: 0.8 × 0.8 = 0.64 is not a 40% discount but a 36% one, which is the trap this line exists to close.

18/60 × 100 = 30% Key: 18 = the part; 60 = the whole; ×100 turns the fraction into a percentage. "18 out of 60" and "18 as a percentage of 60" are the same question, and the fraction is always part ÷ whole.

title: Complex Numbers — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Complex Numbers

Mathematics — A2 (9709). i² = −1. A complex number z = a + bi has real part a and imaginary part b. Two numbers are equal iff both parts match.

Key areas to revise

  • Basics
  • Conjugates
  • Argand Diagram
  • Modulus–Argument Form
  • de Moivre and Roots

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

### Worked example Use i² = −1. The sum (2 + 3i) + (1 − 4i) = 3 − i. The product (2 + 3i)(1 − i) = 2 − 2i + 3i − 3i² = 2 + i + 3 = 5 + i. The modulus of 3 + 4i is √(9 + 16) = 5. The conjugate of 2 + 3i is 2 − 3i, and z multiplied by its conjugate gives |z|² = 13.

Key points to remember

A complex number z = x + iy has real part x and imaginary part y, where i² = −1. To divide, multiply the numerator and denominator by the complex conjugate x − iy of the denominator. The modulus |z| = √(x² + y²) is the distance from the origin on an Argand diagram, and the argument is the angle from the positive real axis.

For a polynomial equation with real coefficients, complex roots occur in conjugate pairs: if 2 + 3i is a root then 2 − 3i is also a root. Use this to factorise a quadratic with no real roots. Sketch the Argand diagram when a question asks about a locus or region, and check that your answer agrees with the picture.

title: Databases and Data Definition — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Databases and Data Definition

Computer Science — A2. A table (relation) stores rows (tuples) and columns (attributes). The primary key uniquely identifies each row; a foreign key references a primary key in another table, creating the relationship. A composite key uses two or more columns together.

Key areas to revise

  • Relational Concepts
  • Normalisation
  • DDL and DML
  • Transactions and Concurrency

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

### Worked example CREATE TABLE Books (BookID INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, Title VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL, Price DECIMAL(6,2)); defines three columns. PRIMARY KEY makes BookID unique and non-empty, and NOT NULL means Title must have a value. VARCHAR(100) holds text up to 100 characters, and DECIMAL(6,2) stores a price with two decimal places. ### Check yourself Write a CREATE TABLE statement for Members with MemberID as the primary key, an Email column that must be unique, and a Joined date column with a default value. Check that each constraint matches what you have been asked to enforce.

title: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Statistics and Data Handling
content:
Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Statistics and Data Handling

Statistics is the art of describing a pile of numbers with a few well-chosen ones: an average to say where the middle lies, a spread to say how tightly the data cluster, and a chart to make the shape visible. The IGCSE questions test exactly that pipeline — classify the data, compute the averages and spread, draw or read the chart, and compare two distributions. This note builds the whole subject from zero: the data types, every average and measure of spread with the frequency-table method, the standard charts, cumulative frequency curves, and histograms with unequal class widths.

Classifying statistical data

TypeMeaningExamples
Qualitative (categorical)describes a quality, not a numberfavourite colour, blood group
Quantitativemeasured or counted as a numberheight, number of siblings
Discretecountable, separate values (usually integers)number of children, shoe size
Continuouscan take any value in a range (measured)height, time, mass

The classification decides which charts and averages are legal: a mode for categorical data, a median for ordered data, class intervals for continuous data. Discrete data are plotted as bar charts with gaps; continuous data as histograms with no gaps (and frequency density on the vertical axis).

Averages and range

mean = sum of values / number of values
median = middle value when ordered (mean of the two middle
         values for an even count)
mode = most frequent value (or class); none if no repeats
range = largest - smallest

quartiles: Q1 = lower quartile (25%), Q3 = upper quartile (75%)
interquartile range (IQR) = Q3 - Q1  (spread of the middle 50%)

The mean uses every value (sensitive to outliers); the median ignores extreme values (robust); the mode is the only average available for categorical data. When comparing two data sets, quote an average and a spread: "school A has a higher median but a larger IQR, so its results are higher on average but less consistent."

Worked example. Find the mean, median, mode and range of: 4, 7, 7, 9, 12, 15, 18.

mean = (4+7+7+9+12+15+18)/7 = 72/7 = 10.3 (3 s.f.)
median = 4th value = 9
mode = 7 (appears twice)
range = 18 - 4 = 14

Worked example 2 (even count). Find the median of 3, 5, 8, 10, 12, 15.

even count: average the 3rd and 4th values
median = (8 + 10)/2 = 9

Averages from frequency tables

mean = sum of (value x frequency) / sum of frequencies
median = the value at position (n + 1)/2 in cumulative order
mode = the value with the highest frequency

Worked example. The table shows goals scored: 0 (5 players), 1 (8), 2 (6), 3 (2). Find the mean and the median.

total players = 5 + 8 + 6 + 2 = 21
total goals = 0 × 5 + 1 × 8 + 2 × 6 + 3 × 2 = 0 + 8 + 12 + 6 = 26
mean = 26/21 = 1.24 (3 s.f.)
median position = (21 + 1)/2 = 11th value
cumulative: 5 (0 goals), 13 (1 goal) - the 11th value is 1
median = 1

For grouped data, use midpoints: the mean = Σ(midpoint × frequency)/Σfrequency, and the median comes from the cumulative frequency curve (below). The grouped mean is an estimate because the midpoint stands in for every value in the class.

Charts and diagrams

  • Bar chart: bars with gaps for categorical or discrete data; height = frequency.
  • Pie chart: angle = (frequency/total) × 360°; label the sectors with the category.
  • Pictogram: a symbol represents a fixed number; a half symbol represents half that number.
  • Stem-and-leaf: a sorted display that keeps the actual values; the key explains the split (e.g. 3|4 means 34).
  • Frequency polygon: plot frequency against the midpoint of each class and join with straight lines.

Worked example (pie chart). 40 students choose a sport: football 16, tennis 10, swimming 8, other 6. Find the angle for football.

angle = (16/40) × 360 = 144 °

Worked example 2 (pie chart reverse). A sector of 72° represents 9 students. How many students in total?

72 ° represents 9  →  360 ° represents 9 × 360/72 = 45 students

Cumulative frequency diagrams

A cumulative frequency table adds frequencies as you move up the classes. Plot cumulative frequency against the upper class boundary and join with a smooth curve; then read positions:

median at n/2
lower quartile at n/4
upper quartile at 3n/4
IQR = Q3 - Q1

Worked example. A cumulative frequency curve for 60 students' marks: Q1 = 42, median = 55, Q3 = 68. Find the IQR and interpret it.

IQR = 68 - 42 = 26 marks
The middle 50% of students scored within 26 marks of each other;

Always read across to the curve and then down to the horizontal axis — and use the class boundaries, not the midpoints, for the plot positions.

Histograms and frequency density

When class widths differ, the height of a bar cannot be the frequency — a wide class would dominate unfairly. Instead, the area of each bar is proportional to the frequency:

frequency density = frequency / class width
frequency = frequency density x class width (area of the bar)

Worked example. Class 0–10 has frequency 20; 10–20 has frequency 30; 20–40 has frequency 40. Find the frequency densities.

0-10: 20/10 = 2.0
10⁻²⁰: 30/10 = 3.0
20-40: 40/20 = 2.0

Reading a histogram backwards is the standard question: measure a bar's width and height, multiply to get the frequency, and read the class from the horizontal axis. Remember that the axes often use class boundaries, so a bar from 20 to 40 covers width 20.

Stem-and-leaf diagrams and frequency polygons

A stem-and-leaf diagram sorts data while keeping every value visible: the stem is the leading digit and the leaf the final digit, with a key such as 3|4 meaning 34. Interpreting one means reading the ordered leaves to find the median, the quartiles and the shape: the median is the middle leaf, Q1 and Q3 sit at the quarter and three-quarter positions, and the distribution's skew shows in where the leaves bunch.

A frequency polygon plots frequency against the midpoint of each class and joins the points with straight lines; it is the grouped-data equivalent of a line graph and makes comparisons between two distributions easy (plot both polygons on the same axes).

Worked example. The leaves for stem 4 are 1, 3, 3, 6, 8 and for stem 5 are 0, 2, 5. List the data in order and find the median.

values: 41, 43, 43, 46, 48, 50, 52, 55
n = 8, so the median is the mean of the 4th and 5th values:
(46 + 48)/2 = 47

Worked example 2 (interpreting). Explain what a long right-hand tail of leaves in a stem-and-leaf diagram indicates.

A long right tail means a few unusually high values: the data
are positively skewed, and the mean will be greater than the
median because the high values pull it upward.

Comparing distributions

Comparison questions want two statements: one about the average (which is higher) and one about the spread (which is more consistent). Use median and IQR together — they are robust to outliers — or mean and standard deviation when the data are symmetric and the syllabus supplies it.

Worked example. Class A: median 62, IQR 18. Class B: median 58, IQR 9. Compare.

Class A has the higher typical score (median 62 vs 58), but its
results are more spread out (IQR 18 vs 9), so Class B is more
consistent even though its middle score is lower.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Averages) Find the mean and range of 12, 15, 11, 19, 13. Answer: mean = 70/5 = 14; range = 19 − 11 = 8.
  2. (Frequency table) Values 1, 2, 3 with frequencies 4, 7, 9. Find the mean. Answer: (4 + 14 + 27)/20 = 45/20 = 2.25.
  3. (Median) Find the median of 2, 4, 4, 6, 9, 10. Answer: (4 + 6)/2 = 5.
  4. (Pie chart) A sector of 90° represents 15 people. Find the total. Answer: 15 × 360/90 = 60.
  5. (Cumulative frequency) For 80 values, where do you read the median? Answer: At cumulative frequency 40, reading across to the curve and down to the axis.
  6. (Histogram) A bar of width 5 has frequency density 4. Find its frequency. Answer: 5 × 4 = 20.
  7. (Frequency density) Class 30–50 has frequency 24. Find the frequency density. Answer: 24/20 = 1.2.
  8. (Compare) Two runners' times: A median 42 s, IQR 3 s; B median 40 s, IQR 8 s. Compare. Answer: B is faster typically (lower median) but less consistent (larger IQR); A is more reliable.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Median without ordering: the median is the middle of the ordered list. Forgetting to sort is the commonest data-handling error.
  • Even-count median: average the two middle values; do not pick one of them.
  • Grouped mean: use midpoints and label the answer an estimate — the midpoint is not the actual mean of the class.
  • Histogram heights: the vertical axis is frequency density, not frequency; area is the frequency. Reading the height as the frequency is the classic histogram error.
  • Cumulative frequency positions: plot against upper class boundaries and read the median at n/2 (not (n+1)/2 on the graph).
  • Pie chart arithmetic: check that the angles sum to 360° before answering the next part.
  • IQR direction: IQR = upper − lower quartile; a negative IQR means the quartiles are swapped.
  • Comparison claims: quote actual values ("median 62 vs 58"), not "better" without evidence.

title: Reading for Main Ideas and Detail — Study Notes
content:
Reading in English means knowing which reading method fits the task. Skimming, scanning and close reading are three different tools, and using the right one saves time and improves understanding.

Skimming

Skimming means reading quickly to get the general idea. Read the title, the first sentence of each paragraph, and any headings. Ask: what is this text about, and who is it for?

Scanning

Scanning means searching for a specific piece of information, such as a date, a name or a number. Move your eyes quickly over the text looking for the key word, and ignore everything else.

Main ideas

The main idea of a paragraph is the point the paragraph makes. It is often in the topic sentence, which is frequently near the start, but it is not always there. Ask: what do the other sentences support?

Supporting details

Supporting details are examples, facts, reasons and explanations that develop the main idea.

  • Main idea: The city is a centre of innovation.
  • Supporting detail: The city hosts three major universities and many technology firms.

Unknown words

When you meet an unfamiliar word:

  • Look at the words around it for clues.
  • Check whether the word is a familiar root with a prefix or suffix.
  • Decide whether you need its exact meaning to answer the question.

Do not stop reading to look up every word. Often the meaning is clear from context.

title: Differentiation — Study Notes
content:
Differentiation

Basic Rules

  • d/dx (xⁿ) = n xⁿ⁻¹
  • d/dx (k) = 0, d/dx (kx) = k

Example: y = 5x² − 3x gives dy/dx = 10x − 3.

Chain Rule

dy/dx = dy/du × du/dx.

Example: y = (3x − 1)⁵: dy/dx = 5(3x − 1)⁴ × 3 = 15(3x − 1)⁴.

Tangents and Normals

The tangent gradient at a point is dy/dx there; the normal gradient is −1/(dy/dx).

Example: y = x² at (2, 4): tangent y = 4x − 4; normal has gradient −1/4.

Stationary Points

Set dy/dx = 0, then classify with the second derivative:

  • d²y/dx² > 0 → minimum
  • d²y/dx² < 0 → maximum
  • d²y/dx² = 0 → test either side

Example: y = x³ − 3x: dy/dx = 3x² − 3 = 0 at x = ±1; d²y/dx² = 6x, so a maximum at x = −1 and a minimum at x = 1.

Rates of Change

dy/dx is a rate: if V = 4/3 πr³, then dV/dr = 4πr² links volume change to radius change.

Exam tips: always restart gradients from the derivative at the exact point, and answer rate questions with units.

title: Probability — Study Notes
content:
Probability

Basic Rules

For an event A with P(A) = p: 0 ≤ p ≤ 1, and P(A′) = 1 − P(A). For mutually exclusive events, probabilities add: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B). For events that can occur together, subtract the overlap:

  • P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B)

Venn Diagrams

Draw the universe first, then the events. Fill from the intersection outwards: if P(A) = 0.6, P(B) = 0.5 and P(A ∩ B) = 0.25, then only-A = 0.35, only-B = 0.25, neither = 0.15. Every region must sum to 1.

Tree Diagrams

Branch probabilities multiply along a path; outcomes at the end of complete paths add. Draw one branch set per stage of the experiment. For two draws without replacement from a bag of 5 red and 3 blue: P(RR) = (5/8)(4/7) = 20/56.

Conditional Probability

P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B) — the probability of A given that B has occurred. The condition shrinks the sample space.

Example: P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.4, P(A ∩ B) = 0.2. Then P(A | B) = 0.2/0.4 = 0.5, so A and B are independent since P(A | B) = P(A).

Independence

A and B are independent exactly when P(A ∩ B) = P(A)·P(B). Do not confuse independent (no influence on probabilities) with mutually exclusive (cannot co-occur). Mutually exclusive events with non-zero probabilities are never independent.

Exam tips: convert every "given that" into a conditional. With trees, label the second-stage branches with conditional probabilities; they are usually different from the first stage when drawing without replacement.

Exam method: combined events

The addition rule gives P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B). For mutually exclusive events the intersection is empty, so P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B). Draw a Venn diagram to place each probability in its region before calculating.

Independent events satisfy P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B). Test independence by checking this equation rather than assuming it, because the question may give the joint probability and ask you to decide.

The conditional probability P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B). Events are independent exactly when P(A | B) = P(A).

Tree diagrams suit sequential events without replacement. Multiply along each branch and add the branches that give the outcome required.

Exam cue: State whether events are independent or mutually exclusive, because the two are different and the formula depends on it.

Worked example: two aces without replacement

Two cards are taken from a standard pack of 52 without replacement. The probability that both are aces is (4/52) × (3/51) = 12/2652 = 1/221. Because the second draw depends on the first, multiply along the branches of the tree diagram and use the reduced totals (51 cards, 3 aces) on the second branch. If the first card were replaced, the answer would be (4/52)² = 1/169 instead.

Exam method: checking a tree diagram

The probabilities on the branches leaving any node must add to 1, so check each node before you multiply. The final probabilities at the ends of the branches must also sum to 1. For a question asking for "at least one", it is usually quicker to find the probability of none and subtract it from 1.

title: Number — Ratio, Rate and Proportion — Study Notes
content:
Number — Ratio, Rate and Proportion

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): ratio notation, sharing, direct & inverse proportion (including squares/cubes), unit rates.

1. Simplifying and sharing ratios

  • Scale both parts by the same factor: 250 g : 0.4 kg = 250 : 400 = 5 : 8.
  • Share $200 in 3 : 5 → 8 parts → $75 : $125.
  • Part–whole: 3 : 5 ⇒ 3/8 of the total. Given one share, find others by scaling.

Example: A : B = 3 : 4 and B : C = 2 : 5 ⇒ A : B : C = 3 : 4 : 10 (make B equal: ×2).

2. Direct proportion

y = kx. Best method: find the unit value, then multiply.

Example: 5 pens cost $3.25 → 1 pen $0.65 → 8 pens $5.20.

Squared/cubed proportion: y ∝ x². y = 54 when x = 3 ⇒ k = 6 ⇒ y = 6x²; at x = 5, y = 150.

3. Inverse proportion

y = k/x (product constant). 4 workers 6 days ⇒ 24 worker-days ⇒ 8 workers take 3 days. Square-law: y ∝ 1/x².

4. Rates

Unit rates (per item, per litre), exchange rates (draw the arrow to the target currency), best buys (price per unit, careful with multi-packs). Speed/density/pressure are compound-measure rates (Mensuration).

Exam tips: write the proportional equation with k before substituting; check proportion type — "more workers, fewer days" = inverse.

Writing and simplifying ratios

A ratio a : b is simplified by dividing both parts by their highest common factor. Ratios with decimals or fractions are multiplied up to whole numbers first. A ratio shared between a total uses the total number of parts as the divisor.

Direct and inverse proportion

In direct proportion, y = kx, so doubling x doubles y. In inverse proportion, y = k ÷ x, so doubling x halves y. Find k from a known pair of values, then use it to answer the question.

Speed, density and rates

Rate questions are solved by identifying the two quantities and the unit of the answer. Speed = distance ÷ time; average speed for a journey is the total distance divided by the total time, not the mean of the speeds. Exchange rates and recipe scaling use the same unitary method: find the value of one unit first.

Worked example: sharing in a ratio

Share 180 in the ratio 2 : 3 : 4. The ratio has 2 + 3 + 4 = 9 parts, so one part is 180 ÷ 9 = 20. The shares are 2 × 20 = 40, 3 × 20 = 60 and 4 × 20 = 80. Check the answer by adding the shares: 40 + 60 + 80 = 180.

Direct and inverse proportion

  • Direct proportion: 5 pens cost 3.50. The cost of one pen is 3.50 ÷ 5 = 0.70, so 12 pens cost 12 × 0.70 = 8.40.
  • Inverse proportion: 4 workers finish a job in 10 days. The total work is 4 × 10 = 40 worker-days. With 5 workers the job takes 40 ÷ 5 = 8 days. More workers means fewer days, so the product of the two quantities stays the same.

Average speed is not the mean of two speeds

A car travels 60 km at 60 km/h and then 60 km at 30 km/h. The first leg takes 1 hour and the second takes 2 hours, so the total distance is 120 km in 3 hours. The average speed is 120 ÷ 3 = 40 km/h, not the mean of 60 and 30, which would be 45 km/h. Always divide total distance by total time.

title: Measures of Variation and Standard Deviation — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Measures of Variation and Standard Deviation

Mathematics — A2. The range is max − min — quick but destroyed by a single outlier. Quartiles split ordered data into quarters: Q₁ at position (n + 1)/4, Q₃ at 3(n + 1)/4 (raw data). The interquartile range, IQR = Q₃ − Q₁, is the spread of the middle 50% and resists outliers. Outliers are commonly flagged as values beyond Q₁ − 1.5·IQR or Q₃ + 1.5·IQR.

Key areas to revise

  • Range and Quartiles
  • Variance and Standard Deviation
  • Grouped Data
  • Combining and Scaling Datasets

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.
