### Worked example Data are 2, 4 and 6. The mean is 4 and the deviations are −2, 0 and 2. The squared deviations sum to 8, so the population variance is 8/3 ≈ 2.67 and the standard deviation is √(8/3) ≈ 1.63. The range is 6 − 2 = 4. ### Check yourself Explain why the standard deviation is more useful than the range for comparing two data sets with the same range. The standard deviation uses every value, so it shows how the data are spread around the mean, while the range uses only the two extremes.

title: Exam technique: Algebra Inequalities
content:
### What earns the marks
For solving, calculate earns marks for each correct rearrangement step with the inequality sign carried through, and the final solution as an inequality or integer list as demanded. For integer-solution questions, list earns marks only for the complete correct set: show the solved inequality first, then enumerate. For combined inequalities, handle each side separately and intersect at the end.
### Traps
Error: forgetting to reverse the sign when dividing by a negative. Correction: circle every division by a negative and flip immediately. Error: answering x < 9 with 9 for the largest integer. Correction: step down one for strict inequalities. Error: including -1 in -1 < n <= 3. Correction: strict ends exclude, slack ends include.
### Worked example
Solve −2x > 6. Divide both sides by −2 and reverse the sign, giving x < −3. For a quadratic x² − 4 < 0, factorise to (x − 2)(x + 2) < 0. The product is negative between the roots, so −2 < x < 2.

title: Artificial Intelligence
content:
Artificial Intelligence

Cambridge International AS & A Level Computer Science 9618: section 18 (Artificial intelligence), examined in Paper 3.

AI Characteristics

Systems exhibiting: planning, learning, reasoning, problem-solving, perception, knowledge representation.

Machine Learning

  • Supervised: learns from labelled data (spam detection)
  • Unsupervised: finds structure in unlabelled data (clustering)
  • Reinforcement: learns by reward signals (game agents)

Training/evaluation loop: fit on training data, test on unseen data to avoid overfitting. Neural networks adjust weights via backpropagation.

Ethics of AI

Bias in training data → unfair outputs; opaque decisions → accountability gaps; job displacement; autonomous weapons.

An AI system learns from its training data. If that data over-represents some groups or reflects past prejudice, the system's outputs can be biased, and it may treat people unfairly without anyone intending it. Developers can reduce this by checking the training data and testing the system on a wide range of cases.

Worked example: a bias scenario

A facial recognition system is trained mostly on photographs of one group of people. When it is tested on a different group it misidentifies people far more often. The cause is sampling bias: the training data did not represent the people the system would be used on. The fix is to collect a training set that reflects the full user population, to test the system on each group separately, and to report the error rate for each group rather than one overall figure.

Bias can also come from the people who label the data. If labellers apply their own assumptions, those assumptions are learned by the model. Name the source of bias in your answer, because marks are given for identifying where the bias enters, not just for saying that it exists.

title: Coordination and Response
content:
Coordination and Response

Cambridge IGCSE Biology 0610, Extended route, topic 14 (statements 14.1–14.5). Nervous coordination and reflex arcs, sense organs and the eye, hormones including insulin and adrenaline, homeostasis, and plant tropic responses.

14.1 Nervous coordination

  • Neurones carry electrical impulses: sensory neurones from receptor to relay neurone, relay neurones within the spinal cord or brain, motor neurones to the effector. A reflex arc bypasses the brain for speed — the pathway is receptor, sensory neurone, relay neurone, motor neurone, effector.
  • The central nervous system is the brain and spinal cord, where impulses are coordinated. Synapses between neurones allow one-way transmission because the neurotransmitter is released from the presynaptic knob only.

14.2 Sense organs and the eye

  • The eye: light passes cornea, pupil, lens, retina. The lens changes shape (accommodation) — thicker for near objects, thinner for distant — controlled by the ciliary muscle and suspensory ligaments. The retina contains rods (dim light, many, not colour-sensitive) and cones (bright light, three types, colour vision).
  • Retinal inverted image is corrected by the brain interpreting the signals as upright.

14.3 to 14.4 Hormones and homeostasis

  • Hormones are chemical messengers in the blood from endocrine glands. Adrenaline prepares the body for action: increased heart rate, more blood to muscles, dilated bronchioles, higher blood glucose.
  • Insulin lowers blood glucose by promoting uptake and conversion to glycogen; glucagon raises it. Diabetes type 1 is caused by too little insulin; type 2 is when cells respond less to insulin.
  • Homeostasis is the maintenance of a constant internal environment. Blood glucose control is a negative feedback loop: rising glucose triggers insulin release, falling glucose triggers glucagon release.

14.5 Tropic responses

  • Phototropism: auxin moves to the shaded side of a shoot, causing cells there to elongate, so the shoot bends towards light. In roots, auxin at high concentration inhibits growth, so the root grows downwards — gravitropism.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Reflex arc reasoning, applied to why you move your hand from a hot plate before you feel pain: the reflex arc through the spinal cord is faster than a pathway up to the brain, so the effector responds first. Explain with the shorter pathway — that comparison is the mark.
  • Accommodation reasoning, applied to focusing on a near object: the ciliary muscle contracts, suspensory ligaments slacken, the lens becomes more curved and refracts light more strongly. State all four steps in order; each link is worth a mark.
  • Negative feedback explanation, applied to blood glucose after a meal: glucose rises, the pancreas detects it, insulin is released into the blood, cells take up more glucose and the liver converts it to glycogen, so glucose falls back to normal. Name the sensor, the effector and the response — a negative feedback answer needs all three.
  • Tropism mechanism, applied to a shoot tip exposed to unilateral light: auxin is redistributed to the shaded side, cells elongate faster there, and the shoot bends towards the light. Mention the inhibitor effect in roots for the full comparison when the question covers both.

Common errors

  • Saying insulin converts glucose to CO₂. It promotes glycogen conversion and uptake.
  • Calling the pupil the light-sensitive part. The retina detects light; the pupil is the opening.
  • Explaining tropism with "the plant wants light". Use auxin and differential growth.

title: IGCSE Physics (OxfordAQA): Particle Model of Matter
content:
Particle Model of Matter

Almost everything in this topic is one idea used repeatedly: matter is made of particles that are in constant random motion, and the energy of that motion explains the state, the temperature, the pressure and the density of a substance. A solid holds its particles in fixed positions, a liquid lets them slide past one another, and a gas lets them fly apart until they collide with a wall. Once you can picture the particles, the equations stop being things to memorise and become descriptions of that picture. This note builds the model, then uses it to explain density, changes of state, internal energy, specific and latent heat, and gas pressure.

3.4.1 Kinetic theory

The kinetic theory of matter states that all matter consists of tiny particles in continuous random motion, and that the energy of this motion increases with temperature. The three states differ in how strongly the particles are held and how much energy they have:

PropertySolidLiquidGas
ArrangementRegular lattice, particles close togetherIrregular, particles still close but free to slideFar apart, random
MotionVibrate about fixed positionsMove past one anotherMove fast in straight lines until they collide
Shape and volumeFixed shape and volumeFixed volume, takes the shape of the containerFills the container; no fixed shape or volume
CompressibilityAlmost incompressibleAlmost incompressibleEasily compressed, because of the empty space between particles
DensityHighestHighLowest
DiffusionVery slowSlowRapid

Density is mass per unit volume, and it explains why a heavy-for-its-size object sinks while a large light one floats.

ρ = m ÷ V

Key: ρ = density (kg/m³); m = mass (kg); V = volume (m³); 1 g/cm³ is 1000 kg/m³, so a conversion is usually needed.

Pressure in a gas comes from the collisions of its particles with the walls of the container. Each collision exerts a tiny force, and the total force spread over the wall's area is the pressure. Anything that increases the rate or the violence of those collisions increases the pressure: raising the temperature makes the particles move faster, and squeezing the gas into a smaller volume makes them hit the walls more often.

For a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature, pressure and volume are inversely proportional, so their product is constant.

p₁ V₁ = p₂ V₂

Key: p₁ and p₂ = pressure before and after (Pa); V₁ and V₂ = volume before and after (m³); the equation holds only while the temperature and the amount of gas stay constant.

Brownian motion is the evidence for the model. Smoke particles seen through a microscope move in a zigzag, random way because they are being struck unevenly by much smaller air molecules that are themselves in random motion. The smoke particles are far too large to move like that on their own, so something invisible must be hitting them.

3.4.2 Energy transfers and particle motion

Internal energy is the total energy in the kinetic and potential stores of all the particles in a substance. Heating a substance transfers energy to its particles and increases its internal energy, and this can happen in two different ways with very different effects.

  • If the energy increases the kinetic energy of the particles, their average speed rises and the temperature rises with it.
  • If the energy is used to overcome the forces holding the particles together, the arrangement changes and the substance changes state, but the temperature stays constant while the change is happening.

That second case is why a mixture of ice and water sits at 0 °C until all the ice has melted. The energy supplied is going into breaking the bonds between particles rather than into making them move faster, so the thermometer does not move even though energy is arriving.

E = m L

Key: E = energy transferred during the change of state (J); m = mass (kg); L = specific latent heat (J/kg), the energy needed to change the state of 1 kg without changing its temperature; the value is called the latent heat of fusion for melting and of vaporisation for boiling.

ΔE = m c Δθ

Key: ΔE = energy transferred to raise the temperature (J); m = mass (kg); c = specific heat capacity (J/kg °C); Δθ = temperature change (°C).

The two equations apply to different parts of the same heating curve. On the sloping sections of a temperature-time graph, ΔE = m c Δθ describes the rise. On the flat sections, where the temperature is constant while the state changes, E = m L describes the energy going in. Reading a graph is therefore a matter of deciding which of the two is happening.

Absolute zero is −273 °C, the temperature at which particles have the least possible kinetic energy. It cannot be reached, and at that temperature a gas would theoretically have zero volume. Converting between kelvin and degrees Celsius needs only one step: T = θ + 273, where T is the temperature in kelvin and θ the temperature in degrees Celsius.

Worked example: density of an irregular object

A stone has a mass of 84 g. When it is lowered into a measuring cylinder the water level rises from 50 cm³ to 82 cm³. Calculate the density of the stone in g/cm³ and in kg/m³.

Volume of the stone = 82 − 50 = 32 cm³. ρ = m ÷ V = 84 ÷ 32 = 2.6 g/cm³, which is 2.6 × 1000 = 2600 kg/m³.

Key: m = mass (g); V = volume displaced (cm³); 84 ÷ 32 = density (g/cm³); 1000 = the number of kilogrammes per cubic metre in one gramme per cubic centimetre.

The displacement method works because the stone takes the place of its own volume of water. It only fails for an object that floats, which needs a sinker, or one that absorbs water, which needs a waterproof coating.

Worked example: heating ice to steam

Calculate the energy needed to turn 0.40 kg of ice at 0 °C into water at 0 °C, taking the specific latent heat of fusion of water as 3.3 × 10⁵ J/kg.

E = m L = 0.40 × 3.3 × 10⁵ = 1.32 × 10⁵ J, or 132 kJ.

Key: m = mass (kg); L = specific latent heat of fusion (J/kg); E = energy (J); 10⁵ means one hundred thousand.

Heating that same water from 0 °C to 100 °C would need ΔE = m c Δθ = 0.40 × 4200 × 100 = 1.68 × 10⁵ J. Boiling it away would need 0.40 × 2.3 × 10⁶ = 9.2 × 10⁵ J, which is several times more again: breaking the forces completely, as in boiling, costs much more than loosening them, as in melting.

Worked example: compressing a gas

A gas occupies 300 cm³ at a pressure of 100 kPa. It is compressed to 120 cm³ at constant temperature. Calculate the new pressure.

p₂ = p₁ V₁ ÷ V₂ = 100 × 300 ÷ 120 = 250 kPa.

Key: p₁ = initial pressure (kPa); V₁ = initial volume (cm³); V₂ = final volume (cm³); p₂ = final pressure, in the same unit as p₁ because the volume units cancel.

The volume fell by a factor of 2.5, so the pressure rose by the same factor. Any consistent volume unit works in this equation, which is why cm³ is acceptable here while the density equation needs m³.

Worked example: a heating curve

A 0.50 kg block of a solid is heated at a steady rate of 200 W. Its temperature rises from 20 °C to 80 °C in 300 s and then stays constant for a further 600 s while it melts. Calculate the specific heat capacity of the solid and its specific latent heat of fusion.

Energy supplied while heating = P t = 200 × 300 = 60,000 J, so c = ΔE ÷ (m Δθ) = 60,000 ÷ (0.50 × 60) = 2000 J/kg °C. Energy supplied while melting = 200 × 600 = 120,000 J, so L = E ÷ m = 120,000 ÷ 0.50 = 2.4 × 10⁵ J/kg.

Key: P = power (W); t = time (s); ΔE = energy supplied (J); m = mass (kg); Δθ = temperature rise (°C); c = specific heat capacity (J/kg °C); L = specific latent heat (J/kg).

The longer flat section than sloping section is the signature of latent heat being the larger quantity, and the ratio of the two energies is the ratio of the two constants for that mass. Reading the graph correctly is worth as many marks as the arithmetic.

Typical mistakes

  • Saying particles in a solid do not move. They vibrate about fixed positions.
  • Describing a gas as having particles that "expand" when heated. The particles themselves do not change size; they move faster and spread further apart.
  • Using E = m c Δθ during a change of state, where the temperature does not change and the latent heat equation applies instead.
  • Mixing grammes and kilogrammes, which puts the density or the energy out by a factor of a thousand.
  • Giving the density in g/cm³ when the question asks for kg/m³, or forgetting to convert.
  • Thinking the temperature must rise whenever energy is supplied. During melting and boiling it does not.
  • Using p₁ V₁ = p₂ V₂ when the temperature is changing; the equation only holds at constant temperature.
  • Describing Brownian motion as the air molecules themselves being seen, when it is the much larger smoke particles that are observed.

Exam-style questions

  1. Explain, in terms of particles, why a gas can be compressed but a liquid cannot. Answer: A gas has large spaces between its particles, so they can be pushed closer together. In a liquid the particles are already touching, so there is almost no empty space to remove.
  2. A metal block has a mass of 2.0 kg and a volume of 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ m³. Calculate its density. Answer: ρ = m ÷ V = 2.0 ÷ 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ = 8000 kg/m³.
  3. Explain why the temperature of melting ice stays at 0 °C even though energy is being supplied. Answer: The energy is used to overcome the forces between the particles and change the state, not to increase their average kinetic energy, so the temperature does not rise until all the ice has melted.
  4. State what is meant by the specific latent heat of vaporisation. Answer: The energy needed to change 1 kg of a substance from liquid to gas at its boiling point, without changing its temperature.
  5. A gas at 120 kPa occupies 0.50 m³. It is allowed to expand to 1.5 m³ at constant temperature. Calculate the new pressure. Answer: p₂ = p₁ V₁ ÷ V₂ = 120 × 0.50 ÷ 1.5 = 40 kPa.
  6. Describe the motion of smoke particles seen in a microscope and explain it. Answer: They move randomly in a zigzag path because air molecules, which are too small to see, collide with them unevenly from all sides. This is evidence that air particles are in continuous random motion.
  7. Calculate the energy needed to raise the temperature of 0.25 kg of water by 40 °C, taking c as 4200 J/kg °C. Answer: ΔE = m c Δθ = 0.25 × 4200 × 40 = 42,000 J.
  8. Explain why a pressurised gas cylinder becomes warm when it is filled quickly. Answer: The gas is compressed quickly, so work is done on it and its particles gain kinetic energy, raising the temperature. In a slow fill the energy is transferred to the surroundings as it happens.

Revision checklist

  • I can describe the arrangement, motion and properties of particles in solids, liquids and gases.
  • I can calculate density and convert between g/cm³ and kg/m³.
  • I can explain gas pressure in terms of collisions with the container walls.
  • I can use p₁ V₁ = p₂ V₂ at constant temperature.
  • I can define internal energy and explain the difference between heating that raises temperature and heating that changes state.
  • I can use E = m L and ΔE = m c Δθ, and decide which one a section of a heating curve needs.
  • I can explain Brownian motion as evidence for random particle motion.
  • I can convert between degrees Celsius and kelvin and explain absolute zero.

title: A Level Mathematics: Sequences and Series
content:
A Level Mathematics: Sequences and Series

This note extends the AS work on arithmetic and geometric sequences into the A2 demands: sums to infinity with their conditions, recurrence relations and their closed forms, the σ notation manipulations, and the applied models — savings, depreciation, loan repayment and pendulum decay. It assumes the AS formulas and concentrates on the reasoning that distinguishes a secure A2 answer: why a series converges, when a model is valid, and how a recurrence becomes a formula.

Recap of the core formulas

arithmetic: u_n = a + (n - 1)d;  S_n = (n/2)[2a + (n - 1)d]
geometric:  u_n = a r^(n - 1);   S_n = a(1 - r^n)/(1 - r)
            S_inf = a/(1 - r) for |r| < 1

Worked example (mixed). The 4th term of a geometric series is 24 and the 7th is 192. Find a, r and S∞ if |r| < 1 (or state that it diverges).

ar³ = 24;  ar⁶ = 192
divide: r³ = 8  →  r = 2;  a = 3
|r| > 1, so the series diverges and S_inf does not exist

Convergence and the sum to infinity

A geometric series converges exactly when |r| < 1, because rⁿ → 0 and the term a rⁿ/(1 − r) vanishes. The condition is worth proving in words: each term is a fixed fraction of the last, so the running total approaches a limit rather than growing without bound.

S_inf = a/(1 - r)   exists only for |r| < 1

recurring decimals are geometric series in disguise

Worked example. Express 0.2̇7̇ (0.272727…) as a fraction.

= 0.27 + 0.0027 + 0.000027 + ...
a = 0.27, r = 0.01
S_inf = 0.27/0.99 = 27/99 = 3/11

Worked example 2 (find the range). For what values of x does 1 + 3x + 9x² + ... converge, and what is the sum?

r = 3x;  convergence needs |3x| < 1  →  |x| < 1/3
S_inf = 1/(1 - 3x)

Recurrence relations

u_(n+1) = a u_n + b

fixed point: L = aL + b  →  L = b/(1 - a)  (a not 1)
converges to L when |a| < 1

Worked example. u₁ = 5 and u_(n+1) = 0.5u_n + 6. Find the limit and the first four terms.

terms: 5, 8.5, 10.25, 11.125
limit L = 6/(1 - 0.5) = 12
the sequence rises towards 12 without reaching it

Worked example 2 (periodic). u_(n+1) = 1/(2 − u_n) with u₁ = 1. Find the first four terms and describe the behaviour.

u2 = 1/(2 - 1) = 1
so every term is 1: a constant sequence, a fixed point

σ notation and manipulation

sum from k = 1 to n of (ak + b) = a n(n+1)/2 + bn

split sums, factor constants, and shift the index as needed

Worked example. Evaluate the sum from k = 1 to 20 of (4k − 3).

= 4(20)(21)/2 - 3(20) = 840 - 60 = 780
check with the arithmetic formula: a = 1, d = 4, n = 20
S = 10(2 + 77) = 790  →  recheck: last term 4(20) - 3 = 77,
first term 1; S = (20/2)(1 + 77) = 780, agreement

Worked example 2 (geometric sum). Evaluate the sum from k = 1 to 8 of 3(2)^(k−1).

a = 3, r = 2, n = 8
S = 3(2⁸ - 1)/(2 - 1) = 3(255) = 765

Applied models

Worked example (savings with interest). 500 pounds is invested at the start of each year at 5% annual interest. Find the value after 10 years.

the first deposit earns 10 years, the last earns 1 year
value = 500(1.05¹⁰ + 1.05⁹ + ... + 1.05)
geometric: a = 500(1.05), r = 1.05, n = 10
S = 525(1.05¹⁰ - 1)/(0.05) = 525 × 12.578 = 6603 pounds

Worked example 2 (depreciation). A machine worth 20000 pounds depreciates 12% per year. When is it worth less than 5000?

20000(0.88)^n < 5000  →  0.88^n < 0.25
n ln 0.88 < ln 0.25  →  n > 1.386/0.1278 = 10.8
so after 11 years

Worked example 3 (bouncing ball). A ball is dropped from 3 m and rebounds to 70% of its previous height. Find the total distance travelled before it stops.

down 3, then up and down 3(0.7), 3(0.7)², ...
total = 3 + 2[3(0.7) + 3(0.7)² + ...]
= 3 + 2[3(0.7)/(1 - 0.7)] = 3 + 2(7) = 17 m

The doubling of the rebound terms is the standard trap: each bounce is travelled twice, up and down, except the initial drop. Sketching the first two bounces on a height axis makes the pattern obvious before any algebra is attempted.

Deriving the sum formulas

Both sum formulas are reconstructable in a few lines, which is worth more than memorising them: a candidate who can derive them never panics in an exam.

arithmetic: S = a + (a + d) + ... + [a + (n - 1)d]
write it backwards and add: 2S = n[2a + (n - 1)d]

geometric: S = a + ar + ... + ar^(n-1); multiply by r and subtract
S(1 - r) = a(1 - r^n)  →  S = a(1 - r^n)/(1 - r)

Worked example. Use the derivation to find S_12 for 4 + 10 + 16 + ...

a = 4, d = 6, n = 12
S = (12/2)[2(4) + 11(6)] = 6(74) = 444

Letting n grow in the geometric formula sends rⁿ → 0 when |r| < 1, leaving a/(1 − r): convergence falls out of the derivation rather than being a separate fact.

When is an arithmetic sum greatest?

If the common difference is negative, the terms eventually become negative and the running total peaks. Finding that peak is a standard A2 question.

terms stop increasing when a + (n - 1)d first becomes negative
sum is greatest just before the terms turn negative

Worked example. Find the greatest value of the sum of 50 + 47 + 44 + ...

d = -3; terms positive while 50 - 3(n - 1) > 0  →  n < 17.67
so keep 17 terms (last term 50 - 48 = 2)
S_17 = (17/2)(50 + 2) = 442

The 18th term is −1, so including it lowers the total: the maximum is at 17 terms. State the reason, not just the number.

Finding the number of terms

Many questions give the first and last terms and ask how many there are. Solve the nth-term formula for n rather than counting.

Worked example. How many terms are in 7, 11, 15, ..., 143?

143 = 7 + (n - 1)4  →  136 = 4(n - 1)  →  n = 35

Worked example 2 (geometric). How many terms of 2, 6, 18, ... are less than 5000?

2(3)^(n-1) < 5000  →  3^(n-1) < 2500
(n - 1) ln 3 < ln 2500  →  n - 1 < 7.13  →  n <= 8

For geometric sequences the log step is compulsory; for arithmetic ones simple rearrangement suffices. Round down for "less than" and up for "at least", and state the counting either way.

Three consecutive terms and the arithmetic mean

Many sequence questions give three consecutive terms involving an unknown and ask for the value that makes the sequence arithmetic or geometric. The condition is the definition, written as an equation.

arithmetic: middle = (first + third)/2
after canceling: the two consecutive differences are equal
geometric: middle² = first x third
after canceling: the two consecutive ratios are equal

Worked example. Find x so that x, x + 3 and 2x + 1 are consecutive terms of an arithmetic sequence.

(x + 3) - x = (2x + 1) - (x + 3)
3 = x - 2  →  x = 5
terms: 5, 8, 11 (difference 3) - check passes

Worked example 2 (geometric). Find x so that 4, x, 9 are consecutive geometric terms.

x² = 36  →  x = 6 or x = -6
both work; the sign changes whether the ratio is positive or negative

The geometric condition gives a square, so both signs survive unless context rules one out. That is exactly why the question usually adds a condition such as "all terms positive".

Formula summary

arithmetic: u_n = a + (n-1)d;  S_n = (n/2)[2a + (n-1)d]
geometric:  u_n = a r^(n-1);   S_n = a(1 - r^n)/(1 - r)
S_inf = a/(1 - r), |r| < 1
recurrence limit: L = b/(1 - a), |a| < 1

In applied questions the model choice decides everything: additive change is arithmetic, proportional change is geometric. Read the wording — "increases by 200 each year" versus "increases by 4% each year" — before writing a single formula, and check the first term corresponds to the first period rather than the starting quantity.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (S∞) Find S∞ of 5 + 2 + 0.8 + ... Answer: r = 0.4; 5/0.6 = 8⅓.
  2. (Convergence) For what x does 2 + 6x + 18x² + ... converge? Answer: |3x| < 1 → |x| < ⅓.
  3. (Recurring decimal) Write 0.4545... as a fraction. Answer: 45/99 = 5/11.
  4. (Recurrence) u_(n+1) = 0.2u_n + 8, find the limit. Answer: 8/0.8 = 10.
  5. (σ) Evaluate Σ from 1 to 10 of 5. Answer: 50.
  6. (σ arithmetic) Evaluate Σ from 1 to 15 of (2k + 1). Answer: 2(120) + 15 = 255.
  7. (Depreciation) 8000 pounds loses 10% annually. Value after 6 years? Answer: 8000(0.9)⁶ = 4252 pounds.
  8. (Unknown n) The sum of 3 + 6 + 12 + ... exceeds 1000 first at which term? Answer: S_n = 3(2ⁿ − 1) > 1000 → 2ⁿ > 334.3 → n = 9.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Using S∞ without checking |r| < 1: a divergent series has no finite sum; saying so earns the mark.
  • Off-by-one in applied models: count how many periods each payment earns; the first deposit earns one more year than the last.
  • Rebound counted once: every bounce after the first contributes twice to the distance.
  • Recurrence limit without the convergence condition: L = b/(1 − a) is only the limit when |a| < 1.
  • Mixing the models: growth uses (1 + r), decay and depreciation use (1 − r); inverting them changes the answer entirely.
  • Logs with a negative base factor: take ln of a positive quantity only; 0.88ⁿ is fine, (−0.88)ⁿ is not.
  • n must be a positive integer: inequality solutions are rounded up for "after how many years" questions.
  • Exact versus approximate: keep fractions and powers until the final money value, then round to the nearest penny or pound as asked.

Equations and symbols

Every relation this topic is examined on, written with its real notation and followed by a key naming each symbol, its unit and what it means. The sections above explain why each one is true; this sheet is the version to revise from, where the answer depends on reproducing the exact form and substituting into it without losing a unit.

Arithmetic and geometric, in both directions

uₙ = a + (n − 1)d and Sₙ = (n/2)(2a + (n − 1)d) = (n/2)(a + l)
Key: uₙ = the nth term; a = the first term; d = the common difference, uₙ₊₁ − uₙ; n = the term number; Sₙ = the sum of the first n terms; l = the last term included, uₙ. The (n − 1) is why the first term has no d added, and the second sum form is Gauss's pairing of the ends.

uₙ = a rⁿ⁻¹ and Sₙ = a(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r), r ≠ 1
Key: a = the first term; r = the common ratio, uₙ₊₁/uₙ; n = the number of terms; Sₙ = the sum of the first n. Each step multiplies by r, so the power is one less than the term number; r = 1 makes every term a and the sum na, which is the excluded case.

S∞ = a/(1 − r), valid only for |r| < 1
Key: S∞ = the sum to infinity; a = the first term; r = the common ratio. The condition is part of the answer, not a footnote: at |r| ≥ 1 the terms do not shrink and no finite sum exists, so writing the value without the condition loses a mark.

remainder after n terms = S∞ − Sₙ = a rⁿ/(1 − r)
Key: S∞ = the infinite sum, a and r as above; Sₙ = the sum of the first n; the difference is the tail still to be added. It shrinks geometrically, which is the algebraic form of the convergence argument.

arⁿ⁻¹ = X ⇒ n = 1 + log(X/a)/log r
Key: a = the first term; r = the common ratio, r > 0 for this form; X = the value of the term whose position is wanted; n = that position. Taking logarithms is the only way to free n from the exponent, and rounding up is usually required because n must be a whole number of terms.

Recurrence relations and their closed forms

uₙ₊₁ = a uₙ + b ⇒ limit L = b/(1 − a), reached only when |a| < 1
Key: uₙ = the current term; a = the multiplier; b = the constant added; L = the fixed point, the value satisfying L = aL + b. A recurrence with |a| < 1 creeps towards L without reaching it, one with |a| > 1 diverges, and |a| = 1 either repeats or drifts linearly.

uₙ = aⁿ⁻¹(u₁ − L) + L
Key: u₁ = the given first term; a, b = the recurrence constants; L = its fixed point b/(1 − a); n = the term number. Subtracting the limit turns the recurrence into a geometric sequence, which is why the closed form has this shape — it is the bridge between the two halves of the topic.

|uₙ − L| = |a|ⁿ⁻¹|u₁ − L|
Key: L = the limit; a = the recurrence multiplier; u₁ = the first term; the modulus is the distance from the limit after n terms. It is how "how many terms until it is within 0.01 of the limit" is answered, by solving an inequality in n with logarithms.

Sums in sigma notation

Σ_{r=1}^{n} r = n(n + 1)/2, Σ r² = n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6, Σ r³ = [n(n + 1)/2]²
Key: Σ = the sum; r = the index running from 1 to n; n = the last index. The three standard results every polynomial sum is built from; the cube sum being the square of the linear sum is worth recognising as a check.

Σ_{r=1}^{n} (A r + B) = A n(n + 1)/2 + B n
Key: A, B = constants; r = the index; n = the number of terms. Sums are linear, so a linear expression splits into the standard r-sum plus a repeated constant — no new formula needed.

Σ_{r=m}^{n} f(r) = Σ_{r=1}^{n} f(r) − Σ_{r=1}^{m−1} f(r)
Key: m = the first index wanted; n = the last; f = the term expression. Subtracting two running totals is the safe way to handle a sum that does not start at 1, rather than re-deriving.

Models and disguised series

0.ẋẏ̇ = a/(1 − r) with a = the repeating block over its place value and r = 10⁻ᵏ
Key: a = the first occurrence of the repeating block as a decimal; r = the ratio between consecutive blocks (10⁻² for a two-digit block, 10⁻³ for three); k = the block length. Every recurring decimal is a geometric series, which is why the fraction is always a rational number.

appreciation or depreciation: Aₙ = A₀(1 ± p/100)ⁿ
Key: Aₙ = the value after n periods; A₀ = the starting value, in the currency unit; p = the percentage change per period; n = the number of periods. It is a geometric sequence with r = 1 ± p/100, so the same convergence and log methods apply.

loan or savings balance: Bₙ₊₁ = Bₙ(1 + i) − R
Key: Bₙ = the balance after n payments, in currency; i = the interest rate per period as a decimal; R = the fixed repayment or withdrawal. This is uₙ₊₁ = auₙ + b with a = 1 + i and b = −R, so its long-term behaviour and closed form come straight from the recurrence results above.

title: Geometry — Angles and Polygons — Study Notes
content:
Geometry — Angles and Polygons

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): angle facts, parallel lines, polygon angles, circle theorems (Extended).

1. Core angle facts

  • Line 180°; point 360°; vertically opposite equal.
  • Parallel lines: corresponding (F), alternate (Z), co-interior (C, sum 180°).
  • Triangle 180°; isosceles/equilateral properties; exterior angle = sum of two remote interior angles.

2. Polygons

Interior angle sum = (n − 2) × 180°. Regular polygon: exterior = 360° ÷ n; interior = 180° − exterior.

Example: regular octagon: exterior 45°, interior 135°.

3. Circle theorems (Extended)

  1. Angle at centre = 2 × angle at circumference (same arc).
  2. Angle in a semicircle = 90°.
  3. Angles in the same segment are equal.
  4. Cyclic quadrilateral: opposite angles sum to 180°.
  5. Tangent ⊥ radius; two tangents from an external point are equal.
  6. Alternate segment theorem.

Quote the reason in brackets every time: "∠ACB = 62° (angles in same segment)".

4. Algebra with angles

Set up equations from the theorem: cyclic quad (2x + 10) + (3x − 5) = 180 ⇒ x = 35.

Exam tips: mark every found angle on the diagram immediately; use radii to create isosceles triangles; never leave a theorem unquoted.

title: System Software and Security — Study Notes
content:
`# System Software and Security

Operating System Roles

  • Manage memory (paging/segmentation, virtual memory to disk)
  • Schedule processes (round robin, priorities)
  • Handle I/O via device drivers and spooling
  • Provide the UI, file systems, and security (users, permissions)

Translators

  • Assembler: assembly → machine code (1:1)
  • Compiler: whole source → machine code, reports all errors, produces standalone executables
  • Interpreter: line-by-line execution, stops at first error, needs the interpreter present

Bytecode + VM (e.g. Java) combines both: compile once, run anywhere the VM exists.

Linkers and Loaders

Static linking copies library code into the executable; dynamic linking binds at runtime (smaller files, shared libraries). The loader places the program in memory, relocating addresses.

IDEs

Editors with syntax highlighting, autocompletion, debugger (breakpoints, stepping, variable watch), and integrated compilation.

Malware and Defences

Viruses, worms, trojans, spyware, phishing. Defences: antivirus (signature + heuristic scanning), firewalls (packet filtering by port/IP), sandboxing, user education, patches.

Exam tips: compare compiler vs interpreter with concrete error-handling differences; explain firewall rules using ports and addresses.

title: Numerical Measures of Central Tendency — Study Notes
content:
Central Tendency: Mean, Median and Mode

The Mean

For data x₁, ..., xₙ the mean is

  • x̄ = Σx/n

For a frequency table with midpoints x and frequencies f: x̄ = Σfx/Σf. The mean uses every value, so a single extreme value drags it — that is its main weakness.

The Median

The median is the middle value: position (n + 1)/2 for ordered raw data. With n even, average the two middle values. The median ignores the size of extreme values, so it describes skewed data more honestly. For grouped data, estimate the median by linear interpolation within the median class.

The Mode

The most frequent value. A dataset may have no mode or several. For grouped data the modal class is the one with the highest frequency density (frequency ÷ class width), not the highest frequency.

Effects of Data Changes

Adding a constant a to every value adds a to the mean and median (the mode too) but leaves the spread untouched. Multiplying every value by b multiplies mean and median by b.

Coding

Subtract a constant and divide by a convenient width: y = (x − a)/b. Then x̄ = b·ȳ + a. Coding simplifies arithmetic and always preserves the relationship — the coded mean decodes exactly.

Example: data 2, 4, 4, 10: mean = 5, median = 4, mode = 4. Change 10 to 100: mean = 27.5, median and mode unchanged — the mean chased the outlier.

Exam tips: always state which average you used and why. When asked to compare two distributions, pair a central measure with a spread measure; a mean without a spread is only half an answer.

title: A Level Mathematics: Coordinate Geometry
content:
A Level Mathematics: Coordinate Geometry

Coordinate geometry is the bridge between algebra and shape: every geometric object is described by an equation, and every geometric question becomes an algebraic one. This note starts from the two measurements that define a straight line — how far and how steep — and builds outwards to circles, tangents, chords and the discriminant conditions that decide whether a line meets a curve at all. The exam almost never asks for a definition; it asks you to combine two or three of these tools in one question, so each one is presented with the situation that calls for it.

Distance, midpoint and gradient

Everything else is built on three formulas. They come from Pythagoras and from averaging, and they are worth being able to derive rather than recall.

for A(x1, y1) and B(x2, y2):
distance AB = √((x2 - x1)² + (y2 - y1)²)     Pythagoras on the step
midpoint   = ((x1 + x2)/2, (y1 + y2)/2)            the averages
gradient m = (y2 - y1)/(x2 - x1)                   rise over run

Worked example. For A(2, −1) and B(8, 7), find the distance AB, the midpoint and the gradient.

distance = √(6² + 8²) = √(100) = 10
midpoint = ((2+8)/2, (-1+7)/2) = (5, 3)
gradient = 8/6 = 4/3

Worked example 2 (finding an unknown). The distance from (1, 2) to (4, k) is 5. Find k.

√(3² + (k-2)²) = 5
9 + (k-2)² = 25
(k-2)² = 16  →  k - 2 = 4 or -4
k = 6 or k = -2

Two answers, not one: the square root in the distance formula hides a sign, and examiners always intend both.

Forms of the equation of a straight line

Three forms, each suited to a different piece of information. Choosing the wrong one costs time, not marks, but the wrong one also invites arithmetic slips.

FormEquationUse when you know
gradient–intercepty = mx + cgradient and intercept, or for sketching
point–gradienty − y1 = m(x − x1)gradient and one point
generalax + by + c = 0the form most mark schemes quote

Worked example. Find the equation of the line through (3, −2) with gradient −1/2, in general form.

y + 2 = (-1/2)(x - 3)
2y + 4 = -x + 3
x + 2y + 1 = 0

Worked example 2 (two points). Find the equation of the line through (1, 4) and (5, 2).

m = (2 - 4)/(5 - 1) = -1/2
y - 4 = -0.5(x - 1)  →  y = -0.5x + 4.5
or x + 2y - 9 = 0

Parallel and perpendicular lines

Parallel means equal gradients. Perpendicular means the gradients multiply to −1, which is the same as one being the negative reciprocal of the other. Recognising that the negative reciprocal is a rotation by 90° prevents the common error of negating without inverting.

parallel: m¹ = m²
perpendicular: m¹ x m² = -1, so m² = -1/m¹

Worked example. Find the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining A(2, 5) and B(6, 1).

midpoint = (4, 3)
gradient AB = (1 - 5)/(6 - 2) = -1
perpendicular gradient = 1
equation: y - 3 = 1(x - 4)  →  y = x - 1

Worked example 2 (proving a right angle). Show that the triangle with vertices P(1, 1), Q(4, 2) and R(3, 5) is right-angled at Q.

gradient PQ = (2 - 1)/(4 - 1) = 1/3
gradient QR = (5 - 2)/(3 - 4) = -3
product = (1/3)(-3) = -1  →  perpendicular, so the angle at Q is 90 degrees

The equation of a circle

A circle is the set of points a fixed distance from a fixed centre, so the distance formula written with an unknown point gives the equation directly.

centre (a, b), radius r:   (x - a)² + (y - b)² = r²
expanded form: x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0
completing the square recovers the centre (-g, -f) and radius √(g² + f² - c)

Worked example. Find the centre and radius of x² + y² − 6x + 8y − 11 = 0.

complete the square in x: x² - 6x = (x - 3)² - 9
in y: y² + 8y = (y + 4)² - 16
so (x - 3)² + (y + 4)² - 9 - 16 - 11 = 0
(x - 3)² + (y + 4)² = 36
centre (3, -4), radius 6

Worked example 2 (finding the equation). Find the equation of the circle with diameter AB where A(1, 2) and B(7, 10).

centre = midpoint = (4, 6)
radius = half of AB = 0.5 √(6² + 8²) = 5
(x - 4)² + (y - 6)² = 25

The diameter shortcut is worth remembering: the angle in a semicircle is a right angle, so any point on the circle sees AB at 90°, which is another route into the same equation.

Tangents, normals and chords

A tangent touches the circle at exactly one point and is perpendicular to the radius there. That single fact generates almost every circle question in the paper.

to find the tangent at P on a circle:
1. gradient of the radius from the centre to P
2. tangent gradient = negative reciprocal
3. use point-gradient form with P

Worked example. Find the tangent to x² + y² = 25 at the point (3, 4).

centre is the origin, so radius gradient = 4/3
tangent gradient = -3/4
y - 4 = (-3/4)(x - 3)
4y - 16 = -3x + 9  →  3x + 4y = 25

Worked example 2 (chord). A chord of the circle x² + y² = 25 lies on the line y = 3. Find its length.

substitute: x² + 9 = 25  →  x² = 16  →  x = +/-4
endpoints (-4, 3) and (4, 3)
length = 8

Worked example 3 (perpendicular from the centre bisects a chord). Use that fact to find the distance from the centre to a chord of length 8 in a circle of radius 5.

half the chord = 4
distance = √(5² - 4²) = 3

Intersections and the discriminant

Substituting a line into a circle gives a quadratic. How many times the line meets the circle is decided by the discriminant, so a tangency condition is a discriminant-equals-zero condition.

substitute y = mx + c into the circle equation
b² - 4ac > 0: two intersections (secant)
b² - 4ac = 0: one intersection (tangent)
b² - 4ac < 0: no intersection

Worked example. Show that the line y = x + 5 is a tangent to x² + y² = 12.5, and find the point of contact.

x² + (x + 5)² = 12.5
2x² + 10x + 25 - 12.5 = 0
2x² + 10x + 12.5 = 0   →  divide by 2: x² + 5x + 6.25 = 0
discriminant = 25 - 25 = 0, so tangent
repeated root: x = -2.5, y = 2.5

Worked example 2 (finding an unknown gradient). Find the values of m for which y = mx is tangent to (x − 3)² + y² = 4.

substitute: (x - 3)² + m² x² = 4
(1 + m²)x² - 6x + 5 = 0
for tangency: 36 - 4(1 + m²)(5) = 0
36 = 20 + 20m²  →  m² = 0.8  →  m = +/- 0.894

Parametric circles and arcs

A circle can also be described by a parameter, which is often the easier form when a point has to move. For a circle of radius r centred at the origin, the point (r cos θ, r sin θ) traces it as θ increases.

x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ  satisfies x² + y² = r²
centre (a, b): x = a + r cos θ, y = b + r sin θ
this is why the modulus-argument form of a complex number is a point on a circle

Worked example. A point moves on x² + y² = 9 with x = 3 cos θ. Find y and the coordinates when θ = 60°.

y = 3 sin θ
at θ = 60: (3 cos 60, 3 sin 60) = (1.5, 2.598)

Worked example 2 (eliminating the parameter). Eliminate θ from x = 2 + 4 cos θ, y = −1 + 4 sin θ.

cos θ = (x - 2)/4;  sin θ = (y + 1)/4
square and add: ((x-2)/4)² + ((y+1)/4)² = 1
(x - 2)² + (y + 1)² = 16

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Distance) Find the distance between (3, −2) and (−1, 4). Answer: √(16 + 36) = √52 = 7.21.
  2. (Midpoint) The midpoint of AB is (5, 1) and A is (2, −3). Find B. Answer: B = (8, 5).
  3. (Line) Find the line through (0, 4) perpendicular to y = 2x + 1. Answer: y = −0.5x + 4.
  4. (Circle) State the centre and radius of (x + 2)² + (y − 5)² = 49. Answer: centre (−2, 5), radius 7.
  5. (Completed square) Find the radius of x² + y² + 4x − 6y = 12. Answer: (x+2)² + (y−3)² = 25, radius 5.
  6. (Tangent) Find the tangent to x² + y² = 20 at (2, 4). Answer: gradient of radius 2, tangent −0.5, so x + 2y = 10.
  7. (Chord) Line y = 2 cuts x² + y² = 13. Find the chord length. Answer: x = ±3, length 6.
  8. (Discriminant) Show y = 2x + 5 does not meet x² + y² = 4. Answer: 5x² + 20x + 21 = 0, discriminant 400 − 420 < 0.
  9. (Circle from diameter) Find the circle with diameter from (0, 0) to (6, 8). Answer: centre (3, 4), radius 5, (x−3)² + (y−4)² = 25.
  10. (Parametric) Eliminate θ from x = cos θ, y = 2 sin θ. Answer: x² + y²/4 = 1, an ellipse.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Perpendicular gradient half-applied: the negative reciprocal of 3 is −1/3, not −3; negating without inverting is the classic slip.
  • Radius squared: (x − a)² + (y − b)² = 49 has radius 7, not 49 — the right-hand side is r².
  • Sign of the centre: (x − 3)² means centre x = +3; students routinely write −3.
  • Completing the square with the constant: the −9 and −16 produced by completing the square must move to the other side, and forgetting them changes the radius.
  • One root from a squared distance: √(k−2)² = 4 gives two values; the geometry usually admits both.
  • Tangent versus normal: a tangent is perpendicular to the radius; the normal is along it. Read which is asked.
  • Intersections solved approximately: the discriminant route gives exact values and the marks; sketching loses the algebra marks.
  • General form left unsimplified: mark schemes quote ax + by + c = 0 with integer coefficients where possible, so clear the fractions.

title: Forces and Equilibrium — Study Notes
content:
Forces and equilibrium

Moment of a force

  • The moment of a force about a point is the force multiplied by the perpendicular distance from the point to the line of action of the force: moment = F × d⊥. Unit: N m.
  • Only the perpendicular component of the force produces a turning effect. A force that passes through the pivot has zero moment.

Principle of moments

For a body in equilibrium the sum of the clockwise moments about any point equals the sum of the anticlockwise moments about that point.

Couples

A couple is two equal and opposite parallel forces whose lines of action do not coincide. It produces a turning effect without a resultant force. The moment of a couple is F × d, where d is the perpendicular separation, and it is the same about every point.

Conditions for equilibrium

  • The resultant force in every direction is zero.
  • The resultant moment about any point is zero.

For three coplanar, non-parallel forces in equilibrium, the lines of action must meet at a single point.

Centre of gravity

The centre of gravity is the point through which the weight of a body appears to act. For a uniform symmetrical body it lies at the geometric centre.

Worked example: a uniform beam of weight 100 N rests horizontally on two supports at its ends. Each support carries half the weight, 50 N, because the beam is symmetrical and in equilibrium.

Exam tips: state the pivot you take moments about. Draw the perpendicular distance, not the slant distance. Show that the resultant force is zero in each direction before you use the principle of moments.

Conditions for equilibrium

A body is in equilibrium when the resultant force on it is zero and the resultant moment about any point is zero. For a body in equilibrium under three coplanar forces, the lines of action meet at a single point. The moment of a force about a pivot is Fd, where d is the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action. Taking moments about the pivot removes the unknown reaction force, which makes this a useful method in exam questions.

Exam tip: show the resolution of forces into horizontal and vertical components before you apply the equilibrium equations.

Worked example: a uniform beam on two supports

A uniform beam of length 4.0 m and weight 120 N rests on two supports, one at each end. Its centre of gravity is at its midpoint, 2.0 m from either support. Taking moments about the left support, the right-hand reaction R2 satisfies R2 × 4.0 = 120 × 2.0, so R2 = 60 N. Vertical equilibrium then gives R1 = 120 − 60 = 60 N. Checking that the two reactions add up to the weight is a quick way to catch an arithmetic or sign error.

Forces and moments in exam questions

Resolve forces into horizontal and vertical components before applying the conditions. For a body in equilibrium, the sum of forces in each direction is zero and the sum of moments about any point is zero. Choosing the pivot at the position of an unknown force removes that force from the moment equation, which often leaves a single equation to solve. A couple (two equal and opposite parallel forces) produces the same moment about every point, so it can be balanced only by another couple, never by a single force.

title: Sequences and Series — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Sequences and Series — Quick Revision Summary

A2 Mathematics: arithmetic and geometric sequences, the sums that go with them, convergence, and the standard results that turn a sigma into a formula. Recognise which type a sequence is before choosing a formula — that is the whole topic.

Arithmetic sequences

u_n = a + (n − 1)d Key: u_n = the nth term; a = first term; d = common difference; n = term number. The (n − 1) is the usual slip.

S_n = n/2 [2a + (n − 1)d] = n/2 (a + l) Key: S_n = sum of the first n terms; a = first term; d = common difference; l = last term. The second form is quicker when the last term is known.

Geometric sequences

u_n = a rⁿ⁻¹ Key: a = first term; r = common ratio; n = term number. The ratio is found by dividing any term by the one before it, and it may be negative.

S_n = a(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r) Key: S_n = sum of the first n terms; a = first term; r = common ratio, r ≠ 1. Use the equivalent a(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1) when r > 1 to keep the arithmetic positive.

S_∞ = a/(1 − r) for |r| < 1 Key: S_∞ = sum to infinity; a = first term; r = common ratio. The modulus condition is the mark: with |r| ≥ 1 the series diverges and the formula does not apply.

Standard summations

Σ r = n(n + 1)/2 Key: r runs from 1 to n; the result is the sum of the first n integers.

Σ r² = n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6 Key: r runs from 1 to n. For a sum that starts at r = 0 or at r = 5, subtract the part you do not want rather than re-deriving.

Recurrence relations

  • A recurrence defines each term from the previous one; list the first few terms to see whether it is arithmetic or geometric.
  • A recurrence of the form u_(n+1) = a u_n + b has a fixed point; the sequence converges to it when |a| < 1.
  • For "find the least n such that S_n > 1000", form the inequality with the sum formula and solve — do not add terms one at a time.

Exam traps

  • Using n instead of n − 1 in the nth term, especially when the sequence is given from u₀.
  • Applying the sum-to-infinity formula to a divergent series.
  • Losing the sign when r is negative — the terms alternate, and the sum formula still works.
  • For a "how many terms" question, checking the answer rounds the right way: too few terms fail the condition, so round up.

title: A Level Physics: Electric Fields and Capacitance
content:
A Level Physics: Electric Fields and Capacitance

Electric fields are the invisible architecture around every charge: the reason a balloon sticks to a wall, the reason a capacitor can store energy in a camera flash, the reason lightning finds a path. This note builds the topic from zero: what a field is and how field lines encode it, uniform and radial fields with their formulas, Coulomb's law and electric potential, and then capacitance — what it means to store charge, where the energy lives, and how a capacitor discharges exponentially. Every formula is derived or justified, and every calculation type is worked in full.

Electric fields and field lines

A field is a region where a force acts on a suitable object: an electric field exerts a force on a charge. Field lines are the map, drawn with three rules: they point in the direction of the force on a positive charge; their density indicates field strength (closer lines, stronger field); and they never cross. A positive point charge has lines radiating outward; a negative charge has them pointing inward; between two parallel plates the lines are equally spaced and parallel — a uniform field.

  • Uniform field: same magnitude and direction everywhere (between charged plates).
  • Radial field: strength falls with distance, direction along the radius (around a point charge or sphere).

Uniform electric fields

Between parallel plates separated by distance d with potential difference V, the field strength is constant:

E = V/d        (V m⁻¹ or N C⁻¹)

force on a charge in the field: F = Q E
so the acceleration of a particle of mass m: a = QE/m

The analogy: the field is a slope; a charge is a ball. Between parallel plates the slope is uniform, so the ball accelerates steadily — exactly like projectile motion with gravity replaced by QE, which is why electron beams deflect in parabolic arcs between deflection plates.

Worked example. Two plates 4.0 cm apart have a p.d. of 200 V. An electron enters the field.

E = V/d = 200/0.040 = 5000 V m⁻¹
force: F = eE = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ x 5000 = 8.0 × 10⁻¹⁶ N
acceleration: a = F/m_e = 8.0 × 10⁻¹⁶/9.11 × 10⁻³¹
            = 8.8 × 10¹⁴ m s⁻²  (toward the positive plate)

Coulomb's law: force between point charges

F = Q1 Q2 / (4 π ε₀ r²)

ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹ (permittivity of free space)
1/(4 π ε₀) = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²
r = separation between the charges (m)

The law is an inverse-square law like gravitation, but with two crucial differences: the force can attract or repel (like charges repel), and the constant is enormously larger. The 10³⁶ ratio between electric and gravitational forces between two protons is why gravity dominates the cosmos while electricity dominates chemistry.

Worked example. Two charges of +3.0 μC and −2.0 μC are 0.15 m apart in air. Find the force.

F = k Q1 Q2/r² = 8.99 × 10⁹ x (3.0 × 10⁻⁶ x 2.0 × 10⁻⁶)/0.15²
  = 8.99 × 10⁹ x 6.0 × 10⁻¹²/0.0225
  = 0.0539/0.0225 = 2.4 N  (attractive)

Electric field of a point charge

From Coulomb's law, the field strength at distance r from a point charge Q is the force per unit charge:

E = Q / (4 π ε₀ r²)        (N C⁻¹)

Compare with gravitational field strength g = GM/r²: same inverse-square shape, different constant and source. Field strength is a vector (direction is the force on a positive charge); field lines are denser near the charge, matching the 1/r² fall.

Worked example. Find the field strength 0.20 m from a +5.0 nC charge.

E = k Q/r² = 8.99 × 10⁹ x 5.0 × 10⁻⁹/0.040
  = 44.95/0.040 = 1.1 × 10³ N C⁻¹ (away from the charge)

Electric potential

Potential is the potential energy per unit charge at a point in a field, measured relative to infinity:

V = Q / (4 π ε₀ r)        (volts, J C⁻¹)

work done moving a charge: W = Q ΔV
relation to field strength: E = - dV/dr  (field is the
potential gradient; the minus sign means E points toward
decreasing potential)

The potential around a positive charge is positive and falls with distance; around a negative charge it is negative and rises toward zero at infinity. Equipotential surfaces are perpendicular to field lines — no work is done moving a charge along one.

Worked example. Find the potential 0.50 m from a −4.0 nC charge and the work needed to move a +2.0 nC charge there from infinity.

V = k Q/r = 8.99 × 10⁹ x (-4.0 × 10⁻⁹)/0.50 = -71.9 V
W = Q ΔV = 2.0 × 10⁻⁹ x (-71.9 - 0) = -1.4 × 10⁻⁷ J
The negative work means the field does the work - the charges attract.

Capacitors and capacitance

A capacitor stores charge on two conductors separated by an insulator. Its capacitance is the charge stored per volt:

C = Q/V        farad (F); 1 F = 1 C V⁻¹

parallel plates: C = ε₀ epsilon_r A/d

epsilon_r = relative permittivity of the dielectric,
A = plate area (m²), d = plate separation (m)

The analogy: a capacitor is a tank for charge, and capacitance is the tank's width — a wide tank (large C) holds more charge for the same pressure (voltage). The dielectric matters: inserting a material with ε_r > 1 (typically 2–10) multiplies the capacitance because the molecules polarise and reduce the effective field between the plates.

Worked example. A parallel-plate capacitor has plates of area 0.020 m² separated by 0.10 mm of air. Find C.

C = ε₀ A/d = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² x 0.020/1.0 × 10⁻⁴
  = 1.77 × 10⁻¹³/1.0 × 10⁻⁴ = 1.77 × 10⁻⁹ F = 1.8 nF

Combining capacitors reverses the resistor rules: capacitors in parallel add (C = C₁ + C₂ — bigger plates), while in series the reciprocals add (1/C = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂).

Worked example (series). Find the total capacitance of 4.0 μF and 12.0 μF in series.

1/C = 1/4.0 + 1/12.0 = 0.25 + 0.0833 = 0.333
C = 3.0 uF   (always smaller than the smallest capacitor)

Energy stored in a capacitor

Charging a capacitor means pushing charge onto a conductor that already repels it — the voltage rises as charge accumulates, so the work done is the area under the Q–V graph, a triangle:

W = (1/2) Q V = (1/2) C V² = Q²/(2C)

The energy is stored in the electric field between the plates. The Q–V graph is a straight line through the origin for a fixed capacitor; the stored energy is the triangular area beneath it — which is why the factor is ½ and not 1.

Worked example. A 100 μF capacitor is charged to 12 V. Find the energy stored and the charge.

Q = C V = 10⁰ × 10⁻⁶ x 12 = 1.2 × 10⁻³ C
W = (1/2) C V² = 0.5 × 10⁰ x 10⁻⁶ x 144 = 7.2 × 10⁻³ J
  = 7.2 mJ

Discharging a capacitor

A capacitor discharging through a resistor follows an exponential decay, like radioactive decay:

Q = Q0 e^(-t/RC)        V = V⁰ e^(-t/RC)        I = I0 e^(-t/RC)

time constant tau = RC   (seconds)
after one tau: about 37% of the starting value remains
after five tau: under 1% remains (effectively discharged)

Worked example. A 470 μF capacitor charged to 9.0 V discharges through 2.2 kΩ. Find the time constant and the voltage after 2.0 s.

tau = R C = 2200 × 470 × 10⁻⁶ = 1.03 s
V = 9.0 x e^(-2.0/1.03) = 9.0 x e^(-1.94)
  = 9.0 × 0.144 = 1.29 V  (1.3 V, 2 s.f.)

The discharge graph questions are standard: plot ln V against t and the gradient is −1/(RC); the area under a current–time graph is the charge that left the capacitor.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Field strength) Two plates 2.0 cm apart have a p.d. of 100 V. Find E. Answer: E = V/d = 100/0.020 = 5000 V m⁻¹.
  2. (Coulomb) Two +2.0 μC charges are 0.10 m apart. Find the force between them. Answer: F = 8.99 × 10⁹ × (2.0 × 10⁻⁶)²/(0.10)² = 8.99 × 10⁹ × 4.0 × 10⁻¹²/0.010 = 3.6 N, repulsive.
  3. (Potential) Explain why electric potential, unlike field strength, is a scalar. Answer: Potential is energy per unit charge, and energy is a scalar; it has sign (positive near positive charge) but no direction. Field strength is a vector because force has direction.
  4. (Capacitance) A capacitor stores 5.0 mC at 25 V. Find its capacitance. Answer: C = Q/V = 5.0 × 10⁻³/25 = 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ F = 200 μF.
  5. (Dielectric) Explain why inserting a dielectric increases capacitance. Answer: The dielectric's molecules polarise, creating an opposing field that reduces the net field for the same charge; since V = Ed falls while Q stays, C = Q/V rises (multiplied by ε_r).
  6. (Energy) A 2.0 μF capacitor is charged to 50 V. Find the energy stored. Answer: W = ½CV² = ½ × 2.0 × 10⁻⁶ × 2500 = 2.5 × 10⁻³ J = 2.5 mJ.
  7. (Discharge) A 2.0 kΩ resistor discharges a 100 μF capacitor. Find the time constant and the percentage remaining after 0.60 s. Answer: τ = RC = 2000 × 100 × 10⁻⁶ = 0.20 s; after 0.60 s = 3τ, remaining fraction = e⁻³ = 0.050, so 5.0%.
  8. (Graph) State how the gradient of a ln V against t graph relates to the time constant. Answer: ln V = ln V₀ − t/RC, so the gradient is −1/(RC) = −1/τ.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • V/d in centimetres: d must be in metres; 4.0 cm is 0.040 m, and the classic factor-of-100 error follows.
  • Charge units: μC = 10⁻⁶ C, nC = 10⁻⁹ C. Substituting μC as C inflates answers by a million.
  • Sign conventions: field strength is defined by the force on a positive charge; around a negative charge the lines point inward. State directions explicitly.
  • E = V/d only in uniform fields: between plates yes; around a point charge use E = kQ/r².
  • Series/parallel reversal: capacitors behave oppositely to resistors — series gives the reciprocals, parallel simply adds.
  • Energy factor ½: W = ½QV, not QV — the voltage rises during charging, so averaging matters. Forgetting the ½ doubles the answer.
  • Time-constant confusion: τ = RC in seconds means R in Ω and C in farads; the pair must be SI.
  • Discharge graph linearisation: a plot of V against t is a curve; only ln V against t is a straight line whose gradient gives −1/τ.
  • Precision: 2 or 3 s.f. with units (N, V m⁻¹, F, J, s); use ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹ from the data sheet.

title: Simulation, Sensors and Real Data — Study Notes
content:
Simulation, Sensors and Real Data

Simulation and Modelling

A simulation is a program that models a real system to test scenarios safely and cheaply: weather models, traffic flows, epidemic spread. Models use abstractions — chosen variables and equations — with a time step. Advantages: no real-world risk, repeatable, faster or slower than real time. Limitations: only as good as the model; rare events may be missed.

Sensors and Signals

Sensors measure physical quantities: temperature (thermistor), light (LDR), pressure, humidity, sound. Most output analogue signals varying continuously; computers need digital values, so an ADC (analogue-to-digital converter) samples the signal. Resolution depends on bits — an 8-bit ADC gives 256 levels. A DAC converts digital output back to analogue for actuators or speakers.

Monitoring vs Control

  • Monitoring: sensors feed data to the computer, which only records, displays or raises alarms — no action taken on the environment.
  • Control: the computer acts via actuators (motors, valves, heaters) based on sensor input — the classic feedback loop.

Real-Time Considerations

Control systems are often real-time: late output can be wrong output. Sampling rate must exceed twice the highest signal frequency (Nyquist) to avoid aliasing.

Exam tips: distinguish monitoring from control with a named example; describe the role of ADC and DAC in a greenhouse system; explain one limitation of a simulation.

Exam method: using simulation output with real data

Sensor readings are noisy, drift over time and can contain missing or impossible values. Before using them, check each reading against a sensible range, remove or flag outliers, and decide how to handle gaps, for example by ignoring them or interpolating between neighbouring readings. State which cleaning step you chose.

A simulation is only as reliable as its assumptions and its inputs. In an exam answer, state one assumption the model makes, explain how it could make the output differ from reality, and suggest a way to test the model against measured data.

Exam cue: When asked to evaluate a simulation, give a specific limitation tied to the scenario in the question rather than a general comment that simulations are approximate.

Worked example: comparing simulation output with real data

A simulation predicts a mean room temperature of 24.0 °C. Sensors in the real room record a mean of 25.3 °C. The difference is 25.3 minus 24.0, which is 1.3 °C. The percentage error is the difference divided by the real value, so 1.3 divided by 25.3 gives about 5.1 per cent. State the direction of the error as well as its size: the model underestimates the real temperature.

Then suggest a cause that the model could plausibly miss, such as heat from windows, occupants or equipment. A good evaluation names one assumption in the simulation and says how changing it would move the output closer to the real data.

Why real-time systems differ from batch simulations

  • A real-time system must respond within a fixed deadline, so a late result is a failure even when it is correct.
  • A batch simulation can run to completion and be checked afterwards, whereas a control system acts on each reading as it arrives.
  • Sampling rate matters: sample too slowly and fast changes are missed entirely, which is an aliasing risk.

title: Data Types and File Organisation — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Data Types and File Organisation

Computer Science — A2. A user-defined type is derived from existing types. An enumerated type lists named values in order: TYPE Months = (Jan, Feb, Mar ...). Internally each value is an integer index starting at 0. Pointer types store a memory address; the dereference operator returns the value at that address, which is how linked structures reference their nodes. Set types store unordered collections of distinct values from an ordinal base type, supporting union, intersection and difference.

Key areas to revise

  • User-Defined Types
  • Records
  • File Organisation
  • Hashing

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

title: AS Level Mathematics: The Normal Distribution
content:
AS Level Mathematics: The Normal Distribution

Many measurements cluster symmetrically about a mean: heights, reaction times, measurement errors, the fill of a production line. The normal distribution is the mathematical shape of that clustering — a symmetric bell curve defined entirely by its mean and standard deviation. This note builds the topic from zero: the shape and its properties, standardising to the standard normal, reading probabilities from tables, working backwards from a probability to an unknown mean or standard deviation, and combining normal variables.

Properties of the normal distribution

X ~ N(mu, σ²)   (mean mu, variance σ²)

symmetric about the mean: P(X < mu) = P(X > mu) = 0.5
total area under the curve = 1
inflection points at mu +/- σ
about 68 per cent within 1 sd, 95 per cent within 2, 99.7 within 3

The notation takes the variance, not the standard deviation: N(10, 4) means mean 10 and standard deviation 2. Writing N(10, 4) while treating 4 as the standard deviation is the single commonest error in the topic.

Worked example. X ~ N(20, 9). State the mean and standard deviation and find P(X < 20).

mu = 20, σ = 3
P(X < 20) = 0.5 by symmetry

Standardising

z = (x - mu)/σ

Z ~ N(0, 1), the standard normal, tabulated in most formula booklets
P(X < x) = P(Z < z) = Φ(z)

Standardising answers "how many standard deviations above the mean is this value?" Every normal probability question reduces to that one number.

Worked example. X ~ N(50, 16). Find P(X < 58).

σ = 4;  z = (58 - 50)/4 = 2
P(Z < 2) = 0.9772

Worked example 2 (above). For the same X, find P(X > 45).

z = (45 - 50)/4 = -1.25
P(Z > -1.25) = P(Z < 1.25) = 0.8944

Between two values

P(a < X < b) = Φ(z_b) - Φ(z_a)

below a value, subtract from 1
between two values, subtract the smaller cumulative from the larger

Worked example. X ~ N(100, 225). Find P(85 < X < 115).

σ = 15
z1 = (85 - 10⁰)/15 = -1;  z2 = (115 - 10⁰)/15 = 1
P = Φ(1) - Φ(-1) = 0.8413 - 0.1587 = 0.6826

Worked example 2 (both tails). X ~ N(30, 25). Find P(X < 25 or X > 38).

σ = 5
z1 = -1  →  Φ = 0.1587
z2 = 1.6  →  Φ = 0.9452, so upper tail = 0.0548
total = 0.2135

Working backwards: finding x from a probability

given P(X < x) = p, find z from the inverse table, then
x = mu + z σ

Worked example. X ~ N(40, 64). Find the value exceeded by 10 per cent of the distribution.

P(X > x) = 0.10  →  P(X < x) = 0.90  →  z = 1.2816
x = 40 + 1.2816(8) = 50.25

Worked example 2 (middle 80 per cent). X ~ N(50, 100). Find the range containing the middle 80 per cent.

tails of 10 per cent each: z = +/-1.2816
x = 50 +/- 1.2816(10)  →  37.2 to 62.8

Finding the mean or standard deviation

When mu or σ is unknown, each probability statement gives an equation in z, and two statements give simultaneous equations.

Worked example 1 (find σ). X ~ N(20, σ²) and P(X > 26) = 0.05. Find σ.

P(X < 26) = 0.95  →  z = 1.6449
(26 - 20)/σ = 1.6449  →  σ = 6/1.6449 = 3.648

Worked example 2 (simultaneous). X ~ N(mu, σ²) with P(X < 10) = 0.20 and P(X < 20) = 0.90. Find mu and σ.

z values: -0.8416 and 1.2816
(mu - 0.8416 σ) = 10
(mu + 1.2816 σ) = 20
subtract: 2.1232 σ = 10  →  σ = 4.71
mu = 10 + 0.8416(4.71) = 13.96

The signs matter: a value below the mean has a negative z, so 10 = mu − 0.8416 σ. Setting both equations up with the same sign convention is what makes the simultaneous solve work.

Combining normal variables

if X ~ N(m¹, s¹²) and Y ~ N(m², s²²) are independent:
X + Y ~ N(m¹ + m², s¹² + s²²)
X - Y ~ N(m¹ - m², s¹² + s²²)
aX + b ~ N(a m¹ + b, a² s¹²)

The variance of a difference adds, exactly as in the probability-distributions topic: independent uncertainties compound in either direction.

Worked example. The masses of apples are N(120, 100) grams and of pears N(150, 144), independent. Find the probability that a random apple and pear together weigh more than 300 g.

T = A + P ~ N(270, 244)
sigma_T = 15.62
z = (300 - 270)/15.62 = 1.921
P(T > 300) = 1 - Φ(1.921) = 0.0274

Worked example 2 (difference). Two machines fill bottles: A ~ N(500, 25) ml, B ~ N(505, 36) ml, independent. Find P(A's fill exceeds B's).

D = A - B ~ N(-5, 61);  σ = 7.81
P(D > 0):  z = (0 + 5)/7.81 = 0.640
P = 1 - 0.7389 = 0.261

Normal approximations and modelling assumptions

The normal model is used for continuous measurements that arise from many small independent influences. Before applying it, check the assumptions: the variable is continuous (or discrete with enough values to ignore the gaps), the distribution is roughly symmetric, and the mean and standard deviation are known or estimable.

Worked example (quality control). A machine produces rods of mean 25.0 mm and standard deviation 0.2 mm. Rods outside 24.7–25.3 mm are scrapped. Find the proportion scrapped.

z1 = (24.7 - 25.0)/0.2 = -1.5  →  0.0668
z2 = (25.3 - 25.0)/0.2 = 1.5   →  upper tail 0.0668
total scrapped = 0.1336, about 13.4 per cent

Interpretation matters: state the proportion and, where asked, the expected number in a batch — 13.4 per cent of 1000 rods is about 134 rods.

Reading the table and using symmetry

The standard normal table gives Φ(z) = P(Z < z) only for positive z. Two symmetries cover every other case:

Φ(-z) = 1 - Φ(z)
P(Z > z) = 1 - Φ(z)
P(-z < Z < z) = 2 Φ(z) - 1

Worked example. Find P(-1.5 < Z < 0.5).

Φ(0.5) = 0.6915;  Φ(-1.5) = 1 - 0.9332 = 0.0668
P = 0.6915 - 0.0668 = 0.6247

Worked example 2 (inverse with symmetry). Find z such that P(Z > z) = 0.75.

Φ(z) = 0.25, so z is negative
z = -0.6745  (the value with Φ = 0.6745 is 0.6745)
check: P(Z > -0.6745) = 1 - 0.25 = 0.75

A rough sketch of the bell with the required region shaded prevents sign errors; the area asked for must match the area you extract from the table.

Normal approximation to the binomial

For a large number of trials the binomial distribution becomes bell-shaped and can be approximated by a normal with the same mean and variance, with a continuity correction because the binomial is discrete.

X ~ B(n, p):  mu = np,  σ² = np(1 - p)
use the normal when np > 5 and n(1 - p) > 5
continuity correction: X >= k becomes X > k - 0.5
                        X <= k becomes X < k + 0.5

Worked example. X ~ B(100, 0.3). Estimate P(X ≥ 35).

mu = 30, σ² = 21, σ = 4.583
with continuity: P(X > 34.5)
z = (34.5 - 30)/4.583 = 0.982
P = 1 - 0.8370 = 0.163

Without the 0.5 shift the estimate is noticeably worse, and the correction is explicitly credited in mark schemes. State both the approximation and the correction.

Is the normal model appropriate?

Before using the bell curve, check four things: the variable is continuous (or a discrete variable with many values); the distribution is roughly symmetric with a single peak; the mean and standard deviation are known or estimated from a large sample; and the values extend, in principle, in both directions. Heights and measurement errors satisfy these; incomes and waiting times do not, because they are skewed.

Worked example. A shop's daily sales figures have a mean of 400 pounds and an sd of 250 pounds, and the normal model gives P(sales < 0) = 0.055. Is the model appropriate?

the calculation implies a 5.5 per cent chance of negative sales,
which is impossible, so the normal model is a poor fit here
sales are right-skewed with a floor at zero; a model with a lower
bound, or a transformation, would be more honest

Recognising when a model fails is examinable: the arithmetic can be flawless and the modelling still wrong, and the marks for that judgement are separate.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Notation) X ~ N(12, 25). State the sd. Answer: 5.
  2. (Standardise) X ~ N(12, 25): find P(X < 17). Answer: z = 1; 0.8413.
  3. (Above) X ~ N(12, 25): find P(X > 9). Answer: z = −0.6; 0.7257.
  4. (Between) X ~ N(12, 25): find P(10 < X < 15). Answer: z = −0.4 and 0.6; 0.7257 − 0.3446 = 0.3811.
  5. (Inverse) X ~ N(12, 25): find the 90th percentile. Answer: z = 1.2816; x = 18.4.
  6. (Unknown σ) X ~ N(50, s²), P(X > 60) = 0.10. Find s. Answer: z = 1.2816; s = 10/1.2816 = 7.80.
  7. (Combination) X ~ N(10, 4), Y ~ N(15, 9), independent. Find P(X + Y < 30). Answer: sum ~ N(25, 13), sd 3.606, z = 1.387, P = 0.917.
  8. (Difference) Same X, Y: find P(Y − X > 10). Answer: D ~ N(5, 13), z = (10 − 5)/3.606 = 1.387; P = 0.083.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Variance mistaken for sd: N(mu, σ²) — square-root the second parameter before standardising.
  • Forgetting the tails: P(X > x) = 1 − Φ(z); the table gives "less than".
  • Wrong z sign: values below the mean have negative z; symmetrise using Φ(−z) = 1 − Φ(z).
  • Subtracting variances of a difference: Var(X − Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) when independent.
  • Not stating independence: combinations need it; without the assumption the variance rule does not hold.
  • Continuity: for a discrete variable approximated by the normal, use a continuity correction (P(X ≥ 5) becomes P(X > 4.5)) — required in A2, and stating it early avoids the habit.
  • Rounding z: use four decimal places from tables or the full calculator value; rounding z to 2 d.p. shifts the probability noticeably.
  • Answer without context: convert the probability into a proportion, a number of items or a percentage, as the question asks.

title: IGCSE Physics: Energy, Work and Power
content:
IGCSE Physics: Energy, Work and Power

Cambridge IGCSE Physics 0625 (2026–2028), Topic 1 Motion, forces and energy, statement 1.7 Energy, work and power. Energy is the currency of every physical process: it is never created or destroyed, only moved between stores and converted between forms. This note builds the whole idea from scratch — stores, transfers, the two energy equations, work, power, the world's energy resources and efficiency — because Paper 4 rewards candidates who can both calculate an energy change and explain where the energy went.

Energy stores and transfers

Think of energy as money held in different bank accounts. It can sit in a store, and it can move between stores along a transfer pathway, but the total across all accounts never changes. The examined stores and transfers are:

Energy storeWhat it meansExample
KineticEnergy of a moving object; more mass or more speed means moreA moving lorry
Gravitational potentialEnergy stored by virtue of height in a gravitational fieldA book on a shelf
Elastic potentialEnergy stored by stretching, compressing or twistingA drawn bow, a compressed spring
Thermal (internal)Energy of the random motion of particles in a substanceHot water in a kettle
ChemicalEnergy stored in chemical bondsFood, fuel, a battery
NuclearEnergy stored in the nucleus of an atomUranium fuel

The four transfer pathways are mechanical work (a force acting over a distance), heating (energy transferred by a temperature difference), radiation (energy carried by waves, mainly infrared and light) and electrical work (charge moving through a potential difference). When a ball is thrown upwards, chemical energy in the muscles does mechanical work on the ball, and that energy becomes kinetic; as the ball rises, kinetic becomes gravitational potential; as it falls back, gravitational potential becomes kinetic again; on impact the kinetic spreads into the thermal stores of the ball, the ground and the air, and some is radiated as sound.

Conservation of energy and Sankey diagrams

The law of conservation of energy states that energy cannot be created or destroyed, and the total energy in a closed system stays constant. This is the most powerful statement in the syllabus: whenever a question says a machine loses energy, it means the energy has been transferred to less useful stores, not destroyed. A Sankey diagram draws the total energy input as one wide arrow, splits it into useful output and wasted arrows, and is drawn so the arrow widths are proportional to the energies.

Useful energy is the energy transferred to the store the device was designed to fill; wasted energy is transferred to stores that were not the goal, usually thermal energy of the surroundings, and it is eventually transferred to the environment, often by radiation. Wasted energy is not destroyed — it has simply become too spread out to be harnessed easily.

Kinetic and gravitational potential energy

Both equations are Supplement statements, and both appear constantly in Paper 4 calculations.

kinetic energy = 1/2 x mass x speed squared        EK = 1/2 m v²
gravitational potential energy = mass x gravitational field strength x height        EP = m g h
  • EK: kinetic energy in joules (J); m: mass in kilograms (kg); v: speed in metres per second (m s⁻¹). Energy is a scalar, so the speed is squared and the direction of travel does not matter.
  • EP: gravitational potential energy in joules (J); g: gravitational field strength in newtons per kilogram (N kg⁻¹, use the value given in the question); h: vertical height in metres (m), measured between the two positions being compared.

Only the difference in height matters. Lifting a 2 kg book from a table to a shelf 0.50 m above it raises EP by 2 × 9.81 × 0.50 = 9.8 J, whatever the height of the room. The sign convention is simple: EP increases as an object rises and decreases as it falls, and the change is ΔEP = m g Δh.

Energy methods are often faster than forces and equations of motion. For a falling object with no air resistance, m g h = ½ m v², and the mass cancels: every object falls at the same rate in a vacuum. For a roller coaster of mass 500 kg dropping 20 m from rest, v = √(2 g h) = √(2 × 9.81 × 20) = 19.8 m s⁻¹.

Work done

Work is done when a force moves an object. It is energy transferred by mechanical work, and it is measured in joules:

work done = force x distance moved in the direction of the force        W = F s
  • W: work done in joules (J). One joule is the work done when a force of 1 newton moves its point of application 1 metre in the direction of the force.
  • F: force in newtons (N); s: distance moved in metres (m), measured in the direction of the force.

Work is a scalar, but the two quantities must line up: carrying a box horizontally at constant height does no work against gravity, because the motion is perpendicular to the weight. Pushing a trolley with 50 N against 20 N of friction over 4 m does 200 J of work in total, of which 80 J goes to heating the bearings and floor through friction and 120 J remains as kinetic energy. If you carry shopping upstairs, the work done against gravity is your weight multiplied by the vertical height gained, not the length of the staircase.

Power

Power measures how fast energy is transferred — the rate of doing work. A car engine that lifts the same load in half the time is twice as powerful.

power = work done / time taken = energy transferred / time taken        P = W / t = E / t
  • P: power in watts (W). One watt is one joule per second (1 W = 1 J s⁻¹). A kilowatt is 1000 W.
