  • W: work done in joules (J); E: energy transferred in joules (J); t: time taken in seconds (s).

Power is a scalar. For a vehicle moving at constant speed against a constant force, the same idea gives P = F v (Supplement), with F in newtons and v in metres per second, giving watts directly. Doubling the speed of a car at constant driving force doubles the power needed; a car climbing a hill at constant speed needs power P = mgv sin θ to raise its weight.

Energy resources and electricity generation

Most electrical energy is generated the same way: a fuel heats water, the steam spins a turbine, and the turbine spins a generator that converts the kinetic energy of rotation into electrical energy. What differs is the energy store the heat comes from.

ResourceStore usedAdvantagesDisadvantages
Coal, oil, gas (fossil fuels)Chemical, burned to give heatReliable, cheap to run, existing infrastructureFinite supply; carbon dioxide and pollutants released; contributes to climate change and acid rain
BiofuelChemical, from plant or animal materialRenewable; carbon dioxide released was recently absorbed by the plantsLand and water needed to grow crops; energy cost of farming and transport
HydroelectricGravitational potential of stored waterRenewable, reliable, no fuel cost, no emissions in useDams flood valleys and disrupt habitats; high construction cost; depends on rainfall
GeothermalThermal energy inside the EarthRenewable, reliable, small land useOnly practical near volcanic regions; drilling cost; possible release of underground gases
Nuclear fuelNuclear, released by fissionVery large energy per kilogram; no carbon dioxide in operationRadioactive waste that must be stored safely for centuries; high decommissioning cost; accident risk
Solar cellsLight radiation converted directly to electricityRenewable, silent, no emissions in use, low maintenanceOutput varies with light and season; expensive to manufacture; large area needed for high output
Solar panels (heating)Light radiation heating water directlyRenewable and cheap to runOnly heats water; ineffective at night and in cloudy climates

Non-renewable resources exist in finite stock and are used faster than they form; renewable resources are replenished as they are used. Supplement statements add the deep connection: the Sun is the principal source for almost all of these resources. Sunlight drives the water cycle behind hydroelectric power and biofuels, heats the ground behind wind and geothermal gradients, and fossil fuels are the remains of organisms that grew in sunlight. The Sun releases energy by nuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium, and research into fusion on Earth aims to provide a fuel that is abundant and produces no long-lived radioactive waste, though sustained fusion power is still experimental.

Efficiency

Efficiency compares what a device delivers with what it is given:

efficiency = useful energy output / total energy input
efficiency = useful power output / total power input

Efficiency has no unit; multiply by 100 for a percentage. No real device is 100 per cent efficient, because some energy is always transferred to thermal stores of the surroundings by friction, resistance and radiation. A filament lamp is about 5 per cent efficient (most energy becomes heat, not light); an electric motor might reach 80 per cent. The most efficient heating device is a simple heater, because its useful output is thermal energy — the same store as its waste. A Sankey diagram makes this visible at a glance, and the arrows must sum to the total input.

Worked example: lifting and efficiency

A crane lifts a 500 kg load through 12 m at constant speed in 20 s. Take g = 9.81 N kg⁻¹.

weight = m g = 500 × 9.81 = 4905 N
useful work = force x distance = 4905 × 12 = 58 860 J
useful power = work / time = 58 860 / 20 = 2943 W (about 2.9 kW)

The motor takes 150 000 J of electrical energy to do this lift. Its efficiency is 58 860 / 150 000 = 0.39, or 39 per cent. The remaining 91 140 J is not destroyed: it warms the motor windings, the cables and the surrounding air.

Second stage, using energy conservation: if the load is dropped from rest through the same 12 m with negligible air resistance, m g h = ½ m v² gives v = √(2 × 9.81 × 12) = 15.3 m s⁻¹. The mass cancels, so any object dropped through 12 m reaches the same speed.

Common mistakes

  • Saying energy is used up or lost; energy is transferred to other stores, and the total is conserved. Examiners award the mark for transferred, not lost.
  • Putting speed rather than speed squared into EK = ½mv², and forgetting the ½.
  • Measuring h in EP = mgh along a slope or a staircase; h is the vertical height difference.
  • Using the wrong mass in W = mg: the mass in kilograms, multiplied by g, never the weight in newtons multiplied by g again.
  • Confusing work done with power: joules measure energy, watts measure the rate of energy transfer.
  • Calculating efficiency as total in over useful out; the useful output goes on top, so efficiency is always less than 1.
  • Forgetting that a percentage efficiency needs multiplying by 100, and leaving the answer as 0.39 when 39 per cent is asked for.
  • Mixing units: power in watts needs energy in joules and time in seconds, so kilowatts and minutes must be converted first.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 4, 3 marks). A ball of mass 0.15 kg is moving at 10 m s⁻¹. Calculate its kinetic energy and the height through which it would need to be raised to store the same energy. Take g = 9.81 N kg⁻¹.

Answer: EK = ½mv² = ½ × 0.15 × 10² = 7.5 J. Setting mgh = 7.5 gives h = 7.5 / (0.15 × 9.81) = 5.1 m.

Question 2 (Paper 4, 4 marks). A 60 kg student runs up a flight of stairs of vertical height 3.0 m in 4.0 s. Calculate the useful power developed. Take g = 10 N kg⁻¹.

Answer: work = mgh = 60 × 10 × 3.0 = 1800 J. Power = 1800 / 4.0 = 450 W. (Real power is higher, because the student also gains kinetic energy and warms their muscles.)

Question 3 (Paper 2 style). A machine takes in 2000 J and delivers 1500 J of useful work. Its efficiency is: A 25 per cent; B 75 per cent; C 133 per cent; D 175 per cent. Answer: B. 1500/2000 = 0.75 = 75 per cent. Option C comes from putting input over output — the classic trap.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 6 marks). Explain why a solar cell is described as renewable, and discuss whether it is a good replacement for a coal-fired power station.

Answer: A solar cell converts light energy directly into electrical energy and consumes no fuel, so its energy source, sunlight, is replenished continuously and it is renewable. It produces no carbon dioxide or pollutants in operation. Against that, output depends on light intensity and falls at night and in cloudy weather, so storage or backup generation is needed; manufacturing the cells is energy-intensive, and a large area is required for high output. Coal is reliable and dispatchable but burns a finite resource, releasing carbon dioxide that drives climate change plus sulfur dioxide and particulates. A balanced conclusion weighs reliability and land use against emissions and fuel sustainability.

Question 5 (Paper 4, 3 marks). A car engine produces a driving force of 2000 N while travelling at 30 m s⁻¹. Calculate the useful power output.

Answer: P = F v = 2000 × 30 = 60 000 W = 60 kW.

Question 6 (Paper 6 style). Suggest how you would determine experimentally the efficiency of an electric motor lifting a small mass.

Answer: Measure the mass with a balance and the height lifted with a ruler, and record the time with a stopwatch. The useful output is mgh, calculated from the measured mass and vertical height. Measure the electrical energy input with a joule meter, or with an ammeter and voltmeter readings and E = V I t. Efficiency is mgh divided by V I t. Repeat for several masses and quote an average, keeping the input voltage constant.

With energy accounted for, the next question is what happens when forces are spread over area and depth: pressure and density.

Equations and symbols

Statement 1.7 is a small set of equations used in a large number of combinations. The two rules that carry most of the marks are that work needs a force along the displacement, and that power is a rate, so every time must be in seconds before dividing.

Work and the energy stores

W = Fd
Key: W = work done (J); F = force in the direction of motion (N); d = distance moved along that direction (m). A force at right angles to the motion does no work.

KE = ½mv²
Key: KE = kinetic energy (J); m = mass (kg); v = speed (m/s). The speed is squared, so doubling the speed quadruples the energy — the reason braking distance rises so steeply.

GPE = mgh
Key: GPE = gravitational potential energy (J); m = mass (kg); g = gravitational field strength (9.8 N/kg); h = height gained (m). A fall is a loss of GPE, so state the sign or the word.

KE lost = GPE gained (no friction)
Key: the conservation statement used to link the two stores. With friction or air resistance, part of the energy is transferred to the thermal store of the surroundings and the equality becomes an inequality.

v = √(2gh)
Key: v = speed at the bottom of a frictionless fall (m/s); g = 9.8 m/s²; h = height fallen (m). It comes from ½mv² = mgh, and the mass cancels — which is why a feather and a hammer match on the Moon.

Power

P = E / t = W / t
Key: P = power (W); E or W = energy transferred or work done (J); t = time taken (s). One watt is one joule per second.

E = Pt
Key: E = energy transferred (J); P = power (W); t = time (s). With P in kilowatts and t in hours the energy comes out in kilowatt-hours, which is what a meter measures.

P = Fv
Key: P = useful power output (W); F = driving force (N); v = constant speed (m/s). For a car at steady speed the driving force equals the total resistive force.

1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J
Key: one kilowatt-hour is the energy of a 1000 W appliance running for one hour; 1 kW × 3600 s = 3.6 MJ.

Efficiency

efficiency = (useful energy output / total energy input) × 100%
Key: both energies in joules (or both powers in watts, since the time cancels); the result is a percentage and can never exceed 100. A figure above 100 means the wrong quantity was used as the input.

wasted energy = input − useful output
Key: the remainder is transferred by friction, air resistance or sound to the thermal store of the surroundings. Energy is not destroyed, so the widths of a Sankey diagram must balance.

useful power of a lifting motor = mgh / t
Key: m = load mass (kg); g = 9.8 N/kg; h = height lifted (m); t = time taken (s). Comparing this with the electrical input VI gives the motor's efficiency.

title: Coordination, Response and Gene Technology — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Coordination, Response and Gene Technology — Quick Revision Summary

This is the fast map of Edexcel International A2 Biology WBI16 Topics 8 and 9. It follows the same order as the full notes so you can cross-reference, and it repeats the specification numbers so you can see which paragraph exists for which point. Use it to organise the topic, not to replace the notes. The topic splits into three big blocks: the nervous system and neurones, the brain, imaging and the pharmacology of the nervous system, and the plant and genetic technologies — coordination in plants, recombinant DNA and GM organisms, and bioinformatics and microarrays.

The nervous system: hierarchy and the reflex arc

The nervous system lets an organism detect a stimulus, send information quickly, and make effectors respond. In mammals it is built from the central and peripheral systems, and its fastest wired responses are the reflex arcs, which are the simplest complete circuits you study in this topic.

  • 8.1 Sensory neurones carry information from receptors toward the central nervous system; relay neurones are in the central nervous system and connect sensory to motor neurones; motor neurones carry impulses from the central nervous system to effectors such as muscles and glands. Schwann cells wrap many axons in myelin, an insulating fatty layer, and myelination increases the speed of conduction. The roles of the three neurone types and the reason for myelination are the core ideas here.
  • 8.2 The nervous system causes effectors to respond to a stimulus through a chain: receptor detects the stimulus, sensory neurone carries the impulse to the central nervous system, relay neurone processes the information and passes it on, motor neurone carries the impulse to the effector, and the effector responds. The pupil example is useful: the iris contains muscles that respond to the amount of light, and the wiring behind that response is the kind of autonomic coordination this part of the topic describes.
  • 8.3 A spinal reflex arc is the simplest complete pathway. The stimulus is detected by a receptor, the sensory neurone enters the spinal cord, the relay neurone in the grey matter connects to the motor neurone, and the motor neurone carries the impulse out to the effector — often a muscle. The grey matter is where the relay neurones and synapses are; the white matter is made of myelinated axons that carry impulses up and down the cord between the spinal cord and the brain. The reflex arc is fast because it is short and involves few synapses, and it is protective because it does not wait for the brain to process the information first.

The practical point is that the reflex arc is not just “a reflex”; it is the minimal circuit that shows how sensory input, central relay and motor output are wired together, and it explains why the grey and white matter of the spinal cord have different functions.

The action potential and how it travels

The nerve impulse is the action potential, a self-propagating electrical signal caused by changes in the permeability of the axon membrane to sodium and potassium ions. The sequence of events is what the exam wants, and the reason myelination speeds conduction is part of the same picture.

  • 8.4 An action potential is conducted along an axon because of changes in membrane permeability to sodium and potassium ions. At rest the membrane is polarised, with the inside negative relative to the outside. When a stimulus is strong enough, voltage-gated sodium channels open and sodium ions enter the axon, depolarising the membrane and generating the rising phase of the action potential. Sodium channels then close and voltage-gated potassium channels open, so potassium ions leave the axon and the membrane repolarises. The sodium-potassium pump restores the resting distribution of ions over time, but the immediate repolarisation is due to potassium leaving, not to the pump. The action potential is all-or-nothing: once the threshold is reached, it fires fully; a stronger stimulus does not make a bigger action potential, only more frequent ones.
  • The propagation happens because the depolarisation of one small region of the membrane changes the voltage in the neighbouring region, opening channels there and so on along the axon. The impulse travels because each section regenerates the signal, not because the same ions travel from one end of the axon to the other. That is why the impulse is an electrochemical wave and not a current flowing the length of the axon like water in a pipe.
  • 8.5 Myelination makes this faster by saltatory conduction. The myelin sheath is interrupted by the nodes of Ranvier, where the axon membrane is exposed. Depolarisation can only happen at these nodes, so the action potential appears to jump from node to node. This is far faster than continuous conduction along an unmyelinated axon of the same diameter, because the signal travels quickly along the insulated internodal regions and is only recharged at the nodes. The comparison is not that myelin makes the ions move faster; it is that the signal regenerates at fewer points along the way.

A frequent mistake is to say that myelination increases the speed by making the ions travel faster, or to forget that the sodium-potassium pump restores the resting conditions after the action potential rather than causing the repolarisation itself. The order of events — sodium in, depolarisation, potassium out, repolarisation, then restoration — is the secure version.

Synapses and the chemical transmission of the signal

Where one neurone meets another, the signal crosses a synapse. The synapse is the point at which the electrical signal becomes chemical for one step and then electrical again, and it is also where drugs and toxins can act. Synaptic transmission is the reason neurones can be modulated, integrated and influenced by chemicals.

  • 8.6 (i) A synapse in nerve impulse transmission has a presynaptic neurone ending with vesicles of neurotransmitter, a synaptic cleft, and a postsynaptic membrane with receptors for the neurotransmitter. When an action potential arrives at the presynaptic ending, calcium channels open, calcium enters, and vesicles fuse with the presynaptic membrane and release neurotransmitter into the cleft. The neurotransmitter diffuses across the cleft and binds to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane, opening ion channels and producing a new change in membrane potential in the postsynaptic neurone. Acetylcholine is the neurotransmitter at the neuromuscular junction and at many other synapses, and its action is a good example of the general scheme.
  • The pupil is a useful illustration. The iris contains muscles whose contraction or relaxation changes the pupil diameter; this is under autonomic control, and the pathway involves synaptic transmission with acetylcholine and, in the relevant part of the autonomic system, noradrenaline, depending on whether the response is constriction or dilation. The point is not to memorise every transmitter at every synapse, but to understand that the synapse is where the signal is passed and where chemicals can modify it.
  • 8.7 Drugs act by influencing nerve impulse transmission, and the specification names several examples. Nicotine mimics acetylcholine at some receptors, stimulating them; lidocaine blocks voltage-gated sodium channels, preventing action potentials and so acting as a local anaesthetic; cobra venom alpha toxin blocks neuromuscular transmission by binding to acetylcholine receptors; L-DOPA is used in Parkinson’s disease because it is a precursor that can be converted to dopamine, which is deficient in that condition; and MDMA, ecstasy, affects neurotransmitter reuptake and release, especially of serotonin, changing mood and perception. The principle is that drugs can mimic, block, enhance or reduce neurotransmitter action, and that the effect depends on which step they influence.

A helpful way to remember the drug examples is to classify them by the step they affect: some mimic a neurotransmitter, some block a receptor, some block ion channels, some change how much neurotransmitter is released or reabsorbed, and some are supplied as precursors. If you can say which step each one affects, you can answer the typical question even if you do not remember the exact detail of every one.

Rods, rhodopsin and the detection of light

The retina is where light is detected, and the rod cell is the model system for how a stimulus is turned into a membrane potential change at the cellular level. This is the place where the idea of a receptor potential and the operation of a G-protein-linked receptor are both visible.

  • 8.8 The mammal detects light with rods in the retina. Rod cells contain the pigment rhodopsin, which is made of opsin and retinal; retinal is the light-absorbing part. When light hits rhodopsin, retinal changes shape, the opsin changes shape, and this activates a transduction pathway that leads to the closure of sodium channels in the rod cell membrane. The result is that sodium ions stop entering as much, the rod cell hyperpolarises, and the pattern of neurotransmitter release at the rod’s synapse changes. This is a case where a stimulus reduces sodium entry rather than increasing it, so the cell hyperpolarises rather than depolarising. The signal is then passed through the retinal wiring to the optic neurones, which carry impulses to the brain.
  • The important concept is that a sensory receptor converts a stimulus into a change in membrane potential, and that the direction of change depends on the receptor. In rods, light causes hyperpolarisation. If you remember that the stimulus closes sodium channels in the rod rather than opening them, you can explain why the signal is generated and why it is not the same as an action potential in an axon.

Habituation and the simple learning of stimulus responses

Not every response is fixed. Habituation is a simple form of learning in which an organism stops responding to a repeated, harmless stimulus, and the specification includes it both as a behaviour and as something you can investigate practically.

  • 8.9 Habituation is a decrease in response to a repeated stimulus that is neither rewarding nor harmful. It is not the same as sensory adaptation, which is a change in the receptor itself; habituation is a change in the nervous system’s response, often at the synapse, so that the repeated stimulus fails to trigger the full response. It is useful because it lets an organism ignore unimportant stimuli and focus on those that matter. The practical investigation is to present a harmless stimulus repeatedly and measure the response over time, looking for the decline.

The organisation of the mammalian nervous system

The nervous system is organised into central and peripheral parts, and the central part is further divided into brain and spinal cord. The structure follows the function: the central system integrates and coordinates, while the peripheral system carries information in and out.

  • 8.10 The mammalian nervous system consists of the central nervous system, CNS, and the peripheral nervous system. The CNS is the brain and spinal cord; it integrates sensory information, coordinates responses, and can initiate behaviour. The peripheral nervous system carries sensory information into the CNS and carries motor commands out to the effectors. The division matters because it tells you which part does the integration and which part does the connecting and carrying.

The brain: structure and function of the main parts

The brain is not a single organ that does one job; its major parts have different functions, and the specification names several of them so you can map structure to role.

  • 8.14 The cerebral hemispheres are the largest part of the brain in mammals and are associated with higher functions such as voluntary movement, sensation, thought, memory, language and consciousness, with different regions specialised for different functions. The hypothalamus links the nervous and endocrine systems; it is involved in homeostasis, including the control of body temperature, hunger, thirst and the release of hormones from the pituitary gland. The pituitary gland is a major endocrine gland under the control of the hypothalamus, releasing hormones that regulate other endocrine glands and other processes. The cerebellum is involved in the coordination of movement, posture and balance, and in the refinement of motor control. The medulla oblongata controls vital automatic functions such as breathing and heart rate. Knowing the role of each part means you can explain what is likely to be affected if one part is damaged.

The exam point is that the brain is a set of specialised regions, not a single uniform structure. If a question asks what function a particular region has, the answer is to name the region’s role rather than to say “it does brain stuff”.

Imaging the living brain

The living brain can be imaged in several ways, and each method gives different information. The exam wants you to compare them by what they show and how they work, not just to list them.

  • 8.15 MRI, magnetic resonance imaging, uses strong magnetic fields and radio waves to build a detailed image of brain structure, and is good for showing anatomy and structural abnormalities. fMRI, functional MRI, detects changes in blood flow related to neural activity, so it shows which areas are active during a task as well as the structure; the idea is that active areas have increased blood flow and changes in oxygenation that the technique detects. PET, positron emission tomography, uses a radioactive tracer to show metabolic activity, so it can reveal which regions are metabolically active. CT, computed tomography, uses X-rays to build a cross-sectional image and is useful for detecting structural problems such as bleeding, fractures and some tumours. The common thread is that each has a different strength: some are better for structure, some for activity, some for acute structural emergencies, and none does everything.

A good comparison answer names what each method shows, what it is best used for, and the fact that they are complementary. Saying “MRI is the best one” without explanation is not enough, because the question is usually about why you would choose one method rather than another.

Imbalances, drugs and the development of new medicines

Disease can arise from the imbalance of naturally occurring brain chemicals, and understanding that imbalance is what lets drugs be developed. Parkinson’s disease and depression are the two named examples, and they illustrate different kinds of problem and different kinds of treatment.

  • 8.16 Imbalances in brain chemicals can contribute to ill health. In Parkinson’s disease, dopamine-secreting neurones in the brain are lost, so dopamine levels fall and movement control is affected. In depression, the regulation of neurotransmitters such as serotonin is thought to be involved, and drugs that affect serotonin can be used in treatment. The development of new drugs follows from understanding these imbalances: if a neurotransmitter is deficient, a precursor or a drug that affects its release, reuptake or receptor action may help. The important conceptual point is that the drug is a response to a biochemical problem, not a random intervention, and that different drugs work by different mechanisms even when they affect the same system.

A common trap is to over-simplify depression as “a serotonin deficiency” in a way that oversells a complex condition. The specification point is that serotonin is involved and that drugs that affect serotonin are used; the exam answer should say that, without pretending the biology is simpler than it is. The safe answer is to say that the imbalance is part of the explanation and that drug treatment targets it.

Coordination in plants: phytochrome, auxin and gibberellins

Plants coordinate their responses too, but they use hormones and light receptors rather than nerves. Phytochrome, auxin and gibberellins are the named examples, and they each work through effects on growth and on transcription, which connects this part of the topic to the gene-technology part later.

  • 8.11 Phytochrome is a plant photoreceptor that exists in two forms that interconvert in response to light. It allows the plant to detect light quality, quantity and duration, and it affects processes such as flowering and germination. Auxin, indoleacetic acid or IAA, is a plant hormone that promotes cell elongation and is involved in tropisms such as phototropism and gravitropism; it is distributed asymmetrically in the shoot so that the shaded side elongates more, bending the shoot toward the light. Gibberellins promote growth, including stem elongation and seed germination, and they bring about their effects partly by affecting transcription, i.e. by switching genes on and off. The link to gene technology is that phytochrome, auxin and gibberellins are not just “plant hormones”; they are part of the plant’s control system for responding to the environment and for development, and some of their effects are at the level of gene expression.

A useful practical image is the shoot bending toward light: auxin moves to the shaded side, the cells there elongate more, and the shoot curves. If you can say that, you have the phototropism story in a form that scores marks.

Core Practical 18 and the production of amylase in germinating grains

Core Practical 18 is about investigating amylase production in germinating cereal grains. The point is to connect enzyme production with germination and with the hormonal control of growth.

  • 8.12 Core Practical 18 investigates the production of amylase in germinating cereal grains. Germinating grains produce amylase to break down starch into sugars that the growing embryo can use. The practical is a way to see enzyme production during germination and to relate it to the hormonal changes that occur as the grain starts to grow. The idea is that the living embryo produces the enzyme, and that the enzyme mobilises the food store for the growing plant.

Recombinant DNA: the technology that joins genes to vectors

Gene technology is the set of methods that let scientists move genes from one organism to another. The first step is making recombinant DNA, and the key tools are restriction endonucleases and DNA ligase.

  • 8.18 Recombinant DNA is DNA made by combining sequences from different sources. Restriction endonucleases are enzymes that cut DNA at specific sequences, often leaving “sticky ends” that are complementary and can base-pair. DNA ligase joins DNA fragments together by forming the bonds between nucleotides in the sugar-phosphate backbone. So the workflow is: cut the gene and the vector with the same restriction enzyme, mix them so the sticky ends pair, and use DNA ligase to seal them together, making a recombinant DNA molecule. The point is that the cutting and joining are sequence-specific and enzyme-catalysed, and that the same enzymes are used to open the vector and to insert the gene.
  • 8.19 Recombinant DNA can be inserted into other cells. The vector is often a plasmid in bacteria, and the recombinant plasmid can be taken up by bacterial cells, which then carry the gene and can express it. Other methods include using viruses as vectors or physical methods such as microinjection or gene guns, depending on the organism and the goal. The important idea is that once the recombinant DNA is inside a host, the host’s molecular machinery can replicate and express the inserted gene, which is what makes the technology useful.

How genes are used to make products

The reason organisms are genetically modified is that they can be turned into factories for substances they would not otherwise make. The specification names the production of drugs by genetically modified organisms as a key example.

  • 8.17 Drugs can be produced using genetically modified organisms — plants, animals and microorganisms. The classic example is the production of human proteins such as insulin by genetically modified bacteria: the human gene is inserted into the bacterium, and the bacterium produces the protein, which can then be purified and used as a medicine. Other products can similarly be made in microorganisms, and sometimes in plants or animals. The point is that the organism is modified once and then used to produce the product, which is why the approach is useful industrially.

Microarrays and the detection of active genes

Not every gene is active at once. Microarrays are the tool for seeing which genes are active in a particular sample, and they connect gene technology to the analysis of gene expression rather than just the sequence of genes.

  • 8.20 Microarrays can be used to identify active genes. A microarray contains many short DNA sequences attached to a solid surface, and a labelled sample of cDNA made from the mRNA of a tissue is hybridised to it. If a gene is active, its cDNA will bind to the corresponding spot, and the label reveals which genes are being expressed and at what relative level. The comparison is between samples — for example a diseased tissue and a healthy one — so you can see which genes are up- or down-regulated. The principle is that the microarray lets you look at many genes at once, rather than one at a time, and that is what makes it useful for profiling gene activity.

Bioinformatics: the computational side of this topic

Bioinformatics is the use of computational tools to handle and interpret biological data, especially large datasets. It is part of this topic because modern biology produces more data than can be handled by hand, and because tools like BLAST let you compare a sequence with everything already known.

  • 8.21 Bioinformatics is the use of computer tools to collect, store, analyse and interpret biological data, especially large datasets such as DNA and protein sequences. It includes sequence alignment, database searching, and the comparison of sequences from different organisms to find similarities and differences. A typical use is to take a newly obtained sequence and see whether similar sequences from other organisms are already known, which can suggest function, evolutionary relationships and the presence of conserved regions. The point is that bioinformatics is not a separate subject from biology; it is the way large biological data are used.

Risks and benefits of genetically modified organisms

Gene technology is powerful, and the specification asks for the risks and benefits, not just the methods. This is the part where an essay-style answer is most likely to come from.

  • 8.22 Genetically modified organisms have both risks and benefits. Benefits can include increased crop yield, improved nutrition, resistance to pests or herbicides, reduced use of chemical inputs, production of medicines, and faster or more targeted research. Risks can include effects on non-target organisms, the spread of genes to wild relatives, the development of resistant pests, and concerns about food safety, patenting and ecological stability. The important point is that the risks and benefits depend on the specific modification, the organism, the environment and the purpose; a blanket statement that GM is good or bad is not an adequate answer. The answer should weigh a concrete benefit against a concrete risk and say what is relevant to the case in question.

A good answer names specific risks and benefits rather than general ones, and it recognises that the same technology can be used in different ways with different outcomes. For example, a herbicide-tolerant crop can reduce the need for some sprays but can also encourage weed resistance; the exam rewards the balanced, specific response.

How the nervous and gene-technology parts fit together

The topic is really two linked stories. The first is how animals coordinate and respond — sensory detection, action potentials, synapses, the brain, imaging and drugs. The second is how plants coordinate with hormones and how genetic technologies let us manipulate genes and measure their activity. The link is that both are about control: the nervous system controls rapid responses, the plant hormones control growth and development, and gene technology lets us read, move and use genes, including the genes that control those responses.

  • Start with the neurone: sensory, relay, motor, Schwann cells and myelination.
  • Move to the impulse: the action potential as sodium in, potassium out, all-or-nothing, and saltatory conduction in myelinated axons.
  • Move to the synapse: vesicles, calcium, neurotransmitter release, receptor binding, and the way drugs can intervene.
  • Move to the brain: CNS and PNS, the roles of the cerebral hemispheres, hypothalamus, pituitary, cerebellum and medulla, and the imaging methods MRI, fMRI, PET and CT.
  • Move to the chemical side: imbalances such as dopamine in Parkinson’s and serotonin in depression, and how drugs are developed in response.
  • Move to plants: phytochrome, auxin and gibberellins, the link to transcription, and the practical on amylase in germinating grains.
  • Move to gene technology: restriction enzymes and ligase, recombinant DNA, insertion into host cells, production of drugs by modified organisms, microarrays for active genes, and bioinformatics.
  • End with the balanced view on GM organisms, specific benefits and risks.

Typical mistakes

  • Saying the sodium-potassium pump repolarises the membrane during the action potential: it restores the resting distribution over time, but repolarisation is due to potassium leaving.
  • Saying myelination makes ions move faster rather than explaining saltatory conduction.
  • Confusing sensory, relay and motor neurones: sensory carry in, relay are in the CNS, motor carry out to effectors.
  • Saying the rod cell depolarises in light: it hyperpolarises because sodium channels close.
  • Treating habituation as the same as sensory adaptation: habituation is a nervous-system change, not a receptor change.
  • Confusing the brain parts: the hypothalamus is not the pituitary, the cerebellum is not the medulla, and the cerebral hemispheres are not all the same function.
  • Listing MRI, fMRI, PET and CT without saying what each shows or why you would choose it.
  • Saying restriction enzymes join DNA: they cut it; ligase joins it.
  • Saying a vector is the gene itself: the vector is the carrier, such as a plasmid.
  • Treating GM organisms as either wholly good or wholly bad without specific risks and benefits.

Exam-style questions

  1. Describe how an action potential is generated and conducted along an axon, and explain the role of myelination. Answer: At rest the axon membrane is polarised; a stimulus opens voltage-gated sodium channels, sodium ions enter and the membrane depolarises; sodium channels then close and potassium channels open, potassium ions leave and the membrane repolarises; the sodium-potassium pump restores the resting ion distribution over time. The action potential is all-or-nothing. Depolarisation in one region triggers it in the next, so the impulse travels. In myelinated axons, depolarisation occurs only at the nodes of Ranvier, so the impulse appears to jump from node to node, making saltatory conduction much faster than in an unmyelinated axon of the same diameter. (6 marks)
  2. Describe synaptic transmission and explain one way in which a drug can interfere with it. Answer: When an action potential reaches the presynaptic ending, calcium channels open, calcium enters, vesicles of neurotransmitter fuse with the presynaptic membrane and release neurotransmitter into the synaptic cleft; the neurotransmitter diffuses across the cleft and binds to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane, opening ion channels and changing the membrane potential of the postsynaptic neurone. A drug such as lidocaine can block voltage-gated sodium channels, preventing action potentials; or a drug such as nicotine can mimic a neurotransmitter and stimulate its receptors. (5 marks)
  3. Explain how rods detect light, including the role of rhodopsin. Answer: Rod cells contain rhodopsin, made of opsin and retinal. Light causes retinal to change shape, altering opsin, which triggers a transduction pathway that closes sodium channels in the rod membrane; sodium entry falls, the rod cell hyperpolarises, and the pattern of neurotransmitter release changes. This change is passed through the retinal wiring to the optic neurones, which carry impulses to the brain. (5 marks)
  4. Describe the functions of the cerebral hemispheres, hypothalamus, pituitary gland, cerebellum and medulla oblongata. Answer: The cerebral hemispheres are involved in higher functions such as voluntary movement, sensation, thought, memory, language and consciousness, with different regions specialised. The hypothalamus links the nervous and endocrine systems and helps control homeostasis, body temperature, hunger, thirst and pituitary hormone release. The pituitary gland releases hormones that regulate other endocrine glands and other processes. The cerebellum coordinates movement, posture and balance and refines motor control. The medulla oblongata controls automatic functions such as breathing and heart rate. (5 marks)
  5. Compare MRI, fMRI, PET and CT scans of the brain. Answer: MRI uses magnetic fields and radio waves to give detailed images of brain structure. fMRI detects changes in blood flow related to neural activity, showing which areas are active during a task. PET uses a radioactive tracer to show metabolic activity in brain regions. CT uses X-rays to produce cross-sectional images, useful for detecting structural problems such as bleeding or fractures. The methods are complementary: some are better for structure, some for activity. (5 marks)
  6. Describe the roles of phytochrome, auxin and gibberellins in plant responses. Answer: Phytochrome is a light receptor that interconverts between forms in response to light and helps the plant detect light, affecting processes such as flowering and germination. Auxin promotes cell elongation and is involved in tropic responses such as phototropism, where asymmetric distribution causes the shoot to bend toward light. Gibberellins promote growth, including stem elongation and seed germination, partly by affecting transcription. (5 marks)
  7. Explain how recombinant DNA is made and how it can be inserted into other cells. Answer: Recombinant DNA is made by cutting a gene and a vector, often a plasmid, with the same restriction endonuclease so they have complementary sticky ends, mixing them so the gene inserts into the vector, and joining them with DNA ligase. The recombinant vector is then inserted into host cells, such as bacteria, where it can be replicated and the inserted gene expressed. (5 marks)
  8. Describe how microarrays are used to identify active genes. Answer: A microarray has many short DNA sequences attached to a solid surface; cDNA made from the mRNA of a sample and labelled is hybridised to the array; if a gene is active, its cDNA binds to the corresponding spot and the label reveals its presence and relative level. Comparing samples, such as diseased and healthy tissue, shows which genes are up- or down-regulated. (4 marks)
  9. Discuss the risks and benefits of genetically modified organisms. Answer: Benefits include increased yield, improved nutrition, pest and herbicide resistance, reduced chemical use, production of medicines and faster research. Risks include effects on non-target organisms, gene flow to wild relatives, pest resistance, food-safety and ecological-stability concerns, and economic and patenting issues. The answer should be specific to the case, because the same technology can have different outcomes depending on the modification, organism and environment. (6 marks)

Use this summary to place each idea before you go into the detail in the full notes. Revise the neurone roles and myelination, the action potential sequence and saltatory conduction, synaptic transmission and the drug examples, the rod and rhodopsin mechanism, the brain regions and the imaging methods, the plant hormones and the practical, and the gene-technology tools and applications. Then check the full notes for the drug names and the microarray details, and move on to the next topic when you can do the calculations and the comparisons without prompting.

title: AS Level Mathematics: Measures of Variation and Standard Deviation
content:
AS Level Mathematics: Measures of Variation and Standard Deviation

Two data sets can share a mean and behave completely differently: one tightly clustered, one wildly spread. Measures of variation quantify that difference. This note builds the topic from zero: the range and interquartile range, the variance and standard deviation with the full calculation from first principles, the frequency-table and coded forms, outliers, and how to compare distributions fairly. Every formula is derived once, because the derivation is what makes it stick.

Why spread matters

Location alone is a half-description. A machine filling 500 g bags with a standard deviation of 2 g is trustworthy; one with a standard deviation of 30 g is not, though both may average 500 g. Spread measures consistency, risk and reliability, and every comparison question rewards naming both a location and a spread.

Range and interquartile range

range = largest - smallest
interquartile range IQR = Q3 - Q1
semi-interquartile range = (Q3 - Q1)/2
MeasureUsesWeakness
RangeOnly the two extremesDestroyed by one outlier
IQRThe middle halfIgnores the tails entirely
Standard deviationEvery valueDragged by outliers; more arithmetic

Worked example. Find the range, IQR and semi-IQR of 12, 15, 18, 21, 25, 30, 44.

range = 44 - 12 = 32
n = 7; median = 21; Q1 = 15; Q3 = 30
IQR = 15;  semi-IQR = 7.5

The 44 stretches the range to 32 while leaving the IQR untouched: exactly the robustness the IQR is chosen for.

Variance and standard deviation defined

variance = mean of the squared deviations from the mean
standard deviation = √(variance)

population form:  σ² = (sum of (x - mu)²)/n
sample form:      s² = (sum of (x - xbar)²)/(n - 1)

Why square the deviations? Signed deviations always sum to zero, so they cannot measure spread; squaring removes the signs and penalises large gaps heavily. The square root returns the answer to the original units, which is why standard deviation, not variance, is quoted in context.

Worked example (full working). Find the standard deviation of 4, 7, 9, 10, 10.

mean = 40/5 = 8
deviations: -4, -1, 1, 2, 2
squares: 16, 1, 1, 4, 4  →  sum 26
variance = 26/5 = 5.2
standard deviation = √(5.2) = 2.28

The computational formula

σ² = (sum of x²)/n - (mean)²

this is algebraically identical to the deviation form but far quicker

Worked example. Repeat the previous calculation with the computational form.

sum x = 40;  mean = 8
sum x² = 16 + 49 + 81 + 100 + 100 = 346
variance = 346/5 - 64 = 69.2 - 64 = 5.2
standard deviation = 2.28  (identical, as it must be)

Frequency tables

mean = (sum of f x)/(sum of f)
variance = (sum of f x²)/(sum of f) - (mean)²

Worked example. Find the mean and standard deviation of the distribution x: 1, 2, 3, 4 with frequencies 2, 5, 8, 5.

sum f = 20
sum fx = 2(1) + 5(2) + 8(3) + 5(4) = 2 + 10 + 24 + 20 = 56  →  mean 2.8
sum fx² = 2(1) + 5(4) + 8(9) + 5(16) = 2 + 20 + 72 + 80 = 174
variance = 174/20 - 7.84 = 8.7 - 7.84 = 0.86
standard deviation = 0.927

For grouped data the midpoint stands in for each class, so the standard deviation is an estimate, like the grouped mean.

Worked example 2 (grouped). Estimate the standard deviation of 0–10 (3), 10–20 (7), 20–30 (10).

midpoints 5, 15, 25;  sum f = 20
sum fx = 15 + 105 + 250 = 370  →  mean 18.5
sum fx² = 3(25) + 7(225) + 10(625) = 75 + 1575 + 6250 = 7900
variance = 7900/20 - 342.25 = 395 - 342.25 = 52.75
standard deviation = 7.26

Coding and the effect on spread

if y = (x - a)/b then:
  mean(y) = (mean(x) - a)/b
  sd(y) = sd(x)/|b|
  variance(y) = variance(x)/b²

shifts (a) do not change spread; scaling (b) scales it

Worked example. The coded values y = (x − 100)/5 have mean 4 and standard deviation 1.2. Find the mean and standard deviation of x.

mean x = 5(4) + 100 = 120
sd x = 5(1.2) = 6

The intuition: adding a constant slides the whole distribution without stretching it; multiplying stretches every gap by the same factor.

Outliers

lower fence = Q1 - 1.5 IQR
upper fence = Q3 + 1.5 IQR
values beyond the fences are outliers

Worked example. With Q1 = 20, Q3 = 32 and a maximum of 60, is 60 an outlier?

IQR = 12; upper fence = 32 + 18 = 50
60 > 50, so yes, 60 is an outlier

Outliers are not automatically errors: they may be genuine extreme values, which is why the median and IQR often summarise skewed data better than the mean and standard deviation.

Comparing distributions properly

A full comparison answers four points: which has the higher typical value, which is more spread, whether either has outliers, and what that means in context.

Worked example. Boys: mean 62, sd 8. Girls: mean 68, sd 4. Compare.

girls have the higher typical mark (68 vs 62)
girls are more consistent (sd 4 vs 8; roughly half the spread)
boys' marks are more widely dispersed, so their range of performance
is broader; the sd ratio 2 suggests boys' marks vary twice as much
about their mean

Never compare standard deviations of data measured in different units or on different scales without converting; here both are marks, so the comparison is valid.

Standard deviation in context

Worked example (quality control). A machine fills bags with mean 500 g and sd 3 g. Assuming a roughly symmetric distribution, about what proportion lies within one standard deviation of the mean?

one sd either side: 497 to 503 g
for a roughly normal shape, about 68 per cent of bags fall in this band
(and about 95 per cent within two sds: 494 to 506 g)

The 68/95/99.7 guide is approximate and only valid for roughly bell-shaped data; stating that condition is part of the answer.

Comparing spread across different units

Standard deviations cannot be compared directly when the scales differ. The coefficient of variation puts them on a common footing by expressing the spread as a fraction of the mean:

coefficient of variation = 100 x sd/mean  (per cent)

A: mean 50 kg, sd 4 kg   →  CV = 8 per cent
B: mean 8000 pounds, sd 400 pounds  →  CV = 5 per cent
B is relatively more consistent despite the larger absolute sd

Worked example. Two athletes' times over a season: A has mean 12.0 s, sd 0.15 s; B has mean 60.0 s, sd 0.60 s (different events). Which is more consistent relative to their event?

CV(A) = 0.15/12.0 × 100 = 1.25 per cent
CV(B) = 0.60/60.0 × 100 = 1.00 per cent
B is relatively more consistent, even though the absolute sd is 4 times larger

Without the coefficient of variation, the comparison would favour A for the wrong reason. State the units and the ratio when answering.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Range) Find the range of 3, 8, 12, 15, 22. Answer: 19.
  2. (IQR) Find the IQR of 5, 6, 9, 11, 14, 18. Answer: Q1 = 6.75, Q3 = 15, IQR = 8.25.
  3. (SD) Find the standard deviation of 2, 4, 4, 6, 9. Answer: mean 5; deviations −3, −1, −1, 1, 4; squares 9, 1, 1, 1, 16 = 28; variance 5.6; sd 2.37.
  4. (Computational) For sum x = 60, sum x² = 800, n = 10, find the sd. Answer: variance = 80 − 36 = 44; sd = 6.63.
  5. (Frequency) x: 0, 1, 2 with f: 4, 3, 3. Find the mean. Answer: 9/10 = 0.9.
  6. (Coding) y = (x − 20)/4 has sd 2.5. Find the sd of x. Answer: 10.
  7. (Outlier) Q1 = 12, Q3 = 20, maximum 45. Is 45 an outlier? Answer: IQR = 8, fence = 32; yes.
  8. (Compare) A: mean 40, sd 5. B: mean 40, sd 12. What differs? Answer: same centre, different spread; B is far more variable.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Forgetting to root: the variance is in squared units; the standard deviation is its square root. Quoting the variance as the sd is a units error.
  • Dividing by n or n − 1: use the convention the question implies; for a population divide by n, for a sample estimate divide by n − 1. Mixing them shifts the answer.
  • Deviation sign errors: the deviations must sum to zero — if they do not, the mean was copied wrongly.
  • Coding with the wrong operation: sd divides by |b|, never subtracts a; shifts do not affect spread.
  • Comparing different units: an sd of 5 marks and an sd of 5 kg are not comparable; convert or use the coefficient of variation.
  • Outlier fences: 1.5 × IQR beyond the quartiles, not beyond the range or the median.
  • Grouped estimates: call them estimates and note that midpoints are assumed uniform within each class.
  • One-sided comparison: a comparison naming only the mean earns half the marks; always add the spread and its interpretation.

Formula summary

range = max - min;  IQR = Q3 - Q1
variance = (sum of x²)/n - (mean)²
standard deviation = √(variance)
coded: mean(x) = b mean(y) + a;  sd(x) = |b| sd(y)
CV = 100 sd/mean

Learn the computational variance form rather than the deviation form: it needs one pass for the sum and one for the sum of squares, and it fails loudly when the mean is wrong because the deviations then do not sum to zero.

Equations and symbols

Every definition and relation these topics are examined on, gathered into one reference sheet, each written with its real notation and followed by a key naming each symbol and what it stands for. The sections above derive them; this is the sheet you revise from when a question has to be turned into algebra quickly and the marks depend on using the right formula, not a nearly-right one.

Range, quartiles and the interquartile range

range = largest − smallest
Key: largest and smallest = the two extreme observations, in the unit of the data; the range is in that same unit and uses only two of the values. That is its weakness as well as its speed: one outlier can double it.

IQR = Q₃ − Q₁ and semi-interquartile range = (Q₃ − Q₁)/2
Key: Q₁ = the lower quartile, the value with a quarter of the data below it; Q₃ = the upper quartile, three quarters below it; IQR = the spread of the middle half, in the data's unit. It ignores the tails entirely, which is why it survives outliers that wreck the range and the standard deviation.

outlier rule: a value below Q₁ − 1.5 × IQR or above Q₃ + 1.5 × IQR
Key: Q₁, Q₃ = the quartiles; IQR = Q₃ − Q₁; 1.5 = the conventional multiplier. An outlier is flagged, not deleted: a question that asks for its effect wants the sentence "with the outlier removed the mean falls and the standard deviation falls sharply".

Variance and standard deviation from first principles

σ² = Σ(x − μ)²/n and σ = √(σ²)
Key: σ² (sigma squared) = the population variance, in the square of the data's unit; x = each observation; μ = the population mean; n = the number of observations; σ = the standard deviation, back in the original unit. Squaring first is essential: signed deviations always sum to zero, so they cannot measure spread on their own.

s² = Σ(x − x̄)²/(n − 1)
Key: s² = the sample variance, an unbiased estimate of σ²; x̄ = the sample mean; n − 1 = the degrees of freedom, because one degree was spent estimating the mean. The two forms differ only in the denominator, and the question's wording ("the data" versus "a sample of") decides which to use.

σ² = Σx²/n − μ² and s² = (Σx² − n x̄²)/(n − 1)
Key: Σx² = the sum of the squared observations; μ, x̄ = the mean; n = the number of observations. The computational forms are algebraically identical to the deviation forms and far quicker — one pass for the sum, one for the squares, no list of deviations.

frequency form: mean = Σfx/Σf, variance = Σfx²/Σf − (mean)²
Key: f = the frequency of each value or class; x = the value, or the midpoint of a class; Σf = the total frequency. For grouped data the midpoint stands in for every value in the class, so both the mean and the standard deviation are estimates and should be described as such.

Coding, combining and comparing

y = (x − a)/b ⇒ ȳ = (x̄ − a)/b, s_y = s_x/|b|, s_y² = s_x²/b²
Key: x = the original variable; a = a constant subtracted (a shift, such as removing 1000 from every salary); b = a constant divisor (a unit change, such as pence to pounds); ȳ, s_y = the mean and standard deviation after coding. A shift moves every value equally and leaves spread untouched; a scale changes the spread by the factor and the variance by its square. The modulus matters because a b < 0 reverses the order of the data but cannot make spread negative.

z = (x − x̄)/s
Key: z = the number of standard deviations a value sits from the mean, dimensionless; x = the value; x̄ = the mean; s = the standard deviation. It is the standardising step of the normal distribution, and it is how two data sets measured in different units are compared fairly.

coefficient of variation = (s/x̄) × 100%
Key: s = the standard deviation; x̄ = the mean, which must be positive and non-zero for the ratio to mean anything; the result is a percentage, dimensionless. It compares relative spread across data sets with different units or very different means, where comparing s directly would mislead.

combined mean = (n₁x̄₁ + n₂x̄₂)/(n₁ + n₂)
Key: n₁, n₂ = the two group sizes; x̄₁, x̄₂ = the two group means; the combination is weighted by size, not a midpoint of the two means. Two classes averaging 60 and 80 do not average 70 unless they have the same number of students.

s² combined = [n₁(s₁² + (x̄₁ − x̄)²) + n₂(s₂² + (x̄₂ − x̄)²)]/(n₁ + n₂)
Key: s₁², s₂² = the within-group variances; x̄₁, x̄₂ = the group means; x̄ = the combined mean; n₁, n₂ = the group sizes. Each group's spread contributes twice: its own variance, plus the squared distance of its mean from the overall mean. The second term is why the combined standard deviation can exceed both group values.

title: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Ratio, Rate and Proportion
content:
Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Ratio, Rate and Proportion

Ratio, rate and proportion are the mathematics of comparison: how two quantities share a whole, how fast one changes with another, and what happens when one stays on the same path to infinity. They appear in nearly every Paper 2, usually as multi-step word problems where the arithmetic is easy and the interpretation is not. This note builds the topic from zero: simplifying and dividing in ratios, the unitary method for direct and inverse proportion, the algebra forms y = kx and y = k/x, and rates — speed, density, flow — with their unit conversions.

Ratio fundamentals

A ratio compares quantities of the same kind. The notation a : b means "a for every b". Equivalent ratios are made by multiplying or dividing all parts by the same number; the simplified ratio has no common factor (other than 1) and, for measurements, the same units.

  • Simplify: 24 : 36 = 2 : 3 (divide both by 12).
  • Three-part: 2 : 3 : 5 means five shares in total; each share is total ÷ 10.
  • Units first: 500 g : 1.5 kg = 500 : 1500 = 1 : 3. Convert before simplifying, never after.

Worked example. Share £84 in the ratio 3 : 4.

total parts = 3 + 4 = 7
one part = 84/7 = 12
shares = 3 × 12 = 36 and 4 × 12 = 48
check: 36 + 48 = 84

Worked example 2 (three parts). A sum of $240 is divided among A, B and C in the ratio 2 : 3 : 5. Find each share.

parts = 2 + 3 + 5 = 10
one part = 240/10 = 24
A = 2 × 24 = 48, B = 3 × 24 = 72, C = 5 × 24 = 120

Combining ratios and ratio changes

Two ratios sharing a middle term can be combined by making that term common:

A : B = 2 : 3 and B : C = 4 : 5
LCM of the B terms (3 and 4) is 12:
A : B = 8 : 12 and B : C = 12 : 15
so A : B : C = 8 : 12 : 15

Worked example (change). A bag contains red and blue counters in the ratio 5 : 3. After 6 red counters are removed, the ratio becomes 1 : 1. Find the original numbers.

let red = 5x, blue = 3x
(5x - 6)/3x = 1  →  5x - 6 = 3x  →  2x = 6  →  x = 3
original: red = 15, blue = 9
check: after removing 6 red, 9 : 9 = 1 : 1

Direct proportion

Two quantities are in direct proportion when one is a constant multiple of the other: double one, double the other. The algebra form is y = kx, a straight line through the origin.

y = k x        k = y/x (the constant of proportionality)
unitary method: find the value of one unit, then multiply

Worked example. 5 pens cost $3.25. Find the cost of 12 pens.

one pen = 3.25/5 = $0.65
12 pens = 12 × 0.65 = $7.80

Worked example 2 (algebra form). y is directly proportional to x, and y = 18 when x = 6. Find y when x = 11.

y = kx  →  18 = 6k  →  k = 3
y = 3 × 11 = 33

Worked example 3 (proportion with powers). The mass of a sphere is proportional to the cube of its radius; a sphere of radius 2 cm has mass 40 g. Find the mass of a sphere of radius 3 cm.

m = k r³  →  40 = k x 8  →  k = 5
m = 5 × 27 = 135 g

Inverse proportion

Inverse proportion means one quantity falls as the other rises: double one, halve the other. The algebra form is y = k/x (the product xy is constant).

y = k/x        x y = k
unitary method: find the total "work" (product), then divide

Worked example. Six workers build a wall in 8 days. How long will 4 workers take (same rate)?

total work = 6 × 8 = 48 worker-days
time for 4 = 48/4 = 12 days

Worked example 2 (algebra). y is inversely proportional to x; y = 5 when x = 4. Find y when x = 10.

xy = k  →  4 × 5 = 20  →  y = 20/10 = 2

The shape on a graph distinguishes the two: direct proportion is a straight line through the origin; inverse proportion is a curve that never touches either axis (a hyperbola).

Rates

A rate compares quantities with different units: speed (distance per time), density (mass per volume), pressure (force per area), flow rate (volume per time). Each is a division, and each can be rearranged.

speed = distance/time        density = mass/volume
pressure = force/area        flow rate = volume/time

average speed over a journey = total distance/total time
(not the average of the speeds, unless the times are equal)

Worked example 1 (speed). A car travels 150 km in 2 hours 30 minutes. Find its average speed in km/h and m/s.

time = 2.5 h
speed = 150/2.5 = 60 km/h
in m/s: 60 × 1000/3600 = 16.7 m/s

Worked example 2 (density). A block of volume 250 cm³ has mass 675 g. Find its density, and the mass of 400 cm³ of the same material.

density = 675/250 = 2.7 g/cm³
mass = 2.7 × 400 = 1080 g = 1.08 kg

Worked example 3 (average speed trap). A cyclist rides 20 km at 20 km/h, then 20 km at 10 km/h. Find the average speed for the whole journey.

time 1 = 20/20 = 1 h;  time 2 = 20/10 = 2 h
total distance = 40 km; total time = 3 h
average speed = 40/3 = 13.3 km/h (not 15!)

Flow rates and filling problems

Flow-rate questions combine a rate with a volume: a tap fills at 4 litres per minute, a pump empties at 6 litres per minute, a pipe delivers water at 2.5 m s⁻¹ through a cross-section. The method is the same division, but the units demand attention — litres per minute into litres and minutes, cubic metres per second into m³ and s, with 1 m³ = 1000 litres and 1 minute = 60 s.

Worked example. A bath holds 180 litres. A tap fills it at 9 litres per minute, but the plug leaks 1.5 litres per minute. How long does the bath take to fill?

net rate = 9 - 1.5 = 7.5 litres per minute
time = 180/7.5 = 24 minutes

Best buys and multi-step comparisons

Ratio reasoning powers the practical comparison questions: which packet is better value, which journey is faster per kilometre, which contract costs less per month. The method is always to reduce both options to the same unit before comparing, and to compare like with like (price per 100 g, cost per km, cost per month).

Worked example. A 750 g box of cereal costs $3.60 and a 1.2 kg box costs $5.28. Which is better value?

large: 5.28/1.2 = $4.40 per kg
small: 3.60/0.75 = $4.80 per kg
better value: the 1.2 kg box (lower cost per kg)

Worked example 2 (multi-step). Two phone contracts: A charges $12 per month plus $0.10 per GB; B charges $20 per month with 15 GB included. For someone using 20 GB per month, which is cheaper over a year?

A: 12 + 0.10 × 20 = $14 per month; yearly = 168
B: $20 per month; yearly = 240
A is cheaper for a 20 GB user by $72 per year.
(check the crossover: 12 + 0.1g = 20 → g = 80 GB, so B
only wins for very heavy users)

The crossover point is a favourite extension: set the two cost expressions equal and solve, then interpret which side of the crossing each customer sits on.

Worked examples: mixed problems

Worked example. A recipe for 4 people uses 300 g of rice. How much is needed for 10 people, and how many people can be served with 2.1 kg?

per person = 300/4 = 75 g
for 10: 750 g
2100 g / 75 = 28 people

Worked example 2 (currency). An exchange rate is £1 = $1.25. Convert £240 to dollars and $500 to pounds.

240 × 1.25 = $300
500/1.25 = £400

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Divide) Share 360 in the ratio 5 : 7. Answer: parts 12; one part 30; shares 150 and 210.
  2. (Simplify with units) Simplify 40 minutes : 2 hours. Answer: 40 : 120 = 1 : 3.
  3. (Direct) 8 m of cloth costs $52. Find the cost of 13 m. Answer: per metre $6.50; 13 × 6.50 = $84.50.
  4. (Inverse) 4 taps fill a tank in 45 minutes. How long for 6 taps? Answer: total = 4 × 45 = 180 tap-minutes; 180/6 = 30 minutes.
  5. (Algebra) y ∝ x² and y = 50 when x = 5. Find y when x = 8. Answer: 50 = k × 25 → k = 2; y = 2 × 64 = 128.
  6. (Rate) A train covers 210 km in 2 h 20 min. Find its average speed. Answer: 2⅓ h; 210 ÷ 7/3 = 90 km/h.
  7. (Density) 150 cm³ of a liquid has mass 120 g. Find the mass of 1 litre. Answer: density 0.8 g/cm³; 1000 cm³ × 0.8 = 800 g.
  8. (Reverse) A map scale is 1 : 50 000. Two points are 7 cm apart on the map. Find the real distance in km. Answer: 7 × 50 000 = 350 000 cm = 3.5 km.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Averaging speeds: average speed is total distance over total time, never the mean of the two speeds unless the times are equal. The classic 20/10 km/h trap answers 15 instead of 13.3.
  • Ratio direction: dividing 84 in 3 : 4 is not 84 × 3/4 for both shares; identify which share is which before writing the answer.
  • Units in ratios: 500 g : 1.5 kg simplifies only after conversion to 500 : 1500 = 1 : 3. Mixing units gives 1 : 0.003.
  • Direct versus inverse: ask "if one doubles, what happens to the other?" Doubling both means direct; one doubling while the other halves means inverse.
  • Proportional to a power: for y ∝ x², doubling x multiplies y by 4; for y ∝ √x it multiplies by √2. Find k from the given pair first.
  • Currency direction: multiplying by the rate converts one way; the reverse needs division. Check with a rough estimate.
  • Time units: 2 h 30 min is 2.5 h, not 2.3 h. Convert minutes to a decimal fraction of an hour before dividing.
  • Rounding mid-calculation: keep full accuracy until the final answer, then round to 3 s.f. or as instructed; money answers usually need 2 decimal places.

Equations and symbols

Every relation this topic is examined on, written with its real notation and followed by a key naming each symbol, its unit and what it means. Restaurant-bill questions, savings plans and areas under curves all reduce to one of these lines with numbers in it.

Ratio and dividing a quantity

a : b : c, simplified by dividing every term by the HCF
Key: a, b, c = the quantities being compared, all in the same unit; HCF = highest common factor. A ratio has no units and no fixed size — 3 : 5 is the same comparison as 6 : 10, which is why simplifying first always shortens the arithmetic.

share of a = total × a/(a + b)
Key: a, b = the ratio parts; total = the quantity being divided. Equivalently each part is total ÷ (a + b) and the share is a times that value — the additive-unitary method, which is safer when there are three or more parts.

1 : n on a map ⇒ real length = map length × n
Key: n = the scale factor, e.g. 1 : 25 000 means 1 cm on the map is 25 000 cm (250 m) on the ground. The same factor applies to lengths only; areas scale by n² and volumes by n³.

similar shapes: lengths a : b ⇒ areas a² : b² and volumes a³ : b³
Key: a : b = the ratio of corresponding lengths; a² : b² = the ratio of corresponding areas; a³ : b³ = the ratio of corresponding volumes. Squaring and cubing the length ratio is what a "the model is 20 times smaller" question is actually asking.

Direct and inverse proportion

y ∝ x ⇒ y = kx
Key: y = the dependent quantity; x = the independent quantity; k = the constant of proportionality, found from one known pair. Direct proportion means doubling x doubles y — a straight line through the origin.

y ∝ 1/x ⇒ y = k/x, so k = xy
Key: the same symbols; k = the constant product. Inverse proportion means doubling x halves y — the curve never reaches either axis.

y ∝ x² ⇒ y = kx²; y ∝ √x ⇒ y = k√x
Key: k = the constant, still found from one pair. The Extended paper's variation questions: write the proportionality, convert it to an equation with k, substitute the known pair, then answer the question asked.

percentage change: new value = original × (1 ± r/100)
Key: r = the percentage rate; the plus sign is an increase, the minus a decrease. Two successive changes multiply their multipliers — a 10% rise then a 10% fall returns to 99% of the original, not 100%.

Rates and compound measures

speed = distance/time, so distance = speed × time and time = distance/speed
Key: speed in m/s or km/h; distance in m or km; time in s or h — the units must match the speed before substituting. The triangle is just this equation rearranged three ways.

average speed = total distance ÷ total time
Key: total distance = the sum of every leg; total time = the sum of every leg's time, including stops. Averaging the two speeds instead of the two journeys is the standard trap and gives a number that is too high.

density = mass/volume, so mass = density × volume
Key: density in g/cm³ or kg/m³; mass in g or kg; volume in cm³ or m³. Convert one unit before dividing, because 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³.

flow rate = volume/time
Key: volume in litres or m³; time in seconds or minutes; the rate in the matching unit per unit time. "How long to fill the tank" is this equation solved for time.

1 m/s = 3.6 km/h
Key: the conversion factor between the two speed units: multiply m/s by 3.6 for km/h, divide km/h by 3.6 for m/s. Worth memorising, because a paper that gives the distance in km and the time in seconds is testing exactly this step.

title: Circular Motion and SHM — Study Notes
content:
Circular Motion and SHM

Uniform circular motion

A particle moving in a circle of radius r at constant speed has a constantly changing velocity, because its direction changes. Angular speed ω is the rate of change of angle in radians per second: ω = 2π/T = 2πf. The linear speed is v = ωr.

Centripetal acceleration and force

The acceleration is directed towards the centre: a = v²/r = ω²r. The resultant force providing it is F = mv²/r = mω²r, also towards the centre. This force does no work, because it is always perpendicular to the velocity, so the kinetic energy stays constant.

Example: a particle on a 0.40 m radius with T = 2.0 s has ω = π rad s⁻¹, v = 1.26 m s⁻¹ and a = π² × 0.40 ≈ 3.9 m s⁻².

Simple harmonic motion as projected circular motion

The displacement of a point moving on a circle, projected onto a diameter, is x = x₀ sin ωt (or cos ωt). Its acceleration is a = −ω²x, always opposite to the displacement, so the defining condition for SHM is that acceleration is proportional to and opposite to displacement.

Solutions: x = x₀ sin ωt starts at the centre; x = x₀ cos ωt starts at an extreme. Time period T = 2π/ω.

Velocity and acceleration:

  • v = ±ω√(x₀² − x²); v_max = ωx₀ at the centre
  • a_max = ω²x₀ at the extremes; a = 0 at the centre

Example: a pendulum with x₀ = 0.02 m and f = 0.5 Hz has a_max = (2π × 0.5)² × 0.02 ≈ 0.20 m s⁻².

Energy in SHM

The total energy is E = ½mω²x₀², constant. It is exchanged between kinetic energy (maximum at the centre) and potential energy (maximum at the extremes). Kinetic energy is at a maximum when displacement is zero, not when acceleration is largest.

Damping and resonance

Damping removes energy from the oscillator. Light damping gives slow decay of amplitude; critical damping returns the system to equilibrium in the shortest time without oscillating; heavy damping is slower still. A system driven at its natural frequency resonates, giving maximum amplitude (playground swings, microwave ovens, bridges that must avoid the wind frequency).

Exam tips: quote a = −ω²x as the defining condition in SHM questions. Time-period questions often need only T = 2π/ω. State which energy is at a maximum and where.

title: Exam technique: Ethics and AI
content:
### What earns the marks
For bias scenarios, the mechanism stated (training data encodes past discrimination) earns the first mark and a concrete mitigation (balanced data plus outcome audits) earns the second. For legislation, the act named plus the offence matched earns both marks: access offences belong to Computer Misuse, copying to Copyright, personal data to Data Protection.
### Traps
Error: data called neutral. Correction: models inherit their training distribution. Error: every offence labelled hacking. Correction: match offence to act. Error: benefits claimed to excuse rights violations. Correction: consent and licensing still required.

title: Mensuration — Area and Volume
content:
Mensuration — Area and Volume

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): units, perimeter/area (incl. sectors), surface area, volume of standard solids, composite shapes.

1. Units

1 m² = 10 000 cm²; 1 m³ = 1 000 000 cm³; 1 litre = 1000 cm³. Convert area/volume factors carefully (square/cube the length factor).

2. Area

  • Triangle ½bh; trapezium ½(a + b)h; parallelogram bh.
  • Circle A = πr²; sector area = (θ/360)πr²; arc = (θ/360) × 2πr.
  • Composites: split, calculate, add/subtract.

3. Volume and surface area

  • Cuboid V = lbh; prism V = cross-section × length.
  • Cylinder V = πr²h; SA = 2πr² + 2πrh.
  • Pyramid V = ⅓ × base area × h.
  • Cone V = ⅓πr²h; SA = πr² + πrl, with l² = r² + h².
  • Sphere V = (4/3)πr³; SA = 4πr².

4. Problem solving

Flow/filling: volume ÷ rate = time. Packing: divide volumes (check edge alignment). Nets for surface area: label every face before adding.

Exam tips: keep π on the calculator until the final answer; for sector problems ask "fraction of the full circle?"; quote units in every answer.

title: Networks and the Internet — Study Notes
content:
Networks and the Internet

The TCP/IP Stack

Four layers: Application (HTTP, FTP, SMTP, DNS), Transport (TCP reliable, connection-oriented with sequence numbers and acknowledgements; UDP fast, connectionless), Internet (IP addressing and routing), Link (physical delivery on the local network). Layering separates concerns so each layer can change independently.

Switching

  • Circuit switching: a dedicated path is held for the call (traditional telephone) — wasteful if idle.
  • Packet switching: data split into packets routed independently; each carries source/destination addresses and a sequence number, reassembled at the destination. Efficient and fault-tolerant; packets may arrive out of order (TCP fixes ordering).

Addressing and Subnetting

IPv4 addresses are 32 bits, written dotted decimal, split into network + host portions by the subnet mask. ANDing an IP with the mask yields the network ID. 192.168.4.0/26 means the first 26 bits are network, leaving 6 host bits: 64 addresses, 62 usable. NAT maps private addresses to one public IP.

Models and Protection

Client-server centralises services (web, email, files); peer-to-peer shares directly (torrents, small LANs). Firewalls filter traffic by rules; proxy servers sit between clients and the internet, caching and filtering; ports identify services (80/443 web, 25 SMTP).

Exam tips: compute usable hosts from a given prefix; trace a packet through the four layers naming one protocol per layer; explain one advantage of packet over circuit switching.

Protocols and switching

A protocol is a set of rules that devices follow to communicate. TCP/IP is the suite used on the internet, and protocols define how data is addressed, formatted and checked for errors.

In circuit switching a dedicated path is set up for the whole call, as in the traditional telephone network. In packet switching the message is split into packets, each carrying a header with source and destination addresses and a sequence number. Packets can take different routes and are reassembled at the destination.

Exam tip: packet switching uses the network efficiently because no path is reserved, but packets can arrive out of order.

title: Alkenes Revision Notes Edexcel IAL AS Chemistry
content:
Alkenes AS Level Chemistry

These revision notes cover Topic 5 Alkenes from the Edexcel International AS Level Chemistry specification, detailing hydrocarbon unsaturation, geometric isomerism, electrophilic addition mechanisms, addition polymerisation, and polymer waste management.

Structure and bonding in alkenes

Alkenes and cycloalkenes are unsaturated hydrocarbons containing a carbon-carbon double bond, which consists of one sigma bond and one pi bond. The general formula for non-cyclic alkenes is CnH2n. A sigma bond is formed by the direct head-on overlap of atomic orbitals along the internuclear axis, providing restricted rotation. A pi bond is formed by the sideways overlap of adjacent p orbitals above and below the plane of the carbon atoms. The carbon atoms of a C=C double bond are planar, with bond angles of approximately 120 degrees due to three regions of electron density repelling each other.

  • General formula for alkenes: CnH2n
  • Unsaturated hydrocarbons possess a carbon-carbon double bond consisting of one sigma bond and one pi bond
  • Cycloalkenes also contain a C=C double bond and are unsaturated hydrocarbons
  • The pi bond electron cloud is susceptible to attack by electrophiles
  • Carbon atoms of the C=C double bond are trigonal planar with 120° bond angles

Geometric isomerism and E-Z naming

Geometric isomerism arises due to the restricted rotation around the C=C double bond caused by the presence of the pi bond. For geometric isomers to exist, each carbon atom of the C=C double bond must be attached to two different groups. When the traditional cis- and trans- naming system breaks down because the groups attached to the double-bonded carbons are not identical or simple, the E-Z naming system must be used. Priorities are assigned to the groups on each carbon using the Cahn-Ingold-Prelog priority rules based on atomic number. The E isomer has the highest priority groups on opposite sides of the double bond, while the Z isomer has the highest priority groups on the same side.

  • Restricted rotation around the C=C double bond prevents free rotation of substituents
  • Each carbon in the double bond must have two different groups attached for geometric isomerism
  • E-Z system is necessary when cis- and trans- terms become ambiguous or break down
  • Priority is determined by higher atomic number attached directly to the double-bonded carbon
  • E means entgegen (opposite sides); Z means zusammen (same side)

Reactions of alkenes

Alkenes undergo addition reactions where the pi bond breaks and two new single bonds form. Hydrogen addition occurs at 150 degrees Celsius using a nickel catalyst to form an alkane through catalytic hydrogenation. Halogens add rapidly at room temperature to produce a di-substituted halogenoalkane. Hydrogen halides add across the double bond to produce mono-substituted halogenoalkanes. Steam addition requires a phosphoric acid catalyst or sulfuric acid catalyst under high temperature and pressure to produce alcohols. Acidified potassium manganate(VII) oxidises the double bond in a cold solution to produce a diol, causing a colour change from purple to colourless.

  • Hydrogenation: Alkene + H2 in the presence of a Ni catalyst forms an alkane
  • Halogenation: Alkene + X2 produces a di-substituted halogenoalkane
  • Hydrohalogenation: Alkene + HX produces a mono-substituted halogenoalkane
  • Hydration: Alkene + H2O(g) with an acid catalyst (H3PO4) produces an alcohol
    • Oxidation: Alkene + acidified KMnO4 produces a diol with a purple to colourless transition

Testing for unsaturation

The qualitative test for the presence of a C=C double bond uses bromine or bromine water. When an orange-brown bromine solution is shaken with an alkene, the bromine adds across the double bond in an electrophilic addition reaction, causing the solution to decolourise from orange-brown to colourless. Alkanes do not react with bromine water in the dark and the solution remains orange-brown.

  • Reagent: Bromine water or liquid bromine
    • Observation with an alkene: Colour changes from orange-brown to colourless
  • Observation with an alkane: No reaction, solution remains orange-brown
