  • Test confirms the presence of an unsaturated carbon-carbon double bond

Mechanisms of electrophilic addition

Electrophilic addition is the characteristic reaction mechanism of alkenes. An electrophile is an electron pair acceptor. The high electron density of the pi bond induces a dipole in non-polar halogen molecules. Curly arrows start from a bond or a lone pair of electrons and point to the electron-deficient site. In the electrophilic addition of bromine to ethene, the pi bond electrons attack the bromine molecule, heterolytically breaking the Br-Br bond and forming a cyclic bromonium ion intermediate or carbocation, followed by attack from the bromide ion. In hydrogen bromide addition, HBr is polar. The hydrogen ion acts as an electrophile, and addition to unsymmetrical alkenes such as propene can yield two possible carbocation intermediates. The major product is formed via the more stable carbocation intermediate. Carbocation stability follows the order: tertiary greater than secondary greater than primary, due to the positive inductive effect of alkyl groups which push electron density towards the positively charged carbon atom.

  • Electrophile definition: An electron pair acceptor
  • Curly arrows must start precisely from a bond or a lone pair
    • Carbocation stability order: tertiary > secondary > primary
  • Primary carbocation has one alkyl group attached to the positively charged carbon
  • Secondary carbocation has two alkyl groups attached
  • Tertiary carbocation has three alkyl groups attached, making it the most stable due to maximum positive inductive effect
  • Major product prediction follows Markovnikov rule: the hydrogen adds to the carbon with more hydrogens already attached

Addition polymerisation

Addition polymerisation involves many small unsaturated alkene molecules, called monomers, joining together to form a long saturated chain called a polymer. The double bond of each monomer opens up to form single covalent bonds with adjacent monomers. To draw the repeat unit given the monomer, change the C=C double bond into a single C-C bond, extend the bonds outside square brackets, and place a letter n outside. To find the monomer from a repeat unit, identify the two-carbon repeat backbone and convert the single bond back into a double bond.

    Polymerisation type: Addition polymerisation of alkenes
  • Monomers contain a carbon-carbon double bond; polymers contain a saturated carbon backbone
  • Repeat unit formula is enclosed in brackets with bonds extending through the brackets
  • Do not leave dangling double bonds inside the repeat unit structure
  • Poly(ethene) and poly(chloroethene) are standard examples of addition polymers

Polymer disposal and environmental management

Chemists limit environmental problems caused by polymer disposal through innovative chemical engineering. Non-biodegradable polymers persist in landfill sites. Biodegradable polymers, such as those made from poly(lactic acid) derived from plant starch, are broken down by microorganisms into natural substances. Incineration of halogen-containing polymers like poly(chloroethene) produces toxic acidic waste gases such as hydrogen chloride. Chemists remove these toxic waste gases by flue gas desulfurisation or base neutralisation, passing the waste gases through alkaline scrubbers containing calcium carbonate or calcium oxide to neutralise the acidic gases before they escape into the atmosphere.

  • Biodegradable polymers degrade naturally via microorganisms
  • Incineration of polymers releases thermal energy but can produce toxic waste gases
  • Poly(chloroethene) combustion produces toxic hydrogen chloride gas
  • Acidic waste gases are removed using alkaline scrubbers or neutralisation towers
  • Calcium carbonate or calcium oxide reacts with HCl to form neutral salts and water

Typical mistakes

  • Mistake: Drawing curly arrows starting from empty space rather than from a bond or lone pair. Correction: Always start curly arrows precisely on a covalent bond line or a pair of non-bonding electrons.
  • Mistake: Forgetting that carbocation stability dictates the major product. Correction: Remember that tertiary carbocations are more stable than secondary, which are more stable than primary, because alkyl groups donate electron density.
  • Mistake: Leaving a double bond inside the repeat unit of an addition polymer. Correction: Convert the double bond into a single bond and ensure the bonds extend outside the square brackets.
  • Mistake: Confusing the E and Z labels by not applying priority rules correctly. Correction: Assign priorities using atomic numbers to the groups on each carbon of the double bond separately.

Exam-style questions

    1. State the general formula for alkenes and define the term unsaturated hydrocarbon. Answer: The general formula is CnH2n. An unsaturated hydrocarbon contains only carbon and hydrogen atoms with at least one carbon-carbon double bond consisting of a sigma and a pi bond. (1 mark for general formula, 1 mark for definition).
    2. Explain why geometric isomerism can occur in pent-2-ene but not in pent-1-ene. Answer: Pent-2-ene has restricted rotation about the C=C double bond and each carbon of the double bond is attached to two different groups (a methyl group and a hydrogen atom on one, an ethyl group and a hydrogen atom on the other). Pent-1-ene has one carbon of the double bond attached to two identical hydrogen atoms, so geometric isomers cannot form. (2 marks).
    3. Outline the mechanism for the electrophilic addition of hydrogen bromide to propene, naming the major product and explaining why it forms in greater yield. Answer: Draw the curly arrow from the C=C pi bond to the hydrogen of HBr, and another arrow from the H-Br bond to the bromine atom. Show two possible carbocation intermediates: a secondary carbocation and a primary carbocation. The major product is 2-bromopropane, which forms via the secondary carbocation because secondary carbocations are more stable than primary carbocations due to the electron-donating inductive effect of two alkyl groups. (4 marks).
    4. Describe the qualitative test to distinguish between hexane and hexene. Answer: Add bromine water to both liquids and shake. Hexene decolourises the orange-brown bromine water to colourless due to electrophilic addition across the double bond. Hexane shows no reaction, and the orange-brown colour remains. (2 marks).
    5. Explain how chemists minimise environmental hazards caused by the disposal of poly(chloroethene). Answer: Poly(chloroethene) is non-biodegradable and produces toxic hydrogen chloride gas upon incineration. Chemists pass the waste gases through alkaline scrubbers or neutralisation towers containing calcium carbonate to react with and neutralise the acidic hydrogen chloride before release. (3 marks).

Use these notes alongside active recall and past paper question practice. Ensure you can draw mechanisms step by step with correct curly arrow origins. Proceed next to review Halogenoalkanes and Reaction Mechanisms.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • E/Z naming, applied to CHBr=CHCl: on each carbon, the group with the higher atomic number takes priority. Br beats H and Cl beats H, so if the two higher-priority groups are on opposite sides, the isomer is E. Compare atomic numbers on the atom attached to the double bond, not the whole group.
  • Markovnikov addition, applied to propene with HBr: the electrophile H⁺ adds to the carbon with more hydrogens, so the carbocation forms on the more substituted carbon. The major product is 2-bromopropane. The stability order is tertiary > secondary > primary carbocation, and that order explains the major product.
  • Mechanism marks: show a curly arrow from the C=C π bond to the H of HBr, then a second curly arrow from the Br⁻ lone pair to the positive carbon. The first arrow is the step that earns the mark, so draw it from the bond, not from a carbon.
  • Bromine water test: decolourisation of orange bromine water shows unsaturation. An alkane does not decolourise it, so an alkene and an alkane are distinguished by this test alone.

title: AS Level Mathematics: Differentiation
content:
AS Level Mathematics: Differentiation

Differentiation measures how fast something changes: the gradient of a curve at a point, the speed of a moving object, the rate at which cost rises with output. It is the central tool of AS mathematics, and this note builds it from zero: the idea of a limit and the gradient function, the power rule with every algebraic case, tangents and normals, stationary points and their classification, increasing and decreasing intervals, and rates of change. Every worked example writes the derivative line before substituting, because the method marks live there.

Gradient as a limit

The gradient of a curve at a point is the gradient of the tangent there. Approximate it with a chord between two nearby points: as the points close up, the chord's gradient approaches the tangent's. That limiting process defines the derivative:

gradient of chord = [f(x + h) - f(x)]/h
derivative = limit as h → 0
notation: dy/dx, f'(x)

For y = x², the chord gradient simplifies to 2x + h, which tends to 2x as h → 0: the derivative of x² is 2x. That single calculation is the model for the general rule.

The power rule

if y = x^n then dy/dx = n x^(n - 1)

constant multiple: d/dx [k f(x)] = k f'(x)
sum: differentiate term by term
constant term: differentiates to 0

Worked example 1. Differentiate y = 4x³ − 2x² + 7x − 5.

dy/dx = 12x² - 4x + 7

Worked example 2 (negative and fractional powers). Differentiate y = 3/x² + √x.

rewrite: y = 3x⁻² + x^(1/2)
dy/dx = -6x⁻³ + (1/2)x^(-1/2)
      = -6/x³ + 1/(2 √(x))

Worked example 3 (expand first). Differentiate y = x²(2x + 1).

expand: y = 2x³ + x²
dy/dx = 6x² + 2x

Worked example 4 (gradient at a point). Find the gradient of y = x³ − 4x at x = 2.

dy/dx = 3x² - 4
at x = 2: 12 - 4 = 8

Tangents and normals

tangent at x = a: gradient m = f'(a), through (a, f(a))
normal: gradient -1/m (perpendicular to the tangent)
equation: y - y1 = m(x - x1)

Worked example. Find the tangent and normal to y = x² − 3x + 1 at x = 4.

point: y = 16 - 12 + 1 = 5  →  (4, 5)
dy/dx = 2x - 3  →  m = 5
tangent: y - 5 = 5(x - 4)  →  y = 5x - 15
normal: gradient -1/5
y - 5 = -1/5 (x - 4)  →  x + 5y = 29

Worked example 2 (tangent through a point). Find where the tangent to y = x³ at (2, 8) crosses the x-axis.

dy/dx = 3x²  →  m = 12
tangent: y - 8 = 12(x - 2)  →  y = 12x - 16
set y = 0: x = 16/12 = 4/3

Stationary points

stationary point: dy/dx = 0
classify with the second derivative:
  d2y/dx2 < 0: maximum
  d2y/dx2 > 0: minimum
  d2y/dx2 = 0: could be either - check the gradient either side

Worked example. Find and classify the stationary points of y = x³ − 3x² + 4.

dy/dx = 3x² - 6x = 3x(x - 2)
stationary at x = 0 and x = 2
points: (0, 4) and (2, 0)
d2y/dx2 = 6x - 6
at x = 0: -6 < 0  →  maximum
at x = 2: +6 > 0  →  minimum

Worked example 2 (unknown coefficient). The curve y = x³ + ax² + b has a stationary point at (2, 1). Find a and b.

point condition: 8 + 4a + b = 1
derivative condition: 3x² + 2ax = 0 at x = 2 → 12 + 4a = 0 → a = -3
substitute: 8 - 12 + b = 1  →  b = 5

Increasing and decreasing functions

increasing where dy/dx > 0
decreasing where dy/dx < 0

Worked example. Find the intervals where y = x³ − 6x² + 9x is increasing.

dy/dx = 3x² - 12x + 9 = 3(x - 1)(x - 3)
positive outside the roots: x < 1 or x > 3
increasing on x < 1 and x > 3; decreasing on 1 < x < 3

Rates of change and kinematics

if s(t) is displacement: velocity v = ds/dt; acceleration a = dv/dt
displacement from velocity: integrate (next topic)

Worked example. A particle's displacement is s = 2t³ − 9t² + 12t (metres, seconds). Find its velocity and acceleration at t = 2.

v = ds/dt = 6t² - 18t + 12
at t = 2: 24 - 36 + 12 = 0 m/s (momentarily at rest)
a = dv/dt = 12t - 18
at t = 2: 24 - 18 = 6 m/s²

Worked example 2 (maximum displacement). With the same s(t), find when the particle is at rest and classify each moment.

v = 0: 6t² - 18t + 12 = 0 → t² - 3t + 2 = 0 → t = 1, 2
a(1) = -6 < 0 → at t = 1 the displacement is a maximum
a(2) = +6 > 0 → at t = 2 the displacement is a minimum

Optimisation problems

Applied maximum/minimum questions follow a fixed routine: write the quantity to optimise as a function of one variable, differentiate, set to zero, solve, and classify (or argue from the context).

Worked example. A rectangular pen is to be made against a wall with 24 m of fencing (three sides). Find the maximum area.

let the two equal sides be x; the third is 24 - 2x
A = x(24 - 2x) = 24x - 2x²
dA/dx = 24 - 4x = 0  →  x = 6
A = 6(24 - 12) = 72 m² (maximum since d2A/dx2 = -4 < 0)

Differentiation from first principles

The definition is examinable and shows why the power rule works. The routine: form f(x + h), subtract f(x), divide by h, simplify, then let h → 0.

Worked example. Differentiate f(x) = x² + 3x from first principles.

f(x + h) = (x + h)² + 3(x + h) = x² + 2xh + h² + 3x + 3h
f(x + h) - f(x) = 2xh + h² + 3h
divide by h: 2x + h + 3
let h → 0: f'(x) = 2x + 3

Worked example 2. Differentiate f(x) = 5x² from first principles.

f(x + h) - f(x) = 5(x² + 2xh + h²) - 5x² = 10xh + 5h²
divide by h: 10x + 5h  →  limit 10x

Concavity and the second derivative

The second derivative describes how the gradient itself is changing. Where d²y/dx² > 0 the gradient is increasing and the curve is concave up (holds water); where it is negative the gradient is decreasing and the curve is concave down. That is exactly why the sign classifies stationary points, and it also answers direct questions about concavity:

d2y/dx2 > 0: concave up / minimum
d2y/dx2 < 0: concave down / maximum
d2y/dx2 = 0: possible point of inflection - test the gradient either side

Worked example. Find where y = x³ − 3x is concave up.

dy/dx = 3x² - 3;  d2y/dx2 = 6x
concave up where 6x > 0  →  x > 0

Sketching curves with calculus

Calculus turns a sketch from guesswork into a list of facts: intercepts, stationary points and their nature, behaviour at the ends, and any asymptotes. A reliable order:

  1. Set x = 0 for the y-intercept; solve y = 0 for the x-intercepts where factorisable.
  2. Differentiate, solve dy/dx = 0, and classify each stationary point.
  3. Use the second derivative sign to fix concavity between the points.
  4. Check the sign of y at the extremes of the sketch (a positive cubic rises to the right).

Worked example. Sketch y = x³ − 3x².

intercepts: y = 0 at x = 0 and x = 3 (x²(x - 3))
dy/dx = 3x² - 6x = 3x(x - 2)
stationary: (0, 0) and (2, -4)
d2y/dx2 = 6x - 6: at 0 negative → maximum; at 2 positive → minimum
The curve rises from the left, peaks at the origin, falls to (2, -4),
then rises, crossing the x-axis at x = 3.

Optimisation with a constraint

Most real optimisation questions give a constraint (fixed perimeter, fixed volume, fixed budget) that must be used to eliminate one variable before differentiating.

Worked example. A closed cylinder has volume 250 cm³. Find the radius that minimises its surface area.

V = π r² h = 250  →  h = 250/(π r²)
S = 2 π r² + 2 π r h = 2 π r² + 500/r
dS/dr = 4 π r - 500/r² = 0
4 π r³ = 500  →  r³ = 39.79  →  r = 3.41 cm
check: d2S/dr2 = 4 π + 1000/r³ > 0  →  minimum

The pattern is always the same: one constraint equation, one quantity to optimise, substitute, differentiate, solve, justify the nature of the stationary point — and answer the question actually asked (here the radius, not the height).

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Differentiate) Differentiate y = 5x⁴ − 3x² + 2. Answer: 20x³ − 6x.
  2. (Negative power) Differentiate y = 4/x. Answer: y = 4x⁻¹ → −4x⁻² = −4/x².
  3. (Gradient) Find the gradient of y = x² + 2x at x = −1. Answer: 2x + 2 → 0.
  4. (Tangent) Find the tangent to y = x² at (3, 9). Answer: m = 6; y = 6x − 9.
  5. (Stationary) Find the stationary point of y = x² − 6x + 5. Answer: 2x − 6 = 0 → x = 3; y = −4; minimum.
  6. (Second derivative) Classify the stationary point of y = x³ at x = 0. Answer: dy/dx = 3x², d²y/dx² = 6x = 0 at x = 0 — the test is inconclusive; the gradient is positive either side, so it is a point of inflection, not an extremum.
  7. (Increasing) Find where y = x² − 4x is decreasing. Answer: 2x − 4 < 0 → x < 2.
  8. (Kinematics) s = t³ − 6t² + 9t. Find the acceleration at t = 1. Answer: v = 3t² − 12t + 9; a = 6t − 12 → −6 m/s².

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Forgetting to rewrite powers: differentiate 1/x and √x only after rewriting as x⁻¹ and x^(1/2); the power rule does not apply to the original form.
  • Dropping the constant: the derivative of a constant is 0 — a leftover +7 in dy/dx is an error.
  • Tangent versus normal: the normal's gradient is −1/m, not −m; and it passes through the same point.
  • Second derivative sign: negative means maximum (the curve is concave down); positive means minimum. Reversing the classification is the classic slip.
  • d²y/dx² = 0: inconclusive, not automatically an inflection — check the gradient either side.
  • Stationary point coordinates: the question wants (x, y), so substitute the x back into the original curve, not the derivative.
  • Rates of change with units: attach units (m/s, m/s², units per item) and interpret the sign in context.
  • Method marks: write dy/dx = ... explicitly before substituting; the derivative itself is credit even if the later arithmetic slips.

Equations and symbols

Every mark in this topic hangs off one rule, one limit and one test. Write the derivative line before substituting — that line is the method mark even when the arithmetic slips.

The definition

gradient of chord = [f(x + h) - f(x)]/h Key: f(x) = the function; h = a small step in x (same unit as x); the quotient is the average gradient over that step. As h tends to zero the chord becomes the tangent, which is the derivative.

if y = x^n then dy/dx = n x^(n - 1) Key: n = the power, which may be negative or fractional once the expression is rewritten; dy/dx = the gradient function. Rewrite 1/x as x⁻¹ and √x as x^(1/2) before applying it — the rule does not work on the original form.

dy/dx = 12x² - 4x + 7 Key: the worked derivative of y = 4x³ − 2x² + 7x − 5: each term differentiated separately, and the constant −5 gone. A surviving constant in dy/dx is always an error.

Tangents, normals and stationary points

stationary point: dy/dx = 0 Key: a stationary point is where the gradient is zero — a maximum, a minimum or a point of inflection. Solve for x, then substitute back into the original curve for y: the answer is a coordinate pair, not just an x.

d2y/dx2 < 0: maximum Key: d²y/dx² = the second derivative, the rate of change of the gradient; a negative value means the gradient is decreasing, so the curve is concave down and the point is a maximum. The minimum is the positive case; zero is inconclusive and needs the gradient tested either side.

increasing where dy/dx > 0 Key: the function rises wherever its gradient is positive and falls where it is negative; solve the inequality in x, and quote the intervals rather than a single value.

Optimisation

V = π r² h = 250 → h = 250/(π r²) Key: V = volume of the closed cylinder (cm³); r = base radius (cm); h = height (cm). This is the constraint step: it eliminates h so the surface area becomes a function of r alone, which is the only way the derivative can be taken.

A = x(24 - 2x) = 24x - 2x² Key: A = area of the pen (m²); x = each of the two equal sides (m); 24 − 2x = the third side (m) from 24 m of fencing. Differentiate, set to zero, and justify the maximum with d²A/dx² < 0.

The slip worth naming

Forgetting to rewrite negative and fractional powers before differentiating, and leaving the constant term in the derivative. Both are avoidable in the first line of working.
