title: AS Level Physics: Superposition
content:
AS Level Physics: Superposition

Superposition is what happens when two waves occupy the same space at the same time: the displacements add, and from that single rule emerge stationary waves, diffraction, interference and the diffraction grating — the four phenomena of this topic. The mental picture to keep is two people shaking ropes that cross: at the crossing, the rope's shape is the sum of both shapes, instant by instant. This note builds each phenomenon from that rule, with the derivations and calculations line by line and the practical skills the papers demand.

The superposition principle

When two or more waves meet, the resultant displacement at any point is the vector sum of the individual displacements at that point. The waves pass through each other unchanged afterwards — they do not bounce off or alter each other. Everything in this topic is that sentence applied to different geometries:

  • Constructive interference: crest meets crest — displacements add, amplitude is a maximum.
  • Destructive interference: crest meets trough — displacements cancel, amplitude is a minimum (zero for equal waves).

Interference is sustained (a stable pattern) only when the sources are coherent: same frequency and a constant phase difference. Two unrelated lamps are incoherent and produce no stable pattern — this distinction is examinable every session.

Stationary waves

A stationary (standing) wave forms when two progressive waves of the same frequency and amplitude travel in opposite directions — classically a wave and its reflection. The pattern oscillates but does not travel: there are fixed points of zero displacement (nodes) and fixed points of maximum displacement (antinodes), and the wave profile stays in place while the medium oscillates within it.

FeatureProgressive waveStationary wave
Energytransferred along the wavestored in the oscillating regions; not transferred
Nodesnonefixed zero-displacement points, half a wavelength apart
Antinodescrests move alongfixed maximum points, half a wavelength apart
Phaseneighbouring points vary smoothly in phaseall points between two adjacent nodes oscillate in phase

Harmonics give the numbers. For a string fixed at both ends (or a pipe closed at both ends), the fundamental has nodes at both ends and one antinode between: the string length L fits half a wavelength, so λ = 2L. The next mode fits a full wavelength (λ = L), the next 3λ/2 (λ = 2L/3), and in general λₙ = 2L/n with fₙ = n v/(2L). For a pipe closed at one end, the closed end is a node and the open end an antinode: the fundamental fits a quarter wavelength, λ = 4L, and only odd harmonics appear, fₙ = n v/(4L) with n = 1, 3, 5 ...

Worked example. A guitar string 0.65 m long has a wave speed of 320 m s⁻¹. Find the fundamental and second harmonic frequencies.

fundamental: λ = 2L = 1.30 m
f1 = v/λ = 320/1.30 = 246 Hz
second harmonic: λ = L = 0.65 m
f2 = 320/0.65 = 492 Hz   (exactly 2 x f1, as expected)

Worked example (closed pipe). A pipe 0.50 m long, closed at one end, has sound speed 340 m s⁻¹. Find the fundamental and state the next allowed frequency.

fundamental: λ = 4L = 2.00 m
f1 = 340/2.00 = 170 Hz
only odd harmonics allowed → next is the 3rd: f3 = 3 × 170 = 510 Hz

Diffraction

Diffraction is the spreading of waves as they pass through a gap or around an obstacle. It is significant when the gap (or obstacle) size is comparable to the wavelength — the wave bends generously around a 1 cm gap if λ is a few centimetres, but barely at all for light through a doorway. The rule to quote: noticeable diffraction requires gap size approximately equal to the wavelength. Consequences: long-wavelength radio diffract around hills; short-wavelength microwaves need line-of-sight aerials; light through everyday doors shows negligible diffraction, which is why shadows exist.

The single-slit pattern is examinable in outline: a broad central maximum of width related to λ/a (slit width a), with the intensity falling away on either side; a narrower slit produces a wider spread. Water waves in a ripple tank photograph the same behaviour macroscopically.

Interference: two sources

Two coherent sources produce a stable pattern of maxima and minima. The controlling quantity is the path difference — the difference in distance from the two sources to the point in question:

  • Constructive (maximum): path difference = nλ (n = 0, 1, 2 ...), i.e. a whole number of wavelengths.
  • Destructive (minimum): path difference = (n + ½)λ — a whole number plus half.

Worked example. Two speakers sit 4.0 m apart, driven in phase at 170 Hz (sound speed 340 m s⁻¹). A listener stands on the perpendicular bisector, then moves until the first minimum. Find the path difference at the first minimum.

λ = v/f = 340/170 = 2.0 m
first minimum: path difference = λ/2 = 1.0 m

On the perpendicular bisector the path difference is zero, so the centre is a maximum; the first minimum occurs where the difference reaches half a wavelength — 1.0 m of extra path.

Young's double-slit experiment

Light through two closely spaced slits forms fringes of alternating bright and dark bands on a screen. The fringe spacing formula, derived from path difference across a distant screen, is the calculation the papers test:

fringe spacing  w  = λ D / d

D = slit-to-screen distance (m)
d = slit separation (m)
λ = wavelength (m)

Worked example 1. Light of wavelength 600 nm falls on slits 0.25 mm apart; the screen is 1.8 m away.

λ = 600 nm = 6.0 × 10⁻⁷ m
d = 0.25 mm = 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ m
w = λ D/d = (6.0 × 10⁻⁷ x 1.8)/(2.5 × 10⁻⁴)
  = 1.08 × 10⁻⁶/2.5 × 10⁻⁴ = 4.32 × 10⁻³ m = 4.3 mm

Worked example 2 (working backwards). Fringe spacing 2.0 mm is measured with D = 2.0 m and λ = 500 nm. Find the slit separation.

d = λ D/w = (5.0 × 10⁻⁷ x 2.0)/(2.0 × 10⁻³)
  = 1.0 × 10⁻⁶/2.0 × 10⁻³ = 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ m = 0.50 mm

Examiner note: the formula assumes small angles and a distant screen; when asked to describe the effect of moving the screen away, the answer is that fringes spread out (w increases with D) — a proportionality answer, not a guess.

The diffraction grating

A diffraction grating has many equally spaced slits; the interference from all of them produces sharp, bright maxima at angles given by

n λ = d sin θ

n = 0, 1, 2, ... (the order)
d = slit spacing (grating spacing), the distance between
    adjacent slits (m)
θ = angle of the maximum from the central beam

The number of orders is a standard question: since sin θ ≤ 1, the maximum order n is the largest integer with nλ ≤ d, i.e. n = floor(d/λ); each order appears twice (either side) plus the central beam.

Worked example 1. A grating has 300 lines per millimetre. Light of wavelength 550 nm is incident normally. Find the angles of the first- and second-order maxima.

grating spacing: d = 1 mm/300 = 3.33 × 10⁻⁶ m
first order (n = 1):
sin θ = λ/d = 5.5 × 10⁻⁷/3.33 × 10⁻⁶ = 0.165
θ = sin-1(0.165) = 9.5 degrees
second order (n = 2):
sin θ = 2 × 0.165 = 0.330
θ = 19.3 degrees

Worked example 2 (counting orders). With the same grating and λ = 550 nm, how many maxima are visible in total?

max order: n λ <= d  →  n <= d/λ = 3.33 × 10⁻⁶/5.5 × 10⁻⁷ = 6.06
largest integer n = 6
orders: -6 to +6 plus n = 0  →  13 maxima in total

Practical skill: measuring d from a grating quoted as N lines per metre, d = 1/N. A grating with 500 lines per mm has d = 2.0 × 10⁻⁶ m. Getting that reciprocal wrong doubles every downstream answer.

Worked examples: comparing the phenomena

Worked example. White light falls on a double slit and, separately, on a diffraction grating. Describe and explain the difference between the two patterns.

double slit: equally spaced fringes; the central fringe is white,
             outer fringes coloured because fringe spacing depends
             on λ - blue (shorter λ) fringes sit closer
             to the centre than red
grating:     sharply defined maxima at angles set by sin θ =
             n λ/d, so each order spreads into a spectrum
             with violet least deviated and red most

Why the marks land: the description names the pattern shape, then the mechanism (spacing proportional to λ) and the colour ordering — explanation, not just observation.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Definitions) State the principle of superposition and define coherence. Answer: When waves meet, the resultant displacement is the sum of the individual displacements. Coherent waves have the same frequency and a constant phase difference.
  2. (Stationary waves) Describe the formation of a stationary wave in a string. Answer: A wave produced at one end travels along the string and reflects at the fixed end; the incident and reflected waves of equal frequency and amplitude superpose; at nodes the two are in antiphase and cancel, at antinodes in phase and reinforce; the pattern oscillates without propagating.
  3. (Closed pipe) The fundamental of a closed pipe is 220 Hz. State the frequency of the next possible harmonic and why. Answer: 660 Hz — closed pipes support odd harmonics only, so the next is the third harmonic, 3 × 220.
  4. (Diffraction) State and explain why long-wave radio signals can be received behind hills but microwave signals cannot. Answer: Radio wavelengths (hundreds of metres) are comparable to hill sizes, so they diffract noticeably around them; microwaves (centimetres) diffract negligibly and need line of sight.
  5. (Double slit) Blue light (450 nm) is replaced by red (650 nm) with no other change. State the effect on fringe spacing and explain. Answer: The spacing increases because w = λD/d and λ has increased; the fringes spread out proportionally.
  6. (Grating) A grating has 600 lines per mm and is illuminated with 500 nm light. Calculate the angle of the first-order maximum. Answer: d = 1/600 000 = 1.67 × 10⁻⁶ m; sin θ = 5.0 × 10⁻⁷/1.67 × 10⁻⁶ = 0.300; θ = 17.5°.
  7. (Orders) In question 6, how many maxima are visible altogether? Answer: d/λ = 3.33, so n = 3; orders −3 to +3 plus the central beam make 7 maxima.
  8. (Practical) Describe how you would measure the fringe spacing of a double-slit pattern. Answer: Measure the distance across several fringes (e.g. from the centre of one bright fringe to the centre of the nth bright fringe) with a ruler or travelling microscope, then divide by n — measuring many fringes reduces the fractional uncertainty.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Grating spacing inversion: 300 lines per mm means d = 3.33 × 10⁻⁶ m, not 3.33 × 10⁻³ m. Write the reciprocal step as its own line.
  • Units in the grating formula: d and λ must both be in metres. Nanometres into the formula directly gives sin θ in the thousands.
  • sin θ vs tan θ: fringe positions at large angles cannot use the small-angle approximation; use sin⁻¹ from the grating equation and w = λD/d only where angles are small.
  • Counting orders: remember the central beam (n = 0) and both sides; and round the order down (floor of d/λ), never up.
  • Node/antinode language: nodes are zero displacement and exist because of antiphase superposition; antinodes vibrate with double amplitude. Swapping the two is a definition mark lost.
  • Closed-pipe harmonics: an open–closed pipe supports odd harmonics only (1st, 3rd, 5th); answering with the second harmonic loses the mark.
  • Incoherent sources: two separate lamps cannot produce a stable interference pattern — coherence is the condition, and it is worth a stated mark.
  • Path difference conditions: maxima at whole wavelengths, minima at half-integer. State the condition in words and symbols.
  • Method marks: write the formula (nλ = d sin θ or w = λD/d) before numbers; a correct formula with failed arithmetic still earns credit.

Equations and symbols

The whole of this topic as equations, each written with its real symbols and each followed by a key naming every symbol and its unit. Where a law has more than one useful form both are given, because which one is quickest depends on which quantities the question hands you. Learn the form here and the algebraic rearrangement becomes mechanical in the exam.

8.1 Wave quantities and stationary waves

v = f λ
Key: v = wave speed (m s⁻¹); f = frequency (Hz); λ = wavelength (m). For a wave crossing a boundary the speed and wavelength change but the frequency is set by the source and does not.

T = 1 / f
Key: T = period, the time for one complete oscillation (s); f = frequency (Hz).

y = y₁ + y₂
Key: y = resultant displacement at a point (m); y₁, y₂ = displacements the two waves would separately produce there (m). The superposition principle itself: displacements add as vectors, so two troughs make a deeper trough and a crest meeting a trough cancels.

node spacing = λ / 2, antinode spacing = λ / 2, node to nearest antinode = λ / 4
Key: λ = wavelength of the waves forming the stationary wave (m). A stationary wave stores energy rather than transporting it, because the two travelling waves carry equal energy in opposite directions.

λ_n = 2 L / n, so f_n = n v / (2 L)
Key: λ_n = wavelength of the nth harmonic (m); L = length of the string or pipe (m); n = 1, 2, 3 … (all integers); f_n = its frequency (Hz); v = wave speed on the string or in the air (m s⁻¹). Applies to a string fixed at both ends and to a pipe open at both ends; f₁ = v/2L is the fundamental, and every harmonic is present.

λ_n = 4 L / n, so f_n = n v / (4 L) with n = 1, 3, 5 …
Key: λ_n = wavelength (m); L = length of the pipe closed at one end (m); n = odd integers only; f_n = frequency (Hz); v = speed of sound (m s⁻¹). A closed end must be a node and an open end an antinode, so only odd harmonics exist — the missing even harmonics are the standard exam trap.

f_n = n f₁
Key: f_n = frequency of the nth harmonic (Hz); f₁ = fundamental frequency (Hz); n = harmonic number. Use it to jump straight from the fundamental to the harmonic a question asks for.

8.2 Diffraction and 8.3 interference

path difference = n λ (constructive), path difference = (n + ½) λ (destructive)
Key: path difference = difference in distance travelled by the two waves to the point (m); λ = wavelength (m); n = 0, 1, 2 … For sources in phase, a whole number of wavelengths arrives in step and reinforces; a half-odd number arrives in antiphase and cancels.

Δφ = 2π Δx / λ
Key: Δφ = phase difference between the two waves at the point (rad); Δx = path difference (m); λ = wavelength (m). The bridge between the two languages of interference: distances in metres and phase in radians, related by 2π per wavelength.

Δφ = 2π Δt / T
Key: Δφ = phase difference (rad); Δt = time delay between the two waves arriving (s); T = period (s). The same idea in time: one whole period of delay is one whole cycle of phase.

w = λ D / d
Key: w = fringe spacing, centre to centre of adjacent bright fringes (m); λ = wavelength (m); D = distance from the double slits to the screen (m); d = separation of the two slits (m). Young's double-slit result, valid when D ≫ d and the fringes are close together.

λ = w d / D
Key: λ = wavelength of the light (m); w = measured fringe spacing (m); d = slit separation (m); D = slit-to-screen distance (m). The measuring form: w and D are easy to measure, d is given, so λ comes out of three lengths.

I ∝ A²
Key: I = intensity, power per unit area (W m⁻²); A = amplitude of the oscillation (m). Doubling the amplitude quadruples the intensity, which is why two identical waves in phase give four times the intensity of one rather than twice.

I = P / (4 π r²)
Key: I = intensity at distance r from a point source (W m⁻²); P = power radiated by the source (W); r = distance from the source (m). The inverse-square law that follows from the energy spreading over a sphere.

coherence: constant phase difference, same frequency
Key: two sources are coherent when the phase difference between them does not vary with time, which requires identical frequency and a fixed path relationship. Independent lamps are not coherent, which is why a stable fringe pattern needs one source split into two paths — a laser, or a single slit feeding a double slit.

8.4 The diffraction grating

d sin θ = n λ
Key: d = grating spacing, the distance between adjacent slits (m); θ = angle between the normal and the nth-order maximum (degrees); n = order of the maximum, 0, 1, 2 …; λ = wavelength (m). Constructive interference from many slits at once, which is why the maxima are sharp where two-slit fringes are broad.

d = 1 / N
Key: d = slit spacing (m); N = number of lines per metre (m⁻¹). For a grating quoted in lines per millimetre, N = 1000 × lines mm⁻¹.

n_max = d / λ (largest integer below it)
Key: n_max = highest order that can be seen; d = slit spacing (m); λ = wavelength (m). It follows from sin θ ≤ 1: an order whose d sin θ would exceed d cannot exist, and the largest integer that fits is the answer.

total maxima = 2 n_max + 1
Key: n_max = highest visible order; the +1 counts the central zero-order maximum; the factor 2 counts the orders on either side of it. The standard final part of a grating question.

sin θ ∝ λ
Key: θ = diffraction angle (degrees); λ = wavelength (m); at fixed order n and spacing d, since sin θ = nλ/d. This is why white light spreads into a spectrum with red deviated most and violet least — the opposite of a prism, where violet is deviated most.

title: Coordinate Geometry — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Coordinate Geometry

Mathematics — AS (9709). Gradient m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁). From ax + by + c = 0, the gradient is −a/b.

Key areas to revise

  • Gradients and Equations of Lines
  • Parallel and Perpendicular
  • Midpoint and Distance
  • Intersections and Bisectors

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

### Worked example For A(1, 2) and B(5, 10), the gradient is (10 − 2)/(5 − 1) = 2. The midpoint is ((1 + 5)/2, (2 + 10)/2) = (3, 6). The length AB = √(4² + 8²) = √80 = 4√5 ≈ 8.94. The line through A with gradient 2 is y − 2 = 2(x − 1), which simplifies to y = 2x and passes through B. ### Check yourself Find the gradient and midpoint of C(−2, 4) and D(4, −2). The gradient is −1 and the midpoint is (1, 1). Check that the perpendicular gradient is 1, the negative reciprocal.

title: Processor Fundamentals — Study Notes
content:
`# Processor Fundamentals

Cambridge International AS & A Level Computer Science 9618: section 4 (Processor fundamentals), examined in AS Paper 1.

The FDE Cycle

  • Fetch: PC → MAR; read memory → MDR; instruction → CIR; PC increments
  • Decode: control unit interprets the opcode
  • Execute: ALU/registers act; results stored; PC may be overwritten (jumps)

Registers

RegisterRole
PCaddress of next instruction
MARaddress being accessed
MDRdata in transit
CIRcurrent instruction
ACCaccumulator results

Buses

  • Address bus: one-way, CPU → memory (width sets addressable space)
  • Data bus: two-way, carries instructions/data
  • Control bus: timing and command signals

Interrupts

Signals that pause the current program (I/O complete, timer, errors). The CPU saves context, runs the ISR, then resumes — enabling multitasking.

Assembly and Addressing

Immediate (#5), direct (address holds value), indirect (address points to address), indexed (base + offset — arrays), relative (PC + offset — jumps).

Example: LDD 100 loads from 100 (direct); LDI 100 loads from the address stored at 100 (indirect).

Exam tips: trace register contents step by step in trace tables; explain the stored program concept — instructions as data in memory.

The fetch-decode-execute cycle and registers

The program counter (PC) holds the address of the next instruction. During fetch, that address is copied to the memory address register (MAR), the instruction is read into the memory data register (MDR) and then into the current instruction register (CIR), and the PC is incremented. During decode the control unit works out what the instruction means, and during execute the ALU or another part of the CPU carries it out.

The accumulator is a register that holds the results of arithmetic and logic operations. Registers are very fast storage inside the CPU, and the CPU uses them so that it does not have to wait for main memory on every step.

Exam tip: learn the purpose of each register in one sentence. Examiners often ask which register holds the address, and which holds the instruction.

Exam method: tracing the fetch-decode-execute cycle

Write the register contents after each stage. In the fetch stage the address in the program counter is copied to the memory address register, the instruction at that address is copied to the memory data register and then to the current instruction register, and the program counter is incremented so that it points to the next instruction. In the decode stage the control unit works out what the instruction means. In the execute stage the instruction is carried out, which may change the accumulator or write a value back to memory.

The program counter is incremented before execution. A jump instruction then overwrites it, which is why a jump changes the order of execution without any special fetch step.

Common errors

  • Saying the program counter holds the instruction. It holds the address of the next instruction, while the current instruction register holds the instruction itself.
  • Describing the buses as storing data. Buses only carry data, addresses and control signals between components.

title: AS Level Chemistry: Alkenes and Addition Reactions
content:
Alkenes AS Level Chemistry

These revision notes cover Topic 5 Alkenes from the Edexcel International AS Level Chemistry specification, detailing hydrocarbon unsaturation, geometric isomerism, electrophilic addition mechanisms, addition polymerisation, and polymer waste management.

Structure and bonding in alkenes

Alkenes and cycloalkenes are unsaturated hydrocarbons containing a carbon-carbon double bond, which consists of one σ bond and one π bond. The general formula for non-cyclic alkenes is CnH2n. A σ bond is formed by the direct head-on overlap of atomic orbitals along the internuclear axis, providing restricted rotation. A π bond is formed by the sideways overlap of adjacent p orbitals above and below the plane of the carbon atoms. The carbon atoms of a C=C double bond are planar, with bond angles of approximately 120 degrees due to three regions of electron density repelling each other.

  • General formula for alkenes: CnH2n
  • Unsaturated hydrocarbons possess a carbon-carbon double bond consisting of one σ bond and one π bond
  • Cycloalkenes also contain a C=C double bond and are unsaturated hydrocarbons
  • The π bond electron cloud is susceptible to attack by electrophiles
  • Carbon atoms of the C=C double bond are trigonal planar with 120° bond angles

Geometric isomerism and E-Z naming

Geometric isomerism arises due to the restricted rotation around the C=C double bond caused by the presence of the π bond. For geometric isomers to exist, each carbon atom of the C=C double bond must be attached to two different groups. When the traditional cis- and trans- naming system breaks down because the groups attached to the double-bonded carbons are not identical or simple, the E-Z naming system must be used. Priorities are assigned to the groups on each carbon using the Cahn-Ingold-Prelog priority rules based on atomic number. The E isomer has the highest priority groups on opposite sides of the double bond, while the Z isomer has the highest priority groups on the same side.

  • Restricted rotation around the C=C double bond prevents free rotation of substituents
  • Each carbon in the double bond must have two different groups attached for geometric isomerism
  • E-Z system is necessary when cis- and trans- terms become ambiguous or break down
  • Priority is determined by higher atomic number attached directly to the double-bonded carbon
  • E means entgegen (opposite sides); Z means zusammen (same side)

Reactions of alkenes

Alkenes undergo addition reactions where the π bond breaks and two new single bonds form. Hydrogen addition occurs at 150 degrees Celsius using a nickel catalyst to form an alkane through catalytic hydrogenation. Halogens add rapidly at room temperature to produce a di-substituted halogenoalkane. Hydrogen halides add across the double bond to produce mono-substituted halogenoalkanes. Steam addition requires a phosphoric acid catalyst or sulfuric acid catalyst under high temperature and pressure to produce alcohols. Acidified potassium manganate(VII) oxidises the double bond in a cold solution to produce a diol, causing a colour change from purple to colourless.

  • Hydrogenation: Alkene + H2 in the presence of a Ni catalyst forms an alkane
  • Halogenation: Alkene + X2 produces a di-substituted halogenoalkane
  • Hydrohalogenation: Alkene + HX produces a mono-substituted halogenoalkane
  • Hydration: Alkene + H2O(g) with an acid catalyst (H3PO4) produces an alcohol
  • Oxidation: Alkene + acidified KMnO4 produces a diol with a purple to colourless transition

Testing for unsaturation

The qualitative test for the presence of a C=C double bond uses bromine or bromine water. When an orange-brown bromine solution is shaken with an alkene, the bromine adds across the double bond in an electrophilic addition reaction, causing the solution to decolourise from orange-brown to colourless. Alkanes do not react with bromine water in the dark and the solution remains orange-brown.

  • Reagent: Bromine water or liquid bromine
  • Observation with an alkene: Colour changes from orange-brown to colourless
  • Observation with an alkane: No reaction, solution remains orange-brown
  • Test confirms the presence of an unsaturated carbon-carbon double bond

Mechanisms of electrophilic addition

Electrophilic addition is the characteristic reaction mechanism of alkenes. An electrophile is an electron pair acceptor. The high electron density of the π bond induces a dipole in non-polar halogen molecules. Curly arrows start from a bond or a lone pair of electrons and point to the electron-deficient site. In the electrophilic addition of bromine to ethene, the π bond electrons attack the bromine molecule, heterolytically breaking the Br-Br bond and forming a cyclic bromonium ion intermediate or carbocation, followed by attack from the bromide ion. In hydrogen bromide addition, HBr is polar. The hydrogen ion acts as an electrophile, and addition to unsymmetrical alkenes such as propene can yield two possible carbocation intermediates. The major product is formed via the more stable carbocation intermediate. Carbocation stability follows the order: tertiary greater than secondary greater than primary, due to the positive inductive effect of alkyl groups which push electron density towards the positively charged carbon atom.

  • Electrophile definition: An electron pair acceptor
  • Curly arrows must start precisely from a bond or a lone pair
  • Carbocation stability order: tertiary > secondary > primary
  • Primary carbocation has one alkyl group attached to the positively charged carbon
  • Secondary carbocation has two alkyl groups attached
  • Tertiary carbocation has three alkyl groups attached, making it the most stable due to maximum positive inductive effect
  • Major product prediction follows Markovnikov rule: the hydrogen adds to the carbon with more hydrogens already attached

Addition polymerisation

Addition polymerisation involves many small unsaturated alkene molecules, called monomers, joining together to form a long saturated chain called a polymer. The double bond of each monomer opens up to form single covalent bonds with adjacent monomers. To draw the repeat unit given the monomer, change the C=C double bond into a single C-C bond, extend the bonds outside square brackets, and place a letter n outside. To find the monomer from a repeat unit, identify the two-carbon repeat backbone and convert the single bond back into a double bond.

  • Polymerisation type: Addition polymerisation of alkenes
  • Monomers contain a carbon-carbon double bond; polymers contain a saturated carbon backbone
  • Repeat unit formula is enclosed in brackets with bonds extending through the brackets
  • Do not leave dangling double bonds inside the repeat unit structure
  • Poly(ethene) and poly(chloroethene) are standard examples of addition polymers

Polymer disposal and environmental management

Chemists limit environmental problems caused by polymer disposal through innovative chemical engineering. Non-biodegradable polymers persist in landfill sites. Biodegradable polymers, such as those made from poly(lactic acid) derived from plant starch, are broken down by microorganisms into natural substances. Incineration of halogen-containing polymers like poly(chloroethene) produces toxic acidic waste gases such as hydrogen chloride. Chemists remove these toxic waste gases by flue gas desulfurisation or base neutralisation, passing the waste gases through alkaline scrubbers containing calcium carbonate or calcium oxide to neutralise the acidic gases before they escape into the atmosphere.

  • Biodegradable polymers degrade naturally via microorganisms
  • Incineration of polymers releases thermal energy but can produce toxic waste gases
  • Poly(chloroethene) combustion produces toxic hydrogen chloride gas
  • Acidic waste gases are removed using alkaline scrubbers or neutralisation towers
  • Calcium carbonate or calcium oxide reacts with HCl to form neutral salts and water

Typical mistakes

  • Mistake: Drawing curly arrows starting from empty space rather than from a bond or lone pair. Correction: Always start curly arrows precisely on a covalent bond line or a pair of non-bonding electrons.
  • Mistake: Forgetting that carbocation stability dictates the major product. Correction: Remember that tertiary carbocations are more stable than secondary, which are more stable than primary, because alkyl groups donate electron density.
  • Mistake: Leaving a double bond inside the repeat unit of an addition polymer. Correction: Convert the double bond into a single bond and ensure the bonds extend outside the square brackets.
  • Mistake: Confusing the E and Z labels by not applying priority rules correctly. Correction: Assign priorities using atomic numbers to the groups on each carbon of the double bond separately.

Exam-style questions

    1. State the general formula for alkenes and define the term unsaturated hydrocarbon. Answer: The general formula is CnH2n. An unsaturated hydrocarbon contains only carbon and hydrogen atoms with at least one carbon-carbon double bond consisting of a σ and a π bond. (1 mark for general formula, 1 mark for definition).
    2. Explain why geometric isomerism can occur in pent-2-ene but not in pent-1-ene. Answer: Pent-2-ene has restricted rotation about the C=C double bond and each carbon of the double bond is attached to two different groups (a methyl group and a hydrogen atom on one, an ethyl group and a hydrogen atom on the other). Pent-1-ene has one carbon of the double bond attached to two identical hydrogen atoms, so geometric isomers cannot form. (2 marks).
    3. Outline the mechanism for the electrophilic addition of hydrogen bromide to propene, naming the major product and explaining why it forms in greater yield. Answer: Draw the curly arrow from the C=C π bond to the hydrogen of HBr, and another arrow from the H-Br bond to the bromine atom. Show two possible carbocation intermediates: a secondary carbocation and a primary carbocation. The major product is 2-bromopropane, which forms via the secondary carbocation because secondary carbocations are more stable than primary carbocations due to the electron-donating inductive effect of two alkyl groups. (4 marks).
    4. Describe the qualitative test to distinguish between hexane and hexene. Answer: Add bromine water to both liquids and shake. Hexene decolourises the orange-brown bromine water to colourless due to electrophilic addition across the double bond. Hexane shows no reaction, and the orange-brown colour remains. (2 marks).
    5. Explain how chemists minimise environmental hazards caused by the disposal of poly(chloroethene). Answer: Poly(chloroethene) is non-biodegradable and produces toxic hydrogen chloride gas upon incineration. Chemists pass the waste gases through alkaline scrubbers or neutralisation towers containing calcium carbonate to react with and neutralise the acidic hydrogen chloride before release. (3 marks).

Use these notes alongside active recall and past paper question practice. Ensure you can draw mechanisms step by step with correct curly arrow origins. Proceed next to review Halogenoalkanes and Reaction Mechanisms.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • E/Z naming, applied to CHBr=CHCl: on each carbon, the group with the higher atomic number takes priority. Br beats H and Cl beats H, so if the two higher-priority groups are on opposite sides, the isomer is E. Compare atomic numbers on the atom attached to the double bond, not the whole group.
  • Markovnikov addition, applied to propene with HBr: the electrophile H⁺ adds to the carbon with more hydrogens, so the carbocation forms on the more substituted carbon. The major product is 2-bromopropane. The stability order is tertiary > secondary > primary carbocation, and that order explains the major product.
  • Mechanism marks: show a curly arrow from the C=C π bond to the H of HBr, then a second curly arrow from the Br⁻ lone pair to the positive carbon. The first arrow is the step that earns the mark, so draw it from the bond, not from a carbon.
  • Bromine water test: decolourisation of orange bromine water shows unsaturation. An alkane does not decolourise it, so an alkene and an alkane are distinguished by this test alone.

title: Edexcel IAL Computer Science: Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning
content:
Edexcel IAL Computer Science: Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning

Pearson Edexcel International Advanced Level in Computer Science, Unit 3 Advanced Computer Science: artificial intelligence — its definitions and techniques, machine learning, and the engineering of AI systems. The AS ethics note touched AI's impact; this note is the technical depth: how models are represented, trained and evaluated, what the major technique families actually do, and where each one fails. Training loops and search traces are walked step by step.

What AI is, precisely

Artificial intelligence is software performing tasks we would call intelligent if a human did them — perception, reasoning, learning, planning, language. The classic distinction: strong AI (general, human-equivalent understanding — not achieved) versus narrow AI (excellent at one defined task — everything deployed today). The test questions: the Turing test (can a machine's conversational behaviour be distinguished from a human's?) and the Chinese Room argument (symbol manipulation without understanding — a philosophical objection worth naming).

Two great families of technique: symbolic AI (search and logic — the system reasons over explicit representations) and machine learning (the system's behaviour is fitted to data). Modern systems mix them.

Search and reasoning

Many AI problems are state-space search: a start state, goal states, and operators moving between states; the task is to find a path. Strategies: uninformed (breadth-first, depth-first — see the graph traversal note) and informed/heuristic (best-first, A* using an evaluation function; minimax for games).

Game playing with minimax, traced on tic-tac-toe:

  Minimax assumes both players play perfectly: MAX maximises the score,
  MIN minimises it.

  Look ahead from a position where MAX can win immediately in one of three
  moves (moves a, b, c):
    move a → terminal +1 (win for MAX)
    move b → after MIN's best reply, 0 (draw)
    move c → after MIN's best reply, -1 (loss)
  MAX chooses move a: min/max over children = +1.

  Alpha-beta pruning cuts branches that cannot change the decision: if move a
  already guarantees +1, MIN's reply to move b is never examined once b's
  subtree provably scores below +1. The search depth decides strength and
  time - "explain the trade-off" is the follow-up mark.

Expert systems

An expert system encodes human expertise as rules over a knowledge base, applied by an inference engine: forward chaining (data-driven: match facts against rules, fire conclusions, repeat — diagnosis) and backward chaining (goal-driven: to prove X, find rules concluding X, prove their conditions — configuration). Uncertainty handling (confidence factors) and explanation facilities (which rules fired) are their design strengths; brittleness outside the encoded knowledge and the knowledge-engineering bottleneck are their limits.

Forward chaining traced (simplified fault diagnosis):

  Knowledge base:
    R1: IF engine_wont_start AND lights_dim        THEN battery_flat
    R2: IF battery_flat                            THEN charge_battery
    R3: IF engine_wont_start AND lights_ok          THEN starter_fault

  Facts: engine_wont_start, lights_dim.
  Cycle 1: R1's conditions match → conclude battery_flat.
  Cycle 2: R2's condition matches → conclude charge_battery.
  Cycle 3: no new rules fire → stop. Output: charge_battery.

  Notice R3 never fires (lights_ok is false) - the matching is exact.

Machine learning, in depth

Machine learning fits behaviour to data. The three learning styles (supervised: labelled examples; unsupervised: structure in unlabelled data; reinforcement: reward-driven trial) and their main methods:

MethodTaskMechanismFailure modes
Decision treesClassification/regressionGreedy splits maximising information gainOverfitting deep trees; unstable to small data changes
k-nearest neighboursClassificationMajority vote of the k closest training pointsCurse of dimensionality; slow at scale
Naive BayesClassification (spam)Posterior probabilities assuming feature independenceIndependence assumption rarely holds exactly
Linear/logistic regressionPrediction/classificationFit weights minimising errorMisses non-linear structure
Neural networksPerception, language, gamesLayers of weighted units trained by backpropagationOpaque; data-hungry; brittle off-distribution
Neural network training, one epoch traced:

  Layer: inputs x1, x2 → weights w → weighted sum → activation → output.
  1. Forward: prediction = f(w1 × 1 + w2 × 2 + bias).
  2. Loss: measure error against the true label (e.g. squared error).
  3. Backpropagation: compute dLoss/dw for each weight (chain rule from the
     output layer backwards).
  4. Update: w <- w - learningRate * dLoss/dw   (gradient descent).
  5. Repeat across all examples; many epochs until validation loss plateaus.

  The activation function must be non-linear (sigmoid, ReLU) or the whole
  network collapses to one linear model - a favourite "why" question.

Overfitting diagnosis: training accuracy 99%, validation 70% - the model
memorised the training set. Remedies: more data, regularization, dropout,
early stopping on the validation curve.

Evaluation is where marks live: a train/validation/test split (or k-fold cross-validation); a confusion matrix (true/false positives/negatives) giving accuracy, precision (of the positives predicted, how many correct), recall (of the real positives, how many found), and F1 balancing them. Class imbalance exposes plain accuracy (a 99%-negative dataset is "99% accurate" predicting all negative); the choice of metric follows the cost of each error — medical screening values recall, spam filtering values precision.

Confusion matrix worked (200 patients, 20 have the disease):

                      predicted +   predicted -
  actual + (20)            16            4
  actual - (180)            8          172

  accuracy  = (16 + 172) / 200 = 0.94
  precision = 16 / (16 + 8)    = 0.667
  recall    = 16 / (16 + 4)    = 0.80

Reading: 94% accuracy LOOKS strong, but a third of positive alarms are false
(24 alarms, 8 wrong) and a fifth of cases are missed (4 of 20). Which number
matters depends on the harm of each error - the medical context says recall.

Applications and their technique

  • Natural language processing — tokenisation, embeddings, sequence models; translation, summarisation, chatbots, sentiment.
  • Computer vision — convolutional networks; classification, detection, segmentation (self-driving perception, medical imaging).
  • Robotics — perception + planning + control; SLAM for mapping and localisation.
  • Recommender systems — collaborative filtering (users like you) and content-based (item similarity).
  • Speech — recognition (audio to text) and synthesis (text to audio).

Worked example: building and evaluating a classifier

Task: flag fraudulent card transactions.

1. Data: 6 months of transactions labelled fraud/legitimate (0.2% fraud -
   heavily imbalanced from the start).
2. Features: amount, time, location distance from last transaction, merchant
   category, spending-rate change. (Feature engineering matters more than the
   model choice at this level.)
3. Split: 60/20/20 train/validation/test, stratified so fraud rate is present
   in all splits.
4. Train several models (logistic regression baseline, decision tree, neural
   net); select on the validation set by RECALL at an acceptable precision -
   missing fraud costs more than a false alarm review.
5. Test once, honestly: confusion matrix on the held-out test set.
6. Deploy with monitoring: live drift detection (feature distributions shift;
   fraud patterns evolve), periodic retraining, and a human-review loop for
   flagged cases.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Saying machine learning "is programmed with rules"; rules are learned from data — that is the definition.
  • Reporting accuracy on imbalanced data without precision/recall; the metric choice is the mark.
  • Testing on training data (or tuning on the test set) — the test set is touched once.
  • Confusing overfitting (high train, low validation) with underfitting (both low) — the diagnosis drives different remedies.
  • Describing neural networks as "simulating the brain" in place of the mechanism: weighted layers, activation, backpropagation.
  • Claiming AI systems understand their outputs; the Chinese Room point and brittleness off-distribution are the honest limits.
  • Forgetting reinforcement learning's exploration/exploitation trade-off in RL answers.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Unit 3, 4 marks). Explain the difference between supervised and unsupervised learning with examples.

Answer: Supervised learning trains on labelled examples — inputs paired with correct outputs — minimising prediction error; e.g. learning spam/ham from emails marked by users. Unsupervised learning finds structure in unlabelled data; e.g. clustering customers by purchasing behaviour with no predefined groups. Supervision needs labelled data (costly) but evaluates against truth; unsupervised discovers patterns a human might not define.

Question 2 (Unit 3, 5 marks). Describe how a neural network is trained.

Answer: Initialise weights randomly; run a forward pass computing a prediction through weighted layers and non-linear activations; compute the loss against the true label; backpropagate the error to find each weight's gradient; update weights against the gradient scaled by the learning rate. Repeat over many examples and epochs until validation performance plateaus, with techniques like early stopping and regularisation against overfitting.

Question 3 (Unit 3, 4 marks). Explain overfitting and two ways to prevent it.

Answer: Overfitting is when a model memorises training data's noise and idiosyncrasies instead of the general pattern — high training accuracy but poor validation/test accuracy. Prevention: use more representative training data; regularise (penalise complexity), use dropout in neural nets, stop training early when the validation curve degrades, and prefer simpler models when performance is comparable.

Question 4 (Unit 3, 5 marks). A disease-screening model has 95% accuracy on data where 2% of patients are positive. Explain why accuracy alone is misleading and which metrics matter.

Answer: Predicting "negative" for everyone yields 98% accuracy while catching nothing — so accuracy hides failure on the minority class. The confusion matrix gives precision (of those flagged, how many truly ill — false alarms' cost) and recall (of the truly ill, how many flagged — missed diagnoses' cost). For screening, recall dominates (a missed case is dangerous); the F1 score balances both, and the confusion matrix itself is the honest picture.

Question 5 (Unit 3, 4 marks). Explain how a recommender system based on collaborative filtering works.

Answer: It builds a user–item matrix of ratings or behaviours, finds users with similar taste patterns (nearest neighbours in that space), and recommends items those similar users rated highly but the target user has not seen. Strength: no item knowledge needed. Weaknesses: cold start (new users/items have no data) and popularity bias (rare items rarely recommended).

Question 6 (Unit 3, 3 marks). Explain the difference between a symbolic expert system and a machine learning system.

Answer: An expert system stores human knowledge as explicit IF–THEN rules applied by an inference engine — transparent and explainable, but limited to encoded knowledge and costly to build. A machine learning system derives its decision function from data — scalable to perceptual tasks and improves with data, but opaque and dependent on data quality, and unable to reason beyond its training distribution.

The last note of the course covers how models and systems meet the physical world: simulation, sensors and real-world data.

title: Circular Measure — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Circular Measure

Mathematics — AS (9709). One radian is the angle subtending an arc equal in length to the radius. π radians = 180°.

Key areas to revise

  • Radians
  • Arc Length
  • Sector Area
  • Segment Area
  • Rearranging

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

### Worked example An arc of a circle of radius r and angle θ in radians has length s = rθ. The sector area is ½r²θ. With r = 5 cm and θ = 0.6 rad, s = 3 cm and the area is 0.5 × 25 × 0.6 = 7.5 cm². To convert, 180° = π radians, so 60° = π/3 ≈ 1.047 radians.

title: Electric Fields and Capacitance — Study Notes
content:
Electric Fields and Capacitance

Edexcel International A Level Physics — Unit 4 (WPH14), sat at A2.

Coulomb's law

The force between two point charges is F = kQ₁Q₂/r², with k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻². Like charges repel and unlike charges attract. The force acts along the line joining the charges.

Example: +2.0 μC and −3.0 μC, 0.30 m apart, attract with F = 0.60 N.

Electric field strength

Field strength E is the force per unit positive charge: E = F/Q, in N C⁻¹ (or V m⁻¹). For a point charge E = kQ/r², radially outward for positive charge.

Uniform field: between parallel plates, E = V/d, with the field constant in magnitude and direction. A charge q in it feels F = qE.

Example: plates 4.0 cm apart with p.d. 600 V have E = 1.5 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹.

Electric potential and potential energy

Electric potential V at a point is the work done per unit positive charge in bringing a small charge from infinity to that point: V = kQ/r for a point charge. Potential is a scalar. Field strength is the negative potential gradient, E = −dV/dr, so a steep potential-distance graph means a strong field. The field points from high to low potential.

Capacitance

Capacitance C = Q/V, measured in farads (C V⁻¹). The energy stored is W = ½QV = ½CV² = ½Q²/C. The area under a graph of V against Q equals the stored energy.

Example: a 10 μF capacitor charged to 200 V stores 0.20 J.

Capacitors in series and parallel

  • In parallel the capacitances add: C = C₁ + C₂.
  • In series the reciprocals add: 1/C = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂. The total is smaller than the smallest.

Discharge: through a resistor R, the charge falls exponentially, Q = Q₀e^(−t/RC). The time constant RC is the time for the charge or p.d. to fall to 37% of its initial value.

Exam tips: convert μF and cm to SI units before calculating. Check whether a question asks for field strength (vector) or potential (scalar). Series capacitors share the charge; parallel capacitors share the p.d.

Worked example: field between parallel plates

Two parallel plates are 0.040 m apart with a potential difference of 2.0 kV. The uniform field strength is E = V/d = 2000/0.040 = 5.0 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹. A proton placed at rest between the plates feels a force F = eE = (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹)(5.0 × 10⁴) = 8.0 × 10⁻¹⁵ N, directed from the positive plate towards the negative plate.

Radial fields and potential

For a point charge, E = Q/(4πε₀r²), so field strength falls with the square of distance. The potential is V = Q/(4πε₀r), which falls only with the first power of distance. Students often mix these two; the field depends on r², the potential on r.

Energy and the electronvolt

The work done in moving a charge Q through a potential difference V is W = QV. A charge accelerated from rest through 500 V gains 500 eV of kinetic energy, which is 8.0 × 10⁻¹⁷ J for an electron. Expressing energies in electronvolts makes many A-level questions faster to work through.

  • Field lines point away from positive charge and towards negative charge, and they never cross.
  • Equipotential surfaces are always perpendicular to field lines.
  • Energy stored in a capacitor is ½CV² = ½QV = ½Q²/C. Choose the form that matches the data given.

title: A Level Mathematics: Numerical Methods
content:
A Level Mathematics: Numerical Methods

Some equations cannot be solved exactly: x = cos x, x³ − x − 1 = 0, e^x = 4x. Numerical methods find the solutions to any required accuracy by iteration and refinement. This note builds the four techniques A2 requires — locating a root by sign change, fixed-point iteration and its convergence, the Newton-Raphson formula with its derivation, and the trapezium rule for integrals that have no elementary antiderivative — together with the failure modes examiners test.

Locating a root: change of sign

if f(a) and f(b) have opposite signs and f is continuous on [a, b],
there is at least one root in (a, b)

Worked example. Show that x³ − x − 1 = 0 has a root between 1 and 2.

f(1) = 1 - 1 - 1 = -1
f(2) = 8 - 2 - 1 = 5
sign change and the cubic is continuous  ->  a root in (1, 2)

The two conditions are both required: continuity rules out a jump, and the sign change forces a crossing. The theorem guarantees at least one root, not exactly one — say "at least" in the answer.

Worked example 2 (narrowing). Show the root lies between 1.3 and 1.4.

f(1.3) = 2.197 - 1.3 - 1 = -0.103
f(1.4) = 2.744 - 1.4 - 1 = 0.344
so the root lies in (1.3, 1.4)

Fixed-point iteration

rearrange f(x) = 0 into x = g(x), then iterate x_(n+1) = g(x_n)

the iteration converges when |g'(x)| < 1 near the root

Worked example. Use x_(n+1) = (x_n + 1)^(1/3) with x₁ = 1.3 to find the root of x³ − x − 1 = 0 to 4 d.p.

x2 = (2.3)^(1/3) = 1.3200
x3 = (2.32)^(1/3) = 1.3238
x4 = 1.3245;  x5 = 1.3246;  x6 = 1.3247
the sequence settles: root = 1.3247 (4 d.p.)

Worked example 2 (testing convergence). For g(x) = (x + 1)^(1/3), show the iteration converges near 1.32.

g'(x) = (1/3)(x + 1)^(-2/3)
at x = 1.32: g' = (1/3)(2.32)^(-2/3) = 0.19 < 1
so the iteration converges

If |g′| > 1 near the root the iteration diverges, and a different rearrangement is needed. The same equation usually has several rearrangements, only some of which converge — that is exactly what the |g′| test decides.

Failure modes of iteration

divergence: |g'| > 1 near the root
oscillation: the sequence jumps between two values
slow convergence: |g'| close to 1

Worked example. The rearrangement x = x³ − 1 for x³ − x − 1 = 0 gives g′(x) = 3x², which is about 5.3 near the root: the iteration diverges rapidly. That is why the cube-root rearrangement, with g′ ≈ 0.19, is used instead.

Newton-Raphson

x_(n+1) = x_n - f(x_n)/f'(x_n)

the tangent at the current point is followed to the x-axis;
the intercept becomes the next estimate

Derivation. The tangent at x_n has equation y − f(x_n) = f′(x_n)(x − x_n). Setting y = 0 gives x = x_n − f(x_n)/f′(x_n), which is the formula.

Worked example. Use Newton-Raphson on f(x) = x³ − x − 1 with x₁ = 1.3.

f'(x) = 3x^2 - 1
x2 = 1.3 - (-0.103)/(4.07) = 1.3 + 0.0253 = 1.3253
x3 = 1.3253 - (0.00053)/(4.2637) = 1.3252
root = 1.3252 (4 d.p.) in two steps, against six for the iteration

Worked example 2 (failure). Explain why x₁ = 0.5 fails for f(x) = x³ − x − 1.

f'(0.5) = -0.25, so x2 = 0.5 - (-1.375)/(-0.25) = 0.5 - 5.5 = -5.0
the tangent is nearly horizontal, so the step overshoots wildly;
the method can diverge when f' is small near the initial guess

State the failure condition explicitly: Newton-Raphson needs f′(x_n) ≠ 0 and a good starting value close to the root.

The trapezium rule

integral from a to b of f(x) dx ~ (h/2)[y_0 + 2(y_1 + ... + y_(n-1)) + y_n]
where h = (b - a)/n and y_i = f(a + ih)

the error: a larger n reduces it; the rule overestimates for a
concave-up curve and underestimates for concave-down

Worked example. Use the trapezium rule with 4 strips to estimate ∫ from 0 to 2 of e^(x²) dx.

h = 0.5; x: 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2
y: 1, 1.2840, 2.7183, 6.4760, 54.5982
I ~ (0.5/2)[1 + 2(1.2840 + 2.7183 + 6.4760) + 54.5982]
  = 0.25[1 + 20.9566 + 54.5982] = 0.25 x 76.5548 = 19.14

Worked example 2 (over or under). Is the estimate above or below the true value here?

e^(x^2) is concave up (its gradient is increasing), so each chord lies
above the curve and the trapezium rule overestimates

Accuracy and error

the error of a trapezium estimate is roughly proportional to h^2
halving h roughly quarters the error

rounding to k decimal places requires the estimate to be stable at
the next place

Worked example. An estimate with h = 0.5 gives 19.14; with h = 0.25 the estimate is 18.92. Estimate the answer to 1 d.p.

the two agree to 1 d.p. at 18.9; quoting 18.9 is defensible, and the
difference indicates the scale of the remaining error

Comparing two step sizes is the standard way to justify an accuracy claim; a single estimate cannot.

Setting up an iteration properly

An iteration question usually hands you the rearrangement; the marks are for using it correctly, showing the iterates, and judging convergence. Three habits cover it:

  • Write the recurrence exactly as given and substitute the stated starting value.
  • Record each iterate to one more decimal place than required.
  • Show two consecutive iterates agreeing at the required accuracy before quoting the root.

Worked example. f(x) = x³ + 2x − 5 has a root near 1.3. Show that x = (5 − 2x)^(1/3) is a valid rearrangement and iterate twice.

from x^3 + 2x - 5 = 0: x^3 = 5 - 2x  ->  x = (5 - 2x)^(1/3)
x2 = (5 - 2.6)^(1/3) = (2.4)^(1/3) = 1.3389
x3 = (5 - 2.6777)^(1/3) = (2.3223)^(1/3) = 1.3241
converging towards about 1.328

Worked example 2 (convergence check). Test |g′| for g(x) = (5 − 2x)^(1/3) near 1.33.

g'(x) = (1/3)(5 - 2x)^(-2/3) x (-2) = -0.667(5 - 2x)^(-2/3)
|g'(1.33)| = 0.667 x (2.34)^(-2/3) = 0.667 x 0.534 = 0.356 < 1
so the iteration converges

Newton-Raphson on other functions

The formula is universal; what changes is the derivative and the care needed with trigonometry and logs.

Worked example. Use Newton-Raphson to solve cos x = x starting from x₁ = 0.7.

f(x) = cos x - x;  f'(x) = -sin x - 1
x2 = 0.7 - (0.7648 - 0.7)/(-0.6442 - 1) = 0.7 + 0.0648/1.6442 = 0.7394
x3 = 0.7394 - (0.7391 - 0.7394)/(-0.6735 - 1) = 0.7391
root = 0.7391 (4 d.p.)

Worked example 2 (log equation). Solve x ln x = 1 from x₁ = 1.5.

f(x) = x ln x - 1;  f'(x) = ln x + 1
x2 = 1.5 - (0.6082 - 1)/(0.4055 + 1) = 1.5 + 0.2788 = 1.7788
x3 = 1.7788 - 0.0423/1.5755 = 1.7519
x4 = 1.7632;  converging to 1.7632

Radians are compulsory in any Newton-Raphson question involving trigonometry; degrees give a value of f′ scaled by π/180 and destroy convergence.

Choosing a starting value

Both iteration and Newton-Raphson need a starting value near the root, and a sketch is the reliable way to find one. Plot or sketch y = left-hand side and y = right-hand side of the rearranged equation; the intersections are the roots, and their approximate positions are the starting values.

Worked example. e^x = 4x has two roots. Sketch and estimate them.

sketch y = e^x and y = 4x: they cross once near x = 0.3 and again
near x = 2.2
checking: e^0.3 = 1.35 against 1.2; e^2.2 = 9.03 against 8.8
so start Newton-Raphson from 0.4 and from 2.2 separately

Two roots require two separate runs; a single guess finds only the root it is near. That is the most common lost mark in equations with several roots.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Sign change) Show x³ + x − 3 = 0 has a root in (1, 2). Answer: f(1) = −1, f(2) = 7; continuous; sign change.
  2. (Iteration) x_(n+1) = (3 − x_n)^(1/3), x₁ = 1. Find x₃. Answer: 1.2599, 1.2020.
  3. (Convergence) g(x) = (3 − x)^(1/3): show |g′| < 1 near 1.21. Answer: |g′| = (1/3)(3 − x)^(−2/3) ≈ 0.21 < 1.
  4. (Newton) f(x) = x² − 5, x₁ = 2. Find x₂. Answer: 2 − (−1)/4 = 2.25.
  5. (Newton again) Find x₃ for the same. Answer: 2.25 − 0.0625/4.5 = 2.2361.
  6. (Newton failure) f(x) = x³, x₁ = −1. What happens? Answer: x₂ = −1 − (−1)/3 = −0.667, converging slowly towards 0; the root is a stationary point, so convergence is linear.
  7. (Trapezium) Estimate ∫₀² x² dx with 2 strips. Answer: h = 1; (1/2)[0 + 2(1) + 4] = 3.
  8. (Error) Is that estimate over or under? Answer: over, since x² is concave up; the true value is 8/3 = 2.667.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Claiming exactly one root: the sign change proves at least one; uniqueness needs monotonicity or a sketch.
  • Iterating too few times: the answer must be stable at the required number of decimal places — show consecutive values agreeing.
  • Calculator in the wrong mode: iteration on a reset calculator silently uses the last answer; store x_n in a variable.
  • Newton with a small derivative: the step overshoots; state the failure rather than ploughing on.
  • Wrong h: h = (b − a)/n, not the number of ordinates; counting strips and counting points are different.
  • Trapezium brackets: the first and last ordinates are counted once, the interior ones twice; a factor-of-two error here is the classic slip.
  • Error direction guessed: justify over/under estimate from the concavity, not from the size of the answer.
  • Accuracy unqualified: "the answer is 1.32" without evidence that later iterations agree is not a numerical-methods answer.

title: IGCSE Mathematics: Sequences and Functions
content:
IGCSE Mathematics: Sequences and Functions

Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580 (2025–2027), section 2 Algebra and graphs: statement 2.7 Sequences and statement 2.13 Functions (Extended). A sequence is a list of numbers generated by a rule; a function is the rule itself. This note builds nth-term rules from scratch — showing why the formula works, not just what it is — then function notation, composite functions and inverse functions, including the domain restrictions that decide whether an inverse exists.

What a sequence is; term-to-term rules

A sequence is an ordered list of numbers. The term-to-term rule gets from one term to the next: add 4, multiply by 2, subtract 1 then double. It tells you what happens step by step but not what the hundredth term is. The position-to-term rule (the nth term) gives any term directly from its position n, and that is the more powerful description.

Sequence: 3, 7, 11, 15, 19, ...

Term-to-term: add 4 each time.
Position-to-term: the terms are 4 less than 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, ..., so the nth term is 4n - 1.

Check: n = 1 gives 4(1) - 1 = 3 ✓;  n = 5 gives 4(5) - 1 = 19 ✓

Linear sequences and the nth term

A linear (arithmetic) sequence has a constant difference d between terms. Its nth term is dn + b, and b is chosen to make the first term correct.

Find the nth term of 5, 8, 11, 14, ...

Constant difference d = 3, so the nth term starts as 3n.
Compare with the sequence: 3, 6, 9, 12, ... is three times the table of 3;
the real sequence is 2 more each time, so b = 2.
nth term:  3n + 2

Check every term: n = 1: 5 ✓   n = 2: 8 ✓   n = 3: 11 ✓
The 50th term is 3(50) + 2 = 152.

Why dn + b always works. Adding d each time from a starting value a means the nth term is a + (n − 1)d, since term n has had (n − 1) additions of d. Expanding gives a + nd − d = nd + (a − d), which is exactly dn + b with b = a − d. Both forms are the same rule; examiners accept either.

Quadratic and special sequences

When the first difference changes but the second difference is constant, the rule is quadratic: an² + bn + c. The method: build the n² sequence, subtract it from the sequence, and finish the linear remainder.

Find the nth term of 2, 5, 10, 17, 26, ...

First differences: 3, 5, 7, 9;  second differences: 2, 2 (constant) → quadratic.
The n² sequence is 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, ...
Subtract: (2-1), (5-4), (10-9), (17-16), (26-25) = 1, 1, 1, 1, 1
So the sequence is n² + 1.

Check: n = 3 gives 9 + 1 = 10 ✓

Other sequences to recognise on sight: the triangular numbers n(n + 1)/2 (1, 3, 6, 10, ...), the square numbers n², the Fibonacci sequence (each term is the sum of the two before it, and it has no simple nth term), and geometric sequences that multiply by a fixed ratio r — their nth term is arⁿ⁻¹ where a is the first term.

Geometric example: 3, 6, 12, 24, ... has a = 3 and r = 2, so the nth term is 3 × 2^(n-1).
The 6th term is 3 × 2⁵ = 96.
Sequence typeExampleRule
Linear (arithmetic)5, 8, 11, 14Constant difference d; nth term dn + b
Quadratic2, 5, 10, 17Constant second difference; nth term an² + bn + c
Geometric3, 6, 12, 24Constant ratio r; nth term arⁿ⁻¹
Triangular numbers1, 3, 6, 10n(n + 1)/2
Square numbers1, 4, 9, 16n²
Fibonacci1, 1, 2, 3, 5Add the two previous terms (no simple nth term)

Choosing the right description is half the battle: check the first differences, then the second, then the ratio, before assuming any rule. Once a candidate rule is found, verify it against every given term — a sequence that matches only the first three terms is not proven.

Function notation

A function is a machine with an input and exactly one output for each input. The notation f(x) = 2x + 3 names the machine f and says what it does to x: multiply by 2, then add 3. Evaluating is substitution: f(4) = 2(4) + 3 = 11. The machine picture matters: one input never gives two outputs, though two inputs may share an output.

  • The domain is the set of allowed inputs; the range is the set of outputs the function actually produces.
  • For f(x) = x² with domain all real numbers, the range is y ⩾ 0, because squares are never negative.
  • For f(x) = 2x + 3 with domain 0 ⩽ x ⩽ 5, the range is 3 ⩽ f(x) ⩽ 13 — substitute the endpoints, since linear functions stretch ranges proportionally.

Questions ask for the range in terms of y or f(x); find the outputs at the domain boundaries and, for quadratics, at the turning point.

Composite functions

A composite function runs one machine after the other. fg(x) means apply g first, then f to the result — the notation reads right to left, like f(g(x)).

Given f(x) = 2x + 1 and g(x) = x², find fg(3), gf(x) and fg(x).

fg(3):  g(3) = 9, then f(9) = 2(9) + 1 = 19.
gf(x):  apply f first:  g(f(x)) = (2x + 1)² = 4x² + 4x + 1.
fg(x):  apply g first:  f(g(x)) = 2x² + 1.

Note fg(x) ≠ gf(x): order matters.

Every line is written out because the most common error is applying the functions in the wrong order — and the composite is not commutative.

Inverse functions

The inverse f⁻¹ undoes f: if f turns 4 into 11, f⁻¹ turns 11 back into 4. Inverse functions exist only for one-to-one functions — ones where different inputs always give different outputs. The graph of y = x² is not one-to-one over all real numbers (both 3 and −3 give 9), so it has no inverse unless the domain is restricted to x ⩾ 0.

Find the inverse of f(x) = (3x - 2)/5:

Write y = (3x - 2)/5 and make x the subject:
5y = 3x - 2          [multiply by 5]
5y + 2 = 3x          [add 2]
x = (5y + 2)/3       [divide by 3]

Swap x and y:  f⁻¹(x) = (5x + 2)/3

Check by composing: f⁻¹(f(x)) = [5((3x - 2)/5) + 2]/3 = [(3x - 2) + 2]/3 = 3x/3 = x  ✓
  • f⁻¹(x) is a single symbol meaning the inverse function; the −1 is not a power and f⁻¹(x) does not mean 1/f(x).
  • The domain of f⁻¹ is the range of f, and the range of f⁻¹ is the domain of f — they swap, exactly as the inputs and outputs swap roles.
  • Graphically, y = f⁻¹(x) is the reflection of y = f(x) in the line y = x.

Worked example: a full function question

Let f(x) = x² + 3 for x ⩾ 0, and g(x) = 4x − 5.

(a) Find f(2):  f(2) = 4 + 3 = 7.

(b) Find fg(x):  f(g(x)) = (4x - 5)² + 3 = 16x² - 40x + 25 + 3 = 16x² - 40x + 28.

(c) Find f⁻¹(x):  y = x² + 3, so x² = y - 3 and x = √(y - 3) (positive root, since x ⩾ 0).
Swap: f⁻¹(x) = √(x - 3).
Domain of f⁻¹: x ⩾ 3, which is exactly the range of f.

(d) Solve f(x) = 30 for x ⩾ 0:
x² + 3 = 30
x² = 27
x = √27 = 3√3 ≈ 5.20        [only the positive root is in the domain]

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Reading fg(x) as f then g. It is g first, then f — the notation runs right to left.
  • Assuming fg = gf; only special cases agree.
  • Treating f⁻¹(x) as 1/f(x). The inverse undoes the function; it is not a reciprocal.
  • Ignoring domain restrictions: with x ⩾ 0 on f(x) = x² + 3, the inverse takes the positive root only, and a negative root answer is wrong.
  • Claiming y = x² has an inverse over all real numbers; it is two-to-one and needs a restricted domain.
  • Building the nth term from the first difference alone without checking every term; a single wrong check sends a whole answer wrong.
  • Writing a geometric nth term as arⁿ instead of arⁿ⁻¹; the first term must be a itself.
  • Stating a range that ignores the turning point of a quadratic: the range of y = (x − 2)² + 1 is y ⩾ 1, not y ⩾ 0.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 2, 3 marks). Find the nth term of 7, 11, 15, 19, ...

Answer: Constant difference 4, so 4n + b; the first term 7 = 4 + b gives b = 3. The nth term is 4n + 3. The 20th term is 83.

Question 2 (Paper 2, 3 marks). A sequence has nth term 5n − 2. Write down the first four terms and the 100th.

Answer: n = 1, 2, 3, 4 give 3, 8, 13, 18; the 100th term is 5(100) − 2 = 498.

Question 3 (Paper 4, 4 marks). f(x) = 3x − 1 and g(x) = x² + 2. Find fg(x), gf(2) and f⁻¹(x).

Answer: fg(x) = 3(x² + 2) − 1 = 3x² + 5. gf(2): f(2) = 5, so g(5) = 27. Inverse: y = 3x − 1 gives x = (y + 1)/3, so f⁻¹(x) = (x + 1)/3.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 4 marks). The second differences of a sequence are constant at 4, and its first two terms are 2 and 7. Find the nth term.

Answer: Constant second difference 4 means the n² coefficient is 4/2 = 2, so the rule starts 2n². The n² sequence gives 2, 8, ... while the sequence is 2, 7, ..., so the remainder is 0, −1, ... a linear part with difference −1: −n + 1. Check: 2n² − n + 1 gives n = 1: 2 ✓ and n = 2: 8 − 2 + 1 = 7 ✓. The nth term is 2n² − n + 1.

Question 5 (Paper 4, 5 marks). f(x) = (x + 4)/(x − 2) for x ≠ 2. Find f⁻¹(x) and the value of x for which f(x) is undefined.

Answer: y = (x + 4)/(x − 2) gives y(x − 2) = x + 4, so yx − 2y = x + 4, yx − x = 2y + 4, x(y − 1) = 2y + 4 and x = (2y + 4)/(y − 1). Swapping: f⁻¹(x) = (2x + 4)/(x − 1). The function itself is undefined at x = 2, where the denominator vanishes; its inverse is undefined at x = 1.

Question 6 (Paper 2, 3 marks). The first three terms of a geometric sequence are 5, 15, 45. Find the 8th term.

Answer: Common ratio r = 15/5 = 3, so the nth term is 5 × 3ⁿ⁻¹ and the 8th term is 5 × 3⁷ = 5 × 2187 = 10 935.

From variables and patterns, the course now turns to the number system itself.

Sequences: terms, term-to-term rules and position rules

A sequence is an ordered list of numbers that follows a rule. Each number in the list is a term, and the position of a term in the list is its term number, written n. Exam questions give a sequence and ask for a missing term, a rule, or a check on whether a particular number belongs to the pattern. The subsections below cover the two kinds of rule and how to move between them.

Reading a sequence and naming its terms

Write the first term as the term with n = 1, the second as n = 2, and so on. In the sequence 5, 8, 11, 14, the first term is 5 and the fourth term is 14. Read the terms from left to right, and keep the positions fixed, because a term that is shifted by one place gives a wrong answer even when the arithmetic is correct.

Term-to-term rules

A term-to-term rule says how to get the next term from the one before it. "Add 3 each time" and "multiply by 2 each time" are term-to-term rules. To use one, start from a known term and apply the rule repeatedly. A term-to-term rule is quick to apply to a few terms, but it is slow to find a term far down the list, which is why the position rule is needed.

Position-to-term rules, or nth term

A position-to-term rule, often called the nth term, gives any term directly from its position n. For the sequence 5, 8, 11, 14, the nth term is 3n + 2. Check it by substitution: n = 1 gives 5, n = 2 gives 8, and n = 4 gives 14. The nth term is the more useful form in an exam, because it finds the 50th term without listing the first 49.

Finding a term from an nth term

Substitute the position into the rule. For the nth term 3n + 2, the 20th term is 3 × 20 + 2 = 62. Write the substitution in full, with the position inside brackets if it is negative or a fraction, and keep the working so that a method mark can be awarded even if the arithmetic slips.

Testing whether a number belongs to a sequence

To check whether a number such as 80 is in the sequence with nth term 3n + 2, set the rule equal to 80 and solve: 3n + 2 = 80, so 3n = 78 and n = 26. Because n is a whole number, 80 is a term, and it is the 26th term. If the solution for n is not a whole number, the number is not in the sequence.

Arithmetic sequences and the common difference

In an arithmetic sequence the difference between consecutive terms is the same every time. This fixed difference is the common difference, written d. For the sequence 5, 8, 11, 14, the common difference is 3. The nth term of any arithmetic sequence has the form dn + c, where d is the common difference and c is found by substituting the first term.

Geometric sequences and the common ratio

In a geometric sequence each term is found by multiplying the previous one by the same number, called the common ratio. The sequence 3, 6, 12, 24 has common ratio 2. A geometric sequence can grow very quickly, so check the ratio by dividing two consecutive terms rather than guessing it from the first two numbers.

Linear and quadratic sequences in depth

Most sequence questions at this level use a linear rule or a quadratic rule. A linear sequence has a constant first difference, and a quadratic sequence has a constant second difference. Recognising which kind a sequence is decides the method, and the subsections below show how to find the rule and how to confirm it.

Finding the nth term of a linear sequence

For a linear sequence, write the common difference as d and the term before the first as a. The nth term is then dn + (a − d). Take the sequence 7, 10, 13, 16. The common difference is 3 and the first term is 7, so the nth term is 3n + (7 − 3), which is 3n + 4. Check the answer against the second term: 3 × 2 + 4 = 10, which matches.

Checking a linear rule with the difference

A quick check on a linear rule is to compare the coefficient of n with the difference between consecutive terms. The coefficient of n must equal the common difference. If the rule is 3n + 4 and the terms increase by 3 each time, the rule is consistent. A mismatch between the coefficient and the difference means the rule is wrong, and the mistake is usually in the constant term.

Quadratic sequences and second differences

Find the first differences, which are the gaps between consecutive terms, and then find the differences between those. If the second differences are constant, the sequence is quadratic. For 4, 7, 12, 19, the first differences are 3, 5, 7, and the second differences are 2, 2. The constant second difference shows that the sequence is quadratic, and the coefficient of n² is half of 2, so it is 1.

Finding the nth term of a quadratic

Write the nth term as an n² + bn + c, where a is half the second difference. Subtract a n² from each term and look at what is left. For 4, 7, 12, 19, subtracting n² leaves 3 for every term, so the remainder is the constant 3 and the nth term is n² + 3. Check n = 2: 2² + 3 = 7, which is the second term.

Special sequences: squares, cubes and triangular numbers

Some sequences should be recognised on sight. The square numbers are 1, 4, 9, 16, with nth term n². The cube numbers are 1, 8, 27, 64, with nth term n³. Triangular numbers are 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, and their nth term is n(n + 1) / 2. A sequence that matches one of these, with a small change, is often a question about adjusting the standard pattern.

Recognising a sequence from its pattern

Some questions give a pattern made of shapes or matchsticks and ask for the number of items in a given step. Write down the number for the first three steps, find the difference or the second difference, and form the rule. For steps that add 4 matchsticks each time, starting from 4 matchsticks, the rule is 4n. Test the rule against a step that is not used to find it, so that a pattern that only fits the first two steps is caught.

Sequences in context

A context question describes a sequence in words, such as the number of tiles in a border or the total of a savings plan that adds the same amount each month. Identify whether the change is by a fixed amount or a fixed factor, write the nth term, and then answer the question in the words of the context. A reply that states "the 12th term is 40" should go on to say what the 40 represents, such as the number of tiles in the 12th border.

Equations and symbols

Two families of formula share this topic: the rules that generate a sequence, and the algebra of function notation. Both are asked as "find the rule", so the sheet is a list of rules with the letters they use.

4n - 1 Key: n = the position of the term in the sequence (1, 2, 3, …); the coefficient 4 is the common difference and −1 is the adjustment that makes n = 1 give the first term, 3. Substitute n to get any term directly; the 20th term here is 79.

3n + 2 Key: n = position; 3 = common difference of 5, 8, 11, 14; +2 makes the first term correct. Every linear sequence can be written dn + b, and b always equals the first term minus d.

n² + 1 Key: n = position; the n² term means the second difference is constant, which is what identifies a quadratic sequence. Build the n² sequence, subtract it, and finish the remaining linear part.

n(n + 1)/2 Key: n = position; the triangular numbers 1, 3, 6, 10, found by adding the integers 1 to n. Recognise the shape rather than deriving it under exam pressure.

arⁿ⁻¹ Key: a = first term; r = common ratio, found by dividing any term by the one before; n = position. The exponent is n − 1, not n: at n = 1 the term must be a itself, and r⁰ = 1 guarantees that.

f(x) = 2x + 3 Key: f = the function's name; x = the input, in the domain; the expression is the rule — multiply by 2, add 3. Evaluating is substitution: f(4) = 11.

fg(x) = 2x² + 1 Key: fg means apply g first (g(x) = x²), then f to the result; the notation reads right to left. fg(x) is not gf(x) — order matters, and swapping it is the standard error.

f⁻¹(x) = (5x + 2)/3 Key: f⁻¹ = the inverse function, the machine that undoes f; the −1 is not a power, and f⁻¹(x) is never 1/f(x). Found by writing y = f(x), making x the subject, then swapping the letters.

f⁻¹(x) = √(x - 3) Key: the inverse of f(x) = x² + 3 on the domain x ⩾ 0; the positive root alone is taken because the original domain excludes negatives. The domain of f⁻¹ is the range of f, here x ⩾ 3.

How the marks are given. Show the substitution, keep the composite order, and state any domain restriction. A range quoted without checking the turning point — y ⩾ 1 for (x − 2)² + 1, not y ⩾ 0 — is the quiet loss on this topic.

title: Transport in Plants
content:
Transport in Plants

Cambridge IGCSE Biology 0610, Extended route, topic 8 (statements 8.1–8.4). Xylem and phloem, water uptake, transpiration and its factors, and translocation between sources and sinks.

8.1 to 8.2 Xylem, phloem and water uptake

  • Xylem vessels carry water and mineral ions upwards from roots to leaves; they are dead, lignified tubes with no end walls, giving a continuous column. Phloem carries sucrose and amino acids both up and down, from source to sink; sieve tube elements are living cells.
  • Water enters root hair cells by osmosis because the cell sap is more concentrated, then moves cell to cell by osmosis until it reaches the xylem.

8.3 Transpiration

  • Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from the leaves through the stomata. It creates a transpiration stream: evaporation from mesophyll cell walls lowers water potential, water moves by osmosis from the xylem, and the whole column is pulled up under tension.
  • Rate increases with higher temperature, lower humidity, more wind and brighter light (stomata open wider). It decreases when stomata close, for example in the dark or when the plant is wilting.

8.4 Translocation

  • Translocation is the movement of sucrose and amino acids in the phloem from sources (leaves, storage organs) to sinks (roots, fruits, growing tips). It requires energy from respiration and is not the same process as the transpiration stream.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Factor analysis, applied to a potometer experiment: the main variables are light, temperature and wind. Explain each: light opens stomata, temperature increases evaporation, wind removes humid air from around the leaf. In an investigation, name which you would control and how.
  • Structure reasoning, applied to why xylem vessels are lignified and dead: lignin strengthens them against collapse under the tension of the transpiration stream, and being dead removes barriers to continuous flow. That two-part answer is worth two marks.
  • Source and sink reasoning, applied to a potato tuber in summer: the leaf is the source and the tuber is the sink; in spring, the tuber becomes the source as stored starch is converted to sucrose and moves out. Sources and sinks change with the season — state the direction in each case.

Common errors

  • Saying transpiration is "the plant sweating". It is evaporation of water vapour, and it is a consequence of gas exchange, not a separate function.
  • Claiming water moves up xylem by root pressure alone. The transpiration pull under tension is the main mechanism at IGCSE level.
  • Confusing translocation (phloem, sugars, both directions) with the transpiration stream (xylem, water, upwards).

content:
IGCSE Biology: Transport in Plants

A tall tree can lift water more than 100 metres from soil to leaf without a single pump — no heart, no muscles, just physics and two sets of microscopic pipes. This note explains the structure of xylem and phloem, how root hair cells take water in, how the transpiration stream pulls a continuous water column up the plant (with the potometer method that measures it), and how sugars are translocated from leaves to the rest of the plant.
