Every mechanism is built from the underlying physical idea first — evaporation, cohesion, osmosis, active transport — then named, so you can reconstruct it in the exam rather than recite it.

Xylem and phloem: the two transport systems

Vascular tissue runs through roots, stems and leaves as veins. Xylem carries water and dissolved mineral ions upwards from the roots to the leaves. Its vessels are dead, hollow tubes made of lignified cells stacked end to end with perforated end walls — wide bore, no cytoplasm, lignin-thickened walls that resist collapse under negative pressure. Phloem carries sucrose (the translocate) and amino acids both up and down the plant, from source (leaves, or storage organs in spring) to sink (roots, fruits, growing tips). Its sieve tubes are living cells with thin walls, perforated sieve plates at the ends, and no nucleus at maturity; each sieve tube element is kept alive by a companion cell packed with mitochondria. Root, stem and leaf arrangement: in roots the xylem sits in a central star; in stems the vascular bundles form a ring near the outside (giving strength); in leaves they branch as veins.

Xylem and phloem compared

FeatureXylemPhloem
CarriesWater and dissolved mineral ionsSucrose and amino acids (translocate)
DirectionUpwards only (roots to leaves)Both directions (source to sink)
CellsDead, hollow, lignified wallsLiving sieve tube elements with companion cells
End wallsPerforated or absentSieve plates with pores
MechanismTranspiration pull and cohesionPressure flow (active loading/unloading)

Water uptake by root hair cells

The root hair is a long extension of an epidermal cell, giving a huge surface area and a thin wall for a short diffusion path. Soil water has a higher water potential than the cell sap of the root cortex cells, so water enters the root hair by osmosis and then passes from cell to cell across the cortex (by osmosis, down the water potential gradient — living layers of the endodermis with their Casparian strip force the symplastic route), until it reaches the xylem. Mineral ions enter by active transport (against their gradient, using carrier proteins and ATP from respiration), which lowers the water potential in the root and helps water follow by osmosis. The whole route: soil solution → root hair → cortex cells → endodermis → xylem. The alternative pathway (through cell walls — the apoplastic route) is blocked at the endodermis by the waterproof Casparian strip, forcing water into the living cells where it can be controlled.

The transpiration stream

Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from the aerial parts of the plant, mainly through the stomata. The mechanism: water evaporates from the spongy mesophyll cell walls into the air spaces of the leaf; this water vapour diffuses out through open stomata down its concentration gradient into the drier air outside. The evaporation pulls the remaining water molecules into the gap (transpiration pull), and because water molecules are cohesive (hydrogen-bonded to each other), they form a continuous column from root to leaf: as molecules leave the top, they pull the next ones up behind them (the cohesion-tension theory). Root pressure and capillary action in the narrow xylem vessels assist. The transpiration stream thus has two consequences: water reaches the leaves for photosynthesis, and dissolved mineral ions travel with it to where they are needed.

Factors affecting transpiration and the potometer

Transpiration increases with: higher temperature (water molecules evaporate faster), lower humidity (steeper diffusion gradient), more wind (water vapour carried away, maintaining the gradient), and higher light intensity (stomata open for carbon dioxide). It decreases when stomata close in darkness, in drought (guard cells lose turgor), or in cold. Xerophytes (cacti, marram grass) have adaptations to cut it: thick cuticle, sunken stomata, rolled leaves, hairs to trap moist air, reduced leaves (spines). The potometer measures water uptake as a proxy for transpiration: a cut leafy shoot is sealed into a capillary tube of water with an air bubble; as the shoot transpires, the bubble moves along the tube; distance moved per minute measures the rate. Keep the apparatus airtight (grease the seal), use the same shoot for all trials, and control temperature, light, humidity and air movement. Note the assumption: uptake ≈ transpiration (some water is used in photosynthesis and growth).

Translocation: moving sugars

Translocation is the movement of sucrose and amino acids in the phloem from source to sink, in both directions depending on the season (down from leaves in summer; up from root stores in spring). Loading sucrose into the sieve tubes at the source (by companion cells, using ATP — active transport) lowers the water potential, water enters by osmosis from the xylem, the pressure rises, and the solution mass-flows towards sinks where sucrose is unloaded (raising water potential, water leaves). This is the pressure-flow hypothesis. Evidence examiners like: aphid stylet experiments (sap collects where the stylet punctures a sieve tube; the exudate is sugary and under pressure), and ringing a stem (removing phloem causes sugars to accumulate above the cut, swelling the bark, while xylem is undisturbed). Sucrose is the transport sugar — not glucose — because it is non-reducing, stable and soluble.

Worked example: potometer data and transpiration reasoning

A potometer's bubble moved 12 cm in 30 minutes at 20 °C in still air. Calculate the rate and predict the effect of a fan. Step 1: rate = distance ÷ time = 12 cm ÷ 30 min = 0.4 cm per minute. Step 2: with a fan, the boundary layer of saturated air around the leaf is swept away, keeping the diffusion gradient steep — the rate increases, perhaps to 0.7 cm/min. Step 3: percent change = (0.7 − 0.4) ÷ 0.4 × 100 = 75 % increase. A second calculation: water loss per day — if 0.4 cm/min over a 12-hour day and the capillary tube bore corresponds to 0.02 cm³ per cm, daily uptake = 0.4 × 60 × 12 × 0.02 = 5.76 cm³. Use the numbers given in any real question, and always quote units (cm per minute, cm³ per hour) — unitless answers lose a mark.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Swapping xylem and phloem: xylem = water up (dead, lignified); phloem = sugars both ways (living, sieve plates). A memory hook: "xylem is for X-tra water".
  • Saying transpiration is "the plant breathing": it is evaporation of water through stomata.
  • Forgetting cohesion in the explanation of the transpiration stream: the continuous hydrogen-bonded column is the whole mechanism.
  • Describing water movement in the xylem as osmosis — xylem is dead, so water movement there is bulk flow under tension, not osmosis.
  • Confusing translocation (sugars in phloem) with transpiration (water vapour loss).
  • In a potometer plan, not mentioning airtight seals or the same shoot for repeats — both are standard control marks.
  • Saying stomata "let water in": they admit carbon dioxide and release oxygen; water loss is a side effect of keeping them open.
  • Writing the source-to-sink direction as one-way only; at A Level the season reversal is examined.

Exam-style questions and answers

Q1. Describe how water moves from the soil into the xylem of a root. (4 marks) Answer: water enters root hair cells by osmosis down the water potential gradient (1); passes through cortex cells from cell to cell (1); endodermis (Casparian strip) blocks the apoplastic route so water passes into living cells (1); enters the xylem where root pressure and transpiration pull move it up (1).

Q2. Explain how four environmental factors affect the rate of transpiration. (4 marks) Answer: higher temperature increases evaporation rate (1); lower humidity steepens the diffusion gradient (1); wind removes saturated air from leaf surfaces (1); light opens stomata so more surface is exposed (1).

Q3. Explain why xylem vessels have lignified walls and no cytoplasm. (2 marks) Answer: lignin strengthens the walls to withstand the negative pressure of the transpiration stream (1); no cytoplasm leaves a clear hollow tube for water flow (1).

Q4. Describe how you would investigate the effect of wind on transpiration using a potometer. (4 marks) Answer: set up the potometer with a cut leafy shoot, ensuring the apparatus is airtight (1); measure the distance the air bubble moves per minute in still air (1); place a fan at a fixed distance and repeat (1); keep temperature, light and humidity constant and repeat for a mean (1).

Q5. Explain the advantage of translocation occurring in both directions in the phloem. (2 marks) Answer: sugars move down from leaves to roots in summer for storage (1); and up from storage organs to growing shoots in spring when leaves are absent (1).

Equations and symbols

The quantitative side of transport in plants is small but examinable: a potometer question is a rate calculation, and the water lost in a day is a rate multiplied by time. Everything here is a measurement of water moving, so the units are always per unit time.

rate = distance ÷ time = 12 cm ÷ 30 min = 0.4 cm per minute Key: rate = rate of water uptake, the proxy for transpiration (cm min⁻¹); distance = movement of the air bubble along the capillary (cm); time = the interval it took (min). Divide, and keep the units — an answer of "0.4" alone loses the mark.

percent change = (0.7 − 0.4) ÷ 0.4 × 100 = 75 % increase Key: 0.7 = the new rate after the change (cm min⁻¹); 0.4 = the original rate (cm min⁻¹); the original always goes on the bottom, and × 100 turns the fraction into a percentage. A decrease comes out negative, so quote the sign.

daily uptake = 0.4 × 60 × 12 × 0.02 = 5.76 cm³ Key: 0.4 = rate from the potometer (cm min⁻¹); 60 = minutes in an hour; 12 = hours of daylight used; 0.02 = the volume each centimetre of capillary holds (cm³ cm⁻¹). Chain the conversions, cancel the units, and state the result as a volume per day.

Why these three are enough. The potometer measures uptake, not transpiration, because a little of the water is used in photosynthesis and growth — say so, and the calculation is complete. The classic slip is multiplying by 24 hours when the question says 12, or forgetting that the bore conversion is a volume per centimetre, not a volume per minute.

title: Electric Fields and Capacitance — Study Notes
content:
Electric Fields and Capacitance

Coulomb's law

The force between two point charges is F = kQ₁Q₂/r², with k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻². Like charges repel and unlike charges attract. The force acts along the line joining the charges.

Example: +2.0 μC and −3.0 μC, 0.30 m apart, attract with F = 0.60 N.

Electric field strength

Field strength E is the force per unit positive charge: E = F/Q, in N C⁻¹ (or V m⁻¹). For a point charge E = kQ/r², radially outward for positive charge.

Uniform field: between parallel plates, E = V/d, with the field constant in magnitude and direction. A charge q in it feels F = qE.

Example: plates 4.0 cm apart with p.d. 600 V have E = 1.5 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹.

Electric potential and potential energy

Electric potential V at a point is the work done per unit positive charge in bringing a small charge from infinity to that point: V = kQ/r for a point charge. Potential is a scalar. Field strength is the negative potential gradient, E = −dV/dr, so a steep potential-distance graph means a strong field. The field points from high to low potential.

Capacitance

Capacitance C = Q/V, measured in farads (C V⁻¹). The energy stored is W = ½QV = ½CV² = ½Q²/C. The area under a graph of V against Q equals the stored energy.

Example: a 10 μF capacitor charged to 200 V stores 0.20 J.

Capacitors in series and parallel

  • In parallel the capacitances add: C = C₁ + C₂.
  • In series the reciprocals add: 1/C = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂. The total is smaller than the smallest.

Discharge: through a resistor R, the charge falls exponentially, Q = Q₀e^(−t/RC). The time constant RC is the time for the charge or p.d. to fall to 37% of its initial value.

Exam tips: convert μF and cm to SI units before calculating. Check whether a question asks for field strength (vector) or potential (scalar). Series capacitors share the charge; parallel capacitors share the p.d.

Worked example: field between parallel plates

Two parallel plates are 0.040 m apart with a potential difference of 2.0 kV. The uniform field strength is E = V/d = 2000/0.040 = 5.0 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹. A proton placed at rest between the plates feels a force F = eE = (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹)(5.0 × 10⁴) = 8.0 × 10⁻¹⁵ N, directed from the positive plate towards the negative plate.

Radial fields and potential

For a point charge, E = Q/(4πε₀r²), so field strength falls with the square of distance. The potential is V = Q/(4πε₀r), which falls only with the first power of distance. Students often mix these two; the field depends on r², the potential on r.

Energy and the electronvolt

The work done in moving a charge Q through a potential difference V is W = QV. A charge accelerated from rest through 500 V gains 500 eV of kinetic energy, which is 8.0 × 10⁻¹⁷ J for an electron. Expressing energies in electronvolts makes many A-level questions faster to work through.

  • Field lines point away from positive charge and towards negative charge, and they never cross.
  • Equipotential surfaces are always perpendicular to field lines.
  • Energy stored in a capacitor is ½CV² = ½QV = ½Q²/C. Choose the form that matches the data given.

title: Probability
content:
Probability

Basic Rules

For an event A with P(A) = p: 0 ≤ p ≤ 1, and P(A′) = 1 − P(A). For mutually exclusive events, probabilities add: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B). For events that can occur together, subtract the overlap:

  • P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B)

Venn Diagrams

Draw the universe first, then the events. Fill from the intersection outwards: if P(A) = 0.6, P(B) = 0.5 and P(A ∩ B) = 0.25, then only-A = 0.35, only-B = 0.25, neither = 0.15. Every region must sum to 1.

Tree Diagrams

Branch probabilities multiply along a path; outcomes at the end of complete paths add. Draw one branch set per stage of the experiment. For two draws without replacement from a bag of 5 red and 3 blue: P(RR) = (5/8)(4/7) = 20/56.

Conditional Probability

P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B) — the probability of A given that B has occurred. The condition shrinks the sample space.

Example: P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.4, P(A ∩ B) = 0.2. Then P(A | B) = 0.2/0.4 = 0.5, so A and B are independent since P(A | B) = P(A).

Independence

A and B are independent exactly when P(A ∩ B) = P(A)·P(B). Do not confuse independent (no influence on probabilities) with mutually exclusive (cannot co-occur). Mutually exclusive events with non-zero probabilities are never independent.

Exam tips: convert every "given that" into a conditional. With trees, label the second-stage branches with conditional probabilities; they are usually different from the first stage when drawing without replacement.

title: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Statistics and Data Handling
content:
Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Statistics and Data Handling

Statistics is the art of describing a pile of numbers with a few well-chosen ones: an average to say where the middle lies, a spread to say how tightly the data cluster, and a chart to make the shape visible. The IGCSE questions test exactly that pipeline — classify the data, compute the averages and spread, draw or read the chart, and compare two distributions. This note builds the whole subject from zero: the data types, every average and measure of spread with the frequency-table method, the standard charts, cumulative frequency curves, and histograms with unequal class widths.

Classifying statistical data

TypeMeaningExamples
Qualitative (categorical)describes a quality, not a numberfavourite colour, blood group
Quantitativemeasured or counted as a numberheight, number of siblings
Discretecountable, separate values (usually integers)number of children, shoe size
Continuouscan take any value in a range (measured)height, time, mass

The classification decides which charts and averages are legal: a mode for categorical data, a median for ordered data, class intervals for continuous data. Discrete data are plotted as bar charts with gaps; continuous data as histograms with no gaps (and frequency density on the vertical axis).

Averages and range

mean = sum of values / number of values
median = middle value when ordered (mean of the two middle
         values for an even count)
mode = most frequent value (or class); none if no repeats
range = largest - smallest

quartiles: Q1 = lower quartile (25%), Q3 = upper quartile (75%)
interquartile range (IQR) = Q3 - Q1  (spread of the middle 50%)

The mean uses every value (sensitive to outliers); the median ignores extreme values (robust); the mode is the only average available for categorical data. When comparing two data sets, quote an average and a spread: "school A has a higher median but a larger IQR, so its results are higher on average but less consistent."

Worked example. Find the mean, median, mode and range of: 4, 7, 7, 9, 12, 15, 18.

mean = (4+7+7+9+12+15+18)/7 = 72/7 = 10.3 (3 s.f.)
median = 4th value = 9
mode = 7 (appears twice)
range = 18 - 4 = 14

Worked example 2 (even count). Find the median of 3, 5, 8, 10, 12, 15.

even count: average the 3rd and 4th values
median = (8 + 10)/2 = 9

Averages from frequency tables

mean = sum of (value x frequency) / sum of frequencies
median = the value at position (n + 1)/2 in cumulative order
mode = the value with the highest frequency

Worked example. The table shows goals scored: 0 (5 players), 1 (8), 2 (6), 3 (2). Find the mean and the median.

total players = 5 + 8 + 6 + 2 = 21
total goals = 0 × 5 + 1 × 8 + 2 × 6 + 3 × 2 = 0 + 8 + 12 + 6 = 26
mean = 26/21 = 1.24 (3 s.f.)
median position = (21 + 1)/2 = 11th value
cumulative: 5 (0 goals), 13 (1 goal) - the 11th value is 1
median = 1

For grouped data, use midpoints: the mean = Σ(midpoint × frequency)/Σfrequency, and the median comes from the cumulative frequency curve (below). The grouped mean is an estimate because the midpoint stands in for every value in the class.

Charts and diagrams

  • Bar chart: bars with gaps for categorical or discrete data; height = frequency.
  • Pie chart: angle = (frequency/total) × 360°; label the sectors with the category.
  • Pictogram: a symbol represents a fixed number; a half symbol represents half that number.
  • Stem-and-leaf: a sorted display that keeps the actual values; the key explains the split (e.g. 3|4 means 34).
  • Frequency polygon: plot frequency against the midpoint of each class and join with straight lines.

Worked example (pie chart). 40 students choose a sport: football 16, tennis 10, swimming 8, other 6. Find the angle for football.

angle = (16/40) × 360 = 144 °

Worked example 2 (pie chart reverse). A sector of 72° represents 9 students. How many students in total?

72 ° represents 9  →  360 ° represents 9 × 360/72 = 45 students

Cumulative frequency diagrams

A cumulative frequency table adds frequencies as you move up the classes. Plot cumulative frequency against the upper class boundary and join with a smooth curve; then read positions:

median at n/2
lower quartile at n/4
upper quartile at 3n/4
IQR = Q3 - Q1

Worked example. A cumulative frequency curve for 60 students' marks: Q1 = 42, median = 55, Q3 = 68. Find the IQR and interpret it.

IQR = 68 - 42 = 26 marks
The middle 50% of students scored within 26 marks of each other;

Always read across to the curve and then down to the horizontal axis — and use the class boundaries, not the midpoints, for the plot positions.

Histograms and frequency density

When class widths differ, the height of a bar cannot be the frequency — a wide class would dominate unfairly. Instead, the area of each bar is proportional to the frequency:

frequency density = frequency / class width
frequency = frequency density x class width (area of the bar)

Worked example. Class 0–10 has frequency 20; 10–20 has frequency 30; 20–40 has frequency 40. Find the frequency densities.

0-10: 20/10 = 2.0
10-20: 30/10 = 3.0
20-40: 40/20 = 2.0

Reading a histogram backwards is the standard question: measure a bar's width and height, multiply to get the frequency, and read the class from the horizontal axis. Remember that the axes often use class boundaries, so a bar from 20 to 40 covers width 20.

Stem-and-leaf diagrams and frequency polygons

A stem-and-leaf diagram sorts data while keeping every value visible: the stem is the leading digit and the leaf the final digit, with a key such as 3|4 meaning 34. Interpreting one means reading the ordered leaves to find the median, the quartiles and the shape: the median is the middle leaf, Q1 and Q3 sit at the quarter and three-quarter positions, and the distribution's skew shows in where the leaves bunch.

A frequency polygon plots frequency against the midpoint of each class and joins the points with straight lines; it is the grouped-data equivalent of a line graph and makes comparisons between two distributions easy (plot both polygons on the same axes).

Worked example. The leaves for stem 4 are 1, 3, 3, 6, 8 and for stem 5 are 0, 2, 5. List the data in order and find the median.

values: 41, 43, 43, 46, 48, 50, 52, 55
n = 8, so the median is the mean of the 4th and 5th values:
(46 + 48)/2 = 47

Worked example 2 (interpreting). Explain what a long right-hand tail of leaves in a stem-and-leaf diagram indicates.

A long right tail means a few unusually high values: the data
are positively skewed, and the mean will be greater than the
median because the high values pull it upward.

Comparing distributions

Comparison questions want two statements: one about the average (which is higher) and one about the spread (which is more consistent). Use median and IQR together — they are robust to outliers — or mean and standard deviation when the data are symmetric and the syllabus supplies it.

Worked example. Class A: median 62, IQR 18. Class B: median 58, IQR 9. Compare.

Class A has the higher typical score (median 62 vs 58), but its
results are more spread out (IQR 18 vs 9), so Class B is more
consistent even though its middle score is lower.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Averages) Find the mean and range of 12, 15, 11, 19, 13. Answer: mean = (12 + 15 + 11 + 19 + 13)/5 = 70/5 = 14; range = largest − smallest = 19 − 11 = 8.
  2. (Frequency table) Values 1, 2, 3 with frequencies 4, 7, 9. Find the mean. Answer: mean = Σfx/Σf = (1 × 4 + 2 × 7 + 3 × 9)/(4 + 7 + 9) = (4 + 14 + 27)/20 = 45/20 = 2.25.
  3. (Median) Find the median of 2, 4, 4, 6, 9, 10. Answer: there are six values, so the median is the mean of the 3rd and 4th: (4 + 6)/2 = 5.
  4. (Pie chart) A sector of 90° represents 15 people. Find the total. Answer: 90° is 90/360 = ¼ of the circle, so the total is 15 ÷ ¼ = 15 × 4 = 60 people.
  5. (Cumulative frequency) For 80 values, where do you read the median? Answer: At cumulative frequency 40, reading across to the curve and down to the axis.
  6. (Histogram) A bar of width 5 has frequency density 4. Find its frequency. Answer: frequency = frequency density × class width = 4 × 5 = 20.
  7. (Frequency density) Class 30–50 has frequency 24. Find the frequency density. Answer: class width = 50 − 30 = 20, so frequency density = frequency/width = 24/20 = 1.2.
  8. (Compare) Two runners' times: A median 42 s, IQR 3 s; B median 40 s, IQR 8 s. Compare. Answer: B is faster typically (lower median) but less consistent (larger IQR); A is more reliable.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Median without ordering: the median is the middle of the ordered list. Forgetting to sort is the commonest data-handling error.
  • Even-count median: average the two middle values; do not pick one of them.
  • Grouped mean: use midpoints and label the answer an estimate — the midpoint is not the actual mean of the class.
  • Histogram heights: the vertical axis is frequency density, not frequency; area is the frequency. Reading the height as the frequency is the classic histogram error.
  • Cumulative frequency positions: plot against upper class boundaries and read the median at n/2 (not (n+1)/2 on the graph).
  • Pie chart arithmetic: check that the angles sum to 360° before answering the next part.
  • IQR direction: IQR = upper − lower quartile; a negative IQR means the quartiles are swapped.
  • Comparison claims: quote actual values ("median 62 vs 58"), not "better" without evidence.

Collecting and classifying data

Every statistical question starts with data, and the type of data decides which averages and diagrams are sensible. Before any calculation, decide where the data came from, what kind of values it holds, and whether the sample is fair. The subsections below set out these decisions in the order an examiner expects them to be made.

Primary and secondary data

Primary data is collected by the person who uses it, for example by a survey or an experiment carried out in class. Secondary data is taken from an existing source such as a census, a published table or a sports website. Primary data suits a question that needs a specific answer, while secondary data is quicker but may not match the exact question being asked. State which kind you have used when you describe an investigation.

Discrete and continuous data

Discrete data takes separate values that are usually counted, such as the number of goals scored or the number of people in a family. Continuous data can take any value in a range and is measured, such as height, mass or time. The distinction matters for grouping: a discrete table can use single values, while a continuous table needs class intervals with clear boundaries such as 10 ≤ t < 20.

Qualitative and quantitative data

Qualitative data describes a quality, such as eye colour or favourite subject, and cannot be averaged. Quantitative data is numerical and can be ordered and added. A mean is only meaningful for quantitative data, so a question that asks for the mean colour is answered by naming the mode or by stating that no mean exists.

Reading the question before the data

Underline what the question asks for before reading the table: a mode, a median, a range, a comparison or a conclusion. Many marks are lost by calculating the right number and then answering a different question. Note the units and the sample size at the same time, because the sample size is needed for a relative frequency and the units for a correct final statement.

Bias in samples and questionnaires

A sample is biased when some members of the population are more likely to be chosen than others. Asking only students in one class about a school-wide question is biased, and so is a question that leads the respondent, such as asking whether people agree that the bus service is too slow. A fair sample is random, large enough to represent the group, and drawn from the whole population being studied.

Judging the reliability of a conclusion

A conclusion is only as reliable as the data behind it. A small sample, an unrepresentative group or a question with an obvious bias weakens any statement drawn from it. A good answer names one weakness and suggests a change, such as taking a larger sample across a wider range of times or places.

Drawing a conclusion from a table

A conclusion must be supported by a number from the table and must answer the question asked. If the mean time for group A is 14 minutes and for group B is 18 minutes, the statement that group B took longer on average is supported, but a statement about all pupils in the school is not, because only two groups were measured.

Averages and spread in depth

The mean, median and mode each describe the centre of a set of data in a different way, and the range and interquartile range describe the spread. A careful answer uses the average that fits the data and the measure of spread that shows how far the values lie from it. The subsections below work through each measure in the form the question is most likely to use.

The mode for discrete and grouped data

The mode is the value that occurs most often. In a discrete frequency table it is the value with the largest frequency. For grouped data it is the modal class, the class with the largest frequency, and the answer is given as a class interval rather than a single value. A data set can have no mode, one mode or several modes.

The median from an ordered list

To find the median, arrange the values in order and locate the middle one. For n values the median is at position (n + 1) ÷ 2. With nine values the median is the fifth value, and with ten values it is the average of the fifth and sixth. Always order the data before counting, because the median taken from an unsorted list is wrong even when the middle value is chosen carefully.

Choosing an average

The mean uses every value, but it is pulled by extreme values. The median is not affected by one very large value, and the mode is the only average that can be used with qualitative data. A typical question asks which average best describes a set of salaries that includes one very large income; the answer is the median, with the reason that the mean is pulled up by the outlier.

The effect of an outlier

An outlier is a value far from the rest of the data. Adding one outlier to a small set changes the mean noticeably but may leave the median and mode unchanged. When an exam question asks for the effect of a change, work out the mean before and after the change, rather than guessing the direction from the size of the new value.

Range as a measure of spread

The range is the largest value minus the smallest value. It is quick to find but depends on only two values, so one outlier can make it large even when the rest of the data are close together. When comparing two data sets, state both the range and the centre, because two sets with the same mean can have very different ranges.

The interquartile range

The interquartile range is the upper quartile minus the lower quartile, the spread of the middle half of the data. It ignores the extreme values at each end and is therefore less affected by outliers than the range. For a list of 12 ordered values, the lower quartile is the median of the lower six values and the upper quartile is the median of the upper six.

Estimating the mean of grouped data

For grouped data the exact values are unknown, so the mean is estimated using the midpoint of each class. Multiply each midpoint by its frequency, add the products and divide by the total frequency: mean = Σfx ÷ Σf, where x is the midpoint. The answer is an estimate, and the working should say so, because the true mean depends on where each value sits inside its class.

Reading charts and diagrams

A chart is a summary of data, and the examiner expects you to read the values it shows, compare them and point out where a chart is misleading. Each diagram type has its own rules for scales, keys and angles. The subsections below cover the diagrams most often used in this topic and the errors that lose marks.

Bar charts and dual bar charts

A bar chart shows the frequency of each category, with equal gaps between the bars. A dual bar chart places two bars side by side for each category, so the two data sets can be compared directly. Read the scale carefully, because a scale that starts at a value other than zero exaggerates small differences between bars.

Pictograms with a key

A pictogram uses a symbol to stand for a number of items, and the key says how many each symbol represents. A symbol that stands for 10 items with 3 and a half symbols shown means 35 items. Partial symbols are the step that most often goes wrong, so divide the partial symbol by its share of the full symbol before multiplying by the key value.

Pie charts and angles

In a pie chart each sector has an angle equal to the frequency divided by the total, multiplied by 360°. A category with frequency 30 out of a total of 120 has an angle of 30 ÷ 120 × 360° = 90°. Working backwards, a sector of 72° in a total of 200 represents 72 ÷ 360 × 200 = 40 items.

Line graphs for time series

A line graph joins points that show a quantity over time, and the gradient shows the rate of change. A steeper line means a faster increase or decrease. When a question asks for the trend, describe the direction and the rate in words, and do not join points across a gap in the time axis without saying so.

Misleading scales and axes

A chart is misleading when its vertical axis does not start at zero, when the bars have different widths, or when a three-dimensional effect distorts the sizes. Each of these changes how large a difference looks. In an exam, name the feature that misleads, state what it does to the picture, and say how the chart should be drawn instead.

Comparing two distributions on one chart

Two distributions can be compared on one chart by using the same scales and the same class intervals. Compare the centre, using a median or mean, and the spread, using a range or interquartile range. A comparison that gives only the higher or lower value of one data set is incomplete, and must be followed by the matching value for the other.

Reading a chart in an exam question

Read the title, the axis labels, the units and the key before answering. Then take each value from the chart and write it in the working so the marker can see where it came from. A correct chart reading with the value written out earns the method marks even when the final statement is worded loosely.

Equations and symbols

Seven formulas cover the whole paper: the three averages with their range and interquartile range, the two histogram relations, and the pie-chart angle. Every one carries the same mark-scheme requirement — substitute, then state the answer in the units of the data, not as a bare number.

mean = sum of values / number of values Key: mean = the arithmetic average, in the same units as the data; sum of values = the total of every reading; number of values = how many readings there are. Uses every value, so one outlier moves it.

median = the value at position (n + 1)/2 in cumulative order Key: n = the number of values; the position is a count through the ordered list, not a value. For an even n the position falls between two values, so average them — picking one of the two is the commonest lost mark.

mode = the value with the highest frequency Key: mode = the most frequent value, in the same units as the data; for grouped data it is the modal class. The only average available for categorical data.

range = largest - smallest Key: largest and smallest = the extreme values of the data set; the range is their difference, in the data's units. It uses only two values, so a single outlier destroys it.

IQR = Q3 - Q1 Key: IQR = interquartile range, the spread of the middle 50% of the data (same units); Q3 = upper quartile at the 75% position; Q1 = lower quartile at the 25% position. A negative IQR means the quartiles have been swapped.

IQR = 68 - 42 = 26 marks Key: 68 = Q3, the mark at the 75% position; 42 = Q1, the mark at the 25% position; 26 marks = the IQR. Interpret it in words: the middle half of the students scored within 26 marks of each other.

frequency density = frequency / class width Key: frequency density = the height of the bar (no units, since it is a count divided by a width); frequency = the number of readings in the class; class width = upper boundary minus lower boundary (in the data's units). Use it only when the class widths differ — with equal widths the height may be the frequency.

frequency = frequency density x class width (area of the bar) Key: the same relation rearranged; reading a histogram backwards means measuring a bar's width and height and multiplying. In a histogram it is the area, never the height, that represents the frequency.

angle = (frequency/total) × 360° Key: frequency = the count in the sector; total = the total count for the whole chart; angle in degrees, and the sectors must sum to 360°. To go the other way, total = frequency × 360/angle.

mean = sum of (value x frequency) / sum of frequencies Key: value = each reading, or the midpoint of a class for grouped data (same units); frequency = how many times it occurs. With midpoints the answer is labelled an estimate, because the midpoint stands in for every value in the class.

title: Exam technique: Ratio, Rate and Proportion
content:
### What earns the marks
For sharing in a ratio, total parts and value of one part each earn a mark: write 5 parts = 600 before splitting. For scales and maps, the real-distance multiplication shown earns the method mark, with each unit conversion (cm to m to km) credited. For proportion with powers, the constant k found first earns the mark: write y = k x squared and solve for k.
### Traps
Error: dividing by 2 and 3 directly for a 2:3 split. Correction: parts first, always. Error: 1.40 hours for 1 h 40 min in speed questions. Correction: 40 min = 2/3 h. Error: linear scaling for an x-squared relation. Correction: square the ratio. Error: inverted map scale (dividing by 50000). Correction: real is bigger than map.

title: Exam technique: Quantum Physics
content:
### What earns the marks
For photons, hf quoted with substitution earns both marks. For photoelectricity, threshold frequency reasoning earns the explanation mark regardless of intensity. For matter waves, h/p quoted earns the method mark; diffraction named as wave proof earns the conclusion.
### Traps
Error: brighter light assumed to beat threshold. Correction: frequency decides, intensity only sets rate. Error: line spectra blamed on heat alone. Correction: discrete levels give lines. Error: electron mass used in photon formula. Correction: photons use hf, electrons use h/p.

title: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Scatter Diagrams and Correlation
content:
Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Scatter Diagrams and Correlation

A scatter diagram plots two measurements for each person or object, one on each axis, and reveals whether they move together. The IGCSE questions ask you to describe that relationship — correlation — draw a line of best fit, and use it to estimate. The arithmetic is light; the marks come from precise language and from the discipline of drawing and reading the line correctly. This note builds the topic from zero: what correlation means and how to describe it, how to draw a line of best fit that earns the marks, how to use it for interpolation and extrapolation, and why correlation is not causation.

What a scatter diagram shows

Each point represents one individual: its horizontal coordinate is one variable (say, hours of revision) and its vertical coordinate the other (say, test score). The pattern of points — the scatter — is the data's message. Bivariate data means two variables measured on the same individuals; the diagram is the quickest way to see whether a relationship exists.

  • Positive correlation: as one variable increases, the other tends to increase (revision time and score).
  • Negative correlation: as one increases, the other tends to decrease (car age and value).
  • No correlation: no pattern — the points form a cloud (shoe size and score).
  • Strength: strong correlation means the points lie close to a line; weak means they are widely scattered around it.

Describing correlation precisely

The mark scheme wants three things in a description: direction (positive or negative), strength (strong, moderate or weak), and the variables named. "There is a strong positive correlation between hours of revision and test score" earns the mark; "the graph goes up" does not.

Worked example. A scatter diagram of 30 cars shows points tightly clustered around a line falling from top-left to bottom-right. Describe the correlation and interpret it.

Strong negative correlation between age and value:
older cars tend to be worth less. The tightness of the
cluster means the relationship is consistent, but individual
cars can still deviate (condition, mileage).

Drawing the line of best fit

A line of best fit summarises the trend. The marks are awarded for a straight line that:

  1. Passes through the middle of the cloud — roughly equal numbers of points above and below.
  2. Follows the trend direction (rising for positive, falling for negative correlation).
  3. Is drawn with a ruler and extends across the plotted range.

A useful anchor: the line should pass close to the mean point (the mean of the x-values, mean of the y-values). It does not have to pass through the origin, and it should not be forced through any single point.

Worked example. Points cluster with mean x = 12 and mean y = 60, trending upward. Describe where the line of best fit should pass and how to check it.

The line should pass through (12, 60) and follow the upward
trend; check by counting points above and below - roughly equal
numbers on each side, with the line through the middle of the
vertical spread at each x.

Using the line: interpolation and extrapolation

Once the line is drawn, estimates are read from it — not from individual points:

  • Interpolation: estimating within the range of the data. Reliable, because the trend is supported by nearby points.
  • Extrapolation: estimating beyond the plotted range. Risky, because nothing guarantees the relationship continues — a straight line cannot describe a curve that turns.

Worked example. A line of best fit passes through (4, 30) and (10, 54). Estimate y when x = 7, and comment on estimating y when x = 30.

gradient = (54 - 30)/(10 - 4) = 24/6 = 4
equation: y = 4x + c; using (4, 30): 30 = 16 + c → c = 14
y = 4x + 14
at x = 7: y = 28 + 14 = 42  (interpolation - reliable)
at x = 30: y = 134 (extrapolation - unreliable; the trend may
not continue that far)

Worked example: from table to diagram to estimate

Data: hours studied (x): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6; marks (y): 35, 42, 50, 55, 63, 70.

Step 1: plot each pair as a point (x horizontal, y vertical).
Step 2: describe - strong positive correlation.
Step 3: draw the line through the middle: the points rise
        about 7 marks per hour; a line from (1, 35) to (6, 70)
        passes through the centre of the cloud.
Step 4: estimate the mark for 3.5 hours: read up from x = 3.5
        to the line, then across: about 53 marks.
Step 5: estimate the hours for 60 marks: read across from y = 60
        to the line, then down: about 4.6 hours.

Note the wording in answers: "from the line of best fit, approximately 53 marks" — the word approximately signals that it is an estimate, which the mark scheme expects.

Correlation and causation

Correlation does not prove cause. Two variables can move together because a third factor drives both (ice-cream sales and drowning rates both rise in summer — heat causes both), or by coincidence in a small sample. Exam questions reward this caution explicitly: state that the correlation shows an association, not that one variable causes the other, unless the data come from a controlled experiment.

Worked example. A study finds a strong positive correlation between the number of books in a home and children's reading scores. Does buying books raise scores?

Not necessarily: households with more books may also have more
educated parents, more time for reading, or higher income - all
of which could raise scores. The correlation is real, but the
causal claim is unsupported by this evidence alone.

A second discipline follows: when a question asks you to comment on a study, name the possible confounding variable rather than simply denying causation. In the books example, income, parental education and available time are all plausible common causes; naming one shows the examiner you understand what a confounding factor is. The same reasoning explains why a strong correlation from a small sample deserves caution: with only a handful of points, a pattern can appear by chance, and a single outlier can create or destroy the apparent trend.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Describe) Points on a scatter diagram trend downward and are tightly clustered. Describe the correlation. Answer: Strong negative correlation — as one variable increases, the other tends to decrease consistently.
  2. (No correlation) Describe a scatter diagram whose points form a random cloud. Answer: No correlation — there is no clear trend between the variables.
  3. (Line) State two features of a correctly drawn line of best fit. Answer: A straight line through the middle of the points with roughly equal numbers above and below, following the trend and drawn with a ruler.
  4. (Estimate) A line of best fit passes through (2, 10) and (6, 26). Estimate y at x = 4. Answer: gradient 4; y = 4x + 2; at x = 4, y = 18.
  5. (Interpolation) Explain why an estimate inside the data range is more reliable than one outside it. Answer: Inside the range the trend is supported by nearby data points (interpolation); outside it (extrapolation) there is no evidence that the relationship continues in the same way.
  6. (Causation) A shop finds that sales of umbrellas and sales of coats rise together. Explain the correlation without claiming that umbrellas cause coat sales. Answer: Both are driven by a third variable — rainy weather — which increases demand for both; the correlation is association, not causation.
  7. (Outlier) One point sits far from the trend. What should you do with it when drawing the line? Answer: Note it as an outlier and draw the line through the main body of points; do not let one point pull the line away from the trend.
  8. (Strength) Two scatter diagrams both show positive correlation; in one the points are close to the line. Compare them. Answer: The tighter diagram shows stronger positive correlation; the looser one shows weaker positive correlation.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Joining the dots: a line of best fit is a single straight line through the trend, never a zigzag connecting points.
  • Forcing through the origin: the line passes through the middle of the cloud; there is no reason for it to start at (0, 0).
  • Reading a point instead of the line: estimates come from the line of best fit, not from the nearest plotted point.
  • Ignoring outliers: one extreme point should not swing the line; note it and fit the main cluster.
  • Weak description: "positive" alone is incomplete — direction and strength, with variables named.
  • Causal language: "revision causes higher scores" overclaims from observational data; write "is associated with" and mention confounding factors.
  • Extrapolating confidently: beyond the data range, state the estimate is unreliable.
  • Axes: plot the explanatory variable on the horizontal axis and the response on the vertical, label both with units, and use the given scales exactly.

Plotting the points: axes, scales and accuracy

A scatter diagram shows two variables plotted against each other, one point for each pair of values. Most of the marks for a plotting question come from setting the axes up correctly and placing each point accurately, so the subsections below take the process one step at a time.

Choosing which variable goes on which axis

The variable that is being explained or predicted goes on the vertical axis, and the variable that does the explaining goes on the horizontal axis. If a question gives a table of hours of revision and test scores, hours go on the x-axis and scores on the y-axis. Check the wording of the question, because an examiner may ask you to read a value from one axis to predict a value on the other.

Choosing a sensible scale

The scale on each axis should spread the data over at least half of the grid in both directions. Use equal steps of 1, 2, 5 or 10 units, and do not start an axis at a value that wastes most of the grid. If the values run from 42 to 58, the axis can start at 40 rather than at 0, provided the axis is labelled clearly so the reader sees that it does not start at zero.

Labelling the axes with name and unit

Each axis needs the name of the quantity and its unit, for example "Mass (kg)" or "Time (minutes)". A diagram without labels or units loses the presentation mark even when every point is correct. Write the scale numbers evenly spaced and make the labels readable, because an unreadable scale makes an estimate from the graph unreliable.

Plotting each point accurately

Plot each pair (x, y) by moving across to x and then up to y, and mark the point with a small neat cross or dot. A point plotted at (3, 7) must sit three units along the horizontal axis and seven units up, not one unit off in either direction. Check the table again after plotting, because a single misread value shows up as a point far away from the rest of the cloud.

Checking the number of points

Count the points on the diagram and compare with the number of rows in the table. A missing point is the most common error, and a diagram with one point missing can still look like a correct pattern. Tick each row of the table as you plot it, which takes a few seconds and protects the mark.

Spotting an outlier before you draw the line

An outlier is a point that lies well away from the general pattern of the others. Identify any outlier before you decide on the trend, because a single extreme point can pull a line of best fit away from where most of the data lies. An outlier is not always an error: note it and say whether it affects the conclusion.

Using a table to check the diagram

Once the diagram is drawn, read two or three points back from the graph and check them against the table. If the graph reads 6 at a point the table lists as 9, there is a plotting mistake that would cost every later estimate. This habit is quick and it turns a plausible but wrong diagram into a checked one.

Describing correlation: strength, direction and the wording examiners expect

Correlation describes the relationship between two variables. The description has two parts, the direction and the strength, and an answer that gives only one of them earns little credit. The subsections below set out the terms in the order a mark scheme checks them.

Positive correlation

Positive correlation means that as one variable increases, the other tends to increase as well. The points rise from left to right on the diagram. Engine size and fuel consumption for cars is a common example, where larger engines tend to use more fuel. Write the description in terms of the two named quantities, not in general words.

Negative correlation

Negative correlation means that as one variable increases, the other tends to decrease. The points fall from left to right. The age of a car and its resale value is an example of a negative relationship. A mark scheme looks for the word "negative" together with the direction of change, so write both.

No correlation

No correlation means that the points show no clear pattern, so knowing one variable does not help predict the other. The points look scattered at random across the grid. Do not say "no correlation" when the points form a loose pattern: if a trend can be seen, describe it with a strength such as weak, and say that it is weak.

Strong and weak correlation

Strong correlation means that the points lie close to a straight line. Weak correlation means that they are spread out around a trend that is still visible. The strength depends on how closely the points cluster, not on how steep the trend is. A steep line of points that are widely scattered is a weak correlation.

Linear and non-linear patterns

A correlation can be described as linear if the points follow a straight line, and the line of best fit is only appropriate for a linear pattern. A curved pattern, such as a set of points that rise and then level off, should be described as a curve, and a straight line should not be drawn through it. Recognising the shape first prevents an inappropriate line from being used for an estimate.

A complete description in one sentence

A complete answer names the two variables, the direction and the strength in one sentence: "There is a strong positive correlation between the hours of revision and the test score." This form is safe in the exam because each element can be checked against the mark scheme. Avoid saying that the points "go up" without naming what they show.

The wording that loses marks

Two phrases lose marks repeatedly. "The more the variable increases, the more the other increases" describes a relationship without stating a direction clearly, and "the points are close" does not say close to what. Replace any vague phrase with the named quantities and the direction of change, and the description becomes precise.

Equations and symbols

The arithmetic of a scatter diagram is the equation of the line of best fit, read in both directions: from the line to an estimate, and from two points back to the line. Keep the meaning of each letter in view, because the exam asks you to interpret the gradient rather than just compute it.

gradient = (54 - 30)/(10 - 4) = 24/6 = 4 Key: 54 and 30 are the y-values of two points on the line; 10 and 4 the matching x-values; the gradient is the change in the vertical variable per unit of the horizontal one, so here the response rises 4 for every 1 of the explanatory variable.

y = 4x + c Key: y = the predicted value on the vertical axis; x = the explanatory variable on the horizontal axis; 4 = the gradient just calculated; c = the intercept, still unknown. Substitute one point to find c.

30 = 16 + c → c = 14 Key: substituting the point (4, 30) into y = 4x + c gives 16 + c = 30, so c = 14. The intercept is where the line would cross x = 0 — meaningful only if x = 0 is inside the data.

y = 4x + 14 Key: the finished line of best fit; use it for every estimate, never the plotted points themselves. From the line, x = 7 gives y = 42 — an interpolation, inside the data range, so reliable.

y = 28 + 14 = 42 Key: the same estimate written out; 28 = 4 × 7 and 14 is the intercept. Showing this line earns the method mark even if the earlier gradient was wrong.

y = 134 Key: the prediction at x = 30, far outside the plotted range. It is an extrapolation: the arithmetic is right and the estimate is unreliable, which is exactly what the question wants you to say.

The language that earns the marks. Name the direction and the strength and the two variables — "strong positive correlation between hours of revision and test score" — and say "approximately" for any value read from the line. Correlation is association, not causation: name the third variable that could drive both.

title: IGCSE Biology: Organisation of the Organism
content:
IGCSE Biology: Organisation of the Organism

Every living thing you will ever meet — from a single bacterium to a blue whale — is built from cells, and this note starts where all biology starts: at the microscope. We begin with the idea that the cell is the smallest unit that can still be called alive, then map the structures inside animal and plant cells, explain what each one actually does, and finish with the specimen-size calculations that Paper 6 loves. Nothing here assumes prior knowledge; each structure is introduced with a physical analogy before the formal term, and every calculation is expanded line by line so you can follow it with no chemistry or maths background at all.

What a cell is, and why it is the unit of life

A cell is the smallest structure that carries out all seven life processes: movement, respiration, sensitivity, growth, reproduction, excretion and nutrition (the mnemonic MRS GREN). A brick is not alive; a single white blood cell is, because it does all seven. Two organisational levels follow. Unicellular organisms (bacteria, Amoeba, yeast) are one cell doing everything. Multicellular organisms (you, an oak tree) are communities of cells that specialise, so the body shows three levels of organisation: cells group into tissues (one job, like muscle tissue), tissues into organs (the stomach), and organs into organ systems (the digestive system).

Cell specialisation means a cell's structure fits its function like a tool fits a job. A red blood cell is a flat biconcave disc with no nucleus, leaving maximum room for haemoglobin. A sperm cell carries a long tail (flagellum) and a packed mitochondria cluster for swimming. A root hair cell pushes out one long extension to maximise surface area for absorption. A palisade cell packs its top half with chloroplasts to catch light. When asked to explain a specialised cell, always write it as: feature, then what the feature does, then why the job needs it.

Animal cell structure

Think of a cell as a factory. The cell membrane is the security door: a thin, selectively permeable layer of lipid and protein that decides what enters and leaves. The cytoplasm is the factory floor: a jelly-like solution of water, salts and enzymes where most reactions happen. The nucleus is the manager's office: it contains genetic material (DNA) and controls the cell's activities by regulating which proteins are made. Mitochondria are the power stations: rod-shaped organelles where aerobic respiration releases energy from glucose. Ribosomes are the assembly lines: tiny structures where proteins are assembled from amino acids. The cytoplasm and cell membrane together carry out most of the life processes; the nucleus stores and passes on genetic information.

Plant cell structure — the three additions

A plant cell has everything an animal cell has, plus three structures an exam will always want named. The cell wall is a rigid layer of cellulose outside the membrane: it gives mechanical strength and stops the cell bursting when water enters. Chloroplasts are the solar panels: they contain the green pigment chlorophyll and are the site of photosynthesis. The permanent vacuole is a storage tank: a large sac of cell sap (dilute sugars, salts and acids) that keeps the cell turgid, pressing the cytoplasm against the wall so leaves stay firm. Learn the comparison as a table — it is the single most reliable three-mark question in Paper 4.

StructureAnimal cellPlant cellJob
Cell membranePresentPresentControls what enters and leaves
Cell wallAbsentPresent (cellulose)Strength and support; prevents bursting
ChloroplastsAbsentPresent (palisade, spongy mesophyll)Photosynthesis in chlorophyll
Permanent vacuoleSmall, temporaryLarge, permanent, cell sapTurgor, storage
NucleusPresentPresentControls activities; stores DNA
MitochondriaPresentPresentAerobic respiration, releases energy
RibosomesPresentPresentProtein synthesis

Bacterial cells: the prokaryote difference

Bacteria are prokaryotes — cells with no nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles. Their DNA is a single circular chromosome free in the cytoplasm, often with small extra rings called plasmids. They have a cell wall (not cellulose — it is murein), a cell membrane, cytoplasm and ribosomes (smaller than eukaryotic ones), and many have a flagellum for swimming and a capsule for protection. The exam answer to "give two differences between a bacterium and a plant cell" is: no nucleus in the bacterium (DNA free in cytoplasm) and no chloroplasts or mitochondria (respiration at the membrane).

Microscopy and magnification

An optical (light) microscope uses glass lenses and visible light; specimens can be living or dead and are often stained (methyl blue for nuclei, iodine for starch) to add contrast. An electron microscope uses a beam of electrons, giving far higher magnification and resolution so organelles such as mitochondria, ribosomes, lysosomes and the endoplasmic reticulum can be seen — but specimens must be dead and in a vacuum. Magnification is how many times larger the image is than the real object; resolution is the minimum distance between two points still seen as separate — a blurry zoomed image has magnification without resolution. The three calculations you must know are written below, and the worked example expands each one.

Size of specimens — the three equations

Equation 1, magnification: magnification = size of image divided by size of real object. Equation 2, real size: real size = image size divided by magnification. Equation 3, image size: image size = real size × magnification. The golden rule of units: convert everything to the same unit before dividing. 1 millimetre (mm) = 1000 micrometres (µm); 1 µm = 1000 nanometres (nm). A common exam device is a scale bar drawn under an image: measure the bar in millimetres with a ruler, note the length it claims to represent in µm, and the magnification is bar length (in µm) ÷ claimed length (in µm). Drawing magnification for Paper 6 is measured the same way: magnification = drawing width (mm) ÷ real width (mm), with the real width first converted from µm by dividing by 1000.

Worked example: specimen size from first principles

An image of a plant cell is 40 mm long in a textbook, and the real cell is 80 µm long. Calculate the magnification. Step 1: write the equation: magnification = image size ÷ real size. Step 2: list what you have: image = 40 mm, real = 80 µm. Step 3: convert to one unit — 40 mm = 40 × 1000 = 40 000 µm. Step 4: divide: 40 000 ÷ 80 = 500. Step 5: write the answer with its × symbol: magnification = ×500. Now the reverse direction. A cell is 12 µm wide and you draw it at ×1500. Step 1: image size = real size × magnification. Step 2: 12 µm × 1500 = 18 000 µm. Step 3: convert to a workable unit: 18 000 ÷ 1000 = 18 mm. Your drawing must be 18 mm wide — measure it with a ruler in the practical. Finally, a bacterium appears 35 mm long in a micrograph at ×20 000. Step 1: real size = 35 mm ÷ 20 000 = 0.00175 mm. Step 2: convert: 0.00175 mm × 1000 = 1.75 µm. Step 3: state the answer: 1.75 µm, which is a sensible bacterium size.

Exam technique: command words and drawing rules

"State" wants one short fact; "describe" wants what you see in a diagram or graph (no reasons); "explain" wants the mechanism with because. For drawings: use clean, unbroken pencil lines with no shading; the drawing should be at least 6 cm wide for a decent magnification; label lines are straight, horizontal, do not cross, and touch the structure named; labels name the structure (write "mitochondrion", not "the power station"). When asked for differences between two diagrams (typical Paper 6), compare like with like: "the plant cell has a cell wall, the animal cell does not" is two marks in one line.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Calling the cell wall "membrane": the membrane is inside the wall; mixing them loses the mark.
  • Writing "chloroplast" on an animal cell diagram — animals have mitochondria, never chloroplasts.
  • Forgetting units after converting: 40 mm ÷ 80 µm is wrong until both are µm; always show the conversion line.
  • Saying magnification and resolution are the same thing; they are different, and Paper 4 has asked for the distinction outright.
  • Shading a drawing or using a ruler-free squiggle: both are explicitly penalised in Paper 6 mark schemes.
  • Label lines crossing each other or drawn as arrows; a line that does not touch the structure scores zero.
  • Writing "cytoplasm" when you mean "cytosol" or vice versa is safe at IGCSE — use "cytoplasm" — but never write "cell sap" for cytoplasm; cell sap is only inside the vacuole.

Exam-style questions and answers

Q1. State two structures found in a plant cell but not in an animal cell. (2 marks) Answer: cell wall (cellulose) and chloroplasts — one mark each; the permanent vacuole is also accepted but do not list more than the question asks.

Q2. A cell is drawn 60 mm wide. The real cell is 150 µm wide. Calculate the magnification and show your working. (3 marks) Answer: 60 mm = 60 000 µm (1); magnification = 60 000 ÷ 150 (1); = ×400 (1).

Q3. Explain why root hair cells are specialised for absorption. (2 marks) Answer: they have a long extension that increases surface area (1), so more water and mineral ions can be absorbed per unit time by diffusion and active transport (1).

Q4. Describe how you would prepare a slide of onion cells for viewing. (4 marks) Answer: peel a thin transparent layer of epidermis (1); place it flat in a drop of water on a slide (1); add a coverslip at an angle without trapping air bubbles (1); view at low power then focus with the fine adjustment (1).

Q5. Explain why the electron microscope was needed to discover ribosomes. (2 marks) Answer: ribosomes are very small (around 20 nm) so need much higher resolution than the light microscope provides (1); the electron microscope's shorter wavelength of electrons gives that resolution (1).

Equations and symbols

The magnification triangle in words, the unit ladder, and the two direction-of-use forms. Paper 6 gives you two of the three quantities and marks the conversion line as much as the arithmetic.

magnification = size of image divided by size of real object Key: magnification = how many times larger the image is (×, no unit); size of image = length measured on the drawing or micrograph (mm); size of real object = the true length of the specimen (µm). Both lengths must be in the same unit before dividing.

real size = image size divided by magnification Key: real size = the specimen's true length (µm or mm, whichever the question asks for); image size = the measured length on the page; magnification = the × value printed on the micrograph. This is the rearrangement used when the micrograph gives ×20 000 and you must name the organelle.

image size = real size × magnification Key: image size = the length your drawing must be (convert to mm for a ruler); real size = the specimen's true length; magnification = the required drawing magnification. A draw-at-×1500 instruction is this line and a conversion, nothing more.

magnification = drawing width (mm) ÷ real width (mm) Key: drawing width = your own pencil drawing, measured with a ruler (mm); real width = the specimen's true width (mm, so divide a µm value by 1000 first). This is the form that earns the "calculate the magnification of your drawing" mark.

1 millimetre (mm) = 1000 micrometres (µm) Key: the first step of the unit ladder; multiply by 1000 to go down, divide by 1000 to go up. A 40 mm image is 40 × 1000 = 40 000 µm, and only then may it be divided by a real size in µm.

1 µm = 1000 nanometres (nm) Key: the second rung, used for organelles: a ribosome at 20 nm is 0.02 µm, which is why a light microscope cannot resolve it. Writing a bacterium's size in nm when the question asked for µm is the commonest unit slip on this topic.

title: Chemical Equilibria A2 Level Chemistry Revision Notes
content:
Chemical Equilibria A2 Level Chemistry Revision Notes

This revision note belongs to Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH14, Topic 13 Chemical Equilibria, covering homogeneous and heterogeneous systems, equilibrium constants Kc and Kp, the factors affecting equilibrium composition and constant values, total entropy links, and reaction extent predictions.

Expressions for Kc in Homogeneous and Heterogeneous Systems

When a reversible reaction takes place in a closed system, it eventually reaches a dynamic equilibrium where the rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction, and the concentrations of reactants and products remain constant. The equilibrium constant Kc allows you to deduce the position of equilibrium quantitatively.

  • Be able to deduce an expression for Kc, for homogeneous and heterogeneous systems, in terms of equilibrium concentrations.
  • For a general homogeneous system where all species are in the same phase, such as aA + bB reversible cC + dD, the expression is Kc = [C]^c [D]^d / ([A]^a [B]^b), where square brackets denote equilibrium concentrations in mol dm⁻³.
  • For heterogeneous systems containing species in different phases, pure solids and pure liquids are omitted from the Kc expression because their concentrations remain essentially constant throughout the reaction. For example, for the decomposition of calcium carbonate, CaCO3(s) reversible CaO(s) + CO2(g), the expression is simply Kc = [CO2].

Expressions for Kp in Homogeneous and Heterogeneous Systems

For systems involving gases, it is often more convenient to use partial pressures rather than concentrations to define the equilibrium position.

  • Be able to deduce an expression for Kp for homogeneous and heterogeneous systems, in terms of equilibrium partial pressures in atm.
  • The mole fraction of a gas in a mixture is calculated as the number of moles of that individual gas divided by the total number of moles of all gases present in the mixture.
  • The partial pressure of an individual gas is its mole fraction multiplied by the total pressure of the gas system, measured in units of atmospheres or atm.
  • For a homogeneous gas phase reaction such as N2O4(g) reversible 2NO2(g), the partial pressure expression is Kp = p(NO2)² / p(N2O4).
  • For a heterogeneous gas-solid equilibrium such as C(s) + CO2(g) reversible 2CO(g), pure solid carbon is omitted from the expression, giving Kp = p(CO)² / p(CO2).

Calculating Equilibrium Constants from Experimental Data

Calculations involving Kc and Kp require systematic tracking of initial moles, change in moles, and equilibrium moles, converting them to concentrations or partial pressures.

  • Be able to calculate a value, with units where appropriate, for the equilibrium constants Kc and Kp for homogeneous and heterogeneous reactions, from experimental data.
  • For Kc calculations, divide equilibrium moles by the total volume in dm³ to find equilibrium concentrations, substitute into the Kc formula, and cancel out units or combine them using indices such as mol⁻² dm⁶.
  • For Kp calculations, find total moles at equilibrium, determine mole fractions for each gas, multiply by total pressure to find partial pressures in atm, substitute into Kp, and derive units like atm or atm².

Worked Example for Kc Calculation

For H2 + I2 reversible 2HI, suppose 1.00 mol of hydrogen and 1.00 mol of iodine are heated in a 2.00 dm³ flask. At equilibrium, 1.60 mol of hydrogen iodide has formed.

  • Step 1: Set up an ICE table. Initial moles: H2 = 1.00, I2 = 1.00, HI = 0.00.
  • Step 2: Equilibrium moles: HI = 1.60. Since stoichiometry shows 2 mol of HI form, 0.80 mol of H2 and 0.80 mol of I2 must have reacted.
  • Step 3: Calculate remaining equilibrium moles: H2 = 1.00 − 0.80 = 0.20 mol; I2 = 1.00 − 0.80 = 0.20 mol.
  • Step 4: Convert to concentrations by dividing by the volume of 2.00 dm³: [HI] = 1.60 ÷ 2.00 = 0.80 mol dm⁻³, [H2] = 0.20 ÷ 2.00 = 0.10 mol dm⁻³, [I2] = 0.20 ÷ 2.00 = 0.10 mol dm⁻³.
  • Step 5: Substitute into Kc expression: Kc = [HI]² / ([H2] × [I2]) = 0.80² / (0.10 × 0.10) = 0.64 / 0.01 = 64. The units cancel out entirely because the number of moles of reactants equals the number of moles of products.

Effects of Changes on Equilibrium Composition

Le Chatelier's principle helps predict how a system responds to external stresses, altering equilibrium composition without changing the constant itself unless temperature changes.

  • Understand how, if at all, a change in temperature, pressure or the presence of a catalyst affects the equilibrium composition in a homogeneous or heterogeneous system.
  • Adding reactant or removing product shifts the position towards the products. Adding product shifts it towards the reactants.
  • Increasing pressure or decreasing volume favours the side of the reaction with fewer gas molecules. Changing the volume has the same effect as changing pressure.
  • Raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium in the endothermic direction. Lowering the temperature shifts it in the exothermic direction.
  • A catalyst changes the rate at which equilibrium is reached by providing an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy, but it has no effect on the equilibrium position or composition.

Independence of Equilibrium Constants from Concentration and Pressure

While altering conditions shifts the position of equilibrium, the underlying constant remains strictly invariant under specific conditions.

  • Understand that the value of the equilibrium constant is not affected by changes in concentration or pressure or by the addition of a catalyst.
  • A change in concentration or pressure shifts the equilibrium composition to counteract the change, but the ratio of products to reactants at the new equilibrium exactly equals the original Kc or Kp value.
  • A catalyst speeds up both the forward and reverse rates equally, leaving the equilibrium constant completely unchanged.

Effect of Temperature on Equilibrium Constants

Temperature is unique because it alters the actual value of the equilibrium constant Kc and Kp, reflecting a change in the position of equilibrium.

  • Know the effect of changing the temperature on the equilibrium constant Kc and Kp for both exothermic and endothermic reactions.
  • Understand that the effect of temperature on the position of equilibrium is explained using a change in the value of the equilibrium constant.
  • For an exothermic forward reaction, raising the temperature decreases the value of Kc and Kp, as the equilibrium shifts to the left. Lowering the temperature increases Kc and Kp.
  • For an endothermic forward reaction, raising the temperature increases the value of Kc and Kp, as the equilibrium shifts to the right. Lowering the temperature decreases Kc and Kp.

Entropy, Total Entropy, and Equilibrium Constants

Thermodynamics links the position of equilibrium to total entropy change and the magnitude of the equilibrium constant.

  • Understand the effect of a change in temperature on the value of Stotal and the magnitude of the equilibrium constant, since Stotal = R ln K.
  • The equation Stotal = R ln K bridges kinetics, equilibrium, and thermodynamics, where R is the universal gas constant and ln K is the natural logarithm of the equilibrium constant.
  • When temperature changes, it alters Stotal, which in turn directly alters the magnitude of K. A larger positive Stotal corresponds to a much larger equilibrium constant, meaning the reaction goes virtually to completion.

Predicting the Extent of Reaction

The numerical value of an equilibrium constant gives immediate insight into whether a reaction proceeds far towards products or stays mostly as reactants.

  • Be able to apply knowledge of the value of equilibrium constants to predict the extent to which a reaction takes place.
  • When an equilibrium constant value is very large, greater than 10 to the power of 10, the numerator is vastly larger than the denominator, indicating that the reaction goes essentially to completion with very few reactants remaining.
  • When an equilibrium constant value is very small, less than 10 to the power of minus 10, the denominator dominates, indicating that virtually no reaction takes place and the system remains almost entirely as reactants.
  • When an equilibrium constant is around 1, significant amounts of both reactants and products are present at equilibrium.

Typical mistakes

  • Mistake: Including pure solids or pure liquids in Kc or Kp expressions. Correction: Omit pure solids and pure liquids because their active masses do not change.
  • Mistake: Forgetting to divide equilibrium moles by volume when calculating Kc. Correction: Always divide moles by the volume in dm³ to obtain concentration values before substituting into Kc.
  • Mistake: Believing that increasing pressure changes the value of Kc. Correction: Pressure changes the position of equilibrium and shifts concentrations, but Kc remains constant at a fixed temperature.
  • Mistake: Using mass in grams instead of mole fractions or partial pressures for Kp calculations. Correction: Always convert mass to moles, find mole fractions, and multiply by total pressure in atm.

Exam-style questions

  1. Write the expression for Kc for the heterogeneous reaction C(s) + H2O(g) reversible CO(g) + H2(g).

    Answer: Kc = [CO] [H2] / [H2O]. Solid carbon is omitted.

  2. State and explain the effect of increasing the temperature on the value of Kc for an endothermic forward reaction.

    Answer: Kc increases. Raising temperature favours the endothermic direction, increasing product concentrations and decreasing reactant concentrations, raising the numerator of Kc.

  3. Calculate the units of Kp for the equilibrium N2(g) + 3H2(g) reversible 2NH3(g) when pressure is measured in atm.

    Answer: Kp = p(NH3)² / (p(N2) × p(H2)³). Units are atm² / (atm × atm³) = atm⁻².

  4. Explain why a catalyst has no effect on the numerical value of Kc.

    Answer: A catalyst speeds up the forward and reverse rates equally by lowering the activation energy, leaving the equilibrium constant ratio unchanged.

  5. Explain what a Kc value of 10 to the power of 15 indicates about the extent of a reaction.

    Answer: The reaction goes almost entirely to completion, with the equilibrium position lying far to the right.

Use these revision notes to test your understanding of equilibrium expressions, unit derivations, and thermodynamic links via Stotal. Next, revise reaction kinetics and acid-base equilibria.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Kc expression, applied to H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g): Kc = [HI]² ÷ ([H₂][I₂]). The units depend on the equation, here none, because the moles cancel. Write the units only when they do not cancel, and state the units explicitly when you give Kc.
  • Kp, applied to N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃: partial pressure of a gas = mole fraction × total pressure. Kp = p(NH₃)² ÷ (p(N₂) × p(H₂)³), and its units are Pa⁻² here. Give the units with Kp, because the pressures do not cancel.
  • Le Chatelier and Kc, applied to an exothermic reaction: raising the temperature moves the equilibrium to the left and decreases Kc. Adding a catalyst does not change Kc, because it speeds up the forward and backward reactions equally. Adding more reactant changes the position but not Kc.
  • Pressure effects: for N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, four gas molecules become two, so higher pressure favours the product. The equilibrium moves to the side with fewer gas molecules, and Kp stays the same at a fixed temperature.

title: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Sets and Venn Diagrams
content:
Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Sets and Venn Diagrams

Set notation is the language of sorting: it describes which elements belong together, which belong to both groups, and which belong to neither. The IGCSE questions are almost always Venn-diagram problems in disguise — a survey of students, a group of numbers, a club membership — and the marks come from filling every region correctly. This note builds the topic from zero: the notation and symbols, the two-set and three-set Venn diagrams and how to shade them, the counting formulas, and the word-problem method that never misses a region.

Set notation and vocabulary

SymbolMeaningExample
∈is an element of3 ∈ {1, 2, 3}
∉is not an element of5 ∉ {1, 2, 3}
ξ (or U)the universal set — everything under discussionξ = {1, 2, ..., 12}
∅the empty setodd multiples of 2 = ∅
A′the complement of A — everything in ξ not in AA′ = ξ A
A ∪ Bunion — in A or B or both{1,2} ∪ {2,3} = {1,2,3}
A ∩ Bintersection — in both{1,2} ∩ {2,3} = {2}
n(A)the number of elements of An({2, 4, 6}) = 3

Two rules follow directly: A ∩ A′ = ∅ (nothing is both in and out), and A ∪ A′ = ξ (everything is one or the other). Subsets: A ⊂ B means every element of A is also in B. The empty set has no elements, so n(∅) = 0, and it is a subset of every set — a fact worth stating explicitly when a question asks whether ∅ ⊂ A is true.

Two-set Venn diagrams

A two-set diagram divides the universal set into four regions: only A, only B, both, and neither. Filling them from the inside out is the reliable method:

  1. Write the number in the intersection (both) first.
