title: Circular Motion and SHM — Study Notes
content:
Circular Motion and SHM

Edexcel International A Level Physics, A2: circular motion in Unit 4 (WPH14) and simple harmonic motion in Unit 5 (WPH15).

Uniform circular motion

A particle moving in a circle of radius r at constant speed has a constantly changing velocity, because its direction changes. Angular speed ω is the rate of change of angle in radians per second: ω = 2π/T = 2πf. The linear speed is v = ωr.

Centripetal acceleration and force

The acceleration is directed towards the centre: a = v²/r = ω²r. The resultant force providing it is F = mv²/r = mω²r, also towards the centre. This force does no work, because it is always perpendicular to the velocity, so the kinetic energy stays constant.

Example: a particle on a 0.40 m radius with T = 2.0 s has ω = π rad s⁻¹, v = 1.26 m s⁻¹ and a = π² × 0.40 ≈ 3.9 m s⁻².

Simple harmonic motion as projected circular motion

The displacement of a point moving on a circle, projected onto a diameter, is x = x₀ sin ωt (or cos ωt). Its acceleration is a = −ω²x, always opposite to the displacement, so the defining condition for SHM is that acceleration is proportional to and opposite to displacement.

Solutions: x = x₀ sin ωt starts at the centre; x = x₀ cos ωt starts at an extreme. Time period T = 2π/ω.

Velocity and acceleration:

  • v = ±ω√(x₀² − x²); v_max = ωx₀ at the centre
  • a_max = ω²x₀ at the extremes; a = 0 at the centre

Example: a pendulum with x₀ = 0.02 m and f = 0.5 Hz has a_max = (2π × 0.5)² × 0.02 ≈ 0.20 m s⁻².

Energy in SHM

The total energy is E = ½mω²x₀², constant. It is exchanged between kinetic energy (maximum at the centre) and potential energy (maximum at the extremes). Kinetic energy is at a maximum when displacement is zero, not when acceleration is largest.

Damping and resonance

Damping removes energy from the oscillator. Light damping gives slow decay of amplitude; critical damping returns the system to equilibrium in the shortest time without oscillating; heavy damping is slower still. A system driven at its natural frequency resonates, giving maximum amplitude (playground swings, microwave ovens, bridges that must avoid the wind frequency).

Exam tips: quote a = −ω²x as the defining condition in SHM questions. Time-period questions often need only T = 2π/ω. State which energy is at a maximum and where.

Worked example: a mass on a string

A 0.50 kg mass on a string of length 0.80 m moves in a horizontal circle at 4.0 m/s. The tension supplies the centripetal force, so T = mv²/r = 0.50 × 4.0² / 0.80 = 10 N. If the same mass is swung in a vertical circle, the tension is least at the top. The minimum speed at the top occurs when the tension falls to zero, giving v = √(gr). Here that is √(9.8 × 0.80) ≈ 2.8 m/s. Below this speed the string goes slack and the mass no longer follows the circle.

Exam method: SHM equations

Use x = A sin(ωt) or x = A cos(ωt), depending on the point at which timing starts. The maximum speed is v₀ = Aω and the maximum acceleration is a₀ = Aω². Use ω = 2π/T, and convert any frequency in hertz by multiplying by 2π before you substitute, because ω is in radians per second. For a simple pendulum at small angles, the period is T = 2π√(L/g) and does not depend on the amplitude.

title: Prepositions and Collocations — Study Notes
content:
Prepositions (in, on, at, for, of) and collocations (words that naturally go together) are not always logical, so they are best learned in phrases rather than one word at a time.

Time prepositions

  • At: a clock time or a specific moment (at 10 a.m., at night).
  • On: a day or a date (on Monday, on 5 May).
  • In: a month, a year or a longer period (in June, in 2020).

Example: The meeting is on Monday at 10 a.m.

Prepositions after adjectives and verbs

Many adjectives and verbs take a fixed preposition:

  • interested in
  • good at
  • depend on
  • listen to
  • belong to

Learn these as complete phrases.

Collocations

Collocations are common word pairings. Learn the verb that goes with the noun:

  • make a decision, make an effort, make a mistake
  • do homework, do the washing, do research
  • take a break, take a photo, take part

Using make where do is needed, or the reverse, is one of the most common errors for learners.

Strategy

  • Keep a notebook of phrases, not single words.
  • Record the preposition or verb with each noun or adjective.
  • Read widely and notice which words appear together in good writing.

title: AS Level Physics: Kinematics
content:
AS Level Physics: Kinematics

Edexcel International A Level Physics, Unit 1 (WPH11) Mechanics and Materials — motion in a straight line and in a plane, and the measurement skills the companion Unit 3 paper (WPH13, Practical Skills in Physics I) examines. Everything in mechanics starts here: quantities with units and directions, the equations of motion, free fall, projectiles and the graphs that describe them. The unit also demands real data-handling skill — uncertainties, error bars, gradients and intercepts — because WPH13 is a written paper that marks your experimental thinking, not your hands.

Quantities, units, scalars and vectors

A physical quantity is a number with a unit, and every unit in mechanics is built from four SI base units: the metre (m), kilogram (kg), second (s) and ampere (A). Speed in m s⁻¹ and force in newtons (1 N = 1 kg m s⁻²) are derived from them. A scalar has size only — distance, speed, mass, time, energy, power. A vector has size and direction — displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, momentum. The distinction is operational, not decorative: vectors add by direction, and every mechanics question that mentions direction is testing it.

  • Two vectors in a line: add if in the same direction, subtract if opposite, and state the direction of the resultant.
  • Two vectors at right angles: the resultant is the hypotenuse, R = √(A² + B²), at an angle θ = tan⁻¹(B/A) to A.
  • Any two vectors: resolve each into perpendicular components with A cos θ and A sin θ, add the components separately, then recombine.

Resolution is the workhorse of A-level mechanics. A force F at angle θ to the horizontal has a horizontal component F cos θ along the motion and a vertical component F sin θ across it; only the component along the motion changes the motion. Sign convention is chosen, not given: for vertical motion taking up as positive makes g = −9.81 m s⁻²; for slopes, taking down the slope as positive is usually simplest.

Motion in a straight line

Uniform motion means constant velocity; accelerated motion means changing velocity. The five quantities in every equation of motion are: displacement s (m), initial velocity u (m s⁻¹), final velocity v (m s⁻¹), acceleration a (m s⁻²), and time t (s). Average velocity is (u + v)/2 only when the acceleration is constant.

QuantityDefinitionUnitScalar or vector
DisplacementDistance from a start point in a stated directionmVector
VelocityRate of change of displacementm s⁻¹Vector
AccelerationRate of change of velocitym s⁻²Vector
SpeedDistance travelled per unit timem s⁻¹Scalar

The equations of motion

For motion with constant acceleration, four equations connect the five quantities. They are valid only while a is constant, and they are all vector equations, so the sign convention must be applied to u, v, a and s consistently.

v = u + a t
s = u t + 1/2 a t²
v² = u² + 2 a s
s = 1/2 (u + v) t
  • Each equation omits one quantity: pick the equation that does not contain the unknown you do not need.
  • Units must be SI before substituting: kilometres to metres, minutes to seconds, km h⁻¹ to m s⁻¹ (divide by 3.6).
  • Direction convention: write one down before touching the algebra — for example, upward positive means a falling object has a = −9.81 m s⁻² and a downward displacement is negative.

Free fall and projectile motion

Free fall is motion under gravity alone. Near the Earth's surface the acceleration is g = 9.81 m s⁻² downwards and is constant (air resistance neglected), so the equations of motion apply directly. An object thrown straight up decelerates at 9.81 m s⁻², stops instantaneously at the top, and falls back with the same acceleration; the time up equals the time down from the same height.

A projectile is any object moving under gravity alone once launched. The key insight is independence of components: the horizontal motion has zero acceleration and constant velocity, while the vertical motion has constant acceleration g. Resolve the launch velocity into u cos θ horizontally and u sin θ vertically, treat the two motions separately with the equations of motion, and combine at the end. At the highest point the vertical velocity is zero but the horizontal velocity is unchanged — the projectile is never at rest. The trajectory is a parabola.

Motion graphs

GraphGradient givesArea gives
Displacement–timeVelocityNot used
Velocity–timeAccelerationChange in displacement
Acceleration–timeNot usedChange in velocity

The equation s = ½(u + v)t is the area of a trapezium under a velocity–time graph, and v² = u² + 2as is what falls out of that geometry — which is why the equations and the graphs never disagree. Curved velocity–time graphs mean changing acceleration; the gradient at a point is found from a tangent drawn with a ruler and evaluated between two distant points on the tangent.

Non-uniform motion: drag and terminal velocity

When a real object falls, air resistance (drag) acts opposite to the motion and grows with speed. The resultant force is weight minus drag, so the acceleration is greatest at the start and falls as speed rises. When drag equals the weight the resultant force is zero and the object continues at terminal velocity. A skydiver reaches terminal velocity in free fall, opens the parachute (which raises drag enormously), and decelerates to a much lower terminal velocity before landing. The same physics sets the thinking and braking distances of a vehicle: thinking distance grows with reaction time and speed; braking distance grows with the square of the speed, because the work the brakes must do is ½mv².

Unit 3 skills: measurement, data and uncertainty

WPH13 examines the practical skills of Units 1 and 2 in writing, using unfamiliar contexts. The marks come from method and analysis, and the analysis rules are fixed.

  • Absolute uncertainty is the precision of the instrument: ±0.5 of the smallest scale division for an analogue scale, ± the smallest reading for a digital one. A length of 24.5 mm on a ruler carries ±0.5 mm.
  • Percentage uncertainty = (absolute uncertainty ÷ measured value) × 100. A small quantity measured with the same instrument carries the biggest percentage uncertainty — which is why measuring a short wire's extension with a ruler is poor method.
  • Combining uncertainties: for a sum or difference, add the absolute uncertainties; for a product or quotient (including powers), add the percentage uncertainties, and for a quantity raised to the power n, multiply its percentage uncertainty by n.
  • Repeat readings reduce random error; the mean is quoted with the uncertainty taken as half the range or the instrument precision, whichever is larger. Systematic errors (zero errors, calibration faults) are corrected at the instrument, never by averaging.
  • Graphs and error bars: plot every point with error bars in both directions where both quantities are uncertain, draw the line of best fit and also the worst acceptable steepest and shallowest lines within the error bars; the gradient's uncertainty comes from their spread.
  • Gradient and intercept: gradient = Δy/Δx taken between two distant points on the line; state it with its unit. The intercept is physical only if the theory predicts one — on a velocity–time graph the intercept is the initial velocity; on a load–extension graph a non-zero intercept suggests the spring was already stretched.
  • Calibration: a known input is applied to an instrument and its output recorded, giving a calibration graph against which unknown readings are converted.
  • Control of variables and safety: identify the independent, dependent and control variables; keep controls fixed and name them; risk assessment links each hazard to a control (falling masses — clamp the stand; long wires under tension — eye protection).

Worked example: equations of motion and uncertainty

A ball is dropped from rest and falls 1.50 m. Neglecting air resistance, take g = 9.81 m s⁻².

v² = u² + 2 a s = 0 + 2 × 9.81 × 1.50 = 29.4, so v = 5.42 m s⁻¹
time: s = u t + 1/2 a t² gives 1.50 = 4.905 t², so t = 0.553 s

Now the uncertainty: if the height is measured as 1.50 ± 0.01 m, its percentage uncertainty is 0.01/1.50 × 100 = 0.67 per cent. Since v = √(2gs), the percentage uncertainty in v is half of that in s, so v = 5.42 ± 0.04 m s⁻¹. Treating powers correctly is the difference between a right and a wrong uncertainty.

Common mistakes

  • Applying the equations of motion when the acceleration is not constant (for example once drag becomes significant).
  • Ignoring sign convention: mixing upward-positive displacements with downward-positive g gives nonsense answers.
  • Forgetting that at the top of a projectile's flight the vertical velocity is zero but the acceleration is still 9.81 m s⁻² downwards.
  • Adding percentage uncertainties for a sum instead of absolute uncertainties, or halving the percentage uncertainty of a square-rooted quantity incorrectly.
  • Joining plotted points with straight lines instead of drawing a smooth line of best fit, or ignoring error bars when asked for uncertainty.
  • Taking the gradient between two plotted points rather than two distant points on the best-fit line.
  • Confusing distance with displacement and speed with velocity in questions that mention direction.
  • Using km h⁻¹ directly in the equations: divide by 3.6 to convert to m s⁻¹ first.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (WPH11, 3 marks). A car accelerates uniformly from 5.0 m s⁻¹ to 15 m s⁻¹ in 6.0 s. Find the acceleration and the distance travelled.

Answer: a = (v − u)/t = (15 − 5.0)/6.0 = 1.7 m s⁻². s = ½(u + v)t = ½(5.0 + 15)(6.0) = 60 m.

Question 2 (WPH11, 4 marks). A stone is thrown vertically upwards at 20 m s⁻¹. Calculate the maximum height and the total time of flight. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².

Answer: At the top v = 0, so v² = u² + 2as gives 0 = 400 − 2(9.81)h, so h = 20.4 m. Time up: v = u + at gives 0 = 20 − 9.81t, so t = 2.04 s; total flight = 2 × 2.04 = 4.08 s (the motion is symmetric when the landing height equals the launch height).

Question 3 (WPH13, 4 marks). A student measures the period of a pendulum as T = 1.98 ± 0.02 s and the length as L = 98.0 ± 0.5 cm. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in g if g = 4π²L/T².

Answer: Percentage uncertainty in L = 0.5/98.0 × 100 = 0.51 per cent. In T = 0.02/1.98 × 100 = 1.01 per cent, doubled for T² = 2.02 per cent. Total for g = 0.51 + 2.02 = 2.5 per cent. The period dominates, so timing more oscillations would improve the result most.

Question 4 (WPH11, 3 marks). A projectile is launched at 30 m s⁻¹ at 30° above the horizontal. Find its initial horizontal and vertical velocity components.

Answer: Horizontal = 30 cos 30° = 26 m s⁻¹; vertical = 30 sin 30° = 15 m s⁻¹. The horizontal component stays constant (no air resistance); the vertical component decreases at 9.81 m s⁻².

Question 5 (WPH13, 3 marks). A graph of extension against load does not pass through the origin. Suggest a reason and an improvement.

Answer: The spring may already have been loaded (its own weight or an unstated mass), or the initial length was measured incorrectly. Measure the spring's original length hanging vertically with no added load, allow it to settle, and take that as the true zero extension; repeat readings at each load and plot a best-fit line.

Question 6 (WPH11, 3 marks). Explain, in terms of forces, why a skydiver reaches a terminal velocity before opening the parachute.

Answer: On leaving the aircraft, weight exceeds drag, so there is a downward resultant force and she accelerates. As speed increases, drag increases, reducing the resultant force and the acceleration. When drag equals the weight the resultant force is zero, so the acceleration is zero and she continues at constant terminal velocity.

Motion is caused by forces — the subject of Dynamics.

title: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Scatter Diagrams and Correlation
content:
Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Scatter Diagrams and Correlation

A scatter diagram plots two measurements for each person or object, one on each axis, and reveals whether they move together. The IGCSE questions ask you to describe that relationship — correlation — draw a line of best fit, and use it to estimate. The arithmetic is light; the marks come from precise language and from the discipline of drawing and reading the line correctly. This note builds the topic from zero: what correlation means and how to describe it, how to draw a line of best fit that earns the marks, how to use it for interpolation and extrapolation, and why correlation is not causation.

What a scatter diagram shows

Each point represents one individual: its horizontal coordinate is one variable (say, hours of revision) and its vertical coordinate the other (say, test score). The pattern of points — the scatter — is the data's message. Bivariate data means two variables measured on the same individuals; the diagram is the quickest way to see whether a relationship exists.

  • Positive correlation: as one variable increases, the other tends to increase (revision time and score).
  • Negative correlation: as one increases, the other tends to decrease (car age and value).
  • No correlation: no pattern — the points form a cloud (shoe size and score).
  • Strength: strong correlation means the points lie close to a line; weak means they are widely scattered around it.

Describing correlation precisely

The mark scheme wants three things in a description: direction (positive or negative), strength (strong, moderate or weak), and the variables named. "There is a strong positive correlation between hours of revision and test score" earns the mark; "the graph goes up" does not.

Worked example. A scatter diagram of 30 cars shows points tightly clustered around a line falling from top-left to bottom-right. Describe the correlation and interpret it.

Strong negative correlation between age and value:
older cars tend to be worth less. The tightness of the
cluster means the relationship is consistent, but individual
cars can still deviate (condition, mileage).

Drawing the line of best fit

A line of best fit summarises the trend. The marks are awarded for a straight line that:

  1. Passes through the middle of the cloud — roughly equal numbers of points above and below.
  2. Follows the trend direction (rising for positive, falling for negative correlation).
  3. Is drawn with a ruler and extends across the plotted range.

A useful anchor: the line should pass close to the mean point (the mean of the x-values, mean of the y-values). It does not have to pass through the origin, and it should not be forced through any single point.

Worked example. Points cluster with mean x = 12 and mean y = 60, trending upward. Describe where the line of best fit should pass and how to check it.

The line should pass through (12, 60) and follow the upward
trend; check by counting points above and below - roughly equal
numbers on each side, with the line through the middle of the
vertical spread at each x.

Using the line: interpolation and extrapolation

Once the line is drawn, estimates are read from it — not from individual points:

  • Interpolation: estimating within the range of the data. Reliable, because the trend is supported by nearby points.
  • Extrapolation: estimating beyond the plotted range. Risky, because nothing guarantees the relationship continues — a straight line cannot describe a curve that turns.

Worked example. A line of best fit passes through (4, 30) and (10, 54). Estimate y when x = 7, and comment on estimating y when x = 30.

gradient = (54 - 30)/(10 - 4) = 24/6 = 4
equation: y = 4x + c; using (4, 30): 30 = 16 + c → c = 14
y = 4x + 14
at x = 7: y = 28 + 14 = 42  (interpolation - reliable)
at x = 30: y = 134 (extrapolation - unreliable; the trend may
not continue that far)

Worked example: from table to diagram to estimate

Data: hours studied (x): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6; marks (y): 35, 42, 50, 55, 63, 70.

Step 1: plot each pair as a point (x horizontal, y vertical).
Step 2: describe - strong positive correlation.
Step 3: draw the line through the middle: the points rise
        about 7 marks per hour; a line from (1, 35) to (6, 70)
        passes through the centre of the cloud.
Step 4: estimate the mark for 3.5 hours: read up from x = 3.5
        to the line, then across: about 53 marks.
Step 5: estimate the hours for 60 marks: read across from y = 60
        to the line, then down: about 4.6 hours.

Note the wording in answers: "from the line of best fit, approximately 53 marks" — the word approximately signals that it is an estimate, which the mark scheme expects.

Correlation and causation

Correlation does not prove cause. Two variables can move together because a third factor drives both (ice-cream sales and drowning rates both rise in summer — heat causes both), or by coincidence in a small sample. Exam questions reward this caution explicitly: state that the correlation shows an association, not that one variable causes the other, unless the data come from a controlled experiment.

Worked example. A study finds a strong positive correlation between the number of books in a home and children's reading scores. Does buying books raise scores?

Not necessarily: households with more books may also have more
educated parents, more time for reading, or higher income - all
of which could raise scores. The correlation is real, but the
causal claim is unsupported by this evidence alone.

A second discipline follows: when a question asks you to comment on a study, name the possible confounding variable rather than simply denying causation. In the books example, income, parental education and available time are all plausible common causes; naming one shows the examiner you understand what a confounding factor is. The same reasoning explains why a strong correlation from a small sample deserves caution: with only a handful of points, a pattern can appear by chance, and a single outlier can create or destroy the apparent trend.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Describe) Points on a scatter diagram trend downward and are tightly clustered. Describe the correlation. Answer: Strong negative correlation — as one variable increases, the other tends to decrease consistently.
  2. (No correlation) Describe a scatter diagram whose points form a random cloud. Answer: No correlation — there is no clear trend between the variables.
  3. (Line) State two features of a correctly drawn line of best fit. Answer: A straight line through the middle of the points with roughly equal numbers above and below, following the trend and drawn with a ruler.
  4. (Estimate) A line of best fit passes through (2, 10) and (6, 26). Estimate y at x = 4. Answer: gradient 4; y = 4x + 2; at x = 4, y = 18.
  5. (Interpolation) Explain why an estimate inside the data range is more reliable than one outside it. Answer: Inside the range the trend is supported by nearby data points (interpolation); outside it (extrapolation) there is no evidence that the relationship continues in the same way.
  6. (Causation) A shop finds that sales of umbrellas and sales of coats rise together. Explain the correlation without claiming that umbrellas cause coat sales. Answer: Both are driven by a third variable — rainy weather — which increases demand for both; the correlation is association, not causation.
  7. (Outlier) One point sits far from the trend. What should you do with it when drawing the line? Answer: Note it as an outlier and draw the line through the main body of points; do not let one point pull the line away from the trend.
  8. (Strength) Two scatter diagrams both show positive correlation; in one the points are close to the line. Compare them. Answer: The tighter diagram shows stronger positive correlation; the looser one shows weaker positive correlation.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Joining the dots: a line of best fit is a single straight line through the trend, never a zigzag connecting points.
  • Forcing through the origin: the line passes through the middle of the cloud; there is no reason for it to start at (0, 0).
  • Reading a point instead of the line: estimates come from the line of best fit, not from the nearest plotted point.
  • Ignoring outliers: one extreme point should not swing the line; note it and fit the main cluster.
  • Weak description: "positive" alone is incomplete — direction and strength, with variables named.
  • Causal language: "revision causes higher scores" overclaims from observational data; write "is associated with" and mention confounding factors.
  • Extrapolating confidently: beyond the data range, state the estimate is unreliable.
  • Axes: plot the explanatory variable on the horizontal axis and the response on the vertical, label both with units, and use the given scales exactly.

Equations and symbols

The arithmetic of a scatter diagram is the equation of the line of best fit, read in both directions: from the line to an estimate, and from two points back to the line. Keep the meaning of each letter in view, because the exam asks you to interpret the gradient rather than just compute it.

gradient = (54 - 30)/(10 - 4) = 24/6 = 4 Key: 54 and 30 are the y-values of two points on the line; 10 and 4 the matching x-values; the gradient is the change in the vertical variable per unit of the horizontal one, so here the response rises 4 for every 1 of the explanatory variable.

y = 4x + c Key: y = the predicted value on the vertical axis; x = the explanatory variable on the horizontal axis; 4 = the gradient just calculated; c = the intercept, still unknown. Substitute one point to find c.

30 = 16 + c → c = 14 Key: substituting the point (4, 30) into y = 4x + c gives 16 + c = 30, so c = 14. The intercept is where the line would cross x = 0 — meaningful only if x = 0 is inside the data.

y = 4x + 14 Key: the finished line of best fit; use it for every estimate, never the plotted points themselves. From the line, x = 7 gives y = 42 — an interpolation, inside the data range, so reliable.

y = 28 + 14 = 42 Key: the same estimate written out; 28 = 4 × 7 and 14 is the intercept. Showing this line earns the method mark even if the earlier gradient was wrong.

y = 134 Key: the prediction at x = 30, far outside the plotted range. It is an extrapolation: the arithmetic is right and the estimate is unreliable, which is exactly what the question wants you to say.

The language that earns the marks. Name the direction and the strength and the two variables — "strong positive correlation between hours of revision and test score" — and say "approximately" for any value read from the line. Correlation is association, not causation: name the third variable that could drive both.

title: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Sets and Venn Diagrams
content:
Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Sets and Venn Diagrams

Set notation is the language of sorting: it describes which elements belong together, which belong to both groups, and which belong to neither. The IGCSE questions are almost always Venn-diagram problems in disguise — a survey of students, a group of numbers, a club membership — and the marks come from filling every region correctly. This note builds the topic from zero: the notation and symbols, the two-set and three-set Venn diagrams and how to shade them, the counting formulas, and the word-problem method that never misses a region.

Set notation and vocabulary

SymbolMeaningExample
∈is an element of3 ∈ {1, 2, 3}
∉is not an element of5 ∉ {1, 2, 3}
ξ (or U)the universal set — everything under discussionξ = {1, 2, ..., 12}
∅the empty setodd multiples of 2 = ∅
A′the complement of A — everything in ξ not in AA′ = ξ A
A ∪ Bunion — in A or B or both{1,2} ∪ {2,3} = {1,2,3}
A ∩ Bintersection — in both{1,2} ∩ {2,3} = {2}
n(A)the number of elements of An({2, 4, 6}) = 3

Two rules follow directly: A ∩ A′ = ∅ (nothing is both in and out), and A ∪ A′ = ξ (everything is one or the other). Subsets: A ⊂ B means every element of A is also in B. The empty set has no elements, so n(∅) = 0, and it is a subset of every set — a fact worth stating explicitly when a question asks whether ∅ ⊂ A is true.

Two-set Venn diagrams

A two-set diagram divides the universal set into four regions: only A, only B, both, and neither. Filling them from the inside out is the reliable method:

  1. Write the number in the intersection (both) first.
  2. Work outward: only A = n(A) − both; only B = n(B) − both.
  3. Neither = total − (only A + only B + both).

Worked example. In a class of 32, 18 study French, 15 study Spanish, and 7 study both. Find the number studying only French, only Spanish, and neither.

both = 7
only French = 18 - 7 = 11
only Spanish = 15 - 7 = 8
neither = 32 - (11 + 8 + 7) = 32 - 26 = 6

Worked example 2 (reverse). In a group, 20 like tea, 14 like coffee and 5 like neither. Everyone likes at least one of the two? Then find n(tea ∩ coffee).

n(T union C) = 20 + 14 - both
total = 20 + 14 - both + 5 = 39 - both
If the group has 30 people: 30 = 39 - both → both = 9

The inclusion–exclusion formula

n(A union B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A intersection B)

for three sets:
n(A u B u C) = n(A) + n(B) + n(C)
             - n(A n B) - n(A n C) - n(B n C)
             + n(A n B n C)

The subtraction corrects double counting; the final addition corrects the triple-counted centre. Knowing the formula lets you answer "how many in total" questions without a full diagram, but a diagram is still the safer route for word problems.

Worked example. A survey of 50 people: 30 read newspapers, 25 read magazines, 12 read both. How many read at least one?

n(N union M) = 30 + 25 - 12 = 43
neither = 50 - 43 = 7

Three-set Venn diagrams

The three-set diagram has eight regions (counting "none of the three"). The fill order that never fails:

  1. Start with the triple intersection (all three).
  2. Find the "exactly two" regions by subtracting the triple from each pair.
  3. Find the "only one" regions by subtracting the pair and triple totals from each set total.
  4. Find "none" from the grand total.

Worked example. 40 students choose subjects: 20 take Maths, 18 take Physics, 15 take Chemistry; 8 take Maths and Physics, 6 take Maths and Chemistry, 5 take Physics and Chemistry; 3 take all three. Find how many take exactly one subject and how many take none.

triple = 3
exactly M and P = 8 - 3 = 5
exactly M and C = 6 - 3 = 3
exactly P and C = 5 - 3 = 2
only M = 20 - (5 + 3 + 3) = 9
only P = 18 - (5 + 2 + 3) = 8
only C = 15 - (3 + 2 + 3) = 7
exactly one = 9 + 8 + 7 = 24
total counted = 24 + 5 + 3 + 2 + 3 = 37
none = 40 - 37 = 3

Sets of numbers and shading

Questions often use number sets inside the universal set: ξ = {1, 2, ..., 20}, A = multiples of 3, B = multiples of 4. List them, then use the same four regions:

A = {3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18}
B = {4, 8, 12, 16, 20}
A n B = {12}
A u B = {3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 12, 15, 16, 18, 20}
neither = {1, 2, 5, 7, 10, 11, 13, 14, 17, 19}

Shading questions ask for a region described in symbols. Translate the symbols into words first: A′ ∩ B means "not in A, but in B" — the part of B outside A. A ∪ B′ means "in A, or outside B" — everything except the part of B that is not in A.

Listing sets and set-builder notation

Sets can be written in three ways, and questions move between them. The roster method lists the elements: A = {2, 4, 6, 8}. The description method states the rule in words: A is the set of even numbers from 2 to 8. Set-builder notation states the rule symbolically: A = {x : x is an even number, 2 ≤ x ≤ 8} — read as "the set of all x such that x is even and between 2 and 8".

  • Roster for finite sets: list every element once, in braces, separated by commas; order does not matter and repeats are not counted twice.
  • Description for patterns: "multiples of 3 less than 30" is clearer than listing ten numbers.
  • Set-builder for precision: the colon means "such that"; the condition after it does the work.

Worked example. Write the set of odd numbers between 1 and 11 in roster and set-builder form, and find its size.

roster: {3, 5, 7, 9}  (strictly between, so 1 and 11 excluded)
set-builder: {x : x odd, 1 < x < 11}
n(A) = 4

Reading the inequalities is the trap: "between" usually excludes the endpoints, "from ... to ..." usually includes them, and the question's wording decides. When in doubt, list both interpretations and choose the one consistent with the other numbers in the question.

Worked examples: word problems

Worked example. In a hostel of 60 students, 35 play football, 28 play basketball, and 12 play both. How many play neither?

at least one = 35 + 28 - 12 = 51
neither = 60 - 51 = 9

Worked example 2 (with a variable). In a group of 25, x people like both tea and coffee, 12 like tea only and 8 like coffee only. Find x if everyone likes at least one.

12 + 8 + x = 25  →  x = 5

Worked example 3 (conditional language). Of 40 students, 24 study History, 18 study Geography and 6 study neither. How many study both?

at least one = 40 - 6 = 34
34 = 24 + 18 - both  →  both = 42 - 34 = 8

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Notation) ξ = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8}; A = {2, 4, 6, 8}; B = {1, 3, 5, 7}. Find A ∩ B and A ∪ B. Answer: A ∩ B = ∅; A ∪ B = ξ.
  2. (Complement) With A = {2, 4, 6, 8} in ξ above, list A′. Answer: {1, 3, 5, 7}.
  3. (Two sets) n(A) = 14, n(B) = 9, n(A ∩ B) = 4. Find n(A ∪ B). Answer: 14 + 9 − 4 = 19.
  4. (Neither) In a class of 30, 17 like cricket, 12 like tennis and 5 like both. Find the number who like neither. Answer: at least one = 24; neither = 6.
  5. (Three sets) 30 students: 15 like Maths, 12 like Physics, 10 like Chemistry; 5 like Maths and Physics, 4 like Maths and Chemistry, 3 like Physics and Chemistry, 2 like all three. Find the number who like exactly one. Answer: only M = 15 − (3 + 2 + 2) = 8; only P = 12 − (3 + 1 + 2) = 6; only C = 10 − (2 + 1 + 2) = 5; total = 19 (with exactly-two counts 3, 2, 1 and triple 2).
  6. (Shading) Describe the region A′ ∩ B in words. Answer: Elements in B but not in A — the part of B outside A.
  7. (Numbers) ξ = {1, ..., 20}; A = even numbers; B = multiples of 5. Find n(A ∩ B). Answer: multiples of 10 in the set = {10, 20}, so 2.
  8. (Reasoning) Explain why n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) is wrong when A and B overlap. Answer: The elements in both sets are counted twice in n(A) + n(B), so the intersection must be subtracted once: n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B).

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Filling the intersection last: start at the centre. Adding both set totals and forgetting the overlap counts shared elements twice.
  • Forgetting the "neither" region: the universal set includes elements outside all named sets; if the question gives a total, subtract to find them.
  • Confusing ∪ and ∩: union is "or" (everything), intersection is "and" (only the middle). A quick mnemonic: ∪ looks like a cup that holds everything.
  • Shading the wrong side for A′: the complement is everything outside A, including parts of other sets and the region outside them all.
  • Triple intersection double subtraction: when subtracting pairs, remember each pair already includes the triple; subtract the triple from each pair before using them.
  • Reading "only": "only A" means A and nothing else — exclude the overlaps. The word only is a region instruction, not decoration.
  • Notation in answers: list elements with braces and commas; do not write 1, 2, 3 as an unbraced list when the answer is a set.
  • Assuming everyone likes something: unless stated, some may be outside both sets — check whether the total equals the sum of the regions.

The four regions: reading a Venn diagram as a counting grid

A two-set Venn diagram is not a picture of two sets. It is a grid with four cells, and every question about it is answered by putting a number in each cell and adding.

Name the four cells before you write anything. For sets A and B inside a universal set ξ, every element is in exactly one of: only A, both, only B, neither. In the figure that is 7, 5, 9 and 4. The moment all four numbers are on the page, every part of the question is a sum:

n(A) = 7 + 5 = 12 Key: n(A) counts everything inside circle A, including the overlap.
n(A ∩ B) = 5 Key: the intersection — the region inside both circles.
n(A ∪ B) = 7 + 5 + 9 = 21 Key: the union — everything inside at least one circle.
n(ξ) = 21 + 4 = 25 Key: the universal set also counts what is in neither set.

Why the formula has a minus sign. Adding n(A) and n(B) counts the overlap twice — once with each circle — so it has to come back off:

n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B) Key: n(A ∪ B) = elements in at least one set; n(A ∩ B) = elements in both. In the figure, 12 + 14 − 5 = 21, which is exactly the sum of the three inner cells. The subtraction is not a rule to remember; it is the double count being removed.

Worked example. In a class of 30, 18 study French, 15 study Spanish and 6 study both. How many study neither?

French only = 18 − 6 = 12
Spanish only = 15 − 6 = 9
at least one = 12 + 6 + 9 = 27
neither = 30 − 27 = 3

Going the other way — "9 study neither" — is the same arithmetic in reverse, and it is the version that appears when the examiner wants an unknown: if the total is 30 and 9 study neither, then 21 study at least one, and 18 + 15 − x = 21 gives x = 12 studying both. Filling the grid from the overlap outwards always works, because the overlap is the only cell that belongs to both circles.

Where marks are lost. Treating "18 study French" as 18 in the French-only region, which double-counts 6. Forgetting the neither region, so the four numbers do not add to the total. And shading the wrong side for A′ ∩ B: the complement of A is everything outside A, so A′ ∩ B is the B-only region, not the overlap.

title: IGCSE Physics: Nuclear Physics
content:
IGCSE Physics: Nuclear Physics

Cambridge IGCSE Physics 0625 (2026–2028), Topic 5 Nuclear physics: statements 5.1 The nuclear model of the atom and 5.2 Radioactivity. Everything in the physical world is built from about a hundred kinds of atom, and almost all the mass of an atom sits in a tiny, dense nucleus. This note builds the nuclear model, then radioactivity from first principles: what the three emissions are, how nuclei decay, how half-life quantifies it, and how radiation is used safely.

The atom and the nuclear model

An atom is mostly empty space: a tiny central nucleus surrounded by electrons that occupy shells around it. The nucleus is about 10 000 times smaller than the atom, yet holds more than 99.9 per cent of its mass. Atoms are neutral because the number of electrons equals the number of protons; if an atom loses or gains electrons it becomes a ion, charged positive or negative.

Supplement: the evidence. In the alpha-particle scattering experiment, alpha particles were fired at an extremely thin gold foil. Most passed straight through, a few were deflected by small angles, and a very small number bounced back. Rutherford concluded that the atom has a small, dense, positively charged nucleus: most alphas met only empty space, those passing near the nucleus were deflected by the positive repulsion, and the rare head-on reversals required a tiny, massive target.

The nucleus: protons, neutrons and isotopes

The nucleus contains protons and neutrons, collectively nucleons. A proton carries one positive charge and one unit of mass; a neutron carries no charge and one unit of mass; an electron carries one negative charge and almost no mass.

ParticleRelative chargeRelative massLocation
Proton+11Nucleus
Neutron01Nucleus
Electron−11/1836 (negligible)Shells around the nucleus

Nuclide notation writes the symbol of the element with the proton number Z (the number of protons, which decides the element) and the nucleon number A (the total number of protons and neutrons) as a superscript and subscript on the left: A over Z beside the symbol. The number of neutrons is A − Z. Isotopes are atoms of the same element (same Z) with different numbers of neutrons (different A), so they have identical chemical properties but different nuclear behaviour.

Supplement: fission and fusion. Nuclear fission splits a heavy nucleus (such as uranium-235) into two lighter nuclei plus neutrons and a large release of energy; a neutron triggers the split and the released neutrons sustain a chain reaction in a reactor. Nuclear fusion joins two light nuclei (such as hydrogen isotopes) into a heavier one, releasing far more energy per kilogram — this powers the Sun and every star. In both, a small loss of mass appears as a large release of energy, in line with mass–energy equivalence, and the sum of the nucleon numbers and of the proton numbers is conserved in any nuclear equation.

Detection of radioactivity

Radioactivity is the spontaneous emission of radiation from unstable nuclei. It cannot be seen, heard or felt, so it is detected by its effects: a Geiger–Müller tube produces an electrical pulse for each ionising particle entering it; photographic film darkens (which is why film badges measure radiation dose); and a cloud chamber shows the tracks of the emissions.

Background radiation is present everywhere and must be subtracted from every measurement: it comes from natural sources (radon gas from rocks and soil, cosmic rays from space, radiation from food and building materials) and from human activity (medical X-rays, fallout from nuclear accidents and weapons tests). A count-rate measurement is corrected by taking the reading with no source present and subtracting it from the source reading (Supplement: count rates are quoted in counts per second or counts per minute, and repeated background readings are averaged before use).

The three types of nuclear emission

Emission from an unstable nucleus is spontaneous and random: nothing external causes a particular nucleus to decay at a particular moment, and no prediction is possible for any single nucleus.

PropertyAlpha (α)Beta (β)Gamma (γ)
NatureHelium nucleus: 2 protons + 2 neutronsFast electron from the nucleusElectromagnetic wave of high frequency
Charge+2−10
Relative mass41/1836 (negligible)0
Ionising powerVery strongModerateWeak
Penetrating powerStopped by paper or a few cm of airStopped by a few mm of aluminiumReduced only by thick lead or many metres of concrete
Effect of a magnetic fieldDeflected slightly (opposite way to beta)Deflected more (opposite way to alpha)Not deflected

Supplement deepens the ionisation ranking: alpha particles are large and doubly charged, so they tear electrons from atoms at every collision and stop quickly; beta particles are small and singly charged and ionise less; gamma rays carry no charge and ionise least, so they travel furthest. The same ranking explains the danger profiles: alpha sources are the least dangerous outside the body (stopped by skin) but the most dangerous if ingested, because their intense ionisation wrecks nearby cells.

Radioactive decay

Decay is the change of an unstable nucleus into a different, more stable nucleus, with the emission of radiation. The nucleus changes identity: emitting alpha reduces the nucleon number by 4 and the proton number by 2; emitting beta converts a neutron into a proton, so the proton number rises by 1 while the nucleon number is unchanged; gamma emission changes the energy of the nucleus but not its identity.

alpha decay:        (A over Z) X  ->  (A-4 over Z-2) Y  +  helium nucleus
beta decay:         (A over Z) X  ->  (A over Z+1) Y  +  electron

In every nuclear equation the total nucleon number and the total charge are the same on both sides — the standard balancing question on Paper 2 and Paper 4. Decay is unaffected by temperature, pressure or chemical state: the nucleus is shielded from ordinary conditions by its electrons.

Half-life

Half-life is the time taken for half the undecayed nuclei of a sample to decay — equivalently, for the count rate to fall to half its original value. It is a fixed property of each isotope, ranging from fractions of a second to billions of years.

after n half-lives:        count rate = starting count rate x (1/2)^(number of half-lives)

From a decay curve, read the time for the rate to halve from any starting point; the half-life is the same at every stage. Radioactive dating uses the ratio of a long-lived isotope to its decay product in rocks (uranium to lead) or in once-living things (carbon-14, half-life 5730 years, absorbed during life and decaying after death). Short-lived isotopes are used as medical tracers, since they deliver a dose that soon disappears.

Safety precautions

Radiation damages living tissue by ionising atoms in cells, which can kill cells or damage DNA and cause cancer. Three simple controls govern all handling:

  • Time: keep exposures short and work quickly with sources.
  • Distance: use tongs and remote handling; the intensity falls sharply with distance from the source.
  • Shielding: store sources in lead-lined boxes; use paper for alpha, aluminium for beta, lead or concrete for gamma.

Sealed sources are never touched or pointed at people; contamination (spreading open sources) is prevented with gloves, trays and careful disposal; workers wear film badges and dose records are kept. Doctors and patients accept a medical dose only when the benefit outweighs the risk — the principle of every risk–benefit question in the paper.

Worked example: half-life calculation

A source has a corrected count rate of 640 counts per minute and a half-life of 8.0 days. What is the rate after 24 days, and how long until it falls below 40 counts per minute?

24 days = 3 half-lives:        640 -> 320 -> 160 -> 80 counts per minute
80 -> 40 needs one more half-life, so 24 + 8 = 32 days total

The physical reasoning: half-living is exponential, never linear. After three half-lives an eighth of the original activity remains, not one third.

Common mistakes

  • Confusing the three emissions: alpha is a helium nucleus (2 protons, 2 neutrons), beta is an electron created in the nucleus, gamma is a wave.
  • Saying radiation becomes safe after a fixed number of days; only the activity falls with half-life, and each isotope has its own.
  • Halving the count rate every half-life from the original instead of from the current value (linear thinking): 100 goes 50, 25, 12.5, not 50, 0, 0.
  • Forgetting to subtract background radiation from raw counts before plotting a decay curve.
  • Balancing a nuclear equation without conserving both the nucleon number and the proton number.
  • Claiming alpha is the most dangerous radiation in every case: it is the most ionising, but the least penetrating — the hazard depends on whether the source is outside or inside the body.
  • Saying isotopes have different chemical properties; the electron arrangement is identical, so the chemistry is identical.
  • Linking decay to temperature or pressure; nuclear decay is unaffected by ordinary physical conditions.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 4, 3 marks). A nucleus of uranium-238 emits an alpha particle. Write the nuclear equation if the product is thorium-234.

Answer: uranium-238 (92 protons) becomes thorium-234 (90 protons) plus a helium nucleus: 238 = 234 + 4 and 92 = 90 + 2, so both totals balance.

Question 2 (Paper 4, 3 marks). A sample's count rate falls from 400 to 50 counts per second in 12 minutes. Calculate the half-life.

Answer: 400 → 200 → 100 → 50 is three half-lives in 12 minutes, so the half-life is 4.0 minutes.

Question 3 (Paper 2 style). Which emission is stopped by a sheet of paper? A alpha; B beta; C gamma; D X-rays. Answer: A. Alpha is stopped by paper, beta by a few millimetres of aluminium, gamma only by thick lead.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 6 marks). Explain why alpha emitters are safe outside the body but extremely dangerous if inhaled.

Answer: Alpha particles are large and doubly charged, so they ionise atoms strongly and are stopped by the dead outer layer of skin or by a sheet of paper, meaning they cannot reach living tissue from outside. If an alpha emitter is inhaled, it lodges in lung tissue and the particles then strike living cells at point-blank range. Their intense ionisation breaks chemical bonds and damages DNA in those cells, which can kill them or cause mutations and cancer. Distance and shielding matter: inside the body there is neither.

Question 5 (Paper 4, 3 marks). State the three standard precautions when handling a radioactive source.

Answer: Keep the time of exposure short; keep well away and handle with long tongs to reduce intensity; store in a lead-lined box with suitable shielding for the emission type (paper for alpha, aluminium for beta, lead for gamma).

Question 6 (Paper 6 style). Describe how you would measure the half-life of a short-lived isotope safely.

Answer: Place the source in a holder a fixed distance from a Geiger–Müller tube connected to a scaler or data logger. Measure the background count rate with no source present and average several readings. Record the source's count rate at regular time intervals until it approaches background, keeping geometry constant. Subtract the background from each reading, plot count rate against time, and read the time for the activity to halve between any two points on the curve. Keep exposure brief, handle the source with tongs, and store it in its shielded box.

The nucleus holds the energy of stars; the last topic of the IGCSE course is where those stars live — Earth and Space.

Equations and symbols

Nuclear decay is described by two bookkeeping rules — the nuclide notation and the conservation of nucleon number and charge — plus the exponential half-life relation. There is no equation for "why" a nucleus decays; the marks are in the accounting.

Nuclide notation

A = Z + N
Key: A = nucleon (mass) number, the total protons plus neutrons; Z = proton (atomic) number, which fixes the element; N = neutron number. Written as A over Z before the symbol, as in ²³⁵₉₂U.

proton number Z = number of protons = number of electrons in a neutral atom
Key: Z decides the element; changing Z changes the element, which is what transmutation means.

isotopes: same Z, different A
Key: isotopes of an element have the same number of protons and different numbers of neutrons, so they behave identically chemically and differently in nuclear decay.

Decay bookkeeping

alpha decay: A → A − 4 and Z → Z − 2
Key: an alpha particle is a helium nucleus, ⁴₂He, so the parent loses two protons and two neutrons. Example: ²³⁸₉₂U → ²³⁴₉₀Th + ⁴₂He.

beta-minus decay: A unchanged and Z → Z + 1
Key: a neutron turns into a proton and an electron, so the nucleon number is unchanged and the proton number rises by one. Example: ¹⁴₆C → ¹⁴₇N + ⁰₋₁e.

gamma emission: A and Z unchanged
Key: a gamma ray is electromagnetic energy released from an excited nucleus; the nucleus loses energy but not particles, so the nuclide stays the same element.

conservation in every decay: ΣA and ΣZ balance on both sides
Key: the totals of nucleon number and of charge must be equal before and after. This is the check that catches a wrong particle on the right-hand side.

Half-life

N = N₀ × (½)^(t / t½)
Key: N = number of nuclei (or count rate) remaining after time t; N₀ = the starting number or rate; t = elapsed time (s, or any unit); t½ = half-life in the same unit as t. After three half-lives, one eighth remains.

t½ = the time for half the nuclei in a sample to decay
Key: a fixed property of the isotope, unaffected by temperature, pressure or chemical state. It is measured from a decay curve as the time for the count rate to halve.

A = ΔN / Δt
Key: A = activity (Bq, decays per second); ΔN = number of decays recorded; Δt = time interval (s). The measured count rate is lower than the activity because the detector only intercepts a fraction of the radiation.

Penetration and ionisation

penetrating power: alpha (less than) beta (less than) gamma
Key: alpha is stopped by paper or a few centimetres of air; beta by a few millimetres of aluminium; gamma is reduced but not stopped by thick lead. Ionising power runs the other way: alpha ionises most strongly because it is the most charged and most massive.

E = mc² (extension, beyond the 0625 requirement)
Key: E = energy released (J); m = mass lost, the mass defect (kg); c = speed of light, 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s. It explains where the energy of a decay comes from, and why a small mass defect is a large energy release.

title: IGCSE Chemistry (OxfordAQA): Organic Chemistry
content:
Organic Chemistry

Organic chemistry is the chemistry of carbon compounds, and there are millions of them because carbon forms four bonds and bonds to itself without limit. That could make the topic a list to memorise, and it is not: a handful of homologous series cover everything the specification asks, and each series has a general formula, a functional group and a predictable set of reactions. This topic starts from crude oil, which is where the fuels come from, then introduces the alkanes and alkenes with the test that separates them, the alcohols and carboxylic acids that follow from them, and finally the polymers — both the synthetic ones made from alkenes and the natural ones such as starch, protein and DNA. Read it as one chain of reasoning rather than four separate topics.

1. Crude oil and fractional distillation

Crude oil is a mixture of hydrocarbons — compounds of carbon and hydrogen only — of different chain lengths. Because the chains differ in length, they have different boiling points, and that is what separates them: fractional distillation heats the oil, lets the vapours rise up a column and draws each fraction off where it condenses.

  • Shorter chains have lower boiling points and condense near the top of the column. They are more flammable and less viscous.
  • Longer chains have higher boiling points and condense near the bottom, where the temperature is highest. They are more viscous and burn less cleanly.
  • The fractions, from top to bottom: refinery gas, petrol, kerosene, diesel, fuel oil and bitumen.

The reason for the trend is the intermolecular forces. Longer molecules have more surface contact with each other, so the forces between them are stronger and more energy is needed to separate them, which raises the boiling point. Viscosity follows the same cause: the chains tangle and slide over each other less easily.

2. Alkanes: the first homologous series

A homologous series is a family of compounds with the same general formula, similar chemical properties and a gradual change in physical properties from one member to the next. The alkanes have the general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, contain only single bonds, and are described as saturated because each carbon has as many hydrogen atoms as it can hold.

CH₄, C₂H₆, C₃H₈ and C₄H₁₀ are methane, ethane, propane and butane. The prefix gives the number of carbons, and that is all the naming you need at this level; the suffix -ane tells you the compound is saturated.

  • Structure: every carbon forms four single bonds, arranged tetrahedrally, so the molecule is not flat.
  • Reactivity: low. Single bonds are strong and there is no functional group for a reagent to attack, so alkanes mainly burn or react with halogens in the presence of ultraviolet light.
  • Physical trend: boiling point rises with chain length for the same intermolecular reason as the fractions above.

3. Combustion: complete and incomplete

Alkanes are used as fuels because they burn exothermically. With plenty of oxygen the combustion is complete and the products are carbon dioxide and water.

CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O Key: CH₄ = methane (g); O₂ = oxygen (g); CO₂ = carbon dioxide (g); H₂O = water (g).

With a limited supply of air the combustion is incomplete. The products then include carbon monoxide, a colourless and odourless gas that is toxic because it binds to haemoglobin and stops the blood carrying oxygen, and sometimes soot, which is unburned carbon.

2CH₄ + 3O₂ → 2CO + 4H₂O Key: CO = carbon monoxide (g); the coefficients show that less oxygen is used per molecule of methane than in complete combustion.

Incomplete combustion also releases less energy per mole of fuel, which is why a badly adjusted burner gives less heat as well as more pollution. Sulfur impurities in fuels produce sulfur dioxide when burned, which dissolves in rainwater to form acid rain; that is a fuel-quality problem rather than a property of the hydrocarbon itself.

4. Cracking: matching supply to demand

Crude oil contains more long-chain fractions than the market wants, and more short-chain ones than it produces naturally. Cracking solves that by breaking long chains into shorter ones, using heat and often a catalyst, and it produces alkenes as well as shorter alkanes — which is where the next section comes from.

C₁₀H₂₂ → C₈H₁₈ + C₂H₄ Key: C₁₀H₂₂ = decane, the long chain being broken; C₈H₁₈ = octane, the shorter alkane produced; C₂H₄ = ethene, the alkene produced.

Check the balance: ten carbons on the left, eight plus two on the right; twenty-two hydrogens on the left, eighteen plus four on the right. Cracking is not a reaction with oxygen or with anything else, so the atoms must simply be redistributed, and a balanced check is the fastest way to catch a wrong product.

5. Alkenes and the bromine water test

Alkenes have the general formula CₙH₂ₙ and contain a carbon–carbon double bond, so they are unsaturated: they can add more atoms without losing any. Ethene is C₂H₄ and propene is C₃H₆.

The test that separates an alkene from an alkane is bromine water. Shake the unknown with orange bromine water: an alkene decolourises it, turning the solution from orange to colourless, because the bromine adds across the double bond. An alkane leaves the colour unchanged, because there is no double bond for the bromine to add to.

C₂H₄ + Br₂ → C₂H₄Br₂ Key: C₂H₄ = ethene (g); Br₂ = bromine, orange in solution; C₂H₄Br₂ = 1,2-dibromoethane, colourless.

That change from orange to colourless is the observation to write. "It goes clear" is accepted; "the bromine water stays orange" for an alkene is not.

6. Addition reactions of alkenes

Because the double bond can open up, alkenes undergo addition reactions in which two species join to make one product and nothing is lost. The four the specification asks for are worth learning as a set, because they all follow the same pattern.

  • With hydrogen an alkene becomes an alkane, over a nickel catalyst: C₂H₄ + H₂ → C₂H₆. This is hydrogenation, the reaction used to harden vegetable oil into margarine.
  • With steam an alkene becomes an alcohol, over a phosphoric acid catalyst at about 300 °C and high pressure: C₂H₄ + H₂O → C₂H₅OH.
  • With bromine it forms a dibromoalkane, as above, which is the test reaction.
  • With hydrogen chloride it forms a chloroalkane: C₂H₄ + HCl → C₂H₅Cl.

In every case the double bond becomes a single bond and the two new atoms attach to the carbons that were double-bonded. Notice that no small molecule is eliminated, which is what distinguishes an addition from a condensation.

7. Alcohols and carboxylic acids

Ethanol, C₂H₅OH, is made in two ways. Fermentation uses yeast on a sugar solution at about 25 to 35 °C in the absence of oxygen: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂. Hydration of ethene is the industrial route described above, and it is faster and purer but needs a catalyst, heat and pressure.

  • Fermentation is cheap and uses renewable sugar, but it is slow and the product is dilute, so it must be distilled.
  • Hydration is fast and gives a concentrated product, but it uses ethene from crude oil, which is not renewable.
  • Ethanol as a fuel burns to carbon dioxide and water and can be blended into petrol, but growing the sugar competes with food crops for land.

Carboxylic acids contain the functional group –COOH. Ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH, is the acid in vinegar, and it behaves like the mineral acids of topic 3.5: it neutralises bases, reacts with carbonates to give carbon dioxide, and reacts with an alcohol to form an ester. That last reaction, esterification, is condensation — two molecules join and a small molecule of water is eliminated.

8. Addition polymerisation

Under the right conditions the double bond of an alkene opens and the molecules join into a long chain without losing any atoms. This is addition polymerisation, and the monomer and the repeating unit have the same empirical formula, which is why the equation is written with the repeat unit in brackets and an n after it.

n C₂H₄ → (–CH₂–CH₂–)ₙ Key: C₂H₄ = ethene, the monomer; the bracket shows the repeating unit; n = the number of monomer units joined, which is large and variable.

  • Poly(ethene) from ethene: bags, bottles and film. It is tough, flexible and unreactive.
  • Poly(propene) from propene: ropes, carpets and food containers.
  • PVC from chloroethene: window frames and pipes, because it is rigid and does not conduct.
  • PTFE from tetrafluoroethene: non-stick coatings, because it is very unreactive and has a low friction surface.

Two consequences follow from the structure. Addition polymers have no functional group to attack, so they are unreactive and do not biodegrade, which is why plastic waste persists. And because the chains are long and tangled, they soften on heating and can be remoulded, which is what makes recycling possible for many of them.

9. Condensation polymers and natural polymers

In condensation polymerisation two different monomers, each with two functional groups, join and eliminate a small molecule — usually water — at every link. Polyesters and nylons are made this way. PET, used in drinks bottles, is made from ethane-1,2-diol and benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid, and the link that forms is an ester link.

PolymerTypeMonomer or monomersWhere it occurs
Poly(ethene)AdditionEtheneSynthetic, from crude oil
PETCondensationA diol and a dicarboxylic acidSynthetic, bottles and fibres
StarchCondensationGlucoseNatural, energy store in plants
CelluloseCondensationGlucoseNatural, plant cell walls
ProteinCondensationAmino acidsNatural, enzymes, muscle and hair
DNACondensationNucleotidesNatural, genetic material

The natural polymers are condensation polymers made by living things. Starch and cellulose are both built from glucose but linked differently, which is why humans can digest starch and not cellulose. Proteins are chains of amino acids joined by peptide links, and the order of those amino acids determines the shape of the protein and therefore its function. DNA is a chain of nucleotides whose order carries the genetic code. All of them are biodegradable, because organisms have enzymes that can break the links — which is precisely what addition polymers lack.

10. Worked example: from monomer to polymer

A sample of poly(ethene) has a relative molecular mass of 8 400. Calculate the number of ethene units in the chain, and state the mass of bromine that would be needed to decolourise 0.020 mol of ethene.

The repeat unit is C₂H₄, with Mᵣ = 2 × 12 + 4 × 1 = 28. The number of units is 8 400 ÷ 28 = 300.

Key: Mᵣ = relative molecular mass, with no unit; 12 and 1 are the relative atomic masses of carbon and hydrogen; the number of units is the polymer's mass divided by the mass of one repeat unit.

Ethene reacts with bromine in a 1:1 ratio, so 0.020 mol of ethene needs 0.020 mol of Br₂. The mass is 0.020 mol × 160 g/mol = 3.2 g, using Mᵣ(Br₂) = 2 × 80 = 160.

Key: mol = amount of substance (mol); 160 g/mol = the relative molecular mass of bromine expressed as grams per mole; 3.2 g = the mass of bromine required.

The two halves of that question are the two skills this topic tests: counting repeat units, and using a mole ratio from an addition reaction. Neither needs the structure drawn out, which is why the calculation is worth practising rather than the drawing.

11. Typical mistakes

  • Writing an alkene's formula with the alkane's general formula. Ethene is C₂H₄, not C₂H₆.
  • Saying bromine water goes colourless for an alkane. It stays orange; only the alkene decolourises it.
  • Forgetting that addition polymerisation loses no atoms, so the empirical formula of the polymer is the same as the monomer's.
  • Drawing a condensation polymer without eliminating the small molecule, which leaves the formula one water too heavy at every link.
  • Claiming all plastics are non-biodegradable. Starch, cellulose and proteins are polymers and all biodegrade; the problem is specific to addition polymers such as poly(ethene).
  • Calling carbon monoxide "just carbon dioxide with less oxygen". It is a different compound with a different effect: it is toxic because it binds to haemoglobin.
  • Using "cracking" and "combustion" interchangeably. Cracking breaks chains without oxygen; combustion reacts the fuel with oxygen.

12. Exam-style questions

  1. Explain why petrol has a lower boiling point than bitumen. Answer: Petrol is a mixture of shorter hydrocarbon chains, which have weaker intermolecular forces between the molecules, so less energy is needed to separate them.
  2. Describe the test that distinguishes ethene from ethane, including the observation. Answer: Shake each gas with orange bromine water; ethene decolourises it, turning it colourless, while ethane leaves it orange.
  3. Write the equation for the complete combustion of propane, C₃H₈. Answer: C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O.
  4. Explain why cracking is used in the oil industry. Answer: It breaks long-chain fractions, for which demand is low, into shorter chains that are in demand as fuels, and it produces alkenes such as ethene, which are needed to make polymers.
  5. State two ways ethanol can be produced and give one advantage of each. Answer: Fermentation of sugar with yeast uses a renewable raw material and is cheap; hydration of ethene is fast and gives a concentrated product.
  6. Name the type of polymerisation that makes poly(ethene) and state what happens to the double bond. Answer: Addition polymerisation; the double bond opens and the molecules join without losing any atoms.
  7. Explain why poly(ethene) does not biodegrade while starch does. Answer: Poly(ethene) has a carbon chain with no functional group that enzymes can attack, so microorganisms cannot break it down, whereas starch has glycosidic links that enzymes can hydrolyse.
  8. 0.050 mol of propene reacts completely with bromine. Calculate the mass of bromine used. Answer: The ratio is 1:1, so 0.050 mol of Br₂ is needed; mass = 0.050 × 160 = 8.0 g.

13. Revision checklist

  • I can define a hydrocarbon and a homologous series.
  • I can explain fractional distillation and the trend in boiling point with chain length.
  • I can write the general formulas of alkanes and alkenes and name the first four of each.
  • I can write complete and incomplete combustion equations.
  • I can explain what cracking does and balance a cracking equation.
  • I can describe the bromine water test and its observation.
  • I can name the four addition reactions of alkenes and their products.
  • I can describe fermentation and hydration as routes to ethanol.
  • I can distinguish addition from condensation polymerisation.
  • I can name two synthetic and three natural polymers with their monomers.
  • I can calculate repeat units and use a 1:1 mole ratio from an addition reaction.

title: Exam technique: Further Trigonometry
content:
### What earns the marks
For multiple solutions, the full period family (180-2x style use of all quadrants) earns both marks. For R-formulae, completing Rcos(x-a) earns the method mark and R and alpha earn one each. For trig proofs, each identity substitution earns stepwise credit.

Quick revision: Data Representation

How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

### Worked example Convert 157 to binary by using place values 128 + 16 + 8 + 4 + 1 = 157, which gives 10011101. Grouping the bits in fours gives 1001 1101, which is 9D in hexadecimal, and 9 × 16 + 13 = 157 confirms it. An 8-bit unsigned number can represent 0 to 255.

Key points to remember

Computers store all data as binary. Convert denary to binary by repeatedly dividing by two or by subtracting place values from 128 down to 1. Hexadecimal groups four bits per digit, so 1111 1010 is FA in hex. Two's complement represents negative integers: invert the bits of the positive value and add one, and the leftmost bit is the sign.

Text is stored using character sets such as ASCII, where each character has a fixed numeric code. Images are stored as pixels, each holding a colour value, and sound as samples of amplitude taken at a sample rate. Show your working for every conversion, because a single wrong bit loses the whole mark.

title: Networking & Communication — Study Notes
content:
Networking & Communication

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): transmission modes, serial/parallel, packet switching, protocols, LAN/WAN, hardware, security layers.

1. Transmission basics

  • Serial: one bit at a time — reliable over distance, cheaper cable.
  • Parallel: several bits at once — faster over short runs; skew/crosstalk limit distance.
  • Simplex / half-duplex / full-duplex direction; bandwidth (bits/s) vs bit rate.

2. Packets

Header (sender/receiver addresses, sequence number) + payload + trailer (checksum). Packet switching: routes vary, packets reassembled at destination; checksum failure → re-request. Benefits: robustness, shared lines; delays/reassembly overhead.

3. Protocols

TCP/IP stack layers (application, transport, network, link). HTTP/HTTPS (TLS encryption), FTP (with login + commands), email: SMTP send, POP3/IMAP retrieve. Bluetooth/Wi-Fi for WPAN/WLAN.

4. Network types & hardware

LAN (site) vs WAN (internet). Router (joins networks, IP), switch (MAC frames within LAN), gateway (protocol translation), NIC, WAP. MAC address (burned-in, layer 2) vs IP address (assigned, layer 3).

5. Security in transmission

Encryption scrambles plaintext → ciphertext (key needed); HTTPS = HTTP over TLS; firewall packet filtering by port/IP; authentication (user+pass, 2FA); access levels.

Exam tips: explain why skew limits parallel over distance; compare MAC vs IP in a table; protocol questions want "rules for communication", not acronyms alone.

Packet switching and protocols

In packet switching, a message is divided into packets. Each packet carries a header with its source and destination addresses and a sequence number, so it can travel by any available route. The packets are reassembled in the correct order at the destination. Packet switching makes efficient use of the network, because no dedicated connection is held open for the whole transmission.

A protocol is an agreed set of rules that devices follow to communicate. TCP/IP is the set of protocols used on the internet. TCP splits data into packets and checks that they arrive, while IP handles addressing and routing between networks.

Exam tip: explain a protocol as a set of rules, and give one example of what it governs, such as addressing or error checking.

Worked example: working out a subnet

A device has the IP address 192.168.1.10 with the subnet mask 255.255.255.0. Applying the mask with a bitwise AND gives the network address 192.168.1.0. The first usable host address is 192.168.1.1 and the last is 192.168.1.254, because the all-zeros address is the network and the all-ones address is the broadcast. Question setters often ask for the broadcast address, which here is 192.168.1.255.

Packets, protocols and layers

  • A message is split into packets. Each packet carries a header with the source and destination addresses and a sequence number so the receiver can rebuild the message in order.
  • Protocols define the rules for each layer. TCP checks for lost packets and requests a resend, while UDP sends without that checking, which suits live video and gaming.

title: Kinematics — Study Notes
content:
Kinematics

This note covers motion in a straight line and projectile motion for the Edexcel International A Level Physics specification, Unit 1 (WPH11), sat at AS. Kinematics describes how position, velocity and acceleration change with time, without asking what causes the motion. Most exam marks come from choosing the right tool, setting a sign convention, and reading graphs correctly.

Definitions

  • Distance and speed are scalars: they have magnitude only.
  • Displacement s and velocity v are vectors: they have magnitude and direction. Displacement is the change in position, measured from a fixed origin.
  • Velocity is the rate of change of displacement: v = ds/dt.
  • Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity: a = dv/dt. An object moving at constant speed around a circle is accelerating, because its direction is changing.

Speed is the magnitude of velocity. An object that travels 60 m in one direction and then 20 m back has a distance of 80 m and a displacement of 40 m.

Interpreting graphs

  • On a displacement–time graph, the gradient is the velocity. A horizontal line means the object is at rest, and a steeper line means a higher speed.
  • On a velocity–time graph, the gradient is the acceleration. A straight line with constant gradient means uniform acceleration. A horizontal line means constant velocity.
  • The area under a velocity–time graph equals the displacement. Area below the time axis counts as negative, so a return journey partly cancels out.
  • On an acceleration–time graph, the area under the line equals the change in velocity.

Worked example. A velocity–time graph rises from 0 to 12 m s⁻¹ in 4 s, stays at 12 m s⁻¹ for 6 s, then falls to 0 in 3 s. The area of the triangle is ½ × 4 × 12 = 24 m, the rectangle is 6 × 12 = 72 m, and the final triangle is ½ × 3 × 12 = 18 m. The total displacement is 114 m. The accelerations are 3 m s⁻² for the first 4 s and −4 m s⁻² for the last 3 s.

SUVAT equations (uniform acceleration only)

SUVAT stands for displacement s, initial velocity u, final velocity v, acceleration a and time t. The four equations below apply only when acceleration is constant.

EquationQuantity not involved
v = u + ats
s = ut + ½at²v
v² = u² + 2ast
s = ½(u + v)ta

Choose the equation that omits the quantity you were not given and do not need. Writing down the list of known and unknown quantities first prevents most errors. Pick a sign convention at the start, normally taking the direction of motion, or up, as positive. For a body falling freely under gravity with up as positive, a = −9.81 m s⁻² (or −9.8 m s⁻² if the question uses g = 9.8).

Worked example. A car accelerates from 5 m s⁻¹ to 25 m s⁻¹ at 2 m s⁻². The time is found from v = u + at: 25 = 5 + 2t, so t = 10 s. The distance follows from v² = u² + 2as: 625 = 25 + 4s, so s = 150 m. Check with s = ½(u + v)t = ½ × 30 × 10 = 150 m.

Non-uniform motion

  • When acceleration is not constant, SUVAT cannot be used. Work from the graphs, or from a displacement function such as s = 3t² − t³, differentiating for velocity and acceleration.
  • Average speed is total distance divided by total time. Average velocity is total displacement divided by total time. These differ whenever the object changes direction.
  • The gradient at a point on a curved graph is the gradient of the tangent at that point. Estimate it by drawing the tangent carefully, and state which point you used.

Projectile motion

A projectile moves under gravity alone, with air resistance ignored. Resolve the launch velocity into two independent components:

  • Horizontal: uₓ = u cos θ. There is no acceleration, so the horizontal velocity stays constant and s = uₓt.
  • Vertical: u_y = u sin θ. The acceleration is g downwards, so SUVAT applies to this component alone.

The two motions share only the time t. At the highest point the vertical velocity is zero, so the time to reach the top is u_y/g. If the object lands at the same height it was launched from, the time of flight is 2u_y/g.

Worked example. A ball is launched at 20 m s⁻¹ at 30° above the horizontal from level ground. uₓ = 20 cos 30° ≈ 17.3 m s⁻¹ and u_y = 20 sin 30° = 10 m s⁻¹. The time of flight is 2 × 10 / 9.81 ≈ 2.04 s. The horizontal range is 17.3 × 2.04 ≈ 35 m. The maximum height is u_y²/(2g) = 100 / 19.62 ≈ 5.1 m.

Exam tips

  • Write the sign convention at the top of your working. Many lost marks come from a sign error in a vertical question.
  • Check whether the question asks for speed or velocity, and distance or displacement. The words decide which quantity to give.
  • Treat the horizontal and vertical motions of a projectile as two one-dimensional problems linked only by time.
  • When a graph is given, say which feature (gradient or area) gives the quantity you want before you calculate it.

title: Bearings and Loci
content:
Mensuration — Bearings and Loci

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): compass bearings, scale drawings, constructions (perpendicular/angle bisectors), loci regions.

1. Bearings

  • Measured clockwise from north; three figures: 065°, 128°, 300°.
  • Back bearing = front bearing ± 180°.
  • Draw a north line at both points; north lines are parallel, giving Z-angles.

Example: B is on bearing 070° from A → A is on bearing 250° from B.

2. Scale drawings

1 cm : 500 m style scales; measure, convert, and quote distances/bearings from your drawing to the accuracy allowed.

3. Constructions

  • Perpendicular bisector of a segment: equal arcs from both ends, join the crossings.
  • Angle bisector: equal arcs from the vertex arms.
  • 60° and 90° constructions with compasses; leave all arcs visible.

4. Loci

Fixed distance from a point = circle; from a line = parallel lines with rounded ends; equidistant from two points = perpendicular bisector; from two lines = angle bisector.

Example: a goat tied by a 5 m rope to a corner of a 4 m × 6 m shed: the reachable region is ¾ circle radius 5 m + two ¼ circles radius 1 m where the rope wraps.

Exam tips: state "clockwise from north" in bearing definitions; shade/label locus regions clearly; use a ruler for construction lines too.
