title: IGCSE Biology: Organisms and their Environment
content:
IGCSE Biology: Organisms and their Environment

Ecology is the accounting of life: where the energy comes from, how much of it moves from level to level, and how the materials (carbon, nitrogen) are endlessly recycled while the energy flows through and out. This note builds food chains and food webs from producers up, explains why only about 10 % of energy passes between levels (with the transfer-efficiency calculations fully worked), traces the carbon and nitrogen cycles step by step, and finishes with population measurement and the factors that control population size. Every cycle is written as a numbered sequence so you can reproduce it in the exam.

Energy flow: producers, consumers and decomposers

Almost all ecosystems are powered by the Sun. Producers (green plants and algae) trap light energy by photosynthesis and convert it into chemical energy in glucose — the base of every food chain. Consumers eat other organisms: primary consumers (herbivores) eat producers; secondary consumers (carnivores) eat herbivores; tertiary consumers eat other carnivores. Decomposers (bacteria and fungi) break down dead organisms and waste, releasing nutrients back to the environment and respiring energy as heat. Detritivores (earthworms, woodlice) feed on detritus (dead material), fragmenting it for decomposers. The flow is one-way: light → chemical energy in producers → consumers → heat lost at every stage; materials, in contrast, cycle.

Food chains, food webs and trophic levels

A food chain shows the transfer of food energy from one trophic level to the next: maize (producer) → locust (primary consumer) → lizard (secondary) → hawk (tertiary). Arrow direction is critical — always point from the organism being eaten to the eater, representing the direction of energy flow. A food web is many interconnected food chains (more realistic); removing one species can cascade through the web — a favourite "explain the consequence" question. Each organism occupies a trophic level: level 1 producers, level 2 primary consumers, and so on. DDT and other persistent poisons accumulate up the chain (biomagnification): the top predator has the highest concentration, which is why raptor eggshells thinned after DDT use.

Pyramids and energy transfer efficiency

Pyramids of numbers count organisms (can be inverted — one tree feeding many caterpillars); pyramids of biomass show the dry mass at each level (usually upright, measured in g/m²); pyramids of energy (kJ/m²/year) are always upright because energy is lost at each transfer. Where does the energy go between levels? Much of the food is not digested (egested in faeces); some is lost in respiration as heat (the largest loss); some goes into growth, but parts are inedible (bones, fur) or become detritus. The result: only about 10 % of the biomass/energy at one level passes to the next. Calculation: if producers contain 20 000 kJ, primary consumers receive about 2 000 kJ, secondary consumers about 200 kJ, tertiary about 20 kJ — divide by 10 at each step. Percentage efficiency = (energy transferred to next level ÷ energy available at this level) × 100. This is why food chains rarely exceed four or five levels: not enough energy remains at the top, and it is why eating lower on the chain (plant-based diets) can feed more people — a linked food-supply question.

Energy at each trophic level

Trophic levelRoleTypical energy (kJ per m² per year)
1Producers (photosynthetic)20 000
2Primary consumers (herbivores)2 000
3Secondary consumers (carnivores)200
4Tertiary consumers (top carnivores)20

Worked example: energy-transfer calculations

A grassland fixes 25 000 kJ per m² per year. Grasshoppers assimilate 2 500 kJ; frogs 250 kJ; snakes 25 kJ. Step 1: check each transfer: 2 500 ÷ 25 000 = 0.10 = 10 %; 250 ÷ 2 500 = 10 %; 25 ÷ 250 = 10 % — consistent with the 10 % rule. Step 2: what happens to the rest? At each level, energy is lost as heat in respiration, in faeces (undigested material), and in uneaten parts. Step 3: question variants: if the snake level must support 10 000 kJ of snake biomass, how much producer is needed? 10 000 → 100 000 (frogs) → 1 000 000 (grasshoppers) → 10 000 000 kJ of grass — show the three multiplications. Step 4: biomass units: dry mass is used (water varies and is not energy), measured by drying samples to constant mass in an oven — a standard Paper 6 method note. Efficiency questions always want the working shown: division by the level below and the percentage written with its unit.

The carbon cycle

Carbon cycles between the atmosphere, living things and the oceans. Step 1: photosynthesis removes carbon dioxide from the air and fixes carbon into glucose and biomass. Step 2: feeding passes carbon along food chains. Step 3: respiration by all organisms returns carbon dioxide to the atmosphere. Step 4: decomposers respire the carbon in dead organisms and waste back to the air as carbon dioxide. Step 5: combustion of fossil fuels (coal, oil, gas) releases carbon that was locked away for millions of years. Step 6: carbon is also stored (sequestered) in fossil fuels, carbonate rocks, oceans (dissolved carbon dioxide and carbonates) and forests. Human impact: burning fossil fuels and deforestation have raised atmospheric carbon dioxide, intensifying the greenhouse effect and global climate change — cutting this cycle's balance is the core of the climate topic.

The nitrogen cycle

Nitrogen is essential for proteins and nucleic acids, and although the air is 78 % nitrogen gas, animals and plants cannot use it directly — the nitrogen cycle has four key bacterial steps. Step 1: nitrogen fixation — nitrogen-fixing bacteria (Rhizobium in root nodules of legumes, Azotobacter in soil) convert nitrogen gas into ammonia and then ammonium compounds in the soil. Step 2: nitrification — nitrifying bacteria (Nitrosomonas: ammonium to nitrite; Nitrobacter: nitrite to nitrate) oxidise ammonium compounds to nitrates, the form plants absorb by root hairs (active transport). Step 3: assimilation — plants take up nitrates and build them into amino acids and proteins; animals obtain nitrogen by eating plants or other animals. Step 4: ammonification — decomposers break down proteins in dead organisms and urea in waste, releasing ammonia/ammonium compounds. Step 5: denitrification — anaerobic bacteria (in waterlogged/poorly aerated soil) convert nitrates back to nitrogen gas, returning it to the air — a loss for farmers, which is why ploughing and drainage (aeration) and fertilisers are used. Fertilisers (natural: manure and compost; artificial: NPK) replace the nitrates removed at harvest.

Populations and population size

A population is all the organisms of one species in an area at a given time; a community is all the populations of different species living together; an ecosystem is the community plus the abiotic (non-living) environment — light, temperature, water, soil pH, mineral ions, carbon dioxide. Population size depends on: birth rate, death rate, immigration and emigration; and it is limited by competition (for light, water, space, nutrients), predation, disease and climate. A typical population growth curve: a lag phase (establishment), a log (exponential) phase (resources plentiful), a stationary phase (births = deaths, resources limiting) and sometimes a decline (resources exhausted). Sampling methods: quadrats (random sampling for plants and slow organisms — throw the quadrat randomly, count within, repeat for a mean), and mark-release-recapture (trap, mark, release, recapture later; population = (number in first catch × number in second catch) ÷ number marked in second catch) for mobile animals. The assumptions of mark-release-recapture: marks do not rub off or harm the animal, the marked animals mix fully with the population, and there are no significant births, deaths or migrations between samplings.

Worked example: population estimation

Ecologists trap 40 mice, mark them and release them. A week later they trap 50 mice, of which 20 are marked. Step 1: the formula — total population = (first catch × second catch) ÷ marked in second catch. Step 2: substitute — (40 × 50) ÷ 20 = 2000 ÷ 20 = 100 mice. Step 3: evaluate the reliability — the sample sizes are small and marks may have rubbed off, giving a wide confidence; repeat the recapture and take a mean. Quadrat example: five 1 m² quadrats contain 12, 15, 9, 14 and 10 dandelions; mean = (12 + 15 + 9 + 14 + 10) ÷ 5 = 60 ÷ 5 = 12 dandelions per m²; for a 200 m² field, the estimated population is 12 × 200 = 2 400. Always show the sum and the division, and quote units (organisms per m²).

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Pointing food-chain arrows from eater to eaten — the arrow shows energy flow, so it points to the eater.
  • Writing that energy "cycles" like carbon: energy flows through and is lost as heat; only materials cycle.
  • Using wet mass for biomass pyramids: dry mass is required because water content varies.
  • Skipping the 10 % rule in energy questions: always divide by 10 (or multiply by 0.1) per level and show it.
  • Confusing nitrogen gas with nitrates: plants absorb nitrates (and ammonium), not atmospheric nitrogen; bacteria convert the gas.
  • Mixing up nitrification (bacteria making nitrates) and denitrification (bacteria releasing nitrogen gas).
  • Confusing population (one species) with community (all species) in definitions.
  • Forgetting the assumptions of mark-release-recapture when evaluating a population estimate.

Exam-style questions and answers

Q1. Explain why food chains rarely have more than five trophic levels. (2 marks) Answer: only about 10 % of energy passes to each successive level (1); so insufficient energy remains at higher levels to support another population (1).

Q2. Describe the role of nitrifying bacteria in the nitrogen cycle. (2 marks) Answer: they oxidise ammonium compounds first to nitrites and then to nitrates (1); the form of nitrogen that plant roots absorb (1).

Q3. A grassland producer level contains 50 000 kJ. Calculate the energy available to secondary consumers. (2 marks) Answer: 50 000 ÷ 10 ÷ 10 (1); = 500 kJ (1).

Q4. Describe how you would estimate the population of dandelions in a field. (3 marks) Answer: use quadrats thrown at random coordinates (1); count dandelions in each and calculate the mean per m² (1); multiply by the total field area (1).

Q5. Explain the effect of deforestation on the carbon cycle and climate. (3 marks) Answer: fewer trees means less photosynthesis removing carbon dioxide (1); burning or rotting trees releases stored carbon (1); atmospheric carbon dioxide rises intensifying the greenhouse effect and global warming (1).

Equations and symbols

Ecology questions look descriptive but are marked on arithmetic: a transfer efficiency, a pyramid step, a mark-release-recapture estimate, a quadrat mean. These five relations cover every calculation in the topic.

Percentage efficiency = (energy transferred to next level ÷ energy available at this level) × 100 Key: energy transferred = energy in the biomass of the next trophic level (kJ m⁻² year⁻¹); energy available = energy in the biomass of the level below (kJ m⁻² year⁻¹); the answer is a percentage, typically about 10 %. Do not divide by the top level and do not forget the × 100.

2 500 ÷ 25 000 = 0.10 = 10 % Key: 2 500 = energy assimilated by grasshoppers (kJ m⁻² year⁻¹); 25 000 = energy fixed by the grassland (kJ m⁻² year⁻¹); 0.10 = the transfer efficiency as a decimal, which is 10 % as a percentage. The same division at each step is the whole 10 % rule.

population = (number in first catch × number in second catch) ÷ number marked in second catch Key: first catch = animals caught, marked and released (individuals); second catch = animals caught on the recapture visit (individuals); marked in second catch = how many of those already carried a mark (individuals); population = estimated total in the habitat (individuals). Assumes marks do not rub off, marked animals mix fully, and no births, deaths or migration between visits.

(40 × 50) ÷ 20 = 2000 ÷ 20 = 100 mice Key: 40 = mice marked and released; 50 = mice in the recapture; 20 = marked mice in the recapture; 100 = estimated population size (mice). If more than half the recapture is marked, the population is small — a sanity check worth one line.

mean = (12 + 15 + 9 + 14 + 10) ÷ 5 = 60 ÷ 5 = 12 dandelions per m² Key: the five counts = dandelions per 1 m² quadrat (individuals m⁻²); 5 = number of quadrats; 12 = mean density (individuals m⁻²). Multiply the mean density by the habitat area to estimate the population — 12 × 200 = 2 400 for a 200 m² field.

12 × 200 = 2 400 Key: 12 = mean density from the quadrats (dandelions per m²); 200 = area of the field (m²); 2 400 = estimated population (dandelions). The mean is only a density; multiplying by the area is the step that turns it into a population, and it is worth a mark of its own.

10 000 → 100 000 (frogs) → 1 000 000 (grasshoppers) → 10 000 000 kJ of grass Key: 10 000 kJ = energy the top level must receive; each arrow is one trophic step backwards, multiplying by 10; 10 000 000 kJ = producer energy needed. Work backwards with × 10, forwards with ÷ 10, and say which direction you used.

title: Functions — Study Notes
content:
Functions

This note builds the functions work used throughout the Edexcel International A Level Mathematics — Pure Mathematics 1 (WMA11) course. A function maps each input in its domain to exactly one output in its range. Notation such as f(x) = 2x + 1 names the rule, and the examiner expects you to state domain, range and inverse clearly.

Domain, range and notation

The domain is the set of inputs the function accepts. Restrictions usually come from denominators (which cannot be zero), square roots (which need a non-negative argument) and logarithms (which need a positive argument). The range is the set of outputs the function actually produces over that domain. For f(x) = x² on all real numbers, the range is f(x) ≥ 0. Writing the domain as x ≥ 0 gives the same range but changes whether an inverse exists.

A many-to-one function, such as x² on all reals, sends two inputs to the same output. A one-to-one function never does. Only one-to-one functions have inverses.

Composite functions

The composite function fg(x) means f(g(x)): apply g first, then f to the result. Order matters, so in general fg(x) and gf(x) are different functions.

Example: f(x) = 2x + 1 and g(x) = x².

  • fg(x) = f(x²) = 2x² + 1
  • gf(x) = g(2x + 1) = (2x + 1)² = 4x² + 4x + 1

When a restriction is involved, check the range of the inner function against the domain of the outer one. If g(x) = x − 3 with domain x ≥ 0 is followed by f(x) = √x, the range of g is x ≥ −3, which is wider than the domain of f, so the composite fg(x) = √(x − 3) needs x ≥ 3 to be defined. The exam often asks for this domain explicitly.

Inverse functions

The inverse f⁻¹ reverses the action of f, so f⁻¹(f(x)) = x. To find it, write y = f(x), swap x and y, then rearrange to make y the subject.

Example: f(x) = 3x − 2. Write y = 3x − 2, swap to x = 3y − 2, then y = (x + 2)/3. So f⁻¹(x) = (x + 2)/3. Check by substituting: f(f⁻¹(x)) = 3 × (x + 2)/3 − 2 = x.

An inverse exists only if f is one-to-one on its domain. If it is not, restrict the domain to make it so. For f(x) = x² with domain x ≥ 0, the inverse is f⁻¹(x) = √x with domain x ≥ 0. Without the restriction, x² would have no single inverse, because both 3 and −3 square to 9.

The domain of f⁻¹ is the range of f, and the range of f⁻¹ is the domain of f. The graph of y = f⁻¹(x) is the reflection of y = f(x) in the line y = x, so a point (a, b) on f becomes (b, a) on f⁻¹. Use this to check an answer: if (2, 5) is on the graph of f, then (5, 2) must be on the graph of f⁻¹.

Transformations of graphs

Each change to the rule moves or stretches the graph in a predictable way. Learn these as a table:

Transformed graphEffect on the graph of y = f(x)
y = f(x) + atranslation by a units up (a < 0: down)
y = f(x + a)translation by a units left (a < 0: right)
y = a f(x)vertical stretch, scale factor a
y = f(ax)horizontal stretch, scale factor 1/a
y = −f(x)reflection in the x-axis
y = f(−x)reflection in the y-axis

The horizontal translation runs against the sign: y = (x − 3)² is the graph of x² moved 3 units to the right. A common error is to move it left. For a sequence of transformations, apply them in the order the question gives, tracking a few key points such as the vertex or the intercepts.

Method for exam questions

  • For a composite function, write out fg(x) and gf(x) separately whenever the question names two functions, and simplify each.
  • For an inverse, state both the rule and its domain. A correct rule with the domain missing loses marks.
  • To show a function has an inverse, argue that it is one-to-one on the stated domain, usually because it is strictly increasing or strictly decreasing there.
  • When sketching y = f⁻¹(x), reflect the graph of f in y = x and mark where the line crosses it, since that point lies on both graphs.

Exam cue: whenever a question says "hence" or "using your answer to part", the composite or inverse from the earlier part is usually the route to the answer, so keep it in simplified form.

title: AS Level Biology: Cell Structure, Reproduction and Development
content:
Cell Structure, Reproduction and Development — AS Level Biology

This revision note belongs to the Edexcel International Advanced Subsidiary (IAS) Biology specification, WBI12 Unit 2, Topic 3 Cell Structure, Reproduction and Development. It covers the cell as the unit of life, eukaryotic and prokaryotic ultrastructure, microscopy and measurement, the cell cycle and mitosis, meiosis and genetic variation, gametes and fertilisation in mammals and flowering plants, stem cells, and the genetic control of development through gene expression, epigenetics and inheritance. Every statement below the topic owns is covered in its own section or paragraph.

1. Cells as the units of life and the levels of organisation

All living organisms are made of cells, and all cells share some common features: a plasma membrane (cell surface membrane) enclosing the cell, cytoplasm in which most chemical reactions occur, and ribosomes for protein synthesis. Differences between cell types are explained from these common features — for example the presence or absence of a cell wall, a nucleus, or membrane-bound organelles decides what a cell can do. In multicellular organisms, cells are organised into tissues, tissues into organs, and organs into organ systems, each level carrying out a particular function. A tissue is a group of similar cells working together; an organ is made of several tissues with a combined function; an organ system is a group of organs whose functions are linked, such as the digestive system. Understanding this hierarchy matters because a structure at one level is shaped by the level below it — the properties of a tissue follow from the cells it contains.

2. Eukaryotic cell ultrastructure and the functions of the organelles

Eukaryotic cells have a membrane-bound nucleus that contains the chromosomes, and a range of membrane-bound organelles, each with a distinct function. The plasma membrane (cell surface membrane) is a phospholipid bilayer with proteins embedded in it, controlling what enters and leaves the cell. The nucleus is surrounded by a double nuclear envelope with nuclear pores, and contains the cell’s DNA; the nucleolus inside the nucleus is the site of ribosome assembly. Ribosomes, made of a large and a small subunit, are the sites of protein synthesis and occur free in the cytoplasm or attached to the rough endoplasmic reticulum. The rough endoplasmic reticulum (rER) is a stack of membrane-bound sacs studded with ribosomes; it synthesises proteins and passes them on in vesicles. The smooth endoplasmic reticulum (sER) lacks ribosomes and synthesises lipids and carbohydrates. Mitochondria have a double membrane, the inner one folded into cristae to increase surface area, and a matrix that contains the enzymes for aerobic respiration; they supply ATP. Centrioles are paired microtubule cylinders that organise the spindle fibres during nuclear division. Lysosomes are membrane-bound sacs containing hydrolytic enzymes that digest worn-out cell components and pathogens. The Golgi apparatus modifies, sorts and packages proteins into vesicles for secretion or for delivery to other parts of the cell; it is also involved in the formation of extracellular enzymes. The cytoskeleton of microtubules and microfilaments maintains cell shape, holds organelles in place and enables movement within the cell.

3. Prokaryotic cell ultrastructure and how to tell the two apart

Prokaryotic cells are much smaller than eukaryotic cells and lack a membrane-bound nucleus. Their genetic material is a single, circular DNA molecule that lies free in the cytoplasm, not associated with histones. The cell wall is made of peptidoglycan and gives rigidity and shape. Many prokaryotes have a protective capsule outside the cell wall. Plasmids are small circles of DNA separate from the main chromosome; they can be transferred between cells and often carry genes for antibiotic resistance. Flagella — rigid helical tails that rotate — give motility in some prokaryotes, and pili help cells attach to surfaces and to each other and mediate conjugation. Prokaryotic ribosomes are 70S, smaller than the 80S ribosomes of eukaryotes. A bacterium therefore shows, in EM images: cell wall, capsule, plasma membrane, circular DNA free in the cytoplasm, 70S ribosomes, plasmids, and, where present, flagella and pili — and none of the membrane-bound organelles found in a eukaryotic cell.

4. Seeing the ultrastructure: light and electron microscopy

A light microscope uses visible light passed through a specimen; its maximum useful magnification is around ×1500 and its resolution is about 0.2 µm, limited by the wavelength of light. An electron microscope uses a beam of electrons, giving far higher resolution and magnification; transmission electron microscopes (TEM) show the internal ultrastructure of thin sections, and scanning electron microscopes (SEM) show the surface detail of a specimen. Staining is essential in light microscopy because most cells are transparent — stains such as methylene blue for animal cells or iodine solution for starch make structures visible and show up nuclei, starch grains and cell walls. The electron microscope can show the organelles listed in 3.3 — nucleus, nucleolus, ribosomes, rER, sER, mitochondria, centrioles, lysosomes, Golgi apparatus — and, in prokaryotes, the cell wall, capsule, plasma membrane, circular DNA, 70S ribosomes, flagella and pili, so that students can recognise the organelles from electron micrographs. In a light microscope the total magnification equals eyepiece magnification × objective magnification; a graticule (eye-piece graticule) fitted with a stage micrometer lets you calibrate it so real sizes can be measured, and specimens can be drawn to scale from the microscope.

5. Core Practical 5 — observing and drawing animal cells

Use a light microscope to make observations and labelled drawings of suitable animal cells, for example cheek epithelial cells. The steps are: sterilise by wiping the mouth, smear a thin layer of cells onto a slide, stain with methylene blue, lower a coverslip at an angle to avoid air bubbles, and observe under the microscope. Draw what you see with the correct relative sizes of nucleus, cytoplasm and cell membrane, label the parts, and add a title and magnification. Core Practical 5 also develops the skill of using a graticule with a microscope to make measurements and understand the concept of scale — the graticule is calibrated against a stage micrometer at each objective, so the real size of a cell or organelle can be calculated from the number of graticule divisions it spans.

6. Cell division: mitosis, the cell cycle and genetic variation by meiosis

Mitosis produces genetically identical daughter cells for growth and asexual reproduction and is one part of the cell cycle, which is the regular sequence of events in a dividing cell: interphase (during which the cell grows, and DNA is replicated — G1, S and G2), mitosis and cytokinesis. Mitosis itself has stages — prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase — in which the copied chromosomes line up on the equator, separate and move to opposite poles, and new nuclei form, followed by division of the cytoplasm. A useful calculation is the mitotic index, the proportion of cells in a sample that are dividing: mitotic index = number of cells undergoing mitosis ÷ total number of cells in the field of view. This is used in Core Practical 6, the root tip squash, to see and count the stages of mitosis. Meiosis, by contrast, produces genetically non-identical gametes and is the source of variation: in metaphase I the homologous chromosomes line up as pairs and assort independently (independent assortment), and in prophase I crossing over exchanges alleles between the chromatids of a homologous pair, so that gametes carry new combinations of alleles. A locus is the fixed position of a gene on a chromosome; genes on the same chromosome are linked and tend to be inherited together, so linked genes do not assort independently.

7. Gametes, fertilisation in mammals and fertilisation in flowering plants

Mammalian gametes are specialised for their function. Sperm are small and motile, with a haploid nucleus, a lot of mitochondria to power the flagellum, and an acrosome at the head containing enzymes that digest a path through the egg’s outer layers. Egg cells are larger, with cytoplasm containing food reserves; the zona pellucida is a glycoprotein layer around the egg that sperm must penetrate. Fertilisation in mammals begins when the acrosome reaction releases enzymes that digest the zona pellucida, then the cortical reaction releases cortical granules into the space around the egg, hardening the zona pellucida and preventing more than one sperm from entering; finally the sperm and egg nuclei fuse, restoring the diploid number. In flowering plants, fertilisation begins with pollination and the growth of a pollen tube from the pollen grain down through the style to the embryo sac; two male nuclei travel down the tube, one fertilising the egg to form the zygote (which develops into the embryo) and one fusing with the two polar nuclei to form the triploid endosperm that will feed the developing seed — double fertilisation, unique to flowering plants.

8. Stem cells and what society does with them

A stem cell is an undifferentiated cell that can divide to produce more stem cells and differentiated cells. Totipotent stem cells can develop into any cell type and form a complete organism; the zygote and the cells of the early embryo up to the 16-cell morula are totipotent. Pluripotent stem cells can give rise to many, but not all, cell types; cells of the blastocyst are pluripotent, and in plants many meristem cells are totipotent, which is why a whole plant can be grown from a single cell or tissue. Stem cells are used medically — for example in bone marrow transplants for leukaemia — and their use raises ethical and social questions: the source of embryonic stem cells, the balance of benefit against risk, and decisions made by individuals, committees and governments all draw on scientific knowledge but also on values. Students should be able to discuss these issues from a range of ethical viewpoints.

9. Gene expression: how one gene makes more than one protein and how proteins control cells

Cells become specialised through differential gene expression — different genes are switched on or off in different cells, producing active mRNA and then proteins that control cell processes or determine cell structure. One gene can give rise to more than one protein through post-transcriptional changes to messenger RNA (mRNA) such as alternative splicing, in which the same primary transcript is spliced in different ways to make different mRNAs and therefore different polypeptides. Transcription factors switch genes on or off by binding to DNA and promoting or blocking transcription, so they control which proteins a cell makes. Epigenetic modification — including DNA methylation and histone modification — alters the activation of certain genes without changing the DNA sequence itself, and these modifications can be passed on following cell division, so that a cell’s gene activity can be inherited by its daughter cells and, in some cases, across generations.

10. Inheritance: alleles, genotypes, phenotypes and how they vary

A gene is a sequence of bases on a DNA molecule that codes for a sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide. The allele is one of the different forms of a gene; the genotype is the alleles an organism has; the phenotype is the observable feature that results from the genotype and the environment. Recessive alleles only show in the phenotype when homozygous; dominant alleles show even in the heterozygous state; codominance is when both alleles in the heterozygote contribute to the phenotype. Sex linkage is the inheritance of a gene carried on the X chromosome, such as red-green colour blindness in humans, which appears more often in males because they have only one X chromosome and so express a recessive allele on it. Some phenotypes are affected by multiple alleles for the same gene, and others by polygenic inheritance, where many genes each contribute a small effect, giving rise to continuous variation in the phenotype — height in humans is a classic example. The environment can also affect phenotype, so that a feature is the result of an interaction between genotype and environment rather than genotype alone.

11. Mutations: how they arise and what they can do

Errors in DNA replication can give rise to mutations — changes to the base sequence of DNA. A substitution replaces one base with another and may change one amino acid or none (because the code is degenerate); an insertion adds one or more bases, and a deletion removes one or more, and these can cause a frameshift that changes every amino acid after the mutation and often produces a non-functional protein. Mutations are the source of new alleles, and some mutations give rise to cancer or genetic disorders, while many have no observable effect. Cystic fibrosis is a genetic disorder caused by a recessive allele; the faulty allele affects chloride ion channels, so the functioning of the gaseous exchange, digestive and reproductive systems is impaired — thick mucus blocks the airways, the pancreas duct is blocked so digestion is affected, and fertility in males is reduced because the vas deferens is absent or blocked.

12. Genetic screening and the questions it raises

Genetic screening can identify carriers of a recessive allele, and prenatal testing — including amniocentesis (sampling the fluid around the embryo) and chorionic villus sampling (taking a sample of placental tissue) — can check an embryo or fetus for genetic disorders. Pre-implantation genetic diagnosis (PGD) is used during IVF to test embryos before implantation so that only unaffected embryos are used. These techniques raise ethical and social questions: the reliability and risk of the test, the right to know or not to know, who decides what is a disorder worth preventing, the cost and access to treatment, and the risk of starting down a path toward selecting traits rather than preventing disease. Students should be able to identify and discuss these issues from religious, moral and social viewpoints.

13. How to use this note and what to revise next

Use these notes by working section by section through the topic, checking that you can name every organelle, state its function, and recognise it in an electron micrograph. Practise the calculations — magnification, real size from image size and magnification, mitotic index, and the index of diversity and the calculations that appear in the genetics sections. Revise by drawing and labelling an animal cell and a plant cell from memory, annotating each organelle with its function, then testing yourself on meiosis and on how variation arises. After this topic, revise Topic 4 Plant structure, biodiversity and conservation, and Topic 5 Energy flow, ecosystems and the environment, because the genetics here underpins inheritance in those later topics.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Magnification, applied to a mitochondrion measuring 4.2 cm on a micrograph at ×20 000: actual size = image size ÷ magnification. 4.2 cm = 42 000 µm, so the real length is 42 000 ÷ 20 000 = 2.1 µm. Convert every unit to µm before you divide, and write the magnification formula out.
  • Prokaryote or eukaryote: a eukaryote has a nucleus, membrane-bound organelles and 80S ribosomes. A prokaryote has a circular DNA loop, no nucleus and 70S ribosomes. Name at least two of these features; a single feature such as the cell wall is not enough because plants and some prokaryotes both have one.
  • Mitosis versus meiosis: mitosis gives two genetically identical diploid cells. Meiosis gives four haploid cells, and genetic variation comes from crossing over in prophase I and independent assortment at metaphase I. Mark schemes award these two sources separately.
  • Mammalian fertilisation: a sperm and an egg fuse to form a diploid zygote, which restores the diploid number. Name the haploid gametes explicitly, because the mark depends on the stage of meiosis that produces them.

Typical mistakes

  • Describing an organelle instead of answering the question. "Mitochondria have cristae" earns nothing when the question asks why a cell needs many of them. State the function — aerobic respiration, so an ATP supply — and link it to the cell's demand, such as the tail of a sperm or the active transport in a kidney cell.
  • Confusing magnification with resolution. Magnification is how much larger the image is than the object; resolution is the smallest distance at which two points are still seen as separate. The electron microscope wins on resolution, and that is why it separates cristae and ribosomes that a light microscope blurs together.
  • Forgetting to convert units in a magnification calculation. Put image size and real size in the same unit before dividing. 1 mm is 1 000 micrometres, and the mark is often for the unit as much as the number.
  • Using the cell wall alone to identify a plant cell. Bacteria and fungi have walls too. Use the cellulose wall together with the chloroplast or the large permanent vacuole, and remember that plant cells lack centrioles.
  • Mixing up mitosis and meiosis. Mitosis: one division, two genetically identical diploid cells, for growth and asexual reproduction. Meiosis: two divisions, four genetically non-identical haploid cells, for gametes.
  • Saying meiosis "creates variation" without naming the source. Crossing over in prophase I and independent assortment in metaphase I are separate marks; the names of the prophase stages are not required.
  • Counting every cell in the mitotic index. Interphase cells belong in the total, never in the numerator: mitotic index = cells in mitosis divided by all cells in the field.
  • Treating epigenetics as a change in the DNA sequence. Methylation and histone modification change which genes are active without altering the base sequence, and the pattern can be passed to daughter cells after division.

Exam-style questions

  1. A nucleus measures 42 mm across on an electron micrograph taken at a magnification of 7 000. Calculate its actual width. Answer: 42 mm = 42 000 micrometres. Actual size = image size divided by magnification = 42 000 / 7 000 = 6 micrometres.
  2. Explain two features of a sperm cell that adapt it for fertilisation. Answer: many mitochondria in the midpiece supply ATP for the flagellum, so the cell can swim to the egg; the acrosome contains hydrolytic enzymes that digest through the zona pellucida so the sperm can reach the egg membrane.
  3. Give three features visible in an electron micrograph that identify a cell as prokaryotic. Answer: circular DNA lying free in the cytoplasm with no nuclear envelope; 70S ribosomes, smaller than eukaryotic 80S ribosomes; no membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria or Golgi; a peptidoglycan cell wall, sometimes with a capsule, plasmids, flagella or pili.
  4. Explain how a protein destined for secretion is made and released. Answer: ribosomes on the rough endoplasmic reticulum synthesise the polypeptide; the rER folds it and packages it into a vesicle; the vesicle fuses with the Golgi apparatus, which modifies the protein, for example by adding carbohydrate; a secretory vesicle carries it to the plasma membrane and releases it by exocytosis.
  5. A root tip squash contains 80 cells in the field of view, of which 12 show visible chromosomes. Calculate the mitotic index. Answer: 12 / 80 = 0.15, or 15 per cent of the cells are in mitosis. A high value in a root tip is expected because the meristem is growing.
  6. Explain how the cortical reaction prevents a second sperm from fertilising the egg. Answer: when the first sperm fuses with the egg membrane, cortical granules release their contents into the space outside the egg; this hardens the zona pellucida and destroys the binding sites, so no further sperm can penetrate.
  7. Explain two ways in which meiosis produces gametes that are genetically different from each other. Answer: crossing over in prophase I exchanges alleles between non-sister chromatids of a homologous pair, so each chromatid carries a new combination; independent assortment in metaphase I means the maternal and paternal chromosomes of each pair line up randomly, giving 2 to the power n different combinations for n pairs.
  8. Explain how one gene can give rise to more than one protein. Answer: the primary transcript can be spliced in different ways, so different mature mRNAs carry different exon combinations; each mRNA is translated into a different polypeptide. Epigenetic modification can also switch the gene on or off in different cells, so the same gene produces protein in one cell type and not in another.

Equations and symbols

Four calculations carry the marks in this topic: real size from a micrograph, total magnification, the mitotic index, and the chromosome arithmetic of meiosis. Each is one line of arithmetic, and each loses marks for a unit that was never converted.

actual size = image size ÷ magnification Key: actual size = the real length of the structure (µm); image size = the measured length on the micrograph, in the same unit (µm); magnification = the stated magnification (×, no unit). Convert millimetres and centimetres to micrometres before dividing: 1 mm = 1000 µm, 1 cm = 10 000 µm.

4.2 cm = 42 000 µm Key: the conversion line that must be written before the division — 4.2 cm × 10 000 = 42 000 µm. Examiners award this step separately, so writing it out protects the mark even if the division slips.

42 000 ÷ 20 000 = 2.1 µm Key: 42 000 µm = image size of the mitochondrion; 20 000 = magnification; 2.1 µm = actual length. The same arithmetic with 7 000 gives 42 000 / 7 000 = 6 micrometres for a nucleus.

mitotic index = number of cells undergoing mitosis ÷ total number of cells in the field of view Key: mitotic index = the proportion of dividing cells (a fraction or a percentage, no unit); the numerator counts only cells with visibly separated chromosomes; the denominator counts every cell in the field, including all the interphase cells. Leaving interphase out of the total is the classic error.

12 / 80 = 0.15 Key: 12 = cells showing visible chromosomes; 80 = all cells in the field; 0.15 = mitotic index, i.e. 15 per cent dividing. A high value is expected in a root tip because the meristem is actively growing.

The symbols of this topic

TermMeaningValue or unit
nhaploid chromosome number23 in humans (no unit)
2ndiploid chromosome number46 in humans
A, T, C, GDNA basespair A–T, C–G
70S, 80Sribosome sizeprokaryote, eukaryote
×magnificationeyepiece × objective

Traps specific to the arithmetic

  • Dividing by the magnification when the question asks for the image size — the same formula rearranged, so read which quantity is unknown.
  • Leaving the answer in centimetres after converting only one side of the division.
  • Counting a cell in anaphase twice because the chromosomes have separated: it is one cell until cytokinesis.

title: AS Level Physics: Work, Energy and Power
content:
AS Level Physics: Work, Energy and Power

Energy is the currency of physics: it is never created or destroyed, only changed in form and moved from place to place, and every calculation in mechanics is really an accounting exercise in that currency. This note builds the energy toolkit from zero: what work actually is (a transfer, not a thing), the conservation principle that governs every process, the two energy formulas you will use daily — kinetic and gravitational potential — and power, the rate at which the currency is spent. Every worked example is a full energy audit with each line shown.

Work: energy in transit

Work is done when a force moves its point of application: energy is transferred from one store to another. The definition that earns the mark:

work done = force x distance moved in the direction of the force
W = F s cos(θ)

W in joules (J), F in newtons (N), s in metres (m)
θ = angle between the force and the displacement

The analogy: pushing a shopping trolley. Push along the direction of travel (θ = 0, cos θ = 1) and all your effort does work; push sideways (θ = 90°, cos θ = 0) and you do no work on its forward motion — you merely warm your arms. One joule is the work done when a force of one newton moves its point of application one metre: 1 J = 1 N m.

Worked example. A woman pushes a trolley with 80 N along 15 m of horizontal floor, the force angled 30° above the horizontal. Find the work done.

W = F s cos(θ) = 80 × 15 x cos(30)
  = 80 × 15 × 0.866 = 1039 J  (2 s.f.: 1.0 kJ)

If instead the question were a box pushed horizontally with 80 N over 15 m, the answer is simply 80 × 15 = 1200 J. Read whether an angle is given; the cos θ line is where method marks live.

Conservation of energy

Energy cannot be created or destroyed; the total energy of a closed system is constant. Energy transfers between stores — kinetic, gravitational potential, elastic potential, thermal, internal — and every real transfer leaks some energy to thermal stores of the surroundings through friction. The exam phrasing: "energy is transferred usefully to X and dissipated to the surroundings as heat" — learn the transfer vocabulary (transferred, dissipated, stored) because the mark schemes use it deliberately.

StoreChange that fills itExample
Kinetican object speeds upa falling stone
Gravitational potentialan object is lifteda book on a shelf
Elastic potentiala spring is stretched or compresseda drawn bow
Thermal (internal)friction, or heatingbrake pads after a descent

Kinetic energy and gravitational potential energy

kinetic energy:  KE = (1/2) m v²
gravitational potential energy (near a planet's surface):
                 GPE = m g h     (change in GPE = m g Δh)

m in kg, v in m s⁻¹, g = 9.81 m s⁻² (or the value given),
h = vertical height change in metres

Two traps live in the definitions. First, h is vertical: moving a box 10 m along a shelf adds no gravitational potential energy however far it slides. Second, GPE is defined as a change — only differences matter, so the question's reference level (where h = 0) is yours to choose; pick the lowest point and every height stays positive.

Worked example 1 (falling object). A 0.50 kg ball is dropped from 20 m. Find its speed just before impact (ignore air resistance).

energy at top:   GPE = m g h = 0.50 × 9.81 × 20 = 98.1 J
energy at bottom: KE = (1/2) m v², and KE = GPE
(1/2)(0.50) v² = 98.1
0.25 v² = 98.1 → v² = 392.4 → v = 19.8 m s⁻¹

Worked example 2 (with friction). A 2.0 kg trolley starts at the top of a 5.0 m slope at 30° and reaches the bottom at 3.0 m s⁻¹. Find the energy dissipated by friction.

vertical height: h = 5.0 sin(30) = 2.5 m
initial GPE = m g h = 2.0 × 9.81 × 2.5 = 49.05 J
final KE = (1/2)(2.0)(3.0)² = 9.0 J
energy lost to friction = 49.05 - 9.0 = 40.05 J
                        = 40 J (2 s.f.)

Note the structure of every friction question: start energy minus end energy is the dissipation. Nothing is destroyed — it went to thermal stores.

Bringing things to rest: work done by braking

A whole family of questions asks how far a vehicle takes to stop, or what force stops it. The engine of the calculation is always the same: the kinetic energy the vehicle loses becomes work done by the braking force.

KE lost = work done by braking
(1/2) m v² = F s        (F = average braking force, s = stopping distance)

Worked example. A 1200 kg car travelling at 20 m s⁻¹ brakes to a halt over 40 m. Find the average braking force.

initial KE = (1/2) m v² = 0.5 × 1200 × 20² = 240 000 J
(1/2) m v² = F s  →  240 000 = F x 40
F = 240 000/40 = 6000 N = 6.0 kN

The same equation rearranged answers the safety version: since KE grows with v², doubling the speed quadruples the energy the brakes must absorb and hence the stopping distance at constant force. That single statement is a full mark in most questions about speed limits.

Power: the rate of transfer

power = work done / time = energy transferred / time
P = W/t          (watts, W; 1 W = 1 J s⁻¹)

also, for a force moving at constant speed:
P = F v          (derivable: W/t = F s/t = F v)

Worked example 1. A motor lifts a 200 kg crate through 8.0 m in 12 s at constant speed. Find its useful power output (g = 9.81 m s⁻²).

useful work = gain in GPE = m g h = 200 × 9.81 × 8.0 = 15 696 J
P = W/t = 15 696/12 = 1308 W = 1.3 kW (2 s.f.)

Worked example 2 (P = Fv). A car engine provides 20 kN of thrust at a steady 30 m s⁻¹. Find the power developed.

P = F v = 20 000 × 30 = 6.0 × 10⁵ W = 600 kW

Efficiency closes the topic: efficiency = useful energy output / total energy input, always a fraction (or ×100%). Real machines are between 0 and 1 — an efficiency of 1.2 is a red flag in your own answer.

Worked example 3 (efficiency). A lift uses 40 kJ of electrical energy to raise a 500 kg load through 6.0 m. Find its efficiency.

useful output = m g h = 500 × 9.81 × 6.0 = 29 430 J
input = 40 kJ = 40 000 J
efficiency = 29 430/40 000 = 0.74  (74%)

Worked examples: the mixed audit

Worked example. A 1.5 kg trolley is pushed by a 6.0 N force along a 4.0 m horizontal track. It starts from rest and ends at 3.0 m s⁻¹. Account for the energy.

work input from the push: W = F s = 6.0 × 4.0 = 24 J
final KE = (1/2)(1.5)(3.0)² = 6.75 J
energy to friction/thermal = 24 - 6.75 = 17.25 J = 17 J (2 s.f.)
comment: most of the push became heat - the track is rough.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Work) A 40 N force acts at 60° to the horizontal, moving a box 5.0 m horizontally. Find the work done. Answer: W = Fs cos θ = 40 × 5.0 × cos 60 = 40 × 5.0 × 0.5 = 100 J.
  2. (Conservation) A cyclist freewheels down a hill. Describe the energy transfers. Answer: Gravitational potential energy is transferred to kinetic energy as the cyclist descends; some energy is dissipated to the thermal stores of the brakes, tyres and air through friction and drag, so the final kinetic energy is slightly less than the initial GPE.
  3. (GPE/KE) A 0.20 kg ball is thrown up at 15 m s⁻¹. Find the maximum height reached (no air resistance). Answer: ½mv² = mgh → h = v²/(2g) = 225/(2 × 9.81) = 11.5 m.
  4. (Power) A crane lifts 800 kg through 12 m at constant speed in 20 s. Find the useful power (g = 9.81). Answer: W = mgh = 800 × 9.81 × 12 = 94 176 J; P = W/t = 4709 W = 4.7 kW.
  5. (Efficiency) A generator takes in 50 kJ and delivers 38 kJ of electrical energy. Find the efficiency and state where the rest goes. Answer: 38/50 = 0.76 (76%); the remaining 12 kJ is dissipated as heat to the surroundings (thermal stores) through friction and electrical resistance.
  6. (P = Fv) A car moves at constant speed against a total drag of 500 N. Find the engine power at 25 m s⁻¹. Answer: P = Fv = 500 × 25 = 12 500 W = 12.5 kW.
  7. (Vertical height) A 3.0 kg suitcase is carried 4.0 m horizontally across a room. Find the change in its GPE. Answer: Zero — the vertical height did not change, and GPE depends only on vertical displacement.
  8. (Full audit) A 1.0 kg block slides 2.0 m down a 25° slope and reaches 2.5 m s⁻¹. Find the energy dissipated. Answer: h = 2.0 sin 25 = 0.845 m; GPE lost = 1.0 × 9.81 × 0.845 = 8.29 J; KE gained = ½ × 1.0 × 6.25 = 3.13 J; dissipated = 8.29 − 3.13 = 5.2 J.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • h is vertical: sliding along a level floor changes no GPE. Convert slope distance to vertical height with sin θ before mgh.
  • Speed squared: KE = ½mv² — doubling v quadruples KE. Candidates who double the energy on doubling speed lose marks in multi-step questions.
  • W = Fs versus W = mgh: the work done by a lifting force equals the gain in GPE only at constant speed; if the load accelerates, some work also becomes KE.
  • Forgetting the energy audit structure: friction questions want input energy minus output energy as a stated subtraction — show both energies first.
  • Power units: kW into W before dividing by seconds (1 kW = 1000 W). 1300 W is 1.3 kW, not 13.
  • Efficiency as a percentage over 100: impossible; check the ratio direction (output over input, never the reverse).
  • g value: use 9.81 m s⁻² unless the paper supplies another value; a question giving g = 10 expects 10.
  • Significant figures and units: answers to 2 or 3 s.f. with units (J, W, m s⁻¹) — unrounded calculator output costs marks.
  • Method visibility: write the formula (W = Fs cos θ, P = W/t) as its own line before substitution; formulae earn credit independently of arithmetic.

title: Hardware and Logic Gates — Study Notes
content:
`# Hardware and Logic Gates

Logic Gates

ABANDORNANDNORXOR
0000110
0101101
1001101
1111000

NOT inverts; NAND is 'AND then NOT'; XOR outputs 1 when inputs differ.

Boolean Algebra Laws

  • De Morgan: (A·B)′ = A′ + B′; (A + B)′ = A′ · B′
  • Distribution: A·(B + C) = A·B + A·C
  • Absorption: A + A·B = A

Example: simplify A + A′B = (A + A′)(A + B) = A + B.

Constructing Circuits

Truth table → Boolean expression → gates. A half adder: S = A XOR B, C = A AND B.

Flip-Flops (Bistables)

  • SR latch: set/reset, invalid state S=R=1
  • JK: like SR but J=K=1 toggles
  • Clock signals synchronise state changes

Von Neumann Model

CPU (ALU, control unit, registers: PC, MAR, MDR, ACC) + memory + I/O, sharing one bus system; instructions fetched–decoded–executed in cycles.

Exam tips: write truth tables fully; simplify before drawing circuits to save gates, and name the law you use.

title: Trigonometry — Study Notes
content:
Trigonometry

Exact Values

Anglesincostan
30°1/2√3/2√3/3
45°√2/2√2/21
60°√3/21/2√3

Key Identities

  • sin²θ + cos²θ = 1
  • tan θ = sin θ / cos θ
  • sec²θ = 1 + tan²θ

Solving Equations

Use the symmetry of the graphs. For sin x = 1/2 in 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π: the acute answer is π/6, and the second solution is π − π/6 = 5π/6.

For cos x = 0.5 in 0° ≤ x ≤ 360°: x = 60° and 360° − 60° = 300°.

Always check the required interval and give every solution.

Graphs and Transformations

y = a sin(bx) + c has amplitude a, period 2π/b, and vertical shift c.

Example: y = 3 sin(2x) has amplitude 3 and period π.

Using Identities

If sin x = 0.6 with x acute, then cos x = √(1 − 0.36) = 0.8 (positive in the first quadrant).

Exam tips: write the general second solution using graph symmetry rather than memorising CAST blindly; square both sides only with care, as it can add false solutions.

Exact values and exam method

Use CAST to find the quadrant signs: all positive in the first quadrant, sine in the second, tangent in the third, cosine in the fourth. Find the acute angle first, then the other solutions in the range the question specifies.

For sin x = k, the solutions in 0° to 360° are α and 180° − α, where α is the acute angle with sin α = |k|. For cos x = k they are α and 360° − α. Always check the range; an answer outside it earns no mark.

Write a sin x + b cos x as R sin(x + α) or R cos(x − α). Expanding gives R = √(a² + b²), and for the sine form tan α = b/a. The maximum value is R, which gives the turning points that exam questions often ask for.

Reciprocal functions: sec x = 1/cos x, cosec x = 1/sin x, cot x = 1/tan x. Use sin²x + cos²x = 1 and 1 + tan²x = sec²x to simplify.

Exam cue: Show the working that gives the acute angle before stating the answers in the required range.

title: Trigonometry — Study Notes
content:
Trigonometry

Edexcel International A Level Mathematics — Pure Mathematics 1 (WMA11), sat at AS.

Exact Values

Anglesincostan
30°1/2√3/2√3/3
45°√2/2√2/21
60°√3/21/2√3

Key Identities

  • sin²θ + cos²θ = 1
  • tan θ = sin θ / cos θ
  • sec²θ = 1 + tan²θ

Solving Equations

Use the symmetry of the graphs. For sin x = 1/2 in 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π: the acute answer is π/6, and the second solution is π − π/6 = 5π/6.

For cos x = 0.5 in 0° ≤ x ≤ 360°: x = 60° and 360° − 60° = 300°.

Always check the required interval and give every solution.

Graphs and Transformations

y = a sin(bx) + c has amplitude a, period 2π/b, and vertical shift c.

Example: y = 3 sin(2x) has amplitude 3 and period π.

Using Identities

If sin x = 0.6 with x acute, then cos x = √(1 − 0.36) = 0.8 (positive in the first quadrant).

Exam tips: write the general second solution using graph symmetry rather than memorising CAST blindly; square both sides only with care, as it can add false solutions.

Exact values and exam method

Use CAST to find the quadrant signs: all positive in the first quadrant, sine in the second, tangent in the third, cosine in the fourth. Find the acute angle first, then the other solutions in the range the question specifies.

For sin x = k, the solutions in 0° to 360° are α and 180° − α, where α is the acute angle with sin α = |k|. For cos x = k they are α and 360° − α. Always check the range; an answer outside it earns no mark.

Write a sin x + b cos x as R sin(x + α) or R cos(x − α). Expanding gives R = √(a² + b²), and for the sine form tan α = b/a. The maximum value is R, which gives the turning points that exam questions often ask for.

Reciprocal functions: sec x = 1/cos x, cosec x = 1/sin x, cot x = 1/tan x. Use sin²x + cos²x = 1 and 1 + tan²x = sec²x to simplify.

Exam cue: Show the working that gives the acute angle before stating the answers in the required range.

Worked example: exact values and a quadrant rule

Use the exact values sin 30° = ½, cos 45° = 1/√2 and tan 60° = √3. For an angle such as 150°, sin 150° = sin(180° − 30°) = sin 30° = ½, because sine is positive in the second quadrant. For 225°, tan 225° = tan 45° = 1, because tangent is positive in the third quadrant.

Draw a quick CAST diagram to decide the sign: all positive in the first quadrant, sine in the second, tangent in the third and cosine in the fourth.

Solving a trigonometric equation

Solve 2cos x = 1 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π. Then cos x = ½, so x = π/3 or x = 2π − π/3 = 5π/3. Always find the principal value first, then use the symmetry of the graph to find the other solutions in the range.

Solve 2sin²x − sin x − 1 = 0 for 0° ≤ x ≤ 360°. Factor as (2 sin x + 1)(sin x − 1) = 0. Then sin x = 1, giving x = 90°, or sin x = −½, giving x = 210° and 330°.

Proving an identity

Show that (sin x + cos x)² = 1 + sin 2x. Expand the left side: sin²x + 2 sin x cos x + cos²x. Use sin²x + cos²x = 1 to get 1 + 2 sin x cos x, and recall sin 2x = 2 sin x cos x, so the left side equals 1 + sin 2x.

Graphs and transformations

  • y = 3 sin 2x + 1 has amplitude 3, period 180° (or π radians), and the maximum value 4 occurs at x = 45°.
  • The range of y = 3 sin 2x + 1 is −2 ≤ y ≤ 4.
  • A horizontal stretch by factor ½ halves the period; a vertical shift of +1 moves the whole graph up by one unit.

Common errors that lose marks

  • Working in degrees when the question uses radians, or the reverse. Check the units in the question before you start.
  • Giving only the principal value and missing the other solutions in the range. Always check the quadrant signs.
  • Squaring both sides of an equation to remove a root, which can add extra solutions. Check each answer in the original equation.

title: IGCSE Mathematics: Inequalities
content:
IGCSE Mathematics: Inequalities

Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580 (2025–2027), section 2 Algebra and graphs, statement 2.6 Inequalities — solving and interpreting linear inequalities, listing integer solutions, and (Extended) regions in the coordinate plane. An inequality describes a range of values rather than one exact value, and solving one follows the same balance principle as solving an equation, with one critical difference: multiplying or dividing by a negative number reverses the inequality sign. This note shows why that happens, writes out every solution line by line, and finishes with the region-shading questions that distinguish Paper 4.

What an inequality says

The four inequality symbols extend the equals sign: < (strictly less than), > (strictly greater than), ⩽ (less than or equal to), ⩾ (greater than or equal to). A solution is a set of values, drawn on a number line with a hollow circle for strict inequalities (the endpoint is excluded) and a solid circle for inclusive ones (the endpoint is included).

StatementMeaningNumber line
x > 3Every value greater than 3, not including 3Hollow circle at 3, arrow to the right
x ⩽ −1Every value up to and including −1Solid circle at −1, arrow to the left
2 ⩽ x < 5Values from 2 up to, but not including, 5Solid circle at 2, hollow at 5, line between

Why the sign flips when multiplying by a negative. Start with the true statement 3 < 5. Multiply both sides by −2 without thinking: −6 < −10 is false, because −10 is further left than −6. The correct statement is −6 > −10. Multiplying by a negative mirrors the number line, which reverses order — so the inequality symbol must reverse too. That single rule causes more lost marks than any other in this topic.

Solving linear inequalities

Use the equation methods unchanged, and remember the one reversal rule:

Solve:  5x - 7 > 3x + 1        (give the solution as an inequality)

5x - 3x > 1 + 7               [add 7 to both sides, subtract 3x from both sides]
2x > 8
x > 4                         [divide by +2: the sign does not reverse]
Solve:  3 - 2x ⩽ 11

-2x ⩽ 11 - 3                  [subtract 3 from both sides]
-2x ⩽ 8
x ⩾ -4                        [divide by -2: the sign REVERSES from ⩽ to ⩾]

The check is direct: x = −4 gives 3 − 2(−4) = 11 ⩽ 11 ✓, and x = 0 gives 3 ⩽ 11 ✓ while x = −5 gives 13 ⩽ 11 ✗ — so the boundary and direction are right.

Solve and list the integer solutions:  2 < (5x - 1)/3 ⩽ 8

Multiply every part by 3:
6 < 5x - 1 ⩽ 24
7 < 5x ⩽ 25                   [add 1 to every part]
7/5 < x ⩽ 5                   [divide every part by +5]

The integers are 2, 3, 4 and 5.

Compound inequalities (a value trapped between two bounds) are solved in one line per operation across all three parts — exactly like a three-pan balance.

Inequalities from word problems

Many questions ask for the greatest or least integer satisfying a condition. Translate carefully: at least means ⩾, at most means ⩽, more than means >, within or no more than means ⩽.

A cinema ticket costs £8. A group has £100 and must keep at least £12 for travel.
How many tickets can they buy?

Let n be the number of tickets:  8n + 12 ⩽ 100
8n ⩽ 88
n ⩽ 11

They can buy at most 11 tickets.

The final answer is a whole number in context: a group cannot buy a fraction of a ticket, so the solution set is the integers up to 11.

Regions in the coordinate plane (Extended)

The line y = mx + c divides the plane into two half-planes: points above it satisfy y > mx + c and points below it satisfy y < mx + c. A region question asks you to shade the set of points satisfying several inequalities at once.

  • Draw the boundary line y = mx + c as a solid line when the inequality includes equality (⩽ or ⩾), and as a dashed line when it is strict (< or >).
  • Test one point not on the line — the origin (0, 0) is easiest when the line misses it. Substitute into the inequality; if it is true, shade the side containing the test point.
  • Shade the side that satisfies every inequality; the answer region is the overlap, and the question often asks for the coordinates of a point inside it.
Shade the region satisfying:  y ⩽ 2x + 1,  y > -x + 2,  x ⩾ 0

Line 1: y = 2x + 1, solid. Test (0, 0): 0 ⩽ 1 true, so shade below-left of this line.
Line 2: y = -x + 2, dashed. Test (0, 0): 0 > 2 false, so shade the side away from the origin.
Line 3: x = 0 (the y-axis), solid, shade to the right.

The solution region is the triangle-like area satisfying all three, e.g. the point (2, 2):
2 ⩽ 5 ✓, 2 > 0 ✓, 2 ⩾ 0 ✓.

Describing a region in words is the reverse skill: read the boundary lines, note whether each is dashed or solid, and translate the shaded side back into an inequality.

Maximum and minimum values over a region (Extended)

Region questions often finish by asking for the largest or smallest value of an expression such as x + 2y for points inside the shaded region. A linear expression grows steadily in one direction across the plane, so over a region bounded by straight lines its extreme values always sit at the corners. The method is therefore exact: find the coordinates of every vertex of the region, substitute each pair into the expression, and pick the largest or smallest result. Do not stop at the corner that looks likely — an untested corner is the usual place a mark is lost.

Worked example: inequality with a parameter

Find the set of values of k for which the equation x² + kx + 9 = 0 has two distinct real roots.

Two distinct real roots require a positive discriminant:  b^2 - 4ac > 0
Here a = 1, b = k, c = 9:
k^2 - 36 > 0
k^2 > 36
k > 6  or  k < -6

This is an inequality inside a quadratic-context question — exactly the blend of topics Paper 4 rewards. If the requirement had been at least one real root, the inequality would be k² ⩾ 36, giving k ⩾ 6 or k ⩽ −6.

Corner points in practice. Take the region x ⩾ 0, y ⩾ 0, x + y ⩽ 6 and y ⩽ x + 2. Its vertices are where the boundary lines meet:

x = 0 with y = 0            gives (0, 0)
y = 0 with x + y = 6        gives (6, 0)
x = 0 with y = x + 2        gives (0, 2)
x + y = 6 with y = x + 2    gives x + (x + 2) = 6, so 2x = 4, x = 2 and y = 4, the corner (2, 4)

Evaluate P = x + 2y at each corner:
(0, 0): P = 0     (6, 0): P = 6     (0, 2): P = 4     (2, 4): P = 10

Maximum P = 10 at (2, 4);  minimum P = 0 at (0, 0).

The minimum sits at the origin only because this region includes it; a region bounded away from the origin puts its minimum at one of the other corners. Substitute every vertex before choosing.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Not reversing the inequality sign after multiplying or dividing by a negative number. −2x < 8 means x > −4.
  • Reversing the sign when multiplying by a positive number, or reversing when subtracting — only multiplication and division by negatives reverse it.
  • Hollow versus solid circles: < and > exclude the endpoint; ⩽ and ⩾ include it. Writing x > 4 when x = 4 works is a boundary error.
  • Flipping the inequality direction mid-solution so the final statement faces the wrong way.
  • Forgetting to reverse in a compound inequality: every part flips when the whole chain is multiplied by a negative.
  • In region questions, drawing a solid boundary for a strict inequality (or a dashed one for ⩽), or shading the wrong side because no test point was used.
  • Reporting a decimal when the question asks for integers: n ⩽ 11.25 means the largest integer is 11, not 11.25.
  • Treating ⩽ as < in a word problem: at most 5 includes 5.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 2, 3 marks). Solve 7 − 3x > 1 and show your solution on a number line.

Answer: −3x > −6, so x < 2 (the sign reverses). Number line: hollow circle at 2, shading to the left.

Question 2 (Paper 2, 3 marks). Solve 2 ⩽ 3x + 5 < 14 and list the integer solutions.

Answer: Subtract 5 throughout: −3 ⩽ 3x < 9. Divide by 3: −1 ⩽ x < 3. The integers are −1, 0, 1, 2.

Question 3 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Find the values of x for which x² − 5x + 4 < 0.

Answer: Factorise: (x − 1)(x − 4) < 0. The quadratic is negative between its roots, so 1 < x < 4. (Test x = 2: 4 − 10 + 4 = −2 < 0 ✓; test x = 0: 4 > 0 ✗.)

Question 4 (Paper 4, 5 marks). Shade the region defined by y > x − 1, y ⩽ 3 and x ⩾ 0, and write down the coordinates of one point in the region.

Answer: Draw y = x − 1 dashed (strict), y = 3 solid and x = 0 solid. The origin test for y > x − 1 gives 0 > −1, true, so shade above the dashed line; y ⩽ 3 shades below the horizontal line; x ⩾ 0 shades right of the y-axis. The overlap is a triangle with vertices (0, 3), (4, 3) and (0, −1); the point (1, 1) lies inside: 1 > 0 ✓, 1 ⩽ 3 ✓, 1 ⩾ 0 ✓.

Question 5 (Paper 4, 4 marks). A rectangle has a perimeter of at most 60 cm and a length of (x + 4) cm. Write an inequality for its width w and find w when x = 8.

Answer: 2[(x + 4) + w] ⩽ 60, so (x + 4) + w ⩽ 30 and w ⩽ 26 − x. With x = 8: w ⩽ 18 cm, and the width must also be positive, so 0 < w ⩽ 18.

Question 6 (Paper 2, 3 marks). The solutions of 5x + a ⩾ 0 include x = −2. Find the smallest integer value of a.

Answer: Substituting x = −2: −10 + a ⩾ 0, so a ⩾ 10. The smallest integer value is 10.

With equations and inequalities mastered, the next stage of algebra is sequences and functions.

title: Organic Chemistry: Carbonyls, Carboxylic Acids and Chirality — Study Notes
content:
Organic Chemistry: Carbonyls, Carboxylic Acids and Chirality

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH14, Topic 15. Aldehydes and ketones contain the carbonyl group, C=O. Their reactions are nucleophilic addition, and the products can be carboxylic acids, alcohols or molecules with a chiral centre.

Carbonyl compounds

  • An aldehyde has the C=O group at the end of a chain (RCHO). A ketone has it inside the chain (RCOR).
  • The carbon of C=O is slightly positive, so nucleophiles attack it. Ketones are less reactive than aldehydes because the two alkyl groups donate electron density.

Reactions and tests

  • Hydrogen cyanide adds across C=O. For ethanal, CH3CHO + HCN gives 2-hydroxypropanenitrile.
  • Sodium tetrahydridoborate(III) (NaBH4) reduces aldehydes to primary alcohols and ketones to secondary alcohols.
  • 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine (2,4-DNPH) gives an orange or yellow precipitate with any carbonyl compound.
  • Tollens' reagent gives a silver mirror with aldehydes but not with ketones.
  • The iodoform test gives a yellow precipitate of triiodomethane with compounds containing CH3CO– or CH3CH(OH)– groups, such as propanone.

Carboxylic acids

  • Carboxylic acids contain –COOH and are weak acids. They are more acidic than alcohols because the carboxylate ion is stabilised by delocalisation.
  • Carboxylic acids react with alcohols in the presence of concentrated sulfuric acid to form esters, in a reversible esterification.
  • Primary alcohols are oxidised to carboxylic acids by heating with acidified potassium dichromate(VI) under reflux.

Chirality

  • A chiral carbon atom has four different groups attached. Molecules with a chiral centre exist as a pair of enantiomers.
  • Enantiomers have identical physical properties except their effect on plane-polarised light: one rotates it clockwise and the other anticlockwise by the same amount.
  • An equimolar mixture of the two enantiomers is a racemic mixture, which is optically inactive.

Exam tip: when describing a nucleophilic addition, show the nucleophile attacking the carbon of C=O and the oxygen gaining the negative charge.

title: AS Level Mathematics: Measures of Variation and Standard Deviation
content:
AS Level Mathematics: Measures of Variation and Standard Deviation

Two data sets can share a mean and behave completely differently: one tightly clustered, one wildly spread. Measures of variation quantify that difference. This note builds the topic from zero: the range and interquartile range, the variance and standard deviation with the full calculation from first principles, the frequency-table and coded forms, outliers, and how to compare distributions fairly. Every formula is derived once, because the derivation is what makes it stick.

Why spread matters

Location alone is a half-description. A machine filling 500 g bags with a standard deviation of 2 g is trustworthy; one with a standard deviation of 30 g is not, though both may average 500 g. Spread measures consistency, risk and reliability, and every comparison question rewards naming both a location and a spread.

Range and interquartile range

range = largest - smallest
interquartile range IQR = Q3 - Q1
semi-interquartile range = (Q3 - Q1)/2
MeasureUsesWeakness
RangeOnly the two extremesDestroyed by one outlier
IQRThe middle halfIgnores the tails entirely
Standard deviationEvery valueDragged by outliers; more arithmetic

Worked example. Find the range, IQR and semi-IQR of 12, 15, 18, 21, 25, 30, 44.

range = 44 - 12 = 32
n = 7; median = 21; Q1 = 15; Q3 = 30
IQR = 15;  semi-IQR = 7.5

The 44 stretches the range to 32 while leaving the IQR untouched: exactly the robustness the IQR is chosen for.

Variance and standard deviation defined

variance = mean of the squared deviations from the mean
standard deviation = √(variance)

population form:  σ² = (sum of (x - mu)²)/n
sample form:      s² = (sum of (x - xbar)²)/(n - 1)

Why square the deviations? Signed deviations always sum to zero, so they cannot measure spread; squaring removes the signs and penalises large gaps heavily. The square root returns the answer to the original units, which is why standard deviation, not variance, is quoted in context.

Worked example (full working). Find the standard deviation of 4, 7, 9, 10, 10.

mean = 40/5 = 8
deviations: -4, -1, 1, 2, 2
squares: 16, 1, 1, 4, 4  →  sum 26
variance = 26/5 = 5.2
standard deviation = √(5.2) = 2.28

The computational formula

σ² = (sum of x²)/n - (mean)²

this is algebraically identical to the deviation form but far quicker

Worked example. Repeat the previous calculation with the computational form.

sum x = 40;  mean = 8
sum x² = 16 + 49 + 81 + 10⁰ + 10⁰ = 346
variance = 346/5 - 64 = 69.2 - 64 = 5.2
standard deviation = 2.28  (identical, as it must be)

Frequency tables

mean = (sum of f x)/(sum of f)
variance = (sum of f x²)/(sum of f) - (mean)²

Worked example. Find the mean and standard deviation of the distribution x: 1, 2, 3, 4 with frequencies 2, 5, 8, 5.

sum f = 20
sum fx = 2(1) + 5(2) + 8(3) + 5(4) = 2 + 10 + 24 + 20 = 56  →  mean 2.8
sum fx² = 2(1) + 5(4) + 8(9) + 5(16) = 2 + 20 + 72 + 80 = 174
variance = 174/20 - 7.84 = 8.7 - 7.84 = 0.86
standard deviation = 0.927

For grouped data the midpoint stands in for each class, so the standard deviation is an estimate, like the grouped mean.

Worked example 2 (grouped). Estimate the standard deviation of 0–10 (3), 10–20 (7), 20–30 (10).

midpoints 5, 15, 25;  sum f = 20
sum fx = 15 + 10⁵ + 250 = 370  →  mean 18.5
sum fx² = 3(25) + 7(225) + 10(625) = 75 + 1575 + 6250 = 7900
variance = 7900/20 - 342.25 = 395 - 342.25 = 52.75
standard deviation = 7.26

Coding and the effect on spread

if y = (x - a)/b then:
  mean(y) = (mean(x) - a)/b
  sd(y) = sd(x)/|b|
  variance(y) = variance(x)/b²

shifts (a) do not change spread; scaling (b) scales it

Worked example. The coded values y = (x − 100)/5 have mean 4 and standard deviation 1.2. Find the mean and standard deviation of x.

mean x = 5(4) + 10⁰ = 120
sd x = 5(1.2) = 6

The intuition: adding a constant slides the whole distribution without stretching it; multiplying stretches every gap by the same factor.

Outliers

lower fence = Q1 - 1.5 IQR
upper fence = Q3 + 1.5 IQR
values beyond the fences are outliers

Worked example. With Q1 = 20, Q3 = 32 and a maximum of 60, is 60 an outlier?

IQR = 12; upper fence = 32 + 18 = 50
60 > 50, so yes, 60 is an outlier

Outliers are not automatically errors: they may be genuine extreme values, which is why the median and IQR often summarise skewed data better than the mean and standard deviation.

Comparing distributions properly

A full comparison answers four points: which has the higher typical value, which is more spread, whether either has outliers, and what that means in context.

Worked example. Boys: mean 62, sd 8. Girls: mean 68, sd 4. Compare.

girls have the higher typical mark (68 vs 62)
girls are more consistent (sd 4 vs 8; roughly half the spread)
boys' marks are more widely dispersed, so their range of performance
is broader; the sd ratio 2 suggests boys' marks vary twice as much
about their mean

Never compare standard deviations of data measured in different units or on different scales without converting; here both are marks, so the comparison is valid.

Standard deviation in context

Worked example (quality control). A machine fills bags with mean 500 g and sd 3 g. Assuming a roughly symmetric distribution, about what proportion lies within one standard deviation of the mean?

one sd either side: 497 to 503 g
for a roughly normal shape, about 68 per cent of bags fall in this band
(and about 95 per cent within two sds: 494 to 506 g)

The 68/95/99.7 guide is approximate and only valid for roughly bell-shaped data; stating that condition is part of the answer.

Comparing spread across different units

Standard deviations cannot be compared directly when the scales differ. The coefficient of variation puts them on a common footing by expressing the spread as a fraction of the mean:

coefficient of variation = 10⁰ x sd/mean  (per cent)

A: mean 50 kg, sd 4 kg   →  CV = 8 per cent
B: mean 8000 pounds, sd 400 pounds  →  CV = 5 per cent
B is relatively more consistent despite the larger absolute sd

Worked example. Two athletes' times over a season: A has mean 12.0 s, sd 0.15 s; B has mean 60.0 s, sd 0.60 s (different events). Which is more consistent relative to their event?

CV(A) = 0.15/12.0 × 10⁰ = 1.25 per cent
CV(B) = 0.60/60.0 × 10⁰ = 1.00 per cent
B is relatively more consistent, even though the absolute sd is 4 times larger

Without the coefficient of variation, the comparison would favour A for the wrong reason. State the units and the ratio when answering.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Range) Find the range of 3, 8, 12, 15, 22. Answer: 19.
  2. (IQR) Find the IQR of 5, 6, 9, 11, 14, 18. Answer: Q1 = 6.75, Q3 = 15, IQR = 8.25.
  3. (SD) Find the standard deviation of 2, 4, 4, 6, 9. Answer: mean 5; deviations −3, −1, −1, 1, 4; squares 9, 1, 1, 1, 16 = 28; variance 5.6; sd 2.37.
  4. (Computational) For sum x = 60, sum x² = 800, n = 10, find the sd. Answer: variance = 80 − 36 = 44; sd = 6.63.
  5. (Frequency) x: 0, 1, 2 with f: 4, 3, 3. Find the mean. Answer: 9/10 = 0.9.
  6. (Coding) y = (x − 20)/4 has sd 2.5. Find the sd of x. Answer: 10.
  7. (Outlier) Q1 = 12, Q3 = 20, maximum 45. Is 45 an outlier? Answer: IQR = 8, fence = 32; yes.
  8. (Compare) A: mean 40, sd 5. B: mean 40, sd 12. What differs? Answer: same centre, different spread; B is far more variable.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Forgetting to root: the variance is in squared units; the standard deviation is its square root. Quoting the variance as the sd is a units error.
  • Dividing by n or n − 1: use the convention the question implies; for a population divide by n, for a sample estimate divide by n − 1. Mixing them shifts the answer.
  • Deviation sign errors: the deviations must sum to zero — if they do not, the mean was copied wrongly.
  • Coding with the wrong operation: sd divides by |b|, never subtracts a; shifts do not affect spread.
  • Comparing different units: an sd of 5 marks and an sd of 5 kg are not comparable; convert or use the coefficient of variation.
  • Outlier fences: 1.5 × IQR beyond the quartiles, not beyond the range or the median.
  • Grouped estimates: call them estimates and note that midpoints are assumed uniform within each class.
  • One-sided comparison: a comparison naming only the mean earns half the marks; always add the spread and its interpretation.

Formula summary

range = max - min;  IQR = Q3 - Q1
variance = (sum of x²)/n - (mean)²
standard deviation = √(variance)
coded: mean(x) = b mean(y) + a;  sd(x) = |b| sd(y)
CV = 10⁰ sd/mean

Learn the computational variance form rather than the deviation form: it needs one pass for the sum and one for the sum of squares, and it fails loudly when the mean is wrong because the deviations then do not sum to zero.

title: Exam technique: Arithmetic and Place Value
content:
### What earns the marks
For HCF and LCM, the prime factorisation of each number earns the method mark; state highest powers for LCM and lowest for HCF. For bounds, half-the-precision stated (0.05 for 1 d.p.) earns the method mark before the bound. For estimation, the rounded line (50 x 20 / 10) must be shown: a bare calculator value scores nothing. For time and money, each conversion step shown earns its mark.
### Traps
Error: 16:80 as a time. Correction: 60 minutes carry. Error: largest rounded value confused with the upper bound (6.34 vs 6.35). Correction: the bound is the first value that rounds away. Error: HCF powers used for LCM. Correction: LCM takes the highest of each prime.
### Worked example
In 4 706 325 the digit 7 is in the hundred-thousands place, so its value is 700 000. For order of operations, 3 + 4 × (10 − 6)² is worked out as 3 + 4 × 4² = 3 + 4 × 16 = 3 + 64 = 67. Brackets and powers come before multiplication, and addition comes last.
### Check yourself
State the value of the digit 6 in 4 706 325, then calculate 20 − 2 × (3 + 4)². The 6 is worth 6000. The second is 20 − 2 × 49 = 20 − 98 = −78, which shows why the brackets must be done first.
