title: IGCSE Chemistry: Metals and Reactivity
content:
IGCSE Chemistry: Metals and Reactivity

Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry 0620 (2026–2028), Extended route, Topic 9 Metals: statements 9.1 Properties of metals, 9.2 Uses of metals, 9.3 Alloys and their properties, 9.4 Reactivity series, 9.5 Corrosion of metals, and 9.6 Extraction of metals. The reactivity series is the spine of this topic — it predicts what metals do with water, acid and oxygen, how they are extracted, and why they corrode. Every prediction below flows from one ordering, and the blast furnace is traced reaction by reaction.

Properties and uses

Metals: good conductors of heat and electricity, malleable (hammer into sheets) and ductile (draw into wire), with high melting points — all from metallic bonding (positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons). Uses follow properties: aluminium — low density (aircraft), corrosion resistance (food containers, overhead cables: light + oxide-protected + conductive); copper — excellent conductivity and ductility (electrical wiring), non-toxic (water pipes).

MetalKey propertyUse
AluminiumLow density; corrosion-resistant oxide layer; conductsAircraft, overhead cables, food containers
CopperExcellent electrical conductivity; ductile; non-toxicElectrical wiring, water pipes
Iron (steel)Strong, cheap; alloyed for hardnessStructures, vehicles, cutlery (stainless)
TungstenVery high melting point (3422 °C)Lamp filaments, cutting tools
TitaniumStrong, low density, corrosion-resistant, biocompatibleAerospace, replacement joints

Alloys

An alloy is a mixture of a metal with other elements (brass = copper + zinc; stainless steel = iron + chromium + nickel). Alloys are harder and stronger than pure metals: atoms of different sizes disrupt the regular layers, so the layers cannot slide over each other easily — this is the complete explanation, and both halves earn marks. Stainless steel's hardness and corrosion resistance suit cutlery.

The reactivity series

The series, memorised in order of decreasing reactivity:

  potassium K, sodium Na, calcium Ca, magnesium Mg, aluminium Al,
  carbon C (reference), zinc Zn, iron Fe, hydrogen H (reference),
  copper Cu, silver Ag, gold Au

Three observations fix a metal's place:

  WITH WATER:
    K, Na, Ca: react with cold water (2K + 2H₂O -> 2KOH + H₂; sodium melts
    and skitters; calcium fizzes steadily)
    Mg: very slowly with cold water, vigorously with steam
       (Mg + H₂O -> MgO + H₂)
    Al, Zn, Fe: react with STEAM only (Fe + H₂O -> Fe₃O₄ + H₂ at red heat)
    Cu, Ag, Au: no reaction even with steam

  WITH DILUTE HCl:
    K..Mg: vigorous (fast fizz of H₂)
    Zn, Fe: steady fizz
    Cu, Ag, Au: no reaction (below hydrogen in the series)

  WITH OXYGEN:
    most metals form oxides; gold does not tarnish at all.

Displacement: a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from its
salt solution:
    Zn(s) + CuSO₄(aq) -> ZnSO₄(aq) + Cu(s)      [zinc plates copper]
    Cu(s) + ZnSO₄(aq) -> no reaction
  Observations: zinc gains a red-brown coating; the blue Cu²⁺ colour fades.

Corrosion and protection

Rusting is the corrosion of iron in the presence of both water and oxygen — the classic two-variable experiment (wet + air = rust; dry air or water without air = none). The product is hydrated iron(III) oxide, Fe₂O₃·xH₂O.

  • Barrier methods: painting, greasing, plastic coating — block water and oxygen reaching the surface.
  • Galvanising: coating with zinc; even scratched, zinc protects because it corrodes preferentially.
  • Sacrificial protection: a more reactive metal (zinc or magnesium) is attached to iron; it corrodes instead of the iron because it loses electrons more readily — used on ships' hulls and underground pipes.
Sacrificial protection explained electron by electron:

  Iron in contact with zinc in damp conditions forms a tiny electrochemical
  cell. Zinc is more reactive, so Zn atoms lose electrons (Zn -> Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻)
  and corrode; the electrons flow to the iron, where oxygen and water take
  them up. The iron is reduced-protected - it cannot corrode while the zinc
  remains. This is why the zinc block is called "sacrificial": it is eaten
  away to save the iron.

Extraction of metals

Ease of extraction tracks the reactivity series: unreactive metals (Cu, Ag, Au) exist as native elements and need no chemical extraction; moderately reactive metals (Zn, Fe) are extracted by reduction with carbon; the most reactive (Al, Mg, Na) are extracted by electrolysis — carbon cannot reduce them.

The blast furnace for iron, reaction by reaction:

  Raw materials: iron ore (haematite, Fe₂O₃), coke (C), limestone (CaCO₃),
                 hot air.

  1. Coke burns to make carbon monoxide (the reducing agent):
       C + O₂ -> CO₂          (exothermic - heats the furnace)
       CO₂ + C -> 2CO          (endothermic; the key reduction agent forms)
  2. Reduction of the ore:
       Fe₂O₃ + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO₂
     (also direct: Fe₂O₃ + 3C -> 2Fe + 3CO at the hottest zone)
  3. Limestone removes sandy impurities (silica):
       CaCO₃ -> CaO + CO₂        (thermal decomposition)
       CaO + SiO₂ -> CaSiO₃     (slag - molten, drained off)

  Slag uses: road building. The molten iron is TAPPED from the bottom;
  slag floats above it (less dense) and is run off separately.

Aluminium extraction (electrolysis of Al₂O₃ in molten cryolite):
  - cryolite (Na₃AlF₆) lowers the melting point from 2050 °C to ~950 °C,
    saving energy;
  - carbon anodes: oxygen liberated reacts with them: C + O₂ -> CO₂, so
    anodes burn away and must be replaced regularly;
  - half-equations:  Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ -> Al  (cathode, reduction)
                     2O²⁻ -> O₂ + 4e⁻  (anode, oxidation)
  - aluminium is used for overhead cables and aircraft: light, resistant
    to corrosion (protective oxide layer), and conductive.

Worked example: reactivity reasoning end to end

Question: metal X does not react with steam but displaces copper from
copper(II) sulfate. Metal Y reacts with cold water. Order X, Y and copper
and justify.

  Y reacts with cold water -> Y is high in the series (like K, Na or Ca).
  X does not react with steam -> X is BELOW the steam-reactive metals (Al,
  Zn, Fe react with steam; Cu, Ag, Au do not) - but X displaces copper ->
  X is MORE reactive than copper. So X sits between iron and copper region:
  e.g. X could be lead. Order: Y > X > copper.

  The displacement alone proves X > Cu; the steam data place X low but not
  at the bottom; combining both observations is the mark.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Writing rust as just iron oxide — it is hydrated iron(III) oxide, and both water AND oxygen are required.
  • Explaining sacrificial protection without electron loss ("zinc is stronger") — the mark is reactivity and electron transfer.
  • Forgetting carbon and hydrogen's places as reference points in the series (they anchor extraction and acid-reaction predictions).
  • Confusing the blast furnace's reducing agents: carbon makes CO, and CO does the reduction — not carbon alone at the top.
  • Missing the limestone/slag step when asked "what removes impurities?"
  • Claiming alloys are harder because "the atoms are bigger" — the layers-disruption explanation is required.
  • Writing electrolysis for iron extraction (that is aluminium) — match method to reactivity.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Explain why gold is found unreactive in the Earth's crust while aluminium is extracted by electrolysis.

Answer: Gold is very low in the reactivity series — it does not react with water, oxygen or dilute acids, so it occurs as the free element and needs no chemical extraction. Aluminium is very reactive: its oxide is too stable for carbon to reduce at workable temperatures, so it must be extracted by electrolysis of molten aluminium oxide in cryolite.

Question 2 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Describe how iron is extracted in the blast furnace, including the role of limestone.

Answer: Coke burns to carbon dioxide, which reacts with more coke to carbon monoxide; the CO reduces haematite: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂. Limestone decomposes to calcium oxide, which reacts with sandy silica impurities to form molten calcium silicate (slag), which floats on the molten iron and is tapped off separately.

Question 3 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Explain sacrificial protection of iron.

Answer: A more reactive metal such as zinc is attached to iron in damp conditions. Zinc loses electrons more readily (Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻) and corrodes instead of the iron; the electrons it releases prevent iron from being oxidised. The zinc block is consumed over time — it is sacrificed — and must be replaced, but the iron stays intact.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 3 marks). Explain why stainless steel is harder than pure iron.

Answer: Stainless steel is an alloy of iron with chromium and nickel. Atoms of different sizes distort the regular layers of iron atoms, so the layers cannot slide over each other easily when stressed — the material resists deformation and is harder and stronger.

Question 5 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Write equations for the reactions of (i) magnesium with steam (ii) zinc with dilute hydrochloric acid (iii) zinc with copper(II) sulfate, and state the observation for (iii).

Answer: (i) Mg + H₂O → MgO + H₂. (ii) Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂. (iii) Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu — the zinc gains a red-brown copper deposit and the blue solution colour fades.

Question 6 (Paper 4, 3 marks). State the conditions needed for iron to rust and describe two methods of prevention.

Answer: Iron needs both water and oxygen (air) in contact with it. Prevention: barrier methods such as painting or greasing that exclude both; galvanising with a zinc coating (which also protects scratches by corroding preferentially); or sacrificial protection with attached zinc or magnesium blocks.

Metals and their reactions shape the environment as well as industry — the next topic is the chemistry of air and water.

title: Respiration, Muscles and the Internal Environment Revision Notes
content:
Quick revision: Respiration, Muscles and the Internal Environment

Biology — A2. Edexcel IAL Biology WBI15, Topic 7. Respiration releases energy as ATP for muscle contraction. Homeostasis keeps the internal environment stable, and the kidney is central to this. The topic links biochemistry to physiology.

Key areas to revise

  • Aerobic respiration
  • Anaerobic respiration in mammals
  • Respiratory quotient
  • Muscle contraction
  • Homeostasis and the kidney

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Core Detailed Revision Notes

Aerobic respiration overall reaction is the splitting of respiratory substrates to release carbon dioxide as a waste product and reuniting hydrogen with atmospheric oxygen with the release of large amounts of energy. Respiration is a stepped process, with each step controlled and catalysed by a specific intracellular enzyme, though specific enzyme names are not required.

Glycolysis takes place in the cytoplasm and involves the phosphorylation of hexoses, production of ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation, reduced coenzyme, pyruvate, and lactate. In anaerobic respiration, pyruvate is converted to lactate, which is later transported to the liver where it is oxidized back to pyruvate or converted to glycogen using oxygen to clear the oxygen debt.

The link reaction and the Krebs cycle take place in the mitochondrial matrix, leading to complete oxidation of glucose and formation of carbon dioxide by decarboxylation, ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation, and reduced NAD and FAD by dehydrogenation. Oxidative phosphorylation occurs at the inner mitochondrial membrane via the electron transport chain, involving chemiosmosis where protons diffuse through ATP synthase down an electrochemical gradient to synthesise ATP.

The respiratory quotient (RQ) is calculated as volume of carbon dioxide produced divided by volume of oxygen consumed over a given time period. Core Practical 15 uses an artificial hydrogen carrier like methylene blue or DCPIP to investigate respiration rates in yeast by timing the color change as it is reduced. Core Practical 16 uses a simple respirometer with soda lime or potassium hydroxide to absorb carbon dioxide, measuring oxygen consumption and calculating rates of respiration and RQ for germinating seeds or small invertebrates.

Muscles, tendons, the skeleton, and ligaments interact to enable movement, operating via antagonistic muscle pairs consisting of extensors and flexors. Mammalian skeletal muscle fibres are composed of myofibrils. Fast twitch fibres contract quickly, rely heavily on anaerobic glycolysis, fatigue rapidly, and have few capillaries and mitochondria. Slow twitch fibres contract slowly, rely on aerobic respiration, resist fatigue, and possess many mitochondria, myoglobin, and capillaries.

Muscle contraction is explained by the sliding filament theory. Action potentials trigger calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Calcium ions bind to troponin, causing tropomyosin to shift and expose myosin-binding sites on actin. Myosin heads bind to actin, forming cross-bridges, and undergo a power stroke using ATP hydrolysis catalysed by ATPase, pulling the actin filament inward and shortening the sarcomere.

Cardiac muscle is myogenic. Normal electrical activity coordinates the heartbeat beginning at the sinoatrial node (SAN) acting as the pacemaker, sending impulses across the atria to the atrioventricular node (AVN), down the bundle of His, and through the Purkyne fibres to contract the ventricles from the apex up. Electrocardiograms (ECGs) record electrical activity and aid in diagnosing abnormal heart rhythms like tachycardia, bradycardia, and fibrillation. Cardiac output equals heart rate multiplied by stroke volume. Variations in ventilation rate and cardiac output enable rapid oxygen delivery and carbon dioxide removal, regulated by the cardiovascular control centre and ventilation centre in the medulla oblongata, influenced by chemoreceptors and baroreceptors.

Adrenaline prepares the body for the fight or flight response by increasing heart rate, dilating airways, and redirecting blood flow. Core Practical 17 investigates the effects of exercise on tidal volume, breathing rate, respiratory minute ventilation, and oxygen consumption using spirometer traces.

Negative feedback returns a system to its set point when deviations occur, maintaining narrow limits essential for homeostasis, whereas positive feedback amplifies the deviation away from the set point. Homeostasis maintains the internal environment in a dynamic equilibrium during exercise, with the hypothalamus acting as the master controller in thermoregulation via shivering, sweating, and vasomotor changes.

The mammalian kidney gross structure includes the cortex, medulla, pelvis, ureter, and renal artery and vein, while microscopic structure features nephrons comprising the Bowman's capsule, proximal convoluted tubule, loop of Henle, distal convoluted tubule, and collecting duct. Urea is produced in the liver from excess deaminated amino acids. Ultrafiltration in the glomerulus under high hydrostatic pressure forces water, glucose, mineral ions, and urea through pores in the capillary endothelium and basement membrane into the Bowman's capsule.

Selective reabsorption occurs in the proximal tubule via active transport of sodium ions linked to co-transport of glucose and amino acids, followed by passive reabsorption of water by osmosis. The loop of Henle acts as a countercurrent multiplier, pumping sodium and chloride ions out of the ascending limb into the medulla to lower water potential, thereby causing water to leave the descending limb and collecting duct by osmosis for high water reabsorption.

Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect changes in blood water potential. If water potential drops, the posterior pituitary gland secretes more antidiuretic hormone (ADH), which increases the permeability of the distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct cells to water by inserting aquaporins, resulting in a smaller volume of concentrated urine via negative feedback. Gene expression can be switched on and off by DNA transcription factors, where peptide hormones act extracellularly via second messenger systems and steroid hormones cross cell membranes to act intracellularly as transcription factors.

Worked example

Calculate the respiratory quotient of an organism that produces 12 cm³ of carbon dioxide and consumes 15 cm³ of oxygen in a set time interval. Step 1: Write the formula RQ = VCO2 / VO2. Step 2: Substitute the values RQ = 12 / 15. Step 3: Calculate the final value giving RQ = 0.8.

Key points to remember

Students often forget that glycolysis does not require oxygen and occurs in the cytoplasm, unlike the link reaction, Krebs cycle, and oxidative phosphorylation which occur exclusively inside mitochondria.

Another common error is confusing the roles of the AVN and SAN in the cardiac cycle, and failing to specify that ADH increases the permeability of the collecting duct to water by stimulating the insertion of aquaporins into the cell membranes.

Always state the direction of ion movement and the active versus passive nature of transport when describing the countercurrent multiplier mechanism in the loop of Henle.

title: Exam technique: Programming and Algorithms
content:
### What earns the marks
For validation, the rejected range stated plus the rejection loop earns both marks. For structure, single entry and exit modules using only sequence, selection and iteration earn the design marks. For traces, each variable tracked per line earns method credit. For testing, the stage named with its setting (isolated module vs live users) earns each mark.
### Traps
Error: fixed FOR loops for unknown-attempt validation. Correction: WHILE-until-valid loops. Error: binary search on unsorted data. Correction: sort first or use linear search. Error: unit and acceptance settings swapped. Correction: unit is isolated with test data; acceptance is live with real users.
### Worked example
A trace table records the value of each variable at each step of an algorithm. For a linear search, the program checks each item in turn and can take up to n comparisons. A binary search on a sorted list halves the search space each time, so 16 sorted items need at most about log₂16 = 4 comparisons. Binary search only works if the list is sorted.
### Check yourself
Trace a binary search for 9 in the sorted list 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13. Record the middle index at each step and state the number of comparisons. It finds 9 at the middle on the first comparison.

Worked example

A ball is dropped from rest and falls 20 m. Taking down as positive, u = 0, s = 20 m and a = 9.81 m s⁻². Then v² = u² + 2as = 392.4, so v ≈ 19.8 m s⁻¹. Using the sign convention with up positive instead gives s = −20 m and a = −9.81 m s⁻², which gives the same answer with the signs consistent.

Common mistakes

  • Using SUVAT for a case with non-uniform acceleration, such as a body with increasing air resistance.
  • Mixing signs, for example taking up as positive but using g = +9.81 m s⁻².
  • Reading a displacement–time gradient as velocity only when it is a straight line. The gradient gives instantaneous velocity at any point on a curve.

title: AS Level Biology: Membranes, Proteins, DNA and Gene Expression
content:
Membranes, Proteins, DNA and Gene Expression — AS Level Biology

This revision note belongs to the Edexcel International Advanced Subsidiary (IAS) Biology specification, WBI11 Unit 1, Topic 2 Membranes, Proteins, DNA and Gene Expression. It covers membrane structure and properties, osmosis and the different kinds of membrane transport, the structure of proteins and how they are built from amino acids, the structure of DNA and RNA and how DNA replicates, the genetic code and how genes work, transcription and translation, mutations and their effects, patterns of inheritance including sex linkage, cystic fibrosis as an example of a gene mutation in humans, and genetic screening and its ethical and social issues. Every statement the topic is responsible for is covered in its own section or paragraph.

1. Cell membranes and the fluid mosaic model

The cell surface membrane (plasma membrane) is a phospholipid bilayer; each phospholipid has a hydrophilic head and two hydrophobic tails, and the heads face out and in while the tails face each other, making a barrier to charged and water-soluble substances. The fluid mosaic model is the accepted interpretation: the membrane is fluid — the phospholipids and proteins can move laterally in the layer — and mosaic because it contains a variety of proteins embedded in or attached to the bilayer, including channel proteins and carrier proteins for transport, receptor proteins for signalling, and proteins for cell recognition. The model is an interpretation of data — it was built from evidence such as electron micrographs and the ability of membranes to fuse and to self-seal — and it explains the structure and properties of cell membranes and how they control what enters and leaves the cell. Cholesterol in the membrane reduces fluidity at high temperatures and prevents the membrane from becoming too rigid at low temperatures.

2. Core Practical 3 — investigating membrane properties

Investigate membrane properties including the effect of alcohol and of temperature on membrane permeability. A typical method uses beetroot cylinders, which contain the red pigment betalain in their vacuoles; as the membrane is damaged, pigment leaks out and the colour of the surrounding solution deepens. Cut cylinders to the same length, wash off surface pigment in distilled water, then place them in water at a range of temperatures or in different concentrations of alcohol for a fixed time, remove the tissue and measure the concentration of pigment in the solution with a colorimeter. As temperature rises or alcohol concentration rises, the membrane proteins denature and the lipid bilayer is disrupted, so permeability increases and more pigment leaks out; a control at room temperature or in distilled water shows the baseline. Record the colorimeter reading for each tube, plot a graph of permeability against temperature or against alcohol concentration, and explain the trend in terms of the effect on membrane proteins and lipids.

3. Osmosis and how water moves across membranes

Osmosis is the net movement of free water molecules through a partially permeable membrane, down a water potential gradient — from higher water potential to lower water potential. Water potential is the tendency of water to move; adding a solute lowers it, so a concentrated solution has a more negative water potential than a dilute one, and pure water has the highest (zero) water potential. If a cell is placed in a solution of higher water potential than its contents, water enters by osmosis and the cell swells; if it is an animal cell it may burst (haemolysis); if it is a plant cell the cell wall prevents bursting and the cell becomes turgid, which supports the plant. In a solution of lower water potential, water leaves and the cell shrinks — animal cells crenate and plant cells become plasmolysed, with the membrane pulling away from the wall. A recommended additional practical is to investigate tissue water potentials using plant tissue (for example potato or onion epidermis) and graded concentrations of a solute: place tissue in solutions of different molarity, note the change in length or mass, and find the concentration at which there is no change — that concentration has the same water potential as the tissue.

4. Passive transport, active transport, endocytosis and exocytosis

Passive transport needs no energy input because substances move down their concentration gradient. Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to one of lower concentration; small, non-polar molecules such as oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse directly through the phospholipid bilayer, while ions and large polar molecules cannot. Facilitated diffusion is the movement of specific particles down their concentration gradient through channel proteins or carrier proteins — channel proteins form water-filled pores for ions, and carrier proteins change shape to carry molecules across. Active transport moves substances against their concentration gradient (from low to high concentration) and needs energy directly from ATP; carrier proteins use ATP to pump substances across, as in the sodium–potassium pump. Endocytosis is the bulk movement of material into the cell inside a vesicle formed from the plasma membrane; phagocytosis takes in solid material and pinocytosis takes in fluid. Exocytosis is the reverse — material is moved out of the cell in a vesicle that fuses with the plasma membrane, as in the secretion of proteins and neurotransmitters. Carrier and channel proteins are involved in facilitated diffusion and active transport; the key difference is that active transport needs ATP and moves substances against their gradient.

5. Protein structure: from amino acid to three-dimensional shape

Amino acids are the monomers of proteins; the basic structure of an amino acid is an amino group, a carboxyl group and a variable R group all attached to a central carbon, with a hydrogen on the remaining bond. There are around 20 amino acids found in proteins, differing only in their R group, and the sequence of amino acids in a protein is its primary structure. Amino acids join by condensation reactions to form peptide bonds, making dipeptides and then polypeptides; a polypeptide chain is a protein’s primary structure and it determines everything about the protein. The secondary structure is the local folding of the chain into alpha-helices and beta-pleated sheets, held by hydrogen bonds between the peptide bonds. The tertiary structure is the overall three-dimensional folding of the whole polypeptide, held by hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, disulfide bonds and hydrophobic interactions; it gives the protein its specific shape and therefore its function. Globular proteins are roughly spherical and usually soluble and active — haemoglobin is the classic example, with four polypeptide chains and a haem group each carrying one oxygen molecule, and it shows quaternary structure (several polypeptides together) plus the importance of the three-dimensional shape for its oxygen-carrying function. Fibrous proteins are long, insoluble and structural — collagen is the example, made of three polypeptide chains wound into a rope-like triple helix, giving strength for tendons, ligaments and skin. The shape of a protein determines its function, so a change to the primary structure can alter the folding and disable the protein.

6. DNA structure and replication

A DNA molecule is made of two nucleotide strands twisted into a double helix. Each nucleotide is made of a deoxyribose sugar, a phosphate group and a base — either adenine (A), cytosine (C), guanine (G) or thymine (T). The two strands run antiparallel and are linked by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases — A pairs with T (two hydrogen bonds) and C pairs with G (three hydrogen bonds). RNA is similar but has ribose instead of deoxyribose, uracil instead of thymine, and is usually single-stranded. The two strands are complementary, so knowing one strand tells you the other, and the two strands separate at replication. DNA replication is semi-conservative: the double helix unzips, each strand acts as a template, and free nucleotides pair with their complementary bases; DNA polymerase joins the nucleotides into a new strand. The result is two identical DNA molecules, each with one old strand and one new strand. Meselson and Stahl’s experiment supported this: they grew bacteria in a medium with a heavy isotope of nitrogen (15N), then moved them to a 14N medium and examined the DNA by centrifugation; the first generation was a single hybrid band (not one heavy and one light, which would be conservative replication), and later generations showed a mixture of hybrid and light bands — exactly what semi-conservative replication predicts and ruling out the conservative and dispersive alternatives.

7. The genetic code and how it works

The genetic code is the set of rules translating the base sequence of mRNA into the amino acid sequence of a protein. It is a triplet code — three bases (a base triplet on DNA, a codon on mRNA) code for one amino acid; it is non-overlapping — each base is read once in order; and it is degenerate — more than one codon can code for the same amino acid, which is why many mutations change a base but not the amino acid. Part of the code is a stop codon that signals the end of translation; there is no amino acid for it. A gene is a sequence of bases on a DNA molecule that codes for a sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide chain. In transcription, the gene is copied into a complementary mRNA molecule by the enzyme RNA polymerase, using the DNA template (antisense) strand; the mRNA is complementary to the template strand and the same as the coding (sense) strand except with uracil in place of thymine. mRNA leaves the nucleus and attaches to ribosomes in the cytoplasm; transfer RNA (tRNA) molecules carry amino acids to the ribosome, each with a three-base anticodon that pairs with the mRNA codon, so the ribosome joins the amino acids into a polypeptide chain in the order of the codons until a stop codon is reached.

8. Mutations: the changes and their effects

A mutation is a change in the DNA base sequence. A substitution replaces one base with another — it may do nothing, change one amino acid, or, rarely, create a stop codon that shortens the protein. An insertion adds one or more bases and a deletion removes one or more; because the code is read in triplets, an insertion or deletion not in a multiple of three causes a frameshift, changing every amino acid after the mutation and usually destroying the protein’s function. Mutations are the only source of new alleles, and most have no observable effect — they may be in non-coding DNA, or a degenerate codon and amino acid may stay the same, or the changed protein still folds and works. Some mutations give rise to cancer (if they affect control of the cell cycle) or to genetic disorders. Ionising radiation such as X-rays and ultraviolet light, and some chemicals such as those in tobacco smoke, can increase the rate of mutation by damaging DNA.

9. Patterns of inheritance: monohybrid crosses, pedigree diagrams and sex linkage

A gene can have different alleles; the genotype is the alleles an organism has, the phenotype is the observable feature. Dominant alleles show in the phenotype even when heterozygous; recessive alleles only show when homozygous. A monohybrid cross is the inheritance of one gene with two alleles; the typical ratios are a 3:1 phenotype ratio in the F2 of a monohybrid cross between two heterozygotes, but only if the alleles are completely dominant and the gene is autosomal. Sex linkage is the inheritance of a gene on the X chromosome — because males have only one X, a recessive allele on it shows in their phenotype even though they are effectively hemizygous; red-green colour blindness and haemophilia are human X-linked conditions that are more common in males. Pedigree diagrams record which family members show a trait and are used to work out whether a trait is dominant or recessive and whether it is autosomal or sex-linked. Codominance is when both alleles are expressed in the heterozygote, as in the ABO blood group system where IA and IB are codominant and i is recessive, giving the four blood groups A, B, AB and O.

10. Cystic fibrosis: a mutation that affects three systems

Cystic fibrosis is caused by a mutation in a gene that codes for a chloride ion channel protein; in the most common form a deletion of three bases removes a single amino acid from the protein, so the channel does not work properly. As a result, chloride ions and water cannot move properly across cell membranes, and the mucus and other secretions become abnormally thick. In the gaseous exchange system the thick mucus blocks the airways and makes it hard to breathe and to clear infections; in the digestive system the pancreatic duct is blocked so digestive enzymes from the pancreas cannot reach the gut, so food is not digested and absorbed properly, and the person may be malnourished; in the reproductive system the vas deferens is often absent or blocked in males, causing infertility. Treatments include physiotherapy and antibiotics for the lungs, and enzyme supplements with meals for digestion, and newer treatments aim to correct the underlying defect.

11. Genetic screening: what it can do and the issues it raises

Genetic screening can identify carriers of recessive alleles (people who have one normal allele and one faulty allele and are unaffected but could pass the allele on), and prenatal testing can check a fetus: amniocentesis takes a sample of amniotic fluid at around 15–17 weeks, and chorionic villus sampling takes a sample of placental tissue at 8–12 weeks. Pre-implantation genetic diagnosis is used with IVF to test embryos before implantation and select unaffected ones. Each raises ethical and social questions — the safety and reliability of the test, the risks of miscarriage with invasive prenatal testing, the right to know or not to know, who decides which conditions to test for, the possible choice to terminate a pregnancy, anxiety and guilt, and the risk that screening could be used to select non-medical traits. Students should be able to identify and discuss these from religious, moral and social viewpoints and to evaluate the implications of prenatal genetic screening.

12. How to use this note and what to revise next

Use these notes by working through each section and checking that you can draw a cell membrane from the fluid mosaic model and label the phospholipid bilayer, the proteins, cholesterol and glycoproteins; state the difference between diffusion, facilitated diffusion and active transport, and give an example of each; outline the steps of DNA extraction (a simple practical with strawberries or onions is useful to remember); and carry out a genetic cross with a Punnett square and interpret the ratios. Revise by drawing protein structure from amino acid to tertiary, then drawing the DNA double helix and explaining semi-conservative replication and the Meselson–Stahl evidence. After this topic, revise Topic 3 Cell structure, reproduction and development, because the same DNA and protein-synthesis processes control cell differentiation and the cell cycle.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Osmosis, applied to a potato cylinder placed in a sugar solution: water moves from the higher water potential to the lower one, down a gradient, through a partially permeable membrane. A cylinder that loses mass has been placed in a solution of lower water potential than its cells. Give the direction of water movement and the reason in the same sentence.
  • Monohybrid cross, applied to two heterozygotes (Aa × Aa): the offspring are 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa, so the phenotypic ratio is 3 : 1. Write the parental genotypes, the gametes and the Punnett square, then state the ratio. A ratio alone earns less than the full working. Key: AA = homozygous dominant; Aa = heterozygote; aa = homozygous recessive; the numbers 1 : 2 : 1 are the expected proportions of those genotypes among the offspring, not counts unless the family is large.
  • Sex linkage, applied to X-linked haemophilia: a carrier mother (XᴴXʰ) and a normal father (XᴴY) have a 50% chance of a son with haemophilia, but a daughter cannot be affected unless her father is affected. Use the X and Y chromosomes explicitly in the genotypes.
  • Mutation effects: a substitution may have no effect because the genetic code is degenerate, while a frameshift changes every codon after the mutation. Name the type of mutation and state whether the change alters the amino acid sequence.

How substances cross a membrane, compared

RouteDirectionProtein neededATP usedExample
Simple diffusionDown the concentration gradientNoNoOxygen into a cell
Facilitated diffusionDown the concentration gradientChannel or carrierNoGlucose into a red blood cell through a carrier
OsmosisDown a water potential gradientNo (partially permeable membrane)NoWater into a root hair cell
Active transportAgainst the concentration gradientCarrier that changes shapeYes, ATP hydrolysedIons reabsorbed in the kidney
Endocytosis and exocytosisInto or out of the cell in a vesicleNo, membrane fusionYesPhagocytosis of a bacterium; secretion of an enzyme

Typical mistakes

  • Writing that active transport "uses energy" and stopping there. The mark is for ATP being hydrolysed to change the shape of the carrier protein, which moves the substance against its gradient.
  • Confusing water potential with solute concentration. Pure water at atmospheric pressure has a water potential of zero, and every solution has a negative value. Water moves from the less negative (higher) water potential to the more negative one.
  • Swapping codon and anticodon. The codon is the triplet on messenger RNA; the anticodon is the triplet on transfer RNA that pairs with it.
  • Saying DNA polymerase unzips the helix. Helicase breaks the hydrogen bonds between the strands; DNA polymerase then adds free nucleotides to the exposed template, always in the 5-prime to 3-prime direction.
  • Claiming the Meselson and Stahl experiment showed dispersive replication. After one generation in nitrogen-15 there was a single hybrid band, and after two generations there were hybrid and light bands. A dispersive model would have given a single intermediate band throughout.
  • Assuming a dominant allele is the more common one. Dominance describes expression in the heterozygote, not frequency in the population.
  • Confusing amniocentesis with chorionic villus sampling. Amniocentesis samples amniotic fluid at about 15 to 17 weeks; chorionic villus sampling takes placental tissue at about 8 to 12 weeks, earlier but with a higher risk of miscarriage.
  • Explaining cystic fibrosis without a mechanism. The mutation changes the chloride channel, so chloride and water cannot cross normally, secretions become thick, and the airways, pancreatic duct and vas deferens are affected. Name the ion, the effect on the secretion and the effect on the organ.

Exam-style questions

  1. Explain why the fluid mosaic model was modified as new evidence appeared. Answer: the model is an interpretation of data, not a direct observation. Freeze-fracture electron micrographs showed proteins embedded within the bilayer rather than coating it, and experiments on membrane fusion showed that proteins move within the membrane, so the model was revised to show a fluid bilayer with proteins partly or wholly embedded.
  2. A potato cylinder loses mass after 30 minutes in 0.6 mol per dm cubed sucrose solution. Explain the loss in terms of water potential. Answer: the sucrose solution has a lower (more negative) water potential than the vacuole contents, so water leaves the cells by osmosis down a water potential gradient through the partially permeable membranes, the cells lose turgor, and the cylinder shrinks.
  3. Distinguish facilitated diffusion from active transport. Answer: both use membrane proteins, but facilitated diffusion moves substances down their concentration gradient through channels or carriers and needs no ATP, while active transport moves them against the gradient using a carrier whose shape is changed by ATP hydrolysis.
  4. Describe the evidence that DNA replication is semi-conservative. Answer: bacteria were grown in nitrogen-15 so that all DNA was heavy, then transferred to nitrogen-14. After one generation all DNA was of intermediate density, which rules out conservative replication; after two generations half the DNA was intermediate and half light, which fits each new molecule keeping one parental strand.
  5. Give the role of the template strand, the codon and the anticodon in protein synthesis. Answer: the template (antisense) strand is the DNA strand that RNA polymerase copies; the codon is the triplet of bases on mRNA that specifies one amino acid; the anticodon on tRNA is complementary to the codon and pairs with it at the ribosome so that the correct amino acid is added.
  6. Explain how a substitution and a deletion affect the polypeptide differently. Answer: a substitution changes one base, so at most one codon changes and, because the code is degenerate, the amino acid sequence may not change at all. A deletion shifts the reading frame, so every codon after the mutation is different and the protein is usually non-functional.
  7. A carrier mother and an unaffected father are expecting a child. Explain the probability that a son is colour blind. Answer: the mother is heterozygous, with one affected X chromosome and one normal X chromosome. A son inherits one of her X chromosomes with equal probability, so half the sons are colour blind. Daughters receive the father's normal X, so none is colour blind, although half are carriers.
  8. Explain how the mutation that causes cystic fibrosis impairs three body systems. Answer: the three-base deletion removes one amino acid from the chloride channel protein, so chloride transport is faulty and water follows less readily. Mucus in the airways becomes thick and blocks gas exchange; the pancreatic duct blocks so digestive enzymes do not reach the gut; the vas deferens is absent or blocked, reducing male fertility.

Factors that change the rate of diffusion and osmosis

Diffusion across a membrane depends on the membrane and on the gradient across it. The rate of net movement rises with the concentration difference, with the surface area available for exchange, and it falls as the diffusion path gets longer. Osmosis is the same process for water alone: net movement of water across a partially permeable membrane, down a water potential gradient.

Key: rate of diffusion ∝ (surface area × concentration difference) ÷ diffusion path length, where ∝ means "is proportional to", surface area is in m², concentration difference in mol m⁻³ and path length in m.

Why surface area changes the rate

The graph holds the concentration difference fixed and changes only the surface area. The steeper line has the larger area, and it moves more molecules per second for the same gradient. Cells that exchange materials quickly, such as the cells lining the small intestine, increase their surface area by folding the membrane, and that is why the same gradient is worked harder by a larger area.

Osmosis in a plant tissue practical

In the plant tissue osmosis practical, cylinders of plant tissue are placed in sucrose solutions of different concentrations and their mass is measured before and after. A gain in mass means water has moved into the cells, which happens when the solution is more dilute than the cell contents; a loss means water has left. The concentration at which the mass does not change is the one at which the solution and the cell sap are isotonic. Reading the result correctly depends on remembering that osmosis follows water potential, not the concentration of the solute alone.

Common errors in the rate answer

Students often say that a larger surface area makes diffusion faster because there is more space, without naming the gradient. A complete answer names the surface area, the concentration difference and the thinness of the membrane, and states that the rate is greater because more molecules cross per unit time.

title: Data Structures
content:
`# Data Structures

Arrays and Lists

Contiguous, indexed, O(1) access; fixed size. 2D arrays: element (i, j) — rows × columns.

Stack (LIFO)

push/pop/peek at one end. Uses: call stacks, undo, expression evaluation, DFS.

Example: evaluating 3 4 + : push 3, push 4, pop both, push 7.

Queue (FIFO)

enqueue at rear, dequeue at front. Uses: print queues, schedulers, BFS. A circular queue reuses vacated slots with head/tail pointers modulo capacity.

Linked List

Nodes with data + pointer. Insert/delete O(1) at a known node; search O(n). Traversal follows next pointers until null.

Hash Table

Hash function maps keys → index. Collisions resolved by chaining or open addressing. Average O(1) lookup, worst O(n).

Complexity

SearchO(n)O(n)O(1) avg
Insert/deleteO(n)O(1)O(1) avg

Exam tips: trace pointers carefully in linked-list diagrams; for circular queues, show head/tail movement and overflow/underflow checks.

title: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Bearings, Constructions and Loci
content:
Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Bearings, Constructions and Loci

Bearings are how navigators describe direction, and geometrical constructions are how geometers draw exact figures with only a ruler and a pair of compasses. Together they fill the practical geometry questions on both papers: a bearing calculated from a diagram, a locus sketched and shaded, a perpendicular bisector constructed and justified. This note builds the topic from zero: the three rules of bearings and the back-bearing calculation, the compass-and-ruler constructions with their standard arcs, scale drawings and their measurements, and the four loci the syllabus requires, with every step shown.

Bearings: the three rules

A bearing is a direction written as a three-figure angle. Three rules define it:

  1. Measured from North (the north line, drawn as an upward arrow).
  2. Clockwise.
  3. Written with three figures — 035°, 090°, 245° (never 35° or 9°).

Bearings are always between 000° and 360°; a direction due east is 090°, due south 180°, due west 270°.

Worked example. A ship sails from A on a bearing of 060° for 12 km to B, then on a bearing of 150° for 8 km to C. Describe the position of C relative to A qualitatively.

060 deg is between north and east; 150 deg is between east and
south. So C lies south-east of A, and the two legs turn 90 deg
(150 - 60 = 90) - the path is two perpendicular legs, making a
right angle at B.

Back bearings

The bearing of A from B is not the bearing of B from A — they differ by 180° (add if under 180°, subtract if 180° or more):

back bearing = bearing + 180  (if bearing < 180)
             = bearing - 180  (if bearing >= 180)

Worked example. The bearing of B from A is 072°. Find the bearing of A from B.

72 + 180 = 252 deg

Worked example 2 (three-figure check). The bearing of P from Q is 310°. Find the bearing of Q from P.

310 - 180 = 130 deg

Bearings with trigonometry

Bearing problems become right-triangle problems once you draw the north lines and mark the angles between the path and north. Use Pythagoras for distances and trigonometry for angles, then convert the angle into a bearing.

Worked example. A boat sails 5 km due north, then 12 km due east. Find its distance and bearing from the start.

distance = sqrt(5^2 + 12^2) = sqrt(169) = 13 km
angle east of north: tan(theta) = 12/5  ->  theta = 67.4 deg
bearing = 067 deg (to the nearest degree)

Worked example 2 (reverse). A helicopter is 9 km from base on a bearing of 145°. How far east and how far south of the base is it?

angle from south = 180 - 145 = 35 deg
east = 9 sin(35) = 5.16 km
south = 9 cos(35) = 7.37 km

Constructions: ruler and compasses only

Constructions are marked on the accuracy of the arcs and the visibility of the construction lines. Keep your compasses sharp and do not rub out the arcs.

ConstructionStandard method (in order)
Perpendicular bisector of ABcompasses wider than half AB: arc from A, same-radius arc from B, both sides; join the two intersections
Angle bisectorarc across both arms from the vertex; same-radius arcs from those two crossings; join the vertex to their intersection
Perpendicular from a point to a linearc from the point cutting the line twice; equal arcs from those cuts; join the point to their intersection
Perpendicular at a point on a lineequal arcs either side of the point; then the perpendicular-bisector method between them
60° anglearc from the endpoint across the line; same radius arc from the crossing; join
Triangle given SSSdraw the base; arcs of the other two lengths from each end; join the intersection

Worked example. Construct the perpendicular bisector of a segment AB of length 8 cm and explain why every point on it is equidistant from A and B.

Construction: arcs of radius > 4 cm from A and from B, above and
below the segment; the two intersections join to form the bisector.
Why: the arcs are circles of equal radius centred at A and B, so
their intersection points are equidistant from A and B; the line
through them is the locus of all such points.

Scale drawings

A scale drawing represents a real situation to a ratio: 1 : 50 000 means 1 cm on paper represents 50 000 cm in reality (0.5 km). The method: convert the scale to a usable unit, measure or construct to scale, then read back with the reverse conversion.

Worked example. A map has scale 1 : 25 000. Two towns are 6.4 cm apart on the map. Find the real distance in km.

6.4 cm x 25 000 = 160 000 cm
160 000 cm = 1600 m = 1.6 km

Worked example 2 (drawing). A field is 400 m by 250 m. Draw it at scale 1 : 5000. What are the drawing dimensions?

400 m = 40 000 cm; /5000 = 8 cm
250 m = 25 000 cm; /5000 = 5 cm
The drawing is 8 cm by 5 cm.

Loci

A locus is the set of all points satisfying a condition. Four standard loci are examinable, and each has its construction:

  • Fixed distance from a point: a circle (arc) of that radius, centred on the point.
  • Equidistant from two points: the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining them.
  • Equidistant from two lines: the angle bisector(s) of the angle between them.
  • Fixed distance from a line: two parallel lines at that distance, one on each side (with semicircular ends for a segment).

Region questions combine loci: "shade the region closer to A than B and within 3 cm of C" means intersect the perpendicular bisector's half-plane with the circle's interior.

Worked example. A goat is tethered to a corner of a 6 m by 4 m shed with a 5 m rope. Describe the region it can reach.

A three-quarter circle of radius 5 m around the corner, minus
the part blocked by the shed: the rope wraps the shed's 4 m and
6 m walls. The reachable region is the quarter circle of radius
5 m outside the shed plus smaller arcs where the rope wraps
(radius 1 m around the far 4 m corner, no reach around the far
6 m corner since 5 - 6 < 0).

Worked examples: bearings and loci together

Worked example. Two radio transmitters A and B are 10 km apart, with B due east of A. A signal is received equally strongly at points equidistant from A and B, and within 6 km of A. Describe the region.

Equidistant from A and B: the perpendicular bisector of AB - a
north-south line 5 km east of A.
Within 6 km of A: a circle of radius 6 km centred at A.
The region is the part of the circle on one side of the bisector:
a circular segment of radius 6 km, cut by the line 5 km from A.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Bearing definition) State the three rules for a bearing. Answer: Measured from north, clockwise, written as three figures.
  2. (Back bearing) The bearing of X from Y is 128°. Find the bearing of Y from X. Answer: 128 + 180 = 308°.
  3. (Calculation) A plane flies 30 km north then 40 km east. Find its distance from the start and its bearing. Answer: distance = √(900 + 1600) = 50 km; tan θ = 40/30 → θ = 53.1°, bearing 053°.
  4. (Components) A ship is 15 km from port on a bearing of 210°. Find its distance west of the port. Answer: angle from south = 210 − 180 = 30°; west = 15 sin 30 = 7.5 km.
  5. (Construction) Describe how to construct the perpendicular bisector of a 6 cm segment. Answer: Set compasses wider than 3 cm; draw arcs from each endpoint, both above and below; join the two crossing points.
  6. (Locus) Describe the locus of points equidistant from the sides of an angle. Answer: The angle bisector — every point on it is the same perpendicular distance from both arms.
  7. (Scale) On a 1 : 20 000 map, a lake is 3.5 cm long. Find its real length in km. Answer: 3.5 × 20 000 = 70 000 cm = 0.7 km.
  8. (Region) Shade the region inside a triangle that is closer to side AB than to side AC and within 2 cm of vertex A. Answer: The intersection of the half-plane on AB's side of the angle bisector of A with the circle of radius 2 cm centred at A.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Two-figure bearings: 35° must be written 035°. Three figures, always.
  • Measuring from the wrong north: bearings start at north, not east. A bearing of 090° is east, not north.
  • Back-bearing addition: add 180 if the bearing is below 180, subtract if above; the result must stay between 000 and 360.
  • Anticlockwise angles: bearing questions are clockwise; a clockwise angle and its anticlockwise partner sum to 360.
  • Rubbing out construction arcs: the arcs are the evidence. Leave them visible and use a sharp pencil.
  • Locus shading: shade the region, not the boundary line; the question usually says "shade the region".
  • Scale unit slips: convert the real measurement to the same unit as the drawing before applying the ratio, and remember 1 km = 100 000 cm.
  • Diagram not to scale: measure only when told to; otherwise calculate. A protractor reading on a "not to scale" diagram earns nothing.

title: Exam technique: Transformations and Vectors
content:
### What earns the marks
For translations and vector arithmetic, each component computed separately earns credit: show x and y lines. For magnitude, the root-of-sum-of-squares line earns the method mark before evaluation. For reflections and rotations, the coordinate rule stated ((y; -x) for 90 degrees clockwise) earns the method mark. For describing transformations, all three of type, centre or line, and size or angle are needed for full marks.
### Traps
Error: writing column vectors as bracket rows that lose a row. Correction: use (x; y) form and keep both components. Error: (100) or 14 for the magnitude of (6; 8). Correction: square, add, then root. Error: (-y; x) for a clockwise rotation. Correction: clockwise is (y; -x). Error: negating both coordinates for a single-axis reflection. Correction: one axis changes, the other stays.
### Worked example
Point A(1; 2) is translated by the vector (3; -1), giving A'(4; 1). Reflecting A' in the x-axis gives (4; -1). Rotating the point (3; -1) 90 degrees clockwise about the origin gives (-1; -3), using the rule (x; y) to (y; -x). Scaling (1; 2) by a factor of 2 from the origin gives (2; 4). Write each coordinate step on its own line.
### Check yourself
A point at (6; 8) has magnitude sqrt(6^2 + 8^2) = sqrt(100) = 10. Explain why the magnitude is never the sum 6 + 8 = 14. The magnitude uses the root of the sum of squares, so the components do not add directly.

### Worked example
Point A(1; 2) is translated by the vector (3; -1), giving A'(4; 1). Reflecting A' in the x-axis gives (4; -1). Rotating the point (3; -1) 90 degrees clockwise about the origin gives (-1; -3), using the rule (x; y) to (y; -x). Scaling (1; 2) by a factor of 2 from the origin gives (2; 4). Write each coordinate step on its own line.
### Check yourself
A point at (6; 8) has magnitude sqrt(6^2 + 8^2) = sqrt(100) = 10. Explain why the magnitude is never the sum 6 + 8 = 14. The magnitude uses the root of the sum of squares, so the components do not add directly.

title: Exam technique: Sine and Cosine Rules
content:
### What earns the marks
For the sine rule, the matched pairs written (b / sin 65 = 7 / sin 40) earn the method mark. For the cosine rule, the full substitution with cos evaluated earns the mark: write a squared = 25 + 64 - 2 x 5 x 8 x 0.5. For the largest angle, identifying the longest side first earns credit. For area, half a b sin C quoted earns the mark on its own.
### Traps
Error: sides paired with wrong angles in the sine rule. Correction: each side faces its angle. Error: 49 given as side a. Correction: root the cosine-rule result. Error: calculator-only acute angle for an obtuse ambiguous case. Correction: subtract from 180 by hand. Error: half a b without sine for a non-right triangle. Correction: area needs the sine factor unless the angle is 90 degrees.

title: Communication and Networking — Study Notes
content:
`# Communication and Networking

Transmission

  • Serial: one bit at a time — cheaper, reliable over distance
  • Parallel: multiple bits simultaneously — fast but suffers skew and crosstalk over long runs
  • Direction: simplex (one way), half-duplex (alternating), full-duplex (both ways)

Packets and Protocols

Data splits into packets with header (addresses, sequence) and trailer (checksum). A protocol is an agreed rule set — without one, devices cannot interpret signals.

  • TCP/IP stack: application → transport → network → link
  • HTTP/HTTPS: web transfer; HTTPS encrypts with TLS
  • FTP: file transfer; SMTP/POP3/IMAP: email

Network Types

  • LAN: small site, privately owned; WAN: large geographic scale (the internet)
  • Topologies: bus, star, mesh (star is most common — central switch)

Hardware

Routers join networks by IP; switches forward frames by MAC within a LAN; gateways translate protocols.

Client-Server vs Peer-to-Peer

Client-server: central services, easy administration, single point of failure. P2P: every node shares files directly — cheap, hard to manage (torrents, blockchain).

Exam tips: explain packet switching with header/trailer details; justify protocol choice per application (email vs streaming).

Network topologies and hardware

In a star topology every device connects to a central switch. If one cable or device fails, the others keep working, but if the central switch fails the whole network stops. In a bus topology all devices share one cable, which is cheap but means a break in the cable disables the network.

A switch connects devices within a local area network (LAN) and sends each frame only to the device it is addressed to, using MAC addresses. A router connects separate networks together and forwards packets using IP addresses. A wireless access point lets wireless devices join a wired LAN.

Exam tip: when comparing topologies, state what happens when one device fails and when the central device fails. Those two cases are the usual differentiators.

Worked example: transfer time and latency

A 2 Mbit file sent over a link of 1 Mbit per second takes 2 seconds to transfer, ignoring overheads. Latency is the delay before the first bit arrives, and it adds to the total time. If the latency is 0.2 seconds, the complete delivery takes about 2.2 seconds. Stating which quantity you are calculating, and the units, earns method marks even when the final figure is slightly off.

Bandwidth and the shared medium

  • Bandwidth is the maximum data rate of a link. Actual throughput is lower when many devices share the medium, because they take turns or collide.
  • Wired connections such as Ethernet usually give more stable speeds than wireless, which is affected by distance, walls and interference.

title: AS Level Mathematics: Coordinate Geometry
content:
AS Level Mathematics: Coordinate Geometry

Coordinate geometry turns shapes into algebra: every line is an equation, every intersection is a simultaneous equation, and every circle is a completed square waiting to happen. This note builds the whole AS toolkit from zero: distance and midpoint, gradients with the parallel and perpendicular rules, the three forms of a line's equation, intersections and perpendicular bisectors, circles in both centre-radius and expanded form, and tangents and normals to circles. Every worked example writes the formula line first, because that is where the method marks are.

Distance and midpoint

distance between (x1, y1) and (x2, y2):
d = √((x2 - x1)² + (y2 - y1)²)

midpoint: ((x1 + x2)/2, (y1 + y2)/2)

The distance formula is Pythagoras in disguise: the horizontal and vertical gaps are the legs of a right triangle, and the distance is the hypotenuse.

Worked example. Find the distance and midpoint of A(1, 2) and B(7, 10).

d = √(6² + 8²) = √(100) = 10
midpoint = ((1 + 7)/2, (2 + 10)/2) = (4, 6)

Gradient and the parallel/perpendicular rules

gradient m = (y2 - y1)/(x2 - x1)   (rise over run)

parallel lines: m¹ = m²
perpendicular lines: m¹ x m² = -1   (m² = -1/m¹)

Worked example. Find the gradient of AB for A(1, 2), B(5, 10), and the gradient of a line perpendicular to it.

m = (10 - 2)/(5 - 1) = 8/4 = 2
perpendicular gradient = -1/2

Worked example 2 (collinearity). Show A(1, 1), B(3, 5), C(5, 9) are collinear.

m(AB) = 4/2 = 2;  m(BC) = 4/2 = 2
equal gradients and a shared point B, so collinear

Equations of straight lines

Three forms, each useful in its own situation:

  • y = mx + c: gradient m, y-intercept c. Use when you know both.
  • y − y₁ = m(x − x₁): point-slope form. Use when you know a point and the gradient.
  • ax + by + c = 0: general form. Rearrange to find m and c when needed.

Worked example 1. Find the equation of the line through (2, 5) with gradient 3.

y - 5 = 3(x - 2)
y = 3x - 6 + 5
y = 3x - 1

Worked example 2 (two points). Find the equation of the line through (1, 4) and (4, 13).

m = (13 - 4)/(4 - 1) = 9/3 = 3
using (1, 4): y - 4 = 3(x - 1)  →  y = 3x + 1

Worked example 3 (perpendicular). Find the line through (2, 1) perpendicular to y = 2x + 3.

perpendicular gradient = -1/2
y - 1 = -1/2 (x - 2)
y = -x/2 + 1 + 1 = -x/2 + 2

Intersections and the perpendicular bisector

Two lines meet where their equations are simultaneously true: set them equal and solve. The perpendicular bisector of AB passes through the midpoint of AB with gradient −1/m(AB).

Worked example. Find where y = 3x − 1 meets y = −x + 7.

3x - 1 = -x + 7
4x = 8  →  x = 2;  y = 3(2) - 1 = 5
intersection: (2, 5)

Worked example 2 (perpendicular bisector). Find the perpendicular bisector of A(1, 2) and B(5, 10).

midpoint = (3, 6)
m(AB) = 8/4 = 2  →  perpendicular gradient = -1/2
y - 6 = -1/2 (x - 3)
y = -x/2 + 3/2 + 6 = -x/2 + 7.5

Circles: centre-radius form

(x - a)² + (y - b)² = r²
centre (a, b), radius r

expanded form x² + y² + 2fx + 2gy + c = 0:
complete the square in x and y to recover the centre and radius

Worked example 1. State the centre and radius of (x − 3)² + (y + 2)² = 25.

centre (3, -2); radius = 5

Worked example 2 (completing the square). Find the centre and radius of x² + y² − 6x + 8y − 11 = 0.

(x² - 6x) + (y² + 8y) = 11
(x - 3)² - 9 + (y + 4)² - 16 = 11
(x - 3)² + (y + 4)² = 36
centre (3, -4), radius 6

Worked example 3 (circle from diameter). AB is a diameter with A(1, 2) and B(7, 10). Find the circle's equation.

centre = midpoint = (4, 6)
radius = half the distance = 10/2 = 5
(x - 4)² + (y - 6)² = 25

Tangents and normals to circles

A tangent to a circle is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact. The method: find the gradient of the radius from the centre to the point, take the negative reciprocal for the tangent, then use the point-slope form.

Worked example. Find the tangent to the circle centre (2, 3) at the point (5, 7).

radius gradient = (7 - 3)/(5 - 2) = 4/3
tangent gradient = -3/4
y - 7 = -3/4 (x - 5)
4y - 28 = -3x + 15
3x + 4y = 43

Worked example 2 (tangent length). From the point P(8, 3), find the length of the tangent to the circle (x − 2)² + (y − 1)² = 13.

centre C(2, 1), radius √(13)
distance PC = √(6² + 2²) = √(40)
tangent² = PC² - r² = 40 - 13 = 27
tangent length = √(27) = 3 √(3) = 5.20

The right angle between radius and tangent makes every tangent-length question a Pythagoras problem in disguise; drawing the radius to the contact point is the step that unlocks it.

Worked example 2 (normal). The normal at a point on a circle is the radius line extended. Find the normal at the same point.

normal gradient = radius gradient = 4/3
y - 7 = 4/3 (x - 5)  →  4x - 3y + 1 = 0 (rearranged)

Circles and lines: intersection problems

Where a line meets a circle, substitute the line into the circle's equation and solve the resulting quadratic. The discriminant then classifies the geometry: two roots mean a secant (two intersection points), one root means a tangent, none means the line misses the circle.

substitute y = mx + c into (x - a)² + (y - b)² = r²
solve for x; each x gives a y from the line
discriminant > 0: two points; = 0: tangent; < 0: no intersection

Worked example. Find the intersection of y = x + 1 with x² + y² = 25.

x² + (x + 1)² = 25
2x² + 2x + 1 - 25 = 0
x² + x - 12 = 0
(x + 4)(x - 3) = 0  →  x = -4 or 3
y = -3 or 4
points: (-4, -3) and (3, 4)

Worked example 2 (tangent condition). Show that y = 2x + 10 is tangent to x² + y² = 20.

x² + (2x + 10)² = 20
5x² + 40x + 100 - 20 = 0
5x² + 40x + 80 = 0  →  x² + 8x + 16 = 0
(x + 4)² = 0: repeated root, so tangent at x = -4, y = 2

Modelling with straight lines

Linear models answer practical questions: when two plans cost the same, how a quantity changes at a constant rate, what a graph's gradient means in context. The method is to identify the two variables, write each relationship as a line, and solve simultaneously — then interpret the answer in the units of the problem.

Worked example. A taxi charges a fixed 3 pounds plus 1.50 pounds per kilometre; a rival charges 6 pounds plus 1.00 pound per kilometre. Find the distance at which the charges are equal.

3 + 1.5d = 6 + 1.0d
0.5d = 3  →  d = 6 km
both charge 12 pounds at 6 km

Worked example 2 (gradient meaning). A graph of value against age for a car is a straight line through (0, 18000) and (4, 10000). Interpret the gradient.

gradient = (10000 - 18000)/4 = -2000
meaning: the car loses 2000 pounds of value per year

Worked examples: mixed coordinate problems

Worked example. The line y = 2x + k is a tangent to the circle x² + y² = 20. Find k.

substitute: x² + (2x + k)² = 20
x² + 4x² + 4kx + k² - 20 = 0
5x² + 4kx + (k² - 20) = 0
tangent: discriminant = 0
16k² - 20(k² - 20) = 0
16k² - 20k² + 400 = 0  →  4k² = 400  →  k = +/-10

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Distance) Find the distance between (2, 1) and (5, 5). Answer: √(9 + 16) = 5.
  2. (Gradient) Find the gradient through (3, 4) and (7, 12). Answer: 8/4 = 2.
  3. (Perpendicular) A line has gradient −⅔. Find the gradient of a perpendicular line. Answer: 3/2.
  4. (Equation) Find the line through (0, 3) with gradient −2. Answer: y = −2x + 3.
  5. (Circle) State the centre and radius of (x + 1)² + (y − 4)² = 9. Answer: centre (−1, 4), radius 3.
  6. (Completing the square) Find the centre and radius of x² + y² + 4x − 2y − 4 = 0. Answer: (x + 2)² + (y − 1)² = 9 → centre (−2, 1), radius 3.
  7. (Tangent) Find the tangent to x² + y² = 25 at (3, 4). Answer: radius gradient 4/3, tangent gradient −3/4; 3x + 4y = 25.
  8. (Midpoint/distance) Show that (1, 2), (5, 6), (9, 10) are collinear. Answer: gradients both 1; shared point → collinear.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Gradient sign errors: (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁) — subtracting in the wrong order flips the sign. Keep the same point first in both differences.
  • Perpendicular as negative: the perpendicular gradient is the negative reciprocal (−1/m), not just −m.
  • Circle sign reversal: (x + 2)² means centre x = −2; (y − 5)² means y = 5. The sign inside is opposite to the centre coordinate.
  • Radius squared: in (x − a)² + (y − b)² = 25 the radius is 5, not 25. Take the square root.
  • Completing the square with coefficients: halve the x-coefficient and subtract its square; forgetting the subtraction changes the radius.
  • Tangent versus normal: tangent is perpendicular to the radius; normal is along the radius. Swapping their gradients inverts the answer.
  • Intersection arithmetic: after finding x, substitute into the simpler equation for y, and check both points when a quadratic gives two solutions.
  • Sketching circles: mark the centre and radius explicitly; a circle without its centre marked cannot be checked.

title: A Level Mathematics: Continuous Random Variables
content:
A Level Mathematics: Continuous Random Variables

A continuous random variable can take any value in an interval, so the probability of one exact value is zero and probabilities are found by integrating over a range. The probability density function replaces the probability table: area under the curve, not height, is probability. This note builds the density function, the cumulative distribution, the mean, the variance and the median from that single idea, and shows the standard exam moves — normalising a density, finding a constant, and reading probabilities off a piecewise curve.

Why density, not probability

If a random variable is a measurement — a length, a waiting time, a mass — there are infinitely many possible values, and giving each a positive probability is impossible because they would have to sum to one. So probability lives in intervals, and the density describes how concentrated it is.

P(a <= X <= b) = integral from a to b of f(x) dx
P(X = c) = 0 for any single value c
f(x) >= 0 everywhere (it is a density, so non-negative)
the total area is 1: integral of f over the whole range = 1

Notice that a density may exceed 1 without contradicting anything: on a narrow support the curve must be tall for its area to reach 1, and no rule forbids that. Only the area is constrained.

The analogy that makes this concrete: the density is like the height of a landscape, and probability is the volume of soil above a patch of ground. A mathematically exact point has no width, so no soil — that is why P(X = c) = 0 even at the peak.

Finding the constant in a density

Most first parts of a question give a density with an unknown constant and require the total area to be one. That single condition fixes the constant and is worth a mark on its own.

set the integral of f over its support equal to 1, solve for k
then check f(x) >= 0 on the support

Worked example. f(x) = kx for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2, and 0 otherwise. Find k.

integral from 0 to 2 of kx dx = k x²/2 evaluated = k(4/2) = 2k
2k = 1  →  k = 0.5

Worked example 2 (quadratic density). f(x) = kx² for 0 ≤ x ≤ 3. Find k and then P(X ≤ 1).

integral = k x³/3 from 0 to 3 = k(27/3) = 9k = 1  →  k = 1/9
P(X <= 1) = (1/9) x³/3 from 0 to 1 = (1/9)(1/3) = 0.0370

Worked example 3 (piecewise). f(x) = kx for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1 and k(2 − x) for 1 < x ≤ 2. Find k.

first part: k/2
second part: k[2x - x²/2] from 1 to 2 = k[(4 - 2) - (2 - 0.5)] = k(0.5)
total: k/2 + k/2 = k = 1  →  k = 1

The cumulative distribution function

The cumulative distribution F(x) is the integral of the density up to x, and it answers every "less than" question directly. Differentiating it recovers the density, which is why the two are always presented together.

F(x) = P(X <= x) = integral from the lower limit to x of f(t) dt
F is non-decreasing, F(lower) = 0, F(upper) = 1
f(x) = F'(x) where F is differentiable

Worked example. For f(x) = x/2 on 0 ≤ x ≤ 2, find F(x) and hence P(X ≤ 1.5).

F(x) = integral of t/2 from 0 to x = x²/4
P(X <= 1.5) = 2.25/4 = 0.5625
check: F(2) = 1

Worked example 2 (from F back to f). Given F(x) = x²/9 on 0 ≤ x ≤ 3, find f(x) and P(1 ≤ X ≤ 2).

f(x) = F'(x) = 2x/9
P(1 <= X <= 2) = F(2) - F(1) = 4/9 - 1/9 = 1/3

The mean and variance

For a continuous variable the sums of the discrete case become integrals, with the same structure: mean is the first moment, variance is the second moment minus the square of the mean.

E(X) = integral of x f(x) dx over the support
E(X²) = integral of x² f(x) dx
Var(X) = E(X²) - [E(X)]^2

Worked example. f(x) = x/2 on 0 ≤ x ≤ 2. Find E(X) and Var(X).

E(X) = integral of x(x/2) = x³/6 from 0 to 2 = 8/6 = 1.333
E(X²) = integral of x²(x/2) = x⁴/8 from 0 to 2 = 16/8 = 2
Var(X) = 2 - (1.333)² = 2 - 1.778 = 0.222

Worked example 2 (uniform special case). For X uniform on [a, b], show E(X) = (a + b)/2.

f(x) = 1/(b - a)
E(X) = (1/(b-a)) integral of x from a to b = (1/(b-a))(b² - a²)/2 = (a + b)/2

The uniform result is worth remembering: the mean is the midpoint and the variance is (b − a)²/12, so a question about a uniform variable can be answered without any integration.

The median and quartiles

The median is the value m with F(m) = 0.5, the lower quartile has F = 0.25 and the upper 0.75. Because a continuous distribution has no lumpy probabilities, these are always found by solving an equation.

median m: F(m) = 0.5
lower quartile: F(q1) = 0.25
upper quartile: F(q3) = 0.75
interquartile range = q3 - q1

Worked example. Find the median of the distribution with f(x) = x/2 on 0 ≤ x ≤ 2.

F(m) = m²/4 = 0.5
m² = 2  →  m = 1.414

Worked example 2 (quartiles). Find the quartiles of the same distribution.

q1²/4 = 0.25  →  q1 = 1
q3²/4 = 0.75  →  q3 = sqrt 3 = 1.732
IQR = 0.732

Worked example 3 (median of a uniform). X is uniform on [2, 10]. State the median and the IQR.

median = 6;  q1 = 4;  q3 = 8;  IQR = 4
for a uniform, the quartiles split the interval into four equal parts

The mode and the shape

The mode of a continuous distribution is where the density is largest — the peak of the curve. It is found by differentiating and setting the derivative to zero, or by inspection when the density is increasing or decreasing throughout.

mode: maximise f(x) on the support
compare f(peak) with the endpoint values, because a density can be largest at an endpoint

Worked example. Find the mode of f(x) = 6x(1 − x) on 0 ≤ x ≤ 1.

f(x) = 6x - 6x²
f'(x) = 6 - 12x = 0  →  x = 0.5
f(0.5) = 1.5, larger than f(0) = f(1) = 0, so the mode is 0.5

Worked example 2 (no stationary point). Find the mode of f(x) = 2x on 0 ≤ x ≤ 1.

f increases throughout the support, so there is no interior maximum
the mode is at the endpoint x = 1

Working backwards from a probability

A frequent final part gives a probability and asks for the value of x that produces it. The method is to set F(k) equal to that probability and solve for k, remembering that the result is a position on the axis, not a probability, so it should carry the units of the variable.

Worked example. For f(x) = x/2 on 0 ≤ x ≤ 2, find the value of k with P(X ≤ k) = 0.8.

F(k) = k²/4 = 0.8
k² = 3.2  →  k = 1.789

Worked example 2 (two-sided). For the same distribution, find the interquartile range directly from the density rather than a table.

q1: q1²/4 = 0.25  →  q1 = 1
q3: q3²/4 = 0.75  →  q3 = 1.732
IQR = 0.732

Percentile questions are the same calculation with a different probability, and a question that says "the 90th percentile" is asking for k with F(k) = 0.9. Reading the wording as a cumulative condition is the whole skill.

One more variant deserves attention: the density may be defined in two pieces, and then P(X ≤ k) depends on which piece k sits in. The routine is to evaluate F at the join first — if the probability asked for is larger than the value at the join, the answer lies in the second piece and the integral starts from the join, carrying the accumulated probability forward. Getting the join wrong is the one error in this topic that produces a plausible but completely wrong number.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Constant) f(x) = k on [0, 5]: find k. Answer: 5k = 1, k = 0.2.
  2. (Probability) For that f, find P(1 ≤ X ≤ 3). Answer: 0.2 × 2 = 0.4.
  3. (Constant) f(x) = kx² on [0, 2]: find k. Answer: 8k/3 = 1, k = 0.375.
  4. (CDF) F(x) = x³/8 on [0, 2]: find f(x). Answer: 3x²/8.
  5. (Mean) f(x) = 0.5 on [0, 2]: find E(X). Answer: 1.
  6. (Variance) Uniform on [0, 4]: find Var(X). Answer: 16/12 = 1.333.
  7. (Median) F(x) = x²/16 on [0, 4]: find the median. Answer: m² = 8, m = 2.828.
  8. (Quartiles) Same F: find the IQR. Answer: q1 = 2, q3 = 3.464, IQR = 1.464.
  9. (Mode) f(x) = 12x²(1 − x) on [0, 1]: find the mode. Answer: f' = 24x − 36x², x = 2/3.
  10. (Interpretation) Explain why P(X = 1.5) = 0 for a continuous variable. Answer: probability is area, and a single point has zero width.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Reading probability off the height: f(x) is a density; only the area is a probability, and f(x) can exceed 1.
  • Integration limits ignored: outside the support the density is zero, so an integral that strays outside must be split.
  • Forgetting the normalising condition: the first mark of a constant question is the integral equal to one.
  • Variance formula misremembered: it is E(X²) − [E(X)]², not E(X²) − E(X) or E(X²) + [E(X)]².
  • Median found by averaging: for a continuous distribution the median solves F(m) = 0.5; it is not the midpoint unless the distribution is uniform.
  • Mode at a stationary point assumed: check the endpoints, because a monotone density peaks at the boundary.
  • F and f confused: F is cumulative (a probability), f is the density; F is the integral of f, not the other way round.
  • Piecewise densities integrated as one piece: a density defined in two parts needs two integrals, one per part.

title: AS Level Biology: Molecules, Transport and Health
content:
Molecules, Transport and Health — AS Level Biology

This revision note belongs to the Edexcel International Advanced Subsidiary (IAS) Biology specification, WBI11 Unit 1, Topic 1 Molecules, Transport and Health. It covers water as a solvent and its structure, carbohydrates and lipids, proteins and their structure and function, gas exchange surfaces and Fick’s law, the mammalian circulatory system and the cardiac cycle, haemoglobin and the oxygen dissociation curve, atherosclerosis and blood clotting, the risk factors for cardiovascular disease, diet, cholesterol and antioxidants, how people use scientific knowledge to reduce risk, the benefits and risks of treatments, and data analysis and evaluation in health studies — plus the gas exchange surfaces and enzyme practical work that support the topic. Every statement the topic is responsible for is covered in its own section or paragraph.

1. Water: structure, properties and why it is the solvent of life

Water is a small molecule with two hydrogen atoms covalently bonded to one oxygen atom; because the oxygen atom is much more electronegative than hydrogen, the shared electrons spend more time near the oxygen, so the molecule is polar — the oxygen end is slightly negative and the hydrogen end slightly positive. This polarity lets water molecules form hydrogen bonds with each other, which gives water its high specific heat capacity, its high latent heat of vaporisation, its cohesion (important for the transpiration stream in plants) and its solvent powers. Water is an excellent solvent because its polarity lets it surround and dissolve ions and polar molecules; ions become hydrated with water molecules around them, and polar molecules such as glucose dissolve readily. In transport, water’s solvent nature lets it carry dissolved substances in blood and in plant tissue fluid and sap, and its dipole nature explains why it can do that — the partial charges interact with the charges of ions and the polar groups of molecules like glucose and amino acids.

2. Carbohydrates: monosaccharides, disaccharides and polysaccharides

Carbohydrates are made of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, with hydrogen and oxygen in the same ratio as in water (2:1). Monosaccharides are the simplest carbohydrates and are the building blocks — glucose, fructose and galactose are hexose monosaccharides with the formula C6H12O6. Disaccharides form when two monosaccharides join by a condensation reaction, losing a water molecule and forming a glycosidic bond; the common ones are maltose (glucose + glucose), sucrose (glucose + fructose) and lactose (glucose + galactose).
