title:
Coordination, Response and Gene Technology — A2 Level Biology

This revision note belongs to the Edexcel International A2 Biology specification, WBI14 Unit 4 Topic 8 Coordination, Response and Gene Technology. It covers the nervous system — sensory, relay and motor neurones, myelination and saltatory conduction, the action potential and its conduction along the axon, the spinal reflex arc, synapses and the role of neurotransmitters, how the pupil dilates and contracts, how drugs influence nerve impulse transmission (nicotine, lidocaine, cobra venom alpha toxin, L-DOPA and Parkinson’s disease, MDMA), how the retina detects light and forms action potentials in the optic neurones, habituation, the central and peripheral nervous systems, hormonal and nervous coordination, the structure and function of the brain (cerebral hemispheres, hypothalamus, pituitary gland, cerebellum, medulla oblongata), how MRI, fMRI, PET and CT are used in diagnosis and investigation of brain structure and function, how imbalances in brain chemicals contribute to ill health (dopamine in Parkinson’s disease, serotonin in depression) and to the development of new drugs, how drugs can be produced using genetically modified organisms, how recombinant DNA is produced and inserted into other cells, how microarrays identify active genes, what bioinformatics is, and the risks and benefits of genetically modified organisms. Every statement the topic is responsible for is covered in its own section or paragraph, with the material set so that a student can revise from it and check themselves against the specification.

1. Sensory, relay and motor neurones, Schwann cells and myelination

The nervous system has three main types of neurone, each with a structure suited to its function. Sensory neurones carry impulses from receptors to the central nervous system; their cell body is off to one side of the axon, halfway along it, and they have a long dendron that carries the impulse from the receptor to the cell body and a long axon that carries it into the CNS. Relay neurones connect sensory and motor neurones within the CNS; their cell body is in the centre of the neurone, and they have many short dendrites and a short axon. Motor neurones carry impulses from the CNS to effectors (muscles or glands); their cell body is in the CNS, and they have a long axon with many short dendrites. All neurones have a cell body containing the nucleus and many mitochondria (to supply ATP), dendrites that carry impulses towards the cell body, and an axon that carries impulses away from the cell body. Many axons are wrapped in Schwann cells, which wrap tightly around the axon in a fatty myelin sheath; the myelin sheath insulates the axon and speeds conduction. The gaps in the myelin sheath are called nodes of Ranvier. The structure of each neurone type reflects what it does — sensory neurones bring information in, relay neurones process it inside the CNS, and motor neurones carry the response out to effectors.

2. The nervous system and how it makes effectors respond to a stimulus

A stimulus is a change in the environment (internal or external) that is detected by a receptor. The receptor converts the stimulus into an electrical signal (a generator potential, then if it reaches threshold an action potential) in a sensory neurone. The impulse travels along the sensory neurone to the CNS, where it is passed to a relay neurone; the relay neurone may synapse with other relay neurones and process the information, then pass the impulse to a motor neurone, which carries it to an effector. The effector — a muscle or a gland — responds: a muscle contracts, or a gland secretes its product. This is the general pathway: stimulus → receptor → sensory neurone → CNS (relay neurone) → motor neurone → effector → response. The response is specific to the stimulus and to the circuitry involved, and rapid because electrical impulses travel fast along neurones.

3. The spinal reflex arc: grey matter, white matter and the withdrawal reflex

A reflex arc is the pathway of neurones that produces a rapid, involuntary response to a stimulus, without involving conscious control. In the spinal reflex arc, a sensory neurone from a receptor (for example in the skin) synapses with a relay neurone in the spinal cord, which in turn synapses with a motor neurone that runs to an effector (for example a muscle). The grey matter of the spinal cord is the inner, butterfly-shaped region where the cell bodies of relay and motor neurones and the synapses between them are found; the white matter is the outer region, made up of myelinated axons that carry impulses up and down the cord, to and from the brain. In the withdrawal reflex, for example touching a hot object, a pain receptor in the skin sends an impulse via a sensory neurone to a relay neurone in the spinal cord, which excites a motor neurone that makes the arm flex (biceps contracts, triceps relaxes) and withdraws from the stimulus. The response is rapid and automatic, and happens before the brain is even aware of the stimulus, because the arc involves only the spinal cord; this protects the body from harm.

4. The action potential: how an impulse is conducted along an axon

An action potential is the nerve impulse — a rapid, transient change in the membrane potential of a neurone, from about −70 mV (resting potential) up to about +40 mV and back, caused by the opening and closing of voltage-gated sodium and potassium ion channels. At rest the inside of the axon is negatively charged relative to the outside (the resting potential), mainly because sodium ions are pumped out and potassium ions are pumped in by the sodium–potassium pump, and the membrane is more permeable to potassium ions than to sodium ions at rest. When a stimulus depolarises the membrane to the threshold, voltage-gated sodium ion channels open, sodium ions flood in, the inside becomes positively charged (depolarisation, up to +40 mV). At about the peak, the sodium channels close and voltage-gated potassium channels open, potassium ions flood out, and the inside returns towards resting (repolarisation); it rises a little too far (hyperpolarisation) before returning to resting. The sodium–potassium pump then restores the resting ion distribution. The all-or-nothing principle applies: once threshold is reached, the action potential fires at full size; a stronger stimulus does not produce a bigger action potential, it produces more of them (greater frequency). During the absolute refractory period, the sodium channels are inactivated and no new action potential can be started, which ensures impulses travel one way and sets a maximum frequency.

5. Myelination and saltatory conduction: why some axons are faster

Myelination speeds up conduction of the action potential. In a myelinated axon the myelin sheath insulates the axon so that ions cannot cross the membrane where it is covered; the action potential can only be generated at the nodes of Ranvier, where the axon is bare. The impulse therefore jumps from node to node — saltatory conduction — and this is much faster than the continuous conduction along an unmyelinated axon, because the impulse does not have to depolarise every part of the membrane. The speed of conduction also depends on the diameter of the axon (larger axons conduct faster because there is less resistance to the flow of ions inside) and on the number of sodium channels and the extent of myelination; the fastest axons in the body are large and heavily myelinated.

6. Synapses: structure, transmission, acetylcholine, and the pupillary reflex

A synapse is the junction between two neurones (or between a neurone and an effector cell) across which the impulse is passed by a chemical neurotransmitter. At a cholinergic synapse, an action potential arriving at the presynaptic neurone opens voltage-gated calcium ion channels; calcium ions enter the presynaptic terminal, causing synaptic vesicles containing the neurotransmitter acetylcholine to fuse with the presynaptic membrane and release their contents by exocytosis into the synaptic cleft. Acetylcholine diffuses across the cleft and binds to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane, opening sodium ion channels so sodium ions enter and depolarise the postsynaptic membrane (this may start an action potential if the threshold is reached). Acetylcholinesterase in the cleft breaks down acetylcholine to stop the signal and recycle the choline. Drugs and toxins can affect the synapse: nicotine mimics acetylcholine and stimulates the postsynaptic receptor; lidocaine blocks voltage-gated sodium channels and stops impulse transmission (used as a local anaesthetic); cobra venom alpha toxin blocks acetylcholine receptors so the muscle cannot be stimulated (paralysis). Meanwhile, the pupil is controlled by two sets of muscles in the iris: circular muscles and radial muscles. In bright light, the parasympathetic nervous system makes the circular muscles of the iris contract, which constricts (makes smaller) the pupil, reducing the light entering the eye; in dim light, the radial muscles contract, dilating (widening) the pupil so more light enters.

7. Drugs and nerve impulse transmission: nicotine, lidocaine, cobra venom alpha toxin, L-DOPA, and MDMA

Many drugs act on the nervous system by influencing nerve impulse transmission. Nicotine stimulates nicotinic acetylcholine receptors in the brain, producing a temporary feeling of alertness and pleasure, and it is addictive because repeated use changes the brain’s reward pathways; it also raises blood pressure and heart rate, and is a carcinogen. Lidocaine is a local anaesthetic that blocks voltage-gated sodium ion channels in sensory neurones, preventing the formation and conduction of action potentials, so pain signals are not sent to the brain — it is used to numb a local area. Cobra venom alpha toxin binds to acetylcholine receptors on the muscle and blocks acetylcholine from binding, so the muscle cannot be stimulated and paralysis results, which can be fatal if the respiratory muscles are paralysed. L-DOPA is used to treat Parkinson’s disease; Parkinson’s is caused by a loss of dopamine-producing neurones in a part of the brain (the substantia nigra), so the level of dopamine falls and movement becomes impaired (tremor, stiffness, slow movement); L-DOPA is a precursor that can cross the blood–brain barrier and is converted to dopamine in the brain, restoring the level and easing the symptoms, at least for a time. MDMA (ecstasy) causes a large release of serotonin from presynaptic neurones and blocks its reuptake, so serotonin levels in the synapse rise sharply, producing a feeling of wellbeing and empathy, but the subsequent depletion of serotonin and damage to serotonin neurones can cause depression and memory problems, and repeated use is harmful.

8. Detecting light: the rod cell, rhodopsin, and how an action potential is generated in the optic neurone

Rods in the retina of mammals detect light and allow us to see in dim light. A rod cell contains the pigment rhodopsin, which is made of a protein (opsin) and a light-absorbing molecule (retinal, a derivative of vitamin A). When light hits rhodopsin, the retinal changes shape (from 11-cis to all-trans retinal), which changes the opsin and causes the rod cell to hyperpolarise — it becomes more negative inside. This hyperpolarisation closes sodium ion channels that are normally open in the dark, so sodium ion entry is reduced and the rod cell hyperpolarises; this in turn reduces the release of the neurotransmitter (glutamate) from the rod cell’s synaptic terminal. The change in transmitter release affects the bipolar neurone, which in turn affects the neurone that runs to the brain (the optic neurone); so the rod cell’s hyperpolarisation to light ultimately leads to action potentials in the optic neurone, which travel to the brain and are interpreted as vision. This is a relatively fine point — light does not itself produce the action potential in the rod, it changes the rod’s membrane potential, and that change is passed on through the retinal circuit to generate action potentials in the optic neurone. Cone cells work similarly but are responsible for colour vision and detail in bright light.

9. Habituation: what it is and how it is investigated

Habituation is a simple form of learning in which a response to a repeated, harmless stimulus decreases over time; the organism learns to ignore the stimulus because it has learned it is not important. For example, a snail initially withdraws into its shell when its shell is tapped, but with repeated tapping the withdrawal response becomes slower and eventually disappears — the snail has habituated to the tap. Habituation is not fatigue of the muscle (if a new stimulus, such as a poke to the body, still produces a strong response, the withdrawal machinery is fine) and not sensory adaptation (the receptor still responds to the stimulus), but a decrease in the synaptic transmission at the synapse between the sensory neurone and the motor neurone that produces the withdrawal. A recommended additional practical is to investigate habituation to a stimulus — for example using the snail withdrawal response, tapping the snail and recording the time to emerge or the frequency of withdrawal, and showing that with repeated harmless taps the response declines and that the decline is not due to muscle fatigue.

10. The central and peripheral nervous systems

The mammalian nervous system consists of the central nervous system (CNS) and the peripheral nervous system (PNS). The CNS is the brain and spinal cord; it integrates information and coordinates responses. The PNS is the network of nerves that connect the CNS to the rest of the body — to receptors and to effectors; it includes the sensory neurones that bring information to the CNS and the motor neurones that carry commands to effectors. The motor part of the PNS can be divided into the voluntary (somatic) nervous system, which controls skeletal muscles consciously, and the autonomic nervous system, which controls involuntary functions such as heart rate, gut movement and the pupils, and which is further divided into the sympathetic (which prepares the body for action — fight or flight) and parasympathetic (which promotes rest and digestion) nervous systems; these two often have opposite effects on the same organ.

11. Coordination in animals: nervous and hormonal control together

Animals coordinate their bodies by both nervous and hormonal control, and the two work together. The nervous system uses electrical impulses that travel fast along neurones and chemical signals (neurotransmitters) across synapses, giving rapid, short-lived responses targeted at specific effectors — good for rapid movements and reflexes. The hormonal system uses hormones carried in the blood, which travel more slowly and affect many cells at once, producing slower, longer-lasting, more widespread responses — good for things like growth, metabolism, reproduction and responding to stress over a longer time. In many situations they act together: for example, in the fight-or-flight response, the sympathetic nervous system acts quickly to increase heart rate, while the hormone adrenaline from the adrenal glands sustains and amplifies the response; in the control of blood glucose, hormones (insulin and glucagon) act more slowly and over longer periods than nervous control would allow. Plants coordinate only by hormones (plant growth substances such as auxin, gibberellin and phytochrome), because they have no nervous system.

12. The human brain: cerebral hemispheres, hypothalamus, pituitary gland, cerebellum, medulla oblongata

The brain controls and coordinates the activities of the body and is the seat of thought, memory and emotion. The cerebral hemispheres are the large, folded upper parts of the brain; they are responsible for higher functions — thought, memory, reasoning, conscious actions, language and sensation — and each hemisphere controls the opposite side of the body. The hypothalamus links the nervous and endocrine systems; it controls the pituitary gland, regulates body temperature, water balance, hunger and thirst, and the sleep cycle, and it plays a central role in homeostasis. The pituitary gland, under the influence of the hypothalamus, releases several hormones that control other endocrine glands and body functions — for example growth hormone, ADH and the hormones that regulate reproduction. The cerebellum is responsible for coordination of movement and balance — it makes sure movements are smooth and coordinated and posture is maintained. The medulla oblongata controls unconscious and automatic functions essential to life — breathing rate, heart rate and the reflex centres for coughing, sneezing and swallowing — and it is where the cardiovascular control centre and the ventilation (breathing) centre are located. Damage to different parts of the brain produces different deficits, and knowing the location and main functions makes it possible to link symptoms to brain regions.

13. Brain imaging: MRI, fMRI, PET and CT — what they show and how they are used

Different imaging techniques give different kinds of information about the brain. Computed tomography (CT) uses X-rays from many angles to produce a cross-sectional image of the brain’s structure; it is good at showing bone, bleeding and structural abnormalities, and it is quick and widely available, but it uses ionising radiation and gives limited soft-tissue contrast. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) uses a strong magnetic field and radio waves to give detailed images of soft tissue; it shows brain structure without ionising radiation and is excellent for detecting tumours, inflammation, demyelination and injury, but it takes longer and is noisy and claustrophobic for the patient. Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) is MRI adapted to show brain function — it detects changes in blood flow and oxygen use that accompany neural activity, so it can show which parts of the brain are active during a task; it has good spatial resolution but poor time resolution because the blood flow change lags the neural activity. Positron emission tomography (PET) uses a radioactive tracer (for example, a labelled glucose) injected into the patient; the tracer accumulates in active tissues and its radioactivity is detected, so PET can show brain activity and metabolism, and it can show neurotransmitter receptors and help in diagnosing and studying disorders such as Alzheimer’s and cancer, but it uses ionising radiation and is expensive. These techniques are used in medical diagnosis (for example to locate a tumour, or to investigate a stroke or a degenerative disease) and in research into brain structure and function — for example to see which areas are involved in a particular task or how activity differs in a disorder.

14. Brain chemicals and disease: dopamine in Parkinson’s disease, serotonin in depression, and new drugs

Imbalances in certain naturally-occurring brain chemicals can contribute to ill health, and understanding these has driven the development of new drugs. Parkinson’s disease is caused by the loss of neurones in the substantia nigra that produce dopamine, a neurotransmitter involved in controlling movement; the resulting dopamine deficiency causes tremor, stiffness, slowness of movement and balance problems. Treatment with L-DOPA (a precursor that crosses the blood–brain barrier and is converted to dopamine) can relieve symptoms, at least for a time, and other drugs may mimic dopamine or prevent its breakdown. Depression is associated with lower levels of the neurotransmitter serotonin (and also noradrenaline) in the brain; selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) block the reuptake of serotonin into the presynaptic neurone, so more serotonin stays in the synapse and helps improve mood, and they are widely used to treat depression and anxiety. New drugs can be developed using this understanding of the role of brain chemicals — for example by targeting the receptors or the synthesis or breakdown of a neurotransmitter — and knowledge of the cause of a disease (such as the dopamine deficiency in Parkinson’s) is what makes targeted treatment possible.

15. Producing drugs using genetically modified organisms

Drugs can be produced using genetically modified organisms (GMOs) — plants, animals and microorganisms. The best-known example is human insulin: the human gene for insulin is inserted into bacteria (usually E. coli) using a plasmid, and the bacteria are grown in large fermenters to produce human insulin, which is then extracted and purified. Human insulin made this way is identical to the insulin made in the human body, so it does not cause the immune reactions that some people had to the animal insulin formerly used. Other products made from GMOs include human growth hormone, clotting factor for haemophiliacs, and enzymes for washing powders; and modified plants and animals are being explored to produce vaccines and other pharmaceuticals. Using GMOs to produce drugs has advantages: the product can be made in large quantities, it can be made more cheaply than by extraction from animals or people, and it can be made identical to the human version. There are concerns, however — about the containment of the GMOs, the possibility of unintended effects, and the ethical questions of modifying organisms in this way.

16. Recombinant DNA: how it is produced (restriction enzymes and DNA ligase) and inserted into other cells

Recombinant DNA is DNA made by joining together pieces of DNA from different sources. Restriction endonucleases (restriction enzymes) cut DNA at specific base sequences, making cuts that can leave complementary ‘sticky ends’ — short single-stranded overhangs that can base-pair with each other — and these sticky ends allow a gene of interest to be joined to a vector (such as a plasmid) cut with the same enzyme. DNA ligase then seals the backbone of the sugar–phosphate chain, joining the gene to the vector to make recombinant DNA. To insert recombinant DNA into other cells, the vector (carrying the gene) is introduced into host cells: bacterial cells can take up plasmids in a process called transformation (which can be helped by making the bacteria competent — for example by calcium chloride treatment and a heat shock); viral vectors can be engineered to carry the gene into the cells they infect, using the virus’s natural ability to enter cells; and other methods such as microinjection or gene guns can put DNA directly into cells. Once inside, the host cell’s machinery may read and express the gene, making the protein it codes for (for example insulin), and if the vector also carries a gene for resistance to an antibiotic, only the cells that took up the vector will survive on antibiotic-containing medium — giving a way to select the transformed cells.

17. Microarrays: how they identify active genes

A microarray (DNA microarray) is a small slide or chip carrying thousands of known DNA sequences (probes), each in a known position. Messenger RNA is extracted from two samples (for example, a diseased tissue and a healthy tissue, or cells treated with a drug and untreated cells), converted to cDNA, and labelled with different coloured fluorescent tags (for example green for one sample and red for the other). The labelled cDNA is mixed and allowed to hybridise to the probes on the microarray: if a gene is active (expressed) in a sample, its cDNA will bind (hybridise) to the complementary probe on the chip. By scanning the chip, the colours and intensities can be read: a green spot means the gene is more active in the green-labelled sample, a red spot means more active in the red-labelled sample, yellow means similar activity in both, and the intensity reflects how active the gene is. By looking at all the spots, researchers can see which genes are active (turned on) or inactive (turned off) in a sample and compare activity between samples — for example to see which genes are active in a cancer cell that are not in a normal cell, or to see how a drug changes gene activity. This makes it possible to identify active genes and to use gene activity patterns for diagnosis and to understand disease and drug action.

18. Bioinformatics: what it is and what it is used for

Bioinformatics is the use of computer technology to collect, store, analyse and interpret biological data, especially large datasets such as DNA and protein sequences, gene expression data from microarrays, and protein structures. It depends on the availability of sequence data — the DNA sequences of genomes and the sequences of proteins — and on databases that store and organise these sequences so they can be compared and searched. Bioinformatics is used to compare sequences to find similarities and differences, to identify genes and their functions (for example by comparing a new sequence with known ones to suggest what it does), to study evolutionary relationships (by building phylogenetic trees from sequence comparisons), to predict the structure and function of proteins from their amino acid sequence, and to analyse gene expression patterns from microarrays. It depends on the work of the Human Genome Project and other sequencing projects, and on the computational tools that turn raw sequence data into useful biological knowledge. Bioinformatics is now part of nearly every area of biology — from identifying a gene, to understanding what it does, to finding targets for drugs, to tracing the evolution of a pathogen.

19. Risks and benefits of genetically modified organisms

Genetically modified organisms (GMOs) — plants, animals and microorganisms — have both benefits and risks. Benefits include: in agriculture, crops can be modified to resist pests (for example Bt crops that produce a bacterial toxin harmful to insect pests but not to people) or herbicides, to tolerate drought or salinity, to improve nutrition (for example golden rice producing beta-carotene, a vitamin A precursor), and to increase yield — which can support food security; in medicine, GM bacteria produce human insulin and other proteins for therapy; in research, GM animals and plants are used to study gene function and disease. Risks and concerns include: the possibility that the modified gene could spread to wild relatives or other organisms (gene flow) and have unintended effects; the potential harm to non-target organisms (for example whether Bt crops affect beneficial insects); the development of resistant pests or weeds; the concentration of control of food and seed in a few companies, and the effect on farmers and on traditional varieties; the long-term effects on ecosystems, which are not fully known; and the ethical questions about modifying organisms, especially animals, and about food that has been genetically modified. These must be weighed case by case: the benefits and risks of each GMO depend on what it is, how it is used, and how it is regulated. The scientific evidence about each GMO is needed to evaluate it properly, and the public has a legitimate role in the decisions because the issues are not only scientific — they include values, economics and the environment.

20. How to use this note and what to revise next

Use these notes by working through each section and checking that you can: describe the structure of sensory, relay and motor neurones; describe the spinal reflex arc, including the roles of grey and white matter; explain how the action potential is generated, including depolarisation, repolarisation, hyperpolarisation, the role of sodium and potassium ions and the sodium–potassium pump, and the all-or-nothing principle; explain how myelination allows saltatory conduction and speeds it up; describe the cholinergic synapse and the roles of calcium, acetylcholine, receptors, acetylcholinesterase; explain the pupillary reflex (circular muscles constrict in bright light, radial muscles dilate in dim); describe how nicotine, lidocaine, cobra venom alpha toxin, L-DOPA and MDMA affect nerve impulse transmission, including examples; describe how rod cells detect light, the role of rhodopsin, opsin, retinal, sodium channels and hyperpolarisation, and how this leads to action potentials in the optic neurone; describe habituation and the evidence for it (the snail withdrawal practical); describe the central and peripheral nervous systems and the sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions; locate and state the functions of the cerebral hemispheres, hypothalamus, pituitary gland, cerebellum and medulla oblongata; explain how MRI, fMRI, PET and CT work and what they are used for; explain the role of dopamine in Parkinson’s disease and serotonin in depression and how the drugs work; describe the production of drugs using GMOs (human insulin as the example); describe how recombinant DNA is made with restriction enzymes and DNA ligase and inserted into cells; describe how microarrays work and what they show; define bioinformatics; and discuss the risks and benefits of GMOs. After this topic, revise Topic 9 the continuation of this unit and the related practicals, and the BIology practicals (Core Practicals 14–18) which reinforce these topics.

This revision note belongs to the Edexcel International A2 Biology specification, WBI14 Unit 4 Topic 8 Coordination, Response and Gene Technology. It covers the nervous system — sensory, relay and motor neurones, myelination and saltatory conduction, the action potential and its conduction along the axon, the spinal reflex arc, synapses and the role of neurotransmitters, how the pupil dilates and contracts, how drugs influence nerve impulse transmission (nicotine, lidocaine, cobra venom alpha toxin, L-DOPA and Parkinson’s disease, MDMA), how the retina detects light and forms action potentials in the optic neurones, habituation, the central and peripheral nervous systems, hormonal and nervous coordination, the structure and function of the brain (cerebral hemispheres, hypothalamus, pituitary gland, cerebellum, medulla oblongata), how MRI, fMRI, PET and CT are used in diagnosis and investigation of brain structure and function, how imbalances in brain chemicals contribute to ill health (dopamine in Parkinson’s disease, serotonin in depression) and to the development of new drugs, how drugs can be produced using genetically modified organisms, how recombinant DNA is produced and inserted into other cells, how microarrays identify active genes, what bioinformatics is, and the risks and benefits of genetically modified organisms. Every statement the topic is responsible for is covered in its own section or paragraph, with the material set so that a student can revise from it and check themselves against the specification.

1. Sensory, relay and motor neurones, Schwann cells and myelination

The nervous system has three main types of neurone, each with a structure suited to its function. Sensory neurones carry impulses from receptors to the central nervous system; their cell body is off to one side of the axon, halfway along it, and they have a long dendron that carries the impulse from the receptor to the cell body and a long axon that carries it into the CNS. Relay neurones connect sensory and motor neurones within the CNS; their cell body is in the centre of the neurone, and they have many short dendrites and a short axon. Motor neurones carry impulses from the CNS to effectors (muscles or glands); their cell body is in the CNS, and they have a long axon with many short dendrites. All neurones have a cell body containing the nucleus and many mitochondria (to supply ATP), dendrites that carry impulses towards the cell body, and an axon that carries impulses away from the cell body. Many axons are wrapped in Schwann cells, which wrap tightly around the axon in a fatty myelin sheath; the myelin sheath insulates the axon and speeds conduction. The gaps in the myelin sheath are called nodes of Ranvier. The structure of each neurone type reflects what it does — sensory neurones bring information in, relay neurones process it inside the CNS, and motor neurones carry the response out to effectors.

2. The nervous system and how it makes effectors respond to a stimulus

A stimulus is a change in the environment (internal or external) that is detected by a receptor. The receptor converts the stimulus into an electrical signal (a generator potential, then if it reaches threshold an action potential) in a sensory neurone. The impulse travels along the sensory neurone to the CNS, where it is passed to a relay neurone; the relay neurone may synapse with other relay neurones and process the information, then pass the impulse to a motor neurone, which carries it to an effector. The effector — a muscle or a gland — responds: a muscle contracts, or a gland secretes its product. This is the general pathway: stimulus → receptor → sensory neurone → CNS (relay neurone) → motor neurone → effector → response. The response is specific to the stimulus and to the circuitry involved, and rapid because electrical impulses travel fast along neurones.

3. The spinal reflex arc: grey matter, white matter and the withdrawal reflex

A reflex arc is the pathway of neurones that produces a rapid, involuntary response to a stimulus, without involving conscious control. In the spinal reflex arc, a sensory neurone from a receptor (for example in the skin) synapses with a relay neurone in the spinal cord, which in turn synapses with a motor neurone that runs to an effector (for example a muscle). The grey matter of the spinal cord is the inner, butterfly-shaped region where the cell bodies of relay and motor neurones and the synapses between them are found; the white matter is the outer region, made up of myelinated axons that carry impulses up and down the cord, to and from the brain. In the withdrawal reflex, for example touching a hot object, a pain receptor in the skin sends an impulse via a sensory neurone to a relay neurone in the spinal cord, which excites a motor neurone that makes the arm flex (biceps contracts, triceps relaxes) and withdraws from the stimulus. The response is rapid and automatic, and happens before the brain is even aware of the stimulus, because the arc involves only the spinal cord; this protects the body from harm.

4. The action potential: how an impulse is conducted along an axon

An action potential is the nerve impulse — a rapid, transient change in the membrane potential of a neurone, from about −70 mV (resting potential) up to about +40 mV and back, caused by the opening and closing of voltage-gated sodium and potassium ion channels. At rest the inside of the axon is negatively charged relative to the outside (the resting potential), mainly because sodium ions are pumped out and potassium ions are pumped in by the sodium–potassium pump, and the membrane is more permeable to potassium ions than to sodium ions at rest. When a stimulus depolarises the membrane to the threshold, voltage-gated sodium ion channels open, sodium ions flood in, the inside becomes positively charged (depolarisation, up to +40 mV). At about the peak, the sodium channels close and voltage-gated potassium channels open, potassium ions flood out, and the inside returns towards resting (repolarisation); it rises a little too far (hyperpolarisation) before returning to resting. The sodium–potassium pump then restores the resting ion distribution. The all-or-nothing principle applies: once threshold is reached, the action potential fires at full size; a stronger stimulus does not produce a bigger action potential, it produces more of them (greater frequency). During the absolute refractory period, the sodium channels are inactivated and no new action potential can be started, which ensures impulses travel one way and sets a maximum frequency.

5. Myelination and saltatory conduction: why some axons are faster

Myelination speeds up conduction of the action potential. In a myelinated axon the myelin sheath insulates the axon so that ions cannot cross the membrane where it is covered; the action potential can only be generated at the nodes of Ranvier, where the axon is bare. The impulse therefore jumps from node to node — saltatory conduction — and this is much faster than the continuous conduction along an unmyelinated axon, because the impulse does not have to depolarise every part of the membrane. The speed of conduction also depends on the diameter of the axon (larger axons conduct faster because there is less resistance to the flow of ions inside) and on the number of sodium channels and the extent of myelination; the fastest axons in the body are large and heavily myelinated.

6. Synapses: structure, transmission, acetylcholine, and the pupillary reflex

A synapse is the junction between two neurones (or between a neurone and an effector cell) across which the impulse is passed by a chemical neurotransmitter. At a cholinergic synapse, an action potential arriving at the presynaptic neurone opens voltage-gated calcium ion channels; calcium ions enter the presynaptic terminal, causing synaptic vesicles containing the neurotransmitter acetylcholine to fuse with the presynaptic membrane and release their contents by exocytosis into the synaptic cleft. Acetylcholine diffuses across the cleft and binds to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane, opening sodium ion channels so sodium ions enter and depolarise the postsynaptic membrane (this may start an action potential if the threshold is reached). Acetylcholinesterase in the cleft breaks down acetylcholine to stop the signal and recycle the choline. Drugs and toxins can affect the synapse: nicotine mimics acetylcholine and stimulates the postsynaptic receptor; lidocaine blocks voltage-gated sodium channels and stops impulse transmission (used as a local anaesthetic); cobra venom alpha toxin blocks acetylcholine receptors so the muscle cannot be stimulated (paralysis). Meanwhile, the pupil is controlled by two sets of muscles in the iris: circular muscles and radial muscles. In bright light, the parasympathetic nervous system makes the circular muscles of the iris contract, which constricts (makes smaller) the pupil, reducing the light entering the eye; in dim light, the radial muscles contract, dilating (widening) the pupil so more light enters.

7. Drugs and nerve impulse transmission: nicotine, lidocaine, cobra venom alpha toxin, L-DOPA, and MDMA

Many drugs act on the nervous system by influencing nerve impulse transmission. Nicotine stimulates nicotinic acetylcholine receptors in the brain, producing a temporary feeling of alertness and pleasure, and it is addictive because repeated use changes the brain’s reward pathways; it also raises blood pressure and heart rate, and is a carcinogen. Lidocaine is a local anaesthetic that blocks voltage-gated sodium ion channels in sensory neurones, preventing the formation and conduction of action potentials, so pain signals are not sent to the brain — it is used to numb a local area. Cobra venom alpha toxin binds to acetylcholine receptors on the muscle and blocks acetylcholine from binding, so the muscle cannot be stimulated and paralysis results, which can be fatal if the respiratory muscles are paralysed. L-DOPA is used to treat Parkinson’s disease; Parkinson’s is caused by a loss of dopamine-producing neurones in a part of the brain (the substantia nigra), so the level of dopamine falls and movement becomes impaired (tremor, stiffness, slow movement); L-DOPA is a precursor that can cross the blood–brain barrier and is converted to dopamine in the brain, restoring the level and easing the symptoms, at least for a time. MDMA (ecstasy) causes a large release of serotonin from presynaptic neurones and blocks its reuptake, so serotonin levels in the synapse rise sharply, producing a feeling of wellbeing and empathy, but the subsequent depletion of serotonin and damage to serotonin neurones can cause depression and memory problems, and repeated use is harmful.

8. Detecting light: the rod cell, rhodopsin, and how an action potential is generated in the optic neurone

Rods in the retina of mammals detect light and allow us to see in dim light. A rod cell contains the pigment rhodopsin, which is made of a protein (opsin) and a light-absorbing molecule (retinal, a derivative of vitamin A). When light hits rhodopsin, the retinal changes shape (from 11-cis to all-trans retinal), which changes the opsin and causes the rod cell to hyperpolarise — it becomes more negative inside. This hyperpolarisation closes sodium ion channels that are normally open in the dark, so sodium ion entry is reduced and the rod cell hyperpolarises; this in turn reduces the release of the neurotransmitter (glutamate) from the rod cell’s synaptic terminal. The change in transmitter release affects the bipolar neurone, which in turn affects the neurone that runs to the brain (the optic neurone); so the rod cell’s hyperpolarisation to light ultimately leads to action potentials in the optic neurone, which travel to the brain and are interpreted as vision. This is a relatively fine point — light does not itself produce the action potential in the rod, it changes the rod’s membrane potential, and that change is passed on through the retinal circuit to generate action potentials in the optic neurone. Cone cells work similarly but are responsible for colour vision and detail in bright light.

9. Habituation: what it is and how it is investigated

Habituation is a simple form of learning in which a response to a repeated, harmless stimulus decreases over time; the organism learns to ignore the stimulus because it has learned it is not important. For example, a snail initially withdraws into its shell when its shell is tapped, but with repeated tapping the withdrawal response becomes slower and eventually disappears — the snail has habituated to the tap. Habituation is not fatigue of the muscle (if a new stimulus, such as a poke to the body, still produces a strong response, the withdrawal machinery is fine) and not sensory adaptation (the receptor still responds to the stimulus), but a decrease in the synaptic transmission at the synapse between the sensory neurone and the motor neurone that produces the withdrawal. A recommended additional practical is to investigate habituation to a stimulus — for example using the snail withdrawal response, tapping the snail and recording the time to emerge or the frequency of withdrawal, and showing that with repeated harmless taps the response declines and that the decline is not due to muscle fatigue.

10. The central and peripheral nervous systems

The mammalian nervous system consists of the central nervous system (CNS) and the peripheral nervous system (PNS). The CNS is the brain and spinal cord; it integrates information and coordinates responses. The PNS is the network of nerves that connect the CNS to the rest of the body — to receptors and to effectors; it includes the sensory neurones that bring information to the CNS and the motor neurones that carry commands to effectors. The motor part of the PNS can be divided into the voluntary (somatic) nervous system, which controls skeletal muscles consciously, and the autonomic nervous system, which controls involuntary functions such as heart rate, gut movement and the pupils, and which is further divided into the sympathetic (which prepares the body for action — fight or flight) and parasympathetic (which promotes rest and digestion) nervous systems; these two often have opposite effects on the same organ.

11. Coordination in animals: nervous and hormonal control together

Animals coordinate their bodies by both nervous and hormonal control, and the two work together. The nervous system uses electrical impulses that travel fast along neurones and chemical signals (neurotransmitters) across synapses, giving rapid, short-lived responses targeted at specific effectors — good for rapid movements and reflexes. The hormonal system uses hormones carried in the blood, which travel more slowly and affect many cells at once, producing slower, longer-lasting, more widespread responses — good for things like growth, metabolism, reproduction and responding to stress over a longer time. In many situations they act together: for example, in the fight-or-flight response, the sympathetic nervous system acts quickly to increase heart rate, while the hormone adrenaline from the adrenal glands sustains and amplifies the response; in the control of blood glucose, hormones (insulin and glucagon) act more slowly and over longer periods than nervous control would allow. Plants coordinate only by hormones (plant growth substances such as auxin, gibberellin and phytochrome), because they have no nervous system.

12. The human brain: cerebral hemispheres, hypothalamus, pituitary gland, cerebellum, medulla oblongata

The brain controls and coordinates the activities of the body and is the seat of thought, memory and emotion. The cerebral hemispheres are the large, folded upper parts of the brain; they are responsible for higher functions — thought, memory, reasoning, conscious actions, language and sensation — and each hemisphere controls the opposite side of the body. The hypothalamus links the nervous and endocrine systems; it controls the pituitary gland, regulates body temperature, water balance, hunger and thirst, and the sleep cycle, and it plays a central role in homeostasis. The pituitary gland, under the influence of the hypothalamus, releases several hormones that control other endocrine glands and body functions — for example growth hormone, ADH and the hormones that regulate reproduction. The cerebellum is responsible for coordination of movement and balance — it makes sure movements are smooth and coordinated and posture is maintained. The medulla oblongata controls unconscious and automatic functions essential to life — breathing rate, heart rate and the reflex centres for coughing, sneezing and swallowing — and it is where the cardiovascular control centre and the ventilation (breathing) centre are located. Damage to different parts of the brain produces different deficits, and knowing the location and main functions makes it possible to link symptoms to brain regions.

13. Brain imaging: MRI, fMRI, PET and CT — what they show and how they are used

Different imaging techniques give different kinds of information about the brain. Computed tomography (CT) uses X-rays from many angles to produce a cross-sectional image of the brain’s structure; it is good at showing bone, bleeding and structural abnormalities, and it is quick and widely available, but it uses ionising radiation and gives limited soft-tissue contrast. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) uses a strong magnetic field and radio waves to give detailed images of soft tissue; it shows brain structure without ionising radiation and is excellent for detecting tumours, inflammation, demyelination and injury, but it takes longer and is noisy and claustrophobic for the patient. Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) is MRI adapted to show brain function — it detects changes in blood flow and oxygen use that accompany neural activity, so it can show which parts of the brain are active during a task; it has good spatial resolution but poor time resolution because the blood flow change lags the neural activity. Positron emission tomography (PET) uses a radioactive tracer (for example, a labelled glucose) injected into the patient; the tracer accumulates in active tissues and its radioactivity is detected, so PET can show brain activity and metabolism, and it can show neurotransmitter receptors and help in diagnosing and studying disorders such as Alzheimer’s and cancer, but it uses ionising radiation and is expensive. These techniques are used in medical diagnosis (for example to locate a tumour, or to investigate a stroke or a degenerative disease) and in research into brain structure and function — for example to see which areas are involved in a particular task or how activity differs in a disorder.

14. Brain chemicals and disease: dopamine in Parkinson’s disease, serotonin in depression, and new drugs

Imbalances in certain naturally-occurring brain chemicals can contribute to ill health, and understanding these has driven the development of new drugs. Parkinson’s disease is caused by the loss of neurones in the substantia nigra that produce dopamine, a neurotransmitter involved in controlling movement; the resulting dopamine deficiency causes tremor, stiffness, slowness of movement and balance problems. Treatment with L-DOPA (a precursor that crosses the blood–brain barrier and is converted to dopamine) can relieve symptoms, at least for a time, and other drugs may mimic dopamine or prevent its breakdown. Depression is associated with lower levels of the neurotransmitter serotonin (and also noradrenaline) in the brain; selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) block the reuptake of serotonin into the presynaptic neurone, so more serotonin stays in the synapse and helps improve mood, and they are widely used to treat depression and anxiety. New drugs can be developed using this understanding of the role of brain chemicals — for example by targeting the receptors or the synthesis or breakdown of a neurotransmitter — and knowledge of the cause of a disease (such as the dopamine deficiency in Parkinson’s) is what makes targeted treatment possible.

15. Producing drugs using genetically modified organisms

Drugs can be produced using genetically modified organisms (GMOs) — plants, animals and microorganisms. The best-known example is human insulin: the human gene for insulin is inserted into bacteria (usually E. coli) using a plasmid, and the bacteria are grown in large fermenters to produce human insulin, which is then extracted and purified. Human insulin made this way is identical to the insulin made in the human body, so it does not cause the immune reactions that some people had to the animal insulin formerly used. Other products made from GMOs include human growth hormone, clotting factor for haemophiliacs, and enzymes for washing powders; and modified plants and animals are being explored to produce vaccines and other pharmaceuticals. Using GMOs to produce drugs has advantages: the product can be made in large quantities, it can be made more cheaply than by extraction from animals or people, and it can be made identical to the human version. There are concerns, however — about the containment of the GMOs, the possibility of unintended effects, and the ethical questions of modifying organisms in this way.

16. Recombinant DNA: how it is produced (restriction enzymes and DNA ligase) and inserted into other cells

Recombinant DNA is DNA made by joining together pieces of DNA from different sources. Restriction endonucleases (restriction enzymes) cut DNA at specific base sequences, making cuts that can leave complementary ‘sticky ends’ — short single-stranded overhangs that can base-pair with each other — and these sticky ends allow a gene of interest to be joined to a vector (such as a plasmid) cut with the same enzyme. DNA ligase then seals the backbone of the sugar–phosphate chain, joining the gene to the vector to make recombinant DNA. To insert recombinant DNA into other cells, the vector (carrying the gene) is introduced into host cells: bacterial cells can take up plasmids in a process called transformation (which can be helped by making the bacteria competent — for example by calcium chloride treatment and a heat shock); viral vectors can be engineered to carry the gene into the cells they infect, using the virus’s natural ability to enter cells; and other methods such as microinjection or gene guns can put DNA directly into cells. Once inside, the host cell’s machinery may read and express the gene, making the protein it codes for (for example insulin), and if the vector also carries a gene for resistance to an antibiotic, only the cells that took up the vector will survive on antibiotic-containing medium — giving a way to select the transformed cells.

17. Microarrays: how they identify active genes

A microarray (DNA microarray) is a small slide or chip carrying thousands of known DNA sequences (probes), each in a known position. Messenger RNA is extracted from two samples (for example, a diseased tissue and a healthy tissue, or cells treated with a drug and untreated cells), converted to cDNA, and labelled with different coloured fluorescent tags (for example green for one sample and red for the other). The labelled cDNA is mixed and allowed to hybridise to the probes on the microarray: if a gene is active (expressed) in a sample, its cDNA will bind (hybridise) to the complementary probe on the chip. By scanning the chip, the colours and intensities can be read: a green spot means the gene is more active in the green-labelled sample, a red spot means more active in the red-labelled sample, yellow means similar activity in both, and the intensity reflects how active the gene is. By looking at all the spots, researchers can see which genes are active (turned on) or inactive (turned off) in a sample and compare activity between samples — for example to see which genes are active in a cancer cell that are not in a normal cell, or to see how a drug changes gene activity. This makes it possible to identify active genes and to use gene activity patterns for diagnosis and to understand disease and drug action.

18. Bioinformatics: what it is and what it is used for

Bioinformatics is the use of computer technology to collect, store, analyse and interpret biological data, especially large datasets such as DNA and protein sequences, gene expression data from microarrays, and protein structures. It depends on the availability of sequence data — the DNA sequences of genomes and the sequences of proteins — and on databases that store and organise these sequences so they can be compared and searched. Bioinformatics is used to compare sequences to find similarities and differences, to identify genes and their functions (for example by comparing a new sequence with known ones to suggest what it does), to study evolutionary relationships (by building phylogenetic trees from sequence comparisons), to predict the structure and function of proteins from their amino acid sequence, and to analyse gene expression patterns from microarrays. It depends on the work of the Human Genome Project and other sequencing projects, and on the computational tools that turn raw sequence data into useful biological knowledge. Bioinformatics is now part of nearly every area of biology — from identifying a gene, to understanding what it does, to finding targets for drugs, to tracing the evolution of a pathogen.

19. Risks and benefits of genetically modified organisms

Genetically modified organisms (GMOs) — plants, animals and microorganisms — have both benefits and risks. Benefits include: in agriculture, crops can be modified to resist pests (for example Bt crops that produce a bacterial toxin harmful to insect pests but not to people) or herbicides, to tolerate drought or salinity, to improve nutrition (for example golden rice producing beta-carotene, a vitamin A precursor), and to increase yield — which can support food security; in medicine, GM bacteria produce human insulin and other proteins for therapy; in research, GM animals and plants are used to study gene function and disease. Risks and concerns include: the possibility that the modified gene could spread to wild relatives or other organisms (gene flow) and have unintended effects; the potential harm to non-target organisms (for example whether Bt crops affect beneficial insects); the development of resistant pests or weeds; the concentration of control of food and seed in a few companies, and the effect on farmers and on traditional varieties; the long-term effects on ecosystems, which are not fully known; and the ethical questions about modifying organisms, especially animals, and about food that has been genetically modified. These must be weighed case by case: the benefits and risks of each GMO depend on what it is, how it is used, and how it is regulated. The scientific evidence about each GMO is needed to evaluate it properly, and the public has a legitimate role in the decisions because the issues are not only scientific — they include values, economics and the environment.

20. How to use this note and what to revise next

Use these notes by working through each section and checking that you can: describe the structure of sensory, relay and motor neurones; describe the spinal reflex arc, including the roles of grey and white matter; explain how the action potential is generated, including depolarisation, repolarisation, hyperpolarisation, the role of sodium and potassium ions and the sodium–potassium pump, and the all-or-nothing principle; explain how myelination allows saltatory conduction and speeds it up; describe the cholinergic synapse and the roles of calcium, acetylcholine, receptors, acetylcholinesterase; explain the pupillary reflex (circular muscles constrict in bright light, radial muscles dilate in dim); describe how nicotine, lidocaine, cobra venom alpha toxin, L-DOPA and MDMA affect nerve impulse transmission, including examples; describe how rod cells detect light, the role of rhodopsin, opsin, retinal, sodium channels and hyperpolarisation, and how this leads to action potentials in the optic neurone; describe habituation and the evidence for it (the snail withdrawal practical); describe the central and peripheral nervous systems and the sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions; locate and state the functions of the cerebral hemispheres, hypothalamus, pituitary gland, cerebellum and medulla oblongata; explain how MRI, fMRI, PET and CT work and what they are used for; explain the role of dopamine in Parkinson’s disease and serotonin in depression and how the drugs work; describe the production of drugs using GMOs (human insulin as the example); describe how recombinant DNA is made with restriction enzymes and DNA ligase and inserted into cells; describe how microarrays work and what they show; define bioinformatics; and discuss the risks and benefits of GMOs. After this topic, revise Topic 9 the continuation of this unit and the related practicals, and the BIology practicals (Core Practicals 14–18) which reinforce these topics.

title: IGCSE Mathematics: Indices and Standard Form
content:
IGCSE Mathematics: Indices and Standard Form

Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580 (2025–2027), section 1 Number: statement 1.3 Powers and roots, 1.7 Indices I (with Extended fractional indices), 1.8 Standard form, E1.18 Surds, and section 2 statement E2.4 Indices II (algebraic indices). Indices are shorthand for repeated multiplication, and their laws are the shortcuts that make large and small numbers manageable. This note derives each law from what it counts, covers standard form arithmetic in full, and finishes with surds and rationalising — an Extended favourite that separates the top grades.

Powers, roots and the vocabulary

In 5³ the base is 5 and the index (plural: indices) is 3; it means 5 × 5 × 5 = 125. A square root reverses a square: √25 = 5 because 5² = 25. A cube root reverses a cube: ³√64 = 4 because 4³ = 64.

  • √16 = 4, the principal (positive) square root, as printed on a calculator. But the equation x² = 16 has two solutions, x = 4 or x = −4, because (−4)² = 16 as well. The question decides which is wanted: a length is positive; a solution of an equation may be negative.
  • Notation: a² is read a squared, a³ a cubed, and aⁿ a to the power n. a² ≠ 2a — a² = a × a while 2a = a + a.

The index laws

Each law is a statement about counting multiplications, so each can be checked by writing the multiplications out.

Law 1:  a^m x a^n = a^(m+n)
Why: a³ x a² = (a x a x a) x (a x a) = a⁵, and 3 + 2 = 5.
Example: 2³ × 2⁵ = 2⁸ = 256; check: 8 × 32 = 256 ✓

Law 2:  a^m ÷ a^n = a^(m-n)
Why: a⁵ ÷ a² = (a x a x a x a x a)/(a x a) = a x a x a = a³, and 5 - 2 = 3.
Example: 5⁷ ÷ 5⁴ = 5³ = 125

Law 3:  (a^m)^n = a^(m n)
Why: (a²)³ = a² x a² x a² = a⁶, and 2 × 3 = 6.
Example: (2x³)² = 2² x (x³)² = 4x⁶        [the power applies to every factor]

Law 4:  a⁰ = 1  (a not zero)
Why: a³ ÷ a³ = a^(3-3) = a⁰, and any number divided by itself is 1.
Example: 7⁰ = 1

Law 5:  a^(-n) = 1/(a^n)
Why: a^(-2) = a^(0-2) = a⁰ ÷ a² = 1/a².
Example: 5^(-2) = 1/25 = 0.04

Fractional indices (Extended). A fractional index is a root: the denominator of the fraction is the root, the numerator is the power.

a^(1/n) = nth root of a        a^(m/n) = (nth root of a)^m

16^(1/2) = √16 = 4
27^(2/3) = (cube root of 27)² = 3² = 9
Check the second: 27^(2/3) squared three times over should give 27² = 729; 9³ = 729 ✓

Indices in algebra (Extended)

The same laws apply when the base is a letter, and every factor in a bracket carries the power:

Simplify:  (2x³)² x⁴ ÷ x⁵

(2x³)² = 4x⁶        [square the 2 and double the index]
4x⁶ x x⁴ = 4x¹⁰     [Law 1: add indices]
4x¹⁰ ÷ x⁵ = 4x⁵     [Law 2: subtract indices]
Solve:  2^x = 32

Write both sides with base 2:  32 = 2⁵
2^x = 2⁵, so x = 5        [matching bases means matching indices]

When the bases differ, rewrite one as a power of the other: 8 = 2³, so 8^x = 2^(3x). Equations like 3^(x+1) = 27^(x−1) become 3^(x+1) = 3^(3x−3), so x + 1 = 3x − 3, giving x = 2.

LawStatementWorked line
Multiplyingaᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ2³ × 2⁵ = 2⁸ = 256
Dividingaᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ5⁷ ÷ 5⁴ = 5³ = 125
Power of a power(aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ(2x³)² = 4x⁶
Zero indexa⁰ = 1 (a not zero)7⁰ = 1
Negative indexa⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ5⁻² = 1/25
Fractional indexa^(m/n) = (ⁿ√a)ᵐ27^(2/3) = 9

Two edge cases deserve care. The zero index says nothing about 0⁰: 0⁰ is undefined, because the pattern a⁰ = 1 holds for every non-zero base while the pattern 0ⁿ = 0 holds for every positive power, and the two patterns collide at the origin. And a negative index never makes a value negative: 2⁻³ = 1/8 is positive, because the minus sign belongs to the position of the power, not to the number itself. Finally, every root can be written as a power — √x = x^(1/2), ³√x = x^(1/3) — which is how a calculator evaluates them and how algebraic roots are simplified in one notation.

Standard form

Standard form writes a number as a × 10ⁿ where 1 ⩽ a < 10 and n is an integer. It handles very large and very small quantities without long strings of zeros.

Write in standard form:

47 382 = 4.7382 × 10⁴        [the decimal point moves 4 places left]
0.0056 = 5.6 × 10^(-3)        [the decimal point moves 3 places right, so n = -3]

Arithmetic in standard form. Multiply or divide the numbers first, then the powers of ten, and adjust back into standard form if needed:

(3 × 10⁵) x (4 × 10^(-2))
= (3 × 4) x (10⁵ × 10^(-2))     [regrouped]
= 12 × 10³
= 1.2 × 10⁴                     [12 is not between 1 and 10, so adjust]

(6 × 10⁸) ÷ (2 × 10³)
= (6 ÷ 2) × 10^(8-3) = 3 × 10⁵

Addition and subtraction need matching powers first: 3 × 10⁵ + 4 × 10⁴ = 30 × 10⁴ + 4 × 10⁴ = 34 × 10⁴ = 3.4 × 10⁵. Real-world uses: the speed of light is 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, the size of an atom is about 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m, and masses, distances and populations in physics and chemistry questions are always quoted this way. A calculator's ×10ˣ key enters the power directly; the answer should be given in the form the question asks, often to 3 s.f.

Surds (Extended)

A surd is a root that cannot be written exactly as a fraction — √2, √3, 3√5. Exact answers in surds are often required on Paper 2, where a calculator cannot help. The laws:

√a x √b = √(ab)        √a ÷ √b = √(a/b)        (√a)² = a

Simplifying. Take out the largest square factor:

√50 = √(25 × 2) = √25 x √2 = 5√2
√72 = √(36 × 2) = 6√2
√(9/16) = √9 / √16 = 3/4

Adding like surds. Only like surds combine, exactly like algebraic terms:

√18 + √8 = 3√2 + 2√2 = 5√2        [simplify first]
2√3 + √5 cannot be combined: they are unlike surds.

Rationalising the denominator. A fraction with a surd underneath is tidied by multiplying top and bottom by the same surd (or its conjugate):

6/√3 = (6 x √3)/(√3 x √3) = 6√3/3 = 2√3

1/(3 + √2): multiply top and bottom by the conjugate (3 - √2):
= (3 - √2)/[(3 + √2)(3 - √2)]
= (3 - √2)/(9 - 2)          [difference of two squares below]
= (3 - √2)/7

The conjugate works because (a + b)(a − b) = a² − b² removes the square root entirely. Expanding surd brackets uses the same identity: (2 + √3)(2 − √3) = 4 − 3 = 1.

Worked example: a combined index calculation

Simplify (2³ × 2⁵) ÷ 2⁴ and check it two ways.

Method 1 (indices): 2³ × 2⁵ = 2⁸, then 2⁸ ÷ 2⁴ = 2⁴ = 16
Method 2 (arithmetic): 2³ × 2⁵ = 8 × 32 = 256;  256 ÷ 16 = 16
Both routes give 16 ✓

Second example: write (3√2)² − √8 in the form k√2.

(3√2)² = 9 × 2 = 18        [square both the 3 and the √2]
√8 = 2√2
18 - 2√2 is already simple; it cannot be written as k√2 because 18 is rational,
so the answer stays 18 - 2√2.

Standard form in a calculation. A red blood cell is 7 × 10⁻⁶ m across and a vein is 2.4 × 10⁻³ m wide. How many cells fit side by side?

2.4 × 10^(-3) ÷ 7 × 10^(-6)
= (2.4 ÷ 7) × 10^(-3 - (-6))        [divide the numbers, subtract the indices]
= 0.342857 × 10³
= 3.43 × 10² (3 s.f.)  ≈ 343 cells

The index arithmetic is the whole question: subtracting −6 gives +3, and a sense-check on the powers alone (10⁻³ ÷ 10⁻⁶ = 10³) says the answer must be in the hundreds — which catches sign slips before they cost the final mark.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Multiplying the base by the index: 2³ is 8, not 6; (2³)² = 2⁶ = 64, not 2⁵.
  • Forgetting to square the coefficient: (2x³)² = 4x⁶, not 2x⁶.
  • Treating a⁻ⁿ as negative rather than reciprocal: 2⁻³ = 1/8.
  • Writing 0.00047 as 4.7 × 10⁻³; it is 4.7 × 10⁻⁴ — count the places the point moves.
  • Leaving a standard-form answer as 12 × 10³; the front number must be between 1 and 10.
  • Giving √16 = ±4 in a simplification; the square root symbol means the principal root, while x² = 16 has both solutions.
  • Rationalising only the surd and not its conjugate partner: 1/(3 + √2) needs (3 − √2) top and bottom.
  • Combining unlike surds: 2√3 + √5 is final; only matching surd parts can be added.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 2, 3 marks). Simplify (3x²)³ ÷ x⁴.

Answer: (3x²)³ = 27x⁶; 27x⁶ ÷ x⁴ = 27x².

Question 2 (Paper 2, 3 marks). Evaluate 8^(2/3).

Answer: ³√8 = 2, and 2² = 4. So 8^(2/3) = 4.

Question 3 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Write 0.000 42 and 63 000 in standard form, then find their product.

Answer: 4.2 × 10⁻⁴ and 6.3 × 10⁴. Product = (4.2 × 6.3) × 10⁰ = 26.46 = 2.646 × 10¹.

Question 4 (Paper 2, 4 marks). Simplify √48 + 3√12.

Answer: √48 = √(16 × 3) = 4√3; 3√12 = 3 × 2√3 = 6√3; total = 10√3.

Question 5 (Paper 2, 4 marks). Rationalise the denominator of 5/(2 + √3).

Answer: Multiply by the conjugate: 5(2 − √3)/[(2 + √3)(2 − √3)] = 5(2 − √3)/(4 − 3) = 5(2 − √3) = 10 − 5√3.

Question 6 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Solve 9^x = 27.

Answer: Write both as powers of 3: 3^(2x) = 3³, so 2x = 3 and x = 3/2. Check: 9^(3/2) = (√9)³ = 3³ = 27 ✓.

From the numbers themselves, the course turns to comparing and sharing them: ratio, rate and proportion.

The powers-of-ten ladder: seeing standard form instead of memorising it

Indices look like a rule to memorise and are really a picture to read. Every quantity in the course sits somewhere on one ladder of powers of ten, and multiplying, dividing and converting all move you up or down that ladder by whole rungs.

One rung, one index. Moving up a rung multiplies by 10, and that is exactly what adding 1 to the index does: 10³ × 10 = 10⁴. Moving down divides by 10 and subtracts 1. Every index law is that sentence applied twice:

aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ Key: a = the base; m and n = the indices (powers). Multiplying adds the indices because each factor contributes its own rungs.
aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ Key: dividing subtracts, because dividing by aⁿ is multiplying by a⁻ⁿ.
(aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ Key: a bracket applied n times multiplies the rungs by n.
a⁰ = 1 and a⁻ⁿ = 1 / aⁿ Key: both follow from the subtraction law: a³ ÷ a³ = a⁰ must be 1, and a² ÷ a⁵ = a⁻³ must be 1/a³.

Standard form is a position on the ladder. A number is in standard form when it is written as

N = A × 10ⁿ Key: A = a number with 1 ≤ A < 10 (one non-zero digit before the point); n = a whole number, positive for large values and negative for small ones. 4.2 × 10³ means four decimal places' worth of rungs above 1: 4,200.

Converting is counting rungs, not guessing the sign. To write 47,500 in standard form, move the point left until one digit remains in front: 4.75, which is three moves, so the index is +3 and the value is 4.75 × 10⁴. To write 0.00062, move the point right until one digit remains in front: 6.2, which is four moves, so the index is −4 and the value is 6.2 × 10⁻⁴. Left is positive, right is negative — the point moving right on a small number gives a negative index, which is the sign students most often flip.

Worked example. A red blood cell has diameter 0.0000072 m and a virus 1.2 × 10⁻⁷ m. Write the cell in standard form and find how many times longer it is.

cell: 0.0000072 = 7.2 × 10⁻⁶ m (six moves right)
ratio: (7.2 × 10⁻⁶) ÷ (1.2 × 10⁻⁷) = (7.2 ÷ 1.2) × 10⁻⁶⁻⁽⁻⁷⁾ = 6.0 × 10¹ = 60

The division law did the work: subtracting a negative index adds. Doing that sum as −6 − 7 = −13 is the error that turns 60 into 0.0000000000006.

Estimating with the ladder. A calculation like (4.9 × 10⁵) × (2.1 × 10³) is roughly 5 × 2 = 10 times 10⁵⁺³ = 10⁸, so about 1.0 × 10⁹ before any calculator. This is how you catch a wrong power of ten — the most common way a correct method still loses the answer mark.

Where marks are lost. Writing 0.42 × 10⁴ or 42 × 10² and calling it standard form: A must be at least 1 and less than 10. Flipping the sign of the index on a small number. And adding indices when multiplying different bases — 2³ × 3² is 8 × 9 = 72, not 6⁵.

Negative and zero indices in depth

A negative index tells you to take a reciprocal, and a zero index gives the value 1. These two rules follow from the index laws, not from memory, so the working below shows how each one is forced. The subsections cover the reasons, the calculator entry, and the common slips that turn a negative power into a negative number.

Why a zero index gives one

Take a number and divide it by itself. Using the division law, a⁵ ÷ a⁵ = a⁰, and the same quotient is 1 because any number divided by itself is 1. So a⁰ = 1 for any non-zero a. The rule is therefore a consequence of the laws already in use, and it is why 5⁰ = 1, 100⁰ = 1 and (−3)⁰ = 1.

Why a negative index is a reciprocal

Divide a power by a larger power of the same base: a² ÷ a⁵ = a^(2−5) = a⁻³. Writing the same quotient as 1/a³ shows that a⁻³ = 1/a³. So a negative index moves the base to the denominator and changes the sign of the index. The value 2⁻³ is 1/2³ = 1/8, which is positive, because a negative index does not make the answer negative.

Negative indices with fractions

The reciprocal rule also works on fractions, where it flips the fraction. (2/3)⁻² = (3/2)² = 9/4. Invert the fraction first, then apply the positive index. A common error is to change only the index and leave the fraction alone, which gives (2/3)⁻² = 4/9 and loses the mark.

Entering negative and fractional powers on a calculator

Use the power key, and enter the negative index in brackets so the calculator reads the whole index as a negative number. For 5⁻², enter 5, the power key and (−2), giving 0.04. A fractional power such as 8^(1/3) is entered with brackets around the fraction, and the calculator returns 2. Check the result by reversing the operation: 2³ = 8 confirms the cube root.

Simplifying expressions with negative powers

To simplify 3x⁻² × 6x⁵, multiply the numbers and add the indices: 18x^(−2+5) = 18x³. To write the answer with only positive indices, move any negative power to the denominator. For example, 4y⁻³ becomes 4/y³. Collect the coefficients first, then deal with the indices, so the final form is easy to check.

Mistakes with negative and zero indices

The commonest errors are treating 2⁻³ as −8, writing a⁰ as 0, and reading (−2)⁻² as −1/4 when the correct value is 1/4. The bracket in (−2)⁻² is what makes the base negative, and an even power of a negative number is positive. Write the bracket in the working so the sign is clear before the reciprocal is taken.

title: Exam technique: Simplifying and Expanding
content:
### What earns the marks
For expansion, calculate earns a mark for every correct pair of products shown before collecting terms. For factorisation, the HCF stated earns the first mark and the fully divided bracket earns the second: partial factorisation scores at most half. For algebraic fractions, factorise first earns the method mark even when cancellation follows.
### Traps
Error: (x + 5)(x - 2) = x squared + 10. Correction: four products, then collect. Error: 3(2x squared - 3x) called fully factorised. Correction: extract x as well. Error: cancelling terms instead of factors in a fraction. Correction: factorise numerator and denominator first.

title: Edexcel IAL Computer Science: Computational Thinking and Programming
content:
Edexcel IAL Computer Science: Computational Thinking and Programming

Pearson Edexcel International Advanced Level in Computer Science, Unit 2 Practical Programming and Problem Solving: computational thinking skills, algorithm design, programming basics and constructs, structured programming, and the program development life cycle with design and testing. This is the unit where knowledge becomes craft — so every algorithm here is refined stage by stage, every trace runs statement by statement, and every test case is chosen with its expected output stated before execution. The Python shown is version 3, as the unit requires.

Computational thinking

  • Abstraction — discard irrelevant detail, model what matters (a timetable models rooms and slots, not paint colours).
  • Decomposition — break a problem into independently solvable parts (an ordering system: stock, basket, payment, delivery).
  • Pattern recognition — spot repetition that generalises (three near-identical report routines become one parameterised function).
  • Algorithmic thinking — express solutions as precise, ordered, unambiguous steps.

These four run through everything below: decomposition yields the module structure, abstraction the data model, patterns the loops and functions, and algorithmic thinking the pseudocode.

Algorithm design and representation

Representations: pseudocode (structured language-independent statements), flowcharts (oval start/end, parallelogram I/O, rectangle process, diamond decision), structure charts (module hierarchy with data couples). Stepwise refinement expands one outline line into steps until each is trivially implementable.

Refinement worked end to end: "process a batch of orders".

Stage 0:   for each order: validate, price, update stock, report.

Stage 1:
  open the order file and the stock file
  for each order in the file:
      validate the order (product exists, quantity positive, credit ok)
      if valid: price it (quantity x unit price, apply discounts)
                update stock (decrement, flag reorders)
                append to the invoice file
      else: append to the error report
  print summary totals

Stage 2 (final pseudocode for one leaf - pricing):

  FUNCTION priceOrder(qty, unitPrice, customerDiscount)
      subtotal <- qty * unitPrice
      IF qty >= 10⁰ THEN
          bulkDiscount <- subtotal * 0.05
      ELSE
          bulkDiscount <- 0
      ENDIF
      total <- subtotal - bulkDiscount
      total <- total * (1 - customerDiscount)
      RETURN total
  ENDFUNCTION

Notice what refinement exposed: two discounts stack - the order of application
must be specified, and the boundary (exactly 10⁰) tested both sides.

Programming basics and constructs

Variables hold typed values; assignment stores the evaluated right-hand side. The three constructs: sequence (statements in order), selection (IF / ELIF / ELSE on boolean conditions; nested selection for layered cases), iteration (FOR over a known count, WHILE while a condition holds — plus the off-by-one and infinite-loop traps). Subprograms: procedures (named actions, no return) and functions (named calculations, return a value); parameters pass data in, return passes results out, and scope keeps locals local.

Python 3 - constructs with line-by-line memory commentary:

  1  def classify(mark):            # function definition; mark is a parameter
  2      if mark >= 70:             # selection: evaluates mark >= 70
  3          return "Distinction"
  4      elif mark >= 50:           # only reached when mark < 70
  5          return "Pass"
  6      else:
  7          return "Fail"
  8
  9  results = []                   # an empty list
 10  for mark in [65, 72, 41]:      # iteration: mark takes each value in turn
 11      results.append(classify(mark))   # call; return value appended
 12  print(results)

Trace:
  line 9:  results = []
  line 10: mark = 65 → classify: 65>=70 false, 65>=50 true → "Pass"
  line 11: results = ["Pass"]
  line 10: mark = 72 → 72>=70 true → "Distinction"
  line 11: results = ["Pass", "Distinction"]
  line 10: mark = 41 → both tests false → "Fail"
  line 11: results = ["Pass", "Distinction", "Fail"]
  line 12: prints ['Pass', 'Distinction', 'Fail']

Definite iteration (FOR) over a list; indefinite iteration (WHILE) for
"read until a sentinel" patterns.

Structured programming discipline: one entry/exit per structure, no wild jumps (goto), top-down design with clear module interfaces, and named constants for magic numbers. Benefits: readability, testability and maintainability — and the exam expects those words attached to the technique.

Program design tools

Before code, the design is expressed in forms the team can review. Structure charts show the module hierarchy: the main program at the top, subtasks beneath, with data couples marking what passes between them — a chart with three levels proves the decomposition. Pseudocode gives each leaf module's exact logic; flowcharts show branch and loop shape at a glance; a data dictionary lists every variable and file field with its type, range and purpose, so modules agree on interfaces before they are coded. Naming conventions, indentation standards and comment discipline are part of the same stage: code is read far more often than written, and the exam gives method marks for showing these artefacts rather than jumping straight to Python.

File handling, validation and data persistence

Python 3 - writing then reading a data file, with validation:

  # write
  with open("temps.txt", "w") as f:        # "w" creates or TRUNCATES
      for reading in [21.5, 19.0, -999]:
          if reading < -50 or reading > 60:      # range validation
              continue                            # skip invalid sensor value
          f.write(str(reading) + "\n")

  # read
  total = 0.0
  count = 0
  with open("temps.txt", "r") as f:        # with closes the file automatically
      for line in f:
          value = float(line)              # type conversion; may raise ValueError
          total += value
          count += 1
  if count > 0:                            # guard the division
      print("mean =", total / count)
  else:
      print("no valid data")

Traps the examiner sets: "w" wiping an existing file where "a" (append) was
meant; reading without closing (the with statement prevents it); averaging
without the empty-file guard; and validating after conversion rather than
before.
