Validation techniques: presence, type, range, length, check digit, list/pick-list, and format (regular expression) checks. Verification: double entry, visual checking, read-back. Input/output at this level is routine-level discipline: every value entering the system passes a check at the boundary.

Program development life cycle

StageActivitiesArtifacts
AnalysisGather requirements; define inputs, outputs, constraintsRequirements specification
DesignDecompose; design data structures and algorithmsStructure charts, pseudocode, data dictionary
ImplementationCode, follow standards, reviewSource code, comments
TestingNormal, boundary, erroneous, edge cases; debugTest plans, test results, bug reports
MaintenanceCorrective, adaptive, perfective changesRevised code and docs

Iterative (agile) development cycles through these stages in small increments with frequent client review; waterfall completes each stage once in order. Agile absorbs change cheaply and shows working software early; waterfall suits fixed-scope contracts with heavy documentation. The exam wants the comparison, not a preference.

Testing worked example: priceOrder above (5% bulk discount at 10⁰+ units).

Test plan rows - each states expected output BEFORE running:

  normal:    qty 50, unit 10.0, disc 0    → 500.00      (no bulk discount)
  boundary:  qty 99, unit 10.0, disc 0    → 990.00      (just below)
  boundary:  qty 10⁰, unit 10.0, disc 0   → 950.00      (bulk fires: 10⁰⁰*0.95)
  boundary:  qty 10¹, unit 10.0, disc 0   → 959.50      (just above)
  erroneous: qty -5, unit 10.0, disc 0    → should be rejected by validation
  edge:      qty 10⁰, unit 0, disc 0.1    → 0.00        (zero price)

Unit testing checks the function in isolation; integration testing checks it
with the stock and invoice modules; acceptance testing checks the customer's
requirements. Black-box testing uses specifications only; white-box testing
uses code structure (statement, branch coverage).

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Design jumps: no decomposition or refinement shown before code loses method marks.
  • WHILE loops with uninitialised or never-updated conditions (infinite loops); FOR loop boundary errors (range(1, n+1) versus range(1, n)).
  • Testing only normal data; boundary and erroneous data carry equal marks.
  • Test results without pre-stated expectations — that is checking, not testing.
  • Confusing procedures with functions (return value) or parameters with arguments at the call site.
  • "w" versus "a" file modes destroying data; and no empty-input guard before division.
  • Stating agile is "better" without the trade-off comparison the question asks for.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Unit 2, 4 marks). Explain abstraction and decomposition with examples from a library system.

Answer: Abstraction models only relevant features — the system tracks loans, members and due dates while ignoring irrelevant details like book cover designs. Decomposition splits the problem into solvable parts — catalogue search, loans/returns, fines, member accounts — each designed and tested independently before integration.

Question 2 (Unit 2, 6 marks). Write pseudocode for a function that returns the median of three numbers.

Answer: FUNCTION median3(a, b, c): IF (a >= b AND a <= c) OR (a <= b AND a >= c) THEN RETURN a; ELSEIF (b >= a AND b <= c) OR (b <= a AND b >= c) THEN RETURN b; ELSE RETURN c; ENDIF. (Alternative: sort the three values and return the middle.)

Question 3 (Unit 2, 4 marks). Describe a test plan for a program calculating exam grades from marks 0–100.

Answer: Normal: 55 → Pass. Boundary: 0, 100, and the grade thresholds 49/50 and 69/70 tested both sides. Erroneous: -1 and 101 rejected by range validation; "abc" rejected by type check. Each test records expected output before execution; failures are logged and retested after fixes.

Question 4 (Unit 2, 4 marks). Compare iterative and waterfall development.

Answer: Iterative development delivers in small cycles with client review after each, so working software appears early and requirement changes are absorbed cheaply — at the cost of less predictable final scope and budget. Waterfall completes analysis, design, implementation and testing in sequence, giving clear milestones and documentation, but testing comes late and changes after design are expensive.

Question 5 (Unit 2, 4 marks). Explain the difference between validation and verification, and give two validation techniques.

Answer: Validation checks data is plausible before storage (range check rejects a mark of 300); verification checks captured data matches the source (double entry of a password). Two further validation techniques: type checks (reject letters in a numeric field) and length checks (reject an 8-digit account number where 10 are required).

Question 6 (Unit 2, 5 marks). Write Python 3 that reads numbers from a file and outputs the largest, handling an empty file.

Answer: largest = None; with open("nums.txt") as f: for line in f: v = float(line); if largest is None or v > largest: largest = v; if largest is None: print("file is empty"); else: print("largest =", largest).

With the craft established, the next note organises what programs manipulate: data types, records and arrays.

title: Geometry — Angles and Polygons — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Geometry — Angles and Polygons

Mathematics — OL. angle facts, parallel lines, polygon angles, circle theorems (Extended).

  • 1. Core angle facts
  • 2. Polygons
  • 3. Circle theorems (Extended)
  • 4. Algebra with angles

How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

Worked example

The interior angle sum of a polygon with n sides is (n − 2) × 180°. For a regular octagon, n = 8, so the sum is 6 × 180° = 1080°. Each interior angle is 1080 ÷ 8 = 135°, and each exterior angle is 360 ÷ 8 = 45°. Exterior angles of any convex polygon always add up to 360°.

Common mistakes

  • Using 360° for the interior sum instead of (n − 2) × 180°.
  • Confusing the angle at the centre with the angle at the circumference. The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference when both subtend the same arc.
  • Writing a reason without naming the theorem. Name it, for example "angles in the same segment" or "opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180°".

title: IGCSE Physics (OxfordAQA): Electricity and Magnetism
content:
Electricity and Magnetism

An electric current is a flow of charge, and every circuit question is asking how that flow is shared, driven and opposed. Potential difference drives the flow, resistance opposes it, and the rules for series and parallel circuits are just consequences of charge being conserved and of energy being transferred per unit charge. Magnetism follows from the same physics: a current is moving charge, moving charge creates a magnetic field, and a current in a magnetic field experiences a force. This note builds the circuit relationships first, then the magnetic ones, so the two halves share one foundation instead of being memorised separately.

3.5.1 Electrical circuits: current and charge

Current is the rate of flow of charge, and charge is measured in coulombs. One ampere is one coulomb per second, so a current of 2 A delivers 2 C every second.

Q = I t

Key: Q = charge (C); I = current (A); t = time (s).

In a series circuit the current is the same at every point, because charge cannot pile up or disappear: whatever leaves the cell must return to it. In a parallel circuit the current splits between the branches, and the current entering the junction equals the total current leaving it. That statement is the conservation of charge, and it is what makes a parallel circuit's total current larger than any one branch's.

Current is measured with an ammeter connected in series with the component, and potential difference with a voltmeter connected in parallel across it. Reversing those two connections is the commonest practical error: an ammeter in parallel shorts the component out, and a voltmeter in series blocks the current.

3.5.1 Electrical circuits: potential difference and resistance

Potential difference is the energy transferred per unit charge between two points, measured in volts. One volt is one joule per coulomb, so a 12 V battery transfers 12 J of energy to every coulomb that passes through it.

V = I R

Key: V = potential difference (V); I = current (A); R = resistance (Ω); the equation is usually used rearranged as R = V ÷ I or I = V ÷ R.

Resistance is a measure of how hard it is for charge to flow through a component. It depends on the material, its length, its cross-sectional area and its temperature: a longer wire has more resistance, a thicker one has less, and a filament lamp's resistance rises as it heats up.

  • Ohmic conductor at constant temperature: current is proportional to potential difference, so the graph of I against V is a straight line through the origin and the resistance is constant.
  • Filament lamp: the line curves, because as the current rises the filament gets hotter and its resistance increases.
  • Diode: negligible current flows in the reverse direction, and beyond a small threshold in the forward direction the current rises steeply.
  • Thermistor: resistance falls as temperature rises, which is why it is used as a temperature sensor.
  • Light-dependent resistor: resistance falls as the light intensity rises.

3.5.1 Electrical circuits: series and parallel

QuantitySeriesParallel
CurrentSame everywhereSplits between branches; the currents add to the total
Potential differenceShared between components; the values add to the supplyThe same across every branch
ResistanceTotal is the sum of the individual resistancesTotal is less than the smallest individual resistance
Effect of adding a componentIncreases the total resistance and reduces the currentProvides another path, so the total resistance falls and the current rises

The parallel rule surprises students because adding a resistor makes the total resistance smaller. It is not a contradiction: the extra branch gives charge a second route, so the same potential difference drives a larger total current, and a larger current for the same potential difference means a smaller resistance. Every lamp in a house is in parallel for the same reason — each one gets the full mains potential difference, and one can be switched off without breaking the others.

3.5.1 Electrical circuits: power and energy

Electrical power is the rate at which a component transfers energy, and energy is what the electricity bill charges for.

P = I V

Key: P = power (W); I = current (A); V = potential difference (V); 1 W = 1 J/s.

E = P t = I V t

Key: E = energy transferred (J); P = power (W); t = time (s); I = current (A); V = potential difference (V).

Combining P = I V with V = I R gives two more forms, P = I² R and P = V² ÷ R, and the useful one depends on what a question fixes. If the current is the same through two resistors, P = I² R shows the larger resistance dissipating more; if the potential difference is the same across them, P = V² ÷ R shows the smaller resistance dissipating more. Choosing the form is half the work.

3.5.2 Magnetism and electromagnetism

A permanent magnet has a north pole and a south pole, and like poles repel while unlike poles attract. A magnetic field is the region where a magnetic force can be felt; field lines run from north to south outside a magnet, and the closer they are the stronger the field. A plotting compass placed in the field lines up along the field line at that point.

An electromagnet is a coil of wire carrying a current, usually wound around an iron core. It has three advantages over a permanent magnet: it can be switched off, its strength can be varied by changing the current, and its polarity can be reversed by reversing the current.

  • The field of a straight wire is a set of concentric circles around the wire, becoming more widely spaced further away.
  • A solenoid produces a field like a bar magnet's, with the field inside the coil strong and uniform.
  • Adding an iron core concentrates the field and makes the electromagnet much stronger.
  • Increasing the current, the number of turns or moving the coil's turns closer together all strengthen the field.

When a current-carrying wire is placed in a magnetic field, it experiences a force, and this is the motor effect. The direction of the force is given by Fleming's left-hand rule: the first finger points along the field, the second finger along the current, and the thumb shows the force. The force is largest when the wire is at right angles to the field and zero when it lies along the field.

The force can be increased by increasing the current, by using a stronger magnetic field, or by having more turns of wire in the field. A simple motor uses this force on a coil, with a commutator reversing the current every half turn so that the coil keeps rotating in the same direction instead of stopping. In a loudspeaker the same effect moves a cone; in a microphone the reverse happens, because a moving coil in a magnetic field induces a current.

Worked example: a series circuit

Two resistors of 4.0 Ω and 6.0 Ω are connected in series to a 12 V battery. Calculate the total resistance, the current and the potential difference across each resistor.

Total resistance = 4.0 + 6.0 = 10 Ω. I = V ÷ R = 12 ÷ 10 = 1.2 A, the same through both. Across the 4.0 Ω resistor, V = I R = 1.2 × 4.0 = 4.8 V; across the 6.0 Ω resistor, V = 1.2 × 6.0 = 7.2 V. The two add to 12 V, which is the check that the work is right.

Key: R = resistance (Ω); V = potential difference (V); I = current (A); the sum of the two potential differences must equal the supply because energy is conserved.

Worked example: a parallel circuit

The same two resistors are now connected in parallel across the same 12 V battery. Calculate the current in each branch and the total current.

Each branch has the full 12 V, so I = 12 ÷ 4.0 = 3.0 A in one and 12 ÷ 6.0 = 2.0 A in the other. Total current = 3.0 + 2.0 = 5.0 A, which is the sum, not the difference.

Key: 12 V = the potential difference across each branch (V); 4.0 Ω and 6.0 Ω = the branch resistances (Ω); 3.0 A and 2.0 A = the branch currents (A); 5.0 A = the total current entering the junction (A).

The total resistance is then 12 ÷ 5.0 = 2.4 Ω, which is smaller than either branch, as the parallel rule requires. If an answer come out larger, the branch currents were added when they should have been used to find the total resistance, or the potential differences were shared.

Worked example: power and energy in a kettle

A kettle draws 10 A from a 230 V supply. Calculate its power, the energy it transfers in 3.0 minutes, and the cost at 30 p per kilowatt-hour.

P = I V = 10 × 230 = 2300 W, or 2.3 kW. t = 3.0 × 60 = 180 s, so E = P t = 2300 × 180 = 414,000 J. In kilowatt-hours that is 2.3 × 0.050 h = 0.115 kWh, costing 0.115 × 0.30 = 3.5 p.

Key: I = current (A); V = potential difference (V); P = power (W); t = time (s or h, depending on the unit of energy wanted); 0.050 h = 3.0 minutes expressed in hours; 0.30 = price in pounds per kilowatt-hour.

Working in joules first and converting afterwards is safer than mixing units, because the joule answer can be checked against the power rating: a 2.3 kW kettle running for three minutes must transfer a few hundred kilojoules, and 414,000 J is that.

Worked example: the motor effect

A wire carrying 2.0 A lies at right angles to a magnetic field. Explain what happens to the force if the current is doubled and the wire is turned to lie along the field.

Doubling the current doubles the force, because the force is proportional to the current. Turning the wire to lie along the field reduces the force to zero, because the force is greatest at right angles to the field and vanishes when the wire is parallel to it.

Key: 2.0 A = the current in the wire (A); right angles = the orientation giving the maximum force; parallel = the orientation giving no force; the direction of the force is found from Fleming's left-hand rule, not from the current alone.

Typical mistakes

  • Adding the currents in a series circuit. The current is the same everywhere in series; it is the potential differences that add.
  • Saying the total resistance in parallel is the sum. It is always less than the smallest branch resistance.
  • Connecting a voltmeter in series or an ammeter in parallel.
  • Treating the resistance of a filament lamp as constant. It rises as the filament heats.
  • Using P = I V when one of the quantities is unknown and needs two steps to find.
  • Forgetting that power in watts multiplied by time in seconds gives joules, not kilowatt-hours.
  • Thinking an electromagnet is stronger with fewer turns, or that reversing the current changes its strength rather than its polarity.
  • Describing the force on a wire in a magnetic field as always present, when it is zero if the wire lies along the field.

Exam-style questions

  1. State the difference between current and potential difference. Answer: Current is the rate of flow of charge, measured in amperes; potential difference is the energy transferred per unit charge between two points, measured in volts.
  2. A current of 0.40 A flows for 5.0 minutes. Calculate the charge that passes. Answer: Q = I t = 0.40 × 300 = 120 C.
  3. Explain why the total resistance of two resistors in parallel is less than either resistance. Answer: Each resistor provides a separate path for charge, so for the same potential difference more current flows in total. A larger total current for the same potential difference means a smaller total resistance.
  4. A 6.0 Ω resistor carries 2.0 A. Calculate the potential difference across it and the power dissipated. Answer: V = I R = 2.0 × 6.0 = 12 V; P = I V = 2.0 × 12 = 24 W.
  5. Describe how to make an electromagnet stronger. Answer: Increase the current, increase the number of turns on the coil, or add an iron core; winding the turns closer together also concentrates the field.
  6. State Fleming's left-hand rule and what it predicts. Answer: With the first finger along the field, the second finger along the current and the thumb at right angles to both, the thumb gives the direction of the force on the wire. It predicts the direction of the motor effect.
  7. Explain why a filament lamp's resistance increases as the current through it rises. Answer: The current heats the filament, and a higher temperature makes the ions in the metal vibrate more, so electrons collide with them more often and the resistance rises.
  8. An electric heater rated at 1500 W runs for 4.0 hours. Calculate the energy used in kilowatt-hours. Answer: 1.5 kW × 4.0 h = 6.0 kWh.

Revision checklist

  • I can define current, charge and potential difference with their units.
  • I can use Q = I t, V = I R and P = I V and rearrange each one.
  • I can describe the current, potential difference and resistance rules for series and parallel circuits.
  • I can sketch and interpret the current-potential difference graphs for a resistor, a filament lamp and a diode.
  • I can calculate energy transferred and convert between joules and kilowatt-hours.
  • I can describe a magnetic field and how to plot it with a compass.
  • I can explain how an electromagnet works and how to strengthen it.
  • I can apply Fleming's left-hand rule to the motor effect and explain how a motor keeps turning.

title: A Level Mathematics: The Poisson Distribution
content:
A Level Mathematics: The Poisson Distribution

The Poisson distribution models the number of events that happen in a fixed interval of time, length, area or volume when those events occur randomly and independently at a constant average rate. Where the binomial counts successes in a fixed number of trials, the Poisson counts arrivals in a continuous window: calls reaching a switchboard in an hour, defects along a length of cable, radioactive decays in a minute. This note derives the formula from the binomial, sets out the two conditions that must hold, and then uses the distribution for the probability and hypothesis-test questions the exam sets.

Where the formula comes from

Imagine slicing the interval into a very large number of tiny sub-intervals. In each slice the chance of an event is tiny but the number of slices is enormous, so the count is binomial with n huge and p tiny. Taking that limit turns nCr p^r (1−p)^(n−r) into the Poisson formula, with the mean λ = np surviving as the only parameter.

X ~ Po(λ):  P(X = r) = e^(-λ) λ^r / r!
mean E(X) = λ
variance Var(X) = λ
so the mean and variance are equal - a diagnostic test for the model

The equality of mean and variance is not a coincidence to memorise; it is the fingerprint of the limit, and it is why an exam question can give you a sample mean and variance and ask whether a Poisson model is plausible.

The three conditions

A Poisson model needs randomness, independence and a constant rate. Naming them is worth marks, and each failure has a characteristic symptom.

1. events occur singly (not in pairs or batches)
2. events occur at random, independently of each other
3. the average rate λ is constant over the interval
then the count in that interval is Poisson

Worked example (checking the model). A shop counts customers arriving per hour. Explain why a Poisson model may be unsuitable.

the arrival rate is not constant: it peaks at lunchtime and is near zero at night
so condition 3 fails and the mean over a whole day is not a single rate
a better model splits the day into periods of roughly constant rate

Calculating probabilities

The formula handles a single value; the cumulative sum handles a range. Because the Poisson has no upper limit, every "at least" question becomes a complement.

P(X = r) = e^(-λ) λ^r / r!
P(X <= r) sums from 0 to r (tables or calculator)
P(X >= r) = 1 - P(X <= r - 1)
P(X < r)  = P(X <= r - 1)

Worked example. X ~ Po(3). Find P(X = 2).

P = e^(-3) × 3² / 2!
= 0.049787 × 9 / 2
= 0.2240

Worked example 2 (at least). For the same X, find P(X ≥ 4).

P(X >= 4) = 1 - P(X <= 3)
P(X <= 3) = 0.049787(1 + 3 + 4.5 + 4.5) = 0.6472
so P(X >= 4) = 0.3528

Worked example 3 (scale change). Calls arrive at 4 per minute. Find the probability of 10 or more calls in two minutes.

the rate scales with the interval: λ = 8 for two minutes
P(X >= 10) = 1 - P(X <= 9) = 1 - 0.7170 = 0.2830

Scaling is the most common source of avoidable error: the parameter must be expressed for the interval the question actually asks about.

Adding independent Poisson variables

If two independent counts each follow a Poisson distribution, their sum does too, and the parameters add. This is why the distribution is so usable: a total across separate sources needs no convolution.

X ~ Po(l1), Y ~ Po(l2), independent
X + Y ~ Po(l1 + l2)
but X - Y is NOT Poisson

Worked example. A website gets 5 hits per minute from Europe and 3 per minute from Asia, independently. Find the probability of more than 10 hits in a minute in total.

total ~ Po(8)
P(X > 10) = 1 - P(X <= 10) = 1 - 0.8159 = 0.1841

The Poisson as an approximation to the binomial

When n is large and p is small, the binomial is well approximated by a Poisson with λ = np. The rule of thumb used in this course is n > 50 and p < 0.05, or np < 5.

X ~ B(n, p) with n large, p small  →  X is approximately Po(np)

Worked example. A factory produces items with a 2% defect rate. In a batch of 200, use a Poisson approximation to find the probability of at most 2 defects.

λ = 200 × 0.02 = 4
P(X <= 2) = e^(-4)(1 + 4 + 8) = 0.018316 × 13 = 0.2381
the exact binomial gives 0.2351, so the approximation is close

Worked example 2 (justifying the approximation). State why the approximation is reasonable here.

n = 200 is large and p = 0.02 is small, with np = 4
so the rare-event limit conditions hold

Hypothesis testing with the Poisson

The structure is identical to the binomial test: state hypotheses, assume the null rate, compute the tail probability, compare with the significance level. The only new step is that the rate may need scaling to the observed interval.

H0: λ = lambda0    H1: λ > lambda0 (or <)
observed count x in the interval
p-value = P(X >= x) or P(X <= x) under Po(lambda0)
reject H0 if the p-value <= the significance level

Worked example. A call centre historically receives 6 calls per hour. In a new hour it receives 12. Test at the 5% level whether the rate has increased.

H0: λ = 6;  H1: λ > 6
X ~ Po(6) under H0
P(X >= 12) = 1 - P(X <= 11) = 1 - 0.9799 = 0.0201
0.0201 < 0.05, so reject H0
there is evidence the rate has increased

Worked example 2 (critical region). For Po(6), find the 5% one-tailed critical region for an increase.

P(X >= 11) = 0.0426 (below 0.05)
P(X >= 10) = 0.0839 (above 0.05)
critical region: X >= 11

Worked example 3 (two intervals). The same centre observes 16 calls over two hours. Test for an increase at 5%.

expected over two hours under H0 = 12, so X ~ Po(12)
P(X >= 16) = 1 - P(X <= 15) = 1 - 0.8444 = 0.1556
0.1556 > 0.05, so do not reject H0

Compare the two: twelve calls in one hour was significant, sixteen in two hours is not, because the expected count doubled. The rate, not the raw count, is what is being tested.

Reading the distribution's shape

The Poisson is skewed to the right when λ is small and becomes almost symmetric as λ grows, which is why small-rate questions usually live in the lower tail and why the normal approximation becomes usable once λ passes about 20. Knowing the shape tells you at a glance whether an answer is plausible: a probability of 0.4 for "more than 10" when λ = 3 should feel wrong before any arithmetic is checked.

A useful sanity check is that the standard deviation is the square root of the mean. For Po(9) the mean is 9 and the standard deviation 3, so counts between 6 and 12 are ordinary and a count of 20 is roughly three and a half standard deviations out — surprising enough to prompt a hypothesis test. That comparison is what turns a bare probability into an interpretation, and interpretation marks are the easiest ones to lose.

Finally, note that the model is about a count in an interval, so the interval has to be defined in the answer. "Three calls per hour" and "three calls per minute" describe different distributions, and a rate quoted per unit time without its unit is not a λ at all.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Definition) State two conditions for a Poisson model. Answer: events occur singly at random, independently, at a constant rate.
  2. (Single value) X ~ Po(2.5): find P(X = 3). Answer: P(X = 3) = e^(−λ)λ³/3! = e^(−2.5) × 15.625/6 = 0.0821 × 2.604 = 0.2138.
  3. (Cumulative) X ~ Po(4): find P(X ≤ 2). Answer: P(X ≤ 2) = e^(−4)(1 + 4 + 8) = 0.0183 × 13 = 0.2381.
  4. (Complement) X ~ Po(5): find P(X ≥ 3). Answer: P(X ≥ 3) = 1 − P(X ≤ 2) = 1 − e^(−5)(1 + 5 + 12.5) = 1 − 0.1247 = 0.8753.
  5. (Scaling) Rate 3 per hour: find P(X = 0) in 20 minutes. Answer: the rate scales with the interval: λ = 3 × 20/60 = 1, so P(X = 0) = e^(−1) = 0.3679.
  6. (Sum) Independent Po(2) and Po(3): find P(total = 4). Answer: independent Poisson variables add, so T ~ Po(2 + 3) = Po(5) and P(T = 4) = e^(−5)5⁴/4! = 0.1755.
  7. (Approximation) B(500, 0.01): approximate P(X = 0). Answer: n is large and p small, so use Po(λ = np = 5): P(X = 0) ≈ e^(−5) = 0.00674.
  8. (Mean/variance) A sample has mean 4.2 and variance 9.1. Comment on the Poisson fit. Answer: variance far exceeds the mean, so the model is doubtful (over-dispersed).
  9. (Test) 9 events observed where 4 expected; test for an increase at 5%. Answer: under H₀, X ~ Po(4); P(X ≥ 9) = 1 − P(X ≤ 8) = 0.0214 < 0.05, so reject H₀ — the observed rate is significantly higher.
  10. (Critical region) Po(3), 5% upper tail: find the critical region. Answer: P(X ≥ 6) = 0.0839 and P(X ≥ 7) = 0.0335; the largest region still at or below 5% starts at 7, so the critical region is X ≥ 7.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Using the wrong interval: λ must match the window asked about; doubling a time doubles the rate.
  • Complement off by one: P(X ≥ 4) = 1 − P(X ≤ 3); subtracting P(X ≤ 4) is the classic error.
  • Treating a difference as Poisson: sums of independent Poisson variables are Poisson, differences are not.
  • Approximation outside its range: np must be small; with np large the Poisson is a poor fit to the binomial.
  • Variance assumed equal to the mean without checking: the test mean = variance is a diagnostic, not a guarantee.
  • Ignoring clustering: events that arrive in bursts break the single-event condition and inflate the variance.
  • r! miscomputed: 0! = 1 and 1! = 1, and a missing factorial term changes the answer entirely.
  • p-value direction: a one-tailed test uses one tail only; doubling it makes a borderline result look significant.

Choosing between a Poisson and a binomial model

Both models count things, and both are discrete, so the choice is a common source of lost marks. The question is always what is fixed: a number of trials, or a length of time, area or volume.

Fixed trials or a continuous window

A binomial model counts successes among a fixed number n of trials, such as 20 items inspected or 12 people surveyed. A Poisson model counts events in a continuous interval, such as calls in an hour or flaws along a metre of wire, where there is no fixed number of trials to count out.

Using the wording of the question

Phrases such as “out of 40” or “of 15 chosen at random” point to a binomial. Phrases such as “in a period of”, “per kilometre” or “per square metre” point to a Poisson. When the wording is unclear, ask whether you could list the trials in advance; if you could, the model is binomial.

Variance as a clue

The binomial variance is np(1 − p), which is smaller than its mean np by the factor 1 − p. The Poisson variance equals its mean. So when p is not small, a Poisson model overstates the spread, and the binomial is the better fit.

A worked choice: binomial

A quality checker tests 40 bolts from a line, and each bolt is faulty independently with probability 0.08. The number of bolts is fixed at 40, so X ~ B(40, 0.08). A Poisson with the same mean would have variance 3.2 instead of 2.944, which is close here, but the binomial is the model the question describes.

A worked choice: Poisson

Bacteria colonies appear on a plate at random, and the average number per square centimetre is known. The area of the plate is not a number of trials, so the count is a Poisson variable with λ proportional to the area of the region counted. Nothing about the plate fixes how many colonies there will be.

Stating the choice in the answer

Write the model as the first line of the solution, with its reason: “X ~ B(40, 0.08), because the sample size is fixed at 40”. A marker can only credit a choice that is written down, and the reason is often worth a mark on its own.

Equations and symbols

One formula does the arithmetic, and one identity checks the model: for a Poisson variable the mean and the variance are the same number λ. Every exam error on this topic is either a λ expressed for the wrong interval or a complement taken one term too far.

P(X = r) = e^(-λ) λ^r / r! Key: X = the number of events counted in the fixed interval (a count, no units); r = the particular count asked about; λ = the mean number of events in that same interval (no units — it is a count, not a rate per second, unless the interval is one second); e = 2.71828…; r! = factorial of r, with 0! = 1.

mean E(X) = λ Key: E(X) = the expected count in the interval; λ = the mean. Read it with the line below: the equality of mean and variance is the fingerprint of the model, and a sample whose variance far exceeds its mean is not Poisson.

variance Var(X) = λ Key: Var(X) = the variance of the count; λ = the same mean. So the standard deviation is √λ, which is the quickest sanity check on an observed count: for λ = 9, counts between 6 and 12 are ordinary.

P(X >= r) = 1 - P(X <= r - 1) Key: the complement rule, because the Poisson has no upper limit; r = the smallest count that counts as "at least". Subtracting P(X ≤ r) instead of P(X ≤ r − 1) is the classic off-by-one and throws the whole tail away.

P = e^(-3) × 3² / 2! Key: λ = 3 for this interval; r = 2; 3² = λ^r; 2! = 2. The arithmetic is 0.049787 × 9 / 2 = 0.2240 — quote four decimal places unless told otherwise.

λ = 200 × 0.02 = 4 Key: 200 = n, the number of trials; 0.02 = p, the probability of the event in one trial; λ = np = 4, the mean of the approximating Poisson. The approximation is used when n is large and p small — n > 50 and p < 0.05, or np < 5.

P(X <= 2) = e^(-4)(1 + 4 + 8) = 0.018316 × 13 = 0.2381 Key: the bracket is λ^r/r! summed for r = 0, 1, 2: 1, 4 and 8 (since 4²/2! = 8); e^(−4) = 0.018316. The exact binomial gives 0.2351, so the approximation is close — say so when a question asks you to comment.

X + Y ~ Po(l1 + l2) Key: X and Y = two independent Poisson counts; l1, l2 = their means; the total count is Poisson with the means added. A difference of two Poisson variables is not Poisson — only sums combine.

X ~ B(n, p) with n large, p small → X is approximately Po(np) Key: B(n, p) = the binomial with n trials and success probability p; np = the Poisson mean that replaces them. State both conditions before using it, because the approximation fails when np is large.

SymbolQuantityUnit
λmean number of events in the stated intervala count (no units) — quote the interval with it
rthe observed or asked-about counta count (no units)
H₀null hypothesis, λ = λ₀a stated mean count for the interval

Scaling is the other half of the topic and it is not a formula but a substitution: a rate of 4 per minute is λ = 8 for a two-minute window, and 12 calls in one hour must be tested against 24 expected in two hours, not against 12. Write the interval beside the λ every time.

title: IGCSE Biology: Excretion in Humans
content:
IGCSE Biology: Excretion in Humans

Metabolism is a messy business: breaking down amino acids leaves toxic ammonia, respiration leaves carbon dioxide, and dead cells leave wastes that would poison the blood if they accumulated. Excretion is the removal of these waste products of metabolism, and the kidney is the chemical processing plant that does most of it — filtering the entire blood volume about 40 times a day and adjusting exactly what is kept. This note defines excretion precisely (against egestion), follows the blood and urine pathways, works through the nephron's filtration-reabsorption-secretion logic, explains kidney failure and dialysis, and shows how the liver's deamination and the urea cycle fit together — with the urine-composition data answers examiners expect.

What excretion is (and what it is not)

Excretion is the removal from organisms of the waste products of metabolism (chemical reactions in cells) — carbon dioxide from respiration, water, and nitrogenous wastes such as urea from the liver. It is NOT egestion (the removal of undigested food as faeces — that material never entered the body's cells), and NOT sweating merely (sweat contains some excretory water and salts, but its main role is temperature regulation). The four mammalian excretory routes: lungs (carbon dioxide and water vapour, exhaled), kidneys (urea, excess water and salts, in urine), skin (water, salts, small urea, in sweat), and the liver processes the toxins first. Being able to classify a given substance's route is a common one-mark question.

The liver, deamination and the urea cycle

The liver receives amino acids from digestion via the hepatic portal vein. Amino acids cannot be stored, so surplus ones are deaminated: the amino group is removed in the liver (using oxygen in a process that also produces carbon dioxide and water), releasing ammonia — highly toxic — which is immediately converted (ornithine/urea cycle) into the much less toxic urea, which enters the blood for the kidneys to excrete. The deaminated remainder (a keto acid) is respired or converted to glycogen or fat for storage. Liver functions in full: deamination and urea production, storing glycogen (and releasing glucose to regulate blood sugar), detoxifying alcohol and drugs (enzymes break them down; chronic alcohol use damages liver cells and reduces detoxification), making bile for fat emulsification, and breaking down old red blood cells (the bile pigment bilirubin being an excretory product of haemoglobin).

The kidneys and the nephron

Each kidney contains about a million nephrons. Blood enters the kidney via the renal artery (high pressure, oxygenated), branches into afferent arterioles, and each feeds a glomerulus — a knot of capillaries inside Bowman's capsule. Filtration: the high pressure forces small molecules (water, glucose, amino acids, salts, urea) out of the blood into the Bowman's capsule, forming the glomerular filtrate; large molecules (proteins, blood cells) stay in the blood. Selective reabsorption: as the filtrate passes along the proximal convoluted tubule, all the glucose and amino acids, most of the water, and some salts are reabsorbed into the peritubular capillaries (glucose and amino acids by active transport, water by osmosis — the proximal tubule is lined with microvilli and packed with mitochondria to power it). Secretion: additional salts and hydrogen ions (and drugs such as penicillin) are secreted from the blood into the tubule. The loop of Henle concentrates the filtrate; the collecting duct adjusts final water reabsorption under the influence of antidiuretic hormone (ADH): more ADH → more water reabsorbed → small volumes of concentrated urine; less ADH → dilute urine. The final fluid is urine: water, urea, salts — normally no glucose.

Urine composition and what it reveals

Normal urine: water, urea, mineral salts, small amounts of other excretory products; no glucose (all reabsorbed at the proximal tubule), no protein (too large to filter). Glucose in urine (glycosuria) indicates diabetes mellitus — insulin deficiency means blood glucose exceeds the kidney's reabsorption capacity (the transport maximum), or renal damage. Protein in urine indicates kidney damage (glomerulitis/nephritis) allowing large molecules through. Dehydration: low water intake or heavy sweating → more water reabsorbed → small volume of dark, concentrated urine, and blood osmotic pressure rises detected by osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus triggering ADH release and thirst. Overhydration: pale, dilute, high-volume urine. Ketones in urine indicate fat breakdown during starvation or uncontrolled diabetes. Reading a urine-composition table against a scenario is a standard Paper 4 data-response question.

Urine composition: normal and diagnostic

SubstanceNormal urinePresence indicates
Water, urea, saltsPresentNormal excretion
GlucoseAbsentDiabetes mellitus or kidney damage
ProteinAbsentKidney damage (large molecules passing the filter)
BloodAbsentInfection, stones or glomerular damage
KetonesAbsentFat breakdown in starvation or uncontrolled diabetes

Kidney failure and dialysis

Kidney failure (from chronic high blood pressure, diabetes, infection or nephrotoxic drugs) means urea and excess salts and water build up in the blood (uraemia), which is fatal without treatment. Two treatments: dialysis (a haemodialysis machine) — the patient's blood is passed over a partially permeable dialysis membrane bathed in dialysis fluid that matches the desired blood composition: no urea, correct glucose and salt concentrations; so urea diffuses out of the blood down its concentration gradient, glucose does not diffuse in (already at the right concentration), and the balance of water and salts is adjusted by pressure and concentration gradients; sessions last several hours, several times a week. Or a kidney transplant — a donor kidney surgically joined to the patient's blood vessels and bladder; success depends on tissue-type matching (HLA antigens) to prevent rejection; immunosuppressant drugs are then needed. Compare in exams: dialysis is regular, time-consuming and diet-restricted but no surgery; transplant restores normal function but needs a matched donor and lifelong immunosuppression.

Worked example: following one molecule and one calculation

Trace a molecule of urea: protein in food → digested to amino acids → absorbed into the blood → deamination in the liver releases ammonia → converted to urea → carried in the blood to the kidney → filtered at the glomerulus into Bowman's capsule → not reabsorbed in the tubule → collects in the collecting duct → drains to the ureter → stored in the bladder → excreted in urine. Now the numbers: a dialysis machine processes 300 cm³ of blood per pass, and the patient has 5 dm³ (5000 cm³) of blood; each hour about 1.5 dm³ passes. If the blood urea concentration is 0.06 g/dm³ and the dialysis fluid contains 0 g/dm³, the concentration gradient drives urea out; after treatment the concentration falls to 0.01 g/dm³. Mass of urea removed per dm³ = 0.06 − 0.01 = 0.05 g; over a 4-hour session treating 12 dm³ of blood-pass volume, up to about 0.6 g is cleared per 12 dm³ processed (use the actual volumes in any question, and show mass = concentration × volume in every calculation).

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Calling faeces an excretory product: it is egested undigested food, never part of metabolism inside cells.
  • Writing that the kidney "makes urea": urea is made in the liver; the kidney only filters and excretes it.
  • Confusing the afferent and efferent arterioles: afferent brings blood to the glomerulus (wider bore, creating filtration pressure); efferent leaves it (narrower, maintaining pressure).
  • Saying glucose is "actively secreted" into the tubule: it is filtered then actively reabsorbed — direction matters.
  • Forgetting the protein-and-blood-cells size rule: too large to be filtered, which is why their presence in urine signals damage.
  • Explaining dialysis as "cleaning the blood with soap": specify the partially permeable membrane, the concentration gradients, and the composition of dialysis fluid (no urea, correct glucose).
  • Leaving ADH out of an osmoregulation/urine-concentration answer — it is usually a mark.
  • Confusing urea (nitrogenous waste, made in liver) with uric acid or ammonia (toxic intermediate, immediately converted).

Exam-style questions and answers

Q1. Define excretion and give two excretory products in mammals with the organ that removes each. (3 marks) Answer: removal of waste products of metabolism (1); carbon dioxide from the lungs (1); urea from the kidneys (1).

Q2. Describe the role of the liver in excretion. (3 marks) Answer: deamination of surplus amino acids removes the amino group (1); ammonia is toxic and is converted to urea (1); urea is released into the blood for the kidneys to filter out (1).

Q3. Describe what happens in the nephron during urine formation. (4 marks) Answer: ultrafiltration at the glomerulus under high pressure (1); small molecules pass into Bowman's capsule while proteins and cells remain (1); selective reabsorption of glucose, amino acids and most water in the proximal tubule (1); water reabsorption in the collecting duct regulated by ADH (1).

Q4. Explain why glucose may appear in the urine of a person with diabetes. (2 marks) Answer: insulin deficiency raises blood glucose above the kidney's reabsorption capacity (1); so not all glucose can be reabsorbed and the excess is excreted (1).

Q5. Compare dialysis with kidney transplantation as treatments for kidney failure. (4 marks) Answer: dialysis regularly filters blood externally without surgery but is time-consuming with diet restrictions (1); transplant restores continuous normal function (1); transplant requires tissue-type matching to prevent rejection (1); transplant recipients take immunosuppressant drugs for life (1).

title: A Level Mathematics: The Binomial Distribution
content:
A Level Mathematics: The Binomial Distribution

A binomial distribution counts successes in a fixed number of independent trials, each with the same probability of success. Coins, multiple-choice guesses, defective items in a sample and free throws all fit the same template, and once a problem is recognised as binomial the calculation is a formula plus a cumulative table. This note builds the distribution from its four conditions, derives the formula from counting, and then uses it for the two things exams actually ask: probabilities and hypothesis tests.

The four conditions

Before writing X ~ B(n, p) you must be able to name the conditions, because most exam questions include a part asking whether the model is appropriate. The conditions are not red tape: drop any one and the formula is simply wrong.

1. a fixed number of trials n
2. each trial has exactly two outcomes (success / failure)
3. the probability of success p is constant for every trial
4. the trials are independent
then X = number of successes has X ~ B(n, p)

Worked example (checking the model). A bag holds 5 red and 15 blue counters. Four counters are taken without replacement. Is the number of red counters binomial?

n = 4 is fixed and each draw is red or not red
but p changes: 5/20, then 5/19 if a red was taken, ...
the trials are not independent, so NOT binomial (it is hypergeometric)

Taking with replacement would fix it: p stays 0.25 on every draw.

The formula, and where it comes from

The probability of a particular sequence of r successes and n − r failures is p^r (1−p)^(n−r), because independence lets you multiply. The number of such sequences is the number of ways to choose which r trials succeed, which is nCr. Multiplying gives the formula.

P(X = r) = nCr p^r (1 - p)^(n - r)
the nCr counts arrangements; the powers give the probability of one arrangement

Worked example. X ~ B(10, 0.3). Find P(X = 3).

P = 10C3 (0.3)³ (0.7)⁷
= 120 × 0.027 × 0.08235
= 120 × 0.002223 = 0.2668

Worked example 2 (a single trial count). A fair die is rolled 8 times. Find the probability of exactly two sixes.

X ~ B(8, 1/6)
P(X = 2) = 8C2 (1/6)² (5/6)⁶ = 28 × 0.02778 × 0.3349 = 0.2605

Worked example 3 (why nCr appears). For n = 3 and r = 1, list the sequences and confirm the coefficient.

sequences: SFF, FSF, FFS - three of them
each has probability p(1-p)²
so P(X = 1) = 3p(1-p)², and 3C1 = 3

Cumulative probabilities

Questions almost always ask for a range, not a single value, and the cumulative distribution is what the calculator or the tables supply. The skill is rewriting the question into the form the table gives you.

P(X <= r) is tabulated directly
P(X >= r) = 1 - P(X <= r - 1)
P(X < r)  = P(X <= r - 1)
P(a <= X <= b) = P(X <= b) - P(X <= a - 1)
P(X = r) = P(X <= r) - P(X <= r - 1)

Worked example. X ~ B(20, 0.4). Find P(X ≥ 8).

P(X >= 8) = 1 - P(X <= 7)
= 1 - 0.4159
= 0.5841

Worked example 2 (between). For the same X, find P(5 ≤ X ≤ 10).

= P(X <= 10) - P(X <= 4)
= 0.8725 - 0.0510
= 0.8215

Worked example 3 (the strict inequality trap). For the same X, find P(X > 6).

P(X > 6) = 1 - P(X <= 6) = 1 - 0.2500 = 0.7500
note this is different from P(X >= 6) = 1 - P(X <= 5) = 0.8746

Mean and variance

The binomial has the simplest mean and variance in the syllabus, and they are worth knowing both forwards and backwards: a question can give the mean and variance and ask for n and p.

E(X) = np
Var(X) = np(1 - p)
standard deviation = √(np(1-p))

Worked example. X ~ B(50, 0.2). Find the mean and standard deviation.

mean = 50 × 0.2 = 10
variance = 10 × 0.8 = 8
sd = 2.828

Worked example 2 (backwards). A binomial variable has mean 12 and variance 9. Find n and p.

np = 12;  np(1-p) = 9
divide: 1 - p = 9/12 = 0.75  →  p = 0.25
then n = 12/0.25 = 48

Hypothesis testing with the binomial

A one-tailed test asks whether p has increased or decreased; the test statistic is the observed count, and the p-value is the probability of a result at least as extreme in the direction of the alternative.

H0: p = p0      H1: p > p0 (or p < p0)
X ~ B(n, p0) under H0
p-value = P(X >= observed) or P(X <= observed)
compare with the significance level; reject H0 if p-value <= alpha

Worked example. A coin is tossed 20 times and lands heads 15 times. Test at the 5% level whether the coin is biased towards heads.

H0: p = 0.5;  H1: p > 0.5
X ~ B(20, 0.5)
P(X >= 15) = 1 - P(X <= 14) = 1 - 0.9793 = 0.0207
0.0207 < 0.05, so reject H0
there is evidence at the 5% level that the coin favours heads

Worked example 2 (two-tailed). The same data tested two-tailed.

double the smaller tail: 2 × 0.0207 = 0.0414
0.0414 < 0.05, so still reject H0 at the 5% level

Worked example 3 (critical region). For X ~ B(20, 0.5), find the critical region for a 5% one-tailed test of p > 0.5.

P(X >= 14) = 0.0577 (above 0.05)
P(X >= 15) = 0.0207 (below 0.05)
critical region: X >= 15

Note that the critical region is chosen so the probability of a Type I error is at most 5%, which is why 14 is excluded even though it is close.

When the model breaks down

Examiners like the question that asks why a binomial model is only an approximation. The usual culprits are dependence, a varying probability, or a fixed sample drawn without replacement from a small population.

SituationProblemEffect
sampling without replacementtrials not independentp drifts; use the hypergeometric instead
clustered data (pupils in classes)responses correlatedvariance underestimated
probability varies between trialsp not constantformula invalid
large n, p near 0.5computation heavynormal approximation is reasonable

Worked example (normal approximation). X ~ B(200, 0.4). Use a normal approximation to estimate P(X ≤ 70).

mean = 80;  variance = 200 × 0.4 × 0.6 = 48;  sd = 6.928
continuity correction: X <= 70 becomes X < 70.5
z = (70.5 - 80)/6.928 = -1.371
P(Z < -1.371) = 0.0852

The continuity correction is compulsory: a discrete count needs a half-unit boundary before it can be treated as continuous.

Expected frequencies and the shape of the distribution

A binomial distribution is not symmetric unless p = 0.5, and that shape decides which tail an exam question is fishing in. The most likely value — the mode — is the integer near (n + 1)p, and expected frequency multiplies the probability by the number of samples taken. Both are quick marks that are frequently missed because students jump straight to the formula.

mode is near (n + 1)p, checked by comparing consecutive probabilities
expected number in a sample of size N = N x P(X = r)

Worked example. X ~ B(12, 0.3). Find the most likely value of X and the expected number of 3s in 500 independent observations.

(n + 1)p = 13 × 0.3 = 3.9, so check r = 3 and r = 4
P(X = 3) = 220 × 0.027 × 0.1176 = 0.2397
P(X = 4) = 495 × 0.0081 × 0.1681 = 0.2311
mode = 3
expected number of 3s = 500 × 0.2397 = 120 (to the nearest whole)

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Model) State the distribution for the number of sixes in 12 rolls of a fair die. Answer: X ~ B(n, p) with n = 12 rolls and p = 1/6 the chance of a six on each, so X ~ B(12, 1/6).
  2. (Single value) X ~ B(8, 0.25): find P(X = 2). Answer: P(X = 2) = ⁸C₂ (0.25)² (0.75)⁶ = 28 × 0.0625 × 0.1780 = 0.3115.
  3. (Cumulative) X ~ B(15, 0.3): find P(X ≤ 4). Answer: P(X ≤ 4) = Σₖ₌₀⁴ ¹⁵Cₖ (0.3)ᵏ (0.7)¹⁵⁻ᵏ = 0.5155 from cumulative binomial tables.
  4. (Complement) Same X: find P(X ≥ 3). Answer: P(X ≥ 3) = 1 − P(X ≤ 2) = 1 − 0.2969 = 0.7031 — the complement, because the tables give the lower tail only.
  5. (Mean) X ~ B(40, 0.35): find E(X) and Var(X). Answer: 14 and 9.1.
  6. (Backwards) Mean 18, variance 12: find n and p. Answer: mean np = 18 and variance np(1 − p) = 12; dividing, 1 − p = 12/18 = 2/3, so p = 1/3 and n = 18 ÷ (1/3) = 54.
  7. (Test) 12 of 20 seeds germinate; test p = 0.5 against p < 0.5 at 5%. Answer: H₀: p = 0.5 against H₁: p < 0.5; under H₀, X ~ B(20, 0.5) and P(X ≤ 12) = 0.8684, which is far above 0.05, so there is no evidence to reject H₀.
  8. (Critical region) X ~ B(10, 0.2): find the 5% critical region for p < 0.2. Answer: the smallest possible tail is P(X ≤ 0) = (0.8)¹⁰ = 0.1074, which already exceeds 0.05, so no critical region exists at the 5% level for this n.
  9. (Approximation) X ~ B(100, 0.5): approximate P(X ≥ 60). Answer: μ = np = 50 and σ = √(np(1 − p)) = √25 = 5; with the continuity correction z = (59.5 − 50)/5 = 1.9, so P(X ≥ 60) ≈ P(Z > 1.9) = 0.0287.
  10. (Assumption) Give one reason a binomial model may fail for defects in boxes of 20. Answer: defects may cluster, so trials are not independent.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Forgetting nCr: the coefficient counts arrangements; without it the answer is the probability of one specific sequence.
  • nCr on the wrong factor: it is p^r (1−p)^(n−r), with the success probability raised to the number of successes.
  • Inequality direction: P(X ≥ 8) uses 1 − P(X ≤ 7), not 1 − P(X ≤ 8).
  • Variance confused with standard deviation: np(1−p) is the variance; the test and the normal approximation need the square root.
  • Continuity correction omitted: any normal approximation to a discrete count needs the half-unit adjustment.
  • One-tailed evidence read as two: halving or doubling the tail without checking the alternative direction is a silent error.
  • Independence asserted, not checked: sampling without replacement from a small population breaks the model, and the question usually invites you to say so.
  • p-value compared with the wrong threshold: the significance level is given as a percentage; 5% means 0.05, not 5.

Equations and symbols

The distribution, its conditions and the four tail identities. Every question on this topic is one of these lines plus a calculator.

P(X = r) = nCr p^r (1 - p)^(n - r) Key: n = number of trials, fixed in advance; p = probability of success in one trial, constant; r = the number of successes asked for; nCr = n!/(r!(n − r)!), the number of orders the successes can occur in. The (1 − p) term is the failures, and its power must be n − r.

X ~ B(n, p) Key: X = the count of successes; the tilde means "is distributed as"; n and p as above. Write this line before calculating — it is often a mark on its own, and it fixes which parameters go into the calculator.

P = 10C3 (0.3)³ (0.7)⁷ Key: n = 10, p = 0.3, r = 3, so the failures are 7 and their probability is 0.7. The coefficient 10C3 = 120 accounts for the order of the three successes among the ten trials.

P(X >= r) = 1 - P(X <= r - 1) Key: a complement, so the two probabilities add to 1; the boundary moves by one because the binomial is discrete. Using 1 − P(X ≤ r) instead is the classic off-by-one error.

P(a <= X <= b) = P(X <= b) - P(X <= a - 1) Key: subtract the part below the interval; again the "− 1" is there because P(X ≤ a − 1) is everything before a. Check with a small case you can list by hand before trusting the calculator.

title: Stoichiometry
content:
Stoichiometry

Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry 0620, Extended route, topic 3 (statements 3.1–3.3). Formulae, equations, the mole, reacting masses, gas volumes, concentration and titration calculations — the highest-weight calculation topic on the paper.

3.1 to 3.2 Formulae and masses

  • An empirical formula is the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms; a molecular formula is the actual number of each atom. Mr of a substance is the sum of the Ar values in its formula.
  • Equations must be balanced and carry state symbols: (s), (l), (g), (aq). Conservation of mass means the number of atoms of each element is the same on both sides.

3.3 The mole

  • One mole of any substance contains 6.02 × 10²³ particles (the Avogadro constant). Moles = mass ÷ Mr. At room temperature and pressure, one mole of any gas occupies 24 dm³.
  • Concentration can be given in g/dm³ or mol/dm³. Moles in solution = concentration (mol/dm³) × volume (dm³), with cm³ ÷ 1000 = dm³.
  • Titration data gives moles of one reagent; the balanced equation gives the ratio; the other reagent's moles and concentration follow. Percentage yield = actual ÷ theoretical × 100.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Reacting masses, applied to 12 g of magnesium burning in oxygen: moles of Mg = 12 ÷ 24 = 0.5 mol. From 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO, 0.5 mol Mg gives 0.5 mol MgO, so mass = 0.5 × 40 = 20 g. Oxygen used = 20 − 12 = 8 g. Always convert to moles first, then use the ratio.
  • Gas volume, applied to 5.6 g of calcium carbonate decomposing: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. Moles of CaCO₃ = 5.6 ÷ 100 = 0.056 mol, so 0.056 mol CO₂ forms. Volume = 0.056 × 24 = 1.34 dm³ (1340 cm³, to 3 significant figures).
  • Titration chain, applied to 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ NaOH needing 22.0 cm³ of HCl: NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O, ratio 1:1. Moles NaOH = 0.100 × 0.0250 = 2.50 × 10⁻³, so moles HCl = 2.50 × 10⁻³, and concentration HCl = 2.50 × 10⁻³ ÷ 0.0220 = 0.114 mol/dm³. Convert cm³ to dm³ before multiplying — that is where most marks are lost.
  • Empirical formula, applied to a compound with 40.0% carbon, 6.7% hydrogen and 53.3% oxygen by mass: divide by Ar to get 3.33 mol C, 6.67 mol H, 3.33 mol O; divide by the smallest (3.33) to get CH₂O. To find the molecular formula, divide Mr by the empirical formula mass: 180 ÷ 30 = 6, so C₆H₁₂O₆.

Common errors

  • Using cm³ directly with mol/dm³ without dividing by 1000.
  • Using 22.4 dm³ (that is at standard temperature and pressure, not room temperature and pressure). IGCSE 0620 uses 24 dm³ at r.t.p.
  • Writing an ionic formula that is not the simplest ratio, or leaving a 1:1 ratio as Mg₂O₂.

title: Exponentials and Logarithms — Study Notes
content:
Exponentials and logarithms

Edexcel International A Level Mathematics — Pure Mathematics 2 (WMA12), sat at AS.

The exponential function e^x and the natural logarithm ln x are inverse functions. They model growth and decay (populations, radioactive decay, cooling) and appear in almost every AS/A2 paper.

The functions

  • e is Euler's number, e = 2.71828... to 4 s.f.
  • y = e^x is always positive, passes through (0, 1), and grows rapidly for large x.
  • y = ln x is defined for x > 0, passes through (1, 0), and is the inverse of e^x: ln(e^x) = x and e^(ln x) = x.
  • The graph of ln x is the reflection of e^x in the line y = x.

Logarithm laws

  • ln(ab) = ln a + ln b
  • ln(a/b) = ln a - ln b
  • ln(a^n) = n ln a
  • The same laws hold for logs to any base; log base a of x = ln x / ln a.

Solving equations

  • To solve e^(kx + c) = d: take ln of both sides, kx + c = ln d, then rearrange.
  • To solve ln(ax + b) = c: exponentiate, ax + b = e^c.
  • To solve a^x = b where a is not e: take logs, x = ln b / ln a.

Modelling

  • Growth/decay: N = N0 e^(kt), k > 0 for growth, k < 0 for decay.
  • Half-life: the time for a quantity to halve, found from ln(0.5) = k t_half.
  • Compound interest and continuously compounded growth use the same form.

Key results

  • The derivative of e^x is e^x; the derivative of ln x is 1/x (know these for later calculus).
  • e^0 = 1, ln 1 = 0, ln e = 1.
  • The curve y = e^x has gradient 1 at x = 0.

title: A Level Mathematics: The Binomial Distribution
content:
A Level Mathematics: The Binomial Distribution

A binomial distribution counts successes in a fixed number of independent trials, each with the same probability of success. Coins, multiple-choice guesses, defective items in a sample and free throws all fit the same template, and once a problem is recognised as binomial the calculation is a formula plus a cumulative table. This note builds the distribution from its four conditions, derives the formula from counting, and then uses it for the two things exams actually ask: probabilities and hypothesis tests.

The four conditions

Before writing X ~ B(n, p) you must be able to name the conditions, because most exam questions include a part asking whether the model is appropriate. The conditions are not red tape: drop any one and the formula is simply wrong.

1. a fixed number of trials n
2. each trial has exactly two outcomes (success / failure)
3. the probability of success p is constant for every trial
4. the trials are independent
then X = number of successes has X ~ B(n, p)

Worked example (checking the model). A bag holds 5 red and 15 blue counters. Four counters are taken without replacement. Is the number of red counters binomial?

n = 4 is fixed and each draw is red or not red
but p changes: 5/20, then 5/19 if a red was taken, ...
the trials are not independent, so NOT binomial (it is hypergeometric)

Taking with replacement would fix it: p stays 0.25 on every draw.

The formula, and where it comes from

The probability of a particular sequence of r successes and n − r failures is p^r (1−p)^(n−r), because independence lets you multiply. The number of such sequences is the number of ways to choose which r trials succeed, which is nCr. Multiplying gives the formula.

P(X = r) = nCr p^r (1 - p)^(n - r)
the nCr counts arrangements; the powers give the probability of one arrangement

Worked example. X ~ B(10, 0.3). Find P(X = 3).

P = 10C3 (0.3)³ (0.7)⁷
= 120 × 0.027 × 0.08235
= 120 × 0.002223 = 0.2668

Worked example 2 (a single trial count). A fair die is rolled 8 times. Find the probability of exactly two sixes.

X ~ B(8, 1/6)
P(X = 2) = 8C2 (1/6)² (5/6)⁶ = 28 × 0.02778 × 0.3349 = 0.2605

Worked example 3 (why nCr appears). For n = 3 and r = 1, list the sequences and confirm the coefficient.

sequences: SFF, FSF, FFS - three of them
each has probability p(1-p)²
so P(X = 1) = 3p(1-p)², and 3C1 = 3

Cumulative probabilities

Questions almost always ask for a range, not a single value, and the cumulative distribution is what the calculator or the tables supply. The skill is rewriting the question into the form the table gives you.

P(X <= r) is tabulated directly
P(X >= r) = 1 - P(X <= r - 1)
P(X < r)  = P(X <= r - 1)
P(a <= X <= b) = P(X <= b) - P(X <= a - 1)
P(X = r) = P(X <= r) - P(X <= r - 1)

Worked example. X ~ B(20, 0.4). Find P(X ≥ 8).

P(X >= 8) = 1 - P(X <= 7)
= 1 - 0.4159
= 0.5841

Worked example 2 (between). For the same X, find P(5 ≤ X ≤ 10).

= P(X <= 10) - P(X <= 4)
= 0.8725 - 0.0510
= 0.8215

Worked example 3 (the strict inequality trap). For the same X, find P(X > 6).

P(X > 6) = 1 - P(X <= 6) = 1 - 0.2500 = 0.7500
note this is different from P(X >= 6) = 1 - P(X <= 5) = 0.8746

Mean and variance

The binomial has the simplest mean and variance in the syllabus, and they are worth knowing both forwards and backwards: a question can give the mean and variance and ask for n and p.

E(X) = np
Var(X) = np(1 - p)
standard deviation = √(np(1-p))

Worked example. X ~ B(50, 0.2). Find the mean and standard deviation.

mean = 50 × 0.2 = 10
variance = 10 × 0.8 = 8
sd = 2.828

Worked example 2 (backwards). A binomial variable has mean 12 and variance 9. Find n and p.

np = 12;  np(1-p) = 9
divide: 1 - p = 9/12 = 0.75  →  p = 0.25
then n = 12/0.25 = 48

Hypothesis testing with the binomial

A one-tailed test asks whether p has increased or decreased; the test statistic is the observed count, and the p-value is the probability of a result at least as extreme in the direction of the alternative.

H0: p = p0      H1: p > p0 (or p < p0)
X ~ B(n, p0) under H0
p-value = P(X >= observed) or P(X <= observed)
compare with the significance level; reject H0 if p-value <= alpha

Worked example. A coin is tossed 20 times and lands heads 15 times. Test at the 5% level whether the coin is biased towards heads.

H0: p = 0.5;  H1: p > 0.5
X ~ B(20, 0.5)
P(X >= 15) = 1 - P(X <= 14) = 1 - 0.9793 = 0.0207
0.0207 < 0.05, so reject H0
there is evidence at the 5% level that the coin favours heads

Worked example 2 (two-tailed). The same data tested two-tailed.

double the smaller tail: 2 × 0.0207 = 0.0414
0.0414 < 0.05, so still reject H0 at the 5% level

Worked example 3 (critical region). For X ~ B(20, 0.5), find the critical region for a 5% one-tailed test of p > 0.5.

P(X >= 14) = 0.0577 (above 0.05)
P(X >= 15) = 0.0207 (below 0.05)
critical region: X >= 15

Note that the critical region is chosen so the probability of a Type I error is at most 5%, which is why 14 is excluded even though it is close.

When the model breaks down

Examiners like the question that asks why a binomial model is only an approximation. The usual culprits are dependence, a varying probability, or a fixed sample drawn without replacement from a small population.

SituationProblemEffect
sampling without replacementtrials not independentp drifts; use the hypergeometric instead
clustered data (pupils in classes)responses correlatedvariance underestimated
probability varies between trialsp not constantformula invalid
large n, p near 0.5computation heavynormal approximation is reasonable

Worked example (normal approximation). X ~ B(200, 0.4). Use a normal approximation to estimate P(X ≤ 70).

mean = 80;  variance = 200 × 0.4 × 0.6 = 48;  sd = 6.928
continuity correction: X <= 70 becomes X < 70.5
z = (70.5 - 80)/6.928 = -1.371
P(Z < -1.371) = 0.0852

The continuity correction is compulsory: a discrete count needs a half-unit boundary before it can be treated as continuous.

Expected frequencies and the shape of the distribution

A binomial distribution is not symmetric unless p = 0.5, and that shape decides which tail an exam question is fishing in. The most likely value — the mode — is the integer near (n + 1)p, and expected frequency multiplies the probability by the number of samples taken. Both are quick marks that are frequently missed because students jump straight to the formula.

mode is near (n + 1)p, checked by comparing consecutive probabilities
expected number in a sample of size N = N x P(X = r)

Worked example. X ~ B(12, 0.3). Find the most likely value of X and the expected number of 3s in 500 independent observations.

(n + 1)p = 13 × 0.3 = 3.9, so check r = 3 and r = 4
P(X = 3) = 220 × 0.027 × 0.1176 = 0.2397
P(X = 4) = 495 × 0.0081 × 0.1681 = 0.2311
mode = 3
expected number of 3s = 500 × 0.2397 = 120 (to the nearest whole)

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Model) State the distribution for the number of sixes in 12 rolls of a fair die. Answer: X ~ B(n, p) with n = 12 rolls and p = 1/6 the chance of a six on each, so X ~ B(12, 1/6).
  2. (Single value) X ~ B(8, 0.25): find P(X = 2). Answer: P(X = 2) = ⁸C₂ (0.25)² (0.75)⁶ = 28 × 0.0625 × 0.1780 = 0.3115.
  3. (Cumulative) X ~ B(15, 0.3): find P(X ≤ 4). Answer: P(X ≤ 4) = Σₖ₌₀⁴ ¹⁵Cₖ (0.3)ᵏ (0.7)¹⁵⁻ᵏ = 0.5155 from cumulative binomial tables.
  4. (Complement) Same X: find P(X ≥ 3). Answer: P(X ≥ 3) = 1 − P(X ≤ 2) = 1 − 0.2969 = 0.7031 — the complement, because the tables give the lower tail only.
  5. (Mean) X ~ B(40, 0.35): find E(X) and Var(X). Answer: 14 and 9.1.
  6. (Backwards) Mean 18, variance 12: find n and p. Answer: mean np = 18 and variance np(1 − p) = 12; dividing, 1 − p = 12/18 = 2/3, so p = 1/3 and n = 18 ÷ (1/3) = 54.
  7. (Test) 12 of 20 seeds germinate; test p = 0.5 against p < 0.5 at 5%. Answer: H₀: p = 0.5 against H₁: p < 0.5; under H₀, X ~ B(20, 0.5) and P(X ≤ 12) = 0.8684, which is far above 0.05, so there is no evidence to reject H₀.
  8. (Critical region) X ~ B(10, 0.2): find the 5% critical region for p < 0.2. Answer: the smallest possible tail is P(X ≤ 0) = (0.8)¹⁰ = 0.1074, which already exceeds 0.05, so no critical region exists at the 5% level for this n.
  9. (Approximation) X ~ B(100, 0.5): approximate P(X ≥ 60). Answer: μ = np = 50 and σ = √(np(1 − p)) = √25 = 5; with the continuity correction z = (59.5 − 50)/5 = 1.9, so P(X ≥ 60) ≈ P(Z > 1.9) = 0.0287.
  10. (Assumption) Give one reason a binomial model may fail for defects in boxes of 20. Answer: defects may cluster, so trials are not independent.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Forgetting nCr: the coefficient counts arrangements; without it the answer is the probability of one specific sequence.
  • nCr on the wrong factor: it is p^r (1−p)^(n−r), with the success probability raised to the number of successes.
  • Inequality direction: P(X ≥ 8) uses 1 − P(X ≤ 7), not 1 − P(X ≤ 8).
  • Variance confused with standard deviation: np(1−p) is the variance; the test and the normal approximation need the square root.
  • Continuity correction omitted: any normal approximation to a discrete count needs the half-unit adjustment.
  • One-tailed evidence read as two: halving or doubling the tail without checking the alternative direction is a silent error.
  • Independence asserted, not checked: sampling without replacement from a small population breaks the model, and the question usually invites you to say so.
  • p-value compared with the wrong threshold: the significance level is given as a percentage; 5% means 0.05, not 5.

Recognising a binomial situation in context

Most binomial marks are lost before any arithmetic starts, because the question was not identified as binomial. The subsections below give a checklist for reading a question and writing the model in the standard form X ~ B(n, p) before you calculate anything.

Writing the model in the form X ~ B(n, p)

Once you decide a situation is binomial, state the model in full: X ~ B(n, p), where X is the number of successes, n is the number of trials and p is the probability of a success on each trial. Define X in words in your answer, for example “X is the number of defective bulbs in a box of 20”. A model with no definition of X loses the communication mark even when the probabilities are right.

Identifying the number of trials, n

The value of n is the fixed number of times the experiment is repeated: the number of bulbs tested, the number of patients treated, or the number of games played. Read the question for the phrase that fixes it, such as “of 20 bulbs chosen at random”. If the question keeps going until a result occurs, the number of trials is not fixed and the binomial model does not apply directly.

Identifying the probability of success, p

The value of p is the probability of the outcome you have chosen to call a success on one trial. It must stay the same for every trial. A fair coin gives p = 0.5, and a bag where 15% of items are faulty gives p = 0.15 for each item drawn with replacement. If the question gives a percentage, convert it to a decimal before you use it in any formula.

Checking for fixed trials

The number of trials must be decided before the experiment starts. Counting the number of successes in a fixed sample is binomial, whereas recording how many trials it takes to get the first success is not. A question about the number of heads in ten tosses is binomial; a question about how many tosses are needed for the first head is a different model. Make the fixed-n check before any other check.

Checking for independent trials

Each trial must not affect the next. Independence is what allows you to multiply the probabilities of several outcomes together, and it is the assumption most often ignored. Drawing items with replacement keeps p constant, and that is what the model needs. Drawing without replacement changes p after each draw, so the binomial model is only an approximation when the sample is small compared with the population.

Worked identification

A survey finds that 30% of adults own a bicycle. Twelve adults are chosen at random from a large town and asked whether they own one. Let X be the number who own a bicycle. Here n = 12, p = 0.3 and the answer is X ~ B(12, 0.3). The population is large, so the probability for each adult stays close to 0.3 and the model is a reasonable one to use. State that assumption, because a marker looks for it.

Probabilities of at least one, and of more than r

Questions that ask for “at least” or “more than” are the ones where the complement saves the most time. The subsections set out the choice between a direct sum and the complement, and the checks that stop an off-by-one error.

Probability of at least one success

“At least one” is the complement of “none”, so P(X ≥ 1) = 1 − P(X = 0) = 1 − qⁿ, where q = 1 − p. For X ~ B(5, 0.2), P(X ≥ 1) = 1 − 0.8⁵ = 1 − 0.32768 = 0.672 to 3 significant figures. Adding the probabilities of X = 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 gives the same answer but takes five calculations instead of one.

Probability of more than r successes

“More than 3” means 4 or more, so P(X > 3) = 1 − P(X ≤ 3). For X ~ B(10, 0.3), P(X ≤ 3) = 0.6496 to 4 decimal places, so P(X > 3) = 0.3504. The number 3 is included in the part you subtract from 1; forgetting that is the typical error on “more than” questions.

Choosing between a direct sum and the complement

Use the complement when the part you do not want is short: “at least one”, “at most one but not zero” and similar phrases. Use a direct sum when the wanted region has only a few terms, such as P(X = 2) + P(X = 3). With a calculator table of cumulative probabilities, most “at most” and “at least” questions reduce to one lookup and one subtraction.

Probability of exactly r on a calculator

For X ~ B(n, p), P(X = r) = ⁿCᵣ pʳ qⁿ⁻ʳ. The combination ⁿCᵣ counts the ways the r successes can be arranged among n trials. For X ~ B(10, 0.3), P(X = 3) = 120 × 0.3³ × 0.7⁷ = 120 × 0.027 × 0.0823543 = 0.2668 to 4 decimal places. Enter the combination with the nCr key so the arrangement count is not mistyped.

The most likely number of successes (the mode)

The most likely value of X is the mode. For a binomial distribution it is the whole number part of (n + 1)p, and if (n + 1)p is itself a whole number there are two modes, (n + 1)p − 1 and (n + 1)p. For X ~ B(10, 0.3), (n + 1)p = 3.3, so the mode is 3. Check against the probabilities: P(X = 3) = 0.2668 is larger than P(X = 2) = 0.2335 and P(X = 4) = 0.2001.

Checking that the probabilities add to 1

A complete check is that P(X = 0) + P(X = 1) + … + P(X = n) = 1. You rarely add every term in an exam, but the check is useful when you build a table of probabilities for a whole distribution. If a column does not total 1 to the rounding used, one of the terms was calculated with the wrong value of q or the wrong combination count.

Equations and symbols

The distribution, its conditions and the four tail identities. Every question on this topic is one of these lines plus a calculator.

P(X = r) = nCr p^r (1 - p)^(n - r) Key: n = number of trials, fixed in advance; p = probability of success in one trial, constant; r = the number of successes asked for; nCr = n!/(r!(n − r)!), the number of orders the successes can occur in. The (1 − p) term is the failures, and its power must be n − r.

X ~ B(n, p) Key: X = the count of successes; the tilde means "is distributed as"; n and p as above. Write this line before calculating — it is often a mark on its own, and it fixes which parameters go into the calculator.

P = 10C3 (0.3)³ (0.7)⁷ Key: n = 10, p = 0.3, r = 3, so the failures are 7 and their probability is 0.7. The coefficient 10C3 = 120 accounts for the order of the three successes among the ten trials.

P(X >= r) = 1 - P(X <= r - 1) Key: a complement, so the two probabilities add to 1; the boundary moves by one because the binomial is discrete. Using 1 − P(X ≤ r) instead is the classic off-by-one error.

P(a <= X <= b) = P(X <= b) - P(X <= a - 1) Key: subtract the part below the interval; again the "− 1" is there because P(X ≤ a − 1) is everything before a. Check with a small case you can list by hand before trusting the calculator.

title: Abstract Data Types — Study Notes
content:
Abstract Data Types

What is an ADT?

An abstract data type is a logical description of a collection of data plus the operations on it, independent of implementation. Stacks, queues, linked lists, binary trees and hash tables are all ADTs; in A Level you must show how they are built from arrays or records with pointers.

Linked Lists

Each node holds a value and a pointer to the next node; a start pointer marks the head and a null marks the end. Insertion rewires two pointers — no shifting — giving O(1) insertion at a known position, but access requires walking the list, O(n).

Stacks and Queues

A stack is LIFO (push and pop at the top); a queue is FIFO (enqueue at the rear, dequeue from the front). Both can be arrays with index pointers or linked lists. Stack uses include call stacks and expression evaluation; queue uses include print buffers and breadth-first search.

Binary Search Trees

Each node has up to two children; left subtree keys are smaller, right subtree keys larger. Search, insert and (average-case) delete are O(log n). An in-order traversal outputs keys in ascending order. A degenerate (linear) tree from sorted input degrades to O(n).

Hash Tables

Covered in file organisation, but as an ADT a hash table pairs a hash function with bucket storage for O(1) average access.

Exam tips: be able to draw a tree after a sequence of insertions and write its three traversals; state the pointer changes for a linked-list insertion; compare ADT operations with Big-O.
