title: A Level Physics: Thermal Physics
content:
A Level Physics: Thermal Physics

Thermal physics is the accountancy of heat: what temperature really measures, how much energy it takes to change a substance's state, and how the invisible motion of billions of particles produces the pressure in a balloon. This note builds the whole subject from zero: thermal equilibrium and the temperature scales, specific heat capacity and specific latent heat with full calorimetry arithmetic, the mole and the equation of state, the kinetic theory that justifies it, and the first law of thermodynamics — the energy bookkeeping rule that governs engines, fridges and stars alike.

Thermal equilibrium

Heat flows from hotter to cooler bodies until no further net transfer occurs — that final state is thermal equilibrium, when both bodies are at the same temperature. The zeroth law of thermodynamics makes the logic precise: if A is in thermal equilibrium with B, and B with C, then A is in equilibrium with C — which is exactly why thermometers work (they reach equilibrium with the thing measured, and the reading transfers). The distinction examiners demand: temperature measures the average random kinetic energy per particle; heat is energy in transit because of a temperature difference. Objects do not contain heat — they contain internal energy.

Temperature scales

The Celsius scale is defined by two fixed points: the melting point of pure ice (0 °C) and the boiling point of pure water (100 °C) at standard pressure. The thermodynamic (Kelvin) scale starts at absolute zero — the temperature at which particles have minimum kinetic energy, −273.15 °C — and its unit, the kelvin, is the same size as the degree Celsius:

T (K) = θ (°C) + 273        (273.15 exact; 273 usual in exams)
temperature change: ΔT in K = Δθ in °C

Every gas-law and kinetic-theory calculation demands kelvin; forgetting the conversion is the single commonest thermal error. A temperature change of 10 °C is a change of 10 K — only absolute values need converting.

Specific heat capacity

Heating a body raises its temperature; the energy needed depends on the substance's own reluctance to change temperature:

E = m c Δθ        (or E = C Δθ for a whole body)

E in J, m in kg, c in J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ (specific heat capacity)
Δθ in °C or K (the same size)
C = m c = heat capacity of the object (J K⁻¹)

The electrical method of measuring c is examinable as a practical: a heater of known power runs for a known time (E = Pt), the temperature rise is recorded, and losses are reduced with insulation and a lid; the graph of temperature against time is extrapolated back to the start to correct for losses during heating.

Worked example 1. A 2.0 kg aluminium block (c = 900 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) is heated from 20 °C to 80 °C by a 500 W heater. Find the energy needed and the minimum heating time.

E = m c Δθ = 2.0 × 900 × 60 = 10⁸ 000 J = 10⁸ kJ
t = E/P = 10⁸ 000/500 = 216 s = 3.6 minutes

Worked example 2 (mixing). 0.50 kg of water at 90 °C is mixed with 0.50 kg of water at 10 °C. Find the final temperature (no losses).

heat lost = heat gained
m c (90 - T) = m c (T - 10)   (same m and c cancel)
90 - T = T - 10 → 10⁰ = 2T → T = 50 °C

The mixing equation is worth learning as a shape: Σ(heat lost) = Σ(heat gained), with each term mcΔθ evaluated from its own temperature difference to the final T.

Specific latent heat

During a change of state, energy goes into breaking intermolecular bonds rather than raising temperature — the heating curve flatlines at the melting or boiling point. The energy for the change:

E = m L        L = specific latent heat (J kg⁻¹)

L_fusion for melting/freezing; L_vaporisation for boiling/condensing

Worked example. A 3.0 kW kettle boils 1.5 kg of water already at 100 °C. How long to boil it dry (L_vap = 2.26 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹)?

E = m L = 1.5 × 2.26 × 10⁶ = 3.39 × 10⁶ J
t = E/P = 3.39 × 10⁶/3000 = 1130 s = 18.8 minutes

Reading a heating curve is a standard question: sloped sections are temperature rise (mcΔθ applies), flat sections are change of state (mL applies), and the flat at 0 °C is melting while the flat at 100 °C is boiling.

The mole

The mole counts particles the way a dozen counts eggs: one mole contains exactly Nₐ = 6.02 × 10²³ particles (Avogadro's constant). The molar mass M is the mass of one mole (numerically the relative atomic mass in grams; in kg mol⁻¹ for calculations).

n = m / M        N = n N_A

n in mol, m in kg (or g consistently with M), M in kg mol⁻¹

Worked example. Find the number of molecules in 8.0 g of oxygen (O₂, M = 0.032 kg mol⁻¹).

n = m/M = 0.008/0.032 = 0.25 mol
N = n N_A = 0.25 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 1.505 × 10²³ molecules
  = 1.5 × 10²³ (2 s.f.)

The equation of state

For a fixed mass of an ideal gas, pressure, volume and temperature obey one master equation:

p V = n R T        (also p V = N k T)

p in pascals (Pa), V in m³, T in kelvin (K)
R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹  (molar gas constant)
k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹ (Boltzmann constant), N = number of molecules

Unit discipline: 1 atm = 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa; 1 cm³ = 10⁻⁶ m³; 1 litre = 10⁻³ m³. The ideal-gas assumptions are examinable: molecules are point particles with negligible volume, intermolecular forces are negligible except during collisions, and collisions are perfectly elastic.

Worked example. 0.40 mol of gas occupies 2.0 × 10⁻³ m³ at 27 °C. Find the pressure.

T = 27 + 273 = 300 K
p = nRT/V = (0.40 × 8.31 × 300)/(2.0 × 10⁻³)
  = 997.2/2.0 × 10⁻³ = 4.99 × 10⁵ Pa = 5.0 × 10⁵ Pa (2 s.f.)

Boyle's, Charles's and the pressure law are all slices of this one equation — if a question gives a change at constant moles, either hold one variable fixed to get the simple law, or write p₁V₁/T₁ = p₂V₂/T₂ for the general case.

Kinetic theory

The kinetic model explains pressure: gas molecules collide elastically with container walls, and each collision transfers momentum; billions per second give a steady average force per unit area — pressure. The model's assumptions (large number of molecules, random motion, elastic collisions, negligible molecular volume, forces only during collisions) justify the ideal-gas behaviour, and the theory links the microscopic to the macroscopic:

p V = (1/3) N m c²        c = root-mean-square speed

mean kinetic energy per molecule = (3/2) k T
so (1/2) m c² = (3/2) k T  →  c = √(3 k T / m)

The rms speed rises with the square root of absolute temperature and falls with molecular mass — hydrogen molecules move faster than oxygen molecules at the same temperature.

Worked example. Find the rms speed of helium atoms (m = 6.6 × 10⁻²⁷ kg) at 300 K.

c = √(3 k T/m) = √(3 × 1.38 × 10⁻²³ × 300/6.6 × 10⁻²⁷)
  = √(1.242 × 10⁻²⁰/6.6 × 10⁻²⁷) = √(1.88 × 10⁶)
  = 1372 m s⁻¹  (2 s.f.: 1.4 × 10³ m s⁻¹)

Internal energy

The internal energy of a substance is the sum of the random kinetic energies of its particles plus the potential energies of their interactions. For an ideal gas (no intermolecular forces) internal energy is purely kinetic and proportional to absolute temperature; for real substances, melting and boiling raise internal energy because potential energy increases as bonds stretch and break. State the split precisely in definitions: internal energy = total random kinetic energy + total intermolecular potential energy.

The first law of thermodynamics

Energy is conserved: the change in a system's internal energy equals the heat added to it plus the work done on it.

ΔU = Q + W

ΔU = change in internal energy (J)
Q = heat energy transferred to the system (J), negative if lost
W = work done ON the system (J), negative if the system does work
    (for a gas: W = -p ΔV under the convention W = work done
     on the system; expanding gas does work, so W is negative)

The sign convention must match your course's — state it in words when you apply the law. Applications the papers love: compressing a gas quickly (W positive, little Q, so ΔU and temperature rise); a gas expanding slowly at constant temperature (ΔU = 0 for an ideal gas, so Q = −W — heat flows in to supply the work done); and refrigerators (work is done to move heat against its natural flow).

Worked example. A gas is compressed so that 500 J of work is done on it while 200 J of heat flows out. Find ΔU and state the temperature change.

W = +500 J (done on the system), Q = -200 J (lost)
ΔU = Q + W = -200 + 500 = +300 J
internal energy rises → temperature rises (for an ideal gas)

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Definitions) Distinguish between temperature and internal energy. Answer: Temperature is proportional to the mean random kinetic energy per molecule; internal energy is the total random kinetic energy plus the intermolecular potential energy of all the particles.
  2. (Kelvin) Convert 27 °C to kelvin and state absolute zero in °C. Answer: T = 27 + 273 = 300 K; absolute zero = −273 °C (−273.15 °C exactly).
  3. (Specific heat) 0.15 kg of a metal at 100 °C is dropped into 0.25 kg of water at 15 °C; the final temperature is 22 °C. Find the metal's specific heat capacity (c_water = 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹). Answer: heat gained by water = 0.25 × 4200 × 7 = 7350 J; metal lost = 0.15 × c × 78 = 7350 → c = 7350/(0.15 × 78) = 628 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ ≈ 630 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.
  4. (Latent heat) Explain why the temperature of boiling water stays constant. Answer: The energy supplied breaks intermolecular bonds during the change of state instead of raising the average kinetic energy of the molecules, so the temperature is unchanged until all the liquid has vaporised.
  5. (Equation of state) 2.0 g of helium (M = 4.0 g mol⁻¹) occupies 0.012 m³ at 300 K. Find the pressure. Answer: n = 2.0/4.0 = 0.50 mol; p = nRT/V = (0.50 × 8.31 × 300)/0.012 = 103 875 Pa ≈ 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa.
  6. (Kinetic theory) State two assumptions of the kinetic model and explain why doubling absolute temperature changes rms speed the way it does. Answer: Molecules are point particles with negligible volume; collisions are perfectly elastic; intermolecular forces are negligible except during collisions (any two). Since c = √(3kT/m), doubling T multiplies c by √2 — speed depends on the square root of absolute temperature.
  7. (First law) A gas expands, doing 300 J of work, while 100 J of heat is supplied. Find ΔU. Answer: W = −300 J (work done by the system), Q = +100 J; ΔU = 100 − 300 = −200 J — internal energy falls and the gas cools.
  8. (Practical) Describe how to determine the specific heat capacity of a metal block electrically. Answer: Place a known-power heater in the block, insulate it, record temperature against time as the heater runs; energy input E = Pt; plot temperature vs time and use the gradient (with m and the extrapolated zero-time temperature) to find c from E = mcΔθ; extrapolating back corrects for heat lost during the experiment.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Celsius in gas laws: pV = nRT demands kelvin. A gas-law calculation with 300 °C is wrong by 273 K at the first step.
  • Δθ in specific heat: E = mcΔθ uses a temperature change; questions giving start and end temperatures need the difference, not a raw value.
  • Latent vs specific heat: during a change of state use mL, not mcΔθ; on a heating curve the flat sections are where Δθ = 0.
  • Molar mass units: grams versus kilograms must match the mass unit in n = m/M; the equation of state with R = 8.31 needs moles and SI units throughout.
  • Pressure units: kPa and atm into Pa, cm³ into m³, before substitution.
  • Internal energy wording: it includes potential energy for real substances; defining it as kinetic only is wrong outside ideal gases.
  • First-law signs: pick a convention and state it — work done on the system is positive in ΔU = Q + W; expanding gas does work on the surroundings (negative W).
  • rms speed vs mean speed: the c in pV = ⅓Nmc² is the root-mean-square speed; it is not the average of speeds (which is smaller).
  • Precision and method: 2 or 3 s.f. with units (J, Pa, K, mol, m s⁻¹); write the formula line before numbers — the physics formulae are credit in their own right.

Equations and symbols

Every relation this topic can be examined on, in the form the mark scheme expects, with a key naming each symbol and its unit. The derivations in the sections above end here: if you can write these from memory and say what each symbol means, the algebra in the exam is bookkeeping.

14.1-14.2 Thermal equilibrium and temperature scales

T(K) = θ(°C) + 273.15
Key: T = thermodynamic temperature (K); θ = Celsius temperature (°C); 273.15 = the offset between the ice point and absolute zero (K). Exams accept 273, and a temperature given as 27 °C becomes 300 K.

ΔT (in K) = Δθ (in °C)
Key: ΔT = temperature change in kelvin (K); Δθ = the same change in degrees Celsius (°C). A change of one kelvin is a change of one degree Celsius, because the scales differ only by their zero — which is why a specific heat capacity in J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ can be used with a temperature difference measured in °C.

thermal equilibrium: no net heat flow between bodies in contact
Key: two bodies are in thermal equilibrium when they are at the same temperature, so no net energy transfers between them; the thermometer reads the same as the body only once this state is reached. The zeroth law in one line: equilibrium is transitive, which is what makes a thermometer possible.

14.3 Specific heat capacity and specific latent heat

E = m c Δθ
Key: E = energy supplied to raise the temperature (J); m = mass of the substance (kg); c = specific heat capacity, the energy needed to raise 1 kg by 1 K (J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹); Δθ = temperature rise (°C or K, the same number). No phase change is allowed during the heating, or some of E goes into breaking bonds instead.

c = E / (m Δθ)
Key: c = specific heat capacity (J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹); E = energy supplied (J); m = mass (kg); Δθ = temperature rise (K). The measuring form, used with an electrical heater where E = V I t.

C = m c
Key: C = heat capacity of the whole object (J K⁻¹); m = its mass (kg); c = specific heat capacity of its material (J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹). Then E = C Δθ for the object as a whole; two objects of the same material have heat capacities in the ratio of their masses.

E = m L
Key: E = energy transferred during a change of state (J); m = mass changing state (kg); L = specific latent heat, the energy per kilogram to change state at constant temperature (J kg⁻¹). Use L_fusion for melting and freezing, L_vaporisation for boiling and condensing; the temperature does not rise while this energy is supplied.

E_total = m c Δθ (heating to the change) + m L (the change itself) + m c Δθ (heating beyond it)
Key: each term is the energy for one stage (J); the symbols are as above. The shape of a heating curve: sloped where a single phase is warming, flat where it changes state.

heat lost = heat gained
Key: in an insulated system, the energy leaving the hotter body (J) equals that entering the colder one, so m₁ c₁ (θ_hot − θ_mix) = m₂ c₂ (θ_mix − θ_cold). The method of mixtures: the only unknown is usually the final temperature, or a specific heat capacity once it is measured.

15.1 The mole

n = m / M
Key: n = amount of substance (mol); m = mass of the sample (kg or g); M = molar mass, the mass of one mole (kg mol⁻¹ or g mol⁻¹). Keep m and M in the same unit — grams with g mol⁻¹, kilograms with kg mol⁻¹.

N = n N_A
Key: N = number of particles (dimensionless); n = amount of substance (mol); N_A = Avogadro constant, 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹. One mole of any substance contains the same number of particles, which is why molar masses compare masses of equal particle counts.

N_A = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹
Key: Avogadro constant: the number of particles in one mole. In this specification it is defined as the number of atoms in 0.012 kg of carbon-12.

15.2 The equation of state

p V = n R T
Key: p = pressure (Pa = N m⁻²); V = volume (m³); n = amount of gas (mol); R = molar gas constant, 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; T = thermodynamic temperature (K). The molar form — use it when the amount is known in moles.

p V = N k T
Key: p = pressure (Pa); V = volume (m³); N = number of molecules; k = Boltzmann constant, 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹; T = temperature (K). The molecular form — use it when the question counts molecules rather than moles.

R = N_A k
Key: R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; N_A = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹; k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹. The bridge between the two forms of the equation of state: dividing pV = NkT by n gives pV = (N/n) kT = N_A k T.

p V / T = constant (for a fixed mass of gas)
Key: p = pressure (Pa); V = volume (m³); T = temperature (K). The combined gas law: states 1 and 2 of the same sample satisfy p₁V₁/T₁ = p₂V₂/T₂, which covers Boyle's, Charles' and the pressure law as special cases.

p = ρ R T / M
Key: p = pressure (Pa); ρ = density of the gas (kg m⁻³); R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; T = temperature (K); M = molar mass (kg mol⁻¹). Since ρ = m/V and n = m/M, the equation of state written in terms of density — the form for "why is hot air less dense".

15.3 Kinetic theory of gases

p V = ⅓ N m ⟨c²⟩
Key: p = pressure (Pa); V = volume (m³); N = number of molecules; m = mass of one molecule (kg); ⟨c²⟩ = mean square speed of the molecules (m² s⁻²). The pressure comes from molecular collisions with the walls: momentum change per collision times collision rate per unit area.

½ m ⟨c²⟩ = (3/2) k T
Key: ½ m ⟨c²⟩ = mean translational kinetic energy of one molecule (J); m = molecular mass (kg); ⟨c²⟩ = mean square speed (m² s⁻²); k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹; T = temperature (K). The mean kinetic energy depends only on temperature, and is the same for every gas at that temperature — heavier molecules simply move more slowly.

⟨c²⟩ = 3 k T / m = 3 p / ρ
Key: ⟨c²⟩ = mean square speed (m² s⁻²); k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹; T = temperature (K); m = mass of one molecule (kg); p = pressure (Pa); ρ = density (kg m⁻³). The second form needs no molecular data at all.

c_rms = √(3 k T / m) = √(3 p / ρ)
Key: c_rms = root-mean-square speed (m s⁻¹); k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹; T = temperature (K); m = mass of one molecule (kg); p = pressure (Pa); ρ = density (kg m⁻³). Take the rms speed rather than the mean speed: the mean of the squared speeds carries the energy.

n = N / V = p / (k T)
Key: n = number density of molecules (m⁻³); N = number of molecules; V = volume (m³); p = pressure (Pa); k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹; T = temperature (K). At s.t.p. this gives about 2.7 × 10²⁵ m⁻³, the number worth remembering for order-of-magnitude checks.

16.1 Internal energy

U = Σ KE + Σ PE of the molecules
Key: U = internal energy of the body (J); Σ KE = total random kinetic energy of its molecules (J); Σ PE = total potential energy from the intermolecular forces (J). For an ideal gas the potential term is negligible, so U depends only on temperature; for a real solid or liquid the potential term dominates the latent heat.

U = (3/2) N k T (ideal monatomic gas)
Key: U = internal energy (J); N = number of molecules; k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹; T = temperature (K). Follows from ½ m ⟨c²⟩ = (3/2) k T multiplied by N molecules — no potential energy to add.

16.2 The first law of thermodynamics

ΔU = q + w
Key: ΔU = increase in internal energy of the system (J); q = heat supplied to the system (J); w = work done on the system (J). The sign convention used throughout this specification — energy in is positive. Get the convention wrong and every answer is out by a sign, so state it in the working.

w = − p ΔV
Key: w = work done on the gas (J); p = pressure (Pa); ΔV = change in volume (m³); the minus sign says that a gas expanding (ΔV positive) does work on its surroundings, so work is done on it negatively. For a constant-pressure process this is the area under a p–V graph.

ΔU = q − p ΔV
Key: ΔU = change in internal energy (J); q = heat supplied to the gas (J); p = pressure (Pa); ΔV = volume change (m³). The expanded first law: heat in, minus the work the gas does by expanding.

q = 0 ⇒ ΔU = w (adiabatic); ΔV = 0 ⇒ ΔU = q (isochoric); ΔT = 0 ⇒ ΔU = 0 (isothermal, ideal gas)
Key: the three named processes as special cases; q = heat exchanged (J); w = work done on the system (J); ΔU = internal energy change (J); ΔV = volume change (m³); ΔT = temperature change (K). An adiabatic change is fast enough, or insulated enough, that no heat flows — a sudden compression, or a gas expanding into a vacuum.

C_p − C_v = R
Key: C_p = molar heat capacity at constant pressure (J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹); C_v = molar heat capacity at constant volume (J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹); R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. At constant pressure some of the heat goes into work of expansion, so more is needed for the same temperature rise — the difference is exactly R per mole.

title: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Angles and Polygons
content:
Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Angles and Polygons

Angles are the simplest measurements in geometry and the most frequently examined: almost every Paper 2 and Paper 4 geometry question ends with a reason written next to a number, and the reason earns as many marks as the calculation. This note builds the whole angle toolkit from zero: the vocabulary of points, lines and angles; the parallel-line rules; the angle sums of triangles, quadrilaterals and polygons; and the full set of circle theorems with the standard reasons examiners accept. Every worked example writes the reason line, because that is how the marks are earned.

Geometrical terms

Geometry has a precise vocabulary, and Paper 2 questions often begin by asking you to use it:

  • Point: a position with no size; named with a capital letter.
  • Line segment: the straight path between two points; a line extends without end.
  • Ray: a line starting at a point and extending in one direction.
  • Parallel lines: always the same distance apart, never meeting (marked with arrows).
  • Perpendicular lines: meeting at 90°.
  • Vertex: a corner where two or more lines meet; vertices in the plural.
  • Polygon: a closed shape with straight sides; regular means all sides equal and all angles equal.

Angle vocabulary: acute (less than 90°), right (90°), obtuse (between 90° and 180°), straight (180°), reflex (between 180° and 360°). Angles on a straight line sum to 180°; angles around a point sum to 360°; vertically opposite angles are equal.

Parallel lines: the three rules

A transversal line crossing two parallel lines creates eight angles, and three relationships do all the work:

RelationshipWhat they look likeRule
Corresponding (F-shape)same position at each intersectionequal
Alternate (Z-shape)opposite sides of the transversal, between the parallelsequal
Co-interior (C-shape)same side of the transversal, between the parallelssum to 180°

Worked example. Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. One angle is 115°. Find the angle in the alternate position and the co-interior angle on the other side.

alternate angle = 115 °            (alternate angles are equal)
co-interior angle = 180 - 115 = 65 ° (co-interior angles sum to 180)

Always write the reason next to each answer: "alternate angles" or "co-interior angles sum to 180°". Paper 2 awards the reason mark explicitly.

Triangles and quadrilaterals

The angle sum of any triangle is 180° (proof: draw a line through one vertex parallel to the opposite side and use alternate angles). Consequences you must know:

  • Exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles.
  • Isosceles triangle: base angles are equal; the angle bisector from the apex is also the perpendicular bisector of the base.
  • Equilateral triangle: all angles 60°.
  • Quadrilateral: interior angles sum to 360° (split into two triangles).

Worked example. A quadrilateral has angles 85°, 95° and 110°. Find the fourth angle.

sum = 360 °
fourth = 360 - (85 + 95 + 110) = 360 - 290 = 70 °

Worked example 2 (exterior angle). In a triangle, an exterior angle is 125° and one opposite interior angle is 48°. Find the other opposite interior angle.

exterior = sum of opposite interiors
125 = 48 + x  →  x = 77 °

Angles in polygons

Any n-sided polygon can be split into (n − 2) triangles from one vertex, so:

interior angle sum = (n - 2) × 180 °

regular polygon: each interior angle = (n - 2) × 180/n
exterior angles of any convex polygon sum to 360 °
regular polygon: each exterior angle = 360/n
interior + exterior = 180 ° at each vertex

Worked example 1. Find the interior angle sum of a decagon (10 sides) and each interior angle of a regular decagon.

sum = (10 - 2) × 180 = 1440 °
each = 1440/10 = 144 °
check with exterior: 360/10 = 36; 180 - 36 = 144 °

Worked example 2 (working backwards). A regular polygon has each interior angle 150°. Find the number of sides.

exterior angle = 180 - 150 = 30 °
n = 360/30 = 12 sides  (a regular dodecagon)

Worked example 3 (exterior angles). A pentagon has exterior angles 70°, 80°, 60°, 90°. Find the fifth.

exterior angles sum to 360 °
fifth = 360 - (70 + 80 + 60 + 90) = 360 - 300 = 60 °

Circle theorems: the full set

Circle theorems are examined every session, and each answer needs its theorem named. Learn them as pictures with their standard reasons:

TheoremStatementReason to write
Angle at the centrethe angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference subtended by the same arcangle at centre = 2 × angle at circumference
Angle in a semicirclethe angle in a semicircle (subtended by a diameter) is 90°angle in a semicircle is 90°
Same segmentangles subtended by the same arc in the same segment are equalangles in the same segment are equal
Cyclic quadrilateralopposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180°opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180°
Tangent–radiusa tangent meets the radius at the point of contact at 90°tangent is perpendicular to the radius
Two tangentstangents from an external point are equal in lengthtangents from an external point are equal
Alternate segmentthe angle between a tangent and a chord equals the angle in the alternate segmentalternate segment theorem

Worked example 1 (centre). The angle at the centre subtended by an arc is 130°. Find the angle at the circumference subtended by the same arc.

angle at circumference = 130/2 = 65 °
(reason: angle at centre = 2 x angle at circumference)

Worked example 2 (cyclic quadrilateral). In a cyclic quadrilateral, one pair of opposite angles is 105° and 75°, and the other pair is 4x and 2x. Find x.

opposite angles sum to 180 °
4x + 2x = 180
6x = 180  →  x = 30
check the first pair: 105 + 75 = 180, consistent

Two disciplines make this safe: pair the angles that sit opposite each other (a diagonal between them), and verify both pairs satisfy the 180° rule before writing the answer.

Worked example 3 (tangent). A tangent touches a circle of radius 5 cm at T; O is the centre and P is a point on the tangent 12 cm from T. Find OP.

The radius OT is perpendicular to the tangent, so triangle OTP
is right-angled at T.
OP² = 5² + 12² = 25 + 144 = 169
OP = 13 cm

Worked example 4 (alternate segment). A tangent and a chord form an angle of 62° at the point of contact. Find the angle in the alternate segment.

alternate segment theorem: the tangent-chord angle equals the
angle in the alternate segment
answer = 62 °

Circle theorems: multi-step problems

Paper 4 circle problems chain two or three theorems. The method: mark every angle you can find with its reason, then use each new angle to unlock the next.

Worked example. O is the centre; A, B, C lie on the circle; angle BAC = 35°. Find angle BOC and angle OBC.

angle BOC = 2 × 35 = 70 °
  (angle at centre = 2 x angle at circumference)
triangle OBC is isosceles (OB = OC = radii)
base angles OBC and OCB are equal:
OBC = (180 - 70)/2 = 55 °

Worked example 2 (semicircle + cyclic). AB is a diameter; C and D lie on the circle; angle ABC = 40°. Find angle ADC.

angle ACB = 90 ° (angle in a semicircle)
angle BAC = 180 - 90 - 40 = 50 °
ABCD is cyclic, so angle ADC = 180 - angle ABC? No - opposite
pairs: A with C, B with D. Angle ADC is opposite angle ABC?
The vertices in order are A, B, C, D, so opposite pairs are
(A, C) and (B, D). Angle ADC is at D, opposite angle ABC at B:
angle ADC = 180 - 40 = 140 °.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Parallel lines) Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal; one co-interior angle is 72°. Find the other. Answer: 108°, because co-interior angles sum to 180°.
  2. (Polygon) Find the interior angle sum of a 15-sided polygon. Answer: (15 − 2) × 180 = 2340°.
  3. (Regular polygon) Each exterior angle of a regular polygon is 24°. Find the number of sides and each interior angle. Answer: n = 360/24 = 15; interior = 180 − 24 = 156°.
  4. (Circle — centre) An angle at the circumference is 28°. Find the angle at the centre subtended by the same arc. Answer: 56°.
  5. (Circle — semicircle) A triangle is inscribed in a semicircle with the diameter as one side; one base angle is 33°. Find the other. Answer: 90° at the circumference, so the other angle is 180 − 90 − 33 = 57°.
  6. (Circle — cyclic) A cyclic quadrilateral has one angle 118°. Find the opposite angle. Answer: 62° (180 − 118).
  7. (Tangent) Two tangents from P touch the circle at A and B; PA = 9 cm. Find PB and explain. Answer: 9 cm — tangents from an external point are equal.
  8. (Multi-step) In a circle, angle ABD = 42° and angle ACD = 42°. What does this tell you about A, B, C, D? Answer: They are concyclic — equal angles subtended by the same chord AD at B and C mean the points lie on the same circle (angles in the same segment).

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Missing reasons: Paper 2 geometry marks include the reason. "x = 65° (angles on a straight line)" scores; a bare "65°" may not.
  • Wrong pairing in cyclic quadrilaterals: opposite angles are the ones separated by a diagonal (A and C, B and D), not adjacent ones. Check both pairs sum to 180°.
  • Alternate versus corresponding: alternate angles form a Z, corresponding an F. Identifying the wrong pattern gives the wrong equality.
  • Interior formula mix-up: interior sum is (n − 2) × 180; each exterior is 360/n. Do not use 360/n for the interior of a regular polygon.
  • Reflex angles: the angle at the centre may be reflex; if the diagram shows an obtuse angle but the geometry demands a reflex one, use 360° − the drawn angle.
  • Assuming radii are parallel or equal to chords: radii are equal to each other, not to chords. Isosceles triangles in circles come from two radii.
  • Tangent–chord angle: the alternate segment theorem requires the angle between the tangent and the chord at the point of contact, not any angle involving the tangent.
  • Diagram not to scale: never measure an angle with a protractor in an exam diagram; the geometry must be calculated. "Diagram not accurately drawn" is a warning, not decoration.

title: IGCSE Mathematics: Sequences and Functions
content:
IGCSE Mathematics: Sequences and Functions

Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580 (2025–2027), section 2 Algebra and graphs: statement 2.7 Sequences and statement 2.13 Functions (Extended). A sequence is a list of numbers generated by a rule; a function is the rule itself. This note builds nth-term rules from scratch — showing why the formula works, not just what it is — then function notation, composite functions and inverse functions, including the domain restrictions that decide whether an inverse exists.

What a sequence is; term-to-term rules

A sequence is an ordered list of numbers. The term-to-term rule gets from one term to the next: add 4, multiply by 2, subtract 1 then double. It tells you what happens step by step but not what the hundredth term is. The position-to-term rule (the nth term) gives any term directly from its position n, and that is the more powerful description.

Sequence: 3, 7, 11, 15, 19, ...

Term-to-term: add 4 each time.
Position-to-term: the terms are 4 less than 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, ..., so the nth term is 4n - 1.

Check: n = 1 gives 4(1) - 1 = 3 ✓;  n = 5 gives 4(5) - 1 = 19 ✓

Linear sequences and the nth term

A linear (arithmetic) sequence has a constant difference d between terms. Its nth term is dn + b, and b is chosen to make the first term correct.

Find the nth term of 5, 8, 11, 14, ...

Constant difference d = 3, so the nth term starts as 3n.
Compare with the sequence: 3, 6, 9, 12, ... is three times the table of 3;
the real sequence is 2 more each time, so b = 2.
nth term:  3n + 2

Check every term: n = 1: 5 ✓   n = 2: 8 ✓   n = 3: 11 ✓
The 50th term is 3(50) + 2 = 152.

Why dn + b always works. Adding d each time from a starting value a means the nth term is a + (n − 1)d, since term n has had (n − 1) additions of d. Expanding gives a + nd − d = nd + (a − d), which is exactly dn + b with b = a − d. Both forms are the same rule; examiners accept either.

Quadratic and special sequences

When the first difference changes but the second difference is constant, the rule is quadratic: an² + bn + c. The method: build the n² sequence, subtract it from the sequence, and finish the linear remainder.

Find the nth term of 2, 5, 10, 17, 26, ...

First differences: 3, 5, 7, 9;  second differences: 2, 2 (constant) → quadratic.
The n² sequence is 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, ...
Subtract: (2-1), (5-4), (10-9), (17-16), (26-25) = 1, 1, 1, 1, 1
So the sequence is n² + 1.

Check: n = 3 gives 9 + 1 = 10 ✓

Other sequences to recognise on sight: the triangular numbers n(n + 1)/2 (1, 3, 6, 10, ...), the square numbers n², the Fibonacci sequence (each term is the sum of the two before it, and it has no simple nth term), and geometric sequences that multiply by a fixed ratio r — their nth term is arⁿ⁻¹ where a is the first term.

Geometric example: 3, 6, 12, 24, ... has a = 3 and r = 2, so the nth term is 3 × 2^(n-1).
The 6th term is 3 × 2⁵ = 96.
Sequence typeExampleRule
Linear (arithmetic)5, 8, 11, 14Constant difference d; nth term dn + b
Quadratic2, 5, 10, 17Constant second difference; nth term an² + bn + c
Geometric3, 6, 12, 24Constant ratio r; nth term arⁿ⁻¹
Triangular numbers1, 3, 6, 10n(n + 1)/2
Square numbers1, 4, 9, 16n²
Fibonacci1, 1, 2, 3, 5Add the two previous terms (no simple nth term)

Choosing the right description is half the battle: check the first differences, then the second, then the ratio, before assuming any rule. Once a candidate rule is found, verify it against every given term — a sequence that matches only the first three terms is not proven.

Function notation

A function is a machine with an input and exactly one output for each input. The notation f(x) = 2x + 3 names the machine f and says what it does to x: multiply by 2, then add 3. Evaluating is substitution: f(4) = 2(4) + 3 = 11. The machine picture matters: one input never gives two outputs, though two inputs may share an output.

  • The domain is the set of allowed inputs; the range is the set of outputs the function actually produces.
  • For f(x) = x² with domain all real numbers, the range is y ⩾ 0, because squares are never negative.
  • For f(x) = 2x + 3 with domain 0 ⩽ x ⩽ 5, the range is 3 ⩽ f(x) ⩽ 13 — substitute the endpoints, since linear functions stretch ranges proportionally.

Questions ask for the range in terms of y or f(x); find the outputs at the domain boundaries and, for quadratics, at the turning point.

Composite functions

A composite function runs one machine after the other. fg(x) means apply g first, then f to the result — the notation reads right to left, like f(g(x)).

Given f(x) = 2x + 1 and g(x) = x², find fg(3), gf(x) and fg(x).

fg(3):  g(3) = 9, then f(9) = 2(9) + 1 = 19.
gf(x):  apply f first:  g(f(x)) = (2x + 1)² = 4x² + 4x + 1.
fg(x):  apply g first:  f(g(x)) = 2x² + 1.

Note fg(x) ≠ gf(x): order matters.

Every line is written out because the most common error is applying the functions in the wrong order — and the composite is not commutative.

Inverse functions

The inverse f⁻¹ undoes f: if f turns 4 into 11, f⁻¹ turns 11 back into 4. Inverse functions exist only for one-to-one functions — ones where different inputs always give different outputs. The graph of y = x² is not one-to-one over all real numbers (both 3 and −3 give 9), so it has no inverse unless the domain is restricted to x ⩾ 0.

Find the inverse of f(x) = (3x - 2)/5:

Write y = (3x - 2)/5 and make x the subject:
5y = 3x - 2          [multiply by 5]
5y + 2 = 3x          [add 2]
x = (5y + 2)/3       [divide by 3]

Swap x and y:  f⁻¹(x) = (5x + 2)/3

Check by composing: f⁻¹(f(x)) = [5((3x - 2)/5) + 2]/3 = [(3x - 2) + 2]/3 = 3x/3 = x  ✓
  • f⁻¹(x) is a single symbol meaning the inverse function; the −1 is not a power and f⁻¹(x) does not mean 1/f(x).
  • The domain of f⁻¹ is the range of f, and the range of f⁻¹ is the domain of f — they swap, exactly as the inputs and outputs swap roles.
  • Graphically, y = f⁻¹(x) is the reflection of y = f(x) in the line y = x.

Worked example: a full function question

Let f(x) = x² + 3 for x ⩾ 0, and g(x) = 4x − 5.

(a) Find f(2):  f(2) = 4 + 3 = 7.

(b) Find fg(x):  f(g(x)) = (4x - 5)² + 3 = 16x² - 40x + 25 + 3 = 16x² - 40x + 28.

(c) Find f⁻¹(x):  y = x² + 3, so x² = y - 3 and x = √(y - 3) (positive root, since x ⩾ 0).
Swap: f⁻¹(x) = √(x - 3).
Domain of f⁻¹: x ⩾ 3, which is exactly the range of f.

(d) Solve f(x) = 30 for x ⩾ 0:
x² + 3 = 30
x² = 27
x = √27 = 3√3 ≈ 5.20        [only the positive root is in the domain]

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Reading fg(x) as f then g. It is g first, then f — the notation runs right to left.
  • Assuming fg = gf; only special cases agree.
  • Treating f⁻¹(x) as 1/f(x). The inverse undoes the function; it is not a reciprocal.
  • Ignoring domain restrictions: with x ⩾ 0 on f(x) = x² + 3, the inverse takes the positive root only, and a negative root answer is wrong.
  • Claiming y = x² has an inverse over all real numbers; it is two-to-one and needs a restricted domain.
  • Building the nth term from the first difference alone without checking every term; a single wrong check sends a whole answer wrong.
  • Writing a geometric nth term as arⁿ instead of arⁿ⁻¹; the first term must be a itself.
  • Stating a range that ignores the turning point of a quadratic: the range of y = (x − 2)² + 1 is y ⩾ 1, not y ⩾ 0.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 2, 3 marks). Find the nth term of 7, 11, 15, 19, ...

Answer: Constant difference 4, so 4n + b; the first term 7 = 4 + b gives b = 3. The nth term is 4n + 3. The 20th term is 83.

Question 2 (Paper 2, 3 marks). A sequence has nth term 5n − 2. Write down the first four terms and the 100th.

Answer: n = 1, 2, 3, 4 give 3, 8, 13, 18; the 100th term is 5(100) − 2 = 498.

Question 3 (Paper 4, 4 marks). f(x) = 3x − 1 and g(x) = x² + 2. Find fg(x), gf(2) and f⁻¹(x).

Answer: fg(x) = 3(x² + 2) − 1 = 3x² + 5. gf(2): f(2) = 5, so g(5) = 27. Inverse: y = 3x − 1 gives x = (y + 1)/3, so f⁻¹(x) = (x + 1)/3.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 4 marks). The second differences of a sequence are constant at 4, and its first two terms are 2 and 7. Find the nth term.

Answer: Constant second difference 4 means the n² coefficient is 4/2 = 2, so the rule starts 2n². The n² sequence gives 2, 8, ... while the sequence is 2, 7, ..., so the remainder is 0, −1, ... a linear part with difference −1: −n + 1. Check: 2n² − n + 1 gives n = 1: 2 ✓ and n = 2: 8 − 2 + 1 = 7 ✓. The nth term is 2n² − n + 1.

Question 5 (Paper 4, 5 marks). f(x) = (x + 4)/(x − 2) for x ≠ 2. Find f⁻¹(x) and the value of x for which f(x) is undefined.

Answer: y = (x + 4)/(x − 2) gives y(x − 2) = x + 4, so yx − 2y = x + 4, yx − x = 2y + 4, x(y − 1) = 2y + 4 and x = (2y + 4)/(y − 1). Swapping: f⁻¹(x) = (2x + 4)/(x − 1). The function itself is undefined at x = 2, where the denominator vanishes; its inverse is undefined at x = 1.

Question 6 (Paper 2, 3 marks). The first three terms of a geometric sequence are 5, 15, 45. Find the 8th term.

Answer: Common ratio r = 15/5 = 3, so the nth term is 5 × 3ⁿ⁻¹ and the 8th term is 5 × 3⁷ = 5 × 2187 = 10 935.

From variables and patterns, the course now turns to the number system itself.

Equations and symbols

Two families of formula share this topic: the rules that generate a sequence, and the algebra of function notation. Both are asked as "find the rule", so the sheet is a list of rules with the letters they use.

4n - 1 Key: n = the position of the term in the sequence (1, 2, 3, …); the coefficient 4 is the common difference and −1 is the adjustment that makes n = 1 give the first term, 3. Substitute n to get any term directly; the 20th term here is 79.

3n + 2 Key: n = position; 3 = common difference of 5, 8, 11, 14; +2 makes the first term correct. Every linear sequence can be written dn + b, and b always equals the first term minus d.

n² + 1 Key: n = position; the n² term means the second difference is constant, which is what identifies a quadratic sequence. Build the n² sequence, subtract it, and finish the remaining linear part.

n(n + 1)/2 Key: n = position; the triangular numbers 1, 3, 6, 10, found by adding the integers 1 to n. Recognise the shape rather than deriving it under exam pressure.

arⁿ⁻¹ Key: a = first term; r = common ratio, found by dividing any term by the one before; n = position. The exponent is n − 1, not n: at n = 1 the term must be a itself, and r⁰ = 1 guarantees that.

f(x) = 2x + 3 Key: f = the function's name; x = the input, in the domain; the expression is the rule — multiply by 2, add 3. Evaluating is substitution: f(4) = 11.

fg(x) = 2x² + 1 Key: fg means apply g first (g(x) = x²), then f to the result; the notation reads right to left. fg(x) is not gf(x) — order matters, and swapping it is the standard error.

f⁻¹(x) = (5x + 2)/3 Key: f⁻¹ = the inverse function, the machine that undoes f; the −1 is not a power, and f⁻¹(x) is never 1/f(x). Found by writing y = f(x), making x the subject, then swapping the letters.

f⁻¹(x) = √(x - 3) Key: the inverse of f(x) = x² + 3 on the domain x ⩾ 0; the positive root alone is taken because the original domain excludes negatives. The domain of f⁻¹ is the range of f, here x ⩾ 3.

How the marks are given. Show the substitution, keep the composite order, and state any domain restriction. A range quoted without checking the turning point — y ⩾ 1 for (x − 2)² + 1, not y ⩾ 0 — is the quiet loss on this topic.

title: Magnetic Fields and Electromagnetism — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Magnetic Fields and Electromagnetism

Physics — A2. F = BIL sin θ (Fleming's left hand: field-index, current-first-finger, force-thumb).

Key areas to revise

  • Force on a Current
  • Force on a Moving Charge
  • Fields from Currents
  • Electromagnetic Induction

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Worked example

A straight wire of length 0.40 m carries a current of 2.5 A at right angles to a uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.12 T. The force is F = BIL sin θ = 0.12 × 2.5 × 0.40 × sin 90° = 0.12 N. Fleming's left hand gives the direction: the field points from the first finger (north to south), the current points along the second finger, and the force is the thumb.

Common mistakes

  • Using θ = 0° when the wire is at right angles to the field. The force is zero only when the wire is parallel to the field.
  • Mixing up the left and right hand rules. The left hand is for motors (force), and the right hand is for generators (induced current).
  • Forgetting that the force on a charge moving in a field is F = BQv, not BIL, unless you convert the current first.

title: Communication and Networking — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Communication and Networking

Computer Science — AS. `# Communication and Networking

Key areas to revise

  • Transmission
  • Packets and Protocols
  • Network Types
  • Hardware
  • Client-Server vs Peer-to-Peer

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

### Worked example A parity bit makes the total number of 1s even (even parity) or odd. For the 7-bit pattern 1011001 there are four 1s, so the even-parity bit is 0. If the receiver counts an odd number of 1s, it knows an error occurred. Packet switching divides data into packets that can take different routes, and each packet is checked before reassembly.

Key points to remember

Data is sent across networks in packets, and each packet is routed separately. Protocols define how devices communicate, and the TCP/IP suite is the set used on the internet. An IP address identifies a device on a network, while a MAC address is fixed to the network hardware.

Network security depends on firewalls that filter traffic, encryption that makes data unreadable to anyone who intercepts it, and user authentication that checks identity. Describe a threat, then say how the security measure prevents it, because an answer with only the name of a method gains little credit.

title: Waves — Study Notes
content:
Waves

Progressive waves

  • A progressive wave transfers energy without transferring matter. Its speed is v = fλ, where f is the frequency and λ the wavelength. Period T = 1/f.
  • Phase difference: two points separated by one wavelength are in phase. Points separated by half a wavelength are in antiphase.

Transverse and longitudinal waves

  • Transverse: the oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer (e.g. light, waves on a string).
  • Longitudinal: the oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer (e.g. sound in air, compressions and rarefactions).

Doppler effect for sound

When a source moves towards an observer, the observed frequency is higher and the wavelength is shorter. When it moves away, the observed frequency is lower and the wavelength is longer. The speed of sound in the medium does not change.

Electromagnetic spectrum

All electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum. In order of increasing wavelength: gamma rays, X-rays, ultraviolet, visible light, infrared, microwaves, radio waves. Frequency increases in the reverse order.

Polarisation

Only transverse waves can be polarised. Polarisation restricts the oscillations to a single plane. Longitudinal waves such as sound cannot be polarised.

Worked example: a wave has frequency 50 Hz and wavelength 6.0 m. Its speed is v = fλ = 50 × 6.0 = 300 m s⁻¹.

Exam tips: learn the spectrum order in terms of wavelength, not frequency. For the Doppler effect, state which way the source moves relative to the observer. Only transverse waves can show polarisation.

Polarisation and the Doppler effect

Only transverse waves can be polarised, because their oscillations can be restricted to one plane. A polariser passes only the component of the oscillation along its transmission axis. Light from a sky or a reflection is partly polarised, which is why polarising filters reduce glare. The Doppler effect for a moving source gives an observed frequency f' = f v/(v ± vs), where the upper sign applies when the source moves away from the observer and the lower sign when it approaches.

Exam tip: longitudinal waves such as sound cannot be polarised, so say so explicitly if a question asks about it.

title: A Level Mathematics: The Poisson Distribution
content:
A Level Mathematics: The Poisson Distribution

The Poisson distribution models the number of events that happen in a fixed interval of time, length, area or volume when those events occur randomly and independently at a constant average rate. Where the binomial counts successes in a fixed number of trials, the Poisson counts arrivals in a continuous window: calls reaching a switchboard in an hour, defects along a length of cable, radioactive decays in a minute. This note derives the formula from the binomial, sets out the two conditions that must hold, and then uses the distribution for the probability and hypothesis-test questions the exam sets.

Where the formula comes from

Imagine slicing the interval into a very large number of tiny sub-intervals. In each slice the chance of an event is tiny but the number of slices is enormous, so the count is binomial with n huge and p tiny. Taking that limit turns nCr p^r (1−p)^(n−r) into the Poisson formula, with the mean λ = np surviving as the only parameter.

X ~ Po(lambda):  P(X = r) = e^(-lambda) lambda^r / r!
mean E(X) = lambda
variance Var(X) = lambda
so the mean and variance are equal - a diagnostic test for the model

The equality of mean and variance is not a coincidence to memorise; it is the fingerprint of the limit, and it is why an exam question can give you a sample mean and variance and ask whether a Poisson model is plausible.

The three conditions

A Poisson model needs randomness, independence and a constant rate. Naming them is worth marks, and each failure has a characteristic symptom.

1. events occur singly (not in pairs or batches)
2. events occur at random, independently of each other
3. the average rate lambda is constant over the interval
then the count in that interval is Poisson

Worked example (checking the model). A shop counts customers arriving per hour. Explain why a Poisson model may be unsuitable.

the arrival rate is not constant: it peaks at lunchtime and is near zero at night
so condition 3 fails and the mean over a whole day is not a single rate
a better model splits the day into periods of roughly constant rate

Calculating probabilities

The formula handles a single value; the cumulative sum handles a range. Because the Poisson has no upper limit, every "at least" question becomes a complement.

P(X = r) = e^(-lambda) lambda^r / r!
P(X <= r) sums from 0 to r (tables or calculator)
P(X >= r) = 1 - P(X <= r - 1)
P(X < r)  = P(X <= r - 1)

Worked example. X ~ Po(3). Find P(X = 2).

P = e^(-3) x 3^2 / 2!
= 0.049787 x 9 / 2
= 0.2240

Worked example 2 (at least). For the same X, find P(X ≥ 4).

P(X >= 4) = 1 - P(X <= 3)
P(X <= 3) = 0.049787(1 + 3 + 4.5 + 4.5) = 0.6472
so P(X >= 4) = 0.3528

Worked example 3 (scale change). Calls arrive at 4 per minute. Find the probability of 10 or more calls in two minutes.

the rate scales with the interval: lambda = 8 for two minutes
P(X >= 10) = 1 - P(X <= 9) = 1 - 0.7170 = 0.2830

Scaling is the most common source of avoidable error: the parameter must be expressed for the interval the question actually asks about.

Adding independent Poisson variables

If two independent counts each follow a Poisson distribution, their sum does too, and the parameters add. This is why the distribution is so usable: a total across separate sources needs no convolution.

X ~ Po(l1), Y ~ Po(l2), independent
X + Y ~ Po(l1 + l2)
but X - Y is NOT Poisson

Worked example. A website gets 5 hits per minute from Europe and 3 per minute from Asia, independently. Find the probability of more than 10 hits in a minute in total.

total ~ Po(8)
P(X > 10) = 1 - P(X <= 10) = 1 - 0.8159 = 0.1841

The Poisson as an approximation to the binomial

When n is large and p is small, the binomial is well approximated by a Poisson with λ = np. The rule of thumb used in this course is n > 50 and p < 0.05, or np < 5.

X ~ B(n, p) with n large, p small  ->  X is approximately Po(np)

Worked example. A factory produces items with a 2% defect rate. In a batch of 200, use a Poisson approximation to find the probability of at most 2 defects.

lambda = 200 x 0.02 = 4
P(X <= 2) = e^(-4)(1 + 4 + 8) = 0.018316 x 13 = 0.2381
the exact binomial gives 0.2351, so the approximation is close

Worked example 2 (justifying the approximation). State why the approximation is reasonable here.

n = 200 is large and p = 0.02 is small, with np = 4
so the rare-event limit conditions hold

Hypothesis testing with the Poisson

The structure is identical to the binomial test: state hypotheses, assume the null rate, compute the tail probability, compare with the significance level. The only new step is that the rate may need scaling to the observed interval.

H0: lambda = lambda0    H1: lambda > lambda0 (or <)
observed count x in the interval
p-value = P(X >= x) or P(X <= x) under Po(lambda0)
reject H0 if the p-value <= the significance level

Worked example. A call centre historically receives 6 calls per hour. In a new hour it receives 12. Test at the 5% level whether the rate has increased.

H0: lambda = 6;  H1: lambda > 6
X ~ Po(6) under H0
P(X >= 12) = 1 - P(X <= 11) = 1 - 0.9799 = 0.0201
0.0201 < 0.05, so reject H0
there is evidence the rate has increased

Worked example 2 (critical region). For Po(6), find the 5% one-tailed critical region for an increase.

P(X >= 11) = 0.0426 (below 0.05)
P(X >= 10) = 0.0839 (above 0.05)
critical region: X >= 11

Worked example 3 (two intervals). The same centre observes 16 calls over two hours. Test for an increase at 5%.

expected over two hours under H0 = 12, so X ~ Po(12)
P(X >= 16) = 1 - P(X <= 15) = 1 - 0.8444 = 0.1556
0.1556 > 0.05, so do not reject H0

Compare the two: twelve calls in one hour was significant, sixteen in two hours is not, because the expected count doubled. The rate, not the raw count, is what is being tested.

Reading the distribution's shape

The Poisson is skewed to the right when λ is small and becomes almost symmetric as λ grows, which is why small-rate questions usually live in the lower tail and why the normal approximation becomes usable once λ passes about 20. Knowing the shape tells you at a glance whether an answer is plausible: a probability of 0.4 for "more than 10" when λ = 3 should feel wrong before any arithmetic is checked.

A useful sanity check is that the standard deviation is the square root of the mean. For Po(9) the mean is 9 and the standard deviation 3, so counts between 6 and 12 are ordinary and a count of 20 is roughly three and a half standard deviations out — surprising enough to prompt a hypothesis test. That comparison is what turns a bare probability into an interpretation, and interpretation marks are the easiest ones to lose.

Finally, note that the model is about a count in an interval, so the interval has to be defined in the answer. "Three calls per hour" and "three calls per minute" describe different distributions, and a rate quoted per unit time without its unit is not a λ at all.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Definition) State two conditions for a Poisson model. Answer: events occur singly at random, independently, at a constant rate.
  2. (Single value) X ~ Po(2.5): find P(X = 3). Answer: e^(−2.5)(15.625/6) = 0.2138.
  3. (Cumulative) X ~ Po(4): find P(X ≤ 2). Answer: 0.2381.
  4. (Complement) X ~ Po(5): find P(X ≥ 3). Answer: 1 − 0.1247 = 0.8753.
  5. (Scaling) Rate 3 per hour: find P(X = 0) in 20 minutes. Answer: λ = 1, so e^(−1) = 0.3679.
  6. (Sum) Independent Po(2) and Po(3): find P(total = 4). Answer: Po(5), P(4) = 0.1755.
  7. (Approximation) B(500, 0.01): approximate P(X = 0). Answer: Po(5), e^(−5) = 0.00674.
  8. (Mean/variance) A sample has mean 4.2 and variance 9.1. Comment on the Poisson fit. Answer: variance far exceeds the mean, so the model is doubtful (over-dispersed).
  9. (Test) 9 events observed where 4 expected; test for an increase at 5%. Answer: P(X ≥ 9) = 0.0214 < 0.05, reject H0.
  10. (Critical region) Po(3), 5% upper tail: find the critical region. Answer: P(X ≥ 7) = 0.0335, P(X ≥ 6) = 0.0839, so X ≥ 7.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Using the wrong interval: λ must match the window asked about; doubling a time doubles the rate.
  • Complement off by one: P(X ≥ 4) = 1 − P(X ≤ 3); subtracting P(X ≤ 4) is the classic error.
  • Treating a difference as Poisson: sums of independent Poisson variables are Poisson, differences are not.
  • Approximation outside its range: np must be small; with np large the Poisson is a poor fit to the binomial.
  • Variance assumed equal to the mean without checking: the test mean = variance is a diagnostic, not a guarantee.
  • Ignoring clustering: events that arrive in bursts break the single-event condition and inflate the variance.
  • r! miscomputed: 0! = 1 and 1! = 1, and a missing factorial term changes the answer entirely.
  • p-value direction: a one-tailed test uses one tail only; doubling it makes a borderline result look significant.

title: Exam technique: Nuclear Physics (A2)
content:
### What earns the marks
For energy, mass defect times c squared with units earns both marks. For decay, ln2 over half-life quoted earns the method mark; activity as lambda N earns the second. For radii, the cube-root rule applied to ratios earns the mark.
### Traps
Error: half-life used as the decay constant. Correction: divide ln2 by it. Error: fission named for the Sun. Correction: fusion powers stars. Error: radius scaled linearly with A. Correction: cube root of nucleon number.
### Worked example
A nucleus has a half-life of 8 days. The decay constant is lambda = ln 2 / 8, which is about 0.087 per day. If the sample holds N = 2.0 x 10^10 nuclei, the activity is A = lambda N, about 1.7 x 10^9 decays per day. Quote the unit with the answer, because the mark depends on it.
### Check yourself
A nucleus with A = 64 has radius r = 1.2 x 64^(1/3) = 4.8 fm. State why doubling A does not double the radius. The radius grows with the cube root of A, so doubling A multiplies r by 2^(1/3), about 1.26.

title: Alkenes Quick Revision
content:
Alkenes

Edexcel International AS Level Chemistry revision notes covering the structure, bonding, isomerism, addition reactions, mechanisms, and polymer disposal of alkenes.

  • Alkenes and cycloalkenes are unsaturated hydrocarbons with a general formula CnH2n containing a carbon-carbon double bond consisting of one σ bond and one π bond.
  • Geometric isomerism arises due to restricted rotation around the C=C double bond and different substituents on each carbon atom of the double bond.
  • The E-Z naming system uses Cahn-Ingold-Prelog priority rules, becoming necessary when the cis- and trans- naming system breaks down due to non-identical groups on the carbon atoms.
  • Alkenes undergo addition reactions including hydrogenation with a nickel catalyst, halogenation to di-halogenoalkanes, addition of hydrogen halides to mono-halogenoalkanes, hydration with steam and an acid catalyst to form alcohols, and oxidation with acidified potassium manganate(VII) to diols.
  • Bromine or bromine water acts as a qualitative test for a C=C double bond, turning from orange/brown to colourless.
  • Electrophilic addition mechanisms for bromine and hydrogen bromide with ethene, and hydrogen bromide with propene, involve curly arrows starting from bonds or lone pairs and proceed via carbocation intermediates whose stability increases in the order primary < secondary < tertiary.
  • Addition polymerisation produces long-chain polymers from alkene monomers, requiring the ability to draw repeat units from monomers and vice versa.
  • Polymer disposal problems are mitigated by developing biodegradable polymers and removing toxic waste gases produced by incineration.

Worked example

Deduce the E-Z isomer designation for (E)-1-bromo-1,2-dichloroethene. Step 1: Assign priorities to the groups attached to each carbon of the C=C double bond using atomic numbers. On carbon 1, bromine (atomic number 35) outranks chlorine (atomic number 17). On carbon 2, chlorine outranks hydrogen (atomic number 1). Step 2: Locate the highest priority groups on each carbon. Since the bromine on carbon 1 and the chlorine on carbon 2 are on opposite sides of the double bond, the isomer is designated as (E).

Key points to remember

Students often forget that a π bond is formed by the sideways overlap of p-orbitals, which restricts rotation and causes geometric isomerism. When drawing curly arrows for electrophilic addition, ensure the arrow starts precisely from the electron source, either a bond or a lone pair, and points to the electron-deficient species. In addition of hydrogen bromide to propene, remember that the major product is formed via the more stable secondary carbocation intermediate rather than the less stable primary carbocation. When naming geometrical isomers, always apply the E-Z priority rules systematically rather than relying on cis and trans prefixes when more than two different groups are attached to the double-bonded carbons.

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

content:
Microbiology, Immunity and Forensics

Edexcel IAL Biology 9BI0 A2, topic 6. Every statement 6.1 to 6.20 is covered below, with its code in the heading. The topic links three big ideas: how microorganisms are grown and measured, how the body defends itself and why pathogens keep finding ways around those defences, and how DNA techniques are used to identify organisms and people.

6.1: Culturing microorganisms with aseptic technique

  • Aseptic technique keeps a culture pure: only the wanted microorganism grows. Sterilise media and equipment first, usually in an autoclave at 121 °C under pressure for about 15 minutes.
  • Work close to a Bunsen flame, flame the inoculating loop until red-hot before and after use, keep Petri dish lids mostly closed, and never pipette by mouth.
  • Incubate cultures inverted at a safe temperature, usually 25 °C for school work, so condensation does not drip onto the agar.

6.2: Measuring the growth of microorganisms

  • Direct cell counts: use a haemocytometer (counting chamber) under a microscope, counting cells in a known volume to get the number per cm³.
  • Viable counts by dilution plating: make a serial dilution, spread known volumes on agar, incubate, and count colonies on plates with about 30 to 300 colonies. Each colony is assumed to grow from one viable cell, so the count shows living cells only.
  • Mass methods: measure the dry mass of cells collected by centrifuging or filtering a known volume of culture.
  • Optical methods (turbidity): a colorimeter or spectrophotometer measures how much light the cloudy culture absorbs. Absorbance rises with cell density, so a calibration curve converts it to cell numbers.

6.3: The bacterial growth curve and the growth rate constant

  • Lag phase: cells adapt to the medium and synthesise enzymes; there is little or no division.
  • Exponential (log) phase: cells divide at a constant rate, so the population doubles each generation. N = N₀ × 2ⁿ, where n is the number of doublings.
  • Stationary phase: births equal deaths, because nutrients run short and waste builds up.
  • Death phase: deaths exceed births and the population falls.
  • Growth rate constant: in exponential growth N = N₀eᵏᵗ. So k = (ln N₂ − ln N₁) ÷ (t₂ − t₁). Plotting ln N against time gives a straight line whose gradient is k.

6.4: Core practical 13: growth of microorganisms in liquid culture

  • Inoculate a sterile liquid medium, take samples at regular intervals, and measure turbidity or cell count each time.
  • Plot the results to show the four phases of the curve, then calculate the exponential growth rate constant from the straight-line part.
  • Safe and ethical use: use only non-pathogenic strains, keep the culture closed, disinfect the bench, and autoclave all used material before disposal.

6.5: Structure of bacteria and viruses

  • Bacteria are cells with a cell wall (peptidoglycan), cell membrane, cytoplasm with ribosomes, and a circular DNA loop, often with plasmids. They have no nucleus.
  • Viruses are not cells. They have a nucleic acid core, either DNA or RNA, surrounded by a protein capsid. Some also have a lipid envelope taken from the host.
  • Comparisons: Ebola virus has single-stranded RNA and an envelope. Tobacco mosaic virus (TMV) has single-stranded RNA in a helical capsid, with no envelope. HIV has two RNA strands, reverse transcriptase and an envelope. Lambda phage, a virus of bacteria, has double-stranded DNA in a head with a tail and no envelope.
  • Lytic cycle: the virus takes over the host cell, makes new viruses, and the cell bursts (lyses) to release them.
  • Latency: the viral genome stays in the host cell without producing new viruses, and can become active later.

6.6: How Mycobacterium tuberculosis and HIV infect human cells

  • Tuberculosis: Mycobacterium tuberculosis is inhaled into the alveoli. Macrophages engulf it, but the bacterium survives inside them and multiplies. The body forms granulomas (tubercles) around the infection, and the lung tissue is destroyed. Symptoms include a persistent cough, fever, night sweats and weight loss. If untreated it can be fatal.
  • HIV: the virus binds to CD4 receptors and a co-receptor on helper T cells. Reverse transcriptase makes DNA from its RNA, which is inserted into the host genome. New viruses bud from the cell. The helper T cell population falls, so the immune system fails and opportunistic infections and cancers take hold (AIDS).

6.7: Routes of entry and barriers

  • Routes: inhalation (airborne droplets), ingestion (contaminated food and water), contact through broken skin or wounds, sexual contact, and vectors such as mosquitoes.
  • Barriers: intact skin (keratin, dryness, and the skin flora that competes with pathogens), stomach acid (pH about 2, which kills many ingested microbes), and gut flora that competes for space and nutrients. Mucus and cilia in the airways trap and move pathogens out.

6.8: Non-specific responses to infection

  • Inflammation: damaged cells release chemicals such as histamine, which dilate blood vessels and make them leaky. The area becomes red, hot and swollen, and white blood cells are recruited to the site.
  • Lysozyme: an enzyme in tears, saliva and mucus that breaks the peptidoglycan of bacterial cell walls.
  • Interferon: proteins released by virus-infected cells that warn neighbouring cells, which then resist viral replication. Interferon is antiviral, not a direct killer of the virus.
  • Phagocytosis: neutrophils and macrophages engulf a pathogen into a phagosome. Lysosomes fuse with it and enzymes digest the contents.

6.9: Antigens, antibodies, plasma cells, macrophages and antigen-presenting cells

  • An antigen is a foreign molecule, usually a protein or glycoprotein on a pathogen's surface, that triggers an immune response.
  • An antibody is a Y-shaped glycoprotein whose binding sites are complementary to one specific antigen. Antibodies mark pathogens for destruction and neutralise toxins.
  • Plasma cells are B cells that have been activated and that secrete antibodies in large amounts.
  • Macrophages and antigen-presenting cells engulf the pathogen, break it down, and display its antigens on their surface (on MHC proteins). This shows helper T cells what to respond to.

6.10: B cells and T cells

  • B effector (plasma) cells secrete antibodies. B memory cells survive for years and give a faster, larger response on the next exposure to the same antigen.
  • T helper cells (CD4) recognise the antigen on an antigen-presenting cell and release cytokines that activate B cells and T killer cells.
  • T killer (cytotoxic, CD8) cells bind to infected or abnormal cells and kill them, for example by releasing perforin.
  • T memory cells persist after the infection and respond quickly if the same pathogen returns.

6.11: Types of immunity

  • Natural active: the person is infected and makes their own antibodies and memory cells.
  • Natural passive: antibodies pass from mother to baby across the placenta or in breast milk. Protection is immediate but short-lived, and no memory cells are formed.
  • Artificial active: vaccination with an antigen, a weakened or dead pathogen, or a toxoid. The person makes antibodies and memory cells without becoming ill.
  • Artificial passive: injected antibodies, such as antivenom or antitoxin. Protection is immediate and short-lived, and the person's own immune system does not learn.

6.12: The evolutionary race between pathogens and hosts

  • Pathogens evolve evasion mechanisms. Antigenic variation changes the surface antigens: influenza and HIV mutate rapidly, so antibodies no longer fit.
  • Other evasion: hiding inside host cells (tuberculosis in macrophages, HIV in T cells), entering latency, and suppressing the immune response.
  • The host responds with new antibodies and T cells, so pathogens and hosts keep evolving against each other. This is the evolutionary race.

6.13: Bacteriostatic and bactericidal antibiotics

  • Bacteriostatic antibiotics stop bacteria growing and dividing, for example by blocking protein synthesis. The immune system then clears the infection.
  • Bactericidal antibiotics kill bacteria, for example penicillin, which stops cell wall synthesis so the cell bursts.
  • Antibiotics do not act on viruses, which use the host cell's machinery.

6.14: Core practical 14: the effect of antibiotics on bacteria

  • Spread a lawn of bacteria on agar, place antibiotic discs on it, and include a control disc with no antibiotic.
  • Incubate, then measure the diameter of each clear zone of inhibition. A larger zone means the bacteria are more sensitive.
  • Use aseptic technique and non-pathogenic strains, and autoclave the plates before disposal.

6.15: Hospital-acquired infections and codes of practice

  • Contributory causes include overuse of broad-spectrum antibiotics, which selects for resistant strains such as MRSA, poor hand hygiene, indwelling catheters, surgical wounds, and immunocompromised patients.
  • Codes of practice respond to these causes: prescribe antibiotics only when needed and according to guidelines, enforce hand hygiene, isolate infected patients, and clean equipment and wards.

6.16: Decomposition and the carbon cycle

  • Bacteria and fungi are the main decomposers. They secrete extracellular enzymes that digest complex organic matter such as cellulose and proteins, then absorb the simpler products.
  • Respiration by decomposers releases carbon dioxide, which returns carbon to the atmosphere for producers. Ammonium released from proteins feeds the nitrogen cycle.

6.17: The polymerase chain reaction (PCR)

  • Each cycle has three steps: denaturation at about 95 °C separates the strands, annealing at about 50 to 65 °C lets primers bind, and extension at about 72 °C is when Taq polymerase builds the new strands.
  • Taq polymerase comes from the heat-tolerant bacterium Thermus aquaticus, so it survives the high temperatures. Around 30 cycles give an exponential increase in the number of copies.

6.18: Gel electrophoresis of DNA fragments

  • DNA carries a negative charge from its phosphate groups, so it moves towards the positive electrode (anode) through a gel.
  • Smaller fragments move faster and further, so fragments separate by length. A DNA ladder of known sizes is run alongside for comparison, and the bands are stained to make them visible.

6.19: DNA profiling for identification and relatedness

  • DNA profiling compares short tandem repeats (STRs) or variable number tandem repeats (VNTRs). These regions vary in length between individuals, so each person gives a distinctive band pattern.
  • Uses include identifying suspects, establishing paternity, and comparing the banding patterns of plants or animals to show how closely related they are.

6.20: Estimating the time of death from forensic evidence

  • Body temperature: the body cools towards the surroundings, so the rate of cooling gives an estimate of time since death.
  • Muscle contraction: rigor mortis sets in over hours, peaks, then fades over about a day or two.
  • Decomposition and succession: bacterial decomposition gives a predictable sequence of changes. Forensic entomology uses the stage of blowfly larvae and the succession of insect species to estimate how long the body has been exposed.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Growth rate, 6.3 applied: a culture grows from 2.0 × 10⁴ cells cm⁻³ at 2 hours to 1.6 × 10⁵ at 5 hours. N₂ ÷ N₁ = 8 = 2³, so three doublings in three hours. k = (ln 1.6 × 10⁵ − ln 2.0 × 10⁴) ÷ 3 = ln 8 ÷ 3 = 0.69 per hour. The doubling time is ln 2 ÷ k = 1.0 hour. Check the answer against the doubling count before you write it down.
  • Viable count, 6.2 applied: 150 colonies grow from 0.1 cm³ of a 10⁻⁵ dilution. That is 150 ÷ 0.1 = 1500 colonies per cm³ in the diluted sample, and multiplying by the dilution factor gives 1.5 × 10⁸ viable cells per cm³. A haemocytometer count would include dead cells, so the two methods can give different numbers from the same culture. Name which one you are using.
  • Log phase, 6.3 applied: plotting ln N against time gives a straight line only during exponential growth. A curve that bends is a sign that the lag, stationary or death phase has been included by mistake. Use only the straight section to find k.
  • Primary and secondary immune response, 6.10 and 6.12 applied: the first exposure has a lag of several days before antibodies peak at a lower level. A second exposure gives a faster, larger and longer-lasting response, because memory cells are already present. Use all three words, faster, larger and longer, to earn the full mark.
  • Antigen presentation, 6.9 applied: helper T cells (CD4) recognise antigen presented on MHC class II proteins, and killer T cells (CD8) recognise it on MHC class I, as on infected body cells. Naming the MHC class shows you understand which cell carries the antigen.
  • Antibiotic action, 6.13 applied: penicillin blocks the cross-linking of peptidoglycan in the cell wall, so a growing cell bursts. An antibiotic that targets a process human cells do not use, such as the bacterial ribosome, is more selective. Resistance arises by chance mutation and is selected for by the antibiotic, so the explanation must say the mutation was already present and survived.
  • PCR, 6.17 applied: after n cycles one DNA molecule has become 2ⁿ molecules. After 30 cycles that is 2³⁰, about 1.07 × 10⁹ copies. This is why a very small sample is enough, and why contamination with foreign DNA is a serious error.
  • Gel electrophoresis, 6.18 applied: the distance moved is roughly linear with the logarithm of the fragment length. Use a DNA ladder to plot log size against distance, then read the unknown band from that graph rather than from the ladder bands by eye.
  • Forensic estimates, 6.20 applied: a time-of-death answer is always a range. Temperature cooling assumes a stable environment, and a hot or wet site or a body wrapped in clothing changes the rate. Say which factor is most uncertain and why.

Exam tip: time-of-death questions are estimates. Name the method, say what it measures, and state the limitation, for example that temperature depends on the environment.

title: Communication and Networking
content:
`# Communication and Networking

Transmission

  • Serial: one bit at a time — cheaper, reliable over distance
  • Parallel: multiple bits simultaneously — fast but suffers skew and crosstalk over long runs
  • Direction: simplex (one way), half-duplex (alternating), full-duplex (both ways)

Packets and Protocols

Data splits into packets with header (addresses, sequence) and trailer (checksum). A protocol is an agreed rule set — without one, devices cannot interpret signals.

  • TCP/IP stack: application → transport → network → link
  • HTTP/HTTPS: web transfer; HTTPS encrypts with TLS
  • FTP: file transfer; SMTP/POP3/IMAP: email

Network Types

  • LAN: small site, privately owned; WAN: large geographic scale (the internet)
  • Topologies: bus, star, mesh (star is most common — central switch)

Hardware

Routers join networks by IP; switches forward frames by MAC within a LAN; gateways translate protocols.

Client-Server vs Peer-to-Peer

Client-server: central services, easy administration, single point of failure. P2P: every node shares files directly — cheap, hard to manage (torrents, blockchain).

Exam tips: explain packet switching with header/trailer details; justify protocol choice per application (email vs streaming).

title: Superposition — Study Notes
content:
Superposition

Principle of superposition

When two or more waves meet at a point, the resultant displacement is the vector sum of the individual displacements. Constructive interference occurs where the waves are in phase; destructive interference occurs where they are in antiphase.

Stationary waves

  • A stationary wave forms when two progressive waves of the same frequency, amplitude and wavelength travel in opposite directions and superpose.
  • Nodes are points of zero amplitude; antinodes are points of maximum amplitude. Adjacent nodes (or antinodes) are separated by λ/2.
  • On a string fixed at both ends, the fundamental frequency is f = v/(2L), so the wavelength is λ = 2L.

Interference

For coherent sources (same frequency and a constant phase difference) with slit separation a and screen distance D, the fringe spacing is Δx = λD/a.

Diffraction

Diffraction is the spreading of a wave after it passes through a gap or round an edge. It is greatest when the gap width is comparable to the wavelength.

Diffraction grating

For a grating with slit spacing d, the angle θ of the nth-order maximum satisfies nλ = d sin θ. A grating with more lines per metre gives a smaller d and larger angles of diffraction.

Worked example: light of wavelength 600 nm passes through two slits 0.30 mm apart, with a screen 1.5 m away. Fringe spacing Δx = λD/a = (600 × 10⁻⁹ × 1.5) ÷ (3.0 × 10⁻⁴) = 3.0 mm.

Exam tips: convert nm and mm to metres before using Δx = λD/a. Check the order n when using a grating. Coherence is a requirement for interference, so state it.

title: Algebra — Inequalities — Quick Revision Summary

Quick revision: Algebra — Inequalities

Mathematics — OL. solving linear inequalities, integer solution sets, shading regions on graphs (linear programming context).

  • 1. Solving
  • 2. Integer solutions
  • 3. Double inequalities
  • 4. Shading regions

How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

Worked example

Solve 2x − 3 < 7. Add 3 to both sides to get 2x < 10, then divide by 2 to get x < 5. If x is an integer and −2 ≤ x < 5, the integer solutions are −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4. The bounds are inclusive on the left and exclusive on the right, so the endpoint −2 is included and 5 is not.

Common mistakes

  • Reversing the inequality sign when you multiply or divide by a negative number, for example in −3x > 6, which gives x < −2.
  • Using a solid line for a strict inequality. Use a dashed line for < or >, and a solid line for ≤ or ≥.
  • Shading the wrong side. Test a point such as (0, 0) and shade the region that makes the inequality true.

title:
Respiration, Muscles and the Internal Environment — Edexcel International A2 Level Biology

This revision note covers the biology topics that sit behind the energy use of cells and animals and behind the maintenance of the internal environment. It is built around the specification statements rather than around a loose theme, so each numbered section reflects one or more things the specification expects a candidate to be able to do. The note is deliberately at exam depth: it explains the reasoning, gives the worked examples and comparisons that examiners look for, and lists the common mistakes that lose marks in this topic. Use it to check what you actually know and to practise the kinds of answer the specification rewards.

1. Why respiration matters and what the topic is for

Respiration is the set of reactions that release energy from nutrient molecules and couple that energy to the work cells do. The main nutrient in most questions is glucose, and the main energy currency that respiration produces is ATP. The practical point is that cells do not get energy directly from glucose; they get it from ATP, and respiration is the process that links the fuel to the currency.
