Glycolysis produces pyruvate, ATP and reduced NAD; the link reaction and Krebs cycle produce reduced NAD and reduced FAD and release CO2; oxidative phosphorylation uses the reduced coenzymes to make ATP and oxygen is the final electron acceptor, forming water. Oxygen is needed so the electron transport chain can continue and the bulk of ATP can be made. (6 marks)
  2. Explain why respiration is an energy-releasing process but still needs to be staged rather than happening in one reaction. Answer: Respiration releases energy from glucose but a single reaction releasing all the energy at once would mostly waste it as heat; the stages release energy in manageable amounts that the cell can use to phosphorylate ADP to ATP, the energy currency for cell work. Stage-by-stage release also allows regulation of the rate to match the cell’s needs. (4 marks)
  3. Describe the sliding filament model of muscle contraction and state the role of ATP in it. Answer: During contraction the actin and myosin filaments slide past each other rather than shortening themselves, so the sarcomere shortens. Myosin heads bind to actin, pivot and pull the thin filament toward the centre, then detach and re-cock. ATP is required for the myosin head to detach from actin and be re-cocked for the next cycle, so the contraction is powered by ATP hydrolysis. (5 marks)
  4. Explain the roles of calcium and ATP in the control of muscle contraction and relaxation. Answer: When a muscle is stimulated, calcium is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum and exposes the binding sites on actin so myosin heads can bind; ATP is used to power the cross-bridge cycle and to detach the myosin heads. Relaxation occurs when calcium is removed and the binding sites are covered again; ATP is still required for detachment, which is why a muscle without ATP stays contracted, as in rigor mortis. (5 marks)
  5. Describe the response of the body during exercise in terms of heart rate and breathing rate, and explain why each increases. Answer: During exercise heart rate increases to deliver more oxygenated blood to the muscles and to remove more carbon dioxide and heat, and breathing rate increases along with breathing depth to bring in more oxygen and remove more carbon dioxide. Both responses increase because the muscles’ ATP demand rises and the supply and waste-removal systems must keep up with the increased metabolism. (5 marks)
  6. Describe how the skin blood vessels help control body temperature and state the direction of the response in each case. Answer: Blood vessels near the skin surface dilate in heat, increasing blood flow near the surface and increasing heat loss to the environment; they constrict in cold, reducing blood flow near the surface and reducing heat loss. This is part of thermoregulation and homeostasis, along with other responses such as sweating or shivering and behavioural changes. (4 marks)
  7. Define homeostasis and explain the principle of negative feedback with one example. Answer: Homeostasis is the maintenance of a stable internal environment within limits. Negative feedback is the control principle in which a change from the set point is detected and the response reduces the change, returning the variable toward the set point; for example in temperature control, if body temperature rises, effectors such as sweating and vasodilation increase heat loss, reducing the temperature back toward normal. (5 marks)
  8. Explain why water and solute balance are part of homeostasis and what happens if the internal environment becomes too concentrated or too dilute. Answer: Cells depend on the water potential of the internal environment; if it becomes too concentrated, water moves out of cells by osmosis, and if it becomes too dilute, water moves into cells. Either change can disrupt cell function, so the concentrations of water and solutes must be controlled. The body loses water in breathing, sweating and urine, so water balance is dynamic and must be regulated. (5 marks)
  9. Explain the link between respiration and muscle activity during exercise and why sustained vigorous exercise can exceed the body’s aerobic capacity for a time. Answer: Muscle activity uses ATP, so respiration must increase to supply ATP; aerobic respiration is efficient and sustainable if oxygen supply is sufficient, but during vigorous exercise oxygen delivery may not keep up with demand, so the muscle relies relatively more on pathways that do not need oxygen and produces different products, which is why breathing and heart rate rise and why the body shifts its metabolism. (5 marks)
  10. State what the kidneys do to help maintain the internal environment. Answer: The kidneys remove waste from the blood and help control water and solute balance by adjusting the composition of the urine, so they are important for maintaining the composition of the internal environment and for disposing of the waste products of metabolism including the CO2-related and other wastes that result from respiration. (4 marks)
  11. Describe one example of negative feedback in the human body and identify the receptor, control centre and effector in that example. Answer: In temperature control, temperature receptors detect a rise in core or skin temperature, the hypothalamus acts as the control centre, and effectors such as sweat glands and skin blood vessels respond by increasing heat loss, returning temperature toward the set point. If temperature falls, effectors such as shivering and vasoconstriction reduce heat loss or increase heat production. (5 marks)

Revise this topic by matching each numbered specification point to one mechanism, one location and one reason. Practise the respiration stages and their products, the sliding filament idea with ATP and calcium, the exercise responses and the thermoregulation responses, and the homeostasis and negative feedback principle with examples. Check that you can say where each process happens and why, not just what happens. Then move on to the next topic and the related practicals, because the practicals are the way the specification ties the ideas to hands-on work.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Respiratory quotient, applied to glucose: RQ = CO₂ released ÷ O₂ consumed. For glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O, so RQ = 6 ÷ 6 = 1.0. Fats give a lower RQ of about 0.7, because they need more oxygen per CO₂ produced. Use the equation to calculate RQ, not a remembered value.
  • ATP yield, applied to glucose: glycolysis gives a net 2 ATP, the link reaction and Krebs cycle give 2 ATP, and reduced coenzymes from all three stages drive oxidative phosphorylation. The total is about 30–32 ATP depending on the shuttle used to bring reduced NAD into the mitochondrion. Quote the stage of each ATP, not just the total.
  • Location of stages: glycolysis takes place in the cytoplasm, the link reaction and Krebs cycle in the matrix, and oxidative phosphorylation on the inner mitochondrial membrane. Oxygen is the final electron acceptor and forms water, so without it the chain stops and ATP production falls.
  • Anaerobic respiration in muscle: without enough oxygen, pyruvate is converted to lactate, which regenerates NAD so glycolysis continues. The oxygen debt is the extra oxygen needed afterwards to convert the lactate back to glucose and to restore ATP and phosphocreatine. Name the reason, not just the product.

title: Statistics — Data Handling — Study Notes
content:
Statistics — Data Handling

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): averages from lists and tables, quartiles/IQR, charts, cumulative frequency, histograms.

1. Averages

  • Mean = Σfx/Σf from frequency tables. Median = middle value (ordered data). Mode = most frequent. Range = max − min.
  • Choose the best average: mode for shoe sizes, median when outliers distort the mean.

Example (table): goals 0,1,2,3 with f 5,8,4,3: mean = (0+8+8+9)/20 = 1.25.

2. Quartiles and IQR

Q₁ at n/4, Q₃ at 3n/4 (position); IQR = Q₃ − Q₁ — less affected by outliers than the range.

3. Charts

Bar charts, pie charts (angle = fraction × 360°), time series, pictograms. Compare data sets with like-for-like totals; comment on trends.

4. Cumulative frequency

Running totals vs upper class boundaries; the curve ends at (max, n). Median at n/2; Q₁/Q₃ at n/4 and 3n/4; box plot from the five-figure summary.

5. Histograms

Bar area ∝ frequency: FD = frequency ÷ class width. Recover frequencies as FD × width; unequal widths need FDs on the axis.

Exam tips: read cumulative-frequency answers with dashed construction lines; always compare spreads, not just averages, when asked to compare data.

Mean, median, mode and range

For ungrouped data, the mean is the sum of values divided by the number of values; the median is the middle value after ordering (the average of the two middle values if there is an even count); the mode is the most frequent value; the range is the largest minus the smallest value.

Frequency tables and grouped data

For a frequency table, the mean is the sum of (value × frequency) divided by the total frequency. For grouped data, use the midpoint of each class as the value and state that the answer is an estimate.

Charts and diagrams

Pie charts use angles: each sector angle is the category frequency divided by the total, multiplied by 360°. Bar charts have gaps between bars; histograms have no gaps, and for unequal class widths the height shown is frequency density.

title: A Level Mathematics: The Binomial Expansion
content:
A Level Mathematics: The Binomial Expansion

The binomial theorem expands (a + b)ⁿ without multiplying out n brackets. AS work covers positive integer powers with nCr coefficients; A2 extends it to negative and fractional powers as an infinite series, valid only inside a stated range of x. This note builds the theorem from Pascal's triangle through to the general term, then handles the negative and fractional cases, the validity condition, and the approximation questions that follow.

Pascal's triangle and nCr

coefficients of (a + b)^n are nCr = n!/(r!(n - r)!)

n = 0:        1
n = 1:       1 1
n = 2:      1 2 1
n = 3:     1 3 3 1
n = 4:    1 4 6 4 1

Each entry is the sum of the two above it. nCr counts the number of ways of choosing r items from n, which is exactly the number of ways the r b's can be selected from n brackets.

The binomial theorem

(a + b)^n = sum from r = 0 to n of nCr a^(n - r) b^r

general term: nCr a^(n - r) b^r

Worked example 1. Expand (2 + 3x)⁴.

coefficients 1, 4, 6, 4, 1
= 2⁴ + 4(2³)(3x) + 6(2²)(3x)² + 4(2)(3x)³ + (3x)⁴
= 16 + 96x + 216x² + 216x³ + 81x⁴

Worked example 2 (a single term). Find the coefficient of x³ in (1 + 2x)⁷.

term with x³: 7C3 (1)⁴ (2x)³ = 35 × 8 x³ = 280x³
coefficient 280

Worked example 3 (the constant term). Find the constant term in (x + 2/x)⁶.

general term: 6Cr x^(6 - r) (2/x)^r = 6Cr 2^r x^(6 - 2r)
constant when 6 - 2r = 0  →  r = 3
6C3 × 2³ = 20 × 8 = 160

Negative and fractional powers

(1 + x)^n = 1 + nx + n(n-1)x²/2! + n(n-1)(n-2)x³/3! + ...

valid for |x| < 1 when n is not a positive integer

The series is infinite, and the validity condition comes from the binomial series converging only for |x| < 1. Always state it.

Worked example 1. Expand (1 + x)^(−1) up to the term in x³.

n = -1: 1 + (-1)x + (-1)(-2)x²/2 + (-1)(-2)(-3)x³/6
= 1 - x + x² - x³,  valid for |x| < 1

Worked example 2 (fractional). Expand (1 + 2x)^(1/2) up to x².

n = 1/2: 1 + (1/2)(2x) + (1/2)(-1/2)(2x)²/2
= 1 + x - (1/8)(4x²) = 1 + x - x²/2
valid for |2x| < 1, i.e. |x| < 1/2

Worked example 3 (leading coefficient). Expand (4 + x)^(1/2) up to x².

factor out the 4: (4 + x)^(1/2) = 2(1 + x/4)^(1/2)
= 2[1 + (1/2)(x/4) + (1/2)(-1/2)(x/4)²/2]
= 2[1 + x/8 - x²/128]
= 2 + x/4 - x²/64,  valid for |x| < 4

The factorisation step is compulsory whenever the constant is not 1: the formula needs (1 + u)^n with |u| < 1, so the leading number must be taken outside.

Validity conditions

for (1 + ax)^n with n not a positive integer: |ax| < 1
after factorising (A + Bx)^n = A^n (1 + Bx/A)^n:
|Bx/A| < 1  →  |x| < |A/B|

Worked example. State the validity range for (3 − 2x)^(−2).

= 3⁻² (1 - 2x/3)⁻²
valid for |2x/3| < 1  →  |x| < 3/2

Approximation

Substituting a small x into a truncated series gives a numerical approximation; the error depends on how small x is and how many terms are kept.

Worked example. Use the first three terms of (1 + x)^(1/2) to estimate √1.02.

x = 0.02: 1 + 0.01 - (0.0004)/8 = 1.00995
calculator value √(1.02) = 1.009950..., agreement to 6 d.p.

Worked example 2 (fraction). Estimate (1.01)^(−1) using three terms and state whether the estimate is above or below the true value.

1 - 0.01 + 0.0001 = 0.9901
true value 1/1.01 = 0.990099...
the estimate 0.9901 is slightly above, since the next term is negative

Why the coefficients are nCr

Expanding (a + b)ⁿ means choosing a or b from each of n brackets and multiplying the choices. A term with r b's arises once for every way of choosing those r brackets from n, and there are nCr such ways. That argument proves the theorem and is itself examinable: it explains both the symmetry of the coefficients (nCr = nC(n−r)) and why the row sums are 2ⁿ.

sum of nCr over r = 0..n = 2^n   (set a = b = 1)
alternating sum = 0                (set a = 1, b = -1)
nCr = nC(n - r)                    (choosing r is choosing which to leave out)

Worked example. Show that the coefficients of x² and x⁴ in (1 + x)⁶ are equal.

6C2 = 15 and 6C4 = 15, as nCr = nC(n - r) with n = 6

Coefficients from products of expansions

A common A2 question multiplies two expansions and asks for one coefficient. Only the pairs that produce the required power matter, so write the contributing terms side by side.

Worked example. Find the coefficient of x² in (1 + x)(1 − 2x)⁵.

(1 - 2x)⁵ = 1 - 10x + 40x² - ...
contributions to x²: 1 × 40x² and x x (-10x)
coefficient = 40 - 10 = 30

Worked example 2 (unknown constant). In the expansion of (2 + kx)⁴ the coefficient of x² is 216. Find k.

x² term: 6(2²)(kx)² = 24k² x²
24k² = 216  →  k² = 9  →  k = 3 or -3

Both roots are usually valid unless the question states k > 0; state both and, if the context fixes the sign, say why.

Partial fractions then a binomial series

When an expression is a rational function, split it into partial fractions first, then expand each piece — each has its own validity range, and the answer takes the intersection.

Worked example. Expand 3/[(1 + x)(2 - x)] up to x² and state the range.

partial fractions: 1/(1 + x) + 1/(2 - x)
first piece: (1 + x)⁻¹ = 1 - x + x² - ...  valid |x| < 1
second: (2 - x)⁻¹ = (1/2)(1 - x/2)⁻¹ = (1/2)(1 + x/2 + x²/4)  valid |x| < 2
sum: 3/2 - x/2 + (3/4)x²
the combined range is the stricter: |x| < 1

The intersection rule is the point: a sum of series is valid only where every piece converges.

Approximation error and checking

Truncating an infinite series leaves an error of the size of the next term, which is why keeping one more term improves the estimate substantially when x is near the edge of the range.

Worked example. Estimate (1.1)^(1/2) with two terms and with three, and compare with the calculator.

two terms: 1 + 0.05 = 1.05
three terms: 1.05 - 0.05²/8 = 1.04875
calculator: 1.0488088...
adding the third term halves the error

Worked example 2. Explain why the series for (1 − 3x)^(1/2) cannot estimate √(1 − 3(0.5)) reliably.

the validity range is |x| < 1/3, and x = 0.5 lies outside it
the series diverges there, so any truncated sum is meaningless

Two unknowns in one expansion

Some questions fix the expansion of (a + bx)ⁿ through two given coefficients. Each coefficient supplies one equation, and the pair is solved simultaneously.

Worked example. In the expansion of (2 + px)⁵ the coefficient of x is 80 and the coefficient of x² is 720. Find p.

x term: 5(2⁴)(px) = 80p x  →  80p = 80  →  p = 1
x² term: 10(2³)(px)² = 80p²  →  80p² = 720  →  p² = 9
contradiction: p = 1 does not satisfy the second equation, so check
the reading of the question - here the consistent pair comes from
solving the x² equation alone for p = +3 or -3, and testing which
reproduces the x coefficient when the constant is also unknown

When both the constant and the coefficient are unknown, write the two coefficient equations and solve them as a pair; a single coefficient cannot determine two unknowns.

Worked example 2. In (1 + ax)ⁿ the coefficient of x is 12 and of x² is 60. Find a and n.

x: na = 12
x²: n(n - 1)a²/2 = 60
substitute a = 12/n: n(n - 1)(144/n²)/2 = 60
72(n - 1)/n = 60  →  72n - 72 = 60n  →  n = 6, a = 2

That pair of equations is the standard exam shape, and eliminating a is always quicker than eliminating n.

Formula summary

(a + b)^n = sum nCr a^(n-r) b^r
general term: nCr a^(n-r) b^r
(1 + x)^n = 1 + nx + n(n-1)x²/2! + ...  (|x| < 1 for n not a
positive integer)
(A + Bx)^n = A^n (1 + Bx/A)^n, valid |Bx/A| < 1

Two habits prevent most lost marks: factorise the leading constant before expanding, and quote the validity range in the same line as the series. A third is to write the general term before substituting anything, because the general term locates the power you need in one step instead of guesswork.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Expand) Expand (1 + x)⁵. Answer: 1 + 5x + 10x² + 10x³ + 5x⁴ + x⁵.
  2. (Coefficient) Find the coefficient of x² in (1 − 3x)⁶. Answer: 15 × 9 = 135.
  3. (Term) Find the term in x⁴ in (2 + x)⁶. Answer: 15(4)x⁴ = 60x⁴.
  4. (Constant) Find the constant term in (2x − 1/x)⁴. Answer: need 4 − 2r = 0 → r = 2; 6(4)(1) = 24.
  5. (Negative power) Expand (1 − x)^(−2) to x³. Answer: 1 + 2x + 3x² + 4x³.
  6. (Fractional) Expand (1 + 3x)^(1/3) to x². Answer: 1 + x − x².
  7. (Validity) State the range for (1 + 5x)^(−1). Answer: |x| < 1/5.
  8. (Approximate) Estimate (0.98)^(−1) to three terms. Answer: 1 + 0.02 + 0.0004 = 1.0204.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Forgetting to factorise: (4 + x)^n must become 4ⁿ(1 + x/4)ⁿ before the series is applied; using the formula directly is wrong.
  • Validity not stated: for negative or fractional powers the range is part of the answer, and a mark is attached to it.
  • Wrong power of the constant: in (2 + 3x)⁴ the term is 4(2³)(3x), not 4(2⁴)(3x).
  • Coefficient versus term: the question may want the coefficient (280) or the whole term (280x³); read it.
  • Rising powers of the wrong part: the r index applies to the second term, with a^(n−r) on the first.
  • nCr on a calculator: use the nCr function, not n!/r!, to avoid overflow and arithmetic slips.
  • Truncated series treated as exact: state the approximation and its limitation; the series is infinite.
  • Sign errors with negative n: alternate signs are expected when n is negative; a run of positive terms signals a slip.

title: Bonding and Structure — Study Notes
content:
Bonding and Structure

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH11, Topic 3. Every statement 3.1 to 3.22 is covered below, with its code in the heading so you can check your own gaps against the specification. The big idea: the type of bonding and the shape of a molecule explain almost every physical property a question can ask about, including melting point, conductivity, solubility and polarity.

3.1 to 3.2: Evidence for ions, and how they form

  • Evidence for ions: ionic compounds conduct electricity only when molten or dissolved, because the ions are then free to move. In electrolysis, a coloured ion such as manganate(VII), MnO₄⁻, migrates to the positive electrode (the anode), which is direct evidence that it carries a negative charge.
  • Electron density maps for ionic compounds show near-spherical regions of electron density around each ion, with a clear drop in density between them.
  • Formation by loss or gain of electrons: sodium loses one electron to form Na⁺ (2,8,1 becomes 2,8), while chlorine gains one to form Cl⁻ (2,8,7 becomes 2,8,8). A metal loses electrons to form a positive ion; a non-metal gains electrons to form a negative ion.

3.3: Dot-and-cross diagrams for ions

  • Show the outer electrons of each atom as dots or crosses. For a cation such as Mg²⁺, the outer shell is empty, so the symbol is written with square brackets and the charge: [Mg]²⁺.
  • For an anion such as O²⁻, the transferred electrons are added to the outer shell, which then holds eight electrons: [O]²⁻ with eight dots and crosses inside the brackets.
  • Always put the charge outside the brackets, and check that the total number of electrons transferred matches the charges.

3.4 to 3.5: Giant ionic lattices and the ionic bond

  • An ionic crystal is a giant lattice of alternating positive and negative ions, repeating in three dimensions. There are no discrete molecules, so the formula, such as NaCl, is only the simplest ratio of ions. In sodium chloride each Na⁺ is surrounded by six Cl⁻ ions and each Cl⁻ by six Na⁺ ions (6:6 coordination).
  • An ionic bond is the strong net electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions. "Net" matters: the attraction between a cation and an anion is partly cancelled by repulsion between like ions, but the attraction wins at the equilibrium distance.

3.6: Effect of ionic radius and ionic charge on bond strength

  • The electrostatic attraction grows with the charge on the ions and falls as the ions get larger, because the centres of charge are further apart.
  • Compare MgO (melting point about 2850 °C) with NaCl (about 800 °C). Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ carry double charges and are small, so their attraction is much stronger than that between the singly charged, larger Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions.

3.7: Trends in ionic radius

  • Down a group, ionic radius increases, because each ion has an additional electron shell. Li⁺ is smaller than Na⁺, which is smaller than K⁺.
  • Across a set of isoelectronic ions, all the species have the same number of electrons (ten, in the series N³⁻, O²⁻, F⁻, Na⁺, Mg²⁺, Al³⁺). The nuclear charge rises from 7 to 13 across the series, so the outer electrons are pulled in more strongly and the radius falls. N³⁻ is the largest and Al³⁺ the smallest.

3.8 to 3.9: Polarisation of ions

  • Polarisation is the distortion of the electron cloud of an anion by a nearby cation. The cation pulls the anion's electron density towards itself, so the bonding stops being purely ionic and gains covalent character.
  • The polarising power of a cation is greatest when it is small and highly charged. Al³⁺ > Mg²⁺ > Na⁺.
  • The polarisability of an anion is greatest when it is large and highly charged, because its outer electrons are held loosely. I⁻ is more polarisable than Br⁻, which is more polarisable than Cl⁻, which is more polarisable than F⁻.
  • Example: aluminium chloride has a low melting point and sublimes, far below what a purely ionic lattice would need. The small, highly charged Al³⁺ polarises the chloride ions strongly, so the bonding is largely covalent.

3.10: Covalent bonding and the evidence for it

  • A covalent bond is the strong electrostatic attraction between two nuclei (both positive) and the shared pair of electrons between them.
  • Evidence: giant atomic structures such as diamond and silicon(IV) oxide have very high melting points, which only strong covalent bonds can explain. Electron density maps for simple molecules such as hydrogen show a build-up of electron density between the two nuclei.

3.11: Dot-and-cross diagrams for covalent substances

  • Multiple bonds: in carbon dioxide, O=C=O, each double bond is two shared pairs. In nitrogen, N≡N, there are three shared pairs.
  • Dative (coordinate) bonds: both electrons in the shared pair come from one atom, the donor, which has a lone pair. The arrow points from donor to acceptor. In the ammonium ion, NH₄⁺, the nitrogen in NH₃ donates its lone pair to H⁺.
  • Aluminium chloride dimer, Al₂Cl₆: each aluminium has four chlorines. Two of the chlorines bridge the two aluminium atoms, and each bridging chlorine forms a dative bond from a chlorine lone pair into the empty orbital of the other aluminium.

3.12: Giant carbon structures: diamond, graphite and graphene

  • Diamond: each carbon forms four single covalent bonds in a tetrahedral giant lattice. It is very hard, has a very high melting point and does not conduct, because there are no free electrons. It is used in cutting and drilling tools.
  • Graphite: each carbon forms three bonds in flat hexagonal sheets. The fourth outer electron on each carbon is delocalised, so graphite conducts along the sheets. The sheets are held by weak forces and slide over each other, so graphite is soft and is used as a lubricant and as electrodes.
  • Graphene: a single sheet of graphite, one atom thick. It is very strong, conducts well and is light and flexible. Applications include electronics, sensors and composite materials.

3.13 to 3.14: Electronegativity and the bonding continuum

  • Electronegativity is the power of an atom to attract the bonding pair of electrons in a covalent bond. Fluorine is the most electronegative element (4.0 on the Pauling scale).
  • The bonding continuum: the bigger the electronegativity difference between two atoms, the more polar the bond. A very small difference gives a non-polar covalent bond, a moderate difference gives a polar covalent bond (as in HCl), and a very large difference gives essentially ionic bonding (as in NaCl). Ionic and covalent bonding are the two ends of this continuum, not separate categories.

3.15: Polar bonds and polar molecules

  • A polar bond has a permanent dipole. A molecule is polar only if its bond dipoles do not cancel, so polar bonds do not automatically make a polar molecule.
  • Carbon tetrachloride, CCl₄: the C–Cl bonds are polar, but the tetrahedral arrangement cancels them, so the molecule is non-polar.
  • Water, H₂O, is bent, so its dipoles add up and the molecule is polar. Carbon dioxide is linear, so its two C=O dipoles cancel and it is non-polar.

3.16 to 3.19: Electron-pair repulsion and molecular shapes

  • Electron-pair repulsion theory: bonding pairs and lone pairs around a central atom repel each other and arrange themselves to be as far apart as possible.
  • Lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs, so lone pairs compress bond angles. The order of repulsion is lone pair to lone pair, then lone pair to bonding pair, then bonding pair to bonding pair.
  • 3.17, bond length and bond angle: bond length is the distance between the nuclei of two bonded atoms. Bond angle is the angle between two bonds at the central atom. Triple bonds are shorter than double bonds, which are shorter than single bonds (C≡C shorter than C=C shorter than C–C).

3.18, the shapes and bond angles of the named species:

SpeciesElectron pairs on central atomShapeBond angle
BeCl₂2 bondingLinear180°
BCl₃3 bondingTrigonal planar120°
CH₄4 bondingTetrahedral109.5°
NH₃3 bonding, 1 loneTrigonal pyramidalabout 107°
NH₄⁺4 bondingTetrahedral109.5°
H₂O2 bonding, 2 loneBentabout 104.5°
CO₂2 bonding (double bonds)Linear180°
PCl₅ (gas)5 bondingTrigonal bipyramidal90° and 120°
SF₆6 bondingOctahedral90°
C₂H₄3 regions around each carbonPlanar around each carbonabout 120°

Applying the same rules to analogous species (3.19): SiH₄ is tetrahedral (109.5°), BF₃ is trigonal planar (120°), PH₃ is pyramidal (about 93°), H₂S is bent (about 92°), XeF₄ is square planar (90°, with two lone pairs), and ClF₃ is T-shaped. Count the electron pairs first, then decide how many are lone pairs.

3.20 to 3.22: Metallic bonding and the properties of metals

  • A metal is a giant lattice of positive metal ions in a sea of delocalised electrons, the outer electrons that are free to move through the whole structure.
  • 3.21, metallic bonding is the strong electrostatic attraction between the metal cations and the delocalised electrons. It is not a bond between two particular atoms.
  • Electrical conduction: the delocalised electrons carry charge through the metal when a voltage is applied.
  • High melting temperature: the attraction is strong and is non-directional, so a lot of energy is needed to overcome it. Magnesium melts at about 650 °C, far above sodium at about 98 °C, because Mg²⁺ carries a double charge and provides two delocalised electrons per atom.
  • Malleability: the layers of ions can slide over each other, and the delocalised electrons keep the ions attracted to each other as they move, so the metal does not shatter.

A* extension: worked reasoning for the hardest bonding questions

  • Bond angles, 3.18 applied: CH₄ is 109.5°, NH₃ about 107°, and H₂O about 104.5°. Each lone pair pushes the bonding pairs closer together, because lone pair to bonding pair repulsion is stronger than bonding pair to bonding pair. So the angle falls by roughly 2.5° per lone pair. An A* answer states the reason in these terms, not just the number.
  • Polarity, 3.15 applied: CH₃Cl is polar, because the C–Cl dipole is not cancelled by the C–H bonds, which point in roughly symmetrical directions but carry much smaller dipoles. CCl₄ is non-polar, because four identical C–Cl dipoles point to the corners of a tetrahedron and cancel exactly. Always say which dipoles cancel and why.
  • Electronegativity and bonding continuum, 3.14 applied: aluminium chloride has an electronegativity difference of about 1.5 between Al and Cl. That is not large enough to make it purely ionic, so it is a polar covalent bond, which is consistent with its low melting point and the polarisation argument in 3.8 to 3.9.
  • Lattice and bond strength, 3.6 applied: when asked to compare two ionic compounds, name both the charge and the radius, and say which one dominates. Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ beat Na⁺ and Cl⁻ on both counts, so MgO has the much higher melting point.
  • Mark-scheme phrasing for metallic bonding (3.21): "giant lattice of positive ions", "sea of delocalised electrons", "strong electrostatic attraction between the ions and the delocalised electrons". Each phrase earns its own mark, so use all three.
  • Graphite versus graphene, 3.12 applied: an electrode question expects you to name the delocalised electron, and a lubricant question expects you to name the weak forces between layers. Give both mechanisms when the question says "explain".

Common errors that lose marks

  • Saying covalent or metallic bonds are "between molecules" (they are within the structure; the forces between molecules are intermolecular forces).
  • Calling a polar bond a polar molecule. Always check the shape before you decide the molecule's polarity.
  • Saying ions "move" in solid ionic compounds. They vibrate in place; only molten or dissolved compounds conduct through ion movement.

title: Quadratics — Study Notes
content:
Quadratics

Cambridge International AS & A Level Mathematics 9709, Paper 1. Quadratic questions ask for a turning point, the roots, or a condition on a parameter. Most multi-part questions use all three, so decide the job of each part before you calculate.

Start from a question

The function is f(x) = 2x² − 8x + 11.

  1. Find the minimum value of f(x) and the value of x at which it occurs.
  2. Find the values of k for which f(x) = k has real roots.
  3. Find the value of m for which the line y = x + m is a tangent to y = f(x).

Part 1. Complete the square: f(x) = 2(x − 2)² + 3. The minimum value is 3, at x = 2.

Part 2. f(x) = k gives 2x² − 8x + (11 − k) = 0. The discriminant is 64 − 8(11 − k) = 8k − 24. Real roots need 8k − 24 ≥ 0, so k ≥ 3, which agrees with Part 1.

Part 3. Substituting y = x + m gives 2x² − 9x + (11 − m) = 0. A tangent needs equal roots, so 81 − 8(11 − m) = 0. That gives 8m − 7 = 0, so m = 7/8.

Turning points and the square

For ax² + bx + c, the turning point is at x = −b/2a. The sign of a decides the type: a > 0 gives a minimum and a < 0 gives a maximum. Example: for 2x² − 12x + 7, the turning point is at x = 3, and the value there is 18 − 36 + 7 = −11.

Solving

Try factorising first. If that fails, use x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac))/2a and simplify the surd. Example: 3x² + 5x − 4 = 0 has discriminant 25 + 48 = 73, so x = (−5 ± √73)/6.

The discriminant counts roots

D = b² − 4ac gives the number of real roots: D > 0 gives two distinct roots, D = 0 gives one repeated root, and D < 0 gives none. Example: 4x² + kx + 9 = 0 has equal roots when k² = 4 × 4 × 9 = 144, so k = ±12. With k = 12 the equation is (2x + 3)² = 0.

A parameter inside the discriminant

When D contains an unknown, form the inequality and solve it. Example: x² + (k − 1)x + 4 = 0 has real roots when (k − 1)² − 16 ≥ 0. So |k − 1| ≥ 4, which gives k ≤ −3 or k ≥ 5.

Sketch, then read the region

For a positive a, the curve is below the x-axis between its roots and above it outside them. Example: 2x² − x − 6 < 0 factorises as (2x + 3)(x − 2) < 0, so −3/2 < x < 2.

Example: 5 − 3x − 2x² ≥ 0. Multiplying by −1 gives 2x² + 3x − 5 ≤ 0, and the inequality reverses. (2x + 5)(x − 1) ≤ 0 gives −5/2 ≤ x ≤ 1.

A line and a curve

Set the two equations equal and rearrange into one quadratic. Example: y = x + 3 and y = 2x² − x meet where 2x² − 2x − 3 = 0. Here D = 28 > 0, so the line cuts the curve at two points.

Traps that cost marks

  • Multiplying an inequality by a negative number and forgetting to reverse it.
  • Using D = 0 for a "no real roots" condition, when it should be D < 0.
  • Giving a single value when the question allows a range of values.
  • Dropping the ± when taking the square root of both sides.

title: International GCSE English as a Second Language: Prepositions and Collocations
content:
International GCSE English as a Second Language: Prepositions and Collocations

Prepositions — at, on, in, by, for, of, with — are the smallest words that cause the biggest problems, because English chooses them by habit rather than by logic. That habit has a name: collocation, the tendency of words to appear together (depend on, good at, by accident). This note builds the full system from zero: the core spatial and temporal prepositions with their reasoning, the adjective, verb and noun collocation tables an exam candidate must know, phrasal verbs for everyday exam topics, and the collocational errors that most often cost accuracy marks in the 9280 writing and speaking papers.

What collocation is: the knife-and-fork analogy

Some words in English come in pairs the way knives and forks do. A native speaker says make a decision, not do a decision, and heavy rain, not strong rain — not because logic demands it, but because that is the established pairing. You cannot compute collocations; you learn them as units, the way you learned football and homework as single items of vocabulary. The good news for exam candidates: the testable collocation set is finite, and the exam repeats the same few hundred pairs every session.

The core three: at, on and in

The most-tested prepositions follow a containment logic: at is a point (a point in space or time), on is a surface or line, in is an enclosed space or a bounded period.

PrepositionTimePlace
atat 7 o'clock, at night, at noon, at the moment, at the weekendat the bus stop, at the door, at school, at home, at work
onon Monday, on 3 May, on my birthday, on Friday morningon the table, on the wall, on the bus (as a passenger), on the second floor
inin May, in 2026, in the morning, in the holidays, in two hoursin the room, in London, in a car (as a passenger), in the garden

The exceptions earn their own marks: at night but in the morning (the day parts take in, night takes at); at the weekend (British) / on the weekend (American); on a bus but in a car; in time (before the deadline) versus on time (exactly at the scheduled moment).

Worked example. "The meeting is ___ Monday ___ 9 am ___ the morning ___ May." Step 1: day → on Monday. Step 2: clock time → at 9 am. Step 3: part of the day → in the morning. Step 4: month → in May. Answers: on / at / in / in. Method visible: decide whether each target is a point (at), a surface/day (on), or an enclosed period (in).

Prepositions of movement and position

  • to / into / onto: to = direction (go to school), into = entering (walk into the room), onto = onto a surface (jump onto the wall).
  • at / to after verbs of position: arrive at (a place), arrive in (a city or country), get to.
  • above / over / under / below: over and under imply vertical opposition (the bridge over the river); above and below are relative levels (the temperature fell below zero).
  • between / among: between two or more distinct things (between the shops), among a group (among the crowd).

Adjective + preposition collocations

This table is the highest-yield collocation list for the exam; learn each adjective with its preposition as one chunk.

AdjectivePrepositionExample
afraid, frightened, scaredofafraid of the dark
good, bad, excellent, betteratgood at mathematics
interestedininterested in history
proudofproud of my sister
responsibleforresponsible for the project
famousforfamous for its beaches
keenonkeen on football
fed up, boredwithfed up with the noise
angry, annoyedwith (a person) / about (a thing)angry with my brother about the mess
marriedtomarried to a teacher
usedtoused to the climate
differentfromdifferent from the others
similartosimilar to mine
polite, kind, rude, generoustokind to animals

Verb + preposition collocations

VerbPrepositionExample
depend, relyonIt depends on the weather.
listentolisten to the radio
applyfor (a job) / to (an institution)apply for the job, apply to university
belongtobelong to my brother
consistofconsist of three parts
arriveat / inarrive at the station, arrive in Spain
explain, suggest, describe, discuss(no to with an object: explain something to someone)explain the problem to me — never "explain me the problem"
succeedinsucceed in passing the exam
apologisefor (something) / to (someone)apologise for being late, apologise to my teacher
pay, wait, ask, thankforpay for the tickets, wait for the bus
thinkabout (consider) / of (have an opinion)think about the offer, think of a better idea

The explain/suggest family is the single most common first-language interference error: these verbs never take a personal indirect object without to. "Explain me the rule" is wrong; "explain the rule to me" is right. Likewise "suggest me a book" is wrong; "suggest a book to me" or "recommend a book to me" is right.

Noun + preposition collocations

  • reason for, cause of, solution to, answer to, invitation to, damage to, effect on, advantage/disadvantage of, increase/decrease in, demand for, opportunity for, experience of/in, attitude to/towards.
  • Prepositional phrases of manner and circumstance: by accident, on purpose, by mistake, at least, at last, in fact, in spite of, due to, because of, according to.

Worked example. Correct the sentence: "She explained me the reason of the delay and asked an apology." Step 1: explain + object + to: "She explained the reason for the delay to me." (reason for, not reason of.) Step 2: ask for an apology — but the meaning is she apologised; the writer wanted "apologised for the delay". Cleanest correction: "She explained the reason for the delay to me and apologised." Two errors in one sentence: verb pattern and noun collocation.

Phrasal verbs for exam topics

Phrasal verbs are verb + particle units whose meaning is not predictable from the parts. The exam themes repeat a manageable set:

Phrasal verbMeaningTheme
look aftercare forfamily, children
grow upbecome an adultidentity, biography
get on withhave a good relationship withpeople, colleagues
find outdiscover informationstudy, research
sign up forenrol incourses, jobs
carry oncontinueany theme
give upstop trying / quithabits, work
cut down onreducehealth, environment
run out ofexhaust the supplyresources, money
take part inparticipateevents, sport
come up withthink of (an idea)study, projects
deal withhandleproblems, stress

Worked examples: collocation decisions

Worked example 1 — gap fill with reasoning. "I am very keen ___ tennis, but I am not very good ___ it. My coach says I need to concentrate ___ my serve and stop worrying ___ losing." Step 1: keen on (adjective collocation) → on. Step 2: good at → at. Step 3: concentrate on → on. Step 4: worry about → about. Answers: on / at / on / about. Every answer is a memorised pair; the reasoning is retrieval, not translation.

Worked example 2 — prepositions of time in a real task. "My course starts ___ September and finishes ___ the end of June. I have exams ___ the first week ___ June, and results come ___ August." Step 1: month → in September. Step 2: fixed phrase → at the end of June. Step 3: a bounded week inside June → in the first week of June (note the second of: week of June). Step 4: in August. Answers: in / at / in / in ... of ... in.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. Fill with at / on / in: "The flight leaves ___ 6:30 ___ Tuesday ___ the morning." Answer: at / on / in.
  2. Fill with adjective collocations: "She is afraid ___ speaking ___ large audiences but is very good ___ writing speeches." Answer: of / to / at. (speak to an audience; good at writing.)
  3. Correct the errors: "He explained me the problem and suggested me to wait." Answer: "He explained the problem to me and suggested that I wait." Why: explain and suggest never take a bare personal object.
  4. Choose: "The solution ___ the problem is a change ___ the law." (of / to / for / in / of) Answer: solution to the problem, change in the law.
  5. Choose the phrasal verb: "If you want to ___ smoking, try to ___ it ___ gradually." Answer: give up ... cut down on ... (give up smoking; cut down on it gradually).
  6. Fill: "We arrived ___ the airport late ___ night ___ the end of the holiday." Answer: at / at / of. (arrive at a point; at night; at the end of.)

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Translating the preposition: "depends of", "married with", "interested on" — the L1 preposition is not the English one. Learn the pairs as chunks and test yourself with gap fills, not translation.
  • explain me / suggest me: the classic transfer error; both verbs need to + person or no person at all.
  • discuss about: discuss takes no preposition ("we discussed the plan"), and "answer to the question" is wrong for the verb ("answer the question" — answer to exists only as a noun: the answer to).
  • Preposition stranding avoided wrongly: "Who did you talk to?" is correct English; "To whom did you talk?" is correct but overly formal for most tasks. Match the register.
  • Time/at-on-in slips: at night / in the morning / on Monday morning — the part-of-day rule (in) and the day-surface rule (on) combine.
  • Strong vs heavy: collocation again — heavy rain, strong wind, big mistake (not strong mistake). Quantifier adjectives are memorised pairs.
  • Phrasal-verb register: "give up the job" is informal; formal writing prefers resign from the post. Choose phrasal verbs for informal tasks and their single-word equivalents for formal ones.
  • Double prepositions: "Where are you going to?" with a destination already stated, or "discuss about" — check each verb's pattern once in the final proofread.

Equations and symbols

For a grammar topic the "equation" is a mapping rule: a type of time or place on the left, the preposition on the right. Learn the mapping, not the translation — the same four rules answer every gap-fill.

day → on Monday Key: left = the category the target belongs to (a named day or date); right = the preposition that category always takes. Collocation, not logic: there is no reason "on" belongs to a day, only that English fixed it that way.

clock time → at 9 am Key: left = a point in time, including at noon, at night, at the weekend (BrE); right = the preposition for points. Change the category and the preposition changes, which is why the decision comes before the word.

part of the day → in the morning Key: left = an enclosed period (morning, afternoon, evening, month, year, season); right = "in". The exception worth memorising is "at night", the one part of the day that behaves like a point.

month → in May Key: left = a month or year; right = "in", because the period encloses the event. Compare "in May" with "on 3 May", where naming the day moves the target into the day category.

keen on (adjective collocation) → on Key: left = the adjective and the preposition it is fixed to (keen on, good at, interested in, worried about); right = the preposition to retrieve. The word after the gap is what tells you which pair you are in — read it before you choose.

title: Kinematics — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Kinematics

Physics — AS. Sign convention matters: take up as positive and g = −9.81 m s⁻² for falling objects.

Key areas to revise

  • Definitions
  • Graphs
  • SUVAT (uniform acceleration only)
  • Projectiles

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Worked example

A ball is dropped from rest and falls 20 m. Taking down as positive, u = 0, s = 20 m and a = 9.81 m s⁻². Then v² = u² + 2as = 392.4, so v ≈ 19.8 m s⁻¹. Using the sign convention with up positive instead gives s = −20 m and a = −9.81 m s⁻², which gives the same answer with the signs consistent.

Common mistakes

  • Using SUVAT for a case with non-uniform acceleration, such as a body with increasing air resistance.
  • Mixing signs, for example taking up as positive but using g = +9.81 m s⁻².
  • Reading a displacement–time gradient as velocity only when it is a straight line. The gradient gives instantaneous velocity at any point on a curve.

Worked example

A ball is dropped from rest and falls 20 m. Taking down as positive, u = 0, s = 20 m and a = 9.81 m s⁻². Then v² = u² + 2as = 392.4, so v ≈ 19.8 m s⁻¹. Using the sign convention with up positive instead gives s = −20 m and a = −9.81 m s⁻², which gives the same answer with the signs consistent.

Common mistakes

  • Using SUVAT for a case with non-uniform acceleration, such as a body with increasing air resistance.
  • Mixing signs, for example taking up as positive but using g = +9.81 m s⁻².
  • Reading a displacement–time gradient as velocity only when it is a straight line. The gradient gives instantaneous velocity at any point on a curve.

title: Coordination, Response and Gene Technology
content:
Quick revision: Coordination, Response and Gene Technology

Biology — A2. Edexcel IAL Biology WBI15, Topic 8. Nervous and hormonal systems coordinate the body, and plants respond to light and gravity using hormones. Gene technology uses enzymes to cut, join and copy DNA for medicine, research and agriculture.

  • 8.1 Sensory neurones carry impulses from receptors to the CNS, relay neurones connect sensory and motor neurones within the CNS, and motor neurones carry impulses from the CNS to effectors, all featuring Schwann cells wrapping around axons to form a myelin sheath that insulates the axon.
  • 8.2 The nervous system causes effectors such as muscles or glands to respond to a stimulus by generating action potentials that travel to neuromuscular junctions or gland endings.
  • 8.3 A spinal reflex arc consists of a receptor, sensory neurone, relay neurone in the grey matter of the spinal cord, motor neurone, and effector, with white matter containing myelinated axons ascending and descending to the brain.
  • 8.4 Action potentials are conducted along an axon via depolarisation caused by voltage-gated sodium ion channels opening and sodium ions rushing in, followed by repolarisation caused by voltage-gated potassium ion channels opening and potassium ions rushing out.
  • 8.5 Myelination allows saltatory conduction where the action potential jumps from one node of Ranvier to the next, drastically increasing the speed of nerve impulse transmission.
  • 8.6 Synapses transmit impulses between neurones using neurotransmitters such as acetylcholine diffusing across the synaptic cleft, and the pupil dilates via radial muscles in dim light and contracts via circular muscles in bright light.
  • 8.7 Drugs affect nerve transmission such as nicotine mimicking acetylcholine, lidocaine blocking voltage-gated sodium channels, cobra venom blocking acetylcholine receptors, L-DOPA acting as a dopamine precursor to treat Parkinson's disease, and MDMA increasing neurotransmitter release.
  • 8.8 Rods in the retina detect light when photon absorption converts cis-retinal to trans-retinal, causing rhodopsin to break down into opsin and retinal, closing sodium cation channels, stopping sodium influx, and hyperpolarising the rod cell to initiate action potentials in optic neurones.
  • 8.9 Habituation is a decrease in response to a repeated stimulus that is harmless, preventing unnecessary energy expenditure.
  • 8.10 The mammalian nervous system consists of the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord) and the peripheral nervous system (cranial and spinal nerves).
  • 8.11 Plant responses are controlled by phytochrome which changes form in red and far-red light affecting transcription, auxin (IAA) which causes cell elongation and affects transcription, and gibberellins which stimulate seed germination by promoting amylase transcription.
  • 8.12 Core Practical 18 investigates the production of amylase in germinating cereal grains by measuring starch breakdown under varying conditions.
  • 8.13 Coordination in animals is brought about through rapid, targeted nervous control and slower, chemical hormonal control travelling in the blood.
  • 8.14 The cerebral hemispheres control conscious thought and sensory processing, the hypothalamus regulates homeostasis, the pituitary gland secretes hormones, the cerebellum coordinates balance and voluntary movement, and the medulla oblongata controls involuntary functions like heart rate and breathing.
  • 8.15 Medical imaging techniques include MRI and CT for structural detail, fMRI for localized brain activity during tasks, and PET for metabolic activity using radioactive tracers.
  • 8.16 Imbalances in brain chemicals cause ill health, such as a shortage of dopamine in Parkinson's disease and low serotonin levels in depression, informing the design of new drugs.
  • 8.17 Therapeutic drugs and proteins can be produced using genetically modified organisms including transgenic plants, animals, and microorganisms like bacteria and yeast.
  • 8.18 Recombinant DNA is produced by using restriction endonucleases to cut DNA at specific palindromic recognition sites to yield sticky or blunt ends, and DNA ligase to join the sugar-phosphate backbones of the DNA insert and vector.
  • 8.19 Recombinant DNA can be inserted into host cells using vectors such as plasmids, bacteriophages, or through methods like electroporation, microinjection, and liposomes.
  • 8.20 Microarrays use fluorescently labelled cDNA to hybridise with fixed single-stranded DNA probes, identifying which genes are actively being transcribed in a cell.
  • 8.21 Bioinformatics is the collection, storage, and computational analysis of large biological datasets such as genomic sequences and amino acid databases using software tools.
  • 8.22 Genetically modified organisms carry risks such as gene transfer to wild relatives and ethical concerns, alongside benefits like increased crop yields, disease resistance, and mass production of essential medical proteins.

Worked example

Explain how lidocaine affects the transmission of a nerve impulse. Step 1: Identify that lidocaine is a local anaesthetic drug. Step 2: Relate its mechanism of action to axonal membranes. Lidocaine binds to and blocks voltage-gated sodium ion channels on the axon membrane. Step 3: State the consequence on the action potential. Sodium ions cannot enter the axon, preventing the membrane from depolarising, so the action potential cannot be generated or propagated along the neurone, blocking pain signals to the CNS.

Key points to remember

Students often confuse hyperpolarisation in rod cells with depolarisation in axons; remember that in the dark rod cells are depolarised and releasing neurotransmitter, but light hyperpolarises them and stops neurotransmitter release.

When describing recombinant DNA, always mention the specific roles of both restriction endonucleases for cutting DNA and DNA ligase for sealing phosphodiester bonds, as omitting either loses credit.

For plant growth factors, make sure to link auxin and gibberellin action directly to transcription and protein synthesis rather than just simple cell stretching.

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

title: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Ratio, Rate and Proportion
content:
Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Ratio, Rate and Proportion

Ratio, rate and proportion are the mathematics of comparison: how two quantities share a whole, how fast one changes with another, and what happens when one stays on the same path to infinity. They appear in nearly every Paper 2, usually as multi-step word problems where the arithmetic is easy and the interpretation is not. This note builds the topic from zero: simplifying and dividing in ratios, the unitary method for direct and inverse proportion, the algebra forms y = kx and y = k/x, and rates — speed, density, flow — with their unit conversions.

Ratio fundamentals

A ratio compares quantities of the same kind. The notation a : b means "a for every b". Equivalent ratios are made by multiplying or dividing all parts by the same number; the simplified ratio has no common factor (other than 1) and, for measurements, the same units.

  • Simplify: 24 : 36 = 2 : 3 (divide both by 12).
  • Three-part: 2 : 3 : 5 means five shares in total; each share is total ÷ 10.
  • Units first: 500 g : 1.5 kg = 500 : 1500 = 1 : 3. Convert before simplifying, never after.

Worked example. Share £84 in the ratio 3 : 4.

total parts = 3 + 4 = 7
one part = 84/7 = 12
shares = 3 × 12 = 36 and 4 × 12 = 48
check: 36 + 48 = 84

Worked example 2 (three parts). A sum of $240 is divided among A, B and C in the ratio 2 : 3 : 5. Find each share.

parts = 2 + 3 + 5 = 10
one part = 240/10 = 24
A = 2 × 24 = 48, B = 3 × 24 = 72, C = 5 × 24 = 120

Combining ratios and ratio changes

Two ratios sharing a middle term can be combined by making that term common:

A : B = 2 : 3 and B : C = 4 : 5
LCM of the B terms (3 and 4) is 12:
A : B = 8 : 12 and B : C = 12 : 15
so A : B : C = 8 : 12 : 15

Worked example (change). A bag contains red and blue counters in the ratio 5 : 3. After 6 red counters are removed, the ratio becomes 1 : 1. Find the original numbers.

let red = 5x, blue = 3x
(5x - 6)/3x = 1  →  5x - 6 = 3x  →  2x = 6  →  x = 3
original: red = 15, blue = 9
check: after removing 6 red, 9 : 9 = 1 : 1

Direct proportion

Two quantities are in direct proportion when one is a constant multiple of the other: double one, double the other. The algebra form is y = kx, a straight line through the origin.

y = k x        k = y/x (the constant of proportionality)
unitary method: find the value of one unit, then multiply

Worked example. 5 pens cost $3.25. Find the cost of 12 pens.

one pen = 3.25/5 = $0.65
12 pens = 12 × 0.65 = $7.80

Worked example 2 (algebra form). y is directly proportional to x, and y = 18 when x = 6. Find y when x = 11.

y = kx  →  18 = 6k  →  k = 3
y = 3 × 11 = 33

Worked example 3 (proportion with powers). The mass of a sphere is proportional to the cube of its radius; a sphere of radius 2 cm has mass 40 g. Find the mass of a sphere of radius 3 cm.

m = k r³  →  40 = k x 8  →  k = 5
m = 5 × 27 = 135 g

Inverse proportion

Inverse proportion means one quantity falls as the other rises: double one, halve the other. The algebra form is y = k/x (the product xy is constant).

y = k/x        x y = k
unitary method: find the total "work" (product), then divide

Worked example. Six workers build a wall in 8 days. How long will 4 workers take (same rate)?

total work = 6 × 8 = 48 worker-days
time for 4 = 48/4 = 12 days

Worked example 2 (algebra). y is inversely proportional to x; y = 5 when x = 4. Find y when x = 10.

xy = k  →  4 × 5 = 20  →  y = 20/10 = 2

The shape on a graph distinguishes the two: direct proportion is a straight line through the origin; inverse proportion is a curve that never touches either axis (a hyperbola).

Rates

A rate compares quantities with different units: speed (distance per time), density (mass per volume), pressure (force per area), flow rate (volume per time). Each is a division, and each can be rearranged.

speed = distance/time        density = mass/volume
pressure = force/area        flow rate = volume/time

average speed over a journey = total distance/total time
(not the average of the speeds, unless the times are equal)

Worked example 1 (speed). A car travels 150 km in 2 hours 30 minutes. Find its average speed in km/h and m/s.

time = 2.5 h
speed = 150/2.5 = 60 km/h
in m/s: 60 × 1000/3600 = 16.7 m/s

Worked example 2 (density). A block of volume 250 cm³ has mass 675 g. Find its density, and the mass of 400 cm³ of the same material.

density = 675/250 = 2.7 g/cm³
mass = 2.7 × 400 = 1080 g = 1.08 kg

Worked example 3 (average speed trap). A cyclist rides 20 km at 20 km/h, then 20 km at 10 km/h. Find the average speed for the whole journey.

time 1 = 20/20 = 1 h;  time 2 = 20/10 = 2 h
total distance = 40 km; total time = 3 h
average speed = 40/3 = 13.3 km/h (not 15!)

Flow rates and filling problems

Flow-rate questions combine a rate with a volume: a tap fills at 4 litres per minute, a pump empties at 6 litres per minute, a pipe delivers water at 2.5 m s⁻¹ through a cross-section. The method is the same division, but the units demand attention — litres per minute into litres and minutes, cubic metres per second into m³ and s, with 1 m³ = 1000 litres and 1 minute = 60 s.

Worked example. A bath holds 180 litres. A tap fills it at 9 litres per minute, but the plug leaks 1.5 litres per minute. How long does the bath take to fill?

net rate = 9 - 1.5 = 7.5 litres per minute
time = 180/7.5 = 24 minutes

Best buys and multi-step comparisons

Ratio reasoning powers the practical comparison questions: which packet is better value, which journey is faster per kilometre, which contract costs less per month. The method is always to reduce both options to the same unit before comparing, and to compare like with like (price per 100 g, cost per km, cost per month).

Worked example. A 750 g box of cereal costs $3.60 and a 1.2 kg box costs $5.28. Which is better value?

large: 5.28/1.2 = $4.40 per kg
small: 3.60/0.75 = $4.80 per kg
better value: the 1.2 kg box (lower cost per kg)

Worked example 2 (multi-step). Two phone contracts: A charges $12 per month plus $0.10 per GB; B charges $20 per month with 15 GB included. For someone using 20 GB per month, which is cheaper over a year?

A: 12 + 0.10 × 20 = $14 per month; yearly = 168
B: $20 per month; yearly = 240
A is cheaper for a 20 GB user by $72 per year.
(check the crossover: 12 + 0.1g = 20 → g = 80 GB, so B
only wins for very heavy users)

The crossover point is a favourite extension: set the two cost expressions equal and solve, then interpret which side of the crossing each customer sits on.

Worked examples: mixed problems

Worked example. A recipe for 4 people uses 300 g of rice. How much is needed for 10 people, and how many people can be served with 2.1 kg?

per person = 300/4 = 75 g
for 10: 750 g
2100 g / 75 = 28 people

Worked example 2 (currency). An exchange rate is £1 = $1.25. Convert £240 to dollars and $500 to pounds.

240 × 1.25 = $300
500/1.25 = £400

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Divide) Share 360 in the ratio 5 : 7. Answer: parts 12; one part 30; shares 150 and 210.
  2. (Simplify with units) Simplify 40 minutes : 2 hours. Answer: 40 : 120 = 1 : 3.
  3. (Direct) 8 m of cloth costs $52. Find the cost of 13 m. Answer: per metre $6.50; 13 × 6.50 = $84.50.
  4. (Inverse) 4 taps fill a tank in 45 minutes. How long for 6 taps? Answer: total = 4 × 45 = 180 tap-minutes; 180/6 = 30 minutes.
  5. (Algebra) y ∝ x² and y = 50 when x = 5. Find y when x = 8. Answer: 50 = k × 25 → k = 2; y = 2 × 64 = 128.
  6. (Rate) A train covers 210 km in 2 h 20 min. Find its average speed. Answer: 2⅓ h; 210 ÷ 7/3 = 90 km/h.
  7. (Density) 150 cm³ of a liquid has mass 120 g. Find the mass of 1 litre. Answer: density 0.8 g/cm³; 1000 cm³ × 0.8 = 800 g.
  8. (Reverse) A map scale is 1 : 50 000. Two points are 7 cm apart on the map. Find the real distance in km. Answer: 7 × 50 000 = 350 000 cm = 3.5 km.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Averaging speeds: average speed is total distance over total time, never the mean of the two speeds unless the times are equal. The classic 20/10 km/h trap answers 15 instead of 13.3.
  • Ratio direction: dividing 84 in 3 : 4 is not 84 × 3/4 for both shares; identify which share is which before writing the answer.
  • Units in ratios: 500 g : 1.5 kg simplifies only after conversion to 500 : 1500 = 1 : 3. Mixing units gives 1 : 0.003.
  • Direct versus inverse: ask "if one doubles, what happens to the other?" Doubling both means direct; one doubling while the other halves means inverse.
  • Proportional to a power: for y ∝ x², doubling x multiplies y by 4; for y ∝ √x it multiplies by √2. Find k from the given pair first.
  • Currency direction: multiplying by the rate converts one way; the reverse needs division. Check with a rough estimate.
  • Time units: 2 h 30 min is 2.5 h, not 2.3 h. Convert minutes to a decimal fraction of an hour before dividing.
  • Rounding mid-calculation: keep full accuracy until the final answer, then round to 3 s.f. or as instructed; money answers usually need 2 decimal places.

title: A Level Physics: Circular Motion and SHM
content:
A Level Physics: Circular Motion and SHM

Circular motion is motion at constant speed but changing velocity — because velocity is a vector, turning is accelerating. This note builds the kinematics of uniform circular motion from zero: angular displacement and angular velocity, the relation v = ωr, centripetal acceleration and the force that causes it, and then the beautiful connection to simple harmonic motion — SHM is literally the shadow of circular motion. Every formula is derived from the geometry, and the standard calculation types (car cornering, vertical circles, conical pendulums, satellite orbits) are worked in full.

Kinematics of uniform circular motion

An object moving in a circle at constant speed has a continuously changing direction, so its velocity changes continuously — it is accelerating. Two measures describe the motion:

angular displacement: theta (radians); one revolution = 2 pi rad
angular velocity: omega = theta/t = 2 pi/T = 2 pi f   (rad s-1)
linear speed: v = omega r        (m s-1)

period T = 2 pi/omega; frequency f = 1/T

The analogy: a point on a record's edge and a point near its centre complete a revolution in the same time, but the edge point travels further — hence v = ωr. Angular velocity is shared; linear speed depends on radius.

Worked example. A wheel of radius 0.30 m spins at 20 revolutions per minute. Find ω and the speed of a point on its rim.

f = 20/60 = 0.333 Hz  ->  omega = 2 pi f = 2.09 rad s-1
v = omega r = 2.09 x 0.30 = 0.63 m s-1

Centripetal acceleration

The acceleration of circular motion points toward the centre — it changes the direction of velocity, not its magnitude. From the geometry of a small angular displacement, the change in velocity points inward with magnitude v²/r:

a = v^2/r = omega^2 r        (directed toward the centre)

centripetal force: F = m a = m v^2/r = m omega^2 r

Derivation sketch worth reproducing in an exam: as the object turns through a small angle θ, the velocity triangle has a small change Δv perpendicular to v, and Δv/v = Δs/r (similar triangles), so Δv/Δt = (v/r)(Δs/Δt) = v²/r. The direction of Δv is toward the centre — hence centripetal.

Worked example. A 1200 kg car rounds a bend of radius 50 m at 15 m s⁻¹. Find the centripetal force.

F = m v^2/r = 1200 x 225/50 = 1200 x 4.5 = 5400 N
The force is provided by friction between tyres and road.

Where the centripetal force comes from

Centripetal force is not a new kind of force — it is the name for whatever real force points toward the centre:

SituationForce providing the centripetal effect
Car on a flat bendstatic friction between tyres and road
Car on a banked trackcomponent of the normal reaction
Satellite in orbitgravitational attraction
Ball on a stringtension in the string
Electron in a magnetic fieldmagnetic force (qvB)
Conical pendulumhorizontal component of tension

The exam favourite is the vertical circle: at the top of a loop, gravity and any normal force both point down and together provide mv²/r; the minimum speed to stay in contact is when the normal force falls to zero, so mg = mv²/r and v_min = √(gr).

Worked example (vertical circle). A ball on a string of length 0.80 m is swung in a vertical circle. Find the minimum speed at the top for the string to stay taut.

at the top: mg + T = mv^2/r; minimum when T = 0
v_min = sqrt(g r) = sqrt(9.81 x 0.80) = sqrt(7.85)
      = 2.8 m s-1

Worked example (banked track). A track is banked at angle θ with no friction. Show that the design speed satisfies tan θ = v²/(rg).

vertical: N cos(theta) = mg
horizontal (centripetal): N sin(theta) = mv^2/r
divide: tan(theta) = v^2/(r g)

Circular motion and SHM: the projection connection

Watch a point moving uniformly around a circle from the side: its shadow on a diameter moves back and forth with simple harmonic motion. This is not an analogy — it is an identity, and it lets you derive every SHM equation from circular motion:

if a particle moves on a circle of radius A with angular
velocity omega, its projection on a diameter has
displacement x = A cos(omega t)  (or A sin, depending on start)
velocity v = -A omega sin(omega t)
acceleration a = -omega^2 A cos(omega t) = -omega^2 x

maximum speed at the centre: v_max = A omega
maximum acceleration at the extremes: a_max = A omega^2

So the SHM angular frequency ω is exactly the angular velocity of the reference circle, and the period T = 2π/ω. The geometry also explains the phase relationships: velocity leads displacement by a quarter turn (90°), acceleration is anti-phase with displacement (180°).

Worked example. A point moves on a circle of radius 0.050 m at 3.0 rad s⁻¹. Find the amplitude, period and maximum speed of its projection.

amplitude A = 0.050 m
T = 2 pi/omega = 6.28/3.0 = 2.1 s
v_max = A omega = 0.050 x 3.0 = 0.15 m s-1

Applications: centrifuges and looping tracks

Circular motion is engineered into everyday machines. A centrifuge spins samples so that the required centripetal force — provided by the container walls — vastly exceeds gravity; denser components need a larger force at the same radius, so they settle outward and separate. The same logic sizes a washing machine's spin cycle (water leaves through the drum holes when the required force exceeds what surface tension can supply) and a car's brake discs (ventilation handles the frictional heat).

A looping track is the vertical-circle problem made physical: at the top of the loop the riders' weight and the track's normal reaction both point inward, providing mv²/r; the design speed is set just above v = √(gr) so the normal reaction never falls to zero and contact is maintained. Rollercoaster designers use the excess above that minimum to create the sensation of lightness without losing the car.

Worked examples: the standard exam types

Worked example 1 (conical pendulum). A 0.20 kg mass on a 1.0 m string moves in a horizontal circle, the string at 30° to the vertical. Find the tension and the period.

vertical: T cos(30) = mg  ->  T = 0.20 x 9.81/0.866 = 2.27 N
radius: r = L sin(30) = 0.50 m
horizontal: T sin(30) = m v^2/r
2.27 x 0.5 = 0.20 x v^2/0.50  ->  v^2 = 2.84  ->  v = 1.69 m s-1
T_period = 2 pi r/v = 6.28 x 0.50/1.69 = 1.86 s

Worked example 2 (satellite). Find the orbital speed of a satellite at radius 7.0 × 10⁶ m around Earth (M = 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg).

GMm/r^2 = mv^2/r  ->  v = sqrt(GM/r)
v = sqrt(6.67 x 10^-11 x 5.97 x 10^24/7.0 x 10^6)
  = sqrt(5.69 x 10^7) = 7.54 x 10^3 m s-1

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Angular velocity) A cyclist's wheel of radius 0.35 m turns at 2.0 revolutions per second. Find the speed of the rim. Answer: ω = 2π × 2.0 = 12.6 rad s⁻¹; v = ωr = 12.6 × 0.35 = 4.4 m s⁻¹.
  2. (Acceleration) State the direction of centripetal acceleration and explain why speed stays constant. Answer: It points toward the centre, perpendicular to the velocity; because the acceleration has no component along the velocity, it changes direction only, not speed.
  3. (Force) A 0.15 kg ball on a 0.60 m string moves at 4.0 m s⁻¹ in a horizontal circle. Find the tension. Answer: T = mv²/r = 0.15 × 16/0.60 = 4.0 N.
  4. (Vertical circle) Explain why a bucket of water can be swung overhead without spilling. Answer: At the top, the water's weight provides the centripetal force; if v ≥ √(gr) the water stays in contact with the bucket base, so it does not fall out.
  5. (Banking) A bend of radius 80 m is banked for 20 m s⁻¹. Find the angle. Answer: tan θ = v²/(rg) = 400/(80 × 9.81) = 0.510; θ = 27°.
  6. (SHM link) Explain how simple harmonic motion can be modelled by the projection of circular motion. Answer: A point moving uniformly on a circle of radius A projects onto a diameter as x = A cos ωt; differentiating gives v and a with a = −ω²x, the defining SHM condition.
  7. (Satellite) Show that the period of a satellite is proportional to r^(3/2). Answer: v = √(GM/r) and T = 2πr/v, so T = 2πr/√(GM/r) = 2π√(r³/GM), hence T ∝ r^(3/2).
  8. (Misconception) A student says a car turning at constant speed has no acceleration. Correct the statement. Answer: Velocity is a vector; its direction changes continuously in a turn, so the car accelerates centripetally toward the centre of the turn even though the speedometer reading is constant.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • The centrifugal fiction: there is no outward force in the inertial frame; the "centrifugal force" felt in a turning car is the inertia of your body, not a force on the car. Never put it on a free-body diagram.
  • v²/r with the wrong r: radius from the centre of the circular path — for a conical pendulum r = L sin θ, not the string length.
  • ω versus v: v = ωr; forgetting the radius converts angular to linear incorrectly. And ω in rad s⁻¹ means revolutions per second × 2π.
  • Units of angle: radians, not degrees, in ω = 2π/T and in the projection equations.
  • Centripetal force is not extra: it is the resultant of the real forces (tension, friction, weight component) — do not add it alongside them.
  • Vertical circles: tension and weight are collinear at top and bottom but not at the sides; resolve properly rather than assuming T = mv²/r everywhere.
  • Period direction: T = 2πr/v uses the circumference; mixing in angular velocity without converting gives factor-of-2π errors.
  • SHM phase: the projection can be sine or cosine depending on the starting point; state your choice and stay consistent.
  • Precision: 2 or 3 s.f. with units (rad s⁻¹, m s⁻¹, N, s); keep π symbolic until the end to avoid rounding drift.

Equations and symbols

Every relation this topic can be examined on, in the form the mark scheme expects, with a key naming each symbol and its unit. The derivations in the sections above end here: if you can write these from memory and say what each symbol means, the algebra in the exam is bookkeeping.

12.1 Kinematics of uniform circular motion

θ = s / r
Key: θ = angular displacement (rad); s = arc length travelled along the circle (m); r = radius of the circle (m). The radian is defined by this ratio, so an angle in radians is a pure number — one complete revolution is 2π rad = 360°.

ω = Δθ / Δt = 2π / T = 2π f
Key: ω = angular velocity (rad s⁻¹); Δθ = angular displacement (rad); Δt = time taken (s); T = period, the time for one revolution (s); f = frequency of revolution (Hz). Uniform circular motion means ω is constant while the direction of the velocity changes continuously.

v = ω r
Key: v = linear speed along the tangent (m s⁻¹); ω = angular velocity (rad s⁻¹); r = radius (m). The same ω for two points on a rotating body gives them speeds in the ratio of their radii — the rim of a wheel moves faster than a point near its hub.

f = 1 / T
Key: f = frequency (Hz); T = period (s). A wheel turning 20 times a minute has f = 20/60 = 0.33 Hz and T = 3.0 s.

a = v² / r = ω² r = ω v
Key: a = centripetal acceleration (m s⁻²); v = speed (m s⁻¹); r = radius (m); ω = angular velocity (rad s⁻¹). Directed towards the centre at every instant; the speed is constant but the velocity is not, because its direction changes, and that change is the acceleration.

F = m a = m v² / r = m ω² r
Key: F = resultant centripetal force (N); m = mass of the moving object (kg); a = centripetal acceleration (m s⁻²); v = speed (m s⁻¹); r = radius (m); ω = angular velocity (rad s⁻¹). Not a new kind of force — it is the name for whatever real force points to the centre: tension, gravity, friction or the normal contact force.

Turning, banking and vertical circles

tan θ = v² / (r g)
Key: θ = angle of banking of the road, or the angle the string makes with the vertical for a conical pendulum (°); v = speed of the vehicle or bob (m s⁻¹); r = radius of the circular path (m); g = 9.81 m s⁻². Derived by dividing the horizontal equation N sin θ = m v²/r by the vertical N cos θ = m g, so the normal force cancels.

at the top of a vertical circle: T + m g = m v² / r
Key: T = tension in the string, or the normal contact force from the track (N); m = mass (kg); g = 9.81 m s⁻²; v = speed at the top (m s⁻¹); r = radius (m). Both the weight and the tension point towards the centre, so they add.

v_min = √(g r)
Key: v_min = minimum speed at the top for the object to stay on its path (m s⁻¹); g = 9.81 m s⁻²; r = radius (m). Found by setting T = 0 at the top: below this speed gravity alone exceeds the required centripetal force and the object leaves the circle.

at the bottom of a vertical circle: T − m g = m v² / r
Key: T = tension (N); m = mass (kg); g = 9.81 m s⁻²; v = speed at the bottom (m s⁻¹); r = radius (m). Here the tension must support the weight as well as provide the centripetal force, so the string is most likely to break at the bottom.

energy between top and bottom: ½ m v_bottom² = ½ m v_top² + m g (2 r)
Key: v_bottom, v_top = speeds at the lowest and highest points (m s⁻¹); m = mass (kg); g = 9.81 m s⁻²; r = radius (m); 2r = the vertical drop. The bridge between the two parts of a looping-track question.

12.2 Linking circular motion to SHM

a = − ω² x
Key: a = acceleration (m s⁻²); ω = angular frequency of the oscillation (rad s⁻¹); x = displacement from the equilibrium position (m). The defining condition of simple harmonic motion: acceleration is proportional to displacement and always directed back towards the centre.

x = A cos(ω t)
Key: x = displacement at time t (m); A = amplitude, the maximum displacement (m); ω = angular frequency (rad s⁻¹); t = time from the start of the motion (s). A sine form with the matching initial condition is equally valid — the physics is the same, only the phase differs.

v = ± ω √(A² − x²)
Key: v = velocity at displacement x (m s⁻¹); ω = angular frequency (rad s⁻¹); A = amplitude (m); x = displacement (m). Fastest at the centre where x = 0, momentarily zero at the extremes where x = ±A.

v_max = ω A, a_max = ω² A
Key: v_max = maximum speed, at the equilibrium position (m s⁻¹); a_max = maximum acceleration, at the extremes (m s⁻²); ω = angular frequency (rad s⁻¹); A = amplitude (m). The two numbers most questions actually ask for.

T = 2 π / ω
Key: T = period of the oscillation (s); ω = angular frequency (rad s⁻¹). The link between the SHM equations and the timing of the motion.

T = 2 π √(m / k)
Key: T = period (s); m = mass on the spring (kg); k = spring constant, force per unit extension (N m⁻¹). Mass–spring oscillator: a stiffer spring or a lighter mass oscillates faster, and amplitude does not affect the period.

T = 2 π √(l / g)
Key: T = period (s); l = length of the simple pendulum (m); g = 9.81 m s⁻². Valid only for small oscillations (a few degrees), where sin θ ≈ θ; the period is independent of the mass of the bob, which is what makes a pendulum a clock.

E_total = ½ m ω² A²
Key: E_total = total energy of the oscillator (J); m = mass (kg); ω = angular frequency (rad s⁻¹); A = amplitude (m). Constant in undamped SHM, exchanged continuously between kinetic and potential forms.

KE = ½ m ω² (A² − x²), PE = ½ m ω² x²
Key: KE = kinetic energy (J); PE = potential energy (J); m = mass (kg); ω = angular frequency (rad s⁻¹); A = amplitude (m); x = displacement (m). The two add to E_total at every point, which is the quickest check on either.

phase: v leads x by π/2, and a is in antiphase with x (π)
Key: x = displacement, v = velocity, a = acceleration of the oscillator; the phase differences are in radians. At the equilibrium position x = 0 while v is greatest and a is zero; at an extreme v = 0 while a is greatest and opposite to x.

G M / r² = v² / r ⇒ v = √(G M / r)
Key: G = gravitational constant, 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²; M = mass of the central body (kg); r = orbital radius from its centre (m); v = orbital speed (m s⁻¹). Circular motion with gravity as the centripetal force — a satellite is simply falling around the planet rather than into it.

T = 2 π √(r³ / (G M))
Key: T = orbital period (s); r = orbital radius (m); G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²; M = mass of the central body (kg). Kepler's third law, obtained by substituting v = 2πr/T into the equation above; r³/T² is the same for every satellite of the same body.

title: IGCSE Biology: Transport in Plants
content:
IGCSE Biology: Transport in Plants

A tall tree can lift water more than 100 metres from soil to leaf without a single pump — no heart, no muscles, just physics and two sets of microscopic pipes. This note explains the structure of xylem and phloem, how root hair cells take water in, how the transpiration stream pulls a continuous water column up the plant (with the potometer method that measures it), and how sugars are translocated from leaves to the rest of the plant. Every mechanism is built from the underlying physical idea first — evaporation, cohesion, osmosis, active transport — then named, so you can reconstruct it in the exam rather than recite it.

Xylem and phloem: the two transport systems

Vascular tissue runs through roots, stems and leaves as veins. Xylem carries water and dissolved mineral ions upwards from the roots to the leaves. Its vessels are dead, hollow tubes made of lignified cells stacked end to end with perforated end walls — wide bore, no cytoplasm, lignin-thickened walls that resist collapse under negative pressure. Phloem carries sucrose (the translocate) and amino acids both up and down the plant, from source (leaves, or storage organs in spring) to sink (roots, fruits, growing tips). Its sieve tubes are living cells with thin walls, perforated sieve plates at the ends, and no nucleus at maturity; each sieve tube element is kept alive by a companion cell packed with mitochondria. Root, stem and leaf arrangement: in roots the xylem sits in a central star; in stems the vascular bundles form a ring near the outside (giving strength); in leaves they branch as veins.

Xylem and phloem compared

FeatureXylemPhloem
CarriesWater and dissolved mineral ionsSucrose and amino acids (translocate)
DirectionUpwards only (roots to leaves)Both directions (source to sink)
CellsDead, hollow, lignified wallsLiving sieve tube elements with companion cells
End wallsPerforated or absentSieve plates with pores
MechanismTranspiration pull and cohesionPressure flow (active loading/unloading)
