Water uptake by root hair cells

The root hair is a long extension of an epidermal cell, giving a huge surface area and a thin wall for a short diffusion path. Soil water has a higher water potential than the cell sap of the root cortex cells, so water enters the root hair by osmosis and then passes from cell to cell across the cortex (by osmosis, down the water potential gradient — living layers of the endodermis with their Casparian strip force the symplastic route), until it reaches the xylem. Mineral ions enter by active transport (against their gradient, using carrier proteins and ATP from respiration), which lowers the water potential in the root and helps water follow by osmosis. The whole route: soil solution → root hair → cortex cells → endodermis → xylem. The alternative pathway (through cell walls — the apoplastic route) is blocked at the endodermis by the waterproof Casparian strip, forcing water into the living cells where it can be controlled.

The transpiration stream

Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from the aerial parts of the plant, mainly through the stomata. The mechanism: water evaporates from the spongy mesophyll cell walls into the air spaces of the leaf; this water vapour diffuses out through open stomata down its concentration gradient into the drier air outside. The evaporation pulls the remaining water molecules into the gap (transpiration pull), and because water molecules are cohesive (hydrogen-bonded to each other), they form a continuous column from root to leaf: as molecules leave the top, they pull the next ones up behind them (the cohesion-tension theory). Root pressure and capillary action in the narrow xylem vessels assist. The transpiration stream thus has two consequences: water reaches the leaves for photosynthesis, and dissolved mineral ions travel with it to where they are needed.

Factors affecting transpiration and the potometer

Transpiration increases with: higher temperature (water molecules evaporate faster), lower humidity (steeper diffusion gradient), more wind (water vapour carried away, maintaining the gradient), and higher light intensity (stomata open for carbon dioxide). It decreases when stomata close in darkness, in drought (guard cells lose turgor), or in cold. Xerophytes (cacti, marram grass) have adaptations to cut it: thick cuticle, sunken stomata, rolled leaves, hairs to trap moist air, reduced leaves (spines). The potometer measures water uptake as a proxy for transpiration: a cut leafy shoot is sealed into a capillary tube of water with an air bubble; as the shoot transpires, the bubble moves along the tube; distance moved per minute measures the rate. Keep the apparatus airtight (grease the seal), use the same shoot for all trials, and control temperature, light, humidity and air movement. Note the assumption: uptake ≈ transpiration (some water is used in photosynthesis and growth).

Translocation: moving sugars

Translocation is the movement of sucrose and amino acids in the phloem from source to sink, in both directions depending on the season (down from leaves in summer; up from root stores in spring). Loading sucrose into the sieve tubes at the source (by companion cells, using ATP — active transport) lowers the water potential, water enters by osmosis from the xylem, the pressure rises, and the solution mass-flows towards sinks where sucrose is unloaded (raising water potential, water leaves). This is the pressure-flow hypothesis. Evidence examiners like: aphid stylet experiments (sap collects where the stylet punctures a sieve tube; the exudate is sugary and under pressure), and ringing a stem (removing phloem causes sugars to accumulate above the cut, swelling the bark, while xylem is undisturbed). Sucrose is the transport sugar — not glucose — because it is non-reducing, stable and soluble.

Worked example: potometer data and transpiration reasoning

A potometer's bubble moved 12 cm in 30 minutes at 20 °C in still air. Calculate the rate and predict the effect of a fan. Step 1: rate = distance ÷ time = 12 cm ÷ 30 min = 0.4 cm per minute. Step 2: with a fan, the boundary layer of saturated air around the leaf is swept away, keeping the diffusion gradient steep — the rate increases, perhaps to 0.7 cm/min. Step 3: percent change = (0.7 − 0.4) ÷ 0.4 × 100 = 75 % increase. A second calculation: water loss per day — if 0.4 cm/min over a 12-hour day and the capillary tube bore corresponds to 0.02 cm³ per cm, daily uptake = 0.4 × 60 × 12 × 0.02 = 5.76 cm³. Use the numbers given in any real question, and always quote units (cm per minute, cm³ per hour) — unitless answers lose a mark.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Swapping xylem and phloem: xylem = water up (dead, lignified); phloem = sugars both ways (living, sieve plates). A memory hook: "xylem is for X-tra water".
  • Saying transpiration is "the plant breathing": it is evaporation of water through stomata.
  • Forgetting cohesion in the explanation of the transpiration stream: the continuous hydrogen-bonded column is the whole mechanism.
  • Describing water movement in the xylem as osmosis — xylem is dead, so water movement there is bulk flow under tension, not osmosis.
  • Confusing translocation (sugars in phloem) with transpiration (water vapour loss).
  • In a potometer plan, not mentioning airtight seals or the same shoot for repeats — both are standard control marks.
  • Saying stomata "let water in": they admit carbon dioxide and release oxygen; water loss is a side effect of keeping them open.
  • Writing the source-to-sink direction as one-way only; at A Level the season reversal is examined.

Exam-style questions and answers

Q1. Describe how water moves from the soil into the xylem of a root. (4 marks) Answer: water enters root hair cells by osmosis down the water potential gradient (1); passes through cortex cells from cell to cell (1); endodermis (Casparian strip) blocks the apoplastic route so water passes into living cells (1); enters the xylem where root pressure and transpiration pull move it up (1).

Q2. Explain how four environmental factors affect the rate of transpiration. (4 marks) Answer: higher temperature increases evaporation rate (1); lower humidity steepens the diffusion gradient (1); wind removes saturated air from leaf surfaces (1); light opens stomata so more surface is exposed (1).

Q3. Explain why xylem vessels have lignified walls and no cytoplasm. (2 marks) Answer: lignin strengthens the walls to withstand the negative pressure of the transpiration stream (1); no cytoplasm leaves a clear hollow tube for water flow (1).

Q4. Describe how you would investigate the effect of wind on transpiration using a potometer. (4 marks) Answer: set up the potometer with a cut leafy shoot, ensuring the apparatus is airtight (1); measure the distance the air bubble moves per minute in still air (1); place a fan at a fixed distance and repeat (1); keep temperature, light and humidity constant and repeat for a mean (1).

Q5. Explain the advantage of translocation occurring in both directions in the phloem. (2 marks) Answer: sugars move down from leaves to roots in summer for storage (1); and up from storage organs to growing shoots in spring when leaves are absent (1).

title: Entropy and Energetics Quick Revision
content:
Entropy and Energetics Quick Revision

Chemistry — A2. Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH14, Topic 12, covering entropy, energetics, and feasibility of reactions. Entropy and enthalpy changes are crucial in determining the spontaneity of a reaction.

  • Entropy measures disorder and randomness, increasing with temperature and phase changes.
  • Gibbs free energy combines enthalpy and entropy to predict reaction feasibility.
  • Total entropy change is the sum of system and surroundings entropy changes.
  • Temperature affects reaction feasibility, with higher temperatures decreasing the magnitude of surroundings entropy change.
  • Worked examples illustrate how to calculate entropy changes and Gibbs free energy.

Worked example

Calculate the total entropy change for a reaction with ΔS_system = 100 J/K and ΔH = -50000 J, at 298 K, using S_surroundings = -ΔH / T, then S_total = ΔS_system + S_surroundings.

Key points to remember

Remember that entropy increases with temperature and phase changes, and that the total entropy change determines reaction spontaneity. Also, recall that the Gibbs free energy equation, ΔG = ΔH - TΔS, is used to predict reaction feasibility. Key: ΔG = Gibbs free energy change (kJ mol⁻¹); ΔH = enthalpy change (kJ mol⁻¹); T = temperature (K); ΔS = entropy change (J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, so divide it by 1000 before combining with ΔH); ΔS_total = ΔS_system + ΔS_surroundings (J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹), with ΔS_surroundings = −ΔH/T. A reaction is feasible when ΔG is negative, which is the same statement as ΔS_total being positive.

How to use this: skim the key points, read the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Born-Haber Cycles and Lattice Energy

A Born-Haber cycle applies Hess's Law to construct an energy level diagram for the formation of an ionic solid from its elements in their standard states. The standard enthalpy change of atomisation, delta_at H, is the enthalpy change when one mole of gaseous atoms is formed from the element under standard conditions. Electron affinity is the enthalpy change when one electron is added to each atom in one mole of gaseous atoms to form one mole of gaseous 1- ions. Lattice energy is defined as the exothermic process for the formation of one mole of an ionic solid from its gaseous ions.

Discrepancies between experimental lattice energy values obtained from Born-Haber cycles and theoretical values calculated from pure electrostatic point-charge models indicate the presence of covalent character. When cations polarise large or highly charged anions, electron density is drawn into the region between the nuclei, leading to partial covalent bonding which releases more energy than predicted by pure ionic models.

Enthalpy of Solution and Hydration

The enthalpy change of solution, delta_sol H, is the enthalpy change when one mole of a solute is dissolved in enough solvent to form an infinitely dilute solution. The enthalpy change of hydration, delta_hyd H, is the enthalpy change when one mole of gaseous ions is dissolved in water to form an infinitely dilute solution. You can use energy cycles combining lattice energy and hydration enthalpies to calculate the enthalpy change of solution.

Ionic charge and radius significantly affect these energetic values. High charge density, resulting from small ionic radius and high ionic charge, leads to more exothermic hydration and lattice energies because of stronger electrostatic attractions between the ions and water molecules or oppositely charged ions.

Thermodynamic Stability versus Kinetic Stability

Thermodynamic stability indicates whether a substance or reaction is feasible based on total entropy change and free energy, showing if a reaction is spontaneous. Kinetic stability refers to the rate of a reaction; a system can be thermodynamically unstable yet kinetically stable if the activation energy barrier is too high for the reaction to proceed at a measurable rate at room temperature.

Additional Worked Example

Calculate the enthalpy change of solution for sodium chloride, given that its lattice energy is +790 kJ / mol and the hydration enthalpies of sodium and chloride ions are −406 kJ / mol and −364 kJ / mol respectively. Using the energy cycle, delta_sol H = lattice energy + sum(delta_hyd H). Therefore, delta_sol H = +790 + (−406 + (−364)) = +790 − 770 = +20 kJ / mol.

More Key Points to Remember

Remember that the total entropy change, delta_S total = delta_S system + delta_S surroundings, must be positive for any spontaneous process. The term delta_S surroundings is calculated using − delta_H / T. Solubility trends down group 2 depend on the relative sizes of the decrease in lattice energy compared to the decrease in hydration enthalpy as cation size increases. Polarisation increases down the group for anions or with smaller cations, driving deviations from theoretical lattice energy calculations.

title: Exam technique: Probability (A2)
content:
### What earns the marks
For conditional probability, the restricted sample space stated earns the method mark. For independence checks, P(A)P(B) compared with P(A and B) earns both marks. For Bayes-style updates, the tree fractions multiplied along branches earn stepwise credit.
### Traps
Error: mutually exclusive assumed independent. Correction: test, never assume. Error: given-condition ignored. Correction: shrink the denominator first. Error: branches added instead of multiplied. Correction: multiply along, add across.
### Worked example
Event A has P(A) = 0.5 and event B has P(B) = 0.4. Given that A and B are independent, P(A and B) = 0.5 × 0.4 = 0.20. If the question instead gives P(A and B) = 0.3, then the events are not independent, because 0.3 does not equal 0.20. The conditional probability is P(A | B) = P(A and B) ÷ P(B) = 0.3 ÷ 0.4 = 0.75.
### Check yourself
Two events are mutually exclusive with P(A) = 0.3 and P(B) = 0.2. Are they independent? No. P(A and B) = 0 but P(A)P(B) = 0.06, so the events are dependent. Mutually exclusive events are always dependent when both have non-zero probability.

### Worked example
Event A has P(A) = 0.5 and event B has P(B) = 0.4. Given that A and B are independent, P(A and B) = 0.5 × 0.4 = 0.20. If the question instead gives P(A and B) = 0.3, then the events are not independent, because 0.3 does not equal 0.20. The conditional probability is P(A | B) = P(A and B) ÷ P(B) = 0.3 ÷ 0.4 = 0.75.

title: Cambridge IGCSE First Language English: Analysing Language Choices
content:
Cambridge IGCSE First Language English: Analysing Language Choices

Writer's effect — the analysis of how a writer uses language to create impact — is the skill that separates a competent reader from a top-band one in Cambridge IGCSE First Language English (0500). The question asks you to choose and explain the language that creates a particular effect, and the mark scheme rewards the link from micro-feature to macro-impact: the exact word, the exact method, the exact effect on the reader. This note builds the analytical system from zero: the vocabulary of literary method, the step-by-step deconstruction of the prompt, the effect vocabulary bank, model answers broken down line by line, and the errors that turn analysis into feature-spotting.

The micro-to-macro principle

Writers create effects with tiny tools: a verb choice, a repeated sound, a sentence that stops short. Analysis means moving from the smallest unit (the word) to the largest (the reader's response, the writer's purpose). The chain every top-band answer follows is:

QUOTATION → METHOD → EFFECT ON THE READER → PURPOSE IN CONTEXT
"clawed"   → verb    → makes the wind feel violent and alive → shows
              choice                   the night as an attack

Candidates who stop at METHOD ("the writer uses a metaphor") score nothing for effect; candidates who leap to PURPOSE without quoting score nothing for evidence. The four-beat chain is the answer structure — practise it until it is automatic.

The method vocabulary: what to look for

CategoryFeaturesWhat it tends to do
Diction (word choice)strong verbs, evaluative adjectives, connotation, register shiftsshapes judgement and sympathy
Figurative languagesimile, metaphor, personification, hyperbole, symbolcreates imagery, comparison, emotional colour
Sensory imagerysight, sound, smell, taste, touchimmerses the reader in a place or moment
Sound devicesalliteration, assonance, onomatopoeia, sibilanceadds mood and rhythm; softens or sharpens tone
Sentence structureshort sentences, long sentences, fragments, listing, repetition, questionscontrols pace, tension and emphasis
Perspective and detailwhat is shown or withheld, focalisation, contrast, juxtapositiondirects sympathy and reveals theme

Diction: reading connotation

Words carry two meanings: the dictionary meaning (denotation) and the associations (connotation). Analysis lives in connotation. Compare: the house stood on the hill / the house perched on the hill / the house crouched on the hill. Perched suggests lightness and elevation; crouched suggests menace, weight, waiting. When you analyse diction, name the connotation direction: what does this word suggest that a neutral word would not?

  • Verbs are the richest targets: in "the river snaked through the valley", snaked suggests sinuous movement and a faint threat — analyse the verb before the adjectives.
  • Evaluative adjectives: "the tiny, defiant crowd" already tells the reader how to feel; identify the judgement embedded in the adjective.
  • Register and tone shifts: a formal description suddenly interrupted by a slang word (or the reverse) creates irony or intimacy.

Figurative language: naming the effect precisely

DeviceDefinitionEffect vocabulary
Similecomparison using like or ascompares X to Y, making it vivid / suggesting it is fragile / threatening
MetaphorX is described as Ytransforms X, implying it shares Y's qualities
Personificationhuman qualities given to a thingbrings X alive / makes nature feel hostile or companionable
Hyperboledeliberate exaggerationintensifies emotion / adds humour / shows obsession
Symbolan object that stands for an ideacompresses the theme into an image the reader carries

The analysis must name what the figure compares or implies and what that does to the reader's feeling. "The sky was a bruise" — metaphor: the sky is described as damaged flesh, so the scene feels injured and threatening, suggesting violence has already happened.

Sentence structure and sound as effects

  • Short sentences: shock, finality, tension. "Then the door opened." A short sentence after long ones lands like a punch.
  • Long sentences: accumulation, calm, overload, dreaminess. Lists and polysyndeton (and ... and ... and ...) create breathlessness or abundance.
  • Fragments: a sentence without a verb or subject ("Silence. Then nothing.") mimics broken thought or stunned reaction.
  • Repetition and rule of three: "he ran and ran and ran" or a tricolon builds emphasis and rhythm.
  • Alliteration and sibilance: repeated sounds create mood — sibilance (s, sh sounds) is soft and secretive or sinister; hard consonants (k, t, g) are aggressive and abrupt.
  • Onomatopoeia: words that sound like their meaning (crash, murmur, hissed) pull the reader's ear into the scene.

Deconstructing the prompt: the five-step routine

  1. Underline the effect words in the question — "How does the writer create the atmosphere of tension in this extract?" Your whole answer serves tension; a brilliant point about humour is off-target.
  2. Skim for the effect, not the features: find the lines where the named effect is strongest (usually the turn in the passage).
  3. Select two to three genuinely strong features — one diction point, one figurative or structural point is usually enough for a full-mark answer.
  4. Build the four-beat chain for each — quotation, method, effect on the reader, purpose in context.
  5. Write in a sequence: open with a sentence that answers the question directly ("The writer creates tension through violent diction and oppressive imagery"), develop each feature as a mini-paragraph, and keep the question's effect word in every other sentence as your anchor.

The effect vocabulary bank

Weak answers say "it makes it interesting". Strong answers have a bank of precise effect phrases. Build yours from this list and use each one only when accurate: creates an atmosphere of ...; conveys a sense of ...; makes the reader feel ...; suggests that ...; implies ...; emphasises ...; highlights ...; draws attention to ...; reinforces the idea that ...; leaves the reader expecting ...; unsettles the reader; evokes sympathy for ...; conveys the character's ...; establishes ...; contrasts with ...; signals a shift from ... to ...

Model answer with top-band breakdown

Extract: "The market was a living thing: breathing steam, groaning trolleys, a heartbeat of a thousand footsteps. I stood very still, and it swallowed me whole."

Model answer: "The writer creates an overwhelming, almost frightening sense of the market's scale through personification and metaphor. The market is described as a living thing, breathing steam and groaning trolleys, so the crowd seems to have one body and one will — the reader feels the place as an organism rather than a location. The metaphor continues with the heartbeat of a thousand footsteps, turning ordinary noise into something alive and relentless, which intensifies the speaker's smallness. That smallness is completed by the final metaphor: the market swallowed me whole. The verb swallowed suggests being consumed without trace, so the reader feels the speaker's helplessness and the city's indifference to the individual."

Breakdown of why it hits the top band: it opens by naming the effect (overwhelming, frightening sense of scale) and the methods; each quotation is brief and exact (living thing, swallowed me whole); each method is named (personification, metaphor, verb choice); every effect is reader-directed (the reader feels ...; intensifies ...; suggests being consumed); and the final clause links to purpose in context (the city's indifference). There is no feature-spotting and no padding.

Worked example: deconstructing a prompt

Prompt: "How does the writer create sympathy for the boy in lines 12-20?"
Step 1: effect anchor = sympathy (not fear, not admiration)
Step 2: find the lines where the boy is shown as vulnerable
Step 3: select features:
        (a) diction: "threadbare", "counted his coins twice"
        (b) contrast: the crowd's indifference against his hope
Step 4: build chains:
        (a) threadbare → adjective → clothes worn thin → poverty visible
            counted his coins twice → verb phrase → care and anxiety
            → the reader sees a child managing scarcity alone
        (b) contrast → juxtaposition of the bustling crowd and the boy
            alone → heightens isolation → the reader's sympathy
Step 5: write: open with the answer, develop (a) then (b), keep
        "sympathy" in the anchor sentence and the final line.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Diction) "The old man shuffled to the window." What does shuffled suggest? Answer: The verb suggests slow, dragging, effortful movement — the man is aged or exhausted, so the reader feels his frailty and perhaps pity.
  2. (Simile) "The silence hung over them like a held breath." Explain the effect. Answer: The simile compares the silence to a held breath, so the quiet feels temporary and full of suspense — the reader expects something to happen or break.
  3. (Sentence structure) "He ran. The corridor stretched and stretched. He ran." How does the structure create tension? Answer: The short, repeated sentences create urgency and breathlessness, while the repetition of stretched mimics the corridor's endlessness, making the reader feel the pursuit dragging on.
  4. (Personification) "The house watched them leave." What is the effect? Answer: Giving the house the human action of watching makes it seem alive and perhaps resentful, so the departure feels observed and uneasy rather than free.
  5. (Combined) "The factory exhaled grey smoke that smothered the gardens." Identify two methods and their effects. Answer: Personification (exhaled) makes the factory seem like a living, breathing force; the metaphor smothered presents the smoke as something that kills life, so the reader feels the pollution as an active threat to the community's homes.
  6. (Purpose in context) Why might a writer describe a character's hands as "bird-bones"? Answer: The metaphor compares the hands to fragile bird bones, suggesting thinness and delicacy, which builds a picture of vulnerability — useful if the writer wants the reader to fear for the character's safety.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Feature-spotting: "There is alliteration and metaphor" with no effect commentary is worth nothing. The method name is the start of the sentence, not the answer.
  • "Makes it interesting": the empty effect phrase. Every effect must be specific — interesting to whom, creating what feeling, suggesting what about the character or theme?
  • Long quotations: quote only the words you analyse (two to six words). A lifted sentence without commentary reads as copying.
  • Analysing the wrong thing: the question's effect word is the anchor. An answer about atmosphere when the question asked about sympathy is off-target however good the analysis.
  • Choosing weak features: not every adjective is worth analysis. Pick features that clearly serve the named effect; one deep point beats three shallow ones.
  • Missing the structure level: most candidates analyse words only. A comment on sentence length, repetition or word order after a diction point adds a whole dimension the mark scheme values.
  • No link to context: the four-beat chain ends at purpose — why the writer wants the reader to feel this here. That final clause is the difference between a good and a top answer.
  • Listing without sequencing: a bulleted list of features cannot show the cumulative effect. Write developed mini-paragraphs and order them from the strongest point to the supporting one.

Structures the mark scheme rewards

English has no equations, but it does have repeatable structures the mark scheme rewards. Each one below is written as its parts — check a draft against them, and any part you have left out is the mark you have not earned yet.

The analysis chain

writer's effect — feature + connotation + reader response
Feature means the named language choice (a word class, a figure, a sentence type); connotation means what that choice suggests beyond its literal meaning; reader response means what the reader now thinks, feels or expects. Three parts, three marks — a paragraph that names a metaphor and stops has earned one of them.

word choice effect — word + its usual associations + what it implies here
The usable method for the "explain how the writer uses language" question: quote a single precise word, state its everyday associations, then say what it suggests about the subject or the speaker in this sentence. Vague adjectives everywhere earn no marks.

imagery — vehicle + tenor + ground
Vehicle means the image used (a "shark"); tenor means the thing described (the journalist); ground means the quality they share (ruthlessness). Naming the ground is what turns "it is a metaphor" into analysis.

sentence effect — length + structure + what it makes the reader do
Length means short or long; structure means simple, compound or complex; effect means the pace or emphasis created. A three-word sentence after two long ones slows the reader down; saying so, and why it matters here, is the mark.

Register and form

register — field + tenor + mode
Field means what the text is about; tenor means the relationship between writer and reader (formal or informal, expert or equal); mode means spoken or written, and how permanent. A speech to peers and a report to a head teacher differ in tenor, and that difference is what "maintain the register" means.

transactional writing — audience + purpose + form (APF)
Audience means exactly who reads it; purpose means persuade, inform, argue, advise or entertain; form means article, letter, speech, report, review. Decide all three before the first sentence, because every later choice — pronoun, heading, sign-off — follows from them.

directed writing mark split — reading (10) + writing (15)
Reading marks come from selecting and developing the bullet points from the passage; writing marks come from register, structure and accuracy. Losing the reading half by inventing material is the commonest way to cap the whole response.

summary — point + supporting detail, in your own words, within the word limit
Point means one fact or idea from the passage; supporting detail means the specific information that proves it; own words means no lifted phrases, which are not credited. Ten points for ten marks, so count them before you write.

Composition

narrative arc — equilibrium + disruption + rising action + climax + resolution
The five movements a 500-word story needs so that it feels shaped rather than listed. Start after the disruption if the word limit is tight — a story that begins with the character waking up spends its first paragraph on nothing.

showing — action + sensory detail + consequence
Action means what a character physically does; sensory detail means one or two senses engaged; consequence means what changes because of it. "She was nervous" tells; "she checked the door twice before sitting" shows — the same information, credited differently.

paragraph function — one idea, one turn, one image
Each paragraph should advance the story once, change the mood once, or plant one image. A paragraph that does none of the three is the one to cut when the word limit bites.

title: Exam technique: Sampling
content:
### What earns the marks
For method choice, random vs stratified vs systematic justified earns the mark. For stratified allocation, the proportion of each stratum applied earns the method mark. For bias discussion, the named source of bias with its effect earns both marks.
### Traps
Error: sample claimed unbiased with no method. Correction: name and justify the method. Error: equal numbers per stratum. Correction: allocate proportionally. Error: population confused with frame. Correction: frame is the list used.
### Worked example
A school has 600 students: 120 in Year 11 and 480 in Year 10. A stratified sample of 50 is needed with proportional allocation. Year 11 gets 120/600 x 50 = 10 students, and Year 10 gets 480/600 x 50 = 40 students. The two numbers add to 50, which confirms the allocation. Random selection then happens inside each group.
### Check yourself
A teacher samples 50 students from the first 50 names on the register. Name the sampling method and the main source of bias. This is a convenience sample, and the bias comes from the register order, which may not represent the whole school.

title: International GCSE English as a Second Language: Prepositions and Collocations
content:
International GCSE English as a Second Language: Prepositions and Collocations

Prepositions — at, on, in, by, for, of, with — are the smallest words that cause the biggest problems, because English chooses them by habit rather than by logic. That habit has a name: collocation, the tendency of words to appear together (depend on, good at, by accident). This note builds the full system from zero: the core spatial and temporal prepositions with their reasoning, the adjective, verb and noun collocation tables an exam candidate must know, phrasal verbs for everyday exam topics, and the collocational errors that most often cost accuracy marks in the 9280 writing and speaking papers.

What collocation is: the knife-and-fork analogy

Some words in English come in pairs the way knives and forks do. A native speaker says make a decision, not do a decision, and heavy rain, not strong rain — not because logic demands it, but because that is the established pairing. You cannot compute collocations; you learn them as units, the way you learned football and homework as single items of vocabulary. The good news for exam candidates: the testable collocation set is finite, and the exam repeats the same few hundred pairs every session.

The core three: at, on and in

The most-tested prepositions follow a containment logic: at is a point (a point in space or time), on is a surface or line, in is an enclosed space or a bounded period.

PrepositionTimePlace
atat 7 o'clock, at night, at noon, at the moment, at the weekendat the bus stop, at the door, at school, at home, at work
onon Monday, on 3 May, on my birthday, on Friday morningon the table, on the wall, on the bus (as a passenger), on the second floor
inin May, in 2026, in the morning, in the holidays, in two hoursin the room, in London, in a car (as a passenger), in the garden

The exceptions earn their own marks: at night but in the morning (the day parts take in, night takes at); at the weekend (British) / on the weekend (American); on a bus but in a car; in time (before the deadline) versus on time (exactly at the scheduled moment).

Worked example. "The meeting is ___ Monday ___ 9 am ___ the morning ___ May." Step 1: day → on Monday. Step 2: clock time → at 9 am. Step 3: part of the day → in the morning. Step 4: month → in May. Answers: on / at / in / in. Method visible: decide whether each target is a point (at), a surface/day (on), or an enclosed period (in).

Prepositions of movement and position

  • to / into / onto: to = direction (go to school), into = entering (walk into the room), onto = onto a surface (jump onto the wall).
  • at / to after verbs of position: arrive at (a place), arrive in (a city or country), get to.
  • above / over / under / below: over and under imply vertical opposition (the bridge over the river); above and below are relative levels (the temperature fell below zero).
  • between / among: between two or more distinct things (between the shops), among a group (among the crowd).

Adjective + preposition collocations

This table is the highest-yield collocation list for the exam; learn each adjective with its preposition as one chunk.

AdjectivePrepositionExample
afraid, frightened, scaredofafraid of the dark
good, bad, excellent, betteratgood at mathematics
interestedininterested in history
proudofproud of my sister
responsibleforresponsible for the project
famousforfamous for its beaches
keenonkeen on football
fed up, boredwithfed up with the noise
angry, annoyedwith (a person) / about (a thing)angry with my brother about the mess
marriedtomarried to a teacher
usedtoused to the climate
differentfromdifferent from the others
similartosimilar to mine
polite, kind, rude, generoustokind to animals

Verb + preposition collocations

VerbPrepositionExample
depend, relyonIt depends on the weather.
listentolisten to the radio
applyfor (a job) / to (an institution)apply for the job, apply to university
belongtobelong to my brother
consistofconsist of three parts
arriveat / inarrive at the station, arrive in Spain
explain, suggest, describe, discuss(no to with an object: explain something to someone)explain the problem to me — never "explain me the problem"
succeedinsucceed in passing the exam
apologisefor (something) / to (someone)apologise for being late, apologise to my teacher
pay, wait, ask, thankforpay for the tickets, wait for the bus
thinkabout (consider) / of (have an opinion)think about the offer, think of a better idea

The explain/suggest family is the single most common first-language interference error: these verbs never take a personal indirect object without to. "Explain me the rule" is wrong; "explain the rule to me" is right. Likewise "suggest me a book" is wrong; "suggest a book to me" or "recommend a book to me" is right.

Noun + preposition collocations

  • reason for, cause of, solution to, answer to, invitation to, damage to, effect on, advantage/disadvantage of, increase/decrease in, demand for, opportunity for, experience of/in, attitude to/towards.
  • Prepositional phrases of manner and circumstance: by accident, on purpose, by mistake, at least, at last, in fact, in spite of, due to, because of, according to.

Worked example. Correct the sentence: "She explained me the reason of the delay and asked an apology." Step 1: explain + object + to: "She explained the reason for the delay to me." (reason for, not reason of.) Step 2: ask for an apology — but the meaning is she apologised; the writer wanted "apologised for the delay". Cleanest correction: "She explained the reason for the delay to me and apologised." Two errors in one sentence: verb pattern and noun collocation.

Phrasal verbs for exam topics

Phrasal verbs are verb + particle units whose meaning is not predictable from the parts. The exam themes repeat a manageable set:

Phrasal verbMeaningTheme
look aftercare forfamily, children
grow upbecome an adultidentity, biography
get on withhave a good relationship withpeople, colleagues
find outdiscover informationstudy, research
sign up forenrol incourses, jobs
carry oncontinueany theme
give upstop trying / quithabits, work
cut down onreducehealth, environment
run out ofexhaust the supplyresources, money
take part inparticipateevents, sport
come up withthink of (an idea)study, projects
deal withhandleproblems, stress

Worked examples: collocation decisions

Worked example 1 — gap fill with reasoning. "I am very keen ___ tennis, but I am not very good ___ it. My coach says I need to concentrate ___ my serve and stop worrying ___ losing." Step 1: keen on (adjective collocation) → on. Step 2: good at → at. Step 3: concentrate on → on. Step 4: worry about → about. Answers: on / at / on / about. Every answer is a memorised pair; the reasoning is retrieval, not translation.

Worked example 2 — prepositions of time in a real task. "My course starts ___ September and finishes ___ the end of June. I have exams ___ the first week ___ June, and results come ___ August." Step 1: month → in September. Step 2: fixed phrase → at the end of June. Step 3: a bounded week inside June → in the first week of June (note the second of: week of June). Step 4: in August. Answers: in / at / in / in ... of ... in.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. Fill with at / on / in: "The flight leaves ___ 6:30 ___ Tuesday ___ the morning." Answer: at / on / in.
  2. Fill with adjective collocations: "She is afraid ___ speaking ___ large audiences but is very good ___ writing speeches." Answer: of / to / at. (speak to an audience; good at writing.)
  3. Correct the errors: "He explained me the problem and suggested me to wait." Answer: "He explained the problem to me and suggested that I wait." Why: explain and suggest never take a bare personal object.
  4. Choose: "The solution ___ the problem is a change ___ the law." (of / to / for / in / of) Answer: solution to the problem, change in the law.
  5. Choose the phrasal verb: "If you want to ___ smoking, try to ___ it ___ gradually." Answer: give up ... cut down on ... (give up smoking; cut down on it gradually).
  6. Fill: "We arrived ___ the airport late ___ night ___ the end of the holiday." Answer: at / at / of. (arrive at a point; at night; at the end of.)

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Translating the preposition: "depends of", "married with", "interested on" — the L1 preposition is not the English one. Learn the pairs as chunks and test yourself with gap fills, not translation.
  • explain me / suggest me: the classic transfer error; both verbs need to + person or no person at all.
  • discuss about: discuss takes no preposition ("we discussed the plan"), and "answer to the question" is wrong for the verb ("answer the question" — answer to exists only as a noun: the answer to).
  • Preposition stranding avoided wrongly: "Who did you talk to?" is correct English; "To whom did you talk?" is correct but overly formal for most tasks. Match the register.
  • Time/at-on-in slips: at night / in the morning / on Monday morning — the part-of-day rule (in) and the day-surface rule (on) combine.
  • Strong vs heavy: collocation again — heavy rain, strong wind, big mistake (not strong mistake). Quantifier adjectives are memorised pairs.
  • Phrasal-verb register: "give up the job" is informal; formal writing prefers resign from the post. Choose phrasal verbs for informal tasks and their single-word equivalents for formal ones.
  • Double prepositions: "Where are you going to?" with a destination already stated, or "discuss about" — check each verb's pattern once in the final proofread.

title: IGCSE Biology: Plant Nutrition
content:
IGCSE Biology: Plant Nutrition

Every food chain on Earth begins with a plant capturing sunlight and turning it into sugar. This note covers photosynthesis from the raw materials to the limiting-factor graphs that decide crop yields, then works through the anatomy of a leaf with each structure tied to the job it performs, and finishes with the mineral requirements of plants and the deficiency symptoms that reveal what is missing. The word equations, the balanced symbol equation and the limiting-factor reasoning are all expanded step by step, because Paper 4 asks for all three almost every year.

The word and symbol equations for photosynthesis

Photosynthesis is the process by which plants make glucose from carbon dioxide and water using light energy trapped by chlorophyll. Word equation: carbon dioxide + water --(light energy, chlorophyll)--> glucose + oxygen. Symbol equation: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O --(light)--> C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂. To balance it from scratch: count the carbons — 6 on the left means C₆ on the right; then the hydrogens — 12 on the left from 6H₂O means H₁₂ in glucose; then the oxygens — 12 on the left (6 × 2) plus 6 from water totals 18; the right side has 6 in glucose plus 6 × 2 = 12 in oxygen, giving 18. Carbon dioxide enters through stomata (pores in the leaf epidermis flanked by guard cells), water is drawn up through xylem in the veins, and the glucose produced is either used in respiration, converted to starch for storage, converted to sucrose for transport, used to make cellulose for cell walls, or used with nitrate ions to make amino acids and proteins.

Chloroplasts, chlorophyll and the role of each factor

Photosynthesis happens in chloroplasts, which are concentrated in the palisade mesophyll layer of the leaf. Chlorophyll is the green pigment that absorbs light energy (mainly in the red and blue wavelengths, reflecting green — which is why leaves look green). The energy is used to power the conversion of carbon dioxide and water into glucose; carbon dioxide is raw material, and water is the hydrogen donor (split in the light-dependent reactions). At IGCSE level, know the three requirements — light, chlorophyll, carbon dioxide — and where each comes from. A variegated leaf (with white non-chlorophyll patches) tested with iodine shows starch only in the green regions, proving chlorophyll is necessary; a destarched plant kept in the dark shows no starch, proving light is necessary.

Limiting factors

The rate of photosynthesis is limited by whichever factor is in shortest supply — the limiting factor. Three are examinable: light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and temperature. As light intensity rises, rate rises proportionally until another factor (usually carbon dioxide) becomes limiting and the graph plateaus. As carbon dioxide rises (from the 0.04 % of the atmosphere), rate rises until light or temperature limits it. Temperature follows the enzyme pattern: rising to an optimum (about 25–30 °C for tropical plants) then falling as enzymes denature. The logic of commercial greenhouses and polytunnels follows directly: add artificial light at night, enrich carbon dioxide to 0.1–0.2 %, and heat to the optimum — but each expense is only worthwhile while that factor is the one limiting. The standard graph questions give a rate-versus-one-factor curve with two or three lines at different levels of a second factor; explain each plateau by naming the new limiting factor.

Leaf structure: form fits function

A cross-section through a leaf reveals adaptations for photosynthesis and gas exchange: a broad flat shape gives maximum light absorption and surface area; a thin lamina keeps a short diffusion path; the upper epidermis is transparent and coated with cuticle (waxy, waterproof, reduces water loss); the palisade mesophyll is a column of tall cells packed with chloroplasts near the top where light is strongest; the spongy mesophyll has irregular cells with air spaces between them for gas circulation; veins contain xylem (water and minerals arriving) and phloem (sugars leaving); stomata on the lower epidermis let carbon dioxide in and oxygen out; guard cells open and close the stomata — opening in light (for photosynthesis) and closing in darkness or when the plant is short of water (to reduce transpiration). The structure-to-function questions reward this chain: feature, then effect on light, gas exchange or water loss.

Mineral requirements and deficiency symptoms

Plants need mineral ions absorbed from the soil solution by root hair cells (by diffusion and active transport). Nitrate ions: needed to make amino acids and therefore proteins and chlorophyll; deficiency causes stunted growth and yellow leaves (chlorosis). Magnesium ions: the central atom in every chlorophyll molecule; deficiency causes yellowing between the leaf veins. Phosphate ions: needed for DNA, RNA, ATP and cell membranes; deficiency causes poor root growth and purplish leaves. Potassium ions: needed for enzymes in respiration and for opening stomata; deficiency causes poor fruit and seed development. Plants grown in hydroponic culture (mineral solution without soil) show exactly these symptoms when one ion is omitted — a standard Paper 6 identification question.

Limiting factors in practice: crops and greenhouses

The same principles scale to agriculture. Growing crops densely shades lower leaves, so light becomes limiting and yields per plant fall even as yield per field rises. Glasshouses trap heat (raising temperature) and allow carbon dioxide enrichment; grow-lights extend the photoperiod. Water stress closes stomata, cutting carbon dioxide entry and thus photosynthesis — irrigation protects yield. But temperature above the optimum denatures the enzymes of the Calvin cycle, and excessive light can bleach chlorophyll (photoinhibition). The examiner's favourite commercial question: "a farmer adds carbon dioxide but yield does not rise — explain why" — the answer: another factor (light or temperature) is now limiting; identify which from the conditions given.

Mineral ions and deficiency at a glance

IonNeeded forDeficiency symptom
NitrateAmino acids, proteins, chlorophyllStunted growth, yellow leaves (chlorosis)
MagnesiumThe chlorophyll moleculeYellowing between the veins
PhosphateDNA, RNA, ATP, membranesPoor root growth, purplish leaves
PotassiumEnzymes of respiration, stomatal openingPoor fruit and seed development

Worked example: reading limiting-factor graphs

A graph shows the rate of photosynthesis versus light intensity at three carbon dioxide concentrations (0.05 %, 0.10 %, 0.20 %): all three lines rise together at low light, then the 0.05 % line plateaus first, followed by the 0.10 %, then the 0.20 %. Step 1: describe the trend in data terms: "rate increases with light intensity initially and then levels off". Step 2: explain the first region: light is limiting — more photons reach chlorophyll, so the light-dependent reactions supply energy faster. Step 3: explain each plateau: above the kink, carbon dioxide concentration is limiting because it is in shortest supply; the higher the carbon dioxide, the higher the plateau. Step 4: name the limiting factor for each line at maximum light: carbon dioxide concentration for all three. Step 5: apply to practice: at the plateau of the 0.05 % curve, adding more light changes nothing; enriching carbon dioxide raises the rate. A second calculation type: comparing rate as a percentage — if rate rises from 20 to 50 arbitrary units, the increase is (50 − 20) ÷ 20 × 100 = 150 %.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Writing the equation with oxygen on the left or forgetting to balance the hydrogens; check every atom before writing "done".
  • Saying plants photosynthesise "to make energy": plants make glucose (chemical energy store); the light energy is converted, not created.
  • Confusing the roles: carbon dioxide is the raw material, water supplies hydrogen, light is the energy source, chlorophyll is the trap.
  • Explaining a plateau without naming the new limiting factor — the word "limiting factor" itself is worth a mark.
  • Describing guard cells as "letting light in": stomata control gas exchange and water loss, not light.
  • Forgetting the cuticle when asked about water loss adaptations.
  • Writing deficiency symptoms without linking the ion to its molecule: magnesium → chlorophyll → yellow leaves; nitrate → protein → stunting.
  • Interpreting a rate graph against temperature without mentioning enzyme denaturation at the peak.

Exam-style questions and answers

Q1. Write the balanced symbol equation for photosynthesis. (2 marks) Answer: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ — one mark for reactants and products, one for correct balancing with light/chlorophyll over the arrow.

Q2. Explain why the rate of photosynthesis levels off as light intensity continues to increase. (2 marks) Answer: another factor becomes limiting (1) — carbon dioxide concentration or temperature in shortest supply (1).

Q3. Describe two ways in which a leaf is adapted for photosynthesis. (4 marks) Answer: broad flat shape for maximum light absorption (1); palisade mesophyll packed with chloroplasts near the upper surface (1); thin lamina for short diffusion path (1); veins bring water by xylem and carry sugars away by phloem (1).

Q4. A plant has yellow leaves with green veins. Identify the missing mineral ion and explain your answer. (2 marks) Answer: magnesium (1) because it is needed to make chlorophyll and its absence causes chlorosis (1).

Q5. Explain how a farmer could increase the rate of photosynthesis in a greenhouse in winter. (3 marks) Answer: add artificial light to raise light intensity (1); heat the greenhouse to the optimum temperature for the enzymes (1); enrich carbon dioxide concentration so it is no longer limiting (1).

title: Differentiation II — Study Notes
content:
Differentiation II

Product and Quotient Rules

  • (uv)′ = u′v + uv′
  • (u/v)′ = (u′v − uv′)/v²

Example: y = x² e^x gives dy/dx = 2x e^x + x² e^x = e^x(2x + x²).

Standard Derivatives

  • sin x → cos x; cos x → −sin x; tan x → sec²x
  • e^x → e^x; ln x → 1/x

Chain Rule Everywhere

d/dx [ln(3x)] = 3/(3x) = 1/x; d/dx [e^(2x)] = 2e^(2x); d/dx [sin²x] = 2 sin x cos x.

Implicit Differentiation

Differentiate both sides w.r.t. x, treating y as a function of x (terms in y pick up dy/dx).

Example: x² + y² = 25 → 2x + 2y(dy/dx) = 0 → dy/dx = −x/y.

Parametric Curves

For x = f(t), y = g(t): dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt).

Example: x = t², y = t³ gives dy/dx = 3t²/2t = 3t/2.

Exam tips: quote the rule you use; for tangent/normal on parametric curves, find t at the point first, and simplify implicit answers using the original equation.

Exam method: exponential, logarithmic and trigonometric rules

The derivative of eˣ is eˣ, and the derivative of e^(kx) is k e^(kx). The derivative of ln x is 1/x, and for ln(f(x)) the chain rule gives f′(x)/f(x). The derivative of sin x is cos x and of cos x is −sin x; for a function of kx, multiply by k.

When a product contains an exponential or trigonometric function, use the product rule d/dx(uv) = u dv/dx + v du/dx. Factorising the result, such as eˣ(1 + x), makes it easier to evaluate at a point.

Quotients use d/dx(u/v) = (v du/dx − u dv/dx)/v². Write tan x as sin x/cos x when the quotient rule is easier, and remember that d/dx(tan x) = sec² x.

Second derivatives follow by differentiating again. Use them to classify stationary points, or to check the concavity of a curve, when the question asks for it.

Exam cue: Show each rule as you apply it. Method marks are awarded for a correct product or chain step even if the final arithmetic is wrong.

title: A Level Mathematics: Further Algebra
content:
A Level Mathematics: Further Algebra

A2 algebra is about rewriting expressions so that they can be handled: splitting a fraction into partial fractions before integrating it, dividing polynomials to expose factors, and using the remainder and factor theorems to find unknowns. This note builds each technique from zero, with the long division written out term by term, because the algebra is the part candidates rush and lose marks on.

Polynomial division

Dividing a polynomial by a linear factor works like numerical long division: divide the leading term, multiply back, subtract, bring down, repeat until the degree of the remainder is lower than the divisor.

Worked example. Divide 2x³ − 5x² + 4x − 7 by (x − 2).

2x^2 into x - 2: 2x^2(x - 2) = 2x^3 - 4x^2;  subtract: -x^2 + 4x - 7
-x into x - 2: -x(x - 2) = -x^2 + 2x;  subtract: 2x - 7
+2 into x - 2: 2(x - 2) = 2x - 4;  subtract: -3
quotient 2x^2 - x + 2 with remainder -3
so 2x^3 - 5x^2 + 4x - 7 = (x - 2)(2x^2 - x + 2) - 3

Worked example 2 (missing terms). Divide x³ + 1 by (x + 1).

write as x^3 + 0x^2 + 0x + 1 to keep the columns aligned
quotient x^2, subtract x^3 + x^2 -> -x^2 + 1
quotient -x, subtract -x^2 - x -> x + 1
quotient +1, subtract x + 1 -> 0
x^3 + 1 = (x + 1)(x^2 - x + 1)

Leaving gaps in the descending powers is the commonest slip; write the zeros in explicitly.

The factor and remainder theorems

remainder theorem: dividing f(x) by (x - a) leaves remainder f(a)
factor theorem: (x - a) is a factor exactly when f(a) = 0
for (ax - b): remainder is f(b/a)

Worked example 1. Find the remainder when f(x) = x³ − 4x + 5 is divided by (x + 2).

f(-2) = -8 + 8 + 5 = 5

Worked example 2 (find a factor). Show that (x − 3) is a factor of x³ − 4x² − 3x + 18.

f(3) = 27 - 36 - 9 + 18 = 0, so (x - 3) is a factor
then divide: x^3 - 4x^2 - 3x + 18 = (x - 3)(x^2 - x - 6)
                                     = (x - 3)(x - 3)(x + 2)

Worked example 3 (unknown constant). f(x) = 2x³ + ax² − 5x + 6 has (x + 2) as a factor. Find a.

f(-2) = -16 + 4a + 10 + 6 = 0
4a = 0  ->  a = 0
check: 2x^3 - 5x + 6 divided by (x + 2) gives 2x^2 - 4x + 3 with no remainder

Partial fractions: distinct linear factors

(px + q)/[(x - a)(x - b)] = A/(x - a) + B/(x - b)

multiply through by the denominator and substitute x = a, x = b
in turn (the cover-up method)

Worked example. Express (5x + 1)/[(x − 1)(x + 2)] in partial fractions.

5x + 1 = A(x + 2) + B(x - 1)
x = 1: 6 = 3A  ->  A = 2
x = -2: -9 = -3B  ->  B = 3
(5x + 1)/[(x - 1)(x + 2)] = 2/(x - 1) + 3/(x + 2)

Worked example 2 (three factors). Express 2/[(x)(x + 1)(x − 2)] in partial fractions.

2 = A(x + 1)(x - 2) + Bx(x - 2) + Cx(x + 1)
x = 0: 2 = -2A  ->  A = -1
x = -1: 2 = 3B  ->  B = 2/3
x = 2: 2 = 6C  ->  C = 1/3
so 2/[...] = -1/x + (2/3)/(x + 1) + (1/3)/(x - 2)

Partial fractions: repeated and improper cases

repeated factor: (px + q)/[(x - a)^2] = A/(x - a) + B/(x - a)^2
improper (degree of numerator >= degree of denominator): divide first

Worked example 1 (repeated). Express (3x + 5)/(x − 1)² in partial fractions.

3x + 5 = A(x - 1) + B
x = 1: 8 = B
compare coefficients of x: 3 = A
so 3/(x - 1) + 8/(x - 1)^2

Worked example 2 (improper). Express (x² + 3x + 2)/(x − 1) in partial fractions.

divide first: (x^2 + 3x + 2)/(x - 1) = x + 4 + 6/(x - 1)
check by multiplying back: (x + 4)(x - 1) + 6 = x^2 + 3x + 2

The division step must come first: writing A + B/(x − 1) for an improper fraction gives the wrong form and cannot be solved consistently.

Inequalities and modulus

|x - a| < b  means  a - b < x < a + b
|x - a| > b  means  x < a - b or x > a + b

rational inequalities: move everything to one side, combine over a
common denominator, then use a sign diagram

Worked example. Solve |2x − 3| < 7.

-7 < 2x - 3 < 7
-4 < 2x < 10
-2 < x < 5

Worked example 2 (rational). Solve (x + 1)/(x − 3) > 2.

(x + 1)/(x - 3) - 2 > 0
(x + 1 - 2x + 6)/(x - 3) > 0
(7 - x)/(x - 3) > 0
critical values x = 3 (undefined) and x = 7
sign test: x = 4 gives 3/1 > 0 true; x = 8 gives -1/5 < 0 false
so 3 < x < 7

Never multiply a rational inequality by the denominator without knowing its sign: multiplying by a negative reverses the inequality, which is why the sign-diagram method is used instead.

Solving cubic equations completely

Once one factor is found by the factor theorem, polynomial division reduces the cubic to a quadratic, and the quadratic gives the remaining roots. The routine never varies:

  1. Try small integer values (±1, ±2, ±3) in f(x) until one gives zero.
  2. Divide by the corresponding linear factor.
  3. Factorise or use the quadratic formula on the quotient.
  4. State every root, including repeats.

Worked example. Solve x³ − 2x² − 5x + 6 = 0.

f(1) = 1 - 2 - 5 + 6 = 0, so (x - 1) is a factor
divide: x^3 - 2x^2 - 5x + 6 = (x - 1)(x^2 - x - 6)
                            = (x - 1)(x - 3)(x + 2)
roots: x = 1, 3, -2

Worked example 2 (repeated root). Solve x³ − 3x + 2 = 0.

f(1) = 0  ->  (x - 1) is a factor
divide: (x - 1)(x^2 + x - 2) = (x - 1)(x + 2)(x - 1)
roots: x = 1 (repeated) and x = -2; the curve touches the axis at x = 1

A repeated root is a tangency, which is why a cubic can have two distinct roots but three real ones counted with multiplicity.

Partial fractions with an irreducible quadratic

for a factor (x^2 + px + q) with no real roots:
(ax + b)/[(x - c)(x^2 + px + q)] = A/(x - c) + (Bx + C)/(x^2 + px + q)

Worked example. Express (3x + 1)/[x(x² + 1)] in partial fractions.

3x + 1 = A(x^2 + 1) + (Bx + C)x
x = 0: 1 = A
compare x^2: 0 = A + B  ->  B = -1
compare x: 3 = C
so 1/x + (-x + 3)/(x^2 + 1)

The numerator over a quadratic factor must be linear (Bx + C); a constant alone cannot satisfy the coefficients in general.

One linear and one quadratic equation

Simultaneous equations where one is a circle or parabola are solved by substitution, producing a quadratic whose roots give the intersection points.

Worked example. Solve y = x + 1 and x² + y² = 25.

substitute: x^2 + (x + 1)^2 = 25
2x^2 + 2x + 1 = 25  ->  x^2 + x - 12 = 0
(x + 4)(x - 3) = 0  ->  x = -4 or 3
points: (-4, -3) and (3, 4)

A line and a curve meet in 0, 1 or 2 points; the discriminant of the substituted quadratic tells you which, without solving — a standard link to the next section.

Surds and rationalising

rationalise 1/(a + sqrt b) by multiplying by (a - sqrt b)/(a - sqrt b)
denominator becomes a^2 - b, which is rational

Worked example. Simplify 3/(2 + √5).

multiply by (2 - sqrt 5)/(2 - sqrt 5):
3(2 - sqrt 5)/(4 - 5) = 3(2 - sqrt 5)/(-1) = 3 sqrt 5 - 6

Worked example 2. Solve x² − 6x + 2 = 0, giving answers in surd form.

x = [6 +/- sqrt(36 - 8)]/2 = (6 +/- sqrt 28)/2 = 3 +/- sqrt 7

Surd answers should be simplified (√28 = 2√7) and, where the question asks, rationalised.

Algebraic fractions and cancelling

Simplifying an algebraic fraction requires factorising both parts first; cancelling terms before factorising is invalid because a sum is not a product.

Worked example. Simplify (x² − 9)/(x² + x − 6).

factorise: (x - 3)(x + 3)/[(x + 3)(x - 2)]
cancel (x + 3): (x - 3)/(x - 2), valid for x not 3 or -2

Worked example 2 (addition). Write 1/(x − 1) + 2/(x + 2) as a single fraction.

common denominator: [(x + 2) + 2(x - 1)]/[(x - 1)(x + 2)]
= (3x)/[(x - 1)(x + 2)]

The excluded values belong in the answer: a cancelled factor leaves a hole in the domain, which the equation's original form still cannot accept.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Remainder) Find the remainder when x³ + 2x − 4 is divided by (x − 1). Answer: 1 + 2 − 4 = −1.
  2. (Factor) Is (x + 3) a factor of x³ + 2x² − 5x + 6? Answer: f(−3) = −27 + 18 + 15 + 6 = 12 ≠ 0, no.
  3. (Unknown) f(x) = x³ + kx − 6 has (x − 2) as a factor. Find k. Answer: 8 + 2k − 6 = 0 → k = −1.
  4. (Partial fractions) Express 7/[(x − 1)(x + 6)]. Answer: 1/(x − 1) − 1/(x + 6).
  5. (Repeated) Express (2x + 1)/(x + 1)². Answer: 2/(x + 1) − 1/(x + 1)².
  6. (Improper) Express (x² + 1)/(x + 1). Answer: x − 1 + 2/(x + 1).
  7. (Modulus) Solve |x − 4| ≥ 3. Answer: x ≤ 1 or x ≥ 7.
  8. (Rational) Solve (x − 2)/(x + 1) < 1. Answer: (x − 2 − x − 1)/(x + 1) < 0 → −3/(x + 1) < 0 → x > −1.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Partial fractions for an improper fraction: divide first; the polynomial part is part of the answer.
  • Repeated factors written once: (x − a)² needs both A/(x − a) and B/(x − a)².
  • Cover-up used on repeating factors: the cover-up method substitutes only for distinct linear factors; for repeats, compare coefficients as well.
  • Sign of the remainder: f(a) gives the remainder when dividing by (x − a); for (x + a) substitute −a.
  • Missing powers in division: write 0x², 0x placeholders so the columns line up.
  • Multiplying inequalities by a variable: the sign may be negative; use a sign diagram instead.
  • Not excluding undefined values: a denominator's zero is never in the solution set; mark it as excluded.
  • Not checking: multiply the partial fractions back, or substitute one value, to confirm the decomposition.

title: IGCSE Mathematics: Fractions, Decimals and Percentages
content:
IGCSE Mathematics: Fractions, Decimals and Percentages

Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580 (2025–2027), section 1 Number: statement 1.4 Fractions, decimals and percentages (equivalence and conversion), 1.13 Percentages (including Extended reverse percentages) and E1.17 Exponential growth and decay. These three representations describe the same quantities, and fluent movement between them is one of the biggest sources of marks in both papers. The note explains why the conversion methods work before showing them, then builds percentages as multipliers — the technique behind most Paper 4 percentage problems.

What a fraction really is

A fraction is a division: 3/4 means 3 divided by 4, or three quarters of a whole. The top (numerator) counts the parts; the bottom (denominator) says how many equal parts the whole is cut into. A proper fraction has a smaller numerator (3/4); an improper fraction has a larger one (7/4); a mixed number combines a whole number with a proper fraction (1 3/4).

Convert 2 3/5 to an improper fraction:

2 wholes = 10 fifths, and 3 more fifths gives 13 fifths:
2 3/5 = (2 × 5 + 3)/5 = 13/5

Equivalent fractions are the same quantity written differently: 3/4 = 6/8 = 15/20, because multiplying top and bottom by the same number is multiplying by 1 (a form of 1, such as 3/3), which changes the look but not the value. Cancelling is the reverse: dividing top and bottom by a common factor. Only factors of the whole numerator and denominator can be cancelled — (x + 3)/(x + 2) cannot be simplified by cancelling the x's, because the top is a sum, not a product.

Converting between fractions, decimals and percentages

Fraction to decimal: divide.  3/8 = 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375
Decimal to fraction: read the place value.  0.47 = 47/100
Fraction to percentage: divide, then multiply by 100.  3/8 = 0.375 = 37.5%
Percentage to fraction: write over 100 and simplify.  45% = 45/100 = 9/20

Recurring decimals. A fraction always produces either a terminating decimal or a recurring one, and every recurring decimal converts back to a fraction by the algebra method:

Write 0.444... (4 recurring) as a fraction:

Let x = 0.444...
Then 10x = 4.444...        [shift the decimal one place]
Subtract:  10x - x = 4.444... - 0.444...
9x = 4
x = 4/9
Write 0.273636... (36 recurring) as a fraction:

Let x = 0.273636...
Two digits repeat, so shift two places:  100x = 27.363636...
100x - x = 27.3636... - 0.2736... = 27.09
99x = 27.09  →  x = 27.09/99 = 301/1100 after multiplying top and bottom by 100 and simplifying

Knowing the common conversions by heart saves time: 1/2 = 0.5 = 50%, 1/4 = 0.25 = 25%, 3/4 = 0.75, 1/5 = 0.2 = 20%, 1/8 = 0.125, 1/3 = 0.333... = 33 1/3%.

FractionDecimalPercentage
1/20.550%
1/40.2525%
3/40.7575%
1/50.220%
1/80.12512.5%
1/30.333...33 1/3%
2/30.666...66 2/3%

These seven values answer a surprising share of Paper 2 questions by inspection, and they anchor every conversion done the long way.

Percentages: the multiplier method

A percentage is a fraction out of 100 — literally per cent, per hundred. Every percentage problem is a multiplication, and the fastest method converts straight to a multiplier.

Find 35% of 240:

35% = 35/100 = 0.35, so  0.35 × 240 = 84

Increase 240 by 35%:
the new value is 135% of the old, so multiply by 1.35:  1.35 × 240 = 324

Decrease 240 by 35%:
the new value is 65% of the old, so multiply by 0.65:   0.65 × 240 = 156

Why the multiplier works. Increasing by 35% means keeping the original 100% and adding 35%, so the result is 135% of the original, which is 1.35 times it. Decreasing by 35% leaves 65%, which is 0.65 times. The multiplier also chains: successive changes multiply, which is why two discounts of 20% are not one discount of 40% (0.8 × 0.8 = 0.64, a 36% total reduction).

One quantity as a percentage of another:  18 out of 60

18/60 × 100 = 30%

Reverse percentages (Extended). Working backwards from a final value needs division:

A price after a 20% increase is £72. Find the original price.

The original is 100%, the new price is 120% of it, so the multiplier is 1.2:
original = 72 / 1.2 = £60

Check: 60 × 1.2 = 72 ✓

The common error is finding 20% of 72 and subtracting; the percentage must be taken from the original 100%, not the final amount.

Percentage change and comparisons

A coat falls from £80 to £56. Find the percentage decrease.

change = 80 - 56 = 24
percentage change = change / original x 100 = 24/80 × 100 = 30%

Percentage change always uses the original value as the denominator. Comparing quantities with different sizes — prices per 100 g, speeds, wages per hour — is done by putting both over a common quantity before comparing.

Exponential growth and decay (Extended)

When a quantity changes by the same percentage each period, it is multiplied by a fixed factor each time, and the result is exponential growth or decay. The multiplier is 1 + r for growth and 1 − r for decay, where r is the rate as a decimal.

After n periods at rate r:
growth:    final = original x (1 + r)^n
decay:     final = original x (1 - r)^n

Why the power. Each period multiplies by the same factor, so n periods multiply n times: an investment of £500 growing 3% a year becomes 500 × 1.03 after one year, 500 × 1.03 × 1.03 after two, and 500 × 1.03ⁿ after n years. The power counts the multiplications.

£500 is invested at 3% compound interest per year for 4 years.

500 × 1.03⁴ = 500 × 1.12550881 = £562.75 (2 d.p.)

Year by year check: 515.00 → 530.45 → 546.36 → 562.75 ✓
A car worth £18 000 depreciates 15% per year. Value after 3 years:

18 000 × 0.85³ = 18 000 × 0.614125 = £11 054.25

Exponential growth graphs climb ever faster and never touch zero; exponential decay graphs fall steeply at first and then level off towards — but never reach — zero (a horizontal asymptote). Doubling and halving questions are solved by logs or trial multiplication: for how many years does £500 at 3% exceed £600? Solve 500 × 1.03ⁿ > 600 by testing values of n, since 1.03ⁿ > 1.2 needs n ⩾ 7 years.

Worked example: a full percentage question

A shop sells a jacket for £84 after a 20% reduction. A further 10% discount is offered for cash.

Original price before the 20% reduction:
84 = original x 0.80
original = 84 / 0.80 = £105

Cash price after the extra 10%:
84 × 0.90 = £75.60

Total percentage saving against the original:
saving = 105 - 75.60 = 29.40
percentage saving = 29.40/105 × 100 = 28%

Check with multipliers: 0.80 × 0.90 = 0.72, so the cash price is 72% of the
original and the saving is 28% ✓

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Finding a percentage of the wrong amount: increase/decrease percentages apply to the original; reverse percentages divide by the multiplier.
  • Adding percentage changes: two 20% discounts give 0.8 × 0.8 = 0.64, a 36% reduction, not 40%.
  • Writing a recurring decimal as a fraction by eye; use the shift-and-subtract method and show it.
  • Cancelling across a sum: 3/4 is not 3 quarters of the top and bottom separately.
  • Using 365 days or 12 months inconsistently in compound problems: the power n counts compounding periods, so match it to the rate.
  • Forgetting that 15% decrease means multiplying by 0.85, not by −0.15 or 0.15.
  • Confusing 33% with 1/3 exactly: 1/3 = 33 1/3%, and the difference matters in exact answers.
  • Deciding an exponential decay value reaches zero; it falls below £1 or 0.001 but never reaches zero.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 2, 3 marks). Express 0.45 as a fraction in its lowest terms.

Answer: 0.45 = 45/100 = 9/20.

Question 2 (Paper 2, 3 marks). Write 0.27 with the 27 recurring as a fraction.

Answer: Let x = 0.272727...; then 100x = 27.2727...; subtracting gives 99x = 27, so x = 27/99 = 3/11.

Question 3 (Paper 4, 4 marks). In a sale, a bike is reduced by 15% to £255. Find the original price.

Answer: £255 represents 85% of the original, so the multiplier is 0.85 and the original price is 255/0.85 = £300. Check: 300 × 0.85 = 255 ✓.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 4 marks). A bacteria culture starts with 2000 and increases by 8% each hour. Find the size after 5 hours.

Answer: 2000 × 1.08⁵ = 2000 × 1.4693280768 = 2938.7 ≈ 2939 bacteria.

Question 5 (Paper 4, 3 marks). A town's population falls from 45 000 to 36 000 over a year. Find the percentage decrease.

Answer: Change = 9000; percentage = 9000/45 000 × 100 = 20%.

Question 6 (Paper 4, 5 marks). A car is bought for £12 000 and depreciates 18% in the first year and 12% in the second. Find its value after two years and the overall percentage loss.

Answer: 12 000 × 0.82 × 0.88 = 12 000 × 0.7216 = £8659.20. Overall loss = £3340.80, which is 3340.80/12 000 × 100 = 27.84% ≈ 27.8%. (Note 0.82 × 0.88 = 0.7216, a 27.84% total fall — not 30%.)

Fractions describe parts; powers and roots describe repeated multiplication — the next topic.

Equations and symbols

The conversion cycle in one place: fraction ↔ decimal ↔ percentage, the multiplier that handles every percentage change, and the mixed-number rule. Non-calculator Paper 2 lives on these.

Fraction to decimal: divide. 3/8 = 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375 Key: the line means "a fraction is a division"; the numerator is divided by the denominator. Terminating here because 8 has only 2 as a prime factor; a denominator with any other prime gives a recurring decimal.

Fraction to percentage: divide, then multiply by 100. 3/8 = 0.375 = 37.5% Key: the decimal comes first, then ×100 moves the point two places; the % sign replaces the "per hundred" you multiplied by. Reversing it, divide by 100 and simplify.

Percentage to fraction: write over 100 and simplify. 45% = 45/100 = 9/20 Key: percent means "per hundred", so the denominator is 100 before simplifying; cancel by the highest common factor, 5 here. Leaving 45/100 is a lost mark in a "give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form" question.

2 3/5 = (2 × 5 + 3)/5 = 13/5 Key: the whole-number part (2) is multiplied by the denominator (5), the numerator (3) is added, and the result goes over the same denominator. This is the step needed before multiplying or dividing mixed numbers.

the new value is 135% of the old, so multiply by 1.35: 1.35 × 240 = 324 Key: 1.35 is the multiplier for an increase of 35% (100% + 35%, as a decimal); 240 is the original. The multiplier chains: 0.8 × 0.8 = 0.64 is not a 40% discount but a 36% one, which is the trap this line exists to close.

18/60 × 100 = 30% Key: 18 = the part; 60 = the whole; ×100 turns the fraction into a percentage. "18 out of 60" and "18 as a percentage of 60" are the same question, and the fraction is always part ÷ whole.

title: A2 Level Biology: Microbiology, Immunity and Forensics
content:
Microbiology, Immunity and Forensics

Edexcel International A Level Biology — Unit 4 (WBI14), Topic 6. Every statement 6.1 to 6.20 is covered below, with its code in the heading. The topic links three big ideas: how microorganisms are grown and measured, how the body defends itself and why pathogens keep finding ways around those defences, and how DNA techniques are used to identify organisms and people.

6.1: Culturing microorganisms with aseptic technique

  • Aseptic technique keeps a culture pure: only the wanted microorganism grows. Sterilise media and equipment first, usually in an autoclave at 121 °C under pressure for about 15 minutes.
  • Work close to a Bunsen flame, flame the inoculating loop until red-hot before and after use, keep Petri dish lids mostly closed, and never pipette by mouth.
  • Incubate cultures inverted at a safe temperature, usually 25 °C for school work, so condensation does not drip onto the agar.

6.2: Measuring the growth of microorganisms

  • Direct cell counts: use a haemocytometer (counting chamber) under a microscope, counting cells in a known volume to get the number per cm³.
  • Viable counts by dilution plating: make a serial dilution, spread known volumes on agar, incubate, and count colonies on plates with about 30 to 300 colonies. Each colony is assumed to grow from one viable cell, so the count shows living cells only.
  • Mass methods: measure the dry mass of cells collected by centrifuging or filtering a known volume of culture.
  • Optical methods (turbidity): a colorimeter or spectrophotometer measures how much light the cloudy culture absorbs. Absorbance rises with cell density, so a calibration curve converts it to cell numbers.

6.3: The bacterial growth curve and the growth rate constant

  • Lag phase: cells adapt to the medium and synthesise enzymes; there is little or no division.
  • Exponential (log) phase: cells divide at a constant rate, so the population doubles each generation. N = N₀ × 2ⁿ, where n is the number of doublings.
  • Stationary phase: births equal deaths, because nutrients run short and waste builds up.
  • Death phase: deaths exceed births and the population falls.
  • Growth rate constant: in exponential growth N = N₀eᵏᵗ. So k = (ln N₂ − ln N₁) ÷ (t₂ − t₁). Plotting ln N against time gives a straight line whose gradient is k.

6.4: Core practical 13: growth of microorganisms in liquid culture

  • Inoculate a sterile liquid medium, take samples at regular intervals, and measure turbidity or cell count each time.
  • Plot the results to show the four phases of the curve, then calculate the exponential growth rate constant from the straight-line part.
  • Safe and ethical use: use only non-pathogenic strains, keep the culture closed, disinfect the bench, and autoclave all used material before disposal.

6.5: Structure of bacteria and viruses

  • Bacteria are cells with a cell wall (peptidoglycan), cell membrane, cytoplasm with ribosomes, and a circular DNA loop, often with plasmids. They have no nucleus.
  • Viruses are not cells. They have a nucleic acid core, either DNA or RNA, surrounded by a protein capsid. Some also have a lipid envelope taken from the host.
  • Comparisons: Ebola virus has single-stranded RNA and an envelope. Tobacco mosaic virus (TMV) has single-stranded RNA in a helical capsid, with no envelope. HIV has two RNA strands, reverse transcriptase and an envelope. λ phage, a virus of bacteria, has double-stranded DNA in a head with a tail and no envelope.
  • Lytic cycle: the virus takes over the host cell, makes new viruses, and the cell bursts (lyses) to release them.
  • Latency: the viral genome stays in the host cell without producing new viruses, and can become active later.

6.6: How Mycobacterium tuberculosis and HIV infect human cells

  • Tuberculosis: Mycobacterium tuberculosis is inhaled into the alveoli. Macrophages engulf it, but the bacterium survives inside them and multiplies. The body forms granulomas (tubercles) around the infection, and the lung tissue is destroyed. Symptoms include a persistent cough, fever, night sweats and weight loss. If untreated it can be fatal.
  • HIV: the virus binds to CD4 receptors and a co-receptor on helper T cells. Reverse transcriptase makes DNA from its RNA, which is inserted into the host genome. New viruses bud from the cell. The helper T cell population falls, so the immune system fails and opportunistic infections and cancers take hold (AIDS).

6.7: Routes of entry and barriers

  • Routes: inhalation (airborne droplets), ingestion (contaminated food and water), contact through broken skin or wounds, sexual contact, and vectors such as mosquitoes.
  • Barriers: intact skin (keratin, dryness, and the skin flora that competes with pathogens), stomach acid (pH about 2, which kills many ingested microbes), and gut flora that competes for space and nutrients. Mucus and cilia in the airways trap and move pathogens out.

6.8: Non-specific responses to infection

  • Inflammation: damaged cells release chemicals such as histamine, which dilate blood vessels and make them leaky. The area becomes red, hot and swollen, and white blood cells are recruited to the site.
  • Lysozyme: an enzyme in tears, saliva and mucus that breaks the peptidoglycan of bacterial cell walls.
  • Interferon: proteins released by virus-infected cells that warn neighbouring cells, which then resist viral replication. Interferon is antiviral, not a direct killer of the virus.
  • Phagocytosis: neutrophils and macrophages engulf a pathogen into a phagosome. Lysosomes fuse with it and enzymes digest the contents.

6.9: Antigens, antibodies, plasma cells, macrophages and antigen-presenting cells

  • An antigen is a foreign molecule, usually a protein or glycoprotein on a pathogen's surface, that triggers an immune response.
  • An antibody is a Y-shaped glycoprotein whose binding sites are complementary to one specific antigen. Antibodies mark pathogens for destruction and neutralise toxins.
  • Plasma cells are B cells that have been activated and that secrete antibodies in large amounts.
  • Macrophages and antigen-presenting cells engulf the pathogen, break it down, and display its antigens on their surface (on MHC proteins). This shows helper T cells what to respond to.

6.10: B cells and T cells

  • B effector (plasma) cells secrete antibodies. B memory cells survive for years and give a faster, larger response on the next exposure to the same antigen.
  • T helper cells (CD4) recognise the antigen on an antigen-presenting cell and release cytokines that activate B cells and T killer cells.
  • T killer (cytotoxic, CD8) cells bind to infected or abnormal cells and kill them, for example by releasing perforin.
  • T memory cells persist after the infection and respond quickly if the same pathogen returns.

6.11: Types of immunity

  • Natural active: the person is infected and makes their own antibodies and memory cells.
  • Natural passive: antibodies pass from mother to baby across the placenta or in breast milk. Protection is immediate but short-lived, and no memory cells are formed.
  • Artificial active: vaccination with an antigen, a weakened or dead pathogen, or a toxoid. The person makes antibodies and memory cells without becoming ill.
  • Artificial passive: injected antibodies, such as antivenom or antitoxin. Protection is immediate and short-lived, and the person's own immune system does not learn.

6.12: The evolutionary race between pathogens and hosts

  • Pathogens evolve evasion mechanisms. Antigenic variation changes the surface antigens: influenza and HIV mutate rapidly, so antibodies no longer fit.
  • Other evasion: hiding inside host cells (tuberculosis in macrophages, HIV in T cells), entering latency, and suppressing the immune response.
  • The host responds with new antibodies and T cells, so pathogens and hosts keep evolving against each other. This is the evolutionary race.

6.13: Bacteriostatic and bactericidal antibiotics

  • Bacteriostatic antibiotics stop bacteria growing and dividing, for example by blocking protein synthesis. The immune system then clears the infection.
  • Bactericidal antibiotics kill bacteria, for example penicillin, which stops cell wall synthesis so the cell bursts.
  • Antibiotics do not act on viruses, which use the host cell's machinery.
