Key: V = terminal p.d. (V); E = e.m.f. (V); I = current (A); r = internal resistance (Ω). This is why a battery reads nearly its e.m.f. on a high-resistance voltmeter and sags when a lamp is connected.

E = I (R + r)
Key: E = e.m.f. (V); I = current (A); R = external load resistance (Ω); r = internal resistance (Ω). The circuit as one loop: the e.m.f. drives the current through both the load and the source.

I = E / (R + r)
Key: I = current (A); E = e.m.f. (V); R = external resistance (Ω); r = internal resistance (Ω). To measure r, vary R, plot 1/I against R: gradient = 1/E and intercept = r/E.

P_output = I² R = E² R / (R + r)²
Key: P_output = power delivered to the external load (W); E = e.m.f. (V); R = load resistance (Ω); r = internal resistance (Ω); I = current (A). Differentiating gives the maximum-power condition below.

R = r gives P_output (max) = E² / (4 r)
Key: R = load resistance at which output power peaks (Ω); r = internal resistance (Ω); E = e.m.f. (V); P_output (max) = greatest power the source can deliver (W). Maximum power transfer — but at this point the efficiency is only 50%, since the source dissipates the same power internally.

Ammeter resistance → 0, voltmeter resistance → ∞
Key: an ideal ammeter is placed in series and must not change the current, so its resistance is zero; an ideal voltmeter is placed in parallel and must not divert current, so its resistance is infinite. A real voltmeter of resistance R_V across a resistor R reads V R_V / (R + R_V), which is always less than the true p.d.

10.2 Kirchhoff's laws

Σ I_in = Σ I_out
Key: currents entering a junction (A) equal currents leaving it. The conservation of charge: charge cannot pile up at a point in a steady circuit.

Σ E = Σ I R
Key: Σ E = sum of e.m.f.s around a closed loop (V); Σ I R = sum of the potential drops around the same loop (V). The conservation of energy: going round a loop returns you to the same potential.

Σ ΔV = 0 around any closed loop
Key: ΔV = potential change across each element (V), counted positive in the direction of travel when the potential rises. The same statement as the line above, written so that sources and resistors are treated alike.

10.3 Potential dividers

V_out = V_in × R₂ / (R₁ + R₂)
Key: V_out = p.d. across the resistor the output is taken from (V); V_in = p.d. across the whole chain (V); R₁ = the other resistor (Ω); R₂ = the resistor across which the output is measured (Ω). The chain carries the same current, so each resistor takes a share of the p.d. in proportion to its resistance.

V₁ / V₂ = R₁ / R₂
Key: V₁, V₂ = p.d.s across the two resistors (V); R₁, R₂ = their resistances (Ω). The ratio form — quicker than the fraction when both outputs are wanted.

V_out = E × R / (R + R_thermistor)
Key: V_out = output p.d. across the fixed resistor R (V); E = supply e.m.f. (V); R = fixed resistance (Ω); R_thermistor = resistance of the thermistor at the current temperature (Ω). A thermistor's resistance falls as temperature rises (negative temperature coefficient), so tapping across the fixed resistor gives an output that rises with temperature and tapping across the thermistor gives one that falls.

V_out = E × R_LDR / (R + R_LDR)
Key: V_out = output p.d. across the LDR (V); E = supply e.m.f. (V); R = fixed series resistance (Ω); R_LDR = resistance of the light-dependent resistor (Ω), which falls as illumination increases. The same divider, with light instead of heat as the input.

V_out = V_in × R₂ / (R₁ + R₂) × R_load / (R_load + R₂)
Key: R_load = resistance of whatever the divider feeds (Ω); the other symbols as above. The loaded-divider correction: a load in parallel with R₂ lowers the effective lower resistance, so the output sags below the unloaded value — the reason a divider is a poor supply for anything drawing current.

Appendix U — Extended worked long answer on the immune response for practice under time pressure

A long answer on the immune response is the kind of question where many candidates have all the pieces but lose marks by not putting them in time order or by not saying the distinctions clearly. The best practice for it is to write the answer from the durable ideas and the immune-process appendix, and to check that the answer has the non-specific first line, the specific response, the timing, the memory and the vaccination link in the right order, with the distinctions in the right places. A model answer starts with the first line: the pathogen has entered through the breach in the skin, the immediate non-specific responses include the local inflammation and the arrival of phagocytes, and phagocytosis is non-specific because it acts against a broad range of pathogens. The answer then moves to the specific response: the antigens on the pathogen are recognised, B cells produce antibodies specific to those antigens, T cells help and control and some T cells are important in dealing with infected cells, and memory B and T cells are formed. The answer then explains why the timing matters: on first exposure the primary response is slower because the specific lymphocytes have to be activated and expanded, but on later exposure the secondary response is faster and stronger because the memory cells are already present. The answer then relates it to vaccination: vaccination exposes the immune system to the antigen without the disease, so the memory is formed without the person having to suffer the infection first.

If you write that answer with those points in that order, you hit the marks the question is after. You hit the non-specific versus specific distinction, because you have said that the first line is non-specific and the specific response is specific. You hit the cell distinction, because you have said that B cells make antibodies and T cells help and control and deal with infected cells. You hit the timing distinction, because you have said that the primary response is slower and the secondary is faster and stronger because of memory. You hit the vaccination link, because you have said that vaccination primes the same memory system without the disease. You hit the process rather than the label, because you have said the sequence in time order and given the reasons for the sequence. If you can write that answer under time pressure, you are ready for the immune-response long question, because you have the kind of answer that question is built from. If you write a shorter answer that only says the body produces white blood cells and antibodies and remembers the pathogen, you have the label but not the reasoning, and the mark is in the reasoning.

The practice for the immune-response question is to write the answer from the durable ideas and then to check the distinctions one by one, because each distinction is a mark and each missing distinction is a lost mark. Check that the non-specific versus specific distinction is there. Check that the B versus T distinction is there. Check that the primary versus secondary timing distinction is there. Check that the memory cell role is there. Check that the vaccination link is there. If all five are there, the answer is ready. If one is missing, the missing one is the thing to practise before the next session, because the missing one is the mark that will be lost on the day. The practice is therefore not just to write the answer once, but to write it, check the distinctions, and practise the missing distinction until it is in the answer under time pressure. That is the practice that makes the immune-response question answerable, and it is the practice the note is designed to support through the durable ideas and the cross-strand and immune-process appendices.

Appendix V — Extended worked long answer on the gene technology techniques for practice under time pressure

A long answer on the gene technology techniques is the kind of question where candidates most often lose marks by knowing the name of each technique but not the principle and the purpose. The best practice for it is to write the answer technique by technique, with the principle and the purpose for each, and then to add the application and the limit if the question asks for it. A model answer starts with restriction enzymes: restriction enzymes cut DNA at specific recognition sequences, and some cuts leave sticky ends, which are short single-stranded overhangs that can base-pair with another piece of DNA cut with the same enzyme, so that the two pieces can be joined by DNA ligase. The answer then says why that matters: the specificity of the cut and the matching of the sticky ends are what make cloning possible, because they let a wanted piece of DNA be inserted into a vector at a predictable place. The next technique is PCR: PCR amplifies a specific DNA sequence in vitro through repeated cycles, and the cycles are denaturation, annealing of primers and extension by a heat-stable polymerase, so that the target sequence doubles each cycle. The answer then says why that matters: PCR lets a small sample of a specific sequence be amplified enough to study or use, and it is used in diagnostics and forensics, but the result is a specific target, not a random copy of the whole genome.

The next technique is gel electrophoresis: gel electrophoresis separates DNA fragments by size in an electric field, and DNA moves toward the positive electrode with smaller fragments moving faster, so the result is a banding pattern by size. The answer then says why that matters: the separation by size is what lets the fragments be resolved and compared, and a gene probe can then be used to detect a specific fragment by hybridisation, with the probe being a labelled complementary sequence. The next technique is the vector and transformation: a vector such as a plasmid carries foreign DNA into a host cell, and transformation is the uptake of the DNA, and a selectable marker lets you identify the transformed cells, with insertional inactivation used when the wanted DNA is inserted into a marker gene so that recombinant cells can be distinguished from non-recombinant ones. The answer then says why that matters: the vector and transformation are what put the DNA into the host, and the marker is what lets you find the cells that took it up, because not all cells do.

If you write that answer with the principle and the purpose for each technique, you hit the marks the question is after. You hit the principle for restriction enzymes, which is cutting at specific sequences and using sticky ends and ligation to join. You hit the purpose for PCR, which is amplifying a specific sequence in vitro by repeated cycles with a heat-stable polymerase. You hit the principle for electrophoresis, which is separation by size in an electric field, with DNA moving to the positive electrode and smaller fragments moving faster. You hit the purpose for the probe, which is detecting a specific fragment by hybridisation with a labelled complementary sequence. You hit the principle and purpose for the vector and transformation and the marker, which is carrying DNA into a host and selecting the cells that took it up, with insertional inactivation as one way to distinguish recombinant from non-recombinant. If you can write that answer under time pressure, you are ready for the gene technology long question, because you have the kind of answer that question is built from. If you write a shorter answer that only names the techniques, you have the labels but not the reasoning, and the mark is in the reasoning.

The practice for the gene technology question is to write the answer technique by technique and then to check that each technique has both the principle and the purpose, because the mark is usually in the principle and the purpose together, not in the name alone. Check that restriction enzymes have the specific cut and the sticky end and the ligation. Check that PCR has the specific amplification and the cycles and the heat-stable polymerase. Check that electrophoresis has the size separation and the movement to the positive electrode and the smaller-faster idea. Check that the probe has the complementary labelled sequence and the hybridisation. Check that the vector and transformation have the carrying of DNA and the selection of transformed cells and the optional insertional inactivation. If all of those are there, the answer is ready. If one is missing, the missing one is the thing to practise before the next session, because the missing one is the mark that will be lost on the day. The practice is therefore to write the answer, check the techniques one by one, and practise the missing technique until its principle and purpose are in the answer under time pressure. That is the practice that makes the gene technology question answerable, and it is the practice the note is designed to support through the durable ideas and the technique-by-technique appendix.

Appendix W — Using the note across both the biology and the forensic strands in one session

The note covers both the biology and the forensic strands of the topic, and a session that uses both at once is often more efficient than one that treats them separately, because the two strands share the recognition, contamination and interpretation ideas and because the session can use the shared ideas to build the precision for both. Start the session with the durable ideas, because those are the framework for both strands, and in particular with the recognition idea, because that is the one that runs through antigen-antibody recognition and DNA profiling recognition in different forms. Say the recognition idea with the antigen-antibody example on one side and the DNA profiling example on the other, and check that you can say the common point and the difference in the same answer. If you can, the session has the framework for both strands in one place, and the rest of the session can fill in the biology detail on one side and the forensic detail on the other without losing the shared idea. The shared idea is the thing that makes the two strands feel like one topic rather than two, and the shared idea is the thing the cross-strand questions are after.

The second part of the session is to practise the biology strand in detail, because the biology strand is the one where the marks are most often lost for lack of sequence and distinction. Practise the immune-response long answer with the non-specific first line, the specific response, the timing, the memory and the vaccination link in the right order. Practise the bacteria-versus-virus distinction, the aseptic-technique reasoning, the growth-curve phases and the growth-factor ideas, and the antigen-antibody and B-cell-T-cell distinctions. Check each practice answer against the model and the appendix that covers the same ground, and note the gaps. If the gaps are small, move on to the forensic strand. If the gaps are large, spend the rest of the session on the largest gap, because the largest gap is the one that will lose the most marks on the biology side. The biology side is the larger of the two strands, and it is the one where most of the marks are, so it is the one that gets the most of the session. The session that gives the biology side the most time is the session that is using the topic the way the marks are distributed.

The third part of the session is to practise the forensic strand in detail, because the forensic strand is the one where the marks are most often lost for lack of interpretation and care reasoning. Practise the DNA profiling answer with the pattern comparison, the identification and exclusion idea, and the interpretation-in-context point. Practise the biological-evidence care answer with the contamination, chain of custody and context ideas. Check each practice answer against the model and the appendix that covers the same ground, and note the gaps. If the gaps are small, move on to the cross-strand question. If the gaps are large, spend the rest of the session on the largest gap, because the largest gap is the one that will lose the most marks on the forensic side. The forensic side is the smaller of the two strands, but it is the one where the interpretation marks are easiest to lose for lack of reasoning, so it is the one that needs the session to be explicit about care and context. The session that gives the forensic side enough time for the care and context reasoning is the session that is using the forensic strand the way the marks are actually earned.

The final part of the session is to do the cross-strand question, because that is the one that tests whether the two strands have been tied together rather than kept as separate lists. Practise the cross-strand answer that relates, for example, the immune recognition of antigens to the forensic comparison of DNA patterns, or the microbiology culturing care to the forensic biological-evidence care. Check that the answer has the common point and the differences, and that it does not treat the two strands as unrelated. If the answer has the common point and the differences, the session has tied the two strands together, and the cross-strand question is answerable. If the answer has only the two strands separately, the session has not yet tied them, and the cross-strand question is still vulnerable. The session that ends with the cross-strand question is the session that tests the tying, and the tying is the thing that makes the topic a connected whole rather than two separate topics. That is the session that uses the note the way it is meant to be used, with both strands in one place and the shared ideas visible across both.

Appendix X — How the note holds up against the kind of mark scheme this specification actually uses

The note is written against the kind of mark scheme this specification actually uses, which is one that rewards reasoning over labels and sequence over lists, and that is the reason the note is long in the way it is long. A mark scheme of this kind does not usually give a mark for a label on its own when the question is asking for the reasoning, because the label is not the reasoning; it gives a mark for the step in the sequence, the distinction in the comparison, or the benefit or issue in the evaluation. If you write the answer to match that kind of mark scheme, you are writing for the marks the exam is actually after, and the note is written to help you write that kind of answer. If you write the answer as if the marks were for labels, you are writing for a different kind of mark scheme, and you will lose the marks that the real one gives for reasoning. The reason the note is long is that the real mark scheme rewards reasoning, and the reasoning takes space to lay out, so the note has the reasoning laid out in the durable ideas, the anchors, the distinctions, the technique-by-technique treatment, the immune-process treatment, the forensic-interpretation treatment and the cross-strand treatment. That is the length that matches the mark scheme, and that is the length that makes the note usable for the exam.

The mark scheme also rewards the distinction between a correct answer and an almost-correct answer, and that is the reason the note has the typical mistakes and the edge cases laid out explicitly. The almost-correct answer is the one that has the label but not the reasoning, the sequence but not the key step, the comparison but not the distinction, or the evaluation but not the specificity. The mark scheme takes marks off the almost-correct answer for the missing step or distinction or specificity, and the note is written to show you what the missing thing is and how to put it in under time pressure. If you can use the note to find the missing thing in your practice answers and put it in, you are practising the thing the mark scheme rewards, which is the difference between the correct answer and the almost-correct one. That is the use of the note against the real mark scheme: to show you the difference the mark scheme cares about, and to give you the material to close the difference under time pressure.

The mark scheme also rewards the ability to answer the question that is actually there, and that is the reason the note has the practice answers shaped for the question shapes rather than for the note itself. The practice answers are shaped for the immune-response question, the gene technology question, the coordination question, the cross-strand question, the description question, the comparison question and the evaluation question, because those are the shapes the mark scheme is built around. If you can write the practice answer in the shape of the question, you are writing for the marks the mark scheme gives, because the mark scheme gives marks for the shape as well as for the content. If you write the answer in the wrong shape, you are writing for a different kind of mark scheme, and you will lose the marks that the real one gives for the shape. The note is written to help you write in the right shape, and that is the use of the practice answers: to model the shape the marks are in, so that you can write in that shape under time pressure on the day.

The final point about the mark scheme is that it is the mark scheme you have to satisfy, not the note, so the note is successful if it helps you write answers that satisfy the mark scheme, not if it is itself a complete summary of everything the specification ever says. The note is long because the mark scheme rewards reasoning, sequence, distinction and specificity, and because those take space to lay out, but the note is only a tool for helping you write the answers the mark scheme rewards, and a tool is only good if it is used well. The use that makes it good is to practise the answers under time pressure, to check the distinctions and the sequence and the reasoning against the note, and to close the gaps before the exam. If you use the note that way, it helps you write the answers the mark scheme rewards, and that is the success the note is aiming for. If you use the note as a thing to read once and then forget, it will not help you write the answers the mark scheme rewards, and that is the use it fails at. The note is long so that you can use it as a practice source, and the practice source is the use that makes it successful, because the practice source is the thing that builds the answers the mark scheme rewards.

Appendix Y — The final end-of-topic checklist for the whole biology-A2 wave in one place

The end-of-topic checklist for the whole wave is the thing that tells you whether the wave is really done or only mostly done, and it is the thing to check after the note is written and before you move on from the wave. The first thing the checklist should confirm is that every specification point in the wave has a place in the note, because if a point has no place, the wave is not done, and the missing point is the thing to add before the wave is finished. For this biology-A2 wave, the checklist is the set of specification points the note is built from: the photosynthesis stages and the ATP story, the light-dependent and light-independent reactions and the chloroplast, the absorption and action spectra and the Rf value, the GPP and NPP and the transfer efficiency, the ecology vocabulary and the biotic and abiotic factors, the succession and the fieldwork methods, the climate evidence and the greenhouse mechanism and the mitigation, the climate models and the limits, the enzyme and temperature and Q10 and the development practical, the evolution and allele frequency and speciation, the receptor and synapse and muscle and homeostasis and the endocrine and plant and gene technology topics. If all of those have a place in the note, the wave is complete in coverage. If one is missing, the missing one is the thing to add, because the missing one is the gap that the exam can test without warning. The note is long enough to cover all of those, and the coverage is the first thing the checklist should confirm.

The second thing the checklist should confirm is that the note is not just covering the coverage but also the precision, because coverage without precision is what loses marks on the day. For this wave, the precision is the sequence and the distinctions: the synaptic calcium step, the sliding-filament idea with ATP and calcium, the insulin-glucagon opposition with negative feedback, the restriction enzyme and PCR and electrophoresis principles, the primary-versus-secondary timing, the non-specific-versus-specific distinction, the B-versus-T distinction, the herd-immunity-as-coverage distinction, the DNA-profiling-as-interpretation distinction, and the cross-strand recognition idea. If all of those are in the note with enough detail to be used under time pressure, the wave is complete in precision. If one is missing, the missing one is the thing to add, because the missing one is the mark that will be lost on the day. The note is long enough to cover all of those, and the precision is the second thing the checklist should confirm.

The third thing the checklist should confirm is that the note is usable under time pressure, because coverage and precision are not enough if they cannot be used under time pressure. For this wave, the usability is the practice answers and the one-page summary: the immune-response long answer, the gene technology long answer, the coordination long answer, the cross-strand answer, the description and comparison answers, the evaluation answers, and the one-page summary of the wave. If all of those can be produced and then checked against the note under time pressure, the wave is complete in usability. If one cannot, the one that cannot is the thing to practise, because the one that cannot is the mark that will be lost on the day. The note is long enough to support all of those, and the usability is the third thing the checklist should confirm. If the wave is complete in coverage, precision and usability, the wave is done, and the note has done its job for the wave. If the wave is missing one of those, the missing one is the thing to finish before the wave is done, and the note is there to finish it.

Appendix Z — Closing the wave: what to do when the wave passes the checklist and what to do when it does not

When the wave passes the checklist, the thing to do is to consolidate and then move on, because the wave is done and the next wave is the thing that now matters. The consolidation is the one-page summary and the four-hour review structure, because those are the things that make the wave reachable on the day and the things that make the wave usable for the exam. If the wave passes the checklist and you also have the one-page summary and the four-hour review structure, the wave is not just done in coverage and precision and usability; it is also done in the form that makes it usable on the day, and that is the form that matters. The move on is to the next wave, which is the thing that the project is actually about, and the wave is the unit of progress. If the wave is done, the next wave is the thing to start, because the project is a set of waves and the waves are the units, and the waves are the thing that build the topic one wave at a time. The thing to do when the wave passes is therefore to consolidate it into the reachable form and then start the next wave, because that is the progress the project is built on.

When the wave does not pass the checklist, the thing to do is to find the missing piece and finish it, because the wave is not done until the missing piece is done, and the missing piece is the gap that will lose marks if it is left open. For this biology-A2 wave, the missing piece is sometimes a coverage gap, sometimes a precision gap, and sometimes a usability gap, and the thing to do is to find which kind of gap it is and finish that kind of gap before moving on. If it is a coverage gap, the thing to do is to add the missing specification point to the note. If it is a precision gap, the thing to do is to add the missing sequence or distinction or reasoning to the note. If it is a usability gap, the thing to do is to add the missing practice answer or one-page-summary piece to the note. The thing to do when the wave does not pass is therefore to find the missing piece and finish the kind of gap it is, because the gap is the thing that stands between the wave and the done state, and the done state is the thing the project is aiming for. The note is there to finish the gap, because the note is the tool for the wave, and the tool is what finishes the gap when the wave is not yet done.

The final thing to do when the wave does not pass is to set a time limit for finishing the gap, because the project is a set of waves and the waves are the units, and a wave that does not finish its gap is a wave that holds up the next wave, and the next wave is the thing that matters to the project. If the gap can be finished in the time limit, finish it and then move on, because that is the progress the project is built on. If the gap cannot be finished in the time limit, the thing to do is to add the reachable part of the gap and leave the rest for the next session, because the reachable part is the part that matters most and the rest can wait, and the project is built on reachable progress more than on perfect progress. The note is long enough to hold both the reachable part and the rest, because the note is the tool for the wave, and the tool is what holds the wave together while the gap is being finished. The wave is therefore finished when the gap is finished or when the reachable part is done and the rest is scheduled, because either way the wave is no longer blocking the next wave, and the next wave is the thing the project is built on. The decision is the thing to make when the wave does not pass, and the note is the tool that makes the decision usable, because the note is the place where the wave lives and the wave is the thing that has to be passed before the next wave can be started.

If one is missing, the missing one is the thing to practise before the next session, because the missing one is the mark that will be lost on the day. The practice is therefore to write the answer, check the techniques one by one, and practise the missing technique until its principle and purpose are in the answer under time pressure. That is the practice that makes the gene technology question answerable, and it is the practice the note is designed to support through the durable ideas and the technique-by-technique appendix.

Appendix W — Using the note across both the biology and the forensic strands in one session

The note covers both the biology and the forensic strands of the topic, and a session that uses both at once is often more efficient than one that treats them separately, because the two strands share the recognition, contamination and interpretation ideas and because the session can use the shared ideas to build the precision for both. Start the session with the durable ideas, because those are the framework for both strands, and in particular with the recognition idea, because that is the one that runs through antigen-antibody recognition and DNA profiling recognition in different forms. Say the recognition idea with the antigen-antibody example on one side and the DNA profiling example on the other, and check that you can say the common point and the difference in the same answer. If you can, the session has the framework for both strands in one place, and the rest of the session can fill in the biology detail on one side and the forensic detail on the other without losing the shared idea. The shared idea is the thing that makes the two strands feel like one topic rather than two, and the shared idea is the thing the cross-strand questions are after.

The second part of the session is to practise the biology strand in detail, because the biology strand is the one where the marks are most often lost for lack of sequence and distinction. Practise the immune-response long answer with the non-specific first line, the specific response, the timing, the memory and the vaccination link in the right order. Practise the bacteria-versus-virus distinction, the aseptic-technique reasoning, the growth-curve phases and the growth-factor ideas, and the antigen-antibody and B-cell-T-cell distinctions. Check each practice answer against the model and the appendix that covers the same ground, and note the gaps. If the gaps are small, move on to the forensic strand. If the gaps are large, spend the rest of the session on the largest gap, because the largest gap is the one that will lose the most marks on the biology side. The biology side is the larger of the two strands, and it is the one where most of the marks are, so it is the one that gets the most of the session. The session that gives the biology side the most time is the session that is using the topic the way the marks are distributed.

The third part of the session is to practise the forensic strand in detail, because the forensic strand is the one where the marks are most often lost for lack of interpretation and care reasoning. Practise the DNA profiling answer with the pattern comparison, the identification and exclusion idea, and the interpretation-in-context point. Practise the biological-evidence care answer with the contamination, chain of custody and context ideas. Check each practice answer against the model and the appendix that covers the same ground, and note the gaps. If the gaps are small, move on to the cross-strand question. If the gaps are large, spend the rest of the session on the largest gap, because the largest gap is the one that will lose the most marks on the forensic side. The forensic side is the smaller of the two strands, but it is the one where the interpretation marks are easiest to lose for lack of reasoning, so it is the one that needs the session to be explicit about care and context. The session that gives the forensic side enough time for the care and context reasoning is the session that is using the forensic strand the way the marks are actually earned.

The final part of the session is to do the cross-strand question, because that is the one that tests whether the two strands have been tied together rather than kept as separate lists. Practise the cross-strand answer that relates, for example, the immune recognition of antigens to the forensic comparison of DNA patterns, or the microbiology culturing care to the forensic biological-evidence care. Check that the answer has the common point and the differences, and that it does not treat the two strands as unrelated. If the answer has the common point and the differences, the session has tied the two strands together, and the cross-strand question is answerable. If the answer has only the two strands separately, the session has not yet tied them, and the cross-strand question is still vulnerable. The session that ends with the cross-strand question is the session that tests the tying, and the tying is the thing that makes the topic a connected whole rather than two separate topics. That is the session that uses the note the way it is meant to be used, with both strands in one place and the shared ideas visible across both.

Appendix X — How the note holds up against the kind of mark scheme this specification actually uses

The note is written against the kind of mark scheme this specification actually uses, which is one that rewards reasoning over labels and sequence over lists, and that is the reason the note is long in the way it is long. A mark scheme of this kind does not usually give a mark for a label on its own when the question is asking for the reasoning, because the label is not the reasoning; it gives a mark for the step in the sequence, the distinction in the comparison, or the benefit or issue in the evaluation. If you write the answer to match that kind of mark scheme, you are writing for the marks the exam is actually after, and the note is written to help you write that kind of answer. If you write the answer as if the marks were for labels, you are writing for a different kind of mark scheme, and you will lose the marks that the real one gives for reasoning. The reason the note is long is that the real mark scheme rewards reasoning, and the reasoning takes space to lay out, so the note has the reasoning laid out in the durable ideas, the anchors, the distinctions, the technique-by-technique treatment, the immune-process treatment, the forensic-interpretation treatment and the cross-strand treatment. That is the length that matches the mark scheme, and that is the length that makes the note usable for the exam.

The mark scheme also rewards the distinction between a correct answer and an almost-correct answer, and that is the reason the note has the typical mistakes and the edge cases laid out explicitly. The almost-correct answer is the one that has the label but not the reasoning, the sequence but not the key step, the comparison but not the distinction, or the evaluation but not the specificity. The mark scheme takes marks off the almost-correct answer for the missing step or distinction or specificity, and the note is written to show you what the missing thing is and how to put it in under time pressure. If you can use the note to find the missing thing in your practice answers and put it in, you are practising the thing the mark scheme rewards, which is the difference between the correct answer and the almost-correct one. That is the use of the note against the real mark scheme: to show you the difference the mark scheme cares about, and to give you the material to close the difference under time pressure.

The mark scheme also rewards the ability to answer the question that is actually there, and that is the reason the note has the practice answers shaped for the question shapes rather than for the note itself. The practice answers are shaped for the immune-response question, the gene technology question, the coordination question, the cross-strand question, the description question, the comparison question and the evaluation question, because those are the shapes the mark scheme is built around. If you can write the practice answer in the shape of the question, you are writing for the marks the mark scheme gives, because the mark scheme gives marks for the shape as well as for the content. If you write the answer in the wrong shape, you are writing for a different kind of mark scheme, and you will lose the marks that the real one gives for the shape. The note is written to help you write in the right shape, and that is the use of the practice answers: to model the shape the marks are in, so that you can write in that shape under time pressure on the day.

The final point about the mark scheme is that it is the mark scheme you have to satisfy, not the note, so the note is successful if it helps you write answers that satisfy the mark scheme, not if it is itself a complete summary of everything the specification ever says. The note is long because the mark scheme rewards reasoning, sequence, distinction and specificity, and because those take space to lay out, but the note is only a tool for helping you write the answers the mark scheme rewards, and a tool is only good if it is used well. The use that makes it good is to practise the answers under time pressure, to check the distinctions and the sequence and the reasoning against the note, and to close the gaps before the exam. If you use the note that way, it helps you write the answers the mark scheme rewards, and that is the success the note is aiming for. If you use the note as a thing to read once and then forget, it will not help you write the answers the mark scheme rewards, and that is the use it fails at. The note is long so that you can use it as a practice source, and the practice source is the use that makes it successful, because the practice source is the thing that builds the answers the mark scheme rewards.

Appendix Y — The final end-of-topic checklist for the whole biology-A2 wave in one place

The end-of-topic checklist for the whole wave is the thing that tells you whether the wave is really done or only mostly done, and it is the thing to check after the note is written and before you move on from the wave. The first thing the checklist should confirm is that every specification point in the wave has a place in the note, because if a point has no place, the wave is not done, and the missing point is the thing to add before the wave is finished. For this biology-A2 wave, the checklist is the set of specification points the note is built from: the photosynthesis stages and the ATP story, the light-dependent and light-independent reactions and the chloroplast, the absorption and action spectra and the Rf value, the GPP and NPP and the transfer efficiency, the ecology vocabulary and the biotic and abiotic factors, the succession and the fieldwork methods, the climate evidence and the greenhouse mechanism and the mitigation, the climate models and the limits, the enzyme and temperature and Q10 and the development practical, the evolution and allele frequency and speciation, the receptor and synapse and muscle and homeostasis and the endocrine and plant and gene technology topics. If all of those have a place in the note, the wave is complete in coverage. If one is missing, the missing one is the thing to add, because the missing one is the gap that the exam can test without warning. The note is long enough to cover all of those, and the coverage is the first thing the checklist should confirm.

The second thing the checklist should confirm is that the note is not just covering the coverage but also the precision, because coverage without precision is what loses marks on the day. For this wave, the precision is the sequence and the distinctions: the synaptic calcium step, the sliding-filament idea with ATP and calcium, the insulin-glucagon opposition with negative feedback, the restriction enzyme and PCR and electrophoresis principles, the primary-versus-secondary timing, the non-specific-versus-specific distinction, the B-versus-T distinction, the herd-immunity-as-coverage distinction, the DNA-profiling-as-interpretation distinction, and the cross-strand recognition idea. If all of those are in the note with enough detail to be used under time pressure, the wave is complete in precision. If one is missing, the missing one is the thing to add, because the missing one is the mark that will be lost on the day. The note is long enough to cover all of those, and the precision is the second thing the checklist should confirm.

The third thing the checklist should confirm is that the note is usable under time pressure, because coverage and precision are not enough if they cannot be used under time pressure. For this wave, the usability is the practice answers and the one-page summary: the immune-response long answer, the gene technology long answer, the coordination long answer, the cross-strand answer, the description and comparison answers, the evaluation answers, and the one-page summary of the wave. If all of those can be produced and then checked against the note under time pressure, the wave is complete in usability. If one cannot, the one that cannot is the thing to practise, because the one that cannot is the mark that will be lost on the day. The note is long enough to support all of those, and the usability is the third thing the checklist should confirm. If the wave is complete in coverage, precision and usability, the wave is done, and the note has done its job for the wave. If the wave is missing one of those, the missing one is the thing to finish before the wave is done, and the note is there to finish it.

Appendix Z — Closing the wave: what to do when the wave passes the checklist and what to do when it does not

When the wave passes the checklist, the thing to do is to consolidate and then move on, because the wave is done and the next wave is the thing that now matters. The consolidation is the one-page summary and the four-hour review structure, because those are the things that make the wave reachable on the day and the things that make the wave usable for the exam. If the wave passes the checklist and you also have the one-page summary and the four-hour review structure, the wave is not just done in coverage and precision and usability; it is also done in the form that makes it usable on the day, and that is the form that matters. The move on is to the next wave, which is the thing that the project is actually about, and the wave is the unit of progress. If the wave is done, the next wave is the thing to start, because the project is a set of waves and the waves are the units, and the waves are the thing that build the topic one wave at a time. The thing to do when the wave passes is therefore to consolidate it into the reachable form and then start the next wave, because that is the progress the project is built on.

When the wave does not pass the checklist, the thing to do is to find the missing piece and finish it, because the wave is not done until the missing piece is done, and the missing piece is the gap that will lose marks if it is left open. For this biology-A2 wave, the missing piece is sometimes a coverage gap, sometimes a precision gap, and sometimes a usability gap, and the thing to do is to find which kind of gap it is and finish that kind of gap before moving on. If it is a coverage gap, the thing to do is to add the missing specification point to the note. If it is a precision gap, the thing to do is to add the missing sequence or distinction or reasoning to the note. If it is a usability gap, the thing to do is to add the missing practice answer or one-page-summary piece to the note. The thing to do when the wave does not pass is therefore to find the missing piece and finish the kind of gap it is, because the gap is the thing that stands between the wave and the done state, and the done state is the thing the project is aiming for. The note is there to finish the gap, because the note is the tool for the wave, and the tool is what finishes the gap when the wave is not yet done.

The final thing to do when the wave does not pass is to set a time limit for finishing the gap, because the project is a set of waves and the waves are the units, and a wave that does not finish its gap is a wave that holds up the next wave, and the next wave is the thing that matters to the project. If the gap can be finished in the time limit, finish it and then move on, because that is the progress the project is built on. If the gap cannot be finished in the time limit, the thing to do is to add the reachable part of the gap and leave the rest for the next session, because the reachable part is the part that matters most and the rest can wait, and the project is built on reachable progress more than on perfect progress. The note is long enough to hold both the reachable part and the rest, because the note is the tool for the wave, and the tool is what holds the wave together while the gap is being finished. The wave is therefore finished when the gap is finished or when the reachable part is done and the rest is scheduled, because either way the wave is no longer blocking the next wave, and the next wave is the thing the project is built on. The decision is the thing to make when the wave does not pass, and the note is the tool that makes the decision usable, because the note is the place where the wave lives and the wave is the thing that has to be passed before the next wave can be started.

title: IGCSE Physics: Waves and Sound
content:
IGCSE Physics: Waves and Sound

Cambridge IGCSE Physics 0625 (2026–2028), Topic 3 Waves: statements 3.1 General properties of waves, 3.2 Light, 3.3 Electromagnetic spectrum and 3.4 Sound. Waves are how energy travels from place to place without moving matter along with it, and everything from a ripple on a pond to a gamma ray obeys the same few rules. This note builds the general wave behaviour first, then light (reflection, refraction, lenses, colour), then the electromagnetic spectrum and finally sound, with the calculations and the ray constructions that Paper 4 and Paper 6 reward.

General properties of waves

A wave transfers energy without transferring matter. Drop a cork into a ripple tank and the ripples pass under it while the cork only bobs: the water moves up and down, not outward. Every wave is described by the same vocabulary:

TermMeaningUnit
AmplitudeMaximum displacement from the rest position; relates to energy (loudness for sound, brightness for light)metre (m)
Wavelength (lambda)Distance between two equivalent points on neighbouring waves, e.g. crest to crestmetre (m)
FrequencyNumber of complete waves passing a point per second; equals the source's number of oscillations per secondhertz (Hz)
PeriodTime for one complete wave to pass a pointsecond (s)
Wave speedDistance a wave crest travels per secondmetre per second (m s⁻¹)
wave speed = frequency x wavelength        v = f lambda
period = 1 / frequency        T = 1 / f
  • v: wave speed in metres per second (m s⁻¹); f: frequency in hertz (Hz, = s⁻¹); lambda: wavelength in metres (m). All scalars, so there are no signs to worry about — but all three quantities must be in SI units before multiplying.

Transverse waves have the vibration perpendicular to the direction of travel: water waves, light and all electromagnetic waves, waves on a shaken rope. Longitudinal waves have the vibration parallel to the direction of travel: sound in air, the push-pull of a slinky. Longitudinal waves show compressions (where particles are pushed together) and rarefactions (where they are spread apart).

Three behaviours describe what happens when waves meet things. Reflection is bouncing off a surface; the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, measured from the normal. Refraction is the change of direction when a wave passes into a different medium at an angle, because its speed changes; moving into a slower medium bends the ray towards the normal and the wavelength shortens while the frequency stays constant. Diffraction is the spreading of waves through a gap or around an obstacle, and it is most pronounced when the gap width is comparable to the wavelength. Ripple tanks demonstrate all three: straight barriers give reflection, shallow regions give refraction, and narrow gaps give circular wavefronts after diffraction (Supplement: wider gaps give less spreading, and an edge produces noticeable diffraction only for longer wavelengths).

Reflection of light

Light travels in straight lines and reflects from smooth surfaces with the law of reflection: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, both measured between the ray and the normal (an imaginary line perpendicular to the surface at the point of incidence). A plane-mirror image is upright, the same size as the object, laterally inverted (left and right swapped), and as far behind the mirror as the object is in front.

Supplement: the ray construction. To locate the image, draw a ray from the object to the mirror, continue it behind the mirror at the same angle, and drop a perpendicular from the image position to the mirror; repeat with a second ray. Where the reflected rays appear to come from behind the mirror is where the image sits. Drawing the construction to scale with a protractor gives the image position exactly.

Refraction of light

When light passes from air into glass at an angle it slows and bends towards the normal; passing back out it speeds up and bends away from the normal. The amount of bending is fixed by the material's refractive index:

refractive index = sin(angle of incidence in vacuum or air) / sin(angle of refraction)        n = sin i / sin r
critical angle:        sin c = 1 / n
  • n: refractive index, a scalar with no unit, always greater than 1 for a material like glass or water.
  • i and r: angles in degrees measured from the normal, not from the surface.
  • c: critical angle in degrees, defined for a ray passing from the material into air.

Total internal reflection happens when a ray inside a material hits the boundary at an angle greater than the critical angle: none of it escapes and all reflects. Two applications are examinable: optical fibres, where light bounces along the core with total internal reflection and carries data over long distances with little loss, and prisms in periscopes and binoculars, where a 45° prism turns light through 90° or 180° by total internal reflection with almost no energy loss compared with a mirror.

Thin lenses and vision

A converging lens brings parallel rays to a focus at its principal focus; a diverging lens spreads them out as if they came from a focus on the near side. Three standard rays build any image on a converging lens:

  • A ray parallel to the axis refracts through the principal focus on the far side.
  • A ray through the centre of the lens passes straight through undeviated.
  • A ray through the near-side principal focus emerges parallel to the axis.

Where two refracted rays cross, a real image forms — it can be shown on a screen. Where they only appear to diverge from a point behind the lens, a virtual image forms — it cannot be caught on a screen and is seen only by looking through the lens. An object beyond twice the focal length gives a smaller inverted real image (a camera); an object between the focus and the lens gives a larger upright virtual image (a magnifying glass, Supplement). Short sight (myopia) is corrected with a diverging lens, long sight (hyperopia) with a converging lens (Supplement).

Dispersion and the electromagnetic spectrum

White light passing through a prism disperses into a spectrum from red to violet because different colours refract by different amounts: red light is refracted least (it travels fastest in glass) and violet most. Light of a single colour is monochromatic (Supplement). The visible spectrum sits inside a much larger family — the electromagnetic spectrum, all waves travelling at 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ in a vacuum, all transverse, arranged by increasing frequency (and decreasing wavelength) as: radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays.

RegionWavelength scaleUsesHazards
Radio wavesmetres to hundreds of metresRadio and TV broadcasting, communicationsLittle evidence of harm at normal levels
Microwavesmillimetres to centimetresMobile phones, satellite communications, microwave ovens, radarHeating of body tissue; dangerous at high intensity
InfraredmicrometresHeating, night-vision cameras, remote controls, optical fibresBurns and skin heating at high intensity
Visible light400–700 nmVision, photography, fibre-optic dataDazzle; eye damage from lasers and the Sun
Ultraviolet10–400 nmFluorescent lamps, sterilisation, security markingSunburn, skin ageing and skin cancer, eye damage
X-rays0.01–10 nmMedical imaging, airport security, detecting cracks in metalIonising: cell damage and cancer risk; dose kept low
Gamma raysbelow 0.01 nmSterilising equipment, cancer radiotherapy, food irradiationIonising: severe cell damage; shielded with lead and concrete

Supplement: signals and communication. An analogue signal varies continuously with the quantity it carries; a digital signal is a stream of on/off pulses. Digital signals are preferred because they can be regenerated without amplifying noise, can be compressed to carry more information, can be encrypted, and can carry text, sound and images in the same stream. Satellite links work by beaming a microwave signal to an orbiting satellite, which amplifies and retransmits it back to a distant ground station.

Sound

Sound is a longitudinal wave produced by vibrating objects and travelling through a medium — air at about 340 m s⁻¹ at room temperature, faster in liquids and fastest in solids, because the particles are closer together and pass the vibration on more quickly. Sound cannot travel through a vacuum. The frequency of a sound sets its pitch (high frequency, high pitch), and the amplitude sets its loudness. The human range of hearing is roughly 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz.

Echoes and distance measurement. Sound reflects from hard surfaces, giving echoes. The depth of the sea under a ship is found by sending a pulse and timing its return:

distance to the surface = (speed of sound x total time) / 2        s = v t / 2

The halving is essential — the pulse travels down and back — and forgetting it is the classic error in this topic. Measuring the time between two microphones a known distance apart gives the speed of sound directly: v = distance/time.

Ultrasound is sound above the human hearing range (above 20 kHz). Its short wavelength means it reflects well from small internal boundaries, which makes it useful for prenatal scanning (reflection at tissue boundaries builds an image), cleaning delicate items (high-energy vibrations dislodge dirt), flaw detection in metal castings (an internal crack reflects the pulse), and sonar depth sounding. All uses share the same principle: send a pulse, time the echo, calculate the distance with s = vt/2.

Worked example: wave calculation and echo depth

A ship's sonar sends ultrasound of frequency 50 kHz. The echo returns from the seabed after 0.12 s. The speed of sound in seawater is 1500 m s⁻¹.

total distance travelled = v t = 1500 x 0.12 = 180 m
depth of the sea = 180 / 2 = 90 m

Second calculation: a ripple tank wave has a wavelength of 0.040 m and the dippers oscillate 25 times per second. The wave speed is v = f λ = 25 × 0.040 = 1.0 m s⁻¹. The frequency of the wave equals the frequency of the source, and it stays unchanged when the wave passes into deeper water — only the speed and the wavelength change there.

Common mistakes

  • Measuring a wavelength from crest to trough; that is half a wavelength. Measure between two equivalent points on neighbouring waves.
  • Forgetting that frequency never changes on refraction. The speed and wavelength change; the frequency is set by the source and stays constant.
  • Mixing up the angle of incidence with its complement: all angles in reflection and refraction are measured from the normal.
  • Using v = fλ with mismatched units: hertz times centimetres gives cm s⁻¹, not m s⁻¹. Convert the wavelength to metres first.
  • Forgetting to halve the total distance in an echo calculation.
  • Drawing a converging lens ray diagram without the two special rays, or putting the image on the wrong side: real images form on the far side where rays actually cross, virtual images on the same side as the object.
  • Claiming light travels slower in a vacuum than in glass; it is fastest in a vacuum and slower in denser media, which is what causes refraction.
  • Describing a digital signal as continuously varying; it is discrete pulses, which is precisely why it resists noise.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 4, 3 marks). A water wave has a frequency of 4.0 Hz and a wavelength of 0.25 m. Calculate its speed and its period.

Answer: v = fλ = 4.0 × 0.25 = 1.0 m s⁻¹. Period T = 1/f = 1/4.0 = 0.25 s.

Question 2 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Explain why sound cannot be heard on the Moon but sunlight still reaches it.

Answer: Sound is a longitudinal wave that needs a medium, because it travels by particles passing vibrations to their neighbours. The Moon is surrounded by a vacuum, with no particles to carry the vibration, so sound cannot travel there. Light is an electromagnetic transverse wave that carries energy without needing a medium, so it crosses the vacuum of space easily.

Question 3 (Paper 2 style). Light passes from air into glass at an angle. Which quantity does not change? A speed; B wavelength; C frequency; D direction. Answer: C. The frequency is set by the source and is unchanged; speed and wavelength both fall in glass and the ray bends.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Ultrasound of speed 1500 m s⁻¹ is used to find the depth of the sea. The echo returns in 0.40 s. Calculate the depth and explain why ultrasound is used rather than audible sound.

Answer: Depth = v t / 2 = 1500 × 0.40 / 2 = 300 m. Ultrasound has a very short wavelength, so it reflects well from small boundaries and gives a clear echo pattern without diffracting uselessly around small features; it also does not interfere with ordinary sound and is harmless at the intensities used.

Question 5 (Paper 6 style). Describe how to measure the speed of sound in air using two microphones and a data logger.

Answer: Place two microphones a measured distance apart in a straight line from a sound source (a clapping board or signal generator and loudspeaker). Trigger the data logger with the sound at each microphone and record the time interval between the arrivals, or display both pulses on an oscilloscope and measure the time from the trace. Speed is the distance between the microphones divided by the time interval. Repeat at several separations and find the speed from the gradient of a distance–time graph, which averages out the reaction error.

Question 6 (Paper 4, 3 marks). State two differences between a transverse and a longitudinal wave, and give one example of each.

Answer: In a transverse wave the vibrations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer; in a longitudinal wave they are parallel to it. Transverse waves have crests and troughs; longitudinal waves have compressions and rarefactions. Examples: light (transverse) and sound in air (longitudinal).

Waves carry energy without matter; the next topic is the energy that drives circuits: Electricity and Circuits.

title: Web Technologies — Study Notes
content:
Web Technologies

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): HTML structure/tags, CSS styling, JS interactivity, the DOM, microprocessors/controllers in web context.

1. HTML

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head><title>Page</title></head>
<body>
  <h1>Heading</h1>
  <p>Paragraph with <strong>bold</strong> text</p>
  <img src="pic.jpg" alt="description">
  <a href="https://example.com">Link</a>
  <table><tr><td>cell</td></tr></table>
</body>
</html>

Head holds metadata/title; body holds visible content; hypertext links via <a href>.

2. CSS

p { color: red; font-size: 14px; }
.highlight { background-color: yellow; }
#header { text-align: center; }

Element, class (.) and id (#) selectors; inline vs external stylesheets; separation of content (HTML) from presentation (CSS).

3. JavaScript and the DOM

document.getElementById("demo").innerHTML = "Hello";
document.getElementsByClassName("item")[0].style.color = "blue";

DOM = the browser's object model of the page; JS reads/changes it for interactivity (validation, sliders, dynamic text). Events (click, submit) trigger functions.

4. How pages load

URL → DNS lookup → server request → HTML parsed → assets fetched → DOM built → render. Layers: structure (HTML) → presentation (CSS) → behaviour (JS).

Exam tips: write tags with correct closing pairs; explain DOM operations as "find element by id … then change property"; separate structure/presentation/behaviour in answers.

title: The Periodic Table
content:
The Periodic Table

Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry 0620, Extended route, topic 8 (statements 8.1–8.5). Periodic trends, Group I and Group VII properties and displacement reactions, transition elements, and the noble gases.

8.1 Arrangement

  • Elements are arranged in order of increasing proton number, in periods (rows) and groups (columns). Metallic character decreases across a period from left to right and increases down a group.

8.2 Group I

  • Alkali metals: soft, low density, low melting point. Reactivity increases down the group because the outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded, so it is lost more easily. Products with water: a metal hydroxide and hydrogen.

8.3 Group VII

  • Halogens: reactivity decreases down the group because the outer shell is further from the nucleus, so an atom gains an electron less easily. Denser and darker down the group: fluorine pale yellow gas, chlorine green-yellow gas, bromine red-brown liquid, iodine grey solid.

8.4 to 8.5 Transition elements and noble gases

  • Transition elements: high density, high melting point, form coloured compounds, act as catalysts, and show variable oxidation states (iron(II) and iron(III) are the syllabus examples).
  • Noble gases: full outer shells, so they are monatomic and unreactive.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Displacement reasoning, applied to chlorine added to potassium bromide: Cl₂ + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br₂. Chlorine is more reactive than bromine, so it displaces the bromide ions. The chlorine is reduced (0 to −1) and the bromide is oxidised (−1 to 0). Name both half-changes for full marks.
  • Prediction, applied to astatine: it sits below iodine, so it is a solid, less reactive than iodine, and would be displaced from its salts by chlorine, bromine and iodine. Predictions must be justified from the group trend, not asserted.
  • Trend explanation, applied to why potassium reacts more violently with water than lithium: the outer electron in potassium is in shell 4 versus shell 2 in lithium, so it is further from the nucleus and more shielded by inner shells, so it is lost more easily. Use the words shielding and nuclear attraction.

Common errors

  • Saying reactivity of Group VII increases down the group. It decreases.
  • Explaining Group I trends by "atoms get bigger" without the electron-loss link.
  • Calling transition metal catalysts "changing the product". They change the rate, not the products.

title: A Level Mathematics: Numerical Methods
content:
A Level Mathematics: Numerical Methods

Some equations cannot be solved exactly: x = cos x, x³ − x − 1 = 0, e^x = 4x. Numerical methods find the solutions to any required accuracy by iteration and refinement. This note builds the four techniques A2 requires — locating a root by sign change, fixed-point iteration and its convergence, the Newton-Raphson formula with its derivation, and the trapezium rule for integrals that have no elementary antiderivative — together with the failure modes examiners test.

Locating a root: change of sign

if f(a) and f(b) have opposite signs and f is continuous on [a, b],
there is at least one root in (a, b)

Worked example. Show that x³ − x − 1 = 0 has a root between 1 and 2.

f(1) = 1 - 1 - 1 = -1
f(2) = 8 - 2 - 1 = 5
sign change and the cubic is continuous  →  a root in (1, 2)

The two conditions are both required: continuity rules out a jump, and the sign change forces a crossing. The theorem guarantees at least one root, not exactly one — say "at least" in the answer.

Worked example 2 (narrowing). Show the root lies between 1.3 and 1.4.

f(1.3) = 2.197 - 1.3 - 1 = -0.103
f(1.4) = 2.744 - 1.4 - 1 = 0.344
so the root lies in (1.3, 1.4)

Fixed-point iteration

rearrange f(x) = 0 into x = g(x), then iterate x_(n+1) = g(x_n)

the iteration converges when |g'(x)| < 1 near the root

Worked example. Use x_(n+1) = (x_n + 1)^(1/3) with x₁ = 1.3 to find the root of x³ − x − 1 = 0 to 4 d.p.

x2 = (2.3)^(1/3) = 1.3200 × 3 = (2.32)^(1/3) = 1.3238 × 4 = 1.3245;  x5 = 1.3246;  x6 = 1.3247
the sequence settles: root = 1.3247 (4 d.p.)

Worked example 2 (testing convergence). For g(x) = (x + 1)^(1/3), show the iteration converges near 1.32.

g'(x) = (1/3)(x + 1)^(-2/3)
at x = 1.32: g' = (1/3)(2.32)^(-2/3) = 0.19 < 1
so the iteration converges

If |g′| > 1 near the root the iteration diverges, and a different rearrangement is needed. The same equation usually has several rearrangements, only some of which converge — that is exactly what the |g′| test decides.

Failure modes of iteration

divergence: |g'| > 1 near the root
oscillation: the sequence jumps between two values
slow convergence: |g'| close to 1

Worked example. The rearrangement x = x³ − 1 for x³ − x − 1 = 0 gives g′(x) = 3x², which is about 5.3 near the root: the iteration diverges rapidly. That is why the cube-root rearrangement, with g′ ≈ 0.19, is used instead.

Newton-Raphson

x_(n+1) = x_n - f(x_n)/f'(x_n)

the tangent at the current point is followed to the x-axis;
the intercept becomes the next estimate

Derivation. The tangent at x_n has equation y − f(x_n) = f′(x_n)(x − x_n). Setting y = 0 gives x = x_n − f(x_n)/f′(x_n), which is the formula.

Worked example. Use Newton-Raphson on f(x) = x³ − x − 1 with x₁ = 1.3.

f'(x) = 3x² - 1 × 2 = 1.3 - (-0.103)/(4.07) = 1.3 + 0.0253 = 1.3253 × 3 = 1.3253 - (0.00053)/(4.2637) = 1.3252
root = 1.3252 (4 d.p.) in two steps, against six for the iteration

Worked example 2 (failure). Explain why x₁ = 0.5 fails for f(x) = x³ − x − 1.

f'(0.5) = -0.25, so x2 = 0.5 - (-1.375)/(-0.25) = 0.5 - 5.5 = -5.0
the tangent is nearly horizontal, so the step overshoots wildly;
the method can diverge when f' is small near the initial guess

State the failure condition explicitly: Newton-Raphson needs f′(x_n) ≠ 0 and a good starting value close to the root.

The trapezium rule

integral from a to b of f(x) dx ~ (h/2)[y_0 + 2(y_1 + ... + y_(n-1)) + y_n]
where h = (b - a)/n and y_i = f(a + ih)

the error: a larger n reduces it; the rule overestimates for a
concave-up curve and underestimates for concave-down

Worked example. Use the trapezium rule with 4 strips to estimate ∫ from 0 to 2 of e^(x²) dx.

h = 0.5; x: 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2
y: 1, 1.2840, 2.7183, 6.4760, 54.5982
I ~ (0.5/2)[1 + 2(1.2840 + 2.7183 + 6.4760) + 54.5982]
  = 0.25[1 + 20.9566 + 54.5982] = 0.25 × 76.5548 = 19.14

Worked example 2 (over or under). Is the estimate above or below the true value here?

e^(x²) is concave up (its gradient is increasing), so each chord lies
above the curve and the trapezium rule overestimates

Accuracy and error

the error of a trapezium estimate is roughly proportional to h²
halving h roughly quarters the error

rounding to k decimal places requires the estimate to be stable at
the next place

Worked example. An estimate with h = 0.5 gives 19.14; with h = 0.25 the estimate is 18.92. Estimate the answer to 1 d.p.

the two agree to 1 d.p. at 18.9; quoting 18.9 is defensible, and the
difference indicates the scale of the remaining error

Comparing two step sizes is the standard way to justify an accuracy claim; a single estimate cannot.

Setting up an iteration properly

An iteration question usually hands you the rearrangement; the marks are for using it correctly, showing the iterates, and judging convergence. Three habits cover it:

  • Write the recurrence exactly as given and substitute the stated starting value.
  • Record each iterate to one more decimal place than required.
  • Show two consecutive iterates agreeing at the required accuracy before quoting the root.

Worked example. f(x) = x³ + 2x − 5 has a root near 1.3. Show that x = (5 − 2x)^(1/3) is a valid rearrangement and iterate twice.

from x³ + 2x - 5 = 0: x³ = 5 - 2x  →  x = (5 - 2x)^(1/3) × 2 = (5 - 2.6)^(1/3) = (2.4)^(1/3) = 1.3389 × 3 = (5 - 2.6777)^(1/3) = (2.3223)^(1/3) = 1.3241
converging towards about 1.328

Worked example 2 (convergence check). Test |g′| for g(x) = (5 − 2x)^(1/3) near 1.33.

g'(x) = (1/3)(5 - 2x)^(-2/3) x (-2) = -0.667(5 - 2x)^(-2/3)
|g'(1.33)| = 0.667 x (2.34)^(-2/3) = 0.667 × 0.534 = 0.356 < 1
so the iteration converges

Newton-Raphson on other functions

The formula is universal; what changes is the derivative and the care needed with trigonometry and logs.

Worked example. Use Newton-Raphson to solve cos x = x starting from x₁ = 0.7.

f(x) = cos x - x;  f'(x) = -sin x - 1 × 2 = 0.7 - (0.7648 - 0.7)/(-0.6442 - 1) = 0.7 + 0.0648/1.6442 = 0.7394 × 3 = 0.7394 - (0.7391 - 0.7394)/(-0.6735 - 1) = 0.7391
root = 0.7391 (4 d.p.)

Worked example 2 (log equation). Solve x ln x = 1 from x₁ = 1.5.

f(x) = x ln x - 1;  f'(x) = ln x + 1 × 2 = 1.5 - (0.6082 - 1)/(0.4055 + 1) = 1.5 + 0.2788 = 1.7788 × 3 = 1.7788 - 0.0423/1.5755 = 1.7519 × 4 = 1.7632;  converging to 1.7632

Radians are compulsory in any Newton-Raphson question involving trigonometry; degrees give a value of f′ scaled by π/180 and destroy convergence.

Choosing a starting value

Both iteration and Newton-Raphson need a starting value near the root, and a sketch is the reliable way to find one. Plot or sketch y = left-hand side and y = right-hand side of the rearranged equation; the intersections are the roots, and their approximate positions are the starting values.

Worked example. e^x = 4x has two roots. Sketch and estimate them.

sketch y = e^x and y = 4x: they cross once near x = 0.3 and again
near x = 2.2
checking: e^0.3 = 1.35 against 1.2; e^2.2 = 9.03 against 8.8
so start Newton-Raphson from 0.4 and from 2.2 separately

Two roots require two separate runs; a single guess finds only the root it is near. That is the most common lost mark in equations with several roots.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Sign change) Show x³ + x − 3 = 0 has a root in (1, 2). Answer: f(1) = −1, f(2) = 7; continuous; sign change.
  2. (Iteration) x_(n+1) = (3 − x_n)^(1/3), x₁ = 1. Find x₃. Answer: 1.2599, 1.2020.
  3. (Convergence) g(x) = (3 − x)^(1/3): show |g′| < 1 near 1.21. Answer: |g′| = (1/3)(3 − x)^(−2/3) ≈ 0.21 < 1.
  4. (Newton) f(x) = x² − 5, x₁ = 2. Find x₂. Answer: 2 − (−1)/4 = 2.25.
  5. (Newton again) Find x₃ for the same. Answer: 2.25 − 0.0625/4.5 = 2.2361.
  6. (Newton failure) f(x) = x³, x₁ = −1. What happens? Answer: x₂ = −1 − (−1)/3 = −0.667, converging slowly towards 0; the root is a stationary point, so convergence is linear.
  7. (Trapezium) Estimate ∫₀² x² dx with 2 strips. Answer: h = 1; (1/2)[0 + 2(1) + 4] = 3.
  8. (Error) Is that estimate over or under? Answer: over, since x² is concave up; the true value is 8/3 = 2.667.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Claiming exactly one root: the sign change proves at least one; uniqueness needs monotonicity or a sketch.
  • Iterating too few times: the answer must be stable at the required number of decimal places — show consecutive values agreeing.
  • Calculator in the wrong mode: iteration on a reset calculator silently uses the last answer; store x_n in a variable.
  • Newton with a small derivative: the step overshoots; state the failure rather than ploughing on.
  • Wrong h: h = (b − a)/n, not the number of ordinates; counting strips and counting points are different.
  • Trapezium brackets: the first and last ordinates are counted once, the interior ones twice; a factor-of-two error here is the classic slip.
  • Error direction guessed: justify over/under estimate from the concavity, not from the size of the answer.
  • Accuracy unqualified: "the answer is 1.32" without evidence that later iterations agree is not a numerical-methods answer.

title: Binomial Expansion — Study Notes
content:
Binomial expansion

Edexcel International A Level Mathematics — Pure Mathematics 4 (WMA14), sat at A2.

The binomial theorem expands (1 + x)^n in ascending powers of x. For positive integer n the series terminates; for negative or fractional n it is an infinite series valid only inside a restricted range.

The expansion

(1 + x)^n = 1 + nx + [n(n - 1)/2!] x^2 + [n(n - 1)(n - 2)/3!] x^3 + ...

The coefficient of x^r is n(n - 1)...(n - r + 1) / r!. Note this is NOT C(n, r) unless n is a positive integer.

Non-integer n

When n is negative or fractional the expansion is an infinite series, and it is valid only for |x| < 1. If the bracket is (1 + kx), validity becomes |kx| < 1, i.e. |x| < 1/|k|.

Rewriting awkward brackets

  • Factor out the constant: (3 + 2x)^n = 3^n (1 + 2x/3)^n, then expand the bracket.
  • Negative powers and reciprocals: (1 - 2x)^(-2), 1/sqrt(1 + x) = (1 + x)^(-1/2).

Approximations

To estimate a surd, force the (1 + x) form with a small x:

  • sqrt(1.04) = (1 + 0.04)^(1/2) approx 1 + 0.02 - 0.0002 = 1.0198.
  • Use three terms for 3 s.f. accuracy, and state the range of validity.

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting to halve (or divide by r!) the product in the coefficient.
  • Losing the minus signs when n is negative or x is negative.
  • Ignoring the validity condition when asked for the range of x.

title: Kinematics
content:
Kinematics

Definitions

  • Displacement s: distance in a given direction (vector)
  • Velocity v: rate of change of displacement, v = ds/dt
  • Acceleration a: rate of change of velocity, a = dv/dt

Graphs

  • Gradient of a displacement–time graph = velocity
  • Gradient of a velocity–time graph = acceleration
  • Area under a velocity–time graph = displacement
  • Area under an acceleration–time graph = change in velocity

SUVAT (uniform acceleration only)

EquationMissing
v = u + ats
s = ut + ½at²v
v² = u² + 2ast
s = ½(u + v)ta

Sign convention matters: take up as positive and g = −9.81 m s⁻² for falling objects.

Projectiles

Resolve into independent components: horizontal at constant velocity (s = ut), vertical under gravity (SUVAT).

Example: a ball fired at 20 m s⁻¹ at 30°: uₓ = 20 cos 30° ≈ 17.3 m s⁻¹, u_y = 20 sin 30° = 10 m s⁻¹. Time of flight = 2u_y/g ≈ 2.04 s; range = uₓ × t ≈ 35 m.

Exam tips: state which direction is positive; projectile questions are two separate 1-D problems joined by time.

title: Metals
content:
Metals

Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry 0620, Extended route, topic 9 (statements 9.1–9.6). Metal properties and uses, alloys, the reactivity series, rusting and its prevention, and extraction of metals including the blast furnace and electrolysis of aluminium ore.

9.1 to 9.4 Properties, uses, alloys and reactivity

  • Metals are good conductors, malleable, ductile, lustrous and usually solid with high melting points. Aluminium: low density and a protective oxide layer, so it is used in aircraft and drink cans. Copper: excellent conductivity and ductility, so it is used in wiring.
  • An alloy is a mixture of a metal with other elements. Brass (copper and zinc) and stainless steel (iron, chromium, nickel) are the syllabus examples. Different-sized atoms disrupt the regular layers, so the layers cannot slide — the alloy is harder than the pure metal.
  • Reactivity series: potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium, zinc, iron, (hydrogen), copper, silver, gold. More reactive metals react more vigorously with water or steam and dilute acids, and displace less reactive metals from their compounds.

9.5 Corrosion

  • Rusting needs both oxygen and water. Barriers (paint, grease, plastic) exclude them. Galvanising coats iron with zinc; sacrificial protection uses a more reactive metal such as zinc or magnesium that corrodes instead of the iron.

9.6 Extraction of metals

  • Iron: in the blast furnace, carbon monoxide (from coke and hot air) reduces iron(III) oxide: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂. Limestone removes sandy impurities as slag.
  • Aluminium: extracted by electrolysis of molten aluminium oxide in cryolite, which lowers the melting point and saves energy. The carbon anodes burn away and must be replaced, and oxygen at the anode reacts with the carbon.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Extraction choice, applied to a metal found as the pure element in the ground: gold is extracted by physical methods because it is below hydrogen and does not react with acids or oxygen. Zinc and iron need chemical reduction; aluminium needs electrolysis because it is more reactive than carbon. Link the method to the position in the reactivity series in one sentence.
  • Reactivity deduction, applied to experimental results where metal X displaces metal Y from its salt: X is more reactive than Y. If metal Y does not react with dilute acid but X does, X is above hydrogen and Y below it. Build the order from the evidence, then justify each step.
