  • Blast furnace chemistry, applied to the role of coke: coke burns in a blast of hot air to make carbon dioxide (exothermic, providing heat), then carbon dioxide reacts with more coke to make carbon monoxide, the actual reducing agent. Distinguish the two roles — heat provider and reducing agent.
  • Rusting protection reasoning, applied to an iron pipe under a ship: a block of magnesium attached to it corrodes instead, because magnesium is more reactive than iron and loses electrons in preference. That is sacrificial protection; name the electron transfer.

Common errors

  • Saying alloys are harder because "they are stronger". The mark is for disrupted layers that cannot slide.
  • Claiming the carbon anode in aluminium extraction is inert. It burns away.
  • Confusing galvanising (a coating) with sacrificial protection (a more reactive metal doing the corroding).

title: Networking & Communication — Study Notes
content:
Networking & Communication

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2023–2025): transmission modes, serial/parallel, packet switching, protocols, LAN/WAN, hardware, security layers.

1. Transmission basics

  • Serial: one bit at a time — reliable over distance, cheaper cable.
  • Parallel: several bits at once — faster over short runs; skew/crosstalk limit distance.
  • Simplex / half-duplex / full-duplex direction; bandwidth (bits/s) vs bit rate.

2. Packets

Header (sender/receiver addresses, sequence number) + payload + trailer (checksum). Packet switching: routes vary, packets reassembled at destination; checksum failure → re-request. Benefits: robustness, shared lines; delays/reassembly overhead.

3. Protocols

TCP/IP stack layers (application, transport, network, link). HTTP/HTTPS (TLS encryption), FTP (with login + commands), email: SMTP send, POP3/IMAP retrieve. Bluetooth/Wi-Fi for WPAN/WLAN.

4. Network types & hardware

LAN (site) vs WAN (internet). Router (joins networks, IP), switch (MAC frames within LAN), gateway (protocol translation), NIC, WAP. MAC address (burned-in, layer 2) vs IP address (assigned, layer 3).

5. Security in transmission

Encryption scrambles plaintext → ciphertext (key needed); HTTPS = HTTP over TLS; firewall packet filtering by port/IP; authentication (user+pass, 2FA); access levels.

Exam tips: explain why skew limits parallel over distance; compare MAC vs IP in a table; protocol questions want "rules for communication", not acronyms alone.

title: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Transformations and Vectors
content:
Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Transformations and Vectors

Transformations move shapes on a grid, and vectors describe those moves with numbers. The exam asks two things: perform a transformation and, more often, describe one completely — with its centre, angle, direction, line or scale factor. This note builds the topic from zero: the four transformations and the full-description checklist for each, enlargement and its effect on area, vector notation with the house column-vector form (x; y), vector arithmetic, and the vector-geometry proofs that show lines are parallel or points are collinear.

The four transformations

TransformationWhat changesWhat must be stated in a description
Translationposition only, no rotation or resizethe column vector of the move
Reflectionmirror imagethe line of reflection (e.g. x = 2, y = x)
Rotationturns about a pointcentre, angle, and direction (clockwise or anticlockwise)
Enlargementresizes about a pointcentre and scale factor

The complete description is the mark: "rotation" alone scores nothing; "rotation 90° anticlockwise about (2, 1)" scores fully.

Translation

A translation moves every point by the same vector. In column form (x; y), x is the horizontal move and y the vertical move; right and up are positive.

Worked example. Triangle A has vertices (1, 1), (3, 1), (1, 4). Translate by (4; −2) and give the image coordinates.

(1, 1) → (5, -1)
(3, 1) → (7, -1)
(1, 4) → (5, 2)

The shape is congruent to the original (same size and shape), and the orientation is unchanged.

Reflection

A reflection flips a shape across a line; the line is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining each point to its image. Common lines: x = a (vertical), y = b (horizontal), y = x, y = −x.

Worked example. Reflect the point (3, 5) in the line y = x.

reflection in y = x swaps the coordinates: (3, 5) → (5, 3)

Worked example 2. Reflect (2, 4) in the line x = 1.

the line x = 1 is vertical; the distance of x = 2 from it is 1,
so the image is 1 unit on the other side: (0, 4)

To find the mirror line from a shape and its image, join a point to its image and draw the perpendicular bisector of that segment.

Rotation

A rotation turns a shape about a fixed centre through a given angle. The four standard angles are 90° and 180° in either direction; 90° clockwise equals 270° anticlockwise.

Worked example. Rotate the point (3, 1) 90° clockwise about the origin.

90 ° clockwise about O: (x, y) → (y, -x)
(3, 1) → (1, -3)

Worked example 2. Rotate (2, 5) 180° about the origin.

180 °: (x, y) → (-x, -y)
(2, 5) → (-2, -5)

For a centre other than the origin, translate the centre to the origin, rotate, then translate back — or count the grid squares from the centre.

Enlargement

An enlargement with centre C and scale factor k maps every point so that its distance from C is multiplied by k. Negative scale factors put the image on the far side of the centre; fractional factors between 0 and 1 shrink the shape.

image distance from centre = k x object distance from centre
area of image = k² x area of object

Worked example. Enlarge the point (2, 3) by scale factor 3 about the origin.

(2, 3) → (6, 9)

Worked example 2 (area). A triangle of area 12 cm² is enlarged by scale factor 2.5. Find the image area.

area factor = k² = 6.25
new area = 12 × 6.25 = 75 cm²

Enlargement is the only transformation that changes area (unless k = 1 or −1); translations, reflections and rotations preserve both shape and size.

Vectors: notation and magnitude

A vector has magnitude and direction. In this course it is written as a column vector (x; y): x is the horizontal component, y the vertical. The same vector can be written as a bold letter a with an arrow above it.

column vector (x; y)
magnitude = √(x² + y²)
direction angle to the horizontal: tan(θ) = y/x
equal vectors have the same components; opposite vectors
negate both components

Worked example. Find the magnitude and direction of the vector (3; 4).

magnitude = √(9 + 16) = 5
tan(θ) = 4/3  →  θ = 53.1 ° above the horizontal

Vector arithmetic and geometry

addition: (a; b) + (c; d) = (a + c; b + d)
subtraction: (a; b) - (c; d) = (a - c; b - d)
scalar multiple: k(a; b) = (ka; kb)

position vector of A relative to O: OA
AB = OB - OA
midpoint of AB: (OA + OB)/2

Worked example. OA = (2; 1), OB = (7; 5). Find AB and the midpoint of AB.

AB = OB - OA = (7 - 2; 5 - 1) = (5; 4)
midpoint = ((2 + 7)/2; (1 + 5)/2) = (4.5; 3)

Worked example 2 (parallel). Show that AB is parallel to CD given A(1, 2), B(5, 8), C(0, 1), D(6, 10).

AB = (5 - 1; 8 - 2) = (4; 6)
CD = (6 - 0; 10 - 1) = (6; 9)
(6; 9) = 1.5 x (4; 6), so CD = 1.5 AB: parallel (and longer)

Parallel vectors are scalar multiples of each other; collinear points occur when AB and AC (or AB and BC) are parallel and share a point.

Combining transformations and invariant points

Two transformations applied in sequence are not the same as the reverse order: a reflection followed by a rotation generally differs from the rotation followed by the reflection. When a question asks for the single transformation equivalent to two, apply both to a convenient point (the origin or a vertex) and to a second point, then identify the transformation that maps the original to the final image. Invariant points are points that do not move: every point on a mirror line is invariant under a reflection, the centre of a rotation is invariant, and no point is invariant under a translation.

Worked example. A shape is reflected in the x-axis and then translated by (0; 3). Find the image of (2, 1) and identify any invariant points.

reflection in the x-axis: (2, 1) → (2, -1)
translation by (0; 3): (2, -1) → (2, 2)
No invariant points: the reflection moved every point off the
axis, and the translation then moved everything upward.

Worked example 2 (invariant line). State the invariant points of a reflection in the line y = 2.

Every point with y-coordinate 2 lies on the mirror line and does
not move: the whole line y = 2 is invariant.

Vectors in context: displacement and velocity

Column vectors describe any quantity with magnitude and direction in two dimensions: displacement (a move from one point to another), velocity (displacement per second) and force (a push in a direction). The arithmetic is identical; only the interpretation changes.

  • Displacement: AB is the vector from A to B; a round trip returns to the start, so the sum of the vectors around a closed polygon is zero.
  • Velocity: a velocity vector (3; −2) means 3 units per second right and 2 units per second down; position after t seconds is the starting position plus t × velocity.
  • Resultant: the sum of two vectors; a vector and its negative cancel.

Worked example. A particle starts at (1, 2) and moves with velocity (3; −1) for 4 seconds. Find its final position.

displacement = 4 x (3; -1) = (12; -4)
final position = (1 + 12; 2 - 4) = (13; -2)

Worked examples: vector proofs

Worked example. In triangle OAB, P is the midpoint of OA and Q is the midpoint of OB. Prove PQ is parallel to AB.

OP = (1/2) OA, OQ = (1/2) OB
PQ = OQ - OP = (1/2)(OB - OA) = (1/2) AB
PQ is a scalar multiple of AB, so PQ is parallel to AB
(and half its length).

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Translation) Translate (2, 3) by (−1; 4). Answer: (1, 7).
  2. (Reflection) Reflect (4, 1) in the x-axis. Answer: (4, −1).
  3. (Rotation) Rotate (5, 2) 90° anticlockwise about the origin. Answer: (−2, 5).
  4. (Enlargement) Enlarge (1, 2) by factor −2 about the origin. Answer: (−2, −4).
  5. (Description) Describe fully the transformation mapping (1, 1) to (3, 5). Answer: Translation by (2; 4) — one of many correct complete descriptions.
  6. (Magnitude) Find the magnitude of (6; 8). Answer: √(36 + 64) = 10.
  7. (Position vectors) OA = (1; 4), OB = (5; 2). Find AB. Answer: (4; −2).
  8. (Collinear) Show A(1, 1), B(3, 4), C(7, 10) are collinear. Answer: AB = (2; 3), AC = (6; 9) = 3 AB — parallel and share A, so collinear.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Incomplete descriptions: "enlargement by 2" omits the centre and loses marks; "reflection" omits the line. State every attribute.
  • Direction of rotation: clockwise and anticlockwise are different transformations; a 90° rotation clockwise is not the same as anticlockwise.
  • Area under enlargement: area scales by k², not k. Doubling the sides quadruples the area.
  • Vector direction: AB = OB − OA, not OA − OB. Reversing the subtraction negates the vector.
  • Column order: (x; y) is horizontal then vertical. Swapping produces a reflection in y = x, not the intended vector.
  • Parallelogram assumptions: equal magnitudes do not imply equal vectors — direction matters too.
  • Negative scale factors: the image lies on the opposite side of the centre; it is not simply "smaller".
  • Collinearity proof: showing parallel is not enough — the segments must also share a point. State it.

Equations and symbols

Every transformation is a coordinate map, and every vector is a column pair. Learn the four rotation maps and the two vector rules, and the topic is arithmetic.

90 ° clockwise about O: (x, y) → (y, -x) Key: (x, y) = the original coordinates; the arrow points to the image's coordinates; O = the origin, the fixed centre. Anticlockwise is the same map with the signs reversed — write the centre down, because a rotation about any other point is not this formula.

180 °: (x, y) → (-x, -y) Key: both coordinates change sign; a half-turn is the only rotation that is also a translation-free "point reflection" in the origin. Check with a point on an axis, where one coordinate stays zero.

reflection in y = x swaps the coordinates: (3, 5) → (5, 3) Key: the line y = x is the mirror; swapping means the image of (x, y) is (y, x). The line is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining each point to its image, which is the definition to quote.

(1, 1) → (5, -1) Key: left = a vertex of the object; right = the matching vertex of the image. Subtract to read off the translation: 5 − 1 = 4 across and −1 − 1 = −2 down, so the column vector is (4; −2).

(3, 1) → (1, -3) Key: this is a 90° clockwise turn about the origin applied to a second vertex — the same map, different numbers. With two vertices mapped you can describe the transformation fully rather than guessing from one.

title: Quantum Physics — Study Notes
content:
Quantum Physics

Photons and photon energy

Electromagnetic radiation travels as photons, each with energy E = hf, where h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s is the Planck constant. Since c = fλ, the energy is also E = hc/λ. Shorter wavelength means higher energy.

Example: a photon of wavelength 500 nm has E = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3.0 × 10⁸)/(5.0 × 10⁻⁷) ≈ 4.0 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, or about 2.5 eV.

The photoelectric effect

When light shines on a metal surface, electrons are emitted only if the frequency of the light is at or above the threshold frequency f₀. Each photon transfers its whole energy to a single electron. Increasing the intensity increases the number of photons per second, so more electrons are emitted, but it does not increase the energy of each electron. The emission is instantaneous, with no time delay.

Wave theory cannot explain the threshold frequency or the lack of a time delay. The photon model explains both.

Einstein's photoelectric equation

hf = φ + E_k(max), where φ is the work function of the metal, the minimum energy needed to free an electron. The threshold frequency is f₀ = φ/h. The stopping potential V_s satisfies eV_s = E_k(max).

Example: a work function of 2.0 eV gives f₀ = (2.0 × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹)/(6.63 × 10⁻³⁴) ≈ 4.8 × 10¹⁴ Hz.

Wave-particle duality

Particles also have wave properties. The de Broglie wavelength of a particle with momentum p is λ = h/p. Electrons diffract through crystal lattices, showing wave behaviour, while photons show particle behaviour in the photoelectric effect. Both are needed to describe the same entities.

Energy levels and line spectra

Electrons in an atom occupy discrete energy levels. When an electron falls from a higher level E₁ to a lower level E₂, it emits a single photon with hf = E₁ − E₂. Absorption happens when a photon with exactly this energy is taken in. Because only specific energies are allowed, the spectrum is a set of sharp lines rather than a continuous band.

Example: a transition from −3.4 eV to −13.6 eV releases 10.2 eV, a wavelength of about 122 nm.

Exam tips: convert eV to joules (1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J) before using E = hf. Say which quantity the intensity changes and which it does not. Quote hf = φ + E_k(max) in photoelectric questions.

title: Exam technique: Forces and Equilibrium
content:
### What earns the marks
For resultants, the vector triangle or Pythagoras with angle earns both marks. For moments, force times perpendicular distance earns each mark. For equilibrium, both zero force and zero moment stated earns the full explanation.
### Traps
Error: one equilibrium condition given alone. Correction: both are required. Error: couple torque taken as force only. Correction: multiply by the separation. Error: upthrust equated to object weight. Correction: it equals displaced fluid weight.

title: A Level Mathematics: Differentiation II
content:
A Level Mathematics: Differentiation II

A2 differentiation adds the rules for products, quotients and functions of functions, then applies them to implicit equations, parametric curves and rates of change. Every rule in this note is stated with the condition for using it and derived where the derivation is short, because the exam tests recognition as much as execution.

The chain rule

if y = f(g(x)) then dy/dx = f'(g(x)) g'(x)

or with u: dy/dx = dy/du x du/dx

Worked example 1. Differentiate y = (3x + 2)⁵.

dy/dx = 5(3x + 2)^4 x 3 = 15(3x + 2)^4

Worked example 2 (trigonometric). Differentiate y = sin(2x).

dy/dx = 2 cos(2x)

Worked example 3 (exponential). Differentiate y = e^(x²).

dy/dx = 2x e^(x^2)

Worked example 4 (power of a trig function). Differentiate y = cos³x.

treat as (cos x)^3: dy/dx = 3(cos x)^2 x (-sin x) = -3 sin x cos^2 x

The product rule

d(uv)/dx = u dv/dx + v du/dx

"first times derivative of second plus second times derivative of first"

Worked example 1. Differentiate y = x² sin x.

dy/dx = 2x sin x + x^2 cos x

Worked example 2. Differentiate y = x ln x.

dy/dx = ln x + x(1/x) = ln x + 1

Worked example 3. Differentiate y = x²e^(3x).

dy/dx = 2x e^(3x) + 3x^2 e^(3x) = x e^(3x)(2 + 3x)

Factorising the answer is not cosmetic: stationary points need the factorised form to be solved.

The quotient rule

d(u/v)/dx = (v du/dx - u dv/dx)/v^2

the numerator's order matters: v times derivative of u minus u times
derivative of v

Worked example 1. Differentiate y = sin x/x.

dy/dx = (x cos x - sin x)/x^2

Worked example 2 (a common form). Differentiate y = (2x + 1)/(x − 3).

dy/dx = [(x - 3)(2) - (2x + 1)(1)]/(x - 3)^2
      = (2x - 6 - 2x - 1)/(x - 3)^2 = -7/(x - 3)^2

Worked example 3 (exponential quotient). Differentiate y = e^x/ln x.

dy/dx = [ln x e^x - e^x(1/x)]/(ln x)^2

Implicit differentiation

differentiate both sides with respect to x, treating y as a function
of x: each y term contributes its derivative times dy/dx

then solve for dy/dx

Worked example 1. Find dy/dx for x² + y² = 25.

2x + 2y dy/dx = 0
 dy/dx = -x/y

Worked example 2 (product inside). Find dy/dx for xy + y² = 6.

differentiate: y + x dy/dx + 2y dy/dx = 0
dy/dx (x + 2y) = -y
dy/dx = -y/(x + 2y)

Worked example 3 (tangent). Find the tangent to x² + xy = 6 at the point (2, 1).

2x + y + x dy/dx = 0
at (2, 1): 4 + 1 + 2 dy/dx = 0  ->  dy/dx = -2.5
tangent: y - 1 = -2.5(x - 2)  ->  5x + 2y = 12

Parametric differentiation

if x = f(t) and y = g(t): dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt)

Worked example. For x = t², y = t³ − t, find dy/dx in terms of t.

dx/dt = 2t;  dy/dt = 3t^2 - 1
dy/dx = (3t^2 - 1)/(2t)

Worked example 2 (tangent). Find the tangent at t = 2.

point: x = 4, y = 6
gradient: (12 - 1)/4 = 2.75
tangent: y - 6 = 2.75(x - 4)  ->  y = 2.75x - 5

Worked example 3 (second derivative). Find d²y/dx² in terms of t for the same curve.

d/dx(dy/dx) = [d/dt(dy/dx)] / (dx/dt)
d/dt[(3t^2 - 1)/(2t)] = (6t x 2t - (3t^2 - 1)2)/(4t^2) = (6t^2 + 2)/(4t^2)
divide by 2t: (6t^2 + 2)/(8t^3)

Stationary points with the new rules

Worked example. Find and classify the stationary point of y = x e^(−x²).

dy/dx = e^(-x^2) + x(-2x)e^(-x^2) = e^(-x^2)(1 - 2x^2)
stationary at x = +/- 1/sqrt 2 = +/- 0.707
at x = 0.707: y = 0.707 e^(-0.5) = 0.429  ->  maximum
by symmetry x = -0.707 is a minimum with y = -0.429

Worked example 2 (product inside a log). Show y = x ln x has a minimum at x = e^(−1).

dy/dx = ln x + 1 = 0  ->  x = e^-1 = 0.368
y = e^-1 ln(e^-1) = -e^-1 = -0.368
second derivative = 1/x > 0 at this point, so minimum

Connected rates of change

chain rule in rate form: dV/dt = dV/dr x dr/dt
strategy: write the quantity as a function of one variable, differentiate,
link the rates, substitute

Worked example. A spherical balloon is inflated so that its volume increases at 100 cm³/s. Find dr/dt when r = 5 cm.

V = (4/3) pi r^3  ->  dV/dr = 4 pi r^2
at r = 5: dV/dr = 100 pi = 314.2
dr/dt = (dV/dt)/(dV/dr) = 100/314.2 = 0.318 cm/s

Worked example 2 (area). A circular ripple's radius grows at 2 cm/s. How fast is the area growing when r = 10 cm?

A = pi r^2  ->  dA/dr = 2 pi r = 62.83
dA/dt = 62.83 x 2 = 125.7 cm2/s

Exponentials and logarithms to other bases

Every exponential can be rewritten with base e, because a = e^(ln a). That one identity turns an unfamiliar derivative into something the chain rule already handles, and it explains why base e is the natural choice: the conversion factor disappears.

y = a^x = e^(x ln a)
dy/dx = ln a x e^(x ln a) = a^x ln a

y = log_a(x);  write x = a^y and differentiate implicitly:
1 = a^y ln a dy/dx   ->   dy/dx = 1/(x ln a)

special cases: d/dx(e^x) = e^x;  d/dx(ln x) = 1/x

The factor ln a is what students leave out. For a = e it equals 1, which is exactly why base-e derivatives come out clean and every other base drags a constant along.

Worked example. Differentiate y = 3^x.

y = e^(x ln 3)
dy/dx = ln 3 x e^(x ln 3) = 3^x ln 3 = 1.0986 x 3^x

Worked example 2 (chain rule inside the exponent). Differentiate y = 2^(x²).

y = e^(x^2 ln 2)
dy/dx = e^(x^2 ln 2) x (2x ln 2) = 2x ln 2 x 2^(x^2) = 1.386 x 2^(x^2)

Worked example 3 (logarithm of a linear function). Differentiate y = ln(3x + 2) and state where the derivative is valid.

inner u = 3x + 2, du/dx = 3
dy/dx = (1/u) x 3 = 3/(3x + 2)
valid for 3x + 2 > 0, i.e. x > -2/3

The second derivative test and curve sketching

At a stationary point the first derivative vanishes, so it cannot distinguish a peak from a trough. The second derivative does: it measures how the gradient itself is changing, which is the curvature of the graph at that point.

Condition at a stationary pointShape of the curveConclusion
d²y/dx² < 0concave down (∩)local maximum
d²y/dx² > 0concave up (∪)local minimum
d²y/dx² = 0test inconclusivecheck the sign of dy/dx either side

Worked example. Find and classify the stationary points of y = x³ − 3x, then sketch the curve.

dy/dx = 3x^2 - 3 = 3(x - 1)(x + 1)
stationary at x = 1 and x = -1
at x = 1:  y = 1 - 3 = -2;  y'' = 6x = 6 > 0  ->  minimum (1, -2)
at x = -1: y = -1 + 3 = 2;  y'' = -6 < 0      ->  maximum (-1, 2)
y intercept: x = 0, y = 0 (also a root)
end behaviour: x -> +inf gives y -> +inf; x -> -inf gives y -> -inf

Worked example 2 (where the test fails). Classify the stationary point of y = x⁴.

dy/dx = 4x^3 = 0 only at x = 0, where y = 0
y'' = 12x^2 = 0 at x = 0, so the test is inconclusive
look at dy/dx: negative for x < 0, positive for x > 0
so the curve falls then rises: (0, 0) is a minimum

The failed case is examinable: y = x³ has no sign change in dy/dx at the origin, so it is a point of inflection, not an extremum. Reporting "stationary point" for x³ without that check loses the mark.

Kinematics with calculus

When displacement is given as a function of time, velocity is its derivative and acceleration the derivative of velocity. Those two definitions replace the constant-acceleration formulas the moment the motion stops being uniform, which is the whole point of the calculus treatment.

s(t) displacement;  v = ds/dt;  a = dv/dt = d^2s/dt^2
reverse: s = integral of v dt;  v = integral of a dt
maximum displacement occurs where v = 0
distance travelled = integral of |v| dt, split where v changes sign

Worked example. A particle moves with s = t³ − 6t² + 9t metres. Find when it is instantaneously at rest and its acceleration at those instants.

v = 3t^2 - 12t + 9 = 3(t - 1)(t - 3)
at rest: t = 1 and t = 3
a = 6t - 12   ->   a(1) = -6 m/s2;  a(3) = 6 m/s2
s(1) = 4 m;  s(3) = 0 m

Worked example 2 (total distance versus displacement). For the same motion, find the distance travelled in 0 ≤ t ≤ 3.

v is positive on (0, 1) and negative on (1, 3)
distance = [s(1) - s(0)] + [s(1) - s(3)] = (4 - 0) + (4 - 0) = 8 m
note the displacement s(3) - s(0) = 0, so displacement alone would report 0

That last result is the standard trap: a question asking for distance needs the sign changes found first, or the positive and negative parts cancel and the answer is nonsense.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Chain) Differentiate (2x − 1)⁴. Answer: 8(2x − 1)³.
  2. (Product) Differentiate x³e^x. Answer: x²e^x(3 + x).
  3. (Quotient) Differentiate (x + 1)/(x − 1). Answer: −2/(x − 1)².
  4. (Implicit) x² + y² = 16: find dy/dx. Answer: −x/y.
  5. (Implicit tangent) Same circle at (2, √12): gradient? Answer: −2/3.46 = −0.577.
  6. (Parametric) x = t², y = 2t + 1: find dy/dx. Answer: 2/(2t) = 1/t.
  7. (Rates) V = s³, ds/dt = 1.5, s = 4. Find dV/dt. Answer: 3s² × 1.5 = 72.
  8. (Stationary) y = x²e^x: find the stationary points. Answer: e^x(x² + 2x) = 0 → x = 0 (min), x = −2 (max).

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Chain rule forgotten: differentiating sin 2x as 2 cos 2x, not cos 2x — the inner derivative is compulsory.
  • Quotient rule order reversed: v du − u dv, not u dv − v du; the sign flips if you swap.
  • Implicit y terms: each differentiated y term needs a dy/dx factor, including products like xy.
  • Parametric dy/dx inverted: it is (dy/dt)/(dx/dt), not the reciprocal.
  • Second derivative by differentiating dy/dx with respect to t: must divide by dx/dt, or the answer is d/dt, not d/dx.
  • Rates linked backwards: dV/dt = dV/dr × dr/dt; inverting gives an answer in the wrong units.
  • Stationary points unfactorised: equations like x e^x(2 + x) = 0 are solved only when factorised.
  • Domain of ln: differentiating ln x is valid only for x > 0; for negative arguments use ln|x|.

title: A2 Level Biology: Microbiology, Immunity and Forensics
content:
Microbiology, Immunity and Forensics

Edexcel International A Level Biology — Unit 4 (WBI14), Topic 6. Every statement 6.1 to 6.20 is covered below, with its code in the heading. The topic links three big ideas: how microorganisms are grown and measured, how the body defends itself and why pathogens keep finding ways around those defences, and how DNA techniques are used to identify organisms and people.

6.1: Culturing microorganisms with aseptic technique

  • Aseptic technique keeps a culture pure: only the wanted microorganism grows. Sterilise media and equipment first, usually in an autoclave at 121 °C under pressure for about 15 minutes.
  • Work close to a Bunsen flame, flame the inoculating loop until red-hot before and after use, keep Petri dish lids mostly closed, and never pipette by mouth.
  • Incubate cultures inverted at a safe temperature, usually 25 °C for school work, so condensation does not drip onto the agar.

6.2: Measuring the growth of microorganisms

  • Direct cell counts: use a haemocytometer (counting chamber) under a microscope, counting cells in a known volume to get the number per cm³.
  • Viable counts by dilution plating: make a serial dilution, spread known volumes on agar, incubate, and count colonies on plates with about 30 to 300 colonies. Each colony is assumed to grow from one viable cell, so the count shows living cells only.
  • Mass methods: measure the dry mass of cells collected by centrifuging or filtering a known volume of culture.
  • Optical methods (turbidity): a colorimeter or spectrophotometer measures how much light the cloudy culture absorbs. Absorbance rises with cell density, so a calibration curve converts it to cell numbers.

6.3: The bacterial growth curve and the growth rate constant

  • Lag phase: cells adapt to the medium and synthesise enzymes; there is little or no division.
  • Exponential (log) phase: cells divide at a constant rate, so the population doubles each generation. N = N₀ × 2ⁿ, where n is the number of doublings.
  • Stationary phase: births equal deaths, because nutrients run short and waste builds up.
  • Death phase: deaths exceed births and the population falls.
  • Growth rate constant: in exponential growth N = N₀eᵏᵗ. So k = (ln N₂ − ln N₁) ÷ (t₂ − t₁). Plotting ln N against time gives a straight line whose gradient is k.

6.4: Core practical 13: growth of microorganisms in liquid culture

  • Inoculate a sterile liquid medium, take samples at regular intervals, and measure turbidity or cell count each time.
  • Plot the results to show the four phases of the curve, then calculate the exponential growth rate constant from the straight-line part.
  • Safe and ethical use: use only non-pathogenic strains, keep the culture closed, disinfect the bench, and autoclave all used material before disposal.

6.5: Structure of bacteria and viruses

  • Bacteria are cells with a cell wall (peptidoglycan), cell membrane, cytoplasm with ribosomes, and a circular DNA loop, often with plasmids. They have no nucleus.
  • Viruses are not cells. They have a nucleic acid core, either DNA or RNA, surrounded by a protein capsid. Some also have a lipid envelope taken from the host.
  • Comparisons: Ebola virus has single-stranded RNA and an envelope. Tobacco mosaic virus (TMV) has single-stranded RNA in a helical capsid, with no envelope. HIV has two RNA strands, reverse transcriptase and an envelope. λ phage, a virus of bacteria, has double-stranded DNA in a head with a tail and no envelope.
  • Lytic cycle: the virus takes over the host cell, makes new viruses, and the cell bursts (lyses) to release them.
  • Latency: the viral genome stays in the host cell without producing new viruses, and can become active later.

6.6: How Mycobacterium tuberculosis and HIV infect human cells

  • Tuberculosis: Mycobacterium tuberculosis is inhaled into the alveoli. Macrophages engulf it, but the bacterium survives inside them and multiplies. The body forms granulomas (tubercles) around the infection, and the lung tissue is destroyed. Symptoms include a persistent cough, fever, night sweats and weight loss. If untreated it can be fatal.
  • HIV: the virus binds to CD4 receptors and a co-receptor on helper T cells. Reverse transcriptase makes DNA from its RNA, which is inserted into the host genome. New viruses bud from the cell. The helper T cell population falls, so the immune system fails and opportunistic infections and cancers take hold (AIDS).

6.7: Routes of entry and barriers

  • Routes: inhalation (airborne droplets), ingestion (contaminated food and water), contact through broken skin or wounds, sexual contact, and vectors such as mosquitoes.
  • Barriers: intact skin (keratin, dryness, and the skin flora that competes with pathogens), stomach acid (pH about 2, which kills many ingested microbes), and gut flora that competes for space and nutrients. Mucus and cilia in the airways trap and move pathogens out.

6.8: Non-specific responses to infection

  • Inflammation: damaged cells release chemicals such as histamine, which dilate blood vessels and make them leaky. The area becomes red, hot and swollen, and white blood cells are recruited to the site.
  • Lysozyme: an enzyme in tears, saliva and mucus that breaks the peptidoglycan of bacterial cell walls.
  • Interferon: proteins released by virus-infected cells that warn neighbouring cells, which then resist viral replication. Interferon is antiviral, not a direct killer of the virus.
  • Phagocytosis: neutrophils and macrophages engulf a pathogen into a phagosome. Lysosomes fuse with it and enzymes digest the contents.

6.9: Antigens, antibodies, plasma cells, macrophages and antigen-presenting cells

  • An antigen is a foreign molecule, usually a protein or glycoprotein on a pathogen's surface, that triggers an immune response.
  • An antibody is a Y-shaped glycoprotein whose binding sites are complementary to one specific antigen. Antibodies mark pathogens for destruction and neutralise toxins.
  • Plasma cells are B cells that have been activated and that secrete antibodies in large amounts.
  • Macrophages and antigen-presenting cells engulf the pathogen, break it down, and display its antigens on their surface (on MHC proteins). This shows helper T cells what to respond to.

6.10: B cells and T cells

  • B effector (plasma) cells secrete antibodies. B memory cells survive for years and give a faster, larger response on the next exposure to the same antigen.
  • T helper cells (CD4) recognise the antigen on an antigen-presenting cell and release cytokines that activate B cells and T killer cells.
  • T killer (cytotoxic, CD8) cells bind to infected or abnormal cells and kill them, for example by releasing perforin.
  • T memory cells persist after the infection and respond quickly if the same pathogen returns.

6.11: Types of immunity

  • Natural active: the person is infected and makes their own antibodies and memory cells.
  • Natural passive: antibodies pass from mother to baby across the placenta or in breast milk. Protection is immediate but short-lived, and no memory cells are formed.
  • Artificial active: vaccination with an antigen, a weakened or dead pathogen, or a toxoid. The person makes antibodies and memory cells without becoming ill.
  • Artificial passive: injected antibodies, such as antivenom or antitoxin. Protection is immediate and short-lived, and the person's own immune system does not learn.

6.12: The evolutionary race between pathogens and hosts

  • Pathogens evolve evasion mechanisms. Antigenic variation changes the surface antigens: influenza and HIV mutate rapidly, so antibodies no longer fit.
  • Other evasion: hiding inside host cells (tuberculosis in macrophages, HIV in T cells), entering latency, and suppressing the immune response.
  • The host responds with new antibodies and T cells, so pathogens and hosts keep evolving against each other. This is the evolutionary race.

6.13: Bacteriostatic and bactericidal antibiotics

  • Bacteriostatic antibiotics stop bacteria growing and dividing, for example by blocking protein synthesis. The immune system then clears the infection.
  • Bactericidal antibiotics kill bacteria, for example penicillin, which stops cell wall synthesis so the cell bursts.
  • Antibiotics do not act on viruses, which use the host cell's machinery.

6.14: Core practical 14: the effect of antibiotics on bacteria

  • Spread a lawn of bacteria on agar, place antibiotic discs on it, and include a control disc with no antibiotic.
  • Incubate, then measure the diameter of each clear zone of inhibition. A larger zone means the bacteria are more sensitive.
  • Use aseptic technique and non-pathogenic strains, and autoclave the plates before disposal.

6.15: Hospital-acquired infections and codes of practice

  • Contributory causes include overuse of broad-spectrum antibiotics, which selects for resistant strains such as MRSA, poor hand hygiene, indwelling catheters, surgical wounds, and immunocompromised patients.
  • Codes of practice respond to these causes: prescribe antibiotics only when needed and according to guidelines, enforce hand hygiene, isolate infected patients, and clean equipment and wards.

6.16: Decomposition and the carbon cycle

  • Bacteria and fungi are the main decomposers. They secrete extracellular enzymes that digest complex organic matter such as cellulose and proteins, then absorb the simpler products.
  • Respiration by decomposers releases carbon dioxide, which returns carbon to the atmosphere for producers. Ammonium released from proteins feeds the nitrogen cycle.

6.17: The polymerase chain reaction (PCR)

  • Each cycle has three steps: denaturation at about 95 °C separates the strands, annealing at about 50 to 65 °C lets primers bind, and extension at about 72 °C is when Taq polymerase builds the new strands.
  • Taq polymerase comes from the heat-tolerant bacterium Thermus aquaticus, so it survives the high temperatures. Around 30 cycles give an exponential increase in the number of copies.

6.18: Gel electrophoresis of DNA fragments

  • DNA carries a negative charge from its phosphate groups, so it moves towards the positive electrode (anode) through a gel.
  • Smaller fragments move faster and further, so fragments separate by length. A DNA ladder of known sizes is run alongside for comparison, and the bands are stained to make them visible.

6.19: DNA profiling for identification and relatedness

  • DNA profiling compares short tandem repeats (STRs) or variable number tandem repeats (VNTRs). These regions vary in length between individuals, so each person gives a distinctive band pattern.
  • Uses include identifying suspects, establishing paternity, and comparing the banding patterns of plants or animals to show how closely related they are.

6.20: Estimating the time of death from forensic evidence

  • Body temperature: the body cools towards the surroundings, so the rate of cooling gives an estimate of time since death.
  • Muscle contraction: rigor mortis sets in over hours, peaks, then fades over about a day or two.
  • Decomposition and succession: bacterial decomposition gives a predictable sequence of changes. Forensic entomology uses the stage of blowfly larvae and the succession of insect species to estimate how long the body has been exposed.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Growth rate, 6.3 applied: a culture grows from 2.0 × 10⁴ cells cm⁻³ at 2 hours to 1.6 × 10⁵ at 5 hours. N₂ ÷ N₁ = 8 = 2³, so three doublings in three hours. k = (ln 1.6 × 10⁵ − ln 2.0 × 10⁴) ÷ 3 = ln 8 ÷ 3 = 0.69 per hour. The doubling time is ln 2 ÷ k = 1.0 hour. Check the answer against the doubling count before you write it down.
  • Viable count, 6.2 applied: 150 colonies grow from 0.1 cm³ of a 10⁻⁵ dilution. That is 150 ÷ 0.1 = 1500 colonies per cm³ in the diluted sample, and multiplying by the dilution factor gives 1.5 × 10⁸ viable cells per cm³. A haemocytometer count would include dead cells, so the two methods can give different numbers from the same culture. Name which one you are using.
  • Log phase, 6.3 applied: plotting ln N against time gives a straight line only during exponential growth. A curve that bends is a sign that the lag, stationary or death phase has been included by mistake. Use only the straight section to find k.
  • Primary and secondary immune response, 6.10 and 6.12 applied: the first exposure has a lag of several days before antibodies peak at a lower level. A second exposure gives a faster, larger and longer-lasting response, because memory cells are already present. Use all three words, faster, larger and longer, to earn the full mark.
  • Antigen presentation, 6.9 applied: helper T cells (CD4) recognise antigen presented on MHC class II proteins, and killer T cells (CD8) recognise it on MHC class I, as on infected body cells. Naming the MHC class shows you understand which cell carries the antigen.
  • Antibiotic action, 6.13 applied: penicillin blocks the cross-linking of peptidoglycan in the cell wall, so a growing cell bursts. An antibiotic that targets a process human cells do not use, such as the bacterial ribosome, is more selective. Resistance arises by chance mutation and is selected for by the antibiotic, so the explanation must say the mutation was already present and survived.
  • PCR, 6.17 applied: after n cycles one DNA molecule has become 2ⁿ molecules. After 30 cycles that is 2³⁰, about 1.07 × 10⁹ copies. This is why a very small sample is enough, and why contamination with foreign DNA is a serious error.
  • Gel electrophoresis, 6.18 applied: the distance moved is roughly linear with the logarithm of the fragment length. Use a DNA ladder to plot log size against distance, then read the unknown band from that graph rather than from the ladder bands by eye.
  • Forensic estimates, 6.20 applied: a time-of-death answer is always a range. Temperature cooling assumes a stable environment, and a hot or wet site or a body wrapped in clothing changes the rate. Say which factor is most uncertain and why.

Exam tip: time-of-death questions are estimates. Name the method, say what it measures, and state the limitation, for example that temperature depends on the environment.

The four types of immunity, compared

TypeHow it is acquiredAntibodies made by the personDuration
Natural activeInfection with the pathogenYesLong, because memory cells remain
Natural passiveAntibodies cross the placenta or arrive in colostrumNoShort, until the transferred antibodies are broken down
Artificial activeVaccination with antigen or an attenuated pathogenYesLong, and boosters raise the secondary response
Artificial passiveInjection of antibodies from another source, such as an antiserumNoShort, but immediate

Typical mistakes

  • Confusing aseptic technique with sterilisation. Apparatus and medium are sterilised before use; aseptic technique is how the worker keeps them sterile while handling them, by flaming the loop, passing the neck of the bottle through the flame and minimising the time the plate is open.
  • Forgetting the dilution factor in a viable count. A count on a diluted sample must be multiplied by the dilution factor and divided by the volume plated, or the answer is out by orders of magnitude. Quote the units as cells per cm cubed.
  • Reading the growth curve without the phase names. Lag phase: cells adapt and synthesise enzymes, so numbers rise slowly. Exponential phase: numbers double at a constant rate. Stationary: growth equals death as nutrients run low and waste builds. Death: death exceeds growth.
  • Saying antibiotics are bactericidal when they are bacteriostatic. Bactericidal antibiotics kill the bacteria; bacteriostatic ones stop them dividing, so the immune system finishes the job. Penicillin is bactericidal because it blocks the cross-linking of peptidoglycan, so growing cells burst.
  • Giving B and T cells the same job. B effector cells make and secrete antibodies and B memory cells make the secondary response faster. T helper cells release cytokines that activate B cells and macrophages, T killer cells destroy infected cells, and T memory cells persist.
  • Describing PCR without its requirements. PCR needs a DNA template, primers, free nucleotides, a heat-stable DNA polymerase and a buffer, with repeated cycles of denaturation, annealing and extension. Each cycle doubles the DNA, so 30 cycles give 2³⁰ copies.
  • Forgetting which electrode DNA moves towards. DNA is negatively charged because of its phosphate groups, so in gel electrophoresis it moves towards the positive electrode, and shorter fragments move further.
  • Giving a single figure for time of death. It is an estimate from several methods, each with a limitation: body temperature depends on the environment, decomposition depends on conditions, and succession depends on the species available.

Exam-style questions

  1. A 0.1 cm cubed sample of a 10⁻⁴ dilution produces 64 colonies. Calculate the number of viable cells in the original culture. Answer: 64 colonies in 0.1 cm cubed is 640 cells per cm cubed in the diluted sample; multiply by the dilution factor 10 000, giving 6.4 times 10⁶ viable cells per cm cubed.
  2. Explain why a viable count can be lower than a total count from a haemocytometer. Answer: a viable count only counts cells that can divide and form a colony, so dead cells and cells that are alive but not dividing are missed; a haemocytometer counts all cells, living and dead, present in the sample.
  3. Describe how you would investigate the effect of different antibiotics on a bacterial culture, naming the variables. Answer: inoculate a lawn of the bacterium evenly over an agar plate using a sterile spreader, place discs soaked in equal volumes of different antibiotic solutions on the surface, incubate at a controlled temperature for a fixed time, and measure the diameter of the clear zone around each disc. Controls: a disc soaked in sterile water, and the same species, incubation temperature and time for every plate. A larger zone means greater inhibition, and repeats give a mean.
  4. Explain how a vaccine produces immunity and why a booster is sometimes needed. Answer: the vaccine presents antigens, which are taken up by antigen-presenting cells; helper T cells activate the specific B cell carrying a matching receptor; the B cell divides into effector cells that secrete antibodies and memory cells that persist. A booster raises the antibody level again through the quicker, larger secondary response, and may be needed when the first dose did not produce enough memory cells or when the pathogen varies.
  5. Explain how HIV and Mycobacterium tuberculosis cause disease. Answer: HIV binds the CD4 receptor on helper T cells, and the virus enters and replicates, eventually destroying the cells; the loss of helper T cells disables the immune response, so opportunistic infections cause AIDS. Mycobacterium tuberculosis is engulfed by macrophages but survives inside them, and the inflammatory response forms tubercles that damage the lung tissue, causing coughing and reduced gas exchange.
  6. Explain how gel electrophoresis separates DNA fragments and what a DNA profile shows. Answer: fragments are cut with restriction enzymes and loaded into a gel; an electric field moves the negatively charged DNA towards the positive electrode, and shorter fragments travel further, so the fragments separate by length. A profile from several loci is a pattern that can identify an individual or show relatedness, because the pattern is inherited.
  7. Explain how PCR amplifies DNA and why contamination is a problem. Answer: the mixture is heated to denature the double helix, cooled so primers anneal to the target sequences, then warmed so DNA polymerase extends the primers; each cycle doubles the number of target molecules. A single foreign DNA molecule can also be amplified, so contamination makes the sample unusable.

Primary and secondary responses: why a second exposure is met faster

The first time the body meets an antigen, the immune system has to find the few B cells whose antibodies fit it, and let those cells divide. This takes days. A second exposure to the same antigen is met much more quickly, because the body keeps memory cells from the first response that are ready to act. The difference is the basis of vaccination.

Key: antigen = a molecule that triggers an immune response; antibody = a protein made by a plasma cell that binds a specific antigen; memory cell = a long-lived B or T cell produced in the first response.

The primary response

On first exposure there is a lag while the correct B cell is selected by clonal selection and divides into plasma cells. Antibody concentration rises to a peak and then falls as the infection is cleared. Because the number of specific B cells is small at the start, the lag is long and the peak is modest.

The secondary response

Memory cells are already present in greater numbers and respond at once. The lag is short, the antibody concentration rises more steeply and reaches a higher peak, and it is maintained for longer. The infection is often cleared before it causes symptoms, which is the protection a vaccine aims to produce.

Comparing the two responses in an answer

Compare the lag, the rate of rise, the peak and the duration for the two exposures, and say why each differs: the number of specific B cells present at the time of exposure. Do not say that the body "learns" in the sense of changing its antibodies; the antibodies are the same, and the difference lies in the number of cells ready to make them.

Equations and symbols

Four calculations carry the quantitative marks in this topic: population growth, the growth rate constant, the viable count with its dilution factor, and the amplification of DNA by PCR. Learn the symbols once and the rest is substitution.

Population growth

N = N₀ × 2ⁿ Key: N = population size after n doublings (cells, or cells cm⁻³); N₀ = starting population at the same units; n = number of doublings (no units). Doubling means n rises by 1 per generation, so the population is exponential, not linear.

N = N₀eᵏᵗ Key: N = population at time t; N₀ = population at t = 0; e = 2.718…; k = growth rate constant (h⁻¹, or s⁻¹ if time is in seconds); t = time (h). This is the continuous form of the same growth, and it is the one that gives k.

k = (ln N₂ − ln N₁) ÷ (t₂ − t₁) Key: k = growth rate constant (h⁻¹); N₁ and N₂ = population at the two sampling times; t₁ and t₂ = those times (h); ln = natural logarithm. It is the gradient of ln N against time, which is why only the straight, exponential section of the graph may be used.

k = (ln 1.6 × 10⁵ − ln 2.0 × 10⁴) ÷ 3 = ln 8 ÷ 3 = 0.69 per hour Key: the worked case: a rise from 2.0 × 10⁴ to 1.6 × 10⁵ cells cm⁻³ over 3 h is an eightfold rise, so ln 8 ÷ 3 = 0.69 h⁻¹. Eightfold is exactly three doublings, which is the check.

doubling time = ln 2 ÷ k Key: doubling time = time for the population to double (h); ln 2 = 0.693; k = growth rate constant (h⁻¹). With k = 0.69 h⁻¹ the doubling time is 1.0 h.

Viable counts and the dilution factor

150 ÷ 0.1 = 1500 colonies per cm³ Key: 150 = colonies counted on the plate; 0.1 = volume plated (cm³); the quotient is the count per cm³ of the diluted sample. Multiply by the dilution factor (10⁵ here) to reach 1.5 × 10⁸ viable cells per cm³ of the original culture — forgetting that step is the classic error.

PCR amplification

2³⁰ Key: 2 = the doubling per cycle; 30 = number of cycles. Thirty cycles give about 1.07 × 10⁹ copies from a single molecule, which is why a trace of DNA is enough and why contamination ruins a sample.

The slip worth naming

A haemocytometer counts live and dead cells together, so a total count is always at least the viable count. State which method produced the number before comparing two counts.

title: Algebra — Sequences and Functions — Study Notes
content:
Sequences and Functions

Sequences as functions

A sequence can be defined by a term-to-term rule (each term from the previous one) or a position-to-term rule (un in terms of n). A linear sequence has un = a + (n − 1)d, and the domain of a sequence is the positive integers.

Function notation

A function f maps each element of its domain to exactly one output. Write f(x) for the output at x, and find values by substitution. The range is the set of outputs the function can produce.

Composite functions

gf(x) means apply f first, then g: gf(x) = g(f(x)). The order matters in general, so fg and gf are usually different.

Example: f(x) = 2x + 3 and g(x) = x². Then gf(x) = (2x + 3)² = 4x² + 12x + 9, while fg(x) = 2x² + 3.

Inverse functions

An inverse exists only when the function is one-to-one. To find f⁻¹(x), write y = f(x), rearrange to make x the subject, then swap x and y. The graph of f⁻¹ is the reflection of the graph of f in the line y = x.

Example: f(x) = 2x + 3 gives y = 2x + 3, so x = (y − 3)/2 and f⁻¹(x) = (x − 3)/2.

Exam technique

  • Write the domain of an inverse function explicitly when the question asks for it.
  • Check a composite function by substituting a simple value such as x = 1.

title: Membranes, Proteins, DNA and Gene Expression — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Membranes, Proteins, DNA and Gene Expression — Quick Revision Summary

Biology — AS Edexcel IAL, WBI12 Unit 1 Topic 2. Membrane structure and the fluid mosaic model, Core Practical 3 on membrane permeability, osmosis and water potential and the different kinds of transport, protein structure from amino acid to tertiary and quaternary, DNA structure and the evidence for semi-conservative replication from Meselson and Stahl, the genetic code and how genes work, transcription and translation and alternative splicing, mutation types and their effects, patterns of inheritance including sex linkage, cystic fibrosis as a gene-mutation disorder, and genetic screening and its ethical and social issues.

  • 2.2 Membrane structure (fluid mosaic model): a phospholipid bilayer with hydrophilic heads out and hydrophobic tails in, proteins (channel, carrier, receptor, recognition) embedded or attached, cholesterol moderating fluidity in animal cells; the membrane is fluid and mosaic, an interpretation of the evidence.
  • 2.3 Core Practical 3: beetroot cylinders in water at different temperatures or in different alcohol concentrations; colourimeter measures the pigment leaked as membranes are damaged — permeability rises with temperature and alcohol as proteins denature and the bilayer is disrupted.
  • 2.4 Osmosis and water potential: osmosis is the net movement of free water through a partially permeable membrane down a water potential gradient; solute lowers water potential; pure water has the highest (zero) water potential; animal cells swell and may haemolyse or crenate; plant cells become turgid (supported) or plasmolysed.
  • 2.5 Passive and active transport: diffusion of small non-polar molecules through the bilayer; facilitated diffusion of ions and large polar molecules through channel and carrier proteins down their gradient; active transport against the gradient using ATP; endocytosis and exocytosis for bulk materials in vesicles.
  • 2.9 Mononucleotides and DNA/RNA structure: a mononucleotide is deoxyribose (or ribose) + phosphate + base (A, C, G, T in DNA; A, C, G, U in RNA); nucleotides join by phosphodiester bonds; two complementary strands hydrogen-bond A–T (two bonds) and C–G (three bonds) in an antiparallel double helix.
  • 2.10 DNA replication (semi-conservative): double helix unzips, each strand is a template, DNA polymerase joins free nucleotides; Meselson and Stahl''s 15N/14N experiment gave a single hybrid band in generation 1 and hybrid + light bands later — exactly what semi-conservative replication predicts and ruling out the conservative and dispersive alternatives.
  • 2.11 Genetic code: triplet, non-overlapping and degenerate — three bases code for one amino acid and several codons can code for the same amino acid; a stop codon signals the end.
  • 2.12 Gene: a sequence of bases on DNA that codes for a sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide.
  • 2.13 Protein synthesis: transcription by RNA polymerase makes mRNA from the template (antisense) strand; mRNA goes to ribosomes; tRNA brings amino acids with anticodons that pair with mRNA codons, building the polypeptide in the order of the codons until a stop codon.
  • 2.14 Mutations: substitution may change one amino acid or none; insertion/deletion (not in threes) causes a frameshift, changing all later amino acids and usually destroying function; some mutations cause cancer or genetic disorders, many do nothing.
  • 2.15 Inheritance: gene, allele, genotype, phenotype, dominant, recessive, codominance, homozygote, heterozygote; monohybrid crosses with ratios; sex linkage on the X chromosome (red-green colour blindness, haemophilia — more common in males); pedigree diagram interpretation.
  • 2.16 Cystic fibrosis: a mutation in a chloride-channel gene (often a three-base deletion removing one amino acid) — chloride and water transport fails, mucus is thick; affects gaseous exchange (blocked airways, infections), digestion (blocked pancreatic duct, poor digestion, malnutrition) and reproduction (absent or blocked vas deferens, male infertility).
  • 2.17 Genetic screening: identifies carriers; prenatal testing (amniocentesis at 15–17 wks, CVS at 8–12 wks); PGD used with IVF to test embryos before implantation — testing for genetic disorders before pregnancy.
  • 2.18 Ethical and social issues: safety and reliability of the test, miscarriage risk with invasive tests, right to know or not to know, what counts as a disorder, choice to terminate, anxiety, access and cost, and the risk of moving from preventing disease to selecting non-medical traits.

Worked example

Monohybrid cross between two heterozygotes (Aa × Aa): Punnett gives AA (¼), Aa (½), aa (¼); phenotype ratio 3 : 1 if A is completely dominant; genotype ratio 1 : 2 : 1. Sex linkage: a carrier female (XᴮXᵇ) and a normal male (XᴮY): sons ½ colour-blind (XᵇY) and ½ normal (XᴮY); daughters ½ carriers (XᴮXᵇ) and ½ normal (XᴮXᴮ), none colour-blind (unless the father is colour-blind). Heterozygosity index: in a population of 20 individuals at one locus, 8 are heterozygotes → H = 8/20 = 0.40.

Key points to remember

Membranes: temperature and alcohol disrupt proteins and the bilayer — permeability rises. Osmosis: water moves from high to low water potential; the direction and whether a cell bursts, crenates, becomes turgid or plasmolysed depends on the water potential of the solution compared with the cell. Transport: diffusion and facilitated diffusion are passive; active transport uses ATP and goes against the gradient; endocytosis and exocytosis use vesicles and ATP. Protein structure: peptide bond from condensation; primary = sequence; secondary = alpha-helix and beta-sheet (hydrogen bonds); tertiary = overall 3D folding with hydrogen, ionic, disulfide and hydrophobic bonds; quaternary = several polypeptides together (haemoglobin). DNA: antiparallel, A–T (2 H-bonds), C–G (3 H-bonds); semi-conservative replication shown by Meselson and Stahl. Protein synthesis: transcription → mRNA; translation on ribosomes with tRNA anticodons; alternative splicing means one gene can make more than one protein. Mutation types: substitution, insertion, deletion (frameshift). Cystic fibrosis: faulty chloride channel → thick mucus → lung, digestion, reproduction problems. Screening: carriers, PGD, amniocentesis, CVS; weigh benefits against ethical and social issues.

How to use this

Read the summary list, then open the full revision notes for any point that feels weak, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself. Revise next by: drawing a cell membrane and labelling the bilayer, proteins and cholesterol; carrying out the beetroot permeability practical and explaining the trend and control variables; drawing DNA, showing base pairing and antiparallel strands, and explaining semi-conservative replication and the Meselson and Stahl evidence; drawing protein synthesis (transcription and translation) with mRNA, tRNA and the ribosome; and working through a monohybrid cross, a sex-linked cross and a pedigree to explain each ratio.

title: Continuous Random Variables — Study Notes
content:
Continuous Random Variables

Probability Density Functions

A continuous variable X is described by a density f(x) with f(x) ≥ 0 and ∫f(x)dx = 1 over all x. Probabilities are areas:

  • P(a ≤ X ≤ b) = ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx

Single points have zero probability, so strict or loose inequalities make no difference: P(X < 2) = P(X ≤ 2).

Finding Unknown Constants

Piecewise densities carry an unknown k: impose that the total area is 1 (and continuity at joins where required). One equation, one unknown.

Example: f(x) = kx on 0 ≤ x ≤ 2. Total area: k·(2²/2) = 2k = 1, so k = ½.

Expectation and Variance

  • E(X) = ∫x·f(x) dx
  • E(X²) = ∫x²·f(x) dx
  • Var(X) = E(X²) − (E(X))²

The mean is the balancing point of the area under the density. For symmetric densities the mean sits at the symmetry point — worth spotting before integrating.

The Median and Mode

The median m solves ∫₋∞ᵐ f(x) dx = 0.5 (left half of the area). The mode is the x maximising f(x). For uniform densities the median is the midpoint.

Uniform Distribution

If f(x) = 1/(b − a) on [a, b], every point is equally likely. Then E(X) = (a + b)/2 and Var(X) = (b − a)²/12 — memorise both; they are quick exam marks.

Exam tips: always verify ∫f = 1 before computing anything else. Sketch the density — area intuitions catch algebra slips. Median questions are integration-to-0.5 questions; set them up before calculating.

Exam method: density functions

A probability density function f must satisfy f(x) ≥ 0 for all x and the total area under it must equal 1, so the integral of f over its whole domain is 1. Use this to find an unknown constant before asking for any probability.

For a continuous variable, P(a ≤ X ≤ b) is the integral of f(x) from a to b. The endpoints carry no probability, so strict and non-strict inequalities give the same answer. Outside the given domain f(x) = 0.

The cumulative distribution function F(x) = P(X ≤ x) is the integral of f from the lower end of the domain up to x. The median m satisfies F(m) = 0.5, and the mode is where f is largest.

Expected value E(X) is the integral of x f(x) over the domain, and the variance is E(X²) minus the square of E(X). Write each integral with its limits before evaluating.

Exam cue: Sketch the density over its domain first. A linear density is a triangle or trapezium, and the area of the shape gives the total probability quickly.

Worked example: the cumulative distribution function

Let X have probability density function f(x) = 2x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1, and zero elsewhere. The cumulative distribution function is F(x) = P(X ≤ x) = ∫ from 0 to x of 2t dt = x² for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1. Then P(0.2 < X < 0.5) = F(0.5) − F(0.2) = 0.25 − 0.04 = 0.21. A probability for a continuous variable is an area under the curve, so the endpoints of an interval do not change its value.

Exam method: state the range and check the total area

Always state the range of x for which the formula applies, and write f(x) = 0 outside it. Before using the density, check that the integral over the full range equals 1; if it does not, the unknown constant has been found incorrectly. Make sure the function is non-negative across the whole range, because a negative value means the function cannot be a density.

title: A Level Mathematics: The Binomial Distribution
content:
A Level Mathematics: The Binomial Distribution

A binomial distribution counts successes in a fixed number of independent trials, each with the same probability of success. Coins, multiple-choice guesses, defective items in a sample and free throws all fit the same template, and once a problem is recognised as binomial the calculation is a formula plus a cumulative table. This note builds the distribution from its four conditions, derives the formula from counting, and then uses it for the two things exams actually ask: probabilities and hypothesis tests.

The four conditions

Before writing X ~ B(n, p) you must be able to name the conditions, because most exam questions include a part asking whether the model is appropriate. The conditions are not red tape: drop any one and the formula is simply wrong.

1. a fixed number of trials n
2. each trial has exactly two outcomes (success / failure)
3. the probability of success p is constant for every trial
4. the trials are independent
then X = number of successes has X ~ B(n, p)

Worked example (checking the model). A bag holds 5 red and 15 blue counters. Four counters are taken without replacement. Is the number of red counters binomial?

n = 4 is fixed and each draw is red or not red
but p changes: 5/20, then 5/19 if a red was taken, ...
the trials are not independent, so NOT binomial (it is hypergeometric)

Taking with replacement would fix it: p stays 0.25 on every draw.

The formula, and where it comes from

The probability of a particular sequence of r successes and n − r failures is p^r (1−p)^(n−r), because independence lets you multiply. The number of such sequences is the number of ways to choose which r trials succeed, which is nCr. Multiplying gives the formula.

P(X = r) = nCr p^r (1 - p)^(n - r)
the nCr counts arrangements; the powers give the probability of one arrangement

Worked example. X ~ B(10, 0.3). Find P(X = 3).

P = 10C3 (0.3)³ (0.7)⁷
= 120 × 0.027 × 0.08235
= 120 × 0.002223 = 0.2668

Worked example 2 (a single trial count). A fair die is rolled 8 times. Find the probability of exactly two sixes.

X ~ B(8, 1/6)
P(X = 2) = 8C2 (1/6)² (5/6)⁶ = 28 × 0.02778 × 0.3349 = 0.2605

Worked example 3 (why nCr appears). For n = 3 and r = 1, list the sequences and confirm the coefficient.

sequences: SFF, FSF, FFS - three of them
each has probability p(1-p)²
so P(X = 1) = 3p(1-p)², and 3C1 = 3

Cumulative probabilities

Questions almost always ask for a range, not a single value, and the cumulative distribution is what the calculator or the tables supply. The skill is rewriting the question into the form the table gives you.

P(X <= r) is tabulated directly
P(X >= r) = 1 - P(X <= r - 1)
P(X < r)  = P(X <= r - 1)
P(a <= X <= b) = P(X <= b) - P(X <= a - 1)
P(X = r) = P(X <= r) - P(X <= r - 1)

Worked example. X ~ B(20, 0.4). Find P(X ≥ 8).

P(X >= 8) = 1 - P(X <= 7)
= 1 - 0.4159
= 0.5841

Worked example 2 (between). For the same X, find P(5 ≤ X ≤ 10).

= P(X <= 10) - P(X <= 4)
= 0.8725 - 0.0510
= 0.8215

Worked example 3 (the strict inequality trap). For the same X, find P(X > 6).

P(X > 6) = 1 - P(X <= 6) = 1 - 0.2500 = 0.7500
note this is different from P(X >= 6) = 1 - P(X <= 5) = 0.8746

Mean and variance

The binomial has the simplest mean and variance in the syllabus, and they are worth knowing both forwards and backwards: a question can give the mean and variance and ask for n and p.

E(X) = np
Var(X) = np(1 - p)
standard deviation = √(np(1-p))

Worked example. X ~ B(50, 0.2). Find the mean and standard deviation.

mean = 50 × 0.2 = 10
variance = 10 × 0.8 = 8
sd = 2.828

Worked example 2 (backwards). A binomial variable has mean 12 and variance 9. Find n and p.

np = 12;  np(1-p) = 9
divide: 1 - p = 9/12 = 0.75  →  p = 0.25
then n = 12/0.25 = 48

Hypothesis testing with the binomial

A one-tailed test asks whether p has increased or decreased; the test statistic is the observed count, and the p-value is the probability of a result at least as extreme in the direction of the alternative.

H0: p = p0      H1: p > p0 (or p < p0)
X ~ B(n, p0) under H0
p-value = P(X >= observed) or P(X <= observed)
compare with the significance level; reject H0 if p-value <= alpha

Worked example. A coin is tossed 20 times and lands heads 15 times. Test at the 5% level whether the coin is biased towards heads.

H0: p = 0.5;  H1: p > 0.5
X ~ B(20, 0.5)
P(X >= 15) = 1 - P(X <= 14) = 1 - 0.9793 = 0.0207
0.0207 < 0.05, so reject H0
there is evidence at the 5% level that the coin favours heads

Worked example 2 (two-tailed). The same data tested two-tailed.

double the smaller tail: 2 × 0.0207 = 0.0414
0.0414 < 0.05, so still reject H0 at the 5% level

Worked example 3 (critical region). For X ~ B(20, 0.5), find the critical region for a 5% one-tailed test of p > 0.5.

P(X >= 14) = 0.0577 (above 0.05)
P(X >= 15) = 0.0207 (below 0.05)
critical region: X >= 15

Note that the critical region is chosen so the probability of a Type I error is at most 5%, which is why 14 is excluded even though it is close.

When the model breaks down

Examiners like the question that asks why a binomial model is only an approximation. The usual culprits are dependence, a varying probability, or a fixed sample drawn without replacement from a small population.

SituationProblemEffect
sampling without replacementtrials not independentp drifts; use the hypergeometric instead
clustered data (pupils in classes)responses correlatedvariance underestimated
probability varies between trialsp not constantformula invalid
large n, p near 0.5computation heavynormal approximation is reasonable

Worked example (normal approximation). X ~ B(200, 0.4). Use a normal approximation to estimate P(X ≤ 70).

mean = 80;  variance = 200 × 0.4 × 0.6 = 48;  sd = 6.928
continuity correction: X <= 70 becomes X < 70.5
z = (70.5 - 80)/6.928 = -1.371
P(Z < -1.371) = 0.0852

The continuity correction is compulsory: a discrete count needs a half-unit boundary before it can be treated as continuous.

Expected frequencies and the shape of the distribution

A binomial distribution is not symmetric unless p = 0.5, and that shape decides which tail an exam question is fishing in. The most likely value — the mode — is the integer near (n + 1)p, and expected frequency multiplies the probability by the number of samples taken. Both are quick marks that are frequently missed because students jump straight to the formula.

mode is near (n + 1)p, checked by comparing consecutive probabilities
expected number in a sample of size N = N x P(X = r)

Worked example. X ~ B(12, 0.3). Find the most likely value of X and the expected number of 3s in 500 independent observations.

(n + 1)p = 13 × 0.3 = 3.9, so check r = 3 and r = 4
P(X = 3) = 220 × 0.027 × 0.1176 = 0.2397
P(X = 4) = 495 × 0.0081 × 0.1681 = 0.2311
mode = 3
expected number of 3s = 500 × 0.2397 = 120 (to the nearest whole)

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Model) State the distribution for the number of sixes in 12 rolls of a fair die. Answer: X ~ B(n, p) with n = 12 rolls and p = 1/6 the chance of a six on each, so X ~ B(12, 1/6).
  2. (Single value) X ~ B(8, 0.25): find P(X = 2). Answer: P(X = 2) = ⁸C₂ (0.25)² (0.75)⁶ = 28 × 0.0625 × 0.1780 = 0.3115.
  3. (Cumulative) X ~ B(15, 0.3): find P(X ≤ 4). Answer: P(X ≤ 4) = Σₖ₌₀⁴ ¹⁵Cₖ (0.3)ᵏ (0.7)¹⁵⁻ᵏ = 0.5155 from cumulative binomial tables.
  4. (Complement) Same X: find P(X ≥ 3). Answer: P(X ≥ 3) = 1 − P(X ≤ 2) = 1 − 0.2969 = 0.7031 — the complement, because the tables give the lower tail only.
  5. (Mean) X ~ B(40, 0.35): find E(X) and Var(X). Answer: 14 and 9.1.
  6. (Backwards) Mean 18, variance 12: find n and p. Answer: mean np = 18 and variance np(1 − p) = 12; dividing, 1 − p = 12/18 = 2/3, so p = 1/3 and n = 18 ÷ (1/3) = 54.
  7. (Test) 12 of 20 seeds germinate; test p = 0.5 against p < 0.5 at 5%. Answer: H₀: p = 0.5 against H₁: p < 0.5; under H₀, X ~ B(20, 0.5) and P(X ≤ 12) = 0.8684, which is far above 0.05, so there is no evidence to reject H₀.
  8. (Critical region) X ~ B(10, 0.2): find the 5% critical region for p < 0.2. Answer: the smallest possible tail is P(X ≤ 0) = (0.8)¹⁰ = 0.1074, which already exceeds 0.05, so no critical region exists at the 5% level for this n.
  9. (Approximation) X ~ B(100, 0.5): approximate P(X ≥ 60). Answer: μ = np = 50 and σ = √(np(1 − p)) = √25 = 5; with the continuity correction z = (59.5 − 50)/5 = 1.9, so P(X ≥ 60) ≈ P(Z > 1.9) = 0.0287.
  10. (Assumption) Give one reason a binomial model may fail for defects in boxes of 20. Answer: defects may cluster, so trials are not independent.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Forgetting nCr: the coefficient counts arrangements; without it the answer is the probability of one specific sequence.
  • nCr on the wrong factor: it is p^r (1−p)^(n−r), with the success probability raised to the number of successes.
  • Inequality direction: P(X ≥ 8) uses 1 − P(X ≤ 7), not 1 − P(X ≤ 8).
  • Variance confused with standard deviation: np(1−p) is the variance; the test and the normal approximation need the square root.
  • Continuity correction omitted: any normal approximation to a discrete count needs the half-unit adjustment.
  • One-tailed evidence read as two: halving or doubling the tail without checking the alternative direction is a silent error.
  • Independence asserted, not checked: sampling without replacement from a small population breaks the model, and the question usually invites you to say so.
  • p-value compared with the wrong threshold: the significance level is given as a percentage; 5% means 0.05, not 5.

Equations and symbols

The distribution, its conditions and the four tail identities. Every question on this topic is one of these lines plus a calculator.

P(X = r) = nCr p^r (1 - p)^(n - r) Key: n = number of trials, fixed in advance; p = probability of success in one trial, constant; r = the number of successes asked for; nCr = n!/(r!(n − r)!), the number of orders the successes can occur in. The (1 − p) term is the failures, and its power must be n − r.

X ~ B(n, p) Key: X = the count of successes; the tilde means "is distributed as"; n and p as above. Write this line before calculating — it is often a mark on its own, and it fixes which parameters go into the calculator.

P = 10C3 (0.3)³ (0.7)⁷ Key: n = 10, p = 0.3, r = 3, so the failures are 7 and their probability is 0.7. The coefficient 10C3 = 120 accounts for the order of the three successes among the ten trials.

P(X >= r) = 1 - P(X <= r - 1) Key: a complement, so the two probabilities add to 1; the boundary moves by one because the binomial is discrete. Using 1 − P(X ≤ r) instead is the classic off-by-one error.

P(a <= X <= b) = P(X <= b) - P(X <= a - 1) Key: subtract the part below the interval; again the "− 1" is there because P(X ≤ a − 1) is everything before a. Check with a small case you can list by hand before trusting the calculator.

title: Algebra — Inequalities — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Algebra — Inequalities

Mathematics — OL. solving linear inequalities, integer solution sets, shading regions on graphs (linear programming context).

  • 1. Solving
  • 2. Integer solutions
  • 3. Double inequalities
  • 4. Shading regions

How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

Worked example

Solve 2x − 3 < 7. Add 3 to both sides to get 2x < 10, then divide by 2 to get x < 5. If x is an integer and −2 ≤ x < 5, the integer solutions are −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4. The bounds are inclusive on the left and exclusive on the right, so the endpoint −2 is included and 5 is not.

Common mistakes

  • Reversing the inequality sign when you multiply or divide by a negative number, for example in −3x > 6, which gives x < −2.
  • Using a solid line for a strict inequality. Use a dashed line for < or >, and a solid line for ≤ or ≥.
  • Shading the wrong side. Test a point such as (0, 0) and shade the region that makes the inequality true.
