title: Nuclear Physics — Study Notes
content:
Nuclear Physics

The nucleus

The nucleus holds protons and neutrons, collectively nucleons. Nuclide notation ᴬZX gives Z protons and A nucleons, so N = A − Z neutrons. Isotopes share Z and differ in N. Nuclear densities are about 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³, so nearly all the mass of an atom sits in a tiny volume.

Mass defect and binding energy (23.1)

The mass of a nucleus is less than the sum of the masses of its separate nucleons. This difference is the mass defect Δm. Energy equivalent to Δm, given by E = Δmc², is the binding energy: the energy released when the nucleus is assembled from separate nucleons, and the energy needed to separate it. In nuclear work, 1 u = 931 MeV.

Example: a mass defect of 0.0300 u corresponds to E = 0.0300 × 931 ≈ 27.9 MeV.

The binding energy per nucleon peaks near iron-56, the most tightly bound nucleus. Energy is released when the nucleons move toward this peak, by fission of heavy nuclei or by fusion of light ones.

Radioactive decay (23.2)

Decay is random and spontaneous. The effect of each type on the nucleus and its penetration are:

TypeWhat changesStopped by
alphaZ − 2, A − 4paper
beta-minusZ + 1, A unchangeda few mm of aluminium
gammano change to Z or Athick lead

The activity A = λN is the rate of decay, in becquerel (Bq). The decay constant λ and the half-life t½ are related by λ = ln 2 / t½. The number of nuclei left after time t is N = N₀e^(−λt).

Example: a sample with t½ = 10 days has 1/8 of its original activity after 30 days, since three half-lives have passed.

Example: with t½ = 5.0 h = 1.8 × 10⁴ s, λ = 0.693 / 1.8 × 10⁴ ≈ 3.9 × 10⁻⁵ s⁻¹.

Fission and fusion

Heavy nuclei split (fission) into lighter nuclei of greater binding energy per nucleon, which releases energy in reactors. Light nuclei merge (fusion), which releases energy in stars.

Exam tips: balance Z and A on both sides of every decay equation. Convert the half-life to seconds before finding λ. Use A = λN, not guesswork with halves, when the number of nuclei is needed.

Worked example: binding energy per nucleon

Carbon-12 has six protons and six neutrons. Adding their masses gives about 12.096 u, while the carbon-12 nucleus has a mass of about 11.997 u once the electrons are removed. The mass defect is therefore about 0.099 u. Using 1 u = 931.5 MeV, the binding energy is about 92 MeV, which is about 7.7 MeV per nucleon. Binding energy per nucleon peaks near iron-56 at about 8.8 MeV. Fusion of light nuclei and fission of heavy nuclei both move products toward that peak, and that shift is why both processes release energy.

Exam method: nuclear equations

Balance the nucleon number and the proton number on each side of the equation separately. Alpha emission lowers the nucleon number by 4 and the proton number by 2. Beta-minus emission (an electron) leaves the nucleon number unchanged and raises the proton number by 1, because a neutron becomes a proton. Write the full symbol with its nucleon and proton numbers so the marker can check both conservation laws.

title: AS Level Mathematics: Numerical Measures of Central Tendency
content:
AS Level Mathematics: Numerical Measures of Central Tendency

Statistics begins with describing data: where its centre lies and how it is spread. This note covers representation of data — tables, histograms, cumulative frequency curves and box plots — and the three averages with their strengths, plus the quartiles and interquartile range that measure spread robustly. The emphasis throughout is on choosing the right representation for the data type and reading values off a graph with the precision the marks require.

Types of data and the right representation

Data typeMeaningUseful displays
QualitativeCategories, no orderBar chart, pie chart
DiscreteCountable valuesBar chart, stem-and-leaf, histogram of counts
ContinuousAny value in a rangeHistogram, cumulative frequency, box plot

A histogram is the display for continuous data grouped into classes; unlike a bar chart, the bars touch because the variable is continuous. For unequal class widths the frequency density is plotted, not the frequency:

frequency density = frequency / class width
area of a bar = frequency (so areas are comparable)

Worked example. A class of width 10 contains 25 items; another of width 20 contains 30. Find the frequency densities.

25/10 = 2.5;  30/20 = 1.5
The narrower class is denser even though it holds fewer items.

The three averages

AverageHow to findStrengthWeakness
MeanSum ÷ countUses every valueDragged by outliers
MedianMiddle of ordered dataResistant to outliersIgnores exact values at the ends
ModeMost frequent valueWorks for categoriesMay not exist or be unique

Worked example. Find all three averages of 4, 7, 7, 9, 13.

mean = 40/5 = 8
median = 7 (third of five ordered values)
mode = 7

Worked example 2 (grouped mean). Estimate the mean of the grouped data: 0–10 (4), 10–20 (9), 20–30 (7).

use midpoints 5, 15, 25
sum = 4(5) + 9(15) + 7(25) = 20 + 135 + 175 = 330
total frequency = 20
estimated mean = 330/20 = 16.5

Grouped means are estimates: the midpoint stands in for every value in its class, so the answer is only as good as the grouping.

Median, quartiles and the interquartile range

median position (n data values) = (n + 1)/2
lower quartile Q1 at position (n + 1)/4
upper quartile Q3 at position 3(n + 1)/4
interquartile range IQR = Q3 - Q1

Worked example. Find the median and IQR of 3, 5, 7, 8, 10, 12, 15, 18.

n = 8; median position 4.5 → average of 4th and 5th = (8 + 10)/2 = 9
Q1 position 2.25 → 5 + 0.25(7 - 5) = 5.5
Q3 position 6.75 → 12 + 0.75(15 - 12) = 14.25
IQR = 14.25 - 5.5 = 8.75

The IQR is the robust measure of spread: it discards the extreme quarter at each end, so one outlier cannot inflate it the way it inflates the range.

Cumulative frequency and box plots

A cumulative frequency curve plots the running total against the upper class boundary. The median, quartiles and any percentile are read off at the corresponding cumulative frequencies.

read the median at n/2, Q1 at n/4, Q3 at 3n/4
(from a cumulative frequency curve, interpolate on the curve)

Worked example. A cumulative frequency curve for 80 students gives Q1 = 42 marks, median = 55, Q3 = 66. Describe the distribution.

IQR = 66 - 42 = 24 marks
the median sits closer to Q1 than Q3? 55 - 42 = 13; 66 - 55 = 11
so the middle half is roughly symmetric, slightly longer tail below
the upper whisker reaches the maximum; compare its length with the
lower whisker to judge skew

Box plot construction. A box from Q1 to Q3 with a line at the median, whiskers to the smallest and largest values that are not outliers. Outliers (beyond 1.5 × IQR from the quartiles) are plotted as separate points.

lower fence = Q1 - 1.5 IQR;  upper fence = Q3 + 1.5 IQR
values outside the fences are outliers

Comparing distributions

A comparison answer needs two parts: a measure of location (median or mean) and a measure of spread (IQR or standard deviation), each with a sentence of interpretation. "School A's median is higher, so its typical student scored more; its IQR is smaller, so its results are more consistent."

Worked example. A: median 62, IQR 18. B: median 58, IQR 9. Compare.

A has the higher typical mark (+4 on the median)
B is more consistent (IQR 9 vs 18)
A's spread suggests a wider mix of abilities; B's results cluster

Choosing and justifying an average

Exam questions ask which average best represents a data set — the answer is a reasoned choice, not a preference:

  • Skewed data or outliers: the median, because it is not dragged by extremes.
  • Categorical data: the mode, because a mean of categories is meaningless.
  • Data where every value should count (e.g. total rainfall per month): the mean.

Worked example. House prices in a street are 180k, 190k, 195k, 200k and 1.2m. Which average represents a typical price?

mean = 393k (dragged up by the 1.2m house)
median = 195k (the middle price)
the median is the honest summary; the mean misrepresents the street

Coding and combined means

Coding simplifies arithmetic without changing the shape of the data. If every value is transformed by y = (x - a)/b, the mean and standard deviation transform the same way, which is why coded means can be decoded exactly.

coded values: y = (x - a)/b
mean(x) = b mean(y) + a
median(x) = b median(y) + a
IQR(x) = b IQR(y)   (spread scales but does not shift)

Worked example. The coded values y = (x - 50)/10 have mean 2.4 and IQR 1.5. Find the mean and IQR of x.

mean x = 10(2.4) + 50 = 74
IQR x = 10(1.5) = 15

Worked example 2 (combined groups). Class A has 20 students with mean mark 60; class B has 30 with mean 70. Find the combined mean.

total marks = 20(60) + 30(70) = 1200 + 2100 = 3300
combined mean = 3300/50 = 66
not the average of 60 and 70, because the groups differ in size

The combined-mean formula is the weighted average: the group sizes are the weights. Averaging two means without weighting is one of the most common arithmetic errors in statistics questions.

Stem-and-leaf diagrams

A stem-and-leaf diagram keeps every value visible while ordering the data, which makes it the quickest route to the median and quartiles without arithmetic. The stem is the leading digit, the leaf the final digit, and a key must be stated.

example key: 3 | 4 means 34

3 | 4 7 9
4 | 1 2 2 5 8
5 | 0 3 6
6 | 1

Reading it: the data are 34, 37, 39, 41, 42, 42, 45, 48, 50, 53, 56, 61. With n = 12, the median sits between the 6th and 7th values, the lower quartile at position 3.25 and the upper at 9.75.

Worked example. Find the median and IQR of the data above.

median = (42 + 45)/2 = 43.5
Q1 = 37 + 0.25(39 - 37) = 37.5
Q3 = 50 + 0.75(53 - 50) = 52.25
IQR = 14.75

Back-to-back stems compare two groups: leaves for one group run left of the stem and for the other to the right, sharing the same stems so the shapes line up. Comparison answers then read off both a location and a spread for each group, exactly as with box plots.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Mean) Find the mean of 12, 15, 9, 18, 16. Answer: 70/5 = 14.
  2. (Median) Find the median of 4, 9, 2, 7, 11, 6. Answer: ordered 2, 4, 6, 7, 9, 11; median (6 + 7)/2 = 6.5.
  3. (Mode) Find the mode of 3, 5, 5, 7, 9, 9, 9. Answer: 9.
  4. (Grouped) Estimate the mean of 0–20 (5), 20–40 (10), 40–60 (5). Answer: (5×10 + 10×30 + 5×50)/20 = 600/20 = 30.
  5. (Quartiles) Find the IQR of 2, 5, 6, 8, 9, 12, 14, 15. Answer: Q1 = 5.5, Q3 = 13.5, IQR = 8.
  6. (Histogram) A bar of height 3 has class width 5. What frequency does it represent? Answer: 3 × 5 = 15.
  7. (Comparison) Two classes: median 55, IQR 10 and median 55, IQR 20. Compare. Answer: same typical mark; the first is more consistent.
  8. (Choice) Which average suits shoe sizes? Answer: the mode, because sizes are categorical/ordinal and the most common size is what a shop stocks.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Not ordering first: the median requires sorted data; taking the middle of the raw list is wrong whenever the data is unsorted.
  • Position versus value: (n + 1)/2 gives the position, not the median; count to that place.
  • Midpoint error: the midpoint of 10–20 is 15, not 10 or 20; open-ended classes make a grouped mean impossible without an assumption, which must be stated.
  • Histogram heights: plot frequency density, not frequency, when class widths differ; areas, not heights, compare.
  • Reading the curve: cumulative frequency is read against the upper boundary; using the lower boundary shifts every quartile.
  • IQR arithmetic: Q3 − Q1, never Q1 − Q3, and never the range.
  • Comparison without spread: a comparison that mentions only the median is half an answer.
  • Mean of grouped data called exact: call it an estimate and say why.

title: Number — Arithmetic and Place Value — Study Notes
content:
Number — Arithmetic and Place Value

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): 1.1 integers & place value; 1.2 fractions/decimals/percentages context; 1.3 powers & roots; HCF/LCM.

1. Types of number

  • Integers: … −2, −1, 0, 1, 2 … Primes: exactly two factors; 2 is the only even prime; 1 is not prime.
  • HCF = product of common prime factors (lowest powers); LCM = all prime factors (highest powers).

Example: 60 = 2²×3×5 and 84 = 2²×3×7 ⇒ HCF = 2²×3 = 12; LCM = 2²×3×5×7 = 420.

2. Place value

In 47 382 the digit 7 has value 7000. Rounding to significant figures: keep n digits, round using the next digit (≥5 up).

Estimation: round inputs to 1 s.f. first — 39.2 × 5.98 ≈ 40 × 6 = 240.

3. Order of operations

BIDMAS. 3 + 4 × 2² = 3 + 16 = 19. Insert brackets yourself when translating words: "3 added to the product of 4 and 2²" = 3 + (4 × 2²).

4. Negative numbers and calculators

Bracket negatives when substituting. Know the ×10ˣ, x², √, ˣ√ and fraction keys; give answers to 3 s.f. unless told otherwise.

5. Bounds (Extended)

Measured to nearest u: UB = +u/2, LB = −u/2. Division p/q: max = UBp ÷ LBq.

Example: 45 cm (nearest cm) in 6 s (nearest s): max speed = 45.5 ÷ 5.5 = 8.27 m/s (3 s.f.).

Exam tips: show prime-factor trees for HCF/LCM; always state rounding units (3 s.f., 1 d.p.); bounds answers quote both limits.

Place value and ordering

Each digit is worth ten times the digit to its right. To order decimals, compare digits from left to right, padding with zeros so every number has the same number of decimal places. Rounding to a given number of decimal places or significant figures looks at the next digit: 5 or more rounds up.

Written methods

Long multiplication and division are set out in columns with place value kept aligned. Estimate first by rounding each number to one significant figure; the estimate shows whether the exact answer is reasonable. Check using the inverse operation.

Order of operations

Brackets, then indices, then division and multiplication from left to right, then addition and subtraction from left to right. For example, 3 + 4 × 2² = 3 + 4 × 4 = 19. Use a calculator's brackets key to enter long expressions in one go.

title: IGCSE Biology: Enzymes
content:
IGCSE Biology: Enzymes

Enzymes are the reason you can digest a meal in hours rather than centuries: they are biological catalysts, proteins that speed up chemical reactions without being consumed. This note starts with the lock-and-key picture of how they work, moves to the factors that change their rate (temperature, pH, substrate concentration, enzyme concentration), gives the graph-reading rules examiners use to separate A-grade answers from C-grade ones, and closes with the Paper 6 enzyme-investigation design you can be asked to write from scratch. Every graph is described in words as well as axes, so you can reconstruct it in the exam.

What an enzyme is, physically

Each enzyme is a globular protein folded so that part of its surface forms a pocket called the active site — a groove whose shape and charge match one particular molecule, the substrate. When substrate meets active site they form an enzyme-substrate complex, the reaction happens (bonds broken or made), and the products leave, freeing the unchanged enzyme to repeat. The lock-and-key analogy imagines the substrate as the key and the active site as the lock; the induced-fit model is the modern refinement — the active site flexes slightly to grip the substrate, straining its bonds so less energy is needed to break them. That lowering of activation energy is the whole catalytic trick: enzymes do not add energy, they lower the hill the reaction must climb.

Specificity and the naming rule

Each enzyme acts on one substrate only, because the active site is complementary to that substrate's shape — this is enzyme specificity. The naming convention is worth a free mark: the enzyme is named after its substrate with the suffix –ase. Starch is digested by carbohydrase (specifically amylase); protein by protease; lipid by lipase; and a specific sugar like lactose by lactase. Maltase digests maltose, sucrase digests sucrose. If a question names a substrate and asks for its enzyme, answer by adding –ase and you will almost always be right.

Temperature and enzyme rate

Temperature works in two stages. Below the optimum, heating increases the kinetic energy of both enzyme and substrate, so they collide more often and with more energy — the rate rises (roughly doubling per 10 °C near the optimum). At the optimum temperature (around 37 °C for human enzymes, 25 °C for many plant enzymes), the rate is fastest. Above the optimum, the bonds holding the tertiary structure (hydrogen and ionic bonds) break: the active site changes shape, the substrate no longer fits, and the enzyme is denatured — this is permanent. The graph of rate against temperature is therefore a steep rise, a rounded peak, then a fall to zero. Exam phrasing: "denatured" must be paired with "active site changes shape" and "substrate no longer fits" to earn all the marks.

pH and enzyme rate

Each enzyme has an optimum pH — around pH 2 for pepsin in the stomach, pH 7–8 for salivary amylase and trypsin in the small intestine. Changing pH alters the charges on the amino acids of the active site; far from the optimum, ionic and hydrogen bonds break and the enzyme denatures, exactly as with temperature. The rate-pH graph is a bell curve centred on the optimum. The trap: do not write that acid "kills" the enzyme or that pH "denatures the substrate" — it is the enzyme's structure that fails.

Substrate and enzyme concentration

With enzyme constant and substrate concentration rising: the rate rises in direct proportion at first (more substrate means more frequent collisions, every active site busy), then the curve levels off (a plateau) when all active sites are occupied — the enzyme is saturated, and adding substrate cannot help. With substrate in excess and enzyme concentration rising: the rate rises linearly and does not plateau while substrate remains available. Recognising which factor is limiting is a standard three-mark "explain the shape of the graph" question: name the limiting factor at each stage (substrate concentration below saturation; number of active sites above it).

Every factor at a glance

FactorEffect on rate below the optimumEffect above the optimumReason
TemperatureRate rises with heatingRate falls to zeroMore energetic collisions, then denaturation of the active site
pHRate rises towards the optimumRate falls to zeroCharges on the active site change, then bonds break
Substrate concentrationRate rises in proportionRate plateausAll active sites occupied — the enzyme is saturated
Enzyme concentrationRate rises in proportionRises while substrate remainsMore active sites available for the substrate

Inhibitors

Competitive inhibitors have a shape similar to the substrate and bind to the active site, blocking it; their effect can be reduced by raising substrate concentration (more substrate outcompetes them). Non-competitive inhibitors bind elsewhere on the enzyme (an allosteric site), changing the active site's shape so the substrate cannot fit; raising substrate concentration does not overcome them. At IGCSE, know both in one line each and be able to say which one is affected by substrate concentration — that distinction is a favourite Paper 2 and Paper 4 probe.

Investigating enzyme rate: the Paper 6 method

A standard investigation: measure 5 cm³ of starch solution into a water bath at a set temperature; add 1 cm³ of amylase solution; start the timer; every 30 seconds take a drop of the mixture and test on a spotting tile with iodine; record the time until the iodine stays yellow-brown (all starch hydrolysed). Rate = 1 ÷ time (the standard reciprocal, in s⁻¹). Variables: independent = temperature (or pH, or enzyme concentration); dependent = time for starch to disappear (converted to rate); controls = volume and concentration of starch, volume and concentration of enzyme, pH (use buffer), identical timing technique. Repeat and take a mean. A water bath (not a Bunsen flame) is required for temperature control, and each test tube must reach the set temperature before mixing.

Worked example: reading and calculating from an enzyme experiment

At 25 °C, starch disappeared in 240 s; at 35 °C, in 120 s; at 45 °C, in 150 s; at 55 °C, in 600 s. Step 1: convert to rate using rate = 1 ÷ time: 1/240 = 0.00417 s⁻¹; 1/120 = 0.00833 s⁻¹; 1/150 = 0.00667 s⁻¹; 1/600 = 0.00167 s⁻¹. Step 2: read the pattern — the rate rises from 25 to 35 °C (kinetic energy up), peaks between 35 and 45 °C, then collapses at 55 °C. Step 3: explain each point as the examiner wants: from 25 to 35 °C, more energetic collisions occur; at the peak the enzyme is at its optimum; at 55 °C the enzyme has denatured, its active site has changed shape and the substrate no longer fits, so the rate is lowest. Step 4: state the trend as a sentence with a number: "the fastest rate was at 35 °C (0.00833 s⁻¹) and the slowest at 55 °C (0.00167 s⁻¹), a five-fold difference." Always quote at least one figure when asked to "use the data".

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Writing that enzymes "are used up" — catalysts are unchanged at the end; say "recovered unchanged".
  • Explaining high temperature as "the enzyme dies" — enzymes are not alive; say the enzyme is denatured because bonds in the tertiary structure break.
  • Forgetting to state "the active site changes shape, so the substrate can no longer fit" — the two extra clauses are the extra marks.
  • Confusing "rate of reaction" with "time taken": rate = 1 ÷ time, so a longer time means a slower rate; plotting time and calling it rate loses interpretation marks.
  • Leaving units off rates (s⁻¹ or per second) or off concentration (mol/dm³) in Paper 4 calculations.
  • In a design question, not controlling pH or temperature — even if you are not investigating them, they must be listed and held constant.
  • Calling the lock-and-key model "wrong": at IGCSE, induced fit is the more precise description, but both are accepted if you explain specificity.
  • Saying competitive inhibitors "kill" enzymes; they only block the active site temporarily.

Exam-style questions and answers

Q1. Explain why the rate of an enzyme-controlled reaction increases as temperature rises from 20 °C to 30 °C. (2 marks) Answer: molecules gain kinetic energy so move faster (1); collisions between enzyme and substrate are more frequent and more energetic, so more enzyme-substrate complexes form (1).

Q2. Explain what happens to an enzyme at 60 °C and why the reaction stops. (3 marks) Answer: the enzyme is denatured (1); bonds maintaining the tertiary structure break so the active site changes shape (1); the substrate no longer fits so no enzyme-substrate complexes form (1).

Q3. Describe how you would investigate the effect of pH on amylase activity. (4 marks) Answer: use buffers to set a range of pH values (1); keep starch concentration, amylase volume and temperature constant (1); time how long starch takes to be hydrolysed, testing with iodine (1); repeat and calculate rate = 1 ÷ time, plot rate against pH (1).

Q4. Explain why adding more substrate eventually stops increasing the reaction rate. (2 marks) Answer: the enzyme becomes saturated — all active sites are occupied at any moment (1), so additional substrate has to wait and cannot raise the rate further (1).

Q5. A reaction takes 40 s. Calculate the rate and state its unit. (2 marks) Answer: rate = 1 ÷ 40 = 0.025 (1); unit s⁻¹ or per second (1).

title: IGCSE Chemistry: Metals and Reactivity
content:
IGCSE Chemistry: Metals and Reactivity

Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry 0620 (2026–2028), Extended route, Topic 9 Metals: statements 9.1 Properties of metals, 9.2 Uses of metals, 9.3 Alloys and their properties, 9.4 Reactivity series, 9.5 Corrosion of metals, and 9.6 Extraction of metals. The reactivity series is the spine of this topic — it predicts what metals do with water, acid and oxygen, how they are extracted, and why they corrode. Every prediction below flows from one ordering, and the blast furnace is traced reaction by reaction.

Properties and uses

Metals: good conductors of heat and electricity, malleable (hammer into sheets) and ductile (draw into wire), with high melting points — all from metallic bonding (positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons). Uses follow properties: aluminium — low density (aircraft), corrosion resistance (food containers, overhead cables: light + oxide-protected + conductive); copper — excellent conductivity and ductility (electrical wiring), non-toxic (water pipes).

MetalKey propertyUse
AluminiumLow density; corrosion-resistant oxide layer; conductsAircraft, overhead cables, food containers
CopperExcellent electrical conductivity; ductile; non-toxicElectrical wiring, water pipes
Iron (steel)Strong, cheap; alloyed for hardnessStructures, vehicles, cutlery (stainless)
TungstenVery high melting point (3422 °C)Lamp filaments, cutting tools
TitaniumStrong, low density, corrosion-resistant, biocompatibleAerospace, replacement joints

Alloys

An alloy is a mixture of a metal with other elements (brass = copper + zinc; stainless steel = iron + chromium + nickel). Alloys are harder and stronger than pure metals: atoms of different sizes disrupt the regular layers, so the layers cannot slide over each other easily — this is the complete explanation, and both halves earn marks. Stainless steel's hardness and corrosion resistance suit cutlery.

The reactivity series

The series, memorised in order of decreasing reactivity:

  potassium K, sodium Na, calcium Ca, magnesium Mg, aluminium Al,
  carbon C (reference), zinc Zn, iron Fe, hydrogen H (reference),
  copper Cu, silver Ag, gold Au

Three observations fix a metal's place:

  WITH WATER:
    K, Na, Ca: react with cold water (2K + 2H₂O → 2KOH + H₂; sodium melts
    and skitters; calcium fizzes steadily)
    Mg: very slowly with cold water, vigorously with steam
       (Mg + H₂O → MgO + H₂)
    Al, Zn, Fe: react with STEAM only (Fe + H₂O → Fe₃O₄ + H₂ at red heat)
    Cu, Ag, Au: no reaction even with steam

  WITH DILUTE HCl:
    K..Mg: vigorous (fast fizz of H₂)
    Zn, Fe: steady fizz
    Cu, Ag, Au: no reaction (below hydrogen in the series)

  WITH OXYGEN:
    most metals form oxides; gold does not tarnish at all.

Displacement: a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from its
salt solution:
    Zn(s) + CuSO₄(aq) → ZnSO₄(aq) + Cu(s)      [zinc plates copper]
    Cu(s) + ZnSO₄(aq) → no reaction
  Observations: zinc gains a red-brown coating; the blue Cu²⁺ colour fades.

Corrosion and protection

Rusting is the corrosion of iron in the presence of both water and oxygen — the classic two-variable experiment (wet + air = rust; dry air or water without air = none). The product is hydrated iron(III) oxide, Fe₂O₃·xH₂O.

  • Barrier methods: painting, greasing, plastic coating — block water and oxygen reaching the surface.
  • Galvanising: coating with zinc; even scratched, zinc protects because it corrodes preferentially.
  • Sacrificial protection: a more reactive metal (zinc or magnesium) is attached to iron; it corrodes instead of the iron because it loses electrons more readily — used on ships' hulls and underground pipes.
Sacrificial protection explained electron by electron:

  Iron in contact with zinc in damp conditions forms a tiny electrochemical
  cell. Zinc is more reactive, so Zn atoms lose electrons (Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻)
  and corrode; the electrons flow to the iron, where oxygen and water take
  them up. The iron is reduced-protected - it cannot corrode while the zinc
  remains. This is why the zinc block is called "sacrificial": it is eaten
  away to save the iron.

Extraction of metals

Ease of extraction tracks the reactivity series: unreactive metals (Cu, Ag, Au) exist as native elements and need no chemical extraction; moderately reactive metals (Zn, Fe) are extracted by reduction with carbon; the most reactive (Al, Mg, Na) are extracted by electrolysis — carbon cannot reduce them.

The blast furnace for iron, reaction by reaction:

  Raw materials: iron ore (haematite, Fe₂O₃), coke (C), limestone (CaCO₃),
                 hot air.

  1. Coke burns to make carbon monoxide (the reducing agent):
       C + O₂ → CO₂          (exothermic - heats the furnace)
       CO₂ + C → 2CO          (endothermic; the key reduction agent forms)
  2. Reduction of the ore:
       Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂
     (also direct: Fe₂O₃ + 3C → 2Fe + 3CO at the hottest zone)
  3. Limestone removes sandy impurities (silica):
       CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂        (thermal decomposition)
       CaO + SiO₂ → CaSiO₃     (slag - molten, drained off)

  Slag uses: road building. The molten iron is TAPPED from the bottom;
  slag floats above it (less dense) and is run off separately.

Aluminium extraction (electrolysis of Al₂O₃ in molten cryolite):
  - cryolite (Na₃AlF₆) lowers the melting point from 2050 °C to ~950 °C,
    saving energy;
  - carbon anodes: oxygen liberated reacts with them: C + O₂ → CO₂, so
    anodes burn away and must be replaced regularly;
  - half-equations:  Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al  (cathode, reduction)
                     2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻  (anode, oxidation)
  - aluminium is used for overhead cables and aircraft: light, resistant
    to corrosion (protective oxide layer), and conductive.

Worked example: reactivity reasoning end to end

Question: metal X does not react with steam but displaces copper from
copper(II) sulfate. Metal Y reacts with cold water. Order X, Y and copper
and justify.

  Y reacts with cold water → Y is high in the series (like K, Na or Ca).
  X does not react with steam → X is BELOW the steam-reactive metals (Al,
  Zn, Fe react with steam; Cu, Ag, Au do not) - but X displaces copper →
  X is MORE reactive than copper. So X sits between iron and copper region:
  e.g. X could be lead. Order: Y > X > copper.

  The displacement alone proves X > Cu; the steam data place X low but not
  at the bottom; combining both observations is the mark.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Writing rust as just iron oxide — it is hydrated iron(III) oxide, and both water AND oxygen are required.
  • Explaining sacrificial protection without electron loss ("zinc is stronger") — the mark is reactivity and electron transfer.
  • Forgetting carbon and hydrogen's places as reference points in the series (they anchor extraction and acid-reaction predictions).
  • Confusing the blast furnace's reducing agents: carbon makes CO, and CO does the reduction — not carbon alone at the top.
  • Missing the limestone/slag step when asked "what removes impurities?"
  • Claiming alloys are harder because "the atoms are bigger" — the layers-disruption explanation is required.
  • Writing electrolysis for iron extraction (that is aluminium) — match method to reactivity.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Explain why gold is found unreactive in the Earth's crust while aluminium is extracted by electrolysis.

Answer: Gold is very low in the reactivity series — it does not react with water, oxygen or dilute acids, so it occurs as the free element and needs no chemical extraction. Aluminium is very reactive: its oxide is too stable for carbon to reduce at workable temperatures, so it must be extracted by electrolysis of molten aluminium oxide in cryolite.

Question 2 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Describe how iron is extracted in the blast furnace, including the role of limestone.

Answer: Coke burns to carbon dioxide, which reacts with more coke to carbon monoxide; the CO reduces haematite: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂. Limestone decomposes to calcium oxide, which reacts with sandy silica impurities to form molten calcium silicate (slag), which floats on the molten iron and is tapped off separately.

Question 3 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Explain sacrificial protection of iron.

Answer: A more reactive metal such as zinc is attached to iron in damp conditions. Zinc loses electrons more readily (Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻) and corrodes instead of the iron; the electrons it releases prevent iron from being oxidised. The zinc block is consumed over time — it is sacrificed — and must be replaced, but the iron stays intact.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 3 marks). Explain why stainless steel is harder than pure iron.

Answer: Stainless steel is an alloy of iron with chromium and nickel. Atoms of different sizes distort the regular layers of iron atoms, so the layers cannot slide over each other easily when stressed — the material resists deformation and is harder and stronger.

Question 5 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Write equations for the reactions of (i) magnesium with steam (ii) zinc with dilute hydrochloric acid (iii) zinc with copper(II) sulfate, and state the observation for (iii).

Answer: (i) Mg + H₂O → MgO + H₂. (ii) Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂. (iii) Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu — the zinc gains a red-brown copper deposit and the blue solution colour fades.

Question 6 (Paper 4, 3 marks). State the conditions needed for iron to rust and describe two methods of prevention.

Answer: Iron needs both water and oxygen (air) in contact with it. Prevention: barrier methods such as painting or greasing that exclude both; galvanising with a zinc coating (which also protects scratches by corroding preferentially); or sacrificial protection with attached zinc or magnesium blocks.

Metals and their reactions shape the environment as well as industry — the next topic is the chemistry of air and water.
