title: Programming Paradigms and Low-Level — Study Notes
content:
Programming Paradigms and Low-Level

Paradigms

  • Procedural: programs as sequences of instructions in procedures — good for straightforward algorithms.
  • Object-oriented: classes encapsulate state (attributes) and behaviour (methods); supports encapsulation, inheritance and polymorphism.
  • Declarative: state what is required, not how (SQL queries, logic programming).
  • Low-level: assembly maps closely to machine code; used where hardware control or timing precision is needed.

Assembly Essentials

The opcode names the operation (LDM load, STR store, ADD, CMP compare, JMP branch, IN/OUT for I/O). The operand names the data. The assembler translates mnemonics to machine code one-to-one; two-pass assemblers resolve forward references via the symbol table.

Addressing Modes

  • Immediate: operand is the constant itself, ADD #5.
  • Direct: operand is the memory address of the data.
  • Indirect: operand is the address OF the address; one extra memory read.
  • Indexed: effective address = base + index register; ideal for arrays.
  • Relative: address given as an offset from the program counter; enables position-independent code.

Fetch-Execute

Fetch: PC gives address, instruction loads into the CIR, PC increments. Decode: control unit interprets the opcode. Execute: the operation runs, possibly updating registers or memory. Interrupts are checked at cycle boundaries.

Exam tips: trace short assembly programs register by register; compute effective addresses for each addressing mode; state one advantage of OOP for large systems.

title: Sequences and Series — Study Notes
content:
Sequences and series

Level note: progressions and sigma notation are Pure 2 (WMA12) in Edexcel, sat at AS; this note is the deeper revision treatment of the same material.

An arithmetic progression (AP) adds a constant difference d each term; a geometric progression (GP) multiplies by a constant ratio r. You must master both closed forms, their sums, and the conditions for an infinite sum.

Arithmetic progression

  • nth term: a_n = a + (n - 1)d.
  • Sum: S_n = n/2 [2a + (n - 1)d] = n/2 (first + last).
  • The difference between consecutive terms is constant: a_{n+1} - a_n = d.

Geometric progression

  • nth term: a_n = a r^(n - 1).
  • Sum: S_n = a(r^n - 1)/(r - 1) = a(1 - r^n)/(1 - r).
  • Sum to infinity: S_inf = a/(1 - r), valid ONLY when |r| < 1.

Sigma notation

  • sum of r from 1 to n = n(n + 1)/2; sum of r^2 = n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6; sum of r^3 = [n(n + 1)/2]^2.
  • sum of a constant c over n terms is cn.
  • Split sums: sum (3r + 1) = 3 sum r + sum 1.

Modelling

  • Arithmetic: hire charges, stacked rows, simple interest.
  • Geometric: depreciation, compound interest, population growth, drug decay.
  • For repeated percentage change, multiplier = (1 + percentage/100) per period.

Exam technique

  • Write the first few terms before committing to a formula.
  • Check the sum formula by substituting n = 1 and n = 2.
  • For 'sum exceeds X' questions solve the inequality and take the first integer.

title: AS Level Physics: Kinematics
content:
AS Level Physics: Kinematics

Edexcel International A Level Physics, Unit 1 (WPH11) Mechanics and Materials — motion in a straight line and in a plane, and the measurement skills the companion Unit 3 paper (WPH13, Practical Skills in Physics I) examines. Everything in mechanics starts here: quantities with units and directions, the equations of motion, free fall, projectiles and the graphs that describe them. The unit also demands real data-handling skill — uncertainties, error bars, gradients and intercepts — because WPH13 is a written paper that marks your experimental thinking, not your hands.

Quantities, units, scalars and vectors

A physical quantity is a number with a unit, and every unit in mechanics is built from four SI base units: the metre (m), kilogram (kg), second (s) and ampere (A). Speed in m s⁻¹ and force in newtons (1 N = 1 kg m s⁻²) are derived from them. A scalar has size only — distance, speed, mass, time, energy, power. A vector has size and direction — displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, momentum. The distinction is operational, not decorative: vectors add by direction, and every mechanics question that mentions direction is testing it.

  • Two vectors in a line: add if in the same direction, subtract if opposite, and state the direction of the resultant.
  • Two vectors at right angles: the resultant is the hypotenuse, R = √(A² + B²), at an angle θ = tan⁻¹(B/A) to A.
  • Any two vectors: resolve each into perpendicular components with A cos θ and A sin θ, add the components separately, then recombine.

Resolution is the workhorse of A-level mechanics. A force F at angle θ to the horizontal has a horizontal component F cos θ along the motion and a vertical component F sin θ across it; only the component along the motion changes the motion. Sign convention is chosen, not given: for vertical motion taking up as positive makes g = −9.81 m s⁻²; for slopes, taking down the slope as positive is usually simplest.

Motion in a straight line

Uniform motion means constant velocity; accelerated motion means changing velocity. The five quantities in every equation of motion are: displacement s (m), initial velocity u (m s⁻¹), final velocity v (m s⁻¹), acceleration a (m s⁻²), and time t (s). Average velocity is (u + v)/2 only when the acceleration is constant.

QuantityDefinitionUnitScalar or vector
DisplacementDistance from a start point in a stated directionmVector
VelocityRate of change of displacementm s⁻¹Vector
AccelerationRate of change of velocitym s⁻²Vector
SpeedDistance travelled per unit timem s⁻¹Scalar

The equations of motion

For motion with constant acceleration, four equations connect the five quantities. They are valid only while a is constant, and they are all vector equations, so the sign convention must be applied to u, v, a and s consistently.

v = u + a t
s = u t + 1/2 a t²
v² = u² + 2 a s
s = 1/2 (u + v) t
  • Each equation omits one quantity: pick the equation that does not contain the unknown you do not need.
  • Units must be SI before substituting: kilometres to metres, minutes to seconds, km h⁻¹ to m s⁻¹ (divide by 3.6).
  • Direction convention: write one down before touching the algebra — for example, upward positive means a falling object has a = −9.81 m s⁻² and a downward displacement is negative.

Free fall and projectile motion

Free fall is motion under gravity alone. Near the Earth's surface the acceleration is g = 9.81 m s⁻² downwards and is constant (air resistance neglected), so the equations of motion apply directly. An object thrown straight up decelerates at 9.81 m s⁻², stops instantaneously at the top, and falls back with the same acceleration; the time up equals the time down from the same height.

A projectile is any object moving under gravity alone once launched. The key insight is independence of components: the horizontal motion has zero acceleration and constant velocity, while the vertical motion has constant acceleration g. Resolve the launch velocity into u cos θ horizontally and u sin θ vertically, treat the two motions separately with the equations of motion, and combine at the end. At the highest point the vertical velocity is zero but the horizontal velocity is unchanged — the projectile is never at rest. The trajectory is a parabola.

Motion graphs

GraphGradient givesArea gives
Displacement–timeVelocityNot used
Velocity–timeAccelerationChange in displacement
Acceleration–timeNot usedChange in velocity

The equation s = ½(u + v)t is the area of a trapezium under a velocity–time graph, and v² = u² + 2as is what falls out of that geometry — which is why the equations and the graphs never disagree. Curved velocity–time graphs mean changing acceleration; the gradient at a point is found from a tangent drawn with a ruler and evaluated between two distant points on the tangent.

Non-uniform motion: drag and terminal velocity

When a real object falls, air resistance (drag) acts opposite to the motion and grows with speed. The resultant force is weight minus drag, so the acceleration is greatest at the start and falls as speed rises. When drag equals the weight the resultant force is zero and the object continues at terminal velocity. A skydiver reaches terminal velocity in free fall, opens the parachute (which raises drag enormously), and decelerates to a much lower terminal velocity before landing. The same physics sets the thinking and braking distances of a vehicle: thinking distance grows with reaction time and speed; braking distance grows with the square of the speed, because the work the brakes must do is ½mv².

Unit 3 skills: measurement, data and uncertainty

WPH13 examines the practical skills of Units 1 and 2 in writing, using unfamiliar contexts. The marks come from method and analysis, and the analysis rules are fixed.

  • Absolute uncertainty is the precision of the instrument: ±0.5 of the smallest scale division for an analogue scale, ± the smallest reading for a digital one. A length of 24.5 mm on a ruler carries ±0.5 mm.
  • Percentage uncertainty = (absolute uncertainty ÷ measured value) × 100. A small quantity measured with the same instrument carries the biggest percentage uncertainty — which is why measuring a short wire's extension with a ruler is poor method.
  • Combining uncertainties: for a sum or difference, add the absolute uncertainties; for a product or quotient (including powers), add the percentage uncertainties, and for a quantity raised to the power n, multiply its percentage uncertainty by n.
  • Repeat readings reduce random error; the mean is quoted with the uncertainty taken as half the range or the instrument precision, whichever is larger. Systematic errors (zero errors, calibration faults) are corrected at the instrument, never by averaging.
  • Graphs and error bars: plot every point with error bars in both directions where both quantities are uncertain, draw the line of best fit and also the worst acceptable steepest and shallowest lines within the error bars; the gradient's uncertainty comes from their spread.
  • Gradient and intercept: gradient = Δy/Δx taken between two distant points on the line; state it with its unit. The intercept is physical only if the theory predicts one — on a velocity–time graph the intercept is the initial velocity; on a load–extension graph a non-zero intercept suggests the spring was already stretched.
  • Calibration: a known input is applied to an instrument and its output recorded, giving a calibration graph against which unknown readings are converted.
  • Control of variables and safety: identify the independent, dependent and control variables; keep controls fixed and name them; risk assessment links each hazard to a control (falling masses — clamp the stand; long wires under tension — eye protection).

Worked example: equations of motion and uncertainty

A ball is dropped from rest and falls 1.50 m. Neglecting air resistance, take g = 9.81 m s⁻².

v² = u² + 2 a s = 0 + 2 × 9.81 × 1.50 = 29.4, so v = 5.42 m s⁻¹
time: s = u t + 1/2 a t² gives 1.50 = 4.905 t², so t = 0.553 s

Now the uncertainty: if the height is measured as 1.50 ± 0.01 m, its percentage uncertainty is 0.01/1.50 × 100 = 0.67 per cent. Since v = √(2gs), the percentage uncertainty in v is half of that in s, so v = 5.42 ± 0.04 m s⁻¹. Treating powers correctly is the difference between a right and a wrong uncertainty.

Common mistakes

  • Applying the equations of motion when the acceleration is not constant (for example once drag becomes significant).
  • Ignoring sign convention: mixing upward-positive displacements with downward-positive g gives nonsense answers.
  • Forgetting that at the top of a projectile's flight the vertical velocity is zero but the acceleration is still 9.81 m s⁻² downwards.
  • Adding percentage uncertainties for a sum instead of absolute uncertainties, or halving the percentage uncertainty of a square-rooted quantity incorrectly.
  • Joining plotted points with straight lines instead of drawing a smooth line of best fit, or ignoring error bars when asked for uncertainty.
  • Taking the gradient between two plotted points rather than two distant points on the best-fit line.
  • Confusing distance with displacement and speed with velocity in questions that mention direction.
  • Using km h⁻¹ directly in the equations: divide by 3.6 to convert to m s⁻¹ first.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (WPH11, 3 marks). A car accelerates uniformly from 5.0 m s⁻¹ to 15 m s⁻¹ in 6.0 s. Find the acceleration and the distance travelled.

Answer: a = (v − u)/t = (15 − 5.0)/6.0 = 1.7 m s⁻². s = ½(u + v)t = ½(5.0 + 15)(6.0) = 60 m.

Question 2 (WPH11, 4 marks). A stone is thrown vertically upwards at 20 m s⁻¹. Calculate the maximum height and the total time of flight. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².

Answer: At the top v = 0, so v² = u² + 2as gives 0 = 400 − 2(9.81)h, so h = 20.4 m. Time up: v = u + at gives 0 = 20 − 9.81t, so t = 2.04 s; total flight = 2 × 2.04 = 4.08 s (the motion is symmetric when the landing height equals the launch height).

Question 3 (WPH13, 4 marks). A student measures the period of a pendulum as T = 1.98 ± 0.02 s and the length as L = 98.0 ± 0.5 cm. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in g if g = 4π²L/T².

Answer: Percentage uncertainty in L = 0.5/98.0 × 100 = 0.51 per cent. In T = 0.02/1.98 × 100 = 1.01 per cent, doubled for T² = 2.02 per cent. Total for g = 0.51 + 2.02 = 2.5 per cent. The period dominates, so timing more oscillations would improve the result most.

Question 4 (WPH11, 3 marks). A projectile is launched at 30 m s⁻¹ at 30° above the horizontal. Find its initial horizontal and vertical velocity components.

Answer: Horizontal = 30 cos 30° = 26 m s⁻¹; vertical = 30 sin 30° = 15 m s⁻¹. The horizontal component stays constant (no air resistance); the vertical component decreases at 9.81 m s⁻².

Question 5 (WPH13, 3 marks). A graph of extension against load does not pass through the origin. Suggest a reason and an improvement.

Answer: The spring may already have been loaded (its own weight or an unstated mass), or the initial length was measured incorrectly. Measure the spring's original length hanging vertically with no added load, allow it to settle, and take that as the true zero extension; repeat readings at each load and plot a best-fit line.

Question 6 (WPH11, 3 marks). Explain, in terms of forces, why a skydiver reaches a terminal velocity before opening the parachute.

Answer: On leaving the aircraft, weight exceeds drag, so there is a downward resultant force and she accelerates. As speed increases, drag increases, reducing the resultant force and the acceleration. When drag equals the weight the resultant force is zero, so the acceleration is zero and she continues at constant terminal velocity.

Motion is caused by forces — the subject of Dynamics.

Equations and symbols

Four equations cover every constant-acceleration problem, and each one is missing exactly one quantity — which is how you choose between them. They are vector equations, so the sign convention written down before the substitution is part of the method, not a preliminary.

v = u + a t Key: u = initial velocity (m s⁻¹); v = final velocity (m s⁻¹); a = acceleration (m s⁻²); t = time (s). Omits s — use it when displacement is neither given nor wanted.

s = u t + 1/2 a t² Key: s = displacement (m); u = initial velocity (m s⁻¹); a = acceleration (m s⁻²); t = time (s). Omits v, and it is the one to use when the time is the unknown.

v² = u² + 2 a s Key: v, u = final and initial velocity (m s⁻¹); a = acceleration (m s⁻²); s = displacement (m). Omits t, which is why it is the fastest route whenever time is neither given nor asked for.

s = 1/2 (u + v) t Key: s = displacement (m); u, v = initial and final velocity (m s⁻¹); t = time (s). This is the area of the trapezium under a velocity–time graph, which is why the equations and the graphs always agree.

R = √(A² + B²) Key: R = the resultant of two perpendicular vectors (units of A and B); A, B = the magnitudes of the two vectors. At an angle to A the direction is θ = tan⁻¹(B/A) — magnitude alone is incomplete for a vector quantity.

1 N = 1 kg m s⁻² Key: the definition of the newton in SI base units, which is how every derived unit in mechanics resolves: check a calculation's units by substituting these and the answer's unit follows.

a = (v − u)/t = (15 − 5.0)/6.0 = 1.7 m s⁻² Key: the worked case — 15 and 5.0 m s⁻¹ are the final and initial velocities, 6.0 s the time, and the answer is positive because the car speeds up in the chosen direction. A negative result would mean deceleration, not an error.

s = ½(u + v)t = ½(5.0 + 15)(6.0) = 60 m Key: the same journey's displacement — the mean velocity 10 m s⁻¹ for 6.0 s. This form is the quickest when both velocities and the time are known.

Quantities, units and the scalar–vector split

QuantityUnitScalar or vector
DisplacementmVector
Velocitym s⁻¹Vector
Accelerationm s⁻²Vector
Speedm s⁻¹Scalar
TimesScalar

Traps specific to the equations

  • Using them while the acceleration is changing — after drag becomes significant they no longer apply.
  • Mixing sign conventions: upward positive with g = +9.81 gives nonsense.
  • Forgetting that at the top of a projectile's flight the vertical velocity is zero but the acceleration is still 9.81 m s⁻² downwards.
  • Feeding km h⁻¹ straight in; divide by 3.6 first.
  • Adding percentage uncertainties for a sum, where absolute uncertainties add.

title: Data Representation — Study Notes
content:
Data Representation

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2023–2025): binary/hex, two's complement, BCD, text/image/sound encoding, file sizes, compression.

1. Number systems

  • Binary place values 128…1; hex digits 0–9, A–F; one hex digit = one nibble (4 bits).
  • Conversions: binary ↔ decimal ↔ hex. 0101 1010 → 5A; FF = 255.
  • BCD: 4 bits per decimal digit — 0029 → 0000 0000 0010 1001. Used in clocks/calculators; easier digit conversions, more bits than pure binary.

2. Two's complement (signed)

MSB is negative: −128 64 32 16 8 4 2 1. −5 = 1111 1011. Range 8-bit: −128…+127.

Negating: invert bits, add 1. Subtraction: add the negated number — 7 − 5 = 7 + (−5) = 0000 0111 + 1111 1011 = 0000 0010.

3. Text

ASCII 7-bit (128 chars) → extended sets; Unicode for all scripts (UTF-8 variable width). Character sets map codes to glyphs; uppercase/lowercase codes differ by one bit.

4. Images and sound

  • Bitmap: pixels; colour depth = bits per pixel. File size (bits) = W × H × depth. Metadata (width, height, depth) stores dimensions.
  • Sound: sample rate (Hz), resolution (bits per sample), track duration × channels. Higher rate/depth = better fidelity, larger files.

5. Compression

  • Lossless (RLE, ZIP): exact restore — text/code must use it. RLE example: AAABBBCC → 3A3B2C; effective with runs.
  • Lossy (JPEG, MP3): discards perceptually minor data — photos/music OK, text never.

Exam tips: show full working in conversions; for size questions write the formula first with units; state the reason a compression type suits the file.

title: Plant Structure and Function, Biodiversity and Conservation — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Plant Structure and Function, Biodiversity and Conservation — Quick Revision Summary

Biology — AS Edexcel IAL, WBI12 Unit 1 Topic 4. Plant cell ultrastructure and the functions of the organelles and cell wall components (cell wall, chloroplasts, amyloplasts, vacuole and tonoplast, plasmodesmata, pits, middle lamella); starch and cellulose and why their structure fits storage and strength; how cellulose microfibril arrangement and secondary thickening give physical properties to xylem and sclerenchyma; the similarities and differences in structure, position and function of sclerenchyma fibres (support, dead, lignified), xylem vessels (support and water/mineral transport, dead, lignified, open tube) and phloem (translocation of organic solutes, living sieve tubes with companion cells, perforated walls); Core Practical 7 transverse sections; the uses of plant fibres and starch in sustainability as replacements for oil-based plastics; water and mineral ions to plants and Core Practical 8 the tensile strength of plant fibres; the conditions for bacterial growth and the aseptic practical on antimicrobial plant substances and zones of inhibition; drug testing from Withering''s digitalis to modern double-blind placebo-controlled trials; classification and the species concept and the three-domain system from molecular evidence; biodiversity and endemism and how they are threatened by human activity; biodiversity measurements (species richness, heterozygosity index = heterozygotes/total, and the index of diversity D = N(N−1)/Σ n(n−1)) and comparing habitats; and the niche and behavioural, anatomical and physiological adaptations.

  • 4.1 Plant cell ultrastructure: cell wall (cellulose microfibrils in a gel matrix — shape, support, prevents bursting when turgid), chloroplast (double membrane, chlorophyll, thylakoid/grana for light reactions, stroma for light-independent reactions), amyloplast (colourless plastid, stores starch), vacuole + tonoplast (large central vacuole with cell sap, turgor and rigidity), plasmodesmata (channels through walls connecting adjacent cells'' cytoplasm), pits (thin regions allowing water/solutes between cells), middle lamella (cements adjacent walls). Ribosomes, nucleus, nucleolus, mitochondria and golgi are present as in animal cells; higher plants lack centrioles.
  • 4.2 EM recognition: recognise plasma membrane, nucleus and nucleolus, chloroplasts (with stacked grana), mitochondria, rER with ribosomes, golgi (dictyosomes), large central vacuole with tonoplast, cell wall and middle lamella, and plasmodesmata; distinguish plant from animal cells (plant has cell wall, chloroplasts, large central vacuole, plasmodesmata, generally no centrioles).
  • 4.3 Starch and cellulose: starch = alpha-glucose polymer (amylose helical, amylopectin branched — compact, insoluble, osmotically inert, good for storage); cellulose = beta-glucose polymer (straight chains, hydrogen bonds between chains make strong microfibrils — structural); both from glucose but different bonds and shape give different roles.
  • 4.4 Microfibrils and secondary thickening: in growing cells microfibrils laid down at right angles to growth direction so the cell expands in length; when growth stops, secondary thickening deposits more cellulose and (in some cells) lignin on the inside, making the wall rigid and waterproof; in sclerenchyma fibres the walls are heavily lignified and the cells die at maturity — strong, flexible, tough — for support and human use; in xylem vessels the walls are lignified with rings, spirals or nets, and the cells are dead with end walls broken down — a continuous tube that resists collapse under transpiration tension.
  • 4.5 Fibres, xylem and phloem: sclerenchyma fibres — long, narrow, thick lignified walls, small lumen, dead, bundles — support and human use; xylem vessels — long open lignified tubes, dead, pits in walls — water and mineral transport plus support; phloem — living sieve tube elements end to end with sieve plates (perforated end walls), little cytoplasm, no nucleus at maturity, each with a companion cell connected by plasmodesmata that keeps it alive and supplies ATP — translocation of sucrose in solution from source (leaves/storage) to sink (growing points, roots, fruits).
  • 4.6 Core Practical 7: cut a thin transverse section with a razor blade, float on water, stain (toluidine blue or iodine) to distinguish lignified xylem, sclerenchyma and phloem, draw a plan diagram of the whole section showing tissue arrangement (not cells), label, title and magnification; then observe and label the cells — thick lignified xylem and sclerenchyma walls, sieve plates and companion cells of phloem, thin-walled cortex and pith cells.
  • 4.7 Plant fibres and starch for sustainability: plant fibres (from sclerenchyma or phloem) are strong, renewable, biodegradable — used in textiles, paper, building materials, composites, replacing oil-based plastics; starch can be processed into bioplastics for packaging, plates and disposable items — renewable and biodegradable, but land, water, energy and food competition must be weighed.
  • 4.8 Water and ions to plants: water for photosynthesis (reactant, medium), transport (solvent), support (turgor) and cooling (transpiration) — enters roots by osmosis, moves up the xylem; nitrate (NO₃⁻) for amino acids, proteins, DNA, chlorophyll — deficiency causes stunted growth and chlorosis of older leaves; calcium for middle lamella and membranes — deficiency gives stunted growth and necrosis of growing points and young leaves; magnesium for chlorophyll — deficiency causes chlorosis of older leaves; Core Practical: grow plants in complete solution and in solutions missing one ion, observe and measure effects over weeks.
  • 4.9 Core Practical 8: tensile strength of a plant fibre — clamp one end, hang weights from the other, add until it breaks, record the weight (force = mass × g) at breaking; repeat for several fibres; compare fibres from different plants or parts; safety: sharp blades, falling weights.
  • 4.10 Bacterial growth conditions: nutrients (carbon, nitrogen, minerals, and for some organic factors), water, suitable temperature (many pathogenic bacteria ~37 °C, many environmental ~25 °C, but ranges vary), oxygen (aerobic, anaerobic, or facultative), suitable pH, time to multiply; cultured in nutrient broth or on agar, at a set temperature, with or without oxygen, in sterile conditions; aseptic technique: sterilise equipment (flame/autoclave), work near a flame for upward air current, cover plates, dispose of cultures by sterilising first.
  • 4.11 Antimicrobial plant substances: substances from plants (e.g. garlic) can inhibit bacteria or fungi; other plants yield useful compounds (aspirin from willow bark, morphine from poppies); modern drugs include many from plants; Core Practical: agar plates, sterile discs or paper discs impregnated with different plant extracts, incubate, measure the zone of inhibition (clear diameter where bacteria did not grow), compare extracts and concentrations; aseptic technique: sterilise discs and loops, work near a flame, spread bacteria in a controlled way, seal plates with tape (not all the way — keep them aerated), incubate at a safe temperature.

Worked example

Index of diversity: in habitat A species counts are 12, 8, 4 (N = 24). Σn(n−1) = (12×11) + (8×7) + (4×3) = 132 + 56 + 12 = 200; N(N−1) = 24×23 = 552; D = 552/200 = 2.76. In habitat B species counts are 20, 1, 1, 1, 1 (N = 24). Σn(n−1) = (20×19) + 4×(1×0) = 380 + 0 = 380; N(N−1) = 552; D = 552/380 = 1.45. So habitat A is more diverse than habitat B — even though both have four species and the same total — because in B one species dominates and the others are rare.

Key points to remember

The structure that makes a plant cell rigid is the cell wall, the large central vacuole and turgor, and the arrangement of cellulose microfibrils; the organelle with stacked membranes for photosynthesis is the chloroplast (grana in the thylakoids, stroma around them); starch stores glucose compactly and insoluble so no osmotic effect; cellulose''s straight beta-glucose chains form hydrogen-bonded microfibrils, strong and supportive; secondary thickening and lignification stiffen walls for support and for the xylem to resist tension; xylem transports water and minerals and supports, phloem translocates sucrose from source to sink; water is essential for photosynthesis, transport, support (turgor) and cooling; nitrate, calcium and magnesium each have a specific role and deficiency gives characteristic symptoms; antibiotic plant substances and the aseptic practical involve zones of inhibition; drug testing progressed from uncontrolled historic trials to double-blind, placebo-controlled, phased, large multi-centre trials; classification is based on relationships using phenotypic and (increasingly) genotypic data, the species concept is a group that can interbreed and produce fertile offspring, and the three-domain system (Archaea, Bacteria, Eukarya) came from molecular evidence (ribosomal RNA); biodiversity is the variety of life, endemism is being restricted to one place, human activity threatens it; biodiversity is measured by species richness, heterozygosity (heterozygotes/total) and the index of diversity D = N(N−1)/Σ n(n−1); the niche is the organism''s role and its adaptations can be behavioural, anatomical or physiological.

Key points to remember

In the heterozygosity index, if a population of 20 individuals at a locus has 8 heterozygotes, H = 8/20 = 0.40, so the higher the number the greater the genetic diversity; in the index of diversity D = N(N−1)/Σ n(n−1), the larger D the more diverse, and the comparison between habitats means you calculate D for each and compare the values, explaining which is more diverse and what that suggests. Distinguish species richness (the number of species) from the index of diversity (which also reflects how even the individuals are among species). In drug testing, the placebo controls for the placebo effect, double-blind avoids bias from patient and clinician expectations, and the phases test safety (Phase 1), efficacy and side effects (Phase 2), and the drug against current treatment or placebo in a large group (Phase 3). The bacteriophage does not belong here — the antimicrobials come from plants, not from viruses; keep plant antimicrobial substances separate from the unrelated concept. The distinction between the habitat (the place) and the niche (the role and resources) is often asked — an organism''s niche is more than where it lives.

How to use this

Read the summary list, then open the full revision notes for any point that feels weak, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself. Revise next by: identifying plant cell ultrastructure and organelles in an EM image and stating each organelle''s function; drawing starch and cellulose and explaining the structure–function link; comparing sclerenchyma fibres, xylem vessels and phloem in a table (structure, position, function); carrying out the transverse section and tensile strength practicals and explaining the variables and safety; describing the conditions for bacterial growth and the aseptic practical; describing the development of drug testing from Withering''s digitalis to modern trials and evaluating the designs; defining classification and the species concept, describing the three-domain system and the molecular evidence for it; defining biodiversity and endemism and listing the threats; carrying out the species richness and heterozygosity and index of diversity calculations including the worked comparison between habitats; and defining niche and giving behavioural, anatomical and physiological adaptations.

title: Cambridge IGCSE First Language English: Analysing Language Choices
content:
Cambridge IGCSE First Language English: Analysing Language Choices

Writer's effect — the analysis of how a writer uses language to create impact — is the skill that separates a competent reader from a top-band one in Cambridge IGCSE First Language English (0500). The question asks you to choose and explain the language that creates a particular effect, and the mark scheme rewards the link from micro-feature to macro-impact: the exact word, the exact method, the exact effect on the reader. This note builds the analytical system from zero: the vocabulary of literary method, the step-by-step deconstruction of the prompt, the effect vocabulary bank, model answers broken down line by line, and the errors that turn analysis into feature-spotting.

The micro-to-macro principle

Writers create effects with tiny tools: a verb choice, a repeated sound, a sentence that stops short. Analysis means moving from the smallest unit (the word) to the largest (the reader's response, the writer's purpose). The chain every top-band answer follows is:

QUOTATION → METHOD → EFFECT ON THE READER → PURPOSE IN CONTEXT
"clawed"   → verb    → makes the wind feel violent and alive → shows
              choice                   the night as an attack

Candidates who stop at METHOD ("the writer uses a metaphor") score nothing for effect; candidates who leap to PURPOSE without quoting score nothing for evidence. The four-beat chain is the answer structure — practise it until it is automatic.

The method vocabulary: what to look for

CategoryFeaturesWhat it tends to do
Diction (word choice)strong verbs, evaluative adjectives, connotation, register shiftsshapes judgement and sympathy
Figurative languagesimile, metaphor, personification, hyperbole, symbolcreates imagery, comparison, emotional colour
Sensory imagerysight, sound, smell, taste, touchimmerses the reader in a place or moment
Sound devicesalliteration, assonance, onomatopoeia, sibilanceadds mood and rhythm; softens or sharpens tone
Sentence structureshort sentences, long sentences, fragments, listing, repetition, questionscontrols pace, tension and emphasis
Perspective and detailwhat is shown or withheld, focalisation, contrast, juxtapositiondirects sympathy and reveals theme

Diction: reading connotation

Words carry two meanings: the dictionary meaning (denotation) and the associations (connotation). Analysis lives in connotation. Compare: the house stood on the hill / the house perched on the hill / the house crouched on the hill. Perched suggests lightness and elevation; crouched suggests menace, weight, waiting. When you analyse diction, name the connotation direction: what does this word suggest that a neutral word would not?

  • Verbs are the richest targets: in "the river snaked through the valley", snaked suggests sinuous movement and a faint threat — analyse the verb before the adjectives.
  • Evaluative adjectives: "the tiny, defiant crowd" already tells the reader how to feel; identify the judgement embedded in the adjective.
  • Register and tone shifts: a formal description suddenly interrupted by a slang word (or the reverse) creates irony or intimacy.

Figurative language: naming the effect precisely

DeviceDefinitionEffect vocabulary
Similecomparison using like or ascompares X to Y, making it vivid / suggesting it is fragile / threatening
MetaphorX is described as Ytransforms X, implying it shares Y's qualities
Personificationhuman qualities given to a thingbrings X alive / makes nature feel hostile or companionable
Hyperboledeliberate exaggerationintensifies emotion / adds humour / shows obsession
Symbolan object that stands for an ideacompresses the theme into an image the reader carries

The analysis must name what the figure compares or implies and what that does to the reader's feeling. "The sky was a bruise" — metaphor: the sky is described as damaged flesh, so the scene feels injured and threatening, suggesting violence has already happened.

Sentence structure and sound as effects

  • Short sentences: shock, finality, tension. "Then the door opened." A short sentence after long ones lands like a punch.
  • Long sentences: accumulation, calm, overload, dreaminess. Lists and polysyndeton (and ... and ... and ...) create breathlessness or abundance.
  • Fragments: a sentence without a verb or subject ("Silence. Then nothing.") mimics broken thought or stunned reaction.
  • Repetition and rule of three: "he ran and ran and ran" or a tricolon builds emphasis and rhythm.
  • Alliteration and sibilance: repeated sounds create mood — sibilance (s, sh sounds) is soft and secretive or sinister; hard consonants (k, t, g) are aggressive and abrupt.
  • Onomatopoeia: words that sound like their meaning (crash, murmur, hissed) pull the reader's ear into the scene.

Deconstructing the prompt: the five-step routine

  1. Underline the effect words in the question — "How does the writer create the atmosphere of tension in this extract?" Your whole answer serves tension; a brilliant point about humour is off-target.
  2. Skim for the effect, not the features: find the lines where the named effect is strongest (usually the turn in the passage).
  3. Select two to three genuinely strong features — one diction point, one figurative or structural point is usually enough for a full-mark answer.
  4. Build the four-beat chain for each — quotation, method, effect on the reader, purpose in context.
  5. Write in a sequence: open with a sentence that answers the question directly ("The writer creates tension through violent diction and oppressive imagery"), develop each feature as a mini-paragraph, and keep the question's effect word in every other sentence as your anchor.

The effect vocabulary bank

Weak answers say "it makes it interesting". Strong answers have a bank of precise effect phrases. Build yours from this list and use each one only when accurate: creates an atmosphere of ...; conveys a sense of ...; makes the reader feel ...; suggests that ...; implies ...; emphasises ...; highlights ...; draws attention to ...; reinforces the idea that ...; leaves the reader expecting ...; unsettles the reader; evokes sympathy for ...; conveys the character's ...; establishes ...; contrasts with ...; signals a shift from ... to ...

Model answer with top-band breakdown

Extract: "The market was a living thing: breathing steam, groaning trolleys, a heartbeat of a thousand footsteps. I stood very still, and it swallowed me whole."

Model answer: "The writer creates an overwhelming, almost frightening sense of the market's scale through personification and metaphor. The market is described as a living thing, breathing steam and groaning trolleys, so the crowd seems to have one body and one will — the reader feels the place as an organism rather than a location. The metaphor continues with the heartbeat of a thousand footsteps, turning ordinary noise into something alive and relentless, which intensifies the speaker's smallness. That smallness is completed by the final metaphor: the market swallowed me whole. The verb swallowed suggests being consumed without trace, so the reader feels the speaker's helplessness and the city's indifference to the individual."

Breakdown of why it hits the top band: it opens by naming the effect (overwhelming, frightening sense of scale) and the methods; each quotation is brief and exact (living thing, swallowed me whole); each method is named (personification, metaphor, verb choice); every effect is reader-directed (the reader feels ...; intensifies ...; suggests being consumed); and the final clause links to purpose in context (the city's indifference). There is no feature-spotting and no padding.

Worked example: deconstructing a prompt

Prompt: "How does the writer create sympathy for the boy in lines 12-20?"
Step 1: effect anchor = sympathy (not fear, not admiration)
Step 2: find the lines where the boy is shown as vulnerable
Step 3: select features:
        (a) diction: "threadbare", "counted his coins twice"
        (b) contrast: the crowd's indifference against his hope
Step 4: build chains:
        (a) threadbare → adjective → clothes worn thin → poverty visible
            counted his coins twice → verb phrase → care and anxiety
            → the reader sees a child managing scarcity alone
        (b) contrast → juxtaposition of the bustling crowd and the boy
            alone → heightens isolation → the reader's sympathy
Step 5: write: open with the answer, develop (a) then (b), keep
        "sympathy" in the anchor sentence and the final line.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Diction) "The old man shuffled to the window." What does shuffled suggest? Answer: The verb suggests slow, dragging, effortful movement — the man is aged or exhausted, so the reader feels his frailty and perhaps pity.
  2. (Simile) "The silence hung over them like a held breath." Explain the effect. Answer: The simile compares the silence to a held breath, so the quiet feels temporary and full of suspense — the reader expects something to happen or break.
  3. (Sentence structure) "He ran. The corridor stretched and stretched. He ran." How does the structure create tension? Answer: The short, repeated sentences create urgency and breathlessness, while the repetition of stretched mimics the corridor's endlessness, making the reader feel the pursuit dragging on.
  4. (Personification) "The house watched them leave." What is the effect? Answer: Giving the house the human action of watching makes it seem alive and perhaps resentful, so the departure feels observed and uneasy rather than free.
  5. (Combined) "The factory exhaled grey smoke that smothered the gardens." Identify two methods and their effects. Answer: Personification (exhaled) makes the factory seem like a living, breathing force; the metaphor smothered presents the smoke as something that kills life, so the reader feels the pollution as an active threat to the community's homes.
  6. (Purpose in context) Why might a writer describe a character's hands as "bird-bones"? Answer: The metaphor compares the hands to fragile bird bones, suggesting thinness and delicacy, which builds a picture of vulnerability — useful if the writer wants the reader to fear for the character's safety.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Feature-spotting: "There is alliteration and metaphor" with no effect commentary is worth nothing. The method name is the start of the sentence, not the answer.
  • "Makes it interesting": the empty effect phrase. Every effect must be specific — interesting to whom, creating what feeling, suggesting what about the character or theme?
  • Long quotations: quote only the words you analyse (two to six words). A lifted sentence without commentary reads as copying.
  • Analysing the wrong thing: the question's effect word is the anchor. An answer about atmosphere when the question asked about sympathy is off-target however good the analysis.
  • Choosing weak features: not every adjective is worth analysis. Pick features that clearly serve the named effect; one deep point beats three shallow ones.
  • Missing the structure level: most candidates analyse words only. A comment on sentence length, repetition or word order after a diction point adds a whole dimension the mark scheme values.
  • No link to context: the four-beat chain ends at purpose — why the writer wants the reader to feel this here. That final clause is the difference between a good and a top answer.
  • Listing without sequencing: a bulleted list of features cannot show the cumulative effect. Write developed mini-paragraphs and order them from the strongest point to the supporting one.

title: Number — Fractions, Decimals and Percentages — Study Notes
content:
Number — Fractions, Decimals and Percentages

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): conversions between fractions, decimals and percentages; percentage change; reverse percentages; compound change.

1. Conversions

Fraction → decimal by division; decimal → percentage ×100. Recurring decimals: let x = 0.7̄, then 10x − x = 7 ⇒ x = 7/9.

Compare fractions by common denominator or by converting to decimals.

2. Operating on fractions

  • Add/subtract: common denominator. 2/3 + 1/4 = 8/12 + 3/12 = 11/12.
  • Multiply: top×top, bottom×bottom. Divide: flip and multiply — 2/3 ÷ 4/5 = 2/3 × 5/4 = 5/6.
  • Of: 3/5 of 45 = 27.

3. Percentage change

change ÷ original × 100. Increase $80 by 15%: 80 × 1.15 = $92.

4. Reverse percentages

Original = new ÷ multiplier. "After a 20% increase a coat is $72" → 72 ÷ 1.2 = $60. "After 12% discount a phone is $440" → 440 ÷ 0.88 = $500.

5. Compound change

Multiplierⁿ. Simple interest I = Prt/100 vs compound P(1 + r/100)ⁿ.

Example: $800 at 3% for 4 years → 800 × 1.03⁴ = $900.41. Successive +10% then −10% ⇒ ×0.99 (net 1% decrease).

Exam tips: identify "increase TO" vs "increase BY"; for reverse questions divide, never subtract the percentage; quote money to 2 d.p.

title: AS Level Chemistry: Bonding and Structure
content:
Bonding and Structure

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH11, Topic 3. Every statement 3.1 to 3.22 is covered below, with its code in the heading so you can check your own gaps against the specification. The big idea: the type of bonding and the shape of a molecule explain almost every physical property a question can ask about, including melting point, conductivity, solubility and polarity.

3.1 to 3.2: Evidence for ions, and how they form

  • Evidence for ions: ionic compounds conduct electricity only when molten or dissolved, because the ions are then free to move. In electrolysis, a coloured ion such as manganate(VII), MnO₄⁻, migrates to the positive electrode (the anode), which is direct evidence that it carries a negative charge.
  • Electron density maps for ionic compounds show near-spherical regions of electron density around each ion, with a clear drop in density between them.
  • Formation by loss or gain of electrons: sodium loses one electron to form Na⁺ (2,8,1 becomes 2,8), while chlorine gains one to form Cl⁻ (2,8,7 becomes 2,8,8). A metal loses electrons to form a positive ion; a non-metal gains electrons to form a negative ion.

3.3: Dot-and-cross diagrams for ions

  • Show the outer electrons of each atom as dots or crosses. For a cation such as Mg²⁺, the outer shell is empty, so the symbol is written with square brackets and the charge: [Mg]²⁺.
  • For an anion such as O²⁻, the transferred electrons are added to the outer shell, which then holds eight electrons: [O]²⁻ with eight dots and crosses inside the brackets.
  • Always put the charge outside the brackets, and check that the total number of electrons transferred matches the charges.

3.4 to 3.5: Giant ionic lattices and the ionic bond

  • An ionic crystal is a giant lattice of alternating positive and negative ions, repeating in three dimensions. There are no discrete molecules, so the formula, such as NaCl, is only the simplest ratio of ions. In sodium chloride each Na⁺ is surrounded by six Cl⁻ ions and each Cl⁻ by six Na⁺ ions (6:6 coordination).
  • An ionic bond is the strong net electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions. "Net" matters: the attraction between a cation and an anion is partly cancelled by repulsion between like ions, but the attraction wins at the equilibrium distance.

3.6: Effect of ionic radius and ionic charge on bond strength

  • The electrostatic attraction grows with the charge on the ions and falls as the ions get larger, because the centres of charge are further apart.
  • Compare MgO (melting point about 2850 °C) with NaCl (about 800 °C). Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ carry double charges and are small, so their attraction is much stronger than that between the singly charged, larger Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions.

3.7: Trends in ionic radius

  • Down a group, ionic radius increases, because each ion has an additional electron shell. Li⁺ is smaller than Na⁺, which is smaller than K⁺.
  • Across a set of isoelectronic ions, all the species have the same number of electrons (ten, in the series N³⁻, O²⁻, F⁻, Na⁺, Mg²⁺, Al³⁺). The nuclear charge rises from 7 to 13 across the series, so the outer electrons are pulled in more strongly and the radius falls. N³⁻ is the largest and Al³⁺ the smallest.

3.8 to 3.9: Polarisation of ions

  • Polarisation is the distortion of the electron cloud of an anion by a nearby cation. The cation pulls the anion's electron density towards itself, so the bonding stops being purely ionic and gains covalent character.
  • The polarising power of a cation is greatest when it is small and highly charged. Al³⁺ > Mg²⁺ > Na⁺.
  • The polarisability of an anion is greatest when it is large and highly charged, because its outer electrons are held loosely. I⁻ is more polarisable than Br⁻, which is more polarisable than Cl⁻, which is more polarisable than F⁻.
  • Example: aluminium chloride has a low melting point and sublimes, far below what a purely ionic lattice would need. The small, highly charged Al³⁺ polarises the chloride ions strongly, so the bonding is largely covalent.

3.10: Covalent bonding and the evidence for it

  • A covalent bond is the strong electrostatic attraction between two nuclei (both positive) and the shared pair of electrons between them.
  • Evidence: giant atomic structures such as diamond and silicon(IV) oxide have very high melting points, which only strong covalent bonds can explain. Electron density maps for simple molecules such as hydrogen show a build-up of electron density between the two nuclei.

3.11: Dot-and-cross diagrams for covalent substances

  • Multiple bonds: in carbon dioxide, O=C=O, each double bond is two shared pairs. In nitrogen, N≡N, there are three shared pairs.
  • Dative (coordinate) bonds: both electrons in the shared pair come from one atom, the donor, which has a lone pair. The arrow points from donor to acceptor. In the ammonium ion, NH₄⁺, the nitrogen in NH₃ donates its lone pair to H⁺.
  • Aluminium chloride dimer, Al₂Cl₆: each aluminium has four chlorines. Two of the chlorines bridge the two aluminium atoms, and each bridging chlorine forms a dative bond from a chlorine lone pair into the empty orbital of the other aluminium.

3.12: Giant carbon structures: diamond, graphite and graphene

  • Diamond: each carbon forms four single covalent bonds in a tetrahedral giant lattice. It is very hard, has a very high melting point and does not conduct, because there are no free electrons. It is used in cutting and drilling tools.
  • Graphite: each carbon forms three bonds in flat hexagonal sheets. The fourth outer electron on each carbon is delocalised, so graphite conducts along the sheets. The sheets are held by weak forces and slide over each other, so graphite is soft and is used as a lubricant and as electrodes.
  • Graphene: a single sheet of graphite, one atom thick. It is very strong, conducts well and is light and flexible. Applications include electronics, sensors and composite materials.

3.13 to 3.14: Electronegativity and the bonding continuum

  • Electronegativity is the power of an atom to attract the bonding pair of electrons in a covalent bond. Fluorine is the most electronegative element (4.0 on the Pauling scale).
  • The bonding continuum: the bigger the electronegativity difference between two atoms, the more polar the bond. A very small difference gives a non-polar covalent bond, a moderate difference gives a polar covalent bond (as in HCl), and a very large difference gives essentially ionic bonding (as in NaCl). Ionic and covalent bonding are the two ends of this continuum, not separate categories.

3.15: Polar bonds and polar molecules

  • A polar bond has a permanent dipole. A molecule is polar only if its bond dipoles do not cancel, so polar bonds do not automatically make a polar molecule.
  • Carbon tetrachloride, CCl₄: the C–Cl bonds are polar, but the tetrahedral arrangement cancels them, so the molecule is non-polar.
  • Water, H₂O, is bent, so its dipoles add up and the molecule is polar. Carbon dioxide is linear, so its two C=O dipoles cancel and it is non-polar.

3.16 to 3.19: Electron-pair repulsion and molecular shapes

  • Electron-pair repulsion theory: bonding pairs and lone pairs around a central atom repel each other and arrange themselves to be as far apart as possible.
  • Lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs, so lone pairs compress bond angles. The order of repulsion is lone pair to lone pair, then lone pair to bonding pair, then bonding pair to bonding pair.
  • 3.17, bond length and bond angle: bond length is the distance between the nuclei of two bonded atoms. Bond angle is the angle between two bonds at the central atom. Triple bonds are shorter than double bonds, which are shorter than single bonds (C≡C shorter than C=C shorter than C–C).

3.18, the shapes and bond angles of the named species:

SpeciesElectron pairs on central atomShapeBond angle
BeCl₂2 bondingLinear180°
BCl₃3 bondingTrigonal planar120°
CH₄4 bondingTetrahedral109.5°
NH₃3 bonding, 1 loneTrigonal pyramidalabout 107°
NH₄⁺4 bondingTetrahedral109.5°
H₂O2 bonding, 2 loneBentabout 104.5°
CO₂2 bonding (double bonds)Linear180°
PCl₅ (gas)5 bondingTrigonal bipyramidal90° and 120°
SF₆6 bondingOctahedral90°
C₂H₄3 regions around each carbonPlanar around each carbonabout 120°

Applying the same rules to analogous species (3.19): SiH₄ is tetrahedral (109.5°), BF₃ is trigonal planar (120°), PH₃ is pyramidal (about 93°), H₂S is bent (about 92°), XeF₄ is square planar (90°, with two lone pairs), and ClF₃ is T-shaped. Count the electron pairs first, then decide how many are lone pairs.

3.20 to 3.22: Metallic bonding and the properties of metals

  • A metal is a giant lattice of positive metal ions in a sea of delocalised electrons, the outer electrons that are free to move through the whole structure.
  • 3.21, metallic bonding is the strong electrostatic attraction between the metal cations and the delocalised electrons. It is not a bond between two particular atoms.
  • Electrical conduction: the delocalised electrons carry charge through the metal when a voltage is applied.
  • High melting temperature: the attraction is strong and is non-directional, so a lot of energy is needed to overcome it. Magnesium melts at about 650 °C, far above sodium at about 98 °C, because Mg²⁺ carries a double charge and provides two delocalised electrons per atom.
  • Malleability: the layers of ions can slide over each other, and the delocalised electrons keep the ions attracted to each other as they move, so the metal does not shatter.

A* extension: worked reasoning for the hardest bonding questions

  • Bond angles, 3.18 applied: CH₄ is 109.5°, NH₃ about 107°, and H₂O about 104.5°. Each lone pair pushes the bonding pairs closer together, because lone pair to bonding pair repulsion is stronger than bonding pair to bonding pair. So the angle falls by roughly 2.5° per lone pair. An A* answer states the reason in these terms, not just the number.
  • Polarity, 3.15 applied: CH₃Cl is polar, because the C–Cl dipole is not cancelled by the C–H bonds, which point in roughly symmetrical directions but carry much smaller dipoles. CCl₄ is non-polar, because four identical C–Cl dipoles point to the corners of a tetrahedron and cancel exactly. Always say which dipoles cancel and why.
  • Electronegativity and bonding continuum, 3.14 applied: aluminium chloride has an electronegativity difference of about 1.5 between Al and Cl. That is not large enough to make it purely ionic, so it is a polar covalent bond, which is consistent with its low melting point and the polarisation argument in 3.8 to 3.9.
  • Lattice and bond strength, 3.6 applied: when asked to compare two ionic compounds, name both the charge and the radius, and say which one dominates. Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ beat Na⁺ and Cl⁻ on both counts, so MgO has the much higher melting point.
  • Mark-scheme phrasing for metallic bonding (3.21): "giant lattice of positive ions", "sea of delocalised electrons", "strong electrostatic attraction between the ions and the delocalised electrons". Each phrase earns its own mark, so use all three.
  • Graphite versus graphene, 3.12 applied: an electrode question expects you to name the delocalised electron, and a lubricant question expects you to name the weak forces between layers. Give both mechanisms when the question says "explain".

Common errors that lose marks

  • Saying covalent or metallic bonds are "between molecules" (they are within the structure; the forces between molecules are intermolecular forces).
  • Calling a polar bond a polar molecule. Always check the shape before you decide the molecule's polarity.
  • Saying ions "move" in solid ionic compounds. They vibrate in place; only molten or dissolved compounds conduct through ion movement.

Exam-style questions

  1. Explain why magnesium oxide has a much higher melting temperature than sodium chloride. Answer: both are giant ionic lattices, but the ions in MgO carry 2+ and 2− charges compared with 1+ and 1− in NaCl, and the Mg2+ and O2− ions are smaller. The electrostatic attraction between the ions is therefore much stronger, so far more energy is needed to break the lattice apart.
  2. Explain why aluminium chloride sublimes at a low temperature while sodium chloride melts at 801 °C. Answer: the Al3+ ion is small and highly charged, so it polarises the Cl− ion strongly. The electron cloud of the chloride is distorted towards the aluminium, giving the Al–Cl bond covalent character and producing discrete Al2Cl6 molecules held by weak London forces. The sodium ion is larger and less charged, so NaCl remains a giant ionic lattice.
  3. Predict the shape and bond angle of SF6 and explain your reasoning. Answer: octahedral, 90°. The sulfur atom has six bonding pairs and no lone pairs, so the six electron pairs repel equally and arrange themselves as far apart as possible.
  4. Carbon dioxide and water both contain polar bonds, yet carbon dioxide is non-polar. Explain. Answer: CO2 is linear and symmetrical, so the two C=O dipoles are equal and opposite and cancel. Water is bent, with two O–H dipoles that do not cancel, so the molecule has a net dipole and is polar.
  5. Explain why graphite conducts electricity but diamond does not. Answer: in graphite each carbon is bonded to three others, leaving one delocalised electron per atom that is free to move along the layers. In diamond every carbon has four covalent bonds, so all the valence electrons are localised in sigma bonds and there are no mobile charge carriers.

title: IGCSE Chemistry: The Periodic Table
content:
IGCSE Chemistry: The Periodic Table

Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry 0620 (2026–2028), Extended route, Topic 8 The Periodic Table: statement 8.1 Arrangement of elements, 8.2 Group I properties, 8.3 Group VII properties, 8.4 Transition elements, and 8.5 Noble gases. The Periodic Table is chemistry's master chart — position predicts behaviour — and this note derives every trend from electron structure rather than asking you to memorise it. Each group's properties are traced down the group with the particle-level reason, because Paper 4 asks "explain the trend", never "state the trend".

Arrangement: periods, groups and the prediction power

Elements are arranged in order of increasing proton number in rows (periods) and columns (groups). Two structural facts run everything: elements in the same group have the same number of outer-shell electrons (hence similar chemistry), and the period number equals the number of occupied shells. Across a period, the character changes from metallic (left) to non-metallic (right); group number gives the ion charge (Group I → +1, Group VII → −1 for monatomic ions).

Group I: the alkali metals

Trend down Group IPatternWhy (electron structure)
ReactivityIncreases (Li < Na < K)The outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded, so it is lost more easily
Melting/boiling pointDecreasesThe metallic bond weakens as ions get larger and the delocalised electrons are further from the nuclei
DensityIncreases (they float or sink accordingly)Mass grows faster than atomic radius
Reactions of Group I with water - the pattern, worked:

  2Li + 2H₂O → 2LiOH + H₂       lithium: steady fizz, floats
  2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂       sodium: vigorous, melts into a ball
  2K  + 2H₂O → 2KOH  + H₂       potassium: lilac flame, skitters

  The products are the group's hydroxide (an alkali, so the name) and
  hydrogen. Down the group the fizzing gets more vigorous - the outer
  electron is lost more easily, so the reaction with water speeds up.

  Burning in oxygen: lithium oxide Li₂O, sodium peroxide Na₂O₂,
  potassium superoxide KO₂ - the pattern of increasing reactivity also
  shows in the oxide formed.

Group VII: the halogens

Trend down Group VIIPatternWhy
ReactivityDecreases (F > Cl > Br > I)The outer shell is further from the nucleus, so an incoming electron is attracted less strongly
ColourDarkens: pale yellow-green gas → red-brown liquid → black solidMolecular size and polarisability increase
Boiling pointIncreasesLarger molecules → stronger intermolecular forces → more energy needed
Displacement reactions - the reactivity rule, worked:

  A more reactive halogen DISPLACES a less reactive halide from solution.

  Cl₂(aq) + 2KBr(aq) → 2KCl(aq) + Br₂(aq)
    chlorine displaces bromine: the solution turns orange-brown.
  Cl₂(aq) + 2KI(aq)  → 2KCl(aq) + I₂(aq)
    iodine formed: with hexane/hexane layer it shows violet.
  Br₂(aq) + 2KI(aq)  → 2KBr(aq) + I₂(aq)
  Br₂(aq) + 2KCl(aq) → no reaction (bromine is less reactive than chlorine)

  Rule: the higher element in the group displaces the lower one's ions.
  Exam answers quote the observation, not just the equation - name the
  colour change.

Group VIII: the noble gases

The noble gases (He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn) are monatomic gases with full outer shells — hence almost completely unreactive. Their existence and inertness are the proof that a full outer shell confers stability — the electron-configuration explanation that underpins all of bonding.

Transition elements

  • Physical: high density, high melting point, strong metallic bonding (partly from their delocalised electrons).
  • Chemical: form coloured compounds (Cu²⁺ blue, Fe²⁺ pale green, Fe³⁺ yellow), show variable oxidation numbers (iron(II) and iron(III)), and act as catalysts (iron in the Haber process, V₂O₅ in the Contact process, nickel in hydrogenation).
Variable oxidation numbers - worked:

  Iron(II) chloride FeCl₂  → iron is +2
  Iron(III) chloride FeCl₃ → iron is +3
  Copper(II) sulfate CuSO₄ → +2 ; copper(I) oxide Cu₂O → +1

  Roman numeral in the NAME = oxidation number. The same element in two
  oxidation states means two families of compounds - a transition-metal
  signature. Colour changes in redox titrations (e.g. MnO₄⁻ purple to
  Mn²⁺ colourless) exploit these states.

The electron-configuration link is worth stating as a rule of its own, because nearly every explanation in this topic reduces to it. The number of outer electrons equals the group number (Group II elements have two outer electrons and form 2+ ions), and the number of occupied shells equals the period number. Similarity within a group is not a coincidence of mass — it is a consequence of identical outer-shell electron arrangements, which is why lithium and potassium, thousands of mass units apart in behaviour terms, give hydroxides of the same formula type and both release hydrogen from water. Across a period, proton number rises while shells stay the same, so the nucleus pulls electrons in more tightly, the atom shrinks, and metallic character gives way to non-metallic — which is why Period 3 runs from sodium's vigorous water chemistry to chlorine's and argon's total inertness.

Worked example: predicting from position

Question: predict the properties of astatine (At, below iodine in Group VII).

  From the trends down the group:
  - state: solid at room temperature (darker than iodine - black),
  - melting point: higher than iodine's,
  - reactivity: LOWER than iodine (outer electron furthest from nucleus),
  - displacement: iodine would displace astatide from solution, and At
    would NOT displace Cl/Br/I.
  - reaction with hydrogen: At₂ + H₂ → 2HAt, less readily than iodine's.

Every prediction cites the trend AND the electron-structure reason - that
pair is the mark scheme.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Explaining Group I reactivity with "gets bigger" alone — the mark is outer electron distance/shielding and ease of loss.
  • Confusing Group I and Group VII trends: Group I reactivity increases down; Group VII decreases — keep the electron argument (lose vs gain) straight.
  • Forgetting the colour observations in displacement answers — the visible change is half the marks.
  • Saying noble gases "have full outer shells so they are stable" without connecting to why that stops bonding.
  • Listing transition-metal properties without examples (coloured compounds: name the ion and its colour).
  • Confusing period number (shells) with group number (outer electrons).
  • Claiming Group I metals float or sink universally — density increases down the group, and lithium floats while others sink in water/oil.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Explain why the reactivity of Group I metals increases down the group.

Answer: Each element down the group has one more occupied shell, so the outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded by inner shells. The electrostatic attraction holding the outer electron weakens, so it is lost more readily in reactions — the metal is more reactive.

Question 2 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Explain why the reactivity of Group VII elements decreases down the group.

Answer: Halogens react by gaining an electron into the outer shell. Down the group the outer shell is further from the nucleus and more shielded, so the attraction for an incoming electron is weaker and it is gained less readily — reactivity falls.

Question 3 (Paper 4, 3 marks). Describe what happens when chlorine is added to potassium iodide solution and name the reaction type.

Answer: The solution turns brown as iodine is displaced: Cl₂ + 2KI → 2KCl + I₂. This is a displacement (redox) reaction — chlorine is more reactive and displaces iodine from its salt.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 3 marks). State three characteristic properties of transition elements and give an example of each.

Answer: Form coloured compounds (copper(II) sulfate is blue); show variable oxidation states (iron(II) and iron(III) compounds); act as catalysts (iron in the Haber process).

Question 5 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Explain why noble gases are unreactive.

Answer: Noble gases have full outer electron shells (2 for helium, 8 for the rest). A full outer shell is energetically stable, so the atoms neither lose, gain nor share electrons — there is no bonding advantage — and they exist as monatomic gases.

Question 6 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Compare the melting points of Group I metals and Group VII elements down each group, explaining both trends.

Answer: Group I metals: melting points decrease down the group — atoms grow larger, the metallic bond between positive ions and delocalised electrons weakens. Group VII elements: melting points increase — molecules get larger (Cl₂ → Br₂ → I₂) and the intermolecular forces between molecules strengthen, so more energy is needed to separate them.

The table's metals deserve their own machinery — extraction, corrosion and the reactivity series.

title: IGCSE Mathematics: Fractions, Decimals and Percentages
content:
IGCSE Mathematics: Fractions, Decimals and Percentages

Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580 (2025–2027), section 1 Number: statement 1.4 Fractions, decimals and percentages (equivalence and conversion), 1.13 Percentages (including Extended reverse percentages) and E1.17 Exponential growth and decay. These three representations describe the same quantities, and fluent movement between them is one of the biggest sources of marks in both papers. The note explains why the conversion methods work before showing them, then builds percentages as multipliers — the technique behind most Paper 4 percentage problems.

What a fraction really is

A fraction is a division: 3/4 means 3 divided by 4, or three quarters of a whole. The top (numerator) counts the parts; the bottom (denominator) says how many equal parts the whole is cut into. A proper fraction has a smaller numerator (3/4); an improper fraction has a larger one (7/4); a mixed number combines a whole number with a proper fraction (1 3/4).

Convert 2 3/5 to an improper fraction:

2 wholes = 10 fifths, and 3 more fifths gives 13 fifths:
2 3/5 = (2 x 5 + 3)/5 = 13/5

Equivalent fractions are the same quantity written differently: 3/4 = 6/8 = 15/20, because multiplying top and bottom by the same number is multiplying by 1 (a form of 1, such as 3/3), which changes the look but not the value. Cancelling is the reverse: dividing top and bottom by a common factor. Only factors of the whole numerator and denominator can be cancelled — (x + 3)/(x + 2) cannot be simplified by cancelling the x's, because the top is a sum, not a product.

Converting between fractions, decimals and percentages

Fraction to decimal: divide.  3/8 = 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375
Decimal to fraction: read the place value.  0.47 = 47/100
Fraction to percentage: divide, then multiply by 100.  3/8 = 0.375 = 37.5%
Percentage to fraction: write over 100 and simplify.  45% = 45/100 = 9/20

Recurring decimals. A fraction always produces either a terminating decimal or a recurring one, and every recurring decimal converts back to a fraction by the algebra method:

Write 0.444... (4 recurring) as a fraction:

Let x = 0.444...
Then 10x = 4.444...        [shift the decimal one place]
Subtract:  10x - x = 4.444... - 0.444...
9x = 4
x = 4/9
Write 0.273636... (36 recurring) as a fraction:

Let x = 0.273636...
Two digits repeat, so shift two places:  100x = 27.363636...
100x - x = 27.3636... - 0.2736... = 27.09
99x = 27.09  ->  x = 27.09/99 = 301/1100 after multiplying top and bottom by 100 and simplifying

Knowing the common conversions by heart saves time: 1/2 = 0.5 = 50%, 1/4 = 0.25 = 25%, 3/4 = 0.75, 1/5 = 0.2 = 20%, 1/8 = 0.125, 1/3 = 0.333... = 33 1/3%.

FractionDecimalPercentage
1/20.550%
1/40.2525%
3/40.7575%
1/50.220%
1/80.12512.5%
1/30.333...33 1/3%
2/30.666...66 2/3%

These seven values answer a surprising share of Paper 2 questions by inspection, and they anchor every conversion done the long way.

Percentages: the multiplier method

A percentage is a fraction out of 100 — literally per cent, per hundred. Every percentage problem is a multiplication, and the fastest method converts straight to a multiplier.

Find 35% of 240:

35% = 35/100 = 0.35, so  0.35 x 240 = 84

Increase 240 by 35%:
the new value is 135% of the old, so multiply by 1.35:  1.35 x 240 = 324

Decrease 240 by 35%:
the new value is 65% of the old, so multiply by 0.65:   0.65 x 240 = 156

Why the multiplier works. Increasing by 35% means keeping the original 100% and adding 35%, so the result is 135% of the original, which is 1.35 times it. Decreasing by 35% leaves 65%, which is 0.65 times. The multiplier also chains: successive changes multiply, which is why two discounts of 20% are not one discount of 40% (0.8 × 0.8 = 0.64, a 36% total reduction).

One quantity as a percentage of another:  18 out of 60

18/60 x 100 = 30%

Reverse percentages (Extended). Working backwards from a final value needs division:

A price after a 20% increase is £72. Find the original price.

The original is 100%, the new price is 120% of it, so the multiplier is 1.2:
original = 72 / 1.2 = £60

Check: 60 x 1.2 = 72 ✓

The common error is finding 20% of 72 and subtracting; the percentage must be taken from the original 100%, not the final amount.

Percentage change and comparisons

A coat falls from £80 to £56. Find the percentage decrease.

change = 80 - 56 = 24
percentage change = change / original x 100 = 24/80 x 100 = 30%

Percentage change always uses the original value as the denominator. Comparing quantities with different sizes — prices per 100 g, speeds, wages per hour — is done by putting both over a common quantity before comparing.

Exponential growth and decay (Extended)

When a quantity changes by the same percentage each period, it is multiplied by a fixed factor each time, and the result is exponential growth or decay. The multiplier is 1 + r for growth and 1 − r for decay, where r is the rate as a decimal.

After n periods at rate r:
growth:    final = original x (1 + r)^n
decay:     final = original x (1 - r)^n

Why the power. Each period multiplies by the same factor, so n periods multiply n times: an investment of £500 growing 3% a year becomes 500 × 1.03 after one year, 500 × 1.03 × 1.03 after two, and 500 × 1.03ⁿ after n years. The power counts the multiplications.

£500 is invested at 3% compound interest per year for 4 years.

500 x 1.03^4 = 500 x 1.12550881 = £562.75 (2 d.p.)

Year by year check: 515.00 -> 530.45 -> 546.36 -> 562.75 ✓
A car worth £18 000 depreciates 15% per year. Value after 3 years:

18 000 x 0.85^3 = 18 000 x 0.614125 = £11 054.25

Exponential growth graphs climb ever faster and never touch zero; exponential decay graphs fall steeply at first and then level off towards — but never reach — zero (a horizontal asymptote). Doubling and halving questions are solved by logs or trial multiplication: for how many years does £500 at 3% exceed £600? Solve 500 × 1.03ⁿ > 600 by testing values of n, since 1.03ⁿ > 1.2 needs n ⩾ 7 years.

Worked example: a full percentage question

A shop sells a jacket for £84 after a 20% reduction. A further 10% discount is offered for cash.

Original price before the 20% reduction:
84 = original x 0.80
original = 84 / 0.80 = £105

Cash price after the extra 10%:
84 x 0.90 = £75.60

Total percentage saving against the original:
saving = 105 - 75.60 = 29.40
percentage saving = 29.40/105 x 100 = 28%

Check with multipliers: 0.80 x 0.90 = 0.72, so the cash price is 72% of the
original and the saving is 28% ✓

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Finding a percentage of the wrong amount: increase/decrease percentages apply to the original; reverse percentages divide by the multiplier.
  • Adding percentage changes: two 20% discounts give 0.8 × 0.8 = 0.64, a 36% reduction, not 40%.
  • Writing a recurring decimal as a fraction by eye; use the shift-and-subtract method and show it.
  • Cancelling across a sum: 3/4 is not 3 quarters of the top and bottom separately.
  • Using 365 days or 12 months inconsistently in compound problems: the power n counts compounding periods, so match it to the rate.
  • Forgetting that 15% decrease means multiplying by 0.85, not by −0.15 or 0.15.
  • Confusing 33% with 1/3 exactly: 1/3 = 33 1/3%, and the difference matters in exact answers.
  • Deciding an exponential decay value reaches zero; it falls below £1 or 0.001 but never reaches zero.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 2, 3 marks). Express 0.45 as a fraction in its lowest terms.

Answer: 0.45 = 45/100 = 9/20.

Question 2 (Paper 2, 3 marks). Write 0.27 with the 27 recurring as a fraction.

Answer: Let x = 0.272727...; then 100x = 27.2727...; subtracting gives 99x = 27, so x = 27/99 = 3/11.

Question 3 (Paper 4, 4 marks). In a sale, a bike is reduced by 15% to £255. Find the original price.

Answer: £255 represents 85% of the original, so the multiplier is 0.85 and the original price is 255/0.85 = £300. Check: 300 × 0.85 = 255 ✓.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 4 marks). A bacteria culture starts with 2000 and increases by 8% each hour. Find the size after 5 hours.

Answer: 2000 × 1.08⁵ = 2000 × 1.4693280768 = 2938.7 ≈ 2939 bacteria.

Question 5 (Paper 4, 3 marks). A town's population falls from 45 000 to 36 000 over a year. Find the percentage decrease.

Answer: Change = 9000; percentage = 9000/45 000 × 100 = 20%.

Question 6 (Paper 4, 5 marks). A car is bought for £12 000 and depreciates 18% in the first year and 12% in the second. Find its value after two years and the overall percentage loss.

Answer: 12 000 × 0.82 × 0.88 = 12 000 × 0.7216 = £8659.20. Overall loss = £3340.80, which is 3340.80/12 000 × 100 = 27.84% ≈ 27.8%. (Note 0.82 × 0.88 = 0.7216, a 27.84% total fall — not 30%.)

Fractions describe parts; powers and roots describe repeated multiplication — the next topic.
