title: A Level Physics: Motion in a Circle and Gravity
content:
A Level Physics: Motion in a Circle and Gravity

Gravity is the weakest of the four fundamental forces and yet it shapes galaxies — because it never cancels: mass has only one sign, so every particle attracts every other. This note builds the gravitational toolkit from zero: the field concept and field lines, Newton's law of gravitation, field strength and potential for a point mass, and then the applications that fill the papers — satellite orbits, escape velocity and the energy bookkeeping of lifting a mass to infinity. Every formula is derived from the inverse-square law, and every calculation type is worked in full.

The gravitational field

A gravitational field is a region in which a mass experiences a force. Field lines point toward the mass creating the field (gravity is always attractive), and their density shows strength — close to a planet the lines are dense (strong field), far away they are sparse. Two field shapes are examinable:

  • Radial field: around a point mass or a spherical planet outside its surface; strength falls with distance.
  • Uniform field: near a planet's surface over small height changes; strength g is effectively constant (the approximation behind mgh).

Newton's law of gravitation

F = G M m / r²

G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻² (gravitational constant)
M, m = the two masses (kg)
r = separation between their centres (m)

The analogy that makes the law intuitive: the force weakens like light spreading from a lamp — doubling the distance spreads the same influence over four times the area, so the force quarters. The law is universal: the same G applies to an apple and the Earth as to two galaxies.

Worked example. Find the gravitational force between two 1000 kg masses 2.0 m apart.

F = G M m/r² = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 1000 × 1000/4.0
  = 6.67 × 10⁻⁵/4.0 = 1.7 × 10⁻⁵ N

Note how tiny it is — gravity only matters when one mass is astronomical, which is why the electric force dominates at particle scales.

Gravitational field strength

Field strength g is force per unit mass (N kg⁻¹), and for a point mass or a spherical body:

g = G M / r²

at a planet's surface: g = G M / R²  (R = planet radius)
variation with height: g falls as 1/r² from the centre

Worked example. Find g at the surface of Mars (M = 6.4 × 10²³ kg, R = 3.4 × 10⁶ m).

g = G M/R² = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 6.4 × 10²³/(3.4 × 10⁶)²
  = 4.27 × 10¹³/1.156 × 10¹³ = 3.7 N kg⁻¹

Worked example 2 (height). At what height above Earth's surface does g fall to half its surface value? (R = 6.4 × 10⁶ m.)

g_surface = GM/R²; half → GM/r² = (1/2) GM/R²
r² = 2 R² → r = R √(2) = 9.05 × 10⁶ m
height = r - R = 2.65 × 10⁶ m  (about 2650 km)

Gravitational potential

Potential is the work done per unit mass in bringing a mass from infinity to that point (zero at infinity by definition). Because gravity attracts, the work is done by the field on the way in, so potential is negative everywhere:

V = - G M / r        (J kg⁻¹)

potential energy of a mass m: U = m V = - G M m / r
work to move between potentials: W = m (V² - V¹)

The negative sign is not a detail — it is the physical statement that masses are bound. The potential well around a planet is a dip; escape means climbing out of it to V = 0 at infinity.

Worked example. Find the potential at Earth's surface (M = 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg, R = 6.37 × 10⁶ m).

V = -GM/R = -(6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 5.97 × 10²⁴)/6.37 × 10⁶
  = -3.98 × 10¹⁴/6.37 × 10⁶ = -6.25 × 10⁷ J kg⁻¹

Escape velocity

To escape a planet's gravity, a body needs enough kinetic energy to climb from the surface potential to zero:

(1/2) m v² = G M m / R  →  v_escape = √(2 G M / R)

Earth: v = √(2 × 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 5.97 × 10²⁴/6.37 × 10⁶)
     = √(1.25 × 10⁸) = 1.12 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹ = 11.2 km s⁻¹

The derivation is worth learning as a pattern: set kinetic energy equal to the depth of the potential well, cancel m, solve for v. Escape speed is independent of the escaping body's mass — a rocket and a molecule need the same speed (though not the same fuel).

The potential well picture explains the sign conventions in one image: near a planet the potential is deeply negative (the bottom of a dip), and moving outward means climbing toward zero. A body with total energy (kinetic plus potential) below zero is bound — it will fall back; a body with total energy at or above zero can coast to infinity. That single inequality, kinetic energy compared with the depth of the well, decides every escape and orbit question, and it is the most reliable way to check an answer's sign and size.

Orbits

A satellite in a circular orbit has gravity as its centripetal force:

G M m / r² = m v² / r   →   v = √(G M / r)

period: T = 2 π r / v = 2 π √(r³/(G M))
(Kepler's third law: T² proportional to r³)

The counter-intuitive exam favourite: a lower orbit means a faster satellite. Since v = √(GM/r), smaller r gives larger v and shorter periods — which is why the International Space Station orbits in about 90 minutes while the Moon takes 27 days.

Worked example. Find the speed and period of a satellite 400 km above Earth's surface.

r = 6.37 × 10⁶ + 4.0 × 10⁵ = 6.77 × 10⁶ m
v = √(GM/r) = √(6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 5.97 × 10²⁴/6.77 × 10⁶)
  = √(5.88 × 10⁷) = 7.67 × 10³ m s⁻¹
T = 2 π r/v = 2 × 3.14 × 6.77 × 10⁶/7.67 × 10³
  = 4.25 × 10⁷/7.67 × 10³ = 5.5 × 10³ s  (about 92 minutes)

Geostationary orbits are the applied case: r ≈ 4.2 × 10⁷ m gives T = 24 hours, the satellite sits above one point on the equator, and it must orbit west-to-east in the equatorial plane.

Worked examples: combined gravity problems

Worked example. Compare the gravitational potential energy of a 500 kg satellite at 400 km altitude with its value at infinity, and find the energy needed to escape from that orbit.

r = 6.77 × 10⁶ m
U_orbit = -GMm/r = -(6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 5.97 × 10²⁴ × 500)/6.77 × 10⁶
        = -1.99 × 10¹⁷/6.77 × 10⁶ = -2.94 × 10¹⁰ J
U_infinity = 0
energy to escape = 0 - (-2.94 × 10¹⁰) = 2.9 × 10¹⁰ J

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Law) State Newton's law of gravitation. Answer: The gravitational force between two point masses is proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centres: F = GMm/r².
  2. (Field strength) Define gravitational field strength. Answer: The force per unit mass on a small test mass at that point, g = F/m, measured in N kg⁻¹.
  3. (Inverse square) State how g changes when the distance from a planet's centre is tripled. Answer: g = GM/r², so tripling r divides g by 9.
  4. (Potential) Explain why gravitational potential is negative. Answer: Potential is defined as zero at infinity; gravity attracts, so the field does work on a mass brought in from infinity, meaning its potential energy — and therefore potential — decreases below zero.
  5. (Escape) Calculate the escape velocity from the Moon (M = 7.35 × 10²² kg, R = 1.74 × 10⁶ m). Answer: v = √(2GM/R) = √(2 × 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 7.35 × 10²²/1.74 × 10⁶) = √(5.63 × 10⁶) = 2.37 × 10³ m s⁻¹ ≈ 2.4 km s⁻¹.
  6. (Orbit) Explain why a satellite in a lower orbit moves faster. Answer: Gravity provides the centripetal force: GMm/r² = mv²/r, so v = √(GM/r); a smaller r gives a larger speed and a shorter period.
  7. (Geostationary) State two conditions for a geostationary orbit. Answer: The period must be 24 hours, the orbit must be equatorial and the satellite must orbit in the same direction as Earth's rotation (west to east) — all three are usually wanted.
  8. (Energy) Explain why the energy needed to move a satellite from a low orbit to a higher one is not simply mgh. Answer: Over large distances g is not constant; the correct treatment uses the change in gravitational potential energy, U = −GMm/r, evaluated at both radii.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • r measured from the centre: the separation is centre-to-centre, so a satellite's r includes the planet's radius. Using altitude alone underestimates r and inflates g and v.
  • Mass cancellation: in orbital and escape calculations m cancels — do not carry a satellite's mass through and then wonder why the answer is huge.
  • Negative potentials: V and U are negative; a "larger" potential energy at a higher orbit is less negative, not more. Work done = m(V₂ − V₁), keeping the signs.
  • g versus G: g = GM/r² is field strength (N kg⁻¹); G is the universal constant (N m² kg⁻²). Confusing the symbols loses marks and factors of mass.
  • Surface approximation: mgh applies only for small heights; over planetary distances use the potential formula.
  • Orbit direction: geostationary requires equatorial, west-to-east, 24 hours — a polar orbit is not geostationary however high it is.
  • Units of G and distances: G in N m² kg⁻², masses in kg, distances in metres — km into m, and planet masses given in scientific notation handled carefully.
  • Precision: 2 or 3 s.f. with units; the data sheet supplies G, Earth's mass and radius — quote them rather than relying on memory.
  • Method marks: write F = GMm/r² or v = √(GM/r) before substituting; formulae earn credit independently of arithmetic.

title: The Normal Distribution — Study Notes
content:
The Normal Distribution

The Model

A continuous distribution with the familiar bell shape, symmetric about the mean, described by two parameters: X ~ N(μ, σ²). The curve is fully determined by μ (centre) and σ (width). Total probability is 1, and because X is continuous, P(X = a) = 0 for any single point — inequalities do not need strictness.

Standardising

Convert any normal variable to the standard normal Z ~ N(0, 1) with

  • Z = (X − μ)/σ

Then read probabilities from the normal table. For X ~ N(50, 4²): P(X > 56) = P(Z > 1.5) = 1 − 0.9332 = 0.0668.

Backwards Problems

Given a probability, find μ or σ. Convert the target percentile to a z-value from the table, then solve (x − μ)/σ = z.

Example: P(X < 30) = 0.15 with unknown σ. From tables z = −1.036, so (30 − μ)/σ = −1.036 — one equation per unknown; use a second condition if both are missing.

Symmetry Shortcuts

P(X > μ) = 0.5. P(X < a) for a above the mean uses the complement. Tables usually give Φ(z) for z ≥ 0 only; use Φ(−z) = 1 − Φ(z).

Normal Approximation to the Binomial

For large n with p near ½, X ~ B(n, p) ≈ N(np, np(1 − p)). The condition usually quoted at this level is np > 5 and n(1 − p) > 5. Apply a continuity correction: to approximate P(X ≥ 12) for a binomial, compute P(Y > 11.5) for the normal Y.

Example: B(100, 0.5) ≈ N(50, 25). P(X ≥ 55) ≈ P(Y > 54.5) = P(Z > 0.9) = 0.1841.

Exam tips: always sketch and shade — the picture prevents complement errors. State the standardisation step explicitly; marks sit in the working. Check whether a question says "mean and standard deviation" (σ) or "variance" (σ²) before standardising.

title: Waves — Study Notes
content:
Waves

Edexcel International A Level Physics — Unit 2 (WPH12), sat at AS.

Progressive waves

  • A progressive wave transfers energy without transferring matter. Its speed is v = fλ, where f is the frequency and λ the wavelength. Period T = 1/f.
  • Phase difference: two points separated by one wavelength are in phase. Points separated by half a wavelength are in antiphase.

Transverse and longitudinal waves

  • Transverse: the oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer (e.g. light, waves on a string).
  • Longitudinal: the oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer (e.g. sound in air, compressions and rarefactions).

Doppler effect for sound

When a source moves towards an observer, the observed frequency is higher and the wavelength is shorter. When it moves away, the observed frequency is lower and the wavelength is longer. The speed of sound in the medium does not change.

Electromagnetic spectrum

All electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum. In order of increasing wavelength: gamma rays, X-rays, ultraviolet, visible light, infrared, microwaves, radio waves. Frequency increases in the reverse order.

Polarisation

Only transverse waves can be polarised. Polarisation restricts the oscillations to a single plane. Longitudinal waves such as sound cannot be polarised.

Worked example: a wave has frequency 50 Hz and wavelength 6.0 m. Its speed is v = fλ = 50 × 6.0 = 300 m s⁻¹.

Exam tips: learn the spectrum order in terms of wavelength, not frequency. For the Doppler effect, state which way the source moves relative to the observer. Only transverse waves can show polarisation.

Polarisation and the Doppler effect

Only transverse waves can be polarised, because their oscillations can be restricted to one plane. A polariser passes only the component of the oscillation along its transmission axis. Light from a sky or a reflection is partly polarised, which is why polarising filters reduce glare. The Doppler effect for a moving source gives an observed frequency f' = f v/(v ± vs), where the upper sign applies when the source moves away from the observer and the lower sign when it approaches.

Exam tip: longitudinal waves such as sound cannot be polarised, so say so explicitly if a question asks about it.

Worked example: wave speed from frequency and wavelength

A sound wave has frequency 680 Hz and wavelength 0.50 m. Using v = fλ, the speed is 680 × 0.50 = 340 m/s, close to the speed of sound in air. For an electromagnetic wave in a vacuum the same relation applies, with v = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s. Take the wavelength from a displacement–distance graph and the period from a displacement–time graph, then use f = 1/T before substituting.

Exam method: reading wave graphs

On a displacement–distance graph, the wavelength is the distance between two adjacent points in phase, such as two successive crests, not the distance between a crest and a trough. On a displacement–time graph, the period is the time for one complete oscillation at a fixed point. Mark the values on the axes carefully, because many lost marks come from reading half a wavelength or half a period.

title: Exam technique: Probability Distributions
content:
### What earns the marks
For distribution tables, probabilities summing to 1 checked earns the first mark. For expectation, each x times p(x) summed earns the method mark. For variance, E(X squared) computed separately then subtracted earns the second mark.
### Traps
Error: sigma used as variance. Correction: sigma is sd; square it. Error: E(X squared) computed as E(X) squared. Correction: square the x values first. Error: function-of-X expectation via E(X) substituted. Correction: sum g(x)p(x) directly.

title: Programming and Algorithms
content:
`# Programming and Algorithms

Design Approaches

  • Top-down (stepwise refinement): decompose into modules — planned structure
  • Object-oriented: classes encapsulating state + behaviour — reusability
  • WAD (write all down): rapid prototyping — evolves during coding

Pseudocode Conventions

DECLARE x : INTEGER
IF x > 10 THEN ... ELSE ... ENDIF
WHILE ... ENDWHILE
FOR i ← 1 TO n ... NEXT i
FUNCTION f(a) RETURNS INTEGER

Searching

  • Linear: check each item, O(n), works unsorted
  • Binary: halve a sorted list each step, O(log n)

Example: 1,000,000 items: binary search needs ≤ 20 comparisons.

Sorting

AlgorithmBestAverageIdea
BubbleO(n)O(n²)swap neighbours
InsertionO(n)O(n²)insert into sorted prefix
MergeO(n log n)O(n log n)divide and merge

Merge sort example: [5,2,9,1] → [5,2][9,1] → [2,5][1,9] → [1,2,5,9].

Recursion

A function calling itself with a base case. Factorial: f(0)=1, f(n)=n·f(n−1). Stack frames handle state.

Exam tips: state the Big-O and justify it; for traces, tabulate variable changes per iteration.

title: Algorithms & Programming — Study Notes
content:
Algorithms & Programming

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2023–2025): pseudocode, flowcharts, standard algorithms (linear/bubble), trace tables, validation & verification.

1. Pseudocode

OUTPUT "Enter n"
INPUT n
IF n MOD 2 = 0 THEN
  OUTPUT "even"
ELSE
  OUTPUT "odd"
ENDIF

FOR i ← 1 TO 10
  total ← total + i
NEXT i

WHILE total < 100
  total ← total + n
ENDWHILE

FUNCTION square(x : INTEGER) RETURNS INTEGER
  RETURN x * x
ENDFUNCTION

Assignment ←, comparison =, MOD/DIV for remainders/quotients.

2. Flowchart symbols

Terminator (oval), process (rectangle), decision (diamond), input/output (parallelogram), flow lines with arrows.

3. Standard algorithms

  • Linear search: check each item until found/end — works unsorted.
  • Bubble sort: repeated adjacent swaps; largest bubbles to the end each pass; n−1 passes max; early exit when no swaps.
  • Counting/totaling patterns; max/min with a running best value.

4. Trace tables

One column per variable; log every assignment in order; watch loop counters and reassignments.

x ← 1; total ← 0
WHILE x <= 4
  total ← total + x * 2
  x ← x + 1
ENDWHILE  // total = 20

5. Validation vs verification

  • Validation: automatic checks on data — range (exam mark 0–100), length (password ≥ 8), type, format (postcode pattern), presence (field not empty), check digit (barcode).
  • Verification: data matches the source — double entry, visual/proof reading.

6. Testing

Normal (typical), abnormal (rejects invalid), boundary (extremes just inside/outside). Test data tables list input → expected output.

Exam tips: write pseudocode with ENDIF/NEXT/ENDWHILE terminators; in trace tables record the condition result too; boundary choices need "just above/below/at" values.

title: Complex Numbers — Study Notes
content:
Complex Numbers

Basics

i² = −1. A complex number z = a + bi has real part a and imaginary part b. Two numbers are equal iff both parts match.

Arithmetic: add/subtract parts; multiply with brackets and replace i² with −1.

Example: (2 + 3i)(1 − i) = 2 − 2i + 3i − 3i² = 5 + i.

Conjugates

z̄ = a − bi. zz̄ = a² + b² (real). Dividing: multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate.

Example: 1/(3 − i) × (3 + i)/(3 + i) = (3 + i)/10.

Argand Diagram

Plot z as the point (a, b). |z| = √(a² + b²) is the modulus (distance from origin); arg z = tan⁻¹(b/a) is the argument (angle). Multiply two numbers: moduli multiply, arguments add.

Modulus–Argument Form

z = r(cos θ + i sin θ), r = |z|, θ = arg z. Useful for powers and roots.

de Moivre and Roots

[r(cos θ + i sin θ)]ⁿ = rⁿ(cos nθ + i sin nθ).

Example: (1 + i)⁸: |1 + i| = √2, arg = π/4, so z⁸ = (√2)⁸ cis 2π = 16.

An nth root gives n evenly spaced solutions, 2π/n apart on a circle of radius r^(1/n).

Exam tips: always give arguments in the required interval; when solving equations, remember complex roots come in conjugate pairs for real polynomials.

Exam method: arithmetic and modulus

Treat i as a symbol with i² = −1 and collect real and imaginary parts separately. When multiplying complex numbers expand like brackets, then replace i² by −1. To divide, multiply the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator, which turns the denominator into a real number.

For z = a + bi the modulus is |z| = √(a² + b²) and the argument is the angle θ in the Argand diagram with tan θ = b/a, placed in the correct quadrant. The conjugate z* = a − bi reverses the sign of the imaginary part, and z z* = a² + b², which is always real.

Equal complex numbers have equal real parts and equal imaginary parts. Use this to solve for unknown real values, comparing coefficients on both sides of an equation.

Exam cue: State the final answer in the form a + bi, and check the sign of the imaginary part after every multiplication.

Worked example: square root of a complex number

Find z such that z² = −9 + 40i. Let z = a + bi. Then a² − b² = −9 and 2ab = 40, so ab = 20. Trying a = 4 and b = 5 gives 16 − 25 = −9, which works. So z = 4 + 5i or z = −(4 + 5i). Check by squaring: (4 + 5i)² = 16 + 40i − 25 = −9 + 40i.

Quadratic equations with complex roots

For x² + 2x + 5 = 0, the discriminant is 4 − 20 = −16, which is negative, so the roots are not real. Use √(−16) = 4i to get x = (−2 ± 4i)/2 = −1 ± 2i. The two roots form a conjugate pair, as they always do when the coefficients are real.

Loci in the Argand diagram

  • |z − 2| = 3 is the circle with centre 2 and radius 3, since it gives the distance of z from the point 2.
  • arg(z) = π/4 is a half-line from the origin at 45° above the positive real axis.
  • |z − 1| = |z + i| is the perpendicular bisector of the points 1 and −i.

Exam point: when a locus question gives an inequality, shade the correct region on the diagram and label the boundary as a solid or dashed line depending on whether it is included.

title: The Normal Distribution — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: The Normal Distribution

Mathematics — A2. A continuous distribution with the familiar bell shape, symmetric about the mean, described by two parameters: X ~ N(μ, σ²). The curve is fully determined by μ (centre) and σ (width). Total probability is 1, and because X is continuous, P(X = a) = 0 for any single point — inequalities do not need strictness.

Key areas to revise

  • The Model
  • Standardising
  • Backwards Problems
  • Symmetry Shortcuts
  • Normal Approximation to the Binomial

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

### Worked example X follows a normal distribution with mean μ and variance σ². Standardise with Z = (X − μ)/σ and read the probability from tables. For Z < 1.5, the table gives 0.9332. The curve is symmetric about the mean, so P(X < μ) = 0.5, and about 68% of values lie within one standard deviation of the mean and about 95% within two. ### Check yourself Find P(Z < −1.5) using symmetry. It equals 1 − 0.9332 = 0.0668. Explain why the symmetry of the curve allows this without a separate table lookup.

title: Exam technique: Simplifying and Expanding
content:
### What earns the marks
For expansion, calculate earns a mark for every correct pair of products shown before collecting terms. For factorisation, the HCF stated earns the first mark and the fully divided bracket earns the second: partial factorisation scores at most half. For algebraic fractions, factorise first earns the method mark even when cancellation follows.
### Traps
Error: (x + 5)(x - 2) = x squared + 10. Correction: four products, then collect. Error: 3(2x squared - 3x) called fully factorised. Correction: extract x as well. Error: cancelling terms instead of factors in a fraction. Correction: factorise numerator and denominator first.
### Worked example
Expand (2x − 3)(x + 4). The four products are 2x², 8x, −3x and −12. Collecting terms gives 2x² + 5x − 12. For factorisation, 6x² − 9x has HCF 3x, so 6x² − 9x = 3x(2x − 3). Check by expanding the answer back to the original expression.

title: Chemistry of the Environment
content:
Chemistry of the Environment

Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry 0620, Extended route, topic 10 (statements 10.1–10.3). Water testing and treatment, fertilisers, air pollution, greenhouse gases and photosynthesis.

10.1 Water

  • Test for water: anhydrous copper(II) sulfate turns from white to blue, or anhydrous cobalt(II) chloride paper turns from blue to pink. Purity is tested by melting point (0 °C) and boiling point (100 °C) — impurities shift both, depression of melting point and elevation of boiling point.

10.2 Fertilisers

  • Ammonium salts and nitrates are used as fertilisers. NPK fertilisers supply nitrogen (for protein), phosphorus (for roots) and potassium (for flowers and fruit).

10.3 Air quality and climate

  • Clean dry air is about 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, with noble gases and about 0.04% carbon dioxide. Pollutants include carbon monoxide (incomplete combustion, toxic), sulfur dioxide (sulfur impurities in fossil fuels, causes acid rain), oxides of nitrogen (from vehicle engines, cause acid rain and photochemical smog), and particulates.
  • Acid rain damages forests, buildings and lakes. Removal methods include flue gas desulfurisation with calcium oxide or calcium carbonate, and catalytic converters in cars that reduce oxides of nitrogen to nitrogen and oxygen.
  • Greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide and methane absorb re-radiated heat and warm the Earth. Photosynthesis: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen, using light and chlorophyll.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Removal chemistry, applied to a catalytic converter: 2CO + 2NO → 2CO₂ + N₂. Carbon monoxide is oxidised to carbon dioxide and nitrogen monoxide is reduced to nitrogen. Name the oxidation and reduction halves separately.
  • Desulfurisation, applied to calcium carbonate removing sulfur dioxide: CaCO₃ + SO₂ → CaSO₃ + CO₂. Explain why this works: calcium carbonate is basic and sulfur dioxide is acidic, an acid–base reaction. That reasoning earns the mark.
  • Experimental design, applied to testing whether a lake is acidic: sample and compare against pure water using universal indicator or a pH meter, and state that a control sample of unpolluted water must be measured with the same method. Naming the control is often the difference mark.
  • Greenhouse reasoning, applied to why methane matters more per molecule than carbon dioxide: methane absorbs more infrared radiation per molecule, so a smaller amount produces a similar warming effect. Quantity AND per-molecule effect both count in an evaluation answer.

Common errors

  • Confusing the water tests: copper(II) sulfate is the white-to-blue test; cobalt(II) chloride is the blue-to-pink test.
  • Describing acid rain without naming its source gases (sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen).
  • Saying catalytic converters "remove carbon dioxide". They convert CO and NO, and can produce more CO₂.

title: Entropy and Energetics Quick Revision
content:
Entropy and Energetics Quick Revision

Chemistry — A2. Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH14, Topic 12, covering entropy, energetics, and feasibility of reactions. Entropy and enthalpy changes are crucial in determining the spontaneity of a reaction.

  • Entropy measures disorder and randomness, increasing with temperature and phase changes.
  • Gibbs free energy combines enthalpy and entropy to predict reaction feasibility.
  • Total entropy change is the sum of system and surroundings entropy changes.
  • Temperature affects reaction feasibility, with higher temperatures decreasing the magnitude of surroundings entropy change.
  • Worked examples illustrate how to calculate entropy changes and Gibbs free energy.

Worked example

Calculate the total entropy change for a reaction with ΔS_system = 100 J/K and ΔH = -50000 J, at 298 K, using S_surroundings = -ΔH / T, then S_total = ΔS_system + S_surroundings.

Key points to remember

Remember that entropy increases with temperature and phase changes, and that the total entropy change determines reaction spontaneity. Also, recall that the Gibbs free energy equation, ΔG = ΔH - TΔS, is used to predict reaction feasibility. Key: ΔG = Gibbs free energy change (kJ mol⁻¹); ΔH = enthalpy change (kJ mol⁻¹); T = temperature (K); ΔS = entropy change (J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, so divide it by 1000 before combining with ΔH); ΔS_total = ΔS_system + ΔS_surroundings (J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹), with ΔS_surroundings = −ΔH/T. A reaction is feasible when ΔG is negative, which is the same statement as ΔS_total being positive.

How to use this: skim the key points, read the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Born-Haber Cycles and Lattice Energy

A Born-Haber cycle applies Hess's Law to construct an energy level diagram for the formation of an ionic solid from its elements in their standard states. The standard enthalpy change of atomisation, delta_at H, is the enthalpy change when one mole of gaseous atoms is formed from the element under standard conditions. Electron affinity is the enthalpy change when one electron is added to each atom in one mole of gaseous atoms to form one mole of gaseous 1- ions. Lattice energy is defined as the exothermic process for the formation of one mole of an ionic solid from its gaseous ions.

Discrepancies between experimental lattice energy values obtained from Born-Haber cycles and theoretical values calculated from pure electrostatic point-charge models indicate the presence of covalent character. When cations polarise large or highly charged anions, electron density is drawn into the region between the nuclei, leading to partial covalent bonding which releases more energy than predicted by pure ionic models.

Enthalpy of Solution and Hydration

The enthalpy change of solution, delta_sol H, is the enthalpy change when one mole of a solute is dissolved in enough solvent to form an infinitely dilute solution. The enthalpy change of hydration, delta_hyd H, is the enthalpy change when one mole of gaseous ions is dissolved in water to form an infinitely dilute solution. You can use energy cycles combining lattice energy and hydration enthalpies to calculate the enthalpy change of solution.

Ionic charge and radius significantly affect these energetic values. High charge density, resulting from small ionic radius and high ionic charge, leads to more exothermic hydration and lattice energies because of stronger electrostatic attractions between the ions and water molecules or oppositely charged ions.

Thermodynamic Stability versus Kinetic Stability

Thermodynamic stability indicates whether a substance or reaction is feasible based on total entropy change and free energy, showing if a reaction is spontaneous. Kinetic stability refers to the rate of a reaction; a system can be thermodynamically unstable yet kinetically stable if the activation energy barrier is too high for the reaction to proceed at a measurable rate at room temperature.

Additional Worked Example

Calculate the enthalpy change of solution for sodium chloride, given that its lattice energy is +790 kJ / mol and the hydration enthalpies of sodium and chloride ions are −406 kJ / mol and −364 kJ / mol respectively. Using the energy cycle, delta_sol H = lattice energy + sum(delta_hyd H). Therefore, delta_sol H = +790 + (−406 + (−364)) = +790 − 770 = +20 kJ / mol.

More Key Points to Remember

Remember that the total entropy change, delta_S total = delta_S system + delta_S surroundings, must be positive for any spontaneous process. The term delta_S surroundings is calculated using − delta_H / T. Solubility trends down group 2 depend on the relative sizes of the decrease in lattice energy compared to the decrease in hydration enthalpy as cation size increases. Polarisation increases down the group for anions or with smaller cations, driving deviations from theoretical lattice energy calculations.

title: Cell Structure, Reproduction and Development
content:
Cell Structure, Reproduction and Development

Edexcel IAL Biology WBI12, Topic 3. Cells are the basic units of life. Their structure reflects their function, and cell division produces the new cells needed for growth, repair and reproduction.

Cell structure

  • Prokaryotic cells have no nucleus; their DNA is a circular loop in the cytoplasm, and their ribosomes are 70S. Eukaryotic cells have a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.
  • The nucleus holds DNA. Mitochondria carry out aerobic respiration. Chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis in plant cells. Rough endoplasmic reticulum has ribosomes and makes proteins; the Golgi apparatus modifies and packages them.
  • Electron microscopes have higher resolution than light microscopes because electrons have a much shorter wavelength than visible light.
  • Magnification = image size ÷ actual size. For an image 40 mm across at a magnification of ×400, the actual size is 0.1 mm.

Cell division

  • The cell cycle has interphase (G1, S and G2) and mitotic division. DNA replicates in the S phase.
  • Mitosis produces two genetically identical diploid daughter cells. It is used for growth and repair.
  • Meiosis has two divisions and produces four genetically different haploid gametes. Crossing over happens in prophase I, and independent assortment happens when homologous pairs line up at metaphase I.

Stem cells and development

  • A totipotent cell can form any cell type, including the cells of the placenta. Embryonic stem cells are pluripotent: they can form any cell type of the body. Adult stem cells are multipotent.
  • Differentiation switches on particular genes so that a cell becomes specialised.

Cancer

  • Cancer results from mutations that disrupt the control of the cell cycle. The cells divide in an uncontrolled way and can form a tumour.

Exam tip: when you compare mitosis and meiosis, name the number of divisions, the number of daughter cells, their ploidy and whether they are genetically identical.

title: Number — Indices and Standard Form — Study Notes
content:
Number — Indices and Standard Form

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): index laws, negative and fractional indices, standard form arithmetic.

1. Index laws

  • aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ; aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ; (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ
  • a⁰ = 1; a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ; a^(1/n) = ⁿ√a; a^(m/n) = (ⁿ√a)ᵐ

Examples: 27^(2/3) = (³√27)² = 9; 5⁻² = 1/25; (2x³)² = 4x⁶.

2. Standard form

a × 10ⁿ with 1 ≤ a < 10.

  • 47 382 = 4.7382 × 10⁴; 0.0056 = 5.6 × 10⁻³
  • Multiplication: multiply a's, add powers. Division: divide a's, subtract powers.

Example: (3 × 10⁵) × (4 × 10⁻²) = 12 × 10³ = 1.2 × 10⁴.

3. Calculator use

Use the ×10ˣ key, not 10 ^; keep working in standard form and convert at the end. Give final answers in the form asked (often 3 s.f. standard form).

4. Solving index equations

Match bases: 2ˣ = 32 ⇒ 2ˣ = 2⁵ ⇒ x = 5. With different bases, rewrite (8 = 2³).

Exam tips: check a is in [1, 10) before writing standard form; in "multiply out" questions apply the power to every factor including coefficients.

title: Quadratics — Study Notes
content:
Quadratics

Cambridge International AS & A Level Mathematics 9709, Paper 1. Quadratic questions usually ask for one of three things: the shape of the curve, the number and position of its roots, or a range of values for a parameter. Identify which one you need before you start.

Completing the square and the turning point

Write ax² + bx + c as a(x + b/2a)² + (c − b²/4a). The turning point is at x = −b/2a, and the sign of a tells you whether it is a minimum (a > 0) or a maximum (a < 0). The same form gives the least or greatest value of the expression.

Example: 2x² − 12x + 7 = 2(x − 3)² − 11. The minimum is at (3, −11), so the least value of the expression is −11.

Solving: factorising, formula or sketch

Try factorising first. If it does not factorise neatly, use x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac))/2a and simplify the surd. A rough sketch shows how many roots to expect and whether the answer is a set of values or an interval.

Example: 3x² + 5x − 4 = 0 does not factorise neatly. Here b² − 4ac = 73, so x = (−5 ± √73)/6.

The discriminant counts roots

The discriminant D = b² − 4ac decides how many real roots an equation has. D > 0 gives two distinct real roots, D = 0 gives one repeated root, and D < 0 gives no real roots. The same test works for intersections: a line and a curve meet where their equations share a solution, so form one quadratic and read its discriminant.

Example: 4x² + kx + 9 = 0 has equal roots when k² − 4(4)(9) = 0, so k² = 144 and k = ±12. Check: with k = 12 the equation becomes (2x + 3)² = 0.

A parameter in the discriminant

When the discriminant contains an unknown constant, write the condition as an equation or inequality and solve it. A quadratic inequality needs a sketch or a sign table to give the final range.

Example: x² + (k − 1)x + 4 = 0 has real roots when (k − 1)² − 16 ≥ 0. Solving gives k − 1 ≤ −4 or k − 1 ≥ 4, so k ≤ −3 or k ≥ 5.

A line meeting a curve, and tangency

Set the two equations equal and rearrange into one quadratic. Two intersections need D > 0, a tangent needs D = 0, and no intersection needs D < 0.

Example: the line y = x + 3 and the curve y = 2x² − x meet where 2x² − 2x − 3 = 0. Here D = 28, so there are two intersection points. For the line y = 4x + c to touch y = x² + 2x + 1, the equation x² − 2x + (1 − c) = 0 needs D = 0, so c = 0. The point of contact is (1, 4).

Solving an inequality from a sketch

Find the roots, sketch the parabola and read off the region. When a is positive, the curve is below the axis between its roots and above it outside them.

Example: 2x² − x − 6 < 0 factorises as (2x + 3)(x − 2) < 0. The curve is below the axis between its roots, so −3/2 < x < 2.

Example: 5 − 3x − 2x² ≥ 0 is the same as 2x² + 3x − 5 ≤ 0, which factorises as (2x + 5)(x − 1) ≤ 0. The solution is −5/2 ≤ x ≤ 1. Multiplying by −1 reverses the inequality, which is the step students most often miss.

Exam technique

  • Name the job first: shape, roots, or a condition on a parameter.
  • Write D = b² − 4ac with its numbers before deciding anything.
  • Give answers in the form the question asks for, such as exact surds or inequalities.
  • For a parameter range, test a value on each side of a boundary to confirm the direction of the inequality.

title: Atomic Structure and the Periodic Table Revision Notes Edexcel IAL AS Chemistry
content:
Atomic Structure and the Periodic Table AS Level Chemistry

These revision notes cover Topic 2 of the Edexcel International Advanced Subsidiary Chemistry specification, Unit 1 (WCH11). They detail subatomic particles, mass spectrometry, ionisation energies, quantum shells, orbitals, and periodic trends across periods 2 and 3.

Subatomic Particles and Isotopes

Atoms consist of a central nucleus containing protons and neutrons, surrounded by electrons in quantum shells. The atomic proton number is the number of protons in the nucleus, which defines the element. The mass number is the total number of protons and neutrons combined. You can determine the number of each subatomic particle in any neutral atom or ion by subtracting the atomic number from the mass number to find neutrons, while electrons equal protons in a neutral atom or are adjusted according to the ionic charge. Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons, resulting in different mass numbers. Isotopes share identical chemical properties because they have the same electron configuration, but they possess different physical properties such as density and mass.

  • Proton: relative mass 1, relative charge +1.
  • Neutron: relative mass 1, relative charge 0.
  • Electron: relative mass 1 / 1836, relative charge −1.
  • Atomic number equals the number of protons.
  • Mass number equals protons plus neutrons.
  • Neutrons = mass number − atomic number.
  • Electrons = protons minus positive charge, or plus negative charge.

Mass Spectrometry and Relative Masses

A mass spectrometer determines the isotopic composition of elements and relative molecular masses of compounds. A vaporised sample is ionised by high-energy electrons to form positive ions, accelerated by an electric field, deflected by a magnetic field according to mass-to-charge ratio, and detected. Ions in a mass spectrometer may occasionally acquire a 2+ charge, producing a signal at half their actual mass-to-charge ratio. Mass spectra display percentage abundance or relative abundance on the vertical axis against mass-to-charge ratio on the horizontal axis. For diatomic molecules such as chlorine, you can predict mass spectra and relative peak heights given isotopic abundances by using probability combinations of isotopes like chlorine-35 and chlorine-37.

  • Relative atomic mass is the weighted mean mass of an atom of an element compared with one-twelfth of the mass of an atom of carbon-12.
  • Relative molecular mass is the sum of relative atomic masses of all atoms in the molecular formula.
  • Formula for relative atomic mass = sum of (isotopic mass × relative abundance) ÷ total abundance.
  • Chlorine-35 and chlorine-37 exist in a 3:1 ratio, producing molecular ion peaks at m/z 70, 72, and 74 with a 9:6:1 ratio.

Worked example: calculate the relative atomic mass of element X with isotopes 24X (78.9%), 25X (10.0%), and 26X (11.1%).

  • Step 1: Multiply each isotopic mass by its percentage abundance. (24 × 78.9) = 1893.6; (25 × 10.0) = 250.0; (26 × 11.1) = 288.6.
  • Step 2: Sum these values. 1893.6 + 250.0 + 288.6 = 2432.2.
  • Step 3: Divide by 100. 2432.2 ÷ 100 = 24.3 to 3 significant figures.

Ionisation Energies and Quantum Evidence

First ionisation energy is the energy required to remove one mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous atoms to form one mole of gaseous 1+ ions. Second and third ionisation energies remove subsequent moles of electrons from 1+ and 2+ gaseous ions respectively. All ionisation energies are endothermic because energy must be put in to overcome the electrostatic attraction between the outer electrons and the positive nucleus. Ionisation energies are influenced by the positive nuclear charge, electron shielding from inner shells, and the distance of the sub-shell from the nucleus. Successive ionisation energies provide decisive evidence for quantum shells and the group number because a large jump occurs when an electron is removed from a shell closer to the nucleus. The first ionisation energy trend across successive elements provides direct evidence for electron sub-shells.

  • First ionisation energy equation: X (g) yields X+ (g) + e−.
  • Second ionisation energy equation: X+ (g) yields X2+ (g) + e−.
  • Endothermic process: ΔH is positive.
  • Nuclear charge increases across a period, increasing attraction.
  • Shielding increases down a group, decreasing attraction.

Orbitals, Sub-shells and Electronic Configurations

An orbital is a region within an atom that can hold up to two electrons with opposite spins. Orbitals in sub-shells each take a single electron before pairing up with two electrons of opposite spin. Orbitals come in different shapes: s-orbitals are spherical, and p-orbitals are dumbbell-shaped along x, y, and z axes. Sub-shells are designated s, p, d, and f. The first four quantum shells hold maximums of 2, 8, 18, and 32 electrons respectively, corresponding to 1, 4, 9, and 16 orbitals. You can predict electronic configurations from hydrogen to krypton inclusive and their ions using s, p, d notation and electron-in-boxes notation. Electronic configuration determines the chemical properties of an element because elements in the same group share outer shell configurations. The Periodic Table is divided into blocks corresponding to the sub-shell containing the highest energy electron.

  • s-block: groups 1 and 2, outer electrons in s-orbitals.
  • p-block: groups 13 to 18, outer electrons in p-orbitals.
  • d-block: transition metals, outer electrons in d-sub-shells.
  • Hunds rule: electrons fill singly before pairing in degenerate orbitals.
  • Transition metal ion formation: 4s electrons are lost before 3d electrons.

Worked example: write the electronic configuration of a titanium atom (atomic number 22) and a titanium 2+ ion.

  • Step 1: Follow the filling order up to 22 electrons. 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d2.
  • Step 2: When forming the 2+ ion, remove electrons from the highest principal quantum number first. Remove 2 electrons from the 4s sub-shell.
  • Step 3: Write the ionic configuration as 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 3d2.

Periodic Trends and Graphical Data

Data represented graphically, including logarithms of first ionisation energies for elements 1 to 36, demonstrate the periodic nature of properties. A periodic property is one that repeats in a regular pattern across periods. Across periods 2 and 3, melting and boiling temperatures depend on structure and bonding: giant metallic structures have high melting points, giant covalent structures have very high melting points due to strong covalent bonds, and simple molecular structures have low melting and boiling points due to weak intermolecular forces. First ionisation energies generally increase across periods due to increasing nuclear charge and constant shielding, with slight drops between group 2 and 13 due to sub-shell changes, and between group 15 and 16 due to spin-pairing repulsion. First ionisation energy decreases down a group due to increased atomic radius and shielding.

  • Period 2 and 3 trends: metallic bonding peaks at group 13, covalent macromolecular peaks at group 14, simple molecules drop sharply at group 15 or 16.
  • Group 2 to 13 drop: outer electron enters a higher-energy p-sub-shell, which is further shielded by the s-sub-shell.
  • Group 15 to 16 drop: pairing of electrons in a p-orbital causes mutual repulsion, making it easier to remove.
  • Logarithm graphs of ionisation energy clearly show the periodicity of quantum shells.

Typical mistakes

  • Mistake: Stating that ionisation energy is exothermic because energy is released. Correction: Ionisation energy is always endothermic because energy is required to overcome the electrostatic attraction between electrons and protons.
  • Mistake: Removing 3d electrons before 4s electrons when ionising transition metal atoms. Correction: Always remove 4s electrons first because the 4s orbital is of higher energy once filling is complete and sits further out.
  • Mistake: Confusing mass number with relative atomic mass. Correction: Mass number is a whole number representing protons plus neutrons in a specific isotope, whereas relative atomic mass is a weighted mean of all naturally occurring isotopes.
  • Mistake: Forgetting that a chlorine mass spectrum has peaks for Cl2 molecules, not just chlorine atoms. Correction: Diatomic chlorine molecules produce molecular ion peaks at m/z 70, 72, and 74 based on combinations of Cl-35 and Cl-37.

Exam-style questions

  1. Define the term first ionisation energy. Answer: The energy required to remove one mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous atoms to form one mole of gaseous 1+ ions. (Earns 2 marks for stating moles of gas and 1+ ions).
  2. Explain why the first ionisation energy of oxygen is lower than that of nitrogen. Answer: Nitrogen has a half-filled 2p3 sub-shell configuration, whereas oxygen has a 2p4 configuration with paired electrons. The mutual repulsion of the paired electrons in oxygen makes the electron easier to remove. (Earns credit for mentioning electron pairing and repulsion).
  3. Calculate the relative atomic mass of magnesium given isotopes: Mg-24 (78.99%), Mg-25 (10.00%), Mg-26 (11.01%). Answer: ((24 × 78.99) + (25 × 10.00) + (26 × 11.01)) ÷ 100 = 24.3 to 1 decimal place. (Earns credit for correct working and units).
  4. State and explain the trend in first ionisation energy down Group 2. Answer: First ionisation energy decreases down Group 2 because atoms have more quantum shells, increasing atomic radius and electron shielding, which outweighs the increased nuclear charge and reduces outer shell attraction. (Earns credit for naming shielding, distance, and attraction).
  5. Write the full electronic configuration for a chromium atom, atomic number 24, using s, p, d notation. Answer: 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s1 3d5. (Earns credit for the stable half-filled d-sub-shell exception).

Use these notes alongside active recall and past paper question practice. Focus next on mastering redox equations and stoichiometry in Topic 3.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Relative atomic mass, applied to chlorine with 75% ³⁵Cl and 25% ³⁷Cl: (35 × 75 + 37 × 25) ÷ 100 = 35.5. Multiply each mass by its abundance as a fraction, then divide by 100. Give the answer to one decimal place when the abundances are given to two significant figures.
  • Electron configuration traps: chromium is [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹ and copper is [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹, because half-filled and full d sub-shells are unusually stable. Fe²⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁶: the 4s electrons are removed first when a transition metal forms an ion, even though 4s fills first.
  • Ionisation energy dip, applied to Mg to Al: aluminium's outer electron is in a 3p sub-shell, which is higher in energy than 3s, so less energy removes it. The dip at O compared with N occurs because O has a paired 2p electron, and the repulsion between the paired electrons makes it easier to remove. Name the sub-shell or the repulsion in the answer.
  • Successive ionisation energies: a large jump between two values shows the electron has moved to a new, inner shell. For example, a jump between the second and third values for an element with two outer electrons identifies it as Group 2.

title: AS Level Chemistry: Formulae, Equations and Amount of Substance
content:
AS Level Chemistry: Formulae, Equations and Amount of Substance

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH11, Topic 1 is the quantitative foundation of the whole course: every later topic, from titrations to equilibria to organic mechanisms, is marked using the ideas here. This topic covers the vocabulary of formulae, relative masses and the mole, balanced and ionic equations with state symbols, concentration in mol dm⁻³ and ppm, empirical and molecular formulae from experimental data, reacting masses, gas volumes including pV = nRT, percentage yield and atom economy, and the two core practicals that turn these ideas into measurements.

The language of formulae

Chemistry names substances at three levels: the particle, the formula and the amount. The vocabulary is examined directly, so learn the definitions precisely.

  • Atom: the smallest particle of an element that can take part in a chemical reaction.
  • Element: a substance containing only one type of atom; it cannot be broken down chemically into anything simpler.
  • Ion: a particle with a charge produced when an atom or group of atoms loses or gains electrons.
  • Molecule: two or more atoms joined by covalent bonds; it is the smallest particle of a covalent substance that can exist independently.
  • Compound: a substance containing two or more elements chemically combined in fixed proportions.
  • Empirical formula: the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound.
  • Molecular formula: the actual number of atoms of each element in one molecule of a compound.

A molecular formula is a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula. Hydrogen peroxide has the empirical formula HO and the molecular formula H₂O₂; ethanoic acid has the empirical formula CH₂O and the molecular formula C₂H₄O₂. Compounds with giant structures, such as sodium chloride or silicon dioxide, have no molecules, so they are described by their empirical formula alone.

Relative masses and the mole

Relative atomic mass, Aᵣ, is the weighted mean mass of the atoms of an element compared with one twelfth of the mass of an atom of carbon-12. Because it is a mean, it takes account of the natural abundances of the isotopes, which is why chlorine has Aᵣ = 35.5 rather than a whole number.

Relative molecular mass, Mᵣ, is the sum of the relative atomic masses in a molecule. For compounds with giant structures, use the term relative formula mass instead: NaCl has a relative formula mass of 23.0 + 35.5 = 58.5. Molar mass, M, is the mass per mole of a substance in g mol⁻¹, and it is numerically equal to Mᵣ or the relative formula mass.

The mole is the unit for amount of substance. One mole contains the Avogadro number of particles, L = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹. Three relationships do nearly all the work in this topic:

RelationshipUse it for
n = m / Mconverting a mass in grams to moles, and back
N = n × Lconverting moles to a number of particles
n = c × V / 1000moles from concentration in mol dm⁻³ and volume in cm³

Worked example. How many molecules are in 4.40 g of carbon dioxide? M(CO₂) = 12.0 + 2(16.0) = 44.0 g mol⁻¹, so n = 4.40 / 44.0 = 0.100 mol. Then N = 0.100 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 6.02 × 10²² molecules. The number of oxygen atoms is twice that, 1.20 × 10²³, because each molecule holds two oxygen atoms.

Balanced equations, state symbols and ionic equations

A balanced equation has the same number of atoms of each element on both sides, and the total charge must balance too. State symbols (s), (l), (g) and (aq) are part of the answer, not decoration: they are how you show that, for example, a reaction produces hydrogen gas rather than hydrogen atoms. Never change a formula to balance an equation; change only the coefficients. Balance the elements that appear once first, leave hydrogen and oxygen until the end, and check by counting a polyatomic ion such as sulfate or nitrate as one unit.

Ionic equations show only the species that change. To construct one, write the full equation, split every soluble ionic compound into its ions, then cancel the ions that appear unchanged on both sides. Those unchanged ions are spectator ions.

Worked example. Silver nitrate solution added to sodium chloride solution:

AgNO3(aq) + NaCl(aq) → AgCl(s) + NaNO3(aq)
Ag+(aq) + NO3−(aq) + Na+(aq) + Cl−(aq) → AgCl(s) + Na+(aq) + NO3−(aq)
Ag+(aq) + Cl−(aq) → AgCl(s)

Sodium and nitrate ions appear on both sides unchanged, so they are spectators. The ionic equation shows the actual change: hydrated silver ions meeting chloride ions to form a white precipitate.

You must be able to link equations to test-tube observations. Displacement reactions, typical acid reactions and precipitation reactions all follow this pattern: the observation is a change in appearance, and the equation explains it.

ObservationIonic equation
Magnesium added to dilute hydrochloric acid: fizzing, metal dissolves, gas pops with a lighted splintMg(s) + 2H+(aq) → Mg2+(aq) + H2(g)
Zinc added to copper(II) sulfate solution: blue colour fades, red-brown solid formsZn(s) + Cu2+(aq) → Zn2+(aq) + Cu(s)
Barium chloride solution added to sodium sulfate solution: white precipitateBa2+(aq) + SO42−(aq) → BaSO4(s)
Calcium carbonate added to nitric acid: fizzing, solid dissolves, gas turns limewater milkyCaCO3(s) + 2H+(aq) → Ca2+(aq) + H2O(l) + CO2(g)

Concentration, dilution and ppm

Concentration is the amount of solute per unit volume of solution. Two units are used and both are examinable:

  • mol dm⁻³ (molarity): moles of solute per cubic decimetre of solution. 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³.
  • g dm⁻³: mass of solute per cubic decimetre of solution.

The bridge between them is molar mass: g dm⁻³ = mol dm⁻³ × M. So 0.250 mol dm⁻³ sodium hydroxide contains 0.250 × 40.0 = 10.0 g dm⁻³.

Worked example. 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ sodium hydroxide is diluted to 250 cm³. The moles of solute do not change: n = 0.100 × 25.0 / 1000 = 2.50 × 10⁻³ mol. The new concentration is 2.50 × 10⁻³ / 0.250 = 0.0100 mol dm⁻³. Diluting tenfold divides the concentration by ten.

Parts per million, ppm, expresses very small proportions and is used for trace gases in the atmosphere and impurities in water. One ppm means one part in a million by mass or by volume, depending on the context:

ppm = (mass of component / mass of sample) × 10⁶

If the atmosphere contains 410 ppm of carbon dioxide and the total pressure is 100 kPa, the partial pressure of carbon dioxide is 410 / 10⁶ × 100 kPa = 0.0410 kPa. The same number treated as a volume fraction gives 0.041 % by volume.

Empirical and molecular formulae from experiment

Experimental data is converted into a formula in four steps: mass, moles, simplify, then scale using the molar mass.

Worked example. A compound contains 40.0 % carbon, 6.7 % hydrogen and 53.3 % oxygen by mass, and its molar mass is 180 g mol⁻¹.

ElementMass in 100 gDivide by AᵣDivide by smallest
C40.040.0 / 12.0 = 3.331
H6.76.7 / 1.0 = 6.672
O53.353.3 / 16.0 = 3.331

The empirical formula is CH₂O, with empirical formula mass 30.0. The molecular formula is (CH₂O)n where n = 180 / 30.0 = 6, so the molecular formula is C6H12O6. Always check that a ratio such as 1 : 1.5 is multiplied through to 2 : 3 before writing a formula.

Two related experiments are examined. In a magnesium oxide determination, a known mass of magnesium is burned in a crucible, the lid is lifted periodically to let air in, and the mass of the white powder is found; the increase in mass is the mass of oxygen that combined. In a water-of-crystallisation determination, a hydrated salt is heated to constant mass and the loss in mass is the water driven off, giving the value of x in a formula such as CuSO4·xH2O. In both cases heating to constant mass is essential, and in both the evaluation should name the errors: some magnesium oxide may escape as smoke, magnesium may react with nitrogen in the air to form a nitride, or the heating may not have removed all the water.

Reacting masses

A reacting-mass calculation follows the same route every time: balance the equation, convert the known mass to moles, use the mole ratio, convert back to a mass.

Worked example. What mass of iron is produced when 8.00 g of iron(III) oxide is reduced by carbon monoxide?

Fe2O3 + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO2

M(Fe₂O₃) = 2(55.8) + 3(16.0) = 159.6 g mol⁻¹, so n(Fe₂O₃) = 8.00 / 159.6 = 0.0501 mol. The ratio is 1 : 2, so n(Fe) = 0.100 mol and m(Fe) = 0.100 × 55.8 = 5.59 g. Notice that the mass of the solid fell: the oxygen was removed as carbon dioxide, and mass is conserved because the carbon dioxide carries it away.

Where two reactant amounts are given, one will be limiting. Calculate the moles of each, divide by the coefficient in the balanced equation, and the smaller quotient is the limiting reactant. The other is in excess and does not take part fully. All product calculations use the limiting reactant.

Gas volumes, molar volume and pV = nRT

One mole of any gas occupies the same volume at the same temperature and pressure. At room temperature and pressure, this molar volume is approximately 24 dm³ mol⁻¹, so 0.0500 mol of any gas occupies 1.20 dm³. Use this only when the conditions are stated as room temperature and pressure.

When conditions differ, use the ideal gas equation:

pV = nRT

In this equation p is in pascals, V in m³, n in moles, T in kelvin and R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Unit conversion causes most lost marks: 1 kPa = 1000 Pa, 1 dm³ = 1 × 10⁻³ m³, and T = θ + 273.

Worked example. A 0.250 g sample of a volatile liquid is vaporised in a syringe at 100 °C and 100 kPa, and occupies 97 cm³. Find its molar mass.

p = 100 000 Pa, V = 97 × 10⁻⁶ m³, T = 373 K. Then n = pV / RT = (100000 × 97 × 10⁻⁶) / (8.31 × 373) = 9.7 / 3099 = 3.13 × 10⁻³ mol. M = m / n = 0.250 / 3.13 × 10⁻³ = 79.9 g mol⁻¹, so the liquid is likely a small molecule such as benzene (Mᵣ = 78).

Percentage yield and atom economy

Percentage yield compares what you actually obtained with the maximum the equation allows:

percentage yield = (actual yield / theoretical yield) × 100

Reasons for a yield below 100 % include incomplete reaction, reversible reactions, loss during transfer or filtration, side reactions producing other products, and impurities in the reactants.

Atom economy asks a different question: how much of the mass of all the reactants ends up in the product you want?

atom economy = (molar mass of desired product / sum of molar masses of all products) × 100

Worked example. Ethene is hydrated to ethanol: C2H4 + H2O → C2H5OH. The only product is ethanol, so the atom economy is 100 %, even though the yield may be well below that because the reaction is reversible. Compare the synthesis of bromoethane from ethene and hydrogen bromide: C2H4 + HBr → C2H5Br also has 100 % atom economy. In a reaction such as CH4 + Cl2 → CH3Cl + HCl, the desired product has Mᵣ = 50.5 and the products total 50.5 + 36.5 = 87.0, so the atom economy is 58.0 %. The HCl is a co-product with little value, which is why industry prefers addition reactions to substitutions.

Core Practical 1: measurement of the molar volume of a gas

A known mass of magnesium ribbon reacts with excess dilute hydrochloric acid and the hydrogen is collected in a gas syringe. The apparatus is assembled and checked for leaks, the acid is added, and the final syringe reading is taken once the reaction has finished and the apparatus has cooled to room temperature.

Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl2(aq) + H2(g)

Calculation. If 0.024 g of magnesium gives 24.0 cm³ of hydrogen, n(Mg) = 0.024 / 24.3 = 9.88 × 10⁻⁴ mol, and the ratio is 1 : 1, so n(H₂) is the same. The molar volume is 24.0 / 9.88 × 10⁻⁴ = 24 300 cm³ mol⁻¹ = 24.3 dm³ mol⁻¹, close to the accepted 24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹ at room temperature and pressure.

Evaluation. The main sources of error are gas escaping before the bung is replaced, a syringe that sticks or leaks, the temperature not being room temperature when the reading is taken, and the small mass of magnesium producing a large percentage uncertainty in mass. Using a larger mass of magnesium reduces the percentage uncertainty but needs a larger syringe.

Typical mistakes

  • Using the mass of a solution rather than the mass of solute, or forgetting to divide by 1000 when converting cm³ to dm³.
  • Rounding an empirical formula ratio such as 1 : 2.5 to 1 : 3 instead of doubling it to 2 : 5.
  • Changing a subscript to balance an equation instead of the coefficient in front of the formula.
  • Leaving state symbols out of an equation when the question asks for a full equation, or including spectator ions in an ionic equation.
  • Forgetting to convert temperature to kelvin, or pressure to pascals, in pV = nRT.
  • Using the actual yield as the theoretical yield in a percentage-yield calculation.
  • Calculating atom economy from the reactants rather than from the products.

Exam-style questions

  1. Define the terms empirical formula and molecular formula, using a compound of your choice to show the difference. Answer: the empirical formula is the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element; the molecular formula is the actual number of atoms of each element in a molecule. Ethanoic acid has the empirical formula CH2O and the molecular formula C2H4O2.
  2. 0.500 g of a hydrated salt, MgSO4·xH2O, is heated to constant mass and 0.244 g of anhydrous magnesium sulfate remains. Find x. Answer: mass of water lost = 0.500 − 0.244 = 0.256 g. n(MgSO4) = 0.244 / 120.4 = 2.03 × 10⁻³ mol; n(H2O) = 0.256 / 18.0 = 1.42 × 10⁻² mol. The ratio is 1.42 × 10⁻² / 2.03 × 10⁻³ = 7.0, so x = 7 and the formula is MgSO4·7H2O.
  3. Write the ionic equation, with state symbols, for the reaction between aqueous sodium carbonate and dilute hydrochloric acid, and state one observation. Answer: CO32−(aq) + 2H+(aq) → CO2(g) + H2O(l); effervescence, and the gas turns limewater milky.
  4. 25.0 cm³ of 0.150 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid is neutralised by 0.100 mol dm⁻³ sodium hydroxide. Calculate the volume of alkali required. Answer: n(HCl) = 0.150 × 25.0 / 1000 = 3.75 × 10⁻³ mol. HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H2O, so n(NaOH) = 3.75 × 10⁻³ mol and V = n / c = 3.75 × 10⁻³ / 0.100 = 0.0375 dm³ = 37.5 cm³.
  5. Explain why the percentage yield of a reaction can be less than 100 %, and why a reaction with a high percentage yield can still have a low atom economy. Answer: the yield is reduced by incomplete reaction, side reactions, losses in transfer and purification, or by the reaction being reversible. Atom economy depends only on the balanced equation, so a reaction can convert nearly all the limiting reactant into products while most of the product mass is an unwanted co-product.

Revise this topic by practising calculations with the units written at every step, because each mark scheme rewards the mole ratio and the correct final unit as much as the numerical answer. Next, move to Atomic Structure and the Periodic Table, where the mole is used again for relative atomic mass and mass spectra.

title: IGCSE Physics: Waves and Sound
content:
IGCSE Physics: Waves and Sound

Cambridge IGCSE Physics 0625 (2026–2028), Topic 3 Waves: statements 3.1 General properties of waves, 3.2 Light, 3.3 Electromagnetic spectrum and 3.4 Sound. Waves are how energy travels from place to place without moving matter along with it, and everything from a ripple on a pond to a gamma ray obeys the same few rules. This note builds the general wave behaviour first, then light (reflection, refraction, lenses, colour), then the electromagnetic spectrum and finally sound, with the calculations and the ray constructions that Paper 4 and Paper 6 reward.

General properties of waves

A wave transfers energy without transferring matter. Drop a cork into a ripple tank and the ripples pass under it while the cork only bobs: the water moves up and down, not outward. Every wave is described by the same vocabulary:

TermMeaningUnit
AmplitudeMaximum displacement from the rest position; relates to energy (loudness for sound, brightness for light)metre (m)
Wavelength (λ)Distance between two equivalent points on neighbouring waves, e.g. crest to crestmetre (m)
FrequencyNumber of complete waves passing a point per second; equals the source's number of oscillations per secondhertz (Hz)
PeriodTime for one complete wave to pass a pointsecond (s)
Wave speedDistance a wave crest travels per secondmetre per second (m s⁻¹)
wave speed = frequency x wavelength        v = fλ
period = 1 / frequency        T = 1 / f
  • v: wave speed in metres per second (m s⁻¹); f: frequency in hertz (Hz, = s⁻¹); λ: wavelength in metres (m). All scalars, so there are no signs to worry about — but all three quantities must be in SI units before multiplying.

Transverse waves have the vibration perpendicular to the direction of travel: water waves, light and all electromagnetic waves, waves on a shaken rope. Longitudinal waves have the vibration parallel to the direction of travel: sound in air, the push-pull of a slinky. Longitudinal waves show compressions (where particles are pushed together) and rarefactions (where they are spread apart).

Three behaviours describe what happens when waves meet things. Reflection is bouncing off a surface; the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, measured from the normal. Refraction is the change of direction when a wave passes into a different medium at an angle, because its speed changes; moving into a slower medium bends the ray towards the normal and the wavelength shortens while the frequency stays constant. Diffraction is the spreading of waves through a gap or around an obstacle, and it is most pronounced when the gap width is comparable to the wavelength. Ripple tanks demonstrate all three: straight barriers give reflection, shallow regions give refraction, and narrow gaps give circular wavefronts after diffraction (Supplement: wider gaps give less spreading, and an edge produces noticeable diffraction only for longer wavelengths).

Reflection of light

Light travels in straight lines and reflects from smooth surfaces with the law of reflection: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, both measured between the ray and the normal (an imaginary line perpendicular to the surface at the point of incidence). A plane-mirror image is upright, the same size as the object, laterally inverted (left and right swapped), and as far behind the mirror as the object is in front.

Supplement: the ray construction. To locate the image, draw a ray from the object to the mirror, continue it behind the mirror at the same angle, and drop a perpendicular from the image position to the mirror; repeat with a second ray. Where the reflected rays appear to come from behind the mirror is where the image sits. Drawing the construction to scale with a protractor gives the image position exactly.

Refraction of light

When light passes from air into glass at an angle it slows and bends towards the normal; passing back out it speeds up and bends away from the normal. The amount of bending is fixed by the material's refractive index:

refractive index = sin(angle of incidence in vacuum or air) / sin(angle of refraction)        n = sin i / sin r
critical angle:        sin c = 1 / n
  • n: refractive index, a scalar with no unit, always greater than 1 for a material like glass or water.
  • i and r: angles in degrees measured from the normal, not from the surface.
  • c: critical angle in degrees, defined for a ray passing from the material into air.

Total internal reflection happens when a ray inside a material hits the boundary at an angle greater than the critical angle: none of it escapes and all reflects. Two applications are examinable: optical fibres, where light bounces along the core with total internal reflection and carries data over long distances with little loss, and prisms in periscopes and binoculars, where a 45° prism turns light through 90° or 180° by total internal reflection with almost no energy loss compared with a mirror.

Thin lenses and vision

A converging lens brings parallel rays to a focus at its principal focus; a diverging lens spreads them out as if they came from a focus on the near side. Three standard rays build any image on a converging lens:

  • A ray parallel to the axis refracts through the principal focus on the far side.
  • A ray through the centre of the lens passes straight through undeviated.
  • A ray through the near-side principal focus emerges parallel to the axis.

Where two refracted rays cross, a real image forms — it can be shown on a screen. Where they only appear to diverge from a point behind the lens, a virtual image forms — it cannot be caught on a screen and is seen only by looking through the lens. An object beyond twice the focal length gives a smaller inverted real image (a camera); an object between the focus and the lens gives a larger upright virtual image (a magnifying glass, Supplement). Short sight (myopia) is corrected with a diverging lens, long sight (hyperopia) with a converging lens (Supplement).

Dispersion and the electromagnetic spectrum

White light passing through a prism disperses into a spectrum from red to violet because different colours refract by different amounts: red light is refracted least (it travels fastest in glass) and violet most. Light of a single colour is monochromatic (Supplement). The visible spectrum sits inside a much larger family — the electromagnetic spectrum, all waves travelling at 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ in a vacuum, all transverse, arranged by increasing frequency (and decreasing wavelength) as: radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays.

RegionWavelength scaleUsesHazards
Radio wavesmetres to hundreds of metresRadio and TV broadcasting, communicationsLittle evidence of harm at normal levels
Microwavesmillimetres to centimetresMobile phones, satellite communications, microwave ovens, radarHeating of body tissue; dangerous at high intensity
InfraredmicrometresHeating, night-vision cameras, remote controls, optical fibresBurns and skin heating at high intensity
Visible light400–700 nmVision, photography, fibre-optic dataDazzle; eye damage from lasers and the Sun
Ultraviolet10–400 nmFluorescent lamps, sterilisation, security markingSunburn, skin ageing and skin cancer, eye damage
X-rays0.01–10 nmMedical imaging, airport security, detecting cracks in metalIonising: cell damage and cancer risk; dose kept low
Gamma raysbelow 0.01 nmSterilising equipment, cancer radiotherapy, food irradiationIonising: severe cell damage; shielded with lead and concrete

Supplement: signals and communication. An analogue signal varies continuously with the quantity it carries; a digital signal is a stream of on/off pulses. Digital signals are preferred because they can be regenerated without amplifying noise, can be compressed to carry more information, can be encrypted, and can carry text, sound and images in the same stream. Satellite links work by beaming a microwave signal to an orbiting satellite, which amplifies and retransmits it back to a distant ground station.

Sound

Sound is a longitudinal wave produced by vibrating objects and travelling through a medium — air at about 340 m s⁻¹ at room temperature, faster in liquids and fastest in solids, because the particles are closer together and pass the vibration on more quickly. Sound cannot travel through a vacuum. The frequency of a sound sets its pitch (high frequency, high pitch), and the amplitude sets its loudness. The human range of hearing is roughly 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz.

Echoes and distance measurement. Sound reflects from hard surfaces, giving echoes. The depth of the sea under a ship is found by sending a pulse and timing its return:

distance to the surface = (speed of sound x total time) / 2        s = v t / 2

The halving is essential — the pulse travels down and back — and forgetting it is the classic error in this topic. Measuring the time between two microphones a known distance apart gives the speed of sound directly: v = distance/time.

Ultrasound is sound above the human hearing range (above 20 kHz). Its short wavelength means it reflects well from small internal boundaries, which makes it useful for prenatal scanning (reflection at tissue boundaries builds an image), cleaning delicate items (high-energy vibrations dislodge dirt), flaw detection in metal castings (an internal crack reflects the pulse), and sonar depth sounding. All uses share the same principle: send a pulse, time the echo, calculate the distance with s = vt/2.

Worked example: wave calculation and echo depth

A ship's sonar sends ultrasound of frequency 50 kHz. The echo returns from the seabed after 0.12 s. The speed of sound in seawater is 1500 m s⁻¹.

total distance travelled = v t = 1500 × 0.12 = 180 m
depth of the sea = 180 / 2 = 90 m

Second calculation: a ripple tank wave has a wavelength of 0.040 m and the dippers oscillate 25 times per second. The wave speed is v = f λ = 25 × 0.040 = 1.0 m s⁻¹. The frequency of the wave equals the frequency of the source, and it stays unchanged when the wave passes into deeper water — only the speed and the wavelength change there.

Common mistakes

  • Measuring a wavelength from crest to trough; that is half a wavelength. Measure between two equivalent points on neighbouring waves.
  • Forgetting that frequency never changes on refraction. The speed and wavelength change; the frequency is set by the source and stays constant.
  • Mixing up the angle of incidence with its complement: all angles in reflection and refraction are measured from the normal.
  • Using v = fλ with mismatched units: hertz times centimetres gives cm s⁻¹, not m s⁻¹. Convert the wavelength to metres first.
  • Forgetting to halve the total distance in an echo calculation.
  • Drawing a converging lens ray diagram without the two special rays, or putting the image on the wrong side: real images form on the far side where rays actually cross, virtual images on the same side as the object.
  • Claiming light travels slower in a vacuum than in glass; it is fastest in a vacuum and slower in denser media, which is what causes refraction.
  • Describing a digital signal as continuously varying; it is discrete pulses, which is precisely why it resists noise.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 4, 3 marks). A water wave has a frequency of 4.0 Hz and a wavelength of 0.25 m. Calculate its speed and its period.

Answer: v = fλ = 4.0 × 0.25 = 1.0 m s⁻¹. Period T = 1/f = 1/4.0 = 0.25 s.

Question 2 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Explain why sound cannot be heard on the Moon but sunlight still reaches it.

Answer: Sound is a longitudinal wave that needs a medium, because it travels by particles passing vibrations to their neighbours. The Moon is surrounded by a vacuum, with no particles to carry the vibration, so sound cannot travel there. Light is an electromagnetic transverse wave that carries energy without needing a medium, so it crosses the vacuum of space easily.

Question 3 (Paper 2 style). Light passes from air into glass at an angle. Which quantity does not change? A speed; B wavelength; C frequency; D direction. Answer: C. The frequency is set by the source and is unchanged; speed and wavelength both fall in glass and the ray bends.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Ultrasound of speed 1500 m s⁻¹ is used to find the depth of the sea. The echo returns in 0.40 s. Calculate the depth and explain why ultrasound is used rather than audible sound.

Answer: Depth = v t / 2 = 1500 × 0.40 / 2 = 300 m. Ultrasound has a very short wavelength, so it reflects well from small boundaries and gives a clear echo pattern without diffracting uselessly around small features; it also does not interfere with ordinary sound and is harmless at the intensities used.

Question 5 (Paper 6 style). Describe how to measure the speed of sound in air using two microphones and a data logger.

Answer: Place two microphones a measured distance apart in a straight line from a sound source (a clapping board or signal generator and loudspeaker). Trigger the data logger with the sound at each microphone and record the time interval between the arrivals, or display both pulses on an oscilloscope and measure the time from the trace. Speed is the distance between the microphones divided by the time interval. Repeat at several separations and find the speed from the gradient of a distance–time graph, which averages out the reaction error.

Question 6 (Paper 4, 3 marks). State two differences between a transverse and a longitudinal wave, and give one example of each.

Answer: In a transverse wave the vibrations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer; in a longitudinal wave they are parallel to it. Transverse waves have crests and troughs; longitudinal waves have compressions and rarefactions. Examples: light (transverse) and sound in air (longitudinal).

Waves carry energy without matter; the next topic is the energy that drives circuits: Electricity and Circuits.

Equations and symbols

One equation, v = fλ, carries the whole of wave physics; the rest of this topic is refraction, the lens and the echo. Frequency and period are reciprocals, so a question that gives one and asks for the other is testing whether you inverted it correctly.

The wave equation

v = fλ
Key: v = wave speed (m/s); f = frequency (Hz, waves per second); λ (λ) = wavelength (m). The speed is set by the medium, so when a wave crosses into a new medium f stays the same and λ changes.

f = 1 / T
Key: f = frequency (Hz); T = period, the time for one complete oscillation (s). A 0.004 s period is 250 Hz.

T = 1 / f
Key: the same relation rearranged; T in seconds, f in hertz.

d = vt
Key: d = distance travelled by the wave (m); v = wave speed (m/s); t = time (s). For an echo the sound travels to the surface and back, so the distance to the surface is half of vt.

s = vt / 2
Key: s = distance to the reflecting surface (m); v = speed of sound in the medium (m/s); t = total time between the pulse and its echo (s). The factor of 2 is the most frequently dropped mark in echo questions.

v(sound in air) ≈ 340 m/s and v(light in vacuum) = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s
Key: the two speeds that explain thunder arriving after lightning; light is nearly a million times faster, so the flash is seen almost instantly.

audible range for a human = 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz
Key: f below 20 Hz is infrasound and above 20 kHz is ultrasound; both are outside human hearing but ultrasound is used in medical scanning and sonar.

Refraction

n = sin i / sin r
Key: n = refractive index of the material (no unit); i = angle of incidence in the less dense medium, measured from the normal (°); r = angle of refraction in the material (°). Both angles are always measured from the normal, never from the surface.

n = 1 / sin c
Key: c = critical angle (°), the angle of incidence in the denser medium for which the refracted ray runs along the surface. A larger n means a smaller critical angle.

n = c / v
Key: c = speed of light in a vacuum (3.0 × 10⁸ m/s); v = speed of light in the material (m/s). Light slows on entering a denser medium, which is what bends it towards the normal.

total internal reflection when i > c
Key: i = angle of incidence inside the denser medium (°); c = critical angle (°). Beyond c no light escapes, which is the rule behind optical fibres and reflecting prisms.

Lenses and images

m = h(image) / h(object)
