  2. Ratio CaCO₃ : CaO is 1 : 1, so moles of calcium oxide = 0.250 mol.
  3. Mass of calcium oxide: m = n × M = 0.250 × 56 = 14.0 g.

The same method handles a ratio that is not 1 : 1. For 4.00 g of hydrogen burning in excess oxygen, 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O: n(H₂) = 4.00 ÷ 2 = 2.00 mol, the ratio is 2 : 2 so n(H₂O) = 2.00 mol, and m = 2.00 × 18 = 36.0 g. Skipping the ratio would give 36.0 g anyway here, which is exactly why an examiner chooses examples where it does not: try methane, CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O, where 1 mol of methane gives 2 mol of water and the missing factor of two is the error being tested.

Two checks catch most mistakes: the mass of the product cannot exceed the total mass of the reactants, and a quick estimate of the molar masses tells you the right order of magnitude before any calculation.

7. Limiting reactants

In a real reaction the reactants are rarely present in exactly the ratio the equation requires, so one of them runs out first. That one is the limiting reactant, and it decides how much product can form; the other is in excess and some of it will be left over.

The method is to convert both amounts to moles, then divide each by its coefficient in the equation. The smallest result is the limiting reactant. For example, 0.20 mol of magnesium is heated with 0.050 mol of oxygen in 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO:

  • Magnesium: 0.20 ÷ 2 = 0.10.
  • Oxygen: 0.050 ÷ 1 = 0.050.

Oxygen gives the smaller value, so oxygen is limiting. Working from it, 0.050 mol of O₂ produces 0.100 mol of MgO, which is m = n × M = 0.100 × 40 = 4.0 g. Working from the magnesium instead would predict 0.20 mol of MgO and 8.0 g, which is more product than the available oxygen allows — the classic error, and the reason the calculation must start from the limiting reactant.

The industrial version of the same idea is using an excess of one reactant deliberately: in the blast furnace, carbon monoxide is supplied in excess so that all the iron oxide is reduced, because unreacted ore is worthless and the gas is cheap.

8. Percentage yield

Yield compares what you actually obtained with the maximum the equation allows, which is the theoretical yield calculated from the limiting reactant:

percentage yield = actual yield ÷ theoretical yield × 100 → Key: both masses are in grams (or both in moles, but never one of each); the result is a percentage of the theoretical maximum.

If 25.0 g of calcium carbonate should give 14.0 g of calcium oxide and a student collects 11.2 g, the yield is 11.2 ÷ 14.0 × 100 = 80.0 %. A yield above 100 % is impossible and always means the product is wet or impure, which is a standard exam question.

Yields are never 100 % in practice, for reasons worth learning as a list: the reaction may be reversible, so it never goes to completion; some product is lost in transferring between vessels, or left on filter paper; side reactions may convert some reactant to a different product; and the product may be impure or partly decomposed during drying. A high yield is a commercial advantage because the reactants were paid for, which is why industrial processes are designed around it.

9. Atom economy

Yield asks how much of the expected product you got. Atom economy asks a different question: of all the atoms you put in, how many ended up in the product you wanted?

percentage atom economy = (Mᵣ of the desired product ÷ total Mᵣ of all reactants) × 100 → Key: Mᵣ = relative formula mass (no units); the denominator is the sum of the Mᵣ of every reactant, as the equation is balanced, and by conservation of mass it equals the total Mᵣ of all products.

For CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂, the desired product is CaO at 56 and the only reactant is CaCO₃ at 100, so the atom economy is 56 ÷ 100 × 100 = 56.0 %. The other 44 %, a whole molecule of carbon dioxide, is waste — which is truthful, because that is what the process produces.

The distinction is worth stating clearly, because examiners test it: a reaction can have a 100 % atom economy and a poor yield if it is slow or reversible, and a reaction can have a poor atom economy and a perfect yield. For example, the preparation of an ester has a low atom economy because water is also produced, yet it may go essentially to completion; the displacement of copper by zinc has a good one but may leave copper behind in the apparatus. Industry prefers a high atom economy because it means less waste to dispose of and less reactant bought per kilogram of product, both of which are cost and environmental arguments.

10. Molar concentration

Concentration is the amount of solute per unit volume of solution, and the working unit is mol/dm³, sometimes written M. One cubic decimetre is one litre, so 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³ and a volume in cm³ is divided by 1000 to become dm³.

c = n ÷ V → Key: c = concentration (mol/dm³); n = amount of solute (mol); V = volume of solution (dm³, not cm³). Rearranged, n = c × V and V = n ÷ c.

For example, 4.0 g of sodium hydroxide dissolved to make 250 cm³ of solution: n = m ÷ M = 4.0 ÷ 40 = 0.100 mol; V = 250 ÷ 1000 = 0.250 dm³; c = n ÷ V = 0.100 ÷ 0.250 = 0.400 mol/dm³. In the other direction, 250 cm³ of 0.200 mol/dm³ copper(II) sulfate contains n = c × V = 0.200 × 0.250 = 0.0500 mol, which is m = n × M = 0.0500 × 160 = 8.0 g of CuSO₄.

Concentration is not the same as amount. A 0.100 mol/dm³ solution in a 25 cm³ pipette contains 0.00250 mol, while the same concentration in a 1 dm³ flask contains 0.100 mol; the concentration is identical, the amount is forty times greater. That confusion is the single commonest error in titration arithmetic.

11. Titration calculations

A titration gives two volumes of solution that just neutralise each other, and one known concentration; the calculation finds the other concentration. The sequence is always the same: moles of the known solution, ratio from the equation, moles of the unknown, then divide by its volume in dm³.

Example, 1 : 1 ratio. 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ sodium hydroxide is neutralised by 20.0 cm³ of hydrochloric acid. NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O, so the ratio is 1 : 1. Moles of alkali: n = c × V = 0.100 × 0.0250 = 0.00250 mol. Moles of acid = 0.00250 mol, and its volume is 20.0 ÷ 1000 = 0.0200 dm³. Then c = n ÷ V = 0.00250 ÷ 0.0200 = 0.125 mol/dm³.

Example, 2 : 1 ratio. The same alkali is neutralised by 12.5 cm³ of sulfuric acid. H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O, so one mole of acid neutralises two moles of alkali. Moles of alkali are still 0.00250 mol, so moles of acid = 0.00250 ÷ 2 = 0.00125 mol, and c = 0.00125 ÷ 0.0125 = 0.100 mol/dm³. Notice how the ratio is applied to moles before the division: dividing the concentration by two instead is the error this example exists to catch.

The practical side matters too. Two concordant titres within 0.1 cm³ are averaged, because a single reading can be spoiled by one drop past the end point, and a titre that is far from the others is discarded rather than averaged in.

12. Gas volumes

One mole of any gas occupies the same volume at the same temperature and pressure, because the volume depends on the number of particles rather than on their mass. At room temperature and pressure that volume is 24 dm³ (24 000 cm³) per mole, so:

n = V ÷ 24 → Key: n = amount of gas (mol); V = volume at room temperature and pressure (dm³); 24 = molar gas volume (dm³/mol) at RTP, and it changes if the temperature or pressure changes.

So 0.0500 mol of carbon dioxide at RTP occupies V = n × 24 = 1.20 dm³, which is 1200 cm³. Combined with a reacting-mass calculation, the same relation answers how much gas a reaction produces: 25.0 g of calcium carbonate decomposes to 0.250 mol of CO₂, which is 0.250 × 24 = 6.00 dm³ at RTP. The temperature has to be stated because 24 dm³ applies at 20 °C and 1 atm; at other conditions the same amount of gas occupies a different volume, which is why the units include the conditions implicitly.

13. Worked examples

Example 1. Calculate the percentage by mass of oxygen in copper(II) sulfate, CuSO₄.

Mᵣ = 63.5 + 32 + (4 × 16) = 159.5. Oxygen contributes 64, so the percentage is 64 ÷ 159.5 × 100 = 40.1 %. Rounding 63.5 to 64 would give 40.0 %, so keep the value you were given.

Example 2. 6.50 g of zinc reacts completely with dilute hydrochloric acid. Calculate the mass of zinc chloride formed. Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂.

n(Zn) = m ÷ M = 6.50 ÷ 65 = 0.100 mol. The ratio Zn : ZnCl₂ is 1 : 1, so n(ZnCl₂) = 0.100 mol. Mᵣ(ZnCl₂) = 65 + (2 × 35.5) = 136, so m = n × M = 0.100 × 136 = 13.6 g. The hydrogen escapes, which is why the mass of the solid product is greater than the mass of zinc that formed it — the chloride ions supplied the extra mass.

Example 3. A reaction has a theoretical yield of 14.0 g and produces 11.2 g. Calculate the percentage yield, and state one reason the yield is below 100 %.

Percentage yield = 11.2 ÷ 14.0 × 100 = 80.0 %. A reason: some product was left behind on the filter paper when it was transferred, or the reaction is reversible and did not go to completion.

Example 4. 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ sodium hydroxide is titrated with sulfuric acid and 12.5 cm³ is needed. Calculate the concentration of the acid, and its mass concentration in g/dm³.

n(NaOH) = c × V = 0.100 × 0.0250 = 0.00250 mol; the ratio in H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O is 1 : 2, so n(H₂SO₄) = 0.00250 ÷ 2 = 0.00125 mol; c = n ÷ V = 0.00125 ÷ 0.0125 = 0.100 mol/dm³. The molar mass of H₂SO₄ is 98, so the mass concentration is 0.100 × 98 = 9.8 g/dm³.

14. Exam-style questions

  1. Magnesium ribbon is burned in a crucible and the mass of the contents increases. Explain the increase in terms of the balanced equation. Answer: the magnesium combines with oxygen from the air, 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO, so oxygen atoms are added to the system; the mass increases by exactly the mass of oxygen that reacted, and mass is conserved because the oxygen was part of the surroundings rather than the crucible.
  2. Calculate the relative formula mass of aluminium sulfate, Al₂(SO₄)₃. Answer: 2 × 27 + 3 × (32 + 4 × 16) = 54 + 3 × 96 = 342.
  3. Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide produced when 50.0 g of calcium carbonate is heated. CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. Answer: n(CaCO₃) = 50.0 ÷ 100 = 0.500 mol; the ratio is 1 : 1 so n(CO₂) = 0.500 mol; m = n × M = 0.500 × 44 = 22.0 g.
  4. Explain why a yield greater than 100 % is impossible. Answer: the theoretical yield is the maximum allowed by the limiting reactant and by conservation of mass, so a measured yield above it means the product is impure or still wet rather than that extra product was formed.
  5. For the reaction 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl, calculate the atom economy. Answer: the desired product is NaCl with Mᵣ = 58.5 and two moles of it are formed, so the product mass is 117; the reactants are 2 × 23 + 71 = 117, so the atom economy is 117 ÷ 117 × 100 = 100 %, because there is only one product.
  6. 0.500 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid is used to make 2.00 dm³ of solution. Calculate the amount of acid in the solution and the mass of hydrogen chloride it contains. Answer: n = c × V = 0.500 × 2.00 = 1.00 mol; m = n × M = 1.00 × 36.5 = 36.5 g of HCl.
  7. 12.0 g of magnesium is burned in 8.00 g of oxygen. Which reactant is limiting, and what mass of magnesium oxide forms? Answer: n(Mg) = 12.0 ÷ 24 = 0.500 mol and 0.500 ÷ 2 = 0.250; n(O₂) = 8.00 ÷ 32 = 0.250 mol and 0.250 ÷ 1 = 0.250; the values are equal, so neither is in excess and 0.500 mol of MgO forms, which is m = 0.500 × 40 = 20.0 g.
  8. A student obtains 3.60 g of copper from 4.00 g of copper(II) oxide reduced by hydrogen, CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O. Calculate the percentage yield. Answer: the theoretical yield is n(CuO) = 4.00 ÷ 79.5 = 0.0503 mol, so m(Cu) = 0.0503 × 63.5 = 3.19 g; the yield would then be 3.60 ÷ 3.19 × 100 = 113 %, which is impossible, so the product must be contaminated — a result worth suspecting rather than accepting.

15. Common mistakes

  • Applying the equation's ratio to grams instead of moles. The ratio is between amounts, so both masses must be converted first.
  • Leaving a volume in cm³ when dividing by it. A concentration in mol/dm³ needs the volume in dm³, so divide by 1000 first.
  • Using the reactant that is in excess to calculate the product. Find the limiting reactant, then calculate from that.
  • Confusing yield with atom economy. Yield compares actual with theoretical product; atom economy compares the wanted product with everything the reaction makes.
  • Forgetting the water in a hydrated salt. CuSO₄·5H₂O has Mᵣ 250, not 160.
  • Rounding relative atomic masses before the last step, which shifts the answer by more than the tolerance allowed.
  • Balancing by changing a subscript. Changing H₂O to H₂O₂ changes the substance rather than the equation.
  • Writing a mass change as a failure of conservation. Name the gas that escaped or the oxygen that joined instead.

16. Exam technique for this topic

  • Write the three steps explicitly, every time: moles of what you know, ratio, moles of what you want. Most of the marks are awarded for the steps, not the final number.
  • Give the unit on every answer, and check it is the unit asked for — mol, g, g/dm³, mol/dm³, dm³ or a percentage.
  • Balance the equation before using it. An unbalanced equation gives the wrong ratio and the rest of the working inherits the error.
  • Quote answers to three significant figures unless the question says otherwise, and keep the unrounded value in the calculator until the end.
  • If the answer comes out absurd — a yield over 100 %, or a product heavier than all the reactants — say so; a sentence of comment often earns a mark on its own.
  • For an "explain" question about a mass change, use the words "closed system" and name what entered or left.

title: Earth & Space
content:
Earth & Space

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2023–2025): Earth & Solar System; stars & the Universe (Extended).

1. Earth, Moon, Sun

Earth rotates 24 h (day/night), orbits 365¼ d (year + leap). Moon orbits Earth ~27.3 d; phases from viewing angle; lunar/solar eclipses when aligned. Seasons from axial tilt (23.5°), not distance.

2. Solar system

Planets (Mercury → Neptune), dwarf planets (Pluto), moons, asteroids, comets (eccentric orbits, tails away from Sun), natural satellites. Gravity keeps orbits; orbital speed & radius relate to the central mass.

3. Orbital motion

Orbital speed v = 2πr/T. T grows with r (Kepler trend). Comets speed up near the Sun (ellipse, Sun at focus).

4. Stars (Extended)

Star formation: nebula → protostar (gravity, KE→thermal) → main sequence (hydrogen fusion: H→He, radiation pressure balances gravity) → red giant → white dwarf (Sun-mass) or supergiant → supernova → neutron star/black hole (massive stars). Elements heavier than iron form in supernovae.

5. Universe (Extended)

The Sun is one star in the Milky Way; the Milky Way is one of billions of galaxies. Redshift: receding galaxies show stretched wavelengths → the Universe is expanding → Big Bang model; CMB is the afterglow. Hubble: farther ⇒ faster recession.

6. Scales

light-year = distance light travels in a year (9.5 × 10¹⁵ m); astronomical unit = Earth–Sun distance (1.5 × 10¹¹ m).

title: Exponentials and Logarithms — Study Notes
content:
Exponentials and logarithms in calculus and modelling

Edexcel International A Level Mathematics — Pure Mathematics 3 (WMA13), sat at A2.

The A2 work on e^x and ln x adds calculus and rates of change to the AS algebraic toolkit.

Differentiation and integration

  • d/dx (e^(kx)) = k e^(kx); so d/dx (e^x) = e^x.
  • d/dx (ln x) = 1/x; by the chain rule d/dx (ln(ax + b)) = a/(ax + b).
  • d/dx (ln(kx)) = 1/x for any constant k > 0.
  • The integral of e^(kx) is (1/k) e^(kx) + c; the integral of 1/x is ln x + c (x > 0).
  • Product rule with logs: d/dx (x ln x) = ln x + 1.

Solving equations

  • ln(x^2) = 4 gives x^2 = e^4, so x = e^2 or x = -e^2 (check the domain).
  • Log equations combine: ln a + ln b = ln(ab); always reject solutions outside the domain.
  • ln(x) = 1 + ln(3) gives ln x = ln(3e), so x = 3e.

Exponential growth and decay

  • If dN/dt = kN then N = N0 e^(kt): the rate of change is proportional to the quantity itself.
  • Examples: population growth, radioactive decay, cooling, compound interest.
  • Doubling time = ln 2 / k; half-life = ln(0.5) / k.

Graphs and limits

  • e^x grows without bound; e^(-x) tends to 0 as x increases (asymptote y = 0).
  • The gradient of e^x at x = 0 is 1.
  • ln x grows slowly; its graph crosses the x-axis at (1, 0).

title: Logic Gates & Boolean Logic — Study Notes
content:
Logic Gates & Boolean Logic

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): six gates, truth tables, logic expressions, building/describing circuits, problem-to-logic mapping.

1. The six gates

ABANDORNANDNORXOR
0000110
0101101
1001101
1111000

NOT inverts. NAND = AND + invert; NOR = OR + invert; XOR = 1 when inputs differ.

2. Truth tables

2 inputs → 4 rows; 3 inputs → 8 rows. Work gate by gate, adding intermediate columns for sub-circuit outputs.

3. Logic expressions

A Boolean expression describes a circuit in logic: X = A AND NOT B, or X = (A OR B) AND C. Brackets fix the order — work out bracketed parts first, then AND, then OR.

  • Circuit → expression: label the output of every gate (P, Q, …), write one expression per gate in order, then combine them at the final gate.
  • Truth table → expression: mark the rows where the output is 1; for each such row write a term that is true only in that row (write NOT for an input that is 0, AND between the inputs); join the terms with OR. For XOR: X = (NOT A AND B) OR (A AND NOT B).
  • Expression → truth table: add an intermediate column for each sub-expression before the output column.
  • Rules used to simplify: A AND 1 = A; A AND 0 = 0; A OR 1 = 1; A OR 0 = A; A AND A = A; A AND NOT A = 0; A OR NOT A = 1; NOT(NOT A) = A; X OR (X AND Y) = X. (AS extension, 9618: De Morgan's laws — NOT(A AND B) = NOT A OR NOT B and NOT(A OR B) = NOT A AND NOT B.)

Example: a light X is on only when switch A is on and switch B is off → X = A AND NOT B, so X = 1 in exactly one row of its truth table (A = 1, B = 0).

4. Problem → logic

Define inputs/outputs first. Alarm rings (X=1) if sensor P triggered AND (door D OR window W): X = P AND (D OR W). Then draw the circuit: OR first, then AND.

5. Describing circuits

Write the expression from a diagram gate by gate; annotate output of each gate (X, Y) before combining.

Exam tips: check your truth table row count before writing; in problem questions, state "input P = 1 means sensor triggered" — definitions earn marks.

title: Molecules, Transport and Health — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Molecules, Transport and Health — Quick Revision Summary

Biology — AS Edexcel IAL, WBI12 Unit 1 Topic 1. Water as a polar solvent and its role in transport, carbohydrates (monosaccharides, disaccharides, polysaccharides including starch, glycogen and cellulose) and their structure and role in energy storage and structure, lipids (triglycerides, saturated and unsaturated) and their roles, proteins and their structure from amino acid to tertiary and quaternary, gas exchange surfaces and Fick''s law and the mammalian lung adaptations, the mammalian heart and circulatory system and the cardiac cycle, haemoglobin and the oxygen dissociation curve and the Bohr effect and fetal haemoglobin, atherosclerosis and blood clotting, risk factors for CVD (diet, blood pressure, smoking, age, gender, inactivity, cholesterol, obesity) and how each acts, diet and antioxidants and cholesterol and the evidence, people using scientific knowledge to reduce risk, the benefits and risks of treatments (antihypertensives, statins, anticoagulants, platelet inhibitors), and the data analysis skills of distinguishing correlation from causation and evaluating study design and sample size — plus the two core practicals (Benedict''s and iodine semi-quantitative tests, DCPIP vitamin C, biuret protein, enzyme factors).

  • 1.1 Water: a dipole — oxygen slightly negative, hydrogen slightly positive — so it forms hydrogen bonds, has high specific heat capacity and high latent heat of vaporisation, is cohesive, and is an excellent solvent for ions and polar molecules (because the partial charges surround and dissolve them); in transport it carries dissolved substances.
  • 1.2 Carbohydrates: monosaccharides (glucose, fructose, galactose — hexoses, C₆H₁₂O₆); disaccharides by condensation forming glycosidic bonds (maltose = glucose+glucose, sucrose = glucose+fructose, lactose = glucose+galactose); polysaccharides: starch (amylose helical and amylopectin branched — glucose storage in plants, compact and insoluble), glycogen (more branched storage in animals, mainly liver and muscle), cellulose (beta-glucose straight chains, hydrogen-bonded into microfibrils — structural).
  • 1.3 Core Practical 1: Benedict''s reagent turns blue → green → yellow → orange → brick-red as reducing sugar concentration increases (heat with the sample, compare with a colour standard chart to estimate); iodine solution turns blue-black with starch — compare intensity with a colour standard to estimate.
  • 1.4 Glycosidic bonds: monosaccharides join by condensation (losing water, forming a glycosidic bond) to make disaccharides and polysaccharides; hydrolysis (adding water) breaks the bond — starch → maltose → glucose; sucrose → glucose + fructose; lactose → glucose + galactose.
  • 1.5 Triglycerides: one glycerol + three fatty acids, joined by ester bonds; saturated fatty acids have no double bonds (straight, pack tight — solid fats), unsaturated have double bonds (kinks, loose packing — liquid oils); roles: energy storage (more energy per gram than carbohydrate), phospholipid bilayer, myelin sheath, waterproof skin layer (subcutaneous fat), steroid hormones.
  • 1.6 Why animals need a heart and circulation: as organisms grow, diffusion alone becomes too slow to supply cells deep inside the body — surface area to volume ratio falls with size, so a mass transport system (heart, blood vessels, blood) moves materials fast.
  • 1.7 Blood vessels: arteries carry blood away from the heart at high pressure — thick muscular, elastic walls, narrow lumen, no valves; veins carry blood to the heart at low pressure — thinner walls, wide lumen, valves to prevent backflow; capillaries are one cell thick with the smallest lumen — thin walls and large total surface area for exchange.
  • 1.8 Cardiac cycle: atrial systole (atria contract, blood into ventricles), ventricular systole (ventricles contract, blood into aorta and pulmonary artery, AV valves close → first heart sound), diastole (heart relaxes, ventricles fill, semilunar valves close → second heart sound); valves ensure one-way flow; left ventricle has a much thicker wall than the right because it pumps to the whole body at higher pressure; the heart is myogenic.
  • 1.9 Haemoglobin and oxygen transport: haemoglobin has four polypeptide chains each with a haem group carrying one O₂ molecule, so one haemoglobin carries four O₂; the oxygen dissociation curve shows saturation rising steeply then levelling; the Bohr effect: higher CO₂ and lower pH lower haemoglobin''s oxygen affinity, so it unloads more O₂ in respiring tissues; fetal haemoglobin has a higher oxygen affinity than adult haemoglobin, so it can take oxygen from adult haemoglobin across the placenta.
  • 1.10 Atherosclerosis: endothelial dysfunction (damage from high blood pressure, smoking chemicals or immune responses) → inflammatory response, white blood cells enter the wall, LDL oxidised and taken up, smooth muscle and fibrous tissue build up → plaque (fibrous cap over a lipid core); the plaque narrows the artery, raises pressure, and can rupture → clot (thrombus) → blocked artery → myocardial infarction (heart attack) or stroke.
  • 1.11 Blood clotting: vessel damage exposes collagen, platelets activate and release thromboplastin, thromboplastin + Ca²⁺ converts prothrombin → thrombin, thrombin converts soluble fibrinogen → insoluble fibrin threads that form a mesh trapping platelets and red blood cells → a clot; clotting prevents blood loss and pathogen entry, but a clot on a ruptured plaque can block a coronary artery and cause a myocardial infarction or a cerebral artery and cause a stroke.

Worked example

Risk calculation from data: a study finds that smokers have a 15% chance of a heart attack by age 70, and non-smokers 4% — the relative risk for smokers = 15/4 = 3.75, so smokers are about 3.75 times as likely to have a heart attack by 70; but this is a correlation — part of the risk is caused by smoking itself (mechanistically, the chemicals damage the endothelium, raise blood pressure and reduce oxygen carried by haemoglobin), and it may also be that smokers differ in other ways (diet, exercise); still, smoking is a causal risk factor, so the relative risk is used as evidence, not proof, and decisions use the whole body of evidence. To evaluate the study, check the sample (is it representative, and large enough, and free from bias in selection or loss of participants) and the method (were the groups comparable, and were confounding factors such as diet and exercise accounted for).

Key points to remember

Risk factors for CVD and how they act: high blood pressure damages endothelium and raises heart strain and atherosclerosis risk; high saturated fat and cholesterol raise LDL and contribute to plaques; smoking introduces chemicals that damage endothelium, raise blood pressure and heart rate and reduce oxygen carried by haemoglobin (carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin); age increases risk as damage accumulates and repair is less efficient; males are at higher risk than females at younger ages; inactivity contributes to blood pressure, obesity and cholesterol; genetics/family history affects baseline risk; obesity (BMI = mass (kg)/height (m)², and waist-to-hip ratio) is a risk factor; high cholesterol (total and LDL) is linked to CVD and HDL is protective. Diet and antioxidants: vitamin C and E (from fruit and vegetables) may reduce risk by preventing oxidation of LDL; evidence for cholesterol causing CVD comes from the biology and from the results of statin trials, which lower cholesterol and reduce events. People use this knowledge — BMI, waist-to-hip ratio, exercise, smoking, diet — to reduce their risk. Benefits and risks of treatments: antihypertensives lower blood pressure (dizziness, fatigue, kidney effects, over-lowering); statins lower cholesterol (muscle pain, digestive upset, rarely liver effects); anticoagulants (warfarin) and platelet inhibitors (aspirin) reduce clotting (bleeding risk, gut bleeding, not for everyone). Distinguish correlation from causation and evaluate study design — sample selection (representative or biased), sample size (small samples less reliable, more chance variation), and whether confounding factors were controlled.

How to use this

Read the summary list, then open the full revision notes for any point that feels weak, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself. Revise next by: drawing a triglyceride and distinguishing saturated and unsaturated; drawing a cholesterol molecule and stating how saturated and unsaturated fats differ; carrying out the Benedict''s, iodine and DCPIP practicals and explaining the variables, the colour standards and the control variables; describing the cardiac cycle and drawing the pressure/volume changes through a heartbeat; sketching the oxygen dissociation curve of haemoglobin, showing the Bohr effect and the fetal haemoglobin curve to the left; describing the stages of atherosclerosis and blood clotting and the enzymes and factors in clotting; listing the risk factors for CVD and stating how each acts; and working through a risk calculation from study data and evaluating the study design.

title: Organic Chemistry: Arenes (Edexcel IAL A2 Chemistry)
content:
Organic Chemistry: Arenes - Edexcel IAL A2 Chemistry

This topic belongs to Edexcel International A-Level Chemistry WCH15, Topic 18, and covers the structure, stability, and characteristic reactions of arenes, specifically benzene, alongside activating and directing effects including phenol.

Structure and Evidence for Benzene

Benzene is an arene with the molecular formula C6H6, possessing a planar ring structure supported by multiple lines of physical and chemical evidence.

  • Thermochemical evidence: The measured enthalpy of hydrogenation of benzene is approximately −208 kJ mol−1, which is significantly less exothermic than the theoretical value of −360 kJ mol−1 calculated for a hypothetical cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene with three isolated double bonds. The difference of about 150 kJ mol−1 is the stabilisation energy, also known as the delocalisation energy, proving benzene is much more stable than the classical Kekule structure.
  • X-ray diffraction data: X-ray crystallography shows that all six carbon-carbon bond lengths in benzene are identical at 0.139 nm, a value intermediate between a typical carbon-carbon single bond (0.154 nm) and a carbon-carbon double bond (0.134 nm).
  • Infrared spectroscopy: IR data shows characteristic carbon-carbon aromatic ring stretching absorptions and aromatic carbon-hydrogen stretching bands.
  • Delocalised model: The delocalised model for the structure of benzene involves the sideways overlap of unhybridised p-orbitals on each of the six carbon atoms, forming a continuous ring of pi-bonds above and below the plane of the carbon ring. Students may represent the structure of benzene as a ring inside a hexagon or as alternating double and single bonds as appropriate in equations and mechanisms.

Resistance to Bromination and Comparison with Alkenes

Benzene displays very different chemical reactivity compared to alkenes due to the nature of its bonding.

  • Resistance to bromination: Benzene is resistant to bromination compared to alkenes because of the delocalisation of pi-bonds in benzene, which spreads the electron density over the whole ring, making it a stable region. In contrast, alkenes possess a localised electron density in their pi-bond situated between two carbon atoms, which polarises approaching electrophiles much more readily.
  • Reactivity consequence: Alkenes undergo electrophilic addition reactions readily at room temperature without a catalyst, whereas benzene undergoes electrophilic substitution reactions and requires a halogen carrier catalyst to polarise non-polar molecules like bromine.

Reactions of Benzene

Benzene undergoes a variety of chemical reactions under specific conditions.

  • Combustion: Benzene burns in oxygen in air with a smoky flame due to its high carbon-to-hydrogen ratio, indicating unburnt carbon particles.
  • Halogenation: Benzene reacts with bromine in the presence of a catalyst such as iron(III) bromide or aluminium bromide.
  • Nitration: Benzene reacts with a mixture of concentrated nitric acid and concentrated sulfuric acids heated to about 50 degrees Celsius.
  • Sulfonation: Benzene reacts with fuming sulfuric acid (sulfuric(VI) acid containing dissolved sulfur trioxide).
  • Friedel-Crafts reactions: Benzene reacts with halogenoalkanes (alkylation) and acyl chlorides (acylation) with anhydrous aluminium chloride as a catalyst.

Mechanisms of Electrophilic Substitution

Electrophilic substitution in benzene proceeds through the generation of an electrophile followed by attack and proton loss.

  • Generation of electrophiles: For nitration, concentrated nitric acid and concentrated sulfuric acid generate the nitronium ion electrophile: HNO3 + 2H2SO4 yields NO2+ + 2HSO4− + H3O+. For halogenation, bromine reacts with an aluminium halide catalyst to generate the Br+ or polarised Br-Br-AlCl3 electrophilic species. For Friedel-Crafts alkylation and acylation, the halogenoalkane or acyl chloride reacts with aluminium chloride, acting as a Lewis acid, to generate a carbocation or acylium ion electrophile: RCl + AlCl3 yields R+ + AlCl4−.
  • Substitution mechanism: The electron-rich pi system of the benzene ring acts as a nucleophile and donates a pair of electrons to the electrophile, forming an unstable arenium intermediate where the positive charge is delocalised over the remaining five carbon atoms of the ring. A base removes a hydrogen ion from the substituted carbon, restoring the stable delocalised pi system of the benzene ring and regenerating the catalyst.

Reactivity of Phenol

Phenol contains a hydroxyl group attached directly to an aromatic ring, significantly altering its reactivity compared to benzene.

  • Reaction with bromine water: Phenol reacts readily with bromine water at room temperature without any halogen carrier catalyst, instantly decolorising the orange bromine water and giving a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol, accompanied by steamy fumes of hydrogen bromide.
  • Reasons for relative ease: The lone pair of electrons on the oxygen atom of the −OH group in phenol overlaps with the pi system of the benzene ring. This partially delocalises the lone pair into the ring, significantly increasing the electron density of the ring compared to benzene. As a result, the benzene ring in phenol is strongly activated, polarizing incoming electrophiles like bromine much more effectively and attracting them faster than benzene can.

Side-Chain Oxidation and Directing Effects

Substituents on the benzene ring affect both the position of further substitution and the reactivity of side chains.

  • Directing effects: Alkyl groups, such as the methyl group in methylbenzene, and activating groups direct a second incoming substituent primarily to the 2- and 4- positions (ortho and para). A nitro group is a deactivating group and directs incoming electrophiles to the 3- (meta) position. Hydroxyl and amino groups are strongly activating.
  • Side-chain oxidation: Hot, acidified potassium manganate(VII) solution oxidises any alkyl side chain on a benzene ring directly to a carboxylic acid group, regardless of the length of the alkyl chain, provided there is at least one benzylic hydrogen atom. For example, methylbenzene is oxidised to benzoic acid.

Typical mistakes

  • Mistake: Stating that benzene undergoes electrophilic addition because it has double bonds. Correction: Benzene undergoes electrophilic substitution to preserve the stable delocalised pi electron system.
  • Mistake: Omitting the catalyst in Friedel-Crafts equations or halogenation. Correction: Always include anhydrous aluminium chloride or iron(III) bromide as catalysts.
  • Mistake: Drawing the positive charge inside the intermediate horseshoe incorrectly. Correction: Ensure the incomplete horseshoe representing the positive charge in the arenium intermediate extends over five carbon atoms and does not touch the carbon bonded to the incoming electrophile and leaving hydrogen.
  • Mistake: Confusing the conditions for phenol bromination with benzene bromination. Correction: Phenol reacts with aqueous bromine without a catalyst at room temperature, whereas benzene requires liquid bromine and a halogen carrier catalyst.

Exam-style questions

  1. Question: State the thermochemical evidence that supports the delocalised model of benzene over the Kekule structure of cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene. Answer: The measured enthalpy of hydrogenation of benzene is approximately −208 kJ mol−1, whereas the theoretical value for cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene is −360 kJ mol−1. The difference of about 150 kJ mol−1 is the delocalisation energy, proving benzene is thermodynamically more stable. (Earns credit by stating both values, their difference, and naming delocalisation energy).
  2. Question: Explain why benzene is resistant to bromination compared to cyclohexene. Answer: Benzene has a delocalised ring of pi-electrons which spreads electron density, whereas cyclohexene has a localised pi-bond between two carbons. The localised electron density in cyclohexene polarises bromine molecules much more readily than the stable delocalised ring of benzene. (Earns credit for contrasting delocalised and localised electron density).
  3. Question: Write the equation for the generation of the electrophile in the nitration of benzene using concentrated nitric and sulfuric acids. Answer: HNO3 + 2H2SO4 yields NO2+ + 2HSO4− + H3O+. (Earns credit for correct reactants, products, and stoichiometry).
  4. Question: Outline the mechanism for the alkylation of benzene with chloromethane in the presence of aluminium chloride. Include curly arrows and the intermediate. Answer: CH3Cl + AlCl3 yields CH3+ + AlCl4−. The benzene ring pi electrons attack the CH3+ electrophile to form the arenium intermediate with a positive charge spread over five carbons, followed by loss of H+ to form methylbenzene and regenerate AlCl3 alongside HCl. (Earns credit for electrophile generation, curly arrows from the ring, correct arenium intermediate structure, and loss of H+).
  5. Question: Explain why phenol reacts with bromine water much more readily than benzene does. Answer: The oxygen atom in the −OH group of phenol has a lone pair of electrons that overlaps with the pi system of the benzene ring. This increases the electron density of the ring, activating it and allowing it to polarise bromine molecules without a catalyst. (Earns credit for mentioning lone pair overlap, increased electron density, and ring activation).

Use these notes alongside active recall of mechanisms, reagent-condition pairs, and thermochemical definitions. Revise next the chemistry of carbonyl compounds, carboxylic acids, and esters to complete your organic chemistry mastery for WCH15.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Evidence for delocalisation, applied to hydrogenation: cyclohexene releases about −120 kJ mol⁻¹, so three double bonds would release about −360 kJ mol⁻¹. Benzene releases only about −208 kJ mol⁻¹, a difference of about 152 kJ mol⁻¹ that is the extra stability from delocalisation.
  • Nitration, applied to benzene: concentrated HNO₃ and H₂SO₄ generate the NO₂⁺ electrophile. The sulfuric acid is a catalyst and dehydrates the nitric acid. Show the electrophile first, then the arrow from the ring to it, then the loss of H⁺ to restore the aromatic ring.
  • Phenol versus benzene, applied to bromination: the lone pair on oxygen donates into the ring, so phenol reacts with aqueous bromine at room temperature without a catalyst and forms 2,4,6-tribromophenol as a white precipitate. Benzene does not react under the same conditions.
  • Directing effects: an electron-donating group such as –OH or –CH₃ directs an incoming electrophile to positions 2, 4 and 6 (ortho and para). A nitro group directs to the meta position and deactivates the ring. Name the group and its effect in the answer.

title: AS Level Biology: Plant Structure and Function, Biodiversity and Conservation
content:
Plant Structure and Function, Biodiversity and Conservation — AS Level Biology

This revision note belongs to the Edexcel International Advanced Subsidiary (IAS) Biology specification, WBI12 Unit 2, Topic 4 Plant Structure and Function, Biodiversity and Conservation. It covers plant cell ultrastructure and the functions of the organelles and cell wall components, starch and cellulose and how their structure fits their role, how cellulose microfibrils and secondary thickening give physical properties to xylem and sclerenchyma fibres, the similarities and differences between sclerenchyma fibres, xylem vessels and phloem and their structure, position and function, the light microscope practical on transverse sections, the uses of plant fibres and starch in sustainability, the importance of water and mineral ions to plants and the practical on mineral deficiency, the tensile strength practical, bacterial growth requirements, antimicrobial plant substances and the aseptic practical, the development of drug testing from Withering’s digitalis to modern three-phased testing, classification and the species concept and the three-domain system, biodiversity and endemism and how they are measured, species richness and the heterozygosity index, the index of diversity and how it is compared between habitats, and the concept of niche and examples of adaptations — behavioural, anatomical and physiological. Every statement the topic is responsible for is covered in its own section or paragraph.

1. Plant cell ultrastructure: what is in a plant cell and why

Plant cells share the common eukaryotic features with animal cells — a plasma membrane (cell surface membrane), cytoplasm and ribosomes — but add several structures that animal cells do not have. The cell wall is a rigid outer layer of cellulose microfibrils embedded in a gel-like matrix; it gives shape and support, prevents the cell from bursting when turgid, and limits uncontrolled expansion. Chloroplasts are double-membraned organelles containing chlorophyll and the enzymes for photosynthesis; inside, stacked membranes (thylakoids, often stacked into grana) carry out the light-dependent reactions, and the surrounding stroma contains the enzymes for the light-independent reactions. Amyloplasts are colourless plastids that store starch; they are found especially in storage organs such as potato tubers. Vacuoles are membrane-bound sacs; a large central vacuole in mature plant cells is filled with cell sap — a watery solution of sugars, salts, pigments and waste — surrounded by the tonoplast membrane, and it maintains turgor pressure and gives the cell its rigidity. Plasmodesmata are thread-like channels through the cell walls of adjacent plant cells, connecting the cytoplasm and allowing communication and transport between cells. Pits are thin regions in the cell wall where the wall is localy thinner or absent, allowing water and solutes to pass between cells; the middle lamella is the layer that cements together the cell walls of adjacent cells. Ribosomes are present (80S in the cytoplasm) and the nucleus, nucleolus, mitochondria and golgi apparatus are all present, as in animal cells, except that plant cells do not have centrioles (higher plants lack them, though they still divide).

2. Recognising plant organelles from electron micrographs

On an electron micrograph of a plant cell you should be able to recognise the plasma membrane, nucleus with nucleolus, chloroplasts with their stacked thylakoid membranes (grana), mitochondria, rough endoplasmic reticulum with ribosomes, golgi (dictyosomes in plants), a large central vacuole with the tonoplast, the cell wall (with middle lamella where two cells meet), and plasmodesmata. Chloroplasts are especially characteristic: the grana appear as stacks of disc-like membranes. Amyloplasts appear as colourless, starch-filled plastids without grana. A good exercise is to label each of these in an EM image and to explain the function of each. Compare the plant cell with an animal cell: plant cells have a cell wall, chloroplasts, a large central vacuole and plasmodesmata, and generally no centrioles, and their shape is more regular because of the wall.

3. Starch and cellulose: polysaccharides that do different jobs

Starch and cellulose are both polymers of glucose, but alpha-glucose for starch and beta-glucose for cellulose, and that difference determines their properties. Alpha-glucose has the hydroxyl groups on the same side of the ring (in the usual representation), so when polymerised with 1,4-glycosidic bonds the chain coils into a helix, forming amylose, and with 1,6-branches forming amylopectin — compact, helical and branched, so starch is an excellent storage material: compact to pack a lot of glucose into little space, and with no osmotic effect, because the large insoluble starch granules do not draw water into the cell by osmosis. Cellulose is made from beta-glucose, in which the hydroxyl on carbon 1 is on the opposite side, so when linked the chain is straight rather than coiled; the linear chains run parallel and form many hydrogen bonds between adjacent chains, making strong cellulose microfibrils. Cellulose microfibrils are the main structural component of the cell wall, giving strength and rigidity; the way they are arranged determines the properties of the cell and of the whole plant. The structure of starch suits it for storage in plant cells; the structure of cellulose suits it for strength and support — two polymers from the same monomer with very different roles because of the different glycosidic bonds and the different shape of the chain.

4. Cellulose microfibrils, secondary thickening and the properties of xylem and sclerenchyma

The physical properties of plant tissues depend on how the cellulose microfibrils are arranged. In a young, growing cell the microfibrils are laid down mainly at right angles to the direction of growth, so the cell can expand in length; when growth stops, the cell can become strengthened by secondary thickening — more cellulose and, in some cells, lignin deposited on the inside of the primary wall — which makes the wall rigid and waterproof. In sclerenchyma fibres, the cells die at maturity and are left with heavily thickened, lignified walls, often with the microfibrils arranged in spiral or ring patterns; the result is strong, flexible but tough fibres that give mechanical support and can be used by humans (for example in textiles and ropes). In xylem vessels, the wall is lignified and the cells are dead at maturity, forming long tubes with the end walls broken down or absent — the vessel elements are linked end to end to form a continuous tube for the transport of water and mineral ions, and the lignified thickening (in rings, spirals or nets) prevents collapse under the negative pressure of the transpiration stream. So the arrangement of cellulose microfibrils and the deposition of lignin determine what a plant part can do: support, flexibility, or transport of water under tension. The secondary thickening of xylem and the lignification of sclerenchyma are the adaptations that let land plants grow tall and stand upright and transport water from the roots to the leaves.

5. Sclerenchyma fibres, xylem vessels and phloem: structure, position and function

Sclerenchyma fibres and xylem vessels provide support and, for xylem, transport; phloem translocates organic solutes. Sclerenchyma fibres are long, narrow cells with thick lignified walls and a small lumen, dead at maturity; they occur in bundles and, because of their strength and flexibility, they give support to stems and leaves and can be used in textiles and ropes. Xylem vessels are long, continuous tubes formed from vessel elements with lignified walls and pits in the walls, dead at maturity with no contents, and their function is transport of water and mineral ions from the roots to the leaves — and they also provide support. Phloem is a living tissue; sieve tube elements are the conducting cells, arranged end to end with perforated end walls (sieve plates) between them, reduced cytoplasm at the edges and no nucleus at maturity; each sieve tube element has a companion cell beside it, connected by plasmodesmata, which keeps the sieve element alive and supplies it with ATP, because the sieve element itself has lost its nucleus and most organelles. Phloem transports organic solutes (mainly sucrose, in solution in water) from sources (leaves, storage organs) to sinks (growing points, roots, developing fruits) by mass flow driven by the pressure gradient built up by the loading of sucrose into the sieve tubes. Compare: sclerenchyma fibres = support, dead, lignified; xylem vessels = support and water/mineral transport, dead, lignified, open tube; phloem = translocation of organic solutes, living sieve tubes with companion cells, perforated end walls, no lignin.

6. Core Practical 7 — transverse sections of roots, stems and leaves

Use a light microscope to make observations, draw and label plan diagrams of transverse sections of roots, stems and leaves, and to observe and label cells of plant tissues, identifying sclerenchyma fibres, phloem, sieve tubes and xylem vessels and their location. To make a transverse section, cut a very thin slice across a stem or root with a razor blade (a sharp blade and a steady hand or a sectioning technique), float the section onto water on a slide, lower a coverslip at an angle, stain if needed (for example with toluidine blue or iodine) to distinguish lignified xylem, sclerenchyma and phloem, and observe under the microscope at several magnifications. In a stem transverse section, note the positions of the epidermis, cortex, the vascular bundles (with xylem toward the inside and phloem toward the outside, and sclerenchyma fibres often outside the phloem in a bundle cap), and the pith in the centre; in roots the vascular tissue is central. Draw a plan diagram (an outline of the whole section showing the arrangement of tissues, not the cells) with the correct relative sizes and positions, label the tissues, give a title and magnification. Then observe and label the cells: look for the thick lignified walls of xylem and sclerenchyma, the sieve plates and companion cells of phloem, and the thin-walled cells of the cortex and pith.

7. Plant fibres and starch in sustainability

Plant fibres and starch can contribute to sustainability and to replacing oil-based plastics. Plant fibres (from sclerenchyma or from phloem fibres) are strong, renewable and biodegradable, and they can be used in textiles, paper, building materials and composites that replace oil-based plastics and synthetic fibres; water transport in plants today parallels the transport of sap and provides a model for how plants already do this. Starch can be used to make bioplastics — for example, starch can be processed into film-forming materials suitable for packaging, plates and disposable items — and because starch is a renewable, biodegradable material made from crops such as potatoes, maize or cassava, it can replace oil-based plastics in some uses. Using plant fibres and starch reduces reliance on oil, is renewable and can be more sustainable if the crops are grown responsibly; but there are trade-offs: land, water and energy for the crops, possible competition with food production, and the need to assess the whole life cycle. The use of plant products to replace oil-based plastics is a topic that connects plant structure (cellulose and starch), to sustainability, to human decisions informed by science.

8. Water and inorganic ions to plants, and mineral deficiency

Plants need water for photosynthesis (a reactant and the medium in which it happens), for transport (water is the solvent for minerals and for sucrose in the phloem), for support (turgor pressure keeps non-woody parts rigid), and for cooling (transpiration). Water enters the roots by osmosis from the soil and moves up the xylem. Inorganic ions are essential: nitrate ions (NO3-) are needed for making amino acids, proteins, DNA and chlorophyll — a deficiency causes stunted growth and yellowing of older leaves (chlorosis); calcium ions are needed for the middle lamella (pectin in the cell wall) and for cell membranes — a deficiency gives stunted growth and necrosis of the growing point and young leaves; magnesium ions are the central atom in chlorophyll — a deficiency causes chlorosis of the older leaves. A recommended additional practical is to investigate plant mineral deficiencies: grow plants in a solution with all minerals (complete) and in solutions missing one of nitrate, calcium or magnesium, observe and measure the effects on growth and leaf colour over weeks, and explain the results in terms of the roles of the missing ion.

9. Core Practical 8 — tensile strength of plant fibres

Determine the tensile strength of plant fibres — the force a fibre can take before it breaks. A typical method: take strands of a plant fibre (for example the fibres from celery stalks or nettle stems, or a piece of a plant stem with visible fibres), clamp one end, hang weights from the other, and add weights until the fibre breaks; record the mass (converted to a force, weight = mass × g) needed to break the fibre. Repeat for several fibres, present the results, and compare fibres from different plants or different parts of a plant. Safety: sharp blades and falling weights. The practical shows how the arrangement of cellulose and lignin gives the fibre its strength, and connects the cell-level structure to a macroscopic useful property.

10. Conditions for bacterial growth

Bacteria need certain conditions to grow: a supply of nutrients (carbon, nitrogen, minerals and, for some, specific organic factors), water, a suitable temperature (most pathogenic bacteria around 37 °C, though many grow across a range), oxygen (some need it — aerobic bacteria — some do not — anaerobic bacteria — and some can manage with or without), a suitable pH, and, for many, time to multiply. In the laboratory these conditions can be met and controlled: cultures are grown in nutrient broth or on agar plates, at a set temperature (often 25 °C for environmental organisms and 37 °C for those that grow at body temperature), with or without oxygen, and in sterile conditions so that only the desired organism grows. Aseptic technique is essential to avoid contaminating the culture or releasing harmful bacteria into the environment — sterilise equipment (by flame or autoclave), work near a flame to create an upward air current, work quickly and cover the plates, and dispose of cultures by sterilising before disposal.

11. Antimicrobial plant substances and the aseptic practical

Substances derived from plants can have antimicrobial and other therapeutic properties. Some plant extracts inhibit the growth of bacteria or fungi — for example, garlic has been traditionally used and does have some antibacterial effects; other plants yield useful compounds (aspirin from willow bark, morphine from poppies, and many modern drugs are derived from plants). A recommended additional practical is to investigate the antimicrobial properties of plants, including aseptic techniques for the safe handling of bacteria: prepare agar plates, use sterile swabs or paper discs impregnated with different plant extracts, incubate and measure the zones of inhibition around the discs — the diameter of the clear zone where bacteria did not grow — and compare the effectiveness of different extracts or the same extract at different concentrations. Use aseptic technique: sterilise the discs and loops, work near a flame, spread the bacteria in a controlled way, seal the plates with tape (but do not seal all the way so they do not become anaerobic), and incubate at a safe temperature. Measure the zones of inhibition and record them, including in a table, and draw a conclusion about which extract is most effective and about concentration.

12. Drug testing: from Withering’s digitalis soup to modern trials

The development of drug testing has moved from historic, uncontrolled methods to contemporary, rigorous protocols. William Withering’s digitalis soup in the 18th century was an early use of a plant-derived medicine — foxglove (Digitalis) — for dropsy (oedema), tested by trial and observation on patients, but with no controls, no placebo, no blinding and no large sample, so the evidence was weak and mixed with other treatments. Modern drug testing uses a sequence of phases: pre-clinical testing in the lab and on animals; clinical trials in humans in three phases — Phase 1 tests safety in a small group, Phase 2 tests efficacy and side effects in a larger group of patients, and Phase 3 tests the drug against the current treatment or a placebo in a large group, in a double-blind trial (neither the patient nor the clinician knows which treatment is being used) so that expectations do not bias the result. Placebos are used to control for the placebo effect (improvement from the belief of being treated). The modern protocol — double-blind, placebo-controlled, multi-centre, large trials — is far more reliable than Withering’s soup, and it protects patients and produces trustworthy evidence. Students should be able to describe this progression and evaluate the designs.

13. Classification: organising life, the species concept and the three domains

Classification is a means of organising the variety of life based on relationships between organisms, using differences and similarities in phenotypes (observable features) and in genotypes (the DNA and the proteins the DNA codes for). It is built around the species concept — a species is a group of organisms that can interbreed and produce fertile offspring — and a hierarchy of groups above it: genus, family, order, class, phylum and kingdom, with organisms grouped because they share common ancestry. The classification has changed as new data — especially molecular evidence from DNA and protein sequences — have come in, leading to critical evaluation of existing groupings and new taxonomic groupings. The three-domain system, based on molecular evidence, divides life into the Archaea, the Bacteria and the Eukarya (which includes all eukaryotes, plants, animals, fungi and protists); the Archaea are distinct from the Bacteria and include organisms that often live in extreme environments, and the evidence from ribosomal RNA sequences and other molecular data led to this reclassification, replacing the older five-kingdom system. The process of critical evaluation of new data by the scientific community — comparing, testing and debating — is what leads to new groupings and to science being self-correcting.

14. Biodiversity, endemism and threats from human activity

Biodiversity is the variety of life — the variety within a habitat, within a species or across the whole planet; it can refer to species richness (the number of different species in a habitat) or to genetic diversity within a species. Endemism is the state of a species being found only in one particular place (an endemic species, such as a plant found only on a particular island). Over time the variety of life has become extensive through evolution, but it is now being threatened by human activity — habitat destruction (deforestation, drainage, conversion to agriculture), over-exploitation (hunting, fishing, logging), pollution, the introduction of invasive species, and climate change, all of which can reduce biodiversity and cause extinctions. Biodiversity matters because it provides ecosystem services, genetic resources for medicines and crops, and is itself valuable; its loss affects ecosystems, food security and human health. Understanding the causes of the loss is important so that conservation measures can be designed to address them.

15. Measuring biodiversity: species richness, genetic diversity and heterozygosity

Biodiversity can be measured in different ways. Species richness — the number of different species in a given area — is one simple measure of biodiversity within a habitat; a habitat with more species is generally more diverse, though this ignores the abundance of each species (a habitat dominated by one common species and several rare ones may have the same species richness as one where all are equally common). Genetic diversity within a species can be measured by the heterozygosity index (also called heterozygosity): the proportion of individuals in a population that are heterozygous at a locus. It is calculated as the number of heterozygotes divided by the number of individuals in the population (for a single locus); a higher heterozygosity means more genetic diversity within that population. This matters because genetic diversity helps a population adapt to changes, resist disease and avoid the problems of inbreeding; loss of genetic diversity raises the risk of extinction.

16. Comparing habitats with the index of diversity

Biodiversity can be compared between different habitats using the formula for the index of diversity, D: D = (N(N−1)) / (Σ n(n−1)), where N is the total number of organisms of all species in the habitat, and n is the number of organisms of a particular species. Calculation: for each species, work out n(n−1); sum these to get Σ n(n−1); then divide N(N−1) by that sum to give D, the index of diversity. Worked example: in a habitat with species counts 10, 15, 5, 2 (N = 32): Σ n(n−1) = (10×9)+(15×14)+(5×4)+(2×1) = 90+210+20+2 = 322; N(N−1) = 32×31 = 992; D = 992 / 322 ≈ 3.08. A larger D means a more diverse habitat, because it reflects both the number of species and how evenly the individuals are distributed among them. To compare habitats, calculate D for each and compare the values, stating which is more diverse and what that suggests. The formula must be applied correctly: calculate n(n−1) for each species, sum them, and divide N(N−1) by the sum.

17. Niche and adaptations: behavioural, anatomical and physiological

A niche is the role of an organism in a habitat — the conditions in which it lives and the resources it uses, and how it interacts with other organisms; it is more than just the physical place (the habitat) where it lives, and no two species can occupy exactly the same niche for long because of competition. Adaptations are features that help an organism survive and reproduce in its niche, and they can be behavioural, anatomical or physiological. Behavioural adaptations are things the organism does — for example migration to avoid harsh conditions, hunting in packs, basking to warm up, or the specific foraging behaviour of a bird. Anatomical (structural) adaptations are physical features of the body — for example the shape of a bird’s beak for its food, the camouflage colours of a prey animal, the thick fur of an arctic mammal, or the long beak of a nectar-feeding bird. Physiological adaptations are internal functions — for example a camel’s ability to tolerate dehydration and to conserve water, the production of venom by a snake, the production of antifreeze proteins in some polar fish, or the specialised nitrogen excretion of desert animals. The concept of niche and the types of adaptation help explain how different organisms fit into their environments and how competition and adaptation shape communities.

18. Hardy-Weinberg, zoos and seed banks: allele frequencies and conservation

The Hardy-Weinberg equation tests whether a population is evolving. In a large population with random mating, no mutation, no migration and no selection, allele frequencies stay constant from generation to generation. Write the frequency of the dominant allele as p and the recessive allele as q. Then p + q = 1, and the genotype frequencies are p squared for the homozygous dominant, 2pq for the heterozygote and q squared for the homozygous recessive, so p squared + 2pq + q squared = 1. The value of the equation is that it gives a null expectation: if the observed genotype frequencies differ significantly from it, one of the assumptions is being broken and the allele frequencies are changing, which is evolution happening in front of you.

A worked use: a recessive condition affects 1 in 10 000 people, so q squared = 0.0001, q = 0.01 and p = 0.99. The carrier frequency is 2pq = 2 times 0.99 times 0.01 = 0.0198, about 1 in 50. That is why a rare recessive allele can be common in carriers while the disease itself stays rare, and it is the calculation the mark scheme wants rather than a guess from the disease frequency.

Conservation of genetic diversity is the other half of this section. Zoos use captive breeding programmes with studbooks to decide which animals pair, so that inbreeding is minimised and unrelated individuals are introduced; they also support scientific research and education, and run reintroduction programmes that prepare animals for the wild. The risks are that captive populations are small, so genetic drift and inbreeding reduce diversity, and that animals bred in captivity may lack the behaviour needed to survive on release. Seed banks store seeds at low temperature and low moisture, testing viability periodically and germinating samples to grow fresh seed, which protects genetic diversity far more cheaply than keeping animals. Their limits are that not all seeds survive drying, so some species need cryopreservation or living collections, and that a bank protects genes rather than the habitat the species needs. Evaluate both by naming what they conserve, what they cost and what they cannot do.

19. How to use this note and what to revise next

Use these notes section by section, checking that you can identify plant cell ultrastructure and organelles in an electron micrograph and state their functions, explain how starch and cellulose differ in structure and role, describe the secondary thickening and the properties of xylem vessels and sclerenchyma fibres, compare sclerenchyma fibres, xylem vessels and phloem in structure, position and function, carry out the transverse section and tensile strength practicals and explain the variables and safety, describe the conditions for bacterial growth and the aseptic practical, describe the development of drug testing from Withering’s digitalis to modern three-phased trials and evaluate the designs, define classification and the species concept, describe the three-domain system and the molecular evidence for it, define biodiversity and endemism and the threats from human activity, carry out the species richness and heterozygosity and index of diversity calculations, and define niche and give behavioural, anatomical and physiological adaptations. After this topic, revise Topic 3 Cell structure, reproduction and development (plant and animal cells, division) and Topic 5 Energy flow, ecosystems and the environment, because classification and biodiversity sit within ecology.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Simpson's index, applied to a quadrat with 10 daisies and 5 dandelions: N = 15, D = 1 − Σ(n ÷ N)² = 1 − [(10 ÷ 15)² + (5 ÷ 15)²] = 1 − (0.444 + 0.111) = 0.556. Use the index to compare two sites; a higher value means greater diversity.
  • Xylem and phloem: xylem transports water and minerals upwards and is made of dead, lignified cells with no end walls, so the water column is continuous. Phloem transports sucrose and amino acids in both directions and is made of living sieve tube elements with companion cells. Name the direction of transport and the living or dead state of the cells.
  • Cellulose versus starch: cellulose is made of β-glucose units linked alternately, which allows hydrogen bonding between chains, forming strong microfibrils. Starch is made of α-glucose, is coiled and is used for storage. The different glucose isomer explains the different shapes and functions.
  • Conservation: a protected area works only if the populations inside it are large enough to be viable. Name the factor, such as a wildlife corridor, that connects populations, because isolated populations lose genetic diversity over time.

Typical mistakes

  • Calling xylem living. Xylem vessels are dead, hollow, lignified tubes with no end walls, which is what allows a continuous water column. Phloem sieve tubes are living and supported by companion cells.
  • Giving sclerenchyma a transport role. Sclerenchyma fibres provide support only; xylem transports water and mineral ions and also supports, and phloem translocates sugars and amino acids.
  • Inverting the heterozygosity index. It is the number of heterozygotes divided by the number of individuals in the population, so it cannot exceed 1. A value of 1 would mean every individual is heterozygous.
  • Reading a diversity index the wrong way round. Use the formula given on the paper and then say which site has the higher diversity; do not assume a small number means a diverse habitat.
  • Missing the assumptions in a Hardy-Weinberg calculation. State that the population is large, mating is random and there is no selection or migration, and say that a significant difference in allele frequency between generations is evidence that one assumption is broken.
  • Claiming aseptic technique keeps everything sterile. Aseptic technique keeps contamination out of the culture and the worker safe: sterilise the loop, flame the neck of the bottle, work near a flame, and dispose of plates in the correct way. The apparatus and the medium are sterilised before use, which is a different step.
  • Describing drug trials without their purpose. A placebo controls for the expectation of improvement, a double-blind design stops the patient or the doctor influencing the result, and the three phases test safety, then effectiveness and dose, then comparison with existing treatment in a larger group.
  • Using the three-domain system without the evidence. Archaea, Bacteria and Eukarya were separated after molecular evidence, particularly ribosomal RNA sequences, showed that the archaea are as different from bacteria as both are from eukaryotes. New data changing a classification is a strength of the system, not a flaw.

Exam-style questions

  1. In a population of 2 000 plants, 120 are heterozygous at a particular locus. Calculate the heterozygosity index. Answer: 120 / 2 000 = 0.06. Only 6 per cent of the population is heterozygous, so the genetic diversity at that locus is low.
  2. A recessive allele causing a disease is present in 1 in 2 500 births. Assuming Hardy-Weinberg conditions, calculate the carrier frequency. Answer: q squared = 1 / 2 500 = 0.0004, so q = 0.02 and p = 0.98. The carrier frequency is 2pq = 2 times 0.98 times 0.02 = 0.0392, about 1 in 25.
  3. Explain how secondary thickening adapts a xylem vessel for its function. Answer: lignin is deposited in the wall, which makes it rigid so the vessel does not collapse under tension, and it makes the wall waterproof so water is not lost sideways; the strengthening also supports the plant.
  4. Describe how you would compare the tensile strength of fibres from two plant stems. Answer: extract fibres of equal length from each stem, clamp each in turn and hang masses from it until it breaks, recording the mass that causes failure. Control fibre length, thickness and the point of attachment, repeat each measurement and compare means. The fibre that withstands the greater mass has the greater tensile strength.
  5. Explain why a seed bank may conserve genetic diversity more effectively than a zoo. Answer: seeds are small, so many individuals and many species can be stored in a small space at low cost, and a large sample preserves more alleles than a small captive population that suffers inbreeding and genetic drift. A zoo is still needed for species whose seed cannot be stored or whose behaviour must be learned.
  6. Explain the evidence that led to the three-domain classification. Answer: comparisons of ribosomal RNA and other molecular sequences showed that archaeal sequences differ from bacterial sequences as much as both differ from eukaryotes, so the archaea were placed in their own domain alongside Bacteria and Eukarya. The classification is based on genotype as well as phenotype, and it is revised when new molecular data are critically evaluated.
  7. Withering's digitalis treatment and a modern double-blind trial are both tests of a drug. Explain two ways in which the modern protocol is an improvement. Answer: the modern trial uses a control group given a placebo, so improvement caused by expectation is separated from the effect of the drug, and it is randomised and double-blind, so neither patient nor doctor knows who received which treatment and bias is removed. It also uses measured doses and larger samples, so the result can be tested statistically.

title: A Level Mathematics: Exponentials and Logarithms
content:
A Level Mathematics: Exponentials and Logarithms

The exponential function eˣ is the one function whose gradient equals its value, which is why it describes any process whose rate of change is proportional to its size: cooling, decay, growth, charging a capacitor, the value of an investment. Its inverse, ln x, is the tool that unlocks equations with the unknown in the exponent. This note builds the pair from zero, links them to calculus, and finishes with the modelling and log-linear graph work that A2 papers test.

Definitions and the laws

log_a x = n  means  a^n = x
ln x = log_e x,  e = 2.718281828...

log(xy) = log x + log y
log(x/y) = log x - log y
log(x^n) = n log x
log_a a = 1;  log_a 1 = 0

e is defined as the value that makes the gradient of aˣ equal to aˣ itself. That single property generates the whole calculus of the topic:

d/dx (e^x) = e^x;  d/dx (e^(kx)) = k e^(kx)
d/dx (ln x) = 1/x;  d/dx (ln(kx)) = 1/x
integral of e^(kx) dx = (1/k) e^(kx) + c
integral of (1/x) dx = ln|x| + c

Worked example. Differentiate y = e^(3x) + ln(5x).

dy/dx = 3e^(3x) + 1/x

Worked example 2. Find ∫ (4e^(2x) + 3/x) dx.

= 2e^(2x) + 3 ln|x| + c

Solving exponential equations

Worked example 1. Solve 7^x = 50.

x ln 7 = ln 50
x = ln 50/ln 7 = 3.912/1.946 = 2.01

Worked example 2 (same base first). Solve 2^(3x−1) = 4^(x+1).

4 = 2², so 4^(x+1) = 2^(2x+2)
3x - 1 = 2x + 2  →  x = 3

Always look for a common base before taking logs: it converts an exponential equation into a linear one and avoids rounding.

Worked example 3 (quadratic in eˣ). Solve e^(2x) − 5e^x + 6 = 0.

let y = e^x: y² - 5y + 6 = 0  →  (y - 2)(y - 3) = 0
y = 2  →  x = ln 2 = 0.693
y = 3  →  x = ln 3 = 1.099

Solving logarithmic equations

Worked example 1. Solve ln(x + 3) + ln(x − 1) = ln 5.

ln[(x + 3)(x - 1)] = ln 5
x² + 2x - 3 = 5  →  x² + 2x - 8 = 0
(x + 4)(x - 2) = 0  →  x = 2 (x = -4 makes an argument negative)

Worked example 2 (different bases). Solve log₂ x + log₄ x = 3.

log_4 x = log_2 x / log_2 4 = (log_2 x)/2
so (3/2) log_2 x = 3  →  log_2 x = 2  →  x = 4

The change-of-base step is compulsory whenever bases differ; check every root against the original domains, and remember that log₂ x is only defined for x > 0 while its squared form can produce spurious negative candidates.

The graphs and their transformations

y = e^x: through (0, 1), increasing, asymptote y = 0
y = ln x: through (1, 0), increasing, asymptote x = 0, domain x > 0
they are reflections in y = x

Worked example. Sketch y = ln(x − 2), stating the asymptote, domain and intercept.

translation 2 right
asymptote x = 2;  domain x > 2
x-intercept: ln(x - 2) = 0  →  x - 2 = 1  →  x = 3

Worked example 2 (reflection). Sketch y = e^(−x) and state its relationship to y = e^x, noting the intercepts and asymptote of each.

reflection in the y-axis; still through (0, 1); asymptote y = 0;
decreasing, a decay curve

Growth and decay models

N = N_0 e^(kt): k > 0 growth, k < 0 decay
half-life = ln 2/|k|;  doubling time = ln 2/k

Newton's cooling: T = T_room + (T_0 - T_room) e^(-kt)

Worked example 1 (half-life). A substance decays as N = 80e^(−0.05t). Find the half-life and the amount after 20 years.

half-life: e^(-0.05t) = 0.5  →  t = ln 2/0.05 = 13.86 years
at t = 20: 80e⁻¹ = 29.4 units

Worked example 2 (cooling). A cup of coffee at 90 °C cools to 60 °C in 10 minutes in a 20 °C room. Find k and the temperature after 25 minutes.

T - 20 = 70e^(-kt);  at t = 10, T = 60: 40 = 70e^(-10k)
e^(-10k) = 4/7  →  k = ln(7/4)/10 = 0.0560
at t = 25: T = 20 + 70e^(-1.4) = 20 + 17.3 = 37.3 °C

Log-linear graphs

If a relationship is exponential, plotting ln y against x gives a straight line whose gradient and intercept reveal the constants. This is how experimental data is tested for exponential behaviour.

y = a b^x  →  ln y = ln a + x ln b
gradient = ln b;  intercept = ln a
y = a x^n  →  ln y = ln a + n ln x  (log-log plot)
gradient = n;  intercept = ln a

Worked example. A graph of ln y against x is a straight line with gradient 0.4 and intercept 1.2. Find the relationship.

ln y = 1.2 + 0.4x
y = e^1.2 x e^(0.4x) = 3.32 e^(0.4x)
so a = 3.32 and the growth rate is 0.4 per unit x

Worked example 2 (power law). A log-log plot of y against x has gradient 2 and intercept 0.693; the intercept is ln a, so a = e^0.693 = 2.

ln y = 0.693 + 2 ln x  →  y = 2x²

Reducing other models to linear form

Some models are linearised by a different transformation. The technique is to rearrange into Y = mX + c and identify what to plot.

y = a/x + b  →  plot y against 1/x: gradient a, intercept b
y = a e^(bx) →  plot ln y against x
y = a x^n    →  plot ln y against ln x

Worked example. Data fits y = p/x + q. What should be plotted on the axes, and how are p and q then found from the graph?

plot y (vertical) against 1/x (horizontal)
gradient = p, intercept = q

Inequalities and exact solutions

Worked example. Solve e^x > 10, giving an exact answer.

x > ln 10

Worked example 2. Solve ln(2x − 1) ≤ 3.

2x - 1 <= e³ and 2x - 1 > 0
1/2 < x <= (e³ + 1)/2 = 10.54

Both boundaries matter: the domain condition gives the strict lower bound, the inequality gives the upper one.

Exponentials in calculus: stationary points

Because e^x differentiates to itself, a product with a polynomial produces clean stationary-point questions.

Worked example. Find and classify the stationary point of y = x e^(−x).

product rule: dy/dx = e^(-x) - x e^(-x) = e^(-x)(1 - x)
stationary where 1 - x = 0  →  x = 1, y = e⁻¹ = 0.368
second derivative: e^(-x)(x - 2); at x = 1 it is -e⁻¹ < 0
so (1, 0.368) is a maximum

Worked example 2. Find the minimum of y = e^x − 3x.

dy/dx = e^x - 3 = 0  →  x = ln 3 = 1.099
y = 3 - 3 ln 3 = 3 - 3.296 = -0.296
second derivative e^x > 0, so it is a minimum

Worked example 3 (integration by recognition). Find ∫ x e^(x²) dx.

the derivative of e^(x²) is 2x e^(x²), so the integral is
(1/2)e^(x²) + c

Comparing growth rates

Exponential growth eventually outpaces any polynomial. That statement is examinable as a comparison of gradients or of long-run behaviour.

Worked example. Show that for large x, e^x grows faster than x³ by comparing their ratio.

consider f(x) = e^x/x³
as x → infinity the ratio tends to infinity (exponential beats polynomial)
equivalently: differentiating repeatedly, e^x keeps its factor of e^x
while the polynomial loses a degree each time

Worked example 2 (doubling). A quantity grows as N = 50e^(0.08t). How long to double?

e^(0.08t) = 2  →  t = ln 2/0.08 = 8.66 years

The doubling time depends only on k, not on the starting value: that is the signature of exponential growth and worth saying in the answer. Halving time behaves the same way, and for decay the ratio ln 2/|k| gives a half-life independent of the initial quantity — which is why radiocarbon dating works on any sample size.

Simultaneous exponential equations

Two exponential equations are solved by taking logs and then treating the result as a linear system in the unknowns.

Worked example. Solve 2^x 3^y = 12 and 2^y 3^x = 18.

take logs: x ln 2 + y ln 3 = ln 12
y ln 2 + x ln 3 = ln 18
rearrange the second: x ln 3 + y ln 2 = ln 18
solve the 2 × 2 system:
from the first: x = (ln 12 - y ln 3)/ln 2
substitute and simplify  →  y = 1, x = 2

Worked example 2 (same base). Solve 9^x = 3^(x+2).

9^x = 3^(2x), so 2x = x + 2  →  x = 2

With two unknowns the log step is compulsory, and the equations are linear in x and y after it; that structure is what makes the pair solvable.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Evaluate) Find ln(e³). Answer: 3.
  2. (Law) Simplify ln 12 − ln 3. Answer: ln 4.
  3. (Solve) Solve 3^(2x) = 81. Answer: 2x = 4 → x = 2.
  4. (Solve logs) Solve log₂(x) + log₂(x − 2) = 3. Answer: x(x − 2) = 8 → x = 4.
  5. (Differentiate) y = e^(2x) ln x. Use the product rule. Answer: 2e^(2x) ln x + e^(2x)/x.
  6. (Integrate) ∫ (1/(2x)) dx. Answer: ½ ln|2x| + c = ½ ln|x| + c′.
  7. (Model) A population is 200e^(0.03t). When does it reach 500? Answer: t = ln(2.5)/0.03 = 30.5.
  8. (Log-linear) ln y = 0.5x + 2. Find y. Answer: y = 7.39e^(0.5x).

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • log(a + b) treated as log a + log b: there is no such law; the sum cannot be split.
