  • Domain ignored: ln of a non-positive number is undefined; reject roots that violate it and say so.
  • Differentiating e^(kx) as ke^x: the factor k multiplies the whole exponential.
  • Integrating 1/x as ln x without the modulus: use ln|x|, since the function is defined on both sides of zero.
  • Half-life sign: with decay k is negative, so half-life is ln 2/|k|; a negative time means the sign was mishandled.
  • Log-linear misread: the intercept is ln a, so a = e^(intercept), not the intercept itself.
  • Base 10 and base e mixed: convert with log_a x = ln x/ln a before combining.
  • Model without interpretation: state the meaning of k in context — a rate per year, per minute, per unit.

Equations and symbols

Every relation this topic is examined on, written with its real notation and followed by a key naming each symbol, its unit and what it means. Where a law has a second useful form both are given, so the rearrangement in the exam is mechanical rather than a thing to rediscover under time pressure.

Definition, laws and change of base

y = aˣ ⇔ x = log_a y
Key: a = base, a > 0 and a ≠ 1; x = the exponent; y = the result, always positive. The logarithm is defined as the inverse of the exponential, which is why log_a y exists only for y > 0 — a positive base can never produce a negative power.

log_a(xy) = log_a x + log_a y
Key: log_a = logarithm to base a; x, y = positive numbers. Multiplication inside becomes addition outside, because aᵐ·aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ.

log_a(x/y) = log_a x − log_a y
Key: the same symbols. Division inside becomes subtraction outside.

log_a(xⁿ) = n log_a x
Key: n = any real power. The law that turns an unknown exponent into a coefficient, and therefore the one that solves every equation of the form aˣ = b.

log_a a = 1 and log_a 1 = 0
Key: a = the base. Both follow from a¹ = a and a⁰ = 1; they are the two anchors most simplification questions use.

a^(log_a x) = x and log_a(aˣ) = x
Key: the inverse pair, valid for x > 0. Composing the two functions returns the input, which is how an exponential equation is cleared.

log_a x = log_b x / log_b a
Key: a = the base wanted; b = any base the calculator offers, usually 10 or e. The change-of-base formula: a calculator computes ln and log, so every other base is converted to one of those.

log_a(1/x) = −log_a x and log_a √x = ½ log_a x
Key: the power law with n = −1 and n = ½. Useful when a reciprocal or a root appears inside a log.

Calculus of exponentials and logarithms

d/dx (eˣ) = eˣ
Key: e = 2.71828…, the base for which the curve's gradient equals its value. This is the property that defines e, not a coincidence about it.

d/dx (e^(kx)) = k e^(kx)
Key: k = constant multiplier of x (any real number). The chain rule applied to the inner function kx.

d/dx (aˣ) = aˣ ln a
Key: a = base > 0; ln a = natural log of the base. Any exponential differentiates to itself times a constant, and that constant is ln a — for a = e it is 1, which recovers the line above.

d/dx (ln x) = 1/x and d/dx (ln kx) = 1/x
Key: x > 0; k > 0 constant. The second result surprises students: ln kx = ln k + ln x, and ln k is a constant, so it differentiates away.

∫ e^(kx) dx = (1/k) e^(kx) + c
Key: k ≠ 0 constant; c = constant of integration. The reverse of the derivative, with the 1/k that undoes the chain rule.

∫ (1/x) dx = ln|x| + c
Key: x ≠ 0; the modulus keeps the antiderivative valid for negative x, where 1/x is still defined but ln x is not. For a definite integral across zero the function is undefined and the integral must be split.

Modelling: growth, decay and log-linear graphs

y = A e^(kx)
Key: y = the quantity at time t; A = its value at t = 0; k = the rate constant (per unit time); k > 0 growth, k < 0 decay. The continuous model — every exponential growth or decay question is this equation with numbers in it.

t½ = ln 2 / |k|
Key: t½ = half-life, the time for y to halve (same time unit as k); k = the rate constant. From A/2 = A e^(kt½), taking logs: kt½ = −ln 2.

ln y = ln A + k x
Key: x = the independent variable; y = the measured quantity; A, k = the model's constants. Taking logs turns the curve into a straight line: plot ln y against x and the gradient is k with intercept ln A.

y = a xⁿ ⇒ ln y = ln a + n ln x
Key: a = coefficient; n = the power. A power law becomes linear on a log–log plot, with gradient n and intercept ln a — the standard way to find an unknown index from data.

y = a bˣ ⇒ log y = log a + x log b
Key: a = value at x = 0; b = the growth factor per unit x. A geometric model becomes linear when log y is plotted against x, with gradient log b.

dy/dx = 0 gives the stationary point of y = A e^(kx)
Key: since A e^(kx) is never zero for finite x, a pure exponential has no stationary point — one exists only where the exponent is a function of x that itself has a turning point, which is the usual exam twist.

title: Integration — Study Notes
content:
Integration

Indefinite Integrals

Reverse the power rule and add a constant: ∫ xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n+1) + c (n ≠ −1).

Examples: ∫ x³ dx = x⁴/4 + c; ∫ 1/x dx = ln|x| + c; ∫ sin x dx = −cos x + c; ∫ e^x dx = e^x + c.

Definite Integrals

∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = [F(x)]ₐᵇ = F(b) − F(a). Constants of integration cancel.

Example: ∫₀¹ 6x² dx = [2x³]₀¹ = 2.

Areas Under Curves

Area between a curve and the x-axis = ∫ₐᵇ y dx, where y ≥ 0. If the curve dips below the axis, split the integral at the roots and add the absolute values.

Example: area between y = x² − 4 and the x-axis: roots ±2, and the area is |∫₋₂² (x² − 4) dx| = 32/3.

Trapezium Rule

A ≈ h/2 [y₀ + 2(y₁ + … + yₙ₋₁) + yₙ], h = (b − a)/n. More strips → better estimate; always an over-estimate for convex curves.

Exam tips: never forget +c on indefinite integrals; for areas with negative regions, sketch first and split.

Rules and exam method

For xⁿ with n ≠ −1, ∫xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + c. Integrate term by term. The special case is ∫(1/x) dx = ln|x| + c. An indefinite integral needs + c; a definite integral does not.

For a definite integral, ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a), where F is any antiderivative. Write the limits as [F(x)] between a and b, and substitute carefully: a negative limit raised to a power needs brackets.

The area between a curve and the x-axis is ∫ y dx when y ≥ 0 over the interval. If the curve lies below the axis the integral is negative, so take the modulus. If the curve crosses the axis, find the root and integrate each part separately, adding the moduli of the parts.

The area between two curves is the integral of (upper − lower) between their intersection points, found by solving the equations simultaneously.

Exam cue: Show the expanded antiderivative before substituting limits; method marks are given for a correct integration even when the arithmetic later slips.

title: A Level Mathematics: Hypothesis Testing
content:
A Level Mathematics: Hypothesis Testing

A hypothesis test is a formal way of deciding whether data are surprising enough to overturn an assumption. The logic is legal rather than mathematical in spirit: assume the claim is true, compute how unlikely the observed evidence would be under that assumption, and reject the claim only if the evidence is unlikely enough. This note sets out the machinery — null and alternative hypotheses, significance levels, tails, critical regions — and then applies it to the binomial and normal cases the exam uses.

The logic of a test

The null hypothesis H0 is the assumption of no change, no effect, no bias: the status quo. The alternative H1 is what you would conclude if the data are too extreme. The significance level α is the risk of rejecting a true H0 that you are willing to accept.

H0: the parameter equals its old value
H1: the parameter is greater, less, or simply different
alpha: the maximum acceptable probability of a Type I error (often 0.05 or 0.01)
test statistic: the observed value computed from the sample
p-value: probability of a result at least as extreme, assuming H0

The analogy that makes the asymmetry clear: a criminal trial presumes innocence. The presumption is not a belief, it is the default that evidence must overcome. Failing to reject H0 is not proof of H0 — it is a verdict of "not proven".

One-tailed and two-tailed tests

The alternative decides the tail. A one-tailed test is used when the direction of the change is specified in advance; a two-tailed test when any change would matter.

AlternativeTest typep-value
p > p0one-tailed, upperP(X ≥ observed)
p < p0one-tailed, lowerP(X ≤ observed)
p ≠ p0two-tailed2 × the smaller tail

Worked example (choosing the alternative). A coin is suspected of favouring heads. Which alternative applies?

the suspicion has a direction, so H1: p > 0.5, a one-tailed upper test
a two-tailed test would be right only if any bias mattered

Errors and their consequences

Every test can go wrong in two ways, and the significance level controls only one of them. Understanding which is which is a frequent exam question and a genuine conceptual point.

Type I error: reject H0 when it is true  (probability alpha)
Type II error: fail to reject H0 when it is false
reducing alpha reduces Type I errors but increases Type II errors
increasing the sample size reduces both

Worked example. A test at the 5% level concludes a die is biased when it is fair. Which error is this?

H0 (fair) was true and was rejected
that is a Type I error, with probability at most 5%

Worked example 2 (effect of sample size). Explain why the same observed proportion can be significant in a large sample and not in a small one.

a larger sample reduces the standard error, so the same deviation
becomes more standard errors away from the null value
the evidence is measured in standard errors, not in raw counts

Testing a binomial proportion

The test statistic is the observed number of successes, the null distribution is binomial, and the p-value is a cumulative binomial probability.

H0: p = p0;  X ~ B(n, p0)
upper tail p-value = P(X >= x)
lower tail p-value = P(X <= x)
reject H0 if p-value <= alpha

Worked example. A manufacturer claims 90% of components are fault-free. In a sample of 20, only 15 are fault-free. Test at the 5% level whether the claim is too high.

H0: p = 0.9;  H1: p < 0.9
X ~ B(20, 0.9)
P(X <= 15) = 0.0432
0.0432 < 0.05, so reject H0
there is evidence the fault-free rate is below 90%

Worked example 2 (critical region). Find the 5% critical region for that test.

P(X <= 15) = 0.0432 (below 0.05)
P(X <= 16) = 0.1330 (above 0.05)
critical region: X <= 15

Worked example 3 (actual significance level). State the actual significance level of that test.

the probability of a Type I error is P(X <= 15) under H0 = 0.0432
so the actual level is 4.32%, just inside the 5% requirement

Testing a normal mean

When the variable is continuous and the population is normal — or the sample is large — the test statistic is standardised with a z-score and compared with critical values.

test statistic z = (x-bar - mu)/(σ/sqrt n)   (σ known)
or z = (x-bar - mu)/(s/sqrt n)                  (σ estimated, large n)
critical values at 5% one-tailed: 1.6449;  two-tailed: 1.96
at 1% one-tailed: 2.3263;  two-tailed: 2.5758

Worked example. A machine fills bags with a mean of 500 g and standard deviation 8 g. A sample of 16 bags has mean 496 g. Test at the 5% level whether the mean has fallen.

H0: mu = 500;  H1: mu < 500
standard error = 8/sqrt 16 = 2
z = (496 - 500)/2 = -2
critical value at 5% one-tailed is -1.6449
-2 < -1.6449, so reject H0: the mean has fallen

Worked example 2 (two-tailed). Same data, tested two-tailed at 5%.

critical values are +/-1.96
|-2| > 1.96, so still reject H0
the evidence is that the mean is not 500, in either direction

Worked example 3 (interpreting a p-value). A test gives z = 1.72 for H1: μ > μ0. Find the p-value and conclude at 5%.

p-value = P(Z > 1.72) = 0.0427
0.0427 < 0.05, so reject H0
the result is significant at the 5% level but not at 1%

Choosing the right test

The exam does not label the test; the shape of the data decides it. Getting the distribution wrong makes every later mark unreachable, so the decision is worth making explicitly.

count of successes in n trials with constant p  →  binomial test
count of events in an interval at a constant rate  →  Poisson test
mean of a continuous measurement  →  normal test (z)
correlation between two variables  →  product-moment test

Worked example. A nurse records the number of patients arriving in an hour on 30 separate days. Which test?

counts of arrivals in equal intervals at a roughly constant rate
use a Poisson test on the mean count, not a binomial test
a normal test on the mean of the 30 counts is also defensible for large n

Writing a conclusion that earns the marks

The final mark of a hypothesis test is for the conclusion, and it has three components: a decision about H0, a reference to the significance level, and the finding stated in the context of the question. Dropping any one of them costs a mark even when the arithmetic is perfect.

Compare these two endings. "0.0201 < 0.05, so reject H0" scores the comparison. "There is sufficient evidence at the 5% level that the call rate has increased" scores the comparison and the interpretation. "The rate has increased" scores neither, because it reports a certainty the test cannot deliver.

The opposite case is often mishandled too. When the p-value is above the level the correct wording is that there is insufficient evidence to reject H0 — never that H0 is true, and never that nothing has happened. A non-significant result from a small sample is weak evidence either way, and saying so is better than overclaiming in either direction.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Hypotheses) A coin might be biased against heads. State H0 and H1. Answer: H0: p = 0.5; H1: p < 0.5.
  2. (Error) Define a Type II error. Answer: failing to reject H0 when it is false.
  3. (Binomial) 8 of 20 seeds germinate; test p = 0.6 against p < 0.6 at 5%. Answer: X ~ B(20, 0.6), so P(X ≤ 8) = 0.0565; since 0.0565 > 0.05 there is insufficient evidence to reject H0.
  4. (Critical region) X ~ B(15, 0.4): 5% lower critical region. Answer: test P(X ≤ c) ≤ 0.05: P(X ≤ 2) = 0.0271 ≤ 0.05, but P(X ≤ 3) = 0.0905 > 0.05, so the critical region is X ≤ 2.
  5. (Actual level) For that region, state the actual significance level. Answer: actual significance level = P(X ≤ 2) = 0.0271 = 2.71%.
  6. (Normal) μ0 = 20, σ = 4, n = 25, mean 21.5: test at 5% one-tailed. Answer: z = (x̄ − μ0)/(σ/√n) = (21.5 − 20)/(4/√25) = 1.5/0.8 = 1.875, and 1.875 > 1.6449, so reject H0.
  7. (Two-tailed) Same data two-tailed: Answer: z = (21.5 − 20)/(4/√25) = 1.875, and 1.875 < 1.96, so do not reject H0.
  8. (p-value) z = 2.4, H1: μ > μ0. Find the p-value. Answer: p-value = P(Z > 2.4) = 1 − 0.9918 = 0.0082.
  9. (Sample size) Why can a larger sample turn a non-significant result significant? Answer: the standard error shrinks, so the same deviation is more standard errors away.
  10. (Conclusion wording) Write a valid conclusion for a rejected H0. Answer: there is sufficient evidence at the 5% level that the mean has fallen.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Concluding H0 is true: failing to reject means the evidence is insufficient; it is never proof of the null.
  • Wrong tail: compute P(X ≥ x) for an increase and P(X ≤ x) for a decrease; using the other tail inverts the conclusion.
  • Doubling without a two-tailed alternative: the p-value is doubled only when H1 is "not equal".
  • p-value compared with the wrong threshold: 5% is 0.05; comparing 0.043 with 5 instead of 0.05 reverses the verdict.
  • Standard error omitted: the z-score divides by σ/√n, not by σ.
  • Critical value for the wrong tail: the 5% one-tailed value is 1.6449, the two-tailed is 1.96; the sign matters too.
  • Type I and Type II swapped: Type I is rejecting a true null — the error the significance level controls.
  • Conclusion beyond the data: a rejected H0 says the parameter has changed, not why, and never that the change is important.

Setting up the hypotheses before any calculation

Hypotheses are the first lines a marker reads, and a wrong direction or a sample statistic written where a parameter belongs loses marks before any arithmetic is checked. The subsections set out how to define the parameter, write H₀ as a single value and read H₁ from the wording of the question.

Defining the parameter in words first

Before writing any symbol, say what the parameter measures. Let p be the proportion of seeds that germinate, or let μ be the mean mass of a bag in grams. The parameter belongs to the population the claim is about, not to the sample you were given. The definition is the line that makes the rest of the working easy to follow, so write it first.

Writing H₀ as a single value

H₀ names one value for the parameter with an equals sign, such as H₀: p = 0.6 or H₀: μ = 50. It is the value the test assumes is true when it calculates the probability of the data. The probability can only be worked out at one specific value, so the test is always carried out at the value stated in H₀, and the working should say so.

Reading the direction of H₁ from the wording

Words map to symbols in a fixed way. “Greater than”, “more than”, “has increased” and “above” give >. “Less than”, “fewer”, “has decreased” and “below” give <. “Different from”, “has changed” and “is not equal to” give ≠. A question that asks whether a proportion has changed, without saying which way, needs H₁: p ≠ p₀, and that choice fixes a two-tailed test.

Hypotheses for a mean from a normal model

When X is normal with a known standard deviation, the hypotheses concern μ, and the variance belongs to the model: X ~ N(μ, σ²). Write the assumption that the population is normal with known σ, or that the sample is large enough for the central limit theorem to apply. The hypotheses for a sample mean are the same as for the population mean, because the test is about μ.

Hypotheses set before the data are used

The direction of H₁ must come from the claim in the question, not from the sample. If the sample mean is 49 and the claim is μ = 50, it is tempting to choose H₁: μ < 50 after looking at the data. That choice invalidates the test, because it lets the data pick the tail. Settle the direction from the wording, and show it in the working before the test statistic.

Equations and symbols

A hypothesis test is a decision rule, and these are its moving parts: the test statistic, the standard error, the tail probability and the comparison that produces the verdict.

The decision

reject H0 if p-value <= alpha Key: H0 = the null hypothesis, the assumption of no change; p-value = the probability of a result at least as extreme, assuming H0 is true; alpha = the significance level, the acceptable risk of rejecting a true H0 (often 0.05 or 0.01). Failing to reject is not proof that H0 is true — it means the evidence was insufficient.

P(X <= 15) = 0.0432 Key: X = number of fault-free components in a sample of 20; 0.0432 = the lower-tail probability under H0: p = 0.9. Because 0.0432 < 0.05 the null is rejected, and the same figure is the actual significance level of the test.

The normal test

standard error = 8/sqrt 16 = 2 Key: 8 = population standard deviation σ (g); 16 = sample size n (bags); 2 = the standard error of the mean (g). The standard error, not σ, is the denominator of the test statistic — omitting the √n is the classic lost mark.

z = (496 - 500)/2 = -2 Key: z = the test statistic, in standard errors; 496 = sample mean (g); 500 = hypothesised mean μ (g); 2 = the standard error (g). Compare |z| with the critical value: 1.6449 one-tailed at 5%, 1.96 two-tailed at 5%.

p-value = P(Z > 1.72) = 0.0427 Key: Z = the standard normal variable; 1.72 = the observed test statistic; 0.0427 = the area beyond it, for an upper-tail alternative. Significant at 5% but not at 1% — say which level you are concluding at.

Errors

A Type I error rejects a true H0 and has probability alpha; a Type II error fails to reject a false H0. Lowering alpha reduces Type I errors and increases Type II; a larger sample reduces both, because it shrinks the standard error so the same deviation counts as more standard errors.

The slip worth naming

Comparing a p-value with 5 instead of 0.05, or doubling the tail without a two-sided alternative. Both reverse a correct conclusion, which is exactly the mark the question is testing.

title: AS Level Chemistry: Halogenoalkanes, Alcohols and Spectra
content:
AS Level Chemistry: Halogenoalkanes, Alcohols and Spectra

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH12, Topic 10 is the largest organic topic in the AS year. It covers how to classify reactions and mechanisms, the chemistry of halogenoalkanes and alcohols with their characteristic substitution, elimination and oxidation reactions, the practical techniques used to prepare and purify a liquid organic compound, and the two spectroscopic methods, mass spectrometry and infrared, that identify what a compound is. The mechanisms are examined with curly arrows, so the drawing and the explanation must both be right.

Classifying reactions and the idea of a mechanism

Every organic reaction belongs to one of these categories, and the classification is often the first mark of a question:

  • Addition: two species combine into one, with nothing lost, as when an alkene adds hydrogen bromide.
  • Elimination: a small molecule is removed from a larger one, leaving a double bond, as when a halogenoalkane forms an alkene.
  • Substitution: one atom or group is replaced by another, as when a halogenoalkane becomes an alcohol.
  • Oxidation: gain of oxygen or loss of hydrogen, as when an alcohol becomes an aldehyde or a carboxylic acid.
  • Reduction: gain of hydrogen or loss of oxygen.
  • Hydrolysis: breaking a bond by reaction with water or aqueous alkali, as in the hydrolysis of a halogenoalkane.
  • Polymerisation: monomers join into a polymer.

A reaction mechanism is a step-by-step description of how the electrons move during a reaction. It shows which bonds break, in what order, and which species are formed on the way. Mechanisms are drawn with curly arrows: a full arrow shows the movement of a pair of electrons, and a half-arrow shows the movement of one electron in a radical reaction. A curly arrow always starts at a bond or at a lone pair and points to where the electrons go.

The type of mechanism depends on bond polarity. When a bond is polar, the more electronegative atom carries a partial negative charge and the other a partial positive charge, so the molecule has an electron-rich site and an electron-poor site. That is an invitation to attack by a species with the opposite character:

  • A nucleophile is an electron-pair donor: it has a lone pair and is attracted to an electron-poor (δ+) carbon. Examples are OH⁻, NH₃, CN⁻ and water.
  • An electrophile is an electron-pair acceptor: it is attracted to an electron-rich site such as a C=C double bond. Examples are HBr, Br₂ and the nitrosonium ion in nitration.

So a polar C–X bond, with δ+ on the carbon, is attacked by nucleophiles and undergoes nucleophilic substitution. A C=C double bond with its exposed π electrons is attacked by electrophiles and undergoes electrophilic addition. Heterolytic fission produces these ions and charged species; homolytic fission produces radicals and leads to radical substitution.

Halogenoalkanes: naming and classification

A halogenoalkane has a halogen atom in place of a hydrogen on an alkane chain. The halogen is named as a prefix (fluoro-, chloro-, bromo-, iodo-) with its position number, and the chain is numbered to give the substituent the lowest number: CH₃CH₂CH₂Cl is 1-chloropropane, and CH₃CHClCH₃ is 2-chloropropane.

Halogenoalkanes are classified by how many carbon atoms are bonded directly to the carbon that carries the halogen:

ClassDefinitionExample
Primary (1°)The C–X carbon is bonded to one other carbonCH₃CH₂Cl, chloroethane
Secondary (2°)The C–X carbon is bonded to two other carbonsCH₃CHClCH₃, 2-chloropropane
Tertiary (3°)The C–X carbon is bonded to three other carbons(CH₃)₃CCl, 2-chloro-2-methylpropane

Reactions of halogenoalkanes

The reagent and the solvent decide whether substitution or elimination happens. Learn the table as a set of conditions, not as separate facts.

Reagent and conditionsProductTypeEquation (with 1-bromopropane)
Aqueous potassium hydroxide, heatAlcoholNucleophilic substitutionC3H7Br + OH⁻ → C3H7OH + Br⁻
Ethanolic potassium hydroxide, heatAlkeneEliminationC3H7Br + OH⁻ → C3H6 + H2O + Br⁻
Aqueous silver nitrate in ethanol, warmAlcohol, with a silver halide precipitateHydrolysisC3H7Br + H2O → C3H7OH + HBr, then Ag+ + Br⁻ → AgBr(s)
Alcoholic ammonia, heated under pressureAmineNucleophilic substitutionC3H7Br + 2NH3 → C3H7NH2 + NH4Br
Alcoholic potassium cyanide, heatNitrileNucleophilic substitutionC3H7Br + CN⁻ → C3H7CN + Br⁻

In the first reaction the hydroxide ion acts as a nucleophile: its lone pair attacks the δ+ carbon and the C–Br bond breaks heterolytically, with the bromide ion leaving. In the second the same ion acts as a base instead, removing a hydrogen from an adjacent carbon and pushing the electrons into a new C=C bond, so the molecule loses HBr and becomes an alkene. The solvent is the switch: water favours substitution, ethanol favours elimination.

Ammonia is used in excess because the first substitution gives an amine, which can itself act as a nucleophile and react again with the halogenoalkane to give a secondary and then a tertiary amine. The cyanide reaction is useful because it lengthens the carbon chain by one carbon: the nitrile can be hydrolysed to a carboxylic acid.

The nucleophilic substitution mechanisms

For a primary halogenoalkane, the mechanism is a one-step bimolecular process. In the exam you draw the displayed formula of the halogenoalkane, place the nucleophile beside it, and use curly arrows.

With aqueous potassium hydroxide. The arrow from the lone pair on the oxygen of OH⁻ points to the δ+ carbon of the C–Br bond. A second arrow starts at the middle of the C–Br bond and points to the bromine, showing the pair leaving with the bromine as Br⁻. The product is the alcohol and the leaving group.

With ammonia. The arrow from the lone pair on the nitrogen of NH₃ points to the δ+ carbon, and a second arrow from the C–Br bond points to the bromine. The initial product is an alkylammonium ion, which loses a proton to give the amine, so the overall equation is a substitution of Br by NH₂. Drawing the ammonium ion is the detail that separates a full-mark answer from a partial one.

The carbon being attacked is electron-poor because bromine is more electronegative than carbon, so the bond is polarised Cδ+–Brδ−. The nucleophile is electron-rich and is attracted to that δ+ carbon, which is why the mechanism is described as nucleophilic substitution rather than electrophilic addition. A secondary or tertiary halogenoalkane may instead react by an ionisation-then-attack route, with a carbocation intermediate; that distinction, SN1 versus SN2, is examined in Unit 4, not here.

Comparing the rates of hydrolysis

The rate of hydrolysis can be followed by warming the halogenoalkane with aqueous silver nitrate in ethanol and timing how long it takes for a precipitate of silver halide to appear. Water is the nucleophile, and the silver ion removes the halide as it is released, which keeps the reaction moving and makes the halide visible.

R-X + H2O → R-OH + HX          then          Ag+(aq) + X-(aq) → AgX(s)
HalidePrecipitate colourRelative rate
Chloro-WhiteSlowest
Bromo-CreamIntermediate
Iodo-Pale yellowFastest

Two comparisons are made. Structurally, tertiary halogenoalkanes hydrolyse faster than secondary, which are faster than primary, because the intermediate carbocation is more stable when more alkyl groups can donate electron density, and because the crowded carbon is more easily approached. Across the halogens, the rate increases from chloro- to bromo- to iodo- because the C–X bond enthalpy decreases down the group: C–Cl is the strongest bond, so it is the hardest to break, and C–I the weakest, so it breaks most readily.

Core Practical 5 carries out exactly this investigation. A measured volume of the halogenoalkane is added to silver nitrate in ethanol at a fixed temperature, and the time to the first appearance of the precipitate is recorded; rate is taken as 1/time. Water baths keep the temperature constant, and the same volumes and concentrations must be used so that the comparison is fair. The evaluation should note that the precipitate appearance is a subjective endpoint, that temperature control is critical because rate is very sensitive to it, and that different halogenoalkanes have different solubilities in ethanol.

Core Practical 6 prepares 2-chloro-2-methylpropane by shaking 2-methylpropan-2-ol with concentrated hydrochloric acid. The tertiary alcohol reacts readily by substitution, and the product separates as an organic layer, which is washed with sodium hydrogencarbonate solution to remove excess acid, dried, and distilled. The boiling temperature of the distillate is checked against the data book value as a test of purity.

Alcohols: naming and classification

An alcohol contains the –OH group. The suffix is -ol with the position number: CH₃CH₂OH is ethanol, CH₃CH₂CH₂OH is propan-1-ol, and CH₃CHOHCH₃ is propan-2-ol.

Alcohols are classified in the same way as halogenoalkanes, by the number of carbons attached to the carbon carrying the –OH group: primary (one), secondary (two), tertiary (three). This classification predicts how each alcohol behaves on oxidation, so it is examined directly.

ClassExampleOxidation product
Primarypropan-1-olPropanal with distillation, propanoic acid under reflux
Secondarypropan-2-olPropanone; no further oxidation under normal conditions
Tertiary2-methylpropan-2-olNo reaction with acidified dichromate at AS level

Reactions of alcohols

Reagent and conditionsProductNotes
Oxygen in air, ignitionCarbon dioxide and waterCombustion; alcohols are fuels
Phosphorus(V) chloride, PCl5, room temperatureChloroalkaneAlso gives misty fumes of HCl and is used as a qualitative test for an –OH group
Concentrated sulfuric acid with potassium bromideBromoalkaneThe HBr generated in situ substitutes the OH
Red phosphorus with iodineIodoalkaneRed phosphorus and iodine generate phosphorus(III) iodide in situ
Concentrated phosphoric acid, heatAlkeneElimination of water (dehydration)
Acidified potassium dichromate(VI), heatAldehyde or carboxylic acid (primary), ketone (secondary)The orange dichromate turns green as it is reduced

For the halogenating agents, the mechanisms are not required, but the equations and the observation are. With PCl₅ the test is the white fumes or misty vapour of hydrogen chloride, which turns damp blue litmus paper red. For the sulfuric acid and potassium bromide route, the acid and the bromide produce hydrogen bromide, which then reacts with the alcohol:

KBr + H2SO4 → KHSO4 + HBr
C2H5OH + HBr → C2H5Br + H2O

Concentrated phosphoric acid dehydrates an alcohol to an alkene, and the alkene can be identified by decolourising bromine water.

Oxidation of alcohols

The oxidising agent is acidified potassium dichromate(VI), written as [O] in equations. The colour change from orange to green is the visual evidence that oxidation has occurred.

Primary alcohols. The product depends on the apparatus. If the aldehyde is distilled off as it forms, it escapes before it can be oxidised further:

C2H5OH + [O] → CH3CHO + H2O

If the mixture is heated under reflux, the aldehyde stays in contact with the oxidising agent and is oxidised again to the carboxylic acid:

C2H5OH + 2[O] → CH3COOH + H2O

Secondary alcohols. Oxidation gives a ketone, which resists further oxidation because the carbonyl carbon has no hydrogen attached:

CH3CHOHCH3 + [O] → CH3COCH3 + H2O

Tertiary alcohols. No reaction with acidified dichromate, because the carbon carrying the OH has no hydrogen to remove and cannot form a C=O bond.

The products are distinguished by tests:

  • Aldehydes reduce Fehling's solution to a brick-red precipitate of copper(I) oxide, and Benedict's solution similarly, on warming. Ketones do not react.
  • Carboxylic acids react with sodium carbonate or sodium hydrogencarbonate to give effervescence of carbon dioxide; aldehydes and ketones do not.
  • Tollens' reagent gives a silver mirror with an aldehyde and no change with a ketone.

Preparing and purifying a liquid organic compound

Five techniques are examined together, because a preparation uses several of them in sequence.

  • Heating under reflux: a vertical condenser returns vapour to the flask, so the mixture can be heated for a long time without losing solvent or volatile product. It is used when the reaction is slow or needs prolonged heating, such as the oxidation of a primary alcohol to a carboxylic acid.
  • Extraction with a solvent using a separating funnel: the product is shaken with a solvent in which it is more soluble than in the reaction mixture, the two layers are allowed to separate, and the layer containing the product is run off. The stopper must be vented during shaking to release pressure.
  • Distillation: separates a volatile product from involatile impurities or from a solvent with a different boiling temperature. The fraction boiling over the expected range is collected.
  • Drying with an anhydrous salt: anhydrous magnesium sulfate or calcium chloride is added to remove traces of water; it clumps and can be filtered off once it stops clumping.
  • Boiling temperature determination: a pure compound boils at a sharp, known temperature. A range that is wide or different from the data book value indicates impurities.

Core Practical 7 oxidises propan-1-ol to propanal and to propanoic acid. For the aldehyde, the oxidising agent is added slowly to the alcohol and the product is distilled off as it forms, collecting the fraction that boils near 48 °C. For the acid, the mixture is heated under reflux, then the acid is separated and purified. The questions on this practical usually ask why the aldehyde must be removed as it forms, and what the observation of the dichromate colour shows.

Mass spectrometry

In a mass spectrometer a molecule is ionised, usually by electron impact, and the ions are separated by mass-to-charge ratio. The most intense peak of the molecular ion, M⁺, gives the relative molecular mass. Fragmentation produces smaller ions, and the pattern of peaks is a fingerprint of the structure.

  • The molecular ion peak is the peak with the highest m/z value (ignoring small isotope peaks), and its m/z equals Mᵣ.
  • A peak at M−15 often indicates the loss of a methyl group, CH₃.
  • A peak at M−29 indicates the loss of an ethyl group, C₂H₅.
  • Peaks at 15, 29, 43 correspond to CH₃⁺, C₂H₅⁺ and C₃H₇⁺, and are common in alkanes and alkyl chains.
  • A peak at m/z 31 is characteristic of CH₂OH⁺ from a primary alcohol.
  • For a chloro- or bromo-compound, the isotope pattern is decisive: chlorine gives peaks two units apart in roughly 3:1 ratio, and bromine gives peaks two units apart in roughly 1:1 ratio, because of the ³⁵Cl/³⁷Cl and ⁷⁹Br/⁸¹Br isotopes.

Worked example. A compound has a molecular ion peak at m/z 74 and major fragments at 43 and 31. Mᵣ = 74 is consistent with C₄H₁₀O (4 × 12 + 10 + 16 = 74). A fragment at 43 corresponds to C₃H₇⁺ (loss of CH₂OH), and a fragment at 31 corresponds to CH₂OH⁺, so the compound is butan-1-ol, a primary alcohol. A secondary alcohol such as butan-2-ol would not give the 31 peak, because it cannot lose a CH₂OH group.

Infrared spectroscopy

Infrared radiation is absorbed by bonds that vibrate with a change in dipole. Different functional groups absorb at different wavenumbers, so an infrared spectrum identifies which groups are present.

BondWavenumber / cm⁻¹Appearance and group
O–H2500–3300, broadBroad absorption, carboxylic acid (with C=O)
O–H3230–3550, broadBroad absorption, alcohol
N–H3300–3500Sharp, amines
C–H2850–3300Stretching in alkanes, alkenes and aldehydes
C=O1680–1750, strongStrong sharp absorption: aldehyde, ketone or carboxylic acid
C=C1620–1680Weak to moderate, alkenes
C–O1000–1300Alcohols, ethers, esters
C–X500–800Halogenoalkanes

Two practical points are examined. First, an absorption at about 1700 cm⁻¹ alone does not distinguish an aldehyde from a ketone from a carboxylic acid: look for the broad O–H absorption of the acid as well, or the aldehyde C–H absorptions near 2700 and 2800 cm⁻¹. Second, the region below about 1500 cm⁻¹ is the fingerprint region, with many overlapping absorptions; it is used to identify a compound by matching its whole spectrum to a known one, not to identify individual groups.

The O–H absorption of an alcohol is broad because hydrogen bonding varies the O–H bond strength across the sample; the carboxylic acid O–H is even broader and extends over a wider range because of strong hydrogen bonding. This is why the shape and position of the broad absorption, not just its presence, carries information.

Core Practical 8: analysis of unknowns

An unknown inorganic or organic substance is identified by a sequence of tests, each chosen to eliminate possibilities. For an organic unknown, the sequence is usually: test for unsaturation with bromine water; test for an alcohol with PCl₅ or by oxidation with acidified dichromate; test for an aldehyde with Fehling's or Tollens' reagent; test for a carboxylic acid with sodium carbonate; then use infrared and mass spectra to confirm the functional groups and the molecular mass. Each positive result should be recorded with its observation, because the observation is the evidence.

Typical mistakes

  • Using aqueous KOH for elimination, or ethanolic KOH for substitution: the solvent decides the reaction.
  • Forgetting that the hydroxide ion is a nucleophile in substitution but a base in elimination.
  • Drawing a curly arrow from the wrong place, or drawing arrows that point to an atom rather than to a bond or lone pair.
  • Thinking a tertiary alcohol oxidises to a ketone; it does not react under these conditions.
  • Distilling a primary alcohol oxidation and expecting the carboxylic acid, or refluxing and expecting the aldehyde.
  • Calling the dichromate colour change a test for an aldehyde; it shows that oxidation has occurred, and Fehling's or Tollens' distinguishes the aldehyde.
  • Confusing the broad O–H absorption of an alcohol with the sharper C=O absorption, or ignoring the fingerprint region.
  • Quoting the base peak as the molecular ion peak; the base peak is the most intense, not necessarily the highest m/z.

Exam-style questions

  1. Explain why 1-iodobutane hydrolyses faster than 1-chlorobutane with aqueous silver nitrate. Answer: the C–I bond has a lower bond enthalpy than the C–Cl bond because the halogen atom is larger and the overlap with the carbon orbital is poorer, so the C–I bond breaks more easily and the iodide is released faster, giving a precipitate sooner.
  2. State the reagent and conditions needed to convert 1-bromopropane into propan-1-ol, and name the mechanism. Answer: aqueous potassium hydroxide, heated; nucleophilic substitution.
  3. Describe how you would obtain propanal from propan-1-ol, including the apparatus and the observation. Answer: warm propan-1-ol with acidified potassium dichromate(VI) and distill the product as it forms, collecting the fraction boiling near 48 °C. The orange dichromate turns green. Distilling the aldehyde off prevents it being oxidised further to propanoic acid.
  4. A compound with the molecular formula C₃H₇Br gives a precipitate with aqueous silver nitrate in ethanol, and on heating with ethanolic potassium hydroxide gives a gas that decolourises bromine water. Identify the type of reaction and explain the observation. Answer: the first is hydrolysis, releasing bromide ions that give a cream precipitate of silver bromide. The second is elimination, producing propene, which decolourises bromine water by electrophilic addition.
  5. A compound shows a strong absorption at 1715 cm⁻¹, a broad absorption at 3000 cm⁻¹ and no absorption at 2500–3300 cm⁻¹. Its mass spectrum has a molecular ion at m/z 58. Identify the compound. Answer: Mᵣ = 58 is consistent with C₃H₆O. The strong 1715 cm⁻¹ absorption is C=O, and the absence of a very broad acid O–H absorption means it is not a carboxylic acid, so it is propanone (or propanal, which would also show aldehyde C–H absorptions near 2700–2800 cm⁻¹).

Revise this topic by working from the functional group outwards: reagent, conditions, product, mechanism, then the observation that proves it. That single chain of reasoning answers most of the questions on halogenoalkanes, alcohols and spectra.

title: IGCSE Physics: Thermal Physics
content:
IGCSE Physics: Thermal Physics

Cambridge IGCSE Physics 0625 (2026–2028), Topic 2 Thermal physics: statements 2.1 Kinetic particle model of matter, 2.2 Thermal properties and temperature, and 2.3 Transfer of thermal energy. Heat is the traffic of energy between hot and cold objects, and the particle model explains every thermal phenomenon in the syllabus: expansion, pressure, changes of state, conduction, convection and radiation. Paper 4 loves the particle explanations as much as the calculations, so both are built here from the same model.

States of matter and changes of state

All matter is made of tiny particles in constant motion, and the three states differ in how those particles are arranged and how they move.

StateArrangementMotionShape and volume
SolidClose-packed regular rows, touchingVibrate about fixed positionsFixed shape and fixed volume
LiquidClose together but disorderedSlide over each otherTakes the shape of the container; fixed volume
GasFar apart, random, filling the containerFast, random, straight-line between collisionsNo fixed shape or volume

When a substance is heated, energy is transferred to its thermal store and the particles move faster. On a heating curve the temperature rises until a change of state begins; during melting or boiling the temperature stays constant while the energy goes into breaking the forces between particles rather than into speed. The names of the changes are: melting (solid to liquid), freezing (liquid to solid), boiling or vaporisation (liquid to gas), condensation (gas to liquid), sublimation (solid straight to gas, as with dry ice).

The particle model of pressure and Brownian motion

Gas pressure arises because particles collide with the walls of their container: each collision gives a tiny push, and billions of pushes per second produce a steady pressure. Squeezing the same particles into a smaller volume raises the collision rate per unit area and so raises the pressure; heating a gas at fixed volume makes the particles move faster and collide harder and more often, again raising the pressure.

Brownian motion is the random jiggling of smoke particles seen under a microscope. The smoke particles are bombarded unevenly by fast-moving invisible air molecules, and the bigger the imbalance of hits at any instant, the bigger the lurch. It is direct evidence that gas particles move randomly and continuously (Supplement: the uneven collisions and their random distribution are the explanation demanded).

The gas laws and the absolute scale of temperature

For a fixed mass of gas, three qualitative rules are examined at Core level: heating a gas at constant pressure makes it expand (and cooling makes it contract); compressing a gas at constant temperature raises its pressure; and the relationships are summarised by the particle model above. The Celsius scale is everyday but its zero is arbitrary; the kelvin scale starts at absolute zero, the temperature at which particles have the minimum possible energy.

temperature in kelvin = temperature in degrees Celsius + 273        T (K) = theta (C) + 273

Supplement: Boyle's law. For a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature, pressure and volume are inversely proportional:

p V = constant        p1 V1 = p2 V2
  • p: pressure in pascals (Pa), positive; V: volume in cubic metres (m³) or any consistent unit. Both are scalars.
  • The product pV stays constant only while the temperature and the amount of gas are fixed.

Doubling the pressure halves the volume; a graph of p against V is a curve (inverse proportion), while a graph of p against 1/V is a straight line through the origin — a standard Paper 4 graph question.

Thermal expansion of solids, liquids and gases

Almost everything expands when heated: the particles move faster and push further apart. Everyday consequences include gaps between railway rails and bridge sections, expansion loops in power cables, the bimetallic strip in a thermostat (two metals expand by different amounts, so the strip bends and breaks a circuit), and the difficulty of undoing a metal jar lid, which can be loosened by running hot water over it so the metal lid expands more than the glass. Liquids expand more than solids for the same temperature rise, and gases expand most of all.

The particle explanation is a Supplement statement: heating increases the average separation of the particles because their increased energy makes them swing wider about their positions in a solid, slide further apart in a liquid, and occupy a larger volume in a gas at the same pressure. Thermometers work because liquids expand predictably with temperature: the liquid column rises in a narrow capillary, making a small volume change visible as a large length change.

Specific heat capacity

Equal masses of different substances need different amounts of energy to warm by the same temperature: water resists temperature change far more than sand, which is why coastal towns have mild climates and why water makes an excellent coolant in car engines and central heating. That property is the specific heat capacity:

energy transferred = mass x specific heat capacity x temperature change        E = m c delta theta
  • E: energy transferred in joules (J); m: mass in kilograms (kg).
  • c: specific heat capacity in joules per kilogram per degree Celsius (J kg⁻¹ °C⁻¹, numerically the same as J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹). A scalar.
  • delta theta: temperature change in degrees Celsius (°C) or kelvin (K). Temperature rises give a positive energy input; falls give energy out.

Supplement: measuring c experimentally. An electrical heater warms a well-lagged block of the substance; an ammeter and voltmeter give the electrical energy E = V I t, and a thermometer gives the temperature rise. Plot temperature against time; the gradient gives the rate of heating, and c = V I t / (m delta theta). Lagging reduces heat loss to the surroundings, the stirrer evens out hot spots, and the same method compares two materials by heating equal masses with the same heater for the same time.

Melting, boiling and evaporation

Melting and boiling happen at fixed temperatures for a pure substance at fixed pressure: 0 °C and 100 °C for pure water at one atmosphere. On a heating curve, plateaus mark the changes of state, and the energy supplied during a plateau is the latent heat: the energy needed to change the state of 1 kg without any temperature change (latent heat of fusion for melting, of vaporisation for boiling). The plateau exists because the energy breaks intermolecular attractions rather than increasing particle speed.

Evaporation is different from boiling and happens at any temperature. Particles at the liquid surface occasionally escape with above-average energy, so the average energy of those left falls and the liquid cools. Evaporation is faster when the temperature is higher, the surface area is larger, and a draught carries vapour away — the three factors Paper 4 expects in an evaporation-and-cooling explanation. Boiling happens throughout the liquid at a fixed temperature, with bubbles of vapour forming internally; evaporation happens only at the surface, at all temperatures, and cools the liquid left behind. Wet skin cools you because the water evaporates and takes the highest-energy particles with it.

Conduction

Conduction is the transfer of energy through a substance without the substance itself moving. In metals, the free electrons carry energy quickly from the hot end to the cold end, which is why metals are good conductors; in non-metals the energy passes only as vibrations handed along the vibrating particles, which is much slower. In gases and most liquids, conduction is poor because the particles are too far apart to pass on vibrations efficiently — hence insulating materials trap air in fibres or foam.

The core practical comparison: rods of different materials are coated with wax at one end and held over a heat source; the wax falls first from the best conductor. Metals come out in order (copper and aluminium good, steel poorer), while wood, plastic and glass barely conduct at all.

Convection

Convection is the transfer of energy by the movement of a fluid itself. Heating a fluid lowers its density: the warm parcel rises, cooler fluid sinks to take its place, and a convection current sets up. This is how radiators heat a room (hot air rises from the radiator, cools at the ceiling and returns down the far wall), how a kettle boils from the bottom, how sea breezes blow from sea to land by day, and how the element of a domestic water heater sits at the bottom so the whole tank warms. Convection requires a fluid — it cannot occur in a solid, and in a vacuum there is no medium at all.

Radiation

Radiation is the transfer of energy by electromagnetic waves, mainly infrared. It needs no medium, so it is the only way energy crosses the vacuum of space — which is why the Sun's heat reaches the Earth. The rate of emission and absorption depends on surface colour and texture: dull black surfaces are the best emitters and the best absorbers; shiny white or silvered surfaces are the poorest and reflect most radiation.

ApplicationSurface choice and reason
House radiatorMatte dark paint: emits radiation well
Hot-water tank and pipesSilvered foil: reduces radiation loss
Thermos flaskSilvered glass walls on both sides: minimises radiated loss in and out
Ice box / cool boxShiny white outside: reflects incoming radiation
Desert survival bagShiny side outwards in hot sun: reflects the Sun's radiation

Supplement: the Earth's energy balance. The Earth absorbs short-wavelength radiation from the Sun and radiates longer-wavelength infrared back to space. At equilibrium the two rates match and the average temperature is steady; greenhouse gases absorb some outgoing infrared and re-radiate it downwards, raising the equilibrium temperature. More greenhouse gas shifts the balance and warms the surface — the physics behind climate change.

Worked example: heating water

A 2.0 kg kettle of water is heated from 15 °C to 100 °C. The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J kg⁻¹ °C⁻¹. The kettle's heater supplies 2400 W.

energy needed = m c delta theta = 2.0 x 4200 x (100 - 15) = 714 000 J
time = energy / power = 714 000 / 2400 = 298 s (about 5.0 minutes)

Real kettles take longer, because some energy warms the kettle body and is lost to the air — which is exactly why the efficiency of a kettle is less than 100 per cent. To boil the water away would need far more energy again, because of the latent heat of vaporisation.

Second calculation: a 0.50 kg block of aluminium (c = 900 J kg⁻¹ °C⁻¹) cools from 80 °C to 25 °C. Energy released = 0.50 × 900 × 55 = 24 750 J ≈ 25 kJ. Cooling gives out the same energy that heating took in; only the sign of the temperature change differs.

Common mistakes

  • Saying heat rises. Heat is energy, not a substance; it is the warm fluid that rises because it is less dense.
  • Confusing temperature with internal energy: temperature measures the average energy per particle, while internal energy is the total energy of all particles.
  • Forgetting that during melting or boiling the temperature stays constant even though energy is still being supplied.
  • Mixing up conduction (through a substance), convection (by a moving fluid) and radiation (by waves, no medium). A vacuum flask blocks all three: silvered walls (radiation), vacuum gap (conduction and convection), foam or stopper (conduction).
  • Using degrees Celsius where kelvin are required in a gas-law calculation; always convert with T = θ + 273 before using pV = constant relationships.
  • Putting mass in grams into E = mcΔθ; the unit J kg⁻¹ °C⁻¹ demands kilograms.
  • Describing evaporation as boiling; evaporation occurs at any temperature, only at the surface, and cools the remaining liquid.
  • Claiming particles expand; it is the average separation between the particles that increases.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 4, 3 marks). A 500 g block of copper (c = 390 J kg⁻¹ °C⁻¹) is heated from 20 °C to 120 °C. Calculate the energy transferred.

Answer: E = mcΔθ = 0.50 × 390 × 100 = 19 500 J = 19.5 kJ.

Question 2 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Explain, using the particle model, why a metal lid on a glass jar loosens under hot water.

Answer: The hot water heats both the lid and the jar. The particles in the metal gain energy and vibrate with greater amplitude, so their average separation increases more than that of the glass particles, because metals expand more than glass for the same temperature rise. The metal lid therefore becomes slightly larger in diameter than the neck of the jar and turns more easily.

Question 3 (Paper 2 style). Which change does not occur at a fixed temperature? A ice melting at 0 °C; B water boiling at 100 °C; C water evaporating from a puddle; D steam condensing at 100 °C. Answer: C. Evaporation occurs at any temperature and is not a fixed-temperature change of state.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 6 marks). Explain how a vacuum flask keeps a drink hot, referring to all three methods of thermal energy transfer.

Answer: The double-walled glass vessel has a vacuum between the walls, and a vacuum contains no particles, so energy cannot be transferred across the gap by conduction or convection. Both walls are silvered to reduce radiation: the shiny surfaces are poor emitters and poor absorbers, so little infrared escapes. The plastic stopper and foam supports are poor conductors and block convection in the air above the liquid. Together these keep energy in the drink for hours.

Question 5 (Paper 6 style). Describe an experiment to compare how well different materials conduct heat.

Answer: Fix rods of equal length and thickness made from the different materials, each coated at the far end with an equal blob of wax, over identical heat sources. Start together and record the time for each wax blob to fall. The shortest time identifies the best conductor. Keep the source, rod dimensions, coating thickness and starting temperature identical so the comparison is fair, and repeat to check the ranking.

Question 6 (Paper 4, 3 marks). A gas is trapped in a sealed syringe at 100 cm³ and 20 °C. It is heated to 87 °C at constant pressure. Find its new volume.

Answer: Convert first: 20 °C = 293 K, 87 °C = 360 K. At constant pressure V/T is constant, so V₂ = 100 × 360/293 = 123 cm³. (For a Core-level answer, the gas expands when heated at constant pressure, and the volume rises by roughly a quarter.)

From heat to the transfer of energy by waves: the next topic is Waves and Sound.

Equations and symbols

Thermal physics at 0625 is built on two energy equations — one for a change of temperature, one for a change of state — plus the power relation that turns either into a rate. The specific heat capacity and specific latent heat values are given in the exam, so the marks are in choosing the right equation and the right mass.

Heating and cooling

E = mcΔθ
Key: E = energy transferred to or from the substance (J); m = mass (kg); c = specific heat capacity (J/(kg °C)); Δθ (delta theta) = temperature change (°C). Use mcΔθ when the temperature changes but the state does not.

c(water) = 4200 J/(kg °C)
Key: the energy needed to raise 1 kg of water by 1 °C. Water's high value is why it is used as a coolant and why coastal climates are mild.

E = mL
Key: E = energy needed to change state (J); m = mass changing state (kg); L = specific latent heat (J/kg). Use it at a melting or boiling point, where the temperature stays constant while the state changes.

L(fusion, water) = 3.34 × 10⁵ J/kg and L(vaporisation, water) = 2.26 × 10⁶ J/kg
Key: L(fusion) melts or freezes 1 kg without changing temperature; L(vaporisation) boils or condenses it. Boiling takes far more energy than melting, which is why steam burns are worse than boiling-water burns at the same temperature.

E(total) = mcΔθ + mL
Key: the two stages of heating ice from below 0 °C to steam above 100 °C, added in sequence: warm the ice, melt it, warm the water, boil it, warm the steam. Each stage uses the equation that matches what is happening.

Rate of energy transfer

P = E / t
Key: P = power of the heater or the rate of energy transfer (W); E = energy transferred (J); t = time (s). Combined with mcΔθ this gives P = mcΔθ / t, the standard heater calculation.

efficiency = (energy gained by the substance / energy supplied) × 100%
Key: the useful gain is mcΔθ (J); the supplied energy is Pt (J). Heat lost to the surroundings is why a measured specific heat capacity often comes out higher than the data-book value.

Temperature and the gas laws

T(K) = θ(°C) + 273
Key: T = thermodynamic temperature (K); θ (theta) = Celsius temperature (°C). Gas-law ratios need kelvin: doubling 20 °C to 40 °C is not a doubling in kelvin.

p / T = constant (volume fixed)
Key: p = gas pressure (Pa); T = temperature (K). Heating a sealed container raises the pressure because the particles move faster and hit the walls harder and more often.

p₁V₁ = p₂V₂ (temperature fixed)
Key: p₁, V₁ = pressure and volume before (Pa, m³); p₂, V₂ = after. Compressing a gas at constant temperature raises its pressure in inverse proportion.

p₁V₁ / T₁ = p₂V₂ / T₂
Key: the combined form, with temperatures in kelvin. Any one of pressure, volume or temperature can be found if the other two change and the third is fixed.

The particle model as a rule set

pressure ∝ rate of collision × momentum change per collision
Key: the qualitative gas model behind every explanation mark: more particles per unit volume, or faster particles, means more forceful collisions with the container walls, hence a higher pressure.

title: Exam technique: Scatter Diagrams
content:
### What earns the marks
For correlation, direction (rising or falling) and strength (tight or spread) each earn a mark: comment on both. For lines of best fit, the mean point plotted first earns the method mark. For estimation questions, naming interpolation versus extrapolation earns a mark before any value, with the reliability comment credited separately.
### Traps
Error: claiming correlation proves causation. Correction: name the confounder (hot weather drives both). Error: trusting extrapolation like interpolation. Correction: outside the range is always less reliable. Error: forcing the line through the origin. Correction: anchor at (mean x, mean y). Error: calling curved association zero correlation. Correction: zero means no pattern at all.
### Worked example
A scatter diagram shows a positive correlation between hours revised and test score. The line of best fit passes through the mean point (x̄, ȳ). If x̄ = 5 and ȳ = 12 with gradient 2, the line is y = 2x + 2. Estimating y for x = 8 is interpolation if 8 lies within the data range, which makes it more reliable than extrapolating beyond the data.
### Check yourself
Explain why the line of best fit should pass through (x̄, ȳ). Check that 2 × 5 + 2 = 12, so the line does pass through the mean point. State whether a prediction at x = 20 would be interpolation or extrapolation, and say why it is less reliable.

title: Quantum Physics
content:
Quantum Physics

Photons

E = hf = hc/λ, h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s.

Example: green light 550 nm: E ≈ 3.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J ≈ 2.3 eV.

The Photoelectric Effect

Light above a threshold frequency ejects electrons instantly; intensity alone does nothing below f₀.

  • Einstein: hf = φ + KE_max (φ = work function)
  • KE_max = eV_s (stopping potential)

Example: sodium φ = 2.3 eV needs λ < 540 nm; 400 nm light gives KE_max = 3.1 − 2.3 = 0.8 eV.

Wave–Particle Duality

de Broglie: λ = h/p = h/(mv). Electrons diffract like waves — electron microscopes exploit short electron wavelengths.

Example: an electron at 10⁶ m s⁻¹: λ ≈ 0.7 nm.

Energy Levels and Line Spectra

Atoms absorb/emit photons matching level gaps: hf = E₁ − E₂. Emission lines are bright; absorption dark.

Example: the Hα line: 3 → 2 transition, 656 nm.

Exam tips: one photon interacts with one electron — that is why intensity cannot release electrons below threshold; convert eV ↔ J with 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹.

title: Further Mechanics — Study Notes
content:
Further mechanics: momentum, impulse and circular motion

Edexcel International A Level Physics — Unit 4 (WPH14), sat at A2.

This unit unifies two big ideas: momentum (with its conservation law) and circular motion (with its centripetal requirement). Both are favourite sources of longer exam questions.

Momentum and impulse

  • Momentum p = mv, a vector measured in kg m/s.
  • Impulse = force x time = change of momentum: F t = m(v - u). Units N s (equivalently kg m/s).
  • Newton's second law in momentum form: F = rate of change of momentum = m(v - u)/t.
  • A force-time graph has area = impulse.

Conservation of momentum

  • In a closed system (no external resultant force) total momentum before = total after. This is a vector law: in two dimensions, resolve along two perpendicular axes.
  • It holds for all collisions, explosions and separations.

Collisions

  • Elastic: total kinetic energy is conserved as well as momentum (e.g. perfectly hard spheres).
  • Inelastic: kinetic energy is not conserved — it transforms into heat, sound and deformation.
  • Perfectly inelastic: the bodies stick together; this gives the maximum kinetic energy loss.
  • In one dimension use simultaneous momentum (and, if elastic, energy) equations.

Circular motion

  • Angular speed: omega = 2 pi / T = 2 pi f = v / r.
  • A body moving in a circle at constant speed still accelerates: centripetal acceleration a = v^2 / r = omega^2 r, directed towards the centre.
  • The centripetal force is the resultant force towards the centre: F = m v^2 / r = m omega^2 r. It is not a new type of force — tension, weight, friction or normal reaction can supply it.

Vertical circles and pendulums

  • For a body on a string in a vertical circle, the string stays taut at the top only if v >= sqrt(g r).
  • Conical pendulum: a mass on a string sweeps a horizontal circle; with string length L at angle theta to the vertical, tan(theta) = v^2/(r g) and the period is T = 2 pi sqrt(L cos(theta)/g).
  • Banked track with no friction: tan(theta) = v^2/(r g); the normal reaction supplies the centripetal force.

Exam technique

  • Momentum is a vector: fix a positive direction and keep signs consistent.
  • Energy is scalar and never negative; check whether the collision is elastic before conserving energy.
  • For circles, draw the force diagram at the point of interest first, then resolve towards the centre.

title: AS Level Mathematics: Sequences and Series
content:
AS Level Mathematics: Sequences and Series

A sequence is an ordered list of numbers generated by a rule; a series is the sum of a sequence. Two families dominate the syllabus: arithmetic (add a constant each time) and geometric (multiply by a constant each time). This note builds the topic from zero: the nth term and sum formulas for both families with derivations, σ notation, recurrence relations, the convergence condition for geometric series, and the applied problems — savings, depreciation, loans — where the formulas earn marks. Every formula is derived once so it can be rebuilt if forgotten.

Arithmetic sequences

nth term: u_n = a + (n - 1)d
sum of n terms: S_n = (n/2)[2a + (n - 1)d] = (n/2)(first + last)

a = first term, d = common difference

Worked example. An arithmetic sequence has first term 5 and common difference 4. Find the 20th term and the sum of the first 20 terms.

u_20 = 5 + 19 × 4 = 81
S_20 = (20/2)(5 + 81) = 10 × 86 = 860

Worked example 2 (working backwards). The 5th term is 17 and the 12th is 45. Find a and d.

u_5: a + 4d = 17
u_12: a + 11d = 45
subtract: 7d = 28  →  d = 4;  a = 17 - 16 = 1

Arithmetic series and the sum formula

The sum formula is Gauss's trick: pair the first and last terms, the second and second-last, and so on; each pair has the same total, and there are n/2 pairs.

Worked example. Find the sum of the first 50 positive even numbers.

a = 2, d = 2, n = 50
last term = 2 + 49 × 2 = 10⁰
S = (50/2)(2 + 10⁰) = 25 × 10² = 2550

Worked example 2 (unknown n). The sum of the first n terms of 3, 7, 11, ... is 210. Find n.

210 = (n/2)[6 + 4(n - 1)] = (n/2)(4n + 2) = 2n² + n
2n² + n - 210 = 0
(2n + 21)(n - 10) = 0  →  n = 10 (n must be positive)

Geometric sequences

nth term: u_n = a r^(n - 1)
sum of n terms: S_n = a(1 - r^n)/(1 - r)   (r not 1)
sum to infinity: S_inf = a/(1 - r)   (only if |r| < 1)

a = first term, r = common ratio

Worked example. A geometric sequence has a = 3 and r = 2. Find the 8th term and the sum of the first 8 terms.

u_8 = 3 × 2⁷ = 384
S_8 = 3(1 - 2⁸)/(1 - 2) = 3(1 - 256)/(-1) = 765

Worked example 2 (working backwards). A geometric sequence has second term 12 and fifth term 96. Find r and a.

u_2 = ar = 12;  u_5 = ar⁴ = 96
divide: r³ = 8  →  r = 2;  a = 6

Sum to infinity and convergence

A geometric series converges only when the ratio has magnitude less than 1: each term is smaller than the last, and the total approaches a finite limit.

if |r| < 1: S_inf = a/(1 - r)
if |r| >= 1: the series diverges (no finite sum)

Worked example. Find the sum to infinity of 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 + ...

a = 8, r = 1/2
S_inf = 8/(1 - 1/2) = 8/(0.5) = 16

Worked example 2 (recurring decimal). Write 0.444... as a fraction using a geometric series.

0.444... = 0.4 + 0.04 + 0.004 + ...
a = 0.4, r = 0.1
S_inf = 0.4/(1 - 0.1) = 0.4/0.9 = 4/9

σ notation and recurrence relations

sum from k = 1 to n of u_k  (σ notation)

recurrence: u_(n+1) = f(u_n), with the first term given

Worked example (σ). Evaluate the sum from k = 1 to 5 of (3k + 1).

terms: 4, 7, 10, 13, 16 (arithmetic, a = 4, d = 3)
S = (5/2)(4 + 16) = 50

Worked example 2 (recurrence). u₁ = 2, u_(n+1) = 3u_n + 1. Find u₄.

u2 = 3(2) + 1 = 7
u3 = 3(7) + 1 = 22
u4 = 3(22) + 1 = 67

Recurrence questions often ask you to prove a sequence is arithmetic or geometric: compute consecutive differences or ratios and show they are constant.

Applied problems

Worked example (savings). A student saves 50 pounds in month 1 and increases the monthly saving by 10 pounds each month. How much is saved in month 12, and in total over the year?

arithmetic: a = 50, d = 10
u_12 = 50 + 11(10) = 160
S_12 = (12/2)(50 + 160) = 6 × 210 = 1260 pounds

Worked example 2 (depreciation). A car worth 18000 pounds loses 15% of its value each year. Find its value after 5 years and the total loss.

geometric: a = 18000, r = 0.85
value after 5 years = 18000 × 0.85⁵ = 18000 × 0.4437 = 7987 pounds
loss = 18000 - 7987 = 10⁰¹³ pounds

Worked example 3 (interest). 1000 pounds is invested at 4% compound interest. Find the value after 10 years and the total interest.

value = 10⁰⁰ x 1.04¹⁰ = 10⁰⁰ x 1.4802 = 1480.24 pounds
interest = 480.24 pounds

Deriving the sum formulas

Knowing where the formulas come from makes them reconstructable under pressure. Write the arithmetic sum forwards and backwards and add:

S = a + (a + d) + ... + [a + (n - 1)d]
S = [a + (n - 1)d] + ... + a
2S = n[2a + (n - 1)d]  (each of the n columns adds to 2a + (n-1)d)
S = (n/2)[2a + (n - 1)d]

The geometric sum is derived by multiplying by r and subtracting, which cancels every intermediate term:

S = a + ar + ar² + ... + ar^(n-1)
rS = ar + ar² + ... + ar^n
S - rS = a - ar^n  →  S(1 - r) = a(1 - r^n)
S = a(1 - r^n)/(1 - r)   (r not 1)

Letting n grow in the geometric formula, rⁿ → 0 whenever |r| < 1, leaving S∞ = a/(1 − r): the same derivation explains convergence, so the condition is not a separate fact to memorise.

Proving a sequence is arithmetic or geometric

Show the consecutive differences or ratios are constant using algebra, not just numbers.

Worked example. The terms of a sequence are 3, 3 + 2k, 3 + 4k, ... Show it is arithmetic and find the sum of the first 10 terms in terms of k.

difference 1: (3 + 2k) - 3 = 2k
difference 2: (3 + 4k) - (3 + 2k) = 2k
constant difference 2k  →  arithmetic with d = 2k
S_10 = (10/2)[2(3) + 9(2k)] = 5(6 + 18k) = 30 + 90k

Worked example 2 (geometric). Show that 2, 2x, 2x², ... is geometric and find the sum to infinity when x = 1/3.

ratio: 2x/2 = x;  2x²/(2x) = x  →  geometric with r = x
with x = 1/3: S_inf = 2/(1 - 1/3) = 3

Combining and interpreting sequences

Some questions give a sequence defined by a rule that is neither purely arithmetic nor geometric, and ask for specific terms or a sum found by splitting it into two familiar parts.

Worked example. Find the sum of the first 20 terms of the sequence whose nth term is 3n + 2ⁿ.

split: arithmetic part 3n (a = 3, d = 3) and geometric part 2^n (a = 2, r = 2)
arithmetic sum: (20/2)[6 + 19 × 3] = 10 × 63 = 630
geometric sum: 2(2²⁰ - 1)/(2 - 1) = 2(10⁴⁸⁵⁷⁶ - 1) = 2097150
total = 630 + 2097150 = 2097780

Worked example 2 (loan style). A student repays a 5000 pound debt in monthly instalments that form an arithmetic sequence: 150 pounds in month 1, rising by 20 pounds each month. After how many months is the debt cleared, and what is the final instalment?

S_n = (n/2)[2(150) + (n - 1)(20)] = 5000
(n/2)(300 + 20n - 20) = 5000
n(280 + 20n) = 10⁰⁰⁰
20n² + 280n - 10⁰⁰⁰ = 0  →  n² + 14n - 500 = 0
n = [-14 + √(196 + 2000)]/2 = (-14 + 46.86)/2 = 16.4
so 17 instalments are needed; the 17th clears the remainder
final (17th) instalment = 150 + 16(20) = 470 pounds

Two modelling habits earn marks here: round n up (16 instalments leave the debt short) and state what the final, part-full payment means. Reading a plan for feasibility — does the sum actually reach the target? — is also examinable: an arithmetic sum with a negative difference peaks and then falls, so a repayment plan built that way may never clear the debt.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Arithmetic) Find the 15th term of 7, 11, 15, ... Answer: a = 7, d = 4; u₁₅ = 7 + 14(4) = 63.
  2. (Sum) Find the sum of the first 30 terms of 2, 5, 8, ... Answer: d = 3; S = 15(4 + 87) = 1365.
  3. (Geometric) Find the 6th term of 2, 6, 18, ... Answer: r = 3; u₆ = 2 × 3⁵ = 486.
  4. (Sum to infinity) Find S∞ for 12 + 6 + 3 + ... Answer: r = ½; S∞ = 12/(1 − ½) = 24.
  5. (Convergence) For what values of r does a geometric series converge? Answer: |r| < 1.
  6. (Recurrence) u₁ = 5, u_(n+1) = 2u_n − 3. Find u₃. Answer: u₂ = 7, u₃ = 11.
  7. (Reverse) The 3rd term of an arithmetic sequence is 11 and the 8th is 31. Find a and d. Answer: 5d = 20 → d = 4; a = 3.
  8. (Applied) A ball is dropped from 2 m and rebounds to 60% of its height each bounce. Find the total distance travelled before it stops. Answer: down 2; up/down 2(0.6) twice... total = 2 + 2(2×0.6)/(1−0.6) = 2 + 6 = 8 m.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • n − 1 versus n: the nth term uses (n − 1)d, not nd. Off-by-one errors are the commonest in this topic.
  • Count versus term: "sum of the first 20 terms" means n = 20; "the 20th term" means u₂₀. Read which is asked.
  • Sign of r: a negative ratio alternates signs; the convergence condition uses |r|, so r = −0.5 converges.
  • Sum to infinity misused: S∞ exists only for |r| < 1; quoting it for a divergent series is a conceptual mark lost.
  • Depreciation versus interest: depreciation multiplies by (1 − rate); interest by (1 + rate). Getting the factor wrong inverts the answer.
  • Solving for n: the quadratic in n has one positive integer root; reject the negative or fractional value explicitly.
  • Recurrence notation: u_(n+1) means the next term; substituting the wrong index shifts the whole sequence.
  • Exact form: where a question asks for an exact answer, keep fractions and powers; decimal approximations lose the final mark.

title: Exam technique: Sampling
content:
### What earns the marks
For method choice, random vs stratified vs systematic justified earns the mark. For stratified allocation, the proportion of each stratum applied earns the method mark. For bias discussion, the named source of bias with its effect earns both marks.
### Traps
Error: sample claimed unbiased with no method. Correction: name and justify the method. Error: equal numbers per stratum. Correction: allocate proportionally. Error: population confused with frame. Correction: frame is the list used.
### Worked example
A school has 600 students: 120 in Year 11 and 480 in Year 10. A stratified sample of 50 is needed with proportional allocation. Year 11 gets 120/600 x 50 = 10 students, and Year 10 gets 480/600 x 50 = 40 students. The two numbers add to 50, which confirms the allocation. Random selection then happens inside each group.
### Check yourself
A teacher samples 50 students from the first 50 names on the register. Name the sampling method and the main source of bias. This is a convenience sample, and the bias comes from the register order, which may not represent the whole school.

### Worked example
A school has 600 students: 120 in Year 11 and 480 in Year 10. A stratified sample of 50 is needed with proportional allocation. Year 11 gets 120/600 x 50 = 10 students, and Year 10 gets 480/600 x 50 = 40 students. The two numbers add to 50, which confirms the allocation. Random selection then happens inside each group.

title: Thermal Physics — Study Notes
content:
Thermal Physics

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2023–2025): kinetic particle model; thermal expansion; specific heat capacity; melting/boiling; conduction, convection, radiation.

1. Kinetic model

Solid: fixed positions, vibrate — fixed shape/volume. Liquid: move around, touching — fixed volume, flows. Gas: far apart, fast random motion — fills container. Brownian motion evidences random molecular motion.

2. Gas pressure and temperature

Pressure from wall collisions. Heating at fixed volume → faster particles → more frequent, harder collisions → higher pressure.

3. Thermal expansion

Heating → particles vibrate more → solids expand slightly (gases expand most). Applications: bimetallic strip (fire alarm/thermostat), gaps in bridges/rails; the liquid-in-glass thermometer.

4. Specific heat capacity

c = ΔE/(mΔθ). Heating: ΔE = mcΔθ.

Example: 2 kg water (c = 4200), 20→80 °C: ΔE = 2×4200×60 = 504 kJ.

High c of water → coolant; temperature rise measured with known heater power P in time t: c = Pt/(mΔθ).

5. State changes

Melting/boiling at fixed temperature despite heating (energy breaks bonds, not temperature). Condensation/ freezing release energy. Impurities raise melting point of mixtures/lower freezing; boiling needs nucleation.

6. Transfer: conduction, convection, radiation

  • Conduction: mainly metals (delocalised electrons + lattice vibration); non-metals poor; insulators trap air.
  • Convection: hot fluid expands, density falls, rises; denser cool fluid sinks — currents.
  • Radiation: infrared EM waves; no medium; matte black best absorber/emitter, shiny silver worst.

Applications: vacuum flask, house insulation, car radiators, solar heating panels.

title: Differentiation — Study Notes
content:
Differentiation

Basic Rules

  • d/dx (xⁿ) = n xⁿ⁻¹
  • d/dx (k) = 0, d/dx (kx) = k

Example: y = 5x² − 3x gives dy/dx = 10x − 3.

Chain Rule

dy/dx = dy/du × du/dx.

Example: y = (3x − 1)⁵: dy/dx = 5(3x − 1)⁴ × 3 = 15(3x − 1)⁴.

Tangents and Normals

The tangent gradient at a point is dy/dx there; the normal gradient is −1/(dy/dx).

Example: y = x² at (2, 4): tangent y = 4x − 4; normal has gradient −1/4.

Stationary Points

Set dy/dx = 0, then classify with the second derivative:

  • d²y/dx² > 0 → minimum
  • d²y/dx² < 0 → maximum
  • d²y/dx² = 0 → test either side

Example: y = x³ − 3x: dy/dx = 3x² − 3 = 0 at x = ±1; d²y/dx² = 6x, so a maximum at x = −1 and a minimum at x = 1.

Rates of Change

dy/dx is a rate: if V = 4/3 πr³, then dV/dr = 4πr² links volume change to radius change.

Exam tips: always restart gradients from the derivative at the exact point, and answer rate questions with units.

Rules and exam method

For y = axⁿ, dy/dx = naxⁿ⁻¹. Differentiate each term of a polynomial separately; a constant term differentiates to zero. Rewrite roots and reciprocals as powers first: √x = x^(1/2) and 1/x² = x⁻².

Product rule: d/dx(uv) = u dv/dx + v du/dx. Quotient rule: d/dx(u/v) = (v du/dx − u dv/dx)/v². Chain rule: dy/dx = dy/du × du/dx. For (ax + b)ⁿ the result is na(ax + b)ⁿ⁻¹.

Stationary points occur where dy/dx = 0. Classify them by the sign of dy/dx either side of the point, or with d²y/dx²: positive gives a minimum, negative a maximum, and zero means use the sign change. The gradient at a point gives the tangent; the normal has the negative reciprocal gradient.

Exam cue: Give the tangent or normal as y − y₁ = m(x − x₁), or simplified to y = mx + c, as the question asks. Check it by substituting the point back into the line.

Worked example: a full stationary-point analysis

Let y = x³ − 3x² − 9x + 5. Then dy/dx = 3x² − 6x − 9 = 3(x − 3)(x + 1). Stationary points occur when dy/dx = 0, so x = 3 or x = −1. The second derivative is d²y/dx² = 6x − 6. At x = −1 it is −12, which is negative, so there is a maximum; at x = 3 it is +12, so there is a minimum. Substitute back into the original equation for the y-coordinates: (−1, 10) is a maximum and (3, −22) is a minimum. Always state both coordinates.

Tangent and normal at a point

At x = 2, y = 8 − 12 − 18 + 5 = −17 and dy/dx = 12 − 12 − 9 = −9. The tangent has gradient −9 through (2, −17), so y + 17 = −9(x − 2). The normal is perpendicular, with gradient 1/9, so y + 17 = (1/9)(x − 2). Keep the equations in the form the question asks for, and do not mix the gradient of the normal with the tangent.

Rates of change: a chain rule example

The volume of a sphere is V = (4/3)πr³. If the radius increases at 0.5 cm/s, find the rate of change of volume when r = 3. dV/dr = 4πr², so dV/dt = dV/dr × dr/dt = 4π(9)(0.5) = 18π cm³/s ≈ 56.5 cm³/s. Linking the rates through the chain rule is the method being tested, so write the link explicitly.

Increasing and decreasing

The sign of dy/dx tells you whether the function is increasing (dy/dx > 0) or decreasing (dy/dx < 0). For y = x³ − 3x² − 9x + 5, the curve increases for x < −1, decreases between −1 and 3, and increases again for x > 3. State these intervals with the correct inequalities; an answer that says "x > −1" for the decreasing part loses the mark.

Common errors

  • Concluding a maximum or minimum from dy/dx = 0 alone without a sign test or second derivative.
  • Substituting the x-value into dy/dx to give the y-coordinate of the stationary point.
  • Using the gradient of the tangent in the normal equation, instead of its negative reciprocal.
  • Forgetting the chain-rule factor when the rate of change question involves two variables.

title: Simulation, Sensors and Real Data — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Simulation, Sensors and Real Data

Computer Science — A2. A simulation is a program that models a real system to test scenarios safely and cheaply: weather models, traffic flows, epidemic spread. Models use abstractions — chosen variables and equations — with a time step. Advantages: no real-world risk, repeatable, faster or slower than real time.
