18. How to use this note and what to revise next

Use these notes section by section, checking that you can identify plant cell ultrastructure and organelles in an electron micrograph and state their functions, explain how starch and cellulose differ in structure and role, describe the secondary thickening and the properties of xylem vessels and sclerenchyma fibres, compare sclerenchyma fibres, xylem vessels and phloem in structure, position and function, carry out the transverse section and tensile strength practicals and explain the variables and safety, describe the conditions for bacterial growth and the aseptic practical, describe the development of drug testing from Withering''s digitalis to modern three-phased trials and evaluate the designs, define classification and the species concept, describe the three-domain system and the molecular evidence for it, define biodiversity and endemism and the threats from human activity, carry out the species richness and heterozygosity and index of diversity calculations, and define niche and give behavioural, anatomical and physiological adaptations. After this topic, revise Topic 3 Cell structure, reproduction and development (plant and animal cells, division) and Topic 5 Energy flow, ecosystems and the environment, because classification and biodiversity sit within ecology.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Simpson's index, applied to a quadrat with 10 daisies and 5 dandelions: N = 15, D = 1 − Σ(n ÷ N)² = 1 − [(10 ÷ 15)² + (5 ÷ 15)²] = 1 − (0.444 + 0.111) = 0.556. Use the index to compare two sites; a higher value means greater diversity.
  • Xylem and phloem: xylem transports water and minerals upwards and is made of dead, lignified cells with no end walls, so the water column is continuous. Phloem transports sucrose and amino acids in both directions and is made of living sieve tube elements with companion cells. Name the direction of transport and the living or dead state of the cells.
  • Cellulose versus starch: cellulose is made of β-glucose units linked alternately, which allows hydrogen bonding between chains, forming strong microfibrils. Starch is made of α-glucose, is coiled and is used for storage. The different glucose isomer explains the different shapes and functions.
  • Conservation: a protected area works only if the populations inside it are large enough to be viable. Name the factor, such as a wildlife corridor, that connects populations, because isolated populations lose genetic diversity over time.

title: Exam technique: Mensuration
content:
### What earns the marks
For circles, sectors and arcs, the fraction of 360 stated earns the method mark: write 60/360 before multiplying. For cylinders, cones and spheres, the formula quoted earns a mark on its own, so write Volume = (1/3) pi r squared h even when confident. For compound shapes, split earns marks: compute each part separately, then add or subtract with a clear statement.
### Traps
Error: 2 pi r used for area. Correction: circumference versus area check first. Error: omitting 1/3 for cones and pyramids. Correction: quote the formula every time. Error: using diameter as radius in a semicircle cut-out. Correction: halve the diameter before any pi work. Error: forgetting the square root in a Pythagoras step. Correction: label squared lines as squared.
### Worked example
A cylinder has radius 3 cm and height 10 cm. Its volume is πr²h = π × 9 × 10 = 90π ≈ 282.7 cm³. A sector of angle 60° in a circle of radius 6 cm has arc length (60/360) × 2π × 6 = 2π cm.
### Check yourself
A trapezium has parallel sides 5 cm and 9 cm and a perpendicular height of 4 cm. Find its area. Use ½(a + b)h = ½ × (5 + 9) × 4 = 28 cm². State the units and show the substitution before the final value.

### Worked example
A rectangle is 8 cm long and 5 cm wide. Its perimeter is 2(8 + 5) = 26 cm and its area is 40 cm². A triangular prism with triangular cross-section area 12 cm² and length 7 cm has volume 12 × 7 = 84 cm³.
### Check yourself
Find the surface area of a cylinder with radius 2 cm and height 5 cm, leaving π in the answer. The curved surface is 2πrh = 20π and the two circles are 2πr² = 8π, giving 28π cm². Show each part before adding them.

title: AS Level Biology: Cell Structure, Reproduction and Development
content:
Cell Structure, Reproduction and Development — AS Level Biology

This revision note belongs to the Edexcel International Advanced Subsidiary (IAS) Biology specification, WBI12 Unit 2, Topic 3 Cell Structure, Reproduction and Development. It covers the cell as the unit of life, eukaryotic and prokaryotic ultrastructure, microscopy and measurement, the cell cycle and mitosis, meiosis and genetic variation, gametes and fertilisation in mammals and flowering plants, stem cells, and the genetic control of development through gene expression, epigenetics and inheritance. Every statement below the topic owns is covered in its own section or paragraph.

1. Cells as the units of life and the levels of organisation

All living organisms are made of cells, and all cells share some common features: a plasma membrane (cell surface membrane) enclosing the cell, cytoplasm in which most chemical reactions occur, and ribosomes for protein synthesis. Differences between cell types are explained from these common features — for example the presence or absence of a cell wall, a nucleus, or membrane-bound organelles decides what a cell can do. In multicellular organisms, cells are organised into tissues, tissues into organs, and organs into organ systems, each level carrying out a particular function. A tissue is a group of similar cells working together; an organ is made of several tissues with a combined function; an organ system is a group of organs whose functions are linked, such as the digestive system. Understanding this hierarchy matters because a structure at one level is shaped by the level below it — the properties of a tissue follow from the cells it contains.

2. Eukaryotic cell ultrastructure and the functions of the organelles

Eukaryotic cells have a membrane-bound nucleus that contains the chromosomes, and a range of membrane-bound organelles, each with a distinct function. The plasma membrane (cell surface membrane) is a phospholipid bilayer with proteins embedded in it, controlling what enters and leaves the cell. The nucleus is surrounded by a double nuclear envelope with nuclear pores, and contains the cell’s DNA; the nucleolus inside the nucleus is the site of ribosome assembly. Ribosomes, made of a large and a small subunit, are the sites of protein synthesis and occur free in the cytoplasm or attached to the rough endoplasmic reticulum. The rough endoplasmic reticulum (rER) is a stack of membrane-bound sacs studded with ribosomes; it synthesises proteins and passes them on in vesicles. The smooth endoplasmic reticulum (sER) lacks ribosomes and synthesises lipids and carbohydrates. Mitochondria have a double membrane, the inner one folded into cristae to increase surface area, and a matrix that contains the enzymes for aerobic respiration; they supply ATP. Centrioles are paired microtubule cylinders that organise the spindle fibres during nuclear division. Lysosomes are membrane-bound sacs containing hydrolytic enzymes that digest worn-out cell components and pathogens. The Golgi apparatus modifies, sorts and packages proteins into vesicles for secretion or for delivery to other parts of the cell; it is also involved in the formation of extracellular enzymes. The cytoskeleton of microtubules and microfilaments maintains cell shape, holds organelles in place and enables movement within the cell.

3. Prokaryotic cell ultrastructure and how to tell the two apart

Prokaryotic cells are much smaller than eukaryotic cells and lack a membrane-bound nucleus. Their genetic material is a single, circular DNA molecule that lies free in the cytoplasm, not associated with histones. The cell wall is made of peptidoglycan and gives rigidity and shape. Many prokaryotes have a protective capsule outside the cell wall. Plasmids are small circles of DNA separate from the main chromosome; they can be transferred between cells and often carry genes for antibiotic resistance. Flagella — rigid helical tails that rotate — give motility in some prokaryotes, and pili help cells attach to surfaces and to each other and mediate conjugation. Prokaryotic ribosomes are 70S, smaller than the 80S ribosomes of eukaryotes. A bacterium therefore shows, in EM images: cell wall, capsule, plasma membrane, circular DNA free in the cytoplasm, 70S ribosomes, plasmids, and, where present, flagella and pili — and none of the membrane-bound organelles found in a eukaryotic cell.

4. Seeing the ultrastructure: light and electron microscopy

A light microscope uses visible light passed through a specimen; its maximum useful magnification is around ×1500 and its resolution is about 0.2 µm, limited by the wavelength of light. An electron microscope uses a beam of electrons, giving far higher resolution and magnification; transmission electron microscopes (TEM) show the internal ultrastructure of thin sections, and scanning electron microscopes (SEM) show the surface detail of a specimen. Staining is essential in light microscopy because most cells are transparent — stains such as methylene blue for animal cells or iodine solution for starch make structures visible and show up nuclei, starch grains and cell walls. The electron microscope can show the organelles listed in 3.3 — nucleus, nucleolus, ribosomes, rER, sER, mitochondria, centrioles, lysosomes, Golgi apparatus — and, in prokaryotes, the cell wall, capsule, plasma membrane, circular DNA, 70S ribosomes, flagella and pili, so that students can recognise the organelles from electron micrographs. In a light microscope the total magnification equals eyepiece magnification × objective magnification; a graticule (eye-piece graticule) fitted with a stage micrometer lets you calibrate it so real sizes can be measured, and specimens can be drawn to scale from the microscope.

5. Core Practical 5 — observing and drawing animal cells

Use a light microscope to make observations and labelled drawings of suitable animal cells, for example cheek epithelial cells. The steps are: sterilise by wiping the mouth, smear a thin layer of cells onto a slide, stain with methylene blue, lower a coverslip at an angle to avoid air bubbles, and observe under the microscope. Draw what you see with the correct relative sizes of nucleus, cytoplasm and cell membrane, label the parts, and add a title and magnification. Core Practical 5 also develops the skill of using a graticule with a microscope to make measurements and understand the concept of scale — the graticule is calibrated against a stage micrometer at each objective, so the real size of a cell or organelle can be calculated from the number of graticule divisions it spans.

6. Cell division: mitosis, the cell cycle and genetic variation by meiosis

Mitosis produces genetically identical daughter cells for growth and asexual reproduction and is one part of the cell cycle, which is the regular sequence of events in a dividing cell: interphase (during which the cell grows, and DNA is replicated — G1, S and G2), mitosis and cytokinesis. Mitosis itself has stages — prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase — in which the copied chromosomes line up on the equator, separate and move to opposite poles, and new nuclei form, followed by division of the cytoplasm. A useful calculation is the mitotic index, the proportion of cells in a sample that are dividing: mitotic index = number of cells undergoing mitosis ÷ total number of cells in the field of view. This is used in Core Practical 6, the root tip squash, to see and count the stages of mitosis. Meiosis, by contrast, produces genetically non-identical gametes and is the source of variation: in metaphase I the homologous chromosomes line up as pairs and assort independently (independent assortment), and in prophase I crossing over exchanges alleles between the chromatids of a homologous pair, so that gametes carry new combinations of alleles. A locus is the fixed position of a gene on a chromosome; genes on the same chromosome are linked and tend to be inherited together, so linked genes do not assort independently.

7. Gametes, fertilisation in mammals and fertilisation in flowering plants

Mammalian gametes are specialised for their function. Sperm are small and motile, with a haploid nucleus, a lot of mitochondria to power the flagellum, and an acrosome at the head containing enzymes that digest a path through the egg’s outer layers. Egg cells are larger, with cytoplasm containing food reserves; the zona pellucida is a glycoprotein layer around the egg that sperm must penetrate. Fertilisation in mammals begins when the acrosome reaction releases enzymes that digest the zona pellucida, then the cortical reaction releases cortical granules into the space around the egg, hardening the zona pellucida and preventing more than one sperm from entering; finally the sperm and egg nuclei fuse, restoring the diploid number. In flowering plants, fertilisation begins with pollination and the growth of a pollen tube from the pollen grain down through the style to the embryo sac; two male nuclei travel down the tube, one fertilising the egg to form the zygote (which develops into the embryo) and one fusing with the two polar nuclei to form the triploid endosperm that will feed the developing seed — double fertilisation, unique to flowering plants.

8. Stem cells and what society does with them

A stem cell is an undifferentiated cell that can divide to produce more stem cells and differentiated cells. Totipotent stem cells can develop into any cell type and form a complete organism; the zygote and the cells of the early embryo up to the 16-cell morula are totipotent. Pluripotent stem cells can give rise to many, but not all, cell types; cells of the blastocyst are pluripotent, and in plants many meristem cells are totipotent, which is why a whole plant can be grown from a single cell or tissue. Stem cells are used medically — for example in bone marrow transplants for leukaemia — and their use raises ethical and social questions: the source of embryonic stem cells, the balance of benefit against risk, and decisions made by individuals, committees and governments all draw on scientific knowledge but also on values. Students should be able to discuss these issues from a range of ethical viewpoints.

9. Gene expression: how one gene makes more than one protein and how proteins control cells

Cells become specialised through differential gene expression — different genes are switched on or off in different cells, producing active mRNA and then proteins that control cell processes or determine cell structure. One gene can give rise to more than one protein through post-transcriptional changes to messenger RNA (mRNA) such as alternative splicing, in which the same primary transcript is spliced in different ways to make different mRNAs and therefore different polypeptides. Transcription factors switch genes on or off by binding to DNA and promoting or blocking transcription, so they control which proteins a cell makes. Epigenetic modification — including DNA methylation and histone modification — alters the activation of certain genes without changing the DNA sequence itself, and these modifications can be passed on following cell division, so that a cell’s gene activity can be inherited by its daughter cells and, in some cases, across generations.

10. Inheritance: alleles, genotypes, phenotypes and how they vary

A gene is a sequence of bases on a DNA molecule that codes for a sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide. The allele is one of the different forms of a gene; the genotype is the alleles an organism has; the phenotype is the observable feature that results from the genotype and the environment. Recessive alleles only show in the phenotype when homozygous; dominant alleles show even in the heterozygous state; codominance is when both alleles in the heterozygote contribute to the phenotype. Sex linkage is the inheritance of a gene carried on the X chromosome, such as red-green colour blindness in humans, which appears more often in males because they have only one X chromosome and so express a recessive allele on it. Some phenotypes are affected by multiple alleles for the same gene, and others by polygenic inheritance, where many genes each contribute a small effect, giving rise to continuous variation in the phenotype — height in humans is a classic example. The environment can also affect phenotype, so that a feature is the result of an interaction between genotype and environment rather than genotype alone.

11. Mutations: how they arise and what they can do

Errors in DNA replication can give rise to mutations — changes to the base sequence of DNA. A substitution replaces one base with another and may change one amino acid or none (because the code is degenerate); an insertion adds one or more bases, and a deletion removes one or more, and these can cause a frameshift that changes every amino acid after the mutation and often produces a non-functional protein. Mutations are the source of new alleles, and some mutations give rise to cancer or genetic disorders, while many have no observable effect. Cystic fibrosis is a genetic disorder caused by a recessive allele; the faulty allele affects chloride ion channels, so the functioning of the gaseous exchange, digestive and reproductive systems is impaired — thick mucus blocks the airways, the pancreas duct is blocked so digestion is affected, and fertility in males is reduced because the vas deferens is absent or blocked.

12. Genetic screening and the questions it raises

Genetic screening can identify carriers of a recessive allele, and prenatal testing — including amniocentesis (sampling the fluid around the embryo) and chorionic villus sampling (taking a sample of placental tissue) — can check an embryo or fetus for genetic disorders. Pre-implantation genetic diagnosis (PGD) is used during IVF to test embryos before implantation so that only unaffected embryos are used. These techniques raise ethical and social questions: the reliability and risk of the test, the right to know or not to know, who decides what is a disorder worth preventing, the cost and access to treatment, and the risk of starting down a path toward selecting traits rather than preventing disease. Students should be able to identify and discuss these issues from religious, moral and social viewpoints.

13. How to use this note and what to revise next

Use these notes by working section by section through the topic, checking that you can name every organelle, state its function, and recognise it in an electron micrograph. Practise the calculations — magnification, real size from image size and magnification, mitotic index, and the index of diversity and the calculations that appear in the genetics sections. Revise by drawing and labelling an animal cell and a plant cell from memory, annotating each organelle with its function, then testing yourself on meiosis and on how variation arises. After this topic, revise Topic 4 Plant structure, biodiversity and conservation, and Topic 5 Energy flow, ecosystems and the environment, because the genetics here underpins inheritance in those later topics.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Magnification, applied to a mitochondrion measuring 4.2 cm on a micrograph at ×20 000: actual size = image size ÷ magnification. 4.2 cm = 42 000 µm, so the real length is 42 000 ÷ 20 000 = 2.1 µm. Convert every unit to µm before you divide, and write the magnification formula out.
  • Prokaryote or eukaryote: a eukaryote has a nucleus, membrane-bound organelles and 80S ribosomes. A prokaryote has a circular DNA loop, no nucleus and 70S ribosomes. Name at least two of these features; a single feature such as the cell wall is not enough because plants and some prokaryotes both have one.
  • Mitosis versus meiosis: mitosis gives two genetically identical diploid cells. Meiosis gives four haploid cells, and genetic variation comes from crossing over in prophase I and independent assortment at metaphase I. Mark schemes award these two sources separately.
  • Mammalian fertilisation: a sperm and an egg fuse to form a diploid zygote, which restores the diploid number. Name the haploid gametes explicitly, because the mark depends on the stage of meiosis that produces them.

Typical mistakes

  • Describing an organelle instead of answering the question. "Mitochondria have cristae" earns nothing when the question asks why a cell needs many of them. State the function — aerobic respiration, so an ATP supply — and link it to the cell's demand, such as the tail of a sperm or the active transport in a kidney cell.
  • Confusing magnification with resolution. Magnification is how much larger the image is than the object; resolution is the smallest distance at which two points are still seen as separate. The electron microscope wins on resolution, and that is why it separates cristae and ribosomes that a light microscope blurs together.
  • Forgetting to convert units in a magnification calculation. Put image size and real size in the same unit before dividing. 1 mm is 1 000 micrometres, and the mark is often for the unit as much as the number.
  • Using the cell wall alone to identify a plant cell. Bacteria and fungi have walls too. Use the cellulose wall together with the chloroplast or the large permanent vacuole, and remember that plant cells lack centrioles.
  • Mixing up mitosis and meiosis. Mitosis: one division, two genetically identical diploid cells, for growth and asexual reproduction. Meiosis: two divisions, four genetically non-identical haploid cells, for gametes.
  • Saying meiosis "creates variation" without naming the source. Crossing over in prophase I and independent assortment in metaphase I are separate marks; the names of the prophase stages are not required.
  • Counting every cell in the mitotic index. Interphase cells belong in the total, never in the numerator: mitotic index = cells in mitosis divided by all cells in the field.
  • Treating epigenetics as a change in the DNA sequence. Methylation and histone modification change which genes are active without altering the base sequence, and the pattern can be passed to daughter cells after division.

Exam-style questions

  1. A nucleus measures 42 mm across on an electron micrograph taken at a magnification of 7 000. Calculate its actual width. Answer: 42 mm = 42 000 micrometres. Actual size = image size divided by magnification = 42 000 / 7 000 = 6 micrometres.
  2. Explain two features of a sperm cell that adapt it for fertilisation. Answer: many mitochondria in the midpiece supply ATP for the flagellum, so the cell can swim to the egg; the acrosome contains hydrolytic enzymes that digest through the zona pellucida so the sperm can reach the egg membrane.
  3. Give three features visible in an electron micrograph that identify a cell as prokaryotic. Answer: circular DNA lying free in the cytoplasm with no nuclear envelope; 70S ribosomes, smaller than eukaryotic 80S ribosomes; no membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria or Golgi; a peptidoglycan cell wall, sometimes with a capsule, plasmids, flagella or pili.
  4. Explain how a protein destined for secretion is made and released. Answer: ribosomes on the rough endoplasmic reticulum synthesise the polypeptide; the rER folds it and packages it into a vesicle; the vesicle fuses with the Golgi apparatus, which modifies the protein, for example by adding carbohydrate; a secretory vesicle carries it to the plasma membrane and releases it by exocytosis.
  5. A root tip squash contains 80 cells in the field of view, of which 12 show visible chromosomes. Calculate the mitotic index. Answer: 12 / 80 = 0.15, or 15 per cent of the cells are in mitosis. A high value in a root tip is expected because the meristem is growing.
  6. Explain how the cortical reaction prevents a second sperm from fertilising the egg. Answer: when the first sperm fuses with the egg membrane, cortical granules release their contents into the space outside the egg; this hardens the zona pellucida and destroys the binding sites, so no further sperm can penetrate.
  7. Explain two ways in which meiosis produces gametes that are genetically different from each other. Answer: crossing over in prophase I exchanges alleles between non-sister chromatids of a homologous pair, so each chromatid carries a new combination; independent assortment in metaphase I means the maternal and paternal chromosomes of each pair line up randomly, giving 2ⁿ different combinations for n pairs.
  8. Explain how one gene can give rise to more than one protein. Answer: the primary transcript can be spliced in different ways, so different mature mRNAs carry different exon combinations; each mRNA is translated into a different polypeptide. Epigenetic modification can also switch the gene on or off in different cells, so the same gene produces protein in one cell type and not in another.

The cell cycle as a graph of DNA content

Interphase is not a rest period. It is the stage in which the cell grows, copies its DNA and checks the copy before it divides. Plotting the amount of DNA in one nucleus against time shows the whole cycle on a single graph, and questions on the cycle are often built on exactly that picture.

Key: C = the DNA content of one haploid set; 2C = the diploid amount before the DNA is copied; 4C = the amount after S phase, when each chromosome consists of two sister chromatids that are still joined.

G1, S and G2: the three parts of interphase

In G1 the cell makes proteins and organelles and grows, and its DNA stays at 2C. In S phase the DNA is replicated semi-conservatively, so the nucleus moves from 2C to 4C. G2 follows: the cell makes the proteins needed for division and checks the replicated DNA for damage before it commits to mitosis. Checkpoints at the end of G1 and G2 can stop the cycle if the DNA is damaged, which is why a fault at these points can lead to uncontrolled division.

Mitosis and the mitotic index

Mitosis returns the nucleus to 2C by separating the sister chromatids at anaphase, so each daughter cell is diploid again. A root tip squash is used to observe it because the cells are fixed and stained, and the chromosomes can be seen at each stage. The mitotic index is the proportion of cells in a sample that are in mitosis: mitotic index = number of cells in mitosis ÷ total number of cells counted. A higher index means more cells are dividing at the moment of fixing; it does not by itself say how long each stage lasts.

Why the graph matters for growth and stem cells

Tissues that replace cells constantly, such as the epidermis, keep their cells cycling. Stem cells are the cells that keep dividing and whose daughters can specialise. Knowing where a cell sits on the graph tells you whether it can copy its DNA at all, which is why many cancer treatments target the cell cycle.

Equations and symbols

Four calculations carry the marks in this topic: real size from a micrograph, total magnification, the mitotic index, and the chromosome arithmetic of meiosis. Each is one line of arithmetic, and each loses marks for a unit that was never converted.

actual size = image size ÷ magnification Key: actual size = the real length of the structure (µm); image size = the measured length on the micrograph, in the same unit (µm); magnification = the stated magnification (×, no unit). Convert millimetres and centimetres to micrometres before dividing: 1 mm = 1000 µm, 1 cm = 10 000 µm.

4.2 cm = 42 000 µm Key: the conversion line that must be written before the division — 4.2 cm × 10 000 = 42 000 µm. Examiners award this step separately, so writing it out protects the mark even if the division slips.

42 000 ÷ 20 000 = 2.1 µm Key: 42 000 µm = image size of the mitochondrion; 20 000 = magnification; 2.1 µm = actual length. The same arithmetic with 7 000 gives 42 000 / 7 000 = 6 micrometres for a nucleus.

mitotic index = number of cells undergoing mitosis ÷ total number of cells in the field of view Key: mitotic index = the proportion of dividing cells (a fraction or a percentage, no unit); the numerator counts only cells with visibly separated chromosomes; the denominator counts every cell in the field, including all the interphase cells. Leaving interphase out of the total is the classic error.

12 / 80 = 0.15 Key: 12 = cells showing visible chromosomes; 80 = all cells in the field; 0.15 = mitotic index, i.e. 15 per cent dividing. A high value is expected in a root tip because the meristem is actively growing.

The symbols of this topic

TermMeaningValue or unit
nhaploid chromosome number23 in humans (no unit)
2ndiploid chromosome number46 in humans
A, T, C, GDNA basespair A–T, C–G
70S, 80Sribosome sizeprokaryote, eukaryote
×magnificationeyepiece × objective

Traps specific to the arithmetic

  • Dividing by the magnification when the question asks for the image size — the same formula rearranged, so read which quantity is unknown.
  • Leaving the answer in centimetres after converting only one side of the division.
  • Counting a cell in anaphase twice because the chromosomes have separated: it is one cell until cytokinesis.

title: IGCSE Mathematics: Inequalities
content:
IGCSE Mathematics: Inequalities

Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580 (2025–2027), section 2 Algebra and graphs, statement 2.6 Inequalities — solving and interpreting linear inequalities, listing integer solutions, and (Extended) regions in the coordinate plane. An inequality describes a range of values rather than one exact value, and solving one follows the same balance principle as solving an equation, with one critical difference: multiplying or dividing by a negative number reverses the inequality sign. This note shows why that happens, writes out every solution line by line, and finishes with the region-shading questions that distinguish Paper 4.

What an inequality says

The four inequality symbols extend the equals sign: < (strictly less than), > (strictly greater than), ⩽ (less than or equal to), ⩾ (greater than or equal to). A solution is a set of values, drawn on a number line with a hollow circle for strict inequalities (the endpoint is excluded) and a solid circle for inclusive ones (the endpoint is included).

StatementMeaningNumber line
x > 3Every value greater than 3, not including 3Hollow circle at 3, arrow to the right
x ⩽ −1Every value up to and including −1Solid circle at −1, arrow to the left
2 ⩽ x < 5Values from 2 up to, but not including, 5Solid circle at 2, hollow at 5, line between

Why the sign flips when multiplying by a negative. Start with the true statement 3 < 5. Multiply both sides by −2 without thinking: −6 < −10 is false, because −10 is further left than −6. The correct statement is −6 > −10. Multiplying by a negative mirrors the number line, which reverses order — so the inequality symbol must reverse too. That single rule causes more lost marks than any other in this topic.

Solving linear inequalities

Use the equation methods unchanged, and remember the one reversal rule:

Solve:  5x - 7 > 3x + 1        (give the solution as an inequality)

5x - 3x > 1 + 7               [add 7 to both sides, subtract 3x from both sides]
2x > 8
x > 4                         [divide by +2: the sign does not reverse]
Solve:  3 - 2x ⩽ 11

-2x ⩽ 11 - 3                  [subtract 3 from both sides]
-2x ⩽ 8
x ⩾ -4                        [divide by -2: the sign REVERSES from ⩽ to ⩾]

The check is direct: x = −4 gives 3 − 2(−4) = 11 ⩽ 11 ✓, and x = 0 gives 3 ⩽ 11 ✓ while x = −5 gives 13 ⩽ 11 ✗ — so the boundary and direction are right.

Solve and list the integer solutions:  2 < (5x - 1)/3 ⩽ 8

Multiply every part by 3:
6 < 5x - 1 ⩽ 24
7 < 5x ⩽ 25                   [add 1 to every part]
7/5 < x ⩽ 5                   [divide every part by +5]

The integers are 2, 3, 4 and 5.

Compound inequalities (a value trapped between two bounds) are solved in one line per operation across all three parts — exactly like a three-pan balance.

Inequalities from word problems

Many questions ask for the greatest or least integer satisfying a condition. Translate carefully: at least means ⩾, at most means ⩽, more than means >, within or no more than means ⩽.

A cinema ticket costs £8. A group has £100 and must keep at least £12 for travel.
How many tickets can they buy?

Let n be the number of tickets:  8n + 12 ⩽ 100
8n ⩽ 88
n ⩽ 11

They can buy at most 11 tickets.

The final answer is a whole number in context: a group cannot buy a fraction of a ticket, so the solution set is the integers up to 11.

Regions in the coordinate plane (Extended)

The line y = mx + c divides the plane into two half-planes: points above it satisfy y > mx + c and points below it satisfy y < mx + c. A region question asks you to shade the set of points satisfying several inequalities at once.

  • Draw the boundary line y = mx + c as a solid line when the inequality includes equality (⩽ or ⩾), and as a dashed line when it is strict (< or >).
  • Test one point not on the line — the origin (0, 0) is easiest when the line misses it. Substitute into the inequality; if it is true, shade the side containing the test point.
  • Shade the side that satisfies every inequality; the answer region is the overlap, and the question often asks for the coordinates of a point inside it.
Shade the region satisfying:  y ⩽ 2x + 1,  y > -x + 2,  x ⩾ 0

Line 1: y = 2x + 1, solid. Test (0, 0): 0 ⩽ 1 true, so shade below-left of this line.
Line 2: y = -x + 2, dashed. Test (0, 0): 0 > 2 false, so shade the side away from the origin.
Line 3: x = 0 (the y-axis), solid, shade to the right.

The solution region is the triangle-like area satisfying all three, e.g. the point (2, 2):
2 ⩽ 5 ✓, 2 > 0 ✓, 2 ⩾ 0 ✓.

Describing a region in words is the reverse skill: read the boundary lines, note whether each is dashed or solid, and translate the shaded side back into an inequality.

Maximum and minimum values over a region (Extended)

Region questions often finish by asking for the largest or smallest value of an expression such as x + 2y for points inside the shaded region. A linear expression grows steadily in one direction across the plane, so over a region bounded by straight lines its extreme values always sit at the corners. The method is therefore exact: find the coordinates of every vertex of the region, substitute each pair into the expression, and pick the largest or smallest result. Do not stop at the corner that looks likely — an untested corner is the usual place a mark is lost.

Worked example: inequality with a parameter

Find the set of values of k for which the equation x² + kx + 9 = 0 has two distinct real roots.

Two distinct real roots require a positive discriminant:  b² - 4ac > 0
Here a = 1, b = k, c = 9:
k² - 36 > 0
k² > 36
k > 6  or  k < -6

This is an inequality inside a quadratic-context question — exactly the blend of topics Paper 4 rewards. If the requirement had been at least one real root, the inequality would be k² ⩾ 36, giving k ⩾ 6 or k ⩽ −6.

Corner points in practice. Take the region x ⩾ 0, y ⩾ 0, x + y ⩽ 6 and y ⩽ x + 2. Its vertices are where the boundary lines meet:

x = 0 with y = 0            gives (0, 0)
y = 0 with x + y = 6        gives (6, 0)
x = 0 with y = x + 2        gives (0, 2)
x + y = 6 with y = x + 2    gives x + (x + 2) = 6, so 2x = 4, x = 2 and y = 4, the corner (2, 4)

Evaluate P = x + 2y at each corner:
(0, 0): P = 0     (6, 0): P = 6     (0, 2): P = 4     (2, 4): P = 10

Maximum P = 10 at (2, 4);  minimum P = 0 at (0, 0).

The minimum sits at the origin only because this region includes it; a region bounded away from the origin puts its minimum at one of the other corners. Substitute every vertex before choosing.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Not reversing the inequality sign after multiplying or dividing by a negative number. −2x < 8 means x > −4.
  • Reversing the sign when multiplying by a positive number, or reversing when subtracting — only multiplication and division by negatives reverse it.
  • Hollow versus solid circles: < and > exclude the endpoint; ⩽ and ⩾ include it. Writing x > 4 when x = 4 works is a boundary error.
  • Flipping the inequality direction mid-solution so the final statement faces the wrong way.
  • Forgetting to reverse in a compound inequality: every part flips when the whole chain is multiplied by a negative.
  • In region questions, drawing a solid boundary for a strict inequality (or a dashed one for ⩽), or shading the wrong side because no test point was used.
  • Reporting a decimal when the question asks for integers: n ⩽ 11.25 means the largest integer is 11, not 11.25.
  • Treating ⩽ as < in a word problem: at most 5 includes 5.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 2, 3 marks). Solve 7 − 3x > 1 and show your solution on a number line.

Answer: −3x > −6, so x < 2 (the sign reverses). Number line: hollow circle at 2, shading to the left.

Question 2 (Paper 2, 3 marks). Solve 2 ⩽ 3x + 5 < 14 and list the integer solutions.

Answer: Subtract 5 throughout: −3 ⩽ 3x < 9. Divide by 3: −1 ⩽ x < 3. The integers are −1, 0, 1, 2.

Question 3 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Find the values of x for which x² − 5x + 4 < 0.

Answer: Factorise: (x − 1)(x − 4) < 0. The quadratic is negative between its roots, so 1 < x < 4. (Test x = 2: 4 − 10 + 4 = −2 < 0 ✓; test x = 0: 4 > 0 ✗.)

Question 4 (Paper 4, 5 marks). Shade the region defined by y > x − 1, y ⩽ 3 and x ⩾ 0, and write down the coordinates of one point in the region.

Answer: Draw y = x − 1 dashed (strict), y = 3 solid and x = 0 solid. The origin test for y > x − 1 gives 0 > −1, true, so shade above the dashed line; y ⩽ 3 shades below the horizontal line; x ⩾ 0 shades right of the y-axis. The overlap is a triangle with vertices (0, 3), (4, 3) and (0, −1); the point (1, 1) lies inside: 1 > 0 ✓, 1 ⩽ 3 ✓, 1 ⩾ 0 ✓.

Question 5 (Paper 4, 4 marks). A rectangle has a perimeter of at most 60 cm and a length of (x + 4) cm. Write an inequality for its width w and find w when x = 8.

Answer: 2[(x + 4) + w] ⩽ 60, so (x + 4) + w ⩽ 30 and w ⩽ 26 − x. With x = 8: w ⩽ 18 cm, and the width must also be positive, so 0 < w ⩽ 18.

Question 6 (Paper 2, 3 marks). The solutions of 5x + a ⩾ 0 include x = −2. Find the smallest integer value of a.

Answer: Substituting x = −2: −10 + a ⩾ 0, so a ⩾ 10. The smallest integer value is 10.

With equations and inequalities mastered, the next stage of algebra is sequences and functions.

title: Waves — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Waves

Physics — AS. A wave transfers energy without net transfer of matter.

Key areas to revise

  • Basics
  • The Wave Equation
  • Intensity
  • Doppler Effect
  • EM Spectrum
  • Polarization

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Worked example

A wave on a rope has a frequency of 500 Hz and a wavelength of 0.68 m. Its speed is v = fλ = 500 × 0.68 = 340 m s⁻¹. The same equation applies to sound and light, but the speed of light in a vacuum is 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ and does not depend on the source. Intensity falls with the inverse square of distance from a point source, so doubling the distance cuts the intensity to one quarter.

Common mistakes

  • Mixing up frequency and wavelength in v = fλ, or leaving wavelength in centimetres while using metres per second.
  • Saying waves carry matter. A wave carries energy, and the particles of the medium oscillate about fixed positions.
  • Assuming polarisation applies to longitudinal waves. Only transverse waves can be polarised.

title: IGCSE Physics: Pressure and Density
content:
IGCSE Physics: Pressure and Density

Cambridge IGCSE Physics 0625 (2026–2028), Topic 1 Motion, forces and energy: statements 1.4 Density and 1.8 Pressure. Density tells you what is inside a given volume; pressure tells you what a force does when it is spread over an area. Both ideas start from everyday experience — why ships float, why snowshoes work, why your ears pop underwater — and both carry straightforward but unit-sensitive calculations that Paper 4 marks reliably. Paper 6 also examines the practical methods used to measure density, so the experimental detail matters as much as the equations.

Density: what it is

Imagine two identical buckets, one filled with feathers and one with sand. They hold the same volume, but the sand packs far more mass into that volume. Density measures exactly that: how much mass is squeezed into each cubic metre of a substance. It is a property of the material, not of the particular sample, which is why a small gold bead and a large gold bar have the same density.

density = mass / volume        ρ = m / V
  • ρ: density in kilograms per cubic metre (kg m⁻³). Density is a scalar, so it has no direction and no sign.
  • m: mass in kilograms (kg); V: volume in cubic metres (m³).

The SI units are easy to get wrong because laboratory data arrives in grams and cubic centimetres. Water has a density of 1.00 g cm⁻³, which is 1000 kg m⁻³: to convert g cm⁻³ to kg m⁻³, multiply by 1000. Typical exam densities run from about 0.5 g cm⁻³ for wood to 19.3 g cm⁻³ for gold, and the density of water is the reference point that decides whether things float.

Measuring density experimentally

The method depends on the shape and state of the sample, and Paper 6 expects you to choose and describe the right one.

SampleMethodKey apparatus and care
Regular solid (cube or cylinder)Measure the mass on a balance; measure the dimensions with a ruler and calculate the volumeMeasure each dimension several times and average; a vernier caliper gives a better length than a ruler
Irregular solidMeasure the mass; find the volume by water displacement in a measuring cylinderRead the bottom of the meniscus at eye level; the volume difference is the sample's volume
LiquidMeasure the mass of a measuring cylinder, add the liquid, read the volume, and find the mass of the liquid by subtractionPouring losses are the main error; use a balance that reads to 0.01 g for small volumes
Object that floats in waterSink it with a thin pin or a heavy sinker and subtract the sinker's own displaced volumeA wax or wood sample cannot be measured by displacement alone because it refuses to submerge

The percentage uncertainty of the result combines the volume and mass measurements, and since volume enters as a product of lengths, a 2 per cent error in a length gives about a 6 per cent error in the volume of a cube. Repeating readings and averaging is the standard control of random error. If the object is soluble in water, use an unsuitable-displacement liquid such as sand or oil instead.

Floating and sinking

An object placed in a liquid sinks if its average density is greater than the liquid's density, and floats if it is less. A floating object displaces its own weight of liquid, so a 1000 kg steel hull floats only because the hull shape encloses a large volume of air and the average density of ship plus air is below that of water. Ice floats on water because ice is less dense (about 0.92 g cm⁻³), which is why lakes freeze from the top.

Supplement: one liquid on another. When two liquids that do not mix are poured together, the denser one sinks below the less dense one, and the boundary stays sharp. Oil (about 0.8 g cm⁻³) floats on water; syrup (about 1.4 g cm⁻³) sinks below it. A carefully poured column of syrup, water and oil layers in the order syrup, water, oil, and a grape that is denser than water but less dense than syrup will float at the syrup–water boundary. The rule is the same in every case: each substance finds the level where the density below it is greater and the density above it is smaller.

Pressure: force spread over area

Pressure is what a force does when it is spread over a surface. The same force over a smaller area produces a greater pressure, which is why a drawing pin drives into a board point-first and why snowshoes stop you sinking into snow. A sharp knife cuts because the small edge area turns a modest force into enormous pressure.

pressure = force / area        p = F / A
  • p: pressure in pascals (Pa). One pascal is one newton per square metre (1 Pa = 1 N m⁻²). Pressure is a scalar.
  • F: force in newtons (N), acting perpendicular to the surface.
  • A: area in square metres (m²) over which the force acts.

Area must be in square metres: 1 cm² = 0.0001 m², so 25 cm² = 0.0025 m². Atmospheric pressure at sea level is about 100 000 Pa (100 kPa), which presses on every square metre with a force of 100 000 N — the reason a vacuum flask is crushed if the air is pumped out, and the reason the body needs equal pressure inside as well.

Pressure is transmitted through liquids: a force applied at one point in a confined liquid is passed on undiminished in every direction, which is the principle of hydraulic brakes and car jacks, where a small force on a small piston gives a large force on a large piston because the pressure is the same on both.

Pressure in a liquid

Supplement. The pressure in a liquid rises with depth because the liquid above presses down. For a liquid of uniform density the increase is:

pressure due to a liquid column = density x gravitational field strength x depth        p = ρ g h
  • p: pressure in pascals (Pa); ρ: density of the liquid in kilograms per cubic metre (kg m⁻³).
  • g: gravitational field strength in newtons per kilogram (N kg⁻¹, use the value given in the question).
  • h: vertical depth below the surface in metres (m). Depth is measured vertically, not along a slope or the container wall.

Only the vertical height of the column counts, which is why the pressure at the bottom of a swimming pool depends only on the water's depth, not on the shape or the width of the pool. The total pressure at depth includes the atmosphere pressing on the surface: total pressure = atmospheric pressure + ρgh. A diver at 20 m in fresh water experiences ρgh = 1000 × 9.81 × 20 = 196 200 Pa from the water alone, about three times atmospheric pressure in total, which is why the ears must be equalised during descent. A manometer measures a pressure difference by the height difference of a liquid column; a barometer measures atmospheric pressure by the height of a mercury column (about 760 mm at sea level).

Worked example: density and pressure together

A rectangular brass block measures 4.0 cm × 5.0 cm × 10.0 cm and has a mass of 1.20 kg.

volume = 0.040 × 0.050 × 0.100 = 0.00020 m³
density = mass / volume = 1.20 / 0.00020 = 6000 kg m⁻³  (6.0 g cm⁻³)

Notice the unit conversion before the division: centimetres were converted to metres first, so the density comes out in kg m⁻³ directly. The same calculation in laboratory units gives the same answer: the volume is 4.0 × 5.0 × 10.0 = 200 cm³ and the mass is 1200 g, so the density is 1200 / 200 = 6.0 g cm⁻³, which converts to 6000 kg m⁻³. Keep the arithmetic in one unit system end to end and the conversion error cannot appear.

Now the block rests on a table on its largest face. The force is its weight, 1.20 × 9.81 = 11.8 N, spread over 5.0 cm × 10.0 cm = 0.0050 m²:

pressure = F / A = 11.8 / 0.0050 = 2350 Pa

Turned onto its smallest face, the area is 4.0 × 5.0 = 0.0020 m² and the pressure rises to 5875 Pa — the same weight, a smaller area, a larger pressure. Finally, the pressure 2.0 m below the surface of a fresh-water lake is ρgh = 1000 × 9.81 × 2.0 = 19 620 Pa, about 20 kPa above atmospheric pressure.

Common mistakes

  • Dividing by mass instead of volume, or reversing the density equation. Density is mass over volume; the heavy object with the same volume has the higher density.
  • Forgetting to convert g cm⁻³ to kg m⁻³ (multiply by 1000) or centimetres to metres before using SI equations. A volume in cm³ must become m³ by dividing by 10⁶.
  • Using area in cm² in p = F/A. The pascal is a newton per square metre, so the area must be in m².
  • Measuring h along the slope of a container or along the wall; depth is the vertical distance below the free surface.
  • Ignoring the atmosphere when asked for the total pressure at a depth: total pressure is atmospheric plus the liquid contribution.
  • Assuming heavy objects sink and light ones float; it is density, not mass, that decides. A huge ship floats on air-filled hull volume.
  • Treating density as a vector or attaching a direction to pressure; both are scalars.
  • Quoting more than two significant figures from readings taken with a ruler or a measuring cylinder, ignoring the precision of the apparatus.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 4, 3 marks). A glass block of mass 150 g has dimensions 5.0 cm × 4.0 cm × 2.0 cm. Calculate its density in g cm⁻³ and in kg m⁻³.

Answer: Volume = 5.0 × 4.0 × 2.0 = 40 cm³. Density = 150 / 40 = 3.75 g cm⁻³ ≈ 3.8 g cm⁻³. In SI units: 3.75 × 1000 = 3750 kg m⁻³.

Question 2 (Paper 4, 3 marks). A student stands on one foot; her weight of 500 N acts on an area of 0.015 m². Calculate the pressure, and state what happens when she stands on both feet with a total area of 0.030 m².

Answer: p = F/A = 500 / 0.015 = 33 000 Pa (33 kPa). On both feet the area doubles, so the pressure halves to about 17 000 Pa. The force is unchanged; only the area changes.

Question 3 (Paper 2 style). An object floats with half its volume submerged in water of density 1000 kg m⁻³. Its density is: A 2000 kg m⁻³; B 1000 kg m⁻³; C 500 kg m⁻³; D zero. Answer: C. Floating means the average density is less than the liquid's; an object that floats with half its volume submerged has an average density of 500 kg m⁻³.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Calculate the pressure due to the water at a depth of 3.0 m in a lake, and the total pressure at that depth. Take g = 10 N kg⁻¹ and atmospheric pressure as 100 kPa.

Answer: p = ρgh = 1000 × 10 × 3.0 = 30 000 Pa = 30 kPa. Total pressure = 100 kPa + 30 kPa = 130 kPa.

Question 5 (Paper 6 style). Describe how you would determine the density of an irregular stone that is denser than water.

Answer: Measure the mass of the dry stone on a balance. Partly fill a measuring cylinder with water and record the volume at eye level with the meniscus bottom. Lower the stone in gently (tied with thread if needed) and record the new volume. The stone's volume is the difference. Density is mass divided by the volume change. Repeat the volume readings and average to reduce random error, and check that no water is splashed out or carried away on the stone.

Question 6 (Paper 4, 3 marks). Explain why a steel needle sinks in water while a steel ship of 10 000 tonnes floats.

Answer: Steel has a density of about 7800 kg m⁻³, far greater than water, so a solid needle sinks. The ship's hull encloses a large volume of air, so the average density of the ship and the air inside it is much less than 1000 kg m⁻³. The ship therefore floats and displaces a weight of water equal to its own weight.

Density decides what floats and pressure decides what pushes; the next stop is the particle model that explains both when matter is heated.

Equations and symbols

Density and pressure share one theme: a quantity spread over a volume or an area. Every equation below is a ratio, so the units of the two quantities must match before dividing.

Density

ρ = m / V
Key: ρ (ρ) = density (kg/m³ or g/cm³); m = mass (kg or g); V = volume (m³ or cm³). 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³.

ρ(water) = 1.0 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³
Key: the reference value that decides floating and sinking for most questions; a body denser than this sinks in water.

V = m / ρ
Key: the same relation rearranged to find a volume (m³ or cm³) from a mass (kg or g) and a density. Useful when a question gives the mass of displaced water.

Pressure on a surface

p = F / A
Key: p = pressure (Pa, where 1 Pa = 1 N/m²); F = force acting perpendicular to the surface (N); A = area of contact (m²). Halving the area doubles the pressure for the same force, which is the whole physics of a sharp blade.

F = pA
Key: F = force on a surface (N); p = pressure (Pa); A = area (m²).

1 kPa = 1000 Pa and 1 MPa = 1 × 10⁶ Pa
Key: prefixes applied to the pascal; atmospheric pressure is about 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa, which is 100 kPa.

Pressure in a liquid

p = ρgh
Key: p = pressure due to the liquid (Pa); ρ (ρ) = density of the liquid (kg/m³); g = 9.8 N/kg; h = depth below the surface (m). The pressure depends on depth and density only — not on the shape or width of the container.

Δp = ρgΔh
Key: Δp = pressure difference between two depths (Pa); Δh = vertical separation of the two points (m). This is the equation behind a manometer reading and behind the pressure on a diver's eardrum.

F₁ / A₁ = F₂ / A₂
Key: F₁, F₂ = forces on the input and output pistons (N); A₁, A₂ = their areas (m² or cm²). The pressure is transmitted unchanged, so a larger area gives a larger force — the hydraulic press.

Upthrust and floating

U = ρ(fluid) × V(displaced) × g
Key: U = upthrust (N); ρ(fluid) = density of the fluid (kg/m³); V(displaced) = volume of fluid pushed aside (m³); g = 9.8 N/kg. This is Archimedes' principle written as an equation.

floating: ρ(object) < ρ(fluid)
Key: ρ(object) = the object's average density, including any trapped air (kg/m³). A steel ship floats because its average density is below water's, not because steel is light.

V(submerged) / V(total) = ρ(object) / ρ(fluid)
Key: V(submerged) = volume below the surface (m³); V(total) = whole volume (m³). A body floating half-submerged in water has half water's density, about 500 kg/m³.

sinking: weight > maximum upthrust
Key: weight = mg (N); maximum upthrust = the upthrust when the body is fully submerged. A body sinks when its density exceeds the fluid's, because even fully submerged the upthrust cannot reach its weight.

title: Edexcel IAL Computer Science: Protocols, Circuit and Packet Switching
content:
Edexcel IAL Computer Science: Protocols, Circuit and Packet Switching

Pearson Edexcel International Advanced Level in Computer Science, Unit 3 Advanced Computer Science: protocols, and circuit switching versus packet switching. The AS networking note traced data across a LAN and the internet; this note goes deeper into the rules themselves — what a protocol specification contains, how the layers compose, and why the telephone model and the packet model make opposite trades. The switching comparison is traced end to end on both models.

What a protocol is

A protocol is an agreed specification governing communication between systems: message format and syntax, semantics (what each field means), timing and sequencing (who speaks when, timeouts, rate), and error handling (detection, correction, retransmission). Without a shared protocol, hardware interoperation is impossible — the exam's "why protocols are needed" question wants those four components, not just "so devices understand each other".

Layering exists so each level can evolve independently and vendors can implement one layer against a stable interface. The TCP/IP model: application (HTTP, SMTP, FTP, DNS), transport (TCP, UDP), internet (IP, ICMP, ARP), network access (Ethernet, Wi-Fi, PPP). The OSI reference model's seven layers (Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application) are the vocabulary examiners use when asking for names — know both, map TCP/IP onto OSI, and explain encapsulation: each layer wraps the one above's data in its own header (and trailer at the data-link layer), and the receiver unwraps in reverse.

Encapsulation traced for sending "Hi" over HTTP:

  Application   : HTTP request headers + "Hi"
  Transport     : TCP header (ports, sequence no.) + HTTP data  = segment
  Internet      : IP header (src/dst addresses) + segment       = packet
  Network access: Ethernet header + trailer (FCS) + packet      = frame

  Receiver unwraps in order: frame → packet → segment → HTTP data.
  Each layer reads only ITS header - the modularity is the point.

ARP bridging the layers: an IP packet needs the destination MAC address on
the LAN; ARP broadcasts "who has 192.168.1.5?" and the owner replies with its
MAC - the address-resolution seam between internet and network-access layers.

The protocol families in depth

ProtocolLayerGuaranteesCostUsed for
TCPTransportReliable, ordered, flow-controlled, connection-oriented (3-way handshake)Round-trips and header overheadHTTP, email, file transfer
UDPTransportNone — best-effort, connectionlessMinimal delayDNS, streaming, gaming, VoIP
IP (v4/v6)InternetBest-effort addressing and routing; fragmentationNo delivery guarantee (IP alone)Everything routed
ICMPInternetError/query messages (ping, TTL exceeded)—Diagnostics
TLSSession/PresentationEncryption, integrity, authentication (certificates)Handshake latency, CPUHTTPS, secure email
The TCP three-way handshake, packet by packet:

  Client                          Server
    | ---- SYN (seq=x) ------------→|    "I want to connect"
    | <--- SYN-ACK (seq=y, ack=x+1) -|    "acknowledged; my sequence is y"
    | ---- ACK (ack=y+1) ----------→|    "confirmed"
  connection ESTABLISHED; data flows with sequence/ack numbers.

Why three steps: each side learns the other's initial sequence number and
both agree the connection exists - a two-way exchange could leave the server
believing in a connection the client never confirmed. Teardown mirrors it
(FIN/ACK), and timeouts recover lost packets - the reliability story.

Circuit switching

In circuit switching, a dedicated physical path is established end to end for the whole conversation and released at the end — the telephone network model. Three phases: circuit establishment (signalling reserves each link), data transfer (the path is exclusive), circuit teardown.

  • Strengths: guaranteed constant bandwidth and latency for the call's duration; no congestion mid-call once established; simple in-call ordering (one path).
  • Weaknesses: the reserved path is wasted during silence (speech is ~40% silence); setup delay before any data flows; a failed link breaks the call with no rerouting; capacity is fixed per circuit.

Packet switching

In packet switching, messages are split into packets, each carrying source/destination addresses and a sequence number; packets travel independently (possibly different routes — datagram approach) or along a pre-agreed virtual circuit, sharing links with other conversations' packets. The receiving end reassembles by sequence number.

One message, both models, traced:

  Message: 1.2 Mbit, links of 1.2 Mbps each.

  CIRCUIT: establish path (say 200 ms signalling), then the message flows on
  its exclusive path: 1.2 Mbit / 1.2 Mbps = 1 s, then teardown. Total ≈ 1.2 s.
  During the transfer no other call can use those links.

  PACKET (1500-byte packets, ~800 packets): packets interleave with other
  traffic. Each hop queues and forwards (store-and-forward: each router
  receives the whole packet, checks it, sends on). If a link is busy, packets
  queue (variable latency - jitter); if a router drops one, only THAT packet
  is retransmitted (TCP). No setup delay; total time depends on congestion.
  A failed route just changes the next hop for later packets.

  Store-and-forward delay per hop = packetSize / linkRate; the end-to-end sum
  plus queueing is the latency - the number a "why is video call laggy?"
  answer quotes.
Circuit switchingPacket switching
PathDedicated, reserved per callShared, per-packet routes
SetupRequired before dataNone (datagram) / light (virtual circuit)
BandwidthGuaranteed constantStatistical; can vary (jitter)
Failure handlingCall drops; no reroutingPackets reroute; lost packets retransmitted
EfficiencyLow during silence/idleHigh — links shared statistically
FitsVoice telephony, constant-rate streamsData networks, the internet, bursty traffic

Modern note the exam appreciates: voice over the internet (VoIP) is packet switching engineered to imitate circuit guarantees — priority queues and reserved capacity give latency-sensitive packets the reserved feel of a circuit.

Worked example: designing a link for a school

Requirement: 40 classrooms, each streaming 2 Mbps video lessons at peak, plus
email/web traffic.

  Peak video demand: 40 × 2 = 80 Mbps, before overheads (add ~20% for
  headers/retransmission): ≈ 96 Mbps.
  Packet switching with a 100 Mbps backbone just fits; a 1 Gbps link gives
  headroom. Circuit switching would reserve 2 Mbps per room regardless of use
  (40 × 2 = 80 Mbps permanently committed) and no room could burst above its
  allocation - wasteful for bursty web traffic.

Choice: packet switching with QoS priority for the video VLAN; the answer
names the burstiness argument (statistical multiplexing) and the QoS trade.

Quality of service on packet networks

Because packet switching offers no inherent guarantee, engineered guarantees are added on top: QoS marks latency-sensitive packets (voice, video) for priority queuing; traffic shaping smooths bursts so links are not overwhelmed; reservation (RSVP-style) holds capacity for a flow; and MPLS gives labelled paths that behave like fast virtual circuits. Each mechanism trades simplicity for predictability — the exam's "how does VoIP work reliably?" answer is exactly this list with priority queuing first.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Describing circuit switching as "faster" universally; it is predictable (guaranteed rate), while packet switching is efficient and burst-friendly — match the claim to the traffic.
  • Forgetting store-and-forward when computing latency: each hop holds the packet, and links serialise it.
  • Saying packets arrive in order; the sequence numbers and reassembly exist because they may not.
  • Listing OSI layers without their function or mis-ordering them (Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application).
  • Confusing IP (best-effort delivery) with TCP (reliability); neither alone is "the internet" — the pairing is.
  • Claiming UDP is unreliable so it is useless; its speed is exactly why real-time services choose it.
  • Leaving handshake/timing out of protocol answers; sequencing and synchronisation are part of what a protocol defines.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Unit 3, 4 marks). Describe the features a protocol must specify.

Answer: Message format/syntax (bit patterns, header fields); semantics (what each field and code means, what actions follow); timing and sequencing (who transmits when, synchronisation, timeouts, rate control); and error handling (detection via checksums, correction or retransmission rules). These four allow independent implementations to interoperate exactly.

Question 2 (Unit 3, 5 marks). Explain encapsulation using the TCP/IP layers.

Answer: Each layer adds its own header to the data from the layer above: the application data gets a TCP header (ports, sequence numbers) forming a segment; the segment gets an IP header (addresses) forming a packet; the packet gets a network-access header and trailer (MAC addresses, checksum) forming a frame. The receiver reverses the process, each layer reading only its own header and passing the payload upward — layering isolates responsibilities so protocols can change independently.

Question 3 (Unit 3, 5 marks). Compare circuit switching and packet switching for a national voice network.

Answer: Circuit switching reserves an exclusive path per call: guaranteed constant bandwidth and latency once established and simple ordering, but setup delay before speech, wasted capacity during silence, and a failed link drops the call. Packet switching shares links statistically: no setup, high efficiency and rerouting around failures, but variable latency (jitter) that voice dislikes unless QoS prioritises it. Traditional telephony chose circuits; modern VoIP chooses packets with engineered priority — the efficiency of sharing wins once jitter can be controlled.

Question 4 (Unit 3, 4 marks). Describe the TCP three-way handshake and explain its purpose.

Answer: The client sends SYN with its initial sequence number; the server replies SYN-ACK acknowledging it and supplying its own sequence number; the client confirms with ACK. Purpose: both sides learn each other's sequence numbers (needed for ordered reassembly), agree the connection exists, and agree parameters — avoiding the half-open connections a two-message exchange would permit.

Question 5 (Unit 3, 4 marks). Explain why the internet uses packet switching rather than circuit switching.

Answer: Internet traffic is bursty — web pages, email and files arrive in irregular bursts with idle gaps. Packet switching shares links statistically, so all conversations use whatever capacity is free at each instant (high utilisation), packets reroute around failures (resilience), and each packet need not hold capacity when silent. Circuit switching would reserve bandwidth through idle periods and block bursts above the reservation. Real-time needs are met with QoS on top rather than dedicated circuits.

Question 6 (Unit 3, 3 marks). Calculate the store-and-forward delay for a 1500-byte packet over three 10 Mbps hops.

Answer: Packet = 1500 × 8 = 12 000 bits. Per hop: 12 000 ÷ 10⁷ = 1.2 ms. Three hops store-and-forward the packet serially (each waits for the whole packet before sending): 3 × 1.2 = 3.6 ms transmission delay, plus any propagation and queueing delay at each router.

The protocols above carry encrypted traffic as often as plain; the security layer on top is the next note's subject.
