   - BOILING POINT RISES (bigger molecules, stronger intermolecular forces);
   - VISCOSITY INCREASES (thicker, flows less easily);
   - VOLATILITY FALLS (evaporates less readily);
   - COMBUSTION gets less clean (more soot/carbon).

Fractional cracking breaks long alkane chains into shorter, more useful ones (alkanes + alkenes): C₁₀H₂₂ → C₈H₁₈ + C₂H₄ — driven by the need for petrol and alkene feedstock.

Alkanes: substitution

Alkanes are generally unreactive (strong, non-polar C–C and C–H bonds) but burn (combustion) and undergo substitution with halogens in UV light.

Complete combustion (all hydrocarbons):
  CH₄ + 2O₂ -> CO₂ + 2H₂O
Incomplete combustion (limited O₂):
  2CH₄ + 3O₂ -> 2CO + 4H₂O   (carbon monoxide - toxic)
  or soot (C) forms - a visible flame with yellow tips.

Chlorination of methane (photochemical substitution):
  CH₄ + Cl₂  --UV light-->  CH₃Cl + HCl
  One H is REPLACED by Cl - the definition of substitution. The UV light
  provides the activation energy to split the Cl-Cl bond into radicals.
  Further substitution gives CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃, CCl₄ - the products are a
  mixture, which is why the reaction is poor for synthesis.

Alkenes: addition

Alkenes react via the C=C double bond in addition reactions — two reactants join to give one product (nothing is lost).

Addition to ethene - each with its conditions:

  + bromine (test for unsaturation):
    C₂H₄ + Br₂ -> C₂H₄Br₂        (1,2-dibromoethane)
    OBSERVATION: orange bromine water is DECOLOURISED - the test that
    distinguishes alkenes from alkanes.

  + hydrogen (nickel catalyst, heat):
    C₂H₄ + H₂ -> C₂H₆            (ethane; hydrogenation - margarine making)

  + steam (phosphoric acid catalyst, heat + pressure):
    C₂H₄ + H₂O -> C₂H₅OH         (ethanol)

In every case the double bond opens to single bonds and the atoms add on -
draw the product by "opening" the C=C and attaching one atom to each carbon.

Alcohols

Two production routes for ethanol, with the trade-off the exam always asks:

1. FERMENTATION of glucose (yeast, no oxygen, 25-35 °C):
     C₆H₁₂O₆ -> 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂
   Advantages: renewable feedstock (sugar/corn), low energy conditions,
   batch process.
   Disadvantages: slow (days), dilute product (needs distilling), depends on
   crop supply and weather.

2. CATALYTIC HYDRATION of ethene (H₃PO₄ catalyst, 300 °C, 60 atm):
     C₂H₄ + H₂O -> C₂H₅OH
   Advantages: fast, continuous, high purity and yield.
   Disadvantages: ethene comes from crude oil (finite), high energy/pressure
   costs.

Ethanol itself: burns cleanly (C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ -> 2CO₂ + 3H₂O) as a fuel;
a solvent (perfumes, paints); in alcoholic drinks.

Carboxylic acids and esters

Carboxylic acids are weak acids: they react with metals (salt + hydrogen), bases (salt + water) and carbonates (salt + water + carbon dioxide — the fizz test that identifies an acid).

Oxidation of ethanol to ethanoic acid:
  ethanol + [O] -> ethanoic acid     e.g. by acidified potassium
  manganate(VII), or by bacterial action in vinegar production (air + 
  Acetobacter).

Esterification (acid + alcohol, concentrated H₂SO₄ catalyst):
  ethanoic acid + ethanol -> ethyl ethanoate + water
  CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O

  Naming esters: the FIRST word comes from the ALCOHOL (ethyl, from ethanol),
  the second from the ACID (ethanoate, from ethanoic acid).
  Propyl methanoate = propanol + methanoic acid.

  Esters: sweet smells (fruits, perfumes), solvents, plasticisers.

Polymers

A monomer is the small molecule that repeats; a polymer is the very long chain of joined monomers. Addition polymerisation joins many alkene molecules by opening the double bonds — nothing else is produced.

Deducing the repeat unit - the master method:

  Monomer: propene, CH₂=CH-CH₃
  1. Open the double bond: -CH₂-CH(CH₃)-
  2. Extend the "bonds" at both ends to show the chain continuing:
     [ -CH₂-CH(CH₃)- ]ₙ

  Reverse (monomer from repeat unit): find the two backbone carbons of one
  unit, restore the double bond between them, and cap the ends with the
  substituents that were drawn.

  poly(ethene):  n CH₂=CH₂ -> [ -CH₂-CH₂- ]ₙ
  poly(propene): n CH₂=CHCH₃ -> [ -CH₂-CH(CH₃)- ]ₙ
  poly(chloroethene) (PVC): n CH₂=CHCl -> [ -CH₂-CHCl- ]ₙ

Condensation polymerisation (two different bifunctional monomers):
  a small molecule (usually water) is LOST at each link.
  Nylon (a polyamide): diamine + dicarboxylic acid -> nylon + water.
  PET (a polyester): diol + dicarboxylic acid -> PET + water.
  Proteins are natural polyamides from amino-acid monomers.

Disposal: plastics are non-biodegradable — landfill accumulates, plastics in the ocean harm wildlife, burning releases toxic gases (HCl from PVC, CO from incomplete combustion). Options: recycling (sorted by type), depolymerisation (PET can be broken back to monomers and re-polymerised), and biodegradable alternatives.

Worked example: one route map, every reaction type

From ethane to ethyl ethanoate:

  ethane --(cracking/heat)--> ethene      [thermal decomposition]
  ethene + steam --(H₃PO₄, 300 °C)--> ethanol   [addition / hydration]
  ethanol + [O] --(bacterial)--> ethanoic acid  [oxidation]
  ethanol + ethanoic acid --(conc. H₂SO₄)--> ethyl ethanoate [esterification]

  Each arrow names its type, conditions and the functional-group change:
  alkane -> alkene (C-C to C=C), alkene -> alcohol (C=C to C-OH),
  alcohol -> acid (-OH to -COOH), acid + alcohol -> ester (-COOH/-OH to
  -COO-). Tracking the functional group through a route map is the skill
  the exam tests.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Forgetting that addition reactions need the C=C — alkanes substitute, alkenes add; mixing them up loses every mark on the question.
  • Bromine water: decolourised by alkenes (addition) but NOT by alkanes — the observation sentence must name the colour loss.
  • Counting general formula wrong for the first members (methane CH₄ fits CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ with n = 1).
  • Writing polymers without the extending bonds at both ends of the repeat unit (it must show continuation).
  • In ester naming, swapping which part comes from the acid and which from the alcohol.
  • Leaving reaction conditions off (UV for substitution, Ni/heat for hydrogenation, concentrated H₂SO₄ for esterification) — conditions are marks.
  • Claiming fermentation is fast/pure — the comparison with catalytic hydration needs both sides.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 4, 3 marks). Define a homologous series and state three general characteristics.

Answer: A homologous series is a family of similar compounds with the same functional group and general formula, each member differing from the next by a CH₂ unit. Characteristics: similar chemical properties; gradual trend in physical properties (boiling point rises with chain length); can be made by similar methods.

Question 2 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Describe the test that distinguishes ethene from ethane, with equations.

Answer: Add aqueous bromine and shake. Ethene decolourises the orange bromine (addition: C₂H₄ + Br₂ → C₂H₄Br₂); ethane shows no change (no reaction in the dark at room temperature). The C=C double bond is responsible for the addition.

Question 3 (Paper 4, 5 marks). Compare fermentation and catalytic hydration as routes to ethanol.

Answer: Fermentation (C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂, yeast, 25–35 °C) uses renewable sugar crops and mild conditions, but is slow, gives dilute ethanol needing distillation, and varies with crop supply. Catalytic hydration (C₂H₄ + H₂O → C₂H₅OH, H₃PO₄, 300 °C, 60 atm) is fast, continuous and high-yield, but depends on crude-oil-derived ethene and costly high-pressure conditions.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Draw the repeat unit of poly(propene) and name the polymerisation type.

Answer: Monomer propene CH₂=CHCH₃ opens at the double bond giving repeat unit [–CH₂–CH(CH₃)–]ₙ, with the chain bonds extending at both ends. This is addition polymerisation — many monomers join with no other product.

Question 5 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Describe how ethyl ethanoate is made and state its uses.

Answer: Warm ethanol with ethanoic acid in the presence of concentrated sulfuric acid catalyst (esterification): CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O. The ester is distilled off. Ethyl ethanoate is used as a solvent (nail-varnish remover), in perfumes and flavourings (sweet smell).

Question 6 (Paper 4, 3 marks). Explain why burning PVC can be more harmful than burning poly(ethene).

Answer: PVC contains chlorine; burning it releases hydrogen chloride gas, which is toxic and forms acidic fumes, plus carbon monoxide from incomplete combustion. Poly(ethene) contains only carbon and hydrogen and burns to CO₂ and water if complete — less acutely toxic though still a CO₂ source.

Organic molecules can be burned as fuels — the next topic is what happens when electrons move instead: electrochemistry.

title: Motion in a Circle and Gravity — Study Notes
content:
Motion in a circle and gravity

Circular motion

  • A body moving in a circle at constant speed has a centripetal acceleration of v²/r, directed towards the centre.
  • The centripetal force is F = mv²/r = mω²r, and it is provided by a real force such as tension, friction or gravity. It does no work on the body, because it is always perpendicular to the velocity.

Gravitational field

The gravitational field strength at a point is the force per unit mass placed at that point: g = F/m. Unit: N kg⁻¹. Field lines point towards the mass that creates the field.

Newton's law of gravitation

F = GMm/r², where r is measured from the centre of each point mass. Doubling the separation reduces the force to one quarter.

Gravitational field of a point mass

g = GM/r². Outside a uniform sphere, its field is the same as that of a point mass at its centre.

Gravitational potential

Gravitational potential at a point is the work done per unit mass in bringing a small mass from infinity to that point. It is always negative, is zero at infinity, and becomes more negative closer to the mass: V = −GM/r. Gravitational potential energy of a mass m is Ep = mV.

Worked example: a 2.0 kg object moves in a circle of radius 0.50 m at 3.0 m s⁻¹. The centripetal force is F = mv²/r = (2.0 × 3.0²) ÷ 0.50 = 36 N.

Exam tips: use r as the distance from the centre, not the surface. State that gravitational potential is negative and rises to zero at infinity. Field strength and potential are different quantities: do not mix their units.

title: Exam technique: System Software and Security
content:
### What earns the marks
For OS roles, each role tied to the scenario earns a mark: paging for oversized workloads, scheduling for shared CPUs. For malware, the propagation method contrasted (self-spreading worms vs host-bound viruses) earns both marks. For hashing, one-way verification plus salt against rainbow tables earns the pair.
### Traps
Error: single-driver answers for whole-OS management. Correction: name memory, processor, devices, security. Error: worms and viruses reversed. Correction: worms roam alone; viruses ride hosts. Error: encryption claimed where hashing belongs. Correction: password checks verify hashes, never decrypt.

title: AS Level Mathematics: Statistics S1 — Correlation and Regression
content:
AS Level Mathematics: Statistics S1 — Correlation and Regression

Statistics S1 turns data into claims about relationships. Two variables measured together can be displayed on a scatter diagram; the strength of any straight-line relationship is measured by the product-moment correlation coefficient; and the line of best fit — the regression line — predicts one variable from the other. This note builds the unit from zero: bivariate data and scatter diagrams, the correlation coefficient with its calculation and interpretation, regression lines and their equations, and the assumptions that make prediction honest.

Bivariate data and scatter diagrams

each observation gives a pair (x, y)
plot y against x; look for direction, strength and shape
PatternMeaning
Points rise left to rightPositive correlation
Points fall left to rightNegative correlation
No patternLittle or no linear correlation
Curved patternA relationship, but not linear

An outlier is a point far from the pattern. It can dominate both the correlation coefficient and the regression line, so it should be identified and its effect discussed, not silently deleted.

The product-moment correlation coefficient

r = Sxy / √(Sxx Syy)

Sxx = sum x² - (sum x)²/n
Syy = sum y² - (sum y)²/n
Sxy = sum xy - (sum x)(sum y)/n

-1 <= r <= 1

Worked example (full calculation). Five pairs give sum x = 20, sum y = 30, sum x² = 90, sum y² = 220, sum xy = 140, n = 5. Find r.

Sxx = 90 - 400/5 = 10
Syy = 220 - 900/5 = 40
Sxy = 140 - 600/5 = 20
r = 20/√(10 × 40) = 20/20 = 1.0  (perfect positive)

Worked example 2. With sum x = 15, sum y = 24, sum x² = 55, sum y² = 130, sum xy = 60, n = 5.

Sxx = 55 - 45 = 10;  Syy = 130 - 115.2 = 14.8
Sxy = 60 - 72 = -12
r = -12/√(148) = -12/12.166 = -0.986

Interpretation is a required sentence, not a number: r = 0.986 means a strong positive linear relationship; r = 0.2 means a weak positive one. Also state that r measures only linear association — a strong curve can give r near zero.

The regression line

y on x:  y = a + bx  with b = Sxy/Sxx and a = ybar - b xbar

x on y (the other regression): x = c + dy with d = Sxy/Syy

There are two regression lines because minimising vertical distances is not the same as minimising horizontal distances. The line of y on x is the one used to predict y from x, and its gradient is always steeper (for |r| < 1) than the x-on-y line.

Worked example. Using the second data set above, find the regression line of y on x.

xbar = 3, ybar = 4.8
b = -12/10 = -1.2
a = 4.8 - (-1.2)(3) = 8.4
y = 8.4 - 1.2x

Worked example 2 (prediction). Use that line to predict y when x = 4, and comment on a prediction at x = 20.

at x = 4: y = 8.4 - 4.8 = 3.6
at x = 20: y = 8.4 - 24 = -15.6, and 20 lies far outside the data
range (1 to 5), so this is extrapolation and unreliable

Interpolation is prediction inside the observed range; extrapolation is outside it. Extrapolation assumes the straight-line pattern continues, which the data cannot support — say so.

Interpreting the gradient and intercept

In context, b is the change in y per unit increase in x, and a is the predicted y when x = 0 (often meaningless: no one weighs 0 kg at 0 cm).

Worked example. A regression of exam mark (y) on hours studied (x) gives y = 30 + 5x. Interpret.

each extra hour of study is associated with 5 more marks
(b is an association, not proof of causation)
the intercept 30 is the predicted mark with no study, but x = 0
may lie outside the data range, so treat it cautiously

Correlation, causation and reliability

A strong correlation never establishes causation. Two variables can move together because a third drives both (ice-cream sales and drowning both rise with temperature), or by coincidence in a small sample.

r measures linear association only
r is unaffected by changing units or swapping x and y
r is sensitive to outliers
r = 0 does not mean no relationship: a symmetric curve can give r = 0

Worked example. A study finds r = 0.85 between shoe size and reading age in children. Explain why this does not mean bigger feet cause better reading.

both increase with age; age is a lurking variable
the correlation is real but confounded, so a causal claim needs a
controlled comparison at a fixed age

Choosing the right summary

S1 questions ask you to select and justify the statistic. The decision table is worth memorising:

SituationBest choiceReason
Outliers presentMedian, IQRRobust to extremes
All values should countMean, sdUses every observation
Two variables, linear patternr and the regression lineMeasures strength and predicts
Curved patternTransform, or do not use rr assumes linearity

Worked example. A data set of salaries has one director earning ten times the rest. Which average and spread should summarise it, and why?

median and IQR: the director's salary drags the mean upward and
inflates the sd, so neither represents a typical employee

Where the least-squares coefficients come from

The regression line is chosen to minimise the sum of squared vertical distances from the points. That criterion produces the formulas already quoted, and knowing why makes them far easier to recall.

minimise sum (y - a - bx)² over a and b
differentiate with respect to a: -2 sum (y - a - bx) = 0
  →  ybar = a + b xbar   (the line passes through the mean point)
differentiate with respect to b: -2 sum x(y - a - bx) = 0
  →  Sxy = b Sxx  →  b = Sxy/Sxx

Two consequences worth stating in an exam: the line always passes through (x̄, ȳ), and if Sxy is zero the gradient is zero — no linear trend, so r = 0 and prediction by the line is useless.

Worked example. Show that the line passes through the mean point for y = 8.4 − 1.2x with x̄ = 3.

y at x = 3: 8.4 - 3.6 = 4.8 = ybar, as the derivation requires

Answering S1 questions the way mark schemes reward

The statistics marks are split between calculation and commentary, and the commentary is where candidates lose most. Four habits cover almost every question:

  • State the statistic with its units and three significant figures.
  • Interpret in context, naming the variables rather than x and y.
  • Qualify every causal claim as an association.
  • For a prediction, say whether it is interpolation or extrapolation.

Worked example. A regression of height y (cm) on age x (years) for 8- to 12-year-olds gives y = 90 + 6x, r = 0.96. Write a full interpretation.

strong positive linear correlation (r = 0.96) between age and height
in this sample; on average each additional year of age is associated
with 6 cm more height; the line explains the data well within the
8-12 range, and a prediction at age 20 would be extrapolation and
unreliable because growth does not continue linearly

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (r meaning) r = −0.9. Interpret. Answer: strong negative linear correlation; as x increases y tends to decrease.
  2. (r range) Can r = 1.2? Answer: no; r lies between −1 and 1.
  3. (Calculation) Sxx = 20, Syy = 45, Sxy = 27. Find r. Answer: r = 27/√900 = 0.9.
  4. (Gradient) Sxy = 27, Sxx = 20. Find b. Answer: 1.35.
  5. (Intercept) b = 1.35, x̄ = 5, ȳ = 10. Find a. Answer: a = 10 − 6.75 = 3.25.
  6. (Prediction) y = 3.25 + 1.35x. Predict y at x = 8. Answer: 14.05.
  7. (Extrapolation) Data covers x = 1 to 10. Is a prediction at x = 50 reliable? Answer: no; extrapolation beyond the data range.
  8. (Causation) r = 0.95 between umbrella sales and rainfall. Does buying umbrellas cause rain? Answer: no; rainfall drives sales, so the correlation is not causal in that direction.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Using the wrong regression line: predict y from x with the y-on-x line, not the x-on-y line.
  • Confusing b and r: the gradient is a rate of change; r is a unitless strength between −1 and 1.
  • Claiming causation: always qualify — "associated with" rather than "causes".
  • Ignoring the outlier: one extreme point can lift or destroy r; comment on its effect.
  • Extrapolating silently: state when a prediction lies outside the data range and that it is unreliable.
  • Rounding r: quote three significant figures and keep full accuracy in Sxy, Sxx, Syy.
  • Swapping Sxy and Syy: the y-on-x gradient divides by Sxx; the x-on-y gradient divides by Syy.
  • Forgetting units in interpretation: "5 more marks per hour" reads as a real claim; "y increases by 5" does not.

Formula summary

Sxx = sum x² - (sum x)²/n;  Syy = sum y² - (sum y)²/n
Sxy = sum xy - (sum x)(sum y)/n
r = Sxy/√(Sxx Syy)
y on x: b = Sxy/Sxx,  a = ybar - b xbar

Compute Sxx, Syy and Sxy first and keep them to four significant figures; every later statistic is a combination of those three, so an early rounding error propagates into r, the gradient and the prediction alike.

title: Exam technique: Nuclear Physics (A2)
content:
### What earns the marks
For energy, mass defect times c squared with units earns both marks. For decay, ln2 over half-life quoted earns the method mark; activity as lambda N earns the second. For radii, the cube-root rule applied to ratios earns the mark.
### Traps
Error: half-life used as the decay constant. Correction: divide ln2 by it. Error: fission named for the Sun. Correction: fusion powers stars. Error: radius scaled linearly with A. Correction: cube root of nucleon number.
### Worked example
A nucleus has a half-life of 8 days. The decay constant is lambda = ln 2 / 8, which is about 0.087 per day. If the sample holds N = 2.0 x 10^10 nuclei, the activity is A = lambda N, about 1.7 x 10^9 decays per day. Quote the unit with the answer, because the mark depends on it.
### Check yourself
A nucleus with A = 64 has radius r = 1.2 x 64^(1/3) = 4.8 fm. State why doubling A does not double the radius. The radius grows with the cube root of A, so doubling A multiplies r by 2^(1/3), about 1.26.

### Worked example
A nucleus has a half-life of 8 days. The decay constant is lambda = ln 2 / 8, which is about 0.087 per day. If the sample holds N = 2.0 x 10^10 nuclei, the activity is A = lambda N, about 1.7 x 10^9 decays per day. Quote the unit with the answer, because the mark depends on it.

title: Algebra — Equations — Study Notes
content:
Equations

Linear equations

Expand any brackets, collect the terms in x on one side and the constants on the other, then divide by the coefficient of x. When fractions appear, multiply every term by the lowest common denominator first.

Simultaneous linear equations

Use elimination (make the coefficient of one variable equal and opposite, then add or subtract) or substitution (rearrange one equation and put it into the other). Check the solution by substituting into the equation you did not use.

Example: 3x + 2y = 12 and x − y = 1. From the second equation x = y + 1. Substituting gives 3y + 3 + 2y = 12, so y = 9/5 and x = 14/5. Check: 3(14/5) + 2(9/5) = 12.

Quadratic equations

Factorise where possible, complete the square, or use the formula x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / 2a. The discriminant b² − 4ac gives the number of real roots: two if positive, one if zero, none if negative.

Equations with algebraic fractions

Multiply through by the product of the denominators, excluding any values that make a denominator zero. The result is often a quadratic.

Example: 2/(x − 1) + 3/(x + 1) = 2. Multiplying by (x − 1)(x + 1) gives 5x − 1 = 2x² − 2, so 2x² − 5x − 1 = 0 and x = (5 ± √33)/4. Neither root equals ±1, so both are valid.

Exam technique

  • Keep answers exact (fractions and surds) unless the question asks for decimals.
  • Substitute each root back into the original equation when fractions are involved.

title: A Level Mathematics: The Binomial Distribution
content:
A Level Mathematics: The Binomial Distribution

A binomial distribution counts successes in a fixed number of independent trials, each with the same probability of success. Coins, multiple-choice guesses, defective items in a sample and free throws all fit the same template, and once a problem is recognised as binomial the calculation is a formula plus a cumulative table. This note builds the distribution from its four conditions, derives the formula from counting, and then uses it for the two things exams actually ask: probabilities and hypothesis tests.

The four conditions

Before writing X ~ B(n, p) you must be able to name the conditions, because most exam questions include a part asking whether the model is appropriate. The conditions are not red tape: drop any one and the formula is simply wrong.

1. a fixed number of trials n
2. each trial has exactly two outcomes (success / failure)
3. the probability of success p is constant for every trial
4. the trials are independent
then X = number of successes has X ~ B(n, p)

Worked example (checking the model). A bag holds 5 red and 15 blue counters. Four counters are taken without replacement. Is the number of red counters binomial?

n = 4 is fixed and each draw is red or not red
but p changes: 5/20, then 5/19 if a red was taken, ...
the trials are not independent, so NOT binomial (it is hypergeometric)

Taking with replacement would fix it: p stays 0.25 on every draw.

The formula, and where it comes from

The probability of a particular sequence of r successes and n − r failures is p^r (1−p)^(n−r), because independence lets you multiply. The number of such sequences is the number of ways to choose which r trials succeed, which is nCr. Multiplying gives the formula.

P(X = r) = nCr p^r (1 - p)^(n - r)
the nCr counts arrangements; the powers give the probability of one arrangement

Worked example. X ~ B(10, 0.3). Find P(X = 3).

P = 10C3 (0.3)³ (0.7)⁷
= 120 × 0.027 × 0.08235
= 120 × 0.002223 = 0.2668

Worked example 2 (a single trial count). A fair die is rolled 8 times. Find the probability of exactly two sixes.

X ~ B(8, 1/6)
P(X = 2) = 8C2 (1/6)² (5/6)⁶ = 28 × 0.02778 × 0.3349 = 0.2605

Worked example 3 (why nCr appears). For n = 3 and r = 1, list the sequences and confirm the coefficient.

sequences: SFF, FSF, FFS - three of them
each has probability p(1-p)²
so P(X = 1) = 3p(1-p)², and 3C1 = 3

Cumulative probabilities

Questions almost always ask for a range, not a single value, and the cumulative distribution is what the calculator or the tables supply. The skill is rewriting the question into the form the table gives you.

P(X <= r) is tabulated directly
P(X >= r) = 1 - P(X <= r - 1)
P(X < r)  = P(X <= r - 1)
P(a <= X <= b) = P(X <= b) - P(X <= a - 1)
P(X = r) = P(X <= r) - P(X <= r - 1)

Worked example. X ~ B(20, 0.4). Find P(X ≥ 8).

P(X >= 8) = 1 - P(X <= 7)
= 1 - 0.4159
= 0.5841

Worked example 2 (between). For the same X, find P(5 ≤ X ≤ 10).

= P(X <= 10) - P(X <= 4)
= 0.8725 - 0.0510
= 0.8215

Worked example 3 (the strict inequality trap). For the same X, find P(X > 6).

P(X > 6) = 1 - P(X <= 6) = 1 - 0.2500 = 0.7500
note this is different from P(X >= 6) = 1 - P(X <= 5) = 0.8746

Mean and variance

The binomial has the simplest mean and variance in the syllabus, and they are worth knowing both forwards and backwards: a question can give the mean and variance and ask for n and p.

E(X) = np
Var(X) = np(1 - p)
standard deviation = √(np(1-p))

Worked example. X ~ B(50, 0.2). Find the mean and standard deviation.

mean = 50 × 0.2 = 10
variance = 10 × 0.8 = 8
sd = 2.828

Worked example 2 (backwards). A binomial variable has mean 12 and variance 9. Find n and p.

np = 12;  np(1-p) = 9
divide: 1 - p = 9/12 = 0.75  →  p = 0.25
then n = 12/0.25 = 48

Hypothesis testing with the binomial

A one-tailed test asks whether p has increased or decreased; the test statistic is the observed count, and the p-value is the probability of a result at least as extreme in the direction of the alternative.

H0: p = p0      H1: p > p0 (or p < p0)
X ~ B(n, p0) under H0
p-value = P(X >= observed) or P(X <= observed)
compare with the significance level; reject H0 if p-value <= alpha

Worked example. A coin is tossed 20 times and lands heads 15 times. Test at the 5% level whether the coin is biased towards heads.

H0: p = 0.5;  H1: p > 0.5
X ~ B(20, 0.5)
P(X >= 15) = 1 - P(X <= 14) = 1 - 0.9793 = 0.0207
0.0207 < 0.05, so reject H0
there is evidence at the 5% level that the coin favours heads

Worked example 2 (two-tailed). The same data tested two-tailed.

double the smaller tail: 2 × 0.0207 = 0.0414
0.0414 < 0.05, so still reject H0 at the 5% level

Worked example 3 (critical region). For X ~ B(20, 0.5), find the critical region for a 5% one-tailed test of p > 0.5.

P(X >= 14) = 0.0577 (above 0.05)
P(X >= 15) = 0.0207 (below 0.05)
critical region: X >= 15

Note that the critical region is chosen so the probability of a Type I error is at most 5%, which is why 14 is excluded even though it is close.

When the model breaks down

Examiners like the question that asks why a binomial model is only an approximation. The usual culprits are dependence, a varying probability, or a fixed sample drawn without replacement from a small population.

SituationProblemEffect
sampling without replacementtrials not independentp drifts; use the hypergeometric instead
clustered data (pupils in classes)responses correlatedvariance underestimated
probability varies between trialsp not constantformula invalid
large n, p near 0.5computation heavynormal approximation is reasonable

Worked example (normal approximation). X ~ B(200, 0.4). Use a normal approximation to estimate P(X ≤ 70).

mean = 80;  variance = 200 × 0.4 × 0.6 = 48;  sd = 6.928
continuity correction: X <= 70 becomes X < 70.5
z = (70.5 - 80)/6.928 = -1.371
P(Z < -1.371) = 0.0852

The continuity correction is compulsory: a discrete count needs a half-unit boundary before it can be treated as continuous.

Expected frequencies and the shape of the distribution

A binomial distribution is not symmetric unless p = 0.5, and that shape decides which tail an exam question is fishing in. The most likely value — the mode — is the integer near (n + 1)p, and expected frequency multiplies the probability by the number of samples taken. Both are quick marks that are frequently missed because students jump straight to the formula.

mode is near (n + 1)p, checked by comparing consecutive probabilities
expected number in a sample of size N = N x P(X = r)

Worked example. X ~ B(12, 0.3). Find the most likely value of X and the expected number of 3s in 500 independent observations.

(n + 1)p = 13 × 0.3 = 3.9, so check r = 3 and r = 4
P(X = 3) = 220 × 0.027 × 0.1176 = 0.2397
P(X = 4) = 495 × 0.0081 × 0.1681 = 0.2311
mode = 3
expected number of 3s = 500 × 0.2397 = 120 (to the nearest whole)

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Model) State the distribution for the number of sixes in 12 rolls of a fair die. Answer: X ~ B(n, p) with n = 12 rolls and p = 1/6 the chance of a six on each, so X ~ B(12, 1/6).
  2. (Single value) X ~ B(8, 0.25): find P(X = 2). Answer: P(X = 2) = ⁸C₂ (0.25)² (0.75)⁶ = 28 × 0.0625 × 0.1780 = 0.3115.
  3. (Cumulative) X ~ B(15, 0.3): find P(X ≤ 4). Answer: P(X ≤ 4) = Σₖ₌₀⁴ ¹⁵Cₖ (0.3)ᵏ (0.7)¹⁵⁻ᵏ = 0.5155 from cumulative binomial tables.
  4. (Complement) Same X: find P(X ≥ 3). Answer: P(X ≥ 3) = 1 − P(X ≤ 2) = 1 − 0.2969 = 0.7031 — the complement, because the tables give the lower tail only.
  5. (Mean) X ~ B(40, 0.35): find E(X) and Var(X). Answer: 14 and 9.1.
  6. (Backwards) Mean 18, variance 12: find n and p. Answer: mean np = 18 and variance np(1 − p) = 12; dividing, 1 − p = 12/18 = 2/3, so p = 1/3 and n = 18 ÷ (1/3) = 54.
  7. (Test) 12 of 20 seeds germinate; test p = 0.5 against p < 0.5 at 5%. Answer: H₀: p = 0.5 against H₁: p < 0.5; under H₀, X ~ B(20, 0.5) and P(X ≤ 12) = 0.8684, which is far above 0.05, so there is no evidence to reject H₀.
  8. (Critical region) X ~ B(10, 0.2): find the 5% critical region for p < 0.2. Answer: the smallest possible tail is P(X ≤ 0) = (0.8)¹⁰ = 0.1074, which already exceeds 0.05, so no critical region exists at the 5% level for this n.
  9. (Approximation) X ~ B(100, 0.5): approximate P(X ≥ 60). Answer: μ = np = 50 and σ = √(np(1 − p)) = √25 = 5; with the continuity correction z = (59.5 − 50)/5 = 1.9, so P(X ≥ 60) ≈ P(Z > 1.9) = 0.0287.
  10. (Assumption) Give one reason a binomial model may fail for defects in boxes of 20. Answer: defects may cluster, so trials are not independent.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Forgetting nCr: the coefficient counts arrangements; without it the answer is the probability of one specific sequence.
  • nCr on the wrong factor: it is p^r (1−p)^(n−r), with the success probability raised to the number of successes.
  • Inequality direction: P(X ≥ 8) uses 1 − P(X ≤ 7), not 1 − P(X ≤ 8).
  • Variance confused with standard deviation: np(1−p) is the variance; the test and the normal approximation need the square root.
  • Continuity correction omitted: any normal approximation to a discrete count needs the half-unit adjustment.
  • One-tailed evidence read as two: halving or doubling the tail without checking the alternative direction is a silent error.
  • Independence asserted, not checked: sampling without replacement from a small population breaks the model, and the question usually invites you to say so.
  • p-value compared with the wrong threshold: the significance level is given as a percentage; 5% means 0.05, not 5.

Recognising a binomial situation in context

Most binomial marks are lost before any arithmetic starts, because the question was not identified as binomial. The subsections below give a checklist for reading a question and writing the model in the standard form X ~ B(n, p) before you calculate anything.

Writing the model in the form X ~ B(n, p)

Once you decide a situation is binomial, state the model in full: X ~ B(n, p), where X is the number of successes, n is the number of trials and p is the probability of a success on each trial. Define X in words in your answer, for example “X is the number of defective bulbs in a box of 20”. A model with no definition of X loses the communication mark even when the probabilities are right.

Identifying the number of trials, n

The value of n is the fixed number of times the experiment is repeated: the number of bulbs tested, the number of patients treated, or the number of games played. Read the question for the phrase that fixes it, such as “of 20 bulbs chosen at random”. If the question keeps going until a result occurs, the number of trials is not fixed and the binomial model does not apply directly.

Identifying the probability of success, p

The value of p is the probability of the outcome you have chosen to call a success on one trial. It must stay the same for every trial. A fair coin gives p = 0.5, and a bag where 15% of items are faulty gives p = 0.15 for each item drawn with replacement. If the question gives a percentage, convert it to a decimal before you use it in any formula.

Checking for fixed trials

The number of trials must be decided before the experiment starts. Counting the number of successes in a fixed sample is binomial, whereas recording how many trials it takes to get the first success is not. A question about the number of heads in ten tosses is binomial; a question about how many tosses are needed for the first head is a different model. Make the fixed-n check before any other check.

Checking for independent trials

Each trial must not affect the next. Independence is what allows you to multiply the probabilities of several outcomes together, and it is the assumption most often ignored. Drawing items with replacement keeps p constant, and that is what the model needs. Drawing without replacement changes p after each draw, so the binomial model is only an approximation when the sample is small compared with the population.

Worked identification

A survey finds that 30% of adults own a bicycle. Twelve adults are chosen at random from a large town and asked whether they own one. Let X be the number who own a bicycle. Here n = 12, p = 0.3 and the answer is X ~ B(12, 0.3). The population is large, so the probability for each adult stays close to 0.3 and the model is a reasonable one to use. State that assumption, because a marker looks for it.

Probabilities of at least one, and of more than r

Questions that ask for “at least” or “more than” are the ones where the complement saves the most time. The subsections set out the choice between a direct sum and the complement, and the checks that stop an off-by-one error.

Probability of at least one success

“At least one” is the complement of “none”, so P(X ≥ 1) = 1 − P(X = 0) = 1 − qⁿ, where q = 1 − p. For X ~ B(5, 0.2), P(X ≥ 1) = 1 − 0.8⁵ = 1 − 0.32768 = 0.672 to 3 significant figures. Adding the probabilities of X = 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 gives the same answer but takes five calculations instead of one.

Probability of more than r successes

“More than 3” means 4 or more, so P(X > 3) = 1 − P(X ≤ 3). For X ~ B(10, 0.3), P(X ≤ 3) = 0.6496 to 4 decimal places, so P(X > 3) = 0.3504. The number 3 is included in the part you subtract from 1; forgetting that is the typical error on “more than” questions.

Choosing between a direct sum and the complement

Use the complement when the part you do not want is short: “at least one”, “at most one but not zero” and similar phrases. Use a direct sum when the wanted region has only a few terms, such as P(X = 2) + P(X = 3). With a calculator table of cumulative probabilities, most “at most” and “at least” questions reduce to one lookup and one subtraction.

Probability of exactly r on a calculator

For X ~ B(n, p), P(X = r) = ⁿCᵣ pʳ qⁿ⁻ʳ. The combination ⁿCᵣ counts the ways the r successes can be arranged among n trials. For X ~ B(10, 0.3), P(X = 3) = 120 × 0.3³ × 0.7⁷ = 120 × 0.027 × 0.0823543 = 0.2668 to 4 decimal places. Enter the combination with the nCr key so the arrangement count is not mistyped.

The most likely number of successes (the mode)

The most likely value of X is the mode. For a binomial distribution it is the whole number part of (n + 1)p, and if (n + 1)p is itself a whole number there are two modes, (n + 1)p − 1 and (n + 1)p. For X ~ B(10, 0.3), (n + 1)p = 3.3, so the mode is 3. Check against the probabilities: P(X = 3) = 0.2668 is larger than P(X = 2) = 0.2335 and P(X = 4) = 0.2001.

Adding independent binomial variables

A question can combine two or more binomial counts, for example the total number of faults from two machines. The result is binomial only under particular conditions, and the subsections below say what those conditions are and how to check them.

Same probability, different numbers of trials

If X ~ B(n, p) and Y ~ B(m, p) are independent, and both use the same probability of success p, then X + Y ~ B(n + m, p). Two batches tested for the same fault, with the same chance of that fault on each item, combine into one larger binomial. The shared p is the key condition: the trials must all be a success or failure with the same chance.

The rule for X + Y

Write the result as X + Y ~ B(n + m, p). For example, X ~ B(4, 0.5) and Y ~ B(6, 0.5), independent, give X + Y ~ B(10, 0.5). Add the trial counts, not the probabilities. The probability of success stays the same because each trial still has the same chance of success.

When the probabilities differ

If X ~ B(n, p) and Y ~ B(m, q) with p ≠ q, the sum is not binomial, and you cannot use the rule above. The number of successes comes from trials that have different chances, so no single p describes all of them. A question that asks for the distribution in this case expects a table of values, not a single binomial statement.

Worked example: two batches

Batch A has 8 items and batch B has 12 items. Each item in either batch is defective with probability 0.05, and the items are independent. Let T be the total number of defective items. Then T ~ B(20, 0.05), because both batches share p = 0.05. The probability of no defective items at all is P(T = 0) = 0.95²⁰ = 0.358 to 3 significant figures.

Why the mean and variance add

The mean of a sum is always the sum of the means, whether or not the variables are independent. The variance of a sum is the sum of the variances only when the variables are independent. For the batch example, E(T) = 20 × 0.05 = 1 and Var(T) = 20 × 0.05 × 0.95 = 0.95, which is the same as adding the separate variances 8 × 0.0475 and 12 × 0.0475.

A one-tailed hypothesis test, step by step

A binomial hypothesis test asks whether an observed count is too unlikely for the claimed probability to be true. The method has the same steps every time, and each step earns its own mark, so write them in order.

State H₀ and H₁ in terms of the parameter

H₀ states the claimed value of p, and H₁ states the direction of the alternative. For a claim that a coin or process produces fewer successes than stated, write H₀: p = 0.4 and H₁: p < 0.4 in your working, with the symbols defined. The hypotheses are always about p, never about X, and H₀ always contains the equals sign.

Find the tail the alternative points to

The direction of H₁ tells you which tail of the distribution is critical. A “less than” alternative uses the lower tail, which contains small values of X. A “greater than” alternative uses the upper tail. Decide the tail before you look at the observed value, because choosing it afterwards invalidates the test.

Compute the probability of the observed value or more extreme

For a lower-tail test, find P(X ≤ x), where x is the observed count, assuming H₀ is true. Suppose X ~ B(12, 0.4) and 1 success is observed. Then P(X ≤ 1) = 0.6¹² + 12 × 0.4 × 0.6¹¹ = 0.00218 + 0.01741 = 0.0196 to 3 significant figures. The working must show both terms, because a single number with no method earns only a fraction of the method marks.

Compare the probability with the significance level

If the probability is less than or equal to the significance level, reject H₀. Here 0.0196 is less than 0.05, so the result is significant at the 5% level and H₀ is rejected. If the question gives a 1% level, the same probability would not be significant, because 0.0196 is greater than 0.01. Always compare with the level the question states.

Write the conclusion in the context of the question

A complete conclusion states what the result means for the claim, not just whether H₀ was rejected. For example: “There is evidence at the 5% level that the proportion of successes is less than 0.4.” Use the word “evidence” and refer to the proportion, because a test gives evidence about a population, not a proof about it.

Find the critical region and the actual significance level

The critical region is the set of values of X that lead to rejection. For B(12, 0.4), P(X ≤ 1) = 0.0196 is at most 0.05 but P(X ≤ 2) = 0.0196 + 66 × 0.16 × 0.6¹⁰ = 0.0835 is more than 0.05, so the critical region at the 5% level is {0, 1}. The actual significance level is 0.0196, which is 1.96%, because the discrete distribution cannot be cut at exactly 5%.

Equations and symbols

The distribution, its conditions and the four tail identities. Every question on this topic is one of these lines plus a calculator.

P(X = r) = nCr p^r (1 - p)^(n - r) Key: n = number of trials, fixed in advance; p = probability of success in one trial, constant; r = the number of successes asked for; nCr = n!/(r!(n − r)!), the number of orders the successes can occur in. The (1 − p) term is the failures, and its power must be n − r.

X ~ B(n, p) Key: X = the count of successes; the tilde means "is distributed as"; n and p as above. Write this line before calculating — it is often a mark on its own, and it fixes which parameters go into the calculator.

P = 10C3 (0.3)³ (0.7)⁷ Key: n = 10, p = 0.3, r = 3, so the failures are 7 and their probability is 0.7. The coefficient 10C3 = 120 accounts for the order of the three successes among the ten trials.

P(X >= r) = 1 - P(X <= r - 1) Key: a complement, so the two probabilities add to 1; the boundary moves by one because the binomial is discrete. Using 1 − P(X ≤ r) instead is the classic off-by-one error.

P(a <= X <= b) = P(X <= b) - P(X <= a - 1) Key: subtract the part below the interval; again the "− 1" is there because P(X ≤ a − 1) is everything before a. Check with a small case you can list by hand before trusting the calculator.

title: AS Level Mathematics: Coordinate Geometry
content:
AS Level Mathematics: Coordinate Geometry

Coordinate geometry turns shapes into algebra: every line is an equation, every intersection is a simultaneous equation, and every circle is a completed square waiting to happen. This note builds the whole AS toolkit from zero: distance and midpoint, gradients with the parallel and perpendicular rules, the three forms of a line's equation, intersections and perpendicular bisectors, circles in both centre-radius and expanded form, and tangents and normals to circles. Every worked example writes the formula line first, because that is where the method marks are.

Distance and midpoint

distance between (x1, y1) and (x2, y2):
d = sqrt((x2 - x1)^2 + (y2 - y1)^2)

midpoint: ((x1 + x2)/2, (y1 + y2)/2)

The distance formula is Pythagoras in disguise: the horizontal and vertical gaps are the legs of a right triangle, and the distance is the hypotenuse.

Worked example. Find the distance and midpoint of A(1, 2) and B(7, 10).

d = sqrt(6^2 + 8^2) = sqrt(100) = 10
midpoint = ((1 + 7)/2, (2 + 10)/2) = (4, 6)

Gradient and the parallel/perpendicular rules

gradient m = (y2 - y1)/(x2 - x1)   (rise over run)

parallel lines: m1 = m2
perpendicular lines: m1 x m2 = -1   (m2 = -1/m1)

Worked example. Find the gradient of AB for A(1, 2), B(5, 10), and the gradient of a line perpendicular to it.

m = (10 - 2)/(5 - 1) = 8/4 = 2
perpendicular gradient = -1/2

Worked example 2 (collinearity). Show A(1, 1), B(3, 5), C(5, 9) are collinear.

m(AB) = 4/2 = 2;  m(BC) = 4/2 = 2
equal gradients and a shared point B, so collinear

Equations of straight lines

Three forms, each useful in its own situation:

  • y = mx + c: gradient m, y-intercept c. Use when you know both.
  • y − y₁ = m(x − x₁): point-slope form. Use when you know a point and the gradient.
  • ax + by + c = 0: general form. Rearrange to find m and c when needed.

Worked example 1. Find the equation of the line through (2, 5) with gradient 3.

y - 5 = 3(x - 2)
y = 3x - 6 + 5
y = 3x - 1

Worked example 2 (two points). Find the equation of the line through (1, 4) and (4, 13).

m = (13 - 4)/(4 - 1) = 9/3 = 3
using (1, 4): y - 4 = 3(x - 1)  ->  y = 3x + 1

Worked example 3 (perpendicular). Find the line through (2, 1) perpendicular to y = 2x + 3.

perpendicular gradient = -1/2
y - 1 = -1/2 (x - 2)
y = -x/2 + 1 + 1 = -x/2 + 2

Intersections and the perpendicular bisector

Two lines meet where their equations are simultaneously true: set them equal and solve. The perpendicular bisector of AB passes through the midpoint of AB with gradient −1/m(AB).

Worked example. Find where y = 3x − 1 meets y = −x + 7.

3x - 1 = -x + 7
4x = 8  ->  x = 2;  y = 3(2) - 1 = 5
intersection: (2, 5)

Worked example 2 (perpendicular bisector). Find the perpendicular bisector of A(1, 2) and B(5, 10).

midpoint = (3, 6)
m(AB) = 8/4 = 2  ->  perpendicular gradient = -1/2
y - 6 = -1/2 (x - 3)
y = -x/2 + 3/2 + 6 = -x/2 + 7.5

Circles: centre-radius form

(x - a)^2 + (y - b)^2 = r^2
centre (a, b), radius r

expanded form x^2 + y^2 + 2fx + 2gy + c = 0:
complete the square in x and y to recover the centre and radius

Worked example 1. State the centre and radius of (x − 3)² + (y + 2)² = 25.

centre (3, -2); radius = 5

Worked example 2 (completing the square). Find the centre and radius of x² + y² − 6x + 8y − 11 = 0.

(x^2 - 6x) + (y^2 + 8y) = 11
(x - 3)^2 - 9 + (y + 4)^2 - 16 = 11
(x - 3)^2 + (y + 4)^2 = 36
centre (3, -4), radius 6

Worked example 3 (circle from diameter). AB is a diameter with A(1, 2) and B(7, 10). Find the circle's equation.

centre = midpoint = (4, 6)
radius = half the distance = 10/2 = 5
(x - 4)^2 + (y - 6)^2 = 25

Tangents and normals to circles

A tangent to a circle is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact. The method: find the gradient of the radius from the centre to the point, take the negative reciprocal for the tangent, then use the point-slope form.

Worked example. Find the tangent to the circle centre (2, 3) at the point (5, 7).

radius gradient = (7 - 3)/(5 - 2) = 4/3
tangent gradient = -3/4
y - 7 = -3/4 (x - 5)
4y - 28 = -3x + 15
3x + 4y = 43

Worked example 2 (tangent length). From the point P(8, 3), find the length of the tangent to the circle (x − 2)² + (y − 1)² = 13.

centre C(2, 1), radius sqrt(13)
distance PC = sqrt(6^2 + 2^2) = sqrt(40)
tangent^2 = PC^2 - r^2 = 40 - 13 = 27
tangent length = sqrt(27) = 3 sqrt(3) = 5.20

The right angle between radius and tangent makes every tangent-length question a Pythagoras problem in disguise; drawing the radius to the contact point is the step that unlocks it.

Worked example 2 (normal). The normal at a point on a circle is the radius line extended. Find the normal at the same point.

normal gradient = radius gradient = 4/3
y - 7 = 4/3 (x - 5)  ->  4x - 3y + 1 = 0 (rearranged)

Circles and lines: intersection problems

Where a line meets a circle, substitute the line into the circle's equation and solve the resulting quadratic. The discriminant then classifies the geometry: two roots mean a secant (two intersection points), one root means a tangent, none means the line misses the circle.

substitute y = mx + c into (x - a)^2 + (y - b)^2 = r^2
solve for x; each x gives a y from the line
discriminant > 0: two points; = 0: tangent; < 0: no intersection

Worked example. Find the intersection of y = x + 1 with x² + y² = 25.

x^2 + (x + 1)^2 = 25
2x^2 + 2x + 1 - 25 = 0
x^2 + x - 12 = 0
(x + 4)(x - 3) = 0  ->  x = -4 or 3
y = -3 or 4
points: (-4, -3) and (3, 4)

Worked example 2 (tangent condition). Show that y = 2x + 10 is tangent to x² + y² = 20.

x^2 + (2x + 10)^2 = 20
5x^2 + 40x + 100 - 20 = 0
5x^2 + 40x + 80 = 0  ->  x^2 + 8x + 16 = 0
(x + 4)^2 = 0: repeated root, so tangent at x = -4, y = 2

Modelling with straight lines

Linear models answer practical questions: when two plans cost the same, how a quantity changes at a constant rate, what a graph's gradient means in context. The method is to identify the two variables, write each relationship as a line, and solve simultaneously — then interpret the answer in the units of the problem.

Worked example. A taxi charges a fixed 3 pounds plus 1.50 pounds per kilometre; a rival charges 6 pounds plus 1.00 pound per kilometre. Find the distance at which the charges are equal.

3 + 1.5d = 6 + 1.0d
0.5d = 3  ->  d = 6 km
both charge 12 pounds at 6 km

Worked example 2 (gradient meaning). A graph of value against age for a car is a straight line through (0, 18000) and (4, 10000). Interpret the gradient.

gradient = (10000 - 18000)/4 = -2000
meaning: the car loses 2000 pounds of value per year

Worked examples: mixed coordinate problems

Worked example. The line y = 2x + k is a tangent to the circle x² + y² = 20. Find k.

substitute: x^2 + (2x + k)^2 = 20
x^2 + 4x^2 + 4kx + k^2 - 20 = 0
5x^2 + 4kx + (k^2 - 20) = 0
tangent: discriminant = 0
16k^2 - 20(k^2 - 20) = 0
16k^2 - 20k^2 + 400 = 0  ->  4k^2 = 400  ->  k = +/-10

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Distance) Find the distance between (2, 1) and (5, 5). Answer: √(9 + 16) = 5.
  2. (Gradient) Find the gradient through (3, 4) and (7, 12). Answer: 8/4 = 2.
  3. (Perpendicular) A line has gradient −⅔. Find the gradient of a perpendicular line. Answer: 3/2.
  4. (Equation) Find the line through (0, 3) with gradient −2. Answer: y = −2x + 3.
  5. (Circle) State the centre and radius of (x + 1)² + (y − 4)² = 9. Answer: centre (−1, 4), radius 3.
  6. (Completing the square) Find the centre and radius of x² + y² + 4x − 2y − 4 = 0. Answer: (x + 2)² + (y − 1)² = 9 → centre (−2, 1), radius 3.
  7. (Tangent) Find the tangent to x² + y² = 25 at (3, 4). Answer: radius gradient 4/3, tangent gradient −3/4; 3x + 4y = 25.
  8. (Midpoint/distance) Show that (1, 2), (5, 6), (9, 10) are collinear. Answer: gradients both 1; shared point → collinear.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Gradient sign errors: (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁) — subtracting in the wrong order flips the sign. Keep the same point first in both differences.
  • Perpendicular as negative: the perpendicular gradient is the negative reciprocal (−1/m), not just −m.
  • Circle sign reversal: (x + 2)² means centre x = −2; (y − 5)² means y = 5. The sign inside is opposite to the centre coordinate.
  • Radius squared: in (x − a)² + (y − b)² = 25 the radius is 5, not 25. Take the square root.
  • Completing the square with coefficients: halve the x-coefficient and subtract its square; forgetting the subtraction changes the radius.
  • Tangent versus normal: tangent is perpendicular to the radius; normal is along the radius. Swapping their gradients inverts the answer.
  • Intersection arithmetic: after finding x, substitute into the simpler equation for y, and check both points when a quadratic gives two solutions.
  • Sketching circles: mark the centre and radius explicitly; a circle without its centre marked cannot be checked.

title: IGCSE Physics (OxfordAQA): Nuclear Physics
content:
Nuclear Physics

Almost all of the mass of an atom sits in a nucleus a hundred thousand times smaller than the atom itself, and almost all of the energy released in a power station or a star comes from rearranging that nucleus. This topic follows the story in four steps: what the nucleus contains, what it emits when it is unstable, what happens when a heavy nucleus splits, and what happens when light nuclei join. Every equation in it is a conservation statement — the mass numbers and the atomic numbers on both sides of a decay must balance — so the arithmetic and the physics are the same thing.

3.7.1 Atomic structure

An atom consists of a nucleus of protons and neutrons, surrounded by electrons arranged in shells. A proton has a relative mass of 1 and a charge of +1, a neutron has a relative mass of 1 and no charge, and an electron has negligible mass and a charge of −1. Nearly all the mass is in the nucleus, while nearly all the volume is the electron cloud.

QuantitySymbolWhat it counts
Atomic (proton) numberZThe number of protons; it identifies the element
Mass (nucleon) numberAProtons plus neutrons
Neutron numberNA minus Z
Charge on the nucleus+ZOne positive unit per proton

An atom is neutral because the number of electrons equals the number of protons. An ion is formed when electrons are gained or lost, which changes the charge but never the element: a chloride ion still has seventeen protons, whatever its charge.

A = Z + N

Key: A = mass number, the number of nucleons; Z = atomic number, the number of protons; N = the number of neutrons; the equation is used rearranged as N = A - Z.

Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. Carbon-12 and carbon-14 both have six protons, so both are carbon, but carbon-14 has eight neutrons rather than six. Isotopes have almost identical chemical properties because chemistry depends on electrons, and different nuclear properties: carbon-14 is radioactive while carbon-12 is not.

3.7.2 Ionizing radiation from the nucleus

An unstable nucleus emits radiation to become more stable. The three types are alpha, beta and gamma, and they differ in what they are, how far they travel and how strongly they ionise.

RadiationWhat it isRange in airStopped byIonising power
AlphaTwo protons and two neutrons (a helium nucleus)A few centimetresA sheet of paper or the dead layer of skinStrongest, because it is large and charged
BetaA fast electron emitted when a neutron turns into a protonA few metresA few millimetres of aluminiumModerate
GammaAn electromagnetic wave of very short wavelengthEffectively unlimited; intensity falls with distanceThick lead or concrete, and only partlyWeakest

Alpha and beta are deflected in electric and magnetic fields in opposite directions, because one is positive and the other negative, while gamma is undeflected because it has no charge. The deflection of alpha is smaller than that of beta because an alpha particle is far more massive.

Every decay changes the nucleus in a way that can be written down and checked. In alpha decay the mass number falls by four and the atomic number by two. In beta decay the mass number is unchanged and the atomic number rises by one, because a neutron has become a proton. Gamma emission changes neither number; it simply carries away energy.

  • Alpha decay of radon-222: the nucleus loses two protons and two neutrons, so mass number 222 - 4 = 218 and atomic number 86 - 2 = 84, giving polonium-218.
  • Beta decay of carbon-14: mass number stays 14, atomic number rises from 6 to 7, giving nitrogen-14.
  • Gamma emission leaves the element unchanged and is written with the same mass and atomic numbers on both sides.

Half-life is the time taken for half of the unstable nuclei in a sample to decay, or for the count rate from it to halve. Nothing about an individual nucleus can be predicted; the half-life is a statement about a very large number of them. Activity is measured in becquerels, one decay per second, and background radiation from rocks, cosmic rays, food and medical sources must be subtracted from a measured count rate before a half-life is calculated.

3.7.3 Nuclear fission

Fission is the splitting of a large nucleus into two smaller ones, releasing energy. It happens when a nucleus such as uranium-235 absorbs a neutron and becomes unstable. The products are two smaller nuclei, two or three further neutrons, and a large amount of energy, which appears as kinetic energy of the fragments.

  • The neutrons released can be absorbed by other uranium nuclei, so the process can sustain a chain reaction.
  • In a nuclear reactor the chain reaction is controlled: control rods made of boron or cadmium absorb surplus neutrons, and a moderator such as graphite or water slows the neutrons so they are more likely to be captured.
  • The energy released heats a coolant, which turns water into steam and drives a turbine, exactly as in a fossil-fuel station.
  • The waste is radioactive for thousands of years, which is why it must be stored and shielded for a very long time.

The mass of the products is slightly less than the mass of the original nucleus plus the neutron, and the difference appears as energy. That is the most important sentence in the topic: the energy released by fission is not created from nothing but converted from mass, in a proportion set by the speed of light squared.

3.7.4 Nuclear fusion

Fusion is the joining together of two light nuclei to form a heavier one, releasing energy. It is the reaction that powers every star, including the Sun, where hydrogen nuclei fuse to form helium at extremely high temperature and pressure.

  • Fusion needs very high temperatures because the nuclei are positively charged and repel each other, so they must be moving fast enough to get close enough for the strong nuclear force to act.
  • It needs very high pressure and density to keep the nuclei close together for long enough to react.
  • The energy released per kilogramme of fuel is much larger than for fission, and the fuel is abundant in seawater.
  • It produces far less long-lived radioactive waste than fission, which is why it is the long-term goal.
  • The difficulty is containment: no material can touch a gas at those temperatures, so magnetic or inertial confinement is required, and no reactor yet produces more energy than it consumes.

Fusion in the Sun and fission in a reactor are opposite ends of the same binding-energy curve: light nuclei release energy when they join, and heavy ones release energy when they split. In both cases the energy comes from the small change in mass.

Worked example: particles in an atom and an ion

Write down the number of protons, neutrons and electrons in a neutral atom of uranium-235, and in the ion U-235 with a charge of 3+.

Neutral atom: protons = 92 (the atomic number of uranium), neutrons = 235 - 92 = 143, electrons = 92. For the 3+ ion, electrons = 92 - 3 = 89, with protons and neutrons unchanged.

Key: 92 = atomic number Z (protons); 235 = mass number A (nucleons); 143 = neutrons, found from N = A - Z; 3 = the charge, which removes three electrons because each electron is -1.

An ion is never a different element: the proton count is what defines the element, and it has not changed. That is why a 3+ uranium ion is still uranium.

Worked example: completing a decay equation

Polonium-210 decays by alpha emission. Write the balanced equation and identify the new element. Its atomic number is 84.

The alpha particle is a helium nucleus, with mass number 4 and atomic number 2. So the daughter has mass number 210 - 4 = 206 and atomic number 84 - 2 = 82. Atomic number 82 is lead, so the equation is Po-210 → Pb-206 + alpha, with 210 = 206 + 4 and 84 = 82 + 2 on the two sides.

Key: 210 and 84 = mass and atomic numbers of the parent; 4 and 2 = mass and atomic numbers of the alpha particle; 206 and 82 = the mass and atomic numbers of the daughter; both totals must match on each side.

Both conservation rules must be checked. An answer that balances the mass numbers but not the atomic numbers has either forgotten that the alpha carries two protons or miscounted the element.

Worked example: half-life

A source has a count rate of 640 counts per minute. After 24 days the count rate is 80 per minute. Calculate the half-life and state the count rate after a further 12 days.

640 halves to 320, then 160, then 80: that is three half-lives, so each is 24 ÷ 3 = 8 days. After a further 12 days, one and a half more half-lives pass, so the rate goes 80 → 40 → 20 in the last half-life, giving 20 counts per minute.

Key: 640 and 80 = count rates (counts per minute); 3 = the number of halvings; 24 days = total time (days); 8 days = one half-life.

Halving is multiplicative, not linear, so the count rate never reaches zero in a finite time. A rate of 0 would be a wrong answer for that reason alone.

Worked example: choosing shielding

A source emits alpha, beta and gamma radiation. Describe the count rate recorded by a detector placed behind paper, then behind aluminium, then behind thick lead.

Behind paper the detector records beta and gamma, because the alpha is stopped: the count falls to about two thirds of the unshielded value if the three are equally intense. Behind aluminium the beta is also stopped, so only gamma is recorded. Behind thick lead the gamma is greatly reduced but not eliminated, so the count falls further but rarely to zero.

Key: paper = the shielding for alpha; aluminium = the shielding for beta; lead = the shielding for gamma; the residual count with lead in place shows that gamma is only attenuated, not absorbed completely.

Typical mistakes

  • Saying an ion is a different element. The proton number is unchanged, so the element is unchanged.
  • Writing the mass number of an alpha particle as 2. It is 4, because it contains two protons and two neutrons.
  • Forgetting that beta decay raises the atomic number by one, because a neutron becomes a proton.
  • Changing the mass number during gamma emission, which changes neither number.
  • Treating half-life as a linear decrease, or predicting that the activity will reach zero.
  • Confusing fission with fusion: heavy nuclei split in fission, light nuclei join in fusion.
  • Claiming fusion needs no energy to start. It needs extremely high temperature because the nuclei repel.
  • Forgetting to subtract background radiation before calculating a half-life from measured counts.

Exam-style questions

  1. State the number of protons, neutrons and electrons in a neutral atom of carbon-14. Answer: Carbon has atomic number Z = 6, so a neutral atom has 6 protons and 6 electrons. The neutrons are N = A - Z = 14 - 6 = 8.
  2. Explain why alpha particles are more ionising than gamma rays but travel a shorter distance. Answer: An alpha particle is large, doubly charged and slow, so it interacts strongly with atoms along its path and ionises many of them, losing its energy quickly. Gamma is uncharged and interacts weakly, so it penetrates much further before being absorbed.
  3. Write the equation for the beta decay of carbon-14 and name the daughter element. Answer: The mass number is unchanged at A = 14, and a neutron turning into a proton raises the atomic number by one: Z = 6 + 1 = 7, which is nitrogen, so carbon-14 → nitrogen-14 + beta.
  4. A sample's activity falls from 800 Bq to 100 Bq in 45 hours. Calculate the half-life. Answer: Halve three times: 800 ÷ 2 = 400, then 400 ÷ 2 = 200, then 200 ÷ 2 = 100. Three half-lives fit into 45 hours, so T = 45 ÷ 3 = 15 hours.
  5. Describe what happens in a controlled chain reaction in a nuclear reactor. Answer: A neutron splits a uranium-235 nucleus and releases more neutrons than one, on average n ≈ 2.4 per fission, and each can split another nucleus. Control rods absorb the surplus so that exactly one neutron per fission causes the next, giving a multiplication factor k = 1 and a steady rate.
  6. Explain why nuclear fusion requires very high temperatures. Answer: The nuclei are positively charged and repel each other. At very high temperatures they move fast enough to overcome that repulsion and get close enough for the strong nuclear force to bind them.
  7. State one similarity and one difference between fission and fusion. Answer: Both release energy from a change in nuclear mass. Fission splits a heavy nucleus and is used in reactors; fusion joins light nuclei, powers stars and is not yet a practical power source.
  8. A detector near a source records 300 counts per minute; the background is 20. After 6 days the reading is 90 counts per minute. Calculate the corrected count rate and the half-life. Answer: Subtract the background first: 300 - 20 = 280 and 90 - 20 = 70. Then 280 ÷ 2 = 140 and 140 ÷ 2 = 70, so two half-lives fit into 6 days and T = 6 ÷ 2 = 3 days.

Revision checklist

  • I can give the mass and charge of each subatomic particle and calculate proton, neutron and electron numbers.
  • I can define isotope and explain why isotopes differ in nuclear but not chemical behaviour.
  • I can compare alpha, beta and gamma in nature, range, penetration and ionising power.
  • I can complete alpha and beta decay equations and check both conservation rules.
  • I can define half-life and calculate it from count-rate data, subtracting background.
  • I can describe fission, a chain reaction and the roles of control rods and moderator.
  • I can describe fusion, the conditions it needs and why it is hard to sustain.
  • I can explain that both fission and fusion release energy from a change in mass.

title: IGCSE Physics: Waves and Sound
content:
IGCSE Physics: Waves and Sound

Cambridge IGCSE Physics 0625 (2026–2028), Topic 3 Waves: statements 3.1 General properties of waves, 3.2 Light, 3.3 Electromagnetic spectrum and 3.4 Sound. Waves are how energy travels from place to place without moving matter along with it, and everything from a ripple on a pond to a gamma ray obeys the same few rules. This note builds the general wave behaviour first, then light (reflection, refraction, lenses, colour), then the electromagnetic spectrum and finally sound, with the calculations and the ray constructions that Paper 4 and Paper 6 reward.

General properties of waves

A wave transfers energy without transferring matter. Drop a cork into a ripple tank and the ripples pass under it while the cork only bobs: the water moves up and down, not outward. Every wave is described by the same vocabulary:

TermMeaningUnit
AmplitudeMaximum displacement from the rest position; relates to energy (loudness for sound, brightness for light)metre (m)
Wavelength (lambda)Distance between two equivalent points on neighbouring waves, e.g. crest to crestmetre (m)
FrequencyNumber of complete waves passing a point per second; equals the source's number of oscillations per secondhertz (Hz)
PeriodTime for one complete wave to pass a pointsecond (s)
Wave speedDistance a wave crest travels per secondmetre per second (m s⁻¹)
wave speed = frequency x wavelength        v = f lambda
period = 1 / frequency        T = 1 / f
  • v: wave speed in metres per second (m s⁻¹); f: frequency in hertz (Hz, = s⁻¹); lambda: wavelength in metres (m). All scalars, so there are no signs to worry about — but all three quantities must be in SI units before multiplying.

Transverse waves have the vibration perpendicular to the direction of travel: water waves, light and all electromagnetic waves, waves on a shaken rope. Longitudinal waves have the vibration parallel to the direction of travel: sound in air, the push-pull of a slinky. Longitudinal waves show compressions (where particles are pushed together) and rarefactions (where they are spread apart).

Three behaviours describe what happens when waves meet things. Reflection is bouncing off a surface; the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, measured from the normal. Refraction is the change of direction when a wave passes into a different medium at an angle, because its speed changes; moving into a slower medium bends the ray towards the normal and the wavelength shortens while the frequency stays constant. Diffraction is the spreading of waves through a gap or around an obstacle, and it is most pronounced when the gap width is comparable to the wavelength. Ripple tanks demonstrate all three: straight barriers give reflection, shallow regions give refraction, and narrow gaps give circular wavefronts after diffraction (Supplement: wider gaps give less spreading, and an edge produces noticeable diffraction only for longer wavelengths).

Reflection of light

Light travels in straight lines and reflects from smooth surfaces with the law of reflection: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, both measured between the ray and the normal (an imaginary line perpendicular to the surface at the point of incidence). A plane-mirror image is upright, the same size as the object, laterally inverted (left and right swapped), and as far behind the mirror as the object is in front.

Supplement: the ray construction. To locate the image, draw a ray from the object to the mirror, continue it behind the mirror at the same angle, and drop a perpendicular from the image position to the mirror; repeat with a second ray. Where the reflected rays appear to come from behind the mirror is where the image sits. Drawing the construction to scale with a protractor gives the image position exactly.

Refraction of light

When light passes from air into glass at an angle it slows and bends towards the normal; passing back out it speeds up and bends away from the normal. The amount of bending is fixed by the material's refractive index:

refractive index = sin(angle of incidence in vacuum or air) / sin(angle of refraction)        n = sin i / sin r
critical angle:        sin c = 1 / n
  • n: refractive index, a scalar with no unit, always greater than 1 for a material like glass or water.
  • i and r: angles in degrees measured from the normal, not from the surface.
  • c: critical angle in degrees, defined for a ray passing from the material into air.

Total internal reflection happens when a ray inside a material hits the boundary at an angle greater than the critical angle: none of it escapes and all reflects. Two applications are examinable: optical fibres, where light bounces along the core with total internal reflection and carries data over long distances with little loss, and prisms in periscopes and binoculars, where a 45° prism turns light through 90° or 180° by total internal reflection with almost no energy loss compared with a mirror.

Thin lenses and vision

A converging lens brings parallel rays to a focus at its principal focus; a diverging lens spreads them out as if they came from a focus on the near side. Three standard rays build any image on a converging lens:

  • A ray parallel to the axis refracts through the principal focus on the far side.
  • A ray through the centre of the lens passes straight through undeviated.
  • A ray through the near-side principal focus emerges parallel to the axis.

Where two refracted rays cross, a real image forms — it can be shown on a screen. Where they only appear to diverge from a point behind the lens, a virtual image forms — it cannot be caught on a screen and is seen only by looking through the lens. An object beyond twice the focal length gives a smaller inverted real image (a camera); an object between the focus and the lens gives a larger upright virtual image (a magnifying glass, Supplement). Short sight (myopia) is corrected with a diverging lens, long sight (hyperopia) with a converging lens (Supplement).

Dispersion and the electromagnetic spectrum

White light passing through a prism disperses into a spectrum from red to violet because different colours refract by different amounts: red light is refracted least (it travels fastest in glass) and violet most. Light of a single colour is monochromatic (Supplement). The visible spectrum sits inside a much larger family — the electromagnetic spectrum, all waves travelling at 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ in a vacuum, all transverse, arranged by increasing frequency (and decreasing wavelength) as: radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays.

RegionWavelength scaleUsesHazards
Radio wavesmetres to hundreds of metresRadio and TV broadcasting, communicationsLittle evidence of harm at normal levels
Microwavesmillimetres to centimetresMobile phones, satellite communications, microwave ovens, radarHeating of body tissue; dangerous at high intensity
InfraredmicrometresHeating, night-vision cameras, remote controls, optical fibresBurns and skin heating at high intensity
Visible light400–700 nmVision, photography, fibre-optic dataDazzle; eye damage from lasers and the Sun
Ultraviolet10–400 nmFluorescent lamps, sterilisation, security markingSunburn, skin ageing and skin cancer, eye damage
X-rays0.01–10 nmMedical imaging, airport security, detecting cracks in metalIonising: cell damage and cancer risk; dose kept low
Gamma raysbelow 0.01 nmSterilising equipment, cancer radiotherapy, food irradiationIonising: severe cell damage; shielded with lead and concrete

Supplement: signals and communication. An analogue signal varies continuously with the quantity it carries; a digital signal is a stream of on/off pulses. Digital signals are preferred because they can be regenerated without amplifying noise, can be compressed to carry more information, can be encrypted, and can carry text, sound and images in the same stream. Satellite links work by beaming a microwave signal to an orbiting satellite, which amplifies and retransmits it back to a distant ground station.

Sound

Sound is a longitudinal wave produced by vibrating objects and travelling through a medium — air at about 340 m s⁻¹ at room temperature, faster in liquids and fastest in solids, because the particles are closer together and pass the vibration on more quickly. Sound cannot travel through a vacuum. The frequency of a sound sets its pitch (high frequency, high pitch), and the amplitude sets its loudness. The human range of hearing is roughly 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz.

Echoes and distance measurement. Sound reflects from hard surfaces, giving echoes. The depth of the sea under a ship is found by sending a pulse and timing its return:

distance to the surface = (speed of sound x total time) / 2        s = v t / 2

The halving is essential — the pulse travels down and back — and forgetting it is the classic error in this topic. Measuring the time between two microphones a known distance apart gives the speed of sound directly: v = distance/time.

Ultrasound is sound above the human hearing range (above 20 kHz). Its short wavelength means it reflects well from small internal boundaries, which makes it useful for prenatal scanning (reflection at tissue boundaries builds an image), cleaning delicate items (high-energy vibrations dislodge dirt), flaw detection in metal castings (an internal crack reflects the pulse), and sonar depth sounding. All uses share the same principle: send a pulse, time the echo, calculate the distance with s = vt/2.

Worked example: wave calculation and echo depth

A ship's sonar sends ultrasound of frequency 50 kHz. The echo returns from the seabed after 0.12 s. The speed of sound in seawater is 1500 m s⁻¹.

total distance travelled = v t = 1500 x 0.12 = 180 m
depth of the sea = 180 / 2 = 90 m

Second calculation: a ripple tank wave has a wavelength of 0.040 m and the dippers oscillate 25 times per second. The wave speed is v = f λ = 25 × 0.040 = 1.0 m s⁻¹. The frequency of the wave equals the frequency of the source, and it stays unchanged when the wave passes into deeper water — only the speed and the wavelength change there.

Common mistakes

  • Measuring a wavelength from crest to trough; that is half a wavelength. Measure between two equivalent points on neighbouring waves.
  • Forgetting that frequency never changes on refraction. The speed and wavelength change; the frequency is set by the source and stays constant.
  • Mixing up the angle of incidence with its complement: all angles in reflection and refraction are measured from the normal.
  • Using v = fλ with mismatched units: hertz times centimetres gives cm s⁻¹, not m s⁻¹. Convert the wavelength to metres first.
  • Forgetting to halve the total distance in an echo calculation.
  • Drawing a converging lens ray diagram without the two special rays, or putting the image on the wrong side: real images form on the far side where rays actually cross, virtual images on the same side as the object.
  • Claiming light travels slower in a vacuum than in glass; it is fastest in a vacuum and slower in denser media, which is what causes refraction.
  • Describing a digital signal as continuously varying; it is discrete pulses, which is precisely why it resists noise.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 4, 3 marks). A water wave has a frequency of 4.0 Hz and a wavelength of 0.25 m. Calculate its speed and its period.

Answer: v = fλ = 4.0 × 0.25 = 1.0 m s⁻¹. Period T = 1/f = 1/4.0 = 0.25 s.

Question 2 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Explain why sound cannot be heard on the Moon but sunlight still reaches it.

Answer: Sound is a longitudinal wave that needs a medium, because it travels by particles passing vibrations to their neighbours. The Moon is surrounded by a vacuum, with no particles to carry the vibration, so sound cannot travel there. Light is an electromagnetic transverse wave that carries energy without needing a medium, so it crosses the vacuum of space easily.

Question 3 (Paper 2 style). Light passes from air into glass at an angle. Which quantity does not change? A speed; B wavelength; C frequency; D direction. Answer: C. The frequency is set by the source and is unchanged; speed and wavelength both fall in glass and the ray bends.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Ultrasound of speed 1500 m s⁻¹ is used to find the depth of the sea. The echo returns in 0.40 s. Calculate the depth and explain why ultrasound is used rather than audible sound.

Answer: Depth = v t / 2 = 1500 × 0.40 / 2 = 300 m. Ultrasound has a very short wavelength, so it reflects well from small boundaries and gives a clear echo pattern without diffracting uselessly around small features; it also does not interfere with ordinary sound and is harmless at the intensities used.

Question 5 (Paper 6 style). Describe how to measure the speed of sound in air using two microphones and a data logger.

Answer: Place two microphones a measured distance apart in a straight line from a sound source (a clapping board or signal generator and loudspeaker). Trigger the data logger with the sound at each microphone and record the time interval between the arrivals, or display both pulses on an oscilloscope and measure the time from the trace. Speed is the distance between the microphones divided by the time interval. Repeat at several separations and find the speed from the gradient of a distance–time graph, which averages out the reaction error.

Question 6 (Paper 4, 3 marks). State two differences between a transverse and a longitudinal wave, and give one example of each.

Answer: In a transverse wave the vibrations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer; in a longitudinal wave they are parallel to it. Transverse waves have crests and troughs; longitudinal waves have compressions and rarefactions. Examples: light (transverse) and sound in air (longitudinal).
