Waves carry energy without matter; the next topic is the energy that drives circuits: Electricity and Circuits.

Equations and symbols

One equation, v = fλ, carries the whole of wave physics; the rest of this topic is refraction, the lens and the echo. Frequency and period are reciprocals, so a question that gives one and asks for the other is testing whether you inverted it correctly.

The wave equation

v = fλ
Key: v = wave speed (m/s); f = frequency (Hz, waves per second); λ (lambda) = wavelength (m). The speed is set by the medium, so when a wave crosses into a new medium f stays the same and λ changes.

f = 1 / T
Key: f = frequency (Hz); T = period, the time for one complete oscillation (s). A 0.004 s period is 250 Hz.

T = 1 / f
Key: the same relation rearranged; T in seconds, f in hertz.

d = vt
Key: d = distance travelled by the wave (m); v = wave speed (m/s); t = time (s). For an echo the sound travels to the surface and back, so the distance to the surface is half of vt.

s = vt / 2
Key: s = distance to the reflecting surface (m); v = speed of sound in the medium (m/s); t = total time between the pulse and its echo (s). The factor of 2 is the most frequently dropped mark in echo questions.

v(sound in air) ≈ 340 m/s and v(light in vacuum) = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s
Key: the two speeds that explain thunder arriving after lightning; light is nearly a million times faster, so the flash is seen almost instantly.

audible range for a human = 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz
Key: f below 20 Hz is infrasound and above 20 kHz is ultrasound; both are outside human hearing but ultrasound is used in medical scanning and sonar.

Refraction

n = sin i / sin r
Key: n = refractive index of the material (no unit); i = angle of incidence in the less dense medium, measured from the normal (°); r = angle of refraction in the material (°). Both angles are always measured from the normal, never from the surface.

n = 1 / sin c
Key: c = critical angle (°), the angle of incidence in the denser medium for which the refracted ray runs along the surface. A larger n means a smaller critical angle.

n = c / v
Key: c = speed of light in a vacuum (3.0 × 10⁸ m/s); v = speed of light in the material (m/s). Light slows on entering a denser medium, which is what bends it towards the normal.

total internal reflection when i (greater than) c
Key: i = angle of incidence inside the denser medium (°); c = critical angle (°). Beyond c no light escapes, which is the rule behind optical fibres and reflecting prisms.

Lenses and images

m = h(image) / h(object)
Key: m = magnification (no unit); h(image) = image height (m or cm); h(object) = object height in the same unit. m greater than 1 means enlarged, less than 1 means diminished.

real image: formed where rays actually meet, and can be projected on a screen
Key: a converging lens gives a real image when the object is beyond the focal length; the image is inverted. A virtual image is where rays only appear to come from, and cannot be projected.

title: IGCSE Physics: Pressure and Density
content:
IGCSE Physics: Pressure and Density

Cambridge IGCSE Physics 0625 (2026–2028), Topic 1 Motion, forces and energy: statements 1.4 Density and 1.8 Pressure. Density tells you what is inside a given volume; pressure tells you what a force does when it is spread over an area. Both ideas start from everyday experience — why ships float, why snowshoes work, why your ears pop underwater — and both carry straightforward but unit-sensitive calculations that Paper 4 marks reliably. Paper 6 also examines the practical methods used to measure density, so the experimental detail matters as much as the equations.

Density: what it is

Imagine two identical buckets, one filled with feathers and one with sand. They hold the same volume, but the sand packs far more mass into that volume. Density measures exactly that: how much mass is squeezed into each cubic metre of a substance. It is a property of the material, not of the particular sample, which is why a small gold bead and a large gold bar have the same density.

density = mass / volume        ρ = m / V
  • ρ: density in kilograms per cubic metre (kg m⁻³). Density is a scalar, so it has no direction and no sign.
  • m: mass in kilograms (kg); V: volume in cubic metres (m³).

The SI units are easy to get wrong because laboratory data arrives in grams and cubic centimetres. Water has a density of 1.00 g cm⁻³, which is 1000 kg m⁻³: to convert g cm⁻³ to kg m⁻³, multiply by 1000. Typical exam densities run from about 0.5 g cm⁻³ for wood to 19.3 g cm⁻³ for gold, and the density of water is the reference point that decides whether things float.

Measuring density experimentally

The method depends on the shape and state of the sample, and Paper 6 expects you to choose and describe the right one.

SampleMethodKey apparatus and care
Regular solid (cube or cylinder)Measure the mass on a balance; measure the dimensions with a ruler and calculate the volumeMeasure each dimension several times and average; a vernier caliper gives a better length than a ruler
Irregular solidMeasure the mass; find the volume by water displacement in a measuring cylinderRead the bottom of the meniscus at eye level; the volume difference is the sample's volume
LiquidMeasure the mass of a measuring cylinder, add the liquid, read the volume, and find the mass of the liquid by subtractionPouring losses are the main error; use a balance that reads to 0.01 g for small volumes
Object that floats in waterSink it with a thin pin or a heavy sinker and subtract the sinker's own displaced volumeA wax or wood sample cannot be measured by displacement alone because it refuses to submerge

The percentage uncertainty of the result combines the volume and mass measurements, and since volume enters as a product of lengths, a 2 per cent error in a length gives about a 6 per cent error in the volume of a cube. Repeating readings and averaging is the standard control of random error. If the object is soluble in water, use an unsuitable-displacement liquid such as sand or oil instead.

Floating and sinking

An object placed in a liquid sinks if its average density is greater than the liquid's density, and floats if it is less. A floating object displaces its own weight of liquid, so a 1000 kg steel hull floats only because the hull shape encloses a large volume of air and the average density of ship plus air is below that of water. Ice floats on water because ice is less dense (about 0.92 g cm⁻³), which is why lakes freeze from the top.

Supplement: one liquid on another. When two liquids that do not mix are poured together, the denser one sinks below the less dense one, and the boundary stays sharp. Oil (about 0.8 g cm⁻³) floats on water; syrup (about 1.4 g cm⁻³) sinks below it. A carefully poured column of syrup, water and oil layers in the order syrup, water, oil, and a grape that is denser than water but less dense than syrup will float at the syrup–water boundary. The rule is the same in every case: each substance finds the level where the density below it is greater and the density above it is smaller.

Pressure: force spread over area

Pressure is what a force does when it is spread over a surface. The same force over a smaller area produces a greater pressure, which is why a drawing pin drives into a board point-first and why snowshoes stop you sinking into snow. A sharp knife cuts because the small edge area turns a modest force into enormous pressure.

pressure = force / area        p = F / A
  • p: pressure in pascals (Pa). One pascal is one newton per square metre (1 Pa = 1 N m⁻²). Pressure is a scalar.
  • F: force in newtons (N), acting perpendicular to the surface.
  • A: area in square metres (m²) over which the force acts.

Area must be in square metres: 1 cm² = 0.0001 m², so 25 cm² = 0.0025 m². Atmospheric pressure at sea level is about 100 000 Pa (100 kPa), which presses on every square metre with a force of 100 000 N — the reason a vacuum flask is crushed if the air is pumped out, and the reason the body needs equal pressure inside as well.

Pressure is transmitted through liquids: a force applied at one point in a confined liquid is passed on undiminished in every direction, which is the principle of hydraulic brakes and car jacks, where a small force on a small piston gives a large force on a large piston because the pressure is the same on both.

Pressure in a liquid

Supplement. The pressure in a liquid rises with depth because the liquid above presses down. For a liquid of uniform density the increase is:

pressure due to a liquid column = density x gravitational field strength x depth        p = ρ g h
  • p: pressure in pascals (Pa); ρ: density of the liquid in kilograms per cubic metre (kg m⁻³).
  • g: gravitational field strength in newtons per kilogram (N kg⁻¹, use the value given in the question).
  • h: vertical depth below the surface in metres (m). Depth is measured vertically, not along a slope or the container wall.

Only the vertical height of the column counts, which is why the pressure at the bottom of a swimming pool depends only on the water's depth, not on the shape or the width of the pool. The total pressure at depth includes the atmosphere pressing on the surface: total pressure = atmospheric pressure + ρgh. A diver at 20 m in fresh water experiences ρgh = 1000 × 9.81 × 20 = 196 200 Pa from the water alone, about three times atmospheric pressure in total, which is why the ears must be equalised during descent. A manometer measures a pressure difference by the height difference of a liquid column; a barometer measures atmospheric pressure by the height of a mercury column (about 760 mm at sea level).

Worked example: density and pressure together

A rectangular brass block measures 4.0 cm × 5.0 cm × 10.0 cm and has a mass of 1.20 kg.

volume = 0.040 x 0.050 x 0.100 = 0.00020 m3
density = mass / volume = 1.20 / 0.00020 = 6000 kg m-3  (6.0 g cm-3)

Notice the unit conversion before the division: centimetres were converted to metres first, so the density comes out in kg m⁻³ directly. The same calculation in laboratory units gives the same answer: the volume is 4.0 × 5.0 × 10.0 = 200 cm³ and the mass is 1200 g, so the density is 1200 / 200 = 6.0 g cm⁻³, which converts to 6000 kg m⁻³. Keep the arithmetic in one unit system end to end and the conversion error cannot appear.

Now the block rests on a table on its largest face. The force is its weight, 1.20 × 9.81 = 11.8 N, spread over 5.0 cm × 10.0 cm = 0.0050 m²:

pressure = F / A = 11.8 / 0.0050 = 2350 Pa

Turned onto its smallest face, the area is 4.0 × 5.0 = 0.0020 m² and the pressure rises to 5875 Pa — the same weight, a smaller area, a larger pressure. Finally, the pressure 2.0 m below the surface of a fresh-water lake is ρgh = 1000 × 9.81 × 2.0 = 19 620 Pa, about 20 kPa above atmospheric pressure.

Common mistakes

  • Dividing by mass instead of volume, or reversing the density equation. Density is mass over volume; the heavy object with the same volume has the higher density.
  • Forgetting to convert g cm⁻³ to kg m⁻³ (multiply by 1000) or centimetres to metres before using SI equations. A volume in cm³ must become m³ by dividing by 10⁶.
  • Using area in cm² in p = F/A. The pascal is a newton per square metre, so the area must be in m².
  • Measuring h along the slope of a container or along the wall; depth is the vertical distance below the free surface.
  • Ignoring the atmosphere when asked for the total pressure at a depth: total pressure is atmospheric plus the liquid contribution.
  • Assuming heavy objects sink and light ones float; it is density, not mass, that decides. A huge ship floats on air-filled hull volume.
  • Treating density as a vector or attaching a direction to pressure; both are scalars.
  • Quoting more than two significant figures from readings taken with a ruler or a measuring cylinder, ignoring the precision of the apparatus.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 4, 3 marks). A glass block of mass 150 g has dimensions 5.0 cm × 4.0 cm × 2.0 cm. Calculate its density in g cm⁻³ and in kg m⁻³.

Answer: Volume = 5.0 × 4.0 × 2.0 = 40 cm³. Density = 150 / 40 = 3.75 g cm⁻³ ≈ 3.8 g cm⁻³. In SI units: 3.75 × 1000 = 3750 kg m⁻³.

Question 2 (Paper 4, 3 marks). A student stands on one foot; her weight of 500 N acts on an area of 0.015 m². Calculate the pressure, and state what happens when she stands on both feet with a total area of 0.030 m².

Answer: p = F/A = 500 / 0.015 = 33 000 Pa (33 kPa). On both feet the area doubles, so the pressure halves to about 17 000 Pa. The force is unchanged; only the area changes.

Question 3 (Paper 2 style). An object floats with half its volume submerged in water of density 1000 kg m⁻³. Its density is: A 2000 kg m⁻³; B 1000 kg m⁻³; C 500 kg m⁻³; D zero. Answer: C. Floating means the average density is less than the liquid's; an object that floats with half its volume submerged has an average density of 500 kg m⁻³.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Calculate the pressure due to the water at a depth of 3.0 m in a lake, and the total pressure at that depth. Take g = 10 N kg⁻¹ and atmospheric pressure as 100 kPa.

Answer: p = ρgh = 1000 × 10 × 3.0 = 30 000 Pa = 30 kPa. Total pressure = 100 kPa + 30 kPa = 130 kPa.

Question 5 (Paper 6 style). Describe how you would determine the density of an irregular stone that is denser than water.

Answer: Measure the mass of the dry stone on a balance. Partly fill a measuring cylinder with water and record the volume at eye level with the meniscus bottom. Lower the stone in gently (tied with thread if needed) and record the new volume. The stone's volume is the difference. Density is mass divided by the volume change. Repeat the volume readings and average to reduce random error, and check that no water is splashed out or carried away on the stone.

Question 6 (Paper 4, 3 marks). Explain why a steel needle sinks in water while a steel ship of 10 000 tonnes floats.

Answer: Steel has a density of about 7800 kg m⁻³, far greater than water, so a solid needle sinks. The ship's hull encloses a large volume of air, so the average density of the ship and the air inside it is much less than 1000 kg m⁻³. The ship therefore floats and displaces a weight of water equal to its own weight.

Density decides what floats and pressure decides what pushes; the next stop is the particle model that explains both when matter is heated.

Equations and symbols

Density and pressure share one theme: a quantity spread over a volume or an area. Every equation below is a ratio, so the units of the two quantities must match before dividing.

Density

ρ = m / V
Key: ρ (rho) = density (kg/m³ or g/cm³); m = mass (kg or g); V = volume (m³ or cm³). 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³.

ρ(water) = 1.0 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³
Key: the reference value that decides floating and sinking for most questions; a body denser than this sinks in water.

V = m / ρ
Key: the same relation rearranged to find a volume (m³ or cm³) from a mass (kg or g) and a density. Useful when a question gives the mass of displaced water.

Pressure on a surface

p = F / A
Key: p = pressure (Pa, where 1 Pa = 1 N/m²); F = force acting perpendicular to the surface (N); A = area of contact (m²). Halving the area doubles the pressure for the same force, which is the whole physics of a sharp blade.

F = pA
Key: F = force on a surface (N); p = pressure (Pa); A = area (m²).

1 kPa = 1000 Pa and 1 MPa = 1 × 10⁶ Pa
Key: prefixes applied to the pascal; atmospheric pressure is about 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa, which is 100 kPa.

Pressure in a liquid

p = ρgh
Key: p = pressure due to the liquid (Pa); ρ (rho) = density of the liquid (kg/m³); g = 9.8 N/kg; h = depth below the surface (m). The pressure depends on depth and density only — not on the shape or width of the container.

Δp = ρgΔh
Key: Δp = pressure difference between two depths (Pa); Δh = vertical separation of the two points (m). This is the equation behind a manometer reading and behind the pressure on a diver's eardrum.

F₁ / A₁ = F₂ / A₂
Key: F₁, F₂ = forces on the input and output pistons (N); A₁, A₂ = their areas (m² or cm²). The pressure is transmitted unchanged, so a larger area gives a larger force — the hydraulic press.

Upthrust and floating

U = ρ(fluid) × V(displaced) × g
Key: U = upthrust (N); ρ(fluid) = density of the fluid (kg/m³); V(displaced) = volume of fluid pushed aside (m³); g = 9.8 N/kg. This is Archimedes' principle written as an equation.

floating: ρ(object) < ρ(fluid)
Key: ρ(object) = the object's average density, including any trapped air (kg/m³). A steel ship floats because its average density is below water's, not because steel is light.

V(submerged) / V(total) = ρ(object) / ρ(fluid)
Key: V(submerged) = volume below the surface (m³); V(total) = whole volume (m³). A body floating half-submerged in water has half water's density, about 500 kg/m³.

sinking: weight > maximum upthrust
Key: weight = mg (N); maximum upthrust = the upthrust when the body is fully submerged. A body sinks when its density exceeds the fluid's, because even fully submerged the upthrust cannot reach its weight.

title: IGCSE Mathematics: Graphs and Coordinate Geometry
content:
IGCSE Mathematics: Graphs and Coordinate Geometry

Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580 (2025–2027), section 2 statements 2.9 Graphs in practical situations, 2.10 Graphs of functions, 2.11 Sketching curves, 2.12 Differentiation (Extended), and section 3 statements 3.1 to 3.7 Coordinate geometry. Graphs turn algebra into pictures and pictures into algebra, and the coordinate geometry of straight lines is the most examined machinery in both papers. This note builds coordinates, gradient, the equation of a line, length and midpoint from scratch, then practical graphs, curves and the first steps of differentiation — with every formula derived rather than asserted.

Coordinates and the Cartesian plane

A point's position is given by an ordered pair (x, y): the x-coordinate says how far right (positive) or left (negative) of the origin, and the y-coordinate says how far up (positive) or down (negative). Order matters: (3, 5) is a different point from (5, 3). The plane is cut into four quadrants by the x-axis and y-axis, and a point on an axis has one coordinate equal to zero. Plotting accurately means counting in the scale given on the axes, marking with a small cross, and labelling the point.

The gradient of a straight line

Gradient measures steepness: how far the line rises or falls for each unit it runs to the right. The word to remember is vertical over horizontal.

gradient = (change in y) / (change in x) = (y2 - y1) / (x2 - x1)
  • Gradient m is a number with no unit: 2 means the line rises 2 units for every 1 unit right.
  • Uphill lines have positive gradient, downhill lines negative; a horizontal line has gradient 0 and a vertical line has undefined gradient (zero run).
  • The gradient between two points is the same wherever the points are taken on a straight line — that constancy is what makes the line straight.

Why the formula works. Take points (1, 2) and (4, 10). Walking from the first to the second you go up 10 − 2 = 8 units and right 4 − 1 = 3 units, so the steepness is 8/3. The formula just records that walk for any two points.

Find the gradient of the line through (-2, 5) and (3, -7):

m = (-7 - 5) / (3 - (-2)) = -12 / 5 = -2.4        [negative: the line falls to the right]

The equation of a straight line

Every straight-line graph can be written as y = mx + c, where m is the gradient and c is the y-intercept (where the line crosses the y-axis). The formula calculates the y-value for any x, and it is the algebraic twin of the drawing.

Find the equation of the line with gradient 2 passing through (1, 5):

y = mx + c gives 5 = 2(1) + c        [substitute the point and the gradient]
5 = 2 + c
c = 3
y = 2x + 3

Given two points instead, find the gradient first, then use one point to find c. Given the intercept and a point, substitute. The form ax + by + d = 0 is the same line rearranged, and gradient-intercept form can always be recovered by solving for y.

Parallel lines never meet, so they have equal gradients: m₁ = m₂. Perpendicular lines meet at right angles, and their gradients multiply to −1:

m1 x m2 = -1        so the perpendicular gradient is  m2 = -1 / m1

Why −1. Rotating a right-angled triangle through 90° swaps its two legs and reverses one direction, turning a rise/run of m into a run/rise of −1/m. If one line has gradient 2, a line at right angles to it has gradient −1/2; if a line has gradient 0 (horizontal), the perpendicular line is vertical with undefined gradient.

Find the equation of the line perpendicular to y = 3x - 4 passing through (3, 0):

perpendicular gradient = -1/3
y = (-1/3)x + c
0 = (-1/3)(3) + c = -1 + c,  so c = 1
y = -x/3 + 1

Length and midpoint of a line segment (Extended)

The distance between two points is Pythagoras applied to the horizontal and vertical gaps; the midpoint is the average of the coordinates.

length = √[(x2 - x1)^2 + (y2 - y1)^2]
midpoint = ((x1 + x2)/2, (y1 + y2)/2)

Why. The horizontal gap is (x₂ − x₁) and the vertical gap is (y₂ − y₁); these are the two shorter sides of a right-angled triangle whose hypotenuse is the distance, so Pythagoras gives the length at once. The midpoint formula is just the average of the two x-values and of the two y-values.

Find the length and midpoint of the segment joining A(-1, 2) and B(5, 8):

horizontal gap = 5 - (-1) = 6;  vertical gap = 8 - 2 = 6
length = √(6^2 + 6^2) = √72 = 6√2 ≈ 8.49
midpoint = ((-1 + 5)/2, (2 + 8)/2) = (2, 5)

Graphs in practical situations

Real data is plotted on axes carrying units, and the shape of the graph tells the story. The skills are reading values, finding gradients and interpreting what sections mean.

GraphVertical axisGradient meansArea means
Distance–timeDistance (m or km)SpeedNot used
Speed–timeSpeed (m s⁻¹)AccelerationDistance travelled
Temperature–timeTemperature (°C)Rate of heating or coolingNot used
Conversion graphsOne unit (e.g. °F)The conversion rateNot used

A horizontal section means the quantity is constant; a steep section means fast change; a curved section means the rate itself is changing. Interpolation reads values inside the plotted range; extrapolation reads beyond it and is unreliable — a distinction the questions like to test. On a distance–time graph for a journey, a stop is flat, a return journey heads down, and the steepest section is the fastest.

Graphs of functions and sketching curves

A function is a machine turning x into y; its graph is all the (x, y) pairs it produces. To sketch, plot a short table of values and recognise the shape:

FunctionShapeKey features
y = mx + cStraight lineGradient m, crossing the y-axis at c
y = ax² + bx + cParabola (U-shape, or ∩ if a is negative)Crosses the x-axis at the roots; turning point on the axis of symmetry midway between the roots
y = x³S-shaped cubicFlattening at the origin; grows steeply both ways
y = k/xHyperbolaTwo branches; the axes are asymptotes the curve approaches but never touches
y = aˣExponential growthPasses through (0, 1); rises ever faster; never touches the x-axis

Quadratics deserve particular care. The graph of y = ax² + bx + c has its turning point where x = −b/(2a), and the y-coordinate follows by substitution. Factorising y = (x − p)(x − q) shows the roots p and q at once, and the axis of symmetry is exactly halfway: x = (p + q)/2.

Solving equations graphically. The roots of f(x) = 0 are where the curve crosses the x-axis. To solve f(x) = g(x), draw both graphs and read the x-coordinates of the intersection points. A rearrangement like x³ − 2x − 5 = 0 becomes y = x³ − 2x and y = 5: where they meet, the equation holds. Answers read from a graph are approximate, so always state them to the accuracy the graph supports.

Gradients of curves and differentiation (Extended)

A curve's gradient changes from point to point, so the straight-line formula does not apply directly. The fix is a limit: take two points on the curve closer and closer together, and the chord between them settles towards the tangent — the line that just touches the curve at that point. Its gradient is the instantaneous rate of change of y with respect to x: how fast y is changing at that exact moment, like a speedometer reading rather than an average speed.

For y = x^n, the gradient function is:  dy/dx = n x^(n-1)
  • dy/dx: the gradient function, meaning the gradient at any value of x; it is read dy by dx.
  • n: the power of x in the term. Multiply by the power, then reduce the power by one: y = x³ gives dy/dx = 3x².
  • A constant term differentiates to zero (its graph is flat), and a constant multiple survives: y = 5x² gives dy/dx = 10x.

Why the rule works. Expand (x + h)ⁿ for a tiny step h, subtract y = xⁿ, and divide by h. For y = x²: [(x + h)² − x²]/h = [x² + 2xh + h² − x²]/h = (2xh + h²)/h = 2x + h. As h shrinks to nothing, this approaches 2x — exactly the rule. The same argument gives nxⁿ⁻¹ for every whole power.

Stationary points are where the gradient is zero — the tops of hills and bottoms of valleys. Solve dy/dx = 0 for x, substitute back for y, then decide which by looking at the curve or the gradient either side: a maximum has positive gradient before and negative after; a minimum the reverse. Maximum and minimum questions are the standard Paper 4 use of differentiation.

Worked example: tangent, stationary point and a practical graph

For the curve y = x² − 4x + 3:

dy/dx = 2x - 4
Stationary point: 2x - 4 = 0, so x = 2;  y = 4 - 8 + 3 = -1. The turning point is (2, -1).
Since the x^2 term is positive the parabola opens upwards, so (2, -1) is a minimum.
Roots: x^2 - 4x + 3 = (x - 1)(x - 3) = 0, so the curve crosses the x-axis at 1 and 3.
Gradient at x = 4: dy/dx = 2(4) - 4 = 4.
Tangent at x = 4: the point is (4, 3), and the tangent has gradient 4:
y - 3 = 4(x - 4), so y = 4x - 13.

The axis of symmetry, x = 2, sits midway between the roots 1 and 3 — everything is consistent, and cross-checking like this catches slips before they cost marks.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Dividing the gradient the wrong way round: it is always (change in y) over (change in x), with the coordinates subtracted in the same order in both.
  • Reading c from where the line crosses the x-axis; the y-intercept is on the y-axis.
  • Assuming parallel and perpendicular lines share a rule: parallel gradients are equal, perpendicular gradients multiply to −1.
  • Forgetting to halve the step in a midpoint, or using the Pythagoras formula without squaring both gaps.
  • Confusing the x-intercepts with the turning point on a quadratic sketch, or sketching y = (x − 2)² as crossing the x-axis at −2 (the root is +2).
  • Treating the asymptote of y = k/x as part of the curve; the curve approaches the axes and never crosses them.
  • Quoting an average speed from a speed–time graph's gradient at one point; the gradient there is acceleration.
  • Differentiating x³ as 3x² and then claiming the gradient of y = x³ is 3 at x = 1 — correct value, but the method mark is for writing dy/dx = 3x² and substituting x = 1.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 2, 3 marks). Find the gradient of the line through (2, 3) and (6, 11).

Answer: m = (11 − 3)/(6 − 2) = 8/4 = 2.

Question 2 (Paper 2, 4 marks). Find the equation of the line with gradient −3 passing through (4, −2).

Answer: y = mx + c gives −2 = −3(4) + c, so c = 10 and the equation is y = −3x + 10.

Question 3 (Paper 4, 4 marks). A line L passes through (1, 2) and (5, 10). Find the equation of the line perpendicular to L through the origin.

Answer: Gradient of L is (10 − 2)/(5 − 1) = 2, so the perpendicular gradient is −1/2. Through the origin c = 0, so y = −x/2.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 5 marks). A car travels at 20 m s⁻¹ for 30 s, then decelerates uniformly to rest in 10 s. Sketch the speed–time graph and find the total distance.

Answer: The graph is a horizontal line at 20 from t = 0 to t = 30, then a straight fall from (30, 20) to (40, 0). Distance = area = rectangle 30 × 20 = 600 m plus triangle ½ × 10 × 20 = 100 m, total 700 m.

Question 5 (Paper 4, 5 marks). For y = x² − 6x + 5, find the coordinates of the turning point and the roots, and sketch the curve.

Answer: dy/dx = 2x − 6 = 0 gives x = 3, y = 9 − 18 + 5 = −4, so the minimum is (3, −4). Roots: (x − 1)(x − 5) = 0 gives x = 1 and x = 5. The parabola opens upward through (1, 0) and (5, 0) with its minimum at (3, −4), crossing the y-axis at (0, 5).

Question 6 (Paper 4, 4 marks). The points A(−2, 1), B(4, 7) and C(10, 1) form a triangle. Show that AB = BC and find the midpoint of AC.

Answer: AB = √[(4 − (−2))² + (7 − 1)²] = √(36 + 36) = √72 = 6√2. BC = √[(10 − 4)² + (1 − 7)²] = √(36 + 36) = √72 = 6√2. The two sides are equal, so the triangle is isosceles. Midpoint of AC = ((−2 + 10)/2, (1 + 1)/2) = (4, 1).

Graphs describe change; sequences describe discrete patterns, and functions describe the machines behind both.

title: Hypothesis Testing — Study Notes
content:
Hypothesis Testing

The Framework

The null hypothesis H₀ is the default claim (no change, p = p₀). The alternative H₁ is what a suspicious observation suggests (p > p₀, p < p₀, or p ≠ p₀). The significance level α is the probability of rejecting a true H₀ — the false-alarm rate, usually 5% or 1%.

Test for a Binomial Proportion

With X ~ B(n, p₀) under H₀, compute the probability of results at least as extreme as the observed count in the direction of H₁.

Example: H₀: p = 0.3 against H₁: p > 0.3, observed 10 successes in n = 20. Compute P(X ≥ 10) under B(20, 0.3). If that tail probability is below α, reject H₀.

One-Tailed vs Two-Tailed

One-tailed tests take the whole α in one direction. Two-tailed tests split α across both tails: compare against α/2 on each side, or equivalently check whether the observation falls in the extreme 2.5% (for α = 5%). Choose the tails from the wording of H₁, not from the data.

Critical Regions

The critical region is the set of values of the test statistic that would lead to rejection. Its boundary is the critical value. For B(20, 0.3) at the 5% level with H₁: p > 0.3, find the smallest k with P(X ≥ k) < 0.05 — that k opens the critical region.

Conclusions in Context

Never just say "reject H₀". Conclude in the language of the problem: "there is sufficient evidence at the 5% level that the proportion has increased". State the significance level, the direction, and the real-world quantity.

Exam tips: define H₀ and H₁ with symbols AND words. Verify which tail the observation sits in before computing. If the observed value lies in the critical region, evidence supports H₁; otherwise there is insufficient evidence — never "prove H₀ true".

Exam method: hypotheses and critical regions

The null hypothesis H₀ states that there is no change or no difference, and the alternative H₁ states the claim being tested. Choose H₁ with a one-tailed test when the question states a direction (greater than or less than), and with a two-tailed test when it asks whether the value has changed.

At the 5% significance level a one-tailed test uses the critical value z = 1.645 for an upper test, and a two-tailed test splits 5% between two tails, giving z = 1.96. Compare the test statistic with the critical value, and reject H₀ when the statistic lies in the critical region.

For a sample mean, the test statistic is z = (x̄ − μ)/(σ/√n), using the population mean stated in H₀. When the sample is large, the Central Limit Theorem lets you use the normal distribution even if the population is not normal.

State the conclusion in the context of the question, for example: there is sufficient evidence at the 5% level to suggest that the mean has increased.

Exam cue: Always state H₀ and H₁ in terms of the population parameter, not the sample statistic, and give a conclusion in words.

title: IGCSE Physics: Earth and Space
content:
IGCSE Physics: Earth and Space

Cambridge IGCSE Physics 0625 (2026–2028), Topic 6 Space physics: statements 6.1 The Earth and the Solar System and 6.2 Stars and the Universe. This final topic scales the mechanics and nuclear physics of the rest of the course up to the largest objects there are. Gravity holds planets in orbit and holds stars together; fusion powers stars; the light from distant galaxies tells us the Universe is expanding. Paper 4 usually has one structured question here, and the calculations are orbital mechanics and redshift.

The Earth: rotation, orbit and seasons

The Earth spins on its axis once every 24 hours, which gives day and night, and it orbits the Sun once every 365.25 days, which gives the year. The Earth's axis is tilted at about 23.5° to the plane of its orbit, and that tilt — not the changing distance from the Sun — causes the seasons: when a hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun its rays strike more directly and the days are longer, so it is summer.

The Moon orbits the Earth in about 27 days. It shines by reflected sunlight, and because we see different fractions of its lit half as it orbits, it shows phases: new moon, crescent, half, gibbous, full. A lunar eclipse occurs when the Earth's shadow falls on the Moon; a solar eclipse when the Moon's shadow falls on the Earth.

Supplement: orbital speed. For a circular orbit of radius r completed in period T:

orbital speed = 2πr / T        v = 2πr / T
  • v: orbital speed in metres per second (m s⁻¹); r: orbital radius in metres (m); T: orbital period in seconds (s). Convert days and years to seconds first.

The Solar System

The Solar System is the Sun and the bodies bound to it by gravity: eight planets (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune), their moons, dwarf planets, asteroids and comets. The four inner planets are small and rocky with few or no moons; the four outer planets are gas giants — large, low density, with many moons and ring systems. Asteroids orbit mainly between Mars and Jupiter; comets have highly elliptical orbits and grow bright tails of gas and dust when near the Sun.

Gravity provides the centripetal force that keeps every planet, moon and satellite in orbit. A planet's orbital speed falls with distance from the Sun (Kepler's laws), and the planets' orbits are ellipses with the Sun at one focus (Supplement: conservation of energy means a planet speeds up at perihelion and slows at aphelion, trading kinetic for gravitational potential energy).

Supplement: light-travel time. Light from the Sun takes about 8 minutes to reach Earth; from the nearest star, about 4.2 years. The light-year is the distance light travels in one year, about 9.5 × 10¹⁵ m, so looking at distant objects is literally looking into the past.

The Sun as a star

The Sun is an ordinary main-sequence star: a sphere of hot gas, about three-quarters hydrogen and one-quarter helium by mass, with a core at roughly 15 million degrees Celsius. Its energy comes from nuclear fusion in the core, where hydrogen nuclei fuse into helium nuclei, and a small loss of mass becomes the radiated energy. That radiation powers the whole Solar System: it drives the water cycle behind hydroelectric power and biofuels, heats the Earth's surface, and — over geological time — built the fossil fuels (Supplement: solar energy is the principal source behind almost every renewable resource on Earth).

The Sun is a medium-sized star about 4.6 billion years old, with enough hydrogen for roughly another 5 billion years of fusion before it swells into a red giant.

Stars and galaxies

A galaxy is a vast collection of stars, gas and dust held together by gravity. The Sun is one of roughly 200 billion stars in the Milky Way, a spiral galaxy, and galaxies themselves are grouped into clusters. The nearest large galaxy to us is Andromeda, about 2.5 million light-years away.

Stars have life cycles set by their mass:

  • Nebula: a huge cloud of gas and dust, pulled inward by gravity.
  • Protostar: the contracting, heating core of the cloud.
  • Main sequence star: when the core is hot enough for hydrogen fusion to start, the outward radiation pressure balances gravity and the star is stable — the Sun's current stage.
  • Red giant or supergiant: when core hydrogen runs low, fusion moves outwards and the star swells and cools at the surface.
  • End state: a star like the Sun sheds its outer layers as a planetary nebula and leaves a white dwarf. A massive star explodes as a supernova and leaves a neutron star, or, for the most massive, a black hole — an object whose gravity is so strong that not even light escapes.

Supernovae matter beyond astrophysics: they create and scatter the elements heavier than helium, so the carbon, oxygen and iron in your body were forged inside stars.

The Universe: redshift, expansion and the Big Bang

Light from distant galaxies is shifted towards the red end of the spectrum: the spectral lines appear at longer wavelengths than the same lines produced in a laboratory. This redshift is a Doppler effect — the galaxies are moving away from us. Crucially, almost every galaxy shows redshift, and the more distant the galaxy, the greater the redshift and the faster it is receding. The conclusion is that the Universe is expanding.

Running the expansion backwards implies that everything was once at one place — the Big Bang, roughly 13.8 billion years ago. Two further pieces of evidence support it: the cosmic microwave background (CMB), faint microwave radiation coming from every direction, which is the cooled remnant of the hot early Universe, and the abundance of light elements (hydrogen and helium) matching the predictions of Big Bang nucleosynthesis.

Supplement: Hubble's law and the age of the Universe. The recession speed of a galaxy is proportional to its distance:

recession speed = Hubble constant x distance        v = H d
  • v: recession speed in metres per second (m s⁻¹); d: distance in metres (m) (often megaparsecs, but convert); H: the Hubble constant in s⁻¹ (quoted as km s⁻¹ per megaparsec).
  • The age of the Universe follows as roughly 1/H: run the expansion back at the present rate.

Worked example: orbital speed and Hubble's law

The Earth orbits the Sun at a radius of 1.5 × 10¹¹ m with a period of 365 days.

T = 365 × 24 × 3600 = 3.15 × 10⁷ s
v = 2πr / T = 2 × 3.14 × 1.5 × 10¹¹ / 3.15 × 10⁷ = 3.0 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹ (about 30 km s⁻¹)

Second calculation: a galaxy is 200 megaparsecs away and Hubble's constant is 70 km s⁻¹ per megaparsec. Its recession speed is v = Hd = 70 × 200 = 14 000 km s⁻¹. The age estimate is 1/H: one megaparsec is 3.1 × 10¹⁹ km, so 1/H = 3.1 × 10¹⁹/70 = 4.4 × 10¹⁷ s ≈ 14 billion years — consistent with the accepted value.

Common mistakes

  • Blaming the seasons on the Earth–Sun distance; it is the axial tilt. The Earth is actually closest to the Sun in January.
  • Confusing the Moon's phases with eclipses: phases are the normal monthly cycle of the lit fraction; eclipses are shadows, and are rare because the Moon's orbit is tilted.
  • Using kilometres and seconds in v = 2πr/T without one consistent unit system; convert the period to seconds and the radius to metres.
  • Calling a light-year a unit of time; it is a distance — the distance light travels in one year.
  • Saying redshift means the galaxies are moving through space away from us; the accepted interpretation is that space itself is expanding, stretching the light.
  • Mixing up redshift and blueshift: receding sources shift to longer (redder) wavelengths; approaching sources shift shorter (bluer) — nearby Andromeda is blueshifted.
  • Placing the Sun at the centre of the Solar System as an absolute; the Sun is the centre of the Solar System, but the Solar System is an ordinary part of the Milky Way.
  • Forgetting that the fusion in stars is hydrogen to helium, which is not the same as the fission of uranium in power stations.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 4, 3 marks). Calculate the orbital speed of a satellite orbiting 7.0 × 10⁶ m from the Earth's centre every 5900 s.

Answer: v = 2πr/T = 2 × 3.14 × 7.0 × 10⁶ / 5900 = 7.5 × 10³ m s⁻¹ (7.5 km s⁻¹).

Question 2 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Explain the evidence from redshift that the Universe is expanding.

Answer: The spectral lines from distant galaxies are shifted towards longer wavelengths than laboratory lines, which by the Doppler effect means the sources are receding. The more distant the galaxy, the greater the redshift and the faster it recedes, so the whole Universe is expanding with every distance growing over time. Reversing that expansion implies all matter was once concentrated at one point — the Big Bang.

Question 3 (Paper 2 style). The seasons on Earth are caused by: A the changing Earth–Sun distance; B the tilt of the Earth's axis; C the Moon's gravity; D the Sun's rotation. Answer: B. The tilt changes the angle of the sunlight and the length of day through the year.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 6 marks). Describe the life cycle of a star like the Sun.

Answer: It begins as a nebula, a cloud of gas and dust. Gravity contracts the cloud and the core heats into a protostar. When the core temperature reaches about 15 million degrees, hydrogen fusion begins and the star joins the main sequence, where radiation pressure from fusion balances gravity and it is stable for billions of years. As core hydrogen depletes, fusion moves outwards, the outer layers expand and cool and the star becomes a red giant. Finally the outer layers are expelled as a planetary nebula, leaving a white dwarf that slowly cools — no fusion, supported by electron degeneracy pressure.

Question 5 (Paper 4, 3 marks). State two pieces of evidence for the Big Bang theory besides the redshift of galaxies.

Answer: The cosmic microwave background radiation — faint microwave radiation arriving from every direction, the cooled afterglow of the hot early Universe. The observed abundances of the light elements, especially hydrogen and helium, match the amounts predicted to have formed in the first minutes after the Big Bang.

Question 6 (Paper 4, 3 marks). Explain why nuclear fusion in the Sun releases energy.

Answer: In fusion, light hydrogen nuclei combine to form a heavier helium nucleus. The product nucleus has slightly less mass than the four protons that formed it; that lost mass is converted into energy in accordance with mass–energy equivalence, and the energy is radiated from the Sun's core. Fusion releases energy for light elements up to iron, which is why it powers stars.

That completes the Cambridge IGCSE 0625 course: the AS notes begin with Edexcel IAL Unit 1 and Kinematics.

Equations and symbols

Earth and space is mostly descriptive, but three quantitative ideas carry the marks: orbital speed, weight on another world, and the distance units that make astronomy's numbers manageable. The cosmological relations are marked as extensions, because 0625 examines the redshift qualitatively.

Orbits

v = 2πr / T
Key: v = orbital speed (m/s); r = orbital radius, measured from the centre of the body being orbited (m); T = orbital period, the time for one complete orbit (s). The 2πr is the circumference of the orbit, so the equation is just speed = distance ÷ time applied to a circle.

a larger orbital radius gives a smaller orbital speed for the same central body
Key: the rule behind a satellite's period rising steeply with height; a geostationary satellite must sit at about 36 000 km above the equator to take exactly 24 hours.

gravitational force provides the centripetal force
Key: the single force keeping a planet or satellite in orbit points towards the centre of the orbit; without it the body would travel in a straight line.

Weight elsewhere

W = mg
Key: W = weight (N); m = mass (kg), unchanged by location; g = gravitational field strength of that body (N/kg). On the Moon g is about 1.6 N/kg, so a 60 kg astronaut weighs about 96 N there and 588 N on Earth.

g(Earth) = 9.8 N/kg and g(Moon) = 1.6 N/kg
Key: the two values used in 0625 questions; weight changes with g while mass does not, which is the whole point of the distinction.

Astronomical distances

1 light year = 9.46 × 10¹⁵ m
Key: the distance light travels in one year, from d = vt with v = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s and t = 3.15 × 10⁷ s. A light year is a distance, not a time.

1 astronomical unit (AU) = 1.5 × 10¹¹ m
Key: the mean Earth–Sun distance, used for distances inside the Solar System; a light year is about 63 000 AU.

orbital period of the planets: T² ∝ r³ (extension)
Key: T = orbital period (s or years); r = orbital radius (m or AU). Kepler's third law, which is why the outer planets take far longer to complete an orbit.

Redshift and the expanding Universe

z = Δλ / λ
Key: z = redshift (no unit); Δλ (Δλ) = increase in wavelength (m); λ = wavelength emitted in the laboratory (m). A larger z means the galaxy is receding faster.

v = H₀ d (extension)
Key: v = recession speed of a galaxy (km/s); H₀ = the Hubble constant (about 70 km/s per Mpc); d = distance to the galaxy (Mpc). Plotting v against d and taking the gradient gives H₀, and 1/H₀ estimates the age of the Universe.

redshift means the source is receding; blueshift means it is approaching
Key: the observed wavelength is stretched when the source moves away and compressed when it moves towards the observer — the same Doppler effect as a passing siren.

title: Continuous Random Variables — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Continuous Random Variables

Mathematics — A2. A continuous variable X is described by a density f(x) with f(x) ≥ 0 and ∫f(x)dx = 1 over all x. Probabilities are areas:

Key areas to revise

  • Probability Density Functions
  • Finding Unknown Constants
  • Expectation and Variance
  • The Median and Mode
  • Uniform Distribution

Core facts to recall

  • Density function: f(x) ≥ 0 everywhere, and the total area under it is 1.
  • Probability: P(a < X < b) = ∫ from a to b of f(x) dx. A single point has zero probability.
  • Mean: E(X) = ∫ x f(x) dx. Variance: Var(X) = E(X²) − [E(X)]².
  • Median m: the area to its left is 0.5, so ∫ from the lower limit to m of f(x) dx = 0.5. Mode: the x-value where f(x) is greatest.
  • Uniform distribution on [a, b]: f(x) = 1 / (b − a), mean (a + b) / 2, variance (b − a)² / 12.

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

title: AS Level Chemistry: Introductory Organic Chemistry and Alkanes
content:
AS Level Chemistry: Introductory Organic Chemistry and Alkanes

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH11, Topic 4 introduces organic chemistry: how carbon compounds are named and drawn, how reactions are classified, how bonds break, and how alkanes are obtained and used. It also carries the safety material on hazard and risk, which is examined in a short-answer question nearly every year. The topic is the vocabulary and grammar of everything that follows, so the mechanisms and IUPAC rules must be exact rather than approximate.

Hazard and risk

A hazard is something with the potential to cause harm: a corrosive acid, a flammable solvent, a toxic gas. Risk is the chance that harm will actually occur when the hazard is used, and it depends on exposure as well as on the hazard itself. A concentrated acid sealed in a bottle is hazardous but carries little risk; the same acid being poured in a busy laboratory carries a real risk.

That distinction is why a risk assessment is made before practical work. It identifies the hazards, decides who might be harmed and how, evaluates the likelihood and severity, and records the controls.

Organic compounds are often hazardous because many are volatile and flammable, and because some are toxic or irritant. Ways to reduce risk include:

  • Working on a smaller scale, which reduces the amount of vapour released and the consequences of a spill.
  • Taking precautions specific to the hazard: a fume cupboard for a volatile toxic liquid, a water bath instead of a naked flame for a flammable solvent, gloves for a corrosive, eye protection at all times.
  • Using an alternative method with less hazardous substances, for example a lower-risk solvent or a reaction that avoids a toxic reagent.
  • Following safe practice for heating: never heat a closed system, and use anti-bump granules or a stirrer to avoid violent boiling.

The question usually asks you to suggest controls for a named procedure, so link each control to the specific hazard rather than listing generic safety advice.

Homologous series and functional groups

A homologous series is a family of organic compounds with the same general formula, the same functional group and similar chemical properties, in which each member differs from the next by a CH₂ unit. Because the formula changes by CH₂, the molar mass changes by 14, and the physical properties change gradually along the series while the chemical properties stay similar.

A functional group is the group of atoms responsible for the characteristic reactions of a compound. The functional groups examined at AS level are:

FamilyFunctional groupGeneral formula
AlkaneC–C and C–H single bonds onlyCₙH₂ₙ₊₂
Cycloalkanering of C–C single bondsCₙH₂ₙ
AlkeneC=C double bondCₙH₂ₙ
HalogenoalkaneC–X (X = Cl, Br, I)CₙH₂ₙ₊₁X
Alcohol–OHCₙH₂ₙ₊₁OH
Aldehyde–CHOCₙH₂ₙO
KetoneC=O between two carbon atomsCₙH₂ₙO
Carboxylic acid–COOHCₙH₂ₙ₊₁COOH

Naming and drawing organic compounds

IUPAC nomenclature follows a fixed sequence of steps. Work through them in order every time.

  1. Find the longest carbon chain containing the functional group; that gives the stem (meth, eth, prop, but, pent, hex...).
  2. Number the chain so that the functional group gets the lowest possible number.
  3. Name and number the substituents, and list them alphabetically (ethyl before methyl), with a multiplier for repeats (di-, tri-).
  4. Add the functional group suffix, with its number: -an- for an alkane, -en- for an alkene, -ol for an alcohol, -al for an aldehyde, -one for a ketone, -oic acid for a carboxylic acid.
  5. Use hyphens between numbers and letters, and commas between numbers.

Worked example. The compound CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₂OH has a four-carbon chain containing the –OH group, numbered from the end nearer the alcohol so that the OH is on carbon 1. There is a methyl group on carbon 3, so the name is 3-methylbutan-1-ol. Numbering from the other end would give 2-methylbutan-4-ol, which is wrong because the principal group must have the lowest number.

Three ways of drawing a compound are examined and you must be able to convert between them:

  • Structural formula: shows how the atoms are grouped, for example CH₃CH₂CH₂OH.
  • Displayed formula: shows every atom and every bond, including the O–H bond, drawn out in full. Required for mechanisms.
  • Skeletal formula: shows the carbon skeleton as a line, with carbon atoms at the ends and vertices and hydrogen atoms attached to carbon implied. Functional groups and the hydrogens on heteroatoms are drawn explicitly.

Where a compound has a double bond, the position is numbered and geometric isomerism may exist; cis and trans (or E and Z) describe the arrangement around the C=C bond and is covered with the alkenes.

Classifying reactions

Every organic reaction can be placed in one of five categories, and the classification is often the first mark of a question.

  • Addition: two molecules join to form one, with no atom lost. Ethene plus bromine gives 1,2-dibromoethane.
  • Substitution: one atom or group is replaced by another. Methane plus chlorine gives chloromethane plus hydrogen chloride.
  • Oxidation: an increase in the oxygen content or a loss of hydrogen, such as a primary alcohol becoming a carboxylic acid.
  • Reduction: a gain of hydrogen or a loss of oxygen, such as an alkene becoming an alkane.
  • Polymerisation: small molecules (monomers) join to form a large molecule (a polymer), as in the addition polymerisation of ethene.

Bond breaking can be classified in the same way. In homolytic fission the shared pair is split equally, one electron going to each atom, producing two free radicals. In heterolytic fission the shared pair goes entirely to one atom, producing a positive and a negative ion. A free radical is a species with an unpaired electron, shown with a single dot, such as Cl·. An electrophile is an electron-pair acceptor, such as HBr or Br₂ in an addition reaction; a nucleophile is an electron-pair donor, such as OH⁻ or NH₃.

Which fission happens depends on the conditions. Ultraviolet light supplies enough energy to break a Cl–Cl bond homolytically, which is why the chlorination of alkanes is a radical reaction; in a polar solvent, heterolytic fission is favoured and produces ions, which is why halogenoalkane hydrolysis is a nucleophilic substitution.

Alkanes and structural isomerism

Alkanes are hydrocarbons: compounds of carbon and hydrogen only. They are saturated, containing single bonds only, and their general formula is CₙH₂ₙ₊₂; cycloalkanes have the general formula CₙH₂ₙ because the ring uses two hydrogens to close.

Structural isomers are molecules with the same molecular formula but different structural formulae. Isomerism arises because the carbon skeleton can be arranged differently, and the number of isomers grows quickly with chain length. The alkanes with up to six carbon atoms are examined directly.

FormulaNumber of structural isomersNames
C4H102butane; 2-methylpropane
C5H123pentane; 2-methylbutane; 2,2-dimethylpropane
C6H145hexane; 2-methylpentane; 3-methylpentane; 2,2-dimethylbutane; 2,3-dimethylbutane

A systematic way to find them all is to take the longest chain first, then shorten the main chain by one carbon and place the removed carbon as a methyl substituent in every distinct position, then shorten again. Never place a methyl group on the end of a chain, because that only lengthens the chain and produces a duplicate.

Obtaining alkanes from crude oil

Crude oil is a mixture of hydrocarbons. It is separated by fractional distillation, which works because the fractions have different boiling temperatures: the larger the molecule, the stronger the London forces and the higher the boiling temperature. The column is hot at the bottom and cooler at the top, so smaller molecules rise further before condensing.

Demand is for short-chain molecules, especially fuels, so longer chains are broken down by cracking. Thermal cracking uses high temperature and pressure; catalytic cracking uses a zeolite catalyst at a lower temperature and pressure. In both cases a long alkane becomes a shorter alkane and an alkene:

C10H22 → C8H18 + C2H4

Reforming rearranges straight-chain alkanes into branched alkanes and cycloalkanes, or converts them into aromatic compounds, without changing the number of carbon atoms. Branched isomers are preferred in petrol because they burn more smoothly and resist premature ignition (knocking). A typical reforming equation shows a straight chain becoming a branched isomer with the same formula, or a cycloalkane plus hydrogen:

C6H14 → cyclo-C6H12 + H2

Combustion and pollution

Alkanes burn in a plentiful supply of oxygen to give carbon dioxide and water:

C3H8 + 5O2 → 3CO2 + 4H2O

With insufficient oxygen, combustion is incomplete and produces carbon monoxide, carbon particulates (soot) and unburned hydrocarbons. Combustion in air at high temperature also produces oxides of nitrogen, because nitrogen and oxygen from the air combine in the hot engine.

PollutantSourceProblem
Carbon monoxideIncomplete combustionToxic: it binds to haemoglobin far more strongly than oxygen does, forming carboxyhaemoglobin, so the blood carries less oxygen and the body is starved of it
Oxides of nitrogen, NO and NO₂Nitrogen and oxygen combining at high temperature in enginesDissolve in rainwater to form nitric acid, contributing to acid rain, which damages buildings, soils and trees and acidifies lakes; also contribute to photochemical smog and respiratory irritation
Sulfur dioxideSulfur impurities in fossil fuelsDissolves to form sulfurous and sulfuric acid, contributing to acid rain
Carbon particulatesIncomplete combustion, especially dieselRespiratory damage; contributes to smog and deposits on buildings
Unburned hydrocarbonsIncomplete combustion and evaporationReact with nitrogen oxides in sunlight to form photochemical smog, and some are carcinogenic
Carbon dioxideComplete combustion of any carbon fuelA greenhouse gas, contributing to climate change

Catalytic converters reduce these emissions by converting carbon monoxide and oxides of nitrogen into carbon dioxide and nitrogen, and oxidising unburned hydrocarbons:

2CO + 2NO → 2CO2 + N2

The catalyst is a ceramic honeycomb coated with platinum, palladium and rhodium. It works best when hot, which is why a cold engine emits more pollution, and it requires unleaded petrol because lead poisons the catalyst.

Alternative fuels and carbon neutrality

Fossil fuels are finite and their combustion adds carbon dioxide that was locked away for millions of years, so alternatives are developed to improve sustainability and reduce emissions. Sustainability means meeting present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs.

  • Bioethanol is produced by fermentation of sugars from crops. It is renewable, but growing the crops uses land, water and fertiliser, and the carbon dioxide released when it burns was recently absorbed by the plants.
  • Hydrogen releases only water when burned or used in a fuel cell, so it produces no carbon dioxide at the point of use. Whether it is low-carbon depends on how it was made: from renewable electricity by electrolysis it is clean, but from methane by steam reforming it is not.
  • Biodiesel from vegetable oils is renewable and can be used in existing diesel engines, but it competes for agricultural land.

Carbon neutrality means that the amount of carbon dioxide released when a fuel is used is balanced by the amount removed from the atmosphere when the fuel was produced. Petrol is not carbon neutral: the carbon in it was stored underground for millions of years and is added to the atmosphere when burned. Bioethanol is often described as carbon neutral because the crops absorbed carbon dioxide as they grew, but it is only truly neutral if the farming, harvesting, transport and distillation are also carbon neutral, and those processes usually burn fossil fuel. Hydrogen made by electrolysis using renewable electricity can be carbon neutral; hydrogen from steam reforming is not.

Reactions of alkanes

Alkanes are relatively unreactive because their C–C and C–H bonds are strong and non-polar. Two reactions are examined.

Combustion. As above: complete combustion gives carbon dioxide and water, incomplete combustion gives carbon monoxide and soot. Alkanes are good fuels because they release a large amount of energy per gram.

Halogenation. In the dark there is no reaction. In the presence of ultraviolet light, a halogen such as chlorine reacts with an alkane in a substitution reaction:

CH4 + Cl2 → CH3Cl + HCl

The reaction is a free radical substitution. It proceeds in three stages, and each must be shown with the correct species and the correct curly half-arrows.

Initiation. Ultraviolet light supplies the energy to break the Cl–Cl bond homolytically, producing two chlorine radicals:

Cl2 → 2Cl·

One half-arrow starts at the middle of the Cl–Cl bond and curves to one chlorine atom, and a second half-arrow curves from the bond to the other chlorine atom, showing one electron going each way.

Propagation. A chlorine radical collides with a methane molecule and removes a hydrogen atom, forming hydrogen chloride and a methyl radical; the methyl radical then reacts with a chlorine molecule to form chloromethane and a new chlorine radical:

Cl· + CH4 → CH3· + HCl
CH3· + Cl2 → CH3Cl + Cl·

Because a chlorine radical is regenerated in the second step, the reaction is a chain reaction. In each propagation step one radical is used and one is produced, so the number of radicals stays constant.

Termination. Two radicals combine and the chain ends:

Cl· + Cl· → Cl2
CH3· + Cl· → CH3Cl
CH3· + CH3· → C2H6

The last termination step explains why ethane is found among the products of the chlorination of methane, even though it is not part of the desired reaction.

Free radical substitution has limited use in synthesis because the reaction does not stop at the first substitution. Chloromethane can react again to give dichloromethane, trichloromethane and tetrachloromethane, and the propagation steps also produce hydrogen chloride and small amounts of ethane, so the product is a mixture that must be separated. To obtain a single product in good yield, a different route such as nucleophilic substitution of an alcohol is preferred.

Typical mistakes

  • Confusing hazard with risk: a hazard is the potential for harm, risk is the chance of it happening.
  • Numbering a chain from the end that gives the substituent the lowest number while ignoring the principal functional group.
  • Writing a radical with a full negative charge instead of a single dot, or forgetting the dot entirely.
  • Showing initiation with a heterolytic split, which would produce ions rather than radicals.
  • Giving the general formula of an alkene (CₙH₂ₙ) for an alkane, or forgetting that cycloalkanes share the alkene's general formula.
  • Missing a structural isomer by placing a methyl group at the end of a chain, which is the same molecule renamed.
  • Describing cracking as the addition of hydrogen, which is hydrogenation, or reforming as breaking molecules into smaller ones.
  • Claiming that a biofuel is automatically carbon neutral without accounting for its production.
  • Leaving ultraviolet light out of the conditions for halogenation, or writing the equation as an addition reaction.

Exam-style questions

  1. Define the terms hazard and risk, and explain why a risk assessment is needed before heating ethanol over a Bunsen burner. Answer: a hazard is something with the potential to cause harm; risk is the chance that harm occurs. Ethanol is volatile and highly flammable, so heating it directly risks a flash fire; a risk assessment identifies that hazard and specifies the control, such as heating in a water bath and keeping the apparatus away from naked flames.
  2. Name the compound CH₃CH₂CH(CH₃)CH₂OH. Answer: the longest chain containing the OH group has four carbons and is numbered from the right so that the OH is on carbon 1; the methyl group is on carbon 3, so the name is 3-methylbutan-1-ol.
  3. Draw and name all the structural isomers of C₅H₁₂. Answer: pentane (a straight chain of five carbons), 2-methylbutane (a four-carbon chain with a methyl on carbon 2), and 2,2-dimethylpropane (a three-carbon chain with two methyls on carbon 2).
  4. Explain why the reaction between methane and chlorine needs ultraviolet light. Answer: the C–H and Cl–Cl bonds are strong and the molecules are non-polar, so collisions at room temperature do not have enough energy to break them. Ultraviolet light provides the energy for homolytic fission of the Cl–Cl bond, which produces chlorine radicals and starts the chain reaction.
  5. Outline the mechanism for the monochlorination of ethane, naming each type of step. Answer: initiation: Cl2 → 2Cl· under UV light. Propagation: Cl· + C2H6 → C2H5· + HCl, then C2H5· + Cl2 → C2H5Cl + Cl·. Termination: Cl· + Cl· → Cl2, C2H5· + Cl· → C2H5Cl, C2H5· + C2H5· → C4H10.

Practise naming and drawing as one skill: take a name, draw the skeletal formula, then the displayed formula, then write the molecular formula, and reverse the process. That fluency is assumed in every later organic topic, especially halogenoalkanes, alcohols and spectra.
