title: Exam technique: Electric Fields and Capacitance
content:
### What earns the marks
For fields, F/Q and V/d chosen by situation earn one mark each. For capacitors, Q = CV quoted earns the method mark; parallel summed directly. For stored energy, half C V squared earns both marks.
### Traps
Error: series and parallel capacitor rules swapped. Correction: parallel adds, series reciprocates. Error: micro prefixes dropped. Correction: carry 10^-6 through. Error: field direction confused. Correction: force on a positive test charge.

title: Measures of Variation and Standard Deviation — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Measures of Variation and Standard Deviation

Mathematics — A2. The range is max − min — quick but destroyed by a single outlier. Quartiles split ordered data into quarters: Q₁ at position (n + 1)/4, Q₃ at 3(n + 1)/4 (raw data). The interquartile range, IQR = Q₃ − Q₁, is the spread of the middle 50% and resists outliers. Outliers are commonly flagged as values beyond Q₁ − 1.5·IQR or Q₃ + 1.5·IQR.

Key areas to revise

  • Range and Quartiles
  • Variance and Standard Deviation
  • Grouped Data
  • Combining and Scaling Datasets

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

title: A Level Physics: Motion in a Circle and Gravity
content:
A Level Physics: Motion in a Circle and Gravity

Gravity is the weakest of the four fundamental forces and yet it shapes galaxies — because it never cancels: mass has only one sign, so every particle attracts every other. This note builds the gravitational toolkit from zero: the field concept and field lines, Newton's law of gravitation, field strength and potential for a point mass, and then the applications that fill the papers — satellite orbits, escape velocity and the energy bookkeeping of lifting a mass to infinity. Every formula is derived from the inverse-square law, and every calculation type is worked in full.

The gravitational field

A gravitational field is a region in which a mass experiences a force. Field lines point toward the mass creating the field (gravity is always attractive), and their density shows strength — close to a planet the lines are dense (strong field), far away they are sparse. Two field shapes are examinable:

  • Radial field: around a point mass or a spherical planet outside its surface; strength falls with distance.
  • Uniform field: near a planet's surface over small height changes; strength g is effectively constant (the approximation behind mgh).

Newton's law of gravitation

F = G M m / r²

G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻² (gravitational constant)
M, m = the two masses (kg)
r = separation between their centres (m)

The analogy that makes the law intuitive: the force weakens like light spreading from a lamp — doubling the distance spreads the same influence over four times the area, so the force quarters. The law is universal: the same G applies to an apple and the Earth as to two galaxies.

Worked example. Find the gravitational force between two 1000 kg masses 2.0 m apart.

F = G M m/r² = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 1000 × 1000/4.0
  = 6.67 × 10⁻⁵/4.0 = 1.7 × 10⁻⁵ N

Note how tiny it is — gravity only matters when one mass is astronomical, which is why the electric force dominates at particle scales.

Gravitational field strength

Field strength g is force per unit mass (N kg⁻¹), and for a point mass or a spherical body:

g = G M / r²

at a planet's surface: g = G M / R²  (R = planet radius)
variation with height: g falls as 1/r² from the centre

Worked example. Find g at the surface of Mars (M = 6.4 × 10²³ kg, R = 3.4 × 10⁶ m).

g = G M/R² = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 6.4 × 10²³/(3.4 × 10⁶)²
  = 4.27 × 10¹³/1.156 × 10¹³ = 3.7 N kg⁻¹

Worked example 2 (height). At what height above Earth's surface does g fall to half its surface value? (R = 6.4 × 10⁶ m.)

g_surface = GM/R²; half → GM/r² = (1/2) GM/R²
r² = 2 R² → r = R √(2) = 9.05 × 10⁶ m
height = r - R = 2.65 × 10⁶ m  (about 2650 km)

Gravitational potential

Potential is the work done per unit mass in bringing a mass from infinity to that point (zero at infinity by definition). Because gravity attracts, the work is done by the field on the way in, so potential is negative everywhere:

V = - G M / r        (J kg⁻¹)

potential energy of a mass m: U = m V = - G M m / r
work to move between potentials: W = m (V² - V¹)

The negative sign is not a detail — it is the physical statement that masses are bound. The potential well around a planet is a dip; escape means climbing out of it to V = 0 at infinity.

Worked example. Find the potential at Earth's surface (M = 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg, R = 6.37 × 10⁶ m).

V = -GM/R = -(6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 5.97 × 10²⁴)/6.37 × 10⁶
  = -3.98 × 10¹⁴/6.37 × 10⁶ = -6.25 × 10⁷ J kg⁻¹

Escape velocity

To escape a planet's gravity, a body needs enough kinetic energy to climb from the surface potential to zero:

(1/2) m v² = G M m / R  →  v_escape = √(2 G M / R)

Earth: v = √(2 × 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 5.97 × 10²⁴/6.37 × 10⁶)
     = √(1.25 × 10⁸) = 1.12 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹ = 11.2 km s⁻¹

The derivation is worth learning as a pattern: set kinetic energy equal to the depth of the potential well, cancel m, solve for v. Escape speed is independent of the escaping body's mass — a rocket and a molecule need the same speed (though not the same fuel).

The potential well picture explains the sign conventions in one image: near a planet the potential is deeply negative (the bottom of a dip), and moving outward means climbing toward zero. A body with total energy (kinetic plus potential) below zero is bound — it will fall back; a body with total energy at or above zero can coast to infinity. That single inequality, kinetic energy compared with the depth of the well, decides every escape and orbit question, and it is the most reliable way to check an answer's sign and size.

Orbits

A satellite in a circular orbit has gravity as its centripetal force:

G M m / r² = m v² / r   →   v = √(G M / r)

period: T = 2 π r / v = 2 π √(r³/(G M))
(Kepler's third law: T² proportional to r³)

The counter-intuitive exam favourite: a lower orbit means a faster satellite. Since v = √(GM/r), smaller r gives larger v and shorter periods — which is why the International Space Station orbits in about 90 minutes while the Moon takes 27 days.

Worked example. Find the speed and period of a satellite 400 km above Earth's surface.

r = 6.37 × 10⁶ + 4.0 × 10⁵ = 6.77 × 10⁶ m
v = √(GM/r) = √(6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 5.97 × 10²⁴/6.77 × 10⁶)
  = √(5.88 × 10⁷) = 7.67 × 10³ m s⁻¹
T = 2 π r/v = 2 × 3.14 × 6.77 × 10⁶/7.67 × 10³
  = 4.25 × 10⁷/7.67 × 10³ = 5.5 × 10³ s  (about 92 minutes)

Geostationary orbits are the applied case: r ≈ 4.2 × 10⁷ m gives T = 24 hours, the satellite sits above one point on the equator, and it must orbit west-to-east in the equatorial plane.

Worked examples: combined gravity problems

Worked example. Compare the gravitational potential energy of a 500 kg satellite at 400 km altitude with its value at infinity, and find the energy needed to escape from that orbit.

r = 6.77 × 10⁶ m
U_orbit = -GMm/r = -(6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 5.97 × 10²⁴ × 500)/6.77 × 10⁶
        = -1.99 × 10¹⁷/6.77 × 10⁶ = -2.94 × 10¹⁰ J
U_infinity = 0
energy to escape = 0 - (-2.94 × 10¹⁰) = 2.9 × 10¹⁰ J

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Law) State Newton's law of gravitation. Answer: The gravitational force between two point masses is proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centres: F = GMm/r².
  2. (Field strength) Define gravitational field strength. Answer: The force per unit mass on a small test mass at that point, g = F/m, measured in N kg⁻¹.
  3. (Inverse square) State how g changes when the distance from a planet's centre is tripled. Answer: g = GM/r², so tripling r divides g by 9.
  4. (Potential) Explain why gravitational potential is negative. Answer: Potential is defined as zero at infinity; gravity attracts, so the field does work on a mass brought in from infinity, meaning its potential energy — and therefore potential — decreases below zero.
  5. (Escape) Calculate the escape velocity from the Moon (M = 7.35 × 10²² kg, R = 1.74 × 10⁶ m). Answer: v = √(2GM/R) = √(2 × 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 7.35 × 10²²/1.74 × 10⁶) = √(5.63 × 10⁶) = 2.37 × 10³ m s⁻¹ ≈ 2.4 km s⁻¹.
  6. (Orbit) Explain why a satellite in a lower orbit moves faster. Answer: Gravity provides the centripetal force: GMm/r² = mv²/r, so v = √(GM/r); a smaller r gives a larger speed and a shorter period.
  7. (Geostationary) State two conditions for a geostationary orbit. Answer: The period must be 24 hours, the orbit must be equatorial and the satellite must orbit in the same direction as Earth's rotation (west to east) — all three are usually wanted.
  8. (Energy) Explain why the energy needed to move a satellite from a low orbit to a higher one is not simply mgh. Answer: Over large distances g is not constant; the correct treatment uses the change in gravitational potential energy, U = −GMm/r, evaluated at both radii.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • r measured from the centre: the separation is centre-to-centre, so a satellite's r includes the planet's radius. Using altitude alone underestimates r and inflates g and v.
  • Mass cancellation: in orbital and escape calculations m cancels — do not carry a satellite's mass through and then wonder why the answer is huge.
  • Negative potentials: V and U are negative; a "larger" potential energy at a higher orbit is less negative, not more. Work done = m(V₂ − V₁), keeping the signs.
  • g versus G: g = GM/r² is field strength (N kg⁻¹); G is the universal constant (N m² kg⁻²). Confusing the symbols loses marks and factors of mass.
  • Surface approximation: mgh applies only for small heights; over planetary distances use the potential formula.
  • Orbit direction: geostationary requires equatorial, west-to-east, 24 hours — a polar orbit is not geostationary however high it is.
  • Units of G and distances: G in N m² kg⁻², masses in kg, distances in metres — km into m, and planet masses given in scientific notation handled carefully.
  • Precision: 2 or 3 s.f. with units; the data sheet supplies G, Earth's mass and radius — quote them rather than relying on memory.
  • Method marks: write F = GMm/r² or v = √(GM/r) before substituting; formulae earn credit independently of arithmetic.

Equations and symbols

Every relation this topic is examined on, written with its real notation and followed by a key naming each symbol, its unit and what it means. The sections above explain why each one is true; this sheet is the version to revise from, where the answer depends on reproducing the exact form and substituting into it without losing a unit.

Circular motion, the kinematics the orbits need

v = ωr and ω = 2π/T
Key: v = the speed along the circular path (m s⁻¹); ω (omega) = the angular velocity (rad s⁻¹); r = the radius of the circle (m); T = the period of one revolution (s). Speed is constant in magnitude but the direction changes continuously, so a body in uniform circular motion is always accelerating.

a = v²/r = ω²r, directed towards the centre; F = mv²/r
Key: a = the centripetal acceleration (m s⁻²); v = speed (m s⁻¹); r = radius (m); ω = angular velocity (rad s⁻¹); F = the resultant force needed (N); m = the mass (kg). The force is not an extra force: it is the net inward force supplied by gravity, tension, friction or a normal reaction, and naming which is the first line of any circular-motion answer.

Gravitational force and field strength

F = GMm/r²
Key: F = the gravitational force between the two masses (N), always attractive; G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², the gravitational constant; M, m = the two masses (kg); r = the distance between their centres (m). The inverse square makes the force fall to a quarter at twice the distance, and r is measured from the centre, never the surface.

g = GM/r², so g at a planet's surface = GM/R²
Key: g = the gravitational field strength (N kg⁻¹, numerically the acceleration of free fall); M = the mass of the planet or star (kg); r = the distance from its centre (m); R = its radius (m). Surface g therefore depends on mass and radius together: a heavier planet with a much larger radius can have the weaker surface field.

g = GM/r² falls as 1/r² from the centre, so half the surface value occurs at r = R√2
Key: g = the field strength at distance r; R = the planet's radius; the √2 comes from solving GM/R² ÷ 2 = GM/r². The height above the surface is then r − R, which is the quantity a "how high" question actually wants.

Potential and energy

V = −GM/r and U = mV = −GMm/r
Key: V = the gravitational potential at distance r (J kg⁻¹), defined as zero at infinity and therefore negative everywhere finite; U = the potential energy of mass m at that point (J); G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²; M, m = the two masses (kg); r = the separation (m). The minus sign is the statement that gravity is attractive and work must be done to separate the masses.

work done in moving between potentials: W = m(V₂ − V₁)
Key: W = the work done on or by the mass (J); m = the mass moved (kg); V₁, V₂ = the potentials at the start and end (J kg⁻¹). Moving away from a planet means V₂ > V₁ (both negative, but less negative), so W is positive — energy must be supplied.

ΔV = g Δh holds only for a uniform field
Key: ΔV = the change in potential (J kg⁻¹); g = the field strength (N kg⁻¹); Δh = the height gained (m). It is the small-distance approximation to GM/r² and fails once the height is a noticeable fraction of the planet's radius — the point a "why not use mgh" question is making.

Escape velocity and orbits

½mv² = GMm/R ⇒ v_escape = √(2GM/R)
Key: v_escape = the minimum launch speed to escape to infinity (m s⁻¹); G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²; M = the mass of the body being escaped (kg); R = the distance from its centre at launch (m). Setting the kinetic energy equal to the depth of the potential well is the whole derivation; the escape speed does not depend on the mass of the escaping object, only on M and R.

orbital speed: GMm/r² = mv²/r ⇒ v = √(GM/r)
Key: v = the orbital speed (m s⁻¹); G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²; M = the mass of the central body (kg); r = the orbital radius from the centre (m). Gravity supplies the centripetal force, which is why a larger orbit means a slower speed — the opposite of the intuition that a bigger orbit needs more speed.

T = 2π√(r³/(GM)), so T² ∝ r³
Key: T = the orbital period (s); r = the orbital radius (m); G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²; M = the central mass (kg). Kepler's third law: the square of the period is proportional to the cube of the radius, which is why a geostationary satellite has one specific radius and not any radius above the equator.

geostationary: T = 24 h ≈ 8.64 × 10⁴ s, orbit in the plane of the equator, same sense as the Earth's rotation
Key: T = the orbital period (s); the two geometric conditions are what make the satellite appear fixed in the sky. A satellite at the right radius but the wrong inclination or direction is merely geosynchronous, not geostationary — the distinction is a standard two-mark point.

title: Ethics and AI — Study Notes
content:
`# Ethics and AI

Professional Bodies

ACM/IEEE-CS and BCS codes: public interest, competence, integrity, avoid harm, respect privacy. Violations cost trust and employment.

Ethical Scenarios

  • Collecting more personal data than needed (privacy)
  • Releasing software with known bugs that risks safety (competence/honesty)
  • Automated decisions without human review (accountability)

Laws: data protection (GDPR-style), computer misuse (unauthorised access is a crime regardless of intent).

AI Characteristics

Systems exhibiting: planning, learning, reasoning, problem-solving, perception, knowledge representation.

Machine Learning

  • Supervised: learns from labelled data (spam detection)
  • Unsupervised: finds structure in unlabelled data (clustering)
  • Reinforcement: learns by reward signals (game agents)

Training/evaluation loop: fit on training data, test on unseen data to avoid overfitting. Neural networks adjust weights via backpropagation.

Ethics of AI

Bias in training data → unfair outputs; opaque decisions → accountability gaps; job displacement; autonomous weapons.

Exam tips: structure ethics answers as: identify the principle → apply to the scenario → give consequences for stakeholders.

title: Exam technique: Integration
content:
### What earns the marks
For indefinite integrals, each term raised correctly plus the constant earns full marks. For definite integrals, the antiderivative quoted earns one mark and the correct upper-minus-lower evaluation earns the next. For area and curve-finding, the limits or the given point used earns the final mark.
### Traps
Error: constant of integration omitted. Correction: +c always for indefinite. Error: limits subtracted backwards. Correction: upper minus lower. Error: power rule inverted on roots. Correction: root x is x to the half, integral goes up.
### Worked example
Find the integral of 6x² − 4x⁻³. Raise each power by one and divide by the new power: 6x² becomes 2x³, and −4x⁻³ becomes 2x⁻² because (−4)/(−2) = 2. Add the constant: 2x³ + 2x⁻² + c. Check by differentiating: 6x² + (−4)x⁻³, which matches the original.
### Check yourself
Evaluate the definite integral of 2x + 1 from 1 to 3. The antiderivative is x² + x, giving (9 + 3) − (1 + 1) = 10. Write both the antiderivative and the subtraction on the paper, because the method mark depends on them.

### Worked example
Find the integral of 6x² − 4x⁻³. Raise each power by one and divide by the new power: 6x² becomes 2x³, and −4x⁻³ becomes 2x⁻² because (−4)/(−2) = 2. Add the constant: 2x³ + 2x⁻² + c. Check by differentiating: 6x² + (−4)x⁻³, which matches the original.
### Check yourself
Evaluate the definite integral of 2x + 1 from 1 to 3. The antiderivative is x² + x, giving (9 + 3) − (1 + 1) = 10. Write both the antiderivative and the subtraction on the paper, because the method mark depends on them.

title: Hardware and Logic Gates — Study Notes
content:
Hardware, Logic Gates and Boolean Algebra

Cambridge International AS & A Level Computer Science 9618 (2026): this note follows syllabus statements 3.1, 3.2 and 15.2. It covers computer components and systems, gate functions and representations, Boolean algebra, adders, SR/JK flip-flops and Karnaugh maps. CPU architecture and the fetch-execute cycle are treated separately under statement 4.1.

1. Computer systems and embedded devices (3.1)

A computer system receives data, processes it, stores data or instructions, and produces output. Input devices convert user actions or measured physical quantities into usable data. A microphone converts sound into an electrical signal; a touchscreen both detects touch input and displays visual output. Output devices present processed results: speakers convert electrical signals into sound, while a laser printer forms a page image and fixes toner to paper. A 3D printer builds an object layer by layer from a digital model. A virtual-reality headset presents a close stereoscopic display and may sense head movement so the scene can respond.

Secondary storage keeps programs and files when power is removed. A magnetic hard disk stores data magnetically on rotating platters and uses moving heads; it offers high capacity but is vulnerable to mechanical shock. Solid-state flash storage stores charge in memory cells and has no moving parts, so it is fast and shock-resistant, though capacity costs more and cells have finite write endurance. An optical reader/writer uses a laser to read or record a disc. Primary memory is directly available to the processor while programs run; it is not a substitute for persistent secondary storage.

An embedded system is a computer built into a larger product to perform a specific or limited set of functions, often for monitoring or control. Benefits include compact size, low power use, reliable repeated operation and lower cost than a general-purpose computer. Limitations include less flexibility, difficulty upgrading or repairing it, and the risk that a failure affects the whole device. Suitability depends on the product and the consequences of failure.

2. Primary memory and buffers (3.1)

RAM is volatile read/write primary memory: its contents are lost when power is removed. It holds programs and data currently in use. ROM is non-volatile and holds instructions that must remain available, such as start-up firmware. Do not confuse ROM with secondary storage: ROM is primary memory with a persistent purpose.

  • PROM can be programmed once after manufacture; it cannot then be erased and rewritten.
  • EPROM can be erased using ultraviolet light and programmed again; conventionally the chip must be removed from its circuit for erasure.
  • EEPROM can be erased and reprogrammed electrically, often while installed. Flash memory is a widely used form of electrically erasable non-volatile memory.

SRAM stores each bit using a bistable circuit and does not need periodic refresh while power is present. It is fast but uses more circuit area per bit, so it is comparatively expensive and lower-density; it is used where speed matters, such as cache. DRAM stores each bit as charge in a capacitor. Charge leaks, so it must be refreshed periodically. DRAM is slower than SRAM but simpler per bit, cheaper and higher-density, making it suitable for main memory. Both SRAM and DRAM are volatile.

A buffer is a temporary memory area holding data during transfer between devices or processes that operate at different rates or transfer different-sized blocks. A printer buffer queues output while the printer works more slowly than the processor can send data. Buffering smooths transfer and lets the sending process continue; it is not permanent storage and does not itself make the receiving device faster.

3. Monitoring, control, sensors and feedback (3.1)

A monitoring system samples sensor readings and records, displays or reports them. It observes a process but does not automatically change it. A control system uses sensor input, compares the measured state with a required condition, and can send an output to an actuator. A temperature sensor may measure a greenhouse; a heater is an actuator. Pressure, infrared and sound sensors are further examples named in the syllabus.

In a feedback control loop, the system measures the result of its action and uses that new measurement to decide what to do next. For a thermostat, the target temperature is compared with the measured temperature: if the room is too cool, the controller switches the heater on; once the target is reached, it switches it off. Feedback helps the controller respond to changing conditions. A one-way system that acts without measuring the result is open-loop, not feedback control.

4. Logic gates and representations (3.2)

A logic gate maps binary input value(s) to a binary output. A NOT gate has one input; the other gates in this syllabus have two inputs. AND is 1 only when both inputs are 1; OR is 1 when at least one input is 1; XOR (EOR) is 1 when exactly one input is 1, so it is 0 when inputs match. NAND is NOT(AND), and NOR is NOT(OR). The prime mark means NOT and parentheses show which operation is complemented.

ABNOT AANDORNANDNORXOR
00100110
01101101
10001101
11011000

The same logic can be represented as a problem, Boolean expression, circuit diagram or truth table. Translate carefully: identify inputs, write the operation and parentheses, then evaluate every input combination. For Y=(A OR B) AND NOT C, evaluate the OR and NOT sub-expressions before the final AND. A circuit must preserve this grouping; a truth table must include all 2ⁿ rows for n inputs and show the output for each row.

5. Boolean algebra and De Morgan's laws (15.2)

Boolean algebra works with values 0 and 1. Here A·B means A AND B, A+B means A OR B, and A' means NOT A. These symbols are not ordinary arithmetic: 1+1=1 because 1 OR 1 is 1. Useful identities include A+0=A, A·1=A, A+A=A, A·A=A, A+A'=1 and A·A'=0. Use identities to simplify a circuit without changing its output for any input.

De Morgan's laws are (A·B)' = A' + B' and (A+B)' = A'·B'. To complement a bracketed expression, complement each input and change AND to OR or OR to AND. Example: (A·(B+C))' = A' + (B'·C'). Check the scope of the complement: A·B' is not the same as (A·B)'. Absorption identities include A+A·B=A and A·(A+B)=A. A truth-table check can confirm a proposed simplification.

6. Adders: half adder and full adder (15.2)

A half adder adds two one-bit inputs A and B. Its Sum output is S=A XOR B; its Carry output is C=A AND B. Thus 0+0 gives S=0,C=0; 0+1 and 1+0 give S=1,C=0; 1+1 gives S=0,C=1. The carry is passed into the next binary column. A half adder has no carry-in input.

A full adder also accepts carry-in Cin. Sum is 1 when an odd number of A, B and Cin are 1: S=A XOR B XOR Cin. Carry-out is 1 when at least two of the three inputs are 1: Cout=(A·B)+(A·Cin)+(B·Cin). For example, 1+1+1 has binary total 3, so S=1 and Cout=1. Keep Sum and Carry as separate outputs; exchanging their gate functions is a common error.

7. Flip-flops and data storage (15.2)

A flip-flop is a bistable circuit: it retains one of two states and therefore stores one bit. The state is retained until an input causes a change. The syllabus includes SR and JK flip-flops. State the circuit convention when interpreting an SR truth table: for a common active-high SR latch made from NOR gates, S=1 sets Q to 1, R=1 resets Q to 0, and S=R=0 holds the previous state. S=R=1 is forbidden for this implementation because it forces both NOR outputs low and violates the complementary-output condition. Other gate implementations may use different active levels; check the diagram before applying this table.

A JK flip-flop removes the SR latch's forbidden input combination: J=0,K=0 holds the current state; J=1,K=0 sets Q=1; J=0,K=1 resets Q=0; J=1,K=1 toggles Q to its complement. Flip-flops provide storage elements in sequential circuits. Distinguish stored state, which depends on previous state, from a combinational gate output, which depends only on current inputs.

8. Karnaugh maps (K-maps) (15.2)

A Karnaugh map is a visual way to simplify a Boolean function from its truth table. Place output values in cells labelled by input combinations. Arrange row and column labels in Gray-code order, for example 00, 01, 11, 10, so neighbouring cells differ in exactly one variable. Groups may wrap across opposite edges because those cells are adjacent; diagonal cells are not adjacent.

Group adjacent 1s in rectangles containing a power of two cells (1, 2, 4, 8, and so on). Use the largest useful groups, and overlap groups if that reduces the expression. Each group gives a product term containing only variables that stay constant throughout the group; variables that change are eliminated. OR the terms together. Every 1 must be covered, and do not include a 0 unless the question explicitly provides a don't-care condition. In a three-input map, minterms 1, 3, 5 and 7 are exactly the rows where C=1; they form a group of four and simplify to C. A K-map can make a multi-variable pattern easier to see than repeated algebra, but the final expression must still match every specified row.

Exam method and common checks

  1. Write input labels and output(s) before filling a truth table; for three inputs list all eight combinations exactly once.
  2. For a circuit, follow wires gate by gate and record intermediate outputs where useful.
  3. For Boolean simplification, preserve parentheses and complement scope; test the result on a truth table when uncertain.
  4. For an adder, calculate the binary total and report Sum and Carry separately.
  5. For a K-map, use Gray-code order, group adjacent 1s in powers of two, and eliminate only variables that change within a group.
  6. For a control-system scenario, name the sensor input, controller decision, actuator output and (if present) feedback measurement.

Syllabus basis: Cambridge International AS & A Level Computer Science 9618 syllabus for 2026, statements 3.1, 3.2 and 15.2; topic boundaries are stated at the start of this note.

title: Probability Distributions — Study Notes
content:
Discrete Random Variables

Probability Distributions

A discrete random variable X takes values xᵢ with probabilities pᵢ where each pᵢ ≥ 0 and Σpᵢ = 1. A probability distribution can be given as a table, a formula, or a function. Any missing probability is found by subtraction.

Example: X = number of heads in 2 fair tosses: P(0) = 1/4, P(1) = 1/2, P(2) = 1/4.

Expectation

The mean of X is

  • E(X) = Σxᵢpᵢ

It is a weighted average — the long-run average value over many repetitions. E(X) need not equal any value X can actually take.

Variance

  • Var(X) = E(X²) − (E(X))²

where E(X²) = Σxᵢ²pᵢ — square the values before multiplying by probabilities. The standard deviation is √Var(X).

Linear Transforms

For constants a and b:

  • E(aX + b) = a·E(X) + b and Var(aX + b) = a²·Var(X)

Adding a constant shifts but does not spread; multiplying scales the spread by |a|.

Independent Variables

If X and Y are independent: E(X + Y) = E(X) + E(Y) and Var(X + Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y). The addition rule for expectation always holds; the variance addition needs independence. The same applies to differences: Var(X − Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) — the subtraction does not cancel spread.

Exam tips: first verify Σp = 1 in any given table. Write E(X²) and (E(X))² separately; merging them is the most common exam error. In games of chance, set the expected profit to zero to find a fair entry fee.

title: Transition Metals and their Chemistry
content:
Transition Metals and their Chemistry

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH15, Topic 17. Transition metals form coloured complex ions, show variable oxidation states and act as catalysts. These properties come from partly filled d orbitals.

Complex ions and ligands

  • A ligand is a species with a lone pair that forms a dative bond to a metal ion. Water, ammonia and chloride are monodentate ligands.
  • Ethane-1,2-diamine is bidentate because it has two donor atoms. EDTA⁴⁻ is hexadentate.
  • The coordination number is the number of coordinate bonds to the central metal ion. Common shapes are octahedral (6), tetrahedral (4), square planar (4) and linear (2, e.g. [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺).

Colour

  • In a ligand field the five d orbitals split into two energy levels. Electrons absorb light to jump between them, and the colour seen is complementary to the colour absorbed.
  • The d-orbital splitting depends on the metal, its oxidation state and the ligands. Ligand exchange changes the colour.

Ligand substitution and isomerism

  • Concentrated HCl converts [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ (blue) into [CuCl₄]²⁻ (yellow-green, tetrahedral).
  • Excess aqueous ammonia converts Cu²⁺ into [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺, a deep blue complex.
  • Square planar [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂] shows cis-trans isomerism. The cis form is the anticancer drug cisplatin.

Catalysis

  • Heterogeneous catalysts (iron in the Haber process) work on a surface. Homogeneous catalysts such as Fe²⁺ in the iodide–peroxydisulfate reaction are in the same phase as the reactants.
  • In the MnO₄⁻ and ethanedioate reaction, Mn²⁺ is the product and catalyses the reaction, so the rate increases as it forms: this is autocatalysis.

Exam tip: when a ligand exchange is asked for, name both the shape and the colour change, and write the complex formula with its charge.

title: AS Level Mathematics: Probability Distributions
content:
AS Level Mathematics: Probability Distributions

A discrete random variable takes a countable set of values, each with a probability. The probability distribution is the complete list of values and probabilities, and from it come the two summaries that matter: the expected value (the long-run average) and the variance (the typical squared spread about it). This note builds the topic from zero: constructing and checking a distribution, E(X) and Var(X) from first principles, the effect of linear transformations, and the linear combinations of random variables that let you combine independent quantities with confidence.

Discrete random variables

X takes values x1, x2, ... with probabilities p1, p2, ...
conditions: 0 <= p_i <= 1 and the probabilities sum to 1

Worked example. A fair die is rolled and X is the score. Write the distribution and verify it.

P(X = k) = 1/6 for k = 1..6
sum = 6 × 1/6 = 1, so it is a valid distribution

Worked example 2 (unknown constant). P(X = 1) = k, P(X = 2) = 2k, P(X = 3) = 3k. Find k.

k + 2k + 3k = 1  →  6k = 1  →  k = 1/6
so P(X = 1) = 1/6, P(X = 2) = 1/3, P(X = 3) = 1/2

Expectation

E(X) = sum of x P(X = x)

the expected value need not be a possible value of X:
the mean of a die is 3.5

Worked example. Find E(X) for the die.

E(X) = (1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6)/6 = 21/6 = 3.5

Worked example 2 (unequal probabilities). X takes 0, 1, 2 with probabilities 0.2, 0.5, 0.3. Find E(X).

E(X) = 0(0.2) + 1(0.5) + 2(0.3) = 0.5 + 0.6 = 1.1

Interpretation: over many repetitions the average outcome approaches 1.1. That long-run reading is what applied questions ("expected profit", "expected number of defects") ask for.

Variance of a discrete random variable

Var(X) = E(X²) - [E(X)]^2
where E(X²) = sum of x² P(X = x)

standard deviation = √(Var(X))

Worked example. Find Var(X) for the die.

E(X²) = (1 + 4 + 9 + 16 + 25 + 36)/6 = 91/6 = 15.167
Var(X) = 15.167 - 12.25 = 2.917
sd = 1.708

Worked example 2. For X = 0, 1, 2 with probabilities 0.2, 0.5, 0.3, find Var(X).

E(X) = 1.1
E(X²) = 0 + 0.5 + 4(0.3) = 1.7
Var(X) = 1.7 - 1.21 = 0.49
sd = 0.7

Linear transformations

E(aX + b) = a E(X) + b
Var(aX + b) = a² Var(X)

sd(aX + b) = |a| sd(X)

The asymmetry is the key idea: adding a constant shifts every value and so shifts the mean but leaves the spread unchanged; multiplying by a scales the mean by a and the spread by |a|, so the variance scales by a².

Worked example. E(X) = 5, Var(X) = 4. Find E(3X + 2) and Var(3X + 2).

E = 3(5) + 2 = 17
Var = 9(4) = 36;  sd = 6

Worked example 2 (finding the transformation). E(Y) = 20 and Var(Y) = 25, where Y = aX + b, E(X) = 4 and Var(X) = 1. Find a and b.

Var: a² (1) = 25  →  a = 5 or -5
if a = 5: 20 = 5(4) + b  →  b = 0
if a = -5: 20 = -20 + b  →  b = 40
both are valid; the sign of a is fixed by context (a positive
scaling is usually implied)

Linear combinations of random variables

E(aX + bY) = a E(X) + b E(Y)          (always, no independence needed)
Var(aX + bY) = a² Var(X) + b² Var(Y)   (only if X, Y independent)
Var(aX - bY) = a² Var(X) + b² Var(Y)   (the variances still add)

The minus sign is where most marks are lost: subtracting random variables adds their variances, because the uncertainty compounds whichever direction the values move.

Worked example. X and Y are independent with E(X) = 10, Var(X) = 9, E(Y) = 4, Var(Y) = 4. Find E(X − Y) and Var(X − Y).

E(X - Y) = 10 - 4 = 6
Var(X - Y) = 9 + 4 = 13   (not 9 - 4)
sd = 3.606

Worked example 2 (three variables). Independent X, Y, Z with variances 2, 3, 5. Find Var(2X + 3Y − Z).

= 4(2) + 9(3) + 1(5) = 8 + 27 + 5 = 40

Worked example 3 (total of identical variables). A fair die is rolled twice; T is the total. Find E(T) and Var(T).

each roll: E = 3.5, Var = 35/12 = 2.917
E(T) = 7;  Var(T) = 2 × 2.917 = 5.833
sd(T) = 2.415  (the spread of a total grows, but by √(2), not 2)

Discrete uniform distribution

X uniform on 1..n: P(X = k) = 1/n
E(X) = (n + 1)/2
Var(X) = (n² - 1)/12

Worked example. X is uniform on 1 to 10. Find E(X) and Var(X).

E(X) = 11/2 = 5.5
Var(X) = (100 - 1)/12 = 8.25

Cumulative distribution functions

The cumulative distribution function F(x) gives the probability that X is at most x. It is a step function for a discrete variable: constant between values, jumping at each value by that value's probability.

F(x) = P(X <= x) = sum of P(X = k) for k <= x

P(X = k) = F(k) - F(k - 1)
P(a < X <= b) = F(b) - F(a)

Worked example. X takes 1, 2, 3 with probabilities 0.2, 0.5, 0.3. Write F(x) and use it to find P(X > 1).

F(1) = 0.2;  F(2) = 0.7;  F(3) = 1
P(X > 1) = 1 - F(1) = 0.8  (equivalently 0.5 + 0.3)

Worked example 2 (recovering probabilities). F(2) = 0.35 and F(3) = 0.8. Find P(X = 3).

P(X = 3) = F(3) - F(2) = 0.8 - 0.35 = 0.45

Reading F correctly requires attention to the inequality: P(X < 3) = F(2) for a discrete variable, while P(X ≤ 3) = F(3). One unit of difference changes the answer.

Expectation from a table and applied profit

When the distribution is given as a table, the calculation is a single weighted total; when it is described in words, the table must be built first.

Worked example. A fair coin is tossed three times and X counts the heads. Find E(X) and Var(X).

X ~ Binomial(3, 1/2) in effect: probabilities 1/8, 3/8, 3/8, 1/8 for 0..3
E(X) = 0 + 3/8 + 6/8 + 3/8 = 12/8 = 1.5
E(X²) = 0 + 3/8 + 12/8 + 9/8 = 24/8 = 3
Var(X) = 3 - 2.25 = 0.75

Worked example 2 (profit). A stall pays 4 pounds to play a game that returns 0, 5 or 20 pounds with probabilities 0.6, 0.3 and 0.1. Find the expected profit per game and whether the stall makes money.

E(return) = 0 + 1.5 + 2.0 = 3.5
profit = return - 4, so E(profit) = 3.5 - 4 = -0.5
players lose 50 pence per game on average, so the stall profits

The transformation rule does the work: E(X − c) = E(X) − c. State the interpretation, not just the number.

Why variances add for independent variables

For independent X and Y, the variance of a sum is the sum of the variances. The proof rests on the fact that independence makes E(XY) = E(X)E(Y), so the cross term in the expansion vanishes:

Var(X + Y) = E[(X + Y)²] - [E(X + Y)]^2
           = E(X²) + 2E(XY) + E(Y²) - [E(X)]^2 - 2E(X)E(Y) - [E(Y)]^2
independence: E(XY) = E(X)E(Y), so the cross terms cancel
           = Var(X) + Var(Y)

For the difference, the same expansion gives Var(X − Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y): the cross term is −2E(XY) + 2E(X)E(Y), which also vanishes. The intuition is that independent errors cannot cancel — a positive error in one is just as likely to meet a positive or negative error in the other, so the uncertainties compound.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Valid distribution) P(X = 1) = 0.3, P(X = 2) = 0.4, P(X = 3) = k. Find k. Answer: 0.3.
  2. (E) X = 1, 3, 5 with probabilities 0.2, 0.5, 0.3. Find E(X). Answer: 0.2 + 1.5 + 1.5 = 3.2.
  3. (Var) For the same X, find Var(X). Answer: E(X²) = 0.2 + 4.5 + 7.5 = 12.2; Var = 12.2 − 10.24 = 1.96.
  4. (Transform) E(X) = 6, Var(X) = 5. Find E(4X − 1) and Var(4X − 1). Answer: 23 and 80.
  5. (Combination) Independent X, Y: Var(X) = 6, Var(Y) = 8. Find Var(2X + Y). Answer: 24 + 8 = 32.
  6. (Combination difference) Same X, Y: Var(X − Y). Answer: 6 + 8 = 14.
  7. (Uniform) X uniform on 1..6. Find Var(X). Answer: (36 − 1)/12 = 2.917.
  8. (Applied) A game pays X with E(X) = 2 and costs 3 to play. Find the expected profit. Answer: E(X − 3) = −1, a loss of 1 per game.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Var(aX) = a Var(X): wrong — the variance scales by a², the standard deviation by |a|.
  • Subtracting variances: Var(X − Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) for independent variables; subtraction never reduces uncertainty.
  • Assuming independence: the variance-addition rule requires it; the expectation rule does not.
  • Using E(X²) as [E(X)]²: they differ by the variance; compute E(X²) from the distribution.
  • Probabilities not summing to 1: the first check on any distribution, and often the way to find an unknown constant.
  • Expectation as a possible value: E(X) need not be attainable (3.5 on a die); say "on average over many trials".
  • Standard deviation units: the variance is in squared units; compare and quote the sd.
  • Negative scaling: if a is negative, E flips sign and sd uses |a|; forgetting the modulus produces a negative standard deviation.

Formula summary

E(X) = sum of x P(X = x);  E(X²) = sum of x² P(X = x)
Var(X) = E(X²) - [E(X)]^2
E(aX + b) = a E(X) + b;  Var(aX + b) = a² Var(X)
E(aX + bY) = a E(X) + b E(Y)
Var(aX + bY) = a² Var(X) + b² Var(Y)   (independent)
F(x) = P(X <= x);  P(X = k) = F(k) - F(k - 1)

Two conditions separate the whole topic: expectations always combine linearly, variances combine linearly only when the variables are independent — and then always with plus signs, whatever the signs in front of the variables. Write the condition before applying the variance rule; it is worth a mark on its own and prevents the commonest mistake in the topic.

Equations and symbols

The whole topic is four rules and one warning: expectation always combines linearly, variance combines linearly only for independent variables, and adding or subtracting them always adds the variances. Write the independence condition before you apply a variance rule — it is worth a mark on its own.

E(X) = sum of x P(X = x) Key: E(X) = the expected value, the long-run average of X (same units as X); x = each possible value; P(X = x) = its probability. The value need not be attainable — 3.5 on a die is the standard example.

Var(X) = E(X²) - [E(X)]^2 Key: Var(X) = the variance, in squared units of X; E(X²) = the sum of x²P(X = x); [E(X)]² is the square of the mean, not the mean itself. The standard deviation is the square root and is back in the data's units.

E(aX + b) = a E(X) + b Key: a = the multiplier applied to every value (no units); b = the constant added to every value (X's units); E(X) = the mean before the change. Shifting every value shifts the mean by exactly the same amount.

Var(aX + b) = a² Var(X) Key: a = the multiplier; b = the constant shift, which does not appear at all because shifting every value leaves the spread unchanged. The variance scales by a², the standard deviation by the modulus of a — quoting a Var(aX) = a Var(X) loses the mark.

E(aX + bY) = a E(X) + b E(Y) Key: X, Y = two random variables; a, b = constants; this holds always, with or without independence, and it is the rule most often needed in applied questions.

Var(aX + bY) = a² Var(X) + b² Var(Y) Key: valid only when X and Y are independent, and the plus sign is unconditional — the variances add however the variables are combined, because uncertainties never cancel.

Var(aX - bY) = a² Var(X) + b² Var(Y) Key: the same rule for a difference: the sign in front of Y affects the expectation and not the variance. Var(X − Y) = 9 + 4 = 13, never 9 − 4.

F(x) = P(X <= x) = sum of P(X = k) for k <= x Key: F(x) = the cumulative distribution function, a probability (no units, between 0 and 1); x = the value asked about; k runs over every possible value at most x. For a discrete variable F is a step function, constant between values and jumping at each one.

P(X = k) = F(k) - F(k - 1) Key: recovers a single probability from the cumulative function; mind the inequality, because P(X < 3) = F(2) while P(X ≤ 3) = F(3) for a discrete variable.

E(X) = (n + 1)/2 and Var(X) = (n² - 1)/12 Key: for a discrete uniform distribution on 1 to n: n = the number of equally likely values (no units); the mean and variance follow from n alone. A fair die has n = 6, so E(X) = 3.5 and Var(X) = 35/12.

title: Formulae, Equations and Amount of Substance — Study Notes
content:
Formulae, Equations and Amount of Substance

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH11, Topic 1. The mole is the bridge between the mass you can weigh and the number of particles a reaction actually uses, so every quantitative question in the course depends on it.

Relative masses and the mole

  • Relative atomic mass (Ar) and relative molecular mass (Mr) are based on the carbon-12 scale.
  • One mole contains the Avogadro constant, 6.02 × 10²³ particles, and the molar mass in g mol⁻¹ equals Mr numerically.
  • Moles: n = m / M. Rearrange to find mass (m = n × M) or molar mass (M = m / n).

Empirical and molecular formulae

  • Convert percentage (or mass) composition to moles, divide by the smallest value and multiply until the ratios are whole numbers.
  • The molecular formula is a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula: n = Mr / Mr(empirical formula).

Equations and reacting masses

  • Balance equations by conserving each element, then use the coefficients as mole ratios.
  • Limiting reagent: work out the moles each reactant could give, then take the smallest.
  • Percentage yield = actual yield / theoretical yield × 100.

Solutions and gases

  • Concentration c = n / V, with V in dm³ (cm³ ÷ 1000). Titration data follow the same route.
  • At room temperature and pressure one mole of gas occupies 24 dm³, so n = V / 24.

Exam tip: write the unit on every line of working, and check that your final answer has the same number of significant figures as the least precise data given.

title: IGCSE Computer Science: Algorithm Design and Problem-Solving
content:
IGCSE Computer Science: Algorithm Design and Problem-Solving

Cambridge IGCSE Computer Science 0478 (2026–2028), Paper 2 Algorithms, Programming and Logic, statement 7 Algorithm design and problem-solving. Writing code is the last 20% of the job; this note is the other 80% — decomposition, abstraction, stepwise refinement, algorithm design and representation, and the testing that proves it works. Every refinement below is shown stage by stage, and the trace tables demonstrate the dry-run technique examiners expect you to produce under time pressure.

The problem-solving cycle

  • 1. Analyse the problem — state precisely what is wanted: the inputs, the required outputs, and any constraints (data ranges, time limits, the algorithm's likely size).
  • 2. Design — decompose into subtasks and design each algorithm (structure charts, pseudocode, flowcharts).
  • 3. Refine — develop each subtask stepwise until every step is a statement a coder could translate directly.
  • 4. Write the code — translate the refined design into a programming language.
  • 5. Test — run normal, boundary, erroneous and extreme data; compare results with expectations.
  • 6. Maintain — fix discovered bugs, adapt to new requirements, improve performance.

Skipping to step 4 is the failure mode this statement exists to cure: code written without a design is where logic errors breed.

Abstraction and decomposition

Decomposition breaks a big problem into smaller, independently solvable subproblems — planning a school trip becomes booking transport, booking accommodation, collecting money, producing a register. Each subtask is solved on its own and recombined. Abstraction is deliberately ignoring detail that does not matter to the task: a seat-booking system models seat numbers and states but not the fabric colour of the seats. Together they keep designs comprehensible — the exam wants a structure chart with named subtasks, not just prose.

Decomposition worked example: a school sports-day results system.

Level 0 (whole problem): record events, score house points, print winners.
Level 1 subtasks:
  1. Input event results (validation included)
  2. Convert places to house points
  3. Accumulate house totals
  4. Determine and print the winning house

Each level-1 subtask decomposes again - refinement of subtask 2:
  2.1  read the event's placing (1st, 2nd, 3rd)
  2.2  look up the points for that placing (5, 3, 1)
  2.3  add the points to the correct house total
  2.4  repeat for each event

At the end of refinement every leaf step is a single statement - that is the
stopping rule for stepwise refinement.

Stepwise refinement

Refinement turns an outline into detail in stages, keeping each stage reviewable. Start with one line; expand the hardest or vaguest part into steps; expand those; stop when each step is trivially translatable. The trace at each stage catches errors while they are cheap.

Refinement stages: "find the mean of a set of numbers".

Stage 0 (outline):     get the numbers, compute the mean, print it.

Stage 1:
  initialise total and count
  get the numbers, adding each to the total and counting it
  compute mean <- total / count
  print mean

Stage 2 (final pseudocode):
  1  total <- 0
  2  count <- 0
  3  INPUT num
  4  WHILE num <> -1              [-1 as a sentinel value meaning "no more"]
  5      total <- total + num
  6      count <- count + 1
  7      INPUT num
  8  ENDWHILE
  9  IF count > 0 THEN
 10      mean <- total / count
 11      OUTPUT mean
 12  ELSE
 13      OUTPUT "no data entered"
 14  ENDIF

Note what refinement surfaced: the empty-input case (line 9). Division by zero
would have been a runtime failure - refinement finds these before coding.

The sentinel (-1) is one way to end input; alternatives are a known count (read exactly n values) or an end-of-file test. State which you use and make sure the sentinel can never be legitimate data.

Representing algorithms

FormWhat it showsBest for
Structure chartWhole problem decomposed into named subtasks and their data linksThe overview; planning who does what
PseudocodeThe logic in structured, language-independent statementsPrecise design and exam answers
FlowchartFlow of control visually: oval start/stop, parallelogram I/O, rectangle process, diamond decisionShowing branches and loops at a glance
Trace tableVariable values statement by statement for given inputsProving correctness before coding
The same algorithm as a flowchart text sketch: reading marks until -1 and
counting passes (mark >= 40).

  (start) → [passes <- 0] → [INPUT mark] → <mark = -1?>
      | no                         | yes
      v                            v
  <mark >= 40?> --yes-→ [passes <- passes + 1] --+
      | no                                       |
      +------------------------------------------+
                                                 v
                                    [INPUT mark] → loop back to <mark = -1?>
  (stop) <- [OUTPUT passes]

Note the two diamonds in sequence: the loop test runs first on every value,
including the very first, and the sentinel is tested BEFORE the pass test so
-1 is never counted as a fail.

Trace tables and dry running

A trace table proves the design with real data before any code runs. One column per variable; one row per statement executed (loops repeat rows); outputs recorded as they happen. Always test at least: normal data, boundary data, and erroneous data.

Trace: count how many of 5 numbers exceed their predecessor.

  1  count <- 0
  2  INPUT previous
  3  FOR i <- 2 TO 5
  4      INPUT current
  5      IF current > previous THEN
  6          count <- count + 1
  7      ENDIF
  8      previous <- current
  9  NEXT i
 10  OUTPUT count

Inputs: 10, 15, 15, 9, 20

Step    i   previous  current  count   comment
1                             0
2             10              0
3       2      10             0
4       2      10      15     0
5       2      10      15     0   15 > 10 TRUE
6       2      10      15     1
8       2      15      15     1   previous tracks the latest
3       3      15             1
4       3      15      15     1
5       3      15      15     1   15 > 15 FALSE (equal is not greater)
8       3      15      15     1
3       4      15             1
4       4      15       9     1
5       4      15       9     1   9 > 15 FALSE
8       4       9       9     1
3       5       9             1
4       5       9      20     1
5       5       9      20     1   20 > 9 TRUE
6       5       9      20     2
8       5      20      20     2
10                        output 2

Boundary check: equal neighbours (15, 15) must NOT count - that row is the one
markers look for.

Testing

  • Normal (valid) data — typical values that should work; checks the happy path.
  • Boundary (extreme) data — values at the edges of validity (0 and 100 for marks, exactly at a threshold); most bugs live here.
  • Erroneous (invalid) data — values the program should reject (negative marks, letters where numbers are expected); checks validation and error handling.

Test data should be chosen deliberately with an expected result stated for each test before running it — otherwise you are checking what the program does, not what it should do. For the mean example above: normal (2, 4, 6 → mean 4), boundary (one value only → the value itself), erroneous (sentinel entered first → "no data entered", not a division by zero).

Iterative (agile) development is examined here too: develop in small iterations, each designing, coding and testing one subtask, then review with the client before the next. Advantages: working software early, changing requirements absorbed cheaply, frequent feedback and testing built in; disadvantages: unclear final scope and budget, and endless change without discipline. Against waterfall (one linear design→build→test→release pass): clear milestones and documentation, but late testing and expensive changes once built.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Jumping straight to code: marks are for analysis, decomposition and refinement stages — show them.
  • Decomposition that is too shallow: subtasks must reach single-statement steps ("input the numbers" is a subtask, not a refinement).
  • Test data without expected outputs; and boundary values are worth as many marks as the normal case.
  • Forgetting the empty-input and division-by-zero case in averages — the most-missed validation mark in Paper 2.
  • Sentinel values that collide with real data (using -1 to stop, when -1 is a valid score).
  • Trace tables that skip loop repetitions or show only the final value; markers want the statement-by-statement rows.
  • Confusing validation (is the data in range?) with verification (is the data the right data — e.g. double entry).
  • Listing agile benefits alone; the question usually wants the comparison against a linear model stated explicitly.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 2, 4 marks). Explain what is meant by decomposition and abstraction, giving an example of each.

Answer: Decomposition splits a problem into smaller subproblems that can be solved separately — an online shop system breaks into stock control, basket, payment and delivery subsystems. Abstraction ignores details irrelevant to the problem — the basket subsystem models items and quantities but not the warehouse's shelf colours, so the design stays manageable.

Question 2 (Paper 2, 4 marks). Refine the step "process the order" into structured pseudocode.

Answer: READ order lines from the file; FOR each line: check the item is in stock; IF in stock THEN add the line total (price × quantity) to orderTotal and reduce stock; ELSE record the item as out of stock; NEXT; apply any discount to orderTotal; OUTPUT orderTotal and the out-of-stock list.

Question 3 (Paper 2, 3 marks). State three types of test data and give one example of each for a program accepting a mark between 0 and 100.

Answer: Normal data — a typical in-range value such as 65. Boundary data — the edge values 0 and 100 (and just outside, 101). Erroneous data — an invalid value such as -5 or the letter "A".

Question 4 (Paper 2, 4 marks). Explain why a trace table is produced before code is written.

Answer: A trace table executes the algorithm step by step on paper, recording each variable's value after every statement, so logic errors — infinite loops, wrong branch conditions, off-by-one errors — are found while the design is still cheap to change. It also provides the expected outputs used later as test data, so the coded program can be checked against a proven result.

Question 5 (Paper 2, 4 marks). Compare iterative development with a waterfall approach.

Answer: Iterative development builds in small cycles with client review after each, delivering working software early and absorbing requirement changes cheaply, at the cost of a less predictable final scope and budget. Waterfall completes each stage before the next, giving fixed milestones, clear documentation and easy planning, but testing happens late and changes after coding are expensive.

Question 6 (Paper 2, 5 marks). Write pseudocode that reads numbers until the user enters 0, then outputs the largest number entered (0 not counted).

Answer: largest <- 0; INPUT num; WHILE num <> 0; IF num > largest THEN; largest <- num; ENDIF; INPUT num; ENDWHILE; OUTPUT largest. (Assumes positive input; a full solution might flag if no positive number was entered.)

These design skills now apply to the two remaining Paper 2 domains: databases and Boolean logic.

title: Transformations and Vectors — Study Notes
content:
Transformations and Vectors

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): reflection, rotation, translation, enlargement (incl. negative SF); vector notation, resultant, magnitude, vector geometry.

1. Transformations — full descriptions

  • Reflection: mirror line (x = 0, y = x, y = −x…).
  • Rotation: centre, angle, direction (anticlockwise positive).
  • Translation: column vector.
  • Enlargement: centre + scale factor; negative SF inverts through the centre.

"Enlargement, SF 2, centre (0, 3)" — every word earns a mark.

2. Combined transformations

Apply right-to-left: "reflect in y = x, then rotate 90°" — rotate the reflected image.

3. Vectors

  • Column vector (x; y); magnitude = √(x² + y²).
  • Resultant by component addition; parallel vectors are scalar multiples.
  • Position vectors: AB = OB − OA.

Example: A(1, 2), B(4, 6): AB = (3; 4), |AB| = 5.

4. Vector geometry

Midpoint of AB = ½(a + b). Prove collinearity: show AB = k·BC (shared point). Prove parallelogram: AB = DC. Use route paths: AC = AB + BC.

Exam tips: tracing paper is allowed for transformations; in proofs, end with a conclusion sentence ("hence A, B, C are collinear").

Translations

A translation moves every point the same distance in the same direction, described by a column vector (x; y): x units across (positive to the right) and y units up (positive upwards). The shape and orientation do not change.

Reflections, rotations and enlargements

A reflection is described by its mirror line, such as x = 2 or y = x. A rotation needs its centre, angle and direction. An enlargement needs its centre and scale factor; a negative scale factor inverts the image. Check the image by measuring its distance from the centre.

Vectors and magnitude

Write a column vector as (x; y). Its magnitude is √(x² + y²). Adding vectors adds the corresponding components, and multiplying by a scalar multiplies each component. The vector from A to B is found as the position vector of B minus the position vector of A.

title: A2 Level Chemistry: Entropy and Energetics
content:
A2 Level Chemistry: Entropy and Energetics

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH14, Topic 12 covers the concept of entropy and energetics, including the relationship between enthalpy, entropy, and the feasibility of reactions. This topic explains that enthalpy alone does not decide whether a reaction happens, and that entropy measures how energy and matter are spread out. The Gibbs energy combines enthalpy and entropy to predict feasibility.

Entropy

Entropy S measures the disorder or the number of ways energy can be dispersed. Its standard unit is J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Entropy increases when a solid melts or dissolves, when a liquid evaporates, and when the number of gas molecules increases. Entropy decreases when gas molecules condense or when a crystal forms from solution.

  • Entropy increases with temperature.
  • Entropy increases as solid, liquid, gas.
  • Perfect crystals at zero kelvin have zero entropy.
  • Standard entropy values are given in data books.
  • The entropy change for a reaction is ΔS = Σ S(products) − Σ S(reactants).

Entropy Changes

Entropy changes occur during changes of state, dissolving of a solid ionic lattice, and reactions in which there is a change in the number of moles from reactants to products.

  • ΔS = +ve for endothermic processes.
  • ΔS = -ve for exothermic processes.
  • ΔS = +ve for increase in moles of gas.
  • ΔS = -ve for decrease in moles of gas.

Total Entropy Change

The total entropy change is ΔS total = ΔS system + ΔS surroundings. For the surroundings, ΔS surroundings = −ΔH / T.

  • ΔS total = ΔS system + ΔS surroundings.
  • ΔS surroundings = −ΔH / T.

Gibbs Free Energy

The Gibbs energy change is ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, where T is in kelvin. ΔH is in J mol⁻¹ and ΔS in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, so convert ΔH from kJ to J before calculating.

  • ΔG = ΔH − TΔS.
  • A reaction is feasible when ΔG is negative.
  • When ΔG = 0 the system is at equilibrium.

Temperature and Feasibility

For a reaction with positive ΔH and positive ΔS, ΔG becomes negative above the temperature T = ΔH / ΔS. High temperature therefore makes the reaction feasible.

  • For a reaction with ΔH positive and ΔS positive, ΔG becomes negative above T = ΔH / ΔS.
  • For a reaction with ΔH positive and ΔS negative, ΔG is always positive, so the reaction is never feasible.

Worked Example

For CaCO3 → CaO + CO2, ΔH = +178 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS = +161 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. The temperature at which ΔG = 0 is T = 178 000 / 161 = 1106 K, so the decomposition becomes feasible above about 1100 K.

Thermodynamic Stability and Kinetic Stability

Thermodynamic stability refers to the feasibility of a reaction, while kinetic stability refers to the rate of the reaction.

  • Thermodynamic stability: ΔG negative.
  • Kinetic stability: slow reaction rate.

Standard Enthalpy Change of Atomisation

The standard enthalpy change of atomisation is the energy required to break one mole of a substance into its constituent atoms.

  • ΔH atomisation = energy required to break one mole of a substance into its constituent atoms.

Electron Affinity

Electron affinity is the energy released when an electron is added to an atom.

  • Electron affinity = energy released when an electron is added to an atom.

Lattice Energy

Lattice energy is the energy released when one mole of an ionic solid is formed from its gaseous ions.

  • Lattice energy = energy released when one mole of an ionic solid is formed from its gaseous ions.

Born-Haber Cycle

A Born-Haber cycle is a diagram that shows the energy changes involved in the formation of an ionic solid from its constituent elements.

  • Born-Haber cycle: diagram showing energy changes involved in the formation of an ionic solid.

Covalent Bonding

Covalent bonding refers to the sharing of electrons between atoms.

  • Covalent bonding: sharing of electrons between atoms.

Polarisation of Anions

Polarisation of anions refers to the distortion of the electron cloud of an anion by a nearby cation.

  • Polarisation of anions: distortion of electron cloud of an anion by a nearby cation.

Enthalpy Change of Solution

Enthalpy change of solution is the energy change involved in the dissolution of a substance.

  • Enthalpy change of solution = energy change involved in the dissolution of a substance.

Enthalpy Change of Hydration

Enthalpy change of hydration is the energy change involved in the hydration of an ion.

  • Enthalpy change of hydration = energy change involved in the hydration of an ion.

Typical Mistakes

  • Forgetting to convert ΔH from kJ to J before calculating ΔG.
  • Not using the correct units for ΔS and ΔH.
  • Not considering the sign of ΔS and ΔH when determining the feasibility of a reaction.

Exam-Style Questions

  1. What is the entropy change for the reaction CaCO3 → CaO + CO2? Answer: ΔS = +161 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
  2. What is the temperature at which the reaction CaCO3 → CaO + CO2 becomes feasible? Answer: T = 1106 K.
  3. What is the lattice energy of an ionic solid? Answer: Lattice energy = energy released when one mole of an ionic solid is formed from its gaseous ions.

To revise this topic, make sure to understand the concepts of entropy, Gibbs free energy, and thermodynamic stability. Practice calculating ΔG and determining the feasibility of reactions. Also, make sure to remember the typical mistakes and how to avoid them. After revising this topic, move on to the next topic, which covers the kinetics of chemical reactions.

Detailed Born-Haber Cycle Calculations

Constructing a Born-Haber cycle requires applying Hess's Law to equate the enthalpy change of formation of an ionic compound to the sum of its stepwise enthalpy changes: atomisation of the metal, first (and subsequent) ionisation energies of the metal, atomisation of the non-metal, electron affinities of the non-metal, and lattice energy. For magnesium chloride, MgCl2, the cycle starts with Mg(s) + Cl2(g) going to MgCl2(s). The steps are: enthalpy of atomisation of Mg, first and second ionisation energies of Mg, twice the enthalpy of atomisation of chlorine (or bond enthalpy of Cl2), twice the first electron affinity of chlorine, and lattice energy. Rearranging the energy level loop allows any single unknown enthalpy term to be calculated.

  • Write the thermochemical equation for formation at the bottom level.
  • Draw upward arrows for endothermic processes: atomisation, ionisation energies, and bond dissociation.
  • Draw downward arrows for exothermic processes: electron affinities and lattice energy.
  • Set the sum of energy changes along the direct route equal to the alternative pathway route.

Worked Example: Born-Haber Cycle for Sodium Chloride

Calculate the lattice energy of sodium chloride, NaCl, using the following standard enthalpy changes: enthalpy of formation of NaCl = −411 kJ mol⁻¹, enthalpy of atomisation of Na = +107 kJ mol⁻¹, first ionisation energy of Na = +496 kJ mol⁻¹, enthalpy of atomisation of Cl2 = +121 kJ mol⁻¹, and first electron affinity of Cl = −364 kJ mol⁻¹. The equation linking these is: ΔHf = ΔHat(Na) + IE1(Na) + 1/2 ΔHdiss(Cl2) + EA1(Cl) + Lattice Energy. Substituting the values: −411 = 107 + 496 + 121 + (−364) + Lattice Energy. Solving gives: −411 = 360 + Lattice Energy, so Lattice Energy = −411 − 360 = −771 kJ mol⁻¹.

Experimental Versus Theoretical Lattice Energies

Perfect ionic model assumes spherical point charges with 100 percent electrostatic attraction. When experimental lattice energies obtained from Born-Haber cycles are more exothermic than theoretical values calculated from electrostatic theory, it indicates that additional bonding character is present. This extra stability arises from partial covalent character caused by the polarisation of the anion.

  • Larger difference between experimental and theoretical values signifies greater covalent character.
  • Polarisation is promoted by small, highly charged cations (high charge density) and large, easily polarisable anions.
  • Fajans' rules help rationalize these trends across different halides and oxides.

Hydration Enthalpies and Enthalpy of Solution

Enthalpy change of solution is the enthalpy change when one mole of a solute dissolves in water to form an infinitely dilute solution. This is related to lattice energy and hydration enthalpies by the equation: ΔHsol = Lattice Energy + Σ ΔHhyd(ions). Because lattice energy is endothermic when viewed as breaking the lattice (positive value) and hydration is exothermic (negative value), the overall enthalpy of solution can be slightly positive, zero, or negative. For sparingly soluble salts, ΔHsol is strongly positive.

  • Hydration enthalpy is always exothermic (negative) due to ion-dipole attractions between the gaseous ions and water molecules.
  • Magnitude of hydration enthalpy increases with increasing ionic charge and decreasing ionic radius.
  • Magnitude of lattice energy also increases with high charge and small radius, meaning lattice energy and hydration enthalpy tend to counteract each other across periodic trends.

Solubility Trends in Group 1 and Group 2 Compounds

The solubility of ionic compounds depends on the balance between lattice energy and hydration enthalpies, alongside the entropy change of the system and surroundings. Down Group 2, both lattice energy and hydration enthalpies decrease in magnitude as the cation radius increases, but hydration enthalpy decreases faster for smaller anions (like sulfates) compared to larger anions (like hydroxides).

  • Group 2 sulfates become less soluble down the group because the hydration enthalpy drops faster than the lattice energy, making ΔHsol increasingly endothermic.
  • Group 2 hydroxides become more soluble down the group because lattice energy decreases more rapidly than hydration enthalpy, making ΔHsol less endothermic or more exothermic.
  • Overall feasibility of dissolving requires calculating ΔStotal using ΔHsol and the entropy change of the solution process.

Typical Mistakes in Energetics and Born-Haber Cycles

  • Omitting the stoichiometric multipliers when using bond enthalpies or atomisation energies for diatomic gases like chlorine or oxygen.
  • Confusing first and second electron affinities, where second electron affinities are endothermic due to repulsion with the incoming electron.
  • Forgetting that lattice energy in standard definitions is exothermic, but must be treated with the correct sign when substituting into energy cycle equations depending on the cycle direction used.

Exam-Style Questions and Worked Solutions

  1. Define the standard enthalpy change of atomisation. Answer: The enthalpy change when one mole of gaseous atoms is formed from the element in its standard state under standard conditions. Credit is earned by mentioning 'one mole of gaseous atoms' and 'element in its standard state'.
  2. Explain why the experimental lattice energy of silver iodide is significantly more exothermic than the theoretical value. Answer: Silver ions have a d-block configuration that polarises the large iodide ion effectively, introducing covalent character which releases extra energy. Credit is earned by linking cation polarisation of the anion to increased stability.
  3. Calculate the enthalpy of solution of potassium chloride given that its lattice energy is −701 kJ mol⁻¹ and the sum of the hydration enthalpies of its ions is −684 kJ mol⁻¹. Answer: ΔHsol = Lattice Energy + Σ ΔHhyd = 701 (if defined as formation) or using standard sign conventions, ΔHsol = −684 − (−701) = +17 kJ mol⁻¹ (or using the exact cycle definition, −701 + 684 = −17 kJ mol⁻¹ depending on data book sign convention for lattice energy release vs absorption). Step for credit: showing ΔHsol = Lattice Energy + Hydration Enthalpies with proper sign substitution.

title: Binomial Distribution — Study Notes
content:
The Binomial Distribution

When Binomial Applies

X ~ B(n, p) counts successes in n independent trials when:

  • a fixed number n of identical trials,
  • each trial ends in success or failure,
  • constant success probability p,
  • trials are independent.

Check all four before using the model — "justifying a binomial model" is a real exam question.

The Formula

P(X = r) = ⁿCᵣ pʳ(1 − p)ⁿ⁻ʳ for r = 0, 1, ..., n. The ⁿCᵣ counts which r of the n trials were the successes.

Example: X ~ B(5, 0.3). P(X = 2) = ¹⁰C₂? No — ⁵C₂ × 0.3² × 0.7³ = 10 × 0.09 × 0.343 = 0.3087.

Cumulative Probabilities

P(X ≤ 2) = P(0) + P(1) + P(2). "At least" questions convert by the complement: P(X ≥ 2) = 1 − P(X ≤ 1). Keep one extra decimal place in intermediate steps to avoid rounding drift.

Expectation and Variance

  • E(X) = np and Var(X) = np(1 − p)

For X ~ B(20, 0.4): E(X) = 8 and Var(X) = 4.8.

Modelling Decisions

If trials are dependent (drawing without replacement from a small population) binomial is not appropriate. If p changes between trials it is not binomial. When n is large and p small, the binomial is approximately Poisson — but at A2 you usually stay exact.

Exam tips: identify n and p in words before touching the calculator. For P(X ≥ k) always rewrite as 1 − P(X ≤ k − 1). Tables give cumulative values — use them rather than summing by hand.

Exam method: binomial probabilities

If X ~ B(n, p) then X counts successes in n independent trials, each with probability p. P(X = r) = nCr p^r (1 - p)^(n - r) for r = 0, 1, ..., n. The mean is np and the variance is np(1 - p).

Check the conditions first: a fixed number of trials, two outcomes, a constant p and independent trials. If any condition fails, the binomial model does not apply.

Exam cue: Always state n and p before calculating, and say which condition you are checking. For P(X ≥ r) or P(X > r), use the complement 1 − P(X ≤ r − 1), read from the cumulative table or calculator, and state the final probability to three significant figures.

Worked example: a binomial probability

A biased coin lands on heads with probability 0.3. Let X be the number of heads in 10 throws, so X ~ B(10, 0.3). The probability of exactly 3 heads is P(X = 3) = C(10, 3) × 0.3³ × 0.7⁷ = 120 × 0.027 × 0.08235 = 0.2668 (to 4 decimal places). The coefficient 120 counts the arrangements of the 3 heads among 10 throws, and it is needed because the heads may fall in any of those positions.

At least one success

For P(X ≥ 1), use the complement: P(X ≥ 1) = 1 − P(X = 0) = 1 − 0.7¹⁰ = 1 − 0.02825 = 0.9718. Examiners look for this shortcut, and writing the full sum from X = 1 to X = 10 is both slower and more error-prone.

Checking the mean and variance

  • Mean: E(X) = np = 10 × 0.3 = 3.
  • Variance: Var(X) = np(1 − p) = 10 × 0.3 × 0.7 = 2.1, so the standard deviation is √2.1 = 1.45 (to 2 decimal places).

Use these values to judge whether a stated answer is sensible: a mean of 3 with a standard deviation of 1.45 means most results fall between 1 and 5.

Exam point: a binomial model needs a fixed number of trials, independence, and the same probability of success on each trial. If the items are drawn without replacement from a small group, the probability changes after each draw and the binomial model is not valid.

title: AS Level Physics: Kinematics
content:
AS Level Physics: Kinematics

Edexcel International A Level Physics, Unit 1 (WPH11) Mechanics and Materials — motion in a straight line and in a plane, and the measurement skills the companion Unit 3 paper (WPH13, Practical Skills in Physics I) examines. Everything in mechanics starts here: quantities with units and directions, the equations of motion, free fall, projectiles and the graphs that describe them. The unit also demands real data-handling skill — uncertainties, error bars, gradients and intercepts — because WPH13 is a written paper that marks your experimental thinking, not your hands.

Quantities, units, scalars and vectors

A physical quantity is a number with a unit, and every unit in mechanics is built from four SI base units: the metre (m), kilogram (kg), second (s) and ampere (A). Speed in m s⁻¹ and force in newtons (1 N = 1 kg m s⁻²) are derived from them. A scalar has size only — distance, speed, mass, time, energy, power. A vector has size and direction — displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, momentum. The distinction is operational, not decorative: vectors add by direction, and every mechanics question that mentions direction is testing it.

  • Two vectors in a line: add if in the same direction, subtract if opposite, and state the direction of the resultant.
  • Two vectors at right angles: the resultant is the hypotenuse, R = √(A² + B²), at an angle θ = tan⁻¹(B/A) to A.
  • Any two vectors: resolve each into perpendicular components with A cos θ and A sin θ, add the components separately, then recombine.

Resolution is the workhorse of A-level mechanics. A force F at angle θ to the horizontal has a horizontal component F cos θ along the motion and a vertical component F sin θ across it; only the component along the motion changes the motion. Sign convention is chosen, not given: for vertical motion taking up as positive makes g = −9.81 m s⁻²; for slopes, taking down the slope as positive is usually simplest.

Motion in a straight line

Uniform motion means constant velocity; accelerated motion means changing velocity. The five quantities in every equation of motion are: displacement s (m), initial velocity u (m s⁻¹), final velocity v (m s⁻¹), acceleration a (m s⁻²), and time t (s). Average velocity is (u + v)/2 only when the acceleration is constant.

QuantityDefinitionUnitScalar or vector
DisplacementDistance from a start point in a stated directionmVector
VelocityRate of change of displacementm s⁻¹Vector
AccelerationRate of change of velocitym s⁻²Vector
SpeedDistance travelled per unit timem s⁻¹Scalar

The equations of motion

For motion with constant acceleration, four equations connect the five quantities. They are valid only while a is constant, and they are all vector equations, so the sign convention must be applied to u, v, a and s consistently.

v = u + a t
s = u t + 1/2 a t^2
v^2 = u^2 + 2 a s
s = 1/2 (u + v) t
  • Each equation omits one quantity: pick the equation that does not contain the unknown you do not need.
  • Units must be SI before substituting: kilometres to metres, minutes to seconds, km h⁻¹ to m s⁻¹ (divide by 3.6).
  • Direction convention: write one down before touching the algebra — for example, upward positive means a falling object has a = −9.81 m s⁻² and a downward displacement is negative.

Free fall and projectile motion

Free fall is motion under gravity alone. Near the Earth's surface the acceleration is g = 9.81 m s⁻² downwards and is constant (air resistance neglected), so the equations of motion apply directly. An object thrown straight up decelerates at 9.81 m s⁻², stops instantaneously at the top, and falls back with the same acceleration; the time up equals the time down from the same height.

A projectile is any object moving under gravity alone once launched. The key insight is independence of components: the horizontal motion has zero acceleration and constant velocity, while the vertical motion has constant acceleration g. Resolve the launch velocity into u cos θ horizontally and u sin θ vertically, treat the two motions separately with the equations of motion, and combine at the end. At the highest point the vertical velocity is zero but the horizontal velocity is unchanged — the projectile is never at rest. The trajectory is a parabola.

Motion graphs

GraphGradient givesArea gives
Displacement–timeVelocityNot used
Velocity–timeAccelerationChange in displacement
Acceleration–timeNot usedChange in velocity

The equation s = ½(u + v)t is the area of a trapezium under a velocity–time graph, and v² = u² + 2as is what falls out of that geometry — which is why the equations and the graphs never disagree. Curved velocity–time graphs mean changing acceleration; the gradient at a point is found from a tangent drawn with a ruler and evaluated between two distant points on the tangent.

Non-uniform motion: drag and terminal velocity

When a real object falls, air resistance (drag) acts opposite to the motion and grows with speed. The resultant force is weight minus drag, so the acceleration is greatest at the start and falls as speed rises. When drag equals the weight the resultant force is zero and the object continues at terminal velocity. A skydiver reaches terminal velocity in free fall, opens the parachute (which raises drag enormously), and decelerates to a much lower terminal velocity before landing. The same physics sets the thinking and braking distances of a vehicle: thinking distance grows with reaction time and speed; braking distance grows with the square of the speed, because the work the brakes must do is ½mv².

Unit 3 skills: measurement, data and uncertainty

WPH13 examines the practical skills of Units 1 and 2 in writing, using unfamiliar contexts. The marks come from method and analysis, and the analysis rules are fixed.

  • Absolute uncertainty is the precision of the instrument: ±0.5 of the smallest scale division for an analogue scale, ± the smallest reading for a digital one. A length of 24.5 mm on a ruler carries ±0.5 mm.
