The same reasoning explains why a strong correlation from a small sample deserves caution: with only a handful of points, a pattern can appear by chance, and a single outlier can create or destroy the apparent trend.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Describe) Points on a scatter diagram trend downward and are tightly clustered. Describe the correlation. Answer: Strong negative correlation — as one variable increases, the other tends to decrease consistently.
  2. (No correlation) Describe a scatter diagram whose points form a random cloud. Answer: No correlation — there is no clear trend between the variables.
  3. (Line) State two features of a correctly drawn line of best fit. Answer: A straight line through the middle of the points with roughly equal numbers above and below, following the trend and drawn with a ruler.
  4. (Estimate) A line of best fit passes through (2, 10) and (6, 26). Estimate y at x = 4. Answer: gradient 4; y = 4x + 2; at x = 4, y = 18.
  5. (Interpolation) Explain why an estimate inside the data range is more reliable than one outside it. Answer: Inside the range the trend is supported by nearby data points (interpolation); outside it (extrapolation) there is no evidence that the relationship continues in the same way.
  6. (Causation) A shop finds that sales of umbrellas and sales of coats rise together. Explain the correlation without claiming that umbrellas cause coat sales. Answer: Both are driven by a third variable — rainy weather — which increases demand for both; the correlation is association, not causation.
  7. (Outlier) One point sits far from the trend. What should you do with it when drawing the line? Answer: Note it as an outlier and draw the line through the main body of points; do not let one point pull the line away from the trend.
  8. (Strength) Two scatter diagrams both show positive correlation; in one the points are close to the line. Compare them. Answer: The tighter diagram shows stronger positive correlation; the looser one shows weaker positive correlation.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Joining the dots: a line of best fit is a single straight line through the trend, never a zigzag connecting points.
  • Forcing through the origin: the line passes through the middle of the cloud; there is no reason for it to start at (0, 0).
  • Reading a point instead of the line: estimates come from the line of best fit, not from the nearest plotted point.
  • Ignoring outliers: one extreme point should not swing the line; note it and fit the main cluster.
  • Weak description: "positive" alone is incomplete — direction and strength, with variables named.
  • Causal language: "revision causes higher scores" overclaims from observational data; write "is associated with" and mention confounding factors.
  • Extrapolating confidently: beyond the data range, state the estimate is unreliable.
  • Axes: plot the explanatory variable on the horizontal axis and the response on the vertical, label both with units, and use the given scales exactly.

title: IGCSE Physics: Forces and Motion
content:
IGCSE Physics: Forces and Motion

Cambridge IGCSE Physics 0625 (2026–2028), Topic 1 Motion, forces and energy: statements 1.2 Motion, 1.3 Mass and weight, 1.5 Forces and 1.6 Momentum. This is the mechanics spine of the whole course, and it is where the Paper 4 structured calculation marks are won and lost. Almost every mechanics question begins the same way: label the velocities, find the resultant force, then choose the equation. The ideas below are built from absolute zero, but the definitions are examinable word for word, so learn them exactly as stated.

Speed, velocity and acceleration

Start with an analogy. A car's speedometer tells you how fast the car is covering ground; it says nothing about which way the car points. That everyday reading is speed. Add a compass direction to it and you have velocity. Speed is a scalar (size only); velocity is a vector (size and direction), and that single distinction runs through the entire course.

QuantityDefinitionSymbol and unitScalar or vector
DistanceTotal length of the path travelleds, metre (m)Scalar
DisplacementDistance in a stated straight-line direction from a start points, metre (m)Vector
SpeedDistance travelled per unit timev, metre per second (m s⁻¹)Scalar
VelocityRate of change of displacement, i.e. speed in a stated directionv, metre per second (m s⁻¹)Vector
AccelerationRate of change of velocitya, metre per second squared (m s⁻²)Vector

The two equations every question uses are:

average speed = total distance travelled / total time taken        v = s / t
acceleration = (final velocity - initial velocity) / time taken    a = (v - u) / t

Here u is the initial velocity, v is the final velocity, and t is the time taken. The SI units must be metres, seconds and metres per second before the equations are used; convert kilometres to metres and minutes to seconds first. The sign convention is the student's choice but must be stated: pick one direction as positive (upwards or forwards is usual), then velocities and accelerations in the opposite direction are negative. A negative acceleration that slows an object is often called a deceleration. An object thrown upwards has g = 9.81 m s⁻² downwards throughout its flight, so if up is positive its acceleration is −9.81 m s⁻² at every point, including the instant it stops at the top.

Average speed over a whole journey is not the average of the speeds. It is total distance divided by total time, so a car that covers 100 km at 50 km h⁻¹ and the next 100 km at 100 km h⁻¹ has an average speed of 200 km in 3 hours, which is 67 km h⁻¹, not 75 km h⁻¹.

Describing motion with graphs

Graphs are the language of this topic, and Paper 4 nearly always carries one. Two kinds do all the work.

FeatureDistance–time graphSpeed–time graph
GradientSpeed (or velocity)Acceleration
Area under the graphNot meaningfulDistance travelled
Horizontal lineObject at restConstant speed, zero acceleration
Straight sloping lineConstant speedConstant acceleration
CurveChanging speed (draw a tangent to find the speed at a point)Changing acceleration

On a distance–time graph the gradient is the distance moved divided by the time taken, which is the speed. On a speed–time graph the gradient is the change in speed divided by the time taken, which is the acceleration, and the area under the graph is made of rectangles (speed × time = distance) and triangles (½ × base × height), so it gives the total distance travelled. Drawing a tangent to a curve at a point is a Paper 6 skill: place the ruler so it just touches the curve, extend the line well past the curve on both sides, and take two distant points on the tangent to work out its gradient.

Paper 6 link. A trolley pulled by a falling mass leaves dots on ticker tape from a 50 Hz timer, so consecutive dots are 0.02 s apart. The distance between successive dots gives the speed over that interval, and a speed–time graph of those speeds has a gradient equal to the trolley's acceleration. Measuring a short distance with a ruler and dividing by 0.02 s is exactly the averaging technique in statement 1.1.

Mass, weight and gravitational field strength

Mass is the amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms with a balance. It does not change wherever the object is taken: the mass of an astronaut is the same on the Moon as on Earth. Weight is the force of gravity on that mass, measured in newtons with a spring balance, and it is a vector because gravity always pulls towards the centre of the attracting body. The astronaut's weight on the Moon is about one sixth of that on Earth because the Moon's gravitational field is weaker.

weight = mass x gravitational field strength        W = m g
  • W: weight in newtons (N). Weight is a vector, and its direction is straight down towards the centre of the Earth.
  • m: mass in kilograms (kg). Mass is a scalar.
  • g: gravitational field strength in newtons per kilogram (N kg⁻¹); on Earth g ≈ 9.81 N kg⁻¹, which is numerically the same as the free-fall acceleration 9.81 m s⁻².

Examination questions give the value of g to use, and many IGCSE papers round it to 10 N kg⁻¹ to keep the arithmetic simple. Always use the value printed in the question, and quote it in your answer when you substitute. Never confuse the two instruments: a balance compares masses and would give the same reading on the Moon, while a newton meter compares weights and would not.

Forces and their effects

A force is a push or a pull, measured in newtons, and it is a vector: direction matters. Forces can change an object's speed, change its direction of travel, or change its shape. Newton's first law states that an object remains at rest, or continues at constant velocity in a straight line, unless a resultant (net) force acts on it. Motion only changes when forces are unbalanced; a book resting on a table has weight and an equal upward normal contact force acting on it, so its resultant force is zero and it does not accelerate.

The resultant force is the single force that has the same effect as all the real forces combined. Two people pushing a trolley the same way add; pushing opposite ways subtract; forces at right angles combine by Pythagoras on the diagonal (Supplement). Newton's second law, in the form examined at IGCSE, is a Supplement statement:

resultant force = mass x acceleration        F = m a
  • F: resultant force in newtons (N), positive in the chosen positive direction.
  • m: mass in kilograms (kg).
  • a: acceleration in metres per second squared (m s⁻²), in the same direction as F.

The equation only works with the resultant force and only in SI units. If a car's engine produces 3000 N while drag is 1000 N, the resultant is 2000 N, and it is that 2000 N that goes into F = ma.

Friction and drag. Friction acts where surfaces touch and always opposes the motion or the tendency to move. Drag (air resistance or water resistance) opposes motion through a fluid and grows as the speed grows. A falling object released from rest therefore accelerates at first, because weight exceeds drag; as speed rises, drag rises until it equals the weight. From that moment the resultant force is zero, the acceleration is zero, and the object falls at terminal velocity. This is a Supplement explanation and it is a regular Paper 4 six-mark question: describe the motion in stages and use the words resultant force, drag and terminal velocity.

Springs and extension. A load hung on a spring stretches it. The relationship is summarised on a load–extension graph: a straight line through the origin shows extension proportional to load, up to the limit of proportionality. The stiffness of the spring is its spring constant:

force = spring constant x extension        F = k x
  • F: force applied to the spring in newtons (N).
  • k: spring constant in newtons per metre (N m⁻¹); larger k means a stiffer spring.
  • x: extension in metres (m). Extension = stretched length − original length, so it is a scalar in practice.

Beyond the limit of proportionality the line curves: the spring is permanently deformed and does not return to its original length when the load is removed. Doubling the load doubles the extension only while the graph is still a straight line. Two identical springs in series share the load and stretch twice as far; in parallel they share the load and stretch half as far (Supplement).

Turning effects of forces: moments

A force that does not act through a pivot makes an object turn. The size of that turning effect is the moment of the force:

moment of a force = force x perpendicular distance from the pivot        M = F d
  • M: moment in newton metres (N m). A moment is a vector in the sense that it turns clockwise or anticlockwise, and that sense must be carried through the calculation as a sign.
  • F: force in newtons (N).
  • d: perpendicular distance from the line of action of the force to the pivot in metres (m).

The word perpendicular is the whole mark. If a 10 N force acts at 30° to a spanner handle, the moment uses the perpendicular component of the force, or equivalently the perpendicular distance. For an object in equilibrium the principle of moments applies: the sum of the clockwise moments about any pivot equals the sum of the anticlockwise moments, and the resultant force is zero. A see-saw balances when the anticlockwise moment of the near child equals the clockwise moment of the far child; moving either child outwards increases that child's moment without changing their weight. Two equal and opposite forces whose lines of action do not coincide form a couple, which produces rotation without translation, as when a steering wheel is turned with both hands.

Centre of gravity and stability

The centre of gravity of an object is the single point through which its entire weight may be taken to act. For a uniform object it is the geometric centre; for a lamina (a flat sheet) it can be found experimentally by the plumb-line method, which is a classic Paper 6 task: hang the lamina freely from one hole, hang a plumb line from the same pin, and mark the line; repeat from a second hole; the lines cross at the centre of gravity.

Stability depends on where that point sits relative to the base. An object topples when the line of action of its weight falls outside its base, because the weight then produces a resultant moment that overturns it. Wide bases and low centres of gravity make objects stable (racing cars carry ballast low; tall trucks are loaded low), and top-heavy objects with narrow bases topple easily.

Momentum and impulse

Momentum is the quantity of motion a moving object carries: a lorry at 20 m s⁻¹ is far harder to stop than a bicycle at the same speed. Momentum is a Supplement statement for 0625 and is a favourite for Paper 4 calculation questions.

momentum = mass x velocity        p = m v
impulse = change in momentum = resultant force x time        F t = m v - m u
  • p: momentum in kilogram metres per second (kg m s⁻¹). Momentum is a vector, in the same direction as the velocity, so the sign convention chosen at the start must be applied to every velocity.
  • m: mass in kilograms (kg); v and u: final and initial velocity in metres per second (m s⁻¹), positive in the chosen positive direction.
  • Impulse: newton seconds (N s), equal to the change in momentum.

The principle of conservation of momentum: in a closed system, where no external resultant force acts, the total momentum before an event equals the total momentum after it. Total means the vector sum: momenta in opposite directions carry opposite signs. This one statement solves collisions, explosions and recoil problems. Newton's second law in its full form is implied here: the resultant force equals the rate of change of momentum, F = (mv − mu)/t, which is why increasing the time of impact reduces the force for the same change in momentum — that is how airbags, crash barriers and landing on a bent knee work.

Worked example: collision and impact force

Collision. A 1200 kg car travelling at 15 m s⁻¹ runs into a stationary 800 kg car and the two lock together. Find their common velocity. Take the first car's direction as positive.

total momentum before = 1200 × 15 + 800 × 0 = 18 000 kg m s⁻¹
total momentum after = (1200 + 800) v = 2000 v
2000 v = 18 000, so v = 9 m s⁻¹, in the original direction

The combined cars move at 9 m s⁻¹ in the direction the first car was travelling. Note that kinetic energy is not conserved in this collision — most of it is lost to sound and deformation — but momentum is always conserved.

Impact force. A 0.50 kg ball travelling at 12 m s⁻¹ hits a wall and rebounds at 8 m s⁻¹ in the opposite direction. The contact lasts 0.050 s. Find the average force on the ball. Take the initial direction as positive, so the rebound velocity is −8 m s⁻¹.

change in momentum = m v - m u = 0.50 x (-8) - 0.50 × 12 = -4.0 - 6.0 = -10 kg m s⁻¹
average force = change in momentum / time = -10 / 0.050 = -200 N

The minus sign shows the force acts opposite to the ball's initial motion, which is what a wall does. The magnitude is 200 N. Getting the sign of the rebound velocity wrong is the single most common error in this topic, and it doubles the answer.

Common mistakes

  • Confusing mass and weight: mass is in kilograms and never changes; weight is in newtons and equals mg. A mass of 5 kg has a weight of about 50 N, not 5 kg.
  • Using the average of speeds for the average speed of a journey; it is always total distance over total time.
  • Reading the wrong quantity from a graph: gradient on a distance–time graph is speed, gradient on a speed–time graph is acceleration, and only the speed–time graph has a meaningful area.
  • Putting any force into F = ma. Only the resultant force gives the acceleration, so add and subtract the forces first.
  • Using a slanted distance in a moment calculation; d is measured perpendicular to the line of action of the force.
  • Losing the sign of a velocity in a momentum calculation. Reversal of direction is a sign change, and the total momentum is a vector sum, not a sum of sizes.
  • Using g = 9.81 when the question says take g = 10 N kg⁻¹, and forgetting to state which value was used.
  • Adding a force in newtons to a momentum in kg m s⁻¹; if the units do not match, the physics does not either.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 4, 3 marks). A cyclist starts from rest and reaches 8.0 m s⁻¹ in 5.0 s. Calculate the average acceleration and the distance travelled.

Answer: a = (v − u)/t = (8.0 − 0)/5.0 = 1.6 m s⁻². Distance = average speed × time = ½(0 + 8.0) × 5.0 = 20 m. (A speed–time graph of the motion is a triangle of area ½ × 5.0 × 8.0 = 20 m.)

Question 2 (Paper 4, 4 marks). A skydiver of mass 80 kg falls. Explain, using forces, why she reaches a terminal velocity, and state the size of the drag force at that moment.

Answer: Weight W = mg = 80 × 9.8 = 784 N downwards (≈ 800 N if g = 10 is taken). At first weight exceeds drag, so there is a downward resultant force and she accelerates. As speed increases, drag increases. When drag equals the weight the resultant force is zero, acceleration is zero, and she falls at constant terminal velocity. The drag force is then 784 N (or 800 N) upwards.

Question 3 (Paper 2 style). Which statement about a ball thrown straight up is correct? A: its acceleration at the top is zero; B: its velocity at the top is zero; C: its momentum at the top is maximum; D: its weight is zero at the top. Answer: B. The velocity is instantaneously zero at the top, but g still acts there, so the acceleration is 9.81 m s⁻² downwards and the weight is unchanged. Paper 2 setters rely on this confusion between velocity and acceleration.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 4 marks). A 1500 kg car travelling at 20 m s⁻¹ brakes to a stop in 4.0 s. Calculate the braking force.

Answer: change in momentum = mv − mu = 1500 × 0 − 1500 × 20 = −30 000 kg m s⁻¹. Force = change in momentum / time = −30 000 / 4.0 = −7500 N. The braking force is 7500 N opposite to the motion.

Question 5 (Paper 6 style). Describe how you would find the centre of gravity of an irregular lamina.

Answer: Hang the lamina from a pin through a hole near its edge so it swings freely. Hang a plumb line from the same pin and, when everything is at rest, mark the plumb-line position on the lamina. Repeat with the lamina hung from a second hole. The point where the two marked lines cross is the centre of gravity. The plumb line marks the vertical through the pivot, and the centre of gravity lies on it in both cases.

Question 6 (Paper 4, 3 marks). A 0.20 kg ball moving at 6.0 m s⁻¹ collides with an identical ball at rest and stops dead. Find the velocity of the second ball after the impact.

Answer: total momentum before = 0.20 × 6.0 = 1.2 kg m s⁻¹. After the impact the first ball has zero momentum, so 0.20 × v = 1.2 and v = 6.0 m s⁻¹ in the original direction.

Momentum, moments and Newton's laws are the tools; the next step is what those forces actually do to energy.

Reading a motion graph line by line

A velocity–time graph is not a picture of the journey. It is a table of two quantities, drawn so that the arithmetic can be done with a ruler. That is the whole idea, and it is why the graph rewards a student who knows what to look for and punishes one who reads it like a map.

Read the graph above in the order the journey happened, and at every segment ask two questions: what is the gradient and what is the area underneath. The answers are always the same two quantities, just measured over different intervals.

SegmentGradient (Δv ÷ Δt)What it meansArea under that segment
0 s to 4 s24 ÷ 4 = 6 m s⁻²Constant acceleration: the velocity rises by 6 m s⁻¹ every second½ × 4 × 24 = 48 m
4 s to 8 s0 ÷ 4 = 0Constant velocity — not at rest. The car is still moving at 24 m s⁻¹4 × 24 = 96 m
8 s to 10 s−24 ÷ 2 = −12 m s⁻²Deceleration: the velocity falls 12 m s⁻¹ each second½ × 2 × 24 = 24 m

a = (v − u) / t Key: a = acceleration (m s⁻²); v = final velocity (m s⁻¹); u = initial velocity (m s⁻¹); t = time taken (s). The gradient is this equation rearranged — nothing more.

Worked example. Find the total distance travelled and the average speed over the ten seconds.

Distance is the area under the whole line, so add the three segments:
s = 48 m + 96 m + 24 m = 168 m

Average speed is total distance over total time, never the mean of the speeds:
vavg = s / t = 168 m ÷ 10 s = 16.8 m s⁻¹

Notice what that number is not. The car spent most of the journey at 24 m s⁻¹, yet its average is 16.8 m s⁻¹, because the first four seconds and the last two were slower. A student who averages 6, 0 and −12 (or 24 and 0) gets a number with no meaning at all.

The self-check that proves the area rule. For the first four seconds, u = 0, a = 6 m s⁻² and t = 4 s, so the equation of motion gives
s = u t + ½ a t² = 0 + ½ × 6 × 4² = 48 m
which is exactly the triangle's area. The area rule is not a separate law — it is that equation, drawn.

Where marks are lost. Three traps account for almost every lost mark on this topic. Reading a flat line as "stopped" (it is constant velocity; only a line on the time axis is stationary). Measuring distance from the height of the line rather than the area under it. And forgetting that a negative velocity means travel in the opposite direction, so a journey out and back has a displacement near zero even though the distance is large — the areas on either side of the axis cancel, and the examiner asks for "distance" or "displacement" precisely to see whether you noticed.

Equations and symbols

Every equation 0625 uses across statements 1.2, 1.3, 1.5 and 1.6, in the form the mark scheme expects. Motion equations assume constant acceleration in a straight line; the force equations are vector equations, so direction is part of the answer.

Motion

v = Δs / Δt
Key: v = speed or velocity (m/s); Δs = change in displacement (m); Δt = time interval (s). Velocity is a vector, so a change of direction is a change of velocity even at constant speed.

a = Δv / Δt = (v − u) / t
Key: a = acceleration (m/s²); v = final velocity (m/s); u = initial velocity (m/s); t = time taken (s). A negative a means deceleration.

v² = u² + 2as
Key: v = final velocity (m/s); u = initial velocity (m/s); a = constant acceleration (m/s²); s = displacement (m). Use it whenever time is neither given nor asked for.

s = ut + ½at²
Key: s = displacement (m); u = initial velocity (m/s); t = time (s); a = acceleration (m/s²). For a body released from rest, u = 0 and the distance is ½at².

s = ½(u + v)t
Key: s = displacement (m); u, v = initial and final velocity (m/s); t = time (s). This is the area under a velocity–time graph for constant acceleration, which is why the area is always a valid route to distance.

g = 9.8 N/kg (9.8 m/s²)
Key: g = gravitational field strength near the Earth's surface; numerically equal to free-fall acceleration, so a dropped body gains 9.8 m/s of speed each second in the absence of air resistance.

Mass, weight and force

W = mg
Key: W = weight (N); m = mass (kg); g = gravitational field strength (N/kg), 9.8 on Earth and about 1.6 on the Moon. Mass stays in kilograms and does not change with location; weight is the force and does.

F = ma
Key: F = resultant force (N); m = mass (kg); a = acceleration (m/s²). F is the resultant after friction and air resistance are subtracted, which is the single most common lost mark in this topic.

R = √(F₁² + F₂²)
Key: R = magnitude of the resultant (N); F₁, F₂ = two perpendicular forces (N). For forces along one line, add them when they point the same way and subtract when they oppose.

Balanced forces: ΣF = 0 implies a = 0
Key: ΣF = the vector sum of all forces (N); a = acceleration (m/s²). Zero resultant means at rest or at constant velocity — never "no forces acting".

Moments and springs

M = F × d
Key: M = moment of the force (N m); F = the force (N); d = the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force (m). A distance measured along a slant gives the wrong moment.

Σ clockwise moments = Σ anticlockwise moments
Key: the principle of moments, for a body in equilibrium. Each term is a force times its perpendicular distance (N m).

F = kx
Key: F = load or tension (N); k = spring constant (N/m or N/cm); x = extension beyond the natural length (m or cm). Valid only up to the limit of proportionality; beyond it the graph curves and the equation stops applying.

k = F / x
Key: k = spring constant (N/m); found as the gradient of the straight part of a force–extension graph, not from a single point beyond the limit.

Momentum

p = mv
Key: p = momentum (kg m/s); m = mass (kg); v = velocity (m/s). Momentum is a vector: opposite directions need opposite signs.

F = Δp / Δt
Key: F = average force acting (N); Δp = change in momentum (kg m/s); Δt = time over which it acts (s). This is the form that explains crumple zones and seatbelts: the same Δp spread over a longer Δt gives a smaller F.

m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂
Key: m₁, m₂ = masses (kg); u₁, u₂ = velocities before the collision (m/s); v₁, v₂ = velocities after (m/s). Total momentum is conserved when no external resultant force acts; kinetic energy is not necessarily conserved.

title: International GCSE English as a Second Language: Word Formation: Prefixes and Suffixes
content:
International GCSE English as a Second Language: Word Formation: Prefixes and Suffixes

Word formation is the skill of building the word a sentence needs from the word you are given — turning decide into decision, happy into unhappy, careful into carefully. It is tested directly in gap-fill tasks across the 9280 papers and it underpins the range mark in writing: a candidate who can deploy accurate, varied word families reads as a competent user of English. This note builds the system from zero: how English derives nouns, verbs, adjectives and adverbs from base words, which prefixes flip meaning, how spelling changes behave, and the decoding procedure that solves every word-formation question under time pressure.

Word families: one idea, four outfits

Most English base words belong to a family whose members are different parts of speech. The first step of any word-formation question is deciding which member the sentence is dressed for.

Base verbNounAdjectiveAdverb
decidedecisiondecisive / decideddecisively
createcreationcreativecreatively
carecarecareful / carelesscarefully
succeedsuccesssuccessfulsuccessfully
developdevelopmentdeveloping / developed—
comparecomparisoncomparablecomparatively
relaterelation / relationshiprelative / relatedrelatively
beautybeautybeautifulbeautifully

The productive pattern: verbs end in -ify, -ise, -en (justify, modernise, widen); nouns of action end in -tion, -ment, -ance, -ence, -ing (decision, development, performance, existence); adjectives end in -ful, -less, -ous, -ive, -able, -ible, -al, -ic (careful, careless, dangerous, active, readable, possible, natural, scientific); adverbs end in -ly (carefully).

Suffixes by part of speech

Part of speechCommon suffixesExamples
Nouns (people)-er, -or, -ist, -ant, -eeteacher, actor, scientist, assistant, employee
Nouns (things/ideas)-tion, -ment, -ness, -ity, -ance, -ence, -ismeducation, achievement, happiness, ability, importance, difference, tourism
Adjectives-ful, -less, -ous, -ive, -able, -ible, -al, -ic, -y, -ishhopeful, hopeless, famous, attractive, comfortable, sensible, cultural, economic, rainy, childish
Adverbs-lyquickly, easily, surprisingly
Verbs-ise/-ize, -ify, -enorganise, simplify, widen

Note the pairs that change meaning with the suffix: -ful (full of) versus -less (without) — hopeful and hopeless; -ous (having the quality) — danger → dangerous. And the -ing/-ed adjective pair: -ing describes the thing that causes (a tiring day), -ed describes the person affected (a tired student).

Prefixes that flip or shift meaning

PrefixMeaningExamples
un-not, reverseunhappy, unable, unlock
in- / im- / il- / ir-notindependent, impossible, illegal, irregular
dis-not, oppositedisagree, dishonest, disappear
mis-wronglymisunderstand, misspell, mislead
re-againrewrite, rebuild, reapply
over- / under-too much / too littleoverestimate, overcrowded, underestimate
pre- / post-before / afterpreview, precaution / postpone, post-war
anti-againstantibiotic, anti-social
co-, ex-, inter-with, out of, betweencooperate, export, international

The negative prefix is chosen by habit as much as by rule: in- becomes im- before m and p (impossible, impatient), il- before l (illegal), ir- before r (irregular). There is no rule for which words take un- rather than in- — unhappy but inactive — so learn negatives as pairs: unhappy, uncomfortable, unfriendly / inactive, inconvenient, informal / dishonest, disrespectful / misbehave.

Spelling changes when adding suffixes

  • Silent -e dropped before a vowel suffix, kept before a consonant suffix: hope + ful → hopeful (the e goes because a vowel follows) but hope + less → hopeless (the e stays because a consonant follows); like + able → likable (e dropped), manage + ment → management (e kept). Compare the same base twice and the rule becomes visible.
  • y → i before a consonant suffix: happy + ness → happiness; beauty + ful → beautiful; but y stays before -ing and -ous: carrying, curious.
  • Final consonant doubled after a single vowel + consonant in stressed syllables: big + er → bigger; begin + ing → beginning; but visit + or → visitor (stress not on last syllable).
  • -ce/-ge keep the e before -a/-o: courage + ous → courageous (the soft c sound is protected).

Worked example. Build the adjective from beauty and the noun from decide. Step 1: beauty ends in a consonant + y → change y to i before -ful: beautiful. Step 2: decide drops the final e before -tion: decision. Both spellings are the marks; the morphology is only the map.

The decoding procedure for gap-fill word formation

  1. Decide the part of speech the gap needs: read the sentence around the gap. After an article or adjective → noun. After a linking verb (is, seems, becomes) → adjective. After a verb object or sentence end → adverb. Before a noun → adjective.
  2. Decide the meaning direction: positive or negative? prefix needed? does the context say although / but / despite (which often signals the opposite meaning)?
  3. Build the word: apply the family suffix, then the prefix if needed.
  4. Spell-check against the three changes: e-drop, y→i, consonant doubling.
  5. Read the finished sentence once — the built word must fit both grammar and meaning.

Worked example 1. "Her ___ (explain) of the theory was completely ___ (understand)." Step 1: after Her + of the theory → noun; explain → explanation (note the -ation after a plain explanation form: explain → explanation, a family with its own spelling). Step 2: after was completely → adjective; understand with the context "completely ... of the theory" and the likely positive framing → understandable. If the sentence had a but clause ("... was completely ___ , so no one followed it"), the negative would be needed: un-understandable is wrong English; use incomprehensible — some negatives cannot be built, which is why step 5 (read it back) exists.

Worked example 2. "The ___ (industry) revolution changed society ___ (dramatic)." Step 1: before the noun revolution → adjective: industry → industrial (the y becomes i before the -al suffix). Step 2: after the verb changed → adverb: dramatic + ally → dramatically (the adjective dramatic gains -ally, not just -ly — read the finished word back and it must sound right). Answer: industrial, dramatically.

Worked example 3 — the double trap. "It is ___ (possible) to finish in ten minutes." Step 1: after is → adjective. Step 2: the context means cannot be done → negative prefix. Step 3: possible takes im- before p: impossible. Many candidates write unpossible — the prefix table exists to prevent exactly that.

Word formation in the writing tasks

The same skill powers the range band in writing and speaking. Families let one idea appear in several grammatical clothes inside one paragraph: "The decision was difficult. We decided slowly and decisively, and the decisive factor was cost." Deciding (or better, deciding not to repeat the root four times) is a range demonstration; the mark scheme rewards varied and accurate structures, and family variation is the cheapest variety available.

  • Upgrade weak adjective stacks: "very big problem" → "significant problem"; "very good results" → "excellent results"; "very tired" → "exhausted". Precision beats intensifiers.
  • Nominalise for formality: "Because prices rose, we lost customers" → "The rise in prices led to a loss of customers." The -tion and -ness nouns are the engine of formal style.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. Build the word: "The ___ (manage) of the company ___ (success) launched a ___ (create) campaign." Answer: management / successfully / creative. Why: after The → noun; after the subject + verb → adverb; before a noun → adjective.
  2. Build with negative prefix: "His answer was ___ (correct) and showed ___ (complete) ___ (understand) of the topic." Answer: "His answer was incorrect and showed complete misunderstanding of the topic." Why: correct takes the negative in- (incorrect); complete is used as an adjective before the noun and needs no prefix (complete, not completely — an adjective describes the noun misunderstanding); understand becomes the noun misunderstanding with the mis- prefix that signals wrongness.
  3. Spelling focus: happy → happiness; big → bigger; beauty → beautiful; decide → decision. Why: y→i, consonant doubling, y→i before -ful, silent-e drop.
  4. Choose the negative: "It is ___ (legal) to park here and ___ (polite) to shout." Answer: illegal / impolite. Why: il- before l, im- before p.
  5. -ing or -ed: "The trip was ___ (exhaust), and the ___ (sleep) children ___ (immediate) fell asleep." Answer: exhausting / sleepy (or sleeping — but sleepy fits tired children) / immediately.
  6. Rewrite with a noun: "He decided to resign because the job was badly paid." Answer: "His decision to resign was caused by the low pay." Why: decide → decision nominalises the clause for formal style.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Right family, wrong form: writing "explaination" or "decission" — the morphology is right but the spelling loses the mark. Learn each family's spelling as vocabulary.
  • Impossible negatives: unpossible, unlegal, unregular. Learn the prefix with the word: impossible, illegal, irregular.
  • -ing / -ed adjectives swapped: "I am boring in this lesson" says the speaker bores others. The person feels -ed; the thing causes -ing.
  • Double suffixes: "carefulness" when carefulness is fine but "beautifulness" is not (beauty → beauty is a noun already; no -ness). When the gap already has the family noun, add nothing.
  • Adverb after linking verbs: "The results were surprising good" → surprisingly good (adverb modifies the adjective), but "The results were surprisingly good" versus "The results were good" — know that after be/seem/become an adjective follows: "The food smells good", not "well".
  • Spelling changes ignored: write the finished word once in the check step; the three changes (e-drop, y→i, doubling) account for most spelling losses.
  • Capital letters and plurals: if the built word starts a sentence it keeps its capital; if the gap sits after a number or many, the noun needs the plural form — a whole-mark detail in note-completion tasks.
  • Over-engineering: sometimes the base word is correct as given (complete in question 2). If the built form sounds wrong read aloud, try the unchanged word.

Derivation patterns, one page

Word formation is a derivation: a base plus an affix gives a new word, and the arrow shows the step. Read each line as an instruction — identify the base, apply the ending the sentence needs, then apply the spelling change. The affix carries the meaning; the spelling carries the mark.

hope + ful → hopeful hope means the base noun; -ful means "full of", an adjective suffix; the silent e is dropped because a vowel suffix follows. The same base with a consonant suffix keeps it: hope + less → hopeless.

happy + ness → happiness happy means base adjective ending in consonant + y; -ness means noun suffix; y becomes i before a consonant suffix. The y stays before -ing and -ous: carrying, curious.

beauty + ful → beautiful beauty means base noun (consonant + y); -ful means adjective suffix; y → i. The adverb then adds -ly: beautifully, with both changes kept.

big + er → bigger big means base adjective, one vowel + one final consonant, stressed on the last syllable; -er means comparative suffix; the consonant doubles. Where the stress is not final the consonant stays single: visit + or → visitor.

manage + ment → management manage means base verb ending in a silent e followed by a consonant suffix; -ment means noun suffix; the e is kept because the suffix begins with a consonant. Contrast like + able → likable, where the vowel suffix drops it.

courage + ous → courageous courage means base noun ending in -ge; -ous means adjective suffix; the e is kept before a vowel suffix so the soft g survives. Drop it and the word reads with a hard g.

decide → decision decide means base verb; the noun is not a suffix added to the whole word but a family member with its own spelling — -sion replaces -de. Learn the family, not the rule: decide, decision, decisive, decisively.

dramatic + ally → dramatically dramatic means adjective ending in -ic; -ally means adverb suffix (not -ly alone). The same pattern gives automatic → automatically, basic → basically. Writing "dramaticly" is the classic spelling loss.

The affix tables in one place

AffixMeaningExample
-ful / -lessfull of / withouthopeful / hopeless
-oushaving the qualitydanger → dangerous
-tion, -sion, -ment, -nessnoun of action or statedecision, achievement, happiness
-er, -or, -ist, -eeperson who does / receivesteacher, actor, employee
un- / in- / im- / il- / ir-notunhappy, inactive, impossible, illegal, irregular
mis- / re- / over- / under-wrongly / again / too much / too littlemisunderstand, rewrite, overestimate, underestimate

Traps specific to the derivation

  • Right family, wrong spelling: explaination, decission, beautifull. The morphology is right; the mark is not.
  • Impossible negatives: unpossible, unlegal, unregular — learn the prefix with the word.
  • -ing versus -ed: the thing is boring, the person is bored.
  • Adding -ness to a word that is already the noun (beautifulness), when the sentence needs the base.

title:
Appendix P — Using the note in a session: what to do first, what to do next, and what to leave for the end

A revision session on this topic works best if it has a clear order, because the topic is long enough that a session without an order can turn into a wandering through details that never adds up to an answer you can produce under time pressure. The first thing to do in a session is to take the durable ideas and say them out loud in your own words with a reason attached, because those are the ideas that hold the topic together and the ideas you most need under time pressure. Say the control idea with the reflex arc and the insulin-glucagon system as the anchors. Say the layered defence idea with the skin barrier and phagocytosis on one side and the antibody and memory cell response on the other. Say the timing idea with the primary and secondary response and vaccination. Say the matching idea with restriction enzymes, PCR and electrophoresis. If you can say those four durable ideas with their reasons and their anchors, you have the framework the session is built on, and the rest of the session is then filling in the detail under that framework rather than trying to hold the whole note in your head at once.

The second thing to do is to pick one comparison or one evaluation question and write the answer from the note under time pressure, then compare it with the model in the exam-style section and with the appendix that covers the same ground. Pick a comparison question such as nervous versus hormonal, primary versus secondary, or specific versus non-specific, or plant versus animal coordination. Pick an evaluation question such as vaccination, monoclonal antibodies, DNA profiling, gene therapy or GM organisms. Write the answer in the time you would have in the exam, and then check whether it has the sequence, the distinctions and the reasoning the model has. If it does, the session has done its job for that question. If it does not, the gap is the thing to practise before the next session, because the gap is the thing that will lose marks on the day. The reason for doing the comparison and evaluation questions in the session is that those are the questions where the marks are most often lost for want of precision, and the session is the place where precision can be built before the exam rather than rescued on the day.

The third thing to do is to use the appendices as the place where you go deeper when a topic needs it, and not as a separate first read. The appendices on practical microbiology, the immune process, forensic interpretation, cross-strand questions and the durable ideas are there because those are the places where the marks are most often lost for lack of depth or lack of connection, and they are the places to spend time when you practise those topics. If you read the main body for coverage and the appendices for depth, you get the best use of the note, because you get both the coverage and the reasoning. If you only read the main body, you may get the labels but not the reasoning. If you only read the appendices, you may get the depth but not the coverage. The session that reads both in the right order gets both, and that is the session that makes the note useful, because the note is long enough to cover the topic fully only if you use it fully.

The final thing to do in a session is to leave the last part of the session for the kind of question you are weakest at, because the last part of the session is the part that will determine what sticks. If you are weakest at evaluation, leave the evaluation question for last and make sure you can give a benefit and an issue for each technology without repeating the same issue in every case. If you are weakest at gene technology, leave the gene technology techniques for last and make sure you can say the principle and the purpose for each one without dropping the key step. If you are weakest at the immune response, leave the primary and secondary response and memory for last and make sure you can say why the secondary response is faster and stronger and what the memory cells do. If you leave the weakest part for last, you are practising the thing you most need to practise while it is still fresh from the session, and that is the practice that makes the difference on the day. The session is then not just a read-through of the note but a targeted practice session that builds the precision the exam is actually after.

Appendix Q — End-of-topic checklist and what “ready” should actually mean

The checklist for the end of the topic is not a list of every detail you can remember; it is a list of the things you should be able to do under time pressure, because that is what “ready” means for this topic. The first thing ready should mean is that you can describe the nervous and hormonal systems well enough to contrast them, with speed, range and duration and one concrete example of each. The second thing ready should mean is that you can describe a receptor well enough to pick one and give its structure, stimulus and transduction, whether it is a rod, a cone, a Pacinian corpuscle or another receptor the question gives you. The third thing ready should mean is that you can describe the synapse and the neuromuscular junction well enough to include the calcium step and the neurotransmitter release, and to say that the neuromuscular junction is a synapse with a muscle as the postsynaptic cell. The fourth thing ready should mean is that you can describe muscle contraction well enough to say that the filaments slide and do not shorten, and that ATP and calcium both matter, and to say how the banding pattern changes.

The fifth thing ready should mean is that you can describe the insulin-glucagon system and homeostasis well enough to say that insulin and glucagon work in opposition and that this is negative feedback, and to say that homeostasis is stability within limits rather than perfect constancy. The sixth thing ready should mean is that you can describe the endocrine control of reproduction and ADH well enough to name the hormones and their functions and to keep ADH in its water-balance role rather than confusing it with the reproductive hormones. The seventh thing ready should mean is that you can describe plant coordination well enough to say that plants use hormones and growth, with auxins and tropic responses as the example, and that plant responses are slower and growth-based compared with animal nerve-and-muscle coordination. The eighth thing ready should mean is that you can describe the gene technology techniques well enough to match each technique to its purpose, including restriction enzymes and sticky ends, PCR, gel electrophoresis, probes, vectors, transformation, selectable markers and insertional inactivation.

The ninth thing ready should mean is that you can describe gene therapy and GM organisms well enough to give a benefit and an issue for each without turning the answer into a slogan, and without treating somatic and germ-line therapy as eth identical. The tenth thing ready should mean is that you can describe vaccination, herd immunity, monoclonal antibodies, epidemiology and forensic biology well enough to give the reasoning behind each, not just the label, including the fact that herd immunity depends on coverage, that monoclonal antibodies are identical antibodies from a cloned line specific to one antigen, that epidemiology studies patterns, causes and control in populations, and that forensic biology and DNA profiling are interpreted in context with attention to sample quality, contamination and the chain of custody. If you can do all ten of those under time pressure, you are ready for the topic in the sense the exam is actually in, because those ten are the things the topic most often tests and the things that carry the marks. If you can only do some of them, that is the gap to fill before the exam, and the note is there to fill it.

The final part of the checklist is to check that the capable things are capable in the right way, which is to say with sequence, with distinctions and with reasoning, not just with labels. For the nervous and hormonal contrast, that means the contrast is actually there, not just a mention of both. For the receptor, that means the structure, stimulus and transduction are actually there, not just the name of the receptor. For the synapse, that means the calcium step and the neurotransmitter release are actually there, not just a mention of the synapse. For the muscle, that means the sliding and the ATP and calcium and banding pattern are actually there, not just a mention of contraction. For the immune system, that means the sequence, the specificity, the memory and the link to vaccination are actually there, not just a mention of antibodies. For the gene technology, that means the principle and the purpose are actually there, not just the name of the technique.
