title: Exam technique: Materials and Deformation
content:
### What earns the marks
For stress and strain, each definition quoted with units or unitless noted earns a mark. For Young modulus, stress over strain earns the method mark with a steel-scale answer. For graphs, area read as stored energy earns the mark.
### Traps
Error: strain given units. Correction: strain is a pure ratio. Error: force-extension gradient called energy. Correction: gradient is stiffness; area is energy. Error: plastic region called elastic. Correction: only the straight line obeys Hooke.
### Worked example
Under a rotation of 90° anticlockwise about the origin, the point (3, 1) maps to (−1, 3). Each point's x and y change places with one sign reversed. Under a reflection in the line y = x, the same point maps to (1, 3), so the coordinates swap. For a translation by vector (2; −3), the point (3, 1) maps to (5, −2).
### Check yourself
Describe the enlargement that maps a triangle with vertices (1, 1), (2, 1), (1, 3) onto one with vertices (2, 2), (4, 2), (2, 6). The scale factor is 2, and the centre must be stated: it is found by joining corresponding points, and the centre is the origin.

title: Forces and Equilibrium — Study Notes
content:
Forces and equilibrium

Moment of a force

  • The moment of a force about a point is the force multiplied by the perpendicular distance from the point to the line of action of the force: moment = F × d⊥. Unit: N m.
  • Only the perpendicular component of the force produces a turning effect. A force that passes through the pivot has zero moment.

Principle of moments

For a body in equilibrium the sum of the clockwise moments about any point equals the sum of the anticlockwise moments about that point.

Couples

A couple is two equal and opposite parallel forces whose lines of action do not coincide. It produces a turning effect without a resultant force. The moment of a couple is F × d, where d is the perpendicular separation, and it is the same about every point.

Conditions for equilibrium

  • The resultant force in every direction is zero.
  • The resultant moment about any point is zero.

For three coplanar, non-parallel forces in equilibrium, the lines of action must meet at a single point.

Centre of gravity

The centre of gravity is the point through which the weight of a body appears to act. For a uniform symmetrical body it lies at the geometric centre.

Worked example: a uniform beam of weight 100 N rests horizontally on two supports at its ends. Each support carries half the weight, 50 N, because the beam is symmetrical and in equilibrium.

Exam tips: state the pivot you take moments about. Draw the perpendicular distance, not the slant distance. Show that the resultant force is zero in each direction before you use the principle of moments.

Conditions for equilibrium

A body is in equilibrium when the resultant force on it is zero and the resultant moment about any point is zero. For a body in equilibrium under three coplanar forces, the lines of action meet at a single point. The moment of a force about a pivot is Fd, where d is the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action. Taking moments about the pivot removes the unknown reaction force, which makes this a useful method in exam questions.

Exam tip: show the resolution of forces into horizontal and vertical components before you apply the equilibrium equations.

title: A2 Level Chemistry: Organic Chemistry: Carbonyls, Carboxylic Acids and Chirality
content:
Organic Chemistry: Carbonyls, Carboxylic Acids and Chirality

Edexcel International A Level Chemistry — Unit 4 (WCH14), Topic 15, covers the concepts of carbonyl compounds, carboxylic acids, and chirality. This topic includes the reactions and tests of aldehydes and ketones, the properties and reactions of carboxylic acids, and the concept of optical isomerism and chirality.

Introduction to Carbonyl Compounds

Carbonyl compounds contain the carbonyl group, C=O. Aldehydes have the C=O group at the end of a chain (RCHO), while ketones have it inside the chain (RCOR). The carbon of C=O is slightly positive, making it susceptible to nucleophilic attack.

  • Aldehydes: RCHO
  • Ketones: RCOR

Reactions of Carbonyl Compounds

Carbonyl compounds undergo nucleophilic addition reactions. The products of these reactions can be carboxylic acids, alcohols, or molecules with a chiral centre.

  • Hydrogen cyanide adds across C=O: RCHO + HCN → RCN
  • Sodium tetrahydridoborate(III) (NaBH4) reduces aldehydes to primary alcohols and ketones to secondary alcohols
  • 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine (2,4-DNPH) gives an orange or yellow precipitate with any carbonyl compound
  • Tollens' reagent gives a silver mirror with aldehydes but not with ketones
  • The iodoform test gives a yellow precipitate of triiodomethane with compounds containing CH3CO– or CH3CH(OH)– groups

Carboxylic Acids

Carboxylic acids contain –COOH and are weak acids. They are more acidic than alcohols because the carboxylate ion is stabilised by delocalisation.

  • Carboxylic acids react with alcohols in the presence of concentrated sulfuric acid to form esters
  • Primary alcohols are oxidised to carboxylic acids by heating with acidified potassium dichromate(VI) under reflux

Chirality and Optical Isomerism

A chiral carbon atom has four different groups attached. Molecules with a chiral centre exist as a pair of enantiomers. Enantiomers have identical physical properties except their effect on plane-polarised light.

  • A chiral carbon atom has four different groups attached
  • Enantiomers have identical physical properties except their effect on plane-polarised light
  • An equimolar mixture of the two enantiomers is a racemic mixture, which is optically inactive

Optical Activity

Optical activity is the ability of a single optical isomer to rotate the plane of polarisation of plane-polarised monochromatic light.

  • Optical activity is measured using a polarimeter
  • The specific rotation of a compound is a characteristic property

Nomenclature of Aldehydes and Ketones

Aldehydes and ketones are named based on the longest continuous chain containing the carbonyl group.

  • Aldehydes: RCHO
  • Ketones: RCOR

Nomenclature of Carboxylic Acids

Carboxylic acids are named based on the longest continuous chain containing the carboxyl group.

  • Carboxylic acids: RCOOH

Nomenclature of Acyl Chlorides and Esters

Acyl chlorides and esters are named based on the longest continuous chain containing the acyl group.

  • Acyl chlorides: RCOCl
  • Esters: RCOOR

Reactions of Acyl Chlorides

Acyl chlorides undergo nucleophilic substitution reactions.

  • Acyl chlorides react with water to form carboxylic acids
  • Acyl chlorides react with alcohols to form esters
  • Acyl chlorides react with concentrated ammonia to form amides
  • Acyl chlorides react with amines to form amides

Hydrolysis of Esters

Esters undergo hydrolysis reactions in acidic and alkaline solutions.

  • Esters react with water in the presence of an acid catalyst to form carboxylic acids and alcohols
  • Esters react with water in the presence of a base to form carboxylic acids and alcohols

Condensation Polymerisation

Polyesters are formed by condensation polymerisation reactions.

  • Polyesters are formed by the reaction of carboxylic acids and alcohols

Mass Spectra

Mass spectra provide information about the molecular mass of a compound.

  • The molecular ion is the ion with the highest mass-to-charge ratio
  • The base peak is the ion with the highest intensity

13C NMR Spectroscopy

13C NMR spectroscopy provides information about the environments of carbon atoms in a molecule.

  • The chemical shift of a carbon atom is a characteristic property
  • The number of peaks in a 13C NMR spectrum is equal to the number of different environments of carbon atoms

Proton NMR Spectroscopy

Proton NMR spectroscopy provides information about the environments of hydrogen atoms in a molecule.

  • The chemical shift of a hydrogen atom is a characteristic property
  • The number of peaks in a proton NMR spectrum is equal to the number of different environments of hydrogen atoms
  • The intensity of a peak is proportional to the number of hydrogen atoms in that environment

Chromatography

Chromatography is a technique used to separate the components of a mixture.

  • Chromatography separates components based on their affinity for a stationary phase and a mobile phase
  • The Rf value is a measure of the distance traveled by a component relative to the distance traveled by the solvent front

Typical Mistakes

  • Confusing the reactions of aldehydes and ketones
  • Forgetting to show the nucleophile attacking the carbon of C=O in nucleophilic addition reactions
  • Not understanding the concept of optical isomerism and chirality

Exam-Style Questions

  1. What is the difference between an aldehyde and a ketone? Answer: An aldehyde has the C=O group at the end of a chain, while a ketone has it inside the chain.
  2. What is the reaction of hydrogen cyanide with an aldehyde? Answer: Hydrogen cyanide adds across C=O to form a cyanohydrin.
  3. What is the specific rotation of a compound? Answer: The specific rotation of a compound is a characteristic property that is measured using a polarimeter.

To revise this topic, make sure to understand the reactions and tests of aldehydes and ketones, the properties and reactions of carboxylic acids, and the concept of optical isomerism and chirality. Practice drawing the structures of aldehydes, ketones, and carboxylic acids, and practice solving problems involving the reactions of these compounds. Also, make sure to understand the concepts of 13C NMR spectroscopy, proton NMR spectroscopy, and chromatography, and practice solving problems involving these techniques. Finally, practice answering exam-style questions to test your understanding of the topic.

Detailed Mechanisms of Nucleophilic Addition: HCN and KCN

The addition of hydrogen cyanide to carbonyl compounds is a classic Edexcel A2 mechanism. Because HCN is a weak acid and provides a very low concentration of cyanide ions, potassium cyanide (KCN) is added to provide a higher concentration of the active nucleophile, CN−. The mechanism proceeds via nucleophilic addition:

  • Step 1: The lone pair on the carbon atom of the cyanide ion (CN−) attacks the slightly positive carbon atom of the carbonyl group (C=O). A curly arrow goes from the lone pair on carbon to the carbonyl carbon.
  • Step 2: Simultaneously, the pi bond of the carbonyl group breaks, with both electrons moving entirely to the oxygen atom. This forms a negatively charged intermediate (an alkoxide ion) and shows a curly arrow from the C=O bond to the oxygen.
  • Step 3: The intermediate accepts a proton (H+) from HCN or from the acidic aqueous environment to form a hydroxy-nitrile (cyanohydrin).

Stereochemical Evidence from Carbonyl Addition to Unsymmetrical Ketones

When an unsymmetrical aldehyde or ketone reacts with hydrogen cyanide, the planar nature of the carbonyl group allows the nucleophile (CN−) to attack from either above or below the plane with equal probability. If the product molecule contains a single chiral centre (i.e., four different groups attached to the central carbon), a racemic mixture of two optical isomers (enantiomers) is formed in equal amounts. This proves that the intermediate is planar around the original carbonyl carbon and provides crucial mechanistic evidence for the reaction pathway.

Physical Properties of Carbonyl Compounds and Carboxylic Acids

Understanding intermolecular forces explains the differing boiling temperatures and water solubilities:

  • Aldehydes and ketones cannot form hydrogen bonds with themselves because they lack a hydrogen atom bonded directly to a strongly electronegative oxygen or nitrogen atom. Their molecules are held together by permanent dipole-dipole attractions and London forces, resulting in lower boiling temperatures than corresponding alcohols or carboxylic acids of similar relative molecular mass.
  • Aldehydes, ketones, and carboxylic acids can form hydrogen bonds with water molecules through their lone pairs on the carbonyl or hydroxyl oxygens, which explains why smaller members of these homologous series are completely soluble in water.
  • Carboxylic acids can form stable hydrogen-bonded dimers with each other in the liquid and vapour phases. This effectively doubles their relative molecular mass during vaporisation, leading to significantly higher boiling temperatures than alcohols of comparable molecular mass.

Comprehensive Analysis of Spectroscopic Data

Examiners frequently test the ability to combine mass spectrometry, carbon-13 NMR, and proton NMR data to deduce molecular structures:

  • Mass Spectrometry: High-resolution mass spectrometry provides accurate relative molecular masses to four decimal places, allowing chemists to distinguish between molecules with the same nominal integer mass (e.g., CO, N2, and C2H4 all have a nominal mass of 28, but accurate masses separate them precisely). Fragmentation patterns reveal structural fragments, such as the loss of 15 (CH3), 17 (OH), or 45 (COOH).
  • Carbon-13 NMR: Each peak in a 13C NMR spectrum corresponds to a carbon atom in a distinct chemical environment. The chemical shift value (measured in ppm) gives information about the types of adjacent atoms or functional groups (e.g., carbon in a C=O group appears around 160 to 220 ppm, while aliphatic sp3 carbons appear between 0 and 50 ppm).
  • Proton (1H) NMR: The number of distinct peaks indicates the number of different hydrogen environments. The relative peak areas (integration traces) show the ratio of hydrogen atoms in each environment. The splitting pattern of each peak is determined by the number of adjacent non-equivalent protons using the (n + 1) rule, where n is the number of protons on adjacent carbon atoms. TMS (tetramethylsilane) is used as an internal reference standard because it produces a single sharp peak at 0 ppm, is inert, volatile, and non-toxic.

Advanced Chromatography Techniques

In addition to basic thin-layer chromatography (TLC) and paper chromatography where Rf values are calculated as the distance travelled by the solute divided by the distance travelled by the solvent front, modern analytical separation relies on column-based methods:

  • High-Performance Liquid Chromatography (HPLC): Uses a liquid mobile phase pumped under high pressure through a tightly packed column containing a solid stationary phase. Components separate based on their differing partition coefficients between the two phases.
  • Gas Chromatography (GC): Uses an inert carrier gas (such as helium or neon) as the mobile phase passing through a column containing a high-boiling liquid stationary phase coated on a solid support. Retention time is the time taken for a component to pass through the column from injection to detection.
  • Coupled Techniques: Both HPLC and GC can be directly coupled with mass spectrometry (HPLC-MS or GC-MS). This allows the chromatographic separation of complex mixtures followed immediately by mass spectral identification of each separated component, widely applied in forensic science, drug testing in sport, and environmental monitoring.

Worked Examples

  1. Worked Example: Calculating Rf Values
    Question: In a TLC experiment, the solvent front travels 8.4 cm from the baseline. A specific organic component travels 3.5 cm from the baseline. Calculate the Rf value for this component.
    Method: Use the formula Rf = (distance travelled by spot) ÷ (distance travelled by solvent front).
    Answer: Rf = 3.5 ÷ 8.4 = 0.42 (no units).
  2. Worked Example: Predicting 1H NMR Splitting
    Question: Predict the splitting pattern for the protons in the CH2 group of ethanol (CH3CH2OH), assuming standard high-resolution conditions.
    Method: Identify the number of non-equivalent protons (n) on the adjacent carbon atom. The adjacent carbon is the CH3 group, which has 3 protons. Apply the (n + 1) rule: 3 + 1 = 4.
    Answer: A quartet.

Common Student Mistakes and Corrections

  • Mistake: Confusing the action of Tollens reagent with Fehling solution on aliphatic aldehydes and aromatic aldehydes.
    Correction: Both Tollens reagent and Fehling solution give positive tests with aliphatic aldehydes (silver mirror and red precipitate respectively). However, aromatic aldehydes like benzaldehyde reduce Tollens reagent to form a silver mirror, but they do NOT reduce Fehling solution.
  • Mistake: Forgetting that carboxylic acids react with carbonates to release carbon dioxide gas, whereas alcohols do not.
    Correction: Always use sodium carbonate or sodium hydrogencarbonate solution to distinguish carboxylic acids from alcohols or phenols, as only carboxylic acids are strong enough acids to liberate carbon dioxide gas with effervescence.
  • Mistake: Misinterpreting peak splitting in proton NMR by counting protons on both sides indiscriminately.
    Correction: The (n + 1) rule only applies to protons on directly adjacent, non-equivalent carbon atoms. Protons separated by oxygen atoms or multiple bonds do not couple.

Exam-Style Questions and Answers

  1. Question: State why 1,1-dichloroethane and 1,2-dichloroethane have different numbers of peaks in their carbon-13 NMR spectra.
    Answer: 1,1-dichloroethane has two carbon environments (the CH3 carbon and the CHCl2 carbon), so it shows 2 peaks in its 13C NMR spectrum. 1,2-dichloroethane has only one carbon environment due to molecular symmetry (both carbons are bonded to a chlorine and a hydrogen and feel the same electronic environment), so it shows only 1 peak.
    Credit Point: Awarded for correctly identifying the carbon environments and linking them directly to the number of observed peaks.
  2. Question: Write an equation for the reaction of propanoyl chloride with concentrated ammonia, and name the organic product.
    Answer: CH3CH2COCl + 2NH3 → CH3CH2CONH2 + NH4Cl. The organic product is propanamide.
    Credit Point: Awarded for correct balanced stoichiometry (including the 2 moles of ammonia to react with the formed HCl) and correct naming of the amide.
  3. Question: Explain why a racemic mixture shows no optical activity when analysed in a polarimeter.
    Answer: A racemic mixture contains equal amounts of two enantiomers. Each enantiomer rotates the plane of plane-polarised light by an equal angle in opposite directions, resulting in the rotations cancelling each other out entirely.
    Credit Point: Awarded for mentioning equal amounts of enantiomers and the equal and opposite rotation of plane-polarised light.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Nucleophilic addition, applied to propanone with HCN and KCN: the cyanide ion attacks the δ+ carbon of the C=O, forming an alkoxide that picks up H⁺. The product is 2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanenitrile. Show the curly arrow from the C=O π bond to the oxygen.
  • Racemic product: the carbonyl carbon is planar, so the cyanide can attack from either face with equal likelihood. Propanal gives a racemic mixture of two enantiomers, and the product has no net optical activity. A chiral centre is one with four different groups attached.
  • Chirality, applied to 2-bromobutane: the second carbon carries H, Br, CH₃ and CH₂CH₃, four different groups, so the molecule is chiral and has two enantiomers that rotate plane-polarised light in opposite directions.
  • Tests: 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine gives an orange precipitate with any carbonyl. Tollens' reagent gives a silver mirror only with aldehydes, and acidified dichromate turns from orange to green with aldehydes. Name the test and the observation together.

title: Cambridge IGCSE First Language English: Analysing Language Choices
content:
Cambridge IGCSE First Language English: Analysing Language Choices

Writer's effect — the analysis of how a writer uses language to create impact — is the skill that separates a competent reader from a top-band one in Cambridge IGCSE First Language English (0500). The question asks you to choose and explain the language that creates a particular effect, and the mark scheme rewards the link from micro-feature to macro-impact: the exact word, the exact method, the exact effect on the reader. This note builds the analytical system from zero: the vocabulary of literary method, the step-by-step deconstruction of the prompt, the effect vocabulary bank, model answers broken down line by line, and the errors that turn analysis into feature-spotting.

The micro-to-macro principle

Writers create effects with tiny tools: a verb choice, a repeated sound, a sentence that stops short. Analysis means moving from the smallest unit (the word) to the largest (the reader's response, the writer's purpose). The chain every top-band answer follows is:

QUOTATION -> METHOD -> EFFECT ON THE READER -> PURPOSE IN CONTEXT
"clawed"   -> verb    -> makes the wind feel violent and alive -> shows
              choice                   the night as an attack

Candidates who stop at METHOD ("the writer uses a metaphor") score nothing for effect; candidates who leap to PURPOSE without quoting score nothing for evidence. The four-beat chain is the answer structure — practise it until it is automatic.

The method vocabulary: what to look for

CategoryFeaturesWhat it tends to do
Diction (word choice)strong verbs, evaluative adjectives, connotation, register shiftsshapes judgement and sympathy
Figurative languagesimile, metaphor, personification, hyperbole, symbolcreates imagery, comparison, emotional colour
Sensory imagerysight, sound, smell, taste, touchimmerses the reader in a place or moment
Sound devicesalliteration, assonance, onomatopoeia, sibilanceadds mood and rhythm; softens or sharpens tone
Sentence structureshort sentences, long sentences, fragments, listing, repetition, questionscontrols pace, tension and emphasis
Perspective and detailwhat is shown or withheld, focalisation, contrast, juxtapositiondirects sympathy and reveals theme

Diction: reading connotation

Words carry two meanings: the dictionary meaning (denotation) and the associations (connotation). Analysis lives in connotation. Compare: the house stood on the hill / the house perched on the hill / the house crouched on the hill. Perched suggests lightness and elevation; crouched suggests menace, weight, waiting. When you analyse diction, name the connotation direction: what does this word suggest that a neutral word would not?

  • Verbs are the richest targets: in "the river snaked through the valley", snaked suggests sinuous movement and a faint threat — analyse the verb before the adjectives.
  • Evaluative adjectives: "the tiny, defiant crowd" already tells the reader how to feel; identify the judgement embedded in the adjective.
  • Register and tone shifts: a formal description suddenly interrupted by a slang word (or the reverse) creates irony or intimacy.

Figurative language: naming the effect precisely

DeviceDefinitionEffect vocabulary
Similecomparison using like or ascompares X to Y, making it vivid / suggesting it is fragile / threatening
MetaphorX is described as Ytransforms X, implying it shares Y's qualities
Personificationhuman qualities given to a thingbrings X alive / makes nature feel hostile or companionable
Hyperboledeliberate exaggerationintensifies emotion / adds humour / shows obsession
Symbolan object that stands for an ideacompresses the theme into an image the reader carries

The analysis must name what the figure compares or implies and what that does to the reader's feeling. "The sky was a bruise" — metaphor: the sky is described as damaged flesh, so the scene feels injured and threatening, suggesting violence has already happened.

Sentence structure and sound as effects

  • Short sentences: shock, finality, tension. "Then the door opened." A short sentence after long ones lands like a punch.
  • Long sentences: accumulation, calm, overload, dreaminess. Lists and polysyndeton (and ... and ... and ...) create breathlessness or abundance.
  • Fragments: a sentence without a verb or subject ("Silence. Then nothing.") mimics broken thought or stunned reaction.
  • Repetition and rule of three: "he ran and ran and ran" or a tricolon builds emphasis and rhythm.
  • Alliteration and sibilance: repeated sounds create mood — sibilance (s, sh sounds) is soft and secretive or sinister; hard consonants (k, t, g) are aggressive and abrupt.
  • Onomatopoeia: words that sound like their meaning (crash, murmur, hissed) pull the reader's ear into the scene.

Deconstructing the prompt: the five-step routine

  1. Underline the effect words in the question — "How does the writer create the atmosphere of tension in this extract?" Your whole answer serves tension; a brilliant point about humour is off-target.
  2. Skim for the effect, not the features: find the lines where the named effect is strongest (usually the turn in the passage).
  3. Select two to three genuinely strong features — one diction point, one figurative or structural point is usually enough for a full-mark answer.
  4. Build the four-beat chain for each — quotation, method, effect on the reader, purpose in context.
  5. Write in a sequence: open with a sentence that answers the question directly ("The writer creates tension through violent diction and oppressive imagery"), develop each feature as a mini-paragraph, and keep the question's effect word in every other sentence as your anchor.

The effect vocabulary bank

Weak answers say "it makes it interesting". Strong answers have a bank of precise effect phrases. Build yours from this list and use each one only when accurate: creates an atmosphere of ...; conveys a sense of ...; makes the reader feel ...; suggests that ...; implies ...; emphasises ...; highlights ...; draws attention to ...; reinforces the idea that ...; leaves the reader expecting ...; unsettles the reader; evokes sympathy for ...; conveys the character's ...; establishes ...; contrasts with ...; signals a shift from ... to ...

Model answer with top-band breakdown

Extract: "The market was a living thing: breathing steam, groaning trolleys, a heartbeat of a thousand footsteps. I stood very still, and it swallowed me whole."

Model answer: "The writer creates an overwhelming, almost frightening sense of the market's scale through personification and metaphor. The market is described as a living thing, breathing steam and groaning trolleys, so the crowd seems to have one body and one will — the reader feels the place as an organism rather than a location. The metaphor continues with the heartbeat of a thousand footsteps, turning ordinary noise into something alive and relentless, which intensifies the speaker's smallness. That smallness is completed by the final metaphor: the market swallowed me whole. The verb swallowed suggests being consumed without trace, so the reader feels the speaker's helplessness and the city's indifference to the individual."

Breakdown of why it hits the top band: it opens by naming the effect (overwhelming, frightening sense of scale) and the methods; each quotation is brief and exact (living thing, swallowed me whole); each method is named (personification, metaphor, verb choice); every effect is reader-directed (the reader feels ...; intensifies ...; suggests being consumed); and the final clause links to purpose in context (the city's indifference). There is no feature-spotting and no padding.

Worked example: deconstructing a prompt

Prompt: "How does the writer create sympathy for the boy in lines 12-20?"
Step 1: effect anchor = sympathy (not fear, not admiration)
Step 2: find the lines where the boy is shown as vulnerable
Step 3: select features:
        (a) diction: "threadbare", "counted his coins twice"
        (b) contrast: the crowd's indifference against his hope
Step 4: build chains:
        (a) threadbare -> adjective -> clothes worn thin -> poverty visible
            counted his coins twice -> verb phrase -> care and anxiety
            -> the reader sees a child managing scarcity alone
        (b) contrast -> juxtaposition of the bustling crowd and the boy
            alone -> heightens isolation -> the reader's sympathy
Step 5: write: open with the answer, develop (a) then (b), keep
        "sympathy" in the anchor sentence and the final line.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Diction) "The old man shuffled to the window." What does shuffled suggest? Answer: The verb suggests slow, dragging, effortful movement — the man is aged or exhausted, so the reader feels his frailty and perhaps pity.
  2. (Simile) "The silence hung over them like a held breath." Explain the effect. Answer: The simile compares the silence to a held breath, so the quiet feels temporary and full of suspense — the reader expects something to happen or break.
  3. (Sentence structure) "He ran. The corridor stretched and stretched. He ran." How does the structure create tension? Answer: The short, repeated sentences create urgency and breathlessness, while the repetition of stretched mimics the corridor's endlessness, making the reader feel the pursuit dragging on.
  4. (Personification) "The house watched them leave." What is the effect? Answer: Giving the house the human action of watching makes it seem alive and perhaps resentful, so the departure feels observed and uneasy rather than free.
  5. (Combined) "The factory exhaled grey smoke that smothered the gardens." Identify two methods and their effects. Answer: Personification (exhaled) makes the factory seem like a living, breathing force; the metaphor smothered presents the smoke as something that kills life, so the reader feels the pollution as an active threat to the community's homes.
  6. (Purpose in context) Why might a writer describe a character's hands as "bird-bones"? Answer: The metaphor compares the hands to fragile bird bones, suggesting thinness and delicacy, which builds a picture of vulnerability — useful if the writer wants the reader to fear for the character's safety.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Feature-spotting: "There is alliteration and metaphor" with no effect commentary is worth nothing. The method name is the start of the sentence, not the answer.
  • "Makes it interesting": the empty effect phrase. Every effect must be specific — interesting to whom, creating what feeling, suggesting what about the character or theme?
  • Long quotations: quote only the words you analyse (two to six words). A lifted sentence without commentary reads as copying.
  • Analysing the wrong thing: the question's effect word is the anchor. An answer about atmosphere when the question asked about sympathy is off-target however good the analysis.
  • Choosing weak features: not every adjective is worth analysis. Pick features that clearly serve the named effect; one deep point beats three shallow ones.
  • Missing the structure level: most candidates analyse words only. A comment on sentence length, repetition or word order after a diction point adds a whole dimension the mark scheme values.
  • No link to context: the four-beat chain ends at purpose — why the writer wants the reader to feel this here. That final clause is the difference between a good and a top answer.
  • Listing without sequencing: a bulleted list of features cannot show the cumulative effect. Write developed mini-paragraphs and order them from the strongest point to the supporting one.

title: Pressure & Density — Study Notes
content:
Pressure & Density

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2023–2025): pressure & pressure differences in fluids, density review (Extended pressure-depth).

1. Pressure basics

p = F/A (Pa = N/m²). Increase F or decrease A to raise pressure; explain applications (snowshoes, knives, hydraulic press).

2. Liquids

  • Pressure increases with depth: p = ρgh (Extended).
  • Same level, same liquid ⇒ same pressure (hydrostatic paradox).
  • Hydraulic systems transmit pressure — force multiplier: F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂.

3. Atmospheric pressure

~10⁵ Pa at sea level; demonstrated by collapsing can, mercury barometer 760 mmHg; decreases with altitude.

4. Density revisited

ρ = m/V; floating condition; upthrust = weight of displaced fluid (qualitative).

5. Gas pressure (particle model)

Particles collide with walls → force per area. Volume ↓ at same T ⇒ pressure ↑ (more frequent collisions). Temperature ↑ ⇒ faster particles ⇒ more frequent, harder impacts.

title: IGCSE Chemistry: Stoichiometry and the Mole
content:
IGCSE Chemistry: Stoichiometry and the Mole

Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry 0620 (2026–2028), Extended route, Topic 3 Stoichiometry: statement 3.1 Formulae, 3.2 Relative masses of atoms and molecules, and 3.3 The mole and the Avogadro constant. Stoichiometry is the accounting of chemistry — it answers "how much?" for every reaction — and it is the single highest-yield calculation topic on Paper 4. Every calculation below is expanded one line at a time with no skipped arithmetic, and each method is stated as a repeatable recipe before the numbers, because the marks sit in the working.

What a chemical formula tells you

Think of a formula as a recipe for one particle of a substance. H₂O says: every molecule of water contains exactly two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom. The small numbers are subscripts — they count atoms inside the particle, and changing them changes the substance entirely (H₂O is water; H₂O₂ is hydrogen peroxide).

  • Empirical formula: the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms in a compound. For glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆) the empirical formula is CH₂O — the ratio 6:12:6 divided by 6.
  • Molecular formula: the actual number of each atom in one molecule (C₆H₁₂O₆).
  • Formula of ionic compounds: the ratio that makes the charges balance. Ca²⁺ and Cl⁻ combine as CaCl₂ because one 2+ ion needs two 1− ions for neutrality.

State symbols appear on every equation and carry a mark: (s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas, (aq) aqueous (dissolved in water).

Equations: balancing and the conservation of mass

Atoms are never created or destroyed in a chemical reaction — mass is conserved. Balancing an equation is simply making the atom count of each element equal on both sides. The master method:

Balance: Al + O2 -> Al2O3   (no state symbols until balanced)

1. List the elements and count each side:
     left:  Al 1, O 2      right: Al 2, O 3
2. Pick the element that appears in the most complex formula and balance it
   first - here Al: put 2 in front of Al:
     2Al + O2 -> Al2O3      left: Al 2, O 2   right: Al 2, O 3
3. Balance O. Left has 2, right has 3. The lowest number both divide into
   is 6 - so aim for 6 O on each side:
     O2 needs 3 molecules (3 x 2 = 6); Al2O3 needs 2 formula units
     (2 x 3 = 6):
     2Al + 3O2 -> 2Al2O3
4. Re-count Al: right now has 4 (2 x 2). Fix the left:
     4Al + 3O2 -> 2Al2O3
5. Final check, every element:
     Al 4 = 4 ✓    O 6 = 6 ✓
6. Add state symbols from the facts you know:
     4Al(s) + 3O2(g) -> 2Al2O3(s)

Rules that never fail: only change the BIG numbers in front (never the
subscripts), never invent atoms, and always re-count at the end.

Relative atomic mass and relative formula mass

You cannot weigh individual atoms, so chemistry compares masses against a standard: one-twelfth the mass of a carbon-12 atom. The relative atomic mass (Aᵣ) is the weighted average mass of an element's atoms on that scale. The relative molecular mass (Mᵣ) (or relative formula mass for ionic compounds) is the sum of the Aᵣ values in the formula.

Worked: find the Mᵣ of calcium carbonate, CaCO₃.

  Aᵣ values from the Periodic Table: Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16
  Mᵣ = 40 + 12 + (3 x 16)
     = 40 + 12 + 48
     = 100

Note the parenthesis: the subscript 3 multiplies ONLY the oxygen.
A common error is 40 + 12 + 16 = 68 - one mark lost to a bracket.

Mᵣ of sulfuric acid, H₂SO₄:
  Mᵣ = (2 x 1) + 32 + (4 x 16)
     = 2 + 32 + 64
     = 98

The mole and the Avogadro constant

A mole is the chemist's counting unit, like "a dozen" — but sized for atoms. One mole of any substance contains 6.02 × 10²³ particles (the Avogadro constant, L). The practical magic: one mole of any substance has a mass in grams equal to its Mᵣ, which turns unweighable atoms into weighable quantities.

The mole triangle - the three relationships and how to rearrange them:

        mass (g)
        /      \
       /        \
    moles x Mᵣ = mass        moles = mass / Mᵣ     Mᵣ = mass / moles

  particles = moles x 6.02 x 10²³

Worked: how many molecules are in 4.4 g of carbon dioxide, CO₂?

Step 1 - Mᵣ of CO₂ = 12 + (2 x 16) = 44
Step 2 - moles = mass / Mᵣ = 4.4 / 44 = 0.1 mol
Step 3 - molecules = 0.1 x 6.02 x 10²³ = 6.02 x 10²² molecules
Step 4 (if asked for ATOMS): each CO₂ has 3 atoms, so
        atoms = 6.02 x 10²² x 3 = 1.806 x 10²³ atoms

"Particles" can mean atoms, molecules or ions - read the question's word.
Question asks forWorking lineWorked number
Moles from massmoles = mass ÷ Mᵣ25 g CaCO₃ → 25 ÷ 100 = 0.25 mol
Mass from molesmass = moles × Mᵣ0.25 mol CO₂ → 0.25 × 44 = 11 g
Particles from molesparticles = moles × 6.02 × 10²³0.25 mol → 1.505 × 10²³ molecules
Gas volume at r.t.p.volume = moles × 24 dm³0.25 mol → 6 dm³
Solution molesmoles = c (mol/dm³) × V (dm³)0.1 × 0.025 = 0.0025 mol
Concentrationc = moles ÷ V (dm³)0.004 mol in 25 cm³ → 0.16 mol/dm³

Reacting masses

The balanced equation is a recipe in moles: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O says 2 moles of hydrogen react with 1 mole of oxygen to make 2 moles of water. Master method for every reacting-mass question: balance the equation → convert given mass to moles → use the equation's ratio → convert back to mass.

Worked: what mass of water forms when 10 g of hydrogen burns in 100 g of
oxygen? And which reactant limits the yield?

Step 1 - balance:  2H₂ + O₂ -> 2H₂O
Step 2 - moles of each reactant:
   H₂:  Mᵣ = 2   ->  moles = 10 / 2  = 5 mol
   O₂:  Mᵣ = 32  ->  moles = 100 / 32 = 3.125 mol
Step 3 - the ratio needed is 2 : 1.
   5 mol H₂ would need 5 / 2 = 2.5 mol O₂.
   We have 3.125 mol O₂ - MORE than needed, so O₂ is in excess and
   H₂ is the LIMITING reactant. All calculations use the limiting one.
Step 4 - moles of water from the limiting reactant:
   ratio H₂ : H₂O = 2 : 2 = 1 : 1  ->  water = 5 mol
Step 5 - mass of water:
   Mᵣ(H₂O) = 18  ->  mass = 5 x 18 = 90 g

Sanity check: 10 + 100 = 110 g in; 90 g water + 10 g unreacted O₂ out
(3.125 - 2.5 = 0.625 mol O₂ left = 0.625 x 32 = 20 g... 
wait - recompute: 100 - 80 = 20 g O₂ left, and 90 + 20 = 110 g ✓)

Percentage yield = (actual mass ÷ theoretical mass) × 100. If the reaction above actually gave 72 g of water: percentage yield = 72 ÷ 90 × 100 = 80%. Percentage purity = (mass of pure product ÷ mass of impure sample) × 100 — a different question, and mixing the two up is a classic lost mark.

Gas volumes

At room temperature and pressure (r.t.p.), one mole of any gas occupies 24 dm³ (24 000 cm³). This connects gas volumes straight to moles.

Worked: what volume of carbon dioxide forms when 25 g of calcium carbonate
decomposes?  CaCO₃ -> CaO + CO₂

Step 1 - balance (already 1:1:1)
Step 2 - moles CaCO₃ = 25 / 100 = 0.25 mol
Step 3 - ratio 1 : 1  ->  CO₂ = 0.25 mol
Step 4 - volume = moles x 24 = 0.25 x 24 = 6 dm³
        (in cm³: 6 x 1000 = 6000 cm³)

The reverse works identically: 480 cm³ of gas = 0.48 dm³
-> moles = 0.48 / 24 = 0.02 mol.

Solutions, concentration and titration

Concentration says how much solute sits in a given volume of solution, in g/dm³ or mol/dm³. The working equations: moles = concentration (mol/dm³) × volume (dm³), and cm³ ÷ 1000 = dm³.

Titration worked in full: 25.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide solution is neutralised
by 20.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ sulfuric acid. Find the NaOH concentration.

  2NaOH + H₂SO₄ -> Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O        [balanced first: ratio 2 : 1]

Step 1 - moles of acid used:
   volume = 20.0 cm³ = 20.0 / 1000 = 0.0200 dm³
   moles H₂SO₄ = 0.100 x 0.0200 = 0.00200 mol
Step 2 - ratio 2 : 1, so:
   moles NaOH = 0.00200 x 2 = 0.00400 mol
Step 3 - concentration of NaOH:
   volume = 25.0 cm³ = 0.0250 dm³
   conc = moles / volume = 0.00400 / 0.0250 = 0.160 mol/dm³

Three marks hide in three places: the balanced ratio (2:1), the cm³ to dm³
conversion, and the final division the right way up.

Titrration technique itself (burette, pipette, indicator, concordant titres) is Paper 6 material — see the experimental techniques note — but the calculation above is pure Paper 4.

Empirical and molecular formulae from data

Worked: a compound contains 40.0% carbon, 6.7% hydrogen and 53.3% oxygen
by mass. Its Mᵣ is 180. Find the empirical and molecular formulae.

Master method: assume 100 g -> divide each percentage by Aᵣ -> divide by the
smallest -> scale to whole numbers.

Step 1 - assume 100 g: C 40.0 g, H 6.7 g, O 53.3 g
Step 2 - convert to moles (Aᵣ: C 12, H 1, O 16):
   C: 40.0 / 12 = 3.33 mol
   H:  6.7 /  1 = 6.70 mol
   O: 53.3 / 16 = 3.33 mol
Step 3 - divide by the smallest (3.33):
   C: 3.33 / 3.33 = 1
   H: 6.70 / 3.33 = 2.01 ≈ 2
   O: 3.33 / 3.33 = 1
Step 4 - empirical formula = CH₂O   (empirical Mᵣ = 12 + 2 + 16 = 30)
Step 5 - molecular formula: 180 / 30 = 6, so multiply by 6
   molecular formula = C₆H₁₂O₆

Check: 6 x 12 + 12 x 1 + 6 x 16 = 72 + 12 + 96 = 180 ✓

Worked example: one problem using every method

10.0 g of magnesium reacts with hydrochloric acid:
  Mg + 2HCl -> MgCl₂ + H₂

(a) moles Mg = 10.0 / 24 = 0.4167 mol
(b) moles HCl needed = 0.4167 x 2 = 0.8333 mol
(c) if HCl is supplied as 2.00 mol/dm³, volume needed =
    0.8333 / 2.00 = 0.4167 dm³ = 416.7 cm³
(d) volume of H₂ at r.t.p. = 0.4167 x 24 = 10.0 dm³
(e) if only 8.4 dm³ of H₂ is collected, percentage yield =
    8.4 / 10.0 x 100 = 84%

One equation, five question shapes - mass, ratio, concentration, gas volume,
yield. The method never changes: moles first, ratio second, back to units.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Changing subscripts to "balance" an equation — that invents a different substance; only front numbers change.
  • Forgetting subscripts when calculating Mᵣ (Mᵣ of CaCO₃ is 100, not 68); bracket the multiplied terms.
  • Skipping the cm³ → dm³ conversion (divide by 1000) in concentration work — the most common single arithmetic slip on Paper 4.
  • Inverting the concentration rearrangement: moles = c × V, so c = moles ÷ V — state the triangle, don't improvise.
  • Using the excess reactant instead of the limiting one in reacting-mass questions; always compare moles ÷ coefficient first.
  • Confusing percentage yield with percentage purity — yield compares actual vs theoretical product; purity compares pure substance vs sample.
  • Dropping the ×10²³ or writing 6.02 × 10⁻²³; the Avogadro constant is positive-indexed and multiplied, not divided, for particle counts.
  • Quoting 24 dm³ without the conditions "at r.t.p."; the molar gas volume only holds there.
  • In empirical formula questions, not scaling 2.01 or 1.99 to whole numbers (2) — ratios are always whole numbers.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 4, 3 marks). Calculate the relative formula mass of ammonium nitrate, NH₄NO₃. (Aᵣ: N = 14, H = 1, O = 16)

Answer: Mᵣ = (2 × 14) + (4 × 1) + (3 × 16) = 28 + 4 + 48 = 80.

Question 2 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Calculate the mass of iron formed when 320 g of iron(III) oxide is reduced by carbon monoxide: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂. (Aᵣ: Fe = 56, O = 16)

Answer: Mᵣ(Fe₂O₃) = (2 × 56) + (3 × 16) = 160. Moles Fe₂O₃ = 320 ÷ 160 = 2 mol. Ratio Fe₂O₃ : Fe = 1 : 2, so Fe = 4 mol. Mass Fe = 4 × 56 = 224 g.

Question 3 (Paper 4, 5 marks). A student neutralises 25.0 cm³ of 0.200 mol/dm³ HNO₃ with Na₂CO₃ solution. Calculate the moles of acid and the mass of anhydrous Na₂CO₃ needed. (Mᵣ Na₂CO₃ = 106)

Answer: Moles HNO₃ = 0.200 × (25.0 ÷ 1000) = 0.200 × 0.025 = 0.00500 mol. Equation: Na₂CO₃ + 2HNO₃ → 2NaNO₃ + H₂O + CO₂, ratio 1 : 2, so moles Na₂CO₃ = 0.00500 ÷ 2 = 0.00250 mol. Mass = 0.00250 × 106 = 0.265 g.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 3 marks). Calculate the volume at r.t.p. of 8.8 g of carbon dioxide.

Answer: Mᵣ(CO₂) = 44; moles = 8.8 ÷ 44 = 0.2 mol; volume = 0.2 × 24 = 4.8 dm³.

Question 5 (Paper 4, 4 marks). An oxide of iron contains 69.9% iron by mass, the rest oxygen. Find its empirical formula. (Aᵣ: Fe = 56, O = 16)

Answer: Assume 100 g: Fe 69.9 g, O 30.1 g. Moles: Fe = 69.9 ÷ 56 = 1.248; O = 30.1 ÷ 16 = 1.881. Divide by the smallest (1.248): Fe 1, O 1.881 ÷ 1.248 = 1.51 ≈ 1.5. Multiply by 2 for whole numbers: Fe₂O₃. Check: (2 × 56) + (3 × 16) = 160; Fe fraction = 112 ÷ 160 = 69.9% ✓.

Question 6 (Paper 4, 3 marks). 0.24 g of magnesium gives 240 cm³ of hydrogen at r.t.p. Calculate the percentage yield if theory predicts 288 cm³.

Answer: Percentage yield = (240 ÷ 288) × 100 = 83.3%.

With the quantitative bookkeeping in place, the next question is what these particles actually are — atomic structure and bonding.

title: Abstract Data Types — Study Notes
content:
Abstract Data Types

What is an ADT?

An abstract data type is a logical description of a collection of data plus the operations on it, independent of implementation. Stacks, queues, linked lists, binary trees and hash tables are all ADTs; in A Level you must show how they are built from arrays or records with pointers.

Linked Lists

Each node holds a value and a pointer to the next node; a start pointer marks the head and a null marks the end. Insertion rewires two pointers — no shifting — giving O(1) insertion at a known position, but access requires walking the list, O(n).

Stacks and Queues

A stack is LIFO (push and pop at the top); a queue is FIFO (enqueue at the rear, dequeue from the front). Both can be arrays with index pointers or linked lists. Stack uses include call stacks and expression evaluation; queue uses include print buffers and breadth-first search.

Binary Search Trees

Each node has up to two children; left subtree keys are smaller, right subtree keys larger. Search, insert and (average-case) delete are O(log n). An in-order traversal outputs keys in ascending order. A degenerate (linear) tree from sorted input degrades to O(n).

Hash Tables

Covered in file organisation, but as an ADT a hash table pairs a hash function with bucket storage for O(1) average access.

Exam tips: be able to draw a tree after a sequence of insertions and write its three traversals; state the pointer changes for a linked-list insertion; compare ADT operations with Big-O.

Abstract data types in practice

An abstract data type is defined by the operations it supports and their behaviour, not by how it is stored. A stack is defined by push, pop and isEmpty; the programmer using it does not need to know whether it is built from an array or a linked list.

Separating the interface from the implementation lets the implementation change without breaking the code that uses it, and makes each part easier to test.

Exam tip: when asked to define an ADT, name the operations and say what each does, not how it is stored.

title: Exam technique: Dynamics
content:
### What earns the marks
For resultant force, subtract opposition before applying F = ma to earn both marks. For collisions, total momentum before equated to total after earns the method mark. For rebounds, the sign change included earns the second mark.
### Traps
Error: friction ignored in acceleration. Correction: use the resultant, not the push alone. Error: rebound treated as stopping. Correction: add the speeds with the sign flip. Error: kinetic energy claimed conserved generally. Correction: momentum always, kinetic only when elastic.

title: Exam technique: Programming and Algorithms
content:
### What earns the marks
For validation, the rejected range stated plus the rejection loop earns both marks. For structure, single entry and exit modules using only sequence, selection and iteration earn the design marks. For traces, each variable tracked per line earns method credit. For testing, the stage named with its setting (isolated module vs live users) earns each mark.
### Traps
Error: fixed FOR loops for unknown-attempt validation. Correction: WHILE-until-valid loops. Error: binary search on unsorted data. Correction: sort first or use linear search. Error: unit and acceptance settings swapped. Correction: unit is isolated with test data; acceptance is live with real users.
### Worked example
A trace table records the value of each variable at each step of an algorithm. For a linear search, the program checks each item in turn and can take up to n comparisons. A binary search on a sorted list halves the search space each time, so 16 sorted items need at most about log₂16 = 4 comparisons. Binary search only works if the list is sorted.
### Check yourself
Trace a binary search for 9 in the sorted list 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13. Record the middle index at each step and state the number of comparisons. It finds 9 at the middle on the first comparison.
