A binary search on a sorted list halves the search space each time, so 16 sorted items need at most about log₂16 = 4 comparisons. Binary search only works if the list is sorted.

title: Integration II — Study Notes
content:
Integration II

Standard Integrals

  • ∫ sin x dx = −cos x + c
  • ∫ cos x dx = sin x + c
  • ∫ e^x dx = e^x + c
  • ∫ 1/x dx = ln|x| + c
  • ∫ sec²x dx = tan x + c

With linear arguments: ∫ e^(3x) dx = e^(3x)/3 + c; ∫ cos 2x dx = sin 2x/2 + c.

Substitution

Reverse of the chain rule. For ∫ 2x e^(x²) dx, let u = x²: du = 2x dx, so the integral is ∫ e^u du = e^(x²) + c.

Integration by Parts

∫ u (dv/dx) dx = uv − ∫ v (du/dx) dx. Choose u to be the part that simplifies when differentiated (LIATE: logs, inverse trig, algebraic, trig, exponential).

Example: ∫ x e^x dx = x e^x − ∫ e^x dx = x e^x − e^x + c.

Partial Fractions

Break rational functions into pieces like ∫ 1/(x+1) dx = ln|x + 1| + c.

Example: ∫ 4x/(x² − 1) dx = ∫ [2/(x − 1) + 2/(x + 1)] dx = 2 ln|x − 1| + 2 ln|x + 1| + c.

Exam tips: definite integrals: substitute limits into the transformed variable directly; for by-parts integrals like ∫ ln x dx, take u = ln x, dv/dx = 1.

Exam method: exponential and reciprocal integrals

The integral of e^(kx) is (1/k) e^(kx) + c, and the integral of e^x is e^x + c. The integral of 1/(ax + b) is (1/a) ln|ax + b| + c. Dividing by the coefficient of x is the step most often missed, so check it by differentiating your answer.

For a definite integral, evaluate the antiderivative at the upper limit, subtract its value at the lower limit, and write the bracket with its limits, such as [e^(2x)/2] from 0 to 1.

When the integrand is a product, integration by parts gives ∫u dv = uv − ∫v du. Choose u to be the part that becomes simpler when differentiated, such as x in x eˣ.

Substitution changes the limits as well as the variable. Either change the limits to the new variable or substitute back before using the original limits; do not mix the two.

Exam cue: Give the answer as an exact value, such as (e² − 1)/2, unless the question asks for a decimal.

Worked example: integration by parts

Find the integral of x e^x with respect to x. Let u = x and dv/dx = e^x, so du/dx = 1 and v = e^x. Then the integral equals x e^x minus the integral of e^x, which is x e^x − e^x + c = (x − 1) e^x + c. Differentiate the answer to check that it returns the integrand.

Definite integrals and area

For a region above the x-axis, the definite integral between the limits gives its area. If part of the curve lies below the axis, that part contributes a negative value to the integral, so the total area is the sum of the absolute values of each part. Sketch the curve first. Integrating across a point where the curve crosses the axis gives the signed net value, not the area.

Checking your answer

  • After integrating, differentiate the answer and confirm that it reproduces the original function.
  • Include the constant of integration on indefinite integrals, and never write it on a definite integral.
  • When a substitution changes the variable, change the limits too, or convert back to x before substituting the original limits.

The integration topic of the Cambridge AS and A Level Mathematics 9709 syllabus expects these methods to be applied to standard forms and to exam-style problems, with the method stated clearly at each step.

title: Exam technique: Integration
content:
### What earns the marks
For indefinite integrals, each term raised correctly plus the constant earns full marks. For definite integrals, the antiderivative quoted earns one mark and the correct upper-minus-lower evaluation earns the next. For area and curve-finding, the limits or the given point used earns the final mark.
### Traps
Error: constant of integration omitted. Correction: +c always for indefinite. Error: limits subtracted backwards. Correction: upper minus lower. Error: power rule inverted on roots. Correction: root x is x to the half, integral goes up.

title: Edexcel IAL Computer Science: File Organisation, Data Types and Floating Point
content:
Edexcel IAL Computer Science: File Organisation, Data Types and Floating Point

Pearson Edexcel International Advanced Level in Computer Science, Unit 3 Advanced Computer Science: files and their organisation and access, user-defined data types, and floating-point representation and manipulation. This note goes beneath the arrays and records of AS into how data physically lives on backing storage and how real numbers are stored and computed — the two topics where exam questions demand mechanism, not definitions. Every pointer movement and every normalisation step is traced on a diagram.

File concepts and access methods

A file is a named collection of records on secondary storage; a record is a collection of fields describing one entity; records may be fixed-length (each record the same size — simple addressing, wasted space for short records) or variable-length (space-efficient, but locating records needs length markers or delimiters). A key field identifies each record uniquely and drives access.

Access methodMechanismStrengthsWeaknesses
SequentialRecords read/written in key order, one after anotherEfficient for batch processing and tape/streamed media; simpleSlow for random queries (average half the file scanned); updates need rewriting
Direct (random)Record located by key → address (hashing or an index)Immediate single-record retrieval regardless of file sizeNeeds hashing/index infrastructure; may leave unused slots
Indexed sequential (ISAM)Sequential file plus an index of keys → addressesBoth fast random lookup and ordered sequential processingIndex maintenance cost; index itself can fragment
Sequential access worked: pay run over a 1000-record file.

  Open file; read record 1, process, write to output; read record 2...;
  one pass, one read per record - O(n) with tiny constants: ideal for batch.

Direct access worked: find one customer account.

  Hash the account number to a slot: address = hash(key); read once at that
  address - O(1). But finding "all accounts in London" needs scanning or a
  secondary index - the query pattern decides the method.

Record address arithmetic (fixed-length):
  record i's byte address = start + i x recordSize
  With 32-byte records starting at byte 100: record 5 = 100 + 5 × 32 = 260.
  Variable-length records break this arithmetic - a pointer table or length
  prefix is needed instead.

File organisation in commercial systems: heap files (unordered, append anywhere), sorted files (binary-searchable, expensive insertion), hashed files (O(1) by key, poor at ranges), clustered files (records grouped by a related key — e.g. all of a customer's orders physically together). The exam wants the choice justified by the workload: point lookup, range scan, or ordered processing.

File maintenance operations: serial update (new transaction file + old master → new master, one pass), random update (locate and rewrite one record), and the failure handling around them (transaction logs keep a recovery trail — the link to the DBMS recovery work in the database note).

File organisation in database systems

Relational tables are files underneath, and the same organisation choices appear as storage-engine decisions. Heap storage appends rows cheaply (good for bulk loads, poor for key lookup); sorted storage supports binary search but rewrites on insertion; hashed storage gives O(1) key access but no ordering; clustered storage groups rows by a related key (all a customer's orders together), making that join a sequential read. Secondary indexes are files of (key, pointer) pairs that restore fast lookup on non-key fields, at the cost of maintaining them on every write. The exam's design question wants the workload named first — point lookup, range scan, ordered report — and the organisation chosen for it.

Worked example: index selection for a query workload

A library table book(ISBN [PK], title, author, year, copies) serves three queries:

  Q1 find by ISBN           → the primary key index already answers this
  Q2 find by author         → secondary index on author (point lookup by name)
  Q3 list all books of a year, in title order → composite index (year, title)
                                so the range scan returns rows already sorted

Writing cost: each additional index slows INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE (every index
must be maintained) and costs storage - so index the read paths the workload
actually uses, not every column. The rule of thumb earns the mark: indexes
serve queries, constraints serve correctness.

User-defined data types

Primitive types cannot express domain structure, so languages offer composition. A record (struct) groups named fields of differing types; enumerated types name a finite set of legal values (DAY = {Mon…Sun}); arrays/sequences group like values; union/variant types hold one of several shapes; and classes bundle records with behaviour (see the OOP note).

Worked: a payroll record type and its use.

  TYPE Employee = RECORD
      empID     : STRING
      name      : STRING
      payGrade  : (A, B, C)          // enumerated: illegal values impossible
      hours     : REAL
      rate      : REAL
  END RECORD

  VAR e : Employee
  e.empID <- "E104"; e.rate <- 12.50; e.hours <- 37.5

  pay <- e.hours * e.rate   // 37.5 × 12.50 = 468.75

Benefits visible here: typed fields prevent "hours = "Tues"" at the type
level; the enum prevents payGrade = "Z"; and grouping means one array element
holds the whole employee - ARRAY[1:500] OF Employee is a payroll file in
memory. Records of records (nested) express containment: a Department record
holds an array of Employee sub-records.

Static versus dynamic typing is the exam's comparison: static types (Pascal, Java) check at compile time, catching whole classes of errors before run and enabling optimisation; dynamic types (Python) defer checks to run time, gaining flexibility at the cost of late error discovery. User-defined types sit on the static side: they make invalid states unrepresentable.

Floating point: representation and manipulation

Recalling the AS construction (value = mantissa × 2^(exponent−bias), normalised with a hidden leading 1), this note adds the manipulation rules and their pitfalls.

Addition in floating point, step by step with rounding:

  x = 1.1011 × 2²   (mantissa 1011, exponent 2)
  y = 1.0110 × 2⁰   (mantissa 0110, exponent 0)

  1. ALIGN: shift the smaller mantissa right by the exponent difference (2),
     truncating bits shifted off the end (this is where precision is lost):
     y' = 0.0101(10...) × 2²   (dropped bits rounded: 10 → round up here)
  2. ADD the mantissas:
     1.1011 + 0.0101 = 10.0000 × 2²
  3. RENORMALISE: 10.0000 × 2² = 1.0000 × 2³
  4. ROUND to the available mantissa bits (here exact), check exponent range.

Multiplication differs: multiply mantissas, ADD exponents, normalise once -
no alignment step, so no alignment truncation:
  (1.1011 × 2²) x (1.0110 × 2⁰):
  mantissas: 1.1011 × 1.0110 = 10.0110(01...) → 1.0011(0) × 2¹ after
  normalise; exponents: 2 + 0 = 1. Result ≈ 1.0011 × 2¹ = 2.375.

Division: divide mantissas, subtract exponents, normalise.

Errors and their names: rounding error (values between representable numbers are rounded — 0.1 is not exactly representable), absorption/cancellation (adding a large and small float loses the small one's digits; subtracting nearly equal values loses significant figures), underflow (result too small for the exponent field → zero or denormal), overflow (too large → infinity). Standards: IEEE 754 defines single (32-bit: 1+8+23) and double (64-bit: 1+11+52) formats, special values (±0, ±∞, NaN), and rounding modes.

Cancellation worked:

  x = 1.0000001 × 2⁷ = 128.000128
  y = 1.0000000 × 2⁷ = 128.000000
  x - y = 0.000128 - exact in this case, but if the mantissa held only 6
  significant bits, x and y would round to the SAME stored value and the
  difference would be 0.000000. "Why is (x + y) - x not always y?" is
  exactly this: the alignment step of x + y may have rounded y away.

Money in floats (again, now with the mechanism): 0.1 + 0.2 in IEEE 754
double = 0.30000000000000004, because 0.1 is stored as 0.1000000000000000055...
and 0.2 as 0.2000000000000000111...; the sum's alignment and rounding leave
the residue. Integer pence avoid the whole class of error.

Worked example: choosing storage for three problems

1. Payroll processed every Friday for 800 employees (all records, in ID
   order): sequential access over a sorted file - one pass, O(n), no index
   maintenance needed.

2. A cashier pulling one account by number on demand: direct access - hash
   the key to an address, O(1) retrieval; the query is always by unique key.

3. A clinic system that takes appointments by patient and occasionally
   lists all patients alphabetically: indexed sequential - the index makes
   the point lookup fast while the ordered scan serves the listing; or a
   database (with the same indexing ideas) if concurrent updates matter.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Saying direct access "reads the record directly from the key" — the key is hashed or looked up in an index to get an address; something must translate one to the other.
  • Quoting record-address arithmetic on variable-length files; it needs a pointer table or length prefix.
  • Forgetting alignment in floating-point addition questions — the exponent difference dictates the right shift, and shifted-off bits are where error enters.
  • Confusing overflow/underflow with rounding error: range failures versus precision loss.
  • Claiming (x + y) − x = y always; cancellation and absorption make float algebra non-associative.
  • Choosing variable-length records when the exam's workload is fixed-size batch processing (or vice versa) without reasoning.
  • Describing enums as "shorthand for numbers"; their point is restricting a field to legal values.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Unit 3, 4 marks). Compare sequential and direct file access.

Answer: Sequential access reads records in order from the start — one pass, efficient for batch processing of whole files (payroll), but finding one record scans on average half the file. Direct access computes a record's location from its key (hashing or index) and reads it immediately — O(1) retrieval for single-record queries (cashier lookups), but it needs the hashing/index infrastructure and suits random rather than ordered workloads.

Question 2 (Unit 3, 4 marks). Explain two differences between fixed-length and variable-length records.

Answer: Fixed-length records reserve the same space for each record, so any record's address is arithmetic (start + i × size) and access is fast, but short records waste space and field sizes are capped. Variable-length records store only what each needs, saving space and allowing long fields, but locating records requires length prefixes or a pointer table and processing is more complex.

Question 3 (Unit 3, 4 marks). Describe how two floating-point numbers are added and where precision can be lost.

Answer: Align the exponents by shifting the smaller mantissa right by their difference (bits shifted off are truncated/rounded), add the mantissas, renormalise the result, and round to the available mantissa bits. Precision is lost during alignment (truncated bits) and the final rounding; if the exponent difference is large, the small number's contribution may vanish entirely (absorption).

Question 4 (Unit 3, 3 marks). Explain why floating-point arithmetic can give (0.1 + 0.2) ≠ 0.3.

Answer: 0.1 and 0.2 have no exact binary representation, so each is stored as the nearest representable mantissa × power of two; their tiny errors propagate through the alignment and addition, and the sum rounds to a value slightly above 0.3 (0.30000000000000004). Float algebra is approximate — a reason to use integer minor units or decimal types for money.

Question 5 (Unit 3, 4 marks). Explain the purpose of user-defined data types and give two examples.

Answer: User-defined types express domain structure that primitives cannot, making invalid data impossible to represent. A record (struct) groups named fields of different types describing one entity (employee: string ID, real rate); an enumerated type names the complete legal value set (payGrade ∈ {A, B, C}), so any other value is rejected at compile time. Both improve readability and safety over loose collections of primitives.

Question 6 (Unit 3, 3 marks). State what overflow and underflow mean in floating-point arithmetic.

Answer: Overflow is a result too large in magnitude for the exponent field to represent — it becomes infinity (or an error). Underflow is a result too small in magnitude for the smallest normal exponent — it becomes zero or a denormal number. Both are range failures of the format, distinct from rounding error, which affects precision within the representable range.

Files store data; databases govern it — the next note is the design and language layer on top.

title: IGCSE Mathematics: Indices and Standard Form
content:
IGCSE Mathematics: Indices and Standard Form

Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580 (2025–2027), section 1 Number: statement 1.3 Powers and roots, 1.7 Indices I (with Extended fractional indices), 1.8 Standard form, E1.18 Surds, and section 2 statement E2.4 Indices II (algebraic indices). Indices are shorthand for repeated multiplication, and their laws are the shortcuts that make large and small numbers manageable. This note derives each law from what it counts, covers standard form arithmetic in full, and finishes with surds and rationalising — an Extended favourite that separates the top grades.

Powers, roots and the vocabulary

In 5³ the base is 5 and the index (plural: indices) is 3; it means 5 × 5 × 5 = 125. A square root reverses a square: √25 = 5 because 5² = 25. A cube root reverses a cube: ³√64 = 4 because 4³ = 64.

  • √16 = 4, the principal (positive) square root, as printed on a calculator. But the equation x² = 16 has two solutions, x = 4 or x = −4, because (−4)² = 16 as well. The question decides which is wanted: a length is positive; a solution of an equation may be negative.
  • Notation: a² is read a squared, a³ a cubed, and aⁿ a to the power n. a² ≠ 2a — a² = a × a while 2a = a + a.

The index laws

Each law is a statement about counting multiplications, so each can be checked by writing the multiplications out.

Law 1:  a^m x a^n = a^(m+n)
Why: a³ x a² = (a x a x a) x (a x a) = a⁵, and 3 + 2 = 5.
Example: 2³ × 2⁵ = 2⁸ = 256; check: 8 × 32 = 256 ✓

Law 2:  a^m ÷ a^n = a^(m-n)
Why: a⁵ ÷ a² = (a x a x a x a x a)/(a x a) = a x a x a = a³, and 5 - 2 = 3.
Example: 5⁷ ÷ 5⁴ = 5³ = 125

Law 3:  (a^m)^n = a^(m n)
Why: (a²)³ = a² x a² x a² = a⁶, and 2 × 3 = 6.
Example: (2x³)² = 2² x (x³)² = 4x⁶        [the power applies to every factor]

Law 4:  a⁰ = 1  (a not zero)
Why: a³ ÷ a³ = a^(3-3) = a⁰, and any number divided by itself is 1.
Example: 7⁰ = 1

Law 5:  a^(-n) = 1/(a^n)
Why: a^(-2) = a^(0-2) = a⁰ ÷ a² = 1/a².
Example: 5^(-2) = 1/25 = 0.04

Fractional indices (Extended). A fractional index is a root: the denominator of the fraction is the root, the numerator is the power.

a^(1/n) = nth root of a        a^(m/n) = (nth root of a)^m

16^(1/2) = √16 = 4
27^(2/3) = (cube root of 27)² = 3² = 9
Check the second: 27^(2/3) squared three times over should give 27² = 729; 9³ = 729 ✓

Indices in algebra (Extended)

The same laws apply when the base is a letter, and every factor in a bracket carries the power:

Simplify:  (2x³)² x⁴ ÷ x⁵

(2x³)² = 4x⁶        [square the 2 and double the index]
4x⁶ x x⁴ = 4x¹⁰     [Law 1: add indices]
4x¹⁰ ÷ x⁵ = 4x⁵     [Law 2: subtract indices]
Solve:  2^x = 32

Write both sides with base 2:  32 = 2⁵
2^x = 2⁵, so x = 5        [matching bases means matching indices]

When the bases differ, rewrite one as a power of the other: 8 = 2³, so 8^x = 2^(3x). Equations like 3^(x+1) = 27^(x−1) become 3^(x+1) = 3^(3x−3), so x + 1 = 3x − 3, giving x = 2.

LawStatementWorked line
Multiplyingaᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ2³ × 2⁵ = 2⁸ = 256
Dividingaᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ5⁷ ÷ 5⁴ = 5³ = 125
Power of a power(aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ(2x³)² = 4x⁶
Zero indexa⁰ = 1 (a not zero)7⁰ = 1
Negative indexa⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ5⁻² = 1/25
Fractional indexa^(m/n) = (ⁿ√a)ᵐ27^(2/3) = 9

Two edge cases deserve care. The zero index says nothing about 0⁰: 0⁰ is undefined, because the pattern a⁰ = 1 holds for every non-zero base while the pattern 0ⁿ = 0 holds for every positive power, and the two patterns collide at the origin. And a negative index never makes a value negative: 2⁻³ = 1/8 is positive, because the minus sign belongs to the position of the power, not to the number itself. Finally, every root can be written as a power — √x = x^(1/2), ³√x = x^(1/3) — which is how a calculator evaluates them and how algebraic roots are simplified in one notation.

Standard form

Standard form writes a number as a × 10ⁿ where 1 ⩽ a < 10 and n is an integer. It handles very large and very small quantities without long strings of zeros.

Write in standard form:

47 382 = 4.7382 × 10⁴        [the decimal point moves 4 places left]
0.0056 = 5.6 × 10^(-3)        [the decimal point moves 3 places right, so n = -3]

Arithmetic in standard form. Multiply or divide the numbers first, then the powers of ten, and adjust back into standard form if needed:

(3 × 10⁵) x (4 × 10^(-2))
= (3 × 4) x (10⁵ × 10^(-2))     [regrouped]
= 12 × 10³
= 1.2 × 10⁴                     [12 is not between 1 and 10, so adjust]

(6 × 10⁸) ÷ (2 × 10³)
= (6 ÷ 2) × 10^(8-3) = 3 × 10⁵

Addition and subtraction need matching powers first: 3 × 10⁵ + 4 × 10⁴ = 30 × 10⁴ + 4 × 10⁴ = 34 × 10⁴ = 3.4 × 10⁵. Real-world uses: the speed of light is 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, the size of an atom is about 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m, and masses, distances and populations in physics and chemistry questions are always quoted this way. A calculator's ×10ˣ key enters the power directly; the answer should be given in the form the question asks, often to 3 s.f.

Surds (Extended)

A surd is a root that cannot be written exactly as a fraction — √2, √3, 3√5. Exact answers in surds are often required on Paper 2, where a calculator cannot help. The laws:

√a x √b = √(ab)        √a ÷ √b = √(a/b)        (√a)² = a

Simplifying. Take out the largest square factor:

√50 = √(25 × 2) = √25 x √2 = 5√2
√72 = √(36 × 2) = 6√2
√(9/16) = √9 / √16 = 3/4

Adding like surds. Only like surds combine, exactly like algebraic terms:

√18 + √8 = 3√2 + 2√2 = 5√2        [simplify first]
2√3 + √5 cannot be combined: they are unlike surds.

Rationalising the denominator. A fraction with a surd underneath is tidied by multiplying top and bottom by the same surd (or its conjugate):

6/√3 = (6 x √3)/(√3 x √3) = 6√3/3 = 2√3

1/(3 + √2): multiply top and bottom by the conjugate (3 - √2):
= (3 - √2)/[(3 + √2)(3 - √2)]
= (3 - √2)/(9 - 2)          [difference of two squares below]
= (3 - √2)/7

The conjugate works because (a + b)(a − b) = a² − b² removes the square root entirely. Expanding surd brackets uses the same identity: (2 + √3)(2 − √3) = 4 − 3 = 1.

Worked example: a combined index calculation

Simplify (2³ × 2⁵) ÷ 2⁴ and check it two ways.

Method 1 (indices): 2³ × 2⁵ = 2⁸, then 2⁸ ÷ 2⁴ = 2⁴ = 16
Method 2 (arithmetic): 2³ × 2⁵ = 8 × 32 = 256;  256 ÷ 16 = 16
Both routes give 16 ✓

Second example: write (3√2)² − √8 in the form k√2.

(3√2)² = 9 × 2 = 18        [square both the 3 and the √2]
√8 = 2√2
18 - 2√2 is already simple; it cannot be written as k√2 because 18 is rational,
so the answer stays 18 - 2√2.

Standard form in a calculation. A red blood cell is 7 × 10⁻⁶ m across and a vein is 2.4 × 10⁻³ m wide. How many cells fit side by side?

2.4 × 10^(-3) ÷ 7 × 10^(-6)
= (2.4 ÷ 7) × 10^(-3 - (-6))        [divide the numbers, subtract the indices]
= 0.342857 × 10³
= 3.43 × 10² (3 s.f.)  ≈ 343 cells

The index arithmetic is the whole question: subtracting −6 gives +3, and a sense-check on the powers alone (10⁻³ ÷ 10⁻⁶ = 10³) says the answer must be in the hundreds — which catches sign slips before they cost the final mark.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Multiplying the base by the index: 2³ is 8, not 6; (2³)² = 2⁶ = 64, not 2⁵.
  • Forgetting to square the coefficient: (2x³)² = 4x⁶, not 2x⁶.
  • Treating a⁻ⁿ as negative rather than reciprocal: 2⁻³ = 1/8.
  • Writing 0.00047 as 4.7 × 10⁻³; it is 4.7 × 10⁻⁴ — count the places the point moves.
  • Leaving a standard-form answer as 12 × 10³; the front number must be between 1 and 10.
  • Giving √16 = ±4 in a simplification; the square root symbol means the principal root, while x² = 16 has both solutions.
  • Rationalising only the surd and not its conjugate partner: 1/(3 + √2) needs (3 − √2) top and bottom.
  • Combining unlike surds: 2√3 + √5 is final; only matching surd parts can be added.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 2, 3 marks). Simplify (3x²)³ ÷ x⁴.

Answer: (3x²)³ = 27x⁶; 27x⁶ ÷ x⁴ = 27x².

Question 2 (Paper 2, 3 marks). Evaluate 8^(2/3).

Answer: ³√8 = 2, and 2² = 4. So 8^(2/3) = 4.

Question 3 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Write 0.000 42 and 63 000 in standard form, then find their product.

Answer: 4.2 × 10⁻⁴ and 6.3 × 10⁴. Product = (4.2 × 6.3) × 10⁰ = 26.46 = 2.646 × 10¹.

Question 4 (Paper 2, 4 marks). Simplify √48 + 3√12.

Answer: √48 = √(16 × 3) = 4√3; 3√12 = 3 × 2√3 = 6√3; total = 10√3.

Question 5 (Paper 2, 4 marks). Rationalise the denominator of 5/(2 + √3).

Answer: Multiply by the conjugate: 5(2 − √3)/[(2 + √3)(2 − √3)] = 5(2 − √3)/(4 − 3) = 5(2 − √3) = 10 − 5√3.

Question 6 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Solve 9^x = 27.

Answer: Write both as powers of 3: 3^(2x) = 3³, so 2x = 3 and x = 3/2. Check: 9^(3/2) = (√9)³ = 3³ = 27 ✓.

From the numbers themselves, the course turns to comparing and sharing them: ratio, rate and proportion.

The powers-of-ten ladder: seeing standard form instead of memorising it

Indices look like a rule to memorise and are really a picture to read. Every quantity in the course sits somewhere on one ladder of powers of ten, and multiplying, dividing and converting all move you up or down that ladder by whole rungs.

One rung, one index. Moving up a rung multiplies by 10, and that is exactly what adding 1 to the index does: 10³ × 10 = 10⁴. Moving down divides by 10 and subtracts 1. Every index law is that sentence applied twice:

aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ Key: a = the base; m and n = the indices (powers). Multiplying adds the indices because each factor contributes its own rungs.
aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ Key: dividing subtracts, because dividing by aⁿ is multiplying by a⁻ⁿ.
(aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ Key: a bracket applied n times multiplies the rungs by n.
a⁰ = 1 and a⁻ⁿ = 1 / aⁿ Key: both follow from the subtraction law: a³ ÷ a³ = a⁰ must be 1, and a² ÷ a⁵ = a⁻³ must be 1/a³.

Standard form is a position on the ladder. A number is in standard form when it is written as

N = A × 10ⁿ Key: A = a number with 1 ≤ A < 10 (one non-zero digit before the point); n = a whole number, positive for large values and negative for small ones. 4.2 × 10³ means four decimal places' worth of rungs above 1: 4,200.

Converting is counting rungs, not guessing the sign. To write 47,500 in standard form, move the point left until one digit remains in front: 4.75, which is three moves, so the index is +3 and the value is 4.75 × 10⁴. To write 0.00062, move the point right until one digit remains in front: 6.2, which is four moves, so the index is −4 and the value is 6.2 × 10⁻⁴. Left is positive, right is negative — the point moving right on a small number gives a negative index, which is the sign students most often flip.

Worked example. A red blood cell has diameter 0.0000072 m and a virus 1.2 × 10⁻⁷ m. Write the cell in standard form and find how many times longer it is.

cell: 0.0000072 = 7.2 × 10⁻⁶ m (six moves right)
ratio: (7.2 × 10⁻⁶) ÷ (1.2 × 10⁻⁷) = (7.2 ÷ 1.2) × 10⁻⁶⁻⁽⁻⁷⁾ = 6.0 × 10¹ = 60

The division law did the work: subtracting a negative index adds. Doing that sum as −6 − 7 = −13 is the error that turns 60 into 0.0000000000006.

Estimating with the ladder. A calculation like (4.9 × 10⁵) × (2.1 × 10³) is roughly 5 × 2 = 10 times 10⁵⁺³ = 10⁸, so about 1.0 × 10⁹ before any calculator. This is how you catch a wrong power of ten — the most common way a correct method still loses the answer mark.

Where marks are lost. Writing 0.42 × 10⁴ or 42 × 10² and calling it standard form: A must be at least 1 and less than 10. Flipping the sign of the index on a small number. And adding indices when multiplying different bases — 2³ × 3² is 8 × 9 = 72, not 6⁵.

Negative and zero indices in depth

A negative index tells you to take a reciprocal, and a zero index gives the value 1. These two rules follow from the index laws, not from memory, so the working below shows how each one is forced. The subsections cover the reasons, the calculator entry, and the common slips that turn a negative power into a negative number.

Why a zero index gives one

Take a number and divide it by itself. Using the division law, a⁵ ÷ a⁵ = a⁰, and the same quotient is 1 because any number divided by itself is 1. So a⁰ = 1 for any non-zero a. The rule is therefore a consequence of the laws already in use, and it is why 5⁰ = 1, 100⁰ = 1 and (−3)⁰ = 1.

Why a negative index is a reciprocal

Divide a power by a larger power of the same base: a² ÷ a⁵ = a^(2−5) = a⁻³. Writing the same quotient as 1/a³ shows that a⁻³ = 1/a³. So a negative index moves the base to the denominator and changes the sign of the index. The value 2⁻³ is 1/2³ = 1/8, which is positive, because a negative index does not make the answer negative.

Negative indices with fractions

The reciprocal rule also works on fractions, where it flips the fraction. (2/3)⁻² = (3/2)² = 9/4. Invert the fraction first, then apply the positive index. A common error is to change only the index and leave the fraction alone, which gives (2/3)⁻² = 4/9 and loses the mark.

Entering negative and fractional powers on a calculator

Use the power key, and enter the negative index in brackets so the calculator reads the whole index as a negative number. For 5⁻², enter 5, the power key and (−2), giving 0.04. A fractional power such as 8^(1/3) is entered with brackets around the fraction, and the calculator returns 2. Check the result by reversing the operation: 2³ = 8 confirms the cube root.

Simplifying expressions with negative powers

To simplify 3x⁻² × 6x⁵, multiply the numbers and add the indices: 18x^(−2+5) = 18x³. To write the answer with only positive indices, move any negative power to the denominator. For example, 4y⁻³ becomes 4/y³. Collect the coefficients first, then deal with the indices, so the final form is easy to check.

Mistakes with negative and zero indices

The commonest errors are treating 2⁻³ as −8, writing a⁰ as 0, and reading (−2)⁻² as −1/4 when the correct value is 1/4. The bracket in (−2)⁻² is what makes the base negative, and an even power of a negative number is positive. Write the bracket in the working so the sign is clear before the reciprocal is taken.

Fractional indices and roots

A fractional index is a root combined with a power, so a^(1/n) is the nth root of a, and a^(m/n) is the nth root of a raised to the mth power. The index laws extend to fractions without any new rule. The subsections below explain the notation, how to evaluate by hand and on a calculator, and how fractional indices appear in equations.

The meaning of a^(1/n)

The index law (a^(1/2))² = a^(1/2 × 2) = a¹ = a shows that a^(1/2) must be the square root of a. In the same way a^(1/3) is the cube root and a^(1/4) is the fourth root. So 16^(1/2) = 4, 27^(1/3) = 3 and 81^(1/4) = 3. The index is the reciprocal of the root.

Evaluating a^(m/n)

Take the root first, then the power, because the root is usually the smaller number. For 8^(2/3), the cube root of 8 is 2, and 2² = 4. Taking the power first gives 8² = 64, and the cube root of 64 is also 4, so the order does not change the answer, but the root first keeps the numbers small and is less error-prone.

Negative fractional indices

A negative fractional index takes a reciprocal of the root. For 16^(−3/4), the fourth root of 16 is 2, so 2³ = 8 and the reciprocal gives 16^(−3/4) = 1/8. Apply the reciprocal last, after the root and power have been found, and write the answer as a fraction if the question asks for an exact value.

Solving an equation with a fractional index

To solve x^(2/3) = 4, raise both sides to the power 3/2, which undoes the 2/3. Then x = 4^(3/2) = (√4)³ = 2³ = 8. Raising both sides to the reciprocal of the index is the step to remember, and the result should be checked by substituting back: 8^(2/3) = 4.

Fractional indices on the calculator

Enter the base, press the power key, and enter the fraction in brackets. For 125^(2/3), the calculator gives 25. Enter the bracket around the index to avoid reading 2 ÷ 3 as a separate step, and check a simple value first, such as 9^(1/2) = 3, so a mis-entered index is spotted.

Why fractional indices matter

Fractional indices let a root be treated with the same index laws as a power. Once a root is written as an index, multiplying and dividing it follows the usual rules. This is why the Extended content treats roots as powers, and it is also the link to surds, which are the roots that are left unevaluated.

title: Enzymes
content:
Enzymes

Cambridge IGCSE Biology 0610, Extended route, topic 5 (statement 5.1). Enzymes as biological catalysts, lock-and-key specificity, and the effects of temperature and pH that top-grade explanations hinge on.

5.1 Enzymes

  • Enzymes are proteins that speed up reactions in living cells without being changed. Each enzyme has an active site with a specific shape; only a substrate with a matching shape binds, which is the lock-and-key model.
  • Rate increases with temperature because particles move faster and collide more often, up to an optimum. Above the optimum, bonds maintaining the enzyme's tertiary structure break and the enzyme is denatured — the active site changes shape permanently.
  • Each enzyme has an optimum pH. Away from it, ionic bonds in the enzyme are disrupted and the active site shape changes; extreme pH also denatures.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Graph interpretation, applied to an enzyme-rate graph against temperature: rate rises to the optimum near 40 °C for human enzymes, then falls steeply to zero. The rise is explained by collision frequency; the fall by denaturation. Both halves are needed for full marks — describing only the rise is the classic incomplete answer.
  • Reasoning chain, applied to pepsin in the stomach: its optimum is around pH 2 because of gastric acid, and at pH 7 it becomes almost inactive. Explain with the active site ionisation, not just "pH changes the rate".
  • Experimental design, applied to an investigation of enzyme concentration: the independent variable is enzyme concentration, the dependent variable the rate of product formation, and the controls include substrate concentration, temperature and pH — all held at the optimum. Naming substrate concentration as a control shows understanding that it must be in excess for enzyme concentration to be the limiting factor.

Common errors

  • Saying enzymes are "used up" or "consumed". They emerge from each reaction unchanged.
  • Saying high temperature "kills" the enzyme. Denaturation is the precise word — enzymes are not alive.
  • Explaining the fall after the optimum with "fewer collisions". Denaturation is the cause.

title: Chemical Equilibria — Study Notes
content:
Chemical Equilibria

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH14, Topic 13. In a closed system a reaction reaches a dynamic equilibrium, where the forward and reverse rates are equal. The equilibrium constant tells you the position of that equilibrium at a given temperature.

The equilibrium constant Kc

  • For aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD, Kc = [C]^c [D]^d / ([A]^a [B]^b). Only species in solution or gas phase appear in the expression.
  • Kc is constant for a given temperature. Changing concentration or pressure shifts the position but not the value of Kc.
  • The units of Kc depend on the stoichiometry. For N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3, Kc has units of mol⁻² dm⁶.

Worked example

  • For H2 + I2 ⇌ 2HI, at equilibrium [HI] = 1.60, [H2] = 0.20 and [I2] = 0.20 mol dm⁻³. Kc = 1.60² / (0.20 × 0.20) = 64.

Partial pressure and Kp

  • In gas equilibria, the partial pressure of a gas is its mole fraction multiplied by the total pressure.
  • Kp uses partial pressures instead of concentrations. For N2O4 ⇌ 2NO2, Kp = p(NO2)² / p(N2O4).

Effect of changes

  • Adding reactant or removing product shifts the position towards the products. Adding product shifts it towards the reactants.
  • Increasing pressure favours the side with fewer gas molecules. Changing the volume has the same effect as changing pressure.
  • Raising the temperature favours the endothermic direction. For an exothermic forward reaction, Kc decreases as temperature rises.
  • A catalyst changes the rate at which equilibrium is reached but not the position or Kc.

Exam tip: a change in temperature is the only change that alters Kc. Concentration, pressure and catalyst changes alter the position or rate, but not the constant.

title: Computational Thinking and Problem-Solving — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Computational Thinking and Problem-Solving

Computer Science — A2. A recursive routine calls itself with a smaller input and a base case that stops the recursion. Elegant for trees and divide-and-conquer, but each call consumes stack space — deep recursion can overflow. Any recursion can be rewritten with a loop and explicit stack.

Key areas to revise

  • Thinking Ahead, Abstractly, Systematically
  • Recursion
  • Searching and Sorting
  • Testing

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

### Worked example When planning a route for a delivery app, decomposition breaks the job into stages such as finding the address, choosing a route and sending a notification. Abstraction removes details that do not matter, such as the colour of the vehicle. Pattern recognition notices that many deliveries follow the same steps, so one algorithm can serve them all. ### Check yourself Give one example of abstraction and one of decomposition from a student's timetable app. Abstraction might hide the room layout, showing only the lesson time. Decomposition might split the app into timetable display, reminders and login.

title: Astronomy and Cosmology — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Astronomy and Cosmology

Physics — A2. Luminosity L is total power radiated (W). Intensity at distance d: I = L/(4πd²) — the key to distances.

Key areas to revise

  • Luminosity and Intensity
  • Wien and Stefan–Boltzmann
  • Hubble's Law
  • The Big Bang

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

### Worked example Hubble's law states v = H₀d, where v is recession speed, d is distance and H₀ is the Hubble constant. With H₀ ≈ 70 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹ and a galaxy 100 Mpc away, v = 70 × 100 = 7000 km s⁻¹. Redshift shows the galaxy is moving away, which supports the expanding-universe model and the age of the universe of about 13.8 billion years.

title: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Statistics and Data Handling
content:
Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Statistics and Data Handling

Statistics is the art of describing a pile of numbers with a few well-chosen ones: an average to say where the middle lies, a spread to say how tightly the data cluster, and a chart to make the shape visible. The IGCSE questions test exactly that pipeline — classify the data, compute the averages and spread, draw or read the chart, and compare two distributions. This note builds the whole subject from zero: the data types, every average and measure of spread with the frequency-table method, the standard charts, cumulative frequency curves, and histograms with unequal class widths.

Classifying statistical data

TypeMeaningExamples
Qualitative (categorical)describes a quality, not a numberfavourite colour, blood group
Quantitativemeasured or counted as a numberheight, number of siblings
Discretecountable, separate values (usually integers)number of children, shoe size
Continuouscan take any value in a range (measured)height, time, mass

The classification decides which charts and averages are legal: a mode for categorical data, a median for ordered data, class intervals for continuous data. Discrete data are plotted as bar charts with gaps; continuous data as histograms with no gaps (and frequency density on the vertical axis).

Averages and range

mean = sum of values / number of values
median = middle value when ordered (mean of the two middle
         values for an even count)
mode = most frequent value (or class); none if no repeats
range = largest - smallest

quartiles: Q1 = lower quartile (25%), Q3 = upper quartile (75%)
interquartile range (IQR) = Q3 - Q1  (spread of the middle 50%)

The mean uses every value (sensitive to outliers); the median ignores extreme values (robust); the mode is the only average available for categorical data. When comparing two data sets, quote an average and a spread: "school A has a higher median but a larger IQR, so its results are higher on average but less consistent."

Worked example. Find the mean, median, mode and range of: 4, 7, 7, 9, 12, 15, 18.

mean = (4+7+7+9+12+15+18)/7 = 72/7 = 10.3 (3 s.f.)
median = 4th value = 9
mode = 7 (appears twice)
range = 18 - 4 = 14

Worked example 2 (even count). Find the median of 3, 5, 8, 10, 12, 15.

even count: average the 3rd and 4th values
median = (8 + 10)/2 = 9

Averages from frequency tables

mean = sum of (value x frequency) / sum of frequencies
median = the value at position (n + 1)/2 in cumulative order
mode = the value with the highest frequency

Worked example. The table shows goals scored: 0 (5 players), 1 (8), 2 (6), 3 (2). Find the mean and the median.

total players = 5 + 8 + 6 + 2 = 21
total goals = 0 × 5 + 1 × 8 + 2 × 6 + 3 × 2 = 0 + 8 + 12 + 6 = 26
mean = 26/21 = 1.24 (3 s.f.)
median position = (21 + 1)/2 = 11th value
cumulative: 5 (0 goals), 13 (1 goal) - the 11th value is 1
median = 1

For grouped data, use midpoints: the mean = Σ(midpoint × frequency)/Σfrequency, and the median comes from the cumulative frequency curve (below). The grouped mean is an estimate because the midpoint stands in for every value in the class.

Charts and diagrams

  • Bar chart: bars with gaps for categorical or discrete data; height = frequency.
  • Pie chart: angle = (frequency/total) × 360°; label the sectors with the category.
  • Pictogram: a symbol represents a fixed number; a half symbol represents half that number.
  • Stem-and-leaf: a sorted display that keeps the actual values; the key explains the split (e.g. 3|4 means 34).
  • Frequency polygon: plot frequency against the midpoint of each class and join with straight lines.

Worked example (pie chart). 40 students choose a sport: football 16, tennis 10, swimming 8, other 6. Find the angle for football.

angle = (16/40) × 360 = 144 °

Worked example 2 (pie chart reverse). A sector of 72° represents 9 students. How many students in total?

72 ° represents 9  →  360 ° represents 9 × 360/72 = 45 students

Cumulative frequency diagrams

A cumulative frequency table adds frequencies as you move up the classes. Plot cumulative frequency against the upper class boundary and join with a smooth curve; then read positions:

median at n/2
lower quartile at n/4
upper quartile at 3n/4
IQR = Q3 - Q1

Worked example. A cumulative frequency curve for 60 students' marks: Q1 = 42, median = 55, Q3 = 68. Find the IQR and interpret it.

IQR = 68 - 42 = 26 marks
The middle 50% of students scored within 26 marks of each other;

Always read across to the curve and then down to the horizontal axis — and use the class boundaries, not the midpoints, for the plot positions.

Histograms and frequency density

When class widths differ, the height of a bar cannot be the frequency — a wide class would dominate unfairly. Instead, the area of each bar is proportional to the frequency:

frequency density = frequency / class width
frequency = frequency density x class width (area of the bar)

Worked example. Class 0–10 has frequency 20; 10–20 has frequency 30; 20–40 has frequency 40. Find the frequency densities.

0-10: 20/10 = 2.0
10-20: 30/10 = 3.0
20-40: 40/20 = 2.0

Reading a histogram backwards is the standard question: measure a bar's width and height, multiply to get the frequency, and read the class from the horizontal axis. Remember that the axes often use class boundaries, so a bar from 20 to 40 covers width 20.

Stem-and-leaf diagrams and frequency polygons

A stem-and-leaf diagram sorts data while keeping every value visible: the stem is the leading digit and the leaf the final digit, with a key such as 3|4 meaning 34. Interpreting one means reading the ordered leaves to find the median, the quartiles and the shape: the median is the middle leaf, Q1 and Q3 sit at the quarter and three-quarter positions, and the distribution's skew shows in where the leaves bunch.

A frequency polygon plots frequency against the midpoint of each class and joins the points with straight lines; it is the grouped-data equivalent of a line graph and makes comparisons between two distributions easy (plot both polygons on the same axes).

Worked example. The leaves for stem 4 are 1, 3, 3, 6, 8 and for stem 5 are 0, 2, 5. List the data in order and find the median.

values: 41, 43, 43, 46, 48, 50, 52, 55
n = 8, so the median is the mean of the 4th and 5th values:
(46 + 48)/2 = 47

Worked example 2 (interpreting). Explain what a long right-hand tail of leaves in a stem-and-leaf diagram indicates.

A long right tail means a few unusually high values: the data
are positively skewed, and the mean will be greater than the
median because the high values pull it upward.

Comparing distributions

Comparison questions want two statements: one about the average (which is higher) and one about the spread (which is more consistent). Use median and IQR together — they are robust to outliers — or mean and standard deviation when the data are symmetric and the syllabus supplies it.

Worked example. Class A: median 62, IQR 18. Class B: median 58, IQR 9. Compare.

Class A has the higher typical score (median 62 vs 58), but its
results are more spread out (IQR 18 vs 9), so Class B is more
consistent even though its middle score is lower.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Averages) Find the mean and range of 12, 15, 11, 19, 13. Answer: mean = (12 + 15 + 11 + 19 + 13)/5 = 70/5 = 14; range = largest − smallest = 19 − 11 = 8.
  2. (Frequency table) Values 1, 2, 3 with frequencies 4, 7, 9. Find the mean. Answer: mean = Σfx/Σf = (1 × 4 + 2 × 7 + 3 × 9)/(4 + 7 + 9) = (4 + 14 + 27)/20 = 45/20 = 2.25.
  3. (Median) Find the median of 2, 4, 4, 6, 9, 10. Answer: there are six values, so the median is the mean of the 3rd and 4th: (4 + 6)/2 = 5.
  4. (Pie chart) A sector of 90° represents 15 people. Find the total. Answer: 90° is 90/360 = ¼ of the circle, so the total is 15 ÷ ¼ = 15 × 4 = 60 people.
  5. (Cumulative frequency) For 80 values, where do you read the median? Answer: At cumulative frequency 40, reading across to the curve and down to the axis.
  6. (Histogram) A bar of width 5 has frequency density 4. Find its frequency. Answer: frequency = frequency density × class width = 4 × 5 = 20.
  7. (Frequency density) Class 30–50 has frequency 24. Find the frequency density. Answer: class width = 50 − 30 = 20, so frequency density = frequency/width = 24/20 = 1.2.
  8. (Compare) Two runners' times: A median 42 s, IQR 3 s; B median 40 s, IQR 8 s. Compare. Answer: B is faster typically (lower median) but less consistent (larger IQR); A is more reliable.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Median without ordering: the median is the middle of the ordered list. Forgetting to sort is the commonest data-handling error.
  • Even-count median: average the two middle values; do not pick one of them.
  • Grouped mean: use midpoints and label the answer an estimate — the midpoint is not the actual mean of the class.
  • Histogram heights: the vertical axis is frequency density, not frequency; area is the frequency. Reading the height as the frequency is the classic histogram error.
  • Cumulative frequency positions: plot against upper class boundaries and read the median at n/2 (not (n+1)/2 on the graph).
  • Pie chart arithmetic: check that the angles sum to 360° before answering the next part.
  • IQR direction: IQR = upper − lower quartile; a negative IQR means the quartiles are swapped.
  • Comparison claims: quote actual values ("median 62 vs 58"), not "better" without evidence.

Collecting and classifying data

Every statistical question starts with data, and the type of data decides which averages and diagrams are sensible. Before any calculation, decide where the data came from, what kind of values it holds, and whether the sample is fair. The subsections below set out these decisions in the order an examiner expects them to be made.

Primary and secondary data

Primary data is collected by the person who uses it, for example by a survey or an experiment carried out in class. Secondary data is taken from an existing source such as a census, a published table or a sports website. Primary data suits a question that needs a specific answer, while secondary data is quicker but may not match the exact question being asked. State which kind you have used when you describe an investigation.

Discrete and continuous data

Discrete data takes separate values that are usually counted, such as the number of goals scored or the number of people in a family. Continuous data can take any value in a range and is measured, such as height, mass or time. The distinction matters for grouping: a discrete table can use single values, while a continuous table needs class intervals with clear boundaries such as 10 ≤ t < 20.

Qualitative and quantitative data

Qualitative data describes a quality, such as eye colour or favourite subject, and cannot be averaged. Quantitative data is numerical and can be ordered and added. A mean is only meaningful for quantitative data, so a question that asks for the mean colour is answered by naming the mode or by stating that no mean exists.

Reading the question before the data

Underline what the question asks for before reading the table: a mode, a median, a range, a comparison or a conclusion. Many marks are lost by calculating the right number and then answering a different question. Note the units and the sample size at the same time, because the sample size is needed for a relative frequency and the units for a correct final statement.

Bias in samples and questionnaires

A sample is biased when some members of the population are more likely to be chosen than others. Asking only students in one class about a school-wide question is biased, and so is a question that leads the respondent, such as asking whether people agree that the bus service is too slow. A fair sample is random, large enough to represent the group, and drawn from the whole population being studied.

Judging the reliability of a conclusion

A conclusion is only as reliable as the data behind it. A small sample, an unrepresentative group or a question with an obvious bias weakens any statement drawn from it. A good answer names one weakness and suggests a change, such as taking a larger sample across a wider range of times or places.

Drawing a conclusion from a table

A conclusion must be supported by a number from the table and must answer the question asked. If the mean time for group A is 14 minutes and for group B is 18 minutes, the statement that group B took longer on average is supported, but a statement about all pupils in the school is not, because only two groups were measured.

Averages and spread in depth

The mean, median and mode each describe the centre of a set of data in a different way, and the range and interquartile range describe the spread. A careful answer uses the average that fits the data and the measure of spread that shows how far the values lie from it. The subsections below work through each measure in the form the question is most likely to use.

The mode for discrete and grouped data

The mode is the value that occurs most often. In a discrete frequency table it is the value with the largest frequency. For grouped data it is the modal class, the class with the largest frequency, and the answer is given as a class interval rather than a single value. A data set can have no mode, one mode or several modes.

The median from an ordered list

To find the median, arrange the values in order and locate the middle one. For n values the median is at position (n + 1) ÷ 2. With nine values the median is the fifth value, and with ten values it is the average of the fifth and sixth. Always order the data before counting, because the median taken from an unsorted list is wrong even when the middle value is chosen carefully.

Choosing an average

The mean uses every value, but it is pulled by extreme values. The median is not affected by one very large value, and the mode is the only average that can be used with qualitative data. A typical question asks which average best describes a set of salaries that includes one very large income; the answer is the median, with the reason that the mean is pulled up by the outlier.

The effect of an outlier

An outlier is a value far from the rest of the data. Adding one outlier to a small set changes the mean noticeably but may leave the median and mode unchanged. When an exam question asks for the effect of a change, work out the mean before and after the change, rather than guessing the direction from the size of the new value.

Range as a measure of spread

The range is the largest value minus the smallest value. It is quick to find but depends on only two values, so one outlier can make it large even when the rest of the data are close together. When comparing two data sets, state both the range and the centre, because two sets with the same mean can have very different ranges.

The interquartile range

The interquartile range is the upper quartile minus the lower quartile, the spread of the middle half of the data. It ignores the extreme values at each end and is therefore less affected by outliers than the range. For a list of 12 ordered values, the lower quartile is the median of the lower six values and the upper quartile is the median of the upper six.

Estimating the mean of grouped data

For grouped data the exact values are unknown, so the mean is estimated using the midpoint of each class. Multiply each midpoint by its frequency, add the products and divide by the total frequency: mean = Σfx ÷ Σf, where x is the midpoint. The answer is an estimate, and the working should say so, because the true mean depends on where each value sits inside its class.

Reading charts and diagrams

A chart is a summary of data, and the examiner expects you to read the values it shows, compare them and point out where a chart is misleading. Each diagram type has its own rules for scales, keys and angles. The subsections below cover the diagrams most often used in this topic and the errors that lose marks.

Bar charts and dual bar charts

A bar chart shows the frequency of each category, with equal gaps between the bars. A dual bar chart places two bars side by side for each category, so the two data sets can be compared directly. Read the scale carefully, because a scale that starts at a value other than zero exaggerates small differences between bars.

Pictograms with a key

A pictogram uses a symbol to stand for a number of items, and the key says how many each symbol represents. A symbol that stands for 10 items with 3 and a half symbols shown means 35 items. Partial symbols are the step that most often goes wrong, so divide the partial symbol by its share of the full symbol before multiplying by the key value.

Pie charts and angles

In a pie chart each sector has an angle equal to the frequency divided by the total, multiplied by 360°. A category with frequency 30 out of a total of 120 has an angle of 30 ÷ 120 × 360° = 90°. Working backwards, a sector of 72° in a total of 200 represents 72 ÷ 360 × 200 = 40 items.

Line graphs for time series

A line graph joins points that show a quantity over time, and the gradient shows the rate of change. A steeper line means a faster increase or decrease. When a question asks for the trend, describe the direction and the rate in words, and do not join points across a gap in the time axis without saying so.

Misleading scales and axes

A chart is misleading when its vertical axis does not start at zero, when the bars have different widths, or when a three-dimensional effect distorts the sizes. Each of these changes how large a difference looks. In an exam, name the feature that misleads, state what it does to the picture, and say how the chart should be drawn instead.

Comparing two distributions on one chart

Two distributions can be compared on one chart by using the same scales and the same class intervals. Compare the centre, using a median or mean, and the spread, using a range or interquartile range. A comparison that gives only the higher or lower value of one data set is incomplete, and must be followed by the matching value for the other.

Reading a chart in an exam question

Read the title, the axis labels, the units and the key before answering. Then take each value from the chart and write it in the working so the marker can see where it came from. A correct chart reading with the value written out earns the method marks even when the final statement is worded loosely.

Cumulative frequency and histograms in practice

A cumulative frequency curve is built from a running total, and it gives the median and quartiles of a grouped data set. A histogram displays the same kind of grouped data with frequency density on the vertical axis, so its bars can have unequal widths. The subsections below set out the steps for each diagram in the order used in a written answer.

Building the cumulative frequency table

Add a column to the grouped table and fill it with the running total of the frequencies. The cumulative frequency at the upper boundary of each class is the total of all frequencies up to and including that class. The final cumulative frequency equals the total number of values, and this check should be made before plotting.

Plotting the cumulative frequency curve

Plot each cumulative frequency against the upper class boundary, and join the points with a smooth curve. The first point is usually placed at the lower boundary of the first class with a cumulative frequency of zero. A ruler-straight line between points is not the expected shape, because the curve shows how the data build up across the range.

Reading the median and quartiles from the curve

The median is read at a cumulative frequency of n ÷ 2, the lower quartile at n ÷ 4 and the upper quartile at 3n ÷ 4. Draw a horizontal line from each of these values to the curve, then a vertical line down to the horizontal axis. The interquartile range is the upper quartile minus the lower quartile, and it should be stated with its units.

Percentiles and other points on the curve

A percentile is read in the same way, with the cumulative frequency given as a percentage of the total. The 90th percentile is at 0.9n, and a question that asks how many values lie above a given value is answered by subtracting the cumulative frequency at that value from the total. Showing the subtraction in the working is what earns the method mark.

Drawing a histogram from a grouped table

For a histogram with unequal class widths, calculate the frequency density for each class as frequency ÷ class width, and plot that on the vertical axis. The horizontal axis is a continuous scale with the class boundaries marked. The bars touch because the data are continuous, and the histogram must have a title, labelled axes and a scale.

Reading a frequency estimate from a histogram

The area of a bar equals the frequency of its class, because the bar's height is the frequency density and its width is the class width. To estimate how many values lie between 20 and 35, add the areas of the bars across that interval, using part of a bar when the interval starts or ends inside a class. This is the most common histogram question, and the working should show each area.

Comparing two histograms and two curves

Two histograms or two cumulative frequency curves are compared by their medians and spreads. A curve lying further to the right has a higher median, and a steeper curve has a smaller interquartile range. A comparison statement names the group, gives the value of the measure for each group and states which is larger, in that order.

Equations and symbols

Seven formulas cover the whole paper: the three averages with their range and interquartile range, the two histogram relations, and the pie-chart angle. Every one carries the same mark-scheme requirement — substitute, then state the answer in the units of the data, not as a bare number.

mean = sum of values / number of values Key: mean = the arithmetic average, in the same units as the data; sum of values = the total of every reading; number of values = how many readings there are. Uses every value, so one outlier moves it.

median = the value at position (n + 1)/2 in cumulative order Key: n = the number of values; the position is a count through the ordered list, not a value. For an even n the position falls between two values, so average them — picking one of the two is the commonest lost mark.

mode = the value with the highest frequency Key: mode = the most frequent value, in the same units as the data; for grouped data it is the modal class. The only average available for categorical data.

range = largest - smallest Key: largest and smallest = the extreme values of the data set; the range is their difference, in the data's units. It uses only two values, so a single outlier destroys it.

IQR = Q3 - Q1 Key: IQR = interquartile range, the spread of the middle 50% of the data (same units); Q3 = upper quartile at the 75% position; Q1 = lower quartile at the 25% position. A negative IQR means the quartiles have been swapped.

IQR = 68 - 42 = 26 marks Key: 68 = Q3, the mark at the 75% position; 42 = Q1, the mark at the 25% position; 26 marks = the IQR. Interpret it in words: the middle half of the students scored within 26 marks of each other.

frequency density = frequency / class width Key: frequency density = the height of the bar (no units, since it is a count divided by a width); frequency = the number of readings in the class; class width = upper boundary minus lower boundary (in the data's units). Use it only when the class widths differ — with equal widths the height may be the frequency.

frequency = frequency density x class width (area of the bar) Key: the same relation rearranged; reading a histogram backwards means measuring a bar's width and height and multiplying. In a histogram it is the area, never the height, that represents the frequency.

angle = (frequency/total) × 360° Key: frequency = the count in the sector; total = the total count for the whole chart; angle in degrees, and the sectors must sum to 360°. To go the other way, total = frequency × 360/angle.

mean = sum of (value x frequency) / sum of frequencies Key: value = each reading, or the midpoint of a class for grouped data (same units); frequency = how many times it occurs. With midpoints the answer is labelled an estimate, because the midpoint stands in for every value in the class.

title: Introduction to Kinetics and Equilibria — Study Notes
content:
Introduction to Kinetics and Equilibria

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH12, Topic 9. Kinetics asks how fast a reaction goes, and equilibria asks how far it goes before the forward and backward reactions balance. Both depend on the same collision ideas.

Rates and collision theory

  • For a reaction to occur, particles must collide with enough energy (the activation energy, Ea) and in the correct orientation.
  • Increasing concentration or pressure increases the frequency of collisions. Increasing temperature raises the proportion of particles with energy above Ea, which has a larger effect than the increase in collision frequency.
  • A catalyst provides an alternative route with a lower Ea; it is not used up.

Measuring rates

  • Rates can be found from the gradient of a concentration–time graph at the start of the reaction (the initial rate).
  • Methods include measuring the volume of gas produced, the change in mass, or the time for a colour change to occur (1/time gives a relative rate).

Dynamic equilibrium

  • In a closed system, the forward and reverse rates become equal. Concentrations stop changing, but the reaction has not stopped.
  • Equilibrium constant Kc = [products]^n / [reactants]^m, with each concentration raised to the power of its coefficient. Kc is constant for a given temperature.

Le Chatelier's principle

  • If a system at equilibrium is disturbed, the position shifts to oppose the change.
  • Increasing temperature favours the endothermic direction. Increasing pressure favours the side with fewer gas molecules. Adding a reactant shifts the position towards products.
  • A catalyst speeds up both directions equally, so it changes the rate of reaching equilibrium but not the equilibrium position or Kc.

Exam tip: say which direction is favoured and why, using the principle. Do not claim that a catalyst increases the yield.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Collision theory, applied to a rate change: raising the temperature increases the fraction of molecules with energy above the activation energy. The number of collisions barely changes, so the increase in rate comes from the larger fraction of successful collisions. Name the activation energy in the answer.
  • Le Chatelier and the Haber process, applied to N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ with ΔH negative: a low temperature favours the product, but the rate is slow, so a compromise temperature of about 450 °C is used with an iron catalyst. The catalyst changes the rate, not the yield.
  • Dynamic equilibrium: the forward and backward rates are equal, and the concentrations are constant. The equilibrium is dynamic, not static, so state both rates are equal and the reactions have not stopped.
  • Common mistake: saying that a catalyst shifts the equilibrium to increase yield. A catalyst lowers the activation energy for both directions, so it reaches equilibrium faster but does not change the yield.

title: AS Level Mathematics: Sequences and Series
content:
AS Level Mathematics: Sequences and Series

A sequence is an ordered list of numbers generated by a rule; a series is the sum of a sequence. Two families dominate the syllabus: arithmetic (add a constant each time) and geometric (multiply by a constant each time). This note builds the topic from zero: the nth term and sum formulas for both families with derivations, σ notation, recurrence relations, the convergence condition for geometric series, and the applied problems — savings, depreciation, loans — where the formulas earn marks. Every formula is derived once so it can be rebuilt if forgotten.

Arithmetic sequences

nth term: u_n = a + (n - 1)d
sum of n terms: S_n = (n/2)[2a + (n - 1)d] = (n/2)(first + last)

a = first term, d = common difference

Worked example. An arithmetic sequence has first term 5 and common difference 4. Find the 20th term and the sum of the first 20 terms.

u_20 = 5 + 19 × 4 = 81
S_20 = (20/2)(5 + 81) = 10 × 86 = 860

Worked example 2 (working backwards). The 5th term is 17 and the 12th is 45. Find a and d.

u_5: a + 4d = 17
u_12: a + 11d = 45
subtract: 7d = 28  →  d = 4;  a = 17 - 16 = 1

Arithmetic series and the sum formula

The sum formula is Gauss's trick: pair the first and last terms, the second and second-last, and so on; each pair has the same total, and there are n/2 pairs.

Worked example. Find the sum of the first 50 positive even numbers.

a = 2, d = 2, n = 50
last term = 2 + 49 × 2 = 100
S = (50/2)(2 + 100) = 25 × 102 = 2550

Worked example 2 (unknown n). The sum of the first n terms of 3, 7, 11, ... is 210. Find n.

210 = (n/2)[6 + 4(n - 1)] = (n/2)(4n + 2) = 2n² + n
2n² + n - 210 = 0
(2n + 21)(n - 10) = 0  →  n = 10 (n must be positive)

Geometric sequences

nth term: u_n = a r^(n - 1)
sum of n terms: S_n = a(1 - r^n)/(1 - r)   (r not 1)
sum to infinity: S_inf = a/(1 - r)   (only if |r| < 1)

a = first term, r = common ratio

Worked example. A geometric sequence has a = 3 and r = 2. Find the 8th term and the sum of the first 8 terms.

u_8 = 3 × 2⁷ = 384
S_8 = 3(1 - 2⁸)/(1 - 2) = 3(1 - 256)/(-1) = 765

Worked example 2 (working backwards). A geometric sequence has second term 12 and fifth term 96. Find r and a.

u_2 = ar = 12;  u_5 = ar⁴ = 96
divide: r³ = 8  →  r = 2;  a = 6

Sum to infinity and convergence

A geometric series converges only when the ratio has magnitude less than 1: each term is smaller than the last, and the total approaches a finite limit.

if |r| < 1: S_inf = a/(1 - r)
if |r| >= 1: the series diverges (no finite sum)

Worked example. Find the sum to infinity of 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 + ...

a = 8, r = 1/2
S_inf = 8/(1 - 1/2) = 8/(0.5) = 16

Worked example 2 (recurring decimal). Write 0.444... as a fraction using a geometric series.

0.444... = 0.4 + 0.04 + 0.004 + ...
a = 0.4, r = 0.1
S_inf = 0.4/(1 - 0.1) = 0.4/0.9 = 4/9

σ notation and recurrence relations

sum from k = 1 to n of u_k  (σ notation)

recurrence: u_(n+1) = f(u_n), with the first term given

Worked example (σ). Evaluate the sum from k = 1 to 5 of (3k + 1).

terms: 4, 7, 10, 13, 16 (arithmetic, a = 4, d = 3)
S = (5/2)(4 + 16) = 50

Worked example 2 (recurrence). u₁ = 2, u_(n+1) = 3u_n + 1. Find u₄.

u2 = 3(2) + 1 = 7
u3 = 3(7) + 1 = 22
u4 = 3(22) + 1 = 67

Recurrence questions often ask you to prove a sequence is arithmetic or geometric: compute consecutive differences or ratios and show they are constant.

Applied problems

Worked example (savings). A student saves 50 pounds in month 1 and increases the monthly saving by 10 pounds each month. How much is saved in month 12, and in total over the year?

arithmetic: a = 50, d = 10
u_12 = 50 + 11(10) = 160
S_12 = (12/2)(50 + 160) = 6 × 210 = 1260 pounds

Worked example 2 (depreciation). A car worth 18000 pounds loses 15% of its value each year. Find its value after 5 years and the total loss.

geometric: a = 18000, r = 0.85
value after 5 years = 18000 × 0.85⁵ = 18000 × 0.4437 = 7987 pounds
loss = 18000 - 7987 = 10013 pounds

Worked example 3 (interest). 1000 pounds is invested at 4% compound interest. Find the value after 10 years and the total interest.

value = 1000 × 1.04¹⁰ = 1000 × 1.4802 = 1480.24 pounds
interest = 480.24 pounds

Deriving the sum formulas

Knowing where the formulas come from makes them reconstructable under pressure. Write the arithmetic sum forwards and backwards and add:

S = a + (a + d) + ... + [a + (n - 1)d]
S = [a + (n - 1)d] + ... + a
2S = n[2a + (n - 1)d]  (each of the n columns adds to 2a + (n-1)d)
S = (n/2)[2a + (n - 1)d]

The geometric sum is derived by multiplying by r and subtracting, which cancels every intermediate term:

S = a + ar + ar² + ... + ar^(n-1)
rS = ar + ar² + ... + ar^n
S - rS = a - ar^n  →  S(1 - r) = a(1 - r^n)
S = a(1 - r^n)/(1 - r)   (r not 1)

Letting n grow in the geometric formula, rⁿ → 0 whenever |r| < 1, leaving S∞ = a/(1 − r): the same derivation explains convergence, so the condition is not a separate fact to memorise.

Proving a sequence is arithmetic or geometric

Show the consecutive differences or ratios are constant using algebra, not just numbers.

Worked example. The terms of a sequence are 3, 3 + 2k, 3 + 4k, ... Show it is arithmetic and find the sum of the first 10 terms in terms of k.

difference 1: (3 + 2k) - 3 = 2k
difference 2: (3 + 4k) - (3 + 2k) = 2k
constant difference 2k  →  arithmetic with d = 2k
S_10 = (10/2)[2(3) + 9(2k)] = 5(6 + 18k) = 30 + 90k

Worked example 2 (geometric). Show that 2, 2x, 2x², ... is geometric and find the sum to infinity when x = 1/3.

ratio: 2x/2 = x;  2x²/(2x) = x  →  geometric with r = x
with x = 1/3: S_inf = 2/(1 - 1/3) = 3

Combining and interpreting sequences

Some questions give a sequence defined by a rule that is neither purely arithmetic nor geometric, and ask for specific terms or a sum found by splitting it into two familiar parts.

Worked example. Find the sum of the first 20 terms of the sequence whose nth term is 3n + 2ⁿ.

split: arithmetic part 3n (a = 3, d = 3) and geometric part 2^n (a = 2, r = 2)
arithmetic sum: (20/2)[6 + 19 × 3] = 10 × 63 = 630
geometric sum: 2(2²⁰ - 1)/(2 - 1) = 2(1048576 - 1) = 2097150
total = 630 + 2097150 = 2097780

Worked example 2 (loan style). A student repays a 5000 pound debt in monthly instalments that form an arithmetic sequence: 150 pounds in month 1, rising by 20 pounds each month. After how many months is the debt cleared, and what is the final instalment?

S_n = (n/2)[2(150) + (n - 1)(20)] = 5000
(n/2)(300 + 20n - 20) = 5000
n(280 + 20n) = 10000
20n² + 280n - 10000 = 0  →  n² + 14n - 500 = 0
n = [-14 + √(196 + 2000)]/2 = (-14 + 46.86)/2 = 16.4
so 17 instalments are needed; the 17th clears the remainder
final (17th) instalment = 150 + 16(20) = 470 pounds

Two modelling habits earn marks here: round n up (16 instalments leave the debt short) and state what the final, part-full payment means. Reading a plan for feasibility — does the sum actually reach the target? — is also examinable: an arithmetic sum with a negative difference peaks and then falls, so a repayment plan built that way may never clear the debt.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Arithmetic) Find the 15th term of 7, 11, 15, ... Answer: a = 7, d = 4; u₁₅ = 7 + 14(4) = 63.
  2. (Sum) Find the sum of the first 30 terms of 2, 5, 8, ... Answer: d = 3; S = 15(4 + 87) = 1365.
  3. (Geometric) Find the 6th term of 2, 6, 18, ... Answer: r = 3; u₆ = 2 × 3⁵ = 486.
  4. (Sum to infinity) Find S∞ for 12 + 6 + 3 + ... Answer: r = ½; S∞ = 12/(1 − ½) = 24.
  5. (Convergence) For what values of r does a geometric series converge? Answer: |r| < 1.
  6. (Recurrence) u₁ = 5, u_(n+1) = 2u_n − 3. Find u₃. Answer: u₂ = 7, u₃ = 11.
  7. (Reverse) The 3rd term of an arithmetic sequence is 11 and the 8th is 31. Find a and d. Answer: 5d = 20 → d = 4; a = 3.
  8. (Applied) A ball is dropped from 2 m and rebounds to 60% of its height each bounce. Find the total distance travelled before it stops. Answer: down 2; up/down 2(0.6) twice... total = 2 + 2(2×0.6)/(1−0.6) = 2 + 6 = 8 m.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • n − 1 versus n: the nth term uses (n − 1)d, not nd. Off-by-one errors are the commonest in this topic.
  • Count versus term: "sum of the first 20 terms" means n = 20; "the 20th term" means u₂₀. Read which is asked.
  • Sign of r: a negative ratio alternates signs; the convergence condition uses |r|, so r = −0.5 converges.
  • Sum to infinity misused: S∞ exists only for |r| < 1; quoting it for a divergent series is a conceptual mark lost.
  • Depreciation versus interest: depreciation multiplies by (1 − rate); interest by (1 + rate). Getting the factor wrong inverts the answer.
  • Solving for n: the quadratic in n has one positive integer root; reject the negative or fractional value explicitly.
  • Recurrence notation: u_(n+1) means the next term; substituting the wrong index shifts the whole sequence.
  • Exact form: where a question asks for an exact answer, keep fractions and powers; decimal approximations lose the final mark.

Equations and symbols

Every relation this topic is examined on, written with its real notation and followed by a key naming each symbol, its unit and what it means. Restaurant-bill questions, savings plans and areas under curves all reduce to one of these lines with numbers in it.

Arithmetic sequences and series

uₙ = a + (n − 1)d
Key: uₙ = the nth term; a = the first term, u₁; d = the common difference, uₙ₊₁ − uₙ; n = the term number, n ≥ 1. The (n − 1) is what makes the first term come out as a: no difference has been added yet.

Sₙ = (n/2)(2a + (n − 1)d) = (n/2)(a + l)
Key: Sₙ = the sum of the first n terms; a = first term; d = common difference; l = the last term, uₙ; n = how many terms are added. The second form is Gauss's pairing: n/2 pairs each summing to a + l.

uₙ = Sₙ − Sₙ₋₁
Key: Sₙ = the sum of the first n terms; Sₙ₋₁ = the sum of the first n − 1. Subtracting the two sums leaves only the nth term — the standard route when a question gives a formula for Sₙ and asks about the sequence.

Geometric sequences and series

uₙ = a rⁿ⁻¹
Key: a = the first term; r = the common ratio, uₙ₊₁/uₙ; n = the term number. Each step multiplies by r, so the power is one less than the term number.

Sₙ = a(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r), r ≠ 1
Key: Sₙ = the sum of the first n terms; a = first term; r = common ratio; n = the number of terms. The equivalent form a(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1) is the same number and is easier when r > 1; r = 1 is excluded because the series is then na.

S∞ = a/(1 − r), valid only for |r| < 1
Key: S∞ = the sum to infinity; a = first term; r = common ratio. The convergence condition is part of the answer: if |r| ≥ 1 the terms do not shrink and the sum diverges, so no finite value exists.

arⁿ⁻¹ = X ⇒ n = 1 + log(X/a)/log r
Key: a = first term; r = common ratio; X = the term whose position is wanted; n = that position. Taking logs of both sides is the only way to get n out of the exponent, and it is what "after how many years" questions require.

uₙ = a(1 + p/100)ⁿ⁻¹
Key: p = the percentage change per period; a = the starting amount; n = the period number. A savings or depreciation model is a geometric sequence: appreciate with p > 0, depreciate with p < 0.

Sigma notation and standard sums

Σ_{r=1}^{n} (A r + B) = A·n(n + 1)/2 + B n
Key: Σ = "sum of"; r = the index running from 1 to n; A, B = constants; n = the number of terms. Every arithmetic series written in sigma notation is this one line, which is why the formula is worth recognising rather than re-deriving.

Σ_{r=1}^{n} r = n(n + 1)/2 and Σ_{r=1}^{n} r² = n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6
Key: n = the last index; r = the index. The two standard results, used to sum any quadratic expression term by term.

Σ_{r=1}^{n} (f(r) ± g(r)) = Σ f(r) ± Σ g(r) and Σ k f(r) = k Σ f(r)
Key: k = a constant; f, g = functions of the index; n = the number of terms. Sums are linear, which is what lets a polynomial be split into the standard sums above.

Recurrence relations and the binomial series

uₙ₊₁ = f(uₙ), with u₁ given
Key: uₙ = the current term; uₙ₊₁ = the next term; f = the rule. A recurrence defines a sequence term by term instead of by a formula in n; to find u₁₀ you iterate, and to describe the long-term behaviour you look for a limit L satisfying L = f(L).

(a + b)ⁿ = Σ_{r=0}^{n} C(n, r) aⁿ⁻ʳ bʳ
Key: a, b = the two terms of the bracket; n = the positive integer power; C(n, r) = n!/(r!(n − r)!), the binomial coefficient; r = the index of the b-power. The (r + 1)th term alone is C(n, r) aⁿ⁻ʳ bʳ, which is how "find the coefficient of x³" is answered without expanding anything.

title: Logic Gates & Boolean Logic — Study Notes
content:
Logic Gates & Boolean Logic

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): six gates, truth tables, building/describing circuits, problem-to-logic mapping.

1. The six gates

ABANDORNANDNORXOR
0000110
0101101
1001101
1111000
