  1. (Hypotheses) A coin might be biased against heads. State H0 and H1. Answer: H0: p = 0.5; H1: p < 0.5.
  2. (Error) Define a Type II error. Answer: failing to reject H0 when it is false.
  3. (Binomial) 8 of 20 seeds germinate; test p = 0.6 against p < 0.6 at 5%. Answer: P(X ≤ 8) = 0.0565, not significant.
  4. (Critical region) X ~ B(15, 0.4): 5% lower critical region. Answer: P(X ≤ 2) = 0.0271, P(X ≤ 3) = 0.0905, so X ≤ 2.
  5. (Actual level) For that region, state the actual significance level. Answer: 2.71%.
  6. (Normal) μ0 = 20, σ = 4, n = 25, mean 21.5: test at 5% one-tailed. Answer: z = 1.875 > 1.6449, reject.
  7. (Two-tailed) Same data two-tailed: Answer: 1.875 < 1.96, do not reject.
  8. (p-value) z = 2.4, H1: μ > μ0. Find the p-value. Answer: 0.0082.
  9. (Sample size) Why can a larger sample turn a non-significant result significant? Answer: the standard error shrinks, so the same deviation is more standard errors away.
  10. (Conclusion wording) Write a valid conclusion for a rejected H0. Answer: there is sufficient evidence at the 5% level that the mean has fallen.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Concluding H0 is true: failing to reject means the evidence is insufficient; it is never proof of the null.
  • Wrong tail: compute P(X ≥ x) for an increase and P(X ≤ x) for a decrease; using the other tail inverts the conclusion.
  • Doubling without a two-tailed alternative: the p-value is doubled only when H1 is "not equal".
  • p-value compared with the wrong threshold: 5% is 0.05; comparing 0.043 with 5 instead of 0.05 reverses the verdict.
  • Standard error omitted: the z-score divides by σ/√n, not by σ.
  • Critical value for the wrong tail: the 5% one-tailed value is 1.6449, the two-tailed is 1.96; the sign matters too.
  • Type I and Type II swapped: Type I is rejecting a true null — the error the significance level controls.
  • Conclusion beyond the data: a rejected H0 says the parameter has changed, not why, and never that the change is important.

title: Atomic Structure and the Periodic Table Revision Notes Edexcel IAL AS Chemistry
content:
Atomic Structure and the Periodic Table AS Level Chemistry

These revision notes cover Topic 2 of the Edexcel International Advanced Subsidiary Chemistry specification. They detail subatomic particles, mass spectrometry, ionisation energies, quantum shells, orbitals, and periodic trends across periods 2 and 3.

Subatomic Particles and Isotopes

Atoms consist of a central nucleus containing protons and neutrons, surrounded by electrons in quantum shells. The atomic proton number is the number of protons in the nucleus, which defines the element. The mass number is the total number of protons and neutrons combined. You can determine the number of each subatomic particle in any neutral atom or ion by subtracting the atomic number from the mass number to find neutrons, while electrons equal protons in a neutral atom or are adjusted according to the ionic charge. Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons, resulting in different mass numbers. Isotopes share identical chemical properties because they have the same electron configuration, but they possess different physical properties such as density and mass.

  • Proton: relative mass 1, relative charge +1.
  • Neutron: relative mass 1, relative charge 0.
  • Electron: relative mass 1 / 1836, relative charge −1.
  • Atomic number equals the number of protons.
  • Mass number equals protons plus neutrons.
  • Neutrons = mass number − atomic number.
  • Electrons = protons minus positive charge, or plus negative charge.

Mass Spectrometry and Relative Masses

A mass spectrometer determines the isotopic composition of elements and relative molecular masses of compounds. A vaporised sample is ionised by high-energy electrons to form positive ions, accelerated by an electric field, deflected by a magnetic field according to mass-to-charge ratio, and detected. Ions in a mass spectrometer may occasionally acquire a 2+ charge, producing a signal at half their actual mass-to-charge ratio. Mass spectra display percentage abundance or relative abundance on the vertical axis against mass-to-charge ratio on the horizontal axis. For diatomic molecules such as chlorine, you can predict mass spectra and relative peak heights given isotopic abundances by using probability combinations of isotopes like chlorine-35 and chlorine-37.

  • Relative atomic mass is the weighted mean mass of an atom of an element compared with one-twelfth of the mass of an atom of carbon-12.
  • Relative molecular mass is the sum of relative atomic masses of all atoms in the molecular formula.
  • Formula for relative atomic mass = sum of (isotopic mass × relative abundance) ÷ total abundance.
  • Chlorine-35 and chlorine-37 exist in a 3:1 ratio, producing molecular ion peaks at m/z 70, 72, and 74 with a 9:6:1 ratio.

Worked example: calculate the relative atomic mass of element X with isotopes 24X (78.9%), 25X (10.0%), and 26X (11.1%).

  • Step 1: Multiply each isotopic mass by its percentage abundance. (24 × 78.9) = 1893.6; (25 × 10.0) = 250.0; (26 × 11.1) = 288.6.
  • Step 2: Sum these values. 1893.6 + 250.0 + 288.6 = 2432.2.
  • Step 3: Divide by 100. 2432.2 ÷ 100 = 24.3 to 3 significant figures.

Ionisation Energies and Quantum Evidence

First ionisation energy is the energy required to remove one mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous atoms to form one mole of gaseous 1+ ions. Second and third ionisation energies remove subsequent moles of electrons from 1+ and 2+ gaseous ions respectively. All ionisation energies are endothermic because energy must be put in to overcome the electrostatic attraction between the outer electrons and the positive nucleus. Ionisation energies are influenced by the positive nuclear charge, electron shielding from inner shells, and the distance of the sub-shell from the nucleus. Successive ionisation energies provide decisive evidence for quantum shells and the group number because a large jump occurs when an electron is removed from a shell closer to the nucleus. The first ionisation energy trend across successive elements provides direct evidence for electron sub-shells.

  • First ionisation energy equation: X (g) yields X+ (g) + e−.
  • Second ionisation energy equation: X+ (g) yields X2+ (g) + e−.
  • Endothermic process: delta H is positive.
  • Nuclear charge increases across a period, increasing attraction.
  • Shielding increases down a group, decreasing attraction.

Orbitals, Sub-shells and Electronic Configurations

An orbital is a region within an atom that can hold up to two electrons with opposite spins. Orbitals in sub-shells each take a single electron before pairing up with two electrons of opposite spin. Orbitals come in different shapes: s-orbitals are spherical, and p-orbitals are dumbbell-shaped along x, y, and z axes. Sub-shells are designated s, p, d, and f. The first four quantum shells hold maximums of 2, 8, 18, and 32 electrons respectively, corresponding to 1, 4, 9, and 16 orbitals. You can predict electronic configurations from hydrogen to krypton inclusive and their ions using s, p, d notation and electron-in-boxes notation. Electronic configuration determines the chemical properties of an element because elements in the same group share outer shell configurations. The Periodic Table is divided into blocks corresponding to the sub-shell containing the highest energy electron.

  • s-block: groups 1 and 2, outer electrons in s-orbitals.
  • p-block: groups 13 to 18, outer electrons in p-orbitals.
  • d-block: transition metals, outer electrons in d-sub-shells.
  • Hunds rule: electrons fill singly before pairing in degenerate orbitals.
  • Transition metal ion formation: 4s electrons are lost before 3d electrons.

Worked example: write the electronic configuration of a titanium atom (atomic number 22) and a titanium 2+ ion.

  • Step 1: Follow the filling order up to 22 electrons. 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d2.
  • Step 2: When forming the 2+ ion, remove electrons from the highest principal quantum number first. Remove 2 electrons from the 4s sub-shell.
  • Step 3: Write the ionic configuration as 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 3d2.

Periodic Trends and Graphical Data

Data represented graphically, including logarithms of first ionisation energies for elements 1 to 36, demonstrate the periodic nature of properties. A periodic property is one that repeats in a regular pattern across periods. Across periods 2 and 3, melting and boiling temperatures depend on structure and bonding: giant metallic structures have high melting points, giant covalent structures have very high melting points due to strong covalent bonds, and simple molecular structures have low melting and boiling points due to weak intermolecular forces. First ionisation energies generally increase across periods due to increasing nuclear charge and constant shielding, with slight drops between group 2 and 13 due to sub-shell changes, and between group 15 and 16 due to spin-pairing repulsion. First ionisation energy decreases down a group due to increased atomic radius and shielding.

  • Period 2 and 3 trends: metallic bonding peaks at group 13, covalent macromolecular peaks at group 14, simple molecules drop sharply at group 15 or 16.
  • Group 2 to 13 drop: outer electron enters a higher-energy p-sub-shell, which is further shielded by the s-sub-shell.
  • Group 15 to 16 drop: pairing of electrons in a p-orbital causes mutual repulsion, making it easier to remove.
  • Logarithm graphs of ionisation energy clearly show the periodicity of quantum shells.

Typical mistakes

  • Mistake: Stating that ionisation energy is exothermic because energy is released. Correction: Ionisation energy is always endothermic because energy is required to overcome the electrostatic attraction between electrons and protons.
  • Mistake: Removing 3d electrons before 4s electrons when ionising transition metal atoms. Correction: Always remove 4s electrons first because the 4s orbital is of higher energy once filling is complete and sits further out.
  • Mistake: Confusing mass number with relative atomic mass. Correction: Mass number is a whole number representing protons plus neutrons in a specific isotope, whereas relative atomic mass is a weighted mean of all naturally occurring isotopes.
  • Mistake: Forgetting that a chlorine mass spectrum has peaks for Cl2 molecules, not just chlorine atoms. Correction: Diatomic chlorine molecules produce molecular ion peaks at m/z 70, 72, and 74 based on combinations of Cl-35 and Cl-37.

Exam-style questions

  1. Define the term first ionisation energy. Answer: The energy required to remove one mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous atoms to form one mole of gaseous 1+ ions. (Earns 2 marks for stating moles of gas and 1+ ions).
  2. Explain why the first ionisation energy of oxygen is lower than that of nitrogen. Answer: Nitrogen has a half-filled 2p3 sub-shell configuration, whereas oxygen has a 2p4 configuration with paired electrons. The mutual repulsion of the paired electrons in oxygen makes the electron easier to remove. (Earns credit for mentioning electron pairing and repulsion).
  3. Calculate the relative atomic mass of magnesium given isotopes: Mg-24 (78.99%), Mg-25 (10.00%), Mg-26 (11.01%). Answer: ((24 × 78.99) + (25 × 10.00) + (26 × 11.01)) ÷ 100 = 24.3 to 1 decimal place. (Earns credit for correct working and units).
  4. State and explain the trend in first ionisation energy down Group 2. Answer: First ionisation energy decreases down Group 2 because atoms have more quantum shells, increasing atomic radius and electron shielding, which outweighs the increased nuclear charge and reduces outer shell attraction. (Earns credit for naming shielding, distance, and attraction).
  5. Write the full electronic configuration for a chromium atom, atomic number 24, using s, p, d notation. Answer: 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s1 3d5. (Earns credit for the stable half-filled d-sub-shell exception).

Use these notes alongside active recall and past paper question practice. Focus next on mastering redox equations and stoichiometry in Topic 3.

title: Nuclear Physics — Study Notes
content:
Nuclear Physics

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): nuclear model, radioactivity, decay types, half-life, safety, fission/fusion (Extended).

1. The nuclear model

Nucleus (protons +, neutrons 0) with orbiting electrons (−). Nuclide notation ᴬ_Z X. Isotopes: same Z, different A. Rutherford scattering established the nuclear model; proton number Z, nucleon number A.

2. Radiation types

TypeNatureRange (air)Stopped by
alpha αhelium nucleus (2p2n)few cmpaper
beta β⁻fast electron~20–30 cmfew mm aluminium
gamma γEM wavevery farthick lead/concrete

Deflection in fields: α/β opposite, γ none. Ionising: α > β > γ. Background radiation: radon, cosmic, rocks, medical, fallout.

3. Decay equations

  • α: A −4, Z −2 (e.g. ²³⁸₉₂U → ²³⁴₉₀Th + α).
  • β⁻: neutron → proton; A same, Z +1 (e.g. ¹⁴₆C → ¹⁴₇N + β⁻).
  • γ: no change to A or Z.

Balance A and Z on both sides — that is the check.

4. Half-life

Time for half the unstable nuclei to decay (random process). Read from a decay curve or count halves: 80 → 40 → 20 over two half-lives.

Example: 800 Bq, half-life 2 h → 200 Bq after 4 h.

5. Safety and uses

Uses: medical tracers (β/γ), sterilisation, thickness gauge (β), dating (C-14), smoke alarms (α). Safety: distance, time, shielding, wear badges, store in lead. Handle with tongs; never point at people.

6. Fission and fusion (Extended)

Fission: heavy nucleus splits (U-235 + neutron), chain reaction controlled by moderators/control rods — power stations. Fusion: light nuclei join (stellar) — needs huge T/P; releases more energy per kg; no long-lived waste.

title: IGCSE Physics: Measurement and Units
content:
IGCSE Physics: Measurement and Units

Cambridge IGCSE Physics 0625 (2026–2028), Topic 1 Motion, forces and energy, statement 1.1 Physical quantities and measurement techniques — plus the experimental skills that Paper 6, Alternative to Practical, examines directly. Every physics result rests on a measurement, and every measurement is uncertain. This note builds the vocabulary of quantities and units, the practical techniques for length, volume and time, and then the full Paper 6 method: variables, safety, tables, graph plotting, gradients and intercepts, conclusions and error analysis. Paper 2 and Paper 4 carry the theory marks; Paper 6 carries these skills as a written exam of their own.

Physical quantities and SI units

A physical quantity is a property that can be measured, and every measurement needs a number and a unit. Physics uses the SI system, whose base units include the metre (m) for length, the kilogram (kg) for mass, the second (s) for time, the ampere (A) for electric current, the kelvin (K) for temperature and the mole (mol) for amount of substance. All other units are derived from these: speed in metres per second (m s⁻¹) is a base unit divided by a base unit, and force in newtons is defined so that 1 N = 1 kg m s⁻².

QuantitySymbolSI unitHow the unit is built
Lengths or lmetre (m)base unit
Massmkilogram (kg)base unit
Timetsecond (s)base unit
VolumeVcubic metre (m³)m³; litres and cm³ are everyday alternatives (1 litre = 0.001 m³)
Speedvmetre per second (m s⁻¹)m ÷ s
Frequencyfhertz (Hz)1 Hz = 1 cycle per second (s⁻¹)
ForceFnewton (N)kg m s⁻²
EnergyEjoule (J)N m = kg m² s⁻²
Pressureppascal (Pa)N m⁻²

Large and small quantities use standard prefixes or standard form: kilo (×1000), centi (÷100), milli (÷1000), micro (÷10⁶). Standard form writes a quantity as a number between 1 and 10 multiplied by a power of ten, so the speed of light is 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. Units obey ordinary algebra: dividing metres by seconds gives m s⁻¹, and a unit written as m/s and one written as m s⁻¹ are the same thing.

Measuring length, area and volume

Length is measured with a ruler or a tape. The three rules of good practice are fixed: place the scale edge along the line being measured, start from the zero mark rather than the worn end of the ruler, and take the reading at eye level directly above the point to avoid parallax error. A ruler reading should be quoted to the nearest half millimetre with an uncertainty of about ±0.5 mm; a vernier caliper or a micrometer screw gauge reads to 0.01 mm and is used when the length is small.

Areas and volumes are calculated from measured lengths. The area of a rectangle is length × width; the volume of a rectangular block is length × width × height; the volume of a cylinder is π r² l. For an irregular solid, the volume is found by displacement: water is poured into a measuring cylinder, the starting volume is read, the object is lowered in, and the rise in level is the object's volume. Read the bottom of the curved meniscus at eye level. The technique fails for objects that float (use a sinker), objects that absorb water or dissolve (use sand or oil), and objects that splash water out on entry (lower them gently on a thread).

Area scales with the square of a length and volume with the cube, so a small length error is amplified: a 2 per cent error in each of the three dimensions of a cube gives about a 6 per cent error in its volume. This is exactly the kind of reasoning Paper 6 rewards in its evaluation questions.

Measuring time intervals

Short times are measured with a stopwatch, and human reaction time of about 0.2 s dominates a single reading. Two standard techniques control it. First, repeat and average: time several oscillations of a pendulum and divide by the number of swings, because the reaction error is then spread over many periods. Second, use a larger quantity: time 20 trolley passes rather than one, or measure the time for 50 dots from a 50 Hz ticker timer, where consecutive dots are 0.02 s apart. Timing devices built into the apparatus — light gates, data loggers and ticker timers — remove reaction time entirely and are the expected answer when a question asks how to improve a timing measurement.

Errors, precision and percentage uncertainty

Every measurement carries an uncertainty, usually taken as the range of the scale: ±0.5 mm on a ruler, ±0.5 s on a stopwatch read to seconds, ±0.5 of the smallest scale division on a measuring cylinder. Two kinds of error behave differently. A random error scatters readings in both directions and is reduced by repeating and averaging; a systematic error shifts every reading the same way — a zero error on a balance, a bent ruler, parallax — and is removed by correcting the instrument, never by averaging. An anomaly is a result that does not fit the pattern; it is discarded only with a stated reason, never because it is inconvenient.

The size of an uncertainty is compared using percentage uncertainty, a technique Paper 6 tests whenever results are combined:

percentage uncertainty in one reading = (uncertainty / reading) x 100
percentage uncertainty in a sum or difference = (largest absolute uncertainty / answer) x 100
percentage uncertainty in a product or quotient = sum of the individual percentage uncertainties

Worked example: a cube of side 2.0 ± 0.05 cm has a mass of 24.0 ± 0.1 g. The side's percentage uncertainty is 0.05/2.0 × 100 = 2.5 per cent, so the volume (a product of three lengths) carries 3 × 2.5 = 7.5 per cent. The mass carries 0.1/24.0 × 100 = 0.4 per cent. The density = mass/volume carries 7.5 + 0.4 = 7.9 per cent, so ρ = 24.0/8.0 = 3.0 g cm⁻³ ± 0.2 g cm⁻³. The volume term dominates: improving the ruler improves the result far more than improving the balance.

Scalars and vectors (Supplement)

A scalar has size only: distance, speed, mass, energy, temperature, pressure. A vector has size and direction: displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, momentum, weight. Vectors are added by direction: two forces in a line add or subtract; two forces at right angles combine by Pythagoras, with the direction found from an angle. If a boat is pushed 3.0 m north and 4.0 m east, its resultant displacement is 5.0 m on a bearing of about 53° from north. Drawing the vector triangle to scale is a complete method on Paper 4 whenever the angle is not 90°.

Paper 6: how the practical exam is written

Paper 6 is a written exam about practical physics; you handle no apparatus but you must think like an experimenter. The question types repeat, and each has a method.

  • Choosing apparatus. Match the instrument to the quantity and its size: a ruler for lengths of centimetres, a micrometer for wires, a measuring cylinder for volumes, a balance for masses. State the range and the precision you expect.
  • Variables. Name the independent variable (what you change), the dependent variable (what you measure) and the control variables (what you keep fixed). A fair test changes one thing only, and every control earns a mark: same material, same temperature, same apparatus, same operator.
  • Safety. Link each hazard to a control: hot water and burners — use tongs and keep hands clear; masses and clamps — secure the clamp to the bench and stand clear of falling masses; lasers and ultrasound — never look into the beam; electricity — low voltages only, and switch off between readings.
  • Tables. Draw a box with a column per quantity and a heading of quantity divided by unit, e.g. length / cm. Numbers sit in the cells without units. Give each column enough rows for repeats, quote consistent significant figures, and record raw readings before any calculated column.
  • Graphs. The independent variable goes on the horizontal axis. Choose a scale that fills at least half the sheet, label both axes with quantity and unit, plot points with a fine cross, and draw a single smooth line of best fit — a thin ruled line for a linear relationship, a smooth curve otherwise. Never join dots dot to dot.
  • Gradient and intercept. The gradient = (change in vertical quantity) / (change in horizontal quantity), taken between two distant points on the line, not between plotted points. For a straight line through the origin the two variables are directly proportional; a non-zero intercept has physical meaning — on a speed–time graph it is the initial speed, on a cooling curve the ambient temperature — and the equation of the line is written as vertical quantity = gradient × horizontal quantity + intercept.
  • Conclusions. State the relationship the graph shows in words and symbols, quote the gradient with its unit, and relate the result to the physics (for example, a load–extension graph through the origin shows extension proportional to load, and its gradient is the spring constant).
  • Evaluation. Name the largest source of uncertainty with a reason, say which way it pushes the answer, and propose a specific improvement — more repeats, a longer measurement interval, a sensor or data logger, a wider range of values — not a vague plea for more care.

Worked example: reading a graph and its gradient

A student measures the speed of a trolley pulled down a runway, plotting speed on the vertical axis against time on the horizontal axis. The plotted points lie close to a straight line crossing the vertical axis at 0.10 m s⁻¹ and passing through (2.0 s, 1.30 m s⁻¹) and (6.0 s, 3.30 m s⁻¹).

gradient = (3.30 - 1.30) / (6.0 - 2.0) = 2.00 / 4.0 = 0.50 m s-2
intercept = 0.10 m s-1
equation: speed = 0.50 x time + 0.10

The gradient is the trolley's acceleration, 0.50 m s⁻², and the intercept is its initial speed, 0.10 m s⁻¹. A conclusion that says only speed increases with time earns no mark; the mark is for the number, its unit and its physical meaning.

Common mistakes

  • Writing a number without its unit, or putting units into the cells of a results table whose heading already carries the unit.
  • Starting a ruler scale from the broken zero end, or reading at an angle and introducing parallax error.
  • Joining plotted points with a zig-zag line instead of drawing one smooth line of best fit, which hides anomalies rather than revealing them.
  • Calculating a gradient between two neighbouring plotted points; use two distant points on the line to shrink the reading error.
  • Reducing a systematic error by repeating readings; averaging shrinks random error only, and a zero error must be corrected at the instrument.
  • Keeping an anomaly with no comment, or discarding one without a stated physical reason.
  • Confusing scalar and vector: adding a speed to a velocity, or giving a direction for energy.
  • Reporting a percentage uncertainty but never saying which measurement dominates the final result.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 6, 3 marks). Describe how you would measure the average speed of a trolley on a runway.

Answer: Mark a fixed distance along the runway and measure it with a metre ruler. Release the trolley from the same point each time and time its passage over the marked distance with light gates and a data logger (or a stopwatch, repeated and averaged to reduce reaction error). Average speed is the distance divided by the time. Repeat for several distances or heights and record results in a table.

Question 2 (Paper 6, 3 marks). A student measures the period of a pendulum once and gets 1.3 s. Suggest two improvements to the method.

Answer: Time 20 complete oscillations and divide by 20, so reaction time error becomes a small fraction of the total; repeat the whole measurement several times and take a mean. Keep the pendulum length fixed and time from the release point to avoid a variable starting condition.

Question 3 (Paper 4, 2 marks). A length is recorded as 2.50 cm. State the instrument used and its uncertainty.

Answer: A ruler reading to 0.1 cm (or a vernier caliper if the precision demands it), with an uncertainty of ±0.05 cm, half the smallest scale division.

Question 4 (Paper 6, 4 marks). The volume of a small stone is found from 30 cm³ to 45 cm³ in a measuring cylinder and its mass is 36 g. Calculate the density and its percentage uncertainty if each volume reading is uncertain by ±0.5 cm³.

Answer: Volume = 15 cm³. The uncertainty in the difference is 0.5 + 0.5 = 1.0 cm³ (worst case for a difference), so the percentage uncertainty is 1.0/15 × 100 = 6.7 per cent. Density = 36/15 = 2.4 g cm⁻³, so the answer is 2.4 g cm⁻³ ± 0.2 g cm³ (about ±7 per cent). Using a larger volume difference would shrink the percentage uncertainty.

Question 5 (Paper 2 style). Which quantity is a vector? A energy; B temperature; C momentum; D pressure. Answer: C. Momentum has size and direction; the rest are scalars.

With measurements trustworthy, the next topic is what heat does to matter: thermal physics.

Equations and symbols

Measurement is the one topic whose equations are mostly about the arithmetic of uncertainty rather than a physical law. Paper 6 marks the method, the significant figures and the uncertainty, so each relation below is given with the symbols it uses and the unit each symbol carries.

Averages and rates

x̄ = (x₁ + x₂ + … + xₙ) / n
Key: x̄ = mean value (same unit as the readings); x₁ … xₙ = individual readings, all in the same unit; n = number of readings (no unit). Anomalous readings are discarded before averaging, never included and then blamed on the mean.

v = d / t
Key: v = average speed (m/s); d = total distance travelled (m); t = total time taken (s). On a two-leg journey this is total distance over total time, not the mean of the two speeds.

T = t / N
Key: T = period of one oscillation (s); t = total time for N oscillations (s); N = number of oscillations counted (no unit). Timing twenty swings and dividing moves the reaction-time error from each swing to the whole interval.

Uncertainty

percentage uncertainty = (Δx / x) × 100%
Key: Δx = absolute uncertainty of the reading, taken as ± half the smallest division for a single reading (same unit as x); x = the reading itself; the result is a percentage (no unit).

percentage uncertainty of a product or quotient = %A + %B
Key: %A, %B = the percentage uncertainties of the measured quantities being multiplied or divided. Adding the percentages is the rule whenever the quantities are combined by × or ÷.

percentage uncertainty of a power = n × (%x)
Key: n = the power to which the quantity is raised (2 for an area, 3 for a volume); %x = the percentage uncertainty in the measured length. This is why a 5% uncertainty in a diameter becomes 15% in a volume.

Geometry needed to find a volume

V = πr²h
Key: V = volume of a cylinder (m³ or cm³); r = radius, half the diameter (m or cm); h = height (m or cm); π = 3.14 (no unit).

V = (4/3)πr³
Key: V = volume of a sphere (m³ or cm³); r = radius (m or cm). The cube is what makes the percentage uncertainty three times the radius's.

A = πr²
Key: A = area of a circle (m² or cm²); r = radius (m or cm).

V = V₂ − V₁
Key: V = volume of an irregular solid (cm³); V₂ = cylinder reading with the solid submerged (cm³); V₁ = cylinder reading before it was added (cm³).

Converting units before substituting

1 km/h = 1000 m / 3600 s = 0.278 m/s
Key: divide a speed in km/h by 3.6 to get m/s. Converting after substituting is the commonest arithmetic error on Paper 2.

1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³
Key: multiply a density in g/cm³ by 1000 to use it with masses in kg and volumes in m³.

1 cm² = 1 × 10⁻⁴ m² and 1 cm³ = 1 × 10⁻⁶ m³
Key: areas scale with the square of the length conversion and volumes with the cube, which is why 100 cm² is 0.01 m², not 1 m².

The one derived quantity this topic measures

ρ = m / V
Key: ρ (rho) = density (kg/m³ or g/cm³); m = mass (kg or g); V = volume (m³ or cm³). The units must match before dividing: 250 g in 30 cm³ is 8.3 g/cm³, which is 8300 kg/m³.

title: Coordinate Geometry — Study Notes
content:
Coordinate geometry of circles

Level note: circles are Pure 2 (WMA12) in Edexcel, sat at AS; this note is the detailed treatment and the AS Coordinate Geometry note covers the same ground.

At A2, coordinate geometry centres on the circle: its equation, tangents, normals and the interaction with straight lines.

Circle equations

  • Centre (a, b), radius r: (x - a)^2 + (y - b)^2 = r^2.
  • General form x^2 + y^2 + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 has centre (-g, -f) and radius sqrt(g^2 + f^2 - c).
  • Always complete the square to find centre and radius.

Tangents and normals

  • The tangent at a point is perpendicular to the radius at that point: gradient of tangent = -1 / (gradient of radius).
  • The normal at a point passes through the centre (it is the radius line extended).
  • For the circle x^2 + y^2 = r^2, the tangent at (x1, y1) is x x1 + y y1 = r^2.

Line and circle

  • Substituting a line into the circle gives a quadratic: two roots = two intersections (secant), one repeated root = tangent, no real roots = no intersection.
  • Tangency condition: the perpendicular distance from the centre to the line equals the radius.
  • Distance from (x0, y0) to ax + by + c = 0 is |ax0 + by0 + c| / sqrt(a^2 + b^2).

Tangent from an external point

The length of a tangent from an external point P to a circle is sqrt(d^2 - r^2), where d is the distance from P to the centre.

title: International GCSE English as a Second Language: Reading for Main Ideas and Detail
content:
International GCSE English as a Second Language: Reading for Main Ideas and Detail

The 9280 reading paper (Paper 1 in the current official numbering) rewards two skills above all others: finding the main idea of a text quickly, and locating precise detail inside it — with a third skill, understanding meaning that is implied rather than stated, deciding the top band. This note builds the complete reading method from zero: how to skim and scan deliberately, how each question type is constructed and answered, how to infer without guessing, and how to prove every answer from the text. Reading speed is a technique, not a talent, and every step below is trainable.

What the reading paper measures

You face a set of texts — factual texts like articles, adverts, emails and reports, and literary texts like stories and extracts — and answer questions that move from explicit to implicit understanding. The question types include short-answer questions, multiple-choice items, note completion and matching tasks; the wording of the instructions (how many words, which text) is binding.

SkillQuestion signalMethod
Explicit meaning"According to the text, what ...?" / "Find and copy ..."scan for the keyword, copy exactly
Main idea"What is the main purpose of ...?" / "Choose the best title"skim first and last lines, repeated nouns
Implicit meaning"What can you infer ...?" / "How does the writer feel ...?"find the evidence line, infer one step beyond it
Vocabulary in context"What does the word X mean here?"replace with each option in the actual sentence

Skimming: the main idea in thirty seconds

Skimming is reading fast for gist, and it has a fixed recipe:

  1. Read the title and any subheadings — they carry the topic and often the writer's stance.
  2. Read the first and last paragraphs in full — English expository writing states its point at the start and repeats it at the end.
  3. Read the first sentence of each middle paragraph — the topic sentence of each paragraph is usually its first one.
  4. Note the nouns that repeat — a word appearing in most paragraphs is the subject of the text.

Worked example. Text: "The town's last cinema closed in 2019, and with it went a ritual ... Six years on, the building is a gym ... Older residents remember Saturday mornings there ... The council now plans a screen in the library ..." Skim recipe applied: title says "The Last Picture Show"; first paragraph gives the closure; the repeated nouns are cinema and town; the last paragraph gives a plan. Main idea: the loss of the town's cinema and how the community is responding. A question asking for the writer's purpose is answered from that shape: to describe what the town lost and what might replace it.

Scanning: the detail in fifteen seconds

Scanning is searching for a specific fact. You are not reading; you are hunting:

  • Underline the question keyword first — names, numbers, dates and unusual nouns scan fastest.
  • Expect paraphrase: the question says "fees", the text says "cost of enrolment". Train yourself to search for meaning, not for the printed word.
  • Search with your finger or cursor down the page — eyes wander less when tracking physically.
  • When you find the region, read the whole sentence around it — the answer is usually one line, and the trap sits in the line before or after.

Worked example. Question: "How much does a student membership cost per month?" Text region: "Membership is 30 pounds a month for adults. Students pay half that, while under-16s go free." Scanning finds membership and cost; the adult price is the distractor; "half that" is the calculation; answer: 15 pounds. The habit of reading the sentence around the hit is what makes the distractor visible.

Question-type recipes

TypeRecipeCommon trap
Short answerfind evidence line → answer in your own words within the word limitcopying ten words when the limit says five
Multiple-choiceanswer from memory of the text first, then match optionsoptions that repeat text words but change meaning
Note completionread the note's grammar → predict answer type → scan → copy the exact word(s)grammar of the answer not fitting the note
Matchingread all statements first → skim the text section → match by meaningmatching on shared words instead of shared meaning
Find and copycopy the exact phrase from the textparaphrasing when the instruction says copy

Implicit meaning: inferring without guessing

An inference question asks what the text implies. The rule that keeps inference honest: every inference must be one small step from a quoted line, never a leap from your own assumptions. The method is three moves: find the evidence line, state what it says literally, then ask "and therefore?" exactly once.

  • Feelings and attitudes: look for the words that carry evaluation (fortunately, sadly, astonishingly), the imagery, and what the writer chooses to mention first and last.
  • Between the lines: "The library's opening hours were cut in March. By August, the study group had dissolved." The text never says the cut killed the group; the inference is exactly one step: the reduced hours contributed to the group's end.
  • Writers' purposes: to inform, to persuade, to entertain, to describe, to warn. Persuasion is detected by evaluative language and one-sided evidence; informing presents facts without judgement.

Worked example — inference with annotation. Text: "When the new road opened, the bakery's morning trade vanished. 'We used to queue out of the door,' Mr Hollis says, staring at the empty counter." Question: How does Mr Hollis feel about the change? Evidence line 1: "morning trade vanished" — a fact with a negative verb. Evidence line 2: "staring at the empty counter" — a physical action that shows loss. One step: he feels sad and nostalgic about the loss of customers. Wrong answers to reject: angry (no evidence of anger), hopeful (opposite of the images). The inference stays anchored to two lines.

Vocabulary in context

When a question asks what a word means in the text, dictionary memory is a trap — many common words carry their less common sense. Method: put each option back into the original sentence and read the sentence aloud in your head. The right option keeps the sentence's meaning intact.

Worked example. "The charity hopes to secure funding before December." Options: (A) lock away (B) obtain (C) guarantee (D) tie up. Substitute: "obtain funding" keeps the sentence identical in meaning; "guarantee funding" changes who does the guaranteeing; "lock away" and "tie up" are literal senses that make the sentence nonsense. Answer: B.

The evidence-line habit

Top-band candidates prove answers. For every question, mark the line that justifies your answer before writing it. This habit (a) prevents answering from memory of the passage's gist, (b) settles arguments between two tempting options — the option with a line behind it wins, and (c) makes checking fast because re-reading one line beats re-reading the text.

Worked examples: full question walk-through

Worked example 1. Text: "Volunteering at the animal shelter takes three hours every Saturday. Most volunteers are students, and the shelter's manager, Ms Oduya, says they are 'the reason we cope with kitten season'. Not everyone stays: the work is smelly and repetitive. But those who stay describe it as the best part of their week."

Q1 (explicit):  How long does a shift last?
                Evidence: "three hours every Saturday" -> 3 hours.

Q2 (detail):    Who volunteers the most?
                Evidence: "Most volunteers are students" -> students.

Q3 (implicit):  What does the quotation suggest about kitten season?
                Evidence: "the reason we cope with kitten season"
                Literal: students help the shelter survive that period.
                One step: kitten season is the busiest and hardest time.
                Answer: it is the shelter's most demanding period.

Q4 (attitude):  What do long-term volunteers think of the work?
                Evidence: "those who stay describe it as the best part
                of their week" -> despite the smell, they love it.

Worked example 2 — multiple-choice on purpose. Question: What is the writer's main purpose in the text above? (A) to advertise the shelter (B) to describe what volunteering there involves (C) to persuade readers to adopt cats (D) to criticise people who quit. Evidence audit: the text states hours, who volunteers, what is hard, how volunteers feel — descriptive facts with one quotation; there is no call to adopt (C), no sales language (A), and the quitters are mentioned neutrally ("not everyone stays"). Answer: B. Method visible: reject options by demanding a line for each.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Skimming) A text about electric buses in a city opens: "The first electric buses arrived in March, and complaints about noise began in April — not from passengers, but from pedestrians who could no longer hear them coming." What is the main idea of the opening? Answer: the new buses brought an unexpected side effect (they are too quiet).
  2. (Scanning) From the shelter text: "The shelter is open weekdays 9–5 and Saturdays 9–1." When can you volunteer on a weekend? Answer: Saturday, 9am to 1pm.
  3. (Inference) "The exam results letter sat unopened on the table for two days." What can you infer about the student? Answer: the student was anxious about opening it — one step from "unopened for two days"; "the student failed" is a guess beyond the evidence.
  4. (Vocabulary in context) "The volunteers maintain the garden every Sunday." Options: keep in good condition / visit / argue about / describe. Answer: keep in good condition.
  5. (Note completion) Note: "Kitten season is the shelter's ____ period." Answer: most demanding (or busiest) — from the manager's quotation; the answer type is an adjective because the note grammar needs one.
  6. (Matching writer purpose) Match each extract to its purpose: (a) "Buy one, get one free — this week only!" (b) "The data show a 12% rise in enrolment." (c) "The waves crashed over the wall as we ran." Answer: (a) to persuade/advertise, (b) to inform, (c) to entertain/describe.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Answering from your own knowledge: the text is the only authority. If the passage says the event was in 1897 and you know it was 1894, the answer is 1897.
  • Gist answering on detail questions: scanning is not reading; a remembered impression is not a located fact. Demand a line for every answer.
  • Inference leaps: "the letter sat unopened" does not prove failure or illness. One step beyond the text is inference; three steps is creative writing.
  • Word-limit losses: "no more than three words" is enforced. Count the words in your answer before moving on.
  • Copy questions paraphrased: "Find and copy one word" means exactly one word from the text, spelled as printed.
  • Matching by shared words: distractor options are built from text words with different meanings. Match meaning; the vocabulary shares are bait.
  • Time sinking: spending five minutes on one inference question starves three easy detail questions. Mark it, move on, return at the end.
  • Ignoring instruction order: questions usually follow the text's order — if question 4's evidence is in paragraph 2, you have probably misread something.

title: Coordinate Geometry — Study Notes
content:
Coordinate Geometry

Distance and midpoint

For A(x₁, y₁) and B(x₂, y₂): length AB = √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²). Midpoint M = ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2).

Gradients

Gradient m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁), where x₂ ≠ x₁. A horizontal line has m = 0; a vertical line has no gradient.

Parallel lines have equal gradients. Perpendicular lines (neither vertical nor horizontal) satisfy m₁ × m₂ = −1.

Equations of a straight line

  • Gradient–intercept form: y = mx + c, where c is the y-intercept.
  • Point–gradient form: y − y₁ = m(x − x₁).
  • General form: ax + by + c = 0, with gradient −a/b.

Example: Find the line through P(2, −1) perpendicular to y = 3x − 4. The perpendicular gradient is −1/3, so y + 1 = −1/3 (x − 2). Multiply by 3: 3y + 3 = −x + 2, giving x + 3y + 1 = 0.

Intersection of two lines

Solve the two equations simultaneously, by substitution or elimination. Lines with equal gradients and no common point are parallel.

Example: y = 2x + 1 and x + y = 7. Substituting gives x + 2x + 1 = 7, so 3x = 6, x = 2 and y = 5. The lines meet at (2, 5).

Circles

A circle with centre (a, b) and radius r has equation (x − a)² + (y − b)² = r².

The expanded form x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 has centre (−g, −f) and radius √(g² + f² − c). Complete the square in x and y to convert between the forms.

Example: x² + y² − 6x + 4y − 3 = 0 has g = −3, f = 2, c = −3. Centre (3, −2), radius √(9 + 4 + 3) = 4.

Tangents

A tangent to a circle is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact. Find the radius gradient from the centre to the point, then take the negative reciprocal for the tangent.

Exam technique

  • Sketch the figure first, and check whether the question asks about a line, a circle or both.
  • Keep exact values (fractions and surds) until the final step unless decimals are requested.
  • Check that a line passes through a given point by substituting its coordinates.

title: A Level Mathematics: Coordinate Geometry
content:
A Level Mathematics: Coordinate Geometry

Coordinate geometry is the bridge between algebra and shape: every geometric object is described by an equation, and every geometric question becomes an algebraic one. This note starts from the two measurements that define a straight line — how far and how steep — and builds outwards to circles, tangents, chords and the discriminant conditions that decide whether a line meets a curve at all. The exam almost never asks for a definition; it asks you to combine two or three of these tools in one question, so each one is presented with the situation that calls for it.

Distance, midpoint and gradient

Everything else is built on three formulas. They come from Pythagoras and from averaging, and they are worth being able to derive rather than recall.

for A(x1, y1) and B(x2, y2):
distance AB = sqrt((x2 - x1)^2 + (y2 - y1)^2)     Pythagoras on the step
midpoint   = ((x1 + x2)/2, (y1 + y2)/2)            the averages
gradient m = (y2 - y1)/(x2 - x1)                   rise over run

Worked example. For A(2, −1) and B(8, 7), find the distance AB, the midpoint and the gradient.

distance = sqrt(6^2 + 8^2) = sqrt(100) = 10
midpoint = ((2+8)/2, (-1+7)/2) = (5, 3)
gradient = 8/6 = 4/3

Worked example 2 (finding an unknown). The distance from (1, 2) to (4, k) is 5. Find k.

sqrt(3^2 + (k-2)^2) = 5
9 + (k-2)^2 = 25
(k-2)^2 = 16  ->  k - 2 = 4 or -4
k = 6 or k = -2

Two answers, not one: the square root in the distance formula hides a sign, and examiners always intend both.

Forms of the equation of a straight line

Three forms, each suited to a different piece of information. Choosing the wrong one costs time, not marks, but the wrong one also invites arithmetic slips.

FormEquationUse when you know
gradient–intercepty = mx + cgradient and intercept, or for sketching
point–gradienty − y1 = m(x − x1)gradient and one point
generalax + by + c = 0the form most mark schemes quote

Worked example. Find the equation of the line through (3, −2) with gradient −1/2, in general form.

y + 2 = (-1/2)(x - 3)
2y + 4 = -x + 3
x + 2y + 1 = 0

Worked example 2 (two points). Find the equation of the line through (1, 4) and (5, 2).

m = (2 - 4)/(5 - 1) = -1/2
y - 4 = -0.5(x - 1)  ->  y = -0.5x + 4.5
or x + 2y - 9 = 0

Parallel and perpendicular lines

Parallel means equal gradients. Perpendicular means the gradients multiply to −1, which is the same as one being the negative reciprocal of the other. Recognising that the negative reciprocal is a rotation by 90° prevents the common error of negating without inverting.

parallel: m1 = m2
perpendicular: m1 x m2 = -1, so m2 = -1/m1

Worked example. Find the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining A(2, 5) and B(6, 1).

midpoint = (4, 3)
gradient AB = (1 - 5)/(6 - 2) = -1
perpendicular gradient = 1
equation: y - 3 = 1(x - 4)  ->  y = x - 1

Worked example 2 (proving a right angle). Show that the triangle with vertices P(1, 1), Q(4, 2) and R(3, 5) is right-angled at Q.

gradient PQ = (2 - 1)/(4 - 1) = 1/3
gradient QR = (5 - 2)/(3 - 4) = -3
product = (1/3)(-3) = -1  ->  perpendicular, so the angle at Q is 90 degrees

The equation of a circle

A circle is the set of points a fixed distance from a fixed centre, so the distance formula written with an unknown point gives the equation directly.

centre (a, b), radius r:   (x - a)^2 + (y - b)^2 = r^2
expanded form: x^2 + y^2 + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0
completing the square recovers the centre (-g, -f) and radius sqrt(g^2 + f^2 - c)

Worked example. Find the centre and radius of x² + y² − 6x + 8y − 11 = 0.

complete the square in x: x^2 - 6x = (x - 3)^2 - 9
in y: y^2 + 8y = (y + 4)^2 - 16
so (x - 3)^2 + (y + 4)^2 - 9 - 16 - 11 = 0
(x - 3)^2 + (y + 4)^2 = 36
centre (3, -4), radius 6

Worked example 2 (finding the equation). Find the equation of the circle with diameter AB where A(1, 2) and B(7, 10).

centre = midpoint = (4, 6)
radius = half of AB = 0.5 sqrt(6^2 + 8^2) = 5
(x - 4)^2 + (y - 6)^2 = 25

The diameter shortcut is worth remembering: the angle in a semicircle is a right angle, so any point on the circle sees AB at 90°, which is another route into the same equation.

Tangents, normals and chords

A tangent touches the circle at exactly one point and is perpendicular to the radius there. That single fact generates almost every circle question in the paper.

to find the tangent at P on a circle:
1. gradient of the radius from the centre to P
2. tangent gradient = negative reciprocal
3. use point-gradient form with P

Worked example. Find the tangent to x² + y² = 25 at the point (3, 4).

centre is the origin, so radius gradient = 4/3
tangent gradient = -3/4
y - 4 = (-3/4)(x - 3)
4y - 16 = -3x + 9  ->  3x + 4y = 25

Worked example 2 (chord). A chord of the circle x² + y² = 25 lies on the line y = 3. Find its length.

substitute: x^2 + 9 = 25  ->  x^2 = 16  ->  x = +/-4
endpoints (-4, 3) and (4, 3)
length = 8

Worked example 3 (perpendicular from the centre bisects a chord). Use that fact to find the distance from the centre to a chord of length 8 in a circle of radius 5.

half the chord = 4
distance = sqrt(5^2 - 4^2) = 3

Intersections and the discriminant

Substituting a line into a circle gives a quadratic. How many times the line meets the circle is decided by the discriminant, so a tangency condition is a discriminant-equals-zero condition.

substitute y = mx + c into the circle equation
b^2 - 4ac > 0: two intersections (secant)
b^2 - 4ac = 0: one intersection (tangent)
b^2 - 4ac < 0: no intersection

Worked example. Show that the line y = x + 5 is a tangent to x² + y² = 12.5, and find the point of contact.

x^2 + (x + 5)^2 = 12.5
2x^2 + 10x + 25 - 12.5 = 0
2x^2 + 10x + 12.5 = 0   ->  divide by 2: x^2 + 5x + 6.25 = 0
discriminant = 25 - 25 = 0, so tangent
repeated root: x = -2.5, y = 2.5

Worked example 2 (finding an unknown gradient). Find the values of m for which y = mx is tangent to (x − 3)² + y² = 4.

substitute: (x - 3)^2 + m^2 x^2 = 4
(1 + m^2)x^2 - 6x + 5 = 0
for tangency: 36 - 4(1 + m^2)(5) = 0
36 = 20 + 20m^2  ->  m^2 = 0.8  ->  m = +/- 0.894

Parametric circles and arcs

A circle can also be described by a parameter, which is often the easier form when a point has to move. For a circle of radius r centred at the origin, the point (r cos θ, r sin θ) traces it as θ increases.

x = r cos theta, y = r sin theta  satisfies x^2 + y^2 = r^2
centre (a, b): x = a + r cos theta, y = b + r sin theta
this is why the modulus-argument form of a complex number is a point on a circle

Worked example. A point moves on x² + y² = 9 with x = 3 cos θ. Find y and the coordinates when θ = 60°.

y = 3 sin theta
at theta = 60: (3 cos 60, 3 sin 60) = (1.5, 2.598)

Worked example 2 (eliminating the parameter). Eliminate θ from x = 2 + 4 cos θ, y = −1 + 4 sin θ.

cos theta = (x - 2)/4;  sin theta = (y + 1)/4
square and add: ((x-2)/4)^2 + ((y+1)/4)^2 = 1
(x - 2)^2 + (y + 1)^2 = 16

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Distance) Find the distance between (3, −2) and (−1, 4). Answer: √(16 + 36) = √52 = 7.21.
  2. (Midpoint) The midpoint of AB is (5, 1) and A is (2, −3). Find B. Answer: B = (8, 5).
  3. (Line) Find the line through (0, 4) perpendicular to y = 2x + 1. Answer: y = −0.5x + 4.
  4. (Circle) State the centre and radius of (x + 2)² + (y − 5)² = 49. Answer: centre (−2, 5), radius 7.
  5. (Completed square) Find the radius of x² + y² + 4x − 6y = 12. Answer: (x+2)² + (y−3)² = 25, radius 5.
  6. (Tangent) Find the tangent to x² + y² = 20 at (2, 4). Answer: gradient of radius 2, tangent −0.5, so x + 2y = 10.
  7. (Chord) Line y = 2 cuts x² + y² = 13. Find the chord length. Answer: x = ±3, length 6.
  8. (Discriminant) Show y = 2x + 5 does not meet x² + y² = 4. Answer: 5x² + 20x + 21 = 0, discriminant 400 − 420 < 0.
  9. (Circle from diameter) Find the circle with diameter from (0, 0) to (6, 8). Answer: centre (3, 4), radius 5, (x−3)² + (y−4)² = 25.
  10. (Parametric) Eliminate θ from x = cos θ, y = 2 sin θ. Answer: x² + y²/4 = 1, an ellipse.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Perpendicular gradient half-applied: the negative reciprocal of 3 is −1/3, not −3; negating without inverting is the classic slip.
  • Radius squared: (x − a)² + (y − b)² = 49 has radius 7, not 49 — the right-hand side is r².
  • Sign of the centre: (x − 3)² means centre x = +3; students routinely write −3.
  • Completing the square with the constant: the −9 and −16 produced by completing the square must move to the other side, and forgetting them changes the radius.
  • One root from a squared distance: √(k−2)² = 4 gives two values; the geometry usually admits both.
  • Tangent versus normal: a tangent is perpendicular to the radius; the normal is along it. Read which is asked.
  • Intersections solved approximately: the discriminant route gives exact values and the marks; sketching loses the algebra marks.
  • General form left unsimplified: mark schemes quote ax + by + c = 0 with integer coefficients where possible, so clear the fractions.

title: Redox Equilibria Revision Notes A2 Chemistry
content:
Redox Equilibria A2 Level Chemistry

This revision note covers Edexcel International A Level Chemistry Topic 16, exploring redox equilibria, standard electrode potentials, electrochemical cells, thermodynamics of redox reactions, cell diagrams, advanced redox titrations, uncertainty analysis, and fuel cells.

Oxidation and Reduction in s-, p- and d-Block Elements

Redox processes involve electron transfer and shifts in oxidation numbers, applying seamlessly across s-, p-, and d-block elements.

  • Oxidation is defined as loss of electrons and an increase in oxidation state. Reduction is gain of electrons and a decrease in oxidation state.
  • The reducing agent is oxidised by losing electrons, whereas the oxidising agent is reduced by gaining electrons.
  • These rules apply whether dealing with simple s-block metal ions, p-block non-metals, or complex d-block transition metal ions showing multiple stable oxidation states.

Standard Electrode Potentials and the Standard Hydrogen Electrode

Standard electrode potentials provide a quantitative measure of a species' tendency to be reduced.

  • Standard electrode potentials, E-zero, are measured strictly at 298 K temperature, 100 kPa pressure of gases, and 1.00 mol dm-3 concentration of ions.
  • The standard hydrogen electrode serves as the universal reference electrode with an E-zero value defined as exactly 0.00 V.
  • A reference electrode is necessary because absolute electrode potentials cannot be measured in isolation; only potential differences can be determined.
  • The standard hydrogen electrode uses platinum foil coated in platinum black, immersed in 1.00 mol dm-3 hydrogen ions, with hydrogen gas bubbled at 100 kPa and 298 K.

Measuring Electrode Potentials and Electrochemical Cells

Different half-cell assemblies are required depending on the physical states of the species involved.

  • For metals or non-metals in contact with their aqueous ions, a metal rod is dipped into a 1.00 mol dm-3 solution of its ions, or an inert platinum electrode is used for non-metals like chlorine gas bubbling over chloride ions.
  • For systems involving ions of the same element with different oxidation numbers, an inert platinum electrode is immersed in a solution containing both species at 1.00 mol dm-3 concentration.
  • CORE PRACTICAL 12 involves investigating electrochemical cells by measuring cell potentials for various metal-metal ion combinations and redox systems.

Cell Diagrams and Standard Cell EMF Calculations

Electrochemical cells can be represented concisely using conventional notation and evaluated mathematically.

  • Cell diagrams use a single vertical line to represent a phase boundary and a double vertical line to represent a salt bridge.
  • Oxidised forms are written closer to the salt bridge in conventional half-cell representations, with the more negative half-cell conventionally written on the left.
  • Calculate standard cell emf, E-zero-cell, using the formula: E-zero-cell = E-zero(reduction) - E-zero(oxidation).

Thermodynamic Feasibility, Entropy, and Equilibrium Constants

Standard electrode potentials connect directly to thermodynamic feasibility, entropy changes, and equilibrium constants.

  • Standard electrode potentials are also known as standard reduction potentials and are listed in an electrochemical series.
  • A positive E-zero-cell value indicates that the forward reaction is thermodynamically feasible under standard conditions.
  • E-zero-cell is directly proportional to the total entropy change, delta-S-total, and to ln K for a reaction, meaning larger positive E-zero values correspond to larger equilibrium constants and greater spontaneity.
  • Standard electrode potentials can predict the thermodynamic feasibility of disproportionation reactions, where a species is simultaneously oxidised and reduced.

Limitations of Standard Electrode Potentials

Thermodynamic predictions do not always match real-world outcomes due to kinetic and condition factors.

  • Predictions made using standard electrode potentials have limitations due to the kinetic stability of systems; a reaction may be thermodynamically feasible with a positive E-zero-cell, but have an activation energy so high that the reaction rate is negligibly slow.
  • Departures from standard conditions, such as non-standard concentrations or temperatures, alter actual electrode potentials according to the Nernst equation, potentially reversing feasibility.

Redox Titrations and Uncertainty Analysis

Volumetric analysis using redox titrations allows accurate determination of concentrations in structured and unstructured problems.

  • CORE PRACTICALS 13a and 13b involve carrying out redox titrations with iron(II) ions and potassium manganate(VII), and with sodium thiosulfate and iodine.
  • Manganate(VII) titrations are self-indicating, turning from purple to colourless at the end point when excess MnO4- ions react to form colourless Mn2+ ions.
  • Iodine-thiosulfate titrations use starch indicator, which forms a deep blue-black complex with iodine and turns colourless at the end point when all iodine is consumed.
  • Discussing the uncertainty of measurements requires evaluating percentage errors of apparatus like burettes and volumetric flasks, and their implications for the validity of final results.

Fuel Cells

Fuel cells convert chemical energy directly into electrical energy through redox reactions.

  • Fuel cells use the energy released on the reaction of a fuel with oxygen to generate a voltage, utilising hydrogen-rich fuels like hydrogen and methanol.
  • In an acidic electrolyte hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell, hydrogen is oxidised at the anode: H2 yields 2H+ + 2e-, and oxygen is reduced at the cathode: O2 + 4H+ + 4e- yields 2H2O.
  • In an alkaline electrolyte hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell, hydrogen reacts at the anode: H2 + 2OH- yields 2H2H2O + 2e-, and oxygen reacts at the cathode: O2 + 2H2O + 4e- yields 4OH-.

Typical Mistakes

  • Mistake: Confusing the left and right sides of a cell diagram. Correction: Remember reduction always occurs at the right-hand electrode and oxidation at the left-hand electrode in conventional notation.
  • Mistake: Omitting the inert platinum electrode in half-cell descriptions containing only aqueous ions. Correction: Always include platinum in phase boundaries if no other solid conductor is present.
  • Mistake: Forgetting that E-zero-cell values are independent of the stoichiometry multipliers used to balance half-equations. Correction: Never multiply E-zero values by balancing coefficients when calculating E-zero-cell.
  • Mistake: Assuming a reaction with a positive E-zero-cell will occur rapidly at room temperature. Correction: Always consider kinetic stability; a positive E-zero only proves thermodynamic feasibility, not reaction rate.

Exam-Style Questions

  1. Question: State the standard conditions required for measuring standard electrode potentials. Answer: 298 K temperature, 100 kPa pressure of gases, and 1.00 mol dm-3 concentration of ions.
  2. Question: Write the conventional cell diagram for a cell formed by Zn(s) / Zn2+(aq) and Cu2+(aq) / Cu(s). Answer: Zn(s) | Zn2+(aq, 1.00 mol dm-3) || Cu2+(aq, 1.00 mol dm-3) | Cu(s).
  3. Question: Calculate the E-zero-cell for zinc and copper given E-zero(Zn2+/Zn) = −0.76 V and E-zero(Cu2+/Cu) = +0.34 V. Answer: E-zero-cell = +0.34 − (−0.76) = +1.10 V.
  4. Question: State the colour change at the end point in a titration of potassium manganate(VII) with iron(II) ions. Answer: From colourless or very pale pink to permanent pale pink.
  5. Question: Write the anode half-equation for an alkaline hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell. Answer: H2 + 2OH- yields 2H2O + 2e-.

Use these notes alongside active practice of past paper calculation questions, ensuring all standard conditions and half-equation balancing steps are memorised. Revise transition metal chemistry next.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Cell EMF, applied to a zinc and copper cell: E(cell) = E(cathode, reduction) − E(anode, oxidation) = +0.34 − (−0.76) = +1.10 V. Zinc is the anode because it has the more negative potential, and it is oxidised. Always identify the anode and cathode before you subtract.
  • Feasibility: ΔG = −nFE, so a positive E(cell) gives a negative ΔG and a feasible reaction. Under non-standard conditions, E changes with concentration, so a reaction can be feasible even when E(cell) under standard conditions is small.
  • Redox titration, applied to Fe²⁺ with acidified MnO₄⁻: 5Fe²⁺ + MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ → 5Fe³⁺ + Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O. The ratio is 5 : 1. The permanganate is its own indicator, so the end point is the first permanent pale pink colour.
  • Limitations of E° values: they apply only under standard conditions and say nothing about the rate. A reaction can be thermodynamically feasible but kinetically slow, so a metal can appear reactive from its potential yet react slowly in practice.

title: IGCSE Mathematics: Arithmetic and Place Value
content:
IGCSE Mathematics: Arithmetic and Place Value

Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580 (2025–2027), section 1 Number: statement 1.1 Types of number, 1.5 Ordering, 1.6 The four operations, 1.9 Estimation, 1.10 Limits of accuracy, 1.14 Using a calculator, 1.15 Time and 1.16 Money. This is the foundation of both papers — Paper 2 (non-calculator) rewards exact written methods, and Paper 4 (calculator) rewards knowing what to type and how to check the answer. Everything here is arithmetic you will use in every other topic, so the methods are written out in full.

Types of number

The number family has its own vocabulary, and the exam expects it precisely.

NameWhat it meansExamples
Natural numbersThe counting numbers1, 2, 3, 4, ...
IntegersWhole numbers, including zero and the negatives... −2, −1, 0, 1, 2 ...
Prime numbersNumbers with exactly two factors: 1 and themselves2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13 ... (2 is the only even prime; 1 is not prime because it has one factor)
Square and cube numbersAn integer times itself, once or twiceSquares 1, 4, 9, 16, 25 ...; cubes 1, 8, 27, 64 ...
Rational numbersAny number that can be written as a fraction p/q with q not zero; equivalently a terminating or recurring decimal3/4, −5, 0.25, 0.333...
Irrational numbersNumbers that cannot be written as a fraction; their decimals never repeat or terminate√2, √3, π

Factors, multiples, HCF and LCM. A factor divides a whole number exactly; a multiple is a number in that number's times table. The highest common factor and lowest common multiple are found from prime factor trees — write each number as a product of primes first:

Find the HCF and LCM of 60 and 84.

60 = 2 × 30 = 2 × 2 × 15 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 5 = 2² × 3 × 5
84 = 2 × 42 = 2 × 2 × 21 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 7 = 2² × 3 × 7

HCF: take each COMMON prime at its LOWEST power:  2² × 3 = 12
LCM: take EVERY prime at its HIGHEST power:       2² × 3 × 5 × 7 = 420

Check: 60 × 84 = HCF x LCM = 12 × 420 = 5040 ✓

Place value and ordering

Each digit is worth ten times the digit to its right. In 47 382 the 7 means 7000, the 3 means 300. In a decimal such as 4.703 the digits to the right of the point are tenths (7/10), hundredths (0/100) and thousandths (3/1000). To order numbers, compare digit by digit from the left, padding with zeros so every number has the same number of decimal places:

Order 0.7, 0.67, 0.706, 0.669 from smallest:

Pad to three decimal places:  0.700, 0.670, 0.706, 0.669
Compare: 0.669 < 0.670 < 0.700 < 0.706
So the order is 0.669, 0.67, 0.7, 0.706.

The symbols are = (equal), ≠ (not equal), > (greater than), < (less than), ⩾ (greater than or equal to) and ⩽ (less than or equal to). On a number line a value increases to the right, so −5 < −2 even though 5 is bigger than 2.

The four operations with integers

Addition and subtraction of negatives follow one rule worth stating clearly: adding a negative is subtracting, and subtracting a negative is adding. So 3 − (−5) = 3 + 5 = 8 and 3 + (−5) = 3 − 5 = −2.

Multiplication and division signs follow from patterns: 3 × (−4) = −12 because three lots of −4 is −12, and (−3) × (−4) = +12 because reversing both directions restores the original. As a rule: same signs give a positive answer; different signs give a negative answer. So (−3) × (−4) = 12, (−24) ÷ 6 = −4 and (−24) ÷ (−6) = 4.

Written methods keep place value aligned: long multiplication multiplies by each digit in turn and adds the partial products; long division subtracts whole multiples at a time. Every calculation can be checked by the inverse operation (subtraction checks addition, division checks multiplication) or by estimation.

The four operations with fractions and decimals

A fraction is a division: 3/4 means 3 divided by 4. Adding and subtracting needs a common denominator; multiplying multiplies tops and bottoms; dividing multiplies by the reciprocal.

Work out  2/3 + 5/8:

The lowest common denominator of 3 and 8 is 24:
2/3 = 8/24        [multiply top and bottom by 8]
5/8 = 15/24       [multiply top and bottom by 3]
8/24 + 15/24 = 23/24
Work out  3/4 × 2/5:

Multiply the numerators and the denominators:
= (3 × 2)/(4 × 5) = 6/20 = 3/10        [cancelled by dividing top and bottom by 2]
Work out  3/4 ÷ 2/5:

Dividing asks how many 2/5 fit into 3/4. Dividing by a fraction is the same as
multiplying by its reciprocal (flip and multiply):
= 3/4 × 5/2 = (3 × 5)/(4 × 2) = 15/8 = 1 7/8

Why flip and multiply works. Dividing by 2 is the same as multiplying by 1/2, so dividing by 2/5 should be multiplying by the number whose relationship to 2/5 mirrors 1/2's relationship to 2 — that is 5/2. Checking with decimals confirms it: 3/4 ÷ 2/5 = 0.75 ÷ 0.4 = 1.875, and 15/8 = 1.875 ✓. The rule is not a trick; it is what division by a fraction means.

Decimals add and subtract with the decimal points aligned; multiply ignoring the points then replace so the total number of decimal places matches; divide by multiplying both numbers by a power of ten first.

Order of operations and brackets

Without a fixed order, an expression like 3 + 4 × 2² would have several answers. The order is: Brackets, Indices, Division and Multiplication (left to right), Addition and Subtraction (left to right).

3 + 4 × 2² = 3 + 4 × 4 = 3 + 16 = 19        [indices first, then multiplication, then addition]
(3 + 4) × 2² = 7 × 4 = 28                   [brackets first: a completely different answer]

Brackets also collect negatives: 2 + 3 × (−4) = 2 − 12 = −10, never (2 + 3) × (−4) = −20. When translating words into algebra, put brackets around each grouped idea before simplifying.

Estimation and rounding

Rounding rules: to a number of decimal places or significant figures, look at the digit after the one you are keeping; 5 or more rounds up, 4 or less stays. Significant figures start at the first non-zero digit. So 0.04752 is 0.048 (2 s.f.), 0.05 (1 s.f.) and 0.0475 (3 s.f.).

Estimation rounds every input to one significant figure before calculating, giving a rough answer that reveals blunders:

Estimate  39.2 × 5.98:

39.2 rounds to 40;  5.98 rounds to 6
40 × 6 = 240

The exact answer 234.416 is close to 240, so it is plausible.

Limits of accuracy (bounds)

A rounded measurement is not exact: a length given as 45 cm to the nearest centimetre is somewhere between 44.5 and 45.5 cm. Those are its bounds — the maximum and minimum the true value could take:

upper bound = measured value + half the unit of accuracy
lower bound = measured value - half the unit of accuracy

Extended questions ask for the bounds of a calculated answer. The rule: to make a quotient as large as possible, divide the largest possible numerator by the smallest possible denominator.

A distance of 45 cm (to the nearest cm) is covered in 6 s (to the nearest s).
Find the bounds of the speed = distance / time.

distance: 44.5 cm to 45.5 cm;  time: 5.5 s to 6.5 s
upper bound of speed = 45.5 / 5.5 = 8.27 cm s⁻¹ (3 s.f.)
lower bound of speed = 44.5 / 6.5 = 6.85 cm s⁻¹ (3 s.f.)

So the speed lies between 6.85 and 8.27 cm s⁻¹. The trap is using 44.5 ÷ 5.5 for the lower bound — dividing two small numbers does not give the smallest quotient; the denominator must be as large as possible.

Time and money

Time works in mixed bases: 60 seconds in a minute, 60 minutes in an hour, 24 hours in a day, 7 days in a week. Timetables use the 24-hour clock to avoid ambiguity (14:35 not 2:35 pm), and durations cross hour boundaries by splitting the subtraction: from 09:45 to 12:20 is 2 hours 35 minutes (09:45 → 12:45 would be 3 hours; subtract 25 minutes). Money calculations use the same arithmetic in decimal form, with unit pricing deciding best buys: divide each price by its quantity and compare. Currency conversion multiplies by the given rate, and the inverse rate checks the answer.

Using a calculator

A scientific calculator follows the order of operations automatically, so use the fraction, bracket and power keys to enter an expression in one go rather than line by line. Know the ×10ˣ key (for standard form), the square and square-root keys, the fraction key and the reciprocal key. Interpret the display: a long decimal may need rounding to 3 s.f., and an answer like 1.23456789e-5 is standard form for 1.23 × 10⁻⁵. Always check a calculator answer against an estimate — that habit catches mistyped entries, which are the most common calculator mark lost.

Worked example: a multi-step calculation

A jacket is reduced by 15% from £84 and then a further 10% is taken off at the till. Find the final price.

First reduction: 15% of 84 = 0.15 × 84 = 12.60
Price after first reduction: 84 - 12.60 = 71.40
Second reduction: 10% of 71.40 = 7.14
Final price: 71.40 - 7.14 = 64.26

Estimate check: 84 down by about 15% is about 71; down 10% is about 64 ✓

Doing it in one step with multipliers gives the same answer: 84 × 0.85 × 0.90 = 64.26 — a method worth knowing for Paper 4, and a check worth doing on Paper 2.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Writing (−3) × (−4) = −12. Two negatives multiply to a positive; check the sign before writing the digits.
  • Evaluating 3 + 4 × 2² as 28 without brackets. Indices and multiplication come before addition.
  • Aligning decimal points wrongly when adding decimals, or keeping the wrong number of decimal places when multiplying.
  • Adding fractions across different denominators: 1/2 + 1/3 is not 2/5. Find a common denominator first.
  • Reversing the bounds rule for division: the minimum quotient divides the smallest numerator by the largest denominator.
  • Rounding too early in a multi-step question and compounding the error; keep all digits until the final line.
  • Confusing factors with multiples: 3 is a factor of 12, 12 is a multiple of 3.
  • Giving 24-hour times as 14.35 rather than 14:35, or treating durations as ordinary decimal hours (2 h 30 min is 2.5 h, but 2 h 45 min is 2.75 h).

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 2, 3 marks). Work out 3 + 4 × 2².

Answer: Indices first: 2² = 4. Then multiplication: 4 × 4 = 16. Then addition: 3 + 16 = 19.

Question 2 (Paper 2, 4 marks). Find the highest common factor and lowest common multiple of 48 and 72.

Answer: 48 = 2⁴ × 3; 72 = 2³ × 3². HCF = 2³ × 3 = 24. LCM = 2⁴ × 3² = 144. Check: 48 × 72 = 3456 = 24 × 144 ✓.

Question 3 (Paper 2, 3 marks). Work out 3/4 − 2/5.

Answer: Common denominator 20: 15/20 − 8/20 = 7/20.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 4 marks). A number is rounded to 2 decimal places as 7.35. Write down the bounds of the number and state which of them could be the exact value of 7.350.

Answer: Bounds are 7.345 ⩽ x < 7.355. Any value in that range rounds to 7.35; 7.350 itself lies inside, so it is possible.

Question 5 (Paper 4, 3 marks). Estimate the value of (29.4 × 5.03)/1.98 and explain your method.

Answer: Round each to 1 s.f.: 30 × 5/2 = 75. The exact value (74.2 to 3 s.f.) is close, so the working is plausible.

Question 6 (Paper 4, 4 marks). A train leaves at 09:50 and arrives at 12:25. Calculate the journey time and the average speed if the journey is 162 km.

Answer: 09:50 to 12:50 would be 3 h; 12:25 is 25 minutes earlier, so the journey is 2 h 35 min (2.583 h). Average speed = 162/2.583 = 62.7 km h⁻¹.

With the number system in hand, the next step is the language of parts of a whole: fractions, decimals and percentages.

title: Poisson Distribution
content:
The Poisson Distribution

The Model

X ~ Po(λ) counts events in a fixed interval of time or space when events occur independently, at a constant average rate λ, and never twice at the same instant. Classic settings: calls per hour at a helpdesk, typos per page, cars per minute at a quiet junction.

The Formula

P(X = r) = e^(−λ) λʳ / r! for r = 0, 1, 2, ...

Example: X ~ Po(2). P(X = 0) = e⁻² ≈ 0.1353. P(X = 1) = 2e⁻² ≈ 0.2707.

Mean and Variance

The defining signature of the Poisson:

  • E(X) = λ and Var(X) = λ — the mean and variance are equal.

If a question gives a mean m, then λ = m; the variance is also m.

Scaling the Interval

If X ~ Po(λ) per hour, then 3 hours gives Y ~ Po(3λ). Rates must be adjusted to the same interval before computing anything. Halving an interval halves λ.

Adding Poissons

If X ~ Po(λ₁) and Y ~ Po(λ₂) are independent, then X + Y ~ Po(λ₁ + λ₂). Two independent queues merging into one server produce a Poisson with summed rate.

Exam tips: check independence and constant rate before modelling — if events cluster (rush hours), Poisson fails. Convert the interval first: a rate of 8 per 20 minutes becomes 24 per hour. In "at least" questions use the complement exactly as with the binomial.
