Standard electrode potentials connect directly to thermodynamic feasibility, entropy changes, and equilibrium constants.

  • Standard electrode potentials are also known as standard reduction potentials and are listed in an electrochemical series.
  • A positive E-zero-cell value indicates that the forward reaction is thermodynamically feasible under standard conditions.
  • E-zero-cell is directly proportional to the total entropy change, delta-S-total, and to ln K for a reaction, meaning larger positive E-zero values correspond to larger equilibrium constants and greater spontaneity.
  • Standard electrode potentials can predict the thermodynamic feasibility of disproportionation reactions, where a species is simultaneously oxidised and reduced.

Limitations of Standard Electrode Potentials

Thermodynamic predictions do not always match real-world outcomes due to kinetic and condition factors.

  • Predictions made using standard electrode potentials have limitations due to the kinetic stability of systems; a reaction may be thermodynamically feasible with a positive E-zero-cell, but have an activation energy so high that the reaction rate is negligibly slow.
  • Departures from standard conditions, such as non-standard concentrations or temperatures, alter actual electrode potentials according to the Nernst equation, potentially reversing feasibility.

Redox Titrations and Uncertainty Analysis

Volumetric analysis using redox titrations allows accurate determination of concentrations in structured and unstructured problems.

  • CORE PRACTICALS 13a and 13b involve carrying out redox titrations with iron(II) ions and potassium manganate(VII), and with sodium thiosulfate and iodine.
  • Manganate(VII) titrations are self-indicating, turning from purple to colourless at the end point when excess MnO4- ions react to form colourless Mn2+ ions.
  • Iodine-thiosulfate titrations use starch indicator, which forms a deep blue-black complex with iodine and turns colourless at the end point when all iodine is consumed.
  • Discussing the uncertainty of measurements requires evaluating percentage errors of apparatus like burettes and volumetric flasks, and their implications for the validity of final results.

Fuel Cells

Fuel cells convert chemical energy directly into electrical energy through redox reactions.

  • Fuel cells use the energy released on the reaction of a fuel with oxygen to generate a voltage, utilising hydrogen-rich fuels like hydrogen and methanol.
  • In an acidic electrolyte hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell, hydrogen is oxidised at the anode: H2 yields 2H+ + 2e-, and oxygen is reduced at the cathode: O2 + 4H+ + 4e- yields 2H2O.
  • In an alkaline electrolyte hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell, hydrogen reacts at the anode: H2 + 2OH- yields 2H2H2O + 2e-, and oxygen reacts at the cathode: O2 + 2H2O + 4e- yields 4OH-.

Typical Mistakes

  • Mistake: Confusing the left and right sides of a cell diagram. Correction: Remember reduction always occurs at the right-hand electrode and oxidation at the left-hand electrode in conventional notation.
  • Mistake: Omitting the inert platinum electrode in half-cell descriptions containing only aqueous ions. Correction: Always include platinum in phase boundaries if no other solid conductor is present.
  • Mistake: Forgetting that E-zero-cell values are independent of the stoichiometry multipliers used to balance half-equations. Correction: Never multiply E-zero values by balancing coefficients when calculating E-zero-cell.
  • Mistake: Assuming a reaction with a positive E-zero-cell will occur rapidly at room temperature. Correction: Always consider kinetic stability; a positive E-zero only proves thermodynamic feasibility, not reaction rate.

Exam-Style Questions

  1. Question: State the standard conditions required for measuring standard electrode potentials. Answer: 298 K temperature, 100 kPa pressure of gases, and 1.00 mol dm-3 concentration of ions.
  2. Question: Write the conventional cell diagram for a cell formed by Zn(s) / Zn2+(aq) and Cu2+(aq) / Cu(s). Answer: Zn(s) | Zn2+(aq, 1.00 mol dm-3) || Cu2+(aq, 1.00 mol dm-3) | Cu(s).
  3. Question: Calculate the E-zero-cell for zinc and copper given E-zero(Zn2+/Zn) = −0.76 V and E-zero(Cu2+/Cu) = +0.34 V. Answer: E-zero-cell = +0.34 − (−0.76) = +1.10 V.
  4. Question: State the colour change at the end point in a titration of potassium manganate(VII) with iron(II) ions. Answer: From colourless or very pale pink to permanent pale pink.
  5. Question: Write the anode half-equation for an alkaline hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell. Answer: H2 + 2OH- yields 2H2O + 2e-.

Use these notes alongside active practice of past paper calculation questions, ensuring all standard conditions and half-equation balancing steps are memorised. Revise transition metal chemistry next.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Cell EMF, applied to a zinc and copper cell: E(cell) = E(cathode, reduction) − E(anode, oxidation) = +0.34 − (−0.76) = +1.10 V. Zinc is the anode because it has the more negative potential, and it is oxidised. Always identify the anode and cathode before you subtract.
  • Feasibility: ΔG = −nFE, so a positive E(cell) gives a negative ΔG and a feasible reaction. Under non-standard conditions, E changes with concentration, so a reaction can be feasible even when E(cell) under standard conditions is small.
  • Redox titration, applied to Fe²⁺ with acidified MnO₄⁻: 5Fe²⁺ + MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ → 5Fe³⁺ + Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O. The ratio is 5 : 1. The permanganate is its own indicator, so the end point is the first permanent pale pink colour.
  • Limitations of E° values: they apply only under standard conditions and say nothing about the rate. A reaction can be thermodynamically feasible but kinetically slow, so a metal can appear reactive from its potential yet react slowly in practice.

title: Waves & Sound
content:
Waves & Sound

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2023–2025): general wave properties; reflection/refraction/diffraction; sound.

1. Wave basics

v = fλ. Transverse (oscillation ⊥ travel — light, water, S-waves) vs longitudinal (parallel — sound, P-waves). Amplitude, wavelength, frequency f = 1/T; wavefront diagrams.

2. Ripple tank behaviours

  • Reflection: angle in = angle out; speed/frequency unchanged, direction changes.
  • Refraction: speed change at boundary bends wavefronts (shallow water slows ripples).
  • Diffraction: spreading through gaps ≈ λ wide; around edges.

3. Electromagnetic spectrum (order)

Radio → micro → IR → visible (red 700 nm – violet 400 nm) → UV → X → gamma. All travel at 3 × 10⁸ m/s in vacuum; transverse; uses and dangers (IR heating; UV skin; X/gamma ionising).

4. Sound

  • Longitudinal; needs a medium (bell in vacuum demo). Speed ~340 m/s air, faster in liquids/solids.
  • Range 20 Hz–20 kHz; ultrasound > 20 kHz (sonar, prenatal scans, cleaning).
  • Pitch ↔ frequency; loudness ↔ amplitude.

5. Echo problems

Distance = (v × t)/2 (there and back).

Example: echo after 0.6 s, v = 340 → cliff 102 m away.

Exam tips: in diagrams always label wavelength as crest-to-crest; for refraction, state "changes speed" first, then direction; quote EM uses with the hazard.

title: Redox Chemistry and Groups 1, 2 and 7
content:
Redox Chemistry and Groups 1, 2 and 7

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH12, Topic 8. Redox reactions involve electron transfer. The same ideas explain the reactions of metals with water and acids, and the displacement reactions of the halogens.

Oxidation states

  • Oxidation state is the charge an atom would have if all bonds were ionic. Elements are 0, simple ions equal their charge, and the sum of oxidation states equals the overall charge.
  • Oxidation is an increase in oxidation state (loss of electrons); reduction is a decrease (gain of electrons).
  • The oxidising agent is reduced; the reducing agent is oxidised.

Redox equations

  • Half-equations balance atoms, then charge, with electrons added to show the transfer. Combine them so that electrons cancel.
  • Example: MnO4⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H2O, and acidified manganate(VII) decolourises when it is reduced.

Group 1 and Group 2

  • Reactivity increases down Group 1 because the outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded, so it is lost more easily.
  • Group 2 metals form M²⁺ ions. Reactivity with water increases down the group: magnesium reacts slowly with cold water, while calcium reacts steadily.
  • The solubility of Group 2 hydroxides and sulfates changes down the group: magnesium sulfate is soluble, barium sulfate is not.

Group 7

  • Halogens are non-metals that form X2 molecules. Oxidising power decreases down the group: chlorine displaces bromide and iodide ions, bromine displaces iodide ions.
  • Halide ions are reducing agents, and reducing power increases down the group. Concentrated sulfuric acid is reduced by HI to hydrogen sulfide, because iodide ions are strong reducing agents.

Tests for halide ions

  • Silver nitrate solution forms precipitates: chloride gives white, bromide cream, iodide yellow. Dilute ammonia distinguishes the first two.

Exam tip: when balancing a redox equation in acid, add H⁺ and H2O before counting electrons, and always check that charge and atoms balance on both sides.

title: Thermal Physics — Study Notes
content:
Thermal Physics

Edexcel International A Level Physics — Unit 5 (WPH15), sat at A2.

Temperature and scales

Thermodynamic temperature is measured in kelvin. The kelvin and Celsius scales have the same size of degree, with T/K = θ/°C + 273. Absolute zero (0 K) is the lowest possible temperature, at which the particles of an ideal gas have minimum kinetic energy.

Example: 25 °C = 298 K.

Specific heat capacity and latent heat

Specific heat capacity c is the energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 K: Q = mcΔθ. Latent heat is the energy needed to change the state of 1 kg without a change in temperature: Q = mL. Melting and boiling absorb energy without a temperature rise, because the energy goes into breaking intermolecular bonds, not into kinetic energy.

Example: warming 2.0 kg of water (c = 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) by 10 K needs 84 kJ. Melting 0.20 kg of ice (L = 334 kJ kg⁻¹) needs 67 kJ.

The mole and Avogadro constant

One mole contains N_A = 6.02 × 10²³ particles. The number of particles is N = nN_A, where n is the amount in moles. Molar mass is the mass of one mole, in kg mol⁻¹ in SI units.

Equation of state for an ideal gas

pV = nRT, where R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ and T must be absolute. Equivalently pV = NkT, with k = R/N_A = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹.

Example: 0.10 mol at 300 K in 2.0 × 10⁻³ m³ has p = nRT/V ≈ 1.2 × 10⁵ Pa.

Kinetic theory

The pressure of an ideal gas comes from molecules colliding with the container walls. The mean kinetic energy of a molecule is ⟨Ek⟩ = 3kT/2, so it depends only on the absolute temperature. At 300 K it is about 6.2 × 10⁻²¹ J.

Internal energy and the first law

The internal energy of an ideal gas is the sum of the kinetic and potential energies of its molecules. For an ideal gas there are no intermolecular forces, so internal energy depends only on temperature. The first law of thermodynamics is ΔU = Q + W, where Q is heat added to the system and W is work done on the system. Heat lost by a system is therefore negative.

Example: a gas has 500 J of work done on it and loses 200 J of heat. ΔU = −200 + 500 = +300 J.

Exam tips: convert to kelvin before using pV = nRT or the kinetic-energy formula. Check the sign convention for W in the question. Use latent heat only when the temperature is constant.

Worked example: pressure of a fixed amount of gas

A sample of 0.50 mol of ideal gas is at 300 K in a container of volume 2.0 × 10⁻³ m³. Using pV = nRT with R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, the pressure is p = (0.50 × 8.31 × 300) ÷ (2.0 × 10⁻³) ≈ 6.2 × 10⁵ Pa. If the same gas is heated to 600 K in a rigid container, the pressure doubles, because for a fixed amount of gas at constant volume p is proportional to T in kelvin. Converting temperatures to kelvin before multiplying is the step examiners check first.

Exam method: units and conversions

Convert cm³ to m³ by dividing by 1 000 000, and convert °C to K by adding 273 (or 273.15). Mass in grams must be turned into kilograms for kinetic energy calculations, and into moles using the molar mass. A quick unit check helps: pressure in pascals multiplied by volume in cubic metres gives joules, the unit of energy.

title: Complex Numbers — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Complex Numbers

Mathematics — A2 (9709). i² = −1. A complex number z = a + bi has real part a and imaginary part b. Two numbers are equal iff both parts match.

Key areas to revise

  • Basics
  • Conjugates
  • Argand Diagram
  • Modulus–Argument Form
  • de Moivre and Roots

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

### Worked example Use i² = −1. The sum (2 + 3i) + (1 − 4i) = 3 − i. The product (2 + 3i)(1 − i) = 2 − 2i + 3i − 3i² = 2 + i + 3 = 5 + i. The modulus of 3 + 4i is √(9 + 16) = 5. The conjugate of 2 + 3i is 2 − 3i, and z multiplied by its conjugate gives |z|² = 13. ### Check yourself Find (1 + 2i)(3 − i). The answer is 5 + 5i. Check by expanding: 3 − i + 6i − 2i² = 3 + 5i + 2 = 5 + 5i.

title: IGCSE Mathematics: Inequalities
content:
IGCSE Mathematics: Inequalities

Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580 (2025–2027), section 2 Algebra and graphs, statement 2.6 Inequalities — solving and interpreting linear inequalities, listing integer solutions, and (Extended) regions in the coordinate plane. An inequality describes a range of values rather than one exact value, and solving one follows the same balance principle as solving an equation, with one critical difference: multiplying or dividing by a negative number reverses the inequality sign. This note shows why that happens, writes out every solution line by line, and finishes with the region-shading questions that distinguish Paper 4.

What an inequality says

The four inequality symbols extend the equals sign: < (strictly less than), > (strictly greater than), ⩽ (less than or equal to), ⩾ (greater than or equal to). A solution is a set of values, drawn on a number line with a hollow circle for strict inequalities (the endpoint is excluded) and a solid circle for inclusive ones (the endpoint is included).

StatementMeaningNumber line
x > 3Every value greater than 3, not including 3Hollow circle at 3, arrow to the right
x ⩽ −1Every value up to and including −1Solid circle at −1, arrow to the left
2 ⩽ x < 5Values from 2 up to, but not including, 5Solid circle at 2, hollow at 5, line between

Why the sign flips when multiplying by a negative. Start with the true statement 3 < 5. Multiply both sides by −2 without thinking: −6 < −10 is false, because −10 is further left than −6. The correct statement is −6 > −10. Multiplying by a negative mirrors the number line, which reverses order — so the inequality symbol must reverse too. That single rule causes more lost marks than any other in this topic.

Solving linear inequalities

Use the equation methods unchanged, and remember the one reversal rule:

Solve:  5x - 7 > 3x + 1        (give the solution as an inequality)

5x - 3x > 1 + 7               [add 7 to both sides, subtract 3x from both sides]
2x > 8
x > 4                         [divide by +2: the sign does not reverse]
Solve:  3 - 2x ⩽ 11

-2x ⩽ 11 - 3                  [subtract 3 from both sides]
-2x ⩽ 8
x ⩾ -4                        [divide by -2: the sign REVERSES from ⩽ to ⩾]

The check is direct: x = −4 gives 3 − 2(−4) = 11 ⩽ 11 ✓, and x = 0 gives 3 ⩽ 11 ✓ while x = −5 gives 13 ⩽ 11 ✗ — so the boundary and direction are right.

Solve and list the integer solutions:  2 < (5x - 1)/3 ⩽ 8

Multiply every part by 3:
6 < 5x - 1 ⩽ 24
7 < 5x ⩽ 25                   [add 1 to every part]
7/5 < x ⩽ 5                   [divide every part by +5]

The integers are 2, 3, 4 and 5.

Compound inequalities (a value trapped between two bounds) are solved in one line per operation across all three parts — exactly like a three-pan balance.

Inequalities from word problems

Many questions ask for the greatest or least integer satisfying a condition. Translate carefully: at least means ⩾, at most means ⩽, more than means >, within or no more than means ⩽.

A cinema ticket costs £8. A group has £100 and must keep at least £12 for travel.
How many tickets can they buy?

Let n be the number of tickets:  8n + 12 ⩽ 100
8n ⩽ 88
n ⩽ 11

They can buy at most 11 tickets.

The final answer is a whole number in context: a group cannot buy a fraction of a ticket, so the solution set is the integers up to 11.

Regions in the coordinate plane (Extended)

The line y = mx + c divides the plane into two half-planes: points above it satisfy y > mx + c and points below it satisfy y < mx + c. A region question asks you to shade the set of points satisfying several inequalities at once.

  • Draw the boundary line y = mx + c as a solid line when the inequality includes equality (⩽ or ⩾), and as a dashed line when it is strict (< or >).
  • Test one point not on the line — the origin (0, 0) is easiest when the line misses it. Substitute into the inequality; if it is true, shade the side containing the test point.
  • Shade the side that satisfies every inequality; the answer region is the overlap, and the question often asks for the coordinates of a point inside it.
Shade the region satisfying:  y ⩽ 2x + 1,  y > -x + 2,  x ⩾ 0

Line 1: y = 2x + 1, solid. Test (0, 0): 0 ⩽ 1 true, so shade below-left of this line.
Line 2: y = -x + 2, dashed. Test (0, 0): 0 > 2 false, so shade the side away from the origin.
Line 3: x = 0 (the y-axis), solid, shade to the right.

The solution region is the triangle-like area satisfying all three, e.g. the point (2, 2):
2 ⩽ 5 ✓, 2 > 0 ✓, 2 ⩾ 0 ✓.

Describing a region in words is the reverse skill: read the boundary lines, note whether each is dashed or solid, and translate the shaded side back into an inequality.

Maximum and minimum values over a region (Extended)

Region questions often finish by asking for the largest or smallest value of an expression such as x + 2y for points inside the shaded region. A linear expression grows steadily in one direction across the plane, so over a region bounded by straight lines its extreme values always sit at the corners. The method is therefore exact: find the coordinates of every vertex of the region, substitute each pair into the expression, and pick the largest or smallest result. Do not stop at the corner that looks likely — an untested corner is the usual place a mark is lost.

Worked example: inequality with a parameter

Find the set of values of k for which the equation x² + kx + 9 = 0 has two distinct real roots.

Two distinct real roots require a positive discriminant:  b² - 4ac > 0
Here a = 1, b = k, c = 9:
k² - 36 > 0
k² > 36
k > 6  or  k < -6

This is an inequality inside a quadratic-context question — exactly the blend of topics Paper 4 rewards. If the requirement had been at least one real root, the inequality would be k² ⩾ 36, giving k ⩾ 6 or k ⩽ −6.

Corner points in practice. Take the region x ⩾ 0, y ⩾ 0, x + y ⩽ 6 and y ⩽ x + 2. Its vertices are where the boundary lines meet:

x = 0 with y = 0            gives (0, 0)
y = 0 with x + y = 6        gives (6, 0)
x = 0 with y = x + 2        gives (0, 2)
x + y = 6 with y = x + 2    gives x + (x + 2) = 6, so 2x = 4, x = 2 and y = 4, the corner (2, 4)

Evaluate P = x + 2y at each corner:
(0, 0): P = 0     (6, 0): P = 6     (0, 2): P = 4     (2, 4): P = 10

Maximum P = 10 at (2, 4);  minimum P = 0 at (0, 0).

The minimum sits at the origin only because this region includes it; a region bounded away from the origin puts its minimum at one of the other corners. Substitute every vertex before choosing.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Not reversing the inequality sign after multiplying or dividing by a negative number. −2x < 8 means x > −4.
  • Reversing the sign when multiplying by a positive number, or reversing when subtracting — only multiplication and division by negatives reverse it.
  • Hollow versus solid circles: < and > exclude the endpoint; ⩽ and ⩾ include it. Writing x > 4 when x = 4 works is a boundary error.
  • Flipping the inequality direction mid-solution so the final statement faces the wrong way.
  • Forgetting to reverse in a compound inequality: every part flips when the whole chain is multiplied by a negative.
  • In region questions, drawing a solid boundary for a strict inequality (or a dashed one for ⩽), or shading the wrong side because no test point was used.
  • Reporting a decimal when the question asks for integers: n ⩽ 11.25 means the largest integer is 11, not 11.25.
  • Treating ⩽ as < in a word problem: at most 5 includes 5.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 2, 3 marks). Solve 7 − 3x > 1 and show your solution on a number line.

Answer: −3x > −6, so x < 2 (the sign reverses). Number line: hollow circle at 2, shading to the left.

Question 2 (Paper 2, 3 marks). Solve 2 ⩽ 3x + 5 < 14 and list the integer solutions.

Answer: Subtract 5 throughout: −3 ⩽ 3x < 9. Divide by 3: −1 ⩽ x < 3. The integers are −1, 0, 1, 2.

Question 3 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Find the values of x for which x² − 5x + 4 < 0.

Answer: Factorise: (x − 1)(x − 4) < 0. The quadratic is negative between its roots, so 1 < x < 4. (Test x = 2: 4 − 10 + 4 = −2 < 0 ✓; test x = 0: 4 > 0 ✗.)

Question 4 (Paper 4, 5 marks). Shade the region defined by y > x − 1, y ⩽ 3 and x ⩾ 0, and write down the coordinates of one point in the region.

Answer: Draw y = x − 1 dashed (strict), y = 3 solid and x = 0 solid. The origin test for y > x − 1 gives 0 > −1, true, so shade above the dashed line; y ⩽ 3 shades below the horizontal line; x ⩾ 0 shades right of the y-axis. The overlap is a triangle with vertices (0, 3), (4, 3) and (0, −1); the point (1, 1) lies inside: 1 > 0 ✓, 1 ⩽ 3 ✓, 1 ⩾ 0 ✓.

Question 5 (Paper 4, 4 marks). A rectangle has a perimeter of at most 60 cm and a length of (x + 4) cm. Write an inequality for its width w and find w when x = 8.

Answer: 2[(x + 4) + w] ⩽ 60, so (x + 4) + w ⩽ 30 and w ⩽ 26 − x. With x = 8: w ⩽ 18 cm, and the width must also be positive, so 0 < w ⩽ 18.

Question 6 (Paper 2, 3 marks). The solutions of 5x + a ⩾ 0 include x = −2. Find the smallest integer value of a.

Answer: Substituting x = −2: −10 + a ⩾ 0, so a ⩾ 10. The smallest integer value is 10.

With equations and inequalities mastered, the next stage of algebra is sequences and functions.

Inequality symbols and the number line

An inequality compares two expressions that are not necessarily equal. There are four symbols, and each one says which side is larger. Reading the symbol correctly is the first step in every inequality question, and most errors in this topic start with a misread symbol rather than with the algebra.

The four inequality symbols

The symbol < means less than, > means greater than, ≤ means less than or equal to, and ≥ means greater than or equal to. The open symbols < and > exclude the boundary value, and the symbols with a bar underneath include it. Write the symbol that matches the wording, because "at least 5" is ≥ 5 and "more than 5" is > 5.

Drawing a number line

Mark the boundary value on a number line with an open circle for < or >, and a filled circle for ≤ or ≥. Shade the side of the line that contains the solutions. A filled circle at 3 with shading to the right shows x ≥ 3, which includes 3 itself. The open circle at 3 with shading to the left shows x < 3, which does not.

Writing a solution set from a number line

To write the inequality from a number line, find the boundary value, decide whether the circle is open or filled, and check the direction of the shading. Shading to the right of the boundary gives a greater-than form, and shading to the left gives a less-than form. Read the direction from the arrow of the shading, not from the side on which the circle sits.

Solutions as whole numbers

Many questions ask for the integers that satisfy an inequality. If x < 4 and x is a positive integer, the solutions are 1, 2 and 3, and 4 is excluded. The boundary value decides the list: x ≤ 4 would include 4. List the values in order, separated by commas, and do not include values that the inequality excludes.

Double inequalities

A double inequality such as −2 < x ≤ 5 states two conditions at once: x is greater than −2 and x is at most 5. On a number line, the two boundaries limit a single shaded section. Keep the inequality in one line when you solve it, and apply every operation to all three parts, so that the middle term is treated the same as the outer two.

Common reading errors

The two errors that cost the most marks are reversing the boundary value by mistake and marking the circle the wrong way. An answer of x ≤ 3 drawn with an open circle is wrong even though the direction is right, because the examiner checks the circle as well as the shading. Check both before you move on to the algebra.

Equations and symbols

An inequality is solved like an equation with one extra rule, and the region questions are all the same line tested against a point. This sheet is the boundary lines and the sign rule — the two places marks are lost.

y = mx + c Key: y and x = the coordinates of a point on the plane (no units); m = the gradient; c = the y-intercept. Drawn solid when the inequality includes equality (⩽ or ⩾) and dashed when it is strict (< or >) — the line style is the first mark of a region question.

y = 2x + 1 Key: the boundary line of y ⩽ 2x + 1, drawn solid because equality is included. Test the origin (0, 0): 0 ⩽ 1 is true, so shade the side containing the origin — testing, never guessing, is what earns the shading mark.

y = -x + 2 Key: the boundary line of y > −x + 2, drawn dashed because the inequality is strict, so points on the line are excluded. Here (0, 0) gives 0 > 2, false, so the region is the side away from the origin.

x = 0 (the y-axis) Key: the boundary of x ⩾ 0; a vertical line has no gradient to quote, which is why the general form breaks down and the line is named instead. Shade to the right of it.

x + y = 6 Key: a boundary written in implicit form; the intercepts are (6, 0) and (0, 6). With y = x + 2 it meets at x + (x + 2) = 6, so x = 2 and y = 4 — corner (2, 4), where the maximum of a linear expression over that region always sits.

x² + kx + 9 = 0 Key: x = the variable; k = the unknown coefficient; the condition "two distinct real roots" becomes b² − 4ac > 0 with a = 1, b = k, c = 9, so k² > 36 and k > 6 or k < −6. The result is a pair of rays, not an interval between them — writing 6 < k < −6 is the standard wrong answer.

The sign rule, in one table

OperationEffect on the sign
Add or subtract the same valueUnchanged
Multiply or divide by a positive numberUnchanged
Multiply or divide by a negative numberReverses: < becomes >, ⩽ becomes ⩾
Reverse the two sidesReverses: 3 < 5 is the same statement as 5 > 3

Traps specific to the algebra

  • Forgetting to reverse when dividing by a negative: −2x ⩽ 8 gives x ⩾ −4.
  • Reversing when subtracting, which is not a reversal at all.
  • Hollow versus solid endpoints: x = 4 does not satisfy x > 4.
  • Reporting 11.25 when the question asks for the greatest integer, which is 11.
  • Shading every inequality's own side instead of their overlap.

title: Coordinate Geometry — Study Notes
content:
Coordinate Geometry

Cambridge International AS & A Level Mathematics 9709, Paper 1. Coordinate questions fall into four types: a shape test, a line from two facts, a meeting point, and a circle. Identify the type from the wording before you touch a formula, because each type has its own first step.

Match the wording to the method

  • "Show that the shape is a rhombus, square or parallelogram": find side lengths and gradients, then compare them. Lengths decide equal sides; gradients decide right angles and parallel sides.
  • "Find the line through … parallel or perpendicular to …": take the gradient from the given line, change it if needed, then build the line from one point.
  • "Find where the line meets the curve or the other line": substitute one equation into the other, then solve the single equation that results.
  • "Find the circle … tangent at …": find the centre and radius first. Tangents are always perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact.

Shape test: lengths first, then gradients

Take P(0, 1), Q(4, 4), R(8, 1) and S(4, −2). Side PQ has change (4, 3), so its length is √(16 + 9) = 5. QR has change (4, −3), length 5. RS has change (−4, −3), length 5, and SP has change (−4, 3), length 5. All four sides are equal.

Equal sides alone do not prove a rhombus when the shape could fold. Check one diagonal: PR has gradient (1 − 1)/(8 − 0) = 0, so it is horizontal. QS is vertical, since Q and S both have x = 4. The diagonals are perpendicular, so PQRS is a rhombus. The midpoints of both diagonals are (4, 1), which confirms the two diagonals bisect each other.

A line from two facts

Find the line through (3, −1) perpendicular to 2x − 5y + 1 = 0. Rearranging gives y = (2/5)x + 1/5, so the given gradient is 2/5. The perpendicular gradient is −5/2. Then y + 1 = −(5/2)(x − 3), which becomes 5x + 2y − 13 = 0.

Check the point: 5(3) + 2(−1) − 13 = 0. Always substitute the point you started from, because it catches sign errors in the gradient step.

Where two lines meet

For 3x + y = 7 and x − 2y = −4, rearrange the first to y = 7 − 3x and substitute into the second: x − 2(7 − 3x) = −4, so 7x = 10 and x = 10/7. Then y = 7 − 30/7 = 19/7. Check in the second equation: 10/7 − 38/7 = −4. The point is (10/7, 19/7).

Two lines with the same gradient and different intercepts never meet, so the substitution leaves a false statement such as 0 = 5. Report that as "no intersection", not as an error in your algebra.

Circles

A circle with centre (2, −3) through (5, 1) has r² = (5 − 2)² + (1 + 3)² = 25. Its equation is (x − 2)² + (y + 3)² = 25, which expands to x² + y² − 4x + 6y − 12 = 0.

The tangent at (5, 1) is perpendicular to the radius. The radius has gradient 4/3, so the tangent has gradient −3/4. Then y − 1 = −(3/4)(x − 5), which gives 3x + 4y − 19 = 0.

To find where the line y = 2x − 1 meets this circle, substitute: (x − 2)² + (2x + 2)² = 25. Expanding gives 5x² + 4x − 17 = 0. The discriminant is 16 + 340 = 356, which is positive, so the line cuts the circle at two points.

Converting between forms

Gradient form y = mx + c is easiest for comparing gradients. Form ax + by + c = 0 is what many final answers need. Going from the centre-radius form to the expanded form means multiplying out both brackets, then collecting the x, y and constant terms.

Traps that cost marks

  • Taking the gradient of the given line as its y-coefficient, rather than −(a/b) in ax + by + c = 0.
  • Forgetting to negate the gradient when the question asks for a perpendicular line.
  • Using the radius value r instead of r² in the circle equation.
  • Leaving a meeting point as one coordinate, when the question asks for both.

title: Differentiation — Study Notes
content:
Differentiation

Cambridge International AS & A Level Mathematics 9709, Paper 1. Differentiation finds how fast y changes with x. Most questions ask for one of three things: a gradient at a point, a tangent or normal, or the nature of a stationary point.

Start from a question

The curve C has equation y = 2x³ − 9x² + 12x − 1.

  1. Find dy/dx.
  2. Find the coordinates of the stationary points and state their nature.
  3. Find the equation of the normal to C at x = 3.

Part 1. dy/dx = 6x² − 18x + 12 = 6(x − 1)(x − 2).

Part 2. dy/dx = 0 at x = 1 and x = 2. When x = 1, y = 4, and when x = 2, y = 3. Next, d²y/dx² = 12x − 18. At (1, 4) this is −6, so the point is a maximum. At (2, 3) it is 6, so the point is a minimum.

Part 3. At x = 3, dy/dx = 6(2)(1) = 12, so the normal has gradient −1/12. Also y = 54 − 81 + 36 − 1 = 8, so the point is (3, 8). The normal is y − 8 = −(x − 3)/12, which gives x + 12y − 99 = 0.

The power rule

If y = axⁿ, then dy/dx = naxⁿ⁻¹, for any rational n. A constant differentiates to zero. Rewrite roots and reciprocals as powers first: 4√x − 6/x² = 4x^(1/2) − 6x⁻², so dy/dx = 2/√x + 12/x³.

Expand before you differentiate

Differentiation works term by term, so multiply out any brackets first. Example: y = (x + 2)(x − 5) = x² − 3x − 10, so dy/dx = 2x − 3.

A zero gradient is not always a turning point

Use the second derivative when it is non-zero at the point. If it is zero, test the sign of dy/dx on each side. Example: y = x⁴ − 4x³ gives dy/dx = 4x²(x − 3). At x = 0 the gradient is negative on both sides, so the curve keeps falling and (0, 0) is not a maximum or minimum. At x = 3 the gradient changes from negative to positive, so (3, −27) is a minimum.

Tangents and normals

Substitute x into the original equation to find y, and into dy/dx to find the gradient. The tangent uses that gradient, and the normal uses its negative reciprocal. Write both as y − y₁ = m(x − x₁) and simplify.

Traps that cost marks

  • Differentiating a product factor by factor instead of expanding it first.
  • Giving the normal the same gradient as the tangent, rather than the negative reciprocal.
  • Giving only the x-value of a stationary point, rather than its coordinates (x, y).
  • Calling a point a maximum or minimum from dy/dx = 0 alone, without checking the nature.

title: A2 Level Biology: Microbiology, Immunity and Forensics
content:
Microbiology, Immunity and Forensics

Edexcel International A Level Biology — Unit 4 (WBI14), Topic 6. Every statement 6.1 to 6.20 is covered below, with its code in the heading. The topic links three big ideas: how microorganisms are grown and measured, how the body defends itself and why pathogens keep finding ways around those defences, and how DNA techniques are used to identify organisms and people.

6.1: Culturing microorganisms with aseptic technique

  • Aseptic technique keeps a culture pure: only the wanted microorganism grows. Sterilise media and equipment first, usually in an autoclave at 121 °C under pressure for about 15 minutes.
  • Work close to a Bunsen flame, flame the inoculating loop until red-hot before and after use, keep Petri dish lids mostly closed, and never pipette by mouth.
  • Incubate cultures inverted at a safe temperature, usually 25 °C for school work, so condensation does not drip onto the agar.

6.2: Measuring the growth of microorganisms

  • Direct cell counts: use a haemocytometer (counting chamber) under a microscope, counting cells in a known volume to get the number per cm³.
  • Viable counts by dilution plating: make a serial dilution, spread known volumes on agar, incubate, and count colonies on plates with about 30 to 300 colonies. Each colony is assumed to grow from one viable cell, so the count shows living cells only.
  • Mass methods: measure the dry mass of cells collected by centrifuging or filtering a known volume of culture.
  • Optical methods (turbidity): a colorimeter or spectrophotometer measures how much light the cloudy culture absorbs. Absorbance rises with cell density, so a calibration curve converts it to cell numbers.

6.3: The bacterial growth curve and the growth rate constant

  • Lag phase: cells adapt to the medium and synthesise enzymes; there is little or no division.
  • Exponential (log) phase: cells divide at a constant rate, so the population doubles each generation. N = N₀ × 2ⁿ, where n is the number of doublings.
  • Stationary phase: births equal deaths, because nutrients run short and waste builds up.
  • Death phase: deaths exceed births and the population falls.
  • Growth rate constant: in exponential growth N = N₀eᵏᵗ. So k = (ln N₂ − ln N₁) ÷ (t₂ − t₁). Plotting ln N against time gives a straight line whose gradient is k.

6.4: Core practical 13: growth of microorganisms in liquid culture

  • Inoculate a sterile liquid medium, take samples at regular intervals, and measure turbidity or cell count each time.
  • Plot the results to show the four phases of the curve, then calculate the exponential growth rate constant from the straight-line part.
  • Safe and ethical use: use only non-pathogenic strains, keep the culture closed, disinfect the bench, and autoclave all used material before disposal.

6.5: Structure of bacteria and viruses

  • Bacteria are cells with a cell wall (peptidoglycan), cell membrane, cytoplasm with ribosomes, and a circular DNA loop, often with plasmids. They have no nucleus.
  • Viruses are not cells. They have a nucleic acid core, either DNA or RNA, surrounded by a protein capsid. Some also have a lipid envelope taken from the host.
  • Comparisons: Ebola virus has single-stranded RNA and an envelope. Tobacco mosaic virus (TMV) has single-stranded RNA in a helical capsid, with no envelope. HIV has two RNA strands, reverse transcriptase and an envelope. λ phage, a virus of bacteria, has double-stranded DNA in a head with a tail and no envelope.
  • Lytic cycle: the virus takes over the host cell, makes new viruses, and the cell bursts (lyses) to release them.
  • Latency: the viral genome stays in the host cell without producing new viruses, and can become active later.

6.6: How Mycobacterium tuberculosis and HIV infect human cells

  • Tuberculosis: Mycobacterium tuberculosis is inhaled into the alveoli. Macrophages engulf it, but the bacterium survives inside them and multiplies. The body forms granulomas (tubercles) around the infection, and the lung tissue is destroyed. Symptoms include a persistent cough, fever, night sweats and weight loss. If untreated it can be fatal.
  • HIV: the virus binds to CD4 receptors and a co-receptor on helper T cells. Reverse transcriptase makes DNA from its RNA, which is inserted into the host genome. New viruses bud from the cell. The helper T cell population falls, so the immune system fails and opportunistic infections and cancers take hold (AIDS).

6.7: Routes of entry and barriers

  • Routes: inhalation (airborne droplets), ingestion (contaminated food and water), contact through broken skin or wounds, sexual contact, and vectors such as mosquitoes.
  • Barriers: intact skin (keratin, dryness, and the skin flora that competes with pathogens), stomach acid (pH about 2, which kills many ingested microbes), and gut flora that competes for space and nutrients. Mucus and cilia in the airways trap and move pathogens out.

6.8: Non-specific responses to infection

  • Inflammation: damaged cells release chemicals such as histamine, which dilate blood vessels and make them leaky. The area becomes red, hot and swollen, and white blood cells are recruited to the site.
  • Lysozyme: an enzyme in tears, saliva and mucus that breaks the peptidoglycan of bacterial cell walls.
  • Interferon: proteins released by virus-infected cells that warn neighbouring cells, which then resist viral replication. Interferon is antiviral, not a direct killer of the virus.
  • Phagocytosis: neutrophils and macrophages engulf a pathogen into a phagosome. Lysosomes fuse with it and enzymes digest the contents.

6.9: Antigens, antibodies, plasma cells, macrophages and antigen-presenting cells

  • An antigen is a foreign molecule, usually a protein or glycoprotein on a pathogen's surface, that triggers an immune response.
  • An antibody is a Y-shaped glycoprotein whose binding sites are complementary to one specific antigen. Antibodies mark pathogens for destruction and neutralise toxins.
  • Plasma cells are B cells that have been activated and that secrete antibodies in large amounts.
  • Macrophages and antigen-presenting cells engulf the pathogen, break it down, and display its antigens on their surface (on MHC proteins). This shows helper T cells what to respond to.

6.10: B cells and T cells

  • B effector (plasma) cells secrete antibodies. B memory cells survive for years and give a faster, larger response on the next exposure to the same antigen.
  • T helper cells (CD4) recognise the antigen on an antigen-presenting cell and release cytokines that activate B cells and T killer cells.
  • T killer (cytotoxic, CD8) cells bind to infected or abnormal cells and kill them, for example by releasing perforin.
  • T memory cells persist after the infection and respond quickly if the same pathogen returns.

6.11: Types of immunity

  • Natural active: the person is infected and makes their own antibodies and memory cells.
  • Natural passive: antibodies pass from mother to baby across the placenta or in breast milk. Protection is immediate but short-lived, and no memory cells are formed.
  • Artificial active: vaccination with an antigen, a weakened or dead pathogen, or a toxoid. The person makes antibodies and memory cells without becoming ill.
  • Artificial passive: injected antibodies, such as antivenom or antitoxin. Protection is immediate and short-lived, and the person's own immune system does not learn.

6.12: The evolutionary race between pathogens and hosts

  • Pathogens evolve evasion mechanisms. Antigenic variation changes the surface antigens: influenza and HIV mutate rapidly, so antibodies no longer fit.
  • Other evasion: hiding inside host cells (tuberculosis in macrophages, HIV in T cells), entering latency, and suppressing the immune response.
  • The host responds with new antibodies and T cells, so pathogens and hosts keep evolving against each other. This is the evolutionary race.

6.13: Bacteriostatic and bactericidal antibiotics

  • Bacteriostatic antibiotics stop bacteria growing and dividing, for example by blocking protein synthesis. The immune system then clears the infection.
  • Bactericidal antibiotics kill bacteria, for example penicillin, which stops cell wall synthesis so the cell bursts.
  • Antibiotics do not act on viruses, which use the host cell's machinery.

6.14: Core practical 14: the effect of antibiotics on bacteria

  • Spread a lawn of bacteria on agar, place antibiotic discs on it, and include a control disc with no antibiotic.
  • Incubate, then measure the diameter of each clear zone of inhibition. A larger zone means the bacteria are more sensitive.
  • Use aseptic technique and non-pathogenic strains, and autoclave the plates before disposal.

6.15: Hospital-acquired infections and codes of practice

  • Contributory causes include overuse of broad-spectrum antibiotics, which selects for resistant strains such as MRSA, poor hand hygiene, indwelling catheters, surgical wounds, and immunocompromised patients.
  • Codes of practice respond to these causes: prescribe antibiotics only when needed and according to guidelines, enforce hand hygiene, isolate infected patients, and clean equipment and wards.

6.16: Decomposition and the carbon cycle

  • Bacteria and fungi are the main decomposers. They secrete extracellular enzymes that digest complex organic matter such as cellulose and proteins, then absorb the simpler products.
  • Respiration by decomposers releases carbon dioxide, which returns carbon to the atmosphere for producers. Ammonium released from proteins feeds the nitrogen cycle.

6.17: The polymerase chain reaction (PCR)

  • Each cycle has three steps: denaturation at about 95 °C separates the strands, annealing at about 50 to 65 °C lets primers bind, and extension at about 72 °C is when Taq polymerase builds the new strands.
  • Taq polymerase comes from the heat-tolerant bacterium Thermus aquaticus, so it survives the high temperatures. Around 30 cycles give an exponential increase in the number of copies.

6.18: Gel electrophoresis of DNA fragments

  • DNA carries a negative charge from its phosphate groups, so it moves towards the positive electrode (anode) through a gel.
  • Smaller fragments move faster and further, so fragments separate by length. A DNA ladder of known sizes is run alongside for comparison, and the bands are stained to make them visible.

6.19: DNA profiling for identification and relatedness

  • DNA profiling compares short tandem repeats (STRs) or variable number tandem repeats (VNTRs). These regions vary in length between individuals, so each person gives a distinctive band pattern.
  • Uses include identifying suspects, establishing paternity, and comparing the banding patterns of plants or animals to show how closely related they are.

6.20: Estimating the time of death from forensic evidence

  • Body temperature: the body cools towards the surroundings, so the rate of cooling gives an estimate of time since death.
  • Muscle contraction: rigor mortis sets in over hours, peaks, then fades over about a day or two.
  • Decomposition and succession: bacterial decomposition gives a predictable sequence of changes. Forensic entomology uses the stage of blowfly larvae and the succession of insect species to estimate how long the body has been exposed.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Growth rate, 6.3 applied: a culture grows from 2.0 × 10⁴ cells cm⁻³ at 2 hours to 1.6 × 10⁵ at 5 hours. N₂ ÷ N₁ = 8 = 2³, so three doublings in three hours. k = (ln 1.6 × 10⁵ − ln 2.0 × 10⁴) ÷ 3 = ln 8 ÷ 3 = 0.69 per hour. The doubling time is ln 2 ÷ k = 1.0 hour. Check the answer against the doubling count before you write it down.
  • Viable count, 6.2 applied: 150 colonies grow from 0.1 cm³ of a 10⁻⁵ dilution. That is 150 ÷ 0.1 = 1500 colonies per cm³ in the diluted sample, and multiplying by the dilution factor gives 1.5 × 10⁸ viable cells per cm³. A haemocytometer count would include dead cells, so the two methods can give different numbers from the same culture. Name which one you are using.
  • Log phase, 6.3 applied: plotting ln N against time gives a straight line only during exponential growth. A curve that bends is a sign that the lag, stationary or death phase has been included by mistake. Use only the straight section to find k.
  • Primary and secondary immune response, 6.10 and 6.12 applied: the first exposure has a lag of several days before antibodies peak at a lower level. A second exposure gives a faster, larger and longer-lasting response, because memory cells are already present. Use all three words, faster, larger and longer, to earn the full mark.
  • Antigen presentation, 6.9 applied: helper T cells (CD4) recognise antigen presented on MHC class II proteins, and killer T cells (CD8) recognise it on MHC class I, as on infected body cells. Naming the MHC class shows you understand which cell carries the antigen.
  • Antibiotic action, 6.13 applied: penicillin blocks the cross-linking of peptidoglycan in the cell wall, so a growing cell bursts. An antibiotic that targets a process human cells do not use, such as the bacterial ribosome, is more selective. Resistance arises by chance mutation and is selected for by the antibiotic, so the explanation must say the mutation was already present and survived.
  • PCR, 6.17 applied: after n cycles one DNA molecule has become 2ⁿ molecules. After 30 cycles that is 2³⁰, about 1.07 × 10⁹ copies. This is why a very small sample is enough, and why contamination with foreign DNA is a serious error.
  • Gel electrophoresis, 6.18 applied: the distance moved is roughly linear with the logarithm of the fragment length. Use a DNA ladder to plot log size against distance, then read the unknown band from that graph rather than from the ladder bands by eye.
  • Forensic estimates, 6.20 applied: a time-of-death answer is always a range. Temperature cooling assumes a stable environment, and a hot or wet site or a body wrapped in clothing changes the rate. Say which factor is most uncertain and why.

Exam tip: time-of-death questions are estimates. Name the method, say what it measures, and state the limitation, for example that temperature depends on the environment.

The four types of immunity, compared

TypeHow it is acquiredAntibodies made by the personDuration
Natural activeInfection with the pathogenYesLong, because memory cells remain
Natural passiveAntibodies cross the placenta or arrive in colostrumNoShort, until the transferred antibodies are broken down
Artificial activeVaccination with antigen or an attenuated pathogenYesLong, and boosters raise the secondary response
Artificial passiveInjection of antibodies from another source, such as an antiserumNoShort, but immediate

Typical mistakes

  • Confusing aseptic technique with sterilisation. Apparatus and medium are sterilised before use; aseptic technique is how the worker keeps them sterile while handling them, by flaming the loop, passing the neck of the bottle through the flame and minimising the time the plate is open.
  • Forgetting the dilution factor in a viable count. A count on a diluted sample must be multiplied by the dilution factor and divided by the volume plated, or the answer is out by orders of magnitude. Quote the units as cells per cm cubed.
  • Reading the growth curve without the phase names. Lag phase: cells adapt and synthesise enzymes, so numbers rise slowly. Exponential phase: numbers double at a constant rate. Stationary: growth equals death as nutrients run low and waste builds. Death: death exceeds growth.
  • Saying antibiotics are bactericidal when they are bacteriostatic. Bactericidal antibiotics kill the bacteria; bacteriostatic ones stop them dividing, so the immune system finishes the job. Penicillin is bactericidal because it blocks the cross-linking of peptidoglycan, so growing cells burst.
  • Giving B and T cells the same job. B effector cells make and secrete antibodies and B memory cells make the secondary response faster. T helper cells release cytokines that activate B cells and macrophages, T killer cells destroy infected cells, and T memory cells persist.
  • Describing PCR without its requirements. PCR needs a DNA template, primers, free nucleotides, a heat-stable DNA polymerase and a buffer, with repeated cycles of denaturation, annealing and extension. Each cycle doubles the DNA, so 30 cycles give 2 to the power 30 copies.
  • Forgetting which electrode DNA moves towards. DNA is negatively charged because of its phosphate groups, so in gel electrophoresis it moves towards the positive electrode, and shorter fragments move further.
  • Giving a single figure for time of death. It is an estimate from several methods, each with a limitation: body temperature depends on the environment, decomposition depends on conditions, and succession depends on the species available.

Exam-style questions

  1. A 0.1 cm cubed sample of a 10 to the power minus 4 dilution produces 64 colonies. Calculate the number of viable cells in the original culture. Answer: 64 colonies in 0.1 cm cubed is 640 cells per cm cubed in the diluted sample; multiply by the dilution factor 10 000, giving 6.4 times 10 to the power 6 viable cells per cm cubed.
  2. Explain why a viable count can be lower than a total count from a haemocytometer. Answer: a viable count only counts cells that can divide and form a colony, so dead cells and cells that are alive but not dividing are missed; a haemocytometer counts all cells, living and dead, present in the sample.
  3. Describe how you would investigate the effect of different antibiotics on a bacterial culture, naming the variables. Answer: inoculate a lawn of the bacterium evenly over an agar plate using a sterile spreader, place discs soaked in equal volumes of different antibiotic solutions on the surface, incubate at a controlled temperature for a fixed time, and measure the diameter of the clear zone around each disc. Controls: a disc soaked in sterile water, and the same species, incubation temperature and time for every plate. A larger zone means greater inhibition, and repeats give a mean.
  4. Explain how a vaccine produces immunity and why a booster is sometimes needed. Answer: the vaccine presents antigens, which are taken up by antigen-presenting cells; helper T cells activate the specific B cell carrying a matching receptor; the B cell divides into effector cells that secrete antibodies and memory cells that persist. A booster raises the antibody level again through the quicker, larger secondary response, and may be needed when the first dose did not produce enough memory cells or when the pathogen varies.
  5. Explain how HIV and Mycobacterium tuberculosis cause disease. Answer: HIV binds the CD4 receptor on helper T cells, and the virus enters and replicates, eventually destroying the cells; the loss of helper T cells disables the immune response, so opportunistic infections cause AIDS. Mycobacterium tuberculosis is engulfed by macrophages but survives inside them, and the inflammatory response forms tubercles that damage the lung tissue, causing coughing and reduced gas exchange.
  6. Explain how gel electrophoresis separates DNA fragments and what a DNA profile shows. Answer: fragments are cut with restriction enzymes and loaded into a gel; an electric field moves the negatively charged DNA towards the positive electrode, and shorter fragments travel further, so the fragments separate by length. A profile from several loci is a pattern that can identify an individual or show relatedness, because the pattern is inherited.
  7. Explain how PCR amplifies DNA and why contamination is a problem. Answer: the mixture is heated to denature the double helix, cooled so primers anneal to the target sequences, then warmed so DNA polymerase extends the primers; each cycle doubles the number of target molecules. A single foreign DNA molecule can also be amplified, so contamination makes the sample unusable.

Equations and symbols

Four calculations carry the quantitative marks in this topic: population growth, the growth rate constant, the viable count with its dilution factor, and the amplification of DNA by PCR. Learn the symbols once and the rest is substitution.

Population growth

N = N₀ × 2ⁿ Key: N = population size after n doublings (cells, or cells cm⁻³); N₀ = starting population at the same units; n = number of doublings (no units). Doubling means n rises by 1 per generation, so the population is exponential, not linear.

N = N₀eᵏᵗ Key: N = population at time t; N₀ = population at t = 0; e = 2.718…; k = growth rate constant (h⁻¹, or s⁻¹ if time is in seconds); t = time (h). This is the continuous form of the same growth, and it is the one that gives k.

k = (ln N₂ − ln N₁) ÷ (t₂ − t₁) Key: k = growth rate constant (h⁻¹); N₁ and N₂ = population at the two sampling times; t₁ and t₂ = those times (h); ln = natural logarithm. It is the gradient of ln N against time, which is why only the straight, exponential section of the graph may be used.

k = (ln 1.6 × 10⁵ − ln 2.0 × 10⁴) ÷ 3 = ln 8 ÷ 3 = 0.69 per hour Key: the worked case: a rise from 2.0 × 10⁴ to 1.6 × 10⁵ cells cm⁻³ over 3 h is an eightfold rise, so ln 8 ÷ 3 = 0.69 h⁻¹. Eightfold is exactly three doublings, which is the check.

doubling time = ln 2 ÷ k Key: doubling time = time for the population to double (h); ln 2 = 0.693; k = growth rate constant (h⁻¹). With k = 0.69 h⁻¹ the doubling time is 1.0 h.

Viable counts and the dilution factor

150 ÷ 0.1 = 1500 colonies per cm³ Key: 150 = colonies counted on the plate; 0.1 = volume plated (cm³); the quotient is the count per cm³ of the diluted sample. Multiply by the dilution factor (10⁵ here) to reach 1.5 × 10⁸ viable cells per cm³ of the original culture — forgetting that step is the classic error.

PCR amplification

2³⁰ Key: 2 = the doubling per cycle; 30 = number of cycles. Thirty cycles give about 1.07 × 10⁹ copies from a single molecule, which is why a trace of DNA is enough and why contamination ruins a sample.

The slip worth naming

A haemocytometer counts live and dead cells together, so a total count is always at least the viable count. State which method produced the number before comparing two counts.

title: IGCSE Mathematics: Fractions, Decimals and Percentages
content:
IGCSE Mathematics: Fractions, Decimals and Percentages

Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580 (2025–2027), section 1 Number: statement 1.4 Fractions, decimals and percentages (equivalence and conversion), 1.13 Percentages (including Extended reverse percentages) and E1.17 Exponential growth and decay. These three representations describe the same quantities, and fluent movement between them is one of the biggest sources of marks in both papers. The note explains why the conversion methods work before showing them, then builds percentages as multipliers — the technique behind most Paper 4 percentage problems.

What a fraction really is

A fraction is a division: 3/4 means 3 divided by 4, or three quarters of a whole. The top (numerator) counts the parts; the bottom (denominator) says how many equal parts the whole is cut into. A proper fraction has a smaller numerator (3/4); an improper fraction has a larger one (7/4); a mixed number combines a whole number with a proper fraction (1 3/4).

Convert 2 3/5 to an improper fraction:

2 wholes = 10 fifths, and 3 more fifths gives 13 fifths:
2 3/5 = (2 × 5 + 3)/5 = 13/5

Equivalent fractions are the same quantity written differently: 3/4 = 6/8 = 15/20, because multiplying top and bottom by the same number is multiplying by 1 (a form of 1, such as 3/3), which changes the look but not the value. Cancelling is the reverse: dividing top and bottom by a common factor. Only factors of the whole numerator and denominator can be cancelled — (x + 3)/(x + 2) cannot be simplified by cancelling the x's, because the top is a sum, not a product.

Converting between fractions, decimals and percentages

Fraction to decimal: divide.  3/8 = 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375
Decimal to fraction: read the place value.  0.47 = 47/100
Fraction to percentage: divide, then multiply by 100.  3/8 = 0.375 = 37.5%
Percentage to fraction: write over 100 and simplify.  45% = 45/100 = 9/20

Recurring decimals. A fraction always produces either a terminating decimal or a recurring one, and every recurring decimal converts back to a fraction by the algebra method:

Write 0.444... (4 recurring) as a fraction:

Let x = 0.444...
Then 10x = 4.444...        [shift the decimal one place]
Subtract:  10x - x = 4.444... - 0.444...
9x = 4
x = 4/9
Write 0.273636... (36 recurring) as a fraction:

Let x = 0.273636...
Two digits repeat, so shift two places:  100x = 27.363636...
100x - x = 27.3636... - 0.2736... = 27.09
99x = 27.09  →  x = 27.09/99 = 301/1100 after multiplying top and bottom by 100 and simplifying

Knowing the common conversions by heart saves time: 1/2 = 0.5 = 50%, 1/4 = 0.25 = 25%, 3/4 = 0.75, 1/5 = 0.2 = 20%, 1/8 = 0.125, 1/3 = 0.333... = 33 1/3%.

FractionDecimalPercentage
1/20.550%
1/40.2525%
3/40.7575%
1/50.220%
1/80.12512.5%
1/30.333...33 1/3%
2/30.666...66 2/3%

These seven values answer a surprising share of Paper 2 questions by inspection, and they anchor every conversion done the long way.

Percentages: the multiplier method

A percentage is a fraction out of 100 — literally per cent, per hundred. Every percentage problem is a multiplication, and the fastest method converts straight to a multiplier.

Find 35% of 240:

35% = 35/100 = 0.35, so  0.35 × 240 = 84

Increase 240 by 35%:
the new value is 135% of the old, so multiply by 1.35:  1.35 × 240 = 324

Decrease 240 by 35%:
the new value is 65% of the old, so multiply by 0.65:   0.65 × 240 = 156

Why the multiplier works. Increasing by 35% means keeping the original 100% and adding 35%, so the result is 135% of the original, which is 1.35 times it. Decreasing by 35% leaves 65%, which is 0.65 times. The multiplier also chains: successive changes multiply, which is why two discounts of 20% are not one discount of 40% (0.8 × 0.8 = 0.64, a 36% total reduction).

One quantity as a percentage of another:  18 out of 60

18/60 × 10⁰ = 30%

Reverse percentages (Extended). Working backwards from a final value needs division:

A price after a 20% increase is £72. Find the original price.

The original is 100%, the new price is 120% of it, so the multiplier is 1.2:
original = 72 / 1.2 = £60

Check: 60 × 1.2 = 72 ✓

The common error is finding 20% of 72 and subtracting; the percentage must be taken from the original 100%, not the final amount.

Percentage change and comparisons

A coat falls from £80 to £56. Find the percentage decrease.

change = 80 - 56 = 24
percentage change = change / original x 100 = 24/80 × 10⁰ = 30%

Percentage change always uses the original value as the denominator. Comparing quantities with different sizes — prices per 100 g, speeds, wages per hour — is done by putting both over a common quantity before comparing.

Exponential growth and decay (Extended)

When a quantity changes by the same percentage each period, it is multiplied by a fixed factor each time, and the result is exponential growth or decay. The multiplier is 1 + r for growth and 1 − r for decay, where r is the rate as a decimal.

After n periods at rate r:
growth:    final = original x (1 + r)^n
decay:     final = original x (1 - r)^n

Why the power. Each period multiplies by the same factor, so n periods multiply n times: an investment of £500 growing 3% a year becomes 500 × 1.03 after one year, 500 × 1.03 × 1.03 after two, and 500 × 1.03ⁿ after n years. The power counts the multiplications.

£500 is invested at 3% compound interest per year for 4 years.

500 × 1.03⁴ = 500 × 1.12550881 = £562.75 (2 d.p.)

Year by year check: 515.00 → 530.45 → 546.36 → 562.75 ✓
A car worth £18 000 depreciates 15% per year. Value after 3 years:

18 000 × 0.85³ = 18 000 × 0.614125 = £11 054.25

Exponential growth graphs climb ever faster and never touch zero; exponential decay graphs fall steeply at first and then level off towards — but never reach — zero (a horizontal asymptote). Doubling and halving questions are solved by logs or trial multiplication: for how many years does £500 at 3% exceed £600? Solve 500 × 1.03ⁿ > 600 by testing values of n, since 1.03ⁿ > 1.2 needs n ⩾ 7 years.

Worked example: a full percentage question

A shop sells a jacket for £84 after a 20% reduction. A further 10% discount is offered for cash.

Original price before the 20% reduction:
84 = original x 0.80
original = 84 / 0.80 = £105

Cash price after the extra 10%:
84 × 0.90 = £75.60

Total percentage saving against the original:
saving = 105 - 75.60 = 29.40
percentage saving = 29.40/105 × 10⁰ = 28%

Check with multipliers: 0.80 × 0.90 = 0.72, so the cash price is 72% of the
original and the saving is 28% ✓

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Finding a percentage of the wrong amount: increase/decrease percentages apply to the original; reverse percentages divide by the multiplier.
  • Adding percentage changes: two 20% discounts give 0.8 × 0.8 = 0.64, a 36% reduction, not 40%.
  • Writing a recurring decimal as a fraction by eye; use the shift-and-subtract method and show it.
  • Cancelling across a sum: 3/4 is not 3 quarters of the top and bottom separately.
  • Using 365 days or 12 months inconsistently in compound problems: the power n counts compounding periods, so match it to the rate.
  • Forgetting that 15% decrease means multiplying by 0.85, not by −0.15 or 0.15.
  • Confusing 33% with 1/3 exactly: 1/3 = 33 1/3%, and the difference matters in exact answers.
  • Deciding an exponential decay value reaches zero; it falls below £1 or 0.001 but never reaches zero.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 2, 3 marks). Express 0.45 as a fraction in its lowest terms.

Answer: 0.45 = 45/100 = 9/20.

Question 2 (Paper 2, 3 marks). Write 0.27 with the 27 recurring as a fraction.

Answer: Let x = 0.272727...; then 100x = 27.2727...; subtracting gives 99x = 27, so x = 27/99 = 3/11.

Question 3 (Paper 4, 4 marks). In a sale, a bike is reduced by 15% to £255. Find the original price.

Answer: £255 represents 85% of the original, so the multiplier is 0.85 and the original price is 255/0.85 = £300. Check: 300 × 0.85 = 255 ✓.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 4 marks). A bacteria culture starts with 2000 and increases by 8% each hour. Find the size after 5 hours.

Answer: 2000 × 1.08⁵ = 2000 × 1.4693280768 = 2938.7 ≈ 2939 bacteria.

Question 5 (Paper 4, 3 marks). A town's population falls from 45 000 to 36 000 over a year. Find the percentage decrease.

Answer: Change = 9000; percentage = 9000/45 000 × 100 = 20%.

Question 6 (Paper 4, 5 marks). A car is bought for £12 000 and depreciates 18% in the first year and 12% in the second. Find its value after two years and the overall percentage loss.

Answer: 12 000 × 0.82 × 0.88 = 12 000 × 0.7216 = £8659.20. Overall loss = £3340.80, which is 3340.80/12 000 × 100 = 27.84% ≈ 27.8%. (Note 0.82 × 0.88 = 0.7216, a 27.84% total fall — not 30%.)

Fractions describe parts; powers and roots describe repeated multiplication — the next topic.
