title: AS Level Physics: Dynamics
content:
AS Level Physics: Dynamics

Edexcel International A Level Physics, Unit 1 (WPH11) Mechanics and Materials — Newton's laws of motion, the conservation of linear momentum, and the behaviour of objects moving through fluids (density, upthrust, viscous drag and terminal velocity). Dynamics answers the question kinematics asks: what makes motion change? The laws are three sentences long and everything else in the unit is their application, so they must be known exactly — including the conditions under which momentum is conserved.

Force and Newton's laws of motion

A force is a push or a pull, measured in newtons (N), and it is a vector. Forces change velocity (they accelerate masses) or change shape. The three laws, in their examinable form:

  • Newton's first law: a body remains at rest or moves with constant velocity in a straight line unless acted on by a resultant external force. It defines inertia — the reluctance of mass to change its state of motion.
  • Newton's second law: the resultant force on a body equals the rate of change of its momentum, in the direction of that force. For constant mass this reduces to F = ma.
  • Newton's third law: when body A exerts a force on body B, body B exerts an equal and opposite force on A. The pair acts on different bodies, always along the same line, and is always the same type of force (gravavitational on gravitational, contact on contact).
resultant force = mass x acceleration        F = m a
  • F: resultant force in newtons (N); m: mass in kilograms (kg); a: acceleration in metres per second squared (m s⁻²). Acceleration is in the direction of the resultant force.

Free-body diagrams are the first mark of nearly every dynamics answer: draw one body, with every force acting on it as an arrow from its centre, labelled (weight, normal reaction, tension, friction, drag, thrust). Resolve the forces along and perpendicular to the direction of motion, apply F = ma along the motion, and use equilibrium (zero resultant) perpendicular to it.

Mass is the quantity of matter and is constant; weight is the gravitational force on that mass, W = mg, and varies with location. The third law pair to an object's weight is the gravitational pull of the object on the Earth — not the normal contact force of the table beneath it.

Momentum and its conservation

Momentum is the product of mass and velocity:

momentum = mass x velocity        p = m v
  • p: momentum in kilogram metres per second (kg m s⁻¹). Momentum is a vector, in the direction of velocity; with a stated sign convention, momenta in opposite directions carry opposite signs.
  • Newton's second law in full form: F = (mv − mu)/t, the rate of change of momentum.

The principle of conservation of linear momentum: when no external resultant force acts on a system, the total momentum of that system remains constant. Collisions, explosions and recoil problems all reduce to one equation: total momentum before = total momentum after, summed as vectors. The condition matters — a ball bouncing off a floor is not momentum-conserving for the ball alone, because the Earth supplies an external force during the bounce.

impulse = change in momentum = force x time        F t = m v - m u
  • Impulse is measured in newton seconds (N s), numerically equal to the momentum change. A force–time graph has an area equal to the impulse; extending the time of impact reduces the peak force for the same impulse — crumple zones, air bags, landing on a bent knee.

Elastic and inelastic collisions

Momentum is conserved in every collision (in an isolated system); kinetic energy is not. A collision is elastic when the total kinetic energy is conserved — idealised gas molecules, and perfectly elastic springs. It is inelastic when kinetic energy is lost to deformation, heat and sound; a collision in which the bodies stick together is completely inelastic, and that is the case where the kinetic energy loss is greatest. Explosions convert stored energy (chemical or elastic) into kinetic energy of the fragments, so the total momentum is conserved while the kinetic energy increases.

Equilibrium and connected bodies

A body is in equilibrium when the resultant force and the resultant moment on it are both zero: it is either at rest or moving with constant velocity. The method is always the same — draw the free-body diagram, resolve along and across the direction of motion, and set the resultant to zero in each direction. For a mass hanging from a string, the tension equals the weight; for a block resting on a slope, the weight resolves into mg sin θ down the slope and mg cos θ into the slope, and the normal reaction balances the latter while friction can balance the former.

Friction acts parallel to a surface and opposes the motion or the tendency to move. The maximum frictional force before slipping is proportional to the normal contact force: F(friction) = mu R, where mu is the coefficient of friction (dimensionless) and R is the normal reaction in newtons. Static friction below that maximum simply matches the applied force, which is why a block on a gentle slope stays put.

Connected bodies share one acceleration, so the fastest method treats the system as a whole first and then separates it. Two masses (3.0 kg and 2.0 kg) joined by a light string over a frictionless pulley accelerate together: the resultant force on the system is the difference in weights, 1.0g, so a = 1.0g/5.0 = 1.96 m s⁻². Cutting the system then gives the tension in the string: for the 3.0 kg mass, 3.0g − T = 3.0a, so T = 23.5 N. The same two answers must hold whichever mass is isolated — a built-in check on the arithmetic.

Fluids: density, upthrust and viscous drag

A fluid is a liquid or a gas, and objects moving through fluids experience forces that solids never show. Density is mass per unit volume, ρ = m/V (kg m⁻³). An object immersed in a fluid is pushed up by an upthrust equal to the weight of fluid displaced (Archimedes' principle), so an object denser than the fluid sinks and one less dense floats; a floating object displaces its own weight of fluid.

Viscous drag is the friction within a fluid: layers of fluid slide over each other and over the object, and the drag grows with speed, viscosity and size. For a small sphere falling slowly through a viscous fluid, Stokes' law gives the drag:

viscous drag = 6 π x viscosity x radius x speed        F = 6 π eta r v
  • F: drag force in newtons (N); eta: viscosity of the fluid in pascal seconds (Pa s); r: radius of the sphere in metres (m); v: speed in metres per second (m s⁻¹). The force acts opposite to the direction of motion.

A falling sphere accelerates until drag + upthrust = weight, and then falls at terminal velocity, which from Stokes' law is v = 2r²(ρ − σ)g/(9η) for a sphere of density ρ in a fluid of density σ. Terminal velocity is reached quickly for small dense spheres in viscous fluids — the principle of the falling-ball viscometer, one of the unit's core practicals. At low speeds the flow around a sphere is smooth and layered (laminar); above a critical speed it becomes chaotic (turbulent), and the drag then rises more steeply with speed. Streamlining delays the onset of turbulence, which is why a golf ball has dimples and a car is shaped the way it is.

Worked example: collision and impulse

A 1200 kg car travelling at 20 m s⁻¹ collides with a stationary 900 kg car and they move together. Find their common velocity and the energy lost.

momentum before = 1200 × 20 = 24 000 kg m s⁻¹
common velocity = 24 000 / (1200 + 900) = 11.4 m s⁻¹
KE before = 1/2 × 1200 × 20² = 240 000 J
KE after = 1/2 × 2100 × 11.4² = 136 000 J
energy lost = 10⁴ 000 J (to deformation, heat and sound)

Momentum is conserved; kinetic energy is not — the collision is inelastic. Second stage: if the impact lasts 0.15 s, the average force on the stationary car is F = mv/t = 900 × 11.4 / 0.15 = 68 400 N, and lengthening the impact with a crumple zone would cut that force sharply.

Common mistakes

  • Using F = ma with one force instead of the resultant; draw the free-body diagram and resolve first.
  • Writing third-law pairs that act on the same body (they never do) or that are different kinds of force.
  • Ignoring direction in momentum problems; a rebound reverses the velocity sign and the total is a vector sum.
  • Assuming kinetic energy is conserved in every collision; only elastic collisions conserve it, and sticking collisions lose the most.
  • Forgetting upthrust when a body moves through a fluid: terminal velocity is reached when drag + upthrust = weight, not when drag = weight, if the fluid's density is not negligible.
  • Using Stokes' law outside its conditions — it assumes laminar flow, slow speeds and a spherical object.
  • Confusing mass and weight in W = mg, or using g in m s⁻² when the question gives g in N kg⁻¹ (numerically equal but state your units).
  • Quoting an impulse as a force: impulse is N s and equals the momentum change; the force depends on the impact time.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (WPH11, 3 marks). A 4.0 kg trolley on a frictionless runway is pulled by a 12 N force. Calculate its acceleration and the distance travelled in 3.0 s from rest.

Answer: a = F/m = 12/4.0 = 3.0 m s⁻². s = ½at² = ½ × 3.0 × 9.0 = 13.5 m ≈ 14 m.

Question 2 (WPH11, 4 marks). A 60 g ball moving at 5.0 m s⁻¹ hits a wall at right angles and rebounds at 3.0 m s⁻¹. The contact lasts 0.020 s. Calculate the average force.

Answer: Taking the initial direction as positive, Δp = 0.060(−3.0) − 0.060(5.0) = −0.48 kg m s⁻¹. Force = Δp/t = −0.48/0.020 = −24 N, i.e. 24 N opposite to the initial motion.

Question 3 (WPH11, 4 marks). Two ice skaters push apart. Skater A (60 kg) moves at 3.0 m s⁻¹. Find the velocity of skater B (75 kg) and explain which principle you used.

Answer: Total momentum before = 0, so 60 × 3.0 + 75 × v = 0 and v = −2.4 m s⁻¹: B moves at 2.4 m s⁻¹ in the opposite direction. The conservation of linear momentum applies because the push is an internal force; the ice's friction is negligible during the push.

Question 4 (WPH11, 3 marks). Explain why a small steel ball bearing falling through glycerine reaches terminal velocity, and state the forces acting at that moment.

Answer: As the ball accelerates, the viscous drag rises with speed (F = 6πηrv). The resultant force is weight minus drag minus upthrust, so the acceleration falls as speed rises. When drag + upthrust equals the weight the resultant force is zero and the ball continues at constant terminal velocity, acted on by three balanced forces: weight down, upthrust and drag up.

Question 5 (WPH13, 3 marks). Describe how you would determine the viscosity of a liquid using a falling-ball method.

Answer: Drop a small steel sphere (radius measured with a micrometer) into a wide measuring cylinder of the liquid and time its fall between two marked lines, where it is already at terminal velocity. Repeat and average the times; calculate v = distance/time. At terminal velocity, 6πηrv = (4/3)πr³(ρ − σ)g, so η = 2r²(ρ − σ)g/(9v). Keep the temperature constant (viscosity depends strongly on it) and use a cylinder at least ten sphere diameters wide to avoid wall effects.

Question 6 (WPH11, 3 marks). A 1500 kg car hits a crash barrier at 15 m s⁻¹ and stops in 0.30 s. Calculate the average force on the car and state one safety feature that reduces this force.

Answer: F = mv/t = 1500 × 15 / 0.30 = 75 000 N = 75 kN. A crumple zone extends the impact time, and for the same momentum change the force falls in proportion to the time.

Forces also change shape — the subject of Materials and Deformation.

title: Exam technique: Mensuration
content:
### What earns the marks
For circles, sectors and arcs, the fraction of 360 stated earns the method mark: write 60/360 before multiplying. For cylinders, cones and spheres, the formula quoted earns a mark on its own, so write Volume = (1/3) pi r squared h even when confident. For compound shapes, split earns marks: compute each part separately, then add or subtract with a clear statement.
### Traps
Error: 2 pi r used for area. Correction: circumference versus area check first. Error: omitting 1/3 for cones and pyramids. Correction: quote the formula every time. Error: using diameter as radius in a semicircle cut-out. Correction: halve the diameter before any pi work. Error: forgetting the square root in a Pythagoras step. Correction: label squared lines as squared.
### Worked example
A cylinder has radius 3 cm and height 10 cm. Its volume is πr²h = π × 9 × 10 = 90π ≈ 282.7 cm³. A sector of angle 60° in a circle of radius 6 cm has arc length (60/360) × 2π × 6 = 2π cm.
### Check yourself
A trapezium has parallel sides 5 cm and 9 cm and a perpendicular height of 4 cm. Find its area. Use ½(a + b)h = ½ × (5 + 9) × 4 = 28 cm². State the units and show the substitution before the final value.

### Worked example
A rectangle is 8 cm long and 5 cm wide. Its perimeter is 2(8 + 5) = 26 cm and its area is 40 cm². A triangular prism with triangular cross-section area 12 cm² and length 7 cm has volume 12 × 7 = 84 cm³.

title: A Level Mathematics: The Poisson Distribution
content:
A Level Mathematics: The Poisson Distribution

The Poisson distribution models the number of events that happen in a fixed interval of time, length, area or volume when those events occur randomly and independently at a constant average rate. Where the binomial counts successes in a fixed number of trials, the Poisson counts arrivals in a continuous window: calls reaching a switchboard in an hour, defects along a length of cable, radioactive decays in a minute. This note derives the formula from the binomial, sets out the two conditions that must hold, and then uses the distribution for the probability and hypothesis-test questions the exam sets.

Where the formula comes from

Imagine slicing the interval into a very large number of tiny sub-intervals. In each slice the chance of an event is tiny but the number of slices is enormous, so the count is binomial with n huge and p tiny. Taking that limit turns nCr p^r (1−p)^(n−r) into the Poisson formula, with the mean λ = np surviving as the only parameter.

X ~ Po(λ):  P(X = r) = e^(-λ) λ^r / r!
mean E(X) = λ
variance Var(X) = λ
so the mean and variance are equal - a diagnostic test for the model

The equality of mean and variance is not a coincidence to memorise; it is the fingerprint of the limit, and it is why an exam question can give you a sample mean and variance and ask whether a Poisson model is plausible.

The three conditions

A Poisson model needs randomness, independence and a constant rate. Naming them is worth marks, and each failure has a characteristic symptom.

1. events occur singly (not in pairs or batches)
2. events occur at random, independently of each other
3. the average rate λ is constant over the interval
then the count in that interval is Poisson

Worked example (checking the model). A shop counts customers arriving per hour. Explain why a Poisson model may be unsuitable.

the arrival rate is not constant: it peaks at lunchtime and is near zero at night
so condition 3 fails and the mean over a whole day is not a single rate
a better model splits the day into periods of roughly constant rate

Calculating probabilities

The formula handles a single value; the cumulative sum handles a range. Because the Poisson has no upper limit, every "at least" question becomes a complement.

P(X = r) = e^(-λ) λ^r / r!
P(X <= r) sums from 0 to r (tables or calculator)
P(X >= r) = 1 - P(X <= r - 1)
P(X < r)  = P(X <= r - 1)

Worked example. X ~ Po(3). Find P(X = 2).

P = e^(-3) × 3² / 2!
= 0.049787 × 9 / 2
= 0.2240

Worked example 2 (at least). For the same X, find P(X ≥ 4).

P(X >= 4) = 1 - P(X <= 3)
P(X <= 3) = 0.049787(1 + 3 + 4.5 + 4.5) = 0.6472
so P(X >= 4) = 0.3528

Worked example 3 (scale change). Calls arrive at 4 per minute. Find the probability of 10 or more calls in two minutes.

the rate scales with the interval: λ = 8 for two minutes
P(X >= 10) = 1 - P(X <= 9) = 1 - 0.7170 = 0.2830

Scaling is the most common source of avoidable error: the parameter must be expressed for the interval the question actually asks about.

Adding independent Poisson variables

If two independent counts each follow a Poisson distribution, their sum does too, and the parameters add. This is why the distribution is so usable: a total across separate sources needs no convolution.

X ~ Po(l1), Y ~ Po(l2), independent
X + Y ~ Po(l1 + l2)
but X - Y is NOT Poisson

Worked example. A website gets 5 hits per minute from Europe and 3 per minute from Asia, independently. Find the probability of more than 10 hits in a minute in total.

total ~ Po(8)
P(X > 10) = 1 - P(X <= 10) = 1 - 0.8159 = 0.1841

The Poisson as an approximation to the binomial

When n is large and p is small, the binomial is well approximated by a Poisson with λ = np. The rule of thumb used in this course is n > 50 and p < 0.05, or np < 5.

X ~ B(n, p) with n large, p small  →  X is approximately Po(np)

Worked example. A factory produces items with a 2% defect rate. In a batch of 200, use a Poisson approximation to find the probability of at most 2 defects.

λ = 200 × 0.02 = 4
P(X <= 2) = e^(-4)(1 + 4 + 8) = 0.018316 × 13 = 0.2381
the exact binomial gives 0.2351, so the approximation is close

Worked example 2 (justifying the approximation). State why the approximation is reasonable here.

n = 200 is large and p = 0.02 is small, with np = 4
so the rare-event limit conditions hold

Hypothesis testing with the Poisson

The structure is identical to the binomial test: state hypotheses, assume the null rate, compute the tail probability, compare with the significance level. The only new step is that the rate may need scaling to the observed interval.

H0: λ = lambda0    H1: λ > lambda0 (or <)
observed count x in the interval
p-value = P(X >= x) or P(X <= x) under Po(lambda0)
reject H0 if the p-value <= the significance level

Worked example. A call centre historically receives 6 calls per hour. In a new hour it receives 12. Test at the 5% level whether the rate has increased.

H0: λ = 6;  H1: λ > 6
X ~ Po(6) under H0
P(X >= 12) = 1 - P(X <= 11) = 1 - 0.9799 = 0.0201
0.0201 < 0.05, so reject H0
there is evidence the rate has increased

Worked example 2 (critical region). For Po(6), find the 5% one-tailed critical region for an increase.

P(X >= 11) = 0.0426 (below 0.05)
P(X >= 10) = 0.0839 (above 0.05)
critical region: X >= 11

Worked example 3 (two intervals). The same centre observes 16 calls over two hours. Test for an increase at 5%.

expected over two hours under H0 = 12, so X ~ Po(12)
P(X >= 16) = 1 - P(X <= 15) = 1 - 0.8444 = 0.1556
0.1556 > 0.05, so do not reject H0

Compare the two: twelve calls in one hour was significant, sixteen in two hours is not, because the expected count doubled. The rate, not the raw count, is what is being tested.

Reading the distribution's shape

The Poisson is skewed to the right when λ is small and becomes almost symmetric as λ grows, which is why small-rate questions usually live in the lower tail and why the normal approximation becomes usable once λ passes about 20. Knowing the shape tells you at a glance whether an answer is plausible: a probability of 0.4 for "more than 10" when λ = 3 should feel wrong before any arithmetic is checked.

A useful sanity check is that the standard deviation is the square root of the mean. For Po(9) the mean is 9 and the standard deviation 3, so counts between 6 and 12 are ordinary and a count of 20 is roughly three and a half standard deviations out — surprising enough to prompt a hypothesis test. That comparison is what turns a bare probability into an interpretation, and interpretation marks are the easiest ones to lose.

Finally, note that the model is about a count in an interval, so the interval has to be defined in the answer. "Three calls per hour" and "three calls per minute" describe different distributions, and a rate quoted per unit time without its unit is not a λ at all.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Definition) State two conditions for a Poisson model. Answer: events occur singly at random, independently, at a constant rate.
  2. (Single value) X ~ Po(2.5): find P(X = 3). Answer: e^(−2.5)(15.625/6) = 0.2138.
  3. (Cumulative) X ~ Po(4): find P(X ≤ 2). Answer: 0.2381.
  4. (Complement) X ~ Po(5): find P(X ≥ 3). Answer: 1 − 0.1247 = 0.8753.
  5. (Scaling) Rate 3 per hour: find P(X = 0) in 20 minutes. Answer: λ = 1, so e^(−1) = 0.3679.
  6. (Sum) Independent Po(2) and Po(3): find P(total = 4). Answer: Po(5), P(4) = 0.1755.
  7. (Approximation) B(500, 0.01): approximate P(X = 0). Answer: Po(5), e^(−5) = 0.00674.
  8. (Mean/variance) A sample has mean 4.2 and variance 9.1. Comment on the Poisson fit. Answer: variance far exceeds the mean, so the model is doubtful (over-dispersed).
  9. (Test) 9 events observed where 4 expected; test for an increase at 5%. Answer: P(X ≥ 9) = 0.0214 < 0.05, reject H0.
  10. (Critical region) Po(3), 5% upper tail: find the critical region. Answer: P(X ≥ 7) = 0.0335, P(X ≥ 6) = 0.0839, so X ≥ 7.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Using the wrong interval: λ must match the window asked about; doubling a time doubles the rate.
  • Complement off by one: P(X ≥ 4) = 1 − P(X ≤ 3); subtracting P(X ≤ 4) is the classic error.
  • Treating a difference as Poisson: sums of independent Poisson variables are Poisson, differences are not.
  • Approximation outside its range: np must be small; with np large the Poisson is a poor fit to the binomial.
  • Variance assumed equal to the mean without checking: the test mean = variance is a diagnostic, not a guarantee.
  • Ignoring clustering: events that arrive in bursts break the single-event condition and inflate the variance.
  • r! miscomputed: 0! = 1 and 1! = 1, and a missing factorial term changes the answer entirely.
  • p-value direction: a one-tailed test uses one tail only; doubling it makes a borderline result look significant.

title: Exam technique: Sequences and Series
content:
### What earns the marks
For AP terms, a + (n-1)d with the brackets evaluated earns the mark; sums use n/2(2a + (n-1)d) quoted. For GP work, the ratio found by division earns one mark and the formula applied earns the next. For sum to infinity, the |r| < 1 check stated earns the method mark.
### Traps
Error: n used instead of (n-1) in terms. Correction: first term needs zero gaps. Error: infinity sums with |r| >= 1. Correction: check convergence first. Error: differentiating S_n for the nth term. Correction: subtract S_{n-1}.
### Worked example
An arithmetic progression has a = 5 and d = 3. The 20th term is a + 19d = 5 + 57 = 62. The sum of the first 20 terms is S₂₀ = (20/2)(2a + 19d) = 10 × 67 = 670. A geometric progression with terms 2, 6, 18 has r = 3, so S₅ = 2(3⁵ − 1)/(3 − 1) = 242. The sum to infinity exists only when |r| < 1, so for r = 1/2 with a = 8 the sum is 8 / (1 − 1/2) = 16.
### Check yourself
State the nth term of a sequence from its sum. Find Sₙ, then subtract Sₙ₋₁. Do not differentiate Sₙ, because the sum is a discrete function.

title: Database Systems — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Database Systems

Computer Science — OL. limitations of file-based systems; relational concepts; SQL (SELECT, FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY, INNER JOIN, SUM, COUNT); DBMS features.

  • 1. File-based problems
  • 2. Relational concepts
  • 3. SQL
  • 4. DBMS features

How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

### Worked example A primary key uniquely identifies each row in a table. A foreign key stores a primary key from another table, which links the two. For Students (StudentID, Name) and Enrolments (EnrolmentID, StudentID, CourseID), StudentID is the foreign key in Enrolments. A query such as SELECT Name FROM Students WHERE Year = 11; returns only the matching rows.

title: Bonding and Structure — Study Notes
content:
Bonding and Structure

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH11, Topic 3. Bonding explains the physical properties of a substance: melting point, conductivity and solubility all follow from the type of bond and the way particles are packed.

Ionic bonding

  • Ionic bonds are the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions in a giant lattice.
  • They have high melting points, are brittle and conduct only when molten or dissolved, because the ions are free to move.

Covalent bonding

  • A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons between two atoms. Simple molecular substances have low melting points because only weak intermolecular forces are overcome.
  • Giant covalent structures such as diamond and silicon(IV) oxide need many strong bonds broken to melt, so they have very high melting points.
  • Graphite conducts because each carbon uses three electrons in bonding, leaving one delocalised electron per atom.

Electronegativity and polarity

  • Electronegativity is the ability of an atom to attract the bonding pair. The difference between two atoms gives a polar bond.
  • A molecule is polar only if its bond dipoles do not cancel. Shape decides this: CO2 is linear and non-polar, while H2O is bent and polar.

Shapes of molecules

  • Electron pairs repel each other, so they arrange themselves as far apart as possible. Lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs.
  • Common shapes: linear (180°), trigonal planar (120°), tetrahedral (109.5°), and bent or pyramidal forms when lone pairs are present.

Metallic bonding

  • Metals consist of positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons, which explains conductivity, malleability and high melting points.

Exam tip: a question asking why a substance conducts must name the mobile particle — ions, delocalised electrons — not just "electrons".

title: Sampling and Estimation
content:
Sampling and Estimation

Populations, Samples, Statistics

A parameter describes the population (μ, σ²); a statistic describes the sample (x̄, s²). A statistic is unbiased if its expectation equals the population parameter: E(x̄) = μ always holds for the sample mean.

Unbiased Variance

The estimator with divisor (n − 1) is the unbiased sample variance:

  • s² = Σ(x − x̄)²/(n − 1)

Why n − 1: deviations are measured from x̄ rather than μ, slightly underestimating spread; the smaller divisor corrects it. At A2, state which estimator you are using — the unbiased one is the default.

Distribution of the Sample Mean

For a sample of size n from a population with mean μ and variance σ²:

  • E(x̄) = μ and Var(x̄) = σ²/n

Averaging shrinks spread — bigger samples give steadier estimates.

Central Limit Theorem

Whatever the population shape, for large n (rule of thumb n ≥ 30) the sample mean is approximately normal: x̄ ~ N(μ, σ²/n). This is why the normal appears constantly in inference.

Example: population mean 50, s.d. 12, n = 36. Then x̄ ~ N(50, 4) and P(x̄ > 51) = P(Z > 0.5) = 0.3085.

Using x̄ to Estimate

Given sample data, estimate μ by x̄ and σ² by the unbiased s². When the population is normal, x̄ is exactly normal for any n — the CLT is only needed for non-normal populations.

Exam tips: distinguish σ²/σ (population) from s²/s (sample) in notation. Standard error means √(σ²/n) — smaller with larger n. Quote probabilities for x̄ with the variance divided by n; forgetting that division is the classic error.

title: AS Level Biology: Plant Structure and Function, Biodiversity and Conservation
content:
Plant Structure and Function, Biodiversity and Conservation — AS Level Biology

This revision note belongs to the Edexcel International Advanced Subsidiary (IAS) Biology specification, WBI12 Unit 2, Topic 4 Plant Structure and Function, Biodiversity and Conservation. It covers plant cell ultrastructure and the functions of the organelles and cell wall components, starch and cellulose and how their structure fits their role, how cellulose microfibrils and secondary thickening give physical properties to xylem and sclerenchyma fibres, the similarities and differences between sclerenchyma fibres, xylem vessels and phloem and their structure, position and function, the light microscope practical on transverse sections, the uses of plant fibres and starch in sustainability, the importance of water and mineral ions to plants and the practical on mineral deficiency, the tensile strength practical, bacterial growth requirements, antimicrobial plant substances and the aseptic practical, the development of drug testing from Withering’s digitalis to modern three-phased testing, classification and the species concept and the three-domain system, biodiversity and endemism and how they are measured, species richness and the heterozygosity index, the index of diversity and how it is compared between habitats, and the concept of niche and examples of adaptations — behavioural, anatomical and physiological. Every statement the topic is responsible for is covered in its own section or paragraph.

1. Plant cell ultrastructure: what is in a plant cell and why

Plant cells share the common eukaryotic features with animal cells — a plasma membrane (cell surface membrane), cytoplasm and ribosomes — but add several structures that animal cells do not have. The cell wall is a rigid outer layer of cellulose microfibrils embedded in a gel-like matrix; it gives shape and support, prevents the cell from bursting when turgid, and limits uncontrolled expansion. Chloroplasts are double-membraned organelles containing chlorophyll and the enzymes for photosynthesis; inside, stacked membranes (thylakoids, often stacked into grana) carry out the light-dependent reactions, and the surrounding stroma contains the enzymes for the light-independent reactions. Amyloplasts are colourless plastids that store starch; they are found especially in storage organs such as potato tubers. Vacuoles are membrane-bound sacs; a large central vacuole in mature plant cells is filled with cell sap — a watery solution of sugars, salts, pigments and waste — surrounded by the tonoplast membrane, and it maintains turgor pressure and gives the cell its rigidity. Plasmodesmata are thread-like channels through the cell walls of adjacent plant cells, connecting the cytoplasm and allowing communication and transport between cells. Pits are thin regions in the cell wall where the wall is localy thinner or absent, allowing water and solutes to pass between cells; the middle lamella is the layer that cements together the cell walls of adjacent cells. Ribosomes are present (80S in the cytoplasm) and the nucleus, nucleolus, mitochondria and golgi apparatus are all present, as in animal cells, except that plant cells do not have centrioles (higher plants lack them, though they still divide).

2. Recognising plant organelles from electron micrographs

On an electron micrograph of a plant cell you should be able to recognise the plasma membrane, nucleus with nucleolus, chloroplasts with their stacked thylakoid membranes (grana), mitochondria, rough endoplasmic reticulum with ribosomes, golgi (dictyosomes in plants), a large central vacuole with the tonoplast, the cell wall (with middle lamella where two cells meet), and plasmodesmata. Chloroplasts are especially characteristic: the grana appear as stacks of disc-like membranes. Amyloplasts appear as colourless, starch-filled plastids without grana. A good exercise is to label each of these in an EM image and to explain the function of each. Compare the plant cell with an animal cell: plant cells have a cell wall, chloroplasts, a large central vacuole and plasmodesmata, and generally no centrioles, and their shape is more regular because of the wall.

3. Starch and cellulose: polysaccharides that do different jobs

Starch and cellulose are both polymers of glucose, but alpha-glucose for starch and beta-glucose for cellulose, and that difference determines their properties. Alpha-glucose has the hydroxyl groups on the same side of the ring (in the usual representation), so when polymerised with 1,4-glycosidic bonds the chain coils into a helix, forming amylose, and with 1,6-branches forming amylopectin — compact, helical and branched, so starch is an excellent storage material: compact to pack a lot of glucose into little space, and with no osmotic effect, because the large insoluble starch granules do not draw water into the cell by osmosis. Cellulose is made from beta-glucose, in which the hydroxyl on carbon 1 is on the opposite side, so when linked the chain is straight rather than coiled; the linear chains run parallel and form many hydrogen bonds between adjacent chains, making strong cellulose microfibrils. Cellulose microfibrils are the main structural component of the cell wall, giving strength and rigidity; the way they are arranged determines the properties of the cell and of the whole plant. The structure of starch suits it for storage in plant cells; the structure of cellulose suits it for strength and support — two polymers from the same monomer with very different roles because of the different glycosidic bonds and the different shape of the chain.

4. Cellulose microfibrils, secondary thickening and the properties of xylem and sclerenchyma

The physical properties of plant tissues depend on how the cellulose microfibrils are arranged. In a young, growing cell the microfibrils are laid down mainly at right angles to the direction of growth, so the cell can expand in length; when growth stops, the cell can become strengthened by secondary thickening — more cellulose and, in some cells, lignin deposited on the inside of the primary wall — which makes the wall rigid and waterproof. In sclerenchyma fibres, the cells die at maturity and are left with heavily thickened, lignified walls, often with the microfibrils arranged in spiral or ring patterns; the result is strong, flexible but tough fibres that give mechanical support and can be used by humans (for example in textiles and ropes). In xylem vessels, the wall is lignified and the cells are dead at maturity, forming long tubes with the end walls broken down or absent — the vessel elements are linked end to end to form a continuous tube for the transport of water and mineral ions, and the lignified thickening (in rings, spirals or nets) prevents collapse under the negative pressure of the transpiration stream. So the arrangement of cellulose microfibrils and the deposition of lignin determine what a plant part can do: support, flexibility, or transport of water under tension. The secondary thickening of xylem and the lignification of sclerenchyma are the adaptations that let land plants grow tall and stand upright and transport water from the roots to the leaves.

5. Sclerenchyma fibres, xylem vessels and phloem: structure, position and function

Sclerenchyma fibres and xylem vessels provide support and, for xylem, transport; phloem translocates organic solutes. Sclerenchyma fibres are long, narrow cells with thick lignified walls and a small lumen, dead at maturity; they occur in bundles and, because of their strength and flexibility, they give support to stems and leaves and can be used in textiles and ropes. Xylem vessels are long, continuous tubes formed from vessel elements with lignified walls and pits in the walls, dead at maturity with no contents, and their function is transport of water and mineral ions from the roots to the leaves — and they also provide support. Phloem is a living tissue; sieve tube elements are the conducting cells, arranged end to end with perforated end walls (sieve plates) between them, reduced cytoplasm at the edges and no nucleus at maturity; each sieve tube element has a companion cell beside it, connected by plasmodesmata, which keeps the sieve element alive and supplies it with ATP, because the sieve element itself has lost its nucleus and most organelles. Phloem transports organic solutes (mainly sucrose, in solution in water) from sources (leaves, storage organs) to sinks (growing points, roots, developing fruits) by mass flow driven by the pressure gradient built up by the loading of sucrose into the sieve tubes. Compare: sclerenchyma fibres = support, dead, lignified; xylem vessels = support and water/mineral transport, dead, lignified, open tube; phloem = translocation of organic solutes, living sieve tubes with companion cells, perforated end walls, no lignin.

6. Core Practical 7 — transverse sections of roots, stems and leaves

Use a light microscope to make observations, draw and label plan diagrams of transverse sections of roots, stems and leaves, and to observe and label cells of plant tissues, identifying sclerenchyma fibres, phloem, sieve tubes and xylem vessels and their location. To make a transverse section, cut a very thin slice across a stem or root with a razor blade (a sharp blade and a steady hand or a sectioning technique), float the section onto water on a slide, lower a coverslip at an angle, stain if needed (for example with toluidine blue or iodine) to distinguish lignified xylem, sclerenchyma and phloem, and observe under the microscope at several magnifications. In a stem transverse section, note the positions of the epidermis, cortex, the vascular bundles (with xylem toward the inside and phloem toward the outside, and sclerenchyma fibres often outside the phloem in a bundle cap), and the pith in the centre; in roots the vascular tissue is central. Draw a plan diagram (an outline of the whole section showing the arrangement of tissues, not the cells) with the correct relative sizes and positions, label the tissues, give a title and magnification. Then observe and label the cells: look for the thick lignified walls of xylem and sclerenchyma, the sieve plates and companion cells of phloem, and the thin-walled cells of the cortex and pith.

7. Plant fibres and starch in sustainability

Plant fibres and starch can contribute to sustainability and to replacing oil-based plastics. Plant fibres (from sclerenchyma or from phloem fibres) are strong, renewable and biodegradable, and they can be used in textiles, paper, building materials and composites that replace oil-based plastics and synthetic fibres; water transport in plants today parallels the transport of sap and provides a model for how plants already do this. Starch can be used to make bioplastics — for example, starch can be processed into film-forming materials suitable for packaging, plates and disposable items — and because starch is a renewable, biodegradable material made from crops such as potatoes, maize or cassava, it can replace oil-based plastics in some uses. Using plant fibres and starch reduces reliance on oil, is renewable and can be more sustainable if the crops are grown responsibly; but there are trade-offs: land, water and energy for the crops, possible competition with food production, and the need to assess the whole life cycle. The use of plant products to replace oil-based plastics is a topic that connects plant structure (cellulose and starch), to sustainability, to human decisions informed by science.

8. Water and inorganic ions to plants, and mineral deficiency

Plants need water for photosynthesis (a reactant and the medium in which it happens), for transport (water is the solvent for minerals and for sucrose in the phloem), for support (turgor pressure keeps non-woody parts rigid), and for cooling (transpiration). Water enters the roots by osmosis from the soil and moves up the xylem. Inorganic ions are essential: nitrate ions (NO3-) are needed for making amino acids, proteins, DNA and chlorophyll — a deficiency causes stunted growth and yellowing of older leaves (chlorosis); calcium ions are needed for the middle lamella (pectin in the cell wall) and for cell membranes — a deficiency gives stunted growth and necrosis of the growing point and young leaves; magnesium ions are the central atom in chlorophyll — a deficiency causes chlorosis of the older leaves. A recommended additional practical is to investigate plant mineral deficiencies: grow plants in a solution with all minerals (complete) and in solutions missing one of nitrate, calcium or magnesium, observe and measure the effects on growth and leaf colour over weeks, and explain the results in terms of the roles of the missing ion.

9. Core Practical 8 — tensile strength of plant fibres

Determine the tensile strength of plant fibres — the force a fibre can take before it breaks. A typical method: take strands of a plant fibre (for example the fibres from celery stalks or nettle stems, or a piece of a plant stem with visible fibres), clamp one end, hang weights from the other, and add weights until the fibre breaks; record the mass (converted to a force, weight = mass × g) needed to break the fibre. Repeat for several fibres, present the results, and compare fibres from different plants or different parts of a plant. Safety: sharp blades and falling weights. The practical shows how the arrangement of cellulose and lignin gives the fibre its strength, and connects the cell-level structure to a macroscopic useful property.

10. Conditions for bacterial growth

Bacteria need certain conditions to grow: a supply of nutrients (carbon, nitrogen, minerals and, for some, specific organic factors), water, a suitable temperature (most pathogenic bacteria around 37 °C, though many grow across a range), oxygen (some need it — aerobic bacteria — some do not — anaerobic bacteria — and some can manage with or without), a suitable pH, and, for many, time to multiply. In the laboratory these conditions can be met and controlled: cultures are grown in nutrient broth or on agar plates, at a set temperature (often 25 °C for environmental organisms and 37 °C for those that grow at body temperature), with or without oxygen, and in sterile conditions so that only the desired organism grows. Aseptic technique is essential to avoid contaminating the culture or releasing harmful bacteria into the environment — sterilise equipment (by flame or autoclave), work near a flame to create an upward air current, work quickly and cover the plates, and dispose of cultures by sterilising before disposal.

11. Antimicrobial plant substances and the aseptic practical

Substances derived from plants can have antimicrobial and other therapeutic properties. Some plant extracts inhibit the growth of bacteria or fungi — for example, garlic has been traditionally used and does have some antibacterial effects; other plants yield useful compounds (aspirin from willow bark, morphine from poppies, and many modern drugs are derived from plants). A recommended additional practical is to investigate the antimicrobial properties of plants, including aseptic techniques for the safe handling of bacteria: prepare agar plates, use sterile swabs or paper discs impregnated with different plant extracts, incubate and measure the zones of inhibition around the discs — the diameter of the clear zone where bacteria did not grow — and compare the effectiveness of different extracts or the same extract at different concentrations. Use aseptic technique: sterilise the discs and loops, work near a flame, spread the bacteria in a controlled way, seal the plates with tape (but do not seal all the way so they do not become anaerobic), and incubate at a safe temperature. Measure the zones of inhibition and record them, including in a table, and draw a conclusion about which extract is most effective and about concentration.

12. Drug testing: from Withering’s digitalis soup to modern trials

The development of drug testing has moved from historic, uncontrolled methods to contemporary, rigorous protocols. William Withering’s digitalis soup in the 18th century was an early use of a plant-derived medicine — foxglove (Digitalis) — for dropsy (oedema), tested by trial and observation on patients, but with no controls, no placebo, no blinding and no large sample, so the evidence was weak and mixed with other treatments. Modern drug testing uses a sequence of phases: pre-clinical testing in the lab and on animals; clinical trials in humans in three phases — Phase 1 tests safety in a small group, Phase 2 tests efficacy and side effects in a larger group of patients, and Phase 3 tests the drug against the current treatment or a placebo in a large group, in a double-blind trial (neither the patient nor the clinician knows which treatment is being used) so that expectations do not bias the result. Placebos are used to control for the placebo effect (improvement from the belief of being treated). The modern protocol — double-blind, placebo-controlled, multi-centre, large trials — is far more reliable than Withering’s soup, and it protects patients and produces trustworthy evidence. Students should be able to describe this progression and evaluate the designs.

13. Classification: organising life, the species concept and the three domains

Classification is a means of organising the variety of life based on relationships between organisms, using differences and similarities in phenotypes (observable features) and in genotypes (the DNA and the proteins the DNA codes for). It is built around the species concept — a species is a group of organisms that can interbreed and produce fertile offspring — and a hierarchy of groups above it: genus, family, order, class, phylum and kingdom, with organisms grouped because they share common ancestry. The classification has changed as new data — especially molecular evidence from DNA and protein sequences — have come in, leading to critical evaluation of existing groupings and new taxonomic groupings. The three-domain system, based on molecular evidence, divides life into the Archaea, the Bacteria and the Eukarya (which includes all eukaryotes, plants, animals, fungi and protists); the Archaea are distinct from the Bacteria and include organisms that often live in extreme environments, and the evidence from ribosomal RNA sequences and other molecular data led to this reclassification, replacing the older five-kingdom system. The process of critical evaluation of new data by the scientific community — comparing, testing and debating — is what leads to new groupings and to science being self-correcting.

14. Biodiversity, endemism and threats from human activity

Biodiversity is the variety of life — the variety within a habitat, within a species or across the whole planet; it can refer to species richness (the number of different species in a habitat) or to genetic diversity within a species. Endemism is the state of a species being found only in one particular place (an endemic species, such as a plant found only on a particular island). Over time the variety of life has become extensive through evolution, but it is now being threatened by human activity — habitat destruction (deforestation, drainage, conversion to agriculture), over-exploitation (hunting, fishing, logging), pollution, the introduction of invasive species, and climate change, all of which can reduce biodiversity and cause extinctions. Biodiversity matters because it provides ecosystem services, genetic resources for medicines and crops, and is itself valuable; its loss affects ecosystems, food security and human health. Understanding the causes of the loss is important so that conservation measures can be designed to address them.

15. Measuring biodiversity: species richness, genetic diversity and heterozygosity

Biodiversity can be measured in different ways. Species richness — the number of different species in a given area — is one simple measure of biodiversity within a habitat; a habitat with more species is generally more diverse, though this ignores the abundance of each species (a habitat dominated by one common species and several rare ones may have the same species richness as one where all are equally common). Genetic diversity within a species can be measured by the heterozygosity index (also called heterozygosity): the proportion of individuals in a population that are heterozygous at a locus. It is calculated as the number of heterozygotes divided by the number of individuals in the population (for a single locus); a higher heterozygosity means more genetic diversity within that population. This matters because genetic diversity helps a population adapt to changes, resist disease and avoid the problems of inbreeding; loss of genetic diversity raises the risk of extinction.

16. Comparing habitats with the index of diversity

Biodiversity can be compared between different habitats using the formula for the index of diversity, D: D = (N(N−1)) / (Σ n(n−1)), where N is the total number of organisms of all species in the habitat, and n is the number of organisms of a particular species. Calculation: for each species, work out n(n−1); sum these to get Σ n(n−1); then divide N(N−1) by that sum to give D, the index of diversity. Worked example: in a habitat with species counts 10, 15, 5, 2 (N = 32): Σ n(n−1) = (10×9)+(15×14)+(5×4)+(2×1) = 90+210+20+2 = 322; N(N−1) = 32×31 = 992; D = 992 / 322 ≈ 3.08. A larger D means a more diverse habitat, because it reflects both the number of species and how evenly the individuals are distributed among them. To compare habitats, calculate D for each and compare the values, stating which is more diverse and what that suggests. The formula must be applied correctly: calculate n(n−1) for each species, sum them, and divide N(N−1) by the sum.

17. Niche and adaptations: behavioural, anatomical and physiological

A niche is the role of an organism in a habitat — the conditions in which it lives and the resources it uses, and how it interacts with other organisms; it is more than just the physical place (the habitat) where it lives, and no two species can occupy exactly the same niche for long because of competition. Adaptations are features that help an organism survive and reproduce in its niche, and they can be behavioural, anatomical or physiological. Behavioural adaptations are things the organism does — for example migration to avoid harsh conditions, hunting in packs, basking to warm up, or the specific foraging behaviour of a bird. Anatomical (structural) adaptations are physical features of the body — for example the shape of a bird’s beak for its food, the camouflage colours of a prey animal, the thick fur of an arctic mammal, or the long beak of a nectar-feeding bird. Physiological adaptations are internal functions — for example a camel’s ability to tolerate dehydration and to conserve water, the production of venom by a snake, the production of antifreeze proteins in some polar fish, or the specialised nitrogen excretion of desert animals. The concept of niche and the types of adaptation help explain how different organisms fit into their environments and how competition and adaptation shape communities.

18. Hardy-Weinberg, zoos and seed banks: allele frequencies and conservation

The Hardy-Weinberg equation tests whether a population is evolving. In a large population with random mating, no mutation, no migration and no selection, allele frequencies stay constant from generation to generation. Write the frequency of the dominant allele as p and the recessive allele as q. Then p + q = 1, and the genotype frequencies are p squared for the homozygous dominant, 2pq for the heterozygote and q squared for the homozygous recessive, so p squared + 2pq + q squared = 1. The value of the equation is that it gives a null expectation: if the observed genotype frequencies differ significantly from it, one of the assumptions is being broken and the allele frequencies are changing, which is evolution happening in front of you.

A worked use: a recessive condition affects 1 in 10 000 people, so q squared = 0.0001, q = 0.01 and p = 0.99. The carrier frequency is 2pq = 2 times 0.99 times 0.01 = 0.0198, about 1 in 50. That is why a rare recessive allele can be common in carriers while the disease itself stays rare, and it is the calculation the mark scheme wants rather than a guess from the disease frequency.

Conservation of genetic diversity is the other half of this section. Zoos use captive breeding programmes with studbooks to decide which animals pair, so that inbreeding is minimised and unrelated individuals are introduced; they also support scientific research and education, and run reintroduction programmes that prepare animals for the wild. The risks are that captive populations are small, so genetic drift and inbreeding reduce diversity, and that animals bred in captivity may lack the behaviour needed to survive on release. Seed banks store seeds at low temperature and low moisture, testing viability periodically and germinating samples to grow fresh seed, which protects genetic diversity far more cheaply than keeping animals. Their limits are that not all seeds survive drying, so some species need cryopreservation or living collections, and that a bank protects genes rather than the habitat the species needs. Evaluate both by naming what they conserve, what they cost and what they cannot do.

19. How to use this note and what to revise next

Use these notes section by section, checking that you can identify plant cell ultrastructure and organelles in an electron micrograph and state their functions, explain how starch and cellulose differ in structure and role, describe the secondary thickening and the properties of xylem vessels and sclerenchyma fibres, compare sclerenchyma fibres, xylem vessels and phloem in structure, position and function, carry out the transverse section and tensile strength practicals and explain the variables and safety, describe the conditions for bacterial growth and the aseptic practical, describe the development of drug testing from Withering’s digitalis to modern three-phased trials and evaluate the designs, define classification and the species concept, describe the three-domain system and the molecular evidence for it, define biodiversity and endemism and the threats from human activity, carry out the species richness and heterozygosity and index of diversity calculations, and define niche and give behavioural, anatomical and physiological adaptations. After this topic, revise Topic 3 Cell structure, reproduction and development (plant and animal cells, division) and Topic 5 Energy flow, ecosystems and the environment, because classification and biodiversity sit within ecology.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Simpson's index, applied to a quadrat with 10 daisies and 5 dandelions: N = 15, D = 1 − Σ(n ÷ N)² = 1 − [(10 ÷ 15)² + (5 ÷ 15)²] = 1 − (0.444 + 0.111) = 0.556. Use the index to compare two sites; a higher value means greater diversity.
  • Xylem and phloem: xylem transports water and minerals upwards and is made of dead, lignified cells with no end walls, so the water column is continuous. Phloem transports sucrose and amino acids in both directions and is made of living sieve tube elements with companion cells. Name the direction of transport and the living or dead state of the cells.
  • Cellulose versus starch: cellulose is made of β-glucose units linked alternately, which allows hydrogen bonding between chains, forming strong microfibrils. Starch is made of α-glucose, is coiled and is used for storage. The different glucose isomer explains the different shapes and functions.
  • Conservation: a protected area works only if the populations inside it are large enough to be viable. Name the factor, such as a wildlife corridor, that connects populations, because isolated populations lose genetic diversity over time.

Typical mistakes

  • Calling xylem living. Xylem vessels are dead, hollow, lignified tubes with no end walls, which is what allows a continuous water column. Phloem sieve tubes are living and supported by companion cells.
  • Giving sclerenchyma a transport role. Sclerenchyma fibres provide support only; xylem transports water and mineral ions and also supports, and phloem translocates sugars and amino acids.
  • Inverting the heterozygosity index. It is the number of heterozygotes divided by the number of individuals in the population, so it cannot exceed 1. A value of 1 would mean every individual is heterozygous.
  • Reading a diversity index the wrong way round. Use the formula given on the paper and then say which site has the higher diversity; do not assume a small number means a diverse habitat.
  • Missing the assumptions in a Hardy-Weinberg calculation. State that the population is large, mating is random and there is no selection or migration, and say that a significant difference in allele frequency between generations is evidence that one assumption is broken.
  • Claiming aseptic technique keeps everything sterile. Aseptic technique keeps contamination out of the culture and the worker safe: sterilise the loop, flame the neck of the bottle, work near a flame, and dispose of plates in the correct way. The apparatus and the medium are sterilised before use, which is a different step.
  • Describing drug trials without their purpose. A placebo controls for the expectation of improvement, a double-blind design stops the patient or the doctor influencing the result, and the three phases test safety, then effectiveness and dose, then comparison with existing treatment in a larger group.
  • Using the three-domain system without the evidence. Archaea, Bacteria and Eukarya were separated after molecular evidence, particularly ribosomal RNA sequences, showed that the archaea are as different from bacteria as both are from eukaryotes. New data changing a classification is a strength of the system, not a flaw.

Exam-style questions

  1. In a population of 2 000 plants, 120 are heterozygous at a particular locus. Calculate the heterozygosity index. Answer: 120 / 2 000 = 0.06. Only 6 per cent of the population is heterozygous, so the genetic diversity at that locus is low.
  2. A recessive allele causing a disease is present in 1 in 2 500 births. Assuming Hardy-Weinberg conditions, calculate the carrier frequency. Answer: q squared = 1 / 2 500 = 0.0004, so q = 0.02 and p = 0.98. The carrier frequency is 2pq = 2 times 0.98 times 0.02 = 0.0392, about 1 in 25.
  3. Explain how secondary thickening adapts a xylem vessel for its function. Answer: lignin is deposited in the wall, which makes it rigid so the vessel does not collapse under tension, and it makes the wall waterproof so water is not lost sideways; the strengthening also supports the plant.
  4. Describe how you would compare the tensile strength of fibres from two plant stems. Answer: extract fibres of equal length from each stem, clamp each in turn and hang masses from it until it breaks, recording the mass that causes failure. Control fibre length, thickness and the point of attachment, repeat each measurement and compare means. The fibre that withstands the greater mass has the greater tensile strength.
  5. Explain why a seed bank may conserve genetic diversity more effectively than a zoo. Answer: seeds are small, so many individuals and many species can be stored in a small space at low cost, and a large sample preserves more alleles than a small captive population that suffers inbreeding and genetic drift. A zoo is still needed for species whose seed cannot be stored or whose behaviour must be learned.
  6. Explain the evidence that led to the three-domain classification. Answer: comparisons of ribosomal RNA and other molecular sequences showed that archaeal sequences differ from bacterial sequences as much as both differ from eukaryotes, so the archaea were placed in their own domain alongside Bacteria and Eukarya. The classification is based on genotype as well as phenotype, and it is revised when new molecular data are critically evaluated.
  7. Withering's digitalis treatment and a modern double-blind trial are both tests of a drug. Explain two ways in which the modern protocol is an improvement. Answer: the modern trial uses a control group given a placebo, so improvement caused by expectation is separated from the effect of the drug, and it is randomised and double-blind, so neither patient nor doctor knows who received which treatment and bias is removed. It also uses measured doses and larger samples, so the result can be tested statistically.

How many quadrats are enough: the species-accumulation curve

Species richness is the number of different species in a habitat. It cannot be counted directly in a large area, so a sample is taken. A single quadrat gives a poor estimate, and the question is how many quadrats are needed before the estimate stops changing. Plotting the cumulative number of species against the number of quadrats answers that question.

Key: species richness = the number of different species recorded; the curve is a running total, so it can only rise or stay level.

Why the curve rises steeply and then levels off

The first few quadrats each contain species not yet seen, so the curve climbs quickly. As sampling continues, most common species have already been recorded and each new quadrat adds fewer. The point where the curve flattens is the point at which more quadrats would add little information, and it is a reasonable sample size for the habitat.

Random placement and bias

Quadrats must be placed at random, for example with random coordinates, so that the sample is not chosen by the person sampling. Placing quadrats where the species look most interesting biases the count upwards for rare species and gives a misleading picture of the habitat. A random sample gives an estimate that can be compared between habitats.

Using the curve in a habitat survey

Two habitats can have different species richness, but a fair comparison needs the same sampling effort in each. If one habitat's curve is still rising at the end of the survey, its true richness has not been reached and the comparison is incomplete. In an answer, state the number of quadrats, say whether the curve had levelled off and explain how that affects confidence in the result.

title: Sampling and Estimation — Study Notes
content:
Sampling and Estimation

Edexcel International A Level Mathematics — Statistics 2 (WST02), sat at A2.

Populations, Samples, Statistics

A parameter describes the population (μ, σ²); a statistic describes the sample (x̄, s²). A statistic is unbiased if its expectation equals the population parameter: E(x̄) = μ always holds for the sample mean.

Unbiased Variance

The estimator with divisor (n − 1) is the unbiased sample variance:

  • s² = Σ(x − x̄)²/(n − 1)

Why n − 1: deviations are measured from x̄ rather than μ, slightly underestimating spread; the smaller divisor corrects it. At A2, state which estimator you are using — the unbiased one is the default.

Distribution of the Sample Mean

For a sample of size n from a population with mean μ and variance σ²:

  • E(x̄) = μ and Var(x̄) = σ²/n

Averaging shrinks spread — bigger samples give steadier estimates.

Central Limit Theorem

Whatever the population shape, for large n (rule of thumb n ≥ 30) the sample mean is approximately normal: x̄ ~ N(μ, σ²/n). This is why the normal appears constantly in inference.

Example: population mean 50, s.d. 12, n = 36. Then x̄ ~ N(50, 4) and P(x̄ > 51) = P(Z > 0.5) = 0.3085.

Using x̄ to Estimate

Given sample data, estimate μ by x̄ and σ² by the unbiased s². When the population is normal, x̄ is exactly normal for any n — the CLT is only needed for non-normal populations.

Exam tips: distinguish σ²/σ (population) from s²/s (sample) in notation. Standard error means √(σ²/n) — smaller with larger n. Quote probabilities for x̄ with the variance divided by n; forgetting that division is the classic error.

Exam method: estimators and sample variance

The sample mean x̄ is an unbiased estimate of the population mean μ. The unbiased estimate of the population variance is s² = Σ(x − x̄)²/(n − 1), which divides by n − 1 rather than n. Using n gives the population variance of the sample, which tends to underestimate the true value.

When the sum of squared deviations is given, divide it by n − 1 directly. When the raw data are given, it is quicker to compute s² = (Σx² − n x̄²)/(n − 1).

A random sample gives each member of the population an equal chance of selection. Bias means the estimator does not equal the parameter on average, so the sample must be random to make the estimate reliable.

The standard error of the sample mean is σ/√n. It decreases as the sample size grows, so larger samples give more precise estimates.

Exam cue: Name the estimator and state whether it is unbiased, because the question often asks for both the value and the reason.

Population and sample

A population is the complete set of items being studied, and a sample is the subset that is actually measured. A sample is used because measuring the whole population is too slow or too costly. A random sample gives every member an equal chance of selection, and a sample that is not random may be biased. A sample statistic, such as the sample mean, is used to estimate a population parameter, such as the population mean.

Worked example: an unbiased estimate of the population variance

A sample of size 5 has values 4, 6, 7, 8 and 10. The sample mean is 35 ÷ 5 = 7. The sum of squared deviations from the mean is 9 + 1 + 0 + 1 + 9 = 20. Dividing by n gives 4, but the unbiased estimate of the population variance divides by n − 1, which gives s² = 20 ÷ 4 = 5. The divisor n − 1 is used because the sample mean is itself estimated from the data, and it corrects the tendency of the divisor n to underestimate the population variance.

Confidence intervals for a mean

For a large sample from a population with known standard deviation σ, a 95% confidence interval for the population mean is the sample mean plus or minus 1.96 multiplied by σ divided by the square root of n. The quantity σ divided by the square root of n is the standard error. A wider interval means less precision, and increasing the sample size narrows the interval. Give the interval as two values and state the confidence level in the conclusion.

title: Magnetism & Electromagnetism — Study Notes
content:
Magnetism & Electromagnetism

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): magnets & fields; magnetic effect of a current; force on a current-carrying conductor; motor effect; electromagnetic induction (Extended); transformers (Extended).

1. Magnets and fields

Iron/steel/cobalt/nickel; like poles repel. Field lines exit N, enter S; compass plotting; plotting compass aligns with field. Induced magnetism: iron (temporary) vs steel (permanent).

2. Electromagnets

Solenoid field like a bar magnet; strength ↑ with current, turns, iron core. Uses: relays, scrapyard crane, electric bell, speaker. Hard/soft magnetic materials choose permanent vs core use.

3. Force on a current-carrying conductor

F = BIL, direction by Fleming's left hand (fIeld, current, force). Reversing current or field reverses force. D.C. motor: coil, commutator reverses current each half-turn for continuous rotation; speed/torque ↑ with current, field strength, turns/area.

4. Electromagnetic induction (Extended)

Induced e.m.f. when a conductor cuts field lines or flux changes. Fleming's right hand (generator). Factors: speed, field strength, turns. A.C. generator: slip rings; dynamo effect; Lenz's law opposes change (direction of induced current).

5. Transformers (Extended)

Vp/Vs = Np/Ns; Pin ≈ Pout (100% assumed): IpVp = IsVs. Step-up raises V, lowers I → lower I²R transmission losses; a.c. required (changing flux).

Magnetic fields and electromagnets

Like magnetic poles repel and unlike poles attract. Outside a bar magnet, field lines run from the north pole to the south pole. A solenoid is a coil of wire; its field is strengthened by increasing the current, increasing the number of turns, or placing a soft iron core inside it. An electromagnet can be switched on and off by the current, unlike a permanent magnet.

A current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field experiences a force, which is the basis of the motor effect used in electric motors.

Exam tip: when asked how to make an electromagnet stronger, give two changes, such as more turns and a larger current.

Worked example: force on a current-carrying conductor

A wire of length 0.5 m carries a current of 3 A at right angles to a magnetic field of flux density 0.2 T. The force is F = B × I × L = 0.2 × 3 × 0.5 = 0.3 N. The force is at right angles to both the field and the current, and the direction can be found with Fleming's left-hand rule: the first finger is the field, the second finger is the current and the thumb is the motion.

Worked example: a transformer

An ideal step-down transformer has 1000 turns on the primary and 100 turns on the secondary. A primary voltage of 230 V gives a secondary voltage of Vs = Vp × Ns ÷ Np = 230 × 100 ÷ 1000 = 23 V. If the primary current is 0.5 A, the secondary current is Is = Ip × Vp ÷ Vs = 0.5 × 230 ÷ 23 = 5 A. The input power is 230 × 0.5 = 115 W and the output power is 23 × 5 = 115 W, so the ideal transformer loses no power. A step-down transformer lowers the voltage and raises the current.

Why a transformer needs alternating current

A transformer works by electromagnetic induction. The changing flux in the iron core induces a voltage in the secondary coil only while the flux is changing. A steady direct current produces a steady flux, so no voltage is induced and the transformer does not work with direct current.

Exam point: quote the transformer equation in the form Vp ÷ Vs = Np ÷ Ns, and check whether the question assumes an ideal transformer, where input and output power are equal.
