title: Quadratics — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Quadratics

Mathematics — AS (9709). A quadratic has the form ax² + bx + c with a ≠ 0. Master three tools: completing the square, the discriminant, and inequalities.

Key areas to revise

  • Completing the Square
  • The Discriminant
  • Quadratic Inequalities
  • Curve and Line Intersections

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Key points to remember

For ax² + bx + c = 0, the roots come from the quadratic formula. The discriminant b² − 4ac decides the type of roots: positive gives two distinct real roots, zero gives one repeated root, and negative gives no real roots. Completing the square writes the expression as a(x + p)² + q, which gives the turning point at (−p, q).

To solve a quadratic inequality, sketch the graph, find where it crosses the x-axis, and read off the range where the curve lies above or below the axis. Use the discriminant to show that a quadratic is always positive or always negative. Show each step, because method marks are given for a correct rearrangement even when the final answer is wrong.

title: Exam technique: Further Algebra
content:
### What earns the marks
For modulus equations, both branches solved earn a mark each. For inequalities, the two-sided split earns the method mark with the and/or structure correct. For equal-roots problems, discriminant zero stated earns the first mark and -b/2a earns the second.
### Traps
Error: one modulus branch only. Correction: split both signs. Error: between-answers for outside-or inequalities. Correction: >= splits outward. Error: non-zero discriminants with equal roots claimed. Correction: equal roots force zero.

title: Energy, Work & Power
content:
Energy, Work & Power

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2023–2025): stores and transfers, KE/PE, work, energy sources, power, efficiency.

1. Energy stores & transfers

Stores: kinetic, gravitational, elastic, chemical, nuclear, thermal. Transfer mechanisms: mechanically, electrically, heating, waves. Energy is conserved overall; transfers via work done.

2. Formulas

  • KE = ½mv²; PE = mgh.
  • Work W = Fd (force along displacement, joules).
  • Power P = W/t = E/t; P = Fv for constant speed.

Example: 0.5 kg at 4 m/s: KE = 4 J. Lift 2 kg by 3 m: PE = 60 J (g = 10).

3. Energy sources

Renewable: solar, wind, hydro, geothermal, biofuel, tidal — replenished. Non-renewable: fossil fuels, nuclear — finite. Discuss reliability, cost, pollution for "evaluate" questions.

4. Efficiency

Efficiency = useful output ÷ total input (×100%). Sankey diagrams show losses.

Example: motor: 150 J useful from 600 J → 25%.

5. Energy-chain problems

Equating KE loss to PE gain: v = √(2gh) for frictionless drop; braking distance grows with v².

Exam tips: define work as "force × distance moved in the direction of the force"; use g = 10 unless told otherwise; efficiency is a ratio — no units.

title: Exam technique: Representation via Numerical Measures
content:
### What earns the marks
For skewness direction, mean vs median comparison stated earns the mark. For box plots, all five values labelled earn one mark and the skew comment earns the second. For outlier checks, the fence calculation shown earns the method mark.
### Traps
Error: skew direction flipped. Correction: tail side names the skew. Error: quartiles mislabeled on plots. Correction: order min, Q1, median, Q3, max. Error: max value called an outlier by eye. Correction: test against the fence.
### Worked example
Data: 2, 4, 5, 5, 6, 7, 20. The mean is 49 / 7 = 7 and the median is 5, so the mean is larger and the skew is positive. The lower half {2, 4, 5} has median 4 (Q1). The upper half {6, 7, 20} has median 7 (Q3). IQR = 3, so the upper fence is 7 + 1.5 × 3 = 11.5, and 20 is an outlier.
### Check yourself
A box plot has its median closer to the lower quartile than to the upper quartile. Which way is the data skewed, and what words should the answer use? The data is positively skewed, because the longer right-hand part of the box shows the upper values are more spread out.

title: Electric Fields and Capacitance — Study Notes
content:
Electric Fields and Capacitance

Coulomb's Law

F = q₁q₂/(4πε₀r²). Field strength E = F/q (N C⁻¹); for a point charge E = q/(4πε₀r²).

Uniform Fields

Between parallel plates: E = V/d, constant.

Example: 2 kV across 5 mm: E = 400 kV m⁻¹. An electron feels F = eE ≈ 6.4 × 10⁻¹⁴ N toward the positive plate.

Potential

V = W/q, scalar; E = −dV/dr. Potential energy of q at V is qV.

Capacitance

C = Q/V (farads). Energy stored: W = ½QV = ½CV².

Combinations: parallel adds (C = C₁ + C₂); series: 1/C = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂ (opposite to resistors).

Example: 10 μF and 20 μF in series: 1/C = 1/10 + 1/20 → C ≈ 6.7 μF.

Charging and Discharging

Exponential: V = V₀ e^(−t/RC). Time constant RC: after one RC, V falls to 37%. Half-life t½ = 0.69 RC.

Exam tips: field points from high to low potential; in discharge problems identify which quantity (V, Q or I) decays — all share the same exponential factor.

title: Exam technique: Transformations and Vectors
content:
### What earns the marks
For translations and vector arithmetic, each component computed separately earns credit: show x and y lines. For magnitude, the root-of-sum-of-squares line earns the method mark before evaluation. For reflections and rotations, the coordinate rule stated ((y; -x) for 90 degrees clockwise) earns the method mark. For describing transformations, all three of type, centre or line, and size or angle are needed for full marks.
### Traps
Error: writing column vectors as bracket rows that lose a row. Correction: use (x; y) form and keep both components. Error: (100) or 14 for the magnitude of (6; 8). Correction: square, add, then root. Error: (-y; x) for a clockwise rotation. Correction: clockwise is (y; -x). Error: negating both coordinates for a single-axis reflection. Correction: one axis changes, the other stays.

title: Coordinate Geometry — Study Notes
content:
Coordinate Geometry

Cambridge International AS & A Level Mathematics 9709, Paper 1. Nearly every question here is the same three-step job: translate the geometry into equations, solve them, then read the answer back against the diagram.

Core results

  • Distance between (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂) is √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²).
  • The midpoint is ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2).
  • Gradient m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁). Parallel lines share a gradient; perpendicular lines satisfy m₁m₂ = −1.

Finding the equation of a line

With a point and a gradient, use y − y₁ = m(x − x₁). With two points, find the gradient first. Give the answer in the form the question requests: y = mx + c, or ax + by + c = 0 with integer coefficients when it asks for that form.

Example: find the line through (−2, 5) perpendicular to 3x − 4y = 1. The given line has gradient 3/4, so the required gradient is −4/3. Then y − 5 = −4/3(x + 2), which rearranges to 4x + 3y − 7 = 0.

Intersections of a line and a curve

Points of intersection satisfy both equations at once, so substitute one into the other. The resulting quadratic has two roots, one repeated root, or no real roots, and the discriminant tells you which. Parallel lines give no intersection, and a repeated root means the line touches the curve.

Example: y = 2x − 1 and x² + y² = 10. Substituting gives 5x² − 4x − 9 = 0, so (5x − 9)(x + 1) = 0. The points are (9/5, 13/5) and (−1, −3).

Circles

A circle with centre (a, b) and radius r has equation (x − a)² + (y − b)² = r². Expanding gives the general form x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0, where the centre is (−g, −f) and the radius is √(g² + f² − c). To test a point, substitute its coordinates: a value below r² means inside, equal means on the circle, above means outside.

Example: x² + y² − 6x + 4y − 12 = 0 has centre (3, −2) and radius √(9 + 4 + 12) = 5.

Tangents and normals

A tangent touches the circle at one point and is perpendicular to the radius through that point. Find the gradient of the radius from the centre, take the negative reciprocal for the tangent, then use the point–gradient form. The normal is the radius itself, so it passes through the centre.

Example: the tangent to (x − 3)² + (y + 2)² = 25 at (7, 1). The radius has gradient 3/4, so the tangent has gradient −4/3, and its equation is 4x + 3y − 31 = 0.

Exam technique

  • Draw a rough diagram first; it shows whether a point should be inside or outside a circle before any algebra is done.
  • With a "show that" instruction, finish with the exact expression that was asked for.
  • To check a tangent, confirm that the distance from the centre to the line equals the radius.

title: Measurement & Units — Study Notes
content:
Measurement & Units

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): 1.1 lengths & volumes; 1.2 density; 1.3 forces & motion context (measurements) — plus measurement techniques, SI units, scalars/vectors.

1. Measuring

  • Length: ruler (mm), vernier calipers (0.1 mm / 0.01 cm), micrometer screw gauge (0.01 mm).
  • Volume: measuring cylinder read at the meniscus bottom; regular solids by calculation; irregular by displacement (eureka can).
  • Time: stopwatch — human reaction time ±0.2 s; measure many oscillations and divide (e.g. 20 T).
  • Pendulum: T = time/oscillations; f = 1/T.

2. SI units and prefixes

QuantityUnitSymbol
lengthmetrem
masskilogramkg
timeseconds
currentampereA
temperaturekelvin (°C used)K

kilo 10³; centi 10⁻²; milli 10⁻³; micro 10⁻⁶; nano 10⁻⁹.

3. Scalars and vectors

Scalars: distance, speed, mass, energy, time. Vectors: displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, weight, momentum. Vector addition by scale diagram (tip-to-tail) or by components.

4. Density

ρ = m/V (kg/m³ or g/cm³; 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³). Determining: mass on balance; volume by displacement. Floating: ρobject < ρfluid.

5. Accuracy and improvements

Avoid parallax (eye level with reading), zero errors (subtract the zero reading), measure multiple laps for small times. Suggest improvements by naming the error and the fix.

Making accurate measurements

The SI base unit of length is the metre (m), and common multiples and submultiples are given in kilometres, centimetres and millimetres. A micrometer screw gauge measures small lengths to about 0.01 mm. A zero error is a reading that is not zero when it should be, and every reading must be corrected by it. Parallax error occurs when the eye is not directly in line with the scale, and it is avoided by reading the scale straight on.

Repeating a measurement and calculating the mean reduces random error. Time many oscillations of a pendulum and divide by the number, to reduce the effect of reaction time on a stopwatch.

Exam tip: give a reading to the same precision as the instrument, and state the unit.

Significant figures and decimal places

Significant figures count from the first non-zero digit. The number 0.00304 has three significant figures, and 4500 to two significant figures is written as 4.5 × 10³. Decimal places count digits after the point. When rounding a measurement, give the answer to the precision of the least precise measurement used in the calculation, and do not show more digits than the data justify.

Worked example: converting between units

To convert 2.5 km into metres, multiply by 1000 to get 2500 m. To convert 450 cm² into m², divide by 10 000, because one square metre is 100 cm × 100 cm, which gives 0.045 m². A common error is to convert a length by 100 when an area or a volume is required. For volume, one cubic metre is 1 000 000 cm³, so 3 m³ is 3 000 000 cm³.

Reading scales and measuring accurately

To read an analogue scale, identify the value of the smallest division, then estimate the reading to a tenth of that division. Record every reading with the same number of decimal places as the scale. A measurement of the thickness of a sheet of paper is made more accurate by measuring many sheets together and dividing by their number, which reduces the effect of the reading error on a single sheet.

title: AS Level Mathematics: Sequences and Series
content:
AS Level Mathematics: Sequences and Series

A sequence is an ordered list of numbers generated by a rule; a series is the sum of a sequence. Two families dominate the syllabus: arithmetic (add a constant each time) and geometric (multiply by a constant each time). This note builds the topic from zero: the nth term and sum formulas for both families with derivations, σ notation, recurrence relations, the convergence condition for geometric series, and the applied problems — savings, depreciation, loans — where the formulas earn marks. Every formula is derived once so it can be rebuilt if forgotten.

Arithmetic sequences

nth term: u_n = a + (n - 1)d
sum of n terms: S_n = (n/2)[2a + (n - 1)d] = (n/2)(first + last)

a = first term, d = common difference

Worked example. An arithmetic sequence has first term 5 and common difference 4. Find the 20th term and the sum of the first 20 terms.

u_20 = 5 + 19 × 4 = 81
S_20 = (20/2)(5 + 81) = 10 × 86 = 860

Worked example 2 (working backwards). The 5th term is 17 and the 12th is 45. Find a and d.

u_5: a + 4d = 17
u_12: a + 11d = 45
subtract: 7d = 28  →  d = 4;  a = 17 - 16 = 1

Arithmetic series and the sum formula

The sum formula is Gauss's trick: pair the first and last terms, the second and second-last, and so on; each pair has the same total, and there are n/2 pairs.

Worked example. Find the sum of the first 50 positive even numbers.

a = 2, d = 2, n = 50
last term = 2 + 49 × 2 = 100
S = (50/2)(2 + 100) = 25 × 102 = 2550

Worked example 2 (unknown n). The sum of the first n terms of 3, 7, 11, ... is 210. Find n.

210 = (n/2)[6 + 4(n - 1)] = (n/2)(4n + 2) = 2n² + n
2n² + n - 210 = 0
(2n + 21)(n - 10) = 0  →  n = 10 (n must be positive)

Geometric sequences

nth term: u_n = a r^(n - 1)
sum of n terms: S_n = a(1 - r^n)/(1 - r)   (r not 1)
sum to infinity: S_inf = a/(1 - r)   (only if |r| < 1)

a = first term, r = common ratio

Worked example. A geometric sequence has a = 3 and r = 2. Find the 8th term and the sum of the first 8 terms.

u_8 = 3 × 2⁷ = 384
S_8 = 3(1 - 2⁸)/(1 - 2) = 3(1 - 256)/(-1) = 765

Worked example 2 (working backwards). A geometric sequence has second term 12 and fifth term 96. Find r and a.

u_2 = ar = 12;  u_5 = ar⁴ = 96
divide: r³ = 8  →  r = 2;  a = 6

Sum to infinity and convergence

A geometric series converges only when the ratio has magnitude less than 1: each term is smaller than the last, and the total approaches a finite limit.

if |r| < 1: S_inf = a/(1 - r)
if |r| >= 1: the series diverges (no finite sum)

Worked example. Find the sum to infinity of 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 + ...

a = 8, r = 1/2
S_inf = 8/(1 - 1/2) = 8/(0.5) = 16

Worked example 2 (recurring decimal). Write 0.444... as a fraction using a geometric series.

0.444... = 0.4 + 0.04 + 0.004 + ...
a = 0.4, r = 0.1
S_inf = 0.4/(1 - 0.1) = 0.4/0.9 = 4/9

σ notation and recurrence relations

sum from k = 1 to n of u_k  (σ notation)

recurrence: u_(n+1) = f(u_n), with the first term given

Worked example (σ). Evaluate the sum from k = 1 to 5 of (3k + 1).

terms: 4, 7, 10, 13, 16 (arithmetic, a = 4, d = 3)
S = (5/2)(4 + 16) = 50

Worked example 2 (recurrence). u₁ = 2, u_(n+1) = 3u_n + 1. Find u₄.

u2 = 3(2) + 1 = 7
u3 = 3(7) + 1 = 22
u4 = 3(22) + 1 = 67

Recurrence questions often ask you to prove a sequence is arithmetic or geometric: compute consecutive differences or ratios and show they are constant.

Applied problems

Worked example (savings). A student saves 50 pounds in month 1 and increases the monthly saving by 10 pounds each month. How much is saved in month 12, and in total over the year?

arithmetic: a = 50, d = 10
u_12 = 50 + 11(10) = 160
S_12 = (12/2)(50 + 160) = 6 × 210 = 1260 pounds

Worked example 2 (depreciation). A car worth 18000 pounds loses 15% of its value each year. Find its value after 5 years and the total loss.

geometric: a = 18000, r = 0.85
value after 5 years = 18000 × 0.85⁵ = 18000 × 0.4437 = 7987 pounds
loss = 18000 - 7987 = 10013 pounds

Worked example 3 (interest). 1000 pounds is invested at 4% compound interest. Find the value after 10 years and the total interest.

value = 1000 × 1.04¹⁰ = 1000 × 1.4802 = 1480.24 pounds
interest = 480.24 pounds

Deriving the sum formulas

Knowing where the formulas come from makes them reconstructable under pressure. Write the arithmetic sum forwards and backwards and add:

S = a + (a + d) + ... + [a + (n - 1)d]
S = [a + (n - 1)d] + ... + a
2S = n[2a + (n - 1)d]  (each of the n columns adds to 2a + (n-1)d)
S = (n/2)[2a + (n - 1)d]

The geometric sum is derived by multiplying by r and subtracting, which cancels every intermediate term:

S = a + ar + ar² + ... + ar^(n-1)
rS = ar + ar² + ... + ar^n
S - rS = a - ar^n  →  S(1 - r) = a(1 - r^n)
S = a(1 - r^n)/(1 - r)   (r not 1)

Letting n grow in the geometric formula, rⁿ → 0 whenever |r| < 1, leaving S∞ = a/(1 − r): the same derivation explains convergence, so the condition is not a separate fact to memorise.

Proving a sequence is arithmetic or geometric

Show the consecutive differences or ratios are constant using algebra, not just numbers.

Worked example. The terms of a sequence are 3, 3 + 2k, 3 + 4k, ... Show it is arithmetic and find the sum of the first 10 terms in terms of k.

difference 1: (3 + 2k) - 3 = 2k
difference 2: (3 + 4k) - (3 + 2k) = 2k
constant difference 2k  →  arithmetic with d = 2k
S_10 = (10/2)[2(3) + 9(2k)] = 5(6 + 18k) = 30 + 90k

Worked example 2 (geometric). Show that 2, 2x, 2x², ... is geometric and find the sum to infinity when x = 1/3.

ratio: 2x/2 = x;  2x²/(2x) = x  →  geometric with r = x
with x = 1/3: S_inf = 2/(1 - 1/3) = 3

Combining and interpreting sequences

Some questions give a sequence defined by a rule that is neither purely arithmetic nor geometric, and ask for specific terms or a sum found by splitting it into two familiar parts.

Worked example. Find the sum of the first 20 terms of the sequence whose nth term is 3n + 2ⁿ.

split: arithmetic part 3n (a = 3, d = 3) and geometric part 2^n (a = 2, r = 2)
arithmetic sum: (20/2)[6 + 19 × 3] = 10 × 63 = 630
geometric sum: 2(2²⁰ - 1)/(2 - 1) = 2(1048576 - 1) = 2097150
total = 630 + 2097150 = 2097780

Worked example 2 (loan style). A student repays a 5000 pound debt in monthly instalments that form an arithmetic sequence: 150 pounds in month 1, rising by 20 pounds each month. After how many months is the debt cleared, and what is the final instalment?

S_n = (n/2)[2(150) + (n - 1)(20)] = 5000
(n/2)(300 + 20n - 20) = 5000
n(280 + 20n) = 10000
20n² + 280n - 10000 = 0  →  n² + 14n - 500 = 0
n = [-14 + √(196 + 2000)]/2 = (-14 + 46.86)/2 = 16.4
so 17 instalments are needed; the 17th clears the remainder
final (17th) instalment = 150 + 16(20) = 470 pounds

Two modelling habits earn marks here: round n up (16 instalments leave the debt short) and state what the final, part-full payment means. Reading a plan for feasibility — does the sum actually reach the target? — is also examinable: an arithmetic sum with a negative difference peaks and then falls, so a repayment plan built that way may never clear the debt.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Arithmetic) Find the 15th term of 7, 11, 15, ... Answer: a = 7, d = 4; u₁₅ = 7 + 14(4) = 63.
  2. (Sum) Find the sum of the first 30 terms of 2, 5, 8, ... Answer: d = 3; S = 15(4 + 87) = 1365.
  3. (Geometric) Find the 6th term of 2, 6, 18, ... Answer: r = 3; u₆ = 2 × 3⁵ = 486.
  4. (Sum to infinity) Find S∞ for 12 + 6 + 3 + ... Answer: r = ½; S∞ = 12/(1 − ½) = 24.
  5. (Convergence) For what values of r does a geometric series converge? Answer: |r| < 1.
  6. (Recurrence) u₁ = 5, u_(n+1) = 2u_n − 3. Find u₃. Answer: u₂ = 7, u₃ = 11.
  7. (Reverse) The 3rd term of an arithmetic sequence is 11 and the 8th is 31. Find a and d. Answer: 5d = 20 → d = 4; a = 3.
  8. (Applied) A ball is dropped from 2 m and rebounds to 60% of its height each bounce. Find the total distance travelled before it stops. Answer: down 2; up/down 2(0.6) twice... total = 2 + 2(2×0.6)/(1−0.6) = 2 + 6 = 8 m.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • n − 1 versus n: the nth term uses (n − 1)d, not nd. Off-by-one errors are the commonest in this topic.
  • Count versus term: "sum of the first 20 terms" means n = 20; "the 20th term" means u₂₀. Read which is asked.
  • Sign of r: a negative ratio alternates signs; the convergence condition uses |r|, so r = −0.5 converges.
  • Sum to infinity misused: S∞ exists only for |r| < 1; quoting it for a divergent series is a conceptual mark lost.
  • Depreciation versus interest: depreciation multiplies by (1 − rate); interest by (1 + rate). Getting the factor wrong inverts the answer.
  • Solving for n: the quadratic in n has one positive integer root; reject the negative or fractional value explicitly.
  • Recurrence notation: u_(n+1) means the next term; substituting the wrong index shifts the whole sequence.
  • Exact form: where a question asks for an exact answer, keep fractions and powers; decimal approximations lose the final mark.

Equations and symbols

Every relation this topic is examined on, written with its real notation and followed by a key naming each symbol, its unit and what it means. Restaurant-bill questions, savings plans and areas under curves all reduce to one of these lines with numbers in it.

Arithmetic sequences and series

uₙ = a + (n − 1)d
Key: uₙ = the nth term; a = the first term, u₁; d = the common difference, uₙ₊₁ − uₙ; n = the term number, n ≥ 1. The (n − 1) is what makes the first term come out as a: no difference has been added yet.

Sₙ = (n/2)(2a + (n − 1)d) = (n/2)(a + l)
Key: Sₙ = the sum of the first n terms; a = first term; d = common difference; l = the last term, uₙ; n = how many terms are added. The second form is Gauss's pairing: n/2 pairs each summing to a + l.

uₙ = Sₙ − Sₙ₋₁
Key: Sₙ = the sum of the first n terms; Sₙ₋₁ = the sum of the first n − 1. Subtracting the two sums leaves only the nth term — the standard route when a question gives a formula for Sₙ and asks about the sequence.

Geometric sequences and series

uₙ = a rⁿ⁻¹
Key: a = the first term; r = the common ratio, uₙ₊₁/uₙ; n = the term number. Each step multiplies by r, so the power is one less than the term number.

Sₙ = a(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r), r ≠ 1
Key: Sₙ = the sum of the first n terms; a = first term; r = common ratio; n = the number of terms. The equivalent form a(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1) is the same number and is easier when r > 1; r = 1 is excluded because the series is then na.

S∞ = a/(1 − r), valid only for |r| < 1
Key: S∞ = the sum to infinity; a = first term; r = common ratio. The convergence condition is part of the answer: if |r| ≥ 1 the terms do not shrink and the sum diverges, so no finite value exists.

arⁿ⁻¹ = X ⇒ n = 1 + log(X/a)/log r
Key: a = first term; r = common ratio; X = the term whose position is wanted; n = that position. Taking logs of both sides is the only way to get n out of the exponent, and it is what "after how many years" questions require.

uₙ = a(1 + p/100)ⁿ⁻¹
Key: p = the percentage change per period; a = the starting amount; n = the period number. A savings or depreciation model is a geometric sequence: appreciate with p > 0, depreciate with p < 0.

Σ notation and standard sums

Σ_{r=1}^{n} (A r + B) = A·n(n + 1)/2 + B n
Key: Σ = "sum of"; r = the index running from 1 to n; A, B = constants; n = the number of terms. Every arithmetic series written in Σ notation is this one line, which is why the formula is worth recognising rather than re-deriving.

Σ_{r=1}^{n} r = n(n + 1)/2 and Σ_{r=1}^{n} r² = n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6
Key: n = the last index; r = the index. The two standard results, used to sum any quadratic expression term by term.

Σ_{r=1}^{n} (f(r) ± g(r)) = Σ f(r) ± Σ g(r) and Σ k f(r) = k Σ f(r)
Key: k = a constant; f, g = functions of the index; n = the number of terms. Sums are linear, which is what lets a polynomial be split into the standard sums above.

Recurrence relations and the binomial series

uₙ₊₁ = f(uₙ), with u₁ given
Key: uₙ = the current term; uₙ₊₁ = the next term; f = the rule. A recurrence defines a sequence term by term instead of by a formula in n; to find u₁₀ you iterate, and to describe the long-term behaviour you look for a limit L satisfying L = f(L).

(a + b)ⁿ = Σ_{r=0}^{n} C(n, r) aⁿ⁻ʳ bʳ
Key: a, b = the two terms of the bracket; n = the positive integer power; C(n, r) = n!/(r!(n − r)!), the binomial coefficient; r = the index of the b-power. The (r + 1)th term alone is C(n, r) aⁿ⁻ʳ bʳ, which is how "find the coefficient of x³" is answered without expanding anything.

title: Waves & Sound — Study Notes
content:
Waves & Sound

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2023–2025): general wave properties; reflection/refraction/diffraction; sound.

1. Wave basics

v = fλ. Transverse (oscillation ⊥ travel — light, water, S-waves) vs longitudinal (parallel — sound, P-waves). Amplitude, wavelength, frequency f = 1/T; wavefront diagrams.

2. Ripple tank behaviours

  • Reflection: angle in = angle out; speed/frequency unchanged, direction changes.
  • Refraction: speed change at boundary bends wavefronts (shallow water slows ripples).
  • Diffraction: spreading through gaps ≈ λ wide; around edges.

3. Electromagnetic spectrum (order)

Radio → micro → IR → visible (red 700 nm – violet 400 nm) → UV → X → gamma. All travel at 3 × 10⁸ m/s in vacuum; transverse; uses and dangers (IR heating; UV skin; X/gamma ionising).

4. Sound

  • Longitudinal; needs a medium (bell in vacuum demo). Speed ~340 m/s air, faster in liquids/solids.
  • Range 20 Hz–20 kHz; ultrasound > 20 kHz (sonar, prenatal scans, cleaning).
  • Pitch ↔ frequency; loudness ↔ amplitude.

5. Echo problems

Distance = (v × t)/2 (there and back).

Example: echo after 0.6 s, v = 340 → cliff 102 m away.

Exam tips: in diagrams always label wavelength as crest-to-crest; for refraction, state "changes speed" first, then direction; quote EM uses with the hazard.

title: Logic Gates & Boolean Logic — Study Notes
content:
Logic Gates & Boolean Logic

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2023–2025): six gates, truth tables, building/describing circuits, problem-to-logic mapping.

1. The six gates

ABANDORNANDNORXOR
0000110
0101101
1001101
1111000

NOT inverts. NAND = AND + invert; NOR = OR + invert; XOR = 1 when inputs differ.

2. Truth tables

2 inputs → 4 rows; 3 inputs → 8 rows. Work gate by gate, adding intermediate columns for sub-circuit outputs.

3. Problem → logic

Define inputs/outputs first. Alarm rings (X=1) if sensor P triggered AND (door D OR window W): X = P AND (D OR W). Then draw the circuit: OR first, then AND.

4. Describing circuits

Write the expression from a diagram gate by gate; annotate output of each gate (X, Y) before combining.

Exam tips: check your truth table row count before writing; in problem questions, state "input P = 1 means sensor triggered" — definitions earn marks.

title: Acid-base Equilibria — Study Notes
content:
Acid-base Equilibria

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH14, Topic 14. Acids and bases are defined by proton transfer. The strength of an acid is given by its dissociation constant, and pH calculations, buffers and titrations all follow from it.

Strong and weak acids

  • A strong acid dissociates completely in water, so [H⁺] equals the acid concentration. For 0.010 mol dm⁻³ HCl, [H⁺] = 0.010 and pH = 2.00.
  • A weak acid dissociates only partly. For HA ⇌ H⁺ + A⁻, Ka = [H⁺][A⁻] / [HA].
  • pKa = −log10 Ka. A smaller pKa means a stronger acid.

pH calculations

  • pH = −log10[H⁺]. For a base, find pOH = −log10[OH⁻] and use pH = 14.00 − pOH at 298 K.
  • Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ mol² dm⁻⁶ at 298 K.
  • For a 0.050 mol dm⁻³ NaOH solution, [OH⁻] = 0.050, pOH = 1.30 and pH = 12.70.

Buffers

  • A buffer contains a weak acid and its conjugate base (for example ethanoic acid and sodium ethanoate). It resists large pH changes.
  • The pH of a buffer is given by pH = pKa + log([A⁻] / [HA]). When [A⁻] = [HA], pH = pKa.
  • Adding a small amount of strong acid is absorbed by the conjugate base, so the pH changes only slightly.

Titrations and indicators

  • Strong acid with strong base: the equivalence point is pH 7.
  • Weak acid with strong base: the equivalence point is above pH 7, so phenolphthalein (pH 8.3 to 10) is suitable.
  • Strong acid with weak base: the equivalence point is below pH 7, so methyl orange (pH 3.1 to 4.4) is suitable.
  • Choose an indicator whose colour change lies within the steep vertical section of the titration curve.

Exam tip: when pH is asked for a weak acid, calculate [H⁺] from Ka and the concentration before taking the logarithm.

title: AS Level Biology: Molecules, Transport and Health
content:
Molecules, Transport and Health — AS Level Biology

This revision note belongs to the Edexcel International Advanced Subsidiary (IAS) Biology specification, WBI11 Unit 1, Topic 1 Molecules, Transport and Health. It covers water as a solvent and its structure, carbohydrates and lipids, proteins and their structure and function, gas exchange surfaces and Fick’s law, the mammalian circulatory system and the cardiac cycle, haemoglobin and the oxygen dissociation curve, atherosclerosis and blood clotting, the risk factors for cardiovascular disease, diet, cholesterol and antioxidants, how people use scientific knowledge to reduce risk, the benefits and risks of treatments, and data analysis and evaluation in health studies — plus the gas exchange surfaces and enzyme practical work that support the topic. Every statement the topic is responsible for is covered in its own section or paragraph.

1. Water: structure, properties and why it is the solvent of life

Water is a small molecule with two hydrogen atoms covalently bonded to one oxygen atom; because the oxygen atom is much more electronegative than hydrogen, the shared electrons spend more time near the oxygen, so the molecule is polar — the oxygen end is slightly negative and the hydrogen end slightly positive. This polarity lets water molecules form hydrogen bonds with each other, which gives water its high specific heat capacity, its high latent heat of vaporisation, its cohesion (important for the transpiration stream in plants) and its solvent powers. Water is an excellent solvent because its polarity lets it surround and dissolve ions and polar molecules; ions become hydrated with water molecules around them, and polar molecules such as glucose dissolve readily. In transport, water’s solvent nature lets it carry dissolved substances in blood and in plant tissue fluid and sap, and its dipole nature explains why it can do that — the partial charges interact with the charges of ions and the polar groups of molecules like glucose and amino acids.

2. Carbohydrates: monosaccharides, disaccharides and polysaccharides

Carbohydrates are made of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, with hydrogen and oxygen in the same ratio as in water (2:1). Monosaccharides are the simplest carbohydrates and are the building blocks — glucose, fructose and galactose are hexose monosaccharides with the formula C6H12O6. Disaccharides form when two monosaccharides join by a condensation reaction, losing a water molecule and forming a glycosidic bond; the common ones are maltose (glucose + glucose), sucrose (glucose + fructose) and lactose (glucose + galactose). Polysaccharides are long chains of monosaccharides; starch in plants is made of two polymers — amylose, a long unbranched helix of glucose, which is compact for storage, and amylopectin, which is branched so that glucose can be added or removed quickly from the ends. Glycogen is similar to amylopectin but more branched, and it is the storage carbohydrate in animals, mainly in liver and muscle cells. Cellulose is a structural polysaccharide of beta-glucose chains forming long, straight fibres that cross-link by hydrogen bonds into strong microfibrils; it forms plant cell walls. Carbohydrates provide and store energy: starch and glycogen store glucose in a compact, insoluble, osmotically inert form, so they do not affect the cell’s water potential, and they can be hydrolysed back to glucose when needed for respiration.

3. Core Practical 1 — semi-quantitative tests for reducing sugars and starch

Use Benedict’s reagent to estimate the concentration of reducing sugars and iodine solution to estimate the concentration of starch, using colour standards. Benedict’s reagent (copper(II) sulfate, sodium carbonate and sodium citrate) turns from blue to green, then yellow, then orange, then brick-red as reducing sugars are heated with it — the colour depends on the concentration of reducing sugar. For a semi-quantitative estimate, prepare a range of known reducing sugar concentrations (for example glucose solutions), heat each with Benedict’s, compare the colour with a colour standard chart, and record the colour or its code for each; then use the standards to estimate the concentration in an unknown. For starch, add iodine solution (iodine in potassium iodide) to the sample; a blue-black colour shows starch, and the intensity of the colour relates to the concentration — compare with colour standards to estimate. State the variables: the independent variable is the sugar or starch concentration, the dependent variable is the colour or colour standard, and controlled variables include the volume, temperature and time of heating.

4. Glycosidic bonds: condensation and hydrolysis

Monosaccharides join by condensation reactions to form disaccharides and polysaccharides, with a glycosidic bond formed between them and a water molecule lost each time. Conversely, polysaccharides and disaccharides can be hydrolysed — split by the addition of water — into their monomers; hydrolysis breaks the glycosidic bond and needs a water molecule for each bond broken. Glucose, fructose and galactose join to make maltose (glucose + glucose), sucrose (glucose + fructose) and lactose (glucose + galactose). Amylose and amylopectin are formed from alpha-glucose units; cellulose is formed from beta-glucose units, and because beta-glucose has a different orientation the chain is straight rather than coiled, so the hydrogen bonds between adjacent chains form strong microfibrils. Hydrolysis of starch gives maltose then glucose; hydrolysis of sucrose gives glucose and fructose; hydrolysis of lactose gives glucose and galactose. This matters in the body: dietary starch is hydrolysed to glucose in the gut by enzymes, and that glucose is used in respiration or stored as glycogen; lactose intolerance is caused by a deficiency of lactase, the enzyme that hydrolyses lactose, so lactose stays in the gut and causes problems.

5. Triglycerides: structure and saturated and unsaturated lipids

A triglyceride is made from one glycerol molecule and three fatty acids, joined by three ester bonds formed in condensation reactions; it is insoluble in water (hydrophobic). Fatty acids have a carboxyl group at one end and a hydrocarbon chain that may be saturated — no double bonds in the chain, so the molecule is straight and packs tightly, and saturated fats (and the triglycerides made from them) are usually solid at room temperature — or unsaturated, with one or more double bonds that kink the chain and prevent tight packing, so unsaturated fats are usually liquid at room temperature (oils). Lipids have several roles: they store energy in a compact, insoluble form (1 g of fat stores more energy than 1 g of carbohydrate), they form the phospholipid bilayer of all cell membranes, they form the myelin sheath around nerve fibres, they form a protective waterproof layer in the skin (subcutaneous fat), and they form steroid hormones. In membranes the phospholipid bilayer controls what enters and leaves the cell; the membrane also has proteins, cholesterol and glycoproteins.

6. Why animals need a heart and circulation

Many animals need a heart and a circulatory system because as an organism grows, diffusion alone is too slow to supply its cells with oxygen and nutrients and to remove waste — the surface area to volume ratio falls as size increases, and diffusion is only effective over short distances. A mass transport system (heart, blood vessels and blood) moves substances rapidly around the body, overcoming the limitations of diffusion. Blood carries oxygen, nutrients, hormones, waste products and defence cells and molecules. In simple organisms (small ones, or those with a large surface area to volume ratio or a thin body wall) exchange can happen directly by diffusion with the environment; larger or more active animals need a specialised exchange surface and a circulation system to move materials there and back.

7. The structure of arteries, veins and capillaries

Blood vessels relate their structure to their function. Arteries carry blood away from the heart at high pressure; they have thick, muscular, elastic walls to withstand and smooth the pressure and to help push the blood on, and a narrow lumen relative to wall thickness; they have no valves (except at the heart). Veins carry blood back to the heart at low pressure; they have thinner walls (less muscle and elastic tissue) and a wide lumen, and they have valves to prevent backflow, helping return blood when pressure is low. Capillaries are the exchange vessels; they have walls only one cell thick, a very narrow lumen just wide enough for red blood cells to pass in single file, slowing the blood and maximising the surface area for the exchange of substances. The structure of each vessel matches the pressure and role it plays.

8. The cardiac cycle and the structure of the mammalian heart

The mammalian heart is a muscular pump with four chambers — two atria (thin-walled, receiving chambers) and two ventricles (thick-walled, pumping chambers), with the left side pumping oxygenated blood to the body and the right side pumping deoxygenated blood to the lungs. The cardiac cycle is the sequence of events in a heartbeat: atrial systole (the atria contract, pushing blood into the ventricles), ventricular systole (the ventricles contract, pushing blood out into the pulmonary artery and aorta, and the atrioventricular valves close to prevent backflow, making the first heart sound), and diastole (the heart relaxes, the ventricles fill, the semilunar valves close, making the second heart sound). The valves ensure one-way flow: the atrioventricular valves (between atria and ventricles) and the semilunar valves (in the aorta and pulmonary artery). The left ventricle has a much thicker wall than the right because it must pump blood at high pressure around the whole body, whereas the right ventricle pumps only to the nearby lungs. The structure of the heart and its operation are shown by dissection (a recommended additional practical), and the heart’s own rhythm is myogenic, starting at the sinoatrial node, though details of that are not needed at IAS.

9. Haemoglobin, oxygen transport and the oxygen dissociation curve

Haemoglobin transports oxygen in red blood cells. Each haemoglobin molecule has four polypeptide chains, each with a haem group that contains an iron ion that can combine with one oxygen molecule, so one haemoglobin can carry four oxygen molecules. The oxygen dissociation curve shows how much oxygen haemoglobin takes up at different oxygen tensions: at high oxygen tension (in the lungs) it becomes almost fully saturated, and at low oxygen tension (in respiring tissues) it releases oxygen; the shape of the curve means a small drop in oxygen tension in the tissues releases a lot of oxygen — this is important. The Bohr effect: as carbon dioxide concentration rises and pH falls, haemoglobin’s affinity for oxygen falls and it releases oxygen more readily — so where respiration is high and CO2 is produced, haemoglobin unloads oxygen. Adult haemoglobin has a lower oxygen affinity than fetal haemoglobin, which has a higher affinity — this lets the fetus pick up oxygen from the mother’s blood across the placenta, because fetal haemoglobin can take oxygen from adult haemoglobin. Carbaminohaemoglobin carries some carbon dioxide as well, so haemoglobin transports both oxygen and carbon dioxide.

10. Atherosclerosis: how it develops and why it matters

Atherosclerosis is the narrowing and hardening of arteries by plaques. The process begins with endothelial dysfunction — damage to the lining of the artery, by high blood pressure, by smoking chemicals, or by immune responses — then an inflammatory response follows, white blood cells (including phagocytes) move into the artery wall, LDL cholesterol is taken up and oxidised, smooth muscle cells multiply and fibrous tissue forms, and a plaque builds up (a fibrous cap over a lipid core). As the plaque grows it narrows the artery, raising blood pressure further and reducing flow; eventually a plaque may rupture, triggering blood clotting and a thrombus, which can block a coronary artery and cause a myocardial infarction (heart attack). The main risk factors — genetics, diet, age, gender, high blood pressure, smoking and inactivity — act through these mechanisms, and the disease shows why passive transport and diffusion alone cannot supply the larger, more active human body and why the heart and blood vessels are needed.

11. Blood clotting and its role in cardiovascular disease

Blood clotting forms a network of insoluble fibrin threads that traps platelets and red blood cells to form a clot and seal a wound. The process: damage to a blood vessel exposes platelets to the collagen in the wall, and they are activated and release thromboplastin; thromboplastin, in the presence of calcium ions, converts prothrombin (an inactive plasma protein) to thrombin; thrombin then catalyses the conversion of soluble fibrinogen to insoluble fibrin, which forms a mesh that traps platelets and red blood cells into a clot. Clotting is needed to prevent blood loss and to stop pathogens entering, but in cardiovascular disease a clot formed on a ruptured plaque can block a coronary artery and cause a myocardial infarction, or travel to block a cerebral artery and cause a stroke. Treatments to reduce clotting include platelet inhibitors such as aspirin, and anticoagulants such as warfarin, which slow the clotting cascade.

12. Risk factors for cardiovascular disease

Many factors increase the risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD), and most act through the mechanisms above. Diet high in saturated fats and cholesterol raises LDL levels and contributes to plaques; high blood pressure damages the endothelium and raises the risk of both atherosclerosis and clotting; age increases risk because damage accumulates and repair is less efficient; males are at higher risk at younger ages than females; smoking introduces chemicals that damage the endothelium and raise blood pressure and heart rate and reduce oxygen carried by haemoglobin; inactivity contributes to high blood pressure, obesity and high cholesterol; and genetics/family history affects a person’s baseline risk. Risk is often the result of several factors combined, and reducing one can help even if others remain. People’s perception of risk is often different from the actual risk — they may underestimate or overestimate the risk from diet and other lifestyle factors, and scientists work to clarify the real risks through studies.

13. Diet, cholesterol and antioxidants and the evidence for them

Dietary antioxidants (such as vitamins C and E from fruits and vegetables) may reduce the risk of CVD by preventing the oxidation of LDL cholesterol — oxidised LDL is taken up more readily by artery walls and contributes to plaque formation. Blood cholesterol level is an important indicator: total cholesterol and LDL cholesterol are linked to CVD, and HDL cholesterol helps remove cholesterol from the artery wall, so high HDL is protective. The evidence that cholesterol causes CVD comes from studies showing a causal relationship between blood cholesterol levels and cardiovascular disease, and from trials of the statins, which lower cholesterol and reduce CVD events. People use scientific knowledge about diet, body mass index (BMI = mass (kg) / height (m) squared) and waist-to-hip ratio (a measure of central obesity), exercise and smoking to reduce their risk of coronary heart disease — and they should distinguish between correlation and causation when interpreting the data, because two things occurring together does not by itself prove one causes the other.

14. Data analysis in health studies: correlation, causation and study design

Health studies use quantitative data on illness and mortality rates to determine health risks. Two things can be correlated without one causing the other — a third factor may cause both, or the relationship may be coincidental — so a key skill is distinguishing correlation from causation. A causal relationship for cholesterol and CVD is supported by mechanistic evidence (the biology above) plus the results of trials. When evaluating the design of studies used to determine health risk factors, consider the sample selection (is it representative, or biased, as in a sample of only one type of person or only volunteers) and the sample size (small samples are less reliable and more easily swayed by chance). Conflicting evidence exists because studies differ in design, in the populations studied, and in the measures used, and scientific decisions draw on the whole body of evidence, not one study.

15. Perceived and actual risk and why people’s views differ

People’s perception of risks is often different from the actual risks — they may underestimate risks due to diet and lifestyle because those risks feel distant and small, or overestimate them because of vivid or recent examples, or because of personal experience, cultural beliefs or poor understanding of the probabilities. Scientific knowledge can clarify the actual risk: for example, many people underestimate the risk from diet and inactivity for coronary heart disease even though the evidence is strong, and the gap between perception and reality is itself a reason to communicate the science clearly. Understanding that perception and reality can diverge is part of evaluating the use of scientific knowledge in making decisions about health, and it explains why public health messages must be carefully designed and evidence-based.

16. Treatments for cardiovascular disease: benefits and risks

Several treatments are used for CVD. Antihypertensives lower blood pressure, reducing the risk of endothelial damage and of heart strain. Statins lower blood cholesterol, reducing plaque formation and the risk of atherosclerosis. Anticoagulants (such as warfarin) and platelet inhibitors (such as aspirin) reduce clot formation, lowering the risk of a clot on a ruptured plaque causing a heart attack or stroke. Each has benefits and risks: antihypertensives can cause dizziness, fatigue or kidney effects and may over-lower pressure; statins can cause muscle pain, digestive upset and, rarely, liver effects; aspirin can cause bleeding, especially in the gut, and is not suitable for everyone. Decisions about treatment balance the degree of risk against the benefit, take the person’s overall risk factors into account, and should be supported by the evidence — and by the science behind the disease, so that treatment targets the actual risk factors.

17. Core Practical 2 — vitamin C content of food and drink

Investigate the vitamin C content of food and drink, using DCPIP (2,6-dichlorophenolindophenol), which is blue when oxidised and colourless when reduced. Ascorbic acid (vitamin C) reduces DCPIP, so as vitamin C is added from a food or drink sample, the blue colour fades; the volume of a known concentration of vitamin C solution needed to decolorise a fixed volume of DCPIP gives a calibration, and the volume of the food or drink needed to decolorise the same DCPIP lets you estimate its vitamin C concentration by comparison. Carry out the test for several drinks (for example fruit juices, boiled and unboiled samples) to compare vitamin C content, and note that heat (boiling) destroys vitamin C, so boiled samples contain much less. Record volumes, identify the independent (volume of sample) and dependent (volume needed to decolorise DCPIP) variables, and control temperature, DCPIP volume and end-point judgement.

18. Proteins: amino acids, peptide bonds and the levels of structure

Amino acids are the monomers of proteins; the basic structure is an amino group, a carboxyl group and a variable R group attached to a central carbon. There are around 20 amino acids, differing in their R group, and the sequence of amino acids in a protein (primary structure) determines its folding and function. Amino acids join by condensation reactions to form peptide bonds, making dipeptides and polypeptides. Secondary structure is local folding into alpha-helices and beta-pleated sheets, held by hydrogen bonds between peptide bonds. Tertiary structure is the overall three-dimensional shape, held by hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, disulfide bonds and hydrophobic interactions; it determines the protein’s function. Haemoglobin is a globular protein with four chains and four haem groups each carrying one oxygen; collagen is a fibrous protein of three polypeptide chains in a triple helix, strong for tendons and skin. Biuret reagent (copper(II) sulfate and sodium hydroxide) turns purple in the presence of peptide bonds, and a semi-quantitative method using it and colour standards can estimate protein concentration — that is a recommended additional practical.

19. Gas exchange surfaces and Fick’s law

An effective gas exchange surface has a large surface area to volume ratio, a thin surface (short diffusion distance) and a difference in concentration between the two sides — the three properties that make diffusion rapid. The rate of diffusion is described by Fick’s law: rate of diffusion = (surface area × concentration difference) / thickness of the surface, so increasing surface area or concentration difference, or decreasing thickness, increases the rate. The mammalian lung is adapted for rapid gaseous exchange: the alveoli provide a huge total surface area (about 70–90 m² in an adult), they are thin-walled (one cell thick, with a shared basement membrane) so the diffusion distance is very short, the air in the alveoli is highly oxygenated while the blood arriving is deoxygenated, so there is a steep concentration gradient, and the constant ventilation and blood flow maintain that gradient. Fick’s law explains why these adaptations matter quantitatively.

20. Enzymes: specificity, catalysing reactions and factors that affect rate

Enzymes are biological catalysts that speed up reactions by lowering the activation energy needed. Their mechanism of action is explained by their three-dimensional structure: the active site has a specific shape that fits the substrate (the lock-and-key model) or changes shape to fit it (the induced-fit model), and specificity comes from the exact shape of the active site — each enzyme works on one or a few substrates. Enzymes are proteins, and heat, pH and the concentrations of enzyme and substrate affect their rate: each enzyme has an optimum temperature and pH; above or below the optimum the rate falls, and extremes denature the enzyme (irreversibly changing the shape of the active site, so it no longer works). Enzyme concentration increases the rate when substrate is in excess, and substrate concentration increases the rate up to a point, after which the enzyme’s active sites are saturated and the rate levels off (maximum rate, Vmax). These effects are investigated in Core Practical 4.

21. Core Practical 4 — factors affecting enzyme rate

Investigate the effect of temperature, pH, enzyme concentration and substrate concentration on the initial rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction. For each factor, choose a suitable enzyme and substrate (for example amylase and starch, or catalase and hydrogen peroxide) and measure the initial rate — the rate in the first part of the reaction, before the substrate is used up or the enzyme denatures. Change the factor being tested in steps, keep the other factors constant (control variables), take several measurements, and calculate the initial rate from the slope of the graph of product formed (or substrate used) against time. For temperature, the rate rises with temperature to an optimum, then falls as the enzyme denatures; for pH, rate is highest at the enzyme’s optimum pH; for enzyme concentration, rate rises linearly with concentration; for substrate concentration, rate rises and then levels off at Vmax. Plot graphs and explain the patterns in terms of collisions, activation energy and denaturation.

22. How to use this note and what to revise next

Use these notes section by section, checking that you can state the structure of a water molecule and explain its polarity, draw the structures of alpha-glucose and beta-glucose and state the difference, carry out the Benedict’s and iodine semi-quantitative tests and explain the variables and the colour standards, draw a triglyceride and distinguish saturated from unsaturated, state the structure and function of arteries, veins and capillaries, describe the cardiac cycle and the structure of the heart, sketch the oxygen dissociation curve and explain the Bohr effect and fetal haemoglobin, describe the stages of atherosclerosis and blood clotting, list the risk factors for CVD and state how each acts, carry out the DCPIP and biuret practicals, describe the properties of a gas exchange surface and apply Fick’s law, and explain enzyme specificity and the effects of temperature, pH and concentrations. After this topic, revise Topic 2 Membranes, proteins, DNA and gene expression, and Topic 3 Cell structure, reproduction and development — the transport and exchange ideas here underpin the circulatory and gas exchange systems in later topics.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Cardiac output, applied to a resting heart: cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume. With a heart rate of 70 beats min⁻¹ and a stroke volume of 70 cm³, the output is 4900 cm³ min⁻¹, or about 4.9 dm³ min⁻¹. Convert the units before you multiply, and state the units of the answer.
  • Glycosidic bonds: condensation forms a glycosidic bond between two monosaccharides and releases one water molecule. Hydrolysis adds a water molecule and breaks the bond. A disaccharide such as maltose from two glucose units therefore has the formula C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁, not two copies of glucose's formula.
  • Triglycerides: one glycerol and three fatty acids form three ester bonds, and three water molecules are released. Saturated fatty acids have no C=C double bonds and pack tightly, so they are solid at room temperature. Unsaturated fatty acids have one or more C=C double bonds, which bend the chain and keep it liquid.
  • Artery, vein and capillary structure: arteries have thick elastic and muscle walls to withstand high pressure, veins have valves and a thinner wall, and capillaries are one cell thick to allow diffusion. Relate each structural feature to its function in the answer, because the mark is for the link.

The tests in Core Practicals 1, 2 and 4, compared

TestDetectsPositive resultWhat makes it semi-quantitative
Benedict's reagent, heatedReducing sugarsBlue to green, yellow, orange or brick-red precipitateComparing the colour with a set of standards made from known concentrations
Iodine solutionStarchOrange-brown to blue-blackJudging the depth of colour against standards
Biuret reagentPeptide bonds, so proteinBlue to purple or lilacColour standards for known protein concentrations
DCPIPVitamin CBlue to colourlessVolume of sample needed to decolourise a fixed volume of DCPIP
Emulsion testLipidMilky white emulsion after adding water to an ethanol extractNone: it is a qualitative test

Statistical analysis for practical papers: spread and significance

Every measurement you make varies, and statistics is the machinery that separates a real difference from the noise of the bench. Start with the mean: the sum of the values divided by the number of values, which locates the centre of a data set. The mean alone hides the spread, though, and spread is what decides whether two data sets really differ. Standard deviation measures that spread: it is the average distance of the individual values from the mean, weighted so that points far from the centre count for more. A small standard deviation means the values cluster tightly around the mean (a precise method); a large one means they scatter (an unreliable method or a genuinely variable system). The formula is standard deviation = the square root of the sum of each value minus the mean, squared, divided by n minus one, where n is the number of values. The n minus one is Bessel's correction: dividing by one fewer than the sample size corrects the bias of estimating spread from a sample rather than the whole population.

Standard error of the mean then estimates how precisely your mean estimates the true population mean: standard error = standard deviation divided by the square root of n. The 95 per cent confidence interval is the mean plus or minus 1.96 times the standard error: if you repeated the experiment many times, 95 of every 100 such intervals would contain the true mean. The practical rule for a quick judgement is that when the 95 per cent confidence intervals of two means do not overlap, the difference is probably significant. On a graph, error bars drawn as plus or minus one standard deviation show the spread of the data; bars drawn as plus or minus two standard error (or 95 per cent confidence) show the precision of the mean — say which you have drawn, because they answer different questions.

Worked example: standard deviation and a t-test from raw data

Ten students each count stomata in one field of view at the leaf surface and one at the leaf underside: surface counts 12, 15, 14, 13, 16 and underside counts 34, 38, 36, 35, 37. Step 1: the means: surface = (12 + 15 + 14 + 13 + 16) / 5 = 70 / 5 = 14; underside = (34 + 38 + 36 + 35 + 37) / 5 = 180 / 5 = 36. Step 2: the standard deviation of the surface counts: deviations from the mean are −2, +1, 0, −1, +2; the squares are 4, 1, 0, 1, 4, which sum to 10; divide by n minus one = 4 to give a variance of 2.5; the square root of 2.5 = 1.58, so the standard deviation is 1.58 stomata per field. Step 3: state the result in the form the examiner wants: mean 14, standard deviation 1.58, n = 5. Step 4: to test whether the surface and underside differ significantly, state a null hypothesis — there is no significant difference between the mean counts at the surface and the underside — then apply the t-test for two means: t equals the difference between the means divided by the square root of the sum of each variance divided by its n. With standard deviations of 1.58 and 1.64 for the two sets and n = 5 in each, t = (36 − 14) / sqrt(2.5 / 5 + 2.7 / 5) = 22 / sqrt(1.04) = 22 / 1.02 = 21.6. Step 5: degrees of freedom = n1 + n2 − 2 = 8; the critical value of t at p = 0.05 for 8 degrees of freedom is 2.306; since 21.6 is far larger than 2.306, the probability that this difference arose by chance is less than 5 per cent, so reject the null hypothesis and conclude that the underside has significantly more stomata. Wording matters: never write that you "proved" a difference; write that the difference is significant at the 5 per cent level.

The chi-squared test does the same job for category counts rather than measurements. If you expect a 3:1 ratio and observe 78 dominant and 22 recessive offspring from 100, the expected values are 75 and 25. Chi-squared = the sum of (observed minus expected) squared divided by expected = (78 − 75)² / 75 + (22 − 25)² / 25 = 9 / 75 + 9 / 25 = 0.12 + 0.36 = 0.48. With one degree of freedom (categories minus one), the critical value at p = 0.05 is 3.84. Since 0.48 is below 3.84, accept the null hypothesis: the data do not differ significantly from a 3:1 ratio. Correlation coefficients work the same way in reverse — a value near plus or minus one indicates a strong association, but correlation is never proof of causation, and confounding variables must be considered.

Presenting and evaluating data

  • Plot the independent variable on the x-axis and the dependent variable on the y-axis, always with units, and choose a scale that fills the graph rather than cramping it into one corner.
  • Join points on a line graph with a smooth line of best fit, not a dot-to-dot zigzag; the line should pass through the mean of any repeated values at each x.
  • Repeat every measurement at least three times and take a mean; a single reading cannot show an anomaly, and anomaly detection is a mark in evaluation questions.
  • Identify anomalies honestly and say whether you would discard them and why; never invent a rule after seeing the data.
  • Control variables must be named with the method of control: not just "temperature" but "water bath set at 25 degrees Celsius".
  • Errors are random (scattered in both directions, reduced by repeats and larger samples) or systematic (biased in one direction, reduced by calibrating the apparatus); percentage error = uncertainty divided by the measured value, times 100.
  • Evaluate with pairs: a limitation and the improvement that answers it — small sample, so increase n; measurement at fixed time points, so record continuously; parallax reading, so read at eye level or use a data logger.
  • Sample size and the t-test: the test assumes roughly normal data and similar variances; small samples make significance hard to reach, so report the actual p threshold used (p = 0.05 is the convention).

Typical mistakes

  • Explaining water's properties from polarity alone. Polarity matters because it allows hydrogen bonds, and it is the hydrogen bonds that give water its high specific heat capacity, its high latent heat of vaporisation and its cohesion.
  • Confusing condensation with hydrolysis. Condensation joins monomers and releases water; hydrolysis adds water and splits the bond. State which one is happening before you name the bond.
  • Describing unsaturated fatty acids as "less healthy" instead of describing their structure. Unsaturated chains contain one or more carbon-carbon double bonds, so the chain kinks, the molecules cannot pack closely, and the substance is liquid at room temperature.
  • Giving the artery wall as "thick" without saying why. The elastic and muscle tissue withstands and smooths high pressure from the ventricles. Capillaries are one cell thick to shorten the diffusion distance, and veins have valves to prevent backflow.
  • Reading the oxygen dissociation curve backwards. A curve shifted to the right shows a lower affinity for oxygen, so haemoglobin unloads oxygen more readily to respiring tissue. That is the Bohr effect, and it is caused by a higher carbon dioxide concentration and lower pH.
  • Treating correlation as causation. A study that finds a statistical association has not shown that one factor causes the other; confounding variables, sample size and study design all have to be evaluated first.
  • Mixing up the treatments for cardiovascular disease. Statins lower blood cholesterol, antihypertensives lower blood pressure, anticoagulants reduce clotting, and platelet inhibitors reduce platelet aggregation. Name the effect, not just the drug.
  • Forgetting the control variables in an enzyme practical. When temperature is the independent variable, pH, enzyme concentration and substrate concentration must be held constant, and the initial rate is measured from the steepest part of the graph, before substrate is used up.

Exam-style questions

  1. Explain why water is an effective solvent for transport in organisms. Answer: the water molecule is a dipole, with a partial negative charge on the oxygen and partial positive charges on the hydrogens, so it attracts ions and polar molecules and surrounds them; this keeps them dissolved and able to move in the bloodstream or in xylem.
  2. A heart beats 75 times a minute with a stroke volume of 70 cm cubed. Calculate the cardiac output in dm cubed per minute. Answer: cardiac output = heart rate times stroke volume = 75 times 70 = 5 250 cm cubed per minute, which is 5.25 dm cubed per minute.
  3. An alveolus has a surface area of 0.02 m squared, a wall thickness of 0.0005 mm and an oxygen concentration difference of 40 units. Use Fick's law to explain what happens to the rate of diffusion if the wall thickens. Answer: rate is proportional to surface area times concentration difference divided by thickness. Thickening the wall increases the diffusion distance, so the rate falls in proportion. Rate = (0.02 times 40) / thickness, so doubling the thickness halves the rate.
  4. Describe the sequence of events that leads to atherosclerosis. Answer: the endothelium is damaged (for example by high blood pressure or smoking); an inflammatory response attracts white blood cells and lipids into the wall; fatty deposits form a plaque (atheroma); the plaque narrows the artery and stiffens it, raising blood pressure; if the plaque ruptures, a clot forms and can block the artery, causing a heart attack or stroke.
  5. Explain the role of haemoglobin in oxygen transport and how the Bohr effect helps a exercising muscle. Answer: haemoglobin binds oxygen in the lungs, where the partial pressure of oxygen is high, and releases it in tissues where it is low. Respiring muscle raises carbon dioxide and lowers pH, which shifts the dissociation curve to the right, lowering the affinity for oxygen so that more oxygen is unloaded where it is needed.
  6. A student tests four solutions with Benedict's reagent and records the time taken to reach a brick-red colour. Explain how this design could be made semi-quantitative and reliable. Answer: fix the volume of solution, the volume of reagent, the temperature of the water bath and the time, then compare each result with a set of standards made from known concentrations. Repeat each measurement and take a mean, and use the same observer or a colorimeter to judge the end point.
  7. Explain why a diet high in saturated fat and low in fruit and vegetables increases the risk of cardiovascular disease. Answer: saturated fat raises low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, which is deposited in artery walls and contributes to plaque formation; fruit and vegetables supply antioxidants that reduce the oxidation of LDL cholesterol, so a low intake removes part of that protection. Both act alongside other risk factors such as smoking, age and inactivity.
  8. Explain the difference between a channel protein and a carrier protein in a membrane. Answer: a channel protein forms a pore through which specific ions or small polar molecules pass down their gradient; a carrier protein binds the substance and changes shape to move it across, which is how active transport can move substances against a gradient using ATP.

Inhibitors: how competitive and non-competitive inhibitors change the rate graph

An enzyme inhibitor slows a reaction by reducing the number of enzyme molecules that are working at a given moment. The two main types act in different places, and the rate graph shows the difference clearly: one can be overcome by adding substrate, the other cannot.

Key: the curves are idealised; the maximum rate is the rate with every active site occupied, and the substrate concentration needed to reach half of it is higher with a competitive inhibitor present.

Competitive inhibition

A competitive inhibitor has a shape similar to the substrate, so it binds to the active site and blocks the substrate from entering. Because the two compete, adding more substrate increases the chance that a substrate molecule meets the active site first. The maximum rate can still be reached, but it takes a higher substrate concentration, so the curve is shifted to the right.

Non-competitive inhibition

A non-competitive inhibitor binds to a site away from the active site, which changes the shape of the enzyme so that the active site no longer fits the substrate well. Adding more substrate does not remove this effect, because the inhibitor is not competing for the active site. The maximum rate falls, so the curve is flattened rather than shifted.

Reading an inhibition graph in an exam

Identify the curve with no inhibitor first. If the inhibited curve reaches the same maximum at high substrate, the inhibitor is competitive. If the maximum itself is lower, it is non-competitive. Name the site of binding and link the shape change to the fall in rate, rather than describing the graph alone.

Equations and symbols

This topic is a set of quantitative relations about surfaces, hearts and data. Each one is a definition, so the mark is for writing it before substituting.

rate of diffusion = (surface area × concentration difference) / thickness of the surface Key: rate of diffusion = amount crossing per unit time (arbitrary units or mol s⁻¹); surface area = area available for exchange (m²); concentration difference = the gradient between the two sides (mol dm⁻³ or arbitrary units); thickness = diffusion distance (m or µm, kept consistent). Fick's law is why an alveolus is thin and folded: halve the thickness and you double the rate.

cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume Key: cardiac output = volume pumped per minute (cm³ min⁻¹ or dm³ min⁻¹); heart rate = beats per minute; stroke volume = volume ejected per beat (cm³). Convert both to the same volume unit before multiplying, and state the unit of the answer.

BMI = mass (kg) / height (m) squared Key: BMI = body mass index (kg m⁻²); mass in kilograms, not pounds; height in metres, not centimetres. A person of 70 kg and 1.75 m has BMI = 70/3.06 = 22.9.

standard error = standard deviation divided by the square root of n Key: standard error = the precision of the mean (same unit as the measurement); standard deviation = spread of the individual values; n = number of measurements. It shrinks as √n, so quadrupling the sample only halves the error.

percentage error = uncertainty divided by the measured value, times 100 Key: uncertainty = half the smallest division of the instrument (or the stated tolerance); measured value = the reading itself. Quote it as a percentage of the reading, not of the range.

t = (36 − 14) / sqrt(2.5 / 5 + 2.7 / 5) Key: the numerator is the difference of the two means (stomata per field); each 2.5 and 2.7 is a variance (standard deviation squared); each 5 is that sample's n. Compare the result with the critical value at n₁ + n₂ − 2 degrees of freedom before you say "significant".

title: Scatter Diagrams and Correlation — Study Notes
content:
Scatter Diagrams and Correlation

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): scatter diagrams, types of correlation, line of best fit, interpolation vs extrapolation.

1. Correlation types

  • Positive: both increase (revision time vs score).
  • Negative: one increases, other decreases (price vs demand).
  • No correlation: random scatter.
  • Strength: strong (tight to a line) vs weak (loose).

2. Line of best fit

Balance points either side of the line; it need not pass through the origin. Use two well-separated points on your line (not necessarily data points) to estimate its gradient and equation.

Example: line through (10, 24) and (50, 60): m = 36/40 = 0.9 → y = 0.9x + 15.

3. Using the line

Interpolation (inside the data range) is reliable; extrapolation (outside) is a risk — say so if asked.

4. Correlation ≠ causation

A third factor may drive both variables (ice-cream sales and drownings both rise with temperature). Describe relationships, don't over-claim.

5. Outliers

Points far from the trend: identify, and comment on their effect on the line; ignore them when drawing the best fit if instructed.

Exam tips: describe correlation in full ("strong positive linear correlation"); quote the equation only from two points on the drawn line, not raw data.

Reading a scatter diagram

Each point plots one pair of values. Positive correlation means y tends to rise as x rises; negative correlation means it falls. The strength of correlation depends on how closely the points cluster around a line. Correlation does not prove causation.

Lines of best fit

Draw a straight line through the middle of the points, with roughly equal numbers of points on each side, and use it to estimate values. Interpolation (inside the data range) is generally reliable; extrapolation (beyond the data) is less so and should be stated as an estimate.

Outliers

A point far from the general pattern is an outlier. Mention it in your answer and state whether it affects the conclusion, rather than ignoring it silently.

Worked example: using a line of best fit

A line of best fit for the data is y = 2x + 1. To predict y when x = 6, substitute to get y = 2 × 6 + 1 = 13. The value x = 6 lies inside the range of the data, so this is interpolation and is usually reliable. If the data only covered x from 0 to 10, predicting y when x = 30 would be extrapolation, which assumes the trend continues beyond the data and is unreliable.

Strength of the relationship

  • Strong positive correlation: the points lie close to a rising line, so the line of best fit is a good model.
  • Weak correlation: the points are scattered widely, so any prediction from the line is of little value.
  • No correlation: the points show no pattern, and a line of best fit should not be used for prediction.

Interpreting the gradient

In a question about height and arm span, the gradient of the line shows how much the second quantity changes for each unit increase in the first. Always include units in the interpretation, for example "each extra centimetre of height is associated with about 1.1 cm of arm span", and avoid saying that height causes arm span.

Exam point: a line of best fit should pass through the mean point (x̄, ȳ) and should have about as many points above it as below it. Reading the value from a graph should be done with a dotted line drawn from the axis to the line and then to the other axis.

title: AS Level Mathematics: Sequences and Series
content:
AS Level Mathematics: Sequences and Series

A sequence is an ordered list of numbers generated by a rule; a series is the sum of a sequence. Two families dominate the syllabus: arithmetic (add a constant each time) and geometric (multiply by a constant each time). This note builds the topic from zero: the nth term and sum formulas for both families with derivations, sigma notation, recurrence relations, the convergence condition for geometric series, and the applied problems — savings, depreciation, loans — where the formulas earn marks. Every formula is derived once so it can be rebuilt if forgotten.

Arithmetic sequences

nth term: u_n = a + (n - 1)d
sum of n terms: S_n = (n/2)[2a + (n - 1)d] = (n/2)(first + last)

a = first term, d = common difference

Worked example. An arithmetic sequence has first term 5 and common difference 4. Find the 20th term and the sum of the first 20 terms.

u_20 = 5 + 19 x 4 = 81
S_20 = (20/2)(5 + 81) = 10 x 86 = 860

Worked example 2 (working backwards). The 5th term is 17 and the 12th is 45. Find a and d.

u_5: a + 4d = 17
u_12: a + 11d = 45
subtract: 7d = 28  ->  d = 4;  a = 17 - 16 = 1

Arithmetic series and the sum formula

The sum formula is Gauss's trick: pair the first and last terms, the second and second-last, and so on; each pair has the same total, and there are n/2 pairs.

Worked example. Find the sum of the first 50 positive even numbers.

a = 2, d = 2, n = 50
last term = 2 + 49 x 2 = 100
S = (50/2)(2 + 100) = 25 x 102 = 2550

Worked example 2 (unknown n). The sum of the first n terms of 3, 7, 11, ... is 210. Find n.

210 = (n/2)[6 + 4(n - 1)] = (n/2)(4n + 2) = 2n^2 + n
2n^2 + n - 210 = 0
(2n + 21)(n - 10) = 0  ->  n = 10 (n must be positive)

Geometric sequences

nth term: u_n = a r^(n - 1)
sum of n terms: S_n = a(1 - r^n)/(1 - r)   (r not 1)
sum to infinity: S_inf = a/(1 - r)   (only if |r| < 1)

a = first term, r = common ratio

Worked example. A geometric sequence has a = 3 and r = 2. Find the 8th term and the sum of the first 8 terms.

u_8 = 3 x 2^7 = 384
S_8 = 3(1 - 2^8)/(1 - 2) = 3(1 - 256)/(-1) = 765

Worked example 2 (working backwards). A geometric sequence has second term 12 and fifth term 96. Find r and a.

u_2 = ar = 12;  u_5 = ar^4 = 96
divide: r^3 = 8  ->  r = 2;  a = 6

Sum to infinity and convergence

A geometric series converges only when the ratio has magnitude less than 1: each term is smaller than the last, and the total approaches a finite limit.

if |r| < 1: S_inf = a/(1 - r)
if |r| >= 1: the series diverges (no finite sum)

Worked example. Find the sum to infinity of 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 + ...

a = 8, r = 1/2
S_inf = 8/(1 - 1/2) = 8/(0.5) = 16

Worked example 2 (recurring decimal). Write 0.444... as a fraction using a geometric series.

0.444... = 0.4 + 0.04 + 0.004 + ...
a = 0.4, r = 0.1
S_inf = 0.4/(1 - 0.1) = 0.4/0.9 = 4/9

Sigma notation and recurrence relations

sum from k = 1 to n of u_k  (sigma notation)

recurrence: u_(n+1) = f(u_n), with the first term given

Worked example (sigma). Evaluate the sum from k = 1 to 5 of (3k + 1).

terms: 4, 7, 10, 13, 16 (arithmetic, a = 4, d = 3)
S = (5/2)(4 + 16) = 50

Worked example 2 (recurrence). u₁ = 2, u_(n+1) = 3u_n + 1. Find u₄.

u2 = 3(2) + 1 = 7
u3 = 3(7) + 1 = 22
u4 = 3(22) + 1 = 67

Recurrence questions often ask you to prove a sequence is arithmetic or geometric: compute consecutive differences or ratios and show they are constant.

Applied problems

Worked example (savings). A student saves 50 pounds in month 1 and increases the monthly saving by 10 pounds each month. How much is saved in month 12, and in total over the year?

arithmetic: a = 50, d = 10
u_12 = 50 + 11(10) = 160
S_12 = (12/2)(50 + 160) = 6 x 210 = 1260 pounds

Worked example 2 (depreciation). A car worth 18000 pounds loses 15% of its value each year. Find its value after 5 years and the total loss.

geometric: a = 18000, r = 0.85
value after 5 years = 18000 x 0.85^5 = 18000 x 0.4437 = 7987 pounds
loss = 18000 - 7987 = 10013 pounds

Worked example 3 (interest). 1000 pounds is invested at 4% compound interest. Find the value after 10 years and the total interest.

value = 1000 x 1.04^10 = 1000 x 1.4802 = 1480.24 pounds
interest = 480.24 pounds

Deriving the sum formulas

Knowing where the formulas come from makes them reconstructable under pressure. Write the arithmetic sum forwards and backwards and add:

S = a + (a + d) + ... + [a + (n - 1)d]
S = [a + (n - 1)d] + ... + a
2S = n[2a + (n - 1)d]  (each of the n columns adds to 2a + (n-1)d)
S = (n/2)[2a + (n - 1)d]

The geometric sum is derived by multiplying by r and subtracting, which cancels every intermediate term:

S = a + ar + ar^2 + ... + ar^(n-1)
rS = ar + ar^2 + ... + ar^n
S - rS = a - ar^n  ->  S(1 - r) = a(1 - r^n)
S = a(1 - r^n)/(1 - r)   (r not 1)

Letting n grow in the geometric formula, rⁿ → 0 whenever |r| < 1, leaving S∞ = a/(1 − r): the same derivation explains convergence, so the condition is not a separate fact to memorise.

Proving a sequence is arithmetic or geometric

Show the consecutive differences or ratios are constant using algebra, not just numbers.

Worked example. The terms of a sequence are 3, 3 + 2k, 3 + 4k, ... Show it is arithmetic and find the sum of the first 10 terms in terms of k.

difference 1: (3 + 2k) - 3 = 2k
difference 2: (3 + 4k) - (3 + 2k) = 2k
constant difference 2k  ->  arithmetic with d = 2k
S_10 = (10/2)[2(3) + 9(2k)] = 5(6 + 18k) = 30 + 90k

Worked example 2 (geometric). Show that 2, 2x, 2x², ... is geometric and find the sum to infinity when x = 1/3.
