ratio: 2x/2 = x;  2x^2/(2x) = x  ->  geometric with r = x
with x = 1/3: S_inf = 2/(1 - 1/3) = 3

Combining and interpreting sequences

Some questions give a sequence defined by a rule that is neither purely arithmetic nor geometric, and ask for specific terms or a sum found by splitting it into two familiar parts.

Worked example. Find the sum of the first 20 terms of the sequence whose nth term is 3n + 2ⁿ.

split: arithmetic part 3n (a = 3, d = 3) and geometric part 2^n (a = 2, r = 2)
arithmetic sum: (20/2)[6 + 19 x 3] = 10 x 63 = 630
geometric sum: 2(2^20 - 1)/(2 - 1) = 2(1048576 - 1) = 2097150
total = 630 + 2097150 = 2097780

Worked example 2 (loan style). A student repays a 5000 pound debt in monthly instalments that form an arithmetic sequence: 150 pounds in month 1, rising by 20 pounds each month. After how many months is the debt cleared, and what is the final instalment?

S_n = (n/2)[2(150) + (n - 1)(20)] = 5000
(n/2)(300 + 20n - 20) = 5000
n(280 + 20n) = 10000
20n^2 + 280n - 10000 = 0  ->  n^2 + 14n - 500 = 0
n = [-14 + sqrt(196 + 2000)]/2 = (-14 + 46.86)/2 = 16.4
so 17 instalments are needed; the 17th clears the remainder
final (17th) instalment = 150 + 16(20) = 470 pounds

Two modelling habits earn marks here: round n up (16 instalments leave the debt short) and state what the final, part-full payment means. Reading a plan for feasibility — does the sum actually reach the target? — is also examinable: an arithmetic sum with a negative difference peaks and then falls, so a repayment plan built that way may never clear the debt.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Arithmetic) Find the 15th term of 7, 11, 15, ... Answer: a = 7, d = 4; u₁₅ = 7 + 14(4) = 63.
  2. (Sum) Find the sum of the first 30 terms of 2, 5, 8, ... Answer: d = 3; S = 15(4 + 87) = 1365.
  3. (Geometric) Find the 6th term of 2, 6, 18, ... Answer: r = 3; u₆ = 2 × 3⁵ = 486.
  4. (Sum to infinity) Find S∞ for 12 + 6 + 3 + ... Answer: r = ½; S∞ = 12/(1 − ½) = 24.
  5. (Convergence) For what values of r does a geometric series converge? Answer: |r| < 1.
  6. (Recurrence) u₁ = 5, u_(n+1) = 2u_n − 3. Find u₃. Answer: u₂ = 7, u₃ = 11.
  7. (Reverse) The 3rd term of an arithmetic sequence is 11 and the 8th is 31. Find a and d. Answer: 5d = 20 → d = 4; a = 3.
  8. (Applied) A ball is dropped from 2 m and rebounds to 60% of its height each bounce. Find the total distance travelled before it stops. Answer: down 2; up/down 2(0.6) twice... total = 2 + 2(2×0.6)/(1−0.6) = 2 + 6 = 8 m.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • n − 1 versus n: the nth term uses (n − 1)d, not nd. Off-by-one errors are the commonest in this topic.
  • Count versus term: "sum of the first 20 terms" means n = 20; "the 20th term" means u₂₀. Read which is asked.
  • Sign of r: a negative ratio alternates signs; the convergence condition uses |r|, so r = −0.5 converges.
  • Sum to infinity misused: S∞ exists only for |r| < 1; quoting it for a divergent series is a conceptual mark lost.
  • Depreciation versus interest: depreciation multiplies by (1 − rate); interest by (1 + rate). Getting the factor wrong inverts the answer.
  • Solving for n: the quadratic in n has one positive integer root; reject the negative or fractional value explicitly.
  • Recurrence notation: u_(n+1) means the next term; substituting the wrong index shifts the whole sequence.
  • Exact form: where a question asks for an exact answer, keep fractions and powers; decimal approximations lose the final mark.

title: IGCSE Mathematics: Indices and Standard Form
content:
IGCSE Mathematics: Indices and Standard Form

Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580 (2025–2027), section 1 Number: statement 1.3 Powers and roots, 1.7 Indices I (with Extended fractional indices), 1.8 Standard form, E1.18 Surds, and section 2 statement E2.4 Indices II (algebraic indices). Indices are shorthand for repeated multiplication, and their laws are the shortcuts that make large and small numbers manageable. This note derives each law from what it counts, covers standard form arithmetic in full, and finishes with surds and rationalising — an Extended favourite that separates the top grades.

Powers, roots and the vocabulary

In 5³ the base is 5 and the index (plural: indices) is 3; it means 5 × 5 × 5 = 125. A square root reverses a square: √25 = 5 because 5² = 25. A cube root reverses a cube: ³√64 = 4 because 4³ = 64.

  • √16 = 4, the principal (positive) square root, as printed on a calculator. But the equation x² = 16 has two solutions, x = 4 or x = −4, because (−4)² = 16 as well. The question decides which is wanted: a length is positive; a solution of an equation may be negative.
  • Notation: a² is read a squared, a³ a cubed, and aⁿ a to the power n. a² ≠ 2a — a² = a × a while 2a = a + a.

The index laws

Each law is a statement about counting multiplications, so each can be checked by writing the multiplications out.

Law 1:  a^m x a^n = a^(m+n)
Why: a³ x a² = (a x a x a) x (a x a) = a⁵, and 3 + 2 = 5.
Example: 2³ × 2⁵ = 2⁸ = 256; check: 8 × 32 = 256 ✓

Law 2:  a^m ÷ a^n = a^(m-n)
Why: a⁵ ÷ a² = (a x a x a x a x a)/(a x a) = a x a x a = a³, and 5 - 2 = 3.
Example: 5⁷ ÷ 5⁴ = 5³ = 125

Law 3:  (a^m)^n = a^(m n)
Why: (a²)³ = a² x a² x a² = a⁶, and 2 × 3 = 6.
Example: (2x³)² = 2² x (x³)² = 4x⁶        [the power applies to every factor]

Law 4:  a⁰ = 1  (a not zero)
Why: a³ ÷ a³ = a^(3-3) = a⁰, and any number divided by itself is 1.
Example: 7⁰ = 1

Law 5:  a^(-n) = 1/(a^n)
Why: a^(-2) = a^(0-2) = a⁰ ÷ a² = 1/a².
Example: 5^(-2) = 1/25 = 0.04

Fractional indices (Extended). A fractional index is a root: the denominator of the fraction is the root, the numerator is the power.

a^(1/n) = nth root of a        a^(m/n) = (nth root of a)^m

16^(1/2) = √16 = 4
27^(2/3) = (cube root of 27)² = 3² = 9
Check the second: 27^(2/3) squared three times over should give 27² = 729; 9³ = 729 ✓

Indices in algebra (Extended)

The same laws apply when the base is a letter, and every factor in a bracket carries the power:

Simplify:  (2x³)² x⁴ ÷ x⁵

(2x³)² = 4x⁶        [square the 2 and double the index]
4x⁶ x x⁴ = 4x¹⁰     [Law 1: add indices]
4x¹⁰ ÷ x⁵ = 4x⁵     [Law 2: subtract indices]
Solve:  2^x = 32

Write both sides with base 2:  32 = 2⁵
2^x = 2⁵, so x = 5        [matching bases means matching indices]

When the bases differ, rewrite one as a power of the other: 8 = 2³, so 8^x = 2^(3x). Equations like 3^(x+1) = 27^(x−1) become 3^(x+1) = 3^(3x−3), so x + 1 = 3x − 3, giving x = 2.

LawStatementWorked line
Multiplyingaᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ2³ × 2⁵ = 2⁸ = 256
Dividingaᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ5⁷ ÷ 5⁴ = 5³ = 125
Power of a power(aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ(2x³)² = 4x⁶
Zero indexa⁰ = 1 (a not zero)7⁰ = 1
Negative indexa⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ5⁻² = 1/25
Fractional indexa^(m/n) = (ⁿ√a)ᵐ27^(2/3) = 9

Two edge cases deserve care. The zero index says nothing about 0⁰: 0⁰ is undefined, because the pattern a⁰ = 1 holds for every non-zero base while the pattern 0ⁿ = 0 holds for every positive power, and the two patterns collide at the origin. And a negative index never makes a value negative: 2⁻³ = 1/8 is positive, because the minus sign belongs to the position of the power, not to the number itself. Finally, every root can be written as a power — √x = x^(1/2), ³√x = x^(1/3) — which is how a calculator evaluates them and how algebraic roots are simplified in one notation.

Standard form

Standard form writes a number as a × 10ⁿ where 1 ⩽ a < 10 and n is an integer. It handles very large and very small quantities without long strings of zeros.

Write in standard form:

47 382 = 4.7382 × 10⁴        [the decimal point moves 4 places left]
0.0056 = 5.6 × 10^(-3)        [the decimal point moves 3 places right, so n = -3]

Arithmetic in standard form. Multiply or divide the numbers first, then the powers of ten, and adjust back into standard form if needed:

(3 × 10⁵) x (4 × 10^(-2))
= (3 × 4) x (10⁵ × 10^(-2))     [regrouped]
= 12 × 10³
= 1.2 × 10⁴                     [12 is not between 1 and 10, so adjust]

(6 × 10⁸) ÷ (2 × 10³)
= (6 ÷ 2) × 10^(8-3) = 3 × 10⁵

Addition and subtraction need matching powers first: 3 × 10⁵ + 4 × 10⁴ = 30 × 10⁴ + 4 × 10⁴ = 34 × 10⁴ = 3.4 × 10⁵. Real-world uses: the speed of light is 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, the size of an atom is about 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m, and masses, distances and populations in physics and chemistry questions are always quoted this way. A calculator's ×10ˣ key enters the power directly; the answer should be given in the form the question asks, often to 3 s.f.

Surds (Extended)

A surd is a root that cannot be written exactly as a fraction — √2, √3, 3√5. Exact answers in surds are often required on Paper 2, where a calculator cannot help. The laws:

√a x √b = √(ab)        √a ÷ √b = √(a/b)        (√a)² = a

Simplifying. Take out the largest square factor:

√50 = √(25 × 2) = √25 x √2 = 5√2
√72 = √(36 × 2) = 6√2
√(9/16) = √9 / √16 = 3/4

Adding like surds. Only like surds combine, exactly like algebraic terms:

√18 + √8 = 3√2 + 2√2 = 5√2        [simplify first]
2√3 + √5 cannot be combined: they are unlike surds.

Rationalising the denominator. A fraction with a surd underneath is tidied by multiplying top and bottom by the same surd (or its conjugate):

6/√3 = (6 x √3)/(√3 x √3) = 6√3/3 = 2√3

1/(3 + √2): multiply top and bottom by the conjugate (3 - √2):
= (3 - √2)/[(3 + √2)(3 - √2)]
= (3 - √2)/(9 - 2)          [difference of two squares below]
= (3 - √2)/7

The conjugate works because (a + b)(a − b) = a² − b² removes the square root entirely. Expanding surd brackets uses the same identity: (2 + √3)(2 − √3) = 4 − 3 = 1.

Worked example: a combined index calculation

Simplify (2³ × 2⁵) ÷ 2⁴ and check it two ways.

Method 1 (indices): 2³ × 2⁵ = 2⁸, then 2⁸ ÷ 2⁴ = 2⁴ = 16
Method 2 (arithmetic): 2³ × 2⁵ = 8 × 32 = 256;  256 ÷ 16 = 16
Both routes give 16 ✓

Second example: write (3√2)² − √8 in the form k√2.

(3√2)² = 9 × 2 = 18        [square both the 3 and the √2]
√8 = 2√2
18 - 2√2 is already simple; it cannot be written as k√2 because 18 is rational,
so the answer stays 18 - 2√2.

Standard form in a calculation. A red blood cell is 7 × 10⁻⁶ m across and a vein is 2.4 × 10⁻³ m wide. How many cells fit side by side?

2.4 × 10^(-3) ÷ 7 × 10^(-6)
= (2.4 ÷ 7) × 10^(-3 - (-6))        [divide the numbers, subtract the indices]
= 0.342857 × 10³
= 3.43 × 10² (3 s.f.)  ≈ 343 cells

The index arithmetic is the whole question: subtracting −6 gives +3, and a sense-check on the powers alone (10⁻³ ÷ 10⁻⁶ = 10³) says the answer must be in the hundreds — which catches sign slips before they cost the final mark.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Multiplying the base by the index: 2³ is 8, not 6; (2³)² = 2⁶ = 64, not 2⁵.
  • Forgetting to square the coefficient: (2x³)² = 4x⁶, not 2x⁶.
  • Treating a⁻ⁿ as negative rather than reciprocal: 2⁻³ = 1/8.
  • Writing 0.00047 as 4.7 × 10⁻³; it is 4.7 × 10⁻⁴ — count the places the point moves.
  • Leaving a standard-form answer as 12 × 10³; the front number must be between 1 and 10.
  • Giving √16 = ±4 in a simplification; the square root symbol means the principal root, while x² = 16 has both solutions.
  • Rationalising only the surd and not its conjugate partner: 1/(3 + √2) needs (3 − √2) top and bottom.
  • Combining unlike surds: 2√3 + √5 is final; only matching surd parts can be added.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 2, 3 marks). Simplify (3x²)³ ÷ x⁴.

Answer: (3x²)³ = 27x⁶; 27x⁶ ÷ x⁴ = 27x².

Question 2 (Paper 2, 3 marks). Evaluate 8^(2/3).

Answer: ³√8 = 2, and 2² = 4. So 8^(2/3) = 4.

Question 3 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Write 0.000 42 and 63 000 in standard form, then find their product.

Answer: 4.2 × 10⁻⁴ and 6.3 × 10⁴. Product = (4.2 × 6.3) × 10⁰ = 26.46 = 2.646 × 10¹.

Question 4 (Paper 2, 4 marks). Simplify √48 + 3√12.

Answer: √48 = √(16 × 3) = 4√3; 3√12 = 3 × 2√3 = 6√3; total = 10√3.

Question 5 (Paper 2, 4 marks). Rationalise the denominator of 5/(2 + √3).

Answer: Multiply by the conjugate: 5(2 − √3)/[(2 + √3)(2 − √3)] = 5(2 − √3)/(4 − 3) = 5(2 − √3) = 10 − 5√3.

Question 6 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Solve 9^x = 27.

Answer: Write both as powers of 3: 3^(2x) = 3³, so 2x = 3 and x = 3/2. Check: 9^(3/2) = (√9)³ = 3³ = 27 ✓.

From the numbers themselves, the course turns to comparing and sharing them: ratio, rate and proportion.

The powers-of-ten ladder: seeing standard form instead of memorising it

Indices look like a rule to memorise and are really a picture to read. Every quantity in the course sits somewhere on one ladder of powers of ten, and multiplying, dividing and converting all move you up or down that ladder by whole rungs.

One rung, one index. Moving up a rung multiplies by 10, and that is exactly what adding 1 to the index does: 10³ × 10 = 10⁴. Moving down divides by 10 and subtracts 1. Every index law is that sentence applied twice:

aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ Key: a = the base; m and n = the indices (powers). Multiplying adds the indices because each factor contributes its own rungs.
aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ Key: dividing subtracts, because dividing by aⁿ is multiplying by a⁻ⁿ.
(aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ Key: a bracket applied n times multiplies the rungs by n.
a⁰ = 1 and a⁻ⁿ = 1 / aⁿ Key: both follow from the subtraction law: a³ ÷ a³ = a⁰ must be 1, and a² ÷ a⁵ = a⁻³ must be 1/a³.

Standard form is a position on the ladder. A number is in standard form when it is written as

N = A × 10ⁿ Key: A = a number with 1 ≤ A < 10 (one non-zero digit before the point); n = a whole number, positive for large values and negative for small ones. 4.2 × 10³ means four decimal places' worth of rungs above 1: 4,200.

Converting is counting rungs, not guessing the sign. To write 47,500 in standard form, move the point left until one digit remains in front: 4.75, which is three moves, so the index is +3 and the value is 4.75 × 10⁴. To write 0.00062, move the point right until one digit remains in front: 6.2, which is four moves, so the index is −4 and the value is 6.2 × 10⁻⁴. Left is positive, right is negative — the point moving right on a small number gives a negative index, which is the sign students most often flip.

Worked example. A red blood cell has diameter 0.0000072 m and a virus 1.2 × 10⁻⁷ m. Write the cell in standard form and find how many times longer it is.

cell: 0.0000072 = 7.2 × 10⁻⁶ m (six moves right)
ratio: (7.2 × 10⁻⁶) ÷ (1.2 × 10⁻⁷) = (7.2 ÷ 1.2) × 10⁻⁶⁻⁽⁻⁷⁾ = 6.0 × 10¹ = 60

The division law did the work: subtracting a negative index adds. Doing that sum as −6 − 7 = −13 is the error that turns 60 into 0.0000000000006.

Estimating with the ladder. A calculation like (4.9 × 10⁵) × (2.1 × 10³) is roughly 5 × 2 = 10 times 10⁵⁺³ = 10⁸, so about 1.0 × 10⁹ before any calculator. This is how you catch a wrong power of ten — the most common way a correct method still loses the answer mark.

Where marks are lost. Writing 0.42 × 10⁴ or 42 × 10² and calling it standard form: A must be at least 1 and less than 10. Flipping the sign of the index on a small number. And adding indices when multiplying different bases — 2³ × 3² is 8 × 9 = 72, not 6⁵.

Negative and zero indices in depth

A negative index tells you to take a reciprocal, and a zero index gives the value 1. These two rules follow from the index laws, not from memory, so the working below shows how each one is forced. The subsections cover the reasons, the calculator entry, and the common slips that turn a negative power into a negative number.

Why a zero index gives one

Take a number and divide it by itself. Using the division law, a⁵ ÷ a⁵ = a⁰, and the same quotient is 1 because any number divided by itself is 1. So a⁰ = 1 for any non-zero a. The rule is therefore a consequence of the laws already in use, and it is why 5⁰ = 1, 100⁰ = 1 and (−3)⁰ = 1.

Why a negative index is a reciprocal

Divide a power by a larger power of the same base: a² ÷ a⁵ = a^(2−5) = a⁻³. Writing the same quotient as 1/a³ shows that a⁻³ = 1/a³. So a negative index moves the base to the denominator and changes the sign of the index. The value 2⁻³ is 1/2³ = 1/8, which is positive, because a negative index does not make the answer negative.

Negative indices with fractions

The reciprocal rule also works on fractions, where it flips the fraction. (2/3)⁻² = (3/2)² = 9/4. Invert the fraction first, then apply the positive index. A common error is to change only the index and leave the fraction alone, which gives (2/3)⁻² = 4/9 and loses the mark.

Entering negative and fractional powers on a calculator

Use the power key, and enter the negative index in brackets so the calculator reads the whole index as a negative number. For 5⁻², enter 5, the power key and (−2), giving 0.04. A fractional power such as 8^(1/3) is entered with brackets around the fraction, and the calculator returns 2. Check the result by reversing the operation: 2³ = 8 confirms the cube root.

Simplifying expressions with negative powers

To simplify 3x⁻² × 6x⁵, multiply the numbers and add the indices: 18x^(−2+5) = 18x³. To write the answer with only positive indices, move any negative power to the denominator. For example, 4y⁻³ becomes 4/y³. Collect the coefficients first, then deal with the indices, so the final form is easy to check.

Mistakes with negative and zero indices

The commonest errors are treating 2⁻³ as −8, writing a⁰ as 0, and reading (−2)⁻² as −1/4 when the correct value is 1/4. The bracket in (−2)⁻² is what makes the base negative, and an even power of a negative number is positive. Write the bracket in the working so the sign is clear before the reciprocal is taken.

Fractional indices and roots

A fractional index is a root combined with a power, so a^(1/n) is the nth root of a, and a^(m/n) is the nth root of a raised to the mth power. The index laws extend to fractions without any new rule. The subsections below explain the notation, how to evaluate by hand and on a calculator, and how fractional indices appear in equations.

The meaning of a^(1/n)

The index law (a^(1/2))² = a^(1/2 × 2) = a¹ = a shows that a^(1/2) must be the square root of a. In the same way a^(1/3) is the cube root and a^(1/4) is the fourth root. So 16^(1/2) = 4, 27^(1/3) = 3 and 81^(1/4) = 3. The index is the reciprocal of the root.

Evaluating a^(m/n)

Take the root first, then the power, because the root is usually the smaller number. For 8^(2/3), the cube root of 8 is 2, and 2² = 4. Taking the power first gives 8² = 64, and the cube root of 64 is also 4, so the order does not change the answer, but the root first keeps the numbers small and is less error-prone.

Negative fractional indices

A negative fractional index takes a reciprocal of the root. For 16^(−3/4), the fourth root of 16 is 2, so 2³ = 8 and the reciprocal gives 16^(−3/4) = 1/8. Apply the reciprocal last, after the root and power have been found, and write the answer as a fraction if the question asks for an exact value.

Solving an equation with a fractional index

To solve x^(2/3) = 4, raise both sides to the power 3/2, which undoes the 2/3. Then x = 4^(3/2) = (√4)³ = 2³ = 8. Raising both sides to the reciprocal of the index is the step to remember, and the result should be checked by substituting back: 8^(2/3) = 4.

Fractional indices on the calculator

Enter the base, press the power key, and enter the fraction in brackets. For 125^(2/3), the calculator gives 25. Enter the bracket around the index to avoid reading 2 ÷ 3 as a separate step, and check a simple value first, such as 9^(1/2) = 3, so a mis-entered index is spotted.

Why fractional indices matter

Fractional indices let a root be treated with the same index laws as a power. Once a root is written as an index, multiplying and dividing it follows the usual rules. This is why the Extended content treats roots as powers, and it is also the link to surds, which are the roots that are left unevaluated.

Standard form in calculations

Standard form writes a number as a × 10ⁿ, where 1 ≤ a < 10 and n is a whole number. It is used to write very large and very small numbers compactly, and it allows multiplication and division to be done by applying the index laws to the powers of ten. The subsections cover converting, multiplying and dividing, adding, and the calculator display.

Converting to and from standard form

To write 47 000 in standard form, move the decimal point until one non-zero digit is in front of it: 4.7. The point moved 4 places left, so the power is 10⁴, giving 4.7 × 10⁴. For 0.00052, the point moves 4 places right to give 5.2, so the power is −4 and the answer is 5.2 × 10⁻⁴. Count the places moved, and remember that a move to the left is a positive power.

Multiplying numbers in standard form

Multiply the number parts and add the powers of ten. (3 × 10⁵) × (2 × 10³) = 6 × 10⁸. If the product of the number parts is 10 or more, rewrite it in standard form and adjust the power. For (4 × 10⁶) × (5 × 10⁴) = 20 × 10¹⁰, which is 2 × 10¹¹ in standard form.

Dividing numbers in standard form

Divide the number parts and subtract the powers of ten. (8 × 10⁹) ÷ (2 × 10³) = 4 × 10⁶. If the number part is not between 1 and 10, adjust it. For (9 × 10⁴) ÷ (3 × 10⁶) = 3 × 10⁻², which is 0.03.

Adding and subtracting in standard form

Write both numbers with the same power of ten before adding or subtracting the number parts. To add 3 × 10⁴ and 5 × 10³, write the first as 30 × 10³, so the sum is (30 + 5) × 10³ = 35 × 10³ = 3.5 × 10⁴. Rewriting the answer in standard form is the step that loses marks when it is left out.

Standard form on the calculator

A calculator shows a standard form answer as a number with E or as a small power-of-ten display, such as 6.0E8, which means 6.0 × 10⁸. Enter a number in standard form with the EXP or ×10ˣ key, not by typing ×10 and the power separately, because the calculator then multiplies the brackets in the wrong order. Convert the display to the written form for the final answer.

Real-world uses of standard form

Standard form is used for distances in space, the mass of atoms and the population of large countries. The Earth is about 1.5 × 10⁸ km from the Sun, and a hydrogen atom has a mass of about 1.7 × 10⁻²⁷ kg. Comparing two such numbers is easy in standard form, because the larger power of ten is the larger number when the number parts are similar.

Surds: simplifying and working with roots

A surd is a root of a number that cannot be written exactly as a whole number or a fraction, such as √2 or √12. The exact form is kept in an answer when the question asks for an exact value, so surds are simplified by taking out any square factor. The subsections cover simplifying, multiplying and dividing surds, adding them, and rationalising a denominator.

Simplifying a surd by its square factor

Find the largest square number that divides the number under the root. √12 = √(4 × 3) = √4 × √3 = 2√3. The square factor 4 comes out of the root as 2, and the remaining 3 stays inside. Always check that the number left inside has no square factor, because an answer like √12 is not fully simplified.

Multiplying and dividing surds

Multiply the numbers inside the roots and simplify the result. √3 × √5 = √15, which has no square factor and is final. For division, √20 ÷ √5 = √(20 ÷ 5) = √4 = 2. The rule works for any two surds that are multiplied or divided, because the square root of a product is the product of the square roots.

Adding and subtracting surds

Surds can be added only when they have the same number under the root, like terms in algebra. 3√2 + 5√2 = 8√2, because both terms are a multiple of √2. But √2 + √3 cannot be simplified and must be left as it is. Simplify each surd first, because √8 + √2 becomes 2√2 + √2 = 3√2 only after √8 is simplified.

Expanding brackets with surds

Expand a bracket with surds in the same way as an ordinary bracket, multiplying each term and then simplifying. (√3 + 1)(√3 − 1) = 3 − √3 + √3 − 1 = 2. The middle terms cancel because they are equal and opposite. For (√5 + 2)², expand as (√5 + 2)(√5 + 2) = 5 + 2√5 + 2√5 + 4 = 9 + 4√5.

Rationalising a denominator

To rationalise a denominator such as 1/√3, multiply the top and bottom by √3. This gives √3/3, which has a whole number in the denominator. For a denominator with two terms, multiply by the conjugate: 1/(√5 + 2) × (√5 − 2)/(√5 − 2) = (√5 − 2)/(5 − 4) = √5 − 2. The conjugate changes the sign of the second term and removes the surd from the denominator.

Checking surd answers

Check a simplified surd by estimating its decimal value on the calculator. √12 should give 3.464…, and 2√3 should give the same value. Also check that no square factor remains inside a root, because the simplified answer is the one the mark scheme expects. An exact answer is not reduced to a decimal unless the question asks for one.

title: Exam technique: Probability (A2)
content:
### What earns the marks
For conditional probability, the restricted sample space stated earns the method mark. For independence checks, P(A)P(B) compared with P(A and B) earns both marks. For Bayes-style updates, the tree fractions multiplied along branches earn stepwise credit.
### Traps
Error: mutually exclusive assumed independent. Correction: test, never assume. Error: given-condition ignored. Correction: shrink the denominator first. Error: branches added instead of multiplied. Correction: multiply along, add across.
### Worked example
Event A has P(A) = 0.5 and event B has P(B) = 0.4. Given that A and B are independent, P(A and B) = 0.5 × 0.4 = 0.20. If the question instead gives P(A and B) = 0.3, then the events are not independent, because 0.3 does not equal 0.20. The conditional probability is P(A | B) = P(A and B) ÷ P(B) = 0.3 ÷ 0.4 = 0.75.
### Check yourself
Two events are mutually exclusive with P(A) = 0.3 and P(B) = 0.2. Are they independent? No. P(A and B) = 0 but P(A)P(B) = 0.06, so the events are dependent. Mutually exclusive events are always dependent when both have non-zero probability.

### Worked example
Event A has P(A) = 0.5 and event B has P(B) = 0.4. Given that A and B are independent, P(A and B) = 0.5 × 0.4 = 0.20. If the question instead gives P(A and B) = 0.3, then the events are not independent, because 0.3 does not equal 0.20. The conditional probability is P(A | B) = P(A and B) ÷ P(B) = 0.3 ÷ 0.4 = 0.75.
### Check yourself
Two events are mutually exclusive with P(A) = 0.3 and P(B) = 0.2. Are they independent? No. P(A and B) = 0 but P(A)P(B) = 0.06, so the events are dependent. Mutually exclusive events are always dependent when both have non-zero probability.

title: A Level Physics: Further Mechanics
content:
A Level Physics: Further Mechanics

Newton's cradle is the whole topic in one toy: a ball arrives, a ball leaves at the same speed, and something invisible has been conserved through the collision. That something is momentum — mass times velocity — and with impulse and energy it lets you analyse every collision, explosion and crash the papers can invent. This note builds the mechanics from zero: the momentum vector and its conservation, impulse as the area under a force–time graph and the physics of why cars crumple, elastic and inelastic collisions with full energy bookkeeping, and the standard problem types solved line by line.

Momentum and its conservation

momentum p = m v        (kg m s⁻¹; a vector)

conservation: in the absence of external forces, the total
momentum of a system stays constant:
  m¹ u1 + m² u2 = m¹ v1 + m² v2

Velocity is a vector, so momentum carries direction: assign positive and negative directions before writing any equation. The conservation law follows from Newton's third law — the forces two bodies exert on each other are equal and opposite for equal times, so the impulses are equal and opposite, so the momentum changes cancel.

Worked example. A 2.0 kg trolley moving at 3.0 m s⁻¹ collides with a stationary 1.0 kg trolley; they stick together. Find the common velocity.

before: 2.0 × 3.0 + 1.0 × 0 = 6.0 kg m s⁻¹
after:  (2.0 + 1.0) v = 3.0 v
3.0 v = 6.0  →  v = 2.0 m s⁻¹ (same direction)

Impulse

impulse = force x time = change in momentum
J = F Δt = Δp = m v - m u

on a force-time graph: impulse = area under the graph

The analogy: catching a ball. A hard catch (short time) means a huge force; moving your hands back (longer time) spreads the same momentum change over more time and reduces the force. That is the entire physics of crumple zones, airbags, seatbelts, helmets, landing mats and bending your knees when you jump down.

Worked example. A 0.16 kg cricket ball arrives at 30 m s⁻¹ and is struck back at 45 m s⁻¹; contact lasts 12 ms. Find the impulse and the average force.

take the incoming direction as negative:
u = -30, v = +45
Δp = m(v - u) = 0.16 x (45 - (-30)) = 0.16 × 75
        = 12 kg m s⁻¹
F = Δp/Δt = 12/0.012 = 1000 N = 1.0 kN

Worked example (graph). A force-time graph shows a triangular pulse rising to 800 N over 0.050 s and falling to zero over the next 0.050 s. Find the impulse and the speed change of a 2.0 kg object.

area = (1/2) x base x height = 0.5 × 0.10 × 800 = 40 N s
Δp = 40 kg m s⁻¹  →  Δv = 40/2.0 = 20 m s⁻¹

Elastic and inelastic collisions

Momentum is conserved in every collision (absent external forces); kinetic energy is conserved only in elastic ones:

ElasticInelastic
Momentumconservedconserved
Kinetic energyconservednot conserved — some becomes heat, sound, deformation
Typical examplegas molecules, billiard-ball idealisationcars sticking together, clay, crumple zones

Explosions run the same conservation law backwards: total momentum before is zero, so the fragments' momenta must cancel.

Worked example (explosion). A 0.50 kg firework at rest explodes into two pieces; the 0.30 kg piece flies at 12 m s⁻¹. Find the velocity of the other piece.

0 = 0.30 × 12 + 0.20 v
0.20 v = -3.6  →  v = -18 m s⁻¹
The 0.20 kg piece moves at 18 m s⁻¹ in the opposite direction.

Worked examples: the full audit

Worked example. A 1500 kg car at 20 m s⁻¹ crashes into a stationary 1000 kg car; they lock together. Find the velocity after impact, the kinetic energy lost, and explain where it went.

momentum: 1500 × 20 = 2500 v  →  v = 12 m s⁻¹
KE before = (1/2) × 1500 × 400 = 300 000 J
KE after  = (1/2) × 2500 × 144 = 180 000 J
lost = 120 000 J = 120 kJ
The energy goes to deformation of the bodies, heat, and sound.

Worked example 2 (elastic check). Two identical trolleys approach each other at 2.0 m s⁻¹ and bounce back at 2.0 m s⁻¹ each. Show the collision is elastic.

momentum before: m(2) + m(-2) = 0; after: m(-2) + m(2) = 0
KE before = (1/2)m(4) + (1/2)m(4) = 4m
KE after  = 4m  - unchanged, so elastic.

Momentum in two dimensions

Momentum is conserved separately in each perpendicular direction. For a collision that is not head-on, resolve the momenta into x and y components before and after, and set up two conservation equations. The geometry is where the marks are: a ball striking a wall at an angle rebounds with its perpendicular component reversed and its parallel component unchanged (for a smooth wall), which is why the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence in the ideal case.

before: p_x = m u cos(θ),  p_y = m u sin(θ)
after a smooth-wall bounce:
  p_x = -m v cos(θ)  (normal component reversed)
  p_y = +m v sin(θ)  (parallel component unchanged)
  |Δp| = 2 m v cos(θ)

Worked example. A 0.20 kg ball hits a smooth wall at 12 m s⁻¹ at 30° to the normal and rebounds elastically at the same speed and angle. Find the impulse on the ball.

Δp = 2 m v cos(θ) = 2 × 0.20 × 12 x cos(30)
        = 4.8 × 0.866 = 4.2 kg m s⁻¹
(directed away from the wall)

Explosions, recoil and rockets

An explosion is a collision reversed: total momentum stays at its initial value (usually zero), so the fragments' momenta must cancel. Recoil problems — a gun, a skateboarder pushing off, an astronaut throwing a tool — are all this one equation. A rocket is the continuous version: it expels gas backward at high speed and gains forward momentum, and it works in a vacuum precisely because it pushes against its own exhaust, not against the air.

recoil: 0 = m¹ v1 + m² v2   →   v2 = -(m¹/m²) v1
rocket thrust: F = (rate of change of momentum of the exhaust)
             = (mass per second) x (exhaust speed)

Worked example. A 4.0 kg rifle fires a 0.020 kg bullet at 400 m s⁻¹. Find the rifle's recoil speed.

0 = 0.020 × 400 + 4.0 v
4.0 v = -8.0  →  v = -2.0 m s⁻¹
The rifle recoils at 2.0 m s⁻¹ opposite to the bullet.

Forces, momentum and safety engineering

Questions about safety devices are impulse questions in disguise: the momentum change is fixed by the crash, so the only variable is time. A seatbelt extends the stopping time, so F = Δp/Δt falls; a crumple zone does the same by deforming; an airbag spreads the force over area as well. When asked to evaluate a design, quantify: if the stopping time triples, the average force falls to a third.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Momentum) Define momentum and state its unit. Answer: Momentum is the product of mass and velocity, p = mv, a vector; unit kg m s⁻¹ (equivalently N s).
  2. (Conservation) A 3.0 kg block at 4.0 m s⁻¹ hits a stationary 1.0 kg block and they move together. Find the final speed. Answer: 3.0 × 4.0 = 4.0v → v = 3.0 m s⁻¹.
  3. (Impulse) A 0.50 kg ball hits a wall at 8.0 m s⁻¹ and rebounds at 6.0 m s⁻¹; contact time 0.020 s. Find the average force. Answer: Δp = 0.50 × (6.0 + 8.0) = 7.0 kg m s⁻¹; F = 7.0/0.020 = 350 N.
  4. (Graph) Explain how to find impulse from a force–time graph. Answer: Impulse is the area under the graph; for a curve, count squares or integrate.
  5. (Elasticity) A collision conserves momentum but not kinetic energy. Classify it and name a real example. Answer: Inelastic; a car crash or two lumps of clay sticking together.
  6. (Explosion) A 60 kg astronaut pushes off a 400 kg spacecraft, moving at 0.50 m s⁻¹ relative to it. Find the spacecraft's recoil speed. Answer: 60 × 0.50 = 400 × v → v = 0.075 m s⁻¹ (opposite direction).
  7. (Safety) Explain how a crumple zone reduces injury. Answer: It deforms, increasing the collision time for a given momentum change; since F = Δp/Δt, the average force falls, reducing injury.
  8. (Energy) In an inelastic collision, where does the lost kinetic energy go? Answer: Into thermal energy, sound and permanent deformation of the materials — energy is conserved overall, but not as kinetic energy.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Dropping signs: momentum is a vector; a rebound reverses sign. The classic error is Δp = m(v − u) with both speeds positive, halving the true impulse.
  • Adding speeds wrongly: for a rebound, the change is v + u in magnitude (with signs, v − (−u)).
  • Assuming KE is conserved: check the type; "they stick together" is always inelastic. Compute KE before and after when asked.
  • External forces: conservation needs no net external force — a collision on a rough surface during a long interval is not the same as an instantaneous impact.
  • Unit of impulse: N s or kg m s⁻¹ are equivalent; force alone (N) is not.
  • Force–time areas: triangles and trapeziums need the correct geometric factors (½ for a triangle), not base × height.
  • Mass in grams: convert to kg before momentum calculations; a factor of 1000 error is common in cricket-ball questions.
  • Precision: 2 or 3 s.f. with units; keep direction words (opposite, same direction) in the answer.

Equations and symbols

Two vectors do all the work here — momentum, which is conserved, and impulse, which is how momentum changes. Direction is part of every symbol, so a sign error is a wrong answer even when the arithmetic is right.

p = m v Key: p = momentum (kg m s⁻¹, equivalent to N s); m = mass (kg); v = velocity (m s⁻¹), with its direction as a sign. Momentum is a vector, so "right" and "left" must be fixed before the first line of any collision question.

J = F Δt = Δp = m v - m u Key: J = impulse (N s); F = average force during contact (N); Δt = duration of contact (s); Δp = change in momentum (kg m s⁻¹); m = mass (kg); u = velocity before (m s⁻¹); v = velocity after (m s⁻¹). A rebound makes u negative, so the change is the sum of the speeds, not their difference.

F = Δp/Δt = 12/0.012 = 1000 N = 1.0 kN Key: 12 kg m s⁻¹ = the momentum change of the struck ball; 0.012 s = the contact time (12 ms); 1000 N = the average force. The whole physics of crumple zones is in this division: fixed Δp, longer Δt, smaller F.

Δv = 40/2.0 = 20 m s⁻¹ Key: 40 N s = the impulse, read as the area under a force–time graph (a triangle here, so ½ x base x height); 2.0 kg = the object's mass; 20 m s⁻¹ = its speed change. The area is the geometric shape's, not base × height for a triangle.

0 = 0.30 × 12 + 0.20 v Key: 0 = the total momentum of the firework before it explodes (at rest); 0.30 kg and 0.20 kg = the two fragments; 12 m s⁻¹ = the velocity of the heavier piece; v = the velocity of the lighter piece (m s⁻¹, negative because it moves the other way). An explosion is conservation with the left side equal to zero.

v2 = -(m¹/m²) v1 Key: m¹ = the mass of the projectile (kg); m² = the mass of the recoiling body (kg); v1 = the projectile's velocity (m s⁻¹); v2 = the recoil velocity (m s⁻¹), negative because it is opposite. The heavier the recoiling body, the slower it moves — 0.020 kg at 400 m s⁻¹ gives a 4.0 kg rifle just 2.0 m s⁻¹.

|Δp| = 2 m v cos(θ) Key: Δp = the change in momentum of a ball bouncing off a smooth wall (kg m s⁻¹); m = its mass (kg); v = its speed (m s⁻¹), unchanged in an elastic bounce; θ = the angle between the velocity and the normal to the wall (degrees). The parallel component is untouched, so only the perpendicular one doubles — hence the factor 2 cos θ.

KE before = (1/2) × 1500 × 400 = 300 000 J Key: 1500 kg = the mass of the moving car; 400 = v², since v = 20 m s⁻¹ (m² s⁻²); 300 000 J = its kinetic energy. Comparing it with the 180 000 J after the crash is the whole energy audit: 120 kJ left the kinetic store as heat, sound and deformation, while momentum stayed exactly conserved.

Two sentences carry marks of their own and belong with the equations: momentum is conserved in every collision, kinetic energy only in elastic ones; and the impulse from a force–time graph is the area beneath it, counted square by square when the line is curved.

title: Waves — Study Notes
content:
Waves

Basics

A wave transfers energy without net transfer of matter.

  • Transverse: oscillation ⊥ propagation (EM waves, water surface)
  • Longitudinal: oscillation ∥ propagation (sound)

The Wave Equation

v = fλ. Frequency f is set by the source; speed v by the medium.

Example: sound at 340 m s⁻¹, f = 512 Hz: λ = 340/512 ≈ 0.66 m.

Intensity

I = P/A. Intensity ∝ amplitude² — doubling the amplitude quadruples the intensity.

Doppler Effect

Observed frequency changes with relative motion: f′ = f(v ± v_o)/(v ∓ v_s). Approaching sources sound higher.

Example: an ambulance passing you: high pitch approaching, low pitch receding.

EM Spectrum

Radio → micro → IR → visible (400–700 nm) → UV → X-ray → gamma. All travel at c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ in vacuum.

Polarization

Only transverse waves can be polarised — proof that light is transverse. Malus' law: I = I₀ cos²θ between polariser axes.

Exam tips: distinguish wave speed (set by medium) from frequency (set by source); in Doppler problems, signs depend on approach or recession.

title: Vectors — Study Notes
content:
Vectors

Components and Arithmetic

A vector a = 3i + 4j has magnitude |a| = √(3² + 4²) = 5. Parallel vectors are scalar multiples; unit vector = a/|a|.

Position and Direction

The line through point A with direction d: r = a + t d. Two lines are parallel if their directions are multiples.

Example: r = (1, 2) + t(3, −1).

Scalar (Dot) Product

a · b = |a||b| cos θ = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂.

Perpendicular ⇔ a · b = 0. Parallel ⇔ cross-multiplied components are equal (in 2D: a₁b₂ − a₂b₁ = 0).

Example: (2, 3) · (−6, 4) = −12 + 12 = 0, so they are perpendicular.

Angle Between Vectors

cos θ = (a · b)/(|a||b|).

Example: between (1, 0) and (1, 1): cos θ = 1/(1 × √2), θ = 45°.

Lines and Points

Foot of perpendicular from P to a line, intersection of two lines, and shortest distances all come from dot products and parameter t.

Exam tips: write column vectors cleanly; check answers by substituting the found t back into both position vectors; keep exact surd magnitudes rather than decimals.

Exam method: components, magnitude and scalar product

A vector in two dimensions is written as a column (x; y), and in three dimensions as (x; y; z) or in unit vector form xi + yj + zk. The magnitude is |a| = √(x² + y² + z²), which is Pythagoras applied in each direction.

The scalar product a · b = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + a₃b₃ is a number, not a vector. It also equals |a||b| cos θ, where θ is the angle between the vectors. Two vectors are perpendicular exactly when their scalar product is zero.

Use the scalar product to find the angle between two vectors: cos θ = (a · b)/(|a||b|). Give the angle in degrees or radians as the question asks.

A unit vector has magnitude 1. Divide a vector by its magnitude to find the unit vector in the same direction.

Exam cue: Write each component with its sign before adding, because a sign slip in the scalar product changes the answer without changing the method.

title: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Probability
content:
Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Probability

Probability measures how likely an event is on a scale from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). The IGCSE questions build from single events to combined ones — two dice, two draws without replacement, "at least one" — and the toolkit is small but must be used precisely: the complement rule, the addition rule for mutually exclusive events, the multiplication rule for independent ones, and tree diagrams for everything with stages. This note builds the topic from zero with every rule justified and every standard question type worked.

The probability scale and notation

P(event) = number of favourable outcomes / total outcomes
         (when outcomes are equally likely)

0 <= P(A) <= 1
P(not A) = 1 - P(A)        (the complement rule)

Probabilities are written as fractions, decimals or percentages — but keep one form within a question. The complement rule is the most powerful single line in the topic: "at least one" is almost always easier as 1 − P(none).

Worked example. A bag has 5 red, 3 blue and 2 green counters. Find P(red) and P(not red).

total = 10
P(red) = 5/10 = 1/2
P(not red) = 1 - 1/2 = 1/2  (check: 3 + 2 = 5 of 10)

Relative frequency and expected frequency

relative frequency = number of times the event occurred
                     / total number of trials

expected number = probability x number of trials

Relative frequency estimates probability from experiment; it approaches the theoretical value as trials increase (the law of large numbers). Questions ask you to compare an experimental relative frequency with a theoretical probability and comment on the discrepancy — small samples fluctuate, large samples converge.

Worked example. A biased die is rolled 200 times; a six appears 50 times. Estimate P(six) and predict the number of sixes in 500 rolls.

relative frequency = 50/200 = 0.25
expected in 500 = 0.25 × 500 = 125

Combined events: the two rules

RuleWhen to use itFormula
Addition (OR)mutually exclusive events — cannot both happenP(A or B) = P(A) + P(B)
Multiplication (AND)independent events — one does not affect the otherP(A and B) = P(A) × P(B)

The words "or" and "and" map onto add and multiply, but the conditions matter: if events are not mutually exclusive, subtract the overlap; if they are not independent, the second probability changes (see trees below).

Worked example 1. A fair die is rolled once. Find P(3 or 4).

mutually exclusive: 1/6 + 1/6 = 2/6 = 1/3

Worked example 2. Two fair coins are tossed. Find P(both heads).

independent: 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4

Worked example 3 (not mutually exclusive). From a standard pack, find P(a heart or a king).

P(heart) = 13/52, P(king) = 4/52, P(heart and king) = 1/52
P(heart or king) = 13/52 + 4/52 - 1/52 = 16/52 = 4/13

Tree diagrams

Trees handle multi-stage experiments, especially without replacement. Multiply along the branches for a sequence, add between branches for alternative ways to get the same outcome.

Worked example 1 (with replacement). A bag has 3 red and 2 blue counters. Two are drawn with replacement. Find P(two red) and P(one of each).

P(RR) = 3/5 × 3/5 = 9/25
P(RB) = 3/5 × 2/5 = 6/25;  P(BR) = 2/5 × 3/5 = 6/25
P(one of each) = 6/25 + 6/25 = 12/25

Worked example 2 (without replacement). Same bag, two counters drawn without replacement. Find P(two red) and P(one of each).

P(RR) = 3/5 × 2/4 = 6/20 = 3/10
P(RB) = 3/5 × 2/4 = 6/20;  P(BR) = 2/5 × 3/4 = 6/20
P(one of each) = 12/20 = 3/5

The denominators drop by one on the second draw without replacement — that is the entire difference, and forgetting it is the standard error.

Sample space diagrams

A sample space diagram lists every possible outcome, so probabilities can be counted rather than guessed. For two dice, a two-way grid of 36 cells shows each pair; shading the cells that satisfy an event turns the question into counting squares. The method protects against the commonest combined-event error — treating non-equally-likely outcomes as equally likely.

Worked example. Two fair dice are rolled. Find P(total = 7).

total outcomes = 6 × 6 = 36
totals of 7: (1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2), (6,1) = 6 outcomes
P(total 7) = 6/36 = 1/6

Worked example 2 (sums). From the same grid, find P(total is more than 10).

totals 11 or 12: (5,6), (6,5), (6,6) = 3 outcomes
P = 3/36 = 1/12

The grid also answers difference and product questions: mark the cells whose difference is 2, or whose product is even, and count. Writing the grid out takes a minute and removes the guesswork from every part of the question.

Two-way tables and Venn diagrams

A two-way table classifies individuals by two attributes at once — boys and girls against glasses and no glasses — with totals in the margins. Reading probabilities from it is a matter of restricting attention to the right row, column or cell:

  • P(A and B): the cell where the row and column meet, over the grand total.
  • P(A or B): the sum of the cells in A plus the cells in B minus the overlap, over the grand total.
  • P(A | B): the A-cell inside B's row (or column) over B's total.

Venn diagrams do the same job for sets: the intersection is "and" (multiply along a branch or read the overlap), the union is "or" (add the regions). Choosing between the two representations is a matter of what the question gives; both are equally valid, and the arithmetic is identical once the numbers sit in the right places.

Conditional probability

Conditional probability asks for the chance of A given that B has happened:

P(A | B) = P(A and B) / P(B)

Two-way tables are the friendliest setting: restrict attention to the row or column named by the condition, then divide by that row or column's total.

Worked example. 60 students: 25 study French, 35 study Spanish, 15 study both. Find P(studies French | studies Spanish).

given Spanish: restrict to the 35 Spanish students
of those, 15 also study French
P(French | Spanish) = 15/35 = 3/7

Worked example 2 (two-way table). A table shows 40 boys (12 play chess) and 30 girls (18 play chess). Find P(plays chess | girl).

restrict to girls: 30; chess players among them: 18
P = 18/30 = 3/5

Independent events and the multiplication rule

Two events are independent when the outcome of one does not change the probability of the other. The test is arithmetic: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B) exactly when they are independent. Questions often give the separate probabilities and ask you to check independence, or give P(A), P(B) and P(A and B) and ask whether the events are independent.

if P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B)  →  independent
if not                        →  not independent (associated)

Worked example. P(rain) = 0.3, P(late) = 0.2, P(rain and late) = 0.06. Are the events independent?

P(rain) x P(late) = 0.3 × 0.2 = 0.06
0.06 = 0.06, so the events are independent.

"At least one" problems

The complement trick: P(at least one) = 1 − P(none).

Worked example. A die is rolled twice. Find P(at least one six).

P(no six) = (5/6) x (5/6) = 25/36
P(at least one six) = 1 - 25/36 = 11/36

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Complement) P(A) = 0.35. Find P(not A). Answer: 0.65.
  2. (Single event) A bag has 4 green and 6 yellow balls. Find P(green). Answer: 4/10 = 2/5.
  3. (Mutually exclusive) A spinner has probabilities 0.2, 0.3, 0.4 and x. Find x. Answer: 1 − 0.9 = 0.1.
  4. (Independent) P(A) = 0.6, P(B) = 0.5, independent. Find P(A and B) and P(A or B). Answer: 0.30; 0.6 + 0.5 − 0.3 = 0.8.
  5. (Tree) Two draws without replacement from 5 red, 3 blue. Find P(both blue). Answer: 3/8 × 2/7 = 6/56 = 3/28.
  6. (At least one) A biased coin has P(head) = 0.4. Tossed twice, find P(at least one head). Answer: 1 − 0.6² = 1 − 0.36 = 0.64.
  7. (Relative frequency) 400 seeds are planted; 340 germinate. Estimate the germination probability. Answer: 340/400 = 0.85.
  8. (Conditional) In a class, 12 of 20 boys and 8 of 15 girls wear glasses. Find P(wears glasses | boy). Answer: 12/20 = 3/5.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Adding when you should multiply: "or" adds (for exclusive events), "and" multiplies (for independent ones). Mixed-up rules produce impossible answers above 1 — a check worth making.
  • Forgetting non-replacement: the second denominator drops by one and the numerator of the taken colour drops too.
  • Probabilities above 1: an answer of 1.2 is always wrong; re-check the rule used.
  • Counting without equally likely outcomes: P = favourable/total only when every outcome is equally likely; loaded dice and biased spinners need empirical or given probabilities.
  • "At least one" done the long way: summing every case wastes time and invites errors; use 1 − P(none).
  • Conditional without restricting: P(A | B) uses the total of B's group, not the grand total. The word "given" is the signal.
  • Not adding alternative branches: one-of-each has two orders (RB and BR); both must be included.
  • Mixing forms: fractions, decimals and percentages within one calculation invite arithmetic slips; choose one form and stay with it.

Equations and symbols

Four rules cover every IGCSE probability question, and each has a condition that decides whether it applies. Learn the condition with the formula — most lost marks are a correct formula used where its condition fails.

P(event) = number of favourable outcomes / total outcomes Key: P = probability, between 0 and 1 with no unit; favourable = outcomes that satisfy the event; total = every outcome in the sample space. Valid only when all outcomes are equally likely — a biased die needs relative frequency instead.

0 <= P(A) <= 1 Key: A = any event; the bounds are the check on every answer. An answer above 1 means two rules were combined wrongly, and an answer below 0 cannot occur.

P(not A) = 1 - P(A) Key: the complement rule — every outcome is either A or not A, so the two probabilities add to 1. This is the route to every "at least one" question: P(at least one) = 1 − P(none).

P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) Key: the addition rule, valid only for mutually exclusive events — those that cannot both happen. When they can, subtract the overlap: P(heart or king) = 13/52 + 4/52 − 1/52.

P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B) Key: the multiplication rule, valid only for independent events — where one outcome does not change the other's probability. With replacement the events are independent; without replacement they are not, and the second denominator drops by one.

P(A | B) = P(A and B) / P(B) Key: A | B = "A given B"; the denominator is the total of B's group, not the grand total. In a two-way table, restrict to B's row or column first and then divide.

relative frequency = number of times the event occurred / total number of trials Key: an estimate of probability from experiment (no unit); it approaches the theoretical value as the number of trials grows, which is the answer to "explain the discrepancy" questions about small samples.

expected number = probability x number of trials Key: probability = the chance of the event in one trial; trials = how many times it is repeated; the answer is a count, so round sensibly when the context needs a whole number.

Which rule, in one table

SituationRule
Two events cannot both happenAdd: P(A) + P(B)
Two events can both happenAdd and subtract the overlap
Two events do not affect each otherMultiply
Draws without replacementMultiply, with the second denominator reduced
"At least one"1 − P(none)
"Given that"Divide by the total of the given group

Traps specific to the rules

  • Adding when the events are independent, or multiplying when they are exclusive.
  • Forgetting the second draw's denominator falls by one.
  • Counting one-of-each in only one order: RB and BR are two branches, both added.
  • Using favourable/total on outcomes that are not equally likely.
  • P(A | B) with the grand total underneath instead of B's total.
  • Mixing fractions, decimals and percentages inside one calculation.

title: Exam technique: Vectors (A2)
content:
### What earns the marks
For line equations, r = a + t b with direction from two points earns the method mark. For intersections, equating components and solving earns one mark and the consistency check earns the second. For angles and distances, the dot-product or cross-product magnitude formula quoted earns the method mark.
### Traps
Error: position vectors used as directions. Correction: subtract to get direction. Error: parameters equated across lines. Correction: different letters per line. Error: inconsistent third component ignored. Correction: verify all three or declare skew.

title: Statistics (S1) — Study Notes
content:
Statistics 1: data, sampling and correlation

S1 is about collecting, summarising and relating data. You must choose sensible models, compute summary statistics quickly, code data, spot outliers and fit a regression line.

Sampling

  • Random sample: every member of the population has equal chance of selection.
  • Systematic: every kth member. Stratified: split population into strata, sample each in proportion.
  • Bias must be avoided: random numbers, representative strata, no convenience sampling.

Averages

  • Mean: x-bar = (sum of x) / n. Sensitive to outliers.
  • Median: the middle value; for n values ordered, position (n + 1)/2. Robust to outliers.
  • Mode: the most frequent value.

Measuring spread

  • Range = largest - smallest.
  • Quartiles: Q1 is the median of the lower half, Q3 the median of the upper half; IQR = Q3 - Q1.
  • Variance = (sum of x^2)/n - (x-bar)^2, and SD = sqrt(variance).
  • The variance uses squared units; the SD returns to the original units.

Coding

For x = a + by: mean of x = a + b x-bar, SD of x = |b| SD of y. Coding never changes the correlation coefficient.

Outliers and box plots

An outlier lies below Q1 - 1.5 x IQR or above Q3 + 1.5 x IQR. Box plots show min, Q1, median, Q3, max (whiskers to the furthest non-outlier).

Correlation and regression

  • The product moment correlation coefficient r measures linear strength: -1 <= r <= 1.
  • r close to +1: strong positive linear; close to -1: strong negative; close to 0: no linear correlation. Correlation is not causation.
  • Regression line of y on x: y = a + bx with b = Sxy / Sxx and a = y-bar - b x-bar. Use it to interpolate, never extrapolate.

title: Exam technique: Representation via Numerical Measures
content:
### What earns the marks
For skewness direction, mean vs median comparison stated earns the mark. For box plots, all five values labelled earn one mark and the skew comment earns the second. For outlier checks, the fence calculation shown earns the method mark.
### Traps
Error: skew direction flipped. Correction: tail side names the skew. Error: quartiles mislabeled on plots. Correction: order min, Q1, median, Q3, max. Error: max value called an outlier by eye. Correction: test against the fence.
### Worked example
Data: 2, 4, 5, 5, 6, 7, 20. The mean is 49 / 7 = 7 and the median is 5, so the mean is larger and the skew is positive. The lower half {2, 4, 5} has median 4 (Q1). The upper half {6, 7, 20} has median 7 (Q3). IQR = 3, so the upper fence is 7 + 1.5 × 3 = 11.5, and 20 is an outlier.

title: IGCSE Computer Science: Programming Concepts and Constructs
content:
IGCSE Computer Science: Programming Concepts and Constructs

Cambridge IGCSE Computer Science 0478 (2026–2028), Paper 2 Algorithms, Programming and Logic and Paper 1 statement 4.2: types of programming language and translators, 8.1 Programming concepts, 8.2 Arrays, and 8.3 File handling. This note builds a programmer's vocabulary from zero: how code becomes machine instructions, the variables-and-constructs model of every imperative program, and how data is organised in arrays and files. Every trace below steps through memory line by line — showing exactly how each variable changes is the skill Paper 2 examines most.

From source code to machine code: translators

A CPU understands only binary machine code — patterns of 0s and 1s unique to its processor family. Humans write source code in a language (Python, C++, Java), so something must convert one to the other: a translator, and there are three kinds.

TranslatorHow it worksResultTrade-off
CompilerTranslates the whole program in one pass, before runningA standalone executable machine-code fileFast to run afterwards; errors reported before execution (C++, Pascal)
InterpreterTranslates and runs one line at a time, in sequenceNo saved executable — the translator is needed every runSlow to run, but great for testing: errors appear exactly where they occur (Python, BASIC)
AssemblerTranslates assembly (human-readable mnemonics for single machine instructions) into machine codeExecutable for one processor familyOne-to-one with machine code: fast and precise, but tied to the hardware
Compiler vs interpreter, step by step, on the same three-line program:

Program:  a = 2 * 3        b = a + 1        print(b)

Compiler:
  1. Read the ENTIRE source file first.
  2. Check syntax of every line; if line 2 is wrong, report it and produce
     nothing - fix it before any code runs.
  3. Emit one machine-code executable.
  4. Run that executable: 18 microseconds of work at full machine speed.

Interpreter:
  1. Take line 1: translate AND execute it - a becomes 6 in memory.
  2. Take line 2: translate AND execute it - b becomes 7.
  3. Take line 3: translate AND execute it - output 7.
  4. If line 2 had failed, line 1 would already have run: execution stops at
     the error, and every run pays the translation cost again.

A syntax error is a grammar mistake the translator refuses; a logic error is
grammar-correct code that computes the wrong thing - translators never catch
those, which is why testing exists.

Levels of programming language

  • Machine code — binary, executed directly, fastest, unreadable to humans, and processor-specific.
  • Assembly language — mnemonics (MOV, ADD, JMP) one per machine instruction; still low-level and hardware-tied, needing an assembler.
  • High-level languages — English-like statements (PRINT, WHILE, INPUT); portable across machines once translated, readable, faster to develop.

The trade-off is always the same: low-level code is small and fast and controls the hardware directly (drivers, embedded systems); high-level code is quick to write and easy to maintain and runs anywhere a translator exists. Fourth-generation languages (SQL, report generators) sit even higher, declaring what is wanted rather than how.

The vocabulary of a program

TermMeaningCambridge pseudocode example
VariableA named memory location whose value can change as the program runsscore <- 0
ConstantA named value fixed for the whole run — used for values like π or tax rates so they are defined once and cannot driftCONSTANT taxRate <- 0.2
Data typeWhat kind of value a variable holds: INTEGER, REAL, CHAR, STRING, BOOLEAN, DATEname : STRING
IdentifierThe name chosen for a variable, constant or proceduretotalPrice, itemCount
AssignmentStoring a value in a variable — the right side is evaluated first, then stored lefttotal <- price * qty
CommentIgnored text explaining the code to human readers// running total

Identifiers have rules worth marks: descriptive names preferred (markScheme not ms), no spaces, cannot start with a digit, and reserved words (PRINT, WHILE, IF) cannot be reused as names.

Sequence: the first construct

Every imperative program executes statements one after another, top to bottom — that is sequence. The trace is the examiner's favourite question type: keep a column per variable and rewrite each row after every statement.

Trace table. Program:

  1  a <- 5
  2  b <- 2 * a
  3  a <- a + b
  4  OUTPUT a, b

Step   statement        a    b    output
start  (nothing)        ?    ?
1      a <- 5           5    ?
2      b <- 2 * a       5    10       [reads a = 5, stores 10]
3      a <- a + b      15    10       [5 + 10 = 15 OVERWRITES the old a]
4      OUTPUT a, b                        15, 10

The trap in line 3: a + b uses the CURRENT values (5 + 10), then the result
replaces a. Assignment destroys the old value - the trace table keeps it honest.

Selection: IF, ELSE and ELSEIF

Selection chooses between paths using a condition — an expression that evaluates TRUE or FALSE. Comparison operators: =, <> (not equal), <, >, <=, >=; combine them with AND, OR, NOT. Conditions in pseudocode are never assignment: IF mark = 50, not mark <- 50.

Worked trace: grading with ELSEIF.

  IF mark >= 70 THEN
      grade <- "A"
  ELSEIF mark >= 60 THEN
      grade <- "B"
  ELSEIF mark >= 50 THEN
      grade <- "C"
  ELSE
      grade <- "U"
  ENDIF

Run with mark = 64:
  Line 1: is 64 >= 70? FALSE - skip to the next branch.
  Line 3: is 64 >= 60? TRUE - grade <- "B", and the whole structure ends.
  (The remaining branches are not even tested: ELSEIF means "else, if".)

Run with mark = 45:
  70? no. 60? no. 50? no - all conditions FALSE, so the ELSE branch runs:
  grade <- "U". ELSE is the guaranteed fallback; with no ELSE, grade would
  keep whatever it held before (possibly nothing).

Nested IF (an IF inside another's branch) handles layered conditions; the exam often asks you to write one and to test both boundary cases (69 and 70, not just 65).

Iteration: WHILE, REPEAT and FOR

Iteration repeats statements. WHILE tests first and repeats while a condition is TRUE — zero repeats possible. REPEAT…UNTIL runs the body at least once, then repeats until the condition becomes TRUE — note the polarity: WHILE repeats while TRUE, UNTIL repeats until TRUE. FOR repeats a counted number of times.

Full memory trace of a WHILE loop: running total of 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5.

  1  total <- 0
  2  count <- 1
  3  WHILE count <= 5
  4      total <- total + count
  5      count <- count + 1
  6  ENDWHILE
  7  OUTPUT total

Step      condition (count <= 5)   total   count
start                            -        -
1                                 0        -
2                                 0        1
3 test 1                          0        1   TRUE → enter body
4   total <- 0 + 1                1        1
5   count <- 1 + 1                1        2
3 test 2                          1        2   TRUE
4   total <- 1 + 2                3        2
5   count <- 2 + 1                3        3
3 test 3                          3        3   TRUE
4   total <- 3 + 3                6        3
5   count <- 3 + 1                6        4
3 test 4                          6        4   TRUE
4   total <- 6 + 4               10⁴
5   count <- 4 + 1               10⁵
3 test 5                         10⁵   TRUE
4   total <- 10 + 5              15        5
5   count <- 5 + 1               15        6
3 test 6                         15        6   FALSE → exit to line 7
7   OUTPUT 15

Two classic bugs visible here: forgetting count <- count + 1 loops forever
(count never reaches 6), and starting count at 0 would run six times.

Off-by-one errors (the loop running once too many or too few) and infinite loops (a condition never updated toward FALSE) are the two most common lost marks — always trace at the boundaries.

Constructing algorithms

Before code comes design. Structure charts break a problem into a main program and subtasks (top-down decomposition); pseudocode expresses the logic in structured English-like statements; flowcharts picture it: oval = start/stop, parallelogram = input/output, rectangle = process, diamond = decision, arrows = flow. Trace tables (as above) dry-run the algorithm to prove it before coding.

Worked example: design then trace. "Read 10 marks and output the highest."

Pseudocode:
  1  highest <- 0
  2  FOR i <- 1 TO 10³      INPUT mark
  4      IF mark > highest THEN
  5          highest <- mark
  6      ENDIF
  7  NEXT i
  8  OUTPUT highest

Trace with inputs 45, 72, 61 (first three of ten):

Step   i   mark   highest   comment
1                  0        no mark can be below 0, safe start
2    1
3         45      0
4   45 > 0 TRUE
5                45
2    2
3         72     45
4   72 > 45 TRUE
5                72
2    3
3         61     72
4   61 > 72 FALSE - highest unchanged
5                72        IF protects the winner

After all ten, line 8 outputs 72.

Procedural decomposition matters in the exam: state the subtasks (input routine, find-max routine, output routine) before writing any of them.

Arrays

An array is one variable holding many values of the same type, each with an index. It replaces dozens of separately named variables (test1, test2, …) and lets loops process the whole collection. In pseudocode an array is declared by type and size; indices in Cambridge pseudocode usually start at 0 (always check the question's convention).

Cambridge pseudocode: declaring and filling an array of 5 marks.

  DECLARE marks : ARRAY[0:4] OF INTEGER       [indices 0, 1, 2, 3, 4]
  FOR i <- 0 TO 4
      INPUT marks[i]
  NEXT i

Memory after entering 12, 47, 33, 58, 21:

  index:   0    1    2    3    4
  value:  12   47   33   58   21

marks[2] means "the value at index 2" = 33. Traps:
  marks[5] is OUT OF RANGE for a 0:4 array - undefined behaviour, and a
  guaranteed lost mark in an exam answer.
  Assigning marks[1] <- 99 overwrites 47 and leaves everything else alone.

Searching an array, step by step (linear search for 58):

  found <- FALSE
  FOR i <- 0 TO 4
      IF marks[i] = 58 THEN
          found <- TRUE
          position <- i
      ENDIF
  NEXT i

  i = 0: marks[0] = 12 - no
  i = 1: marks[1] = 47 - no
  i = 2: marks[2] = 33 - no
  i = 3: marks[3] = 58 - YES: found <- TRUE, position <- 3
  i = 4: still checked (unless the loop is exited early - a fair refinement)

Two-dimensional arrays (ARRAY[0:3, 0:2]) are grids — rows and columns — used for games boards and seating plans; a value is addressed by both indices, e.g. board[2, 1].

File handling

Variables vanish when a program ends; files persist on secondary storage. Text files are read and written sequentially, a line at a time. The pattern is always open → use → close, and you must know the mode:

  • READ mode: open an existing file to get data from it.
  • WRITE mode: create a new file (or wipe an existing one — a classic destructive bug when APPEND was needed).
  • APPEND mode: add to the end of an existing file, keeping what is there.
Worked example: totals and appends. File "scores.txt" holds three lines:
  45
  62
  51

Program:
  1  OPENFILE "scores.txt" FOR READ
  2  total <- 0
  3  WHILE NOT EOF("scores.txt")          [EOF = end of file]
  4      READFILE "scores.txt", score
  5      total <- total + score
  6  ENDWHILE
  7  CLOSEFILE "scores.txt"
  8  OPENFILE "scores.txt" FOR APPEND
  9  WRITEFILE "scores.txt", total
 10  CLOSEFILE "scores.txt"

Memory trace:
  step 2: total = 0
  step 5 (1st read): total = 0 + 45 = 45
  step 5 (2nd read): total = 45 + 62 = 10⁷
  step 5 (3rd read): total = 10⁷ + 51 = 158
  next test: EOF TRUE → exit loop
  line 9 appends 158; the file now holds four lines: 45, 62, 51, 158.

Had line 8 said FOR WRITE, the three scores would be wiped and the file would
hold only 158 - the mode is the whole question.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Using = for comparison inside conditions when the pseudocode expects <- for assignment and = for testing — know which the question's notation uses and be consistent.
  • Forgetting that assignment overwrites: a <- a + b destroys the old a; trace tables must show values before and after.
  • WHILE versus UNTIL polarity: WHILE repeats while the condition is TRUE; UNTIL repeats until it becomes TRUE — writing the wrong one inverts the loop.
  • Infinite loops from a missing or wrongly directed counter update.
  • Off-by-one errors at array and loop boundaries: a 0:4 array has five slots, and FOR i <- 1 TO 10 runs ten times, not eleven.
  • Reading past the end of file or using an open file after CLOSEFILE; always close before reopening in another mode.
  • Opening a data file FOR WRITE when APPEND was required, destroying the data.
  • Confusing a compiler with an interpreter in a comparison answer: whole-program translation versus line-by-line execution is the substance of the mark.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 2, 4 marks). Explain the difference between a compiler and an interpreter.

Answer: A compiler translates the whole source program into machine code before execution, producing a standalone executable that runs fast; syntax errors are all reported before anything runs. An interpreter translates and executes one statement at a time, so the program runs more slowly and must be retranslated each time, but errors appear exactly at the failing line and testing is quicker.

Question 2 (Paper 2, 4 marks). Complete a trace table for: x <- 3; y <- x * 2; x <- x + y; OUTPUT x.

Answer: After line 1, x = 3. After line 2, y = 6 (3 × 2), x = 3. After line 3, x = 3 + 6 = 9. The output is 9.

Question 3 (Paper 2, 6 marks). Write pseudocode to read 20 numbers and output how many are negative.

Answer: count <- 0; FOR i <- 1 TO 20; INPUT num; IF num < 0 THEN; count <- count + 1; ENDIF; NEXT i; OUTPUT count.

Question 4 (Paper 2, 3 marks). An array is declared ARRAY[0:9] OF INTEGER. State how many values it holds, the index of the first and last elements, and the meaning of num[4].

Answer: It holds 10 values; the first is at index 0 and the last at index 9; num[4] is the single value stored at the fifth position (index 4) of the array.

Question 5 (Paper 2, 4 marks). Explain the difference between opening a file FOR WRITE and FOR APPEND, and state one risk of choosing the wrong one.

Answer: FOR WRITE creates a new file and, if the file already exists, erases its previous contents before writing; FOR APPEND keeps the existing contents and adds new data at the end. Choosing WRITE when APPEND was meant destroys all previous records — an unrecoverable data loss unless a backup exists.

Question 6 (Paper 2, 4 marks). Describe what is wrong with: WHILE count <= 10; OUTPUT count; ENDWHILE.

Answer: count is never initialised (no starting value) and never incremented inside the loop, so the condition never changes — if it starts TRUE the loop repeats forever (an infinite loop), and if it is somehow FALSE the loop never runs. Fix: set count <- 1 before the loop and add count <- count + 1 inside it.

With the constructs in hand, the next note turns to the craft itself: designing, refining and testing algorithms.
