title: Quadratics
content:
Quadratics

A quadratic has the form ax² + bx + c with a ≠ 0. Master three tools: completing the square, the discriminant, and inequalities.

Completing the Square

Rewrite x² + bx + c as (x + b/2)² − (b/2)² + c.

Example: x² + 6x + 5 = (x + 3)² − 9 + 5 = (x + 3)² − 4, so the vertex is at (−3, −4).

For a > 1, factor out a first: 2x² + 12x + 19 = 2(x² + 6x) + 19 = 2(x + 3)² − 18 + 19 = 2(x + 3)² + 1.

Vertex form a(x − h)² + k gives the minimum/maximum value k at x = h — this is how you find a maximum area or minimum cost.

The Discriminant

Δ = b² − 4ac decides how the curve meets the x-axis:

ΔRootsGraph
Δ > 0two distinct real rootscrosses x-axis twice
Δ = 0repeated roottouches (tangent)
Δ < 0no real rootsnever meets x-axis

Example: kx² + 4x + 1 = 0 has equal roots when 16 − 4k = 0, so k = 4.

Quadratic Inequalities

Solve by sketching. For x² − 5x + 4 < 0, factorise: (x − 1)(x − 4) < 0, and the curve is below the axis between the roots, so 1 < x < 4.

Tip: flip the inequality when dividing by a negative number, and always sketch to check which interval you need.

Curve and Line Intersections

Set the equations equal; the resulting quadratic's discriminant tells you if the line is a secant (Δ > 0), tangent (Δ = 0) or misses (Δ < 0).

Exam tips: complete the square before reading off turning points; state the discriminant condition explicitly before solving for an unknown coefficient.

title: Magnetism & Electromagnetism — Study Notes
content:
Magnetism & Electromagnetism

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): magnets & fields; magnetic effect of a current; force on a current-carrying conductor; motor effect; electromagnetic induction (Extended); transformers (Extended).

1. Magnets and fields

Iron/steel/cobalt/nickel; like poles repel. Field lines exit N, enter S; compass plotting; plotting compass aligns with field. Induced magnetism: iron (temporary) vs steel (permanent).

2. Electromagnets

Solenoid field like a bar magnet; strength ↑ with current, turns, iron core. Uses: relays, scrapyard crane, electric bell, speaker. Hard/soft magnetic materials choose permanent vs core use.

3. Force on a current-carrying conductor

F = BIL, direction by Fleming's left hand (fIeld, current, force). Reversing current or field reverses force. D.C. motor: coil, commutator reverses current each half-turn for continuous rotation; speed/torque ↑ with current, field strength, turns/area.

4. Electromagnetic induction (Extended)

Induced e.m.f. when a conductor cuts field lines or flux changes. Fleming's right hand (generator). Factors: speed, field strength, turns. A.C. generator: slip rings; dynamo effect; Lenz's law opposes change (direction of induced current).

5. Transformers (Extended)

Vp/Vs = Np/Ns; Pin ≈ Pout (100% assumed): IpVp = IsVs. Step-up raises V, lowers I → lower I²R transmission losses; a.c. required (changing flux).

Magnetic fields and electromagnets

Like magnetic poles repel and unlike poles attract. Outside a bar magnet, field lines run from the north pole to the south pole. A solenoid is a coil of wire; its field is strengthened by increasing the current, increasing the number of turns, or placing a soft iron core inside it. An electromagnet can be switched on and off by the current, unlike a permanent magnet.

A current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field experiences a force, which is the basis of the motor effect used in electric motors.

Exam tip: when asked how to make an electromagnet stronger, give two changes, such as more turns and a larger current.

title: A Level Physics: Oscillations and Waves II
content:
A Level Physics: Oscillations and Waves II

Simple harmonic motion is the master oscillation: the movement of a pendulum, a mass on a spring, a guitar string, a child on a swing — every system that accelerates back toward an equilibrium position with a restoring force proportional to displacement. This note builds SHM from zero: the defining condition and its equations, the displacement, velocity and acceleration graphs and their calculus links, the energy bookkeeping within a cycle, and the real-world finishing topics — damping and resonance — with the applications and disasters that make them examinable.

What simple harmonic motion is

A body performs simple harmonic motion (SHM) when its acceleration is proportional to its displacement from a fixed equilibrium point and always directed toward that point:

a = - ω² x

a = acceleration (m s⁻²), x = displacement from equilibrium (m)
ω = angular frequency (rad s⁻¹); the minus sign means the
acceleration always points back toward equilibrium

The analogy: a ball in a bowl. Push the ball up the side (displacement) and gravity pulls it back with a force proportional to how far up the slope it is — push twice as far, and the restoring force doubles. That proportionality is the whole defining feature; friction-less mass-spring systems and small-angle pendulums obey it.

QuantitySymbolRelation
Displacementxx = A sin(ωt) (from equilibrium at t = 0)
AmplitudeAmaximum displacement
PeriodTT = 2π/ω; mass on a spring: T = 2π√(m/k); pendulum: T = 2π√(L/g)
Frequencyff = 1/T = ω/(2π)
Angular frequencyωω = 2πf = √(k/m) (spring), √(g/L) (pendulum)

SHM equations and graphs

Starting from equilibrium at t = 0, the kinematics follows by differentiation (or by reading the graphs):

displacement:  x = A sin(ω t)
velocity:      v = A ω cos(ω t)
acceleration:  a = - A ω² sin(ω t) = - ω² x

velocity-displacement relation:
v = ω √(A² - x²)

Graph discipline is a mark source in its own right: displacement is a sine wave; velocity leads displacement by a quarter cycle (cosine); acceleration is the inverted displacement (anti-phase, scaled by ω²). At the extremes (x = ±A): velocity is zero and acceleration is maximum; at equilibrium (x = 0): velocity is maximum and acceleration is zero. Learn the four positions (centre, both extremes, mid-point) as a table of states.

Worked example. A mass oscillates with amplitude 0.10 m and frequency 2.0 Hz. Find ω, the maximum speed, and the maximum acceleration.

ω = 2 π f = 2 × 3.14 × 2.0 = 12.6 rad s⁻¹
v_max = A ω = 0.10 × 12.6 = 1.26 m s⁻¹
a_max = A ω² = 0.10 × 158 = 15.8 m s⁻²

Worked example 2 (using v = ω√(A² − x²)). With the same oscillation, find the speed at x = 0.06 m.

v = ω √(A² - x²) = 12.6 x √(0.010 - 0.0036)
  = 12.6 x √(0.0064) = 12.6 × 0.08 = 1.01 m s⁻¹

Worked example 3 (pendulum). Find the period of a 0.90 m pendulum (g = 9.81 m s⁻²).

T = 2 π √(L/g) = 2 × 3.14 x √(0.90/9.81)
  = 6.28 x √(0.0917) = 6.28 × 0.303 = 1.90 s

Energy in simple harmonic motion

Energy shuttles between kinetic and potential stores while the total stays constant (undamped SHM):

total energy:  E = (1/2) m ω² A² = (1/2) k A²
kinetic:       KE = (1/2) m ω² (A² - x²)
potential:     PE = (1/2) m ω² x²   (spring: (1/2) k x²)

The energy curves are examinable as graphs: total energy is a horizontal line over x; KE is an inverted parabola peaking at equilibrium; PE is an upright parabola peaking at the extremes; against time both are sine-squared curves oscillating at twice the frequency of x. Doubling the amplitude quadruples the total energy (E ∝ A²) — a favourite multiple-choice item.

Worked example. A 0.50 kg mass on a spring (k = 200 N m⁻¹) oscillates with amplitude 0.08 m. Find the total energy and the kinetic energy at x = 0.04 m.

E = (1/2) k A² = 0.5 × 200 × 0.0064 = 0.64 J
PE at x = 0.04: (1/2) k x² = 0.5 × 200 × 0.0016 = 0.16 J
KE = E - PE = 0.64 - 0.16 = 0.48 J

Damping

Real oscillations lose energy to drag and friction — damping. The three regimes matter:

  • Light damping: amplitude decays exponentially while the system keeps oscillating at almost the natural frequency (a child's swing gradually slowing).
  • Critical damping: the system returns to equilibrium in the minimum time without overshooting — deliberately engineered for car suspension, door closers and moving-coil meters.
  • Heavy (over) damping: a slow, sluggish return without oscillation.

The energy lost per cycle is the exam phrasing: light damping reduces amplitude gradually because each cycle transfers energy to the surroundings; the total energy falls exponentially with time even though the frequency barely changes.

Resonance

A driven oscillation responds most strongly when the driving frequency matches the system's natural frequency — resonance. The amplitude–frequency curve shows a peak at resonance; sharper peaks mean lighter damping. The mechanism: at resonance the driving force is in phase with the velocity, so energy is transferred most efficiently each cycle.

ApplicationUse or effect
Musical instrumentsair columns and strings resonate at their natural frequencies to amplify sound
Radio tuningan LC circuit selects the broadcast frequency that resonates with it
Microwave ovensdrive water molecules near their resonant absorption frequency
Car suspensiondesigned so road-frequency inputs never match the car's natural frequency; damping controls the peak
Tacoma Narrows (1940)wind-driven resonance (with aeroelastic flutter) destroyed the bridge — the cautionary case study
Bridges and buildingsseismic design detunes natural frequencies from earthquake oscillations

Worked example. Explain why soldiers break step crossing a bridge. Answer: Marching produces a periodic driving force at the step frequency; if it matched the bridge's natural frequency, resonance would build large-amplitude oscillations and structural damage; breaking step makes the driving frequency irregular and removes the coherent input.

Worked examples: combined SHM problems

Worked example. A 0.25 kg mass on a spring completes 20 oscillations in 8.0 s. Find the spring constant k.

T = 8.0/20 = 0.40 s
T = 2 π √(m/k)  →  k = m (2 π/T)²
k = 0.25 x (6.28/0.40)² = 0.25 × 246.4 = 61.6 N m⁻¹
  = 62 N m⁻¹ (2 s.f.)

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Definition) State the defining condition for SHM. Answer: The acceleration is proportional to the displacement from equilibrium and directed toward it: a = −ω²x.
  2. (Graphs) Sketch or describe the velocity–time graph of an oscillating mass starting at maximum displacement. Answer: Velocity is a cosine-like curve starting at zero, reaching extremes of ±v_max as the mass passes equilibrium, one quarter cycle ahead of the displacement.
  3. (Calculations) An oscillator has amplitude 0.12 m and ω = 8.0 rad s⁻¹. Find the maximum acceleration. Answer: a_max = Aω² = 0.12 × 64 = 7.68 m s⁻² ≈ 7.7 m s⁻².
  4. (Energy) State how the total energy of an SHM system depends on amplitude and explain the effect of doubling it. Answer: E = ½kA², so energy is proportional to A²; doubling the amplitude quadruples the total energy.
  5. (Pendulum) Explain why a pendulum clock keeps worse time on a warm day. Answer: Warmth lengthens the pendulum L, and T = 2π√(L/g), so the period increases and the clock runs slow.
  6. (Damping) Distinguish light and critical damping. Answer: Light damping: oscillations continue with amplitude decaying exponentially; critical damping: the system returns to equilibrium in the shortest time without oscillating.
  7. (Resonance) Sketch qualitatively the amplitude–frequency response for a lightly and a heavily damped driven system, and state one use of resonance. Answer: Both peak at the natural frequency; the lightly damped peak is tall and sharp, the heavily damped one short and broad. Use: radio tuning circuits selecting a station's frequency.
  8. (Practical) Describe how you would determine g using a simple pendulum. Answer: Measure pendulum length L from pivot to bob centre; time N complete oscillations with a stopwatch and find T = t/N; repeat for several L values; plot T² against L — the gradient is 4π²/g, so g = 4π²/gradient.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • ω versus f: ω = 2πf. In a = −ω²x the ω is angular frequency; using f directly misses a factor of 4π².
  • Phase of the graphs: at maximum displacement, speed is zero and acceleration is maximum — candidates often invert this. Anchor on the extremes first: nothing moves at the turning points.
  • Energy ∝ A²: doubling amplitude quadruples energy; the amplitude of displacement does not scale energy linearly.
  • Pendulum validity: T = 2π√(L/g) assumes small angles (under about 10°) and a point mass; large angles lengthen the period.
  • Period independence: a pendulum's period is independent of bob mass and amplitude (small angle) — the classic conceptual question.
  • Damping and frequency: damping reduces amplitude and slightly shifts the peak frequency; in light damping the frequency is almost unchanged — do not claim the oscillation stops instantly.
  • Resonance condition: resonance requires the driving frequency to match the natural frequency; merely being "vibrated" does not guarantee it.
  • Spring constant from period: rearrange algebraically first (k = m(2π/T)²) and write the formula line — the rearrangement itself carries marks.
  • Precision: 2 or 3 s.f. with units (rad s⁻¹, m s⁻², N m⁻¹, J); keep π in the working until the final step.

Oscillations: what the equations are telling you

Simple harmonic motion is defined by one condition — acceleration proportional to displacement and directed towards the equilibrium position — and everything else follows from it. This section works from that condition rather than from a list of formulae: why the period is independent of amplitude, where the energy goes, what damping actually does to the motion, and why resonance can be both useful and dangerous.

From the defining condition to the equations

The defining condition is a = −ω²x. The minus sign is the whole of "directed towards the equilibrium position", and the constant ω² is the "proportional to displacement". Differentiate the displacement twice and you get back an acceleration proportional to the displacement: x = A cos(ωt) gives v = −Aω sin(ωt) and a = −Aω² cos(ωt) = −ω²x. So the equation of motion is not an extra assumption; it is the condition written out.

Speed is greatest at the equilibrium position, where the displacement is zero, and zero at the extremes, where the displacement is A. That follows from the velocity expression: v = ±ω√(A² − x²), which is maximum when x = 0 and zero when x = A. Acceleration does the opposite: it is zero at the centre and maximum at the extremes. Students often get these two the wrong way round; the physical picture is that a pendulum moves fastest as it passes the bottom and is momentarily stationary at the top of each swing, while the restoring force is greatest at the extremes.

The period is T = 2π/ω, and for a mass on a spring ω = √(k/m), so T = 2π√(m/k); for a simple pendulum ω = √(g/L), so T = 2π√(L/g). Two consequences are examinable. The period does not depend on amplitude, which is what makes a pendulum a clock: the swings get smaller as the clock runs down, but they take the same time. And the period does depend on mass for a spring but not for a pendulum, because the restoring force for a spring is proportional to the extension while for a pendulum it is proportional to the component of weight, which depends on g and L rather than on the bob's mass.

Energy in SHM, and the shape of the curves

At the extremes the energy is entirely potential — elastic in a spring, gravitational in a pendulum — and the kinetic energy is zero. At the equilibrium position it is entirely kinetic and the potential energy is zero. In between, the two are exchanged. The kinetic energy is ½mv², which with v = ω√(A² − x²) becomes ½mω²(A² − x²); the potential energy is ½mω²x²; and their sum, ½mω²A², is constant. That total is the maximum kinetic energy and also the maximum potential energy, and it is proportional to the square of the amplitude, which is why doubling the amplitude quadruples the energy that must be supplied.

The graphs are worth sketching once and remembering: kinetic energy peaks at the centre and falls to zero at both extremes, potential energy does the reverse, and both are parabolas in x rather than sine curves in t. A graph of total energy against time is a horizontal line if there is no damping — and that flat line is the reason a question asking "why does the amplitude not change?" wants the answer "no energy is lost to the surroundings".

Damping: three cases and one design decision

Damping removes energy from an oscillator, usually to the surroundings as thermal energy. Light damping lets the amplitude decay over many oscillations, and the period is almost unchanged. Heavy damping removes energy so quickly that the system returns to equilibrium without oscillating at all, but slowly. Critical damping is the boundary case: the system returns in the shortest possible time without overshooting (Figure 1).

The engineering examples are chosen because one of the three behaviours is exactly what is wanted. Car suspension is designed to be slightly under critical damping, so that a bump is absorbed quickly without the car bouncing; a door closer is critically damped so the door shuts without slamming; a galvanometer needle is damped so that it settles on a reading quickly rather than swinging past it. A child on a swing wants very light damping, because the point is to keep going.

Resonance, and why the Tacoma Narrows bridge is not the whole story

Every oscillator has a natural frequency. If a periodic driving force is applied at that frequency, the amplitude of the response is maximum — resonance — because each push arrives in step with the motion and adds energy. The amplitude also depends on the damping: lightly damped systems resonate sharply and reach a large amplitude, heavily damped ones have a broad, low peak.

Useful resonance is easy to list: a microwave oven drives water molecules at their resonant frequency, a radio tunes its circuit so that one station's frequency resonates while others do not, and a musical instrument's body resonates to amplify a particular range of notes. Destructive resonance needs the mechanism named: soldiers marching in step across a bridge can drive it at its natural frequency, which is why they break step; a washing machine spinning at a speed that matches its own natural frequency walks across the floor; and a building can be driven by wind or by an earthquake at a frequency close to its own. The remedy in each case is either to change the natural frequency or to add damping, and both are examinable answers.

One caution about the Tacoma Narrows collapse: the popular account says it was simple resonance, but the motion was a torsional flutter, a self-exciting oscillation rather than a response to a periodic driving force at the natural frequency. If you are asked about resonance, use the marching soldiers or the washing machine; if you are asked about Tacoma Narrows, describe aeroelastic flutter and do not claim it as a resonance example.

The graph questions, and how to read them

Three graphs appear repeatedly. A displacement-time graph of SHM is a sine or cosine curve, and its gradient at any point is the velocity; the gradient is steepest at the centre and zero at the extremes. A velocity-time graph is the same curve shifted by a quarter of a period, and its gradient is the acceleration. An acceleration-displacement graph is a straight line through the origin with a negative gradient, whose gradient is −ω² — which is the experimental test for SHM and the reason a question might ask you to show that a motion is simple harmonic by plotting a against x.

When reading any of these, check the axes before anything else. A graph of displacement against time has a period you read horizontally and an amplitude you read vertically; a graph of displacement against position (for a wave, not an oscillator) has a wavelength horizontally. The two look identical and mean completely different things.

Equations and symbols

Simple harmonic motion is one defining condition, its three kinematic consequences, and the energy bookkeeping that follows from them. Note every symbol: ω is angular frequency in rad s⁻¹, not frequency in Hz, and the factor of 2π between them is where most marks are lost.

a = - ω² x Key: a = acceleration (m s⁻²); ω = angular frequency (rad s⁻¹); x = displacement from equilibrium (m). The minus sign is the definition: acceleration always points back toward equilibrium. Proving proportionality to −x is the mark for "show that this is SHM".

x = A sin(ω t) Key: x = displacement (m); A = amplitude, the maximum displacement (m); ω = angular frequency (rad s⁻¹); t = time (s). This form assumes the oscillation starts at equilibrium; starting at maximum displacement gives a cosine.

v = A ω cos(ω t) Key: v = velocity (m s⁻¹); A ω = maximum speed (m s⁻¹); the cosine shows velocity leads displacement by a quarter cycle and is zero at the extremes.

v = ω √(A² - x²) Key: the velocity at a given displacement without needing the time; maximum (Aω) at x = 0, zero at x = ±A. This is the form to use when the question gives a position rather than a clock reading.

ω = 2πf = √(k/m) (spring), √(g/L) (pendulum) Key: ω = angular frequency (rad s⁻¹); f = frequency (Hz); k = spring constant (N m⁻¹); m = mass (kg); g = 9.81 m s⁻²; L = pendulum length (m). The pendulum form assumes small angles and a point mass.

T = 2π√(m/k) Key: T = period (s); m = mass on the spring (kg); k = spring constant (N m⁻¹). Period rises with mass and falls with stiffness, and is independent of amplitude.

ω = 2 π f = 2 × 3.14 × 2.0 = 12.6 rad s⁻¹ Key: f = 2.0 Hz, so ω = 12.6 rad s⁻¹. Substituting f directly into a = −ω²x underestimates the acceleration by 4π² ≈ 39.5.

v_max = A ω Key: v_max = maximum speed (m s⁻¹), reached as the mass passes equilibrium; A = amplitude (m); ω = angular frequency (rad s⁻¹).

a_max = A ω² Key: a_max = maximum acceleration (m s⁻²), reached at the extremes where the restoring force is greatest; A = amplitude (m); ω = angular frequency (rad s⁻¹).

E = (1/2) m ω² A² = (1/2) k A² Key: E = total energy of the oscillation (J); m = mass (kg); ω = angular frequency (rad s⁻¹); A = amplitude (m); k = spring constant (N m⁻¹). Energy is proportional to A², so doubling the amplitude quadruples it.

KE = (1/2) m ω² (A² - x²) Key: KE = kinetic energy at displacement x (J); the bracket is largest at equilibrium, where the speed is greatest, and zero at the extremes.

PE = (1/2) m ω² x² Key: PE = potential energy stored at displacement x (J); for a spring this is (1/2)kx². Adding KE and PE at any x returns the constant total E.

k = m (2 π/T)² Key: k = spring constant (N m⁻¹); m = mass (kg); T = measured period (s). Rearranging first and quoting the rearranged formula is worth a mark, and it is the standard route from a period measurement to k.

The graphs are the answer to half the questions. Displacement is a sine, velocity a cosine, acceleration the inverted displacement; at the extremes the speed is zero and the acceleration is maximum, at equilibrium the reverse. Anchoring on those four positions prevents the phase error that reverses a whole sketch.

title: AS Level Physics: Materials and Deformation
content:
AS Level Physics: Materials and Deformation

Edexcel International A Level Physics, Unit 1 (WPH11) Mechanics and Materials — Hooke's law, stress and strain, Young modulus, elastic and plastic behaviour, and elastic strain energy. This is where mechanics meets the laboratory: the definitions are precise, the graphs carry most of the marks, and the measurement of Young modulus is one of the unit's core practicals and a favourite of WPH13.

Hooke's law

Stretch a spring and it extends; double the load and (at first) the extension doubles. That proportionality is Hooke's law:

force = spring constant x extension        F = k x
  • F: load in newtons (N); k: spring constant (the stiffness) in newtons per metre (N m⁻¹); x: extension in metres (m), where extension = loaded length − original length. Extension is positive for stretching and negative for compression.
  • The law holds only up to the limit of proportionality: beyond it the load–extension graph curves, and past the elastic limit the material is permanently deformed — the extension remains when the load is removed.

A load–extension graph is a straight line through the origin up to the limit of proportionality, and its gradient is the spring constant. Springs in series share the load and add their extensions (1/k = 1/k₁ + 1/k₂); springs in parallel share the load and add their spring constants. Hooke's law applies to all elastic materials, not just coils: a wire, a beam and a rubber band all show the same initial proportionality.

Stress and strain

Extension depends on the size of the sample as well as the material, so materials are compared using quantities that are independent of dimensions. Stress is the force per unit cross-sectional area; strain is the extension per unit original length:

tensile stress = force / cross-sectional area        sigma = F / A
tensile strain = extension / original length        epsilon = x / L
  • Stress (sigma): pascals (Pa = N m⁻²); strain (epsilon): dimensionless, often quoted as a percentage. Both are scalars in a tensile test, but the sign distinguishes tension (positive) from compression (negative).
  • A: cross-sectional area in square metres (m²); L: original length in metres (m); x: extension in metres (m).

Strain has no unit because it is a ratio of two lengths — a common examination trap. Engineering strain uses the original length; so does the AS definition.

Young modulus

The stiffness of a material itself, as opposed to a particular sample, is Young modulus:

Young modulus = stress / strain        E = sigma / epsilon = F L / (A x)
  • E: Young modulus in pascals (Pa), usually quoted in gigapascals (1 GPa = 10⁹ Pa). Steel is about 200 GPa, aluminium about 70 GPa, rubber about 0.01 GPa.
  • E is the gradient of the straight-line (linear) portion of the stress–strain graph, and it is constant for a given material within the limit of proportionality.

Measuring Young modulus (core practical). A long steel wire is clamped at one end, loaded with known masses over a pulley, and its extension measured with a travelling microscope, a vernier scale or an extensometer attached directly to the wire. The long wire is deliberate: a 2 m wire stretches far more than a 30 cm one for the same stress, so the percentage uncertainty in the extension is small. Diameter is measured with a micrometer at several points and orientations and averaged, because A = πd²/4 and the diameter enters squared. Plot load against extension; the gradient is k, and E = FL/(Ax) is evaluated from the gradient and the measured dimensions. The procedure repeats the readings, checks the wire returns to its original length (elastic region), and keeps the load below the limit of proportionality.

Stress–strain and load–extension graphs

FeatureMeaning
Initial straight lineElastic deformation: stress is proportional to strain; gradient = Young modulus; unloaded material returns to its original length
Limit of proportionalityEnd of the straight line: stress and strain are no longer proportional
Elastic limitBeyond this point deformation is plastic: permanent set remains after unloading
Yield pointA sudden large extension for little extra load; the material flows
Ultimate tensile stressThe maximum stress on the graph, where necking begins (the wire thins locally)
Fracture pointThe wire breaks

The area under a load–extension graph is the work done in stretching the sample; the area under a stress–strain graph is the energy stored per unit volume. Material types read straight off the graph: a ductile material (copper) has a long plastic region before breaking; a brittle material (glass, cast iron) fractures with little plastic deformation; a polymeric material (rubber) shows a long, curved elastic region and large strain at low stress.

Elastic strain energy

Work must be done to stretch a material, and while the deformation is elastic that work is stored as elastic strain (potential) energy in the stretched bonds:

elastic strain energy = 1/2 x force x extension        E = 1/2 F x = 1/2 k x^2
  • E: energy in joules (J); F: load in newtons (N); x: extension in metres (m); k: spring constant in newtons per metre (N m⁻¹).
  • It equals the area under the load–extension graph (a triangle, ½ × base × height), and the energy per unit volume is the area under the stress–strain graph, ½ × stress × strain in the linear region.

This is why an elastic band gets warm when stretched repeatedly — hysteresis — and why a bow stores energy in its limbs. On release, the stored energy converts to kinetic energy: ½kx² = ½mv² gives the launch speed of a spring-loaded trolley.

Unit 3 skills: uncertainty in a materials experiment

WPH13 regularly uses a materials experiment as the context for data-analysis questions. The skills it marks:

  • Choosing instruments to match the expected size of the quantity (micrometer for wire diameter, vernier or extensometer for extension), and explaining why (small quantities carry large percentage uncertainties otherwise).
  • Percentage uncertainty propagation for E = FL/(Ax): add the percentage uncertainties of F, L, A and x, remembering that A ∝ d² so the diameter's percentage uncertainty is doubled.
  • Error bars on both axes, best-fit line, and the uncertainty in the gradient from the steepest and shallowest lines through the error bars.
  • Control variables: same wire material and diameter throughout, same temperature, avoid overloading beyond the elastic limit, allow the wire to settle before each reading.
  • Safety: long wires under heavy loads store large energies and can snap — wear eye protection, stand behind a barrier, use a safety cage on the pulley, add masses gently.

Worked example: Young modulus and its uncertainty

A steel wire of length 1.80 m and diameter 0.40 mm extends 2.1 mm under a load of 60 N.

area = pi d^2 / 4 = 3.14 x (0.00040)^2 / 4 = 1.26 × 10⁻⁷ m²
stress = F / A = 60 / 1.26 × 10⁻⁷ = 4.8 × 10⁸ Pa
strain = x / L = 0.0021 / 1.80 = 1.17 × 10⁻³
Young modulus = stress / strain = 4.8 × 10⁸ / 1.17 × 10⁻³ = 4.1 × 10¹¹ Pa (about 400 GPa)

A sanity check flags the result: steel is about 200 GPa, so a value of 400 GPa suggests an error — in fact the extension here is half the realistic value, which is exactly the sort of conclusion an evaluation question wants. Uncertainties: with the extension measured as 2.1 ± 0.1 mm its percentage uncertainty is 4.8 per cent; the diameter 0.40 ± 0.01 mm gives 2.5 per cent, doubled to 5.0 per cent through d²; the length contributes about 0.3 per cent. The total is about 10 per cent, dominated by the extension — so an extensometer rather than a ruler would improve the result most.

Common mistakes

  • Confusing the spring constant (a property of a particular spring, N m⁻¹) with Young modulus (a property of a material, Pa).
  • Using the stretched length instead of the original length in strain, or forgetting to square the diameter when finding the cross-sectional area.
  • Quoting strain with a unit; it is dimensionless.
  • Applying E = FL/(Ax) or F = kx beyond the limit of proportionality.
  • Forgetting the ½ in elastic strain energy: the load rises from zero linearly, so the work is the triangle's area, not the full rectangle.
  • Reading the gradient of a load–extension graph as Young modulus; Young modulus is the gradient of stress against strain. Convert first.
  • Missing that A = πd²/4 means the diameter's uncertainty doubles in the final percentage.
  • Assuming a brittle material stores much energy before fracture; the area under its graph is tiny.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (WPH11, 3 marks). A 2.0 N load stretches a spring from 12.0 cm to 15.0 cm. Calculate the spring constant and the extension produced by a 5.0 N load.

Answer: Extension = 3.0 cm = 0.030 m, so k = F/x = 2.0/0.030 = 67 N m⁻¹. With 5.0 N, x = F/k = 5.0/67 = 0.075 m = 7.5 cm (assuming the limit of proportionality is not exceeded).

Question 2 (WPH11, 4 marks). A copper wire of length 2.00 m and cross-sectional area 0.50 mm² is loaded with 100 N and extends 1.2 mm. Calculate the stress, the strain and Young modulus.

Answer: Stress = F/A = 100 / (0.50 × 10⁻⁶) = 2.0 × 10⁸ Pa. Strain = x/L = 0.0012/2.00 = 6.0 × 10⁻⁴. Young modulus = 2.0 × 10⁸ / 6.0 × 10⁻⁴ = 3.3 × 10¹¹ Pa ≈ 330 GPa.

Question 3 (WPH13, 4 marks). Explain why a long thin wire is used to measure Young modulus, and why the diameter is measured at several positions.

Answer: The extension is proportional to length and inversely proportional to area, so a long thin wire gives a measurable extension under a modest load, keeping the percentage uncertainty in the extension small. The diameter is measured at several positions and in two perpendicular directions and averaged, because the wire's diameter is not perfectly uniform and the area depends on d², so a single unrepresentative measurement would skew the result.

Question 4 (WPH11, 3 marks). A spring of constant 400 N m⁻¹ is compressed by 0.12 m. Calculate the elastic potential energy stored and the speed it can give to a 0.50 kg ball.

Answer: E = ½kx² = ½ × 400 × 0.0144 = 2.9 J. Setting ½mv² = 2.9 gives v = √(2 × 2.9/0.50) = 3.4 m s⁻¹.

Question 5 (WPH11, 4 marks). Describe the difference between elastic and plastic deformation, and explain how a stress–strain graph shows which is occurring.

Answer: In elastic deformation the atoms are displaced slightly from their equilibrium spacing and return when the load is removed, so no permanent change occurs; the stress–strain graph is a straight line whose gradient is Young modulus. In plastic deformation the atomic planes slide over one another, so the material is permanently changed when unloaded; on the graph this is beyond the elastic limit, where the line curves and the strain grows faster than the stress. The limit of proportionality marks the end of the linear region; the elastic limit marks the onset of permanent set.

Question 6 (WPH13, 3 marks). A student's value of Young modulus is 30 per cent below the accepted value. Suggest two likely sources of error.

Answer: The extension was measured with a ruler over too short a gauge length, underestimating it (a systematic underestimate of extension gives an underestimate of E); the wire may already have been stretched beyond its elastic limit on earlier runs, giving extra extension for the same load. Use an extensometer over a longer gauge length, keep loads within the elastic region, and take repeated readings at each load.

Unit 1's remaining strand — energy, power and turning effects — continues the mechanics.

title: Superposition — Study Notes
content:
Superposition

Principle of superposition

When two or more waves meet at a point, the resultant displacement is the vector sum of the individual displacements. Constructive interference occurs where the waves are in phase; destructive interference occurs where they are in antiphase.

Stationary waves

  • A stationary wave forms when two progressive waves of the same frequency, amplitude and wavelength travel in opposite directions and superpose.
  • Nodes are points of zero amplitude; antinodes are points of maximum amplitude. Adjacent nodes (or antinodes) are separated by λ/2.
  • On a string fixed at both ends, the fundamental frequency is f = v/(2L), so the wavelength is λ = 2L.

Interference

For coherent sources (same frequency and a constant phase difference) with slit separation a and screen distance D, the fringe spacing is Δx = λD/a.

Diffraction

Diffraction is the spreading of a wave after it passes through a gap or round an edge. It is greatest when the gap width is comparable to the wavelength.

Diffraction grating

For a grating with slit spacing d, the angle θ of the nth-order maximum satisfies nλ = d sin θ. A grating with more lines per metre gives a smaller d and larger angles of diffraction.

Worked example: light of wavelength 600 nm passes through two slits 0.30 mm apart, with a screen 1.5 m away. Fringe spacing Δx = λD/a = (600 × 10⁻⁹ × 1.5) ÷ (3.0 × 10⁻⁴) = 3.0 mm.

Exam tips: convert nm and mm to metres before using Δx = λD/a. Check the order n when using a grating. Coherence is a requirement for interference, so state it.

The diffraction grating equation

A diffraction grating has many closely spaced slits. Light of wavelength λ leaves the grating at angle θ to form bright maxima when d sin θ = nλ, where d is the slit spacing and n is the order of the maximum. Each order is sharper and more widely separated than a double slit, because the many slits reinforce the bright positions. The number of orders visible is limited by the condition that sin θ cannot exceed 1.

Exam tip: convert the slit spacing to metres before using the grating equation, and note that the central maximum is n = 0.

title: Magnetic Fields and Electromagnetism — Study Notes
content:
Magnetic Fields and Electromagnetism

Edexcel International A Level Physics — Unit 4 (WPH14), sat at A2.

Magnetic flux density

A magnetic field is a region where a magnetic force acts on a magnet, a current-carrying conductor or a moving charge. Its strength is the magnetic flux density B, measured in tesla (T). Field lines run from north to south outside a magnet and never cross.

Force on a current-carrying conductor

A conductor of length L carrying current I at right angles to a field B feels F = BIL. In general F = BIL sin θ, where θ is the angle between the conductor and the field. The force is zero when the conductor is parallel to the field.

Fleming's left-hand rule: First finger = Field (from north to south), seCond finger = Current (conventional, positive to negative), thuMb = Motion (the force). Hold the hand so the three fingers are mutually perpendicular. Check the current direction: it is conventional current, from + to −, not electron flow.

Example: a 0.25 m wire carrying 3.0 A at right angles to a 0.40 T field feels F = 0.40 × 3.0 × 0.25 = 0.30 N.

Force on a moving charge

A charge Q moving with speed v at right angles to B feels F = BQv. The force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so the speed does not change, only the direction. In a uniform field the charge follows a circular path of radius r = mv/BQ. The period T = 2πm/BQ does not depend on the speed.

Velocity selector: crossed electric and magnetic fields give undeflected motion when qE = qvB, so v = E/B.

Magnetic field due to a current

A long straight wire gives B = μ₀I/(2πd), with μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹. Inside a long solenoid of n turns per metre, B = μ₀nI. The field is uniform inside the solenoid and weak outside it.

Electromagnetic induction

Magnetic flux is Φ = BA cos θ, measured in weber (Wb). Faraday's law states that the induced e.m.f. equals the rate of change of flux linkage: ε = −N ΔΦ/Δt. Lenz's law gives the direction: the induced e.m.f. opposes the change that produces it. This is the energy conservation principle, which is why the minus sign appears.

Example: a 200-turn coil whose flux changes by 2.0 mWb in 0.10 s has a mean e.m.f. of 4.0 V.

Alternating currents

For a sinusoidal current, the root-mean-square value is I_rms = I₀/√2, and similarly V_rms = V₀/√2. The mean power is P = I_rms²R = V_rms²/R, and it is the rms value that equals the d.c. value for the same heating effect.

Rectification and smoothing

A diode passes current in one direction only. A half-wave rectifier gives pulses for half of each cycle. A full-wave bridge rectifier uses all of the input, so its output frequency is twice the input frequency. A smoothing capacitor across the output charges at each peak and discharges between peaks, reducing the ripple.

Exam tips: use the rms value for power calculations, not the peak. For Lenz's law, always state the opposing effect in words. Show the angle when the field is not perpendicular to the wire.

title: Exam technique: Magnetic Fields and Electromagnetism
content:
### What earns the marks
For wires, BIL with right-angle condition earns both marks. For selectors, E/B equating the forces earns the method mark. For induction, Lenz opposition stated earns the explanation mark; power conserved in transformers earns the calculation marks.
### Traps
Error: parallel motion assumed to feel force. Correction: only the perpendicular component counts. Error: induced current aiding the change. Correction: it opposes the change. Error: particle path guessed straight. Correction: perpendicular entry gives circular arcs.

title: Exam technique: Nuclear Physics
content:
### What earns the marks
For radiations, alpha-beta-gamma ordered by penetration earns one mark with absorbers earns the second. For half-life, each halving step shown earns stepwise credit. For deflection, mass difference used to explain earns the explanation mark.
### Traps
Error: paper claimed to stop beta. Correction: paper stops alpha only. Error: half-life mass subtracted linearly. Correction: halve each period. Error: closer source assumed lower rate. Correction: closer means higher count rate.

title: AS Level Mathematics: Probability
content:
AS Level Mathematics: Probability

Probability assigns numbers to uncertainty on a scale from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). This note builds the topic from zero: the basic rules, sample spaces and Venn diagrams, mutually exclusive and independent events, tree diagrams for sequences including without-replacement problems, conditional probability in two-way tables, and the counting that makes "equally likely" precise. Every rule is stated with its condition, because most probability errors are conditions applied where they do not hold.

The basic rules

0 <= P(A) <= 1
P(not A) = 1 - P(A)
P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B)   (the addition rule)
P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B|A)            (the multiplication rule)

mutually exclusive: P(A and B) = 0  →  P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B)
independent: P(A and B) = P(A) P(B)

The subtraction of the overlap is the whole point of the addition rule: counting A and B separately counts their intersection twice.

Worked example. In a class of 30, 18 study French, 12 study German and 6 study both. Find the probability a student studies at least one.

P(F or G) = 18/30 + 12/30 - 6/30 = 24/30 = 0.8
so 6 students study neither

Sample spaces and equally likely outcomes

P(event) = (number of favourable outcomes)/(total outcomes)
valid only when all outcomes are equally likely

Worked example. Two fair dice are thrown. Find the probability the total is 7.

36 equally likely pairs; totals of 7: (1,6)(2,5)(3,4)(4,3)(5,2)(6,1)
P = 6/36 = 1/6

Worked example 2 (systematic listing). A bag holds 2 red and 3 blue counters; two are drawn without replacement. List the sample space and find P(both red).

P(RR) = 2/5 × 1/4 = 2/20 = 1/10
systematic listing confirms 20 ordered pairs, 2 of them RR

Venn diagrams

Two overlapping circles inside a rectangle: the rectangle is the sample space, the overlap is "both", the outside is "neither". Every region should be filled so that the totals match.

|A only| = |A| - |A and B|
|neither| = total - |A or B|

Worked example. 40 students: 22 play football, 15 play hockey, 8 play both. Find P(plays exactly one) and P(plays neither).

football only 14; hockey only 7; both 8; neither 40 - 29 = 11
P(exactly one) = 21/40
P(neither) = 11/40

Tree diagrams

Trees handle sequences of events. Multiply along a branch for "and", add across branches for "or". The second-stage probabilities change when items are not replaced.

Worked example (with replacement). A bag holds 3 red and 2 blue counters. Two are drawn with replacement. Find P(exactly one red).

P(RB) = 3/5 × 2/5 = 6/25
P(BR) = 2/5 × 3/5 = 6/25
P(exactly one red) = 12/25

Worked example 2 (without replacement). Same bag, two draws without replacement.

P(RB) = 3/5 × 2/4 = 6/20
P(BR) = 2/5 × 3/4 = 6/20
P(exactly one red) = 12/20 = 3/5
P(both red) = 3/5 × 2/4 = 3/10

Both branches for "exactly one" are needed: the event can happen in either order, and omitting one branch halves the answer.

Conditional probability

P(B | A) = P(A and B)/P(A)

restricting the sample space to A is the same calculation done
by counting within the row of a two-way table

Worked example (two-way table). 50 students: 30 pass maths, 25 pass physics, 20 pass both. Given a student passed maths, find P(they passed physics).

P(P | M) = 20/30 = 2/3
not 20/50: conditioning has already restricted the sample space to the
30 who passed maths

Worked example 2 (tree). Using the without-replacement bag, find the probability the second is red given the first was blue.

after a blue is removed, 3 red and 1 blue remain
P(R | B) = 3/4

Independence and mutual exclusivity

These two ideas are constantly confused and are logically opposite: mutually exclusive events cannot happen together, while independent events do not influence each other.

mutually exclusive: P(A and B) = 0
independent: P(A and B) = P(A) P(B)

if two events with positive probability are mutually exclusive,
they are NOT independent (knowing one happened rules out the other)

Worked example. A fair coin and a fair die are thrown. Show the events are independent.

P(head) = 1/2;  P(six) = 1/6;  P(head and six) = 1/12
(1/2)(1/6) = 1/12, so the product rule holds: independent

Counting and arrangements

When outcomes are equally likely but numerous, counting techniques are quicker than listing.

product rule for choices: m x n ways for two independent choices
arrangements of n distinct items: n!
arrangements of a selection: n!/(n - r)!

Worked example. A password is 2 letters followed by 2 digits. How many passwords are possible, and what is P(all four characters are distinct)?

total = 26 × 26 × 10 × 10 = 67600
first letter has 26 options, second 25; first digit 10, second 9
favourable = 26 × 25 × 10 × 9 = 58500
P = 58500/67600 = 0.865

Set notation and three-region problems

Exam questions use set notation throughout: A ∩ B for "both", A ∪ B for "either", A′ for "not A". Read every symbol before calculating, and fill a Venn diagram innermost region first.

P(A and B) = P(A ∩ B)
P(A or B) = P(A ∪ B)
P(not A) = P(A′)
P(A only) = P(A) - P(A ∩ B)
P(exactly one) = P(A) + P(B) - 2P(A ∩ B)

Worked example. P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.4, P(A ∩ B) = 0.2. Find P(A′ ∩ B′) and P(exactly one).

P(A ∪ B) = 0.5 + 0.4 - 0.2 = 0.7
P(A′ ∩ B′) = 1 - 0.7 = 0.3
P(exactly one) = 0.5 + 0.4 - 2(0.2) = 0.5

Worked example 2 (three sets). 100 students: 50 study maths, 40 physics, 30 chemistry; 20 study maths and physics, 15 physics and chemistry, 10 maths and chemistry, 5 study all three. How many study none?

union = 50 + 40 + 30 - 20 - 15 - 10 + 5 = 80
the +5 adds back the triple overlap, which the three pairwise
subtractions removed three times and the three singles added
twice too many
none = 10⁰ - 80 = 20

The inclusion-exclusion pattern generalises: add the singles, subtract the pairs, add back the triples. Drawing the three-circle diagram and filling from the centre outward is the safest check.

Expected frequency and fairness

Probability becomes practical when multiplied by the number of trials: expected frequency = probability × trials. A large gap between observed and expected frequency is evidence that the model is wrong — the basis of every fairness question.

expected frequency = n P(event)

fair die, 600 rolls: expected sixes = 600 × 1/6 = 10⁰

Worked example. A die is rolled 600 times and a six appears 130 times. Comment on fairness.

expected = 10⁰;  observed = 130
observed exceeds expected by 30 per cent, a large gap
suggesting the die may be biased towards six, though a formal test
would be needed to judge whether the gap is within natural chance
variation

Worked example 2 (expected profit). A raffle sells 500 tickets at 2 pounds; one prize of 300 pounds. Find the organiser's expected profit.

revenue 10⁰⁰; expected payout = 300 (certain)
expected profit = 700 pounds, i.e. 1.40 pounds per ticket

When a game's expected payout exceeds its cost the player profits in the long run; comparing expected value with price is the standard modelling question.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Complement) P(A) = 0.35. Find P(not A). Answer: 0.65.
  2. (Addition) P(A) = 0.4, P(B) = 0.5, P(A∩B) = 0.2. Find P(A∪B). Answer: 0.7.
  3. (Mutually exclusive) P(A) = 0.3, P(B) = 0.4, A and B exclusive. Find P(A or B). Answer: 0.7.
  4. (Independent) P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.3, independent. Find P(A and B). Answer: 0.15.
  5. (Dice) Two dice: P(total ≥ 10). Answer: 6/36 = 1/6.
  6. (Tree) 4 red, 6 blue; two without replacement: P(both blue). Answer: 6/10 × 5/9 = 1/3.
  7. (Conditional) From a two-way table, P(A|B) = 0.4 and P(B) = 0.5. Find P(A and B). Answer: 0.2.
  8. (Counting) How many ways can 3 of 5 books be arranged on a shelf? Answer: 5 × 4 × 3 = 60.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Adding without subtracting the overlap: P(A) + P(B) overcounts the intersection; use the full addition rule.
  • Conditional versus joint: P(A|B) restricts the sample space to B; it is not P(A and B)/P(B) with the wrong denominator.
  • Missing branches: "exactly one" usually has two orders; draw the tree and add both paths.
  • Replacement errors: without replacement, both the numerator and the denominator change on the second draw.
  • Independence assumed: the product rule needs independence, which must be justified (or follows from separate random mechanisms).
  • Mutually exclusive confused with independent: exclusive events with positive probability are dependent.
  • Probabilities not summing: the branches from any node must sum to 1; a total that does not is an arithmetic signal.
  • Decimal rounding: keep exact fractions where asked, and do not round intermediate probabilities.

Formula summary

P(not A) = 1 - P(A)
P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B)
P(A and B) = P(A) P(B|A);  independent: P(A) P(B)
P(B|A) = P(A and B)/P(A)
expected frequency = n P(event)

Every one of these is a rearrangement of the multiplication rule or the addition rule. When a question stalls, ask which two of the three quantities — joint, conditional, marginal — you have, and which the question wants.

title: Exam technique: Programming Concepts
content:
### What earns the marks
To earn full marks on this topic, students need to demonstrate a clear understanding of programming concepts, including variables, data types, selection, iteration, arrays, file handling, and subroutines, as outlined in statements 4.2, 8.1, 8.2, and 8.3. Command words such as calculate, show that, explain, describe, justify, and state are used to assess this understanding. For example, a question may ask students to explain the difference between a WHILE loop and a REPEAT loop, or to describe how to declare and use a 2D array. Working and reasons must be shown to support answers.
### Traps
Common mistakes include using the wrong loop type, such as using a WHILE loop when a REPEAT loop is needed, or vice versa. Another error is failing to declare variables before use, or using the wrong data type. Additionally, students may forget to close files after use, or use the wrong file mode.
### Memory hooks
To remember the different data types, students can use the mnemonic INTEGER, REAL, CHAR, STRING, BOOLEAN, DATE. To recall the difference between a procedure and a function, students can think of a procedure as a recipe that performs a task, while a function is a recipe that returns a value. When working with 2D arrays, students can use the pattern of looping over rows first, then columns.
### Timing
This topic typically accounts for 20-30% of the paper, and students should budget around 30-40 minutes to answer questions on programming concepts. Students should aim to spend around 10-15 minutes on each question, depending on the mark value and complexity.
