title: Algebra — Equations — Study Notes
content:
Algebra — Equations

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): linear equations, simultaneous equations, quadratic formula, completing the square, forming equations from words.

1. Linear equations

3(x − 2) = x + 4 → 3x − 6 = x + 4 → 2x = 10 → x = 5. With fractions, multiply through by the LCD first.

2. Forming equations

Translate shapes/situations: "rectangle length 3 cm more than width, perimeter 34" → 2w + 2(w + 3) = 34 → w = 7.

3. Simultaneous equations

  • Elimination: 2x + y = 7 and x − y = 2 → add → 3x = 9 → x = 3, y = 1.
  • Substitution for linear–quadratic: substitute y = 2x into x² + y² = 20 → 5x² = 20 → x = ±2.

4. Quadratics by formula

x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / 2a.

Example: 2x² − 4x − 3 = 0 → x = (4 ± √(16 + 24))/4 = 2.58 or −0.58 (2 d.p.).

5. Completing the square

x² + bx + c = (x + b/2)² − (b/2)² + c. x² − 6x + 5 = (x − 3)² − 4 → minimum at (3, −4). Use for turning points and for solving when factorising fails.

Exam tips: substitute answers back to verify; in word problems define the unknown clearly ("let w = width in cm"); give quadratic solutions to the accuracy demanded.

title: A Level Mathematics: Vectors
content:
A Level Mathematics: Vectors

A vector is a quantity with both size and direction, and the whole subject is the algebra of arrows. The idea feels abstract until you notice you already use it: a displacement of three miles north-east is a vector, the wind reported as 20 km/h from the west is a vector, and the instruction to walk to a point is a vector. This note builds vectors from components, shows how to add and scale them, then uses the scalar product to measure the angle between two directions — the tool that turns vector algebra into geometry.

What a vector is, and what it is not

A scalar has size alone. A vector has size and direction, and two vectors are equal only if both match. That is why a vector is written with an arrow or in bold, and why reversing the arrow changes the vector into its negative even though the length is unchanged.

vector a has magnitude |a| and direction
-a has the same magnitude, opposite direction
the zero vector 0 has no direction and magnitude 0
a unit vector has magnitude 1 and gives a direction

The distinction matters in mechanics: displacement and velocity are vectors, distance and speed are scalars, and mixing them up is how answers acquire impossible units. A direction given as a bearing is the same information in a different costume, and converting between a compass bearing and a pair of components is a routine exam step.

Components and magnitude

In two dimensions a vector is written as a column of its two components, one per axis. The house convention in this course writes a column vector as (x; y), the first component horizontal and the second vertical.

a = (3; 4)
magnitude |a| = √(3² + 4²) = 5
in three dimensions: a = (x; y; z), |a| = √(x² + y² + z²)

Worked example. Find the magnitude of (6; −8). Draw the reasoning, not just the answer.

|a| = √(36 + 64) = 10
the components form a right triangle with legs 6 and 8, so this is a 3-4-5 triangle scaled by 2

Worked example 2 (unit vector). Find the unit vector in the direction of (6; −8).

divide by the magnitude: (6/10; -8/10) = (0.6; -0.8)
check: 0.36 + 0.64 = 1

Worked example 3 (3-D). Find the magnitude of (2; −3; 6).

√(4 + 9 + 36) = √(49) = 7

Adding, subtracting and scaling

Addition is component by component, and geometrically it is the triangle law: place the tail of the second at the head of the first, and the sum runs from the first tail to the second head. Subtraction is addition of the negative, which gives the vector from one point to another.

a + b = (a1 + b1; a2 + b2)
a - b = (a1 - b1; a2 - b2)
k a = (k a1; k a2)  parallel to a, scaled by k

Worked example. a = (3; 1), b = (−1; 4). Find a + b, a − b and 2a − 3b.

a + b = (2; 5)
a - b = (4; -3)
2a = (6; 2);  3b = (-3; 12)
2a - 3b = (9; -10)

Worked example 2 (parallel condition). Show that (4; −6) and (−2; 3) are parallel.

(4; -6) = -2 x (-2; 3)
one is a scalar multiple of the other, so they are parallel (and antiparallel)

Position vectors and points on a line

A position vector locates a point relative to the origin. The vector from A to B is then the position vector of B minus that of A — a subtraction rule worth memorising because it fixes the direction of every later step.

position vectors a and b for points A and B:
vector AB = b - a
the midpoint of AB has position vector (a + b)/2
a point dividing AB in the ratio m:n has position (n a + m b)/(m + n)

Worked example. A has position vector (2; 1) and B has (8; 5). Find AB and the midpoint.

AB = (8 - 2; 5 - 1) = (6; 4)
midpoint = ((2+8)/2; (1+5)/2) = (5; 3)

Worked example 2 (section formula). P divides AB in the ratio 1:2. Find P.

P = (2a + 1b)/3 = ((4; 2) + (8; 5))/3 = (12; 7)/3 = (4; 2.333)

Worked example 3 (proving three points are collinear). Show that A(1, 1), B(3, 4) and C(7, 10) lie on a line.

AB = (2; 3)
AC = (6; 9) = 3 x (2; 3)
AC is a multiple of AB and they share A, so the three points are collinear

The scalar product

The scalar product (dot product) takes two vectors and returns a number. That number encodes the angle between them, which is why it is the single most useful operation in the topic.

a . b = a1 b1 + a2 b2  (+ a3 b3 in 3-D)
a . b = |a| |b| cos θ
so cos θ = (a . b)/(|a| |b|)

Worked example. Find the angle between a = (3; 4) and b = (5; 0).

a . b = 15 + 0 = 15
|a| = 5, |b| = 5
cos θ = 15/25 = 0.6  →  θ = 53.13 degrees

Worked example 2 (perpendicularity). Find k so that (2; k) is perpendicular to (3; −4).

perpendicular means a . b = 0
6 - 4k = 0  →  k = 1.5

Worked example 3 (3-D angle). Find the angle between (1; 2; 2) and (2; 1; 0).

a . b = 2 + 2 + 0 = 4
|a| = 3, |b| = sqrt 5 = 2.236
cos θ = 4/(3 × 2.236) = 0.596  →  θ = 53.4 degrees

Using vectors in geometry

Geometry proofs become short algebraic arguments once vectors are in play: parallelism is a scalar multiple, equal lengths are equal magnitudes, and a right angle is a zero scalar product. The discipline is to express everything in terms of two base vectors and then compare coefficients.

Geometric statementVector test
PQ is parallel to RSPQ = k RS for some scalar k
PQ has the same length as RS|PQ| = |RS|
angle PQR is a right angleQP . QR = 0
P, Q, R are collinearPQ = k PR

Worked example. In triangle OAB, M is the midpoint of OA and N is the midpoint of OB. Prove MN is parallel to AB.

let OA = a and OB = b
OM = a/2;  ON = b/2
MN = ON - OM = (b - a)/2
AB = b - a
so MN = AB/2: parallel and half the length

A common variant gives two vectors with unknown constants and requires a right angle or a given length. The routine is always the same: write the condition as an equation in the constants, solve it, then check that the solution satisfies any sign or magnitude restriction stated in the question. Two solutions usually appear because a squared length produces a quadratic.

Worked example 2 (right angle inside a shape). With a = (1; 2) and b = (3; −1), show that the diagonals of the parallelogram spanned by a and b are perpendicular.

diagonals are a + b and a - b
a + b = (4; 1);  a - b = (-2; 3)
dot product = -8 + 3 = -5, not zero
so they are not perpendicular - the test is the check, not an assumption

Velocity and displacement vectors

In mechanics, position is a vector function of time and velocity is its rate of change. Constant velocity makes the position a straight line, which is why relative-motion questions reduce to vector subtraction.

position r = r0 + v t
displacement over time t is v t
relative velocity of A with respect to B is vA - vB

Worked example. A boat has velocity (4; 3) m/s relative to the water and the current has velocity (−1; 2) m/s. Find the boat's velocity over the ground and its speed.

resultant = (4 - 1; 3 + 2) = (3; 5)
speed = √(9 + 25) = 5.83 m/s

Worked example 2 (intercept). A particle starts at (1; 2) with velocity (3; −1). Where is it after 4 seconds?

r = (1; 2) + 4(3; -1) = (1 + 12; 2 - 4) = (13; -2)

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Magnitude) Find |(5; −12)|. Answer: √(25 + 144) = 13.
  2. (Unit vector) Find the unit vector of (3; 4). Answer: (0.6; 0.8).
  3. (Addition) a = (2; −3), b = (−4; 1). Find 3a + b. Answer: (6 − 4; −9 + 1) = (2; −8).
  4. (Collinear) Are (1; 2), (4; 8) and (7; 14) collinear? Answer: yes, each step is a multiple of (3; 6).
  5. (Dot product) Find a . b for a = (1; 3), b = (4; −2). Answer: 4 − 6 = −2.
  6. (Angle) Find the angle between (1; 0) and (1; 1). Answer: cos θ = 1/√2, θ = 45°.
  7. (Perpendicular) Find k so (k; 6) is perpendicular to (3; −2). Answer: 3k − 12 = 0, k = 4.
  8. (3-D) Find |(1; 4; 8)|. Answer: √81 = 9.
  9. (Section) P divides AB in ratio 2:1, a = (0; 0), b = (6; 9). Find P. Answer: (2; 3).
  10. (Relative) Velocities (5; 1) and (2; 4). Find the relative velocity of the first with respect to the second. Answer: (3; −3).

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • AB versus BA: AB = b − a; reversing the subtraction gives the wrong direction and the wrong sign in every later step.
  • Magnitude of a sum: |a + b| is not |a| + |b| unless the vectors are parallel; compute the components first.
  • Scalar product sign: an obtuse angle gives a negative dot product, which is information, not an error.
  • Division by a vector: there is no vector division; rearrange using scalar multiples instead.
  • Collinearity without a shared point: parallel vectors alone do not make points collinear — say that they share a point.
  • Degrees and radians: the inverse cosine returns whatever mode the calculator is in; state the unit in the answer.
  • Missing the z component in 3-D: dot products and magnitudes need all three components, including zeros.
  • Arrow notation ignored in proofs: writing a length where a directed vector was needed destroys the argument even when the number is right.

Equations and symbols

Every relation this topic is examined on, written with its real notation and followed by a key naming each symbol, its unit and what it means. The sections above explain why each one is true; this sheet is the version to revise from, where the answer depends on reproducing the exact form and substituting into it without losing a unit.

Components, magnitude and the unit vector

a = (x; y) and |a| = √(x² + y²); in three dimensions a = (x; y; z) and |a| = √(x² + y² + z²)
Key: a = the vector; x, y (and z) = its components along each axis, in the units of the problem; |a| = the magnitude, the length of the arrow, in those same units. The column form (x; y) is the house convention — the first entry is horizontal and the second vertical. The modulus is Pythagoras applied once per dimension.

â = a/|a|, with |â| = 1
Key: â (a-hat) = the unit vector in the direction of a; |a| = the magnitude of a, which must be non-zero. It keeps the direction and discards the length, which is how a direction is quoted independently of how far it is travelled; the check is that its components square and sum to 1.

a ± b = (x₁ ± x₂; y₁ ± y₂) and k a = (k x₁; k y₁)
Key: a, b = two vectors; x₁, x₂ = their components along the same axis; k = a scalar multiplier, which may be negative. Addition is component by component; multiplying by k scales the length by |k| and reverses the direction when k < 0.

Displacement, position and the line

AB = b − a, so |AB| = |b − a|
Key: AB = the vector from point A to point B (with an arrow over it in handwriting); a, b = the position vectors of A and B measured from the origin. "Head minus tail" is the rule; reversing the subtraction gives BA, which is the same length in the opposite direction.

r = a + t d
Key: r = the position vector of a general point on the line; a = the position vector of a known point on it; d = a direction vector along the line; t = a scalar parameter with no unit. Every value of t gives one point, so the line is the set of all such r; parallel lines have parallel d, and a point lies on the line only if its vector satisfies the equation for some single t.

r = a + t(b − a)
Key: a, b = the position vectors of two points on the line; t = the parameter, with t = 0 at A and t = 1 at B. The direction is the displacement between the two given points, which is why two points are enough to write the line.

angle between two lines: cos θ = (d₁·d₂)/(|d₁||d₂|)
Key: d₁, d₂ = the direction vectors of the two lines; θ = the acute angle between them, in degrees or radians. Only the directions matter, so any scalar multiple of either d gives the same angle — take the acute value by using the modulus of the dot product.

The scalar product and what it measures

a·b = x₁x₂ + y₁y₂ (+ z₁z₂) = |a||b| cos θ
Key: a·b = the scalar (dot) product, a pure number with no direction; x₁, x₂ = the components of a and b along each shared axis; |a|, |b| = the magnitudes; θ = the angle between the two vectors. The two expressions are the same quantity: components for arithmetic, magnitudes for geometry.

a ⟂ b ⇔ a·b = 0
Key: ⟂ means perpendicular; a·b = the dot product. When θ = 90°, cos θ = 0, so the product vanishes — the quickest perpendicularity test there is, and the first line of every "find the foot of the perpendicular" question.

a ∥ b ⇔ a = k b for some scalar k
Key: ∥ means parallel; k = the scale factor between them, positive for the same direction and negative for opposite. Component ratios being equal is the practical test, and a dot-product check should never be used for parallelism.

projection of a on b: scalar a·b/|b|, vector ((a·b)/|b|²) b
Key: a = the vector being projected; b = the direction projected onto; the scalar version is a signed length along b's direction, in the units of a; the vector version is that length times a unit vector. It is how a component along a given direction is extracted without drawing a triangle.

area of the parallelogram on a and b = |a||b| sin θ
Key: a, b = the two vectors spanning the parallelogram; θ = the angle between them; the area is in squared units. Since sin²θ = 1 − cos²θ, the area can be recovered from the dot product alone when θ is not given.

title: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Sets and Venn Diagrams
content:
Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Sets and Venn Diagrams

Set notation is the language of sorting: it describes which elements belong together, which belong to both groups, and which belong to neither. The IGCSE questions are almost always Venn-diagram problems in disguise — a survey of students, a group of numbers, a club membership — and the marks come from filling every region correctly. This note builds the topic from zero: the notation and symbols, the two-set and three-set Venn diagrams and how to shade them, the counting formulas, and the word-problem method that never misses a region.

Set notation and vocabulary

SymbolMeaningExample
∈is an element of3 ∈ {1, 2, 3}
∉is not an element of5 ∉ {1, 2, 3}
ξ (or U)the universal set — everything under discussionξ = {1, 2, ..., 12}
∅the empty setodd multiples of 2 = ∅
A′the complement of A — everything in ξ not in AA′ = ξ A
A ∪ Bunion — in A or B or both{1,2} ∪ {2,3} = {1,2,3}
A ∩ Bintersection — in both{1,2} ∩ {2,3} = {2}
n(A)the number of elements of An({2, 4, 6}) = 3

Two rules follow directly: A ∩ A′ = ∅ (nothing is both in and out), and A ∪ A′ = ξ (everything is one or the other). Subsets: A ⊂ B means every element of A is also in B. The empty set has no elements, so n(∅) = 0, and it is a subset of every set — a fact worth stating explicitly when a question asks whether ∅ ⊂ A is true.

Two-set Venn diagrams

A two-set diagram divides the universal set into four regions: only A, only B, both, and neither. Filling them from the inside out is the reliable method:

  1. Write the number in the intersection (both) first.
  2. Work outward: only A = n(A) − both; only B = n(B) − both.
  3. Neither = total − (only A + only B + both).

Worked example. In a class of 32, 18 study French, 15 study Spanish, and 7 study both. Find the number studying only French, only Spanish, and neither.

both = 7
only French = 18 - 7 = 11
only Spanish = 15 - 7 = 8
neither = 32 - (11 + 8 + 7) = 32 - 26 = 6

Worked example 2 (reverse). In a group, 20 like tea, 14 like coffee and 5 like neither. Everyone likes at least one of the two? Then find n(tea ∩ coffee).

n(T union C) = 20 + 14 - both
total = 20 + 14 - both + 5 = 39 - both
If the group has 30 people: 30 = 39 - both -> both = 9

The inclusion–exclusion formula

n(A union B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A intersection B)

for three sets:
n(A u B u C) = n(A) + n(B) + n(C)
             - n(A n B) - n(A n C) - n(B n C)
             + n(A n B n C)

The subtraction corrects double counting; the final addition corrects the triple-counted centre. Knowing the formula lets you answer "how many in total" questions without a full diagram, but a diagram is still the safer route for word problems.

Worked example. A survey of 50 people: 30 read newspapers, 25 read magazines, 12 read both. How many read at least one?

n(N union M) = 30 + 25 - 12 = 43
neither = 50 - 43 = 7

Three-set Venn diagrams

The three-set diagram has eight regions (counting "none of the three"). The fill order that never fails:

  1. Start with the triple intersection (all three).
  2. Find the "exactly two" regions by subtracting the triple from each pair.
  3. Find the "only one" regions by subtracting the pair and triple totals from each set total.
  4. Find "none" from the grand total.

Worked example. 40 students choose subjects: 20 take Maths, 18 take Physics, 15 take Chemistry; 8 take Maths and Physics, 6 take Maths and Chemistry, 5 take Physics and Chemistry; 3 take all three. Find how many take exactly one subject and how many take none.

triple = 3
exactly M and P = 8 - 3 = 5
exactly M and C = 6 - 3 = 3
exactly P and C = 5 - 3 = 2
only M = 20 - (5 + 3 + 3) = 9
only P = 18 - (5 + 2 + 3) = 8
only C = 15 - (3 + 2 + 3) = 7
exactly one = 9 + 8 + 7 = 24
total counted = 24 + 5 + 3 + 2 + 3 = 37
none = 40 - 37 = 3

Sets of numbers and shading

Questions often use number sets inside the universal set: ξ = {1, 2, ..., 20}, A = multiples of 3, B = multiples of 4. List them, then use the same four regions:

A = {3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18}
B = {4, 8, 12, 16, 20}
A n B = {12}
A u B = {3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 12, 15, 16, 18, 20}
neither = {1, 2, 5, 7, 10, 11, 13, 14, 17, 19}

Shading questions ask for a region described in symbols. Translate the symbols into words first: A′ ∩ B means "not in A, but in B" — the part of B outside A. A ∪ B′ means "in A, or outside B" — everything except the part of B that is not in A.

Listing sets and set-builder notation

Sets can be written in three ways, and questions move between them. The roster method lists the elements: A = {2, 4, 6, 8}. The description method states the rule in words: A is the set of even numbers from 2 to 8. Set-builder notation states the rule symbolically: A = {x : x is an even number, 2 ≤ x ≤ 8} — read as "the set of all x such that x is even and between 2 and 8".

  • Roster for finite sets: list every element once, in braces, separated by commas; order does not matter and repeats are not counted twice.
  • Description for patterns: "multiples of 3 less than 30" is clearer than listing ten numbers.
  • Set-builder for precision: the colon means "such that"; the condition after it does the work.

Worked example. Write the set of odd numbers between 1 and 11 in roster and set-builder form, and find its size.

roster: {3, 5, 7, 9}  (strictly between, so 1 and 11 excluded)
set-builder: {x : x odd, 1 < x < 11}
n(A) = 4

Reading the inequalities is the trap: "between" usually excludes the endpoints, "from ... to ..." usually includes them, and the question's wording decides. When in doubt, list both interpretations and choose the one consistent with the other numbers in the question.

Worked examples: word problems

Worked example. In a hostel of 60 students, 35 play football, 28 play basketball, and 12 play both. How many play neither?

at least one = 35 + 28 - 12 = 51
neither = 60 - 51 = 9

Worked example 2 (with a variable). In a group of 25, x people like both tea and coffee, 12 like tea only and 8 like coffee only. Find x if everyone likes at least one.

12 + 8 + x = 25  ->  x = 5

Worked example 3 (conditional language). Of 40 students, 24 study History, 18 study Geography and 6 study neither. How many study both?

at least one = 40 - 6 = 34
34 = 24 + 18 - both  ->  both = 42 - 34 = 8

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Notation) ξ = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8}; A = {2, 4, 6, 8}; B = {1, 3, 5, 7}. Find A ∩ B and A ∪ B. Answer: A ∩ B = ∅; A ∪ B = ξ.
  2. (Complement) With A = {2, 4, 6, 8} in ξ above, list A′. Answer: {1, 3, 5, 7}.
  3. (Two sets) n(A) = 14, n(B) = 9, n(A ∩ B) = 4. Find n(A ∪ B). Answer: 14 + 9 − 4 = 19.
  4. (Neither) In a class of 30, 17 like cricket, 12 like tennis and 5 like both. Find the number who like neither. Answer: at least one = 24; neither = 6.
  5. (Three sets) 30 students: 15 like Maths, 12 like Physics, 10 like Chemistry; 5 like Maths and Physics, 4 like Maths and Chemistry, 3 like Physics and Chemistry, 2 like all three. Find the number who like exactly one. Answer: only M = 15 − (3 + 2 + 2) = 8; only P = 12 − (3 + 1 + 2) = 6; only C = 10 − (2 + 1 + 2) = 5; total = 19 (with exactly-two counts 3, 2, 1 and triple 2).
  6. (Shading) Describe the region A′ ∩ B in words. Answer: Elements in B but not in A — the part of B outside A.
  7. (Numbers) ξ = {1, ..., 20}; A = even numbers; B = multiples of 5. Find n(A ∩ B). Answer: multiples of 10 in the set = {10, 20}, so 2.
  8. (Reasoning) Explain why n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) is wrong when A and B overlap. Answer: The elements in both sets are counted twice in n(A) + n(B), so the intersection must be subtracted once: n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B).

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Filling the intersection last: start at the centre. Adding both set totals and forgetting the overlap counts shared elements twice.
  • Forgetting the "neither" region: the universal set includes elements outside all named sets; if the question gives a total, subtract to find them.
  • Confusing ∪ and ∩: union is "or" (everything), intersection is "and" (only the middle). A quick mnemonic: ∪ looks like a cup that holds everything.
  • Shading the wrong side for A′: the complement is everything outside A, including parts of other sets and the region outside them all.
  • Triple intersection double subtraction: when subtracting pairs, remember each pair already includes the triple; subtract the triple from each pair before using them.
  • Reading "only": "only A" means A and nothing else — exclude the overlaps. The word only is a region instruction, not decoration.
  • Notation in answers: list elements with braces and commas; do not write 1, 2, 3 as an unbraced list when the answer is a set.
  • Assuming everyone likes something: unless stated, some may be outside both sets — check whether the total equals the sum of the regions.

title: AS Level Physics: D.C. Circuits
content:
AS Level Physics: D.C. Circuits

Direct-current circuits are where abstract quantities become measurable: current is charge in motion, potential difference is energy per charge, and resistance is the friction of the electrical world. This note builds the complete circuit toolkit from zero: current and the drift model, potential difference and power, resistance and resistivity, real sources and internal resistance, Kirchhoff's two laws, and potential dividers. Every calculation type is worked line by line, and the practical skills — meters, graphs, and the divider equation — are given the treatment the papers demand.

Electric current: charge in motion

Current is the rate of flow of charge: I = Q/t, measured in amperes (1 A = 1 C s⁻¹). Charge itself comes in quanta of e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. At the microscopic level, current in a metal is the drift of free electrons through a lattice of ions:

I = n A v q

n = charge carrier density (m-3)
A = cross-sectional area of the conductor (m2)
v = drift velocity (m s-1)
q = charge on each carrier (C), = e for electrons

The analogy worth keeping: a garden hose already full of water. Turning the tap (closing the switch) sends water out the far end almost instantly — not because water travels the hose in zero time, but because the hose is full and pressure passes the signal along. So drift velocities are millimetres per second while the lamp lights instantly.

Worked example. A wire of cross-section 1.0 mm² carries 3.0 A. There are 8.5 × 10²⁸ free electrons per m³. Find the drift velocity.

A = 1.0 mm2 = 1.0 x 10-6 m2
v = I/(n A q) = 3.0/(8.5 x 1028 x 1.0 x 10-6 x 1.6 x 10-19)
  = 3.0/(13 600) = 2.2 x 10-4 m s-1  (0.22 mm s-1)

Note the unit conversions: mm² to m² is a factor of 10⁻⁶, and the answer in mm s⁻¹ is a factor of 10³ from m s⁻¹.

Potential difference and power

Potential difference (p.d.) across a component is the energy transferred per unit charge passing through it: V = W/Q, in volts (1 V = 1 J C⁻¹). Electromotive force (e.m.f.) is the energy converted from other forms to electrical energy per unit charge by a source — the same unit, different story (energy in, not energy out). Combine with I = Q/t to get the power equations that run the paper:

W = Q V = I t V
P = W/t = I V = I^2 R = V^2 / R

Worked example. A 12 V heater draws 8.0 A. Find its power and the energy converted in 5.0 minutes.

P = I V = 8.0 x 12 = 96 W
W = P t = 96 x (5.0 x 60) = 96 x 300 = 28 800 J = 29 kJ

Choosing the right power form: use P = IV when you have current and voltage, I²R when current and resistance are known (it shows why heating losses rise with current), V²/R when the voltage is fixed across the component.

Resistance, Ohm's law and resistivity

Resistance is the ratio V/I, in ohms (1 Ω = 1 V A⁻¹). Ohm's law states that current is proportional to potential difference for a metallic conductor at constant temperature — the graph of I against V is a straight line through the origin; the qualification about temperature is examinable. Resistivity is the material's own opposition to current, independent of the wire's shape:

R = rho L / A          so   rho = R A / L

rho in ohm metre (ohm m)
L in m, A in m2

Worked example 1. A nichrome wire of resistivity 1.10 × 10⁻⁶ Ω m is 2.5 m long and 0.20 mm in diameter. Find its resistance.

A = pi r^2 = 3.14 x (1.0 x 10-4)^2 = 3.14 x 10-8 m2
R = rho L/A = (1.10 x 10-6 x 2.5)/(3.14 x 10-8)
  = 2.75 x 10-6/3.14 x 10-8 = 87.6 ohm  (2 s.f.: 88 ohm)

Worked example 2 (temperature). Explain why the resistance of a metal filament rises as it heats up. Answer: The lattice ions vibrate more vigorously with temperature, increasing the rate of collision with drifting electrons; each collision impedes the drift, so the same potential difference drives less current and R = V/I rises. (Semiconductors behave oppositely: more carriers are released, so their resistance falls.)

Practical circuits: sources, internal resistance and meters

A real source has internal resistance r: some energy is converted to heat inside the source itself, so the terminal potential difference is less than the e.m.f. whenever current flows.

e.m.f. = terminal p.d. + lost volts
E = V + I r        ->   V = E - I r

also: E = I (R + r)  for a load resistance R in series with r

The V–I graph of a real source is the standard question: a straight line with y-intercept E and gradient −r. Short-circuit current (V = 0) is E/r.

Worked example. A cell of e.m.f. 1.50 V drives 0.20 A through a 6.0 Ω resistor. Find the internal resistance and the terminal p.d.

E = I(R + r)  ->  1.50 = 0.20(6.0 + r)
7.5 = 6.0 + r  ->  r = 1.5 ohm
terminal p.d.: V = I R = 0.20 x 6.0 = 1.20 V
check: lost volts = I r = 0.20 x 1.5 = 0.30 V, and 1.20 + 0.30 = 1.50 V

Meter rules: an ammeter goes in series (ideally zero resistance) and a voltmeter in parallel with the component (ideally infinite resistance); a real ammeter's small resistance and a real voltmeter's finite one are sources of systematic error worth naming in evaluation questions.

Series and parallel: the recaps that decide marks

SeriesParallel
Currentsame through each componentsplits; total = sum of branches
Voltagesplits; total = sum across componentssame across each branch
ResistanceR = R₁ + R₂ + ...1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + ...

Worked example. Find the total resistance of 6.0 Ω and 3.0 Ω in parallel, then in series with 2.0 Ω.

parallel pair: 1/R = 1/6 + 1/3 = 0.1667 + 0.3333 = 0.5
R_pair = 2.0 ohm
total with the series resistor: R = 2.0 + 2.0 = 4.0 ohm

Kirchhoff's laws

  • First law (charge conservation): the sum of currents entering a junction equals the sum leaving it. ΣI in = ΣI out. The junction rule — charge is not created inside a wire.
  • Second law (energy conservation): the sum of e.m.f.s around any closed loop equals the sum of p.d. drops around it; equivalently the potential changes around a loop sum to zero. ΣE = ΣIR.

The loop method for any network: (1) label current directions (a wrong guess just returns a negative value); (2) write one junction equation per junction you need; (3) write loop equations for enough independent loops; (4) solve the simultaneous equations.

Worked example. A 12 V battery drives two parallel resistors, 4.0 Ω and 6.0 Ω. Find the current from the battery and through each branch.

parallel p.d. is the same: 12 V across both branches
I(4.0) = V/R = 12/4.0 = 3.0 A
I(6.0) = 12/6.0 = 2.0 A
junction rule: I_battery = 3.0 + 2.0 = 5.0 A
check with total resistance: R = (4 x 6)/(4 + 6) = 2.4 ohm
I = 12/2.4 = 5.0 A  (consistent)

Worked example 2 (loop law). A 1.5 V cell and a 2.0 V cell are connected in series aiding, driving 0.10 A through a 33 Ω resistor plus internal resistances of 2.0 Ω total. Verify the loop law.

total e.m.f. = 1.5 + 2.0 = 3.5 V
total resistance = 33 + 2.0 = 35 ohm
I = 3.5/35 = 0.10 A  (matches the given current)
loop check: sum of p.d. drops = 0.10 x 35 = 3.5 V = sum of e.m.f.s

Potential dividers

Two resistors in series across a supply share the supply voltage in proportion to their resistances:

V_out = V_in x R2/(R1 + R2)

(R2 is the resistor across which the output is tapped)

The divider is the backbone of sensor circuits: replace R₂ with a light-dependent resistor or thermistor and the output voltage tracks light level or temperature. The loading caveat is examinable — connecting a finite-resistance voltmeter or load across R₂ changes the effective resistance and lowers V_out below the ideal value.

Worked example 1. A 9.0 V supply has R₁ = 2.0 kΩ and R₂ = 4.0 kΩ. Find the output voltage.

V_out = 9.0 x 4.0/(2.0 + 4.0) = 9.0 x 4/6 = 6.0 V

Worked example 2 (design). You need 3.0 V from a 12 V supply with a 1.0 kΩ total resistance. Choose R₁ and R₂.

V_out/V_in = R2/(R1 + R2) -> 3.0/12 = R2/1000
R2 = 250 ohm,  R1 = 750 ohm

Worked example 3 (thermistor). A thermistor in the lower leg falls from 4.0 kΩ to 1.0 kΩ on heating, with R₁ = 2.0 kΩ across a 9.0 V supply. Find the output voltage before and after heating.

cold:  V_out = 9.0 x 4.0/(2.0 + 4.0) = 6.0 V
hot:   V_out = 9.0 x 1.0/(2.0 + 1.0) = 3.0 V
The falling output signals rising temperature.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Current) A current of 0.50 A flows for 2.0 minutes. Find the charge transferred. Answer: Q = It = 0.50 × 120 = 60 C.
  2. (Power) A 6.0 Ω resistor dissipates 24 W. Find the current through it. Answer: P = I²R → I = √(P/R) = √(24/6.0) = 2.0 A.
  3. (Resistivity) Two wires of the same material have the same resistance; one is twice as long. State how its cross-section compares. Answer: R = ρL/A, so doubling L requires doubling A to keep R — the longer wire must have twice the cross-sectional area.
  4. (Internal resistance) A battery of e.m.f. 6.0 V and internal resistance 0.50 Ω drives a 2.5 Ω load. Find the terminal p.d. Answer: I = E/(R+r) = 6.0/3.0 = 2.0 A; V = IR = 2.0 × 2.5 = 5.0 V (lost volts = 1.0 V).
  5. (Kirchhoff 1) At a junction, 3.0 A and 2.0 A enter; one wire leaves. Find its current. Answer: 5.0 A — charge conservation.
  6. (Kirchhoff 2) State the second law and what it represents. Answer: The sum of e.m.f.s around any closed loop equals the sum of potential differences around it — conservation of energy.
  7. (Divider) A divider has R₁ = 3.0 kΩ and R₂ = 5.0 kΩ across 8.0 V. Find V_out. Answer: V_out = 8.0 × 5.0/8.0 = 5.0 V.
  8. (Sensor) Explain how a potential divider with a thermistor can act as a temperature sensor. Answer: The thermistor's resistance falls as temperature rises, changing the ratio R₂/(R₁+R₂) and hence V_out; the output voltage therefore tracks temperature and can be calibrated to a scale or trigger.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Power formula roulette: choosing P = V²/R when the current is fixed wastes time and marks. Match the formula to the quantities known.
  • Resistivity units: ρ is in Ω m, and areas in the formula are m² — mm² and cm² must be converted (1 mm² = 10⁻⁶ m²).
  • Internal resistance omission: "a battery" in a paper often implies real internal resistance; if the question gives r or a V–I graph, use V = E − Ir.
  • Divider loading: the ideal divider formula assumes no load current; if the question says a resistor is connected across the output, recompute the effective resistance rather than quoting the ideal value.
  • Meter placement: ammeters in series, voltmeters in parallel; a swapped meter is a practical-method mark lost.
  • Junction arithmetic: sum currents entering = leaving; the classic error is subtracting a branch current from itself when directions were assumed wrongly. A negative answer just means the assumed direction is reversed.
  • Series/parallel recognition: redraw circuits before calculating; two resistors across the same two nodes are parallel however the wires are drawn.
  • Significant figures and units: 2 or 3 s.f. with units (A, V, Ω, W, J); keep Ω as the unit for resistance — never ohms written as O or zero.
  • Method marks: state the formula (I = V/R, V = E − Ir, Kirchhoff's law) and the loop/junction you are using before substituting; the law name itself is credit.

Equations and symbols

The whole of this topic as equations, each written with its real symbols and each followed by a key naming every symbol and its unit. Where a law has more than one useful form both are given, because which one is quickest depends on which quantities the question hands you. Learn the form here and the algebraic rearrangement becomes mechanical in the exam.

9.1 Current, charge and drift velocity

I = ΔQ / Δt
Key: I = current (A, where 1 A = 1 C s⁻¹); ΔQ = charge passing a point in the conductor (C); Δt = time taken (s). The definition of current as rate of flow of charge.

Q = I t
Key: Q = charge transferred (C); I = steady current (A); t = time for which it flows (s). The definition rearranged for a constant current — the form used in electrolysis and in electricity-cost questions, where 1 kW h = 3.6 × 10⁶ J.

I = n A v q
Key: I = current (A); n = number density of charge carriers (m⁻³); A = cross-sectional area of the conductor (m²); v = mean drift velocity of the carriers (m s⁻¹); q = charge on each carrier (C), equal to e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C for electrons. Because n is fixed by the metal, a thinner wire must have a larger drift velocity for the same current.

W = Q V = I V t
Key: W = energy transferred electrically (J); Q = charge moved (C); V = potential difference across the component (V); I = current (A); t = time (s).

9.2 Potential difference, e.m.f. and power

V = W / Q
Key: V = potential difference across a component (V, where 1 V = 1 J C⁻¹); W = energy converted from electrical to other forms in that component (J); Q = charge passing through it (C).

E = W / Q
Key: E = electromotive force of the source (V); W = energy converted from chemical, mechanical or light energy into electrical energy per charge (J); Q = charge (C). The distinction the mark scheme rewards: e.m.f. is energy given to the charge inside the source; p.d. is energy taken from the charge in a component.

P = W / t = I V
Key: P = power (W = J s⁻¹); W = energy transferred (J); t = time (s); I = current (A); V = potential difference (V).

P = I² R = V² / R
Key: P = power dissipated as heat in a resistor (W); I = current through it (A); R = its resistance (Ω); V = p.d. across it (V). Use I²R when the current is known and V²/R when the p.d. is fixed — in parallel, V is shared equally, in series the current is.

η = P_useful / P_input × 100%
Key: η = efficiency (%); P_useful = power delivered to the load (W); P_input = total power supplied by the source, E I (W).

9.3 Resistance and resistivity

R = V / I
Key: R = resistance (Ω = V A⁻¹); V = p.d. across the component (V); I = current through it (A). Ohmic only when R is constant as V varies — the I–V graph through the origin is the test.

R = ρ L / A
Key: R = resistance (Ω); ρ = resistivity of the material (Ω m); L = length of the conductor (m); A = cross-sectional area (m²). Resistivity is a property of the material, resistance of the object — doubling the length doubles R but leaves ρ unchanged.

ρ = R A / L
Key: ρ = resistivity (Ω m); R = measured resistance (Ω); A = cross-sectional area (m²); L = measured length (m). The working form of the experiment: plot R against L, gradient = ρ/A, so ρ = gradient × A.

G = 1 / R
Key: G = conductance (S = Ω⁻¹); R = resistance (Ω). Conductance adds directly in parallel, which is why parallel combinations are easier in G.

10.1 Series, parallel, internal resistance and meters

R_series = R₁ + R₂ + R₃ + …
Key: R_series = total resistance (Ω); R₁, R₂ … = individual resistances (Ω). The current is common to all, so the p.d.s add and the resistances add.

1 / R_parallel = 1 / R₁ + 1 / R₂ + 1 / R₃ + …
Key: R_parallel = total resistance (Ω); R₁, R₂ … = branch resistances (Ω). The p.d. is common, so the currents add. For n identical resistors R each, R_parallel = R / n.

R_parallel = R₁ R₂ / (R₁ + R₂)
Key: R_parallel = resistance of the pair (Ω); R₁, R₂ = the two resistances (Ω). The two-resistor shortcut; the total is always smaller than the smaller of the two.

E = V + I r
Key: E = e.m.f. of the source (V); V = terminal potential difference, the p.d. across the external circuit (V); I = current drawn (A); r = internal resistance of the source (Ω). The lost volts are I r, and they exist because the current also flows through the source itself.

V = E − I r
Key: V = terminal p.d. (V); E = e.m.f. (V); I = current (A); r = internal resistance (Ω). This is why a battery reads nearly its e.m.f. on a high-resistance voltmeter and sags when a lamp is connected.

E = I (R + r)
Key: E = e.m.f. (V); I = current (A); R = external load resistance (Ω); r = internal resistance (Ω). The circuit as one loop: the e.m.f. drives the current through both the load and the source.

I = E / (R + r)
Key: I = current (A); E = e.m.f. (V); R = external resistance (Ω); r = internal resistance (Ω). To measure r, vary R, plot 1/I against R: gradient = 1/E and intercept = r/E.

P_output = I² R = E² R / (R + r)²
Key: P_output = power delivered to the external load (W); E = e.m.f. (V); R = load resistance (Ω); r = internal resistance (Ω); I = current (A). Differentiating gives the maximum-power condition below.

R = r gives P_output (max) = E² / (4 r)
Key: R = load resistance at which output power peaks (Ω); r = internal resistance (Ω); E = e.m.f. (V); P_output (max) = greatest power the source can deliver (W). Maximum power transfer — but at this point the efficiency is only 50%, since the source dissipates the same power internally.

Ammeter resistance → 0, voltmeter resistance → ∞
Key: an ideal ammeter is placed in series and must not change the current, so its resistance is zero; an ideal voltmeter is placed in parallel and must not divert current, so its resistance is infinite. A real voltmeter of resistance R_V across a resistor R reads V R_V / (R + R_V), which is always less than the true p.d.

10.2 Kirchhoff's laws

Σ I_in = Σ I_out
Key: currents entering a junction (A) equal currents leaving it. The conservation of charge: charge cannot pile up at a point in a steady circuit.

Σ E = Σ I R
Key: Σ E = sum of e.m.f.s around a closed loop (V); Σ I R = sum of the potential drops around the same loop (V). The conservation of energy: going round a loop returns you to the same potential.

Σ ΔV = 0 around any closed loop
Key: ΔV = potential change across each element (V), counted positive in the direction of travel when the potential rises. The same statement as the line above, written so that sources and resistors are treated alike.

10.3 Potential dividers

V_out = V_in × R₂ / (R₁ + R₂)
Key: V_out = p.d. across the resistor the output is taken from (V); V_in = p.d. across the whole chain (V); R₁ = the other resistor (Ω); R₂ = the resistor across which the output is measured (Ω). The chain carries the same current, so each resistor takes a share of the p.d. in proportion to its resistance.

V₁ / V₂ = R₁ / R₂
Key: V₁, V₂ = p.d.s across the two resistors (V); R₁, R₂ = their resistances (Ω). The ratio form — quicker than the fraction when both outputs are wanted.

V_out = E × R / (R + R_thermistor)
Key: V_out = output p.d. across the fixed resistor R (V); E = supply e.m.f. (V); R = fixed resistance (Ω); R_thermistor = resistance of the thermistor at the current temperature (Ω). A thermistor's resistance falls as temperature rises (negative temperature coefficient), so tapping across the fixed resistor gives an output that rises with temperature and tapping across the thermistor gives one that falls.

V_out = E × R_LDR / (R + R_LDR)
Key: V_out = output p.d. across the LDR (V); E = supply e.m.f. (V); R = fixed series resistance (Ω); R_LDR = resistance of the light-dependent resistor (Ω), which falls as illumination increases. The same divider, with light instead of heat as the input.

V_out = V_in × R₂ / (R₁ + R₂) × R_load / (R_load + R₂)
Key: R_load = resistance of whatever the divider feeds (Ω); the other symbols as above. The loaded-divider correction: a load in parallel with R₂ lowers the effective lower resistance, so the output sags below the unloaded value — the reason a divider is a poor supply for anything drawing current.

title: A Level Mathematics: Differentiation II
content:
A Level Mathematics: Differentiation II

A2 differentiation adds the rules for products, quotients and functions of functions, then applies them to implicit equations, parametric curves and rates of change. Every rule in this note is stated with the condition for using it and derived where the derivation is short, because the exam tests recognition as much as execution.

The chain rule

if y = f(g(x)) then dy/dx = f'(g(x)) g'(x)

or with u: dy/dx = dy/du x du/dx

Worked example 1. Differentiate y = (3x + 2)⁵.

dy/dx = 5(3x + 2)⁴ × 3 = 15(3x + 2)⁴

Worked example 2 (trigonometric). Differentiate y = sin(2x).

dy/dx = 2 cos(2x)

Worked example 3 (exponential). Differentiate y = e^(x²).

dy/dx = 2x e^(x²)

Worked example 4 (power of a trig function). Differentiate y = cos³x.

treat as (cos x)³: dy/dx = 3(cos x)² x (-sin x) = -3 sin x cos² x

The product rule

d(uv)/dx = u dv/dx + v du/dx

"first times derivative of second plus second times derivative of first"

Worked example 1. Differentiate y = x² sin x.

dy/dx = 2x sin x + x² cos x

Worked example 2. Differentiate y = x ln x.

dy/dx = ln x + x(1/x) = ln x + 1

Worked example 3. Differentiate y = x²e^(3x).

dy/dx = 2x e^(3x) + 3x² e^(3x) = x e^(3x)(2 + 3x)

Factorising the answer is not cosmetic: stationary points need the factorised form to be solved.

The quotient rule

d(u/v)/dx = (v du/dx - u dv/dx)/v²

the numerator's order matters: v times derivative of u minus u times
derivative of v

Worked example 1. Differentiate y = sin x/x.

dy/dx = (x cos x - sin x)/x²

Worked example 2 (a common form). Differentiate y = (2x + 1)/(x − 3).

dy/dx = [(x - 3)(2) - (2x + 1)(1)]/(x - 3)²
      = (2x - 6 - 2x - 1)/(x - 3)² = -7/(x - 3)²

Worked example 3 (exponential quotient). Differentiate y = e^x/ln x.

dy/dx = [ln x e^x - e^x(1/x)]/(ln x)²

Implicit differentiation

differentiate both sides with respect to x, treating y as a function
of x: each y term contributes its derivative times dy/dx

then solve for dy/dx

Worked example 1. Find dy/dx for x² + y² = 25.

2x + 2y dy/dx = 0
 dy/dx = -x/y

Worked example 2 (product inside). Find dy/dx for xy + y² = 6.

differentiate: y + x dy/dx + 2y dy/dx = 0
dy/dx (x + 2y) = -y
dy/dx = -y/(x + 2y)

Worked example 3 (tangent). Find the tangent to x² + xy = 6 at the point (2, 1).

2x + y + x dy/dx = 0
at (2, 1): 4 + 1 + 2 dy/dx = 0  →  dy/dx = -2.5
tangent: y - 1 = -2.5(x - 2)  →  5x + 2y = 12

Parametric differentiation

if x = f(t) and y = g(t): dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt)

Worked example. For x = t², y = t³ − t, find dy/dx in terms of t.

dx/dt = 2t;  dy/dt = 3t² - 1
dy/dx = (3t² - 1)/(2t)

Worked example 2 (tangent). Find the tangent at t = 2.

point: x = 4, y = 6
gradient: (12 - 1)/4 = 2.75
tangent: y - 6 = 2.75(x - 4)  →  y = 2.75x - 5

Worked example 3 (second derivative). Find d²y/dx² in terms of t for the same curve.

d/dx(dy/dx) = [d/dt(dy/dx)] / (dx/dt)
d/dt[(3t² - 1)/(2t)] = (6t x 2t - (3t² - 1)2)/(4t²) = (6t² + 2)/(4t²)
divide by 2t: (6t² + 2)/(8t³)

Stationary points with the new rules

Worked example. Find and classify the stationary point of y = x e^(−x²).

dy/dx = e^(-x²) + x(-2x)e^(-x²) = e^(-x²)(1 - 2x²)
stationary at x = +/- 1/sqrt 2 = +/- 0.707
at x = 0.707: y = 0.707 e^(-0.5) = 0.429  →  maximum
by symmetry x = -0.707 is a minimum with y = -0.429

Worked example 2 (product inside a log). Show y = x ln x has a minimum at x = e^(−1).

dy/dx = ln x + 1 = 0  →  x = e⁻¹ = 0.368
y = e⁻¹ ln(e⁻¹) = -e⁻¹ = -0.368
second derivative = 1/x > 0 at this point, so minimum

Connected rates of change

chain rule in rate form: dV/dt = dV/dr x dr/dt
strategy: write the quantity as a function of one variable, differentiate,
link the rates, substitute

Worked example. A spherical balloon is inflated so that its volume increases at 100 cm³/s. Find dr/dt when r = 5 cm.

V = (4/3) π r³  →  dV/dr = 4 π r²
at r = 5: dV/dr = 100 π = 314.2
dr/dt = (dV/dt)/(dV/dr) = 100/314.2 = 0.318 cm/s

Worked example 2 (area). A circular ripple's radius grows at 2 cm/s. How fast is the area growing when r = 10 cm?

A = π r²  →  dA/dr = 2 π r = 62.83
dA/dt = 62.83 × 2 = 125.7 cm²/s

Exponentials and logarithms to other bases

Every exponential can be rewritten with base e, because a = e^(ln a). That one identity turns an unfamiliar derivative into something the chain rule already handles, and it explains why base e is the natural choice: the conversion factor disappears.

y = a^x = e^(x ln a)
dy/dx = ln a x e^(x ln a) = a^x ln a

y = log_a(x);  write x = a^y and differentiate implicitly:
1 = a^y ln a dy/dx   →   dy/dx = 1/(x ln a)

special cases: d/dx(e^x) = e^x;  d/dx(ln x) = 1/x

The factor ln a is what students leave out. For a = e it equals 1, which is exactly why base-e derivatives come out clean and every other base drags a constant along.

Worked example. Differentiate y = 3^x.

y = e^(x ln 3)
dy/dx = ln 3 x e^(x ln 3) = 3^x ln 3 = 1.0986 × 3^x

Worked example 2 (chain rule inside the exponent). Differentiate y = 2^(x²).

y = e^(x² ln 2)
dy/dx = e^(x² ln 2) x (2x ln 2) = 2x ln 2 × 2^(x²) = 1.386 × 2^(x²)

Worked example 3 (logarithm of a linear function). Differentiate y = ln(3x + 2) and state where the derivative is valid.

inner u = 3x + 2, du/dx = 3
dy/dx = (1/u) × 3 = 3/(3x + 2)
valid for 3x + 2 > 0, i.e. x > -2/3

The second derivative test and curve sketching

At a stationary point the first derivative vanishes, so it cannot distinguish a peak from a trough. The second derivative does: it measures how the gradient itself is changing, which is the curvature of the graph at that point.

Condition at a stationary pointShape of the curveConclusion
d²y/dx² < 0concave down (∩)local maximum
d²y/dx² > 0concave up (∪)local minimum
d²y/dx² = 0test inconclusivecheck the sign of dy/dx either side

Worked example. Find and classify the stationary points of y = x³ − 3x, then sketch the curve.

dy/dx = 3x² - 3 = 3(x - 1)(x + 1)
stationary at x = 1 and x = -1
at x = 1:  y = 1 - 3 = -2;  y'' = 6x = 6 > 0  →  minimum (1, -2)
at x = -1: y = -1 + 3 = 2;  y'' = -6 < 0      →  maximum (-1, 2)
y intercept: x = 0, y = 0 (also a root)
end behaviour: x -> +inf gives y -> +inf; x -> -inf gives y -> -inf

Worked example 2 (where the test fails). Classify the stationary point of y = x⁴.

dy/dx = 4x³ = 0 only at x = 0, where y = 0
y'' = 12x² = 0 at x = 0, so the test is inconclusive
look at dy/dx: negative for x < 0, positive for x > 0
so the curve falls then rises: (0, 0) is a minimum

The failed case is examinable: y = x³ has no sign change in dy/dx at the origin, so it is a point of inflection, not an extremum. Reporting "stationary point" for x³ without that check loses the mark.

Kinematics with calculus

When displacement is given as a function of time, velocity is its derivative and acceleration the derivative of velocity. Those two definitions replace the constant-acceleration formulas the moment the motion stops being uniform, which is the whole point of the calculus treatment.

s(t) displacement;  v = ds/dt;  a = dv/dt = d²s/dt²
reverse: s = integral of v dt;  v = integral of a dt
maximum displacement occurs where v = 0
distance travelled = integral of |v| dt, split where v changes sign

Worked example. A particle moves with s = t³ − 6t² + 9t metres. Find when it is instantaneously at rest and its acceleration at those instants.

v = 3t² - 12t + 9 = 3(t - 1)(t - 3)
at rest: t = 1 and t = 3
a = 6t - 12   →   a(1) = -6 m/s²;  a(3) = 6 m/s²
s(1) = 4 m;  s(3) = 0 m

Worked example 2 (total distance versus displacement). For the same motion, find the distance travelled in 0 ≤ t ≤ 3.

v is positive on (0, 1) and negative on (1, 3)
distance = [s(1) - s(0)] + [s(1) - s(3)] = (4 - 0) + (4 - 0) = 8 m
note the displacement s(3) - s(0) = 0, so displacement alone would report 0

That last result is the standard trap: a question asking for distance needs the sign changes found first, or the positive and negative parts cancel and the answer is nonsense.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Chain) Differentiate (2x − 1)⁴. Answer: 8(2x − 1)³.
  2. (Product) Differentiate x³e^x. Answer: x²e^x(3 + x).
  3. (Quotient) Differentiate (x + 1)/(x − 1). Answer: −2/(x − 1)².
  4. (Implicit) x² + y² = 16: find dy/dx. Answer: −x/y.
  5. (Implicit tangent) Same circle at (2, √12): gradient? Answer: −2/3.46 = −0.577.
  6. (Parametric) x = t², y = 2t + 1: find dy/dx. Answer: 2/(2t) = 1/t.
  7. (Rates) V = s³, ds/dt = 1.5, s = 4. Find dV/dt. Answer: 3s² × 1.5 = 72.
  8. (Stationary) y = x²e^x: find the stationary points. Answer: e^x(x² + 2x) = 0 → x = 0 (min), x = −2 (max).

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Chain rule forgotten: differentiating sin 2x as 2 cos 2x, not cos 2x — the inner derivative is compulsory.
  • Quotient rule order reversed: v du − u dv, not u dv − v du; the sign flips if you swap.
  • Implicit y terms: each differentiated y term needs a dy/dx factor, including products like xy.
  • Parametric dy/dx inverted: it is (dy/dt)/(dx/dt), not the reciprocal.
  • Second derivative by differentiating dy/dx with respect to t: must divide by dx/dt, or the answer is d/dt, not d/dx.
  • Rates linked backwards: dV/dt = dV/dr × dr/dt; inverting gives an answer in the wrong units.
  • Stationary points unfactorised: equations like x e^x(2 + x) = 0 are solved only when factorised.
  • Domain of ln: differentiating ln x is valid only for x > 0; for negative arguments use ln|x|.

Equations and symbols

Every rule in this topic is stated once, with its condition, because the exam marks recognition as heavily as execution. The notation is the standard one: y and x the variables, u and v the two factors or the numerator and denominator, t the parameter, dy/dx the derivative of y with respect to x.

dy/dx = f'(g(x)) g'(x) Key: f' = derivative of the outer function; g'(x) = derivative of the inner function; the product of the two is the chain rule. Leaving out the inner derivative is the single commonest lost mark — sin 2x differentiates to 2cos 2x, not cos 2x.

d(uv)/dx = u dv/dx + v du/dx Key: u and v = the two functions being multiplied; du/dx and dv/dx = their derivatives. First times the derivative of the second, plus second times the derivative of the first.

d(u/v)/dx = (v du/dx - u dv/dx)/v² Key: u = numerator; v = denominator; the order in the numerator matters — v du − u dv, and reversing it flips the sign of every answer.

dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt) Key: t = the parameter; x = f(t) and y = g(t) define the curve. Differentiate each with respect to t, then divide — not the reciprocal, and the second derivative needs another division by dx/dt.

2x + 2y dy/dx = 0 Key: implicit differentiation of x² + y² = 25; each differentiated y term carries a dy/dx factor because y is a function of x. Rearranging gives dy/dx = −x/y.

dV/dt = dV/dr x dr/dt Key: V = volume (cm³); r = radius (cm); t = time (s). The chain rule in rate form: differentiate the quantity with respect to the variable you know, then multiply by that variable's rate.

V = (4/3) π r³ → dV/dr = 4 π r² Key: V = volume of a sphere (cm³); r = radius (cm); π = 3.1416. For the 100 cm³ s⁻¹ balloon this gives dr/dt = 100/(4πr²), which is 0.318 cm s⁻¹ at r = 5 cm.

dy/dx = 3x² - 3 = 3(x - 1)(x + 1) Key: the derivative of y = x³ − 3x, factorised so the stationary points x = ±1 can be read off. Factorising is not cosmetic — an unfactorised derivative cannot be solved.

s(t) displacement; v = ds/dt; a = dv/dt = d²s/dt² Key: s = displacement (m); v = velocity (m s⁻¹); a = acceleration (m s⁻²); t = time (s). At rest means v = 0; distance travelled is the integral of the speed, split wherever v changes sign.

d/dx(e^x) = e^x; d/dx(ln x) = 1/x Key: e = 2.71828…; ln x is defined for x > 0 only. For any other base a, the derivative carries a factor ln a: d/dx(aˣ) = aˣ ln a.

Where the marks are lost. A missing inner derivative, a reversed quotient numerator, a missing dy/dx on an implicit y term, and a d²y/dx² obtained by differentiating with respect to t instead of dividing by dx/dt. In kinematics, reporting the displacement when the question asked for distance is the classic: the sign changes must be found first.

title: Exam technique: Poisson Distribution
content:
### What earns the marks
For lambda scaling, the rate times the interval stated earns the first mark. For probabilities, e^-lambda lambda^x / x! with values earns the method mark. For approximations, the condition named (n large, p small, lambda = np) earns credit.
### Traps
Error: unscaled lambda over a new interval. Correction: scale first. Error: binomial coefficients inside Poisson work. Correction: Poisson formula only. Error: mean and variance treated as different. Correction: both equal lambda.
### Worked example
Calls arrive at a rate of 3 per minute, so over 2 minutes λ = 6. The probability of exactly 2 calls is P(X = 2) = e⁻⁶ × 6² / 2! = 18e⁻⁶ ≈ 0.0446. The mean and the variance both equal λ, so the mean number in 2 minutes is 6.
### Check yourself
Explain why the rate must be scaled before you use the formula. The rate is given per minute, but the interval is 2 minutes, so λ must be the rate multiplied by the interval, giving 6 and not 3.

title: Data Structures — Study Notes
content:
`# Data Structures

Arrays and Lists

Contiguous, indexed, O(1) access; fixed size. 2D arrays: element (i, j) — rows × columns.

Stack (LIFO)

push/pop/peek at one end. Uses: call stacks, undo, expression evaluation, DFS.

Example: evaluating 3 4 + : push 3, push 4, pop both, push 7.

Queue (FIFO)

enqueue at rear, dequeue at front. Uses: print queues, schedulers, BFS. A circular queue reuses vacated slots with head/tail pointers modulo capacity.

Linked List

Nodes with data + pointer. Insert/delete O(1) at a known node; search O(n). Traversal follows next pointers until null.

Hash Table

Hash function maps keys → index. Collisions resolved by chaining or open addressing. Average O(1) lookup, worst O(n).

title: Poisson Distribution — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Poisson Distribution

Mathematics — A2. X ~ Po(λ) counts events in a fixed interval of time or space when events occur independently, at a constant average rate λ, and never twice at the same instant. Classic settings: calls per hour at a helpdesk, typos per page, cars per minute at a quiet junction.

Key areas to revise

  • The Model
  • The Formula
  • Mean and Variance
  • Scaling the Interval
  • Adding Poissons

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Key points to remember

If X ~ Po(λ), then P(X = r) = e^(−λ) λʳ / r!. The mean and the variance are both equal to λ. A Poisson model needs events that occur singly, at a constant average rate, independently of one another in a fixed interval.

If X ~ Po(λ) and Y ~ Po(μ) are independent, then X + Y ~ Po(λ + μ). When the time or length interval changes, scale λ to match: a rate of 3 per minute gives λ = 15 for five minutes. Use cumulative tables for P(X ≤ r), and remember that P(X ≥ r) = 1 − P(X ≤ r − 1).

Appendix Q — A full worked example of how the topic’s reasoning comes together in one long answer

A long answer on this topic is best understood by working through a single example from end to end, because that shows how the reasoning, the sequence and the distinctions are meant to come together. Suppose the question asks you to describe how the body responds when a skin infection is beginning to develop, and to explain how the response shows both non-specific and specific defence, and then to relate that to vaccination and to the idea of memory. A good answer starts with the first line: the skin has been breached, the immediate non-specific responses include the local inflammation and the arrival of phagocytes, and phagocytosis is non-specific because it acts against a broad range of pathogens. A good answer then moves to the specific response: the antigens from the pathogen are recognised, B cells produce antibodies specific to those antigens, T cells help and control and some T cells are important in dealing with infected cells, and memory cells are formed. A good answer then explains why this matters: the primary response is slower because the specific lymphocytes have to be activated and expanded, but the secondary response is faster and stronger because the memory cells are already present. And a good answer then relates it to vaccination: vaccination exposes the immune system to the antigen without the disease, so the memory is formed without the person having to suffer the infection first. If you can write that whole sequence from memory, you have the topic as a connected whole, and you have the kind of answer the long questions are after.

If you write that kind of answer with the right distinctions, you hit the marks that the question is really after. You hit the non-specific versus specific distinction, because you have said that the first line is non-specific and the specific response is specific. You hit the process distinction, because you have said that the primary response is slower and the secondary is faster because of memory. You hit the vaccination link, because you have said that vaccination primes the same memory system without the disease. You hit the cell distinction, because you have said that B cells make antibodies and T cells help and control and deal with infected cells. If you can write that whole sequence with those points in it, you are not just labelling; you are reasoning, and the reasoning is what the long-answer marks are about. If you write a shorter answer that only says “the body fights the infection with white blood cells and memory,” you have the label but not the reasoning, and the mark is in the reasoning.

The same kind of integrated answer is what the evaluation and ethics questions want, just with a different content. Suppose the question asks you to evaluate the use of vaccines in controlling an infectious disease, and to consider both benefits and issues. A good answer says that vaccines protect individuals by priming the immune system without disease, and that at high coverage they also protect the population through herd immunity by reducing the spread. A good answer then says that the issues include coverage, exemptions, side effects and public acceptance, and that the balance depends on the disease, the vaccine and the context. A good answer does not say only that vaccines are good or only that they are problematic; it says that the benefit is protection of the individual and, at coverage, the population, and that the issues are real but specific to the case. If you can write that, you have the evaluation. If you write only a slogan one way or the other, you have the label but not the evaluation, and the mark is in the evaluation.

The same kind of integrated answer is what the gene technology questions want when they ask you to relate the technique to the purpose and then to the application and the limits. Suppose the question asks you about PCR and how it is used in a forensic or diagnostic context. A good answer says that PCR amplifies a specific DNA sequence in vitro through repeated cycles, and that the primers define the target and the heat-stable polymerase survives the repeated heating. A good answer then says that this is useful because it lets a small sample be amplified enough to study or use, and that in a forensic or diagnostic context the result is interpreted in context with attention to sample quality and contamination. A good answer does not say only that PCR makes DNA, because that is the label but not the reasoning. It says that PCR amplifies a specific sequence, that is why it is useful, and that the result is interpreted with care. If you can write that, you have the gene technology answer that the question is after, and you have it at the level where the marks are actually given.

The final point about the integrated answer is that it should not be too long, because the exam rewards precision and sequence, not length for its own sake. The example answers above are long enough to earn the marks and not so long that they run out of time or lose focus. If you can write answers of that shape, with the right sequence and the right distinctions and the right level of detail, you are doing the topic as the exam expects it, and you are using the note the way it was meant to be used: as a source of reasoning, not as a script to recite. The length of the note is there to give you enough material to draw from, but the answers you write on the day have to be shaped for the exam, and that shaping is the skill the note is trying to build. If you can write shaped answers from the note, the note has done its job.

Appendix R — The most durable ideas in the topic, and how to hold onto them

The most durable ideas in this topic are the ones you should hold onto first, because they are the ones that carry the most marks and the ones that show up in the most different questions. The first is that the topic is really about control at several levels: detection, coordination, response and regulation, with nervous and hormonal systems as the main animal control systems, homeostasis as the regulation of the internal environment, and gene technology as the manipulation of the DNA that makes all of it possible. The second is that the body defends itself in layers: non-specific first line, then specific response with antibodies and memory, and that the two layers work together rather than one replacing the other. The third is that the immune system is a process with timing, so the primary and secondary responses are different mainly because of memory, and that is why vaccination works. The fourth is that gene technology is about matching techniques to purposes, and that the applications and the limits both matter. If you hold onto those four durable ideas, you can answer a large part of the topic even if you cannot recall every detail, because those four ideas are the framework that the details fit into.

The way to hold onto the durable ideas is to practise them as statements with reasons, not as bare labels. For the control idea, the reason is that different jobs need different speeds, ranges and durations, which is why we have nervous and hormonal systems and why we have immunity and homeostasis and gene technology as separate but related tools. For the layered defence idea, the reason is that the first line is broad and fast and the specific response is targeted and slower to start but stronger on later exposure, and that is why both exist. For the timing idea, the reason is that memory makes the secondary response faster and stronger, and that is why vaccination works. For the gene technology idea, the reason is that each technique is useful for a specific purpose, and that the purpose is what should explain the technique, not the other way around. If you can state those durable ideas with their reasons, you have a framework you can use in many different questions, and that is the use of the framework: to give you something to reach for when the question is not exactly the one you practised.

The worry with durable ideas is that they can sound so general that they become vague, so the way to keep them from becoming vague is to tie each one to one concrete example you can say precisely. For the control idea, tie it to the reflex arc and to the insulin-glucagon system, because those are two concrete cases of control where you can say the detail precisely. For the layered defence idea, tie it to the skin barrier and phagocytosis on one hand and to antibodies and memory cells on the other, because those are two concrete cases where you can say the detail precisely. For the timing idea, tie it to the primary and secondary response and to vaccination, because those are the concrete cases where the timing is most clearly at issue. For the gene technology idea, tie it to restriction enzymes, PCR and electrophoresis, because those are the concrete techniques where the purpose is clearest. If you tie each durable idea to one or two concrete cases you can say precisely, you keep the idea from becoming vague, because the concrete case anchors it. That is the way to hold onto the durable ideas without turning them into slogans, and it is the way to make them useful on the day.

The harder edge cases in this topic are the ones where the specification can ask a question that looks easy but is really testing a precise point, and the point is usually one of the distinctions that is easy to blur when writing fast. One edge case is the difference between the neuromuscular junction and a neurone-to-neurone synapse, because the question can ask you to say what is similar and what is different, and the similar part is the calcium entry and neurotransmitter release, while the different part is that the postsynaptic cell is a muscle fibre and the result is contraction. If you blur that, you lose the marks that depend on seeing both the similarity and the difference. Another edge case is the difference between the structure of a rod and the structure of a cone, because the question can ask you to say how they differ and why, and the difference is that rods are more sensitive and work in dim light without colour, while cones detect colour and work best in brighter light. If you blur that, you lose the marks that depend on the distinction.

Another edge case is the difference between the way a restriction enzyme works and the way a gene probe works, because the question can ask you to say how each contributes to gene technology, and the restriction enzyme cuts at a specific sequence so pieces can be joined, while the gene probe detects a specific sequence by hybridisation. If you blur that, you lose the marks that depend on seeing that one is about cutting and joining and the other is about detecting. Another edge case is the difference between somatic and germ-line gene therapy, because the question can ask you to say why the two are treated differently ethically, and the reason is that somatic treatment affects only the treated individual while germ-line treatment would be inherited and would affect future generations. If you blur that, you lose the marks that depend on the ethical distinction, which is often the whole point of the question.

Another edge case is the difference between herd immunity and individual immunity, because the question can ask you to say why high coverage matters, and the reason is that herd immunity is about reducing transmission through the population, not about making every individual immune. If you blur that, you lose the marks that depend on the population logic, which is often the whole point of the herd immunity question. Another edge case is the difference between the primary and secondary immune response in timing and strength, because the question can ask you to explain why the secondary response is faster and stronger, and the reason is the memory cells from the first exposure. If you blur that, you lose the marks that depend on the memory logic, which is often the whole point of the primary/secondary question.

The way to handle the edge cases is to be precise about the distinction the question is testing, and to say the distinction in a way that makes it clear you are seeing both sides. For the neuromuscular junction versus the synapse, say that the sequence is the same but the postsynaptic cell and the outcome are different. For the rod versus the cone, say that both are photoreceptors but they differ in sensitivity, colour and light level. For the restriction enzyme versus the probe, say that one is for cutting and joining and the other is for detecting. For the somatic versus the germ-line therapy, say that one affects the individual and the other is heritable. For the herd immunity versus the individual immunity, say that one is about coverage and transmission and the other is about the individual. For the primary versus the secondary response, say that one is slower and one is faster and stronger because of memory. If you can say those distinctions precisely, you can answer the edge cases, and the edge cases are the ones that separate a good answer from a very good one.

On the day, the guide to using this note is to use it in time order, from the first idea you reach for to the last. The first thing to reach for is the durable ideas, because those are the ones that give you the framework and keep you from losing the thread. If the question is about coordination, reach for the control idea: detection, coordination, response, with nervous and hormonal systems as the main animal systems, and with homeostasis as the regulation of the internal environment. If the question is about defence, reach for the layered defence idea: non-specific first line, then specific response with antibodies and memory, and the two working together. If the question is about memory, reach for the timing idea: primary is slower, secondary is faster and stronger because of memory, and vaccination works by priming the same memory system. If the question is about gene technology, reach for the matching idea: each technique has a purpose, and the purpose explains the technique. If you can reach for the right durable idea first, you are already in the right place for the answer, and the rest of the answer is then the detail that fits under that idea.

The second thing to reach for is the concrete example that anchors the durable idea, because that is what keeps the answer precise rather than vague. For the control idea, anchor it to the reflex arc or the insulin-glucagon system, whichever the question is about. For the layered defence idea, anchor it to the skin barrier and phagocytosis or to the antibody and memory cell response, whichever the question is about. For the timing idea, anchor it to the primary and secondary response and to vaccination. For the gene technology idea, anchor it to the technique the question is about. If you can anchor the durable idea to a concrete example you can say precisely, you keep the answer precise, and precision is what the marks are about. If you only have the durable idea without the anchor, the answer tends to become vague, and vagueness is what loses marks on the day, even when the idea is right.

The third thing to reach for is the distinction the question is really testing, because that is the mark the question is after. For a coordination question, the distinction may be nervous versus hormonal, or receptor versus effector, or synapse versus neuromuscular junction. For a defence question, the distinction may be non-specific versus specific, or B versus T, or primary versus secondary. For a gene technology question, the distinction may be the purpose of the technique, or somatic versus germ-line, or herd immunity versus individual immunity. If you can reach for the right distinction and say it precisely, you hit the mark the question is after. If you only give the general idea without the distinction, you often leave the mark on the table, because the mark is in the distinction, not in the general idea. The note is written to give you the distinctions as well as the ideas, and that is the use of the length: to make the distinctions available when the question is testing them.

The final thing on the day is to watch the time and the length, because the exam rewards a precise answer of the right length more than a long imprecise one. If you have reached for the durable idea, anchored it to a concrete example, and said the distinction precisely, you have the answer the question wants, and you should stop there and move on, rather than padding it out. If you pad it out, you usually lose precision, and precision is what the mark is after. If you stop at the precise answer, you have the mark, and you have time for the next question. That is the guide to using the note on the day: reach for the durable idea, anchor it, say the distinction, stop at precision, and move on. If you can do that, the note has given you what it was meant to give you: the reasoning that lets you answer the topic under time pressure, which is the only form the exam is in.
