If you pad it out, you usually lose precision, and precision is what the mark is after. If you stop at the precise answer, you have the mark, and you have time for the next question. That is the guide to using the note on the day: reach for the durable idea, anchor it, say the distinction, stop at precision, and move on. If you can do that, the note has given you what it was meant to give you: the reasoning that lets you answer the topic under time pressure, which is the only form the exam is in.

title: A Level Mathematics: Sampling and Estimation
content:
A Level Mathematics: Sampling and Estimation

Statistics works by measuring a sample and reasoning about a population that was never fully measured. That inference is only as good as the sample: a biased sample cannot be rescued by a larger one. This note covers how samples are drawn, what the sampling distribution of the mean is, why the central limit theorem makes normal methods work for almost any population, and how to build and interpret a confidence interval.

Populations, samples and parameters

A parameter describes the population and is usually unknown; a statistic describes the sample and is known. The whole of estimation is the attempt to learn a parameter from a statistic, and naming the two correctly is the first mark in many questions.

parameter: mu (population mean), sigma (population sd), p (proportion)
statistic: x-bar (sample mean), s (sample sd), p-hat (sample proportion)
an estimator is unbiased if its expected value equals the parameter

Worked example. A sample of 40 light bulbs has mean life 1,020 hours. Identify the parameter and the statistic.

statistic: x-bar = 1020 hours (known, from the sample)
parameter: mu, the mean life of all bulbs produced (unknown)
the estimate of mu is 1020 hours, with an uncertainty to be quantified

Sampling methods and bias

The method determines whether the sample can speak for the population at all. Every named method is a compromise between practicality and representativeness, and the exam asks you to identify which compromise a described survey has made.

MethodHow it worksWeakness
simple randomevery member equally likely, chosen by numberneeds a complete list
systematicevery k-th member from a random startperiodic patterns can bias it
stratifiedsample each subgroup in proportionneeds known subgroup sizes
quotafill fixed categories by interviewer choiceinterviewer bias, not random
opportunitywhoever is availablestrongly unrepresentative

Worked example. A surveyor interviews shoppers in a town centre on a weekday morning about working hours. Identify the bias.

people free on a weekday morning are systematically different from the
population: the employed, the housebound and shift workers are under-represented
this is an opportunity sample with selection bias, and no sample size fixes it

The sampling distribution of the mean

Take many samples of size n, compute each mean, and plot them: the result is the sampling distribution, and its spread is smaller than the population's by a factor of √n.

if X has mean mu and variance sigma^2, then x-bar has
mean = mu
variance = sigma^2/n
standard error = sigma/sqrt n

Worked example. A population has mean 50 and standard deviation 12. For samples of 36, find the mean and standard error of the sample mean.

mean of x-bar = 50
standard error = 12/6 = 2

Worked example 2 (effect of quadrupling n). What happens to the standard error if the sample size is quadrupled?

standard error = sigma/sqrt(4n) = (sigma/sqrt n)/2
it halves; quadrupling the sample buys a factor of two in precision

That square-root relationship is why doubling precision costs four times the data, and it is a standard exam comment.

The central limit theorem

Whatever shape the population has, the distribution of the sample mean becomes approximately normal as n grows. That is what licenses normal methods for non-normal populations, and it is the single most important result in the topic.

for large n (in practice n >= 30), x-bar is approximately N(mu, sigma^2/n)
the population itself need not be normal
if the population is already normal, the result is exact for any n

Worked example. A population is strongly skewed with mean 20 and standard deviation 10. Describe the distribution of the mean of samples of 50.

by the central limit theorem, approximately normal
mean 20, standard error 10/sqrt 50 = 1.414
so x-bar is approximately N(20, 2.0)

Confidence intervals for a mean

A confidence interval gives a range of plausible values for the parameter, with a stated long-run success rate. It is not a probability that the parameter lies in this particular interval — the parameter is fixed, the interval is random.

95% interval for mu: x-bar +/- 1.96 (sigma/sqrt n)
99% interval: x-bar +/- 2.5758 (sigma/sqrt n)
with s estimated from the sample, replace sigma by s (large n)
wider interval: more confidence, less precision

Worked example. A sample of 64 measurements has mean 25.4 and known standard deviation 4. Find a 95% confidence interval for the population mean.

standard error = 4/8 = 0.5
margin = 1.96 x 0.5 = 0.98
interval: 25.4 +/- 0.98 = (24.42, 26.38)

Worked example 2 (99%). The same data at 99%.

margin = 2.5758 x 0.5 = 1.288
interval: (24.11, 26.69), wider as expected

Worked example 3 (required sample size). How large a sample is needed for the 95% margin to be at most 0.2?

1.96 x 4/sqrt n <= 0.2
sqrt n >= 39.2
n >= 1537, so the sample must be at least 1537

Confidence intervals for a proportion

The sample proportion is a mean in disguise: each observation is a 0 or 1, so the same machinery applies with p in place of μ.

p-hat = r/n;  standard error = sqrt(p-hat(1 - p-hat)/n)
95% interval: p-hat +/- 1.96 x standard error
valid when n p-hat and n(1 - p-hat) are both at least 5

Worked example. In a sample of 200 voters, 84 support a candidate. Find a 95% confidence interval for the support.

p-hat = 0.42
standard error = sqrt(0.42 x 0.58/200) = sqrt(0.001218) = 0.0349
margin = 1.96 x 0.0349 = 0.0684
interval: (0.352, 0.488)

Worked example 2 (interpretation). A rival claims support is 50%. Does the interval support that claim?

0.5 lies outside (0.352, 0.488)
so at the 95% level the data are not consistent with 50% support

Estimators and their properties

Two properties decide whether an estimator is worth using: unbiasedness (correct on average) and low variance (consistent from sample to sample). The sample mean is unbiased for μ; the sample variance with divisor n is biased, which is why the divisor n − 1 appears.

E(x-bar) = mu  (unbiased)
E(s^2) with divisor n underestimates sigma^2 by a factor (n-1)/n
divisor n - 1 corrects the bias

Worked example. Explain why the divisor n − 1 is used in the sample variance.

deviations are measured from the sample mean, which is itself fitted to the data
that fitting uses up one degree of freedom, so the sum of squares is
systematically too small; dividing by n - 1 instead of n corrects it

Why the standard error is the whole story

Every formula in this topic contains σ/√n somewhere, and the reason is that estimating a mean averages away noise: independent errors partly cancel, and they cancel in proportion to the square root of how many there are. That is why precision is expensive — halving the standard error needs four times the data — and why a very precise interval from a biased sample is worse than useless, since it states a wrong answer with confidence.

The habitual check before trusting any interval is therefore two questions, not one: is the sample random, and is the sample large enough for the approximation used? An interval built from a quota sample answers a question about that quota, not about the population, however narrow it looks.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Parameter) Distinguish a parameter from a statistic. Answer: a parameter describes the population and is unknown; a statistic comes from the sample.
  2. (Method) Name a method that guarantees every member is equally likely. Answer: simple random sampling.
  3. (Bias) Give one weakness of a quota sample. Answer: the interviewer chooses who fills each quota, so selection bias remains.
  4. (Standard error) σ = 15, n = 25: find the standard error. Answer: 3.
  5. (Effect) n increases from 25 to 100: what happens to the standard error? Answer: it halves, from 3 to 1.5.
  6. (CLT) State the central limit theorem. Answer: for large n the sample mean is approximately normal whatever the population shape.
  7. (CI) x̄ = 40, σ = 6, n = 36: 95% interval. Answer: 40 ± 1.96 = (38.04, 41.96).
  8. (Width) How can the interval be made narrower? Answer: increase n, or lower the confidence level.
  9. (Proportion) 60 of 400: 95% interval. Answer: 0.15 ± 1.96(0.01785) = (0.115, 0.185).
  10. (Estimator) Why divide by n − 1? Answer: to correct the bias caused by measuring deviations from the sample mean.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Dividing by n instead of √n: the standard error is σ/√n; using σ/n makes intervals far too narrow.
  • Reading a CI as a probability: the parameter is fixed; the 95% refers to the long-run performance of the method.
  • Assuming normality of the data: it is the sample mean that is approximately normal, by the central limit theorem, not the population.
  • Bias described as variance: a biased sample is wrong however large; a variable one is merely imprecise.
  • Stratified confused with quota: stratified is random within known groups; quota is interviewer-selected.
  • Wrong z for 99%: it is 2.5758, not 2.33 (that is the one-tailed 1% value).
  • Confidence level and sample size traded silently: a narrower interval at the same confidence costs a larger sample.
  • Proportion interval outside [0, 1]: check the validity conditions and truncate, or report that the normal approximation is unsuitable.

title: Quadratics — Study Notes
content:
Quadratics

A quadratic has the form ax² + bx + c with a ≠ 0. Master three tools: completing the square, the discriminant, and inequalities.

Completing the Square

Rewrite x² + bx + c as (x + b/2)² − (b/2)² + c.

Example: x² + 6x + 5 = (x + 3)² − 9 + 5 = (x + 3)² − 4, so the vertex is at (−3, −4).

For a > 1, factor out a first: 2x² + 12x + 19 = 2(x² + 6x) + 19 = 2(x + 3)² − 18 + 19 = 2(x + 3)² + 1.

Vertex form a(x − h)² + k gives the minimum/maximum value k at x = h — this is how you find a maximum area or minimum cost.

The Discriminant

Δ = b² − 4ac decides how the curve meets the x-axis:

ΔRootsGraph
Δ > 0two distinct real rootscrosses x-axis twice
Δ = 0repeated roottouches (tangent)
Δ < 0no real rootsnever meets x-axis

Example: kx² + 4x + 1 = 0 has equal roots when 16 − 4k = 0, so k = 4.

Quadratic Inequalities

Solve by sketching. For x² − 5x + 4 < 0, factorise: (x − 1)(x − 4) < 0, and the curve is below the axis between the roots, so 1 < x < 4.

Tip: flip the inequality when dividing by a negative number, and always sketch to check which interval you need.

Curve and Line Intersections

Set the equations equal; the resulting quadratic's discriminant tells you if the line is a secant (Δ > 0), tangent (Δ = 0) or misses (Δ < 0).

Exam tips: complete the square before reading off turning points; state the discriminant condition explicitly before solving for an unknown coefficient.

Discriminant and inequalities: exam method

For ax² + bx + c = 0 the discriminant is b² − 4ac. Positive gives two distinct real roots, zero gives one repeated root, and negative gives no real roots. Use this without solving the equation when the question asks about the nature of the roots.

To find the values of k for which a quadratic has no real roots, require b² − 4ac < 0 and solve the resulting inequality in k.

To solve a quadratic inequality, find the roots, sketch the U-shaped (a > 0) or inverted-U (a < 0) curve, and read off the region above or below the axis. For x² − 5x + 6 < 0 the roots are 2 and 3, and the solution is 2 < x < 3.

Exam cue: Completing the square gives the turning point (p, q) and shows the minimum or maximum value directly.

Worked example: completing the square with a coefficient

Write 2x² + 8x + 3 in the form a(x + p)² + q. Factor the 2 from the first two terms: 2(x² + 4x) + 3. Complete the square inside the bracket: x² + 4x = (x + 2)² − 4. So the expression is 2((x + 2)² − 4) + 3 = 2(x + 2)² − 5.

The minimum value is −5, reached when x = −2, so the minimum point is (−2, −5). Always factor the leading coefficient out first, otherwise the constant term comes out wrong.

Discriminant and the range of a parameter

The equation x² + kx + 4 = 0 has no real roots when the discriminant is negative: k² − 16 < 0. Solve as a quadratic in k to get −4 < k < 4. Stating the range is the mark-earning step, so write the inequality in full.

If the discriminant equals zero, the line is a tangent to the curve; if it is positive the line cuts the curve at two points.

Tangent to a curve

Find where y = x² − 2x + 3 meets the line y = 2x + k. Substitute to get x² − 4x + (3 − k) = 0. For a tangent the discriminant is zero: 16 − 4(3 − k) = 0, so k = −1. The tangent is y = 2x − 1, touching the curve at x = 2, where y = 3 on both.

Solving a quadratic inequality with a sketch

Solve 2x² − 5x − 3 > 0. Factor as (2x + 1)(x − 3) and find the roots x = −½ and x = 3. The parabola has a positive leading coefficient, so it is above the axis outside the roots. The solution is x < −½ or x > 3. Note the word or: this is two separate intervals, not one.

  • Positive leading coefficient: the expression is positive outside the roots and negative between them.
  • Negative leading coefficient: the reverse is true.
  • If the quadratic has no real roots, the sign never changes, so test one value to decide whether the inequality holds for all x.

title: IGCSE Physics: Electricity and Circuits
content:
IGCSE Physics: Electricity and Circuits

Cambridge IGCSE Physics 0625 (2026–2028), Topic 4 Electricity and magnetism: statements 4.2 Electrical quantities, 4.3 Electric circuits and 4.4 Electrical safety. Electric circuits are the most calculation-dense part of the Paper 4 paper, and every result in them flows from one picture: a battery pushes charge round a circuit, the charge pays a price (p.d.) to get through each component, and the rate of flow is the current. This note builds charge, current, e.m.f., p.d., resistance, energy and power from scratch, then builds real circuits from them and finishes with the mains safety that saves lives.

Electric charge and the electron model

There are two kinds of charge, positive and negative, and the rule is simple: like charges repel, unlike charges attract. Rubbing a polythene rod with a cloth transfers electrons from the cloth to the rod, so the rod becomes negatively charged and the cloth positive; nothing is created — charge is transferred. A conductor (metal, graphite, the human body, tap water) lets charge move through it because it contains free electrons; an insulator (plastic, rubber, dry air, glass) does not. Charging by friction works only when the object is isolated on an insulating support, or the charge leaks away instantly.

Supplement adds the two deeper ideas. Charge is measured in coulombs (C); one coulomb is the charge that flows when a current of 1 ampere passes for 1 second, and the charge on one electron is 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. A charged object also creates an electric field in the space around it — a region where other charges experience a force — and the field of a point charge is drawn as radial lines pointing away from a positive charge and towards a negative one.

Electric current

Electric current is the rate of flow of charge. In metals the charge carriers are free electrons drifting slowly around the circuit while the electric field travels almost at the speed of light, which is why a lamp lights the instant a switch is closed.

current = charge / time        I = Q / t
  • I: current in amperes (A); Q: charge in coulombs (C); t: time in seconds (s). Current is treated as a scalar in circuit calculations.
  • Conventional current flows from the positive terminal, round the circuit, to the negative terminal; electrons drift the opposite way. Both descriptions are accepted, but conventional current is the one used in circuit diagrams.

An ammeter measures current and is connected in series, so the whole current passes through it. Direct current (d.c.) flows in one direction only, as from a battery; alternating current (a.c.) reverses direction repeatedly, as from the mains, which in the UK completes 50 cycles per second at 230 V.

Electromotive force and potential difference

The electromotive force (e.m.f.) of a source is the energy transferred from other forms to electrical energy per unit charge driven round the whole circuit; the potential difference (p.d.) across a component is the energy transferred from electrical to other forms per unit charge passing through that component. Both are measured in volts, and a voltmeter is connected in parallel with the component being measured.

potential difference = energy transferred / charge        V = W / Q
electromotive force = energy transferred from other forms / charge driven
  • V: potential difference in volts (V); W: energy in joules (J); Q: charge in coulombs (C). One volt is one joule per coulomb (1 V = 1 J C⁻¹).

The distinction that earns marks: e.m.f. is about energy supplied to the circuit (a battery's rating, 1.5 V for a dry cell), while p.d. is about energy delivered to a component. In a series circuit the p.d.s across the components add up to the supply e.m.f., because each coulomb spends its energy bit by bit around the loop.

Resistance

Resistance is how much a component opposes current. It is measured in ohms (Ω): a 12 Ω resistor passes less current than a 4 Ω resistor at the same p.d.

resistance = potential difference / current        R = V / I
  • R: resistance in ohms (Ω); V: p.d. across the component in volts (V); I: current through it in amperes (A). Resistance is a scalar.

Resistance is measured by setting up a circuit with the unknown resistor, an ammeter in series and a voltmeter across it, then changing the supply with a variable resistor and taking several pairs of readings. The resistance is found from the gradient of a graph of V against I, which averages the whole data set.

The wire's dimensions matter. A longer wire has greater resistance (resistance is proportional to length); a thicker wire has less (resistance is inversely proportional to cross-sectional area); and the material matters because of how many free electrons it provides. Nichrome wire is used for heating elements because it has a high resistance and resists oxidation when hot.

Supplement: current–voltage graphs. A metallic conductor at constant temperature gives a straight line through the origin — ohmic. A filament lamp curves over: as it heats, its resistance rises, so the graph flattens. A diode conducts in one direction only, giving almost zero current in reverse; a light-dependent resistor falls in resistance as light intensity rises; a thermistor falls in resistance as temperature rises. All three are basis-of-operation questions for sensors.

Electrical energy and power

Every component turns electrical energy into something else — heat in a resistor, light and heat in a lamp, kinetic energy in a motor. The rate of that transfer is electrical power:

electrical power = potential difference x current        P = V I
electrical energy = power x time = V I t        E = V I t
  • P: power in watts (W); V: volts (V); I: amperes (A); E: energy in joules (J); t: time in seconds (s).
  • Combined with R = V/I this gives P = I²R and P = V²/R, useful when the resistance is known instead of the p.d.

The kilowatt-hour is the domestic unit of energy: one kWh is the energy used by a 1000 W device running for one hour (3.6 × 10⁶ J). Electricity bills charge cost = number of kWh × price per kWh, and a Paper 4 question usually asks for the cost of running a named appliance for a stated time.

Circuit components and circuit rules

Circuit diagrams use standard symbols: cell, battery, lamp, resistor, variable resistor, thermistor, LDR, diode, LED, ammeter, voltmeter, switch, motor. The two rules for series and parallel circuits are the spine of every calculation:

SeriesParallel
CurrentThe same through every componentShared between the branches; the branch currents add up to the total
Potential differenceShared between the components; the p.d.s add up to the supplyThe same across every branch
ResistanceR(total) = R1 + R2 + ...1/R(total) = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + ... (Supplement); two equal resistors in parallel give half the resistance of one

Adding lamps in series makes all of them dimmer, because the total resistance rises and the current falls; adding lamps in parallel leaves each at full brightness (each has the full p.d. across it) but draws more current from the supply. A variable resistor in series with a lamp dims it by reducing the current; a potential divider (Supplement) is two resistors in series with the output tapped between them:

output voltage = supply voltage x R2 / (R1 + R2)

A potential divider feeding a sensor gives an output voltage that changes with light or temperature, which is the basis of automatic night lights and thermostats.

Electrical safety

The domestic mains in the UK is 230 V a.c., enough to kill. The three wires in a three-core cable are colour-coded: live (brown) carries the alternating p.d. at about 230 V; neutral (blue) completes the circuit and is held near 0 V; earth (green and yellow) is a safety wire connected to the metal case of the appliance and to the ground.

  • Fuse: a thin wire in the live path that melts and breaks the circuit if the current exceeds its rating, protecting against overheating and fire. Choose a rating just above the normal working current.
  • Circuit breaker: a magnetic or electronic switch that trips and can be reset; faster and reusable, doing the same job as a fuse.
  • Earthing: if a fault connects the live wire to a metal case, the earth wire carries a large current that blows the fuse instead of giving the user a shock.
  • Double insulation: appliances with plastic cases need no earth wire, because no fault can make the case live.

Everyday hazards to name in an exam: frayed cables, damaged plugs, wet hands, water near electrical equipment, overloaded adapters, and touching a live conductor. The physics of the danger is current through the body: even a few tens of milliamperes through the heart can be fatal, and wet skin lowers body resistance and raises that current.

Worked example: a mixed circuit

Two resistors, 6.0 Ω and 3.0 Ω, are connected in parallel across a 12 V supply.

1 / R(total) = 1/6.0 + 1/3.0 = 0.167 + 0.333 = 0.500, so R(total) = 2.0 ohm
total current = V / R = 12 / 2.0 = 6.0 A
current in the 6.0 ohm resistor = 12 / 6.0 = 2.0 A
current in the 3.0 ohm resistor = 12 / 3.0 = 4.0 A   (branch currents add to 6.0 A)
power in the circuit = V I = 12 x 6.0 = 72 W
energy in 5 minutes = P t = 72 x 300 = 21 600 J

Each resistor has the full 12 V across it, as the parallel rule demands. If the two were instead in series, the total resistance would be 9.0 Ω, the current 1.33 A, and each p.d. would add to 12 V — a useful check before trusting any circuit answer.

Common mistakes

  • Putting an ammeter in parallel or a voltmeter in series; ammeters join in series, voltmeters across the component.
  • Using the supply voltage as the p.d. across one component in a series circuit; the supply is shared.
  • Adding resistances in parallel by simple addition; the reciprocals add, so the total is always less than the smallest branch.
  • Confusing current direction with electron drift, or saying charge is used up; the current is the same everywhere in a series circuit, and energy is transferred, not the charge.
  • Using watts and minutes in E = VIt; power in watts needs energy in joules and time in seconds (convert kWh and hours carefully in cost questions).
  • Forgetting that a filament lamp's resistance rises as it heats, so its I–V graph is a curve, not a straight line.
  • Choosing a fuse rating far above the working current for safety; too high a rating defeats the protection.
  • Mixing e.m.f. and p.d.: the battery has an e.m.f.; each component has a p.d. across it.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 4, 3 marks). A lamp is marked 24 W, 12 V. Calculate the current it takes and its resistance.

Answer: P = VI gives I = 24/12 = 2.0 A. R = V/I = 12/2.0 = 6.0 Ω.

Question 2 (Paper 4, 3 marks). A charge of 360 C passes through a lamp in 3.0 minutes. Calculate the current.

Answer: I = Q/t = 360/180 = 2.0 A. (Convert minutes to seconds first.)

Question 3 (Paper 2 style). In a series circuit of two resistors, which statement is true? A the current is largest through the smaller resistor; B the p.d. across each is the same as the supply; C the current is the same in both; D the total resistance is less than either. Answer: C. Current is the same everywhere in series; the p.d. is shared and the total resistance is the sum.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 4 marks). A 3.0 kW kettle runs for 4.0 minutes from 230 V. Find the charge that flows and the energy transferred.

Answer: I = P/V = 3000/230 = 13 A. Q = It = 13 × 240 = 3120 C. Energy = Pt = 3000 × 240 = 720 000 J (0.20 kWh).

Question 5 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Explain why a metal-cased washing machine has an earth wire but a plastic hairdryer does not.

Answer: The metal case is a conductor; if a fault brings the live wire into contact with it, the case would become live at 230 V and anyone touching it would receive a shock. The earth wire connects the case to the ground, so a large fault current flows to earth and melts the fuse, isolating the supply. The hairdryer has a plastic (double-insulated) case which cannot conduct, so no fault can make the outside live and no earth wire is needed.

Question 6 (Paper 6 style). Describe how you would determine the resistance of a coil of wire.

Answer: Connect the coil in series with an ammeter, a cell and a variable resistor, with a voltmeter across the coil. Vary the current and record several pairs of current and p.d. readings. Plot p.d. against current; the gradient is the resistance of the coil. Taking several readings and using the graph removes the effect of random errors and of the coil warming up (which would otherwise change its resistance).

Where charge flows, fields follow: next is Magnetism and Electromagnetism.

Equations and symbols

Statements 4.2 to 4.4 rest on five equations and three circuit rules. Charge, current, voltage and resistance are defined by the first three; the power relations all follow from them, so a question that gives two quantities can almost always be finished without memorising a fourth formula.

Charge, current and voltage

Q = It
Key: Q = charge flowing (C); I = current (A); t = time (s). One coulomb is one ampere for one second.

I = Q / t
Key: I = current (A); Q = charge passing a point (C); t = time (s). Current is a rate of charge flow, not a quantity of charge.

V = W / Q
Key: V = potential difference (V); W = work done or energy transferred (J); Q = charge moved (C). One volt is one joule per coulomb, which is the definition the mark scheme wants.

E = QV
Key: E = energy transferred by the charge (J); Q = charge (C); V = potential difference (V).

Q = Ne
Key: Q = total charge (C); N = number of electrons (no unit); e = elementary charge, 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. Used when a question asks how many electrons carry a given charge.

Resistance and Ohm's law

V = IR
Key: V = potential difference across the component (V); I = current through it (A); R = resistance (Ω). Ohm's law holds only when temperature is constant, which is why a filament lamp's I–V graph curves.

R = V / I
Key: R = resistance (Ω); V = potential difference (V); I = current (A). For a curved I–V graph, R is still V/I at the chosen point, not the gradient.

1 Ω = 1 V / 1 A
Key: the definition of the ohm; a component has 1 Ω when 1 V drives 1 A through it.

Power and energy in a circuit

P = VI
Key: P = power (W); V = potential difference (V); I = current (A).

P = I²R
Key: P = power dissipated as heat (W); I = current (A); R = resistance (Ω). This is the form that explains why transmission cables carry a low current at high voltage.

P = V² / R
Key: P = power (W); V = potential difference (V); R = resistance (Ω). Use it when the current is not given.

E = Pt = VIt
Key: E = energy transferred (J); P = power (W); t = time (s); V = potential difference (V); I = current (A).

cost = P(kW) × t(h) × price per kWh
Key: P in kilowatts (W ÷ 1000); t in hours; the price is per kilowatt-hour. A 2000 W heater for 3 hours uses 6 kWh.

fuse rating: I = P / V
Key: I = normal operating current (A); P = appliance power (W); V = supply voltage (V). Choose the next standard fuse above this value, never below it.

The three circuit rules

series: R(total) = R₁ + R₂ + …
Key: resistances in ohms (Ω); the current is the same everywhere in the series path and the supply voltage divides between the components.

parallel: 1 / R(total) = 1 / R₁ + 1 / R₂ + …
Key: resistances in ohms (Ω); the potential difference is the same across each branch and the current divides. Two 6 Ω resistors in parallel give 3 Ω, which is less than either — a parallel combination always has a lower resistance.

V(total) = V₁ + V₂ (series) and I(total) = I₁ + I₂ (parallel)
Key: the voltage rule for series and the current rule for parallel, both in the units of the quantity. The companion rules — voltage equal in parallel, current equal in series — follow from charge and energy conservation.

title: Mensuration — Bearings and Loci — Study Notes
content:
Mensuration — Bearings and Loci

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): compass bearings, scale drawings, constructions (perpendicular/angle bisectors), loci regions.

1. Bearings

  • Measured clockwise from north; three figures: 065°, 128°, 300°.
  • Back bearing = front bearing ± 180°.
  • Draw a north line at both points; north lines are parallel, giving Z-angles.

Example: B is on bearing 070° from A → A is on bearing 250° from B.

2. Scale drawings

1 cm : 500 m style scales; measure, convert, and quote distances/bearings from your drawing to the accuracy allowed.

3. Constructions

  • Perpendicular bisector of a segment: equal arcs from both ends, join the crossings.
  • Angle bisector: equal arcs from the vertex arms.
  • 60° and 90° constructions with compasses; leave all arcs visible.

4. Loci

Fixed distance from a point = circle; from a line = parallel lines with rounded ends; equidistant from two points = perpendicular bisector; from two lines = angle bisector.

Example: a goat tied by a 5 m rope to a corner of a 4 m × 6 m shed: the reachable region is ¾ circle radius 5 m + two ¼ circles radius 1 m where the rope wraps.

Exam tips: state "clockwise from north" in bearing definitions; shade/label locus regions clearly; use a ruler for construction lines too.

Three-figure bearings

A bearing is measured clockwise from north and written with three figures, so 045° is north-east and 250° is south-west. To find the back bearing, add or subtract 180°. Draw a north line at the starting point and measure the angle carefully with a protractor.

Scale drawings and distance

Use the scale given to convert a map distance to a real distance, and convert back when drawing. Scale 1:50 000 means 1 cm on the map represents 50 000 cm, or 0.5 km. Use Pythagoras or trigonometry to find distances where a direct measurement is not possible.

Loci

The locus of points at a fixed distance from a point is a circle. Points equidistant from two points lie on the perpendicular bisector of the line joining them. Points equidistant from two lines lie on an angle bisector. Shade a region by combining the loci and stating the condition clearly.

title: Database Systems — Study Notes
content:
Database Systems

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2023–2025): limitations of file-based systems; relational concepts; SQL (SELECT, FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY, INNER JOIN, SUM, COUNT); DBMS features.

1. File-based problems

Data repetition (wasted space, inconsistency), fixed queries, no concurrent access control — solved by a DBMS with shared, structured tables.

2. Relational concepts

  • Table, record, field; primary key (unique); secondary key (indexed search field); foreign key links tables.
  • One-to-many relationships via foreign keys; no repeating groups (1NF mindset).

3. SQL

SELECT Title, Year FROM Films
WHERE Genre = 'Sci-Fi' AND Year > 2015
ORDER BY Year DESC;

SELECT Genre, COUNT(*) AS NumFilms, SUM(Rating) AS TotalRating
FROM Films
GROUP BY Genre;

SELECT s.Name, f.Title
FROM Students s INNER JOIN Loans l ON s.StudentID = l.StudentID
INNER JOIN Films f ON l.FilmID = f.FilmID;

WHERE filters rows; GROUP BY aggregates; JOIN combines on matching keys.

4. DBMS features

Data dictionary (schema, types, constraints), query processor, forms/reports, access rights (read/write per user), data integrity (validation rules), backup/recovery.

Exam tips: write SQL keywords uppercase; alias joined tables (s, l, f); when asked "why relational", cite reduced redundancy + flexible queries.

title: AS Level Mathematics: Mechanics M1 — Kinematics, Dynamics and Statics
content:
AS Level Mathematics: Mechanics M1 — Kinematics, Dynamics and Statics

Mechanics describes motion and the forces causing it. M1 covers three linked strands: kinematics (describing motion with graphs and the constant-acceleration equations), dynamics (Newton's second law applied to single particles and connected bodies), and statics (equilibrium of a particle and moments of forces). This note builds each from zero, with the modelling assumptions stated, the sign conventions fixed, and worked examples written out line by line — because in mechanics the marks are in the diagram and the equation, not the answer.

Modelling assumptions and units

standard assumptions unless told otherwise:
  the object is a particle (no size, no rotation)
  air resistance is negligible
  the string is light and inextensible; the pulley is smooth
  g = 9.8 m s⁻² (use 9.81 if the question says so)

State the assumption when you use it: "modelling the stone as a particle, so air resistance is ignored". Marks are awarded for identifying what the model simplifies.

Kinematics: the constant-acceleration equations

v = u + at
s = ut + (1/2) a t²
v² = u² + 2as
s = ((u + v)/2) t

u initial velocity, v final velocity, a acceleration,
s displacement, t time

The equations hold only for constant acceleration. Choose the equation by listing what you know and what you want: exactly one equation omits the quantity you neither know nor need.

Worked example 1. A car accelerates uniformly from 8 m/s to 20 m/s in 6 s. Find the acceleration and the distance.

a = (v - u)/t = (20 - 8)/6 = 2 m/s²
s = ((u + v)/2)t = 14 × 6 = 84 m

Worked example 2 (falling). A stone is dropped from rest from a cliff and takes 3 s to land. Find the height, taking g = 9.8.

u = 0, a = 9.8 (downward positive), t = 3
s = 0 + (1/2)(9.8)(9) = 44.1 m

Worked example 3 (upward). A ball is thrown vertically upwards at 15 m/s. Find the maximum height and the total time in the air.

at the top v = 0: 0 = 225 - 2(9.8)s  →  s = 11.48 m
time up: 0 = 15 - 9.8t  →  t = 1.53 s
total time = 3.06 s (symmetric flight)

Fix the positive direction before substituting. Upward-positive makes g = −9.8; the alternative is consistent arithmetic but must not be mixed mid-question.

Velocity-time and displacement-time graphs

displacement-time: gradient = velocity
velocity-time: gradient = acceleration; area = displacement
speed-time: area = distance

Worked example. A cyclist accelerates from rest to 12 m/s in 5 s, travels at 12 m/s for 10 s, then decelerates to rest in 4 s. Find the total distance.

area 1: (1/2)(5)(12) = 30
area 2: 12 × 10 = 120
area 3: (1/2)(4)(12) = 24
total = 174 m

Area below the time axis is negative displacement: the particle has reversed direction, and distance sums the magnitudes.

Newton's second law and forces

resultant force F = m a
weight W = m g
friction opposes motion: F <= mu R (limiting case F = mu R)
normal reaction R acts perpendicular to the surface

Worked example 1 (horizontal). A 5 kg box is pushed with 30 N along a rough floor with friction 8 N. Find the acceleration.

resultant = 30 - 8 = 22 N
a = 22/5 = 4.4 m/s²

Worked example 2 (on a slope). A 4 kg particle slides down a smooth slope inclined at 30°. Find its acceleration.

component of weight along the slope = 4g sin 30 = 19.6 N
a = 19.6/4 = 4.9 m/s²  (= g sin 30)

Worked example 3 (with friction on a slope). Same slope, friction 6 N.

resultant = 19.6 - 6 = 13.6 N
a = 3.4 m/s²

Connected particles

Two bodies joined by a string have the same magnitude of acceleration (the string is inextensible) and the same tension throughout (the string is light and the pulley smooth). Write one equation per body and add them to eliminate T.

Worked example (pulley). Masses 5 kg and 3 kg hang either side of a smooth pulley. Find the acceleration and the tension.

for 5 kg (downward positive): 5g - T = 5a
for 3 kg (upward positive):   T - 3g = 3a
add: 2g = 8a  →  a = 2.45 m/s²
T = 3(g + a) = 3(9.8 + 2.45) = 36.75 N

Worked example 2 (on a table). A 4 kg block on a smooth table is connected over a pulley to a 2 kg hanging mass. Find the acceleration.

hanging mass: 2g - T = 2a
block: T = 4a
add: 2g = 6a  →  a = 3.27 m/s²

Worked example 3 (lift). A 60 kg person stands in a lift accelerating upward at 2 m/s². Find the reaction force.

R - 60g = 60(2)  →  R = 60(11.8) = 708 N
the person feels heavier; in free fall R would be zero

Statics: equilibrium of a particle

equilibrium: the resultant force is zero
resolve horizontally and vertically, or along and perpendicular to
a slope, and set each total to zero

Worked example. A 10 N weight hangs from two strings making 40° and 50° with the horizontal. Find the tensions.

horizontal: T¹ cos 40 = T² cos 50
vertical: T¹ sin 40 + T² sin 50 = 10
from the first: T² = T¹ cos40/cos50 = 1.1918 T¹
T¹(0.6428) + 1.1918 T¹(0.7660) = 10
T¹(0.6428 + 0.9129) = 10  →  T¹ = 6.43 N, T² = 7.66 N

Moments

moment = force x perpendicular distance from the pivot
for equilibrium of a rigid body: sum of clockwise moments = sum of
anticlockwise moments

Worked example. A uniform plank 4 m long of weight 200 N rests on two supports 1 m from each end. A 300 N load is placed 0.5 m from the left end. Find the reactions.

supports at 1 m and 3 m from the left; load at 0.5 m
moments about the left support:
  load: 300 × 0.5 = 150 anticlockwise
  weight: 200 × 1 = 200 clockwise (weight acts at the centre, 2 m)
  right reaction R2 at 2 m: clockwise
  150 = 200 + 2 R2  →  R2 = -25 N, so the plank would tip
check total: R1 + R2 = 500 needed; with R2 negative the support
cannot hold, so the load must be moved inward - a tipping question

Moments about a support is the standard trick: it eliminates that support's reaction, leaving one unknown. If the required reaction is negative, the body is not in equilibrium and tipping is the intended conclusion.

Friction and limiting equilibrium

Friction is a variable force: it takes whatever value is needed to prevent motion, up to a maximum. Only at the point of slipping does it reach its limiting value.

F <= mu R  on a rough surface
limiting friction: F = mu R   (on the point of moving)
R is found by resolving perpendicular to the surface

Worked example 1 (horizontal, limiting). A 10 kg block rests on a rough horizontal floor with mu = 0.4. Find the smallest horizontal force needed to move it.

R = 10g = 98 N
limiting friction = 0.4 × 98 = 39.2 N
so a force just above 39.2 N starts it moving

Worked example 2 (slope). A block sits on a rough slope inclined at 25° with mu = 0.5. Does it slide?

component down the slope: mg sin 25 = 0.4226 mg
maximum friction: mu mg cos 25 = 0.5 × 0.9063 mg = 0.4531 mg
maximum friction exceeds the driving component, so it stays at rest
and friction takes the value 0.4226 mg

The comparison is the answer: if mu >= tan θ the particle remains in equilibrium on the slope, because the friction ceiling covers the driving component. That inequality is a standard exam demand.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (suvat) u = 4, a = 3, t = 5. Find s. Answer: 20 + 37.5 = 57.5 m.
  2. (suvat) u = 10, v = 30, s = 100. Find a. Answer: 900 = 100 + 200a → a = 4 m/s².
  3. (graph) A v–t graph rises 0 to 20 m/s in 4 s, then falls to 0 in 2 s. Distance? Answer: 40 + 20 = 60 m.
  4. (F = ma) 12 kg, resultant 36 N. Find a. Answer: 3 m/s².
  5. (slope) Smooth slope at 20°, mass 5 kg. Find a. Answer: g sin 20 = 3.35 m/s².
  6. (pulley) 6 kg and 4 kg over a smooth pulley. Find a. Answer: 2g = 10a → 1.96 m/s².
  7. (tension) For that pulley, find T. Answer: T = 4(9.8 + 1.96) = 47.0 N.
  8. (moments) A 2 m lever with a 50 N force at 1.5 m from the pivot balances a force F at 0.5 m. Find F. Answer: 50 × 1.5 = 0.5F → F = 150 N.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • No diagram: draw the forces before writing equations; nearly every mechanics error is a missing or misdirected force.
  • Sign convention drift: fix positive direction once and keep it; a sign flip mid-question produces a wrong acceleration.
  • Using suvat with varying acceleration: the equations need constant a; if a changes, split into stages or use a graph.
  • Forgetting weight on a slope: the component along the slope is mg sin θ; the perpendicular component mg cos θ is balanced by the reaction on a smooth slope.
  • Tension assumed equal to weight: in an accelerating system T ≠ mg; solve the equations.
  • Adding instead of eliminating T: write one equation per body with consistent directions, then add to cancel T.
  • Moments with the wrong distance: the perpendicular distance from the pivot, not the distance along the rod.
  • Units and g: use the g the question gives; mixing 9.8 and 9.81 changes answers at the third figure.

Formula summary

v = u + at;  s = ut + at²/2;  v² = u² + 2as;  s = (u + v)t/2
F = ma;  W = mg;  F = mu R at limiting friction
moment = force x perpendicular distance

Every M1 calculation begins with a diagram showing the forces, the chosen positive direction and the known quantities. The formula is the last step; the model is the first.

title: Materials: Deformation
content:
Materials: Deformation

Hooke's Law

Up to the limit of proportionality, F = kx — extension is proportional to load. k is the spring constant (N m⁻¹).

Springs in series share the load (k_total < each); in parallel, k_total adds.

Stress, Strain, Young Modulus

  • Stress σ = F/A (Pa)
  • Strain ε = x/L (no unit)
  • Young modulus E = σ/ε (Pa) — a material property, independent of shape

Example: a wire of length 2 m, cross-section 1 × 10⁻⁶ m², extends 1 mm under 100 N: E = (F/A)/(x/L) = (10⁸)/(5 × 10⁻⁴) = 2 × 10¹¹ Pa — steel-like.

Force–Extension Graphs

  • Gradient of the linear region = k
  • Area under graph = elastic PE stored = ½Fx (for linear) = ½kx²
  • Beyond the yield point the wire deforms plastically and will not return

Breaking Stress

The maximum stress a material withstands — strong materials have high breaking stress, stiff materials have high E.

Exam tips: convert mm to m and mm² to m² before substituting; the area under a stress–strain graph gives energy per unit volume.

title: AS Level Physics: Dynamics
content:
AS Level Physics: Dynamics

Edexcel International A Level Physics, Unit 1 (WPH11) Mechanics and Materials — Newton's laws of motion, the conservation of linear momentum, and the behaviour of objects moving through fluids (density, upthrust, viscous drag and terminal velocity). Dynamics answers the question kinematics asks: what makes motion change? The laws are three sentences long and everything else in the unit is their application, so they must be known exactly — including the conditions under which momentum is conserved.

Force and Newton's laws of motion

A force is a push or a pull, measured in newtons (N), and it is a vector. Forces change velocity (they accelerate masses) or change shape. The three laws, in their examinable form:

  • Newton's first law: a body remains at rest or moves with constant velocity in a straight line unless acted on by a resultant external force. It defines inertia — the reluctance of mass to change its state of motion.
  • Newton's second law: the resultant force on a body equals the rate of change of its momentum, in the direction of that force. For constant mass this reduces to F = ma.
  • Newton's third law: when body A exerts a force on body B, body B exerts an equal and opposite force on A. The pair acts on different bodies, always along the same line, and is always the same type of force (gravavitational on gravitational, contact on contact).
resultant force = mass x acceleration        F = m a
  • F: resultant force in newtons (N); m: mass in kilograms (kg); a: acceleration in metres per second squared (m s⁻²). Acceleration is in the direction of the resultant force.

Free-body diagrams are the first mark of nearly every dynamics answer: draw one body, with every force acting on it as an arrow from its centre, labelled (weight, normal reaction, tension, friction, drag, thrust). Resolve the forces along and perpendicular to the direction of motion, apply F = ma along the motion, and use equilibrium (zero resultant) perpendicular to it.

Mass is the quantity of matter and is constant; weight is the gravitational force on that mass, W = mg, and varies with location. The third law pair to an object's weight is the gravitational pull of the object on the Earth — not the normal contact force of the table beneath it.

Momentum and its conservation

Momentum is the product of mass and velocity:

momentum = mass x velocity        p = m v
  • p: momentum in kilogram metres per second (kg m s⁻¹). Momentum is a vector, in the direction of velocity; with a stated sign convention, momenta in opposite directions carry opposite signs.
  • Newton's second law in full form: F = (mv − mu)/t, the rate of change of momentum.

The principle of conservation of linear momentum: when no external resultant force acts on a system, the total momentum of that system remains constant. Collisions, explosions and recoil problems all reduce to one equation: total momentum before = total momentum after, summed as vectors. The condition matters — a ball bouncing off a floor is not momentum-conserving for the ball alone, because the Earth supplies an external force during the bounce.

impulse = change in momentum = force x time        F t = m v - m u
  • Impulse is measured in newton seconds (N s), numerically equal to the momentum change. A force–time graph has an area equal to the impulse; extending the time of impact reduces the peak force for the same impulse — crumple zones, air bags, landing on a bent knee.

Elastic and inelastic collisions

Momentum is conserved in every collision (in an isolated system); kinetic energy is not. A collision is elastic when the total kinetic energy is conserved — idealised gas molecules, and perfectly elastic springs. It is inelastic when kinetic energy is lost to deformation, heat and sound; a collision in which the bodies stick together is completely inelastic, and that is the case where the kinetic energy loss is greatest. Explosions convert stored energy (chemical or elastic) into kinetic energy of the fragments, so the total momentum is conserved while the kinetic energy increases.

Equilibrium and connected bodies

A body is in equilibrium when the resultant force and the resultant moment on it are both zero: it is either at rest or moving with constant velocity. The method is always the same — draw the free-body diagram, resolve along and across the direction of motion, and set the resultant to zero in each direction. For a mass hanging from a string, the tension equals the weight; for a block resting on a slope, the weight resolves into mg sin θ down the slope and mg cos θ into the slope, and the normal reaction balances the latter while friction can balance the former.

Friction acts parallel to a surface and opposes the motion or the tendency to move. The maximum frictional force before slipping is proportional to the normal contact force: F(friction) = mu R, where mu is the coefficient of friction (dimensionless) and R is the normal reaction in newtons. Static friction below that maximum simply matches the applied force, which is why a block on a gentle slope stays put.

Connected bodies share one acceleration, so the fastest method treats the system as a whole first and then separates it. Two masses (3.0 kg and 2.0 kg) joined by a light string over a frictionless pulley accelerate together: the resultant force on the system is the difference in weights, 1.0g, so a = 1.0g/5.0 = 1.96 m s⁻². Cutting the system then gives the tension in the string: for the 3.0 kg mass, 3.0g − T = 3.0a, so T = 23.5 N. The same two answers must hold whichever mass is isolated — a built-in check on the arithmetic.

Fluids: density, upthrust and viscous drag

A fluid is a liquid or a gas, and objects moving through fluids experience forces that solids never show. Density is mass per unit volume, ρ = m/V (kg m⁻³). An object immersed in a fluid is pushed up by an upthrust equal to the weight of fluid displaced (Archimedes' principle), so an object denser than the fluid sinks and one less dense floats; a floating object displaces its own weight of fluid.

Viscous drag is the friction within a fluid: layers of fluid slide over each other and over the object, and the drag grows with speed, viscosity and size. For a small sphere falling slowly through a viscous fluid, Stokes' law gives the drag:

viscous drag = 6 π x viscosity x radius x speed        F = 6 π eta r v
  • F: drag force in newtons (N); eta: viscosity of the fluid in pascal seconds (Pa s); r: radius of the sphere in metres (m); v: speed in metres per second (m s⁻¹). The force acts opposite to the direction of motion.

A falling sphere accelerates until drag + upthrust = weight, and then falls at terminal velocity, which from Stokes' law is v = 2r²(ρ − σ)g/(9η) for a sphere of density ρ in a fluid of density σ. Terminal velocity is reached quickly for small dense spheres in viscous fluids — the principle of the falling-ball viscometer, one of the unit's core practicals. At low speeds the flow around a sphere is smooth and layered (laminar); above a critical speed it becomes chaotic (turbulent), and the drag then rises more steeply with speed. Streamlining delays the onset of turbulence, which is why a golf ball has dimples and a car is shaped the way it is.

Worked example: collision and impulse

A 1200 kg car travelling at 20 m s⁻¹ collides with a stationary 900 kg car and they move together. Find their common velocity and the energy lost.

momentum before = 1200 × 20 = 24 000 kg m s⁻¹
common velocity = 24 000 / (1200 + 900) = 11.4 m s⁻¹
KE before = 1/2 × 1200 × 20² = 240 000 J
KE after = 1/2 × 2100 × 11.4² = 136 000 J
energy lost = 104 000 J (to deformation, heat and sound)

Momentum is conserved; kinetic energy is not — the collision is inelastic. Second stage: if the impact lasts 0.15 s, the average force on the stationary car is F = mv/t = 900 × 11.4 / 0.15 = 68 400 N, and lengthening the impact with a crumple zone would cut that force sharply.

Common mistakes

  • Using F = ma with one force instead of the resultant; draw the free-body diagram and resolve first.
  • Writing third-law pairs that act on the same body (they never do) or that are different kinds of force.
  • Ignoring direction in momentum problems; a rebound reverses the velocity sign and the total is a vector sum.
  • Assuming kinetic energy is conserved in every collision; only elastic collisions conserve it, and sticking collisions lose the most.
  • Forgetting upthrust when a body moves through a fluid: terminal velocity is reached when drag + upthrust = weight, not when drag = weight, if the fluid's density is not negligible.
  • Using Stokes' law outside its conditions — it assumes laminar flow, slow speeds and a spherical object.
  • Confusing mass and weight in W = mg, or using g in m s⁻² when the question gives g in N kg⁻¹ (numerically equal but state your units).
  • Quoting an impulse as a force: impulse is N s and equals the momentum change; the force depends on the impact time.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (WPH11, 3 marks). A 4.0 kg trolley on a frictionless runway is pulled by a 12 N force. Calculate its acceleration and the distance travelled in 3.0 s from rest.

Answer: a = F/m = 12/4.0 = 3.0 m s⁻². s = ½at² = ½ × 3.0 × 9.0 = 13.5 m ≈ 14 m.

Question 2 (WPH11, 4 marks). A 60 g ball moving at 5.0 m s⁻¹ hits a wall at right angles and rebounds at 3.0 m s⁻¹. The contact lasts 0.020 s. Calculate the average force.

Answer: Taking the initial direction as positive, Δp = 0.060(−3.0) − 0.060(5.0) = −0.48 kg m s⁻¹. Force = Δp/t = −0.48/0.020 = −24 N, i.e. 24 N opposite to the initial motion.

Question 3 (WPH11, 4 marks). Two ice skaters push apart. Skater A (60 kg) moves at 3.0 m s⁻¹. Find the velocity of skater B (75 kg) and explain which principle you used.

Answer: Total momentum before = 0, so 60 × 3.0 + 75 × v = 0 and v = −2.4 m s⁻¹: B moves at 2.4 m s⁻¹ in the opposite direction. The conservation of linear momentum applies because the push is an internal force; the ice's friction is negligible during the push.

Question 4 (WPH11, 3 marks). Explain why a small steel ball bearing falling through glycerine reaches terminal velocity, and state the forces acting at that moment.

Answer: As the ball accelerates, the viscous drag rises with speed (F = 6πηrv). The resultant force is weight minus drag minus upthrust, so the acceleration falls as speed rises. When drag + upthrust equals the weight the resultant force is zero and the ball continues at constant terminal velocity, acted on by three balanced forces: weight down, upthrust and drag up.

Question 5 (WPH13, 3 marks). Describe how you would determine the viscosity of a liquid using a falling-ball method.

Answer: Drop a small steel sphere (radius measured with a micrometer) into a wide measuring cylinder of the liquid and time its fall between two marked lines, where it is already at terminal velocity. Repeat and average the times; calculate v = distance/time. At terminal velocity, 6πηrv = (4/3)πr³(ρ − σ)g, so η = 2r²(ρ − σ)g/(9v). Keep the temperature constant (viscosity depends strongly on it) and use a cylinder at least ten sphere diameters wide to avoid wall effects.

Question 6 (WPH11, 3 marks). A 1500 kg car hits a crash barrier at 15 m s⁻¹ and stops in 0.30 s. Calculate the average force on the car and state one safety feature that reduces this force.

Answer: F = mv/t = 1500 × 15 / 0.30 = 75 000 N = 75 kN. A crumple zone extends the impact time, and for the same momentum change the force falls in proportion to the time.

Forces also change shape — the subject of Materials and Deformation.

title: Mechanics (M1) — Study Notes
content:
Mechanics 1: forces and motion

Edexcel International A Level Mathematics — Mechanics 1 (WME01), sat at AS.

M1 models particles under constant acceleration and in equilibrium. The whole subject rests on three pillars: the SUVAT equations, Newton's laws, and the turning-effect (moments) of forces.

Kinematics (constant acceleration)

  • v = u + at
  • s = ut + (1/2)at^2
  • v^2 = u^2 + 2as
  • s = (u + v)t / 2
  • A displacement-time graph has gradient = velocity; a velocity-time graph has gradient = acceleration and area = displacement.
  • Free fall: a = g = 9.8 m/s^2 downwards; a ball thrown up decelerates at g on the way up.

Dynamics: Newton's laws

  • First law: a body stays at rest or constant velocity unless a resultant force acts.
  • Second law: F = ma, where F is the resultant force on the particle.
  • Third law: every action has an equal and opposite reaction, acting on DIFFERENT bodies.
  • Weight = mg, acting vertically downwards through the centre of mass.

Connected particles

Treat the system as one body first (F = total mass x a) to find the acceleration, then isolate one particle to find the connecting force (tension in a string, thrust in a tow bar).

Forces at angles

Resolve horizontally and vertically: a force F at angle theta to the horizontal has components F cos(theta) and F sin(theta). Equilibrium means the resultant force in each direction is zero.

Friction

  • F <= mu R, with limiting friction F = mu R when the body is on the point of slipping.
  • Friction opposes motion (or the tendency to motion) and acts along the surface.
  • On a rough inclined plane: R = mg cos(theta) and the component down the plane is mg sin(theta).

Moments

  • Moment of a force = force x perpendicular distance from the pivot.
  • A rigid body in equilibrium has zero resultant force AND zero total moment about any point.
  • Uniform beams have their weight acting at the mid-point.

Quick revision: Differentiation II

Mathematics — A2 (9709). Example: y = x² e^x gives dy/dx = 2x e^x + x² e^x = e^x(2x + x²).

### Worked example Use the chain rule for composite functions. For y = (x² + 1)³, dy/dx = 3(x² + 1)² × 2x = 6x(x² + 1)². At x = 1 this is 6 × 1 × 4 = 24. Check using the derivative of the outer function at the inner value: 3 × 2² × 2 = 24. The product rule gives d/dx(x sin x) = sin x + x cos x.

title: Exam technique: Logic Gates & Boolean Logic
content:
### What earns the marks
For truth tables, every row completed correctly earns stepwise credit. For circuits, each gate output labelled earns one mark before the final column. For expressions, brackets showing the gate order earn the method mark.
### Traps
Error: NAND confused with AND plus NOT placed wrongly. Correction: NAND inverts the AND output. Error: half-filled tables guessed. Correction: list all input combinations. Error: XOR read as OR. Correction: XOR excludes both-1.

title:
Plant Structure and Function, Biodiversity and Conservation — Quick Revision Summary

Biology — AS Edexcel IAL, WBI12 Unit 1 Topic 4. Plant cell ultrastructure and the functions of the organelles and cell wall components (cell wall, chloroplasts, amyloplasts, vacuole and tonoplast, plasmodesmata, pits, middle lamella); starch and cellulose and why their structure fits storage and strength; how cellulose microfibril arrangement and secondary thickening give physical properties to xylem and sclerenchyma; the similarities and differences in structure, position and function of sclerenchyma fibres (support, dead, lignified), xylem vessels (support and water/mineral transport, dead, lignified, open tube) and phloem (translocation of organic solutes, living sieve tubes with companion cells, perforated walls); Core Practical 7 transverse sections; the uses of plant fibres and starch in sustainability as replacements for oil-based plastics; water and mineral ions to plants and Core Practical 8 the tensile strength of plant fibres; the conditions for bacterial growth and the aseptic practical on antimicrobial plant substances and zones of inhibition; drug testing from Withering's digitalis to modern double-blind placebo-controlled trials; classification and the species concept and the three-domain system from molecular evidence; biodiversity and endemism and how they are threatened by human activity; biodiversity measurements (species richness, heterozygosity index = heterozygotes/total, and the index of diversity D = N(N−1)/Σ n(n−1)) and comparing habitats; and the niche and behavioural, anatomical and physiological adaptations.

  • 4.1 Plant cell ultrastructure: cell wall (cellulose microfibrils in a gel matrix — shape, support, prevents bursting when turgid), chloroplast (double membrane, chlorophyll, thylakoid/grana for light reactions, stroma for light-independent reactions), amyloplast (colourless plastid, stores starch), vacuole + tonoplast (large central vacuole with cell sap, turgor and rigidity), plasmodesmata (channels through walls connecting adjacent cells' cytoplasm), pits (thin regions allowing water/solutes between cells), middle lamella (cements adjacent walls). Ribosomes, nucleus, nucleolus, mitochondria and golgi are present as in animal cells; higher plants lack centrioles.
  • 4.2 EM recognition: recognise plasma membrane, nucleus and nucleolus, chloroplasts (with stacked grana), mitochondria, rER with ribosomes, golgi (dictyosomes), large central vacuole with tonoplast, cell wall and middle lamella, and plasmodesmata; distinguish plant from animal cells (plant has cell wall, chloroplasts, large central vacuole, plasmodesmata, generally no centrioles).
  • 4.3 Starch and cellulose: starch = alpha-glucose polymer (amylose helical, amylopectin branched — compact, insoluble, osmotically inert, good for storage); cellulose = beta-glucose polymer (straight chains, hydrogen bonds between chains make strong microfibrils — structural); both from glucose but different bonds and shape give different roles.
  • 4.4 Microfibrils and secondary thickening: in growing cells microfibrils laid down at right angles to growth direction so the cell expands in length; when growth stops, secondary thickening deposits more cellulose and (in some cells) lignin on the inside, making the wall rigid and waterproof; in sclerenchyma fibres the walls are heavily lignified and the cells die at maturity — strong, flexible, tough — for support and human use; in xylem vessels the walls are lignified with rings, spirals or nets, and the cells are dead with end walls broken down — a continuous tube that resists collapse under transpiration tension.
  • 4.5 Fibres, xylem and phloem: sclerenchyma fibres — long, narrow, thick lignified walls, small lumen, dead, bundles — support and human use; xylem vessels — long open lignified tubes, dead, pits in walls — water and mineral transport plus support; phloem — living sieve tube elements end to end with sieve plates (perforated end walls), little cytoplasm, no nucleus at maturity, each with a companion cell connected by plasmodesmata that keeps it alive and supplies ATP — translocation of sucrose in solution from source (leaves/storage) to sink (growing points, roots, fruits).
  • 4.6 Core Practical 7: cut a thin transverse section with a razor blade, float on water, stain (toluidine blue or iodine) to distinguish lignified xylem, sclerenchyma and phloem, draw a plan diagram of the whole section showing tissue arrangement (not cells), label, title and magnification; then observe and label the cells — thick lignified xylem and sclerenchyma walls, sieve plates and companion cells of phloem, thin-walled cortex and pith cells.
  • 4.7 Plant fibres and starch for sustainability: plant fibres (from sclerenchyma or phloem) are strong, renewable, biodegradable — used in textiles, paper, building materials, composites, replacing oil-based plastics; starch can be processed into bioplastics for packaging, plates and disposable items — renewable and biodegradable, but land, water, energy and food competition must be weighed.
  • 4.8 Water and ions to plants: water for photosynthesis (reactant, medium), transport (solvent), support (turgor) and cooling (transpiration) — enters roots by osmosis, moves up the xylem; nitrate (NO₃⁻) for amino acids, proteins, DNA, chlorophyll — deficiency causes stunted growth and chlorosis of older leaves; calcium for middle lamella and membranes — deficiency gives stunted growth and necrosis of growing points and young leaves; magnesium for chlorophyll — deficiency causes chlorosis of older leaves; Core Practical: grow plants in complete solution and in solutions missing one ion, observe and measure effects over weeks.
  • 4.9 Core Practical 8: tensile strength of a plant fibre — clamp one end, hang weights from the other, add until it breaks, record the weight (force = mass × g) at breaking; repeat for several fibres; compare fibres from different plants or parts; safety: sharp blades, falling weights.
  • 4.10 Bacterial growth conditions: nutrients (carbon, nitrogen, minerals, and for some organic factors), water, suitable temperature (many pathogenic bacteria ~37 °C, many environmental ~25 °C, but ranges vary), oxygen (aerobic, anaerobic, or facultative), suitable pH, time to multiply; cultured in nutrient broth or on agar, at a set temperature, with or without oxygen, in sterile conditions; aseptic technique: sterilise equipment (flame/autoclave), work near a flame for upward air current, cover plates, dispose of cultures by sterilising first.
  • 4.11 Antimicrobial plant substances: substances from plants (e.g. garlic) can inhibit bacteria or fungi; other plants yield useful compounds (aspirin from willow bark, morphine from poppies); modern drugs include many from plants; Core Practical: agar plates, sterile discs or paper discs impregnated with different plant extracts, incubate, measure the zone of inhibition (clear diameter where bacteria did not grow), compare extracts and concentrations; aseptic technique: sterilise discs and loops, work near a flame, spread bacteria in a controlled way, seal plates with tape (not all the way — keep them aerated), incubate at a safe temperature.

Worked example

Index of diversity: in habitat A species counts are 12, 8, 4 (N = 24). Σn(n−1) = (12×11) + (8×7) + (4×3) = 132 + 56 + 12 = 200; N(N−1) = 24×23 = 552; D = 552/200 = 2.76. In habitat B species counts are 20, 1, 1, 1, 1 (N = 24). Σn(n−1) = (20×19) + 4×(1×0) = 380 + 0 = 380; N(N−1) = 552; D = 552/380 = 1.45. So habitat A is more diverse than habitat B — even though both have four species and the same total — because in B one species dominates and the others are rare.

Key points to remember

The structure that makes a plant cell rigid is the cell wall, the large central vacuole and turgor, and the arrangement of cellulose microfibrils; the organelle with stacked membranes for photosynthesis is the chloroplast (grana in the thylakoids, stroma around them); starch stores glucose compactly and insoluble so no osmotic effect; cellulose's straight beta-glucose chains form hydrogen-bonded microfibrils, strong and supportive; secondary thickening and lignification stiffen walls for support and for the xylem to resist tension; xylem transports water and minerals and supports, phloem translocates sucrose from source to sink; water is essential for photosynthesis, transport, support (turgor) and cooling; nitrate, calcium and magnesium each have a specific role and deficiency gives characteristic symptoms; antibiotic plant substances and the aseptic practical involve zones of inhibition; drug testing progressed from uncontrolled historic trials to double-blind, placebo-controlled, phased, large multi-centre trials; classification is based on relationships using phenotypic and (increasingly) genotypic data, the species concept is a group that can interbreed and produce fertile offspring, and the three-domain system (Archaea, Bacteria, Eukarya) came from molecular evidence (ribosomal RNA); biodiversity is the variety of life, endemism is being restricted to one place, human activity threatens it; biodiversity is measured by species richness, heterozygosity (heterozygotes/total) and the index of diversity D = N(N−1)/Σ n(n−1); the niche is the organism's role and its adaptations can be behavioural, anatomical or physiological.

Key points to remember

In the heterozygosity index, if a population of 20 individuals at a locus has 8 heterozygotes, H = 8/20 = 0.40, so the higher the number the greater the genetic diversity; in the index of diversity D = N(N−1)/Σ n(n−1), the larger D the more diverse, and the comparison between habitats means you calculate D for each and compare the values, explaining which is more diverse and what that suggests. Distinguish species richness (the number of species) from the index of diversity (which also reflects how even the individuals are among species). In drug testing, the placebo controls for the placebo effect, double-blind avoids bias from patient and clinician expectations, and the phases test safety (Phase 1), efficacy and side effects (Phase 2), and the drug against current treatment or placebo in a large group (Phase 3). The bacteriophage does not belong here — the antimicrobials come from plants, not from viruses; keep plant antimicrobial substances separate from the unrelated concept. The distinction between the habitat (the place) and the niche (the role and resources) is often asked — an organism's niche is more than where it lives.

How to use this

Read the summary list, then open the full revision notes for any point that feels weak, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself. Revise next by: identifying plant cell ultrastructure and organelles in an EM image and stating each organelle's function; drawing starch and cellulose and explaining the structure–function link; comparing sclerenchyma fibres, xylem vessels and phloem in a table (structure, position, function); carrying out the transverse section and tensile strength practicals and explaining the variables and safety; describing the conditions for bacterial growth and the aseptic practical; describing the development of drug testing from Withering's digitalis to modern trials and evaluating the designs; defining classification and the species concept, describing the three-domain system and the molecular evidence for it; defining biodiversity and endemism and listing the threats; carrying out the species richness and heterozygosity and index of diversity calculations including the worked comparison between habitats; and defining niche and giving behavioural, anatomical and physiological adaptations.
