title: Logic Gates & Boolean Logic — Study Notes
content:
Logic Gates & Boolean Logic

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): six gates, truth tables, building/describing circuits, problem-to-logic mapping.

1. The six gates

ABANDORNANDNORXOR
0000110
0101101
1001101
1111000

NOT inverts. NAND = AND + invert; NOR = OR + invert; XOR = 1 when inputs differ.

2. Truth tables

2 inputs → 4 rows; 3 inputs → 8 rows. Work gate by gate, adding intermediate columns for sub-circuit outputs.

3. Logic expressions

A Boolean expression describes a circuit in logic: X = A AND NOT B, or X = (A OR B) AND C. Brackets fix the order — work out bracketed parts first, then AND, then OR.

  • Circuit → expression: label the output of every gate (P, Q, …), write one expression per gate in order, then combine them at the final gate.
  • Truth table → expression: mark the rows where the output is 1; for each such row write a term that is true only in that row (write NOT for an input that is 0, AND between the inputs); join the terms with OR. For XOR: X = (NOT A AND B) OR (A AND NOT B).
  • Expression → truth table: add an intermediate column for each sub-expression before the output column.
  • Rules used to simplify: A AND 1 = A; A AND 0 = 0; A OR 1 = 1; A OR 0 = A; A AND A = A; A AND NOT A = 0; A OR NOT A = 1; NOT(NOT A) = A; X OR (X AND Y) = X. (AS extension, 9618: De Morgan's laws — NOT(A AND B) = NOT A OR NOT B and NOT(A OR B) = NOT A AND NOT B.)

Example: a light X is on only when switch A is on and switch B is off → X = A AND NOT B, so X = 1 in exactly one row of its truth table (A = 1, B = 0).

4. Problem → logic

Define inputs/outputs first. Alarm rings (X=1) if sensor P triggered AND (door D OR window W): X = P AND (D OR W). Then draw the circuit: OR first, then AND.

5. Describing circuits

Write the expression from a diagram gate by gate; annotate output of each gate (X, Y) before combining.

Exam tips: check your truth table row count before writing; in problem questions, state "input P = 1 means sensor triggered" — definitions earn marks.

title: IGCSE Physics: Thermal Physics
content:
IGCSE Physics: Thermal Physics

Cambridge IGCSE Physics 0625 (2026–2028), Topic 2 Thermal physics: statements 2.1 Kinetic particle model of matter, 2.2 Thermal properties and temperature, and 2.3 Transfer of thermal energy. Heat is the traffic of energy between hot and cold objects, and the particle model explains every thermal phenomenon in the syllabus: expansion, pressure, changes of state, conduction, convection and radiation. Paper 4 loves the particle explanations as much as the calculations, so both are built here from the same model.

States of matter and changes of state

All matter is made of tiny particles in constant motion, and the three states differ in how those particles are arranged and how they move.

StateArrangementMotionShape and volume
SolidClose-packed regular rows, touchingVibrate about fixed positionsFixed shape and fixed volume
LiquidClose together but disorderedSlide over each otherTakes the shape of the container; fixed volume
GasFar apart, random, filling the containerFast, random, straight-line between collisionsNo fixed shape or volume

When a substance is heated, energy is transferred to its thermal store and the particles move faster. On a heating curve the temperature rises until a change of state begins; during melting or boiling the temperature stays constant while the energy goes into breaking the forces between particles rather than into speed. The names of the changes are: melting (solid to liquid), freezing (liquid to solid), boiling or vaporisation (liquid to gas), condensation (gas to liquid), sublimation (solid straight to gas, as with dry ice).

The particle model of pressure and Brownian motion

Gas pressure arises because particles collide with the walls of their container: each collision gives a tiny push, and billions of pushes per second produce a steady pressure. Squeezing the same particles into a smaller volume raises the collision rate per unit area and so raises the pressure; heating a gas at fixed volume makes the particles move faster and collide harder and more often, again raising the pressure.

Brownian motion is the random jiggling of smoke particles seen under a microscope. The smoke particles are bombarded unevenly by fast-moving invisible air molecules, and the bigger the imbalance of hits at any instant, the bigger the lurch. It is direct evidence that gas particles move randomly and continuously (Supplement: the uneven collisions and their random distribution are the explanation demanded).

The gas laws and the absolute scale of temperature

For a fixed mass of gas, three qualitative rules are examined at Core level: heating a gas at constant pressure makes it expand (and cooling makes it contract); compressing a gas at constant temperature raises its pressure; and the relationships are summarised by the particle model above. The Celsius scale is everyday but its zero is arbitrary; the kelvin scale starts at absolute zero, the temperature at which particles have the minimum possible energy.

temperature in kelvin = temperature in degrees Celsius + 273        T (K) = theta (C) + 273

Supplement: Boyle's law. For a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature, pressure and volume are inversely proportional:

p V = constant        p1 V1 = p2 V2
  • p: pressure in pascals (Pa), positive; V: volume in cubic metres (m³) or any consistent unit. Both are scalars.
  • The product pV stays constant only while the temperature and the amount of gas are fixed.

Doubling the pressure halves the volume; a graph of p against V is a curve (inverse proportion), while a graph of p against 1/V is a straight line through the origin — a standard Paper 4 graph question.

Thermal expansion of solids, liquids and gases

Almost everything expands when heated: the particles move faster and push further apart. Everyday consequences include gaps between railway rails and bridge sections, expansion loops in power cables, the bimetallic strip in a thermostat (two metals expand by different amounts, so the strip bends and breaks a circuit), and the difficulty of undoing a metal jar lid, which can be loosened by running hot water over it so the metal lid expands more than the glass. Liquids expand more than solids for the same temperature rise, and gases expand most of all.

The particle explanation is a Supplement statement: heating increases the average separation of the particles because their increased energy makes them swing wider about their positions in a solid, slide further apart in a liquid, and occupy a larger volume in a gas at the same pressure. Thermometers work because liquids expand predictably with temperature: the liquid column rises in a narrow capillary, making a small volume change visible as a large length change.

Specific heat capacity

Equal masses of different substances need different amounts of energy to warm by the same temperature: water resists temperature change far more than sand, which is why coastal towns have mild climates and why water makes an excellent coolant in car engines and central heating. That property is the specific heat capacity:

energy transferred = mass x specific heat capacity x temperature change        E = m c delta theta
  • E: energy transferred in joules (J); m: mass in kilograms (kg).
  • c: specific heat capacity in joules per kilogram per degree Celsius (J kg⁻¹ °C⁻¹, numerically the same as J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹). A scalar.
  • delta theta: temperature change in degrees Celsius (°C) or kelvin (K). Temperature rises give a positive energy input; falls give energy out.

Supplement: measuring c experimentally. An electrical heater warms a well-lagged block of the substance; an ammeter and voltmeter give the electrical energy E = V I t, and a thermometer gives the temperature rise. Plot temperature against time; the gradient gives the rate of heating, and c = V I t / (m delta theta). Lagging reduces heat loss to the surroundings, the stirrer evens out hot spots, and the same method compares two materials by heating equal masses with the same heater for the same time.

Melting, boiling and evaporation

Melting and boiling happen at fixed temperatures for a pure substance at fixed pressure: 0 °C and 100 °C for pure water at one atmosphere. On a heating curve, plateaus mark the changes of state, and the energy supplied during a plateau is the latent heat: the energy needed to change the state of 1 kg without any temperature change (latent heat of fusion for melting, of vaporisation for boiling). The plateau exists because the energy breaks intermolecular attractions rather than increasing particle speed.

Evaporation is different from boiling and happens at any temperature. Particles at the liquid surface occasionally escape with above-average energy, so the average energy of those left falls and the liquid cools. Evaporation is faster when the temperature is higher, the surface area is larger, and a draught carries vapour away — the three factors Paper 4 expects in an evaporation-and-cooling explanation. Boiling happens throughout the liquid at a fixed temperature, with bubbles of vapour forming internally; evaporation happens only at the surface, at all temperatures, and cools the liquid left behind. Wet skin cools you because the water evaporates and takes the highest-energy particles with it.

Conduction

Conduction is the transfer of energy through a substance without the substance itself moving. In metals, the free electrons carry energy quickly from the hot end to the cold end, which is why metals are good conductors; in non-metals the energy passes only as vibrations handed along the vibrating particles, which is much slower. In gases and most liquids, conduction is poor because the particles are too far apart to pass on vibrations efficiently — hence insulating materials trap air in fibres or foam.

The core practical comparison: rods of different materials are coated with wax at one end and held over a heat source; the wax falls first from the best conductor. Metals come out in order (copper and aluminium good, steel poorer), while wood, plastic and glass barely conduct at all.

Convection

Convection is the transfer of energy by the movement of a fluid itself. Heating a fluid lowers its density: the warm parcel rises, cooler fluid sinks to take its place, and a convection current sets up. This is how radiators heat a room (hot air rises from the radiator, cools at the ceiling and returns down the far wall), how a kettle boils from the bottom, how sea breezes blow from sea to land by day, and how the element of a domestic water heater sits at the bottom so the whole tank warms. Convection requires a fluid — it cannot occur in a solid, and in a vacuum there is no medium at all.

Radiation

Radiation is the transfer of energy by electromagnetic waves, mainly infrared. It needs no medium, so it is the only way energy crosses the vacuum of space — which is why the Sun's heat reaches the Earth. The rate of emission and absorption depends on surface colour and texture: dull black surfaces are the best emitters and the best absorbers; shiny white or silvered surfaces are the poorest and reflect most radiation.

ApplicationSurface choice and reason
House radiatorMatte dark paint: emits radiation well
Hot-water tank and pipesSilvered foil: reduces radiation loss
Thermos flaskSilvered glass walls on both sides: minimises radiated loss in and out
Ice box / cool boxShiny white outside: reflects incoming radiation
Desert survival bagShiny side outwards in hot sun: reflects the Sun's radiation

Supplement: the Earth's energy balance. The Earth absorbs short-wavelength radiation from the Sun and radiates longer-wavelength infrared back to space. At equilibrium the two rates match and the average temperature is steady; greenhouse gases absorb some outgoing infrared and re-radiate it downwards, raising the equilibrium temperature. More greenhouse gas shifts the balance and warms the surface — the physics behind climate change.

Worked example: heating water

A 2.0 kg kettle of water is heated from 15 °C to 100 °C. The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J kg⁻¹ °C⁻¹. The kettle's heater supplies 2400 W.

energy needed = m c delta theta = 2.0 x 4200 x (100 - 15) = 714 000 J
time = energy / power = 714 000 / 2400 = 298 s (about 5.0 minutes)

Real kettles take longer, because some energy warms the kettle body and is lost to the air — which is exactly why the efficiency of a kettle is less than 100 per cent. To boil the water away would need far more energy again, because of the latent heat of vaporisation.

Second calculation: a 0.50 kg block of aluminium (c = 900 J kg⁻¹ °C⁻¹) cools from 80 °C to 25 °C. Energy released = 0.50 × 900 × 55 = 24 750 J ≈ 25 kJ. Cooling gives out the same energy that heating took in; only the sign of the temperature change differs.

Common mistakes

  • Saying heat rises. Heat is energy, not a substance; it is the warm fluid that rises because it is less dense.
  • Confusing temperature with internal energy: temperature measures the average energy per particle, while internal energy is the total energy of all particles.
  • Forgetting that during melting or boiling the temperature stays constant even though energy is still being supplied.
  • Mixing up conduction (through a substance), convection (by a moving fluid) and radiation (by waves, no medium). A vacuum flask blocks all three: silvered walls (radiation), vacuum gap (conduction and convection), foam or stopper (conduction).
  • Using degrees Celsius where kelvin are required in a gas-law calculation; always convert with T = θ + 273 before using pV = constant relationships.
  • Putting mass in grams into E = mcΔθ; the unit J kg⁻¹ °C⁻¹ demands kilograms.
  • Describing evaporation as boiling; evaporation occurs at any temperature, only at the surface, and cools the remaining liquid.
  • Claiming particles expand; it is the average separation between the particles that increases.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 4, 3 marks). A 500 g block of copper (c = 390 J kg⁻¹ °C⁻¹) is heated from 20 °C to 120 °C. Calculate the energy transferred.

Answer: E = mcΔθ = 0.50 × 390 × 100 = 19 500 J = 19.5 kJ.

Question 2 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Explain, using the particle model, why a metal lid on a glass jar loosens under hot water.

Answer: The hot water heats both the lid and the jar. The particles in the metal gain energy and vibrate with greater amplitude, so their average separation increases more than that of the glass particles, because metals expand more than glass for the same temperature rise. The metal lid therefore becomes slightly larger in diameter than the neck of the jar and turns more easily.

Question 3 (Paper 2 style). Which change does not occur at a fixed temperature? A ice melting at 0 °C; B water boiling at 100 °C; C water evaporating from a puddle; D steam condensing at 100 °C. Answer: C. Evaporation occurs at any temperature and is not a fixed-temperature change of state.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 6 marks). Explain how a vacuum flask keeps a drink hot, referring to all three methods of thermal energy transfer.

Answer: The double-walled glass vessel has a vacuum between the walls, and a vacuum contains no particles, so energy cannot be transferred across the gap by conduction or convection. Both walls are silvered to reduce radiation: the shiny surfaces are poor emitters and poor absorbers, so little infrared escapes. The plastic stopper and foam supports are poor conductors and block convection in the air above the liquid. Together these keep energy in the drink for hours.

Question 5 (Paper 6 style). Describe an experiment to compare how well different materials conduct heat.

Answer: Fix rods of equal length and thickness made from the different materials, each coated at the far end with an equal blob of wax, over identical heat sources. Start together and record the time for each wax blob to fall. The shortest time identifies the best conductor. Keep the source, rod dimensions, coating thickness and starting temperature identical so the comparison is fair, and repeat to check the ranking.

Question 6 (Paper 4, 3 marks). A gas is trapped in a sealed syringe at 100 cm³ and 20 °C. It is heated to 87 °C at constant pressure. Find its new volume.

Answer: Convert first: 20 °C = 293 K, 87 °C = 360 K. At constant pressure V/T is constant, so V₂ = 100 × 360/293 = 123 cm³. (For a Core-level answer, the gas expands when heated at constant pressure, and the volume rises by roughly a quarter.)

From heat to the transfer of energy by waves: the next topic is Waves and Sound.

title: Exam technique: Magnetism and Electromagnetism
content:
### What earns the marks
For electromagnets, turns plus current plus soft iron core earns each mark. For transformers, the turns ratio equation quoted earns the method mark. For induction, rate of change of flux linked to emf size earns the explanation mark.
### Traps
Error: steel chosen for electromagnet cores. Correction: soft iron; steel suits permanent magnets. Error: Fleming hands swapped. Correction: left for motor, right for generator. Error: step-up confused with step-down. Correction: more secondary turns means step-up.
### Worked example
A transformer has 2000 primary turns and 100 secondary turns. The primary is supplied at 240 V. The turns ratio gives Vs = Vp × Ns / Np = 240 × 100 / 2000 = 12 V. More secondary turns than primary turns means a step-up transformer, so the output voltage rises.
### Check yourself
An ideal transformer has 12 V at its secondary and a current of 4.0 A there. Find the primary current when the primary is at 240 V. Power in equals power out, so Ip = (12 × 4.0) / 240 = 0.20 A.

### Worked example
A transformer has 2000 primary turns and 100 secondary turns. The primary is supplied at 240 V. The turns ratio gives Vs = Vp × Ns / Np = 240 × 100 / 2000 = 12 V. More secondary turns than primary turns means a step-up transformer, so the output voltage rises.

title: IGCSE Chemistry: Acids, Bases and Salts
content:
IGCSE Chemistry: Acids, Bases and Salts

Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry 0620 (2026–2028), Extended route, Topic 7 Acids, bases and salts: statement 7.1 The characteristic properties of acids and bases, 7.2 Oxides, and 7.3 Preparation of salts. This note builds from what an acid physically is (a proton donor) through every reaction type worth marks, to the four salt-preparation methods with their procedures — and it is those procedures that carry Paper 6 as well as Paper 4. Every equation is balanced and every calculation line is explicit.

What acids and bases are

The everyday definition: acids taste sour, turn litmus red and react with metals and carbonates; bases are metal oxides or hydroxides that neutralise acids; alkalis are soluble bases (they dissolve to give hydroxide ions). The Extended definition that earns the extra mark: an acid is a proton (H⁺) donor and a base is a proton acceptor — in water an acid donates H⁺ to the solvent, forming H₃O⁺ but conventionally written as H⁺(aq).

Dissociation of acids in water - the strong/weak distinction:

  STRONG acid - fully dissociated (every molecule releases its proton):
    HCl(aq) → H⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq)          [single arrow]
    HNO₃(aq) → H⁺(aq) + NO₃⁻(aq)
    H₂SO₄(aq) → 2H⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq)

  WEAK acid - only partially dissociated (an equilibrium):
    CH₃COOH(aq) ⇌ H⁺(aq) + CH₃COO⁻(aq)   [equilibrium arrow]
    H₂CO₃(aq) ⇌ H⁺(aq) + HCO₃⁻(aq)

Strong vs weak is about the DISOCIATION, not the concentration:
  dilute HCl is strong but dilute; concentrated ethanoic acid is weak but
  concentrated. Strong acids attack metals and carbonates faster (more H⁺
  ions per volume); weak acids are safer (vinegar, lemon juice).

Reactions of acids: the four types

Reacts withProductsWorked equation
MetalsSalt + hydrogenMg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g)
Bases (metal oxides/hydroxides)Salt + waterCuO(s) + H₂SO₄(aq) → CuSO₄(aq) + H₂O(l)
CarbonatesSalt + water + carbon dioxideCaCO₃(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl₂(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g)
Ammonia (alkali)Ammonium saltNH₃(g) + HCl(aq) → NH₄Cl(aq)

Neutralisation is acid + base → salt + water; the ionic essence is H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O. Indicators: litmus (red in acid, blue in alkali), thymolphthalein (colourless in acid, blue in alkali), methyl orange (red in acid, yellow in alkali), universal indicator for a pH estimate. pH measures acidity: pH 7 neutral, below 7 acidic, above 7 alkaline; each unit is a tenfold change in H⁺ concentration.

Oxides: the four classes

  • Basic oxides — metal oxides (CuO, CaO) that react with acids to give salt and water.
  • Acidic oxides — non-metal oxides (SO₂, CO₂, NO₂) that react with alkalis to give salt and water.
  • Amphoteric oxides — react with both acids and alkalis (Al₂O₃, ZnO) — the Extended favourite.
  • Neutral oxides — neither (CO, NO, H₂O).
Amphoteric behaviour worked, both directions:

  Al₂O₃ + 6HCl → 2AlCl₃ + 3H₂O         [acts as a base, with acid]
  Al₂O₃ + 2NaOH → 2NaAlO₂ + H₂O        [acts as an acid, with alkali]

The oxide's character tracks the element's position: metallic oxides basic,
non-metallic oxides acidic, and the metal/metalloid border (Al, Zn) gives
amphoteric behaviour.

Preparation of salts: four methods

The method is chosen by the salt's solubility and the acid type — a decision tree the exam expects you to reason through, not recite.

Decision tree:

  Soluble salt?
  |-- YES → use an ACID + excess INSOLUBLE base/metal/carbonate, then
  |          filter off the excess and crystallise.
  |-- NO  → precipitation: mix two solutions of soluble salts, filter,
             wash and dry the precipitate.

Worked procedure 1 - soluble salt from an insoluble base:
  copper(II) sulfate from copper(II) oxide + dilute sulfuric acid.
  1. Warm dilute H₂SO₄ in a beaker.
  2. Add CuO powder a little at a time with stirring - it reacts and
     dissolves: CuO + H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + H₂O
  3. Keep adding until NO MORE DISSOLVES (the excess solid remains) -
     this guarantees all the acid is used up.
  4. FILTER off the excess CuO (the filtrate is pure copper(II) sulfate
     solution).
  5. Heat the filtrate to the point of crystallisation, leave to cool and
     crystallise; dry the crystals between filter papers.

  The excess-solid trick is the key exam point: a pure salt needs either
  reagent fully consumed, and only an insoluble excess can be filtered off.

Worked procedure 2 - insoluble salt by precipitation:
  barium sulfate from barium chloride + sodium sulfate solutions.
  BaCl₂(aq) + Na₂SO₄(aq) → BaSO₄(s) + 2NaCl(aq)
  Mix solutions, filter the precipitate, wash with distilled water, dry.

Worked procedure 3 - titration (soluble salt from acid + soluble alkali):
  sodium chloride from hydrochloric acid + sodium hydroxide.
  Both are solutions, so there is no excess solid to filter - use EXACT
  volumes from a titration (see the techniques note), then evaporate.

Worked procedure 4 - acid + excess metal (hydrogen given off):
  zinc sulfate from zinc + dilute sulfuric acid; filter excess zinc.

Water of crystallisation

Many salts crystallise with water locked into their lattice — hydrated salts (CuSO₄·5H₂O blue; CoCl₂·6H₂O pink). Heating drives the water off as anhydrous salt (white CuSO₄), and the change is reversible — the water test from the environment topic. In calculations the water counts in the formula mass: Mᵣ of CuSO₄·5H₂O = 160 + 5 × 18 = 250, not 160.

Worked example: a full salt-preparation calculation

10.0 g of calcium carbonate reacts with excess hydrochloric acid:
  CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂

(a) moles CaCO₃ = 10.0 / 100 = 0.100 mol
(b) ratio 1:1 → moles CaCl₂ = 0.100 mol
(c) mass CaCl₂ (Mᵣ = 111) = 0.100 × 111 = 11.1 g   [theoretical yield]
(d) if 9.4 g of dry salt is collected:
    percentage yield = 9.4 / 11.1 × 100 = 84.7%

Where the mass is lost: crystals left in solution, spills, incomplete
reaction, or wet product if not dried - the usual evaluation question.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Confusing acid strength with concentration — strong = fully dissociated; concentrated = lots of acid per volume. The two are independent axes.
  • Writing weak acid dissociation with a single arrow; weak acids are equilibria.
  • Salt formula errors from ion charges: Al³⁺ + Cl⁻ → AlCl₃, not AlCl — check charge balance.
  • Forgetting carbon dioxide in acid + carbonate answers (three products, not two).
  • Adding excess soluble alkali in salt prep (then the salt is contaminated and cannot be filtered) — only insoluble reagents can be used in excess.
  • Leaving water of crystallisation out of formula mass or percentage-composition calculations.
  • Describing neutralisation as "acid + metal" — that is a separate reaction type; neutralisation is acid + base.
  • In precipitation questions, not washing the precipitate (residual soluble ions contaminate it).

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 4, 3 marks). Explain the difference between a strong acid and a concentrated acid.

Answer: A strong acid dissociates completely in water, releasing all its protons (e.g. hydrochloric acid); a concentrated acid contains a large amount of acid per unit volume of solution. A dilute solution of a strong acid is strong but dilute; a concentrated solution of a weak acid (ethanoic) is concentrated but weak.

Question 2 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Write equations for sulfuric acid reacting with (i) magnesium (ii) copper(II) oxide (iii) sodium carbonate.

Answer: (i) Mg + H₂SO₄ → MgSO₄ + H₂. (ii) CuO + H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + H₂O. (iii) Na₂CO₃ + H₂SO₄ → Na₂SO₄ + H₂O + CO₂.

Question 3 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Describe how pure crystals of copper(II) sulfate are prepared from copper(II) oxide and dilute sulfuric acid.

Answer: Warm the dilute acid; add copper(II) oxide with stirring until it no longer dissolves (excess solid ensures all acid reacts); filter off the excess copper(II) oxide; heat the filtrate to the point of crystallisation; leave the solution to cool and crystallise; filter and dry the crystals between filter papers.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 3 marks). Explain why aluminium oxide is described as amphoteric.

Answer: Aluminium oxide reacts with acids to form a salt and water (acting as a base), e.g. Al₂O₃ + 6HCl → 2AlCl₃ + 3H₂O, and also reacts with alkalis to form a salt and water (acting as an acid), e.g. Al₂O₃ + 2NaOH → 2NaAlO₂ + H₂O. Oxides with both behaviours are amphoteric.

Question 5 (Paper 4, 5 marks). Calculate the mass of anhydrous sodium sulfate formed when 21.2 g of sodium carbonate is neutralised by excess sulfuric acid. (Mᵣ: Na₂CO₃ = 106, Na₂SO₄ = 142)

Answer: Na₂CO₃ + H₂SO₄ → Na₂SO₄ + H₂O + CO₂. Moles Na₂CO₃ = 21.2 ÷ 106 = 0.200 mol. Ratio 1:1 → 0.200 mol Na₂SO₄. Mass = 0.200 × 142 = 28.4 g.

Question 6 (Paper 6, 3 marks). A student prepares lead(II) iodide by precipitation. State the reagents and describe the steps after mixing.

Answer: Mix solutions of lead(II) nitrate and potassium iodide. Filter to collect the yellow precipitate; wash it with distilled water to remove soluble nitrate/iodide ions; dry it between filter papers or in a warm oven.

Acids and salts live in the wider map of the elements — the Periodic Table's groups and their trends.

title: Quantum Physics — Study Notes
content:
Quantum Physics

Edexcel International A Level Physics — Unit 2 (WPH12), sat at AS: photons, the photoelectric effect and wave–particle duality.

Photons and photon energy

Electromagnetic radiation travels as photons, each with energy E = hf, where h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s is the Planck constant. Since c = fλ, the energy is also E = hc/λ. Shorter wavelength means higher energy.

Example: a photon of wavelength 500 nm has E = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3.0 × 10⁸)/(5.0 × 10⁻⁷) ≈ 4.0 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, or about 2.5 eV.

The photoelectric effect

When light shines on a metal surface, electrons are emitted only if the frequency of the light is at or above the threshold frequency f₀. Each photon transfers its whole energy to a single electron. Increasing the intensity increases the number of photons per second, so more electrons are emitted, but it does not increase the energy of each electron. The emission is instantaneous, with no time delay.

Wave theory cannot explain the threshold frequency or the lack of a time delay. The photon model explains both.

Einstein's photoelectric equation

hf = φ + E_k(max), where φ is the work function of the metal, the minimum energy needed to free an electron. The threshold frequency is f₀ = φ/h. The stopping potential V_s satisfies eV_s = E_k(max).

Example: a work function of 2.0 eV gives f₀ = (2.0 × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹)/(6.63 × 10⁻³⁴) ≈ 4.8 × 10¹⁴ Hz.

Wave-particle duality

Particles also have wave properties. The de Broglie wavelength of a particle with momentum p is λ = h/p. Electrons diffract through crystal lattices, showing wave behaviour, while photons show particle behaviour in the photoelectric effect. Both are needed to describe the same entities.

Energy levels and line spectra

Electrons in an atom occupy discrete energy levels. When an electron falls from a higher level E₁ to a lower level E₂, it emits a single photon with hf = E₁ − E₂. Absorption happens when a photon with exactly this energy is taken in. Because only specific energies are allowed, the spectrum is a set of sharp lines rather than a continuous band.

Example: a transition from −3.4 eV to −13.6 eV releases 10.2 eV, a wavelength of about 122 nm.

Exam tips: convert eV to joules (1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J) before using E = hf. Say which quantity the intensity changes and which it does not. Quote hf = φ + E_k(max) in photoelectric questions.

Worked example: threshold frequency and stopping voltage

Zinc has a work function of 4.3 eV. Converted to joules, that is 6.9 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, so the threshold frequency is f₀ = φ/h = 6.9 × 10⁻¹⁹ / 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ ≈ 1.04 × 10¹⁵ Hz. Light of frequency 1.5 × 10¹⁵ Hz gives photons of energy 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 1.5 × 10¹⁵ ≈ 9.9 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, or about 6.2 eV. The maximum kinetic energy of the ejected electrons is 6.2 − 4.3 ≈ 1.9 eV, so the stopping voltage is about 1.9 V. Quote values with their units, and keep eV and joules consistent within each step.

Exam method: photon energy and wavelength

Combine E = hf with c = fλ to give E = hc/λ. Convert wavelengths to metres before you substitute into hc, because a wavelength given in nanometres must be multiplied by 10⁻⁹ first. A wrong power of ten is the most common way to lose the final mark, so estimate the answer before you calculate it precisely.

title: Sequences and Series — Study Notes
content:
Sequences and Series

Arithmetic Progressions (AP)

Terms increase by a common difference d.

  • nth term: uₙ = a + (n − 1)d
  • Sum: Sₙ = n/2 [2a + (n − 1)d]

Example: AP 5, 8, 11: the 20th term is 5 + 19 × 3 = 62.

Geometric Progressions (GP)

Terms multiply by a common ratio r.

  • nth term: uₙ = arⁿ⁻¹
  • Sum: Sₙ = a(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r)
  • Sum to infinity (|r| < 1 only): S∞ = a/(1 − r)

Example: a = 8, r = 1/2 gives S∞ = 8/(1/2) = 16.

Binomial Expansion

(1 + x)ⁿ = 1 + nx + n(n − 1)/2! x² + n(n − 1)(n − 2)/3! x³ + …, valid for |x| < 1.

For positive integer n, coefficients come from Pascal's triangle: (1 + 2x)⁴ = 1 + 8x + 24x² + 32x³ + 16x⁴.

Exam tips: identify a, d or r first; for "sum to infinity" questions check |r| < 1 explicitly, and for binomial expansions give terms up to the power asked (usually x² or x³).

Formulae and exam method

Arithmetic progression: the nth term is Tₙ = a + (n − 1)d, where a is the first term and d the common difference. The sum of the first n terms is Sₙ = n/2 [2a + (n − 1)d], or Sₙ = n/2 (a + l) when the last term l is known.

Geometric progression: Tₙ = arⁿ⁻¹, and Sₙ = a(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r) for r ≠ 1. The sum to infinity exists only when |r| < 1, and then S∞ = a/(1 − r).

To find the number of terms, substitute the known sum or term and solve for n. When n sits in an exponent, take logarithms. Check that n is a positive integer.

Sigma notation: Σ from r = 1 to n of (ar + b) is evaluated with the standard sums, but write out the first few terms when the pattern is unclear.

Exam cue: Identify whether the question is AP or GP before choosing a formula, and state the value of r when using the sum to infinity.

Exam method: arithmetic and geometric sums

For an arithmetic sequence with first term a and common difference d, the nth term is a + (n − 1)d and the sum of the first n terms is S_n = n/2 (2a + (n − 1)d). For a geometric sequence with ratio r, the nth term is ar^(n − 1) and S_n = a(1 − r^n)/(1 − r) for r ≠ 1.

The sum to infinity exists only when |r| < 1, and then S∞ = a/(1 − r). If |r| ≥ 1, say so explicitly rather than applying the formula.

Exam cue: Identify whether the sequence is arithmetic or geometric from the common difference or ratio before choosing a formula. Check the number of terms n carefully when you set up the equation.

Worked example: arithmetic progression

The sequence 3, 7, 11, … has first term a = 3 and common difference d = 4. The 20th term is a + 19d = 3 + 76 = 79. The sum of the first 20 terms is Sₙ = n/2 (2a + (n − 1)d) = 10 × (6 + 76) = 820.

Check with the average method: the first and last terms average (3 + 79)/2 = 41, and 41 × 20 = 820.

Worked example: geometric progression

The sequence 5, 10, 20, … has r = 2. The 8th term is 5 × 2⁷ = 640. The sum of the first six terms is 5(2⁶ − 1)/(2 − 1) = 315. Adding them directly gives 5 + 10 + 20 + 40 + 80 + 160 = 315, which confirms the formula.

Sum to infinity

A geometric series has a sum to infinity only when |r| < 1, and then S∞ = a/(1 − r). For 81, 27, 9, … the ratio is 1/3, so S∞ = 81/(2/3) = 121.5. If |r| ≥ 1 the terms do not shrink and the sum does not converge, so say so rather than quoting a formula.

Binomial expansion

For (1 + 2x)⁵, the first terms are 1 + 5(2x) + 10(2x)² + … The coefficient of x² is C(5, 2) × 2² = 10 × 4 = 40. The expansion is valid for |2x| < 1, so the range of x must be stated when the question asks for it.

Common errors that lose marks

  • Using n instead of n − 1 in the n-th term formula, which shifts every term.
  • Confusing the nth term with the sum of the first n terms, a very common error on exam questions that ask for both.
  • Dividing a/(1 − r) when the series starts at a term other than the first, so check the index on the first term before using the formula.
  • Forgetting that the binomial expansion of (a + b)ⁿ has a coefficient C(n, r) on each term, and that the powers of a and b add to n.

title: Electricity: D.C. Circuits — Study Notes
content:
Electricity: D.C. circuits

Edexcel International A Level Physics — Unit 2 (WPH12), sat at AS.

Current and charge

  • Current I = charge Q ÷ time t, so Q = It. Unit: ampere (A), where 1 A = 1 C s⁻¹.
  • Electron drift velocity is very small, but the electric field propagates through the circuit almost at the speed of light.

Potential difference and power

  • Potential difference V = energy transferred ÷ charge. Unit: volt (V), where 1 V = 1 J C⁻¹.
  • Power P = VI = I²R = V²/R. Unit: watt (W).

Resistance and resistivity

R = V/I (Ohm's law for an ohmic conductor, at constant temperature). For a wire of length L and cross-sectional area A, R = ρL/A, where ρ is the resistivity in Ω m. Resistance rises with length and falls with area.

Practical circuits

An ammeter is connected in series with the component it measures. A voltmeter is connected in parallel with the component. An ideal ammeter has zero resistance; an ideal voltmeter has infinite resistance.

Kirchhoff's laws

  • First law: at a junction, the total current entering equals the total current leaving (conservation of charge).
  • Second law: around any closed loop, the sum of the emfs equals the sum of the potential differences (conservation of energy).

Potential dividers

For two resistors R1 and R2 in series across a supply V, the potential difference across R2 is V × R2/(R1 + R2).

Worked example: a 100 Ω and a 300 Ω resistor are in series across 12 V. The current is 12/400 = 0.030 A, and the voltage across the 300 Ω resistor is 0.030 × 300 = 9.0 V.

Exam tips: draw the meter in the correct place, in series or in parallel. Apply Kirchhoff's first law to currents and the second law to loops, with consistent signs. Check that units are converted (e.g. mm² to m²) before using ρL/A.

Resistivity and temperature

For a metallic conductor at constant temperature, resistance is proportional to length and inversely proportional to cross-sectional area. Resistivity, ρ = RA/L, is a property of the material. As temperature rises, the ions in a metal vibrate more and impede the flow of electrons, so resistivity increases. A thermistor behaves differently: its resistance falls as temperature rises, because more charge carriers are released.

Exam tip: when asked to explain a resistance change, relate it to charge carriers and collisions, not just to the formula.

Worked example: resistors in series and in parallel

Two resistors of 4 Ω and 6 Ω in series have a combined resistance of 10 Ω, and the same current flows through each. In parallel, the same two resistors have a combined resistance found from 1/R = 1/4 + 1/6 = 5/12, so R = 2.4 Ω. The combined resistance in parallel is always less than the smallest individual resistance, and adding a branch to a parallel circuit always reduces the total resistance.

Worked example: EMF and internal resistance

A cell with EMF 1.5 V and internal resistance 0.5 Ω supplies a current of 2 A. The terminal potential difference is V = E − Ir = 1.5 − (2 × 0.5) = 0.5 V. Writing V = E − Ir before substituting shows that the energy lost inside the cell is the difference between the EMF and the terminal voltage. A cell with a larger current supplied has a smaller terminal voltage.

The potential divider

Two resistors in series across a supply give an output voltage across one of them that depends on the ratio of the resistances. For a supply of 12 V with resistors of 2 kΩ and 4 kΩ in series, the voltage across the 4 kΩ resistor is 12 × 4 ÷ 6 = 8 V. A thermistor or light-dependent resistor in place of one of the resistors makes this arrangement a sensor, because the output voltage changes with temperature or light level.

title: AS Level Mathematics: Exponentials and Logarithms
content:
AS Level Mathematics: Exponentials and Logarithms

Exponentials describe growth and decay — populations, investments, radioactive isotopes, cooling cups of tea — where the change is proportional to the amount present. Logarithms are their inverses: they turn multiplication into addition and, crucially, let you solve equations where the unknown sits in the exponent. This note builds the topic from zero: the meaning of a logarithm, the three laws with derivations, solving exponential and logarithmic equations including quadratics in disguise, the graph properties and transformations, and the applied growth/decay models.

What a logarithm is

log_a(x) = n  means  a^n = x

common log: log x = log_10 x
natural log: ln x = log_e x,  e = 2.71828...

The logarithm answers "to what power must I raise the base to get this number?" So log₂8 = 3 because 2³ = 8, and log₅(1/25) = −2 because 5⁻² = 1/25. Two identities follow immediately and are always true:

log_a(a) = 1
log_a(1) = 0
a^(log_a x) = x   and   log_a(a^x) = x

Worked example. Evaluate log₃81, log₂(1/8) and ln 1.

3^4 = 81  ->  log_3 81 = 4
2^-3 = 1/8  ->  log_2(1/8) = -3
anything to the power 0 is 1  ->  ln 1 = 0

The three laws of logarithms

product:   log(xy) = log x + log y
quotient:  log(x/y) = log x - log y
power:     log(x^n) = n log x

consequences: log(1/x) = -log x;  log(sqrt x) = (1/2)log x

Why they work. Write x = a^m and y = a^n, so log x = m and log y = n. Then xy = a^(m+n), so log(xy) = m + n = log x + log y. The quotient law follows from a^(m−n) and the power law from (a^m)^n = a^(mn). Each law is a restatement of an index law, which is why logarithms convert products into sums.

Worked example 1 (combine). Write 2 log 3 + log 4 − log 6 as a single logarithm.

2 log 3 = log 9
log 9 + log 4 = log 36
log 36 - log 6 = log 6

Worked example 2 (split). Express log(x³y/√z) in terms of log x, log y and log z.

= 3 log x + log y - (1/2) log z

Worked example 3 (solve). Solve log₂x + log₂(x − 2) = 3.

combine: log_2[x(x - 2)] = 3
x(x - 2) = 2^3 = 8
x^2 - 2x - 8 = 0  ->  (x - 4)(x + 2) = 0
x = 4 or x = -2;  reject x = -2 because log of a negative is undefined
x = 4

Rejecting invalid roots is compulsory: a logarithm only accepts a positive argument, so always check each answer against the original equation.

Solving exponential equations

When the unknown is in the exponent, take logs of both sides and use the power law to bring it down.

Worked example 1. Solve 3^x = 20.

take logs: x log 3 = log 20
x = log 20 / log 3 = 1.301/0.4771 = 2.73

Worked example 2 (different bases). Solve 5^(2x−1) = 7^(x+1).

(2x - 1) log 5 = (x + 1) log 7
2x log 5 - log 5 = x log 7 + log 7
x(2 log 5 - log 7) = log 7 + log 5
x = (log 7 + log 5)/(2 log 5 - log 7)
  = (0.845 + 0.699)/(1.398 - 0.845) = 1.544/0.553 = 2.79

Worked example 3 (quadratic in disguise). Solve 2^(2x) − 5(2^x) + 4 = 0.

let y = 2^x:  y^2 - 5y + 4 = 0  ->  (y - 1)(y - 4) = 0
y = 1  ->  2^x = 1  ->  x = 0
y = 4  ->  2^x = 4  ->  x = 2

The substitution trick is the standard route for any equation where one power is double another: put y = a^x and solve the quadratic, then convert back.

Graphs of exponential and logarithmic functions

FunctionDomainRangeKey points
y = e^xall real xy > 0(0, 1); always increasing; asymptote y = 0
y = e^(−x)all real xy > 0(0, 1); always decreasing; decay
y = ln xx > 0all real y(1, 0); increasing; asymptote x = 0

y = ln x is the reflection of y = e^x in the line y = x, because they are inverse functions. That reflection explains the domain and range swap and the asymptote turning from horizontal to vertical.

Worked example. Sketch y = e^(x−2) + 1, stating the asymptote and intercepts.

translation 2 right, 1 up
asymptote y = 1 (was y = 0)
y-intercept: e^-2 + 1 = 0.135 + 1 = 1.135
no x-intercept (the curve stays above y = 1)

Growth and decay models

exponential model: N = N_0 e^(kt)
  k > 0 growth;  k < 0 decay
half-life: time for N to halve = ln 2 / |k| (decay)
doubling time = ln 2 / k (growth)

Worked example (decay). A radioactive sample decays as N = 500e^(−0.02t) with t in years. Find the initial amount, the amount after 50 years, and the half-life.

t = 0: N = 500
at t = 50: 500e^-1 = 500 x 0.3679 = 184
half-life: 500e^(-0.02t) = 250  ->  e^(-0.02t) = 0.5
-0.02t = ln 0.5 = -0.693  ->  t = 34.7 years

Worked example 2 (growth). Bacteria grow as N = 200e^(0.15t), t in hours. When does the population reach 1000?

200e^(0.15t) = 1000  ->  e^(0.15t) = 5
0.15t = ln 5 = 1.609  ->  t = 10.7 hours

Logarithmic scales in context

Some quantities span so many orders of magnitude that a logarithmic scale is used: pH for acidity, the Richter scale for earthquakes, decibels for sound. A change of 1 on the Richter scale means 10 times the amplitude, so an increase of 3 means 10³ = 1000 times.

Worked example. Two earthquakes differ by 2.4 on the Richter scale. How many times larger is the amplitude of the stronger?

difference 2.4 in log_10  ->  10^2.4 = 251 times

Change of base and log-linearisation

Calculators offer base 10 and base e only, so any other base is converted with the change-of-base formula. The same formula turns a power law into a straight line, which is how experimental data is tested for exponential behaviour.

change of base: log_a(x) = log_b(x)/log_b(a)
so log_2(7) = ln 7 / ln 2 = log 7 / log 2 = 2.807

if y = a x^n then log y = log a + n log x  (straight line in log-log)
if y = a b^x then log y = log a + x log b  (straight line in log-x)

Worked example 1. Evaluate log_5(30).

log 30 / log 5 = 1.477/0.699 = 2.113

Worked example 2 (log-linearisation). Data gives a straight line when log y is plotted against x, with gradient 0.3 and intercept 1.4. Find the model connecting y and x.

log y = 1.4 + 0.3x
so y = 10^1.4 x 10^(0.3x) = 25.1 x 2.00^x
an exponential growth model with a = 25.1 and b = 2.0

Worked example 3 (inequality). Solve 2^x < 100.

take logs (base 2 is increasing, so the inequality is preserved)
x < log_2 100 = log 100/log 2 = 6.64

Taking logs of both sides is safe for any base greater than 1 because the log function is increasing; a base between 0 and 1 would reverse the inequality, which never arises in these models.

Rewriting any exponential in base e

Any exponential a^x can be written as e^(kx), because a = e^(ln a). This is why every growth model in the syllabus uses e: the base is absorbed into the constant.

a^x = e^(x ln a)
so 2^x = e^(0.693x);  5^x = e^(1.609x);  0.8^x = e^(-0.223x)

Worked example. Express y = 300(1.04)^t in the form y = 300e^(kt), and state the annual percentage rate it represents.

1.04 = e^k  ->  k = ln 1.04 = 0.0392
y = 300e^(0.0392t)
the rate is 3.92 per year in continuous-compounding form, while the
annual multiplier is still 1.04 (4 per cent per year)

Worked example 2. A model is N = 80e^(0.25t). Rewrite it as N = 80b^t and find the percentage growth per unit time.

b = e^0.25 = 1.284
N = 80(1.284)^t, so growth is 28.4 per cent per unit time

The two forms describe the same curve; the e-form is convenient for calculus, the b-form for reading off a percentage rate. Converting between them is a standard exam demand.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Evaluate) Find log₄64. Answer: 3, since 4³ = 64.
  2. (Laws) Simplify log 8 + log 5 − log 2. Answer: log(40/2) = log 20.
  3. (Solve log) Solve log₃x = 2. Answer: x = 3² = 9.
  4. (Solve exponential) Solve 2^x = 50. Answer: x = log 50/log 2 = 1.699/0.301 = 5.64.
  5. (Quadratic) Solve e^(2x) − 3e^x + 2 = 0. Answer: y = e^x → y² − 3y + 2 = 0 → y = 1 or 2 → x = 0 or ln 2 = 0.693.
  6. (Combine) Write 3 ln 2 − ln 4 as a single logarithm. Answer: ln 8 − ln 4 = ln 2.
  7. (Inverse) Find the inverse of f(x) = e^(3x). Answer: y = e^(3x) → ln y = 3x → f⁻¹(x) = (ln x)/3.
  8. (Model) A car's value is V = 15000e^(−0.2t). Find its value after 4 years. Answer: 15000e^(−0.8) = 15000 × 0.4493 = 6740 pounds.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • log(x + y) is not log x + log y: the product law applies to products only; there is no law for the log of a sum.
  • Forgetting the domain: logs need a positive argument. Roots that make an argument negative or zero are rejected, explicitly.
  • Dividing by log: log 20/log 3 is not log(20/3); the quotient law is for two logs, not a quotient of logs.
  • Base consistency: mixing log₁₀ and ln inside one equation is an error; convert first (ln x = log x / log e).
  • Power law misuse: (log x)² is not 2 log x. Only log(x²) = 2 log x.
  • Quadratic substitution: after solving for y, the answer is x — convert back and solve the exponential equation.
  • Half-life sign: with a decay model k is negative, so half-life = ln 2/|k|; dropping the modulus gives a negative time.
  • Sketch asymptotes: state the asymptote after transformations; e^x + c has asymptote y = c, not y = 0.

title: International GCSE English as a Second Language: Word Formation: Prefixes and Suffixes
content:
International GCSE English as a Second Language: Word Formation: Prefixes and Suffixes

Word formation is the skill of building the word a sentence needs from the word you are given — turning decide into decision, happy into unhappy, careful into carefully. It is tested directly in gap-fill tasks across the 9280 papers and it underpins the range mark in writing: a candidate who can deploy accurate, varied word families reads as a competent user of English. This note builds the system from zero: how English derives nouns, verbs, adjectives and adverbs from base words, which prefixes flip meaning, how spelling changes behave, and the decoding procedure that solves every word-formation question under time pressure.

Word families: one idea, four outfits

Most English base words belong to a family whose members are different parts of speech. The first step of any word-formation question is deciding which member the sentence is dressed for.

Base verbNounAdjectiveAdverb
decidedecisiondecisive / decideddecisively
createcreationcreativecreatively
carecarecareful / carelesscarefully
succeedsuccesssuccessfulsuccessfully
developdevelopmentdeveloping / developed—
comparecomparisoncomparablecomparatively
relaterelation / relationshiprelative / relatedrelatively
beautybeautybeautifulbeautifully

The productive pattern: verbs end in -ify, -ise, -en (justify, modernise, widen); nouns of action end in -tion, -ment, -ance, -ence, -ing (decision, development, performance, existence); adjectives end in -ful, -less, -ous, -ive, -able, -ible, -al, -ic (careful, careless, dangerous, active, readable, possible, natural, scientific); adverbs end in -ly (carefully).

Suffixes by part of speech

Part of speechCommon suffixesExamples
Nouns (people)-er, -or, -ist, -ant, -eeteacher, actor, scientist, assistant, employee
Nouns (things/ideas)-tion, -ment, -ness, -ity, -ance, -ence, -ismeducation, achievement, happiness, ability, importance, difference, tourism
Adjectives-ful, -less, -ous, -ive, -able, -ible, -al, -ic, -y, -ishhopeful, hopeless, famous, attractive, comfortable, sensible, cultural, economic, rainy, childish
Adverbs-lyquickly, easily, surprisingly
Verbs-ise/-ize, -ify, -enorganise, simplify, widen

Note the pairs that change meaning with the suffix: -ful (full of) versus -less (without) — hopeful and hopeless; -ous (having the quality) — danger → dangerous. And the -ing/-ed adjective pair: -ing describes the thing that causes (a tiring day), -ed describes the person affected (a tired student).

Prefixes that flip or shift meaning

PrefixMeaningExamples
un-not, reverseunhappy, unable, unlock
in- / im- / il- / ir-notindependent, impossible, illegal, irregular
dis-not, oppositedisagree, dishonest, disappear
mis-wronglymisunderstand, misspell, mislead
re-againrewrite, rebuild, reapply
over- / under-too much / too littleoverestimate, overcrowded, underestimate
pre- / post-before / afterpreview, precaution / postpone, post-war
anti-againstantibiotic, anti-social
co-, ex-, inter-with, out of, betweencooperate, export, international

The negative prefix is chosen by habit as much as by rule: in- becomes im- before m and p (impossible, impatient), il- before l (illegal), ir- before r (irregular). There is no rule for which words take un- rather than in- — unhappy but inactive — so learn negatives as pairs: unhappy, uncomfortable, unfriendly / inactive, inconvenient, informal / dishonest, disrespectful / misbehave.

Spelling changes when adding suffixes

  • Silent -e dropped before a vowel suffix, kept before a consonant suffix: hope + ful → hopeful (the e goes because a vowel follows) but hope + less → hopeless (the e stays because a consonant follows); like + able → likable (e dropped), manage + ment → management (e kept). Compare the same base twice and the rule becomes visible.
  • y → i before a consonant suffix: happy + ness → happiness; beauty + ful → beautiful; but y stays before -ing and -ous: carrying, curious.
  • Final consonant doubled after a single vowel + consonant in stressed syllables: big + er → bigger; begin + ing → beginning; but visit + or → visitor (stress not on last syllable).
  • -ce/-ge keep the e before -a/-o: courage + ous → courageous (the soft c sound is protected).

Worked example. Build the adjective from beauty and the noun from decide. Step 1: beauty ends in a consonant + y → change y to i before -ful: beautiful. Step 2: decide drops the final e before -tion: decision. Both spellings are the marks; the morphology is only the map.

The decoding procedure for gap-fill word formation

  1. Decide the part of speech the gap needs: read the sentence around the gap. After an article or adjective → noun. After a linking verb (is, seems, becomes) → adjective. After a verb object or sentence end → adverb. Before a noun → adjective.
  2. Decide the meaning direction: positive or negative? prefix needed? does the context say although / but / despite (which often signals the opposite meaning)?
  3. Build the word: apply the family suffix, then the prefix if needed.
  4. Spell-check against the three changes: e-drop, y→i, consonant doubling.
  5. Read the finished sentence once — the built word must fit both grammar and meaning.

Worked example 1. "Her ___ (explain) of the theory was completely ___ (understand)." Step 1: after Her + of the theory → noun; explain → explanation (note the -ation after a plain explanation form: explain → explanation, a family with its own spelling). Step 2: after was completely → adjective; understand with the context "completely ... of the theory" and the likely positive framing → understandable. If the sentence had a but clause ("... was completely ___ , so no one followed it"), the negative would be needed: un-understandable is wrong English; use incomprehensible — some negatives cannot be built, which is why step 5 (read it back) exists.

Worked example 2. "The ___ (industry) revolution changed society ___ (dramatic)." Step 1: before the noun revolution → adjective: industry → industrial (the y becomes i before the -al suffix). Step 2: after the verb changed → adverb: dramatic + ally → dramatically (the adjective dramatic gains -ally, not just -ly — read the finished word back and it must sound right). Answer: industrial, dramatically.

Worked example 3 — the double trap. "It is ___ (possible) to finish in ten minutes." Step 1: after is → adjective. Step 2: the context means cannot be done → negative prefix. Step 3: possible takes im- before p: impossible. Many candidates write unpossible — the prefix table exists to prevent exactly that.

Word formation in the writing tasks

The same skill powers the range band in writing and speaking. Families let one idea appear in several grammatical clothes inside one paragraph: "The decision was difficult. We decided slowly and decisively, and the decisive factor was cost." Deciding (or better, deciding not to repeat the root four times) is a range demonstration; the mark scheme rewards varied and accurate structures, and family variation is the cheapest variety available.

  • Upgrade weak adjective stacks: "very big problem" → "significant problem"; "very good results" → "excellent results"; "very tired" → "exhausted". Precision beats intensifiers.
  • Nominalise for formality: "Because prices rose, we lost customers" → "The rise in prices led to a loss of customers." The -tion and -ness nouns are the engine of formal style.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. Build the word: "The ___ (manage) of the company ___ (success) launched a ___ (create) campaign." Answer: management / successfully / creative. Why: after The → noun; after the subject + verb → adverb; before a noun → adjective.
  2. Build with negative prefix: "His answer was ___ (correct) and showed ___ (complete) ___ (understand) of the topic." Answer: "His answer was incorrect and showed complete misunderstanding of the topic." Why: correct takes the negative in- (incorrect); complete is used as an adjective before the noun and needs no prefix (complete, not completely — an adjective describes the noun misunderstanding); understand becomes the noun misunderstanding with the mis- prefix that signals wrongness.
  3. Spelling focus: happy → happiness; big → bigger; beauty → beautiful; decide → decision. Why: y→i, consonant doubling, y→i before -ful, silent-e drop.
  4. Choose the negative: "It is ___ (legal) to park here and ___ (polite) to shout." Answer: illegal / impolite. Why: il- before l, im- before p.
  5. -ing or -ed: "The trip was ___ (exhaust), and the ___ (sleep) children ___ (immediate) fell asleep." Answer: exhausting / sleepy (or sleeping — but sleepy fits tired children) / immediately.
  6. Rewrite with a noun: "He decided to resign because the job was badly paid." Answer: "His decision to resign was caused by the low pay." Why: decide → decision nominalises the clause for formal style.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Right family, wrong form: writing "explaination" or "decission" — the morphology is right but the spelling loses the mark. Learn each family's spelling as vocabulary.
  • Impossible negatives: unpossible, unlegal, unregular. Learn the prefix with the word: impossible, illegal, irregular.
  • -ing / -ed adjectives swapped: "I am boring in this lesson" says the speaker bores others. The person feels -ed; the thing causes -ing.
  • Double suffixes: "carefulness" when carefulness is fine but "beautifulness" is not (beauty → beauty is a noun already; no -ness). When the gap already has the family noun, add nothing.
  • Adverb after linking verbs: "The results were surprising good" → surprisingly good (adverb modifies the adjective), but "The results were surprisingly good" versus "The results were good" — know that after be/seem/become an adjective follows: "The food smells good", not "well".
  • Spelling changes ignored: write the finished word once in the check step; the three changes (e-drop, y→i, doubling) account for most spelling losses.
  • Capital letters and plurals: if the built word starts a sentence it keeps its capital; if the gap sits after a number or many, the noun needs the plural form — a whole-mark detail in note-completion tasks.
  • Over-engineering: sometimes the base word is correct as given (complete in question 2). If the built form sounds wrong read aloud, try the unchanged word.

Derivation patterns, one page

Word formation is a derivation: a base plus an affix gives a new word, and the arrow shows the step. Read each line as an instruction — identify the base, apply the ending the sentence needs, then apply the spelling change. The affix carries the meaning; the spelling carries the mark.

hope + ful → hopeful Hope is the base noun; -ful is "full of", an adjective suffix; the silent e is dropped because a vowel suffix follows. The same base with a consonant suffix keeps it: hope + less → hopeless.

happy + ness → happiness Happy is base adjective ending in consonant + y; -ness is noun suffix; y becomes i before a consonant suffix. The y stays before -ing and -ous: carrying, curious.

beauty + ful → beautiful Beauty is base noun (consonant + y); -ful is adjective suffix; y → i. The adverb then adds -ly: beautifully, with both changes kept.

big + er → bigger Big is base adjective, one vowel + one final consonant, stressed on the last syllable; -er is comparative suffix; the consonant doubles. Where the stress is not final the consonant stays single: visit + or → visitor.

manage + ment → management Manage is base verb ending in a silent e followed by a consonant suffix; -ment is noun suffix; the e is kept because the suffix begins with a consonant. Contrast like + able → likable, where the vowel suffix drops it.

courage + ous → courageous Courage is base noun ending in -ge; -ous is adjective suffix; the e is kept before a vowel suffix so the soft g survives. Drop it and the word reads with a hard g.

decide → decision Decide is base verb; the noun is not a suffix added to the whole word but a family member with its own spelling — -sion replaces -de. Learn the family, not the rule: decide, decision, decisive, decisively.

dramatic + ally → dramatically Dramatic is adjective ending in -ic; -ally is adverb suffix (not -ly alone). The same pattern gives automatic → automatically, basic → basically. Writing "dramaticly" is the classic spelling loss.

The affix tables in one place

AffixMeaningExample
-ful / -lessfull of / withouthopeful / hopeless
-oushaving the qualitydanger → dangerous
-tion, -sion, -ment, -nessnoun of action or statedecision, achievement, happiness
-er, -or, -ist, -eeperson who does / receivesteacher, actor, employee
un- / in- / im- / il- / ir-notunhappy, inactive, impossible, illegal, irregular
mis- / re- / over- / under-wrongly / again / too much / too littlemisunderstand, rewrite, overestimate, underestimate

Traps specific to the derivation

  • Right family, wrong spelling: explaination, decission, beautifull. The morphology is right; the mark is not.
  • Impossible negatives: unpossible, unlegal, unregular — learn the prefix with the word.
  • -ing versus -ed: the thing is boring, the person is bored.
  • Adding -ness to a word that is already the noun (beautifulness), when the sentence needs the base.

title: Programming Paradigms and Low-Level
content:
Programming Paradigms and Low-Level

Paradigms

  • Procedural: programs as sequences of instructions in procedures — good for straightforward algorithms.
  • Object-oriented: classes encapsulate state (attributes) and behaviour (methods); supports encapsulation, inheritance and polymorphism.
  • Declarative: state what is required, not how (SQL queries, logic programming).
  • Low-level: assembly maps closely to machine code; used where hardware control or timing precision is needed.

Assembly Essentials

The opcode names the operation (LDM load, STR store, ADD, CMP compare, JMP branch, IN/OUT for I/O). The operand names the data. The assembler translates mnemonics to machine code one-to-one; two-pass assemblers resolve forward references via the symbol table.

Addressing Modes

  • Immediate: operand is the constant itself, ADD #5.
  • Direct: operand is the memory address of the data.
  • Indirect: operand is the address OF the address; one extra memory read.
  • Indexed: effective address = base + index register; ideal for arrays.
  • Relative: address given as an offset from the program counter; enables position-independent code.

Fetch-Execute

Fetch: PC gives address, instruction loads into the CIR, PC increments. Decode: control unit interprets the opcode. Execute: the operation runs, possibly updating registers or memory. Interrupts are checked at cycle boundaries.

Exam tips: trace short assembly programs register by register; compute effective addresses for each addressing mode; state one advantage of OOP for large systems.

title: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Angles and Polygons
content:
Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Angles and Polygons

Angles are the simplest measurements in geometry and the most frequently examined: almost every Paper 2 and Paper 4 geometry question ends with a reason written next to a number, and the reason earns as many marks as the calculation. This note builds the whole angle toolkit from zero: the vocabulary of points, lines and angles; the parallel-line rules; the angle sums of triangles, quadrilaterals and polygons; and the full set of circle theorems with the standard reasons examiners accept. Every worked example writes the reason line, because that is how the marks are earned.

Geometrical terms

Geometry has a precise vocabulary, and Paper 2 questions often begin by asking you to use it:

  • Point: a position with no size; named with a capital letter.
  • Line segment: the straight path between two points; a line extends without end.
  • Ray: a line starting at a point and extending in one direction.
  • Parallel lines: always the same distance apart, never meeting (marked with arrows).
  • Perpendicular lines: meeting at 90°.
  • Vertex: a corner where two or more lines meet; vertices in the plural.
  • Polygon: a closed shape with straight sides; regular means all sides equal and all angles equal.

Angle vocabulary: acute (less than 90°), right (90°), obtuse (between 90° and 180°), straight (180°), reflex (between 180° and 360°). Angles on a straight line sum to 180°; angles around a point sum to 360°; vertically opposite angles are equal.

Parallel lines: the three rules

A transversal line crossing two parallel lines creates eight angles, and three relationships do all the work:

RelationshipWhat they look likeRule
Corresponding (F-shape)same position at each intersectionequal
Alternate (Z-shape)opposite sides of the transversal, between the parallelsequal
Co-interior (C-shape)same side of the transversal, between the parallelssum to 180°

Worked example. Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. One angle is 115°. Find the angle in the alternate position and the co-interior angle on the other side.

alternate angle = 115 deg            (alternate angles are equal)
co-interior angle = 180 - 115 = 65 deg (co-interior angles sum to 180)

Always write the reason next to each answer: "alternate angles" or "co-interior angles sum to 180°". Paper 2 awards the reason mark explicitly.

Triangles and quadrilaterals

The angle sum of any triangle is 180° (proof: draw a line through one vertex parallel to the opposite side and use alternate angles). Consequences you must know:

  • Exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles.
  • Isosceles triangle: base angles are equal; the angle bisector from the apex is also the perpendicular bisector of the base.
  • Equilateral triangle: all angles 60°.
  • Quadrilateral: interior angles sum to 360° (split into two triangles).

Worked example. A quadrilateral has angles 85°, 95° and 110°. Find the fourth angle.

sum = 360 deg
fourth = 360 - (85 + 95 + 110) = 360 - 290 = 70 deg

Worked example 2 (exterior angle). In a triangle, an exterior angle is 125° and one opposite interior angle is 48°. Find the other opposite interior angle.

exterior = sum of opposite interiors
125 = 48 + x  ->  x = 77 deg

Angles in polygons

Any n-sided polygon can be split into (n − 2) triangles from one vertex, so:

interior angle sum = (n - 2) x 180 deg

regular polygon: each interior angle = (n - 2) x 180/n
exterior angles of any convex polygon sum to 360 deg
regular polygon: each exterior angle = 360/n
interior + exterior = 180 deg at each vertex

Worked example 1. Find the interior angle sum of a decagon (10 sides) and each interior angle of a regular decagon.

sum = (10 - 2) x 180 = 1440 deg
each = 1440/10 = 144 deg
check with exterior: 360/10 = 36; 180 - 36 = 144 deg

Worked example 2 (working backwards). A regular polygon has each interior angle 150°. Find the number of sides.

exterior angle = 180 - 150 = 30 deg
n = 360/30 = 12 sides  (a regular dodecagon)

Worked example 3 (exterior angles). A pentagon has exterior angles 70°, 80°, 60°, 90°. Find the fifth.

exterior angles sum to 360 deg
fifth = 360 - (70 + 80 + 60 + 90) = 360 - 300 = 60 deg

Circle theorems: the full set

Circle theorems are examined every session, and each answer needs its theorem named. Learn them as pictures with their standard reasons:

TheoremStatementReason to write
Angle at the centrethe angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference subtended by the same arcangle at centre = 2 × angle at circumference
Angle in a semicirclethe angle in a semicircle (subtended by a diameter) is 90°angle in a semicircle is 90°
Same segmentangles subtended by the same arc in the same segment are equalangles in the same segment are equal
Cyclic quadrilateralopposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180°opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180°
Tangent–radiusa tangent meets the radius at the point of contact at 90°tangent is perpendicular to the radius
Two tangentstangents from an external point are equal in lengthtangents from an external point are equal
Alternate segmentthe angle between a tangent and a chord equals the angle in the alternate segmentalternate segment theorem

Worked example 1 (centre). The angle at the centre subtended by an arc is 130°. Find the angle at the circumference subtended by the same arc.

angle at circumference = 130/2 = 65 deg
(reason: angle at centre = 2 x angle at circumference)

Worked example 2 (cyclic quadrilateral). In a cyclic quadrilateral, one pair of opposite angles is 105° and 75°, and the other pair is 4x and 2x. Find x.

opposite angles sum to 180 deg
4x + 2x = 180
6x = 180  ->  x = 30
check the first pair: 105 + 75 = 180, consistent

Two disciplines make this safe: pair the angles that sit opposite each other (a diagonal between them), and verify both pairs satisfy the 180° rule before writing the answer.

Worked example 3 (tangent). A tangent touches a circle of radius 5 cm at T; O is the centre and P is a point on the tangent 12 cm from T. Find OP.

The radius OT is perpendicular to the tangent, so triangle OTP
is right-angled at T.
OP^2 = 5^2 + 12^2 = 25 + 144 = 169
OP = 13 cm

Worked example 4 (alternate segment). A tangent and a chord form an angle of 62° at the point of contact. Find the angle in the alternate segment.

alternate segment theorem: the tangent-chord angle equals the
angle in the alternate segment
answer = 62 deg

Circle theorems: multi-step problems

Paper 4 circle problems chain two or three theorems. The method: mark every angle you can find with its reason, then use each new angle to unlock the next.

Worked example. O is the centre; A, B, C lie on the circle; angle BAC = 35°. Find angle BOC and angle OBC.

angle BOC = 2 x 35 = 70 deg
  (angle at centre = 2 x angle at circumference)
triangle OBC is isosceles (OB = OC = radii)
base angles OBC and OCB are equal:
OBC = (180 - 70)/2 = 55 deg

Worked example 2 (semicircle + cyclic). AB is a diameter; C and D lie on the circle; angle ABC = 40°. Find angle ADC.

angle ACB = 90 deg (angle in a semicircle)
angle BAC = 180 - 90 - 40 = 50 deg
ABCD is cyclic, so angle ADC = 180 - angle ABC? No - opposite
pairs: A with C, B with D. Angle ADC is opposite angle ABC?
The vertices in order are A, B, C, D, so opposite pairs are
(A, C) and (B, D). Angle ADC is at D, opposite angle ABC at B:
angle ADC = 180 - 40 = 140 deg.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Parallel lines) Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal; one co-interior angle is 72°. Find the other. Answer: 108°, because co-interior angles sum to 180°.
  2. (Polygon) Find the interior angle sum of a 15-sided polygon. Answer: (15 − 2) × 180 = 2340°.
  3. (Regular polygon) Each exterior angle of a regular polygon is 24°. Find the number of sides and each interior angle. Answer: n = 360/24 = 15; interior = 180 − 24 = 156°.
  4. (Circle — centre) An angle at the circumference is 28°. Find the angle at the centre subtended by the same arc. Answer: 56°.
  5. (Circle — semicircle) A triangle is inscribed in a semicircle with the diameter as one side; one base angle is 33°. Find the other. Answer: 90° at the circumference, so the other angle is 180 − 90 − 33 = 57°.
  6. (Circle — cyclic) A cyclic quadrilateral has one angle 118°. Find the opposite angle. Answer: 62° (180 − 118).
  7. (Tangent) Two tangents from P touch the circle at A and B; PA = 9 cm. Find PB and explain. Answer: 9 cm — tangents from an external point are equal.
  8. (Multi-step) In a circle, angle ABD = 42° and angle ACD = 42°. What does this tell you about A, B, C, D? Answer: They are concyclic — equal angles subtended by the same chord AD at B and C mean the points lie on the same circle (angles in the same segment).

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Missing reasons: Paper 2 geometry marks include the reason. "x = 65° (angles on a straight line)" scores; a bare "65°" may not.
  • Wrong pairing in cyclic quadrilaterals: opposite angles are the ones separated by a diagonal (A and C, B and D), not adjacent ones. Check both pairs sum to 180°.
  • Alternate versus corresponding: alternate angles form a Z, corresponding an F. Identifying the wrong pattern gives the wrong equality.
  • Interior formula mix-up: interior sum is (n − 2) × 180; each exterior is 360/n. Do not use 360/n for the interior of a regular polygon.
  • Reflex angles: the angle at the centre may be reflex; if the diagram shows an obtuse angle but the geometry demands a reflex one, use 360° − the drawn angle.
  • Assuming radii are parallel or equal to chords: radii are equal to each other, not to chords. Isosceles triangles in circles come from two radii.
  • Tangent–chord angle: the alternate segment theorem requires the angle between the tangent and the chord at the point of contact, not any angle involving the tangent.
  • Diagram not to scale: never measure an angle with a protractor in an exam diagram; the geometry must be calculated. "Diagram not accurately drawn" is a warning, not decoration.

title: Edexcel IAL Computer Science: Processor Fundamentals and Architecture
content:
Edexcel IAL Computer Science: Processor Fundamentals and Architecture

Pearson Edexcel International Advanced Level in Computer Science, Unit 1 Principles of Computer Science (with Unit 3 systems architecture depth): CPU architecture and the fetch–decode–execute cycle, assembly language and bit manipulation, and processors, parallel processing and virtual machines. Every cycle below is traced register by register, and every assembly instruction is annotated with its effect on memory and the accumulator — because the exam hands you a memory dump and asks for the cycle's exact state at each step.

The stored-program machine

The Von Neumann architecture stores program instructions and data in the same memory, fetched by the CPU over shared buses: CPU (control unit, ALU, registers), main memory, backing storage, and input/output, joined by the address, data and control buses. Its weakness, the Von Neumann bottleneck, is that instruction and data traffic contend for one path — the motivation for caches, pipelines and Harvard-style split paths (separate instruction and data caches) in modern designs.

CPU components and registers

RegisterRole in the cycle
Program counter (PC)Holds the address of the next instruction; incremented after the fetch
Memory address register (MAR)Holds the address being accessed on this bus transfer
Memory data register (MDR/MBR)Holds the instruction or data just fetched or about to be written
Current instruction register (CIR)Holds the instruction being decoded and executed
Accumulator (ACC)Holds the running result of ALU operations

The control unit fetches, decodes and orchestrates; the ALU performs arithmetic and logic; the clock paces each micro-step; the address bus is one-way (CPU → memory/devices), the data bus two-way, the control bus carries read/write/interrupt/clock signals.

The fetch–decode–execute cycle, traced

Memory (opcode / operand; opcode 01 = LOAD, 10 = ADD, 11 = STORE):

  5: 01 001000   LOAD 8
  6: 10 001001   ADD 9
  7: 11 001010   STORE 10
  8: 0000 0101   (5)
  9: 0000 0011   (3)
 10: 0000 0000   (empty)

Cycle 1 - LOAD 8:
  FETCH:   PC = 5 → MAR = 5; control bus READ; MDR = 01 001000;
           CIR = 01 001000; PC = PC + 1 = 6.
  DECODE:  opcode 01 = LOAD: copy memory[operand] to ACC.
  EXECUTE: operand 001000 = 8; MAR = 8; READ; MDR = 5; ACC = 5.

Cycle 2 - ADD 9:
  FETCH:   PC = 6 → MAR = 6; READ; MDR = 10 001001; CIR = same; PC = 7.
  DECODE:  opcode 10 = ADD: ACC = ACC + memory[operand].
  EXECUTE: MAR = 9; READ; MDR = 3; ALU: ACC + MDR = 5 + 3 = 8; ACC = 8.

Cycle 3 - STORE 10:
  FETCH:   PC = 7 → MAR = 7; READ; MDR = 11 001010; CIR = same; PC = 8.
  DECODE:  opcode 11 = STORE: memory[operand] = ACC.
  EXECUTE: MAR = 10; MDR = 8 (from ACC); WRITE; memory[10] = 0000 1000.

Interrupts fit between cycles: complete the current instruction, save the PC,
run the interrupt service routine, restore the PC, resume.

The examiner's checklist: PC → MAR for the fetch; MDR → CIR; PC incremented at fetch (not execute); execute behaviour depends entirely on the opcode; the MAR is reused in execute to address the operand.

Assembly language

Assembly is a thin, human-readable veneer over machine code: one mnemonic per instruction (LOAD, ADD, STORE, JMP, CMP), assembled to binary by an assembler. It is low-level (tied to the processor's instruction set), fast, and used where direct hardware control matters — embedded firmware, drivers, performance-critical inner loops. Instruction sets: CISC (many complex instructions, variable length, microcoded — x86) versus RISC (few simple instructions, one cycle each, hardwired — ARM). Mobile devices favour RISC for power efficiency; the trade-off is instructions-per-task versus cycles-per-instruction.

Assembly concepts with a small program (accumulator machine):

  START:  LOAD  X      ; ACC = value at X
          ADD   Y      ; ACC = ACC + value at Y
          STORE Z      ; Z = ACC
          CMP   K      ; compare ACC with K (sets flags)
          JMPLE DONE   ; jump to DONE if ACC <= K (flag-driven)
          LOAD  Z      ; otherwise adjust
          SUB   K
          STORE Z
  DONE:   HALT

Key ideas the exam tests: labels are addresses (START, DONE are memory
locations); operands address memory; jumps make selection and loops; flags
(Z for zero, C for carry, N for negative, V for overflow) are set by CMP and
tested by conditional jumps - the mechanism behind every IF and WHILE once
compiled.

Bit manipulation (statement 4.3) is done with logical shifts and masks: AND with a mask to extract bits (flags, packed fields), OR to set a bit, XOR to toggle, NOT to invert, shift left/right to multiply/divide by powers of two. Extracting the third byte of a packed word: shift right 16, then AND 0xFF — each step traced in binary in exam answers.

Performance and parallelism

  • Factors: clock speed (ticks per second), cores (independent instruction streams), cache size and levels (L1 fastest/smallest, L3 slowest/largest), bus width (bits per transfer), word length (bits the CPU processes at once), instruction set (CISC/RISC trade-off), and pipelining (overlapping fetch/decode/execute of consecutive instructions — stalls occur on branches).
  • Parallel processing: bit-level (wider words process more bits at once), instruction-level (pipelines and superscalar execution), data-level (SIMD — same operation on many data items: GPU rendering), task-level (different programs or subtasks on different cores). Amdahl's law bounds the gain: the sequential fraction limits speed-up regardless of core count.
  • Virtual machines: a software emulation of another machine. Hardware VMs (hypervisors like VMware/KVM) run several OS instances on one physical host — server consolidation, isolation, easy backup and migration. Language VMs (the JVM, the CLR) execute bytecode portably: compile once to bytecode, run anywhere the VM exists — platform independence at the cost of a translation overhead versus native code.
Worked: a program is 25% sequential. Speed-up with 8 cores (Amdahl):

  speed-up = 1 / (0.25 + 0.75 / 8) = 1 / (0.25 + 0.09375) = 1 / 0.34375 = 2.91

Eight cores give under a threefold gain - the parallel hardware cannot help
the sequential quarter, which is the whole point of the question.

Worked example: one program through the whole stack

Source (high level):     z = x + y
Assembly (low level):    LOAD X / ADD Y / STORE Z
Machine code:            01 001000 / 10 001001 / 11 001010  (as above)

The assembler resolves labels to addresses; the CPU executes each instruction
through fetch-decode-execute; the compiler that produced the assembly chose the
register usage and the instruction order. Three representations, one behaviour -
and the exam question naming "which stage produced which artefact" targets
exactly these three columns.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Saying the PC increments during execute; it increments after the fetch.
  • Confusing MAR (address) with MDR (data) — the most-marked pair in Unit 1.
  • Claiming assembly is "almost high level"; it is one-to-one with machine instructions and hardware-specific.
  • Forgetting that CMP sets flags and conditional jumps read them — without that link, selection and loops have no mechanism.
  • Answering parallelism questions with "more cores = faster" only; Amdahl's law and the type of parallelism (bit/instruction/data/task) are the marks.
  • Describing a language VM as an emulator of hardware only; the JVM executes bytecode — portability is its purpose.
