title: Continuous Random Variables
content:
Continuous Random Variables

Probability Density Functions

A continuous variable X is described by a density f(x) with f(x) ≥ 0 and ∫f(x)dx = 1 over all x. Probabilities are areas:

  • P(a ≤ X ≤ b) = ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx

Single points have zero probability, so strict or loose inequalities make no difference: P(X < 2) = P(X ≤ 2).

Finding Unknown Constants

Piecewise densities carry an unknown k: impose that the total area is 1 (and continuity at joins where required). One equation, one unknown.

Example: f(x) = kx on 0 ≤ x ≤ 2. Total area: k·(2²/2) = 2k = 1, so k = ½.

Expectation and Variance

  • E(X) = ∫x·f(x) dx
  • E(X²) = ∫x²·f(x) dx
  • Var(X) = E(X²) − (E(X))²

The mean is the balancing point of the area under the density. For symmetric densities the mean sits at the symmetry point — worth spotting before integrating.

The Median and Mode

The median m solves ∫₋∞ᵐ f(x) dx = 0.5 (left half of the area). The mode is the x maximising f(x). For uniform densities the median is the midpoint.

Uniform Distribution

If f(x) = 1/(b − a) on [a, b], every point is equally likely. Then E(X) = (a + b)/2 and Var(X) = (b − a)²/12 — memorise both; they are quick exam marks.

Exam tips: always verify ∫f = 1 before computing anything else. Sketch the density — area intuitions catch algebra slips. Median questions are integration-to-0.5 questions; set them up before calculating.

title: IGCSE Biology: Biotechnology and Genetic Modification
content:
IGCSE Biology: Biotechnology and Genetic Modification

Biotechnology is the industrial use of living organisms, cells or their products — from 8000-year-old yeast fermentation to gene-edited crops. This note covers the classical applications (biogas, fermenters, enzymes in industry), then builds genetic modification from the DNA mechanics up: how a gene is cut, copied and inserted; how marker genes screen for success; and every benefit and risk argued with mechanisms rather than slogans. The exam rewards balanced, mechanism-backed arguments, so each claim in the final section carries its biological reasoning.

What biotechnology includes

Classical biotechnology: fermentation — yeast converting glucose to ethanol and carbon dioxide anaerobically (bread, beer, wine), and bacterial fermentation making yoghurt (Lactobacillus converts lactose to lactic acid, lowering pH and setting the milk protein), cheese (rennet and bacteria), and antibiotics (Penicillium moulds in large fermenters). Biogas: anaerobic digestion of sewage, manure and crop waste by methanogenic bacteria produces methane (biogas) for heating and electricity — a renewable fuel that also disposes of waste; small-scale digesters are widely used in developing countries. Enzymes in industry: proteases in biological detergents (digesting protein stains at low temperature), amylases in baking and brewing (breaking starch to sugar), isomerase converting glucose to fructose (a sweeter sugar for low-calorie foods), lactase producing lactose-free milk, and pectinases clarifying fruit juices. Advantages of using enzymes: they work at low temperatures and pressures (saving energy), are specific (fewer by-products), and are biodegradable. Immobilised enzymes (attached to beads or membranes) can be reused continuously and kept out of the product — cutting costs in continuous-flow processes.

Fermenters

Industrial fermentation grows microorganisms in a fermenter (a large sterile stainless-steel vessel) to make products such as antibiotics, single-cell protein (mycoprotein from Fusarium for food), enzymes, vaccines and organic acids. Conditions controlled automatically: temperature (water jacket or cooling coils — microbial respiration releases heat and enzymes denature above the optimum), pH (acids/alkalis added as growth changes the pH), oxygen supply (sterile air pumped in and stirred to keep aerobic organisms respiring and the mixture uniform), nutrients (sterile glucose/mineral broth fed in), and sterility (no contaminating microbes — the vessel is steam-sterilised and the air filtered). Agitation (stirring) keeps nutrients and oxygen evenly distributed and prevents clumping. Batch versus continuous culture: batch is run in cycles and harvested at once; continuous removes product and adds medium continuously for constant output.

Genetic modification: the core technique

Genetic modification (GM, genetic engineering) transfers a gene from one species into another so the recipient expresses a new trait. Step 1: identify and isolate the desired gene — the gene sequence is known, and it is copied many times by the polymerase chain reaction (PCR) or taken from a gene library. Step 2: cut the DNA — restriction endonuclease enzymes cut at specific recognition sequences, often leaving "sticky ends"; the same enzyme cuts the vector (carrier). Step 3: insert the gene into a vector — most often a bacterial plasmid (small circular DNA); DNA ligase joins the sugar-phosphate backbone, forming recombinant DNA. Step 4: transfer into the target organism — the plasmid is taken up by bacteria (transformation), or the gene is inserted into plant cells by Agrobacterium tumefaciens or a gene gun, or into animal embryos by microinjection. Step 5: screen for success — a marker gene (e.g. antibiotic resistance or fluorescent protein) in the vector identifies the transformed cells; only cells containing the recombinant DNA survive the antibiotic or glow. Step 6: grow the modified organism and test the trait. The same gene inserted into a different organism usually works because the genetic code is universal — DNA codes the same amino acids in all living things.

Worked example: making insulin and Bt crops

Human insulin by GM bacteria: Step 1 — the human insulin gene is identified and copied (PCR). Step 2 — restriction enzymes cut the gene and a bacterial plasmid; sticky ends allow pairing. Step 3 — DNA ligase seals the gene into the plasmid, forming recombinant DNA. Step 4 — the plasmid is inserted into E. coli by transformation with heat shock and calcium ions. Step 5 — bacteria are grown in a fermenter with the marker gene confirming success; the bacteria transcribe and translate the human gene and secrete insulin, which is purified. Advantages over pig/bovine insulin: exact human sequence (fewer allergic reactions), unlimited cheap supply, consistent purity. GM crops with examples and mechanisms: Bt crops carry a bacterial gene (from Bacillus thuringiensis) coding for an insecticidal toxin protein, killing pests that eat the plant (less chemical pesticide needed); Golden Rice carries daffodil/bacterial genes for beta-carotene (provitamin A) to combat vitamin A deficiency and blindness; herbicide-tolerant soya survives broad-spectrum weedkiller so weeds can be sprayed on the crop; drought- or salt-tolerant varieties protect yields in marginal lands; virus-resistant papaya protects against ringspot virus. GM animals: fast-growing salmon with a growth-hormone gene; goats producing spider silk proteins in milk; pigs with phytase improving phosphorus uptake to cut phosphate pollution.

GM applications at a glance

OrganismGene addedResult
E. coli bacteriaHuman insulin geneProducing human insulin cheaply in fermenters
Bt crops (maize, cotton)Bacillus thuringiensis toxin geneInsecticidal leaves, less chemical pesticide
Golden Ricebeta-carotene genesProvitamin A, reducing vitamin A deficiency
Herbicide-tolerant soyaHerbicide resistance geneSurvives weedkiller, easier weed control
PapayaVirus coat protein geneResistance to ringspot virus

Benefits and risks — argue with mechanisms

Benefits: higher crop yields and food security (feeding a growing population); crops with added nutrition (Golden Rice addressing vitamin A deficiency); disease-, pest-, drought- and salt-resistant varieties reducing losses and chemical use; faster livestock growth; cheaper pharmaceuticals (insulin, clotting factors); reduced pesticide run-off (Bt crops); bioremediation (bacteria engineered to digest oil spills or break down plastics). Risks and concerns: unintended effects on human health (new proteins might be allergenic or toxic — though tested rigorously); gene transfer to wild relatives creating super-weeds (herbicide resistance escaping into wild populations); harm to non-target species (Bt pollen killing monarch butterfly larvae is the classic study); loss of biodiversity if a few engineered varieties dominate; corporate control of seed (patents raise costs for farmers, who cannot save seed); ethical/religious objections to crossing species boundaries ("playing God"); antibiotic resistance marker genes potentially transferring to pathogens; and monoculture vulnerability. The exam's standard instruction is "evaluate" or "discuss" — give at least two benefits and two risks with biological reasoning, then a justified conclusion. The balance is genuinely contested: the science (gene flow, allergenicity) can be tested, while the ethics and economics are value judgements.

Bioprocessing and other applications

Bioremediation: microorganisms (naturally occurring or engineered) break down pollutants — oil-eating bacteria (Alcanivorax) after spills, digesters breaking down sewage, fungi accumulating heavy metals from contaminated soil (mycoremediation). Gene therapy: replacing or supplementing a faulty gene in a patient's cells to treat genetic disorders (cystic fibrosis trials deliver a functional CFTR gene to airway cells using a viral vector); somatic changes affect only the individual, while germline editing (heritable) is internationally restricted. Cloning: tissue culture micropropagation (growing whole plants from tiny explants — identical, disease-free stock); animal cloning by nuclear transfer (Dolly the sheep — nucleus from a body cell into an enucleated egg); advantages (preserve elite genetics, revive endangered species) and disadvantages (low success rate, reduced diversity, welfare issues). DNA fingerprinting in forensics and paternity: variable DNA regions are amplified by PCR, separated by gel electrophoresis and compared; matching profiles establish identity. Each of these is examinable at mechanism level: be able to state the tool (restriction enzyme, ligase, vector, PCR) and the purpose for each.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Writing that GM "mixes all the genes of two species": only one or a few specific genes are transferred.
  • Confusing restriction enzymes (cut DNA) with ligase (joins DNA fragments) in the technique sequence.
  • Forgetting the vector (plasmid): genes do not enter bacteria by magic — a carrier is required.
  • Leaving out the marker gene when asked "how do scientists know which cells have been modified".
  • Saying fermenters "feed bacteria sugar only": a fermenter controls temperature, pH, oxygen and sterility — name two or more controls for full marks.
  • Answering a GM-evaluation question with only benefits (or only risks): the command word "evaluate" requires both sides plus a judgement.
  • Claiming GM food is "proven safe" or "proven dangerous": the scientific position is that approved GM foods pass rigorous testing, while specific risks (gene flow, allergens) are assessed case by case.
  • Confusing biotechnology (whole organisms/products in industry) with genetic modification (transferring specific genes) — GM is a subset.

Exam-style questions and answers

Q1. Describe how a gene for human growth hormone could be inserted into bacteria. (5 marks) Answer: isolate the gene and copy it (1); cut the gene and a plasmid with the same restriction enzyme (1); sticky ends allow the gene to pair with the plasmid (1); DNA ligase joins them to form recombinant DNA (1); plasmid is taken up by the bacteria which now express the gene (1).

Q2. Explain the role of a marker gene in genetic modification. (2 marks) Answer: the marker (e.g. antibiotic resistance or fluorescence) is inserted alongside the desired gene (1); only cells containing the recombinant DNA survive the antibiotic or glow, identifying successful transformation (1).

Q3. Explain how Bt crops reduce the use of chemical pesticides. (3 marks) Answer: the plants carry a bacterial gene for an insecticidal toxin (1); pests that eat the leaves are killed by the toxin (1); so fewer chemical sprays are needed, reducing run-off and harm to non-target species (1).

Q4. Describe two uses of microorganisms in biotechnology. (4 marks) Answer: yeast ferments glucose to ethanol for bread and alcoholic drinks (1); Penicillium in fermenters produces the antibiotic penicillin (1); bacteria make yoghurt and cheese by converting lactose to lactic acid (1); anaerobic bacteria in biogas digesters produce methane from waste (1).

Q5. Evaluate the use of genetically modified crops. (4 marks) Answer: benefits — higher yields and food security, added nutrients like Golden Rice, less pesticide use with Bt crops (1 per two); risks — gene flow creating super-weeds, effects on non-target insects, corporate control of seed (1 per two); judgement balancing tested benefits against managed risks in regulation (1).

title: IGCSE Physics: Magnetism and Electromagnetism
content:
IGCSE Physics: Magnetism and Electromagnetism

Cambridge IGCSE Physics 0625 (2026–2028), Topic 4 Electricity and magnetism: statements 4.1 Simple phenomena of magnetism and 4.5 Electromagnetic effects. Magnetism and electricity are two faces of one interaction: moving charge makes magnetic fields, and changing magnetic fields make currents. That single loop of cause and effect explains generators, motors, transformers and every device that turns movement into electricity or electricity into movement.

Magnets and magnetic fields

A magnet has two poles, north and south. Like poles repel; unlike poles attract; and a magnet freely suspended turns to line up with the Earth's magnetic field, which is why a compass points north. Magnetic materials (iron, steel, nickel, cobalt) are attracted to magnets; non-magnetic materials are not. Induced magnetism is what happens when a magnetic material near a magnet becomes a magnet itself: a paper clip picked up by a magnet can pick up a second clip. Soft iron makes temporary magnets (it magnetises and demagnetises easily — good for electromagnets and relays); steel makes permanent magnets (hard to demagnetise — good for compass needles).

A magnetic field is the region around a magnet where another magnet experiences a force. Its direction is the direction a north pole would move — out of a north pole and into a south pole. Field lines never cross, and their spacing shows the field strength: close together for a strong field, spread out for a weak one (Supplement: the field is the region of influence, and its strength is represented by the line density). Plotting fields is done with a small plotting compass on a sheet of paper over the magnet; the compass needle traces the lines from pole to pole.

Electromagnetic induction

Move a magnet into a coil of wire and a voltage appears across the coil: this is electromagnetic induction, discovered by Faraday. The induced e.m.f. (and the current it drives if the circuit is closed) is bigger when:

  • the magnet or coil moves faster;
  • the magnet is stronger;
  • the coil has more turns;
  • the coil's core is soft iron (which concentrates the magnetic field).

It is the change in the field that induces a voltage — a stationary magnet inside a coil does nothing. Supplement: Lenz's law. The induced current always flows in a direction that opposes the change producing it: push a north pole in and the coil's near face becomes north to push back; pull it out and the coil becomes south to hold it. Energy conservation demands this — the mechanical work done pushing against the opposition is exactly the electrical energy induced.

The a.c. generator

A generator turns kinetic energy into electrical energy by spinning a coil in a magnetic field (or a magnet inside a coil). As the coil rotates, the amount of magnetic field passing through it changes continuously, so an e.m.f. is induced that rises, falls and reverses, producing alternating current.

  • The coil ends are joined to two slip rings, each touching a brush (a carbon block) that carries the current to the external circuit.
  • Supplement: the e.m.f.–time graph is a sine wave; it is zero when the coil is vertical (moving parallel to the field) and maximum when the coil is horizontal (cutting the field fastest).

A power station generator is the same machine scaled up: steam, water or wind spins the coil, and the faster it spins or the stronger the field, the greater the peak e.m.f.

The magnetic effect of a current

A current in a wire produces a magnetic field around it — the discovery that links electricity and magnetism. The field lines are concentric circles centred on the wire, and the field is stronger closer to the wire. The right-hand grip rule gives the direction: point the thumb along the conventional current and the curled fingers show the direction of the field lines.

Winding the wire into a solenoid (coil) concentrates the field into a pattern just like a bar magnet's: strong and uniform inside the coil, out of one end and into the other. The field is stronger with more turns and a larger current, and an iron core inside the coil makes an electromagnet — a magnet that can be switched on and off, made stronger at will, and loses its magnetism when the current stops.

  • Relay: a small current in an electromagnet's coil attracts a soft-iron armature that closes a second, high-current circuit. It lets a low-voltage circuit switch a dangerous mains circuit safely.
  • Loudspeaker: alternating current in a coil in the field of a permanent magnet makes the coil (attached to the cone) vibrate with the frequency of the current, producing sound waves. The loudspeaker turns electrical energy into sound energy; a microphone does the reverse.

Force on a current-carrying conductor

A wire carrying a current in a magnetic field experiences a force — the principle of the motor and of the moving-coil loudspeaker. The force is largest when the wire is perpendicular to the field and zero when it runs parallel to it.

force on a conductor = magnetic flux density x current x length        F = B I L
  • F: force in newtons (N); B: magnetic flux density in tesla (T); I: current in amperes (A); L: length of wire in the field in metres (m). The force direction is given by Fleming's left-hand rule and is a vector: swap any two of field, current and force and the force reverses.

Fleming's left-hand rule: first finger Field, seCond finger Current, thuMb Motion. The three fingers held mutually at right angles give all three directions. The force can be increased by raising the current, using a stronger magnet, or making the wire longer in the field (more turns on the coil). Supplement: a charged particle moving through a magnetic field is deflected for the same reason, which is how a beam of electrons can be bent on a screen.

The d.c. motor

A coil carrying current in a magnetic field experiences opposite forces on its two sides, producing a turning effect (a couple) that rotates the coil. A simple d.c. motor has the coil, a commutator (a split-ring), brushes, and a permanent-magnet field. The split-ring commutator is the clever part: every half turn it reverses the current in the coil, so the forces always push the same way and the rotation continues instead of stalling at the vertical position.

  • The rotation speeds up with a larger current, a stronger field or more turns on the coil.
  • Energy conversion: electrical energy in, kinetic energy out (plus heat from the coil's resistance).
  • Running the motor in reverse — driving the coil instead of feeding it — turns it into a generator, which is how a bicycle dynamo works.

The transformer

A transformer changes the size of an alternating voltage using electromagnetic induction. It has two coils wound on the same soft-iron core: the alternating current in the primary coil makes an alternating magnetic field in the core, which induces an alternating e.m.f. in the secondary coil.

secondary voltage / primary voltage = secondary turns / primary turns        Vs / Vp = Ns / Np
  • Vp and Vs: voltages in volts (V); Np and Ns: numbers of turns on each coil. A step-up transformer has more turns on the secondary; a step-down has fewer.
  • Supplement: for an ideal transformer, power in = power out, so Vp Ip = Vs Is; stepping the voltage up steps the current down, and vice versa.

Transformers are why the National Grid transmits at 11 000 V or more. For the same power, P = IV means a high voltage needs a small current, and the energy wasted heating the cables is I²R — squaring a small current makes the waste tiny. Power stations therefore step up for transmission and step down again at substations and on poles for safe domestic use. An ideal transformer has no energy losses; real ones lose a little to heating in the coils, to eddy currents in the core (reduced by a laminated core) and to magnetising the core, giving efficiencies of 95 per cent or better.

Worked example: transmission losses

A power station sends 20 MW at 250 V along cables of total resistance 0.10 Ω, and again at 25 000 V.

current at 250 V = P / V = 20 000 000 / 250 = 80 000 A
power wasted = I² R = 80 000² × 0.10 = 640 MW   (impossible in practice - the cable would melt)
current at 25 000 V = 20 000 000 / 25 000 = 800 A
power wasted = 800² × 0.10 = 64 000 W = 64 kW

Stepping the voltage up one hundredfold cuts the current one hundredfold and the wasted power ten thousandfold — 64 kW instead of 640 MW. That is the entire reason the grid uses transformers.

Common mistakes

  • Using Fleming's left-hand rule for generators; the left hand is for motors (force on a current), while generators and induction use the idea that the induced current opposes the change (Lenz's law).
  • Saying a stationary magnet in a coil induces a current; only a changing field does.
  • Forgetting to square the current in the cable-loss equation, or using the transmission voltage instead of the current in I²R.
  • Drawing transformer field lines that do not link both coils; the coils share one core and one magnetic field.
  • Assuming transformers work on d.c.; a steady d.c. produces no changing field and no induced e.m.f. in the secondary.
  • Reversing the turns ratio: step-up means more turns on the secondary, so Vs is bigger than Vp.
  • Mixing up where the force points: current along the second finger, field along the first, motion along the thumb, and all three at right angles.
  • Forgetting that the commutator reverses the current every half turn; without it the coil would stop at the vertical.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 4, 3 marks). A transformer has 500 primary turns and 2000 secondary turns with a 230 V input. Calculate the output voltage and state the transformer type.

Answer: Vs = Vp × Ns/Np = 230 × 2000/500 = 920 V. It is a step-up transformer because the secondary has more turns.

Question 2 (Paper 4, 3 marks). A straight wire carries 4.0 A perpendicular to a 0.25 T field. Find the force on 0.30 m of wire.

Answer: F = BIL = 0.25 × 4.0 × 0.30 = 0.30 N, in the direction given by Fleming's left-hand rule.

Question 3 (Paper 2 style). Which change increases the e.m.f. induced in a coil? A holding the magnet still inside it; B moving the magnet faster; C using fewer turns; D using a weaker magnet. Answer: B. Faster motion means a faster change of field through the coil.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 6 marks). Explain how a transformer works and why the grid transmits power at high voltage.

Answer: The a.c. in the primary coil produces an alternating magnetic field in the soft-iron core. That changing field passes through the secondary coil and induces an alternating e.m.f. in it by electromagnetic induction. The size of the output voltage depends on the turns ratio: Vs/Vp = Ns/Np. For transmission, P = IV, so the same power can be sent at high voltage and low current. The energy wasted heating the cables is I²R, so a smaller current greatly reduces the wasted energy; the voltage is then stepped down with transformers for safe domestic use.

Question 5 (Paper 4, 3 marks). State two ways to increase the turning effect on the coil of a d.c. motor.

Answer: Increase the current, use a stronger magnetic field (or increase the flux density), or wind more turns on the coil. Any two, with the reasoning that the force on each side of the coil is F = BIL, so bigger B or I or L gives a bigger force.

Question 6 (Paper 6 style). Describe an experiment to show the pattern of the magnetic field around a bar magnet.

Answer: Place the bar magnet on a sheet of paper and sprinkle iron filings (or use a small plotting compass). Tap the paper gently; the filings line up along the field. The compass needle is placed at several points and its direction marked with an arrow pointing away from the north pole; the marks are joined into smooth field lines from north to south, close together near the poles where the field is strongest.

Fields move charges and magnets; inside the atom, a different kind of energy is stored: Nuclear Physics next.

Equations and symbols

Two groups of equations share this topic: the force on a current-carrying conductor, and the transformer relations that make the national grid work. The transformer equations are ratios, so the units must match on each side and efficiencies are quoted per second.

Force on a conductor

F = BIL
Key: F = force on the conductor (N); B = magnetic flux density (T, tesla); I = current (A); L = length of conductor inside the field (m). The force is greatest when the conductor is at right angles to the field, and zero when it is parallel to it.

B = F / (IL)
Key: B = magnetic flux density (T); F = force (N); I = current (A); L = length in the field (m). One tesla is one newton per ampere-metre.

F = 0 when the conductor is parallel to the field
Key: the direction rule (Fleming's left hand): first finger = field, second finger = current, thumb = force, all mutually at right angles. Reversing either the current or the field reverses the force.

Transformers

V(s) / V(p) = N(s) / N(p)
Key: V(s) = secondary voltage (V); V(p) = primary voltage (V); N(s) = number of turns on the secondary coil; N(p) = number of turns on the primary. More secondary turns than primary means a step-up transformer.

I(p) / I(s) = N(s) / N(p)
Key: I(p), I(s) = primary and secondary currents (A). A step-up transformer raises the voltage and lowers the current in the same ratio.

V(p) I(p) = V(s) I(s)
Key: the ideal-transformer condition: input power equals output power (W). Real transformers lose some energy to heat in the coils and core, so the output power is slightly lower.

efficiency = (V(s) I(s)) / (V(p) I(p)) × 100%
Key: both products are powers in watts; the result is a percentage below 100 for a real transformer.

P(loss) = I²R
Key: P(loss) = power wasted as heat in the transmission cables (W); I = current in the cables (A); R = cable resistance (Ω). This is why the grid steps voltage up: at ten times the voltage the current falls tenfold and the loss falls a hundredfold.

P = VI (power transmitted)
Key: P = power carried (W); V = transmission voltage (V); I = current (A).

Magnetic rules worth stating as equations of condition

induced e.m.f. requires a changing magnetic field or relative motion
Key: a conductor experiences an induced voltage only while the flux through it changes; a stationary magnet beside a stationary coil induces nothing.

like poles repel, unlike poles attract
Key: the field lines run from a north pole to a south pole outside the magnet; the force between two wires carrying current in the same direction is attractive, and in opposite directions repulsive.

title: Number — Ratio, Rate and Proportion — Study Notes
content:
Number — Ratio, Rate and Proportion

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): ratio notation, sharing, direct & inverse proportion (including squares/cubes), unit rates.

1. Simplifying and sharing ratios

  • Scale both parts by the same factor: 250 g : 0.4 kg = 250 : 400 = 5 : 8.
  • Share $200 in 3 : 5 → 8 parts → $75 : $125.
  • Part–whole: 3 : 5 ⇒ 3/8 of the total. Given one share, find others by scaling.

Example: A : B = 3 : 4 and B : C = 2 : 5 ⇒ A : B : C = 3 : 4 : 10 (make B equal: ×2).

2. Direct proportion

y = kx. Best method: find the unit value, then multiply.

Example: 5 pens cost $3.25 → 1 pen $0.65 → 8 pens $5.20.

Squared/cubed proportion: y ∝ x². y = 54 when x = 3 ⇒ k = 6 ⇒ y = 6x²; at x = 5, y = 150.

3. Inverse proportion

y = k/x (product constant). 4 workers 6 days ⇒ 24 worker-days ⇒ 8 workers take 3 days. Square-law: y ∝ 1/x².

4. Rates

Unit rates (per item, per litre), exchange rates (draw the arrow to the target currency), best buys (price per unit, careful with multi-packs). Speed/density/pressure are compound-measure rates (Mensuration).

Exam tips: write the proportional equation with k before substituting; check proportion type — "more workers, fewer days" = inverse.

Writing and simplifying ratios

A ratio a : b is simplified by dividing both parts by their highest common factor. Ratios with decimals or fractions are multiplied up to whole numbers first. A ratio shared between a total uses the total number of parts as the divisor.

Direct and inverse proportion

In direct proportion, y = kx, so doubling x doubles y. In inverse proportion, y = k ÷ x, so doubling x halves y. Find k from a known pair of values, then use it to answer the question.

Speed, density and rates

Rate questions are solved by identifying the two quantities and the unit of the answer. Speed = distance ÷ time; average speed for a journey is the total distance divided by the total time, not the mean of the speeds. Exchange rates and recipe scaling use the same unitary method: find the value of one unit first.

Mathematics — OL. probability scale, combined events, tree diagrams, conditional probability, relative frequency.

  • 1. Basics
  • 2. Combined events
  • 3. Tree diagrams
  • 4. Conditional probability
  • 5. Relative frequency (experimental)

How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

Key points to remember

Probability is a number from 0 to 1, where 0 is impossible and 1 is certain. For equally likely outcomes, the probability is the number of favourable outcomes divided by the total. The probabilities of all outcomes in a set add up to 1.

For combined events, use a sample space diagram or a tree diagram. Multiply along the branches for "and" and add the results for "or". For the mean of grouped data, use the midpoint of each class and divide the total of the products by the frequency total. Show the formula you use, so the method mark is available.

title: A Level Mathematics: Integration II
content:
A Level Mathematics: Integration II

A2 integration extends the AS power rule to trigonometric and exponential functions, then adds the two general techniques — substitution and integration by parts — plus partial fractions, definite integrals with the new functions, areas, and differential equations. Each technique is presented with its recognition cue: which integrand signals which method is the skill the exam rewards.

Standard integrals to know

integral of sin(ax) dx = -(1/a) cos(ax) + c
integral of cos(ax) dx = (1/a) sin(ax) + c
integral of sec²(ax) dx = (1/a) tan(ax) + c
integral of e^(ax) dx = (1/a) e^(ax) + c
integral of (1/x) dx = ln|x| + c
integral of (1/(ax + b)) dx = (1/a) ln|ax + b| + c

Worked example. Find ∫ (3 sin 2x + 4e^(−x)) dx.

= -(3/2) cos 2x - 4e^(-x) + c

Worked example 2. Find ∫ (1/(3x + 1)) dx.

= (1/3) ln|3x + 1| + c

Trigonometric identities before integrating

Products and even powers of sine and cosine do not integrate directly; use an identity first.

sin² x = (1 - cos 2x)/2
cos² x = (1 + cos 2x)/2
sin A cos B = (1/2)[sin(A + B) + sin(A - B)]

Worked example. Find ∫ sin²x dx.

= integral of (1 - cos 2x)/2 dx = x/2 - (sin 2x)/4 + c

Worked example 2. Find ∫ sin 3x cos x dx.

sin 3x cos x = (1/2)[sin 4x + sin 2x]
integral = -(1/8) cos 4x - (1/4) cos 2x + c

Integration by substitution

let u = g(x), du = g'(x) dx; rewrite the whole integral in u
for definite integrals, change the limits too

Worked example 1. Find ∫ 2x(x² + 1)⁵ dx.

u = x² + 1, du = 2x dx
integral becomes ∫ u⁵ du = u⁶/6 + c = (x² + 1)⁶/6 + c

Worked example 2 (definite). Find ∫ from 0 to 1 of x e^(x²) dx.

u = x², du = 2x dx, so x dx = du/2
limits: x = 0 → u = 0;  x = 1 → u = 1
= (1/2) ∫ from 0 to 1 e^u du = (1/2)(e - 1) = 0.859

Worked example 3 (trigonometric). Find ∫ cos x sin³x dx.

u = sin x, du = cos x dx
∫ u³ du = sin⁴ x/4 + c

Integration by parts

∫ u dv = uv - ∫ v du

choose u to be the part that simplifies when differentiated
(LIATE: logs, inverse trig, algebra, trig, exponential)

Worked example 1. Find ∫ x e^x dx.

u = x, dv = e^x dx  →  du = dx, v = e^x
= x e^x - ∫ e^x dx = x e^x - e^x + c = e^x(x - 1) + c

Worked example 2. Find ∫ x cos x dx.

u = x, dv = cos x dx  →  du = dx, v = sin x
= x sin x - ∫ sin x dx = x sin x + cos x + c

Worked example 3 (logarithm). Find ∫ ln x dx.

u = ln x, dv = dx  →  du = dx/x, v = x
= x ln x - ∫ 1 dx = x ln x - x + c

Worked example 4 (twice). Find ∫ x² e^x dx.

first: u = x², dv = e^x dx  →  x² e^x - 2∫ x e^x dx
second: ∫ x e^x = e^x(x - 1)
result: e^x(x² - 2x + 2) + c

Partial fractions in integration

(px + q)/[(x - a)(x - b)]  →  A/(x - a) + B/(x - b)
integrates to A ln|x - a| + B ln|x - b|

Worked example. Find ∫ 5/[(x − 1)(x + 4)] dx.

partial fractions: 1/(x - 1) - 1/(x + 4)
integral: ln|x - 1| - ln|x + 4| + c = ln|(x - 1)/(x + 4)| + c

Worked example 2 (repeated factor). Find ∫ 3/[(x + 1)²] dx.

= 3 ∫ (x + 1)⁻² dx = -3(x + 1)⁻¹ + c = -3/(x + 1) + c

Areas and volumes

area between curve and x-axis: definite integral (split at crossings)
volume of revolution about the x-axis: V = π ∫ y² dx

Worked example 1. Find the area under y = sin x from 0 to π.

[-cos x] from 0 to π = -(-1) - (-1) = 2 square units

Worked example 2 (volume). The region under y = x from 0 to 2 is rotated about the x-axis. Find the volume.

V = π ∫ from 0 to 2 of x² dx = π [x³/3] = 8 π/3 = 8.38 cubic units

The π multiplies the whole integral; forgetting it is the classic error.

Differential equations

separable: dy/dx = f(x) g(y)  →  ∫ dy/g(y) = ∫ f(x) dx

apply the boundary condition to find the constant

Worked example. Solve dy/dx = xy with y = 3 when x = 0.

∫ dy/y = ∫ x dx
ln|y| = x²/2 + c
y = A e^(x²/2);  at x = 0, y = 3  →  A = 3
y = 3e^(x²/2)

Worked example 2 (rate of cooling). dT/dt = −k(T − 20), T = 90 when t = 0, T = 60 when t = 10. Find T at t = 25.

∫ dT/(T - 20) = -k ∫ dt  →  ln(T - 20) = -kt + c
T - 20 = A e^(-kt);  at t = 0, A = 70
at t = 10: 40 = 70 e^(-10k)  →  k = 0.0560
at t = 25: T = 20 + 70e^(-1.4) = 37.3 °C

Choosing a method: the recognition cues

A2 integration is not a list of tricks to try at random; each integrand shape points at one method. Reading the shape before writing anything is the skill the exam actually tests.

Shape of the integrandMethodWhy
a function times its own derivativesubstitutionthe derivative becomes du
product of two unrelated functionsintegration by partsone factor is integrated, the other differentiated
a rational function with factorable denominatorpartial fractionseach part integrates to a logarithm
even powers of sin and cosdouble-angle identitylowers the power to a single wave
no elementary antiderivative (e.g. e^(−x²))numerical methodthe trapezium rule approximates it

Worked example (cue check). Name the method for each: ∫ 2x(x² + 1)⁵ dx, ∫ x e^x dx, ∫ (3x + 1)/(x² + x) dx.

first: 2x is the derivative of x² + 1  →  substitution u = x² + 1
second: x and e^x are unrelated  →  by parts with u = x
third: denominator factors x(x + 1)  →  partial fractions

Definite integrals with substitution

When a definite integral is evaluated by substitution, the limits belong to the old variable and must be converted to the new one. Forgetting this is the most common single error in the whole topic, and it is invisible if the answer happens to be close.

integral from x = a to x = b of f(x) dx
with u = g(x):  limits become u = g(a) and u = g(b)
then integrate in u with no conversion back

Worked example. Evaluate ∫ from 0 to 2 of x(x² + 1)³ dx.

u = x² + 1, du = 2x dx  →  x dx = du/2
limits: x = 0 → u = 1;  x = 2 → u = 5
integral = (1/2) ∫ from 1 to 5 of u³ du = (1/2)[u⁴/4] from 1 to 5
= (1/8)(625 - 1) = 78

Worked example 2 (by parts, definite). Evaluate ∫ from 0 to 1 of x e^(2x) dx.

u = x, dv = e^(2x) dx  →  du = dx, v = e^(2x)/2
= [x e^(2x)/2] from 0 to 1 - ∫ from 0 to 1 of e^(2x)/2 dx
= e²/2 - 0 - [e^(2x)/4] from 0 to 1
= e²/2 - (e²/4 - 1/4) = (e² + 1)/4 = 2.097

The trapezium rule

When no antiderivative exists in elementary terms, the area is estimated by joining the sampled heights with straight lines. Each strip is a trapezium, so the rule is exact for straight lines and underestimates for curves that bend upwards.

h = (b - a)/n  (width of each strip)
area = (h/2)[y0 + 2(y1 + y2 + ... + y(n-1)) + yn]
first and last heights counted once, all interior heights twice

Worked example. Use the trapezium rule with 4 strips to estimate ∫ from 0 to 1 of e^(−x²) dx.

h = 0.25;  heights at x = 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1
1, 0.9394, 0.7788, 0.5698, 0.3679
sum = 1 + 2(0.9394 + 0.7788 + 0.5698) + 0.3679 = 1 + 4.5760 + 0.3679 = 5.9439
area = (0.25/2)(5.9439) = 0.7430

Worked example 2 (error direction). The curve e^(−x²) is concave down on this interval. State whether the estimate is an over- or underestimate and how to improve it.

Tabulating the heights is worth the thirty seconds it costs. A single transcription error in one of five heights changes the answer but leaves the working looking correct, so the mark scheme cannot help you; writing the sample points in a column and summing them twice is the check that catches it. Mark schemes also accept the rule written in the equivalent form (h/2)(y0 + 2Σ interior + yn), which is often easier to key into a calculator without dropping a term.

chords lie below a concave-down curve, so the rule underestimates
halving h (doubling n) roughly quarters the error
an overestimate would need the curve concave up

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Standard) ∫ cos 3x dx. Answer: (1/3) sin 3x + c.
  2. (Identity) ∫ cos²x dx. Answer: x/2 + (sin 2x)/4 + c.
  3. (Substitution) ∫ 3x²(x³ + 1)⁴ dx. Answer: u = x³ + 1 → (x³ + 1)⁵/5 + c.
  4. (By parts) ∫ x sin x dx. Answer: −x cos x + sin x + c.
  5. (By parts log) ∫ x ln x dx. Answer: (x²/2)ln x − x²/4 + c.
  6. (Partial fractions) ∫ 4/[(x + 1)(x − 1)] dx. Answer: 2 ln|x − 1| − 2 ln|x + 1| + c.
  7. (Volume) y = x² rotated about x-axis from 0 to 1. Answer: π/5.
  8. (Differential equation) dy/dx = 2y, y = 5 at x = 0. Answer: y = 5e^(2x).

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Missing the reciprocal factor: ∫ cos 3x is (1/3)sin 3x, not sin 3x.
  • Integrating products directly: sin x cos x is not sin²x/2 by guesswork — use the identity.
  • Substitution without changing limits: definite integrals must convert the limits to the new variable, or convert back.
  • Wrong choice for u in by parts: choose the part that simplifies when differentiated; x and ln x are the standard picks.
  • Sign errors in by parts: the formula is uv − ∫v du; slipping the minus reverses the answer.
  • Forgetting the modulus in log integrals: ln|x| covers both signs.
  • Volume without π: the π multiplies the entire definite integral of y².
  • Differential equation constants: find the constant from the boundary condition and state the particular solution.

title: A Level Mathematics: The Binomial Distribution
content:
A Level Mathematics: The Binomial Distribution

A binomial distribution counts successes in a fixed number of independent trials, each with the same probability of success. Coins, multiple-choice guesses, defective items in a sample and free throws all fit the same template, and once a problem is recognised as binomial the calculation is a formula plus a cumulative table. This note builds the distribution from its four conditions, derives the formula from counting, and then uses it for the two things exams actually ask: probabilities and hypothesis tests.

The four conditions

Before writing X ~ B(n, p) you must be able to name the conditions, because most exam questions include a part asking whether the model is appropriate. The conditions are not red tape: drop any one and the formula is simply wrong.

1. a fixed number of trials n
2. each trial has exactly two outcomes (success / failure)
3. the probability of success p is constant for every trial
4. the trials are independent
then X = number of successes has X ~ B(n, p)

Worked example (checking the model). A bag holds 5 red and 15 blue counters. Four counters are taken without replacement. Is the number of red counters binomial?

n = 4 is fixed and each draw is red or not red
but p changes: 5/20, then 5/19 if a red was taken, ...
the trials are not independent, so NOT binomial (it is hypergeometric)

Taking with replacement would fix it: p stays 0.25 on every draw.

The formula, and where it comes from

The probability of a particular sequence of r successes and n − r failures is p^r (1−p)^(n−r), because independence lets you multiply. The number of such sequences is the number of ways to choose which r trials succeed, which is nCr. Multiplying gives the formula.

P(X = r) = nCr p^r (1 - p)^(n - r)
the nCr counts arrangements; the powers give the probability of one arrangement

Worked example. X ~ B(10, 0.3). Find P(X = 3).

P = 10C3 (0.3)³ (0.7)⁷
= 120 × 0.027 × 0.08235
= 120 × 0.002223 = 0.2668

Worked example 2 (a single trial count). A fair die is rolled 8 times. Find the probability of exactly two sixes.

X ~ B(8, 1/6)
P(X = 2) = 8C2 (1/6)² (5/6)⁶ = 28 × 0.02778 × 0.3349 = 0.2605

Worked example 3 (why nCr appears). For n = 3 and r = 1, list the sequences and confirm the coefficient.

sequences: SFF, FSF, FFS - three of them
each has probability p(1-p)²
so P(X = 1) = 3p(1-p)², and 3C1 = 3

Cumulative probabilities

Questions almost always ask for a range, not a single value, and the cumulative distribution is what the calculator or the tables supply. The skill is rewriting the question into the form the table gives you.

P(X <= r) is tabulated directly
P(X >= r) = 1 - P(X <= r - 1)
P(X < r)  = P(X <= r - 1)
P(a <= X <= b) = P(X <= b) - P(X <= a - 1)
P(X = r) = P(X <= r) - P(X <= r - 1)

Worked example. X ~ B(20, 0.4). Find P(X ≥ 8).

P(X >= 8) = 1 - P(X <= 7)
= 1 - 0.4159
= 0.5841

Worked example 2 (between). For the same X, find P(5 ≤ X ≤ 10).

= P(X <= 10) - P(X <= 4)
= 0.8725 - 0.0510
= 0.8215

Worked example 3 (the strict inequality trap). For the same X, find P(X > 6).

P(X > 6) = 1 - P(X <= 6) = 1 - 0.2500 = 0.7500
note this is different from P(X >= 6) = 1 - P(X <= 5) = 0.8746

Mean and variance

The binomial has the simplest mean and variance in the syllabus, and they are worth knowing both forwards and backwards: a question can give the mean and variance and ask for n and p.

E(X) = np
Var(X) = np(1 - p)
standard deviation = √(np(1-p))

Worked example. X ~ B(50, 0.2). Find the mean and standard deviation.

mean = 50 × 0.2 = 10
variance = 10 × 0.8 = 8
sd = 2.828

Worked example 2 (backwards). A binomial variable has mean 12 and variance 9. Find n and p.

np = 12;  np(1-p) = 9
divide: 1 - p = 9/12 = 0.75  →  p = 0.25
then n = 12/0.25 = 48

Hypothesis testing with the binomial

A one-tailed test asks whether p has increased or decreased; the test statistic is the observed count, and the p-value is the probability of a result at least as extreme in the direction of the alternative.

H0: p = p0      H1: p > p0 (or p < p0)
X ~ B(n, p0) under H0
p-value = P(X >= observed) or P(X <= observed)
compare with the significance level; reject H0 if p-value <= alpha

Worked example. A coin is tossed 20 times and lands heads 15 times. Test at the 5% level whether the coin is biased towards heads.

H0: p = 0.5;  H1: p > 0.5
X ~ B(20, 0.5)
P(X >= 15) = 1 - P(X <= 14) = 1 - 0.9793 = 0.0207
0.0207 < 0.05, so reject H0
there is evidence at the 5% level that the coin favours heads

Worked example 2 (two-tailed). The same data tested two-tailed.

double the smaller tail: 2 × 0.0207 = 0.0414
0.0414 < 0.05, so still reject H0 at the 5% level

Worked example 3 (critical region). For X ~ B(20, 0.5), find the critical region for a 5% one-tailed test of p > 0.5.

P(X >= 14) = 0.0577 (above 0.05)
P(X >= 15) = 0.0207 (below 0.05)
critical region: X >= 15

Note that the critical region is chosen so the probability of a Type I error is at most 5%, which is why 14 is excluded even though it is close.

When the model breaks down

Examiners like the question that asks why a binomial model is only an approximation. The usual culprits are dependence, a varying probability, or a fixed sample drawn without replacement from a small population.

SituationProblemEffect
sampling without replacementtrials not independentp drifts; use the hypergeometric instead
clustered data (pupils in classes)responses correlatedvariance underestimated
probability varies between trialsp not constantformula invalid
large n, p near 0.5computation heavynormal approximation is reasonable

Worked example (normal approximation). X ~ B(200, 0.4). Use a normal approximation to estimate P(X ≤ 70).

mean = 80;  variance = 200 × 0.4 × 0.6 = 48;  sd = 6.928
continuity correction: X <= 70 becomes X < 70.5
z = (70.5 - 80)/6.928 = -1.371
P(Z < -1.371) = 0.0852

The continuity correction is compulsory: a discrete count needs a half-unit boundary before it can be treated as continuous.

Expected frequencies and the shape of the distribution

A binomial distribution is not symmetric unless p = 0.5, and that shape decides which tail an exam question is fishing in. The most likely value — the mode — is the integer near (n + 1)p, and expected frequency multiplies the probability by the number of samples taken. Both are quick marks that are frequently missed because students jump straight to the formula.

mode is near (n + 1)p, checked by comparing consecutive probabilities
expected number in a sample of size N = N x P(X = r)

Worked example. X ~ B(12, 0.3). Find the most likely value of X and the expected number of 3s in 500 independent observations.

(n + 1)p = 13 × 0.3 = 3.9, so check r = 3 and r = 4
P(X = 3) = 220 × 0.027 × 0.1176 = 0.2397
P(X = 4) = 495 × 0.0081 × 0.1681 = 0.2311
mode = 3
expected number of 3s = 500 × 0.2397 = 120 (to the nearest whole)

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Model) State the distribution for the number of sixes in 12 rolls of a fair die. Answer: X ~ B(12, 1/6).
  2. (Single value) X ~ B(8, 0.25): find P(X = 2). Answer: 28 × 0.0625 × 0.1780 = 0.3115.
  3. (Cumulative) X ~ B(15, 0.3): find P(X ≤ 4). Answer: 0.5155 from tables.
  4. (Complement) Same X: find P(X ≥ 3). Answer: 1 − 0.2969 = 0.7031.
  5. (Mean) X ~ B(40, 0.35): find E(X) and Var(X). Answer: 14 and 9.1.
  6. (Backwards) Mean 18, variance 12: find n and p. Answer: p = 1/3, n = 54.
  7. (Test) 12 of 20 seeds germinate; test p = 0.5 against p < 0.5 at 5%. Answer: P(X ≤ 12) = 0.8684, no evidence to reject.
  8. (Critical region) X ~ B(10, 0.2): find the 5% critical region for p < 0.2. Answer: P(X ≤ 0) = 0.1074 > 0.05, so no region exists at 5%.
  9. (Approximation) X ~ B(100, 0.5): approximate P(X ≥ 60). Answer: μ = 50, σ = 5, z = 1.9, P = 0.0287.
  10. (Assumption) Give one reason a binomial model may fail for defects in boxes of 20. Answer: defects may cluster, so trials are not independent.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Forgetting nCr: the coefficient counts arrangements; without it the answer is the probability of one specific sequence.
  • nCr on the wrong factor: it is p^r (1−p)^(n−r), with the success probability raised to the number of successes.
  • Inequality direction: P(X ≥ 8) uses 1 − P(X ≤ 7), not 1 − P(X ≤ 8).
  • Variance confused with standard deviation: np(1−p) is the variance; the test and the normal approximation need the square root.
  • Continuity correction omitted: any normal approximation to a discrete count needs the half-unit adjustment.
  • One-tailed evidence read as two: halving or doubling the tail without checking the alternative direction is a silent error.
  • Independence asserted, not checked: sampling without replacement from a small population breaks the model, and the question usually invites you to say so.
  • p-value compared with the wrong threshold: the significance level is given as a percentage; 5% means 0.05, not 5.

Equations and symbols

The distribution, its conditions and the four tail identities. Every question on this topic is one of these lines plus a calculator.

P(X = r) = nCr p^r (1 - p)^(n - r) Key: n = number of trials, fixed in advance; p = probability of success in one trial, constant; r = the number of successes asked for; nCr = n!/(r!(n − r)!), the number of orders the successes can occur in. The (1 − p) term is the failures, and its power must be n − r.

X ~ B(n, p) Key: X = the count of successes; the tilde means "is distributed as"; n and p as above. Write this line before calculating — it is often a mark on its own, and it fixes which parameters go into the calculator.

P = 10C3 (0.3)³ (0.7)⁷ Key: n = 10, p = 0.3, r = 3, so the failures are 7 and their probability is 0.7. The coefficient 10C3 = 120 accounts for the order of the three successes among the ten trials.

P(X >= r) = 1 - P(X <= r - 1) Key: a complement, so the two probabilities add to 1; the boundary moves by one because the binomial is discrete. Using 1 − P(X ≤ r) instead is the classic off-by-one error.

P(a <= X <= b) = P(X <= b) - P(X <= a - 1) Key: subtract the part below the interval; again the "− 1" is there because P(X ≤ a − 1) is everything before a. Check with a small case you can list by hand before trusting the calculator.

title: IGCSE Biology: Reproduction
content:
IGCSE Biology: Reproduction

Reproduction is how species persist — and the two strategies, asexual and sexual, trade reliability against variation. This note compares both, then follows plant reproduction from flower structure to pollination, fertilisation and germination, before tracing the human system from gamete production through the menstrual cycle to pregnancy, birth and contraception, and closing with sexually transmitted infections including HIV/AIDS. Every structure is tied to its function and every sequence (pollination → fertilisation → germination; intercourse → fertilisation → implantation) is written in order, because the marks live in the sequence.

The four reproductive hormones

HormoneMade byTargetEffect
FSHPituitary glandOvaryMaturation of a follicle and its egg
OestrogenOvary (follicle)Uterus, pituitaryRebuilds endometrium; triggers the LH surge
LHPituitary glandOvaryCauses ovulation around day 14
ProgesteroneCorpus luteumUterus, pituitaryMaintains the endometrium; inhibits FSH

Asexual and sexual reproduction compared

Asexual reproduction involves one parent and no fusion of gametes: mitosis produces offspring genetically identical to the parent (clones) — binary fission in bacteria, budding in yeast, runners in strawberries, tissue culture for plants. Advantages: rapid, no mate needed, good genes preserved in a stable environment. Disadvantages: no genetic variation, so a disease or environmental change can wipe out the entire clone. Sexual reproduction involves two parents, gametes (sperm and egg) produced by meiosis and fused at fertilisation: offspring are genetically varied (unique combinations of alleles), giving variation on which natural selection acts. Advantage: variation allows adaptation to changing environments; disadvantage: slower, needs a mate and more energy.

Flower structure and function

The flower is the reproductive organ of a plant. Sepals (green, protective bud), petals (often coloured and scented to attract pollinators), stamens (male): anther produces pollen grains (containing male gametes) on a filament, and carpels (female): stigma (sticky, receives pollen), style (tube down which the pollen tube grows), ovary (contains ovules, each with a female gamete), and the ovule becomes the seed after fertilisation. Nectaries at the base of the petals produce sugary nectar to reward pollinators. The structural adaptations for insect pollination: brightly coloured petals, scent, nectar, sticky large pollen grains, and a compact landing platform; for wind pollination: small dull petals (or none), long dangling anthers releasing clouds of light smooth pollen, feathery stigmas to catch pollen, and large amounts of pollen produced.

Pollination, fertilisation and seed formation

Pollination is the transfer of pollen from the anther to the stigma — self-pollination (same flower or plant) gives less variation; cross-pollination (different plant of the same species) increases variation. Agents: insects, wind, water, birds, bats. Fertilisation is the fusion of the male gamete (from the pollen grain) with the female gamete (in the ovule): the pollen grain lands on a compatible stigma, germinates and grows a pollen tube down the style, guided by chemicals from the ovule; the male gamete nucleus travels down the tube and fuses with the egg cell; the zygote divides by mitosis to become the embryo plant; the ovule becomes the seed (with a food store and protective seed coat) and the ovary wall becomes the fruit. Germination requires water (enzyme activation and transport), oxygen (respiration for energy) and a suitable temperature; light is required by some species. Stored starch in the seed is hydrolysed by amylase to glucose for the growing embryo.

The human reproductive system

Male: testes (produce sperm by meiosis and testosterone), scrotum (keeps testes below body temperature for spermatogenesis), sperm duct (vas deferens), prostate gland (secretes seminal fluid feeding sperm), urethra (shared passage), penis. Female: ovaries (produce eggs by meiosis and oestrogen/progesterone), oviducts (fallopian tubes — site of fertilisation, lined with cilia that waft the egg along), uterus (womb — where the embryo implants and develops), endometrium (uterine lining that thickens each cycle), cervix (neck of the uterus), vagina (birth canal). Gametes are haploid (half the chromosome number — 23 in humans) so that at fertilisation the diploid number (46) is restored; the fusion of gametes combines genes from two parents, producing variation.

Menstrual cycle, fertilisation and pregnancy

The cycle takes about 28 days and is controlled by four hormones (FSH, oestrogen, LH, progesterone) as detailed in the coordination note: FSH matures a follicle → oestrogen rebuilds the endometrium and triggers an LH surge → ovulation (day 14) → corpus luteum secretes progesterone maintaining the lining → no fertilisation → hormone levels fall → menstruation. If a sperm fertilises the egg (usually in the oviduct), the zygote divides into a ball of cells (blastocyst) that implants in the endometrium about a week later; the placenta develops, connected to the embryo by the umbilical cord. The placenta allows diffusion of oxygen, glucose, amino acids, water and antibodies (maternal IgG) from mother to fetus, and carbon dioxide, urea and wastes from fetus to mother; it also acts as a barrier to many pathogens and drugs (though not all — alcohol, HIV and some drugs cross). Pregnancy lasts about 40 weeks, ending with birth (parturition): the hormone oxytocin stimulates uterine contractions, and positive feedback (contractions push the baby onto the cervix, causing more oxytocin release) intensifies labour until delivery, followed by the afterbirth (placenta and membranes).

Contraception and fertility

Natural methods: abstinence, rhythm/calendar method (avoiding ovulation days — unreliable due to cycle variation), withdrawal. Hormonal: the combined pill (oestrogen and progesterone inhibit FSH, so no egg matures or ovulates), progesterone-only pill, implants, injections and patches — highly effective but requiring medical oversight. Barrier: condoms (male and female) — block sperm physically AND protect against STIs (the only method that does both), diaphragms with spermicide. Intrauterine devices (IUDs) prevent implantation. Spermicide kills sperm. Surgical: vasectomy (cutting the sperm ducts) and tubal ligation (cutting the oviducts) — permanent. Infertility treatments: hormone therapy to stimulate ovulation, in vitro fertilisation (IVF — eggs fertilised in the lab then implanted), donor gametes, sperm banks; IVF raises ethical questions (multiple embryos, selective reduction, cost, access).

Sexually transmitted infections

STIs spread through sexual contact (body fluids): Chlamydia (bacterial; often symptomless; treated with antibiotics; can cause infertility), Gonorrhoea (bacterial; discharges; antibiotics, but resistant strains emerging), Syphilis (bacterial; sores then organ damage; antibiotics), Genital herpes (viral; recurring sores; no cure, antivirals manage it), HIV (viral; attacks helper T-lymphocytes, destroying the immune system; no cure, but antiretroviral drugs control it), Hepatitis B (viral; liver damage; vaccine available), and HPV (viral; can cause genital warts and cervical cancer; vaccine now given to adolescents). Prevention: condoms reduce transmission, fewer partners, screening, vaccination (hepatitis B, HPV), and education. HIV/AIDS: the virus binds CD4 receptors on helper T-cells, inserts its RNA (reverse transcriptase makes DNA), integrates into the host genome, replicates and destroys the cell; progressive loss of helper T-cells cripples the immune response; the person develops AIDS (acquired immune deficiency syndrome) when opportunistic infections (TB, pneumonia, Kaposi's sarcoma) take hold; transmission: unprotected sex, shared needles, mother to child (during birth or breastfeeding); the epidemic is worst in sub-Saharan Africa; education, condoms, needle exchange, screening of blood supplies and antiretrovirals reduce spread.

Worked example: tracing a cycle and building a contraception comparison

Trace one cycle with a diagram in words: days 1–5 menstruation (low oestrogen and progesterone, endometrium sheds); days 6–13 FSH matures a follicle, rising oestrogen rebuilds the lining; day 14 LH surge causes ovulation; days 15–28 the corpus luteum secretes progesterone maintaining the endometrium; if no fertilisation, corpus luteum degenerates, hormones fall and the cycle restarts. Add fertilisation: sperm meets egg in the oviduct on day 14–15, blastocyst implants around day 21, and the corpus luteum (then placenta) maintains progesterone so no menstruation occurs. Now a comparison question: "compare hormonal and barrier contraception" — hormonal methods do not protect against STIs, do not require action at the time of intercourse, and act by inhibiting ovulation; barrier methods protect against STIs, are used at intercourse, and act by blocking sperm. Comparing two methods on both effectiveness and STI protection is the classic 4-mark structure.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Confusing pollination with fertilisation: pollination is pollen transfer; fertilisation is gamete fusion. They are separate events days apart in plants.
  • Writing that the ovary "contains eggs" loosely: ovaries produce egg cells by meiosis and secrete hormones; ovules (in plants) contain the female gamete.
  • Saying sperm and eggs are diploid: gametes are haploid (n = 23); fertilisation restores 46.
  • Reversing the hormone chain in the menstrual cycle: FSH → follicle/oestrogen → LH surge → ovulation → progesterone → lining maintained.
  • Claiming the placenta "prevents all harmful substances": some drugs, alcohol, HIV and certain pathogens cross it.
  • Writing that condoms "prevent pregnancy and all disease": they greatly reduce STI risk but do not eliminate it.
  • Confusing the site of fertilisation (oviduct) with the site of implantation (uterus/endometrium).
  • Describing birth as purely hormonal: oxytocin causes contractions and positive feedback amplifies labour until delivery.
  • Saying asexual reproduction "produces variation": it produces clones — identical offspring.

Exam-style questions and answers

Q1. Compare asexual and sexual reproduction. (4 marks) Answer: asexual has one parent, sexual two (1); asexual produces genetically identical clones, sexual produces variation (1); asexual is rapid and needs no mate, sexual is slower and needs gamete fusion (1); variation in sexual reproduction aids survival in changing environments (1).

Q2. Describe how a seed is formed after pollination. (4 marks) Answer: pollen grain lands on stigma and germinates (1); pollen tube grows down the style to the ovule (1); male gamete fuses with the egg cell (1); ovule becomes the seed and the ovary becomes the fruit (1).

Q3. Explain the functions of the placenta. (3 marks) Answer: allows oxygen, glucose, amino acids and antibodies to pass from mother to fetus (1); removes carbon dioxide and urea from fetus to mother (1); acts as a barrier to some pathogens and drugs (1).

Q4. Explain how the combined pill prevents pregnancy. (3 marks) Answer: contains oestrogen and progesterone (1); inhibit FSH secretion so follicles do not mature (1); no egg is released so fertilisation cannot occur (1).

Q5. Describe how HIV reduces the body's ability to defend itself against disease. (4 marks) Answer: HIV binds to and enters helper T-lymphocytes (1); uses reverse transcriptase to insert its DNA into the host genome (1); virus replicates and the cell bursts releasing virions (1); loss of helper T-cells means antibody production and phagocyte activation fall, allowing opportunistic infections (1).

Equations and symbols

Reproduction has no algebra, so the "equations" here are the two arrows that earn sequence marks — pollination to germination, and the hormone chain that runs the menstrual cycle — plus the chromosome arithmetic. Learn the order, not the words.

n = 23 Key: n = the haploid chromosome number of a human gamete (23 chromosomes, no unit). Two haploid gametes fuse at fertilisation to restore the diploid number, 2n = 46 — which is why a gamete is never described as diploid.

pollination → fertilisation → germination Key: pollination = transfer of pollen from anther to stigma (an event, not a fusion); fertilisation = fusion of the male gamete from the pollen tube with the egg cell in the ovule; germination = the seed taking up water, activating enzymes and growing. They are three separate events, days apart, and the marks are awarded in that order.

intercourse → fertilisation → implantation Key: fertilisation happens in the oviduct, usually within a day of ovulation; implantation is the blastocyst embedding in the endometrium about a week later. Naming the oviduct as the site of fertilisation and the uterus as the site of implantation is a mark on its own.

FSH → follicle/oestrogen → LH surge → ovulation → progesterone → lining maintained Key: FSH from the pituitary matures a follicle; the follicle secretes oestrogen, which rebuilds the endometrium; oestrogen triggers the LH surge; LH causes ovulation around day 14; the corpus luteum then secretes progesterone, which maintains the lining and inhibits FSH. No fertilisation means the corpus luteum degenerates, both hormones fall, and menstruation follows — the chain read backwards.

The hormones and their targets

HormoneSourceEffect
FSHPituitary glandMatures a follicle and its egg
OestrogenOvary (follicle)Rebuilds the endometrium; triggers the LH surge
LHPituitary glandOvulation, about day 14
ProgesteroneCorpus luteumMaintains the endometrium; inhibits FSH
OxytocinPituitary (posterior)Uterine contractions in labour, amplified by positive feedback

Where the sequence marks are lost

  • Writing "the pollen fertilises the stigma" — pollen lands, a tube grows, gametes fuse. Transfer and fusion are different events.
  • Putting the LH surge before the oestrogen rise, or progesterone before ovulation.
  • Saying the placenta blocks all harmful substances; alcohol, HIV and several drugs cross it.

title: Database Systems — Study Notes
content:
Database Systems

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): limitations of file-based systems; relational concepts; SQL (SELECT, FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY, INNER JOIN, SUM, COUNT); DBMS features.

1. File-based problems

Data repetition (wasted space, inconsistency), fixed queries, no concurrent access control — solved by a DBMS with shared, structured tables.

2. Relational concepts

  • Table, record, field; primary key (unique); secondary key (indexed search field); foreign key links tables.
  • One-to-many relationships via foreign keys; no repeating groups (1NF mindset).

3. SQL

SELECT Title, Year FROM Films
WHERE Genre = 'Sci-Fi' AND Year > 2015
ORDER BY Year DESC;

SELECT Genre, COUNT(*) AS NumFilms, SUM(Rating) AS TotalRating
FROM Films
GROUP BY Genre;

SELECT s.Name, f.Title
FROM Students s INNER JOIN Loans l ON s.StudentID = l.StudentID
INNER JOIN Films f ON l.FilmID = f.FilmID;

WHERE filters rows; GROUP BY aggregates; JOIN combines on matching keys.

4. DBMS features

Data dictionary (schema, types, constraints), query processor, forms/reports, access rights (read/write per user), data integrity (validation rules), backup/recovery.

Exam tips: write SQL keywords uppercase; alias joined tables (s, l, f); when asked "why relational", cite reduced redundancy + flexible queries.

title: Differentiation II — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Differentiation II

Mathematics — A2 (9709). Example: y = x² e^x gives dy/dx = 2x e^x + x² e^x = e^x(2x + x²).

Key areas to revise

  • Product and Quotient Rules
  • Standard Derivatives
  • Chain Rule Everywhere
  • Implicit Differentiation
  • Parametric Curves

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

### Worked example Use the chain rule for composite functions. For y = (x² + 1)³, dy/dx = 3(x² + 1)² × 2x = 6x(x² + 1)². At x = 1 this is 6 × 1 × 4 = 24. Check using the derivative of the outer function at the inner value: 3 × 2² × 2 = 24. The product rule gives d/dx(x sin x) = sin x + x cos x.

Key points to remember

The chain rule differentiates a function of a function: if y = f(g(x)), then dy/dx = f′(g(x)) × g′(x). The product rule for y = uv gives dy/dx = u dv/dx + v du/dx. The quotient rule for y = u/v gives dy/dx = (v du/dx − u dv/dx)/v². Identify the outer and inner functions before you differentiate.

For implicit differentiation, differentiate each term with respect to x, remembering that a term in y gives a dy/dx factor, then rearrange for dy/dx. To classify a stationary point, find the second derivative and check its sign there, or check the gradient either side of the point.

title: Energy Flow, Ecosystems and the Environment - Edexcel International A2 Level Biology
content:
Energy Flow, Ecosystems and the Environment - Edexcel International A2 Level Biology

This revision note belongs to Edexcel International A2 Level Biology WBI14 and covers energy transfers in ecosystems, photosynthesis mechanisms, ecological sampling, community succession, climate change evidence and causes, population genetics, and conservation management.

Photosynthesis and Biochemical Reactions

Photosynthesis is an energy-requiring pathway captured by the overall chemical equation 6CO2 + 6H2O yields C6H12O6 + 6O2, driven by light energy. Light energy splits the strong covalent bonds in water molecules (photolysis), releasing oxygen gas into the atmosphere while storing hydrogen atoms inside glucose by combining them with carbon dioxide. Energy currency within cells relies on photophosphorylation of ADP to synthesize ATP, which undergoes immediate hydrolysis to supply free energy for endergonic biological processes.

  • 5.1 Overall photosynthesis equation: light energy splits H2O, combines hydrogen with CO2 to form glucose, and releases O2.
  • 5.2 Photophosphorylation converts ADP and inorganic phosphate into ATP using energy; ATP hydrolysis releases an immediate supply of energy.
  • 5.3 Light-dependent reactions occur on thylakoid membranes: photons excite electrons in chlorophyll, generating ATP and reduced NADP via cyclic and non-cyclic photophosphorylation, alongside oxygen via photolysis.
  • 5.4 (i) Light-independent reactions (Calvin cycle) occur in the stroma, fixing CO2 onto ribulose bisphosphate (RuBP) via RuBisCO to form glycerate 3-phosphate (GP), which is reduced using ATP and reduced NADP into glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate (GALP).
  • 5.4 (ii) GALP molecules yield simple sugars for respiration and synthesise new biological molecules including polysaccharides, amino acids, proteins, lipids, and nucleic acids.
  • 5.5 Chloroplast structure relates to function: thylakoids provide a large surface area for light absorption and pigment arrays; the stroma contains enzymes for the Calvin cycle; double membranes isolate biochemical pathways.
  • 5.6 Absorption spectrum shows absorbance of light wavelengths by a pigment; action spectrum shows the rate of photosynthesis at different light wavelengths.
  • 5.7 Chloroplast pigments are separated using paper or thin-layer chromatography and identified by calculating Rf values (distance moved by pigment divided by distance moved by solvent front).
  • 5.8 Core Practical 10: Investigate effects of light intensity, light wavelength, temperature, and CO2 availability on photosynthetic rate using an aquatic plant such as Elodea or Cabomba, measuring oxygen bubbles released or volume of gas displaced.

Energy Transfer in Ecosystems

Energy flow through trophic levels begins with primary producers capturing sunlight. Gross primary productivity (GPP) is the total chemical energy fixed by photosynthesis. Net primary productivity (NPP) accounts for respiratory losses (R) and dictates plant tissue available to herbivores.

  • 5.9 (i) The relationship is NPP = GPP − R.
  • 5.9 (ii) Calculation of NPP requires subtracting plant respiration from gross primary productivity.
  • 5.10 Efficiency of biomass and energy transfers between trophic levels is calculated using (Energy or biomass transferred to next trophic level ÷ Energy or biomass received at previous trophic level) × 100%.

Worked example calculation of transfer efficiency: If a producer trophic level contains 15000 kJ m−2 year−1 and primary consumers contain 1400 kJ m−2 year−1, the transfer efficiency is (1400 ÷ 15000) × 100 = 9.33%.

Ecology and Populations

Ecosystems comprise biotic communities and abiotic factors governing species distributions. An organism's ecological niche describes its functional role and interactions within its habitat.

  • 5.11 Population is a group of interbreeding individuals of the same species in a habitat; community is all populations of different species living in a habitat; habitat is the place where an organism lives; ecosystem is a self-sustaining system of living organisms interacting with non-living surroundings.
  • 5.12 Numbers and distributions of organisms are controlled by biotic factors (competition, predation, disease) and abiotic factors (temperature, pH, light intensity, moisture).
  • 5.13 Niche concept accounts for distribution and abundance: no two species can occupy the exact same niche indefinitely without competitive exclusion.
  • 5.14 Core Practical 11: Carry out ecological studies using quadrats for abundance and transects (belt or line) for distribution, recording concurrent abiotic factors using appropriate sensors and meters.
  • 5.15 Succession stages: pioneer species colonise bare substrate, altering abiotic conditions to become less hostile, leading to seral stages of increasing biodiversity until a stable climax community forms.

Climate Change and Environmental Evidence

Anthropogenic activities release greenhouse gases, driving rapid climate change. Multiple proxy records allow scientists to track historical climates and establish causal links.

  • 5.16 Evidence for climate change includes atmospheric CO2 gas records (Mauna Loa curve), temperature records, pollen preservation in peat bogs indicating past flora, and dendrochronology (tree ring width analysis), distinguishing between correlation and causation.
  • 5.17 Anthropogenic climate change is caused by greenhouse gases (carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide, water vapour) absorbing and reradiating infrared radiation back to the Earth's surface (the enhanced greenhouse effect).
  • 5.18 Carbon cycle knowledge is applied to reduce atmospheric CO2 via reforestation, protecting peatlands, reducing fossil fuel combustion, and using carbon capture and storage.
  • 5.19 (i) Data extrapolation allows mathematical models to predict future climate scenarios.
  • 5.19 (ii) Climate models have limitations due to complex feedback loops, incomplete historical datasets, and unpredictable human policy shifts.
  • 5.20 Effects of climate change include shifting rainfall patterns and altered seasonal phenology, impacting animal and plant distribution, development rates, and life cycles.

Metabolic Rates and Evolution

Temperature profoundly influences metabolic rates and enzyme kinetics. Evolutionary mechanisms alter allele frequencies over generations.

  • 5.21 Temperature affects enzyme activity up to an optimum; beyond this, denaturation occurs. Q10 temperature coefficient calculates the rate increase when temperature rises by 10 °C, using formula Q10 = (Rate at (T + 10 °C) ÷ Rate at T).
  • 5.22 Core Practical 12: Investigate temperature effects on organism development (such as seedling growth rate or brine shrimp hatch rates), maintaining ethical use of organisms.
  • 5.23 Evolution is a change in allele frequency within a gene pool over time, driven by gene mutations creating new alleles and natural selection increasing advantageous allele frequencies.
  • 5.24 Geographic, temporal, behavioural, or anatomical isolation reduces gene flow between populations, culminating in allopatric speciation (physical barrier) or sympatric speciation (same habitat, reproductive barrier).
  • 5.25 Scientific conclusions on controversial issues like climate change action and anthropogenic attribution can be influenced by funding sources, political agendas, and underlying stakeholder motives.
  • 5.26 Reforestation and sustainable resources (such as biofuels derived from fast-growing plants) manage the conflict between human economic needs and biological conservation.

Typical mistakes

  • Confusing absorption spectrum and action spectrum: remember absorption measures light energy captured by specific pigments, whereas action spectrum measures overall photosynthetic rate across light wavelengths.
  • Failing to state units in productivity calculations: always specify units such as kJ m−2 year−1 or g m−2 year−1.
  • Stating temperature denaturation destroys primary protein structure: clarify that tertiary and quaternary structures are disrupted via hydrogen and ionic bond breakage, leaving peptide bonds intact.
  • Treating correlation as direct causation in climate proxy data: always mention confounding variables and correlative limits.

Exam-style questions

  1. Explain how non-cyclic photophosphorylation generates ATP and reduced NADP. Answer: Light photons excite electrons in chlorophyll photosystem II; electrons pass down an electron transport chain releasing energy to pump protons and synthesise ATP via ATP synthase; electrons replace those lost from photosystem I where reduced NADP is formed. (3 marks)
  2. Calculate the net primary productivity of a forest where gross primary productivity is 45000 kJ m−2 year−1 and plant respiration is 18000 kJ m−2 year−1. Answer: NPP = GPP − R = 45000 − 18000 = 27000 kJ m−2 year−1. (2 marks)
  3. Describe how allopatric speciation can occur following geographical isolation. Answer: A physical barrier separates a population into two groups; no gene flow occurs between them; different mutations and selection pressures operate in each isolated environment; advantageous alleles accumulate independently until interbreeding can no longer produce fertile offspring. (4 marks)
  4. Explain the term Q10 and how to calculate it. Answer: Q10 is the measure of the rate of reaction when the temperature is increased by 10 °C. Calculated using Q10 = (Rate at (T + 10 °C) ÷ Rate at T). (2 marks)
  5. Discuss why climate models have limitations when predicting future global temperatures. Answer: Models rely on assumptions about future greenhouse gas emissions, human policy changes, and complex feedback loops such as cloud cover or permafrost melting that are difficult to quantify accurately. (3 marks)

Use these revision notes alongside active recall of core practical steps and quantitative calculations for energy efficiencies and Q10 values. Proceed next to topic summaries on human impacts on biogeochemical cycles and global biodiversity.
