title: Edexcel IAL Computer Science: Encryption, Protocols and Digital Certificates
content:
Edexcel IAL Computer Science: Encryption, Protocols and Digital Certificates

Pearson Edexcel International Advanced Level in Computer Science, Unit 3 Advanced Computer Science: encryption, encryption protocols and digital certificates. The AS security note covered threats and defence-in-depth; this note goes into the cryptography itself — how symmetric and asymmetric systems work under the hood, how protocols like TLS compose them into secure channels, and how certificates bind keys to identities. Every exchange below is traced message by message, because the marks sit in the sequence.

The goals of cryptography

Cryptography serves four properties, and each technique below should be read against them: confidentiality (only the intended reader), integrity (detect any change), authentication (prove who sent it), and non-repudiation (the sender cannot deny it). A plain lock (encryption) gives only the first; the rest need hashes, signatures and certificates.

Symmetric encryption under the hood

One shared secret key encrypts and decrypts. Modern ciphers (AES) work by substitution–permutation networks: repeated rounds that substitute bytes (confusion) and shuffle positions (diffusion), each round keyed from the original key by a key schedule — so a single flipped plaintext bit changes roughly half the ciphertext bits after a few rounds. Block ciphers process fixed blocks (AES: 128 bits) in a mode (CBC chains blocks by XOR-ing each plaintext block with the previous ciphertext block, requiring an initialisation vector; ECB — the naive mode — leaks patterns and is unsafe; CTR turns the block cipher into a stream).

One AES-style round, conceptually:

  plaintext block (128 bits)
    -> AddRoundKey (XOR with round key)
    -> SubBytes (substitution table: confusion)
    -> ShiftRows (permute: diffusion)
    -> MixColumns (mix within columns: more diffusion)
  ... 10-14 rounds (key size dependent) ...
  -> ciphertext block

Property worth the mark: encryption itself is deterministic without the IV/mode,
so identical plaintext blocks would give identical ciphertext - the pattern
leak ECB suffers. CBC's XOR of the previous ciphertext block (and a random IV)
breaks that regularity.

The symmetric strengths and weaknesses: very fast (bulk data), strong with adequate key lengths (AES-256); the weakness is the key distribution problem — every pair of communicators needs a shared secret, and every new pair multiplies the keys (n(n−1)/2 pairs) — plus key revocation and rotation logistics.

Asymmetric encryption under the hood

A mathematically related key pair: the public key encrypts (or verifies), the private key decrypts (or signs). RSA's mechanism rests on the trapdoor: multiplying two large primes is easy; factoring their product is computationally infeasible at key sizes of 2048+ bits. Elliptic-curve systems (ECC) give equivalent strength with far smaller keys, suiting mobile and TLS today.

RSA, the shape of the maths (numbers exaggerated for clarity):

  1. Choose primes p = 61, q = 53.  n = p x q = 3233   (public modulus)
  2. phi(n) = (p-1)(q-1) = 3120.
  3. Choose public exponent e = 17 (coprime to 3120).
  4. Compute private exponent d: d x e = 1 mod 3120 -> d = 2753.
  5. Encrypt message m = 65:  c = m^e mod n = 65^17 mod 3233 = 2790.
  6. Decrypt:  m = c^d mod n = 2790^2753 mod 3233 = 65.  ✓

Security: publishing (n = 3233, e = 17) reveals nothing useful WITHOUT
factoring n; with real 2048-bit n, factoring is the infeasible step. Signing
runs the other way: the signer applies d, anyone verifies with e.

Asymmetric strengths: no shared secret to distribute (the public key can be published), enabling signatures and non-repudiation; weakness: orders of magnitude slower than symmetric, so it is used for key exchange and signatures, not bulk data — the hybrid pattern below.

Signatures and hashing, traced:

  Signing a message:
    hash = SHA-256(message)                 (fixed 256-bit digest)
    signature = RSA-encrypt(hash) with the SIGNER'S PRIVATE key
    send (message, signature)

  Verifying:
    compute hash1 = SHA-256(message)
    hash2 = RSA-decrypt(signature) with the signer's PUBLIC key
    match -> the message is unaltered AND only the private-key holder signed
             it (authentication AND non-repudiation).

A hash is one-way and collision-resistant: any edit changes the digest
completely (avalanche), so tampering is detectable even in large documents.
SymmetricAsymmetric
KeysOne shared secretPublic/private pair
SpeedFast (AES)Slow (RSA, ECC) — 100–1000× for bulk
UseBulk data encryptionKey exchange, signatures, certificates
Key distributionHard problem (n(n−1)/2 keys)Public key can be published freely
Non-repudiationNo (either holder could have made the ciphertext)Yes — signatures bind the private key

Hybrid systems and encryption protocols

Real protocols combine the two families: use asymmetric cryptography to authenticate and agree a fresh symmetric session key, then encrypt the conversation symmetrically for speed. The session key is ephemeral — compromising it later decrypts nothing else.

TLS handshake (HTTPS), message by message:

  Client                                    Server
    | --- ClientHello (ciphers, random) ---->|
    | <--- ServerHello (cipher chosen) ------|
    | <--- Certificate (server's public key) |
    | <--- ServerHelloDone ------------------|
    |    [client verifies the CERTIFICATE chain to a trusted CA]
    | --- KeyExchange (pre-master secret     |
    |     encrypted with server's public key)|
    | --- ChangeCipherSpec + Finished ------>|
    | <--- ChangeCipherSpec + Finished ------|
    Both now hold the same symmetric session key (derived from the secret).
    | <========== encrypted application data ==========> |

Why each step matters: Hello negotiates the cipher suite; the certificate
authenticates the server; the key exchange gives confidentiality (only the
private-key holder reads the pre-master secret); Finished confirms both sides
derived the same keys, defeating downgrade tampering.

Related protocols: SSH (encrypted remote shell and transfer, authenticating hosts by keys), IPsec/VPNs (encrypting whole IP tunnels between sites), PGP/GPG (email signing/encryption with a web-of-trust model), WPA2/WPA3 (Wi-Fi link encryption). Each solves the same composition problem for a different layer.

Digital certificates and trust

A digital certificate binds an identity to a public key, issued and signed by a certificate authority (CA) whose own key is trusted by the client's operating system/browser (the trust store). Contents: subject (domain), subject's public key, issuer, validity period, serial number, and the CA's signature. Verification walks the chain from the site's certificate up through intermediates to a trusted root.

  • Issuance: the applicant generates a key pair, sends a CSR (with proof of control over the domain), the CA validates (DV by email/DNS; EV with organisation checks) and signs.
  • Revocation: compromised keys must die early — CRLs (revocation lists) and OCSP (live status queries); browsers check before trusting.
  • Self-signed certificates: usable for testing only; no chain to a trusted root, so browsers warn — the mechanism, not mere "untrustworthiness", is the mark.
  • Trust model weaknesses worth naming: a compromised CA can sign falsely; the system is only as strong as its least careful CA (notable incidents: DigiNotar).
Worked: verifying a certificate chain in a browser, step by step.

1. The server sends its certificate (leaf) plus intermediates.
2. The browser checks the leaf's validity period (not expired/not future).
3. It verifies the CA signature on the leaf using the intermediate's key.
4. It follows intermediates up to a root already in its trust store.
5. It checks the hostname matches the certificate's subject (SAN field).
6. It checks revocation status (OCSP/CRL) for the leaf and intermediates.

Any failure breaks the padlock: expired date (step 2), unknown issuer
(step 4 - self-signed), wrong domain (step 5 - another site's certificate),
or revoked key (step 6 - the compromised-key case).

Worked example: securing a web application end to end

Requirements: users log in, place orders, view invoices.

1. Transport: HTTPS everywhere (TLS 1.3), HSTS so plain HTTP never negotiates -
   protects credentials and cookies in transit.
2. Certificates: a CA-signed certificate with auto-renewal (certbot-style);
   monitor expiry - the classic outage is a lapsed certificate.
3. Passwords: stored as salted bcrypt/argon2 hashes (never reversible
   encryption); 2FA at login for account takeover resistance.
4. Sessions: random session IDs, Secure/HttpOnly/SameSite cookies, short
   expiry; CSRF tokens on state-changing requests.
5. Data at rest: card details tokenised (never stored raw); database backups
   encrypted with keys held separately.
6. Integrity: signed software releases (code-signing certificates) so the
   deployed application is provably what the team built.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Saying asymmetric encryption "is more secure"; it solves key distribution and signatures — security depends on key sizes and protocol design, not the family.
  • Forgetting that hashing alone proves integrity but not authorship; a shared hash proves nothing about who sent it — signatures add the private-key step.
  • Describing certificates as "encryption files"; a certificate is a signed binding of identity to public key.
  • Tracing TLS without the verification steps: the CA chain check and hostname match are the authentication marks.
  • Confusing CRL with OCSP (list pulled periodically vs live per-lookup) or missing revocation entirely.
  • Reusing session keys or calling them permanent; ephemerality limits the blast radius of compromise.
  • Claiming a padlock proves a site is honest; TLS proves the connection is private and the domain is authenticated — not the merchant's intent.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Unit 3, 4 marks). Explain how symmetric and asymmetric encryption are combined in HTTPS.

Answer: Asymmetric encryption authenticates the server (its certificate carries a public key signed by a trusted CA) and encrypts a pre-master secret the client generates, so only the server's private key can read it. Both sides then derive the same ephemeral symmetric session key and encrypt the actual data with a fast symmetric cipher. This gets asymmetric's safe key agreement and symmetric's speed where the bulk flows.

Question 2 (Unit 3, 4 marks). Describe how a digital signature provides authentication and non-repudiation.

Answer: The signer hashes the message and encrypts the digest with their private key; the signature travels with the message. A verifier decrypts the signature with the signer's public key and compares it with their own hash of the message. A match proves the message is unaltered (integrity) and that only the holder of the private key could have signed it (authentication), so the signer cannot later deny it (non-repudiation).

Question 3 (Unit 3, 5 marks). Explain the role of certificate authorities in establishing trust.

Answer: A CA binds an identity to a public key by signing a certificate containing the subject, key, validity period and issuer. Clients hold trusted root CA keys in their trust store, so verifying the chain from the site's certificate up to a root proves the key belongs to that domain. CAs validate applicants (DV/EV), and revocation (CRL/OCSP) ends trust early if keys leak. The model's weakness is that any compromised CA can sign falsely — trust is only as strong as its weakest CA.

Question 4 (Unit 3, 4 marks). Explain the key distribution problem and how it is addressed.

Answer: Symmetric encryption needs every communicating pair to share a secret key in advance; with n users that is n(n−1)/2 keys, and any interception of a distributed key compromises the channel. It is addressed by asymmetric key exchange (publishing a public key lets any party agree a session key securely), key distribution centres/protocols, and hybrid systems where asymmetric agreement hands over an ephemeral symmetric key.

Question 5 (Unit 3, 3 marks). Explain why TLS uses a new session key for each connection.

Answer: Ephemeral keys limit exposure: if a session key is later compromised, only that one session's traffic is decryptable, not past or future ones. Fresh keys also resist replay attacks (old captured traffic under a different key reads as noise) and shrink the value of any single key theft.

Question 6 (Unit 3, 4 marks). A browser warns that a certificate is invalid. Explain three possible causes.

Answer: The certificate has expired (outside its validity period); the chain cannot be verified to a trusted root (self-signed or an untrusted intermediate); the hostname does not match the certificate's subject/SAN (the certificate belongs to another domain); or the certificate has been revoked following key compromise. Each failure corresponds to one check of the verification process.

Cryptography protects channels between machines; the next note covers the software that increasingly acts within them — artificial intelligence.

title: Data Types and File Organisation — Study Notes
content:
Data Types and File Organisation

User-Defined Types

A user-defined type is derived from existing types. An enumerated type lists named values in order: TYPE Months = (Jan, Feb, Mar ...). Internally each value is an integer index starting at 0. Pointer types store a memory address; the dereference operator returns the value at that address, which is how linked structures reference their nodes. Set types store unordered collections of distinct values from an ordinal base type, supporting union, intersection and difference.

Records

A record groups related fields of different types under one identifier, for example a Student record with name : STRING and mark : INTEGER. Arrays of records are the standard structure for storing a table of items in memory.

File Organisation

  • Serial: records in insertion order; searching checks every record. Simple but slow.
  • Sequential: records kept in key order; binary search possible, but insertion needs rewriting.
  • Random (direct): a hashing function converts the key into a storage address, giving near-instant access. A poor hash causes collisions — two keys hashing to the same address — resolved by chaining or overflow areas.

Hashing

A common method is division hashing: Address = Key MOD TableSize. A good hash distributes keys evenly; load factor above roughly 70 percent degrades performance.

Exam tips: state the internal integer representation of enumerated values; define a collision before describing its resolution; compare the three file organisations in terms of search and insert cost.

File organisation and access

Serial files store records in the order they are written and suit sequential processing. Sequential files store records in key order, so a search can stop early. Random (direct) access files calculate a record's address from its key, using a hashing function, so any record can be reached quickly.

Exam tip: state the trade-off: sequential access is simple but slow for searching; direct access is fast but needs a hashing function and can produce collisions.

Worked example: a record definition

A record groups fields of different data types under one name. A record called Book might have Title (string), Pages (integer), Price (real) and InStock (Boolean). Each field is then referred to by the record name and the field name, for example Book.Pages. Records let a program keep related data together and pass it to a procedure as one item.

Worked example: hashing with linear probing

A hash table has 5 slots numbered 0 to 4, and the hash function is h(k) = k mod 5. Insert the keys 12, 27 and 8 in that order. The key 12 gives 12 mod 5 = 2, so it is stored in slot 2. The key 27 also gives 2, which is already occupied, so the next slot 3 is used. The key 8 gives 3, which is occupied, so it moves on to slot 4. A collision happens whenever two keys hash to the same slot, and the probing method determines where the second key is placed.

Comparing file access methods

  • Serial files store records one after another in the order they arrive, so finding one record means reading from the start.
  • Sequential files store records in key order, so a search can stop once it passes the place where the record should be.
  • Random (direct) files use a hash function to calculate the address of a record directly, which gives the fastest access for a single record.

Exam point: when asked to choose a file organisation, state the access pattern the question describes, such as frequent single-record look-ups or regular batch reads in order, and justify the choice from that pattern.

title: Exam technique: Data Handling
content:
### What earns the marks
For averages, the total shown earns a mark before any division. For even-count medians, the two middle values identified earn the method mark. For grouped data, the modal class stated as an interval earns full credit; single numbers score nothing. For cumulative frequency, the position formula (n + 1) / 2 quoted earns the method mark before reading off.
### Traps
Error: total given as the mean. Correction: divide by the count last. Error: 3rd value picked as median of six values. Correction: average the 3rd and 4th. Error: 40th value read for the median of 80. Correction: position 40.5. Error: quartiles read for median and vice versa. Correction: 20th/60th are quartiles at n = 80.
### Worked example
Four values are 2, 3, 3, 5, 8, 9 (six values in total). The median is the average of the 3rd and 4th values: (3 + 5) / 2 = 4. For a mean of 9 from four values, the total must be 36: write the sum first, then divide by 4. Both steps earn their own marks.

title: IGCSE Physics: Forces and Motion
content:
IGCSE Physics: Forces and Motion

Cambridge IGCSE Physics 0625 (2026–2028), Topic 1 Motion, forces and energy: statements 1.2 Motion, 1.3 Mass and weight, 1.5 Forces and 1.6 Momentum. This is the mechanics spine of the whole course, and it is where the Paper 4 structured calculation marks are won and lost. Almost every mechanics question begins the same way: label the velocities, find the resultant force, then choose the equation. The ideas below are built from absolute zero, but the definitions are examinable word for word, so learn them exactly as stated.

Speed, velocity and acceleration

Start with an analogy. A car's speedometer tells you how fast the car is covering ground; it says nothing about which way the car points. That everyday reading is speed. Add a compass direction to it and you have velocity. Speed is a scalar (size only); velocity is a vector (size and direction), and that single distinction runs through the entire course.

QuantityDefinitionSymbol and unitScalar or vector
DistanceTotal length of the path travelleds, metre (m)Scalar
DisplacementDistance in a stated straight-line direction from a start points, metre (m)Vector
SpeedDistance travelled per unit timev, metre per second (m s⁻¹)Scalar
VelocityRate of change of displacement, i.e. speed in a stated directionv, metre per second (m s⁻¹)Vector
AccelerationRate of change of velocitya, metre per second squared (m s⁻²)Vector

The two equations every question uses are:

average speed = total distance travelled / total time taken        v = s / t
acceleration = (final velocity - initial velocity) / time taken    a = (v - u) / t

Here u is the initial velocity, v is the final velocity, and t is the time taken. The SI units must be metres, seconds and metres per second before the equations are used; convert kilometres to metres and minutes to seconds first. The sign convention is the student's choice but must be stated: pick one direction as positive (upwards or forwards is usual), then velocities and accelerations in the opposite direction are negative. A negative acceleration that slows an object is often called a deceleration. An object thrown upwards has g = 9.81 m s⁻² downwards throughout its flight, so if up is positive its acceleration is −9.81 m s⁻² at every point, including the instant it stops at the top.

Average speed over a whole journey is not the average of the speeds. It is total distance divided by total time, so a car that covers 100 km at 50 km h⁻¹ and the next 100 km at 100 km h⁻¹ has an average speed of 200 km in 3 hours, which is 67 km h⁻¹, not 75 km h⁻¹.

Describing motion with graphs

Graphs are the language of this topic, and Paper 4 nearly always carries one. Two kinds do all the work.

FeatureDistance–time graphSpeed–time graph
GradientSpeed (or velocity)Acceleration
Area under the graphNot meaningfulDistance travelled
Horizontal lineObject at restConstant speed, zero acceleration
Straight sloping lineConstant speedConstant acceleration
CurveChanging speed (draw a tangent to find the speed at a point)Changing acceleration

On a distance–time graph the gradient is the distance moved divided by the time taken, which is the speed. On a speed–time graph the gradient is the change in speed divided by the time taken, which is the acceleration, and the area under the graph is made of rectangles (speed × time = distance) and triangles (½ × base × height), so it gives the total distance travelled. Drawing a tangent to a curve at a point is a Paper 6 skill: place the ruler so it just touches the curve, extend the line well past the curve on both sides, and take two distant points on the tangent to work out its gradient.

Paper 6 link. A trolley pulled by a falling mass leaves dots on ticker tape from a 50 Hz timer, so consecutive dots are 0.02 s apart. The distance between successive dots gives the speed over that interval, and a speed–time graph of those speeds has a gradient equal to the trolley's acceleration. Measuring a short distance with a ruler and dividing by 0.02 s is exactly the averaging technique in statement 1.1.

Mass, weight and gravitational field strength

Mass is the amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms with a balance. It does not change wherever the object is taken: the mass of an astronaut is the same on the Moon as on Earth. Weight is the force of gravity on that mass, measured in newtons with a spring balance, and it is a vector because gravity always pulls towards the centre of the attracting body. The astronaut's weight on the Moon is about one sixth of that on Earth because the Moon's gravitational field is weaker.

weight = mass x gravitational field strength        W = m g
  • W: weight in newtons (N). Weight is a vector, and its direction is straight down towards the centre of the Earth.
  • m: mass in kilograms (kg). Mass is a scalar.
  • g: gravitational field strength in newtons per kilogram (N kg⁻¹); on Earth g ≈ 9.81 N kg⁻¹, which is numerically the same as the free-fall acceleration 9.81 m s⁻².

Examination questions give the value of g to use, and many IGCSE papers round it to 10 N kg⁻¹ to keep the arithmetic simple. Always use the value printed in the question, and quote it in your answer when you substitute. Never confuse the two instruments: a balance compares masses and would give the same reading on the Moon, while a newton meter compares weights and would not.

Forces and their effects

A force is a push or a pull, measured in newtons, and it is a vector: direction matters. Forces can change an object's speed, change its direction of travel, or change its shape. Newton's first law states that an object remains at rest, or continues at constant velocity in a straight line, unless a resultant (net) force acts on it. Motion only changes when forces are unbalanced; a book resting on a table has weight and an equal upward normal contact force acting on it, so its resultant force is zero and it does not accelerate.

The resultant force is the single force that has the same effect as all the real forces combined. Two people pushing a trolley the same way add; pushing opposite ways subtract; forces at right angles combine by Pythagoras on the diagonal (Supplement). Newton's second law, in the form examined at IGCSE, is a Supplement statement:

resultant force = mass x acceleration        F = m a
  • F: resultant force in newtons (N), positive in the chosen positive direction.
  • m: mass in kilograms (kg).
  • a: acceleration in metres per second squared (m s⁻²), in the same direction as F.

The equation only works with the resultant force and only in SI units. If a car's engine produces 3000 N while drag is 1000 N, the resultant is 2000 N, and it is that 2000 N that goes into F = ma.

Friction and drag. Friction acts where surfaces touch and always opposes the motion or the tendency to move. Drag (air resistance or water resistance) opposes motion through a fluid and grows as the speed grows. A falling object released from rest therefore accelerates at first, because weight exceeds drag; as speed rises, drag rises until it equals the weight. From that moment the resultant force is zero, the acceleration is zero, and the object falls at terminal velocity. This is a Supplement explanation and it is a regular Paper 4 six-mark question: describe the motion in stages and use the words resultant force, drag and terminal velocity.

Springs and extension. A load hung on a spring stretches it. The relationship is summarised on a load–extension graph: a straight line through the origin shows extension proportional to load, up to the limit of proportionality. The stiffness of the spring is its spring constant:

force = spring constant x extension        F = k x
  • F: force applied to the spring in newtons (N).
  • k: spring constant in newtons per metre (N m⁻¹); larger k means a stiffer spring.
  • x: extension in metres (m). Extension = stretched length − original length, so it is a scalar in practice.

Beyond the limit of proportionality the line curves: the spring is permanently deformed and does not return to its original length when the load is removed. Doubling the load doubles the extension only while the graph is still a straight line. Two identical springs in series share the load and stretch twice as far; in parallel they share the load and stretch half as far (Supplement).

Turning effects of forces: moments

A force that does not act through a pivot makes an object turn. The size of that turning effect is the moment of the force:

moment of a force = force x perpendicular distance from the pivot        M = F d
  • M: moment in newton metres (N m). A moment is a vector in the sense that it turns clockwise or anticlockwise, and that sense must be carried through the calculation as a sign.
  • F: force in newtons (N).
  • d: perpendicular distance from the line of action of the force to the pivot in metres (m).

The word perpendicular is the whole mark. If a 10 N force acts at 30° to a spanner handle, the moment uses the perpendicular component of the force, or equivalently the perpendicular distance. For an object in equilibrium the principle of moments applies: the sum of the clockwise moments about any pivot equals the sum of the anticlockwise moments, and the resultant force is zero. A see-saw balances when the anticlockwise moment of the near child equals the clockwise moment of the far child; moving either child outwards increases that child's moment without changing their weight. Two equal and opposite forces whose lines of action do not coincide form a couple, which produces rotation without translation, as when a steering wheel is turned with both hands.

Centre of gravity and stability

The centre of gravity of an object is the single point through which its entire weight may be taken to act. For a uniform object it is the geometric centre; for a lamina (a flat sheet) it can be found experimentally by the plumb-line method, which is a classic Paper 6 task: hang the lamina freely from one hole, hang a plumb line from the same pin, and mark the line; repeat from a second hole; the lines cross at the centre of gravity.

Stability depends on where that point sits relative to the base. An object topples when the line of action of its weight falls outside its base, because the weight then produces a resultant moment that overturns it. Wide bases and low centres of gravity make objects stable (racing cars carry ballast low; tall trucks are loaded low), and top-heavy objects with narrow bases topple easily.

Momentum and impulse

Momentum is the quantity of motion a moving object carries: a lorry at 20 m s⁻¹ is far harder to stop than a bicycle at the same speed. Momentum is a Supplement statement for 0625 and is a favourite for Paper 4 calculation questions.

momentum = mass x velocity        p = m v
impulse = change in momentum = resultant force x time        F t = m v - m u
  • p: momentum in kilogram metres per second (kg m s⁻¹). Momentum is a vector, in the same direction as the velocity, so the sign convention chosen at the start must be applied to every velocity.
  • m: mass in kilograms (kg); v and u: final and initial velocity in metres per second (m s⁻¹), positive in the chosen positive direction.
  • Impulse: newton seconds (N s), equal to the change in momentum.

The principle of conservation of momentum: in a closed system, where no external resultant force acts, the total momentum before an event equals the total momentum after it. Total means the vector sum: momenta in opposite directions carry opposite signs. This one statement solves collisions, explosions and recoil problems. Newton's second law in its full form is implied here: the resultant force equals the rate of change of momentum, F = (mv − mu)/t, which is why increasing the time of impact reduces the force for the same change in momentum — that is how airbags, crash barriers and landing on a bent knee work.

Worked example: collision and impact force

Collision. A 1200 kg car travelling at 15 m s⁻¹ runs into a stationary 800 kg car and the two lock together. Find their common velocity. Take the first car's direction as positive.

total momentum before = 1200 x 15 + 800 x 0 = 18 000 kg m s-1
total momentum after = (1200 + 800) v = 2000 v
2000 v = 18 000, so v = 9 m s-1, in the original direction

The combined cars move at 9 m s⁻¹ in the direction the first car was travelling. Note that kinetic energy is not conserved in this collision — most of it is lost to sound and deformation — but momentum is always conserved.

Impact force. A 0.50 kg ball travelling at 12 m s⁻¹ hits a wall and rebounds at 8 m s⁻¹ in the opposite direction. The contact lasts 0.050 s. Find the average force on the ball. Take the initial direction as positive, so the rebound velocity is −8 m s⁻¹.

change in momentum = m v - m u = 0.50 x (-8) - 0.50 x 12 = -4.0 - 6.0 = -10 kg m s-1
average force = change in momentum / time = -10 / 0.050 = -200 N

The minus sign shows the force acts opposite to the ball's initial motion, which is what a wall does. The magnitude is 200 N. Getting the sign of the rebound velocity wrong is the single most common error in this topic, and it doubles the answer.

Common mistakes

  • Confusing mass and weight: mass is in kilograms and never changes; weight is in newtons and equals mg. A mass of 5 kg has a weight of about 50 N, not 5 kg.
  • Using the average of speeds for the average speed of a journey; it is always total distance over total time.
  • Reading the wrong quantity from a graph: gradient on a distance–time graph is speed, gradient on a speed–time graph is acceleration, and only the speed–time graph has a meaningful area.
  • Putting any force into F = ma. Only the resultant force gives the acceleration, so add and subtract the forces first.
  • Using a slanted distance in a moment calculation; d is measured perpendicular to the line of action of the force.
  • Losing the sign of a velocity in a momentum calculation. Reversal of direction is a sign change, and the total momentum is a vector sum, not a sum of sizes.
  • Using g = 9.81 when the question says take g = 10 N kg⁻¹, and forgetting to state which value was used.
  • Adding a force in newtons to a momentum in kg m s⁻¹; if the units do not match, the physics does not either.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 4, 3 marks). A cyclist starts from rest and reaches 8.0 m s⁻¹ in 5.0 s. Calculate the average acceleration and the distance travelled.

Answer: a = (v − u)/t = (8.0 − 0)/5.0 = 1.6 m s⁻². Distance = average speed × time = ½(0 + 8.0) × 5.0 = 20 m. (A speed–time graph of the motion is a triangle of area ½ × 5.0 × 8.0 = 20 m.)

Question 2 (Paper 4, 4 marks). A skydiver of mass 80 kg falls. Explain, using forces, why she reaches a terminal velocity, and state the size of the drag force at that moment.

Answer: Weight W = mg = 80 × 9.8 = 784 N downwards (≈ 800 N if g = 10 is taken). At first weight exceeds drag, so there is a downward resultant force and she accelerates. As speed increases, drag increases. When drag equals the weight the resultant force is zero, acceleration is zero, and she falls at constant terminal velocity. The drag force is then 784 N (or 800 N) upwards.

Question 3 (Paper 2 style). Which statement about a ball thrown straight up is correct? A: its acceleration at the top is zero; B: its velocity at the top is zero; C: its momentum at the top is maximum; D: its weight is zero at the top. Answer: B. The velocity is instantaneously zero at the top, but g still acts there, so the acceleration is 9.81 m s⁻² downwards and the weight is unchanged. Paper 2 setters rely on this confusion between velocity and acceleration.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 4 marks). A 1500 kg car travelling at 20 m s⁻¹ brakes to a stop in 4.0 s. Calculate the braking force.

Answer: change in momentum = mv − mu = 1500 × 0 − 1500 × 20 = −30 000 kg m s⁻¹. Force = change in momentum / time = −30 000 / 4.0 = −7500 N. The braking force is 7500 N opposite to the motion.

Question 5 (Paper 6 style). Describe how you would find the centre of gravity of an irregular lamina.

Answer: Hang the lamina from a pin through a hole near its edge so it swings freely. Hang a plumb line from the same pin and, when everything is at rest, mark the plumb-line position on the lamina. Repeat with the lamina hung from a second hole. The point where the two marked lines cross is the centre of gravity. The plumb line marks the vertical through the pivot, and the centre of gravity lies on it in both cases.

Question 6 (Paper 4, 3 marks). A 0.20 kg ball moving at 6.0 m s⁻¹ collides with an identical ball at rest and stops dead. Find the velocity of the second ball after the impact.

Answer: total momentum before = 0.20 × 6.0 = 1.2 kg m s⁻¹. After the impact the first ball has zero momentum, so 0.20 × v = 1.2 and v = 6.0 m s⁻¹ in the original direction.

Momentum, moments and Newton's laws are the tools; the next step is what those forces actually do to energy.

Equations and symbols

Every equation 0625 uses across statements 1.2, 1.3, 1.5 and 1.6, in the form the mark scheme expects. Motion equations assume constant acceleration in a straight line; the force equations are vector equations, so direction is part of the answer.

Motion

v = Δs / Δt
Key: v = speed or velocity (m/s); Δs = change in displacement (m); Δt = time interval (s). Velocity is a vector, so a change of direction is a change of velocity even at constant speed.

a = Δv / Δt = (v − u) / t
Key: a = acceleration (m/s²); v = final velocity (m/s); u = initial velocity (m/s); t = time taken (s). A negative a means deceleration.

v² = u² + 2as
Key: v = final velocity (m/s); u = initial velocity (m/s); a = constant acceleration (m/s²); s = displacement (m). Use it whenever time is neither given nor asked for.

s = ut + ½at²
Key: s = displacement (m); u = initial velocity (m/s); t = time (s); a = acceleration (m/s²). For a body released from rest, u = 0 and the distance is ½at².

s = ½(u + v)t
Key: s = displacement (m); u, v = initial and final velocity (m/s); t = time (s). This is the area under a velocity–time graph for constant acceleration, which is why the area is always a valid route to distance.

g = 9.8 N/kg (9.8 m/s²)
Key: g = gravitational field strength near the Earth's surface; numerically equal to free-fall acceleration, so a dropped body gains 9.8 m/s of speed each second in the absence of air resistance.

Mass, weight and force

W = mg
Key: W = weight (N); m = mass (kg); g = gravitational field strength (N/kg), 9.8 on Earth and about 1.6 on the Moon. Mass stays in kilograms and does not change with location; weight is the force and does.

F = ma
Key: F = resultant force (N); m = mass (kg); a = acceleration (m/s²). F is the resultant after friction and air resistance are subtracted, which is the single most common lost mark in this topic.

R = √(F₁² + F₂²)
Key: R = magnitude of the resultant (N); F₁, F₂ = two perpendicular forces (N). For forces along one line, add them when they point the same way and subtract when they oppose.

Balanced forces: ΣF = 0 implies a = 0
Key: ΣF = the vector sum of all forces (N); a = acceleration (m/s²). Zero resultant means at rest or at constant velocity — never "no forces acting".

Moments and springs

M = F × d
Key: M = moment of the force (N m); F = the force (N); d = the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force (m). A distance measured along a slant gives the wrong moment.

Σ clockwise moments = Σ anticlockwise moments
Key: the principle of moments, for a body in equilibrium. Each term is a force times its perpendicular distance (N m).

F = kx
Key: F = load or tension (N); k = spring constant (N/m or N/cm); x = extension beyond the natural length (m or cm). Valid only up to the limit of proportionality; beyond it the graph curves and the equation stops applying.

k = F / x
Key: k = spring constant (N/m); found as the gradient of the straight part of a force–extension graph, not from a single point beyond the limit.

Momentum

p = mv
Key: p = momentum (kg m/s); m = mass (kg); v = velocity (m/s). Momentum is a vector: opposite directions need opposite signs.

F = Δp / Δt
Key: F = average force acting (N); Δp = change in momentum (kg m/s); Δt = time over which it acts (s). This is the form that explains crumple zones and seatbelts: the same Δp spread over a longer Δt gives a smaller F.

m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂
Key: m₁, m₂ = masses (kg); u₁, u₂ = velocities before the collision (m/s); v₁, v₂ = velocities after (m/s). Total momentum is conserved when no external resultant force acts; kinetic energy is not necessarily conserved.

Quick revision: Differentiation II

Mathematics — A2 (9709). Example: y = x² e^x gives dy/dx = 2x e^x + x² e^x = e^x(2x + x²).

Key areas to revise

  • Product and Quotient Rules
  • Standard Derivatives
  • Chain Rule Everywhere
  • Implicit Differentiation
  • Parametric Curves

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

### Worked example Use the chain rule for composite functions. For y = (x² + 1)³, dy/dx = 3(x² + 1)² × 2x = 6x(x² + 1)². At x = 1 this is 6 × 1 × 4 = 24. Check using the derivative of the outer function at the inner value: 3 × 2² × 2 = 24. The product rule gives d/dx(x sin x) = sin x + x cos x. ### Check yourself Differentiate y = (3x − 1)⁴. The answer is dy/dx = 12(3x − 1)³. Check at x = 1: 12 × 2³ = 96.

title: IGCSE Physics: Thermal Physics
content:
IGCSE Physics: Thermal Physics

Cambridge IGCSE Physics 0625 (2026–2028), Topic 2 Thermal physics: statements 2.1 Kinetic particle model of matter, 2.2 Thermal properties and temperature, and 2.3 Transfer of thermal energy. Heat is the traffic of energy between hot and cold objects, and the particle model explains every thermal phenomenon in the syllabus: expansion, pressure, changes of state, conduction, convection and radiation. Paper 4 loves the particle explanations as much as the calculations, so both are built here from the same model.

States of matter and changes of state

All matter is made of tiny particles in constant motion, and the three states differ in how those particles are arranged and how they move.

StateArrangementMotionShape and volume
SolidClose-packed regular rows, touchingVibrate about fixed positionsFixed shape and fixed volume
LiquidClose together but disorderedSlide over each otherTakes the shape of the container; fixed volume
GasFar apart, random, filling the containerFast, random, straight-line between collisionsNo fixed shape or volume

When a substance is heated, energy is transferred to its thermal store and the particles move faster. On a heating curve the temperature rises until a change of state begins; during melting or boiling the temperature stays constant while the energy goes into breaking the forces between particles rather than into speed. The names of the changes are: melting (solid to liquid), freezing (liquid to solid), boiling or vaporisation (liquid to gas), condensation (gas to liquid), sublimation (solid straight to gas, as with dry ice).

The particle model of pressure and Brownian motion

Gas pressure arises because particles collide with the walls of their container: each collision gives a tiny push, and billions of pushes per second produce a steady pressure. Squeezing the same particles into a smaller volume raises the collision rate per unit area and so raises the pressure; heating a gas at fixed volume makes the particles move faster and collide harder and more often, again raising the pressure.

Brownian motion is the random jiggling of smoke particles seen under a microscope. The smoke particles are bombarded unevenly by fast-moving invisible air molecules, and the bigger the imbalance of hits at any instant, the bigger the lurch. It is direct evidence that gas particles move randomly and continuously (Supplement: the uneven collisions and their random distribution are the explanation demanded).

The gas laws and the absolute scale of temperature

For a fixed mass of gas, three qualitative rules are examined at Core level: heating a gas at constant pressure makes it expand (and cooling makes it contract); compressing a gas at constant temperature raises its pressure; and the relationships are summarised by the particle model above. The Celsius scale is everyday but its zero is arbitrary; the kelvin scale starts at absolute zero, the temperature at which particles have the minimum possible energy.

temperature in kelvin = temperature in degrees Celsius + 273        T (K) = θ (°C) + 273

Supplement: Boyle's law. For a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature, pressure and volume are inversely proportional:

p V = constant        p1 V¹ = p2 V²
  • p: pressure in pascals (Pa), positive; V: volume in cubic metres (m³) or any consistent unit. Both are scalars.
  • The product pV stays constant only while the temperature and the amount of gas are fixed.

Doubling the pressure halves the volume; a graph of p against V is a curve (inverse proportion), while a graph of p against 1/V is a straight line through the origin — a standard Paper 4 graph question.

Thermal expansion of solids, liquids and gases

Almost everything expands when heated: the particles move faster and push further apart. Everyday consequences include gaps between railway rails and bridge sections, expansion loops in power cables, the bimetallic strip in a thermostat (two metals expand by different amounts, so the strip bends and breaks a circuit), and the difficulty of undoing a metal jar lid, which can be loosened by running hot water over it so the metal lid expands more than the glass. Liquids expand more than solids for the same temperature rise, and gases expand most of all.

The particle explanation is a Supplement statement: heating increases the average separation of the particles because their increased energy makes them swing wider about their positions in a solid, slide further apart in a liquid, and occupy a larger volume in a gas at the same pressure. Thermometers work because liquids expand predictably with temperature: the liquid column rises in a narrow capillary, making a small volume change visible as a large length change.

Specific heat capacity

Equal masses of different substances need different amounts of energy to warm by the same temperature: water resists temperature change far more than sand, which is why coastal towns have mild climates and why water makes an excellent coolant in car engines and central heating. That property is the specific heat capacity:

energy transferred = mass x specific heat capacity x temperature change        E = m c Δθ
  • E: energy transferred in joules (J); m: mass in kilograms (kg).
  • c: specific heat capacity in joules per kilogram per degree Celsius (J kg⁻¹ °C⁻¹, numerically the same as J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹). A scalar.
  • Δθ: temperature change in degrees Celsius (°C) or kelvin (K). Temperature rises give a positive energy input; falls give energy out.

Supplement: measuring c experimentally. An electrical heater warms a well-lagged block of the substance; an ammeter and voltmeter give the electrical energy E = V I t, and a thermometer gives the temperature rise. Plot temperature against time; the gradient gives the rate of heating, and c = V I t / (m Δθ). Lagging reduces heat loss to the surroundings, the stirrer evens out hot spots, and the same method compares two materials by heating equal masses with the same heater for the same time.

Melting, boiling and evaporation

Melting and boiling happen at fixed temperatures for a pure substance at fixed pressure: 0 °C and 100 °C for pure water at one atmosphere. On a heating curve, plateaus mark the changes of state, and the energy supplied during a plateau is the latent heat: the energy needed to change the state of 1 kg without any temperature change (latent heat of fusion for melting, of vaporisation for boiling). The plateau exists because the energy breaks intermolecular attractions rather than increasing particle speed.

Evaporation is different from boiling and happens at any temperature. Particles at the liquid surface occasionally escape with above-average energy, so the average energy of those left falls and the liquid cools. Evaporation is faster when the temperature is higher, the surface area is larger, and a draught carries vapour away — the three factors Paper 4 expects in an evaporation-and-cooling explanation. Boiling happens throughout the liquid at a fixed temperature, with bubbles of vapour forming internally; evaporation happens only at the surface, at all temperatures, and cools the liquid left behind. Wet skin cools you because the water evaporates and takes the highest-energy particles with it.

Conduction

Conduction is the transfer of energy through a substance without the substance itself moving. In metals, the free electrons carry energy quickly from the hot end to the cold end, which is why metals are good conductors; in non-metals the energy passes only as vibrations handed along the vibrating particles, which is much slower. In gases and most liquids, conduction is poor because the particles are too far apart to pass on vibrations efficiently — hence insulating materials trap air in fibres or foam.

The core practical comparison: rods of different materials are coated with wax at one end and held over a heat source; the wax falls first from the best conductor. Metals come out in order (copper and aluminium good, steel poorer), while wood, plastic and glass barely conduct at all.

Convection

Convection is the transfer of energy by the movement of a fluid itself. Heating a fluid lowers its density: the warm parcel rises, cooler fluid sinks to take its place, and a convection current sets up. This is how radiators heat a room (hot air rises from the radiator, cools at the ceiling and returns down the far wall), how a kettle boils from the bottom, how sea breezes blow from sea to land by day, and how the element of a domestic water heater sits at the bottom so the whole tank warms. Convection requires a fluid — it cannot occur in a solid, and in a vacuum there is no medium at all.

Radiation

Radiation is the transfer of energy by electromagnetic waves, mainly infrared. It needs no medium, so it is the only way energy crosses the vacuum of space — which is why the Sun's heat reaches the Earth. The rate of emission and absorption depends on surface colour and texture: dull black surfaces are the best emitters and the best absorbers; shiny white or silvered surfaces are the poorest and reflect most radiation.

ApplicationSurface choice and reason
House radiatorMatte dark paint: emits radiation well
Hot-water tank and pipesSilvered foil: reduces radiation loss
Thermos flaskSilvered glass walls on both sides: minimises radiated loss in and out
Ice box / cool boxShiny white outside: reflects incoming radiation
Desert survival bagShiny side outwards in hot sun: reflects the Sun's radiation

Supplement: the Earth's energy balance. The Earth absorbs short-wavelength radiation from the Sun and radiates longer-wavelength infrared back to space. At equilibrium the two rates match and the average temperature is steady; greenhouse gases absorb some outgoing infrared and re-radiate it downwards, raising the equilibrium temperature. More greenhouse gas shifts the balance and warms the surface — the physics behind climate change.

Worked example: heating water

A 2.0 kg kettle of water is heated from 15 °C to 100 °C. The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J kg⁻¹ °C⁻¹. The kettle's heater supplies 2400 W.

energy needed = m c Δθ = 2.0 × 4200 x (10⁰ - 15) = 714 000 J
time = energy / power = 714 000 / 2400 = 298 s (about 5.0 minutes)

Real kettles take longer, because some energy warms the kettle body and is lost to the air — which is exactly why the efficiency of a kettle is less than 100 per cent. To boil the water away would need far more energy again, because of the latent heat of vaporisation.

Second calculation: a 0.50 kg block of aluminium (c = 900 J kg⁻¹ °C⁻¹) cools from 80 °C to 25 °C. Energy released = 0.50 × 900 × 55 = 24 750 J ≈ 25 kJ. Cooling gives out the same energy that heating took in; only the sign of the temperature change differs.

Common mistakes

  • Saying heat rises. Heat is energy, not a substance; it is the warm fluid that rises because it is less dense.
  • Confusing temperature with internal energy: temperature measures the average energy per particle, while internal energy is the total energy of all particles.
  • Forgetting that during melting or boiling the temperature stays constant even though energy is still being supplied.
  • Mixing up conduction (through a substance), convection (by a moving fluid) and radiation (by waves, no medium). A vacuum flask blocks all three: silvered walls (radiation), vacuum gap (conduction and convection), foam or stopper (conduction).
  • Using degrees Celsius where kelvin are required in a gas-law calculation; always convert with T = θ + 273 before using pV = constant relationships.
  • Putting mass in grams into E = mcΔθ; the unit J kg⁻¹ °C⁻¹ demands kilograms.
  • Describing evaporation as boiling; evaporation occurs at any temperature, only at the surface, and cools the remaining liquid.
  • Claiming particles expand; it is the average separation between the particles that increases.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 4, 3 marks). A 500 g block of copper (c = 390 J kg⁻¹ °C⁻¹) is heated from 20 °C to 120 °C. Calculate the energy transferred.

Answer: E = mcΔθ = 0.50 × 390 × 100 = 19 500 J = 19.5 kJ.

Question 2 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Explain, using the particle model, why a metal lid on a glass jar loosens under hot water.

Answer: The hot water heats both the lid and the jar. The particles in the metal gain energy and vibrate with greater amplitude, so their average separation increases more than that of the glass particles, because metals expand more than glass for the same temperature rise. The metal lid therefore becomes slightly larger in diameter than the neck of the jar and turns more easily.

Question 3 (Paper 2 style). Which change does not occur at a fixed temperature? A ice melting at 0 °C; B water boiling at 100 °C; C water evaporating from a puddle; D steam condensing at 100 °C. Answer: C. Evaporation occurs at any temperature and is not a fixed-temperature change of state.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 6 marks). Explain how a vacuum flask keeps a drink hot, referring to all three methods of thermal energy transfer.

Answer: The double-walled glass vessel has a vacuum between the walls, and a vacuum contains no particles, so energy cannot be transferred across the gap by conduction or convection. Both walls are silvered to reduce radiation: the shiny surfaces are poor emitters and poor absorbers, so little infrared escapes. The plastic stopper and foam supports are poor conductors and block convection in the air above the liquid. Together these keep energy in the drink for hours.

Question 5 (Paper 6 style). Describe an experiment to compare how well different materials conduct heat.

Answer: Fix rods of equal length and thickness made from the different materials, each coated at the far end with an equal blob of wax, over identical heat sources. Start together and record the time for each wax blob to fall. The shortest time identifies the best conductor. Keep the source, rod dimensions, coating thickness and starting temperature identical so the comparison is fair, and repeat to check the ranking.

Question 6 (Paper 4, 3 marks). A gas is trapped in a sealed syringe at 100 cm³ and 20 °C. It is heated to 87 °C at constant pressure. Find its new volume.

Answer: Convert first: 20 °C = 293 K, 87 °C = 360 K. At constant pressure V/T is constant, so V₂ = 100 × 360/293 = 123 cm³. (For a Core-level answer, the gas expands when heated at constant pressure, and the volume rises by roughly a quarter.)

From heat to the transfer of energy by waves: the next topic is Waves and Sound.

Equations and symbols

Thermal physics at 0625 is built on two energy equations — one for a change of temperature, one for a change of state — plus the power relation that turns either into a rate. The specific heat capacity and specific latent heat values are given in the exam, so the marks are in choosing the right equation and the right mass.

Heating and cooling

E = mcΔθ
Key: E = energy transferred to or from the substance (J); m = mass (kg); c = specific heat capacity (J/(kg °C)); Δθ (Δθ) = temperature change (°C). Use mcΔθ when the temperature changes but the state does not.

c(water) = 4200 J/(kg °C)
Key: the energy needed to raise 1 kg of water by 1 °C. Water's high value is why it is used as a coolant and why coastal climates are mild.

E = mL
Key: E = energy needed to change state (J); m = mass changing state (kg); L = specific latent heat (J/kg). Use it at a melting or boiling point, where the temperature stays constant while the state changes.

L(fusion, water) = 3.34 × 10⁵ J/kg and L(vaporisation, water) = 2.26 × 10⁶ J/kg
Key: L(fusion) melts or freezes 1 kg without changing temperature; L(vaporisation) boils or condenses it. Boiling takes far more energy than melting, which is why steam burns are worse than boiling-water burns at the same temperature.

E(total) = mcΔθ + mL
Key: the two stages of heating ice from below 0 °C to steam above 100 °C, added in sequence: warm the ice, melt it, warm the water, boil it, warm the steam. Each stage uses the equation that matches what is happening.

Rate of energy transfer

P = E / t
Key: P = power of the heater or the rate of energy transfer (W); E = energy transferred (J); t = time (s). Combined with mcΔθ this gives P = mcΔθ / t, the standard heater calculation.

efficiency = (energy gained by the substance / energy supplied) × 100%
Key: the useful gain is mcΔθ (J); the supplied energy is Pt (J). Heat lost to the surroundings is why a measured specific heat capacity often comes out higher than the data-book value.

Temperature and the gas laws

T(K) = θ(°C) + 273
Key: T = thermodynamic temperature (K); θ (θ) = Celsius temperature (°C). Gas-law ratios need kelvin: doubling 20 °C to 40 °C is not a doubling in kelvin.

p / T = constant (volume fixed)
Key: p = gas pressure (Pa); T = temperature (K). Heating a sealed container raises the pressure because the particles move faster and hit the walls harder and more often.

p₁V₁ = p₂V₂ (temperature fixed)
Key: p₁, V₁ = pressure and volume before (Pa, m³); p₂, V₂ = after. Compressing a gas at constant temperature raises its pressure in inverse proportion.

p₁V₁ / T₁ = p₂V₂ / T₂
Key: the combined form, with temperatures in kelvin. Any one of pressure, volume or temperature can be found if the other two change and the third is fixed.

The particle model as a rule set

pressure ∝ rate of collision × momentum change per collision
Key: the qualitative gas model behind every explanation mark: more particles per unit volume, or faster particles, means more forceful collisions with the container walls, hence a higher pressure.

title: A Level Physics: Astronomy and Cosmology
content:
A Level Physics: Astronomy and Cosmology

Astronomy is physics at the largest scale: measuring the distance to a star by its brightness, its size by its temperature, and the age of the universe by how fast galaxies recede. This note builds the toolkit from zero: luminosity and the inverse-square law, standard candles (Cepheid variables and Type Ia supernovae) and the distance ladder, stellar radii from Stefan's law, Hubble's law and redshift, and the evidence for the Big Bang. Every calculation is worked in full, because the papers test exactly these three or four formulas.

Brightness, luminosity and the inverse-square law

A star's luminosity L is the total power it radiates (watts). What a telescope receives is intensity (or flux) I — power per unit area at the observer's distance:

I = L/(4 π d²)

I in W m⁻², L in W, d in m
doubling the distance quarters the intensity

The analogy: a light bulb's power is fixed, but the same light spreads over a sphere of radius d — four times the area at twice the distance, so a quarter of the brightness per square metre. This one law underlies every distance measurement in astronomy.

Worked example. A star has luminosity 4.0 × 10²⁶ W. Find its intensity at 10 parsecs (1 pc = 3.09 × 10¹⁶ m).

d = 10 × 3.09 × 10¹⁶ = 3.09 × 10¹⁷ m
I = L/(4 π d²) = 4.0 × 10²⁶/(4 × 3.14 x (3.09 × 10¹⁷)²)
  = 4.0 × 10²⁶/(1.20 × 10³⁶) = 3.3 × 10⁻¹⁰ W m⁻²

Standard candles and the distance ladder

A standard candle is an object whose luminosity is known, so its observed intensity gives its distance by rearranging the inverse-square law. Two are examinable:

  • Cepheid variables: pulsating stars whose period of variation is tightly related to their luminosity (longer period, more luminous). Measuring the period gives L; measuring I gives d. Cepheids calibrated the first rungs of the cosmic distance ladder.
  • Type Ia supernovae: exploding white dwarfs that reach a consistent peak luminosity, bright enough to be seen in distant galaxies; they extended the ladder to cosmological distances and revealed the accelerating expansion.
distance from a standard candle:
d = √(L/(4 π I))

Worked example. A Cepheid has luminosity 1.0 × 10²⁹ W and observed intensity 2.5 × 10⁻¹² W m⁻². Find its distance in parsecs.

d = √(L/(4 π I)) = √(1.0 × 10²⁹/(4 × 3.14 × 2.5 × 10⁻¹²))
  = √(1.0 × 10²⁹/3.14 × 10⁻¹¹) = √(3.18 × 10³⁹)
  = 5.64 × 10¹⁹ m
in parsecs: 5.64 × 10¹⁹/3.09 × 10¹⁶ = 1825 pc
          = 1.8 kpc (2 s.f.)

Stellar radii and Stefan's law

A star radiates approximately as a black body. Stefan's law relates its luminosity to its surface area and absolute temperature:

L = 4 π r² σ T⁴

σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴ (Stefan-Boltzmann constant)
r = stellar radius (m), T = surface temperature (K)

so r = √(L/(4 π σ T⁴))

The fourth power is the headline: doubling a star's temperature multiplies its radiated power per square metre by 16. That is why hot blue stars are vastly more luminous than cooler red ones of similar size — and why a red giant can outshine the Sun despite its low temperature, because its radius is enormous.

Worked example. The Sun has L = 3.8 × 10²⁶ W and T = 5800 K. Find its radius.

r = √(L/(4 π σ T⁴))
T⁴ = (5800)⁴ = 1.13 × 10¹⁵
4 π σ T⁴ = 4 × 3.14 × 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ × 1.13 × 10¹⁵
              = 8.05 × 10⁸
r = √(3.8 × 10²⁶/8.05 × 10⁸) = √(4.72 × 10¹⁷)
  = 6.87 × 10⁸ m  (about 7 × 10⁸ m; the accepted value is 6.96 × 10⁸ m)

Worked example 2 (comparison). A star has the same temperature as the Sun but 100 times its luminosity. Find its radius in solar radii.

L = 4 π r² σ T⁴, same T and σ:
r² proportional to L  →  r = 10 R_sun

Redshift and Hubble's law

Light from distant galaxies is shifted toward longer wavelengths — redshift — because the galaxies are receding. For speeds much less than c:

z = Δλ/λ = v/c     (v << c)

Hubble's law: v = H0 d

H0 = Hubble constant (about 70 km s⁻¹ Mpc-1)
d = distance (Mpc)

Worked example 1. A galaxy's spectral line at 656 nm is observed at 689 nm. Find its recession speed.

Δλ = 689 - 656 = 33 nm
z = 33/656 = 0.0503
v = z c = 0.0503 × 3.0 × 10⁸ = 1.51 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹
  = 1.5 × 10⁴ km s⁻¹

Worked example 2. A galaxy at 100 Mpc recedes at 7000 km s⁻¹. Find H₀ and the Hubble time.

H0 = v/d = 7000/100 = 70 km s⁻¹ Mpc-1
Hubble time = 1/H0:
70 km s⁻¹ Mpc-1 = 70 000/(3.09 × 10²²) s⁻¹ = 2.27 × 10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹
t = 1/H0 = 4.4 × 10¹⁷ s = 1.4 × 10¹⁰ years = 14 billion years

The Big Bang and its evidence

Hubble's law implies that galaxies were once much closer together — the universe expanded from a hot, dense state. Three pieces of evidence are examinable:

  • Redshift of galaxies: nearly all galaxies recede, and recession speed increases with distance — expansion from a common origin.
  • Cosmic microwave background (CMB): a uniform 2.7 K radiation filling the sky — the cooled remnant of the hot early universe, predicted before it was found.
  • Abundance of light elements: the observed ratios of hydrogen, helium and lithium match predictions of Big Bang nucleosynthesis.

The expanding universe has no centre: space itself stretches, so every observer sees distant galaxies receding in all directions. The age estimate 1/H₀ assumes constant expansion; accelerating expansion (dark energy) modifies it, and the measured value is about 13.8 billion years.

The theory makes a further testable claim: the CMB should be an almost perfect black-body spectrum with tiny temperature ripples, and it is — the ripples themselves are the seeds of galaxy formation, and their pattern matches the theory's predictions for the mix of ordinary matter, dark matter and dark energy. That agreement across independent observations is why the Big Bang is accepted as the standard cosmological model rather than a single unexplained measurement.

Worked examples: the standard exam types

Worked example. Two stars have the same radius; star A is twice as hot as star B. Find the ratio of their luminosities.

L = 4 π r² σ T⁴; same r and σ
L_A/L_B = (T_A/T_B)⁴ = 2⁴ = 16
Star A is 16 times more luminous.

Worked example 2. A star's luminosity is 4.0 × 10³⁰ W and its surface temperature 10 000 K. Find its radius and compare it with the Sun's (7.0 × 10⁸ m).

T⁴ = (10⁴)⁴ = 1.0 × 10¹⁶
4 π σ T⁴ = 4 × 3.14 × 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ × 1.0 × 10¹⁶ = 7.12 × 10⁹
r = √(4.0 × 10³⁰/7.12 × 10⁹) = √(5.62 × 10²⁰)
  = 2.37 × 10¹⁰ m
r/R_sun = 2.37 × 10¹⁰/7.0 × 10⁸ = 34 solar radii

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Inverse square) A star at 20 pc has intensity I. What is its intensity at 60 pc? Answer: Three times the distance gives 1/9 of the intensity: I/9.
  2. (Luminosity) Define luminosity and state its unit. Answer: The total power radiated by a star across all wavelengths, measured in watts (W).
  3. (Standard candle) Explain how a Cepheid variable is used to find distance. Answer: Its pulsation period determines its luminosity from the period–luminosity relation; comparing that luminosity with the observed intensity gives d = √(L/4πI).
  4. (Stefan) A star has twice the Sun's radius and half its temperature. Compare luminosities. Answer: L ∝ r²T⁴ → (2)² × (1/2)⁴ = 4 × 1/16 = 1/4: the star is a quarter as luminous.
  5. (Redshift) A line at 500 nm appears at 505 nm. Find v. Answer: z = 5/500 = 0.010; v = 0.010 × 3.0 × 10⁸ = 3.0 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹.
  6. (Hubble) A galaxy at 50 Mpc recedes at 3500 km s⁻¹. Find H₀. Answer: H₀ = 3500/50 = 70 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹.
  7. (Age) Estimate the age of the universe from H₀ = 70 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹. Answer: t = 1/H₀ ≈ 14 billion years (with unit conversions: 70 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹ = 2.27 × 10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹).
  8. (Big Bang evidence) State two observations supporting the Big Bang. Answer: The redshift–distance relation (Hubble's law) and the cosmic microwave background; the light-element abundances are a third.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Parsecs versus metres: convert before substituting; 1 pc = 3.09 × 10¹⁶ m, 1 Mpc = 3.09 × 10²² m, 1 AU = 1.50 × 10¹¹ m.
  • Luminosity versus intensity: L is the star's total power; I is what arrives per square metre. The inverse-square law connects them and d must be in metres.
  • T⁴ not T: Stefan's law is a fourth power — doubling temperature multiplies luminosity by 16, not 2. Most arithmetic errors here are exponent slips.
  • Kelvin: surface temperatures in Stefan's law must be absolute; a temperature given in °C needs +273 first.
  • Redshift approximation: z = v/c holds for v ≪ c; at large redshifts the relativistic formula is needed. State the assumption.
  • H₀ units: km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹ — mismatched units in 1/H₀ give absurd ages. Convert km to m and Mpc to m.
  • Hubble time is an estimate: 1/H₀ assumes constant expansion; note the acceleration caveat when discussing the age.
  • Centre of the universe: the Big Bang happened everywhere — there is no centre or edge; expansion stretches space between galaxies.
  • Precision: 2 or 3 s.f. with units (W, W m⁻², m, km s⁻¹, years); the data sheet supplies σ, c and H₀.

Equations and symbols

Astronomy is four formulas and a unit convention. Luminosity, the inverse-square law, Stefan's law and Hubble's law answer almost every question, and the parsec-to-metre conversion decides whether the arithmetic is even in the right ballpark.

Brightness and distance

I = L/(4 π d²) Key: I = intensity or flux received (W m⁻²); L = luminosity, the star's total radiated power (W); d = distance to the star (m); π = 3.14. The 4πd² is the surface of the sphere the light has spread over, so doubling d quarters I.

d = √(L/(4 π I)) Key: the same relation rearranged to give distance in metres; convert to parsecs by dividing by 3.09 × 10¹⁶ m. This is how a standard candle works: L is known from the object's type, I is measured, d follows.

L = 4 π r² σ T⁴ Key: r = stellar radius (m); σ = Stefan–Boltzmann constant, 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴; T = surface temperature (K, absolute — add 273 to °C). The fourth power is why a star twice as hot radiates sixteen times as much per square metre.

r = √(L/(4 π σ T⁴)) Key: the rearranged form that gives a star's radius from its luminosity and temperature. For the Sun, L = 3.8 × 10²⁶ W and T = 5800 K give r = 6.87 × 10⁸ m.

L_A/L_B = (T_A/T_B)⁴ = 2⁴ = 16 Key: the comparison method: with equal radii, luminosity ratio is the fourth power of the temperature ratio. So a star twice as hot as another of the same size is 16 times as luminous — no numbers for L needed.

Redshift and expansion

z = Δλ/λ = v/c Key: z = redshift, a ratio with no units; Δλ = observed minus emitted wavelength (nm); λ = emitted wavelength (nm); v = recession speed (m s⁻¹); c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. Valid only for v much less than c, and that assumption should be stated.

v = H0 d Key: v = recession speed (km s⁻¹); d = distance (Mpc); H0 = Hubble constant, about 70 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹. It is the observational statement that recession speed is proportional to distance.

t = 1/H0 Key: t = Hubble time, the age estimate for the universe (s, then years); H0 must first be converted to s⁻¹ by turning km into m and Mpc into m, giving about 2.27 × 10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹ and hence 14 billion years.

The slip worth naming

Mixing parsecs with metres, and treating T as a first power. Convert to metres before substituting into the inverse-square law, and remember Stefan's law is T⁴ — the exponent slip is where most of the lost marks sit.

title: Web Technologies and Security — Study Notes
content:
Web Technologies and Security

The Three Layers

  • HTML gives structure and content: elements, attributes, forms for user input.
  • CSS gives presentation: selectors, properties, responsive layout.
  • JavaScript gives client-side behaviour: validation before submission, DOM updates without reload.

Server-side scripting (PHP) runs on the server: reads form fields ($_POST), queries the database, outputs HTML. The client never sees PHP source.

SQL Injection

An attack where crafted input changes the meaning of a query. If a login query concatenates the username directly, entering X OR 1=1 can match every row. Defences: parameterised queries (prepared statements) that separate code from data, validation, and least-privilege database accounts.

Encryption

  • Symmetric: one shared key (AES). Fast, but key distribution is the weak point.
  • Asymmetric: public/private key pair (RSA). Anyone encrypts with the public key; only the holder decrypts with the private key. Slower, so used to exchange a symmetric session key.
  • SSL/TLS combines both: certificates verify the server, asymmetric key exchange establishes a symmetric session key, then traffic is encrypted. HTTPS = HTTP over TLS on port 443.

Hashing vs Encryption

Hashing (e.g. SHA-256) is one-way: passwords should be stored hashed with a unique salt, never encrypted reversibly.

Exam tips: explain why parameterised queries stop injection; describe the TLS handshake in three steps; distinguish hashing from encryption with password storage as the example.

title: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Probability
content:
Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Probability

Probability measures how likely an event is on a scale from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). The IGCSE questions build from single events to combined ones — two dice, two draws without replacement, "at least one" — and the toolkit is small but must be used precisely: the complement rule, the addition rule for mutually exclusive events, the multiplication rule for independent ones, and tree diagrams for everything with stages. This note builds the topic from zero with every rule justified and every standard question type worked.

The probability scale and notation

P(event) = number of favourable outcomes / total outcomes
         (when outcomes are equally likely)

0 <= P(A) <= 1
P(not A) = 1 - P(A)        (the complement rule)

Probabilities are written as fractions, decimals or percentages — but keep one form within a question. The complement rule is the most powerful single line in the topic: "at least one" is almost always easier as 1 − P(none).

Worked example. A bag has 5 red, 3 blue and 2 green counters. Find P(red) and P(not red).

total = 10
P(red) = 5/10 = 1/2
P(not red) = 1 - 1/2 = 1/2  (check: 3 + 2 = 5 of 10)

Relative frequency and expected frequency

relative frequency = number of times the event occurred
                     / total number of trials

expected number = probability x number of trials

Relative frequency estimates probability from experiment; it approaches the theoretical value as trials increase (the law of large numbers). Questions ask you to compare an experimental relative frequency with a theoretical probability and comment on the discrepancy — small samples fluctuate, large samples converge.

Worked example. A biased die is rolled 200 times; a six appears 50 times. Estimate P(six) and predict the number of sixes in 500 rolls.

relative frequency = 50/200 = 0.25
expected in 500 = 0.25 × 500 = 125

Combined events: the two rules

RuleWhen to use itFormula
Addition (OR)mutually exclusive events — cannot both happenP(A or B) = P(A) + P(B)
Multiplication (AND)independent events — one does not affect the otherP(A and B) = P(A) × P(B)

The words "or" and "and" map onto add and multiply, but the conditions matter: if events are not mutually exclusive, subtract the overlap; if they are not independent, the second probability changes (see trees below).

Worked example 1. A fair die is rolled once. Find P(3 or 4).

mutually exclusive: 1/6 + 1/6 = 2/6 = 1/3

Worked example 2. Two fair coins are tossed. Find P(both heads).

independent: 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4

Worked example 3 (not mutually exclusive). From a standard pack, find P(a heart or a king).

P(heart) = 13/52, P(king) = 4/52, P(heart and king) = 1/52
P(heart or king) = 13/52 + 4/52 - 1/52 = 16/52 = 4/13

Tree diagrams

Trees handle multi-stage experiments, especially without replacement. Multiply along the branches for a sequence, add between branches for alternative ways to get the same outcome.

Worked example 1 (with replacement). A bag has 3 red and 2 blue counters. Two are drawn with replacement. Find P(two red) and P(one of each).

P(RR) = 3/5 × 3/5 = 9/25
P(RB) = 3/5 × 2/5 = 6/25;  P(BR) = 2/5 × 3/5 = 6/25
P(one of each) = 6/25 + 6/25 = 12/25

Worked example 2 (without replacement). Same bag, two counters drawn without replacement. Find P(two red) and P(one of each).

P(RR) = 3/5 × 2/4 = 6/20 = 3/10
P(RB) = 3/5 × 2/4 = 6/20;  P(BR) = 2/5 × 3/4 = 6/20
P(one of each) = 12/20 = 3/5

The denominators drop by one on the second draw without replacement — that is the entire difference, and forgetting it is the standard error.

Sample space diagrams

A sample space diagram lists every possible outcome, so probabilities can be counted rather than guessed. For two dice, a two-way grid of 36 cells shows each pair; shading the cells that satisfy an event turns the question into counting squares. The method protects against the commonest combined-event error — treating non-equally-likely outcomes as equally likely.

Worked example. Two fair dice are rolled. Find P(total = 7).

total outcomes = 6 × 6 = 36
totals of 7: (1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2), (6,1) = 6 outcomes
P(total 7) = 6/36 = 1/6

Worked example 2 (sums). From the same grid, find P(total is more than 10).

totals 11 or 12: (5,6), (6,5), (6,6) = 3 outcomes
P = 3/36 = 1/12

The grid also answers difference and product questions: mark the cells whose difference is 2, or whose product is even, and count. Writing the grid out takes a minute and removes the guesswork from every part of the question.

Two-way tables and Venn diagrams

A two-way table classifies individuals by two attributes at once — boys and girls against glasses and no glasses — with totals in the margins. Reading probabilities from it is a matter of restricting attention to the right row, column or cell:

  • P(A and B): the cell where the row and column meet, over the grand total.
  • P(A or B): the sum of the cells in A plus the cells in B minus the overlap, over the grand total.
  • P(A | B): the A-cell inside B's row (or column) over B's total.

Venn diagrams do the same job for sets: the intersection is "and" (multiply along a branch or read the overlap), the union is "or" (add the regions). Choosing between the two representations is a matter of what the question gives; both are equally valid, and the arithmetic is identical once the numbers sit in the right places.

Conditional probability

Conditional probability asks for the chance of A given that B has happened:

P(A | B) = P(A and B) / P(B)

Two-way tables are the friendliest setting: restrict attention to the row or column named by the condition, then divide by that row or column's total.

Worked example. 60 students: 25 study French, 35 study Spanish, 15 study both. Find P(studies French | studies Spanish).

given Spanish: restrict to the 35 Spanish students
of those, 15 also study French
P(French | Spanish) = 15/35 = 3/7

Worked example 2 (two-way table). A table shows 40 boys (12 play chess) and 30 girls (18 play chess). Find P(plays chess | girl).

restrict to girls: 30; chess players among them: 18
P = 18/30 = 3/5

Independent events and the multiplication rule

Two events are independent when the outcome of one does not change the probability of the other. The test is arithmetic: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B) exactly when they are independent. Questions often give the separate probabilities and ask you to check independence, or give P(A), P(B) and P(A and B) and ask whether the events are independent.

if P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B)  →  independent
if not                        →  not independent (associated)

Worked example. P(rain) = 0.3, P(late) = 0.2, P(rain and late) = 0.06. Are the events independent?

P(rain) x P(late) = 0.3 × 0.2 = 0.06
0.06 = 0.06, so the events are independent.

"At least one" problems

The complement trick: P(at least one) = 1 − P(none).

Worked example. A die is rolled twice. Find P(at least one six).

P(no six) = (5/6) x (5/6) = 25/36
P(at least one six) = 1 - 25/36 = 11/36

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Complement) P(A) = 0.35. Find P(not A). Answer: 0.65.
  2. (Single event) A bag has 4 green and 6 yellow balls. Find P(green). Answer: 4/10 = 2/5.
  3. (Mutually exclusive) A spinner has probabilities 0.2, 0.3, 0.4 and x. Find x. Answer: 1 − 0.9 = 0.1.
  4. (Independent) P(A) = 0.6, P(B) = 0.5, independent. Find P(A and B) and P(A or B). Answer: 0.30; 0.6 + 0.5 − 0.3 = 0.8.
  5. (Tree) Two draws without replacement from 5 red, 3 blue. Find P(both blue). Answer: 3/8 × 2/7 = 6/56 = 3/28.
  6. (At least one) A biased coin has P(head) = 0.4. Tossed twice, find P(at least one head). Answer: 1 − 0.6² = 1 − 0.36 = 0.64.
  7. (Relative frequency) 400 seeds are planted; 340 germinate. Estimate the germination probability. Answer: 340/400 = 0.85.
  8. (Conditional) In a class, 12 of 20 boys and 8 of 15 girls wear glasses. Find P(wears glasses | boy). Answer: 12/20 = 3/5.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Adding when you should multiply: "or" adds (for exclusive events), "and" multiplies (for independent ones). Mixed-up rules produce impossible answers above 1 — a check worth making.
  • Forgetting non-replacement: the second denominator drops by one and the numerator of the taken colour drops too.
  • Probabilities above 1: an answer of 1.2 is always wrong; re-check the rule used.
  • Counting without equally likely outcomes: P = favourable/total only when every outcome is equally likely; loaded dice and biased spinners need empirical or given probabilities.
  • "At least one" done the long way: summing every case wastes time and invites errors; use 1 − P(none).
  • Conditional without restricting: P(A | B) uses the total of B's group, not the grand total. The word "given" is the signal.
  • Not adding alternative branches: one-of-each has two orders (RB and BR); both must be included.
  • Mixing forms: fractions, decimals and percentages within one calculation invite arithmetic slips; choose one form and stay with it.

title: A Level Mathematics: Hypothesis Testing
content:
A Level Mathematics: Hypothesis Testing

A hypothesis test is a formal way of deciding whether data are surprising enough to overturn an assumption. The logic is legal rather than mathematical in spirit: assume the claim is true, compute how unlikely the observed evidence would be under that assumption, and reject the claim only if the evidence is unlikely enough. This note sets out the machinery — null and alternative hypotheses, significance levels, tails, critical regions — and then applies it to the binomial and normal cases the exam uses.

The logic of a test
