DDL defines structure: CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE, DROP. DML manipulates data: SELECT ... FROM ... WHERE, INSERT INTO, UPDATE, DELETE. Joins combine related tables: FROM Student s JOIN Enrolment e ON s.id = e.StudentID. Aggregates: COUNT, SUM, AVG with GROUP BY and HAVING.

Transactions and Concurrency

A transaction is a unit of work obeying ACID: Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (rules preserved), Isolation (concurrent transactions do not interfere), Durability (committed data survives crashes). Record locking blocks conflicting simultaneous edits; a deadlock occurs when two transactions each hold a lock the other needs.

Exam tips: normalise a small table through 1NF, 2NF, 3NF naming the dependency removed at each step; write a two-table SELECT with JOIN; state which ACID property a scenario breaks.

DDL and DML

Data Definition Language (DDL) creates and changes the structure of a database: CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE and DROP TABLE. Data Manipulation Language (DML) works with the data inside the structure: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE.

Example: CREATE TABLE Student (ID INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, Name VARCHAR(30)); is DDL; INSERT INTO Student VALUES (1, 'Ana'); is DML.

Exam tip: classify each statement by whether it changes structure or changes data.

Worked example: a SELECT query

To list the names of students in Year 11 who study Physics, sorted by surname, a query joins two tables and filters the result: SELECT Name FROM Student INNER JOIN Enrolment ON Student.StudentID = Enrolment.StudentID WHERE Year = 11 AND Subject = 'Physics' ORDER BY Name. Read the question word by word and map each condition onto a clause.

Keys and integrity

  • A primary key uniquely identifies each record in a table and cannot be null.
  • A foreign key holds the primary key of another table, which links the two tables together.
  • A candidate key is any field, or combination of fields, that could serve as the primary key.

Entity-relationship modelling

A one-to-many relationship, such as one teacher and many classes, is shown by placing the primary key of the "one" side in the "many" table. A many-to-many relationship, such as students and courses, needs a third, linking table that holds a foreign key for each side. Without it the database would repeat data or store several values in one field, which breaks normalisation.

Exam point: CREATE TABLE statements declare the data types, the primary key and each foreign key. DROP and ALTER change the structure; INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE and SELECT work with the records.

title: AS Level Physics: Quantum Physics
content:
AS Level Physics: Quantum Physics

Quantum physics begins with a failure: classical physics could not explain why hot objects glow the way they do, why light sometimes knocks electrons out of metal, or why atoms emit sharp lines rather than continuous rainbows. The answers — photons, the photoelectric effect, wave–particle duality and quantised energy levels — rebuilt physics in the twentieth century. This note builds the quantum toolkit from zero: the photon model and its arithmetic, Einstein's photoelectric equation with its graphs, de Broglie's matter waves, and the energy-level picture of the atom that explains every spectrum you will meet.

Why classical physics failed

Classical theory treated light as a continuous wave and predicted that any frequency should eject electrons from a metal if you wait long enough. Experiment said otherwise: below a threshold frequency, no electrons appear however intense the light; above it, electrons appear instantly however faint the light. Similarly, classical theory predicted that hot objects should radiate infinite energy at high frequencies (the ultraviolet catastrophe) — absurd. Planck's and Einstein's fix: energy is exchanged in discrete packets, quanta, each carrying E = hf. The packet idea is the whole foundation.

Photons: energy and momentum

A photon is a quantum of electromagnetic radiation. Its energy is set by its frequency alone:

E = h f = h c / lambda

h = 6.63 x 10-34 J s  (Planck constant)
f = frequency (Hz)
c = 3.0 x 108 m s-1
lambda = wavelength (m)

Photons also carry momentum, p = h/λ — a particle property that waves do not have in classical theory, and the bridge to matter waves later.

Worked example 1. Find the energy of a photon of 500 nm light.

E = hc/lambda = (6.63 x 10-34 x 3.0 x 108)/(5.0 x 10-7)
  = 1.989 x 10-25/5.0 x 10-7 = 3.98 x 10-19 J

Worked example 2 (electronvolts). Convert to electronvolts (1 eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J) and find the photon momentum.

E = 3.98 x 10-19/1.60 x 10-19 = 2.49 eV
p = h/lambda = 6.63 x 10-34/5.0 x 10-7 = 1.33 x 10-27 kg m s-1

Exam conversions deserve care: keV and MeV appear in nuclear contexts, and the eV↔J conversion (multiply or divide by 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹) is a mark waiting to be lost.

The photoelectric effect

Light on a clean metal surface ejects electrons — but only according to rules that demand the photon model:

  • Threshold frequency f₀: below it, no emission at all, whatever the intensity. The photon's energy must exceed the metal's work function φ (the minimum energy to free an electron from the surface).
  • Instantaneity: above f₀, emission begins immediately — one photon transfers all its energy to one electron in one interaction.
  • Intensity effect: above threshold, doubling the intensity doubles the number of photons and hence the photoelectric current (more electrons per second) but does not change their maximum kinetic energy.
  • Frequency effect: raising the frequency above f₀ increases the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons linearly.

Einstein's equation ties the numbers together:

h f = phi + KE_max

phi = work function of the metal (J or eV)
KE_max = maximum kinetic energy of an emitted electron
f0 = threshold frequency: h f0 = phi

Worked example. Sodium has work function 2.3 eV. Light of wavelength 450 nm falls on it. Find whether emission occurs and the maximum kinetic energy.

photon energy: E = hc/lambda = (6.63 x 10-34 x 3.0 x 108)/(4.5 x 10-7)
               = 4.42 x 10-19 J = 2.76 eV
compare: 2.76 eV > 2.3 eV  ->  emission occurs
KE_max = 2.76 - 2.3 = 0.46 eV
       = 0.46 x 1.6 x 10-19 = 7.4 x 10-20 J

Worked example (threshold). Find the threshold wavelength for sodium (φ = 2.3 eV).

h f0 = phi -> f0 = phi/h = (2.3 x 1.6 x 10-19)/6.63 x 10-34
     = 5.55 x 1014 Hz
lambda0 = c/f0 = 3.0 x 108/5.55 x 1014 = 5.4 x 10-7 m = 540 nm

Below 540 nm (higher frequency) sodium emits; above it, nothing. Note the inverse relationship: threshold wavelength corresponds to threshold frequency.

The graphs the papers love

Two plots encode the photoelectric effect and both are examinable:

  • KEₘₐₓ against frequency: a straight line with gradient h, crossing the frequency axis at f₀ and the KE axis at −φ. The gradient is the same for every metal — the metal only moves the intercepts.
  • Stopping potential against frequency: the same shape, since eVₛ = KEₘₐₓ.
  • Current against intensity: linear above threshold (more photons, more electrons).

Worked example. A plot of KEₘₐₓ against frequency has gradient 6.5 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and crosses the axis at 5.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz. Identify Planck's constant and the work function.

gradient = h = 6.5 x 10-34 J s (close to 6.63 x 10-34,
           the difference being experimental error)
phi = h f0 = 6.5 x 10-34 x 5.0 x 1014 = 3.25 x 10-19 J
    = 2.0 eV

Wave–particle duality

The quantum world refuses the wave/particle distinction: light, treated for centuries as a wave, arrives in photon packets; electrons, treated as particles, can diffract. Electron diffraction — beams of electrons producing interference patterns when scattered by crystals — is the evidence that convinced the profession. De Broglie unified the picture: every particle of momentum p has an associated wavelength

lambda = h / p = h / (m v)

Worked example. Find the de Broglie wavelength of an electron accelerated through 100 V.

KE = eV = 1.60 x 10-19 x 100 = 1.60 x 10-17 J
KE = (1/2) m v^2 -> p = sqrt(2 m KE)
p = sqrt(2 x 9.11 x 10-31 x 1.60 x 10-17)
  = sqrt(2.915 x 10-47) = 5.40 x 10-24 kg m s-1
lambda = h/p = 6.63 x 10-34/5.40 x 10-24 = 1.23 x 10-10 m
       = 0.123 nm   (comparable to atomic spacing: electrons
         diffract through crystals)

Why electrons diffract through crystals but footballs do not: the wavelength is only noticeable when it is comparable to the gap it passes through — the same rule as diffraction for waves. A macroscopic ball has such a large momentum that its de Broglie wavelength is immeasurably small.

Energy levels in atoms and line spectra

Electrons in atoms occupy quantised energy levels — only specific energies are allowed. Transitions between them absorb or emit a photon whose energy exactly equals the level difference:

Delta E = E_upper - E_lower = h f = h c / lambda
  • Emission spectrum: an excited atom drops to a lower level and emits a photon; a hot gas produces bright lines at specific wavelengths — a line spectrum.
  • Absorption spectrum: cold gas absorbs those same wavelengths from white light, leaving dark lines at identical positions.
  • Fluorescence: a photon is absorbed (UV, say), some energy is lost as heat, and a lower-energy (visible) photon is emitted — which is why white shirts glow blue under UV light.

The energy-level diagram is the standard question: a vertical scale in eV or J, arrows drawn downward for emission and upward for absorption, each arrow labelled with its transition energy.

Worked example 1. A hydrogen electron falls from level −0.54 eV to −1.51 eV. Find the photon's wavelength.

Delta E = -0.54 - (-1.51) = 0.97 eV
in joules: 0.97 x 1.60 x 10-19 = 1.552 x 10-19 J
lambda = hc/Delta E = (6.63 x 10-34 x 3.0 x 108)/1.552 x 10-19
       = 1.28 x 10-6 m = 1280 nm  (infrared)

Worked example 2. Explain why the spectral lines of an element are sharp rather than continuous.

Electrons occupy quantised levels, so only specific differences
Delta E exist between them; only photons with energy exactly equal
to a difference are emitted or absorbed; since f = Delta E/h, only
specific frequencies appear - sharp lines, not a continuum.

Worked examples: combined quantum calculations

Worked example. A metal has threshold frequency 7.5 × 10¹⁴ Hz. Light of wavelength 300 nm shines on it. Find the work function and the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons.

phi = h f0 = 6.63 x 10-34 x 7.5 x 1014 = 4.97 x 10-19 J
    = 3.1 eV
photon energy: E = hc/lambda = (6.63 x 10-34 x 3.0 x 108)/(3.0 x 10-7)
               = 6.63 x 10-19 J = 4.14 eV
KE_max = E - phi = 6.63 x 10-19 - 4.97 x 10-19 = 1.66 x 10-19 J
       = 1.04 eV

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Photon energy) Calculate the energy of a photon of frequency 5.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz. Answer: E = hf = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 5.0 × 10¹⁴ = 3.3 × 10⁻¹⁹ J (≈ 2.1 eV).
  2. (Photoelectric rules) Explain why red light cannot eject electrons from a given metal however intense it is, while faint blue light can. Answer: Emission requires individual photons above the threshold frequency f₀; red photons have lower frequency and energy below the work function, so no single red photon can free an electron regardless of photon number; blue photons exceed the energy requirement, so each can eject an electron on its own.
  3. (Graph reading) State what the gradient and x-intercept of a KEₘₐₓ against frequency graph represent. Answer: The gradient is Planck's constant h; the x-intercept is the threshold frequency f₀.
  4. (Intensity) The intensity of light above the threshold frequency is doubled. State the effect on (a) the photoelectric current, (b) the maximum kinetic energy. Answer: (a) The current doubles — twice the photons, twice the electrons. (b) The maximum kinetic energy is unchanged — it depends only on frequency and the work function.
  5. (De Broglie) Explain why electrons can be diffracted by crystals but tennis balls cannot. Answer: Diffraction is noticeable when the de Broglie wavelength λ = h/(mv) is comparable to the gap size; electrons have very small momentum and wavelengths of atomic scale, while a tennis ball's momentum makes its wavelength negligibly small.
  6. (Energy levels) An atom transitions between two levels 3.0 eV apart. Find the frequency of the emitted photon. Answer: ΔE = 3.0 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 4.8 × 10⁻¹⁹ J; f = ΔE/h = 4.8 × 10⁻¹⁹/6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ = 7.2 × 10¹⁴ Hz.
  7. (Spectra) Distinguish between an emission and an absorption spectrum. Answer: An emission spectrum shows bright lines on black where excited atoms drop to lower levels; an absorption spectrum shows dark lines on a continuous spectrum where cooler gas absorbs the same wavelengths — the line positions match.
  8. (Explanation) Explain, using photon theory, why photoelectric emission is instantaneous. Answer: One photon transfers all its energy to one electron in a single interaction; there is no gradual accumulation, so emission happens immediately once the photon energy exceeds the work function.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Intensity/frequency confusion: intensity changes the electron count, not their energy; frequency changes their energy. The two-sentence distinction above is worth marks every year.
  • eV/J conversions: 1 eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Work function in eV with photon energy in joules is a guaranteed arithmetic failure — convert before subtracting.
  • Threshold frequency vs threshold wavelength: they are inversely related (f₀ = φ/h, λ₀ = c/f₀); a short threshold wavelength means a high threshold frequency. Do not mix the inequalities.
  • h units: Planck's constant is 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s (or 4.14 × 10⁻¹⁵ eV s); using the wrong pair with the wrong energy unit fails the calculation.
  • Sign errors in ΔE: emission means the electron falls, so ΔE = E_upper − E_lower is positive for the photon. Sketch the level diagram and draw the arrow before calculating.
  • De Broglie with v = fλ confusion: for matter waves λ = h/(mv); substituting the wave speed of sound or light for the electron's speed is a common error.
  • Graph axes: KEₘₐₓ against f has gradient h — but KE against intensity is flat (above threshold, no change). Label what is plotted before reading anything off.
  • Photons of light and electrons are different things: photon energy E = hf for radiation; electron kinetic energy uses ½mv² (non-relativistic). Mixing the two formulas in one question is frequent under pressure.
  • Precision: give answers to 2 or 3 significant figures with units; quote h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s from the data sheet rather than from memory.

title: Coordinate Geometry
content:
Coordinate Geometry

Gradients and Equations of Lines

Gradient m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁). From ax + by + c = 0, the gradient is −a/b.

Point-slope form: y − y₁ = m(x − x₁).

Example: through (4, 3) with m = −1/2: y − 3 = −(x − 4)/2, i.e. y = −x/2 + 5.

Parallel and Perpendicular

  • Parallel lines: equal gradients.
  • Perpendicular lines: m₁m₂ = −1 (gradients are negative reciprocals).

Example: perpendicular to y = 2x + 1 has gradient −1/2.

Midpoint and Distance

Midpoint of (x₁, y₁), (x₂, y₂): ((x₁+x₂)/2, (y₁+y₂)/2).

Distance: √((x₂−x₁)² + (y₂−y₁)²). The line from (0,0) to (3,4) has length 5 — recognise 3-4-5 triangles.

Intersections and Bisectors

Intersections: solve the equations simultaneously. The perpendicular bisector of AB passes through the midpoint of AB with gradient −1/m(AB) — equate distances PA = PB for the locus method.

Exam tips: rationalise gradients as fractions; check perpendicularity by multiplying gradients to get −1.

title: Trigonometry — Sine and Cosine Rules — Study Notes
content:
Trigonometry — Sine and Cosine Rules

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): area formula, sine rule, cosine rule, multi-step bearing and 3-D problems (Extended).

1. Area of a triangle

A = ½ab sin C (C = included angle between sides a and b).

Example: a = 8, b = 5, C = 48° → A = ½ × 8 × 5 × sin 48° = 14.8.

2. Sine rule

a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C. Use when a matching angle–side pair is known.

Example: A = 40°, a = 7, B = 65°: b = 7 sin 65°/sin 40° = 9.98.

Ambiguous case: two triangles possible when finding an angle — check the obtuse option (180° − θ).

3. Cosine rule

a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A. Use with two sides + included angle, or all three sides (then cos A = (b² + c² − a²)/(2bc)).

Example: b = 7, c = 5, A = 52°: a² = 74 − 70 cos 52° = 30.9 → a = 5.56.

4. Bearing problems

Draw both north lines, transfer angles via parallel lines, then pick sine/cosine rule.

Example: QP = 60 km bearing 070° from Q; QR = 45 km bearing 150°. ∠PQR = 80° → PR² = 60² + 45² − 2·60·45 cos 80° → PR = 68.4 km.

5. 3-D trigonometry

Identify the plane containing the required angle; use 3-D Pythagoras d² = x² + y² + z² for space diagonals; angle between a line and a plane uses the projection onto the plane.

Exam tips: state which rule you are using and why; sketch a separate 2-D triangle for 3-D questions; answers to 3 s.f. / bearings as three digits.

The sine rule

For any triangle with sides a, b, c opposite angles A, B, C: a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C. Use it when you know a pair of opposite side and angle (for example, two angles and a side, or a side and its opposite angle with another side). Find the missing angle using the angle sum of 180° first.

The cosine rule

a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A, and cos A = (b² + c² − a²) ÷ 2bc. Use it when you know two sides and the included angle, or all three sides. Careful with negative cosines: an obtuse angle gives a negative cos value.

Area of a triangle

Area = ½ab sin C, using two sides and the included angle. This avoids finding the perpendicular height.

title: A Level Mathematics: Sampling and Estimation
content:
A Level Mathematics: Sampling and Estimation

Statistics works by measuring a sample and reasoning about a population that was never fully measured. That inference is only as good as the sample: a biased sample cannot be rescued by a larger one. This note covers how samples are drawn, what the sampling distribution of the mean is, why the central limit theorem makes normal methods work for almost any population, and how to build and interpret a confidence interval.

Populations, samples and parameters

A parameter describes the population and is usually unknown; a statistic describes the sample and is known. The whole of estimation is the attempt to learn a parameter from a statistic, and naming the two correctly is the first mark in many questions.

parameter: mu (population mean), σ (population sd), p (proportion)
statistic: x-bar (sample mean), s (sample sd), p-hat (sample proportion)
an estimator is unbiased if its expected value equals the parameter

Worked example. A sample of 40 light bulbs has mean life 1,020 hours. Identify the parameter and the statistic.

statistic: x-bar = 1020 hours (known, from the sample)
parameter: mu, the mean life of all bulbs produced (unknown)
the estimate of mu is 1020 hours, with an uncertainty to be quantified

Sampling methods and bias

The method determines whether the sample can speak for the population at all. Every named method is a compromise between practicality and representativeness, and the exam asks you to identify which compromise a described survey has made.

MethodHow it worksWeakness
simple randomevery member equally likely, chosen by numberneeds a complete list
systematicevery k-th member from a random startperiodic patterns can bias it
stratifiedsample each subgroup in proportionneeds known subgroup sizes
quotafill fixed categories by interviewer choiceinterviewer bias, not random
opportunitywhoever is availablestrongly unrepresentative

Worked example. A surveyor interviews shoppers in a town centre on a weekday morning about working hours. Identify the bias.

people free on a weekday morning are systematically different from the
population: the employed, the housebound and shift workers are under-represented
this is an opportunity sample with selection bias, and no sample size fixes it

The sampling distribution of the mean

Take many samples of size n, compute each mean, and plot them: the result is the sampling distribution, and its spread is smaller than the population's by a factor of √n.

if X has mean mu and variance σ², then x-bar has
mean = mu
variance = σ²/n
standard error = σ/sqrt n

Worked example. A population has mean 50 and standard deviation 12. For samples of 36, find the mean and standard error of the sample mean.

mean of x-bar = 50
standard error = 12/6 = 2

Worked example 2 (effect of quadrupling n). What happens to the standard error if the sample size is quadrupled?

standard error = σ/√(4n) = (σ/sqrt n)/2
it halves; quadrupling the sample buys a factor of two in precision

That square-root relationship is why doubling precision costs four times the data, and it is a standard exam comment.

The central limit theorem

Whatever shape the population has, the distribution of the sample mean becomes approximately normal as n grows. That is what licenses normal methods for non-normal populations, and it is the single most important result in the topic.

for large n (in practice n >= 30), x-bar is approximately N(mu, σ²/n)
the population itself need not be normal
if the population is already normal, the result is exact for any n

Worked example. A population is strongly skewed with mean 20 and standard deviation 10. Describe the distribution of the mean of samples of 50.

by the central limit theorem, approximately normal
mean 20, standard error 10/sqrt 50 = 1.414
so x-bar is approximately N(20, 2.0)

Confidence intervals for a mean

A confidence interval gives a range of plausible values for the parameter, with a stated long-run success rate. It is not a probability that the parameter lies in this particular interval — the parameter is fixed, the interval is random.

95% interval for mu: x-bar +/- 1.96 (σ/sqrt n)
99% interval: x-bar +/- 2.5758 (σ/sqrt n)
with s estimated from the sample, replace σ by s (large n)
wider interval: more confidence, less precision

Worked example. A sample of 64 measurements has mean 25.4 and known standard deviation 4. Find a 95% confidence interval for the population mean.

standard error = 4/8 = 0.5
margin = 1.96 × 0.5 = 0.98
interval: 25.4 +/- 0.98 = (24.42, 26.38)

Worked example 2 (99%). The same data at 99%.

margin = 2.5758 × 0.5 = 1.288
interval: (24.11, 26.69), wider as expected

Worked example 3 (required sample size). How large a sample is needed for the 95% margin to be at most 0.2?

1.96 × 4/sqrt n <= 0.2
sqrt n >= 39.2
n >= 1537, so the sample must be at least 1537

Confidence intervals for a proportion

The sample proportion is a mean in disguise: each observation is a 0 or 1, so the same machinery applies with p in place of μ.

p-hat = r/n;  standard error = √(p-hat(1 - p-hat)/n)
95% interval: p-hat +/- 1.96 x standard error
valid when n p-hat and n(1 - p-hat) are both at least 5

Worked example. In a sample of 200 voters, 84 support a candidate. Find a 95% confidence interval for the support.

p-hat = 0.42
standard error = √(0.42 × 0.58/200) = √(0.001218) = 0.0349
margin = 1.96 × 0.0349 = 0.0684
interval: (0.352, 0.488)

Worked example 2 (interpretation). A rival claims support is 50%. Does the interval support that claim?

0.5 lies outside (0.352, 0.488)
so at the 95% level the data are not consistent with 50% support

Estimators and their properties

Two properties decide whether an estimator is worth using: unbiasedness (correct on average) and low variance (consistent from sample to sample). The sample mean is unbiased for μ; the sample variance with divisor n is biased, which is why the divisor n − 1 appears.

E(x-bar) = mu  (unbiased)
E(s²) with divisor n underestimates σ² by a factor (n-1)/n
divisor n - 1 corrects the bias

Worked example. Explain why the divisor n − 1 is used in the sample variance.

deviations are measured from the sample mean, which is itself fitted to the data
that fitting uses up one degree of freedom, so the sum of squares is
systematically too small; dividing by n - 1 instead of n corrects it

Why the standard error is the whole story

Every formula in this topic contains σ/√n somewhere, and the reason is that estimating a mean averages away noise: independent errors partly cancel, and they cancel in proportion to the square root of how many there are. That is why precision is expensive — halving the standard error needs four times the data — and why a very precise interval from a biased sample is worse than useless, since it states a wrong answer with confidence.

The habitual check before trusting any interval is therefore two questions, not one: is the sample random, and is the sample large enough for the approximation used? An interval built from a quota sample answers a question about that quota, not about the population, however narrow it looks.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Parameter) Distinguish a parameter from a statistic. Answer: a parameter describes the population and is unknown; a statistic comes from the sample.
  2. (Method) Name a method that guarantees every member is equally likely. Answer: simple random sampling.
  3. (Bias) Give one weakness of a quota sample. Answer: the interviewer chooses who fills each quota, so selection bias remains.
  4. (Standard error) σ = 15, n = 25: find the standard error. Answer: 3.
  5. (Effect) n increases from 25 to 100: what happens to the standard error? Answer: it halves, from 3 to 1.5.
  6. (CLT) State the central limit theorem. Answer: for large n the sample mean is approximately normal whatever the population shape.
  7. (CI) x̄ = 40, σ = 6, n = 36: 95% interval. Answer: 40 ± 1.96 = (38.04, 41.96).
  8. (Width) How can the interval be made narrower? Answer: increase n, or lower the confidence level.
  9. (Proportion) 60 of 400: 95% interval. Answer: 0.15 ± 1.96(0.01785) = (0.115, 0.185).
  10. (Estimator) Why divide by n − 1? Answer: to correct the bias caused by measuring deviations from the sample mean.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Dividing by n instead of √n: the standard error is σ/√n; using σ/n makes intervals far too narrow.
  • Reading a CI as a probability: the parameter is fixed; the 95% refers to the long-run performance of the method.
  • Assuming normality of the data: it is the sample mean that is approximately normal, by the central limit theorem, not the population.
  • Bias described as variance: a biased sample is wrong however large; a variable one is merely imprecise.
  • Stratified confused with quota: stratified is random within known groups; quota is interviewer-selected.
  • Wrong z for 99%: it is 2.5758, not 2.33 (that is the one-tailed 1% value).
  • Confidence level and sample size traded silently: a narrower interval at the same confidence costs a larger sample.
  • Proportion interval outside [0, 1]: check the validity conditions and truncate, or report that the normal approximation is unsuitable.

title: Energy Flow, Ecosystems and the Environment — Study Notes
content:
Energy Flow, Ecosystems and the Environment

Edexcel IAL Biology WBI14, Topic 5. Energy enters most ecosystems as light, is fixed by photosynthesis and then passes along food chains. Nutrients cycle, and human activity can disrupt those cycles.

Photosynthesis and limiting factors

  • The light-dependent reactions take place on the thylakoid membranes. Light energy splits water (photolysis), releases oxygen and makes ATP and reduced NADP.
  • The light-independent reactions (the Calvin cycle) take place in the stroma. CO₂ is fixed by the enzyme RuBisCO onto ribulose bisphosphate, and the product is reduced to make triose phosphate.
  • Light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and temperature are limiting factors. The factor that is in shortest supply limits the rate.

Energy transfer through trophic levels

  • Gross primary productivity is the total energy fixed by plants. Net primary productivity is the energy left after respiration.
  • Energy is lost between trophic levels: in respiration, as heat, in faeces and urine, and in parts of organisms that are not eaten. Only about 10% of the energy at one trophic level is usually passed on.
  • Energy pyramids are always the right way up, because energy is lost at each step.

Nutrient cycles

  • In the carbon cycle, photosynthesis removes CO₂ from the air and respiration, decomposition and combustion return it.
  • Nitrogen fixing bacteria in root nodules convert nitrogen gas into ammonium ions. Nitrifying bacteria convert ammonium to nitrate, and denitrifying bacteria return nitrogen gas to the air.

Human impact

  • Fertiliser run-off causes eutrophication. Algae grow rapidly, block light, and then die. Decomposers use up the oxygen, and fish and other animals die.
  • Greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide and methane absorb infrared radiation and raise the temperature of the Earth.
  • Pesticides and persistent chemicals become more concentrated at higher trophic levels, which is called biomagnification.

Exam tip: when you explain a limiting factor, name the factor, state which reaction it slows, and say why the rate falls.

title: A Level Mathematics: Hypothesis Testing
content:
A Level Mathematics: Hypothesis Testing

A hypothesis test is a formal way of deciding whether data are surprising enough to overturn an assumption. The logic is legal rather than mathematical in spirit: assume the claim is true, compute how unlikely the observed evidence would be under that assumption, and reject the claim only if the evidence is unlikely enough. This note sets out the machinery — null and alternative hypotheses, significance levels, tails, critical regions — and then applies it to the binomial and normal cases the exam uses.

The logic of a test

The null hypothesis H0 is the assumption of no change, no effect, no bias: the status quo. The alternative H1 is what you would conclude if the data are too extreme. The significance level α is the risk of rejecting a true H0 that you are willing to accept.

H0: the parameter equals its old value
H1: the parameter is greater, less, or simply different
alpha: the maximum acceptable probability of a Type I error (often 0.05 or 0.01)
test statistic: the observed value computed from the sample
p-value: probability of a result at least as extreme, assuming H0

The analogy that makes the asymmetry clear: a criminal trial presumes innocence. The presumption is not a belief, it is the default that evidence must overcome. Failing to reject H0 is not proof of H0 — it is a verdict of "not proven".

One-tailed and two-tailed tests

The alternative decides the tail. A one-tailed test is used when the direction of the change is specified in advance; a two-tailed test when any change would matter.

AlternativeTest typep-value
p > p0one-tailed, upperP(X ≥ observed)
p < p0one-tailed, lowerP(X ≤ observed)
p ≠ p0two-tailed2 × the smaller tail

Worked example (choosing the alternative). A coin is suspected of favouring heads. Which alternative applies?

the suspicion has a direction, so H1: p > 0.5, a one-tailed upper test
a two-tailed test would be right only if any bias mattered

Errors and their consequences

Every test can go wrong in two ways, and the significance level controls only one of them. Understanding which is which is a frequent exam question and a genuine conceptual point.

Type I error: reject H0 when it is true  (probability alpha)
Type II error: fail to reject H0 when it is false
reducing alpha reduces Type I errors but increases Type II errors
increasing the sample size reduces both

Worked example. A test at the 5% level concludes a die is biased when it is fair. Which error is this?

H0 (fair) was true and was rejected
that is a Type I error, with probability at most 5%

Worked example 2 (effect of sample size). Explain why the same observed proportion can be significant in a large sample and not in a small one.

a larger sample reduces the standard error, so the same deviation
becomes more standard errors away from the null value
the evidence is measured in standard errors, not in raw counts

Testing a binomial proportion

The test statistic is the observed number of successes, the null distribution is binomial, and the p-value is a cumulative binomial probability.

H0: p = p0;  X ~ B(n, p0)
upper tail p-value = P(X >= x)
lower tail p-value = P(X <= x)
reject H0 if p-value <= alpha

Worked example. A manufacturer claims 90% of components are fault-free. In a sample of 20, only 15 are fault-free. Test at the 5% level whether the claim is too high.

H0: p = 0.9;  H1: p < 0.9
X ~ B(20, 0.9)
P(X <= 15) = 0.0432
0.0432 < 0.05, so reject H0
there is evidence the fault-free rate is below 90%

Worked example 2 (critical region). Find the 5% critical region for that test.

P(X <= 15) = 0.0432 (below 0.05)
P(X <= 16) = 0.1330 (above 0.05)
critical region: X <= 15

Worked example 3 (actual significance level). State the actual significance level of that test.

the probability of a Type I error is P(X <= 15) under H0 = 0.0432
so the actual level is 4.32%, just inside the 5% requirement

Testing a normal mean

When the variable is continuous and the population is normal — or the sample is large — the test statistic is standardised with a z-score and compared with critical values.

test statistic z = (x-bar - mu)/(σ/sqrt n)   (σ known)
or z = (x-bar - mu)/(s/sqrt n)                  (σ estimated, large n)
critical values at 5% one-tailed: 1.6449;  two-tailed: 1.96
at 1% one-tailed: 2.3263;  two-tailed: 2.5758

Worked example. A machine fills bags with a mean of 500 g and standard deviation 8 g. A sample of 16 bags has mean 496 g. Test at the 5% level whether the mean has fallen.

H0: mu = 500;  H1: mu < 500
standard error = 8/sqrt 16 = 2
z = (496 - 500)/2 = -2
critical value at 5% one-tailed is -1.6449
-2 < -1.6449, so reject H0: the mean has fallen

Worked example 2 (two-tailed). Same data, tested two-tailed at 5%.

critical values are +/-1.96
|-2| > 1.96, so still reject H0
the evidence is that the mean is not 500, in either direction

Worked example 3 (interpreting a p-value). A test gives z = 1.72 for H1: μ > μ0. Find the p-value and conclude at 5%.

p-value = P(Z > 1.72) = 0.0427
0.0427 < 0.05, so reject H0
the result is significant at the 5% level but not at 1%

Choosing the right test

The exam does not label the test; the shape of the data decides it. Getting the distribution wrong makes every later mark unreachable, so the decision is worth making explicitly.

count of successes in n trials with constant p  →  binomial test
count of events in an interval at a constant rate  →  Poisson test
mean of a continuous measurement  →  normal test (z)
correlation between two variables  →  product-moment test

Worked example. A nurse records the number of patients arriving in an hour on 30 separate days. Which test?

counts of arrivals in equal intervals at a roughly constant rate
use a Poisson test on the mean count, not a binomial test
a normal test on the mean of the 30 counts is also defensible for large n

Writing a conclusion that earns the marks

The final mark of a hypothesis test is for the conclusion, and it has three components: a decision about H0, a reference to the significance level, and the finding stated in the context of the question. Dropping any one of them costs a mark even when the arithmetic is perfect.

Compare these two endings. "0.0201 < 0.05, so reject H0" scores the comparison. "There is sufficient evidence at the 5% level that the call rate has increased" scores the comparison and the interpretation. "The rate has increased" scores neither, because it reports a certainty the test cannot deliver.

The opposite case is often mishandled too. When the p-value is above the level the correct wording is that there is insufficient evidence to reject H0 — never that H0 is true, and never that nothing has happened. A non-significant result from a small sample is weak evidence either way, and saying so is better than overclaiming in either direction.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Hypotheses) A coin might be biased against heads. State H0 and H1. Answer: H0: p = 0.5; H1: p < 0.5.
  2. (Error) Define a Type II error. Answer: failing to reject H0 when it is false.
  3. (Binomial) 8 of 20 seeds germinate; test p = 0.6 against p < 0.6 at 5%. Answer: X ~ B(20, 0.6), so P(X ≤ 8) = 0.0565; since 0.0565 > 0.05 there is insufficient evidence to reject H0.
  4. (Critical region) X ~ B(15, 0.4): 5% lower critical region. Answer: test P(X ≤ c) ≤ 0.05: P(X ≤ 2) = 0.0271 ≤ 0.05, but P(X ≤ 3) = 0.0905 > 0.05, so the critical region is X ≤ 2.
  5. (Actual level) For that region, state the actual significance level. Answer: actual significance level = P(X ≤ 2) = 0.0271 = 2.71%.
  6. (Normal) μ0 = 20, σ = 4, n = 25, mean 21.5: test at 5% one-tailed. Answer: z = (x̄ − μ0)/(σ/√n) = (21.5 − 20)/(4/√25) = 1.5/0.8 = 1.875, and 1.875 > 1.6449, so reject H0.
  7. (Two-tailed) Same data two-tailed: Answer: z = (21.5 − 20)/(4/√25) = 1.875, and 1.875 < 1.96, so do not reject H0.
  8. (p-value) z = 2.4, H1: μ > μ0. Find the p-value. Answer: p-value = P(Z > 2.4) = 1 − 0.9918 = 0.0082.
  9. (Sample size) Why can a larger sample turn a non-significant result significant? Answer: the standard error shrinks, so the same deviation is more standard errors away.
  10. (Conclusion wording) Write a valid conclusion for a rejected H0. Answer: there is sufficient evidence at the 5% level that the mean has fallen.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Concluding H0 is true: failing to reject means the evidence is insufficient; it is never proof of the null.
  • Wrong tail: compute P(X ≥ x) for an increase and P(X ≤ x) for a decrease; using the other tail inverts the conclusion.
  • Doubling without a two-tailed alternative: the p-value is doubled only when H1 is "not equal".
  • p-value compared with the wrong threshold: 5% is 0.05; comparing 0.043 with 5 instead of 0.05 reverses the verdict.
  • Standard error omitted: the z-score divides by σ/√n, not by σ.
  • Critical value for the wrong tail: the 5% one-tailed value is 1.6449, the two-tailed is 1.96; the sign matters too.
  • Type I and Type II swapped: Type I is rejecting a true null — the error the significance level controls.
  • Conclusion beyond the data: a rejected H0 says the parameter has changed, not why, and never that the change is important.

Setting up the hypotheses before any calculation

Hypotheses are the first lines a marker reads, and a wrong direction or a sample statistic written where a parameter belongs loses marks before any arithmetic is checked. The subsections set out how to define the parameter, write H₀ as a single value and read H₁ from the wording of the question.

Defining the parameter in words first

Before writing any symbol, say what the parameter measures. Let p be the proportion of seeds that germinate, or let μ be the mean mass of a bag in grams. The parameter belongs to the population the claim is about, not to the sample you were given. The definition is the line that makes the rest of the working easy to follow, so write it first.

Writing H₀ as a single value

H₀ names one value for the parameter with an equals sign, such as H₀: p = 0.6 or H₀: μ = 50. It is the value the test assumes is true when it calculates the probability of the data. The probability can only be worked out at one specific value, so the test is always carried out at the value stated in H₀, and the working should say so.

Reading the direction of H₁ from the wording

Words map to symbols in a fixed way. “Greater than”, “more than”, “has increased” and “above” give >. “Less than”, “fewer”, “has decreased” and “below” give <. “Different from”, “has changed” and “is not equal to” give ≠. A question that asks whether a proportion has changed, without saying which way, needs H₁: p ≠ p₀, and that choice fixes a two-tailed test.

Hypotheses for a mean from a normal model

When X is normal with a known standard deviation, the hypotheses concern μ, and the variance belongs to the model: X ~ N(μ, σ²). Write the assumption that the population is normal with known σ, or that the sample is large enough for the central limit theorem to apply. The hypotheses for a sample mean are the same as for the population mean, because the test is about μ.

Hypotheses set before the data are used

The direction of H₁ must come from the claim in the question, not from the sample. If the sample mean is 49 and the claim is μ = 50, it is tempting to choose H₁: μ < 50 after looking at the data. That choice invalidates the test, because it lets the data pick the tail. Settle the direction from the wording, and show it in the working before the test statistic.

Critical regions and the significance level

A critical region is the set of outcomes that leads to rejecting H₀. For a discrete distribution it is a set of whole numbers, and for a normal test it is a range of z-values. The subsections show how each is built from the significance level, and where the sign and boundary errors come from.

Building a critical region from tail probabilities

For a lower-tail test at level α, find the largest value k with P(X ≤ k) ≤ α, assuming H₀. The critical region is then {0, 1, …, k}. For X ~ B(10, 0.5) at the 5% level, P(X ≤ 1) = 11/1024 = 0.0107 and P(X ≤ 2) = 56/1024 = 0.0547. The second value is greater than 0.05, so k = 1 and the critical region is {0, 1}.

The actual significance level is rarely the stated level

Because X takes only whole-number values, the probability in the critical region is usually below the stated level. Here it is 0.0107, about 1.07%, not 5%. Say so in the working, using the phrase “actual significance level”. A discrete test that falls short of 5% is correct; a candidate who claims the level is exactly 5% makes a false statement.

Critical values for a normal test

For a normal test with known σ, a critical value of z replaces the critical count. The standard values are 1.645 for a one-tailed test at 5%, 2.326 for one-tailed at 1%, 1.96 for two-tailed at 5% and 2.576 for two-tailed at 1%. A lower-tailed test rejects when z ≤ −1.645; an upper-tailed test rejects when z ≥ 1.645. The normal distribution is continuous, so the actual level equals the stated level exactly.

Two-tailed critical regions for a discrete test

For a two-tailed test at 5%, each tail may carry probability at most 0.025. For X ~ B(10, 0.5), P(X ≤ 1) = 0.0107 is at most 0.025, while P(X ≤ 2) = 0.0547 is not. The lower critical region is {0, 1}, and by symmetry the upper one is {9, 10}. The combined probability is 0.0215, which is below 0.05, so the test can reject for 0, 1, 9 or 10 successes.

Checking the boundary and the sign

A common slip is to put the boundary in the wrong region or to use the wrong sign. For a lower-tailed normal test at 5%, the boundary z = −1.645 is itself in the critical region, because the test rejects when z ≤ −1.645. A critical value of +1.645 on a lower-tailed test is the commonest sign error. Write the inequality with the boundary included, then check that its sign matches the tail named in H₁.

p-values, step by step

A p-value gives the same decision as a critical region, but it reports how unlikely the data are on the assumption that H₀ is true, rather than only whether they fall inside a region. Many A2 questions ask for a p-value directly, and some ask for a comparison with the level in a single sentence.

What a p-value is and is not

The p-value is the probability, assuming H₀ is true, of a result at least as extreme as the one observed, in the direction stated in H₁. It is not the probability that H₀ is true, and it is not the probability that the result happened by chance. A p-value of 0.03 means that a result this extreme would occur 3% of the time if H₀ were true.

A p-value for a lower-tailed binomial test

For X ~ B(10, 0.5) with H₁: p < 0.5, suppose 2 successes are observed. The p-value is P(X ≤ 2) = 56/1024 = 0.0547. That is greater than 0.05, so the result is not significant at the 5% level. At the 10% level, 0.0547 is less than 0.10, so H₀ is rejected. The same observation gives different decisions at different levels, which is why the level must always be stated.

A p-value for a two-tailed binomial test

For the same observation with H₁: p ≠ 0.5, the p-value is twice the smaller tail probability: 2 × 0.0547 = 0.1094. A two-tailed p-value is never the value of one tail alone, and it is capped at 1 if doubling would exceed 1. Here 0.1094 is greater than 0.05, so the result is not significant at 5%. A two-tailed p-value is always at least as large as the one-tailed value, which is why a two-tailed test is the harder one to pass.

A p-value for a normal test

Suppose z = −2.1 is found for a lower-tailed normal test. The p-value is Φ(−2.1) = 1 − Φ(2.1) = 1 − 0.9821 = 0.0179. For a two-tailed test the p-value would be 2 × 0.0179 = 0.0357. Use the symmetry of the normal curve, and show the Φ step so that the table lookup can be checked.

Comparing a p-value with the significance level

If the p-value is less than or equal to the significance level, reject H₀. Write the comparison as a statement with both numbers, for example 0.0547 > 0.05, so do not reject H₀. Then give the decision in words, in the context of the question. The comparison in numbers is what the working shows, and the sentence is what the conclusion mark asks for.

The normal test as a standardised calculation

When the population is normal with a known standard deviation, the sample mean is itself normal, and the test standardises it before comparing with a critical value. This section shows the standardisation and the figure that makes the critical region visible.

Standardising the sample mean

If X ~ N(μ, σ²), then the mean of n independent values satisfies X̄ ~ N(μ, σ²/n) when H₀ is true. The test statistic is z = (x̄ − μ₀)/(σ/√n), where μ₀ is the value stated in H₀. Standardising converts any normal model to the standard normal distribution, so the critical values in the tables apply to every normal test.

Using the standard error, not the standard deviation

The denominator is σ/√n, the standard error of the mean, and not σ on its own. Dividing by σ alone gives a z-value that is √n times too small, and the test becomes too cautious. If σ is given, use it directly. If only the sample standard deviation s is given and the sample is large, use s as an estimate of σ and say so in the working.

A worked normal test

A machine fills bags with a mean of 500 g and a known standard deviation of 12 g. A sample of 36 bags has mean 496 g. Test at the 5% level whether the mean fill is less than 500 g. The standard error is 12/√36 = 2, so z = (496 − 500)/2 = −2. The critical value is −1.645, and −2 is less than −1.645, so H₀ is rejected. The p-value is Φ(−2) = 0.0228, which is less than 0.05.

Reading the critical region from the figure

The figure shows the standard normal curve with the lower 5% tail shaded. The boundary at −1.645 separates the critical region from the rest of the curve, and the observed z-value of −2 lies inside the shaded tail, which is why the test rejects H₀. Sketching this shape with the boundary and the observed value marked is a quick check that the direction of the test is right.

Reading the answer back in the units of the question

The conclusion must be in the units of the question: “There is evidence at the 5% level that the mean fill is less than 500 g.” Do not write “the mean is less than 500”, because a test never establishes a fact about the population. Name the quantity the evidence is about, the mean fill mass, and state the level.

Power and the probability of a Type II error

A test that rejects H₀ rarely is also unlikely to detect a real change. The power of a test measures how often it detects a specified change, and it is the quantity that questions about Type II errors ask for.

Defining power

The power of a test is the probability of rejecting H₀ when a specified alternative value is true. A power of 0.149 at p = 0.3 means the test rejects H₀ 14.9% of the time when p really is 0.3. The probability of a Type II error at that value is 1 − power, which is 0.851 here. Power is always calculated at a stated alternative, so name the value of the parameter you used.

Calculating power for a binomial test

Take the lower-tailed test from the previous section: X ~ B(10, 0.5) with H₀: p = 0.5, H₁: p < 0.5 and critical region {0, 1}. To find the power at p = 0.3, use X ~ B(10, 0.3) and find the probability of the critical region. P(X = 0) = 0.7¹⁰ = 0.02825 and P(X = 1) = 10 × 0.3 × 0.7⁹ = 0.12107. Adding these gives 0.1493, so the power is 0.149 to 3 significant figures.

Factors that increase power

Power rises when the sample is larger, when the true value is further from the value in H₀, and when the significance level is larger. A larger sample shrinks the standard error, so a real shift is more likely to land in the critical region. A larger level widens the critical region, but it also raises the chance of a Type I error. This is the trade-off: a test that is hard to pass by chance is also hard to pass when H₁ is true.

Why a non-significant result is not proof

If the power is low, a non-significant result is weak evidence. At p = 0.3 the test above fails to reject H₀ with probability 0.851, so that outcome is very likely even though H₀ is false. A result that does not reject H₀ does not show that p = 0.5. It shows only that the data were not strong enough to reject H₀ at this level.

Sample size and the size of the difference

A test that must detect a small difference needs a large sample. A difference that is large compared with the standard error is detected easily, while a small difference relative to the standard error may not be. In an exam, the question will say whether the power or the Type II error probability is wanted, so check the wording before you calculate, and state the alternative value you used.

Equations and symbols

A hypothesis test is a decision rule, and these are its moving parts: the test statistic, the standard error, the tail probability and the comparison that produces the verdict.

The decision

reject H0 if p-value <= alpha Key: H0 = the null hypothesis, the assumption of no change; p-value = the probability of a result at least as extreme, assuming H0 is true; alpha = the significance level, the acceptable risk of rejecting a true H0 (often 0.05 or 0.01). Failing to reject is not proof that H0 is true — it means the evidence was insufficient.

P(X <= 15) = 0.0432 Key: X = number of fault-free components in a sample of 20; 0.0432 = the lower-tail probability under H0: p = 0.9. Because 0.0432 < 0.05 the null is rejected, and the same figure is the actual significance level of the test.

The normal test

standard error = 8/sqrt 16 = 2 Key: 8 = population standard deviation σ (g); 16 = sample size n (bags); 2 = the standard error of the mean (g). The standard error, not σ, is the denominator of the test statistic — omitting the √n is the classic lost mark.

z = (496 - 500)/2 = -2 Key: z = the test statistic, in standard errors; 496 = sample mean (g); 500 = hypothesised mean μ (g); 2 = the standard error (g). Compare |z| with the critical value: 1.6449 one-tailed at 5%, 1.96 two-tailed at 5%.

p-value = P(Z > 1.72) = 0.0427 Key: Z = the standard normal variable; 1.72 = the observed test statistic; 0.0427 = the area beyond it, for an upper-tail alternative. Significant at 5% but not at 1% — say which level you are concluding at.

Errors

A Type I error rejects a true H0 and has probability alpha; a Type II error fails to reject a false H0. Lowering alpha reduces Type I errors and increases Type II; a larger sample reduces both, because it shrinks the standard error so the same deviation counts as more standard errors.

The slip worth naming

Comparing a p-value with 5 instead of 0.05, or doubling the tail without a two-sided alternative. Both reverse a correct conclusion, which is exactly the mark the question is testing.

title: Exam technique: Algebra Graphs
content:
### What earns the marks
For gradient and equation questions, calculate earns marks for a correct (y2 - y1) / (x2 - x1) computation with substitution shown, then the rearrangement to y = mx + c. For perpendicular lines, state earns the negative-reciprocal gradient explicitly before substituting. For curve questions, describe earns marks for roots, intercept and turning point each stated, and the axis of symmetry as an equation (x = 2, not just 2).
### Traps
Error: answering the midpoint when length is asked. Correction: re-read the final demand before computing. Error: giving the minimum value instead of its x-coordinate. Correction: label every coordinate pair fully. Error: keeping gradient 2 for a perpendicular to y = 2x + 1. Correction: flip and negate first, then substitute.

title: Database Systems — Study Notes
content:
Database Systems

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): limitations of file-based systems; relational concepts; SQL (SELECT, FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY, INNER JOIN, SUM, COUNT); DBMS features.

1. File-based problems

Data repetition (wasted space, inconsistency), fixed queries, no concurrent access control — solved by a DBMS with shared, structured tables.

2. Relational concepts

  • Table, record, field; primary key (unique); secondary key (indexed search field); foreign key links tables.
  • One-to-many relationships via foreign keys; no repeating groups (1NF mindset).

3. SQL

SELECT Title, Year FROM Films
WHERE Genre = 'Sci-Fi' AND Year > 2015
ORDER BY Year DESC;

SELECT Genre, COUNT(*) AS NumFilms, SUM(Rating) AS TotalRating
FROM Films
GROUP BY Genre;

SELECT s.Name, f.Title
FROM Students s INNER JOIN Loans l ON s.StudentID = l.StudentID
INNER JOIN Films f ON l.FilmID = f.FilmID;

WHERE filters rows; GROUP BY aggregates; JOIN combines on matching keys.

4. DBMS features

Data dictionary (schema, types, constraints), query processor, forms/reports, access rights (read/write per user), data integrity (validation rules), backup/recovery.

Exam tips: write SQL keywords uppercase; alias joined tables (s, l, f); when asked "why relational", cite reduced redundancy + flexible queries.

Primary keys, foreign keys and relationships

A primary key uniquely identifies each record in a table, so no two records can share its value. A foreign key is a field in one table that holds the primary key of a related table, and it creates a relationship between the tables. Relationships can be one-to-one, one-to-many or many-to-many. A many-to-many relationship is usually split into two one-to-many relationships through a linking table.

Foreign keys stop a record being added that points to a row which does not exist, which keeps the data consistent. Storing each fact once in the correct table also reduces redundancy, so an update is made in one place only.

Exam tip: when designing a table, name the primary key and say which field links it to another table.

title: A Level Mathematics: Proof
content:
A Level Mathematics: Proof

Proof at A2 extends the AS methods with contradiction, disproof by counter-example in unfamiliar settings, and algebraic arguments about divisibility, parity and inequalities. The examinable skills are choosing a method, setting up general notation, and closing the argument — not spotting a clever trick. This note works through each method with complete examples and the wording mark schemes expect.

The four methods and when to use them

MethodUse whenShape of the argument
DirectThe statement is algebraicStart from definitions, manipulate to the target form
ExhaustionThe domain splits into a few casesCheck each case
Counter-exampleThe statement claims "for all" and looks falseProduce one failing case with arithmetic
ContradictionThe statement is negative or about irrationality/infinityAssume the opposite, derive an impossibility

Choosing badly wastes time: a "prove that there is no largest prime" question cannot be done directly, and a parity statement cannot be done by example.

Proof by contradiction

assume the negation, derive a contradiction with a known truth,
conclude the original statement

Worked example 1 (irrationality of √2). The classic, examinable in full.

assume √(2) = p/q in lowest terms, p and q integers
2q² = p², so p² is even, so p is even: p = 2k
4k² = 2q²  →  q² = 2k², so q is even
p and q both even contradicts "lowest terms"
hence √(2) is irrational

Worked example 2 (no largest prime). Prove there are infinitely many primes.

assume finitely many: p1, p2, ..., pn
consider N = p1 p2 ... pn + 1
N leaves remainder 1 when divided by any π, so no π divides N
so N has a prime factor not in the list: contradiction
hence there are infinitely many primes

Worked example 3 (no rational solution). Prove that x² = 6 has no rational root.

assume x = p/q in lowest terms: p² = 6q²
so 3 divides p², hence 3 divides p: p = 3k
9k² = 6q²  →  3k² = 2q², so 3 divides q², hence q
both divisible by 3 contradicts lowest terms

Disproof by counter-example

Worked example 1. Disprove "if a > b then a² > b²".

take a = 1, b = -3: 1 > -3 but 1 < 9
counter-example disproves the statement

Worked example 2. Disprove "n² + n + 41 is prime for all positive integers n".

n = 41: 1681 + 41 + 41 = 1763 = 41 × 43, not prime

Worked example 3. Disprove "every odd number is prime".

9 is odd and 9 = 3 × 3, not prime

Each disproof is complete with one case; the arithmetic must be shown, not asserted.

Algebraic proof with parity and divisibility

even: 2n;  odd: 2n + 1
"is a multiple of k" means the expression equals k times an integer

Worked example 1. Prove that the difference of the squares of two consecutive odd numbers is a multiple of 8.

(2n + 3)² - (2n + 1)² = (4n² + 12n + 9) - (4n² + 4n + 1) = 8n + 8
= 8(n + 1), a multiple of 8

Worked example 2. Prove that n³ − n is divisible by 6 for all integers n.

n³ - n = n(n - 1)(n + 1), three consecutive integers
one is even, one is a multiple of 3; since 2 and 3 are coprime,
the product is divisible by 6

Worked example 3. Prove that the product of two consecutive even numbers is a multiple of 8.

2n(2n + 2) = 4n(n + 1); n(n + 1) is even, so the product is 8k

Inequalities by completing the square

a squared term is never negative; complete the square to expose a
minimum, then conclude the inequality

Worked example 1. Prove that x² − 4x + 7 > 0 for all real x.

= (x - 2)² + 3 >= 3 > 0

Worked example 2. Prove that 4x − x² − 5 < 0 for all x.

= -(x² - 4x + 5) = -[(x - 2)² + 1] = -(x - 2)² - 1 <= -1 < 0

Worked example 3 (unknown constant). Find the values of k for which x² + kx + k > 0 for all x.

(x + k/2)² + k - k²/4 > 0 requires k - k²/4 > 0
k(1 - k/4) > 0  →  0 < k < 4

The discriminant route gives the same answer (k² − 4k < 0); the completing-the-square route states the minimum explicitly, which is usually clearer in a proof.

Proof by exhaustion

Worked example. Prove that every integer from 1 to 10 is either prime, a square, or the sum of two primes.

1 (square); 2 (prime); 3 (prime); 4 (square); 5 (prime);
6 = 3 + 3; 7 (prime); 8 = 3 + 5; 9 (square); 10 = 3 + 7
all ten cases checked  →  statement proved for this finite domain

Exhaustion is only valid for a finite domain, and the proof is incomplete unless every case is listed. State the domain explicitly.

Setting out a proof for full marks

  • Define every variable with its domain ("let n be an integer").
  • State which method you are using when it is not obvious.
  • Write the algebra in connected steps, each justified.
  • Finish with a sentence tying the result to the claim ("hence ... as required").
  • For contradiction, state the assumption and where the contradiction lies.

Worked example (full structure). Prove that if n is odd then n² + 1 is even.

let n be an odd integer, so n = 2k + 1 for some integer k   [definition]
n² + 1 = 4k² + 4k + 1 + 1 = 4k² + 4k + 2              [algebra]
        = 2(2k² + 2k + 1)                              [target form]
which is even, hence n² + 1 is even whenever n is odd      [conclusion]

Inequalities with the discriminant

"Always positive" or "always negative" quadratics are proved with the discriminant, which is the algebraic form of the completing-the-square argument.

ax² + bx + c > 0 for all x  (a > 0)  <=>  b² - 4ac < 0
ax² + bx + c < 0 for all x  (a < 0)  <=>  b² - 4ac < 0

Worked example. Prove that 2x² − 3x + 4 > 0 for all real x.

a = 2 > 0;  discriminant = 9 - 32 = -23 < 0
no real roots and the parabola opens upward, so it never touches the
x-axis and is positive throughout

Worked example 2 (find the range). Find p such that x² + (p + 1)x + 4 > 0 for all x.

(p + 1)² - 16 < 0  →  -4 < p + 1 < 4  →  -5 < p < 3

Worked example 3 (negative leading coefficient). Prove that −x² + 2x − 5 < 0 for all x.

a = -1 < 0;  discriminant = 4 - 20 = -16 < 0
no real roots and the parabola opens downward, so it stays below the axis

Proving statements about sums and sequences

Closed-form statements about sums are proved by deriving the formula or by induction on the pattern; the derivation is always acceptable and often shorter.

Worked example 1. Prove that the sum of the first n odd numbers is n².

S = 1 + 3 + 5 + ... + (2n - 1), an arithmetic series
a = 1, d = 2: S = (n/2)[2 + 2(n - 1)] = (n/2)(2n) = n²

Worked example 2. Prove that the sum of the first n terms of 2 + 4 + 8 + ... is 2^(n+1) − 2.

geometric with a = 2, r = 2: S = 2(2^n - 1)/(2 - 1) = 2^(n+1) - 2

Worked example 3 (difference of squares). Prove that every odd number greater than 1 is the difference of two squares.

let the odd number be 2n + 1 = (n + 1)² - n²
since (n + 1)² - n² = 2n + 1, the representation always exists

Statements about the roots of a quadratic

Relations between roots and coefficients are provable from the quadratic formula and are a favourite A2 proof.

for ax² + bx + c = 0 with roots alpha and beta:
alpha + beta = -b/a;  alpha beta = c/a

Worked example. Prove that the sum of the roots of x² + px + q = 0 is −p.

roots: (-p +/- √(p² - 4q))/2
sum: [-p + √(...) - p - √(...)]/2 = -2p/2 = -p

Worked example 2. Prove that if one root of x² + bx + c = 0 is twice the other, then 2b² = 9c.

roots k and 2k: sum 3k = -b, product 2k² = c
k = -b/3, so 2b²/9 = c  →  2b² = 9c

Worked example 3 (discriminant). Prove that x² + 2x + 2 = 0 has no real roots.

discriminant = 4 - 8 = -4 < 0, so no real solutions
(equivalently (x + 1)² + 1 = 0 has no real solution)

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Contradiction) Prove √3 is irrational. Answer: assume p/q lowest terms, 3q² = p², 3 | p, then 3 | q — contradiction.
  2. (Counter-example) Disprove "n² − n + 1 is prime for all n". Answer: n = 4 gives 13 (prime) — try n = 5: 21 = 3 × 7, not prime.
  3. (Parity) Prove the sum of two odd numbers is even. Answer: (2m + 1) + (2n + 1) = 2(m + n + 1).
  4. (Divisibility) Prove 5n² + 5n is a multiple of 10. Answer: 5n(n + 1); n(n + 1) is even, so 5 × even = 10k.
  5. (Inequality) Prove x² + 2x + 2 > 0. Answer: (x + 1)² + 1 ≥ 1.
  6. (Constant) Find k so that x² + 2kx + 9 > 0 always. Answer: 4k² < 36 → −3 < k < 3.
  7. (Exhaustion) Prove n² + n is even by cases. Answer: n even → 4k² + 2k; n odd → 4k² + 6k + 2; both even.
  8. (Contradiction) Prove there is no greatest even integer. Answer: if N were greatest, N + 2 is even and larger — contradiction.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Examples offered as proof: only a general algebraic argument proves a universal claim.
  • Undefined variables: "let x be odd" without x = 2k + 1 leaves nothing to manipulate.
  • Contradiction not closed: name the contradiction explicitly — "this contradicts lowest terms".
  • Assuming the conclusion: starting from the statement to be proved and deriving a truth proves nothing unless every step is reversible.
  • Divisibility without coprimality: "divisible by 2 and by 3 hence by 6" needs 2 and 3 coprime; it is true here, but state it.
  • Exhaustion on an infinite domain: cases must cover every possibility; a finite sample is not exhaustion.
  • Counter-example unchecked: show the arithmetic that breaks the claim.
  • Conclusion missing: finish with a sentence; an algebraic derivation alone reads as unfinished.

How a proof is marked: the four lines that earn the marks

At A level the algebra is rarely the hard part — the marking is. A proof is read for four things, in order, and a script that has all the algebra but none of the signposting loses marks that were never in doubt.

Line 1: state what you are working with. Introduce every variable and say what kind of object it is: "let n be an integer", "let x and y be real numbers with x < y". Every mark that depends on parity or divisibility hangs off this line, because without it the algebra could be about anything.

Line 2: the algebra, one implication at a time. Each step must follow from the previous one, and the connector says which way the logic runs. "⇒" means the next line follows; a proof needs that direction, not its converse. Writing = between two expressions that are merely equal in value at the end is not the same as showing one implies the other.

Line 3: name the conclusion. "Therefore n² + n is always even, for every integer n." A proof that stops at the algebra leaves the marker to infer the point, and that inference is the mark.

Line 4: say what the conclusion shows about the original statement. In a contradiction this is the sentence that names what was contradicted; in exhaustion it is "these cases are exhaustive, so the result holds in all cases"; in direct proof it is "as required".

Worked example. Prove that x² + 4x + 7 > 0 for all real x.

Complete the square:
x² + 4x + 7 = (x + 2)² − 4 + 7 = (x + 2)² + 3

Now argue from a fact about squares: (x + 2)² ≥ 0 for every real x, so (x + 2)² + 3 ≥ 3 > 0. Hence x² + 4x + 7 > 0 for all real x.

The line (x + 2)² ≥ 0 is not decoration: it is the only reason the conclusion holds, and the mark scheme wants it written. The same argument answers "show this quadratic has no real roots" — the completed-square form shows the minimum value, and a minimum above zero cannot touch the axis.

The three ways this goes wrong. Assuming the result and working towards something true — that proves nothing, because a false statement can imply a true one. Using "if and only if" when only one direction was proved. And proving the converse: "if n is even then n² is even" is a different statement from "if n² is even then n is even", and only the second needs contradiction.

Reading the question's verbs. "Show that" wants a derivation from given facts. "Prove" wants the argument with its assumptions stated. "Disprove" wants one counter-example and no more. "Determine whether" wants a decision plus its justification — and the mark is for the decision being argued, not merely stated.

title: AS Level Chemistry: Introductory Organic Chemistry and Alkanes
content:
AS Level Chemistry: Introductory Organic Chemistry and Alkanes

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH11, Topic 4 introduces organic chemistry: how carbon compounds are named and drawn, how reactions are classified, how bonds break, and how alkanes are obtained and used. It also carries the safety material on hazard and risk, which is examined in a short-answer question nearly every year. The topic is the vocabulary and grammar of everything that follows, so the mechanisms and IUPAC rules must be exact rather than approximate.

Hazard and risk

A hazard is something with the potential to cause harm: a corrosive acid, a flammable solvent, a toxic gas. Risk is the chance that harm will actually occur when the hazard is used, and it depends on exposure as well as on the hazard itself. A concentrated acid sealed in a bottle is hazardous but carries little risk; the same acid being poured in a busy laboratory carries a real risk.

That distinction is why a risk assessment is made before practical work. It identifies the hazards, decides who might be harmed and how, evaluates the likelihood and severity, and records the controls.

Organic compounds are often hazardous because many are volatile and flammable, and because some are toxic or irritant. Ways to reduce risk include:

  • Working on a smaller scale, which reduces the amount of vapour released and the consequences of a spill.
  • Taking precautions specific to the hazard: a fume cupboard for a volatile toxic liquid, a water bath instead of a naked flame for a flammable solvent, gloves for a corrosive, eye protection at all times.
  • Using an alternative method with less hazardous substances, for example a lower-risk solvent or a reaction that avoids a toxic reagent.
  • Following safe practice for heating: never heat a closed system, and use anti-bump granules or a stirrer to avoid violent boiling.

The question usually asks you to suggest controls for a named procedure, so link each control to the specific hazard rather than listing generic safety advice.

Homologous series and functional groups

A homologous series is a family of organic compounds with the same general formula, the same functional group and similar chemical properties, in which each member differs from the next by a CH₂ unit. Because the formula changes by CH₂, the molar mass changes by 14, and the physical properties change gradually along the series while the chemical properties stay similar.

A functional group is the group of atoms responsible for the characteristic reactions of a compound. The functional groups examined at AS level are:

FamilyFunctional groupGeneral formula
AlkaneC–C and C–H single bonds onlyCₙH₂ₙ₊₂
Cycloalkanering of C–C single bondsCₙH₂ₙ
AlkeneC=C double bondCₙH₂ₙ
HalogenoalkaneC–X (X = Cl, Br, I)CₙH₂ₙ₊₁X
Alcohol–OHCₙH₂ₙ₊₁OH
Aldehyde–CHOCₙH₂ₙO
KetoneC=O between two carbon atomsCₙH₂ₙO
Carboxylic acid–COOHCₙH₂ₙ₊₁COOH

Naming and drawing organic compounds

IUPAC nomenclature follows a fixed sequence of steps. Work through them in order every time.

  1. Find the longest carbon chain containing the functional group; that gives the stem (meth, eth, prop, but, pent, hex...).
  2. Number the chain so that the functional group gets the lowest possible number.
  3. Name and number the substituents, and list them alphabetically (ethyl before methyl), with a multiplier for repeats (di-, tri-).
  4. Add the functional group suffix, with its number: -an- for an alkane, -en- for an alkene, -ol for an alcohol, -al for an aldehyde, -one for a ketone, -oic acid for a carboxylic acid.
  5. Use hyphens between numbers and letters, and commas between numbers.

Worked example. The compound CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₂OH has a four-carbon chain containing the –OH group, numbered from the end nearer the alcohol so that the OH is on carbon 1. There is a methyl group on carbon 3, so the name is 3-methylbutan-1-ol. Numbering from the other end would give 2-methylbutan-4-ol, which is wrong because the principal group must have the lowest number.

Three ways of drawing a compound are examined and you must be able to convert between them:

  • Structural formula: shows how the atoms are grouped, for example CH₃CH₂CH₂OH.
  • Displayed formula: shows every atom and every bond, including the O–H bond, drawn out in full. Required for mechanisms.
  • Skeletal formula: shows the carbon skeleton as a line, with carbon atoms at the ends and vertices and hydrogen atoms attached to carbon implied. Functional groups and the hydrogens on heteroatoms are drawn explicitly.

Where a compound has a double bond, the position is numbered and geometric isomerism may exist; cis and trans (or E and Z) describe the arrangement around the C=C bond and is covered with the alkenes.

Classifying reactions

Every organic reaction can be placed in one of five categories, and the classification is often the first mark of a question.

  • Addition: two molecules join to form one, with no atom lost. Ethene plus bromine gives 1,2-dibromoethane.
  • Substitution: one atom or group is replaced by another. Methane plus chlorine gives chloromethane plus hydrogen chloride.
  • Oxidation: an increase in the oxygen content or a loss of hydrogen, such as a primary alcohol becoming a carboxylic acid.
  • Reduction: a gain of hydrogen or a loss of oxygen, such as an alkene becoming an alkane.
  • Polymerisation: small molecules (monomers) join to form a large molecule (a polymer), as in the addition polymerisation of ethene.

Bond breaking can be classified in the same way. In homolytic fission the shared pair is split equally, one electron going to each atom, producing two free radicals. In heterolytic fission the shared pair goes entirely to one atom, producing a positive and a negative ion. A free radical is a species with an unpaired electron, shown with a single dot, such as Cl·. An electrophile is an electron-pair acceptor, such as HBr or Br₂ in an addition reaction; a nucleophile is an electron-pair donor, such as OH⁻ or NH₃.

Which fission happens depends on the conditions. Ultraviolet light supplies enough energy to break a Cl–Cl bond homolytically, which is why the chlorination of alkanes is a radical reaction; in a polar solvent, heterolytic fission is favoured and produces ions, which is why halogenoalkane hydrolysis is a nucleophilic substitution.

Alkanes and structural isomerism

Alkanes are hydrocarbons: compounds of carbon and hydrogen only. They are saturated, containing single bonds only, and their general formula is CₙH₂ₙ₊₂; cycloalkanes have the general formula CₙH₂ₙ because the ring uses two hydrogens to close.

Structural isomers are molecules with the same molecular formula but different structural formulae. Isomerism arises because the carbon skeleton can be arranged differently, and the number of isomers grows quickly with chain length. The alkanes with up to six carbon atoms are examined directly.

FormulaNumber of structural isomersNames
C4H102butane; 2-methylpropane
C5H123pentane; 2-methylbutane; 2,2-dimethylpropane
C6H145hexane; 2-methylpentane; 3-methylpentane; 2,2-dimethylbutane; 2,3-dimethylbutane

A systematic way to find them all is to take the longest chain first, then shorten the main chain by one carbon and place the removed carbon as a methyl substituent in every distinct position, then shorten again. Never place a methyl group on the end of a chain, because that only lengthens the chain and produces a duplicate.

Obtaining alkanes from crude oil

Crude oil is a mixture of hydrocarbons. It is separated by fractional distillation, which works because the fractions have different boiling temperatures: the larger the molecule, the stronger the London forces and the higher the boiling temperature. The column is hot at the bottom and cooler at the top, so smaller molecules rise further before condensing.

Demand is for short-chain molecules, especially fuels, so longer chains are broken down by cracking. Thermal cracking uses high temperature and pressure; catalytic cracking uses a zeolite catalyst at a lower temperature and pressure. In both cases a long alkane becomes a shorter alkane and an alkene:

C10H22 → C8H18 + C2H4

Reforming rearranges straight-chain alkanes into branched alkanes and cycloalkanes, or converts them into aromatic compounds, without changing the number of carbon atoms. Branched isomers are preferred in petrol because they burn more smoothly and resist premature ignition (knocking). A typical reforming equation shows a straight chain becoming a branched isomer with the same formula, or a cycloalkane plus hydrogen:

C6H14 → cyclo-C6H12 + H2

Combustion and pollution

Alkanes burn in a plentiful supply of oxygen to give carbon dioxide and water:

C3H8 + 5O2 → 3CO2 + 4H2O

With insufficient oxygen, combustion is incomplete and produces carbon monoxide, carbon particulates (soot) and unburned hydrocarbons. Combustion in air at high temperature also produces oxides of nitrogen, because nitrogen and oxygen from the air combine in the hot engine.

PollutantSourceProblem
Carbon monoxideIncomplete combustionToxic: it binds to haemoglobin far more strongly than oxygen does, forming carboxyhaemoglobin, so the blood carries less oxygen and the body is starved of it
Oxides of nitrogen, NO and NO₂Nitrogen and oxygen combining at high temperature in enginesDissolve in rainwater to form nitric acid, contributing to acid rain, which damages buildings, soils and trees and acidifies lakes; also contribute to photochemical smog and respiratory irritation
Sulfur dioxideSulfur impurities in fossil fuelsDissolves to form sulfurous and sulfuric acid, contributing to acid rain
Carbon particulatesIncomplete combustion, especially dieselRespiratory damage; contributes to smog and deposits on buildings
Unburned hydrocarbonsIncomplete combustion and evaporationReact with nitrogen oxides in sunlight to form photochemical smog, and some are carcinogenic
Carbon dioxideComplete combustion of any carbon fuelA greenhouse gas, contributing to climate change

Catalytic converters reduce these emissions by converting carbon monoxide and oxides of nitrogen into carbon dioxide and nitrogen, and oxidising unburned hydrocarbons:

2CO + 2NO → 2CO2 + N²

The catalyst is a ceramic honeycomb coated with platinum, palladium and rhodium. It works best when hot, which is why a cold engine emits more pollution, and it requires unleaded petrol because lead poisons the catalyst.

Alternative fuels and carbon neutrality

Fossil fuels are finite and their combustion adds carbon dioxide that was locked away for millions of years, so alternatives are developed to improve sustainability and reduce emissions. Sustainability means meeting present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs.

  • Bioethanol is produced by fermentation of sugars from crops. It is renewable, but growing the crops uses land, water and fertiliser, and the carbon dioxide released when it burns was recently absorbed by the plants.
  • Hydrogen releases only water when burned or used in a fuel cell, so it produces no carbon dioxide at the point of use. Whether it is low-carbon depends on how it was made: from renewable electricity by electrolysis it is clean, but from methane by steam reforming it is not.
  • Biodiesel from vegetable oils is renewable and can be used in existing diesel engines, but it competes for agricultural land.

Carbon neutrality means that the amount of carbon dioxide released when a fuel is used is balanced by the amount removed from the atmosphere when the fuel was produced. Petrol is not carbon neutral: the carbon in it was stored underground for millions of years and is added to the atmosphere when burned. Bioethanol is often described as carbon neutral because the crops absorbed carbon dioxide as they grew, but it is only truly neutral if the farming, harvesting, transport and distillation are also carbon neutral, and those processes usually burn fossil fuel. Hydrogen made by electrolysis using renewable electricity can be carbon neutral; hydrogen from steam reforming is not.

Reactions of alkanes

Alkanes are relatively unreactive because their C–C and C–H bonds are strong and non-polar. Two reactions are examined.

Combustion. As above: complete combustion gives carbon dioxide and water, incomplete combustion gives carbon monoxide and soot. Alkanes are good fuels because they release a large amount of energy per gram.

Halogenation. In the dark there is no reaction. In the presence of ultraviolet light, a halogen such as chlorine reacts with an alkane in a substitution reaction:

CH4 + Cl2 → CH3Cl + HCl

The reaction is a free radical substitution. It proceeds in three stages, and each must be shown with the correct species and the correct curly half-arrows.

Initiation. Ultraviolet light supplies the energy to break the Cl–Cl bond homolytically, producing two chlorine radicals:

Cl2 → 2Cl·
