One half-arrow starts at the middle of the Cl–Cl bond and curves to one chlorine atom, and a second half-arrow curves from the bond to the other chlorine atom, showing one electron going each way.

Propagation. A chlorine radical collides with a methane molecule and removes a hydrogen atom, forming hydrogen chloride and a methyl radical; the methyl radical then reacts with a chlorine molecule to form chloromethane and a new chlorine radical:

Cl· + CH4 → CH3· + HCl
CH3· + Cl2 → CH3Cl + Cl·

Because a chlorine radical is regenerated in the second step, the reaction is a chain reaction. In each propagation step one radical is used and one is produced, so the number of radicals stays constant.

Termination. Two radicals combine and the chain ends:

Cl· + Cl· → Cl2
CH3· + Cl· → CH3Cl
CH3· + CH3· → C2H6

The last termination step explains why ethane is found among the products of the chlorination of methane, even though it is not part of the desired reaction.

Free radical substitution has limited use in synthesis because the reaction does not stop at the first substitution. Chloromethane can react again to give dichloromethane, trichloromethane and tetrachloromethane, and the propagation steps also produce hydrogen chloride and small amounts of ethane, so the product is a mixture that must be separated. To obtain a single product in good yield, a different route such as nucleophilic substitution of an alcohol is preferred.

Typical mistakes

  • Confusing hazard with risk: a hazard is the potential for harm, risk is the chance of it happening.
  • Numbering a chain from the end that gives the substituent the lowest number while ignoring the principal functional group.
  • Writing a radical with a full negative charge instead of a single dot, or forgetting the dot entirely.
  • Showing initiation with a heterolytic split, which would produce ions rather than radicals.
  • Giving the general formula of an alkene (CₙH₂ₙ) for an alkane, or forgetting that cycloalkanes share the alkene's general formula.
  • Missing a structural isomer by placing a methyl group at the end of a chain, which is the same molecule renamed.
  • Describing cracking as the addition of hydrogen, which is hydrogenation, or reforming as breaking molecules into smaller ones.
  • Claiming that a biofuel is automatically carbon neutral without accounting for its production.
  • Leaving ultraviolet light out of the conditions for halogenation, or writing the equation as an addition reaction.

Exam-style questions

  1. Define the terms hazard and risk, and explain why a risk assessment is needed before heating ethanol over a Bunsen burner. Answer: a hazard is something with the potential to cause harm; risk is the chance that harm occurs. Ethanol is volatile and highly flammable, so heating it directly risks a flash fire; a risk assessment identifies that hazard and specifies the control, such as heating in a water bath and keeping the apparatus away from naked flames.
  2. Name the compound CH₃CH₂CH(CH₃)CH₂OH. Answer: the longest chain containing the OH group has four carbons and is numbered from the right so that the OH is on carbon 1; the methyl group is on carbon 3, so the name is 3-methylbutan-1-ol.
  3. Draw and name all the structural isomers of C₅H₁₂. Answer: pentane (a straight chain of five carbons), 2-methylbutane (a four-carbon chain with a methyl on carbon 2), and 2,2-dimethylpropane (a three-carbon chain with two methyls on carbon 2).
  4. Explain why the reaction between methane and chlorine needs ultraviolet light. Answer: the C–H and Cl–Cl bonds are strong and the molecules are non-polar, so collisions at room temperature do not have enough energy to break them. Ultraviolet light provides the energy for homolytic fission of the Cl–Cl bond, which produces chlorine radicals and starts the chain reaction.
  5. Outline the mechanism for the monochlorination of ethane, naming each type of step. Answer: initiation: Cl2 → 2Cl· under UV light. Propagation: Cl· + C2H6 → C2H5· + HCl, then C2H5· + Cl2 → C2H5Cl + Cl·. Termination: Cl· + Cl· → Cl2, C2H5· + Cl· → C2H5Cl, C2H5· + C2H5· → C4H10.

Practise naming and drawing as one skill: take a name, draw the skeletal formula, then the displayed formula, then write the molecular formula, and reverse the process. That fluency is assumed in every later organic topic, especially halogenoalkanes, alcohols and spectra.

title: Alkenes
content:
Alkenes

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH11, Topic 5. Alkenes contain a carbon–carbon double bond, which makes them far more reactive than alkanes. Their addition reactions are a central part of organic synthesis.

Structure and bonding

  • A C=C double bond consists of one sigma bond and one pi bond. The pi bond is an electron cloud above and below the plane of the atoms, and it is the reactive part.
  • The carbons of a C=C bond are planar, with bond angles of about 120°.

Addition reactions

  • Hydrogen adds across the double bond in the presence of a nickel catalyst to form an alkane.
  • Halogens (for example bromine water) add across the double bond: a colour change from orange to colourless is the test for an alkene.
  • Steam adds across the double bond in the presence of phosphoric acid to form an alcohol.
  • Hydrogen halides add to give halogenoalkanes; with unsymmetrical alkenes the Markovnikov rule predicts the major product.

Polymerisation

  • Addition polymers form when many alkene monomers join together. Poly(ethene) and poly(chloroethene) are examples.
  • The repeat unit is drawn with the double bond opened and the bonds extended through brackets.

Isomerism

  • Restricted rotation about the C=C bond allows E/Z isomers when each carbon carries two different groups.

Exam tip: when drawing a polymer, show the repeat unit with the bonds extending outwards, and do not leave a dangling double bond.

title: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Right-Angled Trigonometry
content:
Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Right-Angled Trigonometry

Right-angled triangles are the most useful triangles in mathematics: Pythagoras relates the three sides, and the sine, cosine and tangent ratios relate sides to angles. Between them they solve every distance and angle problem the IGCSE sets, from ladders against walls to angles of elevation and three-figure bearings. This note builds the topic from zero: Pythagoras with its converse and 3D use, the SOHCAHTOA ratios with the selection method, exact values derived rather than memorised, and the multi-step problems that combine Pythagoras with trigonometry.

Pythagoras' theorem

in a right-angled triangle: a² + b² = c²
where c is the hypotenuse (the side opposite the right angle)

The theorem is a statement about areas: the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides. The converse identifies right angles: if a² + b² = c² for the longest side c, the triangle is right-angled — the standard test for 3-4-5 and 5-12-13 triangles.

Worked example 1. A right-angled triangle has legs 6 cm and 8 cm. Find the hypotenuse.

c² = 6² + 8² = 36 + 64 = 100
c = 10 cm

Worked example 2 (finding a leg). The hypotenuse is 13 cm and one leg is 5 cm. Find the other leg.

a² = 13² - 5² = 169 - 25 = 144
a = 12 cm

Worked example 3 (converse). Is a triangle with sides 7, 24, 25 right-angled?

7² + 24² = 49 + 576 = 625 = 25²
yes - right-angled, with the right angle opposite the 25 side

Pythagoras in three dimensions

In a cuboid, the space diagonal uses Pythagoras twice: first across the base, then up the height.

space diagonal = √(l² + w² + h²)

Worked example. A cuboid is 3 cm by 4 cm by 12 cm. Find the length of the space diagonal.

d = √(9 + 16 + 144) = √(169) = 13 cm

The three ratios: SOHCAHTOA

sin(θ) = opposite/hypotenuse      (SOH)
cos(θ) = adjacent/hypotenuse      (CAH)
tan(θ) = opposite/adjacent       (TOA)

Label the sides relative to the angle in question: the hypotenuse is always opposite the right angle; the opposite is across from the angle; the adjacent is the remaining side touching the angle. The selection method: mark the known side and the wanted side, then ask which ratio contains both.

Worked example 1 (finding a side). In a right-angled triangle, the angle is 35° and the hypotenuse is 12 cm. Find the opposite side.

known: hypotenuse; want: opposite  →  sine
sin(35) = opposite/12
opposite = 12 sin(35) = 12 × 0.574 = 6.88 cm

Worked example 2 (finding a side with cosine). Angle 40°, hypotenuse 20 cm; find the adjacent side.

cos(40) = adjacent/20
adjacent = 20 cos(40) = 20 × 0.766 = 15.3 cm

Worked example 3 (finding an angle). Opposite 5 cm, adjacent 9 cm. Find the angle.

tan(θ) = 5/9 = 0.5556
θ = tan-1(0.5556) = 29.1 °

For angles, use the inverse functions (sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹, tan⁻¹) and check the calculator is in degree mode — a radian-mode calculator turns 90° into 1.57 and ruins the paper.

Exact trigonometric values

Three angles have exact values worth knowing, derived from two special triangles:

Anglesincostan
30°1/2√3/21/√3
45°1/√21/√21
60°√3/21/2√3

Derivation: a 45-45-90 triangle with legs 1 has hypotenuse √2 (Pythagoras), giving sin 45 = 1/√2. An equilateral triangle of side 2 split in half gives a 30-60-90 triangle with sides 1, √3, 2, giving all six values. Deriving them once beats memorising them badly.

Two sanity checks keep the table honest: sine increases from 0 to 1 as the angle grows from 0° to 90°, so sin 30 must be smaller than sin 60; and cosine runs the other way, so cos 30 must be larger than cos 60. If an exact value breaks either ordering, the table has been misremembered.

Worked example. Find the exact value of sin 60° × tan 30°.

sin 60 = √(3)/2;  tan 30 = 1/√(3)
product = (√(3)/2) x (1/√(3)) = 1/2

Angles of elevation and depression

An angle of elevation is measured upward from the horizontal to an object; an angle of depression is measured downward. Both are measured from the observer's eye line, and the angle of depression from A to B equals the angle of elevation from B to A (alternate angles).

Worked example. From a point 40 m from the base of a tower, the angle of elevation to the top is 32°. Find the tower's height.

tan(32) = height/40
height = 40 tan(32) = 40 × 0.625 = 25.0 m

Worked example 2 (depression). A cliff is 60 m high; the angle of depression to a boat is 25°. Find the horizontal distance to the boat.

the angle at the boat is also 25 ° (alternate)
tan(25) = 60/d  →  d = 60/tan(25) = 60/0.466 = 128.7 m

Choosing the method: a decision routine

Most lost trigonometry marks come from choosing the wrong tool, not from arithmetic. The routine below takes ten seconds and removes the guesswork:

  1. Is there a right angle? If not, the question needs the sine or cosine rule (a different topic) — do not force SOHCAHTOA onto a triangle without a right angle.
  2. What do you know — two sides, or a side and an angle? Two sides with no angle means Pythagoras. A side and an angle means trigonometry.
  3. Which ratio? Mark the known side and the target relative to the given angle, then pick the ratio containing both: sin uses opposite and hypotenuse, cos uses adjacent and hypotenuse, tan uses opposite and adjacent.
  4. What is the unknown — a side or an angle? A side comes from multiplying; an angle needs the inverse function.

Worked example. A roof rafter is 4.5 m long and meets the horizontal at 38°. Find the vertical rise and the horizontal run.

rise: sin(38) = rise/4.5  →  rise = 4.5 sin(38) = 2.77 m
run:  cos(38) = run/4.5   →  run = 4.5 cos(38) = 3.55 m
check: 2.77² + 3.55² = 7.67 + 12.60 = 20.27 ~ 4.5²

Worked example 2 (finding the angle of a ladder). A 6 m ladder reaches 5.2 m up a wall. Find the angle it makes with the ground.

sin(θ) = 5.2/6 = 0.867  →  θ = 60.1 °

Multi-step problems: Pythagoras and trigonometry together

Many questions need both tools: Pythagoras to find a side in one triangle, trigonometry to use it in another. The method: draw and label every triangle, find the shared side first, then proceed.

Worked example. A ladder 5 m long leans against a wall, with its foot 2 m from the wall. Find the height reached and the angle the ladder makes with the ground.

height: h² = 5² - 2² = 25 - 4 = 21  →  h = 4.58 m
angle: cos(θ) = 2/5 = 0.4  →  θ = 66.4 °

Worked example 2 (two triangles). From a point P, the angle of elevation to the top of a building is 30°; from a point Q, 20 m closer, it is 45°. Find the height.

let h be the height and x the distance from Q to the base.
tan(45) = h/x  →  h = x
tan(30) = h/(x + 20)
h = (x + 20) tan(30) = (h + 20)(1/√(3))
h √(3) = h + 20  →  h(√(3) - 1) = 20
h = 20/(1.732 - 1) = 20/0.732 = 27.3 m

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Pythagoras) A right-angled triangle has legs 9 and 12. Find the hypotenuse. Answer: √(81 + 144) = √225 = 15.
  2. (Leg) Hypotenuse 17, one leg 8. Find the other. Answer: √(289 − 64) = 15.
  3. (Ratio) Angle 28°, adjacent 15 cm. Find the opposite side. Answer: tan 28 = o/15 → o = 15 × 0.532 = 7.98 cm.
  4. (Angle) Opposite 7, hypotenuse 10. Find the angle. Answer: sin θ = 0.7 → θ = 44.4°.
  5. (Exact) Find cos 30° exactly. Answer: √3/2.
  6. (Elevation) From 25 m away, the angle of elevation to a tree top is 40°. Find the height. Answer: 25 tan 40 = 25 × 0.839 = 21.0 m.
  7. (3D) A cuboid is 2 cm by 3 cm by 6 cm. Find its space diagonal. Answer: √(4 + 9 + 36) = √49 = 7 cm.
  8. (Combined) A ship sails 30 km east then 40 km north. Find its distance from the start and the bearing of its final position. Answer: distance = 50 km; tan θ = 40/30 → θ = 53.1°, bearing 053°.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Calculator mode: check DEG, not RAD or GRAD, before any trigonometric calculation. A radian answer is usually obviously wrong (tiny or huge), but only if you check.
  • Wrong ratio: label the sides relative to the angle before choosing SOH, CAH or TOA; picking by habit is the commonest trigonometry error.
  • Hypotenuse identification: the hypotenuse is opposite the right angle, not necessarily the longest-looking side on the diagram.
  • Pythagoras with the hypotenuse as a leg: c² = a² + b² only when c is the hypotenuse; finding a leg requires subtraction.
  • Rounding early: keep full calculator accuracy until the final answer; round to 3 s.f. (or 1 d.p. for angles unless told otherwise).
  • Angle of depression drawn from the wrong line: it is measured from the horizontal, not from the cliff face; the alternate-angle equality fixes the geometry.
  • Exact values with decimals: "exact" means surds and fractions, not 0.866; leaving √3/2 is required.
  • Missing units and labels: state cm, m, km and degrees; name the side or angle found, especially in multi-step problems.

Label the triangle before you reach for a ratio

Right-angled trigonometry is not three formulas to memorise; it is one decision made three times: which side am I given, which do I want, and which ratio connects them. Every error in this topic is a labelling error made before any calculation starts.

Only the hypotenuse is fixed. It is the side opposite the right angle, and it is always the longest. "Opposite" and "adjacent" are relative to the angle you are working with: in the figure, the side BC is opposite θ and AB is adjacent to it. Put the angle at C instead and those two swap. Annotate the diagram with O, A and H in pencil before choosing anything.

The ratios are ratios, which is why they work at any size. Similar triangles taught that corresponding sides scale together — double every side and the ratio stays the same. That is precisely why sin 30° is ½ for a triangle of any size:

sin θ = opposite / hypotenuse Key: θ = the angle inside the triangle; opposite = the side across from θ; hypotenuse = the side opposite the right angle.
cos θ = adjacent / hypotenuse Key: adjacent = the side next to θ that is not the hypotenuse.
tan θ = opposite / adjacent Key: the only ratio that does not use the hypotenuse.

Choosing in one step. Given an angle and one side, mark on the diagram which two sides the question involves, then read off: two sides with the hypotenuse means sine or cosine; two sides without it means tangent. Use the inverse function when the angle is the unknown.

Worked example. A ladder 5.0 m long leans against a wall, making 68° with the ground. How far up the wall does it reach, and how far is its foot from the wall?

height is opposite the 68° angle, ladder is the hypotenuse:

sin 68° = h / 5.0, so h = 5.0 × sin 68° = 5.0 × 0.9272 = 4.6 m

distance from the wall is adjacent:

cos 68° = d / 5.0, so d = 5.0 × cos 68° = 5.0 × 0.3746 = 1.9 m

Check with Pythagoras: 4.6² + 1.9² = 21.2 + 3.6 = 24.8 ≈ 25 = 5.0². That thirty-second check catches a swapped ratio every time, and the two answers being 4.6 and 1.9 rather than a plausible pair like 4.6 and 4.4 is exactly what the check is for.

The special angles come from two triangles. A 45-45-90 triangle with legs 1 gives sin 45° = 1/√2. Half of an equilateral triangle of side 2 gives sides 1, √3 and 2, hence sin 30° = ½, cos 30° = √3/2 and tan 60° = √3. These are worth deriving once so they are not three more things to memorise.

Where marks are lost. The calculator in radians or grads — check the mode before the first question, not after. Using the adjacent side when the question needs the opposite, because the labels were never written on the diagram. And rounding at 4.6 m then using 4.6 in Pythagoras: keep the full value and round only the answer.

Pythagoras' theorem in more depth

Pythagoras' theorem states that in a right-angled triangle the square of the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides, so c² = a² + b², where c is the hypotenuse. The theorem is used in two directions: to find a missing side when the triangle is known to be right-angled, and to test whether a triangle is right-angled at all. The subsections below cover both directions, the common number patterns, and the errors that cost marks.

Finding the hypotenuse

When the two shorter sides are known, add their squares and take the square root. For a triangle with shorter sides 5 cm and 12 cm, the hypotenuse is √(5² + 12²) = √(25 + 144) = √169 = 13 cm. The hypotenuse is always the longest side and always opposite the right angle, so it is the side that is added, not subtracted, in the calculation.

Finding a shorter side

When the hypotenuse and one shorter side are known, subtract the square of the known shorter side from the square of the hypotenuse, then take the square root. For a hypotenuse of 13 cm and a side of 5 cm, the missing side is √(13² − 5²) = √(169 − 25) = √144 = 12 cm. Write the subtraction out in full, because the most common error in this type of question is to add the squares by mistake.

Testing whether a triangle is right-angled

The converse of Pythagoras' theorem says that if the square of the longest side equals the sum of the squares of the other two, the triangle is right-angled. For sides 6, 8 and 10, the check is 6² + 8² = 36 + 64 = 100 = 10², so the triangle is right-angled. For sides 7, 8 and 10, the check is 49 + 64 = 113, which is greater than 100, so the triangle is acute and not right-angled. Always compare the squares of the longest side with the others.

Pythagorean triples

A Pythagorean triple is a set of three whole numbers that satisfy a² + b² = c². The most used are 3, 4, 5; 5, 12, 13; 8, 15, 17; and 7, 24, 25. Any multiple of a triple is also a triple, so 6, 8, 10 and 9, 12, 15 are triples. Recognising a triple lets you give an exact answer with no square root, which is often what the question wants when the sides are whole numbers.

Pythagoras in a problem with several triangles

Some questions need the theorem twice, because the first right-angled triangle gives a side that is needed in the second. For example, a rectangle 9 cm by 12 cm has a diagonal of √(9² + 12²) = 15 cm. If a second triangle uses that diagonal as one of its sides, the same method applies again. Mark the sides you have found on the diagram before starting the next step, so each calculation has its numbers ready.

Real-world problems with Pythagoras

A ladder leaning against a wall, a diagonal across a field and the straight-line distance between two towns are all Pythagoras problems once the right angle is identified. Draw the triangle, label the hypotenuse as the longest side, and state which right angle the theorem is being used at. A question that describes a route going east then north is a right-angled triangle formed by the two legs and the straight line between the ends.

Rounding and giving the answer

Leave square roots exact if the question asks for an exact answer, and give a decimal to the accuracy the question states. A calculation that gives √50 can be left as 5√2 for an exact answer, or written as 7.07 to 3 significant figures for a decimal answer. Do the rounding only at the last step, because rounding an intermediate square root and then squaring it can change the final answer.

Common errors with Pythagoras

The errors that lose marks are forgetting the square root at the end, adding when the question needs a subtraction, and applying the theorem to a triangle that is not right-angled. Check the answer by reversing the calculation: square the two shorter sides, add them, and confirm the result equals the square of the hypotenuse. A quick reversal catches most slips.

Quick revision: Statistics — Data Handling

Mathematics — OL. averages from lists and tables, quartiles/IQR, charts, cumulative frequency, histograms.

  • 1. Averages
  • 2. Quartiles and IQR
  • 3. Charts
  • 4. Cumulative frequency
  • 5. Histograms

Formulas to learn

  • Mean from a grouped table: sum of f x divided by sum of f, using the class midpoints.
  • Interquartile range: Q3 - Q1. The median is Q2.
  • Histogram height: frequency density = frequency / class width. Area of each bar is proportional to frequency.

Worked example

A cumulative frequency curve has its points plotted against the upper class boundary. Reading the curve at 25 percent of the total gives Q1, at 50 percent gives the median, and at 75 percent gives Q3. The IQR is Q3 minus Q1, and it is less affected by outliers than the range.

How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

title: A Level Mathematics: Permutations and Combinations
content:
A Level Mathematics: Permutations and Combinations

Counting is the part of probability that requires no formula to start with, only a decision: does the order matter? Every question in this topic is answered by that one question. If order matters the count is a permutation; if it does not the count is a combination. Everything else — repetitions, restrictions, arrangements around a circle — is a variation on the same counting principle, and this note sets out each variation with the reasoning behind it.

The multiplication principle

If a choice can be made in a ways and, independently, a second choice in b ways, the pair can be made in a × b ways. That is the whole foundation; the formulas are shortcuts for repeated applications of it.

arrangements of n distinct objects in a row: n! = n x (n-1) x ... x 2 × 1
0! = 1 by convention, so that formulas stay consistent
choosing r from n with order: nPr = n!/(n - r)!
choosing r from n without order: nCr = n!/(r!(n - r)!)

Worked example. A password is 4 distinct letters from the 26-letter alphabet. How many passwords are possible?

order matters, so 26P4 = 26 × 25 × 24 × 23 = 358,800

Worked example 2 (no order). How many ways can 4 students be chosen from 26?

order does not matter, so 26C4 = 14,950

Worked example 3 (a leading zero is not allowed). A code uses four distinct digits from 0 to 9 and cannot begin with zero. How many codes?

first digit: 9 choices (1 to 9)
remaining three: 9P3 = 9 × 8 × 7 = 504
total = 9 × 504 = 4536

Worked example 4 (the link). Explain why nPr = nCr × r!.

every unordered selection of r objects can be arranged in r! orders
so counting ordered selections = counting unordered ones then arranging them

Deciding whether order matters

The decision is not about the words "choose" or "arrange" in the question — those are hints, not rules. The safe test is to imagine two selections differing only by swapping two items: if that counts as a different outcome, order matters.

SituationOrder?Count
finishing order of a raceyesnPr
a committee of 3nonCr
a 4-digit PINyespermutation, with repetition allowed
a hand of cardsnonCr
seating 5 people in a rowyes5!

Worked example. A team of 11 is chosen from 16 players, and one of the 11 is captain. Count the possibilities.

choose the 11: 16C11 = 4368
choose the captain from them: 11 ways
total = 4368 × 11 = 48,048

The multiplication principle is doing the work here: two independent choices, multiplied.

Repetition and identical items

When some objects are identical, arranging them as if all were distinct overcounts by the number of ways the identical ones can be swapped. Dividing by those factorials corrects it.

arrangements of n items with groups of identical items:
n!/(a! b! c! ...) where a, b, c are the group sizes
with repetition allowed, choosing r from n: n^r

Worked example. How many distinct arrangements of the letters in BANANA?

6 letters: B once, A three times, N twice
6!/(1! 3! 2!) = 720/12 = 60

Worked example 2 (repetition allowed). A 3-digit code uses digits 0-9, repeats allowed. How many codes?

10 × 10 × 10 = 1000
if repeats were not allowed: 10 × 9 × 8 = 720

Worked example 3 (identical plus restriction). How many arrangements of the letters of LEVEL begin with L?

fix L at the front; remaining letters E, V, E, L
that is 4 letters with E twice: 4!/2! = 12
but the leading L is one of the two Ls, so there is only one choice for the front
answer 12

Restrictions: the "glue" method

When certain items must be together, treat the group as a single object, arrange the objects, then arrange within the group. When certain items must not be together, count the total and subtract the "together" case.

together: glue the group, arrange the objects, multiply by the internal arrangements
not together: total arrangements minus the together arrangements
specific positions: fix those items first, then arrange the rest

Worked example. Five books, two of which must stand together, are arranged on a shelf. How many orders?

glue the pair: now 4 objects, arranged in 4! = 24 ways
the pair interchange in 2! = 2 ways
total = 48

Worked example 2 (not together). The same five books with the pair not together.

total arrangements = 5! = 120
together = 48
not together = 120 - 48 = 72

Worked example 3 (fixed positions). Four men and three women sit in a row of seven. How many arrangements have all three women together?

glue the women into one block: now 5 objects (4 men + block), 5! = 120
internal arrangements of the women: 3! = 6
total = 720

Circular arrangements

Around a circle, rotations of the same arrangement are not distinguishable, so fixing one item removes the rotational symmetry and the count drops by a factor of n.

n distinct items around a circle: (n - 1)!
a necklace (where reflection also counts as the same): (n - 1)!/2

Worked example. In how many ways can 6 people sit around a round table?

(6 - 1)! = 5! = 120

Worked example 2 (with a fixed seat). How many ways if one particular person must sit in a specified chair?

fix that person, arrange the other 5 around: 5! = 120
the specified chair removes the rotational freedom entirely, so the answer is unchanged here

Worked example 3 (two people together at a round table). Six people, two of whom must sit together.

glue the pair: 5 objects around a circle = 4! = 24
internal order of the pair: 2
total = 48

Combinations with conditions

Committee questions combine cases: choose so many from one group and so many from another, then add the disjoint alternatives. The discipline is to make the cases genuinely disjoint, or the same selection gets counted twice.

choose a from group A and b from group B: C(a-group, a) x C(b-group, b)
several allowed compositions: add the separate cases
at least one: total minus none

Worked example. From 6 men and 5 women, how many committees of 4 contain exactly 2 women?

choose 2 women from 5: 10
choose 2 men from 6: 15
total = 150

Worked example 2 (at least one). How many committees of 4 contain at least one woman?

total committees: 11C4 = 330
none: 6C4 = 15
at least one = 330 - 15 = 315

Worked example 3 (cases added). How many committees of 3 contain more women than men?

3 women: 5C3 = 10
2 women and 1 man: 5C2 × 6C1 = 10 × 6 = 60
total = 70

Counting inside probability

Combinations are usually the denominator of a probability question: count the favourable selections, count all selections, divide. Doing the counting separately from the probability keeps both parts clean and makes partial credit possible.

Worked example. A bag holds 5 red and 7 blue counters. Four are drawn at random. Find the probability of exactly 2 red.

total selections: 12C4 = 495
favourable: 5C2 × 7C2 = 10 × 21 = 210
probability = 210/495 = 0.4242

Worked example 2 (at least one). For the same bag, find the probability of at least one red.

complement: no red means all four blue
7C4 = 35
P(no red) = 35/495 = 0.0707
P(at least one red) = 1 - 0.0707 = 0.9293

Worked example 3 (order matters in the numerator). Three cards are drawn from a standard deck without replacement. Find the probability they are drawn in increasing order of value.

every set of three distinct cards has exactly one increasing order out of 3! orders
so the probability is 1/6, independent of the deck

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Factorial) Evaluate 7!. Answer: 7! = 7 × 6 × 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 5040.
  2. (Permutation) In how many orders can 5 runners finish? Answer: 5P5 = 5! = 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 120.
  3. (Combination) Evaluate 10C3. Answer: 10C3 = 10!/(3! × 7!) = (10 × 9 × 8)/(3 × 2 × 1) = 720/6 = 120.
  4. (Choice) From 8 books, how many ways to choose 3? Answer: 8C3 = 8!/(3! × 5!) = (8 × 7 × 6)/(3 × 2 × 1) = 336/6 = 56.
  5. (Arrangement) How many arrangements of the letters of STATISTICS? Answer: 10!/(3! × 3! × 2!) = 3 628 800/(6 × 6 × 2) = 3 628 800/72 = 50,400.
  6. (Glue) 6 people in a row with two together: Answer: glue the pair: 5! × 2! = 120 × 2 = 240.
  7. (Not together) Same 6, not together: Answer: total − together = 6! − 5! × 2! = 720 − 240 = 480.
  8. (Circle) 7 people around a table: Answer: (n − 1)! = 6! = 720.
  9. (Committee) 3 from 5 men and 4 women, exactly 2 men: Answer: 5C2 × 4C1 = 10 × 4 = 40.
  10. (At least) 4 from the same 9 with at least one woman: Answer: all − none = 9C4 − 5C4 = 126 − 5 = 121.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Using nPr where order does not matter: a committee is unordered; using permutations overcounts by r!.
  • Forgetting to divide by repeated factorials: identical letters need the divisor or the count is inflated.
  • Glue method without the internal factor: the block also has an internal arrangement, and dropping the 2! halves the answer.
  • Circular arrangements with n! instead of (n − 1)!: rotations are the same seating.
  • Adding what should be multiplied: independent stages multiply; alternative cases add.
  • Overlapping cases: cases must be disjoint, or selections are counted twice.
  • "At least one" counted directly: the complement is almost always faster and safer.
  • Restrictions applied after the count: fix the restricted positions first, then count what remains.

Choosing between nPr, nCr and a plain product

Most lost marks in this topic come from using the right formula for the wrong question. Before any calculation, decide whether you are selecting, arranging or doing both, and whether the answer depends on the order. The subsections below set out the decision in the order a careful candidate works through it.

Selecting without arranging: nCr

If you only need to choose a group and the order inside the group does not matter, use ⁿCᵣ = n! / (r!(n − r)!). Choosing a committee of 4 from 10 people gives ¹⁰C₄ = 210. The result counts groups, so two committees with the same members in a different order are the same committee.

Selecting and arranging: nPr

If the chosen items are then placed in distinct positions, the order matters and you use ⁿPᵣ = n! / (n − r)!. Choosing a chair, a vice-chair and a secretary from 10 people gives ¹⁰P₃ = 720. Each committee of 3 from the previous example can be arranged in 3! = 6 ways, so 720 = 120 × 6, which is a useful check.

A plain product for independent choices

When each decision is made separately and the number of options for one does not depend on the others, multiply. Three shirts and four trousers give 3 × 4 = 12 outfits. Do not reach for a combination formula here: nothing is being chosen from a single pool of identical kinds of object.

Checking the order question

Ask whether swapping two chosen items changes the outcome. A password changes if its letters are swapped, so it is an arrangement. A team does not change when two members swap places, so it is a selection. If the words in the question say “the first, second and third” or “positions”, the order matters.

Worked decision

Seven runners compete for gold, silver and bronze. The medals are different, so the order matters and the count is ⁷P₃ = 7 × 6 × 5 = 210. If the question asked for three runners to go through to a final with no ranking, the count would be ⁷C₃ = 35. The same seven people give 210 or 35 depending only on whether the medal order is asked for, so state which one you have chosen before you write the number.

Common error: dividing when you should not

Students often divide by a factorial out of habit. Divide only when items are truly identical or the outcome groups are truly unordered. Dividing ⁷P₃ by 3! to get the medal count gives 35 and throws away the difference between gold and silver, which the question asked you to keep.

Keeping items apart and placing them together

Restriction questions usually ask that certain people or letters are together, or that they are not. Two methods work, and the complement is often shorter. Choose the method from the wording before you start counting.

Together: treat the pair as one object

If two items must sit together, glue them into one block. Arrange the block with the others, then multiply by the number of internal orders of the block. Seven people in a row with two particular people side by side give 6! × 2! = 720 × 2 = 1440 arrangements. Omitting the 2! halves the answer.

Not together: subtract the together cases

For the same seven people with the two not allowed together, the total is 7! = 5040. Subtract the 1440 arrangements in which they are together, giving 5040 − 1440 = 3600. This is usually quicker than building the arrangements directly, because the gaps between people are hard to count without listing them.

Not together: place people in the gaps

An alternative for the same question is to arrange the other five people first, which gives 5! = 120 orders. There are six gaps, including the two ends, and the two special people must go into different gaps. Choose 2 of the 6 gaps in order, 6P2 = 30 ways, and this gives 120 × 30 = 3600. Both methods agree, and showing the second one earns the method marks even if the first has an error.

Letters that must not be adjacent

For the word HEART with the vowels E and A not next to each other, count the arrangements with the vowels together (4! × 2! = 48) and subtract from 5! = 120, giving 72. The same subtraction pattern applies to any pair that must be kept apart.

Position restrictions

If one person must stand at one end, fix that person first and arrange the rest. A person fixed at one end leaves 6 people for 6 places, giving 6! = 720. Fixing the restricted item before counting the free ones avoids double counting, which is the usual cause of an answer that is too large.

Interpreting “together” and “next to”

“Side by side” and “next to each other” mean adjacent in the order given. They do not mean the same chair or a shared seat. Read the wording carefully, because a question about two people sitting “with one seat between them” needs a different count altogether.

Groups, teams and sharing into sets

Questions that divide people or objects into groups are where the difference between labelled and unlabelled groups decides the answer. A group that is named, such as “team A” or “the first group”, is labelled. A group that is only described by its members is unlabelled, and the count must not treat two identical splits as different.

Choosing one team from a pool

Choosing a team of 3 from 10 people is a plain selection, so the count is ¹⁰C₃ = 120. No ordering inside the team is counted, and the team is simply the set of three names.

Two teams with names: labelled groups

If the two teams are called Red and Blue, the choice of Red fixes the rest. Choosing 3 for Red from 6 people and 3 for Blue from the remaining 3 gives ⁶C₃ × ³C₃ = 20 × 1 = 20 ways. The name of each team matters, so there is no further division.

Two identical teams: unlabelled groups

If the two teams are not named, the same 20 splits are counted twice, once with each team as Red. Divide by 2 to get 10 ways to split six people into two unlabelled teams of three. Check that the answer is even, since the teams can be swapped in pairs.

Sharing into several sets of equal size

Dividing 9 people into three unlabelled groups of three gives ⁹C₃ × ⁶C₃ × ³C₃ / 3! = 84 × 20 × 1 / 6 = 280 ways. The divisor 3! is needed because the three groups can be listed in 3! orders without changing the split.

Groups with a fixed member

If a particular person must be in the team, choose the other two from the remaining nine: ⁹C₂ = 36. Fixing the person first removes the need for a subtraction later and keeps the count clear.

Worked example: a committee of mixed teachers

A committee of 4 is chosen from 5 men and 4 women and must contain at least one woman. The complement is the committee with no women, which is all men: ⁵C₄ = 5. The total committees are ⁹C₄ = 126. So the answer is 126 − 5 = 121. Writing the complement out in words, “no women”, stops the most common slip, which is counting the all-women case as if it had been excluded.

Equations and symbols

Every formula here is a shortcut for the multiplication principle, and each one carries a condition that decides whether it applies. The condition is the mark: "order matters" and "items are identical" change the count by a factorial.

n! = n x (n-1) x ... x 2 × 1 Key: n = the number of distinct objects (a count, no units); n! = the number of orders they can be arranged in (a count). The falling product stops at 1, and 0! = 1 by convention so the formulas stay consistent.

nPr = n!/(n - r)! Key: n = how many objects are available; r = how many are being chosen; nPr = the number of ordered selections (a count). Read it as "start at n and write down r factors": 26P4 = 26 × 25 × 24 × 23.

nCr = n!/(r!(n - r)!) Key: n = objects available; r = objects chosen; nCr = the number of unordered selections (a count). The extra r! in the denominator is exactly what removes the orderings — which is the whole difference between a permutation and a combination.

nPr = nCr × r! Key: nPr = ordered selections; nCr = unordered selections; r! = the ways to order each selection. The identity explains both formulas at once: count the sets, then arrange each one.

26P4 = 26 × 25 × 24 × 23 = 358,800 Key: 26 = letters available; 4 = letters chosen without replacement; 358,800 = ordered passwords (a count). The factors fall because each letter is used once — repetition allowed would give 26⁴ instead.

26C4 = 14,950 Key: 26 = students available; 4 = students chosen; 14,950 = unordered groups (a count). The same numbers as the password question, 24 times smaller, because a group of four has 4! orderings that all count as one group.

n!/(a! b! c! ...) Key: n = total items; a, b, c = the sizes of the groups of identical items. Dividing by the factorials of the repeats removes the arrangements that look identical — 6!/(1! 3! 2!) = 60 arrangements of BANANA, not 720.

6!/(1! 3! 2!) = 720/12 = 60 Key: 6 = letters in BANANA; 1! = the single B; 3! = the three As; 2! = the two Ns; 60 = distinct arrangements (a count). Every repeated letter needs its own factorial in the denominator, or the count is inflated.

n^r Key: n = choices available at each stage; r = number of stages; the result counts selections with repetition allowed (a count). It is the multiplication principle applied r times — three digits from 0 to 9 with repeats gives 10³ = 1000.

(n - 1)! Key: n = people or objects around a circle; the result counts distinct circular arrangements (a count), because rotating a seating does not create a new one. For a necklace, where a reflection is also the same, divide once more: (n - 1)!/2.

5! × 2! = 120 × 2 = 240 Key: 5! = the arrangements of four single items plus the glued pair as one object; 2! = the internal orders of the pair; 240 = total arrangements (a count). Gluing without the internal factor halves the answer, which is the classic lost mark in this topic.

title: Algebra — Sequences and Functions — Study Notes
content:
Algebra — Sequences and Functions

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): nth term (linear & quadratic), special sequences, function notation, composites, inverses.

1. Linear sequences

nth term = a + (n − 1)d. 5, 8, 11, … → 3n + 2. Check n = 1, 2, 3.

2. Quadratic sequences

Second difference = 2a → an² + bn + c. 3, 8, 15, 24 … has second difference 2 → n² + bn + c; subtract n² → 2, 4, 6, 8 → 2n; so nth term = n² + 2n.

3. Special sequences

Even/odd, triangular (½n(n+1)), squares, cubes, Fibonacci-type (each term = sum of previous two), geometric (×r).

4. Function notation

f(x) = 2x − 5: f(3) = 1. Solve f(x) = 11 → x = 8.

5. Composite functions

fg(x) = f(g(x)) — g first. f(x) = 2x − 5, g(x) = x²: gf(2) = g(1) = 1; fg(3) = f(9) = 13.

6. Inverse functions

Swap x and y, rearrange. f(x) = 2x − 5 ⇒ f⁻¹(x) = (x + 5)/2. Domain of inverse = range of original. Verify: f⁻¹(f(x)) = x.

Exam tips: write the bracket order explicitly in composites; show the "swap and rearrange" line for inverses — answer-only scores little.

Finding the nth term of a linear sequence

For a sequence with a constant difference d, the nth term is dn + (a − d), where a is the first term. Check the rule by substituting n = 1, 2 and 3 before using it. Given a term value, set the nth term equal to it and solve for n to test whether it belongs to the sequence.

Functions as machines

A function takes an input and gives exactly one output. Composite functions are applied right to left: fg(x) means apply g first, then f. The inverse f⁻¹ reverses each step, found by writing y = f(x), swapping x and y, and rearranging for y.

Domain and range

The domain is the set of allowed inputs; the range is the set of outputs produced. Restrictions usually come from division by zero or from taking square roots of negative numbers. State both when asked to describe a function fully.

Worked examples: sequences

Linear. The sequence 5, 9, 13, 17 has a common difference of 4. The nth term is 4n + 1, since the nth term of a linear sequence is dn + (first term − d). Check the 10th term: 4 × 10 + 1 = 41.

Quadratic. For 2, 6, 12, 20, the first differences are 4, 6, 8 and the second difference is 2. The coefficient of n² is half the second difference, so it is 1. Subtract n² from each term: 1, 2, 3, 4, which is linear with nth term n. So the nth term is n² + n. Check n = 3: 9 + 3 = 12 ✓.

Function notation with composites

Let f(x) = 2x + 3 and g(x) = x − 1. Then fg(x) means f(g(x)) = f(x − 1) = 2(x − 1) + 3 = 2x + 1. Note that gf(x) = g(2x + 3) = 2x + 2, which is different. Composition is not commutative, and questions often ask for both to test whether you apply the inner function first.

Inverse functions

To find f⁻¹(x) for f(x) = 2x + 3: write y = 2x + 3, swap to x = 2y + 3 and solve, giving y = (x − 3)/2. So f⁻¹(x) = (x − 3)/2. Check by substituting: f(f⁻¹(x)) = 2(x − 3)/2 + 3 = x ✓. The graph of f⁻¹ is the reflection of f in the line y = x.

Domain and range

For f(x) = √(x − 2), the expression under the root must be non-negative, so the domain is x ≥ 2. The output of a square root is never negative, so the range is f(x) ≥ 0. For a rational function such as 1/(x − 4), the domain excludes x = 4, and the range excludes y = 0, since the value 0 is never reached.

Common errors

  • Taking the nth term of a quadratic sequence from the first term alone; the second difference must be used.
  • Reversing the order of composition: fg(x) and gf(x) are not the same.
  • Writing the domain as x > 2 when the question allows equality, or stating the range with an inequality in the wrong direction.
  • Forgetting to swap x and y before solving for the inverse.

title: A Level Mathematics: Further Algebra
content:
A Level Mathematics: Further Algebra

A2 algebra is about rewriting expressions so that they can be handled: splitting a fraction into partial fractions before integrating it, dividing polynomials to expose factors, and using the remainder and factor theorems to find unknowns. This note builds each technique from zero, with the long division written out term by term, because the algebra is the part candidates rush and lose marks on.

Polynomial division

Dividing a polynomial by a linear factor works like numerical long division: divide the leading term, multiply back, subtract, bring down, repeat until the degree of the remainder is lower than the divisor.

Worked example. Divide 2x³ − 5x² + 4x − 7 by (x − 2).

2x² into x - 2: 2x²(x - 2) = 2x³ - 4x²;  subtract: -x² + 4x - 7
-x into x - 2: -x(x - 2) = -x² + 2x;  subtract: 2x - 7
+2 into x - 2: 2(x - 2) = 2x - 4;  subtract: -3
quotient 2x² - x + 2 with remainder -3
so 2x³ - 5x² + 4x - 7 = (x - 2)(2x² - x + 2) - 3

Worked example 2 (missing terms). Divide x³ + 1 by (x + 1).

write as x³ + 0x² + 0x + 1 to keep the columns aligned
quotient x², subtract x³ + x² → -x² + 1
quotient -x, subtract -x² - x → x + 1
quotient +1, subtract x + 1 → 0
x³ + 1 = (x + 1)(x² - x + 1)

Leaving gaps in the descending powers is the commonest slip; write the zeros in explicitly.

The factor and remainder theorems

remainder theorem: dividing f(x) by (x - a) leaves remainder f(a)
factor theorem: (x - a) is a factor exactly when f(a) = 0
for (ax - b): remainder is f(b/a)

Worked example 1. Find the remainder when f(x) = x³ − 4x + 5 is divided by (x + 2).

f(-2) = -8 + 8 + 5 = 5

Worked example 2 (find a factor). Show that (x − 3) is a factor of x³ − 4x² − 3x + 18.

f(3) = 27 - 36 - 9 + 18 = 0, so (x - 3) is a factor
then divide: x³ - 4x² - 3x + 18 = (x - 3)(x² - x - 6)
                                     = (x - 3)(x - 3)(x + 2)

Worked example 3 (unknown constant). f(x) = 2x³ + ax² − 5x + 6 has (x + 2) as a factor. Find a.

f(-2) = -16 + 4a + 10 + 6 = 0
4a = 0  →  a = 0
check: 2x³ - 5x + 6 divided by (x + 2) gives 2x² - 4x + 3 with no remainder

Partial fractions: distinct linear factors

(px + q)/[(x - a)(x - b)] = A/(x - a) + B/(x - b)

multiply through by the denominator and substitute x = a, x = b
in turn (the cover-up method)

Worked example. Express (5x + 1)/[(x − 1)(x + 2)] in partial fractions.

5x + 1 = A(x + 2) + B(x - 1)
x = 1: 6 = 3A  →  A = 2
x = -2: -9 = -3B  →  B = 3
(5x + 1)/[(x - 1)(x + 2)] = 2/(x - 1) + 3/(x + 2)

Worked example 2 (three factors). Express 2/[(x)(x + 1)(x − 2)] in partial fractions.

2 = A(x + 1)(x - 2) + Bx(x - 2) + Cx(x + 1)
x = 0: 2 = -2A  →  A = -1
x = -1: 2 = 3B  →  B = 2/3
x = 2: 2 = 6C  →  C = 1/3
so 2/[...] = -1/x + (2/3)/(x + 1) + (1/3)/(x - 2)

Partial fractions: repeated and improper cases

repeated factor: (px + q)/[(x - a)²] = A/(x - a) + B/(x - a)²
improper (degree of numerator >= degree of denominator): divide first

Worked example 1 (repeated). Express (3x + 5)/(x − 1)² in partial fractions.

3x + 5 = A(x - 1) + B
x = 1: 8 = B
compare coefficients of x: 3 = A
so 3/(x - 1) + 8/(x - 1)²

Worked example 2 (improper). Express (x² + 3x + 2)/(x − 1) in partial fractions.

divide first: (x² + 3x + 2)/(x - 1) = x + 4 + 6/(x - 1)
check by multiplying back: (x + 4)(x - 1) + 6 = x² + 3x + 2

The division step must come first: writing A + B/(x − 1) for an improper fraction gives the wrong form and cannot be solved consistently.

Inequalities and modulus

|x - a| < b  means  a - b < x < a + b
|x - a| > b  means  x < a - b or x > a + b

rational inequalities: move everything to one side, combine over a
common denominator, then use a sign diagram

Worked example. Solve |2x − 3| < 7.

-7 < 2x - 3 < 7
-4 < 2x < 10
-2 < x < 5

Worked example 2 (rational). Solve (x + 1)/(x − 3) > 2.

(x + 1)/(x - 3) - 2 > 0
(x + 1 - 2x + 6)/(x - 3) > 0
(7 - x)/(x - 3) > 0
critical values x = 3 (undefined) and x = 7
sign test: x = 4 gives 3/1 > 0 true; x = 8 gives -1/5 < 0 false
so 3 < x < 7

Never multiply a rational inequality by the denominator without knowing its sign: multiplying by a negative reverses the inequality, which is why the sign-diagram method is used instead.

Solving cubic equations completely

Once one factor is found by the factor theorem, polynomial division reduces the cubic to a quadratic, and the quadratic gives the remaining roots. The routine never varies:

  1. Try small integer values (±1, ±2, ±3) in f(x) until one gives zero.
  2. Divide by the corresponding linear factor.
  3. Factorise or use the quadratic formula on the quotient.
  4. State every root, including repeats.

Worked example. Solve x³ − 2x² − 5x + 6 = 0.

f(1) = 1 - 2 - 5 + 6 = 0, so (x - 1) is a factor
divide: x³ - 2x² - 5x + 6 = (x - 1)(x² - x - 6)
                            = (x - 1)(x - 3)(x + 2)
roots: x = 1, 3, -2

Worked example 2 (repeated root). Solve x³ − 3x + 2 = 0.

f(1) = 0  →  (x - 1) is a factor
divide: (x - 1)(x² + x - 2) = (x - 1)(x + 2)(x - 1)
roots: x = 1 (repeated) and x = -2; the curve touches the axis at x = 1

A repeated root is a tangency, which is why a cubic can have two distinct roots but three real ones counted with multiplicity.

Partial fractions with an irreducible quadratic

for a factor (x² + px + q) with no real roots:
(ax + b)/[(x - c)(x² + px + q)] = A/(x - c) + (Bx + C)/(x² + px + q)

Worked example. Express (3x + 1)/[x(x² + 1)] in partial fractions.

3x + 1 = A(x² + 1) + (Bx + C)x
x = 0: 1 = A
compare x²: 0 = A + B  →  B = -1
compare x: 3 = C
so 1/x + (-x + 3)/(x² + 1)

The numerator over a quadratic factor must be linear (Bx + C); a constant alone cannot satisfy the coefficients in general.

One linear and one quadratic equation

Simultaneous equations where one is a circle or parabola are solved by substitution, producing a quadratic whose roots give the intersection points.

Worked example. Solve y = x + 1 and x² + y² = 25.

substitute: x² + (x + 1)² = 25
2x² + 2x + 1 = 25  →  x² + x - 12 = 0
(x + 4)(x - 3) = 0  →  x = -4 or 3
points: (-4, -3) and (3, 4)

A line and a curve meet in 0, 1 or 2 points; the discriminant of the substituted quadratic tells you which, without solving — a standard link to the next section.

Surds and rationalising

rationalise 1/(a + sqrt b) by multiplying by (a - sqrt b)/(a - sqrt b)
denominator becomes a² - b, which is rational

Worked example. Simplify 3/(2 + √5).

multiply by (2 - sqrt 5)/(2 - sqrt 5):
3(2 - sqrt 5)/(4 - 5) = 3(2 - sqrt 5)/(-1) = 3 sqrt 5 - 6

Worked example 2. Solve x² − 6x + 2 = 0, giving answers in surd form.

x = [6 +/- √(36 - 8)]/2 = (6 +/- sqrt 28)/2 = 3 +/- sqrt 7

Surd answers should be simplified (√28 = 2√7) and, where the question asks, rationalised.

Algebraic fractions and cancelling

Simplifying an algebraic fraction requires factorising both parts first; cancelling terms before factorising is invalid because a sum is not a product.

Worked example. Simplify (x² − 9)/(x² + x − 6).

factorise: (x - 3)(x + 3)/[(x + 3)(x - 2)]
cancel (x + 3): (x - 3)/(x - 2), valid for x not 3 or -2

Worked example 2 (addition). Write 1/(x − 1) + 2/(x + 2) as a single fraction.

common denominator: [(x + 2) + 2(x - 1)]/[(x - 1)(x + 2)]
= (3x)/[(x - 1)(x + 2)]

The excluded values belong in the answer: a cancelled factor leaves a hole in the domain, which the equation's original form still cannot accept.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Remainder) Find the remainder when x³ + 2x − 4 is divided by (x − 1). Answer: 1 + 2 − 4 = −1.
  2. (Factor) Is (x + 3) a factor of x³ + 2x² − 5x + 6? Answer: f(−3) = −27 + 18 + 15 + 6 = 12 ≠ 0, no.
  3. (Unknown) f(x) = x³ + kx − 6 has (x − 2) as a factor. Find k. Answer: 8 + 2k − 6 = 0 → k = −1.
  4. (Partial fractions) Express 7/[(x − 1)(x + 6)]. Answer: 1/(x − 1) − 1/(x + 6).
  5. (Repeated) Express (2x + 1)/(x + 1)². Answer: 2/(x + 1) − 1/(x + 1)².
  6. (Improper) Express (x² + 1)/(x + 1). Answer: x − 1 + 2/(x + 1).
  7. (Modulus) Solve |x − 4| ≥ 3. Answer: x ≤ 1 or x ≥ 7.
  8. (Rational) Solve (x − 2)/(x + 1) < 1. Answer: (x − 2 − x − 1)/(x + 1) < 0 → −3/(x + 1) < 0 → x > −1.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Partial fractions for an improper fraction: divide first; the polynomial part is part of the answer.
  • Repeated factors written once: (x − a)² needs both A/(x − a) and B/(x − a)².
  • Cover-up used on repeating factors: the cover-up method substitutes only for distinct linear factors; for repeats, compare coefficients as well.
  • Sign of the remainder: f(a) gives the remainder when dividing by (x − a); for (x + a) substitute −a.
  • Missing powers in division: write 0x², 0x placeholders so the columns line up.
  • Multiplying inequalities by a variable: the sign may be negative; use a sign diagram instead.
  • Not excluding undefined values: a denominator's zero is never in the solution set; mark it as excluded.
  • Not checking: multiply the partial fractions back, or substitute one value, to confirm the decomposition.

title: Nuclear Physics — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Nuclear Physics

Physics — A2. Protons + neutrons (nucleons). Nuclide notation: ᴬZX — Z protons, A nucleons. Isotopes share Z, differ in N.

Key areas to revise

  • The Nucleus
  • Radioactive Decay
  • Mass–Energy
  • Fission and Fusion

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Key relationships

  • Mass defect Δm = difference between the mass of the separate nucleons and the mass of the nucleus.
  • Energy released E = Δm c², and binding energy per nucleon is largest near iron-56.
  • Radioactive decay: activity A = λ N, and half-life T½ = ln 2 / λ.
  • Fission splits heavy nuclei and fusion joins light nuclei; both release energy when the product nuclei have higher binding energy per nucleon.

Common errors

Activity is the number of decays per second, measured in becquerels, and it falls as the number of undecayed nuclei falls. Use the mass defect in kilograms with c in m s⁻¹ to get energy in joules.

title: A2 Level Biology: Respiration, Muscles and the Internal Environment
content:
Respiration, Muscles and the Internal Environment — Edexcel International A2 Level Biology

Edexcel International A Level Biology — Unit 5 (WBI15), Topic 7, covering statements 7.1 to 7.22: glycolysis, the link reaction, the Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation, then muscles and the sliding filament, cardiac output and ventilation, negative feedback and thermoregulation, the kidney and osmoregulation, and the transcription factors that control gene expression. Work through the numbered sections, then test yourself on the mistakes and the exam-style questions at the end.

This revision note covers the biology topics that sit behind the energy use of cells and animals and behind the maintenance of the internal environment. It is built around the specification statements rather than around a loose theme, so each numbered section reflects one or more things the specification expects a candidate to be able to do. The note is deliberately at exam depth: it explains the reasoning, gives the worked examples and comparisons that examiners look for, and lists the common mistakes that lose marks in this topic. Use it to check what you actually know and to practise the kinds of answer the specification rewards.

1. Why respiration matters and what the topic is for

Respiration is the set of reactions that release energy from nutrient molecules and couple that energy to the work cells do. The main nutrient in most questions is glucose, and the main energy currency that respiration produces is ATP. The practical point is that cells do not get energy directly from glucose; they get it from ATP, and respiration is the process that links the fuel to the currency. Understanding respiration therefore means understanding where the energy comes from, how the cell captures it, and how that energy is used in muscles and in the rest of the body.

The topic also connects to the internal environment, because muscles and tissues can only work properly if the internal conditions stay within limits, and because the energy demand of the body changes when muscles work. The link between respiration, muscles and the internal environment is that exercise changes the demand for ATP, which changes the demand for oxygen and fuel and the production of waste, and the internal environment has to respond. If you see the topic as one connected question about supply, demand and control, the parts will fit together rather than staying as separate facts.

2. Aerobic respiration as a sequence of stages, not a single reaction

Aerobic respiration is not one enzyme-controlled reaction but a sequence of stages: the stages are glycolysis, the link reaction, the Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation. Glycolysis happens in the cytoplasm and breaks glucose into pyruvate, producing a small amount of ATP and reduced NAD. The link reaction and the Krebs cycle happen in the mitochondrial matrix and produce reduced coenzymes and carbon dioxide. Oxidative phosphorylation happens in the inner mitochondrial membrane and uses the reduced coenzymes to make the bulk of the ATP and to reduce oxygen to water.

The important idea is that respiration is staged: each stage does a specific job and the stages are connected. Glycolysis starts the breakdown of glucose. The link reaction converts pyruvate and removes carbon dioxide. The Krebs cycle oxidises the acetyl group and harvests hydrogen. Oxidative phosphorylation harvests the energy from the hydrogen and passes it to ATP. A good answer says that respiration is staged, gives the four stages in order, and says where each occurs. It does not say that respiration is a single reaction that turns glucose into ATP in one step, because that is not what happens and it loses marks.

A good answer also says that oxygen is the final electron acceptor in oxidative phosphorylation and that this is why the process is aerobic: without oxygen the chain stops and ATP production from oxidative phosphorylation stops. The link between oxygen and ATP is one of the reasons aerobic respiration yields more ATP than anaerobic alternatives, because the full oxidation is completed and the hydrogen carriers can be re-oxidised at the end of the chain. If you can say that, you have the aerobic idea in a form that scores marks.

3. Glycolysis: the investment and payoff phases and the net yield

Glycolysis is the first stage of respiration and it happens in the cytoplasm. It phosphorylates glucose, splits the phosphorylated intermediate, and then oxidises triose phosphate, producing pyruvate, a small net yield of ATP and reduced NAD. The investment phase uses ATP to phosphorylate glucose and its intermediates; the payoff phase produces the ATP and reduced NAD that make glycolysis worth doing.

The classic net yield for the overall equation taught in this specification is often stated as producing a small amount of ATP per glucose, with the rest coming later from the Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation. The important point is not to memorise only the number but to understand that glycolysis produces pyruvate, ATP and reduced NAD, and that the ATP comes from substrate-level phosphorylation, while the reduced NAD is a carrier of hydrogen that will feed into oxidative phosphorylation if oxygen is available. A good answer says that glycolysis phosphorylates glucose, splits it, oxidises triose phosphate, produces pyruvate and a small amount of ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation and produces reduced NAD. It does not say that glycolysis makes the most ATP, because it does not; that comes later.

The intermediate phosphorylation is the reason glycolysis is not just a simple split. Glucose has to be primed with phosphate so that it can be split and so that the triose phosphate can be oxidised. The ATP investment at the start pays off later, which is why the net yield is what it is. If you can say that, you have the logic of glycolysis rather than just a list of steps.

4. The link reaction and the Krebs cycle: decarboxylation and hydrogen harvesting

The link reaction converts pyruvate into acetyl coenzyme A, releasing carbon dioxide and reducing NAD. The Krebs cycle then oxidises the acetyl group, releasing more carbon dioxide, producing ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation and generating reduced NAD and reduced FAD. The carbon dioxide released in these stages is the CO2 that the cell, and the organism, must dispose of, and the hydrogen carried by the reduced coenzymes is what feeds oxidative phosphorylation.

The link reaction is the bridge between glycolysis and the Krebs cycle. Pyruvate enters the mitochondrion, is oxidised and decarboxylated to form the acetyl group, which is attached to coenzyme A. The Krebs cycle then uses the acetyl group to regenerate oxaloacetate and to produce the reduced coenzymes and substrate-level phosphorylation that are the point of the cycle. A good answer says that the link reaction converts pyruvate to acetyl coenzyme A with release of CO2 and reduced NAD, and that the Krebs cycle oxidises the acetyl group with release of CO2, production of ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation and production of reduced NAD and reduced FAD. It does not say that the Krebs cycle happens in the cytosol, because it happens in the mitochondrial matrix. It also does not say that the Krebs cycle is the stage that uses oxygen, because oxygen is used in oxidative phosphorylation, not in the cycle itself.

The main conceptual point of the Krebs cycle is that it is a cycle that oxidises a two-carbon acetyl group and harvests hydrogen, releasing carbon dioxide along the way. The ATP made by substrate-level phosphorylation in the cycle is small compared with the ATP from oxidative phosphorylation, but the cycle’s real job is to supply the reduced coenzymes. If you can say that, you have the role of the Krebs cycle rather than just a sequence of intermediates.

5. Oxidative phosphorylation and the role of the inner membrane and oxygen

Oxidative phosphorylation is the stage that makes the most ATP and the stage where oxygen is used. It happens on the inner mitochondrial membrane, where the reduced coenzymes deliver hydrogen and the energy from the electrons is used to pump protons, creating a proton gradient that drives ATP synthesis as protons flow back through ATP synthase. Oxygen is the final electron acceptor at the end of the chain, and water is formed.

The key point is that ATP is made by chemiosmosis, not by a single enzyme directly handing a phosphate to ADP. Energy from the electron transport chain is used to pump protons from the matrix to the intermembrane space, and the resulting proton gradient is what drives ATP synthesis when protons flow back through ATP synthase. Oxygen accepts the electrons at the end of the chain and combines with protons to form water, so without oxygen the chain stops and the gradient cannot be maintained. A good answer says that oxidative phosphorylation happens on the inner mitochondrial membrane, that the energy from the electrons pumps protons, that the proton gradient drives ATP synthesis through ATP synthase, and that oxygen is the final electron acceptor forming water. It does not say that ATP is made directly by the electron transport chain itself; it is made by ATP synthase using the proton gradient.

The distinction between the electron transport chain and ATP synthase is important because it is one of the places where a lack of precision loses marks. The chain creates the gradient; ATP synthase uses it. If you keep that distinction clear, you can explain why a poison that blocks the chain, or a lack of oxygen, stops ATP production. The model is also the reason that the inner membrane is folded into cristae: it increases the surface area for the proteins of the chain and for ATP synthase. If you can say that, you have connected the structure to the function.

6. ATP as the energy currency and why respiration is staged

ATP is the immediate energy currency that respiration supplies to the cell. The energy for most cellular processes does not come directly from glucose or food; it comes from the hydrolysis of ATP. Respiration exists so that the energy in food can be used to regenerate ATP, and then the ATP can be used for endergonic processes, active transport, movement and biosynthesis. The role of ATP is to act as a small, reusable and immediately available packet of energy that can be used where and when it is needed.

The reason respiration is staged rather than a single big burn is that staged release is more controllable and more efficient in the biological sense. The energy is not released all at once as heat, but in a way that the cell can use to phosphorylate ADP; the carrier molecules handle the hydrogen and the energy between stages; and the stages can be regulated according to the cell’s needs. A good answer says that respiration is staged so that the energy is released in manageable amounts that the cell can use to make ATP, and that ATP is the energy currency used by the cell. It does not say that the stages are only for historical reasons or that the cell could simply burn glucose in one step for the same practical result, because the control and capture are the point.

The link between ATP and work is that ATP hydrolysis is endergonic to reverse but exergonic in the cell’s direction, so it provides energy for processes that would not otherwise occur. The cell uses ATP to drive active transport, to drive movement including muscle contraction, and to drive biosynthesis, and respiration is what keeps the ATP supply up. If you can say that, you have the currency idea in a form that scores marks.

7. Contraction as sliding filaments, not shortening of the filaments themselves

Muscle contraction works by the sliding filament model, not by the filaments shortening. The actin and myosin filaments slide past one another, so the sarcomere shortens even though the filaments themselves do not get shorter. The thick filaments are myosin, the thin filaments are actin, and the contraction happens when myosin heads bind to actin, pivot, release and re-bind further along, pulling the thin filament past the thick one.

The important point is that contraction is sliding, and that the length of the filaments does not change. A good answer says that during contraction the filaments slide past each other so the sarcomere shortens, that the filaments themselves do not shorten, and that myosin heads bind to actin and pivot to pull the thin filament past the thick one. It does not say that the filaments shorten; it says that they slide. That is one of the most common mistakes in this topic, because it is easy to think that contraction means the filaments get shorter when it actually means they get closer together and the overlap increases.

The energy for the sliding is provided by ATP. ATP is used both to power the power stroke and to detach the myosin head so the cycle can repeat. The calcium ions that are released into the sarcoplasm when the muscle is stimulated allow the myosin head to bind to actin in the first place. The full story is therefore ATP plus calcium plus the filament arrangement, but the most important exam point is the sliding filament idea itself. If you can say that, you have the contraction idea in a form that scores marks.

8. The role of ATP and calcium in the contraction cycle

The contraction cycle uses ATP and calcium. Calcium is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum when the muscle is stimulated, and the calcium allows the myosin head to bind to actin by exposing the binding sites. ATP then is used to break the myosin-actin link and re-cock the myosin head, and another ATP is hydrolysed to position the head for the next stroke. When calcium is removed and the binding sites are covered again, the muscle relaxes.

A good answer says that calcium exposes the actin binding sites so myosin can bind, that ATP is used to break the cross-bridge and re-cock the head, and that the cycle is powered by ATP hydrolysis. It also says that relaxation happens when calcium is removed and the binding sites are covered. It does not say that relaxation uses no ATP, because it does not; the detachment and repositioning of myosin need ATP, and that is one reason rigor mortis happens, because ATP is no longer available and the myosin stays bound. If you can say that, you have the energy story of contraction in a form that scores marks.

The calcium role is essential, not optional. Without calcium, the myosin heads cannot bind to actin and the muscle cannot contract, even if ATP is present. ATP alone is not enough; you need calcium to start the cycle and ATP to keep it going. If you can keep that distinction clear, you can answer the question correctly and avoid the common mistake of saying that ATP alone is what starts contraction.

9. ATP supply during exercise and the limits of aerobic capacity

During exercise the demand for ATP rises, and the rate of respiration must rise to match it. Aerobic respiration can supply ATP for sustained moderate exercise, but when the rate of demand exceeds the rate at which oxygen can be supplied, the muscle shifts toward anaerobic pathways and the balance of products changes. The point is that exercise is a test of the energy supply system and of the system that supports it, including breathing and circulation.

Aerobic respiration is efficient and sustainable, but it depends on oxygen delivery. If oxygen delivery cannot keep up, the cell relies more on pathways that do not need as much oxygen, and this changes the products. A good answer says that aerobic respiration supplies ATP efficiently but needs oxygen, that during strenuous exercise the demand may outstrip oxygen supply, and that this forces a shift in the balance of ATP production. It does not say that the muscle simply switches off aerobic respiration and does nothing else; it says that the balance shifts. The energy story is continuous, not a simple on-off switch.

The practical point is that sustained exercise depends on the ability to deliver oxygen and remove waste, which is why breathing and heart rate rise. The biology here ties respiration, muscle and the internal environment together, because the muscle cannot work unless the supply system keeps up and the internal conditions stay tolerable. If you can see that, you can answer the questions that link the parts, which are often where the higher marks are.

10. The response to exercise: heart rate, breathing rate and breathing volume

During exercise, heart rate, breathing rate and the volume of air breathed per breath all increase. The heart pumps faster and harder to deliver more oxygenated blood to the muscles and to remove more carbon dioxide and heat. Breathing increases in frequency and depth to bring in more oxygen and to remove more carbon dioxide. The point is that the body responds to the higher demand on several fronts at once.

The increase in breathing is not just faster breathing; it is also deeper breathing, so the volume of air exchanged per minute rises more than the rate alone would suggest. The increase in heart rate rises the rate of blood delivery, and a stronger heartbeat can also increase the stroke volume, so the cardiac output rises. A good answer says that during exercise breathing rate and depth increase, that heart rate increases, and that these changes raise the supply of oxygen and the removal of carbon dioxide and heat. It does not say that only breathing rate changes, because depth matters too. It does not say that the heart only beats faster, because the strength of the beat can change as well.

A common mistake is to describe the response to exercise only in terms of breathing, or only in terms of heart rate, when the question asks for both. A good answer gives both and links them, because they are part of the same supply system. The internal environment is what both systems are serving: without the increased supply, the muscles cannot work and the internal conditions would drift out of limits. If you can say that, you have the response in a form that scores marks.

11. Thermoregulation, vasodilation and vasoconstriction, and the control of heat loss

Thermoregulation is the control of body temperature, which is part of homeostasis. The body controls heat loss and heat production to keep temperature within limits. When the body needs to lose heat, blood vessels near the skin surface dilate, allowing more blood flow near the surface so heat is lost to the environment; this is vasodilation. When the body needs to conserve heat, those vessels constrict, reducing blood flow near the surface and reducing heat loss; this is vasoconstriction.

A good answer says that vasodilation increases blood flow near the skin surface and increases heat loss, and that vasoconstriction reduces blood flow near the surface and reduces heat loss. It does not say that vasodilation happens only when it is hot and vasoconstriction only when it is cold, as absolute rules, though that is the typical pattern, because the system is about control, not just a fixed setting. The deeper point is that the skin blood flow is one of the ways the body moves heat around and loses it, and that the control is part of homeostasis.

Other responses to overheating may include sweating, which cools by evaporation, and behavioural changes. Responses to cold include shivering and reducing heat loss by vasoconstriction. The important idea is that the body has both heat-loss and heat-production responses, and that homeothermy is maintained by balancing them. A good answer says that the body controls temperature by adjusting heat loss and heat production, names vasodilation and vasoconstriction as examples of changing heat loss, and mentions that the responses are part of homeostasis. If you can say that, you have the thermoregulation idea in a form that scores marks.

12. The concept of the internal environment and why homeostasis matters

The internal environment is the fluid environment around the cells, and homeostasis is the maintenance of a stable internal environment despite changes outside and inside. The idea is important because cells can only work properly within a limited range of conditions, so the internal environment has to be kept within those limits: water balance, temperature, pH and the concentrations of substances have to be controlled, and respiration and exercise put demands on all of them.

Homeostasis is not a single process but a collection of control systems. Negative feedback is the main control principle, in which a change from the set point is detected and the system acts to bring it back. A good answer says that homeostasis is the maintenance of a stable internal environment, that cells can only function within narrow limits, and that negative feedback is the main control mechanism. It does not say that the internal environment never changes, because it does change; it says that it is kept within limits. That is the difference between a mark-scoring answer and one that treats homeostasis as meaning no change at all.

The link to respiration and muscles is that exercise stresses the internal environment: it produces heat, carbon dioxide and water, changes pH in the tissues and the blood, and demands more fuel and oxygen. Homeostasis has to cope with all of that, and that is why the topic brings together respiration, muscles and internal environment control. If you can say that, you have the unifying idea that makes the topic more than three separate lists.

13. Negative feedback and the way control systems work

Negative feedback is the main control principle in homeostasis. A change away from the set point is detected by a receptor, the information is passed to a control centre, and effectors act to reduce the change and bring the variable back toward the set point. The effect opposes the change, which is why it is called negative feedback. This is the principle behind temperature control, blood glucose control and the control of many other variables.

A good answer describes the components of a negative feedback system: receptor, coordination or control centre and effector, and says that the response reduces the original change. It does not describe positive feedback as the main homeostatic mechanism, because positive feedback amplifies the change and is used in a small number of cases such as childbirth, not as the general principle. The general principle is negative feedback, and the exam questions on this topic usually test that principle. If you can say that, you have the control idea in a form that scores marks.

The point of negative feedback is that it reduces the error from the set point. It does not have to eliminate the change entirely; real systems have a normal range. A good answer therefore does not say that homeostasis keeps every variable exactly constant at all times; it says that it keeps the variable within a normal range by opposing deviations. If you can say that, you have the principle and its limitations both correct.

14. Water and solute balance, and why the internal environment has to manage them

The internal environment has to manage water and solute balance because cells depend on the water potential of their surroundings. If the internal environment is too concentrated, water leaves cells by osmosis; if it is too dilute, water enters cells. Either can disrupt cell function. The control of water and solute balance is therefore part of homeostasis, and it connects to respiration and muscles because the body gains and loses water through breathing, sweating and urine, and because the balance matters for the tissues that are doing the work.

A good answer says that water and solute balance are part of homeostasis, that cells depend on the water potential of the internal environment, and that changes in water potential can move water by osmosis and affect cell function. It does not say that water balance is only about drinking, because the body also loses water in breathing, sweating and urine, and gains it in food and drink. The point is that the balance is dynamic and has to be controlled. If you can say that, you have the water-balance idea in a form that scores marks.

The link to respiration is that breathing loses water vapour, so respiration and breathing are part of the water balance as well as part of the gas exchange. The link to exercise is that sweating loses both water and heat, so the same response that cools can also disturb water balance. If you can see those links, you can answer questions that cross the parts, which are common at this level.

15. The role of the kidneys in the internal environment, briefly and at the right level
