The kidneys are central to the internal environment because they control the composition of the urine and so the balance of water, ions and waste products in the blood. They remove waste from the blood and adjust the water and solute content of the body. In this topic the kidneys matter because they are one of the systems that keeps the internal environment within limits, and because the products of respiration have to be dealt with by the body as a whole.

A good answer describes the kidneys as organs that remove waste from the blood and help control water and solute balance, and links them to homeostasis and to the disposal of waste from respiration. It does not overreach by describing every nephron detail if the question does not ask for it; the key point is the role in the internal environment. The kidneys are part of the disposal and balance system that allows respiration and exercise to happen without wrecking the internal conditions. If you can say that, you have the right level.

The important idea is that the body is an integrated system: respiration makes ATP and produces waste, muscles use ATP and produce heat and waste, and the internal environment systems, including the kidneys, breathing and thermoregulation, keep the whole thing within limits. If you can see the integration, you can answer the questions that ask for the links, which are often the best-marked ones.

16. CPIR and the iodide concentration problem; the direction of control

The basics of thermoregulation include the idea that blood vessel diameter in the skin changes to control heat loss, and that the control is part of homeostasis. The anatomy point that is often tested is which vessels are involved and how they control the flow near the surface. In the skin, arteriole vasodilation and vasoconstriction change the flow to superficial vessels, and the presence of a rich superficial vessel bed lets the skin lose more heat when it is hot and conserve more when it is cold.

A good answer says that vasodilation near the skin surface increases heat loss and vasoconstriction near the skin surface reduces it, and that this is part of the way the body controls temperature. It does not say that the skin is the only place where this happens, or that the control is the only thermoregulatory response, because sweating, shivering and behaviour also matter. The point is to include the skin response correctly as part of the system, not to pretend it is the whole system. If you can say that, you have the idea in a form that scores marks.

The direction of control matters: more flow near the surface when hot, less when cold. A common mistake is to invert the relationship, so the answer says vasodilation happens in the cold, which is wrong. If you keep the direction straight, you can avoid that mistake. The reason the direction matters is that the surface vessels are the main route for losing heat to the environment, so opening them loses heat and closing them conserves it. If you can say that, you have both the direction and the reason.

17. Heat gain, heat loss, and the difference between conserving and producing heat

The body has two broad ways of dealing with cold: conserve the heat it has and make more heat. Vasoconstriction conserves heat by reducing loss from the skin surface. Shivering produces heat by making muscles contract repeatedly, which costs ATP and releases heat. Behavioural changes such as curling up, putting on clothing or moving to a warmer place also help. A good answer says that the body can conserve heat by vasoconstriction and produce heat by shivering and by other means, and that both are part of thermoregulation and homeostasis.

The distinction between conserving and producing heat is useful, because it helps explain why the responses are not all the same kind of thing. Vasoconstriction reduces loss; shivering increases production. A good answer makes that distinction, because it shows that the body has more than one tool for the job and that the tools work differently. If you can say that, you have a better answer than one that just lists “shivering, vasoconstriction” without saying what each does.

The energy angle is important too, because shivering uses ATP and therefore links back to respiration. Shivering keeps you warm by burning fuel, so it is not free; it increases the demand for ATP and therefore for oxygen and fuel. That is the kind of connection that examiners like, because it ties the topic together. If you can say that shivering increases respiratory demand, you have the link between thermoregulation and respiration.

18. The internal environment under exercise stress: what is pushed and what copes

Exercise pushes several variables at once, which is why the topic groups respiration, muscles and the internal environment. Muscles use ATP faster, so respiration must deliver more ATP, which raises the demand for oxygen and fuel and increases the production of carbon dioxide and heat. The heart and lungs respond to meet the oxygen demand and to remove the carbon dioxide. Thermoregulation responds to the heat. Water and solute balance are affected by sweating and by the increased rate of exchange. The overall point is that exercise is a stress test for homeostasis.

A good answer says that exercise raises ATP demand, that respiration and the supply systems respond, that more carbon dioxide and heat are produced, and that the internal environment systems, including breathing, circulation and thermoregulation, have to cope with the change. It does not just list the responses; it says that the internal environment has to keep working despite the stress. That is the unifying idea, and it is why the topic is taught as a unit rather than as three unrelated parts. If you can say that, you have the big picture in a form that scores marks.

A common mistake is to describe the responses as if they were isolated, with no mention of what they are responding to. A good answer links the response to the demand: the heart rate rises because the muscles need more oxygen; the breathing rises because the body needs to supply oxygen and remove carbon dioxide; the cooling responses rise because exercise generates heat. If you can make those links, you are answering at the higher level. The detail is only as good as the reasoning behind it.

19. How to read a respiration question and what examiners want

When a question asks about respiration, the examiner usually wants the pathway and the logic behind it, not just the final number. Say what the stages are, where they are, what they produce and why the process is staged and aerobic. If the question asks about the role of oxygen, say that oxygen is the final electron acceptor and that this is what allows oxidative phosphorylation to continue. If the question asks about ATP yield, say that most ATP comes from oxidative phosphorylation and that glycolysis and the Krebs cycle contribute smaller amounts by substrate-level phosphorylation. If you can do that, you can read the question the way the specification intends.

For muscles, the examiner usually wants the sliding filament idea, the role of ATP and calcium, and the reason the filaments do not shorten. If the question asks about contraction, say that the filaments slide past each other so the sarcomere shortens, that myosin heads bind to actin and pivot, that ATP powers the cycle and is needed for detachment, and that calcium exposes the binding sites. If you can do that, you can answer the muscle questions correctly and avoid the common mistake of saying that the filaments shorten.

For the internal environment, the examiner usually wants homeostasis, negative feedback, the key variables that are controlled, and the way the body responds to exercise or to temperature change. If the question asks about the response to exercise, include both heart rate and breathing rate and volume, and explain what each is doing. If the question asks about thermoregulation, include vasodilation and vasoconstriction and the direction of control. If you can do that, you can answer the internal environment questions at the right level.

20. How the parts connect: respiration powers muscles, muscles stress the internal environment, the internal environment has to cope

The topic is really about a chain: respiration makes ATP, muscles use ATP to do work, and the work changes the internal environment so the control systems have to respond. Respiration supplies ATP from glucose; the ATP is used for muscle contraction and for other cell work; muscle work produces heat and carbon dioxide and stresses the water and solute balance; the body responds by increasing supply and by controlling the internal conditions. The chain is why the topic is grouped together: the parts belong to the same system, even though they are listed under different headings.

A good answer can trace the chain: glucose to respiration to ATP to muscle contraction, muscle contraction to heat and CO2 production, heat to thermoregulation and CO2 to breathing and circulation. It can say that the internal environment system has to keep the body within limits while the muscles demand more and the metabolism produces more waste. It does not treat respiration, muscles and internal environment as three unrelated topics; it treats them as parts of one metabolic and homeostatic picture. That is what the topic is for, and it is what the better questions are testing. If you can see the chain, you can answer the questions that span the parts, which are often where the higher marks are.

21. How to use this note and what to revise next

Use this note by working through each section and checking that you can describe the stages of aerobic respiration and where they occur; explain the reason respiration is staged and aerobic; describe glycolysis, the link reaction and the Krebs cycle; describe oxidative phosphorylation and the role of the inner membrane and oxygen; explain the role of ATP as the energy currency; describe the sliding filament model of contraction and say that the filaments do not shorten; describe the role of ATP and calcium in the contraction cycle; explain ATP supply during exercise and the limits of aerobic capacity; describe the response to exercise in breathing rate, breathing depth and heart rate; describe thermoregulation including vasodilation, vasoconstriction, shivering and other heat-loss and heat-production responses; explain homeostasis and negative feedback; and explain water and solute balance and the role of the kidneys in the internal environment. After this topic, revise the related systems, because the associations matter and the best questions ask for the links.

The note is long because the topic is broad and the specification asks for the biology behind the everyday events of exercise, temperature control and energy supply. A revision note has to cover the respiration pathway, the contraction mechanism, the exercise responses and the homeostasis principles in enough detail to be useful, and it has to link them, because the exam questions do. Study it section by section, check yourself against the specification statements, and practise the kinds of answer that explain rather than list. Then move on to the next topic and the related practicals, because the practicals are the way the specification ties the ideas to hands-on work.

Respirometry: measuring oxygen uptake directly

Gas exchange during respiration can be followed with a respirometer, the practical that links the pathways of respiration to a measurable rate. A conical tube holds germinating seeds (actively respiring), and a small inner tube holds soda lime or potassium hydroxide pellets, which absorb the carbon dioxide the seeds produce. Because carbon dioxide is removed, any change in gas volume inside the sealed apparatus is due to oxygen being used up: as oxygen is consumed, the gas pressure falls and the coloured drop of manometer fluid moves along the capillary towards the tube. The distance moved per unit time, converted to a volume through the bore of the capillary, measures the rate of oxygen uptake. A parallel tube with the same mass of dead (boiled) seeds corrects the reading for changes in atmospheric pressure and temperature, which move the drop without any respiration at all. The whole apparatus sits in a water bath, because even one degree of temperature change alters both respiration rate and gas volume enough to swamp the effect being measured. Variables: independent = temperature or seed type or germination stage; dependent = volume of oxygen consumed per gram per hour; controls = mass of seeds, volume of soda lime, capillary bore, time, and the dead-seed control.

Worked example: from manometer reading to oxygen uptake

Germinating peas with a mass of 1.00 g move the drop 3.0 cm in 30 minutes at 25 degrees Celsius; the dead-seed control moves 0.2 cm in the same period. Step 1: correct for the control: 3.0 − 0.2 = 2.8 cm of movement is due to respiration. Step 2: convert the distance to a volume through the capillary bore: the capillary has an internal radius of 0.5 mm (0.05 cm), so its cross-sectional area = π times the radius squared = 3.14 times 0.05 squared = 3.14 times 0.0025 = 0.00785 cm². Volume = area times distance = 0.00785 times 2.8 = 0.0220 cm³ of oxygen in 30 minutes. Step 3: scale to an hourly, per-gram rate: 0.0220 times 2 = 0.0440 cm³ per hour for 1.00 g, so the rate = 0.044 cm³ of oxygen per gram per hour. Step 4: repeat at 15 and 35 degrees Celsius; between 15 and 25 the rate typically doubles with each 10-degree rise (more kinetic energy, so more frequent successful collisions of enzyme and substrate), then falls away at higher temperatures as the enzymes of the respiratory pathway denature. Step 5: evaluate the method: the apparatus is assumed gas-tight (grease the joints), the drop is assumed to move only because of oxygen use (hence the control), and germinating seeds are compared with equal masses so that the rate can be quoted per gram.

Designing a multivariable investigation (the Unit 6 style): if you want the effects of both temperature and germination stage, run a two-factor design — for example three temperatures crossed with two seed stages — with equal replicates in every cell of the design, so the two factors can be compared without confounding. Analyse each factor with its own comparison (or a two-way analysis of variance), state the null hypotheses separately, and evaluate with paired limitation-and-improvement points: seeds respire at different rates as they germinate, so define the stage by germination length; carbon dioxide absorption is only complete while the soda lime is fresh, so replace it for every run; evaporation from the seeds adds water vapour to the gas, so include a control for that or use a drying agent in the manometer arm.

Typical mistakes

  • Saying that respiration is one reaction that turns glucose straight into ATP, instead of a sequence of stages.
  • Saying the filaments shorten during contraction, instead of sliding past each other.
  • Saying that ATP alone starts contraction, instead of calcium exposing the binding sites first.
  • Saying the Krebs cycle happens in the cytoplasm, or that it is where oxygen is used.
  • Saying ATP is made directly by the electron transport chain, instead of by ATP synthase using the proton gradient.
  • Forgetting that oxygen is the final electron acceptor in oxidative phosphorylation.
  • Saying that breathing rate alone is the response to exercise, forgetting breathing depth and heart rate.
  • Inverting vasodilation and vasoconstriction, so vasodilation is linked to cold and vasoconstriction to heat.
  • Treating homeostasis as meaning the internal environment never changes, instead of staying within limits by negative feedback.
  • Forgetting that sweating and breathing both affect water balance, not just drinking and urine.
  • Saying positive feedback is the main homeostatic mechanism, when negative feedback is.
  • Saying that glycolysis produces most of the ATP from respiration; it does not.
  • Describing thermoregulation responses without saying whether they conserve or produce heat.
  • Missing the link that exercise stresses the internal environment so the control systems have to cope.

Exam-style questions

  1. Describe aerobic respiration and state the role of oxygen in the process. Answer: Aerobic respiration is a sequence of stages: glycolysis in the cytoplasm, the link reaction and the Krebs cycle in the mitochondrial matrix, and oxidative phosphorylation on the inner mitochondrial membrane. Glycolysis produces pyruvate, ATP and reduced NAD; the link reaction and Krebs cycle produce reduced NAD and reduced FAD and release CO2; oxidative phosphorylation uses the reduced coenzymes to make ATP and oxygen is the final electron acceptor, forming water. Oxygen is needed so the electron transport chain can continue and the bulk of ATP can be made. (6 marks)
  2. Explain why respiration is an energy-releasing process but still needs to be staged rather than happening in one reaction. Answer: Respiration releases energy from glucose but a single reaction releasing all the energy at once would mostly waste it as heat; the stages release energy in manageable amounts that the cell can use to phosphorylate ADP to ATP, the energy currency for cell work. Stage-by-stage release also allows regulation of the rate to match the cell’s needs. (4 marks)
  3. Describe the sliding filament model of muscle contraction and state the role of ATP in it. Answer: During contraction the actin and myosin filaments slide past each other rather than shortening themselves, so the sarcomere shortens. Myosin heads bind to actin, pivot and pull the thin filament toward the centre, then detach and re-cock. ATP is required for the myosin head to detach from actin and be re-cocked for the next cycle, so the contraction is powered by ATP hydrolysis. (5 marks)
  4. Explain the roles of calcium and ATP in the control of muscle contraction and relaxation. Answer: When a muscle is stimulated, calcium is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum and exposes the binding sites on actin so myosin heads can bind; ATP is used to power the cross-bridge cycle and to detach the myosin heads. Relaxation occurs when calcium is removed and the binding sites are covered again; ATP is still required for detachment, which is why a muscle without ATP stays contracted, as in rigor mortis. (5 marks)
  5. Describe the response of the body during exercise in terms of heart rate and breathing rate, and explain why each increases. Answer: During exercise heart rate increases to deliver more oxygenated blood to the muscles and to remove more carbon dioxide and heat, and breathing rate increases along with breathing depth to bring in more oxygen and remove more carbon dioxide. Both responses increase because the muscles’ ATP demand rises and the supply and waste-removal systems must keep up with the increased metabolism. (5 marks)
  6. Describe how the skin blood vessels help control body temperature and state the direction of the response in each case. Answer: Blood vessels near the skin surface dilate in heat, increasing blood flow near the surface and increasing heat loss to the environment; they constrict in cold, reducing blood flow near the surface and reducing heat loss. This is part of thermoregulation and homeostasis, along with other responses such as sweating or shivering and behavioural changes. (4 marks)
  7. Define homeostasis and explain the principle of negative feedback with one example. Answer: Homeostasis is the maintenance of a stable internal environment within limits. Negative feedback is the control principle in which a change from the set point is detected and the response reduces the change, returning the variable toward the set point; for example in temperature control, if body temperature rises, effectors such as sweating and vasodilation increase heat loss, reducing the temperature back toward normal. (5 marks)
  8. Explain why water and solute balance are part of homeostasis and what happens if the internal environment becomes too concentrated or too dilute. Answer: Cells depend on the water potential of the internal environment; if it becomes too concentrated, water moves out of cells by osmosis, and if it becomes too dilute, water moves into cells. Either change can disrupt cell function, so the concentrations of water and solutes must be controlled. The body loses water in breathing, sweating and urine, so water balance is dynamic and must be regulated. (5 marks)
  9. Explain the link between respiration and muscle activity during exercise and why sustained vigorous exercise can exceed the body’s aerobic capacity for a time. Answer: Muscle activity uses ATP, so respiration must increase to supply ATP; aerobic respiration is efficient and sustainable if oxygen supply is sufficient, but during vigorous exercise oxygen delivery may not keep up with demand, so the muscle relies relatively more on pathways that do not need oxygen and produces different products, which is why breathing and heart rate rise and why the body shifts its metabolism. (5 marks)
  10. State what the kidneys do to help maintain the internal environment. Answer: The kidneys remove waste from the blood and help control water and solute balance by adjusting the composition of the urine, so they are important for maintaining the composition of the internal environment and for disposing of the waste products of metabolism including the CO2-related and other wastes that result from respiration. (4 marks)
  11. Describe one example of negative feedback in the human body and identify the receptor, control centre and effector in that example. Answer: In temperature control, temperature receptors detect a rise in core or skin temperature, the hypothalamus acts as the control centre, and effectors such as sweat glands and skin blood vessels respond by increasing heat loss, returning temperature toward the set point. If temperature falls, effectors such as shivering and vasoconstriction reduce heat loss or increase heat production. (5 marks)

Revise this topic by matching each numbered specification point to one mechanism, one location and one reason. Practise the respiration stages and their products, the sliding filament idea with ATP and calcium, the exercise responses and the thermoregulation responses, and the homeostasis and negative feedback principle with examples. Check that you can say where each process happens and why, not just what happens. Then move on to the next topic and the related practicals, because the practicals are the way the specification ties the ideas to hands-on work.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Respiratory quotient, applied to glucose: RQ = CO₂ released ÷ O₂ consumed. For glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O, so RQ = 6 ÷ 6 = 1.0. Fats give a lower RQ of about 0.7, because they need more oxygen per CO₂ produced. Use the equation to calculate RQ, not a remembered value.
  • ATP yield, applied to glucose: glycolysis gives a net 2 ATP, the link reaction and Krebs cycle give 2 ATP, and reduced coenzymes from all three stages drive oxidative phosphorylation. The total is about 30–32 ATP depending on the shuttle used to bring reduced NAD into the mitochondrion. Quote the stage of each ATP, not just the total.
  • Location of stages: glycolysis takes place in the cytoplasm, the link reaction and Krebs cycle in the matrix, and oxidative phosphorylation on the inner mitochondrial membrane. Oxygen is the final electron acceptor and forms water, so without it the chain stops and ATP production falls.
  • Anaerobic respiration in muscle: without enough oxygen, pyruvate is converted to lactate, which regenerates NAD so glycolysis continues. The oxygen debt is the extra oxygen needed afterwards to convert the lactate back to glucose and to restore ATP and phosphocreatine. Name the reason, not just the product.

Respiratory quotient: what the CO₂ to O₂ ratio tells you about the fuel

Different respiratory fuels need different amounts of oxygen for the same amount of carbon dioxide released. Measuring both gases in a respirometer gives a ratio that identifies the fuel being used, or the mixture of fuels, in the tissue. This ratio is the respiratory quotient, and it is used both in examinations and in physiology.

Key: RQ = volume of carbon dioxide produced ÷ volume of oxygen consumed; the slope of the line on the graph is the RQ.

Why carbohydrate gives an RQ of 1.0

For glucose the overall equation is C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O. Six molecules of oxygen are used and six of carbon dioxide are released, so the ratio is 1.0. The carbon and oxygen in the fuel are already close to the proportions in carbon dioxide, so little extra oxygen is needed.

Why fat gives an RQ near 0.7

Fats have fewer oxygen atoms per carbon than carbohydrate, so more oxygen is needed to oxidise them completely. The same amount of oxygen therefore releases less carbon dioxide, and the RQ falls to about 0.7. A mixture of fat and carbohydrate gives a value between these, and protein gives a value near 0.9.

Using RQ in a question

Calculate the RQ from the two volumes, then compare the value with the table of fuels. Show the division, state the value to two decimal places, and say which fuel or mixture it indicates. Remember that an RQ above 1.0 can occur when yeast ferments sugar anaerobically, releasing carbon dioxide without using oxygen, so the value then does not identify a fuel.

Equations and symbols

Two pieces of arithmetic sit inside this otherwise descriptive topic: the respirometer calculation that turns a moving drop into an oxygen-uptake rate, and the respiratory quotient that identifies which substrate is being respired. Both are marked on method and on units.

3.0 − 0.2 = 2.8 cm Key: 3.0 cm = the distance the drop moved with living seeds (cm); 0.2 cm = the distance the dead-seed control moved in the same time (cm); 2.8 cm = the movement due to respiration alone. The control is not optional: it removes the effect of changing atmospheric pressure and temperature, which move the drop with no respiration at all.

cross-sectional area = π times the radius squared = 3.14 times 0.05 squared = 3.14 times 0.0025 = 0.00785 cm² Key: π = 3.14 (no units); 0.05 cm = the capillary's internal radius (0.5 mm); 0.00785 cm² = its cross-sectional area. The radius must be in cm to match the distance in cm — the constant source of a factor-of-ten error.

Volume = area times distance = 0.00785 times 2.8 = 0.0220 cm³ Key: 0.00785 cm² = the capillary cross-section; 2.8 cm = the corrected movement; 0.0220 cm³ = the volume of oxygen taken up in 30 minutes. Length becomes volume only through the bore of the tube.

0.0220 times 2 = 0.0440 cm³ Key: 0.0220 cm³ = oxygen used in 30 minutes; 2 = the factor that converts a half hour into an hour (min⁻¹ to h⁻¹); 0.0440 cm³ = oxygen used per hour. State the scaling explicitly — a rate per hour is what the mark scheme asks for.

rate = 0.044 cm³ of oxygen per gram per hour Key: 0.044 cm³ h⁻¹ = oxygen uptake per hour; the mass of tissue = 1.00 g, so the division is by 1 and the rate is expressed per gram (cm³ g⁻¹ h⁻¹). Dividing by mass is what makes two samples of different size comparable, and it is the unit the question expects.

RQ = CO₂ released ÷ O₂ consumed Key: RQ = the respiratory quotient (no units, because it is a ratio of gas volumes or of moles); CO₂ released and O₂ consumed are measured over the same period (cm³ or mol). A quotient needs the same units above and below — mixing volumes with masses is the mistake this definition exists to prevent.

C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O Key: C₆H₁₂O₆ = glucose; O₂ = oxygen consumed; CO₂ and H₂O = the products. The coefficients are the stoichiometry the quotient is built from: six of each gas in and out.

RQ = 6 ÷ 6 = 1.0 Key: 6 = moles of CO₂ produced per mole of glucose; 6 = moles of O₂ consumed; RQ = 1.0, the value for carbohydrate. Fats give about 0.7 because they need more oxygen per carbon dioxide released — so the number itself identifies the substrate, which is why you calculate it rather than quote it.

title: IGCSE Mathematics: Indices and Standard Form
content:
IGCSE Mathematics: Indices and Standard Form

Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580 (2025–2027), section 1 Number: statement 1.3 Powers and roots, 1.7 Indices I (with Extended fractional indices), 1.8 Standard form, E1.18 Surds, and section 2 statement E2.4 Indices II (algebraic indices). Indices are shorthand for repeated multiplication, and their laws are the shortcuts that make large and small numbers manageable. This note derives each law from what it counts, covers standard form arithmetic in full, and finishes with surds and rationalising — an Extended favourite that separates the top grades.

Powers, roots and the vocabulary

In 5³ the base is 5 and the index (plural: indices) is 3; it means 5 × 5 × 5 = 125. A square root reverses a square: √25 = 5 because 5² = 25. A cube root reverses a cube: ³√64 = 4 because 4³ = 64.

  • √16 = 4, the principal (positive) square root, as printed on a calculator. But the equation x² = 16 has two solutions, x = 4 or x = −4, because (−4)² = 16 as well. The question decides which is wanted: a length is positive; a solution of an equation may be negative.
  • Notation: a² is read a squared, a³ a cubed, and aⁿ a to the power n. a² ≠ 2a — a² = a × a while 2a = a + a.

The index laws

Each law is a statement about counting multiplications, so each can be checked by writing the multiplications out.

Law 1:  a^m x a^n = a^(m+n)
Why: a³ x a² = (a x a x a) x (a x a) = a⁵, and 3 + 2 = 5.
Example: 2³ × 2⁵ = 2⁸ = 256; check: 8 × 32 = 256 ✓

Law 2:  a^m ÷ a^n = a^(m-n)
Why: a⁵ ÷ a² = (a x a x a x a x a)/(a x a) = a x a x a = a³, and 5 - 2 = 3.
Example: 5⁷ ÷ 5⁴ = 5³ = 125

Law 3:  (a^m)^n = a^(m n)
Why: (a²)³ = a² x a² x a² = a⁶, and 2 × 3 = 6.
Example: (2x³)² = 2² x (x³)² = 4x⁶        [the power applies to every factor]

Law 4:  a⁰ = 1  (a not zero)
Why: a³ ÷ a³ = a^(3-3) = a⁰, and any number divided by itself is 1.
Example: 7⁰ = 1

Law 5:  a^(-n) = 1/(a^n)
Why: a^(-2) = a^(0-2) = a⁰ ÷ a² = 1/a².
Example: 5^(-2) = 1/25 = 0.04

Fractional indices (Extended). A fractional index is a root: the denominator of the fraction is the root, the numerator is the power.

a^(1/n) = nth root of a        a^(m/n) = (nth root of a)^m

16^(1/2) = √16 = 4
27^(2/3) = (cube root of 27)² = 3² = 9
Check the second: 27^(2/3) squared three times over should give 27² = 729; 9³ = 729 ✓

Indices in algebra (Extended)

The same laws apply when the base is a letter, and every factor in a bracket carries the power:

Simplify:  (2x³)² x⁴ ÷ x⁵

(2x³)² = 4x⁶        [square the 2 and double the index]
4x⁶ x x⁴ = 4x¹⁰     [Law 1: add indices]
4x¹⁰ ÷ x⁵ = 4x⁵     [Law 2: subtract indices]
Solve:  2^x = 32

Write both sides with base 2:  32 = 2⁵
2^x = 2⁵, so x = 5        [matching bases means matching indices]

When the bases differ, rewrite one as a power of the other: 8 = 2³, so 8^x = 2^(3x). Equations like 3^(x+1) = 27^(x−1) become 3^(x+1) = 3^(3x−3), so x + 1 = 3x − 3, giving x = 2.

LawStatementWorked line
Multiplyingaᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ2³ × 2⁵ = 2⁸ = 256
Dividingaᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ5⁷ ÷ 5⁴ = 5³ = 125
Power of a power(aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ(2x³)² = 4x⁶
Zero indexa⁰ = 1 (a not zero)7⁰ = 1
Negative indexa⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ5⁻² = 1/25
Fractional indexa^(m/n) = (ⁿ√a)ᵐ27^(2/3) = 9

Two edge cases deserve care. The zero index says nothing about 0⁰: 0⁰ is undefined, because the pattern a⁰ = 1 holds for every non-zero base while the pattern 0ⁿ = 0 holds for every positive power, and the two patterns collide at the origin. And a negative index never makes a value negative: 2⁻³ = 1/8 is positive, because the minus sign belongs to the position of the power, not to the number itself. Finally, every root can be written as a power — √x = x^(1/2), ³√x = x^(1/3) — which is how a calculator evaluates them and how algebraic roots are simplified in one notation.

Standard form

Standard form writes a number as a × 10ⁿ where 1 ⩽ a < 10 and n is an integer. It handles very large and very small quantities without long strings of zeros.

Write in standard form:

47 382 = 4.7382 × 10⁴        [the decimal point moves 4 places left]
0.0056 = 5.6 × 10^(-3)        [the decimal point moves 3 places right, so n = -3]

Arithmetic in standard form. Multiply or divide the numbers first, then the powers of ten, and adjust back into standard form if needed:

(3 × 10⁵) x (4 × 10^(-2))
= (3 × 4) x (10⁵ × 10^(-2))     [regrouped]
= 12 × 10³
= 1.2 × 10⁴                     [12 is not between 1 and 10, so adjust]

(6 × 10⁸) ÷ (2 × 10³)
= (6 ÷ 2) × 10^(8-3) = 3 × 10⁵

Addition and subtraction need matching powers first: 3 × 10⁵ + 4 × 10⁴ = 30 × 10⁴ + 4 × 10⁴ = 34 × 10⁴ = 3.4 × 10⁵. Real-world uses: the speed of light is 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, the size of an atom is about 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m, and masses, distances and populations in physics and chemistry questions are always quoted this way. A calculator's ×10ˣ key enters the power directly; the answer should be given in the form the question asks, often to 3 s.f.

Surds (Extended)

A surd is a root that cannot be written exactly as a fraction — √2, √3, 3√5. Exact answers in surds are often required on Paper 2, where a calculator cannot help. The laws:

√a x √b = √(ab)        √a ÷ √b = √(a/b)        (√a)² = a

Simplifying. Take out the largest square factor:

√50 = √(25 × 2) = √25 x √2 = 5√2
√72 = √(36 × 2) = 6√2
√(9/16) = √9 / √16 = 3/4

Adding like surds. Only like surds combine, exactly like algebraic terms:

√18 + √8 = 3√2 + 2√2 = 5√2        [simplify first]
2√3 + √5 cannot be combined: they are unlike surds.

Rationalising the denominator. A fraction with a surd underneath is tidied by multiplying top and bottom by the same surd (or its conjugate):

6/√3 = (6 x √3)/(√3 x √3) = 6√3/3 = 2√3

1/(3 + √2): multiply top and bottom by the conjugate (3 - √2):
= (3 - √2)/[(3 + √2)(3 - √2)]
= (3 - √2)/(9 - 2)          [difference of two squares below]
= (3 - √2)/7

The conjugate works because (a + b)(a − b) = a² − b² removes the square root entirely. Expanding surd brackets uses the same identity: (2 + √3)(2 − √3) = 4 − 3 = 1.

Worked example: a combined index calculation

Simplify (2³ × 2⁵) ÷ 2⁴ and check it two ways.

Method 1 (indices): 2³ × 2⁵ = 2⁸, then 2⁸ ÷ 2⁴ = 2⁴ = 16
Method 2 (arithmetic): 2³ × 2⁵ = 8 × 32 = 256;  256 ÷ 16 = 16
Both routes give 16 ✓

Second example: write (3√2)² − √8 in the form k√2.

(3√2)² = 9 × 2 = 18        [square both the 3 and the √2]
√8 = 2√2
18 - 2√2 is already simple; it cannot be written as k√2 because 18 is rational,
so the answer stays 18 - 2√2.

Standard form in a calculation. A red blood cell is 7 × 10⁻⁶ m across and a vein is 2.4 × 10⁻³ m wide. How many cells fit side by side?

2.4 × 10^(-3) ÷ 7 × 10^(-6)
= (2.4 ÷ 7) × 10^(-3 - (-6))        [divide the numbers, subtract the indices]
= 0.342857 × 10³
= 3.43 × 10² (3 s.f.)  ≈ 343 cells

The index arithmetic is the whole question: subtracting −6 gives +3, and a sense-check on the powers alone (10⁻³ ÷ 10⁻⁶ = 10³) says the answer must be in the hundreds — which catches sign slips before they cost the final mark.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Multiplying the base by the index: 2³ is 8, not 6; (2³)² = 2⁶ = 64, not 2⁵.
  • Forgetting to square the coefficient: (2x³)² = 4x⁶, not 2x⁶.
  • Treating a⁻ⁿ as negative rather than reciprocal: 2⁻³ = 1/8.
  • Writing 0.00047 as 4.7 × 10⁻³; it is 4.7 × 10⁻⁴ — count the places the point moves.
  • Leaving a standard-form answer as 12 × 10³; the front number must be between 1 and 10.
  • Giving √16 = ±4 in a simplification; the square root symbol means the principal root, while x² = 16 has both solutions.
  • Rationalising only the surd and not its conjugate partner: 1/(3 + √2) needs (3 − √2) top and bottom.
  • Combining unlike surds: 2√3 + √5 is final; only matching surd parts can be added.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 2, 3 marks). Simplify (3x²)³ ÷ x⁴.

Answer: (3x²)³ = 27x⁶; 27x⁶ ÷ x⁴ = 27x².

Question 2 (Paper 2, 3 marks). Evaluate 8^(2/3).

Answer: ³√8 = 2, and 2² = 4. So 8^(2/3) = 4.

Question 3 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Write 0.000 42 and 63 000 in standard form, then find their product.

Answer: 4.2 × 10⁻⁴ and 6.3 × 10⁴. Product = (4.2 × 6.3) × 10⁰ = 26.46 = 2.646 × 10¹.

Question 4 (Paper 2, 4 marks). Simplify √48 + 3√12.

Answer: √48 = √(16 × 3) = 4√3; 3√12 = 3 × 2√3 = 6√3; total = 10√3.

Question 5 (Paper 2, 4 marks). Rationalise the denominator of 5/(2 + √3).

Answer: Multiply by the conjugate: 5(2 − √3)/[(2 + √3)(2 − √3)] = 5(2 − √3)/(4 − 3) = 5(2 − √3) = 10 − 5√3.

Question 6 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Solve 9^x = 27.

Answer: Write both as powers of 3: 3^(2x) = 3³, so 2x = 3 and x = 3/2. Check: 9^(3/2) = (√9)³ = 3³ = 27 ✓.

From the numbers themselves, the course turns to comparing and sharing them: ratio, rate and proportion.

title: A Level Mathematics: Numerical Methods
content:
A Level Mathematics: Numerical Methods

Some equations cannot be solved exactly: x = cos x, x³ − x − 1 = 0, e^x = 4x. Numerical methods find the solutions to any required accuracy by iteration and refinement. This note builds the four techniques A2 requires — locating a root by sign change, fixed-point iteration and its convergence, the Newton-Raphson formula with its derivation, and the trapezium rule for integrals that have no elementary antiderivative — together with the failure modes examiners test.

Locating a root: change of sign

if f(a) and f(b) have opposite signs and f is continuous on [a, b],
there is at least one root in (a, b)

Worked example. Show that x³ − x − 1 = 0 has a root between 1 and 2.

f(1) = 1 - 1 - 1 = -1
f(2) = 8 - 2 - 1 = 5
sign change and the cubic is continuous  →  a root in (1, 2)

The two conditions are both required: continuity rules out a jump, and the sign change forces a crossing. The theorem guarantees at least one root, not exactly one — say "at least" in the answer.

Worked example 2 (narrowing). Show the root lies between 1.3 and 1.4.

f(1.3) = 2.197 - 1.3 - 1 = -0.103
f(1.4) = 2.744 - 1.4 - 1 = 0.344
so the root lies in (1.3, 1.4)

Fixed-point iteration

rearrange f(x) = 0 into x = g(x), then iterate x_(n+1) = g(x_n)

the iteration converges when |g'(x)| < 1 near the root

Worked example. Use x_(n+1) = (x_n + 1)^(1/3) with x₁ = 1.3 to find the root of x³ − x − 1 = 0 to 4 d.p.

x2 = (2.3)^(1/3) = 1.3200 × 3 = (2.32)^(1/3) = 1.3238 × 4 = 1.3245;  x5 = 1.3246;  x6 = 1.3247
the sequence settles: root = 1.3247 (4 d.p.)

Worked example 2 (testing convergence). For g(x) = (x + 1)^(1/3), show the iteration converges near 1.32.

g'(x) = (1/3)(x + 1)^(-2/3)
at x = 1.32: g' = (1/3)(2.32)^(-2/3) = 0.19 < 1
so the iteration converges

If |g′| > 1 near the root the iteration diverges, and a different rearrangement is needed. The same equation usually has several rearrangements, only some of which converge — that is exactly what the |g′| test decides.

Failure modes of iteration

divergence: |g'| > 1 near the root
oscillation: the sequence jumps between two values
slow convergence: |g'| close to 1

Worked example. The rearrangement x = x³ − 1 for x³ − x − 1 = 0 gives g′(x) = 3x², which is about 5.3 near the root: the iteration diverges rapidly. That is why the cube-root rearrangement, with g′ ≈ 0.19, is used instead.

Newton-Raphson

x_(n+1) = x_n - f(x_n)/f'(x_n)

the tangent at the current point is followed to the x-axis;
the intercept becomes the next estimate

Derivation. The tangent at x_n has equation y − f(x_n) = f′(x_n)(x − x_n). Setting y = 0 gives x = x_n − f(x_n)/f′(x_n), which is the formula.

Worked example. Use Newton-Raphson on f(x) = x³ − x − 1 with x₁ = 1.3.

f'(x) = 3x² - 1 × 2 = 1.3 - (-0.103)/(4.07) = 1.3 + 0.0253 = 1.3253 × 3 = 1.3253 - (0.00053)/(4.2637) = 1.3252
root = 1.3252 (4 d.p.) in two steps, against six for the iteration

Worked example 2 (failure). Explain why x₁ = 0.5 fails for f(x) = x³ − x − 1.

f'(0.5) = -0.25, so x2 = 0.5 - (-1.375)/(-0.25) = 0.5 - 5.5 = -5.0
the tangent is nearly horizontal, so the step overshoots wildly;
the method can diverge when f' is small near the initial guess

State the failure condition explicitly: Newton-Raphson needs f′(x_n) ≠ 0 and a good starting value close to the root.

The trapezium rule

integral from a to b of f(x) dx ~ (h/2)[y_0 + 2(y_1 + ... + y_(n-1)) + y_n]
where h = (b - a)/n and y_i = f(a + ih)

the error: a larger n reduces it; the rule overestimates for a
concave-up curve and underestimates for concave-down

Worked example. Use the trapezium rule with 4 strips to estimate ∫ from 0 to 2 of e^(x²) dx.

h = 0.5; x: 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2
y: 1, 1.2840, 2.7183, 6.4760, 54.5982
I ~ (0.5/2)[1 + 2(1.2840 + 2.7183 + 6.4760) + 54.5982]
  = 0.25[1 + 20.9566 + 54.5982] = 0.25 × 76.5548 = 19.14

Worked example 2 (over or under). Is the estimate above or below the true value here?

e^(x²) is concave up (its gradient is increasing), so each chord lies
above the curve and the trapezium rule overestimates

Accuracy and error

the error of a trapezium estimate is roughly proportional to h²
halving h roughly quarters the error

rounding to k decimal places requires the estimate to be stable at
the next place

Worked example. An estimate with h = 0.5 gives 19.14; with h = 0.25 the estimate is 18.92. Estimate the answer to 1 d.p.

the two agree to 1 d.p. at 18.9; quoting 18.9 is defensible, and the
difference indicates the scale of the remaining error

Comparing two step sizes is the standard way to justify an accuracy claim; a single estimate cannot.

Setting up an iteration properly

An iteration question usually hands you the rearrangement; the marks are for using it correctly, showing the iterates, and judging convergence. Three habits cover it:

  • Write the recurrence exactly as given and substitute the stated starting value.
  • Record each iterate to one more decimal place than required.
  • Show two consecutive iterates agreeing at the required accuracy before quoting the root.

Worked example. f(x) = x³ + 2x − 5 has a root near 1.3. Show that x = (5 − 2x)^(1/3) is a valid rearrangement and iterate twice.

from x³ + 2x - 5 = 0: x³ = 5 - 2x  →  x = (5 - 2x)^(1/3) × 2 = (5 - 2.6)^(1/3) = (2.4)^(1/3) = 1.3389 × 3 = (5 - 2.6777)^(1/3) = (2.3223)^(1/3) = 1.3241
converging towards about 1.328

Worked example 2 (convergence check). Test |g′| for g(x) = (5 − 2x)^(1/3) near 1.33.

g'(x) = (1/3)(5 - 2x)^(-2/3) x (-2) = -0.667(5 - 2x)^(-2/3)
|g'(1.33)| = 0.667 x (2.34)^(-2/3) = 0.667 × 0.534 = 0.356 < 1
so the iteration converges

Newton-Raphson on other functions

The formula is universal; what changes is the derivative and the care needed with trigonometry and logs.

Worked example. Use Newton-Raphson to solve cos x = x starting from x₁ = 0.7.

f(x) = cos x - x;  f'(x) = -sin x - 1 × 2 = 0.7 - (0.7648 - 0.7)/(-0.6442 - 1) = 0.7 + 0.0648/1.6442 = 0.7394 × 3 = 0.7394 - (0.7391 - 0.7394)/(-0.6735 - 1) = 0.7391
root = 0.7391 (4 d.p.)

Worked example 2 (log equation). Solve x ln x = 1 from x₁ = 1.5.

f(x) = x ln x - 1;  f'(x) = ln x + 1 × 2 = 1.5 - (0.6082 - 1)/(0.4055 + 1) = 1.5 + 0.2788 = 1.7788 × 3 = 1.7788 - 0.0423/1.5755 = 1.7519 × 4 = 1.7632;  converging to 1.7632

Radians are compulsory in any Newton-Raphson question involving trigonometry; degrees give a value of f′ scaled by π/180 and destroy convergence.

Choosing a starting value

Both iteration and Newton-Raphson need a starting value near the root, and a sketch is the reliable way to find one. Plot or sketch y = left-hand side and y = right-hand side of the rearranged equation; the intersections are the roots, and their approximate positions are the starting values.

Worked example. e^x = 4x has two roots. Sketch and estimate them.

sketch y = e^x and y = 4x: they cross once near x = 0.3 and again
near x = 2.2
checking: e⁰.3 = 1.35 against 1.2; e².2 = 9.03 against 8.8
so start Newton-Raphson from 0.4 and from 2.2 separately

Two roots require two separate runs; a single guess finds only the root it is near. That is the most common lost mark in equations with several roots.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Sign change) Show x³ + x − 3 = 0 has a root in (1, 2). Answer: f(1) = −1, f(2) = 7; continuous; sign change.
  2. (Iteration) x_(n+1) = (3 − x_n)^(1/3), x₁ = 1. Find x₃. Answer: 1.2599, 1.2020.
  3. (Convergence) g(x) = (3 − x)^(1/3): show |g′| < 1 near 1.21. Answer: |g′| = (1/3)(3 − x)^(−2/3) ≈ 0.21 < 1.
  4. (Newton) f(x) = x² − 5, x₁ = 2. Find x₂. Answer: 2 − (−1)/4 = 2.25.
  5. (Newton again) Find x₃ for the same. Answer: 2.25 − 0.0625/4.5 = 2.2361.
  6. (Newton failure) f(x) = x³, x₁ = −1. What happens? Answer: x₂ = −1 − (−1)/3 = −0.667, converging slowly towards 0; the root is a stationary point, so convergence is linear.
  7. (Trapezium) Estimate ∫₀² x² dx with 2 strips. Answer: h = 1; (1/2)[0 + 2(1) + 4] = 3.
  8. (Error) Is that estimate over or under? Answer: over, since x² is concave up; the true value is 8/3 = 2.667.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Claiming exactly one root: the sign change proves at least one; uniqueness needs monotonicity or a sketch.
  • Iterating too few times: the answer must be stable at the required number of decimal places — show consecutive values agreeing.
  • Calculator in the wrong mode: iteration on a reset calculator silently uses the last answer; store x_n in a variable.
  • Newton with a small derivative: the step overshoots; state the failure rather than ploughing on.
  • Wrong h: h = (b − a)/n, not the number of ordinates; counting strips and counting points are different.
  • Trapezium brackets: the first and last ordinates are counted once, the interior ones twice; a factor-of-two error here is the classic slip.
  • Error direction guessed: justify over/under estimate from the concavity, not from the size of the answer.
  • Accuracy unqualified: "the answer is 1.32" without evidence that later iterations agree is not a numerical-methods answer.

title: Hypothesis Testing — Study Notes
content:
Hypothesis Testing

The Framework

The null hypothesis H₀ is the default claim (no change, p = p₀). The alternative H₁ is what a suspicious observation suggests (p > p₀, p < p₀, or p ≠ p₀). The significance level α is the probability of rejecting a true H₀ — the false-alarm rate, usually 5% or 1%.

Test for a Binomial Proportion

With X ~ B(n, p₀) under H₀, compute the probability of results at least as extreme as the observed count in the direction of H₁.

Example: H₀: p = 0.3 against H₁: p > 0.3, observed 10 successes in n = 20. Compute P(X ≥ 10) under B(20, 0.3). If that tail probability is below α, reject H₀.

One-Tailed vs Two-Tailed

One-tailed tests take the whole α in one direction. Two-tailed tests split α across both tails: compare against α/2 on each side, or equivalently check whether the observation falls in the extreme 2.5% (for α = 5%). Choose the tails from the wording of H₁, not from the data.

Critical Regions

The critical region is the set of values of the test statistic that would lead to rejection. Its boundary is the critical value. For B(20, 0.3) at the 5% level with H₁: p > 0.3, find the smallest k with P(X ≥ k) < 0.05 — that k opens the critical region.

Conclusions in Context

Never just say "reject H₀". Conclude in the language of the problem: "there is sufficient evidence at the 5% level that the proportion has increased". State the significance level, the direction, and the real-world quantity.

Exam tips: define H₀ and H₁ with symbols AND words. Verify which tail the observation sits in before computing. If the observed value lies in the critical region, evidence supports H₁; otherwise there is insufficient evidence — never "prove H₀ true".

title: Permutations and Combinations — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Permutations and Combinations

Mathematics — A2. If a task is done in successive stages with m, n, ... choices at each stage, the total is the product of the choices. This underpins every counting problem: a menu with 4 starters and 6 mains gives 24 meals.

Key areas to revise

  • The Multiplication Principle
  • Permutations — Order Matters
  • Combinations — Order Irrelevant
  • Restricted Permutations
  • Combinations with Constraints

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

### Worked example A permutation is an ordered arrangement, so nPr = n! ÷ (n − r)!. A combination ignores order, so nCr = n! ÷ (r!(n − r)!). Five people in a line can be arranged in 5! = 120 ways. Choosing a committee of 3 from 8 people gives 8C3 = 56, while choosing a ranked top 2 from 5 gives 5P2 = 20. ### Check yourself Find 8C3 without a calculator by writing it as 8 × 7 × 6 ÷ (3 × 2 × 1). The answer is 336 ÷ 6 = 56. Explain why this is a combination and not a permutation. ### Worked example A permutation is an ordered arrangement, so nPr = n! ÷ (n − r)!. A combination ignores order, so nCr = n! ÷ (r!(n − r)!). Five people in a line can be arranged in 5! = 120 ways. Choosing a committee of 3 from 8 people gives 8C3 = 56, while choosing a ranked top 2 from 5 gives 5P2 = 20.

title: IGCSE Computer Science: Hardware and Architecture
content:
IGCSE Computer Science: Hardware and Architecture

Cambridge IGCSE Computer Science 0478 (2026–2028), Paper 1 Computer Systems, Topic 3 Hardware: statement 3.1 Computer architecture, 3.2 Input and output devices, and 3.3 Data storage. This is where the physical machine is opened up: what a CPU actually does with machine code, how instructions and data travel around the system, and how storage technologies differ. Every fetch–execute cycle below is traced register by register, because Paper 1 routinely asks you to follow the cycle through a memory dump — and that question is free marks once you have traced it a dozen times.

Hardware, firmware and software: the layers

Before the parts, the big picture — and the analogy that makes the whole topic click. A computer system is a factory. The hardware is the building and machines (physical, touchable). The software is the list of orders the factory must carry out (instructions, intangible). Firmware is software permanently etched into a chip — like the safety rules bolted to the wall: it survives a power cut and tells the hardware how to start. The operating system is the factory manager, deciding which order runs when and which machine each order may use.

The stored-program concept and Von Neumann architecture

Early machines had to be rewired for every new task. The breakthrough of the stored-program concept is that both the instructions and the data they work on live in the same memory, and the CPU reads instructions from memory and obeys them — no rewiring. In the chef analogy: the recipe (program) and the ingredients (data) sit on the same kitchen shelf; the chef fetches a recipe line, does what it says to the ingredients, and moves to the next line.

Von Neumann architecture is the standard layout built on that idea:

  • CPU — the processor, containing the control unit (CU), the arithmetic logic unit (ALU) and registers.
  • Main memory — RAM (and ROM), holding both program instructions and data.
  • Input and output devices — the system's contact with the outside world.
  • Buses — the cables connecting them: address, data and control.

Its famous weakness is the Von Neumann bottleneck: instructions and data share one memory and one set of buses, so the CPU can fetch only one thing at a time and spends much of its cycle waiting. Caches, pipelining and multiple cores exist largely to hide that bottleneck.

Inside the CPU

The control unit fetches and decodes instructions and orchestrates the rest of the machine; it is the foreman. The ALU performs arithmetic (add, subtract, multiply, divide) and logic (comparisons, AND/OR/NOT); it is the workbench. Registers are tiny, extremely fast storage locations inside the CPU — the foreman's desk, where the handful of items being worked on right now are kept.

RegisterFull nameWhat it holds
PCProgram counterThe memory address of the next instruction to fetch
MARMemory address registerThe address currently being read from or written to
MDRMemory data register (also called MBR)The data or instruction just fetched, or about to be written
CIRCurrent instruction registerThe instruction being decoded and executed
ACCAccumulatorThe result of the last ALU calculation

The clock paces the CPU: each tick synchronises one step, and the clock speed (measured in GHz) is the number of ticks per second. Cache is small, very fast memory inside or beside the CPU holding copies of recently used data and instructions — a cache hit saves a slow trip to RAM. Cores are independent processing units; more cores mean more instructions can be completed simultaneously, provided the software is written to use them.

The buses

BusDirectionCarriesWidth matters because
Address busCPU to memory/peripherals (one-way)Memory addressesMore address lines mean more memory can be addressed (n lines address 2ⁿ locations)
Data busBoth waysInstructions and dataMore lines mean more bits per transfer, so wider = faster
Control busBoth waysSignals: read, write, clock, interrupt, resetCoordinates who does what and when

The fetch–decode–execute cycle

Every program is a list of instructions in memory, and the CPU runs them one at a time in a repeating three-stage cycle. Fetch: get the instruction. Decode: work out what it means. Execute: do it. Then the cycle repeats — millions of times per second.

Memory holds addresses like a street of numbered houses. Suppose memory looks like this before the program runs:

Address   Contents   Meaning
  5       0010 10⁰⁰  LOAD 8        (copy the value at address 8 into the ACC)
  6       0011 10⁰¹  ADD 9         (add the value at address 9 to the ACC)
  7       0100 10¹⁰  STORE 10      (copy the ACC into address 10)
  8       0000 0101  the value 5
  9       0000 0011  the value 3
 10⁰⁰⁰⁰ 0000  (empty)

Trace the whole run, register by register. The first two bits of each instruction are the opcode (the operation) and the remaining six bits are the operand (the address to work on).

Cycle 1 - FETCH of LOAD 8:
  PC = 5. The PC's value is copied to the MAR: MAR = 5.
  The control bus sends a READ signal; memory returns the contents of address 5.
  The instruction arrives in the MDR: MDR = 0010 10⁰⁰.
  The MDR's value is copied to the CIR: CIR = 0010 10⁰⁰. PC is incremented: PC = 6.
Cycle 1 - DECODE:
  The control unit reads the opcode 00 = LOAD: copy the value at the operand address to the ACC.
Cycle 1 - EXECUTE:
  The operand is 01 10⁰⁰ = address 8. MAR = 8; READ; MDR = 0000 0101 (the value 5).
  ACC = 5.

Cycle 2 - FETCH of ADD 9:
  PC = 6 → MAR = 6; READ; MDR = 0011 10⁰¹; CIR = 0011 10⁰¹; PC = 7.
Cycle 2 - DECODE:
  Opcode 01 = ADD: add the value at the operand address to the ACC.
Cycle 2 - EXECUTE:
  Operand 01 10⁰¹ = address 9. MAR = 9; READ; MDR = 0000 0011 (the value 3).
  ALU computes ACC + MDR = 5 + 3 = 8. ACC = 8.

Cycle 3 - FETCH of STORE 10:
  PC = 7 → MAR = 7; READ; MDR = 0100 10¹⁰; CIR = 0100 10¹⁰; PC = 8.
Cycle 3 - DECODE:
  Opcode 10 = STORE: copy the ACC into the operand address.
Cycle 3 - EXECUTE:
  Operand 01 10¹⁰ = address 10. MAR = 10; MDR = 8 (from the ACC); a WRITE signal
  stores it. Address 10 now holds 0000 10⁰⁰. The program stops (STOP instruction).

Notice the pattern examiners look for: PC → MAR → (READ) → MDR → CIR for the fetch, PC incremented after the fetch, and the execute stage differing per opcode. An interrupt (a signal from a device demanding attention, like a keypress or timer) pauses the cycle between instructions: the CPU finishes the current instruction, saves the PC, jumps to an interrupt service routine, then returns.

What makes a processor faster

  • More clock cycles per second (GHz) — each instruction is paced by the clock; more ticks per second means more instructions per second, other things equal.
  • More cores — several CPUs on one chip work on different tasks simultaneously.
  • Larger cache — more of the working data sits close to the CPU, so fewer slow RAM accesses.
  • Wider data bus — more bits move per transfer.
  • Instruction set — the set of operations a CPU understands. RISC processors use few simple instructions, each executed in one clock cycle; CISC processors have many complex instructions, each taking several cycles but needing fewer instructions per task. Say what the difference does: fewer cycles per instruction versus fewer instructions per task.
Worked example: a processor runs at 2.0 GHz and each instruction takes 4 cycles.

2.0 GHz = 2.0 × 10⁹ cycles per second
instructions per second = 2.0 × 10⁹ / 4 = 5.0 × 10⁸

So 500 million instructions per second. Clock speed alone is not the whole story:
a 2.0 GHz CPU needing 4 cycles per instruction matches a 4.0 GHz CPU needing 8.

Embedded systems

An embedded system is a processor built into a device to run one dedicated task — the microcontroller in a washing machine, engine management unit, microwave, traffic light or digital camera. Characteristics: single function, small and cheap, low power, often real-time (must respond within a deadline), and rarely updated. Advantages: low cost, compact, reliable, energy-efficient. Disadvantages: inflexible, hard to upgrade or repair, and a bug affects the whole appliance. The exam wants the trade-off stated, not just a list of examples.

Input and output devices

DeviceTypeTypical use and why it suits it
KeyboardInputEntering text and commands quickly and accurately
Mouse / touchscreenInputDirect graphical manipulation; touchscreens suit kiosks where space or hygiene matters
Scanner / cameraInputDigitising documents and images; OCR software then reads the text
Sensors (temperature, light, pressure, moisture)InputAutomatic measurement in control systems — greenhouses, weather stations, car engines
MicrophoneInputSound capture for recording and voice input
Monitor / projectorOutputVisual display; projectors for audiences, monitors for detail
Printer / plotterOutputHard copy; plotters for large-scale technical drawings
Speakers / headphonesOutputSound reproduction
Actuators (motors, heaters, valves, robotic arms)OutputPhysical action in control systems — the hands of an automated system

The sensor–processor–actuator loop is the heart of every automated system: a sensor measures the world, the microprocessor compares the reading with a target, and the actuator changes the world. Choosing a device is always justified by accuracy, speed, cost and environment.

Primary storage: RAM and ROM

RAMROM
VolatilityVolatile — contents lost on power offNon-volatile — contents survive power off
Read/writeBoth, constantlyRead only (written at manufacture or by special processes)
HoldsThe running OS, open programs and their dataBootstrap/firmware: the start-up instructions that load the OS
Speed/sizeFast, measured in GBFast, but small (MB)

Virtual memory extends RAM by reserving space on the secondary storage device: when RAM fills, less-active pages are swapped to disk. It prevents crashes but is slow, because secondary storage is far slower than RAM — thrashing (constant swapping) can make a machine crawl.

Secondary storage: magnetic, optical and solid state

MediumHow it storesStrengthsWeaknesses
Magnetic (HDD, tape)Magnetised regions on spinning platters or tape, read by headsVery cheap per GB, huge capacityMoving parts: slower, noisy, shock-sensitive; tape is sequential access only
Optical (CD, DVD, Blu-ray)Pits and lands burned by laser, read by reflected lightCheap, portable, long shelf life, good for archiving and distributionLow capacity, slower write speeds, easily scratched
Solid state (SSD, USB flash, memory cards)Electrical charges in NAND flash cellsVery fast, silent, robust (no moving parts), low powerMore expensive per GB, finite number of write cycles

Compare on the four axes examiners name: capacity, speed (access and transfer), cost per GB, durability and portability. Choose by use case — an SSD for video editing, an HDD for a media archive, flash for a phone, optical for distributing software.

Cloud storage keeps data on remote servers reached over a network: accessible anywhere, easy to back up and share, with storage that scales without new hardware. Against that: it needs a connection, costs ongoing fees, gives slower access than local storage, and raises privacy and security concerns because data leaves your control. Local storage is fast and offline but vulnerable to loss or theft and limited by device capacity — most systems use both.

Worked example: choosing storage and reading a memory dump

A school records 200 hours of video per year at 1 GB per hour and wants 5 years of archive with daily access, plus backups.

Capacity needed: 200 × 1 × 5 = 10⁰⁰ GB (about 1 TB), plus backup = 2 TB.

HDD: about £45 per TB, random access for daily retrieval, but a mechanical drive
     is the weak point - keep the backup on a second drive or in the cloud.
SSD: faster and more robust but roughly three times the cost per TB.
Optical: about 25 GB per disc - 80 discs for the archive, sequential retrieval
     only - impractical for daily access.
Cloud: no hardware to fail and off-site backup included, but 2 TB of storage
     for 5 years is an ongoing subscription and every retrieval needs the network.

Choice: working copies on an SSD, archive on one or two HDDs, plus cloud backup.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Saying the fetch stage "executes" the instruction. Fetch retrieves; decode interprets; execute acts — and the PC is incremented during the fetch stage, not the execute stage.
  • Confusing the MAR and the MDR: the MAR holds the address being accessed; the MDR holds the data travelling to or from it.
  • Claiming RAM is permanent because the computer "remembers" files; files live on secondary storage — RAM is volatile.
  • Describing the address bus as two-way; only the data bus is two-way.
  • Listing performance factors without effects: "it has cache" earns nothing; "a larger cache means more data is found without slow RAM access" earns the mark.
  • Calling a sensor an output device; sensors input data, actuators output action.
  • Writing that virtual memory "increases RAM"; it borrows secondary storage and is slower — it prevents out-of-memory failures, not slowness.
  • Forgetting units in capacity calculations (GB vs TB) or mixing up bytes and bits — the classic file-size question trap.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 1, 3 marks). State the purpose of the program counter and the memory address register in the fetch–execute cycle.

Answer: The program counter holds the address of the next instruction to be fetched, so the CPU knows where to look in memory; it is incremented after the fetch. The memory address register holds the address currently being accessed (read from or written to) during the cycle.

Question 2 (Paper 1, 4 marks). Describe what happens to the MDR and CIR during the fetch stage.

Answer: The address in the MAR is sent down the address bus with a READ control signal; memory returns the instruction or data at that address into the memory data register (MDR). The MDR's contents are then copied into the current instruction register (CIR), where the control unit decodes them.

Question 3 (Paper 1, 6 marks). Compare magnetic and solid-state secondary storage for a laptop used for field research.

Answer: Solid state has no moving parts, so it is far more resistant to shock and drops (vital in the field), silent, lighter and much faster, and uses less battery. Against that it costs more per gigabyte and wears out after many write cycles. Magnetic drives offer far more capacity per pound but their spinning platters and heads are damaged by knocks, they are slower and heavier. For field research, robustness and battery life dominate, so solid state is the better choice.

Question 4 (Paper 1, 4 marks). Explain what an embedded system is and give two advantages of using one in a washing machine.

Answer: An embedded system is a processor built into a device to perform one dedicated task, running firmware rather than a general-purpose OS. In a washing machine it is cheap to mass-produce, small enough to fit inside the appliance, low-power, and reliable because there is no general-purpose software to fail — the machine does its one job well and quickly boots each time.

Question 5 (Paper 1, 5 marks). A CPU runs at 3.0 GHz and averages 5 cycles per instruction. Calculate its instruction rate and explain why a 2.0 GHz CPU with 2 cycles per instruction could be faster.

Answer: 3.0 × 10⁹ cycles/second ÷ 5 = 6.0 × 10⁸ instructions per second. The 2.0 GHz CPU gives 2.0 × 10⁹ ÷ 2 = 1.0 × 10⁹ instructions per second — higher despite the lower clock, because instructions per second depends on both clock speed and cycles per instruction, not clock speed alone.

Question 6 (Paper 1, 3 marks). Explain the purpose of virtual memory and one disadvantage of using it.

Answer: When RAM is full, the operating system moves less-active programs and data to a reserved area of secondary storage (the swap file), freeing RAM so programs keep running instead of crashing. Disadvantage: secondary storage is far slower than RAM, so swapping causes noticeable slowdowns — especially thrashing, where the system spends its time swapping rather than working.

With the machine understood at the hardware level, the next question is how it represents everything it knows: data representation.

title: IGCSE Biology: Organisation of the Organism
content:
IGCSE Biology: Organisation of the Organism

Every living thing you will ever meet — from a single bacterium to a blue whale — is built from cells, and this note starts where all biology starts: at the microscope. We begin with the idea that the cell is the smallest unit that can still be called alive, then map the structures inside animal and plant cells, explain what each one actually does, and finish with the specimen-size calculations that Paper 6 loves. Nothing here assumes prior knowledge; each structure is introduced with a physical analogy before the formal term, and every calculation is expanded line by line so you can follow it with no chemistry or maths background at all.

What a cell is, and why it is the unit of life

A cell is the smallest structure that carries out all seven life processes: movement, respiration, sensitivity, growth, reproduction, excretion and nutrition (the mnemonic MRS GREN). A brick is not alive; a single white blood cell is, because it does all seven. Two organisational levels follow. Unicellular organisms (bacteria, Amoeba, yeast) are one cell doing everything. Multicellular organisms (you, an oak tree) are communities of cells that specialise, so the body shows three levels of organisation: cells group into tissues (one job, like muscle tissue), tissues into organs (the stomach), and organs into organ systems (the digestive system).

Cell specialisation means a cell's structure fits its function like a tool fits a job. A red blood cell is a flat biconcave disc with no nucleus, leaving maximum room for haemoglobin. A sperm cell carries a long tail (flagellum) and a packed mitochondria cluster for swimming. A root hair cell pushes out one long extension to maximise surface area for absorption. A palisade cell packs its top half with chloroplasts to catch light. When asked to explain a specialised cell, always write it as: feature, then what the feature does, then why the job needs it.

Animal cell structure

Think of a cell as a factory. The cell membrane is the security door: a thin, selectively permeable layer of lipid and protein that decides what enters and leaves. The cytoplasm is the factory floor: a jelly-like solution of water, salts and enzymes where most reactions happen. The nucleus is the manager's office: it contains genetic material (DNA) and controls the cell's activities by regulating which proteins are made. Mitochondria are the power stations: rod-shaped organelles where aerobic respiration releases energy from glucose. Ribosomes are the assembly lines: tiny structures where proteins are assembled from amino acids. The cytoplasm and cell membrane together carry out most of the life processes; the nucleus stores and passes on genetic information.

Plant cell structure — the three additions

A plant cell has everything an animal cell has, plus three structures an exam will always want named. The cell wall is a rigid layer of cellulose outside the membrane: it gives mechanical strength and stops the cell bursting when water enters. Chloroplasts are the solar panels: they contain the green pigment chlorophyll and are the site of photosynthesis. The permanent vacuole is a storage tank: a large sac of cell sap (dilute sugars, salts and acids) that keeps the cell turgid, pressing the cytoplasm against the wall so leaves stay firm. Learn the comparison as a table — it is the single most reliable three-mark question in Paper 4.

StructureAnimal cellPlant cellJob
Cell membranePresentPresentControls what enters and leaves
Cell wallAbsentPresent (cellulose)Strength and support; prevents bursting
ChloroplastsAbsentPresent (palisade, spongy mesophyll)Photosynthesis in chlorophyll
Permanent vacuoleSmall, temporaryLarge, permanent, cell sapTurgor, storage
NucleusPresentPresentControls activities; stores DNA
MitochondriaPresentPresentAerobic respiration, releases energy
RibosomesPresentPresentProtein synthesis

Bacterial cells: the prokaryote difference

Bacteria are prokaryotes — cells with no nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles. Their DNA is a single circular chromosome free in the cytoplasm, often with small extra rings called plasmids. They have a cell wall (not cellulose — it is murein), a cell membrane, cytoplasm and ribosomes (smaller than eukaryotic ones), and many have a flagellum for swimming and a capsule for protection. The exam answer to "give two differences between a bacterium and a plant cell" is: no nucleus in the bacterium (DNA free in cytoplasm) and no chloroplasts or mitochondria (respiration at the membrane).

Microscopy and magnification

An optical (light) microscope uses glass lenses and visible light; specimens can be living or dead and are often stained (methyl blue for nuclei, iodine for starch) to add contrast. An electron microscope uses a beam of electrons, giving far higher magnification and resolution so organelles such as mitochondria, ribosomes, lysosomes and the endoplasmic reticulum can be seen — but specimens must be dead and in a vacuum. Magnification is how many times larger the image is than the real object; resolution is the minimum distance between two points still seen as separate — a blurry zoomed image has magnification without resolution. The three calculations you must know are written below, and the worked example expands each one.

Size of specimens — the three equations

Equation 1, magnification: magnification = size of image divided by size of real object. Equation 2, real size: real size = image size divided by magnification. Equation 3, image size: image size = real size × magnification. The golden rule of units: convert everything to the same unit before dividing. 1 millimetre (mm) = 1000 micrometres (µm); 1 µm = 1000 nanometres (nm). A common exam device is a scale bar drawn under an image: measure the bar in millimetres with a ruler, note the length it claims to represent in µm, and the magnification is bar length (in µm) ÷ claimed length (in µm). Drawing magnification for Paper 6 is measured the same way: magnification = drawing width (mm) ÷ real width (mm), with the real width first converted from µm by dividing by 1000.

Worked example: specimen size from first principles

An image of a plant cell is 40 mm long in a textbook, and the real cell is 80 µm long. Calculate the magnification. Step 1: write the equation: magnification = image size ÷ real size. Step 2: list what you have: image = 40 mm, real = 80 µm. Step 3: convert to one unit — 40 mm = 40 × 1000 = 40 000 µm. Step 4: divide: 40 000 ÷ 80 = 500. Step 5: write the answer with its × symbol: magnification = ×500. Now the reverse direction. A cell is 12 µm wide and you draw it at ×1500. Step 1: image size = real size × magnification. Step 2: 12 µm × 1500 = 18 000 µm. Step 3: convert to a workable unit: 18 000 ÷ 1000 = 18 mm. Your drawing must be 18 mm wide — measure it with a ruler in the practical. Finally, a bacterium appears 35 mm long in a micrograph at ×20 000. Step 1: real size = 35 mm ÷ 20 000 = 0.00175 mm. Step 2: convert: 0.00175 mm × 1000 = 1.75 µm. Step 3: state the answer: 1.75 µm, which is a sensible bacterium size.

Exam technique: command words and drawing rules

"State" wants one short fact; "describe" wants what you see in a diagram or graph (no reasons); "explain" wants the mechanism with because. For drawings: use clean, unbroken pencil lines with no shading; the drawing should be at least 6 cm wide for a decent magnification; label lines are straight, horizontal, do not cross, and touch the structure named; labels name the structure (write "mitochondrion", not "the power station"). When asked for differences between two diagrams (typical Paper 6), compare like with like: "the plant cell has a cell wall, the animal cell does not" is two marks in one line.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Calling the cell wall "membrane": the membrane is inside the wall; mixing them loses the mark.
  • Writing "chloroplast" on an animal cell diagram — animals have mitochondria, never chloroplasts.
  • Forgetting units after converting: 40 mm ÷ 80 µm is wrong until both are µm; always show the conversion line.
  • Saying magnification and resolution are the same thing; they are different, and Paper 4 has asked for the distinction outright.
  • Shading a drawing or using a ruler-free squiggle: both are explicitly penalised in Paper 6 mark schemes.
  • Label lines crossing each other or drawn as arrows; a line that does not touch the structure scores zero.
  • Writing "cytoplasm" when you mean "cytosol" or vice versa is safe at IGCSE — use "cytoplasm" — but never write "cell sap" for cytoplasm; cell sap is only inside the vacuole.

Exam-style questions and answers

Q1. State two structures found in a plant cell but not in an animal cell. (2 marks) Answer: cell wall (cellulose) and chloroplasts — one mark each; the permanent vacuole is also accepted but do not list more than the question asks.

Q2. A cell is drawn 60 mm wide. The real cell is 150 µm wide. Calculate the magnification and show your working. (3 marks) Answer: 60 mm = 60 000 µm (1); magnification = 60 000 ÷ 150 (1); = ×400 (1).

Q3. Explain why root hair cells are specialised for absorption. (2 marks) Answer: they have a long extension that increases surface area (1), so more water and mineral ions can be absorbed per unit time by diffusion and active transport (1).

Q4. Describe how you would prepare a slide of onion cells for viewing. (4 marks) Answer: peel a thin transparent layer of epidermis (1); place it flat in a drop of water on a slide (1); add a coverslip at an angle without trapping air bubbles (1); view at low power then focus with the fine adjustment (1).

Q5. Explain why the electron microscope was needed to discover ribosomes. (2 marks) Answer: ribosomes are very small (around 20 nm) so need much higher resolution than the light microscope provides (1); the electron microscope's shorter wavelength of electrons gives that resolution (1).

title: Networking & Communication — Study Notes
content:
Networking & Communication

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): transmission modes, serial/parallel, packet switching, protocols, LAN/WAN, hardware, security layers.

1. Transmission basics

  • Serial: one bit at a time — reliable over distance, cheaper cable.
  • Parallel: several bits at once — faster over short runs; skew/crosstalk limit distance.
  • Simplex / half-duplex / full-duplex direction; bandwidth (bits/s) vs bit rate.

2. Packets

Header (sender/receiver addresses, sequence number) + payload + trailer (checksum). Packet switching: routes vary, packets reassembled at destination; checksum failure → re-request. Benefits: robustness, shared lines; delays/reassembly overhead.

3. Protocols

TCP/IP stack layers (application, transport, network, link). HTTP/HTTPS (TLS encryption), FTP (with login + commands), email: SMTP send, POP3/IMAP retrieve. Bluetooth/Wi-Fi for WPAN/WLAN.

4. Network types & hardware

LAN (site) vs WAN (internet). Router (joins networks, IP), switch (MAC frames within LAN), gateway (protocol translation), NIC, WAP. MAC address (burned-in, layer 2) vs IP address (assigned, layer 3).

5. Security in transmission

Encryption scrambles plaintext → ciphertext (key needed); HTTPS = HTTP over TLS; firewall packet filtering by port/IP; authentication (user+pass, 2FA); access levels.

Exam tips: explain why skew limits parallel over distance; compare MAC vs IP in a table; protocol questions want "rules for communication", not acronyms alone.

title: Electric Fields and Capacitance
content:
Electric Fields and Capacitance

Coulomb's Law

F = q₁q₂/(4πε₀r²). Field strength E = F/q (N C⁻¹); for a point charge E = q/(4πε₀r²).

Uniform Fields

Between parallel plates: E = V/d, constant.

Example: 2 kV across 5 mm: E = 400 kV m⁻¹. An electron feels F = eE ≈ 6.4 × 10⁻¹⁴ N toward the positive plate.

Potential

V = W/q, scalar; E = −dV/dr. Potential energy of q at V is qV.

Capacitance

C = Q/V (farads). Energy stored: W = ½QV = ½CV².

Combinations: parallel adds (C = C₁ + C₂); series: 1/C = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂ (opposite to resistors).

Example: 10 μF and 20 μF in series: 1/C = 1/10 + 1/20 → C ≈ 6.7 μF.

Charging and Discharging

Exponential: V = V₀ e^(−t/RC). Time constant RC: after one RC, V falls to 37%. Half-life t½ = 0.69 RC.

Exam tips: field points from high to low potential; in discharge problems identify which quantity (V, Q or I) decays — all share the same exponential factor.

title: IGCSE Physics: Forces and Motion
content:
IGCSE Physics: Forces and Motion

Cambridge IGCSE Physics 0625 (2026–2028), Topic 1 Motion, forces and energy: statements 1.2 Motion, 1.3 Mass and weight, 1.5 Forces and 1.6 Momentum. This is the mechanics spine of the whole course, and it is where the Paper 4 structured calculation marks are won and lost. Almost every mechanics question begins the same way: label the velocities, find the resultant force, then choose the equation. The ideas below are built from absolute zero, but the definitions are examinable word for word, so learn them exactly as stated.

Speed, velocity and acceleration

Start with an analogy. A car's speedometer tells you how fast the car is covering ground; it says nothing about which way the car points. That everyday reading is speed. Add a compass direction to it and you have velocity. Speed is a scalar (size only); velocity is a vector (size and direction), and that single distinction runs through the entire course.

QuantityDefinitionSymbol and unitScalar or vector
DistanceTotal length of the path travelleds, metre (m)Scalar
DisplacementDistance in a stated straight-line direction from a start points, metre (m)Vector
SpeedDistance travelled per unit timev, metre per second (m s⁻¹)Scalar
VelocityRate of change of displacement, i.e. speed in a stated directionv, metre per second (m s⁻¹)Vector
AccelerationRate of change of velocitya, metre per second squared (m s⁻²)Vector

The two equations every question uses are:

average speed = total distance travelled / total time taken        v = s / t
acceleration = (final velocity - initial velocity) / time taken    a = (v - u) / t
