Here u is the initial velocity, v is the final velocity, and t is the time taken. The SI units must be metres, seconds and metres per second before the equations are used; convert kilometres to metres and minutes to seconds first. The sign convention is the student's choice but must be stated: pick one direction as positive (upwards or forwards is usual), then velocities and accelerations in the opposite direction are negative. A negative acceleration that slows an object is often called a deceleration. An object thrown upwards has g = 9.81 m s⁻² downwards throughout its flight, so if up is positive its acceleration is −9.81 m s⁻² at every point, including the instant it stops at the top.

Average speed over a whole journey is not the average of the speeds. It is total distance divided by total time, so a car that covers 100 km at 50 km h⁻¹ and the next 100 km at 100 km h⁻¹ has an average speed of 200 km in 3 hours, which is 67 km h⁻¹, not 75 km h⁻¹.

Describing motion with graphs

Graphs are the language of this topic, and Paper 4 nearly always carries one. Two kinds do all the work.

FeatureDistance–time graphSpeed–time graph
GradientSpeed (or velocity)Acceleration
Area under the graphNot meaningfulDistance travelled
Horizontal lineObject at restConstant speed, zero acceleration
Straight sloping lineConstant speedConstant acceleration
CurveChanging speed (draw a tangent to find the speed at a point)Changing acceleration

On a distance–time graph the gradient is the distance moved divided by the time taken, which is the speed. On a speed–time graph the gradient is the change in speed divided by the time taken, which is the acceleration, and the area under the graph is made of rectangles (speed × time = distance) and triangles (½ × base × height), so it gives the total distance travelled. Drawing a tangent to a curve at a point is a Paper 6 skill: place the ruler so it just touches the curve, extend the line well past the curve on both sides, and take two distant points on the tangent to work out its gradient.

Paper 6 link. A trolley pulled by a falling mass leaves dots on ticker tape from a 50 Hz timer, so consecutive dots are 0.02 s apart. The distance between successive dots gives the speed over that interval, and a speed–time graph of those speeds has a gradient equal to the trolley's acceleration. Measuring a short distance with a ruler and dividing by 0.02 s is exactly the averaging technique in statement 1.1.

Mass, weight and gravitational field strength

Mass is the amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms with a balance. It does not change wherever the object is taken: the mass of an astronaut is the same on the Moon as on Earth. Weight is the force of gravity on that mass, measured in newtons with a spring balance, and it is a vector because gravity always pulls towards the centre of the attracting body. The astronaut's weight on the Moon is about one sixth of that on Earth because the Moon's gravitational field is weaker.

weight = mass x gravitational field strength        W = m g
  • W: weight in newtons (N). Weight is a vector, and its direction is straight down towards the centre of the Earth.
  • m: mass in kilograms (kg). Mass is a scalar.
  • g: gravitational field strength in newtons per kilogram (N kg⁻¹); on Earth g ≈ 9.81 N kg⁻¹, which is numerically the same as the free-fall acceleration 9.81 m s⁻².

Examination questions give the value of g to use, and many IGCSE papers round it to 10 N kg⁻¹ to keep the arithmetic simple. Always use the value printed in the question, and quote it in your answer when you substitute. Never confuse the two instruments: a balance compares masses and would give the same reading on the Moon, while a newton meter compares weights and would not.

Forces and their effects

A force is a push or a pull, measured in newtons, and it is a vector: direction matters. Forces can change an object's speed, change its direction of travel, or change its shape. Newton's first law states that an object remains at rest, or continues at constant velocity in a straight line, unless a resultant (net) force acts on it. Motion only changes when forces are unbalanced; a book resting on a table has weight and an equal upward normal contact force acting on it, so its resultant force is zero and it does not accelerate.

The resultant force is the single force that has the same effect as all the real forces combined. Two people pushing a trolley the same way add; pushing opposite ways subtract; forces at right angles combine by Pythagoras on the diagonal (Supplement). Newton's second law, in the form examined at IGCSE, is a Supplement statement:

resultant force = mass x acceleration        F = m a
  • F: resultant force in newtons (N), positive in the chosen positive direction.
  • m: mass in kilograms (kg).
  • a: acceleration in metres per second squared (m s⁻²), in the same direction as F.

The equation only works with the resultant force and only in SI units. If a car's engine produces 3000 N while drag is 1000 N, the resultant is 2000 N, and it is that 2000 N that goes into F = ma.

Friction and drag. Friction acts where surfaces touch and always opposes the motion or the tendency to move. Drag (air resistance or water resistance) opposes motion through a fluid and grows as the speed grows. A falling object released from rest therefore accelerates at first, because weight exceeds drag; as speed rises, drag rises until it equals the weight. From that moment the resultant force is zero, the acceleration is zero, and the object falls at terminal velocity. This is a Supplement explanation and it is a regular Paper 4 six-mark question: describe the motion in stages and use the words resultant force, drag and terminal velocity.

Springs and extension. A load hung on a spring stretches it. The relationship is summarised on a load–extension graph: a straight line through the origin shows extension proportional to load, up to the limit of proportionality. The stiffness of the spring is its spring constant:

force = spring constant x extension        F = k x
  • F: force applied to the spring in newtons (N).
  • k: spring constant in newtons per metre (N m⁻¹); larger k means a stiffer spring.
  • x: extension in metres (m). Extension = stretched length − original length, so it is a scalar in practice.

Beyond the limit of proportionality the line curves: the spring is permanently deformed and does not return to its original length when the load is removed. Doubling the load doubles the extension only while the graph is still a straight line. Two identical springs in series share the load and stretch twice as far; in parallel they share the load and stretch half as far (Supplement).

Turning effects of forces: moments

A force that does not act through a pivot makes an object turn. The size of that turning effect is the moment of the force:

moment of a force = force x perpendicular distance from the pivot        M = F d
  • M: moment in newton metres (N m). A moment is a vector in the sense that it turns clockwise or anticlockwise, and that sense must be carried through the calculation as a sign.
  • F: force in newtons (N).
  • d: perpendicular distance from the line of action of the force to the pivot in metres (m).

The word perpendicular is the whole mark. If a 10 N force acts at 30° to a spanner handle, the moment uses the perpendicular component of the force, or equivalently the perpendicular distance. For an object in equilibrium the principle of moments applies: the sum of the clockwise moments about any pivot equals the sum of the anticlockwise moments, and the resultant force is zero. A see-saw balances when the anticlockwise moment of the near child equals the clockwise moment of the far child; moving either child outwards increases that child's moment without changing their weight. Two equal and opposite forces whose lines of action do not coincide form a couple, which produces rotation without translation, as when a steering wheel is turned with both hands.

Centre of gravity and stability

The centre of gravity of an object is the single point through which its entire weight may be taken to act. For a uniform object it is the geometric centre; for a lamina (a flat sheet) it can be found experimentally by the plumb-line method, which is a classic Paper 6 task: hang the lamina freely from one hole, hang a plumb line from the same pin, and mark the line; repeat from a second hole; the lines cross at the centre of gravity.

Stability depends on where that point sits relative to the base. An object topples when the line of action of its weight falls outside its base, because the weight then produces a resultant moment that overturns it. Wide bases and low centres of gravity make objects stable (racing cars carry ballast low; tall trucks are loaded low), and top-heavy objects with narrow bases topple easily.

Momentum and impulse

Momentum is the quantity of motion a moving object carries: a lorry at 20 m s⁻¹ is far harder to stop than a bicycle at the same speed. Momentum is a Supplement statement for 0625 and is a favourite for Paper 4 calculation questions.

momentum = mass x velocity        p = m v
impulse = change in momentum = resultant force x time        F t = m v - m u
  • p: momentum in kilogram metres per second (kg m s⁻¹). Momentum is a vector, in the same direction as the velocity, so the sign convention chosen at the start must be applied to every velocity.
  • m: mass in kilograms (kg); v and u: final and initial velocity in metres per second (m s⁻¹), positive in the chosen positive direction.
  • Impulse: newton seconds (N s), equal to the change in momentum.

The principle of conservation of momentum: in a closed system, where no external resultant force acts, the total momentum before an event equals the total momentum after it. Total means the vector sum: momenta in opposite directions carry opposite signs. This one statement solves collisions, explosions and recoil problems. Newton's second law in its full form is implied here: the resultant force equals the rate of change of momentum, F = (mv − mu)/t, which is why increasing the time of impact reduces the force for the same change in momentum — that is how airbags, crash barriers and landing on a bent knee work.

Worked example: collision and impact force

Collision. A 1200 kg car travelling at 15 m s⁻¹ runs into a stationary 800 kg car and the two lock together. Find their common velocity. Take the first car's direction as positive.

total momentum before = 1200 x 15 + 800 x 0 = 18 000 kg m s-1
total momentum after = (1200 + 800) v = 2000 v
2000 v = 18 000, so v = 9 m s-1, in the original direction

The combined cars move at 9 m s⁻¹ in the direction the first car was travelling. Note that kinetic energy is not conserved in this collision — most of it is lost to sound and deformation — but momentum is always conserved.

Impact force. A 0.50 kg ball travelling at 12 m s⁻¹ hits a wall and rebounds at 8 m s⁻¹ in the opposite direction. The contact lasts 0.050 s. Find the average force on the ball. Take the initial direction as positive, so the rebound velocity is −8 m s⁻¹.

change in momentum = m v - m u = 0.50 x (-8) - 0.50 x 12 = -4.0 - 6.0 = -10 kg m s-1
average force = change in momentum / time = -10 / 0.050 = -200 N

The minus sign shows the force acts opposite to the ball's initial motion, which is what a wall does. The magnitude is 200 N. Getting the sign of the rebound velocity wrong is the single most common error in this topic, and it doubles the answer.

Common mistakes

  • Confusing mass and weight: mass is in kilograms and never changes; weight is in newtons and equals mg. A mass of 5 kg has a weight of about 50 N, not 5 kg.
  • Using the average of speeds for the average speed of a journey; it is always total distance over total time.
  • Reading the wrong quantity from a graph: gradient on a distance–time graph is speed, gradient on a speed–time graph is acceleration, and only the speed–time graph has a meaningful area.
  • Putting any force into F = ma. Only the resultant force gives the acceleration, so add and subtract the forces first.
  • Using a slanted distance in a moment calculation; d is measured perpendicular to the line of action of the force.
  • Losing the sign of a velocity in a momentum calculation. Reversal of direction is a sign change, and the total momentum is a vector sum, not a sum of sizes.
  • Using g = 9.81 when the question says take g = 10 N kg⁻¹, and forgetting to state which value was used.
  • Adding a force in newtons to a momentum in kg m s⁻¹; if the units do not match, the physics does not either.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 4, 3 marks). A cyclist starts from rest and reaches 8.0 m s⁻¹ in 5.0 s. Calculate the average acceleration and the distance travelled.

Answer: a = (v − u)/t = (8.0 − 0)/5.0 = 1.6 m s⁻². Distance = average speed × time = ½(0 + 8.0) × 5.0 = 20 m. (A speed–time graph of the motion is a triangle of area ½ × 5.0 × 8.0 = 20 m.)

Question 2 (Paper 4, 4 marks). A skydiver of mass 80 kg falls. Explain, using forces, why she reaches a terminal velocity, and state the size of the drag force at that moment.

Answer: Weight W = mg = 80 × 9.8 = 784 N downwards (≈ 800 N if g = 10 is taken). At first weight exceeds drag, so there is a downward resultant force and she accelerates. As speed increases, drag increases. When drag equals the weight the resultant force is zero, acceleration is zero, and she falls at constant terminal velocity. The drag force is then 784 N (or 800 N) upwards.

Question 3 (Paper 2 style). Which statement about a ball thrown straight up is correct? A: its acceleration at the top is zero; B: its velocity at the top is zero; C: its momentum at the top is maximum; D: its weight is zero at the top. Answer: B. The velocity is instantaneously zero at the top, but g still acts there, so the acceleration is 9.81 m s⁻² downwards and the weight is unchanged. Paper 2 setters rely on this confusion between velocity and acceleration.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 4 marks). A 1500 kg car travelling at 20 m s⁻¹ brakes to a stop in 4.0 s. Calculate the braking force.

Answer: change in momentum = mv − mu = 1500 × 0 − 1500 × 20 = −30 000 kg m s⁻¹. Force = change in momentum / time = −30 000 / 4.0 = −7500 N. The braking force is 7500 N opposite to the motion.

Question 5 (Paper 6 style). Describe how you would find the centre of gravity of an irregular lamina.

Answer: Hang the lamina from a pin through a hole near its edge so it swings freely. Hang a plumb line from the same pin and, when everything is at rest, mark the plumb-line position on the lamina. Repeat with the lamina hung from a second hole. The point where the two marked lines cross is the centre of gravity. The plumb line marks the vertical through the pivot, and the centre of gravity lies on it in both cases.

Question 6 (Paper 4, 3 marks). A 0.20 kg ball moving at 6.0 m s⁻¹ collides with an identical ball at rest and stops dead. Find the velocity of the second ball after the impact.

Answer: total momentum before = 0.20 × 6.0 = 1.2 kg m s⁻¹. After the impact the first ball has zero momentum, so 0.20 × v = 1.2 and v = 6.0 m s⁻¹ in the original direction.

Momentum, moments and Newton's laws are the tools; the next step is what those forces actually do to energy.

title: Differentiation II — Study Notes
content:
Differentiation II

Product and Quotient Rules

  • (uv)′ = u′v + uv′
  • (u/v)′ = (u′v − uv′)/v²

Example: y = x² e^x gives dy/dx = 2x e^x + x² e^x = e^x(2x + x²).

Standard Derivatives

  • sin x → cos x; cos x → −sin x; tan x → sec²x
  • e^x → e^x; ln x → 1/x

Chain Rule Everywhere

d/dx [ln(3x)] = 3/(3x) = 1/x; d/dx [e^(2x)] = 2e^(2x); d/dx [sin²x] = 2 sin x cos x.

Implicit Differentiation

Differentiate both sides w.r.t. x, treating y as a function of x (terms in y pick up dy/dx).

Example: x² + y² = 25 → 2x + 2y(dy/dx) = 0 → dy/dx = −x/y.

Parametric Curves

For x = f(t), y = g(t): dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt).

Example: x = t², y = t³ gives dy/dx = 3t²/2t = 3t/2.

Exam tips: quote the rule you use; for tangent/normal on parametric curves, find t at the point first, and simplify implicit answers using the original equation.

title: Exam technique: Computational Thinking
content:
### What earns the marks
For recursion, the base case quoted plus the shrinking argument earns both marks. For dry runs, each call tracked with its print earns method credit. For strategy choice, the signature named (splitting for divide-and-conquer, retreating for backtracking) earns the mark with a fitting example.
### Traps
Error: base case omitted. Correction: every recursion needs a reachable stop. Error: greedy claimed to backtrack. Correction: greedy never retreats. Error: linear search called divide-and-conquer. Correction: it never divides.

title: Entropy and Energetics Quick Revision
content:
Entropy and Energetics Quick Revision

Chemistry — A2. Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH14, Topic 12, covering entropy, energetics, and feasibility of reactions. Entropy and enthalpy changes are crucial in determining the spontaneity of a reaction.

  • Entropy measures disorder and randomness, increasing with temperature and phase changes.
  • Gibbs free energy combines enthalpy and entropy to predict reaction feasibility.
  • Total entropy change is the sum of system and surroundings entropy changes.
  • Temperature affects reaction feasibility, with higher temperatures decreasing the magnitude of surroundings entropy change.
  • Worked examples illustrate how to calculate entropy changes and Gibbs free energy.

Worked example

Calculate the total entropy change for a reaction with ΔS_system = 100 J/K and ΔH = -50000 J, at 298 K, using S_surroundings = -ΔH / T, then S_total = ΔS_system + S_surroundings.

Key points to remember

Remember that entropy increases with temperature and phase changes, and that the total entropy change determines reaction spontaneity. Also, recall that the Gibbs free energy equation, ΔG = ΔH - TΔS, is used to predict reaction feasibility.

How to use this: skim the key points, read the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Born-Haber Cycles and Lattice Energy

A Born-Haber cycle applies Hess's Law to construct an energy level diagram for the formation of an ionic solid from its elements in their standard states. The standard enthalpy change of atomisation, delta_at H, is the enthalpy change when one mole of gaseous atoms is formed from the element under standard conditions. Electron affinity is the enthalpy change when one electron is added to each atom in one mole of gaseous atoms to form one mole of gaseous 1- ions. Lattice energy is defined as the exothermic process for the formation of one mole of an ionic solid from its gaseous ions.

Discrepancies between experimental lattice energy values obtained from Born-Haber cycles and theoretical values calculated from pure electrostatic point-charge models indicate the presence of covalent character. When cations polarise large or highly charged anions, electron density is drawn into the region between the nuclei, leading to partial covalent bonding which releases more energy than predicted by pure ionic models.

Enthalpy of Solution and Hydration

The enthalpy change of solution, delta_sol H, is the enthalpy change when one mole of a solute is dissolved in enough solvent to form an infinitely dilute solution. The enthalpy change of hydration, delta_hyd H, is the enthalpy change when one mole of gaseous ions is dissolved in water to form an infinitely dilute solution. You can use energy cycles combining lattice energy and hydration enthalpies to calculate the enthalpy change of solution.

Ionic charge and radius significantly affect these energetic values. High charge density, resulting from small ionic radius and high ionic charge, leads to more exothermic hydration and lattice energies because of stronger electrostatic attractions between the ions and water molecules or oppositely charged ions.

Thermodynamic Stability versus Kinetic Stability

Thermodynamic stability indicates whether a substance or reaction is feasible based on total entropy change and free energy, showing if a reaction is spontaneous. Kinetic stability refers to the rate of a reaction; a system can be thermodynamically unstable yet kinetically stable if the activation energy barrier is too high for the reaction to proceed at a measurable rate at room temperature.

Additional Worked Example

Calculate the enthalpy change of solution for sodium chloride, given that its lattice energy is +790 kJ / mol and the hydration enthalpies of sodium and chloride ions are −406 kJ / mol and −364 kJ / mol respectively. Using the energy cycle, delta_sol H = lattice energy + sum(delta_hyd H). Therefore, delta_sol H = +790 + (−406 + (−364)) = +790 − 770 = +20 kJ / mol.

More Key Points to Remember

Remember that the total entropy change, delta_S total = delta_S system + delta_S surroundings, must be positive for any spontaneous process. The term delta_S surroundings is calculated using − delta_H / T. Solubility trends down group 2 depend on the relative sizes of the decrease in lattice energy compared to the decrease in hydration enthalpy as cation size increases. Polarisation increases down the group for anions or with smaller cations, driving deviations from theoretical lattice energy calculations.

title: Databases — Study Notes
content:
`# Databases

Relational Basics

Tables (relations) of records with fields. Keys:

  • Primary key: unique identifier
  • Foreign key: references another table's PK — creates relationships
  • Candidate/secondary keys: other unique identifiers

Normalisation

  • 1NF: atomic values, no repeating groups
  • 2NF: 1NF + no partial dependency on a composite key
  • 3NF: 2NF + no transitive dependencies (non-key → non-key)

Example: (StudentID, Course, CourseFee) has CourseFee depending on Course, not StudentID — move course data to its own table (3NF).

SQL

SELECT name, grade FROM students
  WHERE grade >= 'A' ORDER BY name;
INSERT INTO students VALUES (...);
UPDATE students SET grade = 'B' WHERE id = 5;
DELETE FROM students WHERE id = 5;

Joins combine tables: FROM students s JOIN enrolments e ON s.id = e.sid.

Transactions

ACID: Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (rules hold), Isolation (no interference), Durability (committed = permanent). Record locking prevents conflicting simultaneous edits.

Exam tips: justify each normal form step with the dependency removed; write SQL with correct WHERE clauses to avoid accidental full-table updates.

Primary keys, foreign keys and redundancy

A primary key is a field, or combination of fields, that uniquely identifies each record in a table. A foreign key is a field in one table that holds the primary key of a record in another table. Foreign keys link the tables together and let the database check referential integrity, so that an order cannot refer to a customer who does not exist.

Storing data in one place rather than repeating it in several tables reduces data redundancy. Less redundancy saves storage, and it reduces the chance that an update is made in one copy but not the others. Normalisation is the process of organising tables to remove this repetition.

Exam tip: when asked about a foreign key, say which table it sits in and which primary key it refers to.

title: Exam technique: Sine and Cosine Rules
content:
### What earns the marks
For the sine rule, the matched pairs written (b / sin 65 = 7 / sin 40) earn the method mark. For the cosine rule, the full substitution with cos evaluated earns the mark: write a squared = 25 + 64 - 2 x 5 x 8 x 0.5. For the largest angle, identifying the longest side first earns credit. For area, half a b sin C quoted earns the mark on its own.
### Traps
Error: sides paired with wrong angles in the sine rule. Correction: each side faces its angle. Error: 49 given as side a. Correction: root the cosine-rule result. Error: calculator-only acute angle for an obtuse ambiguous case. Correction: subtract from 180 by hand. Error: half a b without sine for a non-right triangle. Correction: area needs the sine factor unless the angle is 90 degrees.
### Worked example
Two sides are 7 cm and 9 cm, with an included angle of 40 degrees. The cosine rule gives x^2 = 7^2 + 9^2 - 2 x 7 x 9 x cos 40 = 130 - 126 x 0.766 = 33.5, so x is about 5.79 cm. Use the cosine rule when you have two sides and the angle between them.
### Check yourself
A right-angled triangle has legs 6 and 8. Compute the area as one half of 6 x 8 x sin 90 degrees, and the hypotenuse with the cosine rule. The area is 24, and the hypotenuse is sqrt(36 + 64) = 10, because cos 90 degrees is zero.

### Worked example
Two sides are 7 cm and 9 cm, with an included angle of 40 degrees. The cosine rule gives x^2 = 7^2 + 9^2 - 2 x 7 x 9 x cos 40 = 130 - 126 x 0.766 = 33.5, so x is about 5.79 cm. Use the cosine rule when you have two sides and the angle between them.

title: Drugs
content:
Drugs

Cambridge IGCSE Biology 0610, Extended route, topic 15 (statement 15.1). What drugs are, medicinal versus recreational drugs, antibiotic use and resistance, and the effects of alcohol and heroin.

15.1 Drugs

  • A drug is any substance that changes the way the body or mind works. Medicinal drugs treat or prevent disease; recreational drugs are taken for their psychological effects and can be addictive.
  • Antibiotics kill bacteria (bactericidal) or stop them multiplying (bacteriostatic). They do not work against viruses, because viruses use the host cell's own machinery and have no processes for antibiotics to block.
  • Antibiotic resistance arises by random mutation in a bacterial population; antibiotic use selects for resistant bacteria because the non-resistant ones die and the resistant ones reproduce unchecked. Misuse — not finishing a course, unnecessary prescriptions — accelerates resistance.
  • Alcohol is a depressant that slows reaction times and damages liver cells; heroin is an addictive opiate that depresses the central nervous system and carries overdose and infection risks from shared needles.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Selection reasoning, applied to a course of antibiotics stopped early: the most susceptible bacteria die first, leaving behind those with partial resistance, which multiply in the absence of competition. Explain with variation and selection — not "the antibiotics teach bacteria to resist". That misconception loses the mark outright.
  • Stewardship evaluation, applied to proposals to restrict antibiotic use in farming: argue both sides — reduced selection pressure slows resistance, but animal health and welfare may suffer. A top answer weighs both and reaches a justified judgement.
  • Drug classification reasoning, applied to why a vaccine is not an antibiotic: a vaccine stimulates the immune system to make its own antibodies against a virus, while an antibiotic acts directly on bacterial structures. Match the agent to the pathogen type in every case.

Common errors

  • Saying bacteria "become resistant because of antibiotics". Resistance is a random pre-existing mutation that antibiotics select.
  • Claiming antibiotics treat colds. Colds are viral.
  • Describing an overdose risk of heroin without naming respiratory depression as the cause.

title: Earth & Space — Study Notes
content:
Earth & Space

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): Earth & Solar System; stars & the Universe (Extended).

1. Earth, Moon, Sun

Earth rotates 24 h (day/night), orbits 365¼ d (year + leap). Moon orbits Earth ~27.3 d; phases from viewing angle; lunar/solar eclipses when aligned. Seasons from axial tilt (23.5°), not distance.

2. Solar system

Planets (Mercury → Neptune), dwarf planets (Pluto), moons, asteroids, comets (eccentric orbits, tails away from Sun), natural satellites. Gravity keeps orbits; orbital speed & radius relate to the central mass.

3. Orbital motion

Orbital speed v = 2πr/T. T grows with r (Kepler trend). Comets speed up near the Sun (ellipse, Sun at focus).

4. Stars (Extended)

Star formation: nebula → protostar (gravity, KE→thermal) → main sequence (hydrogen fusion: H→He, radiation pressure balances gravity) → red giant → white dwarf (Sun-mass) or supergiant → supernova → neutron star/black hole (massive stars). Elements heavier than iron form in supernovae.

5. Universe (Extended)

The Sun is one star in the Milky Way; the Milky Way is one of billions of galaxies. Redshift: receding galaxies show stretched wavelengths → the Universe is expanding → Big Bang model; CMB is the afterglow. Hubble: farther ⇒ faster recession.

6. Scales

light-year = distance light travels in a year (9.5 × 10¹⁵ m); astronomical unit = Earth–Sun distance (1.5 × 10¹¹ m).

Orbits and the Solar System in more depth

The planets orbit the Sun because the Sun's gravity provides the centripetal force that keeps them on their paths. A moon is a natural satellite that orbits a planet, and an artificial satellite is launched by people. The Earth rotates once on its axis in one day, and it orbits the Sun once in one year. The phases of the Moon are caused by the changing proportion of its sunlit side that we see as it orbits the Earth.

Exam tip: state the object that provides the gravitational force when you describe why an orbit is stable.

title: Thermal Physics
content:
Thermal Physics

Internal Energy

Sum of random kinetic + potential energies of molecules. Temperature rise → KE up; phase change → PE up (bonds stretch) at constant temperature.

Specific Heat and Latent Heat

  • Heating: Q = mcΔθ (c = specific heat capacity)
  • Phase change: Q = mL (L = specific latent heat)

Example: melting 0.2 kg ice: Q = 0.2 × 334,000 ≈ 67 kJ — no temperature change during the change.

Mixtures: heat lost = heat gained.

Gas Laws

  • Boyle: pV = constant (T fixed)
  • Charles: V/T = constant (p fixed)
  • Pressure law: p/T = constant (V fixed)
  • Combined/ideal: pV = nRT, R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹

Example: 2 mol at 300 K in 0.05 m³: p = nRT/V = 2 × 8.31 × 300/0.05 ≈ 100 kPa.

Kinetic Theory

½m⟨c²⟩ = (3/2)kT — temperature measures mean translational KE. Also pV = ⅓Nm⟨c²⟩.

Exam tips: use kelvin in every gas equation; in mixture problems, work per substance with a common final temperature.

title: AS Level Chemistry: Bonding and Structure
content:
Bonding and Structure

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH11, Topic 3. Every statement 3.1 to 3.22 is covered below, with its code in the heading so you can check your own gaps against the specification. The big idea: the type of bonding and the shape of a molecule explain almost every physical property a question can ask about, including melting point, conductivity, solubility and polarity.

3.1 to 3.2: Evidence for ions, and how they form

  • Evidence for ions: ionic compounds conduct electricity only when molten or dissolved, because the ions are then free to move. In electrolysis, a coloured ion such as manganate(VII), MnO₄⁻, migrates to the positive electrode (the anode), which is direct evidence that it carries a negative charge.
  • Electron density maps for ionic compounds show near-spherical regions of electron density around each ion, with a clear drop in density between them.
  • Formation by loss or gain of electrons: sodium loses one electron to form Na⁺ (2,8,1 becomes 2,8), while chlorine gains one to form Cl⁻ (2,8,7 becomes 2,8,8). A metal loses electrons to form a positive ion; a non-metal gains electrons to form a negative ion.

3.3: Dot-and-cross diagrams for ions

  • Show the outer electrons of each atom as dots or crosses. For a cation such as Mg²⁺, the outer shell is empty, so the symbol is written with square brackets and the charge: [Mg]²⁺.
  • For an anion such as O²⁻, the transferred electrons are added to the outer shell, which then holds eight electrons: [O]²⁻ with eight dots and crosses inside the brackets.
  • Always put the charge outside the brackets, and check that the total number of electrons transferred matches the charges.

3.4 to 3.5: Giant ionic lattices and the ionic bond

  • An ionic crystal is a giant lattice of alternating positive and negative ions, repeating in three dimensions. There are no discrete molecules, so the formula, such as NaCl, is only the simplest ratio of ions. In sodium chloride each Na⁺ is surrounded by six Cl⁻ ions and each Cl⁻ by six Na⁺ ions (6:6 coordination).
  • An ionic bond is the strong net electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions. "Net" matters: the attraction between a cation and an anion is partly cancelled by repulsion between like ions, but the attraction wins at the equilibrium distance.

3.6: Effect of ionic radius and ionic charge on bond strength

  • The electrostatic attraction grows with the charge on the ions and falls as the ions get larger, because the centres of charge are further apart.
  • Compare MgO (melting point about 2850 °C) with NaCl (about 800 °C). Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ carry double charges and are small, so their attraction is much stronger than that between the singly charged, larger Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions.

3.7: Trends in ionic radius

  • Down a group, ionic radius increases, because each ion has an additional electron shell. Li⁺ is smaller than Na⁺, which is smaller than K⁺.
  • Across a set of isoelectronic ions, all the species have the same number of electrons (ten, in the series N³⁻, O²⁻, F⁻, Na⁺, Mg²⁺, Al³⁺). The nuclear charge rises from 7 to 13 across the series, so the outer electrons are pulled in more strongly and the radius falls. N³⁻ is the largest and Al³⁺ the smallest.

3.8 to 3.9: Polarisation of ions

  • Polarisation is the distortion of the electron cloud of an anion by a nearby cation. The cation pulls the anion's electron density towards itself, so the bonding stops being purely ionic and gains covalent character.
  • The polarising power of a cation is greatest when it is small and highly charged. Al³⁺ > Mg²⁺ > Na⁺.
  • The polarisability of an anion is greatest when it is large and highly charged, because its outer electrons are held loosely. I⁻ is more polarisable than Br⁻, which is more polarisable than Cl⁻, which is more polarisable than F⁻.
  • Example: aluminium chloride has a low melting point and sublimes, far below what a purely ionic lattice would need. The small, highly charged Al³⁺ polarises the chloride ions strongly, so the bonding is largely covalent.

3.10: Covalent bonding and the evidence for it

  • A covalent bond is the strong electrostatic attraction between two nuclei (both positive) and the shared pair of electrons between them.
  • Evidence: giant atomic structures such as diamond and silicon(IV) oxide have very high melting points, which only strong covalent bonds can explain. Electron density maps for simple molecules such as hydrogen show a build-up of electron density between the two nuclei.

3.11: Dot-and-cross diagrams for covalent substances

  • Multiple bonds: in carbon dioxide, O=C=O, each double bond is two shared pairs. In nitrogen, N≡N, there are three shared pairs.
  • Dative (coordinate) bonds: both electrons in the shared pair come from one atom, the donor, which has a lone pair. The arrow points from donor to acceptor. In the ammonium ion, NH₄⁺, the nitrogen in NH₃ donates its lone pair to H⁺.
  • Aluminium chloride dimer, Al₂Cl₆: each aluminium has four chlorines. Two of the chlorines bridge the two aluminium atoms, and each bridging chlorine forms a dative bond from a chlorine lone pair into the empty orbital of the other aluminium.

3.12: Giant carbon structures: diamond, graphite and graphene

  • Diamond: each carbon forms four single covalent bonds in a tetrahedral giant lattice. It is very hard, has a very high melting point and does not conduct, because there are no free electrons. It is used in cutting and drilling tools.
  • Graphite: each carbon forms three bonds in flat hexagonal sheets. The fourth outer electron on each carbon is delocalised, so graphite conducts along the sheets. The sheets are held by weak forces and slide over each other, so graphite is soft and is used as a lubricant and as electrodes.
  • Graphene: a single sheet of graphite, one atom thick. It is very strong, conducts well and is light and flexible. Applications include electronics, sensors and composite materials.

3.13 to 3.14: Electronegativity and the bonding continuum

  • Electronegativity is the power of an atom to attract the bonding pair of electrons in a covalent bond. Fluorine is the most electronegative element (4.0 on the Pauling scale).
  • The bonding continuum: the bigger the electronegativity difference between two atoms, the more polar the bond. A very small difference gives a non-polar covalent bond, a moderate difference gives a polar covalent bond (as in HCl), and a very large difference gives essentially ionic bonding (as in NaCl). Ionic and covalent bonding are the two ends of this continuum, not separate categories.

3.15: Polar bonds and polar molecules

  • A polar bond has a permanent dipole. A molecule is polar only if its bond dipoles do not cancel, so polar bonds do not automatically make a polar molecule.
  • Carbon tetrachloride, CCl₄: the C–Cl bonds are polar, but the tetrahedral arrangement cancels them, so the molecule is non-polar.
  • Water, H₂O, is bent, so its dipoles add up and the molecule is polar. Carbon dioxide is linear, so its two C=O dipoles cancel and it is non-polar.

3.16 to 3.19: Electron-pair repulsion and molecular shapes

  • Electron-pair repulsion theory: bonding pairs and lone pairs around a central atom repel each other and arrange themselves to be as far apart as possible.
  • Lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs, so lone pairs compress bond angles. The order of repulsion is lone pair to lone pair, then lone pair to bonding pair, then bonding pair to bonding pair.
  • 3.17, bond length and bond angle: bond length is the distance between the nuclei of two bonded atoms. Bond angle is the angle between two bonds at the central atom. Triple bonds are shorter than double bonds, which are shorter than single bonds (C≡C shorter than C=C shorter than C–C).

3.18, the shapes and bond angles of the named species:

SpeciesElectron pairs on central atomShapeBond angle
BeCl₂2 bondingLinear180°
BCl₃3 bondingTrigonal planar120°
CH₄4 bondingTetrahedral109.5°
NH₃3 bonding, 1 loneTrigonal pyramidalabout 107°
NH₄⁺4 bondingTetrahedral109.5°
H₂O2 bonding, 2 loneBentabout 104.5°
CO₂2 bonding (double bonds)Linear180°
PCl₅ (gas)5 bondingTrigonal bipyramidal90° and 120°
SF₆6 bondingOctahedral90°
C₂H₄3 regions around each carbonPlanar around each carbonabout 120°

Applying the same rules to analogous species (3.19): SiH₄ is tetrahedral (109.5°), BF₃ is trigonal planar (120°), PH₃ is pyramidal (about 93°), H₂S is bent (about 92°), XeF₄ is square planar (90°, with two lone pairs), and ClF₃ is T-shaped. Count the electron pairs first, then decide how many are lone pairs.

3.20 to 3.22: Metallic bonding and the properties of metals

  • A metal is a giant lattice of positive metal ions in a sea of delocalised electrons, the outer electrons that are free to move through the whole structure.
  • 3.21, metallic bonding is the strong electrostatic attraction between the metal cations and the delocalised electrons. It is not a bond between two particular atoms.
  • Electrical conduction: the delocalised electrons carry charge through the metal when a voltage is applied.
  • High melting temperature: the attraction is strong and is non-directional, so a lot of energy is needed to overcome it. Magnesium melts at about 650 °C, far above sodium at about 98 °C, because Mg²⁺ carries a double charge and provides two delocalised electrons per atom.
  • Malleability: the layers of ions can slide over each other, and the delocalised electrons keep the ions attracted to each other as they move, so the metal does not shatter.

A* extension: worked reasoning for the hardest bonding questions

  • Bond angles, 3.18 applied: CH₄ is 109.5°, NH₃ about 107°, and H₂O about 104.5°. Each lone pair pushes the bonding pairs closer together, because lone pair to bonding pair repulsion is stronger than bonding pair to bonding pair. So the angle falls by roughly 2.5° per lone pair. An A* answer states the reason in these terms, not just the number.
  • Polarity, 3.15 applied: CH₃Cl is polar, because the C–Cl dipole is not cancelled by the C–H bonds, which point in roughly symmetrical directions but carry much smaller dipoles. CCl₄ is non-polar, because four identical C–Cl dipoles point to the corners of a tetrahedron and cancel exactly. Always say which dipoles cancel and why.
  • Electronegativity and bonding continuum, 3.14 applied: aluminium chloride has an electronegativity difference of about 1.5 between Al and Cl. That is not large enough to make it purely ionic, so it is a polar covalent bond, which is consistent with its low melting point and the polarisation argument in 3.8 to 3.9.
  • Lattice and bond strength, 3.6 applied: when asked to compare two ionic compounds, name both the charge and the radius, and say which one dominates. Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ beat Na⁺ and Cl⁻ on both counts, so MgO has the much higher melting point.
  • Mark-scheme phrasing for metallic bonding (3.21): "giant lattice of positive ions", "sea of delocalised electrons", "strong electrostatic attraction between the ions and the delocalised electrons". Each phrase earns its own mark, so use all three.
  • Graphite versus graphene, 3.12 applied: an electrode question expects you to name the delocalised electron, and a lubricant question expects you to name the weak forces between layers. Give both mechanisms when the question says "explain".

Common errors that lose marks

  • Saying covalent or metallic bonds are "between molecules" (they are within the structure; the forces between molecules are intermolecular forces).
  • Calling a polar bond a polar molecule. Always check the shape before you decide the molecule's polarity.
  • Saying ions "move" in solid ionic compounds. They vibrate in place; only molten or dissolved compounds conduct through ion movement.

Exam-style questions

  1. Explain why magnesium oxide has a much higher melting temperature than sodium chloride. Answer: both are giant ionic lattices, but the ions in MgO carry 2+ and 2− charges compared with 1+ and 1− in NaCl, and the Mg2+ and O2− ions are smaller. The electrostatic attraction between the ions is therefore much stronger, so far more energy is needed to break the lattice apart.
  2. Explain why aluminium chloride sublimes at a low temperature while sodium chloride melts at 801 °C. Answer: the Al3+ ion is small and highly charged, so it polarises the Cl− ion strongly. The electron cloud of the chloride is distorted towards the aluminium, giving the Al–Cl bond covalent character and producing discrete Al2Cl6 molecules held by weak London forces. The sodium ion is larger and less charged, so NaCl remains a giant ionic lattice.
  3. Predict the shape and bond angle of SF6 and explain your reasoning. Answer: octahedral, 90°. The sulfur atom has six bonding pairs and no lone pairs, so the six electron pairs repel equally and arrange themselves as far apart as possible.
  4. Carbon dioxide and water both contain polar bonds, yet carbon dioxide is non-polar. Explain. Answer: CO2 is linear and symmetrical, so the two C=O dipoles are equal and opposite and cancel. Water is bent, with two O–H dipoles that do not cancel, so the molecule has a net dipole and is polar.
  5. Explain why graphite conducts electricity but diamond does not. Answer: in graphite each carbon is bonded to three others, leaving one delocalised electron per atom that is free to move along the layers. In diamond every carbon has four covalent bonds, so all the valence electrons are localised in σ bonds and there are no mobile charge carriers.

title: Intermolecular Forces — Study Notes
content:
Intermolecular Forces

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH12, Topic 7. Intermolecular forces are the attractions between molecules, not the bonds inside them. They determine boiling points, solubility and how molecules pack together.

Types of intermolecular force

  • London (instantaneous dipole–induced dipole) forces exist in all molecules. They grow with the number of electrons, so larger molecules have higher boiling points.
  • Permanent dipole–dipole forces occur between polar molecules, where the partial positive and negative charges attract one another.
  • Hydrogen bonding is a strong dipole–dipole attraction. It occurs when H is bonded to N, O or F and attracts a lone pair on another N, O or F.

Effect on physical properties

  • Boiling point depends on the strength of intermolecular forces: more energy is needed to separate molecules that attract strongly.
  • Water boils at a much higher temperature than hydrogen sulfide because hydrogen bonding is much stronger than the dipole forces between H2S molecules.
  • Branched alkanes have lower boiling points than straight-chain isomers because they have a smaller surface area for London forces.

Solubility

  • Substances dissolve when the new attractions between solute and solvent replace the attractions within each.
  • Polar solvents such as water dissolve ionic and polar solutes; non-polar solvents dissolve non-polar solutes.
  • Ethanol is miscible with water because its –OH group forms hydrogen bonds with water.

Ideal and real gases

  • A real gas deviates from ideal behaviour at high pressure and low temperature, because molecules have volume and attract one another.

Exam tip: when comparing boiling points, name the type of intermolecular force, state whether it is stronger or weaker, and say how much energy is needed to overcome it. Do not say that "bonds break" when a liquid boils.

title: Materials: Deformation — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Materials: Deformation

Physics — AS. Up to the limit of proportionality, F = kx — extension is proportional to load. k is the spring constant (N m⁻¹).

Key areas to revise

  • Hooke's Law
  • Stress, Strain, Young Modulus
  • Force–Extension Graphs
  • Breaking Stress

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Key relationships

  • Stress σ = F / A, measured in pascals, and strain ε = extension / original length, which has no unit.
  • Young modulus E = stress / strain, which is the gradient of the linear part of the stress-strain graph.
  • Within the limit of proportionality, Hooke's law holds: F = k x.
  • The area under a force-extension graph gives the elastic strain energy stored in the material.

Common errors

Strain is a ratio and has no unit. Beyond the elastic limit, the material does not return to its original length, so the Young modulus formula no longer describes the behaviour.

title: Permutations and Combinations — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Permutations and Combinations

Mathematics — A2. If a task is done in successive stages with m, n, ... choices at each stage, the total is the product of the choices. This underpins every counting problem: a menu with 4 starters and 6 mains gives 24 meals.

Key areas to revise

  • The Multiplication Principle
  • Permutations — Order Matters
  • Combinations — Order Irrelevant
  • Restricted Permutations
  • Combinations with Constraints

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

### Worked example A permutation is an ordered arrangement, so nPr = n! ÷ (n − r)!. A combination ignores order, so nCr = n! ÷ (r!(n − r)!). Five people in a line can be arranged in 5! = 120 ways. Choosing a committee of 3 from 8 people gives 8C3 = 56, while choosing a ranked top 2 from 5 gives 5P2 = 20. ### Check yourself Find 8C3 without a calculator by writing it as 8 × 7 × 6 ÷ (3 × 2 × 1). The answer is 336 ÷ 6 = 56. Explain why this is a combination and not a permutation.

title: Exam technique: Continuous Random Variables
content:
### What earns the marks
For pdf constants, total area equals 1 stated earns the method mark. For probabilities, the integral with correct limits earns each mark. For mean and variance, E(X) and E(X squared) - E(X) squared each earn credit stepwise.
### Traps
Error: point probabilities given positive values. Correction: points have zero area. Error: mean mistaken for median. Correction: solve the half-area equation for medians. Error: variance sign reversed. Correction: E(X squared) minus mean squared.

title: Exam technique: Circular Motion and Gravity
content:
### What earns the marks
For circular motion, m v squared over r equated to the providing force earns both marks. For angular speed, 2 pi f quoted earns the mark. For gravity, the inverse square applied to ratios earns the method mark.
### Traps
Error: centrifugal force invoked in inertial frames. Correction: name the real provider (tension, gravity). Error: geostationary period guessed. Correction: 24 h over the equator. Error: lower orbit assumed slower. Correction: lower means faster with shorter period.

title: Chemical Equilibria A2 Level Chemistry Revision Notes
content:
Chemical Equilibria A2 Level Chemistry Revision Notes

This revision note belongs to Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH14, Topic 13 Chemical Equilibria, covering homogeneous and heterogeneous systems, equilibrium constants Kc and Kp, the factors affecting equilibrium composition and constant values, total entropy links, and reaction extent predictions.

Expressions for Kc in Homogeneous and Heterogeneous Systems

When a reversible reaction takes place in a closed system, it eventually reaches a dynamic equilibrium where the rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction, and the concentrations of reactants and products remain constant. The equilibrium constant Kc allows you to deduce the position of equilibrium quantitatively.

  • Be able to deduce an expression for Kc, for homogeneous and heterogeneous systems, in terms of equilibrium concentrations.
  • For a general homogeneous system where all species are in the same phase, such as aA + bB reversible cC + dD, the expression is Kc = [C]^c [D]^d / ([A]^a [B]^b), where square brackets denote equilibrium concentrations in mol dm⁻³.
  • For heterogeneous systems containing species in different phases, pure solids and pure liquids are omitted from the Kc expression because their concentrations remain essentially constant throughout the reaction. For example, for the decomposition of calcium carbonate, CaCO3(s) reversible CaO(s) + CO2(g), the expression is simply Kc = [CO2].

Expressions for Kp in Homogeneous and Heterogeneous Systems

For systems involving gases, it is often more convenient to use partial pressures rather than concentrations to define the equilibrium position.

  • Be able to deduce an expression for Kp for homogeneous and heterogeneous systems, in terms of equilibrium partial pressures in atm.
  • The mole fraction of a gas in a mixture is calculated as the number of moles of that individual gas divided by the total number of moles of all gases present in the mixture.
  • The partial pressure of an individual gas is its mole fraction multiplied by the total pressure of the gas system, measured in units of atmospheres or atm.
  • For a homogeneous gas phase reaction such as N2O4(g) reversible 2NO2(g), the partial pressure expression is Kp = p(NO2)² / p(N2O4).
  • For a heterogeneous gas-solid equilibrium such as C(s) + CO2(g) reversible 2CO(g), pure solid carbon is omitted from the expression, giving Kp = p(CO)² / p(CO2).

Calculating Equilibrium Constants from Experimental Data

Calculations involving Kc and Kp require systematic tracking of initial moles, change in moles, and equilibrium moles, converting them to concentrations or partial pressures.

  • Be able to calculate a value, with units where appropriate, for the equilibrium constants Kc and Kp for homogeneous and heterogeneous reactions, from experimental data.
  • For Kc calculations, divide equilibrium moles by the total volume in dm³ to find equilibrium concentrations, substitute into the Kc formula, and cancel out units or combine them using indices such as mol⁻² dm⁶.
  • For Kp calculations, find total moles at equilibrium, determine mole fractions for each gas, multiply by total pressure to find partial pressures in atm, substitute into Kp, and derive units like atm or atm².

Worked Example for Kc Calculation

For H2 + I2 reversible 2HI, suppose 1.00 mol of hydrogen and 1.00 mol of iodine are heated in a 2.00 dm³ flask. At equilibrium, 1.60 mol of hydrogen iodide has formed.

  • Step 1: Set up an ICE table. Initial moles: H2 = 1.00, I2 = 1.00, HI = 0.00.
  • Step 2: Equilibrium moles: HI = 1.60. Since stoichiometry shows 2 mol of HI form, 0.80 mol of H2 and 0.80 mol of I2 must have reacted.
  • Step 3: Calculate remaining equilibrium moles: H2 = 1.00 − 0.80 = 0.20 mol; I2 = 1.00 − 0.80 = 0.20 mol.
  • Step 4: Convert to concentrations by dividing by the volume of 2.00 dm³: [HI] = 1.60 ÷ 2.00 = 0.80 mol dm⁻³, [H2] = 0.20 ÷ 2.00 = 0.10 mol dm⁻³, [I2] = 0.20 ÷ 2.00 = 0.10 mol dm⁻³.
  • Step 5: Substitute into Kc expression: Kc = [HI]² / ([H2] × [I2]) = 0.80² / (0.10 × 0.10) = 0.64 / 0.01 = 64. The units cancel out entirely because the number of moles of reactants equals the number of moles of products.

Effects of Changes on Equilibrium Composition

Le Chatelier's principle helps predict how a system responds to external stresses, altering equilibrium composition without changing the constant itself unless temperature changes.

  • Understand how, if at all, a change in temperature, pressure or the presence of a catalyst affects the equilibrium composition in a homogeneous or heterogeneous system.
  • Adding reactant or removing product shifts the position towards the products. Adding product shifts it towards the reactants.
  • Increasing pressure or decreasing volume favours the side of the reaction with fewer gas molecules. Changing the volume has the same effect as changing pressure.
  • Raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium in the endothermic direction. Lowering the temperature shifts it in the exothermic direction.
  • A catalyst changes the rate at which equilibrium is reached by providing an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy, but it has no effect on the equilibrium position or composition.

Independence of Equilibrium Constants from Concentration and Pressure

While altering conditions shifts the position of equilibrium, the underlying constant remains strictly invariant under specific conditions.

  • Understand that the value of the equilibrium constant is not affected by changes in concentration or pressure or by the addition of a catalyst.
  • A change in concentration or pressure shifts the equilibrium composition to counteract the change, but the ratio of products to reactants at the new equilibrium exactly equals the original Kc or Kp value.
  • A catalyst speeds up both the forward and reverse rates equally, leaving the equilibrium constant completely unchanged.

Effect of Temperature on Equilibrium Constants

Temperature is unique because it alters the actual value of the equilibrium constant Kc and Kp, reflecting a change in the position of equilibrium.

  • Know the effect of changing the temperature on the equilibrium constant Kc and Kp for both exothermic and endothermic reactions.
  • Understand that the effect of temperature on the position of equilibrium is explained using a change in the value of the equilibrium constant.
  • For an exothermic forward reaction, raising the temperature decreases the value of Kc and Kp, as the equilibrium shifts to the left. Lowering the temperature increases Kc and Kp.
  • For an endothermic forward reaction, raising the temperature increases the value of Kc and Kp, as the equilibrium shifts to the right. Lowering the temperature decreases Kc and Kp.

Entropy, Total Entropy, and Equilibrium Constants

Thermodynamics links the position of equilibrium to total entropy change and the magnitude of the equilibrium constant.

  • Understand the effect of a change in temperature on the value of Stotal and the magnitude of the equilibrium constant, since Stotal = R ln K.
  • The equation Stotal = R ln K bridges kinetics, equilibrium, and thermodynamics, where R is the universal gas constant and ln K is the natural logarithm of the equilibrium constant.
  • When temperature changes, it alters Stotal, which in turn directly alters the magnitude of K. A larger positive Stotal corresponds to a much larger equilibrium constant, meaning the reaction goes virtually to completion.

Predicting the Extent of Reaction

The numerical value of an equilibrium constant gives immediate insight into whether a reaction proceeds far towards products or stays mostly as reactants.

  • Be able to apply knowledge of the value of equilibrium constants to predict the extent to which a reaction takes place.
  • When an equilibrium constant value is very large, greater than 10 to the power of 10, the numerator is vastly larger than the denominator, indicating that the reaction goes essentially to completion with very few reactants remaining.
  • When an equilibrium constant value is very small, less than 10 to the power of minus 10, the denominator dominates, indicating that virtually no reaction takes place and the system remains almost entirely as reactants.
  • When an equilibrium constant is around 1, significant amounts of both reactants and products are present at equilibrium.

Typical mistakes

  • Mistake: Including pure solids or pure liquids in Kc or Kp expressions. Correction: Omit pure solids and pure liquids because their active masses do not change.
  • Mistake: Forgetting to divide equilibrium moles by volume when calculating Kc. Correction: Always divide moles by the volume in dm³ to obtain concentration values before substituting into Kc.
  • Mistake: Believing that increasing pressure changes the value of Kc. Correction: Pressure changes the position of equilibrium and shifts concentrations, but Kc remains constant at a fixed temperature.
  • Mistake: Using mass in grams instead of mole fractions or partial pressures for Kp calculations. Correction: Always convert mass to moles, find mole fractions, and multiply by total pressure in atm.

Exam-style questions

  1. Write the expression for Kc for the heterogeneous reaction C(s) + H2O(g) reversible CO(g) + H2(g).

    Answer: Kc = [CO] [H2] / [H2O]. Solid carbon is omitted.

  2. State and explain the effect of increasing the temperature on the value of Kc for an endothermic forward reaction.

    Answer: Kc increases. Raising temperature favours the endothermic direction, increasing product concentrations and decreasing reactant concentrations, raising the numerator of Kc.

  3. Calculate the units of Kp for the equilibrium N2(g) + 3H2(g) reversible 2NH3(g) when pressure is measured in atm.

    Answer: Kp = p(NH3)² / (p(N2) × p(H2)³). Units are atm² / (atm × atm³) = atm⁻².

  4. Explain why a catalyst has no effect on the numerical value of Kc.

    Answer: A catalyst speeds up the forward and reverse rates equally by lowering the activation energy, leaving the equilibrium constant ratio unchanged.

  5. Explain what a Kc value of 10 to the power of 15 indicates about the extent of a reaction.

    Answer: The reaction goes almost entirely to completion, with the equilibrium position lying far to the right.

Use these revision notes to test your understanding of equilibrium expressions, unit derivations, and thermodynamic links via Stotal. Next, revise reaction kinetics and acid-base equilibria.

title: Exam technique: Coordinate Geometry
content:
### What earns the marks
For lines, the gradient computation shown earns the first mark and the substitution of one point earns the second. For perpendicular bisectors, the midpoint plus the negative-reciprocal gradient each earn a mark. For circles, completing the square to centre-radius form earns the method mark; the root taken last earns the final one.
### Traps
Error: segment equation given for the bisector. Correction: midpoint plus perpendicular gradient. Error: r squared reported as the radius. Correction: root last. Error: intersection x-values presented as points. Correction: substitute back for y.

title: AS Level Mathematics: Proof
content:
AS Level Mathematics: Proof

Proof is the difference between "it works for these numbers" and "it must work for all". AS proof covers four methods — direct proof, proof by exhaustion, proof by counter-example (disproof) and proof by deduction from definitions — plus the algebra of odd, even and consecutive numbers, and completing the square as a tool for inequalities. This note builds each method from zero with templates, full worked examples and the precise wording examiners expect, because proof marks are awarded for structure as much as for algebra.

The language of proof

TermMeaning
ConjectureA statement believed true but not yet proved
TheoremA statement that has been proved
ProofA logical argument from known facts to the conclusion
DisproofOne counter-example that makes the statement false
ExhaustionChecking every possible case

A single counter-example disproves a "for all" statement; no number of examples proves one. That asymmetry is the heart of the topic and the first thing examiners test.

Odd, even and consecutive numbers

even: 2n           (n integer)
odd:  2n + 1       (or 2n - 1)
consecutive integers: n, n + 1, n + 2
consecutive even: 2n, 2n + 2
consecutive odd: 2n + 1, 2n + 3

These forms are not optional decoration: a proof about parity must start from them, because "let the number be x" proves nothing about oddness.

Worked example 1. Prove that the sum of two consecutive odd numbers is a multiple of 4.

let the numbers be 2n + 1 and 2n + 3
sum = 4n + 4 = 4(n + 1)
which is a multiple of 4 for every integer n

Worked example 2. Prove that the product of two odd numbers is odd.

let them be 2m + 1 and 2n + 1
product = 4mn + 2m + 2n + 1 = 2(2mn + m + n) + 1
of the form 2k + 1 with k = 2mn + m + n, an integer
so the product is odd

Worked example 3. Prove that the difference between the squares of consecutive integers is the sum of the integers.

(n + 1)² - n² = n² + 2n + 1 - n² = 2n + 1 = n + (n + 1)

Direct proof

Start from the definitions, manipulate algebraically, and arrive at the required form. Write the conclusion explicitly ("hence ... as required") so the argument is closed.

Worked example. Prove that if x is odd then x² is odd.

let x = 2n + 1
x² = 4n² + 4n + 1 = 2(2n² + 2n) + 1
which is 2k + 1, hence odd

Worked example 2. Prove that the sum of any three consecutive integers is divisible by 3.

n + (n + 1) + (n + 2) = 3n + 3 = 3(n + 1)
which is divisible by 3

Proof by exhaustion

When the domain is small enough to list, check every case. The proof is only complete if the list is genuinely exhaustive — state why nothing is missed.

Worked example. Prove that every prime between 20 and 30 is the sum of two square numbers or state otherwise.

primes in the range: 23, 29
23 = 9 + 14 (not two squares); 25 + (-2)? no
23 = 4 + 19? no; squares below 23: 1, 4, 9, 16
1 + 16 = 17; 4 + 16 = 20; 9 + 16 = 25; 4 + 9 = 13
so 23 is not a sum of two squares; 29: 4 + 25 = 29  yes
conclusion: the conjecture fails for 23; the true statement is
"29 is the only prime between 20 and 30 expressible as a sum of two squares"

Worked example 2. Prove that n² + n is even for all integers n by exhaustion of the two parity cases.

case 1: n even, n = 2k → n² + n = 4k² + 2k = 2(2k² + k), even
case 2: n odd, n = 2k + 1 → 4k² + 4k + 1 + 2k + 1 = 4k² + 6k + 2
        = 2(2k² + 3k + 1), even
both cases covered, so the statement holds for all integers

The two-case parity split is exhaustion in its most common exam form: every integer is even or odd, so the cases exhaust the domain.

Disproof by counter-example

To disprove a "for all" claim, produce one case where it fails and show the arithmetic. One is enough; a hundred confirming cases prove nothing.

Worked example. Disprove: "if n² is a multiple of 4 then n is a multiple of 4."

try n = 6: n² = 36, a multiple of 4? 36/4 = 9, yes
but 6 is not a multiple of 4
so n = 6 is a counter-example and the statement is false

Worked example 2. Disprove: "n² − n + 11 is prime for all positive integers n."

n = 11: 121 - 11 + 11 = 121 = 11², not prime
counter-example n = 11 disproves the conjecture

Proof by completing the square

Inequalities about quadratics are proved by completing the square: a squared term is never negative, so the expression's minimum (or maximum) is visible.

x² + bx + c = (x + b/2)² + c - b²/4
since (x + b/2)² >= 0, the minimum value is c - b²/4

Worked example 1. Prove that x² + 4x + 7 > 0 for all real x.

x² + 4x + 7 = (x + 2)² + 3
(x + 2)² >= 0, so the expression is at least 3 > 0

Worked example 2. Prove that 2x − x² ≤ 1 for all real x.

2x - x² = -(x² - 2x) = -[(x - 1)² - 1] = 1 - (x - 1)²
since (x - 1)² >= 0, this is at most 1

Worked example 3. Find the values of k for which x² + kx + 9 > 0 for all x.

completing the square: (x + k/2)² + 9 - k²/4 > 0 for all x
requires the constant term positive: 9 - k²/4 > 0
k² < 36  →  -6 < k < 6

That last question is the discriminant argument in disguise: "always positive" means no real roots, so b² − 4ac < 0. Either method earns the marks; the completing-the-square route often reads more clearly.

Divisibility and multiples

A statement of the form "is a multiple of k" is proved by putting the expression in the shape k times an integer. Do the algebra first, then identify the factor; never assume the factor exists.

Worked example. Prove that for any integer n, n(n + 1)(n + 2) is a multiple of 6.

among any three consecutive integers there is at least one even
number and exactly one multiple of 3
so the product contains a factor 2 and a factor 3
since 2 and 3 are coprime, the product is divisible by 6

Worked example 2. Prove that 3^(2n) - 1 is a multiple of 8 for positive integers n.

3^(2n) - 1 = 9^n - 1 = (9 - 1)(9^(n-1) + ... + 1)
= 8 x (a positive integer), so divisible by 8

Worked example 3. Prove that the sum of five consecutive integers is always divisible by 5.

n + (n+1) + (n+2) + (n+3) + (n+4) = 5n + 10 = 5(n + 2)

Proof by contradiction: the irrationality of root 2

Contradiction assumes the statement is false, derives an impossibility, and concludes the statement is true. The classic example is examinable and worth knowing in full.

assume √(2) is rational: √(2) = p/q in lowest terms, p, q integers
square: 2 = p²/q²  →  p² = 2q²
so p² is even  →  p is even (a square is even only if its root is)
write p = 2k: 4k² = 2q²  →  q² = 2k²
so q² is even  →  q is even
but p and q cannot both be even if p/q is in lowest terms
contradiction  →  √(2) is irrational

The two logical hinges are that an even square implies an even root, and that "lowest terms" forbids a common factor of 2. State both; the marks live in them.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Parity) Prove that the sum of an odd and an even number is odd. Answer: (2m + 1) + 2n = 2(m + n) + 1, which is odd.
  2. (Consecutive) Prove that the product of two consecutive integers is even. Answer: n(n + 1): one of n, n + 1 is even, so the product is even.
  3. (Direct) Prove that (3n + 1)² − 1 is a multiple of 3. Answer: 9n² + 6n = 3(3n² + 2n).
  4. (Counter-example) Disprove "all primes are odd". Answer: 2 is prime and even.
  5. (Counter-example) Disprove "n² + 1 is prime for all n". Answer: n = 3 gives 10, not prime.
  6. (Completing the square) Prove x² − 6x + 10 > 0. Answer: (x − 3)² + 1 ≥ 1 > 0.
  7. (Exhaustion) Prove that n³ − n is divisible by 6 for n = 1, 2, 3, 4. Answer: 0, 6, 24, 60 — each divisible by 6 (a finite check is exhaustion).
  8. (Discriminant) Find k so that x² + 2kx + 4 = 0 has no real roots. Answer: 4k² − 16 < 0 → k² < 4 → −2 < k < 2.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Proving by example: two or three numbers never prove a "for all" statement; the argument must use algebra with a general n.
  • Not defining the variable: "let n be an integer" and "let n be odd, so n = 2k + 1" are required openings; an undefined x cannot carry a parity argument.
  • Assuming what you must prove: working backwards from the result to a true statement does not prove the original unless every step is reversible — say so if it is.
  • Counter-example not checked: show the arithmetic that makes the case fail; asserting "n = 6 fails" without the calculation loses the mark.
  • Incomplete exhaustion: if the domain has cases you did not cover (e.g. negatives, zero), the proof is incomplete — state the cases and why they exhaust.
  • Completing the square sign: a negative leading coefficient flips the inequality; factor out the minus first.
  • Conclusion missing: close with "hence ... as required"; an unclosed argument reads as unfinished.
  • Notation: write ≡ for identities and ⇒ for implications correctly; mixing them muddles the logic examiners follow.

title: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Transformations and Vectors
content:
Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Transformations and Vectors

Transformations move shapes on a grid, and vectors describe those moves with numbers. The exam asks two things: perform a transformation and, more often, describe one completely — with its centre, angle, direction, line or scale factor. This note builds the topic from zero: the four transformations and the full-description checklist for each, enlargement and its effect on area, vector notation with the house column-vector form (x; y), vector arithmetic, and the vector-geometry proofs that show lines are parallel or points are collinear.

The four transformations

TransformationWhat changesWhat must be stated in a description
Translationposition only, no rotation or resizethe column vector of the move
Reflectionmirror imagethe line of reflection (e.g. x = 2, y = x)
Rotationturns about a pointcentre, angle, and direction (clockwise or anticlockwise)
Enlargementresizes about a pointcentre and scale factor

The complete description is the mark: "rotation" alone scores nothing; "rotation 90° anticlockwise about (2, 1)" scores fully.

Translation

A translation moves every point by the same vector. In column form (x; y), x is the horizontal move and y the vertical move; right and up are positive.

Worked example. Triangle A has vertices (1, 1), (3, 1), (1, 4). Translate by (4; −2) and give the image coordinates.

(1, 1) -> (5, -1)
(3, 1) -> (7, -1)
(1, 4) -> (5, 2)

The shape is congruent to the original (same size and shape), and the orientation is unchanged.

Reflection

A reflection flips a shape across a line; the line is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining each point to its image. Common lines: x = a (vertical), y = b (horizontal), y = x, y = −x.

Worked example. Reflect the point (3, 5) in the line y = x.

reflection in y = x swaps the coordinates: (3, 5) -> (5, 3)

Worked example 2. Reflect (2, 4) in the line x = 1.

the line x = 1 is vertical; the distance of x = 2 from it is 1,
so the image is 1 unit on the other side: (0, 4)

To find the mirror line from a shape and its image, join a point to its image and draw the perpendicular bisector of that segment.

Rotation

A rotation turns a shape about a fixed centre through a given angle. The four standard angles are 90° and 180° in either direction; 90° clockwise equals 270° anticlockwise.

Worked example. Rotate the point (3, 1) 90° clockwise about the origin.

90 deg clockwise about O: (x, y) -> (y, -x)
(3, 1) -> (1, -3)

Worked example 2. Rotate (2, 5) 180° about the origin.

180 deg: (x, y) -> (-x, -y)
(2, 5) -> (-2, -5)

For a centre other than the origin, translate the centre to the origin, rotate, then translate back — or count the grid squares from the centre.

Enlargement

An enlargement with centre C and scale factor k maps every point so that its distance from C is multiplied by k. Negative scale factors put the image on the far side of the centre; fractional factors between 0 and 1 shrink the shape.

image distance from centre = k x object distance from centre
area of image = k^2 x area of object

Worked example. Enlarge the point (2, 3) by scale factor 3 about the origin.

(2, 3) -> (6, 9)

Worked example 2 (area). A triangle of area 12 cm² is enlarged by scale factor 2.5. Find the image area.

area factor = k^2 = 6.25
new area = 12 x 6.25 = 75 cm^2

Enlargement is the only transformation that changes area (unless k = 1 or −1); translations, reflections and rotations preserve both shape and size.

Vectors: notation and magnitude

A vector has magnitude and direction. In this course it is written as a column vector (x; y): x is the horizontal component, y the vertical. The same vector can be written as a bold letter a with an arrow above it.

column vector (x; y)
magnitude = sqrt(x^2 + y^2)
direction angle to the horizontal: tan(theta) = y/x
equal vectors have the same components; opposite vectors
negate both components

Worked example. Find the magnitude and direction of the vector (3; 4).

magnitude = sqrt(9 + 16) = 5
tan(theta) = 4/3  ->  theta = 53.1 deg above the horizontal

Vector arithmetic and geometry

addition: (a; b) + (c; d) = (a + c; b + d)
subtraction: (a; b) - (c; d) = (a - c; b - d)
scalar multiple: k(a; b) = (ka; kb)

position vector of A relative to O: OA
AB = OB - OA
midpoint of AB: (OA + OB)/2

Worked example. OA = (2; 1), OB = (7; 5). Find AB and the midpoint of AB.

AB = OB - OA = (7 - 2; 5 - 1) = (5; 4)
midpoint = ((2 + 7)/2; (1 + 5)/2) = (4.5; 3)

Worked example 2 (parallel). Show that AB is parallel to CD given A(1, 2), B(5, 8), C(0, 1), D(6, 10).

AB = (5 - 1; 8 - 2) = (4; 6)
CD = (6 - 0; 10 - 1) = (6; 9)
(6; 9) = 1.5 x (4; 6), so CD = 1.5 AB: parallel (and longer)

Parallel vectors are scalar multiples of each other; collinear points occur when AB and AC (or AB and BC) are parallel and share a point.

Combining transformations and invariant points

Two transformations applied in sequence are not the same as the reverse order: a reflection followed by a rotation generally differs from the rotation followed by the reflection. When a question asks for the single transformation equivalent to two, apply both to a convenient point (the origin or a vertex) and to a second point, then identify the transformation that maps the original to the final image. Invariant points are points that do not move: every point on a mirror line is invariant under a reflection, the centre of a rotation is invariant, and no point is invariant under a translation.

Worked example. A shape is reflected in the x-axis and then translated by (0; 3). Find the image of (2, 1) and identify any invariant points.

reflection in the x-axis: (2, 1) -> (2, -1)
translation by (0; 3): (2, -1) -> (2, 2)
No invariant points: the reflection moved every point off the
axis, and the translation then moved everything upward.

Worked example 2 (invariant line). State the invariant points of a reflection in the line y = 2.

Every point with y-coordinate 2 lies on the mirror line and does
not move: the whole line y = 2 is invariant.

Vectors in context: displacement and velocity

Column vectors describe any quantity with magnitude and direction in two dimensions: displacement (a move from one point to another), velocity (displacement per second) and force (a push in a direction). The arithmetic is identical; only the interpretation changes.

  • Displacement: AB is the vector from A to B; a round trip returns to the start, so the sum of the vectors around a closed polygon is zero.
  • Velocity: a velocity vector (3; −2) means 3 units per second right and 2 units per second down; position after t seconds is the starting position plus t × velocity.
  • Resultant: the sum of two vectors; a vector and its negative cancel.

Worked example. A particle starts at (1, 2) and moves with velocity (3; −1) for 4 seconds. Find its final position.

displacement = 4 x (3; -1) = (12; -4)
final position = (1 + 12; 2 - 4) = (13; -2)

Worked examples: vector proofs

Worked example. In triangle OAB, P is the midpoint of OA and Q is the midpoint of OB. Prove PQ is parallel to AB.

OP = (1/2) OA, OQ = (1/2) OB
PQ = OQ - OP = (1/2)(OB - OA) = (1/2) AB
PQ is a scalar multiple of AB, so PQ is parallel to AB
(and half its length).

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Translation) Translate (2, 3) by (−1; 4). Answer: (1, 7).
  2. (Reflection) Reflect (4, 1) in the x-axis. Answer: (4, −1).
  3. (Rotation) Rotate (5, 2) 90° anticlockwise about the origin. Answer: (−2, 5).
  4. (Enlargement) Enlarge (1, 2) by factor −2 about the origin. Answer: (−2, −4).
  5. (Description) Describe fully the transformation mapping (1, 1) to (3, 5). Answer: Translation by (2; 4) — one of many correct complete descriptions.
  6. (Magnitude) Find the magnitude of (6; 8). Answer: √(36 + 64) = 10.
  7. (Position vectors) OA = (1; 4), OB = (5; 2). Find AB. Answer: (4; −2).
  8. (Collinear) Show A(1, 1), B(3, 4), C(7, 10) are collinear. Answer: AB = (2; 3), AC = (6; 9) = 3 AB — parallel and share A, so collinear.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Incomplete descriptions: "enlargement by 2" omits the centre and loses marks; "reflection" omits the line. State every attribute.
  • Direction of rotation: clockwise and anticlockwise are different transformations; a 90° rotation clockwise is not the same as anticlockwise.
  • Area under enlargement: area scales by k², not k. Doubling the sides quadruples the area.
  • Vector direction: AB = OB − OA, not OA − OB. Reversing the subtraction negates the vector.
  • Column order: (x; y) is horizontal then vertical. Swapping produces a reflection in y = x, not the intended vector.
  • Parallelogram assumptions: equal magnitudes do not imply equal vectors — direction matters too.
  • Negative scale factors: the image lies on the opposite side of the centre; it is not simply "smaller".
  • Collinearity proof: showing parallel is not enough — the segments must also share a point. State it.

title: Dynamics — Study Notes
content:
Dynamics

Momentum

  • Momentum p = mv. It is a vector, with unit kg m s⁻¹, and it has the same direction as the velocity.
  • Momentum and kinetic energy are different. Momentum is a vector and changes sign with direction. Kinetic energy is a scalar.

Newton's laws of motion

  • First law: a body stays at rest or keeps moving at constant velocity unless a resultant (net) force acts on it.
  • Second law: the resultant force equals the rate of change of momentum, F = ma for constant mass. The acceleration is in the direction of the resultant force.
  • Third law: when body A exerts a force on body B, B exerts an equal and opposite force on A. The two forces are the same type and act on different bodies, so they never cancel.

Weight and mass

Mass is the amount of matter (scalar, kg). Weight is the gravitational force on it, W = mg (vector, N). Mass is the same everywhere; weight changes with the value of g.

Impulse

Impulse = FΔt = Δp = m(v − u). The area under a force–time graph equals the impulse. A longer contact time for the same change in momentum means a smaller average force, which is why airbags and crumple zones work.

Conservation of linear momentum

For a system with no resultant external force, the total momentum before an event equals the total momentum after. In an elastic collision momentum and kinetic energy are both conserved.
