In an inelastic collision only momentum is conserved. In a collision where the bodies stick together, the kinetic energy lost is greatest.

Worked example: a 0.5 kg trolley moving at 4 m s⁻¹ hits a stationary 1.0 kg trolley and they stick together. Total momentum before = 0.5 × 4 = 2.0 kg m s⁻¹. Common velocity = 2.0 / 1.5 ≈ 1.3 m s⁻¹.

Exam tips: choose a positive direction and keep signs consistent in every momentum term. State that the system is isolated before applying conservation. For a recoil question, the two momenta are equal and opposite.

Worked example: explosion and recoil

A 2.0 kg gun at rest fires a 0.020 kg bullet at 300 m s⁻¹. Before the shot, total momentum is zero. After it, the bullet has momentum 0.020 × 300 = 6.0 kg m s⁻¹ forwards, so the gun must recoil with momentum 6.0 kg m s⁻¹ backwards. Its recoil velocity is 6.0/2.0 = 3.0 m s⁻¹. The same reasoning holds for any explosion from rest: the fragments' momenta sum to zero.

Two-dimensional collisions

Momentum is a vector, so it is conserved separately in each perpendicular direction. In a collision where a 2.0 kg ball moving east at 4.0 m s⁻¹ strikes a stationary ball of equal mass at an angle, resolve the momentum of each ball along the original direction and perpendicular to it. Apply conservation in both directions, then combine the components to find the resultant speed or angle.

Kinetic energy in collisions

Kinetic energy is lost in any inelastic collision. For the trolley example above, the initial kinetic energy is ½ × 0.5 × 4² = 4.0 J, and the final kinetic energy is ½ × 1.5 × (1.33)² ≈ 1.33 J. About 2.7 J has been transferred to sound, heat and deformation. Calculate the energies to show that the collision is inelastic, rather than just saying it is.

Impulse and the force–time graph

If a force of 40 N acts for 0.25 s, the impulse is 10 N s. Where the force varies, find the area under the force–time graph: count the squares, or split the area into triangles and rectangles. A large area means a large change in momentum, even if the peak force is modest.

  • Use Δp = m(v − u) with the sign of each velocity included. A ball that bounces back has a negative final velocity relative to its initial motion.
  • For a bounce, the change in momentum is larger than for a ball that stops, because the ball reverses direction.
  • When a question asks for the average force on a ball, use the impulse and the contact time, and state the direction of the force.

Common errors that lose marks

  • Adding the speeds of two bodies moving in opposite directions instead of subtracting, because direction was not included.
  • Treating a non-isolated system as isolated, for example ignoring friction or a gravitational force that acts on the system from outside.
  • Confusing the impulse with the force, or failing to convert the time into seconds.

title: IGCSE Chemistry (OxfordAQA): Trends within the Periodic Table
content:
Trends within the Periodic Table

The Periodic Table is arranged in order of increasing atomic number, and that single decision explains almost every trend the course asks about. Elements in the same group have the same number of electrons in their outer shell, so they react in the same way; the trends down a group come from where that outer shell sits relative to the nucleus. This topic takes the three groups the specification names — Group 1, Group 7 and Group 0 — and works out why reactivity changes in the direction it does, then turns to the block of transition metals, whose properties are different enough that the exam expects you to contrast them with Group 1 in a table. Every trend below is written with its explanation, because the explanation is the mark.

1. What a group is, and what changes down it

A group is a vertical column. Elements in one group have the same number of outer-shell electrons — one for Group 1, seven for Group 7, a full shell for Group 0 — and that number, not the mass, is what decides how an element reacts. Going down a group the atoms get larger: each element has one more shell than the one above it, so the outer electron is further from the nucleus, and the inner shells shield it from the nuclear charge.

  • Down a group, the outer shell is further out and more shielded. The nucleus still attracts the outer electrons, but the pull at the surface is weaker because of the extra distance and the extra shells in between.
  • Across a period, atoms get smaller and the nuclear charge grows. The electrons are added to the same shell, so the pull on that shell increases from left to right.
  • Metals lose electrons, non-metals gain them. A Group 1 atom has one outer electron and loses it easily; a Group 7 atom needs one more and takes it readily. This is why the two groups sit at opposite ends of the table and behave in opposite ways.

2. Group 1: the alkali metals

Lithium, sodium, potassium, rubidium and caesium are soft, low-density metals stored under oil because they react with water and with the air. They are called alkali metals because the hydroxide they form when they react with water is an alkali.

Reactivity increases down the group, and the reason is the outer electron. Going down, that electron is in a shell further from the nucleus and is shielded by more inner shells, so it is held less tightly and is lost more easily. The ion that forms is always 1+, and that is what makes the chemistry so regular: every Group 1 element forms the same compounds with the same formulas.

PropertyTrend down Group 1Reason
Reactivity with waterIncreasesThe outer electron is lost more easily
Melting pointDecreasesThe atoms are larger, so the metallic bonding holds them less strongly
SoftnessIncreasesWeaker metallic bonding, so the metal is easier to cut
DensityGenerally increasesThe atoms are heavier; potassium is the exception, and floats on water

3. Group 1 reactions you must be able to write

Every Group 1 metal reacts in the same three ways, and the equations follow the same pattern, which is why knowing one element is enough to predict the rest.

  • With water it forms the metal hydroxide and hydrogen. Sodium melts into a ball and fizzes; potassium burns with a lilac flame and the reaction is violent enough to be dangerous. 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂
  • With oxygen it forms the metal oxide. 4Na + O₂ → 2Na₂O
  • With chlorine it forms the metal chloride, a white solid. 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl

The observation to quote is the one that changes down the group: lithium fizzes steadily and moves slowly, sodium fizzes vigorously and may melt, potassium ignites the hydrogen it produces. "It reacted" earns nothing; "it moved, fizzing, and shrank to a ball" is the observation the mark scheme pays for.

4. Group 7: the halogens

Fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine and astatine each have seven outer electrons and need one more to complete the shell, so they form 1− ions and pair up as diatomic molecules: F₂, Cl₂, Br₂, I₂. Their appearance and state change steadily down the group, which is a common one-mark question.

HalogenState at room temperatureColour
Fluorine, F₂GasPale yellow
Chlorine, Cl₂GasGreenish yellow
Bromine, Br₂LiquidRed-brown, with an orange vapour
Iodine, I₂SolidGrey-black, giving a purple vapour on heating

Reactivity decreases down the group, which is the opposite of Group 1, and the reason is the same fact read backwards. A halogen reacts by gaining an electron, and the nucleus must attract an electron into its outer shell. Down the group that shell is further from the nucleus and more shielded, so the attraction is weaker, the electron is gained less readily, and the element is less reactive.

5. Displacement: how the trend is tested

A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive one from a solution of its salt. This is the standard practical test of the trend, and it is a redox reaction: the halogen that is displaced is oxidised back to the element, and the halogen doing the displacing is reduced.

  • Chlorine added to potassium bromide solution turns it orange, because bromine is made: Cl₂ + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br₂
  • Chlorine added to potassium iodide solution turns it brown, because iodine is made: Cl₂ + 2KI → 2KCl + I₂
  • Bromine added to potassium iodide solution turns it brown: Br₂ + 2KI → 2KBr + I₂
  • Bromine added to potassium chloride solution does nothing, because chlorine is more reactive and cannot be displaced.

Read the direction of each equation as evidence rather than something to memorise: the element on the left is the more reactive one, and it is the one that ends up in the compound.

6. Group 0: the noble gases

Helium, neon, argon, krypton and xenon have a full outer shell, so they neither lose nor gain electrons readily and are almost completely unreactive. They exist as single atoms rather than molecules, which is why their formulas are written He, Ne and Ar with no subscript.

  • Helium is used in balloons and airships because it is less dense than air and does not burn.
  • Argon fills filament lamps and shields a weld, because being unreactive it will not react with the hot metal.
  • Neon is used in advertising signs, where an electric discharge makes it glow.

Boiling point increases down the group even though reactivity does not change. Larger atoms have more electrons, so the intermolecular forces between their atoms are stronger and more energy is needed to separate them. That is a common exam trap: unreactive does not mean low boiling point.

7. Transition metals: what makes them different

The transition metals sit between Group 2 and Group 3, and they are the metals of everyday life: iron, copper, zinc, nickel, silver, gold. They are not one group in the same sense as Group 1 — their outer shells are similar but not identical — so their properties vary more. The specification asks you to know the typical properties and to contrast them with Group 1.

PropertyGroup 1 metalsTransition metals
HardnessSoft, cut with a knifeHard and strong
DensityLow; lithium, sodium and potassium floatHigh; most sink
Melting pointLow, and falling down the groupHigh, except mercury, which is liquid
ReactivityVery reactive, reacting with cold waterMuch less reactive; many do not react with water at all
CompoundsWhite or colourlessOften coloured
IonsOne charge only, 1+Several charges, for example Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺
Catalytic activityRareCommon

Two of those rows carry most of the marks. Variable oxidation state means the same metal can form more than one compound with different formulas — iron(II) chloride, FeCl₂, and iron(III) chloride, FeCl₃ — which is why the Roman numeral in the name is not decoration. Coloured compounds means a solution of copper(II) sulfate is blue and one of iron(II) sulfate is pale green, so colour becomes evidence for which ion is present.

8. Transition metals as catalysts

A catalyst speeds up a reaction without being used up, and transition metals are the standard examples because their surfaces and their variable oxidation states let them hold reacting species in place. Three named ones are worth learning, because each belongs to a process the specification also covers.

  • Iron catalyses the Haber process, N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃.
  • Vanadium(V) oxide, V₂O₅ catalyses the Contact process, 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃, which makes sulfuric acid.
  • Nickel catalyses the hydrogenation of alkenes, turning an unsaturated oil into a saturated fat.

Note what a catalyst does and does not do: it lowers the activation energy by providing an alternative pathway, so more collisions have enough energy to succeed. It does not change the position of an equilibrium, and it does not change the yield — it only gets the mixture there sooner.

9. Worked example: identifying a metal from its density

A student is given a rectangular bar of an unknown silvery metal. It has a mass of 178 g and a volume of 20.0 cm³. Decide whether it is a Group 1 metal or a transition metal.

ρ = m / V = 178 g ÷ 20.0 cm³ = 8.90 g/cm³

Key: ρ = density (g/cm³); m = mass (g); V = volume (cm³).

The density is 8.90 g/cm³, which is close to copper (8.96 g/cm³) and nickel (8.90 g/cm³) and is far above the Group 1 metals, whose densities are all below 2 g/cm³ and three of which float on water. The metal is therefore a transition metal.

The reasoning matters more than the number: a density near 9 g/cm³ could not belong to a Group 1 element, because those atoms are large and pack loosely, while transition metal atoms are smaller and their metallic bonding pulls them together tightly. If the question gives you the mass and the dimensions instead, find the volume first by multiplying length by width by height, and keep the units consistent before dividing.

10. Typical mistakes

  • Saying reactivity increases down Group 7 as well as Group 1. It increases down Group 1 and decreases down Group 7, and both are explained by the same distance-and-shielding argument.
  • Giving the trend without the reason. "Potassium is more reactive than sodium" is worth one mark; "because its outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded, so it is lost more easily" is worth the second.
  • Writing Group 1 formulas as if the metal were 2+. Sodium chloride is NaCl, not NaCl₂, because the sodium ion is Na⁺.
  • Saying the noble gases have a low boiling point because they are unreactive. The two facts are separate: their boiling points rise down the group with the number of electrons.
  • Assuming every transition metal is magnetic, or that every one is a good catalyst. Manganese and copper are transition metals, and neither is magnetic in the way iron is.
  • Calling a catalyst a reactant, or claiming it increases the yield. It increases the rate and is recovered at the end.

11. Exam-style questions

  1. Explain why potassium reacts more vigorously with water than sodium does. Answer: Potassium's outer electron is in a shell further from the nucleus and is shielded by more inner shells than sodium's, so it is held less tightly and lost more easily, making the reaction faster.
  2. Chlorine is bubbled through potassium bromide solution. State the observation and write the equation. Answer: The colourless solution turns orange-brown as bromine is formed: Cl₂ + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br₂.
  3. Explain why bromine does not displace chlorine from potassium chloride solution. Answer: Chlorine is more reactive than bromine, because its outer shell is closer to the nucleus and less shielded, so chlorine is the one that gains the electron and bromine cannot displace it.
  4. Give two properties that a transition metal has and a Group 1 metal does not. Answer: It forms coloured compounds, and it can form ions with more than one charge (for example Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺). It is also harder and denser with a higher melting point.
  5. Argon is used to fill filament lamps. Explain the property that makes it suitable. Answer: Argon has a full outer shell, so it is unreactive and will not react with the hot filament, which would otherwise burn away.
  6. A 15.0 cm³ sample of a metal has a mass of 134 g. Calculate its density and suggest whether it is a transition metal. Answer: ρ = m / V = 134 ÷ 15.0 = 8.93 g/cm³, which is far above the density of a Group 1 metal and consistent with a transition metal such as copper.
  7. State one use of a transition metal as a catalyst and name the process. Answer: Iron catalyses the Haber process, in which nitrogen and hydrogen react to form ammonia.

12. Revision checklist

  • I can give the group number, outer-shell electron count and ion charge for Groups 1, 7 and 0.
  • I can state the trend in reactivity down Groups 1 and 7 and explain both with distance and shielding.
  • I can write the equations for a Group 1 metal with water, oxygen and chlorine.
  • I can describe the appearance and state of each halogen at room temperature.
  • I can predict the result of any halogen displacement and write its equation.
  • I can explain why noble gas boiling points rise down the group.
  • I can contrast transition metals with Group 1 metals in at least four properties.
  • I can name three transition metal catalysts and the process each is used in.
  • I can calculate a density and use it to argue which family a metal belongs to.

title: IGCSE Biology: Respiration
content:
IGCSE Biology: Respiration

Respiration is the process that keeps every cell alive: the chemical release of energy from glucose inside cells. It is not breathing, it is not combustion, and it happens day and night in every organism. This note separates the definitions that examiners insist on, writes and balances both the aerobic and anaerobic equations from first principles, traces how energy from glucose is transferred to ATP for use in the cell, and covers oxygen debt, the oxygen debt calculation, and the practical methods for measuring respiration rate (the respirometer) that appear in Paper 6.

What respiration is — and what it is not

Respiration is the chemical reactions in cells that break down nutrient molecules (usually glucose) to release energy, which is transferred to ATP. It occurs in every living cell, all the time. Aerobic respiration requires oxygen and releases much more energy per glucose molecule; anaerobic respiration occurs without oxygen and releases much less. Important distinctions: breathing (ventilation) brings oxygen to the lungs and removes carbon dioxide, but respiration happens inside cells; combustion is burning outside the body; and the energy released is used for muscle contraction, active transport, protein synthesis, cell division and maintaining body temperature (mammals and birds are endothermic).

Aerobic respiration: the equation and its stages

Word equation: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy. Symbol equation: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O. Balance check: 6 carbons each side; 12 hydrogens each side (6 × 2 in water); oxygens: 6 + 12 = 18 on the left, 12 + 6 = 18 on the right. The full pathway at A Level and in the supplement: glycolysis (in the cytoplasm) splits glucose into two pyruvate molecules, releasing a small amount of ATP and reduced NAD; the link reaction and Krebs cycle (in the mitochondrial matrix) strip hydrogen and release carbon dioxide; oxidative phosphorylation (on the inner mitochondrial membrane) uses the hydrogen electrons in the electron transfer chain to make large amounts of ATP, with oxygen as the final electron acceptor forming water. The folded cristae of the inner membrane increase surface area for the ATP-generating enzymes — a favourite structure-function question.

Anaerobic respiration in animals and plants

When oxygen is short (sprinting, flooded roots), cells switch to anaerobic respiration. In animals: glucose → lactic acid (+ a little energy), equation C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₃H₆O₃. Only glycolysis runs, so the yield is 2 ATP per glucose versus about 30–32 aerobically. Lactic acid accumulates in muscles, causing fatigue and cramp, and must be broken down later. In plants and yeast: glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide + energy, equation C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂. Yeast fermentation is used industrially to make bread (carbon dioxide raises the dough) and alcoholic drinks (ethanol); both anaerobic equations must balance — check the atoms: C₆ → 2C₃ (animals) or 2C₂ + 2C (yeast, six carbons total), H₁₂ → 6 in two lactic acid molecules or 12 in two ethanol molecules, and the oxygens accordingly.

Oxygen debt

Oxygen debt (excess post-exercise oxygen consumption) is the extra oxygen the body takes in after exercise to restore itself: repaying the lactic acid (oxidising it back to carbon dioxide and water in the liver), resynthesising ATP and phosphocreatine stores, and returning heart rate, breathing rate and body temperature to resting levels. Measure it as the volume of oxygen consumed during recovery minus the resting requirement over the same period. The heavier the exercise, the larger the debt and the longer the recovery — which is exactly the shape of the oxygen-uptake graph before, during and after exercise.

Measuring respiration rate: the respirometer

A respirometer measures oxygen consumption: germinating seeds (actively respiring) are placed in a sealed tube with a small tube of sodium hydroxide solution (which absorbs the carbon dioxide produced, so any gas volume change is due to oxygen use). As oxygen is consumed, gas pressure drops and the coloured drop of liquid in the capillary tube moves towards the apparatus; the distance moved per minute is proportional to the rate of respiration. Control tube: same setup with dead seeds (no respiration) to correct for atmospheric pressure and temperature changes. Variables: independent = temperature or seed type; dependent = distance moved per minute (or volume of oxygen per gram per hour); controls = same mass of seeds, same volume of sodium hydroxide, same time, same apparatus. Use a water bath to set temperature. To calculate actual oxygen consumption, measure the distance moved and convert using the capillary tube's internal volume (volume = π × radius² × distance).

Aerobic and anaerobic compared

FeatureAerobic respirationAnaerobic respiration
OxygenRequiredAbsent or in short supply
SiteCytoplasm and mitochondriaCytoplasm only
Products (animals)Carbon dioxide and waterLactic acid
Products (yeast/plants)Carbon dioxide and waterEthanol and carbon dioxide
Energy per glucoseLarge amount (about 30-32 ATP)Small amount (2 ATP)
EquationC₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂OC₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₃H₆O₃ (animals)

The two pathways also differ in what happens to the hydrogen stripped from glucose. In aerobic respiration the hydrogen is carried by NAD to the inner mitochondrial membrane, where the electron transfer chain passes it to oxygen, forming water and driving the phosphorylation of ADP to ATP — this final step is where most of the ATP comes from. In anaerobic respiration there is no oxygen to accept the hydrogen, so pyruvate itself accepts it (forming lactic acid in animals) or loses carbon dioxide first (forming ethanol in yeast), and the electron transfer chain never runs. That single difference explains the enormous gap in ATP yield, and it is the mechanistic point A Level examiners probe when they ask why lactic acid forms at all.

Worked example: a full anaerobic comparison and the respirometer calculation

An athlete runs 400 m and produces 12 g of lactic acid. What mass of glucose was respired anaerobically? Step 1: the equation: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₃H₆O₃; relative formula masses: glucose 180, lactic acid 90 each, so 180 g of glucose gives 2 × 90 = 180 g of lactic acid. Step 2: ratio 180:180, that is 1:1. Step 3: 12 g lactic acid therefore came from 12 g of glucose. Now the respirometer: in 10 minutes at 25 °C the drop moved 12 mm; at 15 °C it moved 4 mm; dead-seed control moved 1 mm in both cases. Step 1: subtract the control (temperature effects on gas volume): 12 − 1 = 11 mm and 4 − 1 = 3 mm. Step 2: per minute: 11 ÷ 10 = 1.1 mm/min and 3 ÷ 10 = 0.3 mm/min. Step 3: compare: respiration at 25 °C is 1.1 ÷ 0.3 ≈ 3.7 times faster than at 15 °C. Step 4: explain: enzymes of respiration have more kinetic energy at the higher temperature, so more frequent successful collisions.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Defining respiration as "breathing" — it is a chemical process in cells; the distinction is worth a mark almost every year.
  • Writing "energy is released" without saying it is "transferred to ATP" — ATP is the usable energy currency, and the phrasing earns marks.
  • Unbalanced equations: aerobic has 6O₂ and 6H₂O — anything else loses marks.
  • Writing lactic acid as "lactate" only or giving the wrong formula; the symbol equation C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₃H₆O₃ is required at this level.
  • Claiming anaerobic respiration "releases no energy" — it releases less, not none.
  • Explaining oxygen debt as "paying back oxygen": it is the oxygen used to oxidise lactic acid and restore ATP, measured as extra uptake.
  • Forgetting the control (dead seeds) in a respirometer plan — a whole mark for "controls for atmospheric pressure/temperature".
  • Saying the mitochondrion is "where respiration happens" without noting glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm.

Exam-style questions and answers

Q1. Write the word equation for aerobic respiration. (2 marks) Answer: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + (energy transferred to ATP) — one mark for reactants, one for products.

Q2. Compare aerobic and anaerobic respiration in muscle cells. (4 marks) Answer: aerobic uses oxygen, anaerobic does not (1); aerobic in mitochondria and cytoplasm, anaerobic in cytoplasm only (1); aerobic produces carbon dioxide and water, anaerobic produces lactic acid (1); aerobic releases much more energy per glucose (1).

Q3. Explain what happens to lactic acid after exercise. (3 marks) Answer: it is transported to the liver (1); oxidised to carbon dioxide and water or converted back to glycogen (1); the oxygen used in this and in restoring ATP/heat is the oxygen debt (1).

Q4. Describe how you would use a respirometer to compare respiration rates in germinating and dead seeds. (4 marks) Answer: place equal masses in sealed tubes with sodium hydroxide to absorb carbon dioxide (1); record distance moved by the coloured drop per minute (1); run a dead-seed control to correct for pressure/temperature (1); keep temperature constant in a water bath and repeat for means (1).

Q5. Explain why the rate of respiration increases when temperature rises from 15 °C to 25 °C. (2 marks) Answer: enzymes gain kinetic energy (1); more frequent successful collisions, so respiration is faster (1).

title: Numerical Methods — Study Notes
content:
Numerical methods

Edexcel International A Level Mathematics — Pure Mathematics 3 (WMA13), sat at A2.

When an equation cannot be solved algebraically, numerical methods locate roots to required accuracy. You must know three families: change of sign, fixed-point iteration and Newton-Raphson.

Change of sign (decimal search)

If f is continuous and f(a) and f(b) have opposite signs, there is a root in (a, b). Bisection repeatedly halves the interval; a decimal search tests x = 1.0, 1.1, 1.2, ... until the sign changes. The method fails for repeated roots (the graph touches the axis without crossing).

Fixed-point iteration

Rearrange f(x) = 0 into x = g(x), then iterate x_(n+1) = g(x_n). Near the root the iteration converges when |g'(x)| < 1 at the root; if |g'(x)| > 1 it diverges. The iteration staircase/cobweb diagrams show this.

Newton-Raphson

x_(n+1) = x_n - f(x_n) / f'(x_n).

It uses the tangent at the current estimate and converges quadratically (fast), but it can fail: if f'(x_n) = 0 the tangent is vertical, and a poor starting point can send the sequence to a different root or into a loop.

Accuracy and error bounds

  • A sign change over an interval of width w brackets the root to within w; quoting the midpoint gives error at most w/2.
  • Iterate until successive values agree to the required accuracy (e.g. 3 s.f.).
  • Always substitute the final value back into f to confirm f(root) is close to 0.

Choosing a method

  • Bisection: guaranteed on a bracketed interval but slow.
  • Newton-Raphson: fast, needs f' and a good starting value.
  • Iteration: simple, but convergence depends on the rearrangement.

title: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Area, Perimeter and Volume
content:
Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Area, Perimeter and Volume

Measurement questions are the most reliable marks on the paper — provided you convert units correctly and choose the right formula. This note builds the mensuration toolkit from zero: the unit system and its tricky area and volume conversions, the area formulas for every plane shape with derivations, circles, arcs and sectors, the volume and surface area of every solid in the syllabus, and compound shapes — how to add and subtract the pieces. Every worked example shows the substitution and the units, because units and premature rounding are where the marks disappear.

Units of measure

Length, area and volume units are linked by powers of the linear conversion factor:

ConversionLengthAreaVolume
1 m = 100 cm× 100× 100² = 10 000× 100³ = 1 000 000
1 cm = 10 mm× 10× 100× 1000
1 km = 1000 m× 1000× 10⁶× 10⁹

Capacity: 1 litre = 1000 cm³ = 1000 ml; 1 m³ = 1000 litres. The classic trap is converting area with a length factor — 1 m² is 10 000 cm², not 100 cm².

Worked example. Convert 3.5 m² to cm² and 2500 cm³ to litres.

3.5 m² = 3.5 × 10 000 = 35 000 cm²
2500 cm³ = 2500/1000 = 2.5 litres

Area and perimeter of plane shapes

ShapePerimeterArea
Rectangle2(l + w)l × w
Trianglesum of sides½ × base × perpendicular height
Parallelogram2(a + b)base × perpendicular height
Trapeziumsum of sides½(a + b) × h (parallel sides a, b)
Circle2πrπr²

The triangle and parallelogram formulas both need the perpendicular height — not a slanted side. That single word accounts for more lost marks than any other in mensuration.

Worked example. Find the area of a trapezium with parallel sides 7 cm and 11 cm and height 5 cm.

A = (1/2)(a + b) h = 0.5 x (7 + 11) × 5
  = 0.5 × 18 × 5 = 45 cm²

Worked example 2 (triangle). A triangle has sides 6 cm, 8 cm, 10 cm. Is it right-angled, and what is its area?

6² + 8² = 36 + 64 = 100 = 10², so yes - right-angled
at the 6-8 corner. Area = (1/2) × 6 × 8 = 24 cm².

Circles, arcs and sectors

An arc is a fraction of the circumference; a sector is the same fraction of the area. The fraction is the angle over a full turn:

circumference = 2 π r;  area = π r²

arc length  = (θ/360) × 2 π r
sector area = (θ/360) x π r²
perimeter of a sector = arc length + 2r
segment area = sector area - triangle area

Worked example. A sector has radius 9 cm and angle 140°. Find its arc length, sector area and perimeter (π = 3.142).

arc = (140/360) × 2 × 3.142 × 9 = 0.3889 × 56.56 = 21.99 cm
area = (140/360) × 3.142 × 81 = 0.3889 × 254.5 = 98.97 cm²
perimeter = 21.99 + 18 = 39.99 cm = 40.0 cm (3 s.f.)

The perimeter of a sector includes the two radii — students routinely answer only the arc length.

Worked example 2 (segment). Find the area of the segment cut off by a chord in a circle of radius 6 cm when the sector angle is 90°.

sector area = (90/360) × 3.142 × 36 = 28.28 cm²
triangle area = (1/2) × 6 × 6 = 18 cm² (right angle at centre)
segment = 28.28 - 18 = 10.28 cm²

Surface area and volume of solids

SolidVolumeSurface area
Cuboidl × w × h2(lw + lh + wh)
Prism (any cross-section)area of cross-section × length2 × cross-section + perimeter × length
Cylinderπr²h2πr² + 2πrh
Cone⅓πr²hπr² + πrl (l = slant height)
Sphere⁴⁄₃πr³4πr²
Pyramid⅓ × base area × heightsum of face areas

Slant height versus vertical height is the cone trap: volume uses the perpendicular height h, surface area uses the slant height l, and l² = r² + h² connects them.

Worked example 1 (cylinder). A cylinder has radius 4 cm and height 10 cm. Find its volume and total surface area.

V = π r² h = 3.142 × 16 × 10 = 502.7 cm³
SA = 2 π r² + 2 π r h = 2 × 3.142 × 16 + 2 × 3.142 × 4 × 10
   = 100.5 + 251.4 = 351.9 cm²  (352 cm², 3 s.f.)

Worked example 2 (cone). A cone has radius 5 cm and vertical height 12 cm. Find its volume and slant height.

V = (1/3) π r² h = (1/3) × 3.142 × 25 × 12 = 314.2 cm³
l = √(5² + 12²) = √(169) = 13 cm

Worked example 3 (sphere). Find the volume of a sphere of radius 6 cm.

V = (4/3) π r³ = (4/3) × 3.142 × 216 = 904.8 cm³

Compound shapes: add and subtract

Compound figures are split into standard shapes (add) or standard shapes with a piece removed (subtract). The discipline: draw the split lines, label each sub-shape's dimensions, compute each area separately, then combine.

Worked example. An L-shape is made from a 10 cm × 8 cm rectangle with a 4 cm × 3 cm rectangle removed from one corner. Find its area and perimeter.

area = 10 × 8 - 4 × 3 = 80 - 12 = 68 cm²
perimeter: trace the outline:
10 + 8 + 6 + 5 + 4 + 3 = 36 cm
(6 = 10 - 4 along the removed edge; 5 = 8 - 3)

Worked example 2 (semicircle on a rectangle). A running track is a 60 m by 30 m rectangle with a semicircle of diameter 30 m at each end. Find its area.

rectangle = 60 × 30 = 1800 m²
two semicircles = one full circle of radius 15:
  π x 225 = 706.9 m²
total = 1800 + 706.9 = 2507 m²  (2510 m², 3 s.f.)

Worked examples: composite solids

Composite solids combine the standard formulas: a silo is a cylinder with a hemisphere on top; a pencil is a cylinder with a cone; a capsule is a cylinder with two hemispheres. The method: split the solid, compute each volume, add; for surface area, add only the faces that are actually exposed (the join is hidden).

Worked example. A capsule is a cylinder of radius 3 cm and length 10 cm with a hemisphere at each end. Find its total volume and surface area.

cylinder volume = π r² h = 3.142 × 9 × 10 = 282.8 cm³
two hemispheres = one sphere: (4/3) π r³ = (4/3) × 3.142 × 27
               = 113.1 cm³
total volume = 282.8 + 113.1 = 395.9 cm³

surface area: cylinder curved surface 2 π r h = 188.5 cm²
plus one full sphere 4 π r² = 113.1 cm²
total = 301.6 cm²  (the circular joins are internal, not exposed)

Worked example 2 (frustum-free method). A cone of radius 6 cm and height 9 cm has its top 3 cm cut off parallel to the base. Find the volume removed.

the removed cone is similar to the whole cone, scale k = 3/9 = 1/3
volume of whole cone = (1/3) π x 36 × 9 = 339.3 cm³
removed volume = k³ x whole = (1/27) × 339.3 = 12.6 cm³
(the same as computing directly with radius 2 cm and height 3 cm)

Worked examples: reverse problems and density

Worked example. A cylindrical tank of radius 1.5 m holds 20 m³ of water. Find the depth.

V = π r² h  →  h = V/(π r²) = 20/(3.142 × 2.25)
h = 20/7.07 = 2.83 m

Worked example 2 (density). A metal cuboid 5 cm × 4 cm × 2 cm has mass 312 g. Find its density in g cm⁻³ and kg m⁻³.

volume = 5 × 4 × 2 = 40 cm³
density = 312/40 = 7.8 g cm⁻³
in kg m⁻³: 7.8 × 1000 = 7800 kg m⁻³

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Units) Convert 2.4 m² to cm² and 0.75 litres to cm³. Answer: 24 000 cm²; 750 cm³.
  2. (Trapezium) Parallel sides 12 cm and 8 cm, height 6 cm. Find the area. Answer: ½(12 + 8) × 6 = 60 cm².
  3. (Sector) Radius 7 cm, angle 72°. Find arc length and sector area. Answer: arc = (72/360) × 2π × 7 = 8.80 cm; area = (72/360) × π × 49 = 61.6 cm².
  4. (Cylinder) Radius 3 cm, height 12 cm. Find the volume. Answer: π × 9 × 12 = 339 cm³ (3 s.f.).
  5. (Cone) Radius 8 cm, height 15 cm. Find the volume and slant height. Answer: V = ⅓π × 64 × 15 = 1005 cm³; l = √(64 + 225) = 17 cm.
  6. (Sphere) Diameter 10 cm. Find the surface area. Answer: r = 5; SA = 4π × 25 = 314 cm².
  7. (Compound) A rectangle 14 m × 6 m has a semicircle of diameter 6 m removed from one end. Find the area. Answer: 84 − ½π × 9 = 84 − 14.14 = 69.9 m².
  8. (Reverse) A sphere has volume 288 cm³. Find its radius. Answer: 288 = ⁴⁄₃πr³ → r³ = 288 × 3/(4π) = 68.75 → r = 4.10 cm.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Slant versus perpendicular height: triangle/parallelogram areas use perpendicular height; cone surface area uses slant height; cone volume uses perpendicular height.
  • Area unit conversion: 1 m² = 10 000 cm² and 1 cm² = 100 mm². Multiplying by 100 instead of 10 000 is the single most common mensuration error.
  • Sector perimeter: add the two radii to the arc length. The question asks for the perimeter of the sector, not the arc.
  • Using the diameter as radius: halve the diameter first; every circle formula uses r.
  • π precision: use 3.142 or the calculator's π; rounding π to 3 loses accuracy on multi-step questions. Round only the final answer (usually 3 s.f. or as stated).
  • Compound shape subtraction: remove the correct region and keep the outline consistent — recompute the perimeter from the actual boundary, not the sum of the sub-shapes' perimeters.
  • Volume of a prism: cross-section area × length, where the length is perpendicular to the cross-section (a slanted prism uses the perpendicular distance).
  • Units in the answer: cm² for area, cm³ for volume, and capacity conversions (1000 cm³ = 1 litre). A correct number with the wrong unit loses marks on Paper 2.
