title: Introductory Organic Chemistry and Alkanes — Study Notes
content:
Introductory Organic Chemistry and Alkanes

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH11, Topic 4. Organic chemistry is the chemistry of carbon compounds. Alkanes are the simplest family, and their reactions introduce the radical substitution mechanism used throughout the course.

Naming and formulae

  • A homologous series has the same general formula, similar chemical properties and a gradual change in physical properties.
  • Alkanes have the general formula CnH2n+2. Names depend on the longest carbon chain: meth-, eth-, prop-, but-, pent-, hex-.
  • Structural isomers have the same molecular formula but different connectivity, such as butane and methylpropane.

Fossil fuels and cracking

  • Alkanes are obtained from crude oil by fractional distillation; the fractions separate by boiling point, which rises with chain length.
  • Cracking breaks long chains into shorter, more useful alkanes and alkenes, using heat or a catalyst.

Radical substitution

  • Alkanes react with chlorine or bromine under UV light by free-radical substitution.
  • The three stages are initiation (Cl2 → 2Cl•), propagation (a radical reacts with an alkane, regenerating a radical) and termination (two radicals combine).
  • Propagation steps form the product; termination steps are rare, so they do not appear in the main yield.

Combustion

  • Complete combustion gives carbon dioxide and water; limited oxygen gives carbon monoxide or carbon (soot).

Exam tip: when writing a radical mechanism, use a single-headed arrow for each electron moved and always show the radical dot.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Radical substitution, applied to methane and chlorine under UV light: initiation Cl₂ → 2Cl• (homolytic fission, UV required); propagation CH₄ + Cl• → CH₃• + HCl, then CH₃• + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl•; termination when two radicals combine. Each step needs its own equation for the marks.
  • Why a mixture forms: radical substitution is not selective, so chloromethane, dichloromethane and so on all form. Excess methane favours monosubstitution, because a chlorine radical is more likely to meet a methane molecule than a chloromethane molecule.
  • Combustion: complete combustion gives CO₂ and H₂O. Incomplete combustion, with limited oxygen, gives CO, which is toxic because it binds haemoglobin more strongly than oxygen does. State the limited oxygen supply in the answer.
  • Naming: the longest carbon chain gives the parent, and the lowest possible number goes to the first branch. Name branches alphabetically with their numbers, and use di-, tri- for repeated branches, for example 2,2-dimethylpropane.

title: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Right-Angled Trigonometry
content:
Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Right-Angled Trigonometry

Right-angled triangles are the most useful triangles in mathematics: Pythagoras relates the three sides, and the sine, cosine and tangent ratios relate sides to angles. Between them they solve every distance and angle problem the IGCSE sets, from ladders against walls to angles of elevation and three-figure bearings. This note builds the topic from zero: Pythagoras with its converse and 3D use, the SOHCAHTOA ratios with the selection method, exact values derived rather than memorised, and the multi-step problems that combine Pythagoras with trigonometry.

Pythagoras' theorem

in a right-angled triangle: a² + b² = c²
where c is the hypotenuse (the side opposite the right angle)

The theorem is a statement about areas: the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides. The converse identifies right angles: if a² + b² = c² for the longest side c, the triangle is right-angled — the standard test for 3-4-5 and 5-12-13 triangles.

Worked example 1. A right-angled triangle has legs 6 cm and 8 cm. Find the hypotenuse.

c² = 6² + 8² = 36 + 64 = 100
c = 10 cm

Worked example 2 (finding a leg). The hypotenuse is 13 cm and one leg is 5 cm. Find the other leg.

a² = 13² - 5² = 169 - 25 = 144
a = 12 cm

Worked example 3 (converse). Is a triangle with sides 7, 24, 25 right-angled?

7² + 24² = 49 + 576 = 625 = 25²
yes - right-angled, with the right angle opposite the 25 side

Pythagoras in three dimensions

In a cuboid, the space diagonal uses Pythagoras twice: first across the base, then up the height.

space diagonal = √(l² + w² + h²)

Worked example. A cuboid is 3 cm by 4 cm by 12 cm. Find the length of the space diagonal.

d = √(9 + 16 + 144) = √(169) = 13 cm

The three ratios: SOHCAHTOA

sin(θ) = opposite/hypotenuse      (SOH)
cos(θ) = adjacent/hypotenuse      (CAH)
tan(θ) = opposite/adjacent       (TOA)

Label the sides relative to the angle in question: the hypotenuse is always opposite the right angle; the opposite is across from the angle; the adjacent is the remaining side touching the angle. The selection method: mark the known side and the wanted side, then ask which ratio contains both.

Worked example 1 (finding a side). In a right-angled triangle, the angle is 35° and the hypotenuse is 12 cm. Find the opposite side.

known: hypotenuse; want: opposite  →  sine
sin(35) = opposite/12
opposite = 12 sin(35) = 12 × 0.574 = 6.88 cm

Worked example 2 (finding a side with cosine). Angle 40°, hypotenuse 20 cm; find the adjacent side.

cos(40) = adjacent/20
adjacent = 20 cos(40) = 20 × 0.766 = 15.3 cm

Worked example 3 (finding an angle). Opposite 5 cm, adjacent 9 cm. Find the angle.

tan(θ) = 5/9 = 0.5556
θ = tan-1(0.5556) = 29.1 °

For angles, use the inverse functions (sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹, tan⁻¹) and check the calculator is in degree mode — a radian-mode calculator turns 90° into 1.57 and ruins the paper.

Exact trigonometric values

Three angles have exact values worth knowing, derived from two special triangles:

Anglesincostan
30°1/2√3/21/√3
45°1/√21/√21
60°√3/21/2√3

Derivation: a 45-45-90 triangle with legs 1 has hypotenuse √2 (Pythagoras), giving sin 45 = 1/√2. An equilateral triangle of side 2 split in half gives a 30-60-90 triangle with sides 1, √3, 2, giving all six values. Deriving them once beats memorising them badly.

Two sanity checks keep the table honest: sine increases from 0 to 1 as the angle grows from 0° to 90°, so sin 30 must be smaller than sin 60; and cosine runs the other way, so cos 30 must be larger than cos 60. If an exact value breaks either ordering, the table has been misremembered.

Worked example. Find the exact value of sin 60° × tan 30°.

sin 60 = √(3)/2;  tan 30 = 1/√(3)
product = (√(3)/2) x (1/√(3)) = 1/2

Angles of elevation and depression

An angle of elevation is measured upward from the horizontal to an object; an angle of depression is measured downward. Both are measured from the observer's eye line, and the angle of depression from A to B equals the angle of elevation from B to A (alternate angles).

Worked example. From a point 40 m from the base of a tower, the angle of elevation to the top is 32°. Find the tower's height.

tan(32) = height/40
height = 40 tan(32) = 40 × 0.625 = 25.0 m

Worked example 2 (depression). A cliff is 60 m high; the angle of depression to a boat is 25°. Find the horizontal distance to the boat.

the angle at the boat is also 25 ° (alternate)
tan(25) = 60/d  →  d = 60/tan(25) = 60/0.466 = 128.7 m

Choosing the method: a decision routine

Most lost trigonometry marks come from choosing the wrong tool, not from arithmetic. The routine below takes ten seconds and removes the guesswork:

  1. Is there a right angle? If not, the question needs the sine or cosine rule (a different topic) — do not force SOHCAHTOA onto a triangle without a right angle.
  2. What do you know — two sides, or a side and an angle? Two sides with no angle means Pythagoras. A side and an angle means trigonometry.
  3. Which ratio? Mark the known side and the target relative to the given angle, then pick the ratio containing both: sin uses opposite and hypotenuse, cos uses adjacent and hypotenuse, tan uses opposite and adjacent.
  4. What is the unknown — a side or an angle? A side comes from multiplying; an angle needs the inverse function.

Worked example. A roof rafter is 4.5 m long and meets the horizontal at 38°. Find the vertical rise and the horizontal run.

rise: sin(38) = rise/4.5  →  rise = 4.5 sin(38) = 2.77 m
run:  cos(38) = run/4.5   →  run = 4.5 cos(38) = 3.55 m
check: 2.77² + 3.55² = 7.67 + 12.60 = 20.27 ~ 4.5²

Worked example 2 (finding the angle of a ladder). A 6 m ladder reaches 5.2 m up a wall. Find the angle it makes with the ground.

sin(θ) = 5.2/6 = 0.867  →  θ = 60.1 °

Multi-step problems: Pythagoras and trigonometry together

Many questions need both tools: Pythagoras to find a side in one triangle, trigonometry to use it in another. The method: draw and label every triangle, find the shared side first, then proceed.

Worked example. A ladder 5 m long leans against a wall, with its foot 2 m from the wall. Find the height reached and the angle the ladder makes with the ground.

height: h² = 5² - 2² = 25 - 4 = 21  →  h = 4.58 m
angle: cos(θ) = 2/5 = 0.4  →  θ = 66.4 °

Worked example 2 (two triangles). From a point P, the angle of elevation to the top of a building is 30°; from a point Q, 20 m closer, it is 45°. Find the height.

let h be the height and x the distance from Q to the base.
tan(45) = h/x  →  h = x
tan(30) = h/(x + 20)
h = (x + 20) tan(30) = (h + 20)(1/√(3))
h √(3) = h + 20  →  h(√(3) - 1) = 20
h = 20/(1.732 - 1) = 20/0.732 = 27.3 m

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Pythagoras) A right-angled triangle has legs 9 and 12. Find the hypotenuse. Answer: √(81 + 144) = √225 = 15.
  2. (Leg) Hypotenuse 17, one leg 8. Find the other. Answer: √(289 − 64) = 15.
  3. (Ratio) Angle 28°, adjacent 15 cm. Find the opposite side. Answer: tan 28 = o/15 → o = 15 × 0.532 = 7.98 cm.
  4. (Angle) Opposite 7, hypotenuse 10. Find the angle. Answer: sin θ = 0.7 → θ = 44.4°.
  5. (Exact) Find cos 30° exactly. Answer: √3/2.
  6. (Elevation) From 25 m away, the angle of elevation to a tree top is 40°. Find the height. Answer: 25 tan 40 = 25 × 0.839 = 21.0 m.
  7. (3D) A cuboid is 2 cm by 3 cm by 6 cm. Find its space diagonal. Answer: √(4 + 9 + 36) = √49 = 7 cm.
  8. (Combined) A ship sails 30 km east then 40 km north. Find its distance from the start and the bearing of its final position. Answer: distance = 50 km; tan θ = 40/30 → θ = 53.1°, bearing 053°.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Calculator mode: check DEG, not RAD or GRAD, before any trigonometric calculation. A radian answer is usually obviously wrong (tiny or huge), but only if you check.
  • Wrong ratio: label the sides relative to the angle before choosing SOH, CAH or TOA; picking by habit is the commonest trigonometry error.
  • Hypotenuse identification: the hypotenuse is opposite the right angle, not necessarily the longest-looking side on the diagram.
  • Pythagoras with the hypotenuse as a leg: c² = a² + b² only when c is the hypotenuse; finding a leg requires subtraction.
  • Rounding early: keep full calculator accuracy until the final answer; round to 3 s.f. (or 1 d.p. for angles unless told otherwise).
  • Angle of depression drawn from the wrong line: it is measured from the horizontal, not from the cliff face; the alternate-angle equality fixes the geometry.
  • Exact values with decimals: "exact" means surds and fractions, not 0.866; leaving √3/2 is required.
  • Missing units and labels: state cm, m, km and degrees; name the side or angle found, especially in multi-step problems.

Label the triangle before you reach for a ratio

Right-angled trigonometry is not three formulas to memorise; it is one decision made three times: which side am I given, which do I want, and which ratio connects them. Every error in this topic is a labelling error made before any calculation starts.

Only the hypotenuse is fixed. It is the side opposite the right angle, and it is always the longest. "Opposite" and "adjacent" are relative to the angle you are working with: in the figure, the side BC is opposite θ and AB is adjacent to it. Put the angle at C instead and those two swap. Annotate the diagram with O, A and H in pencil before choosing anything.

The ratios are ratios, which is why they work at any size. Similar triangles taught that corresponding sides scale together — double every side and the ratio stays the same. That is precisely why sin 30° is ½ for a triangle of any size:

sin θ = opposite / hypotenuse Key: θ = the angle inside the triangle; opposite = the side across from θ; hypotenuse = the side opposite the right angle.
cos θ = adjacent / hypotenuse Key: adjacent = the side next to θ that is not the hypotenuse.
tan θ = opposite / adjacent Key: the only ratio that does not use the hypotenuse.

Choosing in one step. Given an angle and one side, mark on the diagram which two sides the question involves, then read off: two sides with the hypotenuse means sine or cosine; two sides without it means tangent. Use the inverse function when the angle is the unknown.

Worked example. A ladder 5.0 m long leans against a wall, making 68° with the ground. How far up the wall does it reach, and how far is its foot from the wall?

height is opposite the 68° angle, ladder is the hypotenuse:

sin 68° = h / 5.0, so h = 5.0 × sin 68° = 5.0 × 0.9272 = 4.6 m

distance from the wall is adjacent:

cos 68° = d / 5.0, so d = 5.0 × cos 68° = 5.0 × 0.3746 = 1.9 m

Check with Pythagoras: 4.6² + 1.9² = 21.2 + 3.6 = 24.8 ≈ 25 = 5.0². That thirty-second check catches a swapped ratio every time, and the two answers being 4.6 and 1.9 rather than a plausible pair like 4.6 and 4.4 is exactly what the check is for.

The special angles come from two triangles. A 45-45-90 triangle with legs 1 gives sin 45° = 1/√2. Half of an equilateral triangle of side 2 gives sides 1, √3 and 2, hence sin 30° = ½, cos 30° = √3/2 and tan 60° = √3. These are worth deriving once so they are not three more things to memorise.

Where marks are lost. The calculator in radians or grads — check the mode before the first question, not after. Using the adjacent side when the question needs the opposite, because the labels were never written on the diagram. And rounding at 4.6 m then using 4.6 in Pythagoras: keep the full value and round only the answer.

Pythagoras' theorem in more depth

Pythagoras' theorem states that in a right-angled triangle the square of the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides, so c² = a² + b², where c is the hypotenuse. The theorem is used in two directions: to find a missing side when the triangle is known to be right-angled, and to test whether a triangle is right-angled at all. The subsections below cover both directions, the common number patterns, and the errors that cost marks.

Finding the hypotenuse

When the two shorter sides are known, add their squares and take the square root. For a triangle with shorter sides 5 cm and 12 cm, the hypotenuse is √(5² + 12²) = √(25 + 144) = √169 = 13 cm. The hypotenuse is always the longest side and always opposite the right angle, so it is the side that is added, not subtracted, in the calculation.

Finding a shorter side

When the hypotenuse and one shorter side are known, subtract the square of the known shorter side from the square of the hypotenuse, then take the square root. For a hypotenuse of 13 cm and a side of 5 cm, the missing side is √(13² − 5²) = √(169 − 25) = √144 = 12 cm. Write the subtraction out in full, because the most common error in this type of question is to add the squares by mistake.

Testing whether a triangle is right-angled

The converse of Pythagoras' theorem says that if the square of the longest side equals the sum of the squares of the other two, the triangle is right-angled. For sides 6, 8 and 10, the check is 6² + 8² = 36 + 64 = 100 = 10², so the triangle is right-angled. For sides 7, 8 and 10, the check is 49 + 64 = 113, which is greater than 100, so the triangle is acute and not right-angled. Always compare the squares of the longest side with the others.

Pythagorean triples

A Pythagorean triple is a set of three whole numbers that satisfy a² + b² = c². The most used are 3, 4, 5; 5, 12, 13; 8, 15, 17; and 7, 24, 25. Any multiple of a triple is also a triple, so 6, 8, 10 and 9, 12, 15 are triples. Recognising a triple lets you give an exact answer with no square root, which is often what the question wants when the sides are whole numbers.

Pythagoras in a problem with several triangles

Some questions need the theorem twice, because the first right-angled triangle gives a side that is needed in the second. For example, a rectangle 9 cm by 12 cm has a diagonal of √(9² + 12²) = 15 cm. If a second triangle uses that diagonal as one of its sides, the same method applies again. Mark the sides you have found on the diagram before starting the next step, so each calculation has its numbers ready.

Real-world problems with Pythagoras

A ladder leaning against a wall, a diagonal across a field and the straight-line distance between two towns are all Pythagoras problems once the right angle is identified. Draw the triangle, label the hypotenuse as the longest side, and state which right angle the theorem is being used at. A question that describes a route going east then north is a right-angled triangle formed by the two legs and the straight line between the ends.

Rounding and giving the answer

Leave square roots exact if the question asks for an exact answer, and give a decimal to the accuracy the question states. A calculation that gives √50 can be left as 5√2 for an exact answer, or written as 7.07 to 3 significant figures for a decimal answer. Do the rounding only at the last step, because rounding an intermediate square root and then squaring it can change the final answer.

Common errors with Pythagoras

The errors that lose marks are forgetting the square root at the end, adding when the question needs a subtraction, and applying the theorem to a triangle that is not right-angled. Check the answer by reversing the calculation: square the two shorter sides, add them, and confirm the result equals the square of the hypotenuse. A quick reversal catches most slips.

Trigonometric ratios in more depth

The sine, cosine and tangent ratios connect an angle in a right-angled triangle to the ratio of two sides. They are defined by sin θ = opposite ÷ hypotenuse, cos θ = adjacent ÷ hypotenuse and tan θ = opposite ÷ adjacent, and the calculator supplies the values. The subsections below cover naming the sides, the two directions of use (finding a side and finding an angle), and why the ratios depend only on the angle.

Naming the sides from the angle

The three sides are named from the point of view of the angle θ you are using. The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle and is always the longest. The opposite side is the one across from θ, and the adjacent side is the one next to θ that is not the hypotenuse. The same side is the opposite side for one angle and the adjacent side for the other acute angle, so name the sides again for each angle rather than once for the whole triangle.

Finding a side when an angle is known

Choose the ratio that uses the side you know and the side you want. If the hypotenuse is 10 cm and the angle is 30°, and you want the opposite side, use sin 30° = opposite ÷ 10, so the opposite side is 10 × sin 30° = 10 × 0.5 = 5 cm. Writing the ratio first, with the unknown alone on one side, is the step that keeps the working correct.

Finding an angle from a ratio

When two sides are known, find the ratio and use the inverse function on the calculator. For opposite 7 and adjacent 24, tan θ = 7 ÷ 24 = 0.2917, so θ = tan⁻¹(0.2917) = 16.3° to 1 decimal place. Use sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹ or tan⁻¹ according to the pair of sides, and never take the inverse of a ratio that you have not first worked out.

Setting the calculator to degrees

Every trigonometry question in this note uses degrees, so the calculator must be in degree mode before any value is found. A calculator in radian mode gives sin 30 = −0.988, which is a wrong answer that looks like a real value. Check the mode at the start of each exam and again if an answer looks unreasonable. A quick test is that sin 30 should return 0.5 in degree mode.

Why the ratios depend only on the angle

Two right-angled triangles with the same angle are similar, so the ratio of opposite to hypotenuse is the same in both. A triangle with a hypotenuse of 10 and opposite of 5 has the same sin θ as one with hypotenuse 20 and opposite 10. This is why a table of sine values works for every triangle, and it is the reason the ratios can be used to find unknown sides.

Complementary angles

In a right-angled triangle the two acute angles add to 90°, so each is the complement of the other. This gives sin θ = cos (90° − θ) and cos θ = sin (90° − θ). For example, sin 30° = cos 60° = 0.5. The relationship is useful for checking a value, and it explains why sine and cosine are the same curve shifted by 90°.

Tangent as sine over cosine

The tangent ratio is the sine divided by the cosine, because tan θ = (opposite ÷ hypotenuse) ÷ (adjacent ÷ hypotenuse) = opposite ÷ adjacent. This is the form to use when a question gives the tangent of an angle and asks for a side, and it also explains why tangent is undefined at 90°, where the adjacent side would have length zero.

Trigonometry in three dimensions

Many three-dimensional questions are answered by finding a right-angled triangle inside a solid and then using the methods already covered. The skill is to see the triangle, not to learn a new rule. The subsections below cover the angle between a line and a plane, the diagonal of a solid, and the choice of triangle in a pyramid or cone.

Finding a right-angled triangle inside a solid

In a cuboid, a cone or a pyramid, pick the triangle that contains both the length you want and a length you know. The triangle must have a right angle, and that right angle is often at a vertex where an edge meets the base or where the height meets the base. Draw the triangle on its own, separate from the solid, with the known lengths marked on it. This makes the method the same as the two-dimensional case.

The diagonal of a cuboid

A cuboid with sides 3 cm, 4 cm and 12 cm has a base diagonal of √(3² + 4²) = 5 cm. The space diagonal is then found using the base diagonal and the vertical edge: √(5² + 12²) = √169 = 13 cm. Two applications of Pythagoras give the answer, and the first triangle lies flat on the base while the second stands on its edge.

The angle between a line and the base

To find the angle a space diagonal makes with the base, first find the base diagonal, then use the triangle formed by the vertical height, the base diagonal and the space diagonal. For a box with a base diagonal of 10 cm and a vertical height of 12 cm, the angle is tan θ = 12 ÷ 10 = 1.2, so θ = tan⁻¹(1.2) = 50.2°. The angle is measured between the line and the base, not the vertical.

Heights in pyramids and cones

The vertical height of a pyramid or cone meets the base at a right angle, so it forms a right-angled triangle with a line from the centre of the base to a corner or to the edge. For a square-based pyramid with base side 10 cm, the distance from the centre of the base to a corner is √(5² + 5²) = √50 = 7.07 cm to 2 decimal places. The slant edge then uses that distance and the vertical height.

Choosing the triangle that contains the answer

Ask what you need to find, then identify the triangle whose sides include it. If the question asks for an angle in a plane through the solid, use the triangle in that plane. If it asks for a length along a diagonal of the base, use the triangle in the base. Writing down the triangle you have chosen before any calculation prevents the common error of using lengths from two different triangles in one step.

Sketching a three-dimensional figure

A clear sketch is worth marks, because it shows the examiner which triangle you are using. Draw the solid as a simple outline, use dashed lines for hidden edges, and mark the right angle with a small square. Label the lengths you know and the one you want. A sketch that is a neat outline with the triangle shaded is enough, and it does not need to be drawn to scale.

Checking the three-dimensional answer

A space diagonal must be longer than any edge of the solid, and an angle with the base must lie between 0° and 90°. In the cuboid example, 13 cm is longer than the 12 cm edge, which confirms the calculation. An answer that is shorter than an edge, or an angle above 90° for a line to the base, shows a wrong triangle or a swapped length.

title: Edexcel International A Level Chemistry Kinetics Revision Notes
content:
Kinetics: Edexcel International A Level Chemistry A2 Revision Notes

This topic belongs to Edexcel International A Level Chemistry WCH14 Topic 11 Kinetics. It covers the quantitative study of reaction speeds, the factors affecting them, experimental techniques, rate equations, order of reaction, reaction mechanisms including halogenoalkane hydrolysis, catalysts, core practicals, and the Arrhenius equation to calculate activation energy.

Definitions and Key Terms

To master kinetics, you must learn precise definitions for key terminology used in exam marking points.

  • Rate of reaction is the change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit time, with units mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹.
  • Rate equation is an expression showing how the rate of reaction depends on the concentrations of reactants, given in the form rate = k[A]m[B]n where m and n are the orders with respect to specific substances and are 0, 1 or 2.
  • Order with respect to a substance is the power to which the concentration of that reactant is raised in the rate equation.
  • Overall order of a reaction is the sum of all the individual orders of the reactants in the rate equation (m + n + ...).
  • Rate constant (k) is the proportionality constant that links the rate of reaction to the concentrations in the rate equation at a fixed temperature.
  • Half-life (t1/2) is the time taken for the concentration of a reactant to decrease to half of its initial value.
  • Rate-determining step is the slowest step in a multi-step reaction mechanism, which controls the overall rate of the reaction.
  • Activation energy (Ea) is the minimum kinetic energy that colliding particles must possess for a successful reaction to occur.
  • Heterogeneous catalyst is a catalyst in a different physical state or phase from the reactants, typically providing a solid surface for gas-phase reactions.
  • Homogeneous catalyst is a catalyst in the same physical state or phase as the reactants.

Experimental Techniques and Monitoring Methods

Choosing and justifying the correct experimental technique to obtain rate data is essential for both practical endorsements and written papers.

  • Titration involves quenching reaction aliquots at timed intervals and titrating against a standard solution, suitable for slow reactions like the acid-catalysed iodination of propanone.
  • Colorimetry measures the absorbance of light by a coloured species over time, ideal for reactions involving iodine or transition metal ions.
  • Mass change uses a sensitive balance to track mass loss over time as a gas evolves, suitable for reactions producing carbon dioxide.
  • Volume of gas evolved uses a gas syringe or inverted measuring cylinder over water to measure gas collected per unit time.
  • Initial-rate method involves carrying out separate experiments where different initial concentrations of one reagent are used while others are kept constant, measuring only the initial rate to avoid complications from reactant depletion.
  • Clock reaction is a convenient approximation of the initial-rate method where a single measurement is taken of the time taken for a specific visual change (such as a sudden colour change) to occur, assuming initial rate is proportional to 1 / t provided less than 15 percent of the reaction occurs.
  • Continuous monitoring method generates data over the entire course of a single reaction run to enable concentration-time or volume-time graphs to be plotted.

Deducing Reaction Orders and Calculations

You must be able to deduce the order with respect to a substance using different graphical and numerical representations.

  • Concentration-time graphs show how reactant concentration changes over time. A straight-line downward slope indicates a zero-order reaction with a constant rate. A downward curve with a constant half-life indicates a first-order reaction. A downward curve where the half-life increases as concentration decreases indicates a second-order reaction.
  • Rate-concentration graphs plot rate on the y-axis against concentration on the x-axis. A horizontal straight line parallel to the x-axis indicates zero order (rate is independent of concentration). A straight line passing through the origin indicates first order (rate is directly proportional to concentration). A curve with an increasing gradient (parabola) passing through the origin indicates second order (rate is proportional to concentration squared).
  • Initial-rate calculations compare how changes in initial concentration affect initial rate to find integer orders of 0, 1 or 2.
  • Half-life calculations use data from concentration-time graphs. Identifying a constant half-life is definitive proof that a reaction is first order with respect to that reactant.

Mechanisms and Rate-Determining Steps

The rate equation provides direct evidence for the composition of the rate-determining step and helps deduce reaction pathways.

  • Deducing rate-determining step from a rate equation means any species appearing in the rate equation with a non-zero order must be involved in the rate-determining step or in preceding fast steps that equilibrate before it. Stoichiometric coefficients of reactants in the rate-determining step match their orders in the rate equation.
  • Deducing reaction mechanism uses the rate equation alongside the overall stoichiometric equation. Fast steps before the rate-determining step introduce intermediate concentrations that can be substituted using equilibrium expressions.
  • Hydrolysis of halogenoalkanes provides classic evidence for mechanisms. Primary halogenoalkanes undergo SN2 hydrolysis, which is second-order overall (rate = k[halogenoalkane][OH−]), involving a single concerted step with a transition state. Tertiary halogenoalkanes undergo SN1 hydrolysis, which is first-order overall (rate = k[halogenoalkane]), where the slow rate-determining step is the heterolytic fission of the carbon-halogen bond to form a carbocation intermediate before rapid attack by the nucleophile.
  • Acid-catalysed iodination of propanone involves obtaining data to calculate the order with respect to propanone, hydrogen ions, and iodine. Iodine is found to be zero-order, while propanone and hydrogen ions are first-order. This data proves that neither iodine nor the second step is in the rate-determining step, leading to a mechanism featuring a slow, acid-catalysed tautomerization step forming an enol, followed by rapid reaction with iodine.

Heterogeneous Catalysis in Industry

Solid catalysts function by physical and chemical adsorption of gas-phase reactants.

  • Solid heterogeneous catalysts provide an active surface where reactant molecules are adsorbed.
  • Adsorption weakens internal covalent bonds within the reactant molecules, lowering the activation energy.
  • Reacted species subsequently desorb from the surface, freeing active sites for further catalytic cycles. Examples include iron in the Haber process and platinum, palladium, and rhodium in catalytic converters.

Core Practicals and Activation Energy

Experimental determination of activation energy links rate constants at different temperatures.

  • Core Practical 9a involves following the rate of the iodine-propanone reaction by a titrimetric method, quenching reaction samples with sodium hydrogencarbonate at timed intervals and titrating remaining iodine with standard sodium thiosulfate solution.
  • Core Practical 9b involves investigating a clock reaction, such as the Harcourt-Esson hydrogen peroxide-iodide reaction or the iodine clock, measuring time t for a colour change to appear using varying initial volumes of reagents.
  • Core Practical 10 involves finding the activation energy of a reaction by measuring reaction rates at different temperatures, calculating rate constants k, and applying the Arrhenius equation.
  • Arrhenius equation is given as k = A e^(−Ea / RT), where R is the ideal gas constant (8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹) and T is temperature in Kelvin.
  • Taking natural logarithms yields ln k = (−Ea / R) × (1 / T) + ln A.
  • Plotting ln k on the y-axis against 1 / T on the x-axis produces a straight line with gradient equal to −Ea / R, allowing Ea to be calculated from gradient × (−R).

Typical mistakes

  • Mistake: Assuming the orders in a rate equation match the stoichiometric coefficients in the overall balanced equation. Correction: Remember that rate equations must be determined experimentally, as overall equations show only reactants and products, not the step-by-step mechanism.
  • Mistake: Stating that the rate constant k changes when reactant concentrations are altered. Correction: The rate constant k is only affected by changes in temperature and the addition of a catalyst. Changing concentration alters the rate, not k.
  • Mistake: Forgetting temperature must be in Kelvin when using the Arrhenius equation. Correction: Always convert Celsius to Kelvin by adding 273.15 before calculating 1 / T or using ln k.
  • Mistake: Confusing the units of k for different overall orders. Correction: Derive the units dynamically by rearranging the rate equation: units of k = (units of rate) / (units of concentration) raised to the power of the overall order.

Exam-style questions

  1. Question: The reaction between nitrogen monoxide and hydrogen has the rate equation rate = k[NO]²[H₂]. State the order with respect to NO, the order with respect to H₂, and the overall order of the reaction. Answer: Order with respect to NO is 2; order with respect to H₂ is 1; overall order is 3 (obtained by summing 2 + 1).
  2. Question: Deduce the units of the rate constant k for a third-order overall reaction where rate is measured in mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹ and concentration in mol dm⁻³. Answer: Rearranging gives k = rate / [concentration]³. Units = (mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹) / (mol dm⁻³)³ = s⁻¹ mol⁻² dm⁶.
  3. Question: In an experiment, a student plots a concentration-time graph for a reactant and finds that successive half-lives are constant at 45 seconds. Deduce the order of the reaction with respect to this reactant. Answer: A constant half-life is the defining characteristic of a first-order reaction.
  4. Question: Explain why tertiary halogenoalkanes undergo hydrolysis via an SN1 mechanism whereas primary halogenoalkanes undergo an SN2 mechanism. Answer: Tertiary halogenoalkanes form a relatively stable tertiary carbocation intermediate due to the electron-releasing inductive effect of three alkyl groups, favouring SN1. Primary halogenoalkanes cannot form stable carbocations, so the attack by the nucleophile must occur simultaneously in a concerted SN2 transition state.
  5. Question: A graph of ln k against 1 / T for a reaction gives a straight line with a gradient of −12400 K. Calculate the activation energy Ea in kJ mol⁻¹. Use R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. Answer: Gradient = −Ea / R, so Ea = −(gradient) × R = −(−12400) × 8.31 = 103044 J mol⁻¹ = 103 kJ mol⁻¹ to 3 significant figures.

Use these notes alongside active recall of definitions, rigorous practice of initial-rate data tables, and past paper calculations on the Arrhenius equation. Next, revise Equilibria (Topic 12) to connect reaction kinetics with thermodynamic and dynamic stability.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Order from initial rates, applied to data showing the rate quadruples when [A] doubles with [B] constant: the order with respect to A is 2, because 2² = 4. Read the orders from the experiments, not from the coefficients in the equation, because the orders are found experimentally.
  • Rate constant units, applied to rate = k[A]²: rate is in mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹ and [A]² is in mol² dm⁻⁶, so k is in mol⁻¹ dm³ s⁻¹. If rate = 2.4 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹ at [A] = 0.20 mol dm⁻³, then k = 2.4 × 10⁻³ ÷ 0.040 = 0.060 mol⁻¹ dm³ s⁻¹.
  • Rate-determining step: the slowest step sets the rate, so the orders in the rate equation contain only the species up to and including that step. Catalysts appear in the rate equation if they take part in the rate-determining step.
  • Activation energy from Arrhenius data: a plot of ln k against 1/T gives a straight line with gradient −Ea ÷ R. Use the gradient, and convert the temperature to kelvin before you plot.

title:
Appendix K — Deep practical microbiology: how to think about the culturing and safety questions on the paper

The practical microbiology questions are the ones where candidates most often lose marks by writing a method without the reasoning, or by writing a safety list without the reasoning, or by writing a result description without saying what the result means. The reasoning that the question is really after is usually one of three kinds: why the technique is done that way, what the control is for, or what the observation means about the organism or the condition. If you can answer any of those three in a microbiology context, you can handle the practical question when it appears. If you only know the method and not the reasoning, you are vulnerable on exactly the marks that the practical question is usually built from. The reason for that is that the practical question is not usually a memory test for the method alone; it is a reasoning test about the method, the safety and the interpretation.

For culturing, the reasoning is usually about purity, safety and the reason for the particular setup. A good answer about a culturing method does not just say “spread the inoculum on agar” but says why the inoculum is diluted or isolated, why the plate is incubated in a particular way, why the lid is not fully opened, why the workspace is treated the way it is, and why the waste is disposed of the way it is. If you can say that, you have the reasoning. If you only say “the plate is incubated,” you have the label but not the reasoning, and the mark is in the reasoning. For safety, the reasoning is about what could go wrong and how the procedure prevents it, so a good safety answer is about sterilisation, containment and disposal as connected ideas, not just a list of rules. For interpretation, the reasoning is about what the growth or the lack of growth means, so a good interpretation answer is about the conditions that favour or prevent growth and about the limits of what can be concluded from the result.

The practical microbiology reasoning is also the reasoning that connects back to the theory, because the same ideas that matter in the lab, purity, safety, growth and interpretation, are the ideas that matter in the theory questions. If you can see that the practical and the theory are two views of the same ideas, you can answer the questions that span them, which are often the best-marked ones. If you only see the practical as a separate thing from the theory, you are likely to lose the marks on the questions that ask you to connect the two. The note has covered both, and the length is there so that you have the connection as well as the parts. If you use the note as a set of connected ideas rather than as a set of separate facts, you get the connection, and that is the use of the length.

Appendix L — The immune response as a process with timing, not just as a set of cells and molecules

The immune response is the topic where a candidate can get all the cells and molecules right and still lose marks by not saying the process in time order and by not saying why the timing matters. The process is that on first exposure, the specific lymphocytes have to be activated, expanded and differentiated over time, so the primary response is slow; on later exposure, the memory cells are already present and ready, so the secondary response is fast and strong. The point of the timing is that the immune system is not a single instantaneous event; it is a process with stages, and the stages matter for the comparison between primary and secondary responses and for the explanation of vaccination. If you can say that, you have the immune process in a form that scores marks. If you only say “the body makes antibodies,” you have the label but not the process, and the mark is in the process, because that is what the comparison and the vaccination questions are built from.

The memory idea is the one where the timing matters most, because the mark is often about the difference that memory makes, not just about the existence of memory. A good answer says that memory cells from the first exposure are responsible for the faster and stronger secondary response, and that this is the basis of vaccination, because vaccination produces the memory without the disease. It does not say that the immune system “remembers” in a vague sense without saying what the memory cells do, because the memory cell is the point, and the timing is the point. If you can say that the memory cells are the reason the secondary response is faster, you have the memory idea in a form that scores marks. If you only say “the second time is quicker,” you have the label but not the reasoning, and the reasoning is what the mark is after.

The specificity is the other idea where timing and process meet, because the specific response is specific and the non-specific responses are not, and that distinction matters for the comparison between the first line and the specific response. A good answer says that the first line is non-specific and the specific response is specific, and that the specific response includes antibodies and memory cells, while the first line includes barriers, inflammation and phagocytosis. It does not say that the specific response replaces the first line, because it does not; the two work together, and the mark is often about seeing that the system has both parts and that they have different roles. If you can say that, you have the immune comparison in a form that scores marks. If you only say “the body has specific immunity,” you have the label but not the comparison, and the mark is in the comparison, because that is what the question is usually built from.

Appendix M — Forensic biology as interpretation, and the things that can go wrong with it

Forensic biology is the topic where candidates most often lose marks by treating the evidence as a simple fact rather than as something with an interpretation and a set of things that can go wrong. The precise idea is that biological evidence such as DNA can be used to identify individuals and to link evidence to people or scenes, but the evidence is interpreted, and the interpretation depends on the quality of the sample, on whether it was contaminated, on the chain of custody, and on the context of the question. A good answer says that, and also says that a match or a mismatch is not a simple yes-no answer in the abstract but a result to be interpreted in context. If you can say that, you have the forensic biology idea in a form that scores marks. If you only say “DNA can identify someone,” you have the label but not the reasoning, and the reasoning is what the mark is after.

The things that can go wrong are the other part of the forensic reasoning that is worth saying explicitly, because they are the things that make the evidence meaningful or not. Contamination can make the evidence unreliable. Poor handling can lose or degrade the sample. A broken chain of custody can make the evidence hard to interpret in a legal context. A match in the wrong context can mean something different from a match in the right context. A good answer says that these are the things that matter, and that the value of the evidence depends on them. It does not say that forensic biology is always straightforward, because it is not, and it does not say that it is never reliable, because it can be. If you can say that the evidence has limits as well as value, you have the forensic reasoning in a form that scores marks. If you only have the label of “biological evidence,” you are missing the reasoning that the mark is after.

The identification idea is the one where the forensic topic connects back to the biology, because DNA profiling works because there is variation between individuals in certain DNA regions, and that is a biological fact about variation, not a forensic trick. A good answer says that the method depends on variation between individuals and on the ability to detect and compare those differences, and that the result is a pattern that can be matched or excluded. It does not say that DNA profiling is a magic identification without the variation, because the variation is the point. If you can say that, you have the DNA profiling idea in a form that scores marks. If you only say “DNA fingerprinting identifies people,” you have the label but not the reasoning, and the reasoning is what the mark is after when the question asks about the principle.

Appendix N — How to plan a revision session on this topic so the length of the note becomes an advantage

The length of this note is an advantage if you plan the revision session around it, and a disadvantage if you read it as one long block without a plan. The plan is to work through the note in the order the exam uses the topic: description first, then comparison, then evaluation. For description, work through the organisms, the culturing and safety, the growth curve, the first line of defence, the antigen-antibody idea, the B and T cells, the memory and secondary response, the vaccination and herd immunity, the monoclonal antibodies, the epidemiology, and the forensic biology and DNA profiling. Appendix K — Deep practical microbiology: how to think about the culturing and safety questions on the paper

The practical microbiology questions are the ones where candidates most often lose marks by writing a method without the reasoning, or by writing a safety list without the reasoning, or by writing a result description without saying what the result means. The reasoning that the question is really after is usually one of three kinds: why the technique is done that way, what the control is for, or what the observation means about the organism or the condition. If you can answer any of those three in a microbiology context, you can handle the practical question when it appears. If you only know the method and not the reasoning, you are vulnerable on exactly the marks that the practical question is usually built from. The reason for that is that the practical question is not usually a memory test for the method alone; it is a reasoning test about the method, the safety and the interpretation.

For culturing, the reasoning is usually about purity, safety and the reason for the particular setup. A good answer about a culturing method does not just say “spread the inoculum on agar” but says why the inoculum is diluted or isolated, why the plate is incubated in a particular way, why the lid is not fully opened, why the workspace is treated the way it is, and why the waste is disposed of the way it is. If you can say that, you have the reasoning. If you only say “the plate is incubated,” you have the label but not the reasoning, and the mark is in the reasoning. For safety, the reasoning is about what could go wrong and how the procedure prevents it, so a good safety answer is about sterilisation, containment and disposal as connected ideas, not just a list of rules. For interpretation, the reasoning is about what the growth or the lack of growth means, so a good interpretation answer is about the conditions that favour or prevent growth and about the limits of what can be concluded from the result.

The practical microbiology reasoning is also the reasoning that connects back to the theory, because the same ideas that matter in the lab, purity, safety, growth and interpretation, are the ideas that matter in the theory questions. If you can see that the practical and the theory are two views of the same ideas, you can answer the questions that span them, which are often the best-marked ones. If you only see the practical as a separate thing from the theory, you are likely to lose the marks on the questions that ask you to connect the two. The note has covered both, and the length is there so that you have the connection as well as the parts. If you use the note as a set of connected ideas rather than as a set of separate facts, you get the connection, and that is the use of the length.

Appendix L — The immune response as a process with timing, not just as a set of cells and molecules

The immune response is the topic where a candidate can get all the cells and molecules right and still lose marks by not saying the process in time order and by not saying why the timing matters. The process is that on first exposure, the specific lymphocytes have to be activated, expanded and differentiated over time, so the primary response is slow; on later exposure, the memory cells are already present and ready, so the secondary response is fast and strong. The point of the timing is that the immune system is not a single instantaneous event; it is a process with stages, and the stages matter for the comparison between primary and secondary responses and for the explanation of vaccination. If you can say that, you have the immune process in a form that scores marks. If you only say “the body makes antibodies,” you have the label but not the process, and the mark is in the process, because that is what the comparison and the vaccination questions are built from.

The memory idea is the one where the timing matters most, because the mark is often about the difference that memory makes, not just about the existence of memory. A good answer says that memory cells from the first exposure are responsible for the faster and stronger secondary response, and that this is the basis of vaccination, because vaccination produces the memory without the disease. It does not say that the immune system “remembers” in a vague sense without saying what the memory cells do, because the memory cell is the point, and the timing is the point. If you can say that the memory cells are the reason the secondary response is faster, you have the memory idea in a form that scores marks. If you only say “the second time is quicker,” you have the label but not the reasoning, and the reasoning is what the mark is after.

The specificity is the other idea where timing and process meet, because the specific response is specific and the non-specific responses are not, and that distinction matters for the comparison between the first line and the specific response. A good answer says that the first line is non-specific and the specific response is specific, and that the specific response includes antibodies and memory cells, while the first line includes barriers, inflammation and phagocytosis. It does not say that the specific response replaces the first line, because it does not; the two work together, and the mark is often about seeing that the system has both parts and that they have different roles. If you can say that, you have the immune comparison in a form that scores marks. If you only say “the body has specific immunity,” you have the label but not the comparison, and the mark is in the comparison, because that is what the question is usually built from.

Appendix M — Forensic biology as interpretation, and the things that can go wrong with it

Forensic biology is the topic where candidates most often lose marks by treating the evidence as a simple fact rather than as something with an interpretation and a set of things that can go wrong. The precise idea is that biological evidence such as DNA can be used to identify individuals and to link evidence to people or scenes, but the evidence is interpreted, and the interpretation depends on the quality of the sample, on whether it was contaminated, on the chain of custody, and on the context of the question. A good answer says that, and also says that a match or a mismatch is not a simple yes-no answer in the abstract but a result to be interpreted in context. If you can say that, you have the forensic biology idea in a form that scores marks. If you only say “DNA can identify someone,” you have the label but not the reasoning, and the reasoning is what the mark is after.

The things that can go wrong are the other part of the forensic reasoning that is worth saying explicitly, because they are the things that make the evidence meaningful or not. Contamination can make the evidence unreliable. Poor handling can lose or degrade the sample. A broken chain of custody can make the evidence hard to interpret in a legal context. A match in the wrong context can mean something different from a match in the right context. A good answer says that these are the things that matter, and that the value of the evidence depends on them. It does not say that forensic biology is always straightforward, because it is not, and it does not say that it is never reliable, because it can be. If you can say that the evidence has limits as well as value, you have the forensic reasoning in a form that scores marks. If you only have the label of “biological evidence,” you are missing the reasoning that the mark is after.

The identification idea is the one where the forensic topic connects back to the biology, because DNA profiling works because there is variation between individuals in certain DNA regions, and that is a biological fact about variation, not a forensic trick. A good answer says that the method depends on variation between individuals and on the ability to detect and compare those differences, and that the result is a pattern that can be matched or excluded. It does not say that DNA profiling is a magic identification without the variation, because the variation is the point. If you can say that, you have the DNA profiling idea in a form that scores marks. If you only say “DNA fingerprinting identifies people,” you have the label but not the reasoning, and the reasoning is what the mark is after when the question asks about the principle.
