title: IGCSE Biology: Human Nutrition
content:
IGCSE Biology: Human Nutrition

Nutrition is the taking in of materials for energy, growth and repair — and for humans it runs through a long tube from mouth to anus, with organs that grind, acidify, enzymatically dismantle and finally absorb what you swallow. This note covers the balanced diet (what each nutrient does and what happens without it), the full alimentary canal with the role of every organ, the three types of digestion with each enzyme named against its substrate and end products, and the structure of the small intestine wall down to the villus. Every digestive reaction is written as a hydrolysis equation, and the absorption calculation is worked from first principles.

Starch + H₂O → maltose (amylase), maltose + H₂O → glucose (maltase); protein + H₂O → amino acids (protease); fat + H₂O → fatty acids + glycerol (lipase). Key: H₂O appears on the left of every one of these because hydrolysis is the reaction that splits a bond with water, which is also why the products are smaller molecules than the substrate; the enzyme named in brackets is a catalyst, so it is written above or beside the arrow, never balanced into the equation; and the products, not the substrate, are what the ileum absorbs.

The balanced diet and the six nutrient groups

A balanced diet supplies all the nutrients in the right proportions for health. Carbohydrates (starch, sugars): the main energy source — 17 kJ per gram; deficiency causes fatigue and weight loss. Lipids (fats and oils): concentrated energy store (38 kJ per gram), insulation, waterproofing, cell membranes; excess is linked to obesity and cardiovascular disease. Proteins: growth and repair of tissues, enzymes, antibodies, some hormones; deficiency causes kwashiorkor (swollen belly, poor growth) in children. Vitamins: needed in tiny amounts for enzyme function — vitamin C for blood vessels and wound healing (deficiency: scurvy), vitamin D for calcium absorption (deficiency: rickets, soft bones). Mineral ions: iron for haemoglobin (deficiency: anaemia), calcium for bones and clotting, fluoride for tooth enamel. Water: solvent for all reactions, transport medium, temperature regulation — about 60 % of body mass. Dietary fibre (cellulose): not digested but adds bulk to keep the bowels moving, preventing constipation and bowel cancer risk. Energy needs vary: more for growth, pregnancy, exercise, cold conditions and manual labour; a diet exceeding needs stores fat.

The alimentary canal: organs and their roles

The digestive tract is a muscular tube (the alimentary canal) with accessory organs feeding into it. Mouth: mechanical digestion by teeth (mastication increases surface area), chemical digestion of starch by salivary amylase, swallowing moves the bolus into the oesophagus. Oesophagus: a muscular tube moving food by peristalsis — waves of circular muscle contraction behind the bolus with relaxation in front. Stomach: churns food mechanically, secretes hydrochloric acid (kills bacteria, provides pH 2 for pepsin), mucus (protects the stomach wall from its own acid), and pepsin (begins protein digestion); stores food for 2–4 hours. Small intestine: the main site of chemical digestion and absorption; receives bile from the gall bladder (emulsifies fats into small droplets for lipase) and pancreatic juice (amylase, lipase, protease); its wall has villi. Large intestine: absorbs water and mineral ions from the remaining liquid; the rest becomes faeces, stored in the rectum and egested through the anus. Liver: produces bile. Pancreas: produces digestive enzymes and the hormone insulin. Gall bladder: stores and concentrates bile.

Physical digestion

Physical (mechanical) digestion breaks food into smaller pieces without changing its chemistry: chewing (teeth cut and grind), churning in the stomach (muscular walls mix food with gastric juices), and bile emulsifying fat (breaking large fat globules into tiny droplets). The point is always surface area: enzymes are water-soluble and act only at the surface of food particles, so breaking food down increases the surface area for enzyme action and speeds up digestion. Teeth themselves are specialised: incisors cut, canines tear, premolars and molars grind; each has enamel (hardest substance in the body), dentine, a pulp cavity with nerves and blood, and cement fixing it to the jaw. Dental decay begins when bacteria feed on sugar and produce acid that dissolves enamel; fluoride toothpaste and reducing sugar frequency prevent it.

Chemical digestion: every enzyme, substrate and product

Chemical digestion hydrolyses large insoluble molecules into small soluble ones that can be absorbed. Carbohydrates: salivary amylase (mouth) and pancreatic amylase (small intestine) break starch into maltose; maltase (in the small intestine wall) breaks maltose into glucose. Proteins: pepsin (stomach, in acid) breaks proteins into shorter polypeptides; proteases (trypsin from the pancreas and peptidases in the intestine wall) break polypeptides into amino acids. Lipids: lipase (pancreas and small intestine) breaks emulsified fats into fatty acids and glycerol. Bile salts (from the liver) are not enzymes — they emulsify fat, and the exam wants the difference stated: emulsification is physical, digestion is chemical. Each final product is small and soluble: glucose, amino acids, fatty acids and glycerol.

Absorption: the villus in detail

Absorption is the movement of digested food molecules into the blood. It happens in the small intestine, whose wall is folded into millions of villi (finger-like projections), each villus covered in microvilli — together they multiply the surface area enormously. Each villus has: a single layer of epithelial cells (short diffusion path), a rich blood capillary network (maintaining the concentration gradient by carrying glucose and amino acids away), and a lacteal (a lymph vessel absorbing fatty acids and glycerol). Glucose and amino acids enter the capillaries by diffusion and active transport; fatty acids and glycerol enter the lacteal. The hepatic portal vein carries absorbed nutrients to the liver, where glucose is stored as glycogen and amino acids are processed. Villi structure-to-function is the single most examined link in human nutrition: surface area, thin wall, blood supply — all three clauses earn marks.

Every digestive enzyme at a glance

EnzymeWhere secretedSubstrateProducts
Salivary amylaseSalivary glands (mouth)StarchMaltose
PepsinStomach (in acid, pH 2)ProteinPolypeptides
Pancreatic amylasePancreas (small intestine)StarchMaltose
TrypsinPancreas (small intestine)PolypeptidesShorter peptides, amino acids
LipasePancreas (small intestine)Emulsified fatsFatty acids and glycerol
MaltaseWall of small intestineMaltoseGlucose

Worked example: energy balance and absorption calculations

A meal contains 30 g carbohydrate, 10 g fat and 20 g protein. Step 1: use the energy values: carbohydrate 17 kJ/g, fat 38 kJ/g, protein 17 kJ/g. Step 2: multiply each: 30 × 17 = 510 kJ; 10 × 38 = 380 kJ; 20 × 17 = 340 kJ. Step 3: total: 510 + 380 + 340 = 1230 kJ. Step 4: state the answer with units. Now a mass-balance question: a person eats 10 000 kJ per day and expends 9 500 kJ. The surplus is 500 kJ per day. Since 1 g of fat stores about 38 kJ, the stored fat per week is (500 × 7) ÷ 38 ≈ 92 g per week. An absorption-rate question: if glucose concentration in the gut lumen falls below that in the blood, absorption still occurs because of active transport — name the energy source (respiration in the villus epithelial cells) to secure the mark.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Writing "digestion absorbs food": digestion breaks molecules down; absorption moves the products into the blood. They are different processes in different places.
  • Calling bile an enzyme: bile contains bile salts that emulsify fat physically; it contains no digestive enzymes.
  • Writing the end products wrongly: starch → glucose, protein → amino acids, fat → fatty acids and glycerol (not "sugars and fats").
  • Saying the stomach absorbs food: the stomach absorbs almost nothing except alcohol and some drugs; absorption is the small intestine's job.
  • Forgetting to link villi features to their effect: "thin wall" alone gets nothing without "short diffusion path".
  • Describing peristalsis as "gravity moving food": food moves by muscular contraction even upside down.
  • Writing enzyme names as their substrate (saying "sugarase"); use amylase, maltase, pepsin, protease, lipase as named in the spec.
  • Answering a diet question without a link to deficiency disease: name the disease for the full marks.

Exam-style questions and answers

Q1. Describe the role of the stomach in digestion. (4 marks) Answer: muscular churning physically breaks food up (1); hydrochloric acid provides pH 2 and kills bacteria (1); pepsin hydrolyses proteins into polypeptides (1); mucus protects the stomach wall (1).

Q2. Explain how the structure of a villus is adapted for absorption. (3 marks) Answer: large surface area from folding and microvilli (1); one-cell-thick epithelium gives a short diffusion path (1); rich blood capillary supply maintains a steep concentration gradient (1).

Q3. Name the products of digestion of starch, protein and fat. (3 marks) Answer: glucose (1); amino acids (1); fatty acids and glycerol (1).

Q4. Explain why physical digestion is necessary before chemical digestion. (2 marks) Answer: it increases the surface area of food particles (1); enzymes act on the surface so a larger area speeds up digestion (1).

Q5. Describe the causes and prevention of tooth decay. (3 marks) Answer: bacteria ferment sugar producing acid that dissolves enamel (1); prevention by reducing sugar frequency, brushing and fluoride toothpaste (1); regular dental check-ups (1).

title: IGCSE Chemistry: Stoichiometry and the Mole
content:
IGCSE Chemistry: Stoichiometry and the Mole

Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry 0620 (2026–2028), Extended route, Topic 3 Stoichiometry: statement 3.1 Formulae, 3.2 Relative masses of atoms and molecules, and 3.3 The mole and the Avogadro constant. Stoichiometry is the accounting of chemistry — it answers "how much?" for every reaction — and it is the single highest-yield calculation topic on Paper 4. Every calculation below is expanded one line at a time with no skipped arithmetic, and each method is stated as a repeatable recipe before the numbers, because the marks sit in the working.

What a chemical formula tells you

Think of a formula as a recipe for one particle of a substance. H₂O says: every molecule of water contains exactly two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom. The small numbers are subscripts — they count atoms inside the particle, and changing them changes the substance entirely (H₂O is water; H₂O₂ is hydrogen peroxide).

  • Empirical formula: the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms in a compound. For glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆) the empirical formula is CH₂O — the ratio 6:12:6 divided by 6.
  • Molecular formula: the actual number of each atom in one molecule (C₆H₁₂O₆).
  • Formula of ionic compounds: the ratio that makes the charges balance. Ca²⁺ and Cl⁻ combine as CaCl₂ because one 2+ ion needs two 1− ions for neutrality.

State symbols appear on every equation and carry a mark: (s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas, (aq) aqueous (dissolved in water).

Equations: balancing and the conservation of mass

Atoms are never created or destroyed in a chemical reaction — mass is conserved. Balancing an equation is simply making the atom count of each element equal on both sides. The master method:

Balance: Al + O2 → Al2O3   (no state symbols until balanced)

1. List the elements and count each side:
     left:  Al 1, O 2      right: Al 2, O 3
2. Pick the element that appears in the most complex formula and balance it
   first - here Al: put 2 in front of Al:
     2Al + O2 → Al2O3      left: Al 2, O 2   right: Al 2, O 3
3. Balance O. Left has 2, right has 3. The lowest number both divide into
   is 6 - so aim for 6 O on each side:
     O2 needs 3 molecules (3 × 2 = 6); Al2O3 needs 2 formula units
     (2 × 3 = 6):
     2Al + 3O2 → 2Al2O3
4. Re-count Al: right now has 4 (2 × 2). Fix the left:
     4Al + 3O2 → 2Al2O3
5. Final check, every element:
     Al 4 = 4 ✓    O 6 = 6 ✓
6. Add state symbols from the facts you know:
     4Al(s) + 3O2(g) → 2Al2O3(s)

Rules that never fail: only change the BIG numbers in front (never the
subscripts), never invent atoms, and always re-count at the end.

Relative atomic mass and relative formula mass

You cannot weigh individual atoms, so chemistry compares masses against a standard: one-twelfth the mass of a carbon-12 atom. The relative atomic mass (Aᵣ) is the weighted average mass of an element's atoms on that scale. The relative molecular mass (Mᵣ) (or relative formula mass for ionic compounds) is the sum of the Aᵣ values in the formula.

Worked: find the Mᵣ of calcium carbonate, CaCO₃.

  Aᵣ values from the Periodic Table: Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16
  Mᵣ = 40 + 12 + (3 × 16)
     = 40 + 12 + 48
     = 10⁰

Note the parenthesis: the subscript 3 multiplies ONLY the oxygen.
A common error is 40 + 12 + 16 = 68 - one mark lost to a bracket.

Mᵣ of sulfuric acid, H₂SO₄:
  Mᵣ = (2 × 1) + 32 + (4 × 16)
     = 2 + 32 + 64
     = 98

The mole and the Avogadro constant

A mole is the chemist's counting unit, like "a dozen" — but sized for atoms. One mole of any substance contains 6.02 × 10²³ particles (the Avogadro constant, L). The practical magic: one mole of any substance has a mass in grams equal to its Mᵣ, which turns unweighable atoms into weighable quantities.

The mole triangle - the three relationships and how to rearrange them:

        mass (g)
        /      \
       /        \
    moles x Mᵣ = mass        moles = mass / Mᵣ     Mᵣ = mass / moles

  particles = moles x 6.02 × 10²³

Worked: how many molecules are in 4.4 g of carbon dioxide, CO₂?

Step 1 - Mᵣ of CO₂ = 12 + (2 × 16) = 44
Step 2 - moles = mass / Mᵣ = 4.4 / 44 = 0.1 mol
Step 3 - molecules = 0.1 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 6.02 × 10²² molecules
Step 4 (if asked for ATOMS): each CO₂ has 3 atoms, so
        atoms = 6.02 × 10²² x 3 = 1.806 × 10²³ atoms

"Particles" can mean atoms, molecules or ions - read the question's word.
Question asks forWorking lineWorked number
Moles from massmoles = mass ÷ Mᵣ25 g CaCO₃ → 25 ÷ 100 = 0.25 mol
Mass from molesmass = moles × Mᵣ0.25 mol CO₂ → 0.25 × 44 = 11 g
Particles from molesparticles = moles × 6.02 × 10²³0.25 mol → 1.505 × 10²³ molecules
Gas volume at r.t.p.volume = moles × 24 dm³0.25 mol → 6 dm³
Solution molesmoles = c (mol/dm³) × V (dm³)0.1 × 0.025 = 0.0025 mol
Concentrationc = moles ÷ V (dm³)0.004 mol in 25 cm³ → 0.16 mol/dm³

Reacting masses

The balanced equation is a recipe in moles: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O says 2 moles of hydrogen react with 1 mole of oxygen to make 2 moles of water. Master method for every reacting-mass question: balance the equation → convert given mass to moles → use the equation's ratio → convert back to mass.

Worked: what mass of water forms when 10 g of hydrogen burns in 10⁰ g of
oxygen? And which reactant limits the yield?

Step 1 - balance:  2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O
Step 2 - moles of each reactant:
   H₂:  Mᵣ = 2   →  moles = 10 / 2  = 5 mol
   O₂:  Mᵣ = 32  →  moles = 10⁰ / 32 = 3.125 mol
Step 3 - the ratio needed is 2 : 1.
   5 mol H₂ would need 5 / 2 = 2.5 mol O₂.
   We have 3.125 mol O₂ - MORE than needed, so O₂ is in excess and
   H₂ is the LIMITING reactant. All calculations use the limiting one.
Step 4 - moles of water from the limiting reactant:
   ratio H₂ : H₂O = 2 : 2 = 1 : 1  →  water = 5 mol
Step 5 - mass of water:
   Mᵣ(H₂O) = 18  →  mass = 5 × 18 = 90 g

Sanity check: 10 + 10⁰ = 110 g in; 90 g water + 10 g unreacted O₂ out
(3.125 - 2.5 = 0.625 mol O₂ left = 0.625 × 32 = 20 g... 
wait - recompute: 10⁰ - 80 = 20 g O₂ left, and 90 + 20 = 110 g ✓)

Percentage yield = (actual mass ÷ theoretical mass) × 100. If the reaction above actually gave 72 g of water: percentage yield = 72 ÷ 90 × 100 = 80%. Percentage purity = (mass of pure product ÷ mass of impure sample) × 100 — a different question, and mixing the two up is a classic lost mark.

Gas volumes

At room temperature and pressure (r.t.p.), one mole of any gas occupies 24 dm³ (24 000 cm³). This connects gas volumes straight to moles.

Worked: what volume of carbon dioxide forms when 25 g of calcium carbonate
decomposes?  CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂

Step 1 - balance (already 1:1:1)
Step 2 - moles CaCO₃ = 25 / 10⁰ = 0.25 mol
Step 3 - ratio 1 : 1  →  CO₂ = 0.25 mol
Step 4 - volume = moles x 24 = 0.25 × 24 = 6 dm³
        (in cm³: 6 × 10⁰⁰ = 6000 cm³)

The reverse works identically: 480 cm³ of gas = 0.48 dm³
→ moles = 0.48 / 24 = 0.02 mol.

Solutions, concentration and titration

Concentration says how much solute sits in a given volume of solution, in g/dm³ or mol/dm³. The working equations: moles = concentration (mol/dm³) × volume (dm³), and cm³ ÷ 1000 = dm³.

Titration worked in full: 25.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide solution is neutralised
by 20.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ sulfuric acid. Find the NaOH concentration.

  2NaOH + H₂SO₄ → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O        [balanced first: ratio 2 : 1]

Step 1 - moles of acid used:
   volume = 20.0 cm³ = 20.0 / 10⁰⁰ = 0.0200 dm³
   moles H₂SO₄ = 0.100 × 0.0200 = 0.00200 mol
Step 2 - ratio 2 : 1, so:
   moles NaOH = 0.00200 × 2 = 0.00400 mol
Step 3 - concentration of NaOH:
   volume = 25.0 cm³ = 0.0250 dm³
   conc = moles / volume = 0.00400 / 0.0250 = 0.160 mol/dm³

Three marks hide in three places: the balanced ratio (2:1), the cm³ to dm³
conversion, and the final division the right way up.

Titrration technique itself (burette, pipette, indicator, concordant titres) is Paper 6 material — see the experimental techniques note — but the calculation above is pure Paper 4.

Empirical and molecular formulae from data

Worked: a compound contains 40.0% carbon, 6.7% hydrogen and 53.3% oxygen
by mass. Its Mᵣ is 180. Find the empirical and molecular formulae.

Master method: assume 10⁰ g → divide each percentage by Aᵣ → divide by the
smallest → scale to whole numbers.

Step 1 - assume 10⁰ g: C 40.0 g, H 6.7 g, O 53.3 g
Step 2 - convert to moles (Aᵣ: C 12, H 1, O 16):
   C: 40.0 / 12 = 3.33 mol
   H:  6.7 /  1 = 6.70 mol
   O: 53.3 / 16 = 3.33 mol
Step 3 - divide by the smallest (3.33):
   C: 3.33 / 3.33 = 1
   H: 6.70 / 3.33 = 2.01 ≈ 2
   O: 3.33 / 3.33 = 1
Step 4 - empirical formula = CH₂O   (empirical Mᵣ = 12 + 2 + 16 = 30)
Step 5 - molecular formula: 180 / 30 = 6, so multiply by 6
   molecular formula = C₆H₁₂O₆

Check: 6 × 12 + 12 × 1 + 6 × 16 = 72 + 12 + 96 = 180 ✓

Worked example: one problem using every method

10.0 g of magnesium reacts with hydrochloric acid:
  Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂

(a) moles Mg = 10.0 / 24 = 0.4167 mol
(b) moles HCl needed = 0.4167 × 2 = 0.8333 mol
(c) if HCl is supplied as 2.00 mol/dm³, volume needed =
    0.8333 / 2.00 = 0.4167 dm³ = 416.7 cm³
(d) volume of H₂ at r.t.p. = 0.4167 × 24 = 10.0 dm³
(e) if only 8.4 dm³ of H₂ is collected, percentage yield =
    8.4 / 10.0 × 10⁰ = 84%

One equation, five question shapes - mass, ratio, concentration, gas volume,
yield. The method never changes: moles first, ratio second, back to units.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Changing subscripts to "balance" an equation — that invents a different substance; only front numbers change.
  • Forgetting subscripts when calculating Mᵣ (Mᵣ of CaCO₃ is 100, not 68); bracket the multiplied terms.
  • Skipping the cm³ → dm³ conversion (divide by 1000) in concentration work — the most common single arithmetic slip on Paper 4.
  • Inverting the concentration rearrangement: moles = c × V, so c = moles ÷ V — state the triangle, don't improvise.
  • Using the excess reactant instead of the limiting one in reacting-mass questions; always compare moles ÷ coefficient first.
  • Confusing percentage yield with percentage purity — yield compares actual vs theoretical product; purity compares pure substance vs sample.
  • Dropping the ×10²³ or writing 6.02 × 10⁻²³; the Avogadro constant is positive-indexed and multiplied, not divided, for particle counts.
  • Quoting 24 dm³ without the conditions "at r.t.p."; the molar gas volume only holds there.
  • In empirical formula questions, not scaling 2.01 or 1.99 to whole numbers (2) — ratios are always whole numbers.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 4, 3 marks). Calculate the relative formula mass of ammonium nitrate, NH₄NO₃. (Aᵣ: N = 14, H = 1, O = 16)

Answer: Mᵣ = (2 × 14) + (4 × 1) + (3 × 16) = 28 + 4 + 48 = 80.

Question 2 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Calculate the mass of iron formed when 320 g of iron(III) oxide is reduced by carbon monoxide: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂. (Aᵣ: Fe = 56, O = 16)

Answer: Mᵣ(Fe₂O₃) = (2 × 56) + (3 × 16) = 160. Moles Fe₂O₃ = 320 ÷ 160 = 2 mol. Ratio Fe₂O₃ : Fe = 1 : 2, so Fe = 4 mol. Mass Fe = 4 × 56 = 224 g.

Question 3 (Paper 4, 5 marks). A student neutralises 25.0 cm³ of 0.200 mol/dm³ HNO₃ with Na₂CO₃ solution. Calculate the moles of acid and the mass of anhydrous Na₂CO₃ needed. (Mᵣ Na₂CO₃ = 106)

Answer: Moles HNO₃ = 0.200 × (25.0 ÷ 1000) = 0.200 × 0.025 = 0.00500 mol. Equation: Na₂CO₃ + 2HNO₃ → 2NaNO₃ + H₂O + CO₂, ratio 1 : 2, so moles Na₂CO₃ = 0.00500 ÷ 2 = 0.00250 mol. Mass = 0.00250 × 106 = 0.265 g.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 3 marks). Calculate the volume at r.t.p. of 8.8 g of carbon dioxide.

Answer: Mᵣ(CO₂) = 44; moles = 8.8 ÷ 44 = 0.2 mol; volume = 0.2 × 24 = 4.8 dm³.

Question 5 (Paper 4, 4 marks). An oxide of iron contains 69.9% iron by mass, the rest oxygen. Find its empirical formula. (Aᵣ: Fe = 56, O = 16)

Answer: Assume 100 g: Fe 69.9 g, O 30.1 g. Moles: Fe = 69.9 ÷ 56 = 1.248; O = 30.1 ÷ 16 = 1.881. Divide by the smallest (1.248): Fe 1, O 1.881 ÷ 1.248 = 1.51 ≈ 1.5. Multiply by 2 for whole numbers: Fe₂O₃. Check: (2 × 56) + (3 × 16) = 160; Fe fraction = 112 ÷ 160 = 69.9% ✓.

Question 6 (Paper 4, 3 marks). 0.24 g of magnesium gives 240 cm³ of hydrogen at r.t.p. Calculate the percentage yield if theory predicts 288 cm³.

Answer: Percentage yield = (240 ÷ 288) × 100 = 83.3%.

With the quantitative bookkeeping in place, the next question is what these particles actually are — atomic structure and bonding.

title: Differentiation — Study Notes
content:
Differentiation

Cambridge International AS & A Level Mathematics 9709, Paper 1. Differentiation answers one question: how fast is y changing with x at a given point? Most questions either ask for the gradient function or use it at a particular point.

The power rule

If y = axⁿ then dy/dx = naxⁿ⁻¹, for any rational n. A constant term differentiates to zero. Write roots and reciprocals as powers before you start: √x = x^(1/2) and 1/x² = x⁻².

Example: y = 4√x − 6/x². Rewriting gives y = 4x^(1/2) − 6x⁻², so dy/dx = 2x^(−1/2) + 12x⁻³ = 2/√x + 12/x³.

Expand before you differentiate

Differentiation works term by term, so multiply out any brackets first. Differentiating each factor separately does not give the derivative of the product.

Example: y = (x + 2)(x − 5) = x² − 3x − 10, so dy/dx = 2x − 3.

Tangents and normals

Substitute the x-value into the original curve to get y, and into dy/dx to get the gradient. The tangent uses that gradient; the normal uses the negative reciprocal. Write both in the form y − y₁ = m(x − x₁) and then simplify.

Example: y = x³ − 2x at x = −1. Then y = 1 and dy/dx = 3x² − 2 = 1. The tangent is y = x + 2. The normal has gradient −1 and is y = −x, which also passes through (−1, 1).

Stationary points and their nature

Stationary points are where dy/dx = 0. Solve that equation for x, then use the second derivative: d²y/dx² > 0 gives a minimum and d²y/dx² < 0 gives a maximum. If the second derivative is zero at the point, check the sign of dy/dx on either side of it instead.

Example: y = x³ − 6x² + 9x. Then dy/dx = 3(x − 1)(x − 3), so the stationary points are at x = 1 and x = 3. Since d²y/dx² = 6x − 12, the point at x = 1 is a maximum at (1, 4), and the point at x = 3 is a minimum at (3, 0).

Increasing and decreasing

The curve increases where dy/dx > 0 and decreases where dy/dx < 0. For the example above, dy/dx is positive for x < 1 and for x > 3, and negative between them.

Common errors

  • Differentiating a product factor by factor instead of expanding it first.
  • Forgetting to subtract one from the power, or differentiating a constant to anything other than zero.
  • Giving the tangent without its point, or using the tangent's gradient for the normal.
  • Giving only the x-value of a stationary point instead of its coordinates (x, y).

title:
Coordination, Response and Gene Technology — Quick Revision Summary

This is the fast map of Edexcel International A2 Biology WBI16 Topics 8 and 9. It follows the same order as the full notes so you can cross-reference, and it repeats the specification numbers so you can see which paragraph exists for which point. Use it to organise the topic, not to replace the notes. The topic splits into three big blocks: the nervous system and neurones, the brain, imaging and the pharmacology of the nervous system, and the plant and genetic technologies — coordination in plants, recombinant DNA and GM organisms, and bioinformatics and microarrays.

The nervous system: hierarchy and the reflex arc

The nervous system lets an organism detect a stimulus, send information quickly, and make effectors respond. In mammals it is built from the central and peripheral systems, and its fastest wired responses are the reflex arcs, which are the simplest complete circuits you study in this topic.

  • 8.1 Sensory neurones carry information from receptors toward the central nervous system; relay neurones are in the central nervous system and connect sensory to motor neurones; motor neurones carry impulses from the central nervous system to effectors such as muscles and glands. Schwann cells wrap many axons in myelin, an insulating fatty layer, and myelination increases the speed of conduction. The roles of the three neurone types and the reason for myelination are the core ideas here.
  • 8.2 The nervous system causes effectors to respond to a stimulus through a chain: receptor detects the stimulus, sensory neurone carries the impulse to the central nervous system, relay neurone processes the information and passes it on, motor neurone carries the impulse to the effector, and the effector responds. The pupil example is useful: the iris contains muscles that respond to the amount of light, and the wiring behind that response is the kind of autonomic coordination this part of the topic describes.
  • 8.3 A spinal reflex arc is the simplest complete pathway. The stimulus is detected by a receptor, the sensory neurone enters the spinal cord, the relay neurone in the grey matter connects to the motor neurone, and the motor neurone carries the impulse out to the effector — often a muscle. The grey matter is where the relay neurones and synapses are; the white matter is made of myelinated axons that carry impulses up and down the cord between the spinal cord and the brain. The reflex arc is fast because it is short and involves few synapses, and it is protective because it does not wait for the brain to process the information first.

The practical point is that the reflex arc is not just “a reflex”; it is the minimal circuit that shows how sensory input, central relay and motor output are wired together, and it explains why the grey and white matter of the spinal cord have different functions.

The action potential and how it travels

The nerve impulse is the action potential, a self-propagating electrical signal caused by changes in the permeability of the axon membrane to sodium and potassium ions. The sequence of events is what the exam wants, and the reason myelination speeds conduction is part of the same picture.

  • 8.4 An action potential is conducted along an axon because of changes in membrane permeability to sodium and potassium ions. At rest the membrane is polarised, with the inside negative relative to the outside. When a stimulus is strong enough, voltage-gated sodium channels open and sodium ions enter the axon, depolarising the membrane and generating the rising phase of the action potential. Sodium channels then close and voltage-gated potassium channels open, so potassium ions leave the axon and the membrane repolarises. The sodium-potassium pump restores the resting distribution of ions over time, but the immediate repolarisation is due to potassium leaving, not to the pump. The action potential is all-or-nothing: once the threshold is reached, it fires fully; a stronger stimulus does not make a bigger action potential, only more frequent ones.
  • The propagation happens because the depolarisation of one small region of the membrane changes the voltage in the neighbouring region, opening channels there and so on along the axon. The impulse travels because each section regenerates the signal, not because the same ions travel from one end of the axon to the other. That is why the impulse is an electrochemical wave and not a current flowing the length of the axon like water in a pipe.
  • 8.5 Myelination makes this faster by saltatory conduction. The myelin sheath is interrupted by the nodes of Ranvier, where the axon membrane is exposed. Depolarisation can only happen at these nodes, so the action potential appears to jump from node to node. This is far faster than continuous conduction along an unmyelinated axon of the same diameter, because the signal travels quickly along the insulated internodal regions and is only recharged at the nodes. The comparison is not that myelin makes the ions move faster; it is that the signal regenerates at fewer points along the way.

A frequent mistake is to say that myelination increases the speed by making the ions travel faster, or to forget that the sodium-potassium pump restores the resting conditions after the action potential rather than causing the repolarisation itself. The order of events — sodium in, depolarisation, potassium out, repolarisation, then restoration — is the secure version.

Synapses and the chemical transmission of the signal

Where one neurone meets another, the signal crosses a synapse. The synapse is the point at which the electrical signal becomes chemical for one step and then electrical again, and it is also where drugs and toxins can act. Synaptic transmission is the reason neurones can be modulated, integrated and influenced by chemicals.

  • 8.6 (i) A synapse in nerve impulse transmission has a presynaptic neurone ending with vesicles of neurotransmitter, a synaptic cleft, and a postsynaptic membrane with receptors for the neurotransmitter. When an action potential arrives at the presynaptic ending, calcium channels open, calcium enters, and vesicles fuse with the presynaptic membrane and release neurotransmitter into the cleft. The neurotransmitter diffuses across the cleft and binds to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane, opening ion channels and producing a new change in membrane potential in the postsynaptic neurone. Acetylcholine is the neurotransmitter at the neuromuscular junction and at many other synapses, and its action is a good example of the general scheme.
  • The pupil is a useful illustration. The iris contains muscles whose contraction or relaxation changes the pupil diameter; this is under autonomic control, and the pathway involves synaptic transmission with acetylcholine and, in the relevant part of the autonomic system, noradrenaline, depending on whether the response is constriction or dilation. The point is not to memorise every transmitter at every synapse, but to understand that the synapse is where the signal is passed and where chemicals can modify it.
  • 8.7 Drugs act by influencing nerve impulse transmission, and the specification names several examples. Nicotine mimics acetylcholine at some receptors, stimulating them; lidocaine blocks voltage-gated sodium channels, preventing action potentials and so acting as a local anaesthetic; cobra venom alpha toxin blocks neuromuscular transmission by binding to acetylcholine receptors; L-DOPA is used in Parkinson’s disease because it is a precursor that can be converted to dopamine, which is deficient in that condition; and MDMA, ecstasy, affects neurotransmitter reuptake and release, especially of serotonin, changing mood and perception. The principle is that drugs can mimic, block, enhance or reduce neurotransmitter action, and that the effect depends on which step they influence.

A helpful way to remember the drug examples is to classify them by the step they affect: some mimic a neurotransmitter, some block a receptor, some block ion channels, some change how much neurotransmitter is released or reabsorbed, and some are supplied as precursors. If you can say which step each one affects, you can answer the typical question even if you do not remember the exact detail of every one.

Rods, rhodopsin and the detection of light

The retina is where light is detected, and the rod cell is the model system for how a stimulus is turned into a membrane potential change at the cellular level. This is the place where the idea of a receptor potential and the operation of a G-protein-linked receptor are both visible.

  • 8.8 The mammal detects light with rods in the retina. Rod cells contain the pigment rhodopsin, which is made of opsin and retinal; retinal is the light-absorbing part. When light hits rhodopsin, retinal changes shape, the opsin changes shape, and this activates a transduction pathway that leads to the closure of sodium channels in the rod cell membrane. The result is that sodium ions stop entering as much, the rod cell hyperpolarises, and the pattern of neurotransmitter release at the rod’s synapse changes. This is a case where a stimulus reduces sodium entry rather than increasing it, so the cell hyperpolarises rather than depolarising. The signal is then passed through the retinal wiring to the optic neurones, which carry impulses to the brain.
  • The important concept is that a sensory receptor converts a stimulus into a change in membrane potential, and that the direction of change depends on the receptor. In rods, light causes hyperpolarisation. If you remember that the stimulus closes sodium channels in the rod rather than opening them, you can explain why the signal is generated and why it is not the same as an action potential in an axon.

Habituation and the simple learning of stimulus responses

Not every response is fixed. Habituation is a simple form of learning in which an organism stops responding to a repeated, harmless stimulus, and the specification includes it both as a behaviour and as something you can investigate practically.

  • 8.9 Habituation is a decrease in response to a repeated stimulus that is neither rewarding nor harmful. It is not the same as sensory adaptation, which is a change in the receptor itself; habituation is a change in the nervous system’s response, often at the synapse, so that the repeated stimulus fails to trigger the full response. It is useful because it lets an organism ignore unimportant stimuli and focus on those that matter. The practical investigation is to present a harmless stimulus repeatedly and measure the response over time, looking for the decline.

The organisation of the mammalian nervous system

The nervous system is organised into central and peripheral parts, and the central part is further divided into brain and spinal cord. The structure follows the function: the central system integrates and coordinates, while the peripheral system carries information in and out.

  • 8.10 The mammalian nervous system consists of the central nervous system, CNS, and the peripheral nervous system. The CNS is the brain and spinal cord; it integrates sensory information, coordinates responses, and can initiate behaviour. The peripheral nervous system carries sensory information into the CNS and carries motor commands out to the effectors. The division matters because it tells you which part does the integration and which part does the connecting and carrying.

The brain: structure and function of the main parts

The brain is not a single organ that does one job; its major parts have different functions, and the specification names several of them so you can map structure to role.

  • 8.14 The cerebral hemispheres are the largest part of the brain in mammals and are associated with higher functions such as voluntary movement, sensation, thought, memory, language and consciousness, with different regions specialised for different functions. The hypothalamus links the nervous and endocrine systems; it is involved in homeostasis, including the control of body temperature, hunger, thirst and the release of hormones from the pituitary gland. The pituitary gland is a major endocrine gland under the control of the hypothalamus, releasing hormones that regulate other endocrine glands and other processes. The cerebellum is involved in the coordination of movement, posture and balance, and in the refinement of motor control. The medulla oblongata controls vital automatic functions such as breathing and heart rate. Knowing the role of each part means you can explain what is likely to be affected if one part is damaged.

The exam point is that the brain is a set of specialised regions, not a single uniform structure. If a question asks what function a particular region has, the answer is to name the region’s role rather than to say “it does brain stuff”.

Imaging the living brain

The living brain can be imaged in several ways, and each method gives different information. The exam wants you to compare them by what they show and how they work, not just to list them.

  • 8.15 MRI, magnetic resonance imaging, uses strong magnetic fields and radio waves to build a detailed image of brain structure, and is good for showing anatomy and structural abnormalities. fMRI, functional MRI, detects changes in blood flow related to neural activity, so it shows which areas are active during a task as well as the structure; the idea is that active areas have increased blood flow and changes in oxygenation that the technique detects. PET, positron emission tomography, uses a radioactive tracer to show metabolic activity, so it can reveal which regions are metabolically active. CT, computed tomography, uses X-rays to build a cross-sectional image and is useful for detecting structural problems such as bleeding, fractures and some tumours. The common thread is that each has a different strength: some are better for structure, some for activity, some for acute structural emergencies, and none does everything.

A good comparison answer names what each method shows, what it is best used for, and the fact that they are complementary. Saying “MRI is the best one” without explanation is not enough, because the question is usually about why you would choose one method rather than another.

Imbalances, drugs and the development of new medicines

Disease can arise from the imbalance of naturally occurring brain chemicals, and understanding that imbalance is what lets drugs be developed. Parkinson’s disease and depression are the two named examples, and they illustrate different kinds of problem and different kinds of treatment.

  • 8.16 Imbalances in brain chemicals can contribute to ill health. In Parkinson’s disease, dopamine-secreting neurones in the brain are lost, so dopamine levels fall and movement control is affected. In depression, the regulation of neurotransmitters such as serotonin is thought to be involved, and drugs that affect serotonin can be used in treatment. The development of new drugs follows from understanding these imbalances: if a neurotransmitter is deficient, a precursor or a drug that affects its release, reuptake or receptor action may help. The important conceptual point is that the drug is a response to a biochemical problem, not a random intervention, and that different drugs work by different mechanisms even when they affect the same system.

A common trap is to over-simplify depression as “a serotonin deficiency” in a way that oversells a complex condition. The specification point is that serotonin is involved and that drugs that affect serotonin are used; the exam answer should say that, without pretending the biology is simpler than it is. The safe answer is to say that the imbalance is part of the explanation and that drug treatment targets it.

Coordination in plants: phytochrome, auxin and gibberellins

Plants coordinate their responses too, but they use hormones and light receptors rather than nerves. Phytochrome, auxin and gibberellins are the named examples, and they each work through effects on growth and on transcription, which connects this part of the topic to the gene-technology part later.

  • 8.11 Phytochrome is a plant photoreceptor that exists in two forms that interconvert in response to light. It allows the plant to detect light quality, quantity and duration, and it affects processes such as flowering and germination. Auxin, indoleacetic acid or IAA, is a plant hormone that promotes cell elongation and is involved in tropisms such as phototropism and gravitropism; it is distributed asymmetrically in the shoot so that the shaded side elongates more, bending the shoot toward the light. Gibberellins promote growth, including stem elongation and seed germination, and they bring about their effects partly by affecting transcription, i.e. by switching genes on and off. The link to gene technology is that phytochrome, auxin and gibberellins are not just “plant hormones”; they are part of the plant’s control system for responding to the environment and for development, and some of their effects are at the level of gene expression.

A useful practical image is the shoot bending toward light: auxin moves to the shaded side, the cells there elongate more, and the shoot curves. If you can say that, you have the phototropism story in a form that scores marks.

Core Practical 18 and the production of amylase in germinating grains

Core Practical 18 is about investigating amylase production in germinating cereal grains. The point is to connect enzyme production with germination and with the hormonal control of growth.

  • 8.12 Core Practical 18 investigates the production of amylase in germinating cereal grains. Germinating grains produce amylase to break down starch into sugars that the growing embryo can use. The practical is a way to see enzyme production during germination and to relate it to the hormonal changes that occur as the grain starts to grow. The idea is that the living embryo produces the enzyme, and that the enzyme mobilises the food store for the growing plant.

Recombinant DNA: the technology that joins genes to vectors

Gene technology is the set of methods that let scientists move genes from one organism to another. The first step is making recombinant DNA, and the key tools are restriction endonucleases and DNA ligase.

  • 8.18 Recombinant DNA is DNA made by combining sequences from different sources. Restriction endonucleases are enzymes that cut DNA at specific sequences, often leaving “sticky ends” that are complementary and can base-pair. DNA ligase joins DNA fragments together by forming the bonds between nucleotides in the sugar-phosphate backbone. So the workflow is: cut the gene and the vector with the same restriction enzyme, mix them so the sticky ends pair, and use DNA ligase to seal them together, making a recombinant DNA molecule. The point is that the cutting and joining are sequence-specific and enzyme-catalysed, and that the same enzymes are used to open the vector and to insert the gene.
  • 8.19 Recombinant DNA can be inserted into other cells. The vector is often a plasmid in bacteria, and the recombinant plasmid can be taken up by bacterial cells, which then carry the gene and can express it. Other methods include using viruses as vectors or physical methods such as microinjection or gene guns, depending on the organism and the goal. The important idea is that once the recombinant DNA is inside a host, the host’s molecular machinery can replicate and express the inserted gene, which is what makes the technology useful.

How genes are used to make products

The reason organisms are genetically modified is that they can be turned into factories for substances they would not otherwise make. The specification names the production of drugs by genetically modified organisms as a key example.

  • 8.17 Drugs can be produced using genetically modified organisms — plants, animals and microorganisms. The classic example is the production of human proteins such as insulin by genetically modified bacteria: the human gene is inserted into the bacterium, and the bacterium produces the protein, which can then be purified and used as a medicine. Other products can similarly be made in microorganisms, and sometimes in plants or animals. The point is that the organism is modified once and then used to produce the product, which is why the approach is useful industrially.

Microarrays and the detection of active genes

Not every gene is active at once. Microarrays are the tool for seeing which genes are active in a particular sample, and they connect gene technology to the analysis of gene expression rather than just the sequence of genes.

  • 8.20 Microarrays can be used to identify active genes. A microarray contains many short DNA sequences attached to a solid surface, and a labelled sample of cDNA made from the mRNA of a tissue is hybridised to it. If a gene is active, its cDNA will bind to the corresponding spot, and the label reveals which genes are being expressed and at what relative level. The comparison is between samples — for example a diseased tissue and a healthy one — so you can see which genes are up- or down-regulated. The principle is that the microarray lets you look at many genes at once, rather than one at a time, and that is what makes it useful for profiling gene activity.

Bioinformatics: the computational side of this topic

Bioinformatics is the use of computational tools to handle and interpret biological data, especially large datasets. It is part of this topic because modern biology produces more data than can be handled by hand, and because tools like BLAST let you compare a sequence with everything already known.

  • 8.21 Bioinformatics is the use of computer tools to collect, store, analyse and interpret biological data, especially large datasets such as DNA and protein sequences. It includes sequence alignment, database searching, and the comparison of sequences from different organisms to find similarities and differences. A typical use is to take a newly obtained sequence and see whether similar sequences from other organisms are already known, which can suggest function, evolutionary relationships and the presence of conserved regions. The point is that bioinformatics is not a separate subject from biology; it is the way large biological data are used.

Risks and benefits of genetically modified organisms

Gene technology is powerful, and the specification asks for the risks and benefits, not just the methods. This is the part where an essay-style answer is most likely to come from.

  • 8.22 Genetically modified organisms have both risks and benefits. Benefits can include increased crop yield, improved nutrition, resistance to pests or herbicides, reduced use of chemical inputs, production of medicines, and faster or more targeted research. Risks can include effects on non-target organisms, the spread of genes to wild relatives, the development of resistant pests, and concerns about food safety, patenting and ecological stability. The important point is that the risks and benefits depend on the specific modification, the organism, the environment and the purpose; a blanket statement that GM is good or bad is not an adequate answer. The answer should weigh a concrete benefit against a concrete risk and say what is relevant to the case in question.

A good answer names specific risks and benefits rather than general ones, and it recognises that the same technology can be used in different ways with different outcomes. For example, a herbicide-tolerant crop can reduce the need for some sprays but can also encourage weed resistance; the exam rewards the balanced, specific response.

How the nervous and gene-technology parts fit together

The topic is really two linked stories. The first is how animals coordinate and respond — sensory detection, action potentials, synapses, the brain, imaging and drugs. The second is how plants coordinate with hormones and how genetic technologies let us manipulate genes and measure their activity. The link is that both are about control: the nervous system controls rapid responses, the plant hormones control growth and development, and gene technology lets us read, move and use genes, including the genes that control those responses.

  • Start with the neurone: sensory, relay, motor, Schwann cells and myelination.
  • Move to the impulse: the action potential as sodium in, potassium out, all-or-nothing, and saltatory conduction in myelinated axons.
  • Move to the synapse: vesicles, calcium, neurotransmitter release, receptor binding, and the way drugs can intervene.
  • Move to the brain: CNS and PNS, the roles of the cerebral hemispheres, hypothalamus, pituitary, cerebellum and medulla, and the imaging methods MRI, fMRI, PET and CT.
  • Move to the chemical side: imbalances such as dopamine in Parkinson’s and serotonin in depression, and how drugs are developed in response.
  • Move to plants: phytochrome, auxin and gibberellins, the link to transcription, and the practical on amylase in germinating grains.
  • Move to gene technology: restriction enzymes and ligase, recombinant DNA, insertion into host cells, production of drugs by modified organisms, microarrays for active genes, and bioinformatics.
  • End with the balanced view on GM organisms, specific benefits and risks.

Typical mistakes

  • Saying the sodium-potassium pump repolarises the membrane during the action potential: it restores the resting distribution over time, but repolarisation is due to potassium leaving.
  • Saying myelination makes ions move faster rather than explaining saltatory conduction.
  • Confusing sensory, relay and motor neurones: sensory carry in, relay are in the CNS, motor carry out to effectors.
  • Saying the rod cell depolarises in light: it hyperpolarises because sodium channels close.
  • Treating habituation as the same as sensory adaptation: habituation is a nervous-system change, not a receptor change.
  • Confusing the brain parts: the hypothalamus is not the pituitary, the cerebellum is not the medulla, and the cerebral hemispheres are not all the same function.
  • Listing MRI, fMRI, PET and CT without saying what each shows or why you would choose it.
  • Saying restriction enzymes join DNA: they cut it; ligase joins it.
  • Saying a vector is the gene itself: the vector is the carrier, such as a plasmid.
  • Treating GM organisms as either wholly good or wholly bad without specific risks and benefits.

Exam-style questions

  1. Describe how an action potential is generated and conducted along an axon, and explain the role of myelination. Answer: At rest the axon membrane is polarised; a stimulus opens voltage-gated sodium channels, sodium ions enter and the membrane depolarises; sodium channels then close and potassium channels open, potassium ions leave and the membrane repolarises; the sodium-potassium pump restores the resting ion distribution over time. The action potential is all-or-nothing. Depolarisation in one region triggers it in the next, so the impulse travels. In myelinated axons, depolarisation occurs only at the nodes of Ranvier, so the impulse appears to jump from node to node, making saltatory conduction much faster than in an unmyelinated axon of the same diameter. (6 marks)
  2. Describe synaptic transmission and explain one way in which a drug can interfere with it. Answer: When an action potential reaches the presynaptic ending, calcium channels open, calcium enters, vesicles of neurotransmitter fuse with the presynaptic membrane and release neurotransmitter into the synaptic cleft; the neurotransmitter diffuses across the cleft and binds to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane, opening ion channels and changing the membrane potential of the postsynaptic neurone. A drug such as lidocaine can block voltage-gated sodium channels, preventing action potentials; or a drug such as nicotine can mimic a neurotransmitter and stimulate its receptors. (5 marks)
  3. Explain how rods detect light, including the role of rhodopsin. Answer: Rod cells contain rhodopsin, made of opsin and retinal. Light causes retinal to change shape, altering opsin, which triggers a transduction pathway that closes sodium channels in the rod membrane; sodium entry falls, the rod cell hyperpolarises, and the pattern of neurotransmitter release changes. This change is passed through the retinal wiring to the optic neurones, which carry impulses to the brain. (5 marks)
  4. Describe the functions of the cerebral hemispheres, hypothalamus, pituitary gland, cerebellum and medulla oblongata. Answer: The cerebral hemispheres are involved in higher functions such as voluntary movement, sensation, thought, memory, language and consciousness, with different regions specialised. The hypothalamus links the nervous and endocrine systems and helps control homeostasis, body temperature, hunger, thirst and pituitary hormone release. The pituitary gland releases hormones that regulate other endocrine glands and other processes. The cerebellum coordinates movement, posture and balance and refines motor control. The medulla oblongata controls automatic functions such as breathing and heart rate. (5 marks)
  5. Compare MRI, fMRI, PET and CT scans of the brain. Answer: MRI uses magnetic fields and radio waves to give detailed images of brain structure. fMRI detects changes in blood flow related to neural activity, showing which areas are active during a task. PET uses a radioactive tracer to show metabolic activity in brain regions. CT uses X-rays to produce cross-sectional images, useful for detecting structural problems such as bleeding or fractures. The methods are complementary: some are better for structure, some for activity. (5 marks)
  6. Describe the roles of phytochrome, auxin and gibberellins in plant responses. Answer: Phytochrome is a light receptor that interconverts between forms in response to light and helps the plant detect light, affecting processes such as flowering and germination. Auxin promotes cell elongation and is involved in tropic responses such as phototropism, where asymmetric distribution causes the shoot to bend toward light. Gibberellins promote growth, including stem elongation and seed germination, partly by affecting transcription. (5 marks)
  7. Explain how recombinant DNA is made and how it can be inserted into other cells. Answer: Recombinant DNA is made by cutting a gene and a vector, often a plasmid, with the same restriction endonuclease so they have complementary sticky ends, mixing them so the gene inserts into the vector, and joining them with DNA ligase. The recombinant vector is then inserted into host cells, such as bacteria, where it can be replicated and the inserted gene expressed. (5 marks)
  8. Describe how microarrays are used to identify active genes. Answer: A microarray has many short DNA sequences attached to a solid surface; cDNA made from the mRNA of a sample and labelled is hybridised to the array; if a gene is active, its cDNA binds to the corresponding spot and the label reveals its presence and relative level. Comparing samples, such as diseased and healthy tissue, shows which genes are up- or down-regulated. (4 marks)
  9. Discuss the risks and benefits of genetically modified organisms. Answer: Benefits include increased yield, improved nutrition, pest and herbicide resistance, reduced chemical use, production of medicines and faster research. Risks include effects on non-target organisms, gene flow to wild relatives, pest resistance, food-safety and ecological-stability concerns, and economic and patenting issues. The answer should be specific to the case, because the same technology can have different outcomes depending on the modification, organism and environment. (6 marks)

Use this summary to place each idea before you go into the detail in the full notes. Revise the neurone roles and myelination, the action potential sequence and saltatory conduction, synaptic transmission and the drug examples, the rod and rhodopsin mechanism, the brain regions and the imaging methods, the plant hormones and the practical, and the gene-technology tools and applications. Then check the full notes for the drug names and the microarray details, and move on to the next topic when you can do the calculations and the comparisons without prompting.

Coordination, Response and Gene Technology — Quick Revision Summary

This is the fast map of Edexcel International A2 Biology WBI16 Topics 8 and 9. It follows the same order as the full notes so you can cross-reference, and it repeats the specification numbers so you can see which paragraph exists for which point. Use it to organise the topic, not to replace the notes. The topic splits into three big blocks: the nervous system and neurones, the brain, imaging and the pharmacology of the nervous system, and the plant and genetic technologies — coordination in plants, recombinant DNA and GM organisms, and bioinformatics and microarrays.

The nervous system: hierarchy and the reflex arc

The nervous system lets an organism detect a stimulus, send information quickly, and make effectors respond. In mammals it is built from the central and peripheral systems, and its fastest wired responses are the reflex arcs, which are the simplest complete circuits you study in this topic.

  • 8.1 Sensory neurones carry information from receptors toward the central nervous system; relay neurones are in the central nervous system and connect sensory to motor neurones; motor neurones carry impulses from the central nervous system to effectors such as muscles and glands. Schwann cells wrap many axons in myelin, an insulating fatty layer, and myelination increases the speed of conduction. The roles of the three neurone types and the reason for myelination are the core ideas here.
  • 8.2 The nervous system causes effectors to respond to a stimulus through a chain: receptor detects the stimulus, sensory neurone carries the impulse to the central nervous system, relay neurone processes the information and passes it on, motor neurone carries the impulse to the effector, and the effector responds. The pupil example is useful: the iris contains muscles that respond to the amount of light, and the wiring behind that response is the kind of autonomic coordination this part of the topic describes.
  • 8.3 A spinal reflex arc is the simplest complete pathway. The stimulus is detected by a receptor, the sensory neurone enters the spinal cord, the relay neurone in the grey matter connects to the motor neurone, and the motor neurone carries the impulse out to the effector — often a muscle. The grey matter is where the relay neurones and synapses are; the white matter is made of myelinated axons that carry impulses up and down the cord between the spinal cord and the brain. The reflex arc is fast because it is short and involves few synapses, and it is protective because it does not wait for the brain to process the information first.

The practical point is that the reflex arc is not just “a reflex”; it is the minimal circuit that shows how sensory input, central relay and motor output are wired together, and it explains why the grey and white matter of the spinal cord have different functions.

The action potential and how it travels

The nerve impulse is the action potential, a self-propagating electrical signal caused by changes in the permeability of the axon membrane to sodium and potassium ions. The sequence of events is what the exam wants, and the reason myelination speeds conduction is part of the same picture.

  • 8.4 An action potential is conducted along an axon because of changes in membrane permeability to sodium and potassium ions. At rest the membrane is polarised, with the inside negative relative to the outside. When a stimulus is strong enough, voltage-gated sodium channels open and sodium ions enter the axon, depolarising the membrane and generating the rising phase of the action potential. Sodium channels then close and voltage-gated potassium channels open, so potassium ions leave the axon and the membrane repolarises. The sodium-potassium pump restores the resting distribution of ions over time, but the immediate repolarisation is due to potassium leaving, not to the pump. The action potential is all-or-nothing: once the threshold is reached, it fires fully; a stronger stimulus does not make a bigger action potential, only more frequent ones.
  • The propagation happens because the depolarisation of one small region of the membrane changes the voltage in the neighbouring region, opening channels there and so on along the axon. The impulse travels because each section regenerates the signal, not because the same ions travel from one end of the axon to the other. That is why the impulse is an electrochemical wave and not a current flowing the length of the axon like water in a pipe.
  • 8.5 Myelination makes this faster by saltatory conduction. The myelin sheath is interrupted by the nodes of Ranvier, where the axon membrane is exposed. Depolarisation can only happen at these nodes, so the action potential appears to jump from node to node. This is far faster than continuous conduction along an unmyelinated axon of the same diameter, because the signal travels quickly along the insulated internodal regions and is only recharged at the nodes. The comparison is not that myelin makes the ions move faster; it is that the signal regenerates at fewer points along the way.

A frequent mistake is to say that myelination increases the speed by making the ions travel faster, or to forget that the sodium-potassium pump restores the resting conditions after the action potential rather than causing the repolarisation itself. The order of events — sodium in, depolarisation, potassium out, repolarisation, then restoration — is the secure version.

Synapses and the chemical transmission of the signal

Where one neurone meets another, the signal crosses a synapse. The synapse is the point at which the electrical signal becomes chemical for one step and then electrical again, and it is also where drugs and toxins can act. Synaptic transmission is the reason neurones can be modulated, integrated and influenced by chemicals.

  • 8.6 (i) A synapse in nerve impulse transmission has a presynaptic neurone ending with vesicles of neurotransmitter, a synaptic cleft, and a postsynaptic membrane with receptors for the neurotransmitter. When an action potential arrives at the presynaptic ending, calcium channels open, calcium enters, and vesicles fuse with the presynaptic membrane and release neurotransmitter into the cleft. The neurotransmitter diffuses across the cleft and binds to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane, opening ion channels and producing a new change in membrane potential in the postsynaptic neurone. Acetylcholine is the neurotransmitter at the neuromuscular junction and at many other synapses, and its action is a good example of the general scheme.
  • The pupil is a useful illustration. The iris contains muscles whose contraction or relaxation changes the pupil diameter; this is under autonomic control, and the pathway involves synaptic transmission with acetylcholine and, in the relevant part of the autonomic system, noradrenaline, depending on whether the response is constriction or dilation. The point is not to memorise every transmitter at every synapse, but to understand that the synapse is where the signal is passed and where chemicals can modify it.
  • 8.7 Drugs act by influencing nerve impulse transmission, and the specification names several examples. Nicotine mimics acetylcholine at some receptors, stimulating them; lidocaine blocks voltage-gated sodium channels, preventing action potentials and so acting as a local anaesthetic; cobra venom alpha toxin blocks neuromuscular transmission by binding to acetylcholine receptors; L-DOPA is used in Parkinson’s disease because it is a precursor that can be converted to dopamine, which is deficient in that condition; and MDMA, ecstasy, affects neurotransmitter reuptake and release, especially of serotonin, changing mood and perception. The principle is that drugs can mimic, block, enhance or reduce neurotransmitter action, and that the effect depends on which step they influence.

A helpful way to remember the drug examples is to classify them by the step they affect: some mimic a neurotransmitter, some block a receptor, some block ion channels, some change how much neurotransmitter is released or reabsorbed, and some are supplied as precursors. If you can say which step each one affects, you can answer the typical question even if you do not remember the exact detail of every one.
