content:
Microbiology, Immunity and Forensics

Edexcel International A Level Biology — Unit 4 (WBI14), Topic 6. Every statement 6.1 to 6.20 is covered below, with its code in the heading. The topic links three big ideas: how microorganisms are grown and measured, how the body defends itself and why pathogens keep finding ways around those defences, and how DNA techniques are used to identify organisms and people.

6.1: Culturing microorganisms with aseptic technique

  • Aseptic technique keeps a culture pure: only the wanted microorganism grows. Sterilise media and equipment first, usually in an autoclave at 121 °C under pressure for about 15 minutes.
  • Work close to a Bunsen flame, flame the inoculating loop until red-hot before and after use, keep Petri dish lids mostly closed, and never pipette by mouth.
  • Incubate cultures inverted at a safe temperature, usually 25 °C for school work, so condensation does not drip onto the agar.

6.2: Measuring the growth of microorganisms

  • Direct cell counts: use a haemocytometer (counting chamber) under a microscope, counting cells in a known volume to get the number per cm³.
  • Viable counts by dilution plating: make a serial dilution, spread known volumes on agar, incubate, and count colonies on plates with about 30 to 300 colonies. Each colony is assumed to grow from one viable cell, so the count shows living cells only.
  • Mass methods: measure the dry mass of cells collected by centrifuging or filtering a known volume of culture.
  • Optical methods (turbidity): a colorimeter or spectrophotometer measures how much light the cloudy culture absorbs. Absorbance rises with cell density, so a calibration curve converts it to cell numbers.

6.3: The bacterial growth curve and the growth rate constant

  • Lag phase: cells adapt to the medium and synthesise enzymes; there is little or no division.
  • Exponential (log) phase: cells divide at a constant rate, so the population doubles each generation. N = N₀ × 2ⁿ, where n is the number of doublings.
  • Stationary phase: births equal deaths, because nutrients run short and waste builds up.
  • Death phase: deaths exceed births and the population falls.
  • Growth rate constant: in exponential growth N = N₀eᵏᵗ. So k = (ln N₂ − ln N₁) ÷ (t₂ − t₁). Plotting ln N against time gives a straight line whose gradient is k.

6.4: Core practical 13: growth of microorganisms in liquid culture

  • Inoculate a sterile liquid medium, take samples at regular intervals, and measure turbidity or cell count each time.
  • Plot the results to show the four phases of the curve, then calculate the exponential growth rate constant from the straight-line part.
  • Safe and ethical use: use only non-pathogenic strains, keep the culture closed, disinfect the bench, and autoclave all used material before disposal.

6.5: Structure of bacteria and viruses

  • Bacteria are cells with a cell wall (peptidoglycan), cell membrane, cytoplasm with ribosomes, and a circular DNA loop, often with plasmids. They have no nucleus.
  • Viruses are not cells. They have a nucleic acid core, either DNA or RNA, surrounded by a protein capsid. Some also have a lipid envelope taken from the host.
  • Comparisons: Ebola virus has single-stranded RNA and an envelope. Tobacco mosaic virus (TMV) has single-stranded RNA in a helical capsid, with no envelope. HIV has two RNA strands, reverse transcriptase and an envelope. Lambda phage, a virus of bacteria, has double-stranded DNA in a head with a tail and no envelope.
  • Lytic cycle: the virus takes over the host cell, makes new viruses, and the cell bursts (lyses) to release them.
  • Latency: the viral genome stays in the host cell without producing new viruses, and can become active later.

6.6: How Mycobacterium tuberculosis and HIV infect human cells

  • Tuberculosis: Mycobacterium tuberculosis is inhaled into the alveoli. Macrophages engulf it, but the bacterium survives inside them and multiplies. The body forms granulomas (tubercles) around the infection, and the lung tissue is destroyed. Symptoms include a persistent cough, fever, night sweats and weight loss. If untreated it can be fatal.
  • HIV: the virus binds to CD4 receptors and a co-receptor on helper T cells. Reverse transcriptase makes DNA from its RNA, which is inserted into the host genome. New viruses bud from the cell. The helper T cell population falls, so the immune system fails and opportunistic infections and cancers take hold (AIDS).

6.7: Routes of entry and barriers

  • Routes: inhalation (airborne droplets), ingestion (contaminated food and water), contact through broken skin or wounds, sexual contact, and vectors such as mosquitoes.
  • Barriers: intact skin (keratin, dryness, and the skin flora that competes with pathogens), stomach acid (pH about 2, which kills many ingested microbes), and gut flora that competes for space and nutrients. Mucus and cilia in the airways trap and move pathogens out.

6.8: Non-specific responses to infection

  • Inflammation: damaged cells release chemicals such as histamine, which dilate blood vessels and make them leaky. The area becomes red, hot and swollen, and white blood cells are recruited to the site.
  • Lysozyme: an enzyme in tears, saliva and mucus that breaks the peptidoglycan of bacterial cell walls.
  • Interferon: proteins released by virus-infected cells that warn neighbouring cells, which then resist viral replication. Interferon is antiviral, not a direct killer of the virus.
  • Phagocytosis: neutrophils and macrophages engulf a pathogen into a phagosome. Lysosomes fuse with it and enzymes digest the contents.

6.9: Antigens, antibodies, plasma cells, macrophages and antigen-presenting cells

  • An antigen is a foreign molecule, usually a protein or glycoprotein on a pathogen's surface, that triggers an immune response.
  • An antibody is a Y-shaped glycoprotein whose binding sites are complementary to one specific antigen. Antibodies mark pathogens for destruction and neutralise toxins.
  • Plasma cells are B cells that have been activated and that secrete antibodies in large amounts.
  • Macrophages and antigen-presenting cells engulf the pathogen, break it down, and display its antigens on their surface (on MHC proteins). This shows helper T cells what to respond to.

6.10: B cells and T cells

  • B effector (plasma) cells secrete antibodies. B memory cells survive for years and give a faster, larger response on the next exposure to the same antigen.
  • T helper cells (CD4) recognise the antigen on an antigen-presenting cell and release cytokines that activate B cells and T killer cells.
  • T killer (cytotoxic, CD8) cells bind to infected or abnormal cells and kill them, for example by releasing perforin.
  • T memory cells persist after the infection and respond quickly if the same pathogen returns.

6.11: Types of immunity

  • Natural active: the person is infected and makes their own antibodies and memory cells.
  • Natural passive: antibodies pass from mother to baby across the placenta or in breast milk. Protection is immediate but short-lived, and no memory cells are formed.
  • Artificial active: vaccination with an antigen, a weakened or dead pathogen, or a toxoid. The person makes antibodies and memory cells without becoming ill.
  • Artificial passive: injected antibodies, such as antivenom or antitoxin. Protection is immediate and short-lived, and the person's own immune system does not learn.

6.12: The evolutionary race between pathogens and hosts

  • Pathogens evolve evasion mechanisms. Antigenic variation changes the surface antigens: influenza and HIV mutate rapidly, so antibodies no longer fit.
  • Other evasion: hiding inside host cells (tuberculosis in macrophages, HIV in T cells), entering latency, and suppressing the immune response.
  • The host responds with new antibodies and T cells, so pathogens and hosts keep evolving against each other. This is the evolutionary race.

6.13: Bacteriostatic and bactericidal antibiotics

  • Bacteriostatic antibiotics stop bacteria growing and dividing, for example by blocking protein synthesis. The immune system then clears the infection.
  • Bactericidal antibiotics kill bacteria, for example penicillin, which stops cell wall synthesis so the cell bursts.
  • Antibiotics do not act on viruses, which use the host cell's machinery.

6.14: Core practical 14: the effect of antibiotics on bacteria

  • Spread a lawn of bacteria on agar, place antibiotic discs on it, and include a control disc with no antibiotic.
  • Incubate, then measure the diameter of each clear zone of inhibition. A larger zone means the bacteria are more sensitive.
  • Use aseptic technique and non-pathogenic strains, and autoclave the plates before disposal.

6.15: Hospital-acquired infections and codes of practice

  • Contributory causes include overuse of broad-spectrum antibiotics, which selects for resistant strains such as MRSA, poor hand hygiene, indwelling catheters, surgical wounds, and immunocompromised patients.
  • Codes of practice respond to these causes: prescribe antibiotics only when needed and according to guidelines, enforce hand hygiene, isolate infected patients, and clean equipment and wards.

6.16: Decomposition and the carbon cycle

  • Bacteria and fungi are the main decomposers. They secrete extracellular enzymes that digest complex organic matter such as cellulose and proteins, then absorb the simpler products.
  • Respiration by decomposers releases carbon dioxide, which returns carbon to the atmosphere for producers. Ammonium released from proteins feeds the nitrogen cycle.

6.17: The polymerase chain reaction (PCR)

  • Each cycle has three steps: denaturation at about 95 °C separates the strands, annealing at about 50 to 65 °C lets primers bind, and extension at about 72 °C is when Taq polymerase builds the new strands.
  • Taq polymerase comes from the heat-tolerant bacterium Thermus aquaticus, so it survives the high temperatures. Around 30 cycles give an exponential increase in the number of copies.

6.18: Gel electrophoresis of DNA fragments

  • DNA carries a negative charge from its phosphate groups, so it moves towards the positive electrode (anode) through a gel.
  • Smaller fragments move faster and further, so fragments separate by length. A DNA ladder of known sizes is run alongside for comparison, and the bands are stained to make them visible.

6.19: DNA profiling for identification and relatedness

  • DNA profiling compares short tandem repeats (STRs) or variable number tandem repeats (VNTRs). These regions vary in length between individuals, so each person gives a distinctive band pattern.
  • Uses include identifying suspects, establishing paternity, and comparing the banding patterns of plants or animals to show how closely related they are.

6.20: Estimating the time of death from forensic evidence

  • Body temperature: the body cools towards the surroundings, so the rate of cooling gives an estimate of time since death.
  • Muscle contraction: rigor mortis sets in over hours, peaks, then fades over about a day or two.
  • Decomposition and succession: bacterial decomposition gives a predictable sequence of changes. Forensic entomology uses the stage of blowfly larvae and the succession of insect species to estimate how long the body has been exposed.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Growth rate, 6.3 applied: a culture grows from 2.0 × 10⁴ cells cm⁻³ at 2 hours to 1.6 × 10⁵ at 5 hours. N₂ ÷ N₁ = 8 = 2³, so three doublings in three hours. k = (ln 1.6 × 10⁵ − ln 2.0 × 10⁴) ÷ 3 = ln 8 ÷ 3 = 0.69 per hour. The doubling time is ln 2 ÷ k = 1.0 hour. Check the answer against the doubling count before you write it down.
  • Viable count, 6.2 applied: 150 colonies grow from 0.1 cm³ of a 10⁻⁵ dilution. That is 150 ÷ 0.1 = 1500 colonies per cm³ in the diluted sample, and multiplying by the dilution factor gives 1.5 × 10⁸ viable cells per cm³. A haemocytometer count would include dead cells, so the two methods can give different numbers from the same culture. Name which one you are using.
  • Log phase, 6.3 applied: plotting ln N against time gives a straight line only during exponential growth. A curve that bends is a sign that the lag, stationary or death phase has been included by mistake. Use only the straight section to find k.
  • Primary and secondary immune response, 6.10 and 6.12 applied: the first exposure has a lag of several days before antibodies peak at a lower level. A second exposure gives a faster, larger and longer-lasting response, because memory cells are already present. Use all three words, faster, larger and longer, to earn the full mark.
  • Antigen presentation, 6.9 applied: helper T cells (CD4) recognise antigen presented on MHC class II proteins, and killer T cells (CD8) recognise it on MHC class I, as on infected body cells. Naming the MHC class shows you understand which cell carries the antigen.
  • Antibiotic action, 6.13 applied: penicillin blocks the cross-linking of peptidoglycan in the cell wall, so a growing cell bursts. An antibiotic that targets a process human cells do not use, such as the bacterial ribosome, is more selective. Resistance arises by chance mutation and is selected for by the antibiotic, so the explanation must say the mutation was already present and survived.
  • PCR, 6.17 applied: after n cycles one DNA molecule has become 2ⁿ molecules. After 30 cycles that is 2³⁰, about 1.07 × 10⁹ copies. This is why a very small sample is enough, and why contamination with foreign DNA is a serious error.
  • Gel electrophoresis, 6.18 applied: the distance moved is roughly linear with the logarithm of the fragment length. Use a DNA ladder to plot log size against distance, then read the unknown band from that graph rather than from the ladder bands by eye.
  • Forensic estimates, 6.20 applied: a time-of-death answer is always a range. Temperature cooling assumes a stable environment, and a hot or wet site or a body wrapped in clothing changes the rate. Say which factor is most uncertain and why.

Exam tip: time-of-death questions are estimates. Name the method, say what it measures, and state the limitation, for example that temperature depends on the environment.

title: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Sets and Venn Diagrams
content:
Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Sets and Venn Diagrams

Set notation is the language of sorting: it describes which elements belong together, which belong to both groups, and which belong to neither. The IGCSE questions are almost always Venn-diagram problems in disguise — a survey of students, a group of numbers, a club membership — and the marks come from filling every region correctly. This note builds the topic from zero: the notation and symbols, the two-set and three-set Venn diagrams and how to shade them, the counting formulas, and the word-problem method that never misses a region.

Set notation and vocabulary

SymbolMeaningExample
∈is an element of3 ∈ {1, 2, 3}
∉is not an element of5 ∉ {1, 2, 3}
ξ (or U)the universal set — everything under discussionξ = {1, 2, ..., 12}
∅the empty setodd multiples of 2 = ∅
A′the complement of A — everything in ξ not in AA′ = ξ A
A ∪ Bunion — in A or B or both{1,2} ∪ {2,3} = {1,2,3}
A ∩ Bintersection — in both{1,2} ∩ {2,3} = {2}
n(A)the number of elements of An({2, 4, 6}) = 3

Two rules follow directly: A ∩ A′ = ∅ (nothing is both in and out), and A ∪ A′ = ξ (everything is one or the other). Subsets: A ⊂ B means every element of A is also in B. The empty set has no elements, so n(∅) = 0, and it is a subset of every set — a fact worth stating explicitly when a question asks whether ∅ ⊂ A is true.

Two-set Venn diagrams

A two-set diagram divides the universal set into four regions: only A, only B, both, and neither. Filling them from the inside out is the reliable method:

  1. Write the number in the intersection (both) first.
  2. Work outward: only A = n(A) − both; only B = n(B) − both.
  3. Neither = total − (only A + only B + both).

Worked example. In a class of 32, 18 study French, 15 study Spanish, and 7 study both. Find the number studying only French, only Spanish, and neither.

both = 7
only French = 18 - 7 = 11
only Spanish = 15 - 7 = 8
neither = 32 - (11 + 8 + 7) = 32 - 26 = 6

Worked example 2 (reverse). In a group, 20 like tea, 14 like coffee and 5 like neither. Everyone likes at least one of the two? Then find n(tea ∩ coffee).

n(T union C) = 20 + 14 - both
total = 20 + 14 - both + 5 = 39 - both
If the group has 30 people: 30 = 39 - both → both = 9

The inclusion–exclusion formula

n(A union B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A intersection B)

for three sets:
n(A u B u C) = n(A) + n(B) + n(C)
             - n(A n B) - n(A n C) - n(B n C)
             + n(A n B n C)

The subtraction corrects double counting; the final addition corrects the triple-counted centre. Knowing the formula lets you answer "how many in total" questions without a full diagram, but a diagram is still the safer route for word problems.

Worked example. A survey of 50 people: 30 read newspapers, 25 read magazines, 12 read both. How many read at least one?

n(N union M) = 30 + 25 - 12 = 43
neither = 50 - 43 = 7

Three-set Venn diagrams

The three-set diagram has eight regions (counting "none of the three"). The fill order that never fails:

  1. Start with the triple intersection (all three).
  2. Find the "exactly two" regions by subtracting the triple from each pair.
  3. Find the "only one" regions by subtracting the pair and triple totals from each set total.
  4. Find "none" from the grand total.

Worked example. 40 students choose subjects: 20 take Maths, 18 take Physics, 15 take Chemistry; 8 take Maths and Physics, 6 take Maths and Chemistry, 5 take Physics and Chemistry; 3 take all three. Find how many take exactly one subject and how many take none.

triple = 3
exactly M and P = 8 - 3 = 5
exactly M and C = 6 - 3 = 3
exactly P and C = 5 - 3 = 2
only M = 20 - (5 + 3 + 3) = 9
only P = 18 - (5 + 2 + 3) = 8
only C = 15 - (3 + 2 + 3) = 7
exactly one = 9 + 8 + 7 = 24
total counted = 24 + 5 + 3 + 2 + 3 = 37
none = 40 - 37 = 3

Sets of numbers and shading

Questions often use number sets inside the universal set: ξ = {1, 2, ..., 20}, A = multiples of 3, B = multiples of 4. List them, then use the same four regions:

A = {3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18}
B = {4, 8, 12, 16, 20}
A n B = {12}
A u B = {3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 12, 15, 16, 18, 20}
neither = {1, 2, 5, 7, 10, 11, 13, 14, 17, 19}

Shading questions ask for a region described in symbols. Translate the symbols into words first: A′ ∩ B means "not in A, but in B" — the part of B outside A. A ∪ B′ means "in A, or outside B" — everything except the part of B that is not in A.

Listing sets and set-builder notation

Sets can be written in three ways, and questions move between them. The roster method lists the elements: A = {2, 4, 6, 8}. The description method states the rule in words: A is the set of even numbers from 2 to 8. Set-builder notation states the rule symbolically: A = {x : x is an even number, 2 ≤ x ≤ 8} — read as "the set of all x such that x is even and between 2 and 8".

  • Roster for finite sets: list every element once, in braces, separated by commas; order does not matter and repeats are not counted twice.
  • Description for patterns: "multiples of 3 less than 30" is clearer than listing ten numbers.
  • Set-builder for precision: the colon means "such that"; the condition after it does the work.

Worked example. Write the set of odd numbers between 1 and 11 in roster and set-builder form, and find its size.

roster: {3, 5, 7, 9}  (strictly between, so 1 and 11 excluded)
set-builder: {x : x odd, 1 < x < 11}
n(A) = 4

Reading the inequalities is the trap: "between" usually excludes the endpoints, "from ... to ..." usually includes them, and the question's wording decides. When in doubt, list both interpretations and choose the one consistent with the other numbers in the question.

Worked examples: word problems

Worked example. In a hostel of 60 students, 35 play football, 28 play basketball, and 12 play both. How many play neither?

at least one = 35 + 28 - 12 = 51
neither = 60 - 51 = 9

Worked example 2 (with a variable). In a group of 25, x people like both tea and coffee, 12 like tea only and 8 like coffee only. Find x if everyone likes at least one.

12 + 8 + x = 25  →  x = 5

Worked example 3 (conditional language). Of 40 students, 24 study History, 18 study Geography and 6 study neither. How many study both?

at least one = 40 - 6 = 34
34 = 24 + 18 - both  →  both = 42 - 34 = 8

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Notation) ξ = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8}; A = {2, 4, 6, 8}; B = {1, 3, 5, 7}. Find A ∩ B and A ∪ B. Answer: A ∩ B = ∅; A ∪ B = ξ.
  2. (Complement) With A = {2, 4, 6, 8} in ξ above, list A′. Answer: A′ is everything in ξ that is not in A: ξ = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8} and A = {2, 4, 6, 8}, so A′ = {1, 3, 5, 7}.
  3. (Two sets) n(A) = 14, n(B) = 9, n(A ∩ B) = 4. Find n(A ∪ B). Answer: the overlap is counted twice when the sizes are added, so take it off once: n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B) = 14 + 9 − 4 = 19.
  4. (Neither) In a class of 30, 17 like cricket, 12 like tennis and 5 like both. Find the number who like neither. Answer: at least one = 24; neither = 6.
  5. (Three sets) 30 students: 15 like Maths, 12 like Physics, 10 like Chemistry; 5 like Maths and Physics, 4 like Maths and Chemistry, 3 like Physics and Chemistry, 2 like all three. Find the number who like exactly one. Answer: only M = 15 − (3 + 2 + 2) = 8; only P = 12 − (3 + 1 + 2) = 6; only C = 10 − (2 + 1 + 2) = 5; total = 19 (with exactly-two counts 3, 2, 1 and triple 2).
  6. (Shading) Describe the region A′ ∩ B in words. Answer: Elements in B but not in A — the part of B outside A.
  7. (Numbers) ξ = {1, ..., 20}; A = even numbers; B = multiples of 5. Find n(A ∩ B). Answer: A ∩ B holds the numbers that are both even and a multiple of 5, i.e. multiples of 10; up to 20 those are 10 and 20, so n(A ∩ B) = 2.
  8. (Reasoning) Explain why n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) is wrong when A and B overlap. Answer: The elements in both sets are counted twice in n(A) + n(B), so the intersection must be subtracted once: n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B).

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Filling the intersection last: start at the centre. Adding both set totals and forgetting the overlap counts shared elements twice.
  • Forgetting the "neither" region: the universal set includes elements outside all named sets; if the question gives a total, subtract to find them.
  • Confusing ∪ and ∩: union is "or" (everything), intersection is "and" (only the middle). A quick mnemonic: ∪ looks like a cup that holds everything.
  • Shading the wrong side for A′: the complement is everything outside A, including parts of other sets and the region outside them all.
  • Triple intersection double subtraction: when subtracting pairs, remember each pair already includes the triple; subtract the triple from each pair before using them.
  • Reading "only": "only A" means A and nothing else — exclude the overlaps. The word only is a region instruction, not decoration.
  • Notation in answers: list elements with braces and commas; do not write 1, 2, 3 as an unbraced list when the answer is a set.
  • Assuming everyone likes something: unless stated, some may be outside both sets — check whether the total equals the sum of the regions.

The four regions: reading a Venn diagram as a counting grid

A two-set Venn diagram is not a picture of two sets. It is a grid with four cells, and every question about it is answered by putting a number in each cell and adding.

Name the four cells before you write anything. For sets A and B inside a universal set ξ, every element is in exactly one of: only A, both, only B, neither. In the figure that is 7, 5, 9 and 4. The moment all four numbers are on the page, every part of the question is a sum:

n(A) = 7 + 5 = 12 Key: n(A) counts everything inside circle A, including the overlap.
n(A ∩ B) = 5 Key: the intersection — the region inside both circles.
n(A ∪ B) = 7 + 5 + 9 = 21 Key: the union — everything inside at least one circle.
n(ξ) = 21 + 4 = 25 Key: the universal set also counts what is in neither set.

Why the formula has a minus sign. Adding n(A) and n(B) counts the overlap twice — once with each circle — so it has to come back off:

n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B) Key: n(A ∪ B) = elements in at least one set; n(A ∩ B) = elements in both. In the figure, 12 + 14 − 5 = 21, which is exactly the sum of the three inner cells. The subtraction is not a rule to remember; it is the double count being removed.

Worked example. In a class of 30, 18 study French, 15 study Spanish and 6 study both. How many study neither?

French only = 18 − 6 = 12
Spanish only = 15 − 6 = 9
at least one = 12 + 6 + 9 = 27
neither = 30 − 27 = 3

Going the other way — "9 study neither" — is the same arithmetic in reverse, and it is the version that appears when the examiner wants an unknown: if the total is 30 and 9 study neither, then 21 study at least one, and 18 + 15 − x = 21 gives x = 12 studying both. Filling the grid from the overlap outwards always works, because the overlap is the only cell that belongs to both circles.

Where marks are lost. Treating "18 study French" as 18 in the French-only region, which double-counts 6. Forgetting the neither region, so the four numbers do not add to the total. And shading the wrong side for A′ ∩ B: the complement of A is everything outside A, so A′ ∩ B is the B-only region, not the overlap.

Sets: the building blocks of counting

A set is a well-defined collection of objects, called its elements or members. In IGCSE Mathematics, sets are used to organise numbers and to count how many items share or avoid a property. Questions on this statement test three things: reading and writing set notation, drawing and filling Venn diagrams, and using counting rules without double-counting. The subsections below take these one at a time.

What counts as a set

A set is defined by a rule that tells you, for any object, whether it is in the set or not. "The even numbers less than 10" is a set because every number either is or is not an even number less than 10. A list such as "some tall students" is not a set, because two people might disagree about who is tall. Exam questions always use clear rules, so the first step is to write each set as a list or a rule before counting anything.

Writing a set in roster form

Roster form lists every element between curly brackets, separated by commas. The set of prime numbers less than 12 is {2, 3, 5, 7, 11}. The order of the elements does not matter, and an element is never written twice. Roster form is quickest for small sets, and it is the form the examiner usually expects when a question says "list the elements".

The element and not-element symbols

The symbol ∈ means "is an element of", and ∉ means "is not an element of". So 4 ∈ {1, 2, 3, 4} is true, and 5 ∉ {1, 2, 3, 4} is also true. These symbols are used in statements about membership, and they should be read aloud as whole sentences when you check an answer, because a reversed symbol reverses the meaning of the statement.

The empty set

The empty set, written ∅ or { }, contains no elements at all. The set of whole numbers that are both odd and even is the empty set, because no number has both properties. The empty set is a subset of every set, and in a Venn diagram it is shown by a region with no number in it. Do not confuse ∅ with the set containing zero, {0}, which has one element.

Subsets and the subset symbol

A set A is a subset of a set B when every element of A is also an element of B, and this is written A ⊂ B. For example, {1, 2} ⊂ {1, 2, 3, 4} because both 1 and 2 are in the larger set. Every set is a subset of itself, and the empty set is a subset of every set. A question asking whether one set is a subset of another can be answered by checking each element of the first set in turn.

Equal sets

Two sets are equal when they contain exactly the same elements, whatever order they are listed in. So {3, 1, 2} and {1, 2, 3} are equal, because both contain the numbers 1, 2 and 3 and no others. A repeated element does not make a set bigger, so {1, 1, 2} is the same set as {1, 2}. This is why counting the elements of a set means counting distinct members.

The number of elements in a set

The number of elements in a set A is written n(A). For A = {2, 4, 6, 8}, n(A) = 4. The notation is used in every counting formula in the Venn diagram work later in this note, so write it carefully. A common slip is to count the brackets, the commas or the repeated entries rather than the distinct elements.

Union, intersection and complement

Three operations combine or select sets, and every Venn diagram question uses at least one of them. The union collects everything in either set, the intersection keeps only what is common to both, and the complement takes everything outside a set. The subsections below define each operation, show how it is written, and give a method for working with them.

The universal set

Most set questions give a universal set, written ξ, which contains every element under discussion. The complement of a set is always taken relative to the universal set. If ξ is the set of integers from 1 to 10, then the complement of the even numbers is the odd numbers within those ten integers. Always state the universal set before you find any complement, because the same set has a different complement in a different universe.

Union: everything in either set

The union of A and B, written A ∪ B, is the set of all elements that are in A, or in B, or in both. For A = {1, 2, 3} and B = {3, 4}, the union is A ∪ B = {1, 2, 3, 4}. The element 3 appears once in the answer, even though it is in both sets. The word "or" in mathematics includes the case where both are true, so the union is never smaller than either set on its own.

Intersection: what the two sets share

The intersection of A and B, written A ∩ B, is the set of elements that are in both A and B. For the same sets, A ∩ B = {3}. If two sets have no elements in common, their intersection is the empty set, and the sets are called disjoint. The word "and" in a question such as "students who play both hockey and tennis" points to an intersection.

Complement: everything not in the set

The complement of A, written A′ (read as "A dash"), is the set of all elements of the universal set that are not in A. With ξ = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} and A = {1, 2, 3}, the complement is A′ = {4, 5}. Every element of ξ is in exactly one of A and A′, so the two together account for the whole universal set. This is a useful check when you list a complement by hand.

Combining operations in one expression

Expressions such as (A ∪ B)′ or A ∩ B′ contain more than one operation. Work inside the brackets first, and then apply the outer operation. For A = {1, 2, 3}, B = {3, 4} and ξ = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}, the union A ∪ B is {1, 2, 3, 4}, so its complement is {5}. Writing each stage on a separate line makes the working easy to mark.

Reading the notation in words

Translating between symbols and words is a skill in its own right. A ∪ B is "A or B", A ∩ B is "A and B", and A′ is "not A". A question that asks for "students who do not study French" describes the complement of the French set. Write the set in symbols first, then check your answer against the words of the question before you count.

Identifying the sets from a list

Given a list of properties, the sets are found by reading each property as a rule. For instance, "the multiples of 3 from 1 to 20" is {3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18}. Construct each set from its rule separately, then apply the operation the question asks for. This prevents mixing up the elements of the two sets when the question involves several properties at once.

Checking an answer with the universal set

When a result is a union or an intersection, check that every element is inside the universal set, and that no element of A or B is missing. When a result is a complement, check that it and the original set together make up the universal set with no overlap. These two checks take a few seconds and catch most of the errors made with set operations.

Venn diagrams with two and three sets

A Venn diagram shows sets as overlapping regions inside a rectangle that represents the universal set. Each region holds the elements that belong to exactly the sets that cover it. Once the regions are filled, every set operation and every count can be read from the diagram. The subsections below build the diagram from the information in a question, first for two sets and then for three.

Drawing a two-set Venn diagram

Draw a rectangle for the universal set and two overlapping circles, one for each set. The overlap is the intersection, the rest of each circle is that set without the other, and the area outside both circles is neither set. There are four regions in total, and each one must be labelled before any numbers are entered. Labelling the circles with the set names first avoids confusion when the question changes which set is which.

Filling a two-set diagram from a total

A common question gives the total number of people, the number in each set, and the number in both. Put the number in both sets into the overlap first. Then subtract that number from each circle total to find the number that belong only to that set. The number in neither set is the total minus everything placed in the circles. The order matters: starting with the outer region gives a wrong answer.

Using the counting formula for two sets

The number of elements in a union is given by n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B). The intersection is subtracted because it was counted in both n(A) and n(B). For 15 people in A, 12 in B and 5 in both, n(A ∪ B) = 15 + 12 − 5 = 22. The formula gives the same answer as filling the diagram, and it is quicker when the diagram is not needed.

Reading a diagram with a question about "only"

The phrase "only A" refers to the region inside circle A and outside circle B, which is A ∩ B′. The phrase "neither" refers to the region outside both circles, which is (A ∪ B)′. Students often read "only" as a total of A, which includes the overlap, so check the word carefully. Write the set expression next to each phrase before you read a value from the diagram.

Setting up a three-set Venn diagram

A three-set diagram has three overlapping circles and eight regions, including the one outside all three. Label the circles A, B and C and the regions from the centre outwards. The centre is A ∩ B ∩ C, and the region outside all three is the complement of A ∪ B ∪ C. Filling the centre first is the standard approach, because every other region depends on it.

Filling a three-set diagram step by step

Start from the centre and work outwards. Each pairwise region is found by subtracting the centre from the given total for that pair. Each single-set region is found by subtracting the pairwise and centre values from the total for that set. The region outside all three circles comes last, as the universal total minus everything already placed. Check at the end that the regions add up to the universal total, because an error in one region shows up as a mismatch there.

Using the inclusion–exclusion rule with three sets

For three sets, n(A ∪ B ∪ C) = n(A) + n(B) + n(C) − n(A ∩ B) − n(B ∩ C) − n(A ∩ C) + n(A ∩ B ∩ C). The triple intersection is added back at the end because it was subtracted three times, once in each pairwise term. Use this formula when the question gives the sizes of the sets and their intersections, and draw the diagram only if a region is asked for.

Common errors in Venn diagram questions

The commonest mistakes are filling the outer regions before the centre, forgetting to subtract the overlap from the total of a set, and reading a single region as if it were a whole set. A quick check is to add every region in the diagram and compare the total with the universal set. Where the sum is wrong, go back to the centre and recompute outwards.

Sets of numbers and the notation for each

Several sets of numbers recur throughout IGCSE Mathematics, and each has a standard symbol. Naming the set a number belongs to is how a question about membership is answered, and it is also how a Venn diagram of numbers is labelled. The subsections below introduce each set, show how to write it with set-builder notation, and explain how to decide which set a number belongs to.

The natural numbers and the integers

The natural numbers are the counting numbers 1, 2, 3 and so on, and they are written ℕ. The integers are the whole numbers, positive, negative and zero, and they are written ℤ. Every natural number is an integer, so ℕ is a subset of ℤ. A question that asks whether −4 belongs to ℕ has the answer no, because −4 is an integer but not a natural number.

The rational numbers

The rational numbers are numbers that can be written as a fraction p/q, where p and q are integers and q is not zero. They are written ℚ. The number 0.75 is rational because it equals 3/4, and so is −2 because it equals −2/1. Every integer is rational, so ℤ is a subset of ℚ. A recurring decimal such as 0.333… is also rational, since it can be written as 1/3.

The irrational numbers

An irrational number cannot be written as a fraction of two integers. Examples are √2, √3 and the number π, whose decimal expansion never ends and never repeats. Irrational numbers are not written with a single standard symbol at this level, and a question about them is answered by showing that no fraction equals the number. A square root of a number that is not a perfect square is usually irrational.

The real numbers

The real numbers, written ℝ, are all the numbers that can be placed on a number line. They include the rational and the irrational numbers together. Every number used in IGCSE Mathematics is real, unless the question specifically introduces a non-real quantity. The relationship between the sets is that ℕ ⊂ ℤ ⊂ ℚ ⊂ ℝ, and each set sits inside the one after it.

The prime numbers as a set

The set of prime numbers is {2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, …}, where a prime is a natural number greater than 1 with exactly two factors, 1 and itself. The number 1 is not prime, and 2 is the only even prime. Questions often ask for the primes in a given range, or for the intersection of the primes with another set, such as the odd numbers, which gives every prime except 2.

Set-builder notation

Set-builder notation describes a set by a rule instead of a list. The set {x : x is an integer and −2 < x ≤ 3} is read as "the set of x such that x is an integer and x lies between −2 and 3, not including −2 and including 3". Its elements are {−1, 0, 1, 2, 3}. Read the colon as "such that", and read each inequality as a condition on the element.

Choosing the right set for a number

To decide which sets a number belongs to, check its properties in order. Ask whether it is a counting number, then whether it is a whole number, then whether it is a fraction of integers, and finally whether it is real. The number −3/4 is in ℚ and ℝ, but not in ℕ or ℤ. Writing the list of memberships for each number is a quick way to answer several membership questions at once.

title: Number — Sets — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Number — Sets

Mathematics — OL. A set is a well-defined collection of objects. Set notation and Venn diagrams let you describe groups and count their members precisely.

  • 1. Notation: ∈ means is an element of, ⊂ means is a subset of, ∪ means union (in either set), ∩ means intersection (in both sets), and A′ is the complement of A within the universal set ξ.
  • 2. Venn diagrams: draw the universal set as a rectangle and each set as a circle, and place each element in the correct region.
  • 3. Shading: shade the region that matches the description, and check that every region is covered or excluded correctly.
  • 4. Regions algebra: n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B), because the overlap is counted twice if you add the two sets.
  • 5. Probability links: the same regions give probabilities when each element is equally likely; P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B).

Core facts to recall

  • Start filling a Venn diagram from the centre, the intersection, and work outwards.
  • Check that the numbers in all regions add up to the total in the universal set.

How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

title: AS Level Mathematics: Probability Distributions
content:
AS Level Mathematics: Probability Distributions

A discrete random variable takes a countable set of values, each with a probability. The probability distribution is the complete list of values and probabilities, and from it come the two summaries that matter: the expected value (the long-run average) and the variance (the typical squared spread about it). This note builds the topic from zero: constructing and checking a distribution, E(X) and Var(X) from first principles, the effect of linear transformations, and the linear combinations of random variables that let you combine independent quantities with confidence.

Discrete random variables

X takes values x1, x2, ... with probabilities p1, p2, ...
conditions: 0 <= p_i <= 1 and the probabilities sum to 1

Worked example. A fair die is rolled and X is the score. Write the distribution and verify it.

P(X = k) = 1/6 for k = 1..6
sum = 6 x 1/6 = 1, so it is a valid distribution

Worked example 2 (unknown constant). P(X = 1) = k, P(X = 2) = 2k, P(X = 3) = 3k. Find k.

k + 2k + 3k = 1  ->  6k = 1  ->  k = 1/6
so P(X = 1) = 1/6, P(X = 2) = 1/3, P(X = 3) = 1/2

Expectation

E(X) = sum of x P(X = x)

the expected value need not be a possible value of X:
the mean of a die is 3.5

Worked example. Find E(X) for the die.

E(X) = (1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6)/6 = 21/6 = 3.5

Worked example 2 (unequal probabilities). X takes 0, 1, 2 with probabilities 0.2, 0.5, 0.3. Find E(X).

E(X) = 0(0.2) + 1(0.5) + 2(0.3) = 0.5 + 0.6 = 1.1

Interpretation: over many repetitions the average outcome approaches 1.1. That long-run reading is what applied questions ("expected profit", "expected number of defects") ask for.

Variance of a discrete random variable

Var(X) = E(X^2) - [E(X)]^2
where E(X^2) = sum of x^2 P(X = x)

standard deviation = sqrt(Var(X))

Worked example. Find Var(X) for the die.

E(X^2) = (1 + 4 + 9 + 16 + 25 + 36)/6 = 91/6 = 15.167
Var(X) = 15.167 - 12.25 = 2.917
sd = 1.708

Worked example 2. For X = 0, 1, 2 with probabilities 0.2, 0.5, 0.3, find Var(X).

E(X) = 1.1
E(X^2) = 0 + 0.5 + 4(0.3) = 1.7
Var(X) = 1.7 - 1.21 = 0.49
sd = 0.7

Linear transformations

E(aX + b) = a E(X) + b
Var(aX + b) = a^2 Var(X)

sd(aX + b) = |a| sd(X)

The asymmetry is the key idea: adding a constant shifts every value and so shifts the mean but leaves the spread unchanged; multiplying by a scales the mean by a and the spread by |a|, so the variance scales by a².

Worked example. E(X) = 5, Var(X) = 4. Find E(3X + 2) and Var(3X + 2).

E = 3(5) + 2 = 17
Var = 9(4) = 36;  sd = 6

Worked example 2 (finding the transformation). E(Y) = 20 and Var(Y) = 25, where Y = aX + b, E(X) = 4 and Var(X) = 1. Find a and b.

Var: a^2 (1) = 25  ->  a = 5 or -5
if a = 5: 20 = 5(4) + b  ->  b = 0
if a = -5: 20 = -20 + b  ->  b = 40
both are valid; the sign of a is fixed by context (a positive
scaling is usually implied)

Linear combinations of random variables

E(aX + bY) = a E(X) + b E(Y)          (always, no independence needed)
Var(aX + bY) = a^2 Var(X) + b^2 Var(Y)   (only if X, Y independent)
Var(aX - bY) = a^2 Var(X) + b^2 Var(Y)   (the variances still add)

The minus sign is where most marks are lost: subtracting random variables adds their variances, because the uncertainty compounds whichever direction the values move.

Worked example. X and Y are independent with E(X) = 10, Var(X) = 9, E(Y) = 4, Var(Y) = 4. Find E(X − Y) and Var(X − Y).

E(X - Y) = 10 - 4 = 6
Var(X - Y) = 9 + 4 = 13   (not 9 - 4)
sd = 3.606

Worked example 2 (three variables). Independent X, Y, Z with variances 2, 3, 5. Find Var(2X + 3Y − Z).

= 4(2) + 9(3) + 1(5) = 8 + 27 + 5 = 40

Worked example 3 (total of identical variables). A fair die is rolled twice; T is the total. Find E(T) and Var(T).

each roll: E = 3.5, Var = 35/12 = 2.917
E(T) = 7;  Var(T) = 2 x 2.917 = 5.833
sd(T) = 2.415  (the spread of a total grows, but by sqrt(2), not 2)

Discrete uniform distribution

X uniform on 1..n: P(X = k) = 1/n
E(X) = (n + 1)/2
Var(X) = (n^2 - 1)/12

Worked example. X is uniform on 1 to 10. Find E(X) and Var(X).

E(X) = 11/2 = 5.5
Var(X) = (100 - 1)/12 = 8.25

Cumulative distribution functions

The cumulative distribution function F(x) gives the probability that X is at most x. It is a step function for a discrete variable: constant between values, jumping at each value by that value's probability.

F(x) = P(X <= x) = sum of P(X = k) for k <= x

P(X = k) = F(k) - F(k - 1)
P(a < X <= b) = F(b) - F(a)

Worked example. X takes 1, 2, 3 with probabilities 0.2, 0.5, 0.3. Write F(x) and use it to find P(X > 1).

F(1) = 0.2;  F(2) = 0.7;  F(3) = 1
P(X > 1) = 1 - F(1) = 0.8  (equivalently 0.5 + 0.3)

Worked example 2 (recovering probabilities). F(2) = 0.35 and F(3) = 0.8. Find P(X = 3).

P(X = 3) = F(3) - F(2) = 0.8 - 0.35 = 0.45

Reading F correctly requires attention to the inequality: P(X < 3) = F(2) for a discrete variable, while P(X ≤ 3) = F(3). One unit of difference changes the answer.

Expectation from a table and applied profit

When the distribution is given as a table, the calculation is a single weighted total; when it is described in words, the table must be built first.

Worked example. A fair coin is tossed three times and X counts the heads. Find E(X) and Var(X).

X ~ Binomial(3, 1/2) in effect: probabilities 1/8, 3/8, 3/8, 1/8 for 0..3
E(X) = 0 + 3/8 + 6/8 + 3/8 = 12/8 = 1.5
E(X^2) = 0 + 3/8 + 12/8 + 9/8 = 24/8 = 3
Var(X) = 3 - 2.25 = 0.75

Worked example 2 (profit). A stall pays 4 pounds to play a game that returns 0, 5 or 20 pounds with probabilities 0.6, 0.3 and 0.1. Find the expected profit per game and whether the stall makes money.

E(return) = 0 + 1.5 + 2.0 = 3.5
profit = return - 4, so E(profit) = 3.5 - 4 = -0.5
players lose 50 pence per game on average, so the stall profits

The transformation rule does the work: E(X − c) = E(X) − c. State the interpretation, not just the number.

Why variances add for independent variables

For independent X and Y, the variance of a sum is the sum of the variances. The proof rests on the fact that independence makes E(XY) = E(X)E(Y), so the cross term in the expansion vanishes:

Var(X + Y) = E[(X + Y)^2] - [E(X + Y)]^2
           = E(X^2) + 2E(XY) + E(Y^2) - [E(X)]^2 - 2E(X)E(Y) - [E(Y)]^2
independence: E(XY) = E(X)E(Y), so the cross terms cancel
           = Var(X) + Var(Y)

For the difference, the same expansion gives Var(X − Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y): the cross term is −2E(XY) + 2E(X)E(Y), which also vanishes. The intuition is that independent errors cannot cancel — a positive error in one is just as likely to meet a positive or negative error in the other, so the uncertainties compound.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Valid distribution) P(X = 1) = 0.3, P(X = 2) = 0.4, P(X = 3) = k. Find k. Answer: 0.3.
  2. (E) X = 1, 3, 5 with probabilities 0.2, 0.5, 0.3. Find E(X). Answer: 0.2 + 1.5 + 1.5 = 3.2.
  3. (Var) For the same X, find Var(X). Answer: E(X²) = 0.2 + 4.5 + 7.5 = 12.2; Var = 12.2 − 10.24 = 1.96.
  4. (Transform) E(X) = 6, Var(X) = 5. Find E(4X − 1) and Var(4X − 1). Answer: 23 and 80.
  5. (Combination) Independent X, Y: Var(X) = 6, Var(Y) = 8. Find Var(2X + Y). Answer: 24 + 8 = 32.
  6. (Combination difference) Same X, Y: Var(X − Y). Answer: 6 + 8 = 14.
  7. (Uniform) X uniform on 1..6. Find Var(X). Answer: (36 − 1)/12 = 2.917.
  8. (Applied) A game pays X with E(X) = 2 and costs 3 to play. Find the expected profit. Answer: E(X − 3) = −1, a loss of 1 per game.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Var(aX) = a Var(X): wrong — the variance scales by a², the standard deviation by |a|.
  • Subtracting variances: Var(X − Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) for independent variables; subtraction never reduces uncertainty.
  • Assuming independence: the variance-addition rule requires it; the expectation rule does not.
  • Using E(X²) as [E(X)]²: they differ by the variance; compute E(X²) from the distribution.
  • Probabilities not summing to 1: the first check on any distribution, and often the way to find an unknown constant.
  • Expectation as a possible value: E(X) need not be attainable (3.5 on a die); say "on average over many trials".
  • Standard deviation units: the variance is in squared units; compare and quote the sd.
  • Negative scaling: if a is negative, E flips sign and sd uses |a|; forgetting the modulus produces a negative standard deviation.

Formula summary

E(X) = sum of x P(X = x);  E(X^2) = sum of x^2 P(X = x)
Var(X) = E(X^2) - [E(X)]^2
E(aX + b) = a E(X) + b;  Var(aX + b) = a^2 Var(X)
E(aX + bY) = a E(X) + b E(Y)
Var(aX + bY) = a^2 Var(X) + b^2 Var(Y)   (independent)
F(x) = P(X <= x);  P(X = k) = F(k) - F(k - 1)

Two conditions separate the whole topic: expectations always combine linearly, variances combine linearly only when the variables are independent — and then always with plus signs, whatever the signs in front of the variables. Write the condition before applying the variance rule; it is worth a mark on its own and prevents the commonest mistake in the topic.

title: AS Level Physics: D.C. Circuits
content:
AS Level Physics: D.C. Circuits

Direct-current circuits are where abstract quantities become measurable: current is charge in motion, potential difference is energy per charge, and resistance is the friction of the electrical world. This note builds the complete circuit toolkit from zero: current and the drift model, potential difference and power, resistance and resistivity, real sources and internal resistance, Kirchhoff's two laws, and potential dividers. Every calculation type is worked line by line, and the practical skills — meters, graphs, and the divider equation — are given the treatment the papers demand.

Electric current: charge in motion

Current is the rate of flow of charge: I = Q/t, measured in amperes (1 A = 1 C s⁻¹). Charge itself comes in quanta of e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. At the microscopic level, current in a metal is the drift of free electrons through a lattice of ions:

I = n A v q

n = charge carrier density (m⁻³)
A = cross-sectional area of the conductor (m²)
v = drift velocity (m s⁻¹)
q = charge on each carrier (C), = e for electrons

The analogy worth keeping: a garden hose already full of water. Turning the tap (closing the switch) sends water out the far end almost instantly — not because water travels the hose in zero time, but because the hose is full and pressure passes the signal along. So drift velocities are millimetres per second while the lamp lights instantly.

Worked example. A wire of cross-section 1.0 mm² carries 3.0 A. There are 8.5 × 10²⁸ free electrons per m³. Find the drift velocity.

A = 1.0 mm² = 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ m²
v = I/(n A q) = 3.0/(8.5 × 10²⁸ x 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ x 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹)
  = 3.0/(13 600) = 2.2 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹  (0.22 mm s⁻¹)

Note the unit conversions: mm² to m² is a factor of 10⁻⁶, and the answer in mm s⁻¹ is a factor of 10³ from m s⁻¹.

Potential difference and power

Potential difference (p.d.) across a component is the energy transferred per unit charge passing through it: V = W/Q, in volts (1 V = 1 J C⁻¹). Electromotive force (e.m.f.) is the energy converted from other forms to electrical energy per unit charge by a source — the same unit, different story (energy in, not energy out). Combine with I = Q/t to get the power equations that run the paper:

W = Q V = I t V
P = W/t = I V = I² R = V² / R

Worked example. A 12 V heater draws 8.0 A. Find its power and the energy converted in 5.0 minutes.

P = I V = 8.0 × 12 = 96 W
W = P t = 96 x (5.0 × 60) = 96 × 300 = 28 800 J = 29 kJ

Choosing the right power form: use P = IV when you have current and voltage, I²R when current and resistance are known (it shows why heating losses rise with current), V²/R when the voltage is fixed across the component.

Resistance, Ohm's law and resistivity

Resistance is the ratio V/I, in Ω (1 Ω = 1 V A⁻¹). Ohm's law states that current is proportional to potential difference for a metallic conductor at constant temperature — the graph of I against V is a straight line through the origin; the qualification about temperature is examinable. Resistivity is the material's own opposition to current, independent of the wire's shape:

R = ρ L / A          so   ρ = R A / L

ρ in Ω metre (Ω m)
L in m, A in m²

Worked example 1. A nichrome wire of resistivity 1.10 × 10⁻⁶ Ω m is 2.5 m long and 0.20 mm in diameter. Find its resistance.

A = π r² = 3.14 x (1.0 × 10⁻⁴)² = 3.14 × 10⁻⁸ m²
R = ρ L/A = (1.10 × 10⁻⁶ x 2.5)/(3.14 × 10⁻⁸)
  = 2.75 × 10⁻⁶/3.14 × 10⁻⁸ = 87.6 Ω  (2 s.f.: 88 Ω)

Worked example 2 (temperature). Explain why the resistance of a metal filament rises as it heats up. Answer: The lattice ions vibrate more vigorously with temperature, increasing the rate of collision with drifting electrons; each collision impedes the drift, so the same potential difference drives less current and R = V/I rises. (Semiconductors behave oppositely: more carriers are released, so their resistance falls.)

Practical circuits: sources, internal resistance and meters

A real source has internal resistance r: some energy is converted to heat inside the source itself, so the terminal potential difference is less than the e.m.f. whenever current flows.

e.m.f. = terminal p.d. + lost volts
E = V + I r        →   V = E - I r

also: E = I (R + r)  for a load resistance R in series with r

The V–I graph of a real source is the standard question: a straight line with y-intercept E and gradient −r. Short-circuit current (V = 0) is E/r.

Worked example. A cell of e.m.f. 1.50 V drives 0.20 A through a 6.0 Ω resistor. Find the internal resistance and the terminal p.d.

E = I(R + r)  →  1.50 = 0.20(6.0 + r)
7.5 = 6.0 + r  →  r = 1.5 Ω
terminal p.d.: V = I R = 0.20 × 6.0 = 1.20 V
check: lost volts = I r = 0.20 × 1.5 = 0.30 V, and 1.20 + 0.30 = 1.50 V

Meter rules: an ammeter goes in series (ideally zero resistance) and a voltmeter in parallel with the component (ideally infinite resistance); a real ammeter's small resistance and a real voltmeter's finite one are sources of systematic error worth naming in evaluation questions.

Series and parallel: the recaps that decide marks

SeriesParallel
Currentsame through each componentsplits; total = sum of branches
Voltagesplits; total = sum across componentssame across each branch
ResistanceR = R₁ + R₂ + ...1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + ...

Worked example. Find the total resistance of 6.0 Ω and 3.0 Ω in parallel, then in series with 2.0 Ω.

parallel pair: 1/R = 1/6 + 1/3 = 0.1667 + 0.3333 = 0.5
R_pair = 2.0 Ω
total with the series resistor: R = 2.0 + 2.0 = 4.0 Ω

Kirchhoff's laws

  • First law (charge conservation): the sum of currents entering a junction equals the sum leaving it. ΣI in = ΣI out. The junction rule — charge is not created inside a wire.
  • Second law (energy conservation): the sum of e.m.f.s around any closed loop equals the sum of p.d. drops around it; equivalently the potential changes around a loop sum to zero. ΣE = ΣIR.

The loop method for any network: (1) label current directions (a wrong guess just returns a negative value); (2) write one junction equation per junction you need; (3) write loop equations for enough independent loops; (4) solve the simultaneous equations.

Worked example. A 12 V battery drives two parallel resistors, 4.0 Ω and 6.0 Ω. Find the current from the battery and through each branch.

parallel p.d. is the same: 12 V across both branches
I(4.0) = V/R = 12/4.0 = 3.0 A
I(6.0) = 12/6.0 = 2.0 A
junction rule: I_battery = 3.0 + 2.0 = 5.0 A
check with total resistance: R = (4 × 6)/(4 + 6) = 2.4 Ω
I = 12/2.4 = 5.0 A  (consistent)

Worked example 2 (loop law). A 1.5 V cell and a 2.0 V cell are connected in series aiding, driving 0.10 A through a 33 Ω resistor plus internal resistances of 2.0 Ω total. Verify the loop law.

total e.m.f. = 1.5 + 2.0 = 3.5 V
total resistance = 33 + 2.0 = 35 Ω
I = 3.5/35 = 0.10 A  (matches the given current)
loop check: sum of p.d. drops = 0.10 × 35 = 3.5 V = sum of e.m.f.s

Potential dividers

Two resistors in series across a supply share the supply voltage in proportion to their resistances:

V_out = V_in x R2/(R1 + R2)

(R2 is the resistor across which the output is tapped)

The divider is the backbone of sensor circuits: replace R₂ with a light-dependent resistor or thermistor and the output voltage tracks light level or temperature. The loading caveat is examinable — connecting a finite-resistance voltmeter or load across R₂ changes the effective resistance and lowers V_out below the ideal value.

Worked example 1. A 9.0 V supply has R₁ = 2.0 kΩ and R₂ = 4.0 kΩ. Find the output voltage.

V_out = 9.0 × 4.0/(2.0 + 4.0) = 9.0 × 4/6 = 6.0 V

Worked example 2 (design). You need 3.0 V from a 12 V supply with a 1.0 kΩ total resistance. Choose R₁ and R₂.

V_out/V_in = R2/(R1 + R2) → 3.0/12 = R2/10⁰⁰
R2 = 250 Ω,  R1 = 750 Ω

Worked example 3 (thermistor). A thermistor in the lower leg falls from 4.0 kΩ to 1.0 kΩ on heating, with R₁ = 2.0 kΩ across a 9.0 V supply. Find the output voltage before and after heating.

cold:  V_out = 9.0 × 4.0/(2.0 + 4.0) = 6.0 V
hot:   V_out = 9.0 × 1.0/(2.0 + 1.0) = 3.0 V
The falling output signals rising temperature.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Current) A current of 0.50 A flows for 2.0 minutes. Find the charge transferred. Answer: Q = It = 0.50 × 120 = 60 C.
  2. (Power) A 6.0 Ω resistor dissipates 24 W. Find the current through it. Answer: P = I²R → I = √(P/R) = √(24/6.0) = 2.0 A.
  3. (Resistivity) Two wires of the same material have the same resistance; one is twice as long. State how its cross-section compares. Answer: R = ρL/A, so doubling L requires doubling A to keep R — the longer wire must have twice the cross-sectional area.
  4. (Internal resistance) A battery of e.m.f. 6.0 V and internal resistance 0.50 Ω drives a 2.5 Ω load. Find the terminal p.d. Answer: I = E/(R+r) = 6.0/3.0 = 2.0 A; V = IR = 2.0 × 2.5 = 5.0 V (lost volts = 1.0 V).
  5. (Kirchhoff 1) At a junction, 3.0 A and 2.0 A enter; one wire leaves. Find its current. Answer: 5.0 A — charge conservation.
  6. (Kirchhoff 2) State the second law and what it represents. Answer: The sum of e.m.f.s around any closed loop equals the sum of potential differences around it — conservation of energy.
  7. (Divider) A divider has R₁ = 3.0 kΩ and R₂ = 5.0 kΩ across 8.0 V. Find V_out. Answer: V_out = 8.0 × 5.0/8.0 = 5.0 V.
  8. (Sensor) Explain how a potential divider with a thermistor can act as a temperature sensor. Answer: The thermistor's resistance falls as temperature rises, changing the ratio R₂/(R₁+R₂) and hence V_out; the output voltage therefore tracks temperature and can be calibrated to a scale or trigger.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Power formula roulette: choosing P = V²/R when the current is fixed wastes time and marks. Match the formula to the quantities known.
  • Resistivity units: ρ is in Ω m, and areas in the formula are m² — mm² and cm² must be converted (1 mm² = 10⁻⁶ m²).
  • Internal resistance omission: "a battery" in a paper often implies real internal resistance; if the question gives r or a V–I graph, use V = E − Ir.
  • Divider loading: the ideal divider formula assumes no load current; if the question says a resistor is connected across the output, recompute the effective resistance rather than quoting the ideal value.
  • Meter placement: ammeters in series, voltmeters in parallel; a swapped meter is a practical-method mark lost.
  • Junction arithmetic: sum currents entering = leaving; the classic error is subtracting a branch current from itself when directions were assumed wrongly. A negative answer just means the assumed direction is reversed.
  • Series/parallel recognition: redraw circuits before calculating; two resistors across the same two nodes are parallel however the wires are drawn.
  • Significant figures and units: 2 or 3 s.f. with units (A, V, Ω, W, J); keep Ω as the unit for resistance — never Ω written as O or zero.
  • Method marks: state the formula (I = V/R, V = E − Ir, Kirchhoff's law) and the loop/junction you are using before substituting; the law name itself is credit.

Equations and symbols

The whole of this topic as equations, each written with its real symbols and each followed by a key naming every symbol and its unit. Where a law has more than one useful form both are given, because which one is quickest depends on which quantities the question hands you. Learn the form here and the algebraic rearrangement becomes mechanical in the exam.

9.1 Current, charge and drift velocity

I = ΔQ / Δt
Key: I = current (A, where 1 A = 1 C s⁻¹); ΔQ = charge passing a point in the conductor (C); Δt = time taken (s). The definition of current as rate of flow of charge.

Q = I t
Key: Q = charge transferred (C); I = steady current (A); t = time for which it flows (s). The definition rearranged for a constant current — the form used in electrolysis and in electricity-cost questions, where 1 kW h = 3.6 × 10⁶ J.

I = n A v q
Key: I = current (A); n = number density of charge carriers (m⁻³); A = cross-sectional area of the conductor (m²); v = mean drift velocity of the carriers (m s⁻¹); q = charge on each carrier (C), equal to e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C for electrons. Because n is fixed by the metal, a thinner wire must have a larger drift velocity for the same current.

W = Q V = I V t
Key: W = energy transferred electrically (J); Q = charge moved (C); V = potential difference across the component (V); I = current (A); t = time (s).

9.2 Potential difference, e.m.f. and power

V = W / Q
Key: V = potential difference across a component (V, where 1 V = 1 J C⁻¹); W = energy converted from electrical to other forms in that component (J); Q = charge passing through it (C).

E = W / Q
Key: E = electromotive force of the source (V); W = energy converted from chemical, mechanical or light energy into electrical energy per charge (J); Q = charge (C). The distinction the mark scheme rewards: e.m.f. is energy given to the charge inside the source; p.d. is energy taken from the charge in a component.

P = W / t = I V
Key: P = power (W = J s⁻¹); W = energy transferred (J); t = time (s); I = current (A); V = potential difference (V).

P = I² R = V² / R
Key: P = power dissipated as heat in a resistor (W); I = current through it (A); R = its resistance (Ω); V = p.d. across it (V). Use I²R when the current is known and V²/R when the p.d. is fixed — in parallel, V is shared equally, in series the current is.

η = P_useful / P_input × 100%
Key: η = efficiency (%); P_useful = power delivered to the load (W); P_input = total power supplied by the source, E I (W).

9.3 Resistance and resistivity

R = V / I
Key: R = resistance (Ω = V A⁻¹); V = p.d. across the component (V); I = current through it (A). Ohmic only when R is constant as V varies — the I–V graph through the origin is the test.

R = ρ L / A
Key: R = resistance (Ω); ρ = resistivity of the material (Ω m); L = length of the conductor (m); A = cross-sectional area (m²). Resistivity is a property of the material, resistance of the object — doubling the length doubles R but leaves ρ unchanged.

ρ = R A / L
Key: ρ = resistivity (Ω m); R = measured resistance (Ω); A = cross-sectional area (m²); L = measured length (m). The working form of the experiment: plot R against L, gradient = ρ/A, so ρ = gradient × A.

G = 1 / R
Key: G = conductance (S = Ω⁻¹); R = resistance (Ω). Conductance adds directly in parallel, which is why parallel combinations are easier in G.

10.1 Series, parallel, internal resistance and meters

R_series = R₁ + R₂ + R₃ + …
Key: R_series = total resistance (Ω); R₁, R₂ … = individual resistances (Ω). The current is common to all, so the p.d.s add and the resistances add.

1 / R_parallel = 1 / R₁ + 1 / R₂ + 1 / R₃ + …
Key: R_parallel = total resistance (Ω); R₁, R₂ … = branch resistances (Ω). The p.d. is common, so the currents add. For n identical resistors R each, R_parallel = R / n.

R_parallel = R₁ R₂ / (R₁ + R₂)
Key: R_parallel = resistance of the pair (Ω); R₁, R₂ = the two resistances (Ω). The two-resistor shortcut; the total is always smaller than the smaller of the two.

E = V + I r
Key: E = e.m.f. of the source (V); V = terminal potential difference, the p.d. across the external circuit (V); I = current drawn (A); r = internal resistance of the source (Ω). The lost volts are I r, and they exist because the current also flows through the source itself.

V = E − I r
Key: V = terminal p.d. (V); E = e.m.f. (V); I = current (A); r = internal resistance (Ω). This is why a battery reads nearly its e.m.f. on a high-resistance voltmeter and sags when a lamp is connected.

E = I (R + r)
Key: E = e.m.f. (V); I = current (A); R = external load resistance (Ω); r = internal resistance (Ω). The circuit as one loop: the e.m.f. drives the current through both the load and the source.

I = E / (R + r)
Key: I = current (A); E = e.m.f. (V); R = external resistance (Ω); r = internal resistance (Ω). To measure r, vary R, plot 1/I against R: gradient = 1/E and intercept = r/E.

P_output = I² R = E² R / (R + r)²
Key: P_output = power delivered to the external load (W); E = e.m.f. (V); R = load resistance (Ω); r = internal resistance (Ω); I = current (A). Differentiating gives the maximum-power condition below.

R = r gives P_output (max) = E² / (4 r)
Key: R = load resistance at which output power peaks (Ω); r = internal resistance (Ω); E = e.m.f. (V); P_output (max) = greatest power the source can deliver (W). Maximum power transfer — but at this point the efficiency is only 50%, since the source dissipates the same power internally.

Ammeter resistance → 0, voltmeter resistance → ∞
Key: an ideal ammeter is placed in series and must not change the current, so its resistance is zero; an ideal voltmeter is placed in parallel and must not divert current, so its resistance is infinite. A real voltmeter of resistance R_V across a resistor R reads V R_V / (R + R_V), which is always less than the true p.d.

10.2 Kirchhoff's laws

Σ I_in = Σ I_out
Key: currents entering a junction (A) equal currents leaving it. The conservation of charge: charge cannot pile up at a point in a steady circuit.

Σ E = Σ I R
Key: Σ E = sum of e.m.f.s around a closed loop (V); Σ I R = sum of the potential drops around the same loop (V). The conservation of energy: going round a loop returns you to the same potential.

Σ ΔV = 0 around any closed loop
Key: ΔV = potential change across each element (V), counted positive in the direction of travel when the potential rises. The same statement as the line above, written so that sources and resistors are treated alike.

10.3 Potential dividers

V_out = V_in × R₂ / (R₁ + R₂)
Key: V_out = p.d. across the resistor the output is taken from (V); V_in = p.d. across the whole chain (V); R₁ = the other resistor (Ω); R₂ = the resistor across which the output is measured (Ω). The chain carries the same current, so each resistor takes a share of the p.d. in proportion to its resistance.

V₁ / V₂ = R₁ / R₂
Key: V₁, V₂ = p.d.s across the two resistors (V); R₁, R₂ = their resistances (Ω). The ratio form — quicker than the fraction when both outputs are wanted.

V_out = E × R / (R + R_thermistor)
Key: V_out = output p.d. across the fixed resistor R (V); E = supply e.m.f. (V); R = fixed resistance (Ω); R_thermistor = resistance of the thermistor at the current temperature (Ω). A thermistor's resistance falls as temperature rises (negative temperature coefficient), so tapping across the fixed resistor gives an output that rises with temperature and tapping across the thermistor gives one that falls.

V_out = E × R_LDR / (R + R_LDR)
Key: V_out = output p.d. across the LDR (V); E = supply e.m.f. (V); R = fixed series resistance (Ω); R_LDR = resistance of the light-dependent resistor (Ω), which falls as illumination increases. The same divider, with light instead of heat as the input.

V_out = V_in × R₂ / (R₁ + R₂) × R_load / (R_load + R₂)
Key: R_load = resistance of whatever the divider feeds (Ω); the other symbols as above. The loaded-divider correction: a load in parallel with R₂ lowers the effective lower resistance, so the output sags below the unloaded value — the reason a divider is a poor supply for anything drawing current.
