title: Exponentials and Logarithms — Study Notes
content:
Exponentials and logarithms

The exponential function e^x and the natural logarithm ln x are inverse functions. They model growth and decay (populations, radioactive decay, cooling) and appear in almost every AS/A2 paper.

The functions

  • e is Euler's number, e = 2.71828... to 4 s.f.
  • y = e^x is always positive, passes through (0, 1), and grows rapidly for large x.
  • y = ln x is defined for x > 0, passes through (1, 0), and is the inverse of e^x: ln(e^x) = x and e^(ln x) = x.
  • The graph of ln x is the reflection of e^x in the line y = x.

Logarithm laws

  • ln(ab) = ln a + ln b
  • ln(a/b) = ln a - ln b
  • ln(a^n) = n ln a
  • The same laws hold for logs to any base; log base a of x = ln x / ln a.

Solving equations

  • To solve e^(kx + c) = d: take ln of both sides, kx + c = ln d, then rearrange.
  • To solve ln(ax + b) = c: exponentiate, ax + b = e^c.
  • To solve a^x = b where a is not e: take logs, x = ln b / ln a.

Modelling

  • Growth/decay: N = N0 e^(kt), k > 0 for growth, k < 0 for decay.
  • Half-life: the time for a quantity to halve, found from ln(0.5) = k t_half.
  • Compound interest and continuously compounded growth use the same form.

Key results

  • The derivative of e^x is e^x; the derivative of ln x is 1/x (know these for later calculus).
  • e^0 = 1, ln 1 = 0, ln e = 1.
  • The curve y = e^x has gradient 1 at x = 0.

title: Networks and the Internet — Study Notes
content:
Networks and the Internet

Cambridge International AS & A Level Computer Science 9618: section 14 (Communication and internet technologies), examined in Paper 3.

The TCP/IP Stack

Four layers: Application (HTTP, FTP, SMTP, DNS), Transport (TCP reliable, connection-oriented with sequence numbers and acknowledgements; UDP fast, connectionless), Internet (IP addressing and routing), Link (physical delivery on the local network). Layering separates concerns so each layer can change independently.

Switching

  • Circuit switching: a dedicated path is held for the call (traditional telephone) — wasteful if idle.
  • Packet switching: data split into packets routed independently; each carries source/destination addresses and a sequence number, reassembled at the destination. Efficient and fault-tolerant; packets may arrive out of order (TCP fixes ordering).

Addressing and Subnetting

IPv4 addresses are 32 bits, written dotted decimal, split into network + host portions by the subnet mask. ANDing an IP with the mask yields the network ID. 192.168.4.0/26 means the first 26 bits are network, leaving 6 host bits: 64 addresses, 62 usable. NAT maps private addresses to one public IP.

Models and Protection

Client-server centralises services (web, email, files); peer-to-peer shares directly (torrents, small LANs). Firewalls filter traffic by rules; proxy servers sit between clients and the internet, caching and filtering; ports identify services (80/443 web, 25 SMTP).

Exam tips: compute usable hosts from a given prefix; trace a packet through the four layers naming one protocol per layer; explain one advantage of packet over circuit switching.

Protocols and switching

A protocol is a set of rules that devices follow to communicate. TCP/IP is the suite used on the internet, and protocols define how data is addressed, formatted and checked for errors.

In circuit switching a dedicated path is set up for the whole call, as in the traditional telephone network. In packet switching the message is split into packets, each carrying a header with source and destination addresses and a sequence number. Packets can take different routes and are reassembled at the destination.

Exam tip: packet switching uses the network efficiently because no path is reserved, but packets can arrive out of order.

Exam method: dividing a network into subnets

Take 192.168.1.0/24 and split it into four equal subnets. A /24 prefix leaves 8 host bits, so borrowing 2 bits gives a /26 prefix and 6 host bits, which means 64 addresses per subnet. The four networks are 192.168.1.0, 192.168.1.64, 192.168.1.128 and 192.168.1.192. In each subnet the first address is the network address and the last is the broadcast address, so the usable hosts are 62 per subnet.

Always work out the block size first: 256 minus the last octet of the subnet mask gives the step between subnet addresses. For a mask ending in 192, the step is 64.

Common errors in networking questions

  • Forgetting that the network and broadcast addresses cannot be assigned to hosts, so the usable count is 2 to the power of the host bits, minus 2.
  • Confusing packet switching with circuit switching. Packet switching splits data into packets that may take different routes; circuit switching reserves a fixed path for the whole call.
  • Stating that a router works at the data link layer. Routers forward packets using IP addresses, so they operate at the network layer.

title: Exam technique: Networking & Communication
content:
### What earns the marks
For topologies, the diagram plus one benefit earns one mark each. For addresses, MAC as permanent plus IP as routable earns each mark. For security, firewall plus encryption plus passwords named in context earn full marks.
### Traps
Error: LAN and WAN swapped. Correction: LAN is local, WAN spans distance. Error: MAC claimed to change per network. Correction: MAC is burned in, IP is assigned. Error: HTTP called secure. Correction: HTTPS adds the encryption.

title: Database Systems — Study Notes
content:
Database Systems

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): limitations of file-based systems; relational concepts; SQL (SELECT, FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY, INNER JOIN, SUM, COUNT); DBMS features.

1. File-based problems

Data repetition (wasted space, inconsistency), fixed queries, no concurrent access control — solved by a DBMS with shared, structured tables.

2. Relational concepts

  • Table, record, field; primary key (unique); secondary key (indexed search field); foreign key links tables.
  • One-to-many relationships via foreign keys; no repeating groups (1NF mindset).

3. SQL

SELECT Title, Year FROM Films
WHERE Genre = 'Sci-Fi' AND Year > 2015
ORDER BY Year DESC;

SELECT Genre, COUNT(*) AS NumFilms, SUM(Rating) AS TotalRating
FROM Films
GROUP BY Genre;

SELECT s.Name, f.Title
FROM Students s INNER JOIN Loans l ON s.StudentID = l.StudentID
INNER JOIN Films f ON l.FilmID = f.FilmID;

WHERE filters rows; GROUP BY aggregates; JOIN combines on matching keys.

4. DBMS features

Data dictionary (schema, types, constraints), query processor, forms/reports, access rights (read/write per user), data integrity (validation rules), backup/recovery.

Exam tips: write SQL keywords uppercase; alias joined tables (s, l, f); when asked "why relational", cite reduced redundancy + flexible queries.

Primary keys, foreign keys and relationships

A primary key uniquely identifies each record in a table, so no two records can share its value. A foreign key is a field in one table that holds the primary key of a related table, and it creates a relationship between the tables. Relationships can be one-to-one, one-to-many or many-to-many. A many-to-many relationship is usually split into two one-to-many relationships through a linking table.

Foreign keys stop a record being added that points to a row which does not exist, which keeps the data consistent. Storing each fact once in the correct table also reduces redundancy, so an update is made in one place only.

Exam tip: when designing a table, name the primary key and say which field links it to another table.

Worked example: a two-table database

A school stores pupil details and the subjects each pupil takes. The table Pupil holds PupilID (primary key), Name and Form. The table Enrolment holds EnrolmentID (primary key), PupilID (foreign key referencing Pupil) and SubjectCode. Each enrolment row belongs to exactly one pupil, so the relationship is one-to-many from Pupil to Enrolment. The name is stored once, in Pupil, so moving a pupil to a new form needs one update rather than one per subject.

Validation and data integrity

  • A range check rejects a mark outside 0 to 100. A presence check stops a required field being left empty.
  • A type check rejects text typed into a numeric field, and a length check limits how many characters a field accepts.
  • A referential integrity check refuses an enrolment whose PupilID does not exist in Pupil.

What a database management system does

A DBMS keeps a data dictionary that describes every table and field, controls which users may read or change which data, backs the data up and recovers it after a failure, and manages concurrent access so that two users editing the same record do not corrupt it. Describe each of these with a named example from the question rather than listing the feature in general terms.

title: Electricity: D.C. Circuits — Study Notes
content:
Electricity: D.C. circuits

Current and charge

  • Current I = charge Q ÷ time t, so Q = It. Unit: ampere (A), where 1 A = 1 C s⁻¹.
  • Electron drift velocity is very small, but the electric field propagates through the circuit almost at the speed of light.

Potential difference and power

  • Potential difference V = energy transferred ÷ charge. Unit: volt (V), where 1 V = 1 J C⁻¹.
  • Power P = VI = I²R = V²/R. Unit: watt (W).

Resistance and resistivity

R = V/I (Ohm's law for an ohmic conductor, at constant temperature). For a wire of length L and cross-sectional area A, R = ρL/A, where ρ is the resistivity in Ω m. Resistance rises with length and falls with area.

Practical circuits

An ammeter is connected in series with the component it measures. A voltmeter is connected in parallel with the component. An ideal ammeter has zero resistance; an ideal voltmeter has infinite resistance.

Kirchhoff's laws

  • First law: at a junction, the total current entering equals the total current leaving (conservation of charge).
  • Second law: around any closed loop, the sum of the emfs equals the sum of the potential differences (conservation of energy).

Potential dividers

For two resistors R1 and R2 in series across a supply V, the potential difference across R2 is V × R2/(R1 + R2).

Worked example: a 100 Ω and a 300 Ω resistor are in series across 12 V. The current is 12/400 = 0.030 A, and the voltage across the 300 Ω resistor is 0.030 × 300 = 9.0 V.

Exam tips: draw the meter in the correct place, in series or in parallel. Apply Kirchhoff's first law to currents and the second law to loops, with consistent signs. Check that units are converted (e.g. mm² to m²) before using ρL/A.

title: Exam technique: Sine and Cosine Rules
content:
### What earns the marks
For the sine rule, the matched pairs written (b / sin 65 = 7 / sin 40) earn the method mark. For the cosine rule, the full substitution with cos evaluated earns the mark: write a squared = 25 + 64 - 2 x 5 x 8 x 0.5. For the largest angle, identifying the longest side first earns credit. For area, half a b sin C quoted earns the mark on its own.
### Traps
Error: sides paired with wrong angles in the sine rule. Correction: each side faces its angle. Error: 49 given as side a. Correction: root the cosine-rule result. Error: calculator-only acute angle for an obtuse ambiguous case. Correction: subtract from 180 by hand. Error: half a b without sine for a non-right triangle. Correction: area needs the sine factor unless the angle is 90 degrees.
### Worked example
Two sides are 7 cm and 9 cm, with an included angle of 40 degrees. The cosine rule gives x^2 = 7^2 + 9^2 - 2 x 7 x 9 x cos 40 = 130 - 126 x 0.766 = 33.5, so x is about 5.79 cm. Use the cosine rule when you have two sides and the angle between them.
### Check yourself
A right-angled triangle has legs 6 and 8. Compute the area as one half of 6 x 8 x sin 90 degrees, and the hypotenuse with the cosine rule. The area is 24, and the hypotenuse is sqrt(36 + 64) = 10, because cos 90 degrees is zero.

title: A Level Mathematics: The Binomial Distribution
content:
A Level Mathematics: The Binomial Distribution

A binomial distribution counts successes in a fixed number of independent trials, each with the same probability of success. Coins, multiple-choice guesses, defective items in a sample and free throws all fit the same template, and once a problem is recognised as binomial the calculation is a formula plus a cumulative table. This note builds the distribution from its four conditions, derives the formula from counting, and then uses it for the two things exams actually ask: probabilities and hypothesis tests.

The four conditions

Before writing X ~ B(n, p) you must be able to name the conditions, because most exam questions include a part asking whether the model is appropriate. The conditions are not red tape: drop any one and the formula is simply wrong.

1. a fixed number of trials n
2. each trial has exactly two outcomes (success / failure)
3. the probability of success p is constant for every trial
4. the trials are independent
then X = number of successes has X ~ B(n, p)

Worked example (checking the model). A bag holds 5 red and 15 blue counters. Four counters are taken without replacement. Is the number of red counters binomial?

n = 4 is fixed and each draw is red or not red
but p changes: 5/20, then 5/19 if a red was taken, ...
the trials are not independent, so NOT binomial (it is hypergeometric)

Taking with replacement would fix it: p stays 0.25 on every draw.

The formula, and where it comes from

The probability of a particular sequence of r successes and n − r failures is p^r (1−p)^(n−r), because independence lets you multiply. The number of such sequences is the number of ways to choose which r trials succeed, which is nCr. Multiplying gives the formula.

P(X = r) = nCr p^r (1 - p)^(n - r)
the nCr counts arrangements; the powers give the probability of one arrangement

Worked example. X ~ B(10, 0.3). Find P(X = 3).

P = 10C3 (0.3)³ (0.7)⁷
= 120 × 0.027 × 0.08235
= 120 × 0.002223 = 0.2668

Worked example 2 (a single trial count). A fair die is rolled 8 times. Find the probability of exactly two sixes.

X ~ B(8, 1/6)
P(X = 2) = 8C2 (1/6)² (5/6)⁶ = 28 × 0.02778 × 0.3349 = 0.2605

Worked example 3 (why nCr appears). For n = 3 and r = 1, list the sequences and confirm the coefficient.

sequences: SFF, FSF, FFS - three of them
each has probability p(1-p)²
so P(X = 1) = 3p(1-p)², and 3C1 = 3

Cumulative probabilities

Questions almost always ask for a range, not a single value, and the cumulative distribution is what the calculator or the tables supply. The skill is rewriting the question into the form the table gives you.

P(X <= r) is tabulated directly
P(X >= r) = 1 - P(X <= r - 1)
P(X < r)  = P(X <= r - 1)
P(a <= X <= b) = P(X <= b) - P(X <= a - 1)
P(X = r) = P(X <= r) - P(X <= r - 1)

Worked example. X ~ B(20, 0.4). Find P(X ≥ 8).

P(X >= 8) = 1 - P(X <= 7)
= 1 - 0.4159
= 0.5841

Worked example 2 (between). For the same X, find P(5 ≤ X ≤ 10).

= P(X <= 10) - P(X <= 4)
= 0.8725 - 0.0510
= 0.8215

Worked example 3 (the strict inequality trap). For the same X, find P(X > 6).

P(X > 6) = 1 - P(X <= 6) = 1 - 0.2500 = 0.7500
note this is different from P(X >= 6) = 1 - P(X <= 5) = 0.8746

Mean and variance

The binomial has the simplest mean and variance in the syllabus, and they are worth knowing both forwards and backwards: a question can give the mean and variance and ask for n and p.

E(X) = np
Var(X) = np(1 - p)
standard deviation = √(np(1-p))

Worked example. X ~ B(50, 0.2). Find the mean and standard deviation.

mean = 50 × 0.2 = 10
variance = 10 × 0.8 = 8
sd = 2.828

Worked example 2 (backwards). A binomial variable has mean 12 and variance 9. Find n and p.

np = 12;  np(1-p) = 9
divide: 1 - p = 9/12 = 0.75  →  p = 0.25
then n = 12/0.25 = 48

Hypothesis testing with the binomial

A one-tailed test asks whether p has increased or decreased; the test statistic is the observed count, and the p-value is the probability of a result at least as extreme in the direction of the alternative.

H0: p = p0      H1: p > p0 (or p < p0)
X ~ B(n, p0) under H0
p-value = P(X >= observed) or P(X <= observed)
compare with the significance level; reject H0 if p-value <= alpha

Worked example. A coin is tossed 20 times and lands heads 15 times. Test at the 5% level whether the coin is biased towards heads.

H0: p = 0.5;  H1: p > 0.5
X ~ B(20, 0.5)
P(X >= 15) = 1 - P(X <= 14) = 1 - 0.9793 = 0.0207
0.0207 < 0.05, so reject H0
there is evidence at the 5% level that the coin favours heads

Worked example 2 (two-tailed). The same data tested two-tailed.

double the smaller tail: 2 × 0.0207 = 0.0414
0.0414 < 0.05, so still reject H0 at the 5% level

Worked example 3 (critical region). For X ~ B(20, 0.5), find the critical region for a 5% one-tailed test of p > 0.5.

P(X >= 14) = 0.0577 (above 0.05)
P(X >= 15) = 0.0207 (below 0.05)
critical region: X >= 15

Note that the critical region is chosen so the probability of a Type I error is at most 5%, which is why 14 is excluded even though it is close.

When the model breaks down

Examiners like the question that asks why a binomial model is only an approximation. The usual culprits are dependence, a varying probability, or a fixed sample drawn without replacement from a small population.

SituationProblemEffect
sampling without replacementtrials not independentp drifts; use the hypergeometric instead
clustered data (pupils in classes)responses correlatedvariance underestimated
probability varies between trialsp not constantformula invalid
large n, p near 0.5computation heavynormal approximation is reasonable

Worked example (normal approximation). X ~ B(200, 0.4). Use a normal approximation to estimate P(X ≤ 70).

mean = 80;  variance = 200 × 0.4 × 0.6 = 48;  sd = 6.928
continuity correction: X <= 70 becomes X < 70.5
z = (70.5 - 80)/6.928 = -1.371
P(Z < -1.371) = 0.0852

The continuity correction is compulsory: a discrete count needs a half-unit boundary before it can be treated as continuous.

Expected frequencies and the shape of the distribution

A binomial distribution is not symmetric unless p = 0.5, and that shape decides which tail an exam question is fishing in. The most likely value — the mode — is the integer near (n + 1)p, and expected frequency multiplies the probability by the number of samples taken. Both are quick marks that are frequently missed because students jump straight to the formula.

mode is near (n + 1)p, checked by comparing consecutive probabilities
expected number in a sample of size N = N x P(X = r)

Worked example. X ~ B(12, 0.3). Find the most likely value of X and the expected number of 3s in 500 independent observations.

(n + 1)p = 13 × 0.3 = 3.9, so check r = 3 and r = 4
P(X = 3) = 220 × 0.027 × 0.1176 = 0.2397
P(X = 4) = 495 × 0.0081 × 0.1681 = 0.2311
mode = 3
expected number of 3s = 500 × 0.2397 = 120 (to the nearest whole)

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Model) State the distribution for the number of sixes in 12 rolls of a fair die. Answer: X ~ B(n, p) with n = 12 rolls and p = 1/6 the chance of a six on each, so X ~ B(12, 1/6).
  2. (Single value) X ~ B(8, 0.25): find P(X = 2). Answer: P(X = 2) = ⁸C₂ (0.25)² (0.75)⁶ = 28 × 0.0625 × 0.1780 = 0.3115.
  3. (Cumulative) X ~ B(15, 0.3): find P(X ≤ 4). Answer: P(X ≤ 4) = Σₖ₌₀⁴ ¹⁵Cₖ (0.3)ᵏ (0.7)¹⁵⁻ᵏ = 0.5155 from cumulative binomial tables.
  4. (Complement) Same X: find P(X ≥ 3). Answer: P(X ≥ 3) = 1 − P(X ≤ 2) = 1 − 0.2969 = 0.7031 — the complement, because the tables give the lower tail only.
  5. (Mean) X ~ B(40, 0.35): find E(X) and Var(X). Answer: 14 and 9.1.
  6. (Backwards) Mean 18, variance 12: find n and p. Answer: mean np = 18 and variance np(1 − p) = 12; dividing, 1 − p = 12/18 = 2/3, so p = 1/3 and n = 18 ÷ (1/3) = 54.
  7. (Test) 12 of 20 seeds germinate; test p = 0.5 against p < 0.5 at 5%. Answer: H₀: p = 0.5 against H₁: p < 0.5; under H₀, X ~ B(20, 0.5) and P(X ≤ 12) = 0.8684, which is far above 0.05, so there is no evidence to reject H₀.
  8. (Critical region) X ~ B(10, 0.2): find the 5% critical region for p < 0.2. Answer: the smallest possible tail is P(X ≤ 0) = (0.8)¹⁰ = 0.1074, which already exceeds 0.05, so no critical region exists at the 5% level for this n.
  9. (Approximation) X ~ B(100, 0.5): approximate P(X ≥ 60). Answer: μ = np = 50 and σ = √(np(1 − p)) = √25 = 5; with the continuity correction z = (59.5 − 50)/5 = 1.9, so P(X ≥ 60) ≈ P(Z > 1.9) = 0.0287.
  10. (Assumption) Give one reason a binomial model may fail for defects in boxes of 20. Answer: defects may cluster, so trials are not independent.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Forgetting nCr: the coefficient counts arrangements; without it the answer is the probability of one specific sequence.
  • nCr on the wrong factor: it is p^r (1−p)^(n−r), with the success probability raised to the number of successes.
  • Inequality direction: P(X ≥ 8) uses 1 − P(X ≤ 7), not 1 − P(X ≤ 8).
  • Variance confused with standard deviation: np(1−p) is the variance; the test and the normal approximation need the square root.
  • Continuity correction omitted: any normal approximation to a discrete count needs the half-unit adjustment.
  • One-tailed evidence read as two: halving or doubling the tail without checking the alternative direction is a silent error.
  • Independence asserted, not checked: sampling without replacement from a small population breaks the model, and the question usually invites you to say so.
  • p-value compared with the wrong threshold: the significance level is given as a percentage; 5% means 0.05, not 5.

Recognising a binomial situation in context

Most binomial marks are lost before any arithmetic starts, because the question was not identified as binomial. The subsections below give a checklist for reading a question and writing the model in the standard form X ~ B(n, p) before you calculate anything.

Writing the model in the form X ~ B(n, p)

Once you decide a situation is binomial, state the model in full: X ~ B(n, p), where X is the number of successes, n is the number of trials and p is the probability of a success on each trial. Define X in words in your answer, for example “X is the number of defective bulbs in a box of 20”. A model with no definition of X loses the communication mark even when the probabilities are right.

Identifying the number of trials, n

The value of n is the fixed number of times the experiment is repeated: the number of bulbs tested, the number of patients treated, or the number of games played. Read the question for the phrase that fixes it, such as “of 20 bulbs chosen at random”. If the question keeps going until a result occurs, the number of trials is not fixed and the binomial model does not apply directly.

Identifying the probability of success, p

The value of p is the probability of the outcome you have chosen to call a success on one trial. It must stay the same for every trial. A fair coin gives p = 0.5, and a bag where 15% of items are faulty gives p = 0.15 for each item drawn with replacement. If the question gives a percentage, convert it to a decimal before you use it in any formula.

Checking for fixed trials

The number of trials must be decided before the experiment starts. Counting the number of successes in a fixed sample is binomial, whereas recording how many trials it takes to get the first success is not. A question about the number of heads in ten tosses is binomial; a question about how many tosses are needed for the first head is a different model. Make the fixed-n check before any other check.

Checking for independent trials

Each trial must not affect the next. Independence is what allows you to multiply the probabilities of several outcomes together, and it is the assumption most often ignored. Drawing items with replacement keeps p constant, and that is what the model needs. Drawing without replacement changes p after each draw, so the binomial model is only an approximation when the sample is small compared with the population.

Worked identification

A survey finds that 30% of adults own a bicycle. Twelve adults are chosen at random from a large town and asked whether they own one. Let X be the number who own a bicycle. Here n = 12, p = 0.3 and the answer is X ~ B(12, 0.3). The population is large, so the probability for each adult stays close to 0.3 and the model is a reasonable one to use. State that assumption, because a marker looks for it.

Equations and symbols

The distribution, its conditions and the four tail identities. Every question on this topic is one of these lines plus a calculator.

P(X = r) = nCr p^r (1 - p)^(n - r) Key: n = number of trials, fixed in advance; p = probability of success in one trial, constant; r = the number of successes asked for; nCr = n!/(r!(n − r)!), the number of orders the successes can occur in. The (1 − p) term is the failures, and its power must be n − r.

X ~ B(n, p) Key: X = the count of successes; the tilde means "is distributed as"; n and p as above. Write this line before calculating — it is often a mark on its own, and it fixes which parameters go into the calculator.

P = 10C3 (0.3)³ (0.7)⁷ Key: n = 10, p = 0.3, r = 3, so the failures are 7 and their probability is 0.7. The coefficient 10C3 = 120 accounts for the order of the three successes among the ten trials.

P(X >= r) = 1 - P(X <= r - 1) Key: a complement, so the two probabilities add to 1; the boundary moves by one because the binomial is discrete. Using 1 − P(X ≤ r) instead is the classic off-by-one error.

P(a <= X <= b) = P(X <= b) - P(X <= a - 1) Key: subtract the part below the interval; again the "− 1" is there because P(X ≤ a − 1) is everything before a. Check with a small case you can list by hand before trusting the calculator.

title: Exam technique: Data Handling
content:
### What earns the marks
For averages, the total shown earns a mark before any division. For even-count medians, the two middle values identified earn the method mark. For grouped data, the modal class stated as an interval earns full credit; single numbers score nothing. For cumulative frequency, the position formula (n + 1) / 2 quoted earns the method mark before reading off.
### Traps
Error: total given as the mean. Correction: divide by the count last. Error: 3rd value picked as median of six values. Correction: average the 3rd and 4th. Error: 40th value read for the median of 80. Correction: position 40.5. Error: quartiles read for median and vice versa. Correction: 20th/60th are quartiles at n = 80.

title: Edexcel IAL Computer Science: Computational Thinking and Programming
content:
Edexcel IAL Computer Science: Computational Thinking and Programming

Pearson Edexcel International Advanced Level in Computer Science, Unit 2 Practical Programming and Problem Solving: computational thinking skills, algorithm design, programming basics and constructs, structured programming, and the program development life cycle with design and testing. This is the unit where knowledge becomes craft — so every algorithm here is refined stage by stage, every trace runs statement by statement, and every test case is chosen with its expected output stated before execution. The Python shown is version 3, as the unit requires.

Computational thinking

  • Abstraction — discard irrelevant detail, model what matters (a timetable models rooms and slots, not paint colours).
  • Decomposition — break a problem into independently solvable parts (an ordering system: stock, basket, payment, delivery).
  • Pattern recognition — spot repetition that generalises (three near-identical report routines become one parameterised function).
  • Algorithmic thinking — express solutions as precise, ordered, unambiguous steps.

These four run through everything below: decomposition yields the module structure, abstraction the data model, patterns the loops and functions, and algorithmic thinking the pseudocode.

Algorithm design and representation

Representations: pseudocode (structured language-independent statements), flowcharts (oval start/end, parallelogram I/O, rectangle process, diamond decision), structure charts (module hierarchy with data couples). Stepwise refinement expands one outline line into steps until each is trivially implementable.

Refinement worked end to end: "process a batch of orders".

Stage 0:   for each order: validate, price, update stock, report.

Stage 1:
  open the order file and the stock file
  for each order in the file:
      validate the order (product exists, quantity positive, credit ok)
      if valid: price it (quantity x unit price, apply discounts)
                update stock (decrement, flag reorders)
                append to the invoice file
      else: append to the error report
  print summary totals

Stage 2 (final pseudocode for one leaf - pricing):

  FUNCTION priceOrder(qty, unitPrice, customerDiscount)
      subtotal <- qty * unitPrice
      IF qty >= 100 THEN
          bulkDiscount <- subtotal * 0.05
      ELSE
          bulkDiscount <- 0
      ENDIF
      total <- subtotal - bulkDiscount
      total <- total * (1 - customerDiscount)
      RETURN total
  ENDFUNCTION

Notice what refinement exposed: two discounts stack - the order of application
must be specified, and the boundary (exactly 100) tested both sides.

Programming basics and constructs

Variables hold typed values; assignment stores the evaluated right-hand side. The three constructs: sequence (statements in order), selection (IF / ELIF / ELSE on boolean conditions; nested selection for layered cases), iteration (FOR over a known count, WHILE while a condition holds — plus the off-by-one and infinite-loop traps). Subprograms: procedures (named actions, no return) and functions (named calculations, return a value); parameters pass data in, return passes results out, and scope keeps locals local.

Python 3 - constructs with line-by-line memory commentary:

  1  def classify(mark):            # function definition; mark is a parameter
  2      if mark >= 70:             # selection: evaluates mark >= 70
  3          return "Distinction"
  4      elif mark >= 50:           # only reached when mark < 70
  5          return "Pass"
  6      else:
  7          return "Fail"
  8
  9  results = []                   # an empty list
 10  for mark in [65, 72, 41]:      # iteration: mark takes each value in turn
 11      results.append(classify(mark))   # call; return value appended
 12  print(results)

Trace:
  line 9:  results = []
  line 10: mark = 65 -> classify: 65>=70 false, 65>=50 true -> "Pass"
  line 11: results = ["Pass"]
  line 10: mark = 72 -> 72>=70 true -> "Distinction"
  line 11: results = ["Pass", "Distinction"]
  line 10: mark = 41 -> both tests false -> "Fail"
  line 11: results = ["Pass", "Distinction", "Fail"]
  line 12: prints ['Pass', 'Distinction', 'Fail']

Definite iteration (FOR) over a list; indefinite iteration (WHILE) for
"read until a sentinel" patterns.

Structured programming discipline: one entry/exit per structure, no wild jumps (goto), top-down design with clear module interfaces, and named constants for magic numbers. Benefits: readability, testability and maintainability — and the exam expects those words attached to the technique.

Program design tools

Before code, the design is expressed in forms the team can review. Structure charts show the module hierarchy: the main program at the top, subtasks beneath, with data couples marking what passes between them — a chart with three levels proves the decomposition. Pseudocode gives each leaf module's exact logic; flowcharts show branch and loop shape at a glance; a data dictionary lists every variable and file field with its type, range and purpose, so modules agree on interfaces before they are coded. Naming conventions, indentation standards and comment discipline are part of the same stage: code is read far more often than written, and the exam gives method marks for showing these artefacts rather than jumping straight to Python.

File handling, validation and data persistence

Python 3 - writing then reading a data file, with validation:

  # write
  with open("temps.txt", "w") as f:        # "w" creates or TRUNCATES
      for reading in [21.5, 19.0, -999]:
          if reading < -50 or reading > 60:      # range validation
              continue                            # skip invalid sensor value
          f.write(str(reading) + "\n")

  # read
  total = 0.0
  count = 0
  with open("temps.txt", "r") as f:        # with closes the file automatically
      for line in f:
          value = float(line)              # type conversion; may raise ValueError
          total += value
          count += 1
  if count > 0:                            # guard the division
      print("mean =", total / count)
  else:
      print("no valid data")

Traps the examiner sets: "w" wiping an existing file where "a" (append) was
meant; reading without closing (the with statement prevents it); averaging
without the empty-file guard; and validating after conversion rather than
before.

Validation techniques: presence, type, range, length, check digit, list/pick-list, and format (regular expression) checks. Verification: double entry, visual checking, read-back. Input/output at this level is routine-level discipline: every value entering the system passes a check at the boundary.

Program development life cycle

StageActivitiesArtifacts
AnalysisGather requirements; define inputs, outputs, constraintsRequirements specification
DesignDecompose; design data structures and algorithmsStructure charts, pseudocode, data dictionary
ImplementationCode, follow standards, reviewSource code, comments
TestingNormal, boundary, erroneous, edge cases; debugTest plans, test results, bug reports
MaintenanceCorrective, adaptive, perfective changesRevised code and docs

Iterative (agile) development cycles through these stages in small increments with frequent client review; waterfall completes each stage once in order. Agile absorbs change cheaply and shows working software early; waterfall suits fixed-scope contracts with heavy documentation. The exam wants the comparison, not a preference.

Testing worked example: priceOrder above (5% bulk discount at 100+ units).

Test plan rows - each states expected output BEFORE running:

  normal:    qty 50, unit 10.0, disc 0    -> 500.00      (no bulk discount)
  boundary:  qty 99, unit 10.0, disc 0    -> 990.00      (just below)
  boundary:  qty 100, unit 10.0, disc 0   -> 950.00      (bulk fires: 1000*0.95)
  boundary:  qty 101, unit 10.0, disc 0   -> 959.50      (just above)
  erroneous: qty -5, unit 10.0, disc 0    -> should be rejected by validation
  edge:      qty 100, unit 0, disc 0.1    -> 0.00        (zero price)

Unit testing checks the function in isolation; integration testing checks it
with the stock and invoice modules; acceptance testing checks the customer's
requirements. Black-box testing uses specifications only; white-box testing
uses code structure (statement, branch coverage).

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Design jumps: no decomposition or refinement shown before code loses method marks.
  • WHILE loops with uninitialised or never-updated conditions (infinite loops); FOR loop boundary errors (range(1, n+1) versus range(1, n)).
  • Testing only normal data; boundary and erroneous data carry equal marks.
  • Test results without pre-stated expectations — that is checking, not testing.
  • Confusing procedures with functions (return value) or parameters with arguments at the call site.
  • "w" versus "a" file modes destroying data; and no empty-input guard before division.
  • Stating agile is "better" without the trade-off comparison the question asks for.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Unit 2, 4 marks). Explain abstraction and decomposition with examples from a library system.

Answer: Abstraction models only relevant features — the system tracks loans, members and due dates while ignoring irrelevant details like book cover designs. Decomposition splits the problem into solvable parts — catalogue search, loans/returns, fines, member accounts — each designed and tested independently before integration.

Question 2 (Unit 2, 6 marks). Write pseudocode for a function that returns the median of three numbers.

Answer: FUNCTION median3(a, b, c): IF (a >= b AND a <= c) OR (a <= b AND a >= c) THEN RETURN a; ELSEIF (b >= a AND b <= c) OR (b <= a AND b >= c) THEN RETURN b; ELSE RETURN c; ENDIF. (Alternative: sort the three values and return the middle.)

Question 3 (Unit 2, 4 marks). Describe a test plan for a program calculating exam grades from marks 0–100.

Answer: Normal: 55 → Pass. Boundary: 0, 100, and the grade thresholds 49/50 and 69/70 tested both sides. Erroneous: -1 and 101 rejected by range validation; "abc" rejected by type check. Each test records expected output before execution; failures are logged and retested after fixes.

Question 4 (Unit 2, 4 marks). Compare iterative and waterfall development.

Answer: Iterative development delivers in small cycles with client review after each, so working software appears early and requirement changes are absorbed cheaply — at the cost of less predictable final scope and budget. Waterfall completes analysis, design, implementation and testing in sequence, giving clear milestones and documentation, but testing comes late and changes after design are expensive.

Question 5 (Unit 2, 4 marks). Explain the difference between validation and verification, and give two validation techniques.

Answer: Validation checks data is plausible before storage (range check rejects a mark of 300); verification checks captured data matches the source (double entry of a password). Two further validation techniques: type checks (reject letters in a numeric field) and length checks (reject an 8-digit account number where 10 are required).

Question 6 (Unit 2, 5 marks). Write Python 3 that reads numbers from a file and outputs the largest, handling an empty file.

Answer: largest = None; with open("nums.txt") as f: for line in f: v = float(line); if largest is None or v > largest: largest = v; if largest is None: print("file is empty"); else: print("largest =", largest).

With the craft established, the next note organises what programs manipulate: data types, records and arrays.

title: Microbiology, Immunity and Forensics Revision Notes A2 Biology
content:
Microbiology, Immunity and Forensics A2 Level Biology

This topic belongs to the Edexcel International Advanced Level Biology specification WBI14, covering the growth and control of microorganisms, the immune response against pathogens, infection mechanisms, forensic DNA profiling techniques, and the estimation of time of death in forensic science.

Culturing and Measuring Microorganisms

Microorganisms require precise aseptic techniques to prevent contamination by unwanted microbes and to protect laboratory personnel from potential pathogens. Equipment must be sterilized using an autoclave, inoculating loops passed through a blue Bunsen flame until red hot, and petri dish lids lifted minimally. Growth can be quantified through various direct and indirect methods.

  • 6.1 principles and techniques involved in culturing microorganisms: use sterile nutrient broth or agar plates, incubate at or below 30 °C in school laboratories to prevent growth of human pathogens, and seal petri dishes loosely with adhesive tape to allow oxygen entry and prevent anaerobic conditions that favour harmful pathogens.
  • 6.2 methods of measuring microbial growth: direct cell counts using a haemocytometer with trypan blue to stain dead cells; serial dilution plating to count viable colonies expressed as colony-forming units per cubic centimetre; dry mass measurement following centrifugation and drying; and optical methods using a colorimeter or spectrophotometer to measure turbidity by recording absorbance or percentage transmission.
  • 6.3 phases of a bacterial growth curve: lag phase where cells adjust to the new environment and synthesize necessary enzymes with little population increase; exponential or log phase where cells divide at a constant maximum rate; stationary phase where nutrient depletion and toxic waste accumulation balance the rate of cell division and death; and death phase where cell death exceeds division.
  • 6.3 exponential growth rate constant formula: k = (log10(Nt) − log10(N0)) / (0.301 × t), where Nt is the number of bacteria at time t, N0 is the initial number of bacteria, and t is time.
  • 6.4 Core Practical 13 investigating the rate of growth of microorganisms in a liquid culture: use a spectrophotometer to record absorbance of a yeast or bacterial broth over time at regular intervals, maintaining constant temperature using a water bath and sterile controls, ensuring ethical handling and safe disposal of cultures.

Structure of Pathogens and Infection Mechanisms

Pathogens include both cellular bacteria and non-cellular viruses, each displaying distinct structural features that dictate their interaction with host cells and susceptibility to treatments.

  • 6.5 (i) bacterial structure: single-celled prokaryotes possessing 70S ribosomes, peptidoglycan cell walls, circular DNA, plasmids, and sometimes a capsule or flagella.
  • 6.5 (i) viral structure: acellular entities comprising genetic material enclosed within a protein coat called a capsid, surrounded in some viruses by a membrane envelope derived from host cell membranes. Examples include Ebola virus (filovirus with single-stranded RNA and an envelope), tobacco mosaic virus (rod-shaped helical capsid containing single-stranded RNA without an envelope), human immunodeficiency virus (retrovirus with RNA, capsid, and envelope), and lambda phage (dsDNA virus infecting bacteria with an isometric head and a contractile tail).
  • 6.5 (ii) lytic and latency: lytic cycle involves viral genetic material taking over host machinery to produce new virions, causing host cell lysis and death; latency (lysogeny) involves viral DNA integrating into the host genome as a provirus or prophage, remaining dormant and replicating alongside host DNA without causing immediate symptoms.
  • 6.6 Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection: bacteria are inhaled into the lungs, where they are engulfed by macrophages but can inhibit phagosome-lysosome fusion, surviving and multiplying inside macrophages to form tubercles, causing chronic coughing, tissue destruction, and eventual systemic spread.
  • 6.6 HIV infection: glycoprotein gp120 on the viral envelope binds specifically to CD4 receptors on T helper cells, allowing viral fusion and entry. The viral RNA uses reverse transcriptase to synthesize double-stranded DNA, which integrates into the host genome via integrase, eventually destroying T helper cells and leading to acquired immunodeficiency syndrome.

The Body's Defences and Immunity

The human body employs physical, chemical, and biological barriers alongside multi-tiered immune responses to prevent and combat infection.

  • 6.7 (i) major entry routes for pathogens: gas exchange system, digestive system, reproductive system, and breaks in the skin.
  • 6.7 (ii) protective barriers: keratinized skin forming a tough physical barrier; stomach acid (hydrochloric acid at low pH) denaturing proteins and killing ingested pathogens; gut and skin flora competing with pathogenic microorganisms for resources and space while producing antagonistic chemical substances.
  • 6.8 non-specific responses to infection: inflammation triggered by histamine release from mast cells, causing vasodilation and increased capillary permeability; lysozyme action in tears, saliva, and mucus hydrolyzing peptidoglycan in bacterial cell walls; interferon produced by virus-infected cells to inhibit viral replication in neighbouring cells; and phagocytosis where neutrophils and macrophages engulf and digest foreign particles.
  • 6.9 roles of antigens and antibodies: antigens are molecules that trigger an immune response; antibodies are Y-shaped glycoproteins produced by plasma cells that bind specifically to antigens, promoting agglutination, neutralisation, and opsonisation. Macrophages act as antigen-presenting cells by displaying digested pathogen antigens on their surface using MHC proteins.
  • 6.10 roles of B and T cells: B effector cells differentiate into plasma cells to secrete antibodies, while B memory cells remain long-term for secondary responses; T helper cells release cytokines to activate B cells and killer T cells; T killer (cytotoxic) cells destroy infected host cells by releasing perforin; T memory cells provide long-term immunological memory.
  • 6.11 types of immunity: natural active immunity acquired via infection and primary immune response; natural passive immunity acquired via antibodies crossing the placenta or through breast milk; artificial active immunity acquired via vaccination containing antigens; artificial passive immunity acquired via injection of exogenous antibodies such as antitoxins.
  • 6.12 evolutionary race and evasion mechanisms: pathogens and hosts engage in co-evolutionary arms races; pathogens evade immune responses through antigenic variation (changing surface antigens such as in influenza and HIV), latency (hiding within host cells), and suppression of the host immune system.

Antibiotics and Clinical Practice

Antimicrobial substances are crucial for treating bacterial infections, though misuse has led to widespread resistance and clinical challenges.

  • 6.13 bacteriostatic vs bactericidal antibiotics: bacteriostatic antibiotics inhibit the growth and reproduction of bacteria without killing them, allowing the host immune system to clear the infection; bactericidal antibiotics kill bacteria outright by disrupting vital processes such as cell wall synthesis.
  • 6.14 Core Practical 14 investigate the effect of different antibiotics on bacteria: inoculate an agar plate with a bacterial lawn, place antibiotic-impregnated paper discs on the surface, incubate at 25 °C to 30 °C, and measure the diameter of the clear inhibition zones to calculate area and compare antibiotic effectiveness.
  • 6.15 hospital-acquired infections and prescribing codes: nosocomial infections such as MRSA spread in clinical settings due to vulnerable patients and antibiotic overuse. Codes of practice include strict hand hygiene, thorough cleaning of wards, isolation of infected patients, restricting broad-spectrum antibiotic prescriptions, and completing full courses of prescribed antibiotics to prevent selection for resistant strains.
  • 6.16 microbial decomposition and carbon recycling: saprobiotic microorganisms (bacteria and fungi) secrete extracellular enzymes onto dead organic matter, absorbing soluble products and releasing carbon dioxide back into the atmosphere via respiration, thereby maintaining the global carbon cycle.

Forensic Science and DNA Profiling

Forensic investigations rely on molecular biology techniques and physical evidence to determine genetic relationships and estimate the time of death.

  • 6.17 polymerase chain reaction (PCR): a method used to amplify small quantities of DNA in vitro using cycles of denaturation (94 °C to 95 °C to break hydrogen bonds), annealing (55 °C to 65 °C to allow primers to bind), and extension (72 °C for thermostable Taq DNA polymerase to synthesize new DNA strands).
  • 6.18 gel electrophoresis: a technique that separates DNA fragments based on size by applying an electric current through an agarose gel. Smaller fragments move faster and further toward the positive electrode than larger fragments.
  • 6.19 DNA profiling: analyzes short tandem repeats (STRs) at specific loci. The resulting banding patterns or electropherograms are compared for forensic identification of suspects, paternity testing, and determining genetic relationships in plants and animals.
  • 6.20 determining time of death: examining decomposition stages (fresh, bloated, active decay, advanced decay, skeletal remains); succession of insect species colonising the body (forensic entomology measuring blowfly life cycle stages); cooling rate of body temperature (algor mortis); and degree of muscle contraction (rigor mortis).

Worked Example: Exponential Growth Rate Constant Calculation

Calculate the exponential growth rate constant for a bacterial culture that grows from an initial concentration of 1.0 × 10^3 cells per cm³ to 5.0 × 10^6 cells per cm³ over a period of 12 hours.

  • Step 1: Identify the values: N0 = 1.0 × 10^3, Nt = 5.0 × 10^6, and t = 12 hours.
  • Step 2: Take the log10 of both population values: log10(N0) = 3.0 and log10(Nt) = 6.70.
  • Step 3: Substitute values into the formula k = (log10(Nt) − log10(N0)) / (0.301 × t).
  • Step 4: Calculate the numerator: 6.70 − 3.0 = 3.70.
  • Step 5: Calculate the denominator: 0.301 × 12 = 3.612.
  • Step 6: Divide numerator by denominator: k = 3.70 / 3.612 = 1.024 hours⁻¹.

Typical mistakes

  • Confusing bacteriostatic and bactericidal antibiotics: assuming all antibiotics kill bacteria directly, when bacteriostatic drugs merely halt division while the immune system does the destruction.
  • Misunderstanding viral replication: stating that antibiotics kill viruses, forgetting that viruses lack cellular structures and metabolic pathways targeted by antibiotics.
  • Describing antibiotic resistance incorrectly: writing that individual bacteria mutate in response to antibiotics, rather than recognizing that pre-existing random mutations provide resistance and selection pressure increases the frequency of the resistance allele in the population.
  • Confusing PCR temperatures: stating that Taq polymerase is denatured at 95 °C, when in fact it is heat-stable and only human DNA polymerase would denature at this temperature.

Exam-style questions

  1. Explain why human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection leads to a progressive decline in the immune system. Answer: HIV infects T helper cells by binding gp120 to CD4 receptors. The virus replicates and destroys these cells, reducing cytokine production, which prevents the activation of B cells and cytotoxic T cells, leading to immunodeficiency (AIDS).
  2. Describe how gel electrophoresis separates DNA fragments during DNA profiling. Answer: DNA fragments are loaded into wells in an agarose gel and subjected to an electric current. Because DNA is negatively charged due to phosphate groups, fragments move toward the positive anode. Smaller fragments travel faster and further through the gel mesh than larger fragments.
  3. Explain how natural selection drives the evolution of antibiotic-resistant bacterial populations. Answer: Within a bacterial population, random mutation produces an allele for antibiotic resistance. When the antibiotic is applied, non-resistant bacteria are killed, creating a selection pressure. Resistant bacteria survive, reproduce, and pass on the resistance allele, increasing its frequency in future generations.
  4. State the role of reverse transcriptase in the life cycle of HIV. Answer: Reverse transcriptase is a viral enzyme that catalyzes the transcription of single-stranded viral RNA into double-stranded DNA inside the host cell cytoplasm prior to viral integration.
  5. Outline the stages of a standard bacterial growth curve in a closed liquid culture. Answer: Lag phase (slow growth as cells adjust and synthesize enzymes); exponential phase (rapid cell division at a maximum rate); stationary phase (cell death rate equals division rate due to nutrient depletion and toxin accumulation); death phase (cell death exceeds division as conditions become lethal).

Use these revision notes alongside past paper practice questions. Focus your next revision sessions on mastering core practical calculations, tracing immunological pathways step by step, and applying forensic succession timelines accurately.

title: Respiration, Muscles and the Internal Environment
content:
Respiration, Muscles and the Internal Environment

Edexcel IAL Biology WBI15, Topic 7. Respiration releases energy as ATP for muscle contraction. Homeostasis keeps the internal environment stable, and the kidney is central to this. The topic links biochemistry to physiology.

Aerobic respiration

  • Glycolysis takes place in the cytoplasm. Glucose is split into two pyruvate molecules, with a small net gain of ATP and reduced NAD.
  • The link reaction converts pyruvate to acetyl coenzyme A in the mitochondrial matrix, releasing CO₂.
  • The Krebs cycle takes place in the matrix. It releases CO₂ and produces reduced NAD and FAD, and a little ATP.
  • Oxidative phosphorylation takes place on the inner mitochondrial membrane. Electrons pass along the electron transport chain, a proton gradient forms, and ATP synthase makes ATP. Oxygen is the final electron acceptor.

Anaerobic respiration in mammals

  • Without oxygen, pyruvate is reduced to lactate. This regenerates NAD so that glycolysis can continue, but it gives far less ATP.
  • The oxygen debt is the extra oxygen needed after exercise to oxidise the lactate.

Respiratory quotient

  • RQ = volume of CO₂ produced ÷ volume of O₂ consumed. Carbohydrate gives an RQ of about 1.0 and fat gives about 0.7.

Muscle contraction

  • A sarcomere is the unit between two Z lines. Thick filaments of myosin and thin filaments of actin slide past each other; the sarcomere shortens but the filaments do not change length.
  • Myosin heads bind to actin, and the power stroke pulls the actin along. ATP binds to myosin to break the link, and hydrolysis of ATP resets the head.
  • Calcium ions bind to troponin, which moves tropomyosin and exposes the binding sites on actin.

Homeostasis and the kidney

  • Negative feedback corrects a change from the set point. Receptors detect the change, and effectors bring the level back.
  • In the nephron, ultrafiltration occurs at the Bowman's capsule under high hydrostatic pressure. Glucose and amino acids are reabsorbed by active transport in the proximal convoluted tubule.
  • The loop of Henle creates a salt gradient in the medulla. ADH increases the permeability of the collecting duct, so more water is reabsorbed by osmosis.

Exam tip: when you describe the link between ADH and water reabsorption, follow the steps in order: osmoreceptors, ADH release, collecting duct permeability, water reabsorption.

title: Persuasive and Argumentative Writing — Study Notes
content:
Argumentative writing sets out a clear position, supports it with reasons and evidence, and answers the opposing view. The tone should be measured and confident, not aggressive.

A clear thesis

Your thesis states your position in one sentence. It should be specific and arguable.

Weak and strong thesis statements

  • Weak: "Some people have views about school uniforms."
  • Strong: "School uniforms should be abolished because they limit self-expression without improving learning."

Building the argument

Each paragraph should develop one reason. Start with a topic sentence, give evidence or an example, and explain how the evidence supports your thesis.

Persuasive devices

  • Rhetorical questions make the reader consider a point, often expecting the answer you want.
  • Repetition of a key phrase reinforces your message.
  • A striking example makes an abstract point concrete.

Counter-argument

Acknowledge the opposing view and then rebut it. This shows awareness and makes your case stronger. Use a clear signpost such as "Some argue that... However, ..."

Register and audience

Choose a register that suits the audience and the form. A letter to the editor needs formal vocabulary, a measured tone and no contractions. Avoid slang and text-message abbreviations.

Connectives

Use connectives to show the logic of your argument. "However" introduces contrast, "consequently" introduces a result and "furthermore" adds a point.

title: Transformations and Vectors
content:
Transformations and Vectors

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): reflection, rotation, translation, enlargement (incl. negative SF); vector notation, resultant, magnitude, vector geometry.

1. Transformations — full descriptions

  • Reflection: mirror line (x = 0, y = x, y = −x…).
  • Rotation: centre, angle, direction (anticlockwise positive).
  • Translation: column vector.
  • Enlargement: centre + scale factor; negative SF inverts through the centre.

"Enlargement, SF 2, centre (0, 3)" — every word earns a mark.

2. Combined transformations

Apply right-to-left: "reflect in y = x, then rotate 90°" — rotate the reflected image.

3. Vectors

  • Column vector (x; y); magnitude = √(x² + y²).
  • Resultant by component addition; parallel vectors are scalar multiples.
  • Position vectors: AB = OB − OA.

Example: A(1, 2), B(4, 6): AB = (3; 4), |AB| = 5.

4. Vector geometry

Midpoint of AB = ½(a + b). Prove collinearity: show AB = k·BC (shared point). Prove parallelogram: AB = DC. Use route paths: AC = AB + BC.

Exam tips: tracing paper is allowed for transformations; in proofs, end with a conclusion sentence ("hence A, B, C are collinear").

title: AS Level Biology: Molecules, Transport and Health
content:
Molecules, Transport and Health — AS Level Biology

This revision note belongs to the Edexcel International Advanced Subsidiary (IAS) Biology specification, WBI11 Unit 1, Topic 1 Molecules, Transport and Health. It covers water as a solvent and its structure, carbohydrates and lipids, proteins and their structure and function, gas exchange surfaces and Fick''s law, the mammalian circulatory system and the cardiac cycle, haemoglobin and the oxygen dissociation curve, atherosclerosis and blood clotting, the risk factors for cardiovascular disease, diet, cholesterol and antioxidants, how people use scientific knowledge to reduce risk, the benefits and risks of treatments, and data analysis and evaluation in health studies — plus the gas exchange surfaces and enzyme practical work that support the topic. Every statement the topic is responsible for is covered in its own section or paragraph.

1. Water: structure, properties and why it is the solvent of life

Water is a small molecule with two hydrogen atoms covalently bonded to one oxygen atom; because the oxygen atom is much more electronegative than hydrogen, the shared electrons spend more time near the oxygen, so the molecule is polar — the oxygen end is slightly negative and the hydrogen end slightly positive. This polarity lets water molecules form hydrogen bonds with each other, which gives water its high specific heat capacity, its high latent heat of vaporisation, its cohesion (important for the transpiration stream in plants) and its solvent powers. Water is an excellent solvent because its polarity lets it surround and dissolve ions and polar molecules; ions become hydrated with water molecules around them, and polar molecules such as glucose dissolve readily. In transport, water''s solvent nature lets it carry dissolved substances in blood and in plant tissue fluid and sap, and its dipole nature explains why it can do that — the partial charges interact with the charges of ions and the polar groups of molecules like glucose and amino acids.

2. Carbohydrates: monosaccharides, disaccharides and polysaccharides

Carbohydrates are made of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, with hydrogen and oxygen in the same ratio as in water (2:1). Monosaccharides are the simplest carbohydrates and are the building blocks — glucose, fructose and galactose are hexose monosaccharides with the formula C6H12O6. Disaccharides form when two monosaccharides join by a condensation reaction, losing a water molecule and forming a glycosidic bond; the common ones are maltose (glucose + glucose), sucrose (glucose + fructose) and lactose (glucose + galactose). Polysaccharides are long chains of monosaccharides; starch in plants is made of two polymers — amylose, a long unbranched helix of glucose, which is compact for storage, and amylopectin, which is branched so that glucose can be added or removed quickly from the ends. Glycogen is similar to amylopectin but more branched, and it is the storage carbohydrate in animals, mainly in liver and muscle cells. Cellulose is a structural polysaccharide of beta-glucose chains forming long, straight fibres that cross-link by hydrogen bonds into strong microfibrils; it forms plant cell walls. Carbohydrates provide and store energy: starch and glycogen store glucose in a compact, insoluble, osmotically inert form, so they do not affect the cell''s water potential, and they can be hydrolysed back to glucose when needed for respiration.

3. Core Practical 1 — semi-quantitative tests for reducing sugars and starch

Use Benedict''s reagent to estimate the concentration of reducing sugars and iodine solution to estimate the concentration of starch, using colour standards. Benedict''s reagent (copper(II) sulfate, sodium carbonate and sodium citrate) turns from blue to green, then yellow, then orange, then brick-red as reducing sugars are heated with it — the colour depends on the concentration of reducing sugar. For a semi-quantitative estimate, prepare a range of known reducing sugar concentrations (for example glucose solutions), heat each with Benedict''s, compare the colour with a colour standard chart, and record the colour or its code for each; then use the standards to estimate the concentration in an unknown. For starch, add iodine solution (iodine in potassium iodide) to the sample; a blue-black colour shows starch, and the intensity of the colour relates to the concentration — compare with colour standards to estimate. State the variables: the independent variable is the sugar or starch concentration, the dependent variable is the colour or colour standard, and controlled variables include the volume, temperature and time of heating.

4. Glycosidic bonds: condensation and hydrolysis

Monosaccharides join by condensation reactions to form disaccharides and polysaccharides, with a glycosidic bond formed between them and a water molecule lost each time. Conversely, polysaccharides and disaccharides can be hydrolysed — split by the addition of water — into their monomers; hydrolysis breaks the glycosidic bond and needs a water molecule for each bond broken. Glucose, fructose and galactose join to make maltose (glucose + glucose), sucrose (glucose + fructose) and lactose (glucose + galactose). Amylose and amylopectin are formed from alpha-glucose units; cellulose is formed from beta-glucose units, and because beta-glucose has a different orientation the chain is straight rather than coiled, so the hydrogen bonds between adjacent chains form strong microfibrils. Hydrolysis of starch gives maltose then glucose; hydrolysis of sucrose gives glucose and fructose; hydrolysis of lactose gives glucose and galactose. This matters in the body: dietary starch is hydrolysed to glucose in the gut by enzymes, and that glucose is used in respiration or stored as glycogen; lactose intolerance is caused by a deficiency of lactase, the enzyme that hydrolyses lactose, so lactose stays in the gut and causes problems.

5. Triglycerides: structure and saturated and unsaturated lipids

A triglyceride is made from one glycerol molecule and three fatty acids, joined by three ester bonds formed in condensation reactions; it is insoluble in water (hydrophobic). Fatty acids have a carboxyl group at one end and a hydrocarbon chain that may be saturated — no double bonds in the chain, so the molecule is straight and packs tightly, and saturated fats (and the triglycerides made from them) are usually solid at room temperature — or unsaturated, with one or more double bonds that kink the chain and prevent tight packing, so unsaturated fats are usually liquid at room temperature (oils). Lipids have several roles: they store energy in a compact, insoluble form (1 g of fat stores more energy than 1 g of carbohydrate), they form the phospholipid bilayer of all cell membranes, they form the myelin sheath around nerve fibres, they form a protective waterproof layer in the skin (subcutaneous fat), and they form steroid hormones. In membranes the phospholipid bilayer controls what enters and leaves the cell; the membrane also has proteins, cholesterol and glycoproteins.

6. Why animals need a heart and circulation

Many animals need a heart and a circulatory system because as an organism grows, diffusion alone is too slow to supply its cells with oxygen and nutrients and to remove waste — the surface area to volume ratio falls as size increases, and diffusion is only effective over short distances. A mass transport system (heart, blood vessels and blood) moves substances rapidly around the body, overcoming the limitations of diffusion. Blood carries oxygen, nutrients, hormones, waste products and defence cells and molecules. In simple organisms (small ones, or those with a large surface area to volume ratio or a thin body wall) exchange can happen directly by diffusion with the environment; larger or more active animals need a specialised exchange surface and a circulation system to move materials there and back.

7. The structure of arteries, veins and capillaries

Blood vessels relate their structure to their function. Arteries carry blood away from the heart at high pressure; they have thick, muscular, elastic walls to withstand and smooth the pressure and to help push the blood on, and a narrow lumen relative to wall thickness; they have no valves (except at the heart). Veins carry blood back to the heart at low pressure; they have thinner walls (less muscle and elastic tissue) and a wide lumen, and they have valves to prevent backflow, helping return blood when pressure is low. Capillaries are the exchange vessels; they have walls only one cell thick, a very narrow lumen just wide enough for red blood cells to pass in single file, slowing the blood and maximising the surface area for the exchange of substances. The structure of each vessel matches the pressure and role it plays.

8. The cardiac cycle and the structure of the mammalian heart

The mammalian heart is a muscular pump with four chambers — two atria (thin-walled, receiving chambers) and two ventricles (thick-walled, pumping chambers), with the left side pumping oxygenated blood to the body and the right side pumping deoxygenated blood to the lungs. The cardiac cycle is the sequence of events in a heartbeat: atrial systole (the atria contract, pushing blood into the ventricles), ventricular systole (the ventricles contract, pushing blood out into the pulmonary artery and aorta, and the atrioventricular valves close to prevent backflow, making the first heart sound), and diastole (the heart relaxes, the ventricles fill, the semilunar valves close, making the second heart sound). The valves ensure one-way flow: the atrioventricular valves (between atria and ventricles) and the semilunar valves (in the aorta and pulmonary artery). The left ventricle has a much thicker wall than the right because it must pump blood at high pressure around the whole body, whereas the right ventricle pumps only to the nearby lungs. The structure of the heart and its operation are shown by dissection (a recommended additional practical), and the heart''s own rhythm is myogenic, starting at the sinoatrial node, though details of that are not needed at IAS.

9. Haemoglobin, oxygen transport and the oxygen dissociation curve

Haemoglobin transports oxygen in red blood cells. Each haemoglobin molecule has four polypeptide chains, each with a haem group that contains an iron ion that can combine with one oxygen molecule, so one haemoglobin can carry four oxygen molecules. The oxygen dissociation curve shows how much oxygen haemoglobin takes up at different oxygen tensions: at high oxygen tension (in the lungs) it becomes almost fully saturated, and at low oxygen tension (in respiring tissues) it releases oxygen; the shape of the curve means a small drop in oxygen tension in the tissues releases a lot of oxygen — this is important. The Bohr effect: as carbon dioxide concentration rises and pH falls, haemoglobin''s affinity for oxygen falls and it releases oxygen more readily — so where respiration is high and CO2 is produced, haemoglobin unloads oxygen. Adult haemoglobin has a lower oxygen affinity than fetal haemoglobin, which has a higher affinity — this lets the fetus pick up oxygen from the mother''s blood across the placenta, because fetal haemoglobin can take oxygen from adult haemoglobin. Carbaminohaemoglobin carries some carbon dioxide as well, so haemoglobin transports both oxygen and carbon dioxide.

10. Atherosclerosis: how it develops and why it matters

Atherosclerosis is the narrowing and hardening of arteries by plaques. The process begins with endothelial dysfunction — damage to the lining of the artery, by high blood pressure, by smoking chemicals, or by immune responses — then an inflammatory response follows, white blood cells (including phagocytes) move into the artery wall, LDL cholesterol is taken up and oxidised, smooth muscle cells multiply and fibrous tissue forms, and a plaque builds up (a fibrous cap over a lipid core). As the plaque grows it narrows the artery, raising blood pressure further and reducing flow; eventually a plaque may rupture, triggering blood clotting and a thrombus, which can block a coronary artery and cause a myocardial infarction (heart attack). The main risk factors — genetics, diet, age, gender, high blood pressure, smoking and inactivity — act through these mechanisms, and the disease shows why passive transport and diffusion alone cannot supply the larger, more active human body and why the heart and blood vessels are needed.

11. Blood clotting and its role in cardiovascular disease

Blood clotting forms a network of insoluble fibrin threads that traps platelets and red blood cells to form a clot and seal a wound. The process: damage to a blood vessel exposes platelets to the collagen in the wall, and they are activated and release thromboplastin; thromboplastin, in the presence of calcium ions, converts prothrombin (an inactive plasma protein) to thrombin; thrombin then catalyses the conversion of soluble fibrinogen to insoluble fibrin, which forms a mesh that traps platelets and red blood cells into a clot. Clotting is needed to prevent blood loss and to stop pathogens entering, but in cardiovascular disease a clot formed on a ruptured plaque can block a coronary artery and cause a myocardial infarction, or travel to block a cerebral artery and cause a stroke. Treatments to reduce clotting include platelet inhibitors such as aspirin, and anticoagulants such as warfarin, which slow the clotting cascade.

12. Risk factors for cardiovascular disease

Many factors increase the risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD), and most act through the mechanisms above. Diet high in saturated fats and cholesterol raises LDL levels and contributes to plaques; high blood pressure damages the endothelium and raises the risk of both atherosclerosis and clotting; age increases risk because damage accumulates and repair is less efficient; males are at higher risk at younger ages than females; smoking introduces chemicals that damage the endothelium and raise blood pressure and heart rate and reduce oxygen carried by haemoglobin; inactivity contributes to high blood pressure, obesity and high cholesterol; and genetics/family history affects a person''s baseline risk. Risk is often the result of several factors combined, and reducing one can help even if others remain. People''s perception of risk is often different from the actual risk — they may underestimate or overestimate the risk from diet and other lifestyle factors, and scientists work to clarify the real risks through studies.

13. Diet, cholesterol and antioxidants and the evidence for them

Dietary antioxidants (such as vitamins C and E from fruits and vegetables) may reduce the risk of CVD by preventing the oxidation of LDL cholesterol — oxidised LDL is taken up more readily by artery walls and contributes to plaque formation. Blood cholesterol level is an important indicator: total cholesterol and LDL cholesterol are linked to CVD, and HDL cholesterol helps remove cholesterol from the artery wall, so high HDL is protective. The evidence that cholesterol causes CVD comes from studies showing a causal relationship between blood cholesterol levels and cardiovascular disease, and from trials of the statins, which lower cholesterol and reduce CVD events. People use scientific knowledge about diet, body mass index (BMI = mass (kg) / height (m) squared) and waist-to-hip ratio (a measure of central obesity), exercise and smoking to reduce their risk of coronary heart disease — and they should distinguish between correlation and causation when interpreting the data, because two things occurring together does not by itself prove one causes the other.

14. Data analysis in health studies: correlation, causation and study design

Health studies use quantitative data on illness and mortality rates to determine health risks. Two things can be correlated without one causing the other — a third factor may cause both, or the relationship may be coincidental — so a key skill is distinguishing correlation from causation. A causal relationship for cholesterol and CVD is supported by mechanistic evidence (the biology above) plus the results of trials. When evaluating the design of studies used to determine health risk factors, consider the sample selection (is it representative, or biased, as in a sample of only one type of person or only volunteers) and the sample size (small samples are less reliable and more easily swayed by chance). Conflicting evidence exists because studies differ in design, in the populations studied, and in the measures used, and scientific decisions draw on the whole body of evidence, not one study.

15. Perceived and actual risk and why people''s views differ

People''s perception of risks is often different from the actual risks — they may underestimate risks due to diet and lifestyle because those risks feel distant and small, or overestimate them because of vivid or recent examples, or because of personal experience, cultural beliefs or poor understanding of the probabilities. Scientific knowledge can clarify the actual risk: for example, many people underestimate the risk from diet and inactivity for coronary heart disease even though the evidence is strong, and the gap between perception and reality is itself a reason to communicate the science clearly. Understanding that perception and reality can diverge is part of evaluating the use of scientific knowledge in making decisions about health, and it explains why public health messages must be carefully designed and evidence-based.

16. Treatments for cardiovascular disease: benefits and risks

Several treatments are used for CVD. Antihypertensives lower blood pressure, reducing the risk of endothelial damage and of heart strain. Statins lower blood cholesterol, reducing plaque formation and the risk of atherosclerosis. Anticoagulants (such as warfarin) and platelet inhibitors (such as aspirin) reduce clot formation, lowering the risk of a clot on a ruptured plaque causing a heart attack or stroke. Each has benefits and risks: antihypertensives can cause dizziness, fatigue or kidney effects and may over-lower pressure; statins can cause muscle pain, digestive upset and, rarely, liver effects; aspirin can cause bleeding, especially in the gut, and is not suitable for everyone. Decisions about treatment balance the degree of risk against the benefit, take the person''s overall risk factors into account, and should be supported by the evidence — and by the science behind the disease, so that treatment targets the actual risk factors.

17. Core Practical 2 — vitamin C content of food and drink

Investigate the vitamin C content of food and drink, using DCPIP (2,6-dichlorophenolindophenol), which is blue when oxidised and colourless when reduced. Ascorbic acid (vitamin C) reduces DCPIP, so as vitamin C is added from a food or drink sample, the blue colour fades; the volume of a known concentration of vitamin C solution needed to decolorise a fixed volume of DCPIP gives a calibration, and the volume of the food or drink needed to decolorise the same DCPIP lets you estimate its vitamin C concentration by comparison. Carry out the test for several drinks (for example fruit juices, boiled and unboiled samples) to compare vitamin C content, and note that heat (boiling) destroys vitamin C, so boiled samples contain much less. Record volumes, identify the independent (volume of sample) and dependent (volume needed to decolorise DCPIP) variables, and control temperature, DCPIP volume and end-point judgement.

18. Proteins: amino acids, peptide bonds and the levels of structure

Amino acids are the monomers of proteins; the basic structure is an amino group, a carboxyl group and a variable R group attached to a central carbon. There are around 20 amino acids, differing in their R group, and the sequence of amino acids in a protein (primary structure) determines its folding and function. Amino acids join by condensation reactions to form peptide bonds, making dipeptides and polypeptides. Secondary structure is local folding into alpha-helices and beta-pleated sheets, held by hydrogen bonds between peptide bonds. Tertiary structure is the overall three-dimensional shape, held by hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, disulfide bonds and hydrophobic interactions; it determines the protein''s function. Haemoglobin is a globular protein with four chains and four haem groups each carrying one oxygen; collagen is a fibrous protein of three polypeptide chains in a triple helix, strong for tendons and skin. Biuret reagent (copper(II) sulfate and sodium hydroxide) turns purple in the presence of peptide bonds, and a semi-quantitative method using it and colour standards can estimate protein concentration — that is a recommended additional practical.

19. Gas exchange surfaces and Fick''s law

An effective gas exchange surface has a large surface area to volume ratio, a thin surface (short diffusion distance) and a difference in concentration between the two sides — the three properties that make diffusion rapid. The rate of diffusion is described by Fick''s law: rate of diffusion = (surface area × concentration difference) / thickness of the surface, so increasing surface area or concentration difference, or decreasing thickness, increases the rate. The mammalian lung is adapted for rapid gaseous exchange: the alveoli provide a huge total surface area (about 70–90 m² in an adult), they are thin-walled (one cell thick, with a shared basement membrane) so the diffusion distance is very short, the air in the alveoli is highly oxygenated while the blood arriving is deoxygenated, so there is a steep concentration gradient, and the constant ventilation and blood flow maintain that gradient. Fick''s law explains why these adaptations matter quantitatively.

20. Enzymes: specificity, catalysing reactions and factors that affect rate

Enzymes are biological catalysts that speed up reactions by lowering the activation energy needed. Their mechanism of action is explained by their three-dimensional structure: the active site has a specific shape that fits the substrate (the lock-and-key model) or changes shape to fit it (the induced-fit model), and specificity comes from the exact shape of the active site — each enzyme works on one or a few substrates.
