Enzymes are proteins, and heat, pH and the concentrations of enzyme and substrate affect their rate: each enzyme has an optimum temperature and pH; above or below the optimum the rate falls, and extremes denature the enzyme (irreversibly changing the shape of the active site, so it no longer works). Enzyme concentration increases the rate when substrate is in excess, and substrate concentration increases the rate up to a point, after which the enzyme''s active sites are saturated and the rate levels off (maximum rate, Vmax). These effects are investigated in Core Practical 4.

21. Core Practical 4 — factors affecting enzyme rate

Investigate the effect of temperature, pH, enzyme concentration and substrate concentration on the initial rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction. For each factor, choose a suitable enzyme and substrate (for example amylase and starch, or catalase and hydrogen peroxide) and measure the initial rate — the rate in the first part of the reaction, before the substrate is used up or the enzyme denatures. Change the factor being tested in steps, keep the other factors constant (control variables), take several measurements, and calculate the initial rate from the slope of the graph of product formed (or substrate used) against time. For temperature, the rate rises with temperature to an optimum, then falls as the enzyme denatures; for pH, rate is highest at the enzyme''s optimum pH; for enzyme concentration, rate rises linearly with concentration; for substrate concentration, rate rises and then levels off at Vmax. Plot graphs and explain the patterns in terms of collisions, activation energy and denaturation.

22. How to use this note and what to revise next

Use these notes section by section, checking that you can state the structure of a water molecule and explain its polarity, draw the structures of alpha-glucose and beta-glucose and state the difference, carry out the Benedict''s and iodine semi-quantitative tests and explain the variables and the colour standards, draw a triglyceride and distinguish saturated from unsaturated, state the structure and function of arteries, veins and capillaries, describe the cardiac cycle and the structure of the heart, sketch the oxygen dissociation curve and explain the Bohr effect and fetal haemoglobin, describe the stages of atherosclerosis and blood clotting, list the risk factors for CVD and state how each acts, carry out the DCPIP and biuret practicals, describe the properties of a gas exchange surface and apply Fick''s law, and explain enzyme specificity and the effects of temperature, pH and concentrations. After this topic, revise Topic 2 Membranes, proteins, DNA and gene expression, and Topic 3 Cell structure, reproduction and development — the transport and exchange ideas here underpin the circulatory and gas exchange systems in later topics.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Cardiac output, applied to a resting heart: cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume. With a heart rate of 70 beats min⁻¹ and a stroke volume of 70 cm³, the output is 4900 cm³ min⁻¹, or about 4.9 dm³ min⁻¹. Convert the units before you multiply, and state the units of the answer.
  • Glycosidic bonds: condensation forms a glycosidic bond between two monosaccharides and releases one water molecule. Hydrolysis adds a water molecule and breaks the bond. A disaccharide such as maltose from two glucose units therefore has the formula C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁, not two copies of glucose's formula.
  • Triglycerides: one glycerol and three fatty acids form three ester bonds, and three water molecules are released. Saturated fatty acids have no C=C double bonds and pack tightly, so they are solid at room temperature. Unsaturated fatty acids have one or more C=C double bonds, which bend the chain and keep it liquid.
  • Artery, vein and capillary structure: arteries have thick elastic and muscle walls to withstand high pressure, veins have valves and a thinner wall, and capillaries are one cell thick to allow diffusion. Relate each structural feature to its function in the answer, because the mark is for the link.

The tests in Core Practicals 1, 2 and 4, compared

TestDetectsPositive resultWhat makes it semi-quantitative
Benedict's reagent, heatedReducing sugarsBlue to green, yellow, orange or brick-red precipitateComparing the colour with a set of standards made from known concentrations
Iodine solutionStarchOrange-brown to blue-blackJudging the depth of colour against standards
Biuret reagentPeptide bonds, so proteinBlue to purple or lilacColour standards for known protein concentrations
DCPIPVitamin CBlue to colourlessVolume of sample needed to decolourise a fixed volume of DCPIP
Emulsion testLipidMilky white emulsion after adding water to an ethanol extractNone: it is a qualitative test

Typical mistakes

  • Explaining water's properties from polarity alone. Polarity matters because it allows hydrogen bonds, and it is the hydrogen bonds that give water its high specific heat capacity, its high latent heat of vaporisation and its cohesion.
  • Confusing condensation with hydrolysis. Condensation joins monomers and releases water; hydrolysis adds water and splits the bond. State which one is happening before you name the bond.
  • Describing unsaturated fatty acids as "less healthy" instead of describing their structure. Unsaturated chains contain one or more carbon-carbon double bonds, so the chain kinks, the molecules cannot pack closely, and the substance is liquid at room temperature.
  • Giving the artery wall as "thick" without saying why. The elastic and muscle tissue withstands and smooths high pressure from the ventricles. Capillaries are one cell thick to shorten the diffusion distance, and veins have valves to prevent backflow.
  • Reading the oxygen dissociation curve backwards. A curve shifted to the right shows a lower affinity for oxygen, so haemoglobin unloads oxygen more readily to respiring tissue. That is the Bohr effect, and it is caused by a higher carbon dioxide concentration and lower pH.
  • Treating correlation as causation. A study that finds a statistical association has not shown that one factor causes the other; confounding variables, sample size and study design all have to be evaluated first.
  • Mixing up the treatments for cardiovascular disease. Statins lower blood cholesterol, antihypertensives lower blood pressure, anticoagulants reduce clotting, and platelet inhibitors reduce platelet aggregation. Name the effect, not just the drug.
  • Forgetting the control variables in an enzyme practical. When temperature is the independent variable, pH, enzyme concentration and substrate concentration must be held constant, and the initial rate is measured from the steepest part of the graph, before substrate is used up.

Exam-style questions

  1. Explain why water is an effective solvent for transport in organisms. Answer: the water molecule is a dipole, with a partial negative charge on the oxygen and partial positive charges on the hydrogens, so it attracts ions and polar molecules and surrounds them; this keeps them dissolved and able to move in the bloodstream or in xylem.
  2. A heart beats 75 times a minute with a stroke volume of 70 cm cubed. Calculate the cardiac output in dm cubed per minute. Answer: cardiac output = heart rate times stroke volume = 75 times 70 = 5 250 cm cubed per minute, which is 5.25 dm cubed per minute.
  3. An alveolus has a surface area of 0.02 m squared, a wall thickness of 0.0005 mm and an oxygen concentration difference of 40 units. Use Fick's law to explain what happens to the rate of diffusion if the wall thickens. Answer: rate is proportional to surface area times concentration difference divided by thickness. Thickening the wall increases the diffusion distance, so the rate falls in proportion. Rate = (0.02 times 40) / thickness, so doubling the thickness halves the rate.
  4. Describe the sequence of events that leads to atherosclerosis. Answer: the endothelium is damaged (for example by high blood pressure or smoking); an inflammatory response attracts white blood cells and lipids into the wall; fatty deposits form a plaque (atheroma); the plaque narrows the artery and stiffens it, raising blood pressure; if the plaque ruptures, a clot forms and can block the artery, causing a heart attack or stroke.
  5. Explain the role of haemoglobin in oxygen transport and how the Bohr effect helps a exercising muscle. Answer: haemoglobin binds oxygen in the lungs, where the partial pressure of oxygen is high, and releases it in tissues where it is low. Respiring muscle raises carbon dioxide and lowers pH, which shifts the dissociation curve to the right, lowering the affinity for oxygen so that more oxygen is unloaded where it is needed.
  6. A student tests four solutions with Benedict's reagent and records the time taken to reach a brick-red colour. Explain how this design could be made semi-quantitative and reliable. Answer: fix the volume of solution, the volume of reagent, the temperature of the water bath and the time, then compare each result with a set of standards made from known concentrations. Repeat each measurement and take a mean, and use the same observer or a colorimeter to judge the end point.
  7. Explain why a diet high in saturated fat and low in fruit and vegetables increases the risk of cardiovascular disease. Answer: saturated fat raises low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, which is deposited in artery walls and contributes to plaque formation; fruit and vegetables supply antioxidants that reduce the oxidation of LDL cholesterol, so a low intake removes part of that protection. Both act alongside other risk factors such as smoking, age and inactivity.
  8. Explain the difference between a channel protein and a carrier protein in a membrane. Answer: a channel protein forms a pore through which specific ions or small polar molecules pass down their gradient; a carrier protein binds the substance and changes shape to move it across, which is how active transport can move substances against a gradient using ATP.

title: Exam technique: Oscillations and Waves II
content:
### What earns the marks
For Doppler, approach raising pitch stated earns the mark; v/c quoted earns the calculation marks. For standing waves, half lambda in L for the fundamental earns the method mark. For coherence, constant phase difference stated earns the definition mark.
### Traps
Error: receding claimed to raise frequency. Correction: approach raises, recession lowers. Error: fundamental taken as lambda = L. Correction: L holds half a wave. Error: EM waves given a medium. Correction: they travel through vacuum.

title: AS Level Mathematics: Numerical Measures of Central Tendency
content:
AS Level Mathematics: Numerical Measures of Central Tendency

Statistics begins with describing data: where its centre lies and how it is spread. This note covers representation of data — tables, histograms, cumulative frequency curves and box plots — and the three averages with their strengths, plus the quartiles and interquartile range that measure spread robustly. The emphasis throughout is on choosing the right representation for the data type and reading values off a graph with the precision the marks require.

Types of data and the right representation

Data typeMeaningUseful displays
QualitativeCategories, no orderBar chart, pie chart
DiscreteCountable valuesBar chart, stem-and-leaf, histogram of counts
ContinuousAny value in a rangeHistogram, cumulative frequency, box plot

A histogram is the display for continuous data grouped into classes; unlike a bar chart, the bars touch because the variable is continuous. For unequal class widths the frequency density is plotted, not the frequency:

frequency density = frequency / class width
area of a bar = frequency (so areas are comparable)

Worked example. A class of width 10 contains 25 items; another of width 20 contains 30. Find the frequency densities.

25/10 = 2.5;  30/20 = 1.5
The narrower class is denser even though it holds fewer items.

The three averages

AverageHow to findStrengthWeakness
MeanSum ÷ countUses every valueDragged by outliers
MedianMiddle of ordered dataResistant to outliersIgnores exact values at the ends
ModeMost frequent valueWorks for categoriesMay not exist or be unique

Worked example. Find all three averages of 4, 7, 7, 9, 13.

mean = 40/5 = 8
median = 7 (third of five ordered values)
mode = 7

Worked example 2 (grouped mean). Estimate the mean of the grouped data: 0–10 (4), 10–20 (9), 20–30 (7).

use midpoints 5, 15, 25
sum = 4(5) + 9(15) + 7(25) = 20 + 135 + 175 = 330
total frequency = 20
estimated mean = 330/20 = 16.5

Grouped means are estimates: the midpoint stands in for every value in its class, so the answer is only as good as the grouping.

Median, quartiles and the interquartile range

median position (n data values) = (n + 1)/2
lower quartile Q1 at position (n + 1)/4
upper quartile Q3 at position 3(n + 1)/4
interquartile range IQR = Q3 - Q1

Worked example. Find the median and IQR of 3, 5, 7, 8, 10, 12, 15, 18.

n = 8; median position 4.5 -> average of 4th and 5th = (8 + 10)/2 = 9
Q1 position 2.25 -> 5 + 0.25(7 - 5) = 5.5
Q3 position 6.75 -> 12 + 0.75(15 - 12) = 14.25
IQR = 14.25 - 5.5 = 8.75

The IQR is the robust measure of spread: it discards the extreme quarter at each end, so one outlier cannot inflate it the way it inflates the range.

Cumulative frequency and box plots

A cumulative frequency curve plots the running total against the upper class boundary. The median, quartiles and any percentile are read off at the corresponding cumulative frequencies.

read the median at n/2, Q1 at n/4, Q3 at 3n/4
(from a cumulative frequency curve, interpolate on the curve)

Worked example. A cumulative frequency curve for 80 students gives Q1 = 42 marks, median = 55, Q3 = 66. Describe the distribution.

IQR = 66 - 42 = 24 marks
the median sits closer to Q1 than Q3? 55 - 42 = 13; 66 - 55 = 11
so the middle half is roughly symmetric, slightly longer tail below
the upper whisker reaches the maximum; compare its length with the
lower whisker to judge skew

Box plot construction. A box from Q1 to Q3 with a line at the median, whiskers to the smallest and largest values that are not outliers. Outliers (beyond 1.5 × IQR from the quartiles) are plotted as separate points.

lower fence = Q1 - 1.5 IQR;  upper fence = Q3 + 1.5 IQR
values outside the fences are outliers

Comparing distributions

A comparison answer needs two parts: a measure of location (median or mean) and a measure of spread (IQR or standard deviation), each with a sentence of interpretation. "School A's median is higher, so its typical student scored more; its IQR is smaller, so its results are more consistent."

Worked example. A: median 62, IQR 18. B: median 58, IQR 9. Compare.

A has the higher typical mark (+4 on the median)
B is more consistent (IQR 9 vs 18)
A's spread suggests a wider mix of abilities; B's results cluster

Choosing and justifying an average

Exam questions ask which average best represents a data set — the answer is a reasoned choice, not a preference:

  • Skewed data or outliers: the median, because it is not dragged by extremes.
  • Categorical data: the mode, because a mean of categories is meaningless.
  • Data where every value should count (e.g. total rainfall per month): the mean.

Worked example. House prices in a street are 180k, 190k, 195k, 200k and 1.2m. Which average represents a typical price?

mean = 393k (dragged up by the 1.2m house)
median = 195k (the middle price)
the median is the honest summary; the mean misrepresents the street

Coding and combined means

Coding simplifies arithmetic without changing the shape of the data. If every value is transformed by y = (x - a)/b, the mean and standard deviation transform the same way, which is why coded means can be decoded exactly.

coded values: y = (x - a)/b
mean(x) = b mean(y) + a
median(x) = b median(y) + a
IQR(x) = b IQR(y)   (spread scales but does not shift)

Worked example. The coded values y = (x - 50)/10 have mean 2.4 and IQR 1.5. Find the mean and IQR of x.

mean x = 10(2.4) + 50 = 74
IQR x = 10(1.5) = 15

Worked example 2 (combined groups). Class A has 20 students with mean mark 60; class B has 30 with mean 70. Find the combined mean.

total marks = 20(60) + 30(70) = 1200 + 2100 = 3300
combined mean = 3300/50 = 66
not the average of 60 and 70, because the groups differ in size

The combined-mean formula is the weighted average: the group sizes are the weights. Averaging two means without weighting is one of the most common arithmetic errors in statistics questions.

Stem-and-leaf diagrams

A stem-and-leaf diagram keeps every value visible while ordering the data, which makes it the quickest route to the median and quartiles without arithmetic. The stem is the leading digit, the leaf the final digit, and a key must be stated.

example key: 3 | 4 means 34

3 | 4 7 9
4 | 1 2 2 5 8
5 | 0 3 6
6 | 1

Reading it: the data are 34, 37, 39, 41, 42, 42, 45, 48, 50, 53, 56, 61. With n = 12, the median sits between the 6th and 7th values, the lower quartile at position 3.25 and the upper at 9.75.

Worked example. Find the median and IQR of the data above.

median = (42 + 45)/2 = 43.5
Q1 = 37 + 0.25(39 - 37) = 37.5
Q3 = 50 + 0.75(53 - 50) = 52.25
IQR = 14.75

Back-to-back stems compare two groups: leaves for one group run left of the stem and for the other to the right, sharing the same stems so the shapes line up. Comparison answers then read off both a location and a spread for each group, exactly as with box plots.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Mean) Find the mean of 12, 15, 9, 18, 16. Answer: 70/5 = 14.
  2. (Median) Find the median of 4, 9, 2, 7, 11, 6. Answer: ordered 2, 4, 6, 7, 9, 11; median (6 + 7)/2 = 6.5.
  3. (Mode) Find the mode of 3, 5, 5, 7, 9, 9, 9. Answer: 9.
  4. (Grouped) Estimate the mean of 0–20 (5), 20–40 (10), 40–60 (5). Answer: (5×10 + 10×30 + 5×50)/20 = 600/20 = 30.
  5. (Quartiles) Find the IQR of 2, 5, 6, 8, 9, 12, 14, 15. Answer: Q1 = 5.5, Q3 = 13.5, IQR = 8.
  6. (Histogram) A bar of height 3 has class width 5. What frequency does it represent? Answer: 3 × 5 = 15.
  7. (Comparison) Two classes: median 55, IQR 10 and median 55, IQR 20. Compare. Answer: same typical mark; the first is more consistent.
  8. (Choice) Which average suits shoe sizes? Answer: the mode, because sizes are categorical/ordinal and the most common size is what a shop stocks.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Not ordering first: the median requires sorted data; taking the middle of the raw list is wrong whenever the data is unsorted.
  • Position versus value: (n + 1)/2 gives the position, not the median; count to that place.
  • Midpoint error: the midpoint of 10–20 is 15, not 10 or 20; open-ended classes make a grouped mean impossible without an assumption, which must be stated.
  • Histogram heights: plot frequency density, not frequency, when class widths differ; areas, not heights, compare.
  • Reading the curve: cumulative frequency is read against the upper boundary; using the lower boundary shifts every quartile.
  • IQR arithmetic: Q3 − Q1, never Q1 − Q3, and never the range.
  • Comparison without spread: a comparison that mentions only the median is half an answer.
  • Mean of grouped data called exact: call it an estimate and say why.

title: Chemical Reactions
content:
Chemical Reactions

Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry 0620, Extended route, topic 6 (statements 6.1–6.4). Rates of reaction and collision theory, reversible reactions and equilibrium (including the Haber and Contact processes), and redox.

6.2 Rate of reaction

  • Rates rise with concentration, gas pressure, the surface area of a solid, temperature, and the presence of a catalyst (including enzymes). Measure a rate by mass loss (gas escaping) or gas volume collected against time.
  • Collision theory: reactions happen when particles collide with at least the activation energy and in the correct orientation. Increasing concentration or pressure increases the collision frequency; increasing surface area exposes more particles; a higher temperature gives particles more energy, so a greater proportion of collisions exceed Ea; a catalyst lowers the Ea itself.

6.3 Reversible reactions and equilibrium

  • In a closed system at equilibrium, the forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates and concentrations stay constant. Changing temperature, pressure or concentration shifts the position of equilibrium to oppose the change.
  • Haber process: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, ΔH negative. About 450 °C with an iron catalyst and around 200 atm — a compromise of yield, rate and cost.
  • Contact process: 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃, ΔH negative, about 450 °C with a vanadium(V) oxide catalyst.

6.4 Redox

  • Oxidation is loss of electrons, reduction is gain. In terms of oxygen: oxidation is gain of oxygen, reduction is loss of hydrogen. Oxidation numbers use Roman numerals: copper(II) oxide has copper at +2.
  • Acidified potassium manganate(VII) is purple and turns colourless as it oxidises; potassium iodide is colourless and turns brown (iodine) as it reduces.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Rate graph interpretation, applied to two curves from the same reaction at 20 °C and 40 °C: the 40 °C curve is steeper from the start and levels off at the same total gas volume, because temperature changes the rate but not the amount of product. Compare gradients for rate and final heights for yield.
  • Equilibrium application, applied to the Haber process at higher pressure: four gas molecules of reactants become two of product, so higher pressure shifts the equilibrium to the right and raises yield. Explain with collision frequency and the opposing change, not just "more product".
  • Redox identification, applied to a reaction where carbon reduces copper(II) oxide: copper's oxidation number falls from +2 to 0 (reduction), carbon's rises from 0 to +2 in CO (oxidation). Name both changes — one mark each.
  • Catalyst reasoning: a catalyst lowers the activation energy for BOTH the forward and reverse reactions, so equilibrium is reached faster but the position does not change. That distinction earns the top mark.

Common errors

  • Saying a catalyst increases yield. It only increases speed.
  • Using concentration as the only factor that changes equilibrium — temperature also changes the value of the equilibrium constant.
  • Confusing oxidation numbers with ionic charges. In CuO the copper ion is 2+, and its oxidation number is written +2.

title: Geometry — Congruence and Similarity — Study Notes
content:
Geometry — Congruence and Similarity

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): congruence criteria, similar shapes, scale factors for length/area/volume, symmetry.

1. Congruence

Criteria: SSS, SAS, ASA (AAS), RHS. State the criterion used when proving triangles congruent, then transfer matching sides/angles.

2. Similarity

Equal angles + sides in proportion. Scale factor k = corresponding new ÷ old.

Example: triangles with sides 4, 6, 8 and 6, 9, 12: k = 1.5.

3. Length, area, volume factors

Length ×k; area ×k²; volume ×k³ — including reverse problems.

Example: volumes 250 cm³ and 2000 cm³: k³ = 8 ⇒ k = 2 ⇒ areas ×4.

4. Area/volume calculations from similarity

Find k from a matching length pair, then apply the right power. Watch hidden pairs (radii, heights, slants).

5. Symmetry

Line symmetry (reflect) and rotational symmetry order — for 2-D shapes and 3-D solids (prisms, cubes, pyramids).

Exam tips: write the matching-vertex order in similarity statements (△ABC ~ △DEF); choose which k-power applies before calculating.

Congruent triangles

Two triangles are congruent when they match on one of four conditions: SSS (three sides), SAS (two sides and the included angle), ASA or AAS (two angles and a side), or RHS (right angle, hypotenuse and a side) for right-angled triangles. SSA is not a condition. Name the congruence test in every proof.

Similar shapes and scale factors

Similar shapes have equal angles and proportional sides. The linear scale factor k multiplies lengths, k² multiplies areas and k³ multiplies volumes. To find a missing side, set up the ratio of corresponding sides and cross-multiply.

Transformations in geometry questions

A translation is described by a column vector, a rotation by its centre, angle and direction, a reflection by its mirror line and an enlargement by its centre and scale factor. Image points are checked by measuring the same distance from the centre or the mirror line.

Worked example: proving congruence

Triangles ABC and PQR have AB = PQ, angle B = angle Q and BC = QR. These are two sides and the included angle, so the triangles are congruent by SAS. A correct proof names the criterion and lists the equal parts in the same order as the letters.

The four congruence conditions

  • SSS: three pairs of equal sides.
  • SAS: two pairs of equal sides with the angle between them equal.
  • ASA or AAS: two pairs of equal angles and one pair of equal sides.
  • RHS: a right angle, the hypotenuse and one other side equal, for right-angled triangles only.

SSA is not a valid condition, because the angle may not be the one between the sides, and two different triangles can share those measurements.

Similar shapes and scale factors

If two shapes are similar with scale factor k, every length multiplies by k, every area by k², and every volume by k³. Example: two similar solids have a height ratio 2 : 3. The area ratio is 4 : 9 and the volume ratio is 8 : 27.

To find a missing length, set up the ratio from a known pair: if a side of 6 cm on the small shape matches 9 cm on the large one, the scale factor is 1.5 and an 8 cm side becomes 12 cm.

Symmetry

  • A shape has rotational symmetry of order n if it looks the same after rotations of 360°/n about its centre.
  • A regular hexagon has six lines of symmetry and rotational symmetry of order 6.
  • Count lines of symmetry on the diagram itself, and check each one with a tracing or a mirror image.

title: Measures of Variation and Standard Deviation — Study Notes
content:
Measures of Variation

Range and Quartiles

The range is max − min — quick but destroyed by a single outlier. Quartiles split ordered data into quarters: Q₁ at position (n + 1)/4, Q₃ at 3(n + 1)/4 (raw data). The interquartile range, IQR = Q₃ − Q₁, is the spread of the middle 50% and resists outliers. Outliers are commonly flagged as values beyond Q₁ − 1.5·IQR or Q₃ + 1.5·IQR.

Variance and Standard Deviation

For raw data:

  • variance s² = Σ(x − x̄)²/n (the definitional form)
  • equivalently s² = Σx²/n − x̄² (the computational form)
  • standard deviation s = √(variance)

The standard deviation shares the units of the data; the variance does not. For frequency tables use Σf(x − x̄)²/Σf, or Σfx²/Σf − x̄².

Grouped Data

Use class midpoints as x. The result is an estimate — grouping discards within-class detail.

Combining and Scaling Datasets

Multiplying every value by b multiplies s by |b| and the variance by b². Adding a constant changes nothing in the spread. Two merged datasets: compute combined Σx and Σx² from each part, then apply the computational formula.

Example: data 1, 3, 4, 5, 7: mean 4, Σx² = 100, so variance = 100/5 − 16 = 4 and s = 2.

Exam tips: state units for s. When comparing consistency, the dataset with the smaller standard deviation (relative to its mean) is the more consistent. Always give the comparison sentence, not just the two numbers.

Exam method: variance and standard deviation

The variance is the mean of the squared deviations, or equivalently Var(x) = Σx²/n − x̄². The standard deviation is its square root, and it is in the same units as the data. Using the second form is quicker when the mean is already known.

Adding a constant to every value shifts the mean by that constant but leaves the standard deviation unchanged. Multiplying every value by a constant k multiplies the standard deviation by |k| and the variance by k². Use these rules to avoid recalculating from scratch.

For grouped data, use the class midpoints and the frequencies. The variance is Σfx²/Σf − x̄², with x̄ = Σfx/Σf.

The standard deviation is a measure of spread. Compare two data sets by stating which has the larger spread and linking that to the context of the data.

Exam cue: Show the sum of the values and the sum of squares before dividing, because the method marks depend on those totals.

Worked example: standard deviation from raw data

For the data 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9 there are n = 8 values with mean 5. The sum of the squares is 4 + 16 + 16 + 16 + 25 + 25 + 49 + 81 = 232. The variance is Σx²/n − (x̄)² = 232/8 − 25 = 29 − 25 = 4, and the standard deviation is √4 = 2. Using the formula with the sum of squared deviations gives the same answer and is a useful check on your working.

Exam method: outliers using the interquartile range

The interquartile range is Q3 − Q1. Under the usual rule, a value is an outlier if it lies below Q1 − 1.5 × IQR or above Q3 + 1.5 × IQR. Use the definition given in the question if one is stated, and show the two boundary values in your working. Writing a conclusion in context, such as "the value 40 is an outlier for these hours", gains the communication mark.

title: Quantum Physics — Study Notes
content:
Quantum Physics

Photons and photon energy

Electromagnetic radiation travels as photons, each with energy E = hf, where h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s is the Planck constant. Since c = fλ, the energy is also E = hc/λ. Shorter wavelength means higher energy.

Example: a photon of wavelength 500 nm has E = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3.0 × 10⁸)/(5.0 × 10⁻⁷) ≈ 4.0 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, or about 2.5 eV.

The photoelectric effect

When light shines on a metal surface, electrons are emitted only if the frequency of the light is at or above the threshold frequency f₀. Each photon transfers its whole energy to a single electron. Increasing the intensity increases the number of photons per second, so more electrons are emitted, but it does not increase the energy of each electron. The emission is instantaneous, with no time delay.

Wave theory cannot explain the threshold frequency or the lack of a time delay. The photon model explains both.

Einstein's photoelectric equation

hf = φ + E_k(max), where φ is the work function of the metal, the minimum energy needed to free an electron. The threshold frequency is f₀ = φ/h. The stopping potential V_s satisfies eV_s = E_k(max).

Example: a work function of 2.0 eV gives f₀ = (2.0 × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹)/(6.63 × 10⁻³⁴) ≈ 4.8 × 10¹⁴ Hz.

Wave-particle duality

Particles also have wave properties. The de Broglie wavelength of a particle with momentum p is λ = h/p. Electrons diffract through crystal lattices, showing wave behaviour, while photons show particle behaviour in the photoelectric effect. Both are needed to describe the same entities.

Energy levels and line spectra

Electrons in an atom occupy discrete energy levels. When an electron falls from a higher level E₁ to a lower level E₂, it emits a single photon with hf = E₁ − E₂. Absorption happens when a photon with exactly this energy is taken in. Because only specific energies are allowed, the spectrum is a set of sharp lines rather than a continuous band.

Example: a transition from −3.4 eV to −13.6 eV releases 10.2 eV, a wavelength of about 122 nm.

Exam tips: convert eV to joules (1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J) before using E = hf. Say which quantity the intensity changes and which it does not. Quote hf = φ + E_k(max) in photoelectric questions.

Worked example: threshold frequency and stopping voltage

Zinc has a work function of 4.3 eV. Converted to joules, that is 6.9 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, so the threshold frequency is f₀ = φ/h = 6.9 × 10⁻¹⁹ / 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ ≈ 1.04 × 10¹⁵ Hz. Light of frequency 1.5 × 10¹⁵ Hz gives photons of energy 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 1.5 × 10¹⁵ ≈ 9.9 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, or about 6.2 eV. The maximum kinetic energy of the ejected electrons is 6.2 − 4.3 ≈ 1.9 eV, so the stopping voltage is about 1.9 V. Quote values with their units, and keep eV and joules consistent within each step.

Exam method: photon energy and wavelength

Combine E = hf with c = fλ to give E = hc/λ. Convert wavelengths to metres before you substitute into hc, because a wavelength given in nanometres must be multiplied by 10⁻⁹ first. A wrong power of ten is the most common way to lose the final mark, so estimate the answer before you calculate it precisely.

title: AS Level Biology: Plant Structure and Function, Biodiversity and Conservation
content:
Plant Structure and Function, Biodiversity and Conservation — AS Level Biology

This revision note belongs to the Edexcel International Advanced Subsidiary (IAS) Biology specification, WBI12 Unit 2, Topic 4 Plant Structure and Function, Biodiversity and Conservation. It covers plant cell ultrastructure and the functions of the organelles and cell wall components, starch and cellulose and how their structure fits their role, how cellulose microfibrils and secondary thickening give physical properties to xylem and sclerenchyma fibres, the similarities and differences between sclerenchyma fibres, xylem vessels and phloem and their structure, position and function, the light microscope practical on transverse sections, the uses of plant fibres and starch in sustainability, the importance of water and mineral ions to plants and the practical on mineral deficiency, the tensile strength practical, bacterial growth requirements, antimicrobial plant substances and the aseptic practical, the development of drug testing from Withering''s digitalis to modern three-phased testing, classification and the species concept and the three-domain system, biodiversity and endemism and how they are measured, species richness and the heterozygosity index, the index of diversity and how it is compared between habitats, and the concept of niche and examples of adaptations — behavioural, anatomical and physiological. Every statement the topic is responsible for is covered in its own section or paragraph.

1. Plant cell ultrastructure: what is in a plant cell and why

Plant cells share the common eukaryotic features with animal cells — a plasma membrane (cell surface membrane), cytoplasm and ribosomes — but add several structures that animal cells do not have. The cell wall is a rigid outer layer of cellulose microfibrils embedded in a gel-like matrix; it gives shape and support, prevents the cell from bursting when turgid, and limits uncontrolled expansion. Chloroplasts are double-membraned organelles containing chlorophyll and the enzymes for photosynthesis; inside, stacked membranes (thylakoids, often stacked into grana) carry out the light-dependent reactions, and the surrounding stroma contains the enzymes for the light-independent reactions. Amyloplasts are colourless plastids that store starch; they are found especially in storage organs such as potato tubers. Vacuoles are membrane-bound sacs; a large central vacuole in mature plant cells is filled with cell sap — a watery solution of sugars, salts, pigments and waste — surrounded by the tonoplast membrane, and it maintains turgor pressure and gives the cell its rigidity. Plasmodesmata are thread-like channels through the cell walls of adjacent plant cells, connecting the cytoplasm and allowing communication and transport between cells. Pits are thin regions in the cell wall where the wall is localy thinner or absent, allowing water and solutes to pass between cells; the middle lamella is the layer that cements together the cell walls of adjacent cells. Ribosomes are present (80S in the cytoplasm) and the nucleus, nucleolus, mitochondria and golgi apparatus are all present, as in animal cells, except that plant cells do not have centrioles (higher plants lack them, though they still divide).

2. Recognising plant organelles from electron micrographs

On an electron micrograph of a plant cell you should be able to recognise the plasma membrane, nucleus with nucleolus, chloroplasts with their stacked thylakoid membranes (grana), mitochondria, rough endoplasmic reticulum with ribosomes, golgi (dictyosomes in plants), a large central vacuole with the tonoplast, the cell wall (with middle lamella where two cells meet), and plasmodesmata. Chloroplasts are especially characteristic: the grana appear as stacks of disc-like membranes. Amyloplasts appear as colourless, starch-filled plastids without grana. A good exercise is to label each of these in an EM image and to explain the function of each. Compare the plant cell with an animal cell: plant cells have a cell wall, chloroplasts, a large central vacuole and plasmodesmata, and generally no centrioles, and their shape is more regular because of the wall.

3. Starch and cellulose: polysaccharides that do different jobs

Starch and cellulose are both polymers of glucose, but alpha-glucose for starch and beta-glucose for cellulose, and that difference determines their properties. Alpha-glucose has the hydroxyl groups on the same side of the ring (in the usual representation), so when polymerised with 1,4-glycosidic bonds the chain coils into a helix, forming amylose, and with 1,6-branches forming amylopectin — compact, helical and branched, so starch is an excellent storage material: compact to pack a lot of glucose into little space, and with no osmotic effect, because the large insoluble starch granules do not draw water into the cell by osmosis. Cellulose is made from beta-glucose, in which the hydroxyl on carbon 1 is on the opposite side, so when linked the chain is straight rather than coiled; the linear chains run parallel and form many hydrogen bonds between adjacent chains, making strong cellulose microfibrils. Cellulose microfibrils are the main structural component of the cell wall, giving strength and rigidity; the way they are arranged determines the properties of the cell and of the whole plant. The structure of starch suits it for storage in plant cells; the structure of cellulose suits it for strength and support — two polymers from the same monomer with very different roles because of the different glycosidic bonds and the different shape of the chain.

4. Cellulose microfibrils, secondary thickening and the properties of xylem and sclerenchyma

The physical properties of plant tissues depend on how the cellulose microfibrils are arranged. In a young, growing cell the microfibrils are laid down mainly at right angles to the direction of growth, so the cell can expand in length; when growth stops, the cell can become strengthened by secondary thickening — more cellulose and, in some cells, lignin deposited on the inside of the primary wall — which makes the wall rigid and waterproof. In sclerenchyma fibres, the cells die at maturity and are left with heavily thickened, lignified walls, often with the microfibrils arranged in spiral or ring patterns; the result is strong, flexible but tough fibres that give mechanical support and can be used by humans (for example in textiles and ropes). In xylem vessels, the wall is lignified and the cells are dead at maturity, forming long tubes with the end walls broken down or absent — the vessel elements are linked end to end to form a continuous tube for the transport of water and mineral ions, and the lignified thickening (in rings, spirals or nets) prevents collapse under the negative pressure of the transpiration stream. So the arrangement of cellulose microfibrils and the deposition of lignin determine what a plant part can do: support, flexibility, or transport of water under tension. The secondary thickening of xylem and the lignification of sclerenchyma are the adaptations that let land plants grow tall and stand upright and transport water from the roots to the leaves.

5. Sclerenchyma fibres, xylem vessels and phloem: structure, position and function

Sclerenchyma fibres and xylem vessels provide support and, for xylem, transport; phloem translocates organic solutes. Sclerenchyma fibres are long, narrow cells with thick lignified walls and a small lumen, dead at maturity; they occur in bundles and, because of their strength and flexibility, they give support to stems and leaves and can be used in textiles and ropes. Xylem vessels are long, continuous tubes formed from vessel elements with lignified walls and pits in the walls, dead at maturity with no contents, and their function is transport of water and mineral ions from the roots to the leaves — and they also provide support. Phloem is a living tissue; sieve tube elements are the conducting cells, arranged end to end with perforated end walls (sieve plates) between them, reduced cytoplasm at the edges and no nucleus at maturity; each sieve tube element has a companion cell beside it, connected by plasmodesmata, which keeps the sieve element alive and supplies it with ATP, because the sieve element itself has lost its nucleus and most organelles. Phloem transports organic solutes (mainly sucrose, in solution in water) from sources (leaves, storage organs) to sinks (growing points, roots, developing fruits) by mass flow driven by the pressure gradient built up by the loading of sucrose into the sieve tubes. Compare: sclerenchyma fibres = support, dead, lignified; xylem vessels = support and water/mineral transport, dead, lignified, open tube; phloem = translocation of organic solutes, living sieve tubes with companion cells, perforated end walls, no lignin.

6. Core Practical 7 — transverse sections of roots, stems and leaves

Use a light microscope to make observations, draw and label plan diagrams of transverse sections of roots, stems and leaves, and to observe and label cells of plant tissues, identifying sclerenchyma fibres, phloem, sieve tubes and xylem vessels and their location. To make a transverse section, cut a very thin slice across a stem or root with a razor blade (a sharp blade and a steady hand or a sectioning technique), float the section onto water on a slide, lower a coverslip at an angle, stain if needed (for example with toluidine blue or iodine) to distinguish lignified xylem, sclerenchyma and phloem, and observe under the microscope at several magnifications. In a stem transverse section, note the positions of the epidermis, cortex, the vascular bundles (with xylem toward the inside and phloem toward the outside, and sclerenchyma fibres often outside the phloem in a bundle cap), and the pith in the centre; in roots the vascular tissue is central. Draw a plan diagram (an outline of the whole section showing the arrangement of tissues, not the cells) with the correct relative sizes and positions, label the tissues, give a title and magnification. Then observe and label the cells: look for the thick lignified walls of xylem and sclerenchyma, the sieve plates and companion cells of phloem, and the thin-walled cells of the cortex and pith.

7. Plant fibres and starch in sustainability

Plant fibres and starch can contribute to sustainability and to replacing oil-based plastics. Plant fibres (from sclerenchyma or from phloem fibres) are strong, renewable and biodegradable, and they can be used in textiles, paper, building materials and composites that replace oil-based plastics and synthetic fibres; water transport in plants today parallels the transport of sap and provides a model for how plants already do this. Starch can be used to make bioplastics — for example, starch can be processed into film-forming materials suitable for packaging, plates and disposable items — and because starch is a renewable, biodegradable material made from crops such as potatoes, maize or cassava, it can replace oil-based plastics in some uses. Using plant fibres and starch reduces reliance on oil, is renewable and can be more sustainable if the crops are grown responsibly; but there are trade-offs: land, water and energy for the crops, possible competition with food production, and the need to assess the whole life cycle. The use of plant products to replace oil-based plastics is a topic that connects plant structure (cellulose and starch), to sustainability, to human decisions informed by science.

8. Water and inorganic ions to plants, and mineral deficiency

Plants need water for photosynthesis (a reactant and the medium in which it happens), for transport (water is the solvent for minerals and for sucrose in the phloem), for support (turgor pressure keeps non-woody parts rigid), and for cooling (transpiration). Water enters the roots by osmosis from the soil and moves up the xylem. Inorganic ions are essential: nitrate ions (NO3-) are needed for making amino acids, proteins, DNA and chlorophyll — a deficiency causes stunted growth and yellowing of older leaves (chlorosis); calcium ions are needed for the middle lamella (pectin in the cell wall) and for cell membranes — a deficiency gives stunted growth and necrosis of the growing point and young leaves; magnesium ions are the central atom in chlorophyll — a deficiency causes chlorosis of the older leaves. A recommended additional practical is to investigate plant mineral deficiencies: grow plants in a solution with all minerals (complete) and in solutions missing one of nitrate, calcium or magnesium, observe and measure the effects on growth and leaf colour over weeks, and explain the results in terms of the roles of the missing ion.

9. Core Practical 8 — tensile strength of plant fibres

Determine the tensile strength of plant fibres — the force a fibre can take before it breaks. A typical method: take strands of a plant fibre (for example the fibres from celery stalks or nettle stems, or a piece of a plant stem with visible fibres), clamp one end, hang weights from the other, and add weights until the fibre breaks; record the mass (converted to a force, weight = mass × g) needed to break the fibre. Repeat for several fibres, present the results, and compare fibres from different plants or different parts of a plant. Safety: sharp blades and falling weights. The practical shows how the arrangement of cellulose and lignin gives the fibre its strength, and connects the cell-level structure to a macroscopic useful property.

10. Conditions for bacterial growth

Bacteria need certain conditions to grow: a supply of nutrients (carbon, nitrogen, minerals and, for some, specific organic factors), water, a suitable temperature (most pathogenic bacteria around 37 °C, though many grow across a range), oxygen (some need it — aerobic bacteria — some do not — anaerobic bacteria — and some can manage with or without), a suitable pH, and, for many, time to multiply. In the laboratory these conditions can be met and controlled: cultures are grown in nutrient broth or on agar plates, at a set temperature (often 25 °C for environmental organisms and 37 °C for those that grow at body temperature), with or without oxygen, and in sterile conditions so that only the desired organism grows. Aseptic technique is essential to avoid contaminating the culture or releasing harmful bacteria into the environment — sterilise equipment (by flame or autoclave), work near a flame to create an upward air current, work quickly and cover the plates, and dispose of cultures by sterilising before disposal.

11. Antimicrobial plant substances and the aseptic practical

Substances derived from plants can have antimicrobial and other therapeutic properties. Some plant extracts inhibit the growth of bacteria or fungi — for example, garlic has been traditionally used and does have some antibacterial effects; other plants yield useful compounds (aspirin from willow bark, morphine from poppies, and many modern drugs are derived from plants). A recommended additional practical is to investigate the antimicrobial properties of plants, including aseptic techniques for the safe handling of bacteria: prepare agar plates, use sterile swabs or paper discs impregnated with different plant extracts, incubate and measure the zones of inhibition around the discs — the diameter of the clear zone where bacteria did not grow — and compare the effectiveness of different extracts or the same extract at different concentrations. Use aseptic technique: sterilise the discs and loops, work near a flame, spread the bacteria in a controlled way, seal the plates with tape (but do not seal all the way so they do not become anaerobic), and incubate at a safe temperature. Measure the zones of inhibition and record them, including in a table, and draw a conclusion about which extract is most effective and about concentration.

12. Drug testing: from Withering''s digitalis soup to modern trials

The development of drug testing has moved from historic, uncontrolled methods to contemporary, rigorous protocols. William Withering''s digitalis soup in the 18th century was an early use of a plant-derived medicine — foxglove (Digitalis) — for dropsy (oedema), tested by trial and observation on patients, but with no controls, no placebo, no blinding and no large sample, so the evidence was weak and mixed with other treatments. Modern drug testing uses a sequence of phases: pre-clinical testing in the lab and on animals; clinical trials in humans in three phases — Phase 1 tests safety in a small group, Phase 2 tests efficacy and side effects in a larger group of patients, and Phase 3 tests the drug against the current treatment or a placebo in a large group, in a double-blind trial (neither the patient nor the clinician knows which treatment is being used) so that expectations do not bias the result. Placebos are used to control for the placebo effect (improvement from the belief of being treated). The modern protocol — double-blind, placebo-controlled, multi-centre, large trials — is far more reliable than Withering''s soup, and it protects patients and produces trustworthy evidence. Students should be able to describe this progression and evaluate the designs.

13. Classification: organising life, the species concept and the three domains

Classification is a means of organising the variety of life based on relationships between organisms, using differences and similarities in phenotypes (observable features) and in genotypes (the DNA and the proteins the DNA codes for). It is built around the species concept — a species is a group of organisms that can interbreed and produce fertile offspring — and a hierarchy of groups above it: genus, family, order, class, phylum and kingdom, with organisms grouped because they share common ancestry. The classification has changed as new data — especially molecular evidence from DNA and protein sequences — have come in, leading to critical evaluation of existing groupings and new taxonomic groupings. The three-domain system, based on molecular evidence, divides life into the Archaea, the Bacteria and the Eukarya (which includes all eukaryotes, plants, animals, fungi and protists); the Archaea are distinct from the Bacteria and include organisms that often live in extreme environments, and the evidence from ribosomal RNA sequences and other molecular data led to this reclassification, replacing the older five-kingdom system. The process of critical evaluation of new data by the scientific community — comparing, testing and debating — is what leads to new groupings and to science being self-correcting.

14. Biodiversity, endemism and threats from human activity

Biodiversity is the variety of life — the variety within a habitat, within a species or across the whole planet; it can refer to species richness (the number of different species in a habitat) or to genetic diversity within a species. Endemism is the state of a species being found only in one particular place (an endemic species, such as a plant found only on a particular island). Over time the variety of life has become extensive through evolution, but it is now being threatened by human activity — habitat destruction (deforestation, drainage, conversion to agriculture), over-exploitation (hunting, fishing, logging), pollution, the introduction of invasive species, and climate change, all of which can reduce biodiversity and cause extinctions. Biodiversity matters because it provides ecosystem services, genetic resources for medicines and crops, and is itself valuable; its loss affects ecosystems, food security and human health. Understanding the causes of the loss is important so that conservation measures can be designed to address them.

15. Measuring biodiversity: species richness, genetic diversity and heterozygosity

Biodiversity can be measured in different ways. Species richness — the number of different species in a given area — is one simple measure of biodiversity within a habitat; a habitat with more species is generally more diverse, though this ignores the abundance of each species (a habitat dominated by one common species and several rare ones may have the same species richness as one where all are equally common). Genetic diversity within a species can be measured by the heterozygosity index (also called heterozygosity): the proportion of individuals in a population that are heterozygous at a locus. It is calculated as the number of heterozygotes divided by the number of individuals in the population (for a single locus); a higher heterozygosity means more genetic diversity within that population. This matters because genetic diversity helps a population adapt to changes, resist disease and avoid the problems of inbreeding; loss of genetic diversity raises the risk of extinction.

16. Comparing habitats with the index of diversity

Biodiversity can be compared between different habitats using the formula for the index of diversity, D: D = (N(N−1)) / (Σ n(n−1)), where N is the total number of organisms of all species in the habitat, and n is the number of organisms of a particular species. Calculation: for each species, work out n(n−1); sum these to get Σ n(n−1); then divide N(N−1) by that sum to give D, the index of diversity. Worked example: in a habitat with species counts 10, 15, 5, 2 (N = 32): Σ n(n−1) = (10×9)+(15×14)+(5×4)+(2×1) = 90+210+20+2 = 322; N(N−1) = 32×31 = 992; D = 992 / 322 ≈ 3.08. A larger D means a more diverse habitat, because it reflects both the number of species and how evenly the individuals are distributed among them. To compare habitats, calculate D for each and compare the values, stating which is more diverse and what that suggests. The formula must be applied correctly: calculate n(n−1) for each species, sum them, and divide N(N−1) by the sum.

17. Niche and adaptations: behavioural, anatomical and physiological

A niche is the role of an organism in a habitat — the conditions in which it lives and the resources it uses, and how it interacts with other organisms; it is more than just the physical place (the habitat) where it lives, and no two species can occupy exactly the same niche for long because of competition. Adaptations are features that help an organism survive and reproduce in its niche, and they can be behavioural, anatomical or physiological. Behavioural adaptations are things the organism does — for example migration to avoid harsh conditions, hunting in packs, basking to warm up, or the specific foraging behaviour of a bird. Anatomical (structural) adaptations are physical features of the body — for example the shape of a bird''s beak for its food, the camouflage colours of a prey animal, the thick fur of an arctic mammal, or the long beak of a nectar-feeding bird. Physiological adaptations are internal functions — for example a camel''s ability to tolerate dehydration and to conserve water, the production of venom by a snake, the production of antifreeze proteins in some polar fish, or the specialised nitrogen excretion of desert animals. The concept of niche and the types of adaptation help explain how different organisms fit into their environments and how competition and adaptation shape communities.

18. Hardy-Weinberg, zoos and seed banks: allele frequencies and conservation

The Hardy-Weinberg equation tests whether a population is evolving. In a large population with random mating, no mutation, no migration and no selection, allele frequencies stay constant from generation to generation. Write the frequency of the dominant allele as p and the recessive allele as q. Then p + q = 1, and the genotype frequencies are p squared for the homozygous dominant, 2pq for the heterozygote and q squared for the homozygous recessive, so p squared + 2pq + q squared = 1. The value of the equation is that it gives a null expectation: if the observed genotype frequencies differ significantly from it, one of the assumptions is being broken and the allele frequencies are changing, which is evolution happening in front of you.

A worked use: a recessive condition affects 1 in 10 000 people, so q squared = 0.0001, q = 0.01 and p = 0.99. The carrier frequency is 2pq = 2 times 0.99 times 0.01 = 0.0198, about 1 in 50. That is why a rare recessive allele can be common in carriers while the disease itself stays rare, and it is the calculation the mark scheme wants rather than a guess from the disease frequency.

Conservation of genetic diversity is the other half of this section. Zoos use captive breeding programmes with studbooks to decide which animals pair, so that inbreeding is minimised and unrelated individuals are introduced; they also support scientific research and education, and run reintroduction programmes that prepare animals for the wild. The risks are that captive populations are small, so genetic drift and inbreeding reduce diversity, and that animals bred in captivity may lack the behaviour needed to survive on release. Seed banks store seeds at low temperature and low moisture, testing viability periodically and germinating samples to grow fresh seed, which protects genetic diversity far more cheaply than keeping animals. Their limits are that not all seeds survive drying, so some species need cryopreservation or living collections, and that a bank protects genes rather than the habitat the species needs. Evaluate both by naming what they conserve, what they cost and what they cannot do.

19. How to use this note and what to revise next

Use these notes section by section, checking that you can identify plant cell ultrastructure and organelles in an electron micrograph and state their functions, explain how starch and cellulose differ in structure and role, describe the secondary thickening and the properties of xylem vessels and sclerenchyma fibres, compare sclerenchyma fibres, xylem vessels and phloem in structure, position and function, carry out the transverse section and tensile strength practicals and explain the variables and safety, describe the conditions for bacterial growth and the aseptic practical, describe the development of drug testing from Withering''s digitalis to modern three-phased trials and evaluate the designs, define classification and the species concept, describe the three-domain system and the molecular evidence for it, define biodiversity and endemism and the threats from human activity, carry out the species richness and heterozygosity and index of diversity calculations, and define niche and give behavioural, anatomical and physiological adaptations. After this topic, revise Topic 3 Cell structure, reproduction and development (plant and animal cells, division) and Topic 5 Energy flow, ecosystems and the environment, because classification and biodiversity sit within ecology.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Simpson's index, applied to a quadrat with 10 daisies and 5 dandelions: N = 15, D = 1 − Σ(n ÷ N)² = 1 − [(10 ÷ 15)² + (5 ÷ 15)²] = 1 − (0.444 + 0.111) = 0.556. Use the index to compare two sites; a higher value means greater diversity.
  • Xylem and phloem: xylem transports water and minerals upwards and is made of dead, lignified cells with no end walls, so the water column is continuous. Phloem transports sucrose and amino acids in both directions and is made of living sieve tube elements with companion cells. Name the direction of transport and the living or dead state of the cells.
  • Cellulose versus starch: cellulose is made of β-glucose units linked alternately, which allows hydrogen bonding between chains, forming strong microfibrils. Starch is made of α-glucose, is coiled and is used for storage. The different glucose isomer explains the different shapes and functions.
  • Conservation: a protected area works only if the populations inside it are large enough to be viable. Name the factor, such as a wildlife corridor, that connects populations, because isolated populations lose genetic diversity over time.

Typical mistakes

  • Calling xylem living. Xylem vessels are dead, hollow, lignified tubes with no end walls, which is what allows a continuous water column. Phloem sieve tubes are living and supported by companion cells.
  • Giving sclerenchyma a transport role. Sclerenchyma fibres provide support only; xylem transports water and mineral ions and also supports, and phloem translocates sugars and amino acids.
  • Inverting the heterozygosity index. It is the number of heterozygotes divided by the number of individuals in the population, so it cannot exceed 1. A value of 1 would mean every individual is heterozygous.
  • Reading a diversity index the wrong way round. Use the formula given on the paper and then say which site has the higher diversity; do not assume a small number means a diverse habitat.
  • Missing the assumptions in a Hardy-Weinberg calculation. State that the population is large, mating is random and there is no selection or migration, and say that a significant difference in allele frequency between generations is evidence that one assumption is broken.
  • Claiming aseptic technique keeps everything sterile. Aseptic technique keeps contamination out of the culture and the worker safe: sterilise the loop, flame the neck of the bottle, work near a flame, and dispose of plates in the correct way. The apparatus and the medium are sterilised before use, which is a different step.
  • Describing drug trials without their purpose. A placebo controls for the expectation of improvement, a double-blind design stops the patient or the doctor influencing the result, and the three phases test safety, then effectiveness and dose, then comparison with existing treatment in a larger group.
  • Using the three-domain system without the evidence. Archaea, Bacteria and Eukarya were separated after molecular evidence, particularly ribosomal RNA sequences, showed that the archaea are as different from bacteria as both are from eukaryotes. New data changing a classification is a strength of the system, not a flaw.

Exam-style questions

  1. In a population of 2 000 plants, 120 are heterozygous at a particular locus. Calculate the heterozygosity index. Answer: 120 / 2 000 = 0.06. Only 6 per cent of the population is heterozygous, so the genetic diversity at that locus is low.
  2. A recessive allele causing a disease is present in 1 in 2 500 births. Assuming Hardy-Weinberg conditions, calculate the carrier frequency. Answer: q squared = 1 / 2 500 = 0.0004, so q = 0.02 and p = 0.98. The carrier frequency is 2pq = 2 times 0.98 times 0.02 = 0.0392, about 1 in 25.
  3. Explain how secondary thickening adapts a xylem vessel for its function. Answer: lignin is deposited in the wall, which makes it rigid so the vessel does not collapse under tension, and it makes the wall waterproof so water is not lost sideways; the strengthening also supports the plant.
  4. Describe how you would compare the tensile strength of fibres from two plant stems. Answer: extract fibres of equal length from each stem, clamp each in turn and hang masses from it until it breaks, recording the mass that causes failure. Control fibre length, thickness and the point of attachment, repeat each measurement and compare means. The fibre that withstands the greater mass has the greater tensile strength.
  5. Explain why a seed bank may conserve genetic diversity more effectively than a zoo. Answer: seeds are small, so many individuals and many species can be stored in a small space at low cost, and a large sample preserves more alleles than a small captive population that suffers inbreeding and genetic drift. A zoo is still needed for species whose seed cannot be stored or whose behaviour must be learned.
  6. Explain the evidence that led to the three-domain classification. Answer: comparisons of ribosomal RNA and other molecular sequences showed that archaeal sequences differ from bacterial sequences as much as both differ from eukaryotes, so the archaea were placed in their own domain alongside Bacteria and Eukarya. The classification is based on genotype as well as phenotype, and it is revised when new molecular data are critically evaluated.
  7. Withering's digitalis treatment and a modern double-blind trial are both tests of a drug. Explain two ways in which the modern protocol is an improvement. Answer: the modern trial uses a control group given a placebo, so improvement caused by expectation is separated from the effect of the drug, and it is randomised and double-blind, so neither patient nor doctor knows who received which treatment and bias is removed. It also uses measured doses and larger samples, so the result can be tested statistically.

title: IGCSE Physics: Nuclear Physics
content:
IGCSE Physics: Nuclear Physics

Cambridge IGCSE Physics 0625 (2026–2028), Topic 5 Nuclear physics: statements 5.1 The nuclear model of the atom and 5.2 Radioactivity. Everything in the physical world is built from about a hundred kinds of atom, and almost all the mass of an atom sits in a tiny, dense nucleus. This note builds the nuclear model, then radioactivity from first principles: what the three emissions are, how nuclei decay, how half-life quantifies it, and how radiation is used safely.

The atom and the nuclear model

An atom is mostly empty space: a tiny central nucleus surrounded by electrons that occupy shells around it. The nucleus is about 10 000 times smaller than the atom, yet holds more than 99.9 per cent of its mass. Atoms are neutral because the number of electrons equals the number of protons; if an atom loses or gains electrons it becomes a ion, charged positive or negative.

Supplement: the evidence. In the alpha-particle scattering experiment, alpha particles were fired at an extremely thin gold foil. Most passed straight through, a few were deflected by small angles, and a very small number bounced back. Rutherford concluded that the atom has a small, dense, positively charged nucleus: most alphas met only empty space, those passing near the nucleus were deflected by the positive repulsion, and the rare head-on reversals required a tiny, massive target.

The nucleus: protons, neutrons and isotopes

The nucleus contains protons and neutrons, collectively nucleons. A proton carries one positive charge and one unit of mass; a neutron carries no charge and one unit of mass; an electron carries one negative charge and almost no mass.

ParticleRelative chargeRelative massLocation
Proton+11Nucleus
Neutron01Nucleus
Electron−11/1836 (negligible)Shells around the nucleus

Nuclide notation writes the symbol of the element with the proton number Z (the number of protons, which decides the element) and the nucleon number A (the total number of protons and neutrons) as a superscript and subscript on the left: A over Z beside the symbol. The number of neutrons is A − Z. Isotopes are atoms of the same element (same Z) with different numbers of neutrons (different A), so they have identical chemical properties but different nuclear behaviour.

Supplement: fission and fusion. Nuclear fission splits a heavy nucleus (such as uranium-235) into two lighter nuclei plus neutrons and a large release of energy; a neutron triggers the split and the released neutrons sustain a chain reaction in a reactor. Nuclear fusion joins two light nuclei (such as hydrogen isotopes) into a heavier one, releasing far more energy per kilogram — this powers the Sun and every star. In both, a small loss of mass appears as a large release of energy, in line with mass–energy equivalence, and the sum of the nucleon numbers and of the proton numbers is conserved in any nuclear equation.

Detection of radioactivity

Radioactivity is the spontaneous emission of radiation from unstable nuclei. It cannot be seen, heard or felt, so it is detected by its effects: a Geiger–Müller tube produces an electrical pulse for each ionising particle entering it; photographic film darkens (which is why film badges measure radiation dose); and a cloud chamber shows the tracks of the emissions.

Background radiation is present everywhere and must be subtracted from every measurement: it comes from natural sources (radon gas from rocks and soil, cosmic rays from space, radiation from food and building materials) and from human activity (medical X-rays, fallout from nuclear accidents and weapons tests). A count-rate measurement is corrected by taking the reading with no source present and subtracting it from the source reading (Supplement: count rates are quoted in counts per second or counts per minute, and repeated background readings are averaged before use).

The three types of nuclear emission

Emission from an unstable nucleus is spontaneous and random: nothing external causes a particular nucleus to decay at a particular moment, and no prediction is possible for any single nucleus.

PropertyAlpha (α)Beta (β)Gamma (γ)
NatureHelium nucleus: 2 protons + 2 neutronsFast electron from the nucleusElectromagnetic wave of high frequency
Charge+2−10
Relative mass41/1836 (negligible)0
Ionising powerVery strongModerateWeak
Penetrating powerStopped by paper or a few cm of airStopped by a few mm of aluminiumReduced only by thick lead or many metres of concrete
Effect of a magnetic fieldDeflected slightly (opposite way to beta)Deflected more (opposite way to alpha)Not deflected

Supplement deepens the ionisation ranking: alpha particles are large and doubly charged, so they tear electrons from atoms at every collision and stop quickly; beta particles are small and singly charged and ionise less; gamma rays carry no charge and ionise least, so they travel furthest. The same ranking explains the danger profiles: alpha sources are the least dangerous outside the body (stopped by skin) but the most dangerous if ingested, because their intense ionisation wrecks nearby cells.

Radioactive decay

Decay is the change of an unstable nucleus into a different, more stable nucleus, with the emission of radiation. The nucleus changes identity: emitting alpha reduces the nucleon number by 4 and the proton number by 2; emitting beta converts a neutron into a proton, so the proton number rises by 1 while the nucleon number is unchanged; gamma emission changes the energy of the nucleus but not its identity.

alpha decay:        (A over Z) X  →  (A⁻⁴ over Z-2) Y  +  helium nucleus
beta decay:         (A over Z) X  →  (A over Z+1) Y  +  electron

In every nuclear equation the total nucleon number and the total charge are the same on both sides — the standard balancing question on Paper 2 and Paper 4. Decay is unaffected by temperature, pressure or chemical state: the nucleus is shielded from ordinary conditions by its electrons.

Half-life

Half-life is the time taken for half the undecayed nuclei of a sample to decay — equivalently, for the count rate to fall to half its original value. It is a fixed property of each isotope, ranging from fractions of a second to billions of years.

after n half-lives:        count rate = starting count rate x (1/2)^(number of half-lives)

From a decay curve, read the time for the rate to halve from any starting point; the half-life is the same at every stage. Radioactive dating uses the ratio of a long-lived isotope to its decay product in rocks (uranium to lead) or in once-living things (carbon-14, half-life 5730 years, absorbed during life and decaying after death). Short-lived isotopes are used as medical tracers, since they deliver a dose that soon disappears.

Safety precautions

Radiation damages living tissue by ionising atoms in cells, which can kill cells or damage DNA and cause cancer. Three simple controls govern all handling:

  • Time: keep exposures short and work quickly with sources.
  • Distance: use tongs and remote handling; the intensity falls sharply with distance from the source.
  • Shielding: store sources in lead-lined boxes; use paper for alpha, aluminium for beta, lead or concrete for gamma.

Sealed sources are never touched or pointed at people; contamination (spreading open sources) is prevented with gloves, trays and careful disposal; workers wear film badges and dose records are kept. Doctors and patients accept a medical dose only when the benefit outweighs the risk — the principle of every risk–benefit question in the paper.

Worked example: half-life calculation

A source has a corrected count rate of 640 counts per minute and a half-life of 8.0 days. What is the rate after 24 days, and how long until it falls below 40 counts per minute?

24 days = 3 half-lives:        640 → 320 → 160 → 80 counts per minute
80 → 40 needs one more half-life, so 24 + 8 = 32 days total

The physical reasoning: half-living is exponential, never linear. After three half-lives an eighth of the original activity remains, not one third.

Common mistakes

  • Confusing the three emissions: alpha is a helium nucleus (2 protons, 2 neutrons), beta is an electron created in the nucleus, gamma is a wave.
  • Saying radiation becomes safe after a fixed number of days; only the activity falls with half-life, and each isotope has its own.
  • Halving the count rate every half-life from the original instead of from the current value (linear thinking): 100 goes 50, 25, 12.5, not 50, 0, 0.
  • Forgetting to subtract background radiation from raw counts before plotting a decay curve.
  • Balancing a nuclear equation without conserving both the nucleon number and the proton number.
  • Claiming alpha is the most dangerous radiation in every case: it is the most ionising, but the least penetrating — the hazard depends on whether the source is outside or inside the body.
  • Saying isotopes have different chemical properties; the electron arrangement is identical, so the chemistry is identical.
  • Linking decay to temperature or pressure; nuclear decay is unaffected by ordinary physical conditions.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 4, 3 marks). A nucleus of uranium-238 emits an alpha particle. Write the nuclear equation if the product is thorium-234.

Answer: uranium-238 (92 protons) becomes thorium-234 (90 protons) plus a helium nucleus: 238 = 234 + 4 and 92 = 90 + 2, so both totals balance.

Question 2 (Paper 4, 3 marks). A sample's count rate falls from 400 to 50 counts per second in 12 minutes. Calculate the half-life.

Answer: 400 → 200 → 100 → 50 is three half-lives in 12 minutes, so the half-life is 4.0 minutes.

Question 3 (Paper 2 style). Which emission is stopped by a sheet of paper? A alpha; B beta; C gamma; D X-rays. Answer: A. Alpha is stopped by paper, beta by a few millimetres of aluminium, gamma only by thick lead.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 6 marks). Explain why alpha emitters are safe outside the body but extremely dangerous if inhaled.

Answer: Alpha particles are large and doubly charged, so they ionise atoms strongly and are stopped by the dead outer layer of skin or by a sheet of paper, meaning they cannot reach living tissue from outside. If an alpha emitter is inhaled, it lodges in lung tissue and the particles then strike living cells at point-blank range. Their intense ionisation breaks chemical bonds and damages DNA in those cells, which can kill them or cause mutations and cancer. Distance and shielding matter: inside the body there is neither.

Question 5 (Paper 4, 3 marks). State the three standard precautions when handling a radioactive source.

Answer: Keep the time of exposure short; keep well away and handle with long tongs to reduce intensity; store in a lead-lined box with suitable shielding for the emission type (paper for alpha, aluminium for beta, lead for gamma).

Question 6 (Paper 6 style). Describe how you would measure the half-life of a short-lived isotope safely.

Answer: Place the source in a holder a fixed distance from a Geiger–Müller tube connected to a scaler or data logger. Measure the background count rate with no source present and average several readings. Record the source's count rate at regular time intervals until it approaches background, keeping geometry constant. Subtract the background from each reading, plot count rate against time, and read the time for the activity to halve between any two points on the curve. Keep exposure brief, handle the source with tongs, and store it in its shielded box.

The nucleus holds the energy of stars; the last topic of the IGCSE course is where those stars live — Earth and Space.

Equations and symbols

Nuclear decay is described by two bookkeeping rules — the nuclide notation and the conservation of nucleon number and charge — plus the exponential half-life relation. There is no equation for "why" a nucleus decays; the marks are in the accounting.

Nuclide notation

A = Z + N
Key: A = nucleon (mass) number, the total protons plus neutrons; Z = proton (atomic) number, which fixes the element; N = neutron number. Written as A over Z before the symbol, as in ²³⁵₉₂U.

proton number Z = number of protons = number of electrons in a neutral atom
Key: Z decides the element; changing Z changes the element, which is what transmutation means.

isotopes: same Z, different A
Key: isotopes of an element have the same number of protons and different numbers of neutrons, so they behave identically chemically and differently in nuclear decay.

Decay bookkeeping

alpha decay: A → A − 4 and Z → Z − 2
Key: an alpha particle is a helium nucleus, ⁴₂He, so the parent loses two protons and two neutrons. Example: ²³⁸₉₂U → ²³⁴₉₀Th + ⁴₂He.

beta-minus decay: A unchanged and Z → Z + 1
Key: a neutron turns into a proton and an electron, so the nucleon number is unchanged and the proton number rises by one. Example: ¹⁴₆C → ¹⁴₇N + ⁰₋₁e.

gamma emission: A and Z unchanged
Key: a gamma ray is electromagnetic energy released from an excited nucleus; the nucleus loses energy but not particles, so the nuclide stays the same element.

conservation in every decay: ΣA and ΣZ balance on both sides
Key: the totals of nucleon number and of charge must be equal before and after. This is the check that catches a wrong particle on the right-hand side.

Half-life

N = N₀ × (½)^(t / t½)
Key: N = number of nuclei (or count rate) remaining after time t; N₀ = the starting number or rate; t = elapsed time (s, or any unit); t½ = half-life in the same unit as t. After three half-lives, one eighth remains.

t½ = the time for half the nuclei in a sample to decay
Key: a fixed property of the isotope, unaffected by temperature, pressure or chemical state. It is measured from a decay curve as the time for the count rate to halve.

A = ΔN / Δt
Key: A = activity (Bq, decays per second); ΔN = number of decays recorded; Δt = time interval (s). The measured count rate is lower than the activity because the detector only intercepts a fraction of the radiation.

Penetration and ionisation

penetrating power: alpha < beta < gamma
Key: alpha is stopped by paper or a few centimetres of air; beta by a few millimetres of aluminium; gamma is reduced but not stopped by thick lead. Ionising power runs the other way: alpha ionises most strongly because it is the most charged and most massive.

E = mc² (extension, beyond the 0625 requirement)
