Key: E = energy released (J); m = mass lost, the mass defect (kg); c = speed of light, 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s. It explains where the energy of a decay comes from, and why a small mass defect is a large energy release.

title: Exam technique: Algebra — Equations
content:
### What earns the marks
For linear equations, clearing fractions first earns the method mark. For quadratics, the factorised pair checked by substitution earns both marks. For word problems, the defined unknown plus the formed equation earn one mark each.
### Traps
Error: dividing through by x in quadratics. Correction: factorise, or lose the zero root. Error: unsimplified surds left hanging. Correction: simplify fully for the accuracy mark. Error: negative roots kept for lengths. Correction: reject what the context forbids.

title: A Level Mathematics: Exponentials and Logarithms
content:
A Level Mathematics: Exponentials and Logarithms

The exponential function eˣ is the one function whose gradient equals its value, which is why it describes any process whose rate of change is proportional to its size: cooling, decay, growth, charging a capacitor, the value of an investment. Its inverse, ln x, is the tool that unlocks equations with the unknown in the exponent. This note builds the pair from zero, links them to calculus, and finishes with the modelling and log-linear graph work that A2 papers test.

Definitions and the laws

log_a x = n  means  a^n = x
ln x = log_e x,  e = 2.718281828...

log(xy) = log x + log y
log(x/y) = log x - log y
log(x^n) = n log x
log_a a = 1;  log_a 1 = 0

e is defined as the value that makes the gradient of aˣ equal to aˣ itself. That single property generates the whole calculus of the topic:

d/dx (e^x) = e^x;  d/dx (e^(kx)) = k e^(kx)
d/dx (ln x) = 1/x;  d/dx (ln(kx)) = 1/x
integral of e^(kx) dx = (1/k) e^(kx) + c
integral of (1/x) dx = ln|x| + c

Worked example. Differentiate y = e^(3x) + ln(5x).

dy/dx = 3e^(3x) + 1/x

Worked example 2. Find ∫ (4e^(2x) + 3/x) dx.

= 2e^(2x) + 3 ln|x| + c

Solving exponential equations

Worked example 1. Solve 7^x = 50.

x ln 7 = ln 50
x = ln 50/ln 7 = 3.912/1.946 = 2.01

Worked example 2 (same base first). Solve 2^(3x−1) = 4^(x+1).

4 = 2^2, so 4^(x+1) = 2^(2x+2)
3x - 1 = 2x + 2  ->  x = 3

Always look for a common base before taking logs: it converts an exponential equation into a linear one and avoids rounding.

Worked example 3 (quadratic in eˣ). Solve e^(2x) − 5e^x + 6 = 0.

let y = e^x: y^2 - 5y + 6 = 0  ->  (y - 2)(y - 3) = 0
y = 2  ->  x = ln 2 = 0.693
y = 3  ->  x = ln 3 = 1.099

Solving logarithmic equations

Worked example 1. Solve ln(x + 3) + ln(x − 1) = ln 5.

ln[(x + 3)(x - 1)] = ln 5
x^2 + 2x - 3 = 5  ->  x^2 + 2x - 8 = 0
(x + 4)(x - 2) = 0  ->  x = 2 (x = -4 makes an argument negative)

Worked example 2 (different bases). Solve log₂ x + log₄ x = 3.

log_4 x = log_2 x / log_2 4 = (log_2 x)/2
so (3/2) log_2 x = 3  ->  log_2 x = 2  ->  x = 4

The change-of-base step is compulsory whenever bases differ; check every root against the original domains, and remember that log₂ x is only defined for x > 0 while its squared form can produce spurious negative candidates.

The graphs and their transformations

y = e^x: through (0, 1), increasing, asymptote y = 0
y = ln x: through (1, 0), increasing, asymptote x = 0, domain x > 0
they are reflections in y = x

Worked example. Sketch y = ln(x − 2), stating the asymptote, domain and intercept.

translation 2 right
asymptote x = 2;  domain x > 2
x-intercept: ln(x - 2) = 0  ->  x - 2 = 1  ->  x = 3

Worked example 2 (reflection). Sketch y = e^(−x) and state its relationship to y = e^x, noting the intercepts and asymptote of each.

reflection in the y-axis; still through (0, 1); asymptote y = 0;
decreasing, a decay curve

Growth and decay models

N = N_0 e^(kt): k > 0 growth, k < 0 decay
half-life = ln 2/|k|;  doubling time = ln 2/k

Newton's cooling: T = T_room + (T_0 - T_room) e^(-kt)

Worked example 1 (half-life). A substance decays as N = 80e^(−0.05t). Find the half-life and the amount after 20 years.

half-life: e^(-0.05t) = 0.5  ->  t = ln 2/0.05 = 13.86 years
at t = 20: 80e^-1 = 29.4 units

Worked example 2 (cooling). A cup of coffee at 90 °C cools to 60 °C in 10 minutes in a 20 °C room. Find k and the temperature after 25 minutes.

T - 20 = 70e^(-kt);  at t = 10, T = 60: 40 = 70e^(-10k)
e^(-10k) = 4/7  ->  k = ln(7/4)/10 = 0.0560
at t = 25: T = 20 + 70e^(-1.4) = 20 + 17.3 = 37.3 deg C

Log-linear graphs

If a relationship is exponential, plotting ln y against x gives a straight line whose gradient and intercept reveal the constants. This is how experimental data is tested for exponential behaviour.

y = a b^x  ->  ln y = ln a + x ln b
gradient = ln b;  intercept = ln a
y = a x^n  ->  ln y = ln a + n ln x  (log-log plot)
gradient = n;  intercept = ln a

Worked example. A graph of ln y against x is a straight line with gradient 0.4 and intercept 1.2. Find the relationship.

ln y = 1.2 + 0.4x
y = e^1.2 x e^(0.4x) = 3.32 e^(0.4x)
so a = 3.32 and the growth rate is 0.4 per unit x

Worked example 2 (power law). A log-log plot of y against x has gradient 2 and intercept 0.693; the intercept is ln a, so a = e^0.693 = 2.

ln y = 0.693 + 2 ln x  ->  y = 2x^2

Reducing other models to linear form

Some models are linearised by a different transformation. The technique is to rearrange into Y = mX + c and identify what to plot.

y = a/x + b  ->  plot y against 1/x: gradient a, intercept b
y = a e^(bx) ->  plot ln y against x
y = a x^n    ->  plot ln y against ln x

Worked example. Data fits y = p/x + q. What should be plotted on the axes, and how are p and q then found from the graph?

plot y (vertical) against 1/x (horizontal)
gradient = p, intercept = q

Inequalities and exact solutions

Worked example. Solve e^x > 10, giving an exact answer.

x > ln 10

Worked example 2. Solve ln(2x − 1) ≤ 3.

2x - 1 <= e^3 and 2x - 1 > 0
1/2 < x <= (e^3 + 1)/2 = 10.54

Both boundaries matter: the domain condition gives the strict lower bound, the inequality gives the upper one.

Exponentials in calculus: stationary points

Because e^x differentiates to itself, a product with a polynomial produces clean stationary-point questions.

Worked example. Find and classify the stationary point of y = x e^(−x).

product rule: dy/dx = e^(-x) - x e^(-x) = e^(-x)(1 - x)
stationary where 1 - x = 0  ->  x = 1, y = e^-1 = 0.368
second derivative: e^(-x)(x - 2); at x = 1 it is -e^-1 < 0
so (1, 0.368) is a maximum

Worked example 2. Find the minimum of y = e^x − 3x.

dy/dx = e^x - 3 = 0  ->  x = ln 3 = 1.099
y = 3 - 3 ln 3 = 3 - 3.296 = -0.296
second derivative e^x > 0, so it is a minimum

Worked example 3 (integration by recognition). Find ∫ x e^(x²) dx.

the derivative of e^(x^2) is 2x e^(x^2), so the integral is
(1/2)e^(x^2) + c

Comparing growth rates

Exponential growth eventually outpaces any polynomial. That statement is examinable as a comparison of gradients or of long-run behaviour.

Worked example. Show that for large x, e^x grows faster than x³ by comparing their ratio.

consider f(x) = e^x/x^3
as x -> infinity the ratio tends to infinity (exponential beats polynomial)
equivalently: differentiating repeatedly, e^x keeps its factor of e^x
while the polynomial loses a degree each time

Worked example 2 (doubling). A quantity grows as N = 50e^(0.08t). How long to double?

e^(0.08t) = 2  ->  t = ln 2/0.08 = 8.66 years

The doubling time depends only on k, not on the starting value: that is the signature of exponential growth and worth saying in the answer. Halving time behaves the same way, and for decay the ratio ln 2/|k| gives a half-life independent of the initial quantity — which is why radiocarbon dating works on any sample size.

Simultaneous exponential equations

Two exponential equations are solved by taking logs and then treating the result as a linear system in the unknowns.

Worked example. Solve 2^x 3^y = 12 and 2^y 3^x = 18.

take logs: x ln 2 + y ln 3 = ln 12
y ln 2 + x ln 3 = ln 18
rearrange the second: x ln 3 + y ln 2 = ln 18
solve the 2x2 system:
from the first: x = (ln 12 - y ln 3)/ln 2
substitute and simplify  ->  y = 1, x = 2

Worked example 2 (same base). Solve 9^x = 3^(x+2).

9^x = 3^(2x), so 2x = x + 2  ->  x = 2

With two unknowns the log step is compulsory, and the equations are linear in x and y after it; that structure is what makes the pair solvable.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Evaluate) Find ln(e³). Answer: 3.
  2. (Law) Simplify ln 12 − ln 3. Answer: ln 4.
  3. (Solve) Solve 3^(2x) = 81. Answer: 2x = 4 → x = 2.
  4. (Solve logs) Solve log₂(x) + log₂(x − 2) = 3. Answer: x(x − 2) = 8 → x = 4.
  5. (Differentiate) y = e^(2x) ln x. Use the product rule. Answer: 2e^(2x) ln x + e^(2x)/x.
  6. (Integrate) ∫ (1/(2x)) dx. Answer: ½ ln|2x| + c = ½ ln|x| + c′.
  7. (Model) A population is 200e^(0.03t). When does it reach 500? Answer: t = ln(2.5)/0.03 = 30.5.
  8. (Log-linear) ln y = 0.5x + 2. Find y. Answer: y = 7.39e^(0.5x).

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • log(a + b) treated as log a + log b: there is no such law; the sum cannot be split.
  • Domain ignored: ln of a non-positive number is undefined; reject roots that violate it and say so.
  • Differentiating e^(kx) as ke^x: the factor k multiplies the whole exponential.
  • Integrating 1/x as ln x without the modulus: use ln|x|, since the function is defined on both sides of zero.
  • Half-life sign: with decay k is negative, so half-life is ln 2/|k|; a negative time means the sign was mishandled.
  • Log-linear misread: the intercept is ln a, so a = e^(intercept), not the intercept itself.
  • Base 10 and base e mixed: convert with log_a x = ln x/ln a before combining.
  • Model without interpretation: state the meaning of k in context — a rate per year, per minute, per unit.

Quick revision: Database Systems

Computer Science — OL. limitations of file-based systems; relational concepts; SQL (SELECT, FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY, INNER JOIN, SUM, COUNT); DBMS features.

  • 1. File-based problems
  • 2. Relational concepts
  • 3. SQL
  • 4. DBMS features

How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

### Worked example A primary key uniquely identifies each row in a table. A foreign key stores a primary key from another table, which links the two. For Students (StudentID, Name) and Enrolments (EnrolmentID, StudentID, CourseID), StudentID is the foreign key in Enrolments. A query such as SELECT Name FROM Students WHERE Year = 11; returns only the matching rows. ### Check yourself Explain why a foreign key in Enrolments must match an existing StudentID in Students. Without this link, an enrolment could refer to a student who does not exist, which breaks referential integrity.

title: A Level Physics: Thermal Physics
content:
A Level Physics: Thermal Physics

Thermal physics is the accountancy of heat: what temperature really measures, how much energy it takes to change a substance's state, and how the invisible motion of billions of particles produces the pressure in a balloon. This note builds the whole subject from zero: thermal equilibrium and the temperature scales, specific heat capacity and specific latent heat with full calorimetry arithmetic, the mole and the equation of state, the kinetic theory that justifies it, and the first law of thermodynamics — the energy bookkeeping rule that governs engines, fridges and stars alike.

Thermal equilibrium

Heat flows from hotter to cooler bodies until no further net transfer occurs — that final state is thermal equilibrium, when both bodies are at the same temperature. The zeroth law of thermodynamics makes the logic precise: if A is in thermal equilibrium with B, and B with C, then A is in equilibrium with C — which is exactly why thermometers work (they reach equilibrium with the thing measured, and the reading transfers). The distinction examiners demand: temperature measures the average random kinetic energy per particle; heat is energy in transit because of a temperature difference. Objects do not contain heat — they contain internal energy.

Temperature scales

The Celsius scale is defined by two fixed points: the melting point of pure ice (0 °C) and the boiling point of pure water (100 °C) at standard pressure. The thermodynamic (Kelvin) scale starts at absolute zero — the temperature at which particles have minimum kinetic energy, −273.15 °C — and its unit, the kelvin, is the same size as the degree Celsius:

T (K) = theta (deg C) + 273        (273.15 exact; 273 usual in exams)
temperature change: Delta T in K = Delta theta in deg C

Every gas-law and kinetic-theory calculation demands kelvin; forgetting the conversion is the single commonest thermal error. A temperature change of 10 °C is a change of 10 K — only absolute values need converting.

Specific heat capacity

Heating a body raises its temperature; the energy needed depends on the substance's own reluctance to change temperature:

E = m c Delta theta        (or E = C Delta theta for a whole body)

E in J, m in kg, c in J kg-1 K-1 (specific heat capacity)
Delta theta in deg C or K (the same size)
C = m c = heat capacity of the object (J K-1)

The electrical method of measuring c is examinable as a practical: a heater of known power runs for a known time (E = Pt), the temperature rise is recorded, and losses are reduced with insulation and a lid; the graph of temperature against time is extrapolated back to the start to correct for losses during heating.

Worked example 1. A 2.0 kg aluminium block (c = 900 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) is heated from 20 °C to 80 °C by a 500 W heater. Find the energy needed and the minimum heating time.

E = m c Delta theta = 2.0 x 900 x 60 = 108 000 J = 108 kJ
t = E/P = 108 000/500 = 216 s = 3.6 minutes

Worked example 2 (mixing). 0.50 kg of water at 90 °C is mixed with 0.50 kg of water at 10 °C. Find the final temperature (no losses).

heat lost = heat gained
m c (90 - T) = m c (T - 10)   (same m and c cancel)
90 - T = T - 10 -> 100 = 2T -> T = 50 deg C

The mixing equation is worth learning as a shape: Σ(heat lost) = Σ(heat gained), with each term mcΔθ evaluated from its own temperature difference to the final T.

Specific latent heat

During a change of state, energy goes into breaking intermolecular bonds rather than raising temperature — the heating curve flatlines at the melting or boiling point. The energy for the change:

E = m L        L = specific latent heat (J kg-1)

L_fusion for melting/freezing; L_vaporisation for boiling/condensing

Worked example. A 3.0 kW kettle boils 1.5 kg of water already at 100 °C. How long to boil it dry (L_vap = 2.26 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹)?

E = m L = 1.5 x 2.26 x 10^6 = 3.39 x 10^6 J
t = E/P = 3.39 x 10^6/3000 = 1130 s = 18.8 minutes

Reading a heating curve is a standard question: sloped sections are temperature rise (mcΔθ applies), flat sections are change of state (mL applies), and the flat at 0 °C is melting while the flat at 100 °C is boiling.

The mole

The mole counts particles the way a dozen counts eggs: one mole contains exactly Nₐ = 6.02 × 10²³ particles (Avogadro's constant). The molar mass M is the mass of one mole (numerically the relative atomic mass in grams; in kg mol⁻¹ for calculations).

n = m / M        N = n N_A

n in mol, m in kg (or g consistently with M), M in kg mol-1

Worked example. Find the number of molecules in 8.0 g of oxygen (O₂, M = 0.032 kg mol⁻¹).

n = m/M = 0.008/0.032 = 0.25 mol
N = n N_A = 0.25 x 6.02 x 10^23 = 1.505 x 10^23 molecules
  = 1.5 x 10^23 (2 s.f.)

The equation of state

For a fixed mass of an ideal gas, pressure, volume and temperature obey one master equation:

p V = n R T        (also p V = N k T)

p in pascals (Pa), V in m3, T in kelvin (K)
R = 8.31 J K-1 mol-1  (molar gas constant)
k = 1.38 x 10-23 J K-1 (Boltzmann constant), N = number of molecules

Unit discipline: 1 atm = 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa; 1 cm³ = 10⁻⁶ m³; 1 litre = 10⁻³ m³. The ideal-gas assumptions are examinable: molecules are point particles with negligible volume, intermolecular forces are negligible except during collisions, and collisions are perfectly elastic.

Worked example. 0.40 mol of gas occupies 2.0 × 10⁻³ m³ at 27 °C. Find the pressure.

T = 27 + 273 = 300 K
p = nRT/V = (0.40 x 8.31 x 300)/(2.0 x 10^-3)
  = 997.2/2.0 x 10^-3 = 4.99 x 10^5 Pa = 5.0 x 10^5 Pa (2 s.f.)

Boyle's, Charles's and the pressure law are all slices of this one equation — if a question gives a change at constant moles, either hold one variable fixed to get the simple law, or write p₁V₁/T₁ = p₂V₂/T₂ for the general case.

Kinetic theory

The kinetic model explains pressure: gas molecules collide elastically with container walls, and each collision transfers momentum; billions per second give a steady average force per unit area — pressure. The model's assumptions (large number of molecules, random motion, elastic collisions, negligible molecular volume, forces only during collisions) justify the ideal-gas behaviour, and the theory links the microscopic to the macroscopic:

p V = (1/3) N m c^2        c = root-mean-square speed

mean kinetic energy per molecule = (3/2) k T
so (1/2) m c^2 = (3/2) k T  ->  c = sqrt(3 k T / m)

The rms speed rises with the square root of absolute temperature and falls with molecular mass — hydrogen molecules move faster than oxygen molecules at the same temperature.

Worked example. Find the rms speed of helium atoms (m = 6.6 × 10⁻²⁷ kg) at 300 K.

c = sqrt(3 k T/m) = sqrt(3 x 1.38 x 10^-23 x 300/6.6 x 10^-27)
  = sqrt(1.242 x 10^-20/6.6 x 10^-27) = sqrt(1.88 x 10^6)
  = 1372 m s-1  (2 s.f.: 1.4 x 10^3 m s-1)

Internal energy

The internal energy of a substance is the sum of the random kinetic energies of its particles plus the potential energies of their interactions. For an ideal gas (no intermolecular forces) internal energy is purely kinetic and proportional to absolute temperature; for real substances, melting and boiling raise internal energy because potential energy increases as bonds stretch and break. State the split precisely in definitions: internal energy = total random kinetic energy + total intermolecular potential energy.

The first law of thermodynamics

Energy is conserved: the change in a system's internal energy equals the heat added to it plus the work done on it.

Delta U = Q + W

Delta U = change in internal energy (J)
Q = heat energy transferred to the system (J), negative if lost
W = work done ON the system (J), negative if the system does work
    (for a gas: W = -p Delta V under the convention W = work done
     on the system; expanding gas does work, so W is negative)

The sign convention must match your course's — state it in words when you apply the law. Applications the papers love: compressing a gas quickly (W positive, little Q, so ΔU and temperature rise); a gas expanding slowly at constant temperature (ΔU = 0 for an ideal gas, so Q = −W — heat flows in to supply the work done); and refrigerators (work is done to move heat against its natural flow).

Worked example. A gas is compressed so that 500 J of work is done on it while 200 J of heat flows out. Find ΔU and state the temperature change.

W = +500 J (done on the system), Q = -200 J (lost)
Delta U = Q + W = -200 + 500 = +300 J
internal energy rises -> temperature rises (for an ideal gas)

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Definitions) Distinguish between temperature and internal energy. Answer: Temperature is proportional to the mean random kinetic energy per molecule; internal energy is the total random kinetic energy plus the intermolecular potential energy of all the particles.
  2. (Kelvin) Convert 27 °C to kelvin and state absolute zero in °C. Answer: T = 27 + 273 = 300 K; absolute zero = −273 °C (−273.15 °C exactly).
  3. (Specific heat) 0.15 kg of a metal at 100 °C is dropped into 0.25 kg of water at 15 °C; the final temperature is 22 °C. Find the metal's specific heat capacity (c_water = 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹). Answer: heat gained by water = 0.25 × 4200 × 7 = 7350 J; metal lost = 0.15 × c × 78 = 7350 → c = 7350/(0.15 × 78) = 628 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ ≈ 630 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.
  4. (Latent heat) Explain why the temperature of boiling water stays constant. Answer: The energy supplied breaks intermolecular bonds during the change of state instead of raising the average kinetic energy of the molecules, so the temperature is unchanged until all the liquid has vaporised.
  5. (Equation of state) 2.0 g of helium (M = 4.0 g mol⁻¹) occupies 0.012 m³ at 300 K. Find the pressure. Answer: n = 2.0/4.0 = 0.50 mol; p = nRT/V = (0.50 × 8.31 × 300)/0.012 = 103 875 Pa ≈ 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa.
  6. (Kinetic theory) State two assumptions of the kinetic model and explain why doubling absolute temperature changes rms speed the way it does. Answer: Molecules are point particles with negligible volume; collisions are perfectly elastic; intermolecular forces are negligible except during collisions (any two). Since c = √(3kT/m), doubling T multiplies c by √2 — speed depends on the square root of absolute temperature.
  7. (First law) A gas expands, doing 300 J of work, while 100 J of heat is supplied. Find ΔU. Answer: W = −300 J (work done by the system), Q = +100 J; ΔU = 100 − 300 = −200 J — internal energy falls and the gas cools.
  8. (Practical) Describe how to determine the specific heat capacity of a metal block electrically. Answer: Place a known-power heater in the block, insulate it, record temperature against time as the heater runs; energy input E = Pt; plot temperature vs time and use the gradient (with m and the extrapolated zero-time temperature) to find c from E = mcΔθ; extrapolating back corrects for heat lost during the experiment.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Celsius in gas laws: pV = nRT demands kelvin. A gas-law calculation with 300 °C is wrong by 273 K at the first step.
  • Δθ in specific heat: E = mcΔθ uses a temperature change; questions giving start and end temperatures need the difference, not a raw value.
  • Latent vs specific heat: during a change of state use mL, not mcΔθ; on a heating curve the flat sections are where Δθ = 0.
  • Molar mass units: grams versus kilograms must match the mass unit in n = m/M; the equation of state with R = 8.31 needs moles and SI units throughout.
  • Pressure units: kPa and atm into Pa, cm³ into m³, before substitution.
  • Internal energy wording: it includes potential energy for real substances; defining it as kinetic only is wrong outside ideal gases.
  • First-law signs: pick a convention and state it — work done on the system is positive in ΔU = Q + W; expanding gas does work on the surroundings (negative W).
  • rms speed vs mean speed: the c in pV = ⅓Nmc² is the root-mean-square speed; it is not the average of speeds (which is smaller).
  • Precision and method: 2 or 3 s.f. with units (J, Pa, K, mol, m s⁻¹); write the formula line before numbers — the physics formulae are credit in their own right.

title: Database Systems — Quick Revision Summary

Quick revision: Database Systems

Computer Science — OL. limitations of file-based systems; relational concepts; SQL (SELECT, FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY, INNER JOIN, SUM, COUNT); DBMS features.

  • 1. File-based problems
  • 2. Relational concepts
  • 3. SQL
  • 4. DBMS features

How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

### Worked example A primary key uniquely identifies each row in a table. A foreign key stores a primary key from another table, which links the two. For Students (StudentID, Name) and Enrolments (EnrolmentID, StudentID, CourseID), StudentID is the foreign key in Enrolments. A query such as SELECT Name FROM Students WHERE Year = 11; returns only the matching rows.

Key points to remember

A database stores data in tables made of rows (records) and columns (fields). Each table has a primary key that uniquely identifies each record, and a foreign key links a record to a related table. Normalisation removes repeated data so that each fact is stored once, which reduces errors when data changes.

In SQL, SELECT chooses the fields, FROM names the table and WHERE sets the condition. Use the exact keywords the syllabus names, and write the condition with a comparison operator such as = or >. A query question is usually answered by writing one clear SELECT statement with the correct table and condition.

title: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Statistics and Data Handling
content:
Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Statistics and Data Handling

Statistics is the art of describing a pile of numbers with a few well-chosen ones: an average to say where the middle lies, a spread to say how tightly the data cluster, and a chart to make the shape visible. The IGCSE questions test exactly that pipeline — classify the data, compute the averages and spread, draw or read the chart, and compare two distributions. This note builds the whole subject from zero: the data types, every average and measure of spread with the frequency-table method, the standard charts, cumulative frequency curves, and histograms with unequal class widths.

Classifying statistical data

TypeMeaningExamples
Qualitative (categorical)describes a quality, not a numberfavourite colour, blood group
Quantitativemeasured or counted as a numberheight, number of siblings
Discretecountable, separate values (usually integers)number of children, shoe size
Continuouscan take any value in a range (measured)height, time, mass

The classification decides which charts and averages are legal: a mode for categorical data, a median for ordered data, class intervals for continuous data. Discrete data are plotted as bar charts with gaps; continuous data as histograms with no gaps (and frequency density on the vertical axis).

Averages and range

mean = sum of values / number of values
median = middle value when ordered (mean of the two middle
         values for an even count)
mode = most frequent value (or class); none if no repeats
range = largest - smallest

quartiles: Q1 = lower quartile (25%), Q3 = upper quartile (75%)
interquartile range (IQR) = Q3 - Q1  (spread of the middle 50%)

The mean uses every value (sensitive to outliers); the median ignores extreme values (robust); the mode is the only average available for categorical data. When comparing two data sets, quote an average and a spread: "school A has a higher median but a larger IQR, so its results are higher on average but less consistent."

Worked example. Find the mean, median, mode and range of: 4, 7, 7, 9, 12, 15, 18.

mean = (4+7+7+9+12+15+18)/7 = 72/7 = 10.3 (3 s.f.)
median = 4th value = 9
mode = 7 (appears twice)
range = 18 - 4 = 14

Worked example 2 (even count). Find the median of 3, 5, 8, 10, 12, 15.

even count: average the 3rd and 4th values
median = (8 + 10)/2 = 9

Averages from frequency tables

mean = sum of (value x frequency) / sum of frequencies
median = the value at position (n + 1)/2 in cumulative order
mode = the value with the highest frequency

Worked example. The table shows goals scored: 0 (5 players), 1 (8), 2 (6), 3 (2). Find the mean and the median.

total players = 5 + 8 + 6 + 2 = 21
total goals = 0x5 + 1x8 + 2x6 + 3x2 = 0 + 8 + 12 + 6 = 26
mean = 26/21 = 1.24 (3 s.f.)
median position = (21 + 1)/2 = 11th value
cumulative: 5 (0 goals), 13 (1 goal) - the 11th value is 1
median = 1

For grouped data, use midpoints: the mean = Σ(midpoint × frequency)/Σfrequency, and the median comes from the cumulative frequency curve (below). The grouped mean is an estimate because the midpoint stands in for every value in the class.

Charts and diagrams

  • Bar chart: bars with gaps for categorical or discrete data; height = frequency.
  • Pie chart: angle = (frequency/total) × 360°; label the sectors with the category.
  • Pictogram: a symbol represents a fixed number; a half symbol represents half that number.
  • Stem-and-leaf: a sorted display that keeps the actual values; the key explains the split (e.g. 3|4 means 34).
  • Frequency polygon: plot frequency against the midpoint of each class and join with straight lines.

Worked example (pie chart). 40 students choose a sport: football 16, tennis 10, swimming 8, other 6. Find the angle for football.

angle = (16/40) x 360 = 144 deg

Worked example 2 (pie chart reverse). A sector of 72° represents 9 students. How many students in total?

72 deg represents 9  ->  360 deg represents 9 x 360/72 = 45 students

Cumulative frequency diagrams

A cumulative frequency table adds frequencies as you move up the classes. Plot cumulative frequency against the upper class boundary and join with a smooth curve; then read positions:

median at n/2
lower quartile at n/4
upper quartile at 3n/4
IQR = Q3 - Q1

Worked example. A cumulative frequency curve for 60 students' marks: Q1 = 42, median = 55, Q3 = 68. Find the IQR and interpret it.

IQR = 68 - 42 = 26 marks
The middle 50% of students scored within 26 marks of each other;

Always read across to the curve and then down to the horizontal axis — and use the class boundaries, not the midpoints, for the plot positions.

Histograms and frequency density

When class widths differ, the height of a bar cannot be the frequency — a wide class would dominate unfairly. Instead, the area of each bar is proportional to the frequency:

frequency density = frequency / class width
frequency = frequency density x class width (area of the bar)

Worked example. Class 0–10 has frequency 20; 10–20 has frequency 30; 20–40 has frequency 40. Find the frequency densities.

0-10: 20/10 = 2.0
10-20: 30/10 = 3.0
20-40: 40/20 = 2.0

Reading a histogram backwards is the standard question: measure a bar's width and height, multiply to get the frequency, and read the class from the horizontal axis. Remember that the axes often use class boundaries, so a bar from 20 to 40 covers width 20.

Stem-and-leaf diagrams and frequency polygons

A stem-and-leaf diagram sorts data while keeping every value visible: the stem is the leading digit and the leaf the final digit, with a key such as 3|4 meaning 34. Interpreting one means reading the ordered leaves to find the median, the quartiles and the shape: the median is the middle leaf, Q1 and Q3 sit at the quarter and three-quarter positions, and the distribution's skew shows in where the leaves bunch.

A frequency polygon plots frequency against the midpoint of each class and joins the points with straight lines; it is the grouped-data equivalent of a line graph and makes comparisons between two distributions easy (plot both polygons on the same axes).

Worked example. The leaves for stem 4 are 1, 3, 3, 6, 8 and for stem 5 are 0, 2, 5. List the data in order and find the median.

values: 41, 43, 43, 46, 48, 50, 52, 55
n = 8, so the median is the mean of the 4th and 5th values:
(46 + 48)/2 = 47

Worked example 2 (interpreting). Explain what a long right-hand tail of leaves in a stem-and-leaf diagram indicates.

A long right tail means a few unusually high values: the data
are positively skewed, and the mean will be greater than the
median because the high values pull it upward.

Comparing distributions

Comparison questions want two statements: one about the average (which is higher) and one about the spread (which is more consistent). Use median and IQR together — they are robust to outliers — or mean and standard deviation when the data are symmetric and the syllabus supplies it.

Worked example. Class A: median 62, IQR 18. Class B: median 58, IQR 9. Compare.

Class A has the higher typical score (median 62 vs 58), but its
results are more spread out (IQR 18 vs 9), so Class B is more
consistent even though its middle score is lower.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Averages) Find the mean and range of 12, 15, 11, 19, 13. Answer: mean = 70/5 = 14; range = 19 − 11 = 8.
  2. (Frequency table) Values 1, 2, 3 with frequencies 4, 7, 9. Find the mean. Answer: (4 + 14 + 27)/20 = 45/20 = 2.25.
  3. (Median) Find the median of 2, 4, 4, 6, 9, 10. Answer: (4 + 6)/2 = 5.
  4. (Pie chart) A sector of 90° represents 15 people. Find the total. Answer: 15 × 360/90 = 60.
  5. (Cumulative frequency) For 80 values, where do you read the median? Answer: At cumulative frequency 40, reading across to the curve and down to the axis.
  6. (Histogram) A bar of width 5 has frequency density 4. Find its frequency. Answer: 5 × 4 = 20.
  7. (Frequency density) Class 30–50 has frequency 24. Find the frequency density. Answer: 24/20 = 1.2.
  8. (Compare) Two runners' times: A median 42 s, IQR 3 s; B median 40 s, IQR 8 s. Compare. Answer: B is faster typically (lower median) but less consistent (larger IQR); A is more reliable.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Median without ordering: the median is the middle of the ordered list. Forgetting to sort is the commonest data-handling error.
  • Even-count median: average the two middle values; do not pick one of them.
  • Grouped mean: use midpoints and label the answer an estimate — the midpoint is not the actual mean of the class.
  • Histogram heights: the vertical axis is frequency density, not frequency; area is the frequency. Reading the height as the frequency is the classic histogram error.
  • Cumulative frequency positions: plot against upper class boundaries and read the median at n/2 (not (n+1)/2 on the graph).
  • Pie chart arithmetic: check that the angles sum to 360° before answering the next part.
  • IQR direction: IQR = upper − lower quartile; a negative IQR means the quartiles are swapped.
  • Comparison claims: quote actual values ("median 62 vs 58"), not "better" without evidence.

title: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Bearings, Constructions and Loci
content:
Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Bearings, Constructions and Loci

Bearings are how navigators describe direction, and geometrical constructions are how geometers draw exact figures with only a ruler and a pair of compasses. Together they fill the practical geometry questions on both papers: a bearing calculated from a diagram, a locus sketched and shaded, a perpendicular bisector constructed and justified. This note builds the topic from zero: the three rules of bearings and the back-bearing calculation, the compass-and-ruler constructions with their standard arcs, scale drawings and their measurements, and the four loci the syllabus requires, with every step shown.

Bearings: the three rules

A bearing is a direction written as a three-figure angle. Three rules define it:

  1. Measured from North (the north line, drawn as an upward arrow).
  2. Clockwise.
  3. Written with three figures — 035°, 090°, 245° (never 35° or 9°).

Bearings are always between 000° and 360°; a direction due east is 090°, due south 180°, due west 270°.

Worked example. A ship sails from A on a bearing of 060° for 12 km to B, then on a bearing of 150° for 8 km to C. Describe the position of C relative to A qualitatively.

060 ° is between north and east; 150 ° is between east and
south. So C lies south-east of A, and the two legs turn 90 °
(150 - 60 = 90) - the path is two perpendicular legs, making a
right angle at B.

Back bearings

The bearing of A from B is not the bearing of B from A — they differ by 180° (add if under 180°, subtract if 180° or more):

back bearing = bearing + 180  (if bearing < 180)
             = bearing - 180  (if bearing >= 180)

Worked example. The bearing of B from A is 072°. Find the bearing of A from B.

72 + 180 = 252 °

Worked example 2 (three-figure check). The bearing of P from Q is 310°. Find the bearing of Q from P.

310 - 180 = 130 °

Bearings with trigonometry

Bearing problems become right-triangle problems once you draw the north lines and mark the angles between the path and north. Use Pythagoras for distances and trigonometry for angles, then convert the angle into a bearing.

Worked example. A boat sails 5 km due north, then 12 km due east. Find its distance and bearing from the start.

distance = √(5² + 12²) = √(169) = 13 km
angle east of north: tan(θ) = 12/5  →  θ = 67.4 °
bearing = 067 ° (to the nearest degree)

Worked example 2 (reverse). A helicopter is 9 km from base on a bearing of 145°. How far east and how far south of the base is it?

angle from south = 180 - 145 = 35 °
east = 9 sin(35) = 5.16 km
south = 9 cos(35) = 7.37 km

Constructions: ruler and compasses only

Constructions are marked on the accuracy of the arcs and the visibility of the construction lines. Keep your compasses sharp and do not rub out the arcs.

ConstructionStandard method (in order)
Perpendicular bisector of ABcompasses wider than half AB: arc from A, same-radius arc from B, both sides; join the two intersections
Angle bisectorarc across both arms from the vertex; same-radius arcs from those two crossings; join the vertex to their intersection
Perpendicular from a point to a linearc from the point cutting the line twice; equal arcs from those cuts; join the point to their intersection
Perpendicular at a point on a lineequal arcs either side of the point; then the perpendicular-bisector method between them
60° anglearc from the endpoint across the line; same radius arc from the crossing; join
Triangle given SSSdraw the base; arcs of the other two lengths from each end; join the intersection

Worked example. Construct the perpendicular bisector of a segment AB of length 8 cm and explain why every point on it is equidistant from A and B.

Construction: arcs of radius > 4 cm from A and from B, above and
below the segment; the two intersections join to form the bisector.
Why: the arcs are circles of equal radius centred at A and B, so
their intersection points are equidistant from A and B; the line
through them is the locus of all such points.

Scale drawings

A scale drawing represents a real situation to a ratio: 1 : 50 000 means 1 cm on paper represents 50 000 cm in reality (0.5 km). The method: convert the scale to a usable unit, measure or construct to scale, then read back with the reverse conversion.

Worked example. A map has scale 1 : 25 000. Two towns are 6.4 cm apart on the map. Find the real distance in km.

6.4 cm x 25 000 = 160 000 cm
160 000 cm = 1600 m = 1.6 km

Worked example 2 (drawing). A field is 400 m by 250 m. Draw it at scale 1 : 5000. What are the drawing dimensions?

400 m = 40 000 cm; /5000 = 8 cm
250 m = 25 000 cm; /5000 = 5 cm
The drawing is 8 cm by 5 cm.

Loci

A locus is the set of all points satisfying a condition. Four standard loci are examinable, and each has its construction:

  • Fixed distance from a point: a circle (arc) of that radius, centred on the point.
  • Equidistant from two points: the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining them.
  • Equidistant from two lines: the angle bisector(s) of the angle between them.
  • Fixed distance from a line: two parallel lines at that distance, one on each side (with semicircular ends for a segment).

Region questions combine loci: "shade the region closer to A than B and within 3 cm of C" means intersect the perpendicular bisector's half-plane with the circle's interior.

Worked example. A goat is tethered to a corner of a 6 m by 4 m shed with a 5 m rope. Describe the region it can reach.

A three-quarter circle of radius 5 m around the corner, minus
the part blocked by the shed: the rope wraps the shed's⁴ m and
6 m walls. The reachable region is the quarter circle of radius
5 m outside the shed plus smaller arcs where the rope wraps
(radius 1 m around the far 4 m corner, no reach around the far
6 m corner since 5 - 6 < 0).

Worked examples: bearings and loci together

Worked example. Two radio transmitters A and B are 10 km apart, with B due east of A. A signal is received equally strongly at points equidistant from A and B, and within 6 km of A. Describe the region.

Equidistant from A and B: the perpendicular bisector of AB - a
north-south line 5 km east of A.
Within 6 km of A: a circle of radius 6 km centred at A.
The region is the part of the circle on one side of the bisector:
a circular segment of radius 6 km, cut by the line 5 km from A.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Bearing definition) State the three rules for a bearing. Answer: Measured from north, clockwise, written as three figures.
  2. (Back bearing) The bearing of X from Y is 128°. Find the bearing of Y from X. Answer: a back bearing reverses direction, so add 180° when the bearing is below 180°: 128° + 180° = 308° (if the bearing exceeds 180°, subtract 180° instead).
  3. (Calculation) A plane flies 30 km north then 40 km east. Find its distance from the start and its bearing. Answer: distance = √(900 + 1600) = 50 km; tan θ = 40/30 → θ = 53.1°, bearing 053°.
  4. (Components) A ship is 15 km from port on a bearing of 210°. Find its distance west of the port. Answer: angle from south = 210 − 180 = 30°; west = 15 sin 30 = 7.5 km.
  5. (Construction) Describe how to construct the perpendicular bisector of a 6 cm segment. Answer: set the compasses to more than half the segment — more than 3 cm — and draw arcs from each end both above and below it; the two crossings of the arcs give the points the bisector passes through, so join them, and every point on that line is equidistant from both ends.
  6. (Locus) Describe the locus of points equidistant from the sides of an angle. Answer: The angle bisector — every point on it is the same perpendicular distance from both arms.
  7. (Scale) On a 1 : 20 000 map, a lake is 3.5 cm long. Find its real length in km. Answer: 3.5 × 20 000 = 70 000 cm = 0.7 km.
  8. (Region) Shade the region inside a triangle that is closer to side AB than to side AC and within 2 cm of vertex A. Answer: closer to AB than to AC means the half-plane on AB's side of the angle bisector of angle A, and within 2 cm of A means inside the circle of radius 2 cm centred on A; the shaded region is the intersection of those two, bounded by the bisector and the compass arc.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Two-figure bearings: 35° must be written 035°. Three figures, always.
  • Measuring from the wrong north: bearings start at north, not east. A bearing of 090° is east, not north.
  • Back-bearing addition: add 180 if the bearing is below 180, subtract if above; the result must stay between 000 and 360.
  • Anticlockwise angles: bearing questions are clockwise; a clockwise angle and its anticlockwise partner sum to 360.
  • Rubbing out construction arcs: the arcs are the evidence. Leave them visible and use a sharp pencil.
  • Locus shading: shade the region, not the boundary line; the question usually says "shade the region".
  • Scale unit slips: convert the real measurement to the same unit as the drawing before applying the ratio, and remember 1 km = 100 000 cm.
  • Diagram not to scale: measure only when told to; otherwise calculate. A protractor reading on a "not to scale" diagram earns nothing.

Bearings drawn properly: clockwise from north, three digits, always

A bearing is not an angle inside a triangle — it is a direction on the page, and almost every lost mark on this topic comes from measuring it from the wrong place or turning the wrong way. One drawing fixes the idea for good.

The three rules, in the order they bite. A bearing is measured from the north line at the point you are leaving, it turns clockwise, and it is written with three digits (060°, not 60°, and 025° rather than 25°). The third rule is not fussiness: 070° and 007° are different directions, and the leading zeros are how a reader tells them apart.

The back bearing is the return journey. If B is on a bearing of 060° from A, then A is on a bearing of 240° from B:

back bearing = bearing + 180° (or − 180° if the result would exceed 360°) Key: both are the same line measured from opposite ends. Adding 180° cannot go wrong; subtracting can, so add and then subtract 360° if necessary. For 060°: 60 + 180 = 240°. For 300°: 300 + 180 = 480, and 480 − 360 = 120°.

Worked example. A ship sails 12 km from port P on a bearing of 060°, then 9 km on a bearing of 150°. How far is it from P, and on what bearing?

Draw the two legs nose-to-tail. The turn between them is 150 − 60 = 90°, so the two legs are perpendicular and the distance closes as a right-angled triangle:
distance = √(12² + 9²) = √(144 + 81) = √225 = 15 km

The overall bearing is the angle from north to the closing line, which needs the angle at P inside the triangle: tan θ = 9 / 12, so θ = 36.9°, and the bearing is 60 − 36.9 = 023.1° on the far side — which is why the sketch, not the arithmetic, decides between adding and subtracting. Candidates who skip the sketch get 15 km and then guess the direction.

Where marks are lost. Measuring anticlockwise (bearing 060 becomes the 300° direction). Measuring from the horizontal or from another bearing rather than from north. Writing two digits. And finding the distance with a scale drawing but then reading the bearing off the wrong vertex — the bearing of A from B is not the bearing of B from A, and the question always says which.

title:
Membranes, Proteins, DNA and Gene Expression — AS Level Biology

This revision note belongs to the Edexcel International Advanced Subsidiary (IAS) Biology specification, WBI12 Unit 1, Topic 2 Membranes, Proteins, DNA and Gene Expression. It covers membrane structure and properties, osmosis and the different kinds of membrane transport, the structure of proteins and how they are built from amino acids, the structure of DNA and RNA and how DNA replicates, the genetic code and how genes work, transcription and translation, mutations and their effects, patterns of inheritance including sex linkage, cystic fibrosis as an example of a gene mutation in humans, and genetic screening and its ethical and social issues. Every statement the topic is responsible for is covered in its own section or paragraph.

1. Cell membranes and the fluid mosaic model

The cell surface membrane (plasma membrane) is a phospholipid bilayer; each phospholipid has a hydrophilic head and two hydrophobic tails, and the heads face out and in while the tails face each other, making a barrier to charged and water-soluble substances. The fluid mosaic model is the accepted interpretation: the membrane is fluid — the phospholipids and proteins can move laterally in the layer — and mosaic because it contains a variety of proteins embedded in or attached to the bilayer, including channel proteins and carrier proteins for transport, receptor proteins for signalling, and proteins for cell recognition. The model is an interpretation of data — it was built from evidence such as electron micrographs and the ability of membranes to fuse and to self-seal — and it explains the structure and properties of cell membranes and how they control what enters and leaves the cell. Cholesterol in the membrane reduces fluidity at high temperatures and prevents the membrane from becoming too rigid at low temperatures.

2. Core Practical 3 — investigating membrane properties

Investigate membrane properties including the effect of alcohol and of temperature on membrane permeability. A typical method uses beetroot cylinders, which contain the red pigment betalain in their vacuoles; as the membrane is damaged, pigment leaks out and the colour of the surrounding solution deepens. Cut cylinders to the same length, wash off surface pigment in distilled water, then place them in water at a range of temperatures or in different concentrations of alcohol for a fixed time, remove the tissue and measure the concentration of pigment in the solution with a colorimeter. As temperature rises or alcohol concentration rises, the membrane proteins denature and the lipid bilayer is disrupted, so permeability increases and more pigment leaks out; a control at room temperature or in distilled water shows the baseline. Record the colorimeter reading for each tube, plot a graph of permeability against temperature or against alcohol concentration, and explain the trend in terms of the effect on membrane proteins and lipids.

3. Osmosis and how water moves across membranes

Osmosis is the net movement of free water molecules through a partially permeable membrane, down a water potential gradient — from higher water potential to lower water potential. Water potential is the tendency of water to move; adding a solute lowers it, so a concentrated solution has a more negative water potential than a dilute one, and pure water has the highest (zero) water potential. If a cell is placed in a solution of higher water potential than its contents, water enters by osmosis and the cell swells; if it is an animal cell it may burst (haemolysis); if it is a plant cell the cell wall prevents bursting and the cell becomes turgid, which supports the plant. In a solution of lower water potential, water leaves and the cell shrinks — animal cells crenate and plant cells become plasmolysed, with the membrane pulling away from the wall. A recommended additional practical is to investigate tissue water potentials using plant tissue (for example potato or onion epidermis) and graded concentrations of a solute: place tissue in solutions of different molarity, note the change in length or mass, and find the concentration at which there is no change — that concentration has the same water potential as the tissue.

4. Passive transport, active transport, endocytosis and exocytosis

Passive transport needs no energy input because substances move down their concentration gradient. Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to one of lower concentration; small, non-polar molecules such as oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse directly through the phospholipid bilayer, while ions and large polar molecules cannot. Facilitated diffusion is the movement of specific particles down their concentration gradient through channel proteins or carrier proteins — channel proteins form water-filled pores for ions, and carrier proteins change shape to carry molecules across. Active transport moves substances against their concentration gradient (from low to high concentration) and needs energy directly from ATP; carrier proteins use ATP to pump substances across, as in the sodium–potassium pump. Endocytosis is the bulk movement of material into the cell inside a vesicle formed from the plasma membrane; phagocytosis takes in solid material and pinocytosis takes in fluid. Exocytosis is the reverse — material is moved out of the cell in a vesicle that fuses with the plasma membrane, as in the secretion of proteins and neurotransmitters. Carrier and channel proteins are involved in facilitated diffusion and active transport; the key difference is that active transport needs ATP and moves substances against their gradient.

5. Protein structure: from amino acid to three-dimensional shape

Amino acids are the monomers of proteins; the basic structure of an amino acid is an amino group, a carboxyl group and a variable R group all attached to a central carbon, with a hydrogen on the remaining bond. There are around 20 amino acids found in proteins, differing only in their R group, and the sequence of amino acids in a protein is its primary structure. Amino acids join by condensation reactions to form peptide bonds, making dipeptides and then polypeptides; a polypeptide chain is a protein's primary structure and it determines everything about the protein. The secondary structure is the local folding of the chain into alpha-helices and beta-pleated sheets, held by hydrogen bonds between the peptide bonds. The tertiary structure is the overall three-dimensional folding of the whole polypeptide, held by hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, disulfide bonds and hydrophobic interactions; it gives the protein its specific shape and therefore its function. Globular proteins are roughly spherical and usually soluble and active — haemoglobin is the classic example, with four polypeptide chains and a haem group each carrying one oxygen molecule, and it shows quaternary structure (several polypeptides together) plus the importance of the three-dimensional shape for its oxygen-carrying function. Fibrous proteins are long, insoluble and structural — collagen is the example, made of three polypeptide chains wound into a rope-like triple helix, giving strength for tendons, ligaments and skin. The shape of a protein determines its function, so a change to the primary structure can alter the folding and disable the protein.

6. DNA structure and replication

A DNA molecule is made of two nucleotide strands twisted into a double helix. Each nucleotide is made of a deoxyribose sugar, a phosphate group and a base — either adenine (A), cytosine (C), guanine (G) or thymine (T). The two strands run antiparallel and are linked by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases — A pairs with T (two hydrogen bonds) and C pairs with G (three hydrogen bonds). RNA is similar but has ribose instead of deoxyribose, uracil instead of thymine, and is usually single-stranded. The two strands are complementary, so knowing one strand tells you the other, and the two strands separate at replication. DNA replication is semi-conservative: the double helix unzips, each strand acts as a template, and free nucleotides pair with their complementary bases; DNA polymerase joins the nucleotides into a new strand. The result is two identical DNA molecules, each with one old strand and one new strand. Meselson and Stahl's experiment supported this: they grew bacteria in a medium with a heavy isotope of nitrogen (15N), then moved them to a 14N medium and examined the DNA by centrifugation; the first generation was a single hybrid band (not one heavy and one light, which would be conservative replication), and later generations showed a mixture of hybrid and light bands — exactly what semi-conservative replication predicts and ruling out the conservative and dispersive alternatives.

7. The genetic code and how it works

The genetic code is the set of rules translating the base sequence of mRNA into the amino acid sequence of a protein. It is a triplet code — three bases (a base triplet on DNA, a codon on mRNA) code for one amino acid; it is non-overlapping — each base is read once in order; and it is degenerate — more than one codon can code for the same amino acid, which is why many mutations change a base but not the amino acid. Part of the code is a stop codon that signals the end of translation; there is no amino acid for it. A gene is a sequence of bases on a DNA molecule that codes for a sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide chain. In transcription, the gene is copied into a complementary mRNA molecule by the enzyme RNA polymerase, using the DNA template (antisense) strand; the mRNA is complementary to the template strand and the same as the coding (sense) strand except with uracil in place of thymine. mRNA leaves the nucleus and attaches to ribosomes in the cytoplasm; transfer RNA (tRNA) molecules carry amino acids to the ribosome, each with a three-base anticodon that pairs with the mRNA codon, so the ribosome joins the amino acids into a polypeptide chain in the order of the codons until a stop codon is reached.

8. Mutations: the changes and their effects

A mutation is a change in the DNA base sequence. A substitution replaces one base with another — it may do nothing, change one amino acid, or, rarely, create a stop codon that shortens the protein. An insertion adds one or more bases and a deletion removes one or more; because the code is read in triplets, an insertion or deletion not in a multiple of three causes a frameshift, changing every amino acid after the mutation and usually destroying the protein's function. Mutations are the only source of new alleles, and most have no observable effect — they may be in non-coding DNA, or a degenerate codon and amino acid may stay the same, or the changed protein still folds and works. Some mutations give rise to cancer (if they affect control of the cell cycle) or to genetic disorders. Ionising radiation such as X-rays and ultraviolet light, and some chemicals such as those in tobacco smoke, can increase the rate of mutation by damaging DNA.

9. Patterns of inheritance: monohybrid crosses, pedigree diagrams and sex linkage

A gene can have different alleles; the genotype is the alleles an organism has, the phenotype is the observable feature. Dominant alleles show in the phenotype even when heterozygous; recessive alleles only show when homozygous. A monohybrid cross is the inheritance of one gene with two alleles; the typical ratios are a 3:1 phenotype ratio in the F2 of a monohybrid cross between two heterozygotes, but only if the alleles are completely dominant and the gene is autosomal. Sex linkage is the inheritance of a gene on the X chromosome — because males have only one X, a recessive allele on it shows in their phenotype even though they are effectively hemizygous; red-green colour blindness and haemophilia are human X-linked conditions that are more common in males. Pedigree diagrams record which family members show a trait and are used to work out whether a trait is dominant or recessive and whether it is autosomal or sex-linked. Codominance is when both alleles are expressed in the heterozygote, as in the ABO blood group system where IA and IB are codominant and i is recessive, giving the four blood groups A, B, AB and O.

10. Cystic fibrosis: a mutation that affects three systems

Cystic fibrosis is caused by a mutation in a gene that codes for a chloride ion channel protein; in the most common form a deletion of three bases removes a single amino acid from the protein, so the channel does not work properly. As a result, chloride ions and water cannot move properly across cell membranes, and the mucus and other secretions become abnormally thick. In the gaseous exchange system the thick mucus blocks the airways and makes it hard to breathe and to clear infections; in the digestive system the pancreatic duct is blocked so digestive enzymes from the pancreas cannot reach the gut, so food is not digested and absorbed properly, and the person may be malnourished; in the reproductive system the vas deferens is often absent or blocked in males, causing infertility. Treatments include physiotherapy and antibiotics for the lungs, and enzyme supplements with meals for digestion, and newer treatments aim to correct the underlying defect.

11. Genetic screening: what it can do and the issues it raises

Genetic screening can identify carriers of recessive alleles (people who have one normal allele and one faulty allele and are unaffected but could pass the allele on), and prenatal testing can check a fetus: amniocentesis takes a sample of amniotic fluid at around 15–17 weeks, and chorionic villus sampling takes a sample of placental tissue at 8–12 weeks. Pre-implantation genetic diagnosis is used with IVF to test embryos before implantation and select unaffected ones. Each raises ethical and social questions — the safety and reliability of the test, the risks of miscarriage with invasive prenatal testing, the right to know or not to know, who decides which conditions to test for, the possible choice to terminate a pregnancy, anxiety and guilt, and the risk that screening could be used to select non-medical traits. Students should be able to identify and discuss these from religious, moral and social viewpoints and to evaluate the implications of prenatal genetic screening.

12. How to use this note and what to revise next

Use these notes by working through each section and checking that you can draw a cell membrane from the fluid mosaic model and label the phospholipid bilayer, the proteins, cholesterol and glycoproteins; state the difference between diffusion, facilitated diffusion and active transport, and give an example of each; outline the steps of DNA extraction (a simple practical with strawberries or onions is useful to remember); and carry out a genetic cross with a Punnett square and interpret the ratios. Revise by drawing protein structure from amino acid to tertiary, then drawing the DNA double helix and explaining semi-conservative replication and the Meselson–Stahl evidence. After this topic, revise Topic 3 Cell structure, reproduction and development, because the same DNA and protein-synthesis processes control cell differentiation and the cell cycle.
