title: AS Level Mathematics: Measures of Variation and Standard Deviation
content:
AS Level Mathematics: Measures of Variation and Standard Deviation

Two data sets can share a mean and behave completely differently: one tightly clustered, one wildly spread. Measures of variation quantify that difference. This note builds the topic from zero: the range and interquartile range, the variance and standard deviation with the full calculation from first principles, the frequency-table and coded forms, outliers, and how to compare distributions fairly. Every formula is derived once, because the derivation is what makes it stick.

Why spread matters

Location alone is a half-description. A machine filling 500 g bags with a standard deviation of 2 g is trustworthy; one with a standard deviation of 30 g is not, though both may average 500 g. Spread measures consistency, risk and reliability, and every comparison question rewards naming both a location and a spread.

Range and interquartile range

range = largest - smallest
interquartile range IQR = Q3 - Q1
semi-interquartile range = (Q3 - Q1)/2
MeasureUsesWeakness
RangeOnly the two extremesDestroyed by one outlier
IQRThe middle halfIgnores the tails entirely
Standard deviationEvery valueDragged by outliers; more arithmetic

Worked example. Find the range, IQR and semi-IQR of 12, 15, 18, 21, 25, 30, 44.

range = 44 - 12 = 32
n = 7; median = 21; Q1 = 15; Q3 = 30
IQR = 15;  semi-IQR = 7.5

The 44 stretches the range to 32 while leaving the IQR untouched: exactly the robustness the IQR is chosen for.

Variance and standard deviation defined

variance = mean of the squared deviations from the mean
standard deviation = √(variance)

population form:  σ² = (sum of (x - mu)²)/n
sample form:      s² = (sum of (x - xbar)²)/(n - 1)

Why square the deviations? Signed deviations always sum to zero, so they cannot measure spread; squaring removes the signs and penalises large gaps heavily. The square root returns the answer to the original units, which is why standard deviation, not variance, is quoted in context.

Worked example (full working). Find the standard deviation of 4, 7, 9, 10, 10.

mean = 40/5 = 8
deviations: -4, -1, 1, 2, 2
squares: 16, 1, 1, 4, 4  →  sum 26
variance = 26/5 = 5.2
standard deviation = √(5.2) = 2.28

The computational formula

σ² = (sum of x²)/n - (mean)²

this is algebraically identical to the deviation form but far quicker

Worked example. Repeat the previous calculation with the computational form.

sum x = 40;  mean = 8
sum x² = 16 + 49 + 81 + 100 + 100 = 346
variance = 346/5 - 64 = 69.2 - 64 = 5.2
standard deviation = 2.28  (identical, as it must be)

Frequency tables

mean = (sum of f x)/(sum of f)
variance = (sum of f x²)/(sum of f) - (mean)²

Worked example. Find the mean and standard deviation of the distribution x: 1, 2, 3, 4 with frequencies 2, 5, 8, 5.

sum f = 20
sum fx = 2(1) + 5(2) + 8(3) + 5(4) = 2 + 10 + 24 + 20 = 56  →  mean 2.8
sum fx² = 2(1) + 5(4) + 8(9) + 5(16) = 2 + 20 + 72 + 80 = 174
variance = 174/20 - 7.84 = 8.7 - 7.84 = 0.86
standard deviation = 0.927

For grouped data the midpoint stands in for each class, so the standard deviation is an estimate, like the grouped mean.

Worked example 2 (grouped). Estimate the standard deviation of 0–10 (3), 10–20 (7), 20–30 (10).

midpoints 5, 15, 25;  sum f = 20
sum fx = 15 + 105 + 250 = 370  →  mean 18.5
sum fx² = 3(25) + 7(225) + 10(625) = 75 + 1575 + 6250 = 7900
variance = 7900/20 - 342.25 = 395 - 342.25 = 52.75
standard deviation = 7.26

Coding and the effect on spread

if y = (x - a)/b then:
  mean(y) = (mean(x) - a)/b
  sd(y) = sd(x)/|b|
  variance(y) = variance(x)/b²

shifts (a) do not change spread; scaling (b) scales it

Worked example. The coded values y = (x − 100)/5 have mean 4 and standard deviation 1.2. Find the mean and standard deviation of x.

mean x = 5(4) + 100 = 120
sd x = 5(1.2) = 6

The intuition: adding a constant slides the whole distribution without stretching it; multiplying stretches every gap by the same factor.

Outliers

lower fence = Q1 - 1.5 IQR
upper fence = Q3 + 1.5 IQR
values beyond the fences are outliers

Worked example. With Q1 = 20, Q3 = 32 and a maximum of 60, is 60 an outlier?

IQR = 12; upper fence = 32 + 18 = 50
60 > 50, so yes, 60 is an outlier

Outliers are not automatically errors: they may be genuine extreme values, which is why the median and IQR often summarise skewed data better than the mean and standard deviation.

Comparing distributions properly

A full comparison answers four points: which has the higher typical value, which is more spread, whether either has outliers, and what that means in context.

Worked example. Boys: mean 62, sd 8. Girls: mean 68, sd 4. Compare.

girls have the higher typical mark (68 vs 62)
girls are more consistent (sd 4 vs 8; roughly half the spread)
boys' marks are more widely dispersed, so their range of performance
is broader; the sd ratio 2 suggests boys' marks vary twice as much
about their mean

Never compare standard deviations of data measured in different units or on different scales without converting; here both are marks, so the comparison is valid.

Standard deviation in context

Worked example (quality control). A machine fills bags with mean 500 g and sd 3 g. Assuming a roughly symmetric distribution, about what proportion lies within one standard deviation of the mean?

one sd either side: 497 to 503 g
for a roughly normal shape, about 68 per cent of bags fall in this band
(and about 95 per cent within two sds: 494 to 506 g)

The 68/95/99.7 guide is approximate and only valid for roughly bell-shaped data; stating that condition is part of the answer.

Comparing spread across different units

Standard deviations cannot be compared directly when the scales differ. The coefficient of variation puts them on a common footing by expressing the spread as a fraction of the mean:

coefficient of variation = 100 x sd/mean  (per cent)

A: mean 50 kg, sd 4 kg   →  CV = 8 per cent
B: mean 8000 pounds, sd 400 pounds  →  CV = 5 per cent
B is relatively more consistent despite the larger absolute sd

Worked example. Two athletes' times over a season: A has mean 12.0 s, sd 0.15 s; B has mean 60.0 s, sd 0.60 s (different events). Which is more consistent relative to their event?

CV(A) = 0.15/12.0 × 10⁰ = 1.25 per cent
CV(B) = 0.60/60.0 × 10⁰ = 1.00 per cent
B is relatively more consistent, even though the absolute sd is 4 times larger

Without the coefficient of variation, the comparison would favour A for the wrong reason. State the units and the ratio when answering.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Range) Find the range of 3, 8, 12, 15, 22. Answer: 19.
  2. (IQR) Find the IQR of 5, 6, 9, 11, 14, 18. Answer: Q1 = 6.75, Q3 = 15, IQR = 8.25.
  3. (SD) Find the standard deviation of 2, 4, 4, 6, 9. Answer: mean 5; deviations −3, −1, −1, 1, 4; squares 9, 1, 1, 1, 16 = 28; variance 5.6; sd 2.37.
  4. (Computational) For sum x = 60, sum x² = 800, n = 10, find the sd. Answer: variance = 80 − 36 = 44; sd = 6.63.
  5. (Frequency) x: 0, 1, 2 with f: 4, 3, 3. Find the mean. Answer: 9/10 = 0.9.
  6. (Coding) y = (x − 20)/4 has sd 2.5. Find the sd of x. Answer: 10.
  7. (Outlier) Q1 = 12, Q3 = 20, maximum 45. Is 45 an outlier? Answer: IQR = 8, fence = 32; yes.
  8. (Compare) A: mean 40, sd 5. B: mean 40, sd 12. What differs? Answer: same centre, different spread; B is far more variable.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Forgetting to root: the variance is in squared units; the standard deviation is its square root. Quoting the variance as the sd is a units error.
  • Dividing by n or n − 1: use the convention the question implies; for a population divide by n, for a sample estimate divide by n − 1. Mixing them shifts the answer.
  • Deviation sign errors: the deviations must sum to zero — if they do not, the mean was copied wrongly.
  • Coding with the wrong operation: sd divides by |b|, never subtracts a; shifts do not affect spread.
  • Comparing different units: an sd of 5 marks and an sd of 5 kg are not comparable; convert or use the coefficient of variation.
  • Outlier fences: 1.5 × IQR beyond the quartiles, not beyond the range or the median.
  • Grouped estimates: call them estimates and note that midpoints are assumed uniform within each class.
  • One-sided comparison: a comparison naming only the mean earns half the marks; always add the spread and its interpretation.

Formula summary

range = max - min;  IQR = Q3 - Q1
variance = (sum of x²)/n - (mean)²
standard deviation = √(variance)
coded: mean(x) = b mean(y) + a;  sd(x) = |b| sd(y)
CV = 100 sd/mean

Learn the computational variance form rather than the deviation form: it needs one pass for the sum and one for the sum of squares, and it fails loudly when the mean is wrong because the deviations then do not sum to zero.

title: IGCSE Biology: Biological Molecules
content:
IGCSE Biology: Biological Molecules

Your body is a chemical machine, and the machine runs on four families of large molecules: carbohydrates for fuel and structure, lipids for membranes and long-term energy stores, proteins for everything from muscles to enzymes to antibodies, and nucleic acids (DNA) for information. This note takes each family from its smallest building block to its full structure and function, defines every bond by name, explains the food tests you will perform in Paper 6, and expands the DNA double helix base-by-base. By the end you should be able to look at any food test result or structural diagram and derive the reasoning rather than memorise it.

Elements, small molecules and large molecules

Life is built mainly from carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen (plus smaller amounts of sulfur and phosphorus). Small molecules (glucose, amino acids, fatty acids, nucleotides) join end-to-end to form large molecules (starch, protein, lipid, DNA) in condensation reactions — one molecule of water is removed each time a bond forms. The reverse, splitting a molecule by adding water, is hydrolysis; every digestive enzyme in the body is named after the bond it hydrolyses. Learn the pairing now and it pays off twice: in this topic and again in human nutrition.

Carbohydrates: sugars, starch, glycogen, cellulose

Monosaccharides are single sugars: glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆) is the body's immediate fuel. Disaccharides are two sugars joined: maltose (glucose + glucose), sucrose (glucose + fructose) and lactose (glucose + galactose), each joined by a glycosidic bond formed in condensation. Polysaccharides are long chains: starch (the plant store, a mixture of amylose and amylopectin), glycogen (the animal store, highly branched, in liver and muscle) and cellulose (the plant structural fibre, straight chains that cross-link for strength). Starch is tested with iodine solution: yellow-brown turns blue-black. Function summary: sugars for transport and instant energy; starch and glycogen for storage; cellulose for cell walls.

Lipids: fats, oils and membranes

A lipid is built from one glycerol joined to three fatty acids by ester bonds (three condensation reactions, three water molecules removed). Saturated lipids have no carbon-carbon double bonds in the tails (straight, pack tightly, solid at room temperature — animal fats); unsaturated lipids have one or more double bonds (kinks in the tails, loose packing, liquid — plant oils). Lipids store twice the energy per gram of carbohydrates, form waterproof layers, insulate (blubber, subcutaneous fat), protect organs, and make up the phospholipid bilayer of every cell membrane. The test for lipids is the ethanol emulsion test: dissolve the sample in ethanol, then add water — a milky-white emulsion means lipid present.

Proteins: amino acids to polypeptides

A protein is one or more polypeptide chains folded into a specific 3-D shape. Each amino acid has the same backbone — a central carbon with an amino group (–NH₂), a carboxyl group (–COOH), a hydrogen and a variable R group. In a condensation reaction the –NH₂ of one amino acid reacts with the –COOH of the next, releasing water and forming a peptide bond; repeat it and you have a polypeptide. The sequence of R groups (the primary structure) dictates how the chain folds (secondary and tertiary structure), and that fold dictates function: haemoglobin's shape cradles iron to carry oxygen; enzymes' active sites fit one substrate; antibodies' variable regions fit one antigen; keratin's coil makes hair and nails. The biuret test detects peptide bonds: add biuret solution (sodium hydroxide then copper(II) sulfate) — blue turns to purple if protein is present.

Enzymes as biological molecules (see the Enzymes note for the full kinetics)

Enzymes are globular proteins that act as biological catalysts: they speed reactions without being used up by lowering activation energy. Their active site is a specific-shaped pocket formed by the tertiary structure; only a substrate with a complementary shape fits (the induced-fit model shows the site flexing slightly as the substrate binds). Digestive enzymes hydrolyse their named bonds: carbohydrases (amylase) break glycosidic bonds in starch; proteases (pepsin, trypsin) break peptide bonds in proteins; lipases break ester bonds in lipids. Naming rule: the suffix –ase is an enzyme, the suffix –ose is a sugar, and the stem names the substrate.

Water and mineral ions — the small molecules that matter

Water is the biological solvent for a reason: its molecules are polar (slightly negative oxygen, slightly positive hydrogens), so they surround and dissolve ions and polar molecules, forming the cytoplasm, blood plasma and tissue fluid. Water's high specific heat capacity buffers temperature swings; its high latent heat of vaporisation makes sweating and transpiration effective coolers; its cohesion (hydrogen bonding between molecules) helps the water column in xylem; and it is a reactant in photosynthesis and hydrolysis. Mineral ions have named roles worth memorising: iron for haemoglobin, calcium for bones and clotting and muscle contraction, sodium for nerve impulses, phosphate for DNA and ATP, nitrate for amino acids and chlorophyll in plants, magnesium for chlorophyll, potassium for stomatal opening.

The four food tests at a glance

MoleculeTest reagentPositive resultTechnique note
StarchIodine solutionYellow-brown to blue-blackAdd the solution to the food on a white tile
Reducing sugarBenedict's solutionBlue to brick-red precipitateMust be heated in a water bath; green or orange for lower amounts
ProteinBiuret (sodium hydroxide then copper(II) sulfate)Blue to purpleDo not heat
LipidEthanol then waterWhite milky emulsionShake the sample with ethanol first, then add water

Worked example: the food-test decision tree and one full calculation

A student tests a mystery food for starch, reducing sugars, protein and lipid. Result log: iodine stays orange-brown; Benedict's solution turns from blue to brick-red after heating; biuret turns purple; the emulsion test gives no white cloud. Reading it step by step: iodine unchanged means no starch (the only positive is blue-black). Benedict's brick-red after heating means a reducing sugar is present (glucose gives the strongest red; moderate heat gives yellow-green). Biuret purple means peptide bonds, so protein is present. No emulsion means no lipid. Conclusion: a protein-rich food containing glucose — egg white with sugar, for instance. Now a calculation you can be asked to do with any of these: a 10 g food sample releases 2.5 kJ when burnt under a calorimeter that heated 50 g of water by 12 °C. Energy released = mass of water × specific heat capacity × temperature change = 50 g × 4.2 J/g°C × 12 °C = 2520 J = 2.52 kJ. Because 1 g of lipid yields about 38 kJ and 1 g of carbohydrate about 17 kJ, a high energy per gram means a fatty food.

DNA: the information molecule

DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) is a polymer of nucleotides. Each nucleotide has three parts: a deoxyribose sugar, a phosphate group, and one of four organic bases — adenine (A), thymine (T), cytosine (C), guanine (G). The nucleotides form a long chain by phosphodiester bonds between the sugar of one and the phosphate of the next (one sugar-phosphate backbone on each strand). Two strands then twist into a double helix, held by hydrogen bonds between complementary base pairs: A–T (two hydrogen bonds) and C–G (three hydrogen bonds). The pairing rule is strict and examinable: A only ever bonds with T, C only ever with G. Genes are short sections of DNA whose base sequence codes for the amino acid sequence of a protein; chromosomes are long DNA molecules wound around proteins; a gene is to a chromosome as one sentence is to a book.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Confusing "condensation" with "digestion": condensation builds polymers; digestion (hydrolysis) breaks them; every digestive enzyme performs hydrolysis.
  • Writing the Benedict's result as "turns red" without heating: the test must be heated (water bath), or it scores nothing.
  • Calling a protein's shape "its secondary structure" when the question wants "tertiary structure, which determines the active site".
  • Mixing up the base pairing: writing A–C or G–T in a DNA question is an instant lost mark.
  • Describing iodine for starch as turning "brown to black" — the required wording is "yellow-brown to blue-black".
  • Saying lipids "give more energy because they are bigger" — they store more per gram because their tails are more reduced (more C–H bonds).
  • In Paper 6, omitting the control (a known positive and negative sample) in a food-test plan; examiners award a mark for "compare with a known sample".
  • Writing "DNA is a protein": DNA is a nucleic acid; it is made of nucleotides, not amino acids.

Exam-style questions and answers

Q1. Describe how you would test a food sample for reducing sugar. (3 marks) Answer: dissolve or crush the sample in water and filter (1); add Benedict's solution and heat in a water bath (1); a brick-red (or orange/green) precipitate confirms reducing sugar (1).

Q2. Explain how a change in an amino acid sequence can change an enzyme's function. (3 marks) Answer: the sequence determines the tertiary fold (1); a different R group alters the shape or charge of the active site (1); so the substrate no longer fits and the rate of reaction falls (1).

Q3. State the two base-pairing rules in DNA and the number of hydrogen bonds in each. (2 marks) Answer: A–T with two hydrogen bonds; C–G with three hydrogen bonds (1 per pair).

Q4. Explain why lipids are better energy stores than carbohydrates. (2 marks) Answer: lipid tails contain more carbon-hydrogen bonds per gram so more energy is released per gram on oxidation (1); and they are insoluble so they do not affect water potential in cells (1).

Q5. Describe the role of water in living organisms. (3 marks) Answer: solvent for transport in blood and cytoplasm (1); high specific heat capacity buffers temperature (1); reactant in photosynthesis and hydrolysis, and cohesion aids water movement in xylem (1).

title: A Level Mathematics: Vectors
content:
A Level Mathematics: Vectors

A vector is a quantity with both size and direction, and the whole subject is the algebra of arrows. The idea feels abstract until you notice you already use it: a displacement of three miles north-east is a vector, the wind reported as 20 km/h from the west is a vector, and the instruction to walk to a point is a vector. This note builds vectors from components, shows how to add and scale them, then uses the scalar product to measure the angle between two directions — the tool that turns vector algebra into geometry.

What a vector is, and what it is not

A scalar has size alone. A vector has size and direction, and two vectors are equal only if both match. That is why a vector is written with an arrow or in bold, and why reversing the arrow changes the vector into its negative even though the length is unchanged.

vector a has magnitude |a| and direction
-a has the same magnitude, opposite direction
the zero vector 0 has no direction and magnitude 0
a unit vector has magnitude 1 and gives a direction

The distinction matters in mechanics: displacement and velocity are vectors, distance and speed are scalars, and mixing them up is how answers acquire impossible units. A direction given as a bearing is the same information in a different costume, and converting between a compass bearing and a pair of components is a routine exam step.

Components and magnitude

In two dimensions a vector is written as a column of its two components, one per axis. The house convention in this course writes a column vector as (x; y), the first component horizontal and the second vertical.

a = (3; 4)
magnitude |a| = √(3² + 4²) = 5
in three dimensions: a = (x; y; z), |a| = √(x² + y² + z²)

Worked example. Find the magnitude of (6; −8). Draw the reasoning, not just the answer.

|a| = √(36 + 64) = 10
the components form a right triangle with legs 6 and 8, so this is a 3-4-5 triangle scaled by 2

Worked example 2 (unit vector). Find the unit vector in the direction of (6; −8).

divide by the magnitude: (6/10; -8/10) = (0.6; -0.8)
check: 0.36 + 0.64 = 1

Worked example 3 (3-D). Find the magnitude of (2; −3; 6).

√(4 + 9 + 36) = √(49) = 7

Adding, subtracting and scaling

Addition is component by component, and geometrically it is the triangle law: place the tail of the second at the head of the first, and the sum runs from the first tail to the second head. Subtraction is addition of the negative, which gives the vector from one point to another.

a + b = (a1 + b1; a2 + b2)
a - b = (a1 - b1; a2 - b2)
k a = (k a1; k a2)  parallel to a, scaled by k

Worked example. a = (3; 1), b = (−1; 4). Find a + b, a − b and 2a − 3b.

a + b = (2; 5)
a - b = (4; -3)
2a = (6; 2);  3b = (-3; 12)
2a - 3b = (9; -10)

Worked example 2 (parallel condition). Show that (4; −6) and (−2; 3) are parallel.

(4; -6) = -2 x (-2; 3)
one is a scalar multiple of the other, so they are parallel (and antiparallel)

Position vectors and points on a line

A position vector locates a point relative to the origin. The vector from A to B is then the position vector of B minus that of A — a subtraction rule worth memorising because it fixes the direction of every later step.

position vectors a and b for points A and B:
vector AB = b - a
the midpoint of AB has position vector (a + b)/2
a point dividing AB in the ratio m:n has position (n a + m b)/(m + n)

Worked example. A has position vector (2; 1) and B has (8; 5). Find AB and the midpoint.

AB = (8 - 2; 5 - 1) = (6; 4)
midpoint = ((2+8)/2; (1+5)/2) = (5; 3)

Worked example 2 (section formula). P divides AB in the ratio 1:2. Find P.

P = (2a + 1b)/3 = ((4; 2) + (8; 5))/3 = (12; 7)/3 = (4; 2.333)

Worked example 3 (proving three points are collinear). Show that A(1, 1), B(3, 4) and C(7, 10) lie on a line.

AB = (2; 3)
AC = (6; 9) = 3 x (2; 3)
AC is a multiple of AB and they share A, so the three points are collinear

The scalar product

The scalar product (dot product) takes two vectors and returns a number. That number encodes the angle between them, which is why it is the single most useful operation in the topic.

a . b = a1 b1 + a2 b2  (+ a3 b3 in 3-D)
a . b = |a| |b| cos θ
so cos θ = (a . b)/(|a| |b|)

Worked example. Find the angle between a = (3; 4) and b = (5; 0).

a . b = 15 + 0 = 15
|a| = 5, |b| = 5
cos θ = 15/25 = 0.6  →  θ = 53.13 degrees

Worked example 2 (perpendicularity). Find k so that (2; k) is perpendicular to (3; −4).

perpendicular means a . b = 0
6 - 4k = 0  →  k = 1.5

Worked example 3 (3-D angle). Find the angle between (1; 2; 2) and (2; 1; 0).

a . b = 2 + 2 + 0 = 4
|a| = 3, |b| = sqrt 5 = 2.236
cos θ = 4/(3 × 2.236) = 0.596  →  θ = 53.4 degrees

Using vectors in geometry

Geometry proofs become short algebraic arguments once vectors are in play: parallelism is a scalar multiple, equal lengths are equal magnitudes, and a right angle is a zero scalar product. The discipline is to express everything in terms of two base vectors and then compare coefficients.

Geometric statementVector test
PQ is parallel to RSPQ = k RS for some scalar k
PQ has the same length as RS|PQ| = |RS|
angle PQR is a right angleQP . QR = 0
P, Q, R are collinearPQ = k PR

Worked example. In triangle OAB, M is the midpoint of OA and N is the midpoint of OB. Prove MN is parallel to AB.

let OA = a and OB = b
OM = a/2;  ON = b/2
MN = ON - OM = (b - a)/2
AB = b - a
so MN = AB/2: parallel and half the length

A common variant gives two vectors with unknown constants and requires a right angle or a given length. The routine is always the same: write the condition as an equation in the constants, solve it, then check that the solution satisfies any sign or magnitude restriction stated in the question. Two solutions usually appear because a squared length produces a quadratic.

Worked example 2 (right angle inside a shape). With a = (1; 2) and b = (3; −1), show that the diagonals of the parallelogram spanned by a and b are perpendicular.

diagonals are a + b and a - b
a + b = (4; 1);  a - b = (-2; 3)
dot product = -8 + 3 = -5, not zero
so they are not perpendicular - the test is the check, not an assumption

Velocity and displacement vectors

In mechanics, position is a vector function of time and velocity is its rate of change. Constant velocity makes the position a straight line, which is why relative-motion questions reduce to vector subtraction.

position r = r0 + v t
displacement over time t is v t
relative velocity of A with respect to B is vA - vB

Worked example. A boat has velocity (4; 3) m/s relative to the water and the current has velocity (−1; 2) m/s. Find the boat's velocity over the ground and its speed.

resultant = (4 - 1; 3 + 2) = (3; 5)
speed = √(9 + 25) = 5.83 m/s

Worked example 2 (intercept). A particle starts at (1; 2) with velocity (3; −1). Where is it after 4 seconds?

r = (1; 2) + 4(3; -1) = (1 + 12; 2 - 4) = (13; -2)

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Magnitude) Find |(5; −12)|. Answer: √(25 + 144) = 13.
  2. (Unit vector) Find the unit vector of (3; 4). Answer: (0.6; 0.8).
  3. (Addition) a = (2; −3), b = (−4; 1). Find 3a + b. Answer: (6 − 4; −9 + 1) = (2; −8).
  4. (Collinear) Are (1; 2), (4; 8) and (7; 14) collinear? Answer: yes, each step is a multiple of (3; 6).
  5. (Dot product) Find a . b for a = (1; 3), b = (4; −2). Answer: 4 − 6 = −2.
  6. (Angle) Find the angle between (1; 0) and (1; 1). Answer: cos θ = 1/√2, θ = 45°.
  7. (Perpendicular) Find k so (k; 6) is perpendicular to (3; −2). Answer: 3k − 12 = 0, k = 4.
  8. (3-D) Find |(1; 4; 8)|. Answer: √81 = 9.
  9. (Section) P divides AB in ratio 2:1, a = (0; 0), b = (6; 9). Find P. Answer: (2; 3).
  10. (Relative) Velocities (5; 1) and (2; 4). Find the relative velocity of the first with respect to the second. Answer: (3; −3).

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • AB versus BA: AB = b − a; reversing the subtraction gives the wrong direction and the wrong sign in every later step.
  • Magnitude of a sum: |a + b| is not |a| + |b| unless the vectors are parallel; compute the components first.
  • Scalar product sign: an obtuse angle gives a negative dot product, which is information, not an error.
  • Division by a vector: there is no vector division; rearrange using scalar multiples instead.
  • Collinearity without a shared point: parallel vectors alone do not make points collinear — say that they share a point.
  • Degrees and radians: the inverse cosine returns whatever mode the calculator is in; state the unit in the answer.
  • Missing the z component in 3-D: dot products and magnitudes need all three components, including zeros.
  • Arrow notation ignored in proofs: writing a length where a directed vector was needed destroys the argument even when the number is right.

title: A2 Level Biology: Coordination, Response and Gene Technology
content:
Coordination, Response and Gene Technology — A2 Level Biology

This revision note belongs to the Edexcel International A2 Biology specification, WBI15 Unit 5, Topic 8 Coordination, Response and Gene Technology. It covers the nervous system — sensory, relay and motor neurones, myelination and saltatory conduction, the action potential and its conduction along the axon, the spinal reflex arc, synapses and the role of neurotransmitters, how the pupil dilates and contracts, how drugs influence nerve impulse transmission (nicotine, lidocaine, cobra venom alpha toxin, L-DOPA and Parkinson’s disease, MDMA), how the retina detects light and forms action potentials in the optic neurones, habituation, the central and peripheral nervous systems, hormonal and nervous coordination, the structure and function of the brain (cerebral hemispheres, hypothalamus, pituitary gland, cerebellum, medulla oblongata), how MRI, fMRI, PET and CT are used in diagnosis and investigation of brain structure and function, how imbalances in brain chemicals contribute to ill health (dopamine in Parkinson’s disease, serotonin in depression) and to the development of new drugs, how drugs can be produced using genetically modified organisms, how recombinant DNA is produced and inserted into other cells, how microarrays identify active genes, what bioinformatics is, and the risks and benefits of genetically modified organisms. Every statement the topic is responsible for is covered in its own section or paragraph, with the material set so that a student can revise from it and check themselves against the specification.

1. Sensory, relay and motor neurones, Schwann cells and myelination

The nervous system has three main types of neurone, each with a structure suited to its function. Sensory neurones carry impulses from receptors to the central nervous system; their cell body is off to one side of the axon, halfway along it, and they have a long dendron that carries the impulse from the receptor to the cell body and a long axon that carries it into the CNS. Relay neurones connect sensory and motor neurones within the CNS; their cell body is in the centre of the neurone, and they have many short dendrites and a short axon. Motor neurones carry impulses from the CNS to effectors (muscles or glands); their cell body is in the CNS, and they have a long axon with many short dendrites. All neurones have a cell body containing the nucleus and many mitochondria (to supply ATP), dendrites that carry impulses towards the cell body, and an axon that carries impulses away from the cell body. Many axons are wrapped in Schwann cells, which wrap tightly around the axon in a fatty myelin sheath; the myelin sheath insulates the axon and speeds conduction. The gaps in the myelin sheath are called nodes of Ranvier. The structure of each neurone type reflects what it does — sensory neurones bring information in, relay neurones process it inside the CNS, and motor neurones carry the response out to effectors.

2. The nervous system and how it makes effectors respond to a stimulus

A stimulus is a change in the environment (internal or external) that is detected by a receptor. The receptor converts the stimulus into an electrical signal (a generator potential, then if it reaches threshold an action potential) in a sensory neurone. The impulse travels along the sensory neurone to the CNS, where it is passed to a relay neurone; the relay neurone may synapse with other relay neurones and process the information, then pass the impulse to a motor neurone, which carries it to an effector. The effector — a muscle or a gland — responds: a muscle contracts, or a gland secretes its product. This is the general pathway: stimulus → receptor → sensory neurone → CNS (relay neurone) → motor neurone → effector → response. The response is specific to the stimulus and to the circuitry involved, and rapid because electrical impulses travel fast along neurones.

3. The spinal reflex arc: grey matter, white matter and the withdrawal reflex

A reflex arc is the pathway of neurones that produces a rapid, involuntary response to a stimulus, without involving conscious control. In the spinal reflex arc, a sensory neurone from a receptor (for example in the skin) synapses with a relay neurone in the spinal cord, which in turn synapses with a motor neurone that runs to an effector (for example a muscle). The grey matter of the spinal cord is the inner, butterfly-shaped region where the cell bodies of relay and motor neurones and the synapses between them are found; the white matter is the outer region, made up of myelinated axons that carry impulses up and down the cord, to and from the brain. In the withdrawal reflex, for example touching a hot object, a pain receptor in the skin sends an impulse via a sensory neurone to a relay neurone in the spinal cord, which excites a motor neurone that makes the arm flex (biceps contracts, triceps relaxes) and withdraws from the stimulus. The response is rapid and automatic, and happens before the brain is even aware of the stimulus, because the arc involves only the spinal cord; this protects the body from harm.

4. The action potential: how an impulse is conducted along an axon

An action potential is the nerve impulse — a rapid, transient change in the membrane potential of a neurone, from about −70 mV (resting potential) up to about +40 mV and back, caused by the opening and closing of voltage-gated sodium and potassium ion channels. At rest the inside of the axon is negatively charged relative to the outside (the resting potential), mainly because sodium ions are pumped out and potassium ions are pumped in by the sodium–potassium pump, and the membrane is more permeable to potassium ions than to sodium ions at rest. When a stimulus depolarises the membrane to the threshold, voltage-gated sodium ion channels open, sodium ions flood in, the inside becomes positively charged (depolarisation, up to +40 mV). At about the peak, the sodium channels close and voltage-gated potassium channels open, potassium ions flood out, and the inside returns towards resting (repolarisation); it rises a little too far (hyperpolarisation) before returning to resting. The sodium–potassium pump then restores the resting ion distribution. The all-or-nothing principle applies: once threshold is reached, the action potential fires at full size; a stronger stimulus does not produce a bigger action potential, it produces more of them (greater frequency). During the absolute refractory period, the sodium channels are inactivated and no new action potential can be started, which ensures impulses travel one way and sets a maximum frequency.

5. Myelination and saltatory conduction: why some axons are faster

Myelination speeds up conduction of the action potential. In a myelinated axon the myelin sheath insulates the axon so that ions cannot cross the membrane where it is covered; the action potential can only be generated at the nodes of Ranvier, where the axon is bare. The impulse therefore jumps from node to node — saltatory conduction — and this is much faster than the continuous conduction along an unmyelinated axon, because the impulse does not have to depolarise every part of the membrane. The speed of conduction also depends on the diameter of the axon (larger axons conduct faster because there is less resistance to the flow of ions inside) and on the number of sodium channels and the extent of myelination; the fastest axons in the body are large and heavily myelinated.

6. Synapses: structure, transmission, acetylcholine, and the pupillary reflex

A synapse is the junction between two neurones (or between a neurone and an effector cell) across which the impulse is passed by a chemical neurotransmitter. At a cholinergic synapse, an action potential arriving at the presynaptic neurone opens voltage-gated calcium ion channels; calcium ions enter the presynaptic terminal, causing synaptic vesicles containing the neurotransmitter acetylcholine to fuse with the presynaptic membrane and release their contents by exocytosis into the synaptic cleft. Acetylcholine diffuses across the cleft and binds to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane, opening sodium ion channels so sodium ions enter and depolarise the postsynaptic membrane (this may start an action potential if the threshold is reached). Acetylcholinesterase in the cleft breaks down acetylcholine to stop the signal and recycle the choline. Drugs and toxins can affect the synapse: nicotine mimics acetylcholine and stimulates the postsynaptic receptor; lidocaine blocks voltage-gated sodium channels and stops impulse transmission (used as a local anaesthetic); cobra venom alpha toxin blocks acetylcholine receptors so the muscle cannot be stimulated (paralysis). Meanwhile, the pupil is controlled by two sets of muscles in the iris: circular muscles and radial muscles. In bright light, the parasympathetic nervous system makes the circular muscles of the iris contract, which constricts (makes smaller) the pupil, reducing the light entering the eye; in dim light, the radial muscles contract, dilating (widening) the pupil so more light enters.

7. Drugs and nerve impulse transmission: nicotine, lidocaine, cobra venom alpha toxin, L-DOPA, and MDMA

Many drugs act on the nervous system by influencing nerve impulse transmission. Nicotine stimulates nicotinic acetylcholine receptors in the brain, producing a temporary feeling of alertness and pleasure, and it is addictive because repeated use changes the brain’s reward pathways; it also raises blood pressure and heart rate, and is a carcinogen. Lidocaine is a local anaesthetic that blocks voltage-gated sodium ion channels in sensory neurones, preventing the formation and conduction of action potentials, so pain signals are not sent to the brain — it is used to numb a local area. Cobra venom alpha toxin binds to acetylcholine receptors on the muscle and blocks acetylcholine from binding, so the muscle cannot be stimulated and paralysis results, which can be fatal if the respiratory muscles are paralysed. L-DOPA is used to treat Parkinson’s disease; Parkinson’s is caused by a loss of dopamine-producing neurones in a part of the brain (the substantia nigra), so the level of dopamine falls and movement becomes impaired (tremor, stiffness, slow movement); L-DOPA is a precursor that can cross the blood–brain barrier and is converted to dopamine in the brain, restoring the level and easing the symptoms, at least for a time. MDMA (ecstasy) causes a large release of serotonin from presynaptic neurones and blocks its reuptake, so serotonin levels in the synapse rise sharply, producing a feeling of wellbeing and empathy, but the subsequent depletion of serotonin and damage to serotonin neurones can cause depression and memory problems, and repeated use is harmful.

8. Detecting light: the rod cell, rhodopsin, and how an action potential is generated in the optic neurone

Rods in the retina of mammals detect light and allow us to see in dim light. A rod cell contains the pigment rhodopsin, which is made of a protein (opsin) and a light-absorbing molecule (retinal, a derivative of vitamin A). When light hits rhodopsin, the retinal changes shape (from 11-cis to all-trans retinal), which changes the opsin and causes the rod cell to hyperpolarise — it becomes more negative inside. This hyperpolarisation closes sodium ion channels that are normally open in the dark, so sodium ion entry is reduced and the rod cell hyperpolarises; this in turn reduces the release of the neurotransmitter (glutamate) from the rod cell’s synaptic terminal. The change in transmitter release affects the bipolar neurone, which in turn affects the neurone that runs to the brain (the optic neurone); so the rod cell’s hyperpolarisation to light ultimately leads to action potentials in the optic neurone, which travel to the brain and are interpreted as vision. This is a relatively fine point — light does not itself produce the action potential in the rod, it changes the rod’s membrane potential, and that change is passed on through the retinal circuit to generate action potentials in the optic neurone. Cone cells work similarly but are responsible for colour vision and detail in bright light.

9. Habituation: what it is and how it is investigated

Habituation is a simple form of learning in which a response to a repeated, harmless stimulus decreases over time; the organism learns to ignore the stimulus because it has learned it is not important. For example, a snail initially withdraws into its shell when its shell is tapped, but with repeated tapping the withdrawal response becomes slower and eventually disappears — the snail has habituated to the tap. Habituation is not fatigue of the muscle (if a new stimulus, such as a poke to the body, still produces a strong response, the withdrawal machinery is fine) and not sensory adaptation (the receptor still responds to the stimulus), but a decrease in the synaptic transmission at the synapse between the sensory neurone and the motor neurone that produces the withdrawal. A recommended additional practical is to investigate habituation to a stimulus — for example using the snail withdrawal response, tapping the snail and recording the time to emerge or the frequency of withdrawal, and showing that with repeated harmless taps the response declines and that the decline is not due to muscle fatigue.

10. The central and peripheral nervous systems

The mammalian nervous system consists of the central nervous system (CNS) and the peripheral nervous system (PNS). The CNS is the brain and spinal cord; it integrates information and coordinates responses. The PNS is the network of nerves that connect the CNS to the rest of the body — to receptors and to effectors; it includes the sensory neurones that bring information to the CNS and the motor neurones that carry commands to effectors. The motor part of the PNS can be divided into the voluntary (somatic) nervous system, which controls skeletal muscles consciously, and the autonomic nervous system, which controls involuntary functions such as heart rate, gut movement and the pupils, and which is further divided into the sympathetic (which prepares the body for action — fight or flight) and parasympathetic (which promotes rest and digestion) nervous systems; these two often have opposite effects on the same organ.

11. Coordination in animals: nervous and hormonal control together

Animals coordinate their bodies by both nervous and hormonal control, and the two work together. The nervous system uses electrical impulses that travel fast along neurones and chemical signals (neurotransmitters) across synapses, giving rapid, short-lived responses targeted at specific effectors — good for rapid movements and reflexes. The hormonal system uses hormones carried in the blood, which travel more slowly and affect many cells at once, producing slower, longer-lasting, more widespread responses — good for things like growth, metabolism, reproduction and responding to stress over a longer time. In many situations they act together: for example, in the fight-or-flight response, the sympathetic nervous system acts quickly to increase heart rate, while the hormone adrenaline from the adrenal glands sustains and amplifies the response; in the control of blood glucose, hormones (insulin and glucagon) act more slowly and over longer periods than nervous control would allow. Plants coordinate only by hormones (plant growth substances such as auxin, gibberellin and phytochrome), because they have no nervous system.

12. The human brain: cerebral hemispheres, hypothalamus, pituitary gland, cerebellum, medulla oblongata

The brain controls and coordinates the activities of the body and is the seat of thought, memory and emotion. The cerebral hemispheres are the large, folded upper parts of the brain; they are responsible for higher functions — thought, memory, reasoning, conscious actions, language and sensation — and each hemisphere controls the opposite side of the body. The hypothalamus links the nervous and endocrine systems; it controls the pituitary gland, regulates body temperature, water balance, hunger and thirst, and the sleep cycle, and it plays a central role in homeostasis. The pituitary gland, under the influence of the hypothalamus, releases several hormones that control other endocrine glands and body functions — for example growth hormone, ADH and the hormones that regulate reproduction. The cerebellum is responsible for coordination of movement and balance — it makes sure movements are smooth and coordinated and posture is maintained. The medulla oblongata controls unconscious and automatic functions essential to life — breathing rate, heart rate and the reflex centres for coughing, sneezing and swallowing — and it is where the cardiovascular control centre and the ventilation (breathing) centre are located. Damage to different parts of the brain produces different deficits, and knowing the location and main functions makes it possible to link symptoms to brain regions.

13. Brain imaging: MRI, fMRI, PET and CT — what they show and how they are used

Different imaging techniques give different kinds of information about the brain. Computed tomography (CT) uses X-rays from many angles to produce a cross-sectional image of the brain’s structure; it is good at showing bone, bleeding and structural abnormalities, and it is quick and widely available, but it uses ionising radiation and gives limited soft-tissue contrast. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) uses a strong magnetic field and radio waves to give detailed images of soft tissue; it shows brain structure without ionising radiation and is excellent for detecting tumours, inflammation, demyelination and injury, but it takes longer and is noisy and claustrophobic for the patient. Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) is MRI adapted to show brain function — it detects changes in blood flow and oxygen use that accompany neural activity, so it can show which parts of the brain are active during a task; it has good spatial resolution but poor time resolution because the blood flow change lags the neural activity. Positron emission tomography (PET) uses a radioactive tracer (for example, a labelled glucose) injected into the patient; the tracer accumulates in active tissues and its radioactivity is detected, so PET can show brain activity and metabolism, and it can show neurotransmitter receptors and help in diagnosing and studying disorders such as Alzheimer’s and cancer, but it uses ionising radiation and is expensive. These techniques are used in medical diagnosis (for example to locate a tumour, or to investigate a stroke or a degenerative disease) and in research into brain structure and function — for example to see which areas are involved in a particular task or how activity differs in a disorder.

14. Brain chemicals and disease: dopamine in Parkinson’s disease, serotonin in depression, and new drugs

Imbalances in certain naturally-occurring brain chemicals can contribute to ill health, and understanding these has driven the development of new drugs. Parkinson’s disease is caused by the loss of neurones in the substantia nigra that produce dopamine, a neurotransmitter involved in controlling movement; the resulting dopamine deficiency causes tremor, stiffness, slowness of movement and balance problems. Treatment with L-DOPA (a precursor that crosses the blood–brain barrier and is converted to dopamine) can relieve symptoms, at least for a time, and other drugs may mimic dopamine or prevent its breakdown. Depression is associated with lower levels of the neurotransmitter serotonin (and also noradrenaline) in the brain; selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) block the reuptake of serotonin into the presynaptic neurone, so more serotonin stays in the synapse and helps improve mood, and they are widely used to treat depression and anxiety. New drugs can be developed using this understanding of the role of brain chemicals — for example by targeting the receptors or the synthesis or breakdown of a neurotransmitter — and knowledge of the cause of a disease (such as the dopamine deficiency in Parkinson’s) is what makes targeted treatment possible.

15. Producing drugs using genetically modified organisms

Drugs can be produced using genetically modified organisms (GMOs) — plants, animals and microorganisms. The best-known example is human insulin: the human gene for insulin is inserted into bacteria (usually E. coli) using a plasmid, and the bacteria are grown in large fermenters to produce human insulin, which is then extracted and purified. Human insulin made this way is identical to the insulin made in the human body, so it does not cause the immune reactions that some people had to the animal insulin formerly used. Other products made from GMOs include human growth hormone, clotting factor for haemophiliacs, and enzymes for washing powders; and modified plants and animals are being explored to produce vaccines and other pharmaceuticals. Using GMOs to produce drugs has advantages: the product can be made in large quantities, it can be made more cheaply than by extraction from animals or people, and it can be made identical to the human version. There are concerns, however — about the containment of the GMOs, the possibility of unintended effects, and the ethical questions of modifying organisms in this way.

16. Recombinant DNA: how it is produced (restriction enzymes and DNA ligase) and inserted into other cells

Recombinant DNA is DNA made by joining together pieces of DNA from different sources. Restriction endonucleases (restriction enzymes) cut DNA at specific base sequences, making cuts that can leave complementary ‘sticky ends’ — short single-stranded overhangs that can base-pair with each other — and these sticky ends allow a gene of interest to be joined to a vector (such as a plasmid) cut with the same enzyme. DNA ligase then seals the backbone of the sugar–phosphate chain, joining the gene to the vector to make recombinant DNA. To insert recombinant DNA into other cells, the vector (carrying the gene) is introduced into host cells: bacterial cells can take up plasmids in a process called transformation (which can be helped by making the bacteria competent — for example by calcium chloride treatment and a heat shock); viral vectors can be engineered to carry the gene into the cells they infect, using the virus’s natural ability to enter cells; and other methods such as microinjection or gene guns can put DNA directly into cells. Once inside, the host cell’s machinery may read and express the gene, making the protein it codes for (for example insulin), and if the vector also carries a gene for resistance to an antibiotic, only the cells that took up the vector will survive on antibiotic-containing medium — giving a way to select the transformed cells.

17. Microarrays: how they identify active genes

A microarray (DNA microarray) is a small slide or chip carrying thousands of known DNA sequences (probes), each in a known position. Messenger RNA is extracted from two samples (for example, a diseased tissue and a healthy tissue, or cells treated with a drug and untreated cells), converted to cDNA, and labelled with different coloured fluorescent tags (for example green for one sample and red for the other). The labelled cDNA is mixed and allowed to hybridise to the probes on the microarray: if a gene is active (expressed) in a sample, its cDNA will bind (hybridise) to the complementary probe on the chip. By scanning the chip, the colours and intensities can be read: a green spot means the gene is more active in the green-labelled sample, a red spot means more active in the red-labelled sample, yellow means similar activity in both, and the intensity reflects how active the gene is. By looking at all the spots, researchers can see which genes are active (turned on) or inactive (turned off) in a sample and compare activity between samples — for example to see which genes are active in a cancer cell that are not in a normal cell, or to see how a drug changes gene activity. This makes it possible to identify active genes and to use gene activity patterns for diagnosis and to understand disease and drug action.

18. Bioinformatics: what it is and what it is used for

Bioinformatics is the use of computer technology to collect, store, analyse and interpret biological data, especially large datasets such as DNA and protein sequences, gene expression data from microarrays, and protein structures. It depends on the availability of sequence data — the DNA sequences of genomes and the sequences of proteins — and on databases that store and organise these sequences so they can be compared and searched. Bioinformatics is used to compare sequences to find similarities and differences, to identify genes and their functions (for example by comparing a new sequence with known ones to suggest what it does), to study evolutionary relationships (by building phylogenetic trees from sequence comparisons), to predict the structure and function of proteins from their amino acid sequence, and to analyse gene expression patterns from microarrays. It depends on the work of the Human Genome Project and other sequencing projects, and on the computational tools that turn raw sequence data into useful biological knowledge. Bioinformatics is now part of nearly every area of biology — from identifying a gene, to understanding what it does, to finding targets for drugs, to tracing the evolution of a pathogen.

19. Risks and benefits of genetically modified organisms

Genetically modified organisms (GMOs) — plants, animals and microorganisms — have both benefits and risks. Benefits include: in agriculture, crops can be modified to resist pests (for example Bt crops that produce a bacterial toxin harmful to insect pests but not to people) or herbicides, to tolerate drought or salinity, to improve nutrition (for example golden rice producing beta-carotene, a vitamin A precursor), and to increase yield — which can support food security; in medicine, GM bacteria produce human insulin and other proteins for therapy; in research, GM animals and plants are used to study gene function and disease. Risks and concerns include: the possibility that the modified gene could spread to wild relatives or other organisms (gene flow) and have unintended effects; the potential harm to non-target organisms (for example whether Bt crops affect beneficial insects); the development of resistant pests or weeds; the concentration of control of food and seed in a few companies, and the effect on farmers and on traditional varieties; the long-term effects on ecosystems, which are not fully known; and the ethical questions about modifying organisms, especially animals, and about food that has been genetically modified. These must be weighed case by case: the benefits and risks of each GMO depend on what it is, how it is used, and how it is regulated. The scientific evidence about each GMO is needed to evaluate it properly, and the public has a legitimate role in the decisions because the issues are not only scientific — they include values, economics and the environment.

20. Plant responses: phytochrome, auxin, gibberellins and Core Practical 18

Plants coordinate responses without a nervous system, using pigments and hormones that change gene expression. Phytochrome is a pigment that exists in two interconvertible forms. Red light at about 660 nm converts the inactive form, Pr, into the active form, Pfr; far-red light at about 730 nm converts Pfr back to Pr, and in darkness Pfr slowly reverts. Because daylight is rich in red light, Pfr accumulates during the day, so the ratio of Pfr to Pr tells the plant whether it is in light or shade and how long the night is. Pfr acts as a transcription factor: it enters the nucleus and switches on genes, for example for germination in lettuce seeds or for flowering in long-day plants. A brief flash of red light is enough to trigger germination, and a flash of far-red light immediately afterwards cancels it, which is the classic experimental evidence that phytochrome is the receptor.

Auxin, principally indoleacetic acid or IAA, is made in the shoot tip and moves down the stem. It is transported polarly, from cell to cell, and it accumulates on the shaded side of a shoot in phototropism and on the lower side of a root or shoot in gravitropism. In the shoot, a higher auxin concentration stimulates cell elongation, so the shaded side grows faster and the shoot bends towards the light. In the root the same concentration inhibits elongation, which is why a root bends downwards. Auxin works by binding a receptor that triggers the destruction of repressor proteins, so transcription factors are released and genes for wall-loosening enzymes are transcribed, allowing the cell wall to stretch.

Gibberellins promote stem elongation, seed germination and the transition to flowering. In a germinating cereal grain the embryo releases gibberellin, which diffuses to the aleurone layer and switches on transcription of the gene for amylase. The amylase is secreted into the endosperm, where it hydrolyses starch to maltose, which the embryo respires. Core Practical 18 investigates exactly this: sterilise and soak cereal grains, place them on starch agar with and without gibberellin, leave them to incubate, then flood the plate with iodine solution. Clear zones around the treated grains show that amylase has broken down the starch, and measuring or comparing the zones shows that gibberellin has induced the enzyme.

21. How to use this note and what to revise next

Use these notes by working through each section and checking that you can: describe the structure of sensory, relay and motor neurones; describe the spinal reflex arc, including the roles of grey and white matter; explain how the action potential is generated, including depolarisation, repolarisation, hyperpolarisation, the role of sodium and potassium ions and the sodium–potassium pump, and the all-or-nothing principle; explain how myelination allows saltatory conduction and speeds it up; describe the cholinergic synapse and the roles of calcium, acetylcholine, receptors, acetylcholinesterase; explain the pupillary reflex (circular muscles constrict in bright light, radial muscles dilate in dim); describe how nicotine, lidocaine, cobra venom alpha toxin, L-DOPA and MDMA affect nerve impulse transmission, including examples; describe how rod cells detect light, the role of rhodopsin, opsin, retinal, sodium channels and hyperpolarisation, and how this leads to action potentials in the optic neurone; describe habituation and the evidence for it (the snail withdrawal practical); describe the central and peripheral nervous systems and the sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions; locate and state the functions of the cerebral hemispheres, hypothalamus, pituitary gland, cerebellum and medulla oblongata; explain how MRI, fMRI, PET and CT work and what they are used for; explain the role of dopamine in Parkinson’s disease and serotonin in depression and how the drugs work; describe the production of drugs using GMOs (human insulin as the example); describe how recombinant DNA is made with restriction enzymes and DNA ligase and inserted into cells; describe how microarrays work and what they show; define bioinformatics; and discuss the risks and benefits of GMOs. After this topic, revise the rest of this unit and the related practicals, and the Biology practicals (Core Practicals 14–18) which reinforce these topics.

Worked example: reading an action potential trace

Two electrodes on a giant axon are 30 mm apart. The trace shows an action potential arriving at the first electrode, and the same potential arriving at the second 1.5 ms later. Conduction velocity is distance divided by time, so the answer is 0.030 m divided by 0.0015 s = 20 m per second. Convert millimetres to metres and milliseconds to seconds before dividing, and give the unit, because the mark is for the calculation and the unit together.

The same trace gives information about the refractory period. If the axon cannot fire again for 5 ms after each impulse, the maximum frequency is 1 divided by 0.005 s = 200 impulses per second. That limit, not the size of the stimulus, is why a stronger stimulus cannot raise the frequency indefinitely: the all-or-nothing law means a bigger stimulus does not make a bigger impulse, it can only make more impulses or recruit more axons.

Drugs and nerve transmission, compared

SubstanceSite of actionEffect
NicotineBinds nicotinic acetylcholine receptors on the postsynaptic membraneMimics acetylcholine, so the postsynaptic membrane depolarises; prolonged exposure desensitises the receptor
LidocaineBlocks voltage-gated sodium channels in the axon membraneNo sodium influx means no depolarisation, so no impulse is generated and the area is anaesthetised
Cobra venom alpha toxinBinds nicotinic acetylcholine receptors and blocks themAcetylcholine cannot bind, the postsynaptic membrane is not depolarised, and paralysis follows
L-DOPACrosses the blood-brain barrier and is converted to dopamineReplaces the dopamine that is missing in Parkinson's disease, improving movement control
MDMAIncreases the release of serotonin and blocks its reuptake at synapses in the brainProlongs serotonin signalling, altering mood and perception and raising body temperature

Typical mistakes

  • Making the action potential bigger with a bigger stimulus. The impulse is all-or-nothing; a stronger stimulus increases the frequency of impulses or the number of neurones firing, not the amplitude.
  • Describing depolarisation as potassium leaving the axon. Depolarisation is sodium ions entering through voltage-gated sodium channels. Repolarisation is potassium ions leaving, and the sodium-potassium pump restores the resting distribution afterwards.
  • Saying saltatory conduction is faster because the impulse jumps "through" the myelin. The myelin is an insulator, so the local circuits skip from one node of Ranvier to the next, where the channels are, which is why the impulse travels faster in a myelinated axon.
  • Treating habituation as fatigue. Habituation is a learned decrease in response to a repeated harmless stimulus, as in the snail withdrawal response; the sensory and motor pathways still work, which is why a novel stimulus still produces a response.
  • Using "MRI" for everything. MRI shows structure from the behaviour of hydrogen nuclei in a magnetic field; fMRI shows activity through changes in blood oxygenation; PET shows metabolic activity using a radioactive tracer such as labelled glucose; CT uses X-rays and shows dense tissue such as bone.
  • Explaining a drug's effect without naming the protein or the ion. Say whether it mimics or blocks a receptor, or blocks a channel, and then say what that does to the postsynaptic membrane potential.
  • Confusing nervous and hormonal coordination. Nervous control is electrical along neurones and chemical across synapses, so it is fast, short-lived and targeted. Hormonal control travels in the blood, so it is slower, longer-lasting and widespread.

Exam-style questions

  1. Explain how the myelin sheath increases the speed of conduction. Answer: myelin is a lipid insulator wrapped by Schwann cells, so the membrane cannot depolarise where it is covered. The local circuit current therefore travels from one node of Ranvier to the next, where voltage-gated sodium channels are concentrated, and the impulse is regenerated at each node rather than continuously. This saltatory conduction is faster than conduction in an unmyelinated axon of the same diameter.
  2. Describe the sequence of events at a cholinergic synapse. Answer: the arrival of an action potential depolarises the presynaptic membrane, which opens calcium channels; calcium ions enter and cause vesicles to fuse with the presynaptic membrane and release acetylcholine into the cleft; acetylcholine binds receptors on the postsynaptic membrane, which opens sodium channels and depolarises it; acetylcholinesterase then hydrolyses acetylcholine so the signal ends and the synapse can transmit again.
  3. Explain how a rod cell signals the presence of light. Answer: light is absorbed by rhodopsin, which is retinal bound to opsin. The retinal changes shape, opsin is activated and triggers a cascade that breaks down a messenger molecule, so sodium channels close. Sodium ions stop entering, the cell hyperpolarises, and less neurotransmitter is released, which alters the rate of action potentials in the optic neurone. Rod cells therefore signal light by switching off rather than switching on.
  4. Explain how L-DOPA relieves the symptoms of Parkinson's disease but dopamine itself does not. Answer: dopamine cannot cross the blood-brain barrier, so taken as a drug it does not reach the brain. L-DOPA is its precursor, crosses the barrier using amino acid transporters, and is converted to dopamine by enzymes in the brain, replacing the dopamine that the substantia nigra no longer supplies.
  5. Explain how recombinant DNA is made and inserted into a bacterium. Answer: a restriction endonuclease cuts the gene out of the donor DNA at specific recognition sites, leaving sticky ends; the same enzyme cuts a plasmid vector, giving complementary sticky ends; DNA ligase joins the gene into the plasmid by forming phosphodiester bonds; the recombinant plasmid is inserted into a bacterium, for example by heat shock or electroporation, and the bacterium is selected, often with an antibiotic resistance marker, then grown to produce the protein.
  6. Explain what a microarray shows and why it is useful. Answer: a microarray carries many known DNA probes fixed in a grid. Labelled cDNA made from the mRNA of a sample hybridises to the probes it matches, and the pattern and intensity of the signal show which genes are being transcribed. It therefore compares gene expression between samples, such as healthy and tumour tissue, without testing genes one at a time.
  7. Give two benefits and two risks of using genetically modified organisms, and explain why the answer depends on the GMO. Answer: benefits could include higher yield or reduced pesticide use, and production of human insulin without the risk of animal-derived contamination. Risks could include genes spreading to wild relatives and long-term effects on ecosystems. Each assessment depends on which organism is modified, which gene is inserted and how it is regulated, because a crop modified for drought tolerance is not the same case as a modified animal.

title: Redox Equilibria
content:
Redox Equilibria

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH15, Topic 16. Redox reactions transfer electrons. Standard electrode potentials let you predict whether a reaction is feasible and quantify the reducing and oxidising power of species.

Oxidation and reduction

  • Oxidation is loss of electrons and an increase in oxidation state. Reduction is gain of electrons and a decrease in oxidation state.
  • The reducing agent is oxidised; the oxidising agent is reduced.

Standard electrode potentials

  • Each half-cell has a standard electrode potential, E⁰, measured under standard conditions: 298 K, 1.0 mol dm⁻³ solutions and 100 kPa for gases.
  • E⁰ is measured against the standard hydrogen electrode, which is defined as 0 V.
  • A more positive E⁰ means a stronger oxidising agent on the left of the half-equation. A more negative E⁰ means a stronger reducing agent.

Predicting feasibility

  • E⁰cell = E⁰(reduction) − E⁰(oxidation). A positive E⁰cell means the reaction is feasible under standard conditions.
  • ΔG = −nFE. A negative ΔG (positive E⁰cell) means the reaction is spontaneous.

Redox titrations

  • Manganate(VII) is its own indicator: it is purple in solution and becomes colourless at the end point when Mn²⁺ forms.
  • Acidified dichromate(VI) turns from orange to green as Cr³⁺ forms. Iodine and thiosulfate use starch, which turns blue-black with iodine and loses that colour at the end point.

Exam tip: write the ion-electron half-equations first, balance the electrons, then combine them. The ratio of electrons sets the mole ratio in titration calculations.

content:
IGCSE Biology: Excretion in Humans

Metabolism is a messy business: breaking down amino acids leaves toxic ammonia, respiration leaves carbon dioxide, and dead cells leave wastes that would poison the blood if they accumulated. Excretion is the removal of these waste products of metabolism, and the kidney is the chemical processing plant that does most of it — filtering the entire blood volume about 40 times a day and adjusting exactly what is kept. This note defines excretion precisely (against egestion), follows the blood and urine pathways, works through the nephron's filtration-reabsorption-secretion logic, explains kidney failure and dialysis, and shows how the liver's deamination and the urea cycle fit together — with the urine-composition data answers examiners expect.

What excretion is (and what it is not)

Excretion is the removal from organisms of the waste products of metabolism (chemical reactions in cells) — carbon dioxide from respiration, water, and nitrogenous wastes such as urea from the liver. It is NOT egestion (the removal of undigested food as faeces — that material never entered the body's cells), and NOT sweating merely (sweat contains some excretory water and salts, but its main role is temperature regulation). The four mammalian excretory routes: lungs (carbon dioxide and water vapour, exhaled), kidneys (urea, excess water and salts, in urine), skin (water, salts, small urea, in sweat), and the liver processes the toxins first. Being able to classify a given substance's route is a common one-mark question.

The liver, deamination and the urea cycle

The liver receives amino acids from digestion via the hepatic portal vein. Amino acids cannot be stored, so surplus ones are deaminated: the amino group is removed in the liver (using oxygen in a process that also produces carbon dioxide and water), releasing ammonia — highly toxic — which is immediately converted (ornithine/urea cycle) into the much less toxic urea, which enters the blood for the kidneys to excrete. The deaminated remainder (a keto acid) is respired or converted to glycogen or fat for storage. Liver functions in full: deamination and urea production, storing glycogen (and releasing glucose to regulate blood sugar), detoxifying alcohol and drugs (enzymes break them down; chronic alcohol use damages liver cells and reduces detoxification), making bile for fat emulsification, and breaking down old red blood cells (the bile pigment bilirubin being an excretory product of haemoglobin).

The kidneys and the nephron

Each kidney contains about a million nephrons. Blood enters the kidney via the renal artery (high pressure, oxygenated), branches into afferent arterioles, and each feeds a glomerulus — a knot of capillaries inside Bowman's capsule. Filtration: the high pressure forces small molecules (water, glucose, amino acids, salts, urea) out of the blood into the Bowman's capsule, forming the glomerular filtrate; large molecules (proteins, blood cells) stay in the blood. Selective reabsorption: as the filtrate passes along the proximal convoluted tubule, all the glucose and amino acids, most of the water, and some salts are reabsorbed into the peritubular capillaries (glucose and amino acids by active transport, water by osmosis — the proximal tubule is lined with microvilli and packed with mitochondria to power it). Secretion: additional salts and hydrogen ions (and drugs such as penicillin) are secreted from the blood into the tubule. The loop of Henle concentrates the filtrate; the collecting duct adjusts final water reabsorption under the influence of antidiuretic hormone (ADH): more ADH → more water reabsorbed → small volumes of concentrated urine; less ADH → dilute urine. The final fluid is urine: water, urea, salts — normally no glucose.

Urine composition and what it reveals

Normal urine: water, urea, mineral salts, small amounts of other excretory products; no glucose (all reabsorbed at the proximal tubule), no protein (too large to filter). Glucose in urine (glycosuria) indicates diabetes mellitus — insulin deficiency means blood glucose exceeds the kidney's reabsorption capacity (the transport maximum), or renal damage. Protein in urine indicates kidney damage (glomerulitis/nephritis) allowing large molecules through. Dehydration: low water intake or heavy sweating → more water reabsorbed → small volume of dark, concentrated urine, and blood osmotic pressure rises detected by osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus triggering ADH release and thirst. Overhydration: pale, dilute, high-volume urine. Ketones in urine indicate fat breakdown during starvation or uncontrolled diabetes. Reading a urine-composition table against a scenario is a standard Paper 4 data-response question.

Urine composition: normal and diagnostic

SubstanceNormal urinePresence indicates
Water, urea, saltsPresentNormal excretion
GlucoseAbsentDiabetes mellitus or kidney damage
ProteinAbsentKidney damage (large molecules passing the filter)
BloodAbsentInfection, stones or glomerular damage
KetonesAbsentFat breakdown in starvation or uncontrolled diabetes

Kidney failure and dialysis

Kidney failure (from chronic high blood pressure, diabetes, infection or nephrotoxic drugs) means urea and excess salts and water build up in the blood (uraemia), which is fatal without treatment. Two treatments: dialysis (a haemodialysis machine) — the patient's blood is passed over a partially permeable dialysis membrane bathed in dialysis fluid that matches the desired blood composition: no urea, correct glucose and salt concentrations; so urea diffuses out of the blood down its concentration gradient, glucose does not diffuse in (already at the right concentration), and the balance of water and salts is adjusted by pressure and concentration gradients; sessions last several hours, several times a week. Or a kidney transplant — a donor kidney surgically joined to the patient's blood vessels and bladder; success depends on tissue-type matching (HLA antigens) to prevent rejection; immunosuppressant drugs are then needed. Compare in exams: dialysis is regular, time-consuming and diet-restricted but no surgery; transplant restores normal function but needs a matched donor and lifelong immunosuppression.

Worked example: following one molecule and one calculation

Trace a molecule of urea: protein in food → digested to amino acids → absorbed into the blood → deamination in the liver releases ammonia → converted to urea → carried in the blood to the kidney → filtered at the glomerulus into Bowman's capsule → not reabsorbed in the tubule → collects in the collecting duct → drains to the ureter → stored in the bladder → excreted in urine. Now the numbers: a dialysis machine processes 300 cm³ of blood per pass, and the patient has 5 dm³ (5000 cm³) of blood; each hour about 1.5 dm³ passes. If the blood urea concentration is 0.06 g/dm³ and the dialysis fluid contains 0 g/dm³, the concentration gradient drives urea out; after treatment the concentration falls to 0.01 g/dm³. Mass of urea removed per dm³ = 0.06 − 0.01 = 0.05 g; over a 4-hour session treating 12 dm³ of blood-pass volume, up to about 0.6 g is cleared per 12 dm³ processed (use the actual volumes in any question, and show mass = concentration × volume in every calculation. Key: mass = mass of urea removed (g); concentration = blood urea concentration (g dm⁻³); volume = volume of blood processed by the machine (dm³), so the units cancel to grams.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Calling faeces an excretory product: it is egested undigested food, never part of metabolism inside cells.
  • Writing that the kidney "makes urea": urea is made in the liver; the kidney only filters and excretes it.
  • Confusing the afferent and efferent arterioles: afferent brings blood to the glomerulus (wider bore, creating filtration pressure); efferent leaves it (narrower, maintaining pressure).
  • Saying glucose is "actively secreted" into the tubule: it is filtered then actively reabsorbed — direction matters.
  • Forgetting the protein-and-blood-cells size rule: too large to be filtered, which is why their presence in urine signals damage.
  • Explaining dialysis as "cleaning the blood with soap": specify the partially permeable membrane, the concentration gradients, and the composition of dialysis fluid (no urea, correct glucose).
  • Leaving ADH out of an osmoregulation/urine-concentration answer — it is usually a mark.
  • Confusing urea (nitrogenous waste, made in liver) with uric acid or ammonia (toxic intermediate, immediately converted).

Exam-style questions and answers

Q1. Define excretion and give two excretory products in mammals with the organ that removes each. (3 marks) Answer: removal of waste products of metabolism (1); carbon dioxide from the lungs (1); urea from the kidneys (1).

Q2. Describe the role of the liver in excretion. (3 marks) Answer: deamination of surplus amino acids removes the amino group (1); ammonia is toxic and is converted to urea (1); urea is released into the blood for the kidneys to filter out (1).

Q3. Describe what happens in the nephron during urine formation. (4 marks) Answer: ultrafiltration at the glomerulus under high pressure (1); small molecules pass into Bowman's capsule while proteins and cells remain (1); selective reabsorption of glucose, amino acids and most water in the proximal tubule (1); water reabsorption in the collecting duct regulated by ADH (1).

Q4. Explain why glucose may appear in the urine of a person with diabetes. (2 marks) Answer: insulin deficiency raises blood glucose above the kidney's reabsorption capacity (1); so not all glucose can be reabsorbed and the excess is excreted (1).

Q5. Compare dialysis with kidney transplantation as treatments for kidney failure. (4 marks) Answer: dialysis regularly filters blood externally without surgery but is time-consuming with diet restrictions (1); transplant restores continuous normal function (1); transplant requires tissue-type matching to prevent rejection (1); transplant recipients take immunosuppressant drugs for life (1).

title: Exam technique: Continuous Random Variables
content:
### What earns the marks
For pdf constants, total area equals 1 stated earns the method mark. For probabilities, the integral with correct limits earns each mark. For mean and variance, E(X) and E(X squared) - E(X) squared each earn credit stepwise.
### Traps
Error: point probabilities given positive values. Correction: points have zero area. Error: mean mistaken for median. Correction: solve the half-area equation for medians. Error: variance sign reversed. Correction: E(X squared) minus mean squared.
### Worked example
A pdf is f(x) = kx for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2. Total area is 1, so the integral of kx from 0 to 2 gives 2k = 1 and k = 1/2. Then P(X > 1) is the integral of x/2 from 1 to 2, which is [x²/4] from 1 to 2 = 1 − 1/4 = 3/4. The mean is the integral of x · x/2 from 0 to 2, which is 8/6 = 4/3.
### Check yourself
For the same pdf, state why P(X = 1) is zero before you calculate anything. A single point has zero width, so its area is zero.

### Worked example
A pdf is f(x) = kx for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2. Total area is 1, so the integral of kx from 0 to 2 gives 2k = 1 and k = 1/2. Then P(X > 1) is the integral of x/2 from 1 to 2, which is [x²/4] from 1 to 2 = 1 − 1/4 = 3/4. The mean is the integral of x · x/2 from 0 to 2, which is 8/6 = 4/3.

title: Exam technique: Sequences and Series
content:
### What earns the marks
