For AP terms, a + (n-1)d with the brackets evaluated earns the mark; sums use n/2(2a + (n-1)d) quoted. For GP work, the ratio found by division earns one mark and the formula applied earns the next. For sum to infinity, the |r| < 1 check stated earns the method mark.
### Traps
Error: n used instead of (n-1) in terms. Correction: first term needs zero gaps. Error: infinity sums with |r| >= 1. Correction: check convergence first. Error: differentiating S_n for the nth term. Correction: subtract S_{n-1}.
### Worked example
An arithmetic progression has a = 5 and d = 3. The 20th term is a + 19d = 5 + 57 = 62. The sum of the first 20 terms is S₂₀ = (20/2)(2a + 19d) = 10 × 67 = 670. A geometric progression with terms 2, 6, 18 has r = 3, so S₅ = 2(3⁵ − 1)/(3 − 1) = 242. The sum to infinity exists only when |r| < 1, so for r = 1/2 with a = 8 the sum is 8 / (1 − 1/2) = 16.
### Check yourself
State the nth term of a sequence from its sum. Find Sₙ, then subtract Sₙ₋₁. Do not differentiate Sₙ, because the sum is a discrete function.

### Worked example
An arithmetic progression has a = 5 and d = 3. The 20th term is a + 19d = 5 + 57 = 62. The sum of the first 20 terms is S₂₀ = (20/2)(2a + 19d) = 10 × 67 = 670. A geometric progression with terms 2, 6, 18 has r = 3, so S₅ = 2(3⁵ − 1)/(3 − 1) = 242. The sum to infinity exists only when |r| < 1, so for r = 1/2 with a = 8 the sum is 8 / (1 − 1/2) = 16.

title: IGCSE Physics: Waves and Sound
content:
IGCSE Physics: Waves and Sound

Cambridge IGCSE Physics 0625 (2026–2028), Topic 3 Waves: statements 3.1 General properties of waves, 3.2 Light, 3.3 Electromagnetic spectrum and 3.4 Sound. Waves are how energy travels from place to place without moving matter along with it, and everything from a ripple on a pond to a gamma ray obeys the same few rules. This note builds the general wave behaviour first, then light (reflection, refraction, lenses, colour), then the electromagnetic spectrum and finally sound, with the calculations and the ray constructions that Paper 4 and Paper 6 reward.

General properties of waves

A wave transfers energy without transferring matter. Drop a cork into a ripple tank and the ripples pass under it while the cork only bobs: the water moves up and down, not outward. Every wave is described by the same vocabulary:

TermMeaningUnit
AmplitudeMaximum displacement from the rest position; relates to energy (loudness for sound, brightness for light)metre (m)
Wavelength (λ)Distance between two equivalent points on neighbouring waves, e.g. crest to crestmetre (m)
FrequencyNumber of complete waves passing a point per second; equals the source's number of oscillations per secondhertz (Hz)
PeriodTime for one complete wave to pass a pointsecond (s)
Wave speedDistance a wave crest travels per secondmetre per second (m s⁻¹)
wave speed = frequency x wavelength        v = fλ
period = 1 / frequency        T = 1 / f
  • v: wave speed in metres per second (m s⁻¹); f: frequency in hertz (Hz, = s⁻¹); λ: wavelength in metres (m). All scalars, so there are no signs to worry about — but all three quantities must be in SI units before multiplying.

Transverse waves have the vibration perpendicular to the direction of travel: water waves, light and all electromagnetic waves, waves on a shaken rope. Longitudinal waves have the vibration parallel to the direction of travel: sound in air, the push-pull of a slinky. Longitudinal waves show compressions (where particles are pushed together) and rarefactions (where they are spread apart).

Three behaviours describe what happens when waves meet things. Reflection is bouncing off a surface; the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, measured from the normal. Refraction is the change of direction when a wave passes into a different medium at an angle, because its speed changes; moving into a slower medium bends the ray towards the normal and the wavelength shortens while the frequency stays constant. Diffraction is the spreading of waves through a gap or around an obstacle, and it is most pronounced when the gap width is comparable to the wavelength. Ripple tanks demonstrate all three: straight barriers give reflection, shallow regions give refraction, and narrow gaps give circular wavefronts after diffraction (Supplement: wider gaps give less spreading, and an edge produces noticeable diffraction only for longer wavelengths).

Reflection of light

Light travels in straight lines and reflects from smooth surfaces with the law of reflection: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, both measured between the ray and the normal (an imaginary line perpendicular to the surface at the point of incidence). A plane-mirror image is upright, the same size as the object, laterally inverted (left and right swapped), and as far behind the mirror as the object is in front.

Supplement: the ray construction. To locate the image, draw a ray from the object to the mirror, continue it behind the mirror at the same angle, and drop a perpendicular from the image position to the mirror; repeat with a second ray. Where the reflected rays appear to come from behind the mirror is where the image sits. Drawing the construction to scale with a protractor gives the image position exactly.

Refraction of light

When light passes from air into glass at an angle it slows and bends towards the normal; passing back out it speeds up and bends away from the normal. The amount of bending is fixed by the material's refractive index:

refractive index = sin(angle of incidence in vacuum or air) / sin(angle of refraction)        n = sin i / sin r
critical angle:        sin c = 1 / n
  • n: refractive index, a scalar with no unit, always greater than 1 for a material like glass or water.
  • i and r: angles in degrees measured from the normal, not from the surface.
  • c: critical angle in degrees, defined for a ray passing from the material into air.

Total internal reflection happens when a ray inside a material hits the boundary at an angle greater than the critical angle: none of it escapes and all reflects. Two applications are examinable: optical fibres, where light bounces along the core with total internal reflection and carries data over long distances with little loss, and prisms in periscopes and binoculars, where a 45° prism turns light through 90° or 180° by total internal reflection with almost no energy loss compared with a mirror.

Thin lenses and vision

A converging lens brings parallel rays to a focus at its principal focus; a diverging lens spreads them out as if they came from a focus on the near side. Three standard rays build any image on a converging lens:

  • A ray parallel to the axis refracts through the principal focus on the far side.
  • A ray through the centre of the lens passes straight through undeviated.
  • A ray through the near-side principal focus emerges parallel to the axis.

Where two refracted rays cross, a real image forms — it can be shown on a screen. Where they only appear to diverge from a point behind the lens, a virtual image forms — it cannot be caught on a screen and is seen only by looking through the lens. An object beyond twice the focal length gives a smaller inverted real image (a camera); an object between the focus and the lens gives a larger upright virtual image (a magnifying glass, Supplement). Short sight (myopia) is corrected with a diverging lens, long sight (hyperopia) with a converging lens (Supplement).

Dispersion and the electromagnetic spectrum

White light passing through a prism disperses into a spectrum from red to violet because different colours refract by different amounts: red light is refracted least (it travels fastest in glass) and violet most. Light of a single colour is monochromatic (Supplement). The visible spectrum sits inside a much larger family — the electromagnetic spectrum, all waves travelling at 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ in a vacuum, all transverse, arranged by increasing frequency (and decreasing wavelength) as: radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays.

RegionWavelength scaleUsesHazards
Radio wavesmetres to hundreds of metresRadio and TV broadcasting, communicationsLittle evidence of harm at normal levels
Microwavesmillimetres to centimetresMobile phones, satellite communications, microwave ovens, radarHeating of body tissue; dangerous at high intensity
InfraredmicrometresHeating, night-vision cameras, remote controls, optical fibresBurns and skin heating at high intensity
Visible light400–700 nmVision, photography, fibre-optic dataDazzle; eye damage from lasers and the Sun
Ultraviolet10–400 nmFluorescent lamps, sterilisation, security markingSunburn, skin ageing and skin cancer, eye damage
X-rays0.01–10 nmMedical imaging, airport security, detecting cracks in metalIonising: cell damage and cancer risk; dose kept low
Gamma raysbelow 0.01 nmSterilising equipment, cancer radiotherapy, food irradiationIonising: severe cell damage; shielded with lead and concrete

Supplement: signals and communication. An analogue signal varies continuously with the quantity it carries; a digital signal is a stream of on/off pulses. Digital signals are preferred because they can be regenerated without amplifying noise, can be compressed to carry more information, can be encrypted, and can carry text, sound and images in the same stream. Satellite links work by beaming a microwave signal to an orbiting satellite, which amplifies and retransmits it back to a distant ground station.

Sound

Sound is a longitudinal wave produced by vibrating objects and travelling through a medium — air at about 340 m s⁻¹ at room temperature, faster in liquids and fastest in solids, because the particles are closer together and pass the vibration on more quickly. Sound cannot travel through a vacuum. The frequency of a sound sets its pitch (high frequency, high pitch), and the amplitude sets its loudness. The human range of hearing is roughly 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz.

Echoes and distance measurement. Sound reflects from hard surfaces, giving echoes. The depth of the sea under a ship is found by sending a pulse and timing its return:

distance to the surface = (speed of sound x total time) / 2        s = v t / 2

The halving is essential — the pulse travels down and back — and forgetting it is the classic error in this topic. Measuring the time between two microphones a known distance apart gives the speed of sound directly: v = distance/time.

Ultrasound is sound above the human hearing range (above 20 kHz). Its short wavelength means it reflects well from small internal boundaries, which makes it useful for prenatal scanning (reflection at tissue boundaries builds an image), cleaning delicate items (high-energy vibrations dislodge dirt), flaw detection in metal castings (an internal crack reflects the pulse), and sonar depth sounding. All uses share the same principle: send a pulse, time the echo, calculate the distance with s = vt/2.

Worked example: wave calculation and echo depth

A ship's sonar sends ultrasound of frequency 50 kHz. The echo returns from the seabed after 0.12 s. The speed of sound in seawater is 1500 m s⁻¹.

total distance travelled = v t = 1500 x 0.12 = 180 m
depth of the sea = 180 / 2 = 90 m

Second calculation: a ripple tank wave has a wavelength of 0.040 m and the dippers oscillate 25 times per second. The wave speed is v = f λ = 25 × 0.040 = 1.0 m s⁻¹. The frequency of the wave equals the frequency of the source, and it stays unchanged when the wave passes into deeper water — only the speed and the wavelength change there.

Common mistakes

  • Measuring a wavelength from crest to trough; that is half a wavelength. Measure between two equivalent points on neighbouring waves.
  • Forgetting that frequency never changes on refraction. The speed and wavelength change; the frequency is set by the source and stays constant.
  • Mixing up the angle of incidence with its complement: all angles in reflection and refraction are measured from the normal.
  • Using v = fλ with mismatched units: hertz times centimetres gives cm s⁻¹, not m s⁻¹. Convert the wavelength to metres first.
  • Forgetting to halve the total distance in an echo calculation.
  • Drawing a converging lens ray diagram without the two special rays, or putting the image on the wrong side: real images form on the far side where rays actually cross, virtual images on the same side as the object.
  • Claiming light travels slower in a vacuum than in glass; it is fastest in a vacuum and slower in denser media, which is what causes refraction.
  • Describing a digital signal as continuously varying; it is discrete pulses, which is precisely why it resists noise.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 4, 3 marks). A water wave has a frequency of 4.0 Hz and a wavelength of 0.25 m. Calculate its speed and its period.

Answer: v = fλ = 4.0 × 0.25 = 1.0 m s⁻¹. Period T = 1/f = 1/4.0 = 0.25 s.

Question 2 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Explain why sound cannot be heard on the Moon but sunlight still reaches it.

Answer: Sound is a longitudinal wave that needs a medium, because it travels by particles passing vibrations to their neighbours. The Moon is surrounded by a vacuum, with no particles to carry the vibration, so sound cannot travel there. Light is an electromagnetic transverse wave that carries energy without needing a medium, so it crosses the vacuum of space easily.

Question 3 (Paper 2 style). Light passes from air into glass at an angle. Which quantity does not change? A speed; B wavelength; C frequency; D direction. Answer: C. The frequency is set by the source and is unchanged; speed and wavelength both fall in glass and the ray bends.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Ultrasound of speed 1500 m s⁻¹ is used to find the depth of the sea. The echo returns in 0.40 s. Calculate the depth and explain why ultrasound is used rather than audible sound.

Answer: Depth = v t / 2 = 1500 × 0.40 / 2 = 300 m. Ultrasound has a very short wavelength, so it reflects well from small boundaries and gives a clear echo pattern without diffracting uselessly around small features; it also does not interfere with ordinary sound and is harmless at the intensities used.

Question 5 (Paper 6 style). Describe how to measure the speed of sound in air using two microphones and a data logger.

Answer: Place two microphones a measured distance apart in a straight line from a sound source (a clapping board or signal generator and loudspeaker). Trigger the data logger with the sound at each microphone and record the time interval between the arrivals, or display both pulses on an oscilloscope and measure the time from the trace. Speed is the distance between the microphones divided by the time interval. Repeat at several separations and find the speed from the gradient of a distance–time graph, which averages out the reaction error.

Question 6 (Paper 4, 3 marks). State two differences between a transverse and a longitudinal wave, and give one example of each.

Answer: In a transverse wave the vibrations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer; in a longitudinal wave they are parallel to it. Transverse waves have crests and troughs; longitudinal waves have compressions and rarefactions. Examples: light (transverse) and sound in air (longitudinal).

Waves carry energy without matter; the next topic is the energy that drives circuits: Electricity and Circuits.

Equations and symbols

One equation, v = fλ, carries the whole of wave physics; the rest of this topic is refraction, the lens and the echo. Frequency and period are reciprocals, so a question that gives one and asks for the other is testing whether you inverted it correctly.

The wave equation

v = fλ
Key: v = wave speed (m/s); f = frequency (Hz, waves per second); λ (lambda) = wavelength (m). The speed is set by the medium, so when a wave crosses into a new medium f stays the same and λ changes.

f = 1 / T
Key: f = frequency (Hz); T = period, the time for one complete oscillation (s). A 0.004 s period is 250 Hz.

T = 1 / f
Key: the same relation rearranged; T in seconds, f in hertz.

d = vt
Key: d = distance travelled by the wave (m); v = wave speed (m/s); t = time (s). For an echo the sound travels to the surface and back, so the distance to the surface is half of vt.

s = vt / 2
Key: s = distance to the reflecting surface (m); v = speed of sound in the medium (m/s); t = total time between the pulse and its echo (s). The factor of 2 is the most frequently dropped mark in echo questions.

v(sound in air) ≈ 340 m/s and v(light in vacuum) = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s
Key: the two speeds that explain thunder arriving after lightning; light is nearly a million times faster, so the flash is seen almost instantly.

audible range for a human = 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz
Key: f below 20 Hz is infrasound and above 20 kHz is ultrasound; both are outside human hearing but ultrasound is used in medical scanning and sonar.

Refraction

n = sin i / sin r
Key: n = refractive index of the material (no unit); i = angle of incidence in the less dense medium, measured from the normal (°); r = angle of refraction in the material (°). Both angles are always measured from the normal, never from the surface.

n = 1 / sin c
Key: c = critical angle (°), the angle of incidence in the denser medium for which the refracted ray runs along the surface. A larger n means a smaller critical angle.

n = c / v
Key: c = speed of light in a vacuum (3.0 × 10⁸ m/s); v = speed of light in the material (m/s). Light slows on entering a denser medium, which is what bends it towards the normal.

total internal reflection when i > c
Key: i = angle of incidence inside the denser medium (°); c = critical angle (°). Beyond c no light escapes, which is the rule behind optical fibres and reflecting prisms.

Lenses and images

m = h(image) / h(object)
Key: m = magnification (no unit); h(image) = image height (m or cm); h(object) = object height in the same unit. m greater than 1 means enlarged, less than 1 means diminished.

real image: formed where rays actually meet, and can be projected on a screen
Key: a converging lens gives a real image when the object is beyond the focal length; the image is inverted. A virtual image is where rays only appear to come from, and cannot be projected.

title: Further Trigonometry — Study Notes
content:
Further Trigonometry

Edexcel International A Level Mathematics — Pure Mathematics 3 (WMA13), sat at A2.

Compound Angles

  • sin(A ± B) = sin A cos B ± cos A sin B
  • cos(A ± B) = cos A cos B ∓ sin A sin B

Example: sin 75° = sin(45° + 30°) = (√2/2)(√3/2) + (√2/2)(1/2) = (√6 + √2)/4.

Double Angles

  • sin 2A = 2 sin A cos A
  • cos 2A = cos²A − sin²A = 2cos²A − 1 = 1 − 2sin²A

Example: express 4 sin x cos x in one term: 2 sin 2x.

The R-Form

a sin x + b cos x = R sin(x + α) with R = √(a² + b²) and tan α = b/a.

Example: 3 sin x + 4 cos x = 5 sin(x + 0.927). This instantly gives the maximum 5 and minimum −5.

Reciprocal Functions

sec θ = 1/cos θ, cosec θ = 1/sin θ, cot θ = 1/tan θ. Key identity: 1 + cot²θ = cosec²θ.

Exam tips: choose the cos 2A form that eliminates the unwanted function; when solving with R-form, divide by R before using inverse trig, and translate intervals carefully.

Exam method: reciprocal functions and identities

The reciprocal functions are sec x = 1/cos x, cosec x = 1/sin x and cot x = 1/tan x. Rewrite them in terms of sine and cosine when a question mixes functions, because this usually shows which identity to use.

The Pythagorean identities are sin² x + cos² x = 1, 1 + tan² x = sec² x and 1 + cot² x = cosec² x. Divide the first identity by cos² x or sin² x to obtain the second or third.

To solve an equation such as sec x = 2, first rewrite it as cos x = 1/2, then find the acute angle and the other solutions in the required range. For cos x = k the solutions in 0 to 2π are α and 2π − α, where α is the acute angle.

To prove an identity, work on the more complicated side only, and keep rewriting until it matches the other side.

Exam cue: Give each solution in the range asked for, using exact values such as π/3 when the angle is standard.

Exam method: R-form

To write a sinθ + b cosθ as R sin(θ + α), expand R sin(θ + α) = R sinθ cosα + R cosθ sinα and compare coefficients. This gives R = √(a² + b²) and tan α = b / a, with α in the quadrant where cos α and sin α have the signs of a and b.

Exam cue: Find the maximum and minimum from R, then solve for θ over the stated interval. Give α in the correct quadrant before writing the final angles.

Worked example: solving sin 2x = cos x

Solve sin 2x = cos x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π. Using the double angle formula, 2 sin x cos x = cos x. Move everything to one side and factorise: cos x (2 sin x − 1) = 0. So cos x = 0, giving x = π/2 or 3π/2, or sin x = ½, giving x = π/6 or 5π/6. The four solutions are π/6, π/2, 5π/6 and 3π/2. Dividing both sides by cos x at the start would lose the two solutions where cos x = 0, and that is the most common way to drop marks on this type of question.

Exam method: choosing an identity

Before you start, look at which angles appear. If the question mixes x and 2x, rewrite the double angle first so that everything is in one angle. Always state the range of solutions in the form the question asks for, in radians or degrees, and check that each answer lies inside the range. Substituting each answer back into the original equation is a quick way to catch a sign error.

title: Processor Fundamentals — Study Notes
content:
`# Processor Fundamentals

The FDE Cycle

  • Fetch: PC → MAR; read memory → MDR; instruction → CIR; PC increments
  • Decode: control unit interprets the opcode
  • Execute: ALU/registers act; results stored; PC may be overwritten (jumps)

Registers

RegisterRole
PCaddress of next instruction
MARaddress being accessed
MDRdata in transit
CIRcurrent instruction
ACCaccumulator results

Buses

  • Address bus: one-way, CPU → memory (width sets addressable space)
  • Data bus: two-way, carries instructions/data
  • Control bus: timing and command signals

Interrupts

Signals that pause the current program (I/O complete, timer, errors). The CPU saves context, runs the ISR, then resumes — enabling multitasking.

Assembly and Addressing

Immediate (#5), direct (address holds value), indirect (address points to address), indexed (base + offset — arrays), relative (PC + offset — jumps).

Example: LDD 100 loads from 100 (direct); LDI 100 loads from the address stored at 100 (indirect).

Exam tips: trace register contents step by step in trace tables; explain the stored program concept — instructions as data in memory.

The fetch-decode-execute cycle and registers

The program counter (PC) holds the address of the next instruction. During fetch, that address is copied to the memory address register (MAR), the instruction is read into the memory data register (MDR) and then into the current instruction register (CIR), and the PC is incremented. During decode the control unit works out what the instruction means, and during execute the ALU or another part of the CPU carries it out.

The accumulator is a register that holds the results of arithmetic and logic operations. Registers are very fast storage inside the CPU, and the CPU uses them so that it does not have to wait for main memory on every step.

Exam tip: learn the purpose of each register in one sentence. Examiners often ask which register holds the address, and which holds the instruction.

title: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Angles and Polygons
content:
Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Angles and Polygons

Angles are the simplest measurements in geometry and the most frequently examined: almost every Paper 2 and Paper 4 geometry question ends with a reason written next to a number, and the reason earns as many marks as the calculation. This note builds the whole angle toolkit from zero: the vocabulary of points, lines and angles; the parallel-line rules; the angle sums of triangles, quadrilaterals and polygons; and the full set of circle theorems with the standard reasons examiners accept. Every worked example writes the reason line, because that is how the marks are earned.

Geometrical terms

Geometry has a precise vocabulary, and Paper 2 questions often begin by asking you to use it:

  • Point: a position with no size; named with a capital letter.
  • Line segment: the straight path between two points; a line extends without end.
  • Ray: a line starting at a point and extending in one direction.
  • Parallel lines: always the same distance apart, never meeting (marked with arrows).
  • Perpendicular lines: meeting at 90°.
  • Vertex: a corner where two or more lines meet; vertices in the plural.
  • Polygon: a closed shape with straight sides; regular means all sides equal and all angles equal.

Angle vocabulary: acute (less than 90°), right (90°), obtuse (between 90° and 180°), straight (180°), reflex (between 180° and 360°). Angles on a straight line sum to 180°; angles around a point sum to 360°; vertically opposite angles are equal.

Parallel lines: the three rules

A transversal line crossing two parallel lines creates eight angles, and three relationships do all the work:

RelationshipWhat they look likeRule
Corresponding (F-shape)same position at each intersectionequal
Alternate (Z-shape)opposite sides of the transversal, between the parallelsequal
Co-interior (C-shape)same side of the transversal, between the parallelssum to 180°

Worked example. Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. One angle is 115°. Find the angle in the alternate position and the co-interior angle on the other side.

alternate angle = 115 °            (alternate angles are equal)
co-interior angle = 180 - 115 = 65 ° (co-interior angles sum to 180)

Always write the reason next to each answer: "alternate angles" or "co-interior angles sum to 180°". Paper 2 awards the reason mark explicitly.

Triangles and quadrilaterals

The angle sum of any triangle is 180° (proof: draw a line through one vertex parallel to the opposite side and use alternate angles). Consequences you must know:

  • Exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles.
  • Isosceles triangle: base angles are equal; the angle bisector from the apex is also the perpendicular bisector of the base.
  • Equilateral triangle: all angles 60°.
  • Quadrilateral: interior angles sum to 360° (split into two triangles).

Worked example. A quadrilateral has angles 85°, 95° and 110°. Find the fourth angle.

sum = 360 °
fourth = 360 - (85 + 95 + 110) = 360 - 290 = 70 °

Worked example 2 (exterior angle). In a triangle, an exterior angle is 125° and one opposite interior angle is 48°. Find the other opposite interior angle.

exterior = sum of opposite interiors
125 = 48 + x  →  x = 77 °

Angles in polygons

Any n-sided polygon can be split into (n − 2) triangles from one vertex, so:

interior angle sum = (n - 2) × 180 °

regular polygon: each interior angle = (n - 2) × 180/n
exterior angles of any convex polygon sum to 360 °
regular polygon: each exterior angle = 360/n
interior + exterior = 180 ° at each vertex

Worked example 1. Find the interior angle sum of a decagon (10 sides) and each interior angle of a regular decagon.

sum = (10 - 2) × 180 = 1440 °
each = 1440/10 = 144 °
check with exterior: 360/10 = 36; 180 - 36 = 144 °

Worked example 2 (working backwards). A regular polygon has each interior angle 150°. Find the number of sides.

exterior angle = 180 - 150 = 30 °
n = 360/30 = 12 sides  (a regular dodecagon)

Worked example 3 (exterior angles). A pentagon has exterior angles 70°, 80°, 60°, 90°. Find the fifth.

exterior angles sum to 360 °
fifth = 360 - (70 + 80 + 60 + 90) = 360 - 300 = 60 °

Circle theorems: the full set

Circle theorems are examined every session, and each answer needs its theorem named. Learn them as pictures with their standard reasons:

TheoremStatementReason to write
Angle at the centrethe angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference subtended by the same arcangle at centre = 2 × angle at circumference
Angle in a semicirclethe angle in a semicircle (subtended by a diameter) is 90°angle in a semicircle is 90°
Same segmentangles subtended by the same arc in the same segment are equalangles in the same segment are equal
Cyclic quadrilateralopposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180°opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180°
Tangent–radiusa tangent meets the radius at the point of contact at 90°tangent is perpendicular to the radius
Two tangentstangents from an external point are equal in lengthtangents from an external point are equal
Alternate segmentthe angle between a tangent and a chord equals the angle in the alternate segmentalternate segment theorem

Worked example 1 (centre). The angle at the centre subtended by an arc is 130°. Find the angle at the circumference subtended by the same arc.

angle at circumference = 130/2 = 65 °
(reason: angle at centre = 2 x angle at circumference)

Worked example 2 (cyclic quadrilateral). In a cyclic quadrilateral, one pair of opposite angles is 105° and 75°, and the other pair is 4x and 2x. Find x.

opposite angles sum to 180 °
4x + 2x = 180
6x = 180  →  x = 30
check the first pair: 105 + 75 = 180, consistent

Two disciplines make this safe: pair the angles that sit opposite each other (a diagonal between them), and verify both pairs satisfy the 180° rule before writing the answer.

Worked example 3 (tangent). A tangent touches a circle of radius 5 cm at T; O is the centre and P is a point on the tangent 12 cm from T. Find OP.

The radius OT is perpendicular to the tangent, so triangle OTP
is right-angled at T.
OP² = 5² + 12² = 25 + 144 = 169
OP = 13 cm

Worked example 4 (alternate segment). A tangent and a chord form an angle of 62° at the point of contact. Find the angle in the alternate segment.

alternate segment theorem: the tangent-chord angle equals the
angle in the alternate segment
answer = 62 °

Circle theorems: multi-step problems

Paper 4 circle problems chain two or three theorems. The method: mark every angle you can find with its reason, then use each new angle to unlock the next.

Worked example. O is the centre; A, B, C lie on the circle; angle BAC = 35°. Find angle BOC and angle OBC.

angle BOC = 2 × 35 = 70 °
  (angle at centre = 2 x angle at circumference)
triangle OBC is isosceles (OB = OC = radii)
base angles OBC and OCB are equal:
OBC = (180 - 70)/2 = 55 °

Worked example 2 (semicircle + cyclic). AB is a diameter; C and D lie on the circle; angle ABC = 40°. Find angle ADC.

angle ACB = 90 ° (angle in a semicircle)
angle BAC = 180 - 90 - 40 = 50 °
ABCD is cyclic, so angle ADC = 180 - angle ABC? No - opposite
pairs: A with C, B with D. Angle ADC is opposite angle ABC?
The vertices in order are A, B, C, D, so opposite pairs are
(A, C) and (B, D). Angle ADC is at D, opposite angle ABC at B:
angle ADC = 180 - 40 = 140 °.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Parallel lines) Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal; one co-interior angle is 72°. Find the other. Answer: co-interior angles between parallel lines sum to 180°, so the other angle is 180 − 72 = 108°.
  2. (Polygon) Find the interior angle sum of a 15-sided polygon. Answer: the interior angles of an n-gon sum to (n − 2) × 180°, so (15 − 2) × 180 = 2340°.
  3. (Regular polygon) Each exterior angle of a regular polygon is 24°. Find the number of sides and each interior angle. Answer: exterior angles sum to 360°, so n = 360 ÷ 24 = 15; each interior angle is 180 − 24 = 156°.
  4. (Circle — centre) An angle at the circumference is 28°. Find the angle at the centre subtended by the same arc. Answer: the angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference on the same arc: 2 × 28 = 56°.
  5. (Circle — semicircle) A triangle is inscribed in a semicircle with the diameter as one side; one base angle is 33°. Find the other. Answer: the angle in a semicircle is 90°, so the third angle is 180 − 90 − 33 = 57°.
  6. (Circle — cyclic) A cyclic quadrilateral has one angle 118°. Find the opposite angle. Answer: opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180°, so the opposite angle is 180 − 118 = 62°.
  7. (Tangent) Two tangents from P touch the circle at A and B; PA = 9 cm. Find PB and explain. Answer: tangents drawn from the same external point are equal, so PB = PA = 9 cm.
  8. (Multi-step) In a circle, angle ABD = 42° and angle ACD = 42°. What does this tell you about A, B, C, D? Answer: angle ABD and angle ACD are both 42° and both stand on the chord AD, so they are angles in the same segment; equal angles in the same segment put B and C on the same circle through A and D, so A, B, C and D are concyclic.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Missing reasons: Paper 2 geometry marks include the reason. "x = 65° (angles on a straight line)" scores; a bare "65°" may not.
  • Wrong pairing in cyclic quadrilaterals: opposite angles are the ones separated by a diagonal (A and C, B and D), not adjacent ones. Check both pairs sum to 180°.
  • Alternate versus corresponding: alternate angles form a Z, corresponding an F. Identifying the wrong pattern gives the wrong equality.
  • Interior formula mix-up: interior sum is (n − 2) × 180; each exterior is 360/n. Do not use 360/n for the interior of a regular polygon.
  • Reflex angles: the angle at the centre may be reflex; if the diagram shows an obtuse angle but the geometry demands a reflex one, use 360° − the drawn angle.
  • Assuming radii are parallel or equal to chords: radii are equal to each other, not to chords. Isosceles triangles in circles come from two radii.
  • Tangent–chord angle: the alternate segment theorem requires the angle between the tangent and the chord at the point of contact, not any angle involving the tangent.
  • Diagram not to scale: never measure an angle with a protractor in an exam diagram; the geometry must be calculated. "Diagram not accurately drawn" is a warning, not decoration.

Equations and symbols

Every relation this topic is examined on, written with its real notation and followed by a key naming each symbol, its unit and what it means. The sections above explain why each one is true; this sheet is the version to revise from, where the answer depends on reproducing the exact form and substituting into it without losing a unit.

Angle facts and parallel lines

angles at a point sum to 360°; angles on a straight line sum to 180°; vertically opposite angles are equal
Key: the angle in each case is measured in degrees at the named vertex. These three are the reason every angle chase starts by marking what is already known, not by guessing; a missing step is nearly always one of them.

alternate angles are equal, corresponding angles are equal, co-interior angles sum to 180°
Key: the pairs are formed where a transversal crosses two parallel lines; alternate angles lie on opposite sides in a Z-shape, corresponding angles are in matching positions, co-interior are on the same side inside the parallel lines. Naming the reason is worth a mark on its own, so write it beside the number.

triangle interior angles sum to 180°; exterior angle = sum of the two interior opposite angles
Key: interior angles are inside the triangle at each vertex; the exterior angle is formed by extending one side, and equals the sum of the two angles it does not touch. Quadrilaterals split into two triangles, so their angles sum to 360°.

Polygons

interior angle sum = (n − 2) × 180°
Key: n = the number of sides of the polygon; the result is in degrees. The (n − 2) counts the triangles a polygon can be split into from one vertex, which is the derivation rather than a fact to memorise.

exterior angles of any convex polygon sum to 360°, and for a regular polygon each exterior angle = 360°/n
Key: n = the number of sides; an exterior angle is the turn made at each vertex, so walking round once is a full revolution. Regularity is what makes every exterior angle equal — without it only the total is fixed.

regular polygon: each interior angle = (n − 2) × 180°/n, and interior + exterior = 180° at each vertex
Key: n = the number of sides; the two angles at a vertex lie on a straight line, which is why they add to 180°. The pair gives a fast check: an interior angle of 150° means an exterior of 30°, hence n = 360/30 = 12.

Circle theorems

angle at the centre = 2 × angle at the circumference, standing on the same arc
Key: both angles subtend the same chord; the centre angle is measured at the centre of the circle, the circumference angle at any point on the remaining arc. This is the theorem most others are proved from, so quote it by name.

angle in a semicircle = 90°
Key: the angle is subtended by a diameter at any point on the circumference; it is the centre-angle theorem with the centre angle at 180°. Its converse is how a question proves that a triangle's longest side is a diameter.

angles in the same segment are equal; opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180°
Key: a cyclic quadrilateral has all four vertices on one circle; the segment angles stand on the same chord from the same side. The 180° result is the single most useful one in multi-step problems, because it turns a known angle into the one opposite it.

tangent ⟂ radius at the point of contact; tangents from an external point are equal in length
Key: the tangent touches the circle at exactly one point; the radius is drawn to that point and meets it at 90°, which is what makes Pythagoras available. The equal tangents fact creates the two congruent right triangles that most tangent proofs rely on.

alternate segment theorem: the angle between a tangent and a chord equals the angle in the alternate segment
Key: the chord divides the circle into two segments; the angle is measured between the tangent and the chord at the point of contact, and equals the angle subtended by that chord at any point in the opposite segment. Quote the theorem by name — the reason carries marks.

title: Exam technique: Dynamics
content:
### What earns the marks
For resultant force, subtract opposition before applying F = ma to earn both marks. For collisions, total momentum before equated to total after earns the method mark. For rebounds, the sign change included earns the second mark.
### Traps
Error: friction ignored in acceleration. Correction: use the resultant, not the push alone. Error: rebound treated as stopping. Correction: add the speeds with the sign flip. Error: kinetic energy claimed conserved generally. Correction: momentum always, kinetic only when elastic.
### Worked example
A car of mass 800 kg has a driving force of 2400 N and a resistance of 400 N. The resultant force is 2400 - 400 = 2000 N, so a = F/m = 2000 / 800 = 2.5 m/s^2. Subtract the opposing force before you divide by the mass.
### Check yourself
A 2 kg trolley moving at 3 m/s hits a stationary 1 kg trolley, and they stick together. Total momentum before is 2 x 3 = 6 kg m/s, so the joint speed is 6 / 3 = 2 m/s. Show the momentum equation even when the speed looks obvious.

### Worked example
A car of mass 800 kg has a driving force of 2400 N and a resistance of 400 N. The resultant force is 2400 - 400 = 2000 N, so a = F/m = 2000 / 800 = 2.5 m/s^2. Subtract the opposing force before you divide by the mass.

title: AS Level Chemistry: Intermolecular Forces
content:
AS Level Chemistry: Intermolecular Forces

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH12, Topic 7 explains the forces that hold molecules to one another, as distinct from the covalent bonds inside them. These forces are far weaker than covalent bonds, yet they decide boiling temperature, volatility, solubility and the anomalous behaviour of water, and they are the reason a molecule with polar bonds is not necessarily a polar molecule. Examiners test the explanation rather than the label, so every answer should name the force, say what causes it, and relate it to the property asked about.

Three types of intermolecular force

All intermolecular forces are electrostatic: they arise from the attraction between regions of opposite charge. They differ in what creates those regions.

ForceOriginTypical strength
London forces (instantaneous dipole–induced dipole)Fluctuating electron density in one molecule induces a dipole in a neighbourVery weak, but increases with the number of electrons
Permanent dipole–permanent dipolePermanently polar bonds and an asymmetric shape leave one end of the molecule slightly positive and the other slightly negativeWeak, roughly 5–20 kJ mol⁻¹
Hydrogen bondingA hydrogen atom bonded to N, O or F is attracted to a lone pair on N, O or F in another moleculeStrongest of the three, up to about 40 kJ mol⁻¹

London forces

Electrons are in constant motion, so at any instant the electron distribution in a molecule may be uneven. That creates an instantaneous dipole, which in turn distorts the electron cloud of a neighbouring molecule and induces a dipole in it. The two dipoles then attract. The effect is present in every substance, including the noble gases and non-polar molecules such as methane, and it is the only intermolecular force in a non-polar substance.

The strength of London forces depends on how easily the electron cloud can be distorted, which is called polarisability. Two factors control it:

  • Number of electrons: more electrons means a larger, more polarisable cloud. Iodine (I₂) is a solid and chlorine (Cl₂) a gas at room temperature for this reason.
  • Surface area and shape: a long unbranched chain has more surface contact between neighbouring molecules than a compact branched isomer with the same formula, so it has stronger London forces.

London forces are also the reason why a noble gas such as argon can be liquefied at low temperature, even though its atoms have no permanent dipole and no bonds to break.

Permanent dipole–dipole interactions

A bond between atoms of different electronegativity is polar: the more electronegative atom carries a partial negative charge, δ−, and the less electronegative atom carries δ+. If the molecule is not symmetrical, the individual bond dipoles do not cancel, and the molecule as a whole has a permanent dipole. Neighbouring molecules then line up with opposite ends together, and the attraction is a permanent dipole–permanent dipole interaction.

Hydrogen chloride, HCl, is polar and its molecules attract this way. Carbon dioxide has two polar C=O bonds, but the molecule is linear and symmetrical, so the dipoles cancel exactly and CO₂ has no permanent dipole; its molecules are held only by London forces. Tetrachloromethane, CCl₄, is also symmetrical and non-polar for the same reason, while trichloromethane, CHCl₃, is polar because the fourth substituent is hydrogen rather than chlorine and the symmetry is broken. Whether a molecule is polar therefore needs two checks: are the bonds polar, and is the shape symmetrical?

Hydrogen bonding

Hydrogen bonding is a particularly strong form of permanent dipole attraction. It occurs only when two conditions are satisfied:

  • A hydrogen atom is covalently bonded to a highly electronegative atom, limited to nitrogen, oxygen or fluorine.
  • A lone pair is available on an N, O or F atom in a neighbouring molecule, which the δ+ hydrogen can approach.

The result is a strong attraction between the δ+ hydrogen and the lone pair, often drawn as a dotted line: O–H···O. The bond is directional, which is why hydrogen bonding produces specific structures rather than a random arrangement.

Water, ammonia and hydrogen fluoride all hydrogen bond:

SubstanceHydrogen-bonding unitNumber of hydrogen bonds per molecule in the liquid
H₂OO–H···OTwo hydrogen atoms and two lone pairs allow an extensive network
NH₃N–H···NThree hydrogen atoms but only one lone pair, so fewer bonds than water
HFF–H···FOne hydrogen atom and three lone pairs; chains of HF molecules

Hydrogen bonding is not the same as a covalent bond to hydrogen. It is an intermolecular attraction, so it is broken when a substance melts or boils, while the O–H covalent bond stays intact. That distinction is worth stating explicitly in an answer.

The anomalous properties of water

Water's properties do not follow the pattern of similar molecules, and hydrogen bonding is the explanation.

High melting and boiling temperatures. Compared with hydrogen sulfide, H₂S, which has a similar formula, water boils about 160 °C higher. The molecules of H₂S are held only by London forces and weak dipole–dipole attractions, whereas each water molecule can hydrogen bond to several neighbours. Breaking those attractions needs far more energy, so the melting and boiling temperatures are unusually high, and water is a liquid at room temperature while H₂S is a gas.

Ice is less dense than liquid water. In ice, each water molecule hydrogen bonds to four neighbours in a regular tetrahedral arrangement, which holds the molecules further apart than in the liquid and leaves open hexagonal spaces. When ice melts, much of that open framework collapses and the molecules pack more closely, so liquid water is denser than ice. This is why ice floats, and why a lake freezes from the top, insulating the water beneath and allowing aquatic life to survive.

Hydrogen bonding also gives water a high surface tension, a high specific heat capacity and a high enthalpy of vaporisation, all of which follow from the energy needed to overcome the network of hydrogen bonds.

Predicting hydrogen bonding

To decide whether a molecule can hydrogen bond, look for an O–H, N–H or F–H group and for a lone pair on O, N or F. Ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH, can hydrogen bond because of its O–H group; ethanal, CH₃CHO, has a C=O bond with lone pairs but no hydrogen attached to an electronegative atom, so it cannot donate a hydrogen bond, although its oxygen can accept one. A molecule such as CH₃F has no H–F bond, so it does not hydrogen bond. Methanol and water mix in all proportions because both can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds, whereas methane, with only C–H bonds, cannot.

Intermolecular forces and physical properties

Boiling temperature is a measure of the energy needed to separate molecules, so it reports the strength of the intermolecular forces, not the strength of the covalent bonds. Four trends are examined.

Boiling temperature of alkanes increases with chain length. Each additional CH₂ group adds electrons and surface area, so the London forces between the molecules become stronger and more energy is needed to separate them. Methane boils at −162 °C, ethane at −89 °C and decane at 174 °C.

Branching lowers the boiling temperature. Pentane and 2,2-dimethylpropane have the same molecular formula, but the branched molecule is more compact. Its molecules have less surface contact, so its London forces are weaker and it boils at 9.5 °C compared with 36 °C for pentane. The same reasoning explains why branched isomers have lower boiling temperatures throughout the alkanes.

Alcohols have higher boiling temperatures than alkanes of similar electron count. Ethanol (46 electrons) boils at 78 °C while propane (26 electrons) boils at −42 °C. The comparison is not quite like for like, but the key point is that ethanol molecules hydrogen bond through the O–H group, while propane molecules have only London forces. The hydrogen bonding more than compensates for the smaller number of electrons.

Boiling temperatures of the hydrogen halides are not a simple trend. HF is the highest because of hydrogen bonding. From HCl to HBr to HI, London forces grow as the number of electrons increases, so the boiling temperatures rise in that order: HCl −85 °C, HBr −67 °C, HI −35 °C. HF, at 20 °C, sits far above the smooth trend, and that outlier is the evidence for hydrogen bonding.

Choosing a solvent

Dissolving depends on the solute particles being separated and surrounded by solvent particles, so the solute–solvent attractions must be comparable to the forces they replace. In practice, like dissolves like.

  • Water dissolves ionic compounds because the polar water molecules attract the ions: the partially negative oxygen surrounds a cation and the partially positive hydrogens surround an anion. This is hydration, and it releases hydration enthalpy that helps to compensate for the lattice enthalpy that must be overcome.
  • Water dissolves simple alcohols such as methanol and ethanol, because the alcohol's O–H group can both donate a hydrogen bond to water and accept one from it. As the hydrocarbon chain grows, the non-polar part becomes a larger fraction of the molecule and solubility falls: ethanol mixes with water in all proportions, but hexan-1-ol is only slightly soluble.
  • Water is a poor solvent for halogenoalkanes and other polar organic molecules such as chloroethane. The molecule has a dipole, so it is attracted to water to some extent, but it has no O–H group and cannot hydrogen bond with water, and its hydrocarbon part cannot interact favourably with the water network. The solute–solvent attractions are too weak to overcome the hydrogen bonding between water molecules.
  • Non-aqueous solvents are used when the solute's intermolecular forces resemble the solvent's. Iodine, a non-polar molecule held by London forces, dissolves in hexane, which is also non-polar; bromine dissolves in cyclohexane for the same reason. Propanone is a useful intermediate case, dissolving both polar and many non-polar substances because it has a polar C=O group and a hydrocarbon part.

A good answer states the force between solvent molecules, the force between solute and solvent, and whether the second is strong enough to replace the first.

Typical mistakes

  • Saying a substance has hydrogen bonds when the hydrogen is bonded to carbon; only N–H, O–H and F–H count.
  • Describing hydrogen bonding as a covalent bond, or claiming that boiling water breaks O–H bonds.
  • Assuming that a molecule with polar bonds must be polar, without checking whether the shape cancels the dipoles.
  • Attributing the trend in alkane boiling temperatures to stronger covalent bonds rather than to stronger London forces.
  • Explaining branching by saying the molecule has fewer electrons; the number of electrons is the same, the surface contact is not.
  • Explaining the lower density of ice as an expansion on freezing without mentioning the open hydrogen-bonded lattice.
  • Describing London forces as "weak covalent forces" or as attractions between permanent dipoles.

Exam-style questions

  1. Explain why the boiling temperature of iodine is higher than that of chlorine. Answer: iodine has more electrons and a larger, more polarisable electron cloud, so the London forces between its molecules are stronger; more energy is needed to separate the molecules.
  2. Explain why 2-methylbutane has a lower boiling temperature than pentane. Answer: both have the molecular formula C5H12 and the same number of electrons. 2-methylbutane is more branched and more compact, so its molecules have less surface area in contact, the London forces between them are weaker, and less energy is needed to separate them.
  3. Explain, in terms of intermolecular forces, why ethanol is soluble in water but chloroethane is not. Answer: ethanol has an O–H group and can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds with water, so the solute–solvent attractions are strong enough to replace the hydrogen bonds between water molecules. Chloroethane is polar but has no O–H group, so it cannot hydrogen bond with water; its attractions to water are too weak to compensate for breaking the water–water hydrogen bonds.
  4. Explain why ice is less dense than liquid water. Answer: in ice each water molecule forms hydrogen bonds to four neighbours in a tetrahedral arrangement, producing an open lattice with spaces between the molecules. When ice melts the lattice collapses and the molecules pack more closely, so the liquid is denser.
  5. Identify the strongest intermolecular force in each of the following and justify your answer: (a) HCl, (b) CH₃OH, (c) CCl₄. Answer: (a) permanent dipole–permanent dipole, because the molecule is polar and has no O–H, N–H or F–H group; (b) hydrogen bonding, because of the O–H group; (c) London forces, because the molecule is symmetrical and the bond dipoles cancel, so it is non-polar.

When revising, practise the three-part answer: name the force, explain what causes it in these molecules, then link it to the property in the question. Move on to Introduction to Kinetics and Equilibria next, where the same molecular picture explains why reactions need collisions with sufficient energy.

title: Redox Chemistry and Groups 1, 2 and 7 — Study Notes
content:
Redox Chemistry and Groups 1, 2 and 7

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH12, Topic 8. Every statement 8.1 to 8.28 is covered below, with its code in the heading. Three ideas run through the whole topic: oxidation numbers track electron transfer, the Group 1 and 2 trends follow from atomic size and nuclear charge, and the Group 7 trends are the same ideas applied to halogens.

8.1 to 8.4: Oxidation numbers

  • Rules: an element is 0; a monatomic ion equals its charge; the sum of oxidation numbers equals the overall charge. Oxygen is usually −2 (but −1 in peroxides such as H₂O₂), hydrogen is usually +1 (but −1 in metal hydrides such as NaH), fluorine is always −1, Group 1 is +1 and Group 2 is +2.
  • 8.2: in MnO₄⁻, manganese must be +7, because four oxygens contribute −8 and the ion has a charge of −1.
  • 8.3: write the oxidation number as a Roman numeral in the name: manganese(VII), iron(III), copper(II).
  • 8.4: work backwards from oxidation numbers to a formula. Iron(III) sulfate is Fe₂(SO₄)₃, because Fe³⁺ must balance SO₄²⁻ in a 2:3 ratio.

8.5 to 8.9: Oxidation, reduction and disproportionation

  • 8.5: oxidation is loss of electrons, and it appears as an increase in oxidation number. Reduction is gain of electrons, a decrease in oxidation number. In 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl, sodium is oxidised (0 to +1) and chlorine is reduced (0 to −1). The same idea covers reactions of s-block metals and p-block non-metals.
  • 8.6: an oxidising agent gains electrons and is itself reduced. A reducing agent loses electrons and is itself oxidised.
  • 8.7: disproportionation is when one element in a single species is both oxidised and reduced at the same time. Chlorine in water is the standard example: Cl₂ → Cl⁻ (0 to −1) and HClO (0 to +1).
  • 8.8: oxidation numbers classify reactions. A reaction is redox if any oxidation number changes, and it is a disproportionation if the same element goes both up and down.
  • 8.9: metals form positive ions by losing electrons, so their oxidation number increases. Non-metals form negative ions by gaining electrons, so their oxidation number decreases.

8.10: Half-equations and full ionic equations

  • Write the oxidation and the reduction separately, balance atoms, then balance charge with electrons. For magnesium with chlorine: Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻ and Cl₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻.
  • Add the half-equations so the electrons cancel, then cancel any spectator ions to give the full ionic equation.

8.11 to 8.13: Group 1 and Group 2 trends and reactions

  • 8.11: ionisation energy falls down Groups 1 and 2. The outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded by inner shells, so less energy is needed to remove it.
  • 8.12: reactivity rises down Group 1 (Li to K) and Group 2 (Mg to Ba), for the same reason: the outer electron is removed more easily.
  • 8.13: Group 1 metals burn in oxygen and react vigorously with chlorine and water. Group 2 metals react with oxygen and chlorine to form oxides and chlorides. Magnesium reacts slowly with cold water and readily with steam, while calcium reacts steadily with cold water to form Ca(OH)₂ and hydrogen.

8.14: Reactions of oxides and hydroxides

  • Group 1 oxides dissolve in water to give alkaline hydroxides. Group 2 oxides react less vigorously, and CaO gives a limewater-type solution, Ca(OH)₂.
  • Oxides react with dilute acid to form a salt and water, for example MgO + 2H⁺ → Mg²⁺ + H₂O.
  • Hydroxides neutralise dilute acids: Ca(OH)₂ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + 2H₂O.

8.15: Solubility trends of Group 2 hydroxides and sulfates

  • Hydroxides: solubility increases down the group. Magnesium hydroxide is almost insoluble, calcium hydroxide is slightly soluble, barium hydroxide is quite soluble.
  • Sulfates: solubility decreases down the group. Magnesium sulfate is soluble, barium sulfate is insoluble, which is why acidified barium chloride gives a white precipitate in the sulfate test.

8.16: Thermal stability of nitrates and carbonates

  • Stability increases down each group. A larger cation has a lower charge density, so it polarises the carbonate or nitrate ion less, and the anion breaks down less easily.
  • Carbonates: MCO₃ → MO + CO₂. Group 2 nitrates: 2M(NO₃)₂ → 2MO + 4NO₂ + O₂. Group 1 nitrates (other than lithium) give the nitrite and oxygen: 2NaNO₃ → 2NaNO₂ + O₂.
  • Lithium is the exception: its nitrate decomposes like a Group 2 nitrate, because the small Li⁺ ion polarises the nitrate strongly.

8.17: Flame colours

  • Heat excites outer electrons to higher energy levels. When they fall back, they emit light of a specific wavelength. Lithium is crimson, sodium is yellow-orange, potassium is lilac, calcium is brick red, strontium is red and barium is green.

8.18: Experiments on thermal decomposition

  • Heat a small sample of nitrate or carbonate in a test tube and test the gas. Brown NO₂ shows a nitrate; a glowing splint relit by O₂ shows oxygen. A carbonate gives CO₂, which turns limewater milky.
  • Compare the temperatures needed for decomposition down a group to show the trend in 8.16.

8.19: Identifying ions

  • Carbonate (CO₃²⁻) or hydrogencarbonate (HCO₃⁻): add dilute acid. CO₂ is released and turns limewater milky. Ionic equation: CO₃²⁻ + 2H⁺ → H₂O + CO₂.
  • Sulfate (SO₄²⁻): add acidified barium chloride. A white precipitate of BaSO₄ forms: Ba²⁺ + SO₄²⁻ → BaSO₄. The acid stops carbonate and sulfite interfering.
  • Ammonium (NH₄⁺): add sodium hydroxide and warm. Ammonia is released, turns damp red litmus blue, and gives white fumes with HCl.

8.20 to 8.23: Concentrations, titrations and uncertainty

  • 8.20: concentration in mol dm⁻³ = moles ÷ volume in dm³. To convert to g dm⁻³, multiply by the molar mass.
  • Indicators: methyl orange changes from red to yellow at about pH 3–4, suited to strong acid against weak base. Phenolphthalein changes from colourless to pink at about pH 8–10, suited to weak acid against strong base.
  • 8.21 (core practical 3): titrate hydrochloric acid against a standard alkali, record the titre and use the balanced equation to find the acid's concentration.
  • 8.22: reduce uncertainty by rinsing the pipette and burette, reading the meniscus at eye level, and repeating until two titres agree within 0.10 cm³. A burette reading has an uncertainty of ±0.05 cm³, so a titre has ±0.10 cm³. Calculate the percentage uncertainty as uncertainty ÷ reading × 100.
  • 8.23 (core practical 4): weigh a solid acid such as hydrated ethanedioic acid accurately, dissolve it, make it up to 250 cm³ in a volumetric flask, and use it as a standard solution to find the concentration of sodium hydroxide.

8.24: Trends in Group 7

  • Melting and boiling points rise down the group, because the molecules are larger and have stronger London forces. Fluorine and chlorine are gases, bromine is a liquid, iodine is a solid.
  • Electronegativity falls down the group, because the bonding pair sits further from the nucleus and is shielded more.
  • Reactivity (oxidising power) falls down the group, because the atoms are larger and gain an electron less readily.

8.25: Displacement reactions and colours

  • A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive halide: Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂, and Cl₂ or Br₂ + 2I⁻ → I₂ + halide.
  • Colours: in water, chlorine is pale green-yellow, bromine is orange and iodine is brown. In a non-polar organic solvent such as cyclohexane, bromine stays orange and iodine turns violet.

8.26: Reactions of the halogens, including disproportionation

  • (i) Halogens oxidise Group 1 and 2 metals to halides, for example 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl.
  • (ii) Chlorine with water is a disproportionation: Cl₂ + H₂O ⇌ HCl + HClO. The HClO is the basis of chlorine water treatment.
  • (iii) Chlorine with cold, dilute NaOH gives bleach: Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaClO + H₂O.
  • (iv) With hot concentrated alkali, chlorine disproportionates to chlorate: 3Cl₂ + 6NaOH → 5NaCl + NaClO₃ + 3H₂O.
  • (v) Bromine behaves in the same way with cold alkali. Use the oxidation number of each chlorine to check each product.

8.27: Reactions of halides and hydrogen halides

  • (i) Solid halides with concentrated H₂SO₄ show the reducing trend. NaCl gives HCl only. NaBr is oxidised further to Br₂ and SO₂. NaI is oxidised to I₂ and H₂S. The reducing ability is HI > HBr > HCl.
  • (ii) Silver nitrate with the halide ions in nitric acid: AgCl is white, AgBr is cream, AgI is yellow. AgCl dissolves in dilute aqueous ammonia, AgBr only in concentrated ammonia, and AgI does not dissolve.
  • (iii) Hydrogen halides with ammonia give ammonium halides (NH₃ + HCl → NH₄Cl). With water they give acids.

8.28: Predicting fluorine and astatine

  • Fluorine is the most electronegative element and the strongest oxidising agent in the group. It reacts violently with water, displacing oxygen from it.
  • Astatine is at the bottom of the group, so by the trends it should be a dark, solid, less reactive halogen than iodine, with a lower electronegativity. It is radioactive, so its chemistry is hard to study directly, and predictions come from the trends.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Half-equations in acid, 8.10 applied: dichromate(VI) reduced by iron(II). Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6e⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O, and Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + e⁻ (multiply by 6). Adding gives Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 6Fe²⁺ + 14H⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + 6Fe³⁺ + 7H₂O. Check atoms, then charge: both sides total +24.
  • Titration calculation, 8.20 and 8.22 applied: 25.0 cm³ of an iron(II) solution needs 18.0 cm³ of 0.0200 mol dm⁻³ K₂Cr₂O₇. Moles of dichromate = 0.0200 × 0.0180 = 3.60 × 10⁻⁴ mol. Each dichromate needs six Fe²⁺, so Fe²⁺ = 2.16 × 10⁻³ mol. Concentration = 2.16 × 10⁻³ ÷ 0.0250 = 0.0864 mol dm⁻³. An A* answer shows the ratio from the balanced equation before any arithmetic.
  • Disproportionation, 8.7 and 8.26 applied: chlorine with cold dilute NaOH gives Cl⁻ (0 to −1, reduction) and ClO⁻ (0 to +1, oxidation) in one reaction. Name both oxidation numbers when explaining why a reaction is disproportionation.
  • Group 2 hydroxide solubility, 8.15 applied: solubility rises down the group because hydration enthalpy falls more steeply than lattice enthalpy as the cation grows. Lattice enthalpy depends on the ion sizes and charges; hydration enthalpy depends on how strongly water molecules bind the cation. Both are needed for full marks.
  • Thermal stability, 8.16 applied: a small, highly charged cation such as Mg²⁺ polarises a carbonate ion strongly, which weakens its C–O bonds, so MgCO₃ decomposes at a lower temperature than BaCO₃. Use the word polarisation, not just "smaller ions decompose more easily".
  • Halogen displacement and redox direction, 8.25 and 8.27 applied: chlorine oxidises bromide and iodide, bromine oxidises iodide, but iodine oxidises neither. Read the direction from the reducing trend: iodide is the strongest reducing agent among the halides, which is why concentrated sulfuric acid reduces HI to H₂S.

Common errors that lose marks

  • Using the wrong oxidation number for oxygen in a peroxide or hydrogen in a metal hydride.
  • Confusing reducing ability with reactivity for the halogens: reactivity falls down Group 7, but the reducing ability of the halide ions rises.
  • Writing the test for sulfate without acid. Without acid, carbonate would also give a white precipitate.

title: Mensuration — Bearings and Loci — Study Notes
content:
Mensuration — Bearings and Loci

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): compass bearings, scale drawings, constructions (perpendicular/angle bisectors), loci regions.

1. Bearings

  • Measured clockwise from north; three figures: 065°, 128°, 300°.
  • Back bearing = front bearing ± 180°.
  • Draw a north line at both points; north lines are parallel, giving Z-angles.

Example: B is on bearing 070° from A → A is on bearing 250° from B.

2. Scale drawings

1 cm : 500 m style scales; measure, convert, and quote distances/bearings from your drawing to the accuracy allowed.

3. Constructions

  • Perpendicular bisector of a segment: equal arcs from both ends, join the crossings.
  • Angle bisector: equal arcs from the vertex arms.
  • 60° and 90° constructions with compasses; leave all arcs visible.

4. Loci

Fixed distance from a point = circle; from a line = parallel lines with rounded ends; equidistant from two points = perpendicular bisector; from two lines = angle bisector.

Example: a goat tied by a 5 m rope to a corner of a 4 m × 6 m shed: the reachable region is ¾ circle radius 5 m + two ¼ circles radius 1 m where the rope wraps.

Exam tips: state "clockwise from north" in bearing definitions; shade/label locus regions clearly; use a ruler for construction lines too.

title: IGCSE Computer Science: Databases and SQL
content:
IGCSE Computer Science: Databases and SQL

Cambridge IGCSE Computer Science 0478 (2026–2028), Paper 2 Algorithms, Programming and Logic, statement 9 Databases. Almost every real program stores records — customers, orders, results — and a database is how that is done properly. This note covers the relational model from first principles (tables, keys, relationships), the design rules that stop data going wrong, and the four SQL commands the syllabus examines — SELECT, FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY — with every query parsed clause by clause against a worked dataset.

Why databases, and what a DBMS is

Storing records in ordinary files leads to the classic file problems: the same data duplicated in several files (inconsistency when one copy changes), no way to enforce rules (a mark of 700), updates needing code in every program, and no concurrent access. A database stores structured data once, under shared rules; a database management system (DBMS) is the software that manages it — handling storage, validation rules, security (user accounts and permissions), backup and recovery, and allowing many users to work at once without corrupting data.

The relational model organises data into tables (relations): rows are records, columns are fields, and each field holds one data type. The factory analogy: instead of every department keeping its own customer list, there is one customer table that every department consults — one version of the truth.

Fields, records and data types

ColumnData typeWhy this type
studentIDINTEGER / text codeIdentifies each student; used in relationships
surnameSTRING / VARCHAR(30)Text of bounded length
dobDATEDates need date arithmetic (age checks), not string comparisons
markINTEGERWhole numbers; allows range checks 0–100
averageREALDecimal places needed
isEnrolledBOOLEANTrue/false flag

Choosing types is a mark: types constrain what can be stored (a DATE field rejects "hello"), save space, and make correct operations possible (you cannot average a string field).

Keys

  • Primary key — the field (or combination) that uniquely identifies each record in a table: no duplicates, never empty. StudentID, not surname (two students may share a surname).
  • Foreign key — a field in one table that is the primary key of another, creating a relationship between the tables. In a results table, studentID is a foreign key pointing at the students table.
Two related tables, worked:

STUDENTS                         RESULTS
studentID  surname   class       resultID  studentID  subject   mark
101        Ali       11A         1         101        Maths     72
102        Banda     11A         2         101        Physics   65
103        Chen      11B         3         102        Maths     58

RESULTS.studentID is a foreign key: every value there must match a STUDENTS.
studentID. That referential rule stops a result existing for a student who does
not - and deleting student 102 must deal with their result row (cascade delete
or refuse), which the exam likes to probe.

Relationships come in three shapes: one-to-many (one student, many results — the common case), one-to-one (one student, one locker record) and many-to-many (students and subjects — resolved in practice with a linking table of pairs).

Database design: normalisation and its rules

Normalisation structures tables so that each fact is stored once. First normal form (1NF): no repeating groups — every field holds a single value; a "subjects" field listing "Maths, Physics" is split into separate rows. Second normal form (2NF): 1NF plus no partial dependency — every non-key field depends on the whole key, not part of it. Third normal form (3NF): 2NF plus no transitive dependency — non-key fields must not depend on each other; if a student row holds class and classTeacher, then classTeacher depends on class, not on studentID, so it moves to its own table.

Normalisation worked on one bad table:

Unnormalised:  studentID, name, class, classTeacher, subject, mark
(one row per student with repeating subjects)

1NF - remove repeating groups: one row per student per subject.
  studentID, name, class, classTeacher, subject, mark

2NF - the key is (studentID, subject). name, class and classTeacher depend only
on studentID (part of the key) - split them out:
  STUDENTS: studentID, name, class, classTeacher
  RESULTS:  studentID, subject, mark

3NF - in STUDENTS, classTeacher depends on class, which depends on studentID -
a transitive dependency. Split again:
  STUDENTS: studentID, name, class
  CLASSES:  class, classTeacher
  RESULTS:  studentID, subject, mark

Benefits: no duplicated teacher names to update in fifty rows, no chance of the
same student having two different names, and insertions and deletions no longer
distort unrelated data.

Why it matters earns separate marks: normalisation minimises duplication and therefore the risk of data inconsistency, and prevents update, insertion and deletion anomalies — e.g. deleting the only result of a student would wipe their name if everything sat in one table.

Structured Query Language (SQL)

SQL is the standard language for defining and querying relational databases; it is declarative — you state what you want, and the DBMS works out how. The examined queries have the shape:

SELECT   which columns to show
FROM     which table(s)
WHERE    which rows qualify (a condition)
ORDER BY how to sort the result

Parsing a query against STUDENTS and RESULTS above:

  "List the names of students in class 11A, alphabetically."

  SELECT surname
  FROM STUDENTS
  WHERE class = '11A'
  ORDER BY surname ASC;

  Step 1: FROM - look at the STUDENTS table.
  Step 2: WHERE - keep only rows where class is '11A' (rows 101, 102).
  Step 3: SELECT - from those rows keep just the surname column.
  Step 4: ORDER BY - sort ascending: Ali, Banda.

  Query 2: "List studentID and mark for Maths results, highest mark first."

  SELECT studentID, mark
  FROM RESULTS
  WHERE subject = 'Maths'
  ORDER BY mark DESC;

  Result: (101, 72), (102, 58) - DESC puts the biggest first.
  • Text values go in quotes ('11A'); numbers do not.
  • Conditions use =, <>, <, >, <=, >=, and combine with AND / OR / NOT.
  • SELECT * shows every column; naming columns is better practice and often earns the mark.
  • ORDER BY defaults to ascending; DESC reverses.
  • Useful extras the syllabus allows: COUNT(*), SUM, AVG/MIN/MAX aggregates, GROUP BY to aggregate per category, and LIKE for pattern matching (WHERE surname LIKE 'B%').
Aggregate example: "How many results does each student have, where the count
is at least 2?"

  SELECT studentID, COUNT(*)
  FROM RESULTS
  GROUP BY studentID
  HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2;

  FROM → rows of RESULTS; GROUP BY → one group per studentID (101: 2 rows,
  102: 1 row); HAVING filters groups after aggregation (WHERE filters rows
  before it); SELECT outputs (101, 2).

Data validation and verification at input

Before a record is stored it is checked — validation ensures data is sensible, verification ensures it matches what was intended: presence checks (a required field cannot be empty), type checks (digits only in a phone field), length checks (exactly 8 characters), range checks (mark between 0 and 100), check digits (an ISBN-style computed digit catches transcription slips), and list/pick-list checks (a value must come from an allowed set). Verification includes double entry (typing it twice) and visual checks against the source. The exam wants the technique matched to the error: range check for a mark, check digit for an account number.

Worked example: a complete query set

Table BOOKS: bookID (PK), title, author, year, price

1. All titles costing less than 10 pounds, cheapest first:
   SELECT title, price FROM BOOKS WHERE price < 10 ORDER BY price ASC;

2. Books published after 2015 by "Lee":
   SELECT title, year FROM BOOKS WHERE year > 2015 AND author = 'Lee';

3. How many books has each author written?
   SELECT author, COUNT(*) FROM BOOKS GROUP BY author;

4. The most expensive book:
   SELECT title, price FROM BOOKS ORDER BY price DESC;  (take the first row)

Each query is executed the same way every time: FROM picks the table, WHERE
filters rows, GROUP BY aggregates, HAVING filters groups, SELECT projects
columns, ORDER BY sorts the finished result.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Confusing WHERE with ORDER BY: WHERE filters rows before sorting; ORDER BY only sorts what survives.
  • Forgetting quotes around text values (WHERE class = 11A) or wrongly quoting numbers.
  • Choosing a non-unique field as the primary key (surname); and leaving the primary key empty or duplicated — both are impossible by definition.
  • Saying a foreign key "links tables" without the referential rule: every foreign key value must exist as a primary key in the referenced table.
  • Stopping normalisation at "no duplicate rows" — the anomalies language (update/insert/delete anomaly, transitive dependency) is what the mark scheme wants.
  • Writing SELECT before FROM in analysis answers; the execution order is FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY.
  • Using WHERE to filter an aggregate (WHERE COUNT(*) > 2 fails); aggregates are filtered with HAVING.
  • Mixing validation and verification: validation checks sense (range, type), verification checks accuracy against the source (double entry).

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 2, 3 marks). Explain the difference between a primary key and a foreign key.

Answer: A primary key is the field (or combination) that uniquely identifies each record in its table — it must be unique and never empty. A foreign key is a field in one table whose values are the primary key of another table, creating a link between them and enforcing referential integrity: the database refuses values with no matching record.

Question 2 (Paper 2, 4 marks). A table holds studentID, name, class, classTeacher, subject, mark. Explain the problems with storing classTeacher in this table.

Answer: classTeacher depends on class rather than on the student — a transitive dependency (2NF/3NF violation). The teacher's name is duplicated across every result row of every student in that class: changing one teacher means many updates (update anomaly) and inconsistent copies if only some are changed; deleting a class's only student deletes the teacher record too. Moving class and classTeacher to their own table stores each fact once.

Question 3 (Paper 2, 4 marks). Write SQL to list the titles of all books by "Chen" published after 2020, in alphabetical order.

Answer: SELECT title FROM BOOKS WHERE author = 'Chen' AND year > 2020 ORDER BY title ASC;

Question 4 (Paper 2, 4 marks). State four validation checks and give an example of the data each would reject.

Answer: Presence check — rejects an empty required field. Type check — rejects "abc" in an integer field. Range check — rejects a mark of 150 (outside 0–100). Length check — rejects a 7-character code where 8 are required. (Also acceptable: check digit rejecting a mistyped account number; list check rejecting a subject not offered.)

Question 5 (Paper 2, 3 marks). Explain why a DBMS is used instead of separate data files for each department.

Answer: A DBMS stores each item of data once, eliminating duplicated and inconsistent copies, and centralises the rules: validation on every update, user permissions and audit trails, and backup/recovery. It also lets several users access and update the data concurrently under lock control, without one department overwriting another's work.

Question 6 (Paper 2, 4 marks). Describe the output of: SELECT subject, AVG(mark) FROM RESULTS GROUP BY subject;

Answer: The rows of RESULTS are grouped by subject; for each group the average mark is computed; the output has one row per subject showing the subject name and that group's mean mark — for the sample data: Maths 65 (72 and 58), Physics 65.

The final Paper 2 domain puts logic itself into hardware: Boolean algebra and the gates that compute with truth.

title: IGCSE Biology: Inheritance
content:
IGCSE Biology: Inheritance

Why do you look like your parents but not exactly like either of them? The answer is written in the behaviour of chromosomes during two kinds of cell division, and this note builds it from scratch: DNA and genes first, then mitosis (the copying division), meiosis (the halving-and-shuffling division), and finally the monohybrid cross with every step of a Punnett square worked out loud. The vocabulary — gene, allele, dominant, recessive, homozygous, heterozygous, genotype, phenotype — is defined precisely and paired with a worked cross, because marks are lost when these words are swapped.

Chromosomes, genes and proteins

In the nucleus, DNA is wound around proteins to form chromosomes. A gene is a section of DNA that codes for the sequence of amino acids in a specific protein — and proteins build and run the organism (enzymes, structural proteins like keratin, hormones like insulin). One gene, one polypeptide is the classic summary. Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes (46 total): 22 pairs of autosomes and one pair of sex chromosomes (XX female, XY male). A variant of a gene is an allele — for flower colour there may be a purple allele and a white allele. Chromosomes carry genes in a fixed order (loci), and each body cell has the full diploid set, while gametes carry one of each pair (haploid).

Dominant, recessive and the vocabulary table

TermMeaningExample
GeneSection of DNA coding for a proteinFlower-colour gene
AlleleVariant form of a genePurple allele or white allele
DominantAllele expressed in the phenotype when present with any other alleleB (purple)
RecessiveAllele expressed only when two copies are presentb (white)
HomozygousTwo identical allelesBB or bb
HeterozygousTwo different allelesBb
GenotypeThe allele combination an organism carriesBb
PhenotypeThe observable featurePurple flowers

Key logic to internalise: a recessive phenotype (white) always reveals the genotype (bb), because a white organism must carry two recessive alleles; a dominant phenotype (purple) could be BB or Bb — a test cross (with a homozygous recessive) distinguishes them. That inference is a standard "explain how you would tell" question.

Mitosis: growth and repair

Mitosis produces two genetically identical diploid daughter cells. Purpose: growth, repair of damaged tissues, and asexual reproduction.
