Sequence (learn the order, and what happens at each stage): interphase — the cell grows, DNA replicates (each chromosome now two identical chromatids joined at a centromere) and organelles multiply, using ATP; prophase — chromosomes condense and become visible, the nuclear envelope breaks down; metaphase — chromosomes line up along the equator of the cell, attached to spindle fibres; anaphase — centromeres divide and sister chromatids are pulled to opposite poles; telophase — two nuclei form around each set, and the cytoplasm divides (cytokinesis). The outcome: 2 daughter cells, each with 46 chromosomes in humans, genetically identical to each other and to the parent cell.

Meiosis: variation and gametes

Meiosis produces four genetically different haploid gametes (sex cells) — sperm or egg cells in animals, pollen and ovules in plants. It involves two divisions. Meiosis I: homologous chromosome pairs (one from each parent) pair up along the equator and then separate — this halves the chromosome number (from 46 to 23). Meiosis II: the sister chromatids separate, giving four cells each with 23 single chromosomes. Two sources of variation: crossing over (in prophase I, homologous chromosomes twist and swap sections of DNA, creating new allele combinations on a chromosome) and independent assortment (which member of each pair goes to which daughter cell is random — with 23 pairs, 2²³ ≈ 8.4 million combinations possible before crossing over). Meiosis is therefore the engine of genetic variation: no two gametes are genetically identical. Fertilisation (fusion of two haploid gametes) then restores the diploid number and adds yet more variation, combining the genes of two parents.

Monohybrid inheritance: the master method

A monohybrid cross tracks one gene. Method (memorise the six steps): Step 1: choose symbols — a capital letter for the dominant allele, the same letter lower case for the recessive (B and b). Step 2: write each parent's genotype (e.g. Bb × Bb). Step 3: draw the Punnett square: parental gametes along the top and side (B and b from each). Step 4: fill in the four boxes by combining one allele from each parent (BB, Bb, Bb, bb). Step 5: read off the genotypic ratio (1 BB : 2 Bb : 1 bb) and the phenotypic ratio (3 purple : 1 white). Step 6: state the probabilities as fractions (¾ purple, ¼ white), percentages (75 %, 25 %) or a ratio (3:1), as the question asks. Crossing two heterozygotes always gives 3:1 phenotypic and 1:2:1 genotypic. Crossing a heterozygote with a homozygous recessive (a test cross) gives 1:1 phenotypically.

Worked example: a full monohybrid cross from scratch

In pea plants, tall (T) is dominant over short (t). Cross a heterozygous tall plant with a short plant. Step 1: symbols — T tall, t short. Step 2: genotypes — Tt × tt. Step 3: gametes — the tall parent gives T and t; the short parent gives t only. Step 4: Punnett square (top row T, t; side column t, t): boxes are Tt, tt, Tt, tt. Step 5: genotypic ratio — 2 Tt : 2 tt, simplified 1:1. Step 6: phenotype — 2 tall : 2 short = 1:1 (50 % tall, 50 % short). Second worked cross: two heterozygous tall plants (Tt × Tt): gametes T and t from each; square gives TT, Tt, Tt, tt; genotypic ratio 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt; phenotypic ratio 3 tall : 1 short. If the question asks the chance of a tall offspring from Tt × Tt, the answer is ¾ = 75 %; if it asks the chance of a homozygous tall, it is ¼ = 25 %. Show the square every time — it is a mark in itself.

Sex determination and sex-linked inheritance

Sex is determined by the sex chromosomes: females are XX, males are XY. A Punnett square for XX × XY gives: X from the mother combined with X (daughter) or Y (son) from the father — so the father's sperm determines the sex, 50:50. Sex-linked genes sit on the sex chromosomes (usually the X). Males (XY) express any allele on their single X — so recessive X-linked conditions (colour blindness, haemophilia) are far more common in males. Colour-blindness example: Xᴮ normal, Xᵇ colour-blind. A carrier mother (XᴮXᵇ) × normal father (XᴮY): daughters — XᴮXᴮ (normal), XᴮXᵇ (carrier, normal vision); sons — XᴮY (normal), XᵇY (colour-blind). So half the sons are affected, and no daughter is affected (though half are carriers). Write genotypes with the X superscript attached to the allele — the exam requires showing the X and Y chromosomes explicitly. Haemophilia: blood fails to clot (missing clotting factor VIII); affected males may die from cuts; treated with clotting-factor injections (historically from donated blood — the HIV-contaminated supply scandal).

Codominance and multiple alleles

Not all alleles are simply dominant or recessive. Codominance: both alleles are expressed in the heterozygote (blood groups are the classic example — allele Iᴬ and Iᴮ are codominant, i recessive). Blood-group genotypes: type A = IᴬIᴬ or Iᴬi; type B = IᴮIᴮ or Iᴮi; type AB = IᴬIᴮ (codominant); type O = ii. Multiple alleles: more than two alleles exist in the population (three: Iᴬ, Iᴮ, i), though each individual carries only two. The inheritance squares work the same way — cross Iᴬi × Iᴮi and the four boxes give IᴬIᴮ (AB), Iᴬi (A), Iᴮi (B), ii (O); the phenotypic ratio is 1:1:1:1. Blood typing is used in forensics (paternity testing, crime scenes) and medicine (transfusions must match the ABO group, or antibodies attack the donated cells).

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Swapping gene and allele: a gene is the DNA section; an allele is one variant of it. Mixing them costs the definition mark.
  • Writing "the dominant allele is stronger": dominance describes which allele is expressed in the phenotype, not which is better or more common.
  • Forgetting that the Punnett square needs parental gametes on the outside — filling the square from the parents' phenotypes is a classic error.
  • Leaving ratios as fractions when the question asks "as a ratio" (3:1) or vice versa; answer in the form requested.
  • Writing sex-linked genotypes without the X or Y chromosome (just "Bb") — lose the mark.
  • Claiming mitosis produces variation: mitosis makes identical clones; only meiosis (crossing over, independent assortment) and fertilisation create variation.
  • Confusing crossing over (exchange of DNA between homologous chromosomes) with independent assortment (random orientation of pairs).
  • Saying a carrier "has the disease": a carrier (heterozygous) has a normal phenotype for recessive conditions.

Exam-style questions and answers

Q1. Define the terms allele, genotype and phenotype. (3 marks) Answer: allele — a variant form of a gene (1); genotype — the alleles an organism carries (1); phenotype — the observable feature of the organism (1).

Q2. In pea plants, purple (P) is dominant over white (p). Cross two heterozygous plants and give the phenotypic ratio. (4 marks) Answer: Pp × Pp (1); Punnett square giving PP, Pp, Pp, pp (1); genotypic ratio 1:2:1 (1); phenotypic ratio 3 purple : 1 white (1).

Q3. Explain why males are more likely to be colour-blind than females. (3 marks) Answer: the allele for colour blindness is recessive and carried on the X chromosome (1); males have only one X chromosome so one recessive allele is expressed (1); females need two copies — one from each parent (1).

Q4. Describe the role of meiosis in producing genetic variation. (4 marks) Answer: crossing over in prophase I exchanges DNA between homologous chromosomes (1); independent assortment of pairs at metaphase I gives many combinations (1); four genetically different haploid cells are produced (1); fertilisation then combines genes from two parents (1).

Q5. Explain how a test cross can determine whether a purple-flowered plant is homozygous or heterozygous. (3 marks) Answer: cross with a homozygous recessive (white) plant (1); if all offspring are purple, the parent is homozygous dominant (1); if any white offspring appear (about half), the parent is heterozygous (1).

title: IGCSE Biology (OxfordAQA): Bioenergetics
content:
Bioenergetics

Life needs energy and materials, and this topic is about how a plant captures the first and how both plants and animals move the second around. Five structures in the specification look unrelated — the leaf, the root hair, the alveolus, the villus and the capillary — but they are the same solution to the same problem: a surface must be large, thin and moist, with a steep concentration gradient behind it, or the exchange will be too slow. Photosynthesis makes the sugar, respiration releases the energy, and circulation, digestion and breathing are the transport and supply systems that keep both running. Learn the structures with the reason for their shape and the "explain" questions answer themselves.

1. Photosynthesis

Photosynthesis uses light energy to convert carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen, inside chloroplasts, in cells containing chlorophyll.

6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂   (light energy absorbed by chlorophyll)

Key: CO₂ = carbon dioxide (g), taken in through the stomata; H₂O = water (l), absorbed by the roots; C₆H₁₂O₆ = glucose, used for growth, storage as starch, or converted to cellulose; O₂ = oxygen (g), released as a by-product.

Photosynthesis is endothermic: it takes energy in from light. Respiration is the opposite in that respect, releasing energy from glucose. A plant does both at once, which is why "plants photosynthesise and animals respire" is wrong — a plant respires all day and all night.

  • Light intensity — more light, faster photosynthesis, until another factor becomes limiting.
  • Carbon dioxide concentration — a raw material, so more of it increases the rate up to a point.
  • Temperature — enzymes catalyse the reactions, so the rate rises with temperature until they denature.
  • Amount of chlorophyll — a variegated leaf photosynthesises more slowly in its white areas, which is the classic experiment.

Whichever factor is in shortest supply is the limiting factor, and that is the one a graph plateaus against. A curve that levels off at high light intensity is limited by carbon dioxide or temperature, not by light.

2. Worked example: testing a leaf for starch

A leaf is boiled in ethanol, washed and tested with iodine. Explain why each step is done and predict the result for a leaf kept in the dark for 24 hours.

The leaf is boiled in water to break down the cell membranes, then in ethanol to remove the chlorophyll so the colour change can be seen; iodine solution turns blue-black where starch is present. A leaf kept in the dark cannot photosynthesise, so it uses up its stored starch in respiration and the iodine stays yellow-brown.

Key: ethanol = the solvent that removes chlorophyll, heated in a water bath because ethanol is flammable; iodine = the test for starch; blue-black = starch present; yellow-brown = no starch.

The control matters: a destarched plant proves any starch found was made during the experiment, and a variegated leaf shows that only the green parts photosynthesise. Both are worth a mark in a "describe how you would show" question.

3. Exchange and transport in plants

Water and mineral ions enter through root hair cells, which are long and thin to give a large surface area, and travel up the stem in the xylem. Sugars made in the leaves travel in the phloem. The two tissues form a transport system in a plant that has no pump, which is why transpiration matters: water evaporating from the leaves pulls more water up behind it.

  • Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from leaves, mostly through the stomata. It is fastest when it is warm, dry, windy and bright.
  • Translocation is the movement of sugars and amino acids through the phloem, from sources such as leaves to sinks such as roots, fruits and growing tips.
  • Stomata open in light and close in darkness or drought; guard cells control the pore, balancing carbon dioxide uptake against water loss.

The transpiration rate is measured with a potometer, which measures water uptake rather than water loss — a distinction the exam asks for, because some of the water taken up is used in photosynthesis and some stays in the plant.

4. Circulation in humans

Humans have a double circulatory system: blood passes through the heart twice for each circuit of the body. The right side pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs at low pressure, and the left side pumps oxygenated blood around the body at high pressure. Two circuits mean the blood keeps its pressure on the way to the body, which delivers oxygen faster.

Blood vesselDirectionWall and lumenSpecial feature
ArteryAway from the heartThick muscular wall, narrow lumenWithstands high pressure; elastic recoil maintains flow
VeinTowards the heartThin wall, wide lumenValves prevent backflow at low pressure
CapillaryBetween the twoOne cell thickShort diffusion distance for exchange with tissues

Blood carries red cells (haemoglobin, no nucleus, biconcave), white cells (defence), platelets (clotting) and plasma (dissolved substances, including carbon dioxide and glucose). The heart has four chambers, with valves between atria and ventricles and at the exits, so blood flows one way; the left ventricle has the thickest wall because it pumps furthest.

5. Worked example: cardiac output

A student has a stroke volume of 70 cm³ and a heart rate of 72 beats per minute at rest, and 120 cm³ and 150 beats per minute during exercise. Calculate the cardiac output in each case and in litres per minute.

cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate = 70 × 72 = 5 040 cm³/min = 5.04 dm³/min, and 120 × 150 = 18 000 cm³/min = 18.0 dm³/min.

Key: cardiac output = the volume of blood pumped per minute (cm³/min or dm³/min); stroke volume = the volume pumped per beat (cm³); heart rate = beats per minute (bpm); 1 000 cm³ = 1 dm³ = 1 litre.

During exercise the output roughly triples, and both factors contribute: the heart beats more often and each beat is stronger. That is the physiological reason exercise raises the rate of oxygen delivery to muscles, not just the fact that "the heart beats faster".

6. Digestion

Digestion breaks large insoluble molecules into small soluble ones that can be absorbed. Mechanical digestion — chewing and the churning of the stomach — increases surface area; chemical digestion uses enzymes to hydrolyse bonds.

  • Amylase (salivary and pancreatic) breaks starch into maltose.
  • Protease (stomach pepsin and pancreatic protease) breaks proteins into amino acids.
  • Lipase (pancreatic) breaks fats into fatty acids and glycerol.
  • Bile is made in the liver, stored in the gall bladder and released into the small intestine. It emulsifies fat into small droplets, increasing surface area for lipase, and neutralises stomach acid so the pancreatic enzymes can work.

Absorption happens in the small intestine, whose lining is folded into villi. A villus has a thin wall, a rich blood supply and a lacteal, all of which keep the concentration gradient steep and the diffusion distance short. The colon absorbs water, leaving the remaining material as faeces.

Food testReagentPositive result
StarchIodine solutionBlue-black
Sugar (reducing)Benedict's solution, heatedBrick-red precipitate
ProteinBiuret solutionPurple
FatEthanol and waterCloudy white emulsion

7. Breathing and gas exchange

Breathing moves air in and out of the lungs; respiration is the chemical release of energy in cells. Confusing the two is the most common error in this topic.

  • Inhaling: the intercostal muscles and diaphragm contract, the ribcage moves up and out, the diaphragm flattens, the thorax volume increases and the pressure falls, so air is drawn in.
  • Exhaling: the muscles relax, the ribcage moves down and in, the diaphragm domes upwards, volume falls and pressure rises, so air is pushed out.

Gas exchange happens in the alveoli, which are adapted by having a very large total surface area, walls one cell thick, a moist lining and a dense capillary network. Oxygen diffuses from the air into the blood and carbon dioxide diffuses out, both down their concentration gradients. Smoking damages the alveoli, reducing surface area and causing emphysema.

8. Respiration

Respiration releases energy from glucose in every living cell, all the time. Aerobic respiration uses oxygen and releases far more energy per glucose molecule than anaerobic respiration, which does not use oxygen.

C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O   (aerobic, releases energy)

Key: C₆H₁₂O₆ = glucose; O₂ = oxygen; CO₂ = carbon dioxide; H₂O = water; the energy released drives muscle contraction, active transport and the maintenance of body temperature.

During hard exercise the oxygen supply cannot keep up, so muscles respire anaerobically: glucose → lactic acid, releasing much less energy. Lactic acid builds up and contributes to muscle fatigue. The extra oxygen needed afterwards to break the lactic acid down is the oxygen debt, which is why breathing stays fast after exercise stops.

In yeast, anaerobic respiration produces ethanol and carbon dioxide — fermentation, which is how bread rises and how beer is brewed.

9. Typical mistakes

  • Saying plants only photosynthesise. They respire continuously as well.
  • Writing "breathing releases energy". Breathing is ventilation; respiration releases energy.
  • Claiming anaerobic respiration releases more energy because it is faster. It releases much less per glucose molecule.
  • Forgetting bile's second job. Emulsification is the one everyone remembers; neutralising acid is the other mark.
  • Saying arteries carry oxygenated blood. They carry blood away from the heart — the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood.
  • Giving the transpiration rate as water loss when a potometer measures uptake.
  • Describing a villus as "thin" without saying what that achieves: a short diffusion distance.

10. Exam-style questions

  1. State the word equation for photosynthesis and name the organelle where it happens. Answer: Carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen, using light energy absorbed by chlorophyll, in the chloroplast.
  2. Explain why the rate of photosynthesis stops increasing as light intensity rises. Answer: Light is no longer the limiting factor; another factor such as carbon dioxide concentration or temperature is now in shortest supply.
  3. Explain how the structure of an alveolus speeds up gas exchange. Answer: It has a very large surface area, a wall one cell thick for a short diffusion distance, a moist lining and a good blood supply to maintain a steep concentration gradient.
  4. Give two ways the small intestine is adapted for absorption. Answer: Its lining is folded into villi, which increase surface area, and each villus has a thin wall and a rich blood supply to maintain a concentration gradient.
  5. Calculate the cardiac output of a person with a stroke volume of 80 cm³ and a heart rate of 60 bpm. Answer: 80 × 60 = 4 800 cm³/min, which is 4.8 dm³/min.
  6. Explain why the heart rate stays high after vigorous exercise. Answer: Muscles respired anaerobically and produced lactic acid; the extra oxygen is needed to break it down, which is the oxygen debt.
  7. Compare aerobic and anaerobic respiration in humans. Answer: Aerobic uses oxygen and releases much more energy per glucose, producing carbon dioxide and water; anaerobic happens without oxygen, releases less energy and produces lactic acid.
  8. Explain why a plant wilts faster on a hot, windy day. Answer: High temperature and wind increase the rate of transpiration, so water is lost faster than it is taken up, and the cells lose turgor.

11. Revision checklist

  • I can write the photosynthesis equation and name the limiting factors.
  • I can describe the starch test and explain why each step is done.
  • I can compare xylem and phloem and describe transpiration and translocation.
  • I can label the heart and compare arteries, veins and capillaries.
  • I can calculate cardiac output and explain what changes during exercise.
  • I can name the three digestive enzymes, their substrates and products.
  • I can give the four food tests and their positive results.
  • I can describe the mechanism of inhaling and exhaling.
  • I can compare aerobic and anaerobic respiration and explain oxygen debt.

title: Geometry — Angles and Polygons — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Geometry — Angles and Polygons

Mathematics — OL. angle facts, parallel lines, polygon angles, circle theorems (Extended).

  • 1. Core angle facts
  • 2. Polygons
  • 3. Circle theorems (Extended)
  • 4. Algebra with angles

How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

Worked example

The interior angle sum of a polygon with n sides is (n − 2) × 180°. For a regular octagon, n = 8, so the sum is 6 × 180° = 1080°. Each interior angle is 1080 ÷ 8 = 135°, and each exterior angle is 360 ÷ 8 = 45°. Exterior angles of any convex polygon always add up to 360°. Key: n = the number of sides (no units); (n − 2) × 180° is the interior angle sum in degrees, so a regular polygon's interior angle is that sum ÷ n and its exterior angle is 360° ÷ n.

Common mistakes

  • Using 360° for the interior sum instead of (n − 2) × 180°.
  • Confusing the angle at the centre with the angle at the circumference. The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference when both subtend the same arc.
  • Writing a reason without naming the theorem. Name it, for example "angles in the same segment" or "opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180°".

title: The Normal Distribution — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: The Normal Distribution

Mathematics — A2. A continuous distribution with the familiar bell shape, symmetric about the mean, described by two parameters: X ~ N(μ, σ²). The curve is fully determined by μ (centre) and σ (width). Total probability is 1, and because X is continuous, P(X = a) = 0 for any single point — inequalities do not need strictness.

Key areas to revise

  • The Model
  • Standardising
  • Backwards Problems
  • Symmetry Shortcuts
  • Normal Approximation to the Binomial

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

### Worked example X follows a normal distribution with mean μ and variance σ². Standardise with Z = (X − μ)/σ and read the probability from tables. For Z < 1.5, the table gives 0.9332. The curve is symmetric about the mean, so P(X < μ) = 0.5, and about 68% of values lie within one standard deviation of the mean and about 95% within two.

title: Hypothesis Testing — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Hypothesis Testing

Mathematics — A2. The null hypothesis H₀ is the default claim (no change, p = p₀). The alternative H₁ is what a suspicious observation suggests (p > p₀, p < p₀, or p ≠ p₀). The significance level α is the probability of rejecting a true H₀ — the false-alarm rate, usually 5% or 1%.

Key areas to revise

  • The Framework
  • Test for a Binomial Proportion
  • One-Tailed vs Two-Tailed
  • Critical Regions
  • Conclusions in Context

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

### Worked example A test of a claimed mean has a null hypothesis H₀ and an alternative H₁. Choose a significance level such as 5%, calculate the test statistic and its p-value, then reject H₀ if p < α. A two-tailed test looks for a change in either direction, so the 5% is split between the two tails. ### Check yourself Define a Type I error in words. It is rejecting H₀ when H₀ is actually true. Explain why lowering the significance level reduces the chance of a Type I error but increases the chance of a Type II error.

title: Number — Fractions, Decimals and Percentages — Study Notes
content:
Number — Fractions, Decimals and Percentages

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): conversions between fractions, decimals and percentages; percentage change; reverse percentages; compound change.

1. Conversions

Fraction → decimal by division; decimal → percentage ×100. Recurring decimals: let x = 0.7̄, then 10x − x = 7 ⇒ x = 7/9.

Compare fractions by common denominator or by converting to decimals.

2. Operating on fractions

  • Add/subtract: common denominator. 2/3 + 1/4 = 8/12 + 3/12 = 11/12.
  • Multiply: top×top, bottom×bottom. Divide: flip and multiply — 2/3 ÷ 4/5 = 2/3 × 5/4 = 5/6.
  • Of: 3/5 of 45 = 27.

3. Percentage change

change ÷ original × 100. Increase $80 by 15%: 80 × 1.15 = $92.

4. Reverse percentages

Original = new ÷ multiplier. "After a 20% increase a coat is $72" → 72 ÷ 1.2 = $60. "After 12% discount a phone is $440" → 440 ÷ 0.88 = $500.

5. Compound change

Multiplierⁿ. Simple interest I = Prt/100 vs compound P(1 + r/100)ⁿ.

Example: $800 at 3% for 4 years → 800 × 1.03⁴ = $900.41. Successive +10% then −10% ⇒ ×0.99 (net 1% decrease).

Exam tips: identify "increase TO" vs "increase BY"; for reverse questions divide, never subtract the percentage; quote money to 2 d.p.

Equivalent fractions and simplifying

Multiply or divide the numerator and denominator by the same non-zero number. Simplify by dividing both by their highest common factor. Mixed numbers are converted to improper fractions before multiplying or dividing.

Adding and subtracting fractions

Find the lowest common denominator, rewrite each fraction over it, then add or subtract the numerators only. Multiplying fractions multiplies the numerators and the denominators; dividing multiplies by the reciprocal of the second fraction.

Percentages

To find a percentage of a quantity, multiply by the decimal equivalent: 15% of 240 is 0.15 × 240 = 36. Percentage change is the change divided by the original value, multiplied by 100. Repeated percentage change multiplies by one plus the multiplier each time, so 5% increase twice is × 1.05 × 1.05.

Worked example: reverse percentage

After a 15% increase, a price is 230. The original price is the amount that equals 115% of itself, so divide by 1.15: 230 ÷ 1.15 = 200. Finding 15% of 230 and subtracting it gives 195.50, which is wrong, because 15% is taken of the original price, not the new one.

Compound change

1000 is invested at 4% per year for 3 years. Each year multiplies the value by 1.04, so the final value is 1000 × 1.04 × 1.04 × 1.04 = 1000 × 1.04³ = 1124.86 (to 2 decimal places). Simple interest would give only 1120, so the difference shows why compound growth is treated separately in the examination.

Choosing a method

  • To find a fraction of an amount, divide by the denominator and multiply by the numerator: 3/4 of 80 = 80 ÷ 4 × 3 = 60.
  • To add or subtract fractions, write both over a common denominator first.
  • Write a percentage change as a multiplier: a 20% decrease is multiplier 0.8, and a 5% increase is 1.05.

Exam point: give the final answer in the form the question asks for, such as a fraction in its simplest form or a percentage to 1 decimal place.

title: A Level Mathematics: Coordinate Geometry
content:
A Level Mathematics: Coordinate Geometry

Coordinate geometry is the bridge between algebra and shape: every geometric object is described by an equation, and every geometric question becomes an algebraic one. This note starts from the two measurements that define a straight line — how far and how steep — and builds outwards to circles, tangents, chords and the discriminant conditions that decide whether a line meets a curve at all. The exam almost never asks for a definition; it asks you to combine two or three of these tools in one question, so each one is presented with the situation that calls for it.

Distance, midpoint and gradient

Everything else is built on three formulas. They come from Pythagoras and from averaging, and they are worth being able to derive rather than recall.

for A(x1, y1) and B(x2, y2):
distance AB = √((x2 - x1)² + (y2 - y1)²)     Pythagoras on the step
midpoint   = ((x1 + x2)/2, (y1 + y2)/2)            the averages
gradient m = (y2 - y1)/(x2 - x1)                   rise over run

Worked example. For A(2, −1) and B(8, 7), find the distance AB, the midpoint and the gradient.

distance = √(6² + 8²) = √(100) = 10
midpoint = ((2+8)/2, (-1+7)/2) = (5, 3)
gradient = 8/6 = 4/3

Worked example 2 (finding an unknown). The distance from (1, 2) to (4, k) is 5. Find k.

√(3² + (k-2)²) = 5
9 + (k-2)² = 25
(k-2)² = 16  →  k - 2 = 4 or -4
k = 6 or k = -2

Two answers, not one: the square root in the distance formula hides a sign, and examiners always intend both.

Forms of the equation of a straight line

Three forms, each suited to a different piece of information. Choosing the wrong one costs time, not marks, but the wrong one also invites arithmetic slips.

FormEquationUse when you know
gradient–intercepty = mx + cgradient and intercept, or for sketching
point–gradienty − y1 = m(x − x1)gradient and one point
generalax + by + c = 0the form most mark schemes quote

Worked example. Find the equation of the line through (3, −2) with gradient −1/2, in general form.

y + 2 = (-1/2)(x - 3)
2y + 4 = -x + 3
x + 2y + 1 = 0

Worked example 2 (two points). Find the equation of the line through (1, 4) and (5, 2).

m = (2 - 4)/(5 - 1) = -1/2
y - 4 = -0.5(x - 1)  →  y = -0.5x + 4.5
or x + 2y - 9 = 0

Parallel and perpendicular lines

Parallel means equal gradients. Perpendicular means the gradients multiply to −1, which is the same as one being the negative reciprocal of the other. Recognising that the negative reciprocal is a rotation by 90° prevents the common error of negating without inverting.

parallel: m¹ = m²
perpendicular: m¹ x m² = -1, so m² = -1/m¹

Worked example. Find the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining A(2, 5) and B(6, 1).

midpoint = (4, 3)
gradient AB = (1 - 5)/(6 - 2) = -1
perpendicular gradient = 1
equation: y - 3 = 1(x - 4)  →  y = x - 1

Worked example 2 (proving a right angle). Show that the triangle with vertices P(1, 1), Q(4, 2) and R(3, 5) is right-angled at Q.

gradient PQ = (2 - 1)/(4 - 1) = 1/3
gradient QR = (5 - 2)/(3 - 4) = -3
product = (1/3)(-3) = -1  →  perpendicular, so the angle at Q is 90 degrees

The equation of a circle

A circle is the set of points a fixed distance from a fixed centre, so the distance formula written with an unknown point gives the equation directly.

centre (a, b), radius r:   (x - a)² + (y - b)² = r²
expanded form: x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0
completing the square recovers the centre (-g, -f) and radius √(g² + f² - c)

Worked example. Find the centre and radius of x² + y² − 6x + 8y − 11 = 0.

complete the square in x: x² - 6x = (x - 3)² - 9
in y: y² + 8y = (y + 4)² - 16
so (x - 3)² + (y + 4)² - 9 - 16 - 11 = 0
(x - 3)² + (y + 4)² = 36
centre (3, -4), radius 6

Worked example 2 (finding the equation). Find the equation of the circle with diameter AB where A(1, 2) and B(7, 10).

centre = midpoint = (4, 6)
radius = half of AB = 0.5 √(6² + 8²) = 5
(x - 4)² + (y - 6)² = 25

The diameter shortcut is worth remembering: the angle in a semicircle is a right angle, so any point on the circle sees AB at 90°, which is another route into the same equation.

Tangents, normals and chords

A tangent touches the circle at exactly one point and is perpendicular to the radius there. That single fact generates almost every circle question in the paper.

to find the tangent at P on a circle:
1. gradient of the radius from the centre to P
2. tangent gradient = negative reciprocal
3. use point-gradient form with P

Worked example. Find the tangent to x² + y² = 25 at the point (3, 4).

centre is the origin, so radius gradient = 4/3
tangent gradient = -3/4
y - 4 = (-3/4)(x - 3)
4y - 16 = -3x + 9  →  3x + 4y = 25

Worked example 2 (chord). A chord of the circle x² + y² = 25 lies on the line y = 3. Find its length.

substitute: x² + 9 = 25  →  x² = 16  →  x = +/-4
endpoints (-4, 3) and (4, 3)
length = 8

Worked example 3 (perpendicular from the centre bisects a chord). Use that fact to find the distance from the centre to a chord of length 8 in a circle of radius 5.

half the chord = 4
distance = √(5² - 4²) = 3

Intersections and the discriminant

Substituting a line into a circle gives a quadratic. How many times the line meets the circle is decided by the discriminant, so a tangency condition is a discriminant-equals-zero condition.

substitute y = mx + c into the circle equation
b² - 4ac > 0: two intersections (secant)
b² - 4ac = 0: one intersection (tangent)
b² - 4ac < 0: no intersection

Worked example. Show that the line y = x + 5 is a tangent to x² + y² = 12.5, and find the point of contact.

x² + (x + 5)² = 12.5
2x² + 10x + 25 - 12.5 = 0
2x² + 10x + 12.5 = 0   →  divide by 2: x² + 5x + 6.25 = 0
discriminant = 25 - 25 = 0, so tangent
repeated root: x = -2.5, y = 2.5

Worked example 2 (finding an unknown gradient). Find the values of m for which y = mx is tangent to (x − 3)² + y² = 4.

substitute: (x - 3)² + m² x² = 4
(1 + m²)x² - 6x + 5 = 0
for tangency: 36 - 4(1 + m²)(5) = 0
36 = 20 + 20m²  →  m² = 0.8  →  m = +/- 0.894

Parametric circles and arcs

A circle can also be described by a parameter, which is often the easier form when a point has to move. For a circle of radius r centred at the origin, the point (r cos θ, r sin θ) traces it as θ increases.

x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ  satisfies x² + y² = r²
centre (a, b): x = a + r cos θ, y = b + r sin θ
this is why the modulus-argument form of a complex number is a point on a circle

Worked example. A point moves on x² + y² = 9 with x = 3 cos θ. Find y and the coordinates when θ = 60°.

y = 3 sin θ
at θ = 60: (3 cos 60, 3 sin 60) = (1.5, 2.598)

Worked example 2 (eliminating the parameter). Eliminate θ from x = 2 + 4 cos θ, y = −1 + 4 sin θ.

cos θ = (x - 2)/4;  sin θ = (y + 1)/4
square and add: ((x-2)/4)² + ((y+1)/4)² = 1
(x - 2)² + (y + 1)² = 16

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Distance) Find the distance between (3, −2) and (−1, 4). Answer: √(16 + 36) = √52 = 7.21.
  2. (Midpoint) The midpoint of AB is (5, 1) and A is (2, −3). Find B. Answer: B = (8, 5).
  3. (Line) Find the line through (0, 4) perpendicular to y = 2x + 1. Answer: y = −0.5x + 4.
  4. (Circle) State the centre and radius of (x + 2)² + (y − 5)² = 49. Answer: centre (−2, 5), radius 7.
  5. (Completed square) Find the radius of x² + y² + 4x − 6y = 12. Answer: (x+2)² + (y−3)² = 25, radius 5.
  6. (Tangent) Find the tangent to x² + y² = 20 at (2, 4). Answer: gradient of radius 2, tangent −0.5, so x + 2y = 10.
  7. (Chord) Line y = 2 cuts x² + y² = 13. Find the chord length. Answer: x = ±3, length 6.
  8. (Discriminant) Show y = 2x + 5 does not meet x² + y² = 4. Answer: 5x² + 20x + 21 = 0, discriminant 400 − 420 < 0.
  9. (Circle from diameter) Find the circle with diameter from (0, 0) to (6, 8). Answer: centre (3, 4), radius 5, (x−3)² + (y−4)² = 25.
  10. (Parametric) Eliminate θ from x = cos θ, y = 2 sin θ. Answer: x² + y²/4 = 1, an ellipse.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Perpendicular gradient half-applied: the negative reciprocal of 3 is −1/3, not −3; negating without inverting is the classic slip.
  • Radius squared: (x − a)² + (y − b)² = 49 has radius 7, not 49 — the right-hand side is r².
  • Sign of the centre: (x − 3)² means centre x = +3; students routinely write −3.
  • Completing the square with the constant: the −9 and −16 produced by completing the square must move to the other side, and forgetting them changes the radius.
  • One root from a squared distance: √(k−2)² = 4 gives two values; the geometry usually admits both.
  • Tangent versus normal: a tangent is perpendicular to the radius; the normal is along it. Read which is asked.
  • Intersections solved approximately: the discriminant route gives exact values and the marks; sketching loses the algebra marks.
  • General form left unsimplified: mark schemes quote ax + by + c = 0 with integer coefficients where possible, so clear the fractions.

Equations and symbols

Every relation this topic is examined on, gathered into one reference sheet, each written with its real notation and followed by a key that names every symbol. Nothing here replaces the worked examples above; it is the list you revise from the night before, when you need the form of an answer rather than the reasoning behind it.

Two points: distance, midpoint, gradient

d = √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²)
Key: d = the distance AB, in the units of the axes; (x₁, y₁) = the first point; (x₂, y₂) = the second. Pythagoras on the horizontal and vertical steps. Taking the square root of each square separately is the classic slip — the sum is rooted, not the terms.

M = ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2)
Key: M = the midpoint of AB; the coordinates are the averages, which is why a midpoint question is always "add and halve" and never "subtract and halve".

m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁), x₂ ≠ x₁
Key: m = the gradient, i.e. the rise per unit run (unitless); x₂ ≠ x₁ because a vertical line has no finite gradient. Keep the order of subtraction identical in numerator and denominator, or the sign flips.

Lines: the three forms

y = mx + c
Key: m = gradient; c = y-intercept, the value of y where x = 0. Best when you know the gradient and the intercept, or when you are sketching quickly.

y − y₁ = m(x − x₁)
Key: m = gradient; (x₁, y₁) = one point on the line. Point–gradient form is the version to reach for whenever a question gives a gradient and a point, because it needs no algebra before substituting.

ax + by + c = 0 ⇒ m = −a/b
Key: a, b, c = the integer coefficients of the general form, b ≠ 0 for a non-vertical line; m = the gradient recovered by rearranging. Examiners often state the answer in this form, so converting confidently in both directions is worth practising.

parallel: m₁ = m₂; perpendicular: m₁m₂ = −1 ⇒ m₂ = −1/m₁
Key: m₁ = gradient of the given line; m₂ = gradient of the line you are finding. Perpendicular gradients are negative reciprocals, which flips the sign as well as inverting the fraction — a habit that saves the "find the normal" mark.

perpendicular bisector: through M with gradient −1/m_AB
Key: M = the midpoint of AB; m_AB = the gradient of AB. Two steps, in this order: the midpoint (a point on the line), then the negative reciprocal (its gradient).

Circles

(x − a)² + (y − b)² = r²
Key: (a, b) = the centre; r = the radius, r > 0, in the units of the axes. The signs inside the brackets are the opposite of the centre's coordinates — (x + 2)² means the centre's x is −2.

x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 ⇒ centre (−g, −f), r = √(g² + f² − c)
Key: g = half the x-coefficient; f = half the y-coefficient; c = the constant term; r = the radius, which exists only when g² + f² − c > 0. Completing the square in x and in y recovers both, and the radius is the square root of the whole expression.

circle with diameter AB: centre M and r = ½√((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²)
Key: M = the midpoint of AB (the centre); the radius is half the distance between the endpoints. The alternative test (x − x₁)(x − x₂) + (y − y₁)(y − y₂) = 0 encodes the same circle through the angle-in-a-semicircle fact.

Tangents, chords and intersections

m_tangent = −1/m_radius
Key: m_radius = gradient of the line from the circle's centre to the point of contact; m_tangent = the gradient of the tangent there. A radius meets its tangent at a right angle, so this negative reciprocal is the first line of every tangent question, followed by point–gradient form at the point of contact.

half-chord = √(r² − d²)
Key: r = the radius; d = the perpendicular distance from the centre to the chord. The perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord, so this right-angled triangle gives half the chord length — double it for the whole chord.

tangent length from an external point: L = √(d² − r²)
Key: L = the length of the tangent from the external point to the point of contact; d = the distance from that point to the centre; r = the radius. Tangency again makes a right angle, this time at the point of contact.

line meets circle: Δ = b² − 4ac of the substituted quadratic
Key: Δ = the discriminant of the quadratic left after substituting y = mx + k into the circle's equation; a, b, c = its coefficients. Δ > 0 gives a secant (two points), Δ = 0 a tangent, Δ < 0 no intersection — the same test as for a parabola, because the algebra is identical.

x = a + r cos θ, y = b + r sin θ ⇒ (x − a)² + (y − b)² = r²
Key: (a, b) = the centre; r = the radius; θ (theta) = the parameter, the angle measured anticlockwise from the positive x-direction, in degrees or radians. Squaring and adding eliminates θ through sin²θ + cos²θ = 1, which is how a parametric description is turned back into a Cartesian one.

title: A Level Mathematics: Hypothesis Testing
content:
A Level Mathematics: Hypothesis Testing

A hypothesis test is a formal way of deciding whether data are surprising enough to overturn an assumption. The logic is legal rather than mathematical in spirit: assume the claim is true, compute how unlikely the observed evidence would be under that assumption, and reject the claim only if the evidence is unlikely enough. This note sets out the machinery — null and alternative hypotheses, significance levels, tails, critical regions — and then applies it to the binomial and normal cases the exam uses.

The logic of a test

The null hypothesis H0 is the assumption of no change, no effect, no bias: the status quo. The alternative H1 is what you would conclude if the data are too extreme. The significance level α is the risk of rejecting a true H0 that you are willing to accept.

H0: the parameter equals its old value
H1: the parameter is greater, less, or simply different
alpha: the maximum acceptable probability of a Type I error (often 0.05 or 0.01)
test statistic: the observed value computed from the sample
p-value: probability of a result at least as extreme, assuming H0

The analogy that makes the asymmetry clear: a criminal trial presumes innocence. The presumption is not a belief, it is the default that evidence must overcome. Failing to reject H0 is not proof of H0 — it is a verdict of "not proven".

One-tailed and two-tailed tests

The alternative decides the tail. A one-tailed test is used when the direction of the change is specified in advance; a two-tailed test when any change would matter.

AlternativeTest typep-value
p > p0one-tailed, upperP(X ≥ observed)
p < p0one-tailed, lowerP(X ≤ observed)
p ≠ p0two-tailed2 × the smaller tail

Worked example (choosing the alternative). A coin is suspected of favouring heads. Which alternative applies?

the suspicion has a direction, so H1: p > 0.5, a one-tailed upper test
a two-tailed test would be right only if any bias mattered

Errors and their consequences

Every test can go wrong in two ways, and the significance level controls only one of them. Understanding which is which is a frequent exam question and a genuine conceptual point.

Type I error: reject H0 when it is true  (probability alpha)
Type II error: fail to reject H0 when it is false
reducing alpha reduces Type I errors but increases Type II errors
increasing the sample size reduces both

Worked example. A test at the 5% level concludes a die is biased when it is fair. Which error is this?

H0 (fair) was true and was rejected
that is a Type I error, with probability at most 5%

Worked example 2 (effect of sample size). Explain why the same observed proportion can be significant in a large sample and not in a small one.

a larger sample reduces the standard error, so the same deviation
becomes more standard errors away from the null value
the evidence is measured in standard errors, not in raw counts

Testing a binomial proportion

The test statistic is the observed number of successes, the null distribution is binomial, and the p-value is a cumulative binomial probability.

H0: p = p0;  X ~ B(n, p0)
upper tail p-value = P(X >= x)
lower tail p-value = P(X <= x)
reject H0 if p-value <= alpha

Worked example. A manufacturer claims 90% of components are fault-free. In a sample of 20, only 15 are fault-free. Test at the 5% level whether the claim is too high.

H0: p = 0.9;  H1: p < 0.9
X ~ B(20, 0.9)
P(X <= 15) = 0.0432
0.0432 < 0.05, so reject H0
there is evidence the fault-free rate is below 90%

Worked example 2 (critical region). Find the 5% critical region for that test.

P(X <= 15) = 0.0432 (below 0.05)
P(X <= 16) = 0.1330 (above 0.05)
critical region: X <= 15

Worked example 3 (actual significance level). State the actual significance level of that test.

the probability of a Type I error is P(X <= 15) under H0 = 0.0432
so the actual level is 4.32%, just inside the 5% requirement

Testing a normal mean

When the variable is continuous and the population is normal — or the sample is large — the test statistic is standardised with a z-score and compared with critical values.

test statistic z = (x-bar - mu)/(σ/sqrt n)   (σ known)
or z = (x-bar - mu)/(s/sqrt n)                  (σ estimated, large n)
critical values at 5% one-tailed: 1.6449;  two-tailed: 1.96
at 1% one-tailed: 2.3263;  two-tailed: 2.5758

Worked example. A machine fills bags with a mean of 500 g and standard deviation 8 g. A sample of 16 bags has mean 496 g. Test at the 5% level whether the mean has fallen.

H0: mu = 500;  H1: mu < 500
standard error = 8/sqrt 16 = 2
z = (496 - 500)/2 = -2
critical value at 5% one-tailed is -1.6449
-2 < -1.6449, so reject H0: the mean has fallen

Worked example 2 (two-tailed). Same data, tested two-tailed at 5%.

critical values are +/-1.96
|-2| > 1.96, so still reject H0
the evidence is that the mean is not 500, in either direction

Worked example 3 (interpreting a p-value). A test gives z = 1.72 for H1: μ > μ0. Find the p-value and conclude at 5%.

p-value = P(Z > 1.72) = 0.0427
0.0427 < 0.05, so reject H0
the result is significant at the 5% level but not at 1%

Choosing the right test

The exam does not label the test; the shape of the data decides it. Getting the distribution wrong makes every later mark unreachable, so the decision is worth making explicitly.

count of successes in n trials with constant p  →  binomial test
count of events in an interval at a constant rate  →  Poisson test
mean of a continuous measurement  →  normal test (z)
correlation between two variables  →  product-moment test

Worked example. A nurse records the number of patients arriving in an hour on 30 separate days. Which test?

counts of arrivals in equal intervals at a roughly constant rate
use a Poisson test on the mean count, not a binomial test
a normal test on the mean of the 30 counts is also defensible for large n

Writing a conclusion that earns the marks

The final mark of a hypothesis test is for the conclusion, and it has three components: a decision about H0, a reference to the significance level, and the finding stated in the context of the question. Dropping any one of them costs a mark even when the arithmetic is perfect.

Compare these two endings. "0.0201 < 0.05, so reject H0" scores the comparison. "There is sufficient evidence at the 5% level that the call rate has increased" scores the comparison and the interpretation. "The rate has increased" scores neither, because it reports a certainty the test cannot deliver.

The opposite case is often mishandled too. When the p-value is above the level the correct wording is that there is insufficient evidence to reject H0 — never that H0 is true, and never that nothing has happened. A non-significant result from a small sample is weak evidence either way, and saying so is better than overclaiming in either direction.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Hypotheses) A coin might be biased against heads. State H0 and H1. Answer: H0: p = 0.5; H1: p < 0.5.
  2. (Error) Define a Type II error. Answer: failing to reject H0 when it is false.
  3. (Binomial) 8 of 20 seeds germinate; test p = 0.6 against p < 0.6 at 5%. Answer: X ~ B(20, 0.6), so P(X ≤ 8) = 0.0565; since 0.0565 > 0.05 there is insufficient evidence to reject H0.
  4. (Critical region) X ~ B(15, 0.4): 5% lower critical region. Answer: test P(X ≤ c) ≤ 0.05: P(X ≤ 2) = 0.0271 ≤ 0.05, but P(X ≤ 3) = 0.0905 > 0.05, so the critical region is X ≤ 2.
  5. (Actual level) For that region, state the actual significance level. Answer: actual significance level = P(X ≤ 2) = 0.0271 = 2.71%.
  6. (Normal) μ0 = 20, σ = 4, n = 25, mean 21.5: test at 5% one-tailed. Answer: z = (x̄ − μ0)/(σ/√n) = (21.5 − 20)/(4/√25) = 1.5/0.8 = 1.875, and 1.875 > 1.6449, so reject H0.
  7. (Two-tailed) Same data two-tailed: Answer: z = (21.5 − 20)/(4/√25) = 1.875, and 1.875 < 1.96, so do not reject H0.
  8. (p-value) z = 2.4, H1: μ > μ0. Find the p-value. Answer: p-value = P(Z > 2.4) = 1 − 0.9918 = 0.0082.
  9. (Sample size) Why can a larger sample turn a non-significant result significant? Answer: the standard error shrinks, so the same deviation is more standard errors away.
  10. (Conclusion wording) Write a valid conclusion for a rejected H0. Answer: there is sufficient evidence at the 5% level that the mean has fallen.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Concluding H0 is true: failing to reject means the evidence is insufficient; it is never proof of the null.
  • Wrong tail: compute P(X ≥ x) for an increase and P(X ≤ x) for a decrease; using the other tail inverts the conclusion.
  • Doubling without a two-tailed alternative: the p-value is doubled only when H1 is "not equal".
  • p-value compared with the wrong threshold: 5% is 0.05; comparing 0.043 with 5 instead of 0.05 reverses the verdict.
  • Standard error omitted: the z-score divides by σ/√n, not by σ.
  • Critical value for the wrong tail: the 5% one-tailed value is 1.6449, the two-tailed is 1.96; the sign matters too.
  • Type I and Type II swapped: Type I is rejecting a true null — the error the significance level controls.
  • Conclusion beyond the data: a rejected H0 says the parameter has changed, not why, and never that the change is important.

Equations and symbols

A hypothesis test is a decision rule, and these are its moving parts: the test statistic, the standard error, the tail probability and the comparison that produces the verdict.

The decision

reject H0 if p-value <= alpha Key: H0 = the null hypothesis, the assumption of no change; p-value = the probability of a result at least as extreme, assuming H0 is true; alpha = the significance level, the acceptable risk of rejecting a true H0 (often 0.05 or 0.01). Failing to reject is not proof that H0 is true — it means the evidence was insufficient.

P(X <= 15) = 0.0432 Key: X = number of fault-free components in a sample of 20; 0.0432 = the lower-tail probability under H0: p = 0.9. Because 0.0432 < 0.05 the null is rejected, and the same figure is the actual significance level of the test.

The normal test

standard error = 8/sqrt 16 = 2 Key: 8 = population standard deviation σ (g); 16 = sample size n (bags); 2 = the standard error of the mean (g). The standard error, not σ, is the denominator of the test statistic — omitting the √n is the classic lost mark.

z = (496 - 500)/2 = -2 Key: z = the test statistic, in standard errors; 496 = sample mean (g); 500 = hypothesised mean μ (g); 2 = the standard error (g). Compare |z| with the critical value: 1.6449 one-tailed at 5%, 1.96 two-tailed at 5%.

p-value = P(Z > 1.72) = 0.0427 Key: Z = the standard normal variable; 1.72 = the observed test statistic; 0.0427 = the area beyond it, for an upper-tail alternative. Significant at 5% but not at 1% — say which level you are concluding at.

Errors

A Type I error rejects a true H0 and has probability alpha; a Type II error fails to reject a false H0. Lowering alpha reduces Type I errors and increases Type II; a larger sample reduces both, because it shrinks the standard error so the same deviation counts as more standard errors.

The slip worth naming

Comparing a p-value with 5 instead of 0.05, or doubling the tail without a two-sided alternative. Both reverse a correct conclusion, which is exactly the mark the question is testing.

title: AS Level Physics: Dynamics
content:
AS Level Physics: Dynamics

Edexcel International A Level Physics, Unit 1 (WPH11) Mechanics and Materials — Newton's laws of motion, the conservation of linear momentum, and the behaviour of objects moving through fluids (density, upthrust, viscous drag and terminal velocity). Dynamics answers the question kinematics asks: what makes motion change? The laws are three sentences long and everything else in the unit is their application, so they must be known exactly — including the conditions under which momentum is conserved.

Force and Newton's laws of motion

A force is a push or a pull, measured in newtons (N), and it is a vector. Forces change velocity (they accelerate masses) or change shape. The three laws, in their examinable form:

  • Newton's first law: a body remains at rest or moves with constant velocity in a straight line unless acted on by a resultant external force. It defines inertia — the reluctance of mass to change its state of motion.
  • Newton's second law: the resultant force on a body equals the rate of change of its momentum, in the direction of that force. For constant mass this reduces to F = ma.
  • Newton's third law: when body A exerts a force on body B, body B exerts an equal and opposite force on A. The pair acts on different bodies, always along the same line, and is always the same type of force (gravavitational on gravitational, contact on contact).
resultant force = mass x acceleration        F = m a
  • F: resultant force in newtons (N); m: mass in kilograms (kg); a: acceleration in metres per second squared (m s⁻²). Acceleration is in the direction of the resultant force.

Free-body diagrams are the first mark of nearly every dynamics answer: draw one body, with every force acting on it as an arrow from its centre, labelled (weight, normal reaction, tension, friction, drag, thrust). Resolve the forces along and perpendicular to the direction of motion, apply F = ma along the motion, and use equilibrium (zero resultant) perpendicular to it.

Mass is the quantity of matter and is constant; weight is the gravitational force on that mass, W = mg, and varies with location. The third law pair to an object's weight is the gravitational pull of the object on the Earth — not the normal contact force of the table beneath it.

Momentum and its conservation

Momentum is the product of mass and velocity:

momentum = mass x velocity        p = m v
  • p: momentum in kilogram metres per second (kg m s⁻¹). Momentum is a vector, in the direction of velocity; with a stated sign convention, momenta in opposite directions carry opposite signs.
  • Newton's second law in full form: F = (mv − mu)/t, the rate of change of momentum.

The principle of conservation of linear momentum: when no external resultant force acts on a system, the total momentum of that system remains constant. Collisions, explosions and recoil problems all reduce to one equation: total momentum before = total momentum after, summed as vectors. The condition matters — a ball bouncing off a floor is not momentum-conserving for the ball alone, because the Earth supplies an external force during the bounce.

impulse = change in momentum = force x time        F t = m v - m u
  • Impulse is measured in newton seconds (N s), numerically equal to the momentum change. A force–time graph has an area equal to the impulse; extending the time of impact reduces the peak force for the same impulse — crumple zones, air bags, landing on a bent knee.

Elastic and inelastic collisions

Momentum is conserved in every collision (in an isolated system); kinetic energy is not. A collision is elastic when the total kinetic energy is conserved — idealised gas molecules, and perfectly elastic springs. It is inelastic when kinetic energy is lost to deformation, heat and sound; a collision in which the bodies stick together is completely inelastic, and that is the case where the kinetic energy loss is greatest. Explosions convert stored energy (chemical or elastic) into kinetic energy of the fragments, so the total momentum is conserved while the kinetic energy increases.

Equilibrium and connected bodies

A body is in equilibrium when the resultant force and the resultant moment on it are both zero: it is either at rest or moving with constant velocity. The method is always the same — draw the free-body diagram, resolve along and across the direction of motion, and set the resultant to zero in each direction. For a mass hanging from a string, the tension equals the weight; for a block resting on a slope, the weight resolves into mg sin θ down the slope and mg cos θ into the slope, and the normal reaction balances the latter while friction can balance the former.

Friction acts parallel to a surface and opposes the motion or the tendency to move. The maximum frictional force before slipping is proportional to the normal contact force: F(friction) = mu R, where mu is the coefficient of friction (dimensionless) and R is the normal reaction in newtons. Static friction below that maximum simply matches the applied force, which is why a block on a gentle slope stays put.

Connected bodies share one acceleration, so the fastest method treats the system as a whole first and then separates it. Two masses (3.0 kg and 2.0 kg) joined by a light string over a frictionless pulley accelerate together: the resultant force on the system is the difference in weights, 1.0g, so a = 1.0g/5.0 = 1.96 m s⁻². Cutting the system then gives the tension in the string: for the 3.0 kg mass, 3.0g − T = 3.0a, so T = 23.5 N. The same two answers must hold whichever mass is isolated — a built-in check on the arithmetic.

Fluids: density, upthrust and viscous drag

A fluid is a liquid or a gas, and objects moving through fluids experience forces that solids never show. Density is mass per unit volume, ρ = m/V (kg m⁻³). An object immersed in a fluid is pushed up by an upthrust equal to the weight of fluid displaced (Archimedes' principle), so an object denser than the fluid sinks and one less dense floats; a floating object displaces its own weight of fluid.

Viscous drag is the friction within a fluid: layers of fluid slide over each other and over the object, and the drag grows with speed, viscosity and size. For a small sphere falling slowly through a viscous fluid, Stokes' law gives the drag:

viscous drag = 6 pi x viscosity x radius x speed        F = 6 pi eta r v
  • F: drag force in newtons (N); eta: viscosity of the fluid in pascal seconds (Pa s); r: radius of the sphere in metres (m); v: speed in metres per second (m s⁻¹). The force acts opposite to the direction of motion.

A falling sphere accelerates until drag + upthrust = weight, and then falls at terminal velocity, which from Stokes' law is v = 2r²(ρ − σ)g/(9η) for a sphere of density ρ in a fluid of density σ. Terminal velocity is reached quickly for small dense spheres in viscous fluids — the principle of the falling-ball viscometer, one of the unit's core practicals. At low speeds the flow around a sphere is smooth and layered (laminar); above a critical speed it becomes chaotic (turbulent), and the drag then rises more steeply with speed. Streamlining delays the onset of turbulence, which is why a golf ball has dimples and a car is shaped the way it is.

Worked example: collision and impulse

A 1200 kg car travelling at 20 m s⁻¹ collides with a stationary 900 kg car and they move together. Find their common velocity and the energy lost.

momentum before = 1200 x 20 = 24 000 kg m s-1
common velocity = 24 000 / (1200 + 900) = 11.4 m s-1
KE before = 1/2 x 1200 x 20^2 = 240 000 J
KE after = 1/2 x 2100 x 11.4^2 = 136 000 J
energy lost = 104 000 J (to deformation, heat and sound)

Momentum is conserved; kinetic energy is not — the collision is inelastic. Second stage: if the impact lasts 0.15 s, the average force on the stationary car is F = mv/t = 900 × 11.4 / 0.15 = 68 400 N, and lengthening the impact with a crumple zone would cut that force sharply.

Common mistakes

  • Using F = ma with one force instead of the resultant; draw the free-body diagram and resolve first.
  • Writing third-law pairs that act on the same body (they never do) or that are different kinds of force.
  • Ignoring direction in momentum problems; a rebound reverses the velocity sign and the total is a vector sum.
  • Assuming kinetic energy is conserved in every collision; only elastic collisions conserve it, and sticking collisions lose the most.
  • Forgetting upthrust when a body moves through a fluid: terminal velocity is reached when drag + upthrust = weight, not when drag = weight, if the fluid's density is not negligible.
  • Using Stokes' law outside its conditions — it assumes laminar flow, slow speeds and a spherical object.
  • Confusing mass and weight in W = mg, or using g in m s⁻² when the question gives g in N kg⁻¹ (numerically equal but state your units).
  • Quoting an impulse as a force: impulse is N s and equals the momentum change; the force depends on the impact time.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (WPH11, 3 marks). A 4.0 kg trolley on a frictionless runway is pulled by a 12 N force. Calculate its acceleration and the distance travelled in 3.0 s from rest.

Answer: a = F/m = 12/4.0 = 3.0 m s⁻². s = ½at² = ½ × 3.0 × 9.0 = 13.5 m ≈ 14 m.

Question 2 (WPH11, 4 marks). A 60 g ball moving at 5.0 m s⁻¹ hits a wall at right angles and rebounds at 3.0 m s⁻¹. The contact lasts 0.020 s. Calculate the average force.

Answer: Taking the initial direction as positive, Δp = 0.060(−3.0) − 0.060(5.0) = −0.48 kg m s⁻¹. Force = Δp/t = −0.48/0.020 = −24 N, i.e. 24 N opposite to the initial motion.

Question 3 (WPH11, 4 marks). Two ice skaters push apart. Skater A (60 kg) moves at 3.0 m s⁻¹. Find the velocity of skater B (75 kg) and explain which principle you used.

Answer: Total momentum before = 0, so 60 × 3.0 + 75 × v = 0 and v = −2.4 m s⁻¹: B moves at 2.4 m s⁻¹ in the opposite direction. The conservation of linear momentum applies because the push is an internal force; the ice's friction is negligible during the push.

Question 4 (WPH11, 3 marks). Explain why a small steel ball bearing falling through glycerine reaches terminal velocity, and state the forces acting at that moment.

Answer: As the ball accelerates, the viscous drag rises with speed (F = 6πηrv). The resultant force is weight minus drag minus upthrust, so the acceleration falls as speed rises. When drag + upthrust equals the weight the resultant force is zero and the ball continues at constant terminal velocity, acted on by three balanced forces: weight down, upthrust and drag up.

Question 5 (WPH13, 3 marks). Describe how you would determine the viscosity of a liquid using a falling-ball method.

Answer: Drop a small steel sphere (radius measured with a micrometer) into a wide measuring cylinder of the liquid and time its fall between two marked lines, where it is already at terminal velocity. Repeat and average the times; calculate v = distance/time. At terminal velocity, 6πηrv = (4/3)πr³(ρ − σ)g, so η = 2r²(ρ − σ)g/(9v). Keep the temperature constant (viscosity depends strongly on it) and use a cylinder at least ten sphere diameters wide to avoid wall effects.

Question 6 (WPH11, 3 marks). A 1500 kg car hits a crash barrier at 15 m s⁻¹ and stops in 0.30 s. Calculate the average force on the car and state one safety feature that reduces this force.

Answer: F = mv/t = 1500 × 15 / 0.30 = 75 000 N = 75 kN. A crumple zone extends the impact time, and for the same momentum change the force falls in proportion to the time.

Forces also change shape — the subject of Materials and Deformation.

title: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Sets and Venn Diagrams
content:
Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Sets and Venn Diagrams

Set notation is the language of sorting: it describes which elements belong together, which belong to both groups, and which belong to neither. The IGCSE questions are almost always Venn-diagram problems in disguise — a survey of students, a group of numbers, a club membership — and the marks come from filling every region correctly. This note builds the topic from zero: the notation and symbols, the two-set and three-set Venn diagrams and how to shade them, the counting formulas, and the word-problem method that never misses a region.

Set notation and vocabulary

SymbolMeaningExample
∈is an element of3 ∈ {1, 2, 3}
∉is not an element of5 ∉ {1, 2, 3}
ξ (or U)the universal set — everything under discussionξ = {1, 2, ..., 12}
∅the empty setodd multiples of 2 = ∅
A′the complement of A — everything in ξ not in AA′ = ξ A
A ∪ Bunion — in A or B or both{1,2} ∪ {2,3} = {1,2,3}
A ∩ Bintersection — in both{1,2} ∩ {2,3} = {2}
n(A)the number of elements of An({2, 4, 6}) = 3

Two rules follow directly: A ∩ A′ = ∅ (nothing is both in and out), and A ∪ A′ = ξ (everything is one or the other). Subsets: A ⊂ B means every element of A is also in B. The empty set has no elements, so n(∅) = 0, and it is a subset of every set — a fact worth stating explicitly when a question asks whether ∅ ⊂ A is true.

Two-set Venn diagrams

A two-set diagram divides the universal set into four regions: only A, only B, both, and neither. Filling them from the inside out is the reliable method:

  1. Write the number in the intersection (both) first.
  2. Work outward: only A = n(A) − both; only B = n(B) − both.
  3. Neither = total − (only A + only B + both).

Worked example. In a class of 32, 18 study French, 15 study Spanish, and 7 study both. Find the number studying only French, only Spanish, and neither.

both = 7
only French = 18 - 7 = 11
only Spanish = 15 - 7 = 8
neither = 32 - (11 + 8 + 7) = 32 - 26 = 6

Worked example 2 (reverse). In a group, 20 like tea, 14 like coffee and 5 like neither. Everyone likes at least one of the two? Then find n(tea ∩ coffee).

n(T union C) = 20 + 14 - both
total = 20 + 14 - both + 5 = 39 - both
If the group has 30 people: 30 = 39 - both → both = 9

The inclusion–exclusion formula

n(A union B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A intersection B)

for three sets:
n(A u B u C) = n(A) + n(B) + n(C)
             - n(A n B) - n(A n C) - n(B n C)
             + n(A n B n C)

The subtraction corrects double counting; the final addition corrects the triple-counted centre. Knowing the formula lets you answer "how many in total" questions without a full diagram, but a diagram is still the safer route for word problems.

Worked example. A survey of 50 people: 30 read newspapers, 25 read magazines, 12 read both. How many read at least one?

n(N union M) = 30 + 25 - 12 = 43
neither = 50 - 43 = 7

Three-set Venn diagrams

The three-set diagram has eight regions (counting "none of the three"). The fill order that never fails:

  1. Start with the triple intersection (all three).
  2. Find the "exactly two" regions by subtracting the triple from each pair.
  3. Find the "only one" regions by subtracting the pair and triple totals from each set total.
  4. Find "none" from the grand total.

Worked example. 40 students choose subjects: 20 take Maths, 18 take Physics, 15 take Chemistry; 8 take Maths and Physics, 6 take Maths and Chemistry, 5 take Physics and Chemistry; 3 take all three. Find how many take exactly one subject and how many take none.

triple = 3
exactly M and P = 8 - 3 = 5
exactly M and C = 6 - 3 = 3
exactly P and C = 5 - 3 = 2
only M = 20 - (5 + 3 + 3) = 9
only P = 18 - (5 + 2 + 3) = 8
only C = 15 - (3 + 2 + 3) = 7
exactly one = 9 + 8 + 7 = 24
total counted = 24 + 5 + 3 + 2 + 3 = 37
none = 40 - 37 = 3

Sets of numbers and shading

Questions often use number sets inside the universal set: ξ = {1, 2, ..., 20}, A = multiples of 3, B = multiples of 4. List them, then use the same four regions:

A = {3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18}
B = {4, 8, 12, 16, 20}
A n B = {12}
A u B = {3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 12, 15, 16, 18, 20}
neither = {1, 2, 5, 7, 10, 11, 13, 14, 17, 19}

Shading questions ask for a region described in symbols. Translate the symbols into words first: A′ ∩ B means "not in A, but in B" — the part of B outside A. A ∪ B′ means "in A, or outside B" — everything except the part of B that is not in A.

Listing sets and set-builder notation

Sets can be written in three ways, and questions move between them. The roster method lists the elements: A = {2, 4, 6, 8}. The description method states the rule in words: A is the set of even numbers from 2 to 8. Set-builder notation states the rule symbolically: A = {x : x is an even number, 2 ≤ x ≤ 8} — read as "the set of all x such that x is even and between 2 and 8".

  • Roster for finite sets: list every element once, in braces, separated by commas; order does not matter and repeats are not counted twice.
  • Description for patterns: "multiples of 3 less than 30" is clearer than listing ten numbers.
  • Set-builder for precision: the colon means "such that"; the condition after it does the work.

Worked example. Write the set of odd numbers between 1 and 11 in roster and set-builder form, and find its size.

roster: {3, 5, 7, 9}  (strictly between, so 1 and 11 excluded)
set-builder: {x : x odd, 1 < x < 11}
n(A) = 4

Reading the inequalities is the trap: "between" usually excludes the endpoints, "from ... to ..." usually includes them, and the question's wording decides. When in doubt, list both interpretations and choose the one consistent with the other numbers in the question.

Worked examples: word problems

Worked example. In a hostel of 60 students, 35 play football, 28 play basketball, and 12 play both. How many play neither?

at least one = 35 + 28 - 12 = 51
neither = 60 - 51 = 9

Worked example 2 (with a variable). In a group of 25, x people like both tea and coffee, 12 like tea only and 8 like coffee only. Find x if everyone likes at least one.

12 + 8 + x = 25  →  x = 5

Worked example 3 (conditional language). Of 40 students, 24 study History, 18 study Geography and 6 study neither. How many study both?

at least one = 40 - 6 = 34
34 = 24 + 18 - both  →  both = 42 - 34 = 8

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Notation) ξ = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8}; A = {2, 4, 6, 8}; B = {1, 3, 5, 7}. Find A ∩ B and A ∪ B. Answer: A ∩ B = ∅; A ∪ B = ξ.
  2. (Complement) With A = {2, 4, 6, 8} in ξ above, list A′. Answer: A′ is everything in ξ that is not in A: ξ = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8} and A = {2, 4, 6, 8}, so A′ = {1, 3, 5, 7}.
  3. (Two sets) n(A) = 14, n(B) = 9, n(A ∩ B) = 4. Find n(A ∪ B). Answer: the overlap is counted twice when the sizes are added, so take it off once: n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B) = 14 + 9 − 4 = 19.
  4. (Neither) In a class of 30, 17 like cricket, 12 like tennis and 5 like both. Find the number who like neither. Answer: at least one = 24; neither = 6.
  5. (Three sets) 30 students: 15 like Maths, 12 like Physics, 10 like Chemistry; 5 like Maths and Physics, 4 like Maths and Chemistry, 3 like Physics and Chemistry, 2 like all three. Find the number who like exactly one. Answer: only M = 15 − (3 + 2 + 2) = 8; only P = 12 − (3 + 1 + 2) = 6; only C = 10 − (2 + 1 + 2) = 5; total = 19 (with exactly-two counts 3, 2, 1 and triple 2).
  6. (Shading) Describe the region A′ ∩ B in words. Answer: Elements in B but not in A — the part of B outside A.
  7. (Numbers) ξ = {1, ..., 20}; A = even numbers; B = multiples of 5. Find n(A ∩ B). Answer: A ∩ B holds the numbers that are both even and a multiple of 5, i.e. multiples of 10; up to 20 those are 10 and 20, so n(A ∩ B) = 2.
  8. (Reasoning) Explain why n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) is wrong when A and B overlap. Answer: The elements in both sets are counted twice in n(A) + n(B), so the intersection must be subtracted once: n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B).

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Filling the intersection last: start at the centre. Adding both set totals and forgetting the overlap counts shared elements twice.
  • Forgetting the "neither" region: the universal set includes elements outside all named sets; if the question gives a total, subtract to find them.
  • Confusing ∪ and ∩: union is "or" (everything), intersection is "and" (only the middle). A quick mnemonic: ∪ looks like a cup that holds everything.
  • Shading the wrong side for A′: the complement is everything outside A, including parts of other sets and the region outside them all.
  • Triple intersection double subtraction: when subtracting pairs, remember each pair already includes the triple; subtract the triple from each pair before using them.
  • Reading "only": "only A" means A and nothing else — exclude the overlaps. The word only is a region instruction, not decoration.
  • Notation in answers: list elements with braces and commas; do not write 1, 2, 3 as an unbraced list when the answer is a set.
  • Assuming everyone likes something: unless stated, some may be outside both sets — check whether the total equals the sum of the regions.

The four regions: reading a Venn diagram as a counting grid

A two-set Venn diagram is not a picture of two sets. It is a grid with four cells, and every question about it is answered by putting a number in each cell and adding.

Name the four cells before you write anything. For sets A and B inside a universal set ξ, every element is in exactly one of: only A, both, only B, neither. In the figure that is 7, 5, 9 and 4. The moment all four numbers are on the page, every part of the question is a sum:

n(A) = 7 + 5 = 12 Key: n(A) counts everything inside circle A, including the overlap.
n(A ∩ B) = 5 Key: the intersection — the region inside both circles.
n(A ∪ B) = 7 + 5 + 9 = 21 Key: the union — everything inside at least one circle.
n(ξ) = 21 + 4 = 25 Key: the universal set also counts what is in neither set.

Why the formula has a minus sign. Adding n(A) and n(B) counts the overlap twice — once with each circle — so it has to come back off:

n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B) Key: n(A ∪ B) = elements in at least one set; n(A ∩ B) = elements in both. In the figure, 12 + 14 − 5 = 21, which is exactly the sum of the three inner cells. The subtraction is not a rule to remember; it is the double count being removed.

Worked example. In a class of 30, 18 study French, 15 study Spanish and 6 study both. How many study neither?

French only = 18 − 6 = 12
Spanish only = 15 − 6 = 9
at least one = 12 + 6 + 9 = 27
neither = 30 − 27 = 3

Going the other way — "9 study neither" — is the same arithmetic in reverse, and it is the version that appears when the examiner wants an unknown: if the total is 30 and 9 study neither, then 21 study at least one, and 18 + 15 − x = 21 gives x = 12 studying both. Filling the grid from the overlap outwards always works, because the overlap is the only cell that belongs to both circles.

Where marks are lost. Treating "18 study French" as 18 in the French-only region, which double-counts 6. Forgetting the neither region, so the four numbers do not add to the total. And shading the wrong side for A′ ∩ B: the complement of A is everything outside A, so A′ ∩ B is the B-only region, not the overlap.

Sets: the building blocks of counting

A set is a well-defined collection of objects, called its elements or members. In IGCSE Mathematics, sets are used to organise numbers and to count how many items share or avoid a property. Questions on this statement test three things: reading and writing set notation, drawing and filling Venn diagrams, and using counting rules without double-counting. The subsections below take these one at a time.

What counts as a set

A set is defined by a rule that tells you, for any object, whether it is in the set or not. "The even numbers less than 10" is a set because every number either is or is not an even number less than 10. A list such as "some tall students" is not a set, because two people might disagree about who is tall. Exam questions always use clear rules, so the first step is to write each set as a list or a rule before counting anything.

Writing a set in roster form

Roster form lists every element between curly brackets, separated by commas. The set of prime numbers less than 12 is {2, 3, 5, 7, 11}. The order of the elements does not matter, and an element is never written twice. Roster form is quickest for small sets, and it is the form the examiner usually expects when a question says "list the elements".

The element and not-element symbols

The symbol ∈ means "is an element of", and ∉ means "is not an element of". So 4 ∈ {1, 2, 3, 4} is true, and 5 ∉ {1, 2, 3, 4} is also true. These symbols are used in statements about membership, and they should be read aloud as whole sentences when you check an answer, because a reversed symbol reverses the meaning of the statement.

The empty set

The empty set, written ∅ or { }, contains no elements at all. The set of whole numbers that are both odd and even is the empty set, because no number has both properties. The empty set is a subset of every set, and in a Venn diagram it is shown by a region with no number in it. Do not confuse ∅ with the set containing zero, {0}, which has one element.

Subsets and the subset symbol

A set A is a subset of a set B when every element of A is also an element of B, and this is written A ⊂ B. For example, {1, 2} ⊂ {1, 2, 3, 4} because both 1 and 2 are in the larger set. Every set is a subset of itself, and the empty set is a subset of every set. A question asking whether one set is a subset of another can be answered by checking each element of the first set in turn.

Equal sets

Two sets are equal when they contain exactly the same elements, whatever order they are listed in. So {3, 1, 2} and {1, 2, 3} are equal, because both contain the numbers 1, 2 and 3 and no others. A repeated element does not make a set bigger, so {1, 1, 2} is the same set as {1, 2}. This is why counting the elements of a set means counting distinct members.

The number of elements in a set

The number of elements in a set A is written n(A). For A = {2, 4, 6, 8}, n(A) = 4. The notation is used in every counting formula in the Venn diagram work later in this note, so write it carefully. A common slip is to count the brackets, the commas or the repeated entries rather than the distinct elements.

title: Edexcel IAL Computer Science: Processor Fundamentals and Architecture
content:
Edexcel IAL Computer Science: Processor Fundamentals and Architecture

Pearson Edexcel International Advanced Level in Computer Science, Unit 1 Principles of Computer Science (with Unit 3 systems architecture depth): CPU architecture and the fetch–decode–execute cycle, assembly language and bit manipulation, and processors, parallel processing and virtual machines. Every cycle below is traced register by register, and every assembly instruction is annotated with its effect on memory and the accumulator — because the exam hands you a memory dump and asks for the cycle's exact state at each step.

The stored-program machine

The Von Neumann architecture stores program instructions and data in the same memory, fetched by the CPU over shared buses: CPU (control unit, ALU, registers), main memory, backing storage, and input/output, joined by the address, data and control buses. Its weakness, the Von Neumann bottleneck, is that instruction and data traffic contend for one path — the motivation for caches, pipelines and Harvard-style split paths (separate instruction and data caches) in modern designs.

CPU components and registers

RegisterRole in the cycle
Program counter (PC)Holds the address of the next instruction; incremented after the fetch
Memory address register (MAR)Holds the address being accessed on this bus transfer
Memory data register (MDR/MBR)Holds the instruction or data just fetched or about to be written
Current instruction register (CIR)Holds the instruction being decoded and executed
Accumulator (ACC)Holds the running result of ALU operations
