The control unit fetches, decodes and orchestrates; the ALU performs arithmetic and logic; the clock paces each micro-step; the address bus is one-way (CPU → memory/devices), the data bus two-way, the control bus carries read/write/interrupt/clock signals.

The fetch–decode–execute cycle, traced

Memory (opcode / operand; opcode 01 = LOAD, 10 = ADD, 11 = STORE):

  5: 01 001000   LOAD 8
  6: 10 001001   ADD 9
  7: 11 001010   STORE 10
  8: 0000 0101   (5)
  9: 0000 0011   (3)
 10: 0000 0000   (empty)

Cycle 1 - LOAD 8:
  FETCH:   PC = 5 -> MAR = 5; control bus READ; MDR = 01 001000;
           CIR = 01 001000; PC = PC + 1 = 6.
  DECODE:  opcode 01 = LOAD: copy memory[operand] to ACC.
  EXECUTE: operand 001000 = 8; MAR = 8; READ; MDR = 5; ACC = 5.

Cycle 2 - ADD 9:
  FETCH:   PC = 6 -> MAR = 6; READ; MDR = 10 001001; CIR = same; PC = 7.
  DECODE:  opcode 10 = ADD: ACC = ACC + memory[operand].
  EXECUTE: MAR = 9; READ; MDR = 3; ALU: ACC + MDR = 5 + 3 = 8; ACC = 8.

Cycle 3 - STORE 10:
  FETCH:   PC = 7 -> MAR = 7; READ; MDR = 11 001010; CIR = same; PC = 8.
  DECODE:  opcode 11 = STORE: memory[operand] = ACC.
  EXECUTE: MAR = 10; MDR = 8 (from ACC); WRITE; memory[10] = 0000 1000.

Interrupts fit between cycles: complete the current instruction, save the PC,
run the interrupt service routine, restore the PC, resume.

The examiner's checklist: PC → MAR for the fetch; MDR → CIR; PC incremented at fetch (not execute); execute behaviour depends entirely on the opcode; the MAR is reused in execute to address the operand.

Assembly language

Assembly is a thin, human-readable veneer over machine code: one mnemonic per instruction (LOAD, ADD, STORE, JMP, CMP), assembled to binary by an assembler. It is low-level (tied to the processor's instruction set), fast, and used where direct hardware control matters — embedded firmware, drivers, performance-critical inner loops. Instruction sets: CISC (many complex instructions, variable length, microcoded — x86) versus RISC (few simple instructions, one cycle each, hardwired — ARM). Mobile devices favour RISC for power efficiency; the trade-off is instructions-per-task versus cycles-per-instruction.

Assembly concepts with a small program (accumulator machine):

  START:  LOAD  X      ; ACC = value at X
          ADD   Y      ; ACC = ACC + value at Y
          STORE Z      ; Z = ACC
          CMP   K      ; compare ACC with K (sets flags)
          JMPLE DONE   ; jump to DONE if ACC <= K (flag-driven)
          LOAD  Z      ; otherwise adjust
          SUB   K
          STORE Z
  DONE:   HALT

Key ideas the exam tests: labels are addresses (START, DONE are memory
locations); operands address memory; jumps make selection and loops; flags
(Z for zero, C for carry, N for negative, V for overflow) are set by CMP and
tested by conditional jumps - the mechanism behind every IF and WHILE once
compiled.

Bit manipulation (statement 4.3) is done with logical shifts and masks: AND with a mask to extract bits (flags, packed fields), OR to set a bit, XOR to toggle, NOT to invert, shift left/right to multiply/divide by powers of two. Extracting the third byte of a packed word: shift right 16, then AND 0xFF — each step traced in binary in exam answers.

Performance and parallelism

  • Factors: clock speed (ticks per second), cores (independent instruction streams), cache size and levels (L1 fastest/smallest, L3 slowest/largest), bus width (bits per transfer), word length (bits the CPU processes at once), instruction set (CISC/RISC trade-off), and pipelining (overlapping fetch/decode/execute of consecutive instructions — stalls occur on branches).
  • Parallel processing: bit-level (wider words process more bits at once), instruction-level (pipelines and superscalar execution), data-level (SIMD — same operation on many data items: GPU rendering), task-level (different programs or subtasks on different cores). Amdahl's law bounds the gain: the sequential fraction limits speed-up regardless of core count.
  • Virtual machines: a software emulation of another machine. Hardware VMs (hypervisors like VMware/KVM) run several OS instances on one physical host — server consolidation, isolation, easy backup and migration. Language VMs (the JVM, the CLR) execute bytecode portably: compile once to bytecode, run anywhere the VM exists — platform independence at the cost of a translation overhead versus native code.
Worked: a program is 25% sequential. Speed-up with 8 cores (Amdahl):

  speed-up = 1 / (0.25 + 0.75 / 8) = 1 / (0.25 + 0.09375) = 1 / 0.34375 = 2.91

Eight cores give under a threefold gain - the parallel hardware cannot help
the sequential quarter, which is the whole point of the question.

Worked example: one program through the whole stack

Source (high level):     z = x + y
Assembly (low level):    LOAD X / ADD Y / STORE Z
Machine code:            01 001000 / 10 001001 / 11 001010  (as above)

The assembler resolves labels to addresses; the CPU executes each instruction
through fetch-decode-execute; the compiler that produced the assembly chose the
register usage and the instruction order. Three representations, one behaviour -
and the exam question naming "which stage produced which artefact" targets
exactly these three columns.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Saying the PC increments during execute; it increments after the fetch.
  • Confusing MAR (address) with MDR (data) — the most-marked pair in Unit 1.
  • Claiming assembly is "almost high level"; it is one-to-one with machine instructions and hardware-specific.
  • Forgetting that CMP sets flags and conditional jumps read them — without that link, selection and loops have no mechanism.
  • Answering parallelism questions with "more cores = faster" only; Amdahl's law and the type of parallelism (bit/instruction/data/task) are the marks.
  • Describing a language VM as an emulator of hardware only; the JVM executes bytecode — portability is its purpose.
  • Using a logical shift to halve a negative two's-complement number (must be arithmetic shift, preserving the sign bit).

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Unit 1, 5 marks). Describe the fetch–decode–execute cycle of an instruction that adds the contents of address 200 to the accumulator.

Answer: Fetch: the PC's value is copied to the MAR; a READ signal fetches the instruction from memory into the MDR; it is copied to the CIR; the PC increments. Decode: the control unit interprets the opcode as ADD with operand 200. Execute: MAR ← 200; READ fetches the data into the MDR; the ALU adds MDR to the accumulator and stores the result in it.

Question 2 (Unit 1, 3 marks). Explain the purpose of the MAR and the MDR.

Answer: The MAR holds the memory address currently being read from or written to, driving the address bus. The MDR holds the data or instruction transferred in that access — fetched values arrive there and outgoing values are placed there before a write.

Question 3 (Unit 1, 4 marks). Explain two differences between CISC and RISC processors and state one use for each.

Answer: CISC has many complex instructions, often multi-cycle and microcoded, so programs need fewer instructions — suiting desktops (x86). RISC has few simple instructions, each executed in one clock cycle with hardwired control and heavy pipelining — suiting power-sensitive mobile/embedded devices (ARM). The trade-off: fewer instructions per task versus fewer cycles per instruction.

Question 4 (Unit 1, 4 marks). Explain how 8 cores can fail to give 8× speed-up.

Answer: Amdahl's law: the speed-up is limited by the sequential fraction of the program, which no extra core can accelerate — only the parallel fraction divides among cores. Coordination overhead (thread synchronisation, communication) and memory-bus contention further reduce gains, so real speed-up depends on how much of the work is genuinely parallel.

Question 5 (Unit 1, 4 marks). Describe what a hypervisor provides and one benefit and one drawback of virtualisation.

Answer: A hypervisor runs multiple virtual machines, each with its own OS, on one physical machine by arbitrating CPU, memory and storage. Benefit: server consolidation and isolation — one hardware outlay, VMs start, migrate and snapshot independently. Drawback: each VM competes for shared physical resources, so performance is lower than bare metal, and the hypervisor itself consumes resources and expands the trusted computing base.

Question 6 (Unit 1, 3 marks). Explain how a conditional jump implements IF mark ≥ 50 in assembly.

Answer: CMP compares the accumulator with 50 by subtraction, setting flags (zero, negative, carry, overflow) without storing the result. The test mark ≥ 50 becomes a jump-if-greater-or-equal (reading N and V or C flags) to the "pass" label; if the condition fails, execution falls through to the "fail" code. Flags are the bridge between comparison and branching.

Below the assembly sits the digital logic every instruction is built from: hardware components, gates and Boolean algebra.

title: Membranes, Proteins, DNA and Gene Expression - AS Level Biology
content:
Membranes, Proteins, DNA and Gene Expression - AS Level Biology

These revision notes cover Edexcel International AS Level Biology WBI11 Topic 2, exploring how DNA holds genetic information, how gene expression translates that code into functional proteins, and how cell membranes regulate the internal environment of cells through specialized transport mechanisms.

Cell Membranes and Structure

Cell membranes act as barriers and exchange surfaces, understood scientifically through the fluid mosaic model. This model interprets experimental data regarding lipid and protein mobility to explain membrane properties. The phospholipid bilayer features hydrophilic phosphate heads facing outwards and hydrophobic fatty acid tails facing inwards. Cholesterol molecules fit between phospholipids, regulating membrane fluidity across varying temperatures. Glycoproteins and glycolipids project from the external surface, serving as cell recognition sites and receptors.

  • Fluid mosaic model: interpretation of data showing phospholipid and protein lateral movement.
  • Cholesterol: restricts excessive fluidity at high temperatures and prevents close packing at low temperatures.
  • Glycoproteins and glycolipids: carbohydrate chains attached to proteins or lipids for cell recognition and cell signaling.

Core Practical: Membrane Permeability

Core Practical 3 involves investigating membrane permeability by examining the effects of temperature and alcohol concentration on beetroot cell membranes. Betalain pigment leaks out when cell surface membranes and tonoplasts are damaged. Colorimetry quantifies the amount of pigment released by measuring absorbance.

  • Temperature effect: high temperatures increase kinetic energy, denature membrane proteins, and disrupt the phospholipid bilayer, increasing permeability.
  • Alcohol effect: organic solvents dissolve lipids in the membrane, creating gaps that allow pigment leakage.
  • Method: wash beetroot discs thoroughly to remove loose surface pigment, place in water baths at varying temperatures or alcohol concentrations for a set time, and use a colorimeter with a blue-green filter to measure absorbance.

Transport Across Membranes

Substances move across cell membranes via passive transport mechanisms such as simple diffusion and facilitated diffusion down concentration gradients without metabolic energy. Active transport moves substances against a concentration gradient using carrier proteins and ATP as an immediate source of energy. Endocytosis and exocytosis transport bulk materials into and out of cells via vesicles. Channel proteins provide hydrophilic pores for charged ions, while carrier proteins change shape to transport specific molecules.

  • Simple diffusion: net movement of small, non-polar molecules down a concentration gradient.
  • Facilitated diffusion: passive movement of polar molecules or ions through specific channel or carrier proteins.
  • Active transport: movement against a concentration gradient requiring carrier proteins and ATP hydrolysis.
  • Endocytosis and exocytosis: bulk transport using vesicle formation and fusion, requiring ATP.

Osmosis and Water Potential

Osmosis is the net movement of free water molecules from a region of higher water potential to a region of lower water potential through a partially permeable membrane down a water potential gradient. Water potential is measured in kilopascals (kPa), with pure water having a water potential of 0 kPa. Solute addition lowers water potential into negative values. Recommended additional practical work involves using plant tissue and graded solute concentrations to determine tissue water potentials.

  • Water potential formula concept: Ψ = Ψs + Ψp (solute potential plus pressure potential).
  • Plant tissue practical: immerse plant cylinders in sucrose solutions of varying concentrations, calculate percentage change in mass, and find the point of zero mass change where external water potential equals internal cell water potential.

DNA and RNA Structure

Mononucleotides are the building blocks of nucleic acids, consisting of a pentose sugar (deoxyribose in DNA, ribose in RNA), a phosphate group, and a nitrogenous base (adenine, thymine, cytosine, guanine, or uracil in RNA). Polynucleotides form via condensation reactions creating phosphodiester bonds between the sugar of one nucleotide and the phosphate of the next. DNA is a double helix composed of two antiparallel strands held together by hydrogen bonds between complementary base pairs: adenine pairs with thymine via two hydrogen bonds, and cytosine pairs with guanine via three hydrogen bonds.

  • Mononucleotide components: pentose sugar, phosphate group, nitrogenous base.
  • Bases in DNA: adenine (A), thymine (T), cytosine (C), guanine (G).
  • Bases in RNA: adenine (A), uracil (U), cytosine (C), guanine (G).
  • Bonding: phosphodiester bonds along the backbone; hydrogen bonds between complementary base pairs.

DNA Replication and Meselson-Stahl Experiment

DNA replication is semi-conservative, ensuring genetic continuity. DNA helicase unwinds and unzips the double helix by breaking hydrogen bonds between bases. DNA polymerase catalyses the formation of phosphodiester bonds between free nucleotides, adding them to the 3' end of the growing strand. The Meselson-Stahl experiment provided data supporting semi-conservative replication and refuting conservative and dispersive models by growing bacteria in mediums containing heavy nitrogen (N15) and light nitrogen (N14).

  • Semi-conservative replication: each new DNA molecule contains one original strand and one newly synthesized strand.
  • DNA helicase: unwinds double helix and breaks hydrogen bonds.
  • DNA polymerase: aligns free mononucleotides and forms phosphodiester bonds.
  • Meselson-Stahl findings: after one generation in N14, DNA was a hybrid density (refuting conservative); after two generations, half hybrid and half light density (refuting dispersive).

Protein Synthesis and Genetic Code

A gene is a sequence of bases on a DNA molecule that codes for a sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide chain. The genetic code is a triplet code (three bases code for one amino acid), non-overlapping, and degenerate (multiple codons can code for the same amino acid). Protein synthesis involves transcription in the nucleus and translation on ribosomes. RNA polymerase binds to the promoter, and the DNA template (antisense) strand is transcribed into messenger RNA (mRNA). mRNA travels to ribosomes where transfer RNA (tRNA) molecules with specific anticodons bring amino acids. Start codons initiate translation, and stop codons terminate it.

  • Transcription: RNA polymerase synthesizes pre-mRNA complementary to the antisense DNA strand, which is processed into mature mRNA.
  • Translation: mRNA binds to a ribosome; tRNA anticodons bind to complementary mRNA codons. Peptide bonds form between adjacent amino acids.
  • Code properties: triplet, non-overlapping, degenerate, universal.

Mutations

Errors in DNA replication can cause gene mutations, classified as substitution, insertion, or deletion of bases. A substitution changes a single base, which may be silent, missense, or nonsense. Insertions and deletions cause a frameshift, altering every subsequent triplet codon. Many mutations have no observable effect due to the degenerate nature of the code or if they occur in non-coding regions. However, specific mutations give rise to genetic disorders or cancer.

  • Substitution: one base replaced by another, altering a single codon.
  • Insertion/deletion: addition or loss of bases causing a shift in the reading frame of all downstream codons.
  • Effects: silent (no amino acid change), missense (different amino acid), nonsense (premature stop codon).

Inheritance and Genetics Terminology

Genetics terminology underpins inheritance patterns. A gene is a sequence of DNA coding for a polypeptide; alleles are alternative forms of a gene. Genotype is the genetic makeup, while phenotype is the observable characteristic resulting from genotype and environment. Recessive alleles are expressed only in homozygotes, whereas dominant alleles are expressed in heterozygotes and homozygotes. Codominance occurs when both alleles contribute to the phenotype. Homozygotes possess two identical alleles; heterozygotes possess two different alleles. Monohybrid inheritance examines the transmission of a single gene, and genetic pedigree diagrams track phenotypes across generations. Sex linkage involves genes located on sex chromosomes, typically the X chromosome, such as the gene for red-green colour blindness.

  • Genotype and phenotype: genetic constitution versus expressed physical traits.
  • Homozygote vs heterozygote: matching versus contrasting allele pairs.
  • Codominance: both alleles equally expressed in the phenotype.
  • Sex-linked inheritance: X-linked recessive conditions show higher incidence in males who inherit a single affected X chromosome.

Cystic Fibrosis

Cystic fibrosis is caused by a gene mutation (often a deletion of three nucleotides coding for phenylalanine) affecting the CFTR protein, a chloride ion channel. This impairs water movement across epithelial tissues, producing thick, sticky mucus. In the gaseous exchange system, cilia cannot clear mucus effectively, leading to trapped bacteria and chronic lung infections. In the digestive system, pancreatic ducts become blocked by mucus, preventing digestive enzymes from reaching the small intestine and causing malabsorption. In the reproductive system, thickened cervical mucus or blocked sperm ducts can cause infertility.

  • CFTR protein defect: faulty chloride transport reduces water movement out of cells into mucus.
  • Gaseous exchange: accumulation of viscous mucus leads to frequent bacterial infections and damaged lung tissue.
  • Digestive system: blocked pancreatic ducts reduce enzyme secretion, impairing food digestion and nutrient uptake.

Genetic Screening and Ethics

Genetic screening identifies individuals carrying mutant alleles or affected fetuses. Methods include carrier testing for prospective parents, pre-implantation genetic diagnosis (PGD) during IVF, and prenatal testing via amniocentesis (taking amniotic fluid at 15 to 20 weeks) or chorionic villus sampling (sampling placental tissue at 11 to 14 weeks). Prenatal screening carries risks such as miscarriage. Ethical, moral, and social implications involve debates over the right to life, emotional stress of results, decisions regarding termination, and societal discrimination.

  • Amniocentesis and CVS: invasive prenatal tests to obtain fetal cells for karyotyping or DNA analysis, carrying a small risk of miscarriage.
  • Pre-implantation genetic diagnosis (PGD): screening embryos created via IVF before uterine implantation.
  • Ethical viewpoints: religious beliefs concerning the sanctity of life, moral arguments surrounding disability rights, and social impacts on healthcare resources and insurance access.

Typical mistakes

  • Confusing the sense (coding) and antisense (template) DNA strands: remember that RNA polymerase uses the antisense strand as the template to build complementary mRNA.
  • Stating that water moves down a concentration gradient in osmosis: always state that water moves down a water potential gradient from high to low water potential.
  • Forgetting to mention the exact role of ATP in active transport: state that ATP is hydrolyzed to provide energy for carrier protein conformational change.
  • Describing frameshift mutations for substitutions: substitution mutations alter only a single triplet, whereas insertions and deletions cause frameshifts.

Exam-style questions

  1. Explain why beetroot membrane permeability increases at temperatures above 60 °C. (Answer: High temperatures impart kinetic energy that disrupts the phospholipid bilayer and denatures membrane-bound transport proteins, allowing betalain pigment to leak out.)
  2. Describe the role of tRNA during translation. (Answer: tRNA molecules have a specific anticodon that binds to a complementary codon on mRNA and carry a specific amino acid to the ribosome to build the polypeptide chain.)
  3. Explain how a deletion mutation in the CFTR gene results in thick mucus in individuals with cystic fibrosis. (Answer: The deletion alters the amino acid sequence, leading to a non-functional CFTR chloride ion channel. Chloride ions cannot leave the cell, reducing water movement via osmosis and producing dehydrated, viscous mucus.)
  4. Compare amniocentesis and chorionic villus sampling as methods of prenatal screening. (Answer: Amniocentesis tests amniotic fluid cells and is performed later in pregnancy (15 to 20 weeks) with a slightly lower miscarriage risk, whereas chorionic villus sampling tests placental tissue earlier (11 to 14 weeks) but carries a slightly higher miscarriage risk.)

Use these notes alongside active recall of definitions, core practical method steps, and practice interpreting pedigree diagrams and genetic cross calculations. Review protein synthesis steps next.

title: Exam technique: Permutations and Combinations
content:
### What earns the marks
For counting, the permutation vs combination choice justified earns the method mark. For restricted arrangements, fixing the block first then permuting earns both marks. For probability of selections, the hypergeometric fraction built stepwise earns each mark.
### Traps
Error: P used where order is irrelevant. Correction: C for choose. Error: double counting symmetric selections. Correction: divide by the internal permutations. Error: identical items permuted fully. Correction: divide by repeats factorial.

title: A Level Physics: Oscillations and Waves II
content:
A Level Physics: Oscillations and Waves II

Simple harmonic motion is the master oscillation: the movement of a pendulum, a mass on a spring, a guitar string, a child on a swing — every system that accelerates back toward an equilibrium position with a restoring force proportional to displacement. This note builds SHM from zero: the defining condition and its equations, the displacement, velocity and acceleration graphs and their calculus links, the energy bookkeeping within a cycle, and the real-world finishing topics — damping and resonance — with the applications and disasters that make them examinable.

What simple harmonic motion is

A body performs simple harmonic motion (SHM) when its acceleration is proportional to its displacement from a fixed equilibrium point and always directed toward that point:

a = - ω² x

a = acceleration (m s⁻²), x = displacement from equilibrium (m)
ω = angular frequency (rad s⁻¹); the minus sign means the
acceleration always points back toward equilibrium

The analogy: a ball in a bowl. Push the ball up the side (displacement) and gravity pulls it back with a force proportional to how far up the slope it is — push twice as far, and the restoring force doubles. That proportionality is the whole defining feature; friction-less mass-spring systems and small-angle pendulums obey it.

QuantitySymbolRelation
Displacementxx = A sin(ωt) (from equilibrium at t = 0)
AmplitudeAmaximum displacement
PeriodTT = 2π/ω; mass on a spring: T = 2π√(m/k); pendulum: T = 2π√(L/g)
Frequencyff = 1/T = ω/(2π)
Angular frequencyωω = 2πf = √(k/m) (spring), √(g/L) (pendulum)

SHM equations and graphs

Starting from equilibrium at t = 0, the kinematics follows by differentiation (or by reading the graphs):

displacement:  x = A sin(ω t)
velocity:      v = A ω cos(ω t)
acceleration:  a = - A ω² sin(ω t) = - ω² x

velocity-displacement relation:
v = ω √(A² - x²)

Graph discipline is a mark source in its own right: displacement is a sine wave; velocity leads displacement by a quarter cycle (cosine); acceleration is the inverted displacement (anti-phase, scaled by ω²). At the extremes (x = ±A): velocity is zero and acceleration is maximum; at equilibrium (x = 0): velocity is maximum and acceleration is zero. Learn the four positions (centre, both extremes, mid-point) as a table of states.

Worked example. A mass oscillates with amplitude 0.10 m and frequency 2.0 Hz. Find ω, the maximum speed, and the maximum acceleration.

ω = 2 π f = 2 × 3.14 × 2.0 = 12.6 rad s⁻¹
v_max = A ω = 0.10 × 12.6 = 1.26 m s⁻¹
a_max = A ω² = 0.10 × 158 = 15.8 m s⁻²

Worked example 2 (using v = ω√(A² − x²)). With the same oscillation, find the speed at x = 0.06 m.

v = ω √(A² - x²) = 12.6 x √(0.010 - 0.0036)
  = 12.6 x √(0.0064) = 12.6 × 0.08 = 1.01 m s⁻¹

Worked example 3 (pendulum). Find the period of a 0.90 m pendulum (g = 9.81 m s⁻²).

T = 2 π √(L/g) = 2 × 3.14 x √(0.90/9.81)
  = 6.28 x √(0.0917) = 6.28 × 0.303 = 1.90 s

Energy in simple harmonic motion

Energy shuttles between kinetic and potential stores while the total stays constant (undamped SHM):

total energy:  E = (1/2) m ω² A² = (1/2) k A²
kinetic:       KE = (1/2) m ω² (A² - x²)
potential:     PE = (1/2) m ω² x²   (spring: (1/2) k x²)

The energy curves are examinable as graphs: total energy is a horizontal line over x; KE is an inverted parabola peaking at equilibrium; PE is an upright parabola peaking at the extremes; against time both are sine-squared curves oscillating at twice the frequency of x. Doubling the amplitude quadruples the total energy (E ∝ A²) — a favourite multiple-choice item.

Worked example. A 0.50 kg mass on a spring (k = 200 N m⁻¹) oscillates with amplitude 0.08 m. Find the total energy and the kinetic energy at x = 0.04 m.

E = (1/2) k A² = 0.5 × 200 × 0.0064 = 0.64 J
PE at x = 0.04: (1/2) k x² = 0.5 × 200 × 0.0016 = 0.16 J
KE = E - PE = 0.64 - 0.16 = 0.48 J

Damping

Real oscillations lose energy to drag and friction — damping. The three regimes matter:

  • Light damping: amplitude decays exponentially while the system keeps oscillating at almost the natural frequency (a child's swing gradually slowing).
  • Critical damping: the system returns to equilibrium in the minimum time without overshooting — deliberately engineered for car suspension, door closers and moving-coil meters.
  • Heavy (over) damping: a slow, sluggish return without oscillation.

The energy lost per cycle is the exam phrasing: light damping reduces amplitude gradually because each cycle transfers energy to the surroundings; the total energy falls exponentially with time even though the frequency barely changes.

Resonance

A driven oscillation responds most strongly when the driving frequency matches the system's natural frequency — resonance. The amplitude–frequency curve shows a peak at resonance; sharper peaks mean lighter damping. The mechanism: at resonance the driving force is in phase with the velocity, so energy is transferred most efficiently each cycle.

ApplicationUse or effect
Musical instrumentsair columns and strings resonate at their natural frequencies to amplify sound
Radio tuningan LC circuit selects the broadcast frequency that resonates with it
Microwave ovensdrive water molecules near their resonant absorption frequency
Car suspensiondesigned so road-frequency inputs never match the car's natural frequency; damping controls the peak
Tacoma Narrows (1940)wind-driven resonance (with aeroelastic flutter) destroyed the bridge — the cautionary case study
Bridges and buildingsseismic design detunes natural frequencies from earthquake oscillations

Worked example. Explain why soldiers break step crossing a bridge. Answer: Marching produces a periodic driving force at the step frequency; if it matched the bridge's natural frequency, resonance would build large-amplitude oscillations and structural damage; breaking step makes the driving frequency irregular and removes the coherent input.

Worked examples: combined SHM problems

Worked example. A 0.25 kg mass on a spring completes 20 oscillations in 8.0 s. Find the spring constant k.

T = 8.0/20 = 0.40 s
T = 2 π √(m/k)  →  k = m (2 π/T)²
k = 0.25 x (6.28/0.40)² = 0.25 × 246.4 = 61.6 N m⁻¹
  = 62 N m⁻¹ (2 s.f.)

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Definition) State the defining condition for SHM. Answer: The acceleration is proportional to the displacement from equilibrium and directed toward it: a = −ω²x.
  2. (Graphs) Sketch or describe the velocity–time graph of an oscillating mass starting at maximum displacement. Answer: Velocity is a cosine-like curve starting at zero, reaching extremes of ±v_max as the mass passes equilibrium, one quarter cycle ahead of the displacement.
  3. (Calculations) An oscillator has amplitude 0.12 m and ω = 8.0 rad s⁻¹. Find the maximum acceleration. Answer: a_max = Aω² = 0.12 × 64 = 7.68 m s⁻² ≈ 7.7 m s⁻².
  4. (Energy) State how the total energy of an SHM system depends on amplitude and explain the effect of doubling it. Answer: E = ½kA², so energy is proportional to A²; doubling the amplitude quadruples the total energy.
  5. (Pendulum) Explain why a pendulum clock keeps worse time on a warm day. Answer: Warmth lengthens the pendulum L, and T = 2π√(L/g), so the period increases and the clock runs slow.
  6. (Damping) Distinguish light and critical damping. Answer: Light damping: oscillations continue with amplitude decaying exponentially; critical damping: the system returns to equilibrium in the shortest time without oscillating.
  7. (Resonance) Sketch qualitatively the amplitude–frequency response for a lightly and a heavily damped driven system, and state one use of resonance. Answer: Both peak at the natural frequency; the lightly damped peak is tall and sharp, the heavily damped one short and broad. Use: radio tuning circuits selecting a station's frequency.
  8. (Practical) Describe how you would determine g using a simple pendulum. Answer: Measure pendulum length L from pivot to bob centre; time N complete oscillations with a stopwatch and find T = t/N; repeat for several L values; plot T² against L — the gradient is 4π²/g, so g = 4π²/gradient.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • ω versus f: ω = 2πf. In a = −ω²x the ω is angular frequency; using f directly misses a factor of 4π².
  • Phase of the graphs: at maximum displacement, speed is zero and acceleration is maximum — candidates often invert this. Anchor on the extremes first: nothing moves at the turning points.
  • Energy ∝ A²: doubling amplitude quadruples energy; the amplitude of displacement does not scale energy linearly.
  • Pendulum validity: T = 2π√(L/g) assumes small angles (under about 10°) and a point mass; large angles lengthen the period.
  • Period independence: a pendulum's period is independent of bob mass and amplitude (small angle) — the classic conceptual question.
  • Damping and frequency: damping reduces amplitude and slightly shifts the peak frequency; in light damping the frequency is almost unchanged — do not claim the oscillation stops instantly.
  • Resonance condition: resonance requires the driving frequency to match the natural frequency; merely being "vibrated" does not guarantee it.
  • Spring constant from period: rearrange algebraically first (k = m(2π/T)²) and write the formula line — the rearrangement itself carries marks.
  • Precision: 2 or 3 s.f. with units (rad s⁻¹, m s⁻², N m⁻¹, J); keep π in the working until the final step.

Equations and symbols

Simple harmonic motion is one defining condition, its three kinematic consequences, and the energy bookkeeping that follows from them. Note every symbol: ω is angular frequency in rad s⁻¹, not frequency in Hz, and the factor of 2π between them is where most marks are lost.

a = - ω² x Key: a = acceleration (m s⁻²); ω = angular frequency (rad s⁻¹); x = displacement from equilibrium (m). The minus sign is the definition: acceleration always points back toward equilibrium. Proving proportionality to −x is the mark for "show that this is SHM".

x = A sin(ω t) Key: x = displacement (m); A = amplitude, the maximum displacement (m); ω = angular frequency (rad s⁻¹); t = time (s). This form assumes the oscillation starts at equilibrium; starting at maximum displacement gives a cosine.

v = A ω cos(ω t) Key: v = velocity (m s⁻¹); A ω = maximum speed (m s⁻¹); the cosine shows velocity leads displacement by a quarter cycle and is zero at the extremes.

v = ω √(A² - x²) Key: the velocity at a given displacement without needing the time; maximum (Aω) at x = 0, zero at x = ±A. This is the form to use when the question gives a position rather than a clock reading.

ω = 2πf = √(k/m) (spring), √(g/L) (pendulum) Key: ω = angular frequency (rad s⁻¹); f = frequency (Hz); k = spring constant (N m⁻¹); m = mass (kg); g = 9.81 m s⁻²; L = pendulum length (m). The pendulum form assumes small angles and a point mass.

T = 2π√(m/k) Key: T = period (s); m = mass on the spring (kg); k = spring constant (N m⁻¹). Period rises with mass and falls with stiffness, and is independent of amplitude.

ω = 2 π f = 2 × 3.14 × 2.0 = 12.6 rad s⁻¹ Key: f = 2.0 Hz, so ω = 12.6 rad s⁻¹. Substituting f directly into a = −ω²x underestimates the acceleration by 4π² ≈ 39.5.

v_max = A ω Key: v_max = maximum speed (m s⁻¹), reached as the mass passes equilibrium; A = amplitude (m); ω = angular frequency (rad s⁻¹).

a_max = A ω² Key: a_max = maximum acceleration (m s⁻²), reached at the extremes where the restoring force is greatest; A = amplitude (m); ω = angular frequency (rad s⁻¹).

E = (1/2) m ω² A² = (1/2) k A² Key: E = total energy of the oscillation (J); m = mass (kg); ω = angular frequency (rad s⁻¹); A = amplitude (m); k = spring constant (N m⁻¹). Energy is proportional to A², so doubling the amplitude quadruples it.

KE = (1/2) m ω² (A² - x²) Key: KE = kinetic energy at displacement x (J); the bracket is largest at equilibrium, where the speed is greatest, and zero at the extremes.

PE = (1/2) m ω² x² Key: PE = potential energy stored at displacement x (J); for a spring this is (1/2)kx². Adding KE and PE at any x returns the constant total E.

k = m (2 π/T)² Key: k = spring constant (N m⁻¹); m = mass (kg); T = measured period (s). Rearranging first and quoting the rearranged formula is worth a mark, and it is the standard route from a period measurement to k.

The graphs are the answer to half the questions. Displacement is a sine, velocity a cosine, acceleration the inverted displacement; at the extremes the speed is zero and the acceleration is maximum, at equilibrium the reverse. Anchoring on those four positions prevents the phase error that reverses a whole sketch.

title: AS Level Mathematics: Functions
content:
AS Level Mathematics: Functions

A function is a rule that turns each input into exactly one output — a machine with one chute per item. This note builds the whole AS treatment from zero: function notation with domain and range, the standard graphs and their shapes, composite functions and why order matters, inverses with their reflection in y = x, and the transformation rules that shift, stretch and reflect any graph. The marks in this topic come from precision — writing the correct domain, composing in the right order, and stating the rule for the inverse before using it.

Notation, domain and range

f(x) = 2x + 3      "f of x"
f(4) = 11          substitute 4 for every x
domain: the set of allowed inputs
range: the set of outputs the function actually produces

Domain restrictions matter: f(x) = 1/x is undefined at x = 0; f(x) = √x requires x ≥ 0; a quadratic over the reals has all reals as its domain. The range is found by considering the function's behaviour over its stated domain — for a quadratic, complete the square to find the minimum or maximum.

Worked example. f(x) = x² − 4, domain x ≥ 0. Find the range.

at x = 0: f = -4; the function increases without limit
range: f(x) >= -4

Worked example 2 (reciprocal). g(x) = 3/(x − 2), x ≠ 2. State the domain and range.

domain: all real x except 2
range: all real values except 0 (the fraction can never be 0)

The standard graphs

FunctionShapeFeatures
y = xstraight linegradient 1, through origin
y = x²parabola upwardminimum at origin, symmetric
y = x³cubic, S-shapedpasses through origin, increasing
y = 1/xtwo branches (hyperbola)asymptotes x = 0 and y = 0
y = √xhalf-parabola on its sidedomain x ≥ 0, range y ≥ 0
y = |x|V-shapevertex at origin, domain all reals
y = aˣ (a > 1)exponential growthalways positive, through (0, 1)

Knowing these shapes is the foundation of graph transformations and of estimating solutions graphically.

Composite functions

fg(x) means f(g(x)): apply g first, then f
gf(x) means g(f(x)): apply f first, then g
in general fg(x) is not the same as gf(x)

Worked example. f(x) = 2x + 1, g(x) = x². Find fg(x) and gf(x).

fg(x) = f(g(x)) = f(x^2) = 2x^2 + 1
gf(x) = g(f(x)) = (2x + 1)^2 = 4x^2 + 4x + 1
These differ, so order matters.

Worked example 2 (solving). With the same f and g, solve fg(x) = 19.

2x^2 + 1 = 19
2x^2 = 18  ->  x^2 = 9  ->  x = 3 or x = -3

Inverse functions

The inverse f⁻¹ undoes f: if f(a) = b then f⁻¹(b) = a. To find it, write y = f(x), swap x and y, and rearrange for y.

method: y = f(x)  ->  x = f(y) after swap  ->  y = f^-1(x)

Worked example. Find the inverse of f(x) = 3x − 7.

y = 3x - 7
swap: x = 3y - 7
rearrange: 3y = x + 7  ->  y = (x + 7)/3
f^-1(x) = (x + 7)/3

Worked example 2 (quadratic, restricted domain). f(x) = x² + 2 for x ≥ 0. Find f⁻¹ and its domain.

y = x^2 + 2
swap: x = y^2 + 2  ->  y^2 = x - 2  ->  y = sqrt(x - 2)
(the negative root is rejected because the domain is x >= 0)
f^-1(x) = sqrt(x - 2), domain x >= 2

Two properties worth remembering: the graph of f⁻¹ is the reflection of f in the line y = x, and the domain of f⁻¹ is the range of f (and vice versa).

Transformations of graphs

TransformationEffect on the graphWhat changes
y = f(x) + atranslate up by ay-coordinates +a
y = f(x + a)translate left by ax replaced by x + a (inside: opposite direction)
y = af(x)vertical stretch by ay-coordinates × a
y = f(ax)horizontal stretch by 1/ax-coordinates ÷ a
y = −f(x)reflection in the x-axisy-coordinates negated
y = f(−x)reflection in the y-axisx-coordinates negated

The inside/outside rule is the one that trips candidates: changes outside the bracket affect y and behave as written; changes inside affect x and behave in reverse.

Worked example. The point (3, 5) lies on y = f(x). Find its image under y = f(x − 2) + 1.

f(x - 2) shifts the graph 2 to the right; +1 shifts it up 1
image: (3 + 2, 5 + 1) = (5, 6)

Worked example 2 (stretch). The point (4, 1) is on y = f(x). Find its image under y = f(2x).

horizontal stretch by 1/2: x-coordinate halves
image: (2, 1)

Rational functions and asymptotes

A rational function is a ratio of polynomials, y = p(x)/q(x). Its graph is shaped by two constraints: where the denominator is zero the function is undefined (a vertical asymptote), and for large x the ratio settles to a horizontal asymptote determined by the leading terms.

y = (ax + b)/(cx + d)
vertical asymptote: cx + d = 0  ->  x = -d/c
horizontal asymptote: y -> a/c as x -> +/- infinity
excluded value: the point where the denominator vanishes is
not in the domain

Worked example. Sketch y = 2/(x − 1) and state its domain and range.

vertical asymptote x = 1 (denominator zero)
horizontal asymptote y = 0 (numerator fixed, denominator grows)
domain: x not equal to 1; range: y not equal to 0
the two branches lie in the regions x < 1 and x > 1

Worked example 2 (linear over linear). Sketch y = (x + 1)/(x − 2).

vertical asymptote x = 2
horizontal asymptote y = 1 (leading coefficients 1/1)
intercepts: y = -1/2 at x = 0; x = -1 at y = 0

Exponential and logarithmic graphs

Exponentials and logarithms are inverse functions, and their graphs encode that relationship. y = aˣ (a > 1) rises ever more steeply, passes through (0, 1) and never touches the x-axis — the x-axis is an asymptote. y = log_a x is the reflection in y = x: it passes through (1, 0), has a vertical asymptote at x = 0, and is defined only for x > 0.

  • Growth and decay: y = Ae^(kx) grows for k > 0 and decays for k < 0; the constant A is the value at x = 0.
  • Logarithm laws: log(ab) = log a + log b; log(a/b) = log a − log b; log(aⁿ) = n log a.
  • Solving exponentials: take logs of both sides — 3^x = 20 gives x log 3 = log 20, so x = log 20/log 3 ≈ 2.73.

Worked example. Solve 5^(2x−1) = 40.

(2x - 1) log 5 = log 40
2x - 1 = log 40/log 5 = 1.602/0.699 = 2.292
2x = 3.292  ->  x = 1.65 (3 s.f.)

Worked example 2 (modelling with an exponential). A colony of bacteria doubles every 3 hours, starting at 500. Write the population after t hours and find when it reaches 20 000.

P = 500 x 2^(t/3)
20000 = 500 x 2^(t/3)  ->  40 = 2^(t/3)
log 40 = (t/3) log 2  ->  t/3 = 5.322  ->  t = 16.0 hours

The modelling step — translating "doubles every 3 hours" into 2^(t/3) — is where most marks are lost; write the base (2 for doubling, 0.5 for halving) and the exponent (time divided by the period) explicitly before solving. For decay, the same structure with a base below 1 (or a negative exponent) describes cooling, depreciation and radioactive half-life, so one pattern covers a whole family of questions.

Worked examples: mixed function problems

Worked example. f(x) = x + 2, g(x) = 3x. Find f⁻¹(x), fg(x), and show that f⁻¹(fg(x)) = g(x).

f^-1(x) = x - 2
fg(x) = 3x + 2
f^-1(fg(x)) = (3x + 2) - 2 = 3x = g(x)

Worked example 2 (range of composite). f(x) = x², g(x) = x + 1. Find the range of fg for x ≥ 0.

fg(x) = (x + 1)^2
for x >= 0: x + 1 >= 1  ->  fg(x) >= 1
range: fg(x) >= 1

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Evaluate) f(x) = 2x² − 1. Find f(−3). Answer: 2(9) − 1 = 17.
  2. (Domain) State the domain of g(x) = 1/(x + 4). Answer: x ≠ −4.
  3. (Composite) f(x) = x + 3, g(x) = 2x. Find fg(x). Answer: 2x + 3.
  4. (Inverse) Find the inverse of h(x) = (x − 5)/2. Answer: y = 2x + 5.
  5. (Inverse domain) f(x) = x² + 1 for x ≥ 0. State the domain of f⁻¹. Answer: x ≥ 1 (the range of f).
  6. (Transformation) Describe the transformation y = f(x) → y = f(x + 3) − 2. Answer: translation 3 left and 2 down.
  7. (Point image) (2, 7) is on y = f(x). Find its image on y = 2f(x). Answer: (2, 14).
  8. (Reasoning) Explain why f⁻¹(f(x)) = x. Answer: The inverse undoes the function: applying f then f⁻¹ returns the original input for every x in the domain of f.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Order of composition: fg means g first. Writing f(g(x)) as f(x)g(x) (a product) is a fundamental error.
  • Inside transformations reversed: f(x + 3) moves left, not right; f(2x) compresses horizontally by ½, not stretches by 2.
  • Inverse of a quadratic without restriction: x² has no inverse over all reals because it is not one-to-one; the domain restriction is what makes the inverse valid.
  • Dropping the ± in inverse quadratics: keep the root that matches the stated domain; state which and why.
  • Domain notation: write inequalities or set notation precisely (x ≠ 2; x ≥ 0); "all numbers" is rarely correct.
  • Confusing f⁻¹(x) with 1/f(x): the inverse is not the reciprocal. This is the most common notation trap.
  • Range from the wrong feature: for a quadratic on a restricted domain, evaluate the endpoints and the vertex — the range may be bounded at both ends.
  • Sketch axes: label asymptotes for reciprocal and exponential graphs; an unlabelled sketch loses communication marks.

title: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Area, Perimeter and Volume
content:
Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Area, Perimeter and Volume

Measurement questions are the most reliable marks on the paper — provided you convert units correctly and choose the right formula. This note builds the mensuration toolkit from zero: the unit system and its tricky area and volume conversions, the area formulas for every plane shape with derivations, circles, arcs and sectors, the volume and surface area of every solid in the syllabus, and compound shapes — how to add and subtract the pieces. Every worked example shows the substitution and the units, because units and premature rounding are where the marks disappear.

Units of measure

Length, area and volume units are linked by powers of the linear conversion factor:

ConversionLengthAreaVolume
1 m = 100 cm× 100× 100² = 10 000× 100³ = 1 000 000
1 cm = 10 mm× 10× 100× 1000
1 km = 1000 m× 1000× 10⁶× 10⁹

Capacity: 1 litre = 1000 cm³ = 1000 ml; 1 m³ = 1000 litres. The classic trap is converting area with a length factor — 1 m² is 10 000 cm², not 100 cm².

Worked example. Convert 3.5 m² to cm² and 2500 cm³ to litres.

3.5 m² = 3.5 × 10 000 = 35 000 cm²
2500 cm³ = 2500/1000 = 2.5 litres

Area and perimeter of plane shapes

ShapePerimeterArea
Rectangle2(l + w)l × w
Trianglesum of sides½ × base × perpendicular height
Parallelogram2(a + b)base × perpendicular height
Trapeziumsum of sides½(a + b) × h (parallel sides a, b)
Circle2πrπr²

The triangle and parallelogram formulas both need the perpendicular height — not a slanted side. That single word accounts for more lost marks than any other in mensuration.

Worked example. Find the area of a trapezium with parallel sides 7 cm and 11 cm and height 5 cm.

A = (1/2)(a + b) h = 0.5 x (7 + 11) × 5
  = 0.5 × 18 × 5 = 45 cm²

Worked example 2 (triangle). A triangle has sides 6 cm, 8 cm, 10 cm. Is it right-angled, and what is its area?

6² + 8² = 36 + 64 = 100 = 10², so yes - right-angled
at the 6-8 corner. Area = (1/2) × 6 × 8 = 24 cm².

Circles, arcs and sectors

An arc is a fraction of the circumference; a sector is the same fraction of the area. The fraction is the angle over a full turn:

circumference = 2 π r;  area = π r²

arc length  = (θ/360) × 2 π r
sector area = (θ/360) x π r²
perimeter of a sector = arc length + 2r
segment area = sector area - triangle area

Worked example. A sector has radius 9 cm and angle 140°. Find its arc length, sector area and perimeter (π = 3.142).

arc = (140/360) × 2 × 3.142 × 9 = 0.3889 × 56.56 = 21.99 cm
area = (140/360) × 3.142 × 81 = 0.3889 × 254.5 = 98.97 cm²
perimeter = 21.99 + 18 = 39.99 cm = 40.0 cm (3 s.f.)

The perimeter of a sector includes the two radii — students routinely answer only the arc length.

Worked example 2 (segment). Find the area of the segment cut off by a chord in a circle of radius 6 cm when the sector angle is 90°.

sector area = (90/360) × 3.142 × 36 = 28.28 cm²
triangle area = (1/2) × 6 × 6 = 18 cm² (right angle at centre)
segment = 28.28 - 18 = 10.28 cm²

Surface area and volume of solids

SolidVolumeSurface area
Cuboidl × w × h2(lw + lh + wh)
Prism (any cross-section)area of cross-section × length2 × cross-section + perimeter × length
Cylinderπr²h2πr² + 2πrh
Cone⅓πr²hπr² + πrl (l = slant height)
Sphere⁴⁄₃πr³4πr²
Pyramid⅓ × base area × heightsum of face areas

Slant height versus vertical height is the cone trap: volume uses the perpendicular height h, surface area uses the slant height l, and l² = r² + h² connects them.

Worked example 1 (cylinder). A cylinder has radius 4 cm and height 10 cm. Find its volume and total surface area.

V = π r² h = 3.142 × 16 × 10 = 502.7 cm³
SA = 2 π r² + 2 π r h = 2 × 3.142 × 16 + 2 × 3.142 × 4 × 10
   = 100.5 + 251.4 = 351.9 cm²  (352 cm², 3 s.f.)

Worked example 2 (cone). A cone has radius 5 cm and vertical height 12 cm. Find its volume and slant height.

V = (1/3) π r² h = (1/3) × 3.142 × 25 × 12 = 314.2 cm³
l = √(5² + 12²) = √(169) = 13 cm

Worked example 3 (sphere). Find the volume of a sphere of radius 6 cm.

V = (4/3) π r³ = (4/3) × 3.142 × 216 = 904.8 cm³

Compound shapes: add and subtract

Compound figures are split into standard shapes (add) or standard shapes with a piece removed (subtract). The discipline: draw the split lines, label each sub-shape's dimensions, compute each area separately, then combine.

Worked example. An L-shape is made from a 10 cm × 8 cm rectangle with a 4 cm × 3 cm rectangle removed from one corner. Find its area and perimeter.

area = 10 × 8 - 4 × 3 = 80 - 12 = 68 cm²
perimeter: trace the outline:
10 + 8 + 6 + 5 + 4 + 3 = 36 cm
(6 = 10 - 4 along the removed edge; 5 = 8 - 3)

Worked example 2 (semicircle on a rectangle). A running track is a 60 m by 30 m rectangle with a semicircle of diameter 30 m at each end. Find its area.

rectangle = 60 × 30 = 1800 m²
two semicircles = one full circle of radius 15:
  π x 225 = 706.9 m²
total = 1800 + 706.9 = 2507 m²  (2510 m², 3 s.f.)

Worked examples: composite solids

Composite solids combine the standard formulas: a silo is a cylinder with a hemisphere on top; a pencil is a cylinder with a cone; a capsule is a cylinder with two hemispheres. The method: split the solid, compute each volume, add; for surface area, add only the faces that are actually exposed (the join is hidden).

Worked example. A capsule is a cylinder of radius 3 cm and length 10 cm with a hemisphere at each end. Find its total volume and surface area.

cylinder volume = π r² h = 3.142 × 9 × 10 = 282.8 cm³
two hemispheres = one sphere: (4/3) π r³ = (4/3) × 3.142 × 27
               = 113.1 cm³
total volume = 282.8 + 113.1 = 395.9 cm³

surface area: cylinder curved surface 2 π r h = 188.5 cm²
plus one full sphere 4 π r² = 113.1 cm²
total = 301.6 cm²  (the circular joins are internal, not exposed)

Worked example 2 (frustum-free method). A cone of radius 6 cm and height 9 cm has its top 3 cm cut off parallel to the base. Find the volume removed.

the removed cone is similar to the whole cone, scale k = 3/9 = 1/3
volume of whole cone = (1/3) π x 36 × 9 = 339.3 cm³
removed volume = k³ x whole = (1/27) × 339.3 = 12.6 cm³
(the same as computing directly with radius 2 cm and height 3 cm)

Worked examples: reverse problems and density

Worked example. A cylindrical tank of radius 1.5 m holds 20 m³ of water. Find the depth.

V = π r² h  →  h = V/(π r²) = 20/(3.142 × 2.25)
h = 20/7.07 = 2.83 m

Worked example 2 (density). A metal cuboid 5 cm × 4 cm × 2 cm has mass 312 g. Find its density in g cm⁻³ and kg m⁻³.

volume = 5 × 4 × 2 = 40 cm³
density = 312/40 = 7.8 g cm⁻³
in kg m⁻³: 7.8 × 1000 = 7800 kg m⁻³

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Units) Convert 2.4 m² to cm² and 0.75 litres to cm³. Answer: 24 000 cm²; 750 cm³.
  2. (Trapezium) Parallel sides 12 cm and 8 cm, height 6 cm. Find the area. Answer: ½(12 + 8) × 6 = 60 cm².
  3. (Sector) Radius 7 cm, angle 72°. Find arc length and sector area. Answer: arc = (72/360) × 2π × 7 = 8.80 cm; area = (72/360) × π × 49 = 61.6 cm².
  4. (Cylinder) Radius 3 cm, height 12 cm. Find the volume. Answer: π × 9 × 12 = 339 cm³ (3 s.f.).
  5. (Cone) Radius 8 cm, height 15 cm. Find the volume and slant height. Answer: V = ⅓π × 64 × 15 = 1005 cm³; l = √(64 + 225) = 17 cm.
  6. (Sphere) Diameter 10 cm. Find the surface area. Answer: r = 5; SA = 4π × 25 = 314 cm².
  7. (Compound) A rectangle 14 m × 6 m has a semicircle of diameter 6 m removed from one end. Find the area. Answer: 84 − ½π × 9 = 84 − 14.14 = 69.9 m².
  8. (Reverse) A sphere has volume 288 cm³. Find its radius. Answer: 288 = ⁴⁄₃πr³ → r³ = 288 × 3/(4π) = 68.75 → r = 4.10 cm.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Slant versus perpendicular height: triangle/parallelogram areas use perpendicular height; cone surface area uses slant height; cone volume uses perpendicular height.
  • Area unit conversion: 1 m² = 10 000 cm² and 1 cm² = 100 mm². Multiplying by 100 instead of 10 000 is the single most common mensuration error.
  • Sector perimeter: add the two radii to the arc length. The question asks for the perimeter of the sector, not the arc.
  • Using the diameter as radius: halve the diameter first; every circle formula uses r.
  • π precision: use 3.142 or the calculator's π; rounding π to 3 loses accuracy on multi-step questions. Round only the final answer (usually 3 s.f. or as stated).
  • Compound shape subtraction: remove the correct region and keep the outline consistent — recompute the perimeter from the actual boundary, not the sum of the sub-shapes' perimeters.
  • Volume of a prism: cross-section area × length, where the length is perpendicular to the cross-section (a slanted prism uses the perpendicular distance).
  • Units in the answer: cm² for area, cm³ for volume, and capacity conversions (1000 cm³ = 1 litre). A correct number with the wrong unit loses marks on Paper 2.

Equations and symbols

Every relation this topic is examined on, written with its real notation and followed by a key naming each symbol, its unit and what it means. The sections above explain why each one is true; this sheet is the version to revise from, where the answer depends on reproducing the exact form and substituting into it without losing a unit.

Plane shapes: perimeter and area

rectangle: P = 2(l + w), A = l w
Key: l = length (cm, m); w = width, in the same unit; P = perimeter, in that unit; A = area, in the matching square unit (cm², m²). Both dimensions must be converted to the same unit before multiplying — a mixed mm and cm rectangle is the commonest unit slip.

triangle: A = ½ × base × perpendicular height
Key: base = any side, in cm or m; perpendicular height = the distance from the opposite vertex to that side, measured at 90°. A slanted side is not a height; the words "perpendicular height" are the instruction.

parallelogram: A = b h; trapezium: A = ½(a + b)h
Key: b = base; h = perpendicular height in both; a, b = the two parallel sides of the trapezium, in the same unit. The trapezium formula is the average of the parallel sides times the distance between them, which is why it also handles a triangle when one of them is zero.

circle: C = 2πr = πd, A = πr²
Key: r = radius; d = diameter, so d = 2r; π = 3.14159…; C = circumference (cm); A = area (cm²). The radius is squared in the area and only doubled in the circumference — using r² in both, or d in the area, is the standard confusion.

sector: arc length = (θ/360) × 2πr, area = (θ/360) × πr², perimeter = arc + 2r
Key: θ (theta) = the angle at the centre in degrees; r = radius; the fractions are of the whole circle. The perimeter of a sector includes the two radii, which is the term most often omitted.

Solids: volume and surface area

prism or cylinder: V = A × h and V = πr²h
Key: A = the area of the constant cross-section (cm²); h = the length or height (cm); r = the radius of a circular cross-section; V = volume (cm³). A prism is any solid with the same cross-section throughout, so the first formula covers cuboids, triangular prisms and cylinders alike.

cone: V = ⅓πr²h, curved surface = πrl; sphere: V = (4/3)πr³, surface = 4πr²
Key: r = radius; h = perpendicular height of the cone; l = the slant height, l = √(r² + h²); π = 3.14159…. The ⅓ appears in the cone and pyramid volumes and nowhere else; l is a slant length, never h.

cuboid: surface area = 2(lw + lh + wh)
Key: l, w, h = the three dimensions, in the same unit; the result is in square units. Three pairs of identical faces, which is why each product is doubled — counting six faces individually gets the same answer and fewer marks for method.

pyramid: V = ⅓ × base area × perpendicular height
Key: base area = the area of the polygon forming the base (cm²); perpendicular height = the vertical distance from apex to base, not a slant edge. Slant heights belong to the triangular faces' areas, not the volume.

density = mass/volume, so mass = density × volume
Key: density in g/cm³ or kg/m³; mass in g or kg; volume in cm³ or m³. The units must be consistent: 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³, so a density given in one system with a volume in the other multiplies the answer by a thousand.

Units, scaling and similar solids

1 m = 100 cm ⇒ 1 m² = 10⁴ cm² and 1 m³ = 10⁶ cm³
Key: the linear factor is squared for area and cubed for volume, so a factor of 100 becomes 10,000 and 1,000,000. Converting area with the length factor is the single most expensive unit error in the topic.

similar solids with length ratio k: surface areas in ratio k², volumes in ratio k³
Key: k = the ratio of any pair of corresponding lengths (a scale factor, no unit); areas scale as the square; volumes as the cube. A model at 1:20 therefore has 1/400 of the surface area and 1/8000 of the volume, which is why a scaled-down animal cannot simply be a smaller version of the original.

1 litre = 1000 cm³ = 1000 ml and 1 m³ = 1000 litres
Key: the litre is a capacity unit equal to a cubic decimetre; cm³ and ml are interchangeable. Capacity questions usually give the container's dimensions in cm and the answer in litres, so the division by 1000 is part of the answer.

title: IGCSE Biology: Plant Nutrition
content:
IGCSE Biology: Plant Nutrition

Every food chain on Earth begins with a plant capturing sunlight and turning it into sugar. This note covers photosynthesis from the raw materials to the limiting-factor graphs that decide crop yields, then works through the anatomy of a leaf with each structure tied to the job it performs, and finishes with the mineral requirements of plants and the deficiency symptoms that reveal what is missing. The word equations, the balanced symbol equation and the limiting-factor reasoning are all expanded step by step, because Paper 4 asks for all three almost every year.

The word and symbol equations for photosynthesis

Photosynthesis is the process by which plants make glucose from carbon dioxide and water using light energy trapped by chlorophyll. Word equation: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen (light energy, chlorophyll). Symbol equation: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ (light). Key: CO₂ = carbon dioxide; H₂O = water; C₆H₁₂O₆ = glucose; O₂ = oxygen; the coefficients give 6 C, 12 H and 18 O on each side, which is what balanced means. To balance it from scratch: count the carbons — 6 on the left means C₆ on the right; then the hydrogens — 12 on the left from 6H₂O means H₁₂ in glucose; then the oxygens — 12 on the left (6 × 2) plus 6 from water totals 18; the right side has 6 in glucose plus 6 × 2 = 12 in oxygen, giving 18. Carbon dioxide enters through stomata (pores in the leaf epidermis flanked by guard cells), water is drawn up through xylem in the veins, and the glucose produced is either used in respiration, converted to starch for storage, converted to sucrose for transport, used to make cellulose for cell walls, or used with nitrate ions to make amino acids and proteins.

Chloroplasts, chlorophyll and the role of each factor

Photosynthesis happens in chloroplasts, which are concentrated in the palisade mesophyll layer of the leaf. Chlorophyll is the green pigment that absorbs light energy (mainly in the red and blue wavelengths, reflecting green — which is why leaves look green). The energy is used to power the conversion of carbon dioxide and water into glucose; carbon dioxide is raw material, and water is the hydrogen donor (split in the light-dependent reactions). At IGCSE level, know the three requirements — light, chlorophyll, carbon dioxide — and where each comes from. A variegated leaf (with white non-chlorophyll patches) tested with iodine shows starch only in the green regions, proving chlorophyll is necessary; a destarched plant kept in the dark shows no starch, proving light is necessary.

Limiting factors

The rate of photosynthesis is limited by whichever factor is in shortest supply — the limiting factor. Three are examinable: light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and temperature. As light intensity rises, rate rises proportionally until another factor (usually carbon dioxide) becomes limiting and the graph plateaus. As carbon dioxide rises (from the 0.04 % of the atmosphere), rate rises until light or temperature limits it. Temperature follows the enzyme pattern: rising to an optimum (about 25–30 °C for tropical plants) then falling as enzymes denature. The logic of commercial greenhouses and polytunnels follows directly: add artificial light at night, enrich carbon dioxide to 0.1–0.2 %, and heat to the optimum — but each expense is only worthwhile while that factor is the one limiting. The standard graph questions give a rate-versus-one-factor curve with two or three lines at different levels of a second factor; explain each plateau by naming the new limiting factor.

Leaf structure: form fits function

A cross-section through a leaf reveals adaptations for photosynthesis and gas exchange: a broad flat shape gives maximum light absorption and surface area; a thin lamina keeps a short diffusion path; the upper epidermis is transparent and coated with cuticle (waxy, waterproof, reduces water loss); the palisade mesophyll is a column of tall cells packed with chloroplasts near the top where light is strongest; the spongy mesophyll has irregular cells with air spaces between them for gas circulation; veins contain xylem (water and minerals arriving) and phloem (sugars leaving); stomata on the lower epidermis let carbon dioxide in and oxygen out; guard cells open and close the stomata — opening in light (for photosynthesis) and closing in darkness or when the plant is short of water (to reduce transpiration). The structure-to-function questions reward this chain: feature, then effect on light, gas exchange or water loss.

Mineral requirements and deficiency symptoms

Plants need mineral ions absorbed from the soil solution by root hair cells (by diffusion and active transport). Nitrate ions: needed to make amino acids and therefore proteins and chlorophyll; deficiency causes stunted growth and yellow leaves (chlorosis). Magnesium ions: the central atom in every chlorophyll molecule; deficiency causes yellowing between the leaf veins. Phosphate ions: needed for DNA, RNA, ATP and cell membranes; deficiency causes poor root growth and purplish leaves. Potassium ions: needed for enzymes in respiration and for opening stomata; deficiency causes poor fruit and seed development. Plants grown in hydroponic culture (mineral solution without soil) show exactly these symptoms when one ion is omitted — a standard Paper 6 identification question.

Limiting factors in practice: crops and greenhouses

The same principles scale to agriculture. Growing crops densely shades lower leaves, so light becomes limiting and yields per plant fall even as yield per field rises. Glasshouses trap heat (raising temperature) and allow carbon dioxide enrichment; grow-lights extend the photoperiod. Water stress closes stomata, cutting carbon dioxide entry and thus photosynthesis — irrigation protects yield. But temperature above the optimum denatures the enzymes of the Calvin cycle, and excessive light can bleach chlorophyll (photoinhibition). The examiner's favourite commercial question: "a farmer adds carbon dioxide but yield does not rise — explain why" — the answer: another factor (light or temperature) is now limiting; identify which from the conditions given.

Mineral ions and deficiency at a glance

IonNeeded forDeficiency symptom
NitrateAmino acids, proteins, chlorophyllStunted growth, yellow leaves (chlorosis)
MagnesiumThe chlorophyll moleculeYellowing between the veins
PhosphateDNA, RNA, ATP, membranesPoor root growth, purplish leaves
PotassiumEnzymes of respiration, stomatal openingPoor fruit and seed development

Worked example: reading limiting-factor graphs

A graph shows the rate of photosynthesis versus light intensity at three carbon dioxide concentrations (0.05 %, 0.10 %, 0.20 %): all three lines rise together at low light, then the 0.05 % line plateaus first, followed by the 0.10 %, then the 0.20 %. Step 1: describe the trend in data terms: "rate increases with light intensity initially and then levels off". Step 2: explain the first region: light is limiting — more photons reach chlorophyll, so the light-dependent reactions supply energy faster. Step 3: explain each plateau: above the kink, carbon dioxide concentration is limiting because it is in shortest supply; the higher the carbon dioxide, the higher the plateau. Step 4: name the limiting factor for each line at maximum light: carbon dioxide concentration for all three. Step 5: apply to practice: at the plateau of the 0.05 % curve, adding more light changes nothing; enriching carbon dioxide raises the rate. A second calculation type: comparing rate as a percentage — if rate rises from 20 to 50 arbitrary units, the increase is (50 − 20) ÷ 20 × 100 = 150 %.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Writing the equation with oxygen on the left or forgetting to balance the hydrogens; check every atom before writing "done".
  • Saying plants photosynthesise "to make energy": plants make glucose (chemical energy store); the light energy is converted, not created.
  • Confusing the roles: carbon dioxide is the raw material, water supplies hydrogen, light is the energy source, chlorophyll is the trap.
  • Explaining a plateau without naming the new limiting factor — the word "limiting factor" itself is worth a mark.
  • Describing guard cells as "letting light in": stomata control gas exchange and water loss, not light.
  • Forgetting the cuticle when asked about water loss adaptations.
  • Writing deficiency symptoms without linking the ion to its molecule: magnesium → chlorophyll → yellow leaves; nitrate → protein → stunting.
  • Interpreting a rate graph against temperature without mentioning enzyme denaturation at the peak.

Exam-style questions and answers

Q1. Write the balanced symbol equation for photosynthesis. (2 marks) Answer: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ — one mark for reactants and products, one for correct balancing with light/chlorophyll over the arrow.

Q2. Explain why the rate of photosynthesis levels off as light intensity continues to increase. (2 marks) Answer: another factor becomes limiting (1) — carbon dioxide concentration or temperature in shortest supply (1).

Q3. Describe two ways in which a leaf is adapted for photosynthesis. (4 marks) Answer: broad flat shape for maximum light absorption (1); palisade mesophyll packed with chloroplasts near the upper surface (1); thin lamina for short diffusion path (1); veins bring water by xylem and carry sugars away by phloem (1).

Q4. A plant has yellow leaves with green veins. Identify the missing mineral ion and explain your answer. (2 marks) Answer: magnesium (1) because it is needed to make chlorophyll and its absence causes chlorosis (1).

Q5. Explain how a farmer could increase the rate of photosynthesis in a greenhouse in winter. (3 marks) Answer: add artificial light to raise light intensity (1); heat the greenhouse to the optimum temperature for the enzymes (1); enrich carbon dioxide concentration so it is no longer limiting (1).

title: Dynamics
content:
Dynamics

Newton's Laws

  • A body stays at rest or in uniform motion unless acted on by a resultant force.
  • F = ma — the resultant force equals mass × acceleration.
  • Forces occur in pairs: equal magnitude, opposite direction, on different bodies.

Example: a 2 kg mass with a 10 N resultant accelerates at 5 m s⁻².

Weight and Mass

Weight W = mg — a force in newtons; mass in kg is invariant. A 70 kg person weighs about 687 N.

Momentum

p = mv (vector, kg m s⁻¹). Resultant force = rate of change of momentum: F = Δp/Δt.

Conservation: in a collision with no external forces, total momentum is unchanged.

  • Elastic: kinetic energy also conserved
  • Inelastic: some KE becomes heat/sound

Example: a 3 kg trolley at 4 m s⁻¹ hits a stationary 1 kg trolley and they couple: 12 = 4v, so v = 3 m s⁻¹.

Friction and Connected Bodies

Draw free-body diagrams, then apply F = ma along each axis. For a towed car and trailer, the tow-bar tension appears as an internal pair (equal and opposite).

Exam tips: 'constant velocity' means zero resultant force, not zero friction; impulse questions want FΔt = Δp.

title: Diseases and Immunity
content:
Diseases and Immunity

Cambridge IGCSE Biology 0610, Extended route, topic 10 (statement 10.1). Pathogens and transmission, the body's defences, the immune response, antibodies and vaccination.

10.1 Diseases and immunity

  • Pathogens are microorganisms that cause disease: bacteria produce toxins, viruses invade and destroy host cells. Transmission routes include direct contact, water and food, air droplets, and vectors such as mosquitoes.
  • Non-specific defences: skin as a barrier, mucus and cilia trapping pathogens in the airways, stomach acid killing ingested microbes, and phagocytes engulfing pathogens.
  • The immune response: phagocytes engulf the pathogen and display its antigens; lymphocytes produce antibodies specific to that antigen, which clump the pathogens for destruction and neutralise toxins. Memory lymphocytes remain, so a second exposure produces a faster, stronger response.
  • Vaccination introduces a dead or attenuated pathogen or its antigens, stimulating antibody production and memory cells without causing disease. Herd immunity protects those who cannot be vaccinated.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Primary versus secondary response, applied to an antibody-level graph: the first exposure shows a lag of several days then a modest peak; the second shows a shorter lag and a much higher peak. Explain with memory lymphocytes already present, dividing rapidly and differentiating into plasma cells. Use all three of faster, stronger and longer.
  • Evaluation reasoning, applied to why vaccination of a high proportion of a population protects unvaccinated individuals: with fewer hosts, the pathogen cannot spread easily, so the chance of an unvaccinated person meeting it falls. That is herd immunity — name it and explain the mechanism of reduced transmission.
  • Disease control reasoning, applied to an outbreak: vaccination reduces susceptibility, isolation reduces contact, and vector control removes the route. Match each measure to the transmission stage it interrupts — that matching is the examinable skill.

Common errors

  • Saying antibiotics kill viruses. Antibiotics work on bacteria; viruses are treated by vaccines or not at all.
  • Describing antibodies as killing pathogens directly. They agglutinate and neutralise; phagocytes do the destroying.
  • Forgetting memory cells as the reason the secondary response is faster.

title: Measures of Variation and Standard Deviation — Study Notes
content:
Measures of Variation

Edexcel International A Level Mathematics — Statistics 1 (WST01), sat at AS.

Range and Quartiles

The range is max − min — quick but destroyed by a single outlier. Quartiles split ordered data into quarters: Q₁ at position (n + 1)/4, Q₃ at 3(n + 1)/4 (raw data). The interquartile range, IQR = Q₃ − Q₁, is the spread of the middle 50% and resists outliers. Outliers are commonly flagged as values beyond Q₁ − 1.5·IQR or Q₃ + 1.5·IQR.

Variance and Standard Deviation

For raw data:

  • variance s² = Σ(x − x̄)²/n (the definitional form)
  • equivalently s² = Σx²/n − x̄² (the computational form)
  • standard deviation s = √(variance)

The standard deviation shares the units of the data; the variance does not. For frequency tables use Σf(x − x̄)²/Σf, or Σfx²/Σf − x̄².

Grouped Data

Use class midpoints as x. The result is an estimate — grouping discards within-class detail.

Combining and Scaling Datasets

Multiplying every value by b multiplies s by |b| and the variance by b². Adding a constant changes nothing in the spread. Two merged datasets: compute combined Σx and Σx² from each part, then apply the computational formula.

Example: data 1, 3, 4, 5, 7: mean 4, Σx² = 100, so variance = 100/5 − 16 = 4 and s = 2.

Exam tips: state units for s. When comparing consistency, the dataset with the smaller standard deviation (relative to its mean) is the more consistent. Always give the comparison sentence, not just the two numbers.

Exam method: variance and standard deviation

The variance is the mean of the squared deviations, or equivalently Var(x) = Σx²/n − x̄². The standard deviation is its square root, and it is in the same units as the data. Using the second form is quicker when the mean is already known.

Adding a constant to every value shifts the mean by that constant but leaves the standard deviation unchanged. Multiplying every value by a constant k multiplies the standard deviation by |k| and the variance by k². Use these rules to avoid recalculating from scratch.

For grouped data, use the class midpoints and the frequencies. The variance is Σfx²/Σf − x̄², with x̄ = Σfx/Σf.

The standard deviation is a measure of spread. Compare two data sets by stating which has the larger spread and linking that to the context of the data.

Exam cue: Show the sum of the values and the sum of squares before dividing, because the method marks depend on those totals.

Worked example: standard deviation from raw data

For the data 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9 there are n = 8 values with mean 5. The sum of the squares is 4 + 16 + 16 + 16 + 25 + 25 + 49 + 81 = 232. The variance is Σx²/n − (x̄)² = 232/8 − 25 = 29 − 25 = 4, and the standard deviation is √4 = 2. Using the formula with the sum of squared deviations gives the same answer and is a useful check on your working.

Exam method: outliers using the interquartile range

The interquartile range is Q3 − Q1. Under the usual rule, a value is an outlier if it lies below Q1 − 1.5 × IQR or above Q3 + 1.5 × IQR. Use the definition given in the question if one is stated, and show the two boundary values in your working. Writing a conclusion in context, such as "the value 40 is an outlier for these hours", gains the communication mark.

title: Coordination, Response and Gene Technology
content:
Coordination, Response and Gene Technology - A2 Level Biology

This topic belongs to the Edexcel International AS/A Level Biology specification (WBI15) and covers how nervous and hormonal systems coordinate responses in animals, how plants respond to environmental cues via growth substances, the underlying cellular and molecular mechanisms of nerve transmission and brain function, and advanced gene technology techniques including recombinant DNA, microarrays, and bioinformatics.

Nervous Coordination, Neurones and Reflex Arcs

Animals detect and respond to internal and external stimuli using specialised cells and coordinated nervous pathways. A complete nervous response requires sensory receptors, neurones, synapses, and effectors.

  • 8.1 Sensory neurones transmit electrical impulses from receptors to the central nervous system. Relay neurones are located entirely within the central nervous system and connect sensory neurones to motor neurones. Motor neurones transmit impulses from the central nervous system to effectors such as muscles and glands. Schwann cells wrap around mammalian peripheral nerve axons, forming a fatty myelin sheath composed of multiple layers of cell membrane containing myelin. The gaps between adjacent Schwann cells are called nodes of Ranvier.
  • 8.2 The nervous system causes effectors to respond to a stimulus by generating action potentials along motor neurones that terminate at specialized junctions with effectors, prompting muscle contraction or glandular secretion.
  • 8.3 A spinal reflex arc consists of a receptor, sensory neurone, relay neurone in the grey matter of the spinal cord, motor neurone, and effector. The spinal cord contains an inner region of grey matter, containing cell bodies and synapses, surrounded by white matter, containing myelinated axon tracts running up and down the spinal cord.
  • 8.4 At resting potential, the inside of an axon is at about −70 mV relative to the outside. The sodium-potassium pump actively transports 3 Na⁺ ions out of the axon for every 2 K⁺ ions pumped in, using ATP, maintaining electrochemical gradients. When a stimulus arrives, voltage-gated sodium channels open, causing Na⁺ to flood into the axon down an electrochemical gradient, leading to rapid depolarisation where the interior becomes positive (+40 mV). These sodium channels then close, and voltage-gated potassium channels open, allowing K⁺ ions to diffuse out of the axon, repolarising the membrane. An overshoot hyperpolarisation occurs before the sodium-potassium pump restores the resting potential.
  • 8.5 Myelination acts as an electrical insulator. In myelinated neurones, local circuits of current cannot flow through the thick myelin sheath; instead, depolarisation can only occur at the exposed nodes of Ranvier. This forces the nerve impulse to jump from one node of Ranvier to the next, a process called saltatory conduction, which significantly increases the speed of nerve impulse transmission compared to continuous conduction in unmyelinated axons.

Synapses, Brain Structure and Drug Action

Information transfer between neurones and across effectors occurs at specialised junctions called synapses, modulated by neurotransmitters, neurochemicals, and medical interventions.

  • 8.6 (i) At a cholinergic synapse, an arriving action potential causes voltage-gated calcium ion channels in the presynaptic membrane to open, causing Ca²⁺ to enter the presynaptic knob. This influx causes vesicles containing acetylcholine to fuse with the presynaptic membrane, releasing acetylcholine into the synaptic cleft by exocytosis. Acetylcholine diffuses across the cleft and binds to specific receptor proteins on the postsynaptic membrane, causing sodium ion channels to open, generating a postsynaptic action potential. Acetylcholinesterase then breaks down acetylcholine into choline and ethanoic acid to prevent continuous stimulation. (ii) Pupil dilation (mydriasis) occurs in dim light via contraction of the radial muscles of the iris under sympathetic control. Pupil constriction (miosis) occurs in bright light via contraction of the circular muscles of the iris under parasympathetic control.
  • 8.7 Drugs alter nerve impulse transmission. Nicotine mimics acetylcholine, binding to postsynaptic receptors and keeping sodium channels open, thus stimulating the nervous system. Lidocaine blocks voltage-gated sodium channels, preventing depolarisation and stopping the conduction of nerve impulses, acting as a local anaesthetic. Cobra venom alpha toxin binds irreversibly to acetylcholine receptors on the postsynaptic membrane at neuromuscular junctions, preventing muscle contraction and causing paralysis. L-DOPA is a precursor to dopamine that crosses the blood-brain barrier and is converted into dopamine in the brain to treat Parkinson's disease symptoms. MDMA (ecstasy) increases the concentration of serotonin, dopamine, and noradrenaline in synaptic clefts by reversing the direction of transporter proteins that normally clear them.
  • 8.8 Mammalian retinal rod cells detect light intensity. In the dark, rhodopsin is inactive, cyclic GMP keeps sodium cation channels open, and Na⁺ continually enters the rod cell, causing a depolarised resting state around −40 mV that continuously releases neurotransmitters that inhibit bipolar neurones. Light hits rhodopsin, splitting it into retinal and opsin. Opsin activates a cascade that breaks down cyclic GMP, closing the sodium cation channels.
