Na⁺ can no longer enter, but K⁺ continues to leave, causing hyperpolarisation of the rod cell (down to −70 mV). Neurotransmitter release stops, removing the inhibition on bipolar neurones, which then generate an action potential in the optic neurones.
  • 8.9 Habituation is a learned decrease in response to a repeated stimulus that is determined to be harmless, caused by a reduction in calcium ion channels opening at presynaptic knobs over time, leading to less neurotransmitter release and a smaller postsynaptic response.
  • 8.10 The mammalian nervous system consists of the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord) and the peripheral nervous system (cranial and spinal nerves).
  • 8.14 The human brain comprises specialized regions: the cerebral hemispheres control higher brain functions such as conscious thought, vision, hearing, speech and memory; the hypothalamus coordinates homeostatic responses, osmoregulation, and the autonomic nervous system; the pituitary gland secretes hormones regulating endocrine glands; the cerebellum coordinates balance, posture and fine voluntary muscle movement; and the medulla oblongata controls involuntary autonomic centres including heart rate and breathing rate.
  • 8.15 Medical imaging techniques diagnose brain conditions: magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) uses strong magnetic fields and radio waves to produce high-resolution structural images of soft tissues; functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) measures changes in blood oxygenation and flow to map active brain areas in real time; positron emission tomography (PET) uses radioactive tracers (such as fluorodeoxyglucose) to visualise metabolic activity and chemical pathways in the brain; computed tomography (CT) uses X-rays fired from multiple angles to create cross-sectional structural images.
  • 8.16 Imbalances in brain chemicals cause ill health: a deficiency of dopamine-producing neurones in the substantia nigra leads to Parkinson's disease (treated with L-DOPA), while low serotonin levels in certain brain pathways contribute to clinical depression (treated with Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors, SSRIs). Pharmacists use this understanding to develop targeted new drugs.

Plant Coordination and Gene Technology

Plants coordinate growth responses via hormones such as auxins, gibberellins, and phytochromes. Modern biotechnology utilises enzymes, vectors, and screening tools to manipulate DNA for medicine and agriculture.

  • 8.11 Phytochromes are plant photoreceptors that exist in two interconvertible forms: Pr (absorbs red light at 660 nm) and Pfr (absorbs far-red light at 730 nm). Sunlight converts Pr to Pfr, triggering seed germination, flowering, and stem elongation by influencing transcription factors. Auxins, principally Indoleacetic Acid (IAA), are synthesized in shoot apices and transported basipetally. Auxin promotes cell elongation in shoots by loosening cell walls through proton pumping, activating expansins, whereas high concentrations inhibit root elongation. Gibberellins stimulate seed germination by diffusing to the aleurone layer of cereal grains, inducing transcription of the gene encoding amylase.
  • 8.12 Core Practical 18 involves investigating the production of amylase in germinating cereal grains (such as barley). Grains are cut, sterilized, and incubated on starch agar plates with varying concentrations of gibberellic acid. After incubation, the plates are flooded with iodine solution. A clear zone around the grains indicates starch hydrolysis, demonstrating that gibberellin triggers amylase enzyme production.
  • 8.13 Coordination in animals is achieved through nervous control (rapid, localized, electrical impulses via neurones) and hormonal control (slower, widespread, chemical signals transported in the blood via the endocrine system).
  • 8.17 Drugs and therapeutic proteins can be produced using genetically modified organisms: microorganisms (such as bacteria and yeasts) are cultured in large bioreactors to produce human insulin or antibodies; plants (such as transgenic rice or tobacco) can produce therapeutic proteins or vaccines (

    Gene Technology, Recombinant DNA and Bioinformatics

    Advanced molecular techniques allow scientists to isolate, modify, and amplify specific genes for industrial, agricultural, and medical applications.

    • 8.18 Recombinant DNA is produced by isolating the desired gene using restriction endonucleases (which cut DNA at specific palindromic recognition sequences, producing sticky or blunt ends) and joining it into a prepared plasmid vector using DNA ligase, which catalyses the formation of phosphodiester bonds between the sugar-phosphate backbones.
    • 8.19 Recombinant DNA is inserted into host cells using vectors such as plasmids, bacteriophages, or liposomes, or via direct methods such as electroporation, microinjection, or gene guns, allowing host cells (transformation) to express the foreign protein.
    • 8.20 DNA microarrays consist of a solid glass or silicon slide fixed with thousands of microscopic spots of single-stranded DNA probes corresponding to specific genes. Fluorescently labelled cDNA (derived from mRNA of test and control cells) is washed over the microarray; hybridisation reveals which genes are active or expressed by measuring fluorescence intensity at each spot.
    • 8.21 Bioinformatics involves the collection, storage, and computational analysis of biological data, such as genomic sequences and amino acid structures, using mathematical and statistical algorithms to identify gene functions, evolutionary relationships, and drug-binding sites.
    • 8.22 Genetically modified organisms offer significant benefits, including enhanced crop yields, nutritional fortification (such as Golden Rice), and low-cost pharmaceutical production, but carry risks such as horizontal gene transfer to wild relatives, the creation of invasive species, potential allergenicity, and ethical concerns regarding animal welfare and corporate monopolies.

    Examiner Guidance, Common Mistakes and Exam-Style Practice

    Candidates frequently lose marks in A2 Biology by confusing membrane mechanisms or omitting essential terminology in extended-response questions.

    • Common Mistake: Confusing the roles of sodium and potassium channels during an action potential, or stating that the sodium-potassium pump generates the action potential rather than maintaining the resting potential. Correction: Always state that voltage-gated sodium channels open first for depolarisation, voltage-gated potassium channels open second for repolarisation, and the sodium-potassium pump actively restores the resting electrochemical gradient using ATP.
    • Common Mistake: Describing plant phototropisms simply as 'auxin moving to the dark side' without explaining that IAA is actively transported laterally across the shoot tip, causing differential cell elongation down the shaded flank. Correction: Specify that lateral redistribution of IAA promotes proton pumping into cell walls, lowering pH to activate expansins that loosen cellulose microfibrils.
    • Exam-Style Question and Worked Answer: Explain how cobra venom alpha toxin prevents muscle contraction. Answer: Alpha toxin binds irreversibly to acetylcholine receptors on the postsynaptic membrane at the neuromuscular junction (1 mark). This blocks acetylcholine from binding, preventing the opening of sodium ion channels and stopping the generation of a postsynaptic action potential (1 mark), meaning no depolarisation spreads across the sarcolemma to trigger calcium ion release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum (1 mark).

title: Pressure & Density — Study Notes
content:
Pressure & Density

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): pressure & pressure differences in fluids, density review (Extended pressure-depth).

1. Pressure basics

p = F/A (Pa = N/m²). Increase F or decrease A to raise pressure; explain applications (snowshoes, knives, hydraulic press).

2. Liquids

  • Pressure increases with depth: p = ρgh (Extended).
  • Same level, same liquid ⇒ same pressure (hydrostatic paradox).
  • Hydraulic systems transmit pressure — force multiplier: F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂.

3. Atmospheric pressure

~10⁵ Pa at sea level; demonstrated by collapsing can, mercury barometer 760 mmHg; decreases with altitude.

4. Density revisited

ρ = m/V; floating condition; upthrust = weight of displaced fluid (qualitative).

5. Gas pressure (particle model)

Particles collide with walls → force per area. Volume ↓ at same T ⇒ pressure ↑ (more frequent collisions). Temperature ↑ ⇒ faster particles ⇒ more frequent, harder impacts.

Density in more depth

Density is mass per unit volume, ρ = m/V. Its SI unit is kg/m³, and 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³. An object of a given density will float in a fluid only if the fluid has a higher density. To find the density of an irregular solid, measure its mass on a balance and its volume by displacement of water in a measuring cylinder.

Pressure and depth

Pressure is force per unit area, p = F/A, with unit the pascal (Pa = N/m²). In a liquid, the pressure increases with depth, p = hρg, and acts equally in all directions at a given depth. Atmospheric pressure at sea level is about 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa.

Exam tip: convert the area to m² before you calculate pressure, and use the density in kg/m³ in p = hρg.

title: Binomial Distribution — Study Notes
content:
The Binomial Distribution

When Binomial Applies

X ~ B(n, p) counts successes in n independent trials when:

  • a fixed number n of identical trials,
  • each trial ends in success or failure,
  • constant success probability p,
  • trials are independent.

Check all four before using the model — "justifying a binomial model" is a real exam question.

The Formula

P(X = r) = ⁿCᵣ pʳ(1 − p)ⁿ⁻ʳ for r = 0, 1, ..., n. The ⁿCᵣ counts which r of the n trials were the successes.

Example: X ~ B(5, 0.3). P(X = 2) = ¹⁰C₂? No — ⁵C₂ × 0.3² × 0.7³ = 10 × 0.09 × 0.343 = 0.3087.

Cumulative Probabilities

P(X ≤ 2) = P(0) + P(1) + P(2). "At least" questions convert by the complement: P(X ≥ 2) = 1 − P(X ≤ 1). Keep one extra decimal place in intermediate steps to avoid rounding drift.

Expectation and Variance

  • E(X) = np and Var(X) = np(1 − p)

For X ~ B(20, 0.4): E(X) = 8 and Var(X) = 4.8.

Modelling Decisions

If trials are dependent (drawing without replacement from a small population) binomial is not appropriate. If p changes between trials it is not binomial. When n is large and p small, the binomial is approximately Poisson — but at A2 you usually stay exact.

Exam tips: identify n and p in words before touching the calculator. For P(X ≥ k) always rewrite as 1 − P(X ≤ k − 1). Tables give cumulative values — use them rather than summing by hand.

Exam method: binomial probabilities

If X ~ B(n, p) then X counts successes in n independent trials, each with probability p. P(X = r) = nCr p^r (1 - p)^(n - r) for r = 0, 1, ..., n. The mean is np and the variance is np(1 - p).

Check the conditions first: a fixed number of trials, two outcomes, a constant p and independent trials. If any condition fails, the binomial model does not apply.

title: Energetics — Study Notes
content:
Energetics

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH12, Topic 6. Energetics explains why reactions release or absorb heat, and it provides the enthalpy data that later decides whether a reaction is feasible.

Enthalpy change and types of reaction

  • The enthalpy change ΔH is the heat energy transferred at constant pressure. Exothermic reactions have a negative ΔH; endothermic reactions have a positive ΔH.
  • Standard conditions are 100 kPa and a stated temperature, usually 298 K, with substances in their standard states.
  • Important definitions include standard enthalpy of formation, combustion and neutralisation. Each is written for one mole of the stated substance.

Measuring enthalpy changes

  • In a calorimetry experiment, q = m × c × ΔT, where m is the mass of solution (usually assumed to be 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ for water-based solutions).
  • Convert heat to enthalpy change using moles: ΔH = −q / n. The sign is negative for an exothermic reaction.
  • Sources of error include heat loss to the surroundings and incomplete combustion; the answer is always lower than the data book value for combustion.

Hess's law

  • The total enthalpy change is independent of the route taken. Enthalpy cycles let you find an unknown ΔH from known values.
  • For formation values: ΔH = Σ ΔHf(products) − Σ ΔHf(reactants).

Bond enthalpies

  • Breaking bonds is endothermic; making bonds is exothermic. ΔH ≈ Σ bonds broken − Σ bonds formed.
  • Bond enthalpies are averages over many compounds, so values from bond enthalpy calculations differ from accurate formation data.

Entropy and free energy (introduced)

  • A reaction that increases disorder (more gas molecules, for example) has a positive entropy change, which favours spontaneous change.

Exam tip: a common mistake is to use the wrong sign for ΔH. Always check whether the process is releasing or taking in heat before writing the value.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Calorimetry, applied to burning a fuel: q = m c ΔT. Heating 100 g of water by 10.0 °C gives q = 100 × 4.18 × 10.0 = 4180 J. If 0.0100 mol of fuel was burnt, ΔH = −4180 J ÷ 0.0100 mol = −418 kJ mol⁻¹. The minus sign is required, because the reaction is exothermic.
  • Hess's law, applied to a cycle: ΔH = sum of ΔH(products) − sum of ΔH(reactants), with each enthalpy change taken in its direction in the cycle. Reversing a step changes the sign. Draw the cycle first, then write the equation, so the signs follow from the arrows.
  • Bond enthalpies: ΔH ≈ energy to break bonds − energy released when bonds form. For CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O, use mean values for the bonds involved. The answer is an estimate, because the values are averages across different molecules.
  • Common losses of marks: forgetting that calorimetry gives the heat absorbed by the water, so the sign of ΔH is the opposite of q. Mixing up the units of kJ and J, and giving the answer per gram instead of per mole.

title: IGCSE Mathematics: Inequalities
content:
IGCSE Mathematics: Inequalities

Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580 (2025–2027), section 2 Algebra and graphs, statement 2.6 Inequalities — solving and interpreting linear inequalities, listing integer solutions, and (Extended) regions in the coordinate plane. An inequality describes a range of values rather than one exact value, and solving one follows the same balance principle as solving an equation, with one critical difference: multiplying or dividing by a negative number reverses the inequality sign. This note shows why that happens, writes out every solution line by line, and finishes with the region-shading questions that distinguish Paper 4.

What an inequality says

The four inequality symbols extend the equals sign: < (strictly less than), > (strictly greater than), ⩽ (less than or equal to), ⩾ (greater than or equal to). A solution is a set of values, drawn on a number line with a hollow circle for strict inequalities (the endpoint is excluded) and a solid circle for inclusive ones (the endpoint is included).

StatementMeaningNumber line
x > 3Every value greater than 3, not including 3Hollow circle at 3, arrow to the right
x ⩽ −1Every value up to and including −1Solid circle at −1, arrow to the left
2 ⩽ x < 5Values from 2 up to, but not including, 5Solid circle at 2, hollow at 5, line between

Why the sign flips when multiplying by a negative. Start with the true statement 3 < 5. Multiply both sides by −2 without thinking: −6 < −10 is false, because −10 is further left than −6. The correct statement is −6 > −10. Multiplying by a negative mirrors the number line, which reverses order — so the inequality symbol must reverse too. That single rule causes more lost marks than any other in this topic.

Solving linear inequalities

Use the equation methods unchanged, and remember the one reversal rule:

Solve:  5x - 7 > 3x + 1        (give the solution as an inequality)

5x - 3x > 1 + 7               [add 7 to both sides, subtract 3x from both sides]
2x > 8
x > 4                         [divide by +2: the sign does not reverse]
Solve:  3 - 2x ⩽ 11

-2x ⩽ 11 - 3                  [subtract 3 from both sides]
-2x ⩽ 8
x ⩾ -4                        [divide by -2: the sign REVERSES from ⩽ to ⩾]

The check is direct: x = −4 gives 3 − 2(−4) = 11 ⩽ 11 ✓, and x = 0 gives 3 ⩽ 11 ✓ while x = −5 gives 13 ⩽ 11 ✗ — so the boundary and direction are right.

Solve and list the integer solutions:  2 < (5x - 1)/3 ⩽ 8

Multiply every part by 3:
6 < 5x - 1 ⩽ 24
7 < 5x ⩽ 25                   [add 1 to every part]
7/5 < x ⩽ 5                   [divide every part by +5]

The integers are 2, 3, 4 and 5.

Compound inequalities (a value trapped between two bounds) are solved in one line per operation across all three parts — exactly like a three-pan balance.

Inequalities from word problems

Many questions ask for the greatest or least integer satisfying a condition. Translate carefully: at least means ⩾, at most means ⩽, more than means >, within or no more than means ⩽.

A cinema ticket costs £8. A group has £100 and must keep at least £12 for travel.
How many tickets can they buy?

Let n be the number of tickets:  8n + 12 ⩽ 100
8n ⩽ 88
n ⩽ 11

They can buy at most 11 tickets.

The final answer is a whole number in context: a group cannot buy a fraction of a ticket, so the solution set is the integers up to 11.

Regions in the coordinate plane (Extended)

The line y = mx + c divides the plane into two half-planes: points above it satisfy y > mx + c and points below it satisfy y < mx + c. A region question asks you to shade the set of points satisfying several inequalities at once.

  • Draw the boundary line y = mx + c as a solid line when the inequality includes equality (⩽ or ⩾), and as a dashed line when it is strict (< or >).
  • Test one point not on the line — the origin (0, 0) is easiest when the line misses it. Substitute into the inequality; if it is true, shade the side containing the test point.
  • Shade the side that satisfies every inequality; the answer region is the overlap, and the question often asks for the coordinates of a point inside it.
Shade the region satisfying:  y ⩽ 2x + 1,  y > -x + 2,  x ⩾ 0

Line 1: y = 2x + 1, solid. Test (0, 0): 0 ⩽ 1 true, so shade below-left of this line.
Line 2: y = -x + 2, dashed. Test (0, 0): 0 > 2 false, so shade the side away from the origin.
Line 3: x = 0 (the y-axis), solid, shade to the right.

The solution region is the triangle-like area satisfying all three, e.g. the point (2, 2):
2 ⩽ 5 ✓, 2 > 0 ✓, 2 ⩾ 0 ✓.

Describing a region in words is the reverse skill: read the boundary lines, note whether each is dashed or solid, and translate the shaded side back into an inequality.

Maximum and minimum values over a region (Extended)

Region questions often finish by asking for the largest or smallest value of an expression such as x + 2y for points inside the shaded region. A linear expression grows steadily in one direction across the plane, so over a region bounded by straight lines its extreme values always sit at the corners. The method is therefore exact: find the coordinates of every vertex of the region, substitute each pair into the expression, and pick the largest or smallest result. Do not stop at the corner that looks likely — an untested corner is the usual place a mark is lost.

Worked example: inequality with a parameter

Find the set of values of k for which the equation x² + kx + 9 = 0 has two distinct real roots.

Two distinct real roots require a positive discriminant:  b² - 4ac > 0
Here a = 1, b = k, c = 9:
k² - 36 > 0
k² > 36
k > 6  or  k < -6

This is an inequality inside a quadratic-context question — exactly the blend of topics Paper 4 rewards. If the requirement had been at least one real root, the inequality would be k² ⩾ 36, giving k ⩾ 6 or k ⩽ −6.

Corner points in practice. Take the region x ⩾ 0, y ⩾ 0, x + y ⩽ 6 and y ⩽ x + 2. Its vertices are where the boundary lines meet:

x = 0 with y = 0            gives (0, 0)
y = 0 with x + y = 6        gives (6, 0)
x = 0 with y = x + 2        gives (0, 2)
x + y = 6 with y = x + 2    gives x + (x + 2) = 6, so 2x = 4, x = 2 and y = 4, the corner (2, 4)

Evaluate P = x + 2y at each corner:
(0, 0): P = 0     (6, 0): P = 6     (0, 2): P = 4     (2, 4): P = 10

Maximum P = 10 at (2, 4);  minimum P = 0 at (0, 0).

The minimum sits at the origin only because this region includes it; a region bounded away from the origin puts its minimum at one of the other corners. Substitute every vertex before choosing.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Not reversing the inequality sign after multiplying or dividing by a negative number. −2x < 8 means x > −4.
  • Reversing the sign when multiplying by a positive number, or reversing when subtracting — only multiplication and division by negatives reverse it.
  • Hollow versus solid circles: < and > exclude the endpoint; ⩽ and ⩾ include it. Writing x > 4 when x = 4 works is a boundary error.
  • Flipping the inequality direction mid-solution so the final statement faces the wrong way.
  • Forgetting to reverse in a compound inequality: every part flips when the whole chain is multiplied by a negative.
  • In region questions, drawing a solid boundary for a strict inequality (or a dashed one for ⩽), or shading the wrong side because no test point was used.
  • Reporting a decimal when the question asks for integers: n ⩽ 11.25 means the largest integer is 11, not 11.25.
  • Treating ⩽ as < in a word problem: at most 5 includes 5.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 2, 3 marks). Solve 7 − 3x > 1 and show your solution on a number line.

Answer: −3x > −6, so x < 2 (the sign reverses). Number line: hollow circle at 2, shading to the left.

Question 2 (Paper 2, 3 marks). Solve 2 ⩽ 3x + 5 < 14 and list the integer solutions.

Answer: Subtract 5 throughout: −3 ⩽ 3x < 9. Divide by 3: −1 ⩽ x < 3. The integers are −1, 0, 1, 2.

Question 3 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Find the values of x for which x² − 5x + 4 < 0.

Answer: Factorise: (x − 1)(x − 4) < 0. The quadratic is negative between its roots, so 1 < x < 4. (Test x = 2: 4 − 10 + 4 = −2 < 0 ✓; test x = 0: 4 > 0 ✗.)

Question 4 (Paper 4, 5 marks). Shade the region defined by y > x − 1, y ⩽ 3 and x ⩾ 0, and write down the coordinates of one point in the region.

Answer: Draw y = x − 1 dashed (strict), y = 3 solid and x = 0 solid. The origin test for y > x − 1 gives 0 > −1, true, so shade above the dashed line; y ⩽ 3 shades below the horizontal line; x ⩾ 0 shades right of the y-axis. The overlap is a triangle with vertices (0, 3), (4, 3) and (0, −1); the point (1, 1) lies inside: 1 > 0 ✓, 1 ⩽ 3 ✓, 1 ⩾ 0 ✓.

Question 5 (Paper 4, 4 marks). A rectangle has a perimeter of at most 60 cm and a length of (x + 4) cm. Write an inequality for its width w and find w when x = 8.

Answer: 2[(x + 4) + w] ⩽ 60, so (x + 4) + w ⩽ 30 and w ⩽ 26 − x. With x = 8: w ⩽ 18 cm, and the width must also be positive, so 0 < w ⩽ 18.

Question 6 (Paper 2, 3 marks). The solutions of 5x + a ⩾ 0 include x = −2. Find the smallest integer value of a.

Answer: Substituting x = −2: −10 + a ⩾ 0, so a ⩾ 10. The smallest integer value is 10.

With equations and inequalities mastered, the next stage of algebra is sequences and functions.

Inequality symbols and the number line

An inequality compares two expressions that are not necessarily equal. There are four symbols, and each one says which side is larger. Reading the symbol correctly is the first step in every inequality question, and most errors in this topic start with a misread symbol rather than with the algebra.

The four inequality symbols

The symbol < means less than, > means greater than, ≤ means less than or equal to, and ≥ means greater than or equal to. The open symbols < and > exclude the boundary value, and the symbols with a bar underneath include it. Write the symbol that matches the wording, because "at least 5" is ≥ 5 and "more than 5" is > 5.

Drawing a number line

Mark the boundary value on a number line with an open circle for < or >, and a filled circle for ≤ or ≥. Shade the side of the line that contains the solutions. A filled circle at 3 with shading to the right shows x ≥ 3, which includes 3 itself. The open circle at 3 with shading to the left shows x < 3, which does not.

Writing a solution set from a number line

To write the inequality from a number line, find the boundary value, decide whether the circle is open or filled, and check the direction of the shading. Shading to the right of the boundary gives a greater-than form, and shading to the left gives a less-than form. Read the direction from the arrow of the shading, not from the side on which the circle sits.

Solutions as whole numbers

Many questions ask for the integers that satisfy an inequality. If x < 4 and x is a positive integer, the solutions are 1, 2 and 3, and 4 is excluded. The boundary value decides the list: x ≤ 4 would include 4. List the values in order, separated by commas, and do not include values that the inequality excludes.

Double inequalities

A double inequality such as −2 < x ≤ 5 states two conditions at once: x is greater than −2 and x is at most 5. On a number line, the two boundaries limit a single shaded section. Keep the inequality in one line when you solve it, and apply every operation to all three parts, so that the middle term is treated the same as the outer two.

Common reading errors

The two errors that cost the most marks are reversing the boundary value by mistake and marking the circle the wrong way. An answer of x ≤ 3 drawn with an open circle is wrong even though the direction is right, because the examiner checks the circle as well as the shading. Check both before you move on to the algebra.

Solving linear inequalities step by step

A linear inequality is solved in the same way as a linear equation, with one rule added: the inequality sign changes direction whenever both sides are multiplied or divided by a negative number. The subsections below take the steps in the order an examiner marks them.

Collecting the variable on one side

Add or subtract terms until all the x-terms sit on one side and the constants sit on the other. Adding or subtracting the same quantity from both sides keeps the inequality true, and the sign stays the same. For 3x + 5 > x + 11, subtract x from both sides to get 2x + 5 > 11, then subtract 5 to get 2x > 6.

Dividing by a positive number

Divide both sides by the coefficient of x. When that coefficient is positive, the inequality sign stays the same. From 2x > 6, dividing by 2 gives x > 3, and the solution is every value greater than 3.

Dividing by a negative number

When both sides are divided by a negative number, the sign must flip. From −4x ≥ 12, dividing by −4 gives x ≤ −3. Check this by taking a value from the solution: x = −5 satisfies the original inequality, since −4 × (−5) = 20 is at least 12, and −5 is less than −3.

Multiplying by a fraction or a bracket

To remove a fraction, multiply both sides by the denominator, which is positive in most questions, so the sign stays the same. Expand any bracket before you collect terms. For (x − 2) / 3 < 4, multiply both sides by 3 to get x − 2 < 12, then add 2 to get x < 14.

Checking the solution with a test value

Choose a value that lies inside your solution and substitute it into the original inequality. If x > 3 is correct, the value 4 should make the original statement true. If it does not, the sign was reversed somewhere in the working. A test value takes a few seconds and catches the most common error in this topic.

Writing the answer in the form the question asks for

Give the answer as an inequality in x, such as x < 5, or in the form the question asks for. Keep the variable on the left in the final answer, and make sure the sign matches the direction you found. A correct solution written with the wrong symbol still loses the mark.

Two inequalities together: finding the overlap

Many questions give two inequalities in the same variable and ask for the values that satisfy both. The answer is the overlap of the two solution sets. The subsections below show how to find that overlap and how to present it.

Solving each inequality separately

Solve each inequality on its own first, exactly as you would solve a single inequality, and keep each answer in its own line. If one gives x > 2 and the other gives x ≤ 7, write both results before you combine them. Combining too early is the usual source of a sign error.

Finding the overlap on a number line

Draw both solution sets on the same number line, one above the other, and find where the shading of both overlaps. The overlap is the answer, and it is the only region where both conditions hold at once. Use open or filled circles on each boundary exactly as you would for a single inequality.

Writing the overlap as a double inequality

When the overlap is a bounded interval, write it as a double inequality. For x > 2 and x ≤ 7, the overlap is 2 < x ≤ 7. Put the smaller boundary on the left and keep the inequality symbols in the same direction, so that the expression reads from smallest to largest.

When the two sets do not overlap

Sometimes the two solution sets have no values in common. For x < 1 and x > 5, no number is less than 1 and greater than 5 at once, so the answer is that there is no solution. State this clearly in words, rather than leaving the answer blank, because the examiner gives the mark for recognising it.

Integer solutions of a combined inequality

If the question asks for the whole numbers that satisfy both conditions, list the overlap first and then pick out the integers. For 2 < x ≤ 7 the integers are 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7, and 2 is excluded. Check the endpoints one at a time, because the open and filled circles decide whether each end is in the list.

Inequalities with a variable on both sides

When the variable appears on both sides, collect the x-terms on one side before you solve. Write 5x − 3 ≥ 2x + 9, subtract 2x from both sides to get 3x − 3 ≥ 9, then add 3 to get 3x ≥ 12, and divide by 3 to get x ≥ 4. Each step keeps the variable on the same side, so the sign never needs a second thought.

Checking a combined answer

Test one value from inside the overlap and one value from outside it. The value inside must satisfy both original inequalities, and the value outside must fail at least one of them. This check confirms that the overlap is right and that neither boundary was reversed.

Presenting a two-part answer clearly

Show each solved inequality, then the overlap, then the final answer, in that order. The mark scheme awards the separate solutions and the overlap separately, so a single unexplained line can lose a method mark even when the answer is correct.

Equations and symbols

An inequality is solved like an equation with one extra rule, and the region questions are all the same line tested against a point. This sheet is the boundary lines and the sign rule — the two places marks are lost.

y = mx + c Key: y and x = the coordinates of a point on the plane (no units); m = the gradient; c = the y-intercept. Drawn solid when the inequality includes equality (⩽ or ⩾) and dashed when it is strict (< or >) — the line style is the first mark of a region question.

y = 2x + 1 Key: the boundary line of y ⩽ 2x + 1, drawn solid because equality is included. Test the origin (0, 0): 0 ⩽ 1 is true, so shade the side containing the origin — testing, never guessing, is what earns the shading mark.

y = -x + 2 Key: the boundary line of y > −x + 2, drawn dashed because the inequality is strict, so points on the line are excluded. Here (0, 0) gives 0 > 2, false, so the region is the side away from the origin.

x = 0 (the y-axis) Key: the boundary of x ⩾ 0; a vertical line has no gradient to quote, which is why the general form breaks down and the line is named instead. Shade to the right of it.

x + y = 6 Key: a boundary written in implicit form; the intercepts are (6, 0) and (0, 6). With y = x + 2 it meets at x + (x + 2) = 6, so x = 2 and y = 4 — corner (2, 4), where the maximum of a linear expression over that region always sits.

x² + kx + 9 = 0 Key: x = the variable; k = the unknown coefficient; the condition "two distinct real roots" becomes b² − 4ac > 0 with a = 1, b = k, c = 9, so k² > 36 and k > 6 or k < −6. The result is a pair of rays, not an interval between them — writing 6 < k < −6 is the standard wrong answer.

The sign rule, in one table

OperationEffect on the sign
Add or subtract the same valueUnchanged
Multiply or divide by a positive numberUnchanged
Multiply or divide by a negative numberReverses: < becomes >, ⩽ becomes ⩾
Reverse the two sidesReverses: 3 < 5 is the same statement as 5 > 3

Traps specific to the algebra

  • Forgetting to reverse when dividing by a negative: −2x ⩽ 8 gives x ⩾ −4.
  • Reversing when subtracting, which is not a reversal at all.
  • Hollow versus solid endpoints: x = 4 does not satisfy x > 4.
  • Reporting 11.25 when the question asks for the greatest integer, which is 11.
  • Shading every inequality's own side instead of their overlap.

title: Edexcel IAL Computer Science: Database Concepts and DBMS
content:
Edexcel IAL Computer Science: Database Concepts and DBMS

Pearson Edexcel International Advanced Level in Computer Science, Unit 2 Practical Programming and Problem Solving (with Unit 4 design depth): database concepts — the relational model, keys and relationships — and the functions of a database management system. SQL querying and normalisation appear at Unit 4 depth; this note builds the conceptual foundation every later question assumes. Each design rule is demonstrated on a worked table where breaking it visibly corrupts the data.

From files to databases

Flat files per department lead to classic failures: duplication (the same customer stored in sales and delivery files), inconsistency (one copy updated, one stale), no cross-file querying without bespoke code, weak security (each file its own controls), and concurrent-update hazards (two users editing copies that later overwrite each other). A database stores integrated data once under shared rules; a DBMS manages it — and the comparison question wants those failure modes named.

The relational model

Data lives in tables (relations): rows are records (tuples), columns are fields (attributes) of one type. The model's rules: each field holds one value (no repeating groups), each row is unique, and rows have no order (a table is a set — ordering comes from queries). The design vocabulary: a primary key uniquely identifies each row (never null, never duplicated); a foreign key is a field whose values must match a primary key in another table, creating the relationship and enforcing referential integrity.

Worked tables and their keys:

STUDENT (studentID [PK], name, class)
  S1  Chen   11A
  S2  Ali    11B
  S3  Banda  11A

GRADE (resultID [PK], studentID [FK → STUDENT], subject, mark)
  R1  S1  Maths    72
  R2  S1  Physics  65
  R3  S2  Maths    58

Relationships: STUDENT to GRADE is one-to-many (one student, many grades).
Referential integrity: a GRADE row with studentID S9 would be rejected -
no such student. Deleting S2 must handle their grade R3 (restrict, cascade
or set null) - the delete rule is a design decision the exam probes.

Relationship types: one-to-one (student ↔ locker), one-to-many (student ↔ grades), many-to-many (students ↔ subjects) — resolved with a linking/junction table (ENROLMENT: studentID, subject) so every relationship is physically one-to-many.

DBMS functions

  • Data dictionary / metadata management — stores the schema (tables, types, keys, constraints) that defines valid data.
  • Storage and retrieval — efficient physical management and indexing.
  • Security — accounts, authentication, permissions per user/role, and audit trails.
  • Integrity — enforcing constraints: type, range (CHECK), entity (primary key uniqueness), referential (foreign keys), so bad data cannot be stored regardless of the client.
  • Concurrency control — locking and transaction isolation so simultaneous users cannot corrupt data (lost updates prevented).
  • Recovery / backup — transaction logs and restore after failure.
  • Query facilities — a query language (SQL) and report generation.
Concurrency worked: two clerks updating the same stock level (100).

Without control:                          With locking:
  Clerk A reads 100                        Clerk A reads 100 (row locked)
  Clerk B reads 100                        Clerk B's update WAITS
  Clerk A writes 100 - 10 = 90             Clerk A writes 90 (lock released)
  Clerk B writes 100 - 25 = 75             Clerk B reads 90, writes 65
  Result 75: A's sale LOST - wrong.        Result 65: both sales counted.

Transactions are ACID: Atomic (all-or-nothing), Consistent (rules hold
afterwards), Isolated (concurrent transactions do not interfere), Durable
(committed data survives failure) - the four initials are directly
examinable.

Schema design and normalisation (foundation)

Normalisation removes duplication and the anomalies it causes. 1NF: no repeating groups; every field single-valued. 2NF: 1NF and no partial dependency on part of a composite key. 3NF: 2NF and no transitive dependency (non-key fields must not determine each other). Full treatment with worked conversions sits in the A2 database-design note; the foundation idea here is single fact, single place.

Anomaly worked on an unnormalised order table:
  (orderID, customerName, customerPhone, product, price)

Update anomaly:  customer changes phone - every order row must be updated.
Insert anomaly:  a new customer with no orders cannot be stored.
Delete anomaly:  deleting their only order deletes the customer's details.

Normalised:
  CUSTOMER (customerID [PK], name, phone)
  PRODUCT  (productID [PK], price)
  ORDER    (orderID [PK], customerID [FK], productID [FK], quantity)

Each fact now lives once; the anomalies vanish.

Reading and writing data: the SQL shape

Though examined formally at Unit 4, the query shape appears already at Unit 2: SELECT (columns) FROM (table) WHERE (row filter) ORDER BY (sort), with aggregates COUNT/SUM/AVG/MIN/MAX and GROUP BY. Declarative: state the result wanted, not the procedure. The DBMS's query optimiser chooses the access path — an index turns a table scan into a lookup.

Worked queries on GRADE above:

  "Average mark per subject, highest first":
    SELECT subject, AVG(mark)
    FROM GRADE
    GROUP BY subject
    ORDER BY AVG(mark) DESC;
    → Maths 65, Physics 65   [(72+58)/2 = 65; 65]

  "Students with a mark above 60":
    SELECT studentID, subject, mark
    FROM GRADE
    WHERE mark > 60
    ORDER BY mark DESC;
    → (S1, Maths, 72), (S1, Physics, 65)

Execution order to remember: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING →
SELECT → ORDER BY.
ConceptDefinitionWorked check on the clinic database
EntityA thing about which data is heldPATIENT, DOCTOR, APPOINTMENT
AttributeA property of an entitypatient name, appointment date
Primary keyUnique, non-null identifier of a rowpatientID — no two patients share it
Foreign keyReference to another table's primary keyAPPOINTMENT.patientID must exist in PATIENT
RelationshipAssociation between entitiesPATIENT -< APPOINTMENT >- DOCTOR
ConstraintRule the DBMS enforcesdoctorID + slot UNIQUE stops double booking

Worked example: a database for a small clinic

Requirements: patients, doctors, appointments; one patient sees one doctor
per appointment; track prescriptions.

Design steps:
1. Entities: PATIENT, DOCTOR, APPOINTMENT, PRESCRIPTION.
2. Keys: each gets a surrogate primary key (patientID, doctorID...);
   APPOINTMENT carries patientID and doctorID as foreign keys;
   PRESCRIPTION carries appointmentID.
3. Relationships: PATIENT -< APPOINTMENT >- DOCTOR (many-to-many resolved by
   APPOINTMENT); APPOINTMENT -< PRESCRIPTION (one-to-many).
4. Constraints: appointment date not null; time slot unique per doctor
   (composite unique: doctorID + slot) - double booking becomes impossible at
   the schema level.
5. Security: receptionists insert/read appointments; only doctors read
   prescriptions; audit log for access.

Testing the design: try the three anomalies above on it - each is now
impossible, which is the design's proof.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Calling any column with an ID a "primary key"; the key must be unique and non-null — and chosen deliberately (surrogate vs natural).
  • Explaining foreign keys as "links" without referential integrity: every FK value must exist in the referenced PK.
  • Missing the many-to-many linking table answer; junction tables are the standard resolution.
  • Listing DBMS features without effect — "security" means accounts, permissions and audit; "integrity" means constraints the DBMS enforces.
  • Confusing a database with a DBMS (the data versus the software managing it).
  • Assuming tables have an order; ORDER BY exists precisely because rows are unordered sets.
  • Skipping the delete rule (cascade/restrict/set null) in relationship questions.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Unit 2, 4 marks). Explain two problems of storing the same data in separate department files.

Answer: Duplication leads to inconsistency — when a customer's address changes, each file must be updated separately and stale copies persist, so different departments act on different data. Updates and deletions create anomalies — deleting the last order record may erase the only copy of a customer's details (deletion anomaly), and a new customer cannot be recorded before they order (insertion anomaly).

Question 2 (Unit 2, 4 marks). Explain the roles of primary keys and foreign keys in a relational database.

Answer: A primary key uniquely and non-null identifies each record in its table, enabling reliable retrieval and preventing duplicates. A foreign key in another table references that primary key, creating a relationship and enforcing referential integrity — the DBMS rejects any value with no matching record, and can cascade or restrict deletions so relationships never dangle.

Question 3 (Unit 2, 4 marks). Describe how a DBMS handles two users updating the same record simultaneously.

Answer: Concurrency control locks the record (or uses versioning) when the first transaction begins, so the second waits or operates on a prior version. Isolation ensures one transaction's uncommitted changes are invisible to the other; commit releases the lock and logs the change, so the update is atomic and durable. Without this, interleaved updates produce lost updates.

Question 4 (Unit 2, 3 marks). State what ACID stands for and why it matters.

Answer: Atomic — a transaction completes fully or not at all; Consistent — it leaves the database satisfying all constraints; Isolated — concurrent transactions do not interfere; Durable — committed changes survive failure. Together they guarantee correctness of shared data despite crashes and concurrent users.

Question 5 (Unit 2, 4 marks). A library stores (loanID, memberName, memberPhone, bookTitle, dueDate). Explain one anomaly and how normalisation fixes it.

Answer: MemberPhone depends on the member, not the loan — so a member's phone is duplicated across every loan row; changing it requires many updates and one miss leaves it inconsistent (update anomaly). Splitting into MEMBER(memberID, name, phone) and LOAN(loanID, memberID, bookTitle, dueDate) stores the phone once, with the loan referencing it by key.

Question 6 (Unit 2, 3 marks). Explain the difference between a database and a DBMS.

Answer: The database is the organised collection of integrated data itself — tables of records and their relationships. The DBMS is the software that manages it: creating and enforcing schema rules, handling security, concurrency, backup and query processing. Application programs request data through the DBMS rather than reading files directly.

Unit 2 is complete. A2 builds directly on these foundations — starting with the advanced data structures that generalise arrays and records.

title: IGCSE Computer Science: Algorithm Design and Problem-Solving
content:
IGCSE Computer Science: Algorithm Design and Problem-Solving

Cambridge IGCSE Computer Science 0478 (2026–2028), Paper 2 Algorithms, Programming and Logic, statement 7 Algorithm design and problem-solving. Writing code is the last 20% of the job; this note is the other 80% — decomposition, abstraction, stepwise refinement, algorithm design and representation, and the testing that proves it works. Every refinement below is shown stage by stage, and the trace tables demonstrate the dry-run technique examiners expect you to produce under time pressure.

The problem-solving cycle

  • 1. Analyse the problem — state precisely what is wanted: the inputs, the required outputs, and any constraints (data ranges, time limits, the algorithm's likely size).
  • 2. Design — decompose into subtasks and design each algorithm (structure charts, pseudocode, flowcharts).
  • 3. Refine — develop each subtask stepwise until every step is a statement a coder could translate directly.
  • 4. Write the code — translate the refined design into a programming language.
  • 5. Test — run normal, boundary, erroneous and extreme data; compare results with expectations.
  • 6. Maintain — fix discovered bugs, adapt to new requirements, improve performance.

Skipping to step 4 is the failure mode this statement exists to cure: code written without a design is where logic errors breed.

Abstraction and decomposition

Decomposition breaks a big problem into smaller, independently solvable subproblems — planning a school trip becomes booking transport, booking accommodation, collecting money, producing a register. Each subtask is solved on its own and recombined. Abstraction is deliberately ignoring detail that does not matter to the task: a seat-booking system models seat numbers and states but not the fabric colour of the seats. Together they keep designs comprehensible — the exam wants a structure chart with named subtasks, not just prose.

Decomposition worked example: a school sports-day results system.

Level 0 (whole problem): record events, score house points, print winners.
Level 1 subtasks:
  1. Input event results (validation included)
  2. Convert places to house points
  3. Accumulate house totals
  4. Determine and print the winning house

Each level-1 subtask decomposes again - refinement of subtask 2:
  2.1  read the event's placing (1st, 2nd, 3rd)
  2.2  look up the points for that placing (5, 3, 1)
  2.3  add the points to the correct house total
  2.4  repeat for each event

At the end of refinement every leaf step is a single statement - that is the
stopping rule for stepwise refinement.

Stepwise refinement

Refinement turns an outline into detail in stages, keeping each stage reviewable. Start with one line; expand the hardest or vaguest part into steps; expand those; stop when each step is trivially translatable. The trace at each stage catches errors while they are cheap.

Refinement stages: "find the mean of a set of numbers".

Stage 0 (outline):     get the numbers, compute the mean, print it.

Stage 1:
  initialise total and count
  get the numbers, adding each to the total and counting it
  compute mean <- total / count
  print mean

Stage 2 (final pseudocode):
  1  total <- 0
  2  count <- 0
  3  INPUT num
  4  WHILE num <> -1              [-1 as a sentinel value meaning "no more"]
  5      total <- total + num
  6      count <- count + 1
  7      INPUT num
  8  ENDWHILE
  9  IF count > 0 THEN
 10      mean <- total / count
 11      OUTPUT mean
 12  ELSE
 13      OUTPUT "no data entered"
 14  ENDIF

Note what refinement surfaced: the empty-input case (line 9). Division by zero
would have been a runtime failure - refinement finds these before coding.

The sentinel (-1) is one way to end input; alternatives are a known count (read exactly n values) or an end-of-file test. State which you use and make sure the sentinel can never be legitimate data.

Representing algorithms

FormWhat it showsBest for
Structure chartWhole problem decomposed into named subtasks and their data linksThe overview; planning who does what
PseudocodeThe logic in structured, language-independent statementsPrecise design and exam answers
FlowchartFlow of control visually: oval start/stop, parallelogram I/O, rectangle process, diamond decisionShowing branches and loops at a glance
Trace tableVariable values statement by statement for given inputsProving correctness before coding
The same algorithm as a flowchart text sketch: reading marks until -1 and
counting passes (mark >= 40).

  (start) -> [passes <- 0] -> [INPUT mark] -> <mark = -1?>
      | no                         | yes
      v                            v
  <mark >= 40?> --yes--> [passes <- passes + 1] --+
      | no                                       |
      +------------------------------------------+
                                                 v
                                    [INPUT mark] -> loop back to <mark = -1?>
  (stop) <- [OUTPUT passes]

Note the two diamonds in sequence: the loop test runs first on every value,
including the very first, and the sentinel is tested BEFORE the pass test so
-1 is never counted as a fail.

Trace tables and dry running

A trace table proves the design with real data before any code runs. One column per variable; one row per statement executed (loops repeat rows); outputs recorded as they happen. Always test at least: normal data, boundary data, and erroneous data.

Trace: count how many of 5 numbers exceed their predecessor.

  1  count <- 0
  2  INPUT previous
  3  FOR i <- 2 TO 5
  4      INPUT current
  5      IF current > previous THEN
  6          count <- count + 1
  7      ENDIF
  8      previous <- current
  9  NEXT i
 10  OUTPUT count

Inputs: 10, 15, 15, 9, 20

Step    i   previous  current  count   comment
1                             0
2             10              0
3       2      10             0
4       2      10      15     0
5       2      10      15     0   15 > 10 TRUE
6       2      10      15     1
8       2      15      15     1   previous tracks the latest
3       3      15             1
4       3      15      15     1
5       3      15      15     1   15 > 15 FALSE (equal is not greater)
8       3      15      15     1
3       4      15             1
4       4      15       9     1
5       4      15       9     1   9 > 15 FALSE
8       4       9       9     1
3       5       9             1
4       5       9      20     1
5       5       9      20     1   20 > 9 TRUE
6       5       9      20     2
8       5      20      20     2
10                        output 2

Boundary check: equal neighbours (15, 15) must NOT count - that row is the one
markers look for.

Testing

  • Normal (valid) data — typical values that should work; checks the happy path.
  • Boundary (extreme) data — values at the edges of validity (0 and 100 for marks, exactly at a threshold); most bugs live here.
  • Erroneous (invalid) data — values the program should reject (negative marks, letters where numbers are expected); checks validation and error handling.

Test data should be chosen deliberately with an expected result stated for each test before running it — otherwise you are checking what the program does, not what it should do. For the mean example above: normal (2, 4, 6 → mean 4), boundary (one value only → the value itself), erroneous (sentinel entered first → "no data entered", not a division by zero).

Iterative (agile) development is examined here too: develop in small iterations, each designing, coding and testing one subtask, then review with the client before the next. Advantages: working software early, changing requirements absorbed cheaply, frequent feedback and testing built in; disadvantages: unclear final scope and budget, and endless change without discipline. Against waterfall (one linear design→build→test→release pass): clear milestones and documentation, but late testing and expensive changes once built.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Jumping straight to code: marks are for analysis, decomposition and refinement stages — show them.
  • Decomposition that is too shallow: subtasks must reach single-statement steps ("input the numbers" is a subtask, not a refinement).
  • Test data without expected outputs; and boundary values are worth as many marks as the normal case.
  • Forgetting the empty-input and division-by-zero case in averages — the most-missed validation mark in Paper 2.
  • Sentinel values that collide with real data (using -1 to stop, when -1 is a valid score).
  • Trace tables that skip loop repetitions or show only the final value; markers want the statement-by-statement rows.
  • Confusing validation (is the data in range?) with verification (is the data the right data — e.g. double entry).
  • Listing agile benefits alone; the question usually wants the comparison against a linear model stated explicitly.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 2, 4 marks). Explain what is meant by decomposition and abstraction, giving an example of each.

Answer: Decomposition splits a problem into smaller subproblems that can be solved separately — an online shop system breaks into stock control, basket, payment and delivery subsystems. Abstraction ignores details irrelevant to the problem — the basket subsystem models items and quantities but not the warehouse's shelf colours, so the design stays manageable.

Question 2 (Paper 2, 4 marks). Refine the step "process the order" into structured pseudocode.

Answer: READ order lines from the file; FOR each line: check the item is in stock; IF in stock THEN add the line total (price × quantity) to orderTotal and reduce stock; ELSE record the item as out of stock; NEXT; apply any discount to orderTotal; OUTPUT orderTotal and the out-of-stock list.

Question 3 (Paper 2, 3 marks). State three types of test data and give one example of each for a program accepting a mark between 0 and 100.

Answer: Normal data — a typical in-range value such as 65. Boundary data — the edge values 0 and 100 (and just outside, 101). Erroneous data — an invalid value such as -5 or the letter "A".

Question 4 (Paper 2, 4 marks). Explain why a trace table is produced before code is written.

Answer: A trace table executes the algorithm step by step on paper, recording each variable's value after every statement, so logic errors — infinite loops, wrong branch conditions, off-by-one errors — are found while the design is still cheap to change. It also provides the expected outputs used later as test data, so the coded program can be checked against a proven result.

Question 5 (Paper 2, 4 marks). Compare iterative development with a waterfall approach.

Answer: Iterative development builds in small cycles with client review after each, delivering working software early and absorbing requirement changes cheaply, at the cost of a less predictable final scope and budget. Waterfall completes each stage before the next, giving fixed milestones, clear documentation and easy planning, but testing happens late and changes after coding are expensive.

Question 6 (Paper 2, 5 marks). Write pseudocode that reads numbers until the user enters 0, then outputs the largest number entered (0 not counted).

Answer: largest <- 0; INPUT num; WHILE num <> 0; IF num > largest THEN; largest <- num; ENDIF; INPUT num; ENDWHILE; OUTPUT largest. (Assumes positive input; a full solution might flag if no positive number was entered.)

These design skills now apply to the two remaining Paper 2 domains: databases and Boolean logic.

title: Further Trigonometry — Study Notes
content:
Further Trigonometry

Compound Angles

  • sin(A ± B) = sin A cos B ± cos A sin B
  • cos(A ± B) = cos A cos B ∓ sin A sin B

Example: sin 75° = sin(45° + 30°) = (√2/2)(√3/2) + (√2/2)(1/2) = (√6 + √2)/4.

Double Angles

  • sin 2A = 2 sin A cos A
  • cos 2A = cos²A − sin²A = 2cos²A − 1 = 1 − 2sin²A

Example: express 4 sin x cos x in one term: 2 sin 2x.

The R-Form

a sin x + b cos x = R sin(x + α) with R = √(a² + b²) and tan α = b/a.

Example: 3 sin x + 4 cos x = 5 sin(x + 0.927). This instantly gives the maximum 5 and minimum −5.

Reciprocal Functions

sec θ = 1/cos θ, cosec θ = 1/sin θ, cot θ = 1/tan θ. Key identity: 1 + cot²θ = cosec²θ.

Exam tips: choose the cos 2A form that eliminates the unwanted function; when solving with R-form, divide by R before using inverse trig, and translate intervals carefully.

Exam method: reciprocal functions and identities

The reciprocal functions are sec x = 1/cos x, cosec x = 1/sin x and cot x = 1/tan x. Rewrite them in terms of sine and cosine when a question mixes functions, because this usually shows which identity to use.

The Pythagorean identities are sin² x + cos² x = 1, 1 + tan² x = sec² x and 1 + cot² x = cosec² x. Divide the first identity by cos² x or sin² x to obtain the second or third.

To solve an equation such as sec x = 2, first rewrite it as cos x = 1/2, then find the acute angle and the other solutions in the required range. For cos x = k the solutions in 0 to 2π are α and 2π − α, where α is the acute angle.

To prove an identity, work on the more complicated side only, and keep rewriting until it matches the other side.

Exam cue: Give each solution in the range asked for, using exact values such as π/3 when the angle is standard.

Exam method: R-form

To write a sinθ + b cosθ as R sin(θ + α), expand R sin(θ + α) = R sinθ cosα + R cosθ sinα and compare coefficients. This gives R = √(a² + b²) and tan α = b / a, with α in the quadrant where cos α and sin α have the signs of a and b.

Exam cue: Find the maximum and minimum from R, then solve for θ over the stated interval. Give α in the correct quadrant before writing the final angles.

Worked example: solving sin 2x = cos x

Solve sin 2x = cos x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π. Using the double angle formula, 2 sin x cos x = cos x. Move everything to one side and factorise: cos x (2 sin x − 1) = 0. So cos x = 0, giving x = π/2 or 3π/2, or sin x = ½, giving x = π/6 or 5π/6. The four solutions are π/6, π/2, 5π/6 and 3π/2. Dividing both sides by cos x at the start would lose the two solutions where cos x = 0, and that is the most common way to drop marks on this type of question.

Exam method: choosing an identity

Before you start, look at which angles appear. If the question mixes x and 2x, rewrite the double angle first so that everything is in one angle. Always state the range of solutions in the form the question asks for, in radians or degrees, and check that each answer lies inside the range. Substituting each answer back into the original equation is a quick way to catch a sign error.

title: IGCSE Physics: Electricity and Circuits
content:
IGCSE Physics: Electricity and Circuits

Cambridge IGCSE Physics 0625 (2026–2028), Topic 4 Electricity and magnetism: statements 4.2 Electrical quantities, 4.3 Electric circuits and 4.4 Electrical safety. Electric circuits are the most calculation-dense part of the Paper 4 paper, and every result in them flows from one picture: a battery pushes charge round a circuit, the charge pays a price (p.d.) to get through each component, and the rate of flow is the current. This note builds charge, current, e.m.f., p.d., resistance, energy and power from scratch, then builds real circuits from them and finishes with the mains safety that saves lives.

Electric charge and the electron model

There are two kinds of charge, positive and negative, and the rule is simple: like charges repel, unlike charges attract. Rubbing a polythene rod with a cloth transfers electrons from the cloth to the rod, so the rod becomes negatively charged and the cloth positive; nothing is created — charge is transferred. A conductor (metal, graphite, the human body, tap water) lets charge move through it because it contains free electrons; an insulator (plastic, rubber, dry air, glass) does not. Charging by friction works only when the object is isolated on an insulating support, or the charge leaks away instantly.

Supplement adds the two deeper ideas. Charge is measured in coulombs (C); one coulomb is the charge that flows when a current of 1 ampere passes for 1 second, and the charge on one electron is 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. A charged object also creates an electric field in the space around it — a region where other charges experience a force — and the field of a point charge is drawn as radial lines pointing away from a positive charge and towards a negative one.

Electric current

Electric current is the rate of flow of charge. In metals the charge carriers are free electrons drifting slowly around the circuit while the electric field travels almost at the speed of light, which is why a lamp lights the instant a switch is closed.

current = charge / time        I = Q / t
  • I: current in amperes (A); Q: charge in coulombs (C); t: time in seconds (s). Current is treated as a scalar in circuit calculations.
  • Conventional current flows from the positive terminal, round the circuit, to the negative terminal; electrons drift the opposite way. Both descriptions are accepted, but conventional current is the one used in circuit diagrams.

An ammeter measures current and is connected in series, so the whole current passes through it. Direct current (d.c.) flows in one direction only, as from a battery; alternating current (a.c.) reverses direction repeatedly, as from the mains, which in the UK completes 50 cycles per second at 230 V.

Electromotive force and potential difference

The electromotive force (e.m.f.) of a source is the energy transferred from other forms to electrical energy per unit charge driven round the whole circuit; the potential difference (p.d.) across a component is the energy transferred from electrical to other forms per unit charge passing through that component. Both are measured in volts, and a voltmeter is connected in parallel with the component being measured.

potential difference = energy transferred / charge        V = W / Q
electromotive force = energy transferred from other forms / charge driven
  • V: potential difference in volts (V); W: energy in joules (J); Q: charge in coulombs (C). One volt is one joule per coulomb (1 V = 1 J C⁻¹).

The distinction that earns marks: e.m.f. is about energy supplied to the circuit (a battery's rating, 1.5 V for a dry cell), while p.d. is about energy delivered to a component. In a series circuit the p.d.s across the components add up to the supply e.m.f., because each coulomb spends its energy bit by bit around the loop.

Resistance

Resistance is how much a component opposes current. It is measured in ohms (Ω): a 12 Ω resistor passes less current than a 4 Ω resistor at the same p.d.

resistance = potential difference / current        R = V / I
  • R: resistance in ohms (Ω); V: p.d. across the component in volts (V); I: current through it in amperes (A). Resistance is a scalar.

Resistance is measured by setting up a circuit with the unknown resistor, an ammeter in series and a voltmeter across it, then changing the supply with a variable resistor and taking several pairs of readings. The resistance is found from the gradient of a graph of V against I, which averages the whole data set.

The wire's dimensions matter. A longer wire has greater resistance (resistance is proportional to length); a thicker wire has less (resistance is inversely proportional to cross-sectional area); and the material matters because of how many free electrons it provides. Nichrome wire is used for heating elements because it has a high resistance and resists oxidation when hot.

Supplement: current–voltage graphs. A metallic conductor at constant temperature gives a straight line through the origin — ohmic. A filament lamp curves over: as it heats, its resistance rises, so the graph flattens. A diode conducts in one direction only, giving almost zero current in reverse; a light-dependent resistor falls in resistance as light intensity rises; a thermistor falls in resistance as temperature rises. All three are basis-of-operation questions for sensors.

Electrical energy and power

Every component turns electrical energy into something else — heat in a resistor, light and heat in a lamp, kinetic energy in a motor. The rate of that transfer is electrical power:

electrical power = potential difference x current        P = V I
electrical energy = power x time = V I t        E = V I t
  • P: power in watts (W); V: volts (V); I: amperes (A); E: energy in joules (J); t: time in seconds (s).
  • Combined with R = V/I this gives P = I²R and P = V²/R, useful when the resistance is known instead of the p.d.

The kilowatt-hour is the domestic unit of energy: one kWh is the energy used by a 1000 W device running for one hour (3.6 × 10⁶ J). Electricity bills charge cost = number of kWh × price per kWh, and a Paper 4 question usually asks for the cost of running a named appliance for a stated time.

Circuit components and circuit rules

Circuit diagrams use standard symbols: cell, battery, lamp, resistor, variable resistor, thermistor, LDR, diode, LED, ammeter, voltmeter, switch, motor. The two rules for series and parallel circuits are the spine of every calculation:

SeriesParallel
CurrentThe same through every componentShared between the branches; the branch currents add up to the total
Potential differenceShared between the components; the p.d.s add up to the supplyThe same across every branch
ResistanceR(total) = R1 + R2 + ...1/R(total) = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + ... (Supplement); two equal resistors in parallel give half the resistance of one

Adding lamps in series makes all of them dimmer, because the total resistance rises and the current falls; adding lamps in parallel leaves each at full brightness (each has the full p.d. across it) but draws more current from the supply. A variable resistor in series with a lamp dims it by reducing the current; a potential divider (Supplement) is two resistors in series with the output tapped between them:

output voltage = supply voltage x R2 / (R1 + R2)

A potential divider feeding a sensor gives an output voltage that changes with light or temperature, which is the basis of automatic night lights and thermostats.

Electrical safety

The domestic mains in the UK is 230 V a.c., enough to kill. The three wires in a three-core cable are colour-coded: live (brown) carries the alternating p.d. at about 230 V; neutral (blue) completes the circuit and is held near 0 V; earth (green and yellow) is a safety wire connected to the metal case of the appliance and to the ground.

  • Fuse: a thin wire in the live path that melts and breaks the circuit if the current exceeds its rating, protecting against overheating and fire. Choose a rating just above the normal working current.
  • Circuit breaker: a magnetic or electronic switch that trips and can be reset; faster and reusable, doing the same job as a fuse.
  • Earthing: if a fault connects the live wire to a metal case, the earth wire carries a large current that blows the fuse instead of giving the user a shock.
  • Double insulation: appliances with plastic cases need no earth wire, because no fault can make the case live.

Everyday hazards to name in an exam: frayed cables, damaged plugs, wet hands, water near electrical equipment, overloaded adapters, and touching a live conductor. The physics of the danger is current through the body: even a few tens of milliamperes through the heart can be fatal, and wet skin lowers body resistance and raises that current.

Worked example: a mixed circuit

Two resistors, 6.0 Ω and 3.0 Ω, are connected in parallel across a 12 V supply.

1 / R(total) = 1/6.0 + 1/3.0 = 0.167 + 0.333 = 0.500, so R(total) = 2.0 ohm
total current = V / R = 12 / 2.0 = 6.0 A
current in the 6.0 ohm resistor = 12 / 6.0 = 2.0 A
current in the 3.0 ohm resistor = 12 / 3.0 = 4.0 A   (branch currents add to 6.0 A)
power in the circuit = V I = 12 x 6.0 = 72 W
energy in 5 minutes = P t = 72 x 300 = 21 600 J

Each resistor has the full 12 V across it, as the parallel rule demands. If the two were instead in series, the total resistance would be 9.0 Ω, the current 1.33 A, and each p.d. would add to 12 V — a useful check before trusting any circuit answer.

Common mistakes

  • Putting an ammeter in parallel or a voltmeter in series; ammeters join in series, voltmeters across the component.
  • Using the supply voltage as the p.d. across one component in a series circuit; the supply is shared.
  • Adding resistances in parallel by simple addition; the reciprocals add, so the total is always less than the smallest branch.
  • Confusing current direction with electron drift, or saying charge is used up; the current is the same everywhere in a series circuit, and energy is transferred, not the charge.
  • Using watts and minutes in E = VIt; power in watts needs energy in joules and time in seconds (convert kWh and hours carefully in cost questions).
  • Forgetting that a filament lamp's resistance rises as it heats, so its I–V graph is a curve, not a straight line.
  • Choosing a fuse rating far above the working current for safety; too high a rating defeats the protection.
  • Mixing e.m.f. and p.d.: the battery has an e.m.f.; each component has a p.d. across it.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 4, 3 marks). A lamp is marked 24 W, 12 V. Calculate the current it takes and its resistance.

Answer: P = VI gives I = 24/12 = 2.0 A. R = V/I = 12/2.0 = 6.0 Ω.

Question 2 (Paper 4, 3 marks). A charge of 360 C passes through a lamp in 3.0 minutes. Calculate the current.

Answer: I = Q/t = 360/180 = 2.0 A. (Convert minutes to seconds first.)

Question 3 (Paper 2 style). In a series circuit of two resistors, which statement is true? A the current is largest through the smaller resistor; B the p.d. across each is the same as the supply; C the current is the same in both; D the total resistance is less than either. Answer: C. Current is the same everywhere in series; the p.d. is shared and the total resistance is the sum.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 4 marks). A 3.0 kW kettle runs for 4.0 minutes from 230 V. Find the charge that flows and the energy transferred.

Answer: I = P/V = 3000/230 = 13 A. Q = It = 13 × 240 = 3120 C. Energy = Pt = 3000 × 240 = 720 000 J (0.20 kWh).

Question 5 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Explain why a metal-cased washing machine has an earth wire but a plastic hairdryer does not.

Answer: The metal case is a conductor; if a fault brings the live wire into contact with it, the case would become live at 230 V and anyone touching it would receive a shock. The earth wire connects the case to the ground, so a large fault current flows to earth and melts the fuse, isolating the supply. The hairdryer has a plastic (double-insulated) case which cannot conduct, so no fault can make the outside live and no earth wire is needed.

Question 6 (Paper 6 style). Describe how you would determine the resistance of a coil of wire.

Answer: Connect the coil in series with an ammeter, a cell and a variable resistor, with a voltmeter across the coil. Vary the current and record several pairs of current and p.d. readings. Plot p.d. against current; the gradient is the resistance of the coil. Taking several readings and using the graph removes the effect of random errors and of the coil warming up (which would otherwise change its resistance).

Where charge flows, fields follow: next is Magnetism and Electromagnetism.

title: Exam technique: Magnetism and Electromagnetism
content:
### What earns the marks
For electromagnets, turns plus current plus soft iron core earns each mark. For transformers, the turns ratio equation quoted earns the method mark. For induction, rate of change of flux linked to emf size earns the explanation mark.
### Traps
Error: steel chosen for electromagnet cores. Correction: soft iron; steel suits permanent magnets. Error: Fleming hands swapped. Correction: left for motor, right for generator. Error: step-up confused with step-down. Correction: more secondary turns means step-up.
### Worked example
A transformer has 2000 primary turns and 100 secondary turns. The primary is supplied at 240 V. The turns ratio gives Vs = Vp × Ns / Np = 240 × 100 / 2000 = 12 V. More secondary turns than primary turns means a step-up transformer, so the output voltage rises.
### Check yourself
An ideal transformer has 12 V at its secondary and a current of 4.0 A there. Find the primary current when the primary is at 240 V. Power in equals power out, so Ip = (12 × 4.0) / 240 = 0.20 A.

content:
Quick revision: Integration

Mathematics — AS (9709). Reverse the power rule and add a constant: ∫ xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n+1) + c (n ≠ −1).

Key areas to revise

  • Indefinite Integrals
  • Definite Integrals
  • Areas Under Curves

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Key points to remember

Integration reverses differentiation. For a term ax^n, ∫ax^n dx = a x^(n+1)/(n+1) + c, provided n is not −1. Add the constant of integration c for an indefinite integral, and use a given point on the curve to find it. For a definite integral, evaluate the upper limit minus the lower limit.

The area between a curve and the x-axis from x = a to x = b is ∫y dx. If part of the area lies below the axis, that part gives a negative value, so split the integral at the crossing points, take the absolute value of each part and then add them. Check whether the question asks for an exact value or a decimal to the required accuracy.

title: Magnetic Fields and Electromagnetism — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Magnetic Fields and Electromagnetism

Physics — A2. F = BIL sin θ (Fleming's left hand: field-index, current-first-finger, force-thumb).

Key areas to revise

  • Force on a Current
  • Force on a Moving Charge
  • Fields from Currents
  • Electromagnetic Induction

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Worked example

A straight wire of length 0.40 m carries a current of 2.5 A at right angles to a uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.12 T. The force is F = BIL sin θ = 0.12 × 2.5 × 0.40 × sin 90° = 0.12 N. Fleming's left hand gives the direction: the field points from the first finger (north to south), the current points along the second finger, and the force is the thumb.

Common mistakes

  • Using θ = 0° when the wire is at right angles to the field. The force is zero only when the wire is parallel to the field.
  • Mixing up the left and right hand rules. The left hand is for motors (force), and the right hand is for generators (induced current).
  • Forgetting that the force on a charge moving in a field is F = BQv, not BIL, unless you convert the current first.

Worked example

A straight wire of length 0.40 m carries a current of 2.5 A at right angles to a uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.12 T. The force is F = BIL sin θ = 0.12 × 2.5 × 0.40 × sin 90° = 0.12 N. Fleming's left hand gives the direction: the field points from the first finger (north to south), the current points along the second finger, and the force is the thumb.
