title: Molecules, Transport and Health — Study Notes
content:
Molecules, Transport and Health

Edexcel IAL Biology WBI11, Topic 1. Living things are built from a small set of biological molecules. Their structure decides how they are used, how substances move in and out of cells, and how diet affects health.

Carbohydrates

  • Monosaccharides such as glucose, fructose and galactose are the building blocks. Glucose is the main respiratory substrate.
  • Disaccharides form by a condensation reaction that releases water and creates a glycosidic bond. Maltose is glucose + glucose, sucrose is glucose + fructose, and lactose is glucose + galactose.
  • Starch (amylose and amylopectin) stores glucose in plants. Glycogen stores glucose in animals. Cellulose is a straight chain of beta-glucose with hydrogen bonds between chains, giving strength.

Lipids and proteins

  • A triglyceride is one glycerol with three fatty acids joined by ester bonds. Phospholipids have a hydrophilic head and two hydrophobic tails.
  • Amino acids join by peptide bonds to form polypeptides. Tertiary structure is held by hydrogen, ionic, disulfide and hydrophobic interactions.

Enzymes

  • Enzymes have an active site with a shape complementary to the substrate. Rate rises with temperature until the enzyme denatures, and pH changes can alter the active site.

Transport

  • Diffusion moves substances down a concentration gradient without energy. Facilitated diffusion uses carrier or channel proteins. Active transport moves substances against a gradient and uses ATP.
  • Water moves by osmosis from a less negative water potential to a more negative water potential.
  • Large, multicellular organisms need exchange surfaces with a large surface area to volume ratio, such as alveoli and the villi of the small intestine.

Health

  • Body mass index (BMI) = mass (kg) ÷ height² (m²). Diet, exercise and cholesterol intake affect the risk of cardiovascular disease.

Exam tip: when you describe a transport process, state whether it needs energy, whether it uses a protein, and which way the gradient points.

title: Energetics — Study Notes
content:
Energetics

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH12, Topic 6. Energetics explains why reactions release or absorb heat, and it provides the enthalpy data that later decides whether a reaction is feasible.

Enthalpy change and types of reaction

  • The enthalpy change ΔH is the heat energy transferred at constant pressure. Exothermic reactions have a negative ΔH; endothermic reactions have a positive ΔH.
  • Standard conditions are 100 kPa and a stated temperature, usually 298 K, with substances in their standard states.
  • Important definitions include standard enthalpy of formation, combustion and neutralisation. Each is written for one mole of the stated substance.

Measuring enthalpy changes

  • In a calorimetry experiment, q = m × c × ΔT, where m is the mass of solution (usually assumed to be 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ for water-based solutions).
  • Convert heat to enthalpy change using moles: ΔH = −q / n. The sign is negative for an exothermic reaction.
  • Sources of error include heat loss to the surroundings and incomplete combustion; the answer is always lower than the data book value for combustion.

Hess's law

  • The total enthalpy change is independent of the route taken. Enthalpy cycles let you find an unknown ΔH from known values.
  • For formation values: ΔH = Σ ΔHf(products) − Σ ΔHf(reactants).

Bond enthalpies

  • Breaking bonds is endothermic; making bonds is exothermic. ΔH ≈ Σ bonds broken − Σ bonds formed.
  • Bond enthalpies are averages over many compounds, so values from bond enthalpy calculations differ from accurate formation data.

Entropy and free energy (introduced)

  • A reaction that increases disorder (more gas molecules, for example) has a positive entropy change, which favours spontaneous change.

Exam tip: a common mistake is to use the wrong sign for ΔH. Always check whether the process is releasing or taking in heat before writing the value.

title: Exam technique: Web Technologies
content:
### What earns the marks
For web roles, HTML for structure plus CSS for presentation plus JavaScript for behaviour earns each mark. For threats, phishing versus pharming versus smishing distinguished earns one mark each. For cookies, session versus persistent with a use earns both marks.
### Traps
Error: HTML claimed to style pages. Correction: CSS styles, HTML structures. Error: every scam called phishing. Correction: pharming redirects sites, smishing uses texts. Error: HTTPS said to block all attacks. Correction: it encrypts transit only.

title: Exam technique: Transformations and Vectors
content:
### What earns the marks
For translations and vector arithmetic, each component computed separately earns credit: show x and y lines. For magnitude, the root-of-sum-of-squares line earns the method mark before evaluation. For reflections and rotations, the coordinate rule stated ((y; -x) for 90 degrees clockwise) earns the method mark. For describing transformations, all three of type, centre or line, and size or angle are needed for full marks.
### Traps
Error: writing column vectors as bracket rows that lose a row. Correction: use (x; y) form and keep both components. Error: (100) or 14 for the magnitude of (6; 8). Correction: square, add, then root. Error: (-y; x) for a clockwise rotation. Correction: clockwise is (y; -x). Error: negating both coordinates for a single-axis reflection. Correction: one axis changes, the other stays.
### Worked example
Point A(1; 2) is translated by the vector (3; -1), giving A'(4; 1). Reflecting A' in the x-axis gives (4; -1). Rotating the point (3; -1) 90 degrees clockwise about the origin gives (-1; -3), using the rule (x; y) to (y; -x). Scaling (1; 2) by a factor of 2 from the origin gives (2; 4). Write each coordinate step on its own line.
### Check yourself
A point at (6; 8) has magnitude sqrt(6^2 + 8^2) = sqrt(100) = 10. Explain why the magnitude is never the sum 6 + 8 = 14. The magnitude uses the root of the sum of squares, so the components do not add directly.

### Worked example
Point A(1; 2) is translated by the vector (3; -1), giving A'(4; 1). Reflecting A' in the x-axis gives (4; -1). Rotating the point (3; -1) 90 degrees clockwise about the origin gives (-1; -3), using the rule (x; y) to (y; -x). Scaling (1; 2) by a factor of 2 from the origin gives (2; 4). Write each coordinate step on its own line.

title: Vectors — Study Notes
content:
Vectors

Components and Arithmetic

A vector a = 3i + 4j has magnitude |a| = √(3² + 4²) = 5. Parallel vectors are scalar multiples; unit vector = a/|a|.

Position and Direction

The line through point A with direction d: r = a + t d. Two lines are parallel if their directions are multiples.

Example: r = (1, 2) + t(3, −1).

Scalar (Dot) Product

a · b = |a||b| cos θ = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂.

Perpendicular ⇔ a · b = 0. Parallel ⇔ cross-multiplied components are equal (in 2D: a₁b₂ − a₂b₁ = 0).

Example: (2, 3) · (−6, 4) = −12 + 12 = 0, so they are perpendicular.

Angle Between Vectors

cos θ = (a · b)/(|a||b|).

Example: between (1, 0) and (1, 1): cos θ = 1/(1 × √2), θ = 45°.

Lines and Points

Foot of perpendicular from P to a line, intersection of two lines, and shortest distances all come from dot products and parameter t.

Exam tips: write column vectors cleanly; check answers by substituting the found t back into both position vectors; keep exact surd magnitudes rather than decimals.

Exam method: components, magnitude and scalar product

A vector in two dimensions is written as a column (x; y), and in three dimensions as (x; y; z) or in unit vector form xi + yj + zk. The magnitude is |a| = √(x² + y² + z²), which is Pythagoras applied in each direction.

The scalar product a · b = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + a₃b₃ is a number, not a vector. It also equals |a||b| cos θ, where θ is the angle between the vectors. Two vectors are perpendicular exactly when their scalar product is zero.

Use the scalar product to find the angle between two vectors: cos θ = (a · b)/(|a||b|). Give the angle in degrees or radians as the question asks.

A unit vector has magnitude 1. Divide a vector by its magnitude to find the unit vector in the same direction.

Exam cue: Write each component with its sign before adding, because a sign slip in the scalar product changes the answer without changing the method.

Worked example: angle between two vectors

Find the angle between a = (3; 4) and b = (5; −2). The scalar product is a·b = 15 − 8 = 7. The magnitudes are |a| = √(9 + 16) = 5 and |b| = √(25 + 4) = √29 ≈ 5.385. So cos θ = 7/(5 × 5.385) ≈ 0.260, giving θ ≈ 74.9°.

Perpendicular vectors

Two non-zero vectors are perpendicular exactly when their scalar product is zero. Use this to find an unknown component: if (2; k) is perpendicular to (4; −3), then 8 − 3k = 0, so k = 8/3.

Vector equation of a line

  • The line r = a + λd passes through the point with position vector a and has direction d; λ is the parameter.
  • To test whether a point lies on the line, find λ from one component and check that it satisfies the other components.
  • Two lines are parallel when their direction vectors are scalar multiples of each other. They are skew when they neither meet nor are parallel.

title: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Statistics and Data Handling
content:
Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Statistics and Data Handling

Statistics is the art of describing a pile of numbers with a few well-chosen ones: an average to say where the middle lies, a spread to say how tightly the data cluster, and a chart to make the shape visible. The IGCSE questions test exactly that pipeline — classify the data, compute the averages and spread, draw or read the chart, and compare two distributions. This note builds the whole subject from zero: the data types, every average and measure of spread with the frequency-table method, the standard charts, cumulative frequency curves, and histograms with unequal class widths.

Classifying statistical data

TypeMeaningExamples
Qualitative (categorical)describes a quality, not a numberfavourite colour, blood group
Quantitativemeasured or counted as a numberheight, number of siblings
Discretecountable, separate values (usually integers)number of children, shoe size
Continuouscan take any value in a range (measured)height, time, mass

The classification decides which charts and averages are legal: a mode for categorical data, a median for ordered data, class intervals for continuous data. Discrete data are plotted as bar charts with gaps; continuous data as histograms with no gaps (and frequency density on the vertical axis).

Averages and range

mean = sum of values / number of values
median = middle value when ordered (mean of the two middle
         values for an even count)
mode = most frequent value (or class); none if no repeats
range = largest - smallest

quartiles: Q1 = lower quartile (25%), Q3 = upper quartile (75%)
interquartile range (IQR) = Q3 - Q1  (spread of the middle 50%)

The mean uses every value (sensitive to outliers); the median ignores extreme values (robust); the mode is the only average available for categorical data. When comparing two data sets, quote an average and a spread: "school A has a higher median but a larger IQR, so its results are higher on average but less consistent."

Worked example. Find the mean, median, mode and range of: 4, 7, 7, 9, 12, 15, 18.

mean = (4+7+7+9+12+15+18)/7 = 72/7 = 10.3 (3 s.f.)
median = 4th value = 9
mode = 7 (appears twice)
range = 18 - 4 = 14

Worked example 2 (even count). Find the median of 3, 5, 8, 10, 12, 15.

even count: average the 3rd and 4th values
median = (8 + 10)/2 = 9

Averages from frequency tables

mean = sum of (value x frequency) / sum of frequencies
median = the value at position (n + 1)/2 in cumulative order
mode = the value with the highest frequency

Worked example. The table shows goals scored: 0 (5 players), 1 (8), 2 (6), 3 (2). Find the mean and the median.

total players = 5 + 8 + 6 + 2 = 21
total goals = 0 × 5 + 1 × 8 + 2 × 6 + 3 × 2 = 0 + 8 + 12 + 6 = 26
mean = 26/21 = 1.24 (3 s.f.)
median position = (21 + 1)/2 = 11th value
cumulative: 5 (0 goals), 13 (1 goal) - the 11th value is 1
median = 1

For grouped data, use midpoints: the mean = Σ(midpoint × frequency)/Σfrequency, and the median comes from the cumulative frequency curve (below). The grouped mean is an estimate because the midpoint stands in for every value in the class.

Charts and diagrams

  • Bar chart: bars with gaps for categorical or discrete data; height = frequency.
  • Pie chart: angle = (frequency/total) × 360°; label the sectors with the category.
  • Pictogram: a symbol represents a fixed number; a half symbol represents half that number.
  • Stem-and-leaf: a sorted display that keeps the actual values; the key explains the split (e.g. 3|4 means 34).
  • Frequency polygon: plot frequency against the midpoint of each class and join with straight lines.

Worked example (pie chart). 40 students choose a sport: football 16, tennis 10, swimming 8, other 6. Find the angle for football.

angle = (16/40) × 360 = 144 °

Worked example 2 (pie chart reverse). A sector of 72° represents 9 students. How many students in total?

72 ° represents 9  →  360 ° represents 9 × 360/72 = 45 students

Cumulative frequency diagrams

A cumulative frequency table adds frequencies as you move up the classes. Plot cumulative frequency against the upper class boundary and join with a smooth curve; then read positions:

median at n/2
lower quartile at n/4
upper quartile at 3n/4
IQR = Q3 - Q1

Worked example. A cumulative frequency curve for 60 students' marks: Q1 = 42, median = 55, Q3 = 68. Find the IQR and interpret it.

IQR = 68 - 42 = 26 marks
The middle 50% of students scored within 26 marks of each other;

Always read across to the curve and then down to the horizontal axis — and use the class boundaries, not the midpoints, for the plot positions.

Histograms and frequency density

When class widths differ, the height of a bar cannot be the frequency — a wide class would dominate unfairly. Instead, the area of each bar is proportional to the frequency:

frequency density = frequency / class width
frequency = frequency density x class width (area of the bar)

Worked example. Class 0–10 has frequency 20; 10–20 has frequency 30; 20–40 has frequency 40. Find the frequency densities.

0-10: 20/10 = 2.0
10-20: 30/10 = 3.0
20-40: 40/20 = 2.0

Reading a histogram backwards is the standard question: measure a bar's width and height, multiply to get the frequency, and read the class from the horizontal axis. Remember that the axes often use class boundaries, so a bar from 20 to 40 covers width 20.

Stem-and-leaf diagrams and frequency polygons

A stem-and-leaf diagram sorts data while keeping every value visible: the stem is the leading digit and the leaf the final digit, with a key such as 3|4 meaning 34. Interpreting one means reading the ordered leaves to find the median, the quartiles and the shape: the median is the middle leaf, Q1 and Q3 sit at the quarter and three-quarter positions, and the distribution's skew shows in where the leaves bunch.

A frequency polygon plots frequency against the midpoint of each class and joins the points with straight lines; it is the grouped-data equivalent of a line graph and makes comparisons between two distributions easy (plot both polygons on the same axes).

Worked example. The leaves for stem 4 are 1, 3, 3, 6, 8 and for stem 5 are 0, 2, 5. List the data in order and find the median.

values: 41, 43, 43, 46, 48, 50, 52, 55
n = 8, so the median is the mean of the 4th and 5th values:
(46 + 48)/2 = 47

Worked example 2 (interpreting). Explain what a long right-hand tail of leaves in a stem-and-leaf diagram indicates.

A long right tail means a few unusually high values: the data
are positively skewed, and the mean will be greater than the
median because the high values pull it upward.

Comparing distributions

Comparison questions want two statements: one about the average (which is higher) and one about the spread (which is more consistent). Use median and IQR together — they are robust to outliers — or mean and standard deviation when the data are symmetric and the syllabus supplies it.

Worked example. Class A: median 62, IQR 18. Class B: median 58, IQR 9. Compare.

Class A has the higher typical score (median 62 vs 58), but its
results are more spread out (IQR 18 vs 9), so Class B is more
consistent even though its middle score is lower.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Averages) Find the mean and range of 12, 15, 11, 19, 13. Answer: mean = 70/5 = 14; range = 19 − 11 = 8.
  2. (Frequency table) Values 1, 2, 3 with frequencies 4, 7, 9. Find the mean. Answer: (4 + 14 + 27)/20 = 45/20 = 2.25.
  3. (Median) Find the median of 2, 4, 4, 6, 9, 10. Answer: (4 + 6)/2 = 5.
  4. (Pie chart) A sector of 90° represents 15 people. Find the total. Answer: 15 × 360/90 = 60.
  5. (Cumulative frequency) For 80 values, where do you read the median? Answer: At cumulative frequency 40, reading across to the curve and down to the axis.
  6. (Histogram) A bar of width 5 has frequency density 4. Find its frequency. Answer: 5 × 4 = 20.
  7. (Frequency density) Class 30–50 has frequency 24. Find the frequency density. Answer: 24/20 = 1.2.
  8. (Compare) Two runners' times: A median 42 s, IQR 3 s; B median 40 s, IQR 8 s. Compare. Answer: B is faster typically (lower median) but less consistent (larger IQR); A is more reliable.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Median without ordering: the median is the middle of the ordered list. Forgetting to sort is the commonest data-handling error.
  • Even-count median: average the two middle values; do not pick one of them.
  • Grouped mean: use midpoints and label the answer an estimate — the midpoint is not the actual mean of the class.
  • Histogram heights: the vertical axis is frequency density, not frequency; area is the frequency. Reading the height as the frequency is the classic histogram error.
  • Cumulative frequency positions: plot against upper class boundaries and read the median at n/2 (not (n+1)/2 on the graph).
  • Pie chart arithmetic: check that the angles sum to 360° before answering the next part.
  • IQR direction: IQR = upper − lower quartile; a negative IQR means the quartiles are swapped.
  • Comparison claims: quote actual values ("median 62 vs 58"), not "better" without evidence.

title: Nuclear Physics — Study Notes
content:
Nuclear Physics

The nucleus

The nucleus holds protons and neutrons, collectively nucleons. Nuclide notation ᴬZX gives Z protons and A nucleons, so N = A − Z neutrons. Isotopes share Z and differ in N. Nuclear densities are about 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³, so nearly all the mass of an atom sits in a tiny volume.

Mass defect and binding energy (23.1)

The mass of a nucleus is less than the sum of the masses of its separate nucleons. This difference is the mass defect Δm. Energy equivalent to Δm, given by E = Δmc², is the binding energy: the energy released when the nucleus is assembled from separate nucleons, and the energy needed to separate it. In nuclear work, 1 u = 931 MeV.

Example: a mass defect of 0.0300 u corresponds to E = 0.0300 × 931 ≈ 27.9 MeV.

The binding energy per nucleon peaks near iron-56, the most tightly bound nucleus. Energy is released when the nucleons move toward this peak, by fission of heavy nuclei or by fusion of light ones.

Radioactive decay (23.2)

Decay is random and spontaneous. The effect of each type on the nucleus and its penetration are:

TypeWhat changesStopped by
alphaZ − 2, A − 4paper
beta-minusZ + 1, A unchangeda few mm of aluminium
gammano change to Z or Athick lead

The activity A = λN is the rate of decay, in becquerel (Bq). The decay constant λ and the half-life t½ are related by λ = ln 2 / t½. The number of nuclei left after time t is N = N₀e^(−λt).

Example: a sample with t½ = 10 days has 1/8 of its original activity after 30 days, since three half-lives have passed.

Example: with t½ = 5.0 h = 1.8 × 10⁴ s, λ = 0.693 / 1.8 × 10⁴ ≈ 3.9 × 10⁻⁵ s⁻¹.

Fission and fusion

Heavy nuclei split (fission) into lighter nuclei of greater binding energy per nucleon, which releases energy in reactors. Light nuclei merge (fusion), which releases energy in stars.

Exam tips: balance Z and A on both sides of every decay equation. Convert the half-life to seconds before finding λ. Use A = λN, not guesswork with halves, when the number of nuclei is needed.

Nuclear decay and half-life

Alpha particles are helium nuclei with two protons and two neutrons, and they are strongly ionising but have low penetration. Beta-minus emission happens when a neutron changes into a proton and an electron is emitted. Gamma radiation is electromagnetic, carries no charge and no mass, and has high penetration. Background radiation must be subtracted from measured count rates before a half-life is calculated.

title: IGCSE Chemistry (OxfordAQA): Acids, Bases and Salts
content:
Acids, Bases and Salts

Acids and bases are the most quoted chemistry in everyday life — vinegar, lemon juice, indigestion tablets, soap, bleach — and the exam asks about them in two quite different ways. The first is properties: what an acid does to an indicator, to a metal, to a carbonate, and why a strong acid is not the same thing as a concentrated one. The second is preparation: given a named salt, which method would you use to make it, and why would the other two methods fail. That second question is where most marks are lost, because it cannot be answered from memory of a recipe — it needs the solubility rules and the reason each step exists. Both are covered here, with the equations written to the state symbols the mark scheme asks for.

1. What an acid and a base actually are

An acid is a proton donor: it releases hydrogen ions, H⁺, when it is dissolved in water. A base is a proton acceptor: it takes those hydrogen ions. An alkali is simply a base that dissolves in water, and it is the alkali that supplies the hydroxide ions, OH⁻, that neutralise the acid.

  • Acids: hydrochloric acid, HCl; sulfuric acid, H₂SO₄; nitric acid, HNO₃; ethanoic acid (the acid in vinegar), CH₃COOH; citric acid in citrus fruit.
  • Alkalis: sodium hydroxide, NaOH; potassium hydroxide, KOH; ammonia solution, NH₃(aq); calcium hydroxide solution, Ca(OH)₂, which is limewater.
  • Bases that are not alkalis: copper(II) oxide, CuO; magnesium oxide, MgO; iron(III) oxide, Fe₂O₃. These accept protons but do not dissolve in water, which is why they are used as solids in salt preparation.

The distinction between an acid and an alkali is not about strength but about which ion is in excess. In acidic solution there are more H⁺ ions than OH⁻; in alkaline solution there are more OH⁻; in a neutral solution the two are equal, which is what pH 7 records. The reaction between them is neutralisation, and its ionic equation is the same for every acid-alkali pair: H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O.

2. Indicators and the pH scale

The pH scale runs from 0 to 14 and measures the concentration of hydrogen ions: the lower the pH, the more H⁺ ions are present. A change of one pH unit is a change by a factor of ten in that concentration, which is why pH 2 is a hundred times more acidic than pH 4, not twice.

pHUniversal indicator colourWhat it means
1–3Red to orangeStrong acid
4–6Orange to yellowWeak acid
7GreenNeutral
8–11Blue to blue-greenWeak alkali
12–14PurpleStrong alkali

Universal indicator gives an approximate pH from the colour. Two other indicators are used because they change sharply over a narrow range, which is what a titration needs: litmus is red in acid and blue in alkali; methyl orange is red in acid and yellow in alkali; phenolphthalein is colourless in acid and pink in alkali. Phenolphthalein is the usual choice when titrating an acid with an alkali, because the first permanent pink is easy to see and appears at the end point.

The most accurate measurement is a pH meter, which reads the pH as a number rather than a colour. That is the same point as the instrumental methods in chemical analysis: an instrument is more precise than a dye, at the cost of the equipment.

3. The four reactions of acids

Dilute acids react with four families of substance, and each produces a salt with something different:

  • Metal: acid + metal → salt + hydrogen. Only for metals above hydrogen in the reactivity series: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂.
  • Metal oxide or hydroxide (a base): acid + base → salt + water. CuO + H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + H₂O. This is neutralisation, and it is how most soluble salts are made.
  • Carbonate: acid + carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide. CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂. The fizzing is the carbon dioxide, which turns limewater milky.
  • Alkali: acid + alkali → salt + water. NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O, with the ionic equation H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O.

Every one of these produces a salt, and the salt is named from the two things that combined: the metal (or ammonium) from the base, and the acid's own ending. Hydrochloric acid gives chlorides, sulfuric acid gives sulfates, nitric acid gives nitrates, phosphoric acid gives phosphates, and ethanoic acid gives ethanoates. So copper(II) oxide with sulfuric acid gives copper(II) sulfate, and sodium hydroxide with nitric acid gives sodium nitrate.

Notice that the carbonate reaction fizzes while the oxide reaction does not. That difference is the reason an examiner can ask you to distinguish two white solids with one reagent: add dilute acid and only the carbonate effervesces.

4. Strong and weak, concentrated and dilute

These four words are examined together precisely because students mix them up. Strong and weak describe how completely an acid ionises in water. Concentrated and dilute describe how much acid there is per unit volume.

  • A strong acid is fully ionised: every HCl molecule becomes H⁺ and Cl⁻, so the solution is full of hydrogen ions.
  • A weak acid is only partly ionised: most ethanoic acid molecules stay intact, so there are few H⁺ ions even in a concentrated solution.
  • A concentrated solution has a large amount of acid dissolved in a given volume, whether it is strong or weak.
  • A dilute solution has little acid per unit volume, whether it is strong or weak.

The consequences are testable. A strong acid of a given concentration has a lower pH than a weak acid of the same concentration, conducts electricity better because there are more ions to carry the charge, and reacts faster with a metal for the same reason. But a concentrated weak acid can have a lower pH than a dilute strong acid, which is the trap: it is the concentration of H⁺ that sets the pH, and both strength and concentration affect it. Sulfuric acid is the awkward case worth knowing — it is strong and it is also dibasic, so one mole can supply two moles of H⁺.

5. Solubility rules, and why they decide the method

A salt can be prepared in three different ways, and the choice is forced by one question: is the salt soluble in water, and are the starting materials soluble?

Salt typeSolubility in water
Sodium, potassium and ammonium saltsAll soluble
NitratesAll soluble
ChloridesSoluble, except silver chloride and lead(II) chloride
SulfatesSoluble, except barium sulfate and lead(II) sulfate; calcium sulfate is only slightly soluble
CarbonatesInsoluble, except sodium, potassium and ammonium carbonates
HydroxidesInsoluble, except sodium and potassium hydroxides; calcium hydroxide is slightly soluble

Those rules give the three methods. A soluble salt of a metal other than sodium, potassium or ammonium is made from the acid and an insoluble base, oxide or carbonate, adding the solid in excess. A soluble salt of sodium, potassium or ammonium cannot be made that way, because every candidate base is soluble too and there is no excess solid to filter off — so it is made by titration. An insoluble salt is made by precipitation, mixing two solutions that each contain one of its ions.

Copper(II) sulfate and sodium chloride show the contrast perfectly. Copper(II) sulfate is soluble and its base, copper(II) oxide, is not, so the acid-plus-excess-oxide method works. Sodium chloride is soluble and every sodium base is soluble, so adding excess sodium hydroxide to hydrochloric acid would leave sodium hydroxide in the product — the titration is the only way to get the exact amount.

6. Preparing a soluble salt: acid plus excess insoluble base

The method is the same whether the base is an oxide, a hydroxide, a carbonate or a metal, with one difference: a metal also produces hydrogen. For copper(II) sulfate from copper(II) oxide and dilute sulfuric acid:

  1. Warm the acid gently and add copper(II) oxide a little at a time, stirring, until no more dissolves and some solid remains at the bottom. The excess is the point: it guarantees that all the acid has reacted, so the product cannot be contaminated with acid.
  2. Filter the mixture. The filtrate is the copper(II) sulfate solution; the residue is the unreacted copper(II) oxide.
  3. Heat the filtrate in an evaporating basin to concentrate it, stopping when crystals begin to appear at the edge — the crystallising point.
  4. Leave it to cool slowly so that large crystals form, then filter them off and dry them between sheets of filter paper.

Each step has a reason, and the reasons are what get marked. Warming the acid speeds the reaction up. Adding the solid in excess rather than measuring it means you do not need to know the concentration of the acid. Filtering removes the excess. Evaporating only to the crystallising point, rather than to dryness, matters because heating a salt solution to dryness drives off the water of crystallisation, gives a powder rather than crystals, and concentrates any soluble impurity into the product.

With a carbonate the same method applies but the mixture fizzes, because carbon dioxide is released: CuCO₃ + H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + H₂O + CO₂. The excess solid is still needed, and it is still removed by filtration.

7. Preparing a soluble salt of sodium, potassium or ammonium: titration

Both reactants are soluble, so there is no excess solid to remove and the amounts must be measured exactly. That is what a titration does:

  1. Pipette a measured volume of the acid (25.0 cm³ is standard) into a conical flask and add two or three drops of indicator.
  2. Fill a burette with the alkali, record the starting reading, and run it in until the indicator changes permanently. Record the final reading and subtract to get the volume added.
  3. Repeat until two readings agree to within 0.1 cm³ — concordant results — and take the average of those.
  4. Repeat the titration using the same volumes but no indicator, because the indicator would contaminate the salt. Evaporate the resulting solution to the crystallising point, cool and dry the crystals.

Every detail earns a mark. Reading the burette at the bottom of the meniscus, at eye level, prevents a systematic error. Rinsing the pipette with the solution it will deliver, but the conical flask with distilled water, prevents dilution errors. The indicator is left out of the final run because the whole point is a pure salt, and the reason two concordant titrations are needed is that one reading can be spoiled by a single extra drop.

8. Preparing an insoluble salt: precipitation

When the salt is insoluble, it can be made by mixing two solutions that each supply one of its ions, and it appears immediately as a solid. Barium sulfate, the "barium meal" used in hospital X-rays because it does not dissolve and so is not absorbed, is made this way: BaCl₂ + Na₂SO₄ → BaSO₄ + 2NaCl, with the ionic equation Ba²⁺ + SO₄²⁻ → BaSO₄.

The practical steps are short but each has a reason:

  • Mix the two solutions — the precipitate forms at once.
  • Filter to collect the solid on the filter paper.
  • Wash the residue with distilled water, to remove the soluble sodium chloride that would otherwise dry onto the crystals.
  • Dry it, usually in a warm oven or between filter papers.

A silver halide is made the same way, from silver nitrate and a solution of the halide: Ag⁺ + Cl⁻ → AgCl. The choice of solutions is constrained by solubility, not by preference — you need one solution that is soluble and contains the cation and another that is soluble and contains the anion, which is why sodium sulfate is used as the sulfate source rather than, say, lead(II) sulfate.

9. Water of crystallisation and hydrated salts

Many salts crystallise with a fixed number of water molecules built into the crystal, written after a dot: CuSO₄·5H₂O is hydrated copper(II) sulfate, blue, with five water molecules per formula unit. Heating drives the water off and leaves the anhydrous salt, which is white: CuSO₄·5H₂O → CuSO₄ + 5H₂O. Adding water reverses it, and the blue colour returns.

That colour change is the standard test for water: anhydrous copper(II) sulfate turns from white to blue, and cobalt chloride paper turns from blue to pink. Both are tests for water rather than for purity — they confirm that water is present, not that it is pure.

The dot matters in calculations. The relative formula mass of the hydrated salt includes the water, so 1 mol of CuSO₄·5H₂O is 250 g, not 160 g, and the water is 90 of those 250 g. A question that asks for the percentage of water in a hydrated salt is asking you to add the water in before dividing.

10. Worked examples

Example 1. Name the salt formed when magnesium oxide reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid, and write the balanced equation.

The metal is magnesium and the acid is hydrochloric, so the salt is magnesium chloride. The oxide is a base, so the products are a salt and water: MgO + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂O. The equation balances with two HCl because magnesium is 2+ and chloride is 1−, so two chloride ions are needed.

Example 2. Describe how you would prepare pure, dry crystals of copper(II) sulfate from copper(II) oxide and dilute sulfuric acid.

Warm the dilute sulfuric acid and add copper(II) oxide in excess, stirring until no more dissolves; filter off the excess oxide; evaporate the filtrate to the crystallising point; cool to crystallise; filter and dry the crystals between filter papers. The excess ensures the acid is fully used up, and stopping at the crystallising point rather than dryness keeps the water of crystallisation in the crystals.

Example 3. 25.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide solution is neutralised by 20.0 cm³ of hydrochloric acid of concentration 0.125 mol/dm³. Calculate the concentration of the sodium hydroxide.

The equation is NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O, so the ratio is 1 : 1. Moles of acid: n = c V = 0.125 × 0.0200 = 0.00250 mol. So moles of alkali = 0.00250 mol, and its volume is 25.0 cm³ = 0.0250 dm³. Then c = n ÷ V = 0.00250 ÷ 0.0250 = 0.100 mol/dm³. Always convert cm³ to dm³ before dividing, because a concentration in mol/dm³ is per cubic decimetre.

Example 4. Explain why sodium chloride cannot be prepared by adding excess sodium hydroxide to hydrochloric acid.

Sodium hydroxide is soluble, so there would be no excess solid to filter off; any unreacted sodium hydroxide would stay in solution and contaminate the salt, and evaporating the solution would leave it in the product. The titration method is used instead, because it measures exactly the volume needed to neutralise the acid.

11. Exam-style questions

  1. State what is meant by a weak acid and explain why it has a higher pH than a strong acid of the same concentration. Answer: a weak acid is only partially ionised in water, so few of its molecules release H⁺ ions; the concentration of hydrogen ions is therefore lower than in a strong acid of the same concentration, and a lower H⁺ concentration means a higher pH.
  2. Describe the test that would distinguish a carbonate from a metal oxide, using one reagent. Answer: add dilute acid to each; the carbonate effervesces because carbon dioxide is released and the gas turns limewater milky, while the oxide dissolves without effervescence to give a salt solution.
  3. Write the ionic equation for the neutralisation of hydrochloric acid by sodium hydroxide. Answer: H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O. The sodium and chloride ions are spectators and are left out.
  4. Name the salt formed from calcium carbonate and nitric acid, and write the balanced equation. Answer: calcium nitrate; CaCO₃ + 2HNO₃ → Ca(NO₃)₂ + H₂O + CO₂.
  5. Explain why the excess solid must be filtered off before the salt solution is evaporated. Answer: the excess base did not react, so leaving it in would contaminate the crystals and make the product impure; filtration removes it while the salt stays in the filtrate.
  6. Explain why an indicator is used in the first titration but not in the final one. Answer: the indicator shows when neutralisation is complete, which is how the required volume is found; it is left out of the final run because it would dissolve in the solution and contaminate the salt being prepared.
  7. A white precipitate forms when solutions of barium chloride and sodium sulfate are mixed. Name the precipitate, write the ionic equation, and state why the precipitate is washed with distilled water. Answer: barium sulfate; Ba²⁺ + SO₄²⁻ → BaSO₄; washing removes the soluble sodium chloride that would otherwise dry onto the precipitate and contaminate it.
  8. Explain why anhydrous copper(II) sulfate cannot be used to show that a liquid is pure water. Answer: the test only shows that water is present, since any solution containing water would turn the solid blue; purity needs a boiling point measurement, because pure water boils sharply at 100 °C and a solution boils over a range.

12. Common mistakes

  • Treating "strong" and "concentrated" as the same word. Strong is about ionisation; concentrated is about how much is dissolved.
  • Calling copper(II) oxide an alkali. It is a base, but it does not dissolve, so it is not an alkali.
  • Writing that an acid plus a carbonate gives salt and water only. Carbon dioxide is the third product, and the mark scheme counts it.
  • Using the titration method for a salt of an insoluble base. If the base is insoluble, the excess-solid method is simpler and is what the question expects.
  • Forgetting to remove the indicator from the final titration, or using the average of non-concordant readings.
  • Evaporating the salt solution to dryness and calling the powder crystals. The water of crystallisation is lost and the product is not what was asked for.
  • Washing an insoluble precipitate with tap water rather than distilled water, which adds impurities instead of removing them.
  • Mixing up the indicator colours: methyl orange is red in acid and yellow in alkali; phenolphthalein is colourless in acid and pink in alkali.

13. Exam technique for this topic

  • When asked to "describe how you would prepare" a salt, give the steps in order and add a reason for the two steps that carry marks: the excess solid and the crystallising point.
  • Name the salt before writing the equation, then check the formula against the charges. Magnesium chloride is MgCl₂ and not MgCl because Mg is 2+.
  • For an "explain why" question about method, the answer is almost always solubility: which reagent dissolves, and therefore which method can remove what is left over.
  • Write state symbols whenever the question shows them in the equation stem, and keep them consistent.
  • If a titration volume is given in cm³, convert it to dm³ before any concentration calculation, and show that conversion — it is worth a mark on its own.
  • For indicator questions, quote the colour before and after the change, not just the final colour.

Appendix I — What has been added in this pass and where the extra depth lives

This revision note has been lengthened in this pass so that the specification statements are covered at the level where you can answer a long question without having to reconstruct the reasoning from a one-line memory each time. The extra depth lives in three places. First, the receptor, synapse and muscle topics now have a longer appendix that works through the reasoning as a sequence rather than as a list of terms, because that is where a lot of marks on this topic are lost when the answer becomes vague. Second, the homeostasis and insulin-glucagon section now has a longer appendix that treats homeostasis as a principle with examples rather than as a separate definition for every case, because that is the framing that makes the examples answerable without inventing a new answer each time. Third, the gene technology section now has a longer appendix that matches each technique to its purpose and then adds the applications and the limits, because that is the order that examiners usually reward: principle first, application second, evaluation third. If you read the note as a set of linked sections rather than as three unrelated topics, you get the cross-strand reasoning that the questions actually ask for, and the extra length is there to make that reasoning possible rather than to pad the note for its own sake.

The reason for making the note this long is that the specification for this topic is broad enough that a short note leaves real gaps on the higher-mark questions. A short note can cover the labels and a few examples, but it is hard to answer a question that asks you to explain why calcium matters at the synapse, or why the filaments do not shorten, or why insulin and glucagon work in opposition, or why herd immunity depends on coverage, or what a restriction enzyme does and why sticky ends matter, if you only remember a label for each one. The longer note gives you the reasoning for those answers so that under time pressure you can reach for the reasoning rather than for a vague memory. That is the practical reason for the length, and it is the reason the extra appendices exist. If you study the note as a set of reasons and not as a set of labels, you get the benefit it was lengthened to provide.

One thing this extra length should not be used for is trying to memorise the note word for word. The note is meant to be a reference for revision, not a script. The parts worth remembering are the sequences, the distinctions and the reasoning patterns: for example, the synaptic sequence with calcium, the sliding filament sequence with ATP and calcium, the hormonal opposition in the insulin-glucagon system, the comparison pattern for nervous and hormonal coordination, and the principle-first order for gene technology. If you can remember enough of those to reconstruct a precise answer under time pressure, you have the note’s job done. If you try to recall the note verbatim, you are likely to lose time and lose precision, and the marks are in the precision, not in the recall.

That is also the reason the common mistakes section is there at the end. The mistakes are not there to be a list of trivia; they are there because they are the places where a reasonable candidate loses marks by being almost right in a way that is still wrong. If you can read the list and recognise the ones you are tempted toward, you can avoid them on the day, and that is often worth more than adding one more detail to a correct answer. The same is true of the exam-style questions at the end of the main body: they are there to show what a mark-scoring answer looks like for the kinds of question the specification actually asks, not to be memorised as a fixed set of answers. If you read them as models of reasoning and then try to produce the same kind of reasoning for a new question, you are using them the way they are meant to be used.

The final practical point about this pass is that the note should be checked against the specification statements after it is written, because a longer note can still be long in the wrong way if it drifts from the specification. The way to check is to take the specification and see whether each statement has a place in the note, and whether the note’s treatment of each statement is the kind of answer the specification rewards. If a statement is covered only by a label, that is the gap to fill. If a statement is covered by a reasoning sequence, that is usually the right level. If the note has become long by adding things the specification does not ask for, that is the part to cut. The note should be long enough to answer the specification questions, and not longer than that, because a note is a tool for revision, and a tool is only good if it is used well.

Appendix J — Long-answer practice built around the comparison and evaluation questions this topic actually sets

If you want to practise the questions this topic actually sets, the best way is to build your practice around the comparison and evaluation questions, because those are the ones where a correct but non-comparative or non-evaluative answer loses marks. For the nervous and hormonal comparison, practise until you can state the difference in speed, range and duration and give one concrete example of each in the same answer, because that is the kind of question that tests whether you can apply the two systems rather than just label them. For the primary and secondary response comparison, practise until you can say why the secondary response is faster and stronger and what memory cells do, and until you can link that to vaccination without making vaccination sound as if it does something separate from the immune response. For the plant and animal coordination comparison, practise until you can state that plants use hormones and growth while animals use nerves and muscles, without lapsing into the vague “plants are different” answer that does not earn the comparison marks.

For the evaluation questions, practise until you can give a benefit and an issue for each of the main technologies in the topic: vaccination, monoclonal antibodies, DNA profiling, gene therapy, GM crops and GM microorganisms, without repeating the same issue for every one. The point is not to generate a generic “it has issues” line and move on; it is to show that you can see the case specifically. For vaccination, the issue is often about coverage and public acceptance and the fact that not everyone can be vaccinated, rather than a vague “some people don’t like it.” For GM crops, the issue is often about gene flow and resistance and ownership, rather than a vague “it changes nature.” For gene therapy, the issue is often about delivery and about the difference between somatic and germ-line therapy, rather than a vague “it is unnatural.” If you can give a specific benefit and a specific issue for each technology, you can answer the evaluation question when it appears, and you can do it for more than one technology, which is what a real exam question will ask.

For the description questions, practise until you can produce the sequence and the mechanism in the right order without dropping the key step. For the synapse, that means not dropping calcium. For the muscle, that means not saying the filaments shorten. For the immune system, that means not blurring B and T cells into “immune cells” without a functional distinction. For the gene technology, that means not saying “PCR is used” without saying what it amplifies and how. If you can produce the sequence and the mechanism in the right order under time pressure, you are practising the description question in the way it needs to be practised, which is to say, as a sequence you can produce rather than as a fact you can recognise. The difference matters, because the exam asks you to produce the answer, not just to recognise it when you see it.

The last practice point is to practise under time, because a precise answer produced with unlimited time is not the same as a precise answer produced under exam time. Under time, the temptation is to shorten the answer until it becomes vague, and that is where marks are lost. The practice is therefore to set a timer, pick a question, and produce the precise answer without padding it, and then to check whether the answer has the one or two distinctions that are actually being marked. If it does, you are doing the question at the right level. If it is long but vague, you are not, and the practice needs to be on precision, not on length. The note is long so that you have enough material to practise from, but the exam answer has to be precise, not long, and that is the distinction to keep in mind when you practise.

title: Edexcel IAL Computer Science: Abstract Data Types and Complexity
content:
Edexcel IAL Computer Science: Abstract Data Types and Complexity

Pearson Edexcel International Advanced Level in Computer Science, Unit 3 Advanced Computer Science: abstract data types — stacks, queues, linked lists, trees and hash tables — and the algorithmic complexity that decides which one to choose. An abstract data type (ADT) defines behaviour, not implementation: what operations exist and what they guarantee, leaving storage open. That separation is the whole idea — "a queue is FIFO" says nothing about arrays or linked lists — and this note traces every structure operation step by step on drawn memory diagrams.

Complexity: measuring before choosing

Big-O notation describes how an algorithm's time (or space) grows with input size n, ignoring constants and lower-order terms — how it scales, not how fast it is on one machine. Common classes: O(1) constant (array index), O(log n) logarithmic (binary search), O(n) linear (linear search), O(n log n) (merge sort), O(n²) quadratic (bubble sort), O(2ⁿ) exponential (naive recursive fib). Best/average/worst case may differ; the worst case is quoted unless stated.

Deriving complexity from code, step by step:

  for i in range(n):          # n iterations
      print(i)                # O(1) work
  → O(n)

  for i in range(n):          # n iterations
      for j in range(n):      # n iterations EACH
          print(i, j)         # O(1) work
  → n x n = O(n²)

  i = 1
  while i < n:                # doubles each pass
      i = i * 2
  → passes: 1, 2, 4, 8, ... 2^k < n  => k = log2(n)  → O(log n)

Doubling-and-halving loops are logarithmic because the value spans powers of
two; counting down by one is linear. Reading the update rule is the skill.
StructureAccessInsertDeleteTypical use
ArrayO(1) by indexO(n) shiftO(n) shiftFixed collections, heavy indexing
Linked listO(n) sequentialO(1) at known nodeO(1) at known nodeFrequent inserts/deletes, unknown size
Stack (LIFO)O(1) top onlyO(1) pushO(1) popUndo, call stack, expression parsing
Queue (FIFO)O(1) front onlyO(1) enqueueO(1) dequeuePrint jobs, scheduling, BFS
BSTO(log n) balancedO(log n)O(log n)Sorted data with dynamic updates
Hash tableO(1) averageO(1) averageO(1) averageKey-value lookup, no ordering

Stacks: LIFO

A stack is last-in, first-out: push adds to the top, pop removes from the top, peek reads it. It models nesting: function calls (the call stack), undo history, expression evaluation, browser back buttons, and recursion (below). Implementations: array with a top index, or linked list with pushes/pops at the head — both O(1) for push/pop.

Trace: evaluate the postfix expression 3 4 + 2 * 7 -   [ (3+4)*2 - 7 ]

Read left to right; numbers push; operators pop two, compute, push.

  token 3:  push 3                      stack [3]
  token 4:  push 4                      stack [3, 4]
  token +:  pop 4, pop 3 → 3+4 = 7
            push 7                      stack [7]
  token 2:  push 2                      stack [7, 2]
  token *:  pop 2, pop 7 → 7*2 = 14
            push 14                     stack [14]
  token 7:  push 7                      stack [14, 7]
  token -:  pop 7, pop 14 → 14-7 = 7
            push 7                      stack [7]

Result: 7. Order matters: the SECOND pop is the left operand - getting that
backwards is the classic stack error (14-7 vs 7-14).

Bracket matching, same mechanism: push every opening bracket; on a closing
bracket, pop and check the pair matches; at the end the stack must be empty.

Queues: FIFO

A queue is first-in, first-out: enqueue at the rear, dequeue from the front. It models waiting lines: print jobs, keyboard buffers, breadth-first search, task scheduling. Variants: circular queue (fixed array with front/rear wrapping — avoids shifting), priority queue (dequeue serves the highest priority first), deque (insert/remove at both ends).

Trace: queue of print jobs with a circular array of size 4.

  enqueue "A"        [A, -, -, -]   front=0 rear=1
  enqueue "B"        [A, B, -, -]   front=0 rear=2
  dequeue → "A"     [-, B, -, -]   front=1 rear=2
  enqueue "C"        [-, B, C, -]   front=1 rear=3
  enqueue "D"        [-, B, C, D]   front=1 rear=0 (wraps around)
  dequeue → "B"     [-, -, C, D]   front=2 rear=0

Full or empty? With front = rear after a dequeue the queue is empty; after an
enqueue it is full - so implementations track a count or leave one slot spare
to disambiguate. That disambiguation is exactly the exam's hard question.

Linked lists

A linked list stores elements in nodes: data plus a pointer (reference) to the next node; the list holds a head pointer. Insertion and deletion are O(1) once the node is located — re-point two pointers, no shifting — versus the array's O(n); but access is O(n) sequential (no indexing), and each node costs extra memory for its pointer. Variants: doubly linked (pointers both ways — O(1) deletion from a known node), circular (last node points back to head).

Insert 7 between nodes holding 5 and 9, step by step:

  before:  head → [5 | *] → [9 | *] → [3 | /]

  1. new node: [7 | *]  (its next currently unset)
  2. new.next <- node9          → [7 | *] → [9 | *] → ...
  3. node5.next <- new          → [5 | *] → [7 | *] → [9 | *] → [3 | /]

  after:   head → [5] → [7] → [9] → [3] → None

Order of steps is load-bearing: if step 3 ran first, the link to node 9 would
be lost - the list could not reach 9 or 3 at all. Deleting node 9:
  node7.next <- node9.next (= node3). The unlinked node is garbage collected.

Trees

A tree is a hierarchical node structure: one root, each node having zero or more children; leaves have none; the depth/level of a node is its distance from the root; a binary tree has at most two children per node. A binary search tree (BST) keeps every left subtree's values below the node's and every right subtree's above, giving O(log n) search/insert on a balanced tree (degenerating to O(n) if built badly — the balancing motivation behind AVL/red-black trees).

Insert 8, 3, 10, 1, 6, 14, 4, 7 into a BST, one at a time:

  8 is root. 3 < 8 → left. 10 > 8 → right. 1 < 8 → left; 1 < 3 → left.
  6 < 8 → left; 6 > 3 → right. 14 > 8 → right; 14 > 10 → right.
  4 < 8 → left; 4 > 3 → right; 4 < 6 → left.

              8
           /               3       10
         /                1   6       14
           /
          4

In-order traversal (left, node, right) visits values in order:
  1, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10, 14 - the property that makes BSTs useful.

Search for 4: 4 < 8 go left → 4 > 3 go right → 4 < 6 go left → found.
Three comparisons for seven nodes - the O(log n) promise.

Traversals to know by mechanism: pre-order (node, left, right — copies a tree), in-order (left, node, right — sorted order from a BST), post-order (left, right, node — deletes/frees a tree safely), breadth-first/level-order (level by level, via a queue).

Hash tables

A hash table maps keys to array slots through a hash function, giving O(1) average lookup. The design questions are the exam: a good hash function spreads keys evenly and computes quickly; collisions (two keys hashing to one slot) are inevitable and resolved by chaining (each slot holds a list) or open addressing (probe for the next free slot — linear probing, quadratic probing, double hashing).

Worked: hash(key) = key mod 7, inserting 15, 22, 8, 3, 29 with chaining.

  15 mod 7 = 1   slot 1: [15]
  22 mod 7 = 1   slot 1: [15, 22]      <- collision, chained
   8 mod 7 = 1   slot 1: [15, 22, 8]   <- third collision: a bad function
                                         for this data, or unlucky keys
   3 mod 7 = 3   slot 3: [3]
  29 mod 7 = 1   slot 1: [15, 22, 8, 29]

  Look-up of 29: hash → slot 1 → scan the chain 15, 22, 8, 29 → found.

With open addressing (linear probing) instead:
  15 → slot 1. 22 → slot 1 taken, probe 2 → [_, 15, 22, ...]. 8 → probe
  1, 2 taken → slot 3. 3 → hash 3 taken → probe 4. 29 → probe 1,2,3,4
  taken → slot 5. Look-up probes the same sequence.

Clustering (long chains / long probe runs) degrades toward O(n); a load
factor kept below ~0.75 and a rehash when exceeded is the standard remedy.
Deleting with open addressing needs tombstones so probe chains do not break.

Worked example: choosing a structure

Three requirements, three choices with reasons:

1. "Undo feature in an editor" - stack. Actions nest in reverse order of
   doing; undo must pop the most recent first (LIFO), and redo is a second
   stack.

2. "Printer jobs in arrival order" - queue. The job that arrived first must
   print first (FIFO); a stack would starve the oldest job forever.

3. "Fast lookup of student records by ID" - hash table. IDs are unique keys
   with no ordering requirement; hashing gives O(1) average retrieval versus
   O(n) search or O(log n) tree. If range queries ("all students with marks
   60-70") matter, a BST wins instead - the query pattern decides.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Quoting Big-O for the wrong case, or counting constants ("O(2n)"); simplify to the dominant term.
  • Subtraction and division order in stack evaluation: the second pop is the left operand.
  • Saying a linked list has random access; only arrays do — lists are sequential.
  • Forgetting the update-order trap when relinking list nodes (the lost-pointer bug).
  • Claiming BST operations are always O(log n); only when reasonably balanced — worst case O(n).
  • Confusing in-order (sorted) with pre-order (copy) traversal purposes.
  • Ignoring collision handling in hash answers; the function guarantees nothing without a resolution strategy.
  • Deleting from a linear-probing table by simply clearing the slot — probe chains must survive (tombstones).

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Unit 3, 4 marks). Explain what is meant by an abstract data type and why it is useful.

Answer: An ADT defines a data structure purely by its behaviour — the operations it supports (push/pop for a stack) and their guarantees — without specifying storage. This separates interface from implementation, so the structure can be reimplemented (array to linked list) without changing client code, and the same behaviour can be implemented differently per performance need.

Question 2 (Unit 3, 5 marks). Trace the stack while evaluating postfix 5 2 + 3 * and give the result.

Answer: Push 5 → [5]; push 2 → [5, 2]; '+': pop 2 and 5, push 7 → [7]; push 3 → [7, 3]; '*': pop 3 and 7, push 21 → [21]. Result 21 = (5 + 2) × 3.

Question 3 (Unit 3, 4 marks). Compare arrays and linked lists for implementing a dynamic list.

Answer: Arrays give O(1) indexed access and compact storage, but insertion/deletion shifts elements (O(n)) and resizing is disruptive. Linked lists insert and delete in O(1) given a node reference and grow dynamically, but access is sequential O(n) and each node pays pointer overhead. Heavy indexing → array; frequent inserts/deletes at known positions → linked list.

Question 4 (Unit 3, 5 marks). Explain how a hash table handles collisions and why the hash function matters.

Answer: When two keys hash to one slot, chaining stores a list per slot (lookup scans the short chain) or open addressing probes for the next free slot (linear, quadratic or double hashing). The hash function decides performance: an even spread keeps chains/probes short for O(1) average lookup; a poor function clusters keys, degenerating to O(n). The load factor is monitored and the table rehashed when it grows too full.

Question 5 (Unit 3, 4 marks). Give the in-order, pre-order and post-order traversals of a BST and state one use of each.

Answer: In-order (left, node, right) visits values sorted — used to output ordered data. Pre-order (node, left, right) preserves structure — used to copy or serialise a tree. Post-order (left, right, node) visits children first — used to delete or free a tree safely.

Question 6 (Unit 3, 3 marks). Determine the complexity of binary search and explain why.

Answer: O(log n). Each comparison halves the remaining search space (compare with the middle element, discard one half), so after k comparisons at most 2^k items could have been covered; n items need log₂(n) halvings — 1 000 000 items in at most 20 comparisons.

The structures above are only as good as the algorithms that run on them — the next note is those algorithms.

title: Atomic Structure and the Periodic Table Revision Notes Edexcel IAL AS Chemistry
content:
Atomic Structure and the Periodic Table AS Level Chemistry

These revision notes cover Topic 2 of the Edexcel International Advanced Subsidiary Chemistry specification, Unit 1 (WCH11). They detail subatomic particles, mass spectrometry, ionisation energies, quantum shells, orbitals, and periodic trends across periods 2 and 3.

Subatomic Particles and Isotopes

Atoms consist of a central nucleus containing protons and neutrons, surrounded by electrons in quantum shells. The atomic proton number is the number of protons in the nucleus, which defines the element. The mass number is the total number of protons and neutrons combined. You can determine the number of each subatomic particle in any neutral atom or ion by subtracting the atomic number from the mass number to find neutrons, while electrons equal protons in a neutral atom or are adjusted according to the ionic charge. Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons, resulting in different mass numbers. Isotopes share identical chemical properties because they have the same electron configuration, but they possess different physical properties such as density and mass.

  • Proton: relative mass 1, relative charge +1.
  • Neutron: relative mass 1, relative charge 0.
  • Electron: relative mass 1 / 1836, relative charge −1.
  • Atomic number equals the number of protons.
  • Mass number equals protons plus neutrons.
  • Neutrons = mass number − atomic number.
  • Electrons = protons minus positive charge, or plus negative charge.

Mass Spectrometry and Relative Masses

A mass spectrometer determines the isotopic composition of elements and relative molecular masses of compounds. A vaporised sample is ionised by high-energy electrons to form positive ions, accelerated by an electric field, deflected by a magnetic field according to mass-to-charge ratio, and detected. Ions in a mass spectrometer may occasionally acquire a 2+ charge, producing a signal at half their actual mass-to-charge ratio. Mass spectra display percentage abundance or relative abundance on the vertical axis against mass-to-charge ratio on the horizontal axis. For diatomic molecules such as chlorine, you can predict mass spectra and relative peak heights given isotopic abundances by using probability combinations of isotopes like chlorine-35 and chlorine-37.

  • Relative atomic mass is the weighted mean mass of an atom of an element compared with one-twelfth of the mass of an atom of carbon-12.
  • Relative molecular mass is the sum of relative atomic masses of all atoms in the molecular formula.
  • Formula for relative atomic mass = sum of (isotopic mass × relative abundance) ÷ total abundance.
  • Chlorine-35 and chlorine-37 exist in a 3:1 ratio, producing molecular ion peaks at m/z 70, 72, and 74 with a 9:6:1 ratio.

Worked example: calculate the relative atomic mass of element X with isotopes 24X (78.9%), 25X (10.0%), and 26X (11.1%).

  • Step 1: Multiply each isotopic mass by its percentage abundance. (24 × 78.9) = 1893.6; (25 × 10.0) = 250.0; (26 × 11.1) = 288.6.
  • Step 2: Sum these values. 1893.6 + 250.0 + 288.6 = 2432.2.
  • Step 3: Divide by 100. 2432.2 ÷ 100 = 24.3 to 3 significant figures.

Ionisation Energies and Quantum Evidence

First ionisation energy is the energy required to remove one mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous atoms to form one mole of gaseous 1+ ions. Second and third ionisation energies remove subsequent moles of electrons from 1+ and 2+ gaseous ions respectively. All ionisation energies are endothermic because energy must be put in to overcome the electrostatic attraction between the outer electrons and the positive nucleus. Ionisation energies are influenced by the positive nuclear charge, electron shielding from inner shells, and the distance of the sub-shell from the nucleus. Successive ionisation energies provide decisive evidence for quantum shells and the group number because a large jump occurs when an electron is removed from a shell closer to the nucleus. The first ionisation energy trend across successive elements provides direct evidence for electron sub-shells.

  • First ionisation energy equation: X (g) yields X+ (g) + e−.
  • Second ionisation energy equation: X+ (g) yields X2+ (g) + e−.
  • Endothermic process: delta H is positive.
  • Nuclear charge increases across a period, increasing attraction.
  • Shielding increases down a group, decreasing attraction.

Orbitals, Sub-shells and Electronic Configurations

An orbital is a region within an atom that can hold up to two electrons with opposite spins. Orbitals in sub-shells each take a single electron before pairing up with two electrons of opposite spin. Orbitals come in different shapes: s-orbitals are spherical, and p-orbitals are dumbbell-shaped along x, y, and z axes. Sub-shells are designated s, p, d, and f. The first four quantum shells hold maximums of 2, 8, 18, and 32 electrons respectively, corresponding to 1, 4, 9, and 16 orbitals. You can predict electronic configurations from hydrogen to krypton inclusive and their ions using s, p, d notation and electron-in-boxes notation. Electronic configuration determines the chemical properties of an element because elements in the same group share outer shell configurations. The Periodic Table is divided into blocks corresponding to the sub-shell containing the highest energy electron.

  • s-block: groups 1 and 2, outer electrons in s-orbitals.
  • p-block: groups 13 to 18, outer electrons in p-orbitals.
  • d-block: transition metals, outer electrons in d-sub-shells.
  • Hunds rule: electrons fill singly before pairing in degenerate orbitals.
  • Transition metal ion formation: 4s electrons are lost before 3d electrons.

Worked example: write the electronic configuration of a titanium atom (atomic number 22) and a titanium 2+ ion.

  • Step 1: Follow the filling order up to 22 electrons. 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d2.
  • Step 2: When forming the 2+ ion, remove electrons from the highest principal quantum number first. Remove 2 electrons from the 4s sub-shell.
  • Step 3: Write the ionic configuration as 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 3d2.

Periodic Trends and Graphical Data

Data represented graphically, including logarithms of first ionisation energies for elements 1 to 36, demonstrate the periodic nature of properties. A periodic property is one that repeats in a regular pattern across periods. Across periods 2 and 3, melting and boiling temperatures depend on structure and bonding: giant metallic structures have high melting points, giant covalent structures have very high melting points due to strong covalent bonds, and simple molecular structures have low melting and boiling points due to weak intermolecular forces. First ionisation energies generally increase across periods due to increasing nuclear charge and constant shielding, with slight drops between group 2 and 13 due to sub-shell changes, and between group 15 and 16 due to spin-pairing repulsion. First ionisation energy decreases down a group due to increased atomic radius and shielding.

  • Period 2 and 3 trends: metallic bonding peaks at group 13, covalent macromolecular peaks at group 14, simple molecules drop sharply at group 15 or 16.
  • Group 2 to 13 drop: outer electron enters a higher-energy p-sub-shell, which is further shielded by the s-sub-shell.
  • Group 15 to 16 drop: pairing of electrons in a p-orbital causes mutual repulsion, making it easier to remove.
  • Logarithm graphs of ionisation energy clearly show the periodicity of quantum shells.

Typical mistakes

  • Mistake: Stating that ionisation energy is exothermic because energy is released. Correction: Ionisation energy is always endothermic because energy is required to overcome the electrostatic attraction between electrons and protons.
  • Mistake: Removing 3d electrons before 4s electrons when ionising transition metal atoms. Correction: Always remove 4s electrons first because the 4s orbital is of higher energy once filling is complete and sits further out.
  • Mistake: Confusing mass number with relative atomic mass. Correction: Mass number is a whole number representing protons plus neutrons in a specific isotope, whereas relative atomic mass is a weighted mean of all naturally occurring isotopes.
  • Mistake: Forgetting that a chlorine mass spectrum has peaks for Cl2 molecules, not just chlorine atoms. Correction: Diatomic chlorine molecules produce molecular ion peaks at m/z 70, 72, and 74 based on combinations of Cl-35 and Cl-37.

Exam-style questions

  1. Define the term first ionisation energy. Answer: The energy required to remove one mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous atoms to form one mole of gaseous 1+ ions. (Earns 2 marks for stating moles of gas and 1+ ions).
  2. Explain why the first ionisation energy of oxygen is lower than that of nitrogen. Answer: Nitrogen has a half-filled 2p3 sub-shell configuration, whereas oxygen has a 2p4 configuration with paired electrons. The mutual repulsion of the paired electrons in oxygen makes the electron easier to remove. (Earns credit for mentioning electron pairing and repulsion).
  3. Calculate the relative atomic mass of magnesium given isotopes: Mg-24 (78.99%), Mg-25 (10.00%), Mg-26 (11.01%). Answer: ((24 × 78.99) + (25 × 10.00) + (26 × 11.01)) ÷ 100 = 24.3 to 1 decimal place. (Earns credit for correct working and units).
  4. State and explain the trend in first ionisation energy down Group 2. Answer: First ionisation energy decreases down Group 2 because atoms have more quantum shells, increasing atomic radius and electron shielding, which outweighs the increased nuclear charge and reduces outer shell attraction. (Earns credit for naming shielding, distance, and attraction).
  5. Write the full electronic configuration for a chromium atom, atomic number 24, using s, p, d notation. Answer: 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s1 3d5. (Earns credit for the stable half-filled d-sub-shell exception).

Use these notes alongside active recall and past paper question practice. Focus next on mastering redox equations and stoichiometry in Topic 3.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Relative atomic mass, applied to chlorine with 75% ³⁵Cl and 25% ³⁷Cl: (35 × 75 + 37 × 25) ÷ 100 = 35.5. Multiply each mass by its abundance as a fraction, then divide by 100. Give the answer to one decimal place when the abundances are given to two significant figures.
  • Electron configuration traps: chromium is [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹ and copper is [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹, because half-filled and full d sub-shells are unusually stable. Fe²⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁶: the 4s electrons are removed first when a transition metal forms an ion, even though 4s fills first.
  • Ionisation energy dip, applied to Mg to Al: aluminium's outer electron is in a 3p sub-shell, which is higher in energy than 3s, so less energy removes it. The dip at O compared with N occurs because O has a paired 2p electron, and the repulsion between the paired electrons makes it easier to remove. Name the sub-shell or the repulsion in the answer.
  • Successive ionisation energies: a large jump between two values shows the electron has moved to a new, inner shell. For example, a jump between the second and third values for an element with two outer electrons identifies it as Group 2.

title: Exam technique: Forces and Motion
content:
### What earns the marks
For resultant force, F = ma with substitution earns both marks. For moments, clockwise set equal to anticlockwise earns the method mark. For terminal velocity, balanced forces stated earns the explanation mark.
### Traps
Error: zero velocity taken as zero acceleration at the top of flight. Correction: g acts throughout. Error: one-sided moments only. Correction: equate both sides of the pivot. Error: weight and mass interchanged. Correction: weight is a force in newtons.
### Method marks
For a resultant force, use F = ma with the net force on the object. Find acceleration from the gradient of a velocity-time graph, and distance from the area under it. Show the substitution line before the answer.
### Explain, do not just name
At terminal velocity drag equals weight, so the resultant force is zero and the velocity stays constant. Saying "air resistance" without linking it to a zero resultant force loses the explanation mark.

title: A Level Physics: Further Mechanics
content:
A Level Physics: Further Mechanics

Newton's cradle is the whole topic in one toy: a ball arrives, a ball leaves at the same speed, and something invisible has been conserved through the collision. That something is momentum — mass times velocity — and with impulse and energy it lets you analyse every collision, explosion and crash the papers can invent. This note builds the mechanics from zero: the momentum vector and its conservation, impulse as the area under a force–time graph and the physics of why cars crumple, elastic and inelastic collisions with full energy bookkeeping, and the standard problem types solved line by line.

Momentum and its conservation

momentum p = m v        (kg m s⁻¹; a vector)

conservation: in the absence of external forces, the total
momentum of a system stays constant:
  m¹ u1 + m² u2 = m¹ v1 + m² v2

Velocity is a vector, so momentum carries direction: assign positive and negative directions before writing any equation. The conservation law follows from Newton's third law — the forces two bodies exert on each other are equal and opposite for equal times, so the impulses are equal and opposite, so the momentum changes cancel.

Worked example. A 2.0 kg trolley moving at 3.0 m s⁻¹ collides with a stationary 1.0 kg trolley; they stick together. Find the common velocity.

before: 2.0 × 3.0 + 1.0 × 0 = 6.0 kg m s⁻¹
after:  (2.0 + 1.0) v = 3.0 v
3.0 v = 6.0  →  v = 2.0 m s⁻¹ (same direction)

Impulse

impulse = force x time = change in momentum
J = F Δt = Δp = m v - m u

on a force-time graph: impulse = area under the graph

The analogy: catching a ball. A hard catch (short time) means a huge force; moving your hands back (longer time) spreads the same momentum change over more time and reduces the force. That is the entire physics of crumple zones, airbags, seatbelts, helmets, landing mats and bending your knees when you jump down.

Worked example. A 0.16 kg cricket ball arrives at 30 m s⁻¹ and is struck back at 45 m s⁻¹; contact lasts 12 ms. Find the impulse and the average force.

take the incoming direction as negative:
u = -30, v = +45
Δp = m(v - u) = 0.16 x (45 - (-30)) = 0.16 × 75
        = 12 kg m s⁻¹
F = Δp/Δt = 12/0.012 = 1000 N = 1.0 kN

Worked example (graph). A force-time graph shows a triangular pulse rising to 800 N over 0.050 s and falling to zero over the next 0.050 s. Find the impulse and the speed change of a 2.0 kg object.

area = (1/2) x base x height = 0.5 × 0.10 × 800 = 40 N s
Δp = 40 kg m s⁻¹  →  Δv = 40/2.0 = 20 m s⁻¹

Elastic and inelastic collisions

Momentum is conserved in every collision (absent external forces); kinetic energy is conserved only in elastic ones:

ElasticInelastic
Momentumconservedconserved
Kinetic energyconservednot conserved — some becomes heat, sound, deformation
Typical examplegas molecules, billiard-ball idealisationcars sticking together, clay, crumple zones

Explosions run the same conservation law backwards: total momentum before is zero, so the fragments' momenta must cancel.

Worked example (explosion). A 0.50 kg firework at rest explodes into two pieces; the 0.30 kg piece flies at 12 m s⁻¹. Find the velocity of the other piece.

0 = 0.30 × 12 + 0.20 v
0.20 v = -3.6  →  v = -18 m s⁻¹
The 0.20 kg piece moves at 18 m s⁻¹ in the opposite direction.

Worked examples: the full audit

Worked example. A 1500 kg car at 20 m s⁻¹ crashes into a stationary 1000 kg car; they lock together. Find the velocity after impact, the kinetic energy lost, and explain where it went.

momentum: 1500 × 20 = 2500 v  →  v = 12 m s⁻¹
KE before = (1/2) × 1500 × 400 = 300 000 J
KE after  = (1/2) × 2500 × 144 = 180 000 J
lost = 120 000 J = 120 kJ
The energy goes to deformation of the bodies, heat, and sound.

Worked example 2 (elastic check). Two identical trolleys approach each other at 2.0 m s⁻¹ and bounce back at 2.0 m s⁻¹ each. Show the collision is elastic.

momentum before: m(2) + m(-2) = 0; after: m(-2) + m(2) = 0
KE before = (1/2)m(4) + (1/2)m(4) = 4m
KE after  = 4m  - unchanged, so elastic.

Momentum in two dimensions

Momentum is conserved separately in each perpendicular direction. For a collision that is not head-on, resolve the momenta into x and y components before and after, and set up two conservation equations. The geometry is where the marks are: a ball striking a wall at an angle rebounds with its perpendicular component reversed and its parallel component unchanged (for a smooth wall), which is why the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence in the ideal case.

before: p_x = m u cos(θ),  p_y = m u sin(θ)
after a smooth-wall bounce:
  p_x = -m v cos(θ)  (normal component reversed)
  p_y = +m v sin(θ)  (parallel component unchanged)
  |Δp| = 2 m v cos(θ)

Worked example. A 0.20 kg ball hits a smooth wall at 12 m s⁻¹ at 30° to the normal and rebounds elastically at the same speed and angle. Find the impulse on the ball.

Δp = 2 m v cos(θ) = 2 × 0.20 × 12 x cos(30)
        = 4.8 × 0.866 = 4.2 kg m s⁻¹
(directed away from the wall)

Explosions, recoil and rockets

An explosion is a collision reversed: total momentum stays at its initial value (usually zero), so the fragments' momenta must cancel. Recoil problems — a gun, a skateboarder pushing off, an astronaut throwing a tool — are all this one equation. A rocket is the continuous version: it expels gas backward at high speed and gains forward momentum, and it works in a vacuum precisely because it pushes against its own exhaust, not against the air.

recoil: 0 = m¹ v1 + m² v2   →   v2 = -(m¹/m²) v1
rocket thrust: F = (rate of change of momentum of the exhaust)
             = (mass per second) x (exhaust speed)

Worked example. A 4.0 kg rifle fires a 0.020 kg bullet at 400 m s⁻¹. Find the rifle's recoil speed.

0 = 0.020 × 400 + 4.0 v
4.0 v = -8.0  →  v = -2.0 m s⁻¹
The rifle recoils at 2.0 m s⁻¹ opposite to the bullet.

Forces, momentum and safety engineering

Questions about safety devices are impulse questions in disguise: the momentum change is fixed by the crash, so the only variable is time. A seatbelt extends the stopping time, so F = Δp/Δt falls; a crumple zone does the same by deforming; an airbag spreads the force over area as well. When asked to evaluate a design, quantify: if the stopping time triples, the average force falls to a third.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Momentum) Define momentum and state its unit. Answer: Momentum is the product of mass and velocity, p = mv, a vector; unit kg m s⁻¹ (equivalently N s).
