  2. (Conservation) A 3.0 kg block at 4.0 m s⁻¹ hits a stationary 1.0 kg block and they move together. Find the final speed. Answer: 3.0 × 4.0 = 4.0v → v = 3.0 m s⁻¹.
  3. (Impulse) A 0.50 kg ball hits a wall at 8.0 m s⁻¹ and rebounds at 6.0 m s⁻¹; contact time 0.020 s. Find the average force. Answer: Δp = 0.50 × (6.0 + 8.0) = 7.0 kg m s⁻¹; F = 7.0/0.020 = 350 N.
  4. (Graph) Explain how to find impulse from a force–time graph. Answer: Impulse is the area under the graph; for a curve, count squares or integrate.
  5. (Elasticity) A collision conserves momentum but not kinetic energy. Classify it and name a real example. Answer: Inelastic; a car crash or two lumps of clay sticking together.
  6. (Explosion) A 60 kg astronaut pushes off a 400 kg spacecraft, moving at 0.50 m s⁻¹ relative to it. Find the spacecraft's recoil speed. Answer: 60 × 0.50 = 400 × v → v = 0.075 m s⁻¹ (opposite direction).
  7. (Safety) Explain how a crumple zone reduces injury. Answer: It deforms, increasing the collision time for a given momentum change; since F = Δp/Δt, the average force falls, reducing injury.
  8. (Energy) In an inelastic collision, where does the lost kinetic energy go? Answer: Into thermal energy, sound and permanent deformation of the materials — energy is conserved overall, but not as kinetic energy.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Dropping signs: momentum is a vector; a rebound reverses sign. The classic error is Δp = m(v − u) with both speeds positive, halving the true impulse.
  • Adding speeds wrongly: for a rebound, the change is v + u in magnitude (with signs, v − (−u)).
  • Assuming KE is conserved: check the type; "they stick together" is always inelastic. Compute KE before and after when asked.
  • External forces: conservation needs no net external force — a collision on a rough surface during a long interval is not the same as an instantaneous impact.
  • Unit of impulse: N s or kg m s⁻¹ are equivalent; force alone (N) is not.
  • Force–time areas: triangles and trapeziums need the correct geometric factors (½ for a triangle), not base × height.
  • Mass in grams: convert to kg before momentum calculations; a factor of 1000 error is common in cricket-ball questions.
  • Precision: 2 or 3 s.f. with units; keep direction words (opposite, same direction) in the answer.

title: Ethics, Security & Impact — Study Notes
content:
Ethics, Security & Impact

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2023–2025): ethics & professional codes, security threats, malware, online safety, environmental/employment impact.

1. Ethics and codes

ACM/IEEE-CS/BCS codes: public interest, competence, integrity, privacy. Applying: identify the principle → apply to scenario → stakeholders affected → consequences.

2. Threats

  • Malware: virus (attaches, replicates via host), worm (self-spreads), trojan (disguised), spyware, ransomware.
  • Social: phishing (fake emails/sites), pharming (DNS/hosts redirect), shoulder surfing, brute force.
  • Technical: interception (packet sniffing), SQL injection (malicious input into queries), DoS (flooding services).

3. Defences

Antivirus/antispyware (scan, quarantine), firewalls (port/IP filtering), 2FA + biometrics, strong passwords + managers, encryption (HTTPS, VPN), access levels, patches/updates, user training.

4. Online behaviour

Digital footprint, cyberbullying, fake news, privacy settings, verification of sources.

5. Wider impact

Employment: automation displaces roles but creates IT jobs. Environment: e-waste, energy use vs paperless efficiency. Monitoring: workplace tracking, CCTV — balance with privacy laws (GDPR-style).

Exam tips: name the threat precisely (pharming ≠ phishing), then the matched defence; ethics answers need principle + application, not opinion.

title: IGCSE Chemistry: Atoms, Elements and Compounds
content:
IGCSE Chemistry: Atoms, Elements and Compounds

Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry 0620 (2026–2028), Extended route, Topic 2 Atoms, elements and compounds: statements 2.1 Elements, compounds and mixtures, 2.2 Atomic structure and the Periodic Table, 2.3 Isotopes, 2.4 Ions and ionic bonds, 2.5 Simple molecules and covalent bonds, 2.6 Giant covalent structures, and 2.7 Metallic bonding. This is the foundation everything else stands on: what atoms are made of, why they bond, and how the four bonding types dictate every physical property you will ever be asked to explain. Every electron configuration and isotope calculation is worked digit by digit.

Elements, compounds and mixtures

An element is one kind of atom only (iron, oxygen gas) — it cannot be broken down chemically. A compound is two or more elements chemically joined in fixed proportions, with new properties (water: hydrogen and oxygen, but nothing like either). A mixture is substances physically together, unchanged, separable by physical means. The test-paper distinction: compounds need chemical change to separate (electrolysis); mixtures separate physically (distillation, chromatography, filtration).

Inside the atom

Picture the atom as a sports stadium: the nucleus is a marble at the centre of the pitch, and the electrons are specks of dust whizzing around the stands. Almost all the mass sits in that tiny nucleus; almost all the volume is empty space.

ParticleRelative chargeRelative massLocation
Proton+11Nucleus
Neutron01Nucleus
Electron−11/1836 (negligible)Electron shells around the nucleus

Definitions the exam demands verbatim: the proton (atomic) number is the number of protons in an atom and fixes the element; the mass (nucleon) number is the total of protons plus neutrons. Atoms are neutral because protons = electrons; an ion forms when electrons are lost or gained.

Reading the symbol notation, line by line:  ²³⁵₉₂U

  mass number (top)     = 235 = protons + neutrons
  proton number (bottom)= 92  = protons
  therefore:
    protons   = 92
    electrons = 92 (neutral atom)
    neutrons  = 235 - 92 = 143

Same arithmetic for any species:
  ⁴⁰₂₀Ca²⁺:  protons 20, neutrons 40 - 20 = 20,
             electrons 20 - 2 = 18 (the 2+ charge means 2 electrons LOST)

Electron arrangement, 1 to 20

Electrons occupy shells that fill in a fixed order — first shell 2, second 8, third 8 (for the first twenty elements), then 2. The arrangement is written as comma-separated numbers: sodium (11 electrons) is 2,8,1.

Building every configuration from hydrogen to calcium, step by step:

  H  1        He 2         [first shell full at 2]
  Li 2,1      Be 2,2       B 2,3        C 2,4
  N 2,5       O 2,6        F 2,7        Ne 2,8     [second shell full at 8]
  Na 2,8,1    Mg 2,8,2     Al 2,8,3     Si 2,8,4
  P 2,8,5     S 2,8,6      Cl 2,8,7     Ar 2,8,8   [third shell full at 8]
  K 2,8,8,1   Ca 2,8,8,2   [fourth shell starts after 8 in the third]

Two rules worth a mark each:
  outer-shell electron count = GROUP number  (Cl: 7 outer -> Group VII)
  number of occupied shells = PERIOD number (Cl: 3 shells -> Period 3)
A full outer shell (2 or 8) means the atom is unreactive - the noble gases.

Isotopes and relative atomic mass

Isotopes are atoms of the same element (same proton number) with different numbers of neutrons. They have identical chemical properties — chemistry lives in the electron arrangement, which isotopes share — but different masses. The relative atomic mass is the weighted average of the isotopic masses.

Worked: chlorine exists as ³⁵Cl (75%) and ³⁷Cl (25%). Calculate its Aᵣ.

  Aᵣ = (isotope 1 mass x its fraction) + (isotope 2 mass x its fraction)
     = (35 x 0.75) + (37 x 0.25)
     = 26.25 + 9.25
     = 35.5

Percentages can be used directly with the same arithmetic:
  Aᵣ = (35 x 75 + 37 x 25) / 100 = (2625 + 925) / 100 = 35.5 ✓

If the question gives abundances as 3:1 instead of 75:25, the fractions are
3/4 = 0.75 and 1/4 = 0.25 - convert counts to fractions first.

Ions and ionic bonding

Metals lose electrons, non-metals gain them, and the resulting oppositely charged ions attract — an ionic bond is the electrostatic attraction between cations and anions. The product is a giant ionic lattice: a regular, repeating grid of alternating ions, not individual molecules.

Deduction of ionic formulae by charge balance - worked three times:

  Na (2,8,1) loses 1 electron -> Na⁺       Cl (2,8,7) gains 1 -> Cl⁻
    charges +1 and -1 balance 1:1  ->  NaCl

  Mg (2,8,2) loses 2 -> Mg²⁺               O (2,6) gains 2 -> O²⁻
    charges +2 and -2 balance 1:1  ->  MgO

  Ca (2,8,8,2) loses 2 -> Ca²⁺             Cl (2,8,7) gains 1 -> Cl⁻
    one 2+ needs TWO 1-  ->  CaCl₂

General rule: swap the charge NUMBERS to get the subscripts, then simplify
(Ca²⁺ and O²⁻ -> Ca₂O₂ -> CaO).

Properties follow from structure — the reasoning chain examiners want: ionic compounds have high melting and boiling points because the strong electrostatic forces in the giant lattice take lots of energy to overcome; they conduct electricity when molten or aqueous (ions free to move) but not when solid (ions locked in place); they are often soluble in water (polar water molecules pull ions from the lattice).

Covalent bonds and simple molecules

A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons holding two non-metal atoms together. Each shared pair is one bond; atoms bond until their outer shells are full. Dot-and-cross diagrams draw only the outer-shell electrons, with crosses from one atom and dots from the other.

Dot-and-cross logic for four standard molecules (describe, then draw):

  H₂   each H brings 1 electron; one shared pair fills both 1-electron
       shells -> H-H
  H₂O  O (2,6) needs 2 electrons; each H shares 1 -> two shared pairs,
       two lone pairs on oxygen -> bent shape
  CH₄  C (2,4) needs 4; four H atoms each share 1 -> four shared pairs,
       four lone pairs total on the hydrogens -> tetrahedral
  NH₃  N (2,5) needs 3; three H atoms share -> three shared pairs and ONE
       lone pair on nitrogen -> pyramidal
  HCl  one shared pair between H and Cl (Cl keeps 3 lone pairs)

Simple molecular substances: LOW melting/boiling points - the covalent bonds
INSIDE molecules are strong, but the forces BETWEEN molecules are weak and
need little energy to break. They do not conduct: no free ions or electrons.

The distinction students most often miss: melting a molecular substance breaks intermolecular forces, not covalent bonds. Breaking covalent bonds is a chemical change.

Giant covalent structures

StructureBondingProperties and uses
DiamondEach C bonded to 4 others; giant 3D lattice of strong covalent bondsHardest natural substance; cutting tools, drill bits — no free electrons, so does not conduct
GraphiteEach C bonded to 3 others in flat hexagonal layers; delocalised electrons between layersLayers slide easily — lubricant; conducts electricity — electrodes; soft
Silicon(IV) oxideLike diamond: each Si bonded to 4 O in a giant latticeVery hard, very high melting point; similar to diamond in structure-property terms

The property question is always the same shape: name the structure → name the strong bonds → explain why that gives the property (and where relevant why the other structure differs: graphite's weakly bonded layers slide; its delocalised electrons conduct).

Metallic bonding

Metal atoms pack into a giant lattice of positive ions surrounded by a "sea" of delocalised electrons — electrons detached from their atoms and free to move. The metallic bond is the attraction between the positive ions and that delocalised sea.

  • Electrical and thermal conductivity: the delocalised electrons carry charge (and energy) through the structure.
  • Malleability and ductility: layers of identical ions can slide over each other without breaking the bonding — the electron sea simply re-forms around them (unlike ionic lattices, which shatter when layers shift and like charges align).
  • High melting points: strong attraction throughout the giant lattice (tungsten very high; mercury low because its bonding is weaker).

Worked example: the four bonding types compared on one property set

Question: explain why sodium chloride melts at 801 °C, but methane melts at
-182 °C - even though both contain strong covalent/ionic interactions.

  NaCl: ionic. Giant lattice of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ held by strong electrostatic
        forces throughout. Melting means overcoming these forces everywhere
        at once -> lots of energy -> high temperature.
  Methane (CH₄): simple molecular. Strong covalent bonds INSIDE each molecule
        stay intact on melting; only the weak intermolecular forces BETWEEN
        molecules are overcome -> little energy -> very low temperature.

The structure sentence earns the mark; "because it is ionic" alone does not.
Same shape of answer: diamond vs CO₂ (giant covalent vs simple molecular),
iron vs sodium (both metallic - compare bond strength and ion size).

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Swapping proton number and mass number in symbol notation; the bottom number is always the proton number.
  • Computing neutrons as mass number (it is mass number minus proton number).
  • Writing ion charges as counts (Ca⁺² instead of Ca²⁺) — charge goes top-right after the symbol.
  • Claiming isotopes differ chemically; only physical properties (mass-dependent behaviour like diffusion) differ.
  • Saying ionic compounds conduct when solid — only when molten or in solution, when ions can move.
  • Explaining low melting points of molecular substances by "weak covalent bonds" — the covalent bonds are strong; it is the intermolecular forces that are weak.
  • Forgetting lone pairs in dot-and-cross diagrams (ammonia's and water's lone pairs are marks).
  • Confusing graphite's conductivity (delocalised electrons within layers) with diamond's insulation (all four electrons locked in bonds).
  • Explaining malleability of metals by "layers slide" without mentioning the electron sea re-forming — the bonding must stay intact.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 4, 3 marks). An atom has 16 protons, 16 neutrons and 16 electrons. State the element, its mass number, and the electron arrangement.

Answer: Proton number 16 is sulfur. Mass number = 16 + 16 = 32. Electron arrangement 2,8,6.

Question 2 (Paper 4, 3 marks). Explain why isotopes of an element have the same chemical properties but different physical properties.

Answer: Chemical properties depend on electron arrangement (especially outer-shell electrons), and isotopes have identical electron arrangements since proton number fixes electron count. Physical properties that depend on mass — such as rate of diffusion — differ because isotopes have different numbers of neutrons and therefore different masses.

Question 3 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Describe the bonding in magnesium oxide and explain why it has a high melting point.

Answer: Magnesium atoms (2,8,2) each lose two electrons to become Mg²⁺; oxygen atoms (2,6) each gain two to become O²⁻. The oppositely charged ions form a giant ionic lattice in which each ion is electrostatically attracted to all its neighbours. The strong electrostatic forces throughout the lattice require large amounts of energy to overcome, so the melting point is high (2852 °C).

Question 4 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Explain why graphite conducts electricity but diamond does not, and why graphite is used as a lubricant.

Answer: In graphite each carbon bonds to three others, leaving one delocalised electron per atom free to move within the layers — these carry charge. In diamond every carbon bonds to four others with all electrons locked in bonds, so none are free. As a lubricant: graphite's layers are held only weakly and slide over each other easily while retaining bonding, reducing friction.

Question 5 (Paper 4, 3 marks). Substance A melts at 801 °C and conducts electricity only when molten. Substance B melts at 1610 °C and never conducts. Identify each structure type and explain.

Answer: A is ionic (giant ionic lattice, e.g. sodium chloride): its high melting point reflects strong electrostatic forces between ions, and it conducts only when molten because the ions are then free to move while they are locked in place when solid. B is giant covalent (e.g. silicon(IV) oxide): its higher melting point reflects extensive strong covalent bonds, and it never conducts because there are no free ions or delocalised electrons in any state.

Question 6 (Paper 4, 3 marks). Explain, in terms of structure, why metals are malleable while ionic compounds are brittle.

Answer: In metals, layers of identical positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons can slide without breaking metallic bonding — the electron sea re-forms around the displaced ions. In ionic lattices, shifting a layer brings like charges next to each other; the repulsion splits the crystal — so ionic solids shatter rather than bend.

With the particles and their bonds understood, the next foundations are the states those particles move through and the energy changes when they react.

title: Organic Chemistry: Halogenoalkanes, Alcohols and Spectra — Study Notes
content:
Organic Chemistry: Halogenoalkanes, Alcohols and Spectra

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH12, Topic 10. Halogenoalkanes and alcohols are the first families where a functional group changes the reactivity of the molecule. Spectra are the tools that identify those groups in an unknown compound.

Halogenoalkanes

  • A halogenoalkane has a halogen atom bonded to a carbon atom. The C–X bond is polar because the halogen is more electronegative, so the carbon is slightly positive.
  • Reactivity rises down the group because the C–X bond gets weaker (C–I is weakest), so the iodoalkane reacts fastest.
  • Nucleophilic substitution with aqueous hydroxide ions gives an alcohol. The nucleophile donates a pair of electrons to the carbon atom.
  • Halogenoalkanes can be tested by warming with aqueous silver nitrate in ethanol: the precipitate forms at different rates, and iodoalkanes react fastest.

Alcohols

  • Alcohols contain the –OH group. Primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols depend on how many other carbons are attached to the carbon bearing the –OH.
  • Oxidation of primary alcohols with acidified potassium dichromate(VI) gives aldehydes, which can be oxidised further to carboxylic acids; excess oxidant and heat give the acid.
  • Secondary alcohols oxidise to ketones; tertiary alcohols are not oxidised under these conditions.
  • Dehydration with hot concentrated sulfuric acid or aluminium oxide forms an alkene.

Mass spectrometry

  • The molecular ion peak gives the relative molecular mass. Fragmentation patterns reveal structural features.
  • Peaks at m/z 15 and 29 can indicate CH3 and C2H5 fragments.

Infrared spectroscopy

  • Bonds absorb infrared radiation at characteristic wavenumbers. A broad absorption near 3200–3550 cm⁻¹ indicates an O–H group in an alcohol. A strong absorption near 1700 cm⁻¹ indicates a C=O group.
  • Use tables of characteristic absorptions with the spectrum, rather than memorised single values.

NMR (introduced)

  • The number of peaks in a proton NMR spectrum gives the number of environments of hydrogen atoms; the relative areas give the ratio of hydrogens.

Exam tip: when identifying an unknown, combine evidence: the molecular formula from mass spectrometry, the functional groups from infrared, and the environments from NMR.

title: IGCSE Physics: Nuclear Physics
content:
IGCSE Physics: Nuclear Physics

Cambridge IGCSE Physics 0625 (2026–2028), Topic 5 Nuclear physics: statements 5.1 The nuclear model of the atom and 5.2 Radioactivity. Everything in the physical world is built from about a hundred kinds of atom, and almost all the mass of an atom sits in a tiny, dense nucleus. This note builds the nuclear model, then radioactivity from first principles: what the three emissions are, how nuclei decay, how half-life quantifies it, and how radiation is used safely.

The atom and the nuclear model

An atom is mostly empty space: a tiny central nucleus surrounded by electrons that occupy shells around it. The nucleus is about 10 000 times smaller than the atom, yet holds more than 99.9 per cent of its mass. Atoms are neutral because the number of electrons equals the number of protons; if an atom loses or gains electrons it becomes a ion, charged positive or negative.

Supplement: the evidence. In the alpha-particle scattering experiment, alpha particles were fired at an extremely thin gold foil. Most passed straight through, a few were deflected by small angles, and a very small number bounced back. Rutherford concluded that the atom has a small, dense, positively charged nucleus: most alphas met only empty space, those passing near the nucleus were deflected by the positive repulsion, and the rare head-on reversals required a tiny, massive target.

The nucleus: protons, neutrons and isotopes

The nucleus contains protons and neutrons, collectively nucleons. A proton carries one positive charge and one unit of mass; a neutron carries no charge and one unit of mass; an electron carries one negative charge and almost no mass.

ParticleRelative chargeRelative massLocation
Proton+11Nucleus
Neutron01Nucleus
Electron−11/1836 (negligible)Shells around the nucleus

Nuclide notation writes the symbol of the element with the proton number Z (the number of protons, which decides the element) and the nucleon number A (the total number of protons and neutrons) as a superscript and subscript on the left: A over Z beside the symbol. The number of neutrons is A − Z. Isotopes are atoms of the same element (same Z) with different numbers of neutrons (different A), so they have identical chemical properties but different nuclear behaviour.

Supplement: fission and fusion. Nuclear fission splits a heavy nucleus (such as uranium-235) into two lighter nuclei plus neutrons and a large release of energy; a neutron triggers the split and the released neutrons sustain a chain reaction in a reactor. Nuclear fusion joins two light nuclei (such as hydrogen isotopes) into a heavier one, releasing far more energy per kilogram — this powers the Sun and every star. In both, a small loss of mass appears as a large release of energy, in line with mass–energy equivalence, and the sum of the nucleon numbers and of the proton numbers is conserved in any nuclear equation.

Detection of radioactivity

Radioactivity is the spontaneous emission of radiation from unstable nuclei. It cannot be seen, heard or felt, so it is detected by its effects: a Geiger–Müller tube produces an electrical pulse for each ionising particle entering it; photographic film darkens (which is why film badges measure radiation dose); and a cloud chamber shows the tracks of the emissions.

Background radiation is present everywhere and must be subtracted from every measurement: it comes from natural sources (radon gas from rocks and soil, cosmic rays from space, radiation from food and building materials) and from human activity (medical X-rays, fallout from nuclear accidents and weapons tests). A count-rate measurement is corrected by taking the reading with no source present and subtracting it from the source reading (Supplement: count rates are quoted in counts per second or counts per minute, and repeated background readings are averaged before use).

The three types of nuclear emission

Emission from an unstable nucleus is spontaneous and random: nothing external causes a particular nucleus to decay at a particular moment, and no prediction is possible for any single nucleus.

PropertyAlpha (α)Beta (β)Gamma (γ)
NatureHelium nucleus: 2 protons + 2 neutronsFast electron from the nucleusElectromagnetic wave of high frequency
Charge+2−10
Relative mass41/1836 (negligible)0
Ionising powerVery strongModerateWeak
Penetrating powerStopped by paper or a few cm of airStopped by a few mm of aluminiumReduced only by thick lead or many metres of concrete
Effect of a magnetic fieldDeflected slightly (opposite way to beta)Deflected more (opposite way to alpha)Not deflected

Supplement deepens the ionisation ranking: alpha particles are large and doubly charged, so they tear electrons from atoms at every collision and stop quickly; beta particles are small and singly charged and ionise less; gamma rays carry no charge and ionise least, so they travel furthest. The same ranking explains the danger profiles: alpha sources are the least dangerous outside the body (stopped by skin) but the most dangerous if ingested, because their intense ionisation wrecks nearby cells.

Radioactive decay

Decay is the change of an unstable nucleus into a different, more stable nucleus, with the emission of radiation. The nucleus changes identity: emitting alpha reduces the nucleon number by 4 and the proton number by 2; emitting beta converts a neutron into a proton, so the proton number rises by 1 while the nucleon number is unchanged; gamma emission changes the energy of the nucleus but not its identity.

alpha decay:        (A over Z) X  ->  (A-4 over Z-2) Y  +  helium nucleus
beta decay:         (A over Z) X  ->  (A over Z+1) Y  +  electron

In every nuclear equation the total nucleon number and the total charge are the same on both sides — the standard balancing question on Paper 2 and Paper 4. Decay is unaffected by temperature, pressure or chemical state: the nucleus is shielded from ordinary conditions by its electrons.

Half-life

Half-life is the time taken for half the undecayed nuclei of a sample to decay — equivalently, for the count rate to fall to half its original value. It is a fixed property of each isotope, ranging from fractions of a second to billions of years.

after n half-lives:        count rate = starting count rate x (1/2)^(number of half-lives)

From a decay curve, read the time for the rate to halve from any starting point; the half-life is the same at every stage. Radioactive dating uses the ratio of a long-lived isotope to its decay product in rocks (uranium to lead) or in once-living things (carbon-14, half-life 5730 years, absorbed during life and decaying after death). Short-lived isotopes are used as medical tracers, since they deliver a dose that soon disappears.

Safety precautions

Radiation damages living tissue by ionising atoms in cells, which can kill cells or damage DNA and cause cancer. Three simple controls govern all handling:

  • Time: keep exposures short and work quickly with sources.
  • Distance: use tongs and remote handling; the intensity falls sharply with distance from the source.
  • Shielding: store sources in lead-lined boxes; use paper for alpha, aluminium for beta, lead or concrete for gamma.

Sealed sources are never touched or pointed at people; contamination (spreading open sources) is prevented with gloves, trays and careful disposal; workers wear film badges and dose records are kept. Doctors and patients accept a medical dose only when the benefit outweighs the risk — the principle of every risk–benefit question in the paper.

Worked example: half-life calculation

A source has a corrected count rate of 640 counts per minute and a half-life of 8.0 days. What is the rate after 24 days, and how long until it falls below 40 counts per minute?

24 days = 3 half-lives:        640 -> 320 -> 160 -> 80 counts per minute
80 -> 40 needs one more half-life, so 24 + 8 = 32 days total

The physical reasoning: half-living is exponential, never linear. After three half-lives an eighth of the original activity remains, not one third.

Common mistakes

  • Confusing the three emissions: alpha is a helium nucleus (2 protons, 2 neutrons), beta is an electron created in the nucleus, gamma is a wave.
  • Saying radiation becomes safe after a fixed number of days; only the activity falls with half-life, and each isotope has its own.
  • Halving the count rate every half-life from the original instead of from the current value (linear thinking): 100 goes 50, 25, 12.5, not 50, 0, 0.
  • Forgetting to subtract background radiation from raw counts before plotting a decay curve.
  • Balancing a nuclear equation without conserving both the nucleon number and the proton number.
  • Claiming alpha is the most dangerous radiation in every case: it is the most ionising, but the least penetrating — the hazard depends on whether the source is outside or inside the body.
  • Saying isotopes have different chemical properties; the electron arrangement is identical, so the chemistry is identical.
  • Linking decay to temperature or pressure; nuclear decay is unaffected by ordinary physical conditions.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 4, 3 marks). A nucleus of uranium-238 emits an alpha particle. Write the nuclear equation if the product is thorium-234.

Answer: uranium-238 (92 protons) becomes thorium-234 (90 protons) plus a helium nucleus: 238 = 234 + 4 and 92 = 90 + 2, so both totals balance.

Question 2 (Paper 4, 3 marks). A sample's count rate falls from 400 to 50 counts per second in 12 minutes. Calculate the half-life.

Answer: 400 → 200 → 100 → 50 is three half-lives in 12 minutes, so the half-life is 4.0 minutes.

Question 3 (Paper 2 style). Which emission is stopped by a sheet of paper? A alpha; B beta; C gamma; D X-rays. Answer: A. Alpha is stopped by paper, beta by a few millimetres of aluminium, gamma only by thick lead.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 6 marks). Explain why alpha emitters are safe outside the body but extremely dangerous if inhaled.

Answer: Alpha particles are large and doubly charged, so they ionise atoms strongly and are stopped by the dead outer layer of skin or by a sheet of paper, meaning they cannot reach living tissue from outside. If an alpha emitter is inhaled, it lodges in lung tissue and the particles then strike living cells at point-blank range. Their intense ionisation breaks chemical bonds and damages DNA in those cells, which can kill them or cause mutations and cancer. Distance and shielding matter: inside the body there is neither.

Question 5 (Paper 4, 3 marks). State the three standard precautions when handling a radioactive source.

Answer: Keep the time of exposure short; keep well away and handle with long tongs to reduce intensity; store in a lead-lined box with suitable shielding for the emission type (paper for alpha, aluminium for beta, lead for gamma).

Question 6 (Paper 6 style). Describe how you would measure the half-life of a short-lived isotope safely.

Answer: Place the source in a holder a fixed distance from a Geiger–Müller tube connected to a scaler or data logger. Measure the background count rate with no source present and average several readings. Record the source's count rate at regular time intervals until it approaches background, keeping geometry constant. Subtract the background from each reading, plot count rate against time, and read the time for the activity to halve between any two points on the curve. Keep exposure brief, handle the source with tongs, and store it in its shielded box.

The nucleus holds the energy of stars; the last topic of the IGCSE course is where those stars live — Earth and Space.

Equations and symbols

Nuclear decay is described by two bookkeeping rules — the nuclide notation and the conservation of nucleon number and charge — plus the exponential half-life relation. There is no equation for "why" a nucleus decays; the marks are in the accounting.

Nuclide notation

A = Z + N
Key: A = nucleon (mass) number, the total protons plus neutrons; Z = proton (atomic) number, which fixes the element; N = neutron number. Written as A over Z before the symbol, as in ²³⁵₉₂U.

proton number Z = number of protons = number of electrons in a neutral atom
Key: Z decides the element; changing Z changes the element, which is what transmutation means.

isotopes: same Z, different A
Key: isotopes of an element have the same number of protons and different numbers of neutrons, so they behave identically chemically and differently in nuclear decay.

Decay bookkeeping

alpha decay: A → A − 4 and Z → Z − 2
Key: an alpha particle is a helium nucleus, ⁴₂He, so the parent loses two protons and two neutrons. Example: ²³⁸₉₂U → ²³⁴₉₀Th + ⁴₂He.

beta-minus decay: A unchanged and Z → Z + 1
Key: a neutron turns into a proton and an electron, so the nucleon number is unchanged and the proton number rises by one. Example: ¹⁴₆C → ¹⁴₇N + ⁰₋₁e.

gamma emission: A and Z unchanged
Key: a gamma ray is electromagnetic energy released from an excited nucleus; the nucleus loses energy but not particles, so the nuclide stays the same element.

conservation in every decay: ΣA and ΣZ balance on both sides
Key: the totals of nucleon number and of charge must be equal before and after. This is the check that catches a wrong particle on the right-hand side.

Half-life

N = N₀ × (½)^(t / t½)
Key: N = number of nuclei (or count rate) remaining after time t; N₀ = the starting number or rate; t = elapsed time (s, or any unit); t½ = half-life in the same unit as t. After three half-lives, one eighth remains.

t½ = the time for half the nuclei in a sample to decay
Key: a fixed property of the isotope, unaffected by temperature, pressure or chemical state. It is measured from a decay curve as the time for the count rate to halve.

A = ΔN / Δt
Key: A = activity (Bq, decays per second); ΔN = number of decays recorded; Δt = time interval (s). The measured count rate is lower than the activity because the detector only intercepts a fraction of the radiation.

Penetration and ionisation

penetrating power: alpha < beta < gamma
Key: alpha is stopped by paper or a few centimetres of air; beta by a few millimetres of aluminium; gamma is reduced but not stopped by thick lead. Ionising power runs the other way: alpha ionises most strongly because it is the most charged and most massive.

E = mc² (extension, beyond the 0625 requirement)
Key: E = energy released (J); m = mass lost, the mass defect (kg); c = speed of light, 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s. It explains where the energy of a decay comes from, and why a small mass defect is a large energy release.

title: Motion in a Circle and Gravity — Study Notes
content:
Motion in a circle and gravity

Circular motion

  • A body moving in a circle at constant speed has a centripetal acceleration of v²/r, directed towards the centre.
  • The centripetal force is F = mv²/r = mω²r, and it is provided by a real force such as tension, friction or gravity. It does no work on the body, because it is always perpendicular to the velocity.

Gravitational field

The gravitational field strength at a point is the force per unit mass placed at that point: g = F/m. Unit: N kg⁻¹. Field lines point towards the mass that creates the field.

Newton's law of gravitation

F = GMm/r², where r is measured from the centre of each point mass. Doubling the separation reduces the force to one quarter.

Gravitational field of a point mass

g = GM/r². Outside a uniform sphere, its field is the same as that of a point mass at its centre.

Gravitational potential

Gravitational potential at a point is the work done per unit mass in bringing a small mass from infinity to that point. It is always negative, is zero at infinity, and becomes more negative closer to the mass: V = −GM/r. Gravitational potential energy of a mass m is Ep = mV.

Worked example: a 2.0 kg object moves in a circle of radius 0.50 m at 3.0 m s⁻¹. The centripetal force is F = mv²/r = (2.0 × 3.0²) ÷ 0.50 = 36 N.

Exam tips: use r as the distance from the centre, not the surface. State that gravitational potential is negative and rises to zero at infinity. Field strength and potential are different quantities: do not mix their units.

Gravitational potential and escape velocity

Gravitational potential at a point is the work done per unit mass in moving a small mass from infinity to that point, so φ = -GM/r. Potential is negative because work must be done against gravity to remove a mass to infinity. The change in gravitational potential energy between two radii is GMm(1/r1 - 1/r2). A body escapes a planet when its kinetic energy equals the potential energy needed to reach infinity, which gives the escape speed v = √(2GM/r).

Exam tip: use the zero of potential at infinity, and keep the sign of the potential negative in every calculation.

Worked example: orbital speed and period

A satellite of mass m orbits a planet of mass M at radius r. Gravity provides the centripetal force: GMm/r² = mv²/r, so v = √(GM/r). The orbital period follows from T = 2πr/v, which gives T² = (4π²/GM) r³. This is Kepler's third law in the form used at AS level.

Example: a satellite at radius 7.0 × 10⁶ m around a planet of mass 6.0 × 10²⁴ kg. The speed is v = √((6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 6.0 × 10²⁴)/(7.0 × 10⁶)) = √(5.7 × 10⁷) ≈ 7.6 × 10³ m s⁻¹. The period is T = 2π × 7.0 × 10⁶ / 7.6 × 10³ ≈ 5.8 × 10³ s, about 97 minutes.

Geostationary orbit

A geostationary satellite has a period of exactly 24 hours and orbits in the equatorial plane. Its radius is fixed by the period, so every geostationary satellite has the same radius and speed, regardless of its mass. Its orbit must lie above the equator, which is why communication satellites sit over one point on the ground.

Why orbiting bodies are weightless

Astronauts in orbit are not outside the pull of gravity; gravity supplies their centripetal acceleration. The spacecraft and its occupants fall freely together, so there is no contact force, and the apparent weightlessness follows from that free fall.

Circular motion: banked roads and conical pendulums

On a banked road with no friction, the horizontal component of the normal reaction supplies the centripetal force: N sin θ = mv²/r, while the vertical component balances weight: N cos θ = mg. Dividing gives tan θ = v²/(rg). The design speed depends only on the angle, the radius and g, not on the mass of the vehicle.

  • For a conical pendulum, tension has a vertical component that balances weight and a horizontal component that supplies the centripetal force.
  • Always draw a free-body diagram and resolve forces into components along the radius and the vertical before writing equations.
  • The centripetal force is not an extra force on the diagram; name the real forces that supply it.

Common errors that lose marks

  • Including centripetal force as a separate force in the free-body diagram, which double-counts the force.
  • Using the planet's surface radius where the question gives the distance from the centre, or the reverse.
  • Stating that the satellite is stationary in orbit. It is moving at constant speed, so its velocity changes direction continuously and it is accelerating.

title: IGCSE Biology: Reproduction
content:
IGCSE Biology: Reproduction

Reproduction is how species persist — and the two strategies, asexual and sexual, trade reliability against variation. This note compares both, then follows plant reproduction from flower structure to pollination, fertilisation and germination, before tracing the human system from gamete production through the menstrual cycle to pregnancy, birth and contraception, and closing with sexually transmitted infections including HIV/AIDS. Every structure is tied to its function and every sequence (pollination → fertilisation → germination; intercourse → fertilisation → implantation) is written in order, because the marks live in the sequence.

The four reproductive hormones

HormoneMade byTargetEffect
FSHPituitary glandOvaryMaturation of a follicle and its egg
OestrogenOvary (follicle)Uterus, pituitaryRebuilds endometrium; triggers the LH surge
LHPituitary glandOvaryCauses ovulation around day 14
ProgesteroneCorpus luteumUterus, pituitaryMaintains the endometrium; inhibits FSH

Asexual and sexual reproduction compared

Asexual reproduction involves one parent and no fusion of gametes: mitosis produces offspring genetically identical to the parent (clones) — binary fission in bacteria, budding in yeast, runners in strawberries, tissue culture for plants. Advantages: rapid, no mate needed, good genes preserved in a stable environment. Disadvantages: no genetic variation, so a disease or environmental change can wipe out the entire clone. Sexual reproduction involves two parents, gametes (sperm and egg) produced by meiosis and fused at fertilisation: offspring are genetically varied (unique combinations of alleles), giving variation on which natural selection acts. Advantage: variation allows adaptation to changing environments; disadvantage: slower, needs a mate and more energy.

Flower structure and function

The flower is the reproductive organ of a plant. Sepals (green, protective bud), petals (often coloured and scented to attract pollinators), stamens (male): anther produces pollen grains (containing male gametes) on a filament, and carpels (female): stigma (sticky, receives pollen), style (tube down which the pollen tube grows), ovary (contains ovules, each with a female gamete), and the ovule becomes the seed after fertilisation. Nectaries at the base of the petals produce sugary nectar to reward pollinators. The structural adaptations for insect pollination: brightly coloured petals, scent, nectar, sticky large pollen grains, and a compact landing platform; for wind pollination: small dull petals (or none), long dangling anthers releasing clouds of light smooth pollen, feathery stigmas to catch pollen, and large amounts of pollen produced.

Pollination, fertilisation and seed formation

Pollination is the transfer of pollen from the anther to the stigma — self-pollination (same flower or plant) gives less variation; cross-pollination (different plant of the same species) increases variation. Agents: insects, wind, water, birds, bats. Fertilisation is the fusion of the male gamete (from the pollen grain) with the female gamete (in the ovule): the pollen grain lands on a compatible stigma, germinates and grows a pollen tube down the style, guided by chemicals from the ovule; the male gamete nucleus travels down the tube and fuses with the egg cell; the zygote divides by mitosis to become the embryo plant; the ovule becomes the seed (with a food store and protective seed coat) and the ovary wall becomes the fruit. Germination requires water (enzyme activation and transport), oxygen (respiration for energy) and a suitable temperature; light is required by some species. Stored starch in the seed is hydrolysed by amylase to glucose for the growing embryo.

The human reproductive system

Male: testes (produce sperm by meiosis and testosterone), scrotum (keeps testes below body temperature for spermatogenesis), sperm duct (vas deferens), prostate gland (secretes seminal fluid feeding sperm), urethra (shared passage), penis. Female: ovaries (produce eggs by meiosis and oestrogen/progesterone), oviducts (fallopian tubes — site of fertilisation, lined with cilia that waft the egg along), uterus (womb — where the embryo implants and develops), endometrium (uterine lining that thickens each cycle), cervix (neck of the uterus), vagina (birth canal). Gametes are haploid (half the chromosome number — 23 in humans) so that at fertilisation the diploid number (46) is restored; the fusion of gametes combines genes from two parents, producing variation.

Menstrual cycle, fertilisation and pregnancy

The cycle takes about 28 days and is controlled by four hormones (FSH, oestrogen, LH, progesterone) as detailed in the coordination note: FSH matures a follicle → oestrogen rebuilds the endometrium and triggers an LH surge → ovulation (day 14) → corpus luteum secretes progesterone maintaining the lining → no fertilisation → hormone levels fall → menstruation. If a sperm fertilises the egg (usually in the oviduct), the zygote divides into a ball of cells (blastocyst) that implants in the endometrium about a week later; the placenta develops, connected to the embryo by the umbilical cord. The placenta allows diffusion of oxygen, glucose, amino acids, water and antibodies (maternal IgG) from mother to fetus, and carbon dioxide, urea and wastes from fetus to mother; it also acts as a barrier to many pathogens and drugs (though not all — alcohol, HIV and some drugs cross). Pregnancy lasts about 40 weeks, ending with birth (parturition): the hormone oxytocin stimulates uterine contractions, and positive feedback (contractions push the baby onto the cervix, causing more oxytocin release) intensifies labour until delivery, followed by the afterbirth (placenta and membranes).

Contraception and fertility

Natural methods: abstinence, rhythm/calendar method (avoiding ovulation days — unreliable due to cycle variation), withdrawal. Hormonal: the combined pill (oestrogen and progesterone inhibit FSH, so no egg matures or ovulates), progesterone-only pill, implants, injections and patches — highly effective but requiring medical oversight. Barrier: condoms (male and female) — block sperm physically AND protect against STIs (the only method that does both), diaphragms with spermicide. Intrauterine devices (IUDs) prevent implantation. Spermicide kills sperm. Surgical: vasectomy (cutting the sperm ducts) and tubal ligation (cutting the oviducts) — permanent. Infertility treatments: hormone therapy to stimulate ovulation, in vitro fertilisation (IVF — eggs fertilised in the lab then implanted), donor gametes, sperm banks; IVF raises ethical questions (multiple embryos, selective reduction, cost, access).

Sexually transmitted infections

STIs spread through sexual contact (body fluids): Chlamydia (bacterial; often symptomless; treated with antibiotics; can cause infertility), Gonorrhoea (bacterial; discharges; antibiotics, but resistant strains emerging), Syphilis (bacterial; sores then organ damage; antibiotics), Genital herpes (viral; recurring sores; no cure, antivirals manage it), HIV (viral; attacks helper T-lymphocytes, destroying the immune system; no cure, but antiretroviral drugs control it), Hepatitis B (viral; liver damage; vaccine available), and HPV (viral; can cause genital warts and cervical cancer; vaccine now given to adolescents). Prevention: condoms reduce transmission, fewer partners, screening, vaccination (hepatitis B, HPV), and education. HIV/AIDS: the virus binds CD4 receptors on helper T-cells, inserts its RNA (reverse transcriptase makes DNA), integrates into the host genome, replicates and destroys the cell; progressive loss of helper T-cells cripples the immune response; the person develops AIDS (acquired immune deficiency syndrome) when opportunistic infections (TB, pneumonia, Kaposi's sarcoma) take hold; transmission: unprotected sex, shared needles, mother to child (during birth or breastfeeding); the epidemic is worst in sub-Saharan Africa; education, condoms, needle exchange, screening of blood supplies and antiretrovirals reduce spread.

Worked example: tracing a cycle and building a contraception comparison

Trace one cycle with a diagram in words: days 1–5 menstruation (low oestrogen and progesterone, endometrium sheds); days 6–13 FSH matures a follicle, rising oestrogen rebuilds the lining; day 14 LH surge causes ovulation; days 15–28 the corpus luteum secretes progesterone maintaining the endometrium; if no fertilisation, corpus luteum degenerates, hormones fall and the cycle restarts. Add fertilisation: sperm meets egg in the oviduct on day 14–15, blastocyst implants around day 21, and the corpus luteum (then placenta) maintains progesterone so no menstruation occurs. Now a comparison question: "compare hormonal and barrier contraception" — hormonal methods do not protect against STIs, do not require action at the time of intercourse, and act by inhibiting ovulation; barrier methods protect against STIs, are used at intercourse, and act by blocking sperm. Comparing two methods on both effectiveness and STI protection is the classic 4-mark structure.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Confusing pollination with fertilisation: pollination is pollen transfer; fertilisation is gamete fusion. They are separate events days apart in plants.
  • Writing that the ovary "contains eggs" loosely: ovaries produce egg cells by meiosis and secrete hormones; ovules (in plants) contain the female gamete.
  • Saying sperm and eggs are diploid: gametes are haploid (n = 23); fertilisation restores 46.
  • Reversing the hormone chain in the menstrual cycle: FSH → follicle/oestrogen → LH surge → ovulation → progesterone → lining maintained.
  • Claiming the placenta "prevents all harmful substances": some drugs, alcohol, HIV and certain pathogens cross it.
  • Writing that condoms "prevent pregnancy and all disease": they greatly reduce STI risk but do not eliminate it.
  • Confusing the site of fertilisation (oviduct) with the site of implantation (uterus/endometrium).
  • Describing birth as purely hormonal: oxytocin causes contractions and positive feedback amplifies labour until delivery.
  • Saying asexual reproduction "produces variation": it produces clones — identical offspring.

Exam-style questions and answers

Q1. Compare asexual and sexual reproduction. (4 marks) Answer: asexual has one parent, sexual two (1); asexual produces genetically identical clones, sexual produces variation (1); asexual is rapid and needs no mate, sexual is slower and needs gamete fusion (1); variation in sexual reproduction aids survival in changing environments (1).

Q2. Describe how a seed is formed after pollination. (4 marks) Answer: pollen grain lands on stigma and germinates (1); pollen tube grows down the style to the ovule (1); male gamete fuses with the egg cell (1); ovule becomes the seed and the ovary becomes the fruit (1).

Q3. Explain the functions of the placenta. (3 marks) Answer: allows oxygen, glucose, amino acids and antibodies to pass from mother to fetus (1); removes carbon dioxide and urea from fetus to mother (1); acts as a barrier to some pathogens and drugs (1).

Q4. Explain how the combined pill prevents pregnancy. (3 marks) Answer: contains oestrogen and progesterone (1); inhibit FSH secretion so follicles do not mature (1); no egg is released so fertilisation cannot occur (1).

Q5. Describe how HIV reduces the body's ability to defend itself against disease. (4 marks) Answer: HIV binds to and enters helper T-lymphocytes (1); uses reverse transcriptase to insert its DNA into the host genome (1); virus replicates and the cell bursts releasing virions (1); loss of helper T-cells means antibody production and phagocyte activation fall, allowing opportunistic infections (1).

title: Measures of Variation and Standard Deviation — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Measures of Variation and Standard Deviation

Mathematics — A2. The range is max − min — quick but destroyed by a single outlier. Quartiles split ordered data into quarters: Q₁ at position (n + 1)/4, Q₃ at 3(n + 1)/4 (raw data). The interquartile range, IQR = Q₃ − Q₁, is the spread of the middle 50% and resists outliers. Outliers are commonly flagged as values beyond Q₁ − 1.5·IQR or Q₃ + 1.5·IQR.

Key areas to revise

  • Range and Quartiles
  • Variance and Standard Deviation
  • Grouped Data
  • Combining and Scaling Datasets

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

### Worked example Data are 2, 4 and 6. The mean is 4 and the deviations are −2, 0 and 2. The squared deviations sum to 8, so the population variance is 8/3 ≈ 2.67 and the standard deviation is √(8/3) ≈ 1.63. The range is 6 − 2 = 4.

title: IGCSE Physics: Measurement and Units
content:
IGCSE Physics: Measurement and Units

Cambridge IGCSE Physics 0625 (2026–2028), Topic 1 Motion, forces and energy, statement 1.1 Physical quantities and measurement techniques — plus the experimental skills that Paper 6, Alternative to Practical, examines directly. Every physics result rests on a measurement, and every measurement is uncertain. This note builds the vocabulary of quantities and units, the practical techniques for length, volume and time, and then the full Paper 6 method: variables, safety, tables, graph plotting, gradients and intercepts, conclusions and error analysis. Paper 2 and Paper 4 carry the theory marks; Paper 6 carries these skills as a written exam of their own.

Physical quantities and SI units

A physical quantity is a property that can be measured, and every measurement needs a number and a unit. Physics uses the SI system, whose base units include the metre (m) for length, the kilogram (kg) for mass, the second (s) for time, the ampere (A) for electric current, the kelvin (K) for temperature and the mole (mol) for amount of substance. All other units are derived from these: speed in metres per second (m s⁻¹) is a base unit divided by a base unit, and force in newtons is defined so that 1 N = 1 kg m s⁻².

QuantitySymbolSI unitHow the unit is built
Lengths or lmetre (m)base unit
Massmkilogram (kg)base unit
Timetsecond (s)base unit
VolumeVcubic metre (m³)m³; litres and cm³ are everyday alternatives (1 litre = 0.001 m³)
Speedvmetre per second (m s⁻¹)m ÷ s
Frequencyfhertz (Hz)1 Hz = 1 cycle per second (s⁻¹)
ForceFnewton (N)kg m s⁻²
EnergyEjoule (J)N m = kg m² s⁻²
Pressureppascal (Pa)N m⁻²

Large and small quantities use standard prefixes or standard form: kilo (×1000), centi (÷100), milli (÷1000), micro (÷10⁶). Standard form writes a quantity as a number between 1 and 10 multiplied by a power of ten, so the speed of light is 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. Units obey ordinary algebra: dividing metres by seconds gives m s⁻¹, and a unit written as m/s and one written as m s⁻¹ are the same thing.

Measuring length, area and volume

Length is measured with a ruler or a tape. The three rules of good practice are fixed: place the scale edge along the line being measured, start from the zero mark rather than the worn end of the ruler, and take the reading at eye level directly above the point to avoid parallax error. A ruler reading should be quoted to the nearest half millimetre with an uncertainty of about ±0.5 mm; a vernier caliper or a micrometer screw gauge reads to 0.01 mm and is used when the length is small.

Areas and volumes are calculated from measured lengths. The area of a rectangle is length × width; the volume of a rectangular block is length × width × height; the volume of a cylinder is π r² l. For an irregular solid, the volume is found by displacement: water is poured into a measuring cylinder, the starting volume is read, the object is lowered in, and the rise in level is the object's volume. Read the bottom of the curved meniscus at eye level. The technique fails for objects that float (use a sinker), objects that absorb water or dissolve (use sand or oil), and objects that splash water out on entry (lower them gently on a thread).

Area scales with the square of a length and volume with the cube, so a small length error is amplified: a 2 per cent error in each of the three dimensions of a cube gives about a 6 per cent error in its volume. This is exactly the kind of reasoning Paper 6 rewards in its evaluation questions.

Measuring time intervals

Short times are measured with a stopwatch, and human reaction time of about 0.2 s dominates a single reading. Two standard techniques control it. First, repeat and average: time several oscillations of a pendulum and divide by the number of swings, because the reaction error is then spread over many periods. Second, use a larger quantity: time 20 trolley passes rather than one, or measure the time for 50 dots from a 50 Hz ticker timer, where consecutive dots are 0.02 s apart. Timing devices built into the apparatus — light gates, data loggers and ticker timers — remove reaction time entirely and are the expected answer when a question asks how to improve a timing measurement.

Errors, precision and percentage uncertainty

Every measurement carries an uncertainty, usually taken as the range of the scale: ±0.5 mm on a ruler, ±0.5 s on a stopwatch read to seconds, ±0.5 of the smallest scale division on a measuring cylinder. Two kinds of error behave differently. A random error scatters readings in both directions and is reduced by repeating and averaging; a systematic error shifts every reading the same way — a zero error on a balance, a bent ruler, parallax — and is removed by correcting the instrument, never by averaging. An anomaly is a result that does not fit the pattern; it is discarded only with a stated reason, never because it is inconvenient.

The size of an uncertainty is compared using percentage uncertainty, a technique Paper 6 tests whenever results are combined:

percentage uncertainty in one reading = (uncertainty / reading) x 100
percentage uncertainty in a sum or difference = (largest absolute uncertainty / answer) x 100
percentage uncertainty in a product or quotient = sum of the individual percentage uncertainties

Worked example: a cube of side 2.0 ± 0.05 cm has a mass of 24.0 ± 0.1 g. The side's percentage uncertainty is 0.05/2.0 × 100 = 2.5 per cent, so the volume (a product of three lengths) carries 3 × 2.5 = 7.5 per cent. The mass carries 0.1/24.0 × 100 = 0.4 per cent. The density = mass/volume carries 7.5 + 0.4 = 7.9 per cent, so ρ = 24.0/8.0 = 3.0 g cm⁻³ ± 0.2 g cm⁻³. The volume term dominates: improving the ruler improves the result far more than improving the balance.

Scalars and vectors (Supplement)

A scalar has size only: distance, speed, mass, energy, temperature, pressure. A vector has size and direction: displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, momentum, weight. Vectors are added by direction: two forces in a line add or subtract; two forces at right angles combine by Pythagoras, with the direction found from an angle. If a boat is pushed 3.0 m north and 4.0 m east, its resultant displacement is 5.0 m on a bearing of about 53° from north. Drawing the vector triangle to scale is a complete method on Paper 4 whenever the angle is not 90°.

Paper 6: how the practical exam is written

Paper 6 is a written exam about practical physics; you handle no apparatus but you must think like an experimenter. The question types repeat, and each has a method.

  • Choosing apparatus. Match the instrument to the quantity and its size: a ruler for lengths of centimetres, a micrometer for wires, a measuring cylinder for volumes, a balance for masses. State the range and the precision you expect.
  • Variables. Name the independent variable (what you change), the dependent variable (what you measure) and the control variables (what you keep fixed). A fair test changes one thing only, and every control earns a mark: same material, same temperature, same apparatus, same operator.
  • Safety. Link each hazard to a control: hot water and burners — use tongs and keep hands clear; masses and clamps — secure the clamp to the bench and stand clear of falling masses; lasers and ultrasound — never look into the beam; electricity — low voltages only, and switch off between readings.
  • Tables. Draw a box with a column per quantity and a heading of quantity divided by unit, e.g. length / cm. Numbers sit in the cells without units. Give each column enough rows for repeats, quote consistent significant figures, and record raw readings before any calculated column.
  • Graphs. The independent variable goes on the horizontal axis. Choose a scale that fills at least half the sheet, label both axes with quantity and unit, plot points with a fine cross, and draw a single smooth line of best fit — a thin ruled line for a linear relationship, a smooth curve otherwise. Never join dots dot to dot.
  • Gradient and intercept. The gradient = (change in vertical quantity) / (change in horizontal quantity), taken between two distant points on the line, not between plotted points. For a straight line through the origin the two variables are directly proportional; a non-zero intercept has physical meaning — on a speed–time graph it is the initial speed, on a cooling curve the ambient temperature — and the equation of the line is written as vertical quantity = gradient × horizontal quantity + intercept.
  • Conclusions. State the relationship the graph shows in words and symbols, quote the gradient with its unit, and relate the result to the physics (for example, a load–extension graph through the origin shows extension proportional to load, and its gradient is the spring constant).
  • Evaluation. Name the largest source of uncertainty with a reason, say which way it pushes the answer, and propose a specific improvement — more repeats, a longer measurement interval, a sensor or data logger, a wider range of values — not a vague plea for more care.

Worked example: reading a graph and its gradient

A student measures the speed of a trolley pulled down a runway, plotting speed on the vertical axis against time on the horizontal axis. The plotted points lie close to a straight line crossing the vertical axis at 0.10 m s⁻¹ and passing through (2.0 s, 1.30 m s⁻¹) and (6.0 s, 3.30 m s⁻¹).

gradient = (3.30 - 1.30) / (6.0 - 2.0) = 2.00 / 4.0 = 0.50 m s-2
intercept = 0.10 m s-1
equation: speed = 0.50 x time + 0.10

The gradient is the trolley's acceleration, 0.50 m s⁻², and the intercept is its initial speed, 0.10 m s⁻¹. A conclusion that says only speed increases with time earns no mark; the mark is for the number, its unit and its physical meaning.

Common mistakes

  • Writing a number without its unit, or putting units into the cells of a results table whose heading already carries the unit.
  • Starting a ruler scale from the broken zero end, or reading at an angle and introducing parallax error.
  • Joining plotted points with a zig-zag line instead of drawing one smooth line of best fit, which hides anomalies rather than revealing them.
  • Calculating a gradient between two neighbouring plotted points; use two distant points on the line to shrink the reading error.
  • Reducing a systematic error by repeating readings; averaging shrinks random error only, and a zero error must be corrected at the instrument.
  • Keeping an anomaly with no comment, or discarding one without a stated physical reason.
  • Confusing scalar and vector: adding a speed to a velocity, or giving a direction for energy.
  • Reporting a percentage uncertainty but never saying which measurement dominates the final result.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 6, 3 marks). Describe how you would measure the average speed of a trolley on a runway.

Answer: Mark a fixed distance along the runway and measure it with a metre ruler. Release the trolley from the same point each time and time its passage over the marked distance with light gates and a data logger (or a stopwatch, repeated and averaged to reduce reaction error). Average speed is the distance divided by the time. Repeat for several distances or heights and record results in a table.

Question 2 (Paper 6, 3 marks). A student measures the period of a pendulum once and gets 1.3 s. Suggest two improvements to the method.

Answer: Time 20 complete oscillations and divide by 20, so reaction time error becomes a small fraction of the total; repeat the whole measurement several times and take a mean. Keep the pendulum length fixed and time from the release point to avoid a variable starting condition.

Question 3 (Paper 4, 2 marks). A length is recorded as 2.50 cm. State the instrument used and its uncertainty.

Answer: A ruler reading to 0.1 cm (or a vernier caliper if the precision demands it), with an uncertainty of ±0.05 cm, half the smallest scale division.

Question 4 (Paper 6, 4 marks). The volume of a small stone is found from 30 cm³ to 45 cm³ in a measuring cylinder and its mass is 36 g. Calculate the density and its percentage uncertainty if each volume reading is uncertain by ±0.5 cm³.

Answer: Volume = 15 cm³. The uncertainty in the difference is 0.5 + 0.5 = 1.0 cm³ (worst case for a difference), so the percentage uncertainty is 1.0/15 × 100 = 6.7 per cent. Density = 36/15 = 2.4 g cm⁻³, so the answer is 2.4 g cm⁻³ ± 0.2 g cm³ (about ±7 per cent). Using a larger volume difference would shrink the percentage uncertainty.

Question 5 (Paper 2 style). Which quantity is a vector? A energy; B temperature; C momentum; D pressure. Answer: C. Momentum has size and direction; the rest are scalars.

With measurements trustworthy, the next topic is what heat does to matter: thermal physics.

title: Thermal Physics — Study Notes
content:
Thermal Physics

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): kinetic particle model; thermal expansion; specific heat capacity; melting/boiling; conduction, convection, radiation.

1. Kinetic model

Solid: fixed positions, vibrate — fixed shape/volume. Liquid: move around, touching — fixed volume, flows. Gas: far apart, fast random motion — fills container. Brownian motion evidences random molecular motion.

2. Gas pressure and temperature

Pressure from wall collisions. Heating at fixed volume → faster particles → more frequent, harder collisions → higher pressure.

3. Thermal expansion

Heating → particles vibrate more → solids expand slightly (gases expand most). Applications: bimetallic strip (fire alarm/thermostat), gaps in bridges/rails; the liquid-in-glass thermometer.

4. Specific heat capacity

c = ΔE/(mΔθ). Heating: ΔE = mcΔθ.

Example: 2 kg water (c = 4200), 20→80 °C: ΔE = 2×4200×60 = 504 kJ.

High c of water → coolant; temperature rise measured with known heater power P in time t: c = Pt/(mΔθ).

5. State changes

Melting/boiling at fixed temperature despite heating (energy breaks bonds, not temperature). Condensation/ freezing release energy. Impurities raise melting point of mixtures/lower freezing; boiling needs nucleation.

6. Transfer: conduction, convection, radiation

  • Conduction: mainly metals (delocalised electrons + lattice vibration); non-metals poor; insulators trap air.
  • Convection: hot fluid expands, density falls, rises; denser cool fluid sinks — currents.
  • Radiation: infrared EM waves; no medium; matte black best absorber/emitter, shiny silver worst.

Applications: vacuum flask, house insulation, car radiators, solar heating panels.

title: Probability — Study Notes
content:
Probability

Edexcel International A Level Mathematics — Statistics 1 (WST01), sat at AS.

Basic Rules

For an event A with P(A) = p: 0 ≤ p ≤ 1, and P(A′) = 1 − P(A). For mutually exclusive events, probabilities add: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B). For events that can occur together, subtract the overlap:

  • P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B)

Venn Diagrams

Draw the universe first, then the events. Fill from the intersection outwards: if P(A) = 0.6, P(B) = 0.5 and P(A ∩ B) = 0.25, then only-A = 0.35, only-B = 0.25, neither = 0.15. Every region must sum to 1.

Tree Diagrams

Branch probabilities multiply along a path; outcomes at the end of complete paths add. Draw one branch set per stage of the experiment. For two draws without replacement from a bag of 5 red and 3 blue: P(RR) = (5/8)(4/7) = 20/56.

Conditional Probability

P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B) — the probability of A given that B has occurred. The condition shrinks the sample space.

Example: P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.4, P(A ∩ B) = 0.2. Then P(A | B) = 0.2/0.4 = 0.5, so A and B are independent since P(A | B) = P(A).

Independence

A and B are independent exactly when P(A ∩ B) = P(A)·P(B). Do not confuse independent (no influence on probabilities) with mutually exclusive (cannot co-occur). Mutually exclusive events with non-zero probabilities are never independent.

Exam tips: convert every "given that" into a conditional. With trees, label the second-stage branches with conditional probabilities; they are usually different from the first stage when drawing without replacement.

Exam method: combined events

The addition rule gives P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B). For mutually exclusive events the intersection is empty, so P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B). Draw a Venn diagram to place each probability in its region before calculating.

Independent events satisfy P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B). Test independence by checking this equation rather than assuming it, because the question may give the joint probability and ask you to decide.

The conditional probability P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B). Events are independent exactly when P(A | B) = P(A).

Tree diagrams suit sequential events without replacement. Multiply along each branch and add the branches that give the outcome required.

Exam cue: State whether events are independent or mutually exclusive, because the two are different and the formula depends on it.

Worked example: two aces without replacement

Two cards are taken from a standard pack of 52 without replacement. The probability that both are aces is (4/52) × (3/51) = 12/2652 = 1/221. Because the second draw depends on the first, multiply along the branches of the tree diagram and use the reduced totals (51 cards, 3 aces) on the second branch. If the first card were replaced, the answer would be (4/52)² = 1/169 instead.

Exam method: checking a tree diagram

The probabilities on the branches leaving any node must add to 1, so check each node before you multiply. The final probabilities at the ends of the branches must also sum to 1. For a question asking for "at least one", it is usually quicker to find the probability of none and subtract it from 1.

title: IGCSE Computer Science: Data Representation
content:
IGCSE Computer Science: Data Representation

Cambridge IGCSE Computer Science 0478 (2026–2028), Paper 1 Computer Systems, Topic 1 Data representation: statement 1.1 Number systems, 1.2 Text, sound and images, and 1.3 Data storage and compression. Everything inside a computer — numbers, letters, photographs, music — is stored as patterns of bits, and this note explains exactly how each kind of value becomes binary and how much space it takes. Every conversion and calculation is shown step by step, because in the exam the working carries most of the marks.

Why binary, and how place value works

Computers are built from billions of tiny switches. A switch is either off or on, and those two states are the only thing hardware can reliably store and detect — so all information is encoded with two symbols, 0 and 1. Denary (base 10) has ten digits because we have ten fingers; binary (base 2) has two digits because a switch has two states. The rules of arithmetic are identical — only the number of digits differs.

Place values in binary:   128  64  32  16  8  4  2  1
Example: 1 0 1 1 0 1 1 0
= 128 + 32 + 16 + 4 + 2 = 182 in denary        [add the values of the 1-bits]

Denary to binary, step by step (the subtract-powers method, ideal without a calculator):

Convert 149 to binary:

149 is bigger than 128 -> put a 1 in the 128 column, remainder 149 - 128 = 21
21 is smaller than 64  -> 0
21 is smaller than 32  -> 0
21 is bigger than 16   -> 1, remainder 21 - 16 = 5
5 is smaller than 8    -> 0
5 is bigger than 4     -> 1, remainder 5 - 4 = 1
1 is smaller than 2    -> 0
1 is bigger than 1     -> 1, remainder 0

Reading the columns: 149 = 1001 0101

The reverse direction simply adds the column values, as above. A quick check always exists: convert back.

Hexadecimal

Hexadecimal (base 16) uses sixteen digits: 0–9 then A–F (A = 10 … F = 15). It exists for a practical reason: one hex digit represents exactly four bits (a nibble), so long binary strings become short and readable — memory dumps, error codes, web colours (#FF8800) and MAC addresses are all written in hex because humans can transcribe them without bit-counting errors.

Binary to hex: 1011 0110
Split into nibbles:   1011 = 11 = B    and    0110 = 6
So 1011 0110 = B6 in hex.

Hex to denary: B6
= 11 x 16 + 6 x 1 = 176 + 6 = 182        [16s column and 1s column]

Denary to hex (via binary): 182 = 1011 0110 = B6.
Or directly by division: 182 ÷ 16 = 11 remainder 6 -> digits 11, 6 -> B6.

Binary addition and overflow

Binary addition follows the denary carry rule with one extra fact: 1 + 1 = 10 (write 0, carry 1).

Add 0110 0111 (= 103) and 0011 1010 (= 58), 8-bit, column by column:

bit 0:  1 + 0        = 1                 (write 1, carry 0)
bit 1:  1 + 1        = 0, carry 1        (1 + 1 = 10 in binary)
bit 2:  1 + 0 + 1(c) = 0, carry 1
bit 3:  0 + 1 + 1(c) = 0, carry 1
bit 4:  0 + 1 + 1(c) = 0, carry 1
bit 5:  1 + 1 + 1(c) = 1, carry 1        (three 1s sum to 11: write 1, carry 1)
bit 6:  1 + 0 + 1(c) = 0, carry 1
bit 7:  0 + 0 + 1(c) = 1, carry 0

Result: 1 0 1 0 0 0 0 1 = 1010 0001 = 161. Check: 103 + 58 = 161 ✓
No carry escapes bit 7, so the 8-bit answer is exact and there is no overflow.

Overflow happens when the result needs more bits than the register holds. If the two numbers are added in 8 bits and a carry comes out of the leftmost column, the answer is wrong for that word length:

Unsigned example: 200 + 100 = 300, which is beyond the 8-bit maximum of 255.

  1100 1000 (= 200) + 0110 0100 (= 100) = 1 0010 1100
  The 9th bit is lost, so the 8-bit answer reads 0010 1100 = 44 - wrong.
  A carry out of the most significant bit reveals the overflow.

Signed example (different rule): 127 + 1 = 128, which is outside the signed
range -128 to +127, so even though no carry leaves bit 7 the result overflows:

  0111 1111 (= 127) + 0000 0001 (= 1) = 1000 0000, which reads as -128.
  Two positives summed to a negative: the sign bits reveal the overflow.

Overflow rules differ for signed (two's complement) numbers: there the sign bit is the tell-tale, and adding two negatives that gives a positive (or vice versa) is overflow.

Logical binary shifts

Shifting moves every bit left or right, filling with zeros. Left shift by one multiplies by 2; right shift by one divides by 2 (integer division, discarding the remainder).

0010 1101 (= 45) shifted left one place:  0101 1010 (= 90)      45 x 2 = 90
0010 1101 (= 45) shifted right one place: 0001 0110 (= 22)      45 / 2 = 22 (remainder 1 lost)

Each place shifted doubles or halves the value, so shifting left by n multiplies by 2ⁿ. Bits shifted off the end are lost — which is how quick multiplication can silently overflow.

Two's complement: negative numbers

Hardware needs to store negative integers too. In two's complement the most significant (leftmost) bit is a sign bit and has a negative place value: for 8 bits the columns are −128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1. Think of it as odometer arithmetic: a clock with 8 wheels that wraps around, where the top half of the wheel positions are read as negatives.

Write -5 as an 8-bit two's complement number:

Method: write +5, invert every bit, add 1.

+5      = 0000 0101
invert  = 1111 1010        (each 0 becomes 1 and each 1 becomes 0)
add 1   = 1111 1011        = -5

Check with the column values: -128 + 64 + 32 + 16 + 8 + 2 + 1 = -5 ✓
  • Range of 8-bit two's complement: −128 to +127. (One pattern, 1000 0000, is −128 and there is no positive counterpart — the asymmetry examiners like to test.)
  • Negating (turning x into −x): invert all the bits, then add 1. Negating twice returns the original.
  • Reading a negative directly: 1111 1011 has sign bit 1, so it is negative; the remaining columns sum to 123; the value is −(128 − 123) = −5.

Subtraction becomes addition. Computers do not subtract; they add the negative, which lets one circuit (the adder) do both jobs:

Calculate 7 - 5 in 8-bit two's complement:

7 = 0000 0111
-5 = 1111 1011        (as above)
Add:  0000 0111 + 1111 1011 = (1) 0000 0010
The carry beyond bit 7 is discarded in two's complement addition.
0000 0010 = 2, and 7 - 5 = 2 ✓

Overflow in signed arithmetic: the sign bit is the guide. Adding two positives must not give a negative: 0111 1111 (127) + 0000 0001 = 1000 0000, which reads as −128 — overflow, even though no carry escapes the byte. Two negatives giving a positive is overflow the same way.

Text: character sets

Text is stored as numbers, and a character set is the agreed table mapping numbers to printed symbols. ASCII uses 7 bits per character — 128 codes — covering upper- and lower-case Latin letters, digits, punctuation and control codes (like newline). The code for 'A' is 65, 'a' is 97 and '0' is 48; note that upper- and lower-case letters differ by exactly one bit (32), a fact often examined. Extended ASCII adds a further 128 symbols with 8 bits.

Unicode solves the limitation that 128 symbols cannot cover the world's scripts: it assigns a unique code to well over 100 000 characters from every writing system plus symbols and emoji. UTF-8 stores common characters in 1 byte and rare ones in up to 4 — efficient for web pages, which is why it dominates the internet. More characters per code needs more bits per character, and file size grows accordingly.

Worked example: storing the word "CAT" in ASCII:
C = 67 = 0100 0011
A = 65 = 0100 0001
T = 84 = 0101 0100
Total: 3 characters x 8 bits (stored as bytes) = 24 bits = 3 bytes.

Sound: sampling

Sound is a continuous pressure wave — an analogue signal. To store it, the wave is sampled: measured at regular intervals, and each measurement is rounded to the nearest available level. Two settings decide the quality:

  • Sample rate — how many measurements per second (Hz). Higher rate captures higher frequencies and sounds closer to the original.
  • Sample resolution (bit depth) — how many bits per measurement. More bits means finer rounding of the amplitude, so less distortion.
File size (bits) = sample rate x bit depth x duration in seconds x number of channels

Worked example: 10 seconds of mono CD-quality sound (44 100 Hz, 16 bits):

= 44 100 x 16 x 10 x 1 = 7 056 000 bits
In bytes: 7 056 000 / 8 = 882 000 bytes
In kilobytes: 882 000 / 1024 = 861.3 KB (or /1000 = 882 kB by decimal convention)

Double the sample rate or the bit depth and the file doubles in size.

Raising either setting improves fidelity at the cost of size — the trade-off every sound question turns on.

Images: bitmaps

A bitmap image is a grid of pixels. Two properties set its size and quality: the resolution (pixels across × pixels down) and the colour depth (bits per pixel). With 1 bit per pixel you get black and white; 8 bits give 256 greys or colours; 24 bits (8 per RGB channel) give about 16.7 million colours.

File size (bits) = width in pixels x height in pixels x colour depth

Worked example: 800 x 600 pixels at 24-bit colour:

= 800 x 600 x 24 = 11 520 000 bits
In bytes: 11 520 000 / 8 = 1 440 000 bytes = 1.37 MB (or 1.44 MB decimal)

At 8-bit colour the same image is 800 x 600 x 8 = 3 840 000 bits = 480 000 bytes.

The file also stores metadata: width, height, colour depth and format information, without which the pixels cannot be interpreted. Higher resolution and colour depth improve quality and raise the file size in direct proportion — the same trade-off as sound.

Units of data

UnitSymbolSize
BitbA single 0 or 1
ByteB8 bits
KilobyteKB1024 bytes (binary convention) or 1000 bytes (decimal convention)
MegabyteMB1024 KB
GigabyteGB1024 MB
TerabyteTB1024 GB

The bit/byte distinction is the single most common lost mark in size questions: transmission speeds are quoted in bits per second (Mbps), storage in bytes (MB), and confusing the two is a factor-of-eight error. State which convention you use when the question gives sizes.

Compression

Compression shrinks data for storage or transmission: faster transfer, less bandwidth, lower storage cost. Two families:

LosslessLossy
What it doesRecovers the exact original — redundancy is removed reversiblyDiscards data the human senses are unlikely to miss
MethodsRun-length encoding (RLE), dictionary methods (ZIP, PNG, FLAC)Transform methods throwing away detail (JPEG, MP3)
Used forText, programs, spreadsheets, medical/legal images, archivesPhotographs, music, video, where small losses are acceptable
QualityIdentical to the original after decompressionDegrades with each save; repeated compression compounds the loss
Run-length encoding worked line by line:

Row of pixels: AAAAABBCCCCCCCCDD
Scan for runs:     AAAAA      BB      CCCCCCCC      DD
Count and write:    5A        2B          8C         2D
