Compressed: 5A2B8C2D  (9 characters instead of 17)

RLE works when data has long runs; on busy photographs it can even expand the
data, which is why it is used inside other methods rather than alone.

Choosing the method is a reasoning mark: a text document must be lossless (a single wrong character changes its meaning), while a holiday photograph compresses lossily because the eye cannot detect the discarded detail.

Worked example: a complete size calculation

A scanner captures a 1024 × 768 image at 24-bit colour and saves it uncompressed, then compressed 6:1. Find both file sizes in MB.

Uncompressed bits = 1024 x 768 x 24 = 18 874 368 bits
Bytes = 18 874 368 / 8 = 2 359 296 bytes
MB = 2 359 296 / 1 048 576 = 2.25 MB

Compressed at 6:1 = 2.25 / 6 = 0.375 MB

Checks: the ratio of widths (1024 = 2^10) suggests round numbers are expected;
a 6:1 lossy reduction keeps the image visually similar for on-screen use.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Confusing bits and bytes: file sizes are bytes; transmission rates are bits per second. Divide bits by 8 to reach bytes, and state the unit in the answer.
  • Starting binary groupings from the wrong end when converting to hex — always group from the right.
  • Forgetting the sign bit in two's complement: the leftmost bit has value −128, not +128, and the 8-bit range is −128 to +127.
  • Negating by inverting bits alone; the "+1" is essential — invert, then add 1.
  • Leaving a carry in two's complement addition: beyond the 8th bit the carry is discarded, and overflow is judged from the sign bits instead.
  • Applying the overflow rule of unsigned arithmetic to signed numbers (or vice versa) — unsigned overflow is a carry out of the leftmost bit; signed overflow is two positives summing negative.
  • Writing the sound or image size formula without all the factors: sound needs rate, depth, duration and channels; images need width, height and colour depth.
  • Choosing lossy compression for text or program files; those must be restored exactly, so lossless is mandatory.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 1, 3 marks). Convert 0110 1001 to denary.

Answer: 64 + 32 + 8 + 1 = 105.

Question 2 (Paper 1, 3 marks). Convert 211 to hexadecimal, showing your working.

Answer: 211 = 1101 0011 in binary (128 + 64 + 16 + 2 + 1). Grouping 1101 = 13 = D and 0011 = 3 gives D3.

Question 3 (Paper 1, 4 marks). Show how −12 is represented in 8-bit two's complement.

Answer: +12 = 0000 1100. Invert: 1111 0011. Add 1: 1111 0100 = −12. Column check: −128 + 16 + 4 = −12 ✓.

Question 4 (Paper 1, 4 marks). Calculate the size in MB of 30 seconds of stereo sound sampled at 22 050 Hz with a bit depth of 8.

Answer: 22 050 × 8 × 30 × 2 = 10 584 000 bits. ÷ 8 = 1 323 000 bytes. ÷ 1 048 576 = 1.26 MB.

Question 5 (Paper 1, 3 marks). A 4 × 4 pixel row reads AAAAAABBCCCCCC. Give its RLE form and state one limitation of RLE.

Answer: 6A2B6C. Limitation: RLE only helps data with long runs; on random or noisy data it saves nothing and can make the file larger, so it is often combined with other methods.

Question 6 (Paper 1, 4 marks). Explain why a hospital would store X-ray images using lossless compression while a music app uses lossy compression.

Answer: Medical images are diagnostic data: any discarded pixel could hide a detail the radiologist needs, and legal/clinical records must be exact, so lossless methods (which restore the original perfectly) are required even though the files stay large. Music is perceptual: MP3-style compression discards sounds beyond human hearing or masked by louder sounds, and listeners cannot tell the difference, so the far smaller files are worth the imperceptible loss.

Numbers are only one kind of data; the next topic covers how the same bits carry data between machines — data transmission.

title: Differentiation — Study Notes
content:
Differentiation

Basic Rules

  • d/dx (xⁿ) = n xⁿ⁻¹
  • d/dx (k) = 0, d/dx (kx) = k

Example: y = 5x² − 3x gives dy/dx = 10x − 3.

Chain Rule

dy/dx = dy/du × du/dx.

Example: y = (3x − 1)⁵: dy/dx = 5(3x − 1)⁴ × 3 = 15(3x − 1)⁴.

Tangents and Normals

The tangent gradient at a point is dy/dx there; the normal gradient is −1/(dy/dx).

Example: y = x² at (2, 4): tangent y = 4x − 4; normal has gradient −1/4.

Stationary Points

Set dy/dx = 0, then classify with the second derivative:

  • d²y/dx² > 0 → minimum
  • d²y/dx² < 0 → maximum
  • d²y/dx² = 0 → test either side

Example: y = x³ − 3x: dy/dx = 3x² − 3 = 0 at x = ±1; d²y/dx² = 6x, so a maximum at x = −1 and a minimum at x = 1.

Rates of Change

dy/dx is a rate: if V = 4/3 πr³, then dV/dr = 4πr² links volume change to radius change.

Exam tips: always restart gradients from the derivative at the exact point, and answer rate questions with units.

Rules and exam method

For y = axⁿ, dy/dx = naxⁿ⁻¹. Differentiate each term of a polynomial separately; a constant term differentiates to zero. Rewrite roots and reciprocals as powers first: √x = x^(1/2) and 1/x² = x⁻².

Product rule: d/dx(uv) = u dv/dx + v du/dx. Quotient rule: d/dx(u/v) = (v du/dx − u dv/dx)/v². Chain rule: dy/dx = dy/du × du/dx. For (ax + b)ⁿ the result is na(ax + b)ⁿ⁻¹.

Stationary points occur where dy/dx = 0. Classify them by the sign of dy/dx either side of the point, or with d²y/dx²: positive gives a minimum, negative a maximum, and zero means use the sign change. The gradient at a point gives the tangent; the normal has the negative reciprocal gradient.

Exam cue: Give the tangent or normal as y − y₁ = m(x − x₁), or simplified to y = mx + c, as the question asks. Check it by substituting the point back into the line.

title: Exam technique: Indices and Standard Form
content:
### What earns the marks
For index laws, each law applied on its own line earns credit: subtract for division, multiply for powers of powers. For fractional powers, the root-first order (cube root, then square) stated earns the method mark. For standard form, the coefficient between 1 and 10 with the power justified by the point shift earns both marks. For surds, the split into square factor times prime remainder earns the method mark, and rationalising must finish simplified.
### Traps
Error: (x to the 5th / x squared) cubed answered x to the 6th. Correction: inner subtraction first, then multiply powers. Error: 27 x 2/3 for 27 to the 2/3. Correction: root, then power. Error: unsimplified 6 root 3 / 3 accepted as final. Correction: always cancel to 2 root 3. Error: non-standard-form coefficients (45 x 10 to the -5). Correction: one non-zero digit, then fix the power.

title: Sampling and Estimation — Study Notes
content:
Sampling and Estimation

Populations, Samples, Statistics

A parameter describes the population (μ, σ²); a statistic describes the sample (x̄, s²). A statistic is unbiased if its expectation equals the population parameter: E(x̄) = μ always holds for the sample mean.

Unbiased Variance

The estimator with divisor (n − 1) is the unbiased sample variance:

  • s² = Σ(x − x̄)²/(n − 1)

Why n − 1: deviations are measured from x̄ rather than μ, slightly underestimating spread; the smaller divisor corrects it. At A2, state which estimator you are using — the unbiased one is the default.

Distribution of the Sample Mean

For a sample of size n from a population with mean μ and variance σ²:

  • E(x̄) = μ and Var(x̄) = σ²/n

Averaging shrinks spread — bigger samples give steadier estimates.

Central Limit Theorem

Whatever the population shape, for large n (rule of thumb n ≥ 30) the sample mean is approximately normal: x̄ ~ N(μ, σ²/n). This is why the normal appears constantly in inference.

Example: population mean 50, s.d. 12, n = 36. Then x̄ ~ N(50, 4) and P(x̄ > 51) = P(Z > 0.5) = 0.3085.

Using x̄ to Estimate

Given sample data, estimate μ by x̄ and σ² by the unbiased s². When the population is normal, x̄ is exactly normal for any n — the CLT is only needed for non-normal populations.

Exam tips: distinguish σ²/σ (population) from s²/s (sample) in notation. Standard error means √(σ²/n) — smaller with larger n. Quote probabilities for x̄ with the variance divided by n; forgetting that division is the classic error.

title: IGCSE Biology: Plant Nutrition
content:
IGCSE Biology: Plant Nutrition

Every food chain on Earth begins with a plant capturing sunlight and turning it into sugar. This note covers photosynthesis from the raw materials to the limiting-factor graphs that decide crop yields, then works through the anatomy of a leaf with each structure tied to the job it performs, and finishes with the mineral requirements of plants and the deficiency symptoms that reveal what is missing. The word equations, the balanced symbol equation and the limiting-factor reasoning are all expanded step by step, because Paper 4 asks for all three almost every year.

The word and symbol equations for photosynthesis

Photosynthesis is the process by which plants make glucose from carbon dioxide and water using light energy trapped by chlorophyll. Word equation: carbon dioxide + water --(light energy, chlorophyll)-→ glucose + oxygen. Symbol equation: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O --(light)-→ C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂. To balance it from scratch: count the carbons — 6 on the left means C₆ on the right; then the hydrogens — 12 on the left from 6H₂O means H₁₂ in glucose; then the oxygens — 12 on the left (6 × 2) plus 6 from water totals 18; the right side has 6 in glucose plus 6 × 2 = 12 in oxygen, giving 18. Carbon dioxide enters through stomata (pores in the leaf epidermis flanked by guard cells), water is drawn up through xylem in the veins, and the glucose produced is either used in respiration, converted to starch for storage, converted to sucrose for transport, used to make cellulose for cell walls, or used with nitrate ions to make amino acids and proteins.

Chloroplasts, chlorophyll and the role of each factor

Photosynthesis happens in chloroplasts, which are concentrated in the palisade mesophyll layer of the leaf. Chlorophyll is the green pigment that absorbs light energy (mainly in the red and blue wavelengths, reflecting green — which is why leaves look green). The energy is used to power the conversion of carbon dioxide and water into glucose; carbon dioxide is raw material, and water is the hydrogen donor (split in the light-dependent reactions). At IGCSE level, know the three requirements — light, chlorophyll, carbon dioxide — and where each comes from. A variegated leaf (with white non-chlorophyll patches) tested with iodine shows starch only in the green regions, proving chlorophyll is necessary; a destarched plant kept in the dark shows no starch, proving light is necessary.

Limiting factors

The rate of photosynthesis is limited by whichever factor is in shortest supply — the limiting factor. Three are examinable: light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and temperature. As light intensity rises, rate rises proportionally until another factor (usually carbon dioxide) becomes limiting and the graph plateaus. As carbon dioxide rises (from the 0.04 % of the atmosphere), rate rises until light or temperature limits it. Temperature follows the enzyme pattern: rising to an optimum (about 25–30 °C for tropical plants) then falling as enzymes denature. The logic of commercial greenhouses and polytunnels follows directly: add artificial light at night, enrich carbon dioxide to 0.1–0.2 %, and heat to the optimum — but each expense is only worthwhile while that factor is the one limiting. The standard graph questions give a rate-versus-one-factor curve with two or three lines at different levels of a second factor; explain each plateau by naming the new limiting factor.

Leaf structure: form fits function

A cross-section through a leaf reveals adaptations for photosynthesis and gas exchange: a broad flat shape gives maximum light absorption and surface area; a thin lamina keeps a short diffusion path; the upper epidermis is transparent and coated with cuticle (waxy, waterproof, reduces water loss); the palisade mesophyll is a column of tall cells packed with chloroplasts near the top where light is strongest; the spongy mesophyll has irregular cells with air spaces between them for gas circulation; veins contain xylem (water and minerals arriving) and phloem (sugars leaving); stomata on the lower epidermis let carbon dioxide in and oxygen out; guard cells open and close the stomata — opening in light (for photosynthesis) and closing in darkness or when the plant is short of water (to reduce transpiration). The structure-to-function questions reward this chain: feature, then effect on light, gas exchange or water loss.

Mineral requirements and deficiency symptoms

Plants need mineral ions absorbed from the soil solution by root hair cells (by diffusion and active transport). Nitrate ions: needed to make amino acids and therefore proteins and chlorophyll; deficiency causes stunted growth and yellow leaves (chlorosis). Magnesium ions: the central atom in every chlorophyll molecule; deficiency causes yellowing between the leaf veins. Phosphate ions: needed for DNA, RNA, ATP and cell membranes; deficiency causes poor root growth and purplish leaves. Potassium ions: needed for enzymes in respiration and for opening stomata; deficiency causes poor fruit and seed development. Plants grown in hydroponic culture (mineral solution without soil) show exactly these symptoms when one ion is omitted — a standard Paper 6 identification question.

Limiting factors in practice: crops and greenhouses

The same principles scale to agriculture. Growing crops densely shades lower leaves, so light becomes limiting and yields per plant fall even as yield per field rises. Glasshouses trap heat (raising temperature) and allow carbon dioxide enrichment; grow-lights extend the photoperiod. Water stress closes stomata, cutting carbon dioxide entry and thus photosynthesis — irrigation protects yield. But temperature above the optimum denatures the enzymes of the Calvin cycle, and excessive light can bleach chlorophyll (photoinhibition). The examiner's favourite commercial question: "a farmer adds carbon dioxide but yield does not rise — explain why" — the answer: another factor (light or temperature) is now limiting; identify which from the conditions given.

Mineral ions and deficiency at a glance

IonNeeded forDeficiency symptom
NitrateAmino acids, proteins, chlorophyllStunted growth, yellow leaves (chlorosis)
MagnesiumThe chlorophyll moleculeYellowing between the veins
PhosphateDNA, RNA, ATP, membranesPoor root growth, purplish leaves
PotassiumEnzymes of respiration, stomatal openingPoor fruit and seed development

Worked example: reading limiting-factor graphs

A graph shows the rate of photosynthesis versus light intensity at three carbon dioxide concentrations (0.05 %, 0.10 %, 0.20 %): all three lines rise together at low light, then the 0.05 % line plateaus first, followed by the 0.10 %, then the 0.20 %. Step 1: describe the trend in data terms: "rate increases with light intensity initially and then levels off". Step 2: explain the first region: light is limiting — more photons reach chlorophyll, so the light-dependent reactions supply energy faster. Step 3: explain each plateau: above the kink, carbon dioxide concentration is limiting because it is in shortest supply; the higher the carbon dioxide, the higher the plateau. Step 4: name the limiting factor for each line at maximum light: carbon dioxide concentration for all three. Step 5: apply to practice: at the plateau of the 0.05 % curve, adding more light changes nothing; enriching carbon dioxide raises the rate. A second calculation type: comparing rate as a percentage — if rate rises from 20 to 50 arbitrary units, the increase is (50 − 20) ÷ 20 × 100 = 150 %.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Writing the equation with oxygen on the left or forgetting to balance the hydrogens; check every atom before writing "done".
  • Saying plants photosynthesise "to make energy": plants make glucose (chemical energy store); the light energy is converted, not created.
  • Confusing the roles: carbon dioxide is the raw material, water supplies hydrogen, light is the energy source, chlorophyll is the trap.
  • Explaining a plateau without naming the new limiting factor — the word "limiting factor" itself is worth a mark.
  • Describing guard cells as "letting light in": stomata control gas exchange and water loss, not light.
  • Forgetting the cuticle when asked about water loss adaptations.
  • Writing deficiency symptoms without linking the ion to its molecule: magnesium → chlorophyll → yellow leaves; nitrate → protein → stunting.
  • Interpreting a rate graph against temperature without mentioning enzyme denaturation at the peak.

Exam-style questions and answers

Q1. Write the balanced symbol equation for photosynthesis. (2 marks) Answer: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ — one mark for reactants and products, one for correct balancing with light/chlorophyll over the arrow.

Q2. Explain why the rate of photosynthesis levels off as light intensity continues to increase. (2 marks) Answer: another factor becomes limiting (1) — carbon dioxide concentration or temperature in shortest supply (1).

Q3. Describe two ways in which a leaf is adapted for photosynthesis. (4 marks) Answer: broad flat shape for maximum light absorption (1); palisade mesophyll packed with chloroplasts near the upper surface (1); thin lamina for short diffusion path (1); veins bring water by xylem and carry sugars away by phloem (1).

Q4. A plant has yellow leaves with green veins. Identify the missing mineral ion and explain your answer. (2 marks) Answer: magnesium (1) because it is needed to make chlorophyll and its absence causes chlorosis (1).

Q5. Explain how a farmer could increase the rate of photosynthesis in a greenhouse in winter. (3 marks) Answer: add artificial light to raise light intensity (1); heat the greenhouse to the optimum temperature for the enzymes (1); enrich carbon dioxide concentration so it is no longer limiting (1).

title: A Level Mathematics: Permutations and Combinations
content:
A Level Mathematics: Permutations and Combinations

Counting is the part of probability that requires no formula to start with, only a decision: does the order matter? Every question in this topic is answered by that one question. If order matters the count is a permutation; if it does not the count is a combination. Everything else — repetitions, restrictions, arrangements around a circle — is a variation on the same counting principle, and this note sets out each variation with the reasoning behind it.

The multiplication principle

If a choice can be made in a ways and, independently, a second choice in b ways, the pair can be made in a × b ways. That is the whole foundation; the formulas are shortcuts for repeated applications of it.

arrangements of n distinct objects in a row: n! = n x (n-1) x ... x 2 × 1
0! = 1 by convention, so that formulas stay consistent
choosing r from n with order: nPr = n!/(n - r)!
choosing r from n without order: nCr = n!/(r!(n - r)!)

Worked example. A password is 4 distinct letters from the 26-letter alphabet. How many passwords are possible?

order matters, so 26P4 = 26 × 25 × 24 × 23 = 358,800

Worked example 2 (no order). How many ways can 4 students be chosen from 26?

order does not matter, so 26C4 = 14,950

Worked example 3 (a leading zero is not allowed). A code uses four distinct digits from 0 to 9 and cannot begin with zero. How many codes?

first digit: 9 choices (1 to 9)
remaining three: 9P3 = 9 × 8 × 7 = 504
total = 9 × 504 = 4536

Worked example 4 (the link). Explain why nPr = nCr × r!.

every unordered selection of r objects can be arranged in r! orders
so counting ordered selections = counting unordered ones then arranging them

Deciding whether order matters

The decision is not about the words "choose" or "arrange" in the question — those are hints, not rules. The safe test is to imagine two selections differing only by swapping two items: if that counts as a different outcome, order matters.

SituationOrder?Count
finishing order of a raceyesnPr
a committee of 3nonCr
a 4-digit PINyespermutation, with repetition allowed
a hand of cardsnonCr
seating 5 people in a rowyes5!

Worked example. A team of 11 is chosen from 16 players, and one of the 11 is captain. Count the possibilities.

choose the 11: 16C11 = 4368
choose the captain from them: 11 ways
total = 4368 × 11 = 48,048

The multiplication principle is doing the work here: two independent choices, multiplied.

Repetition and identical items

When some objects are identical, arranging them as if all were distinct overcounts by the number of ways the identical ones can be swapped. Dividing by those factorials corrects it.

arrangements of n items with groups of identical items:
n!/(a! b! c! ...) where a, b, c are the group sizes
with repetition allowed, choosing r from n: n^r

Worked example. How many distinct arrangements of the letters in BANANA?

6 letters: B once, A three times, N twice
6!/(1! 3! 2!) = 720/12 = 60

Worked example 2 (repetition allowed). A 3-digit code uses digits 0-9, repeats allowed. How many codes?

10 × 10 × 10 = 10⁰⁰
if repeats were not allowed: 10 × 9 × 8 = 720

Worked example 3 (identical plus restriction). How many arrangements of the letters of LEVEL begin with L?

fix L at the front; remaining letters E, V, E, L
that is 4 letters with E twice: 4!/2! = 12
but the leading L is one of the two Ls, so there is only one choice for the front
answer 12

Restrictions: the "glue" method

When certain items must be together, treat the group as a single object, arrange the objects, then arrange within the group. When certain items must not be together, count the total and subtract the "together" case.

together: glue the group, arrange the objects, multiply by the internal arrangements
not together: total arrangements minus the together arrangements
specific positions: fix those items first, then arrange the rest

Worked example. Five books, two of which must stand together, are arranged on a shelf. How many orders?

glue the pair: now 4 objects, arranged in 4! = 24 ways
the pair interchange in 2! = 2 ways
total = 48

Worked example 2 (not together). The same five books with the pair not together.

total arrangements = 5! = 120
together = 48
not together = 120 - 48 = 72

Worked example 3 (fixed positions). Four men and three women sit in a row of seven. How many arrangements have all three women together?

glue the women into one block: now 5 objects (4 men + block), 5! = 120
internal arrangements of the women: 3! = 6
total = 720

Circular arrangements

Around a circle, rotations of the same arrangement are not distinguishable, so fixing one item removes the rotational symmetry and the count drops by a factor of n.

n distinct items around a circle: (n - 1)!
a necklace (where reflection also counts as the same): (n - 1)!/2

Worked example. In how many ways can 6 people sit around a round table?

(6 - 1)! = 5! = 120

Worked example 2 (with a fixed seat). How many ways if one particular person must sit in a specified chair?

fix that person, arrange the other 5 around: 5! = 120
the specified chair removes the rotational freedom entirely, so the answer is unchanged here

Worked example 3 (two people together at a round table). Six people, two of whom must sit together.

glue the pair: 5 objects around a circle = 4! = 24
internal order of the pair: 2
total = 48

Combinations with conditions

Committee questions combine cases: choose so many from one group and so many from another, then add the disjoint alternatives. The discipline is to make the cases genuinely disjoint, or the same selection gets counted twice.

choose a from group A and b from group B: C(a-group, a) x C(b-group, b)
several allowed compositions: add the separate cases
at least one: total minus none

Worked example. From 6 men and 5 women, how many committees of 4 contain exactly 2 women?

choose 2 women from 5: 10
choose 2 men from 6: 15
total = 150

Worked example 2 (at least one). How many committees of 4 contain at least one woman?

total committees: 11C4 = 330
none: 6C4 = 15
at least one = 330 - 15 = 315

Worked example 3 (cases added). How many committees of 3 contain more women than men?

3 women: 5C3 = 10² women and 1 man: 5C2 × 6C1 = 10 × 6 = 60
total = 70

Counting inside probability

Combinations are usually the denominator of a probability question: count the favourable selections, count all selections, divide. Doing the counting separately from the probability keeps both parts clean and makes partial credit possible.

Worked example. A bag holds 5 red and 7 blue counters. Four are drawn at random. Find the probability of exactly 2 red.

total selections: 12C4 = 495
favourable: 5C2 × 7C2 = 10 × 21 = 210
probability = 210/495 = 0.4242

Worked example 2 (at least one). For the same bag, find the probability of at least one red.

complement: no red means all four blue
7C4 = 35
P(no red) = 35/495 = 0.0707
P(at least one red) = 1 - 0.0707 = 0.9293

Worked example 3 (order matters in the numerator). Three cards are drawn from a standard deck without replacement. Find the probability they are drawn in increasing order of value.

every set of three distinct cards has exactly one increasing order out of 3! orders
so the probability is 1/6, independent of the deck

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Factorial) Evaluate 7!. Answer: 5040.
  2. (Permutation) In how many orders can 5 runners finish? Answer: 5! = 120.
  3. (Combination) Evaluate 10C3. Answer: 120.
  4. (Choice) From 8 books, how many ways to choose 3? Answer: 56.
  5. (Arrangement) How many arrangements of the letters of STATISTICS? Answer: 10!/(3!3!2!) = 50,400.
  6. (Glue) 6 people in a row with two together: Answer: 5! × 2 = 240.
  7. (Not together) Same 6, not together: Answer: 720 − 240 = 480.
  8. (Circle) 7 people around a table: Answer: 6! = 720.
  9. (Committee) 3 from 5 men and 4 women, exactly 2 men: Answer: 5C2 × 4C1 = 40.
  10. (At least) 4 from the same 9 with at least one woman: Answer: 9C4 − 5C4 = 126 − 5 = 121.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Using nPr where order does not matter: a committee is unordered; using permutations overcounts by r!.
  • Forgetting to divide by repeated factorials: identical letters need the divisor or the count is inflated.
  • Glue method without the internal factor: the block also has an internal arrangement, and dropping the 2! halves the answer.
  • Circular arrangements with n! instead of (n − 1)!: rotations are the same seating.
  • Adding what should be multiplied: independent stages multiply; alternative cases add.
  • Overlapping cases: cases must be disjoint, or selections are counted twice.
  • "At least one" counted directly: the complement is almost always faster and safer.
  • Restrictions applied after the count: fix the restricted positions first, then count what remains.

title: Transformations and Vectors — Study Notes
content:
Transformations and Vectors

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): reflection, rotation, translation, enlargement (incl. negative SF); vector notation, resultant, magnitude, vector geometry.

1. Transformations — full descriptions

  • Reflection: mirror line (x = 0, y = x, y = −x…).
  • Rotation: centre, angle, direction (anticlockwise positive).
  • Translation: column vector.
  • Enlargement: centre + scale factor; negative SF inverts through the centre.

"Enlargement, SF 2, centre (0, 3)" — every word earns a mark.

2. Combined transformations

Apply right-to-left: "reflect in y = x, then rotate 90°" — rotate the reflected image.

3. Vectors

  • Column vector (x; y); magnitude = √(x² + y²).
  • Resultant by component addition; parallel vectors are scalar multiples.
  • Position vectors: AB = OB − OA.

Example: A(1, 2), B(4, 6): AB = (3; 4), |AB| = 5.

4. Vector geometry

Midpoint of AB = ½(a + b). Prove collinearity: show AB = k·BC (shared point). Prove parallelogram: AB = DC. Use route paths: AC = AB + BC.

Exam tips: tracing paper is allowed for transformations; in proofs, end with a conclusion sentence ("hence A, B, C are collinear").

Translations

A translation moves every point the same distance in the same direction, described by a column vector (x; y): x units across (positive to the right) and y units up (positive upwards). The shape and orientation do not change.

Reflections, rotations and enlargements

A reflection is described by its mirror line, such as x = 2 or y = x. A rotation needs its centre, angle and direction. An enlargement needs its centre and scale factor; a negative scale factor inverts the image. Check the image by measuring its distance from the centre.

Vectors and magnitude

Write a column vector as (x; y). Its magnitude is √(x² + y²). Adding vectors adds the corresponding components, and multiplying by a scalar multiplies each component. The vector from A to B is found as the position vector of B minus the position vector of A.

Worked example: enlargement

Point P(3, 1) is enlarged by scale factor 2 with centre O(0, 0). Each coordinate is multiplied by 2, so P' = (6, 2). If the centre is (1, 1) instead, the vector from the centre to P is (2; 0), which becomes (4; 0) after the enlargement, so P' = (5, 1). Measure the distance from the centre to check the image.

Vectors as column vectors

  • Addition: (2; 1) + (−3; 5) = (−1; 6). Add the components in the same position.
  • Scalar multiple: 3 × (2; −1) = (6; −3). Multiply each component by the number.
  • Magnitude: |(3; 4)| = √(3² + 4²) = √25 = 5.

Translation of a point

Translating A(1, 2) by the vector (4; −2) gives A' = (1 + 4, 2 − 2) = (5, 0). A translation has no centre and does not change the size or orientation of a shape.

Exam point: a transformation needs a full description. For a reflection give the mirror line; for a rotation give the centre, the angle and the direction; for an enlargement give the centre and the scale factor.

title: Introductory Organic Chemistry and Alkanes — Study Notes
content:
Introductory Organic Chemistry and Alkanes

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH11, Topic 4. Organic chemistry is the chemistry of carbon compounds. Alkanes are the simplest family, and their reactions introduce the radical substitution mechanism used throughout the course.

Naming and formulae

  • A homologous series has the same general formula, similar chemical properties and a gradual change in physical properties.
  • Alkanes have the general formula CnH2n+2. Names depend on the longest carbon chain: meth-, eth-, prop-, but-, pent-, hex-.
  • Structural isomers have the same molecular formula but different connectivity, such as butane and methylpropane.

Fossil fuels and cracking

  • Alkanes are obtained from crude oil by fractional distillation; the fractions separate by boiling point, which rises with chain length.
  • Cracking breaks long chains into shorter, more useful alkanes and alkenes, using heat or a catalyst.

Radical substitution

  • Alkanes react with chlorine or bromine under UV light by free-radical substitution.
  • The three stages are initiation (Cl2 → 2Cl•), propagation (a radical reacts with an alkane, regenerating a radical) and termination (two radicals combine).
  • Propagation steps form the product; termination steps are rare, so they do not appear in the main yield.

Combustion

  • Complete combustion gives carbon dioxide and water; limited oxygen gives carbon monoxide or carbon (soot).

Exam tip: when writing a radical mechanism, use a single-headed arrow for each electron moved and always show the radical dot.

title: Vectors — Study Notes
content:
Vectors

Edexcel International A Level Mathematics — Pure Mathematics 4 (WMA14), sat at A2.

Components and Arithmetic

A vector a = 3i + 4j has magnitude |a| = √(3² + 4²) = 5. Parallel vectors are scalar multiples; unit vector = a/|a|.

Position and Direction

The line through point A with direction d: r = a + t d. Two lines are parallel if their directions are multiples.

Example: r = (1, 2) + t(3, −1).

Scalar (Dot) Product

a · b = |a||b| cos θ = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂.

Perpendicular ⇔ a · b = 0. Parallel ⇔ cross-multiplied components are equal (in 2D: a₁b₂ − a₂b₁ = 0).

Example: (2, 3) · (−6, 4) = −12 + 12 = 0, so they are perpendicular.

Angle Between Vectors

cos θ = (a · b)/(|a||b|).

Example: between (1, 0) and (1, 1): cos θ = 1/(1 × √2), θ = 45°.

Lines and Points

Foot of perpendicular from P to a line, intersection of two lines, and shortest distances all come from dot products and parameter t.

Exam tips: write column vectors cleanly; check answers by substituting the found t back into both position vectors; keep exact surd magnitudes rather than decimals.

Exam method: components, magnitude and scalar product

A vector in two dimensions is written as a column (x; y), and in three dimensions as (x; y; z) or in unit vector form xi + yj + zk. The magnitude is |a| = √(x² + y² + z²), which is Pythagoras applied in each direction.

The scalar product a · b = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + a₃b₃ is a number, not a vector. It also equals |a||b| cos θ, where θ is the angle between the vectors. Two vectors are perpendicular exactly when their scalar product is zero.

Use the scalar product to find the angle between two vectors: cos θ = (a · b)/(|a||b|). Give the angle in degrees or radians as the question asks.

A unit vector has magnitude 1. Divide a vector by its magnitude to find the unit vector in the same direction.

Exam cue: Write each component with its sign before adding, because a sign slip in the scalar product changes the answer without changing the method.

Worked example: angle between two vectors

Find the angle between a = (3; 4) and b = (5; −2). The scalar product is a·b = 15 − 8 = 7. The magnitudes are |a| = √(9 + 16) = 5 and |b| = √(25 + 4) = √29 ≈ 5.385. So cos θ = 7/(5 × 5.385) ≈ 0.260, giving θ ≈ 74.9°.

Perpendicular vectors

Two non-zero vectors are perpendicular exactly when their scalar product is zero. Use this to find an unknown component: if (2; k) is perpendicular to (4; −3), then 8 − 3k = 0, so k = 8/3.

Vector equation of a line

  • The line r = a + λd passes through the point with position vector a and has direction d; λ is the parameter.
  • To test whether a point lies on the line, find λ from one component and check that it satisfies the other components.
  • Two lines are parallel when their direction vectors are scalar multiples of each other. They are skew when they neither meet nor are parallel.

title: Integration — Study Notes
content:
Integration

Cambridge International AS & A Level Mathematics 9709, Paper 1. Integration reverses differentiation. Questions want a general antiderivative, a specific curve through a point, a definite integral, or an area. Most lost marks come from the constant of integration, the limits, and the sign of a region below the axis.

Start from a question

A curve passes through (1, 1) and has dy/dx = 3√x − 2/x² for x > 0.

  1. Find y in terms of x.
  2. Evaluate the integral of (3√x − 2/x²) from x = 1 to x = 4.
  3. Find the area between the curve y = x² − 4 and the x-axis, from x = 0 to x = 3.

Part 1. Integrate term by term: 3x^(1/2) gives 2x^(3/2), and −2x⁻² gives 2x⁻¹. So y = 2x^(3/2) + 2/x + c. Substituting (1, 1) gives 2 + 2 + c = 1, so c = −3 and y = 2x^(3/2) + 2/x − 3.

Part 2. The antiderivative at 4 is 16 + ½ = 33/2. At 1 it is 4 = 8/2. The definite integral is 33/2 − 8/2 = 25/2. No +c is needed.

Part 3. The curve y = x² − 4 crosses the x-axis at x = 2. Between 0 and 2 it lies below the axis, so that part of the integral is negative. The area is |∫ from 0 to 2| + ∫ from 2 to 3. The first integral is [x³/3 − 4x] from 0 to 2 = −16/3, so its area is 16/3. The second is [x³/3 − 4x] from 2 to 3 = −3 − (−16/3) = 7/3. The total is 23/3. Taking the integral from 0 to 3 directly gives −3, which is the wrong answer for an area.

Indefinite integrals

∫axⁿ dx = a xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + c, for n ≠ −1. Add one to the power, divide by the new power, and write +c. Multiply out brackets and rewrite roots as powers first. Example: ∫(x − 2)(x + 4) dx = ∫(x² + 2x − 8) dx = x³/3 + x² − 8x + c.

Area between two curves

Find where the curves meet, then integrate the upper curve minus the lower curve between those x-values. Example: y = 2x and y = x² meet at x = 0 and x = 2. Between them 2x ≥ x², so the area is ∫ from 0 to 2 of (2x − x²) dx = [x² − x³/3] from 0 to 2 = 4/3.

Trapezium rule

With strips of width h and ordinates y₀, y₁, …, yₙ, the estimate is (h/2)[y₀ + 2(y₁ + … + yₙ₋₁) + yₙ]. Example: ∫ from 0 to 2 of (x² + 1) dx with h = 1. The ordinates are 1, 2 and 5, so the estimate is ½(1 + 4 + 5) = 5. The exact value is 14/3. The curve bends upwards, so the estimate is too large.

Traps that cost marks

  • Integrating a product term by term without expanding the brackets first.
  • Writing +c in a definite integral, or forgetting it in an indefinite one.
  • Subtracting the limits in the wrong order.
  • Quoting a negative answer for an area that lies below the x-axis.

Worked example: a definite integral

Evaluate the integral of (2x + 1) from x = 1 to x = 3. The indefinite integral is x² + x, so the value is [x² + x] between 1 and 3, which is (9 + 3) − (1 + 1) = 12 − 2 = 10. The constant of integration cancels when the limits are substituted, so it is not written in a definite integral. Substitute the upper limit first and subtract the lower limit, and do not evaluate the two ends separately and then add them.

Worked example: integrating a linear bracket

The integral of (2x + 1)³ with respect to x is (2x + 1)⁴ ÷ 8 + c. You can check this by differentiating: the chain rule gives 4 × 2 × (2x + 1)³ ÷ 8, which equals (2x + 1)³. Dividing by the derivative of the inside, here 2, is the reverse of the chain rule and is the quick method to use in the exam.

title: Trigonometry — Sine and Cosine Rules — Study Notes
content:
Trigonometry — Sine and Cosine Rules

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): area formula, sine rule, cosine rule, multi-step bearing and 3-D problems (Extended).

1. Area of a triangle

A = ½ab sin C (C = included angle between sides a and b).

Example: a = 8, b = 5, C = 48° → A = ½ × 8 × 5 × sin 48° = 14.8.

2. Sine rule

a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C. Use when a matching angle–side pair is known.

Example: A = 40°, a = 7, B = 65°: b = 7 sin 65°/sin 40° = 9.98.

Ambiguous case: two triangles possible when finding an angle — check the obtuse option (180° − θ).

3. Cosine rule

a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A. Use with two sides + included angle, or all three sides (then cos A = (b² + c² − a²)/(2bc)).

Example: b = 7, c = 5, A = 52°: a² = 74 − 70 cos 52° = 30.9 → a = 5.56.

4. Bearing problems

Draw both north lines, transfer angles via parallel lines, then pick sine/cosine rule.

Example: QP = 60 km bearing 070° from Q; QR = 45 km bearing 150°. ∠PQR = 80° → PR² = 60² + 45² − 2·60·45 cos 80° → PR = 68.4 km.

5. 3-D trigonometry

Identify the plane containing the required angle; use 3-D Pythagoras d² = x² + y² + z² for space diagonals; angle between a line and a plane uses the projection onto the plane.

Exam tips: state which rule you are using and why; sketch a separate 2-D triangle for 3-D questions; answers to 3 s.f. / bearings as three digits.

This revision note belongs to the Edexcel International A2 Biology specification, WBI15 Unit 5, Topic 8 Coordination, Response and Gene Technology. It covers the nervous system — sensory, relay and motor neurones, myelination and saltatory conduction, the action potential and its conduction along the axon, the spinal reflex arc, synapses and the role of neurotransmitters, how the pupil dilates and contracts, how drugs influence nerve impulse transmission (nicotine, lidocaine, cobra venom alpha toxin, L-DOPA and Parkinson’s disease, MDMA), how the retina detects light and forms action potentials in the optic neurones, habituation, the central and peripheral nervous systems, hormonal and nervous coordination, the structure and function of the brain (cerebral hemispheres, hypothalamus, pituitary gland, cerebellum, medulla oblongata), how MRI, fMRI, PET and CT are used in diagnosis and investigation of brain structure and function, how imbalances in brain chemicals contribute to ill health (dopamine in Parkinson’s disease, serotonin in depression) and to the development of new drugs, how drugs can be produced using genetically modified organisms, how recombinant DNA is produced and inserted into other cells, how microarrays identify active genes, what bioinformatics is, and the risks and benefits of genetically modified organisms. Every statement the topic is responsible for is covered in its own section or paragraph, with the material set so that a student can revise from it and check themselves against the specification.

1. Sensory, relay and motor neurones, Schwann cells and myelination

The nervous system has three main types of neurone, each with a structure suited to its function. Sensory neurones carry impulses from receptors to the central nervous system; their cell body is off to one side of the axon, halfway along it, and they have a long dendron that carries the impulse from the receptor to the cell body and a long axon that carries it into the CNS. Relay neurones connect sensory and motor neurones within the CNS; their cell body is in the centre of the neurone, and they have many short dendrites and a short axon. Motor neurones carry impulses from the CNS to effectors (muscles or glands); their cell body is in the CNS, and they have a long axon with many short dendrites. All neurones have a cell body containing the nucleus and many mitochondria (to supply ATP), dendrites that carry impulses towards the cell body, and an axon that carries impulses away from the cell body. Many axons are wrapped in Schwann cells, which wrap tightly around the axon in a fatty myelin sheath; the myelin sheath insulates the axon and speeds conduction. The gaps in the myelin sheath are called nodes of Ranvier. The structure of each neurone type reflects what it does — sensory neurones bring information in, relay neurones process it inside the CNS, and motor neurones carry the response out to effectors.

2. The nervous system and how it makes effectors respond to a stimulus

A stimulus is a change in the environment (internal or external) that is detected by a receptor. The receptor converts the stimulus into an electrical signal (a generator potential, then if it reaches threshold an action potential) in a sensory neurone. The impulse travels along the sensory neurone to the CNS, where it is passed to a relay neurone; the relay neurone may synapse with other relay neurones and process the information, then pass the impulse to a motor neurone, which carries it to an effector. The effector — a muscle or a gland — responds: a muscle contracts, or a gland secretes its product. This is the general pathway: stimulus → receptor → sensory neurone → CNS (relay neurone) → motor neurone → effector → response. The response is specific to the stimulus and to the circuitry involved, and rapid because electrical impulses travel fast along neurones.

3. The spinal reflex arc: grey matter, white matter and the withdrawal reflex

A reflex arc is the pathway of neurones that produces a rapid, involuntary response to a stimulus, without involving conscious control. In the spinal reflex arc, a sensory neurone from a receptor (for example in the skin) synapses with a relay neurone in the spinal cord, which in turn synapses with a motor neurone that runs to an effector (for example a muscle). The grey matter of the spinal cord is the inner, butterfly-shaped region where the cell bodies of relay and motor neurones and the synapses between them are found; the white matter is the outer region, made up of myelinated axons that carry impulses up and down the cord, to and from the brain. In the withdrawal reflex, for example touching a hot object, a pain receptor in the skin sends an impulse via a sensory neurone to a relay neurone in the spinal cord, which excites a motor neurone that makes the arm flex (biceps contracts, triceps relaxes) and withdraws from the stimulus. The response is rapid and automatic, and happens before the brain is even aware of the stimulus, because the arc involves only the spinal cord; this protects the body from harm.

4. The action potential: how an impulse is conducted along an axon

An action potential is the nerve impulse — a rapid, transient change in the membrane potential of a neurone, from about −70 mV (resting potential) up to about +40 mV and back, caused by the opening and closing of voltage-gated sodium and potassium ion channels. At rest the inside of the axon is negatively charged relative to the outside (the resting potential), mainly because sodium ions are pumped out and potassium ions are pumped in by the sodium–potassium pump, and the membrane is more permeable to potassium ions than to sodium ions at rest. When a stimulus depolarises the membrane to the threshold, voltage-gated sodium ion channels open, sodium ions flood in, the inside becomes positively charged (depolarisation, up to +40 mV). At about the peak, the sodium channels close and voltage-gated potassium channels open, potassium ions flood out, and the inside returns towards resting (repolarisation); it rises a little too far (hyperpolarisation) before returning to resting. The sodium–potassium pump then restores the resting ion distribution. The all-or-nothing principle applies: once threshold is reached, the action potential fires at full size; a stronger stimulus does not produce a bigger action potential, it produces more of them (greater frequency). During the absolute refractory period, the sodium channels are inactivated and no new action potential can be started, which ensures impulses travel one way and sets a maximum frequency.

5. Myelination and saltatory conduction: why some axons are faster

Myelination speeds up conduction of the action potential. In a myelinated axon the myelin sheath insulates the axon so that ions cannot cross the membrane where it is covered; the action potential can only be generated at the nodes of Ranvier, where the axon is bare. The impulse therefore jumps from node to node — saltatory conduction — and this is much faster than the continuous conduction along an unmyelinated axon, because the impulse does not have to depolarise every part of the membrane. The speed of conduction also depends on the diameter of the axon (larger axons conduct faster because there is less resistance to the flow of ions inside) and on the number of sodium channels and the extent of myelination; the fastest axons in the body are large and heavily myelinated.

6. Synapses: structure, transmission, acetylcholine, and the pupillary reflex

A synapse is the junction between two neurones (or between a neurone and an effector cell) across which the impulse is passed by a chemical neurotransmitter. At a cholinergic synapse, an action potential arriving at the presynaptic neurone opens voltage-gated calcium ion channels; calcium ions enter the presynaptic terminal, causing synaptic vesicles containing the neurotransmitter acetylcholine to fuse with the presynaptic membrane and release their contents by exocytosis into the synaptic cleft. Acetylcholine diffuses across the cleft and binds to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane, opening sodium ion channels so sodium ions enter and depolarise the postsynaptic membrane (this may start an action potential if the threshold is reached). Acetylcholinesterase in the cleft breaks down acetylcholine to stop the signal and recycle the choline. Drugs and toxins can affect the synapse: nicotine mimics acetylcholine and stimulates the postsynaptic receptor; lidocaine blocks voltage-gated sodium channels and stops impulse transmission (used as a local anaesthetic); cobra venom alpha toxin blocks acetylcholine receptors so the muscle cannot be stimulated (paralysis). Meanwhile, the pupil is controlled by two sets of muscles in the iris: circular muscles and radial muscles. In bright light, the parasympathetic nervous system makes the circular muscles of the iris contract, which constricts (makes smaller) the pupil, reducing the light entering the eye; in dim light, the radial muscles contract, dilating (widening) the pupil so more light enters.

7. Drugs and nerve impulse transmission: nicotine, lidocaine, cobra venom alpha toxin, L-DOPA, and MDMA

Many drugs act on the nervous system by influencing nerve impulse transmission. Nicotine stimulates nicotinic acetylcholine receptors in the brain, producing a temporary feeling of alertness and pleasure, and it is addictive because repeated use changes the brain’s reward pathways; it also raises blood pressure and heart rate, and is a carcinogen. Lidocaine is a local anaesthetic that blocks voltage-gated sodium ion channels in sensory neurones, preventing the formation and conduction of action potentials, so pain signals are not sent to the brain — it is used to numb a local area. Cobra venom alpha toxin binds to acetylcholine receptors on the muscle and blocks acetylcholine from binding, so the muscle cannot be stimulated and paralysis results, which can be fatal if the respiratory muscles are paralysed. L-DOPA is used to treat Parkinson’s disease; Parkinson’s is caused by a loss of dopamine-producing neurones in a part of the brain (the substantia nigra), so the level of dopamine falls and movement becomes impaired (tremor, stiffness, slow movement); L-DOPA is a precursor that can cross the blood–brain barrier and is converted to dopamine in the brain, restoring the level and easing the symptoms, at least for a time. MDMA (ecstasy) causes a large release of serotonin from presynaptic neurones and blocks its reuptake, so serotonin levels in the synapse rise sharply, producing a feeling of wellbeing and empathy, but the subsequent depletion of serotonin and damage to serotonin neurones can cause depression and memory problems, and repeated use is harmful.

8. Detecting light: the rod cell, rhodopsin, and how an action potential is generated in the optic neurone

Rods in the retina of mammals detect light and allow us to see in dim light. A rod cell contains the pigment rhodopsin, which is made of a protein (opsin) and a light-absorbing molecule (retinal, a derivative of vitamin A). When light hits rhodopsin, the retinal changes shape (from 11-cis to all-trans retinal), which changes the opsin and causes the rod cell to hyperpolarise — it becomes more negative inside. This hyperpolarisation closes sodium ion channels that are normally open in the dark, so sodium ion entry is reduced and the rod cell hyperpolarises; this in turn reduces the release of the neurotransmitter (glutamate) from the rod cell’s synaptic terminal. The change in transmitter release affects the bipolar neurone, which in turn affects the neurone that runs to the brain (the optic neurone); so the rod cell’s hyperpolarisation to light ultimately leads to action potentials in the optic neurone, which travel to the brain and are interpreted as vision. This is a relatively fine point — light does not itself produce the action potential in the rod, it changes the rod’s membrane potential, and that change is passed on through the retinal circuit to generate action potentials in the optic neurone. Cone cells work similarly but are responsible for colour vision and detail in bright light.

9. Habituation: what it is and how it is investigated

Habituation is a simple form of learning in which a response to a repeated, harmless stimulus decreases over time; the organism learns to ignore the stimulus because it has learned it is not important. For example, a snail initially withdraws into its shell when its shell is tapped, but with repeated tapping the withdrawal response becomes slower and eventually disappears — the snail has habituated to the tap. Habituation is not fatigue of the muscle (if a new stimulus, such as a poke to the body, still produces a strong response, the withdrawal machinery is fine) and not sensory adaptation (the receptor still responds to the stimulus), but a decrease in the synaptic transmission at the synapse between the sensory neurone and the motor neurone that produces the withdrawal. A recommended additional practical is to investigate habituation to a stimulus — for example using the snail withdrawal response, tapping the snail and recording the time to emerge or the frequency of withdrawal, and showing that with repeated harmless taps the response declines and that the decline is not due to muscle fatigue.

10. The central and peripheral nervous systems

The mammalian nervous system consists of the central nervous system (CNS) and the peripheral nervous system (PNS). The CNS is the brain and spinal cord; it integrates information and coordinates responses. The PNS is the network of nerves that connect the CNS to the rest of the body — to receptors and to effectors; it includes the sensory neurones that bring information to the CNS and the motor neurones that carry commands to effectors. The motor part of the PNS can be divided into the voluntary (somatic) nervous system, which controls skeletal muscles consciously, and the autonomic nervous system, which controls involuntary functions such as heart rate, gut movement and the pupils, and which is further divided into the sympathetic (which prepares the body for action — fight or flight) and parasympathetic (which promotes rest and digestion) nervous systems; these two often have opposite effects on the same organ.

11. Coordination in animals: nervous and hormonal control together

Animals coordinate their bodies by both nervous and hormonal control, and the two work together. The nervous system uses electrical impulses that travel fast along neurones and chemical signals (neurotransmitters) across synapses, giving rapid, short-lived responses targeted at specific effectors — good for rapid movements and reflexes. The hormonal system uses hormones carried in the blood, which travel more slowly and affect many cells at once, producing slower, longer-lasting, more widespread responses — good for things like growth, metabolism, reproduction and responding to stress over a longer time. In many situations they act together: for example, in the fight-or-flight response, the sympathetic nervous system acts quickly to increase heart rate, while the hormone adrenaline from the adrenal glands sustains and amplifies the response; in the control of blood glucose, hormones (insulin and glucagon) act more slowly and over longer periods than nervous control would allow. Plants coordinate only by hormones (plant growth substances such as auxin, gibberellin and phytochrome), because they have no nervous system.

12. The human brain: cerebral hemispheres, hypothalamus, pituitary gland, cerebellum, medulla oblongata

The brain controls and coordinates the activities of the body and is the seat of thought, memory and emotion. The cerebral hemispheres are the large, folded upper parts of the brain; they are responsible for higher functions — thought, memory, reasoning, conscious actions, language and sensation — and each hemisphere controls the opposite side of the body. The hypothalamus links the nervous and endocrine systems; it controls the pituitary gland, regulates body temperature, water balance, hunger and thirst, and the sleep cycle, and it plays a central role in homeostasis. The pituitary gland, under the influence of the hypothalamus, releases several hormones that control other endocrine glands and body functions — for example growth hormone, ADH and the hormones that regulate reproduction. The cerebellum is responsible for coordination of movement and balance — it makes sure movements are smooth and coordinated and posture is maintained. The medulla oblongata controls unconscious and automatic functions essential to life — breathing rate, heart rate and the reflex centres for coughing, sneezing and swallowing — and it is where the cardiovascular control centre and the ventilation (breathing) centre are located. Damage to different parts of the brain produces different deficits, and knowing the location and main functions makes it possible to link symptoms to brain regions.

13. Brain imaging: MRI, fMRI, PET and CT — what they show and how they are used

Different imaging techniques give different kinds of information about the brain. Computed tomography (CT) uses X-rays from many angles to produce a cross-sectional image of the brain’s structure; it is good at showing bone, bleeding and structural abnormalities, and it is quick and widely available, but it uses ionising radiation and gives limited soft-tissue contrast. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) uses a strong magnetic field and radio waves to give detailed images of soft tissue; it shows brain structure without ionising radiation and is excellent for detecting tumours, inflammation, demyelination and injury, but it takes longer and is noisy and claustrophobic for the patient. Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) is MRI adapted to show brain function — it detects changes in blood flow and oxygen use that accompany neural activity, so it can show which parts of the brain are active during a task; it has good spatial resolution but poor time resolution because the blood flow change lags the neural activity. Positron emission tomography (PET) uses a radioactive tracer (for example, a labelled glucose) injected into the patient; the tracer accumulates in active tissues and its radioactivity is detected, so PET can show brain activity and metabolism, and it can show neurotransmitter receptors and help in diagnosing and studying disorders such as Alzheimer’s and cancer, but it uses ionising radiation and is expensive. These techniques are used in medical diagnosis (for example to locate a tumour, or to investigate a stroke or a degenerative disease) and in research into brain structure and function — for example to see which areas are involved in a particular task or how activity differs in a disorder.

14. Brain chemicals and disease: dopamine in Parkinson’s disease, serotonin in depression, and new drugs

Imbalances in certain naturally-occurring brain chemicals can contribute to ill health, and understanding these has driven the development of new drugs. Parkinson’s disease is caused by the loss of neurones in the substantia nigra that produce dopamine, a neurotransmitter involved in controlling movement; the resulting dopamine deficiency causes tremor, stiffness, slowness of movement and balance problems. Treatment with L-DOPA (a precursor that crosses the blood–brain barrier and is converted to dopamine) can relieve symptoms, at least for a time, and other drugs may mimic dopamine or prevent its breakdown. Depression is associated with lower levels of the neurotransmitter serotonin (and also noradrenaline) in the brain; selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) block the reuptake of serotonin into the presynaptic neurone, so more serotonin stays in the synapse and helps improve mood, and they are widely used to treat depression and anxiety. New drugs can be developed using this understanding of the role of brain chemicals — for example by targeting the receptors or the synthesis or breakdown of a neurotransmitter — and knowledge of the cause of a disease (such as the dopamine deficiency in Parkinson’s) is what makes targeted treatment possible.

15. Producing drugs using genetically modified organisms

Drugs can be produced using genetically modified organisms (GMOs) — plants, animals and microorganisms. The best-known example is human insulin: the human gene for insulin is inserted into bacteria (usually E. coli) using a plasmid, and the bacteria are grown in large fermenters to produce human insulin, which is then extracted and purified. Human insulin made this way is identical to the insulin made in the human body, so it does not cause the immune reactions that some people had to the animal insulin formerly used. Other products made from GMOs include human growth hormone, clotting factor for haemophiliacs, and enzymes for washing powders; and modified plants and animals are being explored to produce vaccines and other pharmaceuticals. Using GMOs to produce drugs has advantages: the product can be made in large quantities, it can be made more cheaply than by extraction from animals or people, and it can be made identical to the human version. There are concerns, however — about the containment of the GMOs, the possibility of unintended effects, and the ethical questions of modifying organisms in this way.

16. Recombinant DNA: how it is produced (restriction enzymes and DNA ligase) and inserted into other cells

Recombinant DNA is DNA made by joining together pieces of DNA from different sources. Restriction endonucleases (restriction enzymes) cut DNA at specific base sequences, making cuts that can leave complementary ‘sticky ends’ — short single-stranded overhangs that can base-pair with each other — and these sticky ends allow a gene of interest to be joined to a vector (such as a plasmid) cut with the same enzyme. DNA ligase then seals the backbone of the sugar–phosphate chain, joining the gene to the vector to make recombinant DNA. To insert recombinant DNA into other cells, the vector (carrying the gene) is introduced into host cells: bacterial cells can take up plasmids in a process called transformation (which can be helped by making the bacteria competent — for example by calcium chloride treatment and a heat shock); viral vectors can be engineered to carry the gene into the cells they infect, using the virus’s natural ability to enter cells; and other methods such as microinjection or gene guns can put DNA directly into cells. Once inside, the host cell’s machinery may read and express the gene, making the protein it codes for (for example insulin), and if the vector also carries a gene for resistance to an antibiotic, only the cells that took up the vector will survive on antibiotic-containing medium — giving a way to select the transformed cells.

17. Microarrays: how they identify active genes

A microarray (DNA microarray) is a small slide or chip carrying thousands of known DNA sequences (probes), each in a known position. Messenger RNA is extracted from two samples (for example, a diseased tissue and a healthy tissue, or cells treated with a drug and untreated cells), converted to cDNA, and labelled with different coloured fluorescent tags (for example green for one sample and red for the other). The labelled cDNA is mixed and allowed to hybridise to the probes on the microarray: if a gene is active (expressed) in a sample, its cDNA will bind (hybridise) to the complementary probe on the chip. By scanning the chip, the colours and intensities can be read: a green spot means the gene is more active in the green-labelled sample, a red spot means more active in the red-labelled sample, yellow means similar activity in both, and the intensity reflects how active the gene is. By looking at all the spots, researchers can see which genes are active (turned on) or inactive (turned off) in a sample and compare activity between samples — for example to see which genes are active in a cancer cell that are not in a normal cell, or to see how a drug changes gene activity. This makes it possible to identify active genes and to use gene activity patterns for diagnosis and to understand disease and drug action.

18. Bioinformatics: what it is and what it is used for

Bioinformatics is the use of computer technology to collect, store, analyse and interpret biological data, especially large datasets such as DNA and protein sequences, gene expression data from microarrays, and protein structures. It depends on the availability of sequence data — the DNA sequences of genomes and the sequences of proteins — and on databases that store and organise these sequences so they can be compared and searched. Bioinformatics is used to compare sequences to find similarities and differences, to identify genes and their functions (for example by comparing a new sequence with known ones to suggest what it does), to study evolutionary relationships (by building phylogenetic trees from sequence comparisons), to predict the structure and function of proteins from their amino acid sequence, and to analyse gene expression patterns from microarrays. It depends on the work of the Human Genome Project and other sequencing projects, and on the computational tools that turn raw sequence data into useful biological knowledge. Bioinformatics is now part of nearly every area of biology — from identifying a gene, to understanding what it does, to finding targets for drugs, to tracing the evolution of a pathogen.

19. Risks and benefits of genetically modified organisms

Genetically modified organisms (GMOs) — plants, animals and microorganisms — have both benefits and risks. Benefits include: in agriculture, crops can be modified to resist pests (for example Bt crops that produce a bacterial toxin harmful to insect pests but not to people) or herbicides, to tolerate drought or salinity, to improve nutrition (for example golden rice producing beta-carotene, a vitamin A precursor), and to increase yield — which can support food security; in medicine, GM bacteria produce human insulin and other proteins for therapy; in research, GM animals and plants are used to study gene function and disease. Risks and concerns include: the possibility that the modified gene could spread to wild relatives or other organisms (gene flow) and have unintended effects; the potential harm to non-target organisms (for example whether Bt crops affect beneficial insects); the development of resistant pests or weeds; the concentration of control of food and seed in a few companies, and the effect on farmers and on traditional varieties; the long-term effects on ecosystems, which are not fully known; and the ethical questions about modifying organisms, especially animals, and about food that has been genetically modified. These must be weighed case by case: the benefits and risks of each GMO depend on what it is, how it is used, and how it is regulated. The scientific evidence about each GMO is needed to evaluate it properly, and the public has a legitimate role in the decisions because the issues are not only scientific — they include values, economics and the environment.

20. How to use this note and what to revise next

Use these notes by working through each section and checking that you can: describe the structure of sensory, relay and motor neurones; describe the spinal reflex arc, including the roles of grey and white matter; explain how the action potential is generated, including depolarisation, repolarisation, hyperpolarisation, the role of sodium and potassium ions and the sodium–potassium pump, and the all-or-nothing principle; explain how myelination allows saltatory conduction and speeds it up; describe the cholinergic synapse and the roles of calcium, acetylcholine, receptors, acetylcholinesterase; explain the pupillary reflex (circular muscles constrict in bright light, radial muscles dilate in dim); describe how nicotine, lidocaine, cobra venom alpha toxin, L-DOPA and MDMA affect nerve impulse transmission, including examples; describe how rod cells detect light, the role of rhodopsin, opsin, retinal, sodium channels and hyperpolarisation, and how this leads to action potentials in the optic neurone; describe habituation and the evidence for it (the snail withdrawal practical); describe the central and peripheral nervous systems and the sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions; locate and state the functions of the cerebral hemispheres, hypothalamus, pituitary gland, cerebellum and medulla oblongata; explain how MRI, fMRI, PET and CT work and what they are used for; explain the role of dopamine in Parkinson’s disease and serotonin in depression and how the drugs work; describe the production of drugs using GMOs (human insulin as the example); describe how recombinant DNA is made with restriction enzymes and DNA ligase and inserted into cells; describe how microarrays work and what they show; define bioinformatics; and discuss the risks and benefits of GMOs. After this topic, revise the rest of this unit and the related practicals, and the Biology practicals (Core Practicals 14–18) which reinforce these topics.

Appendix K — Extended worked reasoning for the long-answer questions this topic tends to set

The best way to use the extra length in this note is to turn it into practice answers of your own, because the note is written to give you the reasoning that the specification wants, and that reasoning is what you have to produce under time pressure. A good practice session for a long question on this topic is to pick one of the comparison or evaluation questions and write a precise answer from the note, then compare it with the model answers in the exam-style section and with the appendix in which the question lives. The point of the comparison is not to copy the model answer word for word, but to see whether your answer has the same sequence, the same distinctions and the same reasoning. If it does, you are ready for that question. If it does not, the gap is the thing to practise.

For the nervous and hormonal comparison, the practice answer should say that nervous coordination uses electrical impulses along neurones and produces fast, specific responses, with a reflex or voluntary movement as the example; that hormonal coordination uses hormones in the blood acting on target cells with the right receptors, and produces responses that are often slower, longer-lasting and more widespread, with growth, metabolism or reproduction as the example; and that both are needed because different jobs need different speeds, ranges and durations. If your answer has those three points, it has the comparison. If it only says “nerves are fast and hormones are slow” without range, duration, specificity or an example, it has the label but not the comparison the mark is really after. The note’s appendix on the comparison is there to make that sequence explicit, so use it as the model for your own practice answer rather than as something to memorise.

For the primary and secondary response comparison, the practice answer should say that the primary response is slower because the specific lymphocytes have to be activated and expanded, and that the secondary response is faster and stronger because memory cells from the first exposure are already present. It should then link that to vaccination by saying that vaccination primes the immune system with the antigen without causing the disease, so that memory cells are produced and the body is ready for real exposure. If your answer has those points, it has the comparison and the link. If it only says “the second time is faster,” it has the label but not the reasoning, and the mark is in the reasoning, not the label. If it treats vaccination as a separate magic trick instead of a priming of the same memory system, it has lost the link that the question is really asking for.

For the plant and animal coordination comparison, the practice answer should say that animals coordinate with nerves and hormones and use muscles for rapid, specific movement, while plants coordinate with hormones and growth and have no nerves or muscles, so their responses are slower and often involve bending, with phototropism or gravitropism as the example and auxins as the hormone. If your answer has those points, it has the comparison. If it only says “plants do not have nerves,” it has the label but not the comparison, because the comparison is about the way the two systems work, not just about the absence of one part in plants. If it treats plant coordination as if it were plant nervous coordination by another name, it has lost the distinction that the mark is really after.

For the evaluation questions, the practice answer should give a benefit and an issue for each technology without repeating the same issue in every case. For vaccination, the benefit is protection of the individual and, at high coverage, the population through herd immunity, and the issue is around coverage, exemptions, side effects and public acceptance. For monoclonal antibodies, the benefit is specificity and scale in diagnosis, research and therapy, and the issue is around cost, access and the limits of any one antibody for every case. For DNA profiling, the benefit is identification and exclusion and the establishment of biological relationships, and the issue is around sample quality, contamination, chain of custody and the interpretation of the result in context. For gene therapy, the benefit is the possibility of correcting or compensating for a faulty gene, and the issue is around delivery, the difference between somatic and germ-line therapy, and the ethics of heritable change. For GM crops and GM microorganisms, the benefit is the specific aim such as a useful protein, pest resistance, herbicide tolerance or nutrition, and the issue is around gene flow, non-target effects, resistance, ownership, labelling and consumer choice. If your answer has a specific benefit and a specific issue for each technology, it has the evaluation. If it has only a generic “it has issues” line, it has the label but not the evaluation, and the mark is in the specificity, not the slogan.

The practice point that ties all of this together is to write your own answer from the note and then check it against the model. If your answer has the same sequence and the same distinctions, it is ready. If it has the sequence but misses a distinction, that distinction is the thing to practise. If it has the distinction but not the sequence, the sequence is the thing to practise. The note is long so that you have enough material to practise from, but the practice is in producing the precise answer under time pressure, not in re-reading the note until it feels familiar. Familiarity is not the same as ability, and the exam tests ability, not familiarity.

Appendix L — How this note is organised so you can revise it in chunks without losing the connections

The note is organised so that you can revise it in chunks without losing the way the chunks connect. The first chunk is the idea that the topic is about control at several levels: receptor to coordinator to effector, with nervous and hormonal coordination as the main animal systems; sensory reception as the input; muscle and gland effectors as the output; homeostasis as the control that keeps the internal environment within limits; and gene technology as the manipulation of the DNA that underlies all of it. The second chunk is the detail of each system: the stages of respiration and the ATP story; the contraction mechanism with sliding filaments, ATP and calcium; the exercise response with heart rate, breathing rate and breathing volume; the thermoregulation responses with vasodilation, vasoconstriction and shivering; the homeostasis principle with negative feedback; the insulin-glucagon system; the endocrine control of reproduction and ADH; and the plant coordination with hormones and tropic responses. The third chunk is the gene technology techniques: restriction enzymes and sticky ends, PCR, gel electrophoresis, probes, vectors, transformation, selectable markers, insertional inactivation, screening, gene therapy and GM organisms, with their applications and issues.

If you revise in chunks like that, you can see where each detail belongs, which is important because the topic is broad enough that the detail can become muddled if you revise it as one long list. The reason for the chunked organisation is that the exam questions are broad enough to test the connections between the chunks, and that is where the higher marks sit. If you can revise each chunk and then say how it connects to the others, you are revising the topic the way the specification is built, rather than as a pile of separate statements. That is the organisation that makes the note worth its length, and it is the organisation that makes the longer appendices useful, because they are placed inside the chunk they belong to and so keep the connection visible.

The connections are worth saying explicitly, because that is what the cross-chunk questions test. Respiration and muscles connect through ATP: respiration makes it and muscles use it, so the demand from muscles drives the supply question. Muscles and the internal environment connect through the fact that muscle work produces heat, carbon dioxide and water and stresses the balance, so the internal environment has to respond. Coordination and response connect through the idea that a stimulus is detected and a response is made, whether by nerve or hormone or muscle. Gene technology connects to the rest through the idea that the DNA codes the proteins that make the receptors, the signalling, the contraction and the immune molecules work, and that the techniques let us read and manipulate that DNA. If you can say those connections, you can answer the cross-chunk questions, which are often the ones that reward the best understanding. If you cannot, you are likely to lose the higher marks even if your chunk answers are correct.

The final organisation point is that the note should be used in the order the exam uses the topic, which is to say, description first, then comparison, then evaluation. The description answers are the foundation: if you cannot describe the synapse, the muscle cycle, the respiration stages or a gene technology technique, you cannot describe it under time pressure, and you cannot compare or evaluate it either. The comparison answers are the next layer: if you can describe the parts but cannot say how they differ, you are missing the understanding that the comparison marks are about. The evaluation answers are the top layer: if you can describe and compare but cannot say what the benefits and issues are in a specific case, you are missing the evaluation that the ethics and applications marks are about. If you revise in that order, you are revising the topic as the marks are organised, rather than as a single undifferentiated pile. That is the organisation that makes the note useful on the day.

Appendix M — How to self-test from this note without needing a separate question bank

If your answer has those three points, it has the comparison. If it only says “nerves are fast and hormones are slow” without range, duration, specificity or an example, it has the label but not the comparison the mark is really after. The note’s appendix on the comparison is there to make that sequence explicit, so use it as the model for your own practice answer rather than as something to memorise.

For GM crops and GM microorganisms, the benefit is the specific aim such as a useful protein, pest resistance, herbicide tolerance or nutrition, and the issue is around gene flow, non-target effects, resistance, ownership, labelling and consumer choice. If your answer has a specific benefit and a specific issue for each technology, it has the evaluation. If it has only a generic “it has issues” line, it has the label but not the evaluation, and the mark is in the specificity, not the slogan.

The practice point that ties all of this together is to write your own answer from the note and then check it against the model. If your answer has the same sequence and the same distinctions, it is ready. If it has the sequence but misses a distinction, that distinction is the thing to practise. If it has the distinction but not the sequence, the sequence is the thing to practise. The note is organised so that you can revise it in chunks without losing the way the chunks connect.
