The third chunk is the gene technology techniques: restriction enzymes and sticky ends, PCR, gel electrophoresis, probes, vectors, transformation, selectable markers, insertional inactivation, screening, gene therapy and GM organisms, with their applications and issues.

Muscles and the internal environment connect through the fact that muscle work produces heat, carbon dioxide and water and stresses the balance, so the internal environment has to respond. title: Exam technique: Probability (A2)
content:
### What earns the marks
For conditional probability, the restricted sample space stated earns the method mark. For independence checks, P(A)P(B) compared with P(A and B) earns both marks. For Bayes-style updates, the tree fractions multiplied along branches earn stepwise credit.
### Traps
Error: mutually exclusive assumed independent. Correction: test, never assume. Error: given-condition ignored. Correction: shrink the denominator first. Error: branches added instead of multiplied. Correction: multiply along, add across.

title: Atomic Structure and the Periodic Table — Study Notes
content:
Atomic Structure and the Periodic Table

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH11, Topic 2. The periodic table is not a list to memorise: its rows and columns follow directly from how electrons fill shells and sub-shells.

Atoms, isotopes and mass spectrometry

  • Protons and neutrons make up the nucleus; the mass number is protons plus neutrons, and the atomic number is the number of protons.
  • Isotopes have the same number of protons and different numbers of neutrons, so the same chemistry but a different mass.
  • Relative atomic mass is the weighted mean of isotopic masses. In a mass spectrum, abundance is read from the peak heights.

Electron configuration

  • Electrons fill orbitals in order of energy: 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d and so on, each orbital holding at most two electrons with opposite spins.
  • Write configurations such as 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ for neon; for transition metals the 4s electrons are lost before the 3d electrons when forming ions.

Periodic trends

  • Ionisation energy increases across a period because nuclear charge rises with similar shielding, and falls down a group as the outer electrons sit further from the nucleus.
  • Atomic radius falls across a period and rises down a group.
  • Successive ionisation energies reveal the group of an element: a large jump appears after the outer-shell electrons are removed.

Electron arrangement and the table

  • Period number = highest principal quantum number in use; group number relates to the number of outer electrons.
  • Blocks: s-block (groups 1-2), p-block (groups 13-18), d-block (transition metals).

Exam tip: when explaining an ionisation energy trend, name the factor (nuclear charge, shielding, distance) and say which way it changes.

title: Cambridge IGCSE First Language English: Analysing Language Choices
content:
Cambridge IGCSE First Language English: Analysing Language Choices

Writer's effect — the analysis of how a writer uses language to create impact — is the skill that separates a competent reader from a top-band one in Cambridge IGCSE First Language English (0500). The question asks you to choose and explain the language that creates a particular effect, and the mark scheme rewards the link from micro-feature to macro-impact: the exact word, the exact method, the exact effect on the reader. This note builds the analytical system from zero: the vocabulary of literary method, the step-by-step deconstruction of the prompt, the effect vocabulary bank, model answers broken down line by line, and the errors that turn analysis into feature-spotting.

The micro-to-macro principle

Writers create effects with tiny tools: a verb choice, a repeated sound, a sentence that stops short. Analysis means moving from the smallest unit (the word) to the largest (the reader's response, the writer's purpose). The chain every top-band answer follows is:

QUOTATION → METHOD → EFFECT ON THE READER → PURPOSE IN CONTEXT
"clawed"   → verb    → makes the wind feel violent and alive → shows
              choice                   the night as an attack

Candidates who stop at METHOD ("the writer uses a metaphor") score nothing for effect; candidates who leap to PURPOSE without quoting score nothing for evidence. The four-beat chain is the answer structure — practise it until it is automatic.

The method vocabulary: what to look for

CategoryFeaturesWhat it tends to do
Diction (word choice)strong verbs, evaluative adjectives, connotation, register shiftsshapes judgement and sympathy
Figurative languagesimile, metaphor, personification, hyperbole, symbolcreates imagery, comparison, emotional colour
Sensory imagerysight, sound, smell, taste, touchimmerses the reader in a place or moment
Sound devicesalliteration, assonance, onomatopoeia, sibilanceadds mood and rhythm; softens or sharpens tone
Sentence structureshort sentences, long sentences, fragments, listing, repetition, questionscontrols pace, tension and emphasis
Perspective and detailwhat is shown or withheld, focalisation, contrast, juxtapositiondirects sympathy and reveals theme

Diction: reading connotation

Words carry two meanings: the dictionary meaning (denotation) and the associations (connotation). Analysis lives in connotation. Compare: the house stood on the hill / the house perched on the hill / the house crouched on the hill. Perched suggests lightness and elevation; crouched suggests menace, weight, waiting. When you analyse diction, name the connotation direction: what does this word suggest that a neutral word would not?

  • Verbs are the richest targets: in "the river snaked through the valley", snaked suggests sinuous movement and a faint threat — analyse the verb before the adjectives.
  • Evaluative adjectives: "the tiny, defiant crowd" already tells the reader how to feel; identify the judgement embedded in the adjective.
  • Register and tone shifts: a formal description suddenly interrupted by a slang word (or the reverse) creates irony or intimacy.

Figurative language: naming the effect precisely

DeviceDefinitionEffect vocabulary
Similecomparison using like or ascompares X to Y, making it vivid / suggesting it is fragile / threatening
MetaphorX is described as Ytransforms X, implying it shares Y's qualities
Personificationhuman qualities given to a thingbrings X alive / makes nature feel hostile or companionable
Hyperboledeliberate exaggerationintensifies emotion / adds humour / shows obsession
Symbolan object that stands for an ideacompresses the theme into an image the reader carries

The analysis must name what the figure compares or implies and what that does to the reader's feeling. "The sky was a bruise" — metaphor: the sky is described as damaged flesh, so the scene feels injured and threatening, suggesting violence has already happened.

Sentence structure and sound as effects

  • Short sentences: shock, finality, tension. "Then the door opened." A short sentence after long ones lands like a punch.
  • Long sentences: accumulation, calm, overload, dreaminess. Lists and polysyndeton (and ... and ... and ...) create breathlessness or abundance.
  • Fragments: a sentence without a verb or subject ("Silence. Then nothing.") mimics broken thought or stunned reaction.
  • Repetition and rule of three: "he ran and ran and ran" or a tricolon builds emphasis and rhythm.
  • Alliteration and sibilance: repeated sounds create mood — sibilance (s, sh sounds) is soft and secretive or sinister; hard consonants (k, t, g) are aggressive and abrupt.
  • Onomatopoeia: words that sound like their meaning (crash, murmur, hissed) pull the reader's ear into the scene.

Deconstructing the prompt: the five-step routine

  1. Underline the effect words in the question — "How does the writer create the atmosphere of tension in this extract?" Your whole answer serves tension; a brilliant point about humour is off-target.
  2. Skim for the effect, not the features: find the lines where the named effect is strongest (usually the turn in the passage).
  3. Select two to three genuinely strong features — one diction point, one figurative or structural point is usually enough for a full-mark answer.
  4. Build the four-beat chain for each — quotation, method, effect on the reader, purpose in context.
  5. Write in a sequence: open with a sentence that answers the question directly ("The writer creates tension through violent diction and oppressive imagery"), develop each feature as a mini-paragraph, and keep the question's effect word in every other sentence as your anchor.

The effect vocabulary bank

Weak answers say "it makes it interesting". Strong answers have a bank of precise effect phrases. Build yours from this list and use each one only when accurate: creates an atmosphere of ...; conveys a sense of ...; makes the reader feel ...; suggests that ...; implies ...; emphasises ...; highlights ...; draws attention to ...; reinforces the idea that ...; leaves the reader expecting ...; unsettles the reader; evokes sympathy for ...; conveys the character's ...; establishes ...; contrasts with ...; signals a shift from ... to ...

Model answer with top-band breakdown

Extract: "The market was a living thing: breathing steam, groaning trolleys, a heartbeat of a thousand footsteps. I stood very still, and it swallowed me whole."

Model answer: "The writer creates an overwhelming, almost frightening sense of the market's scale through personification and metaphor. The market is described as a living thing, breathing steam and groaning trolleys, so the crowd seems to have one body and one will — the reader feels the place as an organism rather than a location. The metaphor continues with the heartbeat of a thousand footsteps, turning ordinary noise into something alive and relentless, which intensifies the speaker's smallness. That smallness is completed by the final metaphor: the market swallowed me whole. The verb swallowed suggests being consumed without trace, so the reader feels the speaker's helplessness and the city's indifference to the individual."

Breakdown of why it hits the top band: it opens by naming the effect (overwhelming, frightening sense of scale) and the methods; each quotation is brief and exact (living thing, swallowed me whole); each method is named (personification, metaphor, verb choice); every effect is reader-directed (the reader feels ...; intensifies ...; suggests being consumed); and the final clause links to purpose in context (the city's indifference). There is no feature-spotting and no padding.

Worked example: deconstructing a prompt

Prompt: "How does the writer create sympathy for the boy in lines 12-20?"
Step 1: effect anchor = sympathy (not fear, not admiration)
Step 2: find the lines where the boy is shown as vulnerable
Step 3: select features:
        (a) diction: "threadbare", "counted his coins twice"
        (b) contrast: the crowd's indifference against his hope
Step 4: build chains:
        (a) threadbare → adjective → clothes worn thin → poverty visible
            counted his coins twice → verb phrase → care and anxiety
            → the reader sees a child managing scarcity alone
        (b) contrast → juxtaposition of the bustling crowd and the boy
            alone → heightens isolation → the reader's sympathy
Step 5: write: open with the answer, develop (a) then (b), keep
        "sympathy" in the anchor sentence and the final line.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Diction) "The old man shuffled to the window." What does shuffled suggest? Answer: The verb suggests slow, dragging, effortful movement — the man is aged or exhausted, so the reader feels his frailty and perhaps pity.
  2. (Simile) "The silence hung over them like a held breath." Explain the effect. Answer: The simile compares the silence to a held breath, so the quiet feels temporary and full of suspense — the reader expects something to happen or break.
  3. (Sentence structure) "He ran. The corridor stretched and stretched. He ran." How does the structure create tension? Answer: The short, repeated sentences create urgency and breathlessness, while the repetition of stretched mimics the corridor's endlessness, making the reader feel the pursuit dragging on.
  4. (Personification) "The house watched them leave." What is the effect? Answer: Giving the house the human action of watching makes it seem alive and perhaps resentful, so the departure feels observed and uneasy rather than free.
  5. (Combined) "The factory exhaled grey smoke that smothered the gardens." Identify two methods and their effects. Answer: Personification (exhaled) makes the factory seem like a living, breathing force; the metaphor smothered presents the smoke as something that kills life, so the reader feels the pollution as an active threat to the community's homes.
  6. (Purpose in context) Why might a writer describe a character's hands as "bird-bones"? Answer: The metaphor compares the hands to fragile bird bones, suggesting thinness and delicacy, which builds a picture of vulnerability — useful if the writer wants the reader to fear for the character's safety.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Feature-spotting: "There is alliteration and metaphor" with no effect commentary is worth nothing. The method name is the start of the sentence, not the answer.
  • "Makes it interesting": the empty effect phrase. Every effect must be specific — interesting to whom, creating what feeling, suggesting what about the character or theme?
  • Long quotations: quote only the words you analyse (two to six words). A lifted sentence without commentary reads as copying.
  • Analysing the wrong thing: the question's effect word is the anchor. An answer about atmosphere when the question asked about sympathy is off-target however good the analysis.
  • Choosing weak features: not every adjective is worth analysis. Pick features that clearly serve the named effect; one deep point beats three shallow ones.
  • Missing the structure level: most candidates analyse words only. A comment on sentence length, repetition or word order after a diction point adds a whole dimension the mark scheme values.
  • No link to context: the four-beat chain ends at purpose — why the writer wants the reader to feel this here. That final clause is the difference between a good and a top answer.
  • Listing without sequencing: a bulleted list of features cannot show the cumulative effect. Write developed mini-paragraphs and order them from the strongest point to the supporting one.

Equations and symbols

This subject has no quantities, so the "equations" here are the structures the mark scheme rewards. Written as formulas they are easier to check your own paragraph against: if a term in the formula is missing from your sentence, that is the mark you have not earned yet.

The analysis chain

writer's effect = feature + connotation + reader response
Key: feature = the named language choice (a word class, a figure, a sentence type); connotation = what that choice suggests beyond its literal meaning; reader response = what the reader now thinks, feels or expects. Three parts, three marks — a paragraph that names a metaphor and stops has earned one of them.

word choice effect = word + its usual associations + what it implies here
Key: the usable method for the "explain how the writer uses language" question: quote a single precise word, state its everyday associations, then say what it suggests about the subject or the speaker in this sentence. Vague adjectives everywhere = no marks.

imagery = vehicle + tenor + ground
Key: vehicle = the image used (a "shark"); tenor = the thing described (the journalist); ground = the quality they share (ruthlessness). Naming the ground is what turns "it is a metaphor" into analysis.

sentence effect = length + structure + what it makes the reader do
Key: length = short or long; structure = simple, compound or complex; effect = the pace or emphasis created. A three-word sentence after two long ones slows the reader down; saying so, and why it matters here, is the mark.

Register and form

register = field + tenor + mode
Key: field = what the text is about; tenor = the relationship between writer and reader (formal or informal, expert or equal); mode = spoken or written, and how permanent. A speech to peers and a report to a head teacher differ in tenor, and that difference is what "maintain the register" means.

transactional writing = audience + purpose + form (APF)
Key: audience = exactly who reads it; purpose = persuade, inform, argue, advise or entertain; form = article, letter, speech, report, review. Decide all three before the first sentence, because every later choice — pronoun, heading, sign-off — follows from them.

directed writing mark split = reading (10) + writing (15)
Key: reading marks come from selecting and developing the bullet points from the passage; writing marks come from register, structure and accuracy. Losing the reading half by inventing material is the commonest way to cap the whole response.

summary = point + supporting detail, in your own words, within the word limit
Key: point = one fact or idea from the passage; supporting detail = the specific information that proves it; own words = no lifted phrases, which are not credited. Ten points for ten marks, so count them before you write.

Composition

narrative arc = equilibrium + disruption + rising action + climax + resolution
Key: the five movements a 500-word story needs so that it feels shaped rather than listed. Start after the disruption if the word limit is tight — a story that begins with the character waking up spends its first paragraph on nothing.

showing = action + sensory detail + consequence
Key: action = what a character physically does; sensory detail = one or two senses engaged; consequence = what changes because of it. "She was nervous" tells; "she checked the door twice before sitting" shows — the same information, credited differently.

paragraph function = one idea, one turn, one image
Key: each paragraph should advance the story once, change the mood once, or plant one image. A paragraph that does none of the three is the one to cut when the word limit bites.

title: Articles and Determiners — Study Notes
content:
Articles (a, an, the) and determiners (some, many, much, each) tell the reader whether a noun is specific, general, countable or uncountable. Small words like these are often where accuracy is lost in writing.

Indefinite article: a and an

Use a or an with a singular countable noun when it is first mentioned or not specific.

  • I bought a bag.
  • He arrived after an hour.

Choose the form by sound, not spelling. Use an before a vowel sound, even when the spelling begins with a consonant: an hour. Use a before a consonant sound, even when the spelling begins with a vowel: a university, a European.

Definite article: the

Use the when both speaker and listener know which thing is meant.

  • The café we visited last week was closed.
  • The sun rises in the east.

No article

Use no article for general plural or uncountable nouns.

  • I like coffee in the morning.
  • Children need sleep.

Determiners with countable and uncountable nouns

  • Many and few go with countable nouns: many books, few students.
  • Much and little go with uncountable nouns: much water, little time.
  • Some and any work with both.

Checking your writing

Ask two questions: is this noun specific to the reader? Is it countable? Those two answers decide the article and the determiner.

title: AS Level Chemistry: Formulae, Equations and Amount of Substance
content:
AS Level Chemistry: Formulae, Equations and Amount of Substance

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH11, Topic 1 is the quantitative foundation of the whole course: every later topic, from titrations to equilibria to organic mechanisms, is marked using the ideas here. This topic covers the vocabulary of formulae, relative masses and the mole, balanced and ionic equations with state symbols, concentration in mol dm⁻³ and ppm, empirical and molecular formulae from experimental data, reacting masses, gas volumes including pV = nRT, percentage yield and atom economy, and the two core practicals that turn these ideas into measurements.

The language of formulae

Chemistry names substances at three levels: the particle, the formula and the amount. The vocabulary is examined directly, so learn the definitions precisely.

  • Atom: the smallest particle of an element that can take part in a chemical reaction.
  • Element: a substance containing only one type of atom; it cannot be broken down chemically into anything simpler.
  • Ion: a particle with a charge produced when an atom or group of atoms loses or gains electrons.
  • Molecule: two or more atoms joined by covalent bonds; it is the smallest particle of a covalent substance that can exist independently.
  • Compound: a substance containing two or more elements chemically combined in fixed proportions.
  • Empirical formula: the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound.
  • Molecular formula: the actual number of atoms of each element in one molecule of a compound.

A molecular formula is a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula. Hydrogen peroxide has the empirical formula HO and the molecular formula H₂O₂; ethanoic acid has the empirical formula CH₂O and the molecular formula C₂H₄O₂. Compounds with giant structures, such as sodium chloride or silicon dioxide, have no molecules, so they are described by their empirical formula alone.

Relative masses and the mole

Relative atomic mass, Aᵣ, is the weighted mean mass of the atoms of an element compared with one twelfth of the mass of an atom of carbon-12. Because it is a mean, it takes account of the natural abundances of the isotopes, which is why chlorine has Aᵣ = 35.5 rather than a whole number.

Relative molecular mass, Mᵣ, is the sum of the relative atomic masses in a molecule. For compounds with giant structures, use the term relative formula mass instead: NaCl has a relative formula mass of 23.0 + 35.5 = 58.5. Molar mass, M, is the mass per mole of a substance in g mol⁻¹, and it is numerically equal to Mᵣ or the relative formula mass.

The mole is the unit for amount of substance. One mole contains the Avogadro number of particles, L = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹. Three relationships do nearly all the work in this topic:

RelationshipUse it for
n = m / Mconverting a mass in grams to moles, and back
N = n × Lconverting moles to a number of particles
n = c × V / 1000moles from concentration in mol dm⁻³ and volume in cm³

Worked example. How many molecules are in 4.40 g of carbon dioxide? M(CO₂) = 12.0 + 2(16.0) = 44.0 g mol⁻¹, so n = 4.40 / 44.0 = 0.100 mol. Then N = 0.100 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 6.02 × 10²² molecules. The number of oxygen atoms is twice that, 1.20 × 10²³, because each molecule holds two oxygen atoms.

Balanced equations, state symbols and ionic equations

A balanced equation has the same number of atoms of each element on both sides, and the total charge must balance too. State symbols (s), (l), (g) and (aq) are part of the answer, not decoration: they are how you show that, for example, a reaction produces hydrogen gas rather than hydrogen atoms. Never change a formula to balance an equation; change only the coefficients. Balance the elements that appear once first, leave hydrogen and oxygen until the end, and check by counting a polyatomic ion such as sulfate or nitrate as one unit.

Ionic equations show only the species that change. To construct one, write the full equation, split every soluble ionic compound into its ions, then cancel the ions that appear unchanged on both sides. Those unchanged ions are spectator ions.

Worked example. Silver nitrate solution added to sodium chloride solution:

AgNO3(aq) + NaCl(aq) → AgCl(s) + NaNO3(aq)
Ag+(aq) + NO3−(aq) + Na+(aq) + Cl−(aq) → AgCl(s) + Na+(aq) + NO3−(aq)
Ag+(aq) + Cl−(aq) → AgCl(s)

Sodium and nitrate ions appear on both sides unchanged, so they are spectators. The ionic equation shows the actual change: hydrated silver ions meeting chloride ions to form a white precipitate.

You must be able to link equations to test-tube observations. Displacement reactions, typical acid reactions and precipitation reactions all follow this pattern: the observation is a change in appearance, and the equation explains it.

ObservationIonic equation
Magnesium added to dilute hydrochloric acid: fizzing, metal dissolves, gas pops with a lighted splintMg(s) + 2H+(aq) → Mg2+(aq) + H2(g)
Zinc added to copper(II) sulfate solution: blue colour fades, red-brown solid formsZn(s) + Cu2+(aq) → Zn2+(aq) + Cu(s)
Barium chloride solution added to sodium sulfate solution: white precipitateBa2+(aq) + SO42−(aq) → BaSO4(s)
Calcium carbonate added to nitric acid: fizzing, solid dissolves, gas turns limewater milkyCaCO3(s) + 2H+(aq) → Ca2+(aq) + H2O(l) + CO2(g)

Concentration, dilution and ppm

Concentration is the amount of solute per unit volume of solution. Two units are used and both are examinable:

  • mol dm⁻³ (molarity): moles of solute per cubic decimetre of solution. 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³.
  • g dm⁻³: mass of solute per cubic decimetre of solution.

The bridge between them is molar mass: g dm⁻³ = mol dm⁻³ × M. So 0.250 mol dm⁻³ sodium hydroxide contains 0.250 × 40.0 = 10.0 g dm⁻³.

Worked example. 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ sodium hydroxide is diluted to 250 cm³. The moles of solute do not change: n = 0.100 × 25.0 / 1000 = 2.50 × 10⁻³ mol. The new concentration is 2.50 × 10⁻³ / 0.250 = 0.0100 mol dm⁻³. Diluting tenfold divides the concentration by ten.

Parts per million, ppm, expresses very small proportions and is used for trace gases in the atmosphere and impurities in water. One ppm means one part in a million by mass or by volume, depending on the context:

ppm = (mass of component / mass of sample) × 10⁶

If the atmosphere contains 410 ppm of carbon dioxide and the total pressure is 100 kPa, the partial pressure of carbon dioxide is 410 / 10⁶ × 100 kPa = 0.0410 kPa. The same number treated as a volume fraction gives 0.041 % by volume.

Empirical and molecular formulae from experiment

Experimental data is converted into a formula in four steps: mass, moles, simplify, then scale using the molar mass.

Worked example. A compound contains 40.0 % carbon, 6.7 % hydrogen and 53.3 % oxygen by mass, and its molar mass is 180 g mol⁻¹.

ElementMass in 100 gDivide by AᵣDivide by smallest
C40.040.0 / 12.0 = 3.331
H6.76.7 / 1.0 = 6.672
O53.353.3 / 16.0 = 3.331

The empirical formula is CH₂O, with empirical formula mass 30.0. The molecular formula is (CH₂O)n where n = 180 / 30.0 = 6, so the molecular formula is C6H12O6. Always check that a ratio such as 1 : 1.5 is multiplied through to 2 : 3 before writing a formula.

Two related experiments are examined. In a magnesium oxide determination, a known mass of magnesium is burned in a crucible, the lid is lifted periodically to let air in, and the mass of the white powder is found; the increase in mass is the mass of oxygen that combined. In a water-of-crystallisation determination, a hydrated salt is heated to constant mass and the loss in mass is the water driven off, giving the value of x in a formula such as CuSO4·xH2O. In both cases heating to constant mass is essential, and in both the evaluation should name the errors: some magnesium oxide may escape as smoke, magnesium may react with nitrogen in the air to form a nitride, or the heating may not have removed all the water.

Reacting masses

A reacting-mass calculation follows the same route every time: balance the equation, convert the known mass to moles, use the mole ratio, convert back to a mass.

Worked example. What mass of iron is produced when 8.00 g of iron(III) oxide is reduced by carbon monoxide?

Fe2O3 + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO2

M(Fe₂O₃) = 2(55.8) + 3(16.0) = 159.6 g mol⁻¹, so n(Fe₂O₃) = 8.00 / 159.6 = 0.0501 mol. The ratio is 1 : 2, so n(Fe) = 0.100 mol and m(Fe) = 0.100 × 55.8 = 5.59 g. Notice that the mass of the solid fell: the oxygen was removed as carbon dioxide, and mass is conserved because the carbon dioxide carries it away.

Where two reactant amounts are given, one will be limiting. Calculate the moles of each, divide by the coefficient in the balanced equation, and the smaller quotient is the limiting reactant. The other is in excess and does not take part fully. All product calculations use the limiting reactant.

Gas volumes, molar volume and pV = nRT

One mole of any gas occupies the same volume at the same temperature and pressure. At room temperature and pressure, this molar volume is approximately 24 dm³ mol⁻¹, so 0.0500 mol of any gas occupies 1.20 dm³. Use this only when the conditions are stated as room temperature and pressure.

When conditions differ, use the ideal gas equation:

pV = nRT

In this equation p is in pascals, V in m³, n in moles, T in kelvin and R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Unit conversion causes most lost marks: 1 kPa = 1000 Pa, 1 dm³ = 1 × 10⁻³ m³, and T = θ + 273.

Worked example. A 0.250 g sample of a volatile liquid is vaporised in a syringe at 100 °C and 100 kPa, and occupies 97 cm³. Find its molar mass.

p = 100 000 Pa, V = 97 × 10⁻⁶ m³, T = 373 K. Then n = pV / RT = (100000 × 97 × 10⁻⁶) / (8.31 × 373) = 9.7 / 3099 = 3.13 × 10⁻³ mol. M = m / n = 0.250 / 3.13 × 10⁻³ = 79.9 g mol⁻¹, so the liquid is likely a small molecule such as benzene (Mᵣ = 78).

Percentage yield and atom economy

Percentage yield compares what you actually obtained with the maximum the equation allows:

percentage yield = (actual yield / theoretical yield) × 10⁰

Reasons for a yield below 100 % include incomplete reaction, reversible reactions, loss during transfer or filtration, side reactions producing other products, and impurities in the reactants.

Atom economy asks a different question: how much of the mass of all the reactants ends up in the product you want?

atom economy = (molar mass of desired product / sum of molar masses of all products) × 10⁰

Worked example. Ethene is hydrated to ethanol: C2H4 + H2O → C2H5OH. The only product is ethanol, so the atom economy is 100 %, even though the yield may be well below that because the reaction is reversible. Compare the synthesis of bromoethane from ethene and hydrogen bromide: C2H4 + HBr → C2H5Br also has 100 % atom economy. In a reaction such as CH4 + Cl2 → CH3Cl + HCl, the desired product has Mᵣ = 50.5 and the products total 50.5 + 36.5 = 87.0, so the atom economy is 58.0 %. The HCl is a co-product with little value, which is why industry prefers addition reactions to substitutions.

Core Practical 1: measurement of the molar volume of a gas

A known mass of magnesium ribbon reacts with excess dilute hydrochloric acid and the hydrogen is collected in a gas syringe. The apparatus is assembled and checked for leaks, the acid is added, and the final syringe reading is taken once the reaction has finished and the apparatus has cooled to room temperature.

Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl2(aq) + H2(g)

Calculation. If 0.024 g of magnesium gives 24.0 cm³ of hydrogen, n(Mg) = 0.024 / 24.3 = 9.88 × 10⁻⁴ mol, and the ratio is 1 : 1, so n(H₂) is the same. The molar volume is 24.0 / 9.88 × 10⁻⁴ = 24 300 cm³ mol⁻¹ = 24.3 dm³ mol⁻¹, close to the accepted 24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹ at room temperature and pressure.

Evaluation. The main sources of error are gas escaping before the bung is replaced, a syringe that sticks or leaks, the temperature not being room temperature when the reading is taken, and the small mass of magnesium producing a large percentage uncertainty in mass. Using a larger mass of magnesium reduces the percentage uncertainty but needs a larger syringe.

Typical mistakes

  • Using the mass of a solution rather than the mass of solute, or forgetting to divide by 1000 when converting cm³ to dm³.
  • Rounding an empirical formula ratio such as 1 : 2.5 to 1 : 3 instead of doubling it to 2 : 5.
  • Changing a subscript to balance an equation instead of the coefficient in front of the formula.
  • Leaving state symbols out of an equation when the question asks for a full equation, or including spectator ions in an ionic equation.
  • Forgetting to convert temperature to kelvin, or pressure to pascals, in pV = nRT.
  • Using the actual yield as the theoretical yield in a percentage-yield calculation.
  • Calculating atom economy from the reactants rather than from the products.

Exam-style questions

  1. Define the terms empirical formula and molecular formula, using a compound of your choice to show the difference. Answer: the empirical formula is the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element; the molecular formula is the actual number of atoms of each element in a molecule. Ethanoic acid has the empirical formula CH2O and the molecular formula C2H4O2.
  2. 0.500 g of a hydrated salt, MgSO4·xH2O, is heated to constant mass and 0.244 g of anhydrous magnesium sulfate remains. Find x. Answer: mass of water lost = 0.500 − 0.244 = 0.256 g. n(MgSO4) = 0.244 / 120.4 = 2.03 × 10⁻³ mol; n(H2O) = 0.256 / 18.0 = 1.42 × 10⁻² mol. The ratio is 1.42 × 10⁻² / 2.03 × 10⁻³ = 7.0, so x = 7 and the formula is MgSO4·7H2O.
  3. Write the ionic equation, with state symbols, for the reaction between aqueous sodium carbonate and dilute hydrochloric acid, and state one observation. Answer: CO32−(aq) + 2H+(aq) → CO2(g) + H2O(l); effervescence, and the gas turns limewater milky.
  4. 25.0 cm³ of 0.150 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid is neutralised by 0.100 mol dm⁻³ sodium hydroxide. Calculate the volume of alkali required. Answer: n(HCl) = 0.150 × 25.0 / 1000 = 3.75 × 10⁻³ mol. HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H2O, so n(NaOH) = 3.75 × 10⁻³ mol and V = n / c = 3.75 × 10⁻³ / 0.100 = 0.0375 dm³ = 37.5 cm³.
  5. Explain why the percentage yield of a reaction can be less than 100 %, and why a reaction with a high percentage yield can still have a low atom economy. Answer: the yield is reduced by incomplete reaction, side reactions, losses in transfer and purification, or by the reaction being reversible. Atom economy depends only on the balanced equation, so a reaction can convert nearly all the limiting reactant into products while most of the product mass is an unwanted co-product.

Revise this topic by practising calculations with the units written at every step, because each mark scheme rewards the mole ratio and the correct final unit as much as the numerical answer. Next, move to Atomic Structure and the Periodic Table, where the mole is used again for relative atomic mass and mass spectra.

title: AS Level Mathematics: Trigonometry
content:
AS Level Mathematics: Trigonometry

Trigonometry at AS level extends the triangle ratios of IGCSE into functions of any angle: the sine and cosine waves that model tides, sound and alternating current, the identities that let you simplify expressions and solve equations, and the sine and cosine rules that handle triangles without a right angle. This note builds the whole topic from zero: the graphs and their properties, exact values, the two core identities, the interval method for solving equations, the sine/cosine rules with the ambiguous case, and transformations of trigonometric graphs. Radian answers are expected wherever the question uses radians.

The three graphs and their properties

FunctionPeriodRangeKey features
sin θ360° (2π)−1 to 10 at 0°, 180°, 360°; maximum at 90°
cos θ360° (2π)−1 to 11 at 0°; 0 at 90°, 270°
tan θ180° (π)all real values0 at 0°, 180°; asymptotes at 90°, 270°

The graphs encode the symmetries the papers test: sin(180° − θ) = sin θ, cos(−θ) = cos θ, sin(−θ) = −sin θ, tan(180° + θ) = tan θ. A quick sketch of the relevant wave inside the required interval solves most equation problems before any algebra.

Worked example. Sketch y = sin x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 360° and mark where sin x = 0.5.

the sine wave crosses 0.5 on its rising part at x = 30 deg
and on its falling part at x = 150 deg (symmetry about 90 deg)
solutions in the interval: x = 30, 150

Exact values

The exact values come from two special triangles and must be known in both degrees and radians:

Anglesincostan
30° = π/61/2√3/21/√3
45° = π/41/√21/√21
60° = π/3√3/21/2√3

Beyond the first quadrant, use the symmetry rules with the reference angle: sin 150° = sin 30° = ½; cos 240° = −cos 60° = −½; tan 135° = −tan 45° = −1. The quadrant sign pattern ("CAST" or a sketch) decides the sign.

Worked example. Find the exact value of cos 300°.

300 deg is in the fourth quadrant; reference angle 60 deg
cos is positive in the fourth quadrant: cos 300 = cos 60 = 1/2

The two identities

sin^2(theta) + cos^2(theta) = 1
tan(theta) = sin(theta)/cos(theta)     (cos theta not 0)

useful rearrangements:
sin^2 = 1 - cos^2;  cos^2 = 1 - sin^2
1 + tan^2 = sec^2 (beyond AS but built from the same identity)

Worked example 1 (simplify). Simplify (1 − cos²θ)/sin θ.

1 - cos^2 = sin^2
sin^2/sin = sin theta   (theta not a multiple of 180 deg)

Worked example 2 (prove). Prove that (sin θ + cos θ)² = 1 + 2 sin θ cos θ.

expand: sin^2 + 2 sin cos + cos^2
rearrange: (sin^2 + cos^2) + 2 sin cos = 1 + 2 sin cos

Worked example 3 (solve with the identity). Solve 2 sin²θ + cos θ = 2 for 0 ≤ θ ≤ 360°.

replace sin^2 = 1 - cos^2:
2(1 - cos^2) + cos = 2
2 - 2cos^2 + cos = 2  ->  -2cos^2 + cos = 0
cos(1 - 2cos) = 0  ->  cos = 0 or cos = 1/2
cos = 0: theta = 90, 270
cos = 1/2: theta = 60, 300

Solving trigonometric equations in an interval

The method that never misses solutions: find the principal value, then use the symmetry of the wave to generate every solution in the interval.

  1. Isolate the trigonometric part (use identities if needed).
  2. Find the principal value with the inverse function.
  3. Use the symmetries: for sin, solutions are θ and 180° − θ (plus 360° steps); for cos, θ and 360° − θ; for tan, θ + 180° steps.
  4. Check every solution lies in the stated interval, and count them.

Worked example. Solve cos 2x = 0.5 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 360°.

let u = 2x, so 0 <= u <= 720
cos u = 0.5  ->  u = 60, 300, 420, 660
x = 30, 150, 210, 330

The doubled-angle trap: the interval for u doubles too. Expand the interval whenever the argument is multiplied.

Worked example 2 (shifted). Solve sin(x − 30°) = 0.6 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 360°.

u = x - 30, so -30 <= u <= 330
sin u = 0.6  ->  u = 36.9 or 143.1
x = 66.9 or 173.1

The sine and cosine rules

sine rule: a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C
cosine rule: a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc cos A
area of a triangle: (1/2) a b sin C

How to choose: two sides and a non-included angle (SSA) or two angles and a side (AAS) use the sine rule; three sides (SSS) or two sides and the included angle (SAS) use the cosine rule. The area formula uses two sides and the included angle.

Worked example 1 (cosine rule). A triangle has sides 8 cm, 11 cm and an included angle of 60°. Find the third side and the area.

a^2 = 8^2 + 11^2 - 2(8)(11)cos 60
    = 64 + 121 - 176(0.5) = 185 - 88 = 97
a = 9.85 cm
area = (1/2)(8)(11) sin 60 = 44 x 0.866 = 38.1 cm2

Worked example 2 (sine rule). In a triangle, angle A = 40°, side a = 7 cm, side b = 10 cm. Find angle B.

sin B / b = sin A / a
sin B = b sin A / a = 10 x 0.643/7 = 0.918
B = 66.7 deg or B = 113.3 deg (ambiguous case)

The ambiguous case

When you know two sides and a non-included angle, the sine rule can produce two valid triangles: angle B could be 66.7° or its supplement 113.3°. Both satisfy the sine rule, and the question must be read to decide which is intended — often a given angle sum rules one out, or the diagram shows an obtuse angle. State both and choose, with a reason.

Worked example. In the triangle above, find the two possible values of angle C and side c.

if B = 66.7: C = 180 - 40 - 66.7 = 73.3 deg
  c/sin 73.3 = 7/sin 40  ->  c = 7 x 0.958/0.643 = 10.4 cm
if B = 113.3: C = 26.7 deg
  c = 7 x 0.449/0.643 = 4.89 cm

Transformations of trigonometric graphs

y = a sin(bx + c) + d
amplitude = |a|;  period = 360/b (or 2 pi/b)
phase shift = -c/b;  vertical shift = d

Worked example. State the amplitude, period and range of y = 3 sin 2x + 1.

amplitude 3; period 360/2 = 180 deg
range: 3 sin 2x ranges -3 to 3, so y ranges 1 - 3 = -2 to 4

Worked example 2 (phase). Describe the transformation y = sin(x + 45°).

a translation of 45 deg to the left (inside the bracket, so the
shift is opposite in sign to the constant)

Worked examples: applied trigonometry

Worked example. A ship sails 30 km on a bearing of 040°, then 20 km on a bearing of 130°. Find its distance and bearing from the start.

the two legs are 90 deg apart (130 - 40), so resolve into east and north
leg 1: east 30 sin 40 = 19.28;  north 30 cos 40 = 22.98
leg 2: east 20 sin 130 = 15.32;  north 20 cos 130 = -12.86
total: east 34.60;  north 10.12
distance = sqrt(34.60^2 + 10.12^2) = sqrt(1197.2 + 102.4) = 36.1 km
bearing: tan(theta) = 34.60/10.12 = 3.419  ->  theta = 73.7 deg
(measured from north towards east)  ->  bearing 074 deg

The component method works for any number of legs; the cosine rule on the included angle is quicker only for exactly two. Either way, bearings are measured clockwise from north at every stage, never from the previous heading.

Radians, arc length and sector area

Radian measure is the natural unit for the trigonometric functions: one radian is the angle subtended at the centre of a circle by an arc equal in length to the radius, and a full turn is 2π radians. The conversions and the two circle formulas are used constantly in P1:

pi radians = 180 deg;  1 radian = 57.3 deg
arc length s = r theta  (theta in radians)
sector area = (1/2) r^2 theta
segment area = sector area - triangle area

Worked example. A sector has radius 6 cm and angle 2 radians. Find its arc length, perimeter and area.

arc = 6 x 2 = 12 cm
perimeter = 12 + 6 + 6 = 24 cm
area = (1/2)(36)(2) = 36 cm2

Worked example 2 (segment). Find the area of the segment cut off by a chord subtending 1.2 radians in a circle of radius 5 cm.

sector = (1/2)(25)(1.2) = 15 cm2
triangle = (1/2)(5)(5) sin 1.2 = 12.5 x 0.932 = 11.65 cm2
segment = 15 - 11.65 = 3.35 cm2

The radian formulas only work in radians; in degrees the arc length is (θ/360)2πr and the sector area (θ/360)πr². Mixing the two is a silent error that costs the accuracy mark.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Exact) Find sin 240° exactly. Answer: third quadrant, reference 60°: −√3/2.
  2. (Identity) Simplify sin²θ/(1 − sin²θ). Answer: sin²θ/cos²θ = tan²θ.
  3. (Solve) Solve tan θ = 1 for 0 ≤ θ ≤ 360°. Answer: θ = 45°, 225°.
  4. (Solve with identity) Solve 3 cos²θ = sin²θ for 0 ≤ θ ≤ 360°. Answer: 3cos² = 1 − cos² → cos² = ¼ → cos = ±½ → θ = 60°, 120°, 240°, 300°.
  5. (Cosine rule) Sides 5 cm and 7 cm with included angle 120°. Find the third side. Answer: a² = 25 + 49 − 70(−0.5) = 109 → a = 10.4 cm.
  6. (Sine rule) A = 35°, B = 80°, a = 9 cm. Find b. Answer: b = 9 sin 80/sin 35 = 9 × 0.985/0.574 = 15.4 cm.
  7. (Area) Find the area of a triangle with sides 6 cm and 9 cm and included angle 50°. Answer: ½ × 54 × sin 50 = 20.7 cm².
  8. (Graph) State the period and amplitude of y = 4 cos 3x. Answer: period 120°, amplitude 4.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Losing solutions: an equation often has more than one solution in the interval; use the symmetry rules or sketch the wave. The commonest mark loss in this topic.
  • Not expanding the interval: for sin 2x over 0 ≤ x ≤ 360°, the argument runs to 720°; solutions are lost without that.
  • Degree/radian mode: the question's units decide the calculator mode; a radian interval (0 to 2π) needs RAD.
  • Wrong rule: sine rule for AAS/SSA, cosine rule for SAS/SSS; using the sine rule on SAS fails silently.
  • Forgetting the ambiguous case: SSA can give two triangles; state both and justify the choice.
  • Identity rearrangement slips: sin² = 1 − cos², not cos² − 1. Sign errors here propagate through the whole solution.
  • Amplitude and period: y = a sin bx has amplitude |a| and period 360/b; the b is not an amplitude.
  • Rounding mid-solution: keep full accuracy until the final answer; angles to 1 d.p. unless told otherwise.

title: Sequences and Series — Study Notes
content:
Sequences and series

An arithmetic progression (AP) adds a constant difference d each term; a geometric progression (GP) multiplies by a constant ratio r. You must master both closed forms, their sums, and the conditions for an infinite sum.

Arithmetic progression

  • nth term: a_n = a + (n - 1)d.
  • Sum: S_n = n/2 [2a + (n - 1)d] = n/2 (first + last).
  • The difference between consecutive terms is constant: a_{n+1} - a_n = d.

Geometric progression

  • nth term: a_n = a r^(n - 1).
  • Sum: S_n = a(r^n - 1)/(r - 1) = a(1 - r^n)/(1 - r).
  • Sum to infinity: S_inf = a/(1 - r), valid ONLY when |r| < 1.

Sigma notation

  • sum of r from 1 to n = n(n + 1)/2; sum of r^2 = n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6; sum of r^3 = [n(n + 1)/2]^2.
  • sum of a constant c over n terms is cn.
  • Split sums: sum (3r + 1) = 3 sum r + sum 1.

Modelling

  • Arithmetic: hire charges, stacked rows, simple interest.
  • Geometric: depreciation, compound interest, population growth, drug decay.
  • For repeated percentage change, multiplier = (1 + percentage/100) per period.

Exam technique

  • Write the first few terms before committing to a formula.
  • Check the sum formula by substituting n = 1 and n = 2.
  • For 'sum exceeds X' questions solve the inequality and take the first integer.

title: Number — Arithmetic and Place Value — Study Notes
content:
Number — Arithmetic and Place Value

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): 1.1 integers & place value; 1.2 fractions/decimals/percentages context; 1.3 powers & roots; HCF/LCM.

1. Types of number

  • Integers: … −2, −1, 0, 1, 2 … Primes: exactly two factors; 2 is the only even prime; 1 is not prime.
  • HCF = product of common prime factors (lowest powers); LCM = all prime factors (highest powers).

Example: 60 = 2²×3×5 and 84 = 2²×3×7 ⇒ HCF = 2²×3 = 12; LCM = 2²×3×5×7 = 420.

2. Place value

In 47 382 the digit 7 has value 7000. Rounding to significant figures: keep n digits, round using the next digit (≥5 up).

Estimation: round inputs to 1 s.f. first — 39.2 × 5.98 ≈ 40 × 6 = 240.

3. Order of operations

BIDMAS. 3 + 4 × 2² = 3 + 16 = 19. Insert brackets yourself when translating words: "3 added to the product of 4 and 2²" = 3 + (4 × 2²).

4. Negative numbers and calculators

Bracket negatives when substituting. Know the ×10ˣ, x², √, ˣ√ and fraction keys; give answers to 3 s.f. unless told otherwise.

5. Bounds (Extended)

Measured to nearest u: UB = +u/2, LB = −u/2. Division p/q: max = UBp ÷ LBq.

Example: 45 cm (nearest cm) in 6 s (nearest s): max speed = 45.5 ÷ 5.5 = 8.27 m/s (3 s.f.).

Exam tips: show prime-factor trees for HCF/LCM; always state rounding units (3 s.f., 1 d.p.); bounds answers quote both limits.

title: Exam technique: Measures of Variation
content:
### What earns the marks
For standard deviation, mean first then the squared-deviation sum earns each mark. For coded data, the y-bar and s_y transformation earns the method mark. For comparisons, mean and spread commented together earns both marks.
### Traps
Error: variance reported as sd. Correction: root last. Error: comparing means only. Correction: comment on spread too. Error: coding applied once then forgotten. Correction: transform consistently.
### Worked example
Five values are 2, 4, 4, 6 and 9. The mean is 25 / 5 = 5. The squared deviations are 9, 1, 1, 1 and 16, which sum to 28. The variance is 28 / 5 = 5.6, and the standard deviation is the square root, about 2.37. Show the squared deviations line on the paper, since the method mark depends on it.
### Check yourself
If each value in the list is increased by 10, state what happens to the mean and to the standard deviation. The mean rises by 10, while the standard deviation is unchanged, because adding a constant does not change the spread.

### Worked example
Five values are 2, 4, 4, 6 and 9. The mean is 25 / 5 = 5. The squared deviations are 9, 1, 1, 1 and 16, which sum to 28. The variance is 28 / 5 = 5.6, and the standard deviation is the square root, about 2.37. Show the squared deviations line on the paper, since the method mark depends on it.

title: Motion in a Circle and Gravity — Study Notes
content:
Motion in a circle and gravity

Circular motion

  • A body moving in a circle at constant speed has a centripetal acceleration of v²/r, directed towards the centre.
  • The centripetal force is F = mv²/r = mω²r, and it is provided by a real force such as tension, friction or gravity. It does no work on the body, because it is always perpendicular to the velocity.

Gravitational field

The gravitational field strength at a point is the force per unit mass placed at that point: g = F/m. Unit: N kg⁻¹. Field lines point towards the mass that creates the field.

Newton's law of gravitation

F = GMm/r², where r is measured from the centre of each point mass. Doubling the separation reduces the force to one quarter.

Gravitational field of a point mass

g = GM/r². Outside a uniform sphere, its field is the same as that of a point mass at its centre.

Gravitational potential

Gravitational potential at a point is the work done per unit mass in bringing a small mass from infinity to that point. It is always negative, is zero at infinity, and becomes more negative closer to the mass: V = −GM/r. Gravitational potential energy of a mass m is Ep = mV.

Worked example: a 2.0 kg object moves in a circle of radius 0.50 m at 3.0 m s⁻¹. The centripetal force is F = mv²/r = (2.0 × 3.0²) ÷ 0.50 = 36 N.

Exam tips: use r as the distance from the centre, not the surface. State that gravitational potential is negative and rises to zero at infinity. Field strength and potential are different quantities: do not mix their units.

Gravitational potential and escape velocity

Gravitational potential at a point is the work done per unit mass in moving a small mass from infinity to that point, so φ = -GM/r. Potential is negative because work must be done against gravity to remove a mass to infinity. The change in gravitational potential energy between two radii is GMm(1/r1 - 1/r2). A body escapes a planet when its kinetic energy equals the potential energy needed to reach infinity, which gives the escape speed v = √(2GM/r).

Exam tip: use the zero of potential at infinity, and keep the sign of the potential negative in every calculation.

title: IGCSE Mathematics: Inequalities
content:
IGCSE Mathematics: Inequalities

Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580 (2025–2027), section 2 Algebra and graphs, statement 2.6 Inequalities — solving and interpreting linear inequalities, listing integer solutions, and (Extended) regions in the coordinate plane. An inequality describes a range of values rather than one exact value, and solving one follows the same balance principle as solving an equation, with one critical difference: multiplying or dividing by a negative number reverses the inequality sign. This note shows why that happens, writes out every solution line by line, and finishes with the region-shading questions that distinguish Paper 4.

What an inequality says

The four inequality symbols extend the equals sign: < (strictly less than), > (strictly greater than), ⩽ (less than or equal to), ⩾ (greater than or equal to). A solution is a set of values, drawn on a number line with a hollow circle for strict inequalities (the endpoint is excluded) and a solid circle for inclusive ones (the endpoint is included).

StatementMeaningNumber line
x > 3Every value greater than 3, not including 3Hollow circle at 3, arrow to the right
x ⩽ −1Every value up to and including −1Solid circle at −1, arrow to the left
2 ⩽ x < 5Values from 2 up to, but not including, 5Solid circle at 2, hollow at 5, line between

Why the sign flips when multiplying by a negative. Start with the true statement 3 < 5. Multiply both sides by −2 without thinking: −6 < −10 is false, because −10 is further left than −6. The correct statement is −6 > −10. Multiplying by a negative mirrors the number line, which reverses order — so the inequality symbol must reverse too. That single rule causes more lost marks than any other in this topic.

Solving linear inequalities

Use the equation methods unchanged, and remember the one reversal rule:

Solve:  5x - 7 > 3x + 1        (give the solution as an inequality)

5x - 3x > 1 + 7               [add 7 to both sides, subtract 3x from both sides]
2x > 8
x > 4                         [divide by +2: the sign does not reverse]
Solve:  3 - 2x ⩽ 11

-2x ⩽ 11 - 3                  [subtract 3 from both sides]
-2x ⩽ 8
x ⩾ -4                        [divide by -2: the sign REVERSES from ⩽ to ⩾]

The check is direct: x = −4 gives 3 − 2(−4) = 11 ⩽ 11 ✓, and x = 0 gives 3 ⩽ 11 ✓ while x = −5 gives 13 ⩽ 11 ✗ — so the boundary and direction are right.

Solve and list the integer solutions:  2 < (5x - 1)/3 ⩽ 8

Multiply every part by 3:
6 < 5x - 1 ⩽ 24
7 < 5x ⩽ 25                   [add 1 to every part]
7/5 < x ⩽ 5                   [divide every part by +5]

The integers are 2, 3, 4 and 5.

Compound inequalities (a value trapped between two bounds) are solved in one line per operation across all three parts — exactly like a three-pan balance.

Inequalities from word problems

Many questions ask for the greatest or least integer satisfying a condition. Translate carefully: at least means ⩾, at most means ⩽, more than means >, within or no more than means ⩽.

A cinema ticket costs £8. A group has £100 and must keep at least £12 for travel.
How many tickets can they buy?

Let n be the number of tickets:  8n + 12 ⩽ 100
8n ⩽ 88
n ⩽ 11

They can buy at most 11 tickets.

The final answer is a whole number in context: a group cannot buy a fraction of a ticket, so the solution set is the integers up to 11.

Regions in the coordinate plane (Extended)

The line y = mx + c divides the plane into two half-planes: points above it satisfy y > mx + c and points below it satisfy y < mx + c. A region question asks you to shade the set of points satisfying several inequalities at once.

  • Draw the boundary line y = mx + c as a solid line when the inequality includes equality (⩽ or ⩾), and as a dashed line when it is strict (< or >).
  • Test one point not on the line — the origin (0, 0) is easiest when the line misses it. Substitute into the inequality; if it is true, shade the side containing the test point.
  • Shade the side that satisfies every inequality; the answer region is the overlap, and the question often asks for the coordinates of a point inside it.
Shade the region satisfying:  y ⩽ 2x + 1,  y > -x + 2,  x ⩾ 0

Line 1: y = 2x + 1, solid. Test (0, 0): 0 ⩽ 1 true, so shade below-left of this line.
Line 2: y = -x + 2, dashed. Test (0, 0): 0 > 2 false, so shade the side away from the origin.
Line 3: x = 0 (the y-axis), solid, shade to the right.

The solution region is the triangle-like area satisfying all three, e.g. the point (2, 2):
2 ⩽ 5 ✓, 2 > 0 ✓, 2 ⩾ 0 ✓.

Describing a region in words is the reverse skill: read the boundary lines, note whether each is dashed or solid, and translate the shaded side back into an inequality.

Maximum and minimum values over a region (Extended)

Region questions often finish by asking for the largest or smallest value of an expression such as x + 2y for points inside the shaded region. A linear expression grows steadily in one direction across the plane, so over a region bounded by straight lines its extreme values always sit at the corners. The method is therefore exact: find the coordinates of every vertex of the region, substitute each pair into the expression, and pick the largest or smallest result. Do not stop at the corner that looks likely — an untested corner is the usual place a mark is lost.

Worked example: inequality with a parameter

Find the set of values of k for which the equation x² + kx + 9 = 0 has two distinct real roots.

Two distinct real roots require a positive discriminant:  b² - 4ac > 0
Here a = 1, b = k, c = 9:
k² - 36 > 0
k² > 36
k > 6  or  k < -6

This is an inequality inside a quadratic-context question — exactly the blend of topics Paper 4 rewards. If the requirement had been at least one real root, the inequality would be k² ⩾ 36, giving k ⩾ 6 or k ⩽ −6.

Corner points in practice. Take the region x ⩾ 0, y ⩾ 0, x + y ⩽ 6 and y ⩽ x + 2. Its vertices are where the boundary lines meet:

x = 0 with y = 0            gives (0, 0)
y = 0 with x + y = 6        gives (6, 0)
x = 0 with y = x + 2        gives (0, 2)
x + y = 6 with y = x + 2    gives x + (x + 2) = 6, so 2x = 4, x = 2 and y = 4, the corner (2, 4)

Evaluate P = x + 2y at each corner:
(0, 0): P = 0     (6, 0): P = 6     (0, 2): P = 4     (2, 4): P = 10

Maximum P = 10 at (2, 4);  minimum P = 0 at (0, 0).

The minimum sits at the origin only because this region includes it; a region bounded away from the origin puts its minimum at one of the other corners. Substitute every vertex before choosing.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Not reversing the inequality sign after multiplying or dividing by a negative number. −2x < 8 means x > −4.
  • Reversing the sign when multiplying by a positive number, or reversing when subtracting — only multiplication and division by negatives reverse it.
  • Hollow versus solid circles: < and > exclude the endpoint; ⩽ and ⩾ include it. Writing x > 4 when x = 4 works is a boundary error.
  • Flipping the inequality direction mid-solution so the final statement faces the wrong way.
  • Forgetting to reverse in a compound inequality: every part flips when the whole chain is multiplied by a negative.
  • In region questions, drawing a solid boundary for a strict inequality (or a dashed one for ⩽), or shading the wrong side because no test point was used.
  • Reporting a decimal when the question asks for integers: n ⩽ 11.25 means the largest integer is 11, not 11.25.
  • Treating ⩽ as < in a word problem: at most 5 includes 5.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 2, 3 marks). Solve 7 − 3x > 1 and show your solution on a number line.

Answer: −3x > −6, so x < 2 (the sign reverses). Number line: hollow circle at 2, shading to the left.

Question 2 (Paper 2, 3 marks). Solve 2 ⩽ 3x + 5 < 14 and list the integer solutions.

Answer: Subtract 5 throughout: −3 ⩽ 3x < 9. Divide by 3: −1 ⩽ x < 3. The integers are −1, 0, 1, 2.

Question 3 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Find the values of x for which x² − 5x + 4 < 0.

Answer: Factorise: (x − 1)(x − 4) < 0. The quadratic is negative between its roots, so 1 < x < 4. (Test x = 2: 4 − 10 + 4 = −2 < 0 ✓; test x = 0: 4 > 0 ✗.)

Question 4 (Paper 4, 5 marks). Shade the region defined by y > x − 1, y ⩽ 3 and x ⩾ 0, and write down the coordinates of one point in the region.

Answer: Draw y = x − 1 dashed (strict), y = 3 solid and x = 0 solid. The origin test for y > x − 1 gives 0 > −1, true, so shade above the dashed line; y ⩽ 3 shades below the horizontal line; x ⩾ 0 shades right of the y-axis. The overlap is a triangle with vertices (0, 3), (4, 3) and (0, −1); the point (1, 1) lies inside: 1 > 0 ✓, 1 ⩽ 3 ✓, 1 ⩾ 0 ✓.

Question 5 (Paper 4, 4 marks). A rectangle has a perimeter of at most 60 cm and a length of (x + 4) cm. Write an inequality for its width w and find w when x = 8.

Answer: 2[(x + 4) + w] ⩽ 60, so (x + 4) + w ⩽ 30 and w ⩽ 26 − x. With x = 8: w ⩽ 18 cm, and the width must also be positive, so 0 < w ⩽ 18.

Question 6 (Paper 2, 3 marks). The solutions of 5x + a ⩾ 0 include x = −2. Find the smallest integer value of a.

Answer: Substituting x = −2: −10 + a ⩾ 0, so a ⩾ 10. The smallest integer value is 10.

With equations and inequalities mastered, the next stage of algebra is sequences and functions.

Inequality symbols and the number line

An inequality compares two expressions that are not necessarily equal. There are four symbols, and each one says which side is larger. Reading the symbol correctly is the first step in every inequality question, and most errors in this topic start with a misread symbol rather than with the algebra.

The four inequality symbols

The symbol < means less than, > means greater than, ≤ means less than or equal to, and ≥ means greater than or equal to. The open symbols < and > exclude the boundary value, and the symbols with a bar underneath include it. Write the symbol that matches the wording, because "at least 5" is ≥ 5 and "more than 5" is > 5.

Drawing a number line

Mark the boundary value on a number line with an open circle for < or >, and a filled circle for ≤ or ≥. Shade the side of the line that contains the solutions. A filled circle at 3 with shading to the right shows x ≥ 3, which includes 3 itself. The open circle at 3 with shading to the left shows x < 3, which does not.

Writing a solution set from a number line

To write the inequality from a number line, find the boundary value, decide whether the circle is open or filled, and check the direction of the shading. Shading to the right of the boundary gives a greater-than form, and shading to the left gives a less-than form. Read the direction from the arrow of the shading, not from the side on which the circle sits.

Solutions as whole numbers

Many questions ask for the integers that satisfy an inequality. If x < 4 and x is a positive integer, the solutions are 1, 2 and 3, and 4 is excluded. The boundary value decides the list: x ≤ 4 would include 4. List the values in order, separated by commas, and do not include values that the inequality excludes.

Double inequalities

A double inequality such as −2 < x ≤ 5 states two conditions at once: x is greater than −2 and x is at most 5. On a number line, the two boundaries limit a single shaded section. Keep the inequality in one line when you solve it, and apply every operation to all three parts, so that the middle term is treated the same as the outer two.

Common reading errors

The two errors that cost the most marks are reversing the boundary value by mistake and marking the circle the wrong way. An answer of x ≤ 3 drawn with an open circle is wrong even though the direction is right, because the examiner checks the circle as well as the shading. Check both before you move on to the algebra.

Solving linear inequalities step by step

A linear inequality is solved in the same way as a linear equation, with one rule added: the inequality sign changes direction whenever both sides are multiplied or divided by a negative number. The subsections below take the steps in the order an examiner marks them.

Collecting the variable on one side

Add or subtract terms until all the x-terms sit on one side and the constants sit on the other. Adding or subtracting the same quantity from both sides keeps the inequality true, and the sign stays the same. For 3x + 5 > x + 11, subtract x from both sides to get 2x + 5 > 11, then subtract 5 to get 2x > 6.

Dividing by a positive number

Divide both sides by the coefficient of x. When that coefficient is positive, the inequality sign stays the same. From 2x > 6, dividing by 2 gives x > 3, and the solution is every value greater than 3.

Dividing by a negative number

When both sides are divided by a negative number, the sign must flip. From −4x ≥ 12, dividing by −4 gives x ≤ −3. Check this by taking a value from the solution: x = −5 satisfies the original inequality, since −4 × (−5) = 20 is at least 12, and −5 is less than −3.

Multiplying by a fraction or a bracket

To remove a fraction, multiply both sides by the denominator, which is positive in most questions, so the sign stays the same. Expand any bracket before you collect terms. For (x − 2) / 3 < 4, multiply both sides by 3 to get x − 2 < 12, then add 2 to get x < 14.

Checking the solution with a test value

Choose a value that lies inside your solution and substitute it into the original inequality. If x > 3 is correct, the value 4 should make the original statement true. If it does not, the sign was reversed somewhere in the working. A test value takes a few seconds and catches the most common error in this topic.

Writing the answer in the form the question asks for

Give the answer as an inequality in x, such as x < 5, or in the form the question asks for. Keep the variable on the left in the final answer, and make sure the sign matches the direction you found. A correct solution written with the wrong symbol still loses the mark.

Equations and symbols

An inequality is solved like an equation with one extra rule, and the region questions are all the same line tested against a point. This sheet is the boundary lines and the sign rule — the two places marks are lost.

y = mx + c Key: y and x = the coordinates of a point on the plane (no units); m = the gradient; c = the y-intercept. Drawn solid when the inequality includes equality (⩽ or ⩾) and dashed when it is strict (< or >) — the line style is the first mark of a region question.

y = 2x + 1 Key: the boundary line of y ⩽ 2x + 1, drawn solid because equality is included. Test the origin (0, 0): 0 ⩽ 1 is true, so shade the side containing the origin — testing, never guessing, is what earns the shading mark.

y = -x + 2 Key: the boundary line of y > −x + 2, drawn dashed because the inequality is strict, so points on the line are excluded. Here (0, 0) gives 0 > 2, false, so the region is the side away from the origin.

x = 0 (the y-axis) Key: the boundary of x ⩾ 0; a vertical line has no gradient to quote, which is why the general form breaks down and the line is named instead. Shade to the right of it.

x + y = 6 Key: a boundary written in implicit form; the intercepts are (6, 0) and (0, 6). With y = x + 2 it meets at x + (x + 2) = 6, so x = 2 and y = 4 — corner (2, 4), where the maximum of a linear expression over that region always sits.

x² + kx + 9 = 0 Key: x = the variable; k = the unknown coefficient; the condition "two distinct real roots" becomes b² − 4ac > 0 with a = 1, b = k, c = 9, so k² > 36 and k > 6 or k < −6. The result is a pair of rays, not an interval between them — writing 6 < k < −6 is the standard wrong answer.

The sign rule, in one table

OperationEffect on the sign
Add or subtract the same valueUnchanged
Multiply or divide by a positive numberUnchanged
Multiply or divide by a negative numberReverses: < becomes >, ⩽ becomes ⩾
Reverse the two sidesReverses: 3 < 5 is the same statement as 5 > 3

Traps specific to the algebra

  • Forgetting to reverse when dividing by a negative: −2x ⩽ 8 gives x ⩾ −4.
  • Reversing when subtracting, which is not a reversal at all.
  • Hollow versus solid endpoints: x = 4 does not satisfy x > 4.
  • Reporting 11.25 when the question asks for the greatest integer, which is 11.
  • Shading every inequality's own side instead of their overlap.

title:
Energy Flow, Ecosystems and the Environment — Quick Revision Summary

This is the fast map of Edexcel International A2 Biology WBI14. It stays in the same order as the full notes so you can cross-reference, and it repeats the specification numbers so you can see which paragraph exists for which point. Use it to organise detail, not to replace the notes. The topic splits into four blocks: the biochemistry of photosynthesis and energy currency, the way energy moves through trophic levels, the ecology of populations and communities and the evidence for climate change, and the wrap-up in metabolic rate and evolution.

Photosynthesis and energy currency

Photosynthesis is the pathway that captures light energy and stores it in chemical form by using that energy to split water, combine the hydrogen with carbon dioxide, and release oxygen. The overall equation is the shorthand: carbon dioxide and water, with light, yield glucose and oxygen. The important conceptual point is that the energy is not just “used” by the plant; it is stored in the bonds of the product, and the water-splitting step is the one that makes oxygen.

  • 5.1 The overall reaction needs light energy to split the strong bonds in water, storing hydrogen in glucose by combining it with carbon dioxide and releasing oxygen to the atmosphere. This is the source of the atmospheric oxygen we breathe and the entry point for energy into ecosystems.
  • 5.2 The immediate energy currency is ATP. Photophosphorylation uses light energy to phosphorylate ADP to ATP, and the hydrolysis of ATP provides a fast, small packet of energy for endergonic processes. This is why the light-dependent and light-independent reactions are linked through ATP and reduced NADP rather than through glucose directly.
  • 5.3 The light-dependent reactions happen on the thylakoid membranes. Light excites electrons in chlorophyll; those electrons are passed down an electron transport chain; their energy is used to make ATP and to reduce NADP to reduced NADP; and water is split by photolysis, releasing oxygen, protons and replacement electrons. Cyclic and non-cyclic photophosphorylation are both used, and the difference matters: non-cyclic produces ATP, reduced NADP, and oxygen, while cyclic makes ATP only and does not produce reduced NADP or oxygen.
  • 5.4 (i) The light-independent reactions, the Calvin cycle, happen in the stroma. The key enzyme RuBisCO fixes carbon dioxide onto ribulose bisphosphate, RuBP, forming glycerate 3-phosphate, GP. GP is then reduced using ATP and reduced NADP to glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate, GALP. Some GALP leaves the cycle to make glucose and other products; some is used to regenerate RuBP so the cycle can continue.
  • 5.4 (ii) The products of the Calvin cycle are simple sugars used in respiration and in the synthesis of new biological molecules — polysaccharides, amino acids, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids. The link between photosynthesis and the rest of metabolism is that the carbohydrates made here are the raw material for everything else the organism builds.

Chloroplast structure and the pigment basis of photosynthesis

Structure and function are linked in the chloroplast. The thylakoids provide the membrane surface for the light-dependent reactions, the stroma holds the enzymes of the Calvin cycle, and the double membrane isolates the biochemical machinery. The pigments are the reason different wavelengths matter, and their separation by chromatography is both a practical skill and a way to understand absorption and action spectra.

  • 5.5 The chloroplast structure matches the function: thylakoids give a large surface area for light absorption and for the pigment arrays and electron transport chain; the stroma contains the enzymes, including RuBisCO, that run the Calvin cycle; and the envelope keeps the internal conditions separated from the cytoplasm.
  • 5.6 The absorption spectrum shows how much light of each wavelength a pigment absorbs; the action spectrum shows the rate of photosynthesis at each wavelength. In an ideal case they track each other because the wavelengths a pigment absorbs are the ones that drive photosynthesis, but the two are not the same concept: one is about the pigment, the other about the whole process.
  • 5.7 Chloroplast pigments can be separated by paper or thin-layer chromatography. The distance each pigment moves compared with the solvent front gives the Rf value: Rf = distance moved by pigment ÷ distance moved by solvent front. The Rf value helps identify the pigment — chlorophylls, carotenoids and xanthophylls all have characteristic Rf values.
  • 5.8 Core Practical 10 investigates the effects of light intensity, light wavelength, temperature and carbon dioxide availability on the rate of photosynthesis using a suitable aquatic plant, measuring oxygen bubbles or gas volume. It is a classic rate experiment, and the point is to see that photosynthesis is affected by more than one factor and that one of them will be limiting at any moment.

Energy transfer between trophic levels

Once light energy is fixed by producers, it moves through the ecosystem when organisms eat one another. The key idea is that energy transfer is inefficient, and the inefficiency is why food chains are short and why top predators are rare. Gross primary productivity and net primary productivity make the accounting explicit.

  • 5.9 (i) Gross primary productivity, GPP, is the total chemical energy fixed by photosynthesis in a given area and time. Net primary productivity, NPP, is GPP minus the energy lost in plant respiration, R. So NPP = GPP − R. NPP is the energy actually available to the next trophic level because it is what remains after the plant has used some of the fixed energy itself.
  • 5.9 (ii) The calculation of NPP is a simple subtraction, but the important understanding is that respiration is the loss and that plants are not perfectly efficient converters of light energy into stored chemical energy, either. A forest can have a high GPP but much of that is respired away, so NPP is what matters for the consumers.
  • 5.10 The efficiency of energy transfer between trophic levels is calculated as (energy or biomass transferred to the next level ÷ energy or biomass received at the previous level) × 100%. The typical figure is well below 100%, often around 10% as a rough guide, because energy is lost in respiration, in egested material, in uneaten parts, and in the energy used by the level itself. This inefficiency is why biomass and energy fall sharply up the trophic levels.

Worked example: if a producer level contains 15000 kJ m−2 year−1 and the primary consumer level contains 1400 kJ m−2 year−1, the transfer efficiency is (1400 ÷ 15000) × 100 = 9.33%. The number itself is not memorable; what matters is that the calculation shows how small the fraction is and why the higher levels get progressively smaller.

Ecology: populations, communities, habitats and niches

Ecology is the study of how organisms interact with each other and with their environment. The basic vocabulary here is the foundation for the rest of the topic, and the specification wants you to know what each term means and how they relate.

  • 5.11 A population is a group of interbreeding individuals of the same species in a habitat; a community is all the populations of different species living and interacting in a habitat; a habitat is the place where an organism lives; and an ecosystem is a self-sustaining system of living organisms interacting with their non-living surroundings. The ecosystem is larger than the community because it includes the abiotic part too.
  • 5.12 The numbers and distribution of organisms are controlled by biotic factors such as competition, predation and disease, and by abiotic factors such as temperature, pH, light intensity and moisture. Which factor limits a population depends on the organism and the environment; in one place it may be food, in another it may be temperature or water.
  • 5.13 The niche concept explains distribution and abundance: a niche is the role of a species in its ecosystem, including the conditions it tolerates, the resources it uses and the interactions it has. Two species cannot indefinitely occupy exactly the same niche, because one will outcompete the other; this is competitive exclusion, and it is one reason species partition resources and why communities can be diverse.
  • 5.14 Core Practical 11 is the fieldwork snapshot: use quadrats to sample abundance and transects, belt or line, to sample distribution, and record abiotic factors at the same time. The point is not just to count organisms but to relate their distribution to the environmental gradient being surveyed. Random sampling is used for abundance where the habitat is uniform; systematic sampling along a transect is used where there is a gradient such as trampling, exposure or moisture.

Succession and communities over time

Communities do not stay the same. After a disturbance or on newly available substrate, a predictable sequence of change occurs, and the endpoint is often a stable community. This is succession, and it matters because it shows that ecosystems are dynamic and that the species present at one time reflect the history of the site, not just the current conditions.

  • 5.15 Succession is the sequence of change from colonisation by pioneer species to a climax community. Pioneer species colonise bare or hostile substrate, change the abiotic conditions — for example by building soil or adding shade — and make the environment less hostile for later species. The community passes through seral stages of increasing complexity and biodiversity until a climax community forms, which is relatively stable and dominated by species adapted to the conditions at that stage.
  • The dynamic point is that succession is not random. It is directional and partly predictable, because the early species modify the environment in ways that favour later ones. Climate change: evidence, causes and modelling

Climate change is the big applied part of this topic, and the specification treats it carefully: it asks for the evidence, the causes, the limitations of models, and the distinction between correlation and causation. This is one of the places where exam questions reward a precise, sceptical answer rather than a confident but vague one.

  • 5.16 Evidence for climate change comes from several independent sources. Atmospheric carbon dioxide records such as the Mauna Loa curve show a rising trend; temperature records show a warming trend; pollen preserved in peat bogs gives information about past vegetation and so past climate; and dendrochronology, tree-ring analysis, gives year-by-year information about growth conditions.   • 5.17 The causes of anthropogenic climate change include the release of greenhouse gases — carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide and water vapour — from human activities. These gases absorb and re-radiate infrared radiation, increasing the amount of energy retained by the atmosphere. This is the enhanced greenhouse effect: the natural greenhouse effect is what makes Earth warm enough to live on, and the enhanced effect is the additional warming from the extra greenhouse gases. To answer well, name the gases and describe the mechanism, not just say “humans cause it”.
  • 5.18 Knowledge of the carbon cycle is used to reduce atmospheric carbon dioxide. Methods include reforestation and afforestation, which increase the removal of CO2 by photosynthesis; protecting peatlands and other carbon-rich ecosystems; reducing fossil fuel combustion; and carbon capture and storage. Each method works by changing the size or direction of a carbon flux, and each has limitations: trees take time to grow and can be lost again, peatlands can be damaged, and capture and storage is not yet universally practical or cheap.
  • 5.19 (i) Data can be extrapolated to make predictions, and models of future climate change are built from such extrapolations and from our understanding of the system. Models are useful precisely because they let us explore the consequences of different scenarios.
  • 5.19 (ii) Models have limitations. The system has complex feedback loops, including cloud cover and ice albedo, that are hard to quantify; historical data are incomplete; and future human behaviour — policy, technology and emissions — is itself unpredictable. A good answer says that models are the best tool available, not that they are perfect, and explains the nature of the uncertainty.
  • 5.20 The effects of climate change include changing rainfall patterns and changes in seasonal cycles, which affect the distribution of species, their development and life cycles. Temperature affects enzyme activity, so it can affect metabolism and development directly as well as shifting the ranges of species.
