Metabolic rate, temperature and evolution

The final block pulls the topic together with two ideas that cut across biology: temperature affects enzyme-controlled metabolism, and evolution is a change in allele frequency. Both are specification points and both are general enough to appear in questions about other topics too.

  • 5.21 Temperature affects enzyme activity up to an optimum; beyond the optimum, enzymes denature because their tertiary and quaternary structures are disrupted by the breakage of hydrogen and ionic bonds. The Q10 temperature coefficient is a way to express how much the rate of a reaction changes with a 10 °C rise: Q10 = rate at T + 10 °C ÷ rate at T. It is not a universal constant; it is a measure that applies to a particular reaction under particular conditions. A common error is to say that high temperature breaks peptide bonds or destroys the primary structure; it does not — it disrupts the higher-order structure that holds the active site in shape.
  • 5.22 Core Practical 12 investigates the effect of temperature on the development of organisms, for example seedling growth rate or brine shrimp hatch rate, while taking into account the ethical use of organisms. The practical point is to measure a rate or a development outcome at different temperatures and to relate it to the effect of temperature on enzyme activity, while using the organisms ethically.
  • 5.23 Evolution is a change in allele frequency in a gene pool over time, brought about by gene mutation creating new alleles and natural selection increasing the frequency of advantageous ones. The important definition is the allele-frequency one: evolution is not “an individual changing during its life”; it is a change in the genetic composition of a population across generations. Mutation provides the variation; selection changes the frequencies.
  • 5.24 Isolation reduces gene flow between populations, allowing them to diverge genetically. Allopatric speciation happens when a physical barrier separates populations so that gene flow stops; sympatric speciation happens in the same habitat through reproductive isolation — differences in timing, behaviour, or genetics that prevent interbreeding. The key difference is the role of a physical barrier: allopatric needs one, sympatric does not. In both cases, the outcome is that populations become so different that they can no longer produce fertile offspring, and they are then distinct species.
  • 5.25 Scientific conclusions about controversial issues can be influenced by who is reaching them. Funding, political agendas and stakeholder motives can affect what conclusions are emphasised or how evidence is interpreted. This is not a claim that science is arbitrary; it is a reason to look at the evidence, the method, and the possible biases, and to distinguish a conclusion that follows from the data from one that is shaped by interests.
  • 5.26 Reforestation and the use of sustainable resources such as biofuels are examples of managing the conflict between human needs and conservation. They try to meet human needs while limiting harm to the environment, and they are practical applications of the ideas in the topic — that ecosystems provide services, that carbon can be kept out of the atmosphere by vegetation and soil, and that trade-offs matter. The point is that conservation is not only about protecting species; it is also about managing the relationship between people and the environment.

Worked examples to practise

These are the sorts of short calculations and comparisons the topic rewards. They are not decoration; they are the most likely exam material from this part of the syllabus.

  • Photosynthesis rate: if an aquatic plant releases 24 bubbles per minute at one light intensity and 48 bubbles per minute at double the intensity, the rate has doubled. The point is to be clear what is being measured and how a change in the independent variable is reflected in the dependent variable. Oxygen production is a proxy for photosynthesis rate; it is not the same as measuring carbon fixed, but it is workable if stated clearly.
  • Efficiency: if producers contain 12000 kJ m−2 year−1 and primary consumers 1500 kJ m−2 year−1, the efficiency is (1500 ÷ 12000) × 100 = 12.5%. Round numbers make the method clear; the actual value does not need to be exactly 10%.

  • Allele frequency: if a population of 200 individuals has 60 individuals with a recessive phenotype and the trait is controlled by a single gene with complete dominance, the frequency of the recessive phenotype is 60 ÷ 200 = 0.30, which is q2 in the Hardy–Weinberg context; the allele frequencies follow from that. This is a bridge to the genetics topic, and it shows that evolution is tracked as a change in allele frequency.

How the pieces fit together

The topic is really about two movements of energy: into ecosystems through photosynthesis and then up through the trophic levels with losses at each step, and the parallel movement of carbon through the carbon cycle. The ecology part places organisms in their populations, communities and environments and explains why they are where they are. The climate change part uses the same system idea — flows, stores, feedbacks — to ask what happens when the energy balance of the planet changes, and what we might do about it.   • Start with the energy: light captured by the pigments of the chloroplast, used to make ATP and reduced NADP, used to fix carbon in the Calvin cycle, ending as sugars that feed respiration and biosynthesis.
  • Move to the transfer: GPP to NPP to the next trophic level, with an efficiency calculation that explains why chains are short.
  • Move to the ecology: populations and communities, biotic and abiotic factors, niche and succession, and the fieldwork methods used to measure them.
  • Move to the change: evidence for climate change, the greenhouse mechanism, the carbon-cycle methods for mitigation, the limits of models, and the biological effects of a warmer, more variable climate.

Typical mistakes

  • Saying the light-dependent reactions make glucose: they make ATP and reduced NADP and oxygen; glucose comes from the Calvin cycle.
  • Confusing absorption spectrum and action spectrum: one is about what the pigment absorbs, the other about the rate of photosynthesis at each wavelength.
  • Using the wrong Rf formula: Rf = distance moved by pigment ÷ distance moved by solvent front. A common variant is to invert it.
  • Treating GPP and NPP as the same thing: NPP is GPP minus respiration, and it is the energy available to consumers.
  • Forgetting to say that transfer efficiency is a percentage and giving the raw fraction alone.
  • Stating that evolution is an individual changing during its lifetime rather than a change in allele frequency in a population.
  • Saying that sympatric speciation needs a physical barrier: it does not; that is allopatric speciation.
  • Saying high temperature breaks peptide bonds or destroys the primary structure of an enzyme: it disrupts the higher-order structure, not the primary sequence.
  • Treating correlation as causation in climate evidence without saying so, or without mentioning the mechanism.
  • Using a single climate indicator as if it proved everything: the evidence is multiple and each line has limitations.

Exam-style questions

  1. Describe the roles of the light-dependent and light-independent reactions of photosynthesis and state where each occurs. Answer: The light-dependent reactions occur on the thylakoid membranes; they use light energy to excite electrons, make ATP and reduced NADP by non-cyclic photophosphorylation, and split water to release oxygen. The light-independent reactions occur in the stroma; they use ATP and reduced NADP to reduce carbon dioxide in the Calvin cycle, producing triose phosphate that can be used to synthesise glucose and other organic molecules. (5 marks)
  2. Explain how gross primary productivity and net primary productivity are related and why net primary productivity is the more important figure for consumers. Answer: GPP is the total energy fixed by photosynthesis; plant respiration uses some of it; NPP is GPP minus respiration, so NPP = GPP − R. NPP is the energy available to the next trophic level because it is what remains after the plant has covered its own respiration, so consumers depend on NPP, not GPP. (4 marks)
  3. Calculate the efficiency of energy transfer if a producer trophic level contains 18000 kJ m−2 year−1 and the primary consumer level contains 1620 kJ m−2 year−1. Answer: Efficiency = (1620 ÷ 18000) × 100 = 9.0%. (2 marks)
  4. Describe how you would investigate the effect of light intensity on the rate of photosynthesis using an aquatic plant, and state one control variable. Answer: Place the aquatic plant in water at a fixed temperature and carbon dioxide concentration; vary the light intensity; count the bubbles of oxygen released per minute or measure the volume of gas collected in a fixed time; keep temperature, carbon dioxide concentration and plant species constant as control variables. (5 marks)
  5. Explain the difference between allopatric and sympatric speciation. Answer: Allopatric speciation occurs when a physical barrier separates populations so gene flow stops and they diverge; sympatric speciation occurs in the same area without a physical barrier, with reproductive isolation such as differences in breeding time or behaviour preventing interbreeding. In both cases the result is that populations become reproductively isolated and form new species. (4 marks)
  6. Describe the evidence for climate change and explain why correlation between two variables is not proof of causation. Answer: Evidence includes rising atmospheric carbon dioxide records, rising temperature records, pollen in peat bogs showing past vegetation, and tree rings. Correlation alone does not prove causation because the two variables could both be affected by a third factor, or the trend could be coincidental; to show causation you need a plausible mechanism and evidence that linking the variables is not better explained by something else. (5 marks)
  7. Explain the effect of temperature on enzyme activity up to and beyond the optimum, and define the Q10 temperature coefficient. Answer: Enzyme activity increases with temperature up to the optimum because molecules have more kinetic energy, but beyond the optimum the enzyme denatures as hydrogen and ionic bonds break and the active site is lost; the primary structure remains intact. Q10 is the factor by which the rate increases when the temperature rises by 10 °C, calculated as rate at T + 10 °C ÷ rate at T. (5 marks)
  8. Describe how reforestation can reduce atmospheric carbon dioxide and state one limitation of this approach. Answer: Trees take up carbon dioxide by photosynthesis and store the carbon in their biomass and in the soil, so planting trees increases the removal of CO2 from the atmosphere and holds it there. Limitation: newly planted trees take time to grow and store significant carbon, forests can be lost to fire or disease, and the land may compete with other uses. (4 marks)

Use this summary to place each idea in the topic before you go into the detail in the full notes. Revise the photosynthesis compartments and their products, the GPP-to-NPP accounting and the efficiency calculation, the ecology vocabulary and fieldwork methods, the climate evidence and the greenhouse mechanism with its mitigation, and the Q10 and allele-frequency ideas that carry into later topics. Then move on to Topic 6: Microbiology, Immunity and Forensics.

Energy Flow, Ecosystems and the Environment — Quick Revision Summary

This is the fast map of Edexcel International A2 Biology WBI14. It stays in the same order as the full notes so you can cross-reference, and it repeats the specification numbers so you can see which paragraph exists for which point. Use it to organise detail, not to replace the notes. The topic splits into four blocks: the biochemistry of photosynthesis and energy currency, the way energy moves through trophic levels, the ecology of populations and communities and the evidence for climate change, and the wrap-up in metabolic rate and evolution.

Photosynthesis and energy currency

Photosynthesis is the pathway that captures light energy and stores it in chemical form by using that energy to split water, combine the hydrogen with carbon dioxide, and release oxygen. The overall equation is the shorthand: carbon dioxide and water, with light, yield glucose and oxygen. The important conceptual point is that the energy is not just “used” by the plant; it is stored in the bonds of the product, and the water-splitting step is the one that makes oxygen.

  • 5.1 The overall reaction needs light energy to split the strong bonds in water, storing hydrogen in glucose by combining it with carbon dioxide and releasing oxygen to the atmosphere. This is the source of the atmospheric oxygen we breathe and the entry point for energy into ecosystems.
  • 5.2 The immediate energy currency is ATP. Photophosphorylation uses light energy to phosphorylate ADP to ATP, and the hydrolysis of ATP provides a fast, small packet of energy for endergonic processes. This is why the light-dependent and light-independent reactions are linked through ATP and reduced NADP rather than through glucose directly.
  • 5.3 The light-dependent reactions happen on the thylakoid membranes. Light excites electrons in chlorophyll; those electrons are passed down an electron transport chain; their energy is used to make ATP and to reduce NADP to reduced NADP; and water is split by photolysis, releasing oxygen, protons and replacement electrons. Cyclic and non-cyclic photophosphorylation are both used, and the difference matters: non-cyclic produces ATP, reduced NADP, and oxygen, while cyclic makes ATP only and does not produce reduced NADP or oxygen.
  • 5.4 (i) The light-independent reactions, the Calvin cycle, happen in the stroma. The key enzyme RuBisCO fixes carbon dioxide onto ribulose bisphosphate, RuBP, forming glycerate 3-phosphate, GP. GP is then reduced using ATP and reduced NADP to glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate, GALP. Some GALP leaves the cycle to make glucose and other products; some is used to regenerate RuBP so the cycle can continue.
  • 5.4 (ii) The products of the Calvin cycle are simple sugars used in respiration and in the synthesis of new biological molecules — polysaccharides, amino acids, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids. The link between photosynthesis and the rest of metabolism is that the carbohydrates made here are the raw material for everything else the organism builds.

Chloroplast structure and the pigment basis of photosynthesis

Structure and function are linked in the chloroplast. The thylakoids provide the membrane surface for the light-dependent reactions, the stroma holds the enzymes of the Calvin cycle, and the double membrane isolates the biochemical machinery. The pigments are the reason different wavelengths matter, and their separation by chromatography is both a practical skill and a way to understand absorption and action spectra.

  • 5.5 The chloroplast structure matches the function: thylakoids give a large surface area for light absorption and for the pigment arrays and electron transport chain; the stroma contains the enzymes, including RuBisCO, that run the Calvin cycle; and the envelope keeps the internal conditions separated from the cytoplasm.
  • 5.6 The absorption spectrum shows how much light of each wavelength a pigment absorbs; the action spectrum shows the rate of photosynthesis at each wavelength. In an ideal case they track each other because the wavelengths a pigment absorbs are the ones that drive photosynthesis, but the two are not the same concept: one is about the pigment, the other about the whole process.
  • 5.7 Chloroplast pigments can be separated by paper or thin-layer chromatography. The distance each pigment moves compared with the solvent front gives the Rf value: Rf = distance moved by pigment ÷ distance moved by solvent front. The Rf value helps identify the pigment — chlorophylls, carotenoids and xanthophylls all have characteristic Rf values.
  • 5.8 Core Practical 10 investigates the effects of light intensity, light wavelength, temperature and carbon dioxide availability on the rate of photosynthesis using a suitable aquatic plant, measuring oxygen bubbles or gas volume. It is a classic rate experiment, and the point is to see that photosynthesis is affected by more than one factor and that one of them will be limiting at any moment.

Energy transfer between trophic levels

Once light energy is fixed by producers, it moves through the ecosystem when organisms eat one another. The key idea is that energy transfer is inefficient, and the inefficiency is why food chains are short and why top predators are rare. Gross primary productivity and net primary productivity make the accounting explicit.

  • 5.9 (i) Gross primary productivity, GPP, is the total chemical energy fixed by photosynthesis in a given area and time. Net primary productivity, NPP, is GPP minus the energy lost in plant respiration, R. So NPP = GPP − R. NPP is the energy actually available to the next trophic level because it is what remains after the plant has used some of the fixed energy itself.
  • 5.9 (ii) The calculation of NPP is a simple subtraction, but the important understanding is that respiration is the loss and that plants are not perfectly efficient converters of light energy into stored chemical energy, either. A forest can have a high GPP but much of that is respired away, so NPP is what matters for the consumers.
  • 5.10 The efficiency of energy transfer between trophic levels is calculated as (energy or biomass transferred to the next level ÷ energy or biomass received at the previous level) × 100%. The typical figure is well below 100%, often around 10% as a rough guide, because energy is lost in respiration, in egested material, in uneaten parts, and in the energy used by the level itself. This inefficiency is why biomass and energy fall sharply up the trophic levels.

Worked example: if a producer level contains 15000 kJ m−2 year−1 and the primary consumer level contains 1400 kJ m−2 year−1, the transfer efficiency is (1400 ÷ 15000) × 100 = 9.33%. The number itself is not memorable; what matters is that the calculation shows how small the fraction is and why the higher levels get progressively smaller.

Ecology: populations, communities, habitats and niches

Ecology is the study of how organisms interact with each other and with their environment. The basic vocabulary here is the foundation for the rest of the topic, and the specification wants you to know what each term means and how they relate.

  • 5.11 A population is a group of interbreeding individuals of the same species in a habitat; a community is all the populations of different species living and interacting in a habitat; a habitat is the place where an organism lives; and an ecosystem is a self-sustaining system of living organisms interacting with their non-living surroundings. The ecosystem is larger than the community because it includes the abiotic part too.
  • 5.12 The numbers and distribution of organisms are controlled by biotic factors such as competition, predation and disease, and by abiotic factors such as temperature, pH, light intensity and moisture. Which factor limits a population depends on the organism and the environment; in one place it may be food, in another it may be temperature or water.
  • 5.13 The niche concept explains distribution and abundance: a niche is the role of a species in its ecosystem, including the conditions it tolerates, the resources it uses and the interactions it has. Two species cannot indefinitely occupy exactly the same niche, because one will outcompete the other; this is competitive exclusion, and it is one reason species partition resources and why communities can be diverse.
  • 5.14 Core Practical 11 is the fieldwork snapshot: use quadrats to sample abundance and transects, belt or line, to sample distribution, and record abiotic factors at the same time. The point is not just to count organisms but to relate their distribution to the environmental gradient being surveyed. Random sampling is used for abundance where the habitat is uniform; systematic sampling along a transect is used where there is a gradient such as trampling, exposure or moisture.

  • Saying high temperature breaks peptide bonds or destroys the primary structure of an enzyme: it disrupts the higher-order structure, not the primary sequence.
  • Treating correlation as causation in climate evidence without saying so, or without mentioning the mechanism.
  • Using a single climate indicator as if it proved everything: the evidence is multiple and each line has limitations.

Exam-style questions

  1. Describe the roles of the light-dependent and light-independent reactions of photosynthesis and state where each occurs. Answer: The light-dependent reactions occur on the thylakoid membranes; they use light energy to excite electrons, make ATP and reduced NADP by non-cyclic photophosphorylation, and split water to release oxygen. The light-independent reactions occur in the stroma; they use ATP and reduced NADP to reduce carbon dioxide in the Calvin cycle, producing triose phosphate that can be used to synthesise glucose and other organic molecules. (5 marks)
  2. Explain how gross primary productivity and net primary productivity are related and why net primary productivity is the more important figure for consumers. Answer: GPP is the total energy fixed by photosynthesis; plant respiration uses some of it; NPP is GPP minus respiration, so NPP = GPP − R. NPP is the energy available to the next trophic level because it is what remains after the plant has covered its own respiration, so consumers depend on NPP, not GPP. (4 marks)
  3. Calculate the efficiency of energy transfer if a producer trophic level contains 18000 kJ m−2 year−1 and the primary consumer level contains 1620 kJ m−2 year−1. Answer: Efficiency = (1620 ÷ 18000) × 100 = 9.0%. (2 marks)
  4. Describe how you would investigate the effect of light intensity on the rate of photosynthesis using an aquatic plant, and state one control variable. Answer: Place the aquatic plant in water at a fixed temperature and carbon dioxide concentration; vary the light intensity; count the bubbles of oxygen released per minute or measure the volume of gas collected in a fixed time; keep temperature, carbon dioxide concentration and plant species constant as control variables. (5 marks)
  5. Explain the difference between allopatric and sympatric speciation. Answer: Allopatric speciation occurs when a physical barrier separates populations so gene flow stops and they diverge; sympatric speciation occurs in the same area without a physical barrier, with reproductive isolation such as differences in breeding time or behaviour preventing interbreeding. In both cases the result is that populations become reproductively isolated and form new species. (4 marks)
  6. Describe the evidence for climate change and explain why correlation between two variables is not proof of causation. Answer: Evidence includes rising atmospheric carbon dioxide records, rising temperature records, pollen in peat bogs showing past vegetation, and tree rings. Correlation alone does not prove causation because the two variables could both be affected by a third factor, or the trend could be coincidental; to show causation you need a plausible mechanism and evidence that linking the variables is not better explained by something else. (5 marks)
  7. Explain the effect of temperature on enzyme activity up to and beyond the optimum, and define the Q10 temperature coefficient. Answer: Enzyme activity increases with temperature up to the optimum because molecules have more kinetic energy, but beyond the optimum the enzyme denatures as hydrogen and ionic bonds break and the active site is lost; the primary structure remains intact. Q10 is the factor by which the rate increases when the temperature rises by 10 °C, calculated as rate at T + 10 °C ÷ rate at T. (5 marks)
  8. Describe how reforestation can reduce atmospheric carbon dioxide and state one limitation of this approach. Answer: Trees take up carbon dioxide by photosynthesis and store the carbon in their biomass and in the soil, so planting trees increases the removal of CO2 from the atmosphere and holds it there. Limitation: newly planted trees take time to grow and store significant carbon, forests can be lost to fire or disease, and the land may compete with other uses. (4 marks)

Use this summary to place each idea in the topic before you go into the detail in the full notes. Revise the photosynthesis compartments and their products, the GPP-to-NPP accounting and the efficiency calculation, the ecology vocabulary and fieldwork methods, the climate evidence and the greenhouse mechanism with its mitigation, and the Q10 and allele-frequency ideas that carry into later topics. Then move on to Topic 6: Microbiology, Immunity and Forensics.

title: AS Level Mathematics: Probability
content:
AS Level Mathematics: Probability

Probability assigns numbers to uncertainty on a scale from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). This note builds the topic from zero: the basic rules, sample spaces and Venn diagrams, mutually exclusive and independent events, tree diagrams for sequences including without-replacement problems, conditional probability in two-way tables, and the counting that makes "equally likely" precise. Every rule is stated with its condition, because most probability errors are conditions applied where they do not hold.

The basic rules

0 <= P(A) <= 1
P(not A) = 1 - P(A)
P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B)   (the addition rule)
P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B|A)            (the multiplication rule)

mutually exclusive: P(A and B) = 0  ->  P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B)
independent: P(A and B) = P(A) P(B)

The subtraction of the overlap is the whole point of the addition rule: counting A and B separately counts their intersection twice.

Worked example. In a class of 30, 18 study French, 12 study German and 6 study both. Find the probability a student studies at least one.

P(F or G) = 18/30 + 12/30 - 6/30 = 24/30 = 0.8
so 6 students study neither

Sample spaces and equally likely outcomes

P(event) = (number of favourable outcomes)/(total outcomes)
valid only when all outcomes are equally likely

Worked example. Two fair dice are thrown. Find the probability the total is 7.

36 equally likely pairs; totals of 7: (1,6)(2,5)(3,4)(4,3)(5,2)(6,1)
P = 6/36 = 1/6

Worked example 2 (systematic listing). A bag holds 2 red and 3 blue counters; two are drawn without replacement. List the sample space and find P(both red).

P(RR) = 2/5 x 1/4 = 2/20 = 1/10
systematic listing confirms 20 ordered pairs, 2 of them RR

Venn diagrams

Two overlapping circles inside a rectangle: the rectangle is the sample space, the overlap is "both", the outside is "neither". Every region should be filled so that the totals match.

|A only| = |A| - |A and B|
|neither| = total - |A or B|

Worked example. 40 students: 22 play football, 15 play hockey, 8 play both. Find P(plays exactly one) and P(plays neither).

football only 14; hockey only 7; both 8; neither 40 - 29 = 11
P(exactly one) = 21/40
P(neither) = 11/40

Tree diagrams

Trees handle sequences of events. Multiply along a branch for "and", add across branches for "or". The second-stage probabilities change when items are not replaced.

Worked example (with replacement). A bag holds 3 red and 2 blue counters. Two are drawn with replacement. Find P(exactly one red).

P(RB) = 3/5 x 2/5 = 6/25
P(BR) = 2/5 x 3/5 = 6/25
P(exactly one red) = 12/25

Worked example 2 (without replacement). Same bag, two draws without replacement.

P(RB) = 3/5 x 2/4 = 6/20
P(BR) = 2/5 x 3/4 = 6/20
P(exactly one red) = 12/20 = 3/5
P(both red) = 3/5 x 2/4 = 3/10

Both branches for "exactly one" are needed: the event can happen in either order, and omitting one branch halves the answer.

Conditional probability

P(B | A) = P(A and B)/P(A)

restricting the sample space to A is the same calculation done
by counting within the row of a two-way table

Worked example (two-way table). 50 students: 30 pass maths, 25 pass physics, 20 pass both. Given a student passed maths, find P(they passed physics).

P(P | M) = 20/30 = 2/3
not 20/50: conditioning has already restricted the sample space to the
30 who passed maths

Worked example 2 (tree). Using the without-replacement bag, find the probability the second is red given the first was blue.

after a blue is removed, 3 red and 1 blue remain
P(R | B) = 3/4

Independence and mutual exclusivity

These two ideas are constantly confused and are logically opposite: mutually exclusive events cannot happen together, while independent events do not influence each other.

mutually exclusive: P(A and B) = 0
independent: P(A and B) = P(A) P(B)

if two events with positive probability are mutually exclusive,
they are NOT independent (knowing one happened rules out the other)

Worked example. A fair coin and a fair die are thrown. Show the events are independent.

P(head) = 1/2;  P(six) = 1/6;  P(head and six) = 1/12
(1/2)(1/6) = 1/12, so the product rule holds: independent

Counting and arrangements

When outcomes are equally likely but numerous, counting techniques are quicker than listing.

product rule for choices: m x n ways for two independent choices
arrangements of n distinct items: n!
arrangements of a selection: n!/(n - r)!

Worked example. A password is 2 letters followed by 2 digits. How many passwords are possible, and what is P(all four characters are distinct)?

total = 26 x 26 x 10 x 10 = 67600
first letter has 26 options, second 25; first digit 10, second 9
favourable = 26 x 25 x 10 x 9 = 58500
P = 58500/67600 = 0.865

Set notation and three-region problems

Exam questions use set notation throughout: A ∩ B for "both", A ∪ B for "either", A′ for "not A". Read every symbol before calculating, and fill a Venn diagram innermost region first.

P(A and B) = P(A ∩ B)
P(A or B) = P(A ∪ B)
P(not A) = P(A′)
P(A only) = P(A) - P(A ∩ B)
P(exactly one) = P(A) + P(B) - 2P(A ∩ B)

Worked example. P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.4, P(A ∩ B) = 0.2. Find P(A′ ∩ B′) and P(exactly one).

P(A ∪ B) = 0.5 + 0.4 - 0.2 = 0.7
P(A′ ∩ B′) = 1 - 0.7 = 0.3
P(exactly one) = 0.5 + 0.4 - 2(0.2) = 0.5

Worked example 2 (three sets). 100 students: 50 study maths, 40 physics, 30 chemistry; 20 study maths and physics, 15 physics and chemistry, 10 maths and chemistry, 5 study all three. How many study none?

union = 50 + 40 + 30 - 20 - 15 - 10 + 5 = 80
the +5 adds back the triple overlap, which the three pairwise
subtractions removed three times and the three singles added
twice too many
none = 100 - 80 = 20

The inclusion-exclusion pattern generalises: add the singles, subtract the pairs, add back the triples. Drawing the three-circle diagram and filling from the centre outward is the safest check.

Expected frequency and fairness

Probability becomes practical when multiplied by the number of trials: expected frequency = probability × trials. A large gap between observed and expected frequency is evidence that the model is wrong — the basis of every fairness question.

expected frequency = n P(event)

fair die, 600 rolls: expected sixes = 600 x 1/6 = 100

Worked example. A die is rolled 600 times and a six appears 130 times. Comment on fairness.

expected = 100;  observed = 130
observed exceeds expected by 30 per cent, a large gap
suggesting the die may be biased towards six, though a formal test
would be needed to judge whether the gap is within natural chance
variation

Worked example 2 (expected profit). A raffle sells 500 tickets at 2 pounds; one prize of 300 pounds. Find the organiser's expected profit.

revenue 1000; expected payout = 300 (certain)
expected profit = 700 pounds, i.e. 1.40 pounds per ticket

When a game's expected payout exceeds its cost the player profits in the long run; comparing expected value with price is the standard modelling question.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Complement) P(A) = 0.35. Find P(not A). Answer: 0.65.
  2. (Addition) P(A) = 0.4, P(B) = 0.5, P(A∩B) = 0.2. Find P(A∪B). Answer: 0.7.
  3. (Mutually exclusive) P(A) = 0.3, P(B) = 0.4, A and B exclusive. Find P(A or B). Answer: 0.7.
  4. (Independent) P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.3, independent. Find P(A and B). Answer: 0.15.
  5. (Dice) Two dice: P(total ≥ 10). Answer: 6/36 = 1/6.
  6. (Tree) 4 red, 6 blue; two without replacement: P(both blue). Answer: 6/10 × 5/9 = 1/3.
  7. (Conditional) From a two-way table, P(A|B) = 0.4 and P(B) = 0.5. Find P(A and B). Answer: 0.2.
  8. (Counting) How many ways can 3 of 5 books be arranged on a shelf? Answer: 5 × 4 × 3 = 60.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Adding without subtracting the overlap: P(A) + P(B) overcounts the intersection; use the full addition rule.
  • Conditional versus joint: P(A|B) restricts the sample space to B; it is not P(A and B)/P(B) with the wrong denominator.
  • Missing branches: "exactly one" usually has two orders; draw the tree and add both paths.
  • Replacement errors: without replacement, both the numerator and the denominator change on the second draw.
  • Independence assumed: the product rule needs independence, which must be justified (or follows from separate random mechanisms).
  • Mutually exclusive confused with independent: exclusive events with positive probability are dependent.
  • Probabilities not summing: the branches from any node must sum to 1; a total that does not is an arithmetic signal.
  • Decimal rounding: keep exact fractions where asked, and do not round intermediate probabilities.

Formula summary

P(not A) = 1 - P(A)
P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B)
P(A and B) = P(A) P(B|A);  independent: P(A) P(B)
P(B|A) = P(A and B)/P(A)
expected frequency = n P(event)

Every one of these is a rearrangement of the multiplication rule or the addition rule. When a question stalls, ask which two of the three quantities — joint, conditional, marginal — you have, and which the question wants.

title: Ratio, Rate and Proportion
content:
Number — Ratio, Rate and Proportion

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): ratio notation, sharing, direct & inverse proportion (including squares/cubes), unit rates.

1. Simplifying and sharing ratios

  • Scale both parts by the same factor: 250 g : 0.4 kg = 250 : 400 = 5 : 8.
  • Share $200 in 3 : 5 → 8 parts → $75 : $125.
  • Part–whole: 3 : 5 ⇒ 3/8 of the total. Given one share, find others by scaling.

Example: A : B = 3 : 4 and B : C = 2 : 5 ⇒ A : B : C = 3 : 4 : 10 (make B equal: ×2).

2. Direct proportion

y = kx. Best method: find the unit value, then multiply.

Example: 5 pens cost $3.25 → 1 pen $0.65 → 8 pens $5.20.

Squared/cubed proportion: y ∝ x². y = 54 when x = 3 ⇒ k = 6 ⇒ y = 6x²; at x = 5, y = 150.

3. Inverse proportion

y = k/x (product constant). 4 workers 6 days ⇒ 24 worker-days ⇒ 8 workers take 3 days. Square-law: y ∝ 1/x².

4. Rates

Unit rates (per item, per litre), exchange rates (draw the arrow to the target currency), best buys (price per unit, careful with multi-packs). Speed/density/pressure are compound-measure rates (Mensuration).

Exam tips: write the proportional equation with k before substituting; check proportion type — "more workers, fewer days" = inverse.

title: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Transformations and Vectors
content:
Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Transformations and Vectors

Transformations move shapes on a grid, and vectors describe those moves with numbers. The exam asks two things: perform a transformation and, more often, describe one completely — with its centre, angle, direction, line or scale factor. This note builds the topic from zero: the four transformations and the full-description checklist for each, enlargement and its effect on area, vector notation with the house column-vector form (x; y), vector arithmetic, and the vector-geometry proofs that show lines are parallel or points are collinear.

The four transformations

TransformationWhat changesWhat must be stated in a description
Translationposition only, no rotation or resizethe column vector of the move
Reflectionmirror imagethe line of reflection (e.g. x = 2, y = x)
Rotationturns about a pointcentre, angle, and direction (clockwise or anticlockwise)
Enlargementresizes about a pointcentre and scale factor

The complete description is the mark: "rotation" alone scores nothing; "rotation 90° anticlockwise about (2, 1)" scores fully.

Translation

A translation moves every point by the same vector. In column form (x; y), x is the horizontal move and y the vertical move; right and up are positive.

Worked example. Triangle A has vertices (1, 1), (3, 1), (1, 4). Translate by (4; −2) and give the image coordinates.

(1, 1) → (5, -1)
(3, 1) → (7, -1)
(1, 4) → (5, 2)

The shape is congruent to the original (same size and shape), and the orientation is unchanged.

Reflection

A reflection flips a shape across a line; the line is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining each point to its image. Common lines: x = a (vertical), y = b (horizontal), y = x, y = −x.

Worked example. Reflect the point (3, 5) in the line y = x.

reflection in y = x swaps the coordinates: (3, 5) → (5, 3)

Worked example 2. Reflect (2, 4) in the line x = 1.

the line x = 1 is vertical; the distance of x = 2 from it is 1,
so the image is 1 unit on the other side: (0, 4)

To find the mirror line from a shape and its image, join a point to its image and draw the perpendicular bisector of that segment.

Rotation

A rotation turns a shape about a fixed centre through a given angle. The four standard angles are 90° and 180° in either direction; 90° clockwise equals 270° anticlockwise.

Worked example. Rotate the point (3, 1) 90° clockwise about the origin.

90 ° clockwise about O: (x, y) → (y, -x)
(3, 1) → (1, -3)

Worked example 2. Rotate (2, 5) 180° about the origin.

180 °: (x, y) → (-x, -y)
(2, 5) → (-2, -5)

For a centre other than the origin, translate the centre to the origin, rotate, then translate back — or count the grid squares from the centre.

Enlargement

An enlargement with centre C and scale factor k maps every point so that its distance from C is multiplied by k. Negative scale factors put the image on the far side of the centre; fractional factors between 0 and 1 shrink the shape.

image distance from centre = k x object distance from centre
area of image = k² x area of object

Worked example. Enlarge the point (2, 3) by scale factor 3 about the origin.

(2, 3) → (6, 9)

Worked example 2 (area). A triangle of area 12 cm² is enlarged by scale factor 2.5. Find the image area.

area factor = k² = 6.25
new area = 12 × 6.25 = 75 cm²

Enlargement is the only transformation that changes area (unless k = 1 or −1); translations, reflections and rotations preserve both shape and size.

Vectors: notation and magnitude

A vector has magnitude and direction. In this course it is written as a column vector (x; y): x is the horizontal component, y the vertical. The same vector can be written as a bold letter a with an arrow above it.

column vector (x; y)
magnitude = √(x² + y²)
direction angle to the horizontal: tan(θ) = y/x
equal vectors have the same components; opposite vectors
negate both components

Worked example. Find the magnitude and direction of the vector (3; 4).

magnitude = √(9 + 16) = 5
tan(θ) = 4/3  →  θ = 53.1 ° above the horizontal

Vector arithmetic and geometry

addition: (a; b) + (c; d) = (a + c; b + d)
subtraction: (a; b) - (c; d) = (a - c; b - d)
scalar multiple: k(a; b) = (ka; kb)

position vector of A relative to O: OA
AB = OB - OA
midpoint of AB: (OA + OB)/2

Worked example. OA = (2; 1), OB = (7; 5). Find AB and the midpoint of AB.

AB = OB - OA = (7 - 2; 5 - 1) = (5; 4)
midpoint = ((2 + 7)/2; (1 + 5)/2) = (4.5; 3)

Worked example 2 (parallel). Show that AB is parallel to CD given A(1, 2), B(5, 8), C(0, 1), D(6, 10).

AB = (5 - 1; 8 - 2) = (4; 6)
CD = (6 - 0; 10 - 1) = (6; 9)
(6; 9) = 1.5 x (4; 6), so CD = 1.5 AB: parallel (and longer)

Parallel vectors are scalar multiples of each other; collinear points occur when AB and AC (or AB and BC) are parallel and share a point.

Combining transformations and invariant points

Two transformations applied in sequence are not the same as the reverse order: a reflection followed by a rotation generally differs from the rotation followed by the reflection. When a question asks for the single transformation equivalent to two, apply both to a convenient point (the origin or a vertex) and to a second point, then identify the transformation that maps the original to the final image. Invariant points are points that do not move: every point on a mirror line is invariant under a reflection, the centre of a rotation is invariant, and no point is invariant under a translation.

Worked example. A shape is reflected in the x-axis and then translated by (0; 3). Find the image of (2, 1) and identify any invariant points.

reflection in the x-axis: (2, 1) → (2, -1)
translation by (0; 3): (2, -1) → (2, 2)
No invariant points: the reflection moved every point off the
axis, and the translation then moved everything upward.

Worked example 2 (invariant line). State the invariant points of a reflection in the line y = 2.

Every point with y-coordinate 2 lies on the mirror line and does
not move: the whole line y = 2 is invariant.

Vectors in context: displacement and velocity

Column vectors describe any quantity with magnitude and direction in two dimensions: displacement (a move from one point to another), velocity (displacement per second) and force (a push in a direction). The arithmetic is identical; only the interpretation changes.

  • Displacement: AB is the vector from A to B; a round trip returns to the start, so the sum of the vectors around a closed polygon is zero.
  • Velocity: a velocity vector (3; −2) means 3 units per second right and 2 units per second down; position after t seconds is the starting position plus t × velocity.
  • Resultant: the sum of two vectors; a vector and its negative cancel.

Worked example. A particle starts at (1, 2) and moves with velocity (3; −1) for 4 seconds. Find its final position.

displacement = 4 x (3; -1) = (12; -4)
final position = (1 + 12; 2 - 4) = (13; -2)

Worked examples: vector proofs

Worked example. In triangle OAB, P is the midpoint of OA and Q is the midpoint of OB. Prove PQ is parallel to AB.

OP = (1/2) OA, OQ = (1/2) OB
PQ = OQ - OP = (1/2)(OB - OA) = (1/2) AB
PQ is a scalar multiple of AB, so PQ is parallel to AB
(and half its length).

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Translation) Translate (2, 3) by (−1; 4). Answer: (1, 7).
  2. (Reflection) Reflect (4, 1) in the x-axis. Answer: reflection in the x-axis maps (x, y) → (x, −y), so (4, 1) → (4, −1).
  3. (Rotation) Rotate (5, 2) 90° anticlockwise about the origin. Answer: a 90° anticlockwise rotation about the origin maps (x, y) → (−y, x), so (5, 2) → (−2, 5).
  4. (Enlargement) Enlarge (1, 2) by factor −2 about the origin. Answer: enlargement about the origin maps (x, y) → k(x, y); with k = −2, (1, 2) → (−2, −4) — the negative factor also puts the image on the opposite side of the centre.
  5. (Description) Describe fully the transformation mapping (1, 1) to (3, 5). Answer: translation vector = image − object = (3 − 1; 5 − 1) = (2; 4), so translation by (2; 4) — one of many correct complete descriptions.
  6. (Magnitude) Find the magnitude of (6; 8). Answer: |v| = √(x² + y²) = √(6² + 8²) = √(36 + 64) = √100 = 10.
  7. (Position vectors) OA = (1; 4), OB = (5; 2). Find AB. Answer: AB = OB − OA = (5; 2) − (1; 4) = (5 − 1; 2 − 4) = (4; −2).
  8. (Collinear) Show A(1, 1), B(3, 4), C(7, 10) are collinear. Answer: AB = (2; 3), AC = (6; 9) = 3 AB — parallel and share A, so collinear.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Incomplete descriptions: "enlargement by 2" omits the centre and loses marks; "reflection" omits the line. State every attribute.
  • Direction of rotation: clockwise and anticlockwise are different transformations; a 90° rotation clockwise is not the same as anticlockwise.
  • Area under enlargement: area scales by k², not k. Doubling the sides quadruples the area.
  • Vector direction: AB = OB − OA, not OA − OB. Reversing the subtraction negates the vector.
  • Column order: (x; y) is horizontal then vertical. Swapping produces a reflection in y = x, not the intended vector.
  • Parallelogram assumptions: equal magnitudes do not imply equal vectors — direction matters too.
  • Negative scale factors: the image lies on the opposite side of the centre; it is not simply "smaller".
  • Collinearity proof: showing parallel is not enough — the segments must also share a point. State it.

Equations and symbols

Every transformation is a coordinate map, and every vector is a column pair. Learn the four rotation maps and the two vector rules, and the topic is arithmetic.

90 ° clockwise about O: (x, y) → (y, -x) Key: (x, y) = the original coordinates; the arrow points to the image's coordinates; O = the origin, the fixed centre. Anticlockwise is the same map with the signs reversed — write the centre down, because a rotation about any other point is not this formula.

180 °: (x, y) → (-x, -y) Key: both coordinates change sign; a half-turn is the only rotation that is also a translation-free "point reflection" in the origin. Check with a point on an axis, where one coordinate stays zero.

reflection in y = x swaps the coordinates: (3, 5) → (5, 3) Key: the line y = x is the mirror; swapping means the image of (x, y) is (y, x). The line is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining each point to its image, which is the definition to quote.

(1, 1) → (5, -1) Key: left = a vertex of the object; right = the matching vertex of the image. Subtract to read off the translation: 5 − 1 = 4 across and −1 − 1 = −2 down, so the column vector is (4; −2).

(3, 1) → (1, -3) Key: this is a 90° clockwise turn about the origin applied to a second vertex — the same map, different numbers. With two vertices mapped you can describe the transformation fully rather than guessing from one.

title: AS Level Mathematics: Sequences and Series
content:
AS Level Mathematics: Sequences and Series

A sequence is an ordered list of numbers generated by a rule; a series is the sum of a sequence. Two families dominate the syllabus: arithmetic (add a constant each time) and geometric (multiply by a constant each time). This note builds the topic from zero: the nth term and sum formulas for both families with derivations, σ notation, recurrence relations, the convergence condition for geometric series, and the applied problems — savings, depreciation, loans — where the formulas earn marks. Every formula is derived once so it can be rebuilt if forgotten.

Arithmetic sequences

nth term: u_n = a + (n - 1)d
sum of n terms: S_n = (n/2)[2a + (n - 1)d] = (n/2)(first + last)

a = first term, d = common difference

Worked example. An arithmetic sequence has first term 5 and common difference 4. Find the 20th term and the sum of the first 20 terms.

u_20 = 5 + 19 × 4 = 81
S_20 = (20/2)(5 + 81) = 10 × 86 = 860

Worked example 2 (working backwards). The 5th term is 17 and the 12th is 45. Find a and d.

u_5: a + 4d = 17
u_12: a + 11d = 45
subtract: 7d = 28  →  d = 4;  a = 17 - 16 = 1

Arithmetic series and the sum formula

The sum formula is Gauss's trick: pair the first and last terms, the second and second-last, and so on; each pair has the same total, and there are n/2 pairs.

Worked example. Find the sum of the first 50 positive even numbers.

a = 2, d = 2, n = 50
last term = 2 + 49 × 2 = 100
S = (50/2)(2 + 100) = 25 × 10² = 2550

Worked example 2 (unknown n). The sum of the first n terms of 3, 7, 11, ... is 210. Find n.

210 = (n/2)[6 + 4(n - 1)] = (n/2)(4n + 2) = 2n² + n
2n² + n - 210 = 0
(2n + 21)(n - 10) = 0  →  n = 10 (n must be positive)

Geometric sequences

nth term: u_n = a r^(n - 1)
sum of n terms: S_n = a(1 - r^n)/(1 - r)   (r not 1)
sum to infinity: S_inf = a/(1 - r)   (only if |r| < 1)

a = first term, r = common ratio

Worked example. A geometric sequence has a = 3 and r = 2. Find the 8th term and the sum of the first 8 terms.

u_8 = 3 × 2⁷ = 384
S_8 = 3(1 - 2⁸)/(1 - 2) = 3(1 - 256)/(-1) = 765

Worked example 2 (working backwards). A geometric sequence has second term 12 and fifth term 96. Find r and a.

u_2 = ar = 12;  u_5 = ar⁴ = 96
divide: r³ = 8  →  r = 2;  a = 6

Sum to infinity and convergence

A geometric series converges only when the ratio has magnitude less than 1: each term is smaller than the last, and the total approaches a finite limit.

if |r| < 1: S_inf = a/(1 - r)
if |r| >= 1: the series diverges (no finite sum)

Worked example. Find the sum to infinity of 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 + ...

a = 8, r = 1/2
S_inf = 8/(1 - 1/2) = 8/(0.5) = 16

Worked example 2 (recurring decimal). Write 0.444... as a fraction using a geometric series.

0.444... = 0.4 + 0.04 + 0.004 + ...
a = 0.4, r = 0.1
S_inf = 0.4/(1 - 0.1) = 0.4/0.9 = 4/9

σ notation and recurrence relations

sum from k = 1 to n of u_k  (σ notation)

recurrence: u_(n+1) = f(u_n), with the first term given

Worked example (σ). Evaluate the sum from k = 1 to 5 of (3k + 1).

terms: 4, 7, 10, 13, 16 (arithmetic, a = 4, d = 3)
S = (5/2)(4 + 16) = 50

Worked example 2 (recurrence). u₁ = 2, u_(n+1) = 3u_n + 1. Find u₄.

u2 = 3(2) + 1 = 7
u3 = 3(7) + 1 = 22
u4 = 3(22) + 1 = 67

Recurrence questions often ask you to prove a sequence is arithmetic or geometric: compute consecutive differences or ratios and show they are constant.

Applied problems

Worked example (savings). A student saves 50 pounds in month 1 and increases the monthly saving by 10 pounds each month. How much is saved in month 12, and in total over the year?

arithmetic: a = 50, d = 10
u_12 = 50 + 11(10) = 160
S_12 = (12/2)(50 + 160) = 6 × 210 = 1260 pounds

Worked example 2 (depreciation). A car worth 18000 pounds loses 15% of its value each year. Find its value after 5 years and the total loss.

geometric: a = 18000, r = 0.85
value after 5 years = 18000 × 0.85⁵ = 18000 × 0.4437 = 7987 pounds
loss = 18000 - 7987 = 10013 pounds

Worked example 3 (interest). 1000 pounds is invested at 4% compound interest. Find the value after 10 years and the total interest.

value = 1000 × 1.04¹⁰ = 1000 × 1.4802 = 1480.24 pounds
interest = 480.24 pounds

Deriving the sum formulas

Knowing where the formulas come from makes them reconstructable under pressure. Write the arithmetic sum forwards and backwards and add:

S = a + (a + d) + ... + [a + (n - 1)d]
S = [a + (n - 1)d] + ... + a
2S = n[2a + (n - 1)d]  (each of the n columns adds to 2a + (n-1)d)
S = (n/2)[2a + (n - 1)d]

The geometric sum is derived by multiplying by r and subtracting, which cancels every intermediate term:

S = a + ar + ar² + ... + ar^(n-1)
rS = ar + ar² + ... + ar^n
S - rS = a - ar^n  →  S(1 - r) = a(1 - r^n)
S = a(1 - r^n)/(1 - r)   (r not 1)

Letting n grow in the geometric formula, rⁿ → 0 whenever |r| < 1, leaving S∞ = a/(1 − r): the same derivation explains convergence, so the condition is not a separate fact to memorise.

Proving a sequence is arithmetic or geometric

Show the consecutive differences or ratios are constant using algebra, not just numbers.

Worked example. The terms of a sequence are 3, 3 + 2k, 3 + 4k, ... Show it is arithmetic and find the sum of the first 10 terms in terms of k.

difference 1: (3 + 2k) - 3 = 2k
difference 2: (3 + 4k) - (3 + 2k) = 2k
constant difference 2k  →  arithmetic with d = 2k
S_10 = (10/2)[2(3) + 9(2k)] = 5(6 + 18k) = 30 + 90k

Worked example 2 (geometric). Show that 2, 2x, 2x², ... is geometric and find the sum to infinity when x = 1/3.

ratio: 2x/2 = x;  2x²/(2x) = x  →  geometric with r = x
with x = 1/3: S_inf = 2/(1 - 1/3) = 3

Combining and interpreting sequences

Some questions give a sequence defined by a rule that is neither purely arithmetic nor geometric, and ask for specific terms or a sum found by splitting it into two familiar parts.

Worked example. Find the sum of the first 20 terms of the sequence whose nth term is 3n + 2ⁿ.

split: arithmetic part 3n (a = 3, d = 3) and geometric part 2^n (a = 2, r = 2)
arithmetic sum: (20/2)[6 + 19 × 3] = 10 × 63 = 630
geometric sum: 2(2²⁰ - 1)/(2 - 1) = 2(1048576 - 1) = 2097150
total = 630 + 2097150 = 2097780

Worked example 2 (loan style). A student repays a 5000 pound debt in monthly instalments that form an arithmetic sequence: 150 pounds in month 1, rising by 20 pounds each month. After how many months is the debt cleared, and what is the final instalment?

S_n = (n/2)[2(150) + (n - 1)(20)] = 5000
(n/2)(300 + 20n - 20) = 5000
n(280 + 20n) = 10000
20n² + 280n - 10000 = 0  →  n² + 14n - 500 = 0
n = [-14 + √(196 + 2000)]/2 = (-14 + 46.86)/2 = 16.4
so 17 instalments are needed; the 17th clears the remainder
final (17th) instalment = 150 + 16(20) = 470 pounds

Two modelling habits earn marks here: round n up (16 instalments leave the debt short) and state what the final, part-full payment means. Reading a plan for feasibility — does the sum actually reach the target? — is also examinable: an arithmetic sum with a negative difference peaks and then falls, so a repayment plan built that way may never clear the debt.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Arithmetic) Find the 15th term of 7, 11, 15, ... Answer: a = 7, d = 4; u₁₅ = 7 + 14(4) = 63.
  2. (Sum) Find the sum of the first 30 terms of 2, 5, 8, ... Answer: d = 3; S = 15(4 + 87) = 1365.
  3. (Geometric) Find the 6th term of 2, 6, 18, ... Answer: r = 3; u₆ = 2 × 3⁵ = 486.
  4. (Sum to infinity) Find S∞ for 12 + 6 + 3 + ... Answer: r = ½; S∞ = 12/(1 − ½) = 24.
  5. (Convergence) For what values of r does a geometric series converge? Answer: |r| < 1.
  6. (Recurrence) u₁ = 5, u_(n+1) = 2u_n − 3. Find u₃. Answer: u₂ = 7, u₃ = 11.
  7. (Reverse) The 3rd term of an arithmetic sequence is 11 and the 8th is 31. Find a and d. Answer: 5d = 20 → d = 4; a = 3.
  8. (Applied) A ball is dropped from 2 m and rebounds to 60% of its height each bounce. Find the total distance travelled before it stops. Answer: down 2; up/down 2(0.6) twice... total = 2 + 2(2×0.6)/(1−0.6) = 2 + 6 = 8 m.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • n − 1 versus n: the nth term uses (n − 1)d, not nd. Off-by-one errors are the commonest in this topic.
  • Count versus term: "sum of the first 20 terms" means n = 20; "the 20th term" means u₂₀. Read which is asked.
  • Sign of r: a negative ratio alternates signs; the convergence condition uses |r|, so r = −0.5 converges.
  • Sum to infinity misused: S∞ exists only for |r| < 1; quoting it for a divergent series is a conceptual mark lost.
  • Depreciation versus interest: depreciation multiplies by (1 − rate); interest by (1 + rate). Getting the factor wrong inverts the answer.
  • Solving for n: the quadratic in n has one positive integer root; reject the negative or fractional value explicitly.
  • Recurrence notation: u_(n+1) means the next term; substituting the wrong index shifts the whole sequence.
  • Exact form: where a question asks for an exact answer, keep fractions and powers; decimal approximations lose the final mark.

title: Circular Measure
content:
Circular Measure

Radians

One radian is the angle subtending an arc equal in length to the radius. π radians = 180°.

  • Degrees → radians: multiply by π/180.
  • Radians → degrees: multiply by 180/π.

Common angles: 30° = π/6, 45° = π/4, 60° = π/3, 90° = π/2, 180° = π, 360° = 2π.

Arc Length

s = rθ (θ in radians).

Example: r = 6, θ = π/3 gives s = 2π.

Sector Area

A = ½r²θ.

Example: r = 5, θ = 1.2 gives A = ½ × 25 × 1.2 = 15.

Segment Area

A = ½r²(θ − sin θ). For r = 2, θ = π/2: A = 2(π/2 − 1) = π − 2.

Rearranging

  • θ = s/r (must be radians)
  • θ = 2A/r²

Exam tips: never mix degrees into s = rθ; convert first. Sketch the sector and mark r and θ before computing, and check whether a question asks for the major or minor sector.

title: Abstract Data Types — Study Notes
content:
Abstract Data Types

What is an ADT?

An abstract data type is a logical description of a collection of data plus the operations on it, independent of implementation. Stacks, queues, linked lists, binary trees and hash tables are all ADTs; in A Level you must show how they are built from arrays or records with pointers.

Linked Lists

Each node holds a value and a pointer to the next node; a start pointer marks the head and a null marks the end. Insertion rewires two pointers — no shifting — giving O(1) insertion at a known position, but access requires walking the list, O(n).

Stacks and Queues

A stack is LIFO (push and pop at the top); a queue is FIFO (enqueue at the rear, dequeue from the front). Both can be arrays with index pointers or linked lists. Stack uses include call stacks and expression evaluation; queue uses include print buffers and breadth-first search.

Binary Search Trees

Each node has up to two children; left subtree keys are smaller, right subtree keys larger. Search, insert and (average-case) delete are O(log n). An in-order traversal outputs keys in ascending order. A degenerate (linear) tree from sorted input degrades to O(n).

Hash Tables

Covered in file organisation, but as an ADT a hash table pairs a hash function with bucket storage for O(1) average access.

Exam tips: be able to draw a tree after a sequence of insertions and write its three traversals; state the pointer changes for a linked-list insertion; compare ADT operations with Big-O.

title: Probability and Statistics II
content:
Probability and Statistics II

Normal Distribution

Continuous, bell-shaped, defined by mean μ and variance σ². Standardise: Z = (X − μ)/σ ~ N(0, 1).

Example: X ~ N(50, 4²). P(X > 56) = P(Z > 1.5) = 1 − 0.9332 = 0.0668.

Backwards problems: given a probability, find μ or σ from the z-value: x = μ + zσ.

Binomial Distribution

Fixed n independent trials, success probability p: P(X = r) = C(n, r) pʳ (1−p)^(n−r). Mean np, variance np(1 − p).

Example: n = 5, p = 0.2: P(X = 2) = 10 × 0.04 × 0.8³ = 0.2048.

Normal Approximation to Binomial

Valid when np > 5 and n(1 − p) > 5. Apply a continuity correction: P(X ≤ 10) becomes P(Y < 10.5) under Y ~ N(np, np(1−p)).

Expectation and Variance Rules

E(aX + b) = aE(X) + b; Var(aX + b) = a² Var(X). For sums: E(X + Y) = E(X) + E(Y).

Exam tips: always sketch the normal curve and shade the region; state the distribution you are using; never forget the continuity correction when approximating a discrete variable.

title: Exam technique: Scatter Diagrams
content:
### What earns the marks
For correlation, direction (rising or falling) and strength (tight or spread) each earn a mark: comment on both. For lines of best fit, the mean point plotted first earns the method mark. For estimation questions, naming interpolation versus extrapolation earns a mark before any value, with the reliability comment credited separately.
### Traps
Error: claiming correlation proves causation. Correction: name the confounder (hot weather drives both). Error: trusting extrapolation like interpolation. Correction: outside the range is always less reliable. Error: forcing the line through the origin. Correction: anchor at (mean x, mean y). Error: calling curved association zero correlation. Correction: zero means no pattern at all.
### Worked example
A scatter diagram shows a positive correlation between hours revised and test score. The line of best fit passes through the mean point (x̄, ȳ). If x̄ = 5 and ȳ = 12 with gradient 2, the line is y = 2x + 2. Estimating y for x = 8 is interpolation if 8 lies within the data range, which makes it more reliable than extrapolating beyond the data.
### Check yourself
Explain why the line of best fit should pass through (x̄, ȳ). Check that 2 × 5 + 2 = 12, so the line does pass through the mean point. State whether a prediction at x = 20 would be interpolation or extrapolation, and say why it is less reliable.

### Worked example
A scatter diagram shows a positive correlation between hours revised and test score. The line of best fit passes through the mean point (x̄, ȳ). If x̄ = 5 and ȳ = 12 with gradient 2, the line is y = 2x + 2. Estimating y for x = 8 is interpolation if 8 lies within the data range, which makes it more reliable than extrapolating beyond the data.

title: Information Representation
content:
`# Information Representation

Number Systems and Ranges

Unsigned binary with n bits stores 0 to 2ⁿ − 1. Two's complement represents negatives: the MSB has value −2ⁿ⁻¹.

Example: 8-bit two's complement of −5: 11111011 (−128 + 64 + 32 + 16 + 8 + 2 + 1).

SystemBaseDigits
Binary20–1
Hexadecimal160–9, A–F
BCD—4 bits per decimal digit

Binary Arithmetic

Add: 0+0=0, 0+1=1, 1+1=0 carry 1, 1+1+1=1 carry 1. Overflow happens when a result exceeds the word size.

Subtraction uses two's complement addition (A − B = A + (−B)).

Text

  • ASCII: 7 bits, 128 characters, English only
  • Unicode: universal scripts; UTF-8 is variable-width (1–4 bytes)

Images and Sound

  • Bitmap: pixels with colour depth (bits per pixel). File size = width × height × depth.
  • Sound: sampling rate (Hz) × bit depth × duration × channels.
  • Resolution trade-off: fidelity vs size.

Compression

  • Lossless (ZIP, run-length encoding): exact reconstruction — required for text/code
  • Lossy (JPEG, MP3): discards perceptually minor data — smaller files

Example: RLE of AAABBBCC → 3A3B2C.

Exam tips: show working for two's complement conversions; state why compression type suits the data (text must be lossless).

title: AS Level Mathematics: Circular Measure
content:
AS Level Mathematics: Circular Measure

Radians measure angles by the arc they cut: one radian is the angle subtended when the arc equals the radius. That definition makes every circle formula simpler — arc length becomes s = rθ and sector area becomes ½r²θ, with no 360 in sight. This note builds the topic from zero: the radian definition and conversions, arc length and sector area with derivations, the segment area formula, and the applied problems (belts, pendulums, cones) that combine circular measure with trigonometry. Every worked example keeps the calculator in radian mode, which is the first habit this topic demands.

Radians and conversion

one full turn = 2 π radians = 360 degrees
π radians = 180 degrees

degrees → radians: multiply by π/180
radians → degrees: multiply by 180/π

common values: 30 ° = π/6, 45 ° = π/4,
60 ° = π/3, 90 ° = π/2, 180 ° = π

Worked example. Convert 150° to radians and 2.4 radians to degrees.

150 x π/180 = 5 π/6 = 2.618 rad
2.4 × 180/π = 137.5 °

Why radians: the arc length formula s = rθ only works when θ is in radians. In degrees the same arc is (θ/360) × 2πr — the same quantity, but with the conversion built in.

Arc length and sector area

arc length: s = r θ
sector area: A = (1/2) r² θ
perimeter of a sector: s + 2r

(θ in radians, r in the same length unit as s)

Worked example 1. A sector has radius 8 cm and angle 1.5 radians. Find the arc length and area.

s = r θ = 8 × 1.5 = 12 cm
A = (1/2) r² θ = 0.5 × 64 × 1.5 = 48 cm²

Worked example 2 (perimeter). Find the perimeter of the same sector.

perimeter = arc + 2 radii = 12 + 16 = 28 cm

Worked example 3 (working backwards). A sector of radius 6 cm has area 27 cm². Find the angle in radians and degrees.

27 = (1/2)(36) θ  →  27 = 18 θ  →  θ = 1.5 rad
in degrees: 1.5 × 180/π = 85.9 °

Segment area

segment area = sector area - triangle area
             = (1/2) r² θ - (1/2) r² sin(θ)
             = (1/2) r² (θ - sin θ)

The triangle is formed by the two radii and the chord; its area uses ½r² sin θ (the sine rule area formula). The subtraction is always the same picture: the segment is the sector with the triangle removed.

Worked example. Find the area of the segment cut off by a chord in a circle of radius 10 cm when the angle at the centre is 1.2 radians.

sector area = (1/2)(10⁰)(1.2) = 60 cm²
triangle area = (1/2)(10⁰) sin(1.2) = 50 × 0.932 = 46.6 cm²
segment = 60 - 46.6 = 13.4 cm²

Worked examples: the standard exam types

Worked example 1 (belt around pulleys). Two pulleys of radius 0.20 m and 0.50 m have centres 1.5 m apart. Find the length of the belt around them (straight sections plus arcs).

straight sections: 2 × 1.5 = 3.0 m (approximately, for the
common external tangents when the radii differ the geometry
needs the tangent length, but the exam version usually gives
equal pulleys or the tangent length directly)
equal-pulley version: belt = 2d + 2 π r = 3.0 + 1.26 = 4.26 m

Worked example 2 (pendulum arc). A pendulum of length 0.80 m swings through 0.6 radians. Find the arc length travelled by the bob.

s = r θ = 0.80 × 0.6 = 0.48 m

Worked example 3 (cone sector). A sector of radius 12 cm and angle 2.0 radians is folded into a cone. Find the base radius.

arc length becomes the base circumference:
s = 12 × 2.0 = 24 cm² π r_base = 24  →  r_base = 24/(2 π) = 3.82 cm

Radian trigonometry and small angles

In radian mode, the trigonometric functions take radian inputs, and small-angle approximations become available: for small θ, sin θ ≈ θ and tan θ ≈ θ (with θ in radians), and cos θ ≈ 1 − θ²/2. These approximations underpin pendulum motion and lens theory later, and they appear in exam questions as "show that for small θ ...".

Worked example. Show that for small θ, the arc length and the chord length are approximately equal.

arc = r θ
chord = 2r sin(θ/2) ~ 2r (θ/2) = r θ  for small θ
so chord ~ arc, with the difference of order θ³

Composite shapes with sectors

Exam figures combine sectors with triangles, rectangles and semicircles. The method is always the same: shade the required region, split it into standard pieces, compute each piece with the radian formulas, then add or subtract. Perimeter questions require the boundary only — internal lines are not part of it.

Worked example. A shape is a rectangle 12 cm by 8 cm with a quarter-circle of radius 8 cm removed from one corner. Find the area and perimeter of the remaining shape.

rectangle area = 96 cm²
quarter circle = (1/4) π r² = (1/4)(3.142)(64) = 50.3 cm²
remaining area = 96 - 50.3 = 45.7 cm²

perimeter: straight edges 12 + 4 + 8 = 24 cm (the 4 cm is the
remaining part of the 8 cm side)
plus the arc: quarter circumference = (1/4)(2 π)(8) = 12.6 cm
total perimeter = 36.6 cm

Worked example 2 (two sectors). Two circles of radius 5 cm have centres 8 cm apart. Find the area common to both.

the overlap is two identical segments. In each circle the chord
subtends an angle θ where cos(θ/2) = 4/5, so θ/2 =
0.6435 and θ = 1.287 rad.
segment area = (1/2)(25)(1.287 - sin 1.287)
             = 12.5(1.287 - 0.960) = 4.09 cm²
common area = 2 × 4.09 = 8.18 cm²

Arc, chord and sector in practice

Three quantities are easy to confuse and each has its own formula. Keep them side by side:

QuantityFormula (θ in radians)What it measures
Arc lengths = r θthe curved boundary
Chord lengthc = 2r sin(θ/2)the straight line joining the arc's ends
Sector areaA = (1/2) r^2 θthe pie-slice region

Worked example. A sector has radius 10 cm and angle 1.0 rad. Find the arc length, chord length and the difference between them.

arc = 10 × 1.0 = 10.0 cm
chord = 2 × 10 x sin(0.5) = 20 × 0.4794 = 9.59 cm
difference = 0.41 cm (the arc bulges beyond the chord)

Worked example (angular speed). A wheel of radius 0.35 m turns at 12 rad s⁻¹. Find the linear speed of a point on its rim and the angle turned in 5 s.

v = r ω = 0.35 × 12 = 4.2 m s⁻¹
angle = ω t = 12 × 5 = 60 rad (about 9.5 full turns)

Angular speed links circular measure to mechanics: one radian per second means one radius of arc per second, so the rim speed is rω. Exam questions on rotating wheels, pulleys and centrifuges all reduce to this one relation, and it also explains why a point near the rim of a wheel moves faster than a point near the hub despite both completing a turn in the same time. The same relation converts between the two ways of measuring rotation: revolutions per minute to radians per second is a factor of 2π/60.

The difference is the sagitta-related gap that appears in lens and bridge questions; it grows as the angle grows, which is why the small-angle approximation fails for large sectors.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Convert) Convert 72° to radians. Answer: 72 × π/180 = 2π/5 ≈ 1.257 rad.
  2. (Arc) Radius 5 cm, θ = 2.0 rad. Find the arc length. Answer: 10 cm.
  3. (Sector) Radius 4 cm, θ = 3.0 rad. Find the area. Answer: ½ × 16 × 3 = 24 cm².
  4. (Reverse) A sector of radius 9 cm has arc length 13.5 cm. Find θ in radians. Answer: θ = 13.5/9 = 1.5 rad.
  5. (Segment) Radius 6 cm, θ = π/3. Find the segment area. Answer: sector = ½ × 36 × π/3 = 6π ≈ 18.85; triangle = ½ × 36 × sin(π/3) = 18 × 0.866 = 15.59; segment ≈ 3.26 cm².
  6. (Perimeter) Find the perimeter of a sector of radius 7 cm and angle 0.8 rad. Answer: arc 5.6 + 14 = 19.6 cm.
  7. (Cone) A sector of radius 10 cm and angle 1.8 rad forms a cone. Find the base radius and slant height. Answer: arc = 18 cm → base radius 18/(2π) = 2.86 cm; slant height = 10 cm.
  8. (Small angle) Use sin θ ≈ θ to estimate sin(0.10) and compare with the calculator value. Answer: ≈ 0.10; calculator 0.0998 — agreement to about 0.2%.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Degree mode: every radians formula requires the calculator in RAD mode. A sin of 1.2 in degree mode gives an entirely different number.
  • Mixing units: s = rθ silently assumes r in metres and s in metres; cm and m mixed in one calculation produces a factor-of-100 error.
  • Half forgotten: sector area is ½r²θ, not r²θ. The ½ comes from the triangle comparison.
  • Angle in degrees in the formula: θ must be radians; convert first, and only convert the final answer back if asked.
  • Perimeter includes the radii: the perimeter of a sector is arc + 2r; the arc alone is not the perimeter.
  • Segment triangle: use ½r² sin θ for the triangle, with θ the same central angle; a different angle changes the answer.
  • Exact versus decimal: when the question says "in terms of π", keep π symbolic; converting to 3.14 loses the required form.
  • Small-angle validity: sin θ ≈ θ is good only for small θ (roughly under 0.2 rad); do not apply it to 1.5 rad.

title: Exam technique: Programming Paradigms
content:
### What earns the marks
For classification, how the computation is expressed decides: machine-mapped is low-level, commanded steps are imperative, wanted results are declarative, data-with-methods is OOP. For OOP benefits, reuse (inheritance) and flexible interfaces (polymorphism) each earn a mark with a mechanism. For errors, TRY plus named EXCEPT earns the handling pair.
### Traps
Error: every language forced into one paradigm. Correction: classify by expression style per snippet. Error: readability sacrificed unknowingly. Correction: assembly trades it for timing control deliberately. Error: unhandled file errors. Correction: wrap risky opens in TRY.

title: Exam technique: Normal Distribution
content:
### What earns the marks
For standardising, Z = (X-mu)/sigma written earns the method mark. For areas, the symmetry or complement step shown earns the second mark. For inverse problems, the z-value from tables stated earns the first mark before unstandardising.
### Traps
Error: variance used as sd in Z. Correction: root the variance first. Error: P(X>a) read directly as the lower tail. Correction: subtract from 1. Error: two unknowns solved from one statement. Correction: need two area statements.

title: Congruence and Similarity
content:
Geometry — Congruence and Similarity

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): congruence criteria, similar shapes, scale factors for length/area/volume, symmetry.

1. Congruence

Criteria: SSS, SAS, ASA (AAS), RHS. State the criterion used when proving triangles congruent, then transfer matching sides/angles.

2. Similarity

Equal angles + sides in proportion. Scale factor k = corresponding new ÷ old.

Example: triangles with sides 4, 6, 8 and 6, 9, 12: k = 1.5.

3. Length, area, volume factors

Length ×k; area ×k²; volume ×k³ — including reverse problems.

Example: volumes 250 cm³ and 2000 cm³: k³ = 8 ⇒ k = 2 ⇒ areas ×4.

4. Area/volume calculations from similarity

Find k from a matching length pair, then apply the right power. Watch hidden pairs (radii, heights, slants).

5. Symmetry

Line symmetry (reflect) and rotational symmetry order — for 2-D shapes and 3-D solids (prisms, cubes, pyramids).

Exam tips: write the matching-vertex order in similarity statements (△ABC ~ △DEF); choose which k-power applies before calculating.

title: Proof — Study Notes
content:
Proof by induction and other formal arguments

Board note: mathematical induction is not in the Edexcel International A Level main specification — it sits in Further Mathematics (FP1, WFM01). Cambridge examines it at A2 (9709).

A2 proof extends the AS toolkit with mathematical induction — the standard method for statements indexed by the positive integers (series formulae, divisibility, inequalities).

The structure of induction

1. Base case: verify the statement directly for n = 1 (or the stated starting value).

2. Inductive step: assume the statement true for n = k (the inductive hypothesis). Prove it true for n = k + 1, using that assumption.

3. Conclusion: by induction the statement is true for all positive integers n >= starting value.

Divisibility inductions

To prove "expression is divisible by m": the base case must divide exactly, and the inductive step writes P(k + 1) = P(k) + m x (something), so divisibility passes from k to k + 1.

Series inductions

To prove a sum formula: write S_{k+1} = S_k + a_{k+1}, substitute the assumed formula for S_k, and simplify to the claimed form with n replaced by k + 1.

When induction is NOT appropriate

  • Statements about all real numbers (use direct proof or contradiction).
  • Finite case lists (use exhaustion).
  • Disproving a universal claim (use a counter-example).

Contradiction and contrapositive

  • To prove "if P then Q" by contradiction: assume P and not Q, and derive nonsense.
  • Contrapositive: prove "if not Q then not P", which is logically equivalent and often cleaner — e.g. "if n^2 is even then n is even" is proved by "if n is odd then n^2 is odd".

title: IGCSE Computer Science: Hardware and Architecture
content:
IGCSE Computer Science: Hardware and Architecture

Cambridge IGCSE Computer Science 0478 (2026–2028), Paper 1 Computer Systems, Topic 3 Hardware: statement 3.1 Computer architecture, 3.2 Input and output devices, and 3.3 Data storage. This is where the physical machine is opened up: what a CPU actually does with machine code, how instructions and data travel around the system, and how storage technologies differ. Every fetch–execute cycle below is traced register by register, because Paper 1 routinely asks you to follow the cycle through a memory dump — and that question is free marks once you have traced it a dozen times.

Hardware, firmware and software: the layers

Before the parts, the big picture — and the analogy that makes the whole topic click. A computer system is a factory. The hardware is the building and machines (physical, touchable). The software is the list of orders the factory must carry out (instructions, intangible). Firmware is software permanently etched into a chip — like the safety rules bolted to the wall: it survives a power cut and tells the hardware how to start. The operating system is the factory manager, deciding which order runs when and which machine each order may use.

The stored-program concept and Von Neumann architecture

Early machines had to be rewired for every new task. The breakthrough of the stored-program concept is that both the instructions and the data they work on live in the same memory, and the CPU reads instructions from memory and obeys them — no rewiring. In the chef analogy: the recipe (program) and the ingredients (data) sit on the same kitchen shelf; the chef fetches a recipe line, does what it says to the ingredients, and moves to the next line.

Von Neumann architecture is the standard layout built on that idea:

  • CPU — the processor, containing the control unit (CU), the arithmetic logic unit (ALU) and registers.
  • Main memory — RAM (and ROM), holding both program instructions and data.
  • Input and output devices — the system's contact with the outside world.
  • Buses — the cables connecting them: address, data and control.

Its famous weakness is the Von Neumann bottleneck: instructions and data share one memory and one set of buses, so the CPU can fetch only one thing at a time and spends much of its cycle waiting. Caches, pipelining and multiple cores exist largely to hide that bottleneck.

Inside the CPU

The control unit fetches and decodes instructions and orchestrates the rest of the machine; it is the foreman. The ALU performs arithmetic (add, subtract, multiply, divide) and logic (comparisons, AND/OR/NOT); it is the workbench. Registers are tiny, extremely fast storage locations inside the CPU — the foreman's desk, where the handful of items being worked on right now are kept.

RegisterFull nameWhat it holds
PCProgram counterThe memory address of the next instruction to fetch
MARMemory address registerThe address currently being read from or written to
MDRMemory data register (also called MBR)The data or instruction just fetched, or about to be written
CIRCurrent instruction registerThe instruction being decoded and executed
ACCAccumulatorThe result of the last ALU calculation

The clock paces the CPU: each tick synchronises one step, and the clock speed (measured in GHz) is the number of ticks per second. Cache is small, very fast memory inside or beside the CPU holding copies of recently used data and instructions — a cache hit saves a slow trip to RAM. Cores are independent processing units; more cores mean more instructions can be completed simultaneously, provided the software is written to use them.

The buses

BusDirectionCarriesWidth matters because
Address busCPU to memory/peripherals (one-way)Memory addressesMore address lines mean more memory can be addressed (n lines address 2ⁿ locations)
Data busBoth waysInstructions and dataMore lines mean more bits per transfer, so wider = faster
Control busBoth waysSignals: read, write, clock, interrupt, resetCoordinates who does what and when

The fetch–decode–execute cycle

Every program is a list of instructions in memory, and the CPU runs them one at a time in a repeating three-stage cycle. Fetch: get the instruction. Decode: work out what it means. Execute: do it. Then the cycle repeats — millions of times per second.

Memory holds addresses like a street of numbered houses. Suppose memory looks like this before the program runs:

Address   Contents   Meaning
  5       0010 1000  LOAD 8        (copy the value at address 8 into the ACC)
  6       0011 1001  ADD 9         (add the value at address 9 to the ACC)
  7       0100 1010  STORE 10      (copy the ACC into address 10)
  8       0000 0101  the value 5
  9       0000 0011  the value 3
 10       0000 0000  (empty)

Trace the whole run, register by register. The first two bits of each instruction are the opcode (the operation) and the remaining six bits are the operand (the address to work on).

Cycle 1 - FETCH of LOAD 8:
  PC = 5. The PC's value is copied to the MAR: MAR = 5.
  The control bus sends a READ signal; memory returns the contents of address 5.
  The instruction arrives in the MDR: MDR = 0010 1000.
  The MDR's value is copied to the CIR: CIR = 0010 1000. PC is incremented: PC = 6.
Cycle 1 - DECODE:
