  The control unit reads the opcode 00 = LOAD: copy the value at the operand address to the ACC.
Cycle 1 - EXECUTE:
  The operand is 01 1000 = address 8. MAR = 8; READ; MDR = 0000 0101 (the value 5).
  ACC = 5.

Cycle 2 - FETCH of ADD 9:
  PC = 6 → MAR = 6; READ; MDR = 0011 1001; CIR = 0011 1001; PC = 7.
Cycle 2 - DECODE:
  Opcode 01 = ADD: add the value at the operand address to the ACC.
Cycle 2 - EXECUTE:
  Operand 01 1001 = address 9. MAR = 9; READ; MDR = 0000 0011 (the value 3).
  ALU computes ACC + MDR = 5 + 3 = 8. ACC = 8.

Cycle 3 - FETCH of STORE 10:
  PC = 7 → MAR = 7; READ; MDR = 0100 1010; CIR = 0100 1010; PC = 8.
Cycle 3 - DECODE:
  Opcode 10 = STORE: copy the ACC into the operand address.
Cycle 3 - EXECUTE:
  Operand 01 1010 = address 10. MAR = 10; MDR = 8 (from the ACC); a WRITE signal
  stores it. Address 10 now holds 0000 1000. The program stops (STOP instruction).

Notice the pattern examiners look for: PC → MAR → (READ) → MDR → CIR for the fetch, PC incremented after the fetch, and the execute stage differing per opcode. An interrupt (a signal from a device demanding attention, like a keypress or timer) pauses the cycle between instructions: the CPU finishes the current instruction, saves the PC, jumps to an interrupt service routine, then returns.

What makes a processor faster

  • More clock cycles per second (GHz) — each instruction is paced by the clock; more ticks per second means more instructions per second, other things equal.
  • More cores — several CPUs on one chip work on different tasks simultaneously.
  • Larger cache — more of the working data sits close to the CPU, so fewer slow RAM accesses.
  • Wider data bus — more bits move per transfer.
  • Instruction set — the set of operations a CPU understands. RISC processors use few simple instructions, each executed in one clock cycle; CISC processors have many complex instructions, each taking several cycles but needing fewer instructions per task. Say what the difference does: fewer cycles per instruction versus fewer instructions per task.
Worked example: a processor runs at 2.0 GHz and each instruction takes 4 cycles.

2.0 GHz = 2.0 × 10⁹ cycles per second
instructions per second = 2.0 × 10⁹ / 4 = 5.0 × 10⁸

So 500 million instructions per second. Clock speed alone is not the whole story:
a 2.0 GHz CPU needing 4 cycles per instruction matches a 4.0 GHz CPU needing 8.

Embedded systems

An embedded system is a processor built into a device to run one dedicated task — the microcontroller in a washing machine, engine management unit, microwave, traffic light or digital camera. Characteristics: single function, small and cheap, low power, often real-time (must respond within a deadline), and rarely updated. Advantages: low cost, compact, reliable, energy-efficient. Disadvantages: inflexible, hard to upgrade or repair, and a bug affects the whole appliance. The exam wants the trade-off stated, not just a list of examples.

Input and output devices

DeviceTypeTypical use and why it suits it
KeyboardInputEntering text and commands quickly and accurately
Mouse / touchscreenInputDirect graphical manipulation; touchscreens suit kiosks where space or hygiene matters
Scanner / cameraInputDigitising documents and images; OCR software then reads the text
Sensors (temperature, light, pressure, moisture)InputAutomatic measurement in control systems — greenhouses, weather stations, car engines
MicrophoneInputSound capture for recording and voice input
Monitor / projectorOutputVisual display; projectors for audiences, monitors for detail
Printer / plotterOutputHard copy; plotters for large-scale technical drawings
Speakers / headphonesOutputSound reproduction
Actuators (motors, heaters, valves, robotic arms)OutputPhysical action in control systems — the hands of an automated system

The sensor–processor–actuator loop is the heart of every automated system: a sensor measures the world, the microprocessor compares the reading with a target, and the actuator changes the world. Choosing a device is always justified by accuracy, speed, cost and environment.

Primary storage: RAM and ROM

RAMROM
VolatilityVolatile — contents lost on power offNon-volatile — contents survive power off
Read/writeBoth, constantlyRead only (written at manufacture or by special processes)
HoldsThe running OS, open programs and their dataBootstrap/firmware: the start-up instructions that load the OS
Speed/sizeFast, measured in GBFast, but small (MB)

Virtual memory extends RAM by reserving space on the secondary storage device: when RAM fills, less-active pages are swapped to disk. It prevents crashes but is slow, because secondary storage is far slower than RAM — thrashing (constant swapping) can make a machine crawl.

Secondary storage: magnetic, optical and solid state

MediumHow it storesStrengthsWeaknesses
Magnetic (HDD, tape)Magnetised regions on spinning platters or tape, read by headsVery cheap per GB, huge capacityMoving parts: slower, noisy, shock-sensitive; tape is sequential access only
Optical (CD, DVD, Blu-ray)Pits and lands burned by laser, read by reflected lightCheap, portable, long shelf life, good for archiving and distributionLow capacity, slower write speeds, easily scratched
Solid state (SSD, USB flash, memory cards)Electrical charges in NAND flash cellsVery fast, silent, robust (no moving parts), low powerMore expensive per GB, finite number of write cycles

Compare on the four axes examiners name: capacity, speed (access and transfer), cost per GB, durability and portability. Choose by use case — an SSD for video editing, an HDD for a media archive, flash for a phone, optical for distributing software.

Cloud storage keeps data on remote servers reached over a network: accessible anywhere, easy to back up and share, with storage that scales without new hardware. Against that: it needs a connection, costs ongoing fees, gives slower access than local storage, and raises privacy and security concerns because data leaves your control. Local storage is fast and offline but vulnerable to loss or theft and limited by device capacity — most systems use both.

Worked example: choosing storage and reading a memory dump

A school records 200 hours of video per year at 1 GB per hour and wants 5 years of archive with daily access, plus backups.

Capacity needed: 200 × 1 × 5 = 1000 GB (about 1 TB), plus backup = 2 TB.

HDD: about £45 per TB, random access for daily retrieval, but a mechanical drive
     is the weak point - keep the backup on a second drive or in the cloud.
SSD: faster and more robust but roughly three times the cost per TB.
Optical: about 25 GB per disc - 80 discs for the archive, sequential retrieval
     only - impractical for daily access.
Cloud: no hardware to fail and off-site backup included, but 2 TB of storage
     for 5 years is an ongoing subscription and every retrieval needs the network.

Choice: working copies on an SSD, archive on one or two HDDs, plus cloud backup.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Saying the fetch stage "executes" the instruction. Fetch retrieves; decode interprets; execute acts — and the PC is incremented during the fetch stage, not the execute stage.
  • Confusing the MAR and the MDR: the MAR holds the address being accessed; the MDR holds the data travelling to or from it.
  • Claiming RAM is permanent because the computer "remembers" files; files live on secondary storage — RAM is volatile.
  • Describing the address bus as two-way; only the data bus is two-way.
  • Listing performance factors without effects: "it has cache" earns nothing; "a larger cache means more data is found without slow RAM access" earns the mark.
  • Calling a sensor an output device; sensors input data, actuators output action.
  • Writing that virtual memory "increases RAM"; it borrows secondary storage and is slower — it prevents out-of-memory failures, not slowness.
  • Forgetting units in capacity calculations (GB vs TB) or mixing up bytes and bits — the classic file-size question trap.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 1, 3 marks). State the purpose of the program counter and the memory address register in the fetch–execute cycle.

Answer: The program counter holds the address of the next instruction to be fetched, so the CPU knows where to look in memory; it is incremented after the fetch. The memory address register holds the address currently being accessed (read from or written to) during the cycle.

Question 2 (Paper 1, 4 marks). Describe what happens to the MDR and CIR during the fetch stage.

Answer: The address in the MAR is sent down the address bus with a READ control signal; memory returns the instruction or data at that address into the memory data register (MDR). The MDR's contents are then copied into the current instruction register (CIR), where the control unit decodes them.

Question 3 (Paper 1, 6 marks). Compare magnetic and solid-state secondary storage for a laptop used for field research.

Answer: Solid state has no moving parts, so it is far more resistant to shock and drops (vital in the field), silent, lighter and much faster, and uses less battery. Against that it costs more per gigabyte and wears out after many write cycles. Magnetic drives offer far more capacity per pound but their spinning platters and heads are damaged by knocks, they are slower and heavier. For field research, robustness and battery life dominate, so solid state is the better choice.

Question 4 (Paper 1, 4 marks). Explain what an embedded system is and give two advantages of using one in a washing machine.

Answer: An embedded system is a processor built into a device to perform one dedicated task, running firmware rather than a general-purpose OS. In a washing machine it is cheap to mass-produce, small enough to fit inside the appliance, low-power, and reliable because there is no general-purpose software to fail — the machine does its one job well and quickly boots each time.

Question 5 (Paper 1, 5 marks). A CPU runs at 3.0 GHz and averages 5 cycles per instruction. Calculate its instruction rate and explain why a 2.0 GHz CPU with 2 cycles per instruction could be faster.

Answer: 3.0 × 10⁹ cycles/second ÷ 5 = 6.0 × 10⁸ instructions per second. The 2.0 GHz CPU gives 2.0 × 10⁹ ÷ 2 = 1.0 × 10⁹ instructions per second — higher despite the lower clock, because instructions per second depends on both clock speed and cycles per instruction, not clock speed alone.

Question 6 (Paper 1, 3 marks). Explain the purpose of virtual memory and one disadvantage of using it.

Answer: When RAM is full, the operating system moves less-active programs and data to a reserved area of secondary storage (the swap file), freeing RAM so programs keep running instead of crashing. Disadvantage: secondary storage is far slower than RAM, so swapping causes noticeable slowdowns — especially thrashing, where the system spends its time swapping rather than working.

With the machine understood at the hardware level, the next question is how it represents everything it knows: data representation.

title: IGCSE Biology: Respiration
content:
IGCSE Biology: Respiration

Respiration is the process that keeps every cell alive: the chemical release of energy from glucose inside cells. It is not breathing, it is not combustion, and it happens day and night in every organism. This note separates the definitions that examiners insist on, writes and balances both the aerobic and anaerobic equations from first principles, traces how energy from glucose is transferred to ATP for use in the cell, and covers oxygen debt, the oxygen debt calculation, and the practical methods for measuring respiration rate (the respirometer) that appear in Paper 6.

What respiration is — and what it is not

Respiration is the chemical reactions in cells that break down nutrient molecules (usually glucose) to release energy, which is transferred to ATP. It occurs in every living cell, all the time. Aerobic respiration requires oxygen and releases much more energy per glucose molecule; anaerobic respiration occurs without oxygen and releases much less. Important distinctions: breathing (ventilation) brings oxygen to the lungs and removes carbon dioxide, but respiration happens inside cells; combustion is burning outside the body; and the energy released is used for muscle contraction, active transport, protein synthesis, cell division and maintaining body temperature (mammals and birds are endothermic).

Aerobic respiration: the equation and its stages

Word equation: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy. Symbol equation: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O. Balance check: 6 carbons each side; 12 hydrogens each side (6 × 2 in water); oxygens: 6 + 12 = 18 on the left, 12 + 6 = 18 on the right. The full pathway at A Level and in the supplement: glycolysis (in the cytoplasm) splits glucose into two pyruvate molecules, releasing a small amount of ATP and reduced NAD; the link reaction and Krebs cycle (in the mitochondrial matrix) strip hydrogen and release carbon dioxide; oxidative phosphorylation (on the inner mitochondrial membrane) uses the hydrogen electrons in the electron transfer chain to make large amounts of ATP, with oxygen as the final electron acceptor forming water. The folded cristae of the inner membrane increase surface area for the ATP-generating enzymes — a favourite structure-function question.

Anaerobic respiration in animals and plants

When oxygen is short (sprinting, flooded roots), cells switch to anaerobic respiration. In animals: glucose → lactic acid (+ a little energy), equation C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₃H₆O₃. Only glycolysis runs, so the yield is 2 ATP per glucose versus about 30–32 aerobically. Lactic acid accumulates in muscles, causing fatigue and cramp, and must be broken down later. In plants and yeast: glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide + energy, equation C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂. Yeast fermentation is used industrially to make bread (carbon dioxide raises the dough) and alcoholic drinks (ethanol); both anaerobic equations must balance — check the atoms: C₆ → 2C₃ (animals) or 2C₂ + 2C (yeast, six carbons total), H₁₂ → 6 in two lactic acid molecules or 12 in two ethanol molecules, and the oxygens accordingly.

Oxygen debt

Oxygen debt (excess post-exercise oxygen consumption) is the extra oxygen the body takes in after exercise to restore itself: repaying the lactic acid (oxidising it back to carbon dioxide and water in the liver), resynthesising ATP and phosphocreatine stores, and returning heart rate, breathing rate and body temperature to resting levels. Measure it as the volume of oxygen consumed during recovery minus the resting requirement over the same period. The heavier the exercise, the larger the debt and the longer the recovery — which is exactly the shape of the oxygen-uptake graph before, during and after exercise.

Measuring respiration rate: the respirometer

A respirometer measures oxygen consumption: germinating seeds (actively respiring) are placed in a sealed tube with a small tube of sodium hydroxide solution (which absorbs the carbon dioxide produced, so any gas volume change is due to oxygen use). As oxygen is consumed, gas pressure drops and the coloured drop of liquid in the capillary tube moves towards the apparatus; the distance moved per minute is proportional to the rate of respiration. Control tube: same setup with dead seeds (no respiration) to correct for atmospheric pressure and temperature changes. Variables: independent = temperature or seed type; dependent = distance moved per minute (or volume of oxygen per gram per hour); controls = same mass of seeds, same volume of sodium hydroxide, same time, same apparatus. Use a water bath to set temperature. To calculate actual oxygen consumption, measure the distance moved and convert using the capillary tube's internal volume (volume = π × radius² × distance).

Aerobic and anaerobic compared

FeatureAerobic respirationAnaerobic respiration
OxygenRequiredAbsent or in short supply
SiteCytoplasm and mitochondriaCytoplasm only
Products (animals)Carbon dioxide and waterLactic acid
Products (yeast/plants)Carbon dioxide and waterEthanol and carbon dioxide
Energy per glucoseLarge amount (about 30-32 ATP)Small amount (2 ATP)
EquationC₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂OC₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₃H₆O₃ (animals)

The two pathways also differ in what happens to the hydrogen stripped from glucose. In aerobic respiration the hydrogen is carried by NAD to the inner mitochondrial membrane, where the electron transfer chain passes it to oxygen, forming water and driving the phosphorylation of ADP to ATP — this final step is where most of the ATP comes from. In anaerobic respiration there is no oxygen to accept the hydrogen, so pyruvate itself accepts it (forming lactic acid in animals) or loses carbon dioxide first (forming ethanol in yeast), and the electron transfer chain never runs. That single difference explains the enormous gap in ATP yield, and it is the mechanistic point A Level examiners probe when they ask why lactic acid forms at all.

Worked example: a full anaerobic comparison and the respirometer calculation

An athlete runs 400 m and produces 12 g of lactic acid. What mass of glucose was respired anaerobically? Step 1: the equation: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₃H₆O₃; relative formula masses: glucose 180, lactic acid 90 each, so 180 g of glucose gives 2 × 90 = 180 g of lactic acid. Step 2: ratio 180:180, that is 1:1. Step 3: 12 g lactic acid therefore came from 12 g of glucose. Now the respirometer: in 10 minutes at 25 °C the drop moved 12 mm; at 15 °C it moved 4 mm; dead-seed control moved 1 mm in both cases. Step 1: subtract the control (temperature effects on gas volume): 12 − 1 = 11 mm and 4 − 1 = 3 mm. Step 2: per minute: 11 ÷ 10 = 1.1 mm/min and 3 ÷ 10 = 0.3 mm/min. Step 3: compare: respiration at 25 °C is 1.1 ÷ 0.3 ≈ 3.7 times faster than at 15 °C. Step 4: explain: enzymes of respiration have more kinetic energy at the higher temperature, so more frequent successful collisions.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Defining respiration as "breathing" — it is a chemical process in cells; the distinction is worth a mark almost every year.
  • Writing "energy is released" without saying it is "transferred to ATP" — ATP is the usable energy currency, and the phrasing earns marks.
  • Unbalanced equations: aerobic has 6O₂ and 6H₂O — anything else loses marks.
  • Writing lactic acid as "lactate" only or giving the wrong formula; the symbol equation C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₃H₆O₃ is required at this level.
  • Claiming anaerobic respiration "releases no energy" — it releases less, not none.
  • Explaining oxygen debt as "paying back oxygen": it is the oxygen used to oxidise lactic acid and restore ATP, measured as extra uptake.
  • Forgetting the control (dead seeds) in a respirometer plan — a whole mark for "controls for atmospheric pressure/temperature".
  • Saying the mitochondrion is "where respiration happens" without noting glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm.

Exam-style questions and answers

Q1. Write the word equation for aerobic respiration. (2 marks) Answer: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + (energy transferred to ATP) — one mark for reactants, one for products.

Q2. Compare aerobic and anaerobic respiration in muscle cells. (4 marks) Answer: aerobic uses oxygen, anaerobic does not (1); aerobic in mitochondria and cytoplasm, anaerobic in cytoplasm only (1); aerobic produces carbon dioxide and water, anaerobic produces lactic acid (1); aerobic releases much more energy per glucose (1).

Q3. Explain what happens to lactic acid after exercise. (3 marks) Answer: it is transported to the liver (1); oxidised to carbon dioxide and water or converted back to glycogen (1); the oxygen used in this and in restoring ATP/heat is the oxygen debt (1).

Q4. Describe how you would use a respirometer to compare respiration rates in germinating and dead seeds. (4 marks) Answer: place equal masses in sealed tubes with sodium hydroxide to absorb carbon dioxide (1); record distance moved by the coloured drop per minute (1); run a dead-seed control to correct for pressure/temperature (1); keep temperature constant in a water bath and repeat for means (1).

Q5. Explain why the rate of respiration increases when temperature rises from 15 °C to 25 °C. (2 marks) Answer: enzymes gain kinetic energy (1); more frequent successful collisions, so respiration is faster (1).

Equations and symbols

The three equations of respiration and the one calculation behind the respirometer. Arrow means "is converted into"; the state symbols are not required at IGCSE, but the balancing is.

C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O Key: C₆H₁₂O₆ = glucose, one molecule; O₂ = oxygen, six molecules; CO₂ = carbon dioxide; H₂O = water. Count the atoms before you write it: 6 carbon, 12 hydrogen and 18 oxygen on each side.

C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₃H₆O₃ Key: C₃H₆O₃ = lactic acid, two molecules from one glucose; no oxygen appears on either side, which is what makes this the anaerobic equation of muscle. The energy released is small and is not shown as a product — write "energy transferred to ATP" in words.

C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂ Key: C₂H₅OH = ethanol; CO₂ = carbon dioxide, which is what raises bread dough and shows as bubbles in yeast experiments. Plants and yeast use this route; animals never do, because they cannot excrete ethanol.

volume = π × radius² × distance Key: volume = oxygen taken up (cm³); π = 3.14; radius = internal radius of the capillary bore (cm, so 0.5 mm becomes 0.05 cm); distance = how far the coloured drop moved (cm). The area of the bore times the distance travelled is the volume, and dividing by the time gives a rate.

11 ÷ 10 = 1.1 mm/min and 3 ÷ 10 = 0.3 mm/min Key: 11 mm and 3 mm are the control-corrected distances the drop moved at 25 °C and at 15 °C; 10 is the time in minutes; the quotients are rates of oxygen uptake. Their ratio, 1.1 ÷ 0.3 ≈ 3.7, is the comparison the question wants, and the dead-seed control is what makes both numbers trustworthy.

title: Number — Ratio, Rate and Proportion — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Number — Ratio, Rate and Proportion

Mathematics — OL. ratio notation, sharing, direct & inverse proportion (including squares/cubes), unit rates.

  • 1. Simplifying and sharing ratios
  • 2. Direct proportion
  • 3. Inverse proportion
  • 4. Rates

How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

Key points to remember

A ratio compares two or more quantities of the same kind and is simplified by dividing each part by the highest common factor. To share a quantity in a given ratio, add the parts of the ratio to find the total, divide the quantity by that total to find one part, then multiply.

A rate compares quantities of different kinds, such as speed in metres per second. Direct proportion means that one quantity doubles when the other doubles, and it is written y = kx. Inverse proportion means that one quantity halves when the other doubles, and it is written y = k/x. Identify which kind of proportion the question describes before you calculate.

title: Coordinate Geometry — Study Notes
content:
Coordinate geometry of circles

At A2, coordinate geometry centres on the circle: its equation, tangents, normals and the interaction with straight lines.

Circle equations

  • Centre (a, b), radius r: (x - a)^2 + (y - b)^2 = r^2.
  • General form x^2 + y^2 + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 has centre (-g, -f) and radius sqrt(g^2 + f^2 - c).
  • Always complete the square to find centre and radius.

Tangents and normals

  • The tangent at a point is perpendicular to the radius at that point: gradient of tangent = -1 / (gradient of radius).
  • The normal at a point passes through the centre (it is the radius line extended).
  • For the circle x^2 + y^2 = r^2, the tangent at (x1, y1) is x x1 + y y1 = r^2.

Line and circle

  • Substituting a line into the circle gives a quadratic: two roots = two intersections (secant), one repeated root = tangent, no real roots = no intersection.
  • Tangency condition: the perpendicular distance from the centre to the line equals the radius.
  • Distance from (x0, y0) to ax + by + c = 0 is |ax0 + by0 + c| / sqrt(a^2 + b^2).

Tangent from an external point

The length of a tangent from an external point P to a circle is sqrt(d^2 - r^2), where d is the distance from P to the centre.

title: AS Level Mathematics: Exponentials and Logarithms
content:
AS Level Mathematics: Exponentials and Logarithms

Exponentials describe growth and decay — populations, investments, radioactive isotopes, cooling cups of tea — where the change is proportional to the amount present. Logarithms are their inverses: they turn multiplication into addition and, crucially, let you solve equations where the unknown sits in the exponent. This note builds the topic from zero: the meaning of a logarithm, the three laws with derivations, solving exponential and logarithmic equations including quadratics in disguise, the graph properties and transformations, and the applied growth/decay models.

What a logarithm is

log_a(x) = n  means  a^n = x

common log: log x = log_10 x
natural log: ln x = log_e x,  e = 2.71828...

The logarithm answers "to what power must I raise the base to get this number?" So log₂8 = 3 because 2³ = 8, and log₅(1/25) = −2 because 5⁻² = 1/25. Two identities follow immediately and are always true:

log_a(a) = 1
log_a(1) = 0
a^(log_a x) = x   and   log_a(a^x) = x

Worked example. Evaluate log₃81, log₂(1/8) and ln 1.

3⁴ = 81  →  log_3 81 = 4
2⁻³ = 1/8  →  log_2(1/8) = -3
anything to the power 0 is 1  →  ln 1 = 0

The three laws of logarithms

product:   log(xy) = log x + log y
quotient:  log(x/y) = log x - log y
power:     log(x^n) = n log x

consequences: log(1/x) = -log x;  log(sqrt x) = (1/2)log x

Why they work. Write x = a^m and y = a^n, so log x = m and log y = n. Then xy = a^(m+n), so log(xy) = m + n = log x + log y. The quotient law follows from a^(m−n) and the power law from (a^m)^n = a^(mn). Each law is a restatement of an index law, which is why logarithms convert products into sums.

Worked example 1 (combine). Write 2 log 3 + log 4 − log 6 as a single logarithm.

2 log 3 = log 9
log 9 + log 4 = log 36
log 36 - log 6 = log 6

Worked example 2 (split). Express log(x³y/√z) in terms of log x, log y and log z.

= 3 log x + log y - (1/2) log z

Worked example 3 (solve). Solve log₂x + log₂(x − 2) = 3.

combine: log_2[x(x - 2)] = 3
x(x - 2) = 2³ = 8
x² - 2x - 8 = 0  →  (x - 4)(x + 2) = 0
x = 4 or x = -2;  reject x = -2 because log of a negative is undefined
x = 4

Rejecting invalid roots is compulsory: a logarithm only accepts a positive argument, so always check each answer against the original equation.

Solving exponential equations

When the unknown is in the exponent, take logs of both sides and use the power law to bring it down.

Worked example 1. Solve 3^x = 20.

take logs: x log 3 = log 20
x = log 20 / log 3 = 1.301/0.4771 = 2.73

Worked example 2 (different bases). Solve 5^(2x−1) = 7^(x+1).

(2x - 1) log 5 = (x + 1) log 7
2x log 5 - log 5 = x log 7 + log 7
x(2 log 5 - log 7) = log 7 + log 5
x = (log 7 + log 5)/(2 log 5 - log 7)
  = (0.845 + 0.699)/(1.398 - 0.845) = 1.544/0.553 = 2.79

Worked example 3 (quadratic in disguise). Solve 2^(2x) − 5(2^x) + 4 = 0.

let y = 2^x:  y² - 5y + 4 = 0  →  (y - 1)(y - 4) = 0
y = 1  →  2^x = 1  →  x = 0
y = 4  →  2^x = 4  →  x = 2

The substitution trick is the standard route for any equation where one power is double another: put y = a^x and solve the quadratic, then convert back.

Graphs of exponential and logarithmic functions

FunctionDomainRangeKey points
y = e^xall real xy > 0(0, 1); always increasing; asymptote y = 0
y = e^(−x)all real xy > 0(0, 1); always decreasing; decay
y = ln xx > 0all real y(1, 0); increasing; asymptote x = 0

y = ln x is the reflection of y = e^x in the line y = x, because they are inverse functions. That reflection explains the domain and range swap and the asymptote turning from horizontal to vertical.

Worked example. Sketch y = e^(x−2) + 1, stating the asymptote and intercepts.

translation 2 right, 1 up
asymptote y = 1 (was y = 0)
y-intercept: e⁻² + 1 = 0.135 + 1 = 1.135
no x-intercept (the curve stays above y = 1)

Growth and decay models

exponential model: N = N_0 e^(kt)
  k > 0 growth;  k < 0 decay
half-life: time for N to halve = ln 2 / |k| (decay)
doubling time = ln 2 / k (growth)

Worked example (decay). A radioactive sample decays as N = 500e^(−0.02t) with t in years. Find the initial amount, the amount after 50 years, and the half-life.

t = 0: N = 500
at t = 50: 500e⁻¹ = 500 × 0.3679 = 184
half-life: 500e^(-0.02t) = 250  →  e^(-0.02t) = 0.5
-0.02t = ln 0.5 = -0.693  →  t = 34.7 years

Worked example 2 (growth). Bacteria grow as N = 200e^(0.15t), t in hours. When does the population reach 1000?

200e^(0.15t) = 1000  →  e^(0.15t) = 5
0.15t = ln 5 = 1.609  →  t = 10.7 hours

Logarithmic scales in context

Some quantities span so many orders of magnitude that a logarithmic scale is used: pH for acidity, the Richter scale for earthquakes, decibels for sound. A change of 1 on the Richter scale means 10 times the amplitude, so an increase of 3 means 10³ = 1000 times.

Worked example. Two earthquakes differ by 2.4 on the Richter scale. How many times larger is the amplitude of the stronger?

difference 2.4 in log_10  →  10^2.4 = 251 times

Change of base and log-linearisation

Calculators offer base 10 and base e only, so any other base is converted with the change-of-base formula. The same formula turns a power law into a straight line, which is how experimental data is tested for exponential behaviour.

change of base: log_a(x) = log_b(x)/log_b(a)
so log_2(7) = ln 7 / ln 2 = log 7 / log 2 = 2.807

if y = a x^n then log y = log a + n log x  (straight line in log-log)
if y = a b^x then log y = log a + x log b  (straight line in log-x)

Worked example 1. Evaluate log_5(30).

log 30 / log 5 = 1.477/0.699 = 2.113

Worked example 2 (log-linearisation). Data gives a straight line when log y is plotted against x, with gradient 0.3 and intercept 1.4. Find the model connecting y and x.

log y = 1.4 + 0.3x
so y = 10^1.4 × 10^(0.3x) = 25.1 × 2.00^x
an exponential growth model with a = 25.1 and b = 2.0

Worked example 3 (inequality). Solve 2^x < 100.

take logs (base 2 is increasing, so the inequality is preserved)
x < log_2 100 = log 100/log 2 = 6.64

Taking logs of both sides is safe for any base greater than 1 because the log function is increasing; a base between 0 and 1 would reverse the inequality, which never arises in these models.

Rewriting any exponential in base e

Any exponential a^x can be written as e^(kx), because a = e^(ln a). This is why every growth model in the syllabus uses e: the base is absorbed into the constant.

a^x = e^(x ln a)
so 2^x = e^(0.693x);  5^x = e^(1.609x);  0.8^x = e^(-0.223x)

Worked example. Express y = 300(1.04)^t in the form y = 300e^(kt), and state the annual percentage rate it represents.

1.04 = e^k  →  k = ln 1.04 = 0.0392
y = 300e^(0.0392t)
the rate is 3.92 per year in continuous-compounding form, while the
annual multiplier is still 1.04 (4 per cent per year)

Worked example 2. A model is N = 80e^(0.25t). Rewrite it as N = 80b^t and find the percentage growth per unit time.

b = e^0.25 = 1.284
N = 80(1.284)^t, so growth is 28.4 per cent per unit time

The two forms describe the same curve; the e-form is convenient for calculus, the b-form for reading off a percentage rate. Converting between them is a standard exam demand.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Evaluate) Find log₄64. Answer: 3, since 4³ = 64.
  2. (Laws) Simplify log 8 + log 5 − log 2. Answer: log(40/2) = log 20.
  3. (Solve log) Solve log₃x = 2. Answer: x = 3² = 9.
  4. (Solve exponential) Solve 2^x = 50. Answer: x = log 50/log 2 = 1.699/0.301 = 5.64.
  5. (Quadratic) Solve e^(2x) − 3e^x + 2 = 0. Answer: y = e^x → y² − 3y + 2 = 0 → y = 1 or 2 → x = 0 or ln 2 = 0.693.
  6. (Combine) Write 3 ln 2 − ln 4 as a single logarithm. Answer: ln 8 − ln 4 = ln 2.
  7. (Inverse) Find the inverse of f(x) = e^(3x). Answer: y = e^(3x) → ln y = 3x → f⁻¹(x) = (ln x)/3.
  8. (Model) A car's value is V = 15000e^(−0.2t). Find its value after 4 years. Answer: 15000e^(−0.8) = 15000 × 0.4493 = 6740 pounds.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • log(x + y) is not log x + log y: the product law applies to products only; there is no law for the log of a sum.
  • Forgetting the domain: logs need a positive argument. Roots that make an argument negative or zero are rejected, explicitly.
  • Dividing by log: log 20/log 3 is not log(20/3); the quotient law is for two logs, not a quotient of logs.
  • Base consistency: mixing log₁₀ and ln inside one equation is an error; convert first (ln x = log x / log e).
  • Power law misuse: (log x)² is not 2 log x. Only log(x²) = 2 log x.
  • Quadratic substitution: after solving for y, the answer is x — convert back and solve the exponential equation.
  • Half-life sign: with a decay model k is negative, so half-life = ln 2/|k|; dropping the modulus gives a negative time.
  • Sketch asymptotes: state the asymptote after transformations; e^x + c has asymptote y = c, not y = 0.

Equations and symbols

Every relation this topic is examined on, written with its real notation and followed by a key naming each symbol, its unit and what it means. Where a law has a second useful form both are given, so the rearrangement in the exam is mechanical rather than a thing to rediscover under time pressure.

What a logarithm is

log_a x = n ⇔ aⁿ = x
Key: a = base (a > 0, a ≠ 1); x = the number, x > 0; n = the logarithm, the power a must be raised to. Read it aloud as "a to what power gives x" and most of the difficulty disappears.

log_a a = 1 and log_a 1 = 0
Key: a = the base. Consequences of a¹ = a and a⁰ = 1; a log question that stalls usually stalls because one of these was not used.

a^(log_a x) = x and log_a(aˣ) = x
Key: the two functions are inverses, so each undoes the other. Graphically the curves y = aˣ and y = log_a x are reflections of one another in the line y = x.

log x means log_10 x, and ln x means log_e x
Key: log = common logarithm, base 10; ln = natural logarithm, base e = 2.71828…; e is the base for which the exponential has gradient equal to its value. The calculator has keys for exactly these two, which is why change of base exists.

The three laws and their consequences

log_a(xy) = log_a x + log_a y
Key: x, y > 0; a = base. Addition outside the log is multiplication inside it.

log_a(x/y) = log_a x − log_a y
Key: the same symbols. Subtraction outside is division inside — the law that collapses a fraction into one log.

log_a(xⁿ) = n log_a x
Key: n = any real index. Brings a power down in front, which is how 3ˣ = 20 is solved: x log 3 = log 20.

log_a(1/x) = −log_a x and log_a √x = ½ log_a x
Key: the power law with n = −1 and n = ½. A reciprocal flips the sign; a square root halves the value.

log_a x = log_b x / log_b a
Key: b = any convenient base, 10 or e on a calculator. Change of base; the special case log_a b = 1 / log_b a falls out by putting x = b.

Solving, modelling and scale

aˣ = b ⇒ x = log b / log a
Key: a > 0, b > 0; the logs may be to any base provided both are the same. Take logs of both sides, then use the power law — never guess the exponent.

A = P(1 + r/100)ⁿ
Key: A = amount after n periods; P = principal; r = percentage rate per period; n = number of periods. Compound growth, where the growth factor is 1 + r/100 and the model is geometric rather than exponential.

A = P e^(rt)
Key: A = amount after time t; P = initial amount; r = continuous growth rate per unit time (r < 0 for decay); t = time. Continuous compounding, the bridge between the geometric model and e.

t½ = ln 2 / k
Key: t½ = half-life; k = decay constant in y = A e^(−kt). Follows from ½ = e^(−kt½); the half-life does not depend on the starting amount.

ln y = ln A + k x
Key: plotting ln y against x gives gradient k and intercept ln A. Log-linearisation: how a curve is proved to be exponential and its constants extracted from experimental data.

pH = −log₁₀[H⁺]
Key: pH = acidity on the logarithmic scale; [H⁺] = hydrogen ion concentration in mol dm⁻³. The standard logarithmic scale in context: pH 3 is ten times more acidic than pH 4, not twice.

title: IGCSE Biology (OxfordAQA): Inheritance
content:
Inheritance

Every cell in your body carries the same set of instructions, written in DNA and packaged into chromosomes, and this topic is about how that set is copied, halved, shuffled and sometimes changed. Two divisions do the copying and halving; alleles decide which version of a characteristic appears; a genetic cross predicts the odds; and genetic engineering and cloning are the technologies that follow once you can read and cut DNA. The exam treats the cross as arithmetic — set out the gametes, fill the grid, read the ratio — so the worked examples below are the ones to practise rather than the vocabulary.

1. Sexual and asexual reproduction

Sexual reproduction involves two parents and the fusion of gametes, so the offspring are genetically different from each other and from their parents. Asexual reproduction involves one parent and no gamete fusion, so the offspring are genetically identical clones.

FeatureSexualAsexual
ParentsTwoOne
GametesFused (sperm and egg)None
OffspringGenetically variedGenetically identical clones
ExamplesHumans, flowering plantsBacteria, strawberry runners, potato tubers
AdvantageVariation helps a population survive a changeFast, and needs only one parent

Some organisms do both depending on conditions — aphids reproduce asexually in summer when food is plentiful and sexually in autumn, which is variation exactly when it is useful.

2. Cell division: mitosis and meiosis

Mitosis produces two genetically identical diploid cells and is used for growth, repair and asexual reproduction. Meiosis produces four genetically different haploid gametes and happens only in the reproductive organs.

  • Diploid means two copies of each chromosome, one from each parent; human body cells are diploid with 46 chromosomes.
  • Haploid means one copy of each chromosome; human gametes are haploid with 23.
  • Meiosis halves the chromosome number so that fertilisation restores the diploid number, and it shuffles the chromosomes and their alleles, which is where genetic variation comes from.
  • Mitosis copies the chromosomes first, then divides once, so each new cell has the full set.

The order of events matters: in meiosis the chromosomes line up in pairs and are pulled apart twice, so four cells result; in mitosis they line up singly and are pulled apart once, so two cells result.

3. Genetic variation

A gene is a section of DNA that codes for a characteristic. Different versions of the same gene are alleles, and the combination an organism carries is its genotype; the characteristic you can see is its phenotype.

  • Dominant alleles are expressed even when only one copy is present, written with a capital letter.
  • Recessive alleles are expressed only when two copies are present, written with a lower-case letter.
  • Homozygous means two identical alleles (AA or aa); heterozygous means two different alleles (Aa).
  • Co-dominance means both alleles are expressed, as in AB blood group or a roan coat.

Variation comes from three sources: the genes inherited from two parents, meiosis shuffling the alleles, and mutation. Environmental factors such as diet and exercise also affect phenotype, which is why identical twins are not perfectly identical.

4. Worked example: a monohybrid cross

Two heterozygous parents (Aa × Aa) have children. A is the dominant allele for free earlobes; a gives attached earlobes. Predict the ratio of phenotypes and the probability that a child has attached earlobes.

Each parent's gametes are A and a, so the grid gives AA, Aa, Aa and aa: the ratio is 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa. Three of the four combinations carry at least one A, so 3 have free earlobes and 1 has attached — a phenotype ratio of 3 : 1. The probability of attached earlobes is 1 in 4, or 25 %.

Key: A = dominant allele (free earlobes); a = recessive allele (attached earlobes); AA and Aa = free earlobes because A is expressed; aa = attached earlobes because both alleles are recessive.

Now run it the other way. If the couple has four children, each child independently has a 25 % chance, so the expected number with attached earlobes is 4 × 0.25 = 1 — but a family of four can easily have none or two. Expected numbers are probabilities multiplied by the number of children, not a promise.

5. Genetic disorders

Some disorders are caused by a single gene and are inherited in a predictable pattern, which is why a genetic cross can estimate the risk.

  • Cystic fibrosis is caused by a recessive allele. A person inherits it only with two copies (cc); a carrier (Cc) has one copy and no symptoms, so two carrier parents have a 1 in 4 chance of an affected child.
  • Polydactyly — extra fingers or toes — is caused by a dominant allele, so a person with one copy has the condition and can pass it to half their children.

Genetic screening tests for these alleles before or during pregnancy, and for embryos during IVF. It gives parents information, and raises the ethical question of what to do with it; the exam asks for both sides, so give one benefit and one concern rather than a verdict.

6. Genetic manipulation and cloning

Genetic engineering moves a gene from one organism to another. A human gene for insulin, for example, is cut out with an enzyme, inserted into a bacterial plasmid using another enzyme, and the bacteria are grown in a fermenter to produce insulin.

  • Advantages: insulin is produced in large quantities, is identical to human insulin so fewer reactions occur, and the process does not depend on animal pancreases.
  • Concerns: the long-term effects of genetically modified organisms on ecosystems are uncertain, and some people object on ethical or religious grounds.
  • Cloning by embryo transplant takes a fertilised egg, splits it into several embryos and implants them into surrogates, producing identical offspring. Adult cell cloning transfers the nucleus of a body cell into an egg cell with its nucleus removed.
  • Cloning plants by cuttings or tissue culture is cheap and preserves a desirable variety, but the whole crop is equally vulnerable to one disease.

7. Typical mistakes

  • Saying meiosis produces two cells. It produces four, each with half the chromosome number.
  • Writing "a recessive allele is weaker". It is not weaker; it is simply not expressed when a dominant allele is present.
  • Giving a genotype ratio when the question asks for a phenotype ratio, or forgetting to say which phenotype is which.
  • Claiming a 3 : 1 ratio guarantees three of one and one of the other in a family of four.
  • Confusing a carrier with an affected person. A carrier has one copy of a recessive allele and no symptoms.
  • Describing genetic engineering as "breeding". Breeding selects existing alleles; engineering moves a gene between species.
  • Saying clones are "identical in every way". They share genotype, but environment still affects phenotype.

8. Exam-style questions

  1. Compare mitosis and meiosis in terms of the cells produced. Answer: Mitosis gives two genetically identical diploid cells; meiosis gives four genetically different haploid gametes.
  2. Explain why meiosis is important for sexual reproduction. Answer: It halves the chromosome number so that fertilisation restores the diploid number, and it creates genetic variation by shuffling alleles.
  3. A heterozygous brown-eyed parent (Bb) has children with a blue-eyed parent (bb). What proportion of the children would be expected to have blue eyes? Answer: The gametes are B and b from one parent and b and b from the other, giving Bb, Bb, bb and bb — so 50 % would be expected to have blue eyes.
  4. Two carriers of cystic fibrosis have a child. State the probability the child is affected and explain. Answer: 1 in 4, or 25 %: both parents are Cc, so one combination in four is cc, and cc is the only genotype that gives the condition.
  5. Explain why two parents with the same phenotype can have a child with a different one. Answer: Both parents may be heterozygous carriers of a recessive allele, so the child can inherit the recessive allele from each and show the recessive phenotype.
  6. Give one advantage and one concern of genetic engineering. Answer: Advantage: insulin can be produced in large amounts and is identical to human insulin. Concern: the long-term effects of releasing genetically modified organisms into the environment are uncertain.
  7. Explain why cloning a plant produces a crop that is uniformly vulnerable. Answer: The plants are genetically identical, so none of them carries resistance to a disease that the others lack, and the whole crop can be lost together.

9. Revision checklist

  • I can compare sexual and asexual reproduction.
  • I can compare mitosis and meiosis and say where each happens.
  • I can define gene, allele, genotype, phenotype, homozygous and heterozygous.
  • I can complete a Punnett square and give a phenotype ratio and a probability.
  • I can explain cystic fibrosis and polydactyly as recessive and dominant inheritance.
  • I can describe genetic engineering of insulin and give one advantage and one concern.
  • I can describe embryo transplant and adult cell cloning.

title: Probability Distributions
content:
Discrete Random Variables

Probability Distributions

A discrete random variable X takes values xᵢ with probabilities pᵢ where each pᵢ ≥ 0 and Σpᵢ = 1. A probability distribution can be given as a table, a formula, or a function. Any missing probability is found by subtraction.

Example: X = number of heads in 2 fair tosses: P(0) = 1/4, P(1) = 1/2, P(2) = 1/4.

Expectation

The mean of X is

  • E(X) = Σxᵢpᵢ

It is a weighted average — the long-run average value over many repetitions. E(X) need not equal any value X can actually take.

Variance

  • Var(X) = E(X²) − (E(X))²

where E(X²) = Σxᵢ²pᵢ — square the values before multiplying by probabilities. The standard deviation is √Var(X).

Linear Transforms

For constants a and b:

  • E(aX + b) = a·E(X) + b and Var(aX + b) = a²·Var(X)

Adding a constant shifts but does not spread; multiplying scales the spread by |a|.

Independent Variables

If X and Y are independent: E(X + Y) = E(X) + E(Y) and Var(X + Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y). The addition rule for expectation always holds; the variance addition needs independence. The same applies to differences: Var(X − Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) — the subtraction does not cancel spread.

Exam tips: first verify Σp = 1 in any given table. Write E(X²) and (E(X))² separately; merging them is the most common exam error. In games of chance, set the expected profit to zero to find a fair entry fee.

title: The Normal Distribution — Study Notes
content:
The Normal Distribution

Edexcel International A Level Mathematics — Statistics 1 (WST01), sat at AS. The normal-approximation section continues in Statistics 2 (WST02) at A2.

The Model

A continuous distribution with the familiar bell shape, symmetric about the mean, described by two parameters: X ~ N(μ, σ²). The curve is fully determined by μ (centre) and σ (width). Total probability is 1, and because X is continuous, P(X = a) = 0 for any single point — inequalities do not need strictness.

Standardising

Convert any normal variable to the standard normal Z ~ N(0, 1) with

  • Z = (X − μ)/σ

Then read probabilities from the normal table. For X ~ N(50, 4²): P(X > 56) = P(Z > 1.5) = 1 − 0.9332 = 0.0668.

Backwards Problems

Given a probability, find μ or σ. Convert the target percentile to a z-value from the table, then solve (x − μ)/σ = z.

Example: P(X < 30) = 0.15 with unknown σ. From tables z = −1.036, so (30 − μ)/σ = −1.036 — one equation per unknown; use a second condition if both are missing.

Symmetry Shortcuts

P(X > μ) = 0.5. P(X < a) for a above the mean uses the complement. Tables usually give Φ(z) for z ≥ 0 only; use Φ(−z) = 1 − Φ(z).

Normal Approximation to the Binomial

For large n with p near ½, X ~ B(n, p) ≈ N(np, np(1 − p)). The condition usually quoted at this level is np > 5 and n(1 − p) > 5. Apply a continuity correction: to approximate P(X ≥ 12) for a binomial, compute P(Y > 11.5) for the normal Y.

Example: B(100, 0.5) ≈ N(50, 25). P(X ≥ 55) ≈ P(Y > 54.5) = P(Z > 0.9) = 0.1841.

Exam tips: always sketch and shade — the picture prevents complement errors. State the standardisation step explicitly; marks sit in the working. Check whether a question says "mean and standard deviation" (σ) or "variance" (σ²) before standardising.

Exam method: standardising and symmetry

For X ~ N(μ, σ²) the standard score is z = (x − μ)/σ, and Z ~ N(0, 1). Note that the second parameter is the variance, so take the square root to get σ before standardising. Many errors come from using 25 instead of 5 when the variance is 25.

Probabilities are found from the standard normal table or calculator using Φ(z) = P(Z ≤ z). Because the curve is symmetric about 0, Φ(−z) = 1 − Φ(z), and P(Z > z) = 1 − Φ(z).

For a probability between two values, P(a < X < b) = Φ(z_b) − Φ(z_a). Standardise each limit separately and subtract.

To find a value from a probability, read the z-value from the table with the required area, and then rearrange z = (x − μ)/σ to find x.

Exam cue: Sketch the curve and shade the area asked for, then match it to the table value, since the sketch catches sign errors.

Standardising a normal variable

If X follows a normal distribution with mean μ and standard deviation σ, then Z = (X − μ) ÷ σ follows the standard normal distribution with mean 0 and standard deviation 1. Standardising allows any normal probability to be read from the standard normal table. For example, if X is normal with mean 50 and standard deviation 4, then P(X > 54) = P(Z > 1), which the table gives as about 0.1587.

Worked example: finding a value from a probability

Suppose P(X < k) = 0.9 for a normal variable with mean 20 and standard deviation 3. The table gives the z-value 1.2816 for a probability of 0.9, so k = 20 + 1.2816 × 3 = 23.85. When the probability is less than 0.5, the z-value is negative, so take care with the sign. Sketch the normal curve and shade the area you need before you use the table, because the sketch shows whether the answer should be above or below the mean.

Symmetry and the 68-95-99 rule

The normal curve is symmetric about the mean, so P(Z < −a) = P(Z > a). Roughly 68% of values lie within one standard deviation of the mean, 95% within two and 99.7% within three. These approximate figures are useful for checking whether a calculated probability is reasonable.

title: IGCSE Biology: Gas Exchange in Humans
content:
IGCSE Biology: Gas Exchange in Humans

Every cell in your body needs oxygen and must be rid of carbon dioxide, and the surface where that trade happens is astonishingly thin and large: the alveoli, together about the size of a tennis court, packed into your chest behind a set of muscles and airways built like an inverted tree. This note traces the anatomy from nose to alveolus, explains the mechanism of breathing with the pressure changes named, works through the diffusion of the two gases across the alveolar-capillary membrane, and closes with how exercise and lung diseases change the picture — plus the Paper 6 spirometry and data-response skills.

The airway anatomy and its adaptations

Air enters through the nose or mouth; the nasal cavity warms, moistens and filters it (hairs and mucus trap particles and microbes). It passes the pharynx, through the larynx (voice box), down the trachea (windpipe), into the two bronchi (one per lung), then branching bronchioles, and finally into clusters of alveoli. The trachea and bronchi are held open by C-shaped rings of cartilage, lined with ciliated epithelium and mucus-secreting goblet cells: mucus traps pathogens and dust, and the cilia sweep it upwards to the throat to be swallowed (the mucociliary escalator — smoking paralyses the cilia). Bronchioles have smooth muscle in their walls to control airflow (they constrict in asthma). The lungs themselves are spongy, elastic, and sit in the pleural cavity with a fluid layer that reduces friction as they inflate.

Alveoli: the exchange surface

Each alveolus is a tiny air sac with features that maximise gas exchange: an enormous combined surface area (about 70 m² in an adult); walls one cell thick (thin squamous epithelium) giving a very short diffusion path; a dense capillary network around each sac maintaining steep concentration gradients (blood flow constantly sweeps oxygen away and brings carbon dioxide); and a moist lining so gases dissolve before diffusing. Ventilation keeps the gradients fresh: oxygen concentration in alveolar air stays higher than in deoxygenated blood arriving, so oxygen diffuses in; carbon dioxide concentration in the blood stays higher than in alveolar air, so carbon dioxide diffuses out. Partial pressure gradients, not "attraction", drive the movement — always answer in terms of gradients.

Breathing (ventilation) mechanism

Inhalation is active: the external intercostal muscles contract (ribcage up and out) and the diaphragm contracts (flattens from dome to lower), enlarging the thoracic volume; the lungs stretch with it, pressure inside falls below atmospheric pressure, and air rushes in down the pressure gradient. Exhalation at rest is passive: the intercostals and diaphragm relax, elastic recoil of the lungs reduces thoracic volume, pressure rises above atmospheric, and air is pushed out. During exercise, forced exhalation uses the internal intercostals and abdominal muscles. The pressure story is the mark: volume up → pressure down → air in; volume down → pressure up → air out. Tidal volume is the volume per breath at rest (about 0.5 dm³); breathing rate rises and tidal volume deepens during exercise; minute ventilation = tidal volume × breathing rate.

Gas exchange in the alveolus

Oxygen: inhaled air brings oxygen to a high partial pressure in the alveolus; deoxygenated blood arriving in the capillary has low oxygen partial pressure; oxygen therefore dissolves in the moist alveolar surface and diffuses across the alveolar epithelium, the thin interstitial space, and the capillary endothelium into the plasma, then into red blood cells where it binds haemoglobin (forming oxyhaemoglobin) — keeping free oxygen low and the gradient steep. Carbon dioxide: produced by respiration in tissues, carried in plasma (as hydrogencarbonate ions and dissolved gas) and partly bound to haemoglobin; its partial pressure in capillary blood exceeds that in alveolar air, so it diffuses the opposite way and is exhaled. The whole exchange depends on the thinness of the barrier (two cells thick at most), the large surface area, and constant blood flow and ventilation maintaining gradients.

Ventilation data at a glance

MeasurementAt rest (typical)During vigorous exercise
Tidal volume (per breath)0.5 dm³2.0-3.0 dm³
Breathing rate12-16 breaths per minute30-40 breaths per minute
Minute ventilation7-8 dm³ per minute60-100 dm³ per minute
Vital capacity4-5 dm³Unchanged (trained athletes higher)

Effects of exercise on gas exchange

During exercise, muscles respire faster and produce more carbon dioxide; the brain detects rising carbon dioxide (via chemoreceptors) and increases breathing rate and depth, and heart rate, to deliver oxygen faster and remove carbon dioxide. Tidal volume and breathing rate both rise, so minute ventilation increases dramatically; gas exchange remains efficient because the gradients are steeper (more carbon dioxide arriving keeps its gradient high) and blood flow is faster. Oxygen debt after exercise (covered in the respiration note) is the extra oxygen consumed for recovery. The trained athlete has a larger vital capacity (maximum volume exhaled after a maximum inhalation), more efficient ventilation, and a lower resting heart rate — all standard data-response comparison points.

Lung disease and smoking

Asthma: bronchioles constrict (smooth muscle spasm), narrowing the airways; triggers include allergens, cold air, exercise; symptoms wheezing and breathlessness; treated with inhalers (bronchodilators). Emphysema: alveolar walls break down and merge, destroying surface area and elasticity; permanent breathlessness; strongly linked to smoking. Lung cancer: uncontrolled cell division in the airways forming tumours that block air flow; smoking (tar and carcinogens) is the main risk factor. Smoking's mechanisms: carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin irreversibly in preference to oxygen, reducing oxygen transport; tar paralyses cilia and deposits in alveoli causing chronic cough and infections; nicotine constricts vessels and raises heart rate, increasing heart disease risk; particulates irritate and inflame the airways. The comparison questions reward "disease → structural change → functional effect".

Worked example: spirometry and ventilation calculations

A student records tidal volume 0.5 dm³ at rest with a breathing rate of 14 breaths per minute. Step 1: minute ventilation = tidal volume × rate = 0.5 × 14 = 7.0 dm³/min. Step 2: during exercise, tidal volume rises to 2.0 dm³ and rate to 32: ventilation = 2.0 × 32 = 64 dm³/min. Step 3: interpret: ventilation increased 64 ÷ 7.0 ≈ 9-fold, supplying the extra oxygen demanded by respiring muscles and clearing the extra carbon dioxide. Step 4: if the question gives a spirometer trace (a loop of volume against time), read tidal volume from the peak-to-trough amplitude at rest, count peaks for breathing rate, and use vital capacity from the highest peak to the lowest trough — then apply the same formula. Percentage change of ventilation = (64 − 7) ÷ 7 × 100 = 814 % increase — quote the multiplier (about nine times) as well as the percentage for clarity.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Saying air is "sucked into the lungs": air moves in because thoracic pressure falls below atmospheric pressure — use pressure language.
  • Confusing the diaphragm's action: it contracts and flattens on inhalation, relaxes and domes on exhalation.
  • Describing gas exchange as "osmosis": gases move by diffusion down partial pressure gradients.
  • Forgetting the moisture lining of the alveoli — gases must dissolve before they diffuse.
  • Writing that emphysema "blocks the alveoli" — the correct description is walls break down, reducing surface area and elasticity.
  • Leaving cilia and mucus out of an airway-adaptation question — they are marks for protection.
  • In a ventilation calculation, mixing up tidal volume and vital capacity; and forgetting units (dm³ per minute).
  • Explaining exercise response as "the lungs grow bigger": breathing rate and depth increase, but lung structure does not change.

Exam-style questions and answers

Q1. Describe how the alveoli are adapted for gas exchange. (4 marks) Answer: large surface area (1); walls one cell thick for a short diffusion path (1); dense capillary network maintains steep concentration gradients (1); moist lining so gases dissolve (1).

Q2. Explain how the intercostal muscles and diaphragm cause inhalation. (3 marks) Answer: external intercostals contract lifting the ribcage up and out (1); diaphragm contracts and flattens (1); thoracic volume increases so pressure falls below atmospheric and air enters (1).

Q3. Explain why smoking increases the risk of lung infections. (3 marks) Answer: tar paralyses cilia so mucus is not swept away (1); pathogens accumulate in the airways (1); carbon monoxide reduces oxygen transport weakening defences (1).

Q4. Calculate the minute ventilation of a person with a tidal volume of 0.4 dm³ breathing 18 times per minute. (2 marks) Answer: 0.4 × 18 (1); = 7.2 dm³ per minute (1).

Q5. Compare gas exchange in a healthy person and someone with emphysema. (4 marks) Answer: healthy alveoli have a huge surface area and thin walls (1); in emphysema walls break down so surface area falls (1); elasticity is lost so air is not expelled efficiently (1); oxygen diffusion rate drops causing breathlessness (1).

Equations and symbols

Two relations carry the whole of the ventilation arithmetic, and Paper 6 asks for both. Learn them as words first — the symbols are only shorthand for the measurements a spirometer trace gives you.

minute ventilation = tidal volume × breathing rate Key: minute ventilation = volume of air moved in or out per minute (dm³ min⁻¹); tidal volume = volume breathed in one breath at rest (dm³); breathing rate = breaths per minute (min⁻¹). Multiply, never divide: a big tidal volume at a slow rate and a small one at a fast rate can give the same minute ventilation.

minute ventilation = 0.5 × 14 = 7.0 dm³/min Key: 0.5 = tidal volume at rest (dm³); 14 = breathing rate at rest (breaths per minute); 7.0 = minute ventilation (dm³ min⁻¹). This is the at-rest figure every comparison starts from.

ventilation = 2.0 × 32 = 64 dm³/min Key: 2.0 = tidal volume during vigorous exercise (dm³); 32 = breathing rate during exercise (breaths per minute); 64 = minute ventilation during exercise (dm³ min⁻¹). Both factors rise, which is why the product rises so sharply.

Percentage change of ventilation = (64 − 7) ÷ 7 × 100 = 814 % Key: 64 = new minute ventilation (dm³ min⁻¹); 7 = original minute ventilation (dm³ min⁻¹); 814 % = the percentage increase. Divide by the original value, not the new one, and quote the multiplier as well — an 814 % rise is about nine times.

0.4 × 18 = 7.2 dm³ per minute Key: 0.4 = tidal volume (dm³); 18 = breathing rate (breaths per minute); 7.2 = minute ventilation (dm³ min⁻¹). The standard two-mark calculation: one mark for multiplying the two measurements, one for the unit.

Where the question gives a spirometer trace instead of numbers, read the quantities off it and use the same relations: tidal volume is the peak-to-trough amplitude of one resting cycle (dm³), breathing rate is the number of cycles in a minute (min⁻¹), and vital capacity is the height from the deepest trough to the highest peak (dm³). Vital capacity is not part of minute ventilation — mixing the two up is the commonest lost mark in this calculation.

title: A Level Mathematics: Vectors
content:
A Level Mathematics: Vectors

A vector is a quantity with both size and direction, and the whole subject is the algebra of arrows. The idea feels abstract until you notice you already use it: a displacement of three miles north-east is a vector, the wind reported as 20 km/h from the west is a vector, and the instruction to walk to a point is a vector. This note builds vectors from components, shows how to add and scale them, then uses the scalar product to measure the angle between two directions — the tool that turns vector algebra into geometry.

What a vector is, and what it is not

A scalar has size alone. A vector has size and direction, and two vectors are equal only if both match. That is why a vector is written with an arrow or in bold, and why reversing the arrow changes the vector into its negative even though the length is unchanged.

vector a has magnitude |a| and direction
-a has the same magnitude, opposite direction
the zero vector 0 has no direction and magnitude 0
a unit vector has magnitude 1 and gives a direction

The distinction matters in mechanics: displacement and velocity are vectors, distance and speed are scalars, and mixing them up is how answers acquire impossible units. A direction given as a bearing is the same information in a different costume, and converting between a compass bearing and a pair of components is a routine exam step.

Components and magnitude

In two dimensions a vector is written as a column of its two components, one per axis. The house convention in this course writes a column vector as (x; y), the first component horizontal and the second vertical.

a = (3; 4)
magnitude |a| = sqrt(3^2 + 4^2) = 5
in three dimensions: a = (x; y; z), |a| = sqrt(x^2 + y^2 + z^2)

Worked example. Find the magnitude of (6; −8). Draw the reasoning, not just the answer.

|a| = sqrt(36 + 64) = 10
the components form a right triangle with legs 6 and 8, so this is a 3-4-5 triangle scaled by 2

Worked example 2 (unit vector). Find the unit vector in the direction of (6; −8).

divide by the magnitude: (6/10; -8/10) = (0.6; -0.8)
check: 0.36 + 0.64 = 1

Worked example 3 (3-D). Find the magnitude of (2; −3; 6).

sqrt(4 + 9 + 36) = sqrt(49) = 7

Adding, subtracting and scaling

Addition is component by component, and geometrically it is the triangle law: place the tail of the second at the head of the first, and the sum runs from the first tail to the second head. Subtraction is addition of the negative, which gives the vector from one point to another.

a + b = (a1 + b1; a2 + b2)
a - b = (a1 - b1; a2 - b2)
k a = (k a1; k a2)  parallel to a, scaled by k

Worked example. a = (3; 1), b = (−1; 4). Find a + b, a − b and 2a − 3b.

a + b = (2; 5)
a - b = (4; -3)
2a = (6; 2);  3b = (-3; 12)
2a - 3b = (9; -10)

Worked example 2 (parallel condition). Show that (4; −6) and (−2; 3) are parallel.

(4; -6) = -2 x (-2; 3)
one is a scalar multiple of the other, so they are parallel (and antiparallel)

Position vectors and points on a line

A position vector locates a point relative to the origin. The vector from A to B is then the position vector of B minus that of A — a subtraction rule worth memorising because it fixes the direction of every later step.

position vectors a and b for points A and B:
vector AB = b - a
the midpoint of AB has position vector (a + b)/2
a point dividing AB in the ratio m:n has position (n a + m b)/(m + n)

Worked example. A has position vector (2; 1) and B has (8; 5). Find AB and the midpoint.

AB = (8 - 2; 5 - 1) = (6; 4)
midpoint = ((2+8)/2; (1+5)/2) = (5; 3)

Worked example 2 (section formula). P divides AB in the ratio 1:2. Find P.

P = (2a + 1b)/3 = ((4; 2) + (8; 5))/3 = (12; 7)/3 = (4; 2.333)

Worked example 3 (proving three points are collinear). Show that A(1, 1), B(3, 4) and C(7, 10) lie on a line.

AB = (2; 3)
AC = (6; 9) = 3 x (2; 3)
AC is a multiple of AB and they share A, so the three points are collinear

The scalar product

The scalar product (dot product) takes two vectors and returns a number. That number encodes the angle between them, which is why it is the single most useful operation in the topic.

a . b = a1 b1 + a2 b2  (+ a3 b3 in 3-D)
a . b = |a| |b| cos theta
so cos theta = (a . b)/(|a| |b|)

Worked example. Find the angle between a = (3; 4) and b = (5; 0).

a . b = 15 + 0 = 15
|a| = 5, |b| = 5
cos theta = 15/25 = 0.6  ->  theta = 53.13 degrees

Worked example 2 (perpendicularity). Find k so that (2; k) is perpendicular to (3; −4).

perpendicular means a . b = 0
6 - 4k = 0  ->  k = 1.5

Worked example 3 (3-D angle). Find the angle between (1; 2; 2) and (2; 1; 0).

a . b = 2 + 2 + 0 = 4
|a| = 3, |b| = sqrt 5 = 2.236
cos theta = 4/(3 x 2.236) = 0.596  ->  theta = 53.4 degrees

Using vectors in geometry

Geometry proofs become short algebraic arguments once vectors are in play: parallelism is a scalar multiple, equal lengths are equal magnitudes, and a right angle is a zero scalar product. The discipline is to express everything in terms of two base vectors and then compare coefficients.

Geometric statementVector test
PQ is parallel to RSPQ = k RS for some scalar k
PQ has the same length as RS|PQ| = |RS|
angle PQR is a right angleQP . QR = 0
P, Q, R are collinearPQ = k PR

Worked example. In triangle OAB, M is the midpoint of OA and N is the midpoint of OB. Prove MN is parallel to AB.

let OA = a and OB = b
OM = a/2;  ON = b/2
MN = ON - OM = (b - a)/2
AB = b - a
so MN = AB/2: parallel and half the length

A common variant gives two vectors with unknown constants and requires a right angle or a given length. The routine is always the same: write the condition as an equation in the constants, solve it, then check that the solution satisfies any sign or magnitude restriction stated in the question. Two solutions usually appear because a squared length produces a quadratic.

Worked example 2 (right angle inside a shape). With a = (1; 2) and b = (3; −1), show that the diagonals of the parallelogram spanned by a and b are perpendicular.

diagonals are a + b and a - b
a + b = (4; 1);  a - b = (-2; 3)
dot product = -8 + 3 = -5, not zero
so they are not perpendicular - the test is the check, not an assumption

Velocity and displacement vectors

In mechanics, position is a vector function of time and velocity is its rate of change. Constant velocity makes the position a straight line, which is why relative-motion questions reduce to vector subtraction.

position r = r0 + v t
displacement over time t is v t
relative velocity of A with respect to B is vA - vB

Worked example. A boat has velocity (4; 3) m/s relative to the water and the current has velocity (−1; 2) m/s. Find the boat's velocity over the ground and its speed.

resultant = (4 - 1; 3 + 2) = (3; 5)
speed = sqrt(9 + 25) = 5.83 m/s

Worked example 2 (intercept). A particle starts at (1; 2) with velocity (3; −1). Where is it after 4 seconds?

r = (1; 2) + 4(3; -1) = (1 + 12; 2 - 4) = (13; -2)

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Magnitude) Find |(5; −12)|. Answer: √(25 + 144) = 13.
  2. (Unit vector) Find the unit vector of (3; 4). Answer: (0.6; 0.8).
  3. (Addition) a = (2; −3), b = (−4; 1). Find 3a + b. Answer: (6 − 4; −9 + 1) = (2; −8).
  4. (Collinear) Are (1; 2), (4; 8) and (7; 14) collinear? Answer: yes, each step is a multiple of (3; 6).
  5. (Dot product) Find a . b for a = (1; 3), b = (4; −2). Answer: 4 − 6 = −2.
  6. (Angle) Find the angle between (1; 0) and (1; 1). Answer: cos θ = 1/√2, θ = 45°.
  7. (Perpendicular) Find k so (k; 6) is perpendicular to (3; −2). Answer: 3k − 12 = 0, k = 4.
  8. (3-D) Find |(1; 4; 8)|. Answer: √81 = 9.
  9. (Section) P divides AB in ratio 2:1, a = (0; 0), b = (6; 9). Find P. Answer: (2; 3).
  10. (Relative) Velocities (5; 1) and (2; 4). Find the relative velocity of the first with respect to the second. Answer: (3; −3).

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • AB versus BA: AB = b − a; reversing the subtraction gives the wrong direction and the wrong sign in every later step.
  • Magnitude of a sum: |a + b| is not |a| + |b| unless the vectors are parallel; compute the components first.
  • Scalar product sign: an obtuse angle gives a negative dot product, which is information, not an error.
  • Division by a vector: there is no vector division; rearrange using scalar multiples instead.
  • Collinearity without a shared point: parallel vectors alone do not make points collinear — say that they share a point.
  • Degrees and radians: the inverse cosine returns whatever mode the calculator is in; state the unit in the answer.
  • Missing the z component in 3-D: dot products and magnitudes need all three components, including zeros.
  • Arrow notation ignored in proofs: writing a length where a directed vector was needed destroys the argument even when the number is right.

title: AS Level Mathematics: Probability Distributions
content:
AS Level Mathematics: Probability Distributions

A discrete random variable takes a countable set of values, each with a probability. The probability distribution is the complete list of values and probabilities, and from it come the two summaries that matter: the expected value (the long-run average) and the variance (the typical squared spread about it). This note builds the topic from zero: constructing and checking a distribution, E(X) and Var(X) from first principles, the effect of linear transformations, and the linear combinations of random variables that let you combine independent quantities with confidence.

Discrete random variables

X takes values x1, x2, ... with probabilities p1, p2, ...
conditions: 0 <= p_i <= 1 and the probabilities sum to 1

Worked example. A fair die is rolled and X is the score. Write the distribution and verify it.

P(X = k) = 1/6 for k = 1..6
sum = 6 × 1/6 = 1, so it is a valid distribution

Worked example 2 (unknown constant). P(X = 1) = k, P(X = 2) = 2k, P(X = 3) = 3k. Find k.

k + 2k + 3k = 1  →  6k = 1  →  k = 1/6
so P(X = 1) = 1/6, P(X = 2) = 1/3, P(X = 3) = 1/2

Expectation

E(X) = sum of x P(X = x)

the expected value need not be a possible value of X:
the mean of a die is 3.5

Worked example. Find E(X) for the die.

E(X) = (1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6)/6 = 21/6 = 3.5

Worked example 2 (unequal probabilities). X takes 0, 1, 2 with probabilities 0.2, 0.5, 0.3. Find E(X).

E(X) = 0(0.2) + 1(0.5) + 2(0.3) = 0.5 + 0.6 = 1.1

Interpretation: over many repetitions the average outcome approaches 1.1. That long-run reading is what applied questions ("expected profit", "expected number of defects") ask for.

Variance of a discrete random variable

Var(X) = E(X²) - [E(X)]^2
where E(X²) = sum of x² P(X = x)

standard deviation = √(Var(X))

Worked example. Find Var(X) for the die.

E(X²) = (1 + 4 + 9 + 16 + 25 + 36)/6 = 91/6 = 15.167
Var(X) = 15.167 - 12.25 = 2.917
sd = 1.708

Worked example 2. For X = 0, 1, 2 with probabilities 0.2, 0.5, 0.3, find Var(X).

E(X) = 1.1
E(X²) = 0 + 0.5 + 4(0.3) = 1.7
Var(X) = 1.7 - 1.21 = 0.49
sd = 0.7

Linear transformations

E(aX + b) = a E(X) + b
Var(aX + b) = a² Var(X)

sd(aX + b) = |a| sd(X)

The asymmetry is the key idea: adding a constant shifts every value and so shifts the mean but leaves the spread unchanged; multiplying by a scales the mean by a and the spread by |a|, so the variance scales by a².

Worked example. E(X) = 5, Var(X) = 4. Find E(3X + 2) and Var(3X + 2).

E = 3(5) + 2 = 17
Var = 9(4) = 36;  sd = 6

Worked example 2 (finding the transformation). E(Y) = 20 and Var(Y) = 25, where Y = aX + b, E(X) = 4 and Var(X) = 1. Find a and b.

Var: a² (1) = 25  →  a = 5 or -5
if a = 5: 20 = 5(4) + b  →  b = 0
if a = -5: 20 = -20 + b  →  b = 40
both are valid; the sign of a is fixed by context (a positive
scaling is usually implied)

Linear combinations of random variables

E(aX + bY) = a E(X) + b E(Y)          (always, no independence needed)
Var(aX + bY) = a² Var(X) + b² Var(Y)   (only if X, Y independent)
Var(aX - bY) = a² Var(X) + b² Var(Y)   (the variances still add)

The minus sign is where most marks are lost: subtracting random variables adds their variances, because the uncertainty compounds whichever direction the values move.

Worked example. X and Y are independent with E(X) = 10, Var(X) = 9, E(Y) = 4, Var(Y) = 4. Find E(X − Y) and Var(X − Y).

E(X - Y) = 10 - 4 = 6
Var(X - Y) = 9 + 4 = 13   (not 9 - 4)
sd = 3.606

Worked example 2 (three variables). Independent X, Y, Z with variances 2, 3, 5. Find Var(2X + 3Y − Z).

= 4(2) + 9(3) + 1(5) = 8 + 27 + 5 = 40

Worked example 3 (total of identical variables). A fair die is rolled twice; T is the total. Find E(T) and Var(T).

each roll: E = 3.5, Var = 35/12 = 2.917
E(T) = 7;  Var(T) = 2 × 2.917 = 5.833
sd(T) = 2.415  (the spread of a total grows, but by √(2), not 2)

Discrete uniform distribution

X uniform on 1..n: P(X = k) = 1/n
E(X) = (n + 1)/2
Var(X) = (n² - 1)/12

Worked example. X is uniform on 1 to 10. Find E(X) and Var(X).

E(X) = 11/2 = 5.5
Var(X) = (100 - 1)/12 = 8.25

Cumulative distribution functions

The cumulative distribution function F(x) gives the probability that X is at most x. It is a step function for a discrete variable: constant between values, jumping at each value by that value's probability.

F(x) = P(X <= x) = sum of P(X = k) for k <= x

P(X = k) = F(k) - F(k - 1)
P(a < X <= b) = F(b) - F(a)

Worked example. X takes 1, 2, 3 with probabilities 0.2, 0.5, 0.3. Write F(x) and use it to find P(X > 1).

F(1) = 0.2;  F(2) = 0.7;  F(3) = 1
P(X > 1) = 1 - F(1) = 0.8  (equivalently 0.5 + 0.3)

Worked example 2 (recovering probabilities). F(2) = 0.35 and F(3) = 0.8. Find P(X = 3).

P(X = 3) = F(3) - F(2) = 0.8 - 0.35 = 0.45

Reading F correctly requires attention to the inequality: P(X < 3) = F(2) for a discrete variable, while P(X ≤ 3) = F(3). One unit of difference changes the answer.

Expectation from a table and applied profit

When the distribution is given as a table, the calculation is a single weighted total; when it is described in words, the table must be built first.

Worked example. A fair coin is tossed three times and X counts the heads. Find E(X) and Var(X).

X ~ Binomial(3, 1/2) in effect: probabilities 1/8, 3/8, 3/8, 1/8 for 0..3
E(X) = 0 + 3/8 + 6/8 + 3/8 = 12/8 = 1.5
E(X²) = 0 + 3/8 + 12/8 + 9/8 = 24/8 = 3
Var(X) = 3 - 2.25 = 0.75

Worked example 2 (profit). A stall pays 4 pounds to play a game that returns 0, 5 or 20 pounds with probabilities 0.6, 0.3 and 0.1. Find the expected profit per game and whether the stall makes money.

E(return) = 0 + 1.5 + 2.0 = 3.5
profit = return - 4, so E(profit) = 3.5 - 4 = -0.5
players lose 50 pence per game on average, so the stall profits

The transformation rule does the work: E(X − c) = E(X) − c. State the interpretation, not just the number.

Why variances add for independent variables

For independent X and Y, the variance of a sum is the sum of the variances. The proof rests on the fact that independence makes E(XY) = E(X)E(Y), so the cross term in the expansion vanishes:

Var(X + Y) = E[(X + Y)²] - [E(X + Y)]^2
           = E(X²) + 2E(XY) + E(Y²) - [E(X)]^2 - 2E(X)E(Y) - [E(Y)]^2
independence: E(XY) = E(X)E(Y), so the cross terms cancel
           = Var(X) + Var(Y)

For the difference, the same expansion gives Var(X − Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y): the cross term is −2E(XY) + 2E(X)E(Y), which also vanishes. The intuition is that independent errors cannot cancel — a positive error in one is just as likely to meet a positive or negative error in the other, so the uncertainties compound.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Valid distribution) P(X = 1) = 0.3, P(X = 2) = 0.4, P(X = 3) = k. Find k. Answer: 0.3.
  2. (E) X = 1, 3, 5 with probabilities 0.2, 0.5, 0.3. Find E(X). Answer: 0.2 + 1.5 + 1.5 = 3.2.
  3. (Var) For the same X, find Var(X). Answer: E(X²) = 0.2 + 4.5 + 7.5 = 12.2; Var = 12.2 − 10.24 = 1.96.
  4. (Transform) E(X) = 6, Var(X) = 5. Find E(4X − 1) and Var(4X − 1). Answer: 23 and 80.
  5. (Combination) Independent X, Y: Var(X) = 6, Var(Y) = 8. Find Var(2X + Y). Answer: 24 + 8 = 32.
  6. (Combination difference) Same X, Y: Var(X − Y). Answer: 6 + 8 = 14.
  7. (Uniform) X uniform on 1..6. Find Var(X). Answer: (36 − 1)/12 = 2.917.
  8. (Applied) A game pays X with E(X) = 2 and costs 3 to play. Find the expected profit. Answer: E(X − 3) = −1, a loss of 1 per game.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Var(aX) = a Var(X): wrong — the variance scales by a², the standard deviation by |a|.
  • Subtracting variances: Var(X − Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) for independent variables; subtraction never reduces uncertainty.
  • Assuming independence: the variance-addition rule requires it; the expectation rule does not.
  • Using E(X²) as [E(X)]²: they differ by the variance; compute E(X²) from the distribution.
  • Probabilities not summing to 1: the first check on any distribution, and often the way to find an unknown constant.
  • Expectation as a possible value: E(X) need not be attainable (3.5 on a die); say "on average over many trials".
  • Standard deviation units: the variance is in squared units; compare and quote the sd.
  • Negative scaling: if a is negative, E flips sign and sd uses |a|; forgetting the modulus produces a negative standard deviation.

Formula summary

E(X) = sum of x P(X = x);  E(X²) = sum of x² P(X = x)
Var(X) = E(X²) - [E(X)]^2
E(aX + b) = a E(X) + b;  Var(aX + b) = a² Var(X)
E(aX + bY) = a E(X) + b E(Y)
Var(aX + bY) = a² Var(X) + b² Var(Y)   (independent)
