F(x) = P(X <= x);  P(X = k) = F(k) - F(k - 1)

Two conditions separate the whole topic: expectations always combine linearly, variances combine linearly only when the variables are independent — and then always with plus signs, whatever the signs in front of the variables. Write the condition before applying the variance rule; it is worth a mark on its own and prevents the commonest mistake in the topic.

title: A Level Mathematics: Permutations and Combinations
content:
A Level Mathematics: Permutations and Combinations

Counting is the part of probability that requires no formula to start with, only a decision: does the order matter? Every question in this topic is answered by that one question. If order matters the count is a permutation; if it does not the count is a combination. Everything else — repetitions, restrictions, arrangements around a circle — is a variation on the same counting principle, and this note sets out each variation with the reasoning behind it.

The multiplication principle

If a choice can be made in a ways and, independently, a second choice in b ways, the pair can be made in a × b ways. That is the whole foundation; the formulas are shortcuts for repeated applications of it.

arrangements of n distinct objects in a row: n! = n x (n-1) x ... x 2 × 1
0! = 1 by convention, so that formulas stay consistent
choosing r from n with order: nPr = n!/(n - r)!
choosing r from n without order: nCr = n!/(r!(n - r)!)

Worked example. A password is 4 distinct letters from the 26-letter alphabet. How many passwords are possible?

order matters, so 26P4 = 26 × 25 × 24 × 23 = 358,800

Worked example 2 (no order). How many ways can 4 students be chosen from 26?

order does not matter, so 26C4 = 14,950

Worked example 3 (a leading zero is not allowed). A code uses four distinct digits from 0 to 9 and cannot begin with zero. How many codes?

first digit: 9 choices (1 to 9)
remaining three: 9P3 = 9 × 8 × 7 = 504
total = 9 × 504 = 4536

Worked example 4 (the link). Explain why nPr = nCr × r!.

every unordered selection of r objects can be arranged in r! orders
so counting ordered selections = counting unordered ones then arranging them

Deciding whether order matters

The decision is not about the words "choose" or "arrange" in the question — those are hints, not rules. The safe test is to imagine two selections differing only by swapping two items: if that counts as a different outcome, order matters.

SituationOrder?Count
finishing order of a raceyesnPr
a committee of 3nonCr
a 4-digit PINyespermutation, with repetition allowed
a hand of cardsnonCr
seating 5 people in a rowyes5!

Worked example. A team of 11 is chosen from 16 players, and one of the 11 is captain. Count the possibilities.

choose the 11: 16C11 = 4368
choose the captain from them: 11 ways
total = 4368 × 11 = 48,048

The multiplication principle is doing the work here: two independent choices, multiplied.

Repetition and identical items

When some objects are identical, arranging them as if all were distinct overcounts by the number of ways the identical ones can be swapped. Dividing by those factorials corrects it.

arrangements of n items with groups of identical items:
n!/(a! b! c! ...) where a, b, c are the group sizes
with repetition allowed, choosing r from n: n^r

Worked example. How many distinct arrangements of the letters in BANANA?

6 letters: B once, A three times, N twice
6!/(1! 3! 2!) = 720/12 = 60

Worked example 2 (repetition allowed). A 3-digit code uses digits 0-9, repeats allowed. How many codes?

10 × 10 × 10 = 1000
if repeats were not allowed: 10 × 9 × 8 = 720

Worked example 3 (identical plus restriction). How many arrangements of the letters of LEVEL begin with L?

fix L at the front; remaining letters E, V, E, L
that is 4 letters with E twice: 4!/2! = 12
but the leading L is one of the two Ls, so there is only one choice for the front
answer 12

Restrictions: the "glue" method

When certain items must be together, treat the group as a single object, arrange the objects, then arrange within the group. When certain items must not be together, count the total and subtract the "together" case.

together: glue the group, arrange the objects, multiply by the internal arrangements
not together: total arrangements minus the together arrangements
specific positions: fix those items first, then arrange the rest

Worked example. Five books, two of which must stand together, are arranged on a shelf. How many orders?

glue the pair: now 4 objects, arranged in 4! = 24 ways
the pair interchange in 2! = 2 ways
total = 48

Worked example 2 (not together). The same five books with the pair not together.

total arrangements = 5! = 120
together = 48
not together = 120 - 48 = 72

Worked example 3 (fixed positions). Four men and three women sit in a row of seven. How many arrangements have all three women together?

glue the women into one block: now 5 objects (4 men + block), 5! = 120
internal arrangements of the women: 3! = 6
total = 720

Circular arrangements

Around a circle, rotations of the same arrangement are not distinguishable, so fixing one item removes the rotational symmetry and the count drops by a factor of n.

n distinct items around a circle: (n - 1)!
a necklace (where reflection also counts as the same): (n - 1)!/2

Worked example. In how many ways can 6 people sit around a round table?

(6 - 1)! = 5! = 120

Worked example 2 (with a fixed seat). How many ways if one particular person must sit in a specified chair?

fix that person, arrange the other 5 around: 5! = 120
the specified chair removes the rotational freedom entirely, so the answer is unchanged here

Worked example 3 (two people together at a round table). Six people, two of whom must sit together.

glue the pair: 5 objects around a circle = 4! = 24
internal order of the pair: 2
total = 48

Combinations with conditions

Committee questions combine cases: choose so many from one group and so many from another, then add the disjoint alternatives. The discipline is to make the cases genuinely disjoint, or the same selection gets counted twice.

choose a from group A and b from group B: C(a-group, a) x C(b-group, b)
several allowed compositions: add the separate cases
at least one: total minus none

Worked example. From 6 men and 5 women, how many committees of 4 contain exactly 2 women?

choose 2 women from 5: 10
choose 2 men from 6: 15
total = 150

Worked example 2 (at least one). How many committees of 4 contain at least one woman?

total committees: 11C4 = 330
none: 6C4 = 15
at least one = 330 - 15 = 315

Worked example 3 (cases added). How many committees of 3 contain more women than men?

3 women: 5C3 = 10
2 women and 1 man: 5C2 × 6C1 = 10 × 6 = 60
total = 70

Counting inside probability

Combinations are usually the denominator of a probability question: count the favourable selections, count all selections, divide. Doing the counting separately from the probability keeps both parts clean and makes partial credit possible.

Worked example. A bag holds 5 red and 7 blue counters. Four are drawn at random. Find the probability of exactly 2 red.

total selections: 12C4 = 495
favourable: 5C2 × 7C2 = 10 × 21 = 210
probability = 210/495 = 0.4242

Worked example 2 (at least one). For the same bag, find the probability of at least one red.

complement: no red means all four blue
7C4 = 35
P(no red) = 35/495 = 0.0707
P(at least one red) = 1 - 0.0707 = 0.9293

Worked example 3 (order matters in the numerator). Three cards are drawn from a standard deck without replacement. Find the probability they are drawn in increasing order of value.

every set of three distinct cards has exactly one increasing order out of 3! orders
so the probability is 1/6, independent of the deck

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Factorial) Evaluate 7!. Answer: 7! = 7 × 6 × 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 5040.
  2. (Permutation) In how many orders can 5 runners finish? Answer: 5P5 = 5! = 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 120.
  3. (Combination) Evaluate 10C3. Answer: 10C3 = 10!/(3! × 7!) = (10 × 9 × 8)/(3 × 2 × 1) = 720/6 = 120.
  4. (Choice) From 8 books, how many ways to choose 3? Answer: 8C3 = 8!/(3! × 5!) = (8 × 7 × 6)/(3 × 2 × 1) = 336/6 = 56.
  5. (Arrangement) How many arrangements of the letters of STATISTICS? Answer: 10!/(3! × 3! × 2!) = 3 628 800/(6 × 6 × 2) = 3 628 800/72 = 50,400.
  6. (Glue) 6 people in a row with two together: Answer: glue the pair: 5! × 2! = 120 × 2 = 240.
  7. (Not together) Same 6, not together: Answer: total − together = 6! − 5! × 2! = 720 − 240 = 480.
  8. (Circle) 7 people around a table: Answer: (n − 1)! = 6! = 720.
  9. (Committee) 3 from 5 men and 4 women, exactly 2 men: Answer: 5C2 × 4C1 = 10 × 4 = 40.
  10. (At least) 4 from the same 9 with at least one woman: Answer: all − none = 9C4 − 5C4 = 126 − 5 = 121.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Using nPr where order does not matter: a committee is unordered; using permutations overcounts by r!.
  • Forgetting to divide by repeated factorials: identical letters need the divisor or the count is inflated.
  • Glue method without the internal factor: the block also has an internal arrangement, and dropping the 2! halves the answer.
  • Circular arrangements with n! instead of (n − 1)!: rotations are the same seating.
  • Adding what should be multiplied: independent stages multiply; alternative cases add.
  • Overlapping cases: cases must be disjoint, or selections are counted twice.
  • "At least one" counted directly: the complement is almost always faster and safer.
  • Restrictions applied after the count: fix the restricted positions first, then count what remains.

Choosing between nPr, nCr and a plain product

Most lost marks in this topic come from using the right formula for the wrong question. Before any calculation, decide whether you are selecting, arranging or doing both, and whether the answer depends on the order. The subsections below set out the decision in the order a careful candidate works through it.

Selecting without arranging: nCr

If you only need to choose a group and the order inside the group does not matter, use ⁿCᵣ = n! / (r!(n − r)!). Choosing a committee of 4 from 10 people gives ¹⁰C₄ = 210. The result counts groups, so two committees with the same members in a different order are the same committee.

Selecting and arranging: nPr

If the chosen items are then placed in distinct positions, the order matters and you use ⁿPᵣ = n! / (n − r)!. Choosing a chair, a vice-chair and a secretary from 10 people gives ¹⁰P₃ = 720. Each committee of 3 from the previous example can be arranged in 3! = 6 ways, so 720 = 120 × 6, which is a useful check.

A plain product for independent choices

When each decision is made separately and the number of options for one does not depend on the others, multiply. Three shirts and four trousers give 3 × 4 = 12 outfits. Do not reach for a combination formula here: nothing is being chosen from a single pool of identical kinds of object.

Checking the order question

Ask whether swapping two chosen items changes the outcome. A password changes if its letters are swapped, so it is an arrangement. A team does not change when two members swap places, so it is a selection. If the words in the question say “the first, second and third” or “positions”, the order matters.

Worked decision

Seven runners compete for gold, silver and bronze. The medals are different, so the order matters and the count is ⁷P₃ = 7 × 6 × 5 = 210. If the question asked for three runners to go through to a final with no ranking, the count would be ⁷C₃ = 35. The same seven people give 210 or 35 depending only on whether the medal order is asked for, so state which one you have chosen before you write the number.

Common error: dividing when you should not

Students often divide by a factorial out of habit. Divide only when items are truly identical or the outcome groups are truly unordered. Dividing ⁷P₃ by 3! to get the medal count gives 35 and throws away the difference between gold and silver, which the question asked you to keep.

Equations and symbols

Every formula here is a shortcut for the multiplication principle, and each one carries a condition that decides whether it applies. The condition is the mark: "order matters" and "items are identical" change the count by a factorial.

n! = n x (n-1) x ... x 2 × 1 Key: n = the number of distinct objects (a count, no units); n! = the number of orders they can be arranged in (a count). The falling product stops at 1, and 0! = 1 by convention so the formulas stay consistent.

nPr = n!/(n - r)! Key: n = how many objects are available; r = how many are being chosen; nPr = the number of ordered selections (a count). Read it as "start at n and write down r factors": 26P4 = 26 × 25 × 24 × 23.

nCr = n!/(r!(n - r)!) Key: n = objects available; r = objects chosen; nCr = the number of unordered selections (a count). The extra r! in the denominator is exactly what removes the orderings — which is the whole difference between a permutation and a combination.

nPr = nCr × r! Key: nPr = ordered selections; nCr = unordered selections; r! = the ways to order each selection. The identity explains both formulas at once: count the sets, then arrange each one.

26P4 = 26 × 25 × 24 × 23 = 358,800 Key: 26 = letters available; 4 = letters chosen without replacement; 358,800 = ordered passwords (a count). The factors fall because each letter is used once — repetition allowed would give 26⁴ instead.

26C4 = 14,950 Key: 26 = students available; 4 = students chosen; 14,950 = unordered groups (a count). The same numbers as the password question, 24 times smaller, because a group of four has 4! orderings that all count as one group.

n!/(a! b! c! ...) Key: n = total items; a, b, c = the sizes of the groups of identical items. Dividing by the factorials of the repeats removes the arrangements that look identical — 6!/(1! 3! 2!) = 60 arrangements of BANANA, not 720.

6!/(1! 3! 2!) = 720/12 = 60 Key: 6 = letters in BANANA; 1! = the single B; 3! = the three As; 2! = the two Ns; 60 = distinct arrangements (a count). Every repeated letter needs its own factorial in the denominator, or the count is inflated.

n^r Key: n = choices available at each stage; r = number of stages; the result counts selections with repetition allowed (a count). It is the multiplication principle applied r times — three digits from 0 to 9 with repeats gives 10³ = 1000.

(n - 1)! Key: n = people or objects around a circle; the result counts distinct circular arrangements (a count), because rotating a seating does not create a new one. For a necklace, where a reflection is also the same, divide once more: (n - 1)!/2.

5! × 2! = 120 × 2 = 240 Key: 5! = the arrangements of four single items plus the glued pair as one object; 2! = the internal orders of the pair; 240 = total arrangements (a count). Gluing without the internal factor halves the answer, which is the classic lost mark in this topic.

title: Exam technique: Ratio, Rate and Proportion
content:
### What earns the marks
For sharing in a ratio, total parts and value of one part each earn a mark: write 5 parts = 600 before splitting. For scales and maps, the real-distance multiplication shown earns the method mark, with each unit conversion (cm to m to km) credited. For proportion with powers, the constant k found first earns the mark: write y = k x squared and solve for k.
### Traps
Error: dividing by 2 and 3 directly for a 2:3 split. Correction: parts first, always. Error: 1.40 hours for 1 h 40 min in speed questions. Correction: 40 min = 2/3 h. Error: linear scaling for an x-squared relation. Correction: square the ratio. Error: inverted map scale (dividing by 50000). Correction: real is bigger than map.
### Worked example
Share £120 in the ratio 2 : 3 : 7. The total parts are 12, so one part is £10 and the shares are £20, £30 and £70. Check: 20 + 30 + 70 = 120. For speed, 150 km in 2.5 hours gives 150 ÷ 2.5 = 60 km/h. Direct proportion means y = kx, so doubling x doubles y.
### Check yourself
Share £45 in the ratio 1 : 4. Find each share and check that they add up to £45. The shares are £9 and £36, because there are 5 parts and each is £9.

Quick revision: Hypothesis Testing

Mathematics — A2. The null hypothesis H₀ is the default claim (no change, p = p₀). The alternative H₁ is what a suspicious observation suggests (p > p₀, p < p₀, or p ≠ p₀). The significance level α is the probability of rejecting a true H₀ — the false-alarm rate, usually 5% or 1%.

Key areas to revise

  • The Framework
  • Test for a Binomial Proportion
  • One-Tailed vs Two-Tailed
  • Critical Regions
  • Conclusions in Context

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

### Worked example A test of a claimed mean has a null hypothesis H₀ and an alternative H₁. Choose a significance level such as 5%, calculate the test statistic and its p-value, then reject H₀ if p < α. A two-tailed test looks for a change in either direction, so the 5% is split between the two tails. ### Check yourself Define a Type I error in words. It is rejecting H₀ when H₀ is actually true. Explain why lowering the significance level reduces the chance of a Type I error but increases the chance of a Type II error. ### Worked example A test of a claimed mean has a null hypothesis H₀ and an alternative H₁. Choose a significance level such as 5%, calculate the test statistic and its p-value, then reject H₀ if p < α. A two-tailed test looks for a change in either direction, so the 5% is split between the two tails.

title: Introduction to Kinetics and Equilibria — Study Notes
content:
Introduction to Kinetics and Equilibria

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH12, Topic 9. Kinetics asks how fast a reaction goes, and equilibria asks how far it goes before the forward and backward reactions balance. Both depend on the same collision ideas.

Rates and collision theory

  • For a reaction to occur, particles must collide with enough energy (the activation energy, Ea) and in the correct orientation.
  • Increasing concentration or pressure increases the frequency of collisions. Increasing temperature raises the proportion of particles with energy above Ea, which has a larger effect than the increase in collision frequency.
  • A catalyst provides an alternative route with a lower Ea; it is not used up.

Measuring rates

  • Rates can be found from the gradient of a concentration–time graph at the start of the reaction (the initial rate).
  • Methods include measuring the volume of gas produced, the change in mass, or the time for a colour change to occur (1/time gives a relative rate).

Dynamic equilibrium

  • In a closed system, the forward and reverse rates become equal. Concentrations stop changing, but the reaction has not stopped.
  • Equilibrium constant Kc = [products]^n / [reactants]^m, with each concentration raised to the power of its coefficient. Kc is constant for a given temperature.

Le Chatelier's principle

  • If a system at equilibrium is disturbed, the position shifts to oppose the change.
  • Increasing temperature favours the endothermic direction. Increasing pressure favours the side with fewer gas molecules. Adding a reactant shifts the position towards products.
  • A catalyst speeds up both directions equally, so it changes the rate of reaching equilibrium but not the equilibrium position or Kc.

Exam tip: say which direction is favoured and why, using the principle. Do not claim that a catalyst increases the yield.

title: A Level Mathematics: Hypothesis Testing
content:
A Level Mathematics: Hypothesis Testing

A hypothesis test is a formal way of deciding whether data are surprising enough to overturn an assumption. The logic is legal rather than mathematical in spirit: assume the claim is true, compute how unlikely the observed evidence would be under that assumption, and reject the claim only if the evidence is unlikely enough. This note sets out the machinery — null and alternative hypotheses, significance levels, tails, critical regions — and then applies it to the binomial and normal cases the exam uses.

The logic of a test

The null hypothesis H0 is the assumption of no change, no effect, no bias: the status quo. The alternative H1 is what you would conclude if the data are too extreme. The significance level α is the risk of rejecting a true H0 that you are willing to accept.

H0: the parameter equals its old value
H1: the parameter is greater, less, or simply different
alpha: the maximum acceptable probability of a Type I error (often 0.05 or 0.01)
test statistic: the observed value computed from the sample
p-value: probability of a result at least as extreme, assuming H0

The analogy that makes the asymmetry clear: a criminal trial presumes innocence. The presumption is not a belief, it is the default that evidence must overcome. Failing to reject H0 is not proof of H0 — it is a verdict of "not proven".

One-tailed and two-tailed tests

The alternative decides the tail. A one-tailed test is used when the direction of the change is specified in advance; a two-tailed test when any change would matter.

AlternativeTest typep-value
p > p0one-tailed, upperP(X ≥ observed)
p < p0one-tailed, lowerP(X ≤ observed)
p ≠ p0two-tailed2 × the smaller tail

Worked example (choosing the alternative). A coin is suspected of favouring heads. Which alternative applies?

the suspicion has a direction, so H1: p > 0.5, a one-tailed upper test
a two-tailed test would be right only if any bias mattered

Errors and their consequences

Every test can go wrong in two ways, and the significance level controls only one of them. Understanding which is which is a frequent exam question and a genuine conceptual point.

Type I error: reject H0 when it is true  (probability alpha)
Type II error: fail to reject H0 when it is false
reducing alpha reduces Type I errors but increases Type II errors
increasing the sample size reduces both

Worked example. A test at the 5% level concludes a die is biased when it is fair. Which error is this?

H0 (fair) was true and was rejected
that is a Type I error, with probability at most 5%

Worked example 2 (effect of sample size). Explain why the same observed proportion can be significant in a large sample and not in a small one.

a larger sample reduces the standard error, so the same deviation
becomes more standard errors away from the null value
the evidence is measured in standard errors, not in raw counts

Testing a binomial proportion

The test statistic is the observed number of successes, the null distribution is binomial, and the p-value is a cumulative binomial probability.

H0: p = p0;  X ~ B(n, p0)
upper tail p-value = P(X >= x)
lower tail p-value = P(X <= x)
reject H0 if p-value <= alpha

Worked example. A manufacturer claims 90% of components are fault-free. In a sample of 20, only 15 are fault-free. Test at the 5% level whether the claim is too high.

H0: p = 0.9;  H1: p < 0.9
X ~ B(20, 0.9)
P(X <= 15) = 0.0432
0.0432 < 0.05, so reject H0
there is evidence the fault-free rate is below 90%

Worked example 2 (critical region). Find the 5% critical region for that test.

P(X <= 15) = 0.0432 (below 0.05)
P(X <= 16) = 0.1330 (above 0.05)
critical region: X <= 15

Worked example 3 (actual significance level). State the actual significance level of that test.

the probability of a Type I error is P(X <= 15) under H0 = 0.0432
so the actual level is 4.32%, just inside the 5% requirement

Testing a normal mean

When the variable is continuous and the population is normal — or the sample is large — the test statistic is standardised with a z-score and compared with critical values.

test statistic z = (x-bar - mu)/(σ/sqrt n)   (σ known)
or z = (x-bar - mu)/(s/sqrt n)                  (σ estimated, large n)
critical values at 5% one-tailed: 1.6449;  two-tailed: 1.96
at 1% one-tailed: 2.3263;  two-tailed: 2.5758

Worked example. A machine fills bags with a mean of 500 g and standard deviation 8 g. A sample of 16 bags has mean 496 g. Test at the 5% level whether the mean has fallen.

H0: mu = 500;  H1: mu < 500
standard error = 8/sqrt 16 = 2
z = (496 - 500)/2 = -2
critical value at 5% one-tailed is -1.6449
-2 < -1.6449, so reject H0: the mean has fallen

Worked example 2 (two-tailed). Same data, tested two-tailed at 5%.

critical values are +/-1.96
|-2| > 1.96, so still reject H0
the evidence is that the mean is not 500, in either direction

Worked example 3 (interpreting a p-value). A test gives z = 1.72 for H1: μ > μ0. Find the p-value and conclude at 5%.

p-value = P(Z > 1.72) = 0.0427
0.0427 < 0.05, so reject H0
the result is significant at the 5% level but not at 1%

Choosing the right test

The exam does not label the test; the shape of the data decides it. Getting the distribution wrong makes every later mark unreachable, so the decision is worth making explicitly.

count of successes in n trials with constant p  →  binomial test
count of events in an interval at a constant rate  →  Poisson test
mean of a continuous measurement  →  normal test (z)
correlation between two variables  →  product-moment test

Worked example. A nurse records the number of patients arriving in an hour on 30 separate days. Which test?

counts of arrivals in equal intervals at a roughly constant rate
use a Poisson test on the mean count, not a binomial test
a normal test on the mean of the 30 counts is also defensible for large n

Writing a conclusion that earns the marks

The final mark of a hypothesis test is for the conclusion, and it has three components: a decision about H0, a reference to the significance level, and the finding stated in the context of the question. Dropping any one of them costs a mark even when the arithmetic is perfect.

Compare these two endings. "0.0201 < 0.05, so reject H0" scores the comparison. "There is sufficient evidence at the 5% level that the call rate has increased" scores the comparison and the interpretation. "The rate has increased" scores neither, because it reports a certainty the test cannot deliver.

The opposite case is often mishandled too. When the p-value is above the level the correct wording is that there is insufficient evidence to reject H0 — never that H0 is true, and never that nothing has happened. A non-significant result from a small sample is weak evidence either way, and saying so is better than overclaiming in either direction.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Hypotheses) A coin might be biased against heads. State H0 and H1. Answer: H0: p = 0.5; H1: p < 0.5.
  2. (Error) Define a Type II error. Answer: failing to reject H0 when it is false.
  3. (Binomial) 8 of 20 seeds germinate; test p = 0.6 against p < 0.6 at 5%. Answer: X ~ B(20, 0.6), so P(X ≤ 8) = 0.0565; since 0.0565 > 0.05 there is insufficient evidence to reject H0.
  4. (Critical region) X ~ B(15, 0.4): 5% lower critical region. Answer: test P(X ≤ c) ≤ 0.05: P(X ≤ 2) = 0.0271 ≤ 0.05, but P(X ≤ 3) = 0.0905 > 0.05, so the critical region is X ≤ 2.
  5. (Actual level) For that region, state the actual significance level. Answer: actual significance level = P(X ≤ 2) = 0.0271 = 2.71%.
  6. (Normal) μ0 = 20, σ = 4, n = 25, mean 21.5: test at 5% one-tailed. Answer: z = (x̄ − μ0)/(σ/√n) = (21.5 − 20)/(4/√25) = 1.5/0.8 = 1.875, and 1.875 > 1.6449, so reject H0.
  7. (Two-tailed) Same data two-tailed: Answer: z = (21.5 − 20)/(4/√25) = 1.875, and 1.875 < 1.96, so do not reject H0.
  8. (p-value) z = 2.4, H1: μ > μ0. Find the p-value. Answer: p-value = P(Z > 2.4) = 1 − 0.9918 = 0.0082.
  9. (Sample size) Why can a larger sample turn a non-significant result significant? Answer: the standard error shrinks, so the same deviation is more standard errors away.
  10. (Conclusion wording) Write a valid conclusion for a rejected H0. Answer: there is sufficient evidence at the 5% level that the mean has fallen.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Concluding H0 is true: failing to reject means the evidence is insufficient; it is never proof of the null.
  • Wrong tail: compute P(X ≥ x) for an increase and P(X ≤ x) for a decrease; using the other tail inverts the conclusion.
  • Doubling without a two-tailed alternative: the p-value is doubled only when H1 is "not equal".
  • p-value compared with the wrong threshold: 5% is 0.05; comparing 0.043 with 5 instead of 0.05 reverses the verdict.
  • Standard error omitted: the z-score divides by σ/√n, not by σ.
  • Critical value for the wrong tail: the 5% one-tailed value is 1.6449, the two-tailed is 1.96; the sign matters too.
  • Type I and Type II swapped: Type I is rejecting a true null — the error the significance level controls.
  • Conclusion beyond the data: a rejected H0 says the parameter has changed, not why, and never that the change is important.

Setting up the hypotheses before any calculation

Hypotheses are the first lines a marker reads, and a wrong direction or a sample statistic written where a parameter belongs loses marks before any arithmetic is checked. The subsections set out how to define the parameter, write H₀ as a single value and read H₁ from the wording of the question.

Defining the parameter in words first

Before writing any symbol, say what the parameter measures. Let p be the proportion of seeds that germinate, or let μ be the mean mass of a bag in grams. The parameter belongs to the population the claim is about, not to the sample you were given. The definition is the line that makes the rest of the working easy to follow, so write it first.

Writing H₀ as a single value

H₀ names one value for the parameter with an equals sign, such as H₀: p = 0.6 or H₀: μ = 50. It is the value the test assumes is true when it calculates the probability of the data. The probability can only be worked out at one specific value, so the test is always carried out at the value stated in H₀, and the working should say so.

Reading the direction of H₁ from the wording

Words map to symbols in a fixed way. “Greater than”, “more than”, “has increased” and “above” give >. “Less than”, “fewer”, “has decreased” and “below” give <. “Different from”, “has changed” and “is not equal to” give ≠. A question that asks whether a proportion has changed, without saying which way, needs H₁: p ≠ p₀, and that choice fixes a two-tailed test.

Hypotheses for a mean from a normal model

When X is normal with a known standard deviation, the hypotheses concern μ, and the variance belongs to the model: X ~ N(μ, σ²). Write the assumption that the population is normal with known σ, or that the sample is large enough for the central limit theorem to apply. The hypotheses for a sample mean are the same as for the population mean, because the test is about μ.

Hypotheses set before the data are used

The direction of H₁ must come from the claim in the question, not from the sample. If the sample mean is 49 and the claim is μ = 50, it is tempting to choose H₁: μ < 50 after looking at the data. That choice invalidates the test, because it lets the data pick the tail. Settle the direction from the wording, and show it in the working before the test statistic.

Critical regions and the significance level

A critical region is the set of outcomes that leads to rejecting H₀. For a discrete distribution it is a set of whole numbers, and for a normal test it is a range of z-values. The subsections show how each is built from the significance level, and where the sign and boundary errors come from.

Building a critical region from tail probabilities

For a lower-tail test at level α, find the largest value k with P(X ≤ k) ≤ α, assuming H₀. The critical region is then {0, 1, …, k}. For X ~ B(10, 0.5) at the 5% level, P(X ≤ 1) = 11/1024 = 0.0107 and P(X ≤ 2) = 56/1024 = 0.0547. The second value is greater than 0.05, so k = 1 and the critical region is {0, 1}.

The actual significance level is rarely the stated level

Because X takes only whole-number values, the probability in the critical region is usually below the stated level. Here it is 0.0107, about 1.07%, not 5%. Say so in the working, using the phrase “actual significance level”. A discrete test that falls short of 5% is correct; a candidate who claims the level is exactly 5% makes a false statement.

Critical values for a normal test

For a normal test with known σ, a critical value of z replaces the critical count. The standard values are 1.645 for a one-tailed test at 5%, 2.326 for one-tailed at 1%, 1.96 for two-tailed at 5% and 2.576 for two-tailed at 1%. A lower-tailed test rejects when z ≤ −1.645; an upper-tailed test rejects when z ≥ 1.645. The normal distribution is continuous, so the actual level equals the stated level exactly.

Two-tailed critical regions for a discrete test

For a two-tailed test at 5%, each tail may carry probability at most 0.025. For X ~ B(10, 0.5), P(X ≤ 1) = 0.0107 is at most 0.025, while P(X ≤ 2) = 0.0547 is not. The lower critical region is {0, 1}, and by symmetry the upper one is {9, 10}. The combined probability is 0.0215, which is below 0.05, so the test can reject for 0, 1, 9 or 10 successes.

Checking the boundary and the sign

A common slip is to put the boundary in the wrong region or to use the wrong sign. For a lower-tailed normal test at 5%, the boundary z = −1.645 is itself in the critical region, because the test rejects when z ≤ −1.645. A critical value of +1.645 on a lower-tailed test is the commonest sign error. Write the inequality with the boundary included, then check that its sign matches the tail named in H₁.

p-values, step by step

A p-value gives the same decision as a critical region, but it reports how unlikely the data are on the assumption that H₀ is true, rather than only whether they fall inside a region. Many A2 questions ask for a p-value directly, and some ask for a comparison with the level in a single sentence.

What a p-value is and is not

The p-value is the probability, assuming H₀ is true, of a result at least as extreme as the one observed, in the direction stated in H₁. It is not the probability that H₀ is true, and it is not the probability that the result happened by chance. A p-value of 0.03 means that a result this extreme would occur 3% of the time if H₀ were true.

A p-value for a lower-tailed binomial test

For X ~ B(10, 0.5) with H₁: p < 0.5, suppose 2 successes are observed. The p-value is P(X ≤ 2) = 56/1024 = 0.0547. That is greater than 0.05, so the result is not significant at the 5% level. At the 10% level, 0.0547 is less than 0.10, so H₀ is rejected. The same observation gives different decisions at different levels, which is why the level must always be stated.

A p-value for a two-tailed binomial test

For the same observation with H₁: p ≠ 0.5, the p-value is twice the smaller tail probability: 2 × 0.0547 = 0.1094. A two-tailed p-value is never the value of one tail alone, and it is capped at 1 if doubling would exceed 1. Here 0.1094 is greater than 0.05, so the result is not significant at 5%. A two-tailed p-value is always at least as large as the one-tailed value, which is why a two-tailed test is the harder one to pass.

A p-value for a normal test

Suppose z = −2.1 is found for a lower-tailed normal test. The p-value is Φ(−2.1) = 1 − Φ(2.1) = 1 − 0.9821 = 0.0179. For a two-tailed test the p-value would be 2 × 0.0179 = 0.0357. Use the symmetry of the normal curve, and show the Φ step so that the table lookup can be checked.

Comparing a p-value with the significance level

If the p-value is less than or equal to the significance level, reject H₀. Write the comparison as a statement with both numbers, for example 0.0547 > 0.05, so do not reject H₀. Then give the decision in words, in the context of the question. The comparison in numbers is what the working shows, and the sentence is what the conclusion mark asks for.

The normal test as a standardised calculation

When the population is normal with a known standard deviation, the sample mean is itself normal, and the test standardises it before comparing with a critical value. This section shows the standardisation and the figure that makes the critical region visible.

Standardising the sample mean

If X ~ N(μ, σ²), then the mean of n independent values satisfies X̄ ~ N(μ, σ²/n) when H₀ is true. The test statistic is z = (x̄ − μ₀)/(σ/√n), where μ₀ is the value stated in H₀. Standardising converts any normal model to the standard normal distribution, so the critical values in the tables apply to every normal test.

Using the standard error, not the standard deviation

The denominator is σ/√n, the standard error of the mean, and not σ on its own. Dividing by σ alone gives a z-value that is √n times too small, and the test becomes too cautious. If σ is given, use it directly. If only the sample standard deviation s is given and the sample is large, use s as an estimate of σ and say so in the working.

A worked normal test

A machine fills bags with a mean of 500 g and a known standard deviation of 12 g. A sample of 36 bags has mean 496 g. Test at the 5% level whether the mean fill is less than 500 g. The standard error is 12/√36 = 2, so z = (496 − 500)/2 = −2. The critical value is −1.645, and −2 is less than −1.645, so H₀ is rejected. The p-value is Φ(−2) = 0.0228, which is less than 0.05.

Reading the critical region from the figure

The figure shows the standard normal curve with the lower 5% tail shaded. The boundary at −1.645 separates the critical region from the rest of the curve, and the observed z-value of −2 lies inside the shaded tail, which is why the test rejects H₀. Sketching this shape with the boundary and the observed value marked is a quick check that the direction of the test is right.

Reading the answer back in the units of the question

The conclusion must be in the units of the question: “There is evidence at the 5% level that the mean fill is less than 500 g.” Do not write “the mean is less than 500”, because a test never establishes a fact about the population. Name the quantity the evidence is about, the mean fill mass, and state the level.

Equations and symbols

A hypothesis test is a decision rule, and these are its moving parts: the test statistic, the standard error, the tail probability and the comparison that produces the verdict.

The decision

reject H0 if p-value <= alpha Key: H0 = the null hypothesis, the assumption of no change; p-value = the probability of a result at least as extreme, assuming H0 is true; alpha = the significance level, the acceptable risk of rejecting a true H0 (often 0.05 or 0.01). Failing to reject is not proof that H0 is true — it means the evidence was insufficient.

P(X <= 15) = 0.0432 Key: X = number of fault-free components in a sample of 20; 0.0432 = the lower-tail probability under H0: p = 0.9. Because 0.0432 < 0.05 the null is rejected, and the same figure is the actual significance level of the test.

The normal test

standard error = 8/sqrt 16 = 2 Key: 8 = population standard deviation σ (g); 16 = sample size n (bags); 2 = the standard error of the mean (g). The standard error, not σ, is the denominator of the test statistic — omitting the √n is the classic lost mark.

z = (496 - 500)/2 = -2 Key: z = the test statistic, in standard errors; 496 = sample mean (g); 500 = hypothesised mean μ (g); 2 = the standard error (g). Compare |z| with the critical value: 1.6449 one-tailed at 5%, 1.96 two-tailed at 5%.

p-value = P(Z > 1.72) = 0.0427 Key: Z = the standard normal variable; 1.72 = the observed test statistic; 0.0427 = the area beyond it, for an upper-tail alternative. Significant at 5% but not at 1% — say which level you are concluding at.

Errors

A Type I error rejects a true H0 and has probability alpha; a Type II error fails to reject a false H0. Lowering alpha reduces Type I errors and increases Type II; a larger sample reduces both, because it shrinks the standard error so the same deviation counts as more standard errors.

The slip worth naming

Comparing a p-value with 5 instead of 0.05, or doubling the tail without a two-sided alternative. Both reverse a correct conclusion, which is exactly the mark the question is testing.

title: Exam technique: Sampling
content:
### What earns the marks
For method choice, random vs stratified vs systematic justified earns the mark. For stratified allocation, the proportion of each stratum applied earns the method mark. For bias discussion, the named source of bias with its effect earns both marks.
### Traps
Error: sample claimed unbiased with no method. Correction: name and justify the method. Error: equal numbers per stratum. Correction: allocate proportionally. Error: population confused with frame. Correction: frame is the list used.

title: Poisson Distribution — Study Notes
content:
The Poisson Distribution

The Model

X ~ Po(λ) counts events in a fixed interval of time or space when events occur independently, at a constant average rate λ, and never twice at the same instant. Classic settings: calls per hour at a helpdesk, typos per page, cars per minute at a quiet junction.

The Formula

P(X = r) = e^(−λ) λʳ / r! for r = 0, 1, 2, ...

Example: X ~ Po(2). P(X = 0) = e⁻² ≈ 0.1353. P(X = 1) = 2e⁻² ≈ 0.2707.

Mean and Variance

The defining signature of the Poisson:

  • E(X) = λ and Var(X) = λ — the mean and variance are equal.

If a question gives a mean m, then λ = m; the variance is also m.

Scaling the Interval

If X ~ Po(λ) per hour, then 3 hours gives Y ~ Po(3λ). Rates must be adjusted to the same interval before computing anything. Halving an interval halves λ.

Adding Poissons

If X ~ Po(λ₁) and Y ~ Po(λ₂) are independent, then X + Y ~ Po(λ₁ + λ₂). Two independent queues merging into one server produce a Poisson with summed rate.

Exam tips: check independence and constant rate before modelling — if events cluster (rush hours), Poisson fails. Convert the interval first: a rate of 8 per 20 minutes becomes 24 per hour. In "at least" questions use the complement exactly as with the binomial.

title: A Level Mathematics: The Poisson Distribution
content:
A Level Mathematics: The Poisson Distribution

The Poisson distribution models the number of events that happen in a fixed interval of time, length, area or volume when those events occur randomly and independently at a constant average rate. Where the binomial counts successes in a fixed number of trials, the Poisson counts arrivals in a continuous window: calls reaching a switchboard in an hour, defects along a length of cable, radioactive decays in a minute. This note derives the formula from the binomial, sets out the two conditions that must hold, and then uses the distribution for the probability and hypothesis-test questions the exam sets.

Where the formula comes from

Imagine slicing the interval into a very large number of tiny sub-intervals. In each slice the chance of an event is tiny but the number of slices is enormous, so the count is binomial with n huge and p tiny. Taking that limit turns nCr p^r (1−p)^(n−r) into the Poisson formula, with the mean λ = np surviving as the only parameter.

X ~ Po(λ):  P(X = r) = e^(-λ) λ^r / r!
mean E(X) = λ
variance Var(X) = λ
so the mean and variance are equal - a diagnostic test for the model

The equality of mean and variance is not a coincidence to memorise; it is the fingerprint of the limit, and it is why an exam question can give you a sample mean and variance and ask whether a Poisson model is plausible.

The three conditions

A Poisson model needs randomness, independence and a constant rate. Naming them is worth marks, and each failure has a characteristic symptom.

1. events occur singly (not in pairs or batches)
2. events occur at random, independently of each other
3. the average rate λ is constant over the interval
then the count in that interval is Poisson

Worked example (checking the model). A shop counts customers arriving per hour. Explain why a Poisson model may be unsuitable.

the arrival rate is not constant: it peaks at lunchtime and is near zero at night
so condition 3 fails and the mean over a whole day is not a single rate
a better model splits the day into periods of roughly constant rate

Calculating probabilities

The formula handles a single value; the cumulative sum handles a range. Because the Poisson has no upper limit, every "at least" question becomes a complement.

P(X = r) = e^(-λ) λ^r / r!
P(X <= r) sums from 0 to r (tables or calculator)
P(X >= r) = 1 - P(X <= r - 1)
P(X < r)  = P(X <= r - 1)

Worked example. X ~ Po(3). Find P(X = 2).

P = e^(-3) × 3² / 2!
= 0.049787 × 9 / 2
= 0.2240

Worked example 2 (at least). For the same X, find P(X ≥ 4).

P(X >= 4) = 1 - P(X <= 3)
P(X <= 3) = 0.049787(1 + 3 + 4.5 + 4.5) = 0.6472
so P(X >= 4) = 0.3528

Worked example 3 (scale change). Calls arrive at 4 per minute. Find the probability of 10 or more calls in two minutes.

the rate scales with the interval: λ = 8 for two minutes
P(X >= 10) = 1 - P(X <= 9) = 1 - 0.7170 = 0.2830

Scaling is the most common source of avoidable error: the parameter must be expressed for the interval the question actually asks about.

Adding independent Poisson variables

If two independent counts each follow a Poisson distribution, their sum does too, and the parameters add. This is why the distribution is so usable: a total across separate sources needs no convolution.

X ~ Po(l1), Y ~ Po(l2), independent
X + Y ~ Po(l1 + l2)
but X - Y is NOT Poisson

Worked example. A website gets 5 hits per minute from Europe and 3 per minute from Asia, independently. Find the probability of more than 10 hits in a minute in total.

total ~ Po(8)
P(X > 10) = 1 - P(X <= 10) = 1 - 0.8159 = 0.1841

The Poisson as an approximation to the binomial

When n is large and p is small, the binomial is well approximated by a Poisson with λ = np. The rule of thumb used in this course is n > 50 and p < 0.05, or np < 5.

X ~ B(n, p) with n large, p small  →  X is approximately Po(np)

Worked example. A factory produces items with a 2% defect rate. In a batch of 200, use a Poisson approximation to find the probability of at most 2 defects.

λ = 200 × 0.02 = 4
P(X <= 2) = e^(-4)(1 + 4 + 8) = 0.018316 × 13 = 0.2381
the exact binomial gives 0.2351, so the approximation is close

Worked example 2 (justifying the approximation). State why the approximation is reasonable here.

n = 200 is large and p = 0.02 is small, with np = 4
so the rare-event limit conditions hold

Hypothesis testing with the Poisson

The structure is identical to the binomial test: state hypotheses, assume the null rate, compute the tail probability, compare with the significance level. The only new step is that the rate may need scaling to the observed interval.

H0: λ = lambda0    H1: λ > lambda0 (or <)
observed count x in the interval
p-value = P(X >= x) or P(X <= x) under Po(lambda0)
reject H0 if the p-value <= the significance level

Worked example. A call centre historically receives 6 calls per hour. In a new hour it receives 12. Test at the 5% level whether the rate has increased.

H0: λ = 6;  H1: λ > 6
X ~ Po(6) under H0
P(X >= 12) = 1 - P(X <= 11) = 1 - 0.9799 = 0.0201
0.0201 < 0.05, so reject H0
there is evidence the rate has increased

Worked example 2 (critical region). For Po(6), find the 5% one-tailed critical region for an increase.

P(X >= 11) = 0.0426 (below 0.05)
P(X >= 10) = 0.0839 (above 0.05)
critical region: X >= 11

Worked example 3 (two intervals). The same centre observes 16 calls over two hours. Test for an increase at 5%.

expected over two hours under H0 = 12, so X ~ Po(12)
P(X >= 16) = 1 - P(X <= 15) = 1 - 0.8444 = 0.1556
0.1556 > 0.05, so do not reject H0

Compare the two: twelve calls in one hour was significant, sixteen in two hours is not, because the expected count doubled. The rate, not the raw count, is what is being tested.

Reading the distribution's shape

The Poisson is skewed to the right when λ is small and becomes almost symmetric as λ grows, which is why small-rate questions usually live in the lower tail and why the normal approximation becomes usable once λ passes about 20. Knowing the shape tells you at a glance whether an answer is plausible: a probability of 0.4 for "more than 10" when λ = 3 should feel wrong before any arithmetic is checked.

A useful sanity check is that the standard deviation is the square root of the mean. For Po(9) the mean is 9 and the standard deviation 3, so counts between 6 and 12 are ordinary and a count of 20 is roughly three and a half standard deviations out — surprising enough to prompt a hypothesis test. That comparison is what turns a bare probability into an interpretation, and interpretation marks are the easiest ones to lose.

Finally, note that the model is about a count in an interval, so the interval has to be defined in the answer. "Three calls per hour" and "three calls per minute" describe different distributions, and a rate quoted per unit time without its unit is not a λ at all.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Definition) State two conditions for a Poisson model. Answer: events occur singly at random, independently, at a constant rate.
  2. (Single value) X ~ Po(2.5): find P(X = 3). Answer: e^(−2.5)(15.625/6) = 0.2138.
  3. (Cumulative) X ~ Po(4): find P(X ≤ 2). Answer: 0.2381.
  4. (Complement) X ~ Po(5): find P(X ≥ 3). Answer: 1 − 0.1247 = 0.8753.
  5. (Scaling) Rate 3 per hour: find P(X = 0) in 20 minutes. Answer: λ = 1, so e^(−1) = 0.3679.
  6. (Sum) Independent Po(2) and Po(3): find P(total = 4). Answer: Po(5), P(4) = 0.1755.
  7. (Approximation) B(500, 0.01): approximate P(X = 0). Answer: Po(5), e^(−5) = 0.00674.
  8. (Mean/variance) A sample has mean 4.2 and variance 9.1. Comment on the Poisson fit. Answer: variance far exceeds the mean, so the model is doubtful (over-dispersed).
  9. (Test) 9 events observed where 4 expected; test for an increase at 5%. Answer: P(X ≥ 9) = 0.0214 < 0.05, reject H0.
  10. (Critical region) Po(3), 5% upper tail: find the critical region. Answer: P(X ≥ 7) = 0.0335, P(X ≥ 6) = 0.0839, so X ≥ 7.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Using the wrong interval: λ must match the window asked about; doubling a time doubles the rate.
  • Complement off by one: P(X ≥ 4) = 1 − P(X ≤ 3); subtracting P(X ≤ 4) is the classic error.
  • Treating a difference as Poisson: sums of independent Poisson variables are Poisson, differences are not.
  • Approximation outside its range: np must be small; with np large the Poisson is a poor fit to the binomial.
  • Variance assumed equal to the mean without checking: the test mean = variance is a diagnostic, not a guarantee.
  • Ignoring clustering: events that arrive in bursts break the single-event condition and inflate the variance.
  • r! miscomputed: 0! = 1 and 1! = 1, and a missing factorial term changes the answer entirely.
  • p-value direction: a one-tailed test uses one tail only; doubling it makes a borderline result look significant.

Equations and symbols

One formula does the arithmetic, and one identity checks the model: for a Poisson variable the mean and the variance are the same number λ. Every exam error on this topic is either a λ expressed for the wrong interval or a complement taken one term too far.

P(X = r) = e^(-λ) λ^r / r! Key: X = the number of events counted in the fixed interval (a count, no units); r = the particular count asked about; λ = the mean number of events in that same interval (no units — it is a count, not a rate per second, unless the interval is one second); e = 2.71828…; r! = factorial of r, with 0! = 1.

mean E(X) = λ Key: E(X) = the expected count in the interval; λ = the mean. Read it with the line below: the equality of mean and variance is the fingerprint of the model, and a sample whose variance far exceeds its mean is not Poisson.

variance Var(X) = λ Key: Var(X) = the variance of the count; λ = the same mean. So the standard deviation is √λ, which is the quickest sanity check on an observed count: for λ = 9, counts between 6 and 12 are ordinary.

P(X >= r) = 1 - P(X <= r - 1) Key: the complement rule, because the Poisson has no upper limit; r = the smallest count that counts as "at least". Subtracting P(X ≤ r) instead of P(X ≤ r − 1) is the classic off-by-one and throws the whole tail away.

P = e^(-3) × 3² / 2! Key: λ = 3 for this interval; r = 2; 3² = λ^r; 2! = 2. The arithmetic is 0.049787 × 9 / 2 = 0.2240 — quote four decimal places unless told otherwise.

λ = 200 × 0.02 = 4 Key: 200 = n, the number of trials; 0.02 = p, the probability of the event in one trial; λ = np = 4, the mean of the approximating Poisson. The approximation is used when n is large and p small — n > 50 and p < 0.05, or np < 5.

P(X <= 2) = e^(-4)(1 + 4 + 8) = 0.018316 × 13 = 0.2381 Key: the bracket is λ^r/r! summed for r = 0, 1, 2: 1, 4 and 8 (since 4²/2! = 8); e^(−4) = 0.018316. The exact binomial gives 0.2351, so the approximation is close — say so when a question asks you to comment.

X + Y ~ Po(l1 + l2) Key: X and Y = two independent Poisson counts; l1, l2 = their means; the total count is Poisson with the means added. A difference of two Poisson variables is not Poisson — only sums combine.

X ~ B(n, p) with n large, p small → X is approximately Po(np) Key: B(n, p) = the binomial with n trials and success probability p; np = the Poisson mean that replaces them. State both conditions before using it, because the approximation fails when np is large.

SymbolQuantityUnit
λmean number of events in the stated intervala count (no units) — quote the interval with it
rthe observed or asked-about counta count (no units)
H₀null hypothesis, λ = λ₀a stated mean count for the interval

Scaling is the other half of the topic and it is not a formula but a substitution: a rate of 4 per minute is λ = 8 for a two-minute window, and 12 calls in one hour must be tested against 24 expected in two hours, not against 12. Write the interval beside the λ every time.

title: Electrochemistry
content:
Electrochemistry

Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry 0620, Extended route, topic 4 (statements 4.1–4.2). Electrolysis of molten and aqueous electrolytes, electrode products, half-equations, electroplating and fuel cells.

4.1 Electrolysis

  • Electrolysis is the breakdown of an ionic compound, when molten or in aqueous solution, by the passage of electricity. Cations (positive ions) move to the cathode (negative electrode) and are reduced; anions (negative ions) move to the anode (positive electrode) and are oxidised.
  • Molten lead(II) bromide: Pb²⁺ → Pb at the cathode (grey lead forms), 2Br⁻ → Br₂ at the anode (brown bromine vapour). Only the ions of the compound are present, so the products are unambiguous.
  • Concentrated aqueous sodium chloride: hydrogen at the cathode, chlorine at the anode, sodium hydroxide left in solution. Dilute sulfuric acid: hydrogen at the cathode, oxygen at the anode (water is preferentially discharged over the sulfate ion).
  • Aqueous copper(II) sulfate with inert electrodes: copper at the cathode, oxygen at the anode. With copper electrodes the anode dissolves instead, so the concentration stays constant — this is electroplating and industrial copper refining.
  • Half-equations (Extended): 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂; 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻; Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu. Include electrons on the correct side and balance charge as well as atoms.

4.2 Hydrogen–oxygen fuel cells

  • A hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell uses hydrogen and oxygen to produce electricity, with water as the only product. Advantages: no carbon dioxide at the point of use, high efficiency. Disadvantages: hydrogen is hard to store and transport, and producing it may itself burn fossil fuels.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Product prediction, applied to molten aluminium oxide: Al³⁺ → Al at the cathode, O²⁻ → O₂ at the anode. The Extended rule is that in aqueous solutions the hydrogen ion discharges in preference to a metal low in the reactivity series, and the hydroxide ion in preference to most anions. State the rule you are applying.
  • Electroplating, applied to plating a key with silver: the key is the cathode (it must be negative so Ag⁺ ions deposit on it), the silver object is the anode (it dissolves to replace the Ag⁺ used up), and the electrolyte is a soluble silver salt such as silver nitrate. Name all three — a three-mark question.
  • Mass deposited calculation, applied to a current plating with copper for a given time: moles of copper = mass ÷ 64. From Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu, two moles of electrons are needed per mole of copper. The reasoning marks come from linking the mass to the half-equation, not from the arithmetic alone.

Common errors

  • Swapping anode and cathode. The anode is positive and oxidation happens there; the cathode is negative and reduction happens there.
  • Writing half-equations with unbalanced charge.
  • Saying the anode "loses mass" for inert electrodes in dilute sulfuric acid — it is the water that is oxidised, and oxygen gas forms.

How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

### Worked example Solve 3(x − 2) = 2x + 5. Expand to 3x − 6 = 2x + 5, then subtract 2x and add 6 to get x = 11. Check by substitution: 3(11 − 2) = 27 and 2(11) + 5 = 27. For rearranging, make t the subject of v = u + at by subtracting u and dividing by a, giving t = (v − u)/a.

title: Algebra — Inequalities — Study Notes
content:
Algebra — Inequalities

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): solving linear inequalities, integer solution sets, shading regions on graphs (linear programming context).

1. Solving

Like equations, but reverse the sign when multiplying/dividing by a negative: −2x ≥ 6 ⇒ x ≤ −3.

Example: 3x − 5 < 2x + 1 ⇒ x < 6.

2. Integer solutions

−1 ≤ x < 4 ⇒ x ∈ {−1, 0, 1, 2, 3}. Closed endpoint for ≤/≥, open for </>.

3. Double inequalities

Handle both sides: −3 < 2x + 1 ≤ 7 → −4 < 2x ≤ 6 → −2 < x ≤ 3.

4. Shading regions

  • Draw the boundary line: dashed for </>, solid for ≤/≥.
  • Test a point (usually (0,0)) to pick the wanted side; shade the unwanted side or label the wanted region.
  • Feasible region satisfies all constraints simultaneously.

Example: y ≤ 2x + 1: solid line, test (0,0): 0 ≤ 1 ✓ → region containing origin.

Exam tips: never divide by an unknown sign — move x terms first; list integer solutions inside curly brackets; state which region you shade.

Solving linear inequalities

Inequalities are solved like equations, with one crucial exception: multiplying or dividing both sides by a negative number reverses the inequality sign. Answers are written as a single inequality such as x > 3, or as a set such as -2 < x ≤ 5 when two bounds are given.

Representing inequalities on a number line

An open circle marks a strict bound (< or >) that is not included; a filled circle marks an inclusive bound (≤ or ≥). Shade the region that satisfies the statement.

Regions on a coordinate grid

Draw each boundary line as a solid line for ≤ or ≥ and a dashed line for < or >. Test a point such as (0, 0) if it is not on the line; shade the side that makes the inequality true. Where several regions are required, the wanted region is the overlap of all the shaded areas. Integer points inside a region are counted when a question asks for them.

Worked example: solving a linear inequality

Solve 3x − 7 < 2x + 4. Subtract 2x from both sides to get x − 7 < 4, then add 7 to get x < 11. The solution set is every number less than 11, which has no lower bound.

Double inequalities and integer solutions

Solve −3 ≤ 2x + 1 < 7. Subtract 1 from each part: −4 ≤ 2x < 6. Divide each part by 2: −2 ≤ x < 3. The integer solutions are −2, −1, 0, 1 and 2. Remember that the ≤ sign includes −2 and the < sign excludes 3.

Multiplying or dividing by a negative number

Solve 8 − 3x > 2. Subtract 8: −3x > −6. Divide by −3 and reverse the sign: x < 2. Forgetting to reverse the sign is the most common lost mark in this topic.

Quadratic inequalities

Solve x² − x − 6 ≤ 0. Factorise to (x − 3)(x + 2) ≤ 0. The expression is zero at x = 3 and x = −2, and it is negative between them. The solution is −2 ≤ x ≤ 3. Sketch the parabola to see which region is below the axis.

Shading regions on a grid

  • Draw a boundary line as a solid line for ≤ or ≥, and as a dashed line for < or >.
  • Test a point that is not on the line, usually (0, 0) if the line does not pass through it, to decide which side to shade.
  • If the question asks for a region bounded by several inequalities, shade each one lightly and leave the overlap clear.

title: Organic Nitrogen Compounds: Amines, Amides, Amino Acids and Proteins — Study Notes
content:
Organic Nitrogen Compounds: Amines, Amides, Amino Acids and Proteins

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH15, Topic 19. Amines, amides, amino acids and proteins contain nitrogen. The lone pair on nitrogen controls basicity, and the amide and peptide links join molecules into polymers.

Amines

  • Primary amines have one alkyl group on the nitrogen, for example ethylamine.
  • Alkyl groups push electron density onto nitrogen, so ethylamine is a stronger base than ammonia.
  • In phenylamine the lone pair is delocalised into the ring, so it is a weaker base than ammonia.
  • Amines form salts with acids: CH₃NH₂ + HCl gives CH₃NH₃⁺Cl⁻.
  • Preparation: a haloalkane heated with excess ethanolic ammonia gives a primary amine. The excess ammonia limits further substitution. A nitrile reduced by LiAlH₄ gives a primary amine.

Amides

  • An acyl chloride reacts with ammonia or an amine to form an amide. Ethanoyl chloride with ammonia gives ethanamide.
  • Hydrolysis of an amide with hot dilute acid gives a carboxylic acid and an ammonium salt.

Amino acids and zwitterions

  • Amino acids contain –NH₂ and –COOH. In the solid and near neutral pH they exist as zwitterions, ⁺H₃NCH(R)COO⁻, with no net charge.
  • At the isoelectric point the zwitterion has no net charge. In strong acid it is a cation; in alkali it is an anion.
  • Amino acids can be separated by electrophoresis because their charge depends on pH.

Peptides and proteins

  • A peptide link forms when the –COOH of one amino acid condenses with the –NH₂ of another, releasing water.
  • Proteins have primary (sequence), secondary (alpha helices and beta sheets, held by hydrogen bonds) and tertiary structures. Complete hydrolysis with hot acid gives amino acids.

Exam tip: when comparing base strength, explain the availability of the nitrogen lone pair, not just the names of the groups.

title: A Level Mathematics: The Binomial Distribution
content:
A Level Mathematics: The Binomial Distribution

A binomial distribution counts successes in a fixed number of independent trials, each with the same probability of success. Coins, multiple-choice guesses, defective items in a sample and free throws all fit the same template, and once a problem is recognised as binomial the calculation is a formula plus a cumulative table. This note builds the distribution from its four conditions, derives the formula from counting, and then uses it for the two things exams actually ask: probabilities and hypothesis tests.

The four conditions

Before writing X ~ B(n, p) you must be able to name the conditions, because most exam questions include a part asking whether the model is appropriate. The conditions are not red tape: drop any one and the formula is simply wrong.

1. a fixed number of trials n
2. each trial has exactly two outcomes (success / failure)
3. the probability of success p is constant for every trial
4. the trials are independent
then X = number of successes has X ~ B(n, p)

Worked example (checking the model). A bag holds 5 red and 15 blue counters. Four counters are taken without replacement. Is the number of red counters binomial?

n = 4 is fixed and each draw is red or not red
but p changes: 5/20, then 5/19 if a red was taken, ...
the trials are not independent, so NOT binomial (it is hypergeometric)

Taking with replacement would fix it: p stays 0.25 on every draw.

The formula, and where it comes from

The probability of a particular sequence of r successes and n − r failures is p^r (1−p)^(n−r), because independence lets you multiply. The number of such sequences is the number of ways to choose which r trials succeed, which is nCr. Multiplying gives the formula.

P(X = r) = nCr p^r (1 - p)^(n - r)
the nCr counts arrangements; the powers give the probability of one arrangement

Worked example. X ~ B(10, 0.3). Find P(X = 3).

P = 10C3 (0.3)³ (0.7)⁷
= 120 × 0.027 × 0.08235
= 120 × 0.002223 = 0.2668

Worked example 2 (a single trial count). A fair die is rolled 8 times. Find the probability of exactly two sixes.

X ~ B(8, 1/6)
P(X = 2) = 8C2 (1/6)² (5/6)⁶ = 28 × 0.02778 × 0.3349 = 0.2605

Worked example 3 (why nCr appears). For n = 3 and r = 1, list the sequences and confirm the coefficient.

sequences: SFF, FSF, FFS - three of them
each has probability p(1-p)²
so P(X = 1) = 3p(1-p)², and 3C1 = 3

Cumulative probabilities

Questions almost always ask for a range, not a single value, and the cumulative distribution is what the calculator or the tables supply. The skill is rewriting the question into the form the table gives you.

P(X <= r) is tabulated directly
P(X >= r) = 1 - P(X <= r - 1)
P(X < r)  = P(X <= r - 1)
P(a <= X <= b) = P(X <= b) - P(X <= a - 1)
P(X = r) = P(X <= r) - P(X <= r - 1)

Worked example. X ~ B(20, 0.4). Find P(X ≥ 8).

P(X >= 8) = 1 - P(X <= 7)
= 1 - 0.4159
= 0.5841

Worked example 2 (between). For the same X, find P(5 ≤ X ≤ 10).

= P(X <= 10) - P(X <= 4)
= 0.8725 - 0.0510
= 0.8215

Worked example 3 (the strict inequality trap). For the same X, find P(X > 6).

P(X > 6) = 1 - P(X <= 6) = 1 - 0.2500 = 0.7500
note this is different from P(X >= 6) = 1 - P(X <= 5) = 0.8746

Mean and variance

The binomial has the simplest mean and variance in the syllabus, and they are worth knowing both forwards and backwards: a question can give the mean and variance and ask for n and p.

E(X) = np
Var(X) = np(1 - p)
standard deviation = √(np(1-p))

Worked example. X ~ B(50, 0.2). Find the mean and standard deviation.

mean = 50 × 0.2 = 10
variance = 10 × 0.8 = 8
sd = 2.828

Worked example 2 (backwards). A binomial variable has mean 12 and variance 9. Find n and p.

np = 12;  np(1-p) = 9
divide: 1 - p = 9/12 = 0.75  →  p = 0.25
then n = 12/0.25 = 48

Hypothesis testing with the binomial

A one-tailed test asks whether p has increased or decreased; the test statistic is the observed count, and the p-value is the probability of a result at least as extreme in the direction of the alternative.

H0: p = p0      H1: p > p0 (or p < p0)
X ~ B(n, p0) under H0
p-value = P(X >= observed) or P(X <= observed)
compare with the significance level; reject H0 if p-value <= alpha

Worked example. A coin is tossed 20 times and lands heads 15 times. Test at the 5% level whether the coin is biased towards heads.

H0: p = 0.5;  H1: p > 0.5
X ~ B(20, 0.5)
P(X >= 15) = 1 - P(X <= 14) = 1 - 0.9793 = 0.0207
0.0207 < 0.05, so reject H0
there is evidence at the 5% level that the coin favours heads

Worked example 2 (two-tailed). The same data tested two-tailed.

double the smaller tail: 2 × 0.0207 = 0.0414
0.0414 < 0.05, so still reject H0 at the 5% level

Worked example 3 (critical region). For X ~ B(20, 0.5), find the critical region for a 5% one-tailed test of p > 0.5.

P(X >= 14) = 0.0577 (above 0.05)
P(X >= 15) = 0.0207 (below 0.05)
critical region: X >= 15

Note that the critical region is chosen so the probability of a Type I error is at most 5%, which is why 14 is excluded even though it is close.

When the model breaks down

Examiners like the question that asks why a binomial model is only an approximation. The usual culprits are dependence, a varying probability, or a fixed sample drawn without replacement from a small population.

SituationProblemEffect
sampling without replacementtrials not independentp drifts; use the hypergeometric instead
clustered data (pupils in classes)responses correlatedvariance underestimated
probability varies between trialsp not constantformula invalid
large n, p near 0.5computation heavynormal approximation is reasonable

Worked example (normal approximation). X ~ B(200, 0.4). Use a normal approximation to estimate P(X ≤ 70).

mean = 80;  variance = 200 × 0.4 × 0.6 = 48;  sd = 6.928
continuity correction: X <= 70 becomes X < 70.5
z = (70.5 - 80)/6.928 = -1.371
P(Z < -1.371) = 0.0852

The continuity correction is compulsory: a discrete count needs a half-unit boundary before it can be treated as continuous.

Expected frequencies and the shape of the distribution

A binomial distribution is not symmetric unless p = 0.5, and that shape decides which tail an exam question is fishing in. The most likely value — the mode — is the integer near (n + 1)p, and expected frequency multiplies the probability by the number of samples taken. Both are quick marks that are frequently missed because students jump straight to the formula.

mode is near (n + 1)p, checked by comparing consecutive probabilities
expected number in a sample of size N = N x P(X = r)

Worked example. X ~ B(12, 0.3). Find the most likely value of X and the expected number of 3s in 500 independent observations.

(n + 1)p = 13 × 0.3 = 3.9, so check r = 3 and r = 4
P(X = 3) = 220 × 0.027 × 0.1176 = 0.2397
P(X = 4) = 495 × 0.0081 × 0.1681 = 0.2311
mode = 3
expected number of 3s = 500 × 0.2397 = 120 (to the nearest whole)

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Model) State the distribution for the number of sixes in 12 rolls of a fair die. Answer: X ~ B(n, p) with n = 12 rolls and p = 1/6 the chance of a six on each, so X ~ B(12, 1/6).
  2. (Single value) X ~ B(8, 0.25): find P(X = 2). Answer: P(X = 2) = ⁸C₂ (0.25)² (0.75)⁶ = 28 × 0.0625 × 0.1780 = 0.3115.
  3. (Cumulative) X ~ B(15, 0.3): find P(X ≤ 4). Answer: P(X ≤ 4) = Σₖ₌₀⁴ ¹⁵Cₖ (0.3)ᵏ (0.7)¹⁵⁻ᵏ = 0.5155 from cumulative binomial tables.
  4. (Complement) Same X: find P(X ≥ 3). Answer: P(X ≥ 3) = 1 − P(X ≤ 2) = 1 − 0.2969 = 0.7031 — the complement, because the tables give the lower tail only.
  5. (Mean) X ~ B(40, 0.35): find E(X) and Var(X). Answer: 14 and 9.1.
  6. (Backwards) Mean 18, variance 12: find n and p. Answer: mean np = 18 and variance np(1 − p) = 12; dividing, 1 − p = 12/18 = 2/3, so p = 1/3 and n = 18 ÷ (1/3) = 54.
  7. (Test) 12 of 20 seeds germinate; test p = 0.5 against p < 0.5 at 5%. Answer: H₀: p = 0.5 against H₁: p < 0.5; under H₀, X ~ B(20, 0.5) and P(X ≤ 12) = 0.8684, which is far above 0.05, so there is no evidence to reject H₀.
  8. (Critical region) X ~ B(10, 0.2): find the 5% critical region for p < 0.2. Answer: the smallest possible tail is P(X ≤ 0) = (0.8)¹⁰ = 0.1074, which already exceeds 0.05, so no critical region exists at the 5% level for this n.
  9. (Approximation) X ~ B(100, 0.5): approximate P(X ≥ 60). Answer: μ = np = 50 and σ = √(np(1 − p)) = √25 = 5; with the continuity correction z = (59.5 − 50)/5 = 1.9, so P(X ≥ 60) ≈ P(Z > 1.9) = 0.0287.
  10. (Assumption) Give one reason a binomial model may fail for defects in boxes of 20. Answer: defects may cluster, so trials are not independent.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Forgetting nCr: the coefficient counts arrangements; without it the answer is the probability of one specific sequence.
  • nCr on the wrong factor: it is p^r (1−p)^(n−r), with the success probability raised to the number of successes.
  • Inequality direction: P(X ≥ 8) uses 1 − P(X ≤ 7), not 1 − P(X ≤ 8).
  • Variance confused with standard deviation: np(1−p) is the variance; the test and the normal approximation need the square root.
  • Continuity correction omitted: any normal approximation to a discrete count needs the half-unit adjustment.
  • One-tailed evidence read as two: halving or doubling the tail without checking the alternative direction is a silent error.
  • Independence asserted, not checked: sampling without replacement from a small population breaks the model, and the question usually invites you to say so.
  • p-value compared with the wrong threshold: the significance level is given as a percentage; 5% means 0.05, not 5.

Recognising a binomial situation in context

Most binomial marks are lost before any arithmetic starts, because the question was not identified as binomial. The subsections below give a checklist for reading a question and writing the model in the standard form X ~ B(n, p) before you calculate anything.

Writing the model in the form X ~ B(n, p)

Once you decide a situation is binomial, state the model in full: X ~ B(n, p), where X is the number of successes, n is the number of trials and p is the probability of a success on each trial. Define X in words in your answer, for example “X is the number of defective bulbs in a box of 20”. A model with no definition of X loses the communication mark even when the probabilities are right.

Identifying the number of trials, n

The value of n is the fixed number of times the experiment is repeated: the number of bulbs tested, the number of patients treated, or the number of games played. Read the question for the phrase that fixes it, such as “of 20 bulbs chosen at random”. If the question keeps going until a result occurs, the number of trials is not fixed and the binomial model does not apply directly.

Identifying the probability of success, p

The value of p is the probability of the outcome you have chosen to call a success on one trial. It must stay the same for every trial. A fair coin gives p = 0.5, and a bag where 15% of items are faulty gives p = 0.15 for each item drawn with replacement. If the question gives a percentage, convert it to a decimal before you use it in any formula.

Checking for fixed trials

The number of trials must be decided before the experiment starts. Counting the number of successes in a fixed sample is binomial, whereas recording how many trials it takes to get the first success is not. A question about the number of heads in ten tosses is binomial; a question about how many tosses are needed for the first head is a different model. Make the fixed-n check before any other check.

Checking for independent trials

Each trial must not affect the next. Independence is what allows you to multiply the probabilities of several outcomes together, and it is the assumption most often ignored. Drawing items with replacement keeps p constant, and that is what the model needs. Drawing without replacement changes p after each draw, so the binomial model is only an approximation when the sample is small compared with the population.

Worked identification

A survey finds that 30% of adults own a bicycle. Twelve adults are chosen at random from a large town and asked whether they own one. Let X be the number who own a bicycle. Here n = 12, p = 0.3 and the answer is X ~ B(12, 0.3). The population is large, so the probability for each adult stays close to 0.3 and the model is a reasonable one to use. State that assumption, because a marker looks for it.

Probabilities of at least one, and of more than r

Questions that ask for “at least” or “more than” are the ones where the complement saves the most time. The subsections set out the choice between a direct sum and the complement, and the checks that stop an off-by-one error.

Probability of at least one success

“At least one” is the complement of “none”, so P(X ≥ 1) = 1 − P(X = 0) = 1 − qⁿ, where q = 1 − p. For X ~ B(5, 0.2), P(X ≥ 1) = 1 − 0.8⁵ = 1 − 0.32768 = 0.672 to 3 significant figures. Adding the probabilities of X = 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 gives the same answer but takes five calculations instead of one.

Probability of more than r successes

“More than 3” means 4 or more, so P(X > 3) = 1 − P(X ≤ 3). For X ~ B(10, 0.3), P(X ≤ 3) = 0.6496 to 4 decimal places, so P(X > 3) = 0.3504. The number 3 is included in the part you subtract from 1; forgetting that is the typical error on “more than” questions.

Choosing between a direct sum and the complement

Use the complement when the part you do not want is short: “at least one”, “at most one but not zero” and similar phrases. Use a direct sum when the wanted region has only a few terms, such as P(X = 2) + P(X = 3). With a calculator table of cumulative probabilities, most “at most” and “at least” questions reduce to one lookup and one subtraction.

Probability of exactly r on a calculator

For X ~ B(n, p), P(X = r) = ⁿCᵣ pʳ qⁿ⁻ʳ. The combination ⁿCᵣ counts the ways the r successes can be arranged among n trials. For X ~ B(10, 0.3), P(X = 3) = 120 × 0.3³ × 0.7⁷ = 120 × 0.027 × 0.0823543 = 0.2668 to 4 decimal places. Enter the combination with the nCr key so the arrangement count is not mistyped.

The most likely number of successes (the mode)

The most likely value of X is the mode. For a binomial distribution it is the whole number part of (n + 1)p, and if (n + 1)p is itself a whole number there are two modes, (n + 1)p − 1 and (n + 1)p. For X ~ B(10, 0.3), (n + 1)p = 3.3, so the mode is 3. Check against the probabilities: P(X = 3) = 0.2668 is larger than P(X = 2) = 0.2335 and P(X = 4) = 0.2001.

Adding independent binomial variables

A question can combine two or more binomial counts, for example the total number of faults from two machines. The result is binomial only under particular conditions, and the subsections below say what those conditions are and how to check them.

Same probability, different numbers of trials

If X ~ B(n, p) and Y ~ B(m, p) are independent, and both use the same probability of success p, then X + Y ~ B(n + m, p). Two batches tested for the same fault, with the same chance of that fault on each item, combine into one larger binomial. The shared p is the key condition: the trials must all be a success or failure with the same chance.

The rule for X + Y

Write the result as X + Y ~ B(n + m, p). For example, X ~ B(4, 0.5) and Y ~ B(6, 0.5), independent, give X + Y ~ B(10, 0.5). Add the trial counts, not the probabilities. The probability of success stays the same because each trial still has the same chance of success.

When the probabilities differ

If X ~ B(n, p) and Y ~ B(m, q) with p ≠ q, the sum is not binomial, and you cannot use the rule above. The number of successes comes from trials that have different chances, so no single p describes all of them. A question that asks for the distribution in this case expects a table of values, not a single binomial statement.

Worked example: two batches

Batch A has 8 items and batch B has 12 items. Each item in either batch is defective with probability 0.05, and the items are independent. Let T be the total number of defective items. Then T ~ B(20, 0.05), because both batches share p = 0.05. The probability of no defective items at all is P(T = 0) = 0.95²⁰ = 0.358 to 3 significant figures.

Why the mean and variance add

The mean of a sum is always the sum of the means, whether or not the variables are independent. The variance of a sum is the sum of the variances only when the variables are independent. For the batch example, E(T) = 20 × 0.05 = 1 and Var(T) = 20 × 0.05 × 0.95 = 0.95, which is the same as adding the separate variances 8 × 0.0475 and 12 × 0.0475.

Equations and symbols

The distribution, its conditions and the four tail identities. Every question on this topic is one of these lines plus a calculator.

P(X = r) = nCr p^r (1 - p)^(n - r) Key: n = number of trials, fixed in advance; p = probability of success in one trial, constant; r = the number of successes asked for; nCr = n!/(r!(n − r)!), the number of orders the successes can occur in. The (1 − p) term is the failures, and its power must be n − r.

X ~ B(n, p) Key: X = the count of successes; the tilde means "is distributed as"; n and p as above. Write this line before calculating — it is often a mark on its own, and it fixes which parameters go into the calculator.
