P = 10C3 (0.3)³ (0.7)⁷ Key: n = 10, p = 0.3, r = 3, so the failures are 7 and their probability is 0.7. The coefficient 10C3 = 120 accounts for the order of the three successes among the ten trials.

P(X >= r) = 1 - P(X <= r - 1) Key: a complement, so the two probabilities add to 1; the boundary moves by one because the binomial is discrete. Using 1 − P(X ≤ r) instead is the classic off-by-one error.

P(a <= X <= b) = P(X <= b) - P(X <= a - 1) Key: subtract the part below the interval; again the "− 1" is there because P(X ≤ a − 1) is everything before a. Check with a small case you can list by hand before trusting the calculator.

title: IGCSE Computer Science: Programming Concepts and Constructs
content:
IGCSE Computer Science: Programming Concepts and Constructs

Cambridge IGCSE Computer Science 0478 (2026–2028), Paper 2 Algorithms, Programming and Logic and Paper 1 statement 4.2: types of programming language and translators, 8.1 Programming concepts, 8.2 Arrays, and 8.3 File handling. This note builds a programmer's vocabulary from zero: how code becomes machine instructions, the variables-and-constructs model of every imperative program, and how data is organised in arrays and files. Every trace below steps through memory line by line — showing exactly how each variable changes is the skill Paper 2 examines most.

From source code to machine code: translators

A CPU understands only binary machine code — patterns of 0s and 1s unique to its processor family. Humans write source code in a language (Python, C++, Java), so something must convert one to the other: a translator, and there are three kinds.

TranslatorHow it worksResultTrade-off
CompilerTranslates the whole program in one pass, before runningA standalone executable machine-code fileFast to run afterwards; errors reported before execution (C++, Pascal)
InterpreterTranslates and runs one line at a time, in sequenceNo saved executable — the translator is needed every runSlow to run, but great for testing: errors appear exactly where they occur (Python, BASIC)
AssemblerTranslates assembly (human-readable mnemonics for single machine instructions) into machine codeExecutable for one processor familyOne-to-one with machine code: fast and precise, but tied to the hardware
Compiler vs interpreter, step by step, on the same three-line program:

Program:  a = 2 * 3        b = a + 1        print(b)

Compiler:
  1. Read the ENTIRE source file first.
  2. Check syntax of every line; if line 2 is wrong, report it and produce
     nothing - fix it before any code runs.
  3. Emit one machine-code executable.
  4. Run that executable: 18 microseconds of work at full machine speed.

Interpreter:
  1. Take line 1: translate AND execute it - a becomes 6 in memory.
  2. Take line 2: translate AND execute it - b becomes 7.
  3. Take line 3: translate AND execute it - output 7.
  4. If line 2 had failed, line 1 would already have run: execution stops at
     the error, and every run pays the translation cost again.

A syntax error is a grammar mistake the translator refuses; a logic error is
grammar-correct code that computes the wrong thing - translators never catch
those, which is why testing exists.

Levels of programming language

  • Machine code — binary, executed directly, fastest, unreadable to humans, and processor-specific.
  • Assembly language — mnemonics (MOV, ADD, JMP) one per machine instruction; still low-level and hardware-tied, needing an assembler.
  • High-level languages — English-like statements (PRINT, WHILE, INPUT); portable across machines once translated, readable, faster to develop.

The trade-off is always the same: low-level code is small and fast and controls the hardware directly (drivers, embedded systems); high-level code is quick to write and easy to maintain and runs anywhere a translator exists. Fourth-generation languages (SQL, report generators) sit even higher, declaring what is wanted rather than how.

The vocabulary of a program

TermMeaningCambridge pseudocode example
VariableA named memory location whose value can change as the program runsscore <- 0
ConstantA named value fixed for the whole run — used for values like pi or tax rates so they are defined once and cannot driftCONSTANT taxRate <- 0.2
Data typeWhat kind of value a variable holds: INTEGER, REAL, CHAR, STRING, BOOLEAN, DATEname : STRING
IdentifierThe name chosen for a variable, constant or proceduretotalPrice, itemCount
AssignmentStoring a value in a variable — the right side is evaluated first, then stored lefttotal <- price * qty
CommentIgnored text explaining the code to human readers// running total

Identifiers have rules worth marks: descriptive names preferred (markScheme not ms), no spaces, cannot start with a digit, and reserved words (PRINT, WHILE, IF) cannot be reused as names.

Sequence: the first construct

Every imperative program executes statements one after another, top to bottom — that is sequence. The trace is the examiner's favourite question type: keep a column per variable and rewrite each row after every statement.

Trace table. Program:

  1  a <- 5
  2  b <- 2 * a
  3  a <- a + b
  4  OUTPUT a, b

Step   statement        a    b    output
start  (nothing)        ?    ?
1      a <- 5           5    ?
2      b <- 2 * a       5    10       [reads a = 5, stores 10]
3      a <- a + b      15    10       [5 + 10 = 15 OVERWRITES the old a]
4      OUTPUT a, b                        15, 10

The trap in line 3: a + b uses the CURRENT values (5 + 10), then the result
replaces a. Assignment destroys the old value - the trace table keeps it honest.

Selection: IF, ELSE and ELSEIF

Selection chooses between paths using a condition — an expression that evaluates TRUE or FALSE. Comparison operators: =, <> (not equal), <, >, <=, >=; combine them with AND, OR, NOT. Conditions in pseudocode are never assignment: IF mark = 50, not mark <- 50.

Worked trace: grading with ELSEIF.

  IF mark >= 70 THEN
      grade <- "A"
  ELSEIF mark >= 60 THEN
      grade <- "B"
  ELSEIF mark >= 50 THEN
      grade <- "C"
  ELSE
      grade <- "U"
  ENDIF

Run with mark = 64:
  Line 1: is 64 >= 70? FALSE - skip to the next branch.
  Line 3: is 64 >= 60? TRUE - grade <- "B", and the whole structure ends.
  (The remaining branches are not even tested: ELSEIF means "else, if".)

Run with mark = 45:
  70? no. 60? no. 50? no - all conditions FALSE, so the ELSE branch runs:
  grade <- "U". ELSE is the guaranteed fallback; with no ELSE, grade would
  keep whatever it held before (possibly nothing).

Nested IF (an IF inside another's branch) handles layered conditions; the exam often asks you to write one and to test both boundary cases (69 and 70, not just 65).

Iteration: WHILE, REPEAT and FOR

Iteration repeats statements. WHILE tests first and repeats while a condition is TRUE — zero repeats possible. REPEAT…UNTIL runs the body at least once, then repeats until the condition becomes TRUE — note the polarity: WHILE repeats while TRUE, UNTIL repeats until TRUE. FOR repeats a counted number of times.

Full memory trace of a WHILE loop: running total of 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5.

  1  total <- 0
  2  count <- 1
  3  WHILE count <= 5
  4      total <- total + count
  5      count <- count + 1
  6  ENDWHILE
  7  OUTPUT total

Step      condition (count <= 5)   total   count
start                            -        -
1                                 0        -
2                                 0        1
3 test 1                          0        1   TRUE -> enter body
4   total <- 0 + 1                1        1
5   count <- 1 + 1                1        2
3 test 2                          1        2   TRUE
4   total <- 1 + 2                3        2
5   count <- 2 + 1                3        3
3 test 3                          3        3   TRUE
4   total <- 3 + 3                6        3
5   count <- 3 + 1                6        4
3 test 4                          6        4   TRUE
4   total <- 6 + 4               10        4
5   count <- 4 + 1               10        5
3 test 5                         10        5   TRUE
4   total <- 10 + 5              15        5
5   count <- 5 + 1               15        6
3 test 6                         15        6   FALSE -> exit to line 7
7   OUTPUT 15

Two classic bugs visible here: forgetting count <- count + 1 loops forever
(count never reaches 6), and starting count at 0 would run six times.

Off-by-one errors (the loop running once too many or too few) and infinite loops (a condition never updated toward FALSE) are the two most common lost marks — always trace at the boundaries.

Constructing algorithms

Before code comes design. Structure charts break a problem into a main program and subtasks (top-down decomposition); pseudocode expresses the logic in structured English-like statements; flowcharts picture it: oval = start/stop, parallelogram = input/output, rectangle = process, diamond = decision, arrows = flow. Trace tables (as above) dry-run the algorithm to prove it before coding.

Worked example: design then trace. "Read 10 marks and output the highest."

Pseudocode:
  1  highest <- 0
  2  FOR i <- 1 TO 10
  3      INPUT mark
  4      IF mark > highest THEN
  5          highest <- mark
  6      ENDIF
  7  NEXT i
  8  OUTPUT highest

Trace with inputs 45, 72, 61 (first three of ten):

Step   i   mark   highest   comment
1                  0        no mark can be below 0, safe start
2    1
3         45      0
4   45 > 0 TRUE
5                45
2    2
3         72     45
4   72 > 45 TRUE
5                72
2    3
3         61     72
4   61 > 72 FALSE - highest unchanged
5                72        IF protects the winner

After all ten, line 8 outputs 72.

Procedural decomposition matters in the exam: state the subtasks (input routine, find-max routine, output routine) before writing any of them.

Arrays

An array is one variable holding many values of the same type, each with an index. It replaces dozens of separately named variables (test1, test2, …) and lets loops process the whole collection. In pseudocode an array is declared by type and size; indices in Cambridge pseudocode usually start at 0 (always check the question's convention).

Cambridge pseudocode: declaring and filling an array of 5 marks.

  DECLARE marks : ARRAY[0:4] OF INTEGER       [indices 0, 1, 2, 3, 4]
  FOR i <- 0 TO 4
      INPUT marks[i]
  NEXT i

Memory after entering 12, 47, 33, 58, 21:

  index:   0    1    2    3    4
  value:  12   47   33   58   21

marks[2] means "the value at index 2" = 33. Traps:
  marks[5] is OUT OF RANGE for a 0:4 array - undefined behaviour, and a
  guaranteed lost mark in an exam answer.
  Assigning marks[1] <- 99 overwrites 47 and leaves everything else alone.

Searching an array, step by step (linear search for 58):

  found <- FALSE
  FOR i <- 0 TO 4
      IF marks[i] = 58 THEN
          found <- TRUE
          position <- i
      ENDIF
  NEXT i

  i = 0: marks[0] = 12 - no
  i = 1: marks[1] = 47 - no
  i = 2: marks[2] = 33 - no
  i = 3: marks[3] = 58 - YES: found <- TRUE, position <- 3
  i = 4: still checked (unless the loop is exited early - a fair refinement)

Two-dimensional arrays (ARRAY[0:3, 0:2]) are grids — rows and columns — used for games boards and seating plans; a value is addressed by both indices, e.g. board[2, 1].

File handling

Variables vanish when a program ends; files persist on secondary storage. Text files are read and written sequentially, a line at a time. The pattern is always open → use → close, and you must know the mode:

  • READ mode: open an existing file to get data from it.
  • WRITE mode: create a new file (or wipe an existing one — a classic destructive bug when APPEND was needed).
  • APPEND mode: add to the end of an existing file, keeping what is there.
Worked example: totals and appends. File "scores.txt" holds three lines:
  45
  62
  51

Program:
  1  OPENFILE "scores.txt" FOR READ
  2  total <- 0
  3  WHILE NOT EOF("scores.txt")          [EOF = end of file]
  4      READFILE "scores.txt", score
  5      total <- total + score
  6  ENDWHILE
  7  CLOSEFILE "scores.txt"
  8  OPENFILE "scores.txt" FOR APPEND
  9  WRITEFILE "scores.txt", total
 10  CLOSEFILE "scores.txt"

Memory trace:
  step 2: total = 0
  step 5 (1st read): total = 0 + 45 = 45
  step 5 (2nd read): total = 45 + 62 = 107
  step 5 (3rd read): total = 107 + 51 = 158
  next test: EOF TRUE -> exit loop
  line 9 appends 158; the file now holds four lines: 45, 62, 51, 158.

Had line 8 said FOR WRITE, the three scores would be wiped and the file would
hold only 158 - the mode is the whole question.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Using = for comparison inside conditions when the pseudocode expects <- for assignment and = for testing — know which the question's notation uses and be consistent.
  • Forgetting that assignment overwrites: a <- a + b destroys the old a; trace tables must show values before and after.
  • WHILE versus UNTIL polarity: WHILE repeats while the condition is TRUE; UNTIL repeats until it becomes TRUE — writing the wrong one inverts the loop.
  • Infinite loops from a missing or wrongly directed counter update.
  • Off-by-one errors at array and loop boundaries: a 0:4 array has five slots, and FOR i <- 1 TO 10 runs ten times, not eleven.
  • Reading past the end of file or using an open file after CLOSEFILE; always close before reopening in another mode.
  • Opening a data file FOR WRITE when APPEND was required, destroying the data.
  • Confusing a compiler with an interpreter in a comparison answer: whole-program translation versus line-by-line execution is the substance of the mark.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 2, 4 marks). Explain the difference between a compiler and an interpreter.

Answer: A compiler translates the whole source program into machine code before execution, producing a standalone executable that runs fast; syntax errors are all reported before anything runs. An interpreter translates and executes one statement at a time, so the program runs more slowly and must be retranslated each time, but errors appear exactly at the failing line and testing is quicker.

Question 2 (Paper 2, 4 marks). Complete a trace table for: x <- 3; y <- x * 2; x <- x + y; OUTPUT x.

Answer: After line 1, x = 3. After line 2, y = 6 (3 × 2), x = 3. After line 3, x = 3 + 6 = 9. The output is 9.

Question 3 (Paper 2, 6 marks). Write pseudocode to read 20 numbers and output how many are negative.

Answer: count <- 0; FOR i <- 1 TO 20; INPUT num; IF num < 0 THEN; count <- count + 1; ENDIF; NEXT i; OUTPUT count.

Question 4 (Paper 2, 3 marks). An array is declared ARRAY[0:9] OF INTEGER. State how many values it holds, the index of the first and last elements, and the meaning of num[4].

Answer: It holds 10 values; the first is at index 0 and the last at index 9; num[4] is the single value stored at the fifth position (index 4) of the array.

Question 5 (Paper 2, 4 marks). Explain the difference between opening a file FOR WRITE and FOR APPEND, and state one risk of choosing the wrong one.

Answer: FOR WRITE creates a new file and, if the file already exists, erases its previous contents before writing; FOR APPEND keeps the existing contents and adds new data at the end. Choosing WRITE when APPEND was meant destroys all previous records — an unrecoverable data loss unless a backup exists.

Question 6 (Paper 2, 4 marks). Describe what is wrong with: WHILE count <= 10; OUTPUT count; ENDWHILE.

Answer: count is never initialised (no starting value) and never incremented inside the loop, so the condition never changes — if it starts TRUE the loop repeats forever (an infinite loop), and if it is somehow FALSE the loop never runs. Fix: set count <- 1 before the loop and add count <- count + 1 inside it.

With the constructs in hand, the next note turns to the craft itself: designing, refining and testing algorithms.

title: AS Level Mathematics: Functions
content:
AS Level Mathematics: Functions

A function is a rule that turns each input into exactly one output — a machine with one chute per item. This note builds the whole AS treatment from zero: function notation with domain and range, the standard graphs and their shapes, composite functions and why order matters, inverses with their reflection in y = x, and the transformation rules that shift, stretch and reflect any graph. The marks in this topic come from precision — writing the correct domain, composing in the right order, and stating the rule for the inverse before using it.

Notation, domain and range

f(x) = 2x + 3      "f of x"
f(4) = 11          substitute 4 for every x
domain: the set of allowed inputs
range: the set of outputs the function actually produces

Domain restrictions matter: f(x) = 1/x is undefined at x = 0; f(x) = √x requires x ≥ 0; a quadratic over the reals has all reals as its domain. The range is found by considering the function's behaviour over its stated domain — for a quadratic, complete the square to find the minimum or maximum.

Worked example. f(x) = x² − 4, domain x ≥ 0. Find the range.

at x = 0: f = -4; the function increases without limit
range: f(x) >= -4

Worked example 2 (reciprocal). g(x) = 3/(x − 2), x ≠ 2. State the domain and range.

domain: all real x except 2
range: all real values except 0 (the fraction can never be 0)

The standard graphs

FunctionShapeFeatures
y = xstraight linegradient 1, through origin
y = x²parabola upwardminimum at origin, symmetric
y = x³cubic, S-shapedpasses through origin, increasing
y = 1/xtwo branches (hyperbola)asymptotes x = 0 and y = 0
y = √xhalf-parabola on its sidedomain x ≥ 0, range y ≥ 0
y = |x|V-shapevertex at origin, domain all reals
y = aˣ (a > 1)exponential growthalways positive, through (0, 1)

Knowing these shapes is the foundation of graph transformations and of estimating solutions graphically.

Composite functions

fg(x) means f(g(x)): apply g first, then f
gf(x) means g(f(x)): apply f first, then g
in general fg(x) is not the same as gf(x)

Worked example. f(x) = 2x + 1, g(x) = x². Find fg(x) and gf(x).

fg(x) = f(g(x)) = f(x²) = 2x² + 1
gf(x) = g(f(x)) = (2x + 1)² = 4x² + 4x + 1
These differ, so order matters.

Worked example 2 (solving). With the same f and g, solve fg(x) = 19.

2x² + 1 = 19
2x² = 18  →  x² = 9  →  x = 3 or x = -3

Inverse functions

The inverse f⁻¹ undoes f: if f(a) = b then f⁻¹(b) = a. To find it, write y = f(x), swap x and y, and rearrange for y.

method: y = f(x)  →  x = f(y) after swap  →  y = f⁻¹(x)

Worked example. Find the inverse of f(x) = 3x − 7.

y = 3x - 7
swap: x = 3y - 7
rearrange: 3y = x + 7  →  y = (x + 7)/3
f⁻¹(x) = (x + 7)/3

Worked example 2 (quadratic, restricted domain). f(x) = x² + 2 for x ≥ 0. Find f⁻¹ and its domain.

y = x² + 2
swap: x = y² + 2  →  y² = x - 2  →  y = √(x - 2)
(the negative root is rejected because the domain is x >= 0)
f⁻¹(x) = √(x - 2), domain x >= 2

Two properties worth remembering: the graph of f⁻¹ is the reflection of f in the line y = x, and the domain of f⁻¹ is the range of f (and vice versa).

Transformations of graphs

TransformationEffect on the graphWhat changes
y = f(x) + atranslate up by ay-coordinates +a
y = f(x + a)translate left by ax replaced by x + a (inside: opposite direction)
y = af(x)vertical stretch by ay-coordinates × a
y = f(ax)horizontal stretch by 1/ax-coordinates ÷ a
y = −f(x)reflection in the x-axisy-coordinates negated
y = f(−x)reflection in the y-axisx-coordinates negated

The inside/outside rule is the one that trips candidates: changes outside the bracket affect y and behave as written; changes inside affect x and behave in reverse.

Worked example. The point (3, 5) lies on y = f(x). Find its image under y = f(x − 2) + 1.

f(x - 2) shifts the graph 2 to the right; +1 shifts it up 1
image: (3 + 2, 5 + 1) = (5, 6)

Worked example 2 (stretch). The point (4, 1) is on y = f(x). Find its image under y = f(2x).

horizontal stretch by 1/2: x-coordinate halves
image: (2, 1)

Rational functions and asymptotes

A rational function is a ratio of polynomials, y = p(x)/q(x). Its graph is shaped by two constraints: where the denominator is zero the function is undefined (a vertical asymptote), and for large x the ratio settles to a horizontal asymptote determined by the leading terms.

y = (ax + b)/(cx + d)
vertical asymptote: cx + d = 0  →  x = -d/c
horizontal asymptote: y → a/c as x → +/- infinity
excluded value: the point where the denominator vanishes is
not in the domain

Worked example. Sketch y = 2/(x − 1) and state its domain and range.

vertical asymptote x = 1 (denominator zero)
horizontal asymptote y = 0 (numerator fixed, denominator grows)
domain: x not equal to 1; range: y not equal to 0
the two branches lie in the regions x < 1 and x > 1

Worked example 2 (linear over linear). Sketch y = (x + 1)/(x − 2).

vertical asymptote x = 2
horizontal asymptote y = 1 (leading coefficients 1/1)
intercepts: y = -1/2 at x = 0; x = -1 at y = 0

Exponential and logarithmic graphs

Exponentials and logarithms are inverse functions, and their graphs encode that relationship. y = aˣ (a > 1) rises ever more steeply, passes through (0, 1) and never touches the x-axis — the x-axis is an asymptote. y = log_a x is the reflection in y = x: it passes through (1, 0), has a vertical asymptote at x = 0, and is defined only for x > 0.

  • Growth and decay: y = Ae^(kx) grows for k > 0 and decays for k < 0; the constant A is the value at x = 0.
  • Logarithm laws: log(ab) = log a + log b; log(a/b) = log a − log b; log(aⁿ) = n log a.
  • Solving exponentials: take logs of both sides — 3^x = 20 gives x log 3 = log 20, so x = log 20/log 3 ≈ 2.73.

Worked example. Solve 5^(2x−1) = 40.

(2x - 1) log 5 = log 40
2x - 1 = log 40/log 5 = 1.602/0.699 = 2.292
2x = 3.292  →  x = 1.65 (3 s.f.)

Worked example 2 (modelling with an exponential). A colony of bacteria doubles every 3 hours, starting at 500. Write the population after t hours and find when it reaches 20 000.

P = 500 × 2^(t/3)
20000 = 500 × 2^(t/3)  →  40 = 2^(t/3)
log 40 = (t/3) log 2  →  t/3 = 5.322  →  t = 16.0 hours

The modelling step — translating "doubles every 3 hours" into 2^(t/3) — is where most marks are lost; write the base (2 for doubling, 0.5 for halving) and the exponent (time divided by the period) explicitly before solving. For decay, the same structure with a base below 1 (or a negative exponent) describes cooling, depreciation and radioactive half-life, so one pattern covers a whole family of questions.

Worked examples: mixed function problems

Worked example. f(x) = x + 2, g(x) = 3x. Find f⁻¹(x), fg(x), and show that f⁻¹(fg(x)) = g(x).

f⁻¹(x) = x - 2
fg(x) = 3x + 2
f⁻¹(fg(x)) = (3x + 2) - 2 = 3x = g(x)

Worked example 2 (range of composite). f(x) = x², g(x) = x + 1. Find the range of fg for x ≥ 0.

fg(x) = (x + 1)²
for x >= 0: x + 1 >= 1  →  fg(x) >= 1
range: fg(x) >= 1

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Evaluate) f(x) = 2x² − 1. Find f(−3). Answer: 2(9) − 1 = 17.
  2. (Domain) State the domain of g(x) = 1/(x + 4). Answer: x ≠ −4.
  3. (Composite) f(x) = x + 3, g(x) = 2x. Find fg(x). Answer: 2x + 3.
  4. (Inverse) Find the inverse of h(x) = (x − 5)/2. Answer: y = 2x + 5.
  5. (Inverse domain) f(x) = x² + 1 for x ≥ 0. State the domain of f⁻¹. Answer: x ≥ 1 (the range of f).
  6. (Transformation) Describe the transformation y = f(x) → y = f(x + 3) − 2. Answer: translation 3 left and 2 down.
  7. (Point image) (2, 7) is on y = f(x). Find its image on y = 2f(x). Answer: (2, 14).
  8. (Reasoning) Explain why f⁻¹(f(x)) = x. Answer: The inverse undoes the function: applying f then f⁻¹ returns the original input for every x in the domain of f.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Order of composition: fg means g first. Writing f(g(x)) as f(x)g(x) (a product) is a fundamental error.
  • Inside transformations reversed: f(x + 3) moves left, not right; f(2x) compresses horizontally by ½, not stretches by 2.
  • Inverse of a quadratic without restriction: x² has no inverse over all reals because it is not one-to-one; the domain restriction is what makes the inverse valid.
  • Dropping the ± in inverse quadratics: keep the root that matches the stated domain; state which and why.
  • Domain notation: write inequalities or set notation precisely (x ≠ 2; x ≥ 0); "all numbers" is rarely correct.
  • Confusing f⁻¹(x) with 1/f(x): the inverse is not the reciprocal. This is the most common notation trap.
  • Range from the wrong feature: for a quadratic on a restricted domain, evaluate the endpoints and the vertex — the range may be bounded at both ends.
  • Sketch axes: label asymptotes for reciprocal and exponential graphs; an unlabelled sketch loses communication marks.

Equations and symbols

Every relation this topic is examined on, written with its real notation and followed by a key naming each symbol, its unit and what it means. Where a statement has a second useful form both are given, so a rearrangement in the exam is mechanical rather than something to rediscover under time pressure.

Notation, domain and range

f: x ↦ f(x), with domain D_f and range R_f
Key: f = the function (the rule); x = an input drawn from the domain; f(x) = the single output; D_f = the set of allowed inputs; R_f = the set of outputs actually produced. A function is only fully specified when all three of rule, domain and range are given — an answer that states the rule alone loses the mark.

f(x) = √(x − a) ⇒ D_f = {x : x ≥ a}
Key: a = the value under the root where the expression becomes zero. A square root is real only when its argument is non-negative, and that inequality is the domain.

f(x) = k/x ⇒ D_f = {x : x ≠ 0}
Key: k = any non-zero constant. Division by zero is undefined, so the excluded value is removed from the domain and becomes a vertical asymptote on the graph.

Composite functions

(g ∘ f)(x) = g(f(x))
Key: f = the function applied first (the inner one); g = applied second (the outer one). Order matters: f then g is not the same as g then f, and the notation is read right-to-left, which is the single most common source of lost marks here.

D_{g∘f} = {x ∈ D_f : f(x) ∈ D_g}
Key: D_f = domain of the inner function; D_g = domain of the outer function. The composite exists only where the inner output is a legal input for the outer function, so every restriction from either function survives.

(f ∘ g)(x) ≠ (g ∘ f)(x) in general
Key: f, g = two functions. Composition is not commutative; a question that asks for both is testing exactly this, and the two answers differing is the expected result, not an error.

Inverse functions

y = f(x) ⇔ x = f⁻¹(y), with D_{f⁻¹} = R_f and R_{f⁻¹} = D_f
Key: f⁻¹ = the inverse function; D and R = domain and range. To find the rule: write y = f(x), rearrange to make x the subject, then swap the letters. The domain and range exchange, which is why an inverse can fail to exist until the domain is restricted.

f⁻¹(f(x)) = x and f(f⁻¹(x)) = x
Key: the two compositions that define an inverse: each function undoes the other. A quick check on any answer — compose them and you must return to the input.

y = f⁻¹(x) is the reflection of y = f(x) in the line y = x
Key: the line y = x = the mirror. Every point (a, b) on the graph of f appears as (b, a) on the graph of f⁻¹, which is the geometric statement of swapping the variables.

f(x) = x² on x ≥ 0 ⇒ f⁻¹(x) = √x
Key: the restriction x ≥ 0 is what makes the squaring function one-to-one. Without it the parabola fails the horizontal-line test and no inverse function exists; the restricted domain is the mark.

Transformations of graphs

y = f(x) + a ⇒ translation by a in the y-direction
Key: a = the number added outside the function; positive moves up. Every point rises by a, so the shape is unchanged.

y = f(x + a) ⇒ translation by −a in the x-direction
Key: a = the number added inside the bracket; the graph moves opposite to the sign. This is the rule students invert under pressure: f(x + 3) moves the curve 3 to the left.

y = a f(x) ⇒ stretch parallel to the y-axis, scale factor a; y = f(ax) ⇒ stretch parallel to the x-axis, scale factor 1/a
Key: a = the multiplier, a > 0. Outside the function multiplies heights; inside multiplies inputs, so it compresses horizontally by the reciprocal.

y = −f(x) reflects in the x-axis; y = f(−x) reflects in the y-axis
Key: the minus sign's position decides the mirror. Outside negates the output (vertical flip); inside negates the input (horizontal flip).

f(x) = a(x − h)² + k ⇒ R_f = [k, ∞) for a > 0, and (−∞, k] for a < 0
Key: a = the coefficient controlling width and direction; h = the x-coordinate of the vertex; k = its y-coordinate (the minimum or maximum value). Completing the square reads the range straight off the completed form.

y = (ax + b)/(cx + d) ⇒ vertical asymptote x = −d/c, horizontal asymptote y = a/c
Key: a, b, c, d = the four coefficients, c ≠ 0. The excluded input gives the vertical asymptote; the ratio of the leading coefficients gives the horizontal one, which is the value the function approaches as x grows.

title: Transition Metals and their Chemistry - A2 Chemistry
content:
Transition Metals and their Chemistry - A2 Level

This topic belongs to the Edexcel International Advanced Level (IAL) Chemistry specification, Unit 5 (WCH15), and covers the electronic configurations, variable oxidation states, complex ion formation, ligand exchange, colour changes, standard electrode potentials of vanadium and chromium systems, catalysis, and practical preparations associated with d-block transition elements of Period 4 from scandium to zinc.

Definition and Electronic Configurations of Transition Metals

Transition metals are defined as d-block elements that form one or more stable ions with incompletely-filled d-orbitals. Scandium and zinc are in the d-block but are not true transition metals because Sc3+ has an empty d-orbital (3d0) and Zn2+ has a completely filled d-orbital (3d10). To deduce electronic configurations of Period 4 atoms and ions from Sc to Zn, remember that the 4s orbital fills before 3d, but when positive ions are formed, electrons are always removed from the 4s orbital before the 3d orbitals.

  • Transition metals are d-block elements forming stable ions with incompletely-filled d-orbitals (17.1).
  • Electronic configuration rules: fill 4s then 3d, empty 4s before 3d when forming ions (17.2).
  • Example atom Ti (atomic number 22): 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d2 (17.2).
  • Example ion Fe2+ (atomic number 26): 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 3d6, with the two 4s electrons removed (17.2).
  • Example ion Cu+ (atomic number 29): 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 3d10 (17.2).
  • Variable oxidation numbers occur because the 4s and 3d sub-shells have very similar energies, allowing different numbers of electrons to be lost or involved in bonding with minimal energy penalty (17.3).

Complex Ions, Ligands, and Coordination Numbers

A complex ion consists of a central metal ion surrounded by species called ligands. A ligand is a species containing at least one lone pair of electrons that forms a dative covalent (coordinate) bond to the central metal ion. The coordination number is the total number of coordinate bonds formed to the central metal ion. The nature and size of ligands determine the spatial arrangement and geometry of the resulting complex ion.

  • Ligand definition: a species with a lone pair that forms a dative covalent bond to a metal ion (17.4, 17.5).
  • Complex ion definition: a central metal ion surrounded by ligands (17.6).
  • Coordination number: the number of coordinate bonds to the central metal ion (17.10).
  • Monodentate ligands donate one pair of electrons; H2O, OH− and NH3 act as monodentate ligands (17.12).
  • Six-fold coordination complexes have an octahedral shape, such as [M(H2O)6]n+, [M(OH)6]n−, and [M(NH3)6]n+ (17.13).
  • Tetrahedral complexes form with relatively large ligands such as Cl−, for example [CuCl4]2− and [CoCl4]2−, due to steric hindrance preventing six chloride ions from packing around the small metal centre (17.14).
  • Square planar complexes are also formed by transition metal ions; cis-platin, [Pt(NH3)2Cl2], is a square planar complex used in cancer treatment supplied as a single active cis isomer rather than a mixture with the inactive trans form (17.15).
  • Bidentate ligands have two donor atoms donating two lone pairs, such as ethane-1,2-diamine (NH2CH2CH2NH2). Hexadentate ligands have six donor atoms, such as EDTA4− (17.16).
  • Haemoglobin is an iron(II) complex containing a polydentate porphyrin ring ligand; ligand exchange occurs when an oxygen molecule bound to haemoglobin in the lungs is replaced by a carbon monoxide molecule in the body tissues (17.17).

Colour and d-Orbital Splitting

Aqueous solutions of transition metal ions are usually coloured because the presence of surrounding ligands causes the five degenerate d-orbitals to split into two different energy levels. When white light passes through the solution, electrons absorb specific frequencies of visible light to jump from the lower d-orbitals to the higher d-orbitals. The colour observed is due to the remaining unabsorbed wavelengths transmitted or reflected. A lack of colour in some aqueous ions or complex ions, such as Sc3+ (3d0) or Zn2+ (3d10), occurs because their d-orbitals are either completely empty or completely full, so d-d electronic transitions are impossible.

  • Aqueous solutions of transition metal ions are usually coloured (17.7).
  • Colour arises from the splitting of the energy levels of d-orbitals by the electrostatic field of surrounding ligands (17.8).
  • Lack of colour in ions like Sc3+ (3d0) and Zn2+ (3d10) is due to empty or full d-orbitals preventing d-d electron transitions (17.9).
  • Colour changes in transition metal ions arise from changes in oxidation number, changes in ligand, or changes in the coordination number of the complex (17.11).

Vanadium and Chromium Redox Chemistry

Vanadium exhibits four stable oxidation states in aqueous solution, each with a characteristic colour: +5 (yellow, VO2+), +4 (blue, VO2+), +3 (green, V3+), and +2 (violet, V2+). These oxidation states can be interconverted via redox reactions using zinc metal in acidic conditions as a reducing agent, driven by standard electrode potential (Eo) values. Similarly, chromium chemistry involves the interconversion of Cr3+ and dichromate(VI) ions, Cr2O7 2−. Dichromate(VI) ions can be reduced using zinc in acid and produced by oxidising Cr3+ with hydrogen peroxide in alkaline conditions followed by acidification. In aqueous solution, dichromate(VI) ions exist in a pH-dependent equilibrium with chromate(VI) ions.

  • Vanadium oxidation states and colours: +5 is yellow (VO2+), +4 is blue (VO2+), +3 is green (V3+), and +2 is violet (V2+) (17.18).
  • Redox interconversion of vanadium oxidation states is achieved using zinc in acidic solution, evaluated through relevant Eo values where Zn/Zn2+ is sufficiently negative to reduce V5+ down to V2+ (17.19).
  • Dchromate(VI) ions (Cr2O7 2−) can be reduced to Cr3+ and further to Cr2+ using zinc in acidic conditions (17.20i).
  • Dichromate(VI) ions can be produced by the oxidation of Cr3+ ions using hydrogen peroxide in alkaline conditions, followed by subsequent acidification (17.20ii).
  • Dichromate(VI) ion equilibrium with chromate(VI): Cr2O7 2− + H2O <→ 2CrO4 2− + 2H+ (17.21). Adding acid shifts this equilibrium left towards orange dichromate; adding alkali shifts it right towards yellow chromate.

Reactions of Aqueous Transition Metal Ions with Hydroxide and Ammonia

Aqueous metal ions react with sodium hydroxide and aqueous ammonia to produce precipitates, which may show amphoteric behaviour or dissolve in excess reagent due to ligand exchange. You must know the exact observations and write balanced ionic equations for Cr3+(aq), Mn2+(aq), Fe2+(aq), Fe3+(aq), Co2+(aq), Ni2+(aq), Cu2+(aq), and Zn2+(aq).

  • Cr3+(aq) + 3OH−(aq) → Cr(OH)3(H2O)3(s) (grey-green precipitate). Excess OH− gives [Cr(OH)6]3− (dark green solution) demonstrating amphoteric behaviour (17.22, 17.23).
  • Cr3+(aq) with NH3(aq): grey-green precipitate of Cr(OH)3(H2O)3, insoluble in excess ammonia (17.22).
  • Mn2+(aq) + 2OH−(aq) → Mn(OH)2(s) (off-white precipitate, turns brown on standing in air due to oxidation). Insoluble in excess OH− and excess NH3 (17.22).
  • Fe2+(aq) + 2OH−(aq) → Fe(OH)2(s) (green precipitate, turns brown on surface in air). Insoluble in excess OH− and excess NH3 (17.22).
  • Fe3+(aq) + 3OH−(aq) → Fe(OH)3(s) (rusty-brown precipitate). Insoluble in excess OH− and excess NH3 (17.22).
  • Co2+(aq) + 2OH−(aq) → Co(OH)2(s) (blue precipitate, turns pink on standing). Insoluble in excess OH−. With excess NH3, forms [Co(NH3)6]2+ (pale yellow solution turning brown) via ligand exchange (17.22, 17.23, 17.24).
  • Ni2+(aq) + 2OH−(aq) → Ni(OH)2(s) (green precipitate). Insoluble in excess OH−. With excess NH3, dissolves to form [Ni(NH3)6]2+ (blue solution) (17.22, 17.23).
  • Cu2+(aq) + 2OH−(aq) → Cu(OH)2(s) (pale blue precipitate). Insoluble in excess OH−. With excess NH3, dissolves to form [Cu(NH3)4(H2O)2]2+ (deep blue solution) (17.22, 17.23, 17.24).
  • Zn2+(aq) + 2OH−(aq) → Zn(OH)2(s) (white precipitate). Dissolves in excess OH− to form [Zn(OH)4]2− (colourless solution) demonstrating amphoteric behaviour (17.22, 17.23).
  • Zn2+(aq) with excess NH3(aq): white precipitate dissolves to form [Zn(NH3)4]2+ (colourless solution) (17.22, 17.23).
  • Deprotonation reactions involve aqueous metal ions losing protons from coordinated water molecules to form neutral hydroxide precipitates (17.23).

Specific Ligand Exchange Reactions and Entropy

Ligand exchange occurs when one ligand in a complex is replaced by another, accompanied by a distinct colour change and often a change in coordination number. The thermodynamic stability of complex ions is significantly enhanced when monodentate ligands are replaced by bidentate or hexadentate ligands, known as the chelate effect. This can be understood in terms of the positive increase in entropy (Ssystem) because there are more free moles of product species than reactant species in solution.

  • Formation of [Cu(NH3)4(H2O)2]2+ (deep blue) from [Cu(H2O)6]2+ (pale blue) proceeds via an intermediate Cu(OH)2(H2O)4 precipitate upon adding ammonia, which then redissolves in excess ammonia (17.24i).
  • Formation of [CuCl4]2− (yellow-green) from [Cu(H2O)6]2+ (blue) occurs upon adding concentrated hydrochloric acid, resulting in a change in coordination number from 6 to 4 and a shape change from octahedral to tetrahedral (17.24ii).
  • Formation of [CoCl4]2− (blue) from [Co(H2O)6]2+ (pink) occurs on adding concentrated hydrochloric acid, changing coordination number from 6 to 4 and shape from octahedral to tetrahedral (17.24iii).
  • Substitution of monodentate ligands by bidentate or hexadentate ligands leads to a more stable complex ion due to a positive increase in system entropy (Ssystem), as the number of independent particles in solution increases (17.25).

Catalysis by Transition Metals

Transition metals and their compounds are exceptionally effective catalysts, operating as either heterogeneous catalysts (in a different phase from reactants, with reactions occurring on the catalyst surface) or homogeneous catalysts (in the same phase as reactants, proceeding via intermediate species). V2O5 acts as a heterogeneous catalyst in the Contact process for manufacturing sulfur trioxide. Catalytic converters in vehicles use solid platinum/rhodium heterogeneous catalysts to remove carbon monoxide and nitrogen monoxide emissions via adsorption, bond weakening, reaction, and desorption. Homogeneous catalysis is exemplified by Fe2+ catalysing the reaction between iodide and peroxydisulfate ions, and Mn2+ autocatalysing the reaction between manganate(VII) and ethanedioate ions.

  • Heterogeneous catalyst: in a different phase from reactants; reaction occurs at the active sites on the surface of the catalyst (17.26, 17.27).
  • V2O5 acts as a heterogeneous catalyst in the Contact process by being reduced from V(V) to V(IV) by SO2, then reoxidised back to V(V) by O2: SO2 + V2O5 → SO3 + V2O4, followed by V2O4 + 0.5O2 → V2O5 (17.28).
  • Catalytic converter mechanism: 1. Adsorption of CO and NO molecules onto the metal surface, weakening covalent bonds. 2. Chemical reaction between adsorbed species to form CO2 and N2. 3. Desorption of product molecules from the surface (17.29).
  • Homogeneous catalyst: in the same phase as reactants, proceeding through distinct intermediate species (17.30).
  • Role of Fe2+ in catalysing reaction between I− and S2O8 2−: Fe2+ reduces S2O8 2− to SO4 2− forming Fe3+ intermediate (S2O8 2− + 2Fe2+ → 2SO4 2− + 2Fe3+), then Fe3+ oxidises I− back to I2 regenerating Fe2+ (2Fe3+ + 2I− → 2Fe2+ + I2) (17.31).
  • Role of Mn2+ in autocatalysing reaction between MnO4 − and C2O4 2−: reaction starts very slowly, but the Mn2+ product acts as a catalyst, speeding up the reaction as its concentration increases (autocatalysis) (17.32).
  • Core Practical 14: The preparation of a transition metal complex, such as potassium tris(oxalato)ferrate(III) trihydrate, involving ligand substitution, precipitation, recrystallisation, and percentage yield calculation (17.33).

Typical mistakes

  • Mistake: Removing electrons from 3d orbitals before 4s orbitals when writing ion configurations. Correction: Always fill 4s before 3d, but remove electrons from the 4s orbital first when forming positive ions.
  • Mistake: Stating that Sc3+ or Zn2+ solutions are coloured. Correction: They are colourless because they do not have incompletely-filled d-orbitals to permit d-d electron transitions.
  • Mistake: Confusing coordination number with the number of ligands. Correction: Coordination number is the total number of coordinate bonds, which equals the number of monodentate ligands, but is double the number of bidentate ligands.
  • Mistake: Omitting phase or charge when writing complex ion formulas. Correction: Always enclose the complex in square brackets with the overall charge outside, e.g., [Cu(NH3)4(H2O)2]2+.
  • Mistake: Forgetting that cis-platin must be supplied as a single isomer. Correction: Cis-platin is supplied specifically as the cis isomer because only this form binds to DNA to inhibit cancer cell replication.

Exam-style questions

  1. Deduce the ground state electronic configuration of a cobalt(II) atom (atomic number 27) and a cobalt(III) ion. (2 marks)

    Answer: Co atom is 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d7 (1 mark). Co3+ ion is 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 3d6, with electrons removed from 4s first (1 mark).

  2. Explain why aqueous copper(II) sulfate is blue, whereas aqueous scandium(III) chloride is colourless. (3 marks)

    Answer: Cu2+ has an incompletely-filled 3d9 configuration; d-orbitals split in the ligand field, allowing d-d electron transitions which absorb specific frequencies of visible light (2 marks). Sc3+ has a 3d0 configuration with no d-electrons, so no d-d transitions are possible, making it colourless (1 mark).

  3. Describe what you would observe when excess aqueous ammonia is added dropwise to an aqueous solution containing copper(II) ions. Write ionic equations for the reactions that occur. (4 marks)

    Answer: Observations: pale blue solution forms a pale blue precipitate of Cu(OH)2, which then dissolves in excess ammonia to form a deep blue solution (2 marks). Equations: Cu2+(aq) + 2OH−(aq) → Cu(OH)2(s) followed by Cu(OH)2(s) + 4NH3(aq) + 2H2O(l) → [Cu(NH3)4(H2O)2]2+(aq) + 2OH−(aq) (2 marks).

  4. Explain why the substitution of six monodentate water ligands by three bidentate ethane-1,2-diamine ligands in a complex ion is thermodynamically favoured by entropy. (2 marks)

    Answer: There is an increase in the total number of independent particles/molecules in solution from 4 reactants to 7 products (1 mark), leading to a positive entropy change (Ssystem > 0) making the complex more stable (1 mark).

  5. Outline how V2O5 acts as a heterogeneous catalyst in the Contact process, including chemical equations. (3 marks)

    Answer: V2O5 is in a different phase (solid) from the gaseous reactants (1 mark). It oxidises SO2 to SO3, being reduced itself: SO2 + V2O5 → SO3 + V2O4 (1 mark). The V2O4 is then reoxidised by oxygen back to V2O5: V2O4 + 0.5O2 → V2O5 (1 mark).

Use these revision notes alongside active recall of colour changes, precipitation reactions, and equation writing. Practise balancing redox equations for vanadium and chromium, and ensure you can explain the chelate effect using entropy arguments before moving on to past paper practice.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Colour, applied to [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺: the d-orbitals split into two energy levels in an octahedral complex. The complex absorbs light that promotes an electron across that gap, and the colour seen is the complementary colour. A change in ligand changes the splitting, and so changes the colour.
  • Ligand exchange with entropy, applied to [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ with excess NH₃: [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ + 4NH₃ → [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺ + 4H₂O. The number of particles is unchanged, so ΔS is about zero. Compare this with EDTA, where the chelate gives an increase in the number of particles and a positive ΔS.
  • Vanadium oxidation states: V²⁺ is lilac, V³⁺ green, VO²⁺ blue and VO₂⁺ yellow. A reduction from VO₂⁺ to VO²⁺ and then to V³⁺ can be followed by the colour change, which is why it is used in redox titrations.
  • Catalysis: the contact process uses V₂O₅ in SO₂ + ½O₂ → SO₃, where the vanadium changes oxidation state in the cycle, V(V) to V(IV) and back. Haber uses iron. Name the oxidation state change in the cycle, because mark schemes award it separately.

title: Edexcel IAL Computer Science: Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning
content:
Edexcel IAL Computer Science: Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning

Pearson Edexcel International Advanced Level in Computer Science, Unit 3 Advanced Computer Science: artificial intelligence — its definitions and techniques, machine learning, and the engineering of AI systems. The AS ethics note touched AI's impact; this note is the technical depth: how models are represented, trained and evaluated, what the major technique families actually do, and where each one fails. Training loops and search traces are walked step by step.

What AI is, precisely

Artificial intelligence is software performing tasks we would call intelligent if a human did them — perception, reasoning, learning, planning, language. The classic distinction: strong AI (general, human-equivalent understanding — not achieved) versus narrow AI (excellent at one defined task — everything deployed today). The test questions: the Turing test (can a machine's conversational behaviour be distinguished from a human's?) and the Chinese Room argument (symbol manipulation without understanding — a philosophical objection worth naming).

Two great families of technique: symbolic AI (search and logic — the system reasons over explicit representations) and machine learning (the system's behaviour is fitted to data). Modern systems mix them.

Search and reasoning

Many AI problems are state-space search: a start state, goal states, and operators moving between states; the task is to find a path. Strategies: uninformed (breadth-first, depth-first — see the graph traversal note) and informed/heuristic (best-first, A* using an evaluation function; minimax for games).

Game playing with minimax, traced on tic-tac-toe:

  Minimax assumes both players play perfectly: MAX maximises the score,
  MIN minimises it.

  Look ahead from a position where MAX can win immediately in one of three
  moves (moves a, b, c):
    move a -> terminal +1 (win for MAX)
    move b -> after MIN's best reply, 0 (draw)
    move c -> after MIN's best reply, -1 (loss)
  MAX chooses move a: min/max over children = +1.

  Alpha-beta pruning cuts branches that cannot change the decision: if move a
  already guarantees +1, MIN's reply to move b is never examined once b's
  subtree provably scores below +1. The search depth decides strength and
  time - "explain the trade-off" is the follow-up mark.

Expert systems

An expert system encodes human expertise as rules over a knowledge base, applied by an inference engine: forward chaining (data-driven: match facts against rules, fire conclusions, repeat — diagnosis) and backward chaining (goal-driven: to prove X, find rules concluding X, prove their conditions — configuration). Uncertainty handling (confidence factors) and explanation facilities (which rules fired) are their design strengths; brittleness outside the encoded knowledge and the knowledge-engineering bottleneck are their limits.

Forward chaining traced (simplified fault diagnosis):

  Knowledge base:
    R1: IF engine_wont_start AND lights_dim        THEN battery_flat
    R2: IF battery_flat                            THEN charge_battery
    R3: IF engine_wont_start AND lights_ok          THEN starter_fault

  Facts: engine_wont_start, lights_dim.
  Cycle 1: R1's conditions match -> conclude battery_flat.
  Cycle 2: R2's condition matches -> conclude charge_battery.
  Cycle 3: no new rules fire -> stop. Output: charge_battery.

  Notice R3 never fires (lights_ok is false) - the matching is exact.

Machine learning, in depth

Machine learning fits behaviour to data. The three learning styles (supervised: labelled examples; unsupervised: structure in unlabelled data; reinforcement: reward-driven trial) and their main methods:

MethodTaskMechanismFailure modes
Decision treesClassification/regressionGreedy splits maximising information gainOverfitting deep trees; unstable to small data changes
k-nearest neighboursClassificationMajority vote of the k closest training pointsCurse of dimensionality; slow at scale
Naive BayesClassification (spam)Posterior probabilities assuming feature independenceIndependence assumption rarely holds exactly
Linear/logistic regressionPrediction/classificationFit weights minimising errorMisses non-linear structure
Neural networksPerception, language, gamesLayers of weighted units trained by backpropagationOpaque; data-hungry; brittle off-distribution
Neural network training, one epoch traced:

  Layer: inputs x1, x2 -> weights w -> weighted sum -> activation -> output.
  1. Forward: prediction = f(w1x1 + w2x2 + bias).
  2. Loss: measure error against the true label (e.g. squared error).
  3. Backpropagation: compute dLoss/dw for each weight (chain rule from the
     output layer backwards).
  4. Update: w <- w - learningRate * dLoss/dw   (gradient descent).
  5. Repeat across all examples; many epochs until validation loss plateaus.

  The activation function must be non-linear (sigmoid, ReLU) or the whole
  network collapses to one linear model - a favourite "why" question.

Overfitting diagnosis: training accuracy 99%, validation 70% - the model
memorised the training set. Remedies: more data, regularization, dropout,
early stopping on the validation curve.

Evaluation is where marks live: a train/validation/test split (or k-fold cross-validation); a confusion matrix (true/false positives/negatives) giving accuracy, precision (of the positives predicted, how many correct), recall (of the real positives, how many found), and F1 balancing them. Class imbalance exposes plain accuracy (a 99%-negative dataset is "99% accurate" predicting all negative); the choice of metric follows the cost of each error — medical screening values recall, spam filtering values precision.

Confusion matrix worked (200 patients, 20 have the disease):

                      predicted +   predicted -
  actual + (20)            16            4
  actual - (180)            8          172

  accuracy  = (16 + 172) / 200 = 0.94
  precision = 16 / (16 + 8)    = 0.667
  recall    = 16 / (16 + 4)    = 0.80

Reading: 94% accuracy LOOKS strong, but a third of positive alarms are false
(24 alarms, 8 wrong) and a fifth of cases are missed (4 of 20). Which number
matters depends on the harm of each error - the medical context says recall.

Applications and their technique

  • Natural language processing — tokenisation, embeddings, sequence models; translation, summarisation, chatbots, sentiment.
  • Computer vision — convolutional networks; classification, detection, segmentation (self-driving perception, medical imaging).
  • Robotics — perception + planning + control; SLAM for mapping and localisation.
  • Recommender systems — collaborative filtering (users like you) and content-based (item similarity).
  • Speech — recognition (audio to text) and synthesis (text to audio).

Worked example: building and evaluating a classifier

Task: flag fraudulent card transactions.

1. Data: 6 months of transactions labelled fraud/legitimate (0.2% fraud -
   heavily imbalanced from the start).
2. Features: amount, time, location distance from last transaction, merchant
   category, spending-rate change. (Feature engineering matters more than the
   model choice at this level.)
3. Split: 60/20/20 train/validation/test, stratified so fraud rate is present
   in all splits.
4. Train several models (logistic regression baseline, decision tree, neural
   net); select on the validation set by RECALL at an acceptable precision -
   missing fraud costs more than a false alarm review.
5. Test once, honestly: confusion matrix on the held-out test set.
6. Deploy with monitoring: live drift detection (feature distributions shift;
   fraud patterns evolve), periodic retraining, and a human-review loop for
   flagged cases.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Saying machine learning "is programmed with rules"; rules are learned from data — that is the definition.
  • Reporting accuracy on imbalanced data without precision/recall; the metric choice is the mark.
  • Testing on training data (or tuning on the test set) — the test set is touched once.
  • Confusing overfitting (high train, low validation) with underfitting (both low) — the diagnosis drives different remedies.
  • Describing neural networks as "simulating the brain" in place of the mechanism: weighted layers, activation, backpropagation.
  • Claiming AI systems understand their outputs; the Chinese Room point and brittleness off-distribution are the honest limits.
  • Forgetting reinforcement learning's exploration/exploitation trade-off in RL answers.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Unit 3, 4 marks). Explain the difference between supervised and unsupervised learning with examples.

Answer: Supervised learning trains on labelled examples — inputs paired with correct outputs — minimising prediction error; e.g. learning spam/ham from emails marked by users. Unsupervised learning finds structure in unlabelled data; e.g. clustering customers by purchasing behaviour with no predefined groups. Supervision needs labelled data (costly) but evaluates against truth; unsupervised discovers patterns a human might not define.

Question 2 (Unit 3, 5 marks). Describe how a neural network is trained.

Answer: Initialise weights randomly; run a forward pass computing a prediction through weighted layers and non-linear activations; compute the loss against the true label; backpropagate the error to find each weight's gradient; update weights against the gradient scaled by the learning rate. Repeat over many examples and epochs until validation performance plateaus, with techniques like early stopping and regularisation against overfitting.

Question 3 (Unit 3, 4 marks). Explain overfitting and two ways to prevent it.

Answer: Overfitting is when a model memorises training data's noise and idiosyncrasies instead of the general pattern — high training accuracy but poor validation/test accuracy. Prevention: use more representative training data; regularise (penalise complexity), use dropout in neural nets, stop training early when the validation curve degrades, and prefer simpler models when performance is comparable.

Question 4 (Unit 3, 5 marks). A disease-screening model has 95% accuracy on data where 2% of patients are positive. Explain why accuracy alone is misleading and which metrics matter.

Answer: Predicting "negative" for everyone yields 98% accuracy while catching nothing — so accuracy hides failure on the minority class. The confusion matrix gives precision (of those flagged, how many truly ill — false alarms' cost) and recall (of the truly ill, how many flagged — missed diagnoses' cost). For screening, recall dominates (a missed case is dangerous); the F1 score balances both, and the confusion matrix itself is the honest picture.

Question 5 (Unit 3, 4 marks). Explain how a recommender system based on collaborative filtering works.

Answer: It builds a user–item matrix of ratings or behaviours, finds users with similar taste patterns (nearest neighbours in that space), and recommends items those similar users rated highly but the target user has not seen. Strength: no item knowledge needed. Weaknesses: cold start (new users/items have no data) and popularity bias (rare items rarely recommended).

Question 6 (Unit 3, 3 marks). Explain the difference between a symbolic expert system and a machine learning system.

Answer: An expert system stores human knowledge as explicit IF–THEN rules applied by an inference engine — transparent and explainable, but limited to encoded knowledge and costly to build. A machine learning system derives its decision function from data — scalable to perceptual tasks and improves with data, but opaque and dependent on data quality, and unable to reason beyond its training distribution.

The last note of the course covers how models and systems meet the physical world: simulation, sensors and real-world data.

title: Functions — Study Notes
content:
Functions

A function maps each input in the domain to exactly one output in the range.

Composite Functions

fg(x) means f(g(x)) — apply g first, then f. Order matters.

Example: f(x) = 2x + 1, g(x) = x². Then fg(x) = 2x² + 1 but gf(x) = (2x + 1)².

Inverse Functions

f⁻¹ reverses f: f⁻¹f(x) = x. To find it, swap x and y in y = f(x) and rearrange.

Example: f(x) = 3x − 2 gives f⁻¹(x) = (x + 2)/3.

An inverse exists only if f is one-one. If not, restrict the domain (e.g. f(x) = x² for x ≥ 0 has f⁻¹(x) = √x). Graphically, y = f⁻¹(x) is the reflection of y = f(x) in the line y = x, and the range of f becomes the domain of f⁻¹.

Transformations

NotationEffect on y = f(x)
f(x) + atranslation up by a
f(x + a)translation left by a
a f(x)vertical stretch, factor a
f(ax)horizontal stretch, factor 1/a
−f(x)reflection in the x-axis
f(−x)reflection in the y-axis

Exam tips: state the domain of any inverse; when combining transformations, translations inside the bracket act in the opposite direction to the sign.

Composite and inverse functions: exam method

fg(x) means f(g(x)): apply g first, then f, so read the composite from the right. Check that the output of g lies in the domain of f before you combine them; restricted domains are a common examiner target.

To find f⁻¹(x), write y = f(x), swap x and y, then rearrange to make y the subject. The domain of f⁻¹ is the range of f. A function has an inverse only if it is one-to-one on the domain given; restrict the domain (for example x ≥ 0 for a quadratic) when the question asks for it.

The graph of f⁻¹ is the reflection of the graph of f in the line y = x, so the point (a, b) on f becomes (b, a) on f⁻¹. Use this to check an answer.

Exam cue: State the domain and range of an inverse when asked, and write fg and gf separately when order matters.

title: Exam technique: Web Technologies and Security
content:
### What earns the marks
For trust, the CA signature chain described earns both marks: CA binds key to identity, browsers check against roots. For bulk data, symmetric speed plus asymmetric key exchange earns the hybrid pair. For verification, re-hash and compare stated earns the integrity mark with mismatch meaning change.
### Traps
Error: encryption claimed to stop phishing. Correction: valid TLS carries fake sites too; check identity. Error: hashes claimed to prove authorship. Correction: hashes prove integrity, signatures prove authorship. Error: self-claims accepted as trust. Correction: only CA signatures establish it.

title: Quadratics — Study Notes
content:
Quadratics

A quadratic has the form ax² + bx + c with a ≠ 0. Master three tools: completing the square, the discriminant, and inequalities.

Completing the Square

Rewrite x² + bx + c as (x + b/2)² − (b/2)² + c.

Example: x² + 6x + 5 = (x + 3)² − 9 + 5 = (x + 3)² − 4, so the vertex is at (−3, −4).

For a > 1, factor out a first: 2x² + 12x + 19 = 2(x² + 6x) + 19 = 2(x + 3)² − 18 + 19 = 2(x + 3)² + 1.

Vertex form a(x − h)² + k gives the minimum/maximum value k at x = h — this is how you find a maximum area or minimum cost.

The Discriminant

Δ = b² − 4ac decides how the curve meets the x-axis:

ΔRootsGraph
Δ > 0two distinct real rootscrosses x-axis twice
Δ = 0repeated roottouches (tangent)
Δ < 0no real rootsnever meets x-axis

Example: kx² + 4x + 1 = 0 has equal roots when 16 − 4k = 0, so k = 4.

Quadratic Inequalities

Solve by sketching. For x² − 5x + 4 < 0, factorise: (x − 1)(x − 4) < 0, and the curve is below the axis between the roots, so 1 < x < 4.

Tip: flip the inequality when dividing by a negative number, and always sketch to check which interval you need.

Curve and Line Intersections

Set the equations equal; the resulting quadratic's discriminant tells you if the line is a secant (Δ > 0), tangent (Δ = 0) or misses (Δ < 0).

Exam tips: complete the square before reading off turning points; state the discriminant condition explicitly before solving for an unknown coefficient.

title: Dynamics — Study Notes
content:
Dynamics

Newton's Laws

  • A body stays at rest or in uniform motion unless acted on by a resultant force.
  • F = ma — the resultant force equals mass × acceleration.
  • Forces occur in pairs: equal magnitude, opposite direction, on different bodies.

Example: a 2 kg mass with a 10 N resultant accelerates at 5 m s⁻².

Weight and Mass

Weight W = mg — a force in newtons; mass in kg is invariant. A 70 kg person weighs about 687 N.

Momentum

p = mv (vector, kg m s⁻¹). Resultant force = rate of change of momentum: F = Δp/Δt.

Conservation: in a collision with no external forces, total momentum is unchanged.

  • Elastic: kinetic energy also conserved
  • Inelastic: some KE becomes heat/sound

Example: a 3 kg trolley at 4 m s⁻¹ hits a stationary 1 kg trolley and they couple: 12 = 4v, so v = 3 m s⁻¹.

Friction and Connected Bodies

Draw free-body diagrams, then apply F = ma along each axis. For a towed car and trailer, the tow-bar tension appears as an internal pair (equal and opposite).

Exam tips: 'constant velocity' means zero resultant force, not zero friction; impulse questions want FΔt = Δp.

title: Motion in a Circle and Gravity
content:
Motion in a Circle and Gravity

Circular Motion

Angular speed ω = v/r = 2π/T (rad s⁻¹). Centripetal acceleration a = v²/r = ω²r, always directed to the centre; centripetal force F = mv²/r.

Example: a 0.5 kg ball on a 1 m string at 2 m s⁻¹ needs F = 2 N inward.

Gravitational Field

Newton's law: F = Gm₁m₂/r², G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².

Field strength g = GM/r². At Earth's surface g ≈ 9.81 N kg⁻¹.

Orbits

For a circular orbit, gravity supplies the centripetal force: GMm/r² = mv²/r, so v = √(GM/r) — higher orbits move slower but have longer periods (Kepler's third law: T² ∝ r³).

Geostationary satellites: T = 24 h, r ≈ 42,300 km from the centre.

Potential

Gravitational potential φ = −GM/r (zero at infinity). Potential gradient gives field strength: g = −dφ/dr.

Exam tips: speed in orbit is independent of the satellite's own mass; don't confuse g at the surface with orbital equations using r from the planet's centre.

title: AS Level Mathematics: Proof
content:
AS Level Mathematics: Proof

Proof is the difference between "it works for these numbers" and "it must work for all". AS proof covers four methods — direct proof, proof by exhaustion, proof by counter-example (disproof) and proof by deduction from definitions — plus the algebra of odd, even and consecutive numbers, and completing the square as a tool for inequalities. This note builds each method from zero with templates, full worked examples and the precise wording examiners expect, because proof marks are awarded for structure as much as for algebra.

The language of proof

TermMeaning
ConjectureA statement believed true but not yet proved
TheoremA statement that has been proved
ProofA logical argument from known facts to the conclusion
DisproofOne counter-example that makes the statement false
ExhaustionChecking every possible case

A single counter-example disproves a "for all" statement; no number of examples proves one. That asymmetry is the heart of the topic and the first thing examiners test.

Odd, even and consecutive numbers

even: 2n           (n integer)
odd:  2n + 1       (or 2n - 1)
consecutive integers: n, n + 1, n + 2
consecutive even: 2n, 2n + 2
consecutive odd: 2n + 1, 2n + 3

These forms are not optional decoration: a proof about parity must start from them, because "let the number be x" proves nothing about oddness.

Worked example 1. Prove that the sum of two consecutive odd numbers is a multiple of 4.

let the numbers be 2n + 1 and 2n + 3
sum = 4n + 4 = 4(n + 1)
which is a multiple of 4 for every integer n

Worked example 2. Prove that the product of two odd numbers is odd.

let them be 2m + 1 and 2n + 1
product = 4mn + 2m + 2n + 1 = 2(2mn + m + n) + 1
of the form 2k + 1 with k = 2mn + m + n, an integer
so the product is odd

Worked example 3. Prove that the difference between the squares of consecutive integers is the sum of the integers.

(n + 1)² - n² = n² + 2n + 1 - n² = 2n + 1 = n + (n + 1)

Direct proof

Start from the definitions, manipulate algebraically, and arrive at the required form. Write the conclusion explicitly ("hence ... as required") so the argument is closed.

Worked example. Prove that if x is odd then x² is odd.

let x = 2n + 1
x² = 4n² + 4n + 1 = 2(2n² + 2n) + 1
which is 2k + 1, hence odd

Worked example 2. Prove that the sum of any three consecutive integers is divisible by 3.

n + (n + 1) + (n + 2) = 3n + 3 = 3(n + 1)
which is divisible by 3

Proof by exhaustion

When the domain is small enough to list, check every case. The proof is only complete if the list is genuinely exhaustive — state why nothing is missed.

Worked example. Prove that every prime between 20 and 30 is the sum of two square numbers or state otherwise.

primes in the range: 23, 29
23 = 9 + 14 (not two squares); 25 + (-2)? no
23 = 4 + 19? no; squares below 23: 1, 4, 9, 16
1 + 16 = 17; 4 + 16 = 20; 9 + 16 = 25; 4 + 9 = 13
so 23 is not a sum of two squares; 29: 4 + 25 = 29  yes
conclusion: the conjecture fails for 23; the true statement is
"29 is the only prime between 20 and 30 expressible as a sum of two squares"

Worked example 2. Prove that n² + n is even for all integers n by exhaustion of the two parity cases.

case 1: n even, n = 2k → n² + n = 4k² + 2k = 2(2k² + k), even
case 2: n odd, n = 2k + 1 → 4k² + 4k + 1 + 2k + 1 = 4k² + 6k + 2
        = 2(2k² + 3k + 1), even
both cases covered, so the statement holds for all integers

The two-case parity split is exhaustion in its most common exam form: every integer is even or odd, so the cases exhaust the domain.

Disproof by counter-example

To disprove a "for all" claim, produce one case where it fails and show the arithmetic. One is enough; a hundred confirming cases prove nothing.

Worked example. Disprove: "if n² is a multiple of 4 then n is a multiple of 4."

try n = 6: n² = 36, a multiple of 4? 36/4 = 9, yes
but 6 is not a multiple of 4
so n = 6 is a counter-example and the statement is false

Worked example 2. Disprove: "n² − n + 11 is prime for all positive integers n."

n = 11: 121 - 11 + 11 = 121 = 11², not prime
counter-example n = 11 disproves the conjecture

Proof by completing the square

Inequalities about quadratics are proved by completing the square: a squared term is never negative, so the expression's minimum (or maximum) is visible.

x² + bx + c = (x + b/2)² + c - b²/4
since (x + b/2)² >= 0, the minimum value is c - b²/4

Worked example 1. Prove that x² + 4x + 7 > 0 for all real x.

x² + 4x + 7 = (x + 2)² + 3
(x + 2)² >= 0, so the expression is at least 3 > 0

Worked example 2. Prove that 2x − x² ≤ 1 for all real x.

2x - x² = -(x² - 2x) = -[(x - 1)² - 1] = 1 - (x - 1)²
since (x - 1)² >= 0, this is at most 1

Worked example 3. Find the values of k for which x² + kx + 9 > 0 for all x.

completing the square: (x + k/2)² + 9 - k²/4 > 0 for all x
requires the constant term positive: 9 - k²/4 > 0
k² < 36  →  -6 < k < 6

That last question is the discriminant argument in disguise: "always positive" means no real roots, so b² − 4ac < 0. Either method earns the marks; the completing-the-square route often reads more clearly.

Divisibility and multiples

A statement of the form "is a multiple of k" is proved by putting the expression in the shape k times an integer. Do the algebra first, then identify the factor; never assume the factor exists.

Worked example. Prove that for any integer n, n(n + 1)(n + 2) is a multiple of 6.

among any three consecutive integers there is at least one even
number and exactly one multiple of 3
so the product contains a factor 2 and a factor 3
since 2 and 3 are coprime, the product is divisible by 6

Worked example 2. Prove that 3^(2n) - 1 is a multiple of 8 for positive integers n.

3^(2n) - 1 = 9^n - 1 = (9 - 1)(9^(n-1) + ... + 1)
= 8 x (a positive integer), so divisible by 8

Worked example 3. Prove that the sum of five consecutive integers is always divisible by 5.

n + (n+1) + (n+2) + (n+3) + (n+4) = 5n + 10 = 5(n + 2)

Proof by contradiction: the irrationality of root 2

Contradiction assumes the statement is false, derives an impossibility, and concludes the statement is true. The classic example is examinable and worth knowing in full.

assume √(2) is rational: √(2) = p/q in lowest terms, p, q integers
square: 2 = p²/q²  →  p² = 2q²
so p² is even  →  p is even (a square is even only if its root is)
write p = 2k: 4k² = 2q²  →  q² = 2k²
so q² is even  →  q is even
but p and q cannot both be even if p/q is in lowest terms
contradiction  →  √(2) is irrational

The two logical hinges are that an even square implies an even root, and that "lowest terms" forbids a common factor of 2. State both; the marks live in them.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Parity) Prove that the sum of an odd and an even number is odd. Answer: (2m + 1) + 2n = 2(m + n) + 1, which is odd.
  2. (Consecutive) Prove that the product of two consecutive integers is even. Answer: n(n + 1): one of n, n + 1 is even, so the product is even.
  3. (Direct) Prove that (3n + 1)² − 1 is a multiple of 3. Answer: 9n² + 6n = 3(3n² + 2n).
  4. (Counter-example) Disprove "all primes are odd". Answer: 2 is prime and even.
  5. (Counter-example) Disprove "n² + 1 is prime for all n". Answer: n = 3 gives 10, not prime.
  6. (Completing the square) Prove x² − 6x + 10 > 0. Answer: (x − 3)² + 1 ≥ 1 > 0.
  7. (Exhaustion) Prove that n³ − n is divisible by 6 for n = 1, 2, 3, 4. Answer: 0, 6, 24, 60 — each divisible by 6 (a finite check is exhaustion).
  8. (Discriminant) Find k so that x² + 2kx + 4 = 0 has no real roots. Answer: 4k² − 16 < 0 → k² < 4 → −2 < k < 2.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Proving by example: two or three numbers never prove a "for all" statement; the argument must use algebra with a general n.
  • Not defining the variable: "let n be an integer" and "let n be odd, so n = 2k + 1" are required openings; an undefined x cannot carry a parity argument.
  • Assuming what you must prove: working backwards from the result to a true statement does not prove the original unless every step is reversible — say so if it is.
  • Counter-example not checked: show the arithmetic that makes the case fail; asserting "n = 6 fails" without the calculation loses the mark.
  • Incomplete exhaustion: if the domain has cases you did not cover (e.g. negatives, zero), the proof is incomplete — state the cases and why they exhaust.
  • Completing the square sign: a negative leading coefficient flips the inequality; factor out the minus first.
  • Conclusion missing: close with "hence ... as required"; an unclosed argument reads as unfinished.
  • Notation: write ≡ for identities and ⇒ for implications correctly; mixing them muddles the logic examiners follow.

The three shapes of a proof — and how to choose between them

A proof is not a longer calculation; it is an argument with a shape. There are only three shapes in this specification, each fits a different kind of statement, and recognising which one a question wants is most of the mark.

Shape 1: direct proof. Start from the definition, do algebra, arrive at the thing you were asked to show. It is the right choice whenever the statement is about all numbers of a kind, because a variable stands for all of them at once. "The sum of two consecutive integers is odd" is three lines: let them be n and n + 1, then n + (n + 1) = 2n + 1, which is odd by definition.

Shape 2: exhaustion. When there are finitely many cases, check them all and say so. It is a real proof — but only because the list is complete.

Shape 3: contradiction. When the statement denies something ("there is no greatest prime", "√2 is irrational"), assume the opposite and show it cannot stand. The template above is the whole method; the work is entirely in step 2.

The sentence that makes step 2 work. Whatever you deduce must contradict something already established — a definition, a theorem you have proved, or the assumption you made in step 1. In the √2 proof the contradiction is that a fraction is shown to be reducible when it was written in lowest terms, and the words that carry it are "but this contradicts the assumption that a and b have no common factor".

Why a counter-example is not a proof. One example can disprove a universal statement and can never prove one: "n² + n + 41 is prime for n = 1, 2, 3" is true and worthless, because n = 41 breaks it. If a question says "prove", an example earns nothing; if it says "disprove", one counter-example is a complete answer.

Worked example. Prove that if n² is even then n is even.

Suppose instead that n is odd. Then n = 2k + 1 for some integer k, so
n² = (2k + 1)² = 4k² + 4k + 1 = 2(2k² + 2k) + 1
which is odd, because it is one more than a multiple of 2. But we were told n² is even, and a number cannot be both odd and even — a contradiction. Therefore n cannot be odd, so n is even. ∎

Two details earn marks that students routinely drop: stating the form of the variable ("n = 2k + 1 for some integer k", not "n is odd so write it as something odd"), and naming the contradiction rather than stopping at the algebra. The ∎ is optional; the sentence that says what was contradicted is not.

Where marks are lost. Assuming what you are proving (writing "n² = 2m and n = 2k" straight away). Using the converse by accident — proving "n even ⇒ n² even" when the question asked the other way round. And ending with "therefore it is true" without saying what is true and why the assumption failed.

Equations and symbols

The algebraic moves that carry a P1 proof. Each line is a rewrite of one expression, so the marks are for the factorisation at the end, not the expansion.

sum = 4n + 4 = 4(n + 1) Key: sum = the combined expression from two consecutive even numbers; 4n + 4 is the unsimplified result; 4(n + 1) is the form that proves divisibility by 4. Always finish in the "k × integer" shape the question names.

product = 4mn + 2m + 2n + 1 = 2(2mn + m + n) + 1 Key: m, n = integers, so 2m + 1 and 2n + 1 are the two odd numbers; the final form is 2k + 1 with k = 2mn + m + n, which is the definition of odd. The factorisation, not the arithmetic, is the proof.

(n + 1)² - n² = n² + 2n + 1 - n² = 2n + 1 = n + (n + 1) Key: the difference of consecutive squares; the result is the sum of the same two numbers, which is the identity being proved. Two independent routes to 2n + 1 is stronger than one.

n + (n + 1) + (n + 2) = 3n + 3 = 3(n + 1) Key: three consecutive integers; the middle term is n + 1, so the sum is three times the middle. The last form proves divisibility by 3 for every n without testing any value.

let x = 2n + 1 Key: the standard opening for an odd number; n is an integer, so 2n is even and 2n + 1 is odd. State "for some integer n" — the clause is part of the proof, not decoration.

title: IGCSE Chemistry: Rates, Equilibrium and Redox
content:
IGCSE Chemistry: Rates, Equilibrium and Redox

Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry 0620 (2026–2028), Extended route, Topic 6 Chemical reactions: statement 6.1 Physical and chemical changes, 6.2 Rate of reaction, 6.3 Reversible reactions and equilibrium, and 6.4 Redox. Three questions meet here: how fast a reaction goes, how far it goes, and what happens to the electrons. Each section below works from the particle model to the exam wording, with collision theory as the engine of every rate explanation and the Haber and Contact processes traced condition by condition.

Physical and chemical changes

A physical change alters form without changing the substance — no new material is made (melting, dissolving, evaporation), and it is usually reversible. A chemical change makes new substances with new properties — new bonds form and old ones break (burning, rusting, reacting acid with metal), is often harder to reverse, and usually involves an energy change. The decisive question: "has a new substance formed?"

Rate of reaction: the measurement

Rate is how fast a reaction happens: rate = change in quantity ÷ time. Measure it by how fast a reactant disappears or a product appears.

Three standard measurement methods, each with its apparatus:

  1. MASS CHANGE (balance + flask): a gas escapes, so mass falls.
     rate = loss of mass / time. Good for CO₂ from acid + carbonate.
     Limitation: only works when the gas escapes and is not toxic.
  2. GAS VOLUME (gas syringe): collect the gas; read volume at intervals.
     rate = volume of gas / time. Works for any gaseous product.
     Limitation: gas may leak past the plunger; syringe may stick.
  3. COLOUR CHANGE / TURBIDITY (colorimeter or cross-on-paper): for
     thiosulfate + acid (sulfur precipitate clouds the solution); time how
     long a marked cross disappears from view.
  4. TEMPERATURE CHANGE for neutralisation-type reactions (thermometer).

Reading rate from a graph: the rate at any moment is the GRADIENT of the
tangent to the curve. Steep = fast; the curve flattens as reactants are used
up and collisions become rarer.

Rate and collision theory

Particles react when they collide with enough energy (≥ the activation energy) in the right orientation. Anything that increases the frequency or energy of successful collisions increases the rate.

FactorParticle-level explanationEffect on graph
ConcentrationMore particles per volume → more frequent collisionsSteeper initial gradient, same final product
Pressure (gases)Same as concentration: particles closer togetherSteeper initial gradient
Surface areaPowder exposes more particles to collide at onceSteeper initial gradient, same final product
TemperatureParticles move faster (more frequent collisions) AND a bigger fraction exceed EₐSteeper initial gradient; often reaches the same final product
CatalystProvides an alternative route with LOWER activation energy; more particles can react on collision; unchanged at the endSteeper initial gradient, same final product

Enzymes are biological catalysts — same mechanism, protein shaped to fit the substrate; denatured by high temperature (shape changes, substrate no longer fits).
