must name the halving and the sorted-data precondition.

Sorting algorithms compared

Before the traces, the comparison the exam wants in one place. Each algorithm's mechanism dictates its complexity and its niche; the traces below then show why each number is what it is.

SortBestAverageWorstSpaceStableBest niche
BubbleO(n)O(n²)O(n²)O(1)YesTeaching; tiny nearly-sorted sets (early-exit pass)
InsertionO(n)O(n²)O(n²)O(1)YesNearly-sorted or small data
SelectionO(n²)O(n²)O(n²)O(1)NoFew writes available (n swaps total)
MergeO(n log n)O(n log n)O(n log n)O(n)YesGuaranteed performance; linked lists; external sorting

Sorting: bubble, insertion, selection, merge

Data: [24, 12, 31, 19] - sort ascending with each algorithm's mechanism.

BUBBLE SORT - swap adjacent out-of-order pairs, pass by pass:
  pass 1: [24,12] swap -> [12,24,31,19]; [24,31] ok; [31,19] swap ->
          [12,24,19,31]  (largest value 31 has "bubbled" to the end)
  pass 2: [12,24] ok; [24,19] swap -> [12,19,24,31]; end is sorted
  pass 3: [12,19] ok; [19,24] ok -> sorted, no swaps means done.
  Worst case O(n^2): reverse-ordered data swaps at every comparison.

INSERTION SORT - build a sorted left portion, insert each next value:
  start [24 | 12 31 19]        (left portion [24])
  insert 12: 12 < 24 -> shift -> [12 24 | 31 19]
  insert 31: 31 >= 24 -> place  -> [12 24 31 | 19]
  insert 19: 19 < 31, 19 < 24, 19 > 12 -> [12 19 24 31]
  Fast on nearly-sorted data (few shifts); worst case O(n^2).

SELECTION SORT - find the minimum of the unsorted part, swap to its front:
  [24 12 31 19] min=12 -> swap with 24 -> [12 | 24 31 19]
  [24 31 19]   min=19 -> swap with 24 -> [12 19 | 31 24]
  [31 24]      min=24 -> swap with 31 -> [12 19 24 31]
  Always O(n^2) comparisons, but only n swaps - good when writes are costly.

MERGE SORT - divide in half recursively, then merge sorted halves:
  [24 12 31 19] -> [24 12] [31 19] -> [24] [12] [31] [19]
  merge -> [12 24] [19 31] -> merge -> [12 19 24 31]
  Every level merges n items, and there are log n levels: O(n log n) always,
  at the cost of O(n) extra memory.

Choosing: small or nearly-sorted data → insertion; minimal memory and small n → selection; guaranteed performance and memory available → merge; tiny arrays with expensive swaps → bubble (mostly pedagogical). The exam asks for the comparison and a reason.

Recursion

A recursive function calls itself on a smaller instance, with a base case ending the recursion. Every recursion is equivalent to iteration plus an explicit stack (the call stack does the pushing). Two rules for correctness: each call must move toward the base case, and the base case must be reachable.

Recursive factorial, traced through the call stack:

  def factorial(n):
      if n <= 1: return 1        # base case
      return n * factorial(n-1)  # recursive case

  factorial(4):
    4 * factorial(3)
        3 * factorial(2)
            2 * factorial(1)
                1                 # base case reached; returns start
            2 * 1 = 2
        3 * 2 = 6
    4 * 6 = 24

Stack depth is n (each call waits for the return below it). A missing base
case never terminates - and deep recursion on large n overflows the stack,
which is why iterative solutions are preferred for deep, simple loops.

Trace table alternative for factorial(4): n=4 -> 24, n=3 -> 6, n=2 -> 2,
n=1 -> 1 (returns), then the multiplications unwind: 2, 6, 24.
Recursive binary search on [12, 19, 24, 31, 38, 44, 52, 67, 71, 89]:

  def bsearch(lo, hi, target):
      if lo > hi: return -1          # base case: empty range
      mid = (lo + hi) // 2
      if data[mid] == target: return mid
      if data[mid] > target: return bsearch(lo, mid-1, target)   # left
      return bsearch(mid+1, hi, target)                          # right

  Search for 31: mid=4 (38) -> 31 < 38 -> recurse left [0..3];
  mid=1 (19) -> 31 > 19 -> recurse right [2..3]; mid=2 (24) -> right [3..3];
  mid=3 (31) -> found. Four recursive calls, each halving the range.

Graphs and traversal

A graph is nodes (vertices) joined by edges — modelling networks, maps, dependencies. Terminology: undirected/directed, weighted (edges carry costs), path, cycle, connected. Storage: adjacency matrix (n×n grid — O(1) edge check, O(n²) space) versus adjacency list (list of neighbours per node — O(V+E) space, faster to iterate edges).

Graph: A connected to B, C; B to D; C to D; D to E.  Start at A.

BREADTH-FIRST SEARCH (queue; visit level by level):
  queue [A]; visit A -> neighbours B, C -> queue [B, C]
  visit B -> neighbour D -> queue [C, D]
  visit C -> neighbour D (already queued/visited) -> queue [D]
  visit D -> neighbour E -> queue [E]
  visit E -> queue []
  Order: A, B, C, D, E. Finds SHORTEST PATH in unweighted graphs (level order).

DEPTH-FIRST SEARCH (stack or recursion; dive to the end, then backtrack):
  visit A -> B (first neighbour)
  visit B -> D
  visit D -> E
  visit E -> backtrack to D -> backtrack to B -> backtrack to A
  visit C -> D already visited -> backtrack
  Order: A, B, D, E, C. Detects CYCLES and solves maze-like problems.

Both mark nodes visited - without that, cycles make them loop forever.
Complexity: O(V + E) with adjacency lists - every vertex and edge processed
once.

Dijkstra's algorithm (weighted shortest path) extends BFS with a priority queue: keep tentative distances from the source, always settle the nearest unsettled node, and relax (shorten) its neighbours' distances; O((V+E) log V) with a heap. The trace question walks one node's relaxation exactly this way.

Worked example: algorithm choice for three problems

1. Find a name in an unsorted phone book (data streams in):
   linear search - no ordering to exploit; O(n).

2. Find a name in a sorted directory of 10^6 entries:
   binary search - O(log n) is about 20 comparisons; sorting once with
   merge sort (O(n log n)) then searching many times amortises quickly.

3. Find the shortest route between two towns on a weighted map:
   Dijkstra - BFS ignores the road distances; a greedy relaxation over a
   priority queue computes the true shortest path; complexity
   O((V+E) log V).

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Applying binary search to unsorted data; the sorted precondition is part of the answer.
  • Complexity claims without the mechanism ("bubble sort is O(n²)" needs nested loops and the swap rule).
  • Confusing best/average/worst case; quote worst unless asked.
  • Recursion without a reachable base case, or not moving toward it.
  • Forgetting the call stack's cost: recursion uses O(n) stack space even when the algorithm is O(1) in its own memory.
  • BFS versus DFS purpose swap: BFS = shortest unweighted path; DFS = cycles, connectivity, exhaustive paths.
  • Unmarked visited sets in graph traversal — infinite loops on cycles.
  • Merge sort's memory cost omitted; it is O(n) extra space, the standard trade against in-place O(n²) sorts.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Unit 3, 4 marks). Trace bubble sort on [5, 3, 4, 1] for one pass and describe what the pass achieves.

Answer: Compare 5 and 3 → swap [3, 5, 4, 1]; 5 and 4 → swap [3, 4, 5, 1]; 5 and 1 → swap [3, 4, 1, 5]. The largest value (5) has bubbled to its final position; each pass places one more element, so n−1 passes complete the sort — O(n²).

Question 2 (Unit 3, 4 marks). Explain why binary search is O(log n) and state its precondition.

Answer: Each comparison discards half the remaining range (compare against the middle, keep one half), so the number of comparisons grows with the number of halvings needed to reach one element — log₂n: a million items need at most 20. Precondition: the data must be sorted by the searched key.

Question 3 (Unit 3, 5 marks). Write a recursive algorithm to compute the sum of an array and explain its base case.

Answer: FUNCTION sum(a, n): IF n = 0 THEN RETURN 0; ELSE RETURN a[n] + sum(a, n−1); ENDIF. The base case n = 0 returns 0 (empty array sums to zero), guaranteeing termination; each recursive call shrinks n by one toward it. Recursion depth is n, so iterative summation avoids stack growth for huge arrays.

Question 4 (Unit 3, 5 marks). Compare BFS and DFS on an undirected graph.

Answer: BFS uses a queue and explores level by level, visiting all neighbours before descending — giving the shortest path in unweighted graphs and O(V+E) time, at the cost of queue memory. DFS uses a stack (or recursion) and dives along one path to its end before backtracking — suiting cycle detection, topological ordering and exhaustive search, with memory proportional to the deepest path. Both must mark visited vertices to terminate on cycles.

Question 5 (Unit 3, 4 marks). Compare adjacency matrices and adjacency lists.

Answer: An adjacency matrix is a V×V grid giving O(1) edge-existence checks but O(V²) space — wasteful for sparse graphs. An adjacency list stores each vertex's neighbours, using O(V+E) space and fast edge iteration, but checking one edge takes O(degree). Dense graphs with frequent edge queries favour matrices; sparse graphs favour lists.

Question 6 (Unit 3, 3 marks). Explain how Dijkstra's algorithm finds a shortest path and state its limitation.

Answer: It maintains tentative distances from the source, repeatedly settling the unvisited node with the smallest distance and relaxing its edges (updating neighbour distances when the new route is shorter). Once a node is settled its distance is final. Limitation: it requires non-negative edge weights — negative weights break the greedy finality, needing Bellman-Ford instead.

Algorithms need code to run on; the next note covers how programming paradigms structure that code.

title: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Statistics and Data Handling
content:
Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Statistics and Data Handling

Statistics is the art of describing a pile of numbers with a few well-chosen ones: an average to say where the middle lies, a spread to say how tightly the data cluster, and a chart to make the shape visible. The IGCSE questions test exactly that pipeline — classify the data, compute the averages and spread, draw or read the chart, and compare two distributions. This note builds the whole subject from zero: the data types, every average and measure of spread with the frequency-table method, the standard charts, cumulative frequency curves, and histograms with unequal class widths.

Classifying statistical data

TypeMeaningExamples
Qualitative (categorical)describes a quality, not a numberfavourite colour, blood group
Quantitativemeasured or counted as a numberheight, number of siblings
Discretecountable, separate values (usually integers)number of children, shoe size
Continuouscan take any value in a range (measured)height, time, mass

The classification decides which charts and averages are legal: a mode for categorical data, a median for ordered data, class intervals for continuous data. Discrete data are plotted as bar charts with gaps; continuous data as histograms with no gaps (and frequency density on the vertical axis).

Averages and range

mean = sum of values / number of values
median = middle value when ordered (mean of the two middle
         values for an even count)
mode = most frequent value (or class); none if no repeats
range = largest - smallest

quartiles: Q1 = lower quartile (25%), Q3 = upper quartile (75%)
interquartile range (IQR) = Q3 - Q1  (spread of the middle 50%)

The mean uses every value (sensitive to outliers); the median ignores extreme values (robust); the mode is the only average available for categorical data. When comparing two data sets, quote an average and a spread: "school A has a higher median but a larger IQR, so its results are higher on average but less consistent."

Worked example. Find the mean, median, mode and range of: 4, 7, 7, 9, 12, 15, 18.

mean = (4+7+7+9+12+15+18)/7 = 72/7 = 10.3 (3 s.f.)
median = 4th value = 9
mode = 7 (appears twice)
range = 18 - 4 = 14

Worked example 2 (even count). Find the median of 3, 5, 8, 10, 12, 15.

even count: average the 3rd and 4th values
median = (8 + 10)/2 = 9

Averages from frequency tables

mean = sum of (value x frequency) / sum of frequencies
median = the value at position (n + 1)/2 in cumulative order
mode = the value with the highest frequency

Worked example. The table shows goals scored: 0 (5 players), 1 (8), 2 (6), 3 (2). Find the mean and the median.

total players = 5 + 8 + 6 + 2 = 21
total goals = 0 × 5 + 1 × 8 + 2 × 6 + 3 × 2 = 0 + 8 + 12 + 6 = 26
mean = 26/21 = 1.24 (3 s.f.)
median position = (21 + 1)/2 = 11th value
cumulative: 5 (0 goals), 13 (1 goal) - the 11th value is 1
median = 1

For grouped data, use midpoints: the mean = Σ(midpoint × frequency)/Σfrequency, and the median comes from the cumulative frequency curve (below). The grouped mean is an estimate because the midpoint stands in for every value in the class.

Charts and diagrams

  • Bar chart: bars with gaps for categorical or discrete data; height = frequency.
  • Pie chart: angle = (frequency/total) × 360°; label the sectors with the category.
  • Pictogram: a symbol represents a fixed number; a half symbol represents half that number.
  • Stem-and-leaf: a sorted display that keeps the actual values; the key explains the split (e.g. 3|4 means 34).
  • Frequency polygon: plot frequency against the midpoint of each class and join with straight lines.

Worked example (pie chart). 40 students choose a sport: football 16, tennis 10, swimming 8, other 6. Find the angle for football.

angle = (16/40) × 360 = 144 °

Worked example 2 (pie chart reverse). A sector of 72° represents 9 students. How many students in total?

72 ° represents 9  →  360 ° represents 9 × 360/72 = 45 students

Cumulative frequency diagrams

A cumulative frequency table adds frequencies as you move up the classes. Plot cumulative frequency against the upper class boundary and join with a smooth curve; then read positions:

median at n/2
lower quartile at n/4
upper quartile at 3n/4
IQR = Q3 - Q1

Worked example. A cumulative frequency curve for 60 students' marks: Q1 = 42, median = 55, Q3 = 68. Find the IQR and interpret it.

IQR = 68 - 42 = 26 marks
The middle 50% of students scored within 26 marks of each other;

Always read across to the curve and then down to the horizontal axis — and use the class boundaries, not the midpoints, for the plot positions.

Histograms and frequency density

When class widths differ, the height of a bar cannot be the frequency — a wide class would dominate unfairly. Instead, the area of each bar is proportional to the frequency:

frequency density = frequency / class width
frequency = frequency density x class width (area of the bar)

Worked example. Class 0–10 has frequency 20; 10–20 has frequency 30; 20–40 has frequency 40. Find the frequency densities.

0-10: 20/10 = 2.0
10-20: 30/10 = 3.0
20-40: 40/20 = 2.0

Reading a histogram backwards is the standard question: measure a bar's width and height, multiply to get the frequency, and read the class from the horizontal axis. Remember that the axes often use class boundaries, so a bar from 20 to 40 covers width 20.

Stem-and-leaf diagrams and frequency polygons

A stem-and-leaf diagram sorts data while keeping every value visible: the stem is the leading digit and the leaf the final digit, with a key such as 3|4 meaning 34. Interpreting one means reading the ordered leaves to find the median, the quartiles and the shape: the median is the middle leaf, Q1 and Q3 sit at the quarter and three-quarter positions, and the distribution's skew shows in where the leaves bunch.

A frequency polygon plots frequency against the midpoint of each class and joins the points with straight lines; it is the grouped-data equivalent of a line graph and makes comparisons between two distributions easy (plot both polygons on the same axes).

Worked example. The leaves for stem 4 are 1, 3, 3, 6, 8 and for stem 5 are 0, 2, 5. List the data in order and find the median.

values: 41, 43, 43, 46, 48, 50, 52, 55
n = 8, so the median is the mean of the 4th and 5th values:
(46 + 48)/2 = 47

Worked example 2 (interpreting). Explain what a long right-hand tail of leaves in a stem-and-leaf diagram indicates.

A long right tail means a few unusually high values: the data
are positively skewed, and the mean will be greater than the
median because the high values pull it upward.

Comparing distributions

Comparison questions want two statements: one about the average (which is higher) and one about the spread (which is more consistent). Use median and IQR together — they are robust to outliers — or mean and standard deviation when the data are symmetric and the syllabus supplies it.

Worked example. Class A: median 62, IQR 18. Class B: median 58, IQR 9. Compare.

Class A has the higher typical score (median 62 vs 58), but its
results are more spread out (IQR 18 vs 9), so Class B is more
consistent even though its middle score is lower.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Averages) Find the mean and range of 12, 15, 11, 19, 13. Answer: mean = (12 + 15 + 11 + 19 + 13)/5 = 70/5 = 14; range = largest − smallest = 19 − 11 = 8.
  2. (Frequency table) Values 1, 2, 3 with frequencies 4, 7, 9. Find the mean. Answer: mean = Σfx/Σf = (1 × 4 + 2 × 7 + 3 × 9)/(4 + 7 + 9) = (4 + 14 + 27)/20 = 45/20 = 2.25.
  3. (Median) Find the median of 2, 4, 4, 6, 9, 10. Answer: there are six values, so the median is the mean of the 3rd and 4th: (4 + 6)/2 = 5.
  4. (Pie chart) A sector of 90° represents 15 people. Find the total. Answer: 90° is 90/360 = ¼ of the circle, so the total is 15 ÷ ¼ = 15 × 4 = 60 people.
  5. (Cumulative frequency) For 80 values, where do you read the median? Answer: At cumulative frequency 40, reading across to the curve and down to the axis.
  6. (Histogram) A bar of width 5 has frequency density 4. Find its frequency. Answer: frequency = frequency density × class width = 4 × 5 = 20.
  7. (Frequency density) Class 30–50 has frequency 24. Find the frequency density. Answer: class width = 50 − 30 = 20, so frequency density = frequency/width = 24/20 = 1.2.
  8. (Compare) Two runners' times: A median 42 s, IQR 3 s; B median 40 s, IQR 8 s. Compare. Answer: B is faster typically (lower median) but less consistent (larger IQR); A is more reliable.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Median without ordering: the median is the middle of the ordered list. Forgetting to sort is the commonest data-handling error.
  • Even-count median: average the two middle values; do not pick one of them.
  • Grouped mean: use midpoints and label the answer an estimate — the midpoint is not the actual mean of the class.
  • Histogram heights: the vertical axis is frequency density, not frequency; area is the frequency. Reading the height as the frequency is the classic histogram error.
  • Cumulative frequency positions: plot against upper class boundaries and read the median at n/2 (not (n+1)/2 on the graph).
  • Pie chart arithmetic: check that the angles sum to 360° before answering the next part.
  • IQR direction: IQR = upper − lower quartile; a negative IQR means the quartiles are swapped.
  • Comparison claims: quote actual values ("median 62 vs 58"), not "better" without evidence.

Collecting and classifying data

Every statistical question starts with data, and the type of data decides which averages and diagrams are sensible. Before any calculation, decide where the data came from, what kind of values it holds, and whether the sample is fair. The subsections below set out these decisions in the order an examiner expects them to be made.

Primary and secondary data

Primary data is collected by the person who uses it, for example by a survey or an experiment carried out in class. Secondary data is taken from an existing source such as a census, a published table or a sports website. Primary data suits a question that needs a specific answer, while secondary data is quicker but may not match the exact question being asked. State which kind you have used when you describe an investigation.

Discrete and continuous data

Discrete data takes separate values that are usually counted, such as the number of goals scored or the number of people in a family. Continuous data can take any value in a range and is measured, such as height, mass or time. The distinction matters for grouping: a discrete table can use single values, while a continuous table needs class intervals with clear boundaries such as 10 ≤ t < 20.

Qualitative and quantitative data

Qualitative data describes a quality, such as eye colour or favourite subject, and cannot be averaged. Quantitative data is numerical and can be ordered and added. A mean is only meaningful for quantitative data, so a question that asks for the mean colour is answered by naming the mode or by stating that no mean exists.

Reading the question before the data

Underline what the question asks for before reading the table: a mode, a median, a range, a comparison or a conclusion. Many marks are lost by calculating the right number and then answering a different question. Note the units and the sample size at the same time, because the sample size is needed for a relative frequency and the units for a correct final statement.

Bias in samples and questionnaires

A sample is biased when some members of the population are more likely to be chosen than others. Asking only students in one class about a school-wide question is biased, and so is a question that leads the respondent, such as asking whether people agree that the bus service is too slow. A fair sample is random, large enough to represent the group, and drawn from the whole population being studied.

Judging the reliability of a conclusion

A conclusion is only as reliable as the data behind it. A small sample, an unrepresentative group or a question with an obvious bias weakens any statement drawn from it. A good answer names one weakness and suggests a change, such as taking a larger sample across a wider range of times or places.

Drawing a conclusion from a table

A conclusion must be supported by a number from the table and must answer the question asked. If the mean time for group A is 14 minutes and for group B is 18 minutes, the statement that group B took longer on average is supported, but a statement about all pupils in the school is not, because only two groups were measured.

Averages and spread in depth

The mean, median and mode each describe the centre of a set of data in a different way, and the range and interquartile range describe the spread. A careful answer uses the average that fits the data and the measure of spread that shows how far the values lie from it. The subsections below work through each measure in the form the question is most likely to use.

The mode for discrete and grouped data

The mode is the value that occurs most often. In a discrete frequency table it is the value with the largest frequency. For grouped data it is the modal class, the class with the largest frequency, and the answer is given as a class interval rather than a single value. A data set can have no mode, one mode or several modes.

The median from an ordered list

To find the median, arrange the values in order and locate the middle one. For n values the median is at position (n + 1) ÷ 2. With nine values the median is the fifth value, and with ten values it is the average of the fifth and sixth. Always order the data before counting, because the median taken from an unsorted list is wrong even when the middle value is chosen carefully.

Choosing an average

The mean uses every value, but it is pulled by extreme values. The median is not affected by one very large value, and the mode is the only average that can be used with qualitative data. A typical question asks which average best describes a set of salaries that includes one very large income; the answer is the median, with the reason that the mean is pulled up by the outlier.

The effect of an outlier

An outlier is a value far from the rest of the data. Adding one outlier to a small set changes the mean noticeably but may leave the median and mode unchanged. When an exam question asks for the effect of a change, work out the mean before and after the change, rather than guessing the direction from the size of the new value.

Range as a measure of spread

The range is the largest value minus the smallest value. It is quick to find but depends on only two values, so one outlier can make it large even when the rest of the data are close together. When comparing two data sets, state both the range and the centre, because two sets with the same mean can have very different ranges.

The interquartile range

The interquartile range is the upper quartile minus the lower quartile, the spread of the middle half of the data. It ignores the extreme values at each end and is therefore less affected by outliers than the range. For a list of 12 ordered values, the lower quartile is the median of the lower six values and the upper quartile is the median of the upper six.

Estimating the mean of grouped data

For grouped data the exact values are unknown, so the mean is estimated using the midpoint of each class. Multiply each midpoint by its frequency, add the products and divide by the total frequency: mean = Σfx ÷ Σf, where x is the midpoint. The answer is an estimate, and the working should say so, because the true mean depends on where each value sits inside its class.

Equations and symbols

Seven formulas cover the whole paper: the three averages with their range and interquartile range, the two histogram relations, and the pie-chart angle. Every one carries the same mark-scheme requirement — substitute, then state the answer in the units of the data, not as a bare number.

mean = sum of values / number of values Key: mean = the arithmetic average, in the same units as the data; sum of values = the total of every reading; number of values = how many readings there are. Uses every value, so one outlier moves it.

median = the value at position (n + 1)/2 in cumulative order Key: n = the number of values; the position is a count through the ordered list, not a value. For an even n the position falls between two values, so average them — picking one of the two is the commonest lost mark.

mode = the value with the highest frequency Key: mode = the most frequent value, in the same units as the data; for grouped data it is the modal class. The only average available for categorical data.

range = largest - smallest Key: largest and smallest = the extreme values of the data set; the range is their difference, in the data's units. It uses only two values, so a single outlier destroys it.

IQR = Q3 - Q1 Key: IQR = interquartile range, the spread of the middle 50% of the data (same units); Q3 = upper quartile at the 75% position; Q1 = lower quartile at the 25% position. A negative IQR means the quartiles have been swapped.

IQR = 68 - 42 = 26 marks Key: 68 = Q3, the mark at the 75% position; 42 = Q1, the mark at the 25% position; 26 marks = the IQR. Interpret it in words: the middle half of the students scored within 26 marks of each other.

frequency density = frequency / class width Key: frequency density = the height of the bar (no units, since it is a count divided by a width); frequency = the number of readings in the class; class width = upper boundary minus lower boundary (in the data's units). Use it only when the class widths differ — with equal widths the height may be the frequency.

frequency = frequency density x class width (area of the bar) Key: the same relation rearranged; reading a histogram backwards means measuring a bar's width and height and multiplying. In a histogram it is the area, never the height, that represents the frequency.

angle = (frequency/total) × 360° Key: frequency = the count in the sector; total = the total count for the whole chart; angle in degrees, and the sectors must sum to 360°. To go the other way, total = frequency × 360/angle.

mean = sum of (value x frequency) / sum of frequencies Key: value = each reading, or the midpoint of a class for grouped data (same units); frequency = how many times it occurs. With midpoints the answer is labelled an estimate, because the midpoint stands in for every value in the class.

title: AS Level Mathematics: Functions
content:
AS Level Mathematics: Functions

A function is a rule that turns each input into exactly one output — a machine with one chute per item. This note builds the whole AS treatment from zero: function notation with domain and range, the standard graphs and their shapes, composite functions and why order matters, inverses with their reflection in y = x, and the transformation rules that shift, stretch and reflect any graph. The marks in this topic come from precision — writing the correct domain, composing in the right order, and stating the rule for the inverse before using it.

Notation, domain and range

f(x) = 2x + 3      "f of x"
f(4) = 11          substitute 4 for every x
domain: the set of allowed inputs
range: the set of outputs the function actually produces

Domain restrictions matter: f(x) = 1/x is undefined at x = 0; f(x) = √x requires x ≥ 0; a quadratic over the reals has all reals as its domain. The range is found by considering the function's behaviour over its stated domain — for a quadratic, complete the square to find the minimum or maximum.

Worked example. f(x) = x² − 4, domain x ≥ 0. Find the range.

at x = 0: f = -4; the function increases without limit
range: f(x) >= -4

Worked example 2 (reciprocal). g(x) = 3/(x − 2), x ≠ 2. State the domain and range.

domain: all real x except 2
range: all real values except 0 (the fraction can never be 0)

The standard graphs

FunctionShapeFeatures
y = xstraight linegradient 1, through origin
y = x²parabola upwardminimum at origin, symmetric
y = x³cubic, S-shapedpasses through origin, increasing
y = 1/xtwo branches (hyperbola)asymptotes x = 0 and y = 0
y = √xhalf-parabola on its sidedomain x ≥ 0, range y ≥ 0
y = |x|V-shapevertex at origin, domain all reals
y = aˣ (a > 1)exponential growthalways positive, through (0, 1)

Knowing these shapes is the foundation of graph transformations and of estimating solutions graphically.

Composite functions

fg(x) means f(g(x)): apply g first, then f
gf(x) means g(f(x)): apply f first, then g
in general fg(x) is not the same as gf(x)

Worked example. f(x) = 2x + 1, g(x) = x². Find fg(x) and gf(x).

fg(x) = f(g(x)) = f(x²) = 2x² + 1
gf(x) = g(f(x)) = (2x + 1)² = 4x² + 4x + 1
These differ, so order matters.

Worked example 2 (solving). With the same f and g, solve fg(x) = 19.

2x² + 1 = 19
2x² = 18  →  x² = 9  →  x = 3 or x = -3

Inverse functions

The inverse f⁻¹ undoes f: if f(a) = b then f⁻¹(b) = a. To find it, write y = f(x), swap x and y, and rearrange for y.

method: y = f(x)  →  x = f(y) after swap  →  y = f⁻¹(x)

Worked example. Find the inverse of f(x) = 3x − 7.

y = 3x - 7
swap: x = 3y - 7
rearrange: 3y = x + 7  →  y = (x + 7)/3
f⁻¹(x) = (x + 7)/3

Worked example 2 (quadratic, restricted domain). f(x) = x² + 2 for x ≥ 0. Find f⁻¹ and its domain.

y = x² + 2
swap: x = y² + 2  →  y² = x - 2  →  y = √(x - 2)
(the negative root is rejected because the domain is x >= 0)
f⁻¹(x) = √(x - 2), domain x >= 2

Two properties worth remembering: the graph of f⁻¹ is the reflection of f in the line y = x, and the domain of f⁻¹ is the range of f (and vice versa).

Transformations of graphs

TransformationEffect on the graphWhat changes
y = f(x) + atranslate up by ay-coordinates +a
y = f(x + a)translate left by ax replaced by x + a (inside: opposite direction)
y = af(x)vertical stretch by ay-coordinates × a
y = f(ax)horizontal stretch by 1/ax-coordinates ÷ a
y = −f(x)reflection in the x-axisy-coordinates negated
y = f(−x)reflection in the y-axisx-coordinates negated

The inside/outside rule is the one that trips candidates: changes outside the bracket affect y and behave as written; changes inside affect x and behave in reverse.

Worked example. The point (3, 5) lies on y = f(x). Find its image under y = f(x − 2) + 1.

f(x - 2) shifts the graph 2 to the right; +1 shifts it up 1
image: (3 + 2, 5 + 1) = (5, 6)

Worked example 2 (stretch). The point (4, 1) is on y = f(x). Find its image under y = f(2x).

horizontal stretch by 1/2: x-coordinate halves
image: (2, 1)

Rational functions and asymptotes

A rational function is a ratio of polynomials, y = p(x)/q(x). Its graph is shaped by two constraints: where the denominator is zero the function is undefined (a vertical asymptote), and for large x the ratio settles to a horizontal asymptote determined by the leading terms.

y = (ax + b)/(cx + d)
vertical asymptote: cx + d = 0  →  x = -d/c
horizontal asymptote: y → a/c as x → +/- infinity
excluded value: the point where the denominator vanishes is
not in the domain

Worked example. Sketch y = 2/(x − 1) and state its domain and range.

vertical asymptote x = 1 (denominator zero)
horizontal asymptote y = 0 (numerator fixed, denominator grows)
domain: x not equal to 1; range: y not equal to 0
the two branches lie in the regions x < 1 and x > 1

Worked example 2 (linear over linear). Sketch y = (x + 1)/(x − 2).

vertical asymptote x = 2
horizontal asymptote y = 1 (leading coefficients 1/1)
intercepts: y = -1/2 at x = 0; x = -1 at y = 0

Exponential and logarithmic graphs

Exponentials and logarithms are inverse functions, and their graphs encode that relationship. y = aˣ (a > 1) rises ever more steeply, passes through (0, 1) and never touches the x-axis — the x-axis is an asymptote. y = log_a x is the reflection in y = x: it passes through (1, 0), has a vertical asymptote at x = 0, and is defined only for x > 0.

  • Growth and decay: y = Ae^(kx) grows for k > 0 and decays for k < 0; the constant A is the value at x = 0.
  • Logarithm laws: log(ab) = log a + log b; log(a/b) = log a − log b; log(aⁿ) = n log a.
  • Solving exponentials: take logs of both sides — 3^x = 20 gives x log 3 = log 20, so x = log 20/log 3 ≈ 2.73.

Worked example. Solve 5^(2x−1) = 40.

(2x - 1) log 5 = log 40
2x - 1 = log 40/log 5 = 1.602/0.699 = 2.292
2x = 3.292  →  x = 1.65 (3 s.f.)

Worked example 2 (modelling with an exponential). A colony of bacteria doubles every 3 hours, starting at 500. Write the population after t hours and find when it reaches 20 000.

P = 500 × 2^(t/3)
20000 = 500 × 2^(t/3)  →  40 = 2^(t/3)
log 40 = (t/3) log 2  →  t/3 = 5.322  →  t = 16.0 hours

The modelling step — translating "doubles every 3 hours" into 2^(t/3) — is where most marks are lost; write the base (2 for doubling, 0.5 for halving) and the exponent (time divided by the period) explicitly before solving. For decay, the same structure with a base below 1 (or a negative exponent) describes cooling, depreciation and radioactive half-life, so one pattern covers a whole family of questions.

Worked examples: mixed function problems

Worked example. f(x) = x + 2, g(x) = 3x. Find f⁻¹(x), fg(x), and show that f⁻¹(fg(x)) = g(x).

f⁻¹(x) = x - 2
fg(x) = 3x + 2
f⁻¹(fg(x)) = (3x + 2) - 2 = 3x = g(x)

Worked example 2 (range of composite). f(x) = x², g(x) = x + 1. Find the range of fg for x ≥ 0.

fg(x) = (x + 1)²
for x >= 0: x + 1 >= 1  →  fg(x) >= 1
range: fg(x) >= 1

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Evaluate) f(x) = 2x² − 1. Find f(−3). Answer: 2(9) − 1 = 17.
  2. (Domain) State the domain of g(x) = 1/(x + 4). Answer: x ≠ −4.
  3. (Composite) f(x) = x + 3, g(x) = 2x. Find fg(x). Answer: 2x + 3.
  4. (Inverse) Find the inverse of h(x) = (x − 5)/2. Answer: y = 2x + 5.
  5. (Inverse domain) f(x) = x² + 1 for x ≥ 0. State the domain of f⁻¹. Answer: x ≥ 1 (the range of f).
  6. (Transformation) Describe the transformation y = f(x) → y = f(x + 3) − 2. Answer: translation 3 left and 2 down.
  7. (Point image) (2, 7) is on y = f(x). Find its image on y = 2f(x). Answer: (2, 14).
  8. (Reasoning) Explain why f⁻¹(f(x)) = x. Answer: The inverse undoes the function: applying f then f⁻¹ returns the original input for every x in the domain of f.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Order of composition: fg means g first. Writing f(g(x)) as f(x)g(x) (a product) is a fundamental error.
  • Inside transformations reversed: f(x + 3) moves left, not right; f(2x) compresses horizontally by ½, not stretches by 2.
  • Inverse of a quadratic without restriction: x² has no inverse over all reals because it is not one-to-one; the domain restriction is what makes the inverse valid.
  • Dropping the ± in inverse quadratics: keep the root that matches the stated domain; state which and why.
  • Domain notation: write inequalities or set notation precisely (x ≠ 2; x ≥ 0); "all numbers" is rarely correct.
  • Confusing f⁻¹(x) with 1/f(x): the inverse is not the reciprocal. This is the most common notation trap.
  • Range from the wrong feature: for a quadratic on a restricted domain, evaluate the endpoints and the vertex — the range may be bounded at both ends.
  • Sketch axes: label asymptotes for reciprocal and exponential graphs; an unlabelled sketch loses communication marks.

title: Information Representation — Study Notes
content:
`# Information Representation

Number Systems and Ranges

Unsigned binary with n bits stores 0 to 2ⁿ − 1. Two's complement represents negatives: the MSB has value −2ⁿ⁻¹.

Example: 8-bit two's complement of −5: 11111011 (−128 + 64 + 32 + 16 + 8 + 2 + 1).

SystemBaseDigits
Binary20–1
Hexadecimal160–9, A–F
BCD—4 bits per decimal digit

Binary Arithmetic

Add: 0+0=0, 0+1=1, 1+1=0 carry 1, 1+1+1=1 carry 1. Overflow happens when a result exceeds the word size.

Subtraction uses two's complement addition (A − B = A + (−B)).

Text

  • ASCII: 7 bits, 128 characters, English only
  • Unicode: universal scripts; UTF-8 is variable-width (1–4 bytes)

Images and Sound

  • Bitmap: pixels with colour depth (bits per pixel). File size = width × height × depth.
  • Sound: sampling rate (Hz) × bit depth × duration × channels.
  • Resolution trade-off: fidelity vs size.

Compression

  • Lossless (ZIP, run-length encoding): exact reconstruction — required for text/code
  • Lossy (JPEG, MP3): discards perceptually minor data — smaller files

Example: RLE of AAABBBCC → 3A3B2C.

Exam tips: show working for two's complement conversions; state why compression type suits the data (text must be lossless).

Binary and hexadecimal worked conversion

To convert the denary number 156 to binary, subtract the place values from the largest downwards: 156 = 128 + 16 + 8 + 4, so the binary value is 10011100. Each binary digit is a bit, and the place values double from right to left: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128.

Hexadecimal groups four bits at a time, so one hexadecimal digit represents a value from 0 to 15. Split 10011100 into 1001 and 1100 to get 9 and 12, which is 9C in hexadecimal. Hexadecimal is used to write memory addresses and colour codes because it is shorter than binary and converts to it directly.

Exam tip: show the place-value working, not just the answer. Examiners award method marks for the subtraction or the grouping.

Worked example: sound file size

A mono recording lasts 60 seconds, is sampled at 8000 samples per second and uses 16 bits per sample. The file size in bits is 8000 multiplied by 16 multiplied by 60, which is 7,680,000 bits. Dividing by 8 gives 960,000 bytes, or about 960 kB. Doubling the sample rate or recording in stereo doubles the file size, so check each factor separately.

Worked example: image file size

An image is 800 pixels wide and 600 pixels high, with 24 bits of colour per pixel. The total is 800 multiplied by 600 multiplied by 24, which is 11,520,000 bits, or 1,440,000 bytes. Reducing the colour depth to 8 bits cuts the file to one third of that size, but the image can then show fewer distinct colours.

Lossy and lossless compression compared

  • Lossless compression finds repeated patterns and can rebuild the original exactly, so it suits text and program files.
  • Lossy compression discards detail the eye or ear is least likely to notice, so it produces much smaller files for photographs and music.

title: Continuous Random Variables — Study Notes
content:
Continuous Random Variables

Edexcel International A Level Mathematics — Statistics 2 (WST02), sat at A2.

Probability Density Functions

A continuous variable X is described by a density f(x) with f(x) ≥ 0 and ∫f(x)dx = 1 over all x. Probabilities are areas:

  • P(a ≤ X ≤ b) = ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx

Single points have zero probability, so strict or loose inequalities make no difference: P(X < 2) = P(X ≤ 2).

Finding Unknown Constants

Piecewise densities carry an unknown k: impose that the total area is 1 (and continuity at joins where required). One equation, one unknown.

Example: f(x) = kx on 0 ≤ x ≤ 2. Total area: k·(2²/2) = 2k = 1, so k = ½.

Expectation and Variance

  • E(X) = ∫x·f(x) dx
  • E(X²) = ∫x²·f(x) dx
  • Var(X) = E(X²) − (E(X))²

The mean is the balancing point of the area under the density. For symmetric densities the mean sits at the symmetry point — worth spotting before integrating.

The Median and Mode

The median m solves ∫₋∞ᵐ f(x) dx = 0.5 (left half of the area). The mode is the x maximising f(x). For uniform densities the median is the midpoint.

Uniform Distribution

If f(x) = 1/(b − a) on [a, b], every point is equally likely. Then E(X) = (a + b)/2 and Var(X) = (b − a)²/12 — memorise both; they are quick exam marks.

Exam tips: always verify ∫f = 1 before computing anything else. Sketch the density — area intuitions catch algebra slips. Median questions are integration-to-0.5 questions; set them up before calculating.

Exam method: density functions

A probability density function f must satisfy f(x) ≥ 0 for all x and the total area under it must equal 1, so the integral of f over its whole domain is 1. Use this to find an unknown constant before asking for any probability.

For a continuous variable, P(a ≤ X ≤ b) is the integral of f(x) from a to b. The endpoints carry no probability, so strict and non-strict inequalities give the same answer. Outside the given domain f(x) = 0.

The cumulative distribution function F(x) = P(X ≤ x) is the integral of f from the lower end of the domain up to x. The median m satisfies F(m) = 0.5, and the mode is where f is largest.

Expected value E(X) is the integral of x f(x) over the domain, and the variance is E(X²) minus the square of E(X). Write each integral with its limits before evaluating.

Exam cue: Sketch the density over its domain first. A linear density is a triangle or trapezium, and the area of the shape gives the total probability quickly.

Worked example: the cumulative distribution function

Let X have probability density function f(x) = 2x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1, and zero elsewhere. The cumulative distribution function is F(x) = P(X ≤ x) = ∫ from 0 to x of 2t dt = x² for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1. Then P(0.2 < X < 0.5) = F(0.5) − F(0.2) = 0.25 − 0.04 = 0.21. A probability for a continuous variable is an area under the curve, so the endpoints of an interval do not change its value.

Exam method: state the range and check the total area

Always state the range of x for which the formula applies, and write f(x) = 0 outside it. Before using the density, check that the integral over the full range equals 1; if it does not, the unknown constant has been found incorrectly. Make sure the function is non-negative across the whole range, because a negative value means the function cannot be a density.

title: Poisson Distribution — Study Notes
content:
The Poisson Distribution

The Model

X ~ Po(λ) counts events in a fixed interval of time or space when events occur independently, at a constant average rate λ, and never twice at the same instant. Classic settings: calls per hour at a helpdesk, typos per page, cars per minute at a quiet junction.

The Formula

P(X = r) = e^(−λ) λʳ / r! for r = 0, 1, 2, ...

Example: X ~ Po(2). P(X = 0) = e⁻² ≈ 0.1353. P(X = 1) = 2e⁻² ≈ 0.2707.

Mean and Variance

The defining signature of the Poisson:

  • E(X) = λ and Var(X) = λ — the mean and variance are equal.

If a question gives a mean m, then λ = m; the variance is also m.

Scaling the Interval

If X ~ Po(λ) per hour, then 3 hours gives Y ~ Po(3λ). Rates must be adjusted to the same interval before computing anything. Halving an interval halves λ.

Adding Poissons

If X ~ Po(λ₁) and Y ~ Po(λ₂) are independent, then X + Y ~ Po(λ₁ + λ₂). Two independent queues merging into one server produce a Poisson with summed rate.

Exam tips: check independence and constant rate before modelling — if events cluster (rush hours), Poisson fails. Convert the interval first: a rate of 8 per 20 minutes becomes 24 per hour. In "at least" questions use the complement exactly as with the binomial.

Exam method: Poisson probabilities

If X ~ Po(λ), then P(X = r) = e^(−λ) λʳ / r! for r = 0, 1, 2, … The mean and the variance are both equal to λ, so the parameter is found directly from either quantity given in the question.

Use the calculator's Poisson function or the formula with the exact value of e^(−λ). When a question asks for P(X ≤ r) or P(X ≥ r), add the separate probabilities, or subtract the complement from 1.

The rate must match the interval. If events occur at 4 per hour and the question asks about a 30-minute period, the new mean is 2. Always rescale λ to the period in the question.

A Poisson model is appropriate for counts of events that occur randomly and independently at a constant average rate.

Exam cue: Check the rescaling of λ first; it is the most common error in Poisson questions, and it costs the whole question.

title: Poisson Distribution — Study Notes
content:
The Poisson Distribution

Edexcel International A Level Mathematics — Statistics 2 (WST02), sat at A2.

The Model

Mean and Variance

The defining signature of the Poisson:

  • E(X) = λ and Var(X) = λ — the mean and variance are equal.
