If you can say that the topic has both a small-scale and a large-scale side, and that the large-scale side depends on the same kinds of reasoning, you have the topic as a connected whole rather than as three unrelated lists. That is the view that the higher marks are after, because the higher marks are about the connections, not just the parts.

Appendix H — Forensic biology and the reasoning behind the evidence, not just the evidence types

Forensic biology is the part of the topic where candidates most often lose marks by listing evidence types without saying why they matter or what their limits are. The precise idea is that forensic biology uses biological evidence, especially DNA, to help identify individuals and to link evidence to people, objects or scenes, and that the evidence is interpreted rather than taken as a simple yes-no answer on its own. A good answer says that, and also says that the value of the evidence depends on how it was collected, whether it was contaminated, and whether the interpretation matches the question. If you can say that, you have the forensic biology idea in a form that scores marks. If you only say “DNA can identify people,” you have the label but not the reasoning, and the mark is in the reasoning about interpretation and limits.

DNA profiling is the technique in this topic where the reasoning about the method matters as much as the result. DNA profiling compares patterns of variation in DNA from different samples, and a match can identify a person or link a sample to a scene, while a mismatch can exclude a person. The result depends on the quality of the sample and the comparison, and on the context, so it is not a simple absolute proof in every sense without context. A good answer says that DNA profiling compares the patterns of variation in DNA, that the differences between individuals are what make it possible, and that the result is interpreted in context. It does not say that DNA profiling is proof in a magic sense, because the context and the sample quality matter. If you can say that, you have the DNA profiling idea in a form that scores marks. If you only say “DNA fingerprinting identifies someone,” you have the label but not the reasoning, and the mark is in the reasoning about the pattern and the interpretation.

The care with biological evidence is the other idea in this topic that is worth saying explicitly, because it is the idea that connects forensics to the same reasoning as microbiology culturing. Contamination, chain of custody and context are all things that affect whether the evidence is meaningful, and a candidate who cannot say that is usually left with only the label of “biological evidence” and no reasoning about what makes it reliable or not. A good answer says that biological evidence has to be collected and preserved properly, that contamination must be avoided, that the chain of custody matters, and that the interpretation depends on the context. If you can say that, you have the forensic care idea in a form that scores marks. If you only say “blood is evidence,” you have the label but not the reasoning, and the reasoning is what the mark is after when the question asks about handling or interpretation.

Appendix I — Typical mistakes, revisited with the reasoning behind them

The mistakes in this topic are worth revisiting with the reasoning behind them, because that is the way to stop making them under time pressure. The reason candidates say all bacteria are pathogens is that they are thinking of disease, not of the whole group. The fix is to remember that bacteria include harmless and useful ones as well. The reason candidates say viruses are cells is that they are thinking of “small living thing” rather than of the cell structure. The fix is to remember that viruses are particles with genetic material and a coat and no independent metabolism. The reason candidates say aseptic technique is just about tidiness is that they are thinking of neatness rather than of controlling the movement of microbes. The fix is to remember that aseptic technique is about purity and containment at the same time. The reason candidates say microbial growth is a steady increase is that they are thinking of “more and more” rather of the limits that end exponential growth. The fix is to remember the phases and the reasons for the shape.

The reason candidates say the first line of defence is always enough is that they are thinking of “the body has defences” rather of the fact that pathogens can still get through. The fix is to remember that the first line is non-specific and often insufficient, which is why the specific response exists. The reason candidates say antibodies kill pathogens in one uniform way is that they are thinking of “antibodies are the good guys” rather of the different roles antibodies play. The fix is to remember neutralisation, marking and aiding removal as different roles. The reason candidates blur B cells and T cells is that they are thinking of “lymphocytes” as one thing rather than of the different roles the two kinds play. The fix is to remember antibody production for B cells and cell-mediated roles for T cells, with memory as the shared outcome. The reason candidates say herd immunity means every individual is immune is that they are thinking of “everyone is protected” rather of the transmission logic. The fix is to remember coverage and reduced spread.

The reason candidates say DNA profiling is absolute proof without context is that they are thinking of “DNA is unique” rather of the interpretation of the sample. The fix is to remember sample quality, contamination, chain of custody and the context of the comparison. The reason candidates say the mere presence of blood is proof of guilt or innocence is that they are thinking of “blood is incriminating” rather of the meaning of the evidence. The fix is to remember that presence is not the same as a meaningful match, and that the evidence has to be interpreted. If you can remember the reasoning behind each mistake, you are less likely to make it when you are writing fast, because the reasoning gives you something to reach for instead of the vague wrong idea. That is the use of revisiting the mistakes with the reasoning behind them, and it is the use that matters on the day.

Appendix J — How the three strands of the topic connect when the question crosses them

The three strands of the topic, microbes, immunity and forensics, are connected in a way that the cross-strand questions test, and the connection is the reasoning you have to be able to move between. Microbiology gives you the pathogens and the way they grow and spread, and the practical care that matters with living cultures. Immunity gives you the defence system that fights them, from barriers and phagocytosis through antibodies and memory cells. Forensics gives you the use of biological evidence, especially DNA, to identify and link, with the care and interpretation that make the evidence meaningful. If you can move between these strands, you can answer the cross-strand questions, which are often the ones where the marks are concentrated because they test understanding rather than labels.

The cleanest cross-strand connection is the reasoning about contamination, because it appears in microbiology culturing and in forensic evidence for different but related reasons. In microbiology, contamination ruins the purity of the culture and can introduce the wrong organism. In forensics, contamination can make the evidence unreliable or misleading. In both cases, the reasoning is that the result is only as good as the way it was obtained and handled, and that the meaning depends on the context. If you can say that, you can answer the cross-strand question that asks you to compare or relate the care needed in the two cases, because you have the reasoning rather than a separate label for each.

Another cross-strand connection is the reasoning about recognition, because the same idea of recognition appears in antigens and antibodies and in DNA profiling, though in different forms. In immunity, the body recognises antigens and produces specific antibodies. In DNA profiling, the method compares patterns of variation in DNA that distinguish individuals. In both cases, the idea is that the system can tell one thing from another by recognising specific features, and that the result is meaningful only if the recognition is reliable and the comparison is relevant. If you can say that, you can answer the cross-strand question that asks you to relate the two kinds of recognition, because you have the reasoning rather than a set of unrelated labels.

The final cross-strand connection is the reasoning about memory and specificity in immunity and the reasoning about identification and variation in forensics. Both strands are about telling things apart and responding to them in a way that is specific and useful: the immune system tells one antigen from another and remembers it; the forensic method tells one individual’s DNA pattern from another’s and uses that to identify or exclude. If you can say that, you have the cross-strand view that makes the topic a connected whole, and that is the view that the higher-mark questions are after. If you only see the three strands as separate, you are likely to lose the marks on the questions that span them. The note is long enough to cover the strands separately and together, and that is the use of the length: to make the connections visible as well as the parts.

title: Sequences and Functions
content:
Algebra — Sequences and Functions

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): nth term (linear & quadratic), special sequences, function notation, composites, inverses.

1. Linear sequences

nth term = a + (n − 1)d. 5, 8, 11, … → 3n + 2. Check n = 1, 2, 3.

2. Quadratic sequences

Second difference = 2a → an² + bn + c. 3, 8, 15, 24 … has second difference 2 → n² + bn + c; subtract n² → 2, 4, 6, 8 → 2n; so nth term = n² + 2n.

3. Special sequences

Even/odd, triangular (½n(n+1)), squares, cubes, Fibonacci-type (each term = sum of previous two), geometric (×r).

4. Function notation

f(x) = 2x − 5: f(3) = 1. Solve f(x) = 11 → x = 8.

5. Composite functions

fg(x) = f(g(x)) — g first. f(x) = 2x − 5, g(x) = x²: gf(2) = g(1) = 1; fg(3) = f(9) = 13.

6. Inverse functions

Swap x and y, rearrange. f(x) = 2x − 5 ⇒ f⁻¹(x) = (x + 5)/2. Domain of inverse = range of original. Verify: f⁻¹(f(x)) = x.

Exam tips: write the bracket order explicitly in composites; show the "swap and rearrange" line for inverses — answer-only scores little.

title: Forces and Equilibrium — Study Notes
content:
Forces and equilibrium

Edexcel International A Level Physics — Unit 1 (WPH11), sat at AS.

Moment of a force

  • The moment of a force about a point is the force multiplied by the perpendicular distance from the point to the line of action of the force: moment = F × d⊥. Unit: N m.
  • Only the perpendicular component of the force produces a turning effect. A force that passes through the pivot has zero moment.

Principle of moments

For a body in equilibrium the sum of the clockwise moments about any point equals the sum of the anticlockwise moments about that point.

Couples

A couple is two equal and opposite parallel forces whose lines of action do not coincide. It produces a turning effect without a resultant force. The moment of a couple is F × d, where d is the perpendicular separation, and it is the same about every point.

Conditions for equilibrium

  • The resultant force in every direction is zero.
  • The resultant moment about any point is zero.

For three coplanar, non-parallel forces in equilibrium, the lines of action must meet at a single point.

Centre of gravity

The centre of gravity is the point through which the weight of a body appears to act. For a uniform symmetrical body it lies at the geometric centre.

Worked example: a uniform beam of weight 100 N rests horizontally on two supports at its ends. Each support carries half the weight, 50 N, because the beam is symmetrical and in equilibrium.

Exam tips: state the pivot you take moments about. Draw the perpendicular distance, not the slant distance. Show that the resultant force is zero in each direction before you use the principle of moments.

Conditions for equilibrium

A body is in equilibrium when the resultant force on it is zero and the resultant moment about any point is zero. For a body in equilibrium under three coplanar forces, the lines of action meet at a single point. The moment of a force about a pivot is Fd, where d is the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action. Taking moments about the pivot removes the unknown reaction force, which makes this a useful method in exam questions.

Exam tip: show the resolution of forces into horizontal and vertical components before you apply the equilibrium equations.

Worked example: a uniform beam on two supports

A uniform beam of length 4.0 m and weight 120 N rests on two supports, one at each end. Its centre of gravity is at its midpoint, 2.0 m from either support. Taking moments about the left support, the right-hand reaction R2 satisfies R2 × 4.0 = 120 × 2.0, so R2 = 60 N. Vertical equilibrium then gives R1 = 120 − 60 = 60 N. Checking that the two reactions add up to the weight is a quick way to catch an arithmetic or sign error.

Forces and moments in exam questions

Resolve forces into horizontal and vertical components before applying the conditions. For a body in equilibrium, the sum of forces in each direction is zero and the sum of moments about any point is zero. Choosing the pivot at the position of an unknown force removes that force from the moment equation, which often leaves a single equation to solve. A couple (two equal and opposite parallel forces) produces the same moment about every point, so it can be balanced only by another couple, never by a single force.

title: Exam technique: Sets
content:
### What earns the marks
For Venn problems, the union formula n(A union B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A intersect B) quoted earns the method mark; subtracting the intersection corrects the double count explicitly. For neither, the subtraction from the universal set shown earns the final mark. For notation, the complement symbol with the correct parent set earns precision marks.
### Traps
Error: adding all three Venn counts including the intersection. Correction: the overlap was counted twice, subtract once. Error: element confused with subset (2 vs {2}). Correction: only a set can be a subset. Error: empty set equated with {0}. Correction: {0} has one element; the empty set has none. Error: modal-style single numbers for grouped answers. Correction: classes are intervals.

title: Oscillations and Waves II — Study Notes
content:
Oscillations and Waves II

Simple harmonic motion (17.1)

A body oscillates with simple harmonic motion when its acceleration is proportional to its displacement x and directed towards the equilibrium position: a = −ω²x. The angular frequency is ω = 2πf, and the displacement is x = x₀ sin ωt, where x₀ is the amplitude.

The velocity is v = ±ω√(x₀² − x²), and the maximum acceleration is a₀ = ω²x₀. Velocity is zero at the extremes and maximum at equilibrium. Acceleration is maximum at the extremes and zero at equilibrium.

Example: amplitude 0.030 m and frequency 2.0 Hz give a₀ = (2π × 2.0)² × 0.030 ≈ 4.7 m s⁻².

Energy in SHM (17.2)

Kinetic energy is greatest at the equilibrium position, where speed is greatest. Potential energy is greatest at the extremes. The total energy is constant: E = ½mω²x₀², and it is shared between kinetic and potential energy as the body oscillates.

Example: a 0.20 kg mass with ω = 10 rad s⁻¹ and x₀ = 0.050 m has E = ½ × 0.20 × 10² × 0.050² = 0.025 J.

Damping, forced oscillations and resonance (17.3)

Damping removes energy from an oscillator. Light damping gives decaying oscillations. Critical damping returns the system to equilibrium in the shortest time without oscillating. Heavy damping is also non-oscillatory but slower.

A forced oscillator is driven by a periodic force. When the driving frequency equals the natural frequency, the amplitude is at its maximum, which is resonance. Greater damping lowers the peak and broadens the resonance curve.

Exam tips: state which quantity is maximum or zero at each point of the cycle. For resonance, always name the driving frequency relative to the natural frequency.

Waves: the superposition ideas

Progressive vs Stationary

Progressive waves transfer energy; stationary waves store it in loops. Stationary patterns arise from two identical waves travelling in opposite directions (reflections on strings, air columns).

PropertyProgressiveStationary
Amplitudesame for all pointsvaries: nodes zero, antinodes max
Phasevaries along wavesame within a loop, π flip across nodes
Energytransferredtrapped

Harmonics

A string fixed at both ends: f₁ = v/2L, then 2f₁, 3f₁… Closed pipes resonate at odd multiples; open pipes at all multiples.

Superposition Applications

  • Young's double slit: x = λD/a — evidence light is a wave
  • Diffraction grating: d sin θ = nλ — resolution of spectra
  • Noise-cancelling headphones: destructive interference of antiphase sound

Polarization Applications

Polaroid sunglasses cut glare from horizontal surfaces; stress analysis in plastics; LCD screens control light with twisted polarizers. Malus' law I = I₀cos²θ.

Exam tips: 'explain' marks want the physics: path difference, phase, node/antinode conditions — not just formula substitution.

title: Waves & Sound — Study Notes
content:
Waves & Sound

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): general wave properties; reflection/refraction/diffraction; sound.

1. Wave basics

v = fλ. Transverse (oscillation ⊥ travel — light, water, S-waves) vs longitudinal (parallel — sound, P-waves). Amplitude, wavelength, frequency f = 1/T; wavefront diagrams.

2. Ripple tank behaviours

  • Reflection: angle in = angle out; speed/frequency unchanged, direction changes.
  • Refraction: speed change at boundary bends wavefronts (shallow water slows ripples).
  • Diffraction: spreading through gaps ≈ λ wide; around edges.

3. Electromagnetic spectrum (order)

Radio → micro → IR → visible (red 700 nm – violet 400 nm) → UV → X → gamma. All travel at 3 × 10⁸ m/s in vacuum; transverse; uses and dangers (IR heating; UV skin; X/gamma ionising).

4. Sound

  • Longitudinal; needs a medium (bell in vacuum demo). Speed ~340 m/s air, faster in liquids/solids.
  • Range 20 Hz–20 kHz; ultrasound > 20 kHz (sonar, prenatal scans, cleaning).
  • Pitch ↔ frequency; loudness ↔ amplitude.

5. Echo problems

Distance = (v × t)/2 (there and back).

Example: echo after 0.6 s, v = 340 → cliff 102 m away.

Exam tips: in diagrams always label wavelength as crest-to-crest; for refraction, state "changes speed" first, then direction; quote EM uses with the hazard.

Wave equation and sound

The wave equation is v = fλ, where v is the wave speed, f the frequency and λ the wavelength. Sound is a longitudinal wave that needs a medium, so it cannot travel through a vacuum. All electromagnetic waves travel at the speed of light in a vacuum, about 3 × 10⁸ m/s. In reflection the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. For an echo, the sound travels to the reflecting surface and back, so the distance to the surface is half the total distance travelled.

Worked example: wave equation

A sound wave has frequency 500 Hz and travels at 340 m s⁻¹ in air. Using v = fλ, the wavelength is λ = 340/500 = 0.68 m. Doubling the frequency to 1000 Hz halves the wavelength to 0.34 m. The speed is fixed by the medium, not by the frequency, so the product fλ stays constant.

Echo calculations

A reflected sound returns after a time t. The distance to the reflecting surface is d = vt/2, because the sound travels to the surface and back. Forgetting the factor of one half doubles the answer, which is the most common error in echo questions.

Reflection, refraction and diffraction

  • Reflection: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, both measured from the normal, not from the surface.
  • Refraction: a wave changes speed and direction at a boundary between media, but its frequency stays the same.
  • Diffraction: spreading is greatest when the gap or obstacle is comparable to the wavelength. Low-pitched sound, with its longer wavelength, bends around a doorway more than high-pitched speech does.

These are the wave properties examined in the wave topic of the Cambridge IGCSE 0625 and AS 9702 syllabi. Name each property precisely and apply it to a labelled diagram.

title: Pressure & Density — Study Notes
content:
Pressure & Density

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): pressure & pressure differences in fluids, density review (Extended pressure-depth).

1. Pressure basics

p = F/A (Pa = N/m²). Increase F or decrease A to raise pressure; explain applications (snowshoes, knives, hydraulic press).

2. Liquids

  • Pressure increases with depth: p = ρgh (Extended).
  • Same level, same liquid ⇒ same pressure (hydrostatic paradox).
  • Hydraulic systems transmit pressure — force multiplier: F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂.

3. Atmospheric pressure

~10⁵ Pa at sea level; demonstrated by collapsing can, mercury barometer 760 mmHg; decreases with altitude.

4. Density revisited

ρ = m/V; floating condition; upthrust = weight of displaced fluid (qualitative).

5. Gas pressure (particle model)

Particles collide with walls → force per area. Volume ↓ at same T ⇒ pressure ↑ (more frequent collisions). Temperature ↑ ⇒ faster particles ⇒ more frequent, harder impacts.

title: A Level Physics: Circular Motion and SHM
content:
A Level Physics: Circular Motion and SHM

Circular motion is motion at constant speed but changing velocity — because velocity is a vector, turning is accelerating. This note builds the kinematics of uniform circular motion from zero: angular displacement and angular velocity, the relation v = ωr, centripetal acceleration and the force that causes it, and then the beautiful connection to simple harmonic motion — SHM is literally the shadow of circular motion. Every formula is derived from the geometry, and the standard calculation types (car cornering, vertical circles, conical pendulums, satellite orbits) are worked in full.

Kinematics of uniform circular motion

An object moving in a circle at constant speed has a continuously changing direction, so its velocity changes continuously — it is accelerating. Two measures describe the motion:

angular displacement: θ (radians); one revolution = 2 π rad
angular velocity: ω = θ/t = 2 π/T = 2 π f   (rad s⁻¹)
linear speed: v = ω r        (m s⁻¹)

period T = 2 π/ω; frequency f = 1/T

The analogy: a point on a record's edge and a point near its centre complete a revolution in the same time, but the edge point travels further — hence v = ωr. Angular velocity is shared; linear speed depends on radius.

Worked example. A wheel of radius 0.30 m spins at 20 revolutions per minute. Find ω and the speed of a point on its rim.

f = 20/60 = 0.333 Hz  →  ω = 2 π f = 2.09 rad s⁻¹
v = ω r = 2.09 × 0.30 = 0.63 m s⁻¹

Centripetal acceleration

The acceleration of circular motion points toward the centre — it changes the direction of velocity, not its magnitude. From the geometry of a small angular displacement, the change in velocity points inward with magnitude v²/r:

a = v²/r = ω² r        (directed toward the centre)

centripetal force: F = m a = m v²/r = m ω² r

Derivation sketch worth reproducing in an exam: as the object turns through a small angle θ, the velocity triangle has a small change Δv perpendicular to v, and Δv/v = Δs/r (similar triangles), so Δv/Δt = (v/r)(Δs/Δt) = v²/r. The direction of Δv is toward the centre — hence centripetal.

Worked example. A 1200 kg car rounds a bend of radius 50 m at 15 m s⁻¹. Find the centripetal force.

F = m v²/r = 1200 × 225/50 = 1200 × 4.5 = 5400 N
The force is provided by friction between tyres and road.

Where the centripetal force comes from

Centripetal force is not a new kind of force — it is the name for whatever real force points toward the centre:

SituationForce providing the centripetal effect
Car on a flat bendstatic friction between tyres and road
Car on a banked trackcomponent of the normal reaction
Satellite in orbitgravitational attraction
Ball on a stringtension in the string
Electron in a magnetic fieldmagnetic force (qvB)
Conical pendulumhorizontal component of tension

The exam favourite is the vertical circle: at the top of a loop, gravity and any normal force both point down and together provide mv²/r; the minimum speed to stay in contact is when the normal force falls to zero, so mg = mv²/r and v_min = √(gr).

Worked example (vertical circle). A ball on a string of length 0.80 m is swung in a vertical circle. Find the minimum speed at the top for the string to stay taut.

at the top: mg + T = mv²/r; minimum when T = 0
v_min = √(g r) = √(9.81 × 0.80) = √(7.85)
      = 2.8 m s⁻¹

Worked example (banked track). A track is banked at angle θ with no friction. Show that the design speed satisfies tan θ = v²/(rg).

vertical: N cos(θ) = mg
horizontal (centripetal): N sin(θ) = mv²/r
divide: tan(θ) = v²/(r g)

Circular motion and SHM: the projection connection

Watch a point moving uniformly around a circle from the side: its shadow on a diameter moves back and forth with simple harmonic motion. This is not an analogy — it is an identity, and it lets you derive every SHM equation from circular motion:

if a particle moves on a circle of radius A with angular
velocity ω, its projection on a diameter has
displacement x = A cos(ω t)  (or A sin, depending on start)
velocity v = -A ω sin(ω t)
acceleration a = -ω² A cos(ω t) = -ω² x

maximum speed at the centre: v_max = A ω
maximum acceleration at the extremes: a_max = A ω²

So the SHM angular frequency ω is exactly the angular velocity of the reference circle, and the period T = 2π/ω. The geometry also explains the phase relationships: velocity leads displacement by a quarter turn (90°), acceleration is anti-phase with displacement (180°).

Worked example. A point moves on a circle of radius 0.050 m at 3.0 rad s⁻¹. Find the amplitude, period and maximum speed of its projection.

amplitude A = 0.050 m
T = 2 π/ω = 6.28/3.0 = 2.1 s
v_max = A ω = 0.050 × 3.0 = 0.15 m s⁻¹

Applications: centrifuges and looping tracks

Circular motion is engineered into everyday machines. A centrifuge spins samples so that the required centripetal force — provided by the container walls — vastly exceeds gravity; denser components need a larger force at the same radius, so they settle outward and separate. The same logic sizes a washing machine's spin cycle (water leaves through the drum holes when the required force exceeds what surface tension can supply) and a car's brake discs (ventilation handles the frictional heat).

A looping track is the vertical-circle problem made physical: at the top of the loop the riders' weight and the track's normal reaction both point inward, providing mv²/r; the design speed is set just above v = √(gr) so the normal reaction never falls to zero and contact is maintained. Rollercoaster designers use the excess above that minimum to create the sensation of lightness without losing the car.

Worked examples: the standard exam types

Worked example 1 (conical pendulum). A 0.20 kg mass on a 1.0 m string moves in a horizontal circle, the string at 30° to the vertical. Find the tension and the period.

vertical: T cos(30) = mg  →  T = 0.20 × 9.81/0.866 = 2.27 N
radius: r = L sin(30) = 0.50 m
horizontal: T sin(30) = m v²/r
2.27 × 0.5 = 0.20 x v²/0.50  →  v² = 2.84  →  v = 1.69 m s⁻¹
T_period = 2 π r/v = 6.28 × 0.50/1.69 = 1.86 s

Worked example 2 (satellite). Find the orbital speed of a satellite at radius 7.0 × 10⁶ m around Earth (M = 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg).

GMm/r² = mv²/r  →  v = √(GM/r)
v = √(6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ x 5.97 × 10²⁴/7.0 × 10⁶)
  = √(5.69 × 10⁷) = 7.54 × 10³ m s⁻¹

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Angular velocity) A cyclist's wheel of radius 0.35 m turns at 2.0 revolutions per second. Find the speed of the rim. Answer: ω = 2π × 2.0 = 12.6 rad s⁻¹; v = ωr = 12.6 × 0.35 = 4.4 m s⁻¹.
  2. (Acceleration) State the direction of centripetal acceleration and explain why speed stays constant. Answer: It points toward the centre, perpendicular to the velocity; because the acceleration has no component along the velocity, it changes direction only, not speed.
  3. (Force) A 0.15 kg ball on a 0.60 m string moves at 4.0 m s⁻¹ in a horizontal circle. Find the tension. Answer: T = mv²/r = 0.15 × 16/0.60 = 4.0 N.
  4. (Vertical circle) Explain why a bucket of water can be swung overhead without spilling. Answer: At the top, the water's weight provides the centripetal force; if v ≥ √(gr) the water stays in contact with the bucket base, so it does not fall out.
  5. (Banking) A bend of radius 80 m is banked for 20 m s⁻¹. Find the angle. Answer: tan θ = v²/(rg) = 400/(80 × 9.81) = 0.510; θ = 27°.
  6. (SHM link) Explain how simple harmonic motion can be modelled by the projection of circular motion. Answer: A point moving uniformly on a circle of radius A projects onto a diameter as x = A cos ωt; differentiating gives v and a with a = −ω²x, the defining SHM condition.
  7. (Satellite) Show that the period of a satellite is proportional to r^(3/2). Answer: v = √(GM/r) and T = 2πr/v, so T = 2πr/√(GM/r) = 2π√(r³/GM), hence T ∝ r^(3/2).
  8. (Misconception) A student says a car turning at constant speed has no acceleration. Correct the statement. Answer: Velocity is a vector; its direction changes continuously in a turn, so the car accelerates centripetally toward the centre of the turn even though the speedometer reading is constant.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • The centrifugal fiction: there is no outward force in the inertial frame; the "centrifugal force" felt in a turning car is the inertia of your body, not a force on the car. Never put it on a free-body diagram.
  • v²/r with the wrong r: radius from the centre of the circular path — for a conical pendulum r = L sin θ, not the string length.
  • ω versus v: v = ωr; forgetting the radius converts angular to linear incorrectly. And ω in rad s⁻¹ means revolutions per second × 2π.
  • Units of angle: radians, not degrees, in ω = 2π/T and in the projection equations.
  • Centripetal force is not extra: it is the resultant of the real forces (tension, friction, weight component) — do not add it alongside them.
  • Vertical circles: tension and weight are collinear at top and bottom but not at the sides; resolve properly rather than assuming T = mv²/r everywhere.
  • Period direction: T = 2πr/v uses the circumference; mixing in angular velocity without converting gives factor-of-2π errors.
  • SHM phase: the projection can be sine or cosine depending on the starting point; state your choice and stay consistent.
  • Precision: 2 or 3 s.f. with units (rad s⁻¹, m s⁻¹, N, s); keep π symbolic until the end to avoid rounding drift.

Equations and symbols

Every relation this topic can be examined on, in the form the mark scheme expects, with a key naming each symbol and its unit. The derivations in the sections above end here: if you can write these from memory and say what each symbol means, the algebra in the exam is bookkeeping.

12.1 Kinematics of uniform circular motion

θ = s / r
Key: θ = angular displacement (rad); s = arc length travelled along the circle (m); r = radius of the circle (m). The radian is defined by this ratio, so an angle in radians is a pure number — one complete revolution is 2π rad = 360°.

ω = Δθ / Δt = 2π / T = 2π f
Key: ω = angular velocity (rad s⁻¹); Δθ = angular displacement (rad); Δt = time taken (s); T = period, the time for one revolution (s); f = frequency of revolution (Hz). Uniform circular motion means ω is constant while the direction of the velocity changes continuously.

v = ω r
Key: v = linear speed along the tangent (m s⁻¹); ω = angular velocity (rad s⁻¹); r = radius (m). The same ω for two points on a rotating body gives them speeds in the ratio of their radii — the rim of a wheel moves faster than a point near its hub.

f = 1 / T
Key: f = frequency (Hz); T = period (s). A wheel turning 20 times a minute has f = 20/60 = 0.33 Hz and T = 3.0 s.

a = v² / r = ω² r = ω v
Key: a = centripetal acceleration (m s⁻²); v = speed (m s⁻¹); r = radius (m); ω = angular velocity (rad s⁻¹). Directed towards the centre at every instant; the speed is constant but the velocity is not, because its direction changes, and that change is the acceleration.

F = m a = m v² / r = m ω² r
Key: F = resultant centripetal force (N); m = mass of the moving object (kg); a = centripetal acceleration (m s⁻²); v = speed (m s⁻¹); r = radius (m); ω = angular velocity (rad s⁻¹). Not a new kind of force — it is the name for whatever real force points to the centre: tension, gravity, friction or the normal contact force.

Turning, banking and vertical circles

tan θ = v² / (r g)
Key: θ = angle of banking of the road, or the angle the string makes with the vertical for a conical pendulum (°); v = speed of the vehicle or bob (m s⁻¹); r = radius of the circular path (m); g = 9.81 m s⁻². Derived by dividing the horizontal equation N sin θ = m v²/r by the vertical N cos θ = m g, so the normal force cancels.

at the top of a vertical circle: T + m g = m v² / r
Key: T = tension in the string, or the normal contact force from the track (N); m = mass (kg); g = 9.81 m s⁻²; v = speed at the top (m s⁻¹); r = radius (m). Both the weight and the tension point towards the centre, so they add.

v_min = √(g r)
Key: v_min = minimum speed at the top for the object to stay on its path (m s⁻¹); g = 9.81 m s⁻²; r = radius (m). Found by setting T = 0 at the top: below this speed gravity alone exceeds the required centripetal force and the object leaves the circle.

at the bottom of a vertical circle: T − m g = m v² / r
Key: T = tension (N); m = mass (kg); g = 9.81 m s⁻²; v = speed at the bottom (m s⁻¹); r = radius (m). Here the tension must support the weight as well as provide the centripetal force, so the string is most likely to break at the bottom.

energy between top and bottom: ½ m v_bottom² = ½ m v_top² + m g (2 r)
Key: v_bottom, v_top = speeds at the lowest and highest points (m s⁻¹); m = mass (kg); g = 9.81 m s⁻²; r = radius (m); 2r = the vertical drop. The bridge between the two parts of a looping-track question.

12.2 Linking circular motion to SHM

a = − ω² x
Key: a = acceleration (m s⁻²); ω = angular frequency of the oscillation (rad s⁻¹); x = displacement from the equilibrium position (m). The defining condition of simple harmonic motion: acceleration is proportional to displacement and always directed back towards the centre.

x = A cos(ω t)
Key: x = displacement at time t (m); A = amplitude, the maximum displacement (m); ω = angular frequency (rad s⁻¹); t = time from the start of the motion (s). A sine form with the matching initial condition is equally valid — the physics is the same, only the phase differs.

v = ± ω √(A² − x²)
Key: v = velocity at displacement x (m s⁻¹); ω = angular frequency (rad s⁻¹); A = amplitude (m); x = displacement (m). Fastest at the centre where x = 0, momentarily zero at the extremes where x = ±A.

v_max = ω A, a_max = ω² A
Key: v_max = maximum speed, at the equilibrium position (m s⁻¹); a_max = maximum acceleration, at the extremes (m s⁻²); ω = angular frequency (rad s⁻¹); A = amplitude (m). The two numbers most questions actually ask for.

T = 2 π / ω
Key: T = period of the oscillation (s); ω = angular frequency (rad s⁻¹). The link between the SHM equations and the timing of the motion.

T = 2 π √(m / k)
Key: T = period (s); m = mass on the spring (kg); k = spring constant, force per unit extension (N m⁻¹). Mass–spring oscillator: a stiffer spring or a lighter mass oscillates faster, and amplitude does not affect the period.

T = 2 π √(l / g)
Key: T = period (s); l = length of the simple pendulum (m); g = 9.81 m s⁻². Valid only for small oscillations (a few degrees), where sin θ ≈ θ; the period is independent of the mass of the bob, which is what makes a pendulum a clock.

E_total = ½ m ω² A²
Key: E_total = total energy of the oscillator (J); m = mass (kg); ω = angular frequency (rad s⁻¹); A = amplitude (m). Constant in undamped SHM, exchanged continuously between kinetic and potential forms.

KE = ½ m ω² (A² − x²), PE = ½ m ω² x²
Key: KE = kinetic energy (J); PE = potential energy (J); m = mass (kg); ω = angular frequency (rad s⁻¹); A = amplitude (m); x = displacement (m). The two add to E_total at every point, which is the quickest check on either.

phase: v leads x by π/2, and a is in antiphase with x (π)
Key: x = displacement, v = velocity, a = acceleration of the oscillator; the phase differences are in radians. At the equilibrium position x = 0 while v is greatest and a is zero; at an extreme v = 0 while a is greatest and opposite to x.

G M / r² = v² / r ⇒ v = √(G M / r)
Key: G = gravitational constant, 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²; M = mass of the central body (kg); r = orbital radius from its centre (m); v = orbital speed (m s⁻¹). Circular motion with gravity as the centripetal force — a satellite is simply falling around the planet rather than into it.

T = 2 π √(r³ / (G M))
Key: T = orbital period (s); r = orbital radius (m); G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²; M = mass of the central body (kg). Kepler's third law, obtained by substituting v = 2πr/T into the equation above; r³/T² is the same for every satellite of the same body.

title: A Level Mathematics: Permutations and Combinations
content:
A Level Mathematics: Permutations and Combinations

Counting is the part of probability that requires no formula to start with, only a decision: does the order matter? Every question in this topic is answered by that one question. If order matters the count is a permutation; if it does not the count is a combination. Everything else — repetitions, restrictions, arrangements around a circle — is a variation on the same counting principle, and this note sets out each variation with the reasoning behind it.

The multiplication principle

If a choice can be made in a ways and, independently, a second choice in b ways, the pair can be made in a × b ways. That is the whole foundation; the formulas are shortcuts for repeated applications of it.

arrangements of n distinct objects in a row: n! = n x (n-1) x ... x 2 x 1
0! = 1 by convention, so that formulas stay consistent
choosing r from n with order: nPr = n!/(n - r)!
choosing r from n without order: nCr = n!/(r!(n - r)!)

Worked example. A password is 4 distinct letters from the 26-letter alphabet. How many passwords are possible?

order matters, so 26P4 = 26 x 25 x 24 x 23 = 358,800

Worked example 2 (no order). How many ways can 4 students be chosen from 26?

order does not matter, so 26C4 = 14,950

Worked example 3 (a leading zero is not allowed). A code uses four distinct digits from 0 to 9 and cannot begin with zero. How many codes?

first digit: 9 choices (1 to 9)
remaining three: 9P3 = 9 x 8 x 7 = 504
total = 9 x 504 = 4536

Worked example 4 (the link). Explain why nPr = nCr × r!.

every unordered selection of r objects can be arranged in r! orders
so counting ordered selections = counting unordered ones then arranging them

Deciding whether order matters

The decision is not about the words "choose" or "arrange" in the question — those are hints, not rules. The safe test is to imagine two selections differing only by swapping two items: if that counts as a different outcome, order matters.

SituationOrder?Count
finishing order of a raceyesnPr
a committee of 3nonCr
a 4-digit PINyespermutation, with repetition allowed
a hand of cardsnonCr
seating 5 people in a rowyes5!

Worked example. A team of 11 is chosen from 16 players, and one of the 11 is captain. Count the possibilities.

choose the 11: 16C11 = 4368
choose the captain from them: 11 ways
total = 4368 x 11 = 48,048

The multiplication principle is doing the work here: two independent choices, multiplied.

Repetition and identical items

When some objects are identical, arranging them as if all were distinct overcounts by the number of ways the identical ones can be swapped. Dividing by those factorials corrects it.

arrangements of n items with groups of identical items:
n!/(a! b! c! ...) where a, b, c are the group sizes
with repetition allowed, choosing r from n: n^r

Worked example. How many distinct arrangements of the letters in BANANA?

6 letters: B once, A three times, N twice
6!/(1! 3! 2!) = 720/12 = 60

Worked example 2 (repetition allowed). A 3-digit code uses digits 0-9, repeats allowed. How many codes?

10 x 10 x 10 = 1000
if repeats were not allowed: 10 x 9 x 8 = 720

Worked example 3 (identical plus restriction). How many arrangements of the letters of LEVEL begin with L?

fix L at the front; remaining letters E, V, E, L
that is 4 letters with E twice: 4!/2! = 12
but the leading L is one of the two Ls, so there is only one choice for the front
answer 12

Restrictions: the "glue" method

When certain items must be together, treat the group as a single object, arrange the objects, then arrange within the group. When certain items must not be together, count the total and subtract the "together" case.

together: glue the group, arrange the objects, multiply by the internal arrangements
not together: total arrangements minus the together arrangements
specific positions: fix those items first, then arrange the rest

Worked example. Five books, two of which must stand together, are arranged on a shelf. How many orders?

glue the pair: now 4 objects, arranged in 4! = 24 ways
the pair interchange in 2! = 2 ways
total = 48

Worked example 2 (not together). The same five books with the pair not together.

total arrangements = 5! = 120
together = 48
not together = 120 - 48 = 72

Worked example 3 (fixed positions). Four men and three women sit in a row of seven. How many arrangements have all three women together?

glue the women into one block: now 5 objects (4 men + block), 5! = 120
internal arrangements of the women: 3! = 6
total = 720

Circular arrangements

Around a circle, rotations of the same arrangement are not distinguishable, so fixing one item removes the rotational symmetry and the count drops by a factor of n.

n distinct items around a circle: (n - 1)!
a necklace (where reflection also counts as the same): (n - 1)!/2

Worked example. In how many ways can 6 people sit around a round table?

(6 - 1)! = 5! = 120

Worked example 2 (with a fixed seat). How many ways if one particular person must sit in a specified chair?

fix that person, arrange the other 5 around: 5! = 120
the specified chair removes the rotational freedom entirely, so the answer is unchanged here

Worked example 3 (two people together at a round table). Six people, two of whom must sit together.

glue the pair: 5 objects around a circle = 4! = 24
internal order of the pair: 2
total = 48

Combinations with conditions

Committee questions combine cases: choose so many from one group and so many from another, then add the disjoint alternatives. The discipline is to make the cases genuinely disjoint, or the same selection gets counted twice.

choose a from group A and b from group B: C(a-group, a) x C(b-group, b)
several allowed compositions: add the separate cases
at least one: total minus none

Worked example. From 6 men and 5 women, how many committees of 4 contain exactly 2 women?

choose 2 women from 5: 10
choose 2 men from 6: 15
total = 150

Worked example 2 (at least one). How many committees of 4 contain at least one woman?

total committees: 11C4 = 330
none: 6C4 = 15
at least one = 330 - 15 = 315

Worked example 3 (cases added). How many committees of 3 contain more women than men?

3 women: 5C3 = 10
2 women and 1 man: 5C2 x 6C1 = 10 x 6 = 60
total = 70

Counting inside probability

Combinations are usually the denominator of a probability question: count the favourable selections, count all selections, divide. Doing the counting separately from the probability keeps both parts clean and makes partial credit possible.

Worked example. A bag holds 5 red and 7 blue counters. Four are drawn at random. Find the probability of exactly 2 red.

total selections: 12C4 = 495
favourable: 5C2 x 7C2 = 10 x 21 = 210
probability = 210/495 = 0.4242

Worked example 2 (at least one). For the same bag, find the probability of at least one red.

complement: no red means all four blue
7C4 = 35
P(no red) = 35/495 = 0.0707
P(at least one red) = 1 - 0.0707 = 0.9293

Worked example 3 (order matters in the numerator). Three cards are drawn from a standard deck without replacement. Find the probability they are drawn in increasing order of value.

every set of three distinct cards has exactly one increasing order out of 3! orders
so the probability is 1/6, independent of the deck

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Factorial) Evaluate 7!. Answer: 5040.
  2. (Permutation) In how many orders can 5 runners finish? Answer: 5! = 120.
  3. (Combination) Evaluate 10C3. Answer: 120.
  4. (Choice) From 8 books, how many ways to choose 3? Answer: 56.
  5. (Arrangement) How many arrangements of the letters of STATISTICS? Answer: 10!/(3!3!2!) = 50,400.
  6. (Glue) 6 people in a row with two together: Answer: 5! × 2 = 240.
  7. (Not together) Same 6, not together: Answer: 720 − 240 = 480.
  8. (Circle) 7 people around a table: Answer: 6! = 720.
  9. (Committee) 3 from 5 men and 4 women, exactly 2 men: Answer: 5C2 × 4C1 = 40.
  10. (At least) 4 from the same 9 with at least one woman: Answer: 9C4 − 5C4 = 126 − 5 = 121.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Using nPr where order does not matter: a committee is unordered; using permutations overcounts by r!.
  • Forgetting to divide by repeated factorials: identical letters need the divisor or the count is inflated.
  • Glue method without the internal factor: the block also has an internal arrangement, and dropping the 2! halves the answer.
  • Circular arrangements with n! instead of (n − 1)!: rotations are the same seating.
  • Adding what should be multiplied: independent stages multiply; alternative cases add.
  • Overlapping cases: cases must be disjoint, or selections are counted twice.
  • "At least one" counted directly: the complement is almost always faster and safer.
  • Restrictions applied after the count: fix the restricted positions first, then count what remains.

title: Work, Energy and Power
content:
Work, Energy and Power

Work

W = Fs cos θ — force × displacement in the force's direction. Unit: joule (J).

Example: 100 N over 5 m in the same direction: W = 500 J. At 60°: 100 × 5 × cos 60° = 250 J.

Energy Forms

  • Kinetic energy: Ek = ½mv²
  • Gravitational PE: Ep = mgh
  • Elastic PE: ½kx² (spring, Hooke's law region)

Conservation of Energy

Energy changes between forms but the total stays constant (no external work).

Falling from height h: mgh = ½mv², so v = √(2gh) — independent of mass.

Example: a 0.5 kg ball dropped from 4 m hits at v = √(2 × 9.81 × 4) ≈ 8.9 m s⁻¹.

Power

P = W/t = Fv. Unit: watt (W = J s⁻¹).

Example: a 750 N runner at 6 m s⁻¹ outputs P = 4500 W.

Efficiency

Efficiency = useful output / total input × 100%.

Exam tips: energy questions are solved with energy, not kinematics, when forces vary; always ask 'where did the missing energy go?' — usually heat or sound.

title: Differentiation — Study Notes
content:
Differentiation

Edexcel International A Level Mathematics — Pure Mathematics 1 (WMA11), sat at AS. Differentiation finds how fast y changes with x. Most questions ask for one of three things: a gradient at a point, a tangent or normal, or the nature of a stationary point.

Start from a question

The curve C has equation y = 2x³ − 9x² + 12x − 1.

  1. Find dy/dx.
  2. Find the coordinates of the stationary points and state their nature.
  3. Find the equation of the normal to C at x = 3.

Part 1. dy/dx = 6x² − 18x + 12 = 6(x − 1)(x − 2).

Part 2. dy/dx = 0 at x = 1 and x = 2. When x = 1, y = 4, and when x = 2, y = 3. Next, d²y/dx² = 12x − 18. At (1, 4) this is −6, so the point is a maximum. At (2, 3) it is 6, so the point is a minimum.

Part 3. At x = 3, dy/dx = 6(2)(1) = 12, so the normal has gradient −1/12. Also y = 54 − 81 + 36 − 1 = 8, so the point is (3, 8). The normal is y − 8 = −(x − 3)/12, which gives x + 12y − 99 = 0.

The power rule

If y = axⁿ, then dy/dx = naxⁿ⁻¹, for any rational n. A constant differentiates to zero. Rewrite roots and reciprocals as powers first: 4√x − 6/x² = 4x^(1/2) − 6x⁻², so dy/dx = 2/√x + 12/x³.

Expand before you differentiate

Differentiation works term by term, so multiply out any brackets first. Example: y = (x + 2)(x − 5) = x² − 3x − 10, so dy/dx = 2x − 3.

A zero gradient is not always a turning point

Use the second derivative when it is non-zero at the point. If it is zero, test the sign of dy/dx on each side. Example: y = x⁴ − 4x³ gives dy/dx = 4x²(x − 3). At x = 0 the gradient is negative on both sides, so the curve keeps falling and (0, 0) is not a maximum or minimum. At x = 3 the gradient changes from negative to positive, so (3, −27) is a minimum.

Tangents and normals

Substitute x into the original equation to find y, and into dy/dx to find the gradient. The tangent uses that gradient, and the normal uses its negative reciprocal. Write both as y − y₁ = m(x − x₁) and simplify.

Traps that cost marks

  • Differentiating a product factor by factor instead of expanding it first.
  • Giving the normal the same gradient as the tangent, rather than the negative reciprocal.
  • Giving only the x-value of a stationary point, rather than its coordinates (x, y).
  • Calling a point a maximum or minimum from dy/dx = 0 alone, without checking the nature.

Worked example: the chain rule

Differentiate y = (3x − 2)⁵. Treat this as an outer power of an inner linear function. The derivative of the outer function, with the inside kept as a single unit, is 5(3x − 2)⁴. Multiply by the derivative of the inside, which is 3. So dy/dx = 15(3x − 2)⁴. Forgetting the factor 3 from the inside is the most frequent error on this type of question, and it loses the accuracy mark even when the power rule has been applied correctly.

Worked example: the product rule

For y = x² sin x, let u = x² and v = sin x. Then dy/dx = u dv/dx + v du/dx = x² cos x + 2x sin x. Write the two products out separately and then collect like terms. If the question asks for the gradient at a particular point, substitute only after the derivative has been simplified, because substituting first makes it harder to spot an algebra slip.

title: Trigonometry — Sine and Cosine Rules — Study Notes
content:
Trigonometry — Sine and Cosine Rules

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): area formula, sine rule, cosine rule, multi-step bearing and 3-D problems (Extended).

1. Area of a triangle

A = ½ab sin C (C = included angle between sides a and b).

Example: a = 8, b = 5, C = 48° → A = ½ × 8 × 5 × sin 48° = 14.8.

2. Sine rule

a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C. Use when a matching angle–side pair is known.

Example: A = 40°, a = 7, B = 65°: b = 7 sin 65°/sin 40° = 9.98.

Ambiguous case: two triangles possible when finding an angle — check the obtuse option (180° − θ).

3. Cosine rule

a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A. Use with two sides + included angle, or all three sides (then cos A = (b² + c² − a²)/(2bc)).

Example: b = 7, c = 5, A = 52°: a² = 74 − 70 cos 52° = 30.9 → a = 5.56.

4. Bearing problems

Draw both north lines, transfer angles via parallel lines, then pick sine/cosine rule.

Example: QP = 60 km bearing 070° from Q; QR = 45 km bearing 150°. ∠PQR = 80° → PR² = 60² + 45² − 2·60·45 cos 80° → PR = 68.4 km.

5. 3-D trigonometry

Identify the plane containing the required angle; use 3-D Pythagoras d² = x² + y² + z² for space diagonals; angle between a line and a plane uses the projection onto the plane.

Exam tips: state which rule you are using and why; sketch a separate 2-D triangle for 3-D questions; answers to 3 s.f. / bearings as three digits.

The sine rule

For any triangle with sides a, b, c opposite angles A, B, C: a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C. Use it when you know a pair of opposite side and angle (for example, two angles and a side, or a side and its opposite angle with another side). Find the missing angle using the angle sum of 180° first.

The cosine rule

a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A, and cos A = (b² + c² − a²) ÷ 2bc. Use it when you know two sides and the included angle, or all three sides. Careful with negative cosines: an obtuse angle gives a negative cos value.

Area of a triangle

Area = ½ab sin C, using two sides and the included angle. This avoids finding the perpendicular height.

Worked example: the sine rule

In triangle ABC, side a = 7 cm is opposite angle A = 40°, and angle B = 65°. Find side b, which is opposite B: b = a × sin B ÷ sin A = 7 × sin 65° ÷ sin 40° = 7 × 0.9063 ÷ 0.6428 = 9.87 cm (to 2 decimal places).

Worked example: the cosine rule

Triangle PQR has PQ = 5 cm, PR = 8 cm and the included angle P = 60°. The side QR is found from a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A: QR² = 8² + 5² − 2 × 8 × 5 × cos 60° = 64 + 25 − 20 = 69, so QR = √69 = 8.31 cm.

Area and 3-D problems

  • Area of a triangle = ½ × a × b × sin C, where C is the angle between sides a and b. With a = 8, b = 5 and C = 60°, the area is ½ × 8 × 5 × sin 60° = 17.32 cm².
  • In a 3-D question, first find a triangle that contains the unknown and two known values, then apply the sine or cosine rule to that triangle only.

Exam point: use the sine rule when you have a matching pair (a side and the angle opposite it). Use the cosine rule when you have two sides and the included angle, or three sides.

title: Kinetics
content:
Kinetics

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH14, Topic 11. Kinetics links the rate of a reaction to the concentrations of the reactants, and the rate constant to temperature. Rate equations come from experiments, not from the balanced equation.

Rate equations and order

  • The rate equation has the form rate = k[A]^m[B]^n. The powers m and n are the orders with respect to A and B, and they must be found from experimental data.
  • A first-order reaction has rate proportional to concentration: doubling [A] doubles the rate. A second-order reaction gives a quadrupled rate when [A] doubles.
  • A zero-order reaction has a rate that does not depend on the concentration of that reactant, because the reactant is not involved in the rate-determining step or the reaction surface is saturated.
  • The overall order is the sum of the individual orders.

Initial rates

  • Using the initial rates method, keep all but one concentration constant and compare the rates. The ratio of rates gives the order for the changed reactant.

Rate constant and units

  • The rate constant k is the proportionality constant in the rate equation. Its units depend on the overall order: for rate in mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹, a first-order k is in s⁻¹ and a second-order k is in dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹.
  • k changes only with temperature (and with a catalyst, which lowers Ea). Concentration changes alter the rate, not k.

Half-life

  • For a first-order reaction, the half-life is constant and given by t½ = ln 2 / k = 0.693 / k.

Arrhenius equation

  • The Arrhenius equation k = A e^(−Ea/RT) relates the rate constant to temperature. Taking natural logarithms gives ln k = ln A − Ea/(RT).
  • A plot of ln k against 1/T is a straight line with gradient −Ea/R, which allows the activation energy to be found.

Mechanisms

  • A reaction mechanism is a series of steps. The slowest step is the rate-determining step, and the rate equation is predicted from its stoichiometry.

Exam tip: when asked for the rate equation, use the data and state the order for each reactant; do not simply copy the coefficients from the balanced equation.

title: Human Nutrition
content:
Human Nutrition

Cambridge IGCSE Biology 0610, Extended route, topic 7 (statements 7.1–7.5). Balanced diets and nutrient functions, the digestive system, physical and chemical digestion, and absorption in the small intestine.

7.1 Diet

  • A balanced diet contains the right proportions of carbohydrate, protein, lipids, vitamins, minerals, fibre and water. Carbohydrates and lipids provide energy; protein builds and repairs tissues; vitamins and minerals regulate body processes; fibre adds bulk; water is a solvent and coolant.
  • Deficiency diseases: scurvy (vitamin C), rickets (vitamin D), anaemia (iron), kwashiorkor (protein).

7.2 to 7.4 Digestion

  • The alimentary canal runs mouth → oesophagus → stomach → small intestine → large intestine → rectum. The liver produces bile, the pancreas produces pancreatic juice, and both empty into the small intestine.
  • Physical digestion: chewing breaks food into smaller pieces; bile emulsifies fats into smaller droplets, increasing the surface area for enzymes. Bile is alkaline, neutralising stomach acid so enzymes work at their optimum.
  • Chemical digestion by enzymes: amylase (salivary, pancreatic) breaks starch to maltose; pepsin (stomach, acidic) breaks proteins to smaller polypeptides; trypsin (pancreatic, alkaline) continues protein digestion; lipase (pancreatic) breaks emulsified fats to fatty acids and glycerol. Each enzyme works best at the pH of its site.

7.5 Absorption

  • Absorption happens in the small intestine: villi have a large surface area, a one-cell-thick wall, a rich blood supply to carry products away, and lacteals for fatty acids and glycerol. Glucose and amino acids pass into the blood capillaries.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Enzyme site reasoning, applied to why pepsin works in the stomach but trypsin in the small intestine: pepsin's optimum is pH 2 (gastric acid) and trypsin's is about pH 8 (bile neutralises the acid). State the pH of each site and the enzyme's optimum — the matching is the explanation.
  • Adaptation chains, applied to villus features: large surface area increases the rate of absorption; thin wall shortens the diffusion path; the blood supply maintains the concentration gradient by carrying products away. One structure, one function, one mark — write them as separate sentences.
  • Fat absorption reasoning, applied to fatty acids and glycerol: they are lipid-soluble, so they pass into the lacteal rather than the blood capillary, and are then carried in the lymphatic system before entering the bloodstream. Naming the lacteal and the route both earn marks.

Common errors

  • Calling bile an enzyme. It is not — it is a salt emulsion that prepares fats for lipase.
  • Saying absorption happens in the large intestine. Water is absorbed there; nutrients are absorbed in the small intestine.
  • Confusing digestion (breaking down) with absorption (moving into blood).

title: AS Level Mathematics: Measures of Variation and Standard Deviation
content:
AS Level Mathematics: Measures of Variation and Standard Deviation

Two data sets can share a mean and behave completely differently: one tightly clustered, one wildly spread. Measures of variation quantify that difference. This note builds the topic from zero: the range and interquartile range, the variance and standard deviation with the full calculation from first principles, the frequency-table and coded forms, outliers, and how to compare distributions fairly. Every formula is derived once, because the derivation is what makes it stick.

Why spread matters

Location alone is a half-description. A machine filling 500 g bags with a standard deviation of 2 g is trustworthy; one with a standard deviation of 30 g is not, though both may average 500 g. Spread measures consistency, risk and reliability, and every comparison question rewards naming both a location and a spread.

Range and interquartile range

range = largest - smallest
interquartile range IQR = Q3 - Q1
semi-interquartile range = (Q3 - Q1)/2
MeasureUsesWeakness
RangeOnly the two extremesDestroyed by one outlier
IQRThe middle halfIgnores the tails entirely
Standard deviationEvery valueDragged by outliers; more arithmetic

Worked example. Find the range, IQR and semi-IQR of 12, 15, 18, 21, 25, 30, 44.

range = 44 - 12 = 32
n = 7; median = 21; Q1 = 15; Q3 = 30
IQR = 15;  semi-IQR = 7.5

The 44 stretches the range to 32 while leaving the IQR untouched: exactly the robustness the IQR is chosen for.

Variance and standard deviation defined

variance = mean of the squared deviations from the mean
standard deviation = sqrt(variance)

population form:  sigma^2 = (sum of (x - mu)^2)/n
sample form:      s^2 = (sum of (x - xbar)^2)/(n - 1)

Why square the deviations? Signed deviations always sum to zero, so they cannot measure spread; squaring removes the signs and penalises large gaps heavily. The square root returns the answer to the original units, which is why standard deviation, not variance, is quoted in context.

Worked example (full working). Find the standard deviation of 4, 7, 9, 10, 10.

mean = 40/5 = 8
deviations: -4, -1, 1, 2, 2
squares: 16, 1, 1, 4, 4  ->  sum 26
variance = 26/5 = 5.2
standard deviation = sqrt(5.2) = 2.28

The computational formula

sigma^2 = (sum of x^2)/n - (mean)^2

this is algebraically identical to the deviation form but far quicker

Worked example. Repeat the previous calculation with the computational form.

sum x = 40;  mean = 8
sum x^2 = 16 + 49 + 81 + 100 + 100 = 346
variance = 346/5 - 64 = 69.2 - 64 = 5.2
standard deviation = 2.28  (identical, as it must be)

Frequency tables

mean = (sum of f x)/(sum of f)
variance = (sum of f x^2)/(sum of f) - (mean)^2

Worked example. Find the mean and standard deviation of the distribution x: 1, 2, 3, 4 with frequencies 2, 5, 8, 5.

sum f = 20
sum fx = 2(1) + 5(2) + 8(3) + 5(4) = 2 + 10 + 24 + 20 = 56  ->  mean 2.8
sum fx^2 = 2(1) + 5(4) + 8(9) + 5(16) = 2 + 20 + 72 + 80 = 174
variance = 174/20 - 7.84 = 8.7 - 7.84 = 0.86
standard deviation = 0.927

For grouped data the midpoint stands in for each class, so the standard deviation is an estimate, like the grouped mean.

Worked example 2 (grouped). Estimate the standard deviation of 0–10 (3), 10–20 (7), 20–30 (10).

midpoints 5, 15, 25;  sum f = 20
sum fx = 15 + 105 + 250 = 370  ->  mean 18.5
sum fx^2 = 3(25) + 7(225) + 10(625) = 75 + 1575 + 6250 = 7900
variance = 7900/20 - 342.25 = 395 - 342.25 = 52.75
standard deviation = 7.26

Coding and the effect on spread

if y = (x - a)/b then:
  mean(y) = (mean(x) - a)/b
  sd(y) = sd(x)/|b|
  variance(y) = variance(x)/b^2

shifts (a) do not change spread; scaling (b) scales it

Worked example. The coded values y = (x − 100)/5 have mean 4 and standard deviation 1.2. Find the mean and standard deviation of x.

mean x = 5(4) + 100 = 120
sd x = 5(1.2) = 6

The intuition: adding a constant slides the whole distribution without stretching it; multiplying stretches every gap by the same factor.

Outliers

lower fence = Q1 - 1.5 IQR
upper fence = Q3 + 1.5 IQR
values beyond the fences are outliers

Worked example. With Q1 = 20, Q3 = 32 and a maximum of 60, is 60 an outlier?

IQR = 12; upper fence = 32 + 18 = 50
60 > 50, so yes, 60 is an outlier

Outliers are not automatically errors: they may be genuine extreme values, which is why the median and IQR often summarise skewed data better than the mean and standard deviation.

Comparing distributions properly

A full comparison answers four points: which has the higher typical value, which is more spread, whether either has outliers, and what that means in context.

Worked example. Boys: mean 62, sd 8. Girls: mean 68, sd 4. Compare.

girls have the higher typical mark (68 vs 62)
girls are more consistent (sd 4 vs 8; roughly half the spread)
boys' marks are more widely dispersed, so their range of performance
is broader; the sd ratio 2 suggests boys' marks vary twice as much
about their mean

Never compare standard deviations of data measured in different units or on different scales without converting; here both are marks, so the comparison is valid.

Standard deviation in context

Worked example (quality control). A machine fills bags with mean 500 g and sd 3 g. Assuming a roughly symmetric distribution, about what proportion lies within one standard deviation of the mean?

one sd either side: 497 to 503 g
for a roughly normal shape, about 68 per cent of bags fall in this band
(and about 95 per cent within two sds: 494 to 506 g)

The 68/95/99.7 guide is approximate and only valid for roughly bell-shaped data; stating that condition is part of the answer.

Comparing spread across different units

Standard deviations cannot be compared directly when the scales differ. The coefficient of variation puts them on a common footing by expressing the spread as a fraction of the mean:

coefficient of variation = 100 x sd/mean  (per cent)

A: mean 50 kg, sd 4 kg   ->  CV = 8 per cent
B: mean 8000 pounds, sd 400 pounds  ->  CV = 5 per cent
B is relatively more consistent despite the larger absolute sd

Worked example. Two athletes' times over a season: A has mean 12.0 s, sd 0.15 s; B has mean 60.0 s, sd 0.60 s (different events). Which is more consistent relative to their event?

CV(A) = 0.15/12.0 x 100 = 1.25 per cent
CV(B) = 0.60/60.0 x 100 = 1.00 per cent
B is relatively more consistent, even though the absolute sd is 4 times larger

Without the coefficient of variation, the comparison would favour A for the wrong reason. State the units and the ratio when answering.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Range) Find the range of 3, 8, 12, 15, 22. Answer: 19.
  2. (IQR) Find the IQR of 5, 6, 9, 11, 14, 18. Answer: Q1 = 6.75, Q3 = 15, IQR = 8.25.
  3. (SD) Find the standard deviation of 2, 4, 4, 6, 9. Answer: mean 5; deviations −3, −1, −1, 1, 4; squares 9, 1, 1, 1, 16 = 28; variance 5.6; sd 2.37.
  4. (Computational) For sum x = 60, sum x² = 800, n = 10, find the sd. Answer: variance = 80 − 36 = 44; sd = 6.63.
  5. (Frequency) x: 0, 1, 2 with f: 4, 3, 3. Find the mean. Answer: 9/10 = 0.9.
  6. (Coding) y = (x − 20)/4 has sd 2.5. Find the sd of x. Answer: 10.
  7. (Outlier) Q1 = 12, Q3 = 20, maximum 45. Is 45 an outlier? Answer: IQR = 8, fence = 32; yes.
  8. (Compare) A: mean 40, sd 5. B: mean 40, sd 12. What differs? Answer: same centre, different spread; B is far more variable.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Forgetting to root: the variance is in squared units; the standard deviation is its square root. Quoting the variance as the sd is a units error.
  • Dividing by n or n − 1: use the convention the question implies; for a population divide by n, for a sample estimate divide by n − 1. Mixing them shifts the answer.
  • Deviation sign errors: the deviations must sum to zero — if they do not, the mean was copied wrongly.
  • Coding with the wrong operation: sd divides by |b|, never subtracts a; shifts do not affect spread.
  • Comparing different units: an sd of 5 marks and an sd of 5 kg are not comparable; convert or use the coefficient of variation.
  • Outlier fences: 1.5 × IQR beyond the quartiles, not beyond the range or the median.
  • Grouped estimates: call them estimates and note that midpoints are assumed uniform within each class.
  • One-sided comparison: a comparison naming only the mean earns half the marks; always add the spread and its interpretation.

Formula summary

range = max - min;  IQR = Q3 - Q1
variance = (sum of x^2)/n - (mean)^2
standard deviation = sqrt(variance)
coded: mean(x) = b mean(y) + a;  sd(x) = |b| sd(y)
CV = 100 sd/mean

Learn the computational variance form rather than the deviation form: it needs one pass for the sum and one for the sum of squares, and it fails loudly when the mean is wrong because the deviations then do not sum to zero.

title: A Level Mathematics: The Binomial Expansion
content:
A Level Mathematics: The Binomial Expansion

The binomial theorem expands (a + b)ⁿ without multiplying out n brackets. AS work covers positive integer powers with nCr coefficients; A2 extends it to negative and fractional powers as an infinite series, valid only inside a stated range of x. This note builds the theorem from Pascal's triangle through to the general term, then handles the negative and fractional cases, the validity condition, and the approximation questions that follow.

Pascal's triangle and nCr

coefficients of (a + b)^n are nCr = n!/(r!(n - r)!)

n = 0:        1
n = 1:       1 1
n = 2:      1 2 1
n = 3:     1 3 3 1
n = 4:    1 4 6 4 1

Each entry is the sum of the two above it. nCr counts the number of ways of choosing r items from n, which is exactly the number of ways the r b's can be selected from n brackets.

The binomial theorem

(a + b)^n = sum from r = 0 to n of nCr a^(n - r) b^r

general term: nCr a^(n - r) b^r

Worked example 1. Expand (2 + 3x)⁴.

coefficients 1, 4, 6, 4, 1
= 2⁴ + 4(2³)(3x) + 6(2²)(3x)² + 4(2)(3x)³ + (3x)⁴
= 16 + 96x + 216x² + 216x³ + 81x⁴

Worked example 2 (a single term). Find the coefficient of x³ in (1 + 2x)⁷.

term with x³: 7C3 (1)⁴ (2x)³ = 35 × 8 x³ = 280x³
coefficient 280

Worked example 3 (the constant term). Find the constant term in (x + 2/x)⁶.

general term: 6Cr x^(6 - r) (2/x)^r = 6Cr 2^r x^(6 - 2r)
constant when 6 - 2r = 0  →  r = 3
6C3 × 2³ = 20 × 8 = 160

Negative and fractional powers

(1 + x)^n = 1 + nx + n(n-1)x²/2! + n(n-1)(n-2)x³/3! + ...

valid for |x| < 1 when n is not a positive integer

The series is infinite, and the validity condition comes from the binomial series converging only for |x| < 1. Always state it.

Worked example 1. Expand (1 + x)^(−1) up to the term in x³.

n = -1: 1 + (-1)x + (-1)(-2)x²/2 + (-1)(-2)(-3)x³/6
= 1 - x + x² - x³,  valid for |x| < 1

Worked example 2 (fractional). Expand (1 + 2x)^(1/2) up to x².

n = 1/2: 1 + (1/2)(2x) + (1/2)(-1/2)(2x)²/2
= 1 + x - (1/8)(4x²) = 1 + x - x²/2
valid for |2x| < 1, i.e. |x| < 1/2

Worked example 3 (leading coefficient). Expand (4 + x)^(1/2) up to x².

factor out the 4: (4 + x)^(1/2) = 2(1 + x/4)^(1/2)
= 2[1 + (1/2)(x/4) + (1/2)(-1/2)(x/4)²/2]
= 2[1 + x/8 - x²/128]
= 2 + x/4 - x²/64,  valid for |x| < 4

The factorisation step is compulsory whenever the constant is not 1: the formula needs (1 + u)^n with |u| < 1, so the leading number must be taken outside.

Validity conditions

for (1 + ax)^n with n not a positive integer: |ax| < 1
after factorising (A + Bx)^n = A^n (1 + Bx/A)^n:
|Bx/A| < 1  →  |x| < |A/B|

Worked example. State the validity range for (3 − 2x)^(−2).

= 3⁻² (1 - 2x/3)⁻²
valid for |2x/3| < 1  →  |x| < 3/2

Approximation

Substituting a small x into a truncated series gives a numerical approximation; the error depends on how small x is and how many terms are kept.

Worked example. Use the first three terms of (1 + x)^(1/2) to estimate √1.02.

x = 0.02: 1 + 0.01 - (0.0004)/8 = 1.00995
calculator value √(1.02) = 1.009950..., agreement to 6 d.p.

Worked example 2 (fraction). Estimate (1.01)^(−1) using three terms and state whether the estimate is above or below the true value.

1 - 0.01 + 0.0001 = 0.9901
true value 1/1.01 = 0.990099...
the estimate 0.9901 is slightly above, since the next term is negative

Why the coefficients are nCr

Expanding (a + b)ⁿ means choosing a or b from each of n brackets and multiplying the choices. A term with r b's arises once for every way of choosing those r brackets from n, and there are nCr such ways. That argument proves the theorem and is itself examinable: it explains both the symmetry of the coefficients (nCr = nC(n−r)) and why the row sums are 2ⁿ.

sum of nCr over r = 0..n = 2^n   (set a = b = 1)
alternating sum = 0                (set a = 1, b = -1)
nCr = nC(n - r)                    (choosing r is choosing which to leave out)

Worked example. Show that the coefficients of x² and x⁴ in (1 + x)⁶ are equal.

6C2 = 15 and 6C4 = 15, as nCr = nC(n - r) with n = 6

Coefficients from products of expansions

A common A2 question multiplies two expansions and asks for one coefficient. Only the pairs that produce the required power matter, so write the contributing terms side by side.

Worked example. Find the coefficient of x² in (1 + x)(1 − 2x)⁵.

(1 - 2x)⁵ = 1 - 10x + 40x² - ...
contributions to x²: 1 × 40x² and x x (-10x)
coefficient = 40 - 10 = 30

Worked example 2 (unknown constant). In the expansion of (2 + kx)⁴ the coefficient of x² is 216. Find k.

x² term: 6(2²)(kx)² = 24k² x²
24k² = 216  →  k² = 9  →  k = 3 or -3

Both roots are usually valid unless the question states k > 0; state both and, if the context fixes the sign, say why.

Partial fractions then a binomial series

When an expression is a rational function, split it into partial fractions first, then expand each piece — each has its own validity range, and the answer takes the intersection.

Worked example. Expand 3/[(1 + x)(2 - x)] up to x² and state the range.

partial fractions: 1/(1 + x) + 1/(2 - x)
first piece: (1 + x)⁻¹ = 1 - x + x² - ...  valid |x| < 1
second: (2 - x)⁻¹ = (1/2)(1 - x/2)⁻¹ = (1/2)(1 + x/2 + x²/4)  valid |x| < 2
sum: 3/2 - x/2 + (3/4)x²
the combined range is the stricter: |x| < 1

The intersection rule is the point: a sum of series is valid only where every piece converges.

Approximation error and checking

Truncating an infinite series leaves an error of the size of the next term, which is why keeping one more term improves the estimate substantially when x is near the edge of the range.

Worked example. Estimate (1.1)^(1/2) with two terms and with three, and compare with the calculator.

two terms: 1 + 0.05 = 1.05
three terms: 1.05 - 0.05²/8 = 1.04875
calculator: 1.0488088...
adding the third term halves the error

Worked example 2. Explain why the series for (1 − 3x)^(1/2) cannot estimate √(1 − 3(0.5)) reliably.

the validity range is |x| < 1/3, and x = 0.5 lies outside it
the series diverges there, so any truncated sum is meaningless

Two unknowns in one expansion

Some questions fix the expansion of (a + bx)ⁿ through two given coefficients. Each coefficient supplies one equation, and the pair is solved simultaneously.

Worked example. In the expansion of (2 + px)⁵ the coefficient of x is 80 and the coefficient of x² is 720. Find p.

x term: 5(2⁴)(px) = 80p x  →  80p = 80  →  p = 1
x² term: 10(2³)(px)² = 80p²  →  80p² = 720  →  p² = 9
contradiction: p = 1 does not satisfy the second equation, so check
the reading of the question - here the consistent pair comes from
solving the x² equation alone for p = +3 or -3, and testing which
reproduces the x coefficient when the constant is also unknown

When both the constant and the coefficient are unknown, write the two coefficient equations and solve them as a pair; a single coefficient cannot determine two unknowns.

Worked example 2. In (1 + ax)ⁿ the coefficient of x is 12 and of x² is 60. Find a and n.

x: na = 12
x²: n(n - 1)a²/2 = 60
substitute a = 12/n: n(n - 1)(144/n²)/2 = 60
72(n - 1)/n = 60  →  72n - 72 = 60n  →  n = 6, a = 2

That pair of equations is the standard exam shape, and eliminating a is always quicker than eliminating n.

Formula summary

(a + b)^n = sum nCr a^(n-r) b^r
general term: nCr a^(n-r) b^r
(1 + x)^n = 1 + nx + n(n-1)x²/2! + ...  (|x| < 1 for n not a
positive integer)
(A + Bx)^n = A^n (1 + Bx/A)^n, valid |Bx/A| < 1

Two habits prevent most lost marks: factorise the leading constant before expanding, and quote the validity range in the same line as the series. A third is to write the general term before substituting anything, because the general term locates the power you need in one step instead of guesswork.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Expand) Expand (1 + x)⁵. Answer: 1 + 5x + 10x² + 10x³ + 5x⁴ + x⁵.
  2. (Coefficient) Find the coefficient of x² in (1 − 3x)⁶. Answer: 15 × 9 = 135.
  3. (Term) Find the term in x⁴ in (2 + x)⁶. Answer: 15(4)x⁴ = 60x⁴.
  4. (Constant) Find the constant term in (2x − 1/x)⁴. Answer: need 4 − 2r = 0 → r = 2; 6(4)(1) = 24.
  5. (Negative power) Expand (1 − x)^(−2) to x³. Answer: 1 + 2x + 3x² + 4x³.
  6. (Fractional) Expand (1 + 3x)^(1/3) to x². Answer: 1 + x − x².
  7. (Validity) State the range for (1 + 5x)^(−1). Answer: |x| < 1/5.
  8. (Approximate) Estimate (0.98)^(−1) to three terms. Answer: 1 + 0.02 + 0.0004 = 1.0204.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Forgetting to factorise: (4 + x)^n must become 4ⁿ(1 + x/4)ⁿ before the series is applied; using the formula directly is wrong.
  • Validity not stated: for negative or fractional powers the range is part of the answer, and a mark is attached to it.
  • Wrong power of the constant: in (2 + 3x)⁴ the term is 4(2³)(3x), not 4(2⁴)(3x).
  • Coefficient versus term: the question may want the coefficient (280) or the whole term (280x³); read it.
  • Rising powers of the wrong part: the r index applies to the second term, with a^(n−r) on the first.
  • nCr on a calculator: use the nCr function, not n!/r!, to avoid overflow and arithmetic slips.
  • Truncated series treated as exact: state the approximation and its limitation; the series is infinite.
  • Sign errors with negative n: alternate signs are expected when n is negative; a run of positive terms signals a slip.

Equations and symbols

Three forms and one condition. The general term locates a coefficient without expanding anything, the infinite series handles negative and fractional powers, and the validity range is a mark of its own.

(a + b)^n = sum from r = 0 to n of nCr a^(n - r) b^r Key: a = the first term of the bracket; b = the second term; n = the index, a positive integer here; r = the term counter running 0 to n; nCr = n!/(r!(n − r)!), the binomial coefficient. Powers of a fall while powers of b rise, and the two always add to n.

general term: nCr a^(n - r) b^r Key: r = which term you want, counted from 0; a, b = the two terms of the bracket; n = the index. Write this line before substituting anything — the constant term is where the power of x is zero, and the coefficient of x³ is where the power is 3.

(1 + x)^n = 1 + nx + n(n-1)x²/2! + n(n-1)(n-2)x³/3! + ... Key: n = the index, which may be negative or fractional; x = the variable, subject to |x| < 1; the factorials in the denominators come from the falling product, which is why the series never terminates. Each new coefficient multiplies the previous one by the next factor in the falling product and divides by the next integer.

valid for |x| < 1 Key: x = the whole variable part of the bracket, not just the letter; |x| < 1 = the condition under which the infinite series converges. For (1 + 2x)^(1/2) the condition is |2x| < 1, so |x| < 1/2 — quoting the wrong range costs the mark even when the series is right.

(A + Bx)^n = A^n (1 + Bx/A)^n, valid |Bx/A| < 1 Key: A = the constant term (must be taken outside); B = the coefficient of x; n = the index. This factorisation is compulsory whenever A ≠ 1, because the standard series only exists for a bracket starting with 1 — and it generates the range |x| < |A/B|.

|Bx/A| < 1 → |x| < |A/B| Key: A = the constant term of the bracket; B = the coefficient of x; the result is the validity range (no units). For (3 − 2x)^(−2) this gives |x| < 3/2.

sum of nCr over r = 0..n = 2^n Key: nCr = the binomial coefficients of row n; 2ⁿ = their total. It follows from setting a = b = 1 in the theorem, and the alternating sum is zero by setting a = 1, b = −1.

nCr = nC(n - r) Key: nCr = choosing r from n; nC(n − r) = choosing which to leave out. That symmetry is why the coefficients of a row read the same forwards and backwards — 6C2 = 15 and 6C4 = 15.

24k² = 216 → k² = 9 → k = 3 or -3 Key: 24k² = the coefficient of x² in (2 + kx)⁴, from 6(2²)(kx)²; 216 = the stated coefficient; k = ±3 (no units). Both roots are valid unless the question fixes k > 0, so quote both and say why one is rejected if it is.
