na = 12 Key: n = the index; a = the coefficient of x inside the bracket; 12 = the given coefficient of x in (1 + ax)ⁿ. One coefficient gives one equation, so a second (n(n − 1)a²/2 = 60) is needed — eliminating a by substituting a = 12/n gives n = 6, a = 2.

title: AS Level Mathematics: Probability Distributions
content:
AS Level Mathematics: Probability Distributions

A discrete random variable takes a countable set of values, each with a probability. The probability distribution is the complete list of values and probabilities, and from it come the two summaries that matter: the expected value (the long-run average) and the variance (the typical squared spread about it). This note builds the topic from zero: constructing and checking a distribution, E(X) and Var(X) from first principles, the effect of linear transformations, and the linear combinations of random variables that let you combine independent quantities with confidence.

Discrete random variables

X takes values x1, x2, ... with probabilities p1, p2, ...
conditions: 0 <= p_i <= 1 and the probabilities sum to 1

Worked example. A fair die is rolled and X is the score. Write the distribution and verify it.

P(X = k) = 1/6 for k = 1..6
sum = 6 × 1/6 = 1, so it is a valid distribution

Worked example 2 (unknown constant). P(X = 1) = k, P(X = 2) = 2k, P(X = 3) = 3k. Find k.

k + 2k + 3k = 1  →  6k = 1  →  k = 1/6
so P(X = 1) = 1/6, P(X = 2) = 1/3, P(X = 3) = 1/2

Expectation

E(X) = sum of x P(X = x)

the expected value need not be a possible value of X:
the mean of a die is 3.5

Worked example. Find E(X) for the die.

E(X) = (1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6)/6 = 21/6 = 3.5

Worked example 2 (unequal probabilities). X takes 0, 1, 2 with probabilities 0.2, 0.5, 0.3. Find E(X).

E(X) = 0(0.2) + 1(0.5) + 2(0.3) = 0.5 + 0.6 = 1.1

Interpretation: over many repetitions the average outcome approaches 1.1. That long-run reading is what applied questions ("expected profit", "expected number of defects") ask for.

Variance of a discrete random variable

Var(X) = E(X²) - [E(X)]^2
where E(X²) = sum of x² P(X = x)

standard deviation = √(Var(X))

Worked example. Find Var(X) for the die.

E(X²) = (1 + 4 + 9 + 16 + 25 + 36)/6 = 91/6 = 15.167
Var(X) = 15.167 - 12.25 = 2.917
sd = 1.708

Worked example 2. For X = 0, 1, 2 with probabilities 0.2, 0.5, 0.3, find Var(X).

E(X) = 1.1
E(X²) = 0 + 0.5 + 4(0.3) = 1.7
Var(X) = 1.7 - 1.21 = 0.49
sd = 0.7

Linear transformations

E(aX + b) = a E(X) + b
Var(aX + b) = a² Var(X)

sd(aX + b) = |a| sd(X)

The asymmetry is the key idea: adding a constant shifts every value and so shifts the mean but leaves the spread unchanged; multiplying by a scales the mean by a and the spread by |a|, so the variance scales by a².

Worked example. E(X) = 5, Var(X) = 4. Find E(3X + 2) and Var(3X + 2).

E = 3(5) + 2 = 17
Var = 9(4) = 36;  sd = 6

Worked example 2 (finding the transformation). E(Y) = 20 and Var(Y) = 25, where Y = aX + b, E(X) = 4 and Var(X) = 1. Find a and b.

Var: a² (1) = 25  →  a = 5 or -5
if a = 5: 20 = 5(4) + b  →  b = 0
if a = -5: 20 = -20 + b  →  b = 40
both are valid; the sign of a is fixed by context (a positive
scaling is usually implied)

Linear combinations of random variables

E(aX + bY) = a E(X) + b E(Y)          (always, no independence needed)
Var(aX + bY) = a² Var(X) + b² Var(Y)   (only if X, Y independent)
Var(aX - bY) = a² Var(X) + b² Var(Y)   (the variances still add)

The minus sign is where most marks are lost: subtracting random variables adds their variances, because the uncertainty compounds whichever direction the values move.

Worked example. X and Y are independent with E(X) = 10, Var(X) = 9, E(Y) = 4, Var(Y) = 4. Find E(X − Y) and Var(X − Y).

E(X - Y) = 10 - 4 = 6
Var(X - Y) = 9 + 4 = 13   (not 9 - 4)
sd = 3.606

Worked example 2 (three variables). Independent X, Y, Z with variances 2, 3, 5. Find Var(2X + 3Y − Z).

= 4(2) + 9(3) + 1(5) = 8 + 27 + 5 = 40

Worked example 3 (total of identical variables). A fair die is rolled twice; T is the total. Find E(T) and Var(T).

each roll: E = 3.5, Var = 35/12 = 2.917
E(T) = 7;  Var(T) = 2 × 2.917 = 5.833
sd(T) = 2.415  (the spread of a total grows, but by √(2), not 2)

Discrete uniform distribution

X uniform on 1..n: P(X = k) = 1/n
E(X) = (n + 1)/2
Var(X) = (n² - 1)/12

Worked example. X is uniform on 1 to 10. Find E(X) and Var(X).

E(X) = 11/2 = 5.5
Var(X) = (100 - 1)/12 = 8.25

Cumulative distribution functions

The cumulative distribution function F(x) gives the probability that X is at most x. It is a step function for a discrete variable: constant between values, jumping at each value by that value's probability.

F(x) = P(X <= x) = sum of P(X = k) for k <= x

P(X = k) = F(k) - F(k - 1)
P(a < X <= b) = F(b) - F(a)

Worked example. X takes 1, 2, 3 with probabilities 0.2, 0.5, 0.3. Write F(x) and use it to find P(X > 1).

F(1) = 0.2;  F(2) = 0.7;  F(3) = 1
P(X > 1) = 1 - F(1) = 0.8  (equivalently 0.5 + 0.3)

Worked example 2 (recovering probabilities). F(2) = 0.35 and F(3) = 0.8. Find P(X = 3).

P(X = 3) = F(3) - F(2) = 0.8 - 0.35 = 0.45

Reading F correctly requires attention to the inequality: P(X < 3) = F(2) for a discrete variable, while P(X ≤ 3) = F(3). One unit of difference changes the answer.

Expectation from a table and applied profit

When the distribution is given as a table, the calculation is a single weighted total; when it is described in words, the table must be built first.

Worked example. A fair coin is tossed three times and X counts the heads. Find E(X) and Var(X).

X ~ Binomial(3, 1/2) in effect: probabilities 1/8, 3/8, 3/8, 1/8 for 0..3
E(X) = 0 + 3/8 + 6/8 + 3/8 = 12/8 = 1.5
E(X²) = 0 + 3/8 + 12/8 + 9/8 = 24/8 = 3
Var(X) = 3 - 2.25 = 0.75

Worked example 2 (profit). A stall pays 4 pounds to play a game that returns 0, 5 or 20 pounds with probabilities 0.6, 0.3 and 0.1. Find the expected profit per game and whether the stall makes money.

E(return) = 0 + 1.5 + 2.0 = 3.5
profit = return - 4, so E(profit) = 3.5 - 4 = -0.5
players lose 50 pence per game on average, so the stall profits

The transformation rule does the work: E(X − c) = E(X) − c. State the interpretation, not just the number.

Why variances add for independent variables

For independent X and Y, the variance of a sum is the sum of the variances. The proof rests on the fact that independence makes E(XY) = E(X)E(Y), so the cross term in the expansion vanishes:

Var(X + Y) = E[(X + Y)²] - [E(X + Y)]^2
           = E(X²) + 2E(XY) + E(Y²) - [E(X)]^2 - 2E(X)E(Y) - [E(Y)]^2
independence: E(XY) = E(X)E(Y), so the cross terms cancel
           = Var(X) + Var(Y)

For the difference, the same expansion gives Var(X − Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y): the cross term is −2E(XY) + 2E(X)E(Y), which also vanishes. The intuition is that independent errors cannot cancel — a positive error in one is just as likely to meet a positive or negative error in the other, so the uncertainties compound.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Valid distribution) P(X = 1) = 0.3, P(X = 2) = 0.4, P(X = 3) = k. Find k. Answer: ΣP(X = x) = 1, so k = 1 − 0.3 − 0.4 = 0.3.
  2. (E) X = 1, 3, 5 with probabilities 0.2, 0.5, 0.3. Find E(X). Answer: E(X) = ΣxP(X = x) = 1(0.2) + 3(0.5) + 5(0.3) = 0.2 + 1.5 + 1.5 = 3.2.
  3. (Var) For the same X, find Var(X). Answer: Var(X) = Σx²P(X = x) − [E(X)]² = 1(0.2) + 9(0.5) + 25(0.3) − 3.2² = 0.2 + 4.5 + 7.5 − 10.24 = 1.96.
  4. (Transform) E(X) = 6, Var(X) = 5. Find E(4X − 1) and Var(4X − 1). Answer: E(4X − 1) = 4E(X) − 1 = 24 − 1 = 23; Var(4X − 1) = 4²Var(X) = 16 × 5 = 80.
  5. (Combination) Independent X, Y: Var(X) = 6, Var(Y) = 8. Find Var(2X + Y). Answer: Var(2X + Y) = 2²Var(X) + Var(Y) = 4(6) + 8 = 32 — the variances add because X and Y are independent, and the constant is squared.
  6. (Combination difference) Same X, Y: Var(X − Y). Answer: 6 + 8 = 14.
  7. (Uniform) X uniform on 1..6. Find Var(X). Answer: (36 − 1)/12 = 2.917.
  8. (Applied) A game pays X with E(X) = 2 and costs 3 to play. Find the expected profit. Answer: E(X − 3) = −1, a loss of 1 per game.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Var(aX) = a Var(X): wrong — the variance scales by a², the standard deviation by |a|.
  • Subtracting variances: Var(X − Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) for independent variables; subtraction never reduces uncertainty.
  • Assuming independence: the variance-addition rule requires it; the expectation rule does not.
  • Using E(X²) as [E(X)]²: they differ by the variance; compute E(X²) from the distribution.
  • Probabilities not summing to 1: the first check on any distribution, and often the way to find an unknown constant.
  • Expectation as a possible value: E(X) need not be attainable (3.5 on a die); say "on average over many trials".
  • Standard deviation units: the variance is in squared units; compare and quote the sd.
  • Negative scaling: if a is negative, E flips sign and sd uses |a|; forgetting the modulus produces a negative standard deviation.

Formula summary

E(X) = sum of x P(X = x);  E(X²) = sum of x² P(X = x)
Var(X) = E(X²) - [E(X)]^2
E(aX + b) = a E(X) + b;  Var(aX + b) = a² Var(X)
E(aX + bY) = a E(X) + b E(Y)
Var(aX + bY) = a² Var(X) + b² Var(Y)   (independent)
F(x) = P(X <= x);  P(X = k) = F(k) - F(k - 1)

Two conditions separate the whole topic: expectations always combine linearly, variances combine linearly only when the variables are independent — and then always with plus signs, whatever the signs in front of the variables. Write the condition before applying the variance rule; it is worth a mark on its own and prevents the commonest mistake in the topic.

Equations and symbols

The whole topic is four rules and one warning: expectation always combines linearly, variance combines linearly only for independent variables, and adding or subtracting them always adds the variances. Write the independence condition before you apply a variance rule — it is worth a mark on its own.

E(X) = sum of x P(X = x) Key: E(X) = the expected value, the long-run average of X (same units as X); x = each possible value; P(X = x) = its probability. The value need not be attainable — 3.5 on a die is the standard example.

Var(X) = E(X²) - [E(X)]^2 Key: Var(X) = the variance, in squared units of X; E(X²) = the sum of x²P(X = x); [E(X)]² is the square of the mean, not the mean itself. The standard deviation is the square root and is back in the data's units.

E(aX + b) = a E(X) + b Key: a = the multiplier applied to every value (no units); b = the constant added to every value (X's units); E(X) = the mean before the change. Shifting every value shifts the mean by exactly the same amount.

Var(aX + b) = a² Var(X) Key: a = the multiplier; b = the constant shift, which does not appear at all because shifting every value leaves the spread unchanged. The variance scales by a², the standard deviation by the modulus of a — quoting a Var(aX) = a Var(X) loses the mark.

E(aX + bY) = a E(X) + b E(Y) Key: X, Y = two random variables; a, b = constants; this holds always, with or without independence, and it is the rule most often needed in applied questions.

Var(aX + bY) = a² Var(X) + b² Var(Y) Key: valid only when X and Y are independent, and the plus sign is unconditional — the variances add however the variables are combined, because uncertainties never cancel.

Var(aX - bY) = a² Var(X) + b² Var(Y) Key: the same rule for a difference: the sign in front of Y affects the expectation and not the variance. Var(X − Y) = 9 + 4 = 13, never 9 − 4.

F(x) = P(X <= x) = sum of P(X = k) for k <= x Key: F(x) = the cumulative distribution function, a probability (no units, between 0 and 1); x = the value asked about; k runs over every possible value at most x. For a discrete variable F is a step function, constant between values and jumping at each one.

P(X = k) = F(k) - F(k - 1) Key: recovers a single probability from the cumulative function; mind the inequality, because P(X < 3) = F(2) while P(X ≤ 3) = F(3) for a discrete variable.

E(X) = (n + 1)/2 and Var(X) = (n² - 1)/12 Key: for a discrete uniform distribution on 1 to n: n = the number of equally likely values (no units); the mean and variance follow from n alone. A fair die has n = 6, so E(X) = 3.5 and Var(X) = 35/12.

title: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Transformations and Vectors
content:
Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Transformations and Vectors

Transformations move shapes on a grid, and vectors describe those moves with numbers. The exam asks two things: perform a transformation and, more often, describe one completely — with its centre, angle, direction, line or scale factor. This note builds the topic from zero: the four transformations and the full-description checklist for each, enlargement and its effect on area, vector notation with the house column-vector form (x; y), vector arithmetic, and the vector-geometry proofs that show lines are parallel or points are collinear.

The four transformations

TransformationWhat changesWhat must be stated in a description
Translationposition only, no rotation or resizethe column vector of the move
Reflectionmirror imagethe line of reflection (e.g. x = 2, y = x)
Rotationturns about a pointcentre, angle, and direction (clockwise or anticlockwise)
Enlargementresizes about a pointcentre and scale factor

The complete description is the mark: "rotation" alone scores nothing; "rotation 90° anticlockwise about (2, 1)" scores fully.

Translation

A translation moves every point by the same vector. In column form (x; y), x is the horizontal move and y the vertical move; right and up are positive.

Worked example. Triangle A has vertices (1, 1), (3, 1), (1, 4). Translate by (4; −2) and give the image coordinates.

(1, 1) → (5, -1)
(3, 1) → (7, -1)
(1, 4) → (5, 2)

The shape is congruent to the original (same size and shape), and the orientation is unchanged.

Reflection

A reflection flips a shape across a line; the line is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining each point to its image. Common lines: x = a (vertical), y = b (horizontal), y = x, y = −x.

Worked example. Reflect the point (3, 5) in the line y = x.

reflection in y = x swaps the coordinates: (3, 5) → (5, 3)

Worked example 2. Reflect (2, 4) in the line x = 1.

the line x = 1 is vertical; the distance of x = 2 from it is 1,
so the image is 1 unit on the other side: (0, 4)

To find the mirror line from a shape and its image, join a point to its image and draw the perpendicular bisector of that segment.

Rotation

A rotation turns a shape about a fixed centre through a given angle. The four standard angles are 90° and 180° in either direction; 90° clockwise equals 270° anticlockwise.

Worked example. Rotate the point (3, 1) 90° clockwise about the origin.

90 ° clockwise about O: (x, y) → (y, -x)
(3, 1) → (1, -3)

Worked example 2. Rotate (2, 5) 180° about the origin.

180 °: (x, y) → (-x, -y)
(2, 5) → (-2, -5)

For a centre other than the origin, translate the centre to the origin, rotate, then translate back — or count the grid squares from the centre.

Enlargement

An enlargement with centre C and scale factor k maps every point so that its distance from C is multiplied by k. Negative scale factors put the image on the far side of the centre; fractional factors between 0 and 1 shrink the shape.

image distance from centre = k x object distance from centre
area of image = k² x area of object

Worked example. Enlarge the point (2, 3) by scale factor 3 about the origin.

(2, 3) → (6, 9)

Worked example 2 (area). A triangle of area 12 cm² is enlarged by scale factor 2.5. Find the image area.

area factor = k² = 6.25
new area = 12 × 6.25 = 75 cm²

Enlargement is the only transformation that changes area (unless k = 1 or −1); translations, reflections and rotations preserve both shape and size.

Vectors: notation and magnitude

A vector has magnitude and direction. In this course it is written as a column vector (x; y): x is the horizontal component, y the vertical. The same vector can be written as a bold letter a with an arrow above it.

column vector (x; y)
magnitude = √(x² + y²)
direction angle to the horizontal: tan(θ) = y/x
equal vectors have the same components; opposite vectors
negate both components

Worked example. Find the magnitude and direction of the vector (3; 4).

magnitude = √(9 + 16) = 5
tan(θ) = 4/3  →  θ = 53.1 ° above the horizontal

Vector arithmetic and geometry

addition: (a; b) + (c; d) = (a + c; b + d)
subtraction: (a; b) - (c; d) = (a - c; b - d)
scalar multiple: k(a; b) = (ka; kb)

position vector of A relative to O: OA
AB = OB - OA
midpoint of AB: (OA + OB)/2

Worked example. OA = (2; 1), OB = (7; 5). Find AB and the midpoint of AB.

AB = OB - OA = (7 - 2; 5 - 1) = (5; 4)
midpoint = ((2 + 7)/2; (1 + 5)/2) = (4.5; 3)

Worked example 2 (parallel). Show that AB is parallel to CD given A(1, 2), B(5, 8), C(0, 1), D(6, 10).

AB = (5 - 1; 8 - 2) = (4; 6)
CD = (6 - 0; 10 - 1) = (6; 9)
(6; 9) = 1.5 x (4; 6), so CD = 1.5 AB: parallel (and longer)

Parallel vectors are scalar multiples of each other; collinear points occur when AB and AC (or AB and BC) are parallel and share a point.

Combining transformations and invariant points

Two transformations applied in sequence are not the same as the reverse order: a reflection followed by a rotation generally differs from the rotation followed by the reflection. When a question asks for the single transformation equivalent to two, apply both to a convenient point (the origin or a vertex) and to a second point, then identify the transformation that maps the original to the final image. Invariant points are points that do not move: every point on a mirror line is invariant under a reflection, the centre of a rotation is invariant, and no point is invariant under a translation.

Worked example. A shape is reflected in the x-axis and then translated by (0; 3). Find the image of (2, 1) and identify any invariant points.

reflection in the x-axis: (2, 1) → (2, -1)
translation by (0; 3): (2, -1) → (2, 2)
No invariant points: the reflection moved every point off the
axis, and the translation then moved everything upward.

Worked example 2 (invariant line). State the invariant points of a reflection in the line y = 2.

Every point with y-coordinate 2 lies on the mirror line and does
not move: the whole line y = 2 is invariant.

Vectors in context: displacement and velocity

Column vectors describe any quantity with magnitude and direction in two dimensions: displacement (a move from one point to another), velocity (displacement per second) and force (a push in a direction). The arithmetic is identical; only the interpretation changes.

  • Displacement: AB is the vector from A to B; a round trip returns to the start, so the sum of the vectors around a closed polygon is zero.
  • Velocity: a velocity vector (3; −2) means 3 units per second right and 2 units per second down; position after t seconds is the starting position plus t × velocity.
  • Resultant: the sum of two vectors; a vector and its negative cancel.

Worked example. A particle starts at (1, 2) and moves with velocity (3; −1) for 4 seconds. Find its final position.

displacement = 4 x (3; -1) = (12; -4)
final position = (1 + 12; 2 - 4) = (13; -2)

Worked examples: vector proofs

Worked example. In triangle OAB, P is the midpoint of OA and Q is the midpoint of OB. Prove PQ is parallel to AB.

OP = (1/2) OA, OQ = (1/2) OB
PQ = OQ - OP = (1/2)(OB - OA) = (1/2) AB
PQ is a scalar multiple of AB, so PQ is parallel to AB
(and half its length).

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Translation) Translate (2, 3) by (−1; 4). Answer: add the translation vector: (2, 3) + (−1, 4) = (2 − 1, 3 + 4) = (1, 7).
  2. (Reflection) Reflect (4, 1) in the x-axis. Answer: reflection in the x-axis negates the y-coordinate: x′ = x = 4 and y′ = −y = −1, so the image is (4, −1).
  3. (Rotation) Rotate (5, 2) 90° anticlockwise about the origin. Answer: a 90° anticlockwise turn about the origin maps (x, y) → (−y, x): x′ = −y = −2 and y′ = x = 5, so the image is (−2, 5).
  4. (Enlargement) Enlarge (1, 2) by factor −2 about the origin. Answer: enlargement about the origin maps (x, y) → k(x, y) with k = −2, so (1, 2) becomes (−2, −4); the negative factor puts the image on the opposite side of the centre.
  5. (Description) Describe fully the transformation mapping (1, 1) to (3, 5). Answer: translation vector = image − object = (3 − 1; 5 − 1) = (2; 4), so translation by (2; 4) — one of many correct complete descriptions.
  6. (Magnitude) Find the magnitude of (6; 8). Answer: |v| = √(x² + y²) = √(6² + 8²) = √(36 + 64) = √100 = 10.
  7. (Position vectors) OA = (1; 4), OB = (5; 2). Find AB. Answer: AB = OB − OA = (5; 2) − (1; 4) = (5 − 1; 2 − 4) = (4; −2).
  8. (Collinear) Show A(1, 1), B(3, 4), C(7, 10) are collinear. Answer: AB = (2; 3), AC = (6; 9) = 3 AB — parallel and share A, so collinear.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Incomplete descriptions: "enlargement by 2" omits the centre and loses marks; "reflection" omits the line. State every attribute.
  • Direction of rotation: clockwise and anticlockwise are different transformations; a 90° rotation clockwise is not the same as anticlockwise.
  • Area under enlargement: area scales by k², not k. Doubling the sides quadruples the area.
  • Vector direction: AB = OB − OA, not OA − OB. Reversing the subtraction negates the vector.
  • Column order: (x; y) is horizontal then vertical. Swapping produces a reflection in y = x, not the intended vector.
  • Parallelogram assumptions: equal magnitudes do not imply equal vectors — direction matters too.
  • Negative scale factors: the image lies on the opposite side of the centre; it is not simply "smaller".
  • Collinearity proof: showing parallel is not enough — the segments must also share a point. State it.

Translations: moving a shape without changing it

A translation slides every point of a shape the same distance in the same direction. The shape keeps its size, its shape and its orientation, so the image is congruent to the object. The description needs a column vector, written (x; y), where x is the movement to the right and y is the movement up. Negative values move left or down.

Reading a column vector

The vector (3; −2) means move 3 units to the right and 2 units down. Read the top number first, as the horizontal movement, and the bottom number second, as the vertical movement. Swapping the two numbers is one of the most common errors, and it moves the shape to a completely different place.

Translating a point

To translate a point, add the vector to its coordinates. The point A(1, 4) under the translation (3; −2) becomes A′(1 + 3, 4 − 2) = A′(4, 2). Work out each coordinate separately and check that the sign of each movement is right before you write the answer.

Translating a whole shape

A triangle is translated by translating each of its three vertices and joining the new points with straight lines. Drawing only one vertex, or moving the shape by eye, loses the mark. Check the result by counting the squares between each object point and its image: every pair should show the same horizontal and vertical movement.

Working backwards from an image

A question may give the image and ask for the vector. Take one point and its image, and find the change in x and the change in y. If P(2, 5) maps to P′(7, 1), the vector is (7 − 2; 1 − 5) = (5; −4). Check with a second point before you write the vector down.

Translations and the notation of the answer

The answer to a translation question must give the vector, not a verbal description alone. "Move 5 right and 4 down" is acceptable in words, but the examiner expects the column vector form (5; −4), which is what the syllabus asks for. Write it in brackets with a semicolon between the two numbers.

Common errors with translations

The commonest errors are reversing the direction of the movement, moving only the x-coordinate, and rotating the shape by mistake when a translation was asked for. A translation never turns the shape over and never changes its size, so an image that looks rotated or stretched is wrong. Check each answer against the rule that the shape is unchanged.

Reflections: the mirror line and the image

A reflection flips a shape over a mirror line. Every point of the image is the same distance from the mirror line as the matching point of the object, on the opposite side. The size and shape are unchanged, but the orientation is reversed. A full description needs the equation of the mirror line, and a mark is lost for any answer that names no line.

Reflection in the x-axis and y-axis

Reflection in the x-axis sends (x, y) to (x, −y), so the sign of the y-coordinate changes. Reflection in the y-axis sends (x, y) to (−x, y). Learn these two rules as fixed facts, because they are the quickest marks in the topic.

Reflection in a line such as y = x

Reflection in the line y = x swaps the two coordinates: (x, y) maps to (y, x). Reflection in y = −x sends (x, y) to (−y, −x). Test a single point to confirm the rule before you apply it to the whole shape, since a sign slip here changes every vertex.

Using the perpendicular distance

For a mirror line that is not a standard axis, each point of the image lies on the perpendicular from the object point to the line, at the same distance beyond the line. Draw the perpendicular with a set square so the image is placed accurately, and count the squares on each side to check.

Finding the mirror line from an object and image

When the question asks for the mirror line, join each point to its image. All those joining lines are parallel, and the mirror line is the perpendicular bisector of each joining segment. Read the line from the diagram, then give its equation, for example x = 2 or y = x.

Invariant points under reflection

A point is invariant under a reflection if it does not move, which happens when it lies on the mirror line. Any point on the mirror line maps to itself, so it is a useful check: if a vertex you expected to stay fixed has moved, the reflection has been drawn in the wrong place.

Common errors with reflections

The commonest errors are reflecting in the wrong axis, giving the mirror line as a point rather than a line, and forgetting that the image is the reverse of the object. A reflection that leaves the shape the same way round as the object is a translation or a rotation, not a reflection, so check the orientation of the image.

Rotations: centre, angle and direction

A rotation turns a shape about a fixed point, the centre of rotation, through a given angle in a given direction. The size and shape are unchanged. A complete description has three parts: the centre, the angle and the direction, and a mark is lost for any part that is missing.

The three parts of a rotation

Write the rotation as "rotation through 90° clockwise about (0, 0)". Omitting the centre, or describing the rotation without its direction, does not earn the full mark even when the image is drawn correctly.

Clockwise and anticlockwise

Anticlockwise is the positive direction in mathematics, and clockwise is the negative. Confirm the direction by tracing the movement of one vertex from its object position to its image before you finalise the answer. Many lost marks come from drawing the image in the opposite direction.

Rotations about the origin by 90° and 180°

A 90° anticlockwise rotation about the origin sends (x, y) to (−y, x). A 180° rotation sends (x, y) to (−x, −y). A 90° clockwise rotation sends (x, y) to (y, −x). Check the rule on one vertex before you draw the whole image.

Rotating a shape by drawing

To rotate a shape by drawing, measure the distance from each vertex to the centre, and rotate the line through the given angle. Use tracing paper or a protractor, and check that every vertex is the same distance from the centre as its original. A vertex that lies at a different distance has been placed wrongly.

Finding the centre of rotation

When the question gives the object and the image and asks for the centre, the centre is the point that is the same distance from an object point and its image. Draw the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining a point to its image, and repeat with a second point. The two bisectors cross at the centre.

Common errors with rotations

The commonest errors are rotating about the wrong point, using the wrong sign for the angle, and changing the size of the shape. A rotation keeps every length the same, so a rotated image that looks bigger or smaller than the object has been enlarged, and the answer is wrong.

Equations and symbols

Every transformation is a coordinate map, and every vector is a column pair. Learn the four rotation maps and the two vector rules, and the topic is arithmetic.

90 ° clockwise about O: (x, y) → (y, -x) Key: (x, y) = the original coordinates; the arrow points to the image's coordinates; O = the origin, the fixed centre. Anticlockwise is the same map with the signs reversed — write the centre down, because a rotation about any other point is not this formula.

180 °: (x, y) → (-x, -y) Key: both coordinates change sign; a half-turn is the only rotation that is also a translation-free "point reflection" in the origin. Check with a point on an axis, where one coordinate stays zero.

reflection in y = x swaps the coordinates: (3, 5) → (5, 3) Key: the line y = x is the mirror; swapping means the image of (x, y) is (y, x). The line is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining each point to its image, which is the definition to quote.

(1, 1) → (5, -1) Key: left = a vertex of the object; right = the matching vertex of the image. Subtract to read off the translation: 5 − 1 = 4 across and −1 − 1 = −2 down, so the column vector is (4; −2).

(3, 1) → (1, -3) Key: this is a 90° clockwise turn about the origin applied to a second vertex — the same map, different numbers. With two vertices mapped you can describe the transformation fully rather than guessing from one.

title: Nuclear Physics
content:
Nuclear Physics

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2023–2025): nuclear model, radioactivity, decay types, half-life, safety, fission/fusion (Extended).

1. The nuclear model

Nucleus (protons +, neutrons 0) with orbiting electrons (−). Nuclide notation ᴬ_Z X. Isotopes: same Z, different A. Rutherford scattering established the nuclear model; proton number Z, nucleon number A.

2. Radiation types

TypeNatureRange (air)Stopped by
alpha αhelium nucleus (2p2n)few cmpaper
beta β⁻fast electron~20–30 cmfew mm aluminium
gamma γEM wavevery farthick lead/concrete

Deflection in fields: α/β opposite, γ none. Ionising: α > β > γ. Background radiation: radon, cosmic, rocks, medical, fallout.

3. Decay equations

  • α: A −4, Z −2 (e.g. ²³⁸₉₂U → ²³⁴₉₀Th + α).
  • β⁻: neutron → proton; A same, Z +1 (e.g. ¹⁴₆C → ¹⁴₇N + β⁻).
  • γ: no change to A or Z.

Balance A and Z on both sides — that is the check.

4. Half-life

Time for half the unstable nuclei to decay (random process). Read from a decay curve or count halves: 80 → 40 → 20 over two half-lives.

Example: 800 Bq, half-life 2 h → 200 Bq after 4 h.

5. Safety and uses

Uses: medical tracers (β/γ), sterilisation, thickness gauge (β), dating (C-14), smoke alarms (α). Safety: distance, time, shielding, wear badges, store in lead. Handle with tongs; never point at people.

6. Fission and fusion (Extended)

Fission: heavy nucleus splits (U-235 + neutron), chain reaction controlled by moderators/control rods — power stations. Fusion: light nuclei join (stellar) — needs huge T/P; releases more energy per kg; no long-lived waste.

title: IGCSE Computer Science: Networking and Data Transmission
content:
IGCSE Computer Science: Networking and Data Transmission

Cambridge IGCSE Computer Science 0478 (2026–2028), Paper 1 Computer Systems: statement 2.1 Types and methods of data transmission, 2.2 Methods of error detection, 2.3 Encryption, and 3.4 Network hardware. This note explains how data travels between machines — the modes and media it moves over, how errors in transit are spotted and fixed, how it is kept secret from eavesdroppers, and the hardware that carries it. Every parity bit and checksum below is worked line by line, because Paper 1 asks you to produce the check bits, not just name the method.

Why network computers at all

Networking lets machines share resources and communicate: shared files, printers and internet connections; centralised backup and security; email and messaging; and collaboration on the same data. The three sizes you must distinguish: a LAN (local area network) covers one site — a school or office — over its own cabling; a WLAN is a LAN using wireless links; a WAN (wide area network) spans many sites over public infrastructure such as telephone lines and fibre, with the internet the largest WAN of all.

Two ways to organise a LAN. In a client–server network, dedicated servers hold shared files, user accounts and backups, and clients request services from them: central control, easy backups, better security, but expensive hardware and an administrator is required — a server failure can stop everyone. In a peer-to-peer network every computer is equal and shares its own resources: cheap and simple, but no central control, each machine backed up separately, and security is harder to enforce.

Serial and parallel transmission

Serial sends one bit at a time down a single wire (or channel). It needs fewer wires, so it is cheaper and works over long distances without the signals interfering with each other; modern systems use serial links for almost everything outside the chip (USB, Ethernet, SATA). Parallel sends several bits at once — one per wire. It looks faster, and is over very short distances such as the paths inside a computer, but over long cables the wires pick up each other's signals (crosstalk) and the pulses arrive at slightly different times (skew), so the receiving end misreads them. Memory buses and internal data paths stay parallel; anything long-distance is serial.

Simplex, half-duplex and full-duplex

ModeDirectionExample
SimplexOne direction onlyKeyboard to computer; a TV broadcast
Half-duplexBoth directions, but one way at a timeWalkie-talkie; older Ethernet hubs
Full-duplexBoth directions simultaneouslyTelephone call; modern switched Ethernet

Two more distinctions the syllabus names. Synchronous transmission sends a continuous stream of data with a shared clock signal synchronising sender and receiver — fast and efficient for large transfers. Asynchronous transmission sends one character at a time wrapped in a start bit and stop bit (with a parity bit), so no shared clock is needed; it is slower because of the overhead but simple and cheap for bursty traffic such as a keyboard. Baseband means the whole medium carries a single digital signal (ordinary Ethernet); broadband splits the medium into several frequency channels so different signals travel at once (the cable TV and ADSL line into a house).

Transmission media

MediumHow it carries dataStrengthsWeaknesses
Twisted pair (Ethernet cable)Electrical pulses in paired copper wiresCheap, easy to install, fine for LANsLimited distance and speed; electrical interference
Coaxial cableElectrical pulses in a shielded copper coreBetter shielding than twisted pair; TV and cable networksThicker, dearer, still limited bandwidth compared with fibre
Fibre opticPulses of laser light down glass fibresHuge bandwidth, very long distances, immune to electrical interference, hard to tapExpensive; needs specialist skills to join and repair
Wireless (radio, microwave, infrared)Electromagnetic waves through the airMobility; no cabling costInterference and obstacles; slower; eavesdropping risk; coverage limits

Bandwidth is the maximum data rate of a link, in bits per second (bps, kbps, Mbps, Gbps) — the width of the pipe. Latency is the delay before data arrives. High bandwidth with high latency still feels sluggish: size of pipe versus distance the water travels. Time to send a file is roughly file size in bits divided by bandwidth:

Worked example: how long to send a 45 MB file over an 8 Mbps link?

45 MB = 45 × 8 = 360 megabits                [bytes to bits: multiply by 8]
360 / 8 = 45 seconds

Note the two eights doing different jobs: one converts bytes to bits,
the other is the 8 Mbps bandwidth. Confusing them is the classic error.

Error detection: parity

Signals degrade in transit — crosstalk, interference, dirty connectors — so receiving systems must check whether what arrived is what was sent. The simplest method, parity checking, appends one extra bit (the parity bit) to each byte so that the number of 1-bits in the group is always odd (odd parity) or always even (even parity). The sender works the bit out; the receiver recounts.

Send 0110 1011 with EVEN parity.

Count the 1-bits: 0+1+1+0+1+0+1+1 = 5 ones (odd).
For the group to have an even number of ones, the parity bit must be 1.
Transmitted byte (with parity bit at the front): 1 0110 1011

Now suppose one bit is flipped in transit: 1 0010 1011.
The receiver counts the ones: 1+0+0+1+0+1+0+1+1 = 5 (odd), but even parity was
agreed, so an error is detected and the byte is retransmitted.

With ODD parity for the same byte, the parity bit would be 0 (already 5 ones),
and the receiver expects an odd total.

Parity catches any single bit flip (the total changes parity), but two flips cancel out and pass unnoticed — a limitation worth a mark on its own.

Error detection: checksums

A checksum covers a whole block of data rather than one byte. The sender adds the data values together and sends the sum (or its complement) with the block; the receiver repeats the addition and compares. A corrupted value gives a different total.

Send the block 25, 47, 12 with a checksum.

Sender: 25 + 47 + 12 = 84. Transmit 25, 47, 12, 84.
Suppose 47 is corrupted to 48.
Receiver: 25 + 48 + 12 = 85, which does not match the received checksum 84:
error detected, request retransmission.

A plain sum can miss compensating errors (25 up by 1 and 12 down by 1), so real
systems use the one's complement of the sum, which catches more patterns.

Checksums detect most multi-bit errors in a block but not all; they are used together with retransmission (below), not instead of it.

Error correction and ARQ

Automatic repeat request (ARQ) is the protocol that turns detection into recovery. The receiver acknowledges each correctly received packet with an ACK; a corrupted packet gets a NAK (negative acknowledgement), and the sender resends it. If the packet or its ACK is lost entirely, the sender's timeout expires and it resends anyway. Sequence numbers on packets let the receiver spot duplicates caused by those resends and discard them. Stop-and-wait ARQ sends one packet and waits for its ACK before the next; continuous ARQ keeps a window of packets flowing and retransmits only the missing ones — faster on long links.

Error-correcting codes go further: extra bits are added so the receiver can repair a single-bit error without retransmission (vital where no return channel exists, such as on CDs). The trade-off in every method: more check bits means more reliability and less room for data.

Encryption

Anything crossing a network can be intercepted, so sensitive data is encrypted: the readable plain text is scrambled by an algorithm (a cipher) using a key into unreadable cipher text; the receiver uses a key to decrypt it back. The algorithm is public — the security lives in the key, like a lock whose design everyone knows but whose key you alone hold.

Symmetric encryptionAsymmetric encryption
KeysOne shared secret key for both encrypting and decryptingA matched pair: a public key (encrypts) and a private key (decrypts)
SpeedFast, suited to bulk dataSlow, suited to short messages and key exchange
ProblemGetting the shared key to the other party securely in the first placeNothing is secret to distribute, but the private key must be kept safe
ExamplesAES, DESRSA

Real systems combine them: HTTPS uses the asymmetric pair to agree a symmetric session key, then encrypts the whole conversation with the fast cipher. Hashing is a third tool — a one-way function producing a fixed-length value (the hash) from any input; it cannot be reversed, so passwords are stored as hashes (with a salt against rainbow tables) and any change to a message changes its hash, proving integrity. Digital certificates issued by certificate authorities bind a public key to a real identity, so a browser knows it is talking to the genuine bank and not an impostor.

Network hardware (statement 3.4)

  • Network interface card (NIC) — gives a device a network connection and a MAC address; it frames data onto the medium.
  • Switch — connects devices within a LAN and forwards each frame only to the port holding the destination MAC address; filters traffic and reduces collisions.
  • Router — connects different networks (your LAN to the internet) and forwards packets between them by choosing the best path using IP addresses.
  • Wireless access point — lets Wi-Fi devices join the wired LAN.
  • Hub — an older, simple repeater broadcasting every frame to all ports; largely replaced by switches.

Two addresses appear in exam answers and they belong to different layers: the MAC address is the permanent hardware identifier of a NIC used within a LAN, while the IP address is the logical address of a device on a network, used by routers to deliver packets across networks. Domains and DNS sit on top of that (see the internet note).

Worked example: a school LAN sends a file from room 1 to a server.

The file is split into numbered packets. Each packet is given the server's IP
address. The sending switch looks up the server's MAC address and forwards the
frame within the LAN. Along the way each packet may take a different route;
the server uses the sequence numbers to reassemble the file in order, and ACKs
any packet that fails its checksum so the sender retransmits only that packet.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Saying parity "corrects" errors; parity detects most single-bit errors — correction needs error-correcting codes or retransmission.
  • Getting the parity bit backwards: count the existing ones first; even parity needs the total to be even, so an odd count means the parity bit is 1.
  • Claiming two flipped bits are detected by parity; they change the count by two, which parity cannot see.
  • Confusing bandwidth with latency, or forgetting to convert bytes to bits (×8) before dividing by a bits-per-second rate.
  • Describing a router's job as "connects computers in a LAN" — that is the switch; the router connects networks and routes packets by IP address.
  • Swapping MAC and IP: MAC is fixed hardware identity on a LAN; IP is logical and can change, and is what routing uses.
  • Saying symmetric encryption is more secure than asymmetric (or vice versa); they are secure in different ways — the exam wants the key-distribution and speed trade-off.
  • Forgetting the timeout case in ARQ questions: a lost packet or lost ACK is recovered by the sender's timer, not by a NAK.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 1, 4 marks). Describe the difference between serial and parallel transmission and state one use for each.

Answer: Serial transmission sends the bits of a byte one after another down a single channel, so it is cheaper, immune to crosstalk between wires and reliable over long distances — used for USB, Ethernet and all long-distance links. Parallel transmission sends several bits simultaneously down multiple channels, which is faster over short distances but suffers skew and crosstalk over long cables — used for data buses inside a computer.

Question 2 (Paper 1, 3 marks). The byte 1011 0010 is to be sent using odd parity. State the parity bit and the transmitted group.

Answer: The byte contains five 1-bits (odd). Odd parity requires an odd total, so the parity bit is 0 and the transmitted group is 0 1011 0010 (parity bit shown first).

Question 3 (Paper 1, 4 marks). Explain how ARQ recovers from (i) a corrupted packet and (ii) a lost packet.

Answer: (i) The receiver's checksum test fails, so it returns a NAK; the sender retransmits that packet. (ii) No packet arrives, so no ACK is returned; the sender's timeout expires and it retransmits. In both cases the packet carries a sequence number so the receiver can discard duplicates and reassemble the data in order.

Question 4 (Paper 1, 4 marks). Explain why a bank uses asymmetric encryption to start a secure connection but symmetric encryption to transfer the data.

Answer: Asymmetric encryption (a public/private key pair) needs no shared secret to be distributed, so the bank can safely agree a session key with any customer who encrypts with the bank's published public key — only the bank's private key decrypts it. That process is slow, so once the session key is agreed both sides switch to fast symmetric encryption for the bulk of the transaction, which is efficient for large amounts of data.

Question 5 (Paper 1, 2 marks). Calculate the time to send a 12 MB file over a 4 Mbps link.

Answer: 12 MB = 96 megabits (12 × 8), and 96 ÷ 4 = 24 seconds.

Question 6 (Paper 1, 4 marks). Compare a switch and a router in a school network.

Answer: A switch connects devices within the LAN and forwards each frame only to the port of the destination MAC address, keeping local traffic off the rest of the network. A router connects the school LAN to other networks such as the internet and forwards packets between them, choosing routes using IP addresses. A switch works within one network; a router works between networks.

With the data safely moved, the next question is what runs on the machines: the software and the operating system that manages everything.

title: Organic Chemistry: Arenes
content:
Organic Chemistry: Arenes

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH15, Topic 18. Benzene is an arene. Its delocalised ring of six pi electrons makes it stable, so it reacts by electrophilic substitution rather than addition.

Structure and stability

  • Benzene is C₆H₆ with a planar ring. All six C–C bonds are the same length (0.139 nm), intermediate between single and double bonds.
  • The measured enthalpy of hydrogenation is about −208 kJ mol⁻¹, compared with −360 kJ mol⁻¹ for a hypothetical cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene. The difference, about 150 kJ mol⁻¹, is the delocalisation energy.

Electrophilic substitution

  • The pi electron cloud is electron-rich, so the ring is a nucleophile and attacks electrophiles.
  • Nitration: concentrated HNO₃ and concentrated H₂SO₄ at about 50 °C. The electrophile is NO₂⁺, and nitrobenzene forms.
  • Halogenation: Br₂ with an AlBr₃ or FeBr₃ halogen carrier. The carrier polarises Br₂ to give Br⁺.
  • Friedel–Crafts alkylation uses a haloalkane and AlCl₃ to add an alkyl group. Friedel–Crafts acylation uses an acyl chloride and AlCl₃ to form a phenyl ketone.

Directing effects

  • Alkyl groups, including –CH₃, direct a second substituent to the 2- and 4- (ortho and para) positions.
  • A –NO₂ group directs to the 3- (meta) position.
  • –OH and –NH₂ are strongly activating: phenol reacts with bromine water at room temperature to give a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol.

Side-chain oxidation

  • Hot, acidified KMnO₄ oxidises an alkyl side chain on the ring to a carboxylic acid group. Methylbenzene forms benzoic acid.

Exam tip: when describing a mechanism, show the electrophile, the arenium intermediate with its positive charge spread over the ring, and the loss of H⁺ to restore the delocalised ring.

title: A Level Mathematics: Permutations and Combinations
content:
A Level Mathematics: Permutations and Combinations

Counting is the part of probability that requires no formula to start with, only a decision: does the order matter? Every question in this topic is answered by that one question. If order matters the count is a permutation; if it does not the count is a combination. Everything else — repetitions, restrictions, arrangements around a circle — is a variation on the same counting principle, and this note sets out each variation with the reasoning behind it.

The multiplication principle

If a choice can be made in a ways and, independently, a second choice in b ways, the pair can be made in a × b ways. That is the whole foundation; the formulas are shortcuts for repeated applications of it.

arrangements of n distinct objects in a row: n! = n x (n-1) x ... x 2 × 1
0! = 1 by convention, so that formulas stay consistent
choosing r from n with order: nPr = n!/(n - r)!
choosing r from n without order: nCr = n!/(r!(n - r)!)

Worked example. A password is 4 distinct letters from the 26-letter alphabet. How many passwords are possible?

order matters, so 26P4 = 26 × 25 × 24 × 23 = 358,800

Worked example 2 (no order). How many ways can 4 students be chosen from 26?

order does not matter, so 26C4 = 14,950

Worked example 3 (a leading zero is not allowed). A code uses four distinct digits from 0 to 9 and cannot begin with zero. How many codes?

first digit: 9 choices (1 to 9)
remaining three: 9P3 = 9 × 8 × 7 = 504
total = 9 × 504 = 4536

Worked example 4 (the link). Explain why nPr = nCr × r!.

every unordered selection of r objects can be arranged in r! orders
so counting ordered selections = counting unordered ones then arranging them

Deciding whether order matters

The decision is not about the words "choose" or "arrange" in the question — those are hints, not rules. The safe test is to imagine two selections differing only by swapping two items: if that counts as a different outcome, order matters.

SituationOrder?Count
finishing order of a raceyesnPr
a committee of 3nonCr
a 4-digit PINyespermutation, with repetition allowed
a hand of cardsnonCr
seating 5 people in a rowyes5!

Worked example. A team of 11 is chosen from 16 players, and one of the 11 is captain. Count the possibilities.

choose the 11: 16C11 = 4368
choose the captain from them: 11 ways
total = 4368 × 11 = 48,048

The multiplication principle is doing the work here: two independent choices, multiplied.

Repetition and identical items

When some objects are identical, arranging them as if all were distinct overcounts by the number of ways the identical ones can be swapped. Dividing by those factorials corrects it.

arrangements of n items with groups of identical items:
n!/(a! b! c! ...) where a, b, c are the group sizes
with repetition allowed, choosing r from n: n^r

Worked example. How many distinct arrangements of the letters in BANANA?

6 letters: B once, A three times, N twice
6!/(1! 3! 2!) = 720/12 = 60

Worked example 2 (repetition allowed). A 3-digit code uses digits 0-9, repeats allowed. How many codes?

10 × 10 × 10 = 1000
if repeats were not allowed: 10 × 9 × 8 = 720

Worked example 3 (identical plus restriction). How many arrangements of the letters of LEVEL begin with L?

fix L at the front; remaining letters E, V, E, L
that is 4 letters with E twice: 4!/2! = 12
but the leading L is one of the two Ls, so there is only one choice for the front
answer 12

Restrictions: the "glue" method

When certain items must be together, treat the group as a single object, arrange the objects, then arrange within the group. When certain items must not be together, count the total and subtract the "together" case.

together: glue the group, arrange the objects, multiply by the internal arrangements
not together: total arrangements minus the together arrangements
specific positions: fix those items first, then arrange the rest

Worked example. Five books, two of which must stand together, are arranged on a shelf. How many orders?

glue the pair: now 4 objects, arranged in 4! = 24 ways
the pair interchange in 2! = 2 ways
total = 48

Worked example 2 (not together). The same five books with the pair not together.

total arrangements = 5! = 120
together = 48
not together = 120 - 48 = 72

Worked example 3 (fixed positions). Four men and three women sit in a row of seven. How many arrangements have all three women together?

glue the women into one block: now 5 objects (4 men + block), 5! = 120
internal arrangements of the women: 3! = 6
total = 720

Circular arrangements

Around a circle, rotations of the same arrangement are not distinguishable, so fixing one item removes the rotational symmetry and the count drops by a factor of n.

n distinct items around a circle: (n - 1)!
a necklace (where reflection also counts as the same): (n - 1)!/2

Worked example. In how many ways can 6 people sit around a round table?

(6 - 1)! = 5! = 120

Worked example 2 (with a fixed seat). How many ways if one particular person must sit in a specified chair?

fix that person, arrange the other 5 around: 5! = 120
the specified chair removes the rotational freedom entirely, so the answer is unchanged here

Worked example 3 (two people together at a round table). Six people, two of whom must sit together.

glue the pair: 5 objects around a circle = 4! = 24
internal order of the pair: 2
total = 48

Combinations with conditions

Committee questions combine cases: choose so many from one group and so many from another, then add the disjoint alternatives. The discipline is to make the cases genuinely disjoint, or the same selection gets counted twice.

choose a from group A and b from group B: C(a-group, a) x C(b-group, b)
several allowed compositions: add the separate cases
at least one: total minus none

Worked example. From 6 men and 5 women, how many committees of 4 contain exactly 2 women?

choose 2 women from 5: 10
choose 2 men from 6: 15
total = 150

Worked example 2 (at least one). How many committees of 4 contain at least one woman?

total committees: 11C4 = 330
none: 6C4 = 15
at least one = 330 - 15 = 315

Worked example 3 (cases added). How many committees of 3 contain more women than men?

3 women: 5C3 = 10
2 women and 1 man: 5C2 × 6C1 = 10 × 6 = 60
total = 70

Counting inside probability

Combinations are usually the denominator of a probability question: count the favourable selections, count all selections, divide. Doing the counting separately from the probability keeps both parts clean and makes partial credit possible.

Worked example. A bag holds 5 red and 7 blue counters. Four are drawn at random. Find the probability of exactly 2 red.

total selections: 12C4 = 495
favourable: 5C2 × 7C2 = 10 × 21 = 210
probability = 210/495 = 0.4242

Worked example 2 (at least one). For the same bag, find the probability of at least one red.

complement: no red means all four blue
7C4 = 35
P(no red) = 35/495 = 0.0707
P(at least one red) = 1 - 0.0707 = 0.9293

Worked example 3 (order matters in the numerator). Three cards are drawn from a standard deck without replacement. Find the probability they are drawn in increasing order of value.

every set of three distinct cards has exactly one increasing order out of 3! orders
so the probability is 1/6, independent of the deck

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Factorial) Evaluate 7!. Answer: 7! = 7 × 6 × 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 5040.
  2. (Permutation) In how many orders can 5 runners finish? Answer: 5P5 = 5! = 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 120.
  3. (Combination) Evaluate 10C3. Answer: 10C3 = 10!/(3! × 7!) = (10 × 9 × 8)/(3 × 2 × 1) = 720/6 = 120.
  4. (Choice) From 8 books, how many ways to choose 3? Answer: 8C3 = 8!/(3! × 5!) = (8 × 7 × 6)/(3 × 2 × 1) = 336/6 = 56.
  5. (Arrangement) How many arrangements of the letters of STATISTICS? Answer: 10!/(3! × 3! × 2!) = 3 628 800/(6 × 6 × 2) = 3 628 800/72 = 50,400.
  6. (Glue) 6 people in a row with two together: Answer: glue the pair: 5! × 2! = 120 × 2 = 240.
  7. (Not together) Same 6, not together: Answer: total − together = 6! − 5! × 2! = 720 − 240 = 480.
  8. (Circle) 7 people around a table: Answer: (n − 1)! = 6! = 720.
  9. (Committee) 3 from 5 men and 4 women, exactly 2 men: Answer: 5C2 × 4C1 = 10 × 4 = 40.
  10. (At least) 4 from the same 9 with at least one woman: Answer: all − none = 9C4 − 5C4 = 126 − 5 = 121.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Using nPr where order does not matter: a committee is unordered; using permutations overcounts by r!.
  • Forgetting to divide by repeated factorials: identical letters need the divisor or the count is inflated.
  • Glue method without the internal factor: the block also has an internal arrangement, and dropping the 2! halves the answer.
  • Circular arrangements with n! instead of (n − 1)!: rotations are the same seating.
  • Adding what should be multiplied: independent stages multiply; alternative cases add.
  • Overlapping cases: cases must be disjoint, or selections are counted twice.
  • "At least one" counted directly: the complement is almost always faster and safer.
  • Restrictions applied after the count: fix the restricted positions first, then count what remains.

Equations and symbols

Every formula here is a shortcut for the multiplication principle, and each one carries a condition that decides whether it applies. The condition is the mark: "order matters" and "items are identical" change the count by a factorial.

n! = n x (n-1) x ... x 2 × 1 Key: n = the number of distinct objects (a count, no units); n! = the number of orders they can be arranged in (a count). The falling product stops at 1, and 0! = 1 by convention so the formulas stay consistent.

nPr = n!/(n - r)! Key: n = how many objects are available; r = how many are being chosen; nPr = the number of ordered selections (a count). Read it as "start at n and write down r factors": 26P4 = 26 × 25 × 24 × 23.

nCr = n!/(r!(n - r)!) Key: n = objects available; r = objects chosen; nCr = the number of unordered selections (a count). The extra r! in the denominator is exactly what removes the orderings — which is the whole difference between a permutation and a combination.

nPr = nCr × r! Key: nPr = ordered selections; nCr = unordered selections; r! = the ways to order each selection. The identity explains both formulas at once: count the sets, then arrange each one.

26P4 = 26 × 25 × 24 × 23 = 358,800 Key: 26 = letters available; 4 = letters chosen without replacement; 358,800 = ordered passwords (a count). The factors fall because each letter is used once — repetition allowed would give 26⁴ instead.

26C4 = 14,950 Key: 26 = students available; 4 = students chosen; 14,950 = unordered groups (a count). The same numbers as the password question, 24 times smaller, because a group of four has 4! orderings that all count as one group.

n!/(a! b! c! ...) Key: n = total items; a, b, c = the sizes of the groups of identical items. Dividing by the factorials of the repeats removes the arrangements that look identical — 6!/(1! 3! 2!) = 60 arrangements of BANANA, not 720.

6!/(1! 3! 2!) = 720/12 = 60 Key: 6 = letters in BANANA; 1! = the single B; 3! = the three As; 2! = the two Ns; 60 = distinct arrangements (a count). Every repeated letter needs its own factorial in the denominator, or the count is inflated.

n^r Key: n = choices available at each stage; r = number of stages; the result counts selections with repetition allowed (a count). It is the multiplication principle applied r times — three digits from 0 to 9 with repeats gives 10³ = 1000.

(n - 1)! Key: n = people or objects around a circle; the result counts distinct circular arrangements (a count), because rotating a seating does not create a new one. For a necklace, where a reflection is also the same, divide once more: (n - 1)!/2.

5! × 2! = 120 × 2 = 240 Key: 5! = the arrangements of four single items plus the glued pair as one object; 2! = the internal orders of the pair; 240 = total arrangements (a count). Gluing without the internal factor halves the answer, which is the classic lost mark in this topic.

title: Algebra — Simplifying and Expanding — Study Notes
content:
Algebra — Simplifying and Expanding

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): substitution, collecting like terms, expanding brackets, factorising (common factor, quadratics, difference of two squares), algebraic fractions.

1. Substitution

a = 3, b = −2: 2a² − b = 2(9) + 2 = 20. Always bracket substituted negatives.

2. Collecting like terms

5x + 3y − 2x + y = 3x + 4y. Terms need identical letter parts (x² and x are not like terms).

3. Expanding

  • Single: 3(2x − 5) = 6x − 15.
  • Double: (x + 3)(x − 4) = x² − x − 12 (grid or FOIL).
  • Cubic products: (x+2)³ = x³ + 6x² + 12x + 8.

4. Factorising

  • Common factor: 6x²y − 9xy² = 3xy(2x − 3y).
  • Quadratics: x² − 5x + 6 = (x − 2)(x − 3) (two numbers ×6, sum −5).
  • Harder: 6x² + 7x + 2 = (3x + 2)(2x + 1) — split the middle term.
  • Difference of two squares: 9x² − 25 = (3x − 5)(3x + 5).

5. Algebraic fractions

Factorise top and bottom fully, then cancel: (x² − 9)/(x + 3) = (x − 3). To add, use a common denominator: 1/(x+1) + 2/(x−1) = (3x + 1)/((x+1)(x−1)).

Exam tips: always factorise out the highest common factor including the number; check expansion by substituting x = 1 into both forms.

Core facts to recall

  • Angular speed: ω = 2π / T. Linear speed v = ωr, and the centripetal acceleration is a = ω²r = v² / r.
  • SHM displacement: x = A cos ωt for a body released from maximum displacement. The maximum speed is v = ωA.
  • Acceleration is always directed to the equilibrium position: a = −ω²x.
  • Spring-mass period: T = 2π√(m / k). Simple pendulum period: T = 2π√(l / g) for small angles.
  • Energy: kinetic and potential energy trade places, while total energy stays constant when there is no damping.

title: IGCSE Computer Science: Automated Systems, Robotics and AI
content:
IGCSE Computer Science: Automated Systems, Robotics and AI

Cambridge IGCSE Computer Science 0478 (2026–2028), Paper 1 Computer Systems, Topic 6 Automated and emerging technologies: statement 6.1 Automated systems, 6.2 Robotics, and 6.3 Artificial intelligence. This is where the machine stops waiting for instructions and acts on its own — sensing, deciding and moving. Every feedback loop below is traced step by step, and the AI section separates what the syllabus actually expects (machine learning, natural language processing, robotics) from the hype, because examiners reward precise terminology over vague claims.

What makes a system automated

An automated system measures and controls a process with little or no human intervention. The architecture is always the same loop, and once you see it you can analyse any example the exam gives:

  • Input (sensors) — measure the real world: temperature, light, pressure, humidity, proximity, pH.
  • Processing — a microprocessor compares each measurement against a target (the set point) and decides what to do.
  • Output (actuators) — change the real world: motors, heaters, pumps, valves, lights, robotic arms.
  • Feedback — the sensors keep measuring the effect of the actuators, closing the loop so the system corrects itself.
Worked trace: a greenhouse temperature control system.

Set point: 22 degrees C. The sensor reads the air every 10 seconds.

1. 09:00:00  reading 18 C - below the set point.
   Processing: heating required. Actuators: heater ON, roof vent CLOSED.
2. 09:00:30  reading 21 C - still below (within the 2 C dead zone margin).
   Processing: continue heating.
3. 09:01:10  reading 23 C - above the set point.
   Processing: heater OFF (switching now, not at 22, avoids rapid cycling),
   roof vent OPEN to cool.
4. 09:03:00  reading 22 C - within the dead zone between 21 and 23.
   Processing: change nothing - the dead zone prevents constant switching,
   which would wear the heater out.

The loop repeats indefinitely. The set point is the target, the dead zone is
the tolerance band that stops the actuators chattering, and the feedback is the
sensor readings that drive each decision.

Closed-loop systems use feedback (as above); open-loop systems act without measuring the result — a toaster runs for a fixed time regardless of how brown the bread is. The exam asks you to say which a system is and justify it: if the output feeds back into the next decision, it is closed-loop.

Transducers: where physical change becomes data

Sensors and actuators are both transducers — devices that convert one form of energy into another — and knowing which way the conversion runs is the cleanest way to keep them straight. A sensor converts a physical quantity into an electrical signal the processor can read (temperature into resistance, light into voltage, sound into a varying current). An actuator does the reverse: it converts the processor's electrical signal into physical action (voltage into motion in a motor, into heat in a heater, into light in an LED).

Conversion direction, always:

  physical quantity -→ electrical signal     SENSOR (input)
  electrical signal -→ physical action       ACTUATOR (output)

Examples worked through:
  A thermistor in a greenhouse: temperature rises → resistance falls → the
  analogue voltage changes → an analogue-to-digital converter (ADC) turns it
  into a binary number the processor compares with the set point.

  A motor on a roof vent: the processor outputs a digital command → a digital-
  to-analogue converter (DAC) and driver circuit produce a varying current →
  the motor turns the vent.

Many real devices are both at once in different roles: a microphone is a sensor
(sound → electricity) and a speaker is an actuator (electricity → sound).

Where automation is used

DomainExampleSensorsActuators
ManufacturingRobotic assembly linePosition, proximity, visionRobot arms, conveyors, welders
AgricultureAutomatic irrigationSoil moisture, rain, temperaturePumps, valves
HomeCentral heatingThermostat, timerBoiler, radiator valves
TrafficAdaptive traffic lightsInductive loop detectors, camerasSignal lamps
MedicineInsulin pumpGlucose sensorPump actuator

Benefits: consistent quality, output in dangerous or monotonous conditions, 24-hour working, long-run cost per unit falls, and precise control improves yield. Costs: high capital outlay, jobs lost or changed, expensive and disruptive breakdowns, and loss of human judgement when the unexpected happens — a self-driving vehicle's edge cases are the modern form of that risk.

Robotics

A robot is a programmable machine that can sense, process and act on its environment to carry out tasks, often autonomously. The syllabus separates the types: fixed robots (a welding arm bolted to a factory floor — precise and strong, one workspace), mobile robots (warehouse robots, rovers — move themselves, need navigation), and autonomous robots (self-driving cars, drones — make decisions without continuous human control).

Inside any robot, the same loop as any automated system: sensors (cameras, LiDAR, ultrasonic, gyroscopes, encoders on the motors), a processor running control software, and actuators (motors, servos, grippers) — plus a power supply (battery) and a communication link for supervision.

  • Industrial uses: welding, painting and assembly (consistent quality, no fatigue, hazardous-environment work); picking and packing; bomb disposal and deep-sea or space exploration where humans cannot go.
  • Domestic and service uses: vacuum cleaners, lawn mowers, surgical robots, warehouse logistics, companionship and care.
  • Advantages: repeatable precision, tireless, work in danger, cheaper than labour at volume.
  • Disadvantages: very expensive to design and install, rigid when the task changes, maintenance needs skilled engineers, and they displace workers — the social consequence earns its own marks.

Artificial intelligence and machine learning

Artificial intelligence (AI) is software that appears to make intelligent decisions — solving problems and carrying out tasks in ways we would call clever if a human did them. Machine learning (ML) is the subset the syllabus emphasises: instead of being explicitly programmed with rules, the system is given data and learns patterns from it, improving with experience.

An analogy before the mechanics: teaching a child to recognise cats does not mean listing ear shapes and whisker counts. Show the child thousands of labelled pictures and the rules form themselves inside their head. Machine learning does exactly that with numbers.

How a machine learning model is trained, step by step:

1. Collect data: thousands of emails labelled "spam" or "not spam" by humans.
2. Choose features: word frequencies, sender reputation, link count, subject
   line patterns - measurable properties of each email.
3. Split the data: most for training, some held back for testing.
4. TRAINING: the algorithm adjusts its internal weights to fit the training
   data. It predicts each email's label; each wrong prediction nudges the
   weights; repeat over the dataset many times. The weights ARE the learned
   model - no human wrote the rules.
5. TESTING: run the trained model on the held-back data it has never seen and
   measure accuracy (correct predictions / total predictions). High training
   accuracy but low test accuracy means overfitting - it memorised the
   examples rather than learning the pattern.
6. DEPLOYMENT: new emails are classified by the model; correct and incorrect
   feedback can be fed back in so it keeps improving.

Key: accuracy = correct predictions ÷ total predictions tested, × 100 for a percentage and no units; the figure means something only on the held-back test set, and a wide gap between training and test accuracy is the definition of overfitting. In the vehicle trace the 4 m s⁻² is a deceleration, the a in v² = u² + 2as, where u = speed when braking begins (m s⁻¹), v = final speed (m s⁻¹, zero to stop) and s = stopping distance (m).

The three kinds of learning the syllabus names: supervised learning trains on labelled data (the spam example; predicting house prices from past sales); unsupervised learning finds structure in unlabelled data (customer segmentation — "these shoppers behave alike"); reinforcement learning learns by trial and reward (a game-playing program gets points for winning and adjusts its strategy).

Other AI applications in the syllabus: natural language processing (NLP) — understanding and generating human language: translation, voice assistants, chatbots, spam filtering; speech recognition — turning spoken audio into text (dictation, voice control); expert systems — a knowledge base of facts plus an inference engine applying rules to reach a conclusion (medical diagnosis support, fault finding); computer vision — interpreting images (face recognition, self-driving perception, medical imaging); autonomous vehicles — combining sensors, vision and decision-making to navigate.

Advantages of AI systemsDisadvantages of AI systems
Fast decisions over huge data volumesTraining needs vast data and computing power
Consistent, no fatigue or emotionNo common sense; fails on cases unlike its training data
Handles dangerous or dull workJob displacement across many industries
Improves with more dataBiased training data produces biased decisions — and they are hard to challenge
Available 24/7Cannot explain its reasoning well; accountability is unclear

Worked example: applying the loop to an autonomous vehicle

Approaching a pedestrian crossing:

1. SENSORS: cameras, radar and LiDAR continuously measure distance to the
   crossing, the pedestrian's position and speed, and the car's own speed.
2. PROCESSING: the AI classifies the objects (camera vision: "pedestrian at
   kerb"), predicts likely movement from the training data, and compares this
   with safety rules - minimum stopping distance for current speed and grip.
3. DECISION: predicted conflict - begin braking now, at 4 m/s², and warn.
4. ACTUATORS: brake and steering systems carry out the decision.
5. FEEDBACK: sensors keep measuring; if the pedestrian steps back, the plan
   updates; if the road is wet, the sensors' distance readings lengthen the
   braking margin.

Every one of these five stages can be a separate exam answer.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Calling any machine with a motor a "robot"; the syllabus sense is a programmable machine that senses, processes and acts — and "autonomous" requires decisions without continuous human control.
  • Describing open-loop systems as using feedback; if the output is not measured to adjust the next action, the loop is open (a toaster), regardless of how clever it looks.
  • Confusing the sensor and the actuator in a scenario: sensors measure (input), actuators move or heat (output) — thermostats sense, heaters act.
  • Saying machine learning "is programmed with rules"; the whole point is that the rules are learned from data — the trained weights are the program.
  • Skipping the training/testing split when explaining ML; measuring on unseen data is what distinguishes learning from memorising.
  • Equating AI with robots (or robots with AI): AI is software that can run without a robot, and many robots run purely on fixed programs with no learning.
  • Listing advantages only; the disadvantages (job losses, bias, data hunger, no common sense) carry equal marks.
  • Forgetting the feedback loop when describing any control system — "the sensor keeps measuring the effect" is the sentence examiners look for.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 1, 4 marks). Describe the input, process and output stages of an automatic door.

Answer: Input: a motion or proximity sensor detects a person approaching (and a pressure sensor may detect someone standing on the mat). Processing: the microprocessor compares the sensor reading with its trigger condition and checks safety sensors before acting. Output: an actuator (an electric motor) slides the door open; a timer or sensor then closes it. Feedback: the sensors keep monitoring so the door stays open while the beam is broken.

Question 2 (Paper 1, 3 marks). Explain the difference between a closed-loop and an open-loop system, giving one example of each.

Answer: A closed-loop system measures its output and feeds that back to adjust its actions — a central heating system measures room temperature and switches the boiler accordingly. An open-loop system acts without measuring the result — a toaster runs for a fixed time regardless of how brown the toast is.

Question 3 (Paper 1, 4 marks). Describe how a machine learning system is trained to detect fraudulent bank transactions.

Answer: Collect a large dataset of past transactions each labelled fraudulent or genuine by humans. Choose features such as amount, location, time and spending pattern. The algorithm trains on most of the data, adjusting its internal weights each time its prediction is wrong, until the predictions fit. The model is then tested on held-back transactions it has never seen to measure accuracy, before being used to score new transactions — with feedback from confirmed cases improving it over time.

Question 4 (Paper 1, 4 marks). Discuss the impact of introducing robots into a car factory.

Answer: For the firm: consistent weld quality, output day and night without fatigue, safer handling of painting fumes and heavy parts, and lower unit costs at volume — offset by very high installation costs, expensive breakdowns and rigidity when the product changes. For workers: dangerous and repetitive jobs are replaced, but assembly jobs are lost and remaining roles demand higher skills, so retraining is needed and communities dependent on the plant can suffer.

Question 5 (Paper 1, 3 marks). State three differences between a robot and an AI system.

Answer: A robot is hardware that physically senses and acts in the world; AI is software that makes decisions and may never have a physical form. Robots follow explicit programs; AI systems (especially machine learning) derive behaviour from data. A robot can run with no AI at all (a fixed assembly arm), and AI can exist with no robot (a spam filter).

The counterpart to systems that act on their own is the people who attack them: cyber security.

title: Data Representation — Study Notes
content:
Data Representation

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): binary/hex, two's complement, BCD, text/image/sound encoding, file sizes, compression.

1. Number systems

  • Binary place values 128…1; hex digits 0–9, A–F; one hex digit = one nibble (4 bits).
  • Conversions: binary ↔ decimal ↔ hex. 0101 1010 → 5A; FF = 255.
  • BCD: 4 bits per decimal digit — 0029 → 0000 0000 0010 1001. Used in clocks/calculators; easier digit conversions, more bits than pure binary.

2. Two's complement (signed)

MSB is negative: −128 64 32 16 8 4 2 1. −5 = 1111 1011. Range 8-bit: −128…+127.

Negating: invert bits, add 1. Subtraction: add the negated number — 7 − 5 = 7 + (−5) = 0000 0111 + 1111 1011 = 0000 0010.

3. Text

ASCII 7-bit (128 chars) → extended sets; Unicode for all scripts (UTF-8 variable width). Character sets map codes to glyphs; uppercase/lowercase codes differ by one bit.

4. Images and sound

  • Bitmap: pixels; colour depth = bits per pixel. File size (bits) = W × H × depth. Metadata (width, height, depth) stores dimensions.
  • Sound: sample rate (Hz), resolution (bits per sample), track duration × channels. Higher rate/depth = better fidelity, larger files.

5. Compression

  • Lossless (RLE, ZIP): exact restore — text/code must use it. RLE example: AAABBBCC → 3A3B2C; effective with runs.
  • Lossy (JPEG, MP3): discards perceptually minor data — photos/music OK, text never.

Exam tips: show full working in conversions; for size questions write the formula first with units; state the reason a compression type suits the file.

Binary addition and overflow

Binary addition follows the same carry rule as denary, except that 1 + 1 = 10 (0 carry 1). For example, 0110 + 0111 = 1101. A register or storage location has a fixed number of bits, so a result that needs more bits than are available overflows and gives a wrong answer. Programmers and examiners look for an overflow error when the carry out of the leftmost bit is set.

Exam tip: state the number of bits used. Overflow depends on that width, not on the value of the numbers alone.

title: Exam technique: Measures of Variation
content:
### What earns the marks
For standard deviation, mean first then the squared-deviation sum earns each mark. For coded data, the y-bar and s_y transformation earns the method mark. For comparisons, mean and spread commented together earns both marks.
### Traps
Error: variance reported as sd. Correction: root last. Error: comparing means only. Correction: comment on spread too. Error: coding applied once then forgotten. Correction: transform consistently.
### Worked example
Five values are 2, 4, 4, 6 and 9. The mean is 25 / 5 = 5. The squared deviations are 9, 1, 1, 1 and 16, which sum to 28. The variance is 28 / 5 = 5.6, and the standard deviation is the square root, about 2.37. Show the squared deviations line on the paper, since the method mark depends on it.
### Check yourself
If each value in the list is increased by 10, state what happens to the mean and to the standard deviation. The mean rises by 10, while the standard deviation is unchanged, because adding a constant does not change the spread.
