title: A Level Mathematics: Further Algebra
content:
A Level Mathematics: Further Algebra

A2 algebra is about rewriting expressions so that they can be handled: splitting a fraction into partial fractions before integrating it, dividing polynomials to expose factors, and using the remainder and factor theorems to find unknowns. This note builds each technique from zero, with the long division written out term by term, because the algebra is the part candidates rush and lose marks on.

Polynomial division

Dividing a polynomial by a linear factor works like numerical long division: divide the leading term, multiply back, subtract, bring down, repeat until the degree of the remainder is lower than the divisor.

Worked example. Divide 2x³ − 5x² + 4x − 7 by (x − 2).

2x² into x - 2: 2x²(x - 2) = 2x³ - 4x²;  subtract: -x² + 4x - 7
-x into x - 2: -x(x - 2) = -x² + 2x;  subtract: 2x - 7
+2 into x - 2: 2(x - 2) = 2x - 4;  subtract: -3
quotient 2x² - x + 2 with remainder -3
so 2x³ - 5x² + 4x - 7 = (x - 2)(2x² - x + 2) - 3

Worked example 2 (missing terms). Divide x³ + 1 by (x + 1).

write as x³ + 0x² + 0x + 1 to keep the columns aligned
quotient x², subtract x³ + x² → -x² + 1
quotient -x, subtract -x² - x → x + 1
quotient +1, subtract x + 1 → 0
x³ + 1 = (x + 1)(x² - x + 1)

Leaving gaps in the descending powers is the commonest slip; write the zeros in explicitly.

The factor and remainder theorems

remainder theorem: dividing f(x) by (x - a) leaves remainder f(a)
factor theorem: (x - a) is a factor exactly when f(a) = 0
for (ax - b): remainder is f(b/a)

Worked example 1. Find the remainder when f(x) = x³ − 4x + 5 is divided by (x + 2).

f(-2) = -8 + 8 + 5 = 5

Worked example 2 (find a factor). Show that (x − 3) is a factor of x³ − 4x² − 3x + 18.

f(3) = 27 - 36 - 9 + 18 = 0, so (x - 3) is a factor
then divide: x³ - 4x² - 3x + 18 = (x - 3)(x² - x - 6)
                                     = (x - 3)(x - 3)(x + 2)

Worked example 3 (unknown constant). f(x) = 2x³ + ax² − 5x + 6 has (x + 2) as a factor. Find a.

f(-2) = -16 + 4a + 10 + 6 = 0
4a = 0  →  a = 0
check: 2x³ - 5x + 6 divided by (x + 2) gives 2x² - 4x + 3 with no remainder

Partial fractions: distinct linear factors

(px + q)/[(x - a)(x - b)] = A/(x - a) + B/(x - b)

multiply through by the denominator and substitute x = a, x = b
in turn (the cover-up method)

Worked example. Express (5x + 1)/[(x − 1)(x + 2)] in partial fractions.

5x + 1 = A(x + 2) + B(x - 1)
x = 1: 6 = 3A  →  A = 2
x = -2: -9 = -3B  →  B = 3
(5x + 1)/[(x - 1)(x + 2)] = 2/(x - 1) + 3/(x + 2)

Worked example 2 (three factors). Express 2/[(x)(x + 1)(x − 2)] in partial fractions.

2 = A(x + 1)(x - 2) + Bx(x - 2) + Cx(x + 1)
x = 0: 2 = -2A  →  A = -1
x = -1: 2 = 3B  →  B = 2/3
x = 2: 2 = 6C  →  C = 1/3
so 2/[...] = -1/x + (2/3)/(x + 1) + (1/3)/(x - 2)

Partial fractions: repeated and improper cases

repeated factor: (px + q)/[(x - a)²] = A/(x - a) + B/(x - a)²
improper (degree of numerator >= degree of denominator): divide first

Worked example 1 (repeated). Express (3x + 5)/(x − 1)² in partial fractions.

3x + 5 = A(x - 1) + B
x = 1: 8 = B
compare coefficients of x: 3 = A
so 3/(x - 1) + 8/(x - 1)²

Worked example 2 (improper). Express (x² + 3x + 2)/(x − 1) in partial fractions.

divide first: (x² + 3x + 2)/(x - 1) = x + 4 + 6/(x - 1)
check by multiplying back: (x + 4)(x - 1) + 6 = x² + 3x + 2

The division step must come first: writing A + B/(x − 1) for an improper fraction gives the wrong form and cannot be solved consistently.

Inequalities and modulus

|x - a| < b  means  a - b < x < a + b
|x - a| > b  means  x < a - b or x > a + b

rational inequalities: move everything to one side, combine over a
common denominator, then use a sign diagram

Worked example. Solve |2x − 3| < 7.

-7 < 2x - 3 < 7
-4 < 2x < 10
-2 < x < 5

Worked example 2 (rational). Solve (x + 1)/(x − 3) > 2.

(x + 1)/(x - 3) - 2 > 0
(x + 1 - 2x + 6)/(x - 3) > 0
(7 - x)/(x - 3) > 0
critical values x = 3 (undefined) and x = 7
sign test: x = 4 gives 3/1 > 0 true; x = 8 gives -1/5 < 0 false
so 3 < x < 7

Never multiply a rational inequality by the denominator without knowing its sign: multiplying by a negative reverses the inequality, which is why the sign-diagram method is used instead.

Solving cubic equations completely

Once one factor is found by the factor theorem, polynomial division reduces the cubic to a quadratic, and the quadratic gives the remaining roots. The routine never varies:

  1. Try small integer values (±1, ±2, ±3) in f(x) until one gives zero.
  2. Divide by the corresponding linear factor.
  3. Factorise or use the quadratic formula on the quotient.
  4. State every root, including repeats.

Worked example. Solve x³ − 2x² − 5x + 6 = 0.

f(1) = 1 - 2 - 5 + 6 = 0, so (x - 1) is a factor
divide: x³ - 2x² - 5x + 6 = (x - 1)(x² - x - 6)
                            = (x - 1)(x - 3)(x + 2)
roots: x = 1, 3, -2

Worked example 2 (repeated root). Solve x³ − 3x + 2 = 0.

f(1) = 0  →  (x - 1) is a factor
divide: (x - 1)(x² + x - 2) = (x - 1)(x + 2)(x - 1)
roots: x = 1 (repeated) and x = -2; the curve touches the axis at x = 1

A repeated root is a tangency, which is why a cubic can have two distinct roots but three real ones counted with multiplicity.

Partial fractions with an irreducible quadratic

for a factor (x² + px + q) with no real roots:
(ax + b)/[(x - c)(x² + px + q)] = A/(x - c) + (Bx + C)/(x² + px + q)

Worked example. Express (3x + 1)/[x(x² + 1)] in partial fractions.

3x + 1 = A(x² + 1) + (Bx + C)x
x = 0: 1 = A
compare x²: 0 = A + B  →  B = -1
compare x: 3 = C
so 1/x + (-x + 3)/(x² + 1)

The numerator over a quadratic factor must be linear (Bx + C); a constant alone cannot satisfy the coefficients in general.

One linear and one quadratic equation

Simultaneous equations where one is a circle or parabola are solved by substitution, producing a quadratic whose roots give the intersection points.

Worked example. Solve y = x + 1 and x² + y² = 25.

substitute: x² + (x + 1)² = 25
2x² + 2x + 1 = 25  →  x² + x - 12 = 0
(x + 4)(x - 3) = 0  →  x = -4 or 3
points: (-4, -3) and (3, 4)

A line and a curve meet in 0, 1 or 2 points; the discriminant of the substituted quadratic tells you which, without solving — a standard link to the next section.

Surds and rationalising

rationalise 1/(a + sqrt b) by multiplying by (a - sqrt b)/(a - sqrt b)
denominator becomes a² - b, which is rational

Worked example. Simplify 3/(2 + √5).

multiply by (2 - sqrt 5)/(2 - sqrt 5):
3(2 - sqrt 5)/(4 - 5) = 3(2 - sqrt 5)/(-1) = 3 sqrt 5 - 6

Worked example 2. Solve x² − 6x + 2 = 0, giving answers in surd form.

x = [6 +/- √(36 - 8)]/2 = (6 +/- sqrt 28)/2 = 3 +/- sqrt 7

Surd answers should be simplified (√28 = 2√7) and, where the question asks, rationalised.

Algebraic fractions and cancelling

Simplifying an algebraic fraction requires factorising both parts first; cancelling terms before factorising is invalid because a sum is not a product.

Worked example. Simplify (x² − 9)/(x² + x − 6).

factorise: (x - 3)(x + 3)/[(x + 3)(x - 2)]
cancel (x + 3): (x - 3)/(x - 2), valid for x not 3 or -2

Worked example 2 (addition). Write 1/(x − 1) + 2/(x + 2) as a single fraction.

common denominator: [(x + 2) + 2(x - 1)]/[(x - 1)(x + 2)]
= (3x)/[(x - 1)(x + 2)]

The excluded values belong in the answer: a cancelled factor leaves a hole in the domain, which the equation's original form still cannot accept.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Remainder) Find the remainder when x³ + 2x − 4 is divided by (x − 1). Answer: 1 + 2 − 4 = −1.
  2. (Factor) Is (x + 3) a factor of x³ + 2x² − 5x + 6? Answer: f(−3) = −27 + 18 + 15 + 6 = 12 ≠ 0, no.
  3. (Unknown) f(x) = x³ + kx − 6 has (x − 2) as a factor. Find k. Answer: 8 + 2k − 6 = 0 → k = −1.
  4. (Partial fractions) Express 7/[(x − 1)(x + 6)]. Answer: 1/(x − 1) − 1/(x + 6).
  5. (Repeated) Express (2x + 1)/(x + 1)². Answer: 2/(x + 1) − 1/(x + 1)².
  6. (Improper) Express (x² + 1)/(x + 1). Answer: x − 1 + 2/(x + 1).
  7. (Modulus) Solve |x − 4| ≥ 3. Answer: x ≤ 1 or x ≥ 7.
  8. (Rational) Solve (x − 2)/(x + 1) < 1. Answer: (x − 2 − x − 1)/(x + 1) < 0 → −3/(x + 1) < 0 → x > −1.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Partial fractions for an improper fraction: divide first; the polynomial part is part of the answer.
  • Repeated factors written once: (x − a)² needs both A/(x − a) and B/(x − a)².
  • Cover-up used on repeating factors: the cover-up method substitutes only for distinct linear factors; for repeats, compare coefficients as well.
  • Sign of the remainder: f(a) gives the remainder when dividing by (x − a); for (x + a) substitute −a.
  • Missing powers in division: write 0x², 0x placeholders so the columns line up.
  • Multiplying inequalities by a variable: the sign may be negative; use a sign diagram instead.
  • Not excluding undefined values: a denominator's zero is never in the solution set; mark it as excluded.
  • Not checking: multiply the partial fractions back, or substitute one value, to confirm the decomposition.

Equations and symbols

Every technique in this topic is one of five statements: the division identity, the two theorems, the partial-fraction form and the modulus rule. Learn the form and the case it does not cover, because the incomplete form is what loses the marks.

2x³ - 5x² + 4x - 7 = (x - 2)(2x² - x + 2) - 3 Key: the division identity dividend = divisor × quotient + remainder. The remainder (−3) is a constant because the divisor is linear; if the remainder had an x in it, the division is unfinished. Write 0x² and 0x placeholders when a power is missing, or the columns misalign.

remainder theorem: dividing f(x) by (x - a) leaves remainder f(a) Key: f(x) = the polynomial; a = the value that makes the divisor zero. For a divisor (x + a) substitute −a, and for (ax − b) substitute b/a — the sign error here is the commonest in the topic.

factor theorem: (x - a) is a factor exactly when f(a) = 0 Key: the same substitution, read the other way: a remainder of zero means no remainder, so the divisor divides exactly. It is also the fastest route to an unknown coefficient: substitute the root, set the result to zero, solve.

(px + q)/[(x - a)(x - b)] = A/(x - a) + B/(x - b) Key: p, q = coefficients of the numerator; a, b = the roots of the denominator; A, B = the constants to find. Multiply through by the denominator and substitute x = a then x = b (the cover-up method) — valid only while the factors are distinct.

repeated factor: (px + q)/[(x - a)²] = A/(x - a) + B/(x - a)² Key: a squared factor needs both fractions, not one; cover-up finds B, and comparing coefficients of x finds A. Writing only A/(x − a) leaves a decomposition that cannot satisfy the coefficients.

improper (degree of numerator >= degree of denominator): divide first Key: the polynomial part is part of the answer — (x² + 3x + 2)/(x − 1) = x + 4 + 6/(x − 1). Skipping the division gives a form with no solution.

|x - a| < b means a - b < x < a + b Key: | | = modulus, the distance from x to a ignoring sign; b = the radius of the interval, so the answer is one interval for < and two rays for >. Solve −b < x − a < b, and never drop the modulus without writing both directions.

The forms, by case

DenominatorForm to write
Distinct linear factorsA/(x − a) + B/(x − b)
Repeated linear factorA/(x − a) + B/(x − a)²
Irreducible quadraticA/(x − c) + (Bx + C)/(x² + px + q)
Improper fractionDivide first, then decompose the remainder

Traps specific to the algebra

  • Cover-up used on a repeated factor, which gives only one of the two constants.
  • A constant numerator over an irreducible quadratic; it must be linear.
  • Multiplying an inequality by a variable whose sign is unknown — use a sign diagram instead.
  • Cancelling terms before factorising, which is invalid because a sum is not a product.
  • Leaving out the excluded values where a cancelled factor's denominator was zero.

title: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Transformations and Vectors
content:
Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Transformations and Vectors

Transformations move shapes on a grid, and vectors describe those moves with numbers. The exam asks two things: perform a transformation and, more often, describe one completely — with its centre, angle, direction, line or scale factor. This note builds the topic from zero: the four transformations and the full-description checklist for each, enlargement and its effect on area, vector notation with the house column-vector form (x; y), vector arithmetic, and the vector-geometry proofs that show lines are parallel or points are collinear.

The four transformations

TransformationWhat changesWhat must be stated in a description
Translationposition only, no rotation or resizethe column vector of the move
Reflectionmirror imagethe line of reflection (e.g. x = 2, y = x)
Rotationturns about a pointcentre, angle, and direction (clockwise or anticlockwise)
Enlargementresizes about a pointcentre and scale factor

The complete description is the mark: "rotation" alone scores nothing; "rotation 90° anticlockwise about (2, 1)" scores fully.

Translation

A translation moves every point by the same vector. In column form (x; y), x is the horizontal move and y the vertical move; right and up are positive.

Worked example. Triangle A has vertices (1, 1), (3, 1), (1, 4). Translate by (4; −2) and give the image coordinates.

(1, 1) → (5, -1)
(3, 1) → (7, -1)
(1, 4) → (5, 2)

The shape is congruent to the original (same size and shape), and the orientation is unchanged.

Reflection

A reflection flips a shape across a line; the line is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining each point to its image. Common lines: x = a (vertical), y = b (horizontal), y = x, y = −x.

Worked example. Reflect the point (3, 5) in the line y = x.

reflection in y = x swaps the coordinates: (3, 5) → (5, 3)

Worked example 2. Reflect (2, 4) in the line x = 1.

the line x = 1 is vertical; the distance of x = 2 from it is 1,
so the image is 1 unit on the other side: (0, 4)

To find the mirror line from a shape and its image, join a point to its image and draw the perpendicular bisector of that segment.

Rotation

A rotation turns a shape about a fixed centre through a given angle. The four standard angles are 90° and 180° in either direction; 90° clockwise equals 270° anticlockwise.

Worked example. Rotate the point (3, 1) 90° clockwise about the origin.

90 ° clockwise about O: (x, y) → (y, -x)
(3, 1) → (1, -3)

Worked example 2. Rotate (2, 5) 180° about the origin.

180 °: (x, y) → (-x, -y)
(2, 5) → (-2, -5)

For a centre other than the origin, translate the centre to the origin, rotate, then translate back — or count the grid squares from the centre.

Enlargement

An enlargement with centre C and scale factor k maps every point so that its distance from C is multiplied by k. Negative scale factors put the image on the far side of the centre; fractional factors between 0 and 1 shrink the shape.

image distance from centre = k x object distance from centre
area of image = k² x area of object

Worked example. Enlarge the point (2, 3) by scale factor 3 about the origin.

(2, 3) → (6, 9)

Worked example 2 (area). A triangle of area 12 cm² is enlarged by scale factor 2.5. Find the image area.

area factor = k² = 6.25
new area = 12 × 6.25 = 75 cm²

Enlargement is the only transformation that changes area (unless k = 1 or −1); translations, reflections and rotations preserve both shape and size.

Vectors: notation and magnitude

A vector has magnitude and direction. In this course it is written as a column vector (x; y): x is the horizontal component, y the vertical. The same vector can be written as a bold letter a with an arrow above it.

column vector (x; y)
magnitude = √(x² + y²)
direction angle to the horizontal: tan(θ) = y/x
equal vectors have the same components; opposite vectors
negate both components

Worked example. Find the magnitude and direction of the vector (3; 4).

magnitude = √(9 + 16) = 5
tan(θ) = 4/3  →  θ = 53.1 ° above the horizontal

Vector arithmetic and geometry

addition: (a; b) + (c; d) = (a + c; b + d)
subtraction: (a; b) - (c; d) = (a - c; b - d)
scalar multiple: k(a; b) = (ka; kb)

position vector of A relative to O: OA
AB = OB - OA
midpoint of AB: (OA + OB)/2

Worked example. OA = (2; 1), OB = (7; 5). Find AB and the midpoint of AB.

AB = OB - OA = (7 - 2; 5 - 1) = (5; 4)
midpoint = ((2 + 7)/2; (1 + 5)/2) = (4.5; 3)

Worked example 2 (parallel). Show that AB is parallel to CD given A(1, 2), B(5, 8), C(0, 1), D(6, 10).

AB = (5 - 1; 8 - 2) = (4; 6)
CD = (6 - 0; 10 - 1) = (6; 9)
(6; 9) = 1.5 x (4; 6), so CD = 1.5 AB: parallel (and longer)

Parallel vectors are scalar multiples of each other; collinear points occur when AB and AC (or AB and BC) are parallel and share a point.

Combining transformations and invariant points

Two transformations applied in sequence are not the same as the reverse order: a reflection followed by a rotation generally differs from the rotation followed by the reflection. When a question asks for the single transformation equivalent to two, apply both to a convenient point (the origin or a vertex) and to a second point, then identify the transformation that maps the original to the final image. Invariant points are points that do not move: every point on a mirror line is invariant under a reflection, the centre of a rotation is invariant, and no point is invariant under a translation.

Worked example. A shape is reflected in the x-axis and then translated by (0; 3). Find the image of (2, 1) and identify any invariant points.

reflection in the x-axis: (2, 1) → (2, -1)
translation by (0; 3): (2, -1) → (2, 2)
No invariant points: the reflection moved every point off the
axis, and the translation then moved everything upward.

Worked example 2 (invariant line). State the invariant points of a reflection in the line y = 2.

Every point with y-coordinate 2 lies on the mirror line and does
not move: the whole line y = 2 is invariant.

Vectors in context: displacement and velocity

Column vectors describe any quantity with magnitude and direction in two dimensions: displacement (a move from one point to another), velocity (displacement per second) and force (a push in a direction). The arithmetic is identical; only the interpretation changes.

  • Displacement: AB is the vector from A to B; a round trip returns to the start, so the sum of the vectors around a closed polygon is zero.
  • Velocity: a velocity vector (3; −2) means 3 units per second right and 2 units per second down; position after t seconds is the starting position plus t × velocity.
  • Resultant: the sum of two vectors; a vector and its negative cancel.

Worked example. A particle starts at (1, 2) and moves with velocity (3; −1) for 4 seconds. Find its final position.

displacement = 4 x (3; -1) = (12; -4)
final position = (1 + 12; 2 - 4) = (13; -2)

Worked examples: vector proofs

Worked example. In triangle OAB, P is the midpoint of OA and Q is the midpoint of OB. Prove PQ is parallel to AB.

OP = (1/2) OA, OQ = (1/2) OB
PQ = OQ - OP = (1/2)(OB - OA) = (1/2) AB
PQ is a scalar multiple of AB, so PQ is parallel to AB
(and half its length).

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Translation) Translate (2, 3) by (−1; 4). Answer: add the translation vector: (2, 3) + (−1, 4) = (2 − 1, 3 + 4) = (1, 7).
  2. (Reflection) Reflect (4, 1) in the x-axis. Answer: reflection in the x-axis negates the y-coordinate: x′ = x = 4 and y′ = −y = −1, so the image is (4, −1).
  3. (Rotation) Rotate (5, 2) 90° anticlockwise about the origin. Answer: a 90° anticlockwise turn about the origin maps (x, y) → (−y, x): x′ = −y = −2 and y′ = x = 5, so the image is (−2, 5).
  4. (Enlargement) Enlarge (1, 2) by factor −2 about the origin. Answer: enlargement about the origin maps (x, y) → k(x, y) with k = −2, so (1, 2) becomes (−2, −4); the negative factor puts the image on the opposite side of the centre.
  5. (Description) Describe fully the transformation mapping (1, 1) to (3, 5). Answer: translation vector = image − object = (3 − 1; 5 − 1) = (2; 4), so translation by (2; 4) — one of many correct complete descriptions.
  6. (Magnitude) Find the magnitude of (6; 8). Answer: |v| = √(x² + y²) = √(6² + 8²) = √(36 + 64) = √100 = 10.
  7. (Position vectors) OA = (1; 4), OB = (5; 2). Find AB. Answer: AB = OB − OA = (5; 2) − (1; 4) = (5 − 1; 2 − 4) = (4; −2).
  8. (Collinear) Show A(1, 1), B(3, 4), C(7, 10) are collinear. Answer: AB = (2; 3), AC = (6; 9) = 3 AB — parallel and share A, so collinear.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Incomplete descriptions: "enlargement by 2" omits the centre and loses marks; "reflection" omits the line. State every attribute.
  • Direction of rotation: clockwise and anticlockwise are different transformations; a 90° rotation clockwise is not the same as anticlockwise.
  • Area under enlargement: area scales by k², not k. Doubling the sides quadruples the area.
  • Vector direction: AB = OB − OA, not OA − OB. Reversing the subtraction negates the vector.
  • Column order: (x; y) is horizontal then vertical. Swapping produces a reflection in y = x, not the intended vector.
  • Parallelogram assumptions: equal magnitudes do not imply equal vectors — direction matters too.
  • Negative scale factors: the image lies on the opposite side of the centre; it is not simply "smaller".
  • Collinearity proof: showing parallel is not enough — the segments must also share a point. State it.

Translations: moving a shape without changing it

A translation slides every point of a shape the same distance in the same direction. The shape keeps its size, its shape and its orientation, so the image is congruent to the object. The description needs a column vector, written (x; y), where x is the movement to the right and y is the movement up. Negative values move left or down.

Reading a column vector

The vector (3; −2) means move 3 units to the right and 2 units down. Read the top number first, as the horizontal movement, and the bottom number second, as the vertical movement. Swapping the two numbers is one of the most common errors, and it moves the shape to a completely different place.

Translating a point

To translate a point, add the vector to its coordinates. The point A(1, 4) under the translation (3; −2) becomes A′(1 + 3, 4 − 2) = A′(4, 2). Work out each coordinate separately and check that the sign of each movement is right before you write the answer.

Translating a whole shape

A triangle is translated by translating each of its three vertices and joining the new points with straight lines. Drawing only one vertex, or moving the shape by eye, loses the mark. Check the result by counting the squares between each object point and its image: every pair should show the same horizontal and vertical movement.

Working backwards from an image

A question may give the image and ask for the vector. Take one point and its image, and find the change in x and the change in y. If P(2, 5) maps to P′(7, 1), the vector is (7 − 2; 1 − 5) = (5; −4). Check with a second point before you write the vector down.

Translations and the notation of the answer

The answer to a translation question must give the vector, not a verbal description alone. "Move 5 right and 4 down" is acceptable in words, but the examiner expects the column vector form (5; −4), which is what the syllabus asks for. Write it in brackets with a semicolon between the two numbers.

Common errors with translations

The commonest errors are reversing the direction of the movement, moving only the x-coordinate, and rotating the shape by mistake when a translation was asked for. A translation never turns the shape over and never changes its size, so an image that looks rotated or stretched is wrong. Check each answer against the rule that the shape is unchanged.

Reflections: the mirror line and the image

A reflection flips a shape over a mirror line. Every point of the image is the same distance from the mirror line as the matching point of the object, on the opposite side. The size and shape are unchanged, but the orientation is reversed. A full description needs the equation of the mirror line, and a mark is lost for any answer that names no line.

Reflection in the x-axis and y-axis

Reflection in the x-axis sends (x, y) to (x, −y), so the sign of the y-coordinate changes. Reflection in the y-axis sends (x, y) to (−x, y). Learn these two rules as fixed facts, because they are the quickest marks in the topic.

Reflection in a line such as y = x

Reflection in the line y = x swaps the two coordinates: (x, y) maps to (y, x). Reflection in y = −x sends (x, y) to (−y, −x). Test a single point to confirm the rule before you apply it to the whole shape, since a sign slip here changes every vertex.

Using the perpendicular distance

For a mirror line that is not a standard axis, each point of the image lies on the perpendicular from the object point to the line, at the same distance beyond the line. Draw the perpendicular with a set square so the image is placed accurately, and count the squares on each side to check.

Finding the mirror line from an object and image

When the question asks for the mirror line, join each point to its image. All those joining lines are parallel, and the mirror line is the perpendicular bisector of each joining segment. Read the line from the diagram, then give its equation, for example x = 2 or y = x.

Invariant points under reflection

A point is invariant under a reflection if it does not move, which happens when it lies on the mirror line. Any point on the mirror line maps to itself, so it is a useful check: if a vertex you expected to stay fixed has moved, the reflection has been drawn in the wrong place.

Common errors with reflections

The commonest errors are reflecting in the wrong axis, giving the mirror line as a point rather than a line, and forgetting that the image is the reverse of the object. A reflection that leaves the shape the same way round as the object is a translation or a rotation, not a reflection, so check the orientation of the image.

Equations and symbols

Every transformation is a coordinate map, and every vector is a column pair. Learn the four rotation maps and the two vector rules, and the topic is arithmetic.

90 ° clockwise about O: (x, y) → (y, -x) Key: (x, y) = the original coordinates; the arrow points to the image's coordinates; O = the origin, the fixed centre. Anticlockwise is the same map with the signs reversed — write the centre down, because a rotation about any other point is not this formula.

180 °: (x, y) → (-x, -y) Key: both coordinates change sign; a half-turn is the only rotation that is also a translation-free "point reflection" in the origin. Check with a point on an axis, where one coordinate stays zero.

reflection in y = x swaps the coordinates: (3, 5) → (5, 3) Key: the line y = x is the mirror; swapping means the image of (x, y) is (y, x). The line is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining each point to its image, which is the definition to quote.

(1, 1) → (5, -1) Key: left = a vertex of the object; right = the matching vertex of the image. Subtract to read off the translation: 5 − 1 = 4 across and −1 − 1 = −2 down, so the column vector is (4; −2).

(3, 1) → (1, -3) Key: this is a 90° clockwise turn about the origin applied to a second vertex — the same map, different numbers. With two vertices mapped you can describe the transformation fully rather than guessing from one.

title: The Normal Distribution
content:
The Normal Distribution

The Model

A continuous distribution with the familiar bell shape, symmetric about the mean, described by two parameters: X ~ N(μ, σ²). The curve is fully determined by μ (centre) and σ (width). Total probability is 1, and because X is continuous, P(X = a) = 0 for any single point — inequalities do not need strictness.

Standardising

Convert any normal variable to the standard normal Z ~ N(0, 1) with

  • Z = (X − μ)/σ

Then read probabilities from the normal table. For X ~ N(50, 4²): P(X > 56) = P(Z > 1.5) = 1 − 0.9332 = 0.0668.

Backwards Problems

Given a probability, find μ or σ. Convert the target percentile to a z-value from the table, then solve (x − μ)/σ = z.

Example: P(X < 30) = 0.15 with unknown σ. From tables z = −1.036, so (30 − μ)/σ = −1.036 — one equation per unknown; use a second condition if both are missing.

Symmetry Shortcuts

P(X > μ) = 0.5. P(X < a) for a above the mean uses the complement. Tables usually give Φ(z) for z ≥ 0 only; use Φ(−z) = 1 − Φ(z).

Normal Approximation to the Binomial

For large n with p near ½, X ~ B(n, p) ≈ N(np, np(1 − p)). The condition usually quoted at this level is np > 5 and n(1 − p) > 5. Apply a continuity correction: to approximate P(X ≥ 12) for a binomial, compute P(Y > 11.5) for the normal Y.

Example: B(100, 0.5) ≈ N(50, 25). P(X ≥ 55) ≈ P(Y > 54.5) = P(Z > 0.9) = 0.1841.

Exam tips: always sketch and shade — the picture prevents complement errors. State the standardisation step explicitly; marks sit in the working. Check whether a question says "mean and standard deviation" (σ) or "variance" (σ²) before standardising.

title: Ethics, Security & Impact — Study Notes
content:
Ethics, Security & Impact

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): ethics & professional codes, security threats, malware, online safety, environmental/employment impact.

1. Ethics and codes

ACM/IEEE-CS/BCS codes: public interest, competence, integrity, privacy. Applying: identify the principle → apply to scenario → stakeholders affected → consequences.

2. Threats

  • Malware: virus (attaches, replicates via host), worm (self-spreads), trojan (disguised), spyware, ransomware.
  • Social: phishing (fake emails/sites), pharming (DNS/hosts redirect), shoulder surfing, brute force.
  • Technical: interception (packet sniffing), SQL injection (malicious input into queries), DoS (flooding services).

3. Defences

Antivirus/antispyware (scan, quarantine), firewalls (port/IP filtering), 2FA + biometrics, strong passwords + managers, encryption (HTTPS, VPN), access levels, patches/updates, user training.

4. Online behaviour

Digital footprint, cyberbullying, fake news, privacy settings, verification of sources.

5. Wider impact

Employment: automation displaces roles but creates IT jobs. Environment: e-waste, energy use vs paperless efficiency. Monitoring: workplace tracking, CCTV — balance with privacy laws (GDPR-style).

Exam tips: name the threat precisely (pharming ≠ phishing), then the matched defence; ethics answers need principle + application, not opinion.

title: Exam technique: Congruence and Similarity
content:
### What earns the marks
For similarity lengths, calculate earns marks for the scale factor stated (larger over smaller, matched pairs) and then applied. For area and volume, the squared and cubed factors stated earn the method mark before any multiplication: write k squared or k cubed explicitly. For symmetry, count earns marks per correct count with the reasoning (vertices, rotation step 360 / n). For congruence, name earns the test (SSS, SAS, ASA, RHS) with the matching parts listed.
### Traps
Error: adding the length difference instead of scaling. Correction: similarity always multiplies. Error: using k instead of k squared for area or k cubed for volume. Correction: write the power first. Error: equal angles claimed as congruence. Correction: angles alone prove similarity; a matching side upgrades it.

title: AS Level Mathematics: Trigonometry
content:
AS Level Mathematics: Trigonometry

Trigonometry at AS level extends the triangle ratios of IGCSE into functions of any angle: the sine and cosine waves that model tides, sound and alternating current, the identities that let you simplify expressions and solve equations, and the sine and cosine rules that handle triangles without a right angle. This note builds the whole topic from zero: the graphs and their properties, exact values, the two core identities, the interval method for solving equations, the sine/cosine rules with the ambiguous case, and transformations of trigonometric graphs. Radian answers are expected wherever the question uses radians.

The three graphs and their properties

FunctionPeriodRangeKey features
sin θ360° (2π)−1 to 10 at 0°, 180°, 360°; maximum at 90°
cos θ360° (2π)−1 to 11 at 0°; 0 at 90°, 270°
tan θ180° (π)all real values0 at 0°, 180°; asymptotes at 90°, 270°

The graphs encode the symmetries the papers test: sin(180° − θ) = sin θ, cos(−θ) = cos θ, sin(−θ) = −sin θ, tan(180° + θ) = tan θ. A quick sketch of the relevant wave inside the required interval solves most equation problems before any algebra.

Worked example. Sketch y = sin x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 360° and mark where sin x = 0.5.

the sine wave crosses 0.5 on its rising part at x = 30 °
and on its falling part at x = 150 ° (symmetry about 90 °)
solutions in the interval: x = 30, 150

Exact values

The exact values come from two special triangles and must be known in both degrees and radians:

Anglesincostan
30° = π/61/2√3/21/√3
45° = π/41/√21/√21
60° = π/3√3/21/2√3

Beyond the first quadrant, use the symmetry rules with the reference angle: sin 150° = sin 30° = ½; cos 240° = −cos 60° = −½; tan 135° = −tan 45° = −1. The quadrant sign pattern ("CAST" or a sketch) decides the sign.

Worked example. Find the exact value of cos 300°.

300 ° is in the fourth quadrant; reference angle 60 °
cos is positive in the fourth quadrant: cos 300 = cos 60 = 1/2

The two identities

sin²(θ) + cos²(θ) = 1
tan(θ) = sin(θ)/cos(θ)     (cos θ not 0)

useful rearrangements:
sin² = 1 - cos²;  cos² = 1 - sin²
1 + tan² = sec² (beyond AS but built from the same identity)

Worked example 1 (simplify). Simplify (1 − cos²θ)/sin θ.

1 - cos² = sin²
sin²/sin = sin θ   (θ not a multiple of 180 °)

Worked example 2 (prove). Prove that (sin θ + cos θ)² = 1 + 2 sin θ cos θ.

expand: sin² + 2 sin cos + cos²
rearrange: (sin² + cos²) + 2 sin cos = 1 + 2 sin cos

Worked example 3 (solve with the identity). Solve 2 sin²θ + cos θ = 2 for 0 ≤ θ ≤ 360°.

replace sin² = 1 - cos²:
2(1 - cos²) + cos = 2
2 - 2cos² + cos = 2  →  -2cos² + cos = 0
cos(1 - 2cos) = 0  →  cos = 0 or cos = 1/2
cos = 0: θ = 90, 270
cos = 1/2: θ = 60, 300

Solving trigonometric equations in an interval

The method that never misses solutions: find the principal value, then use the symmetry of the wave to generate every solution in the interval.

  1. Isolate the trigonometric part (use identities if needed).
  2. Find the principal value with the inverse function.
  3. Use the symmetries: for sin, solutions are θ and 180° − θ (plus 360° steps); for cos, θ and 360° − θ; for tan, θ + 180° steps.
  4. Check every solution lies in the stated interval, and count them.

Worked example. Solve cos 2x = 0.5 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 360°.

let u = 2x, so 0 <= u <= 720
cos u = 0.5  →  u = 60, 300, 420, 660
x = 30, 150, 210, 330

The doubled-angle trap: the interval for u doubles too. Expand the interval whenever the argument is multiplied.

Worked example 2 (shifted). Solve sin(x − 30°) = 0.6 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 360°.

u = x - 30, so -30 <= u <= 330
sin u = 0.6  →  u = 36.9 or 143.1
x = 66.9 or 173.1

The sine and cosine rules

sine rule: a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C
cosine rule: a² = b² + c² - 2bc cos A
area of a triangle: (1/2) a b sin C

How to choose: two sides and a non-included angle (SSA) or two angles and a side (AAS) use the sine rule; three sides (SSS) or two sides and the included angle (SAS) use the cosine rule. The area formula uses two sides and the included angle.

Worked example 1 (cosine rule). A triangle has sides 8 cm, 11 cm and an included angle of 60°. Find the third side and the area.

a² = 8² + 11² - 2(8)(11)cos 60
    = 64 + 121 - 176(0.5) = 185 - 88 = 97
a = 9.85 cm
area = (1/2)(8)(11) sin 60 = 44 × 0.866 = 38.1 cm²

Worked example 2 (sine rule). In a triangle, angle A = 40°, side a = 7 cm, side b = 10 cm. Find angle B.

sin B / b = sin A / a
sin B = b sin A / a = 10 × 0.643/7 = 0.918
B = 66.7 ° or B = 113.3 ° (ambiguous case)

The ambiguous case

When you know two sides and a non-included angle, the sine rule can produce two valid triangles: angle B could be 66.7° or its supplement 113.3°. Both satisfy the sine rule, and the question must be read to decide which is intended — often a given angle sum rules one out, or the diagram shows an obtuse angle. State both and choose, with a reason.

Worked example. In the triangle above, find the two possible values of angle C and side c.

if B = 66.7: C = 180 - 40 - 66.7 = 73.3 °
  c/sin 73.3 = 7/sin 40  →  c = 7 × 0.958/0.643 = 10.4 cm
if B = 113.3: C = 26.7 °
  c = 7 × 0.449/0.643 = 4.89 cm

Transformations of trigonometric graphs

y = a sin(bx + c) + d
amplitude = |a|;  period = 360/b (or 2 π/b)
phase shift = -c/b;  vertical shift = d

Worked example. State the amplitude, period and range of y = 3 sin 2x + 1.

amplitude 3; period 360/2 = 180 °
range: 3 sin 2x ranges -3 to 3, so y ranges 1 - 3 = -2 to 4

Worked example 2 (phase). Describe the transformation y = sin(x + 45°).

a translation of 45 ° to the left (inside the bracket, so the
shift is opposite in sign to the constant)

Worked examples: applied trigonometry

Worked example. A ship sails 30 km on a bearing of 040°, then 20 km on a bearing of 130°. Find its distance and bearing from the start.

the two legs are 90 ° apart (130 - 40), so resolve into east and north
leg 1: east 30 sin 40 = 19.28;  north 30 cos 40 = 22.98
leg 2: east 20 sin 130 = 15.32;  north 20 cos 130 = -12.86
total: east 34.60;  north 10.12
distance = √(34.60² + 10.12²) = √(1197.2 + 10².4) = 36.1 km
bearing: tan(θ) = 34.60/10.12 = 3.419  →  θ = 73.7 °
(measured from north towards east)  →  bearing 074 °

The component method works for any number of legs; the cosine rule on the included angle is quicker only for exactly two. Either way, bearings are measured clockwise from north at every stage, never from the previous heading.

Radians, arc length and sector area

Radian measure is the natural unit for the trigonometric functions: one radian is the angle subtended at the centre of a circle by an arc equal in length to the radius, and a full turn is 2π radians. The conversions and the two circle formulas are used constantly in P1:

π radians = 180 °;  1 radian = 57.3 °
arc length s = r θ  (θ in radians)
sector area = (1/2) r² θ
segment area = sector area - triangle area

Worked example. A sector has radius 6 cm and angle 2 radians. Find its arc length, perimeter and area.

arc = 6 × 2 = 12 cm
perimeter = 12 + 6 + 6 = 24 cm
area = (1/2)(36)(2) = 36 cm²

Worked example 2 (segment). Find the area of the segment cut off by a chord subtending 1.2 radians in a circle of radius 5 cm.

sector = (1/2)(25)(1.2) = 15 cm²
triangle = (1/2)(5)(5) sin 1.2 = 12.5 × 0.932 = 11.65 cm²
segment = 15 - 11.65 = 3.35 cm²

The radian formulas only work in radians; in degrees the arc length is (θ/360)2πr and the sector area (θ/360)πr². Mixing the two is a silent error that costs the accuracy mark.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Exact) Find sin 240° exactly. Answer: third quadrant, reference 60°: −√3/2.
  2. (Identity) Simplify sin²θ/(1 − sin²θ). Answer: sin²θ/cos²θ = tan²θ.
  3. (Solve) Solve tan θ = 1 for 0 ≤ θ ≤ 360°. Answer: θ = 45°, 225°.
  4. (Solve with identity) Solve 3 cos²θ = sin²θ for 0 ≤ θ ≤ 360°. Answer: 3cos² = 1 − cos² → cos² = ¼ → cos = ±½ → θ = 60°, 120°, 240°, 300°.
  5. (Cosine rule) Sides 5 cm and 7 cm with included angle 120°. Find the third side. Answer: a² = 25 + 49 − 70(−0.5) = 109 → a = 10.4 cm.
  6. (Sine rule) A = 35°, B = 80°, a = 9 cm. Find b. Answer: b = 9 sin 80/sin 35 = 9 × 0.985/0.574 = 15.4 cm.
  7. (Area) Find the area of a triangle with sides 6 cm and 9 cm and included angle 50°. Answer: ½ × 54 × sin 50 = 20.7 cm².
  8. (Graph) State the period and amplitude of y = 4 cos 3x. Answer: period 120°, amplitude 4.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Losing solutions: an equation often has more than one solution in the interval; use the symmetry rules or sketch the wave. The commonest mark loss in this topic.
  • Not expanding the interval: for sin 2x over 0 ≤ x ≤ 360°, the argument runs to 720°; solutions are lost without that.
  • Degree/radian mode: the question's units decide the calculator mode; a radian interval (0 to 2π) needs RAD.
  • Wrong rule: sine rule for AAS/SSA, cosine rule for SAS/SSS; using the sine rule on SAS fails silently.
  • Forgetting the ambiguous case: SSA can give two triangles; state both and justify the choice.
  • Identity rearrangement slips: sin² = 1 − cos², not cos² − 1. Sign errors here propagate through the whole solution.
  • Amplitude and period: y = a sin bx has amplitude |a| and period 360/b; the b is not an amplitude.
  • Rounding mid-solution: keep full accuracy until the final answer; angles to 1 d.p. unless told otherwise.

title: Number — Sets — Study Notes
content:
Number — Sets

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): set notation, Venn diagrams, shading, universal set, subsets.

1. Notation

  • ∈ belongs to; ∉ not in; ∅ empty set; ξ (or U) universal set; n(A) = number of elements.
  • A ∩ B intersection (AND); A ∪ B union (OR); A′ complement (NOT A).
  • A ⊆ B: every element of A is in B.

2. Venn diagrams

Fill the intersection first, then work outwards. Two sets: only A, both, only B, neither.

Example: 30 students; 18 maths, 15 physics, 7 both ⇒ neither = 30 − (11 + 7 + 8) = 4.

3. Shading

For A ∩ B′ shade where A and outside-B overlap. (A ∪ B)′ = A′ ∩ B′ (De Morgan) — check every region.

4. Regions algebra

With region variables x, y, z: use the totals to form equations, e.g. n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B).

5. Probability links

P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B) — inclusion–exclusion from the diagram.

Exam tips: "neither" sits outside both circles — subtract from the universal set last; label regions with numbers, not expressions, as you fill.

title: AS Level Physics: Superposition
content:
AS Level Physics: Superposition

Superposition is what happens when two waves occupy the same space at the same time: the displacements add, and from that single rule emerge stationary waves, diffraction, interference and the diffraction grating — the four phenomena of this topic. The mental picture to keep is two people shaking ropes that cross: at the crossing, the rope's shape is the sum of both shapes, instant by instant. This note builds each phenomenon from that rule, with the derivations and calculations line by line and the practical skills the papers demand.

The superposition principle

When two or more waves meet, the resultant displacement at any point is the vector sum of the individual displacements at that point. The waves pass through each other unchanged afterwards — they do not bounce off or alter each other. Everything in this topic is that sentence applied to different geometries:

  • Constructive interference: crest meets crest — displacements add, amplitude is a maximum.
  • Destructive interference: crest meets trough — displacements cancel, amplitude is a minimum (zero for equal waves).

Interference is sustained (a stable pattern) only when the sources are coherent: same frequency and a constant phase difference. Two unrelated lamps are incoherent and produce no stable pattern — this distinction is examinable every session.

Stationary waves

A stationary (standing) wave forms when two progressive waves of the same frequency and amplitude travel in opposite directions — classically a wave and its reflection. The pattern oscillates but does not travel: there are fixed points of zero displacement (nodes) and fixed points of maximum displacement (antinodes), and the wave profile stays in place while the medium oscillates within it.

FeatureProgressive waveStationary wave
Energytransferred along the wavestored in the oscillating regions; not transferred
Nodesnonefixed zero-displacement points, half a wavelength apart
Antinodescrests move alongfixed maximum points, half a wavelength apart
Phaseneighbouring points vary smoothly in phaseall points between two adjacent nodes oscillate in phase

Harmonics give the numbers. For a string fixed at both ends (or a pipe closed at both ends), the fundamental has nodes at both ends and one antinode between: the string length L fits half a wavelength, so λ = 2L. The next mode fits a full wavelength (λ = L), the next 3λ/2 (λ = 2L/3), and in general λₙ = 2L/n with fₙ = n v/(2L). For a pipe closed at one end, the closed end is a node and the open end an antinode: the fundamental fits a quarter wavelength, λ = 4L, and only odd harmonics appear, fₙ = n v/(4L) with n = 1, 3, 5 ...

Worked example. A guitar string 0.65 m long has a wave speed of 320 m s⁻¹. Find the fundamental and second harmonic frequencies.

fundamental: lambda = 2L = 1.30 m
f1 = v/lambda = 320/1.30 = 246 Hz
second harmonic: lambda = L = 0.65 m
f2 = 320/0.65 = 492 Hz   (exactly 2 x f1, as expected)

Worked example (closed pipe). A pipe 0.50 m long, closed at one end, has sound speed 340 m s⁻¹. Find the fundamental and state the next allowed frequency.

fundamental: lambda = 4L = 2.00 m
f1 = 340/2.00 = 170 Hz
only odd harmonics allowed -> next is the 3rd: f3 = 3 x 170 = 510 Hz

Diffraction

Diffraction is the spreading of waves as they pass through a gap or around an obstacle. It is significant when the gap (or obstacle) size is comparable to the wavelength — the wave bends generously around a 1 cm gap if λ is a few centimetres, but barely at all for light through a doorway. The rule to quote: noticeable diffraction requires gap size approximately equal to the wavelength. Consequences: long-wavelength radio diffract around hills; short-wavelength microwaves need line-of-sight aerials; light through everyday doors shows negligible diffraction, which is why shadows exist.

The single-slit pattern is examinable in outline: a broad central maximum of width related to λ/a (slit width a), with the intensity falling away on either side; a narrower slit produces a wider spread. Water waves in a ripple tank photograph the same behaviour macroscopically.

Interference: two sources

Two coherent sources produce a stable pattern of maxima and minima. The controlling quantity is the path difference — the difference in distance from the two sources to the point in question:

  • Constructive (maximum): path difference = nλ (n = 0, 1, 2 ...), i.e. a whole number of wavelengths.
  • Destructive (minimum): path difference = (n + ½)λ — a whole number plus half.

Worked example. Two speakers sit 4.0 m apart, driven in phase at 170 Hz (sound speed 340 m s⁻¹). A listener stands on the perpendicular bisector, then moves until the first minimum. Find the path difference at the first minimum.

lambda = v/f = 340/170 = 2.0 m
first minimum: path difference = lambda/2 = 1.0 m

On the perpendicular bisector the path difference is zero, so the centre is a maximum; the first minimum occurs where the difference reaches half a wavelength — 1.0 m of extra path.

Young's double-slit experiment

Light through two closely spaced slits forms fringes of alternating bright and dark bands on a screen. The fringe spacing formula, derived from path difference across a distant screen, is the calculation the papers test:

fringe spacing  w  = lambda D / d

D = slit-to-screen distance (m)
d = slit separation (m)
lambda = wavelength (m)

Worked example 1. Light of wavelength 600 nm falls on slits 0.25 mm apart; the screen is 1.8 m away.

lambda = 600 nm = 6.0 x 10-7 m
d = 0.25 mm = 2.5 x 10-4 m
w = lambda D/d = (6.0 x 10-7 x 1.8)/(2.5 x 10-4)
  = 1.08 x 10-6/2.5 x 10-4 = 4.32 x 10-3 m = 4.3 mm

Worked example 2 (working backwards). Fringe spacing 2.0 mm is measured with D = 2.0 m and λ = 500 nm. Find the slit separation.

d = lambda D/w = (5.0 x 10-7 x 2.0)/(2.0 x 10-3)
  = 1.0 x 10-6/2.0 x 10-3 = 5.0 x 10-4 m = 0.50 mm

Examiner note: the formula assumes small angles and a distant screen; when asked to describe the effect of moving the screen away, the answer is that fringes spread out (w increases with D) — a proportionality answer, not a guess.

The diffraction grating

A diffraction grating has many equally spaced slits; the interference from all of them produces sharp, bright maxima at angles given by

n lambda = d sin theta

n = 0, 1, 2, ... (the order)
d = slit spacing (grating spacing), the distance between
    adjacent slits (m)
theta = angle of the maximum from the central beam

The number of orders is a standard question: since sin θ ≤ 1, the maximum order n is the largest integer with nλ ≤ d, i.e. n = floor(d/λ); each order appears twice (either side) plus the central beam.

Worked example 1. A grating has 300 lines per millimetre. Light of wavelength 550 nm is incident normally. Find the angles of the first- and second-order maxima.

grating spacing: d = 1 mm/300 = 3.33 x 10-6 m
first order (n = 1):
sin theta = lambda/d = 5.5 x 10-7/3.33 x 10-6 = 0.165
theta = sin-1(0.165) = 9.5 degrees
second order (n = 2):
sin theta = 2 x 0.165 = 0.330
theta = 19.3 degrees

Worked example 2 (counting orders). With the same grating and λ = 550 nm, how many maxima are visible in total?

max order: n lambda <= d  ->  n <= d/lambda = 3.33 x 10-6/5.5 x 10-7 = 6.06
largest integer n = 6
orders: -6 to +6 plus n = 0  ->  13 maxima in total

Practical skill: measuring d from a grating quoted as N lines per metre, d = 1/N. A grating with 500 lines per mm has d = 2.0 × 10⁻⁶ m. Getting that reciprocal wrong doubles every downstream answer.

Worked examples: comparing the phenomena

Worked example. White light falls on a double slit and, separately, on a diffraction grating. Describe and explain the difference between the two patterns.

double slit: equally spaced fringes; the central fringe is white,
             outer fringes coloured because fringe spacing depends
             on lambda - blue (shorter lambda) fringes sit closer
             to the centre than red
grating:     sharply defined maxima at angles set by sin theta =
             n lambda/d, so each order spreads into a spectrum
             with violet least deviated and red most

Why the marks land: the description names the pattern shape, then the mechanism (spacing proportional to λ) and the colour ordering — explanation, not just observation.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Definitions) State the principle of superposition and define coherence. Answer: When waves meet, the resultant displacement is the sum of the individual displacements. Coherent waves have the same frequency and a constant phase difference.
  2. (Stationary waves) Describe the formation of a stationary wave in a string. Answer: A wave produced at one end travels along the string and reflects at the fixed end; the incident and reflected waves of equal frequency and amplitude superpose; at nodes the two are in antiphase and cancel, at antinodes in phase and reinforce; the pattern oscillates without propagating.
  3. (Closed pipe) The fundamental of a closed pipe is 220 Hz. State the frequency of the next possible harmonic and why. Answer: 660 Hz — closed pipes support odd harmonics only, so the next is the third harmonic, 3 × 220.
  4. (Diffraction) State and explain why long-wave radio signals can be received behind hills but microwave signals cannot. Answer: Radio wavelengths (hundreds of metres) are comparable to hill sizes, so they diffract noticeably around them; microwaves (centimetres) diffract negligibly and need line of sight.
  5. (Double slit) Blue light (450 nm) is replaced by red (650 nm) with no other change. State the effect on fringe spacing and explain. Answer: The spacing increases because w = λD/d and λ has increased; the fringes spread out proportionally.
  6. (Grating) A grating has 600 lines per mm and is illuminated with 500 nm light. Calculate the angle of the first-order maximum. Answer: d = 1/600 000 = 1.67 × 10⁻⁶ m; sin θ = 5.0 × 10⁻⁷/1.67 × 10⁻⁶ = 0.300; θ = 17.5°.
  7. (Orders) In question 6, how many maxima are visible altogether? Answer: d/λ = 3.33, so n = 3; orders −3 to +3 plus the central beam make 7 maxima.
  8. (Practical) Describe how you would measure the fringe spacing of a double-slit pattern. Answer: Measure the distance across several fringes (e.g. from the centre of one bright fringe to the centre of the nth bright fringe) with a ruler or travelling microscope, then divide by n — measuring many fringes reduces the fractional uncertainty.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Grating spacing inversion: 300 lines per mm means d = 3.33 × 10⁻⁶ m, not 3.33 × 10⁻³ m. Write the reciprocal step as its own line.
  • Units in the grating formula: d and λ must both be in metres. Nanometres into the formula directly gives sin θ in the thousands.
  • sin θ vs tan θ: fringe positions at large angles cannot use the small-angle approximation; use sin⁻¹ from the grating equation and w = λD/d only where angles are small.
  • Counting orders: remember the central beam (n = 0) and both sides; and round the order down (floor of d/λ), never up.
  • Node/antinode language: nodes are zero displacement and exist because of antiphase superposition; antinodes vibrate with double amplitude. Swapping the two is a definition mark lost.
  • Closed-pipe harmonics: an open–closed pipe supports odd harmonics only (1st, 3rd, 5th); answering with the second harmonic loses the mark.
  • Incoherent sources: two separate lamps cannot produce a stable interference pattern — coherence is the condition, and it is worth a stated mark.
  • Path difference conditions: maxima at whole wavelengths, minima at half-integer. State the condition in words and symbols.
  • Method marks: write the formula (nλ = d sin θ or w = λD/d) before numbers; a correct formula with failed arithmetic still earns credit.

title: Forces & Motion
content:
Forces & Motion

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2023–2025): motion (speed, acceleration, graphs); mass & weight; density link; force basics (F = ma, resultant); momentum (Extended); turning effects; equilibrium.

1. Kinematics

  • Speed = distance/time; average speed = (u + v)/2 for uniform acceleration.
  • Acceleration a = (v − u)/t.
  • SUVAT (uniform a): v = u + at; s = ut + ½at²; v² = u² + 2as.

2. Motion graphs

  • Distance–time: gradient = speed.
  • Speed–time: gradient = acceleration; area = distance. Negative gradient = deceleration.
  • Free fall 1: g ≈ 9.8 m/s² (use 10) — v = gt from rest.

3. Mass, weight, density

W = mg (g ≈ 10 N/kg). Weight acts at the centre of mass; mass is invariant. Density ρ = m/V.

4. Newton's laws and resultant force

  • Resultant: colinear addition/subtraction; perpendicular by Pythagoras.
  • F = ma. Terminal velocity: drag grows with speed until it balances weight.
  • Third law pairs: equal magnitude, opposite direction, different bodies.

5. Momentum (Extended)

p = mv; impulse Ft = Δ(mv); conservation: Σpbefore = Σpafter (explosions, collisions).

Example: 2 kg at 3 m/s hits 1 kg at rest, combined 1 m/s: 6 = 3v ⇒ v = 2 m/s.

6. Moments and equilibrium

  • Moment = F × perpendicular distance from pivot.
  • Principle of moments: Σclockwise = Σanticlockwise.
  • Equilibrium: resultant force = 0 and resultant moment = 0.

Example: 100 N at 0.3 m balances F at 0.5 m: F = 60 N.

title: Scatter Diagrams and Correlation
content:
Scatter Diagrams and Correlation

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): scatter diagrams, types of correlation, line of best fit, interpolation vs extrapolation.

1. Correlation types

  • Positive: both increase (revision time vs score).
  • Negative: one increases, other decreases (price vs demand).
  • No correlation: random scatter.
  • Strength: strong (tight to a line) vs weak (loose).

2. Line of best fit

Balance points either side of the line; it need not pass through the origin. Use two well-separated points on your line (not necessarily data points) to estimate its gradient and equation.

Example: line through (10, 24) and (50, 60): m = 36/40 = 0.9 → y = 0.9x + 15.

3. Using the line

Interpolation (inside the data range) is reliable; extrapolation (outside) is a risk — say so if asked.

4. Correlation ≠ causation

A third factor may drive both variables (ice-cream sales and drownings both rise with temperature). Describe relationships, don't over-claim.

5. Outliers

Points far from the trend: identify, and comment on their effect on the line; ignore them when drawing the best fit if instructed.

Exam tips: describe correlation in full ("strong positive linear correlation"); quote the equation only from two points on the drawn line, not raw data.

title: Exam technique: Logic Gates & Boolean Logic
content:
### What earns the marks
For full marks, ensure you understand the command words: calculate for truth tables, show that for circuit construction, explain and describe for logic expressions. Justify and state are used for problem-to-logic mapping, where defining inputs and outputs earns marks. See statement 10.
### Traps
Error: incorrect truth table row count. Correction: check the number of inputs to determine the row count. Error: writing NOT before a gate. Correction: NOT inverts the output, not the input. Error: incorrect order of operations in logic expressions. Correction: brackets first, then AND, then OR.
### Memory hooks
To remember the six gates, use the mnemonic AND, OR, and NOT to create the others. For truth tables, use the pattern 2 inputs = 4 rows, 3 inputs = 8 rows. To sanity-check a logic expression, plug in values from the truth table.
### Timing
This topic accounts for approximately 10% of the paper. Budget 10-15 minutes to answer questions on logic gates and Boolean logic.

title: AS Level Biology: Cell Structure, Reproduction and Development
content:
Cell Structure, Reproduction and Development — AS Level Biology

This revision note belongs to the Edexcel International Advanced Subsidiary (IAS) Biology specification, WBI12 Unit 2, Topic 3 Cell Structure, Reproduction and Development. It covers the cell as the unit of life, eukaryotic and prokaryotic ultrastructure, microscopy and measurement, the cell cycle and mitosis, meiosis and genetic variation, gametes and fertilisation in mammals and flowering plants, stem cells, and the genetic control of development through gene expression, epigenetics and inheritance. Every statement below the topic owns is covered in its own section or paragraph.

1. Cells as the units of life and the levels of organisation

All living organisms are made of cells, and all cells share some common features: a plasma membrane (cell surface membrane) enclosing the cell, cytoplasm in which most chemical reactions occur, and ribosomes for protein synthesis. Differences between cell types are explained from these common features — for example the presence or absence of a cell wall, a nucleus, or membrane-bound organelles decides what a cell can do. In multicellular organisms, cells are organised into tissues, tissues into organs, and organs into organ systems, each level carrying out a particular function. A tissue is a group of similar cells working together; an organ is made of several tissues with a combined function; an organ system is a group of organs whose functions are linked, such as the digestive system. Understanding this hierarchy matters because a structure at one level is shaped by the level below it — the properties of a tissue follow from the cells it contains.

2. Eukaryotic cell ultrastructure and the functions of the organelles

Eukaryotic cells have a membrane-bound nucleus that contains the chromosomes, and a range of membrane-bound organelles, each with a distinct function. The plasma membrane (cell surface membrane) is a phospholipid bilayer with proteins embedded in it, controlling what enters and leaves the cell. The nucleus is surrounded by a double nuclear envelope with nuclear pores, and contains the cell’s DNA; the nucleolus inside the nucleus is the site of ribosome assembly. Ribosomes, made of a large and a small subunit, are the sites of protein synthesis and occur free in the cytoplasm or attached to the rough endoplasmic reticulum. The rough endoplasmic reticulum (rER) is a stack of membrane-bound sacs studded with ribosomes; it synthesises proteins and passes them on in vesicles. The smooth endoplasmic reticulum (sER) lacks ribosomes and synthesises lipids and carbohydrates. Mitochondria have a double membrane, the inner one folded into cristae to increase surface area, and a matrix that contains the enzymes for aerobic respiration; they supply ATP. Centrioles are paired microtubule cylinders that organise the spindle fibres during nuclear division. Lysosomes are membrane-bound sacs containing hydrolytic enzymes that digest worn-out cell components and pathogens. The Golgi apparatus modifies, sorts and packages proteins into vesicles for secretion or for delivery to other parts of the cell; it is also involved in the formation of extracellular enzymes. The cytoskeleton of microtubules and microfilaments maintains cell shape, holds organelles in place and enables movement within the cell.

3. Prokaryotic cell ultrastructure and how to tell the two apart

Prokaryotic cells are much smaller than eukaryotic cells and lack a membrane-bound nucleus. Their genetic material is a single, circular DNA molecule that lies free in the cytoplasm, not associated with histones. The cell wall is made of peptidoglycan and gives rigidity and shape. Many prokaryotes have a protective capsule outside the cell wall. Plasmids are small circles of DNA separate from the main chromosome; they can be transferred between cells and often carry genes for antibiotic resistance. Flagella — rigid helical tails that rotate — give motility in some prokaryotes, and pili help cells attach to surfaces and to each other and mediate conjugation. Prokaryotic ribosomes are 70S, smaller than the 80S ribosomes of eukaryotes. A bacterium therefore shows, in EM images: cell wall, capsule, plasma membrane, circular DNA free in the cytoplasm, 70S ribosomes, plasmids, and, where present, flagella and pili — and none of the membrane-bound organelles found in a eukaryotic cell.

4. Seeing the ultrastructure: light and electron microscopy

A light microscope uses visible light passed through a specimen; its maximum useful magnification is around ×1500 and its resolution is about 0.2 µm, limited by the wavelength of light. An electron microscope uses a beam of electrons, giving far higher resolution and magnification; transmission electron microscopes (TEM) show the internal ultrastructure of thin sections, and scanning electron microscopes (SEM) show the surface detail of a specimen. Staining is essential in light microscopy because most cells are transparent — stains such as methylene blue for animal cells or iodine solution for starch make structures visible and show up nuclei, starch grains and cell walls. The electron microscope can show the organelles listed in 3.3 — nucleus, nucleolus, ribosomes, rER, sER, mitochondria, centrioles, lysosomes, Golgi apparatus — and, in prokaryotes, the cell wall, capsule, plasma membrane, circular DNA, 70S ribosomes, flagella and pili, so that students can recognise the organelles from electron micrographs. In a light microscope the total magnification equals eyepiece magnification × objective magnification; a graticule (eye-piece graticule) fitted with a stage micrometer lets you calibrate it so real sizes can be measured, and specimens can be drawn to scale from the microscope.

5. Core Practical 5 — observing and drawing animal cells

Use a light microscope to make observations and labelled drawings of suitable animal cells, for example cheek epithelial cells. The steps are: sterilise by wiping the mouth, smear a thin layer of cells onto a slide, stain with methylene blue, lower a coverslip at an angle to avoid air bubbles, and observe under the microscope. Draw what you see with the correct relative sizes of nucleus, cytoplasm and cell membrane, label the parts, and add a title and magnification. Core Practical 5 also develops the skill of using a graticule with a microscope to make measurements and understand the concept of scale — the graticule is calibrated against a stage micrometer at each objective, so the real size of a cell or organelle can be calculated from the number of graticule divisions it spans.

6. Cell division: mitosis, the cell cycle and genetic variation by meiosis

Mitosis produces genetically identical daughter cells for growth and asexual reproduction and is one part of the cell cycle, which is the regular sequence of events in a dividing cell: interphase (during which the cell grows, and DNA is replicated — G1, S and G2), mitosis and cytokinesis. Mitosis itself has stages — prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase — in which the copied chromosomes line up on the equator, separate and move to opposite poles, and new nuclei form, followed by division of the cytoplasm. A useful calculation is the mitotic index, the proportion of cells in a sample that are dividing: mitotic index = number of cells undergoing mitosis ÷ total number of cells in the field of view. This is used in Core Practical 6, the root tip squash, to see and count the stages of mitosis. Meiosis, by contrast, produces genetically non-identical gametes and is the source of variation: in metaphase I the homologous chromosomes line up as pairs and assort independently (independent assortment), and in prophase I crossing over exchanges alleles between the chromatids of a homologous pair, so that gametes carry new combinations of alleles. A locus is the fixed position of a gene on a chromosome; genes on the same chromosome are linked and tend to be inherited together, so linked genes do not assort independently.

7. Gametes, fertilisation in mammals and fertilisation in flowering plants

Mammalian gametes are specialised for their function. Sperm are small and motile, with a haploid nucleus, a lot of mitochondria to power the flagellum, and an acrosome at the head containing enzymes that digest a path through the egg’s outer layers. Egg cells are larger, with cytoplasm containing food reserves; the zona pellucida is a glycoprotein layer around the egg that sperm must penetrate. Fertilisation in mammals begins when the acrosome reaction releases enzymes that digest the zona pellucida, then the cortical reaction releases cortical granules into the space around the egg, hardening the zona pellucida and preventing more than one sperm from entering; finally the sperm and egg nuclei fuse, restoring the diploid number. In flowering plants, fertilisation begins with pollination and the growth of a pollen tube from the pollen grain down through the style to the embryo sac; two male nuclei travel down the tube, one fertilising the egg to form the zygote (which develops into the embryo) and one fusing with the two polar nuclei to form the triploid endosperm that will feed the developing seed — double fertilisation, unique to flowering plants.

8. Stem cells and what society does with them

A stem cell is an undifferentiated cell that can divide to produce more stem cells and differentiated cells. Totipotent stem cells can develop into any cell type and form a complete organism; the zygote and the cells of the early embryo up to the 16-cell morula are totipotent. Pluripotent stem cells can give rise to many, but not all, cell types; cells of the blastocyst are pluripotent, and in plants many meristem cells are totipotent, which is why a whole plant can be grown from a single cell or tissue. Stem cells are used medically — for example in bone marrow transplants for leukaemia — and their use raises ethical and social questions: the source of embryonic stem cells, the balance of benefit against risk, and decisions made by individuals, committees and governments all draw on scientific knowledge but also on values. Students should be able to discuss these issues from a range of ethical viewpoints.

9. Gene expression: how one gene makes more than one protein and how proteins control cells

Cells become specialised through differential gene expression — different genes are switched on or off in different cells, producing active mRNA and then proteins that control cell processes or determine cell structure. One gene can give rise to more than one protein through post-transcriptional changes to messenger RNA (mRNA) such as alternative splicing, in which the same primary transcript is spliced in different ways to make different mRNAs and therefore different polypeptides. Transcription factors switch genes on or off by binding to DNA and promoting or blocking transcription, so they control which proteins a cell makes. Epigenetic modification — including DNA methylation and histone modification — alters the activation of certain genes without changing the DNA sequence itself, and these modifications can be passed on following cell division, so that a cell’s gene activity can be inherited by its daughter cells and, in some cases, across generations.

10. Inheritance: alleles, genotypes, phenotypes and how they vary

A gene is a sequence of bases on a DNA molecule that codes for a sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide. The allele is one of the different forms of a gene; the genotype is the alleles an organism has; the phenotype is the observable feature that results from the genotype and the environment. Recessive alleles only show in the phenotype when homozygous; dominant alleles show even in the heterozygous state; codominance is when both alleles in the heterozygote contribute to the phenotype. Sex linkage is the inheritance of a gene carried on the X chromosome, such as red-green colour blindness in humans, which appears more often in males because they have only one X chromosome and so express a recessive allele on it. Some phenotypes are affected by multiple alleles for the same gene, and others by polygenic inheritance, where many genes each contribute a small effect, giving rise to continuous variation in the phenotype — height in humans is a classic example. The environment can also affect phenotype, so that a feature is the result of an interaction between genotype and environment rather than genotype alone.

11. Mutations: how they arise and what they can do

Errors in DNA replication can give rise to mutations — changes to the base sequence of DNA. A substitution replaces one base with another and may change one amino acid or none (because the code is degenerate); an insertion adds one or more bases, and a deletion removes one or more, and these can cause a frameshift that changes every amino acid after the mutation and often produces a non-functional protein. Mutations are the source of new alleles, and some mutations give rise to cancer or genetic disorders, while many have no observable effect. Cystic fibrosis is a genetic disorder caused by a recessive allele; the faulty allele affects chloride ion channels, so the functioning of the gaseous exchange, digestive and reproductive systems is impaired — thick mucus blocks the airways, the pancreas duct is blocked so digestion is affected, and fertility in males is reduced because the vas deferens is absent or blocked.

12. Genetic screening and the questions it raises

Genetic screening can identify carriers of a recessive allele, and prenatal testing — including amniocentesis (sampling the fluid around the embryo) and chorionic villus sampling (taking a sample of placental tissue) — can check an embryo or fetus for genetic disorders. Pre-implantation genetic diagnosis (PGD) is used during IVF to test embryos before implantation so that only unaffected embryos are used. These techniques raise ethical and social questions: the reliability and risk of the test, the right to know or not to know, who decides what is a disorder worth preventing, the cost and access to treatment, and the risk of starting down a path toward selecting traits rather than preventing disease. Students should be able to identify and discuss these issues from religious, moral and social viewpoints.

13. How to use this note and what to revise next

Use these notes by working section by section through the topic, checking that you can name every organelle, state its function, and recognise it in an electron micrograph. Practise the calculations — magnification, real size from image size and magnification, mitotic index, and the index of diversity and the calculations that appear in the genetics sections. Revise by drawing and labelling an animal cell and a plant cell from memory, annotating each organelle with its function, then testing yourself on meiosis and on how variation arises. After this topic, revise Topic 4 Plant structure, biodiversity and conservation, and Topic 5 Energy flow, ecosystems and the environment, because the genetics here underpins inheritance in those later topics.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Magnification, applied to a mitochondrion measuring 4.2 cm on a micrograph at ×20 000: actual size = image size ÷ magnification. 4.2 cm = 42 000 µm, so the real length is 42 000 ÷ 20 000 = 2.1 µm. Convert every unit to µm before you divide, and write the magnification formula out.
  • Prokaryote or eukaryote: a eukaryote has a nucleus, membrane-bound organelles and 80S ribosomes. A prokaryote has a circular DNA loop, no nucleus and 70S ribosomes. Name at least two of these features; a single feature such as the cell wall is not enough because plants and some prokaryotes both have one.
  • Mitosis versus meiosis: mitosis gives two genetically identical diploid cells. Meiosis gives four haploid cells, and genetic variation comes from crossing over in prophase I and independent assortment at metaphase I. Mark schemes award these two sources separately.
  • Mammalian fertilisation: a sperm and an egg fuse to form a diploid zygote, which restores the diploid number. Name the haploid gametes explicitly, because the mark depends on the stage of meiosis that produces them.

Typical mistakes

  • Describing an organelle instead of answering the question. "Mitochondria have cristae" earns nothing when the question asks why a cell needs many of them. State the function — aerobic respiration, so an ATP supply — and link it to the cell's demand, such as the tail of a sperm or the active transport in a kidney cell.
  • Confusing magnification with resolution. Magnification is how much larger the image is than the object; resolution is the smallest distance at which two points are still seen as separate. The electron microscope wins on resolution, and that is why it separates cristae and ribosomes that a light microscope blurs together.
  • Forgetting to convert units in a magnification calculation. Put image size and real size in the same unit before dividing. 1 mm is 1 000 micrometres, and the mark is often for the unit as much as the number.
  • Using the cell wall alone to identify a plant cell. Bacteria and fungi have walls too. Use the cellulose wall together with the chloroplast or the large permanent vacuole, and remember that plant cells lack centrioles.
  • Mixing up mitosis and meiosis. Mitosis: one division, two genetically identical diploid cells, for growth and asexual reproduction. Meiosis: two divisions, four genetically non-identical haploid cells, for gametes.
  • Saying meiosis "creates variation" without naming the source. Crossing over in prophase I and independent assortment in metaphase I are separate marks; the names of the prophase stages are not required.
  • Counting every cell in the mitotic index. Interphase cells belong in the total, never in the numerator: mitotic index = cells in mitosis divided by all cells in the field.
  • Treating epigenetics as a change in the DNA sequence. Methylation and histone modification change which genes are active without altering the base sequence, and the pattern can be passed to daughter cells after division.

Exam-style questions

  1. A nucleus measures 42 mm across on an electron micrograph taken at a magnification of 7 000. Calculate its actual width. Answer: 42 mm = 42 000 micrometres. Actual size = image size divided by magnification = 42 000 / 7 000 = 6 micrometres.
  2. Explain two features of a sperm cell that adapt it for fertilisation. Answer: many mitochondria in the midpiece supply ATP for the flagellum, so the cell can swim to the egg; the acrosome contains hydrolytic enzymes that digest through the zona pellucida so the sperm can reach the egg membrane.
  3. Give three features visible in an electron micrograph that identify a cell as prokaryotic. Answer: circular DNA lying free in the cytoplasm with no nuclear envelope; 70S ribosomes, smaller than eukaryotic 80S ribosomes; no membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria or Golgi; a peptidoglycan cell wall, sometimes with a capsule, plasmids, flagella or pili.
  4. Explain how a protein destined for secretion is made and released. Answer: ribosomes on the rough endoplasmic reticulum synthesise the polypeptide; the rER folds it and packages it into a vesicle; the vesicle fuses with the Golgi apparatus, which modifies the protein, for example by adding carbohydrate; a secretory vesicle carries it to the plasma membrane and releases it by exocytosis.
  5. A root tip squash contains 80 cells in the field of view, of which 12 show visible chromosomes. Calculate the mitotic index. Answer: 12 / 80 = 0.15, or 15 per cent of the cells are in mitosis. A high value in a root tip is expected because the meristem is growing.
  6. Explain how the cortical reaction prevents a second sperm from fertilising the egg. Answer: when the first sperm fuses with the egg membrane, cortical granules release their contents into the space outside the egg; this hardens the zona pellucida and destroys the binding sites, so no further sperm can penetrate.
  7. Explain two ways in which meiosis produces gametes that are genetically different from each other. Answer: crossing over in prophase I exchanges alleles between non-sister chromatids of a homologous pair, so each chromatid carries a new combination; independent assortment in metaphase I means the maternal and paternal chromosomes of each pair line up randomly, giving 2 to the power n different combinations for n pairs.
  8. Explain how one gene can give rise to more than one protein. Answer: the primary transcript can be spliced in different ways, so different mature mRNAs carry different exon combinations; each mRNA is translated into a different polypeptide. Epigenetic modification can also switch the gene on or off in different cells, so the same gene produces protein in one cell type and not in another.

title: Cambridge IGCSE First Language English: Reading for Information and Inference
content:
Cambridge IGCSE First Language English: Reading for Information and Inference

Paper 1 of Cambridge IGCSE First Language English (0500) is a reading paper: you meet one or more unseen passages and answer questions that move from what the text says to what it means. The assessment separates two skills — reading for explicit meaning (facts stated on the page) and reading for implicit meaning and inference (facts you must work out) — and both are trainable with method rather than intuition. This note builds the complete reading method from zero: how to annotate a passage, how to answer each question type in the form the mark scheme rewards, and how to infer exactly one step beyond the evidence without drifting into guesswork.

What Paper 1 is testing

The passages are usually narrative, descriptive or discursive extracts from fiction, journalism, travel writing, autobiography or speeches. The questions ask you to retrieve information, infer meaning and attitude, and explain how the writer achieves effects.
