Error: n used instead of (n-1) in terms. Correction: first term needs zero gaps. Error: infinity sums with |r| >= 1. Correction: check convergence first. Error: differentiating S_n for the nth term. Correction: subtract S_{n-1}.
### Worked example
An arithmetic progression has a = 5 and d = 3. The 20th term is a + 19d = 5 + 57 = 62. The sum of the first 20 terms is S₂₀ = (20/2)(2a + 19d) = 10 × 67 = 670. A geometric progression with terms 2, 6, 18 has r = 3, so S₅ = 2(3⁵ − 1)/(3 − 1) = 242. The sum to infinity exists only when |r| < 1, so for r = 1/2 with a = 8 the sum is 8 / (1 − 1/2) = 16.
### Check yourself
State the nth term of a sequence from its sum. Find Sₙ, then subtract Sₙ₋₁. Do not differentiate Sₙ, because the sum is a discrete function.

### Worked example
An arithmetic progression has a = 5 and d = 3. The 20th term is a + 19d = 5 + 57 = 62. The sum of the first 20 terms is S₂₀ = (20/2)(2a + 19d) = 10 × 67 = 670. A geometric progression with terms 2, 6, 18 has r = 3, so S₅ = 2(3⁵ − 1)/(3 − 1) = 242. The sum to infinity exists only when |r| < 1, so for r = 1/2 with a = 8 the sum is 8 / (1 − 1/2) = 16.
### Check yourself
State the nth term of a sequence from its sum. Find Sₙ, then subtract Sₙ₋₁. Do not differentiate Sₙ, because the sum is a discrete function.

title: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Congruence and Similarity
content:
Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Congruence and Similarity

Two shapes are congruent when they are identical in shape and size; they are similar when they are the same shape but a different size. Those two ideas power a whole family of exam questions: proving triangles congruent, finding missing lengths with scale factors, and scaling areas and volumes — where the factors square and cube. This note builds the topic from zero: the four congruence tests with how to write a proof, the similarity rules and the length–area–volume factor chain, and symmetry (line and rotational) with its order and practical counting.

Congruence: identical in every way

Congruent shapes have the same side lengths and the same angles — one can be moved onto the other by translation, rotation or reflection (but not enlargement). Triangles are the workhorse, and four tests prove congruence:

TestWhat you need
SSSthree pairs of corresponding sides equal
SAStwo pairs of sides and the included angle equal
ASA (or AAS)two pairs of angles and a corresponding side equal
RHSright angle, hypotenuse and one other side equal

Note what is not a test: AAA proves similarity, not congruence (same shape, different size), and SSA is not valid in general (the ambiguous case). Writing a congruence proof means listing the three equalities with reasons and naming the test.

Worked example. In triangles ABC and PQR: AB = PQ, angle ABC = angle PQR, BC = QR. Prove the triangles are congruent.

AB = PQ       (given)
angle ABC = angle PQR  (given, the included angle)
BC = QR       (given)
Therefore triangles ABC and PQR are congruent (SAS).

Worked example 2 (RHS). Two right-angled triangles share a hypotenuse of 13 cm, and each has one shorter side 5 cm. Are they congruent?

Right angle: given; hypotenuse 13 = 13; one side 5 = 5.
RHS applies, so the triangles are congruent - in fact both
have the third side √(169 - 25) = 12 cm.

Similarity: same shape, scaled size

Two shapes are similar when corresponding angles are equal and corresponding sides are in the same ratio. For triangles, any one of these proves similarity:

  • AAA (or AA): two pairs of equal angles suffice (the third follows from the angle sum).
  • All three sides in the same ratio (SSS similarity).
  • Two sides in the same ratio with the included angle equal (SAS similarity).

The scale factor k compares corresponding lengths:

k = length in image / length in original
missing length = corresponding length x k

Worked example. Triangles ABC and DEF are similar with AB = 6 cm, DE = 9 cm, BC = 8 cm. Find EF.

k = DE/AB = 9/6 = 1.5
EF = BC x k = 8 × 1.5 = 12 cm

Worked example 2 (working backwards). Similar rectangles have areas 50 cm² and 200 cm²; the smaller is 5 cm wide. Find the width of the larger.

area factor = 200/50 = 4
length factor k = √(4) = 2
width = 5 × 2 = 10 cm

The length–area–volume factor chain

This is the highest-yield similarity result in the syllabus: if the length scale factor is k, then areas scale by k² and volumes by k³.

QuantityFactorExample (k = 3)
Lengthksides triple
Areak²areas multiply by 9
Volumek³volumes multiply by 27

Worked example. Two similar bottles hold 250 ml and 2000 ml. The smaller is 12 cm tall. Find the height of the larger and the ratio of their surface areas.

volume factor = 2000/250 = 8
k = cube root of 8 = 2
height = 12 × 2 = 24 cm
area factor = k² = 4, so the larger has 4 times the surface area.

Worked example 2 (reverse). Two similar solids have surface areas in the ratio 9 : 25. Find the ratio of their volumes.

area factor 9/25 → k = √(9/25) = 3/5
volume ratio = k³ = 27/125

Similarity in real geometry: triangles in circles and parallel lines

Similar triangles hide inside diagrams. Two standard configurations:

  • Parallel lines cutting a triangle: a line parallel to one side of a triangle creates a smaller similar triangle (corresponding angles equal).
  • Intersecting chords and the "bow-tie": two chords crossing inside a circle create similar triangles because angles in the same segment are equal — this is the route to the intersecting-chords result.

Worked example. In triangle ABC, DE is parallel to BC with D on AB and E on AC. AD = 4 cm, DB = 6 cm, DE = 5 cm. Find BC.

Triangles ADE and ABC are similar (DE parallel BC gives
corresponding angles).
k = AB/AD = (4 + 6)/4 = 2.5
BC = DE x k = 5 × 2.5 = 12.5 cm

Symmetry: lines and rotation

Symmetry is examined as counting and as reasoning:

  • Line (reflective) symmetry: a line about which the shape maps onto itself. Count the lines: a square has 4, an equilateral triangle 3, a rectangle 2, a regular n-gon n, a circle infinitely many.
  • Rotational symmetry: the shape maps onto itself when rotated about a centre by less than 360°. The order is the number of distinct positions in a full turn (a square has order 4; a parallelogram order 2; a scalene triangle order 1 or none).
  • Regular polygons: n lines of symmetry and rotational symmetry of order n.

Worked example. State the line and rotational symmetry of a regular hexagon and of an isosceles trapezium.

regular hexagon: 6 lines of symmetry; rotational order 6
isosceles trapezium: 1 line of symmetry (vertical through the
midpoints of the parallel sides); rotational order 1 (none)

Writing congruence and similarity proofs for marks

Proof questions are marked on structure as much as conclusion, and the structure has three parts: name the pair of triangles you are comparing (in corresponding order); list every equality with its reason (given, common side, vertically opposite, alternate angles, radii of the same circle); and finish with the test that the equalities satisfy. A proof that reaches the right conclusion without naming the test loses the final mark, and one that names equalities out of correspondence order cannot be followed.

Triangle ABC and triangle PQR:
  AB = PQ        (given)
  angle B = angle Q (given)
  BC = QR        (common/given)
Therefore ABC is congruent to PQR (SAS).

For similarity, the same scaffold with a different finish: two pairs of equal angles (or equivalent ratios of sides) and the word "similar" with the test named. State the correspondence explicitly — writing ABC similar to PQR means A matches P, B matches Q, C matches R — because the next part of the question will expect you to use those pairings to form ratios.

Worked examples: mixed congruence and similarity

Worked example. A photograph 15 cm by 10 cm is enlarged so its longer side becomes 24 cm. Find the shorter side and the ratio of areas.

k = 24/15 = 1.6
shorter side = 10 × 1.6 = 16 cm
area ratio = k² = 2.56
(new area is 2.56 times the old)

Worked example 2. Explain why all circles are similar but not all rectangles are.

Circles: every circle is a scaled copy of every other (same shape,
different radius), so they are similar.
Rectangles: only those with the same length-to-width ratio are
similar; a 2 × 1 rectangle and a 3 × 1 rectangle have different
ratios, so they are not similar.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Congruence test) State the four tests for congruent triangles. Answer: SSS, SAS, ASA (or AAS), RHS.
  2. (Proof) Triangles ABC and XYZ have AB = XY, AC = XZ and angle BAC = angle YXZ. Are they congruent? Which test? Answer: Yes — SAS, because the equal angles are included between the equal sides.
  3. (Scale factor) Two similar triangles have corresponding sides 5 cm and 8 cm. Find the area factor. Answer: k = 8/5 = 1.6; area factor = 2.56.
  4. (Volumes) Two similar cones have heights 6 cm and 15 cm. Find the ratio of their volumes. Answer: k = 2.5; volume ratio = 2.5³ = 15.625 (or 125 : 8).
  5. (Reverse) Two similar solids have volumes in the ratio 64 : 27. Find the ratio of their surface areas. Answer: k = 4/3; area ratio = 16/9.
  6. (Parallel line) In a triangle, a line parallel to the base divides the other two sides in the ratio 3 : 2 (from the vertex). If the base is 15 cm, find the parallel segment. Answer: k = 3/(3 + 2) = 0.6; segment = 9 cm.
  7. (Symmetry) State the symmetry of a regular octagon. Answer: 8 lines of symmetry; rotational symmetry of order 8.
  8. (Reasoning) A student says two rectangles with the same perimeter are similar. Give a counterexample. Answer: A 4 × 2 rectangle (perimeter 12) and a 5 × 1 rectangle (perimeter 12) are not similar — their side ratios differ.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • AAA as congruence: three equal angles prove similarity, not congruence. Size can differ.
  • SSA: two sides and a non-included angle do not determine a unique triangle — never cite it as a congruence test.
  • Area factor as k: areas scale by k², volumes by k³. Doubling lengths quadruples areas and octuples volumes — the most common Paper 4 error.
  • Square-root confusion: from an area ratio take the square root to get k; from a volume ratio take the cube root.
  • Correspondence: match corresponding vertices in the order named (ABC to PQR means A↔P, B↔Q, C↔R). Mixing the order produces wrong ratios.
  • Rotational order 1: a shape with no rotational symmetry has order 1, not 0 — one full turn always maps a shape onto itself.
  • Line symmetry count: a rectangle has 2 lines, a square 4; do not assume all quadrilaterals have the same.
  • Proof formatting: list each equality with its reason and finish with the test name. The structure is the mark scheme.

title: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Bearings, Constructions and Loci
content:
Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Bearings, Constructions and Loci

Bearings are how navigators describe direction, and geometrical constructions are how geometers draw exact figures with only a ruler and a pair of compasses. Together they fill the practical geometry questions on both papers: a bearing calculated from a diagram, a locus sketched and shaded, a perpendicular bisector constructed and justified. This note builds the topic from zero: the three rules of bearings and the back-bearing calculation, the compass-and-ruler constructions with their standard arcs, scale drawings and their measurements, and the four loci the syllabus requires, with every step shown.

Bearings: the three rules

A bearing is a direction written as a three-figure angle. Three rules define it:

  1. Measured from North (the north line, drawn as an upward arrow).
  2. Clockwise.
  3. Written with three figures — 035°, 090°, 245° (never 35° or 9°).

Bearings are always between 000° and 360°; a direction due east is 090°, due south 180°, due west 270°.

Worked example. A ship sails from A on a bearing of 060° for 12 km to B, then on a bearing of 150° for 8 km to C. Describe the position of C relative to A qualitatively.

060 ° is between north and east; 150 ° is between east and
south. So C lies south-east of A, and the two legs turn 90 °
(150 - 60 = 90) - the path is two perpendicular legs, making a
right angle at B.

Back bearings

The bearing of A from B is not the bearing of B from A — they differ by 180° (add if under 180°, subtract if 180° or more):

back bearing = bearing + 180  (if bearing < 180)
             = bearing - 180  (if bearing >= 180)

Worked example. The bearing of B from A is 072°. Find the bearing of A from B.

72 + 180 = 252 °

Worked example 2 (three-figure check). The bearing of P from Q is 310°. Find the bearing of Q from P.

310 - 180 = 130 °

Bearings with trigonometry

Bearing problems become right-triangle problems once you draw the north lines and mark the angles between the path and north. Use Pythagoras for distances and trigonometry for angles, then convert the angle into a bearing.

Worked example. A boat sails 5 km due north, then 12 km due east. Find its distance and bearing from the start.

distance = √(5² + 12²) = √(169) = 13 km
angle east of north: tan(θ) = 12/5  →  θ = 67.4 °
bearing = 067 ° (to the nearest degree)

Worked example 2 (reverse). A helicopter is 9 km from base on a bearing of 145°. How far east and how far south of the base is it?

angle from south = 180 - 145 = 35 °
east = 9 sin(35) = 5.16 km
south = 9 cos(35) = 7.37 km

Constructions: ruler and compasses only

Constructions are marked on the accuracy of the arcs and the visibility of the construction lines. Keep your compasses sharp and do not rub out the arcs.

ConstructionStandard method (in order)
Perpendicular bisector of ABcompasses wider than half AB: arc from A, same-radius arc from B, both sides; join the two intersections
Angle bisectorarc across both arms from the vertex; same-radius arcs from those two crossings; join the vertex to their intersection
Perpendicular from a point to a linearc from the point cutting the line twice; equal arcs from those cuts; join the point to their intersection
Perpendicular at a point on a lineequal arcs either side of the point; then the perpendicular-bisector method between them
60° anglearc from the endpoint across the line; same radius arc from the crossing; join
Triangle given SSSdraw the base; arcs of the other two lengths from each end; join the intersection

Worked example. Construct the perpendicular bisector of a segment AB of length 8 cm and explain why every point on it is equidistant from A and B.

Construction: arcs of radius > 4 cm from A and from B, above and
below the segment; the two intersections join to form the bisector.
Why: the arcs are circles of equal radius centred at A and B, so
their intersection points are equidistant from A and B; the line
through them is the locus of all such points.

Scale drawings

A scale drawing represents a real situation to a ratio: 1 : 50 000 means 1 cm on paper represents 50 000 cm in reality (0.5 km). The method: convert the scale to a usable unit, measure or construct to scale, then read back with the reverse conversion.

Worked example. A map has scale 1 : 25 000. Two towns are 6.4 cm apart on the map. Find the real distance in km.

6.4 cm x 25 000 = 160 000 cm
160 000 cm = 1600 m = 1.6 km

Worked example 2 (drawing). A field is 400 m by 250 m. Draw it at scale 1 : 5000. What are the drawing dimensions?

400 m = 40 000 cm; /5000 = 8 cm
250 m = 25 000 cm; /5000 = 5 cm
The drawing is 8 cm by 5 cm.

Loci

A locus is the set of all points satisfying a condition. Four standard loci are examinable, and each has its construction:

  • Fixed distance from a point: a circle (arc) of that radius, centred on the point.
  • Equidistant from two points: the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining them.
  • Equidistant from two lines: the angle bisector(s) of the angle between them.
  • Fixed distance from a line: two parallel lines at that distance, one on each side (with semicircular ends for a segment).

Region questions combine loci: "shade the region closer to A than B and within 3 cm of C" means intersect the perpendicular bisector's half-plane with the circle's interior.

Worked example. A goat is tethered to a corner of a 6 m by 4 m shed with a 5 m rope. Describe the region it can reach.

A three-quarter circle of radius 5 m around the corner, minus
the part blocked by the shed: the rope wraps the shed's⁴ m and
6 m walls. The reachable region is the quarter circle of radius
5 m outside the shed plus smaller arcs where the rope wraps
(radius 1 m around the far 4 m corner, no reach around the far
6 m corner since 5 - 6 < 0).

Worked examples: bearings and loci together

Worked example. Two radio transmitters A and B are 10 km apart, with B due east of A. A signal is received equally strongly at points equidistant from A and B, and within 6 km of A. Describe the region.

Equidistant from A and B: the perpendicular bisector of AB - a
north-south line 5 km east of A.
Within 6 km of A: a circle of radius 6 km centred at A.
The region is the part of the circle on one side of the bisector:
a circular segment of radius 6 km, cut by the line 5 km from A.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Bearing definition) State the three rules for a bearing. Answer: Measured from north, clockwise, written as three figures.
  2. (Back bearing) The bearing of X from Y is 128°. Find the bearing of Y from X. Answer: a back bearing reverses direction, so add 180° when the bearing is below 180°: 128° + 180° = 308° (if the bearing exceeds 180°, subtract 180° instead).
  3. (Calculation) A plane flies 30 km north then 40 km east. Find its distance from the start and its bearing. Answer: distance = √(900 + 1600) = 50 km; tan θ = 40/30 → θ = 53.1°, bearing 053°.
  4. (Components) A ship is 15 km from port on a bearing of 210°. Find its distance west of the port. Answer: angle from south = 210 − 180 = 30°; west = 15 sin 30 = 7.5 km.
  5. (Construction) Describe how to construct the perpendicular bisector of a 6 cm segment. Answer: set the compasses to more than half the segment — more than 3 cm — and draw arcs from each end both above and below it; the two crossings of the arcs give the points the bisector passes through, so join them, and every point on that line is equidistant from both ends.
  6. (Locus) Describe the locus of points equidistant from the sides of an angle. Answer: The angle bisector — every point on it is the same perpendicular distance from both arms.
  7. (Scale) On a 1 : 20 000 map, a lake is 3.5 cm long. Find its real length in km. Answer: 3.5 × 20 000 = 70 000 cm = 0.7 km.
  8. (Region) Shade the region inside a triangle that is closer to side AB than to side AC and within 2 cm of vertex A. Answer: closer to AB than to AC means the half-plane on AB's side of the angle bisector of angle A, and within 2 cm of A means inside the circle of radius 2 cm centred on A; the shaded region is the intersection of those two, bounded by the bisector and the compass arc.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Two-figure bearings: 35° must be written 035°. Three figures, always.
  • Measuring from the wrong north: bearings start at north, not east. A bearing of 090° is east, not north.
  • Back-bearing addition: add 180 if the bearing is below 180, subtract if above; the result must stay between 000 and 360.
  • Anticlockwise angles: bearing questions are clockwise; a clockwise angle and its anticlockwise partner sum to 360.
  • Rubbing out construction arcs: the arcs are the evidence. Leave them visible and use a sharp pencil.
  • Locus shading: shade the region, not the boundary line; the question usually says "shade the region".
  • Scale unit slips: convert the real measurement to the same unit as the drawing before applying the ratio, and remember 1 km = 100 000 cm.
  • Diagram not to scale: measure only when told to; otherwise calculate. A protractor reading on a "not to scale" diagram earns nothing.

Bearings drawn properly: clockwise from north, three digits, always

A bearing is not an angle inside a triangle — it is a direction on the page, and almost every lost mark on this topic comes from measuring it from the wrong place or turning the wrong way. One drawing fixes the idea for good.

The three rules, in the order they bite. A bearing is measured from the north line at the point you are leaving, it turns clockwise, and it is written with three digits (060°, not 60°, and 025° rather than 25°). The third rule is not fussiness: 070° and 007° are different directions, and the leading zeros are how a reader tells them apart.

The back bearing is the return journey. If B is on a bearing of 060° from A, then A is on a bearing of 240° from B:

back bearing = bearing + 180° (or − 180° if the result would exceed 360°) Key: both are the same line measured from opposite ends. Adding 180° cannot go wrong; subtracting can, so add and then subtract 360° if necessary. For 060°: 60 + 180 = 240°. For 300°: 300 + 180 = 480, and 480 − 360 = 120°.

Worked example. A ship sails 12 km from port P on a bearing of 060°, then 9 km on a bearing of 150°. How far is it from P, and on what bearing?

Draw the two legs nose-to-tail. The turn between them is 150 − 60 = 90°, so the two legs are perpendicular and the distance closes as a right-angled triangle:
distance = √(12² + 9²) = √(144 + 81) = √225 = 15 km

The overall bearing is the angle from north to the closing line, which needs the angle at P inside the triangle: tan θ = 9 / 12, so θ = 36.9°, and the bearing is 60 − 36.9 = 023.1° on the far side — which is why the sketch, not the arithmetic, decides between adding and subtracting. Candidates who skip the sketch get 15 km and then guess the direction.

Where marks are lost. Measuring anticlockwise (bearing 060 becomes the 300° direction). Measuring from the horizontal or from another bearing rather than from north. Writing two digits. And finding the distance with a scale drawing but then reading the bearing off the wrong vertex — the bearing of A from B is not the bearing of B from A, and the question always says which.

Bearings in more depth

A bearing gives a direction as an angle measured clockwise from north, written as three figures. Bearings are the commonest context for angle questions in navigation, and they combine with the sine and cosine rules when the journey is not at right angles. The subsections below cover measuring, reversing and using bearings in a calculation, which are the three skills the mark scheme checks.

Measuring a bearing with a protractor

Place the centre of the protractor on the point where the bearing starts, with the zero line pointing north. Read the angle clockwise from north to the line that joins the start point to the target. A bearing of 65° is read on the outer scale of a protractor when the north line points up the page. Always check which scale you are reading, because the inner scale gives the anticlockwise angle and loses marks.

Three-figure bearings in exam answers

Exam bearings are written with exactly three figures, so a bearing of 8° is written 008°, and 65° is written 065°. The three-figure form is required even when the answer has a leading zero. A bearing given with two figures will normally be marked wrong, so write the final answer in the form the question asks for and keep the degree sign.

The bearing of A from B and of B from A

The bearing of B from A and the bearing of A from B are not the same. The first is measured at A, the second at B. They differ by exactly 180°, so if the bearing of B from A is 070°, the bearing of A from B is 250°. Draw a north line at each point, because the question usually asks for one direction and the reversed direction is the common error.

Back bearings

A back bearing is the bearing of the start point from the end point, and it is found by adding or subtracting 180°. If the bearing is less than 180°, add 180°. If it is more than 180°, subtract 180°. The back bearing is used when a journey is reversed, and it is also used as a check on a diagram, since the two north lines at the points are parallel.

Bearings with trigonometry

A bearing often describes one side of a triangle, and the other sides are found with the sine or cosine rule. Put the north lines on the diagram, mark the bearing as an angle between the north line and the side, and then find the interior angle of the triangle. Once the angle is known, the rule is applied in the usual way, and the bearings are only used to find that angle.

A worked navigation problem

A ship sails 12 km on a bearing of 040° and then 9 km on a bearing of 130°. The angle between the two legs at the turning point is found from the bearings: the turn is 130° − 040° = 090°, so the path is at right angles and the distance back to the start is √(12² + 9²) = 15 km. Each step uses one bearing to find an angle, and then Pythagoras or a rule gives the length.

Checking a bearing answer

A bearing must lie between 000° and 360°. Check that the answer is measured clockwise from north, that it has three figures, and that a diagram drawn to scale agrees with the value. A bearing of 200° points roughly south-south-west, so a diagram showing it pointing north-east is a sign that the angle was measured from the wrong line.

title: Coordination, Response and Gene Technology — Study Notes
content:
Coordination, Response and Gene Technology

Edexcel IAL Biology WBI15, Topic 8. Nervous and hormonal systems coordinate the body, and plants respond to light and gravity using hormones. Gene technology uses enzymes to cut, join and copy DNA for medicine, research and agriculture.

Nervous coordination

  • A reflex arc passes information from a receptor along a sensory neurone, through a relay neurone in the spinal cord, and along a motor neurone to an effector. It is fast and does not need conscious control.
  • The resting potential is about −70 mV. The sodium-potassium pump moves three Na⁺ out and two K⁺ in, maintaining the gradient.
  • An action potential is a rapid depolarisation as voltage-gated sodium channels open, followed by repolarisation as potassium channels open. The myelin sheath allows saltatory conduction.
  • At a cholinergic synapse, an action potential causes Ca²⁺ to enter the presynaptic knob. Vesicles of acetylcholine fuse with the membrane, and the transmitter diffuses across the cleft and binds to receptors. Acetylcholinesterase breaks it down.

Hormonal coordination

  • Insulin is released from β cells when blood glucose is high. It increases glucose uptake and glycogenesis, and lowers blood glucose.
  • Glucagon is released from α cells when blood glucose is low. It stimulates glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.
  • Adrenaline prepares the body for fight or flight by raising heart rate and glucose release.

Plant responses

  • Auxin is made in the shoot tip and moves to the shaded side of a shoot. Cells on that side elongate faster, so the shoot bends towards the light (positive phototropism).
  • Roots show positive gravitropism and shoots show negative gravitropism.

Gene technology

  • Restriction endonucleases cut DNA at specific palindromic sequences. Many leave sticky ends that are complementary to each other.
  • DNA ligase joins the sugar-phosphate backbone of two DNA fragments. Plasmids are used as vectors to carry the gene into bacteria.
  • Reverse transcriptase makes complementary DNA (cDNA) from mRNA, so the cDNA has no introns.
  • In PCR, the sample is heated to separate the strands, primers anneal, and Taq polymerase extends the new strands. Each cycle doubles the amount of DNA.

Exam tip: for a question on synapses, give the steps in order: action potential, calcium entry, vesicle fusion, diffusion, binding, and then removal of the transmitter.

title: IGCSE Mathematics: Fractions, Decimals and Percentages
content:
IGCSE Mathematics: Fractions, Decimals and Percentages

Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580 (2025–2027), section 1 Number: statement 1.4 Fractions, decimals and percentages (equivalence and conversion), 1.13 Percentages (including Extended reverse percentages) and E1.17 Exponential growth and decay. These three representations describe the same quantities, and fluent movement between them is one of the biggest sources of marks in both papers. The note explains why the conversion methods work before showing them, then builds percentages as multipliers — the technique behind most Paper 4 percentage problems.

What a fraction really is

A fraction is a division: 3/4 means 3 divided by 4, or three quarters of a whole. The top (numerator) counts the parts; the bottom (denominator) says how many equal parts the whole is cut into. A proper fraction has a smaller numerator (3/4); an improper fraction has a larger one (7/4); a mixed number combines a whole number with a proper fraction (1 3/4).

Convert 2 3/5 to an improper fraction:

2 wholes = 10 fifths, and 3 more fifths gives 13 fifths:
2 3/5 = (2 × 5 + 3)/5 = 13/5

Equivalent fractions are the same quantity written differently: 3/4 = 6/8 = 15/20, because multiplying top and bottom by the same number is multiplying by 1 (a form of 1, such as 3/3), which changes the look but not the value. Cancelling is the reverse: dividing top and bottom by a common factor. Only factors of the whole numerator and denominator can be cancelled — (x + 3)/(x + 2) cannot be simplified by cancelling the x's, because the top is a sum, not a product.

Converting between fractions, decimals and percentages

Fraction to decimal: divide.  3/8 = 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375
Decimal to fraction: read the place value.  0.47 = 47/100
Fraction to percentage: divide, then multiply by 100.  3/8 = 0.375 = 37.5%
Percentage to fraction: write over 100 and simplify.  45% = 45/100 = 9/20

Recurring decimals. A fraction always produces either a terminating decimal or a recurring one, and every recurring decimal converts back to a fraction by the algebra method:

Write 0.444... (4 recurring) as a fraction:

Let x = 0.444...
Then 10x = 4.444...        [shift the decimal one place]
Subtract:  10x - x = 4.444... - 0.444...
9x = 4
x = 4/9
Write 0.273636... (36 recurring) as a fraction:

Let x = 0.273636...
Two digits repeat, so shift two places:  100x = 27.363636...
100x - x = 27.3636... - 0.2736... = 27.09
99x = 27.09  →  x = 27.09/99 = 301/1100 after multiplying top and bottom by 100 and simplifying

Knowing the common conversions by heart saves time: 1/2 = 0.5 = 50%, 1/4 = 0.25 = 25%, 3/4 = 0.75, 1/5 = 0.2 = 20%, 1/8 = 0.125, 1/3 = 0.333... = 33 1/3%.

FractionDecimalPercentage
1/20.550%
1/40.2525%
3/40.7575%
1/50.220%
1/80.12512.5%
1/30.333...33 1/3%
2/30.666...66 2/3%

These seven values answer a surprising share of Paper 2 questions by inspection, and they anchor every conversion done the long way.

Percentages: the multiplier method

A percentage is a fraction out of 100 — literally per cent, per hundred. Every percentage problem is a multiplication, and the fastest method converts straight to a multiplier.

Find 35% of 240:

35% = 35/100 = 0.35, so  0.35 × 240 = 84

Increase 240 by 35%:
the new value is 135% of the old, so multiply by 1.35:  1.35 × 240 = 324

Decrease 240 by 35%:
the new value is 65% of the old, so multiply by 0.65:   0.65 × 240 = 156

Why the multiplier works. Increasing by 35% means keeping the original 100% and adding 35%, so the result is 135% of the original, which is 1.35 times it. Decreasing by 35% leaves 65%, which is 0.65 times. The multiplier also chains: successive changes multiply, which is why two discounts of 20% are not one discount of 40% (0.8 × 0.8 = 0.64, a 36% total reduction).

One quantity as a percentage of another:  18 out of 60

18/60 × 100 = 30%

Reverse percentages (Extended). Working backwards from a final value needs division:

A price after a 20% increase is £72. Find the original price.

The original is 100%, the new price is 120% of it, so the multiplier is 1.2:
original = 72 / 1.2 = £60

Check: 60 × 1.2 = 72 ✓

The common error is finding 20% of 72 and subtracting; the percentage must be taken from the original 100%, not the final amount.

Percentage change and comparisons

A coat falls from £80 to £56. Find the percentage decrease.

change = 80 - 56 = 24
percentage change = change / original x 100 = 24/80 × 100 = 30%

Percentage change always uses the original value as the denominator. Comparing quantities with different sizes — prices per 100 g, speeds, wages per hour — is done by putting both over a common quantity before comparing.

Exponential growth and decay (Extended)

When a quantity changes by the same percentage each period, it is multiplied by a fixed factor each time, and the result is exponential growth or decay. The multiplier is 1 + r for growth and 1 − r for decay, where r is the rate as a decimal.

After n periods at rate r:
growth:    final = original x (1 + r)^n
decay:     final = original x (1 - r)^n

Why the power. Each period multiplies by the same factor, so n periods multiply n times: an investment of £500 growing 3% a year becomes 500 × 1.03 after one year, 500 × 1.03 × 1.03 after two, and 500 × 1.03ⁿ after n years. The power counts the multiplications.

£500 is invested at 3% compound interest per year for 4 years.

500 × 1.03⁴ = 500 × 1.12550881 = £562.75 (2 d.p.)

Year by year check: 515.00 → 530.45 → 546.36 → 562.75 ✓
A car worth £18 000 depreciates 15% per year. Value after 3 years:

18 000 × 0.85³ = 18 000 × 0.614125 = £11 054.25

Exponential growth graphs climb ever faster and never touch zero; exponential decay graphs fall steeply at first and then level off towards — but never reach — zero (a horizontal asymptote). Doubling and halving questions are solved by logs or trial multiplication: for how many years does £500 at 3% exceed £600? Solve 500 × 1.03ⁿ > 600 by testing values of n, since 1.03ⁿ > 1.2 needs n ⩾ 7 years.

Worked example: a full percentage question

A shop sells a jacket for £84 after a 20% reduction. A further 10% discount is offered for cash.

Original price before the 20% reduction:
84 = original x 0.80
original = 84 / 0.80 = £105

Cash price after the extra 10%:
84 × 0.90 = £75.60

Total percentage saving against the original:
saving = 105 - 75.60 = 29.40
percentage saving = 29.40/105 × 100 = 28%

Check with multipliers: 0.80 × 0.90 = 0.72, so the cash price is 72% of the
original and the saving is 28% ✓

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Finding a percentage of the wrong amount: increase/decrease percentages apply to the original; reverse percentages divide by the multiplier.
  • Adding percentage changes: two 20% discounts give 0.8 × 0.8 = 0.64, a 36% reduction, not 40%.
  • Writing a recurring decimal as a fraction by eye; use the shift-and-subtract method and show it.
  • Cancelling across a sum: 3/4 is not 3 quarters of the top and bottom separately.
  • Using 365 days or 12 months inconsistently in compound problems: the power n counts compounding periods, so match it to the rate.
  • Forgetting that 15% decrease means multiplying by 0.85, not by −0.15 or 0.15.
  • Confusing 33% with 1/3 exactly: 1/3 = 33 1/3%, and the difference matters in exact answers.
  • Deciding an exponential decay value reaches zero; it falls below £1 or 0.001 but never reaches zero.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 2, 3 marks). Express 0.45 as a fraction in its lowest terms.

Answer: 0.45 = 45/100 = 9/20.

Question 2 (Paper 2, 3 marks). Write 0.27 with the 27 recurring as a fraction.

Answer: Let x = 0.272727...; then 100x = 27.2727...; subtracting gives 99x = 27, so x = 27/99 = 3/11.

Question 3 (Paper 4, 4 marks). In a sale, a bike is reduced by 15% to £255. Find the original price.

Answer: £255 represents 85% of the original, so the multiplier is 0.85 and the original price is 255/0.85 = £300. Check: 300 × 0.85 = 255 ✓.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 4 marks). A bacteria culture starts with 2000 and increases by 8% each hour. Find the size after 5 hours.

Answer: 2000 × 1.08⁵ = 2000 × 1.4693280768 = 2938.7 ≈ 2939 bacteria.

Question 5 (Paper 4, 3 marks). A town's population falls from 45 000 to 36 000 over a year. Find the percentage decrease.

Answer: Change = 9000; percentage = 9000/45 000 × 100 = 20%.

Question 6 (Paper 4, 5 marks). A car is bought for £12 000 and depreciates 18% in the first year and 12% in the second. Find its value after two years and the overall percentage loss.

Answer: 12 000 × 0.82 × 0.88 = 12 000 × 0.7216 = £8659.20. Overall loss = £3340.80, which is 3340.80/12 000 × 100 = 27.84% ≈ 27.8%. (Note 0.82 × 0.88 = 0.7216, a 27.84% total fall — not 30%.)

Fractions describe parts; powers and roots describe repeated multiplication — the next topic.

Fractions in practice: simplifying, adding and dividing

Most lost marks on fraction questions come from skipping one small step. Simplify early, find a common denominator before adding, and turn a division into a multiplication by the reciprocal. Each subsection below gives one rule and one fully worked number.

Simplifying by the highest common factor

To simplify a fraction, divide the numerator and the denominator by their highest common factor. For example, 6/8 has a highest common factor of 2, so 6/8 = 3/4. A fraction is fully simplified when the numerator and denominator share no factor except 1. Check this before you give a final answer, because an unsimplified fraction usually loses the accuracy mark.

Adding and subtracting fractions

Fractions can only be added or subtracted once they share a denominator. Write each over the lowest common multiple of the denominators. For 2/3 + 3/4, the common denominator is 12, so the sum is 8/12 + 9/12 = 17/12. Leave an improper fraction as a mixed number if the question asks for one: 17/12 = 1 5/12.

Multiplying fractions

Multiply the numerators together and the denominators together. Cancel common factors first, because it keeps the numbers small. For 2/3 × 3/5, the 3 on the top and the 3 on the bottom cancel, leaving 2/5. Do not add the denominators when multiplying, which is a common error.

Dividing fractions: keep, change, flip

To divide by a fraction, multiply by its reciprocal. Keep the first fraction, change the division to multiplication, and flip the second fraction. For 3/4 ÷ 2/5, write 3/4 × 5/2 = 15/8 = 1 7/8. A whole number divided by a fraction works the same way once the whole number is written over 1.

Converting between mixed numbers and improper fractions

To write a mixed number as an improper fraction, multiply the whole number by the denominator, add the numerator, and keep the denominator. So 2 3/5 = (2 × 5 + 3)/5 = 13/5. To go the other way, divide the numerator by the denominator: 13 ÷ 5 gives 2 remainder 3, so 13/5 = 2 3/5. Use whichever form the question's wording suggests.

Finding a fraction of an amount

To find a fraction of a quantity, divide by the denominator and then multiply by the numerator. Three eighths of 240 is 240 ÷ 8 = 30, then 30 × 3 = 90. Writing the fraction as a single multiplication, 3/8 × 240 = 90, gives the same answer and is quicker on a calculator.

Fractions in word problems

When a question says "two fifths of the class walk to school", the phrase "of" means multiply. Identify the whole first, because the fraction applies to that whole. If a quantity is left after a fraction is taken, subtract the fraction from 1 before you multiply. For example, if 3/8 of the money is spent, 1 − 3/8 = 5/8 is left.

Decimals in practice: place value, rounding and estimating

Decimal questions test place value more than arithmetic. Know which digit is the tenths, the hundredths and the thousandths, and round only once you have the final value. The subsections below cover the rules that appear most often in papers.

Rounding to decimal places and significant figures

To round to a number of decimal places, look at the digit after the last one you keep. If it is 5 or more, round up. For example, 0.004 56 rounded to 3 decimal places is 0.005, while rounded to 2 significant figures it is 0.0046. Significant figures count from the first non-zero digit, so the leading zeros in 0.004 56 do not count.

Multiplying and dividing by powers of ten

Multiplying by 10 moves every digit one place to the left, so 3.27 × 100 = 327. Dividing by 10 moves the digits one place to the right, so 0.5 ÷ 10 = 0.05. Use this rule instead of long multiplication when the multiplier is a power of ten. It is also how you check that a decimal point is in a sensible position.

Terminating and recurring decimals

A fraction in its simplest form gives a terminating decimal if its denominator has no prime factors other than 2 and 5. So 1/4 = 0.25 terminates, while 1/3 = 0.333… recurs. Recurring decimals are written with a dot or a line over the repeating digits. Knowing which fractions terminate helps you decide whether a decimal answer is exact.

Converting a recurring decimal to a fraction (Extended)

Let x = 0.363636…. Multiply by 100 because two digits repeat, so 100x = 36.363636…. Subtract the first equation from the second: 99x = 36, so x = 36/99. Simplify by 9 to get x = 4/11. The method works because the repeating part cancels out exactly.

Ordering decimals

To order decimals, compare the digits place by place, starting from the left. Pad the numbers with zeros so they have the same number of decimal places. Writing 0.7, 0.07 and 0.707 as 0.700, 0.070 and 0.707 makes the order clear: 0.07 is smallest, then 0.7, then 0.707. A common mistake is to think 0.707 is smaller than 0.7 because it has more digits.

Decimals in money and measurement

Money is written to two decimal places, so £4.5 should be written as £4.50 when you give a final answer. Measurements in decimal form convert with a power of ten: 3.5 km = 3.5 × 1000 m = 3500 m. Check that the unit in your answer matches the unit the question asks for.

Estimating answers before calculating

To estimate, round each number to one significant figure and calculate the result. For 49.8 × 0.31, use 50 × 0.3 = 15, which tells you the true answer should be close to 15. An estimate is a check, not an answer. If your calculator gives a value far from the estimate, you have probably mistyped a number or put the decimal point in the wrong place.

Equations and symbols

The conversion cycle in one place: fraction ↔ decimal ↔ percentage, the multiplier that handles every percentage change, and the mixed-number rule. Non-calculator Paper 2 lives on these.

Fraction to decimal: divide. 3/8 = 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375 Key: the line means "a fraction is a division"; the numerator is divided by the denominator. Terminating here because 8 has only 2 as a prime factor; a denominator with any other prime gives a recurring decimal.

Fraction to percentage: divide, then multiply by 100. 3/8 = 0.375 = 37.5% Key: the decimal comes first, then ×100 moves the point two places; the % sign replaces the "per hundred" you multiplied by. Reversing it, divide by 100 and simplify.

Percentage to fraction: write over 100 and simplify. 45% = 45/100 = 9/20 Key: percent means "per hundred", so the denominator is 100 before simplifying; cancel by the highest common factor, 5 here. Leaving 45/100 is a lost mark in a "give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form" question.

2 3/5 = (2 × 5 + 3)/5 = 13/5 Key: the whole-number part (2) is multiplied by the denominator (5), the numerator (3) is added, and the result goes over the same denominator. This is the step needed before multiplying or dividing mixed numbers.

the new value is 135% of the old, so multiply by 1.35: 1.35 × 240 = 324 Key: 1.35 is the multiplier for an increase of 35% (100% + 35%, as a decimal); 240 is the original. The multiplier chains: 0.8 × 0.8 = 0.64 is not a 40% discount but a 36% one, which is the trap this line exists to close.

18/60 × 100 = 30% Key: 18 = the part; 60 = the whole; ×100 turns the fraction into a percentage. "18 out of 60" and "18 as a percentage of 60" are the same question, and the fraction is always part ÷ whole.

title: Acids, Bases and Salts
content:
Acids, Bases and Salts

Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry 0620, Extended route, topic 7 (statements 7.1–7.3). Acid and base properties, strong versus weak acids, oxide classification, and the preparation of soluble and insoluble salts with full practical detail.

7.1 Acids and bases

  • An acid is a proton (H⁺) donor; a base is a proton acceptor. An alkali is a soluble base. Neutralisation is H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O.
  • Acid reactions: with metals to give a salt and hydrogen; with bases to give a salt and water; with carbonates to give a salt, water and carbon dioxide.
  • Strong acids (hydrochloric, sulfuric, nitric) are fully dissociated in water; weak acids (ethanoic, carbonic) are only partly dissociated. Both can be dilute or concentrated — strength and concentration are different ideas.

7.2 Oxides

  • Basic oxides are metal oxides such as CuO; acidic oxides are non-metal oxides such as SO₂; amphoteric oxides react with both acids and bases — Al₂O₃ and ZnO are the syllabus examples.

7.3 Preparation of salts

  • Soluble salts by titration: dissolve the acid, use a pipette and burette with an indicator, add alkali until neutralised, then evaporate to crystallise.
  • Soluble salts from an excess insoluble reactant: add excess metal or insoluble base or carbonate to the acid, filter off the excess, evaporate the filtrate.
  • Insoluble salts by precipitation: mix two solutions whose ions combine to form an insoluble salt; filter, wash and dry. Silver chloride and barium sulfate are the standard examples.
  • Hydrated salts contain water of crystallisation (CuSO₄·5H₂O); heating drives it off to give the anhydrous salt, which turns blue again with water.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Method choice, applied to making pure copper sulfate crystals from copper oxide and dilute sulfuric acid: copper oxide is insoluble, so add it in excess to the acid, filter, then crystallise. You cannot titrate here — there is no soluble base to measure. Justify the choice of method in one sentence; that justification is the mark.
  • Purity reasoning, applied to crystals dried too quickly: crystals coated with impure surface moisture give a melting point below the pure value and a broad range. A pure substance melts sharply at a single temperature — quote the sharp range as the evidence.
  • Strong versus weak, applied to equal concentrations of hydrochloric and ethanoic acid: hydrochloric acid has a lower pH and a greater temperature rise when reacting with the same mass of magnesium, because it is fully dissociated and supplies more H⁺ per mole. Name dissociation as the reason.

Common errors

  • Confusing strong (fully dissociated) with concentrated (lots of solute per dm³).
  • Forgetting to filter off the excess solid when preparing a salt from an insoluble reactant.
  • Choosing titration for a preparation where one reactant is insoluble.

title: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Bearings, Constructions and Loci
content:
Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Bearings, Constructions and Loci

Bearings are how navigators describe direction, and geometrical constructions are how geometers draw exact figures with only a ruler and a pair of compasses. Together they fill the practical geometry questions on both papers: a bearing calculated from a diagram, a locus sketched and shaded, a perpendicular bisector constructed and justified. This note builds the topic from zero: the three rules of bearings and the back-bearing calculation, the compass-and-ruler constructions with their standard arcs, scale drawings and their measurements, and the four loci the syllabus requires, with every step shown.

Bearings: the three rules

A bearing is a direction written as a three-figure angle. Three rules define it:

  1. Measured from North (the north line, drawn as an upward arrow).
  2. Clockwise.
  3. Written with three figures — 035°, 090°, 245° (never 35° or 9°).

Bearings are always between 000° and 360°; a direction due east is 090°, due south 180°, due west 270°.

Worked example. A ship sails from A on a bearing of 060° for 12 km to B, then on a bearing of 150° for 8 km to C. Describe the position of C relative to A qualitatively.

060 ° is between north and east; 150 ° is between east and
south. So C lies south-east of A, and the two legs turn 90 °
(150 - 60 = 90) - the path is two perpendicular legs, making a
right angle at B.

Back bearings

The bearing of A from B is not the bearing of B from A — they differ by 180° (add if under 180°, subtract if 180° or more):

back bearing = bearing + 180  (if bearing < 180)
             = bearing - 180  (if bearing >= 180)

Worked example. The bearing of B from A is 072°. Find the bearing of A from B.

72 + 180 = 252 °

Worked example 2 (three-figure check). The bearing of P from Q is 310°. Find the bearing of Q from P.

310 - 180 = 130 °

Bearings with trigonometry

Bearing problems become right-triangle problems once you draw the north lines and mark the angles between the path and north. Use Pythagoras for distances and trigonometry for angles, then convert the angle into a bearing.

Worked example. A boat sails 5 km due north, then 12 km due east. Find its distance and bearing from the start.

distance = √(5² + 12²) = √(169) = 13 km
angle east of north: tan(θ) = 12/5  →  θ = 67.4 °
bearing = 067 ° (to the nearest degree)

Worked example 2 (reverse). A helicopter is 9 km from base on a bearing of 145°. How far east and how far south of the base is it?

angle from south = 180 - 145 = 35 °
east = 9 sin(35) = 5.16 km
south = 9 cos(35) = 7.37 km

Constructions: ruler and compasses only

Constructions are marked on the accuracy of the arcs and the visibility of the construction lines. Keep your compasses sharp and do not rub out the arcs.

ConstructionStandard method (in order)
Perpendicular bisector of ABcompasses wider than half AB: arc from A, same-radius arc from B, both sides; join the two intersections
Angle bisectorarc across both arms from the vertex; same-radius arcs from those two crossings; join the vertex to their intersection
Perpendicular from a point to a linearc from the point cutting the line twice; equal arcs from those cuts; join the point to their intersection
Perpendicular at a point on a lineequal arcs either side of the point; then the perpendicular-bisector method between them
60° anglearc from the endpoint across the line; same radius arc from the crossing; join
Triangle given SSSdraw the base; arcs of the other two lengths from each end; join the intersection

Worked example. Construct the perpendicular bisector of a segment AB of length 8 cm and explain why every point on it is equidistant from A and B.

Construction: arcs of radius > 4 cm from A and from B, above and
below the segment; the two intersections join to form the bisector.
Why: the arcs are circles of equal radius centred at A and B, so
their intersection points are equidistant from A and B; the line
through them is the locus of all such points.

Scale drawings

A scale drawing represents a real situation to a ratio: 1 : 50 000 means 1 cm on paper represents 50 000 cm in reality (0.5 km). The method: convert the scale to a usable unit, measure or construct to scale, then read back with the reverse conversion.

Worked example. A map has scale 1 : 25 000. Two towns are 6.4 cm apart on the map. Find the real distance in km.

6.4 cm x 25 000 = 160 000 cm
160 000 cm = 1600 m = 1.6 km

Worked example 2 (drawing). A field is 400 m by 250 m. Draw it at scale 1 : 5000. What are the drawing dimensions?

400 m = 40 000 cm; /5000 = 8 cm
250 m = 25 000 cm; /5000 = 5 cm
The drawing is 8 cm by 5 cm.

Loci

A locus is the set of all points satisfying a condition. Four standard loci are examinable, and each has its construction:

  • Fixed distance from a point: a circle (arc) of that radius, centred on the point.
  • Equidistant from two points: the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining them.
  • Equidistant from two lines: the angle bisector(s) of the angle between them.
  • Fixed distance from a line: two parallel lines at that distance, one on each side (with semicircular ends for a segment).

Region questions combine loci: "shade the region closer to A than B and within 3 cm of C" means intersect the perpendicular bisector's half-plane with the circle's interior.

Worked example. A goat is tethered to a corner of a 6 m by 4 m shed with a 5 m rope. Describe the region it can reach.

A three-quarter circle of radius 5 m around the corner, minus
the part blocked by the shed: the rope wraps the shed's⁴ m and
6 m walls. The reachable region is the quarter circle of radius
5 m outside the shed plus smaller arcs where the rope wraps
(radius 1 m around the far 4 m corner, no reach around the far
6 m corner since 5 - 6 < 0).

Worked examples: bearings and loci together

Worked example. Two radio transmitters A and B are 10 km apart, with B due east of A. A signal is received equally strongly at points equidistant from A and B, and within 6 km of A. Describe the region.

Equidistant from A and B: the perpendicular bisector of AB - a
north-south line 5 km east of A.
Within 6 km of A: a circle of radius 6 km centred at A.
The region is the part of the circle on one side of the bisector:
a circular segment of radius 6 km, cut by the line 5 km from A.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Bearing definition) State the three rules for a bearing. Answer: Measured from north, clockwise, written as three figures.
  2. (Back bearing) The bearing of X from Y is 128°. Find the bearing of Y from X. Answer: a back bearing reverses direction, so add 180° when the bearing is below 180°: 128° + 180° = 308° (if the bearing exceeds 180°, subtract 180° instead).
  3. (Calculation) A plane flies 30 km north then 40 km east. Find its distance from the start and its bearing. Answer: distance = √(900 + 1600) = 50 km; tan θ = 40/30 → θ = 53.1°, bearing 053°.
  4. (Components) A ship is 15 km from port on a bearing of 210°. Find its distance west of the port. Answer: angle from south = 210 − 180 = 30°; west = 15 sin 30 = 7.5 km.
  5. (Construction) Describe how to construct the perpendicular bisector of a 6 cm segment. Answer: set the compasses to more than half the segment — more than 3 cm — and draw arcs from each end both above and below it; the two crossings of the arcs give the points the bisector passes through, so join them, and every point on that line is equidistant from both ends.
  6. (Locus) Describe the locus of points equidistant from the sides of an angle. Answer: The angle bisector — every point on it is the same perpendicular distance from both arms.
  7. (Scale) On a 1 : 20 000 map, a lake is 3.5 cm long. Find its real length in km. Answer: 3.5 × 20 000 = 70 000 cm = 0.7 km.
  8. (Region) Shade the region inside a triangle that is closer to side AB than to side AC and within 2 cm of vertex A. Answer: closer to AB than to AC means the half-plane on AB's side of the angle bisector of angle A, and within 2 cm of A means inside the circle of radius 2 cm centred on A; the shaded region is the intersection of those two, bounded by the bisector and the compass arc.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Two-figure bearings: 35° must be written 035°. Three figures, always.
  • Measuring from the wrong north: bearings start at north, not east. A bearing of 090° is east, not north.
  • Back-bearing addition: add 180 if the bearing is below 180, subtract if above; the result must stay between 000 and 360.
  • Anticlockwise angles: bearing questions are clockwise; a clockwise angle and its anticlockwise partner sum to 360.
  • Rubbing out construction arcs: the arcs are the evidence. Leave them visible and use a sharp pencil.
  • Locus shading: shade the region, not the boundary line; the question usually says "shade the region".
  • Scale unit slips: convert the real measurement to the same unit as the drawing before applying the ratio, and remember 1 km = 100 000 cm.
  • Diagram not to scale: measure only when told to; otherwise calculate. A protractor reading on a "not to scale" diagram earns nothing.

Bearings drawn properly: clockwise from north, three digits, always

A bearing is not an angle inside a triangle — it is a direction on the page, and almost every lost mark on this topic comes from measuring it from the wrong place or turning the wrong way. One drawing fixes the idea for good.

The three rules, in the order they bite. A bearing is measured from the north line at the point you are leaving, it turns clockwise, and it is written with three digits (060°, not 60°, and 025° rather than 25°). The third rule is not fussiness: 070° and 007° are different directions, and the leading zeros are how a reader tells them apart.

The back bearing is the return journey. If B is on a bearing of 060° from A, then A is on a bearing of 240° from B:

back bearing = bearing + 180° (or − 180° if the result would exceed 360°) Key: both are the same line measured from opposite ends. Adding 180° cannot go wrong; subtracting can, so add and then subtract 360° if necessary. For 060°: 60 + 180 = 240°. For 300°: 300 + 180 = 480, and 480 − 360 = 120°.

Worked example. A ship sails 12 km from port P on a bearing of 060°, then 9 km on a bearing of 150°. How far is it from P, and on what bearing?

Draw the two legs nose-to-tail. The turn between them is 150 − 60 = 90°, so the two legs are perpendicular and the distance closes as a right-angled triangle:
distance = √(12² + 9²) = √(144 + 81) = √225 = 15 km

The overall bearing is the angle from north to the closing line, which needs the angle at P inside the triangle: tan θ = 9 / 12, so θ = 36.9°, and the bearing is 60 − 36.9 = 023.1° on the far side — which is why the sketch, not the arithmetic, decides between adding and subtracting. Candidates who skip the sketch get 15 km and then guess the direction.

Where marks are lost. Measuring anticlockwise (bearing 060 becomes the 300° direction). Measuring from the horizontal or from another bearing rather than from north. Writing two digits. And finding the distance with a scale drawing but then reading the bearing off the wrong vertex — the bearing of A from B is not the bearing of B from A, and the question always says which.

Bearings in more depth

A bearing gives a direction as an angle measured clockwise from north, written as three figures. Bearings are the commonest context for angle questions in navigation, and they combine with the sine and cosine rules when the journey is not at right angles. The subsections below cover measuring, reversing and using bearings in a calculation, which are the three skills the mark scheme checks.

Measuring a bearing with a protractor

Place the centre of the protractor on the point where the bearing starts, with the zero line pointing north. Read the angle clockwise from north to the line that joins the start point to the target. A bearing of 65° is read on the outer scale of a protractor when the north line points up the page. Always check which scale you are reading, because the inner scale gives the anticlockwise angle and loses marks.

Three-figure bearings in exam answers

Exam bearings are written with exactly three figures, so a bearing of 8° is written 008°, and 65° is written 065°. The three-figure form is required even when the answer has a leading zero. A bearing given with two figures will normally be marked wrong, so write the final answer in the form the question asks for and keep the degree sign.

The bearing of A from B and of B from A

The bearing of B from A and the bearing of A from B are not the same. The first is measured at A, the second at B. They differ by exactly 180°, so if the bearing of B from A is 070°, the bearing of A from B is 250°. Draw a north line at each point, because the question usually asks for one direction and the reversed direction is the common error.

Back bearings

A back bearing is the bearing of the start point from the end point, and it is found by adding or subtracting 180°. If the bearing is less than 180°, add 180°. If it is more than 180°, subtract 180°. The back bearing is used when a journey is reversed, and it is also used as a check on a diagram, since the two north lines at the points are parallel.

Bearings with trigonometry

A bearing often describes one side of a triangle, and the other sides are found with the sine or cosine rule. Put the north lines on the diagram, mark the bearing as an angle between the north line and the side, and then find the interior angle of the triangle. Once the angle is known, the rule is applied in the usual way, and the bearings are only used to find that angle.

A worked navigation problem

A ship sails 12 km on a bearing of 040° and then 9 km on a bearing of 130°. The angle between the two legs at the turning point is found from the bearings: the turn is 130° − 040° = 090°, so the path is at right angles and the distance back to the start is √(12² + 9²) = 15 km. Each step uses one bearing to find an angle, and then Pythagoras or a rule gives the length.

Checking a bearing answer

A bearing must lie between 000° and 360°. Check that the answer is measured clockwise from north, that it has three figures, and that a diagram drawn to scale agrees with the value. A bearing of 200° points roughly south-south-west, so a diagram showing it pointing north-east is a sign that the angle was measured from the wrong line.

Geometrical constructions with ruler and compasses

A construction is a drawing made with a ruler and a pair of compasses only, with no protractor and no measurement. The method is what gets the mark, so the arcs must be left visible on the final diagram. The subsections below give the standard constructions the syllabus asks for, with the steps for each and the checks that show the result is accurate.

The perpendicular bisector of a line

To construct the perpendicular bisector of a line AB, open the compasses to more than half the length of AB. Draw an arc from A above and below the line, then draw the same arc from B so that the two pairs of arcs cross at two points. The line joining those two crossing points is the perpendicular bisector. It cuts AB into two equal parts at a right angle.

The bisector of an angle

To bisect an angle, put the compass point on the vertex and draw an arc that cuts both arms of the angle. From each of those two points draw a further arc of equal radius, so the arcs cross inside the angle. The line from the vertex through the crossing point bisects the angle into two equal parts. The construction works for any angle, because the two triangles formed are congruent.

A perpendicular from a point to a line

To draw the perpendicular from a point P to a line, place the compass on P and draw an arc that cuts the line at two points. Then construct the perpendicular bisector of those two points. The bisector passes through P and meets the line at right angles, so it is the required perpendicular. This method works whether P is above or below the line.

Constructing 60° and 90° angles

A 60° angle is constructed by drawing an equilateral triangle. Draw a line, put the compass on one end, and mark an arc of radius equal to the line. From the other end draw a second arc of the same radius to cross it. Joining the crossing point to the two ends gives an equilateral triangle, so the angle at the end is 60°. A 90° angle is constructed as a perpendicular to a line through a point on it.

Constructing a triangle from three sides

To construct a triangle with sides 6 cm, 5 cm and 4 cm, draw the 6 cm base. Open the compass to 5 cm, place the point at one end, and draw an arc. Open to 4 cm, place the point at the other end, and draw a second arc to cross the first. Join the crossing point to the two ends. A triangle is fixed by its three sides, so the construction gives one unique shape.

Accuracy and the arcs left on the diagram

Examiners check the construction arcs, not only the final line. Leave every arc visible, use a sharp pencil, and keep the compass radius constant when it is supposed to be constant. A line drawn without its construction arcs can earn no method marks, even if it is in the correct place. Make the arcs light but clear, so a marker can see which steps were followed.

Common construction errors

The commonest errors are opening the compass by different amounts for arcs that should be equal, forgetting that the perpendicular bisector needs arcs from both ends, and drawing a bisector from the wrong vertex. Check each construction by measuring afterwards: the bisected parts should be equal, and the angle at a right-angle construction should be 90° when you check it with a protractor.

Loci: the set of points that obey a rule

A locus is the set of all points that satisfy a given condition. In this note, loci are drawn with ruler and compasses, and the answer is a region or a line that a student must shade or describe. The subsections below cover the standard loci the syllabus names: points at a fixed distance, points equidistant from two points or two lines, and combined loci that give a region.

A locus defined by a fixed distance

The locus of points that are exactly 3 cm from a fixed point O is a circle of radius 3 cm with centre O. Every point on the circle is 3 cm from O, and no other point is. The locus of points within 3 cm of O is the region inside that circle, including the circle itself. Read the word "exactly" as a circle and the words "within" or "less than" as a region.

Points equidistant from two points

The locus of points equidistant from two points A and B is the perpendicular bisector of AB. Every point on that line is the same distance from A as from B. A question that asks for the points closer to A than to B asks for the half-plane on A's side of the bisector, so the answer is a region and not just the line.

Points equidistant from two lines

The locus of points equidistant from two intersecting lines is the pair of angle bisectors of the angles between them. The bisector of the angle between two lines passes through their intersection point. For two parallel lines, the locus is the single line midway between them, parallel to both.

Combining loci to find a region

Many questions ask for the region that satisfies two or more conditions at once. Draw each locus on the same diagram, using a light line for each. The required region is where all the conditions are true at the same time, so it is the overlap of the individual regions. Shade it and label it, since the marks are given for the correct region and not just for the lines.

Loci with a distance from a line

The locus of points at a fixed distance from a straight line is two lines, one on each side, parallel to the original line and at that distance. Within a given distance the region is the strip between those two lines. This type of question is often combined with a circle or a perpendicular bisector, so draw the strip first and then the other constraint.

Reading a locus question in words

The key phrases are "equidistant", "closer to", "within", "at a fixed distance" and "at equal distances from". Each phrase maps to one locus: equidistant from points gives a bisector, equidistant from lines gives an angle bisector, and within a distance gives a circle or a strip. Underline the phrase in the question, name its locus, and then construct it.

Checking a locus diagram

Test a point in each region of your answer and confirm it satisfies the conditions. A point inside the shaded area must be closer to the stated point, and a point outside it must fail. Leaving the construction arcs visible also lets the marker check the construction, so keep them even when the answer is a shaded region.

Scale drawings and scale factors

A scale drawing represents a real object or place at a reduced or enlarged size, and the scale tells you how each length in the drawing relates to the real length. The syllabus asks for scale drawings in statement 4.3, and the work involves ratios, unit conversion and the scale factor for areas. The subsections below go through each of these, with a method for each type of question.

Writing a scale as a ratio

A scale is often written as a ratio such as 1 : 50 or 1 cm to 2 m. In a ratio 1 : 50, one unit on the drawing represents 50 of the same units in reality. The two lengths must be in the same units before the ratio is used, because 1 cm to 2 m is 1 : 200, not 1 : 2. Convert first, then apply the ratio.

Reading a scale drawing

To find a real length from a drawing, measure the length on the drawing and multiply by the scale factor. A wall that measures 6 cm on a plan drawn to 1 : 50 is 6 × 50 = 300 cm, or 3 m, in reality. Keep track of the units throughout, and convert the final answer to the units the question asks for.

Making a scale drawing

To draw a room 4 m by 3 m at a scale of 1 cm to 1 m, divide each real length by the scale: 4 m becomes 4 cm and 3 m becomes 3 cm. Draw a rectangle 4 cm by 3 cm and label the scale on the drawing. A scale drawing that does not state its scale can be marked as incomplete, so always write it on the drawing.

Scale factors for lengths

A scale factor relates a length on the drawing to the corresponding real length. Given a scale of 1 : 25, the scale factor is 25, meaning every real length is 25 times its length on the drawing. If the drawing is an enlargement, the scale factor is greater than 1, and if it is a reduction it is less than 1, so read the direction of the change before using the value.

Scale factors for areas

When lengths are scaled by a factor k, areas are scaled by k². A square on a plan with side 2 cm at a scale of 1 : 100 has a real side of 200 cm, so its real area is 200² = 40 000 cm², or 4 m². The drawn area is 2² = 4 cm². The real area is 100² = 10 000 times the drawn area, which is the square of the length scale factor.

Map scales and bearings together

A map scale is used with bearings in navigation questions. A point 5 cm from a town on a map at 1 : 100 000 is 5 × 100 000 = 500 000 cm, or 5 km, from it. The bearing is measured on the map with a protractor in the usual way. Combining the scale and the bearing gives the position of one point relative to another, which is a common exam question.

Checking a scale answer

Confirm that the answer has the right order of magnitude. A distance of 3 km on a plan at 1 : 1000 should be drawn about 3 m, and a drawing that makes it 3 mm is wrong by a factor of 1000. Also check that area answers have units squared, since a common mistake is to scale the lengths correctly and forget to square the scale factor for the area.

title: Operating Systems — Study Notes
content:
Operating Systems

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): OS roles, memory/process management, hardware–software layer, interrupts, buffers, utility software.

1. What an OS does

Manages memory, processes/files, I/O via drivers, security (users, permissions), and provides the UI (CLI/GUI) between user, applications and hardware.

2. Memory and process management

  • Paging/segmentation move programs in/out; virtual memory extends RAM to disk when RAM is full.
  • Multitasking: scheduler gives each process time slices; context switching saves/restores state.

3. Interrupts and buffers

Interrupts signal events (I/O complete, timer); CPU saves context, services via ISR, resumes. Buffers hold data in transit (printing) so slow devices don't block the CPU; spooling queues jobs.

4. Utility software

Disk formatter, defragmenter (reduces head movement on HDDs; unnecessary for SSD), backup scheduler, compression, antivirus, file compression.

5. UI and drivers

CLI: precise, scriptable, low overhead. GUI: icons/windows, discoverable, more resources. Device drivers translate OS calls to hardware specifics — each device needs its own.

Exam tips: "manage" verbs earn marks: manages memory, manages processes, manages peripherals; explain virtual memory by RAM-full scenario, not definition alone.

Interrupts and scheduling

An interrupt is a signal that tells the processor to stop its current task and deal with an event, such as a key press, a timer ending or an error. The processor saves the state of the current task, runs the interrupt service routine, and then resumes the task it was doing. Interrupts let the processor respond to devices without checking them constantly.

The operating system manages several programs at once through scheduling. Each program receives processor time in turn, which gives the impression that they run at the same time. Memory management keeps each program's data separate, and the operating system provides a user interface and manages files and devices.

Exam tip: describe the steps of an interrupt in order: save state, run the routine, restore state.

title: Organic Chemistry: Carbonyls, Carboxylic Acids and Chirality
content:
Organic Chemistry: Carbonyls, Carboxylic Acids and Chirality

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH14, Topic 15. Aldehydes and ketones contain the carbonyl group, C=O. Their reactions are nucleophilic addition, and the products can be carboxylic acids, alcohols or molecules with a chiral centre.

Carbonyl compounds

  • An aldehyde has the C=O group at the end of a chain (RCHO). A ketone has it inside the chain (RCOR).
  • The carbon of C=O is slightly positive, so nucleophiles attack it. Ketones are less reactive than aldehydes because the two alkyl groups donate electron density.

Reactions and tests

  • Hydrogen cyanide adds across C=O. For ethanal, CH3CHO + HCN gives 2-hydroxypropanenitrile.
  • Sodium tetrahydridoborate(III) (NaBH4) reduces aldehydes to primary alcohols and ketones to secondary alcohols.
  • 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine (2,4-DNPH) gives an orange or yellow precipitate with any carbonyl compound.
  • Tollens' reagent gives a silver mirror with aldehydes but not with ketones.
  • The iodoform test gives a yellow precipitate of triiodomethane with compounds containing CH3CO– or CH3CH(OH)– groups, such as propanone.

Carboxylic acids

  • Carboxylic acids contain –COOH and are weak acids. They are more acidic than alcohols because the carboxylate ion is stabilised by delocalisation.
  • Carboxylic acids react with alcohols in the presence of concentrated sulfuric acid to form esters, in a reversible esterification.
  • Primary alcohols are oxidised to carboxylic acids by heating with acidified potassium dichromate(VI) under reflux.

Chirality

  • A chiral carbon atom has four different groups attached. Molecules with a chiral centre exist as a pair of enantiomers.
  • Enantiomers have identical physical properties except their effect on plane-polarised light: one rotates it clockwise and the other anticlockwise by the same amount.
  • An equimolar mixture of the two enantiomers is a racemic mixture, which is optically inactive.

Exam tip: when describing a nucleophilic addition, show the nucleophile attacking the carbon of C=O and the oxygen gaining the negative charge.

title: Exam technique: Simulation, Sensors and Real Data
content:
### What earns the marks
For control systems, sensor plus actuator plus loop type each earn a mark: feedback reads back every cycle. For conversions, the direction named (ADC into the controller) earns the mark with resolution tied to bit depth. For regimes, the hazard speed matched to sampling earns the design mark.
### Traps
Error: DAC into the controller. Correction: sensors are analog, controllers digital: ADC. Error: batch uploads for flood alerts. Correction: fast hazards need real-time sensing. Error: tripling identical sensors for redundancy. Correction: diversify physics so failures stay independent.

title: AS Level Mathematics: Quadratics
content:
AS Level Mathematics: Quadratics

A quadratic is a curve you already know from everyday life: the path of a thrown ball, the profit curve of a business, the shape of a satellite dish. Algebraically it is any expression ax² + bx + c with a ≠ 0, and this note builds every technique the AS papers test: solving by factorising, completing the square and the formula; using the discriminant to count roots without solving; reading the vertex and intercepts off a sketch; and solving simultaneous and inequality problems where the quadratic meets a line. Every step is shown line by line, because the method marks live in the middle.

The three forms of a quadratic

FormExpressionWhat it reveals
Standardax² + bx + cthe y-intercept is c
Factoriseda(x − p)(x − q)roots at x = p and x = q
Completed squarea(x + h)² + kvertex at (−h, k); minimum or maximum k

The sign of a decides the shape: a > 0 opens upward (a minimum), a < 0 opens downward (a maximum). The axis of symmetry runs through the vertex, halfway between the roots.

Solving by factorising

Look for two numbers that multiply to ac and add to b, then split the middle term and factorise in pairs.

Worked example. Solve 2x² + 7x + 3 = 0.

ac = 6, b = 7: numbers 6 and 1
2x² + 6x + x + 3 = 0
2x(x + 3) + 1(x + 3) = 0
(2x + 1)(x + 3) = 0
x = -1/2 or x = -3

Worked example 2 (difference of squares). Solve 9x² − 25 = 0.

(3x - 5)(3x + 5) = 0
x = 5/3 or x = -5/3

Completing the square

Write x² + bx + c as (x + b/2)² − (b/2)² + c. The method: halve the coefficient of x, square the bracket, subtract the square of that half.

Worked example. Write x² − 6x + 11 in completed-square form and state the vertex.

x² - 6x + 11 = (x - 3)² - 9 + 11
              = (x - 3)² + 2
vertex: (3, 2); minimum value 2 at x = 3

Worked example 2 (leading coefficient not 1). Write 2x² + 8x + 5 in completed-square form.

factor out 2: 2(x² + 4x) + 5
complete inside: 2[(x + 2)² - 4] + 5
= 2(x + 2)² - 8 + 5 = 2(x + 2)² - 3
vertex: (-2, -3); minimum -3

Worked example 3 (solving by completing the square). Solve x² + 4x − 1 = 0, giving exact answers.

(x + 2)² - 4 - 1 = 0
(x + 2)² = 5
x + 2 = +/- √(5)
x = -2 +/- √(5)

The quadratic formula and the discriminant

x = (-b +/- √(b² - 4ac)) / (2a)

discriminant D = b² - 4ac
D > 0: two distinct real roots
D = 0: one repeated root (the curve touches the x-axis)
D < 0: no real roots (the curve misses the x-axis)

Worked example. Solve 3x² − 5x − 2 = 0 using the formula.

a = 3, b = -5, c = -2
D = 25 + 24 = 49
x = (5 +/- 7)/6
x = 12/6 = 2 or x = -2/6 = -1/3

Worked example 2 (discriminant). Find the values of k for which x² + kx + 9 = 0 has equal roots.

equal roots: D = 0
k² - 36 = 0
k = 6 or k = -6

Sketching a quadratic

A sketch needs four features: the shape (up or down from the sign of a), the y-intercept (c), the roots (from factorising or the formula) and the vertex (from completing the square or the midpoint of the roots). Mark them, then draw a smooth curve through them.

Worked example. Sketch y = x² − 4x + 3.

a = 1 > 0: opens upward
y-intercept: (0, 3)
roots: x² - 4x + 3 = (x - 1)(x - 3) → x = 1, 3
vertex: (x - 2)² - 1 → (2, -1)
axis of symmetry: x = 2

Simultaneous equations: a line and a curve

The method: make one variable the subject in the line, substitute into the curve, solve the resulting quadratic, then find the partner values. Two solutions mean the line cuts the curve twice; one means it is a tangent; none means it misses.

Worked example. Solve y = x² − 1 and y = 3x − 3.

x² - 1 = 3x - 3
x² - 3x + 2 = 0
(x - 1)(x - 2) = 0  →  x = 1 or x = 2
y = 3(1) - 3 = 0  and  y = 3(2) - 3 = 3
solutions: (1, 0) and (2, 3)

Worked example 2 (tangency condition). Find k such that y = 2x + k is tangent to y = x² + 3.

x² + 3 = 2x + k  →  x² - 2x + (3 - k) = 0
tangent: D = 0  →  4 - 4(3 - k) = 0
4 - 12 + 4k = 0  →  4k = 8  →  k = 2

Quadratic inequalities

Solve the corresponding equation first, sketch the parabola, then read which x-values satisfy the inequality.

Worked example. Solve x² − x − 6 < 0.

roots: (x - 3)(x + 2) = 0  →  x = 3, x = -2
the parabola opens upward, so it is below the axis between
the roots:  -2 < x < 3

Worked example 2 (outside). Solve x² − 4 ≥ 0.
