NPP is the energy available to the next trophic level because it is what remains after the plant has covered its own respiration, so consumers depend on NPP, not GPP. (4 marks)
  3. Calculate the efficiency of energy transfer if a producer trophic level contains 18000 kJ m−2 year−1 and the primary consumer level contains 1620 kJ m−2 year−1. Answer: Efficiency = (1620 ÷ 18000) × 100 = 9.0%. (2 marks)
  4. Describe how you would investigate the effect of light intensity on the rate of photosynthesis using an aquatic plant, and state one control variable. Answer: Place the aquatic plant in water at a fixed temperature and carbon dioxide concentration; vary the light intensity; count the bubbles of oxygen released per minute or measure the volume of gas collected in a fixed time; keep temperature, carbon dioxide concentration and plant species constant as control variables. (5 marks)
  5. Explain the difference between allopatric and sympatric speciation. Answer: Allopatric speciation occurs when a physical barrier separates populations so gene flow stops and they diverge; sympatric speciation occurs in the same area without a physical barrier, with reproductive isolation such as differences in breeding time or behaviour preventing interbreeding. In both cases the result is that populations become reproductively isolated and form new species. (4 marks)
  6. Describe the evidence for climate change and explain why correlation between two variables is not proof of causation. Answer: Evidence includes rising atmospheric carbon dioxide records, rising temperature records, pollen in peat bogs showing past vegetation, and tree rings. Correlation alone does not prove causation because the two variables could both be affected by a third factor, or the trend could be coincidental; to show causation you need a plausible mechanism and evidence that linking the variables is not better explained by something else. (5 marks)
  7. Explain the effect of temperature on enzyme activity up to and beyond the optimum, and define the Q10 temperature coefficient. Answer: Enzyme activity increases with temperature up to the optimum because molecules have more kinetic energy, but beyond the optimum the enzyme denatures as hydrogen and ionic bonds break and the active site is lost; the primary structure remains intact. Q10 is the factor by which the rate increases when the temperature rises by 10 °C, calculated as rate at T + 10 °C ÷ rate at T. (5 marks)
  8. Describe how reforestation can reduce atmospheric carbon dioxide and state one limitation of this approach. Answer: Trees take up carbon dioxide by photosynthesis and store the carbon in their biomass and in the soil, so planting trees increases the removal of CO2 from the atmosphere and holds it there. Limitation: newly planted trees take time to grow and store significant carbon, forests can be lost to fire or disease, and the land may compete with other uses. (4 marks)

Use this summary to place each idea in the topic before you go into the detail in the full notes. Revise the photosynthesis compartments and their products, the GPP-to-NPP accounting and the efficiency calculation, the ecology vocabulary and fieldwork methods, the climate evidence and the greenhouse mechanism with its mitigation, and the Q10 and allele-frequency ideas that carry into later topics. Then move on to Topic 6: Microbiology, Immunity and Forensics.

title: Binomial Distribution — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Binomial Distribution

Mathematics — A2. X ~ B(n, p) counts successes in n independent trials when:

Key areas to revise

  • When Binomial Applies
  • The Formula
  • Cumulative Probabilities
  • Expectation and Variance
  • Modelling Decisions

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

### Worked example For X ~ B(n, p), P(X = r) = nCr pʳ(1 − p)ⁿ⁻ʳ, with mean np and variance np(1 − p). For n = 5 and p = 0.2, P(X = 2) = 10 × 0.2² × 0.8³ = 10 × 0.04 × 0.512 = 0.2048. The mean is 5 × 0.2 = 1.

Key points to remember

If X ~ B(n, p), then P(X = r) = ⁿCᵣ pʳ(1 − p)ⁿ⁻ʳ. The mean is np and the variance is np(1 − p). Check the conditions first: a fixed number of independent trials, two outcomes, and a constant probability of success.

Use cumulative probabilities for P(X ≤ r) or P(X ≥ r). For P(X ≥ r), subtract P(X ≤ r − 1) from 1, and watch whether the wording says more than or at least, because that changes the boundary value. A normal approximation needs both np and n(1 − p) to be large (usually above 5), and then a continuity correction must be applied.

title: Tenses in Context — Study Notes
content:
Tense choice depends on time, not only on the verb. The same action can be described with different tenses, and the difference changes the meaning. Learn the tenses by the situations where you use them.

Present simple

Use the present simple for facts, general truths and routines.

  • Water boils at 100 degrees Celsius.
  • The bus leaves at seven every morning.

Past simple

Use the past simple for a finished action at a stated or clearly understood past time.

  • She went to the cinema yesterday evening.
  • We moved to Leeds in 2015.

Present perfect

Use the present perfect for an action connected to now. It is common with since, for and ever, and when the exact time is not important.

  • I have lived in London since 2019. (It continues now.)
  • Have you ever tried sushi?

Compare: I lived in London in 2019. This finishes in the past and does not connect to now.

Past continuous

Use the past continuous for an action in progress at a past moment, often interrupted by a shorter action.

  • When the phone rang, I was taking a shower.

Future forms

Use will have plus a past participle for an action completed before a future time.

  • By next summer, they will have finished the course.

Common errors

  • Using the past simple with since: write "I have lived here since 2019", not "I lived here since 2019".
  • Forgetting that a general fact uses the present simple even in a past context.

title: Exam technique: Forces and Motion
content:
### What earns the marks
For resultant force, F = ma with substitution earns both marks. For moments, clockwise set equal to anticlockwise earns the method mark. For terminal velocity, balanced forces stated earns the explanation mark.
### Traps
Error: zero velocity taken as zero acceleration at the top of flight. Correction: g acts throughout. Error: one-sided moments only. Correction: equate both sides of the pivot. Error: weight and mass interchanged. Correction: weight is a force in newtons.

title: Data Representation — Study Notes
content:
Data Representation

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): binary/hex, two's complement, BCD, text/image/sound encoding, file sizes, compression.

1. Number systems

  • Binary place values 128…1; hex digits 0–9, A–F; one hex digit = one nibble (4 bits).
  • Conversions: binary ↔ decimal ↔ hex. 0101 1010 → 5A; FF = 255.
  • BCD: 4 bits per decimal digit — 0029 → 0000 0000 0010 1001. Used in clocks/calculators; easier digit conversions, more bits than pure binary.

2. Two's complement (signed)

MSB is negative: −128 64 32 16 8 4 2 1. −5 = 1111 1011. Range 8-bit: −128…+127.

Negating: invert bits, add 1. Subtraction: add the negated number — 7 − 5 = 7 + (−5) = 0000 0111 + 1111 1011 = 0000 0010.

3. Text

ASCII 7-bit (128 chars) → extended sets; Unicode for all scripts (UTF-8 variable width). Character sets map codes to glyphs; uppercase/lowercase codes differ by one bit.

4. Images and sound

  • Bitmap: pixels; colour depth = bits per pixel. File size (bits) = W × H × depth. Metadata (width, height, depth) stores dimensions.
  • Sound: sample rate (Hz), resolution (bits per sample), track duration × channels. Higher rate/depth = better fidelity, larger files.

5. Compression

  • Lossless (RLE, ZIP): exact restore — text/code must use it. RLE example: AAABBBCC → 3A3B2C; effective with runs.
  • Lossy (JPEG, MP3): discards perceptually minor data — photos/music OK, text never.

Exam tips: show full working in conversions; for size questions write the formula first with units; state the reason a compression type suits the file.

title: Thermal Physics
content:
Thermal Physics

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2023–2025): kinetic particle model; thermal expansion; specific heat capacity; melting/boiling; conduction, convection, radiation.

1. Kinetic model

Solid: fixed positions, vibrate — fixed shape/volume. Liquid: move around, touching — fixed volume, flows. Gas: far apart, fast random motion — fills container. Brownian motion evidences random molecular motion.

2. Gas pressure and temperature

Pressure from wall collisions. Heating at fixed volume → faster particles → more frequent, harder collisions → higher pressure.

3. Thermal expansion

Heating → particles vibrate more → solids expand slightly (gases expand most). Applications: bimetallic strip (fire alarm/thermostat), gaps in bridges/rails; the liquid-in-glass thermometer.

4. Specific heat capacity

c = ΔE/(mΔθ). Heating: ΔE = mcΔθ.

Example: 2 kg water (c = 4200), 20→80 °C: ΔE = 2×4200×60 = 504 kJ.

High c of water → coolant; temperature rise measured with known heater power P in time t: c = Pt/(mΔθ).

5. State changes

Melting/boiling at fixed temperature despite heating (energy breaks bonds, not temperature). Condensation/ freezing release energy. Impurities raise melting point of mixtures/lower freezing; boiling needs nucleation.

6. Transfer: conduction, convection, radiation

  • Conduction: mainly metals (delocalised electrons + lattice vibration); non-metals poor; insulators trap air.
  • Convection: hot fluid expands, density falls, rises; denser cool fluid sinks — currents.
  • Radiation: infrared EM waves; no medium; matte black best absorber/emitter, shiny silver worst.

Applications: vacuum flask, house insulation, car radiators, solar heating panels.

title: A Level Physics: Magnetic Fields and Electromagnetism
content:
A Level Physics: Magnetic Fields and Electromagnetism

Magnetism and electricity are one phenomenon seen from two sides: every current makes a magnetic field, and every changing magnetic field makes a current. This note builds the subject from zero: what a magnetic field is and how flux density measures it, the forces on currents and on moving charges with their right-hand rules, the fields produced by wires and solenoids, electromagnetic induction through Faraday's and Lenz's laws, and the alternating-current ideas — rms values, rectification and smoothing — that connect the physics to the mains supply. Every calculation type is worked in full.

The magnetic field and flux density

A magnetic field is a region where a magnetic force acts on moving charges, currents and magnetic materials. Field lines run from north to south outside a magnet and never cross; their density indicates strength. The strength of the field is measured by the magnetic flux density B, in tesla (T): one tesla is one newton per ampere-metre of conductor, or one weber per square metre. Magnetic flux Φ through an area is the field passing through it:

Φ = B A cos(θ)        weber (Wb)

θ = angle between the field and the NORMAL to the area
flux linkage = N Φ        (N turns of a coil)

Force on a current-carrying conductor

F = B I L sin(θ)

B in T, I in A, L = length of conductor in the field (m)
θ = angle between the current and the field

The force is maximum when the current is perpendicular to the field (sin 90° = 1) and zero when parallel. Its direction comes from Fleming's left-hand rule: first finger = field, second finger = current, thumb = force (all mutually perpendicular). The analogy: think of the wire as a sail in a river of field lines — the force is perpendicular to both the flow and the sail.

Worked example. A 0.20 m wire carrying 3.0 A sits perpendicular to a 0.50 T field. Find the force.

F = B I L = 0.50 × 3.0 × 0.20 = 0.30 N

Force on a moving charge

F = B Q v sin(θ)

for a charge moving perpendicular to the field:
F = B Q v, and this force is centripetal:
B Q v = m v²/r  →  r = m v/(B Q)

A charged particle moving perpendicular to a uniform field follows a circular path; the radius grows with momentum and shrinks with field strength and charge. This is the working principle of the mass spectrometer (ions of different mass follow different radii) and the cyclotron.

Worked example. An electron moves at 2.0 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ perpendicular to a 0.10 T field. Find the force and the radius of its path.

F = B e v = 0.10 × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 2.0 × 10⁶ = 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁴ N
r = m v/(B e) = (9.11 × 10⁻³¹ × 2.0 × 10⁶)/(0.10 × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹)
  = 1.82 × 10⁻²⁴/1.6 × 10⁻²⁰ = 1.14 × 10⁻⁴ m  (0.11 mm)

Magnetic fields due to currents

  • Straight wire: concentric circular field lines around the wire; the right-hand grip rule (thumb along current, fingers curl with the field) gives direction; strength falls with distance, B = μ₀I/(2πr).
  • Solenoid: a uniform field inside, like a bar magnet, with the field direction set by the right-hand grip rule; adding an iron core concentrates the field (an electromagnet).
  • Parallel wires: currents in the same direction attract, opposite directions repel — a direct consequence of each wire's field acting on the other's current.

Worked example. Find the flux density 0.050 m from a long straight wire carrying 10 A (μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹).

B = μ₀ I/(2 π r) = (4 π x 10⁻⁷ × 10)/(2 π x 0.050)
  = (2 × 10⁻⁶)/0.050 = 4.0 × 10⁻⁵ T

Electromagnetic induction

Faraday's law: the induced e.m.f. is proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux linkage. Lenz's law: the induced current opposes the change producing it (a statement of energy conservation — the induced current's field pushes back).

ε = - N dPhi/dt

moving a rod of length L at speed v perpendicular to B:
ε = B L v

rotating coil (peak e.m.f.): ε₀ = N B A ω

Worked example. A 0.50 m rod moves at 4.0 m s⁻¹ perpendicular to a 0.20 T field. Find the induced e.m.f.

ε = B L v = 0.20 × 0.50 × 4.0 = 0.40 V

Worked example (flux change). A 200-turn coil of area 0.010 m² sits in a 0.50 T field; the field is reversed in 0.10 s. Find the average e.m.f.

initial flux linkage: N B A = 200 × 0.50 × 0.010 = 1.0 Wb-turn
field reversed: change = 2 × 1.0 = 2.0 Wb-turn
ε = change/time = 2.0/0.10 = 20 V

Alternating current: peak and rms values

Mains electricity is sinusoidal: the voltage and current reverse direction periodically. The average of a sine wave is zero, so power calculations use the root-mean-square value, which is the steady d.c. value that would deliver the same power:

V_rms = V_0/√(2) = 0.707 V_0
I_rms = I_0/√(2)

average power: P = V_rms I_rms = I_rms² R = V_rms²/R

Worked example. A 230 V rms mains supply feeds a 2.0 kW heater. Find the peak voltage and the rms current.

V_0 = 230 x √(2) = 325 V
I_rms = P/V_rms = 2000/230 = 8.7 A

Rectification and smoothing

A diode allows current in one direction only, so a single diode halves the a.c. wave (half-wave rectification); a bridge of four diodes produces full-wave rectification — the output always has the same polarity. A capacitor in parallel with the load then smooths the output: it charges at the peaks and discharges through the load between them, reducing the ripple. Larger capacitance and larger load resistance give less ripple (τ = RC longer relative to the cycle).

  • Half-wave: one diode; half the wave is missing; more ripple.
  • Full-wave: bridge of four diodes; both halves used; easier to smooth.
  • Smoothing: capacitor across the load; ripple reduced as C and R increase.

Worked examples: combined electromagnetism

Worked example. A generator coil of 50 turns and area 0.020 m² rotates at 60 rad s⁻¹ in a 0.40 T field. Find the peak e.m.f. and the rms e.m.f.

ε₀ = N B A ω = 50 × 0.40 × 0.020 × 60
         = 24 V
epsilon_rms = 24/√(2) = 17 V

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Force on wire) A 0.30 m wire carrying 2.0 A is perpendicular to a 0.80 T field. Find the force. Answer: F = BIL = 0.80 × 2.0 × 0.30 = 0.48 N.
  2. (Direction) State Fleming's left-hand rule. Answer: With the first finger along the field and the second along the current, the thumb points along the force — used for motors (the left hand gives the force on the conductor).
  3. (Charge) Explain why a moving charge in a uniform magnetic field moves in a circle. Answer: The magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work and changes only direction; a constant perpendicular force produces circular motion with r = mv/(BQ).
  4. (Solenoid) Describe the magnetic field inside a current-carrying solenoid. Answer: Strong, uniform, and directed along the axis; outside it resembles a bar magnet's field, with the end determined by the right-hand grip rule.
  5. (Faraday) State Faraday's law and Lenz's law. Answer: The induced e.m.f. is proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux linkage; the induced current opposes the change that produces it.
  6. (Lenz) Explain why Lenz's law is a consequence of energy conservation. Answer: If the induced current aided the change, it would generate energy from nothing; opposing it means work must be done to produce the change, and that work becomes electrical energy.
  7. (rms) An a.c. supply has peak voltage 340 V. Find the rms voltage. Answer: V_rms = 340/√2 = 240 V.
  8. (Smoothing) Explain how a capacitor smooths a rectified output. Answer: The capacitor charges as the rectified voltage rises to its peak and discharges through the load as the voltage falls, filling the gaps between peaks and reducing the ripple.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Angle in F = BIL sin θ: θ is between the current and the field; perpendicular means sin θ = 1. A wire parallel to the field feels no force.
  • Left hand versus right hand: use the left-hand rule for the force on a current (motor effect) and the right-hand grip rule for the field around a current. Mixing them reverses the answer.
  • Flux versus flux density: Φ = BA (weber), B is tesla; flux linkage multiplies by N turns. Do not call B flux.
  • Change of flux sign: reversing a field doubles the change (from +BA to −BA), a factor candidates often forget.
  • rms factor: peak over √2; the peak is rms × √2. Power uses rms values, not peak.
  • Induced e.m.f. needs change: a stationary coil in a steady field induces nothing; there must be a changing flux linkage (movement, rotation, or a changing current).
  • Lenz direction questions: state the opposing field direction and then the current direction; the reasoning chain is the mark.
  • Rectification understanding: diodes conduct one way only; a bridge gives full-wave, a single diode half-wave — do not claim a single diode gives full-wave output.
  • Precision and units: tesla, weber, volt; 2 or 3 s.f.; μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹ from the data sheet.

title: IGCSE English as a Second Language: Listening Strategies
AS Level Mathematics: Differentiation
content:
AS Level Mathematics: Differentiation

Differentiation measures how fast something changes: the gradient of a curve at a point, the speed of a moving object, the rate at which cost rises with output. It is the central tool of AS mathematics, and this note builds it from zero: the idea of a limit and the gradient function, the power rule with every algebraic case, tangents and normals, stationary points and their classification, increasing and decreasing intervals, and rates of change. Every worked example writes the derivative line before substituting, because the method marks live there.

Gradient as a limit

The gradient of a curve at a point is the gradient of the tangent there. Approximate it with a chord between two nearby points: as the points close up, the chord's gradient approaches the tangent's. That limiting process defines the derivative:

gradient of chord = [f(x + h) - f(x)]/h
derivative = limit as h -> 0
notation: dy/dx, f'(x)

For y = x², the chord gradient simplifies to 2x + h, which tends to 2x as h → 0: the derivative of x² is 2x. That single calculation is the model for the general rule.

The power rule

if y = x^n then dy/dx = n x^(n - 1)

constant multiple: d/dx [k f(x)] = k f'(x)
sum: differentiate term by term
constant term: differentiates to 0

Worked example 1. Differentiate y = 4x³ − 2x² + 7x − 5.

dy/dx = 12x^2 - 4x + 7

Worked example 2 (negative and fractional powers). Differentiate y = 3/x² + √x.

rewrite: y = 3x^-2 + x^(1/2)
dy/dx = -6x^-3 + (1/2)x^(-1/2)
      = -6/x^3 + 1/(2 sqrt(x))

Worked example 3 (expand first). Differentiate y = x²(2x + 1).

expand: y = 2x^3 + x^2
dy/dx = 6x^2 + 2x

Worked example 4 (gradient at a point). Find the gradient of y = x³ − 4x at x = 2.

dy/dx = 3x^2 - 4
at x = 2: 12 - 4 = 8

Tangents and normals

tangent at x = a: gradient m = f'(a), through (a, f(a))
normal: gradient -1/m (perpendicular to the tangent)
equation: y - y1 = m(x - x1)

Worked example. Find the tangent and normal to y = x² − 3x + 1 at x = 4.

point: y = 16 - 12 + 1 = 5  ->  (4, 5)
dy/dx = 2x - 3  ->  m = 5
tangent: y - 5 = 5(x - 4)  ->  y = 5x - 15
normal: gradient -1/5
y - 5 = -1/5 (x - 4)  ->  x + 5y = 29

Worked example 2 (tangent through a point). Find where the tangent to y = x³ at (2, 8) crosses the x-axis.

dy/dx = 3x^2  ->  m = 12
tangent: y - 8 = 12(x - 2)  ->  y = 12x - 16
set y = 0: x = 16/12 = 4/3

Stationary points

stationary point: dy/dx = 0
classify with the second derivative:
  d2y/dx2 < 0: maximum
  d2y/dx2 > 0: minimum
  d2y/dx2 = 0: could be either - check the gradient either side

Worked example. Find and classify the stationary points of y = x³ − 3x² + 4.

dy/dx = 3x^2 - 6x = 3x(x - 2)
stationary at x = 0 and x = 2
points: (0, 4) and (2, 0)
d2y/dx2 = 6x - 6
at x = 0: -6 < 0  ->  maximum
at x = 2: +6 > 0  ->  minimum

Worked example 2 (unknown coefficient). The curve y = x³ + ax² + b has a stationary point at (2, 1). Find a and b.

point condition: 8 + 4a + b = 1
derivative condition: 3x^2 + 2ax = 0 at x = 2 -> 12 + 4a = 0 -> a = -3
substitute: 8 - 12 + b = 1  ->  b = 5

Increasing and decreasing functions

increasing where dy/dx > 0
decreasing where dy/dx < 0

Worked example. Find the intervals where y = x³ − 6x² + 9x is increasing.

dy/dx = 3x^2 - 12x + 9 = 3(x - 1)(x - 3)
positive outside the roots: x < 1 or x > 3
increasing on x < 1 and x > 3; decreasing on 1 < x < 3

Rates of change and kinematics

if s(t) is displacement: velocity v = ds/dt; acceleration a = dv/dt
displacement from velocity: integrate (next topic)

Worked example. A particle's displacement is s = 2t³ − 9t² + 12t (metres, seconds). Find its velocity and acceleration at t = 2.

v = ds/dt = 6t^2 - 18t + 12
at t = 2: 24 - 36 + 12 = 0 m/s (momentarily at rest)
a = dv/dt = 12t - 18
at t = 2: 24 - 18 = 6 m/s2

Worked example 2 (maximum displacement). With the same s(t), find when the particle is at rest and classify each moment.

v = 0: 6t^2 - 18t + 12 = 0 -> t^2 - 3t + 2 = 0 -> t = 1, 2
a(1) = -6 < 0 -> at t = 1 the displacement is a maximum
a(2) = +6 > 0 -> at t = 2 the displacement is a minimum

Optimisation problems

Applied maximum/minimum questions follow a fixed routine: write the quantity to optimise as a function of one variable, differentiate, set to zero, solve, and classify (or argue from the context).

Worked example. A rectangular pen is to be made against a wall with 24 m of fencing (three sides). Find the maximum area.

let the two equal sides be x; the third is 24 - 2x
A = x(24 - 2x) = 24x - 2x^2
dA/dx = 24 - 4x = 0  ->  x = 6
A = 6(24 - 12) = 72 m2 (maximum since d2A/dx2 = -4 < 0)

Differentiation from first principles

The definition is examinable and shows why the power rule works. The routine: form f(x + h), subtract f(x), divide by h, simplify, then let h → 0.

Worked example. Differentiate f(x) = x² + 3x from first principles.

f(x + h) = (x + h)^2 + 3(x + h) = x^2 + 2xh + h^2 + 3x + 3h
f(x + h) - f(x) = 2xh + h^2 + 3h
divide by h: 2x + h + 3
let h -> 0: f'(x) = 2x + 3

Worked example 2. Differentiate f(x) = 5x² from first principles.

f(x + h) - f(x) = 5(x^2 + 2xh + h^2) - 5x^2 = 10xh + 5h^2
divide by h: 10x + 5h  ->  limit 10x

Concavity and the second derivative

The second derivative describes how the gradient itself is changing. Where d²y/dx² > 0 the gradient is increasing and the curve is concave up (holds water); where it is negative the gradient is decreasing and the curve is concave down. That is exactly why the sign classifies stationary points, and it also answers direct questions about concavity:

d2y/dx2 > 0: concave up / minimum
d2y/dx2 < 0: concave down / maximum
d2y/dx2 = 0: possible point of inflection - test the gradient either side

Worked example. Find where y = x³ − 3x is concave up.

dy/dx = 3x^2 - 3;  d2y/dx2 = 6x
concave up where 6x > 0  ->  x > 0

Sketching curves with calculus

Calculus turns a sketch from guesswork into a list of facts: intercepts, stationary points and their nature, behaviour at the ends, and any asymptotes. A reliable order:

  1. Set x = 0 for the y-intercept; solve y = 0 for the x-intercepts where factorisable.
  2. Differentiate, solve dy/dx = 0, and classify each stationary point.
  3. Use the second derivative sign to fix concavity between the points.
  4. Check the sign of y at the extremes of the sketch (a positive cubic rises to the right).

Worked example. Sketch y = x³ − 3x².

intercepts: y = 0 at x = 0 and x = 3 (x^2(x - 3))
dy/dx = 3x^2 - 6x = 3x(x - 2)
stationary: (0, 0) and (2, -4)
d2y/dx2 = 6x - 6: at 0 negative -> maximum; at 2 positive -> minimum
The curve rises from the left, peaks at the origin, falls to (2, -4),
then rises, crossing the x-axis at x = 3.

Optimisation with a constraint

Most real optimisation questions give a constraint (fixed perimeter, fixed volume, fixed budget) that must be used to eliminate one variable before differentiating.

Worked example. A closed cylinder has volume 250 cm³. Find the radius that minimises its surface area.

V = pi r^2 h = 250  ->  h = 250/(pi r^2)
S = 2 pi r^2 + 2 pi r h = 2 pi r^2 + 500/r
dS/dr = 4 pi r - 500/r^2 = 0
4 pi r^3 = 500  ->  r^3 = 39.79  ->  r = 3.41 cm
check: d2S/dr2 = 4 pi + 1000/r^3 > 0  ->  minimum

The pattern is always the same: one constraint equation, one quantity to optimise, substitute, differentiate, solve, justify the nature of the stationary point — and answer the question actually asked (here the radius, not the height).

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Differentiate) Differentiate y = 5x⁴ − 3x² + 2. Answer: 20x³ − 6x.
  2. (Negative power) Differentiate y = 4/x. Answer: y = 4x⁻¹ → −4x⁻² = −4/x².
  3. (Gradient) Find the gradient of y = x² + 2x at x = −1. Answer: 2x + 2 → 0.
  4. (Tangent) Find the tangent to y = x² at (3, 9). Answer: m = 6; y = 6x − 9.
  5. (Stationary) Find the stationary point of y = x² − 6x + 5. Answer: 2x − 6 = 0 → x = 3; y = −4; minimum.
  6. (Second derivative) Classify the stationary point of y = x³ at x = 0. Answer: dy/dx = 3x², d²y/dx² = 6x = 0 at x = 0 — the test is inconclusive; the gradient is positive either side, so it is a point of inflection, not an extremum.
  7. (Increasing) Find where y = x² − 4x is decreasing. Answer: 2x − 4 < 0 → x < 2.
  8. (Kinematics) s = t³ − 6t² + 9t. Find the acceleration at t = 1. Answer: v = 3t² − 12t + 9; a = 6t − 12 → −6 m/s².

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Forgetting to rewrite powers: differentiate 1/x and √x only after rewriting as x⁻¹ and x^(1/2); the power rule does not apply to the original form.
  • Dropping the constant: the derivative of a constant is 0 — a leftover +7 in dy/dx is an error.
  • Tangent versus normal: the normal's gradient is −1/m, not −m; and it passes through the same point.
  • Second derivative sign: negative means maximum (the curve is concave down); positive means minimum. Reversing the classification is the classic slip.
  • d²y/dx² = 0: inconclusive, not automatically an inflection — check the gradient either side.
  • Stationary point coordinates: the question wants (x, y), so substitute the x back into the original curve, not the derivative.
  • Rates of change with units: attach units (m/s, m/s², units per item) and interpret the sign in context.
  • Method marks: write dy/dx = ... explicitly before substituting; the derivative itself is credit even if the later arithmetic slips.

title: IGCSE Computer Science: Data Representation
content:
IGCSE Computer Science: Data Representation

Cambridge IGCSE Computer Science 0478 (2026–2028), Paper 1 Computer Systems, Topic 1 Data representation: statement 1.1 Number systems, 1.2 Text, sound and images, and 1.3 Data storage and compression. Everything inside a computer — numbers, letters, photographs, music — is stored as patterns of bits, and this note explains exactly how each kind of value becomes binary and how much space it takes. Every conversion and calculation is shown step by step, because in the exam the working carries most of the marks.

Why binary, and how place value works

Computers are built from billions of tiny switches. A switch is either off or on, and those two states are the only thing hardware can reliably store and detect — so all information is encoded with two symbols, 0 and 1. Denary (base 10) has ten digits because we have ten fingers; binary (base 2) has two digits because a switch has two states. The rules of arithmetic are identical — only the number of digits differs.

Place values in binary:   128  64  32  16  8  4  2  1
Example: 1 0 1 1 0 1 1 0
= 128 + 32 + 16 + 4 + 2 = 182 in denary        [add the values of the 1-bits]

Denary to binary, step by step (the subtract-powers method, ideal without a calculator):

Convert 149 to binary:

149 is bigger than 128 → put a 1 in the 128 column, remainder 149 - 128 = 21
21 is smaller than 64  → 0
21 is smaller than 32  → 0
21 is bigger than 16   → 1, remainder 21 - 16 = 5
5 is smaller than 8    → 0
5 is bigger than 4     → 1, remainder 5 - 4 = 1
1 is smaller than 2    → 0
1 is bigger than 1     → 1, remainder 0

Reading the columns: 149 = 1001 0101

The reverse direction simply adds the column values, as above. A quick check always exists: convert back.

Hexadecimal

Hexadecimal (base 16) uses sixteen digits: 0–9 then A–F (A = 10 … F = 15). It exists for a practical reason: one hex digit represents exactly four bits (a nibble), so long binary strings become short and readable — memory dumps, error codes, web colours (#FF8800) and MAC addresses are all written in hex because humans can transcribe them without bit-counting errors.

Binary to hex: 1011 0110
Split into nibbles:   1011 = 11 = B    and    0110 = 6
So 1011 0110 = B6 in hex.

Hex to denary: B6
= 11 × 16 + 6 × 1 = 176 + 6 = 182        [16s column and 1s column]

Denary to hex (via binary): 182 = 1011 0110 = B6.
Or directly by division: 182 ÷ 16 = 11 remainder 6 → digits 11, 6 → B6.

Binary addition and overflow

Binary addition follows the denary carry rule with one extra fact: 1 + 1 = 10 (write 0, carry 1).

Add 0110 0111 (= 103) and 0011 1010 (= 58), 8-bit, column by column:

bit 0:  1 + 0        = 1                 (write 1, carry 0)
bit 1:  1 + 1        = 0, carry 1        (1 + 1 = 10 in binary)
bit 2:  1 + 0 + 1(c) = 0, carry 1
bit 3:  0 + 1 + 1(c) = 0, carry 1
bit 4:  0 + 1 + 1(c) = 0, carry 1
bit 5:  1 + 1 + 1(c) = 1, carry 1        (three 1s sum to 11: write 1, carry 1)
bit 6:  1 + 0 + 1(c) = 0, carry 1
bit 7:  0 + 0 + 1(c) = 1, carry 0

Result: 1 0 1 0 0 0 0 1 = 1010 0001 = 161. Check: 103 + 58 = 161 ✓
No carry escapes bit 7, so the 8-bit answer is exact and there is no overflow.

Overflow happens when the result needs more bits than the register holds. If the two numbers are added in 8 bits and a carry comes out of the leftmost column, the answer is wrong for that word length:

Unsigned example: 200 + 100 = 300, which is beyond the 8-bit maximum of 255.

  1100 1000 (= 200) + 0110 0100 (= 100) = 1 0010 1100
  The 9th bit is lost, so the 8-bit answer reads 0010 1100 = 44 - wrong.
  A carry out of the most significant bit reveals the overflow.

Signed example (different rule): 127 + 1 = 128, which is outside the signed
range -128 to +127, so even though no carry leaves bit 7 the result overflows:

  0111 1111 (= 127) + 0000 0001 (= 1) = 1000 0000, which reads as -128.
  Two positives summed to a negative: the sign bits reveal the overflow.

Overflow rules differ for signed (two's complement) numbers: there the sign bit is the tell-tale, and adding two negatives that gives a positive (or vice versa) is overflow.

Logical binary shifts

Shifting moves every bit left or right, filling with zeros. Left shift by one multiplies by 2; right shift by one divides by 2 (integer division, discarding the remainder).

0010 1101 (= 45) shifted left one place:  0101 1010 (= 90)      45 × 2 = 90
0010 1101 (= 45) shifted right one place: 0001 0110 (= 22)      45 / 2 = 22 (remainder 1 lost)

Each place shifted doubles or halves the value, so shifting left by n multiplies by 2ⁿ. Bits shifted off the end are lost — which is how quick multiplication can silently overflow.

Two's complement: negative numbers

Hardware needs to store negative integers too. In two's complement the most significant (leftmost) bit is a sign bit and has a negative place value: for 8 bits the columns are −128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1. Think of it as odometer arithmetic: a clock with 8 wheels that wraps around, where the top half of the wheel positions are read as negatives.

Write -5 as an 8-bit two's complement number:

Method: write +5, invert every bit, add 1.

+5      = 0000 0101
invert  = 1111 1010        (each 0 becomes 1 and each 1 becomes 0)
add 1   = 1111 1011        = -5

Check with the column values: -128 + 64 + 32 + 16 + 8 + 2 + 1 = -5 ✓
  • Range of 8-bit two's complement: −128 to +127. (One pattern, 1000 0000, is −128 and there is no positive counterpart — the asymmetry examiners like to test.)
  • Negating (turning x into −x): invert all the bits, then add 1. Negating twice returns the original.
  • Reading a negative directly: 1111 1011 has sign bit 1, so it is negative; the remaining columns sum to 123; the value is −(128 − 123) = −5.

Subtraction becomes addition. Computers do not subtract; they add the negative, which lets one circuit (the adder) do both jobs:

Calculate 7 - 5 in 8-bit two's complement:

7 = 0000 0111
-5 = 1111 1011        (as above)
Add:  0000 0111 + 1111 1011 = (1) 0000 0010
The carry beyond bit 7 is discarded in two's complement addition.
0000 0010 = 2, and 7 - 5 = 2 ✓

Overflow in signed arithmetic: the sign bit is the guide. Adding two positives must not give a negative: 0111 1111 (127) + 0000 0001 = 1000 0000, which reads as −128 — overflow, even though no carry escapes the byte. Two negatives giving a positive is overflow the same way.

Text: character sets

Text is stored as numbers, and a character set is the agreed table mapping numbers to printed symbols. ASCII uses 7 bits per character — 128 codes — covering upper- and lower-case Latin letters, digits, punctuation and control codes (like newline). The code for 'A' is 65, 'a' is 97 and '0' is 48; note that upper- and lower-case letters differ by exactly one bit (32), a fact often examined. Extended ASCII adds a further 128 symbols with 8 bits.

Unicode solves the limitation that 128 symbols cannot cover the world's scripts: it assigns a unique code to well over 100 000 characters from every writing system plus symbols and emoji. UTF-8 stores common characters in 1 byte and rare ones in up to 4 — efficient for web pages, which is why it dominates the internet. More characters per code needs more bits per character, and file size grows accordingly.

Worked example: storing the word "CAT" in ASCII:
C = 67 = 0100 0011
A = 65 = 0100 0001
T = 84 = 0101 0100
Total: 3 characters x 8 bits (stored as bytes) = 24 bits = 3 bytes.

Sound: sampling

Sound is a continuous pressure wave — an analogue signal. To store it, the wave is sampled: measured at regular intervals, and each measurement is rounded to the nearest available level. Two settings decide the quality:

  • Sample rate — how many measurements per second (Hz). Higher rate captures higher frequencies and sounds closer to the original.
  • Sample resolution (bit depth) — how many bits per measurement. More bits means finer rounding of the amplitude, so less distortion.
File size (bits) = sample rate x bit depth x duration in seconds x number of channels

Worked example: 10 seconds of mono CD-quality sound (44 100 Hz, 16 bits):

= 44 100 × 16 × 10 × 1 = 7 056 000 bits
In bytes: 7 056 000 / 8 = 882 000 bytes
In kilobytes: 882 000 / 1024 = 861.3 KB (or /1000 = 882 kB by decimal convention)

Double the sample rate or the bit depth and the file doubles in size.

Raising either setting improves fidelity at the cost of size — the trade-off every sound question turns on.

Images: bitmaps

A bitmap image is a grid of pixels. Two properties set its size and quality: the resolution (pixels across × pixels down) and the colour depth (bits per pixel). With 1 bit per pixel you get black and white; 8 bits give 256 greys or colours; 24 bits (8 per RGB channel) give about 16.7 million colours.

File size (bits) = width in pixels x height in pixels x colour depth

Worked example: 800 × 600 pixels at 24-bit colour:

= 800 × 600 × 24 = 11 520 000 bits
In bytes: 11 520 000 / 8 = 1 440 000 bytes = 1.37 MB (or 1.44 MB decimal)

At 8-bit colour the same image is 800 × 600 × 8 = 3 840 000 bits = 480 000 bytes.

The file also stores metadata: width, height, colour depth and format information, without which the pixels cannot be interpreted. Higher resolution and colour depth improve quality and raise the file size in direct proportion — the same trade-off as sound.

Units of data

UnitSymbolSize
BitbA single 0 or 1
ByteB8 bits
KilobyteKB1024 bytes (binary convention) or 1000 bytes (decimal convention)
MegabyteMB1024 KB
GigabyteGB1024 MB
TerabyteTB1024 GB

The bit/byte distinction is the single most common lost mark in size questions: transmission speeds are quoted in bits per second (Mbps), storage in bytes (MB), and confusing the two is a factor-of-eight error. State which convention you use when the question gives sizes.

Compression

Compression shrinks data for storage or transmission: faster transfer, less bandwidth, lower storage cost. Two families:

LosslessLossy
What it doesRecovers the exact original — redundancy is removed reversiblyDiscards data the human senses are unlikely to miss
MethodsRun-length encoding (RLE), dictionary methods (ZIP, PNG, FLAC)Transform methods throwing away detail (JPEG, MP3)
Used forText, programs, spreadsheets, medical/legal images, archivesPhotographs, music, video, where small losses are acceptable
QualityIdentical to the original after decompressionDegrades with each save; repeated compression compounds the loss
Run-length encoding worked line by line:

Row of pixels: AAAAABBCCCCCCCCDD
Scan for runs:     AAAAA      BB      CCCCCCCC      DD
Count and write:    5A        2B          8C         2D
Compressed: 5A2B8C2D  (9 characters instead of 17)

RLE works when data has long runs; on busy photographs it can even expand the
data, which is why it is used inside other methods rather than alone.

Choosing the method is a reasoning mark: a text document must be lossless (a single wrong character changes its meaning), while a holiday photograph compresses lossily because the eye cannot detect the discarded detail.

Worked example: a complete size calculation

A scanner captures a 1024 × 768 image at 24-bit colour and saves it uncompressed, then compressed 6:1. Find both file sizes in MB.

Uncompressed bits = 1024 × 768 × 24 = 18 874 368 bits
Bytes = 18 874 368 / 8 = 2 359 296 bytes
MB = 2 359 296 / 1 048 576 = 2.25 MB

Compressed at 6:1 = 2.25 / 6 = 0.375 MB

Checks: the ratio of widths (1024 = 2¹⁰) suggests round numbers are expected;
a 6:1 lossy reduction keeps the image visually similar for on-screen use.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Confusing bits and bytes: file sizes are bytes; transmission rates are bits per second. Divide bits by 8 to reach bytes, and state the unit in the answer.
  • Starting binary groupings from the wrong end when converting to hex — always group from the right.
  • Forgetting the sign bit in two's complement: the leftmost bit has value −128, not +128, and the 8-bit range is −128 to +127.
  • Negating by inverting bits alone; the "+1" is essential — invert, then add 1.
  • Leaving a carry in two's complement addition: beyond the 8th bit the carry is discarded, and overflow is judged from the sign bits instead.
  • Applying the overflow rule of unsigned arithmetic to signed numbers (or vice versa) — unsigned overflow is a carry out of the leftmost bit; signed overflow is two positives summing negative.
  • Writing the sound or image size formula without all the factors: sound needs rate, depth, duration and channels; images need width, height and colour depth.
  • Choosing lossy compression for text or program files; those must be restored exactly, so lossless is mandatory.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 1, 3 marks). Convert 0110 1001 to denary.

Answer: 64 + 32 + 8 + 1 = 105.

Question 2 (Paper 1, 3 marks). Convert 211 to hexadecimal, showing your working.

Answer: 211 = 1101 0011 in binary (128 + 64 + 16 + 2 + 1). Grouping 1101 = 13 = D and 0011 = 3 gives D3.

Question 3 (Paper 1, 4 marks). Show how −12 is represented in 8-bit two's complement.

Answer: +12 = 0000 1100. Invert: 1111 0011. Add 1: 1111 0100 = −12. Column check: −128 + 16 + 4 = −12 ✓.

Question 4 (Paper 1, 4 marks). Calculate the size in MB of 30 seconds of stereo sound sampled at 22 050 Hz with a bit depth of 8.

Answer: 22 050 × 8 × 30 × 2 = 10 584 000 bits. ÷ 8 = 1 323 000 bytes. ÷ 1 048 576 = 1.26 MB.

Question 5 (Paper 1, 3 marks). A 4 × 4 pixel row reads AAAAAABBCCCCCC. Give its RLE form and state one limitation of RLE.

Answer: 6A2B6C. Limitation: RLE only helps data with long runs; on random or noisy data it saves nothing and can make the file larger, so it is often combined with other methods.

Question 6 (Paper 1, 4 marks). Explain why a hospital would store X-ray images using lossless compression while a music app uses lossy compression.

Answer: Medical images are diagnostic data: any discarded pixel could hide a detail the radiologist needs, and legal/clinical records must be exact, so lossless methods (which restore the original perfectly) are required even though the files stay large. Music is perceptual: MP3-style compression discards sounds beyond human hearing or masked by louder sounds, and listeners cannot tell the difference, so the far smaller files are worth the imperceptible loss.

Numbers are only one kind of data; the next topic covers how the same bits carry data between machines — data transmission.

title: AS Level Mathematics: Integration
content:
AS Level Mathematics: Integration

Integration is differentiation in reverse: it recovers a function from its gradient, and it accumulates a rate into a total — the area under a curve, the distance from a velocity, the cost from a marginal. This note builds the topic from zero: the indefinite integral and the constant of integration, the power rule, definite integrals and the fundamental theorem, areas above and below the axis, the area between two curves, and kinematics. Every worked example shows the antiderivative line before any substitution of limits.

The indefinite integral

if dy/dx = x^n then y = x^(n+1)/(n+1) + c   (n not -1)

integral of x^n dx = x^(n+1)/(n+1) + c
integral of k f(x) dx = k integral of f(x) dx
integral of a sum = sum of integrals

The +c is mandatory for indefinite integrals: every antiderivative differs by a constant, and the constant is fixed by a boundary condition (a point on the curve).

Worked example 1. Find ∫(6x² − 4x + 3) dx.

= 6x^3/3 - 4x^2/2 + 3x + c
= 2x^3 - 2x^2 + 3x + c

Worked example 2 (negative and fractional powers). Find ∫(1/x² + √x) dx.

rewrite: integral of (x^-2 + x^(1/2)) dx
= -x^-1 + (2/3)x^(3/2) + c
= -1/x + (2/3)x^(3/2) + c

Worked example 3 (finding c). dy/dx = 3x² + 2 and the curve passes through (1, 5). Find y.

y = x^3 + 2x + c
5 = 1 + 2 + c  ->  c = 2
y = x^3 + 2x + 2

Definite integrals and area

integral from a to b of f(x) dx = F(b) - F(a)

area under the curve between x = a and x = b (above the axis)
= definite integral; a negative value means the region is
below the x-axis, and the area is the magnitude

Worked example. Evaluate ∫ from 1 to 3 of (2x + 1) dx.

antiderivative: x^2 + x
F(3) = 9 + 3 = 12;  F(1) = 1 + 1 = 2
value = 12 - 2 = 10

Worked example 2 (area under a curve). Find the area under y = x² between x = 0 and x = 3.

integral: x^3/3
from 0 to 3: 27/3 - 0 = 9 square units

Worked example 3 (below the axis). Find the area between y = x² − 4 and the x-axis from x = 0 to x = 2.

integral: x^3/3 - 4x
from 0 to 2: 8/3 - 8 = -16/3
the value is negative because the region is below the axis;
area = 16/3 = 5.33 square units

Areas crossing the axis

When a curve crosses the x-axis inside the interval, integrate each piece separately and add the magnitudes — a single integral would cancel positive and negative areas.

Worked example. Find the total area between y = x² − 1 and the x-axis from x = −2 to x = 2.

crossings at x = -1 and x = 1
piece 1 (-2 to -1): F = x^3/3 - x; F(-1) - F(-2) = (2/3) - (-2/3) = 4/3
piece 2 (-1 to 1): F(1) - F(-1) = (-2/3) - (2/3) = -4/3 -> magnitude 4/3
piece 3 (1 to 2): F(2) - F(1) = (2/3) - (-2/3) = 4/3
total area = 4/3 + 4/3 + 4/3 = 4 square units

Area between two curves

area between y = f(x) and y = g(x) from a to b
= integral of (f(x) - g(x)) dx from a to b
where f is the upper curve and g the lower

Worked example. Find the area between y = x² and y = x from x = 0 to x = 1.

upper curve on this interval is y = x
integral of (x - x^2) dx = x^2/2 - x^3/3
from 0 to 1: 1/2 - 1/3 = 1/6 square units

Worked example 2 (intersections). Find the area enclosed by y = x² and y = 2x.

intersections: x^2 = 2x -> x(x - 2) = 0 -> x = 0, 2
upper on (0, 2) is y = 2x
integral of (2x - x^2) dx = x^2 - x^3/3
from 0 to 2: 4 - 8/3 = 4/3 square units

Kinematics with integration

velocity v = ds/dt  ->  displacement s = integral of v dt
acceleration a = dv/dt  ->  velocity v = integral of a dt

definite integral of v from t1 to t2 = displacement
integral of |v| = distance travelled

Worked example. A particle has velocity v = 3t² − 6t (m/s). Find its displacement from t = 0 to t = 3 and its distance travelled.

s = integral of (3t^2 - 6t) dt = t^3 - 3t^2
from 0 to 3: 27 - 27 = 0  ->  net displacement zero
sign of v: 3t(t - 2), negative between 0 and 2, positive after
distance = |integral 0 to 2| + integral 2 to 3
= |8 - 12| + (27 - 27) - (8 - 12) = 4 + 4 = 8 m

The distinction between displacement and distance is examinable: displacement is the signed integral, distance is the sum of the absolute pieces.

Worked examples: mixed integration

Worked example. The curve y = f(x) has f'(x) = 6x − 4 and passes through (2, 3). Find f(x) and the area under the curve from x = 1 to x = 2.

f(x) = 3x^2 - 4x + c;  3 = 12 - 8 + c -> c = -1
f(x) = 3x^2 - 4x - 1
area = integral 1 to 2: x^3 - 2x^2 - x
F(2) = 8 - 8 - 2 = -2; F(1) = 1 - 2 - 1 = -2
area = -2 - (-2) = 0  (the curve is below the axis and the
signed areas cancel); the geometric area needs the crossing
checked - a useful reminder to sketch first

Integrating expressions that need rearranging

Integration has no product or quotient rule at AS level, so expressions must first be written as sums of powers. Two standard rearrangements cover almost every case:

product: expand, then integrate term by term
quotient with a single term denominator: divide through first

(x + 2)(x - 5) = x^2 - 3x - 10
(3x^2 + 4x)/x = 3x + 4
sqrt(x)(x + 1) = x^(3/2) + x^(1/2)

Worked example. Find ∫ (x + 3)(x − 1) dx.

expand: x^2 + 2x - 3
integrate: x^3/3 + x^2 - 3x + c

Worked example 2. Find ∫ (4x³ + 2x)/x dx.

divide: 4x^2 + 2
integrate: (4/3)x^3 + 2x + c

Two boundary conditions

When the second derivative is given, integrate twice and use two pieces of information to fix both constants. The order matters: the first integration produces the gradient function and its constant, the second the curve and its constant.

Worked example. d²y/dx² = 6x, dy/dx = 2 when x = 1, and y = 5 when x = 1. Find y.

first: dy/dx = 3x^2 + c;  2 = 3 + c  ->  c = -1, so dy/dx = 3x^2 - 1
second: y = x^3 - x + k;  5 = 1 - 1 + k  ->  k = 5
y = x^3 - x + 5

Finding limits and constants from area information

Area questions are often inverted: the area is given and a limit or coefficient must be found. Set up the definite integral with the unknown, evaluate, and solve the resulting equation — rejecting any root outside the geometric context.

Worked example. The area under y = kx² from x = 0 to x = 3 is 36. Find k.

integral: kx^3/3
from 0 to 3: 27k/3 = 9k
9k = 36  ->  k = 4

Worked example 2 (unknown upper limit). The area under y = 2x from x = 0 to x = a is 25. Find a.

integral: x^2;  from 0 to a: a^2 = 25
a = 5  (the negative root is rejected: a is an x-coordinate to
the right of the origin in this setup)

Kinematics: recovering velocity from acceleration

Worked example. A particle starts from rest with acceleration a = 6t − 4 (m/s²). Find its velocity at t = 3 and the distance travelled in the first 3 seconds.

v = integral of (6t - 4) dt = 3t^2 - 4t + c
at rest at t = 0: c = 0  ->  v = 3t^2 - 4t
v(3) = 27 - 12 = 15 m/s
distance = integral of |v| from 0 to 3
v = 0 at t = 0 and t = 4/3; v is negative on (0, 4/3)
piece 1: [t^3 - 2t^2] from 0 to 4/3 = 64/27 - 32/9 = -32/27 -> 32/27
piece 2: [t^3 - 2t^2] from 4/3 to 3 = (27 - 18) - (-32/27) = 9 + 32/27
distance = 32/27 + 9 + 32/27 = 9 + 64/27 = 11.4 m

The sign analysis is the whole question: sketch v against t, mark where it crosses zero, and integrate each piece with its sign removed.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Indefinite) Find ∫(4x³ − 2) dx. Answer: x⁴ − 2x + c.
  2. (Negative power) Find ∫x⁻² dx. Answer: −x⁻¹ + c = −1/x + c.
  3. (Definite) Evaluate ∫ from 0 to 2 of 3x² dx. Answer: [x³] = 8.
  4. (Area) Find the area under y = x + 2 from x = 0 to x = 3. Answer: [x²/2 + 2x] = 4.5 + 6 = 10.5.
  5. (Below axis) Find the area between y = x − 3 and the x-axis from x = 0 to x = 2. Answer: integral = [x²/2 − 3x] = 2 − 6 = −4; area 4.
  6. (Between curves) Find the area between y = x² and y = x³ from 0 to 1. Answer: upper is x²; ∫(x² − x³) = 1/3 − 1/4 = 1/12.
  7. (Constant) dy/dx = 4x and y = 7 when x = 1. Find y. Answer: y = 2x² + c → 7 = 2 + c → c = 5 → y = 2x² + 5.
  8. (Kinematics) v = 2t + 1. Find the displacement from t = 0 to t = 4. Answer: [t² + t] = 16 + 4 = 20 m.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Forgetting +c: an indefinite integral without the constant loses a mark; with a boundary condition, the constant is required for the answer.
  • Power rule reversal: integrate xⁿ to x^(n+1)/(n+1); adding one and dividing is the opposite of differentiating, and mixing them up produces nonsense.
  • Limits order: F(b) − F(a), never the reverse. A negative area often means the limits were swapped.
  • Ignoring crossings: a definite integral over a region that crosses the axis gives the signed area; split at the crossings and add magnitudes for the geometric area.
  • Wrong upper curve: subtract lower from upper; sketching between the intersection points avoids the sign error.
  • Distance versus displacement: displacement is the signed integral; distance sums the absolute pieces. Read which is asked.
  • Expanding before integrating: products must be expanded or divided first; there is no product rule for integration at AS level.
  • Units: areas are square units, displacements in metres; attach and interpret units in applied questions.

title: Scatter Diagrams and Correlation — Study Notes
content:
Scatter Diagrams and Correlation

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): scatter diagrams, types of correlation, line of best fit, interpolation vs extrapolation.

1. Correlation types

  • Positive: both increase (revision time vs score).
  • Negative: one increases, other decreases (price vs demand).
  • No correlation: random scatter.
  • Strength: strong (tight to a line) vs weak (loose).

2. Line of best fit

Balance points either side of the line; it need not pass through the origin. Use two well-separated points on your line (not necessarily data points) to estimate its gradient and equation.

Example: line through (10, 24) and (50, 60): m = 36/40 = 0.9 → y = 0.9x + 15.

3. Using the line

Interpolation (inside the data range) is reliable; extrapolation (outside) is a risk — say so if asked.

4. Correlation ≠ causation

A third factor may drive both variables (ice-cream sales and drownings both rise with temperature). Describe relationships, don't over-claim.

5. Outliers

Points far from the trend: identify, and comment on their effect on the line; ignore them when drawing the best fit if instructed.

Exam tips: describe correlation in full ("strong positive linear correlation"); quote the equation only from two points on the drawn line, not raw data.

title: A2 Level Biology: Microbiology, Immunity and Forensics
content:
Microbiology, Immunity and Forensics

Edexcel International A Level Biology — Unit 4 (WBI14), Topic 6. Every statement 6.1 to 6.20 is covered below, with its code in the heading. The topic links three big ideas: how microorganisms are grown and measured, how the body defends itself and why pathogens keep finding ways around those defences, and how DNA techniques are used to identify organisms and people.

6.1: Culturing microorganisms with aseptic technique

  • Aseptic technique keeps a culture pure: only the wanted microorganism grows. Sterilise media and equipment first, usually in an autoclave at 121 °C under pressure for about 15 minutes.
  • Work close to a Bunsen flame, flame the inoculating loop until red-hot before and after use, keep Petri dish lids mostly closed, and never pipette by mouth.
  • Incubate cultures inverted at a safe temperature, usually 25 °C for school work, so condensation does not drip onto the agar.

6.2: Measuring the growth of microorganisms

  • Direct cell counts: use a haemocytometer (counting chamber) under a microscope, counting cells in a known volume to get the number per cm³.
  • Viable counts by dilution plating: make a serial dilution, spread known volumes on agar, incubate, and count colonies on plates with about 30 to 300 colonies. Each colony is assumed to grow from one viable cell, so the count shows living cells only.
  • Mass methods: measure the dry mass of cells collected by centrifuging or filtering a known volume of culture.
  • Optical methods (turbidity): a colorimeter or spectrophotometer measures how much light the cloudy culture absorbs. Absorbance rises with cell density, so a calibration curve converts it to cell numbers.

6.3: The bacterial growth curve and the growth rate constant

  • Lag phase: cells adapt to the medium and synthesise enzymes; there is little or no division.
  • Exponential (log) phase: cells divide at a constant rate, so the population doubles each generation. N = N₀ × 2ⁿ, where n is the number of doublings.
  • Stationary phase: births equal deaths, because nutrients run short and waste builds up.
  • Death phase: deaths exceed births and the population falls.
  • Growth rate constant: in exponential growth N = N₀eᵏᵗ. So k = (ln N₂ − ln N₁) ÷ (t₂ − t₁). Plotting ln N against time gives a straight line whose gradient is k.

6.4: Core practical 13: growth of microorganisms in liquid culture

  • Inoculate a sterile liquid medium, take samples at regular intervals, and measure turbidity or cell count each time.
  • Plot the results to show the four phases of the curve, then calculate the exponential growth rate constant from the straight-line part.
  • Safe and ethical use: use only non-pathogenic strains, keep the culture closed, disinfect the bench, and autoclave all used material before disposal.

6.5: Structure of bacteria and viruses

  • Bacteria are cells with a cell wall (peptidoglycan), cell membrane, cytoplasm with ribosomes, and a circular DNA loop, often with plasmids. They have no nucleus.
  • Viruses are not cells. They have a nucleic acid core, either DNA or RNA, surrounded by a protein capsid. Some also have a lipid envelope taken from the host.
  • Comparisons: Ebola virus has single-stranded RNA and an envelope. Tobacco mosaic virus (TMV) has single-stranded RNA in a helical capsid, with no envelope. HIV has two RNA strands, reverse transcriptase and an envelope. Lambda phage, a virus of bacteria, has double-stranded DNA in a head with a tail and no envelope.
  • Lytic cycle: the virus takes over the host cell, makes new viruses, and the cell bursts (lyses) to release them.
  • Latency: the viral genome stays in the host cell without producing new viruses, and can become active later.

6.6: How Mycobacterium tuberculosis and HIV infect human cells

  • Tuberculosis: Mycobacterium tuberculosis is inhaled into the alveoli. Macrophages engulf it, but the bacterium survives inside them and multiplies. The body forms granulomas (tubercles) around the infection, and the lung tissue is destroyed. Symptoms include a persistent cough, fever, night sweats and weight loss. If untreated it can be fatal.
  • HIV: the virus binds to CD4 receptors and a co-receptor on helper T cells. Reverse transcriptase makes DNA from its RNA, which is inserted into the host genome. New viruses bud from the cell. The helper T cell population falls, so the immune system fails and opportunistic infections and cancers take hold (AIDS).

6.7: Routes of entry and barriers

  • Routes: inhalation (airborne droplets), ingestion (contaminated food and water), contact through broken skin or wounds, sexual contact, and vectors such as mosquitoes.
  • Barriers: intact skin (keratin, dryness, and the skin flora that competes with pathogens), stomach acid (pH about 2, which kills many ingested microbes), and gut flora that competes for space and nutrients. Mucus and cilia in the airways trap and move pathogens out.

6.8: Non-specific responses to infection

  • Inflammation: damaged cells release chemicals such as histamine, which dilate blood vessels and make them leaky. The area becomes red, hot and swollen, and white blood cells are recruited to the site.
  • Lysozyme: an enzyme in tears, saliva and mucus that breaks the peptidoglycan of bacterial cell walls.
  • Interferon: proteins released by virus-infected cells that warn neighbouring cells, which then resist viral replication. Interferon is antiviral, not a direct killer of the virus.
  • Phagocytosis: neutrophils and macrophages engulf a pathogen into a phagosome. Lysosomes fuse with it and enzymes digest the contents.

6.9: Antigens, antibodies, plasma cells, macrophages and antigen-presenting cells

  • An antigen is a foreign molecule, usually a protein or glycoprotein on a pathogen's surface, that triggers an immune response.
  • An antibody is a Y-shaped glycoprotein whose binding sites are complementary to one specific antigen. Antibodies mark pathogens for destruction and neutralise toxins.
  • Plasma cells are B cells that have been activated and that secrete antibodies in large amounts.
  • Macrophages and antigen-presenting cells engulf the pathogen, break it down, and display its antigens on their surface (on MHC proteins). This shows helper T cells what to respond to.

6.10: B cells and T cells

  • B effector (plasma) cells secrete antibodies. B memory cells survive for years and give a faster, larger response on the next exposure to the same antigen.
  • T helper cells (CD4) recognise the antigen on an antigen-presenting cell and release cytokines that activate B cells and T killer cells.
  • T killer (cytotoxic, CD8) cells bind to infected or abnormal cells and kill them, for example by releasing perforin.
  • T memory cells persist after the infection and respond quickly if the same pathogen returns.

6.11: Types of immunity

  • Natural active: the person is infected and makes their own antibodies and memory cells.
  • Natural passive: antibodies pass from mother to baby across the placenta or in breast milk. Protection is immediate but short-lived, and no memory cells are formed.
  • Artificial active: vaccination with an antigen, a weakened or dead pathogen, or a toxoid. The person makes antibodies and memory cells without becoming ill.
  • Artificial passive: injected antibodies, such as antivenom or antitoxin. Protection is immediate and short-lived, and the person's own immune system does not learn.

6.12: The evolutionary race between pathogens and hosts

  • Pathogens evolve evasion mechanisms. Antigenic variation changes the surface antigens: influenza and HIV mutate rapidly, so antibodies no longer fit.
  • Other evasion: hiding inside host cells (tuberculosis in macrophages, HIV in T cells), entering latency, and suppressing the immune response.
  • The host responds with new antibodies and T cells, so pathogens and hosts keep evolving against each other. This is the evolutionary race.

6.13: Bacteriostatic and bactericidal antibiotics

  • Bacteriostatic antibiotics stop bacteria growing and dividing, for example by blocking protein synthesis. The immune system then clears the infection.
  • Bactericidal antibiotics kill bacteria, for example penicillin, which stops cell wall synthesis so the cell bursts.
  • Antibiotics do not act on viruses, which use the host cell's machinery.

6.14: Core practical 14: the effect of antibiotics on bacteria

  • Spread a lawn of bacteria on agar, place antibiotic discs on it, and include a control disc with no antibiotic.
  • Incubate, then measure the diameter of each clear zone of inhibition. A larger zone means the bacteria are more sensitive.
  • Use aseptic technique and non-pathogenic strains, and autoclave the plates before disposal.

6.15: Hospital-acquired infections and codes of practice

  • Contributory causes include overuse of broad-spectrum antibiotics, which selects for resistant strains such as MRSA, poor hand hygiene, indwelling catheters, surgical wounds, and immunocompromised patients.
  • Codes of practice respond to these causes: prescribe antibiotics only when needed and according to guidelines, enforce hand hygiene, isolate infected patients, and clean equipment and wards.

6.16: Decomposition and the carbon cycle

  • Bacteria and fungi are the main decomposers. They secrete extracellular enzymes that digest complex organic matter such as cellulose and proteins, then absorb the simpler products.
  • Respiration by decomposers releases carbon dioxide, which returns carbon to the atmosphere for producers. Ammonium released from proteins feeds the nitrogen cycle.

6.17: The polymerase chain reaction (PCR)

  • Each cycle has three steps: denaturation at about 95 °C separates the strands, annealing at about 50 to 65 °C lets primers bind, and extension at about 72 °C is when Taq polymerase builds the new strands.
  • Taq polymerase comes from the heat-tolerant bacterium Thermus aquaticus, so it survives the high temperatures. Around 30 cycles give an exponential increase in the number of copies.

6.18: Gel electrophoresis of DNA fragments

  • DNA carries a negative charge from its phosphate groups, so it moves towards the positive electrode (anode) through a gel.
  • Smaller fragments move faster and further, so fragments separate by length. A DNA ladder of known sizes is run alongside for comparison, and the bands are stained to make them visible.

6.19: DNA profiling for identification and relatedness

  • DNA profiling compares short tandem repeats (STRs) or variable number tandem repeats (VNTRs). These regions vary in length between individuals, so each person gives a distinctive band pattern.
  • Uses include identifying suspects, establishing paternity, and comparing the banding patterns of plants or animals to show how closely related they are.

6.20: Estimating the time of death from forensic evidence

  • Body temperature: the body cools towards the surroundings, so the rate of cooling gives an estimate of time since death.
  • Muscle contraction: rigor mortis sets in over hours, peaks, then fades over about a day or two.
  • Decomposition and succession: bacterial decomposition gives a predictable sequence of changes. Forensic entomology uses the stage of blowfly larvae and the succession of insect species to estimate how long the body has been exposed.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Growth rate, 6.3 applied: a culture grows from 2.0 × 10⁴ cells cm⁻³ at 2 hours to 1.6 × 10⁵ at 5 hours. N₂ ÷ N₁ = 8 = 2³, so three doublings in three hours. k = (ln 1.6 × 10⁵ − ln 2.0 × 10⁴) ÷ 3 = ln 8 ÷ 3 = 0.69 per hour. The doubling time is ln 2 ÷ k = 1.0 hour. Check the answer against the doubling count before you write it down.
  • Viable count, 6.2 applied: 150 colonies grow from 0.1 cm³ of a 10⁻⁵ dilution. That is 150 ÷ 0.1 = 1500 colonies per cm³ in the diluted sample, and multiplying by the dilution factor gives 1.5 × 10⁸ viable cells per cm³. A haemocytometer count would include dead cells, so the two methods can give different numbers from the same culture. Name which one you are using.
  • Log phase, 6.3 applied: plotting ln N against time gives a straight line only during exponential growth. A curve that bends is a sign that the lag, stationary or death phase has been included by mistake. Use only the straight section to find k.
  • Primary and secondary immune response, 6.10 and 6.12 applied: the first exposure has a lag of several days before antibodies peak at a lower level. A second exposure gives a faster, larger and longer-lasting response, because memory cells are already present. Use all three words, faster, larger and longer, to earn the full mark.
  • Antigen presentation, 6.9 applied: helper T cells (CD4) recognise antigen presented on MHC class II proteins, and killer T cells (CD8) recognise it on MHC class I, as on infected body cells. Naming the MHC class shows you understand which cell carries the antigen.
  • Antibiotic action, 6.13 applied: penicillin blocks the cross-linking of peptidoglycan in the cell wall, so a growing cell bursts. An antibiotic that targets a process human cells do not use, such as the bacterial ribosome, is more selective. Resistance arises by chance mutation and is selected for by the antibiotic, so the explanation must say the mutation was already present and survived.
  • PCR, 6.17 applied: after n cycles one DNA molecule has become 2ⁿ molecules. After 30 cycles that is 2³⁰, about 1.07 × 10⁹ copies. This is why a very small sample is enough, and why contamination with foreign DNA is a serious error.
  • Gel electrophoresis, 6.18 applied: the distance moved is roughly linear with the logarithm of the fragment length. Use a DNA ladder to plot log size against distance, then read the unknown band from that graph rather than from the ladder bands by eye.
  • Forensic estimates, 6.20 applied: a time-of-death answer is always a range. Temperature cooling assumes a stable environment, and a hot or wet site or a body wrapped in clothing changes the rate. Say which factor is most uncertain and why.

Exam tip: time-of-death questions are estimates. Name the method, say what it measures, and state the limitation, for example that temperature depends on the environment.

The four types of immunity, compared

TypeHow it is acquiredAntibodies made by the personDuration
Natural activeInfection with the pathogenYesLong, because memory cells remain
Natural passiveAntibodies cross the placenta or arrive in colostrumNoShort, until the transferred antibodies are broken down
Artificial activeVaccination with antigen or an attenuated pathogenYesLong, and boosters raise the secondary response
Artificial passiveInjection of antibodies from another source, such as an antiserumNoShort, but immediate

Typical mistakes

  • Confusing aseptic technique with sterilisation. Apparatus and medium are sterilised before use; aseptic technique is how the worker keeps them sterile while handling them, by flaming the loop, passing the neck of the bottle through the flame and minimising the time the plate is open.
  • Forgetting the dilution factor in a viable count. A count on a diluted sample must be multiplied by the dilution factor and divided by the volume plated, or the answer is out by orders of magnitude. Quote the units as cells per cm cubed.
  • Reading the growth curve without the phase names. Lag phase: cells adapt and synthesise enzymes, so numbers rise slowly. Exponential phase: numbers double at a constant rate. Stationary: growth equals death as nutrients run low and waste builds. Death: death exceeds growth.
  • Saying antibiotics are bactericidal when they are bacteriostatic. Bactericidal antibiotics kill the bacteria; bacteriostatic ones stop them dividing, so the immune system finishes the job. Penicillin is bactericidal because it blocks the cross-linking of peptidoglycan, so growing cells burst.
  • Giving B and T cells the same job. B effector cells make and secrete antibodies and B memory cells make the secondary response faster. T helper cells release cytokines that activate B cells and macrophages, T killer cells destroy infected cells, and T memory cells persist.
  • Describing PCR without its requirements. PCR needs a DNA template, primers, free nucleotides, a heat-stable DNA polymerase and a buffer, with repeated cycles of denaturation, annealing and extension. Each cycle doubles the DNA, so 30 cycles give 2 to the power 30 copies.
  • Forgetting which electrode DNA moves towards. DNA is negatively charged because of its phosphate groups, so in gel electrophoresis it moves towards the positive electrode, and shorter fragments move further.
  • Giving a single figure for time of death. It is an estimate from several methods, each with a limitation: body temperature depends on the environment, decomposition depends on conditions, and succession depends on the species available.

Exam-style questions

  1. A 0.1 cm cubed sample of a 10 to the power minus 4 dilution produces 64 colonies. Calculate the number of viable cells in the original culture. Answer: 64 colonies in 0.1 cm cubed is 640 cells per cm cubed in the diluted sample; multiply by the dilution factor 10 000, giving 6.4 times 10 to the power 6 viable cells per cm cubed.
  2. Explain why a viable count can be lower than a total count from a haemocytometer. Answer: a viable count only counts cells that can divide and form a colony, so dead cells and cells that are alive but not dividing are missed; a haemocytometer counts all cells, living and dead, present in the sample.
  3. Describe how you would investigate the effect of different antibiotics on a bacterial culture, naming the variables. Answer: inoculate a lawn of the bacterium evenly over an agar plate using a sterile spreader, place discs soaked in equal volumes of different antibiotic solutions on the surface, incubate at a controlled temperature for a fixed time, and measure the diameter of the clear zone around each disc. Controls: a disc soaked in sterile water, and the same species, incubation temperature and time for every plate. A larger zone means greater inhibition, and repeats give a mean.
  4. Explain how a vaccine produces immunity and why a booster is sometimes needed. Answer: the vaccine presents antigens, which are taken up by antigen-presenting cells; helper T cells activate the specific B cell carrying a matching receptor; the B cell divides into effector cells that secrete antibodies and memory cells that persist. A booster raises the antibody level again through the quicker, larger secondary response, and may be needed when the first dose did not produce enough memory cells or when the pathogen varies.
  5. Explain how HIV and Mycobacterium tuberculosis cause disease. Answer: HIV binds the CD4 receptor on helper T cells, and the virus enters and replicates, eventually destroying the cells; the loss of helper T cells disables the immune response, so opportunistic infections cause AIDS. Mycobacterium tuberculosis is engulfed by macrophages but survives inside them, and the inflammatory response forms tubercles that damage the lung tissue, causing coughing and reduced gas exchange.
  6. Explain how gel electrophoresis separates DNA fragments and what a DNA profile shows. Answer: fragments are cut with restriction enzymes and loaded into a gel; an electric field moves the negatively charged DNA towards the positive electrode, and shorter fragments travel further, so the fragments separate by length. A profile from several loci is a pattern that can identify an individual or show relatedness, because the pattern is inherited.
  7. Explain how PCR amplifies DNA and why contamination is a problem. Answer: the mixture is heated to denature the double helix, cooled so primers anneal to the target sequences, then warmed so DNA polymerase extends the primers; each cycle doubles the number of target molecules. A single foreign DNA molecule can also be amplified, so contamination makes the sample unusable.

title: Algebra — Sequences and Functions — Study Notes
content:
Algebra — Sequences and Functions

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): nth term (linear & quadratic), special sequences, function notation, composites, inverses.

1. Linear sequences

nth term = a + (n − 1)d. 5, 8, 11, … → 3n + 2. Check n = 1, 2, 3.

2. Quadratic sequences

Second difference = 2a → an² + bn + c. 3, 8, 15, 24 … has second difference 2 → n² + bn + c; subtract n² → 2, 4, 6, 8 → 2n; so nth term = n² + 2n.

3. Special sequences

Even/odd, triangular (½n(n+1)), squares, cubes, Fibonacci-type (each term = sum of previous two), geometric (×r).

4. Function notation

f(x) = 2x − 5: f(3) = 1. Solve f(x) = 11 → x = 8.

5. Composite functions

fg(x) = f(g(x)) — g first. f(x) = 2x − 5, g(x) = x²: gf(2) = g(1) = 1; fg(3) = f(9) = 13.

6. Inverse functions

Swap x and y, rearrange. f(x) = 2x − 5 ⇒ f⁻¹(x) = (x + 5)/2. Domain of inverse = range of original. Verify: f⁻¹(f(x)) = x.

Exam tips: write the bracket order explicitly in composites; show the "swap and rearrange" line for inverses — answer-only scores little.

title: A Level Mathematics: Exponentials and Logarithms
content:
A Level Mathematics: Exponentials and Logarithms

The exponential function eˣ is the one function whose gradient equals its value, which is why it describes any process whose rate of change is proportional to its size: cooling, decay, growth, charging a capacitor, the value of an investment. Its inverse, ln x, is the tool that unlocks equations with the unknown in the exponent. This note builds the pair from zero, links them to calculus, and finishes with the modelling and log-linear graph work that A2 papers test.

Definitions and the laws

log_a x = n  means  a^n = x
ln x = log_e x,  e = 2.718281828...

log(xy) = log x + log y
log(x/y) = log x - log y
log(x^n) = n log x
log_a a = 1;  log_a 1 = 0

e is defined as the value that makes the gradient of aˣ equal to aˣ itself. That single property generates the whole calculus of the topic:

d/dx (e^x) = e^x;  d/dx (e^(kx)) = k e^(kx)
d/dx (ln x) = 1/x;  d/dx (ln(kx)) = 1/x
integral of e^(kx) dx = (1/k) e^(kx) + c
integral of (1/x) dx = ln|x| + c

Worked example. Differentiate y = e^(3x) + ln(5x).

dy/dx = 3e^(3x) + 1/x

Worked example 2. Find ∫ (4e^(2x) + 3/x) dx.

= 2e^(2x) + 3 ln|x| + c

Solving exponential equations

Worked example 1. Solve 7^x = 50.

x ln 7 = ln 50
x = ln 50/ln 7 = 3.912/1.946 = 2.01

Worked example 2 (same base first). Solve 2^(3x−1) = 4^(x+1).

4 = 2², so 4^(x+1) = 2^(2x+2)
3x - 1 = 2x + 2  →  x = 3

Always look for a common base before taking logs: it converts an exponential equation into a linear one and avoids rounding.

Worked example 3 (quadratic in eˣ). Solve e^(2x) − 5e^x + 6 = 0.

let y = e^x: y² - 5y + 6 = 0  →  (y - 2)(y - 3) = 0
y = 2  →  x = ln 2 = 0.693
y = 3  →  x = ln 3 = 1.099

Solving logarithmic equations

Worked example 1. Solve ln(x + 3) + ln(x − 1) = ln 5.

ln[(x + 3)(x - 1)] = ln 5
x² + 2x - 3 = 5  →  x² + 2x - 8 = 0
(x + 4)(x - 2) = 0  →  x = 2 (x = -4 makes an argument negative)

Worked example 2 (different bases). Solve log₂ x + log₄ x = 3.

log_4 x = log_2 x / log_2 4 = (log_2 x)/2
so (3/2) log_2 x = 3  →  log_2 x = 2  →  x = 4

The change-of-base step is compulsory whenever bases differ; check every root against the original domains, and remember that log₂ x is only defined for x > 0 while its squared form can produce spurious negative candidates.

The graphs and their transformations

y = e^x: through (0, 1), increasing, asymptote y = 0
y = ln x: through (1, 0), increasing, asymptote x = 0, domain x > 0
they are reflections in y = x

Worked example. Sketch y = ln(x − 2), stating the asymptote, domain and intercept.

translation 2 right
asymptote x = 2;  domain x > 2
x-intercept: ln(x - 2) = 0  →  x - 2 = 1  →  x = 3

Worked example 2 (reflection). Sketch y = e^(−x) and state its relationship to y = e^x, noting the intercepts and asymptote of each.

reflection in the y-axis; still through (0, 1); asymptote y = 0;
decreasing, a decay curve

Growth and decay models

N = N_0 e^(kt): k > 0 growth, k < 0 decay
half-life = ln 2/|k|;  doubling time = ln 2/k

Newton's cooling: T = T_room + (T_0 - T_room) e^(-kt)

Worked example 1 (half-life). A substance decays as N = 80e^(−0.05t). Find the half-life and the amount after 20 years.

half-life: e^(-0.05t) = 0.5  →  t = ln 2/0.05 = 13.86 years
at t = 20: 80e⁻¹ = 29.4 units

Worked example 2 (cooling). A cup of coffee at 90 °C cools to 60 °C in 10 minutes in a 20 °C room. Find k and the temperature after 25 minutes.

T - 20 = 70e^(-kt);  at t = 10, T = 60: 40 = 70e^(-10k)
e^(-10k) = 4/7  →  k = ln(7/4)/10 = 0.0560
at t = 25: T = 20 + 70e^(-1.4) = 20 + 17.3 = 37.3 °C

Log-linear graphs

If a relationship is exponential, plotting ln y against x gives a straight line whose gradient and intercept reveal the constants. This is how experimental data is tested for exponential behaviour.

y = a b^x  →  ln y = ln a + x ln b
gradient = ln b;  intercept = ln a
y = a x^n  →  ln y = ln a + n ln x  (log-log plot)
gradient = n;  intercept = ln a

Worked example. A graph of ln y against x is a straight line with gradient 0.4 and intercept 1.2. Find the relationship.

ln y = 1.2 + 0.4x
y = e¹.2 x e^(0.4x) = 3.32 e^(0.4x)
so a = 3.32 and the growth rate is 0.4 per unit x

Worked example 2 (power law). A log-log plot of y against x has gradient 2 and intercept 0.693; the intercept is ln a, so a = e^0.693 = 2.

ln y = 0.693 + 2 ln x  →  y = 2x²

Reducing other models to linear form

Some models are linearised by a different transformation. The technique is to rearrange into Y = mX + c and identify what to plot.

y = a/x + b  →  plot y against 1/x: gradient a, intercept b
y = a e^(bx) →  plot ln y against x
y = a x^n    →  plot ln y against ln x

Worked example. Data fits y = p/x + q. What should be plotted on the axes, and how are p and q then found from the graph?

plot y (vertical) against 1/x (horizontal)
gradient = p, intercept = q

Inequalities and exact solutions

Worked example. Solve e^x > 10, giving an exact answer.

x > ln 10

Worked example 2. Solve ln(2x − 1) ≤ 3.

2x - 1 <= e³ and 2x - 1 > 0
1/2 < x <= (e³ + 1)/2 = 10.54

Both boundaries matter: the domain condition gives the strict lower bound, the inequality gives the upper one.

Exponentials in calculus: stationary points

Because e^x differentiates to itself, a product with a polynomial produces clean stationary-point questions.

Worked example. Find and classify the stationary point of y = x e^(−x).
