product rule: dy/dx = e^(-x) - x e^(-x) = e^(-x)(1 - x)
stationary where 1 - x = 0  →  x = 1, y = e⁻¹ = 0.368
second derivative: e^(-x)(x - 2); at x = 1 it is -e⁻¹ < 0
so (1, 0.368) is a maximum

Worked example 2. Find the minimum of y = e^x − 3x.

dy/dx = e^x - 3 = 0  →  x = ln 3 = 1.099
y = 3 - 3 ln 3 = 3 - 3.296 = -0.296
second derivative e^x > 0, so it is a minimum

Worked example 3 (integration by recognition). Find ∫ x e^(x²) dx.

the derivative of e^(x²) is 2x e^(x²), so the integral is
(1/2)e^(x²) + c

Comparing growth rates

Exponential growth eventually outpaces any polynomial. That statement is examinable as a comparison of gradients or of long-run behaviour.

Worked example. Show that for large x, e^x grows faster than x³ by comparing their ratio.

consider f(x) = e^x/x³
as x → infinity the ratio tends to infinity (exponential beats polynomial)
equivalently: differentiating repeatedly, e^x keeps its factor of e^x
while the polynomial loses a degree each time

Worked example 2 (doubling). A quantity grows as N = 50e^(0.08t). How long to double?

e^(0.08t) = 2  →  t = ln 2/0.08 = 8.66 years

The doubling time depends only on k, not on the starting value: that is the signature of exponential growth and worth saying in the answer. Halving time behaves the same way, and for decay the ratio ln 2/|k| gives a half-life independent of the initial quantity — which is why radiocarbon dating works on any sample size.

Simultaneous exponential equations

Two exponential equations are solved by taking logs and then treating the result as a linear system in the unknowns.

Worked example. Solve 2^x 3^y = 12 and 2^y 3^x = 18.

take logs: x ln 2 + y ln 3 = ln 12
y ln 2 + x ln 3 = ln 18
rearrange the second: x ln 3 + y ln 2 = ln 18
solve the 2 × 2 system:
from the first: x = (ln 12 - y ln 3)/ln 2
substitute and simplify  →  y = 1, x = 2

Worked example 2 (same base). Solve 9^x = 3^(x+2).

9^x = 3^(2x), so 2x = x + 2  →  x = 2

With two unknowns the log step is compulsory, and the equations are linear in x and y after it; that structure is what makes the pair solvable.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Evaluate) Find ln(e³). Answer: 3.
  2. (Law) Simplify ln 12 − ln 3. Answer: ln 4.
  3. (Solve) Solve 3^(2x) = 81. Answer: 2x = 4 → x = 2.
  4. (Solve logs) Solve log₂(x) + log₂(x − 2) = 3. Answer: x(x − 2) = 8 → x = 4.
  5. (Differentiate) y = e^(2x) ln x. Use the product rule. Answer: 2e^(2x) ln x + e^(2x)/x.
  6. (Integrate) ∫ (1/(2x)) dx. Answer: ½ ln|2x| + c = ½ ln|x| + c′.
  7. (Model) A population is 200e^(0.03t). When does it reach 500? Answer: t = ln(2.5)/0.03 = 30.5.
  8. (Log-linear) ln y = 0.5x + 2. Find y. Answer: y = 7.39e^(0.5x).

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • log(a + b) treated as log a + log b: there is no such law; the sum cannot be split.
  • Domain ignored: ln of a non-positive number is undefined; reject roots that violate it and say so.
  • Differentiating e^(kx) as ke^x: the factor k multiplies the whole exponential.
  • Integrating 1/x as ln x without the modulus: use ln|x|, since the function is defined on both sides of zero.
  • Half-life sign: with decay k is negative, so half-life is ln 2/|k|; a negative time means the sign was mishandled.
  • Log-linear misread: the intercept is ln a, so a = e^(intercept), not the intercept itself.
  • Base 10 and base e mixed: convert with log_a x = ln x/ln a before combining.
  • Model without interpretation: state the meaning of k in context — a rate per year, per minute, per unit.

title: AS Level Mathematics: Integration
content:
AS Level Mathematics: Integration

Integration is differentiation in reverse: it recovers a function from its gradient, and it accumulates a rate into a total — the area under a curve, the distance from a velocity, the cost from a marginal. This note builds the topic from zero: the indefinite integral and the constant of integration, the power rule, definite integrals and the fundamental theorem, areas above and below the axis, the area between two curves, and kinematics. Every worked example shows the antiderivative line before any substitution of limits.

The indefinite integral

if dy/dx = x^n then y = x^(n+1)/(n+1) + c   (n not -1)

integral of x^n dx = x^(n+1)/(n+1) + c
integral of k f(x) dx = k integral of f(x) dx
integral of a sum = sum of integrals

The +c is mandatory for indefinite integrals: every antiderivative differs by a constant, and the constant is fixed by a boundary condition (a point on the curve).

Worked example 1. Find ∫(6x² − 4x + 3) dx.

= 6x³/3 - 4x²/2 + 3x + c
= 2x³ - 2x² + 3x + c

Worked example 2 (negative and fractional powers). Find ∫(1/x² + √x) dx.

rewrite: integral of (x⁻² + x^(1/2)) dx
= -x⁻¹ + (2/3)x^(3/2) + c
= -1/x + (2/3)x^(3/2) + c

Worked example 3 (finding c). dy/dx = 3x² + 2 and the curve passes through (1, 5). Find y.

y = x³ + 2x + c
5 = 1 + 2 + c  →  c = 2
y = x³ + 2x + 2

Definite integrals and area

integral from a to b of f(x) dx = F(b) - F(a)

area under the curve between x = a and x = b (above the axis)
= definite integral; a negative value means the region is
below the x-axis, and the area is the magnitude

Worked example. Evaluate ∫ from 1 to 3 of (2x + 1) dx.

antiderivative: x² + x
F(3) = 9 + 3 = 12;  F(1) = 1 + 1 = 2
value = 12 - 2 = 10

Worked example 2 (area under a curve). Find the area under y = x² between x = 0 and x = 3.

integral: x³/3
from 0 to 3: 27/3 - 0 = 9 square units

Worked example 3 (below the axis). Find the area between y = x² − 4 and the x-axis from x = 0 to x = 2.

integral: x³/3 - 4x
from 0 to 2: 8/3 - 8 = -16/3
the value is negative because the region is below the axis;
area = 16/3 = 5.33 square units

Areas crossing the axis

When a curve crosses the x-axis inside the interval, integrate each piece separately and add the magnitudes — a single integral would cancel positive and negative areas.

Worked example. Find the total area between y = x² − 1 and the x-axis from x = −2 to x = 2.

crossings at x = -1 and x = 1
piece 1 (-2 to -1): F = x³/3 - x; F(-1) - F(-2) = (2/3) - (-2/3) = 4/3
piece 2 (-1 to 1): F(1) - F(-1) = (-2/3) - (2/3) = -4/3 → magnitude 4/3
piece 3 (1 to 2): F(2) - F(1) = (2/3) - (-2/3) = 4/3
total area = 4/3 + 4/3 + 4/3 = 4 square units

Area between two curves

area between y = f(x) and y = g(x) from a to b
= integral of (f(x) - g(x)) dx from a to b
where f is the upper curve and g the lower

Worked example. Find the area between y = x² and y = x from x = 0 to x = 1.

upper curve on this interval is y = x
integral of (x - x²) dx = x²/2 - x³/3
from 0 to 1: 1/2 - 1/3 = 1/6 square units

Worked example 2 (intersections). Find the area enclosed by y = x² and y = 2x.

intersections: x² = 2x → x(x - 2) = 0 → x = 0, 2
upper on (0, 2) is y = 2x
integral of (2x - x²) dx = x² - x³/3
from 0 to 2: 4 - 8/3 = 4/3 square units

Kinematics with integration

velocity v = ds/dt  →  displacement s = integral of v dt
acceleration a = dv/dt  →  velocity v = integral of a dt

definite integral of v from t1 to t2 = displacement
integral of |v| = distance travelled

Worked example. A particle has velocity v = 3t² − 6t (m/s). Find its displacement from t = 0 to t = 3 and its distance travelled.

s = integral of (3t² - 6t) dt = t³ - 3t²
from 0 to 3: 27 - 27 = 0  →  net displacement zero
sign of v: 3t(t - 2), negative between 0 and 2, positive after
distance = |integral 0 to 2| + integral 2 to 3
= |8 - 12| + (27 - 27) - (8 - 12) = 4 + 4 = 8 m

The distinction between displacement and distance is examinable: displacement is the signed integral, distance is the sum of the absolute pieces.

Worked examples: mixed integration

Worked example. The curve y = f(x) has f'(x) = 6x − 4 and passes through (2, 3). Find f(x) and the area under the curve from x = 1 to x = 2.

f(x) = 3x² - 4x + c;  3 = 12 - 8 + c → c = -1
f(x) = 3x² - 4x - 1
area = integral 1 to 2: x³ - 2x² - x
F(2) = 8 - 8 - 2 = -2; F(1) = 1 - 2 - 1 = -2
area = -2 - (-2) = 0  (the curve is below the axis and the
signed areas cancel); the geometric area needs the crossing
checked - a useful reminder to sketch first

Integrating expressions that need rearranging

Integration has no product or quotient rule at AS level, so expressions must first be written as sums of powers. Two standard rearrangements cover almost every case:

product: expand, then integrate term by term
quotient with a single term denominator: divide through first

(x + 2)(x - 5) = x² - 3x - 10
(3x² + 4x)/x = 3x + 4
√(x)(x + 1) = x^(3/2) + x^(1/2)

Worked example. Find ∫ (x + 3)(x − 1) dx.

expand: x² + 2x - 3
integrate: x³/3 + x² - 3x + c

Worked example 2. Find ∫ (4x³ + 2x)/x dx.

divide: 4x² + 2
integrate: (4/3)x³ + 2x + c

Two boundary conditions

When the second derivative is given, integrate twice and use two pieces of information to fix both constants. The order matters: the first integration produces the gradient function and its constant, the second the curve and its constant.

Worked example. d²y/dx² = 6x, dy/dx = 2 when x = 1, and y = 5 when x = 1. Find y.

first: dy/dx = 3x² + c;  2 = 3 + c  →  c = -1, so dy/dx = 3x² - 1
second: y = x³ - x + k;  5 = 1 - 1 + k  →  k = 5
y = x³ - x + 5

Finding limits and constants from area information

Area questions are often inverted: the area is given and a limit or coefficient must be found. Set up the definite integral with the unknown, evaluate, and solve the resulting equation — rejecting any root outside the geometric context.

Worked example. The area under y = kx² from x = 0 to x = 3 is 36. Find k.

integral: kx³/3
from 0 to 3: 27k/3 = 9k
9k = 36  →  k = 4

Worked example 2 (unknown upper limit). The area under y = 2x from x = 0 to x = a is 25. Find a.

integral: x²;  from 0 to a: a² = 25
a = 5  (the negative root is rejected: a is an x-coordinate to
the right of the origin in this setup)

Kinematics: recovering velocity from acceleration

Worked example. A particle starts from rest with acceleration a = 6t − 4 (m/s²). Find its velocity at t = 3 and the distance travelled in the first 3 seconds.

v = integral of (6t - 4) dt = 3t² - 4t + c
at rest at t = 0: c = 0  →  v = 3t² - 4t
v(3) = 27 - 12 = 15 m/s
distance = integral of |v| from 0 to 3
v = 0 at t = 0 and t = 4/3; v is negative on (0, 4/3)
piece 1: [t³ - 2t²] from 0 to 4/3 = 64/27 - 32/9 = -32/27 → 32/27
piece 2: [t³ - 2t²] from 4/3 to 3 = (27 - 18) - (-32/27) = 9 + 32/27
distance = 32/27 + 9 + 32/27 = 9 + 64/27 = 11.4 m

The sign analysis is the whole question: sketch v against t, mark where it crosses zero, and integrate each piece with its sign removed.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Indefinite) Find ∫(4x³ − 2) dx. Answer: integrate term by term and add the constant: ∫4x³ dx = x⁴ and ∫2 dx = 2x, so the result is x⁴ − 2x + c.
  2. (Negative power) Find ∫x⁻² dx. Answer: raise the power by one and divide by the new power: ∫x⁻² dx = x⁻¹/(−1) + c = −1/x + c.
  3. (Definite) Evaluate ∫ from 0 to 2 of 3x² dx. Answer: integrate, then substitute the limits: ∫₀² 3x² dx = [x³]₀² = 2³ − 0³ = 8.
  4. (Area) Find the area under y = x + 2 from x = 0 to x = 3. Answer: [x²/2 + 2x] = 4.5 + 6 = 10.5.
  5. (Below axis) Find the area between y = x − 3 and the x-axis from x = 0 to x = 2. Answer: integral = [x²/2 − 3x] = 2 − 6 = −4; area 4.
  6. (Between curves) Find the area between y = x² and y = x³ from 0 to 1. Answer: upper is x²; ∫(x² − x³) = 1/3 − 1/4 = 1/12.
  7. (Constant) dy/dx = 4x and y = 7 when x = 1. Find y. Answer: y = 2x² + c → 7 = 2 + c → c = 5 → y = 2x² + 5.
  8. (Kinematics) v = 2t + 1. Find the displacement from t = 0 to t = 4. Answer: [t² + t] = 16 + 4 = 20 m.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Forgetting +c: an indefinite integral without the constant loses a mark; with a boundary condition, the constant is required for the answer.
  • Power rule reversal: integrate xⁿ to x^(n+1)/(n+1); adding one and dividing is the opposite of differentiating, and mixing them up produces nonsense.
  • Limits order: F(b) − F(a), never the reverse. A negative area often means the limits were swapped.
  • Ignoring crossings: a definite integral over a region that crosses the axis gives the signed area; split at the crossings and add magnitudes for the geometric area.
  • Wrong upper curve: subtract lower from upper; sketching between the intersection points avoids the sign error.
  • Distance versus displacement: displacement is the signed integral; distance sums the absolute pieces. Read which is asked.
  • Expanding before integrating: products must be expanded or divided first; there is no product rule for integration at AS level.
  • Units: areas are square units, displacements in metres; attach and interpret units in applied questions.

Reverse differentiation and the constant of integration

Integration undoes differentiation. Every indefinite integral is found by asking which function differentiates to the one given, and every answer carries a constant of integration, because a constant disappears when a function is differentiated.

Integrating powers of x

For any power other than −1, ∫xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + c. Raise the power by one and divide by the new power. For example ∫x³ dx = x⁴/4 + c, and ∫x⁻² dx = x⁻¹/(−1) + c = −1/x + c. Students often forget to add one to the power, which gives a result that does not differentiate back to the start.

Integrating a sum and a constant multiple

Integrate term by term and keep constant multipliers outside. ∫(3x² − 4x + 5) dx = x³ − 2x² + 5x + c. Check it by differentiating: 3x² − 4x + 5 is returned exactly, which is the test that the answer is correct.

Why the constant of integration is needed

The derivative of x³ + 7 is the same as the derivative of x³ − 2, so the integral of 3x² must be x³ plus some unknown constant. Writing +c records that the answer is a whole family of curves, one for each value of c. A question that gives one point on the curve fixes c, and that step is worth marks in its own right.

Integrating (ax + b)ⁿ

When the bracket is linear, the chain rule runs backwards and needs one extra division by a. ∫(2x + 3)⁴ dx = (2x + 3)⁵/(2 × 5) + c = (2x + 3)⁵/10 + c. Differentiating (2x + 3)⁵/10 gives 5 × 2 × (2x + 3)⁴/10, which is (2x + 3)⁴, so the answer is confirmed.

Integrating expressions that need rearranging

Expand brackets and split fractions before integrating, because the power rule works only on single powers. (x + 1)² is x² + 2x + 1 before integration, so ∫(x + 1)² dx = x³/3 + x² + x + c. Writing (x + 1)² as a power of a bracket and applying the linear rule gives the same answer, but expanding is the safer route when the bracket is not linear.

Checking an integral by differentiating

Differentiate the answer and compare it with the integrand. If the two do not match, the error is in the power, the division or a missing coefficient. This check takes a few seconds and catches most sign and division slips before they reach the final line.

Equations and symbols

Integration is four formulas and two decisions: which power rule, and whether the answer is signed. Learn the rule with its condition attached — the exception at n = −1 is the mark most often lost.

integral of x^n dx = x^(n+1)/(n+1) + c Key: x = the variable of integration (no units for a pure function); n = the power, any real number except −1; c = the constant of integration, fixed by a boundary condition. Raise the power by one, then divide by the new power — the reverse of differentiating, and n = −1 is excluded because it would divide by zero.

if dy/dx = x^n then y = x^(n+1)/(n+1) + c (n not -1) Key: dy/dx = the gradient function; y = the function recovered from it; n = the power; c = the constant. The same statement read from the other end: differentiating the answer returns the question.

integral of k f(x) dx = k integral of f(x) dx Key: k = a constant multiplier (no units); f(x) = the function being integrated. Constants pass through the integral sign, which is why a polynomial is integrated term by term.

integral from a to b of f(x) dx = F(b) - F(a) Key: a = the lower limit; b = the upper limit; f(x) = the integrand; F(x) = any antiderivative of f(x). Upper value minus lower value, never the reverse — a negative area usually means the limits were swapped.

velocity v = ds/dt Key: v = velocity (m s⁻¹); s = displacement (m); t = time (s). The gradient form; integrate it in reverse to recover displacement.

displacement s = integral of v dt Key: s = displacement (m); v = velocity (m s⁻¹); t = time (s). The signed integral, so motion backwards subtracts from the total.

acceleration a = dv/dt Key: a = acceleration (m s⁻²); v = velocity (m s⁻¹); t = time (s). The link that lets a question give acceleration and ask for velocity or displacement.

velocity v = integral of a dt Key: v = velocity (m s⁻¹); a = acceleration (m s⁻²); t = time (s). Integrate, then use "starts from rest" or a stated value to fix the constant.

integral of |v| = distance travelled Key: |v| = the magnitude of the velocity, so every piece counts positive (m s⁻¹); the integral gives distance (m), not displacement. Split the integral wherever v = 0, because that is where the sign changes.

9k = 36 → k = 4 Key: 9k = the definite integral of kx² from 0 to 3, written with the unknown constant k; 36 = the given area (square units); k = 4 (no units). The inverted-area question: set the integral equal to the stated area and solve, rather than integrating a known function.

title: Continuous Random Variables — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Continuous Random Variables

Mathematics — A2. A continuous variable X is described by a density f(x) with f(x) ≥ 0 and ∫f(x)dx = 1 over all x. Probabilities are areas:

Key areas to revise

  • Probability Density Functions
  • Finding Unknown Constants
  • Expectation and Variance
  • The Median and Mode
  • Uniform Distribution

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

title: Information Representation — Study Notes
content:
`# Information Representation

Number Systems and Ranges

Unsigned binary with n bits stores 0 to 2ⁿ − 1. Two's complement represents negatives: the MSB has value −2ⁿ⁻¹.

Example: 8-bit two's complement of −5: 11111011 (−128 + 64 + 32 + 16 + 8 + 2 + 1).

SystemBaseDigits
Binary20–1
Hexadecimal160–9, A–F
BCD—4 bits per decimal digit

Binary Arithmetic

Add: 0+0=0, 0+1=1, 1+1=0 carry 1, 1+1+1=1 carry 1. Overflow happens when a result exceeds the word size.

Subtraction uses two's complement addition (A − B = A + (−B)).

Text

  • ASCII: 7 bits, 128 characters, English only
  • Unicode: universal scripts; UTF-8 is variable-width (1–4 bytes)

Images and Sound

  • Bitmap: pixels with colour depth (bits per pixel). File size = width × height × depth.
  • Sound: sampling rate (Hz) × bit depth × duration × channels.
  • Resolution trade-off: fidelity vs size.

Compression

  • Lossless (ZIP, run-length encoding): exact reconstruction — required for text/code
  • Lossy (JPEG, MP3): discards perceptually minor data — smaller files

Example: RLE of AAABBBCC → 3A3B2C.

Exam tips: show working for two's complement conversions; state why compression type suits the data (text must be lossless).

Binary and hexadecimal worked conversion

To convert the denary number 156 to binary, subtract the place values from the largest downwards: 156 = 128 + 16 + 8 + 4, so the binary value is 10011100. Each binary digit is a bit, and the place values double from right to left: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128.

Hexadecimal groups four bits at a time, so one hexadecimal digit represents a value from 0 to 15. Split 10011100 into 1001 and 1100 to get 9 and 12, which is 9C in hexadecimal. Hexadecimal is used to write memory addresses and colour codes because it is shorter than binary and converts to it directly.

Exam tip: show the place-value working, not just the answer. Examiners award method marks for the subtraction or the grouping.

title: IGCSE Mathematics: Sequences and Functions
content:
IGCSE Mathematics: Sequences and Functions

Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580 (2025–2027), section 2 Algebra and graphs: statement 2.7 Sequences and statement 2.13 Functions (Extended). A sequence is a list of numbers generated by a rule; a function is the rule itself. This note builds nth-term rules from scratch — showing why the formula works, not just what it is — then function notation, composite functions and inverse functions, including the domain restrictions that decide whether an inverse exists.

What a sequence is; term-to-term rules

A sequence is an ordered list of numbers. The term-to-term rule gets from one term to the next: add 4, multiply by 2, subtract 1 then double. It tells you what happens step by step but not what the hundredth term is. The position-to-term rule (the nth term) gives any term directly from its position n, and that is the more powerful description.

Sequence: 3, 7, 11, 15, 19, ...

Term-to-term: add 4 each time.
Position-to-term: the terms are 4 less than 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, ..., so the nth term is 4n - 1.

Check: n = 1 gives 4(1) - 1 = 3 ✓;  n = 5 gives 4(5) - 1 = 19 ✓

Linear sequences and the nth term

A linear (arithmetic) sequence has a constant difference d between terms. Its nth term is dn + b, and b is chosen to make the first term correct.

Find the nth term of 5, 8, 11, 14, ...

Constant difference d = 3, so the nth term starts as 3n.
Compare with the sequence: 3, 6, 9, 12, ... is three times the table of 3;
the real sequence is 2 more each time, so b = 2.
nth term:  3n + 2

Check every term: n = 1: 5 ✓   n = 2: 8 ✓   n = 3: 11 ✓
The 50th term is 3(50) + 2 = 152.

Why dn + b always works. Adding d each time from a starting value a means the nth term is a + (n − 1)d, since term n has had (n − 1) additions of d. Expanding gives a + nd − d = nd + (a − d), which is exactly dn + b with b = a − d. Both forms are the same rule; examiners accept either.

Quadratic and special sequences

When the first difference changes but the second difference is constant, the rule is quadratic: an² + bn + c. The method: build the n² sequence, subtract it from the sequence, and finish the linear remainder.

Find the nth term of 2, 5, 10, 17, 26, ...

First differences: 3, 5, 7, 9;  second differences: 2, 2 (constant) → quadratic.
The n² sequence is 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, ...
Subtract: (2-1), (5-4), (10⁻⁹), (17-16), (26-25) = 1, 1, 1, 1, 1
So the sequence is n² + 1.

Check: n = 3 gives 9 + 1 = 10 ✓

Other sequences to recognise on sight: the triangular numbers n(n + 1)/2 (1, 3, 6, 10, ...), the square numbers n², the Fibonacci sequence (each term is the sum of the two before it, and it has no simple nth term), and geometric sequences that multiply by a fixed ratio r — their nth term is arⁿ⁻¹ where a is the first term.

Geometric example: 3, 6, 12, 24, ... has a = 3 and r = 2, so the nth term is 3 × 2^(n-1).
The 6th term is 3 × 2⁵ = 96.
Sequence typeExampleRule
Linear (arithmetic)5, 8, 11, 14Constant difference d; nth term dn + b
Quadratic2, 5, 10, 17Constant second difference; nth term an² + bn + c
Geometric3, 6, 12, 24Constant ratio r; nth term arⁿ⁻¹
Triangular numbers1, 3, 6, 10n(n + 1)/2
Square numbers1, 4, 9, 16n²
Fibonacci1, 1, 2, 3, 5Add the two previous terms (no simple nth term)

Choosing the right description is half the battle: check the first differences, then the second, then the ratio, before assuming any rule. Once a candidate rule is found, verify it against every given term — a sequence that matches only the first three terms is not proven.

Function notation

A function is a machine with an input and exactly one output for each input. The notation f(x) = 2x + 3 names the machine f and says what it does to x: multiply by 2, then add 3. Evaluating is substitution: f(4) = 2(4) + 3 = 11. The machine picture matters: one input never gives two outputs, though two inputs may share an output.

  • The domain is the set of allowed inputs; the range is the set of outputs the function actually produces.
  • For f(x) = x² with domain all real numbers, the range is y ⩾ 0, because squares are never negative.
  • For f(x) = 2x + 3 with domain 0 ⩽ x ⩽ 5, the range is 3 ⩽ f(x) ⩽ 13 — substitute the endpoints, since linear functions stretch ranges proportionally.

Questions ask for the range in terms of y or f(x); find the outputs at the domain boundaries and, for quadratics, at the turning point.

Composite functions

A composite function runs one machine after the other. fg(x) means apply g first, then f to the result — the notation reads right to left, like f(g(x)).

Given f(x) = 2x + 1 and g(x) = x², find fg(3), gf(x) and fg(x).

fg(3):  g(3) = 9, then f(9) = 2(9) + 1 = 19.
gf(x):  apply f first:  g(f(x)) = (2x + 1)² = 4x² + 4x + 1.
fg(x):  apply g first:  f(g(x)) = 2x² + 1.

Note fg(x) ≠ gf(x): order matters.

Every line is written out because the most common error is applying the functions in the wrong order — and the composite is not commutative.

Inverse functions

The inverse f⁻¹ undoes f: if f turns 4 into 11, f⁻¹ turns 11 back into 4. Inverse functions exist only for one-to-one functions — ones where different inputs always give different outputs. The graph of y = x² is not one-to-one over all real numbers (both 3 and −3 give 9), so it has no inverse unless the domain is restricted to x ⩾ 0.

Find the inverse of f(x) = (3x - 2)/5:

Write y = (3x - 2)/5 and make x the subject:
5y = 3x - 2          [multiply by 5]
5y + 2 = 3x          [add 2]
x = (5y + 2)/3       [divide by 3]

Swap x and y:  f⁻¹(x) = (5x + 2)/3

Check by composing: f⁻¹(f(x)) = [5((3x - 2)/5) + 2]/3 = [(3x - 2) + 2]/3 = 3x/3 = x  ✓
  • f⁻¹(x) is a single symbol meaning the inverse function; the −1 is not a power and f⁻¹(x) does not mean 1/f(x).
  • The domain of f⁻¹ is the range of f, and the range of f⁻¹ is the domain of f — they swap, exactly as the inputs and outputs swap roles.
  • Graphically, y = f⁻¹(x) is the reflection of y = f(x) in the line y = x.

Worked example: a full function question

Let f(x) = x² + 3 for x ⩾ 0, and g(x) = 4x − 5.

(a) Find f(2):  f(2) = 4 + 3 = 7.

(b) Find fg(x):  f(g(x)) = (4x - 5)² + 3 = 16x² - 40x + 25 + 3 = 16x² - 40x + 28.

(c) Find f⁻¹(x):  y = x² + 3, so x² = y - 3 and x = √(y - 3) (positive root, since x ⩾ 0).
Swap: f⁻¹(x) = √(x - 3).
Domain of f⁻¹: x ⩾ 3, which is exactly the range of f.

(d) Solve f(x) = 30 for x ⩾ 0:
x² + 3 = 30
x² = 27
x = √27 = 3√3 ≈ 5.20        [only the positive root is in the domain]

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Reading fg(x) as f then g. It is g first, then f — the notation runs right to left.
  • Assuming fg = gf; only special cases agree.
  • Treating f⁻¹(x) as 1/f(x). The inverse undoes the function; it is not a reciprocal.
  • Ignoring domain restrictions: with x ⩾ 0 on f(x) = x² + 3, the inverse takes the positive root only, and a negative root answer is wrong.
  • Claiming y = x² has an inverse over all real numbers; it is two-to-one and needs a restricted domain.
  • Building the nth term from the first difference alone without checking every term; a single wrong check sends a whole answer wrong.
  • Writing a geometric nth term as arⁿ instead of arⁿ⁻¹; the first term must be a itself.
  • Stating a range that ignores the turning point of a quadratic: the range of y = (x − 2)² + 1 is y ⩾ 1, not y ⩾ 0.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 2, 3 marks). Find the nth term of 7, 11, 15, 19, ...

Answer: Constant difference 4, so 4n + b; the first term 7 = 4 + b gives b = 3. The nth term is 4n + 3. The 20th term is 83.

Question 2 (Paper 2, 3 marks). A sequence has nth term 5n − 2. Write down the first four terms and the 100th.

Answer: n = 1, 2, 3, 4 give 3, 8, 13, 18; the 100th term is 5(100) − 2 = 498.

Question 3 (Paper 4, 4 marks). f(x) = 3x − 1 and g(x) = x² + 2. Find fg(x), gf(2) and f⁻¹(x).

Answer: fg(x) = 3(x² + 2) − 1 = 3x² + 5. gf(2): f(2) = 5, so g(5) = 27. Inverse: y = 3x − 1 gives x = (y + 1)/3, so f⁻¹(x) = (x + 1)/3.

Question 4 (Paper 4, 4 marks). The second differences of a sequence are constant at 4, and its first two terms are 2 and 7. Find the nth term.

Answer: Constant second difference 4 means the n² coefficient is 4/2 = 2, so the rule starts 2n². The n² sequence gives 2, 8, ... while the sequence is 2, 7, ..., so the remainder is 0, −1, ... a linear part with difference −1: −n + 1. Check: 2n² − n + 1 gives n = 1: 2 ✓ and n = 2: 8 − 2 + 1 = 7 ✓. The nth term is 2n² − n + 1.

Question 5 (Paper 4, 5 marks). f(x) = (x + 4)/(x − 2) for x ≠ 2. Find f⁻¹(x) and the value of x for which f(x) is undefined.

Answer: y = (x + 4)/(x − 2) gives y(x − 2) = x + 4, so yx − 2y = x + 4, yx − x = 2y + 4, x(y − 1) = 2y + 4 and x = (2y + 4)/(y − 1). Swapping: f⁻¹(x) = (2x + 4)/(x − 1). The function itself is undefined at x = 2, where the denominator vanishes; its inverse is undefined at x = 1.

Question 6 (Paper 2, 3 marks). The first three terms of a geometric sequence are 5, 15, 45. Find the 8th term.

Answer: Common ratio r = 15/5 = 3, so the nth term is 5 × 3ⁿ⁻¹ and the 8th term is 5 × 3⁷ = 5 × 2187 = 10 935.

From variables and patterns, the course now turns to the number system itself.

title: A Level Mathematics: The Poisson Distribution
content:
A Level Mathematics: The Poisson Distribution

The Poisson distribution models the number of events that happen in a fixed interval of time, length, area or volume when those events occur randomly and independently at a constant average rate. Where the binomial counts successes in a fixed number of trials, the Poisson counts arrivals in a continuous window: calls reaching a switchboard in an hour, defects along a length of cable, radioactive decays in a minute. This note derives the formula from the binomial, sets out the two conditions that must hold, and then uses the distribution for the probability and hypothesis-test questions the exam sets.

Where the formula comes from

Imagine slicing the interval into a very large number of tiny sub-intervals. In each slice the chance of an event is tiny but the number of slices is enormous, so the count is binomial with n huge and p tiny. Taking that limit turns nCr p^r (1−p)^(n−r) into the Poisson formula, with the mean λ = np surviving as the only parameter.

X ~ Po(λ):  P(X = r) = e^(-λ) λ^r / r!
mean E(X) = λ
variance Var(X) = λ
so the mean and variance are equal - a diagnostic test for the model

The equality of mean and variance is not a coincidence to memorise; it is the fingerprint of the limit, and it is why an exam question can give you a sample mean and variance and ask whether a Poisson model is plausible.

The three conditions

A Poisson model needs randomness, independence and a constant rate. Naming them is worth marks, and each failure has a characteristic symptom.

1. events occur singly (not in pairs or batches)
2. events occur at random, independently of each other
3. the average rate λ is constant over the interval
then the count in that interval is Poisson

Worked example (checking the model). A shop counts customers arriving per hour. Explain why a Poisson model may be unsuitable.

the arrival rate is not constant: it peaks at lunchtime and is near zero at night
so condition 3 fails and the mean over a whole day is not a single rate
a better model splits the day into periods of roughly constant rate

Calculating probabilities

The formula handles a single value; the cumulative sum handles a range. Because the Poisson has no upper limit, every "at least" question becomes a complement.

P(X = r) = e^(-λ) λ^r / r!
P(X <= r) sums from 0 to r (tables or calculator)
P(X >= r) = 1 - P(X <= r - 1)
P(X < r)  = P(X <= r - 1)

Worked example. X ~ Po(3). Find P(X = 2).

P = e^(-3) × 3² / 2!
= 0.049787 × 9 / 2
= 0.2240

Worked example 2 (at least). For the same X, find P(X ≥ 4).

P(X >= 4) = 1 - P(X <= 3)
P(X <= 3) = 0.049787(1 + 3 + 4.5 + 4.5) = 0.6472
so P(X >= 4) = 0.3528

Worked example 3 (scale change). Calls arrive at 4 per minute. Find the probability of 10 or more calls in two minutes.

the rate scales with the interval: λ = 8 for two minutes
P(X >= 10) = 1 - P(X <= 9) = 1 - 0.7170 = 0.2830

Scaling is the most common source of avoidable error: the parameter must be expressed for the interval the question actually asks about.

Adding independent Poisson variables

If two independent counts each follow a Poisson distribution, their sum does too, and the parameters add. This is why the distribution is so usable: a total across separate sources needs no convolution.

X ~ Po(l1), Y ~ Po(l2), independent
X + Y ~ Po(l1 + l2)
but X - Y is NOT Poisson

Worked example. A website gets 5 hits per minute from Europe and 3 per minute from Asia, independently. Find the probability of more than 10 hits in a minute in total.

total ~ Po(8)
P(X > 10) = 1 - P(X <= 10) = 1 - 0.8159 = 0.1841

The Poisson as an approximation to the binomial

When n is large and p is small, the binomial is well approximated by a Poisson with λ = np. The rule of thumb used in this course is n > 50 and p < 0.05, or np < 5.

X ~ B(n, p) with n large, p small  →  X is approximately Po(np)

Worked example. A factory produces items with a 2% defect rate. In a batch of 200, use a Poisson approximation to find the probability of at most 2 defects.

λ = 200 × 0.02 = 4
P(X <= 2) = e^(-4)(1 + 4 + 8) = 0.018316 × 13 = 0.2381
the exact binomial gives 0.2351, so the approximation is close

Worked example 2 (justifying the approximation). State why the approximation is reasonable here.

n = 200 is large and p = 0.02 is small, with np = 4
so the rare-event limit conditions hold

Hypothesis testing with the Poisson

The structure is identical to the binomial test: state hypotheses, assume the null rate, compute the tail probability, compare with the significance level. The only new step is that the rate may need scaling to the observed interval.

H0: λ = lambda0    H1: λ > lambda0 (or <)
observed count x in the interval
p-value = P(X >= x) or P(X <= x) under Po(lambda0)
reject H0 if the p-value <= the significance level

Worked example. A call centre historically receives 6 calls per hour. In a new hour it receives 12. Test at the 5% level whether the rate has increased.

H0: λ = 6;  H1: λ > 6
X ~ Po(6) under H0
P(X >= 12) = 1 - P(X <= 11) = 1 - 0.9799 = 0.0201
0.0201 < 0.05, so reject H0
there is evidence the rate has increased

Worked example 2 (critical region). For Po(6), find the 5% one-tailed critical region for an increase.

P(X >= 11) = 0.0426 (below 0.05)
P(X >= 10) = 0.0839 (above 0.05)
critical region: X >= 11

Worked example 3 (two intervals). The same centre observes 16 calls over two hours. Test for an increase at 5%.

expected over two hours under H0 = 12, so X ~ Po(12)
P(X >= 16) = 1 - P(X <= 15) = 1 - 0.8444 = 0.1556
0.1556 > 0.05, so do not reject H0

Compare the two: twelve calls in one hour was significant, sixteen in two hours is not, because the expected count doubled. The rate, not the raw count, is what is being tested.

Reading the distribution's shape

The Poisson is skewed to the right when λ is small and becomes almost symmetric as λ grows, which is why small-rate questions usually live in the lower tail and why the normal approximation becomes usable once λ passes about 20. Knowing the shape tells you at a glance whether an answer is plausible: a probability of 0.4 for "more than 10" when λ = 3 should feel wrong before any arithmetic is checked.

A useful sanity check is that the standard deviation is the square root of the mean. For Po(9) the mean is 9 and the standard deviation 3, so counts between 6 and 12 are ordinary and a count of 20 is roughly three and a half standard deviations out — surprising enough to prompt a hypothesis test. That comparison is what turns a bare probability into an interpretation, and interpretation marks are the easiest ones to lose.

Finally, note that the model is about a count in an interval, so the interval has to be defined in the answer. "Three calls per hour" and "three calls per minute" describe different distributions, and a rate quoted per unit time without its unit is not a λ at all.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Definition) State two conditions for a Poisson model. Answer: events occur singly at random, independently, at a constant rate.
  2. (Single value) X ~ Po(2.5): find P(X = 3). Answer: P(X = 3) = e^(−λ)λ³/3! = e^(−2.5) × 15.625/6 = 0.0821 × 2.604 = 0.2138.
  3. (Cumulative) X ~ Po(4): find P(X ≤ 2). Answer: P(X ≤ 2) = e^(−4)(1 + 4 + 8) = 0.0183 × 13 = 0.2381.
  4. (Complement) X ~ Po(5): find P(X ≥ 3). Answer: P(X ≥ 3) = 1 − P(X ≤ 2) = 1 − e^(−5)(1 + 5 + 12.5) = 1 − 0.1247 = 0.8753.
  5. (Scaling) Rate 3 per hour: find P(X = 0) in 20 minutes. Answer: the rate scales with the interval: λ = 3 × 20/60 = 1, so P(X = 0) = e^(−1) = 0.3679.
  6. (Sum) Independent Po(2) and Po(3): find P(total = 4). Answer: independent Poisson variables add, so T ~ Po(2 + 3) = Po(5) and P(T = 4) = e^(−5)5⁴/4! = 0.1755.
  7. (Approximation) B(500, 0.01): approximate P(X = 0). Answer: n is large and p small, so use Po(λ = np = 5): P(X = 0) ≈ e^(−5) = 0.00674.
  8. (Mean/variance) A sample has mean 4.2 and variance 9.1. Comment on the Poisson fit. Answer: variance far exceeds the mean, so the model is doubtful (over-dispersed).
  9. (Test) 9 events observed where 4 expected; test for an increase at 5%. Answer: under H₀, X ~ Po(4); P(X ≥ 9) = 1 − P(X ≤ 8) = 0.0214 < 0.05, so reject H₀ — the observed rate is significantly higher.
  10. (Critical region) Po(3), 5% upper tail: find the critical region. Answer: P(X ≥ 6) = 0.0839 and P(X ≥ 7) = 0.0335; the largest region still at or below 5% starts at 7, so the critical region is X ≥ 7.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Using the wrong interval: λ must match the window asked about; doubling a time doubles the rate.
  • Complement off by one: P(X ≥ 4) = 1 − P(X ≤ 3); subtracting P(X ≤ 4) is the classic error.
  • Treating a difference as Poisson: sums of independent Poisson variables are Poisson, differences are not.
  • Approximation outside its range: np must be small; with np large the Poisson is a poor fit to the binomial.
  • Variance assumed equal to the mean without checking: the test mean = variance is a diagnostic, not a guarantee.
  • Ignoring clustering: events that arrive in bursts break the single-event condition and inflate the variance.
  • r! miscomputed: 0! = 1 and 1! = 1, and a missing factorial term changes the answer entirely.
  • p-value direction: a one-tailed test uses one tail only; doubling it makes a borderline result look significant.

Choosing between a Poisson and a binomial model

Both models count things, and both are discrete, so the choice is a common source of lost marks. The question is always what is fixed: a number of trials, or a length of time, area or volume.

Fixed trials or a continuous window

A binomial model counts successes among a fixed number n of trials, such as 20 items inspected or 12 people surveyed. A Poisson model counts events in a continuous interval, such as calls in an hour or flaws along a metre of wire, where there is no fixed number of trials to count out.

Using the wording of the question

Phrases such as “out of 40” or “of 15 chosen at random” point to a binomial. Phrases such as “in a period of”, “per kilometre” or “per square metre” point to a Poisson. When the wording is unclear, ask whether you could list the trials in advance; if you could, the model is binomial.

Variance as a clue

The binomial variance is np(1 − p), which is smaller than its mean np by the factor 1 − p. The Poisson variance equals its mean. So when p is not small, a Poisson model overstates the spread, and the binomial is the better fit.

A worked choice: binomial

A quality checker tests 40 bolts from a line, and each bolt is faulty independently with probability 0.08. The number of bolts is fixed at 40, so X ~ B(40, 0.08). A Poisson with the same mean would have variance 3.2 instead of 2.944, which is close here, but the binomial is the model the question describes.

A worked choice: Poisson

Bacteria colonies appear on a plate at random, and the average number per square centimetre is known. The area of the plate is not a number of trials, so the count is a Poisson variable with λ proportional to the area of the region counted. Nothing about the plate fixes how many colonies there will be.

Stating the choice in the answer

Write the model as the first line of the solution, with its reason: “X ~ B(40, 0.08), because the sample size is fixed at 40”. A marker can only credit a choice that is written down, and the reason is often worth a mark on its own.

Setting λ for the interval in the question

λ is the mean count for the interval the question asks about, and that interval is often not the one in which the rate is given. Most wrong answers on Poisson questions come from using a rate for the wrong length of time or distance.

The rate and the interval

If events occur at a rate r per unit of time and the question concerns an interval of length t in the same unit, then λ = rt. The rate and the interval must use the same unit before you multiply.

Scaling down to a shorter interval

Calls arrive at 6 per hour. For a 10-minute interval, the time is one sixth of an hour, so λ = 6 × 10/60 = 1. The probability of no calls in those 10 minutes is then e⁻¹ = 0.3679, not e⁻⁶.

Scaling up to a longer interval

Defects occur at 1.5 per kilometre of cable. For a 8 km stretch, λ = 1.5 × 8 = 12. Doubling the length doubles the mean, and the variance doubles with it, so a longer stretch is more spread out as well as higher.

Rates per area or volume

Flaws appear at 3 per square metre on a sheet. For a region of 4.5 m², λ = 3 × 4.5 = 13.5. The same method works for volume, provided the rate is given per unit of volume and the region is measured in the same units.

Keeping λ and the interval together

λ has no unit of its own because it is a count, but it always refers to a named interval. Writing “λ = 3 for 15 minutes” keeps the reference; writing a bare “λ = 3” invites the wrong interval to be used later in the same question.

A worked example

Emails arrive at a server at 12 per hour, at random and independently. Find the probability of exactly 2 arrivals in a 15-minute period. The interval is 0.25 hours, so λ = 12 × 0.25 = 3. Then P(X = 2) = e⁻³ × 3²/2! = 0.2240, which matches the value a student gets by scaling the rate first, not by using 12 directly.

Estimating λ from data and checking the fit

Exam questions often give observed counts and ask for an estimate of λ, then ask whether the Poisson model is reasonable. The sample mean does the estimating, and the sample variance does the checking.

The sample mean as an estimate of λ

If counts x₁, x₂, … xₙ are observed over equal intervals, the sample mean x̄ is the natural estimate of λ. For a Poisson variable the mean of the population is λ, so the sample mean is the value that best matches the data. The estimate is only meaningful when every observation covers the same interval.

Comparing the sample mean and variance

For a Poisson model the sample variance should be close to the sample mean. A variance well above the mean suggests events that cluster, which breaks the independence condition. A variance well below the mean suggests events that are more evenly spaced than chance would give.

Reading a frequency table

Suppose 20 one-minute intervals give counts of 0 in 6 intervals, 1 in 9, 2 in 4 and 3 in 1. Then Σfx = 20, so x̄ = 20/20 = 1.0. Also Σfx² = 34, so the sample variance is 34/20 − 1.0² = 0.7. The variance is a little below the mean, which is not strong evidence against the model with only 20 intervals.

Using the estimate to find a probability

Once λ is estimated, the fitted model gives probabilities. With λ̂ = 1.0, the fitted probability of no events in one minute is e⁻¹ = 0.368, which can be compared with the observed proportion of intervals with no events, here 6/20 = 0.30. Close agreement supports the model; a large gap is a reason to doubt it.

Why a poor fit is a conclusion, not a failure

A question that asks whether the Poisson model is suitable is testing judgement. Say which feature of the data is inconsistent with the model, such as the variance being much larger than the mean, and link it to the condition it breaks. A vague “the model is not good” earns little credit.

Sampling over equal intervals

The method depends on equal intervals. If some counts cover two minutes and others one minute, the counts are not comparable, and they must be rescaled to a common interval before the mean or variance is calculated. Checking the interval for each observation is the first step of the estimate.

A two-tailed Poisson test

A two-tailed test asks whether the rate has changed in either direction, so H₁ is λ ≠ λ₀. The method is the same as the one-tailed test, with a critical region in each tail, and the discreteness of the distribution makes the arithmetic less tidy.

Setting up H₀ and H₁

H₀ states the rate, λ = λ₀, and H₁ states that the rate differs, λ ≠ λ₀. Write the distribution under H₀ as X ~ Po(λ₀), with λ₀ stated for the interval observed, before any probability is calculated.

Splitting the significance level

A 5% two-tailed test puts about 2.5% in each tail. Because the Poisson takes only whole-number values, an exact split is usually impossible. The rule is that each tail probability must be no more than 2.5%, and the critical region is the largest one that satisfies this.

Finding the two critical regions

For X ~ Po(6), the lower tail gives P(X ≤ 1) = 0.0174, which is at most 0.025, while P(X ≤ 2) = 0.0620 is too large. The upper tail gives P(X ≥ 11) = 0.0426, which is too large, and P(X ≥ 12) = 0.0201, which is acceptable. The critical region is X ≤ 1 or X ≥ 12.

Why the actual significance level is below 5%

The combined probability of the critical region under H₀ is about 0.0174 + 0.0201 = 0.037, or 3.7%. The test is therefore slightly more conservative than 5%, because the next value in either tail would push its probability above 2.5%. State the actual significance level when it differs from the nominal one; a marker looks for this.

A worked two-tailed example

A machine usually produces 6 faults per shift. In a shift with 13 faults, test at the 5% level whether the rate has changed. The observed value 13 is greater than 12, so it lies in the upper critical region, and H₀ is rejected. In a shift with 9 faults, the value is outside the region, so the result is not significant.

Writing the conclusion in context

Say what the test shows about the rate, not about the individual count: “There is evidence at the 5% level that the mean number of faults per shift has changed.” Avoid saying that the rate has been shown to be 6, because the test never proves that a hypothesis is true.

Equations and symbols

One formula does the arithmetic, and one identity checks the model: for a Poisson variable the mean and the variance are the same number λ. Every exam error on this topic is either a λ expressed for the wrong interval or a complement taken one term too far.

P(X = r) = e^(-λ) λ^r / r! Key: X = the number of events counted in the fixed interval (a count, no units); r = the particular count asked about; λ = the mean number of events in that same interval (no units — it is a count, not a rate per second, unless the interval is one second); e = 2.71828…; r! = factorial of r, with 0! = 1.

mean E(X) = λ Key: E(X) = the expected count in the interval; λ = the mean. Read it with the line below: the equality of mean and variance is the fingerprint of the model, and a sample whose variance far exceeds its mean is not Poisson.

variance Var(X) = λ Key: Var(X) = the variance of the count; λ = the same mean. So the standard deviation is √λ, which is the quickest sanity check on an observed count: for λ = 9, counts between 6 and 12 are ordinary.

P(X >= r) = 1 - P(X <= r - 1) Key: the complement rule, because the Poisson has no upper limit; r = the smallest count that counts as "at least". Subtracting P(X ≤ r) instead of P(X ≤ r − 1) is the classic off-by-one and throws the whole tail away.

P = e^(-3) × 3² / 2! Key: λ = 3 for this interval; r = 2; 3² = λ^r; 2! = 2. The arithmetic is 0.049787 × 9 / 2 = 0.2240 — quote four decimal places unless told otherwise.

λ = 200 × 0.02 = 4 Key: 200 = n, the number of trials; 0.02 = p, the probability of the event in one trial; λ = np = 4, the mean of the approximating Poisson. The approximation is used when n is large and p small — n > 50 and p < 0.05, or np < 5.

P(X <= 2) = e^(-4)(1 + 4 + 8) = 0.018316 × 13 = 0.2381 Key: the bracket is λ^r/r! summed for r = 0, 1, 2: 1, 4 and 8 (since 4²/2! = 8); e^(−4) = 0.018316. The exact binomial gives 0.2351, so the approximation is close — say so when a question asks you to comment.

X + Y ~ Po(l1 + l2) Key: X and Y = two independent Poisson counts; l1, l2 = their means; the total count is Poisson with the means added. A difference of two Poisson variables is not Poisson — only sums combine.

X ~ B(n, p) with n large, p small → X is approximately Po(np) Key: B(n, p) = the binomial with n trials and success probability p; np = the Poisson mean that replaces them. State both conditions before using it, because the approximation fails when np is large.

SymbolQuantityUnit
λmean number of events in the stated intervala count (no units) — quote the interval with it
rthe observed or asked-about counta count (no units)
H₀null hypothesis, λ = λ₀a stated mean count for the interval

Scaling is the other half of the topic and it is not a formula but a substitution: a rate of 4 per minute is λ = 8 for a two-minute window, and 12 calls in one hour must be tested against 24 expected in two hours, not against 12. Write the interval beside the λ every time.

title: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Area, Perimeter and Volume
content:
Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Area, Perimeter and Volume

Measurement questions are the most reliable marks on the paper — provided you convert units correctly and choose the right formula. This note builds the mensuration toolkit from zero: the unit system and its tricky area and volume conversions, the area formulas for every plane shape with derivations, circles, arcs and sectors, the volume and surface area of every solid in the syllabus, and compound shapes — how to add and subtract the pieces. Every worked example shows the substitution and the units, because units and premature rounding are where the marks disappear.

Units of measure

Length, area and volume units are linked by powers of the linear conversion factor:

ConversionLengthAreaVolume
1 m = 100 cm× 100× 100² = 10 000× 100³ = 1 000 000
1 cm = 10 mm× 10× 100× 1000
1 km = 1000 m× 1000× 10⁶× 10⁹

Capacity: 1 litre = 1000 cm³ = 1000 ml; 1 m³ = 1000 litres. The classic trap is converting area with a length factor — 1 m² is 10 000 cm², not 100 cm².

Worked example. Convert 3.5 m² to cm² and 2500 cm³ to litres.

3.5 m² = 3.5 × 10⁰⁰⁰ = 35 000 cm²
2500 cm³ = 2500/10⁰⁰ = 2.5 litres

Area and perimeter of plane shapes

ShapePerimeterArea
Rectangle2(l + w)l × w
Trianglesum of sides½ × base × perpendicular height
Parallelogram2(a + b)base × perpendicular height
Trapeziumsum of sides½(a + b) × h (parallel sides a, b)
Circle2πrπr²

The triangle and parallelogram formulas both need the perpendicular height — not a slanted side. That single word accounts for more lost marks than any other in mensuration.

Worked example. Find the area of a trapezium with parallel sides 7 cm and 11 cm and height 5 cm.

A = (1/2)(a + b) h = 0.5 x (7 + 11) × 5
  = 0.5 × 18 × 5 = 45 cm²

Worked example 2 (triangle). A triangle has sides 6 cm, 8 cm, 10 cm. Is it right-angled, and what is its area?

6² + 8² = 36 + 64 = 10⁰ = 10², so yes - right-angled
at the 6-8 corner. Area = (1/2) × 6 × 8 = 24 cm².

Circles, arcs and sectors

An arc is a fraction of the circumference; a sector is the same fraction of the area. The fraction is the angle over a full turn:

circumference = 2 π r;  area = π r²

arc length  = (θ/360) × 2 π r
sector area = (θ/360) x π r²
perimeter of a sector = arc length + 2r
segment area = sector area - triangle area

Worked example. A sector has radius 9 cm and angle 140°. Find its arc length, sector area and perimeter (π = 3.142).

arc = (140/360) × 2 × 3.142 × 9 = 0.3889 × 56.56 = 21.99 cm
area = (140/360) × 3.142 × 81 = 0.3889 × 254.5 = 98.97 cm²
perimeter = 21.99 + 18 = 39.99 cm = 40.0 cm (3 s.f.)

The perimeter of a sector includes the two radii — students routinely answer only the arc length.

Worked example 2 (segment). Find the area of the segment cut off by a chord in a circle of radius 6 cm when the sector angle is 90°.

sector area = (90/360) × 3.142 × 36 = 28.28 cm²
triangle area = (1/2) × 6 × 6 = 18 cm² (right angle at centre)
segment = 28.28 - 18 = 10.28 cm²

Surface area and volume of solids

SolidVolumeSurface area
Cuboidl × w × h2(lw + lh + wh)
Prism (any cross-section)area of cross-section × length2 × cross-section + perimeter × length
Cylinderπr²h2πr² + 2πrh
Cone⅓πr²hπr² + πrl (l = slant height)
Sphere⁴⁄₃πr³4πr²
Pyramid⅓ × base area × heightsum of face areas

Slant height versus vertical height is the cone trap: volume uses the perpendicular height h, surface area uses the slant height l, and l² = r² + h² connects them.

Worked example 1 (cylinder). A cylinder has radius 4 cm and height 10 cm. Find its volume and total surface area.

V = π r² h = 3.142 × 16 × 10 = 502.7 cm³
SA = 2 π r² + 2 π r h = 2 × 3.142 × 16 + 2 × 3.142 × 4 × 10
   = 10⁰.5 + 251.4 = 351.9 cm²  (352 cm², 3 s.f.)

Worked example 2 (cone). A cone has radius 5 cm and vertical height 12 cm. Find its volume and slant height.

V = (1/3) π r² h = (1/3) × 3.142 × 25 × 12 = 314.2 cm³
l = √(5² + 12²) = √(169) = 13 cm

Worked example 3 (sphere). Find the volume of a sphere of radius 6 cm.

V = (4/3) π r³ = (4/3) × 3.142 × 216 = 904.8 cm³

Compound shapes: add and subtract

Compound figures are split into standard shapes (add) or standard shapes with a piece removed (subtract). The discipline: draw the split lines, label each sub-shape's dimensions, compute each area separately, then combine.

Worked example. An L-shape is made from a 10 cm × 8 cm rectangle with a 4 cm × 3 cm rectangle removed from one corner. Find its area and perimeter.

area = 10 × 8 - 4 × 3 = 80 - 12 = 68 cm²
perimeter: trace the outline:
10 + 8 + 6 + 5 + 4 + 3 = 36 cm
(6 = 10 - 4 along the removed edge; 5 = 8 - 3)

Worked example 2 (semicircle on a rectangle). A running track is a 60 m by 30 m rectangle with a semicircle of diameter 30 m at each end. Find its area.

rectangle = 60 × 30 = 1800 m²
two semicircles = one full circle of radius 15:
  π x 225 = 706.9 m²
total = 1800 + 706.9 = 2507 m²  (2510 m², 3 s.f.)

Worked examples: composite solids

Composite solids combine the standard formulas: a silo is a cylinder with a hemisphere on top; a pencil is a cylinder with a cone; a capsule is a cylinder with two hemispheres. The method: split the solid, compute each volume, add; for surface area, add only the faces that are actually exposed (the join is hidden).

Worked example. A capsule is a cylinder of radius 3 cm and length 10 cm with a hemisphere at each end. Find its total volume and surface area.

cylinder volume = π r² h = 3.142 × 9 × 10 = 282.8 cm³
two hemispheres = one sphere: (4/3) π r³ = (4/3) × 3.142 × 27
               = 113.1 cm³
total volume = 282.8 + 113.1 = 395.9 cm³

surface area: cylinder curved surface 2 π r h = 188.5 cm²
plus one full sphere 4 π r² = 113.1 cm²
total = 301.6 cm²  (the circular joins are internal, not exposed)

Worked example 2 (frustum-free method). A cone of radius 6 cm and height 9 cm has its top 3 cm cut off parallel to the base. Find the volume removed.

the removed cone is similar to the whole cone, scale k = 3/9 = 1/3
volume of whole cone = (1/3) π x 36 × 9 = 339.3 cm³
removed volume = k³ x whole = (1/27) × 339.3 = 12.6 cm³
(the same as computing directly with radius 2 cm and height 3 cm)

Worked examples: reverse problems and density

Worked example. A cylindrical tank of radius 1.5 m holds 20 m³ of water. Find the depth.

V = π r² h  →  h = V/(π r²) = 20/(3.142 × 2.25)
h = 20/7.07 = 2.83 m

Worked example 2 (density). A metal cuboid 5 cm × 4 cm × 2 cm has mass 312 g. Find its density in g cm⁻³ and kg m⁻³.

volume = 5 × 4 × 2 = 40 cm³
density = 312/40 = 7.8 g cm⁻³
in kg m⁻³: 7.8 × 10⁰⁰ = 7800 kg m⁻³

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Units) Convert 2.4 m² to cm² and 0.75 litres to cm³. Answer: 24 000 cm²; 750 cm³.
  2. (Trapezium) Parallel sides 12 cm and 8 cm, height 6 cm. Find the area. Answer: ½(12 + 8) × 6 = 60 cm².
  3. (Sector) Radius 7 cm, angle 72°. Find arc length and sector area. Answer: arc = (72/360) × 2π × 7 = 8.80 cm; area = (72/360) × π × 49 = 61.6 cm².
  4. (Cylinder) Radius 3 cm, height 12 cm. Find the volume. Answer: π × 9 × 12 = 339 cm³ (3 s.f.).
  5. (Cone) Radius 8 cm, height 15 cm. Find the volume and slant height. Answer: V = ⅓π × 64 × 15 = 1005 cm³; l = √(64 + 225) = 17 cm.
  6. (Sphere) Diameter 10 cm. Find the surface area. Answer: r = 5; SA = 4π × 25 = 314 cm².
  7. (Compound) A rectangle 14 m × 6 m has a semicircle of diameter 6 m removed from one end. Find the area. Answer: 84 − ½π × 9 = 84 − 14.14 = 69.9 m².
  8. (Reverse) A sphere has volume 288 cm³. Find its radius. Answer: 288 = ⁴⁄₃πr³ → r³ = 288 × 3/(4π) = 68.75 → r = 4.10 cm.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Slant versus perpendicular height: triangle/parallelogram areas use perpendicular height; cone surface area uses slant height; cone volume uses perpendicular height.
  • Area unit conversion: 1 m² = 10 000 cm² and 1 cm² = 100 mm². Multiplying by 100 instead of 10 000 is the single most common mensuration error.
  • Sector perimeter: add the two radii to the arc length. The question asks for the perimeter of the sector, not the arc.
  • Using the diameter as radius: halve the diameter first; every circle formula uses r.
  • π precision: use 3.142 or the calculator's π; rounding π to 3 loses accuracy on multi-step questions. Round only the final answer (usually 3 s.f. or as stated).
  • Compound shape subtraction: remove the correct region and keep the outline consistent — recompute the perimeter from the actual boundary, not the sum of the sub-shapes' perimeters.
  • Volume of a prism: cross-section area × length, where the length is perpendicular to the cross-section (a slanted prism uses the perpendicular distance).
  • Units in the answer: cm² for area, cm³ for volume, and capacity conversions (1000 cm³ = 1 litre). A correct number with the wrong unit loses marks on Paper 2.

title: IGCSE Chemistry: Chemical Energetics
content:
IGCSE Chemistry: Chemical Energetics

Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry 0620 (2026–2028), Extended route, Topic 5 Chemical energetics, statement 5.1 Exothermic and endothermic reactions. This note covers the energy accounting of reactions: where the energy goes when bonds break and form, how to read and draw reaction pathway diagrams, and how to calculate enthalpy changes from bond energies. Every calculation is worked line by line, and the sign convention — where most marks are lost — is derived from the physics rather than memorised.

Exothermic and endothermic: the physical picture

Every chemical reaction involves breaking bonds in the reactants and making new bonds in the products. Breaking bonds takes energy in (you must pull atoms apart against their attraction); making bonds releases energy out (atoms fall into each other's attraction). The overall energy change is the balance between the two — like a bank account with deposits and withdrawals.

  • Exothermic reactions release more energy than they absorb — the products have lower energy than the reactants, the temperature of the surroundings rises. Examples: combustion, neutralisation, respiration.
  • Endothermic reactions absorb more than they release — products have higher energy, surroundings cool. Examples: thermal decomposition, photosynthesis, dissolving ammonium nitrate.

Definitions to write exactly: an enthalpy change (ΔH) is the heat energy change at constant pressure; ΔH is negative for exothermic reactions (the system loses energy to the surroundings) and positive for endothermic reactions (the system gains). The activation energy (Eₐ) is the minimum energy colliding particles need to react — the hill every reaction must climb first, even exothermic ones.

Reaction pathway diagrams

Exothermic profile (combustion of methane):

  energy
    |  *  <- reactants (CH₄ + 2O₂) at higher energy
    |   \
    |    \  Eₐ (activation energy: reactants to the peak)
    |     \_
    |       * <- transition state (the hill's peak)
    |        \
    |         \  ΔH negative (downhill overall)
    |          \
    |           *  <- products (CO₂ + 2H₂O) at lower energy
    +---------------- reaction path

Endothermic profile (thermal decomposition):

  energy
    |             *  <- products at HIGHER energy
    |            /   ΔH positive (uphill overall)
    |           /
    |       * <- transition state
    |      /
    |  *  <- reactants
    +---------------- reaction path

Drawing rules that earn marks:
  - label BOTH energy levels (reactants and products),
  - draw Eₐ from reactants up to the peak,
  - draw ΔH as the DIFFERENCE between reactant and product levels
    (arrow down for exothermic, up for endothermic),
  - label the axes (energy against reaction path).
BondBond energy (kJ/mol)BondBond energy (kJ/mol)
H-H436O-H464
Cl-Cl242C-H413
O=O498C=O (in CO₂)805
C-C348H-Cl431

These are average values for the bonds in many environments; an exam supplies the table it expects you to use, so always take numbers from the question. The arithmetic above stays identical whichever numbers arrive.

Calculating enthalpy changes from bond energies

Master method: ΔH = (energy needed to break all reactant bonds) − (energy released making all product bonds). Bond energies are always positive quantities; the sign of ΔH comes out of the subtraction.

Worked: calculate ΔH for the combustion of methane using bond energies.
  CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O

  Bond energies (kJ/mol): C-H 413, O=O 498, C=O 805, O-H 464

Step 1 - count and list bonds BROKEN (reactants):
  4 x C-H  = 4 × 413 = 1652 kJ
  2 x O=O  = 2 × 498 =  996 kJ
  total in = 2648 kJ

Step 2 - count and list bonds MADE (products):
  2 x C=O  = 2 × 805 = 1610 kJ   (CO₂ has two C=O double bonds)
  4 x O-H  = 4 × 464 = 1856 kJ   (2 H₂O x two O-H each)
  total out = 3466 kJ

Step 3 - subtract:
  ΔH = 2648 - 3466 = -818 kJ per mole of CH₄

Step 4 - sign check: negative = energy released = exothermic ✓
  (combustion must be exothermic - a positive answer means a counting error)

Common counting errors flagged: CO₂ contains TWO C=O bonds (not one); each
water has TWO O-H bonds, and there are TWO waters (four O-H in total).

The master method for any energetics question

1. Write the BALANCED equation first (unbalanced = wrong bond counts).
2. Draw out or list every bond in reactants and products.
3. Multiply each bond energy by the number of those bonds.
4. ΔH = bonds broken − bonds made.
5. Check the sign matches the reaction type (combustion: negative).

Worked mini-example: H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl
  broken: H-H 436 + Cl-Cl 242 = 678
  made:   2 x H-Cl 2 × 431 = 862
  ΔH = 678 - 862 = -184 kJ/mol  (exothermic ✓)

Worked example: an enthalpy cycle question from scratch

Enthalpy of combustion is measured in a calorimeter; the same data can be
reached through a cycle. Example: given
  (1) C(s) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g)                ΔH = -394 kJ/mol
  (2) H₂(g) + 1/2 O₂(g) → H₂O(l)           ΔH = -286 kJ/mol
  (3) C(s) + 2H₂(g) → CH₄(g)               ΔH = -75 kJ/mol
find the enthalpy of combustion of methane.

Target: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O

Method: combine the given equations so they add to the target.
  Reverse (3): CH₄ → C + 2H₂       ΔH = +75      (sign flips on reversal)
  Keep (1):    C + O₂ → CO₂        ΔH = -394
  2 x (2):     2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O    ΔH = 2 x -286 = -572
  ------------------------------------------------------------
  Add: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O
  ΔH = +75 - 394 - 572 = -891 kJ/mol

Sanity check: combustion must be exothermic - a negative answer is the
signature. The sign-flip-on-reversal rule and the multiply-everything rule
are where the marks live.

Everyday energy changes

Instant cold packs (ammonium nitrate dissolving in water — endothermic, the pack cools); self-heating cans (calcium oxide + water — exothermic); hand warmers (iron oxidation — exothermic); the energy value of fuels (calorimetry: energy = mass of water × 4.2 J/g°C × temperature rise). These applied questions always ask for the particle-level reason as well as the sign.

Calorimetry worked: burning 0.5 g of a fuel heats 10⁰ g of water from
22.0 °C to 32.0 °C. Calculate the energy released per gram.

  energy = mass x specific heat x ΔT
         = 10⁰ x 4.2 x (32.0 - 22.0)
         = 10⁰ x 4.2 × 10
         = 4200 J = 4.2 kJ
  per gram: 4.2 kJ / 0.5 g = 8.4 kJ/g

Watch the units: 4.2 is J/g°C (so the answer starts in joules); the question
may want kJ - divide by 10⁰⁰ and say so.

Calorimetry questions also probe assumptions: heat is lost to the surroundings and to the calorimeter itself, so measured temperature rises underestimate the true enthalpy change; insulation and a lid reduce that loss. Incomplete combustion (carbon monoxide or soot forming instead of carbon dioxide) releases less energy than the complete-combustion value, which is why experimental answers fall below data-book figures. Stating these two effects is often the last mark on a fuel-comparison question.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Getting ΔH's sign backwards: exothermic = negative (energy leaves the system); endothermic = positive. Bond energy method: broken − made, not the reverse.
  • Subtracting bond energies the wrong way round — the formula is energy in (broken) minus energy out (made).
  • Forgetting to multiply by the number of bonds (four C-H, not one).
  • Confusing activation energy with enthalpy change: Eₐ is the reactant-to-peak height (always positive); ΔH is reactant-to-product difference.
  • Drawing an exothermic profile with products above reactants (or forgetting to label levels/axes).
  • Claiming bond making absorbs energy — making bonds releases; breaking absorbs.
  • Mixing J and kJ in calorimetry (4.2 J/g°C × g × °C gives joules).

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 4, 3 marks). Define enthalpy change and state the sign of ΔH for (i) combustion (ii) thermal decomposition.

Answer: Enthalpy change is the heat energy change at constant pressure during a reaction. (i) Combustion is exothermic, so ΔH is negative. (ii) Thermal decomposition is endothermic, so ΔH is positive.

Question 2 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Explain, in terms of bonds, why combustion is exothermic.

Answer: Combustion breaks the bonds in the fuel and in oxygen (absorbing energy) and makes new bonds in carbon dioxide and water (releasing energy). The energy released forming the very strong C=O and O-H bonds in the products exceeds the energy absorbed breaking the reactant bonds, so net energy is released to the surroundings and ΔH is negative.

Question 3 (Paper 4, 5 marks). Calculate ΔH for 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O using bond energies: H-H 436, O=O 498, O-H 464 kJ/mol.

Answer: Broken: 2 × H-H = 872; 1 × O=O = 498; total = 1370 kJ. Made: 4 × O-H = 1856 kJ. ΔH = 1370 − 1856 = −486 kJ per mole of reaction as written (−243 kJ per mole of H₂).

Question 4 (Paper 4, 4 marks). Draw and label a reaction pathway diagram for an endothermic reaction, identifying activation energy and ΔH.

Answer: Axes: energy (y) against reaction path (x). Products are drawn above reactants. Eₐ is the vertical arrow from reactants up to the peak of the curve (positive, the energy needed to start the reaction). ΔH is the vertical arrow between reactant and product levels, pointing up (positive) since products have higher energy.

Question 5 (Paper 4, 3 marks). A student burns 1.0 g of ethanol and heats 200 g of water by 15.0 °C. Calculate the energy released and give it in kJ/g. (c = 4.2 J/g°C)

Answer: Energy = 200 × 4.2 × 15.0 = 12 600 J = 12.6 kJ. Per gram of ethanol: 12.6 ÷ 1.0 = 12.6 kJ/g.

Question 6 (Paper 2, 2 marks). Explain why an instant cold pack feels cold.

Answer: The pack dissolves an endothermic salt (ammonium nitrate): the dissolving process absorbs heat energy from the surroundings to break the solute's lattice, so the pack and hand lose thermal energy and feel cold.

Energy decides whether a reaction can happen at all; whether it actually does — and how fast — is the next topic.

title: Thermal Physics — Study Notes
content:
Thermal Physics

Temperature and scales

Thermodynamic temperature is measured in kelvin. The kelvin and Celsius scales have the same size of degree, with T/K = θ/°C + 273. Absolute zero (0 K) is the lowest possible temperature, at which the particles of an ideal gas have minimum kinetic energy.

Example: 25 °C = 298 K.

Specific heat capacity and latent heat

Specific heat capacity c is the energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 K: Q = mcΔθ. Latent heat is the energy needed to change the state of 1 kg without a change in temperature: Q = mL. Melting and boiling absorb energy without a temperature rise, because the energy goes into breaking intermolecular bonds, not into kinetic energy.

Example: warming 2.0 kg of water (c = 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) by 10 K needs 84 kJ. Melting 0.20 kg of ice (L = 334 kJ kg⁻¹) needs 67 kJ.

The mole and Avogadro constant

One mole contains N_A = 6.02 × 10²³ particles. The number of particles is N = nN_A, where n is the amount in moles. Molar mass is the mass of one mole, in kg mol⁻¹ in SI units.

Equation of state for an ideal gas

pV = nRT, where R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ and T must be absolute. Equivalently pV = NkT, with k = R/N_A = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹.

Example: 0.10 mol at 300 K in 2.0 × 10⁻³ m³ has p = nRT/V ≈ 1.2 × 10⁵ Pa.

Kinetic theory

The pressure of an ideal gas comes from molecules colliding with the container walls. The mean kinetic energy of a molecule is ⟨Ek⟩ = 3kT/2, so it depends only on the absolute temperature. At 300 K it is about 6.2 × 10⁻²¹ J.

Internal energy and the first law

The internal energy of an ideal gas is the sum of the kinetic and potential energies of its molecules. For an ideal gas there are no intermolecular forces, so internal energy depends only on temperature. The first law of thermodynamics is ΔU = Q + W, where Q is heat added to the system and W is work done on the system. Heat lost by a system is therefore negative.

Example: a gas has 500 J of work done on it and loses 200 J of heat. ΔU = −200 + 500 = +300 J.

Exam tips: convert to kelvin before using pV = nRT or the kinetic-energy formula. Check the sign convention for W in the question. Use latent heat only when the temperature is constant.

title: A Level Mathematics: Proof
content:
A Level Mathematics: Proof

Proof at A2 extends the AS methods with contradiction, disproof by counter-example in unfamiliar settings, and algebraic arguments about divisibility, parity and inequalities. The examinable skills are choosing a method, setting up general notation, and closing the argument — not spotting a clever trick. This note works through each method with complete examples and the wording mark schemes expect.

The four methods and when to use them

MethodUse whenShape of the argument
DirectThe statement is algebraicStart from definitions, manipulate to the target form
ExhaustionThe domain splits into a few casesCheck each case
Counter-exampleThe statement claims "for all" and looks falseProduce one failing case with arithmetic
ContradictionThe statement is negative or about irrationality/infinityAssume the opposite, derive an impossibility

Choosing badly wastes time: a "prove that there is no largest prime" question cannot be done directly, and a parity statement cannot be done by example.

Proof by contradiction

assume the negation, derive a contradiction with a known truth,
conclude the original statement

Worked example 1 (irrationality of √2). The classic, examinable in full.

assume √(2) = p/q in lowest terms, p and q integers
2q² = p², so p² is even, so p is even: p = 2k
4k² = 2q²  →  q² = 2k², so q is even
p and q both even contradicts "lowest terms"
hence √(2) is irrational

Worked example 2 (no largest prime). Prove there are infinitely many primes.

assume finitely many: p1, p2, ..., pn
consider N = p1 p2 ... pn + 1
N leaves remainder 1 when divided by any π, so no π divides N
so N has a prime factor not in the list: contradiction
hence there are infinitely many primes

Worked example 3 (no rational solution). Prove that x² = 6 has no rational root.

assume x = p/q in lowest terms: p² = 6q²
so 3 divides p², hence 3 divides p: p = 3k
9k² = 6q²  →  3k² = 2q², so 3 divides q², hence q
both divisible by 3 contradicts lowest terms

Disproof by counter-example

Worked example 1. Disprove "if a > b then a² > b²".

take a = 1, b = -3: 1 > -3 but 1 < 9
counter-example disproves the statement

Worked example 2. Disprove "n² + n + 41 is prime for all positive integers n".

n = 41: 1681 + 41 + 41 = 1763 = 41 × 43, not prime

Worked example 3. Disprove "every odd number is prime".

9 is odd and 9 = 3 × 3, not prime

Each disproof is complete with one case; the arithmetic must be shown, not asserted.

Algebraic proof with parity and divisibility

even: 2n;  odd: 2n + 1
"is a multiple of k" means the expression equals k times an integer

Worked example 1. Prove that the difference of the squares of two consecutive odd numbers is a multiple of 8.

(2n + 3)² - (2n + 1)² = (4n² + 12n + 9) - (4n² + 4n + 1) = 8n + 8
= 8(n + 1), a multiple of 8

Worked example 2. Prove that n³ − n is divisible by 6 for all integers n.

n³ - n = n(n - 1)(n + 1), three consecutive integers
one is even, one is a multiple of 3; since 2 and 3 are coprime,
the product is divisible by 6

Worked example 3. Prove that the product of two consecutive even numbers is a multiple of 8.

2n(2n + 2) = 4n(n + 1); n(n + 1) is even, so the product is 8k

Inequalities by completing the square

a squared term is never negative; complete the square to expose a
minimum, then conclude the inequality

Worked example 1. Prove that x² − 4x + 7 > 0 for all real x.

= (x - 2)² + 3 >= 3 > 0

Worked example 2. Prove that 4x − x² − 5 < 0 for all x.

= -(x² - 4x + 5) = -[(x - 2)² + 1] = -(x - 2)² - 1 <= -1 < 0

Worked example 3 (unknown constant). Find the values of k for which x² + kx + k > 0 for all x.

(x + k/2)² + k - k²/4 > 0 requires k - k²/4 > 0
k(1 - k/4) > 0  →  0 < k < 4

The discriminant route gives the same answer (k² − 4k < 0); the completing-the-square route states the minimum explicitly, which is usually clearer in a proof.

Proof by exhaustion

Worked example. Prove that every integer from 1 to 10 is either prime, a square, or the sum of two primes.

1 (square); 2 (prime); 3 (prime); 4 (square); 5 (prime);
6 = 3 + 3; 7 (prime); 8 = 3 + 5; 9 (square); 10 = 3 + 7
all ten cases checked  →  statement proved for this finite domain

Exhaustion is only valid for a finite domain, and the proof is incomplete unless every case is listed. State the domain explicitly.

Setting out a proof for full marks

  • Define every variable with its domain ("let n be an integer").
  • State which method you are using when it is not obvious.
  • Write the algebra in connected steps, each justified.
  • Finish with a sentence tying the result to the claim ("hence ... as required").
  • For contradiction, state the assumption and where the contradiction lies.

Worked example (full structure). Prove that if n is odd then n² + 1 is even.

let n be an odd integer, so n = 2k + 1 for some integer k   [definition]
n² + 1 = 4k² + 4k + 1 + 1 = 4k² + 4k + 2              [algebra]
        = 2(2k² + 2k + 1)                              [target form]
which is even, hence n² + 1 is even whenever n is odd      [conclusion]

Inequalities with the discriminant

"Always positive" or "always negative" quadratics are proved with the discriminant, which is the algebraic form of the completing-the-square argument.

ax² + bx + c > 0 for all x  (a > 0)  <=>  b² - 4ac < 0
ax² + bx + c < 0 for all x  (a < 0)  <=>  b² - 4ac < 0

Worked example. Prove that 2x² − 3x + 4 > 0 for all real x.

a = 2 > 0;  discriminant = 9 - 32 = -23 < 0
no real roots and the parabola opens upward, so it never touches the
x-axis and is positive throughout

Worked example 2 (find the range). Find p such that x² + (p + 1)x + 4 > 0 for all x.

(p + 1)² - 16 < 0  →  -4 < p + 1 < 4  →  -5 < p < 3

Worked example 3 (negative leading coefficient). Prove that −x² + 2x − 5 < 0 for all x.

a = -1 < 0;  discriminant = 4 - 20 = -16 < 0
no real roots and the parabola opens downward, so it stays below the axis

Proving statements about sums and sequences

Closed-form statements about sums are proved by deriving the formula or by induction on the pattern; the derivation is always acceptable and often shorter.

Worked example 1. Prove that the sum of the first n odd numbers is n².

S = 1 + 3 + 5 + ... + (2n - 1), an arithmetic series
a = 1, d = 2: S = (n/2)[2 + 2(n - 1)] = (n/2)(2n) = n²

Worked example 2. Prove that the sum of the first n terms of 2 + 4 + 8 + ... is 2^(n+1) − 2.

geometric with a = 2, r = 2: S = 2(2^n - 1)/(2 - 1) = 2^(n+1) - 2

Worked example 3 (difference of squares). Prove that every odd number greater than 1 is the difference of two squares.

let the odd number be 2n + 1 = (n + 1)² - n²
since (n + 1)² - n² = 2n + 1, the representation always exists

Statements about the roots of a quadratic

Relations between roots and coefficients are provable from the quadratic formula and are a favourite A2 proof.

for ax² + bx + c = 0 with roots alpha and beta:
alpha + beta = -b/a;  alpha beta = c/a

Worked example. Prove that the sum of the roots of x² + px + q = 0 is −p.

roots: (-p +/- √(p² - 4q))/2
sum: [-p + √(...) - p - √(...)]/2 = -2p/2 = -p

Worked example 2. Prove that if one root of x² + bx + c = 0 is twice the other, then 2b² = 9c.

roots k and 2k: sum 3k = -b, product 2k² = c
k = -b/3, so 2b²/9 = c  →  2b² = 9c

Worked example 3 (discriminant). Prove that x² + 2x + 2 = 0 has no real roots.

discriminant = 4 - 8 = -4 < 0, so no real solutions
(equivalently (x + 1)² + 1 = 0 has no real solution)

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Contradiction) Prove √3 is irrational. Answer: assume p/q lowest terms, 3q² = p², 3 | p, then 3 | q — contradiction.
  2. (Counter-example) Disprove "n² − n + 1 is prime for all n". Answer: n = 4 gives 13 (prime) — try n = 5: 21 = 3 × 7, not prime.
  3. (Parity) Prove the sum of two odd numbers is even. Answer: (2m + 1) + (2n + 1) = 2(m + n + 1).
  4. (Divisibility) Prove 5n² + 5n is a multiple of 10. Answer: 5n(n + 1); n(n + 1) is even, so 5 × even = 10k.
  5. (Inequality) Prove x² + 2x + 2 > 0. Answer: (x + 1)² + 1 ≥ 1.
  6. (Constant) Find k so that x² + 2kx + 9 > 0 always. Answer: 4k² < 36 → −3 < k < 3.
  7. (Exhaustion) Prove n² + n is even by cases. Answer: n even → 4k² + 2k; n odd → 4k² + 6k + 2; both even.
  8. (Contradiction) Prove there is no greatest even integer. Answer: if N were greatest, N + 2 is even and larger — contradiction.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Examples offered as proof: only a general algebraic argument proves a universal claim.
  • Undefined variables: "let x be odd" without x = 2k + 1 leaves nothing to manipulate.
  • Contradiction not closed: name the contradiction explicitly — "this contradicts lowest terms".
  • Assuming the conclusion: starting from the statement to be proved and deriving a truth proves nothing unless every step is reversible.
  • Divisibility without coprimality: "divisible by 2 and by 3 hence by 6" needs 2 and 3 coprime; it is true here, but state it.
