  • Luminosity and Intensity
  • Wien and Stefan–Boltzmann
  • Hubble's Law
  • The Big Bang

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

### Worked example Hubble's law states v = H₀d, where v is recession speed, d is distance and H₀ is the Hubble constant. With H₀ ≈ 70 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹ and a galaxy 100 Mpc away, v = 70 × 100 = 7000 km s⁻¹. Redshift shows the galaxy is moving away, which supports the expanding-universe model and the age of the universe of about 13.8 billion years. ### Check yourself A galaxy is 200 Mpc away with H₀ = 70. Calculate its recession speed. The answer is 14 000 km s⁻¹. Explain why a more distant galaxy recedes faster.

title: Exam technique: Circular Motion and SHM
content:
### What earns the marks
For SHM acceleration, minus omega squared x with direction stated earns both marks. For periods, the correct root form quoted earns the method mark. For energy, equilibrium named for max KE earns the mark; resonance at natural frequency earns the explanation.
### Traps
Error: sign dropped in a = -omega squared x. Correction: acceleration points to equilibrium. Error: pendulum and spring formulae swapped. Correction: root(L/g) versus root(m/k). Error: resonance blamed on damping alone. Correction: matching frequencies drive it.

title: Information Representation — Study Notes
content:
`# Information Representation

Cambridge International AS & A Level Computer Science 9618: section 1 (Information representation), examined in AS Paper 1.

Number Systems and Ranges

Unsigned binary with n bits stores 0 to 2ⁿ − 1. Two's complement represents negatives: the MSB has value −2ⁿ⁻¹.

Example: 8-bit two's complement of −5: 11111011 (−128 + 64 + 32 + 16 + 8 + 2 + 1).

SystemBaseDigits
Binary20–1
Hexadecimal160–9, A–F
BCD—4 bits per decimal digit

Binary Arithmetic

Add: 0+0=0, 0+1=1, 1+1=0 carry 1, 1+1+1=1 carry 1. Overflow happens when a result exceeds the word size.

Subtraction uses two's complement addition (A − B = A + (−B)).

Text

  • ASCII: 7 bits, 128 characters, English only
  • Unicode: universal scripts; UTF-8 is variable-width (1–4 bytes)

Images and Sound

  • Bitmap: pixels with colour depth (bits per pixel). File size = width × height × depth.
  • Sound: sampling rate (Hz) × bit depth × duration × channels.
  • Resolution trade-off: fidelity vs size.

Compression

  • Lossless (ZIP, run-length encoding): exact reconstruction — required for text/code
  • Lossy (JPEG, MP3): discards perceptually minor data — smaller files

Example: RLE of AAABBBCC → 3A3B2C.

Exam tips: show working for two's complement conversions; state why compression type suits the data (text must be lossless).

Binary and hexadecimal worked conversion

To convert the denary number 156 to binary, subtract the place values from the largest downwards: 156 = 128 + 16 + 8 + 4, so the binary value is 10011100. Each binary digit is a bit, and the place values double from right to left: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128.

Hexadecimal groups four bits at a time, so one hexadecimal digit represents a value from 0 to 15. Split 10011100 into 1001 and 1100 to get 9 and 12, which is 9C in hexadecimal. Hexadecimal is used to write memory addresses and colour codes because it is shorter than binary and converts to it directly.

Exam tip: show the place-value working, not just the answer. Examiners award method marks for the subtraction or the grouping.

Worked example: sound file size

A mono recording lasts 60 seconds, is sampled at 8000 samples per second and uses 16 bits per sample. The file size in bits is 8000 multiplied by 16 multiplied by 60, which is 7,680,000 bits. Dividing by 8 gives 960,000 bytes, or about 960 kB. Doubling the sample rate or recording in stereo doubles the file size, so check each factor separately.

Worked example: image file size

An image is 800 pixels wide and 600 pixels high, with 24 bits of colour per pixel. The total is 800 multiplied by 600 multiplied by 24, which is 11,520,000 bits, or 1,440,000 bytes. Reducing the colour depth to 8 bits cuts the file to one third of that size, but the image can then show fewer distinct colours.

Lossy and lossless compression compared

  • Lossless compression finds repeated patterns and can rebuild the original exactly, so it suits text and program files.
  • Lossy compression discards detail the eye or ear is least likely to notice, so it produces much smaller files for photographs and music.

title: IGCSE Computer Science: Automated Systems, Robotics and AI
content:
IGCSE Computer Science: Automated Systems, Robotics and AI

Cambridge IGCSE Computer Science 0478 (2026–2028), Paper 1 Computer Systems, Topic 6 Automated and emerging technologies: statement 6.1 Automated systems, 6.2 Robotics, and 6.3 Artificial intelligence. This is where the machine stops waiting for instructions and acts on its own — sensing, deciding and moving. Every feedback loop below is traced step by step, and the AI section separates what the syllabus actually expects (machine learning, natural language processing, robotics) from the hype, because examiners reward precise terminology over vague claims.

What makes a system automated

An automated system measures and controls a process with little or no human intervention. The architecture is always the same loop, and once you see it you can analyse any example the exam gives:

  • Input (sensors) — measure the real world: temperature, light, pressure, humidity, proximity, pH.
  • Processing — a microprocessor compares each measurement against a target (the set point) and decides what to do.
  • Output (actuators) — change the real world: motors, heaters, pumps, valves, lights, robotic arms.
  • Feedback — the sensors keep measuring the effect of the actuators, closing the loop so the system corrects itself.
Worked trace: a greenhouse temperature control system.

Set point: 22 degrees C. The sensor reads the air every 10 seconds.

1. 09:00:00  reading 18 C - below the set point.
   Processing: heating required. Actuators: heater ON, roof vent CLOSED.
2. 09:00:30  reading 21 C - still below (within the 2 C dead zone margin).
   Processing: continue heating.
3. 09:01:10  reading 23 C - above the set point.
   Processing: heater OFF (switching now, not at 22, avoids rapid cycling),
   roof vent OPEN to cool.
4. 09:03:00  reading 22 C - within the dead zone between 21 and 23.
   Processing: change nothing - the dead zone prevents constant switching,
   which would wear the heater out.

The loop repeats indefinitely. The set point is the target, the dead zone is
the tolerance band that stops the actuators chattering, and the feedback is the
sensor readings that drive each decision.

Closed-loop systems use feedback (as above); open-loop systems act without measuring the result — a toaster runs for a fixed time regardless of how brown the bread is. The exam asks you to say which a system is and justify it: if the output feeds back into the next decision, it is closed-loop.

Transducers: where physical change becomes data

Sensors and actuators are both transducers — devices that convert one form of energy into another — and knowing which way the conversion runs is the cleanest way to keep them straight. A sensor converts a physical quantity into an electrical signal the processor can read (temperature into resistance, light into voltage, sound into a varying current). An actuator does the reverse: it converts the processor's electrical signal into physical action (voltage into motion in a motor, into heat in a heater, into light in an LED).

Conversion direction, always:

  physical quantity -→ electrical signal     SENSOR (input)
  electrical signal -→ physical action       ACTUATOR (output)

Examples worked through:
  A thermistor in a greenhouse: temperature rises → resistance falls → the
  analogue voltage changes → an analogue-to-digital converter (ADC) turns it
  into a binary number the processor compares with the set point.

  A motor on a roof vent: the processor outputs a digital command → a digital-
  to-analogue converter (DAC) and driver circuit produce a varying current →
  the motor turns the vent.

Many real devices are both at once in different roles: a microphone is a sensor
(sound → electricity) and a speaker is an actuator (electricity → sound).

Where automation is used

DomainExampleSensorsActuators
ManufacturingRobotic assembly linePosition, proximity, visionRobot arms, conveyors, welders
AgricultureAutomatic irrigationSoil moisture, rain, temperaturePumps, valves
HomeCentral heatingThermostat, timerBoiler, radiator valves
TrafficAdaptive traffic lightsInductive loop detectors, camerasSignal lamps
MedicineInsulin pumpGlucose sensorPump actuator

Benefits: consistent quality, output in dangerous or monotonous conditions, 24-hour working, long-run cost per unit falls, and precise control improves yield. Costs: high capital outlay, jobs lost or changed, expensive and disruptive breakdowns, and loss of human judgement when the unexpected happens — a self-driving vehicle's edge cases are the modern form of that risk.

Robotics

A robot is a programmable machine that can sense, process and act on its environment to carry out tasks, often autonomously. The syllabus separates the types: fixed robots (a welding arm bolted to a factory floor — precise and strong, one workspace), mobile robots (warehouse robots, rovers — move themselves, need navigation), and autonomous robots (self-driving cars, drones — make decisions without continuous human control).

Inside any robot, the same loop as any automated system: sensors (cameras, LiDAR, ultrasonic, gyroscopes, encoders on the motors), a processor running control software, and actuators (motors, servos, grippers) — plus a power supply (battery) and a communication link for supervision.

  • Industrial uses: welding, painting and assembly (consistent quality, no fatigue, hazardous-environment work); picking and packing; bomb disposal and deep-sea or space exploration where humans cannot go.
  • Domestic and service uses: vacuum cleaners, lawn mowers, surgical robots, warehouse logistics, companionship and care.
  • Advantages: repeatable precision, tireless, work in danger, cheaper than labour at volume.
  • Disadvantages: very expensive to design and install, rigid when the task changes, maintenance needs skilled engineers, and they displace workers — the social consequence earns its own marks.

Artificial intelligence and machine learning

Artificial intelligence (AI) is software that appears to make intelligent decisions — solving problems and carrying out tasks in ways we would call clever if a human did them. Machine learning (ML) is the subset the syllabus emphasises: instead of being explicitly programmed with rules, the system is given data and learns patterns from it, improving with experience.

An analogy before the mechanics: teaching a child to recognise cats does not mean listing ear shapes and whisker counts. Show the child thousands of labelled pictures and the rules form themselves inside their head. Machine learning does exactly that with numbers.

How a machine learning model is trained, step by step:

1. Collect data: thousands of emails labelled "spam" or "not spam" by humans.
2. Choose features: word frequencies, sender reputation, link count, subject
   line patterns - measurable properties of each email.
3. Split the data: most for training, some held back for testing.
4. TRAINING: the algorithm adjusts its internal weights to fit the training
   data. It predicts each email's label; each wrong prediction nudges the
   weights; repeat over the dataset many times. The weights ARE the learned
   model - no human wrote the rules.
5. TESTING: run the trained model on the held-back data it has never seen and
   measure accuracy (correct predictions / total predictions). High training
   accuracy but low test accuracy means overfitting - it memorised the
   examples rather than learning the pattern.
6. DEPLOYMENT: new emails are classified by the model; correct and incorrect
   feedback can be fed back in so it keeps improving.

The three kinds of learning the syllabus names: supervised learning trains on labelled data (the spam example; predicting house prices from past sales); unsupervised learning finds structure in unlabelled data (customer segmentation — "these shoppers behave alike"); reinforcement learning learns by trial and reward (a game-playing program gets points for winning and adjusts its strategy).

Other AI applications in the syllabus: natural language processing (NLP) — understanding and generating human language: translation, voice assistants, chatbots, spam filtering; speech recognition — turning spoken audio into text (dictation, voice control); expert systems — a knowledge base of facts plus an inference engine applying rules to reach a conclusion (medical diagnosis support, fault finding); computer vision — interpreting images (face recognition, self-driving perception, medical imaging); autonomous vehicles — combining sensors, vision and decision-making to navigate.

Advantages of AI systemsDisadvantages of AI systems
Fast decisions over huge data volumesTraining needs vast data and computing power
Consistent, no fatigue or emotionNo common sense; fails on cases unlike its training data
Handles dangerous or dull workJob displacement across many industries
Improves with more dataBiased training data produces biased decisions — and they are hard to challenge
Available 24/7Cannot explain its reasoning well; accountability is unclear

Worked example: applying the loop to an autonomous vehicle

Approaching a pedestrian crossing:

1. SENSORS: cameras, radar and LiDAR continuously measure distance to the
   crossing, the pedestrian's position and speed, and the car's own speed.
2. PROCESSING: the AI classifies the objects (camera vision: "pedestrian at
   kerb"), predicts likely movement from the training data, and compares this
   with safety rules - minimum stopping distance for current speed and grip.
3. DECISION: predicted conflict - begin braking now, at 4 m/s², and warn.
4. ACTUATORS: brake and steering systems carry out the decision.
5. FEEDBACK: sensors keep measuring; if the pedestrian steps back, the plan
   updates; if the road is wet, the sensors' distance readings lengthen the
   braking margin.

Every one of these five stages can be a separate exam answer.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Calling any machine with a motor a "robot"; the syllabus sense is a programmable machine that senses, processes and acts — and "autonomous" requires decisions without continuous human control.
  • Describing open-loop systems as using feedback; if the output is not measured to adjust the next action, the loop is open (a toaster), regardless of how clever it looks.
  • Confusing the sensor and the actuator in a scenario: sensors measure (input), actuators move or heat (output) — thermostats sense, heaters act.
  • Saying machine learning "is programmed with rules"; the whole point is that the rules are learned from data — the trained weights are the program.
  • Skipping the training/testing split when explaining ML; measuring on unseen data is what distinguishes learning from memorising.
  • Equating AI with robots (or robots with AI): AI is software that can run without a robot, and many robots run purely on fixed programs with no learning.
  • Listing advantages only; the disadvantages (job losses, bias, data hunger, no common sense) carry equal marks.
  • Forgetting the feedback loop when describing any control system — "the sensor keeps measuring the effect" is the sentence examiners look for.

Exam-style questions and answers

Question 1 (Paper 1, 4 marks). Describe the input, process and output stages of an automatic door.

Answer: Input: a motion or proximity sensor detects a person approaching (and a pressure sensor may detect someone standing on the mat). Processing: the microprocessor compares the sensor reading with its trigger condition and checks safety sensors before acting. Output: an actuator (an electric motor) slides the door open; a timer or sensor then closes it. Feedback: the sensors keep monitoring so the door stays open while the beam is broken.

Question 2 (Paper 1, 3 marks). Explain the difference between a closed-loop and an open-loop system, giving one example of each.

Answer: A closed-loop system measures its output and feeds that back to adjust its actions — a central heating system measures room temperature and switches the boiler accordingly. An open-loop system acts without measuring the result — a toaster runs for a fixed time regardless of how brown the toast is.

Question 3 (Paper 1, 4 marks). Describe how a machine learning system is trained to detect fraudulent bank transactions.

Answer: Collect a large dataset of past transactions each labelled fraudulent or genuine by humans. Choose features such as amount, location, time and spending pattern. The algorithm trains on most of the data, adjusting its internal weights each time its prediction is wrong, until the predictions fit. The model is then tested on held-back transactions it has never seen to measure accuracy, before being used to score new transactions — with feedback from confirmed cases improving it over time.

Question 4 (Paper 1, 4 marks). Discuss the impact of introducing robots into a car factory.

Answer: For the firm: consistent weld quality, output day and night without fatigue, safer handling of painting fumes and heavy parts, and lower unit costs at volume — offset by very high installation costs, expensive breakdowns and rigidity when the product changes. For workers: dangerous and repetitive jobs are replaced, but assembly jobs are lost and remaining roles demand higher skills, so retraining is needed and communities dependent on the plant can suffer.

Question 5 (Paper 1, 3 marks). State three differences between a robot and an AI system.

Answer: A robot is hardware that physically senses and acts in the world; AI is software that makes decisions and may never have a physical form. Robots follow explicit programs; AI systems (especially machine learning) derive behaviour from data. A robot can run with no AI at all (a fixed assembly arm), and AI can exist with no robot (a spam filter).

The counterpart to systems that act on their own is the people who attack them: cyber security.

title: Acid-base Equilibria
content:
Acid-base Equilibria

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH14, Topic 14. Acids and bases are defined by proton transfer. The strength of an acid is given by its dissociation constant, and pH calculations, buffers and titrations all follow from it.

Strong and weak acids

  • A strong acid dissociates completely in water, so [H⁺] equals the acid concentration. For 0.010 mol dm⁻³ HCl, [H⁺] = 0.010 and pH = 2.00.
  • A weak acid dissociates only partly. For HA ⇌ H⁺ + A⁻, Ka = [H⁺][A⁻] / [HA].
  • pKa = −log10 Ka. A smaller pKa means a stronger acid.

pH calculations

  • pH = −log10[H⁺]. For a base, find pOH = −log10[OH⁻] and use pH = 14.00 − pOH at 298 K.
  • Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ mol² dm⁻⁶ at 298 K.
  • For a 0.050 mol dm⁻³ NaOH solution, [OH⁻] = 0.050, pOH = 1.30 and pH = 12.70.

Buffers

  • A buffer contains a weak acid and its conjugate base (for example ethanoic acid and sodium ethanoate). It resists large pH changes.
  • The pH of a buffer is given by pH = pKa + log([A⁻] / [HA]). When [A⁻] = [HA], pH = pKa.
  • Adding a small amount of strong acid is absorbed by the conjugate base, so the pH changes only slightly.

Titrations and indicators

  • Strong acid with strong base: the equivalence point is pH 7.
  • Weak acid with strong base: the equivalence point is above pH 7, so phenolphthalein (pH 8.3 to 10) is suitable.
  • Strong acid with weak base: the equivalence point is below pH 7, so methyl orange (pH 3.1 to 4.4) is suitable.
  • Choose an indicator whose colour change lies within the steep vertical section of the titration curve.

Exam tip: when pH is asked for a weak acid, calculate [H⁺] from Ka and the concentration before taking the logarithm.

title: A Level Physics: Nuclear Physics
content:
A Level Physics: Nuclear Physics

Nuclear physics studies the dense heart of the atom: what the nucleus contains, why some nuclei fly apart, and how the mass of a nucleus is less than the sum of its parts — the most famous equation in physics. This note builds the subject from zero: nuclear composition and notation, the three kinds of radiation and their detection, mass defect and binding energy with the binding-energy curve, and radioactive decay as an exponential process with its own vocabulary (activity, decay constant, half-life). Every calculation type is worked line by line.

Atoms, nuclei and radiation

An atom is a tiny nucleus surrounded by electrons. The nucleus contains protons (positive) and neutrons (neutral); the notation uses X with atomic number Z (protons) above and mass number A (nucleons: protons + neutrons) below. Isotopes share Z but differ in N; they are chemically identical (same electron configuration) but physically different (different mass and nuclear stability).

Three kinds of emission come from unstable nuclei:

PropertyAlpha (α)Beta-minus (β⁻)Gamma (γ)
What it ishelium nucleus (2 protons + 2 neutrons)fast electron from the nucleushigh-energy photon
Notation⁴₂He⁰₋₁e⁰₀γ
Charge+2e−1e0
Speedup to ~0.05cup to ~0.99cc
Range in aira few cma few metreshundreds of metres
Ionisingstrongly (double charge, slow)moderatelyweakly
Deflectionslight, in magnetic/electric fieldsgreater, opposite direction to αnone
Stopped bypaperthin aluminiumlead or thick concrete

Nuclear equations balance on two counts: nucleon number A and proton number Z both conserved. In beta-minus decay a neutron turns into a proton plus an electron plus an antineutrino (n → p + e⁻ + ν̄), which is why A stays the same while Z rises by one.

Worked example. Complete: ²³⁸₉₂U → ²³⁴₉₀Th + ? Answer: the missing particle has A = 238 − 234 = 4 and Z = 92 − 90 = 2 → an alpha particle ⁴₂He. For ¹⁴₆C → ¹⁴₇N + ?: A = 0, Z = −1 → beta-minus ⁰₋₁e (plus an antineutrino).

Mass defect and nuclear binding energy

Every nucleus weighs less than its separated nucleons — the mass defect Δm. That missing mass is the energy released when the nucleus assembled, by Einstein's mass–energy equivalence:

E = Delta m c^2        c = 3.0 x 10^8 m s-1

binding energy = energy needed to separate a nucleus into
                 its individual nucleons
binding energy per nucleon = binding energy / A

The atomic mass unit, u, is defined so that 1 u = 1.661 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, equivalent to 931.5 MeV of energy. The binding-energy-per-nucleon curve is the map of nuclear energy: it rises steeply to a maximum near iron-56 (about 8.8 MeV per nucleon) and falls slowly for heavier nuclei. Consequences, both examinable:

  • Fission: a heavy nucleus (uranium) splitting toward the middle of the curve releases energy — each fragment is more tightly bound.
  • Fusion: light nuclei (hydrogen isotopes) joining toward the peak also release energy — this powers stars.

Worked example 1. Find the binding energy of a helium-4 nucleus (mass 4.0026 u) given proton mass 1.0073 u and neutron mass 1.0087 u.

separate nucleons: 2(1.0073) + 2(1.0087) = 4.0320 u
nucleus: 4.0026 u
mass defect: Delta m = 4.0320 - 4.0026 = 0.0294 u
binding energy = 0.0294 x 931.5 = 27.4 MeV
per nucleon = 27.4/4 = 6.85 MeV

Worked example 2 (joules). Convert the mass defect 0.0294 u to joules.

Delta m = 0.0294 x 1.661 x 10^-27 = 4.88 x 10^-29 kg
E = Delta m c^2 = 4.88 x 10^-29 x (3.0 x 10^8)^2
  = 4.88 x 10^-29 x 9.0 x 10^16 = 4.39 x 10^-12 J

Radioactive decay

Radioactive decay is spontaneous and random: no external condition (temperature, pressure, chemistry) changes when a given nucleus decays. What is predictable is the behaviour of huge numbers of nuclei — an exponential law:

N = N0 e^(-lambda t)

N = number of undecayed nuclei; N0 at t = 0
lambda = decay constant (s-1)

activity A = lambda N    (becquerel, Bq; 1 Bq = 1 decay per second)
A = A0 e^(-lambda t)

half-life t_half = ln(2)/lambda = 0.693/lambda

The decay constant is the probability per unit time that any one nucleus decays. The half-life is the time for half the present nuclei to decay — a fixed fraction, not a fixed number. On a graph of N against t, read the half-life directly as the time to fall from any value to half of it; the gradient of ln N against t is −λ.

Worked example 1. A sample has activity 8000 Bq. After 6.0 hours the activity is 1000 Bq. Find the half-life.

8000 -> 1000 is three halvings (8 -> 4 -> 2 -> 1)
three half-lives = 6.0 hours  ->  t_half = 2.0 hours

Worked example 2 (decay constant). Find λ and the number of nuclei in a 1000 Bq sample with that half-life.

lambda = 0.693/t_half = 0.693/(2.0 x 3600) = 9.6 x 10-5 s-1
A = lambda N -> N = A/lambda = 1000/9.6 x 10-5 = 1.04 x 10^7 nuclei

Worked example 3 (exponential). A sample of 4.0 × 10¹⁰ nuclei has λ = 2.0 × 10⁻⁶ s⁻¹. How many remain after one hour?

N = N0 e^(-lambda t) = 4.0 x 10^10 x e^(-2.0 x 10-6 x 3600)
  = 4.0 x 10^10 x e^(-0.0072) = 4.0 x 10^10 x 0.9928
  = 3.97 x 10^10  (only 0.7% decayed - short times barely dent N)

Worked examples: interpreting decay data

Worked example. A student measures count rate against time and finds it falls from 640 counts per minute to 40 in 30 minutes. Explain why count rate is used instead of activity directly, and find the half-life.

640 -> 320 -> 160 -> 80 -> 40 : four halvings in 30 min
t_half = 30/4 = 7.5 minutes
why counts: a detector records only the fraction of decays that
reach it (geometric efficiency), so the count rate is proportional
to activity but not equal to it - proportional, so halvings work.

Fission, fusion and the binding-energy curve

The curve of binding energy per nucleon against nucleon number is the energy map of the nucleus. It rises steeply through the light nuclei, peaks near iron-56 at about 8.8 MeV per nucleon, and falls slowly for the heaviest nuclei. Any process that moves nucleons toward the peak releases energy: splitting a heavy nucleus (fission) and joining light nuclei (fusion) both climb toward iron. The energy released is the difference in total binding energy between the starting nucleus and the products.

energy released = (binding energy of products)
                - (binding energy of reactants)

for fission of one U-235 nucleus: about 200 MeV is released;
it appears as the kinetic energy of the two fragments
(and some neutrons) plus gamma radiation

Worked example. Estimate the energy released when one uranium-235 nucleus fissions into fragments whose binding energy per nucleon averages 8.5 MeV, given U-235 has about 7.6 MeV per nucleon.

change per nucleon = 8.5 - 7.6 = 0.9 MeV
235 nucleons take part (approximately)
energy = 235 x 0.9 = 211 MeV
       = 211 x 10^6 x 1.6 x 10^-19 = 3.4 x 10^-11 J

Fusion in the Sun is the same arithmetic in reverse: four protons combine through a chain of reactions into helium-4, releasing about 26.7 MeV per nucleus formed — small per nucleus but astronomical in total because the Sun fuses about 600 million tonnes of hydrogen every second.

Detecting radiation and handling it safely

Radiation is detected by its ionising effect: a Geiger-Muller tube counts individual particles or photons (each gives a click or count), a cloud chamber shows tracks as condensed droplets along ionisation paths, and a photographic film badge darkens cumulatively with dose. Every measurement must subtract background radiation — the constant low level from cosmic rays, rocks, radon gas and medical sources — recorded with no source present.

  • Alpha: dangerous only if inhaled or swallowed (it is stopped by skin but deposits all its energy in a small volume of tissue); handled with gloves and no eating in the lab.
  • Beta: stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium or by thick clothing; eye protection and distance matter.
  • Gamma: penetrates deeply; lead shielding, distance and limiting exposure time are the protections (dose falls with the inverse square of distance).
  • General rules: minimise time near a source, maximise distance, use shielding, and never point a source at anyone. Tracers in medicine use short-half-life isotopes (technetium-99m, t½ = 6 hours) so activity falls quickly after use.

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Structure) Define isotope and state one pair of isotopes. Answer: Isotopes are nuclei of the same element (same proton number Z) with different numbers of neutrons (different mass number A) — e.g. carbon-12 and carbon-14.
  2. (Radiation) Explain why alpha radiation is more ionising than gamma. Answer: An alpha particle has double charge and moves slowly, so it exerts strong Coulomb forces on nearby electrons over a longer interaction time, stripping many electrons; gamma photons interact only occasionally.
  3. (Equations) Complete: ²¹⁰₈₄Po → ²⁰⁶₈₂Pb + X. Answer: X has A = 4, Z = 2 → ⁴₂He (alpha).
  4. (Binding energy) Explain, in terms of binding energy per nucleon, why fusion releases energy. Answer: Light nuclei have low binding energy per nucleon; fusing them moves products toward the peak of the curve near iron, where each nucleon is more tightly bound; the difference in total binding energy is released.
  5. (Mass defect) State what mass defect represents. Answer: The difference between the mass of a nucleus and the total mass of its separate nucleons; it equals the energy released when the nucleus formed (E = Δmc²), and also the energy required to disassemble it.
  6. (Decay law) Define activity and the decay constant. Answer: Activity is the rate of decay of a sample (decays per second, Bq); the decay constant is the probability per unit time that a given nucleus decays, with A = λN.
  7. (Half-life) A sample's activity drops from 2000 Bq to 250 Bq in 12 days. Find the half-life. Answer: 2000 → 250 is three halvings; t½ = 12/3 = 4 days.
  8. (Randomness) Explain why radioactive decay is described as random yet its rate is predictable. Answer: Each nucleus decays spontaneously with no known trigger, so no individual decay can be predicted; but for a large population the probability per unit time (λ) is constant, so the number decaying per second — the activity — follows A = λN predictably.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Conservation bookkeeping: A and Z both balance in nuclear equations; beta decay keeps A constant while Z changes — write both numbers at every arrow.
  • u to joules: 1 u = 1.661 × 10⁻²⁷ kg; 1 u = 931.5 MeV. Use one route consistently; mixing MeV and joules mid-question fails.
  • Binding energy direction: energy is released when a tightly bound nucleus forms and required to split it; the sign of ΔE follows the arrow.
  • Half-life arithmetic: it is the time to halve the current amount, not to reach zero; count the halvings (80 → 20 is two halvings).
  • ln 2 versus base-2: N = N₀(½)^(t/t½) and N = N₀e^(−λt) are the same law; λ = 0.693/t½ converts between them. Do not apply e-folding time as a half-life.
  • Activity vs count rate: count rate is proportional to activity but reduced by detector geometry and absorption; background radiation must be subtracted before analysis.
  • Decay units: λ in s⁻¹ (or per the time unit given), A in Bq; hours and minutes into seconds when mixing with s⁻¹.
  • Ignoring neutrinos: beta decay equations in modern syllabuses include the antineutrino; omitting it is an accuracy loss where the paper's data sheet includes it.
  • Precision: 2 or 3 s.f. with units; quote c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ and Nₐ = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ from the data sheet.

title: Excretion in Humans
content:
Excretion in Humans

Cambridge IGCSE Biology 0610, Extended route, topic 13 (statement 13.1). What excretion is, the excretory products and organs, and how urea is formed and removed.

13.1 Excretion in humans

  • Excretion is the removal of the waste products of metabolism, toxic substances and excess substances. This is different from egestion, which is the removal of undigested food as faeces.
  • Carbon dioxide from respiration is excreted by the lungs; urea from the breakdown of excess amino acids is excreted by the kidneys in urine; water and some salts leave in sweat and urine; heat is lost through the skin.
  • The liver deaminates excess amino acids, removing the amino group to form ammonia, which is converted into the less toxic urea. Urea travels in the blood to the kidneys.
  • The kidney filters blood, and the useful glucose, water and ions are reabsorbed; urea, excess water and salts form urine, which passes down the ureters to the bladder.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Reasoning chain, applied to why the liver is the site of deamination: amino acids come from excess dietary protein or from the breakdown of body proteins, and removing the amino group produces ammonia, which is toxic. The liver converts it to urea, which is far less toxic and can be carried safely in the blood. Name ammonia, its toxicity, and the conversion — each is a separate mark.
  • Organ identification, applied to which organs excrete which waste: lungs (carbon dioxide and water), kidneys (urea, excess water and salts), skin (water, salts and small urea). A complete answer names the product with each organ, not the organ alone.
  • Distinction reasoning, applied to a colostomy patient whose faeces contain no urea: faeces are egested, not excreted — the undigested material never entered the body's cells, so it carries no metabolic waste. State the excretion-versus-egestion distinction explicitly.

Common errors

  • Calling faeces an excretory product. Egestion is not excretion.
  • Saying the kidneys remove carbon dioxide. That is the lungs' job.
  • Forgetting that urea comes from amino acids, not from fats or carbohydrates.

title: AS Level Chemistry: Alkenes and Addition Reactions
content:
Alkenes AS Level Chemistry

These revision notes cover Topic 5 Alkenes from the Edexcel International AS Level Chemistry specification, detailing hydrocarbon unsaturation, geometric isomerism, electrophilic addition mechanisms, addition polymerisation, and polymer waste management.

Structure and bonding in alkenes

Alkenes and cycloalkenes are unsaturated hydrocarbons containing a carbon-carbon double bond, which consists of one σ bond and one π bond. The general formula for non-cyclic alkenes is CnH2n. A σ bond is formed by the direct head-on overlap of atomic orbitals along the internuclear axis, providing restricted rotation. A π bond is formed by the sideways overlap of adjacent p orbitals above and below the plane of the carbon atoms. The carbon atoms of a C=C double bond are planar, with bond angles of approximately 120 degrees due to three regions of electron density repelling each other.

  • General formula for alkenes: CnH2n
  • Unsaturated hydrocarbons possess a carbon-carbon double bond consisting of one σ bond and one π bond
  • Cycloalkenes also contain a C=C double bond and are unsaturated hydrocarbons
  • The π bond electron cloud is susceptible to attack by electrophiles
  • Carbon atoms of the C=C double bond are trigonal planar with 120° bond angles

Geometric isomerism and E-Z naming

Geometric isomerism arises due to the restricted rotation around the C=C double bond caused by the presence of the π bond. For geometric isomers to exist, each carbon atom of the C=C double bond must be attached to two different groups. When the traditional cis- and trans- naming system breaks down because the groups attached to the double-bonded carbons are not identical or simple, the E-Z naming system must be used. Priorities are assigned to the groups on each carbon using the Cahn-Ingold-Prelog priority rules based on atomic number. The E isomer has the highest priority groups on opposite sides of the double bond, while the Z isomer has the highest priority groups on the same side.

  • Restricted rotation around the C=C double bond prevents free rotation of substituents
  • Each carbon in the double bond must have two different groups attached for geometric isomerism
  • E-Z system is necessary when cis- and trans- terms become ambiguous or break down
  • Priority is determined by higher atomic number attached directly to the double-bonded carbon
  • E means entgegen (opposite sides); Z means zusammen (same side)

Reactions of alkenes

Alkenes undergo addition reactions where the π bond breaks and two new single bonds form. Hydrogen addition occurs at 150 degrees Celsius using a nickel catalyst to form an alkane through catalytic hydrogenation. Halogens add rapidly at room temperature to produce a di-substituted halogenoalkane. Hydrogen halides add across the double bond to produce mono-substituted halogenoalkanes. Steam addition requires a phosphoric acid catalyst or sulfuric acid catalyst under high temperature and pressure to produce alcohols. Acidified potassium manganate(VII) oxidises the double bond in a cold solution to produce a diol, causing a colour change from purple to colourless.

  • Hydrogenation: Alkene + H2 in the presence of a Ni catalyst forms an alkane
  • Halogenation: Alkene + X2 produces a di-substituted halogenoalkane
  • Hydrohalogenation: Alkene + HX produces a mono-substituted halogenoalkane
  • Hydration: Alkene + H2O(g) with an acid catalyst (H3PO4) produces an alcohol
    • Oxidation: Alkene + acidified KMnO4 produces a diol with a purple to colourless transition

Testing for unsaturation

The qualitative test for the presence of a C=C double bond uses bromine or bromine water. When an orange-brown bromine solution is shaken with an alkene, the bromine adds across the double bond in an electrophilic addition reaction, causing the solution to decolourise from orange-brown to colourless. Alkanes do not react with bromine water in the dark and the solution remains orange-brown.

  • Reagent: Bromine water or liquid bromine
    • Observation with an alkene: Colour changes from orange-brown to colourless
  • Observation with an alkane: No reaction, solution remains orange-brown
  • Test confirms the presence of an unsaturated carbon-carbon double bond

Mechanisms of electrophilic addition

Electrophilic addition is the characteristic reaction mechanism of alkenes. An electrophile is an electron pair acceptor. The high electron density of the π bond induces a dipole in non-polar halogen molecules. Curly arrows start from a bond or a lone pair of electrons and point to the electron-deficient site. In the electrophilic addition of bromine to ethene, the π bond electrons attack the bromine molecule, heterolytically breaking the Br-Br bond and forming a cyclic bromonium ion intermediate or carbocation, followed by attack from the bromide ion. In hydrogen bromide addition, HBr is polar. The hydrogen ion acts as an electrophile, and addition to unsymmetrical alkenes such as propene can yield two possible carbocation intermediates. The major product is formed via the more stable carbocation intermediate. Carbocation stability follows the order: tertiary greater than secondary greater than primary, due to the positive inductive effect of alkyl groups which push electron density towards the positively charged carbon atom.

  • Electrophile definition: An electron pair acceptor
  • Curly arrows must start precisely from a bond or a lone pair
    • Carbocation stability order: tertiary > secondary > primary
  • Primary carbocation has one alkyl group attached to the positively charged carbon
  • Secondary carbocation has two alkyl groups attached
  • Tertiary carbocation has three alkyl groups attached, making it the most stable due to maximum positive inductive effect
  • Major product prediction follows Markovnikov rule: the hydrogen adds to the carbon with more hydrogens already attached

Addition polymerisation

Addition polymerisation involves many small unsaturated alkene molecules, called monomers, joining together to form a long saturated chain called a polymer. The double bond of each monomer opens up to form single covalent bonds with adjacent monomers. To draw the repeat unit given the monomer, change the C=C double bond into a single C-C bond, extend the bonds outside square brackets, and place a letter n outside. To find the monomer from a repeat unit, identify the two-carbon repeat backbone and convert the single bond back into a double bond.

    Polymerisation type: Addition polymerisation of alkenes
  • Monomers contain a carbon-carbon double bond; polymers contain a saturated carbon backbone
  • Repeat unit formula is enclosed in brackets with bonds extending through the brackets
  • Do not leave dangling double bonds inside the repeat unit structure
  • Poly(ethene) and poly(chloroethene) are standard examples of addition polymers

Polymer disposal and environmental management

Chemists limit environmental problems caused by polymer disposal through innovative chemical engineering. Non-biodegradable polymers persist in landfill sites. Biodegradable polymers, such as those made from poly(lactic acid) derived from plant starch, are broken down by microorganisms into natural substances. Incineration of halogen-containing polymers like poly(chloroethene) produces toxic acidic waste gases such as hydrogen chloride. Chemists remove these toxic waste gases by flue gas desulfurisation or base neutralisation, passing the waste gases through alkaline scrubbers containing calcium carbonate or calcium oxide to neutralise the acidic gases before they escape into the atmosphere.

  • Biodegradable polymers degrade naturally via microorganisms
  • Incineration of polymers releases thermal energy but can produce toxic waste gases
  • Poly(chloroethene) combustion produces toxic hydrogen chloride gas
  • Acidic waste gases are removed using alkaline scrubbers or neutralisation towers
  • Calcium carbonate or calcium oxide reacts with HCl to form neutral salts and water

Typical mistakes

  • Mistake: Drawing curly arrows starting from empty space rather than from a bond or lone pair. Correction: Always start curly arrows precisely on a covalent bond line or a pair of non-bonding electrons.
  • Mistake: Forgetting that carbocation stability dictates the major product. Correction: Remember that tertiary carbocations are more stable than secondary, which are more stable than primary, because alkyl groups donate electron density.
  • Mistake: Leaving a double bond inside the repeat unit of an addition polymer. Correction: Convert the double bond into a single bond and ensure the bonds extend outside the square brackets.
  • Mistake: Confusing the E and Z labels by not applying priority rules correctly. Correction: Assign priorities using atomic numbers to the groups on each carbon of the double bond separately.

Exam-style questions

    1. State the general formula for alkenes and define the term unsaturated hydrocarbon. Answer: The general formula is CnH2n. An unsaturated hydrocarbon contains only carbon and hydrogen atoms with at least one carbon-carbon double bond consisting of a σ and a π bond. (1 mark for general formula, 1 mark for definition).
    2. Explain why geometric isomerism can occur in pent-2-ene but not in pent-1-ene. Answer: Pent-2-ene has restricted rotation about the C=C double bond and each carbon of the double bond is attached to two different groups (a methyl group and a hydrogen atom on one, an ethyl group and a hydrogen atom on the other). Pent-1-ene has one carbon of the double bond attached to two identical hydrogen atoms, so geometric isomers cannot form. (2 marks).
    3. Outline the mechanism for the electrophilic addition of hydrogen bromide to propene, naming the major product and explaining why it forms in greater yield. Answer: Draw the curly arrow from the C=C π bond to the hydrogen of HBr, and another arrow from the H-Br bond to the bromine atom. Show two possible carbocation intermediates: a secondary carbocation and a primary carbocation. The major product is 2-bromopropane, which forms via the secondary carbocation because secondary carbocations are more stable than primary carbocations due to the electron-donating inductive effect of two alkyl groups. (4 marks).
    4. Describe the qualitative test to distinguish between hexane and hexene. Answer: Add bromine water to both liquids and shake. Hexene decolourises the orange-brown bromine water to colourless due to electrophilic addition across the double bond. Hexane shows no reaction, and the orange-brown colour remains. (2 marks).
    5. Explain how chemists minimise environmental hazards caused by the disposal of poly(chloroethene). Answer: Poly(chloroethene) is non-biodegradable and produces toxic hydrogen chloride gas upon incineration. Chemists pass the waste gases through alkaline scrubbers or neutralisation towers containing calcium carbonate to react with and neutralise the acidic hydrogen chloride before release. (3 marks).

Use these notes alongside active recall and past paper question practice. Ensure you can draw mechanisms step by step with correct curly arrow origins. Proceed next to review Halogenoalkanes and Reaction Mechanisms.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • E/Z naming, applied to CHBr=CHCl: on each carbon, the group with the higher atomic number takes priority. Br beats H and Cl beats H, so if the two higher-priority groups are on opposite sides, the isomer is E. Compare atomic numbers on the atom attached to the double bond, not the whole group.
  • Markovnikov addition, applied to propene with HBr: the electrophile H⁺ adds to the carbon with more hydrogens, so the carbocation forms on the more substituted carbon. The major product is 2-bromopropane. The stability order is tertiary > secondary > primary carbocation, and that order explains the major product.
  • Mechanism marks: show a curly arrow from the C=C π bond to the H of HBr, then a second curly arrow from the Br⁻ lone pair to the positive carbon. The first arrow is the step that earns the mark, so draw it from the bond, not from a carbon.
  • Bromine water test: decolourisation of orange bromine water shows unsaturation. An alkane does not decolourise it, so an alkene and an alkane are distinguished by this test alone.

title: Exam technique: Information Representation
content:
### What earns the marks
For two complement, inversion plus one stated earns the method mark before the value. For floating point, mantissa plus exponent roles stated earn one mark each. For normalisation, the leading-bit rule quoted earns the precision mark.
### Traps
Error: sign bit ignored in range. Correction: an n-bit signed range tops at 2^(n-1) - 1. Error: larger exponent read as more precision. Correction: exponent sets range, mantissa sets precision. Error: normalised form guessed. Correction: mantissa starts with 0.1 or 1.0 pattern per the scheme.
### Worked example
Write -45 in 8-bit two's complement. First write 45 in binary: 00101101. Invert every bit to get 11010010, then add 1 to get 11010011. Check: the sign bit has weight -128, so the value is -128 + 64 + 16 + 2 + 1 = -45, which matches.
### Check yourself
State the range of an 8-bit two's complement integer, and say which bit sets the sign. The range is -128 to +127, and the leftmost bit is the sign bit with weight -128.

### Worked example
Write -45 in 8-bit two's complement. First write 45 in binary: 00101101. Invert every bit to get 11010010, then add 1 to get 11010011. Check: the sign bit has weight -128, so the value is -128 + 64 + 16 + 2 + 1 = -45, which matches.
### Check yourself
State the range of an 8-bit two's complement integer, and say which bit sets the sign. The range is -128 to +127, and the leftmost bit is the sign bit with weight -128.

title: Exam technique: Communication and Networking
content:
### What earns the marks
For switching and protocols, describe earns marks for the mechanism plus its consequence: packets carry addresses and sequence numbers so routers forward independently and the receiver reassembles. For TCP vs UDP, justify earns marks for matching reliability to the use case, not for declaring one better. For security, name earns the control plus what it inspects: packet-filtering checks headers against rules.
### Traps
Error: circuit-switching features credited to packet switching. Correction: dedicated path and guaranteed bandwidth are circuit properties. Error: TCP recommended for live video. Correction: delay hurts more than loss there, so UDP. Error: claiming wireless uses collision detection. Correction: senders cannot listen while sending, so avoidance (RTS/CTS).
### Worked example
A local area network of computers in one room connects to the internet through a router. The router uses the IP address to send packets to the correct network. Each computer's network card has a MAC address that is fixed at manufacture, and a switch uses it to deliver frames within the local network.
### Check yourself
Explain the difference between an IP address and a MAC address. An IP address is logical and can change, for example when a device joins another network. A MAC address is physical and identifies the network card itself.
