title: Experimental Techniques and Chemical Analysis
content:
Experimental Techniques and Chemical Analysis

Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry 0620, Extended route, topic 12 (statements 12.1–12.5). Apparatus and measurement, titration, chromatography and Rf, separation and purification, and the tests for ions and gases. Practical skills are examined directly in Paper 5 or 6.

12.1 to 12.2 Apparatus and titration

  • Measure time with a stopwatch, temperature with a thermometer, mass with a balance, volume of liquids with a burette, pipette or measuring cylinder. A volumetric pipette delivers one exact volume; a burette delivers a variable, measured volume.
  • Titration setup: rinse the burette with the solution it will hold, fill above zero, run out to remove the air bubble in the tip, record the initial reading at eye level with the meniscus. Swirl throughout and wash down near the endpoint.

12.3 Chromatography

  • Separation happens because components differ in solubility in the solvent and attraction to the paper. Rf = distance moved by substance ÷ distance moved by the solvent. Colourless substances are located with a locating agent such as ninhydrin.

12.4 Separation and purification

  • Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid; crystallisation obtains a dissolved solid; simple distillation obtains a solvent; fractional distillation separates miscible liquids with close boiling points. Purity is assessed by a sharp melting or boiling point.

12.5 Ion and gas tests

  • Carbonate + dilute acid → carbon dioxide (turns limewater milky). Halides with acidified silver nitrate: white (Cl⁻), cream (Br⁻), yellow (I⁻). Sulfate with acidified barium chloride → white precipitate. Nitrate + sodium hydroxide + aluminium foil → ammonia. Flame tests: lithium/calcium red, sodium yellow, potassium lilac, copper(II) green-blue, barium light green.
  • Aqueous cations with aqueous sodium hydroxide: copper(II) gives a blue precipitate soluble in excess only in ammonia; iron(II) pale green, iron(III) red-brown, aluminium white soluble in excess, zinc white soluble in excess. Ammonia: copper(II) deep blue solution, zinc white precipitate soluble in excess.
  • Gases: hydrogen relights a glowing splint with a squeaky pop; oxygen relights a glowing splint; carbon dioxide turns limewater milky; ammonia turns damp red litmus paper blue; chlorine bleaches damp litmus.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Rf calculation, applied to a spot moving 3.6 cm while the solvent moves 9.0 cm: Rf = 3.6 ÷ 9.0 = 0.40. Rf has no unit and is always less than 1. Two spots with the same Rf on the same chromatogram are likely the same substance — say "on the same chromatogram", because Rf values are not comparable between different runs.
  • Evaluation reasoning, applied to a titration with titres of 22.35, 22.40 and 24.10 cm³: the 24.10 cm³ titre is a concordant outlier — discard it, because the first two agree within 0.10 cm³ and the third does not. Average the concordant titres: (22.35 + 22.40) ÷ 2 = 22.375 cm³, reported as 22.38 cm³.
  • Plan-a-method questions: name the independent variable (what you change), the dependent variable (what you measure) and the control variables (what you keep the same). Then give the safety point and one improvement. Structure answers in that order and every part of the question gets its mark.
  • Ion identification, applied to a white solid giving a yellow precipitate with silver nitrate that dissolves in excess ammonia: the halide is iodide. Write the full test, observation and conclusion as a chain — Cambridge marks each link separately, and skipping the observation loses the middle marks.

Common errors

  • Calling the milky limewater precipitate "a white precipitate in the test tube". The observation is that limewater turns milky.
  • Forgetting to state that the burette reading is taken at eye level to avoid parallax error.
  • Reporting Rf to the wrong precision or without showing the division.

title: Superposition — Study Notes
content:
Superposition

Principle of superposition

When two or more waves meet at a point, the resultant displacement is the vector sum of the individual displacements. Constructive interference occurs where the waves are in phase; destructive interference occurs where they are in antiphase.

Stationary waves

  • A stationary wave forms when two progressive waves of the same frequency, amplitude and wavelength travel in opposite directions and superpose.
  • Nodes are points of zero amplitude; antinodes are points of maximum amplitude. Adjacent nodes (or antinodes) are separated by λ/2.
  • On a string fixed at both ends, the fundamental frequency is f = v/(2L), so the wavelength is λ = 2L.

Interference

For coherent sources (same frequency and a constant phase difference) with slit separation a and screen distance D, the fringe spacing is Δx = λD/a.

Diffraction

Diffraction is the spreading of a wave after it passes through a gap or round an edge. It is greatest when the gap width is comparable to the wavelength.

Diffraction grating

For a grating with slit spacing d, the angle θ of the nth-order maximum satisfies nλ = d sin θ. A grating with more lines per metre gives a smaller d and larger angles of diffraction.

Worked example: light of wavelength 600 nm passes through two slits 0.30 mm apart, with a screen 1.5 m away. Fringe spacing Δx = λD/a = (600 × 10⁻⁹ × 1.5) ÷ (3.0 × 10⁻⁴) = 3.0 mm.

Exam tips: convert nm and mm to metres before using Δx = λD/a. Check the order n when using a grating. Coherence is a requirement for interference, so state it.

The diffraction grating equation

A diffraction grating has many closely spaced slits. Light of wavelength λ leaves the grating at angle θ to form bright maxima when d sin θ = nλ, where d is the slit spacing and n is the order of the maximum. Each order is sharper and more widely separated than a double slit, because the many slits reinforce the bright positions. The number of orders visible is limited by the condition that sin θ cannot exceed 1.

Exam tip: convert the slit spacing to metres before using the grating equation, and note that the central maximum is n = 0.

Two-source interference: a worked calculation

Two coherent loudspeakers emit sound of frequency 680 Hz. The speed of sound is 340 m s⁻¹, so λ = v/f = 340/680 = 0.50 m. A listener walks along a line parallel to the line joining the speakers. At a point where the path difference is 0.75 m, the waves arrive in antiphase, because 0.75 is an odd multiple of λ/2 (0.25 m). The listener hears a minimum there.

Use the path difference, not the distance from one source, to decide the outcome. Path difference = nλ gives a maximum; path difference = (n + ½)λ gives a minimum. Writing the test as a multiple of λ, and not as a raw distance, is the step examiners look for.

Phase difference and path difference

A phase difference of 360° (2π radians) corresponds to a path difference of one wavelength. A phase difference of 180° corresponds to a path difference of λ/2. In general, phase difference = (path difference / λ) × 360°. Questions often give one and ask for the other, so be ready to convert between them.

  • Coherence needs a constant phase difference, which is why two independent light bulbs do not produce a stable fringe pattern.
  • Monochromatic light is needed for sharp fringes, because each wavelength produces its own fringe spacing and the patterns blur together.
  • Fringe spacing is directly proportional to wavelength and to screen distance, and inversely proportional to slit separation. Halving a doubles the spacing.

Stationary waves: harmonics on a pipe

An open pipe has antinodes at both ends, so its fundamental wavelength is 2L and its harmonics are f, 2f, 3f and so on. A pipe closed at one end has a node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end, so its fundamental wavelength is 4L, and it produces only odd harmonics: f, 3f, 5f.

Example: a pipe of length 0.85 m, open at both ends, with speed of sound 340 m s⁻¹. The fundamental is f = v/(2L) = 340/1.7 = 200 Hz, and the second harmonic is 400 Hz.

Common errors that lose marks

  • Using the slit spacing a where the question gives the slit-to-screen distance D, or the reverse. Read the labels in the diagram before substituting.
  • Stating that a stationary wave transfers energy along the string. It does not: energy is confined between the nodes, and the wave transfers no net energy along the medium.
  • Calling the points between two adjacent nodes "in phase" without qualification. Particles between the same two nodes are in phase; particles either side of a node are in antiphase.

title: International GCSE English as a Second Language: Writing Tasks and Themes
content:
International GCSE English as a Second Language: Writing Tasks and Themes

OxfordAQA International GCSE English as a Second Language (9280) assesses writing in a paper of its own (Paper 2 in the current official numbering — some older revision materials list the writing component first, so always check the code on your question paper). This note builds the whole writing skill set from zero: how to read the task, how to choose register, how to plan in five minutes, and how to write each task type — functional and transactional writing, short-form responses, extended discursive writing and narrative writing — across the three exam themes. Every task on this paper is a communication problem, not a grammar test, and the marks follow from solving that problem in the right tone.

What the Writing paper asks of you

The writing component carries 60 marks, is 1 hour 15 minutes long, and counts for 30% of the qualification. Its tasks are progressive: shorter functional writing first, then short-form responses, then one or two extended pieces that may be discursive or narrative. The exact task list and word limits are printed on your paper, so this note teaches the task types rather than guessing a fixed layout — and the word limit given in the question is always binding.

FeatureWhat it means for you
Duration and marks1 hour 15 minutes, 60 marks, 30% of the grade. Roughly one minute of planning per ten minutes of writing.
Task progressionShort functional tasks first (emails, notes, forms), then extended discursive or narrative writing. The later tasks carry more marks — save time for them.
The themesEverything you write sits under one of three theme areas, so vocabulary preparation is finite and examinable.
What earns marksTask fulfilment (did you do what was asked?), register (is the tone right for the reader?), organisation (is it structured?), and linguistic range and accuracy.

The three themes and their topic banks

Every question is drawn from the three OxfordAQA theme areas. You cannot predict the exact topic, but you can prepare vocabulary, examples and opinions for each theme bank, and that preparation is the single highest-return revision you can do for this paper.

ThemeTypical topicsVocabulary to prepare
Identity and cultureFamily life, traditions and festivals, food, personal identity, hobbies, music and film, cultural differencesdescribing habits and routines, comparing traditions, giving opinions about culture, describing people and places from your own experience
Local, national, international and global areas of interestYour town and region, travel and tourism, the environment, technology, news and current events, sportdescribing places, cause and effect language for problems (pollution, congestion), proposing solutions, comparing locations
Current and future study and employmentSchool subjects, exams, ambitions, jobs and careers, work experience, skills, further studydescribing plans and ambitions, talking about ability and skills, justifying choices, writing about the future with will, going to, would like to

The efficient way to revise: for each theme, prepare ten nouns, ten verbs, five adjectives, two personal examples and one opinion with a reason. That is a working vocabulary of about eighty items, and it covers almost anything the paper can ask.

The APF framework: Audience, Purpose, Form

Before writing a single sentence, three decisions control everything else. The exam rewards candidates who make these decisions visibly, because the marker can see that the writing is shaped rather than dumped.

  1. Audience — who reads this? A friend, a teacher, a stranger, an employer, a newspaper reader. This decides formality, pronouns (I and you versus one and people), abbreviations (don't versus do not), and how much you explain.
  2. Purpose — why am I writing? To persuade, inform, request, describe, entertain, complain, advise, or apply. Purpose decides the opening move and the content order: a complaint states the problem then the desired fix; a persuasive piece states the position then the reasons.
  3. Form — what shape does this text have? Email, letter, article, review, report, story. Form decides the layout features the marker looks for: greeting and sign-off on an email, headline and opening hook on an article, a clear introduction and conclusion on an essay.

Worked example of the APF decision: the task says, "Your school is thinking about banning mobile phones. Write an article for the school magazine giving your views." Audience: your classmates and teachers (semi-formal, first person plural we). Purpose: persuade with reasons and examples. Form: article, so you need a headline, a hook opening, paragraphs with linking, and a closing line that lands the point. Once those three answers exist, the plan writes itself.

Register and tone: the formal–informal continuum

Register is the difference between "Hiya, can't come, sorry!" and "Dear Mr Ahmed, I am writing to apologise for my absence." Neither is wrong in itself; each is wrong for the wrong reader. Markers describe the top band as a consistent register suited to audience and purpose — the key word is consistent. One slang phrase in an otherwise formal letter breaks that consistency and costs marks.

FeatureInformal (friend, peer)Formal (teacher, employer, institution)
OpeningHi ..., How are you?Dear Mr/Ms ..., I am writing to ...
Contractionsdon't, I'm, can'tdo not, I am, cannot
QuestionsDirect and chatty: What do you think?Polite forms: I would be grateful if you could ...
OpinionI reckon ..., To be honest ...In my opinion ..., It seems to me that ...
ClosingSee you soon! Best wishesYours sincerely / Yours faithfully

One rule of thumb saves many marks: match the formality of the task, and never mix the two columns inside one text.

Functional and transactional writing: format skeletons

Functional tasks (emails, letters, notes, messages, short articles) are marked for doing the job: covering every content point in the prompt, using the right form, and keeping the register right. A skeleton for each form means your brain can spend its energy on language instead of layout.

  • Email to a friend: greeting → reaction to their news → answers to their questions (one per bullet in the prompt) → your news/questions → closing line.
  • Formal letter or email: Dear ... → why you are writing (one sentence) → the content points in logical order, one paragraph each → what you want to happen → Yours sincerely, name.
  • Article: headline → hook (a question, a surprising fact, a short scene) → two or three paragraphs each making one point → closing line that echoes the hook.
  • Review: what it is → description → evaluation with reasons → recommendation and who it suits.
  • Report: title → introduction stating the scope → findings under clear headings → recommendation.

For every content point in the prompt, write one developed sentence or more. Under-developed content is the most common reason a competent writer scores mid-band: the marker counts content points and how fully each is covered.

Short-form responses: from notes to sentences

Short-form tasks give you information in notes, a table, or a picture and ask for connected sentences. The skill is expansion: each note must become real grammar, not a list with a capital letter.

  • Step 1 — read every note and mark the content points; one sentence minimum per point.
  • Step 2 — add the missing grammar: articles (a, the), pronouns to avoid repetition, a verb in the right tense, connectors (because, so, although, however).
  • Step 3 — check the target reader: if the task says "write to your English-speaking friend", contractions and questions are welcome; if it says "write to the school principal", they are not.

Worked example. The task: "Your friend wants to know about your new school. Use these notes to write a message: new school / big / near home / walk 10 minutes / favourite subject science / teacher good / start football club next month." A weak answer copies the notes. A top-band answer expands every point with grammar and personality: "My new school is really big — there are about a thousand students! The best part is that it's near home, so I only walk ten minutes every morning. My favourite subject is science because the teacher explains everything clearly and lets us do experiments. I've also started a football club — well, it opens next month, and I can't wait." Every note became a sentence; the register is friendly; the message reads like a message.

Extended discursive writing: the argument engine

Discursive tasks (an essay, an opinion article, a for-and-against discussion) reward organisation above fancy vocabulary. The marker needs to find your position, your reasons and your ending without hunting. Build the piece from modules:

  1. Introduction (2-3 sentences): restate the topic in your own words and give your position or the question you will explore. Never copy the prompt wording.
  2. Body paragraph 1: strongest reason. Topic sentence (the point) → explanation (why it is true) → example (a specific case, ideally personal or local) → link back to the position.
  3. Body paragraph 2: second reason, same four-beat shape.
  4. Body paragraph 3 (optional): the other side of the argument, then why your position still wins. This concession move reads as sophisticated thinking.
  5. Conclusion (2-3 sentences): restate the position in fresh words and end with the consequence or a call to action.

Model paragraph with top-band breakdown: "Some people believe that homework should be abolished because it causes stress. In my view, however, homework teaches students to work independently, a skill they will need at university and at work. For example, when I prepared for my maths exam last term, the practice I did at home was what moved my grade from a C to an A. Therefore, rather than abolishing homework, schools should limit its quantity." Why it scores: the topic sentence names the counter-argument, the contrast word however marks the writer's position, the explanation states the reason in abstract terms (independence), the example grounds it in a specific personal case, and the final sentence turns the concession into a balanced recommendation. That is the whole engine: point, reason, example, link — used once per paragraph.

Narrative writing: story craft under time pressure

Narrative tasks ask for a story, and the marker rewards a controlled arc over an ambitious plot. Three moves separate top-band stories from mid-band ones: a clear structure, controlled tense, and concrete detail instead of abstract claims.

  • The arc: opening situation (who, where, when) → an incident that changes things → rising tension in two or three beats → a climax moment → a short resolution or closing image. Plan all five before writing.
  • Tense control: past simple for events (I opened the door), past continuous for background (The rain was falling), past perfect for earlier events (I had forgotten my keys). Choose one main past tense and stay there; tense drift is a classic accuracy loss.
  • Showing, not telling: instead of "I was nervous", write "My hands were shaking as I unfolded the paper." Concrete detail (hands, paper, rain) lets the reader feel the emotion the writer claims.
  • Sentence variation: mix short dramatic sentences ("The door opened.") with longer flowing ones. Sentence control is explicitly rewarded in the writing criteria.

Worked example of turning telling into showing. Weak: "The market was busy and colourful and I felt excited." Top-band: "The market was a wall of noise: vendors shouting prices, scooters threading between the stalls, the smell of grilled corn drifting over everything. I stood on my toes, grinning, trying to see everything at once." The second version names concrete sounds and smells, uses a colon and participles, and shows the excitement through behaviour (standing on toes, grinning) rather than the adjective excited.

The five-minute plan

Planning is not wasted time; it is where the marks are decided. For every extended task, spend five minutes on a grid: APF in one corner (who, why, what form), then five content beats (for discursive: position, reason 1, reason 2, other side, conclusion; for narrative: situation, incident, rising tension, climax, resolution). Under each beat, jot one keyword or example. The writing stage then becomes transcription with style — and the marker sees structure immediately.

Worked examples: task to top-band answer

Worked example 1 — functional task. "You have won a place on a summer course in another country. Write an email to the course organiser. Say why you chose the course, ask two questions about accommodation and food, and explain your travel arrangements."

APF:  Audience = adult organiser (formal, no slang)
      Purpose  = inform + request information (cover all three bullets)
      Form     = email: greeting, clear paragraphs, sign-off
Plan: 1 why chosen  2 question: accommodation  3 question: food
      4 travel arrangements  5 closing

Model answer: "Dear Ms Carter, I am writing to confirm my place on the International Summer Course in July and to say how delighted I am to have been accepted. I chose this course because I hope to study engineering at university, and the robotics module is exactly the experience I need. I would be grateful if you could tell me a little about the accommodation. Will students stay with host families or in a residence? I also have a question about food: will it be possible to provide vegetarian meals? As for my travel, I will fly from Kuala Lumpur on 2 July and expect to arrive at the airport at about three o'clock in the afternoon. Thank you for your help. Yours sincerely, Amir Rahman." Why it scores: every bullet is covered and developed (the reason is specific — robotics and engineering; the questions are polite and precise; the travel gives a date, a route and a time), the register is consistently formal (I am writing, I would be grateful, no contractions), and the form features (greeting, sign-off, clear paragraphing) are all present.

Worked example 2 — discursive task. "Some students think that school uniforms should be banned. Write an article for your school magazine giving your views."

Plan: position = keep uniforms (with a change: student input on design)
      P1 identity/equality argument + example of bullying over clothes
      P2 practical argument (cost, mornings) + example
      P3 concession: freedom matters — answer it with the design compromise
      Conclusion: keep, but reform

Model opening and body paragraph: "Should we all dress the same? Every September the uniform debate returns to our school, and this year I think we can answer it honestly: uniforms should stay, but they should change. The strongest reason is equality. When everyone wears the same clothes, nobody is judged for what their parents can afford. At my old school, a classmate was mocked for wearing the same jacket every day; with a uniform, that cruelty simply had no surface to attach to." Why it scores: the headline question hooks, the opening states a nuanced position (stay, but change), and the first body paragraph runs the point–reason–example–link engine with a concrete story instead of a vague claim.

Exam-style questions and answers

Practise each of these in timed conditions, planning with APF first.

  1. (Functional, 12 marks worth of practice) Your English-speaking friend has invited you to a festival in their country. Write an email: thank them, ask about what to wear and what to bring, explain why you are looking forward to it. Answer outline: informal register, three developed paragraphs, two clear questions, contractions and a warm closing.
  2. (Short-form) Notes: library / opens 8am / new computers / free wifi / quiet room upstairs. Write four sentences for the school website. Answer outline: expand each note with articles, linking and a positive recommendation sentence.
  3. (Discursive) "Public transport should be free for everyone." Write an article giving your views. Answer outline: position (free for students and the elderly at least), reasons (cost of living, pollution, congestion), concession (who pays — taxation), conclusion (phased scheme).
  4. (Narrative) Write a story that begins: "The letter had been sitting on the table for three days." Answer outline: five-beat arc, past-tense control, showing detail in the climax, closing image.
  5. (Review) A travel website wants reviews of places in your area. Write a review of a place visitors should see. Answer outline: identify the place, describe it, evaluate with reasons, recommend to a named type of visitor.
  6. (Formal letter) You want a part-time job at a local café. Write a letter explaining why you are suitable and asking for an interview. Answer outline: formal opening, two skill examples with evidence, polite request, Yours sincerely.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Register drift: starting formally ("Dear Sir") and ending informally ("See ya!"). Pick one register in the plan and check it at the end.
  • Bullet copying: answering a content-point prompt as a list. Every point needs a full, developed sentence — the marker looks for development, not mention.
  • Wrong form: writing an essay when the task asked for an email. The form features (greeting, sign-off, headline) are easy marks and easy to lose.
  • Ignoring the word limit: the limit on the paper is binding. Under-length answers cap your content marks; long answers eat the time later tasks need.
  • Memorised paragraphs: examiners read thousands of scripts; a pasted "global warming is one of the biggest problems" paragraph without task-specific detail reads as filler and cannot reach the top band.
  • Time management: spending 30 minutes on the short task and 10 on the extended one inverts the mark distribution. Budget roughly 15 minutes for short tasks and the remainder for extended writing, with 5 minutes to check.
  • Theme blindness: not preparing vocabulary for the three themes leaves you translating in the exam. Translation costs accuracy, range and time at once.
  • Final check failure: the last three minutes should hunt only for verb tenses, subject–verb agreement, articles and spelling of your most-used theme words.

Equations and symbols

The writing paper is marked on content, organisation and language, so the "equations" below are the structures that win each of those. Each is followed by a key defining every term in it — check a draft against them and the missing term is the mark you are about to lose.

Answer structures

developed point = point + detail + example or consequence
Key: point = the claim in one sentence; detail = the specifics (who, when, how much); example or consequence = what follows from it. A list of undeveloped points scores in the lowest content band however long it is.

paragraph = topic sentence + support + link
Key: topic sentence = the paragraph's one idea, stated first; support = two or three sentences of detail; link = a connective that carries the reader to the next paragraph. Organisation marks are given for exactly this shape, visible at a glance.

formal email or letter = salutation + purpose + details + closing
Key: salutation = Dear Mr/Ms + surname, or Dear Sir/Madam if unknown; purpose = why you are writing, in the first line; details = the numbered points from the task; closing = Yours sincerely (named) or Yours faithfully (unnamed). Wrong closing with the wrong salutation costs a register mark.

review = summary + evaluation + recommendation
Key: summary = what the thing is; evaluation = what worked and what did not, with reasons; recommendation = who should try it and why. A review that only describes has not reviewed.

article = headline + hook + development + conclusion
Key: headline = short and specific; hook = a question, a statistic or a striking detail that makes the reader continue; development = two or three paragraphs each making one point; conclusion = a closing thought, not a summary of what has just been said.

Language control

tense frame: narrative = past simple; discursive = present simple; future plans = will or going to
Key: the dominant tense of each task type. Choose it in the plan and keep it: tense drift mid-paragraph is the single most common language-band limiter in this paper.

connective ladder = addition (moreover) → contrast (however) → cause (therefore) → example (for instance) → conclusion (in conclusion)
Key: the five functions a linking word can perform. Using the right function with the wrong word ("although" for "therefore") reads as a content error as well as a language one.

word budget: plan 10%, write 80%, check 10% of the time allowed
Key: the split that keeps a candidate inside the word limit without losing the checking pass. Under-length answers lose content marks; over-length answers lose accuracy marks to unchecked errors.

range = simple + compound + complex sentence in every paragraph
Key: simple = one clause; compound = two main clauses joined by and/but/so; complex = a main clause plus a subordinate clause (because, although, which). The language band rewards variety, and variety is countable — one of each per paragraph is the target.

title: Circular Measure — Study Notes
content:
Circular Measure

Edexcel International A Level Mathematics — Pure Mathematics 1 (WMA11), sat at AS: radian measure, arc length, and the areas and perimeters of sectors and segments. Every formula here takes its angle in radians — that is the single fact most marks hinge on.

Radians

One radian is the angle at the centre of a circle subtended by an arc whose length equals the radius. The full circumference is 2πr, so a full turn is 2π radians and π radians = 180°.

  • Degrees → radians: multiply by π/180. Example: 150° = 150π/180 = 5π/6 ≈ 2.618 rad.
  • Radians → degrees: multiply by 180/π. Example: 1.5 rad = 1.5 × 180/π ≈ 85.9°.

Learn the common values: 30° = π/6, 45° = π/4, 60° = π/3, 90° = π/2, 180° = π, 360° = 2π. Leave answers in terms of π unless the question asks for a decimal — and when it does, give three significant figures.

Arc Length

s = rθ (θ in radians).

Example: r = 6, θ = π/3 gives s = 6 × π/3 = 2π.

A chord splits the circumference into a minor arc and a major arc, and their lengths add to 2πr. If a question gives the major angle, use θ_major = 2π − θ_minor before substituting.

Sector Area

A = ½r²θ.

Example: r = 5, θ = 1.2 gives A = ½ × 25 × 1.2 = 15.

Minor and major sector areas add to πr². The perimeter of a sector is P = 2r + s = 2r + rθ — the two straight edges count, so an arc length alone is not a perimeter.

Segment Area

A = ½r²(θ − sin θ). For r = 2, θ = π/2: A = 2(π/2 − 1) = π − 2.

The segment is the sector minus the triangle ½r²sin θ — that subtraction is where the formula comes from, and writing it down earns method marks even if the arithmetic slips. Its perimeter is the arc plus the chord, with chord length 2r sin(θ/2).

Putting It Together

Worked example: a sector has radius 8 cm and angle 1.1 rad. Arc length s = 8 × 1.1 = 8.8 cm. Area A = ½ × 64 × 1.1 = 35.2 cm². Perimeter P = 2 × 8 + 8.8 = 24.8 cm.

Rearranging

  • θ = s/r (must be radians)
  • θ = 2A/r²
  • r = s/θ, and r = √(2A/θ) — isolate the squared term first, then take the positive root only, since a radius is a length.

Exam traps: never mix degrees into s = rθ or A = ½r²θ — convert first, and check the calculator is in radian mode. Sketch the sector and mark r and θ before computing. Read whether the question asks for the major or the minor arc, sector, or segment, and confirm area answers carry squared units while arcs and perimeters are plain lengths.

Worked example: arc length and sector area

A sector has radius 5 cm and angle 0.8 radians. The arc length is rθ = 5 × 0.8 = 4 cm. The sector area is ½r²θ = ½ × 25 × 0.8 = 10 cm².

Both formulas need the angle in radians. If the question gives degrees, convert first: 60° = π/3 radians, and 1 radian is about 57.3°. Writing a degree value into rθ is one of the most common lost marks in this topic.

Exact answers with π

For radius 6 cm and angle π/3, the arc length is 6 × π/3 = 2π cm, and the sector area is ½ × 36 × π/3 = 6π cm². Leave answers in terms of π when the question asks for an exact value, and give a decimal only if it asks for one.

Segment area

A segment is the region between a chord and an arc. Its area is the sector area minus the area of the triangle formed by the two radii and the chord, so segment = ½r²(θ − sin θ).

Example: with r = 5 and θ = 0.8, sin 0.8 is about 0.7174, so the segment area is ½ × 25 × (0.8 − 0.7174) = 1.03 cm² to 2 decimal places. Keep sin θ in your calculator, not rounded, until the final line.

Finding an angle or radius from a perimeter or arc

If an arc has length 12 cm on a circle of radius 4 cm, the angle is θ = 12/4 = 3 radians. If the perimeter of a sector is given, the perimeter is 2r + rθ, so set that expression equal to the known value and solve for the unknown.

  • Check that the answer is reasonable: an angle of 3 radians is less than π, so the sector must be less than a half-disc.
  • Sketch the sector and label the radii and the angle before you substitute.
  • When a question combines two sectors or a sector with a triangle, find each area separately and then add or subtract, stating which operation you used.

title: Analysing Language Choices — Study Notes
content:
Language analysis asks how a writer uses words to create an effect. A device is only worth naming if you explain what it does and why the writer chose it.

Identifying devices

Name the device precisely, then move straight to its effect.

Common devices

  • Simile: a comparison using like or as, for example "like a black curtain drawn across the sky".
  • Metaphor: a direct comparison with no like or as.
  • Personification: giving human qualities to something non-human, for example "the city devoured the last of the daylight".
  • Onomatopoeia: a word that imitates a sound, such as buzz or crack.
  • Hyperbole: deliberate exaggeration for effect.

Explaining the effect

A strong comment has three parts: the word or phrase, what it suggests, and the reader's likely response.

Word-level analysis

  • Consider connotations: the feelings a word carries beyond its literal meaning.
  • Compare a chosen word with a plausible alternative to show why this one works better.
  • Notice verbs and adjectives, since they often carry the emotional weight of a description.

Sentence-level analysis

  • A short sentence after several long ones creates emphasis or sudden impact.
  • A list of three can build rhythm or momentum.
  • A rhetorical question makes the reader pause and consider the point.

Structuring your answer

Choose two or three clear examples rather than listing everything. Each paragraph should name the device, quote the words, and explain the effect in full sentences.

title: Algebra — Graphs — Study Notes
content:
Algebra — Graphs

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): straight lines (gradient, intercept), key curves (quadratic, cubic, reciprocal, exponential), tangents, kinematic reading.

1. Straight lines

  • Gradient m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁).
  • y = mx + c; parallel ⇒ equal m; perpendicular ⇒ m₁m₂ = −1.

Example: through (2, −1) parallel to y = 3x + 1: y + 1 = 3(x − 2) ⇒ y = 3x − 7.

2. Drawing curves

Table of values, plot, smooth curve. Parabola symmetry axis x = −b/2a. Recognise reciprocal y = 1/x (two branches) and exponential y = aˣ (through (0,1)).

3. Interpreting

  • Roots = x-intercepts; y-intercept from x = 0.
  • Turning points of quadratics by completing the square.

4. Tangents and rates

Gradient of tangent at a point = instantaneous rate: draw a large triangle, rise/run. Area under a speed–time graph = distance (trapezium estimate).

5. Graphical solutions

Simultaneous: intersection points. Quadratic = line: intersections give roots. Read off carefully to the accuracy allowed.

Exam tips: quote gradients as fractions where exact; when estimating a tangent gradient, use a triangle spanning at least 4 grid squares.

Plotting and reading straight-line graphs

A table of values is set up from the equation, points are plotted and joined with a ruler. For y = mx + c, m is the gradient and c the y-intercept. The gradient is the change in y divided by the change in x, measured on a large triangle drawn on the line, not between two points read from a table.

Quadratic and cubic curves

Curves are drawn freehand as smooth curves through plotted points. Turning points, roots (where the curve cuts the x-axis) and the y-intercept are read directly from the graph. A quadratic has one turning point; a cubic can have up to two.

Using graphs to solve equations

To solve f(x) = k, draw the line y = k and read the x-coordinates where it meets the curve. Intersections of two graphs give simultaneous solutions. Always state the solutions to the accuracy the question asks for.

Worked example: gradient and equation of a line

A line passes through (1, 3) and (4, −3). The gradient is (−3 − 3)/(4 − 1) = −6/3 = −2. Substituting into y = mx + c with the point (1, 3) gives 3 = −2 + c, so c = 5 and the equation is y = −2x + 5.

A parallel line has the same gradient, so a line through (0, 1) parallel to this one is y = −2x + 1. A perpendicular line has gradient 1/2.

Turning points of a quadratic

For y = x² − 6x + 5, complete the square: y = (x − 3)² − 4. The minimum turning point is (3, −4), and the curve crosses the x-axis where (x − 3)² = 4, that is at x = 1 and x = 5. Sketch the curve through these points and label the turning point.

Gradient of a curve at a point

Between two points on a curve, the average rate of change is the gradient of the chord. To estimate the gradient at a point, draw a tangent by eye and find its gradient from two clearly read points on the tangent, using a large triangle. The answer will only be as accurate as your tangent.

Reading a graph in context

A distance–time graph has gradient equal to speed, so a horizontal section means the object is stationary. A speed–time graph has gradient equal to acceleration, and the area under it equals the distance travelled. Always state the units of the gradient, for example m/s or m/s².

  • Plot points carefully and join curves with a smooth line, not straight segments.
  • When a question asks you to use a graph to solve an equation, draw the line y = (the right-hand side) and read off the x-values where the curve crosses it.

title: Quadratics — Study Notes
content:
Quadratics

Edexcel International A Level Mathematics — Pure Mathematics 1 (WMA11), sat at AS. Quadratic questions ask for a turning point, the roots, or a condition on a parameter. Most multi-part questions use all three, so decide the job of each part before you calculate.

Start from a question

The function is f(x) = 2x² − 8x + 11.

  1. Find the minimum value of f(x) and the value of x at which it occurs.
  2. Find the values of k for which f(x) = k has real roots.
  3. Find the value of m for which the line y = x + m is a tangent to y = f(x).

Part 1. Complete the square: f(x) = 2(x − 2)² + 3. The minimum value is 3, at x = 2.

Part 2. f(x) = k gives 2x² − 8x + (11 − k) = 0. The discriminant is 64 − 8(11 − k) = 8k − 24. Real roots need 8k − 24 ≥ 0, so k ≥ 3, which agrees with Part 1.

Part 3. Substituting y = x + m gives 2x² − 9x + (11 − m) = 0. A tangent needs equal roots, so 81 − 8(11 − m) = 0. That gives 8m − 7 = 0, so m = 7/8.

Turning points and the square

For ax² + bx + c, the turning point is at x = −b/2a. The sign of a decides the type: a > 0 gives a minimum and a < 0 gives a maximum. Example: for 2x² − 12x + 7, the turning point is at x = 3, and the value there is 18 − 36 + 7 = −11.

Solving

Try factorising first. If that fails, use x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac))/2a and simplify the surd. Example: 3x² + 5x − 4 = 0 has discriminant 25 + 48 = 73, so x = (−5 ± √73)/6.

The discriminant counts roots

D = b² − 4ac gives the number of real roots: D > 0 gives two distinct roots, D = 0 gives one repeated root, and D < 0 gives none. Example: 4x² + kx + 9 = 0 has equal roots when k² = 4 × 4 × 9 = 144, so k = ±12. With k = 12 the equation is (2x + 3)² = 0.

A parameter inside the discriminant

When D contains an unknown, form the inequality and solve it. Example: x² + (k − 1)x + 4 = 0 has real roots when (k − 1)² − 16 ≥ 0. So |k − 1| ≥ 4, which gives k ≤ −3 or k ≥ 5.

Sketch, then read the region

For a positive a, the curve is below the x-axis between its roots and above it outside them. Example: 2x² − x − 6 < 0 factorises as (2x + 3)(x − 2) < 0, so −3/2 < x < 2.

Example: 5 − 3x − 2x² ≥ 0. Multiplying by −1 gives 2x² + 3x − 5 ≤ 0, and the inequality reverses. (2x + 5)(x − 1) ≤ 0 gives −5/2 ≤ x ≤ 1.

A line and a curve

Set the two equations equal and rearrange into one quadratic. Example: y = x + 3 and y = 2x² − x meet where 2x² − 2x − 3 = 0. Here D = 28 > 0, so the line cuts the curve at two points.

Traps that cost marks

  • Multiplying an inequality by a negative number and forgetting to reverse it.
  • Using D = 0 for a "no real roots" condition, when it should be D < 0.
  • Giving a single value when the question allows a range of values.
  • Dropping the ± when taking the square root of both sides.

title: Exam technique: Ratio, Rate and Proportion
content:
### What earns the marks
For sharing in a ratio, total parts and value of one part each earn a mark: write 5 parts = 600 before splitting. For scales and maps, the real-distance multiplication shown earns the method mark, with each unit conversion (cm to m to km) credited. For proportion with powers, the constant k found first earns the mark: write y = k x squared and solve for k.
### Traps
Error: dividing by 2 and 3 directly for a 2:3 split. Correction: parts first, always. Error: 1.40 hours for 1 h 40 min in speed questions. Correction: 40 min = 2/3 h. Error: linear scaling for an x-squared relation. Correction: square the ratio. Error: inverted map scale (dividing by 50000). Correction: real is bigger than map.
### Worked example
Share £120 in the ratio 2 : 3 : 7. The total parts are 12, so one part is £10 and the shares are £20, £30 and £70. Check: 20 + 30 + 70 = 120. For speed, 150 km in 2.5 hours gives 150 ÷ 2.5 = 60 km/h. Direct proportion means y = kx, so doubling x doubles y.
### Check yourself
Share £45 in the ratio 1 : 4. Find each share and check that they add up to £45. The shares are £9 and £36, because there are 5 parts and each is £9.

### Worked example
Share £120 in the ratio 2 : 3 : 7. The total parts are 12, so one part is £10 and the shares are £20, £30 and £70. Check: 20 + 30 + 70 = 120. For speed, 150 km in 2.5 hours gives 150 ÷ 2.5 = 60 km/h. Direct proportion means y = kx, so doubling x doubles y.

title: Oscillations and Waves II — Study Notes
content:
Oscillations and Waves II

Progressive vs Stationary

Progressive waves transfer energy; stationary waves store it in loops. Stationary patterns arise from two identical waves travelling in opposite directions (reflections on strings, air columns).

PropertyProgressiveStationary
Amplitudesame for all pointsvaries: nodes zero, antinodes max
Phasevaries along wavesame within a loop, π flip across nodes
Energytransferredtrapped

Harmonics

A string fixed at both ends: f₁ = v/2L, then 2f₁, 3f₁… Closed pipes resonate at odd multiples; open pipes at all multiples.

Superposition Applications

  • Young's double slit: x = λD/a — evidence light is a wave
  • Diffraction grating: d sin θ = nλ — resolution of spectra
  • Noise-cancelling headphones: destructive interference of antiphase sound

Polarization Applications

Polaroid sunglasses cut glare from horizontal surfaces; stress analysis in plastics; LCD screens control light with twisted polarizers. Malus' law I = I₀cos²θ.

Exam tips: 'explain' marks want the physics: path difference, phase, node/antinode conditions — not just formula substitution.

title: Work, Energy and Power — Study Notes
content:
Work, energy and power

Work

  • Work done = force × displacement in the direction of the force, W = Fs cos θ. Unit: joule (J), where 1 J = 1 N m.
  • No work is done by a force that acts perpendicular to the displacement, such as the normal contact force on a body moving along a horizontal surface.

Energy stores and transfers

Gravitational potential energy, kinetic energy, elastic potential energy, chemical energy and thermal energy are energy stores. Work done transfers energy from one store to another.

Conservation of energy

Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred. Where only conservative forces such as gravity act, the total mechanical energy is constant. Where non-conservative forces such as friction or air resistance act, the energy they dissipate appears as thermal energy.

Kinetic and gravitational potential energy

  • Kinetic energy: Ek = ½mv².
  • Gravitational potential energy change near the Earth's surface: ΔEp = mgΔh.

Power and efficiency

  • Power = work done ÷ time = energy transferred ÷ time. Unit: watt (W), where 1 W = 1 J s⁻¹.
  • Efficiency = useful energy output ÷ total energy input × 100%. It is always less than 100%.

Worked example: a 2.0 kg object falls freely from rest through 5.0 m. Its speed at the bottom, from energy conservation: ½mv² = mgh, so v = √(2gh) = √(2 × 9.81 × 5.0) ≈ 9.9 m s⁻¹.

Exam tips: check whether the question says air resistance is negligible before using conservation of energy. Always convert minutes to seconds in power calculations. Give efficiency as a percentage.

content:

  • Energy Levels and Line Spectra

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

title: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Transformations and Vectors
content:
Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics: Transformations and Vectors

Transformations move shapes on a grid, and vectors describe those moves with numbers. The exam asks two things: perform a transformation and, more often, describe one completely — with its centre, angle, direction, line or scale factor. This note builds the topic from zero: the four transformations and the full-description checklist for each, enlargement and its effect on area, vector notation with the house column-vector form (x; y), vector arithmetic, and the vector-geometry proofs that show lines are parallel or points are collinear.

The four transformations

TransformationWhat changesWhat must be stated in a description
Translationposition only, no rotation or resizethe column vector of the move
Reflectionmirror imagethe line of reflection (e.g. x = 2, y = x)
Rotationturns about a pointcentre, angle, and direction (clockwise or anticlockwise)
Enlargementresizes about a pointcentre and scale factor

The complete description is the mark: "rotation" alone scores nothing; "rotation 90° anticlockwise about (2, 1)" scores fully.

Translation

A translation moves every point by the same vector. In column form (x; y), x is the horizontal move and y the vertical move; right and up are positive.

Worked example. Triangle A has vertices (1, 1), (3, 1), (1, 4). Translate by (4; −2) and give the image coordinates.

(1, 1) → (5, -1)
(3, 1) → (7, -1)
(1, 4) → (5, 2)

The shape is congruent to the original (same size and shape), and the orientation is unchanged.

Reflection

A reflection flips a shape across a line; the line is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining each point to its image. Common lines: x = a (vertical), y = b (horizontal), y = x, y = −x.

Worked example. Reflect the point (3, 5) in the line y = x.

reflection in y = x swaps the coordinates: (3, 5) → (5, 3)

Worked example 2. Reflect (2, 4) in the line x = 1.

the line x = 1 is vertical; the distance of x = 2 from it is 1,
so the image is 1 unit on the other side: (0, 4)

To find the mirror line from a shape and its image, join a point to its image and draw the perpendicular bisector of that segment.

Rotation

A rotation turns a shape about a fixed centre through a given angle. The four standard angles are 90° and 180° in either direction; 90° clockwise equals 270° anticlockwise.

Worked example. Rotate the point (3, 1) 90° clockwise about the origin.

90 ° clockwise about O: (x, y) → (y, -x)
(3, 1) → (1, -3)

Worked example 2. Rotate (2, 5) 180° about the origin.

180 °: (x, y) → (-x, -y)
(2, 5) → (-2, -5)

For a centre other than the origin, translate the centre to the origin, rotate, then translate back — or count the grid squares from the centre.

Enlargement

An enlargement with centre C and scale factor k maps every point so that its distance from C is multiplied by k. Negative scale factors put the image on the far side of the centre; fractional factors between 0 and 1 shrink the shape.

image distance from centre = k x object distance from centre
area of image = k² x area of object

Worked example. Enlarge the point (2, 3) by scale factor 3 about the origin.

(2, 3) → (6, 9)

Worked example 2 (area). A triangle of area 12 cm² is enlarged by scale factor 2.5. Find the image area.

area factor = k² = 6.25
new area = 12 × 6.25 = 75 cm²

Enlargement is the only transformation that changes area (unless k = 1 or −1); translations, reflections and rotations preserve both shape and size.

Vectors: notation and magnitude

A vector has magnitude and direction. In this course it is written as a column vector (x; y): x is the horizontal component, y the vertical. The same vector can be written as a bold letter a with an arrow above it.

column vector (x; y)
magnitude = √(x² + y²)
direction angle to the horizontal: tan(θ) = y/x
equal vectors have the same components; opposite vectors
negate both components

Worked example. Find the magnitude and direction of the vector (3; 4).

magnitude = √(9 + 16) = 5
tan(θ) = 4/3  →  θ = 53.1 ° above the horizontal

Vector arithmetic and geometry

addition: (a; b) + (c; d) = (a + c; b + d)
subtraction: (a; b) - (c; d) = (a - c; b - d)
scalar multiple: k(a; b) = (ka; kb)

position vector of A relative to O: OA
AB = OB - OA
midpoint of AB: (OA + OB)/2

Worked example. OA = (2; 1), OB = (7; 5). Find AB and the midpoint of AB.

AB = OB - OA = (7 - 2; 5 - 1) = (5; 4)
midpoint = ((2 + 7)/2; (1 + 5)/2) = (4.5; 3)

Worked example 2 (parallel). Show that AB is parallel to CD given A(1, 2), B(5, 8), C(0, 1), D(6, 10).

AB = (5 - 1; 8 - 2) = (4; 6)
CD = (6 - 0; 10 - 1) = (6; 9)
(6; 9) = 1.5 x (4; 6), so CD = 1.5 AB: parallel (and longer)

Parallel vectors are scalar multiples of each other; collinear points occur when AB and AC (or AB and BC) are parallel and share a point.

Combining transformations and invariant points

Two transformations applied in sequence are not the same as the reverse order: a reflection followed by a rotation generally differs from the rotation followed by the reflection. When a question asks for the single transformation equivalent to two, apply both to a convenient point (the origin or a vertex) and to a second point, then identify the transformation that maps the original to the final image. Invariant points are points that do not move: every point on a mirror line is invariant under a reflection, the centre of a rotation is invariant, and no point is invariant under a translation.

Worked example. A shape is reflected in the x-axis and then translated by (0; 3). Find the image of (2, 1) and identify any invariant points.

reflection in the x-axis: (2, 1) → (2, -1)
translation by (0; 3): (2, -1) → (2, 2)
No invariant points: the reflection moved every point off the
axis, and the translation then moved everything upward.

Worked example 2 (invariant line). State the invariant points of a reflection in the line y = 2.

Every point with y-coordinate 2 lies on the mirror line and does
not move: the whole line y = 2 is invariant.

Vectors in context: displacement and velocity

Column vectors describe any quantity with magnitude and direction in two dimensions: displacement (a move from one point to another), velocity (displacement per second) and force (a push in a direction). The arithmetic is identical; only the interpretation changes.

  • Displacement: AB is the vector from A to B; a round trip returns to the start, so the sum of the vectors around a closed polygon is zero.
  • Velocity: a velocity vector (3; −2) means 3 units per second right and 2 units per second down; position after t seconds is the starting position plus t × velocity.
  • Resultant: the sum of two vectors; a vector and its negative cancel.

Worked example. A particle starts at (1, 2) and moves with velocity (3; −1) for 4 seconds. Find its final position.

displacement = 4 x (3; -1) = (12; -4)
final position = (1 + 12; 2 - 4) = (13; -2)

Worked examples: vector proofs

Worked example. In triangle OAB, P is the midpoint of OA and Q is the midpoint of OB. Prove PQ is parallel to AB.

OP = (1/2) OA, OQ = (1/2) OB
PQ = OQ - OP = (1/2)(OB - OA) = (1/2) AB
PQ is a scalar multiple of AB, so PQ is parallel to AB
(and half its length).

Exam-style questions and answers

  1. (Translation) Translate (2, 3) by (−1; 4). Answer: add the translation vector: (2, 3) + (−1, 4) = (2 − 1, 3 + 4) = (1, 7).
  2. (Reflection) Reflect (4, 1) in the x-axis. Answer: reflection in the x-axis negates the y-coordinate: x′ = x = 4 and y′ = −y = −1, so the image is (4, −1).
  3. (Rotation) Rotate (5, 2) 90° anticlockwise about the origin. Answer: a 90° anticlockwise turn about the origin maps (x, y) → (−y, x): x′ = −y = −2 and y′ = x = 5, so the image is (−2, 5).
  4. (Enlargement) Enlarge (1, 2) by factor −2 about the origin. Answer: enlargement about the origin maps (x, y) → k(x, y) with k = −2, so (1, 2) becomes (−2, −4); the negative factor puts the image on the opposite side of the centre.
  5. (Description) Describe fully the transformation mapping (1, 1) to (3, 5). Answer: translation vector = image − object = (3 − 1; 5 − 1) = (2; 4), so translation by (2; 4) — one of many correct complete descriptions.
  6. (Magnitude) Find the magnitude of (6; 8). Answer: |v| = √(x² + y²) = √(6² + 8²) = √(36 + 64) = √100 = 10.
  7. (Position vectors) OA = (1; 4), OB = (5; 2). Find AB. Answer: AB = OB − OA = (5; 2) − (1; 4) = (5 − 1; 2 − 4) = (4; −2).
  8. (Collinear) Show A(1, 1), B(3, 4), C(7, 10) are collinear. Answer: AB = (2; 3), AC = (6; 9) = 3 AB — parallel and share A, so collinear.

Typical mistakes and exam traps

  • Incomplete descriptions: "enlargement by 2" omits the centre and loses marks; "reflection" omits the line. State every attribute.
  • Direction of rotation: clockwise and anticlockwise are different transformations; a 90° rotation clockwise is not the same as anticlockwise.
  • Area under enlargement: area scales by k², not k. Doubling the sides quadruples the area.
  • Vector direction: AB = OB − OA, not OA − OB. Reversing the subtraction negates the vector.
  • Column order: (x; y) is horizontal then vertical. Swapping produces a reflection in y = x, not the intended vector.
  • Parallelogram assumptions: equal magnitudes do not imply equal vectors — direction matters too.
  • Negative scale factors: the image lies on the opposite side of the centre; it is not simply "smaller".
  • Collinearity proof: showing parallel is not enough — the segments must also share a point. State it.

Translations: moving a shape without changing it

A translation slides every point of a shape the same distance in the same direction. The shape keeps its size, its shape and its orientation, so the image is congruent to the object. The description needs a column vector, written (x; y), where x is the movement to the right and y is the movement up. Negative values move left or down.

Reading a column vector

The vector (3; −2) means move 3 units to the right and 2 units down. Read the top number first, as the horizontal movement, and the bottom number second, as the vertical movement. Swapping the two numbers is one of the most common errors, and it moves the shape to a completely different place.

Translating a point

To translate a point, add the vector to its coordinates. The point A(1, 4) under the translation (3; −2) becomes A′(1 + 3, 4 − 2) = A′(4, 2). Work out each coordinate separately and check that the sign of each movement is right before you write the answer.

Translating a whole shape

A triangle is translated by translating each of its three vertices and joining the new points with straight lines. Drawing only one vertex, or moving the shape by eye, loses the mark. Check the result by counting the squares between each object point and its image: every pair should show the same horizontal and vertical movement.

Working backwards from an image

A question may give the image and ask for the vector. Take one point and its image, and find the change in x and the change in y. If P(2, 5) maps to P′(7, 1), the vector is (7 − 2; 1 − 5) = (5; −4). Check with a second point before you write the vector down.

Translations and the notation of the answer

The answer to a translation question must give the vector, not a verbal description alone. "Move 5 right and 4 down" is acceptable in words, but the examiner expects the column vector form (5; −4), which is what the syllabus asks for. Write it in brackets with a semicolon between the two numbers.

Common errors with translations

The commonest errors are reversing the direction of the movement, moving only the x-coordinate, and rotating the shape by mistake when a translation was asked for. A translation never turns the shape over and never changes its size, so an image that looks rotated or stretched is wrong. Check each answer against the rule that the shape is unchanged.

Equations and symbols

Every transformation is a coordinate map, and every vector is a column pair. Learn the four rotation maps and the two vector rules, and the topic is arithmetic.

90 ° clockwise about O: (x, y) → (y, -x) Key: (x, y) = the original coordinates; the arrow points to the image's coordinates; O = the origin, the fixed centre. Anticlockwise is the same map with the signs reversed — write the centre down, because a rotation about any other point is not this formula.

180 °: (x, y) → (-x, -y) Key: both coordinates change sign; a half-turn is the only rotation that is also a translation-free "point reflection" in the origin. Check with a point on an axis, where one coordinate stays zero.

reflection in y = x swaps the coordinates: (3, 5) → (5, 3) Key: the line y = x is the mirror; swapping means the image of (x, y) is (y, x). The line is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining each point to its image, which is the definition to quote.

(1, 1) → (5, -1) Key: left = a vertex of the object; right = the matching vertex of the image. Subtract to read off the translation: 5 − 1 = 4 across and −1 − 1 = −2 down, so the column vector is (4; −2).

(3, 1) → (1, -3) Key: this is a 90° clockwise turn about the origin applied to a second vertex — the same map, different numbers. With two vertices mapped you can describe the transformation fully rather than guessing from one.

title: Functions — Study Notes
content:
Functions

This note builds the functions work used throughout the Cambridge AS & A Level Mathematics 9709 course. A function maps each input in its domain to exactly one output in its range. Notation such as f(x) = 2x + 1 names the rule, and the examiner expects you to state domain, range and inverse clearly.

Domain, range and notation

The domain is the set of inputs the function accepts. Restrictions usually come from denominators (which cannot be zero), square roots (which need a non-negative argument) and logarithms (which need a positive argument). The range is the set of outputs the function actually produces over that domain. For f(x) = x² on all real numbers, the range is f(x) ≥ 0. Writing the domain as x ≥ 0 gives the same range but changes whether an inverse exists.

A many-to-one function, such as x² on all reals, sends two inputs to the same output. A one-to-one function never does. Only one-to-one functions have inverses.

Composite functions

The composite function fg(x) means f(g(x)): apply g first, then f to the result. Order matters, so in general fg(x) and gf(x) are different functions.

Example: f(x) = 2x + 1 and g(x) = x².

  • fg(x) = f(x²) = 2x² + 1
  • gf(x) = g(2x + 1) = (2x + 1)² = 4x² + 4x + 1

When a restriction is involved, check the range of the inner function against the domain of the outer one. If g(x) = x − 3 with domain x ≥ 0 is followed by f(x) = √x, the range of g is x ≥ −3, which is wider than the domain of f, so the composite fg(x) = √(x − 3) needs x ≥ 3 to be defined. The exam often asks for this domain explicitly.

Inverse functions

The inverse f⁻¹ reverses the action of f, so f⁻¹(f(x)) = x. To find it, write y = f(x), swap x and y, then rearrange to make y the subject.

Example: f(x) = 3x − 2. Write y = 3x − 2, swap to x = 3y − 2, then y = (x + 2)/3. So f⁻¹(x) = (x + 2)/3. Check by substituting: f(f⁻¹(x)) = 3 × (x + 2)/3 − 2 = x.

An inverse exists only if f is one-to-one on its domain. If it is not, restrict the domain to make it so. For f(x) = x² with domain x ≥ 0, the inverse is f⁻¹(x) = √x with domain x ≥ 0. Without the restriction, x² would have no single inverse, because both 3 and −3 square to 9.

The domain of f⁻¹ is the range of f, and the range of f⁻¹ is the domain of f. The graph of y = f⁻¹(x) is the reflection of y = f(x) in the line y = x, so a point (a, b) on f becomes (b, a) on f⁻¹. Use this to check an answer: if (2, 5) is on the graph of f, then (5, 2) must be on the graph of f⁻¹.

Transformations of graphs

Each change to the rule moves or stretches the graph in a predictable way. Learn these as a table:

Transformed graphEffect on the graph of y = f(x)
y = f(x) + atranslation by a units up (a < 0: down)
y = f(x + a)translation by a units left (a < 0: right)
y = a f(x)vertical stretch, scale factor a
y = f(ax)horizontal stretch, scale factor 1/a
y = −f(x)reflection in the x-axis
y = f(−x)reflection in the y-axis

The horizontal translation runs against the sign: y = (x − 3)² is the graph of x² moved 3 units to the right. A common error is to move it left. For a sequence of transformations, apply them in the order the question gives, tracking a few key points such as the vertex or the intercepts.

Method for exam questions

  • For a composite function, write out fg(x) and gf(x) separately whenever the question names two functions, and simplify each.
  • For an inverse, state both the rule and its domain. A correct rule with the domain missing loses marks.
  • To show a function has an inverse, argue that it is one-to-one on the stated domain, usually because it is strictly increasing or strictly decreasing there.
  • When sketching y = f⁻¹(x), reflect the graph of f in y = x and mark where the line crosses it, since that point lies on both graphs.

Exam cue: whenever a question says "hence" or "using your answer to part", the composite or inverse from the earlier part is usually the route to the answer, so keep it in simplified form.

title: Numerical Measures of Central Tendency
content:
Central Tendency: Mean, Median and Mode

The Mean

For data x₁, ..., xₙ the mean is

  • x̄ = Σx/n

For a frequency table with midpoints x and frequencies f: x̄ = Σfx/Σf. The mean uses every value, so a single extreme value drags it — that is its main weakness.

The Median

The median is the middle value: position (n + 1)/2 for ordered raw data. With n even, average the two middle values. The median ignores the size of extreme values, so it describes skewed data more honestly. For grouped data, estimate the median by linear interpolation within the median class.

The Mode

The most frequent value. A dataset may have no mode or several. For grouped data the modal class is the one with the highest frequency density (frequency ÷ class width), not the highest frequency.

Effects of Data Changes

Adding a constant a to every value adds a to the mean and median (the mode too) but leaves the spread untouched. Multiplying every value by b multiplies mean and median by b.

Coding

Subtract a constant and divide by a convenient width: y = (x − a)/b. Then x̄ = b·ȳ + a. Coding simplifies arithmetic and always preserves the relationship — the coded mean decodes exactly.

Example: data 2, 4, 4, 10: mean = 5, median = 4, mode = 4. Change 10 to 100: mean = 27.5, median and mode unchanged — the mean chased the outlier.

Exam tips: always state which average you used and why. When asked to compare two distributions, pair a central measure with a spread measure; a mean without a spread is only half an answer.

title: Nuclear Physics — Study Notes
content:
Nuclear Physics

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): nuclear model, radioactivity, decay types, half-life, safety, fission/fusion (Extended).

1. The nuclear model

Nucleus (protons +, neutrons 0) with orbiting electrons (−). Nuclide notation ᴬ_Z X. Isotopes: same Z, different A. Rutherford scattering established the nuclear model; proton number Z, nucleon number A.

2. Radiation types

TypeNatureRange (air)Stopped by
alpha αhelium nucleus (2p2n)few cmpaper
beta β⁻fast electron~20–30 cmfew mm aluminium
gamma γEM wavevery farthick lead/concrete

Deflection in fields: α/β opposite, γ none. Ionising: α > β > γ. Background radiation: radon, cosmic, rocks, medical, fallout.

3. Decay equations

  • α: A −4, Z −2 (e.g. ²³⁸₉₂U → ²³⁴₉₀Th + α).
  • β⁻: neutron → proton; A same, Z +1 (e.g. ¹⁴₆C → ¹⁴₇N + β⁻).
  • γ: no change to A or Z.

Balance A and Z on both sides — that is the check.

4. Half-life

Time for half the unstable nuclei to decay (random process). Read from a decay curve or count halves: 80 → 40 → 20 over two half-lives.

Example: 800 Bq, half-life 2 h → 200 Bq after 4 h.

5. Safety and uses

Uses: medical tracers (β/γ), sterilisation, thickness gauge (β), dating (C-14), smoke alarms (α). Safety: distance, time, shielding, wear badges, store in lead. Handle with tongs; never point at people.

6. Fission and fusion (Extended)

Fission: heavy nucleus splits (U-235 + neutron), chain reaction controlled by moderators/control rods — power stations. Fusion: light nuclei join (stellar) — needs huge T/P; releases more energy per kg; no long-lived waste.

Nuclear decay and half-life

Alpha particles are helium nuclei with two protons and two neutrons, and they are strongly ionising but have low penetration. Beta-minus emission happens when a neutron changes into a proton and an electron is emitted. Gamma radiation is electromagnetic, carries no charge and no mass, and has high penetration. Background radiation must be subtracted from measured count rates before a half-life is calculated.

title: Exam technique: Probability (A2)
content:
### What earns the marks
For conditional probability, the restricted sample space stated earns the method mark. For independence checks, P(A)P(B) compared with P(A and B) earns both marks. For Bayes-style updates, the tree fractions multiplied along branches earn stepwise credit.
### Traps
Error: mutually exclusive assumed independent. Correction: test, never assume. Error: given-condition ignored. Correction: shrink the denominator first. Error: branches added instead of multiplied. Correction: multiply along, add across.
### Worked example
Event A has P(A) = 0.5 and event B has P(B) = 0.4. Given that A and B are independent, P(A and B) = 0.5 × 0.4 = 0.20. If the question instead gives P(A and B) = 0.3, then the events are not independent, because 0.3 does not equal 0.20. The conditional probability is P(A | B) = P(A and B) ÷ P(B) = 0.3 ÷ 0.4 = 0.75.
### Check yourself
Two events are mutually exclusive with P(A) = 0.3 and P(B) = 0.2. Are they independent? No. P(A and B) = 0 but P(A)P(B) = 0.06, so the events are dependent. Mutually exclusive events are always dependent when both have non-zero probability.
